title: Plaque telling story of African-Caribbean prisoners in Britain stolen within days
summary: Descendants say theft from Portchester Castle reflects spirit of racism that has haunted ‘generation after generation’
text: The theft of a plaque in Hampshire that told the little-known story of African-Caribbean prisoners in 18th-century Britain reflects the enduring racism that has fuelled centuries of atrocities against Black and Indigenous Caribbean people, their descendants say. Drummer Ronald Raymond McDonald was part of a delegation that travelled from Belize and elsewhere to Portchester Castle last week to honour their ancestors: 2,500 men, women and children transported to Britain as prisoners of war in 1796. McDonald, whose Garifuna ancestors from St Vincent and the Grenadines were among the prisoners, said he was heartbroken to learn that the plaque had been stolen and a nearby bench vandalised with hateful graffiti. “Why would somebody do something like that when people are simply honouring their ancestors … It’s very sad,” he said. The plaque, installed at the castle, commemorated the more than 2,000 prisoners held there, marking an extraordinary chapter of Black British history: one of the largest known arrivals of African-Caribbean people in Britain before the Windrush era. The unveiling was part of a ceremony organised by the St Vincent and the Grenadines 2nd Generation (SV2G), in partnership with the University of Warwick and English Heritage, and was attended by Caribbean communities, diplomats, researchers and heritage organisations. But days later, English Heritage staff discovered the plaque was missing. They said a padlock to one of the castle gates had been removed and the incident had been reported to police. Garifuna advocate Princess Eulogia said the theft reflected “a spirit of racism that haunts generation after generation and hides in plain sight”. It was time, she said, to recognise that “we are all connected” and to end the hate. Queen Mother Chief Freda Paulino-Sideroff, who is Garifuna and had travelled to the UK for the ceremony, was returning home to the US when she learned of the theft. “Hate will never define who we are as a people. We are resilient survivors of our ancestors who have endured,” she said. In the 1700s, her Garifuna ancestors were expelled from St Vincent by British forces and left to perish on the barren island of Baliceaux as Britain sought to crush decades of resistance to colonisation. Emilio ‘Sásamu’ Thomas, a Garifuna cultural ambassador who also travelled from Belize for the ceremony, echoed Paulino-Sideroff’s defiance, saying Garifuna people would not allow themselves to be victimised. His message to the perpetrators, he said, was: “Whatever pain that they are experiencing, we’re here to help them to relieve that pain.” The missing plaque was meant to honour the prisoners, whose story, researchers say, had been largely lost to history. They came from a coalition that included formerly enslaved Africans, Caribbean-born people, Indigenous people and French soldiers who fought against British control of St Lucia, St Vincent and the Grenadines and Grenada. Their defeat and removal helped strengthen British rule in the region. It was unveiled on 9 October, exactly 230 years after one of the ships carrying the prisoners was wrecked at Rapparee Cove in Devon, with many of those on board losing their lives. Iona Keen of English Heritage called the removal an act of vandalism, while University of Warwick professor Katherine Astbury said the plaque was intended to provide a visible memorial of the prisoners, and a reminder of “an important, forgotten part of Caribbean history”. The incident comes during Black History Month and amid renewed debate over slavery reparations. Campaigner and author Sir Patrick Vernon said vandalism of memorials representing Black British history had occurred repeatedly over decades, citing damage to other memorials. He described the theft as symbolic of an “ongoing battle and the legacy of enslavement”. Jacqueline Roberts, SV2G chief executive, said the theft could not erase history, and stressed the importance of continuing research to uncover more hidden stories. “Our history is intertwined with British history,” she said. “It’s important to understand that part of our journey, because it is part of the complexity of our identity, and affects our sense of belonging.” Anthony Severin, St Lucia’s high commissioner and chair of the Caribbean community diplomatic caucus in the UK, described the theft as a “desecration of the memory and spirit of our commemorated ancestors”. He pledged that the plaque “whether returned or replaced, will remain affixed to the walls of Portchester Castle”.

title: US corporate lobbyists mounted ‘blitz’ to dilute landmark EU deforestation law, report finds
summary: Environmental watchdog Mighty Earth reveals two-year effort to postpone and weaken EU Deforestation Regulation
text: US corporate lobbyists launched a two-year “blitz” to postpone and weaken the world’s most progressive legislation to protect forests, according to a new investigation by the environmental watchdog Mighty Earth. Major US firms and trade associations, including Cargill, Bunge, Mondelēz and the US Soybean Export Council, as well as numerous other US firms and organizations, sought to influence the EU Deforestation Regulation (EUDR) in more than 350 meetings, the advocacy group found. US company representatives and industry groups deny there was a concerted campaign to derail the deforestation rules, saying their meetings with EU officials raised legitimate concerns around implementation. The EUDR prohibits imports of commodities such as cattle, cocoa, coffee, oil palm, rubber, soya and wood from deforested land. When the ban was put forward in 2003, the then European environment commissioner, Virginijus Sinkevičius, described it as “the most ambitious legislative attempt to tackle these issues worldwide ever” and some US lawmakers said it should be a model for similar rules in the United States. In the years since, its official implementation has been delayed twice and the original goal to rigorously trace the origin of commodities has been revised so much that some of its initial supporters claimed the policy has been in effect “dismantled”. The law will come into effect in December. Lobbyists from many countries, including Brazil and several EU nations, are known to have contributed to this dilution. Mighty Earth has provided the most detailed analysis yet of the role of organisations from the United States. It found 24 major US companies, trade associations and industry organizations discussed the EUDR in at least 173 meetings with members of the European parliament and 178 meetings with senior European Commission officials between July 2024 and July 2026. The US organisations with the highest number of meetings with the European Commission were the National Alliance of Forest Owners, Advanced Woody Biomass Alliance, the US Soybean Export Council, Bunge, the American Chamber of Commerce to the European Union and Cargill. Cargill had two meetings, Bunge one meeting and Mondlēz eight meetings. Mighty Earth said lobbying was also conducted through the US Congress, the US Department of Agriculture, the Office of the US Trade Representative and the White House. Two weeks after a July 2025 meeting at a Scottish golf course between Trump and the president of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, the two sides released a joint statement that promised the US special treatment with regard to the EUDR. The commission stated the US “poses negligible risk to global deforestation” (even though many of its biggest financial and trading companies have been repeatedly implicated in destruction of the Amazon and similar biomes). The statement also talked about the EU working “to address the concerns of US producers and exporters regarding EUDR, with a view to avoiding undue impact on US-EU trade”. Mighty Earth said its investigation highlighted the need for the EU to adopt greater transparency about lobbying activities and to give more access to civil society to ensure balance. “Our analysis found a relentless and aggressive campaign by major US businesses, trade bodies and government officials, going all the way to President Trump, who offered to personally intervene, to further pressure EU policymakers,” Isabel Fernandez, senior adviser for Mighty Earth, said. “Some of the companies lobbying the EU, include the most egregious who are still linked to the illegal clearing of forests for commodities, such as soy that make their way into European markets.” Earlier this year a delegation of Trump administration officials went to EU capitals arguing the law would put the US off exporting to the European market because it would raise costs for US producers. In an opinion piece published in Agence France, Andrew Puzder, the US ambassador to the EU, said the law was: “… sold as a bold strike against global forest loss. In reality it will impose significant regulatory compliance costs while producing inconsequential environmental benefit when enforced against countries that pose no deforestation risk.” US corporate organisations said their engagement was designed to better understand and enhance the EUDR. The American Chamber of Commerce to the EU said it had raised concerns about EUDR implementation challenges, such as IT system shortcomings and a lack of clarity around the obligations of companies. But a spokesperson said its role had been constructive: “AmCham EU has consistently supported the EUDR’s objective of tackling global deforestation and promoting sustainable supply chains ... We have asked to allow sufficient time for companies and authorities to prepare and ensure the regulation can be effectively enforced without undermining its environmental objectives.” The US Soybean Export Council said it was focused on ways to support industry compliance with the EU’s rules. “USSEC does not seek delay or exemption; rather we favour a transition period as the Regulation comes into force. This would allow companies, control authorities, the European Commission, and the entire value chain to gain experience and learnings on how compliance works in practice, allowing for greater understanding and adaptations to implementation if needed moving forwards,” a spokesperson said. The agribusiness company Bunge said it was committed to deforestation-free supply chains and was investing in monitoring and traceability that had, it said, achieved 100% traceability to farm for both direct and indirect soy sourcing in priority areas of Argentina, Brazil and Paraguay. A spokesperson said: “Bunge supports the objectives of the European Union Deforestation Regulation while observing our own non-deforestation commitment and strengthening responsible sourcing. We are also in contact with relevant EU bodies and national competent authorities via sector organizations and directly to request clarification on certain specific complex scenarios regarding the practical implementation requirements of the EUDR.” Cargill and Mondelēz did not send an on-the-record response to the Guardian’s request for a comment.

title: Fake Linda and me: the Agatha Christie-worthy mystery of the fraudster who stole my byline
summary: How a string of bizarre events led writer Linda Geddes to don her sleuthing cap and dig into a world of shadowy impersonators
text: It started with an entirely ordinary interaction on LinkedIn. Someone had tagged me in a post, saying how much they’d enjoyed contributing to a New York Post article I’d written about “chronoworking”. As the author of a book about circadian rhythms, it was exactly the sort of subject I might write about. Except I’d never heard of this person, let alone interviewed them. I clicked on the link and my stomach dropped. There, above an article about people who organise their working lives around their biological clocks, was my name: Linda Geddes. It was the latest in a string of increasingly bizarre events that had begun three weeks earlier, when a friend who works as an editor at the scientific journal Nature texted to ask whether I’d been pitching stories to one of her colleagues. I hadn’t. It turned out that someone had been approaching Nature editors using my name and an email address that wasn’t mine, referencing articles I’d previously written to make their pitches more convincing. Worse, the journal had recently encountered another impersonator posing as Caroline Williams, a former colleague of mine. That person had convinced an editor at Science to commission and publish an article under Caroline’s name, receiving about $1,000 for it. Further digging revealed that Fake Linda had also pitched a story to Science, unsuccessfully. Then, last week, an editor at Nature Medicine contacted me to ask whether I’d been pitching to them and Nature Health as well. I donned my sleuthing cap and discovered a potential link between Fake Linda and Fake Caroline. Entering my impersonator’s email address into Outlook.com’s account recovery system revealed a partially obscured Gmail recovery address. An editor at Science had independently discovered the same address pattern associated with Fake Caroline’s email. As someone whose livelihood depends on the reputation I’ve spent decades building, I find this deeply unsettling. Someone is potentially making money by passing themselves off as me, while putting my professional credibility at risk. Apart from one interview conducted by email, the quotes in the New York Post article were lifted from previously published features, without attribution. Many of Fake Linda’s pitches also bear the hallmarks of AI-assisted writing. Even unsuccessful pitches could damage relationships with editors. The New York Post has since removed the article, conducted an internal review and referred the matter to the appropriate authorities, a spokesperson said. What I find particularly baffling is the motive. Freelance science journalism is hardly a lucrative profession, and is quite niche. My best guess is that a struggling freelancer is impersonating more established peers to boost their earnings, perhaps using AI to make the process more efficient. But how would they receive payment without revealing their identity? Other possibilities have crossed my mind. Could it be a PR professional trying to secure coverage for a client, or someone testing how easily publishers can be fooled? Perhaps it is someone with a personal grudge. But as Caroline put it: “Why us? We’re nice!” Dr Simon Miller, the director of policy, strategy and communications at the UK fraud prevention service Cifas, is equally bemused. “Ordinarily, if you’re seeking to defraud, you’re seeking to do it at scale, in a relatively light-touch way, using mechanised, industrialised processes,” he said. “This is tantalisingly unusual. It’s almost the stuff of Agatha Christie, but with 21st-century technology.” Journalists are far from the only people finding their names attached to work they didn’t produce. In April, Prof Eric Topol, of the Scripps Institute in California, discovered his name on a scientific paper he knew nothing about. Four of his five supposed co-authors were similarly unaware of the paper, while the fifth could not be identified. Within hours of Topol flagging the incident on X, the journal’s website had disappeared. Topol, who is a bestselling author, said he has discovered at least 12 books on Amazon with his name on that he didn’t write, including several cookbooks. “I don’t even know how to cook,” he said. Particularly upsetting was when a patient told him he’d read his supposed memoir. “They said: ‘I was reading it, and a lot of those things don’t seem to be accurate.’ That’s how I found out about it.” Leslie McIntosh, a vice-president of research integrity and security at Digital Science, said someone might add a respected name to a scientific paper without permission to make the work appear more credible. Fraudsters also sometimes added respected researchers as editors to make bogus journals appear legitimate and attract publication fees. Even more nightmarish would be someone deliberately publishing misleading information under someone else’s name to damage their reputation. “If their name ended up on a retracted paper, they would then have to explain that retraction,” she said. Employers are encountering yet another form of impersonation. Jamie Collier, a researcher at Google Threat Intelligence, said criminals had used stolen personal information to secure remote jobs under other people’s names, sometimes without the victim’s knowledge. Generative AI is making such deception easier, “mainly by stripping away the usual tell-tale red flags that hiring managers relied on to spot fraud,” Collier said. Large language models can generate convincing CVs, tailored cover letters and fabricated evidence of professional experience. “Real-time video filters and voice-cloning tools are the next step. While live deepfakes are still relatively nascent … threat actors are already testing them to bypass quick video screenings and mask regional accents,” Collier said. The Society of Authors and the Writers’ Guild of Great Britain have warned of increasingly sophisticated scams involving people impersonating literary agents and publishers, in an attempt to get writers to part with money or sign away their rights. The Society of Authors’ chief executive, Anna Ganley, said she personally received between five and 10 scam emails a day, supposedly from book festivals, literary agents, publishers and others. Some writers had lost thousands of pounds after responding to genuine-sounding offers. “It’s incredibly difficult for writers, because you are often looking for opportunities to market your books,” she said. Unlike those scams, Fake Linda’s activities seem like a lot of work for relatively small financial gain. But the latest technology could make such impersonations easier. Miller said: “AI is allowing criminals to create sophisticated impersonations at unprecedented speed and scale.” Or multiple impersonations. I’ve since identified a third science journalist, Sara Novak, with a potential link to Fake Linda and Fake Caroline. Fake Sara apparently pitched a story to Chemical and Engineering News in August, which was declined. When Real Sara shared her impersonator’s email address with me, I discovered it links to the same masked recovery address. The consequences extend beyond those being impersonated. “The risk for journals and publishers is huge,” said Dr Ben Johnson, the chief editor at Nature Health, who turned down a pitch by Fake Linda. “People trust the Nature brand as a source of evidence-based quality information. If an AI-generated story from a fake journalist is submitted then I will likely spend hours editing it from AI slop into Nature prose, including all the fake quotes from people never interviewed.” All of this raises uncomfortable questions about how you can be sure you know who you’re dealing with when communicating online. When I emailed the New York Post about my impersonator, it agreed to help rectify the situation, then asked: “I see that you’re emailing me from a Guardian email address. Is there any other info you can provide to verify who you are?” After discovering that Science had inadvertently published a news story by Fake Caroline, its managing news editor, John Travis, said his team had started running all pitches and drafts through AI detectors, “though they are not perfect”. “We also require Zoom calls for any new writers,” he said. The experience has also put editors at Nature on higher alert. “Sadly, for early career freelancers, this makes me less likely to commission news stories from journalists that I haven’t worked with before,” Johnson said. “I will also have to try to find the time to have a call with new freelancers before they write, to check they are who they say they are.” Even video calls are no guarantee of identity. Google Threat Intelligence recently documented North Korea-linked hackers using real-time deepfakes to lure executives into Zoom calls with trusted peers. “They faked video and audio glitches to get the target to download a ‘troubleshooting tool’ that wiped out their credentials and wallets,” Collier said. Miller advises independently checking unexpected approaches through an established email address or telephone number. McIntosh advocates several layers of verification, like the multiple identity checks at airports. “You have to have multiple ways to ensure and triangulate that you’re speaking to the person you think you’re speaking to,” she said. For people whose identities have been hijacked, Miller advises warning professional networks and monitoring for further impersonation attempts. There may also be legal remedies. Rupert Earle, senior counsel at the London law firm Bates Wells, said that under UK law, impersonating someone to secure paid work could constitute fraud. Victims could also have civil claims for “passing off” – misleading people into believing that work or services come from an established person or business – or false attribution, if work they didn’t create was published under their name. However, identifying the perpetrator and taking legal action can be difficult, particularly when the publications are overseas and the impersonator’s location is unknown. Despite uncovering several clues linking Fake Linda and Fake Caroline, we still don’t know who is behind the accounts. But the hunt for Fake Linda continues. I’ll be reporting the incident to the UK’s Report Fraud service. I’ve also sent a cease-and-desist email to my impersonator, demanding they stop. For such a prolific writer, they’ve gone surprisingly quiet.

title: ‘Is this too little, too late?’: Cornell students on school’s response to gang-rape allegations
summary: Students say the school is more interested in scapegoating fraternities than in committing to institutional change
text: In the wake of a lawsuit over an alleged gang-rape that took place at Cornell University in 2024, the school announced this week that it would be suspending parties and social gatherings at fraternity houses for the remainder of the academic year. Last month, a former student, referred to in court documents by the pseudonym “Jane Doe”, filed a civil lawsuit against multiple parties, including the university, accusing seven members of the Chi Phi fraternity of sexually assaulting her at a party at their fraternity house on campus in October 2024. All of the men named in the lawsuit have denied wrongdoing, and none have been criminally charged. In a letter to the Cornell community, the school’s president, Michael Kotlikoff, said that the ban on frat parties will be “provide time for a thorough review of fraternity life at Cornell to determine whether and how it can safely continue”. The Guardian spoke with several undergraduate students at Cornell about the university’s decision, as well as their handling of the alleged assault and its aftermath. The measure, which Kotlikoff referred to as an effort to “strengthen campus safety”, was announced on 13 October in a letter to the Cornell community. While some students welcome the ban on frat parties, others argue that the move is an attempt by the administration to avoid a perception of culpability in the case. When asked for comment, Cornell referred the Guardian to Kotlikoff’s letter to the community from 13 October, in which he said: “I have spent the past weeks listening to students, faculty, staff, parents, alumni, and trustees, who have shared their feelings of deep connection and sympathy with Jane Doe, anger and frustration that this could happen at Cornell, and outrage at the broader prevalence of sexual violence against women in our society. These conversations, and campus protests, have underscored my deep conviction that we must do better: that the time for meaningful and lasting change at Cornell, and at campuses across the country, is now.” A sophomore at Cornell’s school of industrial and labor relations, who asked to remain anonymous, supports the school’s latest decision. She acknowledged that Greek life “wasn’t something that really added to my experience at Cornell” and that the ban was “so necessary in light of Jane Doe’s experience”. The student added that while she is not in Greek life herself, many of her friends are. “I think it’s been upsetting for people that are super involved in Greek life,” she said, noting that some members of Greek life feel that they’re being penalized for the actions of others. They “think that [the ban is] somewhat unnecessary because this happened two years ago, and it’s a completely different group of people”. “I have many friends that have opposing viewpoints,” she said. Some students argued that the opposition is the point, and believe that the administration’s decision was intended to further a divide between the student body. “The fact that [the administration] thinks a one-year moratorium will solve this is, I wouldn’t say it’s misguided. I would say it is purposefully manipulative to the student body,” said Jack Huber, a sophomore at the school of industrial and labor relations and member of Students for a Democratic Cornell (SDC), an independent, student-run organization that advocates for free speech on campus. “I believe it’s a very intentional choice, because what it’s done is create a sentiment that many students are angry, and are blaming protesters for their inability to party. “Cornell is not ready to commit itself to institutional change, and is using this moratorium to essentially scapegoat fraternities when this is a campus-wide issue,” he added. Huber added that issues of sexual assault will remain until the school has implemented an independent judicial system, which was previously in effect from 1969 to 2020. Huber said that school’s current judiciary process operates as “a tool to be used to sweep incidences of sexual violence under the rug because they harm Cornell’s reputation, and persecute protesters because they harm the board of trustees’ investments”. “That’s the system that allowed essays to get written by two of the [Cornell 7]” he said. SDC is demanding that the administration rewrite a portion of its student code of conduct to require independent hearings and minimum sanctions for sexual assault. Darius Pierce, a sophomore at Cornell’s college of architecture, art and planning, remembered hearing about the incident, which had resulted in Chi Phi being disbarred and removed from campus during his first few weeks of college in 2025. “I was walking past the Chi Phi house, heading back to campus, and a person in my group pointed out [the house] and I asked why I’ve never heard of them, and they explained that there was an issue with ketamine and assault at that house, and that was it,” he said. “No one ever expanded upon that. I hadn’t heard anything about it until the story broke with the Cornell Sun.” Like Huber, Pierce believes that the administration’s decision to ban frat parties is an attempt to “cover up for their own faults and own mistakes”. “They’re trying to make it seem like they’re actually responding to [the alleged assault] and taking action instead of addressing the real issue,” he said. Following the alleged assault, Cornell issued a statement in November 2024 informing the community that there would be an internal investigation while the Cornell University Police Department continued their criminal investigation. Per Jane Doe’s lawsuit, Cornell University Police did not end up pursuing criminal charges. The investigation was reopened in September 2026 in response to public outrage. None of the defendants in the civil lawsuit have been charged and all have denied wrongdoing. Pierce, who rushed a fraternity but decided not to join one, also spoke of the endemic culture of drinking and substance use he has witnessed within Greek life at Cornell. He recalled an experience at a fraternity party where “this group of girls kept screaming that it was their first time doing coke at that frat party, and that these frat guys were just handing out lines of coke like candy”. “If you go to a frat, you plan on drinking,” Pierce said. “But it seems like for women specifically who go to these frats, they’re kind of pressured to do more.” The Guardian previously reported on how Jane Doe’s lawsuit has reignited debates over Greek life and the relationship between fraternity parties, drinking culture and sexual assault. A 2019 survey from the Association of American Universities revealed that a quarter of undergraduate women reported experiencing nonconsensual sexual conduct, with fraternities being the setting where it was most likely to occur. At Cornell, 35% of undergraduate women reported experiencing nonconsensual sexual contact since arriving at school, according to a 2025 survey conducted by the university. Saya Taylor, a sophomore who is also a member of SDC, believes that the frat ban is a “Band-Aid” solution to a much deeper problem. “They’re trying to give the appearance that they are changing when they are not,” she said. “Cornell University does not want this to [have] a lasting impact.” In addition to the fraternity ban, Kotlikoff also announced that the university would be adding a case manager to Cornell’s office of civil rights to help those who report sexual misconduct at the school navigate the processes. He also pledged that Cornell would work with the New York state police and allow their trauma-informed criminal investigators, who are independent of Cornell, to investigate allegations. The sophomore believes that this week’s announcement is a step in the right direction. “For the vast majority, people like me, we want justice and we want the administration to change the structural way that they address sexual assault,” she said. But others need more convincing. “Is this too little, too late? The answer there is a resounding yes,” said Huber. “Jane Doe never got the justice she deserved in the moment.” • Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organizations. In the US, Rainn offers support on 800-656-4673. In the UK, Rape Crisis offers support on 0808 500 2222. In Australia, support is available at 1800Respect (1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found at ibiblio.org/rcip/internl.html

title: Briton threatened with deportation from Sweden over Brexit rules goes into hiding
summary: Mark Smith, who has severe health issues, says he was told three times he needed to do nothing in order to remain after Brexit
text: A seriously ill British man living in Sweden has been forced into hiding amid fears he will be deported as a result of what he says is a government Brexit residency error. Mark Smith, 60, who has had heart attacks, strokes, severe headaches and chronically high blood pressure that has been difficult to treat, was told on the phone he should leave Sweden by 17 October as he was an “alien” without permission to stay. Terrified of deportation, he and his wife have moved out of their home in Falkenberg, in south-west Sweden, to a caravan park. “We are in hiding, we daren’t go back to our apartment. We are scared to go out as we don’t know if the police will come and take us,” Smith said. A court ruled on 12 October that a decision on deportation would not be suspended but gave him until 20 October to “submit his application for a retrial” in relation to “the grounds for the decision on indefinite deportation”. Smith has been in Sweden since 2017 and says he was told by authorities he did not need to do anything to stay after Brexit in 2020. He worked, had private health insurance, supported his wife and registered on the population register administered by the national tax authority, as required under Swedish rules. He was unaware, however, that Sweden was among 13 of the 27 EU member states that required Britons living in the country before Brexit to make a formal application to remain. Other countries, such as Spain, did not opt for that system and just required Britons to declare they were a resident. Smith said: “I asked the tax authorities three times on different occasions if I had to do anything because of Brexit and they said no, telling me I had to wait for five years to apply for permanent residency. “Because it was the tax authority, a government body, I took it for granted that what they told me was correct,” he added. David Milstead, a British-Swedish volunteer citizens’ rights activist working through the Brits in Sweden group, said Smith’s case was typical of many Britons living in Sweden. Milstead said: “Mark’s experience is far from unusual. I have encountered many British citizens who actively sought information from the Swedish authorities about their residence rights after Brexit, only to receive vague, unhelpful answers, sometimes being told that they needed to do nothing.” They include the 78-year-old widow Joyce Thomas, whose husband also inquired about Brexit residency and was told by the tax authorities there was nothing to do, and who is now fighting a removal order. Smith had a minor heart attack on Wednesday night but wanted his situation publicised because he said the British government needed to know what was happening to expats in Sweden, “not just to me but others”. His wife, Petra, said his health conditions had left him so vulnerable she was not sure “if he will last until Christmas”. She said: “He has been told he can’t drive, he can’t fly – what do they expect him to do? Get up and walk to England? Come on, Sweden, we need to step back from all of this and be better.” After 12 years together, she said deportation would be devastating for her and her 15-year-old son who has special needs, who Smith co-parents. “It is wrong what they are doing, I feel ashamed to be Swedish. What they are doing is racist to British people,” Petra said. Milstead said Smith’s case was “depressingly familiar” and should warrant the urgent attention of the European Commission, which has previously said Sweden was not breaking any laws. “A gentleman with Mark’s serious health conditions should not be having to fight deportation. It is difficult to understand how the European Commission has concluded that Sweden’s treatment of late applications under the [Brexit] withdrawal agreement does not warrant a challenge,” he said. “Sweden stands out so starkly from other EU countries, and there are serious questions that remain unanswered, particularly about proportionality and the treatment of vulnerable people. These are precisely the kinds of cases where the protections of the withdrawal agreement ought to matter most.” The Scandinavian country has found itself under mounting pressure over its approach to the withdrawal agreements having deported 458 Britons, including one man who had been in the country since he was 10 years old, and a 65-year-old man married to a Swede with no family or property in the UK. Sweden has also issued removal orders to a man with dementia who is in 24-hour care and who has been in the country for 25 years. Under the legally binding treaty, it was agreed governments would communicate the Brexit residency rules, consider late applications on reasonable grounds, and exercise “proportionate” decisions including in the case of vulnerable people. Smith’s troubles began in 2021 when he started to get ill and applied for sickness benefit. He was told by officials that he should have applied for post-Brexit residency. The couple immediately did so; they recall making the application at the end of 2021, in time for Sweden’s 31 December 2021 deadline. They waited more than two years to hear back and when they did it was a rejection on the grounds that they were not married and therefore did not have a family connection to merit his residency in Sweden. They were married in 2023 and had been living together since 2017. It is not clear if Smith applied for the specific Brexit residency or through the usual immigration route, an important difference and one that may not have been made clear to British protected by the withdrawal agreement. Family connections are not a criteria under free movement rights, which apply to any individual regardless of marital status, so campaigners believe they have a strong case. Smith said: “We were so much in love, we lived together, we did everything together, even now we hold hands walking down the streets. We wanted to get married, we wanted to do it the right way. I wanted to ask Petra’s father for permission and have him give her away, but two weeks after he gave me permission to marry his daughter, he passed. “So we were looking into marriage but things just kept happening. But we don’t understand why this matters.” They also said they had not been given the full court paperwork from the first case appealing against the migration agency’s decision, so they appealed to a higher courtwithout the full arguments against them. After speaking to a judge this week, Petra has had assurances that all the paperwork will be sent to them by post, but they feel angry that they were not apprised of the information that the migration agency was arguing before the courts. Sweden’s migration agency has said there is no evidence Sweden has taken an extreme approach to the withdrawal agreement. The UK Foreign Office has raised concerns about Sweden’s approach to the withdrawal agreement with the European Commission on numerous occasions, but has been told Sweden is not breaching the agreement. A spokesperson said: “We are in touch with Mr Smith and are providing consular support. We know this is a distressing and challenging time for those concerned and we are urgently raising the situation with both the Swedish authorities and the European Commission.” The Foreign Office welcomed a statement by Sweden’s former migration minister Johan Forssell in August that Sweden would examine “additional measures” that would address the issue of Brexit deportation, and a similar declaration by Magdalena Andersson, who is on track to form the new government.

title: The people who are transforming Philly’s vacant lots into green spaces
summary: The organization We Are the Seeds began planting as part of a push to return land sovereignty to Indigenous people
text: Xiao Hui Star kneeled on her haunches, with her hands in the dirt as she cleared a spot to plant a flowering perennial in late summer. Surrounding her was a native garden replete with golden sunflowers, beans, squash, pawpaw and corn. She ruffled tufts of sweetgrass, which emitted a vanilla-like fragrance. Birds fluttered by and swooped down into a small bath filled with hard clam shells. Sandwiched between a brick home and a playground in west Philadelphia in Pennsylvania, the native garden featured plants endemic to the region. “These are very special endangered varieties that we are rematriating back to the soil,” said Star, who is part of Rhode Island’s Narragansett tribe. She is also the manager of new initiatives at the Philadelphia-based organization We Are the Seeds, which hosts public events and education on Indigenous arts and culture. “Who knows how many centuries it’s been since a Lenape corn or a Nanticoke squash have grown in this soil.” Unlike a typical garden plot, the 2,250 sq ft Seeds Indigenous listening garden sits atop a longtime vacant lot. In April, the organization began planting on the city-owned lot as an act of the LandBack movement – an Indigenous campaign of returning sovereignty and stewardship of land to Native people. Native plants offer food and shelter to the local insects and birds that evolved along with them over thousands of years. They also require less water than exotic plants, since they thrive in the soil and weather of the local environment. Over the past six months, We Are the Seeds has converted three vacant lots in Philadelphia into native gardens. They hope that their project will serve as a model that inspires others to transform some of the 40,000 vacant lots in the city into green spaces. “That’s where the growth would go,” said the organization’s co-founder and director Tailinh Agoyo, who is also Star’s sister. “That’s where the ripple effect would happen.” Studies show that revitalizing vacant property can lead to less violence and improved mental health in the area. The seeds – including maypop and garden phlox, among others – come from organizations that save and propagate heirloom plants to promote agriculture biodiversity, such as Experimental Farm Network, Truelove Seeds and the Seed Savers Exchange. We Are the Seeds’ native gardens are tended by Indigenous people – Star and her father Tchin, an artist and educator. The city of Philadelphia has also ramped up efforts to address its vacant lots, which are a result of decades of redlining and disinvestment. In April, the city launched a pilot program, Lotscapes, to transform 10 of the city’s 8,000 vacant lots into green spaces. Launched through the city’s office of clean and green initiatives and the Bloomberg-funded innovation team, the program aims to make it easier for community members to legally transform vacant land in their neighborhoods by applying for licensing or ownership. “The ultimate objective”, said Casey Kuklick, the city’s office of clean and green initiatives deputy director, “is to scale the ability of community groups to be able to … access land in the first place from a legal perspective”. For the pilot program, the city has partnered with community organizations to envision how to revitalize the land. In the current design stage, community members are choosing whether to transform the lots in their neighborhoods into gardens, gathering spaces with benches and tables, and areas with interactive structures. In the Strawberry Mansion neighborhood, the city is working with a health center to create interactive elements for a future green space that will also serve students from the elementary school next door. ‘You can’t eat concrete’ When Star set out to transform vacant lots to native gardens, she searched on a city website for all of the properties owned by the Philadelphia land bank, a public agency that acquires vacant and tax-delinquent properties. She made a list of vacant lots with ample sunlight and took soil samples of her top options to ascertain their toxicity levels. The west Philadelphia lot she chose was a sparse lot with a lawn mowed by the Philadelphia Horticultural Society, a non-profit that maintains some vacant lots in the city; it lacked features that grounded the community and honored the native plants. We Are the Seeds was inspired to create native gardens in Philadelphia after helping the Indigenous-led Ashawaug Farm in Rhode Island develop their branding and education initiative. Transforming vacant lots “was the way we could implement our big ideas right away without having to deal with a lot of legal [hurdles]”, said Agoyo. “We just wanted to get our seeds in the ground.” They hope to secure a mortgage and deed to the land through the state law adverse possession, which allows people to gain possession of vacant land if they have tended it as a garden for at least 10 years. Before assuming management of the land, We Are the Seeds spoke with community members who enthusiastically supported the garden’s development. They also received support from the city council district. In April, the organization hosted an opening ceremony at the lot where Indigenous dancers performed the corn dance. Neighbors from a nearby community garden participated in the dance, and a youth football team helped cast seeds after completing practice at the field next door. While the garden is not designed for sustenance, neighbors are welcome to take corn and herbs from the land. “Part of the vision for the garden is for not just Indigenous people, but for all people to come and have that reconnection to the land, because we cannot survive without the land,” Star said. “You can’t eat concrete.” The organization has received funding from the Philadelphia-based non-profit People’s Media Fund to erect a podcast studio where they will interview community members about their connection to the land. They will also archive audio recordings from Philadelphians about their Indigenous ancestry. In the future, the garden will feature sculptures and soundscapes. Agoyo hopes that native gardens soon spread throughout the city. “Start in your backyard. There’s just so much that we can all do individually to make a difference,” said Agoyo. “ I want everybody to feel what we feel when we come here, when we see something has grown or taken shape.”

title: How the quirky puffin became a symbol of the climate crisis – and hope
summary: In an extract from his new book, the nature historian explains how technology could help the seabird survive
text: For centuries human beings have exploited puffins, harvesting them by the thousand on their breeding grounds for their food and feathers. Over time, though, this relationship has changed, so that today we have come to love them, celebrating their quirky character and comical appearance and giving them a central place in our affections – a journey described by the environmental historian Dr Rob Lambert as the shift “from use to delight”. How ironic, then, that just as we have come to truly appreciate them, our own existence now threatens theirs. The climate crisis threatens almost all the world’s roughly 11,000 species of birds, but its consequences have particularly dire significance for seabirds, whose life cycle is so intimately connected to the timing and abundance of their food supplies. Warming oceans result in fish such as sand eels shifting their range into cooler waters, and thus either declining or disappearing from the seas around seabird breeding colonies. If puffins need to travel further to their feeding areas, or take longer to find and catch food once they get there, then their chicks have a lower chance of fledging. Even if they do, they are less likely to survive the following winter. Our changing climate has already led to an increase in the frequency and severity of extreme weather events such as autumn and winter storms, which leads to a higher mortality of birds outside the breeding season. It is often forgotten that the climate crisis is not the only negative factor affecting these birds’ lives. As we have seen, increased marine pollution, especially from oil and plastic, along with less severe yet still serious issues such as disturbance and predation, are already reducing the puffin’s breeding success at many once-thriving colonies. The dire prediction that nine out of 10 puffins could disappear before the middle of this century is hopefully pessimistic, yet we do know that serious declines are already occurring. In early 2026, BBC News reported that following that winter’s severe storms hundreds of dead and dying puffins, guillemots and razorbills had been washed up on beaches in Cornwall, Scotland and north-east England. Conservation organisations have also reported more than 20,000 stranded birds, mostly puffins, along the Atlantic coasts of France, Spain and Portugal. Samuel Wrobel, the RSPB’s senior marine officer, noted that this was the worst wreck for over a decade, since the catastrophic events of winter 2013-14, and warned that “after the impact of avian flu this is the last thing our seabirds need”. Moreover, as most birds are likely to have died at sea, so will never be found, the true death toll is likely to be much higher. Peter Harrison has spent his life watching, painting and studying seabirds, and has a special affection for the puffin. I asked him what he thought about the species’ future, and he began by confirming the many threats the birds face, including a reduction in their prey due to the climate crisis, threats to nest sites and the resulting lower breeding success. Rather to my surprise, however, Harrison feels some optimism for the puffin’s future, pointing to that famous legal victory that stopped industrial sand eel fishing in the waters around England and Scotland. He is also enthusiastic about the use of technology to track the movements and survival of all seabirds, including the puffin, since this began in the 1980s. “Prior to that time, there was a huge void in our knowledge of what puffins and other seabirds did in their non-breeding period,” he says. “They simply went to sea, only to reappear again in their breeding areas the following season. Rapid technological advances over the last four decades have greatly increased our understanding of their movements, revealing details of seabird distribution and behaviour at sea, including important foraging areas.” And as he points out, this knowledge does not just benefit the puffin. “Auks – including puffins – fulfil a role as important canaries in the cage, indicators of global health and sustainability. If auks are doing well, the oceans will be doing well,” Harrison says. The one thing we have on our side, Harrison believes, is that, unlike landbirds which often only live for a few years, even small seabirds can live for several decades. As he notes, although they might have gone through bad times, seabirds have in the past shown that they can make a rapid comeback, especially if we are able to rid their breeding islands of invasive predators. Scientists have a crucial role to play, too. In 2004 BirdLife International developed the BirdLife Seabird Tracking Database (STDB) to collate tracking data using a range of different, and rapidly improving, technologies that can track the presence and movements of seabirds when they are away from their breeding colonies, as they are for most of their lives. The records enabled them to identify six previously unrecognised oceanic routes used by the birds on their journeys: the Atlantic Ocean, North Indian Ocean, East Ocean, West Pacific Ocean, Pacific Ocean, and the Southern Ocean Flyways. The data obtained is also used for seabird research and conservation by BirdLife scientists and their collaborators throughout the world. As Dr Stephen Kress, the scientist who has devoted his life to successfully bringing back puffins to the US, points out: “Seabirds were once abundant along the coastlines of North America and throughout the world, but the declines we’re seeing in their populations are directly related to things humans are doing – they would be fine if we weren’t tampering with their world and messing things up. “And so I feel that we have an ethical responsibility as stewards of the Earth to do something where we can. That’s why we’ve developed these restoration techniques. If we hadn’t done that, we wouldn’t be documenting puffin recovery, we’d be documenting extinction.” Yet perhaps we can maintain at least a small fragment of hope for the future not just of the puffin, but of all the world’s seabirds. They may be outside our day-to-day experience for much of our – and their – lives, yet the huge affection for the puffin, held by millions of people around the world, must surely count for something. This is an edited extract from The Puffin by Stephen Moss published by Vintage at £14.99. To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.

title: Key player in false Talarico rumor has history of online posts invoking Nazi Germany
summary: Ryan Amacher, who played role in bid to damage campaign, has also made antisemitic and racist posts on social media
text: An influencer who played a key role in hoax claims that James Talarico was in a mental health facility has a long history of social media posts that favorably invoke Nazi Germany, express antisemitism and anti-Black racism, criticize miscegenation and call for “remigration” of refugees. On X, the Lake Oswego, Oregon, resident Ryan Amacher, known online as Rhein Amacher, has described Muslims as “sub-human”, claimed that Black Africans are “monkeys” with low IQ, characterized immigrants as “vermin” and expressed support for the far right, including Germany’s AfD and the UK’s Tommy Robinson. His attempt to damage Talarico’s campaign with false claims about a supposed inpatient admission to an Ohio facility fell apart quickly on Sunday night, but not before his claims were boosted by a staffer on the campaign of Talarico’s Republican rival, Ken Paxton. Since working for the Trump campaign in 2024, he has remained in the milieu of Republican politics and rightwing influencers. Neither Amacher nor the Paxton campaign responded to requests for comment. Last week, Amacher phoned the Lindner Center of Hope, a psychiatric hospital in Mason, Ohio, three times, trying to confirm a false rumor that Talarico had been admitted there. The rumor apparently began with a 9 October post by an anonymous X account, TickleTexts, which claimed Talarico had been “hospitalized at Lindner Center for HOPE”, and was picked up by the Republican fundraiser Caroline Wren, who falsely tied it to a private flight between Ohio and Austin. Before calling, Amacher had posted as fact that Talarico “was hospitalized at the @LindnerCtrHope” and tagged the hospital asking it to confirm. In the full recording of the second call, he gives his name as “Tim”, says he wants to send a care package to his cousin, and offers a four-digit patient code. “I simply made one up (2244) in an attempt to bypass the facility’s security restrictions to discuss the patient,” he later wrote on X. For most of the six-minute call the employee tells him she has no record of Talarico. In its final seconds she says a man that looks like Talarico “was just discharged this evening”. An excerpt of the recording was incorporated into a 47-second clip that Nick Sortor posted on Sunday afternoon under the headline “Ohio mental hospital CONFIRMS James Talarico was discharged from the facility earlier this week”. Amacher posted his own version minutes later, and Elon Musk replied with a characteristic “!!”. Amacher had first offered the recording to Blaze Media and the Daily Mail, which reportedly declined to run it, and said in an X Space that evening that influencers are “not held to the same journalistic standards”. By Tuesday he had reportedly pulled out of an interview with the writer and podcaster Jesse Singal, saying his attorney had given him a “stand down order”. The purported legal advice coincides with coverage of the fiasco, which has included speculation that Amacher’s attempt to access private health information may land him in legal trouble. Previous coverage, however, has not probed Amacher’s long history of extremist commentary. ‘Modern Freikorps volunteers are needed’ Amacher often invokes Nazi Germany, and the paramilitary movement that preceded it, with apparent admiration. “In 1919, Germany’s defeated soldiers came home only to be stabbed in the back by socialists and communists who wanted to burn the nation down and install a Soviet-style dictatorship,” he wrote on 29 July, over an AI-generated image of German soldiers beneath Soviet flags beside uniformed men under crescent moons at Berlin’s Brandenburg Gate. In a follow-up post he wrote: “Modern Freikorps volunteers are needed to step up to purge the German nation of the filth destroying it from within.” An AI-generated image accompanying it showed a masked soldier wearing “Freikorps” and “Deutsches Reich” patches, with the black, white and red flag of imperial Germany flying over the Reichstag. The Freikorps were paramilitary units of demobilized soldiers that crushed leftwing uprisings in Germany after the first world war. In January 1919, Freikorps troops murdered the communist leaders Rosa Luxemburg and Karl Liebknecht. In June, Amacher told critics to “read up on the German Freikorps after 1919–and what became of Luxemburg and Liebknecht”. “History has a way of repeating itself when revolutionary movements collide with a nation pushed to the brink,” he added. The Freikorps are widely seen as an ideological ancestor of Adolf Hitler’s Nazi party, though he later turned against them. In July, replying to a post that said “we fought the wrong enemy in WW2, just like General Patton said before the jews assassinated him in 1945”, Amacher wrote: “We should have immediately re-armed the German Wehrmacht and auxiliary troops and joined forces to defeat Soviet communism, once and for all!” Patton died in December 1945 after a car crash in occupied Germany; conspiratorial claims that he was assassinated have long been debunked. When fellow influencer Cam Higby complained in February that saying Nick Shirley was not a Nazi had led others to call him one, Amacher replied that “a colleague’s great-grandfather served as a paramilitary adjunct in Germany’s ‘other’ military force (not the Wehrmacht)”. He went on: “By your logic, does that make him a Nazi? Asking for a friend…” and attaching an “OK” emoji. He has captioned a photo of a figure skater with her right arm raised “Heil yes!” and offered to recruit a man “straight into my elite Panzer division”. Panzer divisions were armored tank units in Nazi Germany’s army. In July 2025 he joked that his ancestors “fled to Argentina as well, but way back in 1945, departing from the Deutsches Reich”. He has also called for the return of the late Spanish dictator Francisco Franco, writing: “Bring back Francisco Franco!” in July under a post claiming that “African military-aged males by the THOUSANDS” were entering the Spanish enclave of Ceuta. And he has praised Germany’s AfD, which the country’s domestic intelligence agency labeled a “confirmed rightwing extremist” force last year. “The @AfD is the ONLY party left that will actually SAVE Germany from destruction,” he wrote in April. “We will restore traditional German societal norms, identity, and culture.” ‘He looks like a Jew’ In January, replying to a post attacking the San Francisco Democrat Scott Wiener, Amacher wrote: “He looks like a Jew–I’m guessing he is a Jew!,” and included a nose emoji. In May 2025, after another user wrote of a man that “He’s also jewish, no surprise there”, Amacher replied: “A ginger Jew? Worst of both worlds…” Under a December post blaming Somali Muslims in Minnesota for “the largest theft of tax payer dollars in American History”, he wrote: “Both peoples are despicable, but the Somalis are ahead of the Jews by far!” He has told a pro-Israel account that it was “a hollowed-out puppet dancing on Zionist strings” whose loyalty was “to a parasitic regime halfway across the world”, and written that “Zionist infiltrators have sunk their claws deep into U.S. policy”. Another recurring subject is George Soros, the Jewish financier who is a frequent target of antisemitic conspiracy theories. Amacher has called him “a spawn of the Devil himself”, and in February 2025 wrote that Soros “allegedly turned in his own people during WWII just to save his own skin”, a claim factcheckers have repeatedly debunked. ‘Monkeys typically have an estimated IQ below 70’ In June, TickleTexts, the anonymous account that started the Talarico rumor, baselessly claimed, “as a born South African”, that “some villages believe r*ping a 6 month old baby girl will cure their AIDS”. Amacher replied: “Monkeys typically have an estimated IQ below 70.” Replying in January to a post about a Somali asylum seeker who, it claimed, had raped a 10-year-old girl in Denmark, he wrote: “Seriously, f*ck international obligations! These people are sub-human animals meant for zoos for viewing purposes only!” In February, he wrote that a dog said to have led police in Louisville, Kentucky, to a missing three-year-old had “demonstrated an intelligence far superior to that of any illegal Somali invader!” In June, he credited Nick Shirley, whose videos about Somali-run daycare centers in Minnesota set off a national panic, with exposing a “mastermind” who, Amacher wrote, had “funded the savage, low-IQ black Tusken Raiders fleecing Minnesota taxpayers”. In January, under a post about Trump’s claim that fraud in Minnesota could reach $80bn, he proposed “one-way, remigration flights back to Somalia as starters!” ‘Future super predators in the making’ In June 2025, after another user told the Hodgetwins, a pair of Black conservative YouTubers, that they were “NO longer welcome”, Amacher wrote: “I’m waiting for their response of, ‘hey sorry, blame it on my negro brain!’” On 7 October he replied to a comment about “the white girl in the front” of an image: “Getting strong mudshark vibes with that one.” “Mudshark” is a racist slur for a white woman who partners with Black men. Last November, under a post about “a mob of black ‘kids’” accused of attacking a pregnant woman in Chicago, he wrote: “F*cking savages and future super predators in the making!” In May, replying to a post about a weekend of shootings in Chicago, he wrote: “You can’t override biology or selectively breed out the ‘predator’ gene in certain populations.” In June, under a post claiming that “the biggest scandal in American history” was “convincing millions of people that Michelle Obama is beautiful”, Amacher wrote: “Hey now–‘BIG Mike’ ain’t playing around! No monkey business here…” The reference to “Big Mike” probably comes from a baseless conspiracy theory that Michelle Obama is a man. That month, Karmelo Anthony was convicted of murder in Texas for the 2025 stabbing of a fellow student, 17-year-old Austin Metcalf. Replying to a video of a crowd of Anthony’s supporters, most of them Black, outside the trial, Amacher wrote: “I hope none of these animals breed.” ‘Remigration is the ONLY answer’ Since November 2025, Amacher has used the word “remigration” in more than 30 posts. The term, promoted by Europe’s far right, describes the mass deportation of migrants; plans discussed at a meeting in Potsdam attended by AfD members included people with German citizenship. Last month Germany’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz, accused the AfD of pursuing an “ethnic cleansing” policy. “The word for 2026 is remigration!” Amacher posted in January. Asked by another user in November 2025 what should happen to Muslims in America, he replied: “Remigration to native homelands for those with insufficient loyalties.” In April he shared an AfD video with the comment: “Remigration is the ONLY answer–great video by the @AfD!” In June, under a post complaining about the Muslim call to prayer in Dearborn, Michigan, he wrote: “These sub-humans must be forcibly extracted from America and shipped off in crates back to the Middle East.” He has also cheered Jake Lang, a pardoned January 6 rioter who has led anti-Muslim protests. Replying last November to a post about clashes between Muslim residents and Christian protesters in Dearborn, where rightwing influencers have staged anti-Islam rallies, Amacher wrote: “Jake is the general leading our generation’s Crusade to save our nation’s cultural identity and heritage. Brave, fearsome, and ready to drive out the foreign invaders!” When Lang led a protest in Plano, Texas, in December “against the Islamic takeover of America”, Amacher tagged him in a post calling him “the leader for the next Crusades!” On 21 December he wrote that he had texted Lang to confirm he was “not Jewish”. Earlier this month, he posted: “We need another Crusades–except on our own home turf!” Two national guard members were shot in Washington DC last November, and an Afghan man, Rahmanullah Lakanwal, was arrested as the suspect. That evening Amacher wrote that the attacker “should be publicly executed in Lafayette Square using bacon grease, with the entire nation watching”. He added: “This will send a clear message to third world invaders that we will not tolerate their presence!” Other posts urge that migrants be shot, or rounded up by ordinary citizens. Under a June 2025 post by the British far-right activist Tommy Robinson about a defaced statue of Joan of Arc in Paris, he wrote: “These invaders don’t deserve deportation–better yet, shoot them and save the cost!” This June he wrote that “those uncivilized savages can leave Britain on their own–or be removed at gunpoint by a mob of furious native Britons”. Replying in April to Nick Sortor’s post that “hard choices are going to have to be made soon”, he wrote that if the federal government would not deport “these third-world invaders, then we, the American people, will have no choice but to hunt them down ourselves, round them up like the illegal trash they are, and throw their asses back across the border where they belong!” “Bounty hunters get paid to track down bail jumpers and hand them over,” he wrote in July. “We should be able to do the exact same thing with illegal immigrants–hunt them down, turn them in to @ICEgov, and get rewarded.” Public records show Amacher has used two first names. Oregon business filings list Ryan David Amacher, at a house in Lake Oswego, as the registered agent of Amacher & Company LLC, formed in 2012. In 2018, a letter from “Ryan Amacher” calling for the repeal of US immigration law drew a rebuttal in the Lake Oswego Review. By 2024 he was signing himself Rhein: federal campaign finance records list “Rhein Amacher”, at the same address, as the company’s president, and his columns in the Review now carry that name. Last year a Portland police dispatcher logged a call from “RYAN AMACHER” at the city’s ICE facility, while officers ran a records check on “Rhein David” Amacher. The Daily Mail has reported that his “real name is Ryan”. Until now, Amacher has been a lower-tier player in a rightwing influencer economy whose currency includes live streams of contentious events, tendentious coverage of perceived political foes, and disinformation campaigns. Even now, his social media following is relatively modest. His biggest platform is X, where his follower count (about 35,000) is dwarfed by those of similar rightwing creators such as Nick Shirley (1.8m), Nick Sortor (1.6m) and Katie Daviscourt (512,000). His first brushes with broader notoriety came during anti-ICE protests in his native Portland, Oregon, last year, when his antagonism toward protesters extended to the self-confessed theft of leaf blowers and other items from an abandoned protest camp.

title: Insults, odd obsessions and rambling thoughts: a week in Trump rallies
summary: President has hit red states to drum up Republican support – and his increasingly strange performances are on full display
text: Montana, Tennessee, Alaska. In the run-up to an election, a Republican president typically wouldn’t be campaigning in these traditionally red states. These aren’t normal times, however, and Donald Trump, an unpopular president leading an unpopular party, has held rallies in those states in the last week, seeking to drum up support. But a series of eccentric performances from the president means his behavior has been the focus, rather than any of the candidates he is backing. Trump, 80, has used his appearances to muse about animals’ opposition to the second amendment, to call one Republican candidate “nerdy”, and to demonstrate a hitherto unexpressed fascination with “asses” – men’s and babies’, in particular. Along the way Trump has repeated his lie that 2020 was a rigged election, claimed, falsely, that he has secured $21tn in foreign investment in the US, and issued dark warnings about Democrats. Let’s take a look. Syracuse, New York. Friday Trump was supposed to be in Syracuse to support Bruce Blakeman, the Republican candidate for New York governor, whom he introduced to the crowd in a confusing way. Trump told the crowd of Blakeman: “I’ve just known him just for a second. I’ve known him for a long time, years.” Aside from his entirely contradictory explanation of his relationship with Blakeman, Trump went on to claim that, in New York: “You can no longer say: ‘Mother – hi, mom’. It’s: ‘Hi gestating – hi, gestating. I love you so much, gestating.’” People are still allowed to say mother in New York. Trump continued by talking about one of the things closest to his heart, spending 15 minutes complaining about how he did not win the Nobel peace prize, despite having “settled eight wars”. “Pakistan and India. I called them up, I said: ‘If you guys don’t stop killing each other I’m going to charge you 250% in tariffs and we’re not going to trade with you. They said no, no, no, you cannot do that. I said, yes, I can,” Trump said. India has repeatedly denied that a ceasefire was reached because of any intervention from Trump. Clarksville, Tennessee. Saturday A day later, Trump appeared in Clarksville. There, he adopted a strange method of talking to the audience, saying there was “such love”, before adding: “I mean, it’s amazing. When you stand up here, it’s just like… the love. I could say the stupidest things and you clap: “Oh, I love you so … .’” Trump continued: “It’s true. But we don’t say the stupidest things. We say things of common sense. We say things that make sense, and we probably are mostly conservative, but it’s not really conservative. It’s things of common sense.” Youngstown, Ohio. Tuesday Speaking in Ohio, Trump said he had recently learned that Jon Husted, the Republican senator running for re-election in the state, played football at university. Trump continued: “I don’t do this with men very often. I started examining [Husted’s] body, because I didn’t know he was a great athlete. And I looked and I watched up and down. I looked at his ass and I looked at the whole – and then I looked at his hands. Look at his hands. He’s got these, like, claws.” Later, Trump praised Husted, 59, for having a good jawline, before turning his attention to insulting immigrants from Somalia. Trump claimed that those people “come from a part of the world that only knows how to kill each other” and said that in Somalia people were “low IQ” and “don’t have pants to wear”. Wasilla, Alaska. Tuesday Trump was in Alaska to rally support for Dan Sullivan, the Republican senator. It was revealing that he was there at all: this should be deep red territory. Yet the Democratic candidate, Mary Peltola, is running neck and neck against Sullivan, something which prompted Trump to call Peltola, a native American former tribal judge, “a whack job”. During a meandering speech, Trump also granted pardons, on stage, to two Alaska auto shop owners, who previously pleaded guilty to violating the Clean Air Act. “When you give somebody a pardon, they say that means – and I don’t know how this works and why it’s an expression, but it’s well used, that means you’re as clean as a newborn baby’s ass,” Trump said. He added of that phrase: “I never understood that. Why is that so clean? But they – they – they felt that was the definition of cleanliness.” The White House did not respond to a request for comment. Bullhead City, Arizona. Wednesday After praising Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad al-Thani, the emir of Qatar, as “young” and “handsome” (Sheikh Tamim is 46), Trump turned his attention the Arizona Republicans he was in Bullhead City to support, including Alex Kolodin, a member of the Arizona house of representatives who is seeking higher office. “Everybody also needs to get out and vote for Alex Kolodin, a warrior for election integrity, as your next secretary of state,” Trump said. “Alex, good luck. You look good. Central casting, actually. You want a secretary of state to look exactly like that, a little bit nerdy, and that’s good.” It was reminiscent of Trump’s repeated complaints about Ken Paxton, his handpicked nominee for US Senate in Texas. Trump has repeatedly said he does not like how Paxton talks, dresses, or looks. During his remarks, Trump also managed to add to questions about his health, insult yet another person he knows, and let the crowd know their life was less important than his. “I travel with more doctors than any human being. If people get sick in the audience, they don’t – they leave them alone,” Trump said. “You know what they call them? Collateral damage. If that person right over there, a friend of mine – he looks like shit, actually, he looks – he looks like he’s ready to have a heart attack. If he actually had a heart attack, you know what my doctors would do that follow the president, all presidents? “They would leave him alone. I’d say please help him. No, sir, we can’t leave your side. I said but he’s dying of a heart attack. Sir, he’s collateral damage. Can you believe it? They got, like, six ambulances and they won’t use one for anybody else. Anyway – but let’s hope we never have that problem.” Kalispell, Montana. Wednesday Trump made a fairly desperate plea to voters, invoking the long-time Republican fear-mongering that Democrats will ban guns – something which is very much not a position of the Democratic party. “You know who would love that to happen? Some of the wild animals you have up here that like – that like eating you,” Trump said. “We talked about that with Tim [Sheehy, US senator for Montana] and Steve [Daines, the other US senator for Montana] on the plane. That was my first question, I say: ‘When you walk out in the woods here, do you always have a gun, Tim?’ He said: ‘Actually – actually, yes.’ I said: ‘What about you, Steve?’ He said: ‘Yes, we’re intelligent people.’ “You know, the animals would be very, very happy to see you without guns. They would gain a lot of weight. And leave the law-abiding Americans defenseless while they set loose the savage criminals into your communities.” Even for a president known for eccentricities, Trump’s fascination with backsides, the appearance of his friends, and animals, has raised eyebrows. And with two weeks to go until the midterm elections, there will be more appearances to come.

title: Two people killed in light aircraft crash near Loch Lomond
summary: Police Scotland says boy, 16, and 80-year-old man died in incident north-east of village of Drymen in Stirling
text: A 16-year-old boy and an 80-year-old man have been killed in a light aircraft crash near Loch Lomond in Scotland. Emergency services were called to reports of an incident north-east of the village of Drymen, Stirling, at about 4.45pm on Friday. Police said the next of kin of the boy and the man, who were pronounced dead at the scene, had been informed. After the crash, temporary airspace restrictions, including drones, were in place around the village. Police Scotland said its Air Accidents Investigation Branch (AAIB) had been informed, and inquiries were taking place to establish the full circumstances of the incident. Restrictions were likely to be in place for some time, police said, to allow the AAIB to conduct its investigation. The Piper Tomahawk II aircraft took off from Glasgow airport on Friday afternoon at 4.17pm, according to data from online flight-tracking tools. The tracking data showed the plane circled before coming down north of Drymen. The plane stopped transmitting at 4.37pm, according to the data. Earlier in the day, the plane had taken off from Cumbernauld airport at 11.46am, before flying to Glasgow airport. It stayed there until about 1pm, then embarked on a flight north-east to Newport-on-Tay, opposite Dundee, before turning round and heading back to Glasgow. It was on the ground at the airport for just over an hour before it took off again and began its final flight. Gavin Birch-Williams, the managing director of Glasgow airport, said: “We are aware of an incident involving a light aircraft that departed from Glasgow airport. “This is a deeply tragic event, and the thoughts and heartfelt sympathies from all at Glasgow airport are with the friends and families affected.” In a statement, the AAIB said: “An investigation has begun into an accident involving a light aircraft which occurred on 16 October 2026. “A team has travelled to the accident site near Drymen, north of Glasgow, to make inquiries and gather evidence as part of the process of conducting a safety investigation.” Officers warned it was a criminal offence to fly in restricted airspace.
