title: Ministers must be honest about Russian threat to UK, says former Foreign Office head
summary: Peter Ricketts calls for more resilience in protecting banking, energy and water systems from cyber-assaults
text: Ministers need to be honest with the British public about the immediate threat posed by Russia, which could soon lead to lives being lost, a former national security adviser has said. Peter Ricketts, who advised David Cameron when he was prime minister, became the latest figure to warn about the scale of the threat posed by “hybrid attacks” from Vladimir Putin’s forces. The peer, who is the former top civil servant in the Foreign Office, said banking systems, energy or water supplies could be targeted by Kremlin cyber-assaults. He called for further investment in resilience for key sectors. It comes in a week where the heads of MI5 and the British army have warned about the danger posed by Moscow. Lord Ricketts also dismissed Andy Burnham’s claim he wanted to be a “bridge” between the US and Ukraine. Relations between Washington and Kyiv deteriorated sharply this week after Donald Trump waived a number of economic sanctions on Russia and suggested Ukraine needed a new leader. Speaking to BBC Radio 4’s Today programme, Ricketts said: “I think they’ve really got to start a conversation with the British people about what may be coming, because not only is Putin trying to break morale in Ukraine, he’s also trying to undermine morale in European countries.” In response to a question over the impact of disruption by Russia, he added: “I’m not saying there’s going to be industrial war with tanks rolling across the north German plain. “But these hybrid attacks are getting more reckless, more dangerous. One day, people are going to land up being killed somewhere, and so we are going to have to look at responding in that sense and finding the money to do it.” Speaking about Burnham’s comments at prime minister’s questions this week saying he wanted to be a bridge between Washington and Kyiv, Ricketts said: “I don’t really go on this bridge business. I mean, I don’t think in Trump’s current mood there’s any influence that Britain can have in the short term.” Ricketts’s comments join those by the director general of MI5, Sir Ken McCallum, and the chief of the general staff, Gen Sir Roly Walker, in the last few days about Russia. On Tuesday, McCallum said MI5 was devoting more resources to combating threats from hostile states than it did during the cold war and described Russia as the “number one aggressor”. And on Friday, Walker told 700 troops at Catterick garrison in North Yorkshire that politicians would soon need to have a “frank conversation” about the “sacrifices” that would be needed to prioritise defence and security. Walker, a former special forces commander, said soldiers would probably need to fight in a war, given the “extreme jeopardy in the world at the moment”. The warnings come after a difficult week for Kyiv, with the US appearing to withdraw support. Trump said the decision to pause sanctions was in the US “national interest”, despite previously signing them into law in September. Last week, he lifted restrictions on Russian diesel amid spiralling fuel prices in the US ahead of the midterm elections. He also suggested Ukraine needed a new president. Volodymyr Zelenskyy hit back this week during an EU summit, saying it was nice to be among “real leaders”. There are also concerns that the US has withdrawn intelligence sharing with Ukraine, leaving towns and cities across the country vulnerable to attack. Ricketts said the government should spend more money on protections for key infrastructure in Britain, including energy, transport, air traffic control and defence. He said: “They all need better protection, and that’s an argument that needs to be had with the British people because we need to find the money to do it.”

title: ‘Countries are defying gravity’: how much longer can global economy resist chaos?
summary: Sky-high oil prices and geopolitical turmoil have made less of a dent than feared … just don’t bank on it to last
text: Inside the vast, glass-walled Queen Sirikit conference centre in Bangkok, the air-conditioned atmosphere was calm as policymakers from more than 100 countries gathered this week for the International Monetary Fund’s annual meeting – and contemplated the surprising strength of the global economy. A small army of smiling, uniformed Thai staff were on hand to explain the baffling geography of the heavily guarded building, where lunch options were as cosmopolitan as the delegates – including, improbably, a Burger King. “Resilience” was the buzzword at one event after another, after six months in which sky-high oil prices and geopolitical chaos have made less of a dent in the global economy than first feared. Growth has not fallen off a cliff, buoyed up by the AI investment boom; stock markets haven’t crashed. “We had Covid, the war in Ukraine, supply-chain shocks, the war in Iran, and the alarm bells go off. And yet we haven’t had that massive synchronised crisis. So I think there’s this feeling that a lot of countries are sort of defying gravity at all income levels,” said Clemence Landers, the vice-president of the Washington-based Center for Global Development. Yet the IMF was also keen to remind delegates that the resilience of the past six months had been bought at a cost and may not last. The message – “Resilience under strain, urgent choices” – leapt out from the front page of its flagship publication, the World Economic Outlook (WEO). According to IMF experts, the cost of the energy support measures governments have put in place to protect their citizens from soaring oil prices, as a result of Donald Trump’s war in Iran, has been an extraordinary 0.5% of global GDP. It said many countries would be unable to sustain support on this scale for much longer – and some had already begun to phase out subsidies, exposing the public to more of the costs of the conflict. The IMF urged governments to limit the costs and let market signals do their work, by sticking to temporary, targeted measures, rather than across-the-board subsidies. Aside from how to cope with the practicalities of a conflict that has persisted far longer than many governments had hoped – and whose end point remains elusive – the IMF was also keen to highlight two pressing risks. The first was what it sees as the unsustainable state of the public finances, particularly in the world’s richest countries. The WEO projected the highest budget deficits this year for advanced economies since the depths of the Covid pandemic. That means government debt in these countries is expected to keep rising – from 108% of GDP last year, to 115% of GDP in five years’ time. “Public debt is high in many economies, and fiscal buffers that could otherwise have helped meet rising spending pressures from ageing populations, climate change and national security needs have instead been used to absorb the repeated shocks,” the WEO said. Anxiety about spendthrift governments appears to have been one factor driving the recent sell-off of government bonds – pushing up yields, or interest rates, to their highest levels in decades; though it also reflects higher expectations for inflation and growth. The IMF’s managing director, Kristalina Georgieva, lamented: “Too many countries, they did not use the post-pandemic recovery to rebuild fiscal buffers, and each new shock has pushed debt levels higher.” Fretting that this leaves governments exposed when the next shock comes, as well as pushing up the share of tax revenues required just to service debt, Georgieva repeatedly implored governments – not least Washington – to tighten their belts. “What is our loudest call to policymakers right now? Make urgent repairs to the fiscal house before the cracks widen,” she said. It seems a message unlikely to land well with voters buffeted by one shock after another. The US Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, did not bother to travel to Bangkok to hear it; nor to oversee the meeting of G20 finance ministers, of whom he is formally the chair this year. The UK chancellor, John Healey, stepped in to chair the meeting instead. He spent much of his brief time in Bangkok stressing the importance of standing shoulder to shoulder with Ukraine – which the US has notably not been doing of late. Russia’s delegation was allowed to attend the G20 meeting, to the deep discomfort of UK delegates. The UK received a positive review from Georgieva and her colleagues, for setting out a plan to balance the books; though she conceded the bond markets had not rewarded its prudence. “The UK is actually one country where action to reduce the deficit has been taken decisively,” she said. Asked why the UK’s bond yields have not fallen accordingly, Georgieva said London’s status as a global financial centre tended to put the UK under additional scrutiny. “Traditionally we’ve seen more attention, in relative terms in the UK, to what the government is doing. [There is] a bit more sensitivity, and I think the government recognises they need to stay the course.” Unusually, no communique was issued after the G20 meeting: a stark signal of how difficult it has become to reach multilateral agreement in the current fissiparous period. The UK will take over the G20 presidency next year and has ambitious plans, on AI regulation and international development; but Bessent’s no-show was a reminder of the tough task they face in rekindling multilateralism. The other alarming message the IMF was keen to land, concerned the threat of an AI market crash. As Georgieva put it in a blogpost on Friday: “The risk is that expectations may run rapidly ahead of productivity gains, setting the stage for near-term disappointment.” The Federal Reserve chair, Kevin Warsh, while professing himself an optimist about the long-term gains of “superintelligence”, as he insisted on calling it, put it another way: “We really don’t know what the market structure is going to be of these new technologies. Who’s going to get to make the money? What are the consequences for those that bet that they were going to make money, but the market structure doesn’t allow it?” And AI is not just a stock market phenomenon but a huge driver of real-world exports, of the hardware and infrastructure necessary – albeit the benefits are heavily concentrated in a small number of economies, including Taiwan and South Korea. The knock-on effects, then, would be significant. It is a familiar fear; but in its twice-yearly Global Financial Stability Review, the IMF laid out in detail the rising levels of debt being used to finance the AI boom; the intricate financial linkages between the companies involved; and the increasingly leveraged position of the investors – including hedge funds – backing them up. As far back as the Wall Street crash of almost a century ago, the economist JK Galbraith was highlighting the fact that leverage – betting with borrowed money, effectively – tends to amplify booms and busts. And as ministers met in the Thai capital, elsewhere in Asia there were tremors that may suggest Georgieva’s fear of “near-term disappointment” may already be gripping some investors. South Korea’s Kospi share index recorded its biggest weekly loss since October 2008, at the height of the financial crisis, tumbling by 14.5% during the week, as traders ditched chip manufacturers such as Samsung and SK Hynix. Analysts reported that questions around the borrowing, spending commitments and future profitability of AI companies unsettled the markets. Bonds issued by the datacentre CoreWeave slumped almost to distressed levels as these worries swirled. Expectations of future increases in US interest rates also rose, after data showing that consumer price inflation rose in September, as did inflation at the US factory gate. US tech stocks were also hit, knocking 2% off the Nasdaq index between Monday and Thursday. It was just the latest of a series of market wobbles of late, and finance ministers and central bankers probably gave it little thought as they were whisked in air-conditioned comfort back to their capitals this weekend. But if the boom does turn to bust, sending shock waves through the global economy, they won’t be able to say they weren’t warned that the “resilience” we have been enjoying rests on shaky foundations.

title: All the president’s women: a familiar downward trajectory in Trump’s team
summary: Half of the women on Trump’s team have been replaced by men, while men facing misconduct allegations remain
text: Donald Trump is not, by any measure, a feminist. He has said so himself. But the president has often pointed to his hiring and promoting of women in an attempt to stave off criticism of both his policies and personal conduct over the years. During his second term, however, there is one common characteristic among most of those who have departed the Trump administration. In the space of just a few months, half of his eight high-level female officials have either resigned or been fired. All have been replaced by men. Several other women in his administration have also departed, whether voluntarily or involuntarily. On Friday, Trump was forced to deny reports that he was considering replacing Susie Wiles, his White House chief of staff, and the first woman to do the job. “She’s gonna be here for a long time,” he claimed. Numerous top male officials, meanwhile, from Trump’s defense secretary Pete Hegseth, who has on multiple occasions courted global condemnation, to the widely ridiculed FBI director Kash Patel, have survived intense scrutiny and repeated calls for their resignation – and yet remain in post. Katie Zacharia The latest female casualty was White House press secretary Katie Zacharia, who was fired on Friday just five days into the role. After a rocky start to her tenure, sparked by a widely panned first White House press briefing on Tuesday, she had also faced questions over her legal credentials after admitting she did not pass the bar exam. The ensuing semantics battle over whether or not she is a lawyer, or an attorney, placed her in a pickle – even with the rightwing cable network Fox News. Zacharia had taken over from Karoline Leavitt, who said in August that she had chosen to resign from the role after 20 months so she could spend more time with her young family. Kristi Noem In terms of firings, the first domino to fall was former homeland security secretary Kristi Noem, who was the face of Trump’s mass deportation campaign until she was unceremoniously sacked on 5 March. Her tenure was plagued by controversy, in large part amid national uproar over federal immigration enforcement operations that killed two US citizens in Minneapolis (one of whom Noem called a “domestic terrorist”, with no evidence), and coincided with a sharp decline in national support for Trump’s immigration agenda. Her suggestion at a congressional hearing in March that Trump had known about her decision to approve a contract for a $220m ad campaign to encourage immigrants to “self-deport” – which prominently featured Noem on horseback – reportedly left Trump “pissed” and appeared to be the straw that broke the camel’s back. There had also been scrutiny of general leadership failures under Noem, as well as questions the influence of her adviser, Corey Lewandowski, who also left his role when she was ousted. Noem was repurposed as special envoy to the so-called “Shield of the Americas” coalition and, after that arrangement expired last month, is now serving in a vaguely defined advisory role. She was succeeded as DHS secretary by Markwayne Mullin. Pam Bondi Next fell former attorney general and Trump loyalist Pam Bondi, who was pushed out in April after a turbulent 14 months that saw the president increasingly frustrated over her mishandling of the Department of Justice’s long-awaited release of the Epstein files. The Epstein issue became a huge political liability for Trump and infuriated his Maga base, and he also felt that Bondi had failed to sufficiently prosecute his political enemies. Bondi revealed a month after she was ousted that she had been diagnosed with thyroid cancer. Her deputy, Todd Blanche, assumed the role in August. It’s worth noting that commerce secretary Howard Lutnick faced public scrutiny after details emerged surrounding his past ties to Jeffrey Epstein and visits to his private island emerged. By contrast, the White House supported him after Democrats called for his resignation. Lori Chavez-DeRemer Also in April, former labor secretary Lori Chavez-DeRemer stepped down after a Department of Labor inspector general investigation led to a series of allegations of misconduct, including having an affair with a subordinate and drinking alcohol on the job. She was replaced by Keith Sonderling. Kash Patel has also been alleged to have been intoxicated or absent on the job. He has denied these allegations, and remains FBI director. Tulsi Gabbard A month later, in May, Tulsi Gabbard resigned from her position as Trump’s national intelligence director. While she officially cited her husband’s rare cancer diagnosis, Gabbard was reportedly forced out after a tumultuous stint in which she was largely sidelined as Trump launched attacks on Venezuela and Iran. She had previously testified to Congress that Iran was not building a nuclear weapon. Gabbard was replaced on an acting basis by Bill Pulte, a Trump loyalist with no previous experience in the intelligence sphere, and eventually by Jay Clayton. Kimberly Guilfoyle Earlier this week, the Trump administration asked longtime Trump ally Kimberly Guilfoyle to step down from her position as US ambassador to Greece after weeks of reports that she sought payment from a Trump donor in exchange for access to administration officials. *** The only senior male official to have been somewhat punished by Trump since his return to office is Mike Waltz. The then-national security adviser was fired in May last year after inadvertently adding a journalist to a Signal group chat in which Hegseth disclosed secret war plans. Waltz had been on thin ice with Trump for a while, and the president was reportedly annoyed by Waltz’s hawkish stance on Iran. Signalgate merely sealed his fate. But he didn’t disappear to some obscure advisory role; Waltz was nominated to the position of US ambassador to the United Nations. Hegseth, meanwhile, was allowed to ride out the controversy and – several controversies later, including allegations of war crimes – remains in post. Democrats have highlighted the double standard that Trump only seems to fire women in his administration – even those who are ultra-loyal to him, and decidedly less incompetent than some of their male colleagues. “If you’re a man in the Trump administration, it seems that they reward misconduct,” Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, the Democratic congresswoman, observed in April. “I wouldn’t say I’m a feminist,” Trump said in a 2018 interview. “I mean, I think that would be, maybe, going too far. I’m for women. I’m for men. I’m for everyone.” But not everyone gets to stick around.

title: Honeybees are barging aside wild pollinators in hunt for pollen and nectar, study finds
summary: As a surge in beekeepers has lead to increased numbers of honeybees, researchers record them pushing bumblebees and other rival species away from flowers
text: Honeybees are outcompeting wild pollinators for resources by aggressively bumping into them and chasing them away from flowers, research has shown. The study, by researchers from Anglia Ruskin University, found that areas where there were higher concentrations of honeybees had fewer wild pollinators, such as bumblebees, solitary bees and hoverflies. Honeybees were also most likely to instigate, and win, competitive interactions, pushing out rivals to collect more pollen and nectar. The number of managed bees has risen in the UK, as campaigns to “save the bees” resonate with the public, leading to a boom in hobbyists setting up beehives. The number of registered beekeepers has more than doubled, from 19,000 in 2010 to 47,000 in 2025, according to the National Bee Unit. However, there are growing concerns that this growth in managed honeybees is harming other, wild, pollinators including bumblebees, by increasing competition for food and passing on diseases, especially in areas where there are fewer flowers or an especially high density of hives. To better understand the nature of this competition, the study in Cambridgeshire observed pollinators over a two-year period as they foraged on bramble and ivy in areas close to honeybee colonies. The study documented the outcomes of 300 interactions between flower visitors from five groups: honeybees, bumblebees, solitary bees, hoverflies and “other”, which included types of flower-visiting and pollinating flies, butterflies, beetles and wasps. In each interaction, the study noted where an individual “won”, by gaining access to a resource, “lost”, or if a resource was shared. Honeybees won in most of the encounters across both plant species. Past research has suggested that honeybees outcompete other pollinators indirectly, by taking up resources. However, the Cambridgeshire study provides evidence that they are posing a more direct form of competition, known as “interference competition”, where a species might attack or chase others away. “That’s important because, of course, it means that the wild pollinators are facing a challenge from both those types of competition from honeybees,” said Victoria Buckle, lead author of the study and a PhD researcher at Anglia Ruskin University. Honeybees were actively avoided by other flower visitors in 28.4% of interactions on bramble and 35.6% on ivy. In competitive interactions won by a honeybee, the honeybee either displaced other flower visitors – for example, by landing on them or pushing them off flowers – or chased them away, in about 20% of cases. Bumblebees were also observed displacing other pollinators, though Buckle believes this was probably not intentional, and was instead a reflection of their less coordinated movements as they fly through confined spaces. “They bumble along the patch and then they’ll mistakenly bump into another pollinator and it just falls off a flower,” Buckle said. “With the honeybees, the aggression was more overt. You could tell that they’re specifically trying to move the other one off the flower.” The reasons for honeybees’ aggressive behaviour is likely to relate to the way in which they organise their social groups, said Buckle, adding: “Some castes of bees can be guard bees, so they have that capacity within them to show threat and aggression, to guard their hives and to look after the brood.” The only pollinator able to hold its own against honeybees was the ivy bee, which was first recorded in the UK in 2001 and feeds mainly on the nectar of ivy flowers. It was seen displacing and chasing honeybees. The study also found that higher temperatures led to an increased number of competitive interactions, probably because nectar was drying up and plants were going into heat stress. Given that mean summer temperatures are predicted to rise by up to 4C in the UK by 2080, such competition is likely to become more frequent, said Buckle. More research is needed to examine how wild pollinators can be better protected, she added. “A lot of beekeepers are environmentally minded and they want to make sure that they’re not impinging or having an impact on other pollinators,” Buckle said. “This research is important because it helps guide our planning and best practices for conservation.”

title: Stinky business: south London bike shop hit by ‘unbearable’ stench from Thames Water sewer
summary: Owner and mechanics fear for their health and future of the Herne Hill shop with no date for fixing problem
text: The leafy south London neighbourhood of Herne Hill is a haven for cyclists who can often be seen lapping the local parks and refuelling at the many cafes that line the suburban streets. But there is something foul in the air of this corner of the capital – and for once it’s not the traffic fumes hitting bicycle riders. A toxic stench thought to be caused by untreated sewage stuck in Thames Water drains has been emanating from the subterranean depths for months, most likely caused by the summer’s lack of rain. The stink is so acrid that the Bicyclenation shop has had to bar some customers and its mechanics have been forced to work on the pavement outside. The owner of the shop, Tamas Polocz, has repeatedly complained to Thames Water since the smell first hit the shop in June and caused his colleague Nick to vomit. Last week the troubled water company told Polocz it accepted that a mains sewer directly beneath the shop was to blame, but it has yet to offer him and his team of 11 any date for resolving the problem. Polocz and his colleagues have been left fearing for their physical and mental health after repeated exposure to the gassy stench. And the outlook for the business is bleak. The odour comes in putrid wafts that occur at least five times a day, according to a “smell chart” used to log the time and duration of each incident with a description. The words used include “cabbage”, “teargas”, “onions”, “spicy BBQ” and repeated references to “shit”. When the Guardian first arrived at the shop there was a whiff of rotten eggs but not enough to stop mechanics working inside and customers milling about. But within minutes we were overpowered by a repulsive gas that hit the back of the throat and left us scurrying outside, gagging for air. “It’s unbearable,” said Polocz. “You can’t be in the shop when it comes.” He added: “It has a really strong physical presence. This is a smell you take home with you. It’s in your hair, on your skin, sometimes it feels it’s inside your skin. When you go home and cough, you taste it again.” The ordeal comes after record-breaking temperatures and drought prompted calls for a radical overhaul of an outdated sewage system, just as the Great Stink ushered in new sanitation in the Victorian era. Thames Water initially suggested the Herne Hill smell was due to a gas leak. But extensive tests by the local gas supplier ruled that out. Polocz said he had been battling the company every week. “Thames Water have always tried to push me away, or blame others. When they finally accepted liability last week I just broke down. But we still don’t have a date for fixing it.” The exact cause of the stench remains unknown, but a Thames Water engineer told Polocz it was likely to be linked to the lack of rain. The engineer also told him that a cast-iron ventilation pipe that had previously drawn odours away from the shop had not been replaced. Experts warn that during dry periods, untreated sewage builds up in pipes with no rainwater to flush it out. Microbial activity in the sewage causes foul-smelling gas to be emitted in wafts, in a similar process to the one that causes flatulence in human digestion. Prof Barbara Evans, the chair of public health engineering at Leeds University, said: “It sounds like methane and it’s probably unsafe working conditions. Biological processes are cyclical just like in your digestive system, which is why sewer smells come in wafts.” When Polocz woke up to rainfall, he was hopeful it would flush away the stench. “I looked out through the window at home and thought, oh good, but it didn’t make any difference. Even after the rain there was still the smell. Maybe the rain will eventually clear it, but we don’t know. Something is happening down there that is pushing the smell up.” Evans said: “The first flushes of rain will probably make things smell worse because it just stirs things up. It needs a lot of rain to clear. There might be some blockage there but it’s impossible to know without a proper inspection.” Harriet Talbot, a board member of Bicyclenation, said: “You can’t run a business relying on the weather.” She helped set up a webpage asking for customers to sign up for a collect and repair service to help the shop survive. Polocz said the shop was currently unsustainable because staff had to evacuate so frequently. “We have to do half a day in the shop and half outside on the pavement. But now the cold weather is coming, we can’t keep doing that.” And the stress from the stink is taking its toll. Polocz said: “I’m 49, but today I feel 62-ish. We have guys calling in sick. It affects you both physically and mentally.” Polocz said he laid in bed at night worrying how he would be able to keep the shop going. “The last thought of the day and the first thought of the day are now both the same,” he said. “And I wake up at night thinking: what are we going to do about it? I try to listen to a podcast, but I still keep thinking about the smell. Somehow I’m going to get through this and change back to normal.” Polocz’s plight is likely to add to calls for an overhaul of London’s Victorian sewage system. Evans said: “This underlines the need for a rethink of our sewers. The system was designed for a climate that we just don’t currently have any more.” The Guardian asked Thames Water when the problem would be fixed, why it had taken so long to resolve, and whether the company would apologise to Polocz. A spokesperson replied: “Our teams are investigating the source of an odour reported at a bike shop. Initial investigations have confirmed there are no blockages in the sewers surrounding the property. Odour monitors are to be installed, which will enable engineers to detect, measure and track odorous gases in real time and help determine the exact cause.”

title: ‘I cannot carry all of this alone’: the couples kept apart by the war in Gaza
summary: Families have been scattered, fathers separated from their children, and couples unable to reunite and marry
text: Wijdan Abu Matar, 43, was forced to leave Gaza in November 2023 with her eight children for medical treatment, while her injured husband, Hatem, remained behind. Wijdan and her family were living in the Nuseirat refugee camp when the Gaza war began with the 7 October 2023 Hamas attack on Israel. Ten days later, on 17 October that year, an Israeli strike hit the al-Muhandseen tower, near their home, injuring Wijdan and every member of her family. “We were sitting together, just about to start lunch when the bombing happened,” Wijdan recalled. “The ceiling collapsed over our heads. Everything went dark. I couldn’t see anything. I just started screaming the names of my sons and daughters.” Her daughter Nour, 15, suffered the most serious injuries, including a fractured skull and bleeding in the brain. Five-year-old Amna suffered severe burns to her chest. The family was initially separated after the strike. Nour spent about 33 days in intensive care, with Wijdan by her side. Amna and Aysel, three and a half, were at a different hospital for 15 days. On 30 November 2023, Wijdan travelled with Nour to a hospital in Egypt for treatment. For months, the family remained scattered across Egypt, receiving medical treatment and staying with other relatives. “I felt completely helpless,” Wijdan said. “There was a fire in my heart because I was away from my husband and my family was scattered.” Eventually, Wijdan managed to bring her children together in an apartment in Egypt. Three years on, however, she is still separated from her husband, who remains in Gaza. “I have become both the mother and the father to my children,” she said. “The responsibility is exhausting me, and I am constantly worried about my husband.” Hatem suffered a serious leg injury that limits his mobility and is now displaced in a tent in Nuseirat. Even speaking to him is difficult because of Gaza’s unreliable internet connection. “When he manages to get online, he calls me and the children. He tells me, ‘I am counting the days until I can see you again.’ I can see the tears in his eyes,” Wijdan says. Wijdan has no regular source of income and relies on donations. Hatem stopped receiving a salary 10 months ago and his injury prevents him from working. In Egypt, life is difficult for Wijdan and her family. She says she cannot afford transportation to send five of her children to school. “I see my children’s future slipping away in front of me, and there is nothing I can do.” Nour still requires medical treatment, but Wijdan often cannot afford her medication. She sometimes considers returning to Gaza to be with Hatem, but fears exposing her children to further suffering. “I dream of getting my children the treatment they need, and I hope we can reunite with my husband as soon as possible so he can also receive treatment,” Wijdan said. “I cannot carry all of this alone. Psychologically, I am exhausted. I have lost 35 members of my family in this war.” Since the war began with Hamas’s attack on Israel that killed 1,200 people, at least 73,783 Palestinians have been killed and 174,738 wounded, according to the health ministry. Earlier this year an independent UN inquiry found that Israel continues to commit genocide by deliberately targeting Palestinian children in Gaza. Sami Abu Tabaq, a 29-year-old Palestinian photojournalist, was forced to leave the Gaza Strip in April 2024, leaving behind his family and his fiancee, Ola. “Loneliness kills me every day,” he said. “Life away from the woman I love and my family is incredibly hard. I’m desperately waiting for the day God brings us together again.” Sami became engaged to Ola five months before the war began. They had met by chance when he chose her family’s home as a location for a photoshoot. Before the war, they saw each other constantly. They went to the sea, had dinner at restaurants in Gaza, and spent months preparing the house where they planned to live after their wedding, which was scheduled for November 2023. Sami and his family fled their home in Tal al-Zaatar, Jabaliya, early on in the war. Their home was badly damaged and later destroyed, along with the house Sami and Ola had been planning to move into once they got married. When his sister decided to flee south with her children, Sami accompanied her but he could not reach Ola to say goodbye. The separation became unbearable. Days, sometimes weeks, passed without Sami knowing whether Ola was alive. Once, he saw reports that an entire residential block near her home in Gaza City had been bombed. “I almost lost my mind. I had never felt so helpless,” he said. Unable to return north, he asked his brother to check on her. Eventually, his brother confirmed that she and her family were alive. Sami continued working as a photojournalist from southern Gaza. Four journalists who had shared his tent were later killed, including Hamza al-Dahdouh, a son of the Al Jazeera journalist Wael al-Dahdouh. As Israel threatened a ground invasion of Rafah in 2024, Ola began urging Sami to leave Gaza, fearing he would be killed. Sami paid a company coordinating exits at the time for both of them to cross into Egypt. But Ola could not reach southern Gaza to travel through Rafah. “She told me, ‘You go, and I’ll follow you,’” Sami said. “And here we are, still waiting, nearly two and a half years later.” They still have not managed to get married. By his second day in Egypt, Sami was overwhelmed by guilt. “The overthinking kills me,” he said. “I felt ashamed to turn on the lights or eat proper food while my fiancee and my family were struggling to find the most basic things.” In Egypt, his life has become dominated by loneliness and sleeplessness. “There is safety in Egypt and there are beautiful places, but I stay home. Happiness has no meaning without her. I cannot enjoy anything while she is not here,” he said. Despite the war, Ola completed her bachelor’s degree in nursing at the Islamic University of Gaza. She has also endured enormous loss: her cousin, the journalist Ayat Khadoura, was killed, along with about 50 other members of her extended family. From Egypt, Sami tries to create moments of happiness for her. For her latest birthday, he contacted her brother in Gaza and secretly arranged a cake, gift and flowers. “When she woke up and saw everything, she was so happy. I love her reaction when she’s happy.” The only problem was the flowers. “They were artificial,” he said. “I wasn’t happy with them, but natural flowers can’t get into Gaza because Israel does not allow them in.” Sami says he has tried every possible way to get Ola out, without success. She is now applying for scholarships abroad, hoping education might provide a route to evacuation and, eventually, to him. Sami recently travelled to Mecca for Umrah, where one prayer remained constantly on his mind. “I prayed, ‘God, please bring us together soon,’” he said. “But one thing I know for sure: I will wait for her for the rest of my life, until God brings us together.”

title: Plan to make firms pay more to train older workers than youth apprentices in England
summary: Exclusive: Ministers considering overhaul of apprenticeship funding scheme to tackle youth jobs crisis
text: Employers in England are to be forced to pay more to train an older worker than a youth apprentice under plans being drawn up by the government to tackle the youth jobs crisis. The Guardian understands ministers plan to overhaul Labour’s apprenticeship funding scheme to increase the cost of training by 25% for a worker over the age of 25 in order to encourage businesses to train young people instead. Aiming to reverse a 40% drop in youth apprenticeship starts over the past decade, the proposal is being developed as part of the government response to Alan Milburn’s review into why so many young people are out of work. With his final report delayed until after the budget, the former Labour cabinet minister this week signalled that boosting access to apprenticeships would be critical for fixing the first rungs of the career ladder for young people. The chancellor, John Healey, is preparing to include measures to tackle soaring youth unemployment in his highly anticipated tax and spending statement to the Commons in less than a fortnight’s time. After a rise in the number of young people not in education, employment or training to almost 1 million, Andy Burnham has made supporting youth job opportunities central to his agenda for power, including sweeping changes to retool technical education and apprenticeships. Ministers have been clear they want to rebalance the apprenticeship system back towards younger people. More than half of new starts are now for over-25s and the number of under-19s enrolling has almost halved in a decade. Under the changes being planned to the growth and skills levy – the £4bn a year tax used to fund the national apprenticeship system – employers in England will face a new “co-investment” rule restricting the funding they can access. Aiming to tip the balance to incentivise youth apprenticeships, the change is controversial because employers have for years been told by successive governments they were free to spend their levy funds on training as they saw fit. “Employers are not going to like it,” said one senior policy expert close to the government. “They were told ‘it’s your money, you get to decide’. But the system is not working at the moment.” Earlier this year Labour revamped the apprenticeship levy introduced by the Conservatives in 2017, with changes handing more flexibility to employers over the types of training the system can be used for – including new foundation apprenticeships and shorter courses. Under the levy, large employers (those with yearly wage costs totalling more than £3m) must pay 0.5% of their total annual pay bill into a dedicated digital pot that they can draw from to fund training and assessment costs. Following the proposed change, money from the pot would still be available to cover eligible training costs for apprentices aged 16 to 24. However, for older apprentices, the funds would cover only 75% of the cost and employers would need to pay for the remainder. It is believed the measure is under consideration for a phased launch from the start of the next academic year, in September 2027. Labour has been warned that its skills strategy to tackle youth unemployment risks failure without a change in course. Official figures show its flagship foundation apprenticeship scheme has enrolled just 160 young people in the first eight months, against an ambition for 30,000 starts over the course of the parliament. This month the Fabian Society thinktank called on ministers to increase the rate of the growth and skills levy to 0.7% to raise an additional £2.5bn, which could be used to target more funding towards youth apprenticeships. However, it is understood that ministers are wary of heaping additional costs on businesses after the backlash suffered over employer national insurance contributions and as firms press for budget support to help them hire more young people. Alongside tight constraints on the public finances, this has shifted the focus to restricting levy funds as a way to support young people without further adding to the costs for the public purse. A Department for Work and Pensions spokesperson said: “We remain determined to address the 40% decline in apprenticeship starts among young people and give them the skills they need to succeed. “We are already pivoting the system towards the next generation, including by creating 50,000 additional apprenticeships for young people, and introducing a new hiring payment of £2,000 for SMEs who take on a 16-24-year-old apprentice. “The Milburn review is due in the autumn. We will not pre-empt its findings.”

title: Palantir patient data tech rejected by many NHS trusts in England
summary: Exclusive: health bodies across country say controversial US firm’s data platform no better than systems already in use
text: NHS organisations that care for millions of people in England are rejecting Palantir’s patient data technology, according to freedom of information responses that reveal health bosses believe they can find better or equal alternatives in many cases. Some health bodies said the £330m federated data platform (FDP) operated by the controversial US company had made it easier to manage waiting lists and has improved surgery scheduling. But, from Gateshead to Truro, others said they were declining to use it or had carried out trials and reverted to old systems. A Suffolk trust said other systems “supercede” the FDP’s functionality, while Greater Manchester’s care board called the Palantir system “duplicative” and “retrograde”. The responses come as Andy Burnham’s government faces a crunch decision about whether to exercise a break clause in the seven-year NHS-Palantir deal, which was intended to better integrate the health system’s data to improve clinical accuracy and efficiency. Protests against the US firm’s role have also focused on its other contracts with the Israeli military and Donald Trump’s homeland security forces. There is also dispute over evidence for the system’s effectiveness and public concern about the involvement in the NHS of a company cofounded by the tech billionaire Peter Thiel, who said in 2023: “The NHS makes people sick.” According to more than two dozen FOI responses reviewed by the Guardian, 16 trusts and health boards declared they do not use it, following its introduction in March 2024. They include the University hospitals of North Midlands NHS trust, which said it will not use it primarily because “it does not appear to provide functionality over and above what we have already” and Dorset HealthCare university trust said it “will not be adopting or going live with the FDP”. Humber Teaching NHS foundation trust said: “We have no plans to use it.” Cambridgeshire and Peterborough NHS foundation trust said it has used the system but it has “not offered significant improvements on local systems”. Avon and Wiltshire mental health partnership NHS trust said it had yet to find an FDP tool that offered significantly more than its existing capabilities and University hospitals Birmingham NHS foundation trust, which cares for more than 2 million people, said it had no plans to use it, citing “limited expected benefit over existing solutions”. The FOIs were gathered by Medact, a health campaign that opposes Palantir’s role in the NHS, and posted to a public transparency website, WhatDoTheyKnow. Palantir has previously challenged claims that other software could be just as effective, with its senior vice-president, the former Labour MP Tom Watson, saying last week: “If there are companies that can do it, they would have taken part in free and open competition” to run the FDP. Watson, a Labour peer and former minister alongside Burnham, was appointed as Palantir’s chief lobbyist last month amid a wave of opposition to the Palantir deal. He warned his former colleagues in Labour not to let “mob rule … lead procurement practices”. But two parliamentary select committees have urged the government to end Palantir’s contract, including the Commons’ science and technology committee. Martin Wrigley, a Liberal Democrat member of the committee, said the NHS boards’ responses “justify what I have been saying for the last year, which is that Palantir’s system is just not that good”. “Once again we have proven that centrally dictating a solution to the NHS can’t work,” he said. “We have to get back to developing interoperability so each trust has its own software but with a set of standards for how they interact. Palantir are great sales people but they over-promise and under-deliver.” Dr Rhiannon Mihranian Osborne, a spokesperson for Medact, said the FOIs showed alternatives existed, a safe transition away from Palantir was possible and “the government has no excuse to extend the contract”. “Instead of outsourcing key NHS functions to big tech companies, the government must back NHS innovation and the highly skilled NHS data professionals who work alongside doctors and nurses to deliver care in the public interest,” she said. Palantir accused Medact of “slanted analysis” and of “misleading the public”. “The FDP is, objectively, a successful programme,” a spokesperson said, adding that its purpose was to provide trusts with tools to draw on depending on their existing capabilities and needs. “It is one of just 20% of major government programmes with a green delivery rating, with ministers stating that it ‘is significantly exceeding its benefits forecast and has exceeded every target’.” It said NHS trusts, including Chelsea and Westminster, Leicester, Northampton, Bath, North Cumbria, Croydon, Great Western, Dorset, Chesterfield, Ashford and St Peters and Norfolk have publicly praised the FDP. Palantir also points to NHS data that shows trusts using the FDP have carried out 117,000 additional operations and a 14.3% reduction in discharge delays for long-stay patients. NHS England has, however, had to add a caveat to its statistics, making clear it cannot draw conclusions about cause and effect as other variables have not been controlled for. The government’s national data guardian for health and social care, Dr Nicola Byrne, this week urged ministers to give substantial weight to the “trust factor” when deciding on Palantir’s fate. More than 44,000 people have filed legal objections to their health data being shared with, stored in or used by the FDP. Byrne, a government-appointed watchdog, said there was evidence “a significant number of local organisations” were reluctant to adopt the FDP including due to concerns about Palantir and “a preference for other solutions”. Sophie Don, the chief executive of Voror, a patient data company that bid unsuccessfully against Palantir, said: “Of course Palantir isn’t the only company that can do this. It doesn’t surprise me that it is making things harder … If NHS staff are choosing not to use it, it’s a clear sign it’s not creating value. There are many home-grown systems that would release much more value to the NHS than the [Palantir] platform.” A spokesperson for NHS England said: “137 NHS trusts have now reported benefits from the wide range of tools available on the platform – helping staff join-up and improve care for patients, and work more efficiently.”

title: Russell Brand’s trial: what we’ve heard and seen so far
summary: Accused of assaulting six women, the former comedian and presenter denies all charges
text: Russell Brand’s trial at Southwark crown court began this week, with widespread media coverage. The former comedian and presenter is accused of assaulting six women. He denies all charges. Here are five things we have learned so far: ‘Indiscriminate and voracious’: the prosecution sets out its case Brand faces three charges of rape, three of sexual assault and one of indecent assault against six women, in allegations spanning 10 years from 1999 to 2009. He denies all the charges and has pleaded not guilty. Jury selection began on Monday but the prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones KC opened the case on Wednesday. She told the court that Brand, 51, was a ruthless, calculated and manipulative predator with an “indiscriminate and voracious” desire for sexual contact. His methods varied, she argued, and women were just a means to an end for him. “Sometimes he might tell women what they wanted to hear, be nice, be kind. Sometimes he might have appeared interested in their cause, sometimes he might even have made sexual advances within minutes of meeting them, identified someone young and impressionable where he was performing – but every time he had identified his target, he was intent on trying to fulfil his sexual desire,” Karmy-Jones said. ‘I was like a zombie’: court hears first women’s accounts The court has so far heard from two of the six women who have made allegations against Brand. Both women have given evidence from behind a screen, and the trial judge, Mr Justice Bennathan, has told the jury that the measure was quite standard, saying: “Don’t hold it against anyone.” The earliest allegation Brand faces is from a woman who claims the TV personality raped her after a fringe cabaret show at the 1999 Labour party conference in Bournemouth. She broke down in tears in the witness box on Thursday as she told how Brand was “monster-like” when he pushed her on to a bed in a hotel room in an attack that left her feeling as if she couldn’t breathe. “I was like a zombie on the bed. All I could think was he’s inside me and the quicker the better,” she said. Brand is accused of indecently assaulting the second alleged victim, who told the court on Friday that he transformed into a “wild-eyed maniac” when he tried to drag her into a men’s toilets for a sexual encounter. The woman, who was working for MTV at the time, alleged she “wrenched” herself free, saying: “I emerged relatively unscathed. He didn’t manage to rape me.” 'No power imbalance': Brand sets out his defence The court heard that in prepared statements in police interviews, Brand denied all the allegations. He said he had never engaged in nonconsensual sexual activity, and suggested some accounts may have been reinvented or imagined after a 2023 documentary about his alleged sexual misconduct. His defence barrister, Ian Winter KC, suggested to the first complainant that Brand was a “very young-looking boy” and there was “no power imbalance” during their alleged encounter in 1999. He suggested to the second complainant that Brand had “invited” her into the toilet for a consensual sexual encounter and that it had been a “short-lived, very, very minor incident”. 'I pray for everybody': Brand puts faith in Christian image Brand has arrived at court with his wife, Laura, on three of the five days the case has been sitting. His security guard and members of his entourage have sat in the public gallery each day. Arriving at Southwark crown court on Friday in his signature dark suit, cross necklace and long scarf, the actor said: “Obviously it’s an extraordinary and stressful situation, but it is also an exploration of truth and justice and, as I’ve said before, I pray for everybody involved. “It’s in a way very, very sad but hopefully it can bring about some conclusions that are beneficial.” In court, Brand has sat upright with his hands in his lap, appearing to listen intently to the evidence. Journalists sitting in the press gallery, directly behind the glass dock, have caught glimpses of his reflection as he stares ahead. Occasionally, he has been spotted clutching prayer beads. The court case as content Brand has arrived at court each morning to a large crowd of photographers and journalists from across the world. There has been widespread international coverage of the case, including in the US, where Brand now lives with his wife and children. Each day there have been at least 20 journalists crammed into court 3 where the trial is taking place, and about 30 more have been watching on a screen in another courtroom in the building. Some have accessed the case remotely via CVP link. There are at least five daily podcasts covering the trial, and several journalists from the same outlets have been angling to get into court.

title: Brexit’s back – but are British voters ready to contemplate a reversal?
summary: As Andy Burnham talks up closer alignment with the EU and a poll suggests half in UK would rejoin, the B-word is back on the agenda
text: In February 2016, days after David Cameron announced the UK would hold a referendum on leaving the EU, he told workers in Slough not to imagine they could change their minds a few years down the line if they did not like how things panned out. Voting to stay in or leave was a once in a generation thing, he said. “This is a decision that lasts for life.” Well times change, as the last prime minister but five could testify. A decade after Britain told Brussels where to go, Brexit is back on the political agenda. After years in which many politicians avoided any mention of the B-word, Andy Burnham broke the omertà in his party conference speech last month, saying he would look again at Britain’s relationship with Europe. This week he went further, insisting the current arrangement must change: “Sticking with the status quo is not good enough for Britain.” Among a range of options on the table, he has been clear, is the possibility of going “all the way” and rejoining the EU. There are pressing economic reasons Burnham has been talking up closer alignment, as the EU works out its position on the UK’s access to its protectionist “Made in Europe” legislation, which the prime minister has said could hurt British manufacturing. But after years of bitter division and political dysfunction in the fallout from the vote, are the British public really ready to talk about Brexit again – and even to contemplate reversing it? Polling evidence may suggest so. A “megapoll” of more than 11,000 people published this month found that half of Britons now support rejoining the EU, with only 28% opposed, and the remainder undecided. Almost 60% think it was wrong to leave. Sliced some ways, the numbers are even more striking: a More in Common survey in June to mark a decade since the vote found that if another referendum was held today across Britain’s 632 constituencies, just 11 would vote to leave (even in Clacton, Nigel Farage’s constituency, 52% supported rejoining). What changed? To the polling expert Rob Ford, a professor of political science at the University of Manchester, there are several key reasons, from demographic change to buyers’ remorse. Brexiters are fewer in number – “a lot of leave voters have died, bluntly” – and both young people entering the electorate and those who did not vote in 2016 skew heavily in favour of Europe. And with the project widely considered a disappointment at best, a proportion of those who opted to leave have switched positions. “Although each is a relatively slow moving and relatively small incremental force, add them together over a decade and it adds up to quite a lot of change,” said Ford. Given the divisiveness and turbulence of the past decade – and the fact many Labour MPs represent constituencies that voted to leave – it is little wonder that some senior Labour figures have expressed nervousness about reopening the debate. “[Burnham] definitely needs to proceed with caution because we don’t want to restoke division,” one cabinet minister told the Guardian. But the view from formerly Brexit-supporting areas is not necessarily what it was. “Hull East voted 74% leave in the referendum, however I believe the mood has changed,” said Karl Turner, the Labour MP for the constituency since 2010 (he now sits as an independent after having the whip withdrawn). “Constituents tell me they expected Brexit to improve their lives; instead many face higher costs and fewer opportunities.” As a result, he said, they were “increasingly ready to consider the practical benefits of rejoining the EU”. Ford added: “Andy Burnham looks at the data and says, well, I’ve got an electoral coalition that’s 80% remain and becoming more so. The parties to my left that I need to squeeze have a [position] that is even more remain than that. “And the overall balance of opinion in the country is now nudging up towards 60% in favour of remain, sometimes even higher in terms of how many think Brexit is a mistake. Why wouldn’t I move in a pro-remain direction? It’s the direction of travel of the country. The art of leadership is getting out ahead of the trends that are happening and using them to your advantage.” Sara Hobolt, a professor in the department of government at London School of Economics, agrees that the polling data today suggests Brexit could be an effective general election rallying cry for Labour. “This is an issue that a lot of people were quite upset with Keir Starmer and his government for not talking about it. It is something that definitely mobilises the base.” While Labour supporters and those the party wants to win back from other progressive parties overwhelmingly support remain, she points out, the Conservative party is now much more divided on the issue, having lost many of its hardline Brexiters to Reform. “That means that [by putting Brexit back on the agenda] you can potentially do more damage to the right than the left. “But I think probably the main thing for Andy Burnham is that this has been seen in his electoral base as something [that has been overlooked]. ‘You talk about growth? Why are you not talking about Brexit?’ Because overwhelmingly remainers think that a lot of the economic problems we’ve faced over the last decade are due to Brexit.” But if uniting the left before a Westminster election is one thing, winning a future Brexit referendum is a whole other challenge, as the experience of 2016 showed. “There clearly is support for rejoining the EU,” says the More in Commondirector, Luke Tryl, “the question is, how resilient would that be in the face of a referendum campaign?” One factor is, inevitably, Brexit weariness, he says. “The British public are tired. They’ve lurched from crisis to crisis, from row to row, and I think, for some, just the idea of reopening the wounds [is unwelcome]. I think in a campaign rejoin, if it got to that, would start ahead, but I don’t think the headline polling we are seeing now would remain where it is once it was subject to a full back and forth.” Ford agrees – noting that the EU will be resistant to serious discussions so long as there is the prospect of a wholesale reversal under a future Reform government. The risk of bringing up Brexit is not just because the subject is neuralgic to many, he says. “One of the problems during the Brexit years was it was just simply impossible to get a conversation going about all the other pressing issues that mattered. “There is a risk for Burnham, if this thing starts to take life of its own yet again, that the big difficult conversations he wants to have about some of the longstanding structural problems in British society will be harder to have because for a lot of people in the political conversation, Brexit is like catnip – they’ll run straight to it. And then you’re not able to get them to pay attention to the issues you want them to pay attention to.”

title: Home Office denies British baby living in Thailand chance to meet great-grandfather in UK
summary: British father would like to take his family to Lancashire to see ill relative but officials refused visa for his partner, a refugee from Myanmar
text: The Home Office has denied a great-grandfather from Lancashire the chance of meeting his five-month-old British great-grandson, who lives abroad. William Cross was born in Thailand on 30 April to parents Matthew Cross, 31, who is from Burnley in Lancashire, and Khin Thant Zin, known as Jue Jue, also 31, a refugee who fled persecution in Myanmar to Thailand. The family live on the island of Koh Tao, famous for its diving schools and a centre for turtle conservation. It is a popular tourism spot and Cross, a mechanical engineer, opened a steakhouse restaurant there 15 months ago. He met Zin on the island and the couple are now engaged. She works in the restaurant managing social media and human resources. Cross’s parents have visited the family in Thailand and have met their grandson. But William’s great-grandfather George Kerr, 74, who lives in Clayton-le-Moors in Lancashire, has multiple health problems and so is unable to fly out to Thailand to meet the baby. Instead, a large family gathering was planned in Burnley for Christmas. Cross said: “My grandfather suffers from ill health and sadly he is unable to travel. He and I have been extremely close all my life and I’m desperate for him to meet his grandchild.” The family have just signed a lease on a new home and have bought some land on the island for later development. They assumed that organising a short trip to the UK for a family Christmas would be straightforward. But the Home Office refused Zin’s visitor visa application, which means the family will be unable to travel. Officials said they were not satisfied she was a “genuine visitor”, and that there was no evidence Zin would return to Thailand because she had not shown evidence of significant family ties there, and she was unable to show sufficient evidence of her income. “Jue Jue has never had a bank account,” Cross said. “Her brother and sister both live on Koh Tao and her mum is planning to move here when her younger sister has finished school in Myanmar.” The visitor visa application process is expensive and cumbersome. “They required documentation from my family to be financial guarantors while we’re in the UK. Passport photos of my grandfather, my mum and dad and me, a typed letter from each of us confirming our commitment to sponsorship, a formal letter of invitation from my parents saying they would be comfortable with my partner being in my home,” Cross said. “We had to travel to Phuket, a journey of two nights and three days from Koh Tao on a ferry and buses, which cost us £400, to complete biometric screening required for the visitor visa application.” There is no right of appeal against this visa refusal so the couple are preparing a new application, although the Home Office refusal letter warns that future applications are likely to be refused “unless the circumstances of your application change”. They also need to buy and provide evidence of return flight tickets even though they don’t know whether the new visa application will be granted. They have to make the long journey from the island on ferry and buses a second time to repeat the biometrics. “By the time we send our next application, the whole thing will have cost us £3,000 with no guarantee of it being accepted,” Cross said. The family are still hoping that baby William will be able to meet his great-grandfather at Christmas. Temperatures on the island rarely fall below 25C, so back in Burnley his relatives have bought warm baby clothes in the hope he will get a chance to wear them. A Home Office spokesperson said: “We do not routinely comment on individual cases. All visa applications are carefully considered on their individual merits, in line with the immigration rules and based on the information and evidence provided by the applicant.”

title: Country diary: The challenge of making a thatched roof pine-marten proof | Tom Allan
summary: Glenisla, Angus: Damage by squirrels is common; the mustelid less so. Still, as a local told me, ‘you cannae blame them wanting somewhere to live’
text: That the thatch is thick with moss and crusted with the brittle fronds of lichen is not unusual for a roof of this age. What’s puzzling me is the hole in its centre. It is about 10in wide – a dark scoop, as if someone has taken a giant ladle to the roof. When I climb the ladder for a closer look, I can see toothmarks on the reed. I also see that the hole does not go all the way through – the animal obviously gave up after an exploratory burrow. “It was probably the pine marten,” says Pam Aitchison, the owner of this thatched roundhouse in a glen just south of the Cairngorms, which I am here to re-thatch. She fed it peanut butter and jam sandwiches for a while, but stopped when she became concerned that it might be damaging the roof. This is a first for me in 14 years working on thatched roofs. Damage by squirrels is fairly common. They can chew through reed, wire netting, roof battens and even lead chimney flashings. Rats and jackdaws are familiar culprits too, but pine martens – less so. They are a regular presence in this glen, though. Bruce, a semi-retired plumber who lives up the track, had a pair of martens nesting in the roof of his garage for a few summers. Initially, he tried various ways of keeping them out, but in the end he decided to live with them. “They’ll squeeze through anything,” he said. “You cannae blame them wanting somewhere to live.” The tightly packed new thatch I am laying should, I hope, be less inviting to the mustelids than the soft surface of the old reed. I set to work fixing in place the bundles of water reed, which has come from just down the road, in Tayside (unlike the majority of thatching reed in the UK, which is imported from overseas). It was harvested from Britain’s largest continuous reedbed – an 11-mile-long arc of Phragmites planted in the early 19th century. Originally intended as a flood defence, it is now managed by the RSPB, and contains a quarter of Britain’s population of bearded tits, as well as marsh harriers and water rails. Thatch can be a home for wildlife before it goes on the roof, too. • Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024 is published by Guardian Faber; order at guardianbookshop.com and get a 15% discount

title: Trump pauses new Russia sanctions passed by Congress amid deepening row with Ukraine
summary: President signed the legislation championed by late senator Lindsey Graham last month but has waived the restrictions as they were due to come into effect
text: Donald Trump has put on hold a sweeping new sanctions package targeting the Russian economy, telling Congress the pause on the legislation passed by both chambers was in the national interest. In an executive order on Friday, the US president said he was waiving many ⁠sanctions, restrictions and duties ⁠on Russia, in a move that comes as he has been publicly criticising ⁠Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy, including suggesting that Ukraine needs a new leader. The move was greeted by Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev, who wrote on social media: “The Trump administration’s suspension of the Graham Act is an important and truly historic moment.” Trump signed the legislation last month, after Congress passed the measure in an act of rare bipartisan agreement. It sought to clamp down more quickly on the flow of financial resources fuelling Russia’s war against Ukraine. The legislation – whose ‌primary backer in ‌Congress was the late senator Lindsey Graham – sanctions Russian officials, banks and a shadow fleet of tankers that keeps Russian energy moving and was due to be implemented in two days. It also directs Trump to impose up to 100% tariffs on the top five importers of Russian oil or natural gas, with an exception for countries that import less than 15% of Russia’s natural gas exports and have taken significant steps to reduce those imports. Friday’s announcement comes a week after Trump said the US had agreed to purchase diesel from Russia to try to bring down global energy prices, upending years of US and western pressure on the Kremlin to end its war against Ukraine. Trump said last week that Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1m tons “immediately thereafter”. Russia would deliver an additional 3m tons “within a short period of time” after that, he wrote. The president has face widespread criticism after making the announcement, with a dozen US senators – including six Republicans – calling on Trump ⁠to rescind his diesel deal. A letter from the bipartisan group of lawmakers sent on Tuesday urged Trump to execute the sanctions authorities included in the legislation passed last month, called the “Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026”. Under the legislation he signed into law, Trump had until 18 October to impose the sanctions and tariffs on Russian energy, or waive them. The administration had not told lawmakers whether it would impose the sanctions or issue a waiver. Zelenskyy said on Friday the diesel deal would mean cash “will start flowing back into Russia”, as he met European leaders in Brussels. Trump ⁠blindsided Zelenskyy last weekend by announcing that Ukraine and Russia had agreed not to target each other’s energy facilities. Facing midterm elections next month, Trump has blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries for pushing up energy prices that could cost his Republican party its thin majorities in the US ‌Senate and House of Representatives. Trump’s administration is suspected of withholding intelligence from Ukraine on incoming Russian ballistic missile strikes, and of throttling Starshield, the military version of the Starlink satellite internet network, to prevent it from being used on drones flying faster than 100mph (161km/h). Neither has officially been confirmed. The US sanctions legislation has also become a campaign centerpiece for Senator Darline Graham, Lindsey Graham’s sister appointed to serve out the remaining months of his term, who is also running to replace him in the Senate more permanently. In a debate earlier this week with South Carolina Democratic nominee Annie Andrews, Graham – who has Trump’s endorsement and is expected to campaign with him in South Carolina next week – said she had been “so proud” to help get the measure passed but acknowledged it was Trump’s purview as to how he implemented it. “It gives the president tools that he can use, if he so chooses, to end the war through economic sanctions,” Graham said during the debate in Columbia. “So that’s up to him as to whether or not he wants to use it, or whether he wants to use something else, but I think the purpose of it is to bring down the gas prices and ultimately end the war. And when the war ends, gas prices will fall.” With Reuters and the Associated Press

title: Mexican judge sentences three men to 158 years in prison for murders of Australian and US surfers​
summary: Australian ​brothers Jake ​and Callum Robinson, and ​their ‌American friend ​Carter Rhoad, were killed while on a surf trip in Baja California in 2024
text: A Mexican ⁠judge ⁠has sentenced three men to 158 years ⁠and nine months in prison each for ⁠the murder of two Australian ‌brothers ‌and their American friend during ‌a 2024 surf trip to the state of Baja California. The ‌defendants were declared guilty a week ago of homicide, aggravated robbery, robbery with violence and vehicle theft ⁠with violence, crimes committed against Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, and their ‌American friend Carter Rhoad. Rhoad and the Robinsons were shot dead in a suspected robbery while travelling through Mexico. They were camping in a remote beachside area near the city of Ensenada when they were attacked on 27 April 2024. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Their bodies were found days later in a clifftop well with gunshot wounds to the heads. Jesus Gerardo – known as “El Kekas” – was accused of leading the attack. His surname has not been disclosed for legal reasons. Two other defendants, Irineo Francisco and Angel Jesus, were also found guilty and have been sentenced. The families of the victims followed the sentencing hearing via video link. Prosecutors had requested damages of more than $100,000 but the judge ruled against it and said any compensation would have to be pursued through civil proceedings. The brothers’ parents, Martin and Debra Robinson, travelled from Australia to the port city of Ensenada for the trial, which began on 7 September. They have established a foundation in their sons’ names to carry on their legacy. The Callum and Jake Robinson Foundation aims to “help people live bigger, shine brighter and love harder in their honour”. Callum, the older of the two brothers, moved to the US as a professional lacrosse player and has been remembered for his loving nature and passion for the environment, having been involved in coastal cleanups. Jake, a doctor, was set to take up a position at Geelong hospital after returning to Australia. He has been remembered for his academic success, his passion for sport, particularly cricket and surfing, and his compassion. Baja California is one of Mexico’s most violent states, plagued by organised crime and drug trafficking, although cartel activity does not usually affect tourists. Other foreign visitors have, however, been targeted in criminal attacks on Mexico’s Pacific coast. Two Australian surfers, Dean Lucas and Adam Coleman, were killed in 2015 while travelling through the north-western state of Sinaloa. Their bodies were later burned.

title: Mimicking populists will not ease cost of living or boost productivity, Mathias Cormann warns
summary: Former minister and OECD head urges Australia not to adopt migration caps, with research showing migrants boost employment
text: Australia’s mainstream political parties are being warned not to adopt populist policies such as migration caps to address voters’ grievances over the cost of living. Instead, Australia’s longest-serving finance minister, Mathias Cormann, is urging politicians to deliver housing, real wage growth and lower energy costs by boosting productivity. Now the secretary general for the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), Cormann will deliver an address to the Centre for Independent Studies on Saturday night spruiking productivity as the only way to reliably lower the cost of living over the long term. Though not directly named in his address, One Nation – which largely runs on an anti-immigration platform – has surged in popularity since the 2025 federal election, with its primary vote reaching 25%, according to the latest Guardian Essential poll, rising above the Coalition’s 22%. While populist parties may have gained traction by speaking to real grievances about rising energy bills, home ownership and real incomes going backwards, Cormann is expected to warn Labor and the Coalition not to follow suit. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email “Mainstream parties that respond to a populist surge by adopting its economics do not recover their voters. They lose twice: once to the original, which the electorate will always prefer to the copy, and once to the centre, which has nowhere else to go,” he will say in his address. “The lesson is consistent: deliver homes, lower energy costs, real wage growth and a credible budget, and the populist tide recedes. “Mimic the populists, and you simply confirm that they were right all along. The way to defeat populism is to solve the problems it feeds on.” Cormann will point to “arbitrary migration caps” imposed regardless of their effect on business, hospitals, aged care or universities. He will acknowledge more Australians now than any time in the past 20 years say the migration intake is too high and may support such policies, with many attributing their concerns to housing. But the answer is to address housing supply, infrastructure, services and the composition of the migration intake, he will say. According to OECD research across Australia’s regions, in places where more migrants arrived, employment among Australian-born workers grew faster, not slower, with no measurable effect on their wages. Without migration, Australia’s working-age population would decrease as the number of older people grows. “An ageing country that chooses to shrink its working-age population while promising to spend more on health, care and defence has not developed a plan – it has put forward a contradiction,” Cormann will say. Tariffs, which have been imposed by US president Donald Trump and proposed by One Nation, would also fail to address the cost of living and could instead raise costs for farmers, miners and builders, Cormann will say. He believes Australia can only grow its way out of the issue through productivity. “There is no shortcut to a lower cost of living. There is no populist shortcut, through tariffs and caps and state banks,” he will say. “There is only the long way round: an economy that produces more, competes harder and grows faster than its costs … anyone offering you a quicker route is offering you a poorer country.”
