title: Ukraine war briefing: Russia building non-negotiable ‘security zone’ inside Ukrainian border, Putin declares
summary: Russian president says area will not be part of any potential peace talks while Kremlin puts its size at spanning 660km. What we know on day 1,697
text: Russia is establishing a “security zone” inside Ukraine along the border and it will be non-negotiable in any ⁠future talks with Kyiv, Vladimir Putin has said. The Russian president, wearing military uniform and speaking during a visit to a command post, said the operation ⁠was in response to Ukraine’s ⁠2024-25 incursion into Russia’s western Kursk region. “The Russian armed forces were tasked not only with expelling the enemy from our land but also with establishing a security zone ⁠in the adjacent territory. This task is being carried out successfully,” he said in televised comments on Friday. “Our goal is to ensure the absolute security of Russia’s border regions ⁠for the future, and we do not plan to make this a subject for potential peace negotiations with Ukraine.” The planned ‌security zone spanned 660km (410 ‌miles), of which 70% was currently under Russia’s control, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said. Peskov did not say how deep it would ‌reach inside Ukraine. The zone requires Russia to carve out land in the Sumy and Kharkiv regions, which are not among those it is illegally claiming as its own territory. Donald Trump has put on hold a sweeping new sanctions package targeting the Russian economy, telling the US Congress the pause on the legislation which passed both chambers was in the national interest. The US president said in an executive order on Friday he was waiving many ⁠sanctions, restrictions and duties ⁠on Russia, in a move that comes as he has been publicly criticising ⁠Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy. Zelenskyy said the Ukrainian military’s access to the Starlink satellite internet service had not yet been fully restored, as media reports suggested the order to throttle the service had come from within the White House. Zelenskyy met European leaders on Friday in Brussels and asked the EU for another €70bn ($79bn/£59bn) next year to fund Ukraine’s defence against Russia, report Jennifer Rankin and Andrew Roth. Hours earlier Trump called Ukraine’s renewed strikes on Russian oil refineries “a disgrace” after his purported “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine failed to take hold. A Russian ⁠airstrike on Kherson in southern ⁠Ukraine killed one ⁠person and ‌injured ‌19 others, the governor ‌said on Saturday. The person ‌killed was an ambulance driver and ⁠a child was among the injured, Oleksandr Prokudin said ‌on Telegram. Russian attacks on Friday killed at least eight people and injured 60 ⁠across Ukraine, hit two shopping centres and cut power to more than 1 million people after strikes on the energy grid, ⁠officials said. Two were kiled and 12 more wounded in attacks on three districts of the eastern city of Kharkiv, governor Oleh Syniehubov ⁠said. Further Russian strikes through the evening injured nine, officials said. Attacks in Kramatorsk in the eastern Donetsk region killed two and another two were killed in south-eastern Dnipropetrovsk region. A drone strike on a food-processing facility killed one person and wounded eight in the north-western region of Volyn, according to governor Roman Romaniuk, leaving 370,000 people temporarily without power. Drone attacks also struck a customs terminal and torched about 10 trucks in the town of Kovel, he said. Other attacks hit at least two shopping centres – one in the northern city of Sumy and another in the neighbouring region of ⁠Rivne, officials said. The attacks came as a new report showed that civilian casualties from Russia’s invasion have climbed steeply. At least 328 civilians were killed and 2,105 wounded last month – a total that is 85% higher than in September last year, the report from the UN human rights office in Kyiv said on Friday. It said intensifying Russian attacks in October already had killed dozens of civilians, including children. “The first two weeks of October were among the deadliest periods for civilians in years,” said Danielle Bell, the UN office head. As Russian missiles and drones have systematically slammed into power plants in Kyiv and Kharkiv this week, the rolling blackouts and water outages have increasingly resembled a supposed Russian blueprint to destroy life in major Ukrainian cities seen by the Guardian, writes Andrew Roth in this analysis.

title: Brush fires set homes ablaze in southern California as it braces for more hot weather
summary: Hot, windy weather stokes fires in southern California as utilities shut off power to 150,000 customers as precaution
text: A fast-moving fire spread into neighborhoods in southern California on Friday as the region braces for more hot, windy weather that will amplify fire dangers through Saturday. Several structures could be seen ablaze in video footage captured by local news helicopters as firefighters worked to wrangle the more than 465 acre Norte fire, which erupted in Orange county on Friday. At least six homes were destroyed, according to Mark Backoff, a division chief with the Orange county fire authority (OCFA). “Due to topography features and the weather, this fire rapidly grew,” he said in a video update Friday afternoon. “We continue to be engaged in the firefight and we have additional resources coming.” Photos taken by the local TV news station showed a row of houses at the end of a cul-de-sac reduced to blackened debris. Others were coated red by fire retardant. Roughly 16,000 people in the coastal communities of San Juan Capistrano and San Clemente were under mandatory evacuation orders by Friday afternoon. Flames aggressively ripped across the brush-covered hillsides, shrouding the sky in thick smoke. Sirens wailed through the city streets, as the hum of helicopters and aircraft echoed from above. Nine schools in the area dismissed early, as the OCFA urged all residents under the order to leave quickly. In a Friday evening press conference, officials said two firefighters were injured battling the blaze due to heat exhaustion. While the fire continued to burn out of control; authorities said the objective was to limit its further spread and keep the fire within its current footprint. Just to the south, a blaze dubbed the Henderson fire, which erupted in San Diego Marine Corps training base Camp Pendleton on Thursday, swept across more than 2,000 acres by Friday afternoon Videos of the incident shared by the California department of forestry and fire protection showed a wall of flames that thrashed in the strong winds alongside the Interstate 5. The major highway was closed in both directions by California Highway Patrol for part of the afternoon, as plumes of thick black smoke clouded visibility. The blaze was 20% contained by Friday evening. A blaze in Malibu, west of Los Angeles, covered roughly 146 acres and was 39% contained on Friday evening. Evacuation orders and warnings for a large swathe of the Santa Monica Mountains were still in effect. Facing daytime highs of up to 92F (33C) with wind gusts reaching up to 65mph, fire officials said “crews will continue to protect structures and build containment” in a Friday morning update, adding that fire progression and flare ups could occur under increasing winds. More than 7,200 structures remained under threat, but none have been reported damaged or destroyed by the Bryson fire. Lindsey Horvath, the Los Angeles county supervisor, thanked firefighters “who held the line to make sure that despite these challenging winds, no lives or structures were put in harm’s way” by the blaze. Local residents were asked to keep roads clear to make it easier for emergency responders to operate. There were “only minor injuries” to the more than 400 firefighters working to contain the Bryson blaze, Anthony Morrone, the Los Angeles fire chief, said during a press conference held on Friday morning. The blazes broke out during a high wind event that has increased fire risks across southern California. Dry, warm and gusty north-east winds known as Santa Anas, which blow from the interior of southern California toward the coast and offshore, could continue through Saturday, according to the National Weather Service, and the potential for extreme fire behavior and rapid spread may still rise. As the firefight continues, California governor Gavin Newsom secured a Fire Management Assistance Grant from the Federal Emergency Management agency to help support crews working to suppress Orange county’s Norte fire. “By securing this federal assistance, we are ensuring our local and state partners have the critical resources they need,” he said in an issued statement. In anticipation of the extreme weather event, California’s office of emergency services also pre-positoned resources statewide. “It’s a pretty widespread event of elevated fire weather, so the whole SoCal region should really be on alert,” said Rose Schoenfeld, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service. Fire hazards typically rise in southern California during this time of year, and risks are expected to remain high into November. If there aren’t significant rains, they could extend longer. Because some of the state’s worst wildfires in recent years have been sparked by power equipment, utilities proactively shut off power to more than 150,000 customers across the state. In Los Angeles, the mayor, Karen Bass, who faced criticism for her city’s response to deadly fires in 2025, directed the fire department to deploy personnel and equipment ahead of the winds. The fire department also requested assistance from the state’s office of emergency services. Schoenfeld said the Santa Ana winds are not going to be as strong as those that fueled a deadly firestorm in early 2025, that destroyed thousands of homes and killed more than 30 people when gusts reached up to 100mph. But she still urged residents to be ready. “We are still in red flag conditions through 8pm [Saturday] evening,” Horvath said. “It’s important that we stay vigilant and stay prepared.”

title: Uncovering the secrets of New Zealand’s elusive ‘jungle penguins’
summary: The tawaki, or Fiordland crested penguin, known for its prominent yellow eyebrows, has for years baffled scientists with its unusual habits
text: Deep in the misty fjords of New Zealand’s South Island, a team of researchers is trying to catch one of the world’s most elusive penguins: the forest-dwelling tawaki, or Fiordland crested penguin. For weeks, researchers stand sentry each day over a burrow on Eleanor Island, hoping to corner the female bird so they can retrieve data from its tagging device. But this penguin has developed a clever exit strategy – digging multiple tunnels to elude its captors. The Tutoko I prepares for a research trip during its annual Fiordland crested penguin nest survey around Doubtful Sound “It took us about four days to recapture that bird,” says Dr Thomas Mattern, a research fellow at the University of Otago and chair of the Tawaki Project, a scientific initiative established to study the population. “We plugged all the holes around the nest so that it could not escape, until we finally could recover that device,” he adds. In a first for the species, Tawaki Project researchers are conducting long-term population counts, unlocking secrets about the bird’s breeding and foraging habits, and what threats they might face. The project is New Zealand’s most comprehensive mapping of tawaki nests. Over September, it mapped 93 nests across two islands in Fiordland, and has now mapped 1,200 nests across nine fjords in the past 12 years. Its mapping shows the tawaki population is roughly three times bigger than earlier surveys suggest, says Mattern, pictured below at Precipice Cove. Dr Thomas Mattern searches for tawaki near Precipice Cove during a research trip with the Tawaki Project The Māori name for crested penguins, tawaki, is a catch-all for several species around New Zealand and the sub-Antarctic region, but the focus of this annual voyage is on the declining species that inhabits remote Fiordland, New Zealand’s largest national park, which is Unesco heritage listed. Until German-born Mattern and his wife, Ursula Ellenberg, founded the volunteer research project in 2014, almost nothing was known about Fiordland’s tawaki, which stands half a metre tall, and features prominent yellow eyebrows. “Tawaki are a ghost,” Mattern says of the penguin’s enigmatic behaviour. But “they are the most amazing penguin species … They do not fit any penguin mould. What we know about penguins, you throw it all out of the window.” Clockwise from top left: A tawaki taking shelter. A research vessel at anchor near the Shelter Islands. Dr Thomas Mattern looks for penguins. A nest tag on Eleanor Island Unlike most penguins, the Fiordland tawaki do not breed in colonies, preferring instead to build single burrows deep in dense rainforest, sometimes at high elevations. While some other species can nest in forests, tawaki are unique because they nest exclusively in forests, Mattern says, describing them as “proper jungle penguins”. Its hunting habits are also unusual. Some groups fish entirely within the fjords, while others hunt in the ocean. The tawaki’s habits have baffled scientists “When you think you have them nailed down, you go to a different fjord, and they show behaviour that just does not conform to any of the ideas you have developed so far,” Mattern says. ‘Absolutely zero sense’ Tawaki have also become infamous among scientists for their baffling journey to feed before they go through their annual “catastrophic moult” – the scientific term for when animals shed and replace all their feathers in one go. All penguins moult after breeding season and before they do, they eat vast quantities of food to put on weight. Despite an abundance of food around the fjords in December (when breeding season ends), tawaki undertake a 5,000 to 7,000km return trip to the sub-Antarctic region to feed. “These emaciated tawaki, that have just said goodbye to their chicks, hop in the water and travel halfway to Antarctica, which makes absolutely zero sense because there should be more than enough food in the water just outside their breeding area,” Mattern says. “They are running a marathon, while trying to gain weight.” Researchers Owen Dabkowski and Mandy Abernethy explore a nest on Eleanor Island Mattern believes tawaki are likely acting on ancient instinct, heading to grounds where all other crested penguin species feed. The Tawaki Project is funded by public donations and international grants, and supported by local volunteers, such as Richard Abernathy, the owner of tourism company Fiordland Expeditions, who donates his boat and time to the expedition for several weeks a year. “Since 2018, we’ve been chasing penguins all over Fiordland,” says Abernathy whose ability to find nests in surprising places has earned him the nickname “sniffer dog”. Together, their efforts have “shed light on the most understudied species” in New Zealand, Mattern says. In 2020, the International Union for Conservation of Nature’s Red List moved tawaki up in status from “vulnerable” to “near-threatened” because the researchers were able to develop a better picture of their populations, estimated to be in the region of 12,00 to 15,000 mature birds. A tawaki swims in Charles Sound in Fiordland But risks remain, including from commercial fishing practices. “[We’re] looking at survival rates … to determine whether the population is stable,” says Mattern. “If they’re going down, then we need to kick into gear to improve the situation for them.”

title: China’s tourists flock to experience a pretend typhoon as ‘dark tourism’ flourishes
summary: The concept of ‘paying to suffer’ soars in popularity, with simulated disasters proving a modern twist on visiting sites of historic tragedies
text: When Leon Lv was looking for somewhere to travel last year, she turned to the Chinese social media app RedNote for ideas. The algorithm took her to videos of people struggling to survive typhoon-strength winds and flash floods. “I never experienced a typhoon. I don’t know how it will feel and what will happen. I just have seen it on the news,” says the 28-year-old from Chongqing in south-west China. “So that’s why I want to go there to have a safe place to experience it and learn something.” She travelled more than 1,300km to Hangzhou in the east, and joined a group of 20 to take part in a disaster simulation that featured a typhoon-fuelled flooding scenario. Standing in a simulated flood, her mind momentarily went blank as hundreds of tonnes of water swept people off their feet, and carried them towards a safety barrier. As the surge hit, she forgot she was in a simulation. “One thing I learned is how to stay calm and protect myself during a flood. I learned how to use the right body position to stay safe,” she says. “No book and no school [can] teach me like that.” Across Chinese social platforms phrases like “paying to suffer”, or “paying to buy fear” are trending online as part of a wave of interest in experiences known as “dark tourism”. Lvxing Base, a company in Hangzhou offering simulated disaster experiences has gone viral. The founders spent 10 years making documentaries in some of the world’s most extreme environments. At a 200,000 square metre facility, which opened in 2024, they simulate extreme weather conditions like typhoons and mudslides, giving participants the experience of what it would be like in a disaster. “I don’t deny that many people come because they want excitement,” says general manager Wang Kuanghan. They want to see what this place is like, what a real typhoon and torrential rain feel like, and whether they themselves can withstand it. Most of our individual customers are between 20 and 30 years old.” It plans to open five more centres across China within the next three years. It also plans to create earthquake and fire simulations. The offerings are not limited to private companies. At Beijing’s Haidian public safety museum, tourists experience simulated earthquakes, tsunamis and fires using a 4D theatre, equipped with moving platforms and sound effects. Last year the southern Chinese city of Guangzhou opened a five-storey centre to teach visitors how to respond to emergencies and disasters. Its earthquake simulator can recreate ground shaking equivalent to a 7.2 magnitude quake. Extreme weather has become increasingly common in China. In 2025, China recorded its highest number of hot days since records began, and was hit by 10 typhoons, well above the long-term annual average. China’s ministry of emergencies reported that 67 million people were affected by such disasters across the country. In 2024, local governments were instructed to promote immersive disaster education, instructing safety centres, museums and training bases to use simulations to teach people how to respond in a real crisis. ‘A new generation of travellers’ “The new generation of Chinese travellers want to experience a place rather than simply see famous attractions,” says Robert Li, director of the School of Hotel and Tourism Management at the Chinese University of Hong Kong. But some travellers have found a way to blend the two approaches; rather than indulging in the white-knuckle ride of a simulated typhoon, they are travelling to real sites of death and destruction. In May 2008 a magnitude 8.0 earthquake devastated towns in China’s Sichuan province, killing more than 70,000 people. Alice*, a 30-year-old writer from Sichuan walked around Beichuan, one of the affected towns, the ruins of which the government had preserved. Metal beams hold collapsed buildings in place for the public to visit. She saw the site where schools collapsed, crushing students inside. In Yingxue close to the epicentre, a broken clock surrounded by the remains of a middle school is frozen at 2.28, the moment the earthquake struck. “I felt scared because of the power of nature and how many children and students could not escape from it,” says Alice, who plans to start a Chinese language Substack account detailing her journeys into tragedy. “Everything was so broken. It became like a ghost town, because nobody lives in the old town any more.” Alice believes dark tourism helps a country reconcile with its past, even if the government decides what can be remembered. In recent years, tour guide Samantha Wang has seen an increase in Chinese tourists attending the Nanjing Massacre Memorial Hall. In 1937 the Japanese Imperial army captured Nanjing, and Chinese official accounts say 300,000 civilians and soldiers were killed over weeks of massacres. Japan’s official position is that it acknowledges that large numbers of civilians were killed but says the number of victims is “difficult to determine”. Entry to the hall is free but tourists must book online The local government reserves 25,000 places a day. In August, tickets to attend the museum are frequently sold out in advance, she says. “There are more tragic sites in China, and I see more people interested to know about that. That’s a new trend” says Wang. Inside the memorial hall hang photos of victims. “They [visitors] feel sad when they see those pictures, when they see those kids who were killed … After the visit, they feel relieved, and they feel encouraged that they should work harder to make China stronger,” she says. *Name has been changed Additional reporting by Yu-chen Li in Taipei

title: Shooter in fatal Bend, Oregon, school shooting was former student there
summary: One teacher and three children killed after Griffin J John II, 16, barged into elementary school and began shooting
text: The 16-year-old who barged into an elementary school in Bend, Oregon, and unleashed a barrage of gunfire that killed a teacher and three children was a former student at Silver Rail elementary, officials confirmed in a Friday press conference. The heavily armed shooter, identified as Griffin J John II, climbed over a fence and onto the school’s property before shooting through a set of locked doors to enter the building. The shooter, a former special needs learner, beelined toward a special education classroom left of the entrance doors, firing as many as 15 rounds. All of the victims from Thursday’s shooting were in that room: five-year-old Rhoam Summer, two other students, aged eight and 11, whom authorities have not identified, and 25-year-old teacher Megan Lambert. Lambert, from central Oregon, had regarded Silver Rail as a “dream job”, her family said in a statement read by police. “She always fought for the underdog and those with special needs.” The shooting also left a seven-year-old in serious condition, police said, and 54-year-old educator Becky Drury with serious, but non-life-threatening, injuries. A 36-year-old Silver Rail parent, identified by relatives as Kaylub Giamanco, heard the gunshots as he was driving by and entered the school. He saw an educator in a scuffle with the shooter, at which point he intervened, shooting and killing the teen. Police say the teacher threw her phone at the shooter before tackling him, as she fought to disarm him. “She almost certainly helped prevent more bloodshed,” Bend police chief Mike Krantz said. Authorities recovered 44 more rounds of ammunition in the shooter’s backpack. Police have not offered a motive, citing the continuing investigation. Candlelight vigils and memorials have sprung up around Bend, as the city has been thrust into a gruesome, but tragically familiar American story. Outside the school on Friday, a steady stream of people arrived to deliver flowers in front of the campus. They left dozens of bouquets, teddy bears, Minnie Mouse stuffed animals and a pumpkin. Most people stopped by for just a moment to pay their respects. Some sat, and parents held their children and cried together. It was eerily quiet at a time when the campus would normally be teeming with activity, said Joe Camarlinghi, father of a third grader at the school. Fabiola Caseres, who runs a local preschool and came by to deliver flowers, said the sadness was palpable all around the close-knit city. “It just feels so heavy,” she said. “Everybody is looking like deer in the headlights. It’s so sad, and you can’t stop thinking about the kids. They’re supposed to come home.” Thursday’s events mark the most deadly school shooting since the September 2024 mass killing at Apalachee high school in Georgia, where a 14-year-old shooter killed two teachers and two students. Although a motive in this school shooting remains unclear, the age of the shooter points to a troubling pattern. Some of the most recent high-profile shootings on and off school campuses have been carried out by teenagers and young adults, many of whom are a part of nihilistic online communities where posters praise, and seek to emulate, prior shooters like those who carried out attacks at Columbine high school, in Christchurch in New Zealand and at Virginia Tech. In May, two teenagers who met and were radicalized online shot and killed three people at a mosque in San Diego before shooting themselves. In their manifesto, they explicitly named the Apalachee high school shooters as their inspiration. The city of Bend, home to about 100,000 residents, held a candlelit vigil on Thursday night. Hundreds of people gathered in Bend’s Drake Park as the sun set. Oregon governor Tina Kotek and Bend mayor Melanie Kebler attended the vigil. “There is power and love in this park tonight,” Kotek said. “On behalf of everyone who lives in Oregon, I am so sorry for what you are experiencing today. No parent, no family, no community should have to have this kind of day.” All schools in Bend and La Pine, a neighboring city, were closed on Friday.

title: Cloudy with a chance of moths: bogong swarms are bamboozling weather radars across NSW
summary: Radar systems designed for rain, hail and snow are picking up bogong moths migrating to the Australian Alps
text: It was during Sydney’s Olympic Games in 2000, people say, that a swarm of bogong moths attracted by stadium lights was so huge that meteorologists mistook it for rain. Fast forward 26 years and the bogongs are back in big numbers. And, this time, they are firmly on the radar. “Every single night, particularly across eastern New South Wales and around Sydney, widespread rain is appearing on the imagery,” the ABC’s meteorologist has reported. “The only problem is, many nights (it’s appearing where) there hasn’t been a drop of rain (on the ground).” Weather radars, designed for rain, hail or snow, may be picking up swarms of moths on their long-distance migration to the Australian Alps. Radio pulses, designed to hit water particles and bounce back as “echoes” on the rain radar screen, may be reflecting off insect bodies and wings instead. A Bureau of Meteorology spokesperson says it is possible radars across eastern NSW are detecting bogong moths, as large numbers of insects can look like very light widespread rain, particularly near sunrise and sunset. Radars have been showing increased echoes that aren’t rain, the spokesperson says, however completely attributing the effect to moths was challenging, given other factors, such as temperature inversions, can cause similar effects. That radar data could be “absolute gold” for scientists, says Dr Kate Umbers, who has been working to understand where bogong moths breed and the routes they take. After all, researchers have tried numerous tactics – from tagging tiny moths, to collecting stories and newspaper reports – to trace the moths’ journey across hundreds of kilometres. Umbers, an associate professor in zoology at Western Sydney University and the managing director of Invertebrates Australia, says it poses all sorts of interesting possibilities and questions, including: “How many bogong moths equals heavy rain?” Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email But moths are far from the only flying animal able to be picked up by radar. Prof Justin Welbergen, an ecologist who specialises in flying foxes at Western Sydney University, has been using radar data to track the movements of flying foxes, both in near real time and retrospectively. It began, Welbergen says, because he had been researching the coordinated nightly departure of bats from their roosts, and happened to check the weather radar while in Melbourne. “I decided to look at the weather radar to see if I could see any signal of the flying foxes in the radar – and there it was. And the rest was history.” Flying fox emergences are highly organised events, where the hungriest individuals leave first, he says. “Adult females were followed by their young, and then the adult males would be the last ones to leave, only after all the females had left.” The animals show up clearly in radar data as “a big bag of water”, emerging at about the same time each night around dusk, and flying in predictable directions, Welbergen says. With those insights, researchers built a working prototype that allows them to track and count flying foxes using radar data – in near real time with the help of a computer algorithm, and even reconstruct historical movements over several decades with data from weather stations. A similar initiative in the United States, called BirdCast, relies on weather radar to track bird migrations. Welbergen hopes to expand the flying fox prototype, known as “Aerocast”, in collaboration with other researchers and organisations, for tracking other aerial animals, such as birds and even bogong moths. Although dependent on radar coverage and quality, it is a promising tool for conservation, which could be used to detect signals of important ecological events, such as mass flowering or extreme heat. Like bogong moths, flying foxes are difficult to track across the landscape because of their extreme mobility. “Flying foxes travel all over the place, all the time. They congregate in these roosts, and the individuals that are there may not be there the next day.” It is not the only thing the two species have in common, Welbergen says. “They often emerge from these central locations at predictable places, and predictable times of the day and year,” he says. “So our techniques for detecting flying foxes, I expect, are readily transferable to moths as well, because [on the radar] flying foxes are effectively just giant moths.” In the meantime, Umbers has been delighted to have the help of millions of research assistants across Sydney and Canberra as the latest bogong wave passes through. “For us, having that many eyes on this species at one time is the best possible scenario we could hope for in trying to understand them.” It has been a worrying few years since populations collapsed, but the small, brown critters are not out of the woods just yet. Their alpine habitat remains threatened by global heating, and an abundance of sightings in cities may not necessarily equate to a population boom overall. Still, Umbers says it is “wonderful” that a new cohort of Australians are getting acquainted with a bogong moth storm. “There’s a lot of people alive that have never seen this,” she says. “The moths are saying: don’t forget about us, look after us, look how amazing and impactful and epic we can be.”

title: Trump in Georgia falsely claims election of Jon Ossoff was illegitimate
summary: President appears at rally for struggling Mike Collins, dismisses critics and touts ‘most successful’ two-year run
text: At a rally in north Georgia, Donald Trump again claimed that the 2020 election in Georgia was fraudulent, alleging that the election of US senator Jon Ossoff was illegitimate. Ossoff, who faces US congressman Mike Collins in November, does not represent Georgia’s values, Trump said. “And he was never elected,” Trump added. Ossoff has maintained a consistent lead against Collins, with most recent polling showing him with a nine-point lead against his Republican rival. Trump claimed he was about to complete the “most successful” two-year run of a president in history, touting stock market gains, low unemployment and poverty rates and the establishment of “Trump accounts” for newborns. Trump again said that American voters would receive a $5,000 government check if Republicans hold the US House of Representatives, claiming that $21tn in foreign manufacturing investments pledged on his watch would offset the trillion-dollar cost. Most of those pledges remain unfulfilled. Trump also touted his immigration record and the overthrow of the Venezuelan government. “Forty-eight hours, and that war was done,” Trump said. He described the early days of the war on Iran from the perspective of Oval Office meetings and damage reports, particularly of strikes against Iranian leadership. “They’ll blow up Israel, they’ll blow up the Middle East,” Trump said of Iran and the imperatives of launching attacks. “Iran is the only country where nobody wants to be president.” The Iran war has caused a spike in gasoline and diesel prices. Trump was dismissive of critics citing the increased cost of living on his watch, describing the term “affordability” as Democratic propaganda. “In the past 17 months, zero illegal aliens have been admitted into the United States,” he said. An undocumented migrant is rarely “admitted” in any official way. Trump returned to his regular themes at the rally, which began at about 2pm. About 1,200 people packed grandstands at Dalton municipal airport. Trump took the stage at about 4.20pm, 80 minutes after his scheduled start, with about 300 people standing unshaded in the Georgia afternoon sun. His supporters were undaunted. “Donald Trump is the greatest president of all time,” said Tracy Spencer of Chattanooga, Tennessee, as she awaited the president’s arrival in Marine One. Asked how she addresses the increasing criticism of the president from disillusioned conservatives, she scoffed. “Well, none of my friends and family are expressing that to me, because they know better,” she said. “But I have heard the rumors that there are some people that think that, and I would say to those people that growth doesn’t happen overnight and that there are growing pains.” Trump obliquely discussed his administration’s attacks on anti-discrimination policies he terms “DEI” while describing the “handsomeness” of a US soldier he encountered at the White House. “Everything is based on merit,” Trump said. “I really have my difficulties with the supreme court, but … our country now is based on merit.” Two protesters briefly unfurled a banner with an anti-ICE slogan. They were hustled out of the grandstands quickly by security. The assault of a protester in Ohio by Trump supporters in the stands on Monday was not repeated.

title: Family of US man who died on Six Flags ride question if death was preventable
summary: Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem died after reportedly ‘passing out’ and falling off Goliath rollercoaster in Georgia while beside niece
text: The family of a man who was ejected from a rollercoaster at a Six Flags amusement park in Georgia and died has publicly questioned whether the death could have been prevented. Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem was riding the Goliath rollercoaster at Six Flags Over Georgia near Atlanta alongside his niece during a family trip to celebrate her birthday when he was thrown from the ride. His niece witnessed her uncle’s death, a relative told the Atlanta ABC News affiliate WSB-TV. “A large part of me does believe, you know, it was a freak accident, but the other part of me questions … could this have been prevented?” Joshua Nelson, Kariem’s brother-in-law, told the outlet. Nelson, whose daughter was seated beside Kariem, shared her account of the terrifying moments leading up to her uncle’s death. “She said he fainted, or passed – her words were ‘he passed out,’” Nelson said. “And then they went up and down, up and down, up and down – and she said it went up again and his latch, I guess, snapped or came loose and he fell,” Nelson remarked. During the celebratory family outing, Kariem had expressed his excitement about riding the Goliath, which was one of his favorite attractions, according to Nelson. Nelson said that he hoped Kariem did not experience pain during his final moments. Kariem was an educator and a father to a 10-year-old daughter. According to Atlanta public schools, Kariem started his career at Wesley International Academy as a technology teacher before being promoted to an information technology manager. Georgia authorities as of Friday were still investigating the circumstances of Kariem’s death at Six Flags Over Georgia, which opened its gates Friday evening for the first time since the incident. Cobb county police department’s major crimes unit has launched an investigation. Since Kariem’s death, Six Flags temporarily closed nine rollercoasters across six amusement parks around the US. Deaths such as Kariem’s are rare. But his death has prompted some to call for federal oversight of amusement parks, which in the US has been left to individual states, as the New York Times reported.

title: Oregon shooting victims: three boys and female teacher killed at elementary school
summary: Father of five-year-old Rhoam Summer says family ‘broken and lost’, while seven-year-old and 54-year-old in hospital
text: Authorities are investigating a shooting at an elementary school in Bend, Oregon, where a 16-year-old shooter killed four people before being shot dead by a bystander. The shooting took place on Thursday afternoon at Silver Rail elementary school, about 125 miles (200km) south-east of Portland. Here is what we know so far about the four victims, including three children aged five, eight and 11, and a 25-year old teacher, as well as the two people injured. Rhoam Summer In a Facebook group post, Rhoam Summer’s father Kelik Summer posted about his five-year old son’s death, saying that Thursday was “the worst day of my life.” He added: “My son Rhoam was killed in a school shooting. We are broken and lost, but are surrounded by friends and family who are keeping us safe.” Rhoam’s grandfather Bryan Jolly also confirmed his grandson’s death to the New York Times. Jolly described the tragedy as “senseless and a shock”, adding that Rhoam was “in my house a lot and in my garden with me and wrestling with me on the couch”. “He was very bright and very mischievous and very fun-loving, and totally without fear,” Jolly said. A separate GoFundMe page that appears to have been set up by friends of Rhoam’s family said: “In the wake of an unimaginable tragedy, the Summer family is grieving the heartbreaking loss of their sweet five-year-old son, Rhoam. There are no words that can ease the pain of losing a child, and no family should ever have to experience a loss like this.” Bend police also confirmed Rhoam’s identity on Friday afternoon. Eight-year old boy Police are not releasing his identification at his family’s request. Eleven-year old boy Police are not releasing his identification at his family’s request. Megan Lambert Twenty-five-year old Megan Lambert, a teacher at the school, was identified as another victim killed in the shooting, Bend police said on Friday. In a statement shared with Bend police, Lambert’s family said: “Megan was a native central Oregonian. She grew up in Bend. She had a passion for playing sports, especially volleyball. She was a volleyball coach. She actually turned down pay for her first season as a coach, so families who couldn’t afford to participate could have the chance to play the sport she loved.” “Her goal was to be an educator, and teach in the school district she loved growing up in … Silver Rail was her first job as a teacher, though she subbed there for many years … She loved Silver Rail. This was her dream job. Megan was compassionate and had a huge heart,” her family added. The Central Oregon Volleyball Club website lists Megan as a local high school coach and describes her as a “blessing” who has done “so much for her team”. Saylor Graham Seven-year old Saylor Graham was injured in the shooting, according to several GoFundMe accounts set up by co-workers and friends of her family. “The family is focused on being at the hospital while their child fights for their life,” one account said. “Right now, they are carrying the impossible weight of traveling to and from the hospital, staying near their child, caring for their other child, trying to keep up their household, and missing work during this crisis,” it added. A business partner of Saylor’s mother, Danielle Graham, declined to be interviewed but confirmed Saylor’s identity to the Guardian. Meanwhile, Bend police said on Friday that a seven-year old girl who was shot “is receiving life-saving care” at Oregon Health & Science University hospital in Portland, adding: “She is in serious but stable condition.” Becky Drury Fifty-four-year old Becky Drury was also injured in the shooting, with her mother-in-law Yvonne Drury posting on Facebook: “Our wonderful daughter-in-law, Becky was shot thr[ough] her left arm and right hand, and is recovering in the hospital after surgery this afternoon.” In the same post, Becky’s son Will Drury said: “Her left arm took a lot of damage so there’s a long recovery and more surgeries ahead. Her right hand took a hit as well, which also required surgery, but it is much less severe. The good news is she will be OK and we all get to keep that magnificent woman we love so much in our lives.” Bend police said on Friday: “The injured 54-year-old female teacher suffered serious but non-life-threatening injuries and is currently receiving treatment at St Charles Bend [hospital].”

title: Bystander who killed Oregon shooter identified as father of girls at elementary school
summary: Kaylub Giamanco, who was reportedly driving home when he heard gunshots, ‘not seeking recognition’, family says
text: Details are beginning to emerge about Kaylub Giamanco, the man who brought the deadly shooting at elementary school in Bend, Oregon on Thursday, to an end by fatally shooting the 16-year-old suspect in the midst of a violent rampage. While police have declined to release the man’s identity, Giamanco’s family issued a statement on Friday confirming that he shot and killed the suspect, identified Friday as Griffin J John II, a former Silver Rail student. Giamanco is a lifelong resident of Bend with two daughters at Silver Rail elementary, where three children – aged five, eight and 11 – and a teacher were killed, and a seven-year-old child and another teacher injured. Police detailed Giamanco’s actions in a Friday press conference. Giamanco was driving by the school when he heard gunfire and saw the gunman entering the school. Armed with a .40-caliber pistol he is licensed to carry, Giamanco pulled over, followed the gunman into the school and witnessed the shooter in a scuffle with a teacher. Giamanco then fired his weapon, killing the assailant, police said. “The tragedy at Silver Rail elementary has devastated the Bend community,” Giamanco’s family said in a statement, asking for privacy and declining further media interviews. “He is not seeking recognition, but instead wishes to express his gratitude to the first responders, school personnel, and community for the outpouring of love and support.” Speaking briefly to reporters on Friday, Giamanco’s mother read the statement from her phone and said her son appreciated the support but wanted to remain private. “Yes, my brother shot the shooter in yesterday’s events at the Bend elementary school,” Kameron Giamanco wrote in a public Facebook post on Friday that reiterated the family’s request for privacy in the aftermath of the traumatic event. “He’s an absolute HERO. However, we are not speaking to media at this time. He’s not ready, nor is the family.” Though she did not name him, Oregon’s governor, Tina Kotek, praised the man who followed the shooter into the school during a news conference on Thursday. “To the community member who heroically intervened to stop further loss of life,” she said, “your actions carry a heavy emotional burden, and I just want you to know that my thoughts are with you as well.” Authorities are still investigating what led to the deadly attack, and have not released a motive. The suspect was using a pump-action shotgun purchased by his mother, according to reporting from the Associated Press. “This is going to be a long investigation,” Bend’s police chief, Mike Krantz, said, adding that the police would maintain a large presence at the school for the next few days. • This story was updated on 16 October 2026 to correct the name of the shooter. His name was Griffin J John II, not John Griffin II. Anna Betts and Abené Clayton contributed reporting

title: Reform councillor resigns after being filmed making racist remarks
summary: Alan Feeney, who sat on Solihull and Birmingham councils, said there was ‘no excuse’ for his comments
text: Alan Feeney has resigned as a Reform councillor for Solihull and Birmingham after backlash over racist comments that were captured in an undercover investigation. In a Facebook post on Friday, Feeney wrote: “There is no excuse for my comments. With responsibility comes accountability, and it is for that reason that I have resigned every post I hold on both Solihull borough council and Birmingham city council.” Earlier this week, an ITV investigation revealed secretly recorded footage of Feeney making racist comments about Asian homeowners, calling them “parasites”, and stating that “no more than 1% of [the] British population can be non-white”, during a local election campaign. Feeney has apologised for his comments. “My remarks were wrong, offensive and completely unacceptable. They do not reflect the standards that the public rightly expects from an elected representative, and I take full responsibility for what I said,” he wrote in a Facebook post. “The comments do not reflect my true beliefs or opinions, particularly of the communities mentioned in the report. These are communities I have supported countless times in my personal and professional life over many years, many of whom I have been lucky enough to call friends.” Earlier this year, Feeney won seats in the Shard End ward of Birmingham city council and the Castle Bromwich ward of Solihull metropolitan borough council, and was then appointed deputy mayor of Solihull. Following the ITV investigation, which is part of a longer series on Reform UK, Feeney announced on Facebook that he was leaving Reform for “personal reasons”, but kept his seats as an independent councillor before resigning. In a Facebook post, Feeney wrote: “Byelections will be held on a timescale laid out by those councils in the due course. I hope that in time these councils, and the communities they serve can heal and move on.” Secretly filmed footage showed Feeney making racist remarks alongside two other Reform candidates who went on to become councillors, Jamie Campbell and Chris Whelan, while canvassing during May’s local elections. Both Campbell and Whelan have also resigned after the fallout from the investigation. Nigel Farage has repeatedly pledged to rid Reform of “extremists” and “bigots”. The party says it carries out vetting checks on everyone who wants to stand for election. The clips from ITV’s year-long undercover investigation showed Feeney calling Asian homeowners “parasites”, and stating that “no more than 1% of [the] British population can be non-white”. In a Facebook post Feeney wrote: “I understand that my words have caused hurt and anger, particularly among those from the communities I serve. For that, I am deeply sorry. I will be undertaking intensive personal analysis to understand how these sentiments could have taken root, and ensure they can never do so again.” Alan Feeney and Reform UK have been approached for comment.

title: Oregon elementary school shooting: what we know so far
summary: The rural Oregon city of Bend was rocked by a mass shooting at an elementary school that killed three students and a teacher. Here’s what we know about the tragedy
text: A 16-year-old gunman opened fire at the Silver Rail elementary school in Bend, Oregon, on Thursday, killing three children and a teacher. The student victims were aged five, eight and 11. All of the victims were shot in the same classroom. On Friday, the youngest victim was identified as Rhoam Summer, age five. His family said he was a fast runner and fearless climber who loved reading and his stuffed animals. “He never met a stuffie that he didn’t think needed to be rescued and cared for,” said his aunt, Swan Sheridan, who described him as “a little ball of energy from the moment he was born”. The names of the other student victims have not been released. The teacher who was killed has been identified as 25-year-old Megan Lambert. In a statement read by officials on Friday, her family said she grew up in Bend, graduated from Boise State University and had a passion for sports, especially volleyball, and was a local coach. They said she was funny and opinionated, and “fought for the underdog” and “those with special needs”. “Meg loved those children,” the family said. The 16-year-old shooter has been identified as Griffin J John II, a former student at the school. Griffin was killed at the scene. Police have yet to offer a motive. Police said that an armed bystander pursued the suspect and shot him inside the school shortly before officers arrived. On Friday, that bystander was identified by his family as Kaylub Giamanco, a lifelong resident of Bend with two daughters at Silver Rail elementary. His family and others have called him a “hero”. Two other victims, a seven-year-old student and a 54-year-old teacher, remain hospitalized. As of Friday afternoon, authorities said the student was receiving “life-saving care”, while the teacher was described as having “significant” but non-life-threatening injuries, police said. The wounded teacher was identified by family as Becky Drury. Her mother-in-law, Yvonne Drury, said on Facebook that she had injuries to her left arm and right hand and was recovering from surgery. Police arrived at the school at 1.02pm local time after receiving multiple reports of a shooting. One 911 caller reported an individual armed with a long gun firing upon their car. At a news conference on Friday, police said the shooter climbed over a fence and onto the school’s property, before shooting through a set of locked doors and forcing entry into the building. He fired as many as 15 shots from a 12-gauge shotgun before he was stopped, police said. The attack has rocked the small city of Bend, which is home to 100,000 residents and is located on the Deschutes River, about 170 miles (275km) south-east of Portland. All public schools in the district, and the campuses of Oregon State University-Cascades and Central Oregon Community College, were closed on Friday. Hundreds of people gathered at nearby Drake Park on Thursday night at a somber candlelight ceremony to remember the victims. Some attenders called on authorities to harden gun laws in Oregon, already some of the tightest in the nation. Officials have praised the swift actions of law enforcement officers and of the community member who intervened. The Oregon governor, Tina Kotek, praised the intervention as heroic and extended her thoughts to the bystander. “Your actions carry a heavy emotional burden,” she said on Thursday evening. The FBI is helping local authorities investigate the shooting, according to the agency’s director, Kash Patel. The Associated Press contributed reporting

title: Katie Zacharia’s five days as press secretary expose flaws in Trump’s TV-driven hiring
summary: The president reportedly chose Zacharia after seeing her on television, but her first press briefing and disastrous interviews sealed her fate
text: And so Katie Zacharia joins the mayfly ranks of Liz Truss, Anthony Scaramucci, New Coke, CNN+ and Quibi. To say she burned twice as bright and half as long would be too kind. She went out like a firework on a soggy night. The White House confirmed on Friday that Zacharia was leaving her role as press secretary after just five days on the job. No one was surprised after a lacklustre press briefing debut and scrutiny over her legal credentials. But even more importantly, Zacharia lived by the sword and died in the one arena that Donald Trump truly cares about: television. She reportedly got the job by closely monitoring the US president’s public schedule and tracked his active hours on Truth Social to predict exactly when he would be watching TV. She then timed her own appearances on air to make sure she caught his eye. The fact that she fitted the glossy blond aesthetic from what Trump calls “central casting” also helped. But TV also proved her undoing. On Thursday, Zacharia gave a series of interviews to Trump-friendly outlets in a desperate bid for redemption. Instead, she sealed her own fate with more hapless performances. She must have expected Fox News host Sean Hannity, who has even spoken at Trump rallies, to give her an easy ride. But even he was sceptical when she admitted she had “stepped up to the plate with very little prep time” for the first briefing. Hannity asked: “Am I hearing that you think the staff should have prepped you better?” Zacharia rejected the notion that she had only taken questions from conservative outlets, incorrectly asserting that the Daily Mail is “not known to be a conservative outlet”. Hannity also quizzed her about her dubious legal credentials, saying: “Why not just say: ‘I went to Pepperdine law school, and then took a different career path, and I took the bar once and didn’t pass?’” Zacharia tried again on Fox & Friends but ran into host Lawrence Jones, who said: “You know, Katie, it’s been a tough week for you. It’s not an easy job to be the press secretary and you never want to be the story.” He also asked: “Do you think you still have the confidence of the president?” Zacharia responded: “I’m standing here,” referring to the fact that she was speaking from the White House North Lawn. Her exit hours later was met with widespread ridicule – and a measure of human compassion for someone whom Trump had subjected to a very public humiliation. Scaramucci, who lasted only 11 days as White House communications director during Trump’s first term, tweeted: “Records are made to be broken. But I take no pleasure in other people’s pain.” Joe Lockhart, a former White House press secretary under Bill Clinton, said in a phone interview: “It’s hard to generate sympathy for this woman, but there was no way for her to succeed. It takes years to be ready to do that job. Not days, not hours. I spent 20 years preparing for my first briefing from the very first campaign I did. It was very unfair for her, but very bad judgment on her part to think she could wander out there and smile.” The fiasco was also a reminder of Trump’s woeful judgment as a manager whose chief criteria are looks and loyalty. During his 2015 presidential campaign, he promised that he would only hire “the best people”, comparing his future administration to corporate boardrooms. His first national security adviser, Michael Flynn, resigned after 23 days. His second term has featured incompetents such as Kristi Noem, fired as homeland security secretary after multiple controversies, Robert F Kennedy Jr, a health secretary who spent years promoting anti-scientific claims about vaccine safety, and Pete Hegseth, a defence secretary who bungled the Iran war and announced a livestreamed execution only to be overruled by his boss. Kurt Bardella, a political commentator, said: “It shows the limitations of the president making decisions like this based solely on: ‘Oh, I liked watching this clip of her on this segment in the most friendly environment possible.’ We’ve seen this time and again with this president selecting figures for very meaningful, important and substantive positions solely based on cable news, and just look at how the war in Iran is going to know that ain’t working out too good.” Trump also entrusted tech bro Elon Musk to take a chainsaw to the federal government. His choice of personnel has had damaging consequences for US institutions. The position of White House press secretary is the latest example. Lockhart added: “It one more time shows how Trump cheapens everything he touches. He wants everything to be in his image. He tears down the East Wing. He puts his name on the Kennedy Center. Now he has tried to put someone in that job who reflects him, not the country and the values and the power of this country. “He has cheapened another institution. I hold that room somewhat dear, and it’s sad to watch each of these things get remade in his image because he is cheap, tawdry, corrupt, and he has managed to make the United States reflect those values around the world rather than the ones we knew about for 250 years before him.” Zacharia will survive and maybe thrive as a “former White House press secretary” in rightwing media, just as Scaramucci still makes the most of his “former” title. Meanwhile, the hunt is on, presumably, for a successor who can at least look reporters in the eye and not get into a tangle about their credentials. But the cold truth is that the job of White House press secretary is superfluous when Trump is a word machine who holds two-hour campaign rallies, turns social media into a stream of consciousness and takes calls from reporters on his mobile phone. Playing the role of Trump’s spokesperson carries the inherent risk of inadvertently factchecking him. “He’s certainly remade the job because all the press secretary does now is repeat what the president says and tell him how brilliant he was in saying it,” Lockhart concluded. “It used to be that credibility was the currency in the room. It’s impossible to be credible when you’re working for someone who lies almost every time he speaks.”

title: Healey backs pro-growth case for Heathrow third runway after Burnham ducks issue
summary: Chancellor says government will study responses to public consultation, with airports being ‘big part of jobs and growth’
text: John Healey has said there is a pro-growth case for going ahead with a third runway at Heathrow despite the prime minister declining to back it. Healey’s predecessor as chancellor, Rachel Reeves, put approval of the long-planned runway at the heart of her “growth speech” last year, saying it would “make Britain the world’s best-connected place to do business”. However, since arriving in No 10 in July, Andy Burnham has ducked the issue of whether the runway should go ahead, suggesting it should be “a matter for London and Londoners”. A recent Sunday Times report suggested the prime minister had told the transport secretary, Heidi Alexander, that he was “unconvinced” by arguments for the megaproject. Asked for his views in Bangkok this week, Healey said the government would study responses to a public consultation, which recently closed. He appeared to strike a markedly more positive note than Burnham, however. “I think in recent decades, and this is true in Heathrow and airports right across the UK, that they have been a big part of jobs and growth. And the case for a third runway at Heathrow has always been a case for growth,” he said. Healey has insisted economic growth is his and Burnham’s “number one mission” in government. Heathrow’s chief executive, Thomas Woldbye, has warned that investors could reassess their backing for the £33bn infrastructure project if it does not receive the prime minister’s support. “Our shareholders would like to do this,” he said earlier this week. “They do think that things are taking a long time, and so far they have decided to be OK with that … But of course we cannot wait for ever.” The airport’s owners include Qatar’s investment authority; the French private equity firm Ardian; Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund and Singapore’s sovereign wealth fund, GIC. They are expected to decide in the coming months whether to apply for formal planning permission. Healey voted in favour of the third runway when the question was put to the House of Commons in 2018. The chancellor was in Bangkok to attend the International Monetary Fund annual meetings but has returned to London to put the finishing touches to his 28 October budget. The UK was praised by the IMF this week for taking action to cut its deficit, while other large economies have opted not to do so. The IMF’s managing director, Kristalina Georgieva, urged Healey to “stay the course” in his budget. On Thursday, official figures showed the UK economy unexpectedly continued to grow in August.

title: New York man charged with rape and lethal fentanyl dosing of college student
summary: Prosecutors allege Moises Freire gave two students at FIT the opioid, saying it was cocaine, and raped one as she overdosed
text: A man raped a student at New York’s Fashion Institute of Technology (FIT) after giving her a dose of fentanyl that rendered her unconscious and ultimately killed her, federal prosecutors allege. That student’s friend also experienced an overdose and nearly died after taking the potent synthetic opiate, leading to charges against three men, the US Department of Justice said in a statement on Thursday. Moises Freire, 19, faces counts of participating in a conspiracy to distribute fentanyl and of distributing a deadly drug with intent to commit rape. Meanwhile, 18-year-old Brian Peralta Cabrera was also charged in connection with the drug conspiracy. A third defendant in the case, Harry Rosales Pino, pleaded guilty in September to plotting to distribute narcotics resulting in death and serious bodily injury. He was tentatively scheduled to be sentenced on 15 December in one of the latest prominent criminal cases in the US justice system to involve fentanyl, a primary driver of drug-related deaths in the country, according to the federal government. Freire was not a student at FIT but brought fentanyl to the dorm room of two women that he was visiting there on 18 March. He lied that the substance was pure cocaine, prosecutors contend. Though he had referred to the fentanyl in question as “straight poison”, he successfully urged the women to take the drug and both quickly slipped into unconsciousness, prosecutors maintained. Prosecutors said the woman whom Freire is accused of raping went into a coma and died on 21 March. He, Peralta and Rosales were charged and pleaded not guilty to initial charges, which omitted the rape allegation. A transcript from an April federal court hearing shows a prosecutor alleged that Rosales sold the fentanyl at the center of the case to Peralta. Peralta in turn dealt it to Freire, who gave it to the two women at FIT, that prosecutor said. Rosales pleaded out on 16 September. And updated charges against Peralta and Freire, which contained the rape allegation against Freire, were filed on Thursday. Neither Freire, described as being from the Bronx, nor Peralta – of Queens – had been arraigned on those superseding charges on Friday. They remained in federal custody pending the outcome of the case. The charging documents against Freire and Peralta do not name either of the women whom prosecutors said were drugged, but multiple media reports identified the dead woman as Annabel Richter. The New York Post quoted Richter’s mom, Flavia Rocha, as saying her daughter “was full of life”. “She knew loads about music and art and had a contagious laughter,” Rocha told the Post. “Her presence filled the room. For us, her family and her friends, she was and always will be, our beloved Bel.” Rocha also reportedly said: “I don’t want to think of a world in which crimes against women would be too many to count. Bel and I would often discuss how women who suffered violence would rarely have a voice. I hope that Annabel’s story brings awareness, and meets justice.” The documents also do not identify FIT, which is part of the State University of New York (Suny) system. However, the April court hearing’s transcript shows that Freire’s lawyer, Mitchell Schwartz, mentioned FIT by name. Furthermore, at that hearing, the assistant US attorney Ariana Bloom, of the southern district of New York in Manhattan, provided gut-wrenching details about the rape allegations against Freire. Bloom said Freire admitted in writing that he raped the woman who later died while she was unconscious. As he put it, he had sex with her, realized she was unconscious only afterward – and then saw her friend on the floor in a similar state “with her eyes rolled back in her head”, Bloom recounted. Freire then sent pictures to others of the women while they were passed out, waited about 40 minutes and only then alerted building security to the situation, Bloom said. It was determined that the women had overdosed – one fatally – after being taken to a hospital. Bloom said Freire himself never called an ambulance. She also said a friend of Freire had warned him that the fentanyl he gave to the women “doesn’t look like coke”. “The defendant’s friend … told him to give that shit to the ‘sluts’, meaning the girls, and don’t take it yourself,” Bloom said. Bloom also argued: “Once things started going south, instead of calling 911 or alerting someone or prioritizing their lives, he took time to take pictures of them and to protect himself.” A message to FIT’s campus community from the university president, Jason Schupbach, said Thursday’s charges “reflect what a horrific tragedy this was” while bringing “accountability and justice for those involved”. Schupbach’s message highlighted various security policies in place at FIT. And it also said both students mentioned in Thursday’s superseding charges were given Narcan, a drug that can reverse the effects of opiate overdoses. Schupbach said Narcan kits were “stationed in the lobbies of each of the residence halls” at FIT – and that public safety supervisors on campus were now required to carry the opioid antidonte on them “at all times as part of their uniform”. “We continue to provide education and programming to our community on healthy relationships, and awareness campaigns on misconduct, and sexual health,” Schupbach’s message said. And “we will continue to keep you informed as appropriate, but it is important to reiterate that we all must ensure that we continue to protect the safety of the victims and their families’ privacy and the sanctity of the ongoing legal proceedings”. The Associated Press contributed reporting • Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organizations. In the US, Rainn offers support on 800-656-4673. In the UK, Rape Crisis offers support on 0808 500 2222. In Australia, support is available at 1800Respect (1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found at ibiblio.org/rcip/internl.html

title: Who could replace Katie Zacharia as White House press secretary?

text: The White House is without a press secretary again after the ousting of Katie Zacharia, just five days into her appointment as Donald Trump’s spokesperson. Zacharia’s departure comes just months after Karoline Leavitt unexpectedly resigned as the White House press secretary to focus on her family. Once again, a sharp-elbowed race inside Trump’s world to take on one of the most prominent positions in the administration has kicked off. Here are some of the possible contenders. Stephen Cheung Cheung currently serves as the White House communications director, and worked closely with Leavitt throughout the second Trump administration. Anna Kelly Kelly already works at the White House as the principal deputy press secretary, working under Leavitt. She was previously a spokesperson for Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign, and before that, she served as national press secretary for the Republican National Committee. Katie Miller As the wife of Stephen Miller, a top White House aide and immigration policy architect, Katie Miller has a front-row seat to the administration’s movements. And as an influential conservative podcast host, Katie has spent a lot of time interviewing cabinet officials and rightwing media figures. Before launching her podcast, Katie was a communications director for the so-called “department of government efficiency” (Doge). She was former vice-president Mike Pence’s press secretary from 2019 to 2021. Taylor Budowich Budowich is a former White House deputy chief of staff, who worked alongside Miller and Dan Scavino. He left the White House last year to join the private sector. Alongside Leavitt, Budowich was one of the defendants in the case brought by the Associated Press after the outlet was banned from the press rotation for refusing to refer to the Gulf of Mexico as the “Gulf of America”. Scott Jennings Jennings is a longtime conservative commentator and Trump ally who often defends the president and members of his administration on network television and online. He now serves as an on-air political contributor on CNN. Jennings was rumored to be in the running to replace Leavitt but ultimately passed over for Zacharia. Alina Habba Habba is a loyal ally of the president who served as his personal lawyer before becoming a short-lived US attorney for New Jersey. A federal judge ultimately ruled her appointment was unlawful. But Habba has been one of Trump’s most vocal defenders on conservative outlets. According to the New York Post, citing sources within the administration, Habba was an early frontrunner to replace Leavitt. title: Brazilian Amazon deforestation falls to lowest on record as pivotal vote looms
summary: Forest clearance at smallest total since records began in 1988 in success for Lula ahead of presidential run-off
text: Deforestation in the Brazilian Amazon has fallen to its lowest level since records began, new government data shows. But whether this globally important success is maintained or reversed is on a knife edge ahead of a presidential election run-off on 25 October between two candidates with sharply different visions for the future of the rainforest and how that affects relations with the US under Donald Trump. The incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, fell behind in the first round of voting despite an impressive record in slowing the destruction of the Amazon while also reducing poverty and food insecurity. He is up against Flávio Bolsonaro, son of the former president Jair Bolsonaro. The Prodes satellite data series, which is considered the most accurate measure of deforestation, showed forest clearance in the Amazon fell by 41.8% over the past year to 3,335 square kilometres, the lowest value since the start of such measurements in 1988. This beats the previous record low by 1,236 sq km, equivalent to an area the size of Rio de Janeiro. Since 2022, the year before the start of the Lula administration, the deforestation rate has slowed by 71.2%, according to the data collated by Brazil’s National Institute for Space Research. This was largely as a result of stronger enforcement measures and state investments in environmental agencies. The Brazilian states with the worst records in 2026 were Pará, which registered 33.9% of all Amazon deforestation in the year, Mato Grosso (25.5%) and Amazonas (15.7%). However, even in those places the figures were down by more than 45% on the previous year. The state where the problem grew worse (up 0.4%) was Roraima, which is a Bolsonaro stronghold. Outside the Amazon, the neighbouring biome of the Cerrado – an area of savannah – registered its lowest annual deforestation since 2001, at 5,516 sq km. This is significant as the Cerrado has long been treated as an area of environmental sacrifice, where soya and beef producers could clear more forest than they were allowed to do in the Amazon. Over the past four years, Cerrado deforestation has fallen by 48.4%. These spectacular results, which brought some conservationists to tears, stand in sharp contrast to the 2019-23 term of Jair Bolsonaro, who oversaw a 59.5% increase in Amazon deforestation, roughly equivalent to destroying more than a million trees a day, through cuts to forest protection agencies, reduced implementation of penalties for environmental crimes, and verbal encouragement for illegal miners, loggers and land grabbers. Bolsonaro was then convicted for attempting a coup but his son has vowed to release his father and let him take any position in government that he chooses. The younger Bolsonaro has followed his father’s example in courting support from predatory landowners in the Amazon and other extractivist interests while ignoring the climate crisis in his manifesto. The former environment minister Marina Silva, who has arguably done more than anyone to defend the rainforest, has warned that Flávio Bolsonaro will try to finish his father’s “perverse project” to destroy the Amazon. The stark contrast between the two candidates is evident in the electoral results map in the Amazon, where Bolsonaro secured the most votes near areas of degraded forest, mines, ranches and soya monocultures, while Lula’s support was higher in big cities or areas of forest where the vegetation was relatively intact. It is also evident in their very different relations to the US. Lula has warned that Trump is trying to colonise the country and capture its resources. He defends the Amazon as a sovereign asset for Brazil, an important home for Indigenous peoples and an essential element in global efforts to stabilise the climate. The Bolsonaro family, by contrast, has close ties to the US. Flavio’s brother Eduardo has lived in Texas since last year and called upon the Trump administration to impose punitive tariffs on his own country. Jair has saluted the US flag and led chants of “USA, USA”. If the family secure power, they are expected to shift Brazil’s trade priorities, particularly when it comes to critical minerals, from China and Europe to the US. The biggest difference, however, is likely to be the far right’s willingness to exploit natural resources in the Amazon and elsewhere in Brazil and then sell them to the highest bidder, regardless of environmental and social concerns. Conservation groups said the new deforestation data showed how much was at stake in the presidential run-off. Marcio Astrini, the executive secretary of the Climate Observatory, said: “The figure makes it clear that putting an end to forest destruction in Brazil is entirely possible. “However, everything depends on the election result. The country will decide whether we move toward the end of deforestation or toward the end of the forest.”

title: Katie Zacharia fired after five days as White House press secretary
summary: Zacharia hosted widely panned first briefing on Tuesday and faced scrutiny after admitting she didn’t pass bar exam
text: Donald Trump’s new press secretary, Katie Zacharia, was fired on Friday, just five days after she assumed the role, according to a White House official. Zacharia confirmed her departure from the White House on Friday evening. “President Trump is a kind, wonderful, gracious, thoughtful, enthusiastic, and hardworking man. I wish more Americans appreciated him. No one will ever make America great the way he has and continues to,” she wrote on social media. “It was an honor to work for him.” Zacharia, a little-known conservative political commentator prior to her selection as the president’s chief spokesperson, came under immediate scrutiny after a widely panned inaugural briefing on Tuesday. The 14-minute exchange was soon followed by a barrage of questions over her legal credentials after she admitted she did not pass the bar exam. In an interview on Thursday, Zacharia detailed her whirlwind sprint to the podium to replace Karoline Leavitt as the White House press secretary, stepping into the role as the president faces multiple headwinds just weeks before the midterm elections next month. On Friday, Trump signaled that Zacharia’s tenure would be short-lived, telling reporters that he had asked his embattled press secretary to “reconsider” the job. “I said: ‘Is this for you, Katie? Because honestly, you don’t need it,’” Trump said, speaking outside the White House. “I said to her: ‘Honestly, if I were you, I’d reconsider. You think about it, but I would reconsider.’” During her first – and apparently only – press briefing, Zacharia stumbled through prepared remarks highlighting Trump’s accomplishments in his presidency. She made a notable gaffe when she called her husband “the president”. Members of the White House press corps were left puzzled when she departed the podium after only taking questions from three predominantly conservative media outlets. She spent the next hours and days trying to clarify swirling questions about her résumé, after reports emerged revealing that Zacharia, whom Trump has referred to as an “attorney”, had never passed the bar exam. She later confirmed that she took the bar once and failed. Zacharia graduated from Pepperdine University’s law school in California, and repeatedly called herself a lawyer. She defended using the term to describe herself professionally, claiming there was a difference between a “lawyer” and an “attorney”, a title reserved for those licensed to practice law. She had previously shared social media posts identifying herself as an “attorney”. And when the White House officially announced her appointment, the statement described her as an “attorney”. Over the last few days, Zacharia has spoken with members of the media in an effort to try to move past the criticism and make the case that she was ready to take on the role as the president’s chief spokesperson. In an unexpectedly tough interview on Thursday evening, Fox host Sean Hannity grilled Zacharia about her first press briefing, asking bluntly: “What happened?” Zacharia sought to explain that she had had little time to prep in the days between accepting the job and holding her first press briefing and argued that the conservative Daily Mail, one of only three outlets she took questions from, was “not known to be a conservative outlet”. Hannity, a Trump ally, also pressed her on her decision to identify herself as a “lawyer”. “Why get into this long, drawn-out definition of the difference between a lawyer and an attorney? Because I don’t think most people see much of a distinction,” he asked. In a Friday appearance on Fox & Friends, host Lawrence Jones continued, telling Zacharia: “You know, Katie, it’s been a tough week for you. It’s not an easy job to be the press secretary, and you never want to be the story.” Jones then asked: “Do you think you still have the confidence of the president?” “I’m standing here,” Zacharia replied, referring to the fact that she was speaking from the White House north lawn. She said she hoped to “build the trust and confidence of everyone around me” but could not say when her next press briefing would be.
