title: Case against Leon Black dismissed after plaintiff said she was ‘medically incapable of continuing’
summary: In civil suit, ‘Jane Doe’ alleged billionaire raped her after being ‘handed off’ by Jeffrey Epstein. Black denied the allegations and called claims a fabrication
text: A federal judge has agreed to dismiss a lawsuit brought against Leon Black after the plaintiff in the case, who had accused the private equity billionaire of rape, said she was “medically incapable of continuing” and at risk of “acute psychiatric crisis”, including suicide. The woman known only as “Jane Doe”, who claimed in a lawsuit that was first filed in July 2023 that she had been “handed off” to Black by his associate Jeffrey Epstein and then sexually assaulted by him, had been acting without a lawyer in the case. Doe has alleged that the assault occurred in 2002, when she was a teenager. “My request [to dismiss the case with prejudice] is not a concession concerning the truth of my allegations, a retraction of my statements, or an acceptance of defendant’s disputed positions; it reflects only the medical reality that I can no longer safely pursue this litigation,” Doe wrote in a legal filing submitted to the court on 12 October. An attorney for Black, who has strongly denied Doe’s allegations, said his team was pleased that the judge had dismissed the lawsuit. Susan Estrich, Black’s lawyer, said in a statement that the lawsuit should never have been brought in the first place and repeated earlier claims that Doe’s complaint was a “work of fiction” filled with lies and fabrications. In a legal filing, Black’s lawyer Michael Carlinsky said Doe’s request to dismiss the case – which Black did not oppose – “has been made voluntarily by Ms Doe without any settlement, compromise, or inducement by Mr Black”. The Wall Street billionaire, who was Epstein’s friend and former client, has separately come under fire in Washington, where the US House of Representatives voted unanimously in September to hold him in criminal contempt for defying two congressional subpoenas ordered by the House oversight committee, which is investigating Epstein, his relationships to powerful people and the government’s handling of Epstein investigations. One of the congressional subpoenas that Black was accused of violating would have forced him to hand over all nondisclosure agreements to which he was a party. Black attended a voluntary closed-door interview with the oversight committee in June but walked out shortly after it started and was accused by members of stonewalling. He then declined to appear for a subsequent congressional deposition. Black’s lawyers have said he was being targeted by a “political witch-hunt” and filed a lawsuit against the oversight committee to block the subpoenas, claiming the committee was exceeding its authority. The contempt resolution has been referred to the US Department of Justice, though it is not clear if the department will pursue criminal prosecution. Black has emerged as a key target of congressional investigators because of his relationship with Epstein, who provided financial services to Black between 2012 and 2017. After Epstein pleaded guilty to Florida state prostitution charges in 2008, including procuring a minor, Black became Epstein’s largest client, paying him a total of roughly $170m in fees, according to an investigation by the Senate finance committee’s ranking member, Ron Wyden. In his statement before the oversight committee in June, Black wrote: “I did not know about this nefarious activity until Epstein was charged with trafficking in July 2019.” But Black acknowledged that he did know about Epstein pleading guilty in “2008 to state charges relating to prostitution involving a minor”. Epstein died in prison in 2019 after he was charged with sex trafficking. The dismissal of the Doe v Black lawsuit comes at what could have been a critical moment in the case, which was being heard in the southern district of New York. Both sides had been ordered to review thousands of pages of documents that were due to be unsealed, which were related both to that case as well as a separate class-action lawsuit brought by Epstein victims against JP Morgan, in which Doe received a financial settlement. The review process required both sides to examine documents and propose redactions before they were to be made public. In a recent filing, Doe said she needed legal assistance to complete the task. In response to that request, Judge Jessica Clarke suggested Doe contact the City Bar Justice Center, which is described as a pro bono legal service to low-income clients. In a later eight-page letter requesting the dismissal of her case against Black, Doe, who said she is autistic and has post-traumatic stress disorder, said that on reflection she believed neither additional time nor limited legal assistance could “address the medical danger associated with my continued substantive participation”. “My treating physician has expressed serious concern about the effects of the litigation over an extended period and has repeatedly advised that I disengage,” she wrote. Doe said her autism and PTSD materially affected her ability to “process complex, ambiguous, rapidly changing, and socially mediated information under adversarial pressure”. She added that – because she was representing herself in the case – she had been exposed through the redaction process to thousands of pages containing “graphic accounts of sexual trauma, [and] intimate medical and familial information”. Doe had initially been represented by lawyers at the Wigdor law firm, which is known for representing sexual assault victims. Her former attorneys withdrew from the case in April 2025. Black’s legal team said they intended to continue to pursue litigation against Wigdor over legal fees, which is a position Wigdor is expected to challenge. Doe faced significant setbacks over the course of her lawsuit against Black, but also some victories. Clarke, the judge who was presiding over the lawsuit, sanctioned Doe and her former lawyer at Wigdor in April for “serious, sanctionable misconduct in this case” and said the lawyer had “repeatedly lied to the court and opposing counsel”. But the judge also ruled at the time that the high-stakes lawsuit could proceed. The case was dismissed with prejudice, which means Doe cannot bring the matter to court again. The Guardian sought a comment from Doe but she did not reply to an email request.

title: No 10 leaves option open to impose Chinese EV tariffs if UK joins EU scheme
summary: Beijing warns against ‘discriminatory’ step after France drops opposition to British role in Made in Europe package
text: No 10 has left the door open to imposing tariffs on Chinese-made electric vehicles as part of the Made in Europe package, prompting a warning from Beijing that such a move would be “discriminatory”. Downing Street said on Friday that it would “welcome the objective to have the UK included in the Industrial Accelerator Act” after France dropped its opposition to Britain joining the scheme. The aim of the rules is to curb subsidised Chinese imports by giving EU-made products preferential treatment, but the UK and others such as Norway are worried about being left at a disadvantage if excluded from the scheme. The price for joining would be aligning with the EU’s tariffs on Chinese EVs imposed by the bloc in 2024, according to a Franco-German proposal on Thursday night that said the UK would have to dynamically align with EU trade defence measures. The Chinese embassy in London said it was “firmly opposed to any discriminatory practice involving tariff hikes or restrictive measures on Chinese products”. “We have expressed serious concern to the UK side regarding the reports in question,” it said, adding that “trade protectionism runs counter to WTO rules and market principles”. This week, the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, said he would not be coerced into aligning with the EU’s policy. However, the government has been desperate to be included in the Made in Europe package, fearing billions of pounds of trade in the car industry could be lost if the UK is locked out of supply chains in the EU. Asked whether the UK accepted it would have to put tariffs on Chinese-made vehicles in order to join Made in Europe, a No 10 spokesperson said it was “premature to speculate” on the terms of any deal with the bloc and there was “still a European process to run”. They added: “But more broadly, on the principle, the UK obviously has its own trade policy and it keeps all tariffs under review. And we work closely with the British automotive sector to make sure that that approach reflects their best interests.” Chinese EVs are increasingly popular, with BYD sales up 78% year on year in September, Chery up 660% and the lesser-known Changan up by more than 3,000% in terms of market share. EU lawmakers are expected to finalise the Industrial Accelerator Act, known as Made in Europe legislation, by the end of the year or early 2027. But MEPs have already tabled 5,100 amendments, including one embracing the UK and giving Andy Burnham time to secure the deal he wants. Earlier this week the boss of Mercedes-Benz, Ola Källenius, who is also the president of the European car trade body ACEA, warned that locking the UK out of legislation would amount to a “deliberate choice” by EU leaders to “hurt” the car industry across the bloc. According to the new Franco-German proposal, there would be “an opt-in to further include European partners who were part of the EU single market as of 1 January 2020”, which includes the UK and Norway. This would be provided those third countries accepted “dynamic alignment on the EU’s conditions related to third countries’ investments and on relevant EU trade defence measures”. Tariffs could help UK-based manufacturers by preventing cut-price Chinese models flooding the market but they could also push up prices for consumers and harm British manufacturers trying to sell vehicles to China in the case of an escalating trade war. About 80% of UK-made cars are exported, with more than half going to the EU and 6% to China. Earlier on Thursday the trade minister, Anas Sarwar, hinted that the UK was minded to align on tariffs. He told Politico the UK and the EU must “work together and act in lockstep” to tackle China’s dominance in the automotive sector. A car industry source said the EU “has recently shown that it is possible to have a dialogue with the Chinese and get some form of safeguarding in place” without retaliation. China opposes the expansion of EV tariffs. In the past few months it has made what European Commission officials called “bloodcurdling threats” to launch a trade war over the latest plan to impose quotas on Chinese hybrid cars. While quotas can be introduced within months under World Trade Organization rules, it could take more than a year to impose tariffs on Chinese cars, with strict processes to be followed, starting with notification of an investigation and followed by evidence-gathering and sharing over alleged harms China might be causing to the British car industry. Liam Byrne, the Labour chair of the parliamentary business committee, has said imposing tariffs on Chinese EVs would be “a small price to pay” to save the industry in both the UK and the EU. At a conference in London on Thursday night, he said the UK “urgently needs” a new strategy on China to ensure that British and European manufacturing “does not die”. Byrne, who has been leading an investigation into the UK’s position on China, was highly critical of the government’s approach, which he believes is naive and based on false hopes that China will change its export policy. “Our China strategy is simply not where it needs to be. The UK urgently needs a coherent China strategy, which it does not have today,” he said.

title: Starlink access still not fully restored for Ukraine’s military, says Zelenskyy
summary: Ukrainian president says US limiting access was a ‘dangerous and unpleasant surprise’, amid reports the order came from inside White House
text: Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said the Ukrainian military’s access to the Starlink satellite internet service has not yet been fully restored, as media reports suggested the order to throttle the service had come from within the White House. Zelenskyy met European leaders on Friday in Brussels, where he asked the EU for another €70bn (£60bn) next year to fund Ukraine’s defence against Russia. The meeting offered an important opportunity for Zelenskyy and Europe to align their strategies, as Zelenskyy once again found himself embroiled in a major quarrel with the US president, Donald Trump. Hours earlier, Trump had called Ukraine’s renewed strikes on Russian oil refineries “a disgrace” and criticised ⁠Zelenskyy, after a purported “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine failed to take hold. “All he’s doing is making the world oil price higher,” Trump told the Newsmax television channel. “Well, I think that’s a disgrace.” Energy analysts told the BBC that the US-Israeli war on Iran was having the biggest impact on diesel export volumes, although the Ukraine war was also significant. Trump’s administration is suspected of withholding intelligence from Ukraine on incoming Russian ballistic missile strikes, and of throttling Starshield, the military version of the Starlink satellite internet network, to prevent it from being used on drones flying faster than 100mph. Neither has officially been confirmed. Speaking after meeting EU leaders on Friday, Zelenskyy said that Starshield had not yet returned to normal. “Our defence ministry is in touch and my partners, they told me that there were signals from the White House that they would return these capabilities,” Zelenskyy said. “Have they returned to the previous speed limits? No. But is it coming back now? Yes.” Reuters on Friday reported that the order to throttle Starshield had come from inside the White House, according to two US officials and a western official briefed on the matter. They did not identify the White House official who had made the decision, but said the Pentagon had been informed that the SpaceX Starshield service for the Ukrainian military had to be slowed. Trump said on Friday he did not think either ⁠he or ⁠Elon Musk was responsible for Ukraine losing Starshield access and that any limits were not imposed by the US. Starshield is produced by Musk’s SpaceX but controlled by the US government. Zelenskyy called it a “very dangerous and unpleasant surprise” that speeds had been reduced on Starlink, which Ukraine uses to support its most effective air defence systems against Russian jet-powered drones. Russian attacks killed at least eight people and injured 60 ⁠across Ukraine on Friday, hitting two shopping centres and temporarily power to more than 1 million people, ⁠officials said. When Zelenskyy arrived for talks with EU leaders, he was applauded by the heads of state and government of the bloc’s 27 countries. Zelenskyy later said he had heard “only support”, when asked about reports that European leaders had asked him to dial down his criticism of Trump. According to a transcript of his remarks, he told EU leaders that the war would cost €155bn in 2027. “And we need at least €70bn more from you – for defence, for weapons, and for our resilience,” he said. “This is a realistic amount.” The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, agreed with Zelenskyy that “it is clear that we have a gap of €70bn that has to be covered” for 2027, although she expected Ukraine’s other partners – which she did not name – to cover part of the sum. The EU is currently giving Ukraine regular payments from a €90bn funding plan agreed last December that was intended to cover two-thirds of Kyiv’s civilian and military needs for 2026-27. The remaining third was to be filled by other “international partners”, such as the UK, Canada, Norway and Japan. The realisation that Kyiv again risks a financial crunch has put Russia’s €210bn assets frozen inside the EU back on the table. The EU takes the profits from those assets to support Ukraine, but last year decided against using the funds themselves, instead opting for an EU-backed €90bn loan. Belgium, which hosts the vast majority of the Russian funds, remains strongly opposed to using the frozen assets, fearing it will be left to carry the financial burden if the plan goes wrong. But Zelenskyy said there could be an alternative. “We need something like a special EU-controlled custodian to reduce the risk of them being unfrozen and divided up among those who clearly do not want what is best for Europe or an end to this war,” he said. The European Commission, a strong backer of last year’s rejected frozen assets plan, has been reluctant to propose new variants – such as an EU-controlled custodian – because it fears running into same opposition from Belgium and other sceptical member states. Before the summit, Belgium’s prime minister, Bart De Wever, said Zelenskyy would “probably look everybody straight in the eye and say: thank you for the €90bn, but that money is going to run out because a war is a very costly thing”.

title: Amber Guyger, police officer who murdered black neighbor in his home, released from prison
summary: Guyger, convicted of murder of Botham Jean in Dallas in 2018, served seven years of 10-year sentence
text: The former Dallas police officer who was convicted of murdering Botham Jean after entering his apartment and shooting him in 2018 was released from prison on Friday morning after spending seven years in prison. Amber Guyger, 38, regained her freedom a little more than two weeks after the Texas board of pardons and paroles approved her release, despite opposition from Jean’s family. The former officer was sentenced to 10 years in prison after her murder conviction on 1 October 2019. Her parole was approved exactly seven years after that verdict. The case against Guyger drew national attention after she fatally shot Jean, 26, inside his own Dallas apartment in September 2018. During her trial, Guyger maintained that she had accidentally parked on the fourth floor of the garage at the apartment complex where she and Jean lived. Jean’s apartment was located one floor above hers. Guyger testified that she believed she was entering her own residence when she walked into Jean’s apartment. According to her account, she attempted to unlock the door with her key when it pushed open. She claimed she mistook Jean for a burglar and fired her weapon because she feared for her life. Jean had been eating ice-cream and watching television in his apartment when Guyger entered and shot him dead. Guyger was taken into custody three days after the deadly shooting and was subsequently dismissed from the Dallas police department before standing trial. A jury found her guilty of murder. She faced a possible sentence of life imprisonment. Jurors ultimately gave her a 10-year prison term. Prosecutors had pushed for a minimum of 28 years, choosing that number to represent the age Jean would have reached at the time. Guyger first sought parole in 2024. But the parole board denied her request. When she became eligible to apply again, the board reversed course and granted her parole, allowing her to complete the remainder of her sentence under supervision. After the decision granting her parole, Jean’s family released a statement to CBS News Texas expressing their continued grief and requesting privacy. “Two days ago, the family of Botham Jean lovingly remembered their son and brother and celebrated his life on what would have been his birthday,” it read. “Today, it was reported that Amber Guyger will be paroled and will serve the remainder of her sentence under supervision. The family of Botham Jean respectfully requests privacy at this time as they process this development and continue to navigate their grief.” It continued: “To the many well-wishers who continue to say Botham’s name, honor his life, and carry his memory forward, the family extends their heartfelt gratitude for your continued love and support.” While Guyger’s release on Friday marks the end of her time in custody after the 2018 killing, she remains subject to supervision for the remainder of her sentence.

title: Met police investigating row over founding of Your Party
summary: Inquiry said to have been launched after force received report ‘relating to alleged unauthorised access of a political party’s database’
text: Police are carrying out a criminal investigation into a row over the founding of Your Party, which split the leftwing party as it was established last year. A spokesperson for London’s Metropolitan police said they had launched an investigation after they received a report in September 2025 “relating to the alleged unauthorised access of a political party’s database”, the Politico website reported. Your Party was founded in summer 2025 by the former Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn and the former Labour MP Zarah Sultana, both of whom now sit as Your Party MPs in the House of Commons. But relations between the different factions in the party have been strained since its creation in July last year. That September Sultana revealed a new membership portal on X, and encouraged members to become paying members for £55. Corbyn described the site as a “false membership system” and told supporters to ignore an email requesting funds. Sultana said her only aim had been to “safeguard the grassroots involvement that is essential to building this party”, and later accused the party of being run by a “sexist boys’ club”. Officers had now arrested a man on suspicion of an offence under the 1990 Computer Misuse Act, a police spokesperson told Politico. The man was released pending further inquiries and has not been charged. Officers also previously interviewed a woman in her 30s under caution in connection with the same investigation. The spokesperson added: “The investigation continues.” The police spokesperson did not name any political party in their statement, and the spokesperson did not confirm which political party their investigation was related to. Sources told the Guardian that the investigation was linked to the long-running dispute connected to the establishment of Your Party. Neither the man arrested nor the woman interviewed by police are MPs and neither have been charged with an offence. Neither Corbyn nor Sultana were accused of wrongdoing, Politico reported. In January, it emerged that the Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) advised the party that while it was taking no further action over the Your Party membership portal launch, it may have involved “serious criminal activity” and should be referred to the police. A Your Party spokesperson said: “It would not be appropriate to comment any further about ongoing police investigations.” They also said: “We can reassure our members and supporters that our systems are secure and that this was an isolated incident.” Your Party has struggled to make a widespread national impact since it was founded, while the Green party of England and Wales, rebranded as an eco-socialist party, has seen its membership quadruple. In February, Corbyn won a comprehensive victory to become the de facto leader of the leftwing startup party. He said Your Party would work with the Green party and others to push for a “coordinated left-flank offensive” against Reform and Labour. Sultana was also voted on to the party’s leadership committee under its collective leadership model. Corbyn-backed candidates took 14 of the 24 available places on the party’s central executive committee (CEC). Sultana-backed candidates took seven of the seats and three went to independents.

title: UK national security adviser under pressure over wife’s comment on supporting Palestine Action
summary: Author Sarah Helm, married to Jonathan Powell, wrote to back novelist Sally Rooney’s support of proscribed direct action group
text: The UK’s national security adviser, Jonathan Powell, is under pressure to distance himself from a comment made by his wife, the award-winning writer Sarah Helm, in support of Palestine Action. The post was made in defence of the critically acclaimed Irish novelist Sally Rooney, who said she had been forced to pull her books from shelves in the UK after pledging proceeds from their sales to Palestine Action. Helm, a former Sunday Times journalist and diplomatic editor at the Independent who spent many years covering the Middle East, wrote on X indicating support for the direct action group, which was proscribed last year. Under terror laws, this could constitute a criminal offence, carrying a maximum penalty of 14 years in prison. The ban has so far resulted in more than 3,700 arrests for backing the group, with more than 2,250 people formally charged as terrorists. In response to comments by the broadcaster Adam Boulton that Rooney’s support for Palestine was “anti-Jewish”, Helm wrote: “God help us authors who support Palestine and Palestine Action. Sounds like Adam would have all our books swept off the shelves in a jiffy.” Police said the post was “in the process of being assessed” to determine whether an investigation was required. Downing Street distanced itself from Helm’s post on Friday, with a spokesperson saying: “These views are held by an individual who does not represent the government in any capacity.” Helm’s works include a book about the women imprisoned by the Nazis at the Ravensbrück concentration camp, and Loyalty, a play about the Iraq war, inspired by her husband’s decade as the chief of staff to the then prime minister, Tony Blair. The author, who is writing a book about Gaza, married Powell in 2007. He was appointed in 2024 as a national security adviser under Keir Starmer. According to government guidance, being married to a suspected or convicted terrorist would normally result in the revocation of security clearance. Under the vetting framework for a job as national security adviser, being married to someone tied to a proscribed terrorist organisation is viewed as creating an automatic, unmitigated national security risk. Responding to questions about Powell’s position after his wife’s comments, a government spokesperson said: “These views are held by an individual who does not represent the government in any capacity.” A spokesperson for Defend Our Juries, a free speech group which supports the right for people to protest peacefully, thanked Helm for “defying this absurdly authoritarian ban”. “How can Andy Burnham’s government possibly defend this ban in the supreme court next month when his own national security adviser’s wife has openly defied it? This unprecedented attack on free speech in our country is plainly unsustainable,” they said. “We know of 36 people who have been arrested and had their homes raided for similarly expressing support for Palestine Action on social media. “We hope Sarah will not face the same treatment for standing up for free speech and Palestinian lives. But her defiance further exposes the absurdity of a ban that cannot be enforced against everyone who challenges it. There are simply too many of us who will continue to defy this unjust law until the government is forced to see sense and abandon it.” However, the Campaign Against Antisemitism called for Helm to “face the full force of the law”. A spokesperson said: “This is gobsmacking. Clearly, the police need to investigate and Sarah Helm must face the full force of the law, just like others who appear to express support for any proscribed terrorist organisation. “But this raises extremely serious questions for Jonathan Powell and the government. Spouses are entitled to independent views, but plainly Mr Powell, who leads on our country’s national security and has been intricately involved in our Middle East diplomacy, must publicly denounce this rhetoric if he is to continue in post.” A Met Police spokesperson said: “We have been made aware of an X post on Thursday, 15 October referencing Palestine Action. It is in the process of being assessed to determine whether any further police investigation may be required. Hundreds of writers have signed an open letter in support of Rooney, whose books include Normal People and Conversations With Friends, warning that “a country that bans its writers for speaking out is not a free country”. The letter has been signed by 419 novelists, poets, editors and illustrators including Ali Smith, Kamila Shamsie, Robert Macfarlane, Daisy Johnson, Eliza Clark, Jeanette Winterson, Alice Oseman, Derek Landy, Louise O’Neill, AM Dassu and Nikesh Shukla. The letter states: “As authors, illustrators, poets, and editors, we stand with Sally Rooney and Faber Books, and condemn a government whose actions, and inactions, have led to her books being pulled from sale in the UK. “Writers already face book bans worldwide and at home. It is unconscionable that a government can now effectively ban a single author for protesting that government’s own conflation of protest with terrorism. What future governments might do with this power should frighten us all.” Rooney said she had made the decision to withdraw from the UK market with her publisher, Faber, after learning that passing earnings on to her for the sale of her books in the UK could constitute a serious criminal offence. In a letter shared with the Guardian, Rooney said she was “wholly prepared to accept the consequences”. Faber will continue to sell Rooney’s books in other countries.

title: Brazil’s Lula says he now backs lowering age of criminal responsibility to 16
summary: Lula reverses position on age of responsibility for ‘heinous’ crimes in what many see as a desperate electoral gambit
text: Brazil’s president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, has announced that he now supports lowering the age of criminal responsibility for “heinous” crimes from 18 to 16, reversing a longstanding policy in what is widely seen as a desperate electoral gambit. The U-turn, which Lula announced during a Thursday night interview with TV Globo, comes with the presidential runoff in just over a week. The incumbent faces an uphill battle to overturn the first-round victory of his opponent, the far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro, who remains slightly ahead at the polls. Both the senator and his father, the former president, Jair Bolsonaro, have long supported lowering the age of criminal responsibility – they want it reduced to 14 rather than 16 – but Lula and his party have always opposed the change. After repeated opinion polls, the latest of them this week, showed that 80% of the population supports lowering the age, Lula said: “My view, as a Brazilian citizen, is that for any and every heinous crime, I am in favour of lowering the age.” He answered “yes” when the reporter asked whether he meant lowering it to 16. The list of crimes classified as “heinous” under Brazilian law is extensive, ranging from murder and rape to the falsification of medicines and drug trafficking – the offence for which about a quarter of the 816,000 people serving prison sentences in Brazil were incarcerated. Human rights organisations and security experts have long criticised proposals to lower the age of criminal responsibility, arguing that they do little to tackle violence while increasing recruitment into organised crime in Brazil’s overcrowded prisons. On Thursday, before Lula’s interview, the proposal had been discussed in the senate. The Episcopal Conference of Brazil, a Catholic bishops’ organisation, had criticised it for “not addressing the causes of violence”, adding that placing young people “prematurely in the prison system tends to deepen cycles of violence and exclusion, undermining their rehabilitation”. The columnist Josias de Souza wrote in his UOL column that, by reversing his longstanding position, Lula “decided to change himself. It was no ordinary transformation. On public security, Lula turned himself inside out. He began defending what he had always rejected.” The incumbent has doubled down in recent days in an effort to overturn Bolsonaro’s 2.2 million-vote first-round lead by appealing to independents and undecided voters. He has secured congressional approval for a shorter working week – a proposal on which Bolsonaro himself U-turned and decided to support at the last minute, when it appeared ready to pass – and debt relief for microentrepreneurs, as well as promising free public transport on weekends.

title: NHS staff investigated over potential accessing of tiger victim’s records
summary: Yorkshire ambulance service says workers may have accessed or attempted to access information ‘without legitimate reason’
text: NHS staff may have accessed the medical records of a man killed by a tiger at a wildlife park “without legitimate permission”, an ambulance trust has said. Yorkshire ambulance service NHS trust has launched an investigation into two members of staff at the trust, which responded to emergency calls on Saturday when William Chapman climbed into the tiger enclosure at Yorkshire Wildlife Park. There may have been “two instances involving two members of staff accessing or attempting to access incident/medical information without a legitimate reason”, the ambulance service said after being contacted by HSJ, the trade publication for NHS policy. Chapman, 23, was mauled to death by the 200kg male Siberian tiger named Altai at the zoo after climbing into its enclosure. The park reopened on Friday after being closed since the attack. An inquest opening on Thursday heard how Chapman had schizophrenia and had experienced bouts of psychosis but was “highly functioning and independent with no care requirements”. His family, who did not attend the hearing at Doncaster coroner’s court, expressed concerns about his contact with mental health services before his death. Rotherham, Doncaster and South Humber NHS foundation trust has launched an investigation into its contact with him. The inquest heard Chapman was a self-employed online trader who was living in Doncaster at the time of his death. An initial postmortem found that he died from multiple traumatic injuries. The coroner’s officer Caitlin Brookes said: “He was approached by the tiger and the ensuing physical contact between the tiger and Mr Chapman led to him sustaining multiple traumatic injuries which rapidly led to his death.” Park staff secured the tiger and Yorkshire ambulance service paramedics attended and confirmed Chapman’s death at the scene. The senior coroner Nicola Mundy said her office was awaiting a more substantial report on the extent of Chapman’s injuries ahead of a full inquest on 18 March. The potential breach of Chapman’s medical records happened after the attack and has been reported to the Information Commissioner’s Office. The trust said it had “identified an information governance concern in relation to this tragic incident at Yorkshire Wildlife Park and William’s family has been informed of our ongoing investigation into this. We believe there may have been two instances involving two members of staff accessing or attempting to access incident/medical information following this incident without a legitimate reason to do so.” It said: “We take the confidentiality and security of patient information extremely seriously and have robust systems in place to protect information, and this concern has been identified as a result of our proactive audits.” Ahead of reopening on Friday, Yorkshire Wildlife Park said safety was the “highest priority”, and it thanked members of the public who had sent “messages of support and love for our team at this time”. Wildlife and zoo experts have told the Guardian it is unlikely the wildlife park could have done anything to prevent the death.

title: Six-figure payout for senior civil servant sacked over Peter Mandelson vetting
summary: Former head of Foreign Office Olly Robbins applied for judicial review after Keir Starmer dismissed him in April
text: Olly Robbins, the former head of the Foreign Office sacked by Keir Starmer over his role in vetting Peter Mandelson, has received a six-figure payout from the government over his dismissal. Robbins had applied to the high court for a judicial review of the prime minister’s decision to remove him as the top civil servant at the Foreign Office after he was dismissed in April. He was removed from his post by Starmer after the Guardian’s disclosure that he had overturned a recommendation from UK Security Vetting (UKSV) to deny clearance for Mandelson. In a statement on Friday, Robbins said he was “grateful for all the support and good wishes from former colleagues, friends and strangers, which have helped me and my family during this difficult time”. He added: “I want to thank the FDA [union] for their assistance in reaching this settlement and I am looking forward to moving on to the next chapter of my life.” Dave Penman, general secretary of the FDA, which represents senior civil servants, said: “This settlement may bring an end to the judicial review proceedings, but this whole unprecedented affair has damaged the bond of trust between civil servants and ministers, which is essential to the effective running of government. “The scapegoating of Sir Oliver, to mask the misjudgment of the previous prime minister, marked one of the lowest points in the recent history of civil service-ministerial relations – which is quite the feat. “We urge the government to clarify quickly the issues raised by this affair over ministerial involvement in the vetting process.” The government will ultimately have to publish how much it has given Robbins in a settlement, which is believed to be six figures but not as much as the record £860,000 given to former cabinet secretary Chris Wormald after he was forced out by Starmer after just a year in post. At the time of his dismissal, Downing Street said Robbins had lost the confidence of Starmer and Yvette Cooper, then foreign secretary, due to his handling of the vetting of Mandelson, who was sacked over the extent of his links to the convicted child sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. The Guardian later revealed that Mandelson’s associations with senior figures in China, Russia and Israel had been among the concerns raised by UKSV when it concluded he should be denied clearance. His relationship with Epstein was not among the reasons. Robbins’ legal submission had made the case that Starmer had no statutory authority to dismiss him as the head of the diplomatic service, and that there had been “no fair procedure” and “no process at all” in the dismissal. It also said Robbins had been given “irrational” reasons for being fired. There had been strong support for Robbins within Whitehall, with senior civil servants said to believe he had in effect been sacked for doing what No 10 wanted by swiftly passing Mandelson through vetting, and that the focus should instead have been on the prime minister’s initial decision. The Commons foreign affairs select committee has previously said that Robbins believed he was “delivering the outcome that was wanted” and concluded that his dismissal “seems to have been taken without full due process and the establishment of the facts”. Questions remain about the defence Robbins mounted, both of his own actions and the system through which the national security establishment vets people, and the lack of mitigation put in place to get around the security concerns. The Foreign Office refused to hand over a summary of Mandelson’s security vetting to the official tasked with compiling documents detailing his appointment as ambassador to the US, in response to a Commons motion forcing the release of documents linked to the process.

title: Israeli settlers attack olive farmers and Washington Post journalist in West Bank
summary: Settlers hurl rocks at Palestinians and beat photographer Heidi Levine as part of yearly attacks to disrupt harvest
text: Israeli settlers have attacked Palestinians across the occupied West Bank in a coordinated movement to disrupt the annual olive harvest, burning cars and trees and injuring Palestinians and a Washington Post photographer. Masked settlers wielding clubs and other weapons attacked people attempting to harvest their olives in West Bank towns on Friday. Palestinian authorities said they recorded attacks in eight villages, and injuries among at least 20 people. It was the latest series of attacks in a deadly campaign of Israeli settler violence against Palestinians in recent months, violence which has drawn accusations of “ethnic cleansing”, including from the British government. In the town of Abu Falah, near Ramallah, at least 80 settlers, some of whom were carrying firearms or clubs, gathered to stop Palestinians from harvesting their olives, using slingshots to hurl rocks at the farmers in view of Israeli military vehicles. When some of the Palestinians then picked up rocks to defend themselves, the Israeli military fired teargas in their direction. The Israeli Foreign Press Association said in a statement: “This is the latest in a long line of violent attacks by Israeli settlers against journalists and other civilians in the occupied West Bank. Yet our repeated calls for action to confront this lawlessness have been ignored by Israeli authorities.” Among those injured was the Washington Post photographer Heidi Levine, who was beaten by settlers in an attack that lasted more than 10 minutes, according to witnesses. Settlers stole her passport, phone, wallet and equipment. “I was attacked, pushed to the ground. Luckily, I had my flak jacket and helmet, otherwise I probably wouldn’t even be here, because they just kept kicking and kicking me,” Levine said from a hospital bed in Ramallah. She said the attack ended when her Palestinian colleagues intervened to save her. In a statement, the Washington Post said Levine had been wearing visible markings clearly identifying her as a journalist. The office of Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, said that the facts surrounding the attack on Levine were “unclear”, suggesting the attack was the fault of “200 Arabs and far-left activists” who confronted Israeli youths. The office added that it condemned “violence against anyone”. There has been a surge of settler violence against Palestinians over the past month. Settlers have carried out at least 170 attacks since 27 September, around the start of the annual olive harvest, according to Yesh Din, an Israeli rights group. Every year, settlers attack Palestinians trying to harvest their olives, but there has been a rise in violence this year as Israel’s elections approach at the end of October. At least four Palestinians had been killed and more than 100 others injured over the past month, Palestinian authorities said. Thousands of trees have been damaged. Israel imposed new rules on the olive harvest this year, barring Palestinians from harvesting their trees located in Area C, an area under the Israeli military’s control, which comprises most of the West Bank’s agricultural land. The new orders prohibit Palestinians from entering about 8,800 hectares (21,800 acres) of agricultural land – a 30% increase from the year prior – without the approval of the Israeli military. By contrast, the military gave Israeli citizens access to more land this year. The rights group Peace Now says the military decreased the amount of land Israeli citizens were prohibited, for the purpose of preventing settler violence, from entering from about 1,070 hectares in 2025 to 680 hectares in 2026. The olive harvest is an economic lifeline for Palestinians and has grown in importance since Israel revoked work permits for many Palestinians in the West Bank after the Hamas-led attack on 7 October 2023. Photos and videos showed large swathes of agricultural land with uprooted olive trees in Kufur Malek, outside Ramallah, where Israeli bulldozers razed trees. Settlers rarely face accountability for their violence, even when well-documented. Rights groups say settlers enjoy the protection of the Israeli military, which intervenes only if Palestinians try to defend themselves. Netanyahu, has on occasion condemned the violence, which he says is due to just about 100 settlers, but he has taken few steps to stop it. Settlements have rapidly expanded across the West Bank under his rightwing government, leading to international condemnation. The UN and most countries judge settlements to be in violation of international law. Friday’s attack in Abu Falah followed a similar attack hours earlier near the West Bank village of Turmus Ayya, where settlers burned three cars after attacking Palestinians harvesting olives. Videos shared by the Israeli rights group B’tselem showed hundreds of bags of olives “violently” stolen by Israeli settlers from Palestinians and taken to Israeli olive presses. Sarit Michaeli, an independent activist, said settlers were stealing Palestinians’ olive crop on a scale “never seen before in my 22-year history of working on this issue”. A spokesperson for the US embassy in Jerusalem said it was aware of reports of the attack and declined to comment further due to privacy laws.

title: If livestreaming an execution is an outrage, is looking at old photos of them OK? | Brief letters
summary: Brief letters: Death penalty | Sir Charles Evans | Tautological traps | Spousal annoyance | Placenames
text: In view of the worldwide revulsion at Pete Hegseth’s decision to livestream a judicial killing (‘Medieval’ and ‘disturbing’: US plan to livestream execution elicits global condemnation, 9 October), how come there were photos of two more – a man awaiting execution in an electric chair in 1928 and conspirators in the assassination of Abraham Lincoln on the gallows in 1865 – on page 8 of last Saturday’s paper (next to your article on whether Christa Pike’s botched execution might help to end the death penalty in the US). I’m glad they weren’t filmed. Nick Hopkinson Tockwith, North Yorkshire • I was very disappointed to see a write-up about the famed Pen-y-Gwryd Hotel, framed around the first ascent of Everest, make no mention of Sir Charles Evans, who lived just miles away in Capel Curig and whose tankard hangs behind the bar (The Welsh mountain inn that helped conquer Everest, 15 October). He was a hero of British mountaineering who is too often absent from commentary, and the reason the hotel was part of the story in the first place. William Purkhardt Godalming, Surrey • I believe the Guardian has fallen into a tautological trap (Letters, 11 October). You report that zoos must “follow strict safety procedures to protect their animals and human staff and visitors” (Report, 12 October). One wonders who on the staff is not human. Charles Foster Chalfont St Peter, Buckinghamshire • Further to my wife’s letter about winding me up with her Brummie “Sainsers” (9 October): “Sainsers” I can bear; a Birmingham accent I can bear; her impersonation of one, as a Scot, is more than I can bear. Rob Hutchinson Newport, Isle of Wight • I have long thought that the upper and lower levels of the Compton stand at Lord’s cricket ground should have been named after the Dorset villages of Over and Nether Compton (Letters, 15 October). Peter Malpass Bristol • Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Please email us your letter and it will be considered for publication in our letters section.

title: Trump urges new press secretary to ‘reconsider’ taking job: ‘Is this for you, Katie?’
summary: Katie Zacharia had a rough start as she fumbled first press conference and faced questions from media about her professional background
text: Donald Trump has urged Katie Zacharia, his new White House press secretary, to “reconsider” taking the job after she faced intense scrutiny from news outlets, including the rightwing cable network Fox News. Speaking with reporters outside the White House on Friday, the US president said Zacharia had been “treated very badly by the media” after she stumbled through a 14-minute press conference on Tuesday and questions arose over her legal credentials. “I said, ‘Is this for you, Katie? Because honestly, you don’t need it,’” Trump recalled to reporters. “I said to her, ‘Honestly, if I were you, I’d reconsider. You think about it, but I would reconsider.’” During an appearance on the rightwing Fox News network earlier on Friday morning – her fifth day as Trump’s chief spokesperson – Zacharia was asked whether she still had the confidence of the US president. “I’m standing here,” she replied. It comes as Zacharia, who describes herself as a lawyer, faces scrutiny over her professional background after admitting she did not pass the bar exam. On Thursday evening, the Fox host Sean Hannity grilled Zacharia about her first press briefing in which she read directly from notes and occasionally stumbled over her words for 14 minutes. “What happened?” Hannity – a close ally of Trump – asked Zacharia. “How did you feel it went personally?” Zacharia quickly defended herself, saying she had little time to prep between accepting the job and holding her first press briefing and then insisted the conservative Daily Mail, one of only three outlets she took questions from, was “not known to be a conservative outlet”. Pushback on Zacharia continued on Friday morning when the Fox & Friends host Lawrence Jones said: “You know, Katie, it’s been a tough week for you. It’s not an easy job to be the press secretary, and you never want to be the story. Zacharia, a former conservative commentator, detailed the whirlwind sprint to install her as Trump’s new press secretary in an interview with the Guardian on Thursday. She replaces Karoline Leavitt, who left her role in August. Zacharia previously served as an adviser to Trump Media Group, which owns the president’s Truth Social platform, and also had a brief stint as a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security. Her introduction to the White House press corps has been rocky – between a press briefing criticized for being too short and allegations that she misrepresented herself as a lawyer. Zacharia, who graduated from Pepperdine University’s law school, had called herself a “lawyer”, and Trump identified Zacharia as an “attorney” when announcing her appointment. She had previously shared social media posts that also identified her as an “attorney”, which she defended on Hannity by saying “they were retweets”. But reports emerged this week revealing Zacharia never passed the bar exam, which she later confirmed. Zacharia has said she identified herself as a “lawyer”, not an “attorney”, to distinguish herself from a licensed legal adviser. “Why get into this long-drawn-out definition of the difference between a lawyer and an attorney? Because I don’t think most people see much of a distinction,” Hannity said. Trump told reporters on Friday that both Hannity and other Fox hosts had been “a little tough” on his new press secretary. “Sean [Hannity] was a little bit tough, and I saw Fox & Friends this morning; they were a little tough. She’s been treated, I would say, pretty nastily,” the president said. The US president said he was going to let Zacharia make the decision whether to stay or not. “Maybe it’s not for her,” Trump said, adding that he wanted her “to be happy”.

title: India’s Cockroach Janta party leader arrested amid crackdown on protests
summary: Abhijeet Dipke was detained before planned anti-government demonstrations in Delhi
text: The leader of the Cockroach Janta party (CJP) youth movement, Abhijeet Dipke, was detained by police on Friday and then later formally arrested as authorities cracked down on fresh anti-government protests in the Indian capital. Dipke was detained before a planned Friday evening demonstration he had called in central Delhi, urging supporters of the movement to come out and hold up the Indian flag. On Saturday local media reported he was arrested “to prevent a breach of the peace”, with broadcasters NDTV and India Today saying he would be called before a special executive ⁠magistrate later in the day. The Cockroach movement initially emerged back in May as online satire, but has since grown into one of the most substantial challenges to the powerful Modi government over its 12-year rule. Alongside student groups and opposition parties, its supporters have in the past month been out on the streets across India’s biggest cities calling for the resignation of the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, who is accused of overseeing a revision of India’s electoral rolls that allegedly favours the ruling Narendra Modi government with the deletion of 130m names. The election commission and Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) deny the claims. The authorities, particularly in Delhi, have met the recent protests with a draconian crackdown, including bans on public gatherings, the deployment of tens of thousands of police, and detentions of thousands last weekend. Friday’s protest was called by Dipke after the arrest and jailing of two of his fellow CJP leaders, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka. They were sentenced to five days in jail this week for jumping police barricades and holding a brief protest – including waving the Indian flag – at a site recently restricted by police for demonstrations in Delhi. At a press conference on Thursday, Dipke condemned the “repressive” attempts to silence the CJP movement and called on supporters to come out and show Narendra Modi “that we are not afraid”. He added: “If waving the Indian national flag lands you in jail, we are ready.” Delhi police had once again taken extreme measures to try to prevent Friday’s demonstration, due to be held at a park in a busy commercial centre in the heart of Delhi, from going ahead. Police were deployed en masse to the area and a police notice was sent to Dipke instructing him to call off the protest. The Delhi local authority also shut down the park where the protest was due to take place. When Dipke refused to call it off, police detained him en route, just as people began to assemble for the protest. In videos captured of his arrest, the CJP leader was seen holding an Indian flag aloft and saying: “I have not broken any law right now … how can you detain me?” as he was led away by dozens of police officers. In a post after his detention, the CJP posted on social media: “This government is so scared of the youth waving national flag.” Neha Bora, a student leader who has become a figurehead of the protests, was also detained on Friday as she began a march in the centre of the capital. Despite Dipke’s detention, about 2,000 protesters still gathered and unfurled flags at the protest around Delhi’s Connaught Place. Among them was 23-year-old Sanna, who said the brutal police crackdown on peaceful protests over recent weeks demonstrated that India was “on a pathway to dictatorship under the Modi government”. “We are only out here to peacefully hold up the Indian flag and they treat us as if we are criminals, not citizens exercising our democratic rights,” she said. “Gyanesh Kumar must resign, and no matter what the police do, detaining us or crushing our skulls, we still won’t stop protesting until he is gone.” Smaller protests also took place in Mumbai, Bengaluru and Patna on Friday. The BJP has claimed that the Cockroach movement and the political opposition alliance have been holding protests to cause “anarchy” in the country. “Their sole intention is to stage a coup in the country,” said the BJP’s national spokesperson, Sambit Patra. The authorities have also gone to unusual lengths to punish figures who have been seen at the recent protests calling for Kumar’s resignation. In Mumbai, the Bollywood actor Imran Khan was given a notice to leave the country after he was detained by police while attending a demonstration last weekend. Khan, who holds a US passport, was told to leave the country by the end of the month, an order he is now challenging in the courts.

title: Extreme heatwaves in Europe not changing Britons’ holiday plans, say travel bosses
summary: Hot summer getaways are still popular – but tourism industry fears impact of rising jet fuel costs and squeezed household incomes
text: After a year marked by extreme heat and war sending fuel prices skywards, British travel executives hoped for solace in Madeira’s benign subtropical climate, separated by hundreds of miles of blue sea from the overtourism protests and six-hour EU-entry queues seen on the Portuguese mainland. As bosses admitted, holidays will be ever less affordable, AI is coming for their jobs, and the visitable world is shrinking – not least those parts where tourists remain welcome. Some of the bigger anxieties in spring, such as widespread border chaos and planes running out of fuel, have not come to pass; others now appear chronic issues. New supplies of jet fuel, a major concern after the US first attacked Iran in February, have been established – but the cost is staying far higher for longer than most expected. “Fuel is a huge part of any holiday and people are going to have to reckon with the cost,” said Neil Swanson, Tui UK & Ireland managing director, among the attendees at the Abta convention. Tui and airlines such as easyJet and Ryanair escaped the worst immediate impact by having secured much of their 2026 fuel supply at a fixed price. But the latter airlines are now slashing capacity for winter. “It’s not great for consumers, who are going to have to pay a lot more for their holidays. But airlines are going to be less and less hedged and prices are going to go up,” Swanson added. The oil price impact goes beyond jet fuel, said Mark Tanzer, the chief executive of Abta: “The bigger worry is the squeeze on household incomes that’s going to come through their domestic costs. It will be a much tighter market.” Perhaps surprisingly, numbers have held up – but customers have been leaving it ever later to book, he said, whether in search of a deal or because of uncertainty from disruption, war or weather. Despite the intense heat, mass travel firms are clear that the template has not changed: most customers still want a hot holiday, in summer, on the beach. Garry Wilson, the chief executive of easyJet Holidays, said: “Will there be long-term effects on demand? Perhaps. But in the short-term, no, we don’t see it.” Growing “shoulder season” travel outside the school holidays for those who can, including city breaks, are driven by price more than climate, several people suggest. And talk of “coolcations” or people turning towards northern climes cuts little ice here. “We’re not seeing any of that,” said Swanson. “Nothing’s changed, the destinations are the same.” When Tunisia was forecast a 10-day stretch of 45C temperatures this summer, Tui offered customers the chance to switch their holiday elsewhere. Swanson said: “We didn’t get the interest and take-up. People were expecting it to be hot and were happy to go there, and we’re not seeing any change in demand. Brits like a warm holiday – if it’s got a pool and air-conditioning, that works for them.” Neither does Wilson see many heading north. Citing easyJet destinations such as Tromsø in Norway or Malmö in Sweden, he said: “They’re all very nice to launch, but we send more customers to Majorca in a week than those in a year.” Outbound holidays prospered in the heatwave, he suggested. “People thought: ‘You know what, we maybe don’t need to go away.’ But it became apparent that the UK doesn’t have the infrastructure to cope … people actually were going abroad to escape the heat in the UK.” For now, the big firms see little change in destinations, Swanson said, but added: “We’ll keep it under review. Who knows where the temperature’s going to go in the next few years?” More people could get priced out. At last year’s convention, the Spanish tourist board started pushing its cooler northern destinations; but, said Tanzer, “I’m not sure the north has 100m beds” to accommodate the visitors who predominantly go to Spain’s south, east and islands. He added: “Certain types of holiday could become more expensive just because there’s limited availability. If the snow is higher up the mountain, there’s going to be fewer skiing holidays and the price is going to go up – there’s little room at the top.” Tui has not been immune. Its river cruises in Europe were marooned when the Danube’s water levels dipped last month to the point where some passengers spent most of their return Austro-Hungarian cruise on a boat-replacement bus. Katy Berzins, the head of river cruises at Tui, said: “Every year has highs and lows and it’s part of river cruising, rivers are changeable.” But 2026, she said, was “unprecedented”. The division is expanding nonetheless. Two new ships are joining its fleet – initially destined for the Seine and the Douro – that are built with lower draught levels (the vessel’s vertical depth below the surface), meaning they are able to keep sailing in shallower rivers. Others are seeing faster change. James Thornton, the chief executive of Intrepid Travel, said the firm no longer sold active travel group tours in southern Europe in the summer; few had wanted to trek or cycle in that level of heat. Last year, Thornton said, there were 185 different extreme weather-related incidents that affected Intrepid holidaymakers around the world. “When we first started, there would be a handful.” Intrepid has long wrestled with its own impact on climate: for years, before offsetting fell into disrepute, it paid millions to offset its emissions. That did not cover the biggest factor, the flights taken by its customers to reach Intrepid tours – not entirely dissimilar from how an airport might declare itself net zero. Instead now the firm has a decarbonisation fund for local projects: “Ultimately you can’t have sustainable travel, you can only limit the impact,” Thornton said. Having grown from backpacking to a A$1bn annual business, its own footprint is becoming significant. This year the firm is launching Timor-Leste, or East Timor. Thornton said: “Some customers have done 30 to 40 trips, so they’re often looking for places that they haven’t been able to travel to.” Asked about overtourism, Thornton said: “We’re definitely worried about it.” Intrepid tries to advertise the less visited destinations, he added. “We call it the not-hot list – drawing out the places where the infrastructure is available and the locals are willing to welcome travellers.” Rising tourist taxes around the world underline that many places feel they have more than enough visitors. For Wilson, it is “grossly unfair”; destinations such as Mallorca, he said, “built enormous economic positions on the back of mass tourism, and then pull up the bridge and put on an extra tax. All that does is go back to the days of travel being only for the rich.” How many of the UK outbound travel industry remain in sufficient paid work to afford it may also be in question. Shaun Morton, the chief executive of On the Beach, laid off 20% of the Manchester-based online agency’s staff this summer to “automate and streamline” processes. He told delegates: “You’ve got the technology, people, processes and you hold them all dear … We just started to ask not how do we get 10% more out of that, but how do we get 10 times that, you know?” He added that “very bright people with a sharp head with technology” probably would keep their jobs longest, but acknowledged: “They’re worried, because they can see a little bit further ahead than everyone else.” The Guardian’s travel to the convention in Madeira was provided by Abta
