title: Shooter kills three children and one teacher at Oregon elementary school
summary: Two people critical in hospital as officials in Bend say 16-year-old suspect shot dead by bystander
text: Schools in Bend, Oregon, will be closed on Friday after a 16-year-old shooter opened fire at an elementary school in the city on Thursday, killing three children and a teacher before he was shot dead by a community member. The children killed at Silver Rail elementary school were aged five, eight and 11, officials said. A seven-year-old and a 54-year-old were also hospitalized with critical injuries, according to police. The shooter, who was a Bend resident, has not been publicly identified and early on Friday the identities of those killed, those wounded and the armed bystander who followed the teen into the school and shot him were not publicly known. Officials said they are still investigating if the perpetrator had ties to the school. He shot his way through a locked gate into the school grounds and through locked doors to gain access to the premises, the authorities said. Children and staff who heard gunfire rushed to lock classroom doors and hide. The deadly shooting has rocked the city of 100,000 residents located on the Deschutes River, roughly 170 miles south-east of Portland, in central Oregon. “Please hold your children, hold your loved ones tight tonight. Let them talk. Let them cry. Let them know we are going to rally and care for one another in this community,” said Steven Cook, the superintendent of Bend-La Pine Schools. “We will get through this – but not yet. We must grieve for the loss of our community members.” At 1.02pm, police responded to Silver Rail elementary school after receiving several reports about an active shooter. One 911 caller reported an individual armed with a long gun firing at their car. Police did not specify the firearm’s make. Dozens of callers stated the shooter had entered the school, continuing the attack inside. By the time officers arrived on scene, the suspected assailant had been shot and killed by the bystander, who apprehended him inside. The attacker used a pump-action shotgun, according to a law enforcement official briefed on the shooting. The official spoke to the Associated Press on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to publicly discuss the investigation. In the aftermath of the tragedy, children were taken by bus to a nearby church serving as a reunification center for families. Parents hugged, kissed and held their kids’ hands as they walked to their cars, with some bringing along favorite stuffed animals or other comfort items from home. The school serves kindergarten through fifth grade, roughly ages five to 11, and has about 450 students and 40 staff members, officials said. Oregon’s governor, Tina Kotek, praised the intervention as heroic and extended her thoughts to the bystander. “Your actions carry a heavy emotional burden,” she said on Thursday evening. Classes, sports and extracurriculars were canceled Friday for all 32 schools in the Bend-La Pine district. The FBI is helping local authorities investigate the shooting, according to the agency’s director, Kash Patel. The shooting began about an hour before the school day was set to end. “A school should be a safe place where children can learn and feel secure,” said Bend’s mayor, Melanie Kebler. “Like so many in our community, I’m struggling to make sense of a loss that feels unimaginable.” Gun control advocate Gabrielle Giffords, ⁠a former congresswoman who survived a mass shooting in 2011, said in a statement she was “heartbroken” by the shooting. “This cannot continue to be a reality in our country. Leaders at every level must step up and act,” Giffords said. Thursday’s shooting is the latest event in a grim history of recurring gun violence at schools across the US. According to Everytown for Gun Safety, there have been at least 100 incidents of gunfire on school grounds across the country in 2026, resulting in 33 deaths. Oregon has passed several gun safety measures in recent years, including a law that requires gun owners to undergo a criminal background check and safety training before being approved for a firearm permit.

title: Sharks, rays and wobbegongs: South Australian algal bloom killed more than 8,000 creatures
summary: ‘Unprecedented’ mass mortality event that began in 2025 may have led to the collapse of some populations, ecologists fear
text: More than 8,000 sharks and rays died during South Australia’s toxic algal bloom, the largest known mass mortality globally, with endangered species among the fatalities. Prof Charlie Huveneers, a shark ecologist at Flinders University, said the bloom had potentially led to the collapse of some local populations. “The scale of the harmful algal bloom is unprecedented, the number and diversity of shark and ray species impacted is something never seen before.” Documented losses included about 4,460 southern fiddler rays, 850 Port Jackson sharks, 670 cobbler wobbegongs and 650 western shovelnose rays, according to an analysis of citizen science and government records led by Janine Baker, a marine ecologist. When people in South Australia think of sharks, they typically have white sharks or bronze whalers in mind, Huveneers said. But there were more than 50 species of sharks and rays found in state waters, including many small endemic species. In all, 31 species of sharks, rays, skates and stingarees were recorded in the algal bloom death toll, including coastal stingarees (listed as endangered by the International Union for Conservation of Nature) and pygmy thornback skates, two species found only in South Australian waters. Vulnerable Melbourne skates were also among the dead. While little is known about these smaller, range-restricted species, it was possible that a large proportion of individual creatures were affected by the bloom. Affected species ranged from skates and stingarees, roughly the size of a dinner plate, to bronze whalers and white sharks that grow to several metres. While benthic species – those living on or near the sea floor – dominated the death toll, even sharks capable of large-scale movements like white sharks were also affected by the harmful bloom. “People might be aware of the Port Jackson sharks, southern eagle rays, fiddler rays – and there was certainly a lot of them washing up – but we also had a lot of species that people had never seen or heard about, like cobbler wobbegongs,” Huveneers said. “One of the surprising things with the bloom is that it didn’t just impact a couple of species but a whole range of sharks and rays. And that suggests that sharks and rays are highly susceptible to these blooms.” In some areas, previously common species were now rarely seen, he said. While Port Jackson sharks on the east coast undertook large migrations, some of the South Australian populations stay put year-round, which put them at greater risk. Sharks and rays were among more than 800 species affected by Australia’s first bloom of Karenia cristata, a rare and toxic type of algae deadly to marine life. “For many of the sharks and rays impacted, both adults and juveniles showed signs of blood pooling under the skin and blood leakage from the orifices,” the report said. Eighteen months on from the start of the algal bloom’s spread, surveys and reports are beginning to measure the scale of the devastation, including the catastrophic decline in giant cuttlefish and the deaths of thousands of sea dragons, pipefishes and seahorses – research made possible through the contributions of citizen scientists and divers. The numbers were likely an underestimate, given they exclude shark eggs and animals that died offshore. But understanding the impact was the first step towards supporting the recovery of sharks, rays and their ecosystems, Huveneers said. The state’s environment department is finalising a comprehensive assessment of the bloom’s impact on nearshore marine biodiversity, including sharks and rays, to guide its recovery efforts. “Citizen science initiatives provide critical information on the ecological effects of the algal bloom that will inform expected recovery timelines and actions, and design of impact monitoring programs,” a department spokesperson said. Prof Culum Brown, a fish and shark researcher at Macquarie University, said Australia was a hotspot for shark diversity and the algal bloom had “affected pretty much the entire food web, all the way to the top” There was growing concern for sharks and rays across the board in society, especially in Australia, he said. “To see these deaths at this sort of scale is pretty heartbreaking.”

title: Just 14% of Albertans want independence from Canada. Can a conference in a Calgary ballroom change that?
summary: WeUnify’s Reclaiming Alberta brought together ardent supporters of separating from Canada while highlighting key disagreements – not least how close an independent Albert should be to the US
text: The debate began with a simple question in a dark Calgary hotel ballroom: does Alberta need Canada? By the time the audience was asked to vote at the end, more than three-quarters had answered no – a decisive measure of the convictions of a room packed with some of Alberta’s most ardent independence supporters, some of whom had paid C$900 (£480) for a “visionary” weekend pass. But outside the comfort of the ballroom, the debate is far from settled. Across the province, the forthcoming 19 October referendum on separatism has divided communities, prompting accusations of treason and grift and, at times, bitter feuds between former allies. One recent poll shows support for independence at only 14%. You wouldn’t know it from the WeUnify’s Reclaiming Alberta conference though. “This is a matter of survival,” conservative activist and broadcaster Faytene Grasseschi told the crowd, which erupted into applause after she said Alberta’s oil resources had been “usurped” by the federal government and the Canada she had been born into “doesn’t exist any more”. In the main halls outside the ballroom, attendees milled around the vendor stalls. A handful donned a $6,500 (£4,925) helmet that resembles white colanders hastily attached to a bike helmet, bathing the user’s head in red LED light supposedly for treatment of “Parkinson’s, Alzheimer’s, dementia, traumatic brain injury, [and] brain fog”. Others took in sales pitches about the need for gold and silver as paper money “fails”. But the busiest stall belonged to the group Let’s Talk Alberta. It says it is neither a political party nor a campaign organisation but its five bound pamphlets include a 52-page volume titled Every Argument to Stay is a Reason to Leave. The pamphlets were written by its founder, Chris Scott, a cafe owner who attracted widespread attention during the Covid-19 pandemic after he was arrested for violating public health orders. After a lengthy legal battle, he was acquitted. On stage, Scott told the crowd the push for independence would be a “wake-up call” for the rest of the country and reflected a fight against what many in the movement see as an entrenched political elite – a fight that needed to happen “come hell or high water”. After initial efforts to bring a referendum question on independence were derailed by First Nations groups, Albertans will now be voting on the question of whether Alberta should remain part of Canada or whether the provincial government should begin the legal process to hold a second, binding referendum on separation. With just days to go, the foot soldiers and the faithful of the independence movement have begun their final pitches for what they envision will one day be a wealthy, “anti-woke” nation – one unshackled from the control of the federal government, or even a vassal of the United States. The conference, which was organised by the WeUnify movement, brought together Alberta separatists, veterans of the pandemic-era “freedom movement” and conservatives united by a distrust of established institutions. Speakers reserved their harshest words for Justin Trudeau, who, despite resigning as prime minister more than a year ago, remains a bugbear for the separatist movement. Sheane Meikle, a volunteer with Let’s Talk Alberta, said the independence movement was gaining support. “We’re getting far fewer Trudeau salutes when we wave flags on the side of the road,” he said – a reference to the raised middle finger. Meikle, 58, has spent months travelling the province with Scott, adding more than 32,000 miles to his van as part of a quest to convince sceptical Albertans of the benefits of separation. The referendum had been “longtime coming” for the movement, he said. “Even if the results don’t go our way, it doesn’t mean we’re done. This is a movement now that’s sustained.” Not everyone agreed the conference was the best idea, though. Keith Wilson, one of the principal intellectual and legal architects of Alberta’s modern separatist movement, admitted in an interview that he regretted participating. “It’s just an echo chamber in there – I’m not changing any minds that are already made up for separatism. I shouldn’t be here. I should be out campaigning.” In September Wilson brought together 45 unnamed contributors to publish the Alberta Transition Plan, a 214-page blueprint for turning Alberta from a province into an independent country. “We have everything. Alberta is an economic powerhouse. But we’re also on the ground with our face in our dirt and our arms tied behind our backs because of Ottawa,” he said, referring to a longstanding belief that the federal government continues to exert unfair influence over the oil-rich province. “That’s how many Albertans feel, and that’s why they want change.” His blueprint, however, has drawn criticism for leaving major questions about the costs and practicalities of independence unresolved. The University of Calgary’s School of Public Policy recently estimated that the costs associated with separation could cost Alberta between C$50bn and C$170bn over its first five years and warned substantial annual deficits were possible. Nor have the secessionists built the political machinery that could bring it about. The campaign has no official leader, nor an organised movement under the guise of a political party. No elected officials have campaigned for independence. Unlike Quebec, where independence parties have run explicitly on the idea and won, Alberta has only ever elected a separatist candidate once, and he lost his seat months later. In previous elections, separatist parties have won an average popular vote of 1%. In the absence of coherent leadership, prominent figures have been thrust into the limelight, often with chaotic results. Jeff Rath, a bombastic lawyer linked to the Alberta Prosperity Project, is embroiled in legal battles over allegations that millions of dollars in disputed First Nations trust funds were mishandled. Mitch Sylvestre, head of the Alberta Prosperity Project and owner of a sporting goods store, told the Toronto Star he fears King Charles will have him assassinated. David Parker, a longtime rightwing political organizer, was at the centre of a voter-data scandal that exposed the personal information of nearly 3 million Albertans and remains under investigation. But for Meikle and others, the movement is “grassroots” and would only be damaged by the presence of elected officials. “We just need our politicians to get out of the way and stop being so biased towards this movement,” he said. “They shouldn’t be using taxpayer money to campaign against us.” For many here, the coronavirus pandemic remains an animating force. Some of the panellists and speakers were prominent lawyers who challenged and in some cases won cases against the government for overreach in shutdown laws. It was the pandemic – and the political atmosphere that followed it – that got Betty Field, a retiree who worked in the oil sector, interested in the independence movement. Her husband, Gord Pick, chimed in that even supporters of federalism should vote against unity “to put a little fear of God into Ottawa”. But the lack of a leader has led to divergence over messaging and strategy. In early October, the Globe and Mail reported on ties between the Alberta separatists movement and Republican operatives, and meetings between those unelected Albertans and White House staff. Among items allegedly discussed were oil revenues that could be directed to the US in exchange for assistance establishing a new country, as well as Alberta’s fresh water resources. “We wouldn’t want to be part of the US,” said Pick. “Why trade one overlord in Ottawa for another in Washington?” Outside, fresh off their weekly dinner of liver and onions – “just the best in Calgary, hands down!” – friends Vera Patten and Lisette Bourget stand in the waning sun, smoking a cigarette. When a conference attender offers to hold the door for them, Patten says politely: “Oh we’re not with you.” “I hope they lose,” she adds after a small crowd, also out for a smoke, returns back inside. “It’s just disgusting. I can’t believe how they’re trying to break up this country.” A veteran of the oil industry, Patten has lived in Calgary for decades and says only damage can come from separation. “This needs to stop, and I’m hopeful that after the vote – that they lose.” Wilson said the movement had other plans. “The separatist movement in Alberta started before my parents were born – and they’re dead,” he said. “Because if you’re a separatist, you see a better opportunity for your friends, neighbours and your grandkids. And you never give up on that. Even if the vote goes poorly, it will not end. In the same way that winters won’t end and springs won’t end, this movement won’t end either. It’s here to stay.”

title: ‘We should all be worried’: calls grow to limit London rollout of robotaxis
summary: Protest planned at Wayve HQ as Uber drivers fear for their future and city’s politicians demand TfL should have power over licences
text: For passengers in Britain who want to try the latest ride, robotaxis are eagerly awaited: more than 100,000 are on Uber’s waitlist in London after the first UK services started in September. Others view them with trepidation. “I think we should all be worried,” said Florentina Ghiuzan, an Uber driver from Essex. “I was shocked TfL approved it so soon. I knew change would come. But I thought it would come with a solution for us.” London’s rollout is facing mounting opposition, from drivers fearing for their future and the capital’s politicians, with a critical report demanding Transport for London (TfL) is given full powers to permit or suspend operations. Drivers will this weekend protest outside the headquarters and depot of Wayve, which has partnered with Uber to supply London’s first autonomous cabs for hire. The direct action marks the latest salvo between unions and the global tech companies, whose driverless cars trials expanded this week to Manchester, with fears that hundreds of thousands of driver jobs could be lost. Although only a handful of driverless cars now ply the streets, Uber has announced plans to deploy 100,000 Nvidia robotaxis worldwide starting next year, and its senior executives have talked about all new cars being autonomous by 2040. In San Francisco, Waymo’s fully autonomous cars already operate more than a quarter of all rides. The mayor of London, Sadiq Khan, and bosses at TfL have expressed unease, and the London assembly’s transport committee has called for the government to devolve authority over autonomous taxi services. In a report published this week, the committee said there was “considerable uncertainty around many of the claimed benefits of autonomous passenger vehicles”, and fears over the impact on public transport and congestion, as well as safeguarding and accessibility for disabled passengers. The chair, Caroline Russell, said they were not convinced that London should welcome robotaxis. “Rather than just accepting the autonomous passenger service model proposed by operators, London should be looking at the transport problems it is trying to solve and then considering what solutions this technology could provide,” she said. TfL is understood to see little benefit in the addition of robotaxi services to its crowded city streets, even if the numbers turn out to be relatively few in comparison to the wider traffic. For the robotaxi companies, London is a tempting challenge to crack. Commercially, it is one of the biggest private hire markets in the world and a foothold in Europe; logistically, it is a tricky test bed to prove their vehicles are viable anywhere. Compared with the grid system of US cities in particular, it presents narrower, twisting and unruly streets, without the kind of rules on jaywalking that give cars priority on the road. Under current rules, TfL licenses passenger services, but the government decides whether autonomous vehicles can operate. TfL has approved the start of Uber and Wayve’s limited robotaxi services, which retain a human safety driver in the front seat. As it stands, when it comes to fully autonomous passenger services, the Department for Transport would issue permits for robotaxis with TfL only able to grant or refuse consent, rather than regulate their usage on London’s streets. That has alarmed TfL, which sees parallels with when Uber first started business in London, creating problems few had considered, and was twice rebuffed in licence renewals as not a “fit and proper” operator. Quite how driverless cars will affect the capital’s transport ecosystem is unknown – and TfL wants to retain the power to intervene. City hall is also concerned about the social implications of more than 100,000 licensed drivers losing income or a living. Those at the frontline in the App Drivers and Couriers Union (ADCU) are planning protests outside Wayve’s London base from this Saturday. Their members include Ghiuzan, 42, who started working as a driver four years ago after going back to college. She said: “Our earnings are the same or even lower since I started – and with the robotaxis on the market it could get even worse.” Ghiuzan said she was notified of the start of autonomous services as an Uber customer – but received no notification as a driver. She thinks people will switch to robotaxis: “Young people like them, it’s new, and you don’t have to pay the driver … I might have other skills, but for lots of drivers who are older and have done it their whole life, it’s going to be quite a challenge.” Faisal Osman, 51, from east London, has been an Uber driver for 12 years, after switching from a long commute to an IT engineering job to allow him to work nights when he had children. He knows four other engineers who joined Uber: “We all used to talk about AI taking our jobs in IT. We thought, we’re not earning as much driving but we’ll be safe for a while, support the family, pay the bills. But robocabs are a massive concern. “People might be interested but it will decimate the livelihoods of many people including me – I really wanted some authorities to say no.” Abdurzak Hadi, an Uber driver and theLondon chair of the ADCU, said Saturday’s protests would follow a similar action held at Waymo’s base in Park Royal in August. He said: “For me as a driver, I’m thinking about competing with a machine that’s not going to get tired, and could work 24 hours a day. “But as a Londoner with family, I’m thinking about safety. As licensed drivers we’re taught by TfL about safeguarding, looking out for a vulnerable child, or for abuse. Or looking after passengers who can only read your lips. We’re a safety net. But losing my job – that’s also losing a safety net for my family.” A recent report from the Centre for British Progress thinktank said more than 400,000 UK drivers (121,000 in London) would soon find “much of this work obsolete”, and urged the government to tax autonomous vehicles to help pay for the social consequences and economic losses. The GMB union has demanded a “just transition” to help drivers reskill and find new work. Speaking at the Labour conference last month, the GMB’s Mark Betteridge said the union was not against change but added: “The people who do these jobs will know the reality far better of what change will look like … Drivers tell us they want some sort of transition plan to get through this.” The roads minister, Justin Madders, told the meeting that autonomous vehicles could bring “opportunities for well-paid and unionised jobs” and the government wanted Britain to be a “world leader” in the technology. But, he added: “Sometimes government hasn’t worked on the impact on workers … We’re absolutely committed to making sure that doesn’t happen that time.” An Uber spokesperson said: “Drivers and AVs [automated vehicles], which we believe will also offer considerable benefits to cities, are both expected to grow side by side for quite some time. That said, we shouldn’t hide that autonomous mobility will impact workers, riders, and the communities they live in. “We are in conversations with the government and local stakeholders to ensure we can realise the promise of AVs while not leaving drivers and communities behind.” Uber said it had not significantly increased its share of fares in London but VAT changes meant drivers were keeping less of the fares customers paid, and it said it was the only private hire operator in the UK recognising its drivers as workers with employment protections. Wayve said that with Uber it was taking a “deliberately phased approach”, and had engaged extensively with political leaders, community organisations and accessibility advocates. A spokesperson said its robotaxis could “make a positive contribution to London’s transport system, helping to improve road safety, expand connectivity and give people more ways to travel. “There is clear excitement in the potential for this technology to support safer, more accessible journeys, provided it is introduced responsibly and in partnership with the city. We have a positive, constructive relationship with TfL and we’re working pragmatically together to ensure any future services meet its expectations.” A spokesperson for Khan said the mayor was committed to ensuring that Londoners benefitted from the opportunities new technologies could bring but shared “concerns about potential impacts on safety, congestion and jobs”, as any changes needed to “work for our world-leading transport system – including taxi and private hire services, and those who drive them”.

title: ‘Clean air is not a favour’: Indonesia’s neighbours fed up with acrid haze as Singapore threatens to prosecute
summary: Millions affected by smoke from wildfires as schools close, respiratory illnesses soar and diplomatic tensions rise
text: Singapore is threatening to prosecute companies responsible for some of the worst fires in years in neighbouring Indonesia, as the region grows increasingly frustrated with a persistent, acrid haze that could result in diplomatic relations fraying. Lawrence Wong, the Singaporean prime minister, said his government was distributing masks to vulnerable citizens and working with countries in the region to deal with the smoke. “At the same time, we are looking into which companies may be responsible for the fires,” he said in a Facebook post on Thursday, adding that he was exploring the idea of “joint action with other countries”. Singapore has no plantations or forests of its own, but several companies with concessions in Indonesia are reportedly based in the city-state. Haze is a persistent problem in Indonesia, but drier-than-usual conditions mean the thick smoke has been drifting into nearby Singapore, Malaysia, Brunei and Timor-Leste, and as far afield as the Philippines and Vietnam. Millions are affected, with school closures, respiratory illness spiking and air pollution indexes reaching unhealthy levels. Malaysians and Singaporeans have been sharing images online of their cities, with skyscrapers disappearing into the smog, and frustration with the region’s most populous country is boiling over. “Year after year, the haze comes back. It affects our health, closes schools, hurts businesses, and costs us billions,” a veteran Malaysian social activist and former politician wrote in a public letter this week. Lee Lam Thye said that real enforcement and “not just polite words” were needed. “Those responsible must be named, investigated, and punished. Clean air is not a favour. It is a basic right.” While Indonesia regularly battles wildfires in the dry season, these blazes are the most intense in more than a decade and exacerbated by slash-and-burn practices to clear land for agriculture, including palm oil, of which Indonesia is the world’s largest producer. Regional diplomats have offered to help Indonesia, but their offers have not always been immediately accepted. On Monday, an Indonesian official said the country was “still capable of handling it”. By the end of the week, Jakarta said it would accept assistance. Such delicate diplomacy is routine among the region’s Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean), which is built on quiet engagement and non-interference. A meeting of regional foreign ministers in the Philippines is due next month, but that might be too late. Nerves are fraying. In remarks that went viral on social media, Syahganda Nainggolan, the head of Indonesia’s government communication agency, hit back at the criticism on Saturday. “We don’t only send haze,” he said, “the oxygen in Singapore and Malaysia comes from our forests.” Rare strong words came earlier this month from Anwar Ibrahim, the Malaysian prime minister. He said he had been in contact with Indonesia’s president, Prabowo Subianto, “who agreed to take the necessary steps, and this commitment must be followed by immediate and effective action from the Indonesian side to tackle the root causes of the haze”. At the same time, pressure is growing on Jakarta to declare a national disaster, first from civil society groups but now also from Indonesian politicians and neighbours. According to the Jakarta Post, Indonesian students have been holding protests across Kalimantan and Sumatra, demanding accountability and government action. In one video posted online, a child in a mask stands outside under a dark orange sky and calls on the local and national government to help. He holds a sign that says: “Save our little lungs”. The country has dispatched firefighters and announced a crackdown on arsonists, but declaring a disaster would unlock funds and help thousands with medical expenses. On Friday, the Indonesian forestry ministry said four firefighters were killed in a national park in Java. Longtime onlookers say the issue is not just firefighting, but targeting the companies involved. In recent years, several attempts to take legal action against the companies exacerbating “transboundary haze” have failed, both locally and internationally, and posed a diplomatic minefield. Haze is complex for Singapore and Malaysia, as they host companies working in Indonesia. A Greenpeace report published this month identified businesses based in Singapore and Malaysia that it claimed were linked to burning land in Indonesia. Ultimately, Indonesians bear the brunt of the blazes. The health ministry has reported nearly 280,000 people in the country with respiratory infections linked to the fires, with children under five accounting for more than 60,000. Michelle Dyonisius, a campaigner at Amnesty International Indonesia, said rights groups and civil society organisations were ramping up pressure on the government to declare a national disaster emergency. “It has been going on for months, affecting millions and millions of people, including abroad,” she said. “I think there is a refusal to acknowledge the gravity of the issue at hand and also the belief that it is under control. But considering the gravity of the issue and all of the people affected, it seems quite naive to remain in that position.”

title: Digested week: No Nobel again for Trump but he looks a cert to retain Fifa peace prize | John Crace
summary: With his war in Iran and siding with Russia, it’s hard to think of someone who has done more to make the world a safer place
text: Monday It might have been more, shall we say, diplomatic if Donald Trump had taken some deep breaths after finding out he had been overlooked for the Nobel peace prize for the second year running before virtually declaring war on Norway. But maybe we should just be grateful he refrained from rubbishing the South African human rights activist Navi Pillay, who picked up the award, and shelved his plans to livestream the execution of the Norwegian prize committee. There again, you can understand his frustration. It’s hard to think of someone who has done more to make the world a safer place. Where would we be had not The Donald started a war with Iran which he shows no sign of knowing how to finish and which has forced up the price of global energy? And it was so good to see him intervening so positively in Russia’s war with Ukraine by appearing to side with the aggressor. These are just the things everyone is looking for in a Nobel peace laureate. The president is also put out that no one has noticed he has personally ended eight global conflicts; though it would be helpful if he could let us know which ones. Are they ones he has personally started – Trump appears disappointed that Argentina hasn’t invaded the Falklands again – or ones that only he knows about. During a press conference at Chequers in 2025, he claimed to have brought about a lasting peace between Albania and Azerbaijan. Maybe there are other wars going on we just don’t know about. Perhaps Australia and New Zealand have been bombing each other for years with neither side noticing. And perhaps the border between France and Italy has been a no-go zone ever since the fight between Zinedine Zidane and Marco Materazzi in the 2006 World Cup final. Still, Trump looks a cert to retain Gianni Infantino’s Fifa peace prize – if only because it seems likely to be scrapped, making him the only winner. Tuesday We may be facing higher levels of global threat and energy costs, but the political outlook isn’t all bleak. You’d need to have a major sense of humour failure not to be enjoying Reform sliding in the polls and falling out with one another. Things seemed to start going wrong when the Guardian exposed Nigel Farage’s £5m bung from the Thai-based crypto-billionaire Christopher Harborne. Nige has still not come up with a convincing explanation of how the money would be spent. Other than maintaining an expensive lifestyle. Then there was the Channel 4 sting when two of Farage’s closest political allies were caught allegedly trying to take an illegal overseas donation. Nige’s excuse? He wasn’t listening to his conversation with the donor. Who hasn’t dozed off when there’s £500,000 at stake? Since then everyone in Reform appears hell-bent on being the worst versions of themselves as the party loses support by tacking ever further to the right. On Monday, Robert Jenrick declared he would personally be happy to give the order for the Royal Navy to blow every small boat crossing the Channel out of the water. This was too much for Zia Yusuf. Zia is widely loathed within the Reform elite but no one has found a way of saying no to his money, so he gets to call himself the bogus title of shadow home secretary. His main objection to Honest Bob’s plan is that he wasn’t the one to think of it first. Meanwhile, Nige just sits back and pockets the money. Seemingly unable to stop his party collapsing around him. Wednesday After several years of consultation, the Bank of England has announced the four animals, insects and birds that will appear on the new banknotes. What goes on what denomination has yet to be decided, but the ones chosen are the European hedgehog, the barn owl, the buff-tailed bumblebee and the Atlantic puffin. And while I’d have quite liked to have seen my much-missed dog Herbie, who died last year, on one of the notes, they all seem reasonable choices to me. I guess the last thing the Bank wanted was to start a war between cat and dog lovers. But not everyone is happy. Partly because they are mad but mostly because they don’t apparently understand how the selection process worked. It was the public who got to choose both the theme of the banknotes and the actual creatures. Needless to say, leading the charge against the new notes are Kemi Badenoch and Nigel Farage, who see the hedgehog and the puffin as some kind of woke symbols. A country going to the barn owls and the bumblebees. They have moaned, what was wrong with having Winston Churchill? Are we now ashamed of our past? No, you halfwits. You don’t have to plaster Churchill’s face on everything to prove you are British. Most of us are secure enough in our identity not to need countless flags and symbols as a reminder. It’s just nice to have a change from time to time. And how many people used to see Churchill’s face on a £5 note and feel a well of pride every time you wanted to buy a sandwich? For that matter, how many people even use cash these days? Mind you, once AI has mined all our data from our emails and bank accounts we could be back to a cash and letter-writing society. Thursday In one of his last conversations with a close friend, Jeffrey Archer was asked if he had any regrets. While he admitted to having some flaws, Archer went on to say that there was nothing he would change. I find that remarkable. I’m not expecting him to apologise for having invented so much of his life – a fantasist is going to fantasise – and he had every right to be proud of his book sales. But not to feel a tiny bit of regret about having lied on oath and being sent to prison. Or feel guilty for the lives he ruined as a result of his lies. That feels borderline sociopathic. Isn’t it human to wish you had done some things differently? I’ve been thinking about this now I’ve turned 70. There’s a lot about my life that I love – family, friends, job – but I have a lasting sadness and guilt about my 20s that I find hard to forgive. The waste, the self-destruction, the damage I did to myself and others. Many of those who knew me had doubts I would even live to 30. I had those doubts, too. And sometimes didn’t much care either way. So yes, I have a whole decade I would love to have done differently. The repair job has been a lifetime’s work and it’s still ongoing. It will probably always be thus. Friday The Celebrity Traitors continues to be addictive television. A class above the civilian version, partly because we all know something about the celebs, but mainly because the game is different. The civilians are playing for money, the celebs are playing for screen time. That’s why Amol Rajan was gutted to be banished inside 24 hours. The one exception was Richard E Grant, who didn’t care one way or the other. Since his wife died he’s become more disinhibited. The worst has already happened to him. Halfway in, Maya Jama and James Acaster are making great traitors. Maya because she’s so hard to read as her face doesn’t move, James because he genuinely believes he’s too nice to be a traitor while stabbing his friends in the back. I’m amazed Jerry Hall is still in. Not because she’s particularly suspicious but more because she’s incredibly annoying. And why has no one asked her what it was like being married to Rupert Murdoch? The faithful who is playing a blinder is Sharon Rooney. So far she has said and done nothing to attract the film crew, which means she’s likely to be around for a while yet. Being boring is not a bad strategy. I’d like to see a version of The Traitors for politicians, and in my forthcoming shows (Birmingham MAC on 31 October, Huntingdon theatre in Worcester on 26 November) I will be inviting the audience to offer suggestions for possible contestants. So please come along and let’s see if we can make it happen. On Tuesday 1 December, join John Crace and Pippa Crerar as they skewer the biggest stories from Westminster and beyond, as part of the Guardian’s year in review event. Joined by fellow Guardian writers, expect candid conversations, witty remarks and surprises as they look back on the year-defining stories of 2026. Book tickets here or at theguardian.live

title: ‘Too big to rig’: No Kings movement heads to the polls to boost early voting
summary: Coalition has planned more than 3,000 events on Saturday to encourage voting before election day
text: The coalition that has drawn millions of Americans into the streets to fight for democracy over the past two years is shifting its strategy this weekend. On Saturday, No Kings organizers and partners will hold thousands of events across all 50 states and Washington DC to get people to the polls early for the US midterm elections. With high-stakes races that will determine control of Congress, organizers say getting out the vote before election day can ease burdens on election workers and build confidence in voters, allowing them to avoid hiccups such as long lines and potential election threats. Organizers hope to not only make Saturday the largest single day of early voting in US history, but also build a volunteer network ready to defend the results of the 3 November midterm elections – should actors choose to undermine election results. “Saturday will be an anti-election sabotage effort,” said Ezra Levin, co-founder of the progressive group Indivisible, part of the No Kings coalition. “The single best thing you can do to push back against sabotage is to massively increase the vote and do it early.” From the streets to the polls No Kings began as a protest movement during Donald Trump’s second presidential term, organizing three days of nationwide protests beginning in the summer of 2025 that brought people out to protest a government shutdown, federal layoffs, immigration enforcement, foreign wars, fatal ICE shootings and military deployments in US cities, among other issues. Organizers said those protests did what they were built to do – show that Americans would not quietly surrender their rights. And now, ahead of the midterms, they plan to direct this energy into casting ballots. “No Kings needs to be more than just getting people together every couple of months on a Saturday and marching,” said Hunter Dunn, an organizer with 50501, a decentralized anti-fascist protest network that is also part of the No Kings coalition. “The goal of it isn’t just to demonstrate people power. It’s to channel people power into something useful.” A large early vote turnout gives voters time to fix problems with registration and narrows the window for interference, organizers said. They worry that fears over Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), Customs and Border Protection (CBP), the FBI, or armed militants at the polls could intimidate voters or force voters to stay home. They want to make the results “simply too big to rig”, Dunn said. Leah Greenberg, an Indivisible co-founder, said the authoritarian playbook relies on creating “fear and uncertainty and confusion and chaos around the process of voting”, partly to manufacture grounds for contesting results later. Voting early interrupts that and “ensures that voting is a season rather than a single day”, she said. Voting as a collective activity At the heart of the thousands of events scheduled for Saturday is a goal to make voting a communal activity. That’s why the formats of Saturday’s events vary widely, from big-city rallies and concerts to festivals and block parties, voter registration tables and people lining long stretches of highway. In states where early voting will already be under way on Saturday – about half the US – Levin said local groups will hold get-out-the-vote kick-offs and knock on doors. Where it has yet to begin, some will throw superhero-themed parties built around the message that voting is a superpower. Others have registered “paws to the polls” events, walking their dogs to vote together. In the handful of states without in-person early voting – New Hampshire, Alabama and Mississippi – Greenberg said participants will focus on helping people make a plan for election day. Sarah Parker, a 50501 organizer in Florida, said small gatherings matter even in conservative places such as Sarasota, where rallies will be paired with virtual events and “education rallies” on why voting matters and how to become a poll monitor. “Even if you’re one or two people, you’re still creating change,” she said, noting that a passing driver might pull over and join. Poll walks, in which neighbors head to vote together, also serve a practical purpose amid rising threats at polling places. “Going as a group helps people be a lot more safe than going alone,” Dunn said. A response to redistricting The day of action is also a response to the fallout from the supreme court’s gutting of the Voting Rights Act in April. Soon after the decision, several Republican-led states moved to redraw congressional maps to favor the party, and in the process dilute Black voting power. Saturday’s flagship event, to be held in Atlanta, will highlight the effect of redistricting across the south. “Black voters are under attack,” said LaTosha Brown, co-founder of Black Voters Matter Fund, the organization hosting the flagship event, in a press briefing. She pointed to the FBI’s removal of about 650 boxes of 2020 election records from Fulton county, Georgia, in January, and a justice department push to obtain the names and home addresses of nearly 3,000 poll workers. “There is a full-fledged effort under way to steal this election,” she said. Damon Hewitt, president of the Lawyers’ Committee for Civil Rights Under Law, said his group is watching for last-minute voter purges, attempts to seize ballots or equipment after the election, and intimidation at polling places. Last month, the group was part of a suit that stopped a Trump executive order that would have restricted delivery of mail-in ballots. Also, in Atlanta, local 50501 organizers expect to train more than 400 poll monitors and election defenders to ensure smooth voting and counting processes for voters and local election officials. Preparing to take to the streets – again Saturday’s organizers are also recruiting election defenders – volunteers trained to respond if results are challenged. Greenberg said the coalition is preparing people “to mass-mobilize on a rapid-response basis, if necessary, to respond to election sabotage”. Levin pointed to Hungary, where he said Viktor Orbán lost power this spring after thousands of local groups drove turnout to record levels. “The thing you can do about it is ensure that the margins are just so big that it’s impossible to rig,” he said. Saturday will be judged on a single measure, Levin said. “Did we boost the early vote to the highest level it’s ever been in a midterm? Full stop. That is the question.”

title: Flash floods destroy villages in central Nepal
summary: Landslide blocks river and triggers downstream flooding, while summer temperatures persist in Portugal
text: Flash floods have swept through Nepal’s central Gorkha district after a pre-dawn landslide on 11 October blocked the Budhi Gandaki River, triggering severe downstream flooding. Two villages in the worst-affected Chumanubri rural municipality were reportedly destroyed, with homes, roads and bridges washed away. Part of a hydropower station was also damaged. After river levels surged from 2 metres to nearly 8.5 metres within hours, the national disaster risk reduction and management authority reported that 204 homes were damaged, and more than 650 people had been affected. More than 100 foreign trekkers were stranded in the popular hiking region. The floods come just two months after catastrophic flooding and landslides devastated parts of the country on the border with Tibet, leaving thousands dead or missing. An exceptionally deep area of low pressure barrelled towards Iceland this week. The central pressure was measured at 931mb on 14 October. The pressure plummeted by 49mb in 24 hours, meeting the thresholds for explosive cyclogenesis, or a weather bomb. The system brought sustained winds of 55–60mph to the southern shores of the island before moving north-east through the North Atlantic towards Norway. However, Iceland was spared the strongest winds as the track of the storm meant they remained out at sea. The system also affected areas beyond Iceland: a 108mph gust was recorded at Bealach Na Bà, in the Scottish Highlands, in association with a trailing 1,000-mile cold front that stretched from Norway to the mid-Atlantic. Summer-like conditions have extended even further into meteorological autumn in Portugal. After temperatures of 40C at the end of September, on 14 October a maximum of 35.6C was recorded in the southern town of Mora, representing a climatological anomaly of more than 10C. The heat was not localised, with numerous stations recording temperatures well into the mid-30s celsius. The latest forecasts show that the high pressure and unseasonably warm upper air temperatures will remain in place for the next few days. Looking further ahead, however, temperatures are expected to slowly return towards the average around the middle of next week.

title: Museum releases historical photos of island where Amelia Earhart may have crashed
summary: Images from New Zealand aerial survey of Nikumaroro in 1938 offer new clues over aviator’s disappearance
text: A New Zealand museum has released nearly 50 photos from a 1938 aerial survey of the island where Amelia Earhart is believed to have crash-landed, offering amateur sleuths new evidence to scour for traces of the pioneering aviator and her plane. The black-and-white images were published by the Air Force Museum of New Zealand after renewed interest in one of the biggest mysteries of the 20th century, spurred by a US expedition to the Pacific atoll of Nikumaroro in search of new clues. While some low-resolution copies have been uploaded on blogs, the Air Force Museum of New Zealand said it had received several requests for the photos and had released the full set of 47 images in digital high-resolution format on its website. The negatives were found more than a decade ago by Matthew O’Sullivan, the keeper of photographs at the museum in Christchurch. Earhart’s most prominent investigator, Ric Gillespie, described the images as a “goldmine” in his blog, saying they were a complete set of aerial photos taken on 1 December 1938 by an amphibious biplane during a New Zealand survey of Pacific islands that was looking for suitable airbase locations. What happened to Earhart and her navigator Fred Noonan when they disappeared on 2 July 1937 during an attempt to circumnavigate the globe at the equator has been a stop-and-start search over eight decades, filled with false leads. A leading theory is that the aviator, who broke several records including becoming the first woman to fly a nonstop solo trip across the Atlantic, ran out of fuel and was marooned on Nikumaroro, then known as Gardner Island. The hypothesis is that she survived for a while, drinking rainwater and eating fish and turtles, based on signs of a castaway’s campsite and artefacts, including glass from a jar that is thought to have contained cosmetic cream. This week, archaeologists and scientists from Earhart’s former benefactor, Purdue University in Indianapolis, are searching a part of the island for the “Taraia Object”, an elongated shape in a lagoon named after the part of the island where it was first noticed in a 2020 satellite image. Other longtime Earhart explorers, including Gillespie, are not convinced, saying it is probably a fallen tree and not the wreckage of her Lockheed Model 10-E Electra. The small atoll has been visited dozens of times. In their latest update on Nikumaroro, which is part of the archipelago country of Kiribati, the expedition said severe weather had hampered their metal-detecting but that they would release an update within 48 hours. “Despite Thursday’s weather delay, the expedition remains on schedule, with two more days of field operations planned – and an update on the identification of the Taraia Object expected,” Purdue University said. Rick Pettigrew, the expedition lead and executive director of the Archaeological Legacy Institute, said: “We understand the tremendous interest in what we’re doing at Nikumaroro, and we appreciate everyone’s patience. This is a complex scientific process. You don’t simply arrive at a site and immediately identify what’s there. We have to carefully collect the data, analyse it and reach sound conclusions.” The New Zealand military images are some of the earliest photographic evidence of the island. There is no immediate sign of an object in the Taraia area.

title: Trump calls Ukraine’s renewed strikes on Russian oil refineries ‘a disgrace’
summary: US president says Zelenskyy ‘more difficult ​to deal with ​than Putin’ after ‘energy ceasefire’ collapses
text: Donald Trump has called Ukraine’s renewed strikes on Russian oil refineries “a disgrace” and criticised Volodymyr ⁠Zelenskyy after an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine failed to take hold. Ukraine resumed strikes on Russian oil refineries ⁠after Zelenskyy said Kyiv was abandoning a ceasefire unilaterally declared by Trump on Sunday, having briefly halted its attacks to demonstrate its readiness for peace talks. Russia had continued its strikes on Ukrainian power plants. In an interview with Newsmax aired on Thursday, the US president said: “All he’s doing is making the world oil price higher. Well, I think that’s a disgrace. “There are a lot ‌of targets you can ‌hit, but when you shoot at diesel refineries where you make, you know, ‌diesel oil, and we need that, and the world needs that, then he’s not doing a good service for the world.” Relations between Kyiv and Washington have soured since Trump announced an easing sanctions on Russia in exchange for Moscow releasing large amounts of diesel on to global markets. Zelenskyy criticised the agreement, which was widely interpreted as an attempt to curb high fuel prices before the US midterm elections, saying it would allow Russia to press on with its full-scale invasion of Ukraine that began more than four and a half years ago. US efforts under Trump to end the war have made no progress. Trump repeated to Newsmax his views of the two leaders involved in the conflict. “I’m not a big fan of Zelenskyy,” Trump said. “I think they actually both would like to see it ⁠end, but I think I find Zelenskyy to be more difficult to deal with than Putin.” Arriving in Brussels to meet EU leaders on Friday, Zelenskyy did not comment on Trump’s latest remarks. He said he was “so thankful that we have such huge support from the EU” and its leaders, whom he described as “real leaders”. He went on to say that Ukraine wanted to end the war as quickly as possible, but “we don’t see now signals from [the] Russian side that they are ready for this”. Kyiv’s relationship with Washington was strained further this week when Ukraine said Starlink services had been restricted, in effect hobbling Ukrainian drone strike missions and crucial air defences with a flick of the switch. During a visit to London this week, the Ukrainian president said the sudden restriction of Starlink had left him feeling personally betrayed by Trump and lamented losing a partner. The British defence secretary, Wes Streeting, said on Thursday that his US counterpart, Pete Hegseth, had assured him in a face-to-face meeting that the vital satellite communications system had been restored. In an interview with the BBC, he said it was unclear what had caused the disruption, but added: “This is not the first time we’ve seen a falling out between Washington and Kyiv.” Amid growing doubts about long-term US commitment to Ukraine, European leaders declared their support for Zelenskyy. Standing alongside the Ukrainian leader in Brussels, the European Council president, António Costa, said Ukraine could “count on us not only to support you in war” but also in the path to negotiating EU membership. The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, said the EU had supported Trump’s energy ceasefire, “but we have seen that Russia did not respect it, not a single minute” and instead had escalated its attacks. She said the EU intended to increase pressure on Russia, promising a 22nd round of sanctions, adding: “We will not lift any sanctions unless Russia stops the war.” The promise of further European sanctions against Russia comes weeks after the EU lifted sanctions against two prominent Russian oligarchs at the request of France and Luxembourg. After meeting Zelenskyy, the French president, Emmanuel Macron, said it was “crucial” that Ukraine received “all the means necessary to protect itself”. The Polish prime minister, Donald Tusk, posted online: “I can reassure you, dear Ukrainian friends and President Zelenskyy: YOU ARE NOT ALONE.” As Zelenskyy met Macron in Brussels, he said that the Kremlin had “launched yet another vile drone strike on Ukrainian energy infrastructure” in the city of Lutsk, which caused blackouts. The Kremlin, meanwhile, accused Ukraine of derailing US peace efforts by resuming its strikes on refineries.

title: Trump wants more Afrikaner refugees while others are stuck due to his ‘cruel’ policies
summary: Thousands of vetted and approved refugees are suffering as Trump restricts quotas and prioritizes white South Africans
text: Donald Trump plans to once more severely restrict the number of refugees admitted to the US, announcing a limit of just 17,500 people in fiscal year 2027 – and that, again, those let in will be “primarily” white South Africans. Refugee rights groups are alarmed and infuriated at the decision last month by the US president to exclude almost every other demographic. They claim the decision will continue to leave thousands of refugees stuck in dangerous situations around the globe, many of whom were already vetted and approved for entry, in favor of a very small quota dominated by Afrikaners, an Afrikaans-speaking white ethnic group descended from Dutch and French colonial settlers to South Africa. This despite low take-up of US refugee slots by Afrikaners, prompting extraordinary measures from the government to attract them even in the face of apparent lack of interest, the Guardian revealed this week, and the greatness of need in other countries. During his first and second terms, Trump has signed various executive orders and his administration made significant policy decisions to halt nearly all refugee admissions, except for white South Africans. The refugee cap determination, published on 25 September, is just the latest move in undermining legal migration while also changing the demographics of who can come into the country. “What is lost is the focus on humanitarian need,” said Kennji Kizuka, the director of policy for the International Rescue Committee (IRC), a global humanitarian and non-governmental organization headquartered in New York, which works with refugees worldwide. “We built up over decades this humanitarian system that was meant to try to avoid politicized decisions around which kind of refugees to admit.” Some refugees slated to arrive to the US before Trump took office already “had travel plans that were canceled at the last minute”, Kizuka added. “They were ready to go and then everything was pulled out from underneath them.” The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) referred all questions to the state department. “President Trump has been very clear that we are prioritizing the resettlement of Afrikaners in South Africa who are escaping government-sponsored race-based discrimination, a US policy indicated in E.O. 14204,” a state department spokesperson said in a statement. In a statement, a White House spokesperson, Anna Kelly, said: “President Trump has provided a lifeline for Afrikaners, who are being raped, maimed, killed, and driven off their property across South Africa. “While the South African government and many in the media have brushed off the horrific lived experiences of this community, the Trump administration continues to process applications for refugee status because the president has a humanitarian heart,” Kelly added. For fiscal year 2026, which ended on 30 September, the Trump administration capped the refugee limit at 17,500. The US only accepted 16,292 refugees total during that time – nearly all were white Afrikaners, except for five from Afghanistan. The overall cap was 125,000 under Joe Biden. Trump and his allies have falsely claimed there is a “white genocide” against the white minority population, which led South Africa during the apartheid years. In February 2025, Trump signed an executive order claiming that Afrikaners are victims of “unjust racial discrimination”. There is no proof that there is a “white genocide” in South Africa and the new South African ambassador to the US, an Afrikaner himself, has also said the phenomenon does not exist. Groups in the US working with refugees view the administration’s moves as discriminatory. “Hundreds of thousands of refugees who are in the US refugee admissions program pipeline are impacted,” said Mevlüde Akay Alp, senior litigation attorney with the International Refugee Assistance Project (IRAP), a legal non-profit based in New York that advocates for the human rights of refugees and displaced people. “It’s particularly cruel to see the way in which the government has prioritized new white Afrikaners to the program without even considering these people who had gone through years of processing and had been promised safety here in the United States.” The refugee admission process can be excruciatingly long, with refugees required to undergo vetting, interviews and background checks – processes that can take years. Thousands of refugees were already in the queue to be admitted to the US when Trump halted the bulk of refugee arrivals but started rushing Afrikaners through. The US government said it will accept refugees on case-by-case exceptions, such as with the South Africans. But a lawsuit filed by IRAP last year, representing a number of refugees and refugee resettlement organizations, accuses the government of refusing to tell refugees and their attorneys what those exceptions would be and how a refugee could qualify. “Nobody else, including any of our plaintiffs, have any way of requesting an exception for themselves, no matter how dire their situation or how strong their connections to the United States are,” said Alp. An appeals court mostly sided with the Trump administration, but IRAP challenged that decision, bouncing the case back to a Washington state federal court. The legal battle continues. For many families, the administration’s decisions have been a devastating blow. Vartush and her family, who are being helped by IRC, are currently stuck in this limbo. Vartush, who requested that only her first name be used due to fear of jeopardizing her son’s refugee admission process, is a 70-year-old US citizen living in California. Vartush is an ethnic Armenian Christian, who was living in Iran with her family. She recounted how she and much of her family fled Iran and arrived in the US in 2009 under the refugee admissions program due to religious persecution. But delays and the lengthy refugee admission process kept her adult son in Iran. Finally in 2024, Vartush’s son and his fiancee were approved to take the next step in the refugee admission process. His fiancee went first and arrived in the US at the end of 2024. His trip was supposed to be next – he sold his belongings and prepared to leave, with IRC resettlement case managers requesting to expedite his case, citing his clinical depression. But then Trump came back into office and radically changed policy, halting the possibility for Vartush’s son to arrive in the US and be reunited with the rest of his family. “He suffers from depression,” Vartush said through an interpreter. “But obviously that got even worse.” The current US war in Iran has only deepened the family’s stress and deteriorated the son’s mental health. Vartush calls him daily to wake him up, she said. She said her son is despondent, with little hope of reuniting with his family as his case remains stuck. “The war itself brought a lot of anxiety,” Vartush said. “We have fear and anxiety, especially with his depression, I’m very worried that one day he might do something to himself.” Other people stuck in this limbo include some who are involved in the IRAP lawsuit against the administration. Their names have all been changed as part of the lawsuit, due to fear of jeopardizing their pending refugee case and, in some cases, for fear of violent retaliation by groups persecuting them. From Iraq: Sara and her son Sixty-year-old Sara and her 19-year-old son, who is disabled, are currently stuck in Jordan, despite being conditionally approved for US refugee resettlement, according to her court declaration. They desperately want to join Sara’s older son, now a US citizen who has been in Idaho since 2012 after arriving in the country as a refugee. In January 2025, Sara and her teenage son sold some of their items for the trip, began taking an American cultural orientation course and even purchased some baby clothes, as Sara’s son in Idaho is married and preparing to welcome his first child. “I wanted to make sure to be ready for the day that I received the call from the US government that we would travel to the United States,” Sara said in her court declaration. She and the son who is now in the US lived in Basra during the US war in Iraq, before her second son was born. As fighting near their home was intensifying, Sara’s husband dropped her and her son at her parents for their safety. But when he drove away, his car was bombed, killing him. Her brother-in-law, a member of an influential militia network, then demanded that she give him her house and custody of her son and fired a gun at her house, the court declaration says, and eventually Sara and the son fled to Jordan. In Jordan she gave birth to her younger son, who suffers from a birth defect in his brain. They have lived in Jordan for years and had applied for refugee status back in 2014, but Sara said they face discrimination and extortion in Jordan as Iraqi refugees. “I know that there are many other refugees prevented from traveling who are suffering through things that are even more difficult than my situation,” Sara wrote. From the Congo: Miriam’s 10-year-old son In the mid-2000s, Miriam and her family fled the Democratic Republic of the Congo after being persecuted by paramilitary groups, a filing by IRAP attorneys said. They arrived in a refugee camp in neighboring Burundi and spent nearly 15 years there. During that time, Miriam and her family were accepted to the US refugee admissions programs and began the lengthy process of vetting, background checks and interviews. Meanwhile, she gave birth to her youngest son. According to a court filing, Miriam was “erroneously” advised by staff at the UN that adding the baby to their family’s refugee application at that point would delay the process. In 2021, Miriam and her family finally received tickets to fly and settle in the US. But when they arrived at the plane, Miriam’s youngest son, who was five years old by then, was prevented from boarding. According to the court filing, his name was not listed on the flight manifest. Miriam had to leave her child behind and fly to the US with the rest of her family. The boy has remained without any relatives in the Burundi refugee camp. Miriam’s attorneys have been battling to bring him to the US, but the case has moved very slowly, partly due to delays caused by the first Trump administration’s anti-refugee policies, IRAP attorneys allege, and is stuck. “Miriam speaks to her son every day, often multiple times, so that he knows that she is thinking of him and feels emotionally supported,” the filing reads. “But the separation has caused Miriam and her son unbearable frustration and emotional pain. “Miriam believes the US government is purposely neglecting her and her family because they do not want her to be here and do not value her family in the same way that they value white Afrikaners, just because of her race,” the court filing reads. From El Salvador: Marcos’s stepdaughter Marcos, a 59-year-old Salvadorian man, has been in the US for more than 25 years and currently lives in California. For 10 years, he has been attempting to help his stepdaughter move to the US through the refugee program for Central American minors, according to his court declaration. In 2010, he met his wife, who is also from El Salvador. According to his court declaration, Marcos’s wife had to flee El Salvador and leave her daughter behind, because of domestic violence at the hands of her daughter’s biological father. Life has been difficult for his stepdaughter in El Salvador. When she was 12 or 13 years old, she had to abandon school for several years after being threatened by gangs – they tried to extort her family by threatening to hurt her unless her mother, already in the US, paid them, the lawsuit said. In 2016, Marcos began the refugee resettlement process for his stepdaughter. But the process stalled due to the first Trump administration’s limits to refugee admissions. Marcos restarted the process in 2022 and finally, in early 2025, Marcos was informed his stepdaughter could enter the US in February. “My wife and I started preparing for her arrival,” Marcos wrote in his declaration. “I started preparing her room in our home. I painted her room a dark pink color. “My wife also bought our daughter new clothes to wear. We also bought her a new computer so that she could be prepared for her studies here in the United States,” he added. But Trump suspended all refugee arrivals just before his stepdaughter’s arrival. Now, Marcos, his wife and his stepdaughter are in limbo, worried about her wellbeing and wondering whether she will ever be able to come to be with her mother.

title: Jenrick claims Farage has done more to stand against racism than ‘almost anybody’
summary: Reform MP defends leader after ITV footage shows official warning Farage he is ‘protecting’ candidate over racist David Lammy comments
text: Robert Jenrick has sought to defend Reform UK against fresh allegations that it hosts extremists by claiming that Nigel Farage has “probably done more than almost anybody to stand against racism and the far right”. The remarks came after Farage was berated by a Reform official for “protecting” a mayoral candidate who was accused of making racist remarks about the former Labour deputy prime minister David Lammy. The exchange emerged in an undercover investigation by ITV Exposure, which has also shown councillors and election candidates for Reform making threats of extreme violence and expressing racist, Islamophobic and misogynistic views. In the latest footage released by ITV, a senior Reform official is seen warning Farage that he was “protecting” a high-profile mayoral candidate accused of making racist comments about Lammy. Sarah Pochin, one of two female MPs for Reform, is also seen complaining that other party officials “are so fucking chauvinistic” and that “they just exclude you if you are a woman”. Jenrick, the party’s Treasury spokesperson and MP for Newark, told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme on Friday: “[Farage] is the most heavily scrutinised figure in British politics, and he’s someone who’s probably done more than almost anybody else to stand against racism and the far right, and to protect our politics from that over the course of my lifetime. “And this documentary failed to besmirch his character, which presumably was the ultimate objective.” Farage has made repeated promises over the last two years to rid Reform of “extremists” and “bigots” and introduce vetting. The party says it carries out vetting checks on everyone who wants to stand for election. However, the first clips from ITV’s year-long undercover investigation showed Alan Feeney, a Reform councillor and deputy mayor of Solihull, calling Asian homeowners “parasites”, and stating that “no more than 1% of [the] British population can be non-white”. Further footage released on Thursday shows Farage discussing the case of Chris Parry, a retired rear admiral picked to contest the Hampshire and the Solent mayoral election for the party. The party stood by Parry for months after it emerged he had said the former foreign secretary should “go home to the Caribbean” last year, and suggested that at least eight other politicians from minority ethnic backgrounds did not have a primary loyalty to the UK. Reform eventually suspended him in March after the Guardian revealed other remarks by Parry, but clips from the ITV documentary show Farage pushing back against senior advisers who said the candidate had to be sacked. They included Ed Sumner, Reform’s head of communications, who had told another press officer in an earlier discussion that Parry was “clearly a racist”. In a conversation between Farage and Sumner, which was recorded by the undercover reporter, the Reform leader said Parry “must apologise to Lammy” and was told that a text had been written for the candidate. “He must do it and move on … Tell him that from me,” Farage said, to which Sumner said: “You’re protecting him.” To laughter, Farage replied: “It’s showing a bit of … bit of sorrow. Look, ‘I’m sorry’ is probably a good thing to hear. Just take the fucking deal. Trouble is he’s a rear admiral. That’s the problem.” Jenrick defended Reform’s vetting policy. “In my experience, all political parties have bad apples. I mean, you can see that’s plain to see from the conduct of other political parties. In fact, Councillor Feeney, the one that you presented before I came online, was for a short time a Reform councillor, but for a much greater time a Conservative councillor.” He added: “We actually have very strong vetting, and we invest a huge amount in it, and it’s improving all the time. I don’t know what the vetting is like in every other political party. I can say in the Conservative party, because it was my former party, there is absolutely no vetting whatsoever by the central party for local councillors.”

title: Ofgem could force energy suppliers to pay rivals if they lure customers with cheaper deals
summary: Regulator for Great Britain weighs up reintroducing market stabilisation charge to prevent firms going bust
text: Energy suppliers could be forced to pay a charge to rivals if they lure customers with cheaper deals, as the industry regulator for Great Britain attempts to prevent suppliers going bust this winter. Ofgem has published a consultation on a proposal to reintroduce the market stabilisation charge (MSC), which aims to prevent suppliers failing if there is customer exodus, as it frets over the impact of sharp swings in energy prices linked to the conflict in the Middle East. The charge was last activated between April 2022 and March 2024, when Russia’s invasion of Ukraine sparked soaring wholesale prices that caused more than 30 energy companies to go bust. “We’re preparing for what is likely to be a difficult winter for many households,” said Neil Kenward, the interim director general of markets at Ofgem. “While the energy market is stronger than it was during the energy crisis, volatility remains and the market stabilisation charge helps to protect consumers from that volatility. “In volatile market conditions, it’s important that suppliers can continue to secure the energy their customers need without taking unsustainable risks.” Under the mechanism, the MSC would be triggered if wholesale prices fall more than 10%. At that point, suppliers who win customers by being able to then offer cheap deals would have to compensate rivals 85% of the drop in wholesale rates. “When wholesale prices fall sharply, suppliers that have bought energy in advance for customers on default tariffs can face losses if large numbers of customers switch to cheaper fixed deals,” Ofgem said. When Ofgem last activated the MSC in 2022 Martin Lewis, the founder of the consumer advice site MoneySavingExpert, swore at the regulator on a press call and said the mechanism sold consumers “down the river” because it would deter competition. He later posted an apology for his “emotional rant” on the social media platform X. Reacting to Ofgem’s consultation, Lewis said on Friday that consumers’ will not get as good deals if wholesale prices drop because the mechanism acts as a “switching penalty”. He added: “The new supplier can’t pass a chunk of the saving from lower wholesale rates on to you, because it has to hand much of it to your old supplier. The cheap fixes and switcher deals offered will be a lot more expensive, in order to protect energy firms’ profits. It ain’t good for consumers.” He questioned the need to reintroduce the mechanism, pointing out that many energy companies have made significant profits since last time it was triggered. “The supplier market is pretty stable, and I doubt we are at the domino risk of suppliers going bust in the way they did in the early 20s,” he said. “Protecting them over winter by effectively dampening competition … feels raw. I don’t like it.” Ofgem said that reactivating the MSC would not “automatically create charges or increase customer bills”. The consultation is seeking views on how the mechanism should operate, including trigger levels, notice periods and deactivation arrangements. “The MSC supports responsible energy purchasing and helps reduce the risk of instability in the market during periods of significant price volatility,” Kenward said. “By acting now, we can help maintain a stable and resilient energy market and protect consumers from the costs and disruption that can arise when markets become unstable.” Households are facing the highest energy charges in three years this winter after rising market wholesale prices pushed up the government’s price cap from this month. About 22m homes are paying the equivalent of £1,723 a year for typical gas and electricity usage between October and December, up from £1,663 for the July to September period. Ofgem’s quarterly energy price cap is forecast to climb by the equivalent of a further £149 a year in January, according to energy consultants at Cornwall Insight, which would put the average annual bill at £1,872. The chancellor, John Healey, is planning a major intervention to cut energy bills for poorer households in this month’s budget.
