title: Revealed: VW, Ford and Tesla batteries linked to destructive deforestation of indigenous lands
summary: Mines in supply chains of western carmakers linked to widespread deforestation of primary rainforest in nickel-rich lands inhabited by Tolaki people in Indonesia
text: Volkswagen, Ford and Tesla are among the electric carmakers whose batteries may contain nickel mined in indigenous woodlands plagued by deforestation, an analysis has found, highlighting the struggle to make vehicles that are free from environmental destruction. Corporate disclosures and trade flows from the last two years show mines in the battery supply chains of automotive giants are linked to the loss of trees in Sulawesi, a wildlife hotspot in Indonesia that houses the world’s largest nickel deposits. The metal is widely used in cathodes in car batteries because it boosts energy density and increases range. Ore from the Cahaya and Hengjaya mines was traced through regional smelters and Chinese processing plants run by Zhejiang Huayou Cobalt, a cathode manufacturer that supplies CATL, the world’s largest battery maker. Huayou’s corporate reports list US and European carmakers as end-users, while additional corporate files and trade data show a separate route from Huayou to LG, a South Korean group that also supplies battery products to leading carmakers, via Poland. Satellite analysis shows the mines have led to widespread deforestation of primary rainforest in nickel-rich lands inhabited by the indigenous Tolaki people. “We used to ask the forest for protection in return for our offerings,” said Wadimula, a Tolaki elder whose home sits on the edge of the 21,000-hectare Cahaya mining concession. “Destroying it means destroying our own life.” Electric vehicles are less environmentally harmful than fossil fuel-burning engines, which spew gases that foul the air and heat the planet, but western carmakers have struggled to clean up supply chains for batteries built with critical minerals from Africa, Asia and South America. Environmental groups warn that a failure to curb the boom of material-hungry SUVs is exacerbating the destruction by increasing the quantity mined. Ore from the two mining concessions is sent to a nickel smelter in an industrial complex in Morowali, on Indonesia’s eastern coast, operated by Huayou’s local subsidiary, where limonite is refined into mixed hydroxide precipitate, the primary raw material used to make battery cathodes. In 2024, $606m worth of mixed hydroxide precipitate was shipped from the Morowali plant to ports in China, followed by further shipments worth $470m in 2025. The processed ore was transported overland to Huayou cathode manufacturing sites in Quzhou, near Shanghai, and Yulin, near the border with Vietnam. Public filings do not disclose specific volumes or timings of sales from Huayou to CATL, which would be needed to directly connect specific ore shipments to car batteries, but Huayou confirmed group-level supplies to CATL in response to a regulatory inquiry by the Shanghai Stock Exchange in 2024. Chengdu B&M, a downstream subsidiary of Huayou, has also confirmed the supply of “large quantities” to CATL. The investigation, published in partnership with Voxeurop and other European media partners, traced shipments from mines and refineries in Sulawesi to China, and then again from Huayou cathode and CATL battery factories to the assembly lines of carmakers in the US and Europe. Volkswagen’s facility in Braunschweig, for instance, received a shipment in October 2024 of 24 tonnes of cell modules worth about $390,000, according to data from Volza, a trade platform. The shift to a carbon-free economy is pushing up demand for critical minerals in countries with weak environmental safeguards, though experts have argued the mining boom can be tempered without slowing the shift away from dirty fuels. In 2023, a report found lithium demand in the US transport sector could be reduced by 18% to 66% compared with a business-as-usual scenario, by improving public transport, walking and cycling more, and buying smaller cars. Better recycling could bring demand reductions as high as 92%, the report found. Global demand for nickel is set to double to 5.5m tonnes by 2040, according to the International Energy Agency, much of it mined in Indonesia and then refined in China. The loss of trees in mining concessions means the carbon footprint of nickel from the worst mines may be up to 500 times greater than previously reported, a study in Nature Communications found last year. The Cahaya and Hengjaya mines are located in woodlands designated as “production forest”, which are intended for forestry rather than industrial activities. However, successive Indonesian governments have weakened safeguards and carved out exemptions for miners as demand for nickel has soared. Nickel mining may be responsible for two-thirds of the forest loss recorded since 2001 within the area encompassed by the Cahaya concession, and over half of the loss in the Hengjaya concession, spatial analysis conducted by geospatial firm The TreeMap suggests. Sulawesi Cahaya Mineral (SCM), the company that operates the Cahaya mine, contributed to clearing an additional 330 hectares of forest in 2024, according to an analysis by Auriga, an Indonesian nonprofit. The same year, it delivered 11m tonnes of limonite ore – almost all of its production – to Huayou’s smelter. Deliveries increased to nearly 12.5m tonnes throughout 2025. The plant also continued to receive ore from the Hengjaya mine by road, local lorry drivers said. SCM received two administrative sanctions last year for illegally clearing more than 450 hectares of forest beyond the boundaries of its permitted clearing area. The company is a subsidiary of Merdeka Battery Materials, part of a group whose shareholders include Huayou and CATL. The carmakers identified as end-users of Huayou cathodes or recipients of shipments from CATL include Volkswagen, Volvo, Ford, General Motors, Tesla, BMW, Stellantis and Hyundai. Mercedes-Benz was separately linked to Huayou. Many of the companies said they did not source nickel directly, they assessed and mitigated adverse impacts, and they required suppliers to comply with responsible sourcing standards. They declined to share the results of on-site audits. Volkswagen, Europe’s leading manufacturer, which powered one-quarter of its vehicles with CATL systems in 2024, said it could not rule out that the companies may fall within its supply chain. Volkswagen said: “We take potential risks in our supply chain very seriously. However, due to contractual obligations with our business partners, we cannot disclose specific details on our supplier relationships or their supply chain.” Ford said: “We are committed to protecting human rights and the environment. We are reviewing the allegations and will determine any appropriate next steps based on that review.” Mercedes-Benz said: “We take reports of environmental and social harm in raw material supply chains – including nickel from Indonesia – seriously and assess them as part of our risk-based due diligence.” Renault Group said: “We have identified a nickel mining site in Sulawesi, Indonesia, as being a tier-n supplier (eg. indirect) in our battery supply chain. We have engaged with the relevant business partners to verify some ESG information concerning Sulawesi Cahaya Mineral.” Volvo Cars said: “During 2025, we conducted […] onsite audits […] on suppliers [who are] part of our battery supply chains, two of them located in Indonesia […] with further battery supply chain partners during 2026 and onward.” General Motors said: “We are aware that nickel mining in Indonesia presents significant environmental, human-rights and community-related risks.” Stellantis said: “We are aware of the environmental and social challenges associated with nickel production in Indonesia, including risks related to deforestation, biodiversity loss and ecosystem degradation.” Hyundai said: “We recognise the importance of protecting forests, biodiversity and local communities. We regularly monitor and assess our suppliers, including mineral suppliers, to ensure compliance.” CATL, Huayou, SCM and Tesla did not respond to requests for comment. Tsingshan, the main shareholder of Nickel Industries, which operates Hengjaya mine, did not respond to a request for comment. This investigation was supported by Journalismfund Europe and The Pulitzer Center. Lorenzo Di Stasi and James Jackson contributed reporting.

title: UK could quickly re-enter EU with ‘Switzerland plus’ deal, senior MEP says
summary: Bernd Lange, who was involved in Brexit talks, says deal could be negotiated within months of any decision to deepen ties
text: The UK could re-enter the EU in a “Switzerland plus” package that could be negotiated within months of any decision to deepen ties with the bloc, the head of a European parliament committee has said. Bernd Lange, who was heavily involved in Brexit negotiations, said: “I would love to see the UK back.” He said the EU missed the UK in decision-making because of its strong history of promoting open markets and democracy. A Swiss style arrangement is often considered a halfway house to full membership of the bloc but involves free movement and regulatory alignment. Switzerland is not a member of the EU but it struck a deal last year cementing its “frictionless access” to the single market across more than 100 agreements with a new framework deal. This gives it access to the EU’s electricity market, space programmes, Erasmus and the Digital Europe research programme, and participation in the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control. In exchange, Switzerland agreed to the free movement of people and to pay €375m (£326m) a year into the EU’s economic and cohesion funds. Lange, a German MEP who has an important role in the European legislative process as chair of the European parliament’s trade committee, said the Switzerland framework could be a model for the UK, but it was a “passive” agreement that would not involve the country in EU decision-making. “As a step by step [process], of course, there are a lot of possibilities, but I would love to have the UK come back also in the political decision-making process and politically be engaged. So we have the model of Switzerland … Switzerland plus, I would say, as that has some kinds of engagement but not the full membership.” He said the decision about what relationship the UK wanted with the EU was entirely “in the hands of the UK”, but if it opted for something like Switzerland plus, an agreement could be achieved quickly, notwithstanding political hiccups. He was speaking in London, where his schedule includes a meeting with the trade minister, Anas Sarwar, who is part of a team working on the UK’s new position on EU relations. Lange also threw his weight behind Andy Burnham’s call for the EU not to lock the UK out of Made in Europe legislation that would restrict UK suppliers from inclusion in public procurement tenders as well as some corporate contracts such as car fleets. French and German leaders were reportedly close on Thursday to agreeing a proposal that the UK could be included, provided it aligned with the EU’s 2024 tariffs on imports of Chinese electric vehicles. This week the boss of Mercedes said the EU would be making a “deliberate choice” to harm the EU car industry if it did not allow the UK into the Made in Europe package. Burnham has backing from the Netherlands, Germany and Italy. France, which came up with the legislative proposals, was opposed, saying it needed to get the legislation on the books urgently to guard against cheap competition from China, and that allowing the UK and other allied countries in could hold up the lawmaking. Lange said the UK should “of course” be included because it was already aligned with the EU on environmental standards and employment laws. He said France’s position was “not rational” and “also so emotional” but could be born from the desire to be seen as putting France first before next April’s presidential elections, in which Marine Le Pen, who is opposed to globalism, could take power. Locking the UK out of Made in Europe could also cause a legal dispute over the trade and cooperation agreement that allows UK goods to be sold in the single market without barriers as long as they the meet the bloc’s standards. The Made in Europe package, or the Industrial Accelerator Act, is expected to get political approval by the end of the year or early 2027, meaning Burnham does not have much time to get clauses inserted designating the UK as European for the purposes of the legislation. But Lange said there could be time after that, given the processes of the European parliament, where three committees have scrutinising powers. “There are 5,100 amendments,” he said, referring to the protracted process ahead, including one on UK inclusion.

title: Four years after the promises of Cop15, our biodiversity targets are slipping away
summary: ​The world pledged to halt biodiversity loss by 2030, but as Cop17 delegates meet in Armenia next week the outlook is bleak and optimism has faded
text: The world has lost its way on nature once again. Next week, biodiversity Cop17 begins in Yerevan, Armenia, and expectations are low. Very low. Almost four years ago, governments reached an historic agreement at the biodiversity Cop15 to halt the destruction of Earth’s ecosystems – to rapturous applause in Montreal, Canada. I still remember the excitement in the hall in the early hours of that freezing December morning. Governments had never met a self-mandated target on biodiversity loss, but there was a sense after the Covid-19 pandemic that this time really would be different. The 23-point deal included targets to protect 30% of the planet for nature, restore 30% of the planet’s degraded terrestrial, inland water, coastal and marine ecosystems, and tackle $500bn of environmentally damaging subsidies. Almost every country in the world, apart from the US and the Vatican, backed it. Yes, the agreement was flawed, and barely matched what the science tells us we need to do to stop biodiversity loss. But it was a serious, considered plan to tackle the underlying causes of the largest loss of life since the dinosaurs (this time, humans are the asteroid). Since then, though, action has fallen short. More on why that is, what it means and what is at stake at Cop17, after this week’s climate headlines. Essential reads A perfect storm: how the super El Niño is devastating the fishing industry ‘We need less point scoring’: What party conference season taught us about UK climate action ‘I didn’t want to write about this’: the man who first saw chimps waging civil war In focus The summit in Yerevan is about assessing progress towards the targets, and the scorecard does not look good. In preparatory meetings governments have acknowledged (pdf) that they are way off track from meeting any of the targets. The traffic-light system used to rate actions towards the targets from countries is awash with yellow, orange and red. “Unless collective implementation accelerates rapidly, the 2030 targets and mission will not be achieved,” the pre-Cop17 report reads. “Parties and other actors have taken action to address all 23 targets; however, no target presents a fully positive picture. The available evidence indicates that there are gaps in the collective progress. Without urgently addressing these gaps and barriers, it will not be possible to meet the 2030 targets and mission, in turn placing achievement of the 2050 goals and vision [to live in harmony with nature] in jeopardy.” This time, it is hard to be too angry with some governments. Countries including Kazakhstan have used the agreement to drive a major rewilding effort, bringing back the caspian tiger. The EU did attempt to enact the targets with the nature restoration law – but it quickly became a culture-wars issue. Swathes of the world, though, have turned against action on the environment. Donald Trump’s return to the White House has been catastrophic for the conservation sector, caught in his administration clampdown on the climate and “woke” policies. Through USAID and partner organisations, the US government provided, on average, 12.1% of the world’s biodiversity funding between 2015 and 2022, according to the OECD. Almost all of that has gone, hitting everything from anti-rhino poaching initiatives in east Africa, to efforts to combat illegal fishing in the Galápagos. Power has also drained out of multilateral organisations such as the UN. Tech billionaires and the architects of AI are more powerful than many countries. Trump’s second term has seen a return to might-is-right politics that is dismissive of the international cooperation needed to make an agreement like this a reality. So what next? Cop17 in Armenia is likely to be a moment where the calamity of the last four years crystallises – and governments must try to pick up the pieces. “There’s a massive gap between countries agreeing to do something and actually doing it,” says Zac Goldsmith, who was UK environment minister when that landmark Cop15 deal was reached in 2022. “That’s where we are today.” Read more: • More than half of countries are ignoring biodiversity pledges – analysis • We launched a war on nature. Now we are in a climate war zone | Rebecca Solnit • ‘We can’t make it better again’: what Europe’s wildfires tell us about the climate crisis • To read the complete version of this newsletter – subscribe to receive Down to Earth in your inbox every Thursday.

title: Friday briefing: How Manchester City’s ​financial scandal could upend the whole football league
summary: In today’s newsletter: Manchester City’s disgrace reaches far beyond sport, exposing not just a crisis in football but also raising questions about foreign owned British institutions
text: Good morning. It’s a sporting scandal of colossal proportions, with the juiciest details still to come. Manchester City’s ascent from mediocre to majestic changed the landscape of British football. Now, that pace looks set to be matched by a sudden, plummeting fall. The club has been found guilty of breaching football finance rules to the tune of hundreds of millions of pounds, with ramifications poised to spill far beyond Manchester (the club denies the allegations, and says it will appeal). Foreign state ownership makes this an international relations issue, not just a sporting one. The prime minister has been dragged into the sleaze-fest, and the stream of stories shows no sign of slowing. Meanwhile, the Mancunian club has the chutzpah to sit at the top of the Premier League, much to the repulsion of my Manchester United-supporting boyfriend. With the help of Guardian football writer Jonathan Wilson, today’s First Edition delivers everything you need to know about the crisis engulfing the beautiful game, and believe me, this one’s not just for the footie fans. That’s after the headlines. Five big stories Ukraine | Wes Streeting urged the US to stand by Ukraine on his visit to the American capital and sought to cool tensions between the two countries in the wake of the Starlink row that is threatening to set back Kyiv’s war effort. UK news | Jeffrey Donaldson has been sentenced to 15 years for sexual offences against two women who were children when he abused them, completing what was described as a “catastrophic descent into disgrace”. Hacking | An Israeli advertising agency has been serving millions of online adverts that allow “zero-click” spyware to be used against targets, researchers at a Canadian university have said. UK news | A woman has alleged Russell Brand told her “it’s just fun” as he raped her in a hotel room at the 1999 Labour party conference, a court has heard. US news | Donald Trump has shelved a widely condemned plan to livestream the execution of a disabled man by firing squad. In depth: ‘There was a sense that the panel felt lied to by City’ To some (Manchester City fans, mostly), it was a sporting success story for the ages. After decades of underachievement, a middle-of-the-road club transformed into England’s best performing – and top title-winning – team. Others grumbled that City’s success was a sad indictment of the state of modern football. The club’s change in fortunes came shortly after they were bought by the Abu Dhabi United Group, a private equity group owned by the Gulf state’s vice president. Billionaires had already gutted the topflight of its heart, now governments with entire GDPs to burn had descended. Except, of course, the cash injection at Manchester City breached strict Premier League limits. Financial fair play rules, introduced by the league in 2013, aimed to keep a lid on spending so that clubs – financed by, say, a fossil-fuel rich state – couldn’t simply spend billions for immediate dominance. Only, that’s precisely what Manchester City did. According to an independent panel, they secretly boosted their income by a staggering £900m between 2009 and 2018. When he first flicked through the panel’s 40-page verdict summary, Wilson was surprised by the “incredibly strong language it used for a dry legal document”. The word “sham” is repeated eight times. “There was a clear sense that the panel felt systematically lied to by City,” says Wilson. The real spice is likely to come in the yet-to-be-published appendices to the verdict, which will probably contain names, companies and detailed figures. These recent revelations didn’t come out of nowhere. Back in November 2018, German newspaper Der Spiegel published a four-part series on Manchester City (“Bending the Rules to the Tune of Millions” was the first headline). The paper’s bombshell reporting was based on data released in The Football Leaks, a website containing millions of documents on allegedly murky financial transactions in the sport, made public by Portuguese whistleblower (and convicted hacker) Rui Pinto. UEFA conducted an investigation, and in 2020 found the club guilty, though the punishments (a two-year ban from European competitions and a €30m fine) were watered down on appeal. Meanwhile, Manchester City kept on winning. “There was wide recognition that Manchester City had gotten away with it by dragging out the process,” Wilson tells me – the Court of Arbitration for Sport found the club showed a “blatant disregard” to Uefa’s investigation. “There was a sense then that football could not really handle situations like these,” Wilson says. Then, last month, the Premier League announcement came: Manchester City was guilty of 114 charges. It’s understood these offences correlate to information already in the public domain: that Manchester City inflated the value of sponsorship deals to channel extra cash into the club; that secret payments were made to senior club figures and player agents. These were a contravention of financial rules, and the club “made concerted efforts to stop and frustrate” Premier League investigations. The club has maintained its innocence, and intends to appeal. *** A sizeable punishment? Even allowing time for Manchester City to appeal, a sanction decision is expected around Christmas. Fines, point-docking, transfer bans, suspension and expulsion are all being discussed, though Premier League rules dictate there’s no limit to the penalties that could be dished out. The sheer scale of the rule-breaking means there’s little precedent for comparison. Everton were docked six points for a £20 million rule breach. Apply the same metrics, and Manchester City would lose hundreds. Knocking that much off their tally in a single season is “functionally identical” to a much softer sentence, says Wilson. (Points reset every season, and last year, league-toppers Arsenal finished on just 85.) “It leads to the conclusion that expulsion from the Premier League might be the only logical outcome,” says Wilson. He’d also like them stripped of their titles, and to see an investigation launched immediately into the club’s finances from 2018 until now. Expulsion would be complicated. The complex structure of English football means if Manchester City did get booted out of the Premier League, there’s no guarantee the club would find a place in a lower league. And, even if it’s recommended by the panel, Premier League clubs would need to vote it through on a two-thirds majority. “That vote is unpredictable, as some club owners have business ties in Abu Dhabi or fear setting a precedent where clubs can vote out rivals,” says Wilson. *** How worried should Man City be? Off the pitch, there’s the prospect of civil litigation lingering too: Liverpool, Arsenal, Manchester United and Tottenham Hotspur each submitted formal legal notices before a September 2024 deadline, which reserves them the right to claim compensation for losses caused by City’s rule breaches. When Everton breached financial rules in the 2021/22 season Burnley successfully claimed close to £40m from the Merseyside club. The sums at stake in this instance could be eye-watering. Plus there’s the prospect of possible criminal proceedings. Tom Forster KC, a financial crime barrister, suggested that Manchester City “has a great deal to be worried about on this front”. Then there’s the political fallout, which is still taking shape. Andy Burnham was mayor of Greater Manchester through this period, a time during which Abu Dhabi made serious investments in the city. “That can be viewed either as benevolent community building or as a calculated investment, expecting returns and local influence,” says Wilson. Either way, it’s not ideal for the new prime minister. Plus, Burnham’s initial response to the judgment raised eyebrows, saying he’d be “really concerned” if the owners were forced to sell. “His skepticism of the charges sounded like comments from a fan on a message board rather than a measured politician,” says Wilson. Clarifications from Number 10 soon followed, and Burnham committed to publishing details of his dealings with Manchester City. Yesterday, he requested a “manual trawl” of records from his time as Greater Manchester Mayor, after two hospitality dinners with Manchester City’s chair were found to be absent from the combined authority’s digital register. *** What does this mean for English football? The ramifications for English football are clear. The Premier League faces a massive problem: the success of its top side is built on foul play. And not just between 2009 and 2018, Wilson reckons. “Even if we assume City complied cleanly after the leaks emerged, their success since remains predicated on that unfair advantage. That’s a lot of titles – and a lot of prize money – won under compromised conditions. As it stands, this is “hugely damaging” to the Premier League’s reputation and fan trust, Wilson says. Football is the UK’s most popular sport, and is worth billions to the economy. If faith is lost in the sport, that’s a real problem. On the other hand, football is just a ballgame without the drama, spectacle and narrative – to which this debacle adds plenty. Especially, Wilson says, “if the outcome demonstrates that the Premier League is willing to enforce its regulations against even its most dominant team.” But there’s a story much bigger than football here. Manchester City (and Saudi Arabia’s Newcastle United for that matter) aren’t the only British institutions quasi-owned by foreign governments. Qatar, Saudi and China own the bulk of Heathrow Airport; through state-owned EDF, France claims significant chunks of UK energy infrastructure. Royal Mail, meanwhile, is owned by a Czech billionaire; more than 70% of the English water industry is in foreign ownership. “This case illustrates the extent of foreign state influence over major British institutions,” says Wilson, “tracing back to New Labour policies that encouraged foreign state investment without sufficient safeguards against geopolitical manipulation.” But, if the Premier League holds course, its response could be just as symbolic. “In a broader societal landscape where massive wealth often overrides accountability, this would represent a major British institution taking a stand to enforce rule of law and regulatory compliance.” What else we’ve been enjoying I enjoyed Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett’s column on the return of Girls, and what it could look like now its protagonists are more women than girls them. Poppy Noor, newsletters team I don’t get a chance to dance these days. So I found Lyndsey Winship’s piece on which music is the best to get down to both absolutely fascinating and a potent reminder to get myself ‘out out’. Lucinda Everett, newsletters team If you’ve used the term “greedflation” you’re borrowing a term from Isabella Weber, who is quickly becoming one of the most sought-after economists of her generation. Our own Michael Segalov interviewed her, and the piece out this morning provides a rare bit of hope. Poppy Maya Yang’s report about a loophole that lets private firms catch protected sand tiger sharks in the US and sell them to foreign aquariums is a shocking but important read. Lucinda I thought Zoe Williams was superb on Sally Rooney’s courage and humanity. Poppy Sport Football | Brazilians Evanilson and Rayan scored as Bournemouth eased to a 3-0 win over Sturm Graz of Austria in their first-ever home European tie; Sunderland came from behind to beat Torreense 2-1; Crystal Palace and Celtic both defeated. title: Like dinosaur eggs in the sand: the pterosaur museum built to thrive in the Gobi desert
summary: How architects worked with harsh environment to create sustainable building in location where fossils were found
text: Viewed from afar, the silver-hued Hami Pterosaur Museum almost looks like a space base on Mars. Viewed from above, it resembles a collection of dinosaur eggs in the sand. Nestled in the Gobi desert, in north-west China, the new tourist attraction showcases hundreds of impressive fossils of pterosaurs, ancient flying reptiles related to dinosaurs. But far from reflecting its prehistoric exhibits, the building itself is a modern-day architectural specimen. Designed with underground exhibition halls, giant light funnels and sprawling solar farms, the museum is able to operate sustainably while withstanding an extremely harsh environment. The Hami region is notorious for its scorching summers. Air temperatures can exceed 55C (131F), while the surface ground temperature can reach 80C, says Wang Xiaolin, the director of the museum and a palaeontologist at the Chinese Academy of Sciences. Violent winds and sandstorms terrorise the area frequently, according to Xiaolin, who has carried out excavation work in Hami for 20 years. Despite the intimidating conditions, building the museum in the area is important from a scientific perspective because this is where the fossils were buried and found, Xiaolin says. Keeping the fossils local protects the fragile relics and lets visitors see them in their geological context, he adds. Visitors to the five exhibition halls can expect to see precious fossils discovered by Xiaolin’s team, including one that has preserved the upper and lower jaws, as well as the soft-tissue structures of the head crest of a pterosaur that roamed the area roughly 130m years ago. Most of the 8,000-sq metre museum is built 8 metres into the ground where temperatures are much lower, which helps it stay cool in summer, says Huai Kaifeng, an architect at Beijing-based Turenscape, which designed the project. In winter, when temperatures can drop below -20C, the design also helps the museum stay warm. Being largely underground, with seven above-ground entrances, allows the museum to use its energy as efficiently as possible, says Wang Yujia, a landscape architect and associate professor at the University of Nebraska–Lincoln in the US, who is not involved in the project. Most of it is able to avoid direct exposure to wind, sand and solar heat and the large temperature swings between day and night in the desert. “This all means that you need much, much less air-conditioning,” Yujia says. Although air-conditioners have been installed to provide backup, the museum has natural ventilation shafts that allow cool air to sink and hot air to rise and escape. The museum can cut its electricity usage on air conditioning by 94% compared with an above-ground counterpart, according to estimates by Turenscape. This equates to a saving of 223,421kWh of electricity annually – enough to power an average UK home for 89 years. But the underground space in the desert presented another challenge for the architects: lighting. The team used giant, translucent, ceiling-to-floor funnels to let in as much natural light as possible. These structures slash the museum’s need for artificial lighting by nearly 50%, saving 84,672kWh of electricity a year, according to Turenscape. The museum was one of the last designs completed by the late Chinese landscape architect Kongjian Yu, the founder of Turenscape. Yu was the brain behind China’s “sponge cities”, a concept that uses nature to prevent flooding in urban areas. The museum has its own micro power grid, featuring a solar farm and batteries to store energy. The solar farm is about 1km from the museum, with an outline resembling that of a pterosaur when viewed from above. It is expected to generate more than 22.4GWh of electricity a year, enough to meet the museum’s own demand, Huai says. The museum is still connected to the power grid of the nearby city of Hami to ensure its energy security, he notes. The museum is also connected to Hami’s water-supplying network, but it has a recycling system on site to collect, process and reuse its grey water. “Water is precious out here in the Gobi,” Xiaolin says. For Yujia, the museum is a good example of how a building can be designed to adapt to its natural environment rather than fight against it. Although technology enables people to build luxury resorts in a desert and keep them cool, such projects require huge amounts of energy and resources, he says. “It makes sense to work as much as possible with the environmental conditions that are already there, instead of relying entirely on technology to isolate the building from them.” Examples include a floating exhibition pavilion built in Rotterdam to address rising sea levels, and a giant park with a tilted ground in Bangkok that aims to prevent urban flooding, and a home shaped like a snail’s shell in Iran to help its inhabitants stay cool. The concept is important for arid areas. “These places are not cities, you don’t necessarily have the basic infrastructure or the resources you desire even if you pay, because money is not magic,” Yujia adds. Designing buildings and parks to combat natural disasters was a lasting theme throughout Yu’s career, and for Jiinyi Hwang, the chief architect at Turenscape, the museum is no exception. “Our world is drying. Deserts and arid zones are expanding. Cities are warming. More and more of the built environment is being pushed into climates that were once considered unbuildable,” Hwang says. “If we keep designing with the same assumptions – sealed boxes, glass facades and mechanical climate control – we will consume the very resources these landscapes cannot spare.”

title: Commercial kitchen staff exposed to high levels of air pollution, study finds
summary: US research says nitrogen dioxide in restaurants that cook with gas can exceed WHO limits, which also affects diners
text: Each time we enjoy a meal out or order a takeaway, someone cooks for us in a commercial kitchen. In the UK, 3.6 million people work in catering and hospitality. In the US it is estimated at close to 16 million. A first-of-its-kind study in the US has found catering staff can experience high air pollution at work – and that this can affect diners too. Dr Drew Michanowicz, senior author of the study at non-profit research institute PSE Healthy Energy, said: “I was motivated by what we have learned over the years about what just 30 minutes of gas cooking can do to air quality in homes with the realisation that millions of people cook for a living for hours on end.” The researchers measured air pollution in 27 kitchens including fine-dining and casual full-service restaurants, those serving pizza and Chinese cuisine, catering facilities and kitchens in senior-living communities, universities and schools. Although the kitchens met US legal limits for air pollution in workplaces, nitrogen dioxide in 17 kitchens was greater than the World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines for indoor air. All of these kitchens cooked with fossil-gas or propane. Nitrogen dioxide is a pollutant in diesel exhaust, which has led to many UK and European cities introducing clean air and low-emission zones. Three all-electric kitchens, a full-service restaurant, a school cafeteria, and a conference centre kitchen were part of the study. These had the lowest air pollution, indicating benefits from decarbonisation in catering and ending fossil-gas combustion. The electric kitchens also had the lowest temperatures, an obvious benefit for staff welfare. This summer’s European heatwave forced some restaurants in the UK to cut hours or close due sweltering conditions. Christopher Galarza, a chef who worked with the researchers, said: “I’ve worked in kitchens where the heat was so intense that you would finish a shift drenched in sweat, dehydrated and physically spent.” The study also found air pollution did not stay in the kitchen. Median concentrations in dining areas were greater than WHO guidelines for outdoor air pollution. Dr Yannai Kashtan, first author of the study from PSE Heathy Energy, said: “It is difficult to contextualise the relative risk to diners, but as a diner in a restaurant with gas-fired appliances you may be exposed to elevated levels of nitrogen dioxide.” One result surprised the research team. Kashtan said: “In two-thirds of the gas kitchens, we measured higher levels of pollution overnight and in the early morning, when all the appliances were off. The culprit? Pilot lights that burn 24/7, whether or not ventilation is on.” In the UK many commercial kitchens have automatic systems that cut off gas when ventilation is not operating. Michanowicz said commercial-grade cooking appliances were not included in US energy efficiency regulations that led to pilot lights being phased out in the residential sector. “In most full-service kitchens with multiple appliances like ranges, griddles, fryers, ovens, steamers, and broilers, upwards of 20-30 small flames may be constantly burning,” said Michanowicz. In the study, air pollution from pilot lights spread into dining areas, increasing exposure for cleaners and other workers and the health risk for other people in multi-use buildings.

title: Repairing Brexit economic damage should be Burnham’s top priority, business chief says
summary: Shevaun Haviland argues PM is right to revisit Labour’s EU red lines as current trading relationship is bad for business
text: Repairing the economic damage of Brexit should be the top priority for Andy Burnham as he reconsiders Labour’s red lines on EU membership, the head of one of Britain’s leading business groups has said. Shevaun Haviland, the director general of the British Chambers of Commerce (BCC), said she welcomed the prime minister reopening the Brexit battle lines despite the uncertainty it could create, arguing that the UK’s current trading relationship with the EU was bad for business. “We do think it’s right, because of what we know from the evidence of how businesses feel it’s not working,” she said. Highlighting the continuing economic hit from Brexit, Haviland said more than half of bosses surveyed by the business lobby group believed the deal negotiated by Boris Johnson’s government and enacted in 2021 was not helping them. “We expected it to be very difficult at the beginning, when [companies] were getting used to the new rules, and then it would sort of get easier as it went to along. But actually, that has not happened,” she said. Economists estimate the cost to the UK economy has been up to £240bn so far, with national income per head between 6% and 8% lower than it would have been had the UK not left the EU. The Office for Budget Responsibility estimates a long-term hit of about 4% of gross domestic product. At Labour’s conference in Liverpool last month, Burnham said Brexit had done “more harm than good” as he pledged to reassess Britain’s relationship with the EU. He opened the door to options including fully rejoining the bloc, and this week he said failing to pursue a better deal with the EU would be a “major dereliction of duty”. In an interview with the Guardian in Norwich alongside the head of the Norfolk Chambers of Commerce (NCC) chief executive, Nova Fairbanks, Haviland said the government had to take into account business frustrations with Brexit. She said the BCC would also consult its 50,000 members, who collectively employ more than 6 million people across the UK, on a range of options for Britain’s relationship, including rejoining the EU. “We are 10 years since the referendum,” Haviland said. “We would say the language of Brexit needs to move on. That’s gone. What businesses understand is what we had before and what we’ve got now. “We’re apolitical, it’s not a political question. It is an economic question. So we are going to set out the options, from the where we are to the most extreme. And in consultation with our chambers, and our partners, we will see where people are.” Fairbanks said it was clear that some Brexit-backing bosses recognised the economic damage. “It would be very interesting to see how many businesses that were very much pro-Brexit are still pro-Brexit, because I’ve certainly not heard any change of heart from those that were against Brexit. I think they are still very much: ‘We need to be closer to Europe.’” Speaking on the sidelines of an NCC trade fair at the Norfolk Showground, the business leaders said companies were coming under growing pressure from rising energy prices and other effects of the war in the Middle East. Haviland called on the chancellor, John Healey, to take bold action at this month’s budget to support firms despite concerns at the heart of government about the pressure on the public finances amid jitters in the bond market. “This rumour about a sort of ‘steady as she goes’ budget, and ‘let’s not upset the apple cart’. Business don’t really want just a ‘steady as she goes’. They want to see some action that will relieve some of those costs that will drive that fly wheel [of the British economy],” she said. “You can’t just trot along in a crouch position effectively. And surely the markets will be happy to see some spending cuts by the government, and some investment in private-sector growth?” Haviland called for action on energy bills, business rates and taxes on employment to help companies recruit more young people. “In your energy bill, about 40% of your energy is actually energy. The other 60% is about tax. So the government can get some of that out,” she said. “The big test for the chancellor is to put his money where his mouth is for business at the budget. Just showing that he genuinely believes that the wealth creators are the job creators – which is business.”

title: Country diary: A three-day perambulation around my own parish | Simon Lockett
summary: Golden Valley, Herefordshire: Even vicars can get stuck too much behind a desk, and the 800th anniversary of St Francis of Assisi’s death is a good excuse to strike out, and speak to local people
text: I was sitting at my desk again, with the dull hum and the blue glow of the screen. It seems that every occupation traps people at their desk, and being a vicar is no different. But I wanted to resist, and it happened to be the 800th anniversary of Saint Francis of Assisi’s death. With Jesus of Galilee as inspiration, Saint Francis was known for his vow of simplicity, his love of the Earth and his critique of the wealth accumulated by the religious elite at the expense of the poor. He was also horrified by the Fifth Crusade, so he travelled to Egypt, hoping to make peace. Francis also walked the walk, as it were, sleeping in caves in the Umbrian hills, taking nothing with him. No sitting at the desk for Francis. So I decided to do the same, spending three days walking the bridleways, holloways, footpaths and country lanes of the Golden Valley, speaking to people along the way. My sanctuary for the night was one of my parish churches – Madley, Tyberton, then Peterchurch, with its very welcome underfloor heating. The conversations were rich. People love Saint Francis because of his love of animals. Some found his actions, such as disrobing before a bishop – a sign of his rejection of church corruption – “extreme”. Thomas, a young farmer, challenged me when I said Francis’s rejection of wealth inspired me. Thomas spoke of the importance of “the posture of the heart” towards wealth – that riches can be used for good. The children in the primary school loved the story of Francis taming a wolf. But the conversation that stayed with me most took place looking over the valley, with Bill, a businessman out walking his dog. We chatted about Saint Francis, and he bemoaned the culture that was taking hold in his business. His wish was for a Franciscan simplicity. Instead of a company that cherished belonging, community and purpose, one that was relational and people-oriented, it had become full of policies, programmes and technique. Simplicity had given way to complexity. I walked on through an oak wood, buzzards mewing overhead, a complexity of relationships that had led to simplicity. Ecology and Saint Francis have much to teach us. • Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024, is available now at guardianbookshop.com
