title: France drops opposition to UK being included in ‘Made in Europe’ legislation
summary: British government must however align with the European Union’s position over tariffs on Chinese EVs
text: France has dropped its opposition to the UK being included in the EU’s “Made in Europe” legislation as long as the British government aligns with the bloc’s position over tariffs on Chinese EVs. In a breakthrough for Andy Burnham, France on Thursday came round to backing Germany, which has always supported the UK’s calls to be designated European for the purposes of the Industrial Accelerator Act. The legislation, which is in its draft stage, is designed to protect domestic manufacturing from cheap Chinese competition. According to a joint Franco-German paper seen by the Guardian, the two countries are now proposing that for the car industry specifically the UK could be included in Made in Europe. “For the automotive sector, ‘Made in Europe’ should comprise the EU27 and an opt-in to further include European partners who were part of the EU single market as of 01/01/2020, subject to an agreement on full reciprocity – i.e. adopting the European preference scheme relevant to the automotive sector,” it says in a clear reference to the UK, which was still in the single market as an EU member in January 2020. It would also include Norway, which is in the single market but not a member of the EU. The paper added that the opt-in would come with conditions, including alignment on trade defence measures, which have included tariffs on Chinese EVs imposed by the EU in 2024 and any future trade barriers, such as the quota deal being finalised with China on its exports of hybrid cars. The paper says that “as well as relevant anti-circumvention measures”, these “opt-in” countries would have to accept “dynamic alignment on the EU’s conditions related to third countries’ investments and on relevant EU trade defence measures”. Liam Byrne, the chair of the UK’s business, innovation, science and trade committee, said he believed aligning with the EU on trade defence measures was a small price to pay to save British manufacturing. “Sometimes politics is the least worst choice – aligning with Europe on trade defence against an over-subsidised China is the way we deliver for all of us,” he said. “Tariffs on these would be a small price to pay for the protection of a European manufacturing industry which safeguards jobs across supply chains in the UK and makes us less prone to coercion from China in the future.” On Wednesday the head of Mercedes implored EU leaders to let the UK join the package. Locking the UK out of the EU’s flagship industrial Made in Europe legislation would amount to a “deliberate choice” by EU leaders to “hurt” the car industry across the bloc, the head of Mercedes-Benz said. The UK has been under pressure for weeks to align with the EU on tariffs on Chinese vehicles, but this week the business secretary Jonathan Reynolds said he would not be coerced into aligning with the EU’s policy. However the government has been desperate to be included in the Made in Europe package, fearing billions of pounds of trade in the car industry could be lost if the UK was locked out of supply chains in the EU. Earlier on Thursday trade minister Anas Sarwar hinted that the UK was minded to align on tariffs. He told Politico the UK and the EU must “work together and act in lockstep” to tackle China’s dominance in the automotive sector. Bernd Lange, the chair of the European parliament’s influential international trade committee, told the Guardian the UK should “of course” be included in the Made in Europe legislation, calling France’s opposition “not rational”. A Downing Street spokesperson said it had yet to see the detail but saw the development as positive. “This is a Franco-German proposal and there is still a European process to run, but if confirmed, we welcome the objective to have UK included in the Industrial Accelerator Act and this would be good news for the British automotive industry and the jobs and investment it supports across the UK.”

title: Farage accused of ‘protecting’ Reform candidate over racist slurs against David Lammy
summary: Exclusive: ITV investigation shows leader stood by mayoral candidate who said Labour MP should ‘go home to the Caribbean’
text: Nigel Farage was told by a senior Reform official that he was “protecting” a high-profile mayoral candidate accused of making racist comments about David Lammy, an undercover investigation has revealed. The latest footage from an undercover investigation by ITV also shows Sarah Pochin, one of two female MPs for Reform, complaining that other party officials “are so fucking chauvinistic” and that “they just exclude you if you are a woman”. Other footage shows Farage himself discussing the case of Chris Parry, a retired rear admiral picked to contest the Hampshire and the Solent mayoral election for the party. The party stood by Parry for months after it emerged that he had said the former foreign secretary should “go home to the Caribbean” last year, and suggested that at least eight other politicians from minority ethnic backgrounds do not have a primary loyalty towards the UK. However, while Reform eventually suspended him in March after the Guardian revealed other remarks by Parry, clips from an ITV documentary show Farage pushing back against senior advisers who said the candidate had to be sacked. They included Ed Sumner, Reform’s head of communications, who had told another press officer in an earlier disucussion that Parry was “clearly a racist”. “He needs to go, I’m getting rid of him,” Sumner was filmed saying when the controversy broke last December. However, Parry was still the candidate three weeks later, while Farage told a press conference that the candidate could stay if he apologised. In a conversation between Farage and Sumner, which was recorded by the undercover reporter, the Reform leader said that Parry “must apologise to Lammy” and was told that a text had been written for the candidate. “He must do it and move on … Tell him that from me,” Farage said, to which Sumner said: “You’re protecting him.” To laughter, Farage replied: “It’s showing a bit of … bit of sorrow. Look, ‘I’m sorry’ is probably a good thing to hear. Just take the fucking deal. Trouble is he’s a rear admiral. That’s the problem.” Parry was suspended on 26 March after the Guardian reported that he had described members of a Jewish neighbourhood watch group as “cosplayers” and likened them to “Islamists on horseback”. Bridget Phillipson, the Labour party chair, said these “latest shocking and deeply disturbing revelations go right to the top of Reform”, adding: “Nigel Farage needs to wake up and realise the buck stops with him. He also must urgently explain why he allegedly stood by a blatant racist instead of kicking him out of his party.” The revelations are the latest in a number of recent controversies for Reform. The full ITV documentary, Undercover: A Year in Reform, airs on Sunday. A number of councillors have already stood down after segments from the investigation aired on Wednesday showed them making graphic threats of extreme violence and expressing racist and misogynistic views. The undercover reporter for ITV also met Pochin, Reform’s MP for Runcorn and Helsby, at a time when she was the party’s only female member of parliament. When Pochin was told that a new female press officer was starting work, she was recorded as saying: “Oh thank fuck for that. God! We so need women press officers … They are so fucking chauvinistic. “I go out on all the shows and go: ‘Oh no, it’s lovely, oh they’re all so welcoming.’ Shit … they just exclude you if you’re a woman. It’s really tough being a girl with all of this alpha male shit going on.” Pochin did not provide a statement when approached by ITV. Reform UK used a statement issued on Thursday to accuse ITV and the company behind the documentary, Hardcash Productions, of using “extreme methods of deception”. It said: “They have infiltrated our workplace including commissioning an undercover journalist to provide altered identification documents, a false address, and false credentials so that they could be given access to Reform’s headquarters, computer systems, and spy on its employees. “That same journalist did not limit themselves to recording candid conversations in the workplace. That journalist also sought to find out sensitive security information, travel arrangements, and financial information outside of the scope of this investigation.” Reform went on to claim that ITV had failed to address this in correspondence, despite this conduct being drawn to its attention. “This is at a time when Nigel Farage and other members of Reform are being targeted by individuals who wished them harm and caused a security issue which was documented during the course of the undercover investigation,” it added. “There is no room for racism in Reform UK. We always respect due process of investigations and whilst these are ongoing it would not be appropriate to comment on individual cases.” When approached for comment, Parry referred the Guardian to a statement given to ITV. In it he said: “I would urge people to go back to the original contexts and tweets to see what was said and why. They related to reparations and failures by the police and government. They will see I always exercise my right to criticise anyone in power or the public eye whom I judge to be acting against the interests of the British people.”

title: Chris Davies obituary
summary: Other lives: Professor of engineering whose work on light metals established him as a leading researcher in the field
text: My brother, Chris Davies, who has died aged 61 of cancer, was an academic metallurgist whose research helped to bring about a better understanding of why metals behave the way they do – and therefore how to control their properties during manufacturing. Much of his research took place at Monash University in Australia, where he had moved from the UK in the early 1990s. In particular, his work on the behaviour of light metals and alloys fed into the development of lighter, stronger and more reliable materials used in the making of aircraft, vehicles and medical devices. Chris’s studies also helped to support advances in 3D printing by providing insights into how companies can produce high-performance metal components more efficiently, with less waste and lower energy consumption. Born in Cardiff, Chris was the son of Jack and his wife, Margaret (nee Powell), both teachers of English. He attended Cardiff high school and then gained a degree in engineering at Imperial College London, where he stayed on to do a PhD. In 1992 he moved to Vancouver in Canada to do two years of postdoctoral research at the University of British Columbia, before joining Monash in Melbourne in 1994 and remaining there until his death, initially in a teaching role but thereafter specialising mainly in research. In addition, Chris held a number of leadership roles at Monash over the years, including as associate dean of research, deputy dean of external engagements and deputy dean of operations in the Faculty of Engineering. He was president of the Academic Board from 2016 to 2019, and in 2025 was named to the Monash Honour Roll, a mark of the esteem in which he was held for his integrity, humour and unwavering commitment. Beyond his life in academia Chris loved reading, enjoyed print making, painting and drawing and appreciated music of all genres. He was an avid sports fan, having played club hockey in his younger days, and was a member of the Cardiff Nomads Angling Club. He is survived by his second wife, Sam (nee Lipscombe), whom he married in 2011, a son, Calum, from his first marriage to Louise (nee Hehir), which ended in divorce, and his siblings, Graham and me.

title: Norman McCubbin obituary
summary: Other lives: Particle physicist who worked for many years on projects related to the Large Hadron Collider
text: My brother Norman McCubbin, who has died aged 77, was a scientist who worked at the forefront of experimental particle physics. A leading light in experiments that took place on the Large Hadron Collider, the world’s biggest and most powerful particle accelerator at the European Organization for Nuclear Research (Cern) in Switzerland, he spent the last five years of his working life as director of the particle physics department at the Rutherford Appleton Laboratory (RAL) in Oxfordshire, until his retirement in 2012. Afterwards he became a tutor to undergraduates at St Anne’s College, Oxford, and was still in that role at his death. Norman was born in Pinner, Middlesex, the first child of Hugh, an accountant, and his wife, Pat (nee Rosenberg). The family moved to Leicester, where his brothers, Richard and I, were born, and then in 1958 to Kenya for Hugh to take up a post as finance director of the Kenya Farmers’ Association . When Hugh joined the UN’s World Food Programme, the family moved to Lesotho and later, Taiwan, while Norman went to Repton school in Derbyshire as a boarder. After moving on to New College, Oxford, he gained a first-class physics degree and took a PhD. Between 1973 and 1979 he was a postdoctoral research associate at the University of Lancaster and then at RAL, working with the laboratory on the first hadron collider at Cern to study the dynamics of proton-proton collisions. He then worked at Cern as a senior (then principal) scientific officer, where he concentrated on the collisions of heavy ions. From 1990 to 1999 Norman led RAL’s Zeus experiment in Hamburg, studying the structure of the proton, and from 1999 to 2003 he was computing coordinator for the Atlas experiment at the Large Hadron Collider. Later he became divisional head of RAL’s particle physics department while continuing with some of his work at Cern until, in 2007, he became the department’s director. In retirement as a stipendiary lecturer in physics at Oxford, he was a popular tutor, relishing the core subjects of thermodynamics, statistical mechanics, relativity and symmetries. More prosaically, he relished answering questions, via video from New Zealand, from his ever-curious seven-year-old great-nephew Hugh, about issues such as gravity, centrifugal force and quantum entanglement. Despite his dedication to his work, family and friendship always came first for Norman. We all basked in his warmth, love, humour and kindness, as well as that illuminating intelligence he wore so lightly. He is survived by me and Richard, two nieces, two nephews, three great-nephews and a great-niece.

title: US justice department sues California over alleged noncitizen voting
summary: DoJ had demanded that LA county confirm citizenship of people on list in thumb drive, but officials refused
text: The US Department of Justice sued California on Thursday, seeking a court order to prevent the state from tabulating certain ballots cast in the midterm elections. The suit came two days after the department made a specious demand to the state. On Tuesday, the department sent election officials in Los Angeles county a thumb drive with a handwritten password purporting to contain the names of noncitizens registered to vote. The department asked officials to confirm the citizenship of anyone on the list and set aside ballots from those whose status could not be confirmed. It gave the state 48 hours – an extremely narrow window – to take action. It did not provide details on how it came up with the names on the list. In its lawsuit, filed in federal court in the central district of California, the justice department said it had provided the state with more than 20,000 names of likely noncitizens. The Los Angeles county clerk and recorder, Dean Logan, said his office would not review the list, in part because it didn’t consider the USB drive secure. “The Department of Justice has not provided the underlying evidence, source, or methodology supporting its assertions that individuals identified in its records are ineligible to vote,” Logan said in a statement. “We cannot withhold or refuse to count ballots based solely on unverified allegations, nor can we disregard the legal requirements governing our election – and we certainly have no authority to act on records that are outside of our jurisdiction.” In a statement on Wednesday, the California secretary of state, Shirley Weber, a Democrat, said the justice department had not provided the list of voters to her office. “The [justice department’s] relentless efforts to unlawfully gain access to states’ protected voter data and purge voter rolls serve only to cause chaos and fuel public distrust in our elections,” Weber said. Justice department lawyers are asking the court to order the state not to count votes from those it had flagged. “This Court should enjoin California from presently tabulating vote-by-mail ballots from likely noncitizens in the upcoming federal election until the voter’s citizenship status can be determined,” the lawsuit said. “This Court should order California (1) to set aside vote-by-mail ballots from persons identified by the Federal Government likely to be noncitizens and (2) to independently – or in collaboration with the Federal Government – verify their citizenship status (beyond relying on unverified statements of citizenship necessary to registering) before tabulating their vote-by-mail ballot.” The request to block tabulation comes amid concerns that Donald Trump and his allies will interfere in the counting of votes in the midterm elections, in which Republicans are expected to lose seats in Congress. The Trump administration’s methodology for identifying noncitizens has come under scrutiny. Earlier this year, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) said there could be as many as 278,000 noncitizens on the rolls in four states, including more than 190,000 in California and about 16,000 in Nevada. Officials at the DHS refused to share their methodology with Nevada election officials and later turned over just 185 names of people it had a strong belief were noncitizens. When Nevada officials investigated, they found every one of those people was a citizen. Richard Hasen, an election law scholar at UCLA, described the justice department’s efforts in California as “a nice publicity stunt that gets attention for [the justice department] and reinforces the notion among the president’s most ardent supporters that California is not doing enough to combat voter fraud”. “The Department of Justice has no standing to tell states and localities to go in and remove voters from voting rolls in the midst of an election. In fact, the National Voter Registration Act bars systematic purges of ineligible voters in the 90-day period before the election,” he wrote in a blogpost. “The purpose of this provision, unsurprisingly, is to stop false positives, that is the removal of eligible voters who are mistakenly flagged as noncitizens. A rushed process would almost certainly lead to disenfranchisement.”

summary: Woman claims comedian ‘pranced around like an ostrich’ before forcing himself on her in hotel room attack
text: Russell Brand transformed into a “monster” when he allegedly made a woman take half-naked photographs of him before raping her in a hotel room at a Labour party conference, a court has heard. The 51-year-old comedian has denied attacking the woman, who broke down in tears in the witness box at Southwark crown court as she told how she could not fight him off. “He was really heavy,” she said. “I couldn’t struggle. I couldn’t breathe. I know he raped me, I know I said: ‘No, no, I don’t want this.’” Brand faces three charges of rape, three of sexual assault and one of indecent assault against six women, in allegations spanning 10 years from 1999 to 2009. He denies all the charges and has pleaded not guilty. Brand fixed his gaze on one of the TV screens in court on Thursday morning as a video of the woman’s interview from 27 September 2023 was played. She told police she met Brand at a fringe cabaret event that he was performing in during the Labour party conference in Bournemouth in 1999. She was not attracted to the then unknown performer, whom she assumed was gay and who showered her with compliments. But she found him polite and intelligent, and the pair spoke about their work before going back to her hotel room to continue their conversation. The woman said she “froze” in the run-down single room when she returned from the toilet to find that Brand was partly naked and “prancing around” like an ostrich. She said she asked him why he had undressed, and he told her: “Don’t worry, I’m mostly naked at home.” The woman told how she became “frightened” when Brand made her take half-naked photographs of him. “I took pictures of him on my camera – he made me take them,” she said. “I remember feeling: ‘What on earth have I got myself into?’” She told police he then raped her in an attack that lasted up to 10 minutes and left her feeling scared, in pain, and as if she couldn’t breathe. “He did rape, he did push me on the bed,” she told police. “He did pull my clothes off, he took my trousers off. “I remember him on me, very heavy. I know I said no. I kind of drifted out of my head. I couldn’t get out of the situation – ‘do I shout, do I scream?’ He was very heavy, I couldn’t breathe, it didn’t take long.” She described his body as snake-like and “disgusting” and said his tongue was “horrible” like a lizard. “I’m saying ‘no, no’ but I was really scared,” she told police. “I know he groped me. I know he was touching me, I know he grabbed my breasts. I know he tried to kiss me and I moved my neck. I didn’t want his mouth on mine. “He was just pulling my trousers down and pulling my underwear off, and he was inside me. It was not nice, it was painful and it hurt.” Giving evidence from behind a screen in the afternoon, the woman added: “I was like a zombie on the bed. All I could think was he’s inside me and the quicker the better.” In tense exchanges during cross-examination with the defence barrister, Ian Winter KC, the woman denied that Brand had persuaded her to have sex. “He was frightening, he seemed menacing at that point,” she replied. “He’s scary. I didn’t know what to do.” She rejected Winter’s suggestion that she had fallen under the spell of Brand, whom the barrister described as charismatic with a magnetic personality. The judge, Mr Justice Bennathan, had to interrupt the lawyer during one exchange to object to one of his questions, saying: “Shush please. I’m the judge, you have to let me talk.” The woman told the court Brand was a “completely different persona” in the hotel room. When pressed further by the prosecutor, Riel Karmy-Jones, the woman said: “He just changed suddenly from camp, friendly and effeminate to monster-like. “I felt very scared in that moment. He was big, I felt threatened and he’s half naked. And while I’m naive, I didn’t think at that moment his intentions were good. “He was just dark and arrogant and performing – he was scary, he was demanding. He was the centre of the show, it was like it was back on stage – he wasn’t the [same] person I was chatting to.” The woman told police she closed her eyes during the attack and that Brand made her feel sick and dirty. She recalled: “He was making noises, a lot of noises of enjoyment and saying how pretty I was. I remember him complimenting me, saying: ‘Are you enjoying it’? I remember him asking me. Obviously I didn’t answer.” She alleged that Brand spoke as the attack was unfolding. She told police: “He was just saying: ‘We’re having fun, it’s fine, it’s all good, don’t worry about it, it’s just fun, it’s normal.’” The woman, who had been a victim of abuse in the past, said Brand made her compare earlier experiences, and it “stuck in her head … is this what abusers do?” She told police: “It was almost like to convince me it’s all OK and that I’d enjoy it, that I’d have to learn to enjoy it.” In the aftermath, she said Brand acted “like nothing was wrong”, wrote down his email address, and suggested that his mother might like to meet her. She told the court: “He is so arrogant in his mindset that he’s God’s gift that I must’ve enjoyed it and I must’ve wanted more.” The following morning, she banged her head against the wall because she felt numb. She told police she had had nightmares about being pregnant and said she kept quiet about the incident for years as she watched Brand becoming “more and more famous”. The woman said a 2023 Dispatches documentary about allegations of sexual misconduct by Brand “triggered” her to go to police. Brand denies the allegations. The trial continues.

title: The water torture goes on at Thames. Sector-wide reform isn’t moving much faster | Nils Pratley
summary: If ‘public control’ bit is delaying overhaul, that needs to be nailed down sharpish or continued uncertainty could be costly
text: It is strange now to recall that Thames Water had a prominent slot on what was known as “Sue’s shit list” – the internal Labour dossier, compiled by Keir Starmer’s first chief of staff, Sue Gray, of potential crises that could erupt at short notice and force the incoming administration to make some big decisions quickly. That was July 2024. Here we are – more than two years later – and the Thames script has barely advanced. We’re still waiting to see if the financial crisis at the over-indebted, under-performing water company will be resolved by a creditor-led recapitalisation, special administration or something else. Now Thames is seeking another £2.4bn slug of funding from creditors to stay afloat for another year and survive yet more back and forth between ministers, regulators and those same lenders. The new mystery element in the talks is what the prime minister, Andy Burnham, actually means by “greater public control”. Still, Thames was an outlier – albeit a biggie – one might say. At least the government in 2024 cracked on with the job of deciding how to overhaul the wider water sector in England and Wales. Indeed it did: Sir Jon Cunliffe, a former deputy governor of the Bank of England, was commissioned to review what was needed and his detailed report landed in summer last year. The centrepiece was the abolition of Ofwat, the regulator. Steve Reed, the environment secretary at the time, embraced Cunliffe’s proposals and declared the “the biggest overhaul of water regulation in a generation” via a new water bill. Game on? Not exactly. The bill, which should have arrived this autumn, was delayed by the change of PM. Burnham has promised a “strengthened” version, which presumably will include the “public control” elements. In the meantime, Ofwat is still in place, and nobody knows which bits of the Environment Agency will be absorbed into the new super-regulator, or what the new body’s formal status will be. Will it, for example, be as formally independent as Ofwat, or will it be under a tighter ministerial leash? Credit rating agencies have noticed the uncertainty. In dry language, Moody’s on Thursday issued a report noting that regulatory changes “appears to have stalled”, that “political scrutiny is heightened and may cause further delay” and the “potential increase in business risk will require stronger financial ratios to maintain credit quality”. Moody’s, note, did not downgrade its assessment of the “stability and predictability” of UK water regulation, as it did in late-2024. But it did tiptoe up to the line: one of its slides at Thursday’s conference warned: “Our score could fall further.” Why does Moody’s opinion matter? Simply because rating agencies influence the price at which companies can borrow, which can itself affect the financing costs passed on to customers in bills. The government should take the hint and decide what it actually wants from water reform. Emma Hardy, the water minister, at least indicated to the same conference that a formal transition plan to the regulator is coming soon. But that’s not the same as an actual water bill, which would reveal if the rest of the Cunliffe changes have survived. It is, of course, entirely fair for an incoming PM to review what he wants from a bill. But the “public control” bit, if that’s delaying everything, needs to be nailed down sharpish. Is it simply the Cunliffe-compliant idea of greater powers of influence for mayors and local authorities? Or bigger changes to match the summer rhetoric? It’s impossible to tell – but it’s all taking far too long. And make a decision one way or another on Thames. Half a parliament to address a supposedly urgent 2024 problem is extreme water torture.

title: Albania’s prime minister vows not to resign over student-led protests
summary: Demonstrators demand resignation of Edi Rama after three days of clashes in capital Tirana
text: Albania’s prime minister has said he will not resign as a protest movement, initially prompted by a proposal to build a Trump family-backed resort in the Balkan state, turned violent with clashes convulsing the capital for a third consecutive day. Speaking on Thursday after calls by students who this week assumed control of the anti-government demonstrations that have rattled Tirana since June, Edi Rama said: “Governments are changed through democratic elections. We had elections last year, not a revolution.” Rama’s comments to Reuters came hours before fresh clashes erupted outside the education ministry, where riot police responded to rock-throwing youths with teargas and water cannon. “My responsibility is to listen, address legitimate concerns and keep Albania moving forward,” he added. The alternative, he argued, would be tantamount “to a betrayal of the Albanians who gave me a strong mandate to complete negotiations on European Union membership … I will not allow violence to derail Albania’s European future.” Rama, who won a historic fourth term last year, has vowed to get what was once the continent’s most isolated Stalinist state into the 27-member bloc by 2030. The unrest – in contrast to the largely peaceful protests of recent months – marks the veteran leader’s biggest challenge yet. On Thursday, after a night of running street battles between demonstrators and riot police, residents awoke to see the facades of shops smashed and traffic signals destroyed, with government buildings and banks burned and ransacked. An estimated 89 people, including 61 police officers, were injured. The renewed violence has created an atmosphere of unpredictability amid predictions that public patience may finally be running out for the socialist government after 13 years in power. “Young Albanians are tired of all the corruption, tired of all the arrogance. They want to live in a better country and they are not afraid to use violence,” said Afrim Krasniqi, the director of the Albanian Institute for Political Studies in Tirana. “There is no prognosis. Nobody can say what will come next.” But Rama, who emerged from the protest movement himself – becoming the face of state violence when he dared to criticise Albania’s first-post-communist government 30 years ago – also doubled down. “Students are the future. They are the ones who look ahead, who want to go further and faster,” he said as he visited the fire-damaged premises of Tirana’s College of Europe on Thursday. “Today, this is the ruin left by hands that are not, and can never be, the hands of students. These are the hands that try to push Albania down every time Albania tries to rise.” While he was willing to talk with the younger generation about the rising costs of education – a central complaint that has also spurred the unrest – vandalism would not be tolerated, he said. For nearly five months, demonstrators have gathered daily outside Rama’s office, prompted by plans for a controversial tourism complex championed by the US president’s son-in-law Jared Kushner. The venture foresees construction along pristine coastline deemed a conservation zone of unique natural beauty, including the uninhabited island of Sazan. Labelled the “flamingo revolution” because of the risk posed by the development to wildlife and delicate ecosystems, the rallies have attracted crowds big and small. They, too, have demanded the prime minister resign. Despite the opposition, Rama has steadfastly refused to back down, defending the project as a “gift” that will boost the economy and provide badly needed jobs by transforming Albania into a high-end tourist destination. But Krasniqi said he believed the protest movement was at an inflection point – even if the demonstrations had also been inspired by similar student unrest sweeping Europe, particularly France. “I think this week we reached a turning point,” he said. “The government had more than four months to talk to people, who every day have been out on the street. It chose to belittle and dismiss them instead. And now students have joined in, and they appear to have the upper hand.” For the first time, Krasniqi said, he had heard young people saying they were prepared to be hurt or go to jail if that was the price “for ensuring democracy”. “Their demands are very different to the [flamingo] protesters. They want better education, better university buildings, a society that offers them hope. They also don’t believe Albania should be for sale.” At €4bn (€3.37bn), the Trump family-backed resort would be the biggest investment the nation has seen. Last week, addressing the controversy triggered by the project, Kushner admitted he and his investment firm, Affinity Partners, were “betting on a country that has never had a project of this scale”. “There are no guarantees,” he said. “We are taking that risk because we believe in Albania and we believe in Albanians. If successful, the project would represent approximately €4bn of investment and create significant jobs, economic activity and international visibility for Albania.” This week environmentalists, who first led the charge against the development, begged to differ. Months after the protests began, people still felt as exercised about a venture many believed would only benefit the elite, said Aleksandër Trajçe, who heads the country’s leading conservation group, the Protection and Preservation of Natural Environment in Albania. “Anger over the [Kushner] project has prepared the ground for the violence we are seeing, because day after day protesters have been faced with the arrogance of a government that has refused to listen to them, or give an inch.”

title: Texas sued after glitch delays almost 600,000 voter registrations
summary: Voting registration organizations accuse Texas officials of failing to ensure eligible voters can register properly
text: Texas election officials are struggling to process a massive backlog of nearly 600,000 voter registration applications after a major state computer system failure, just days before early voting is set to open on Monday and amid concerns about widespread voter suppression. The disruption has raised serious concerns about the state’s voter registration system, with voting rights organizations accusing Texas officials of failing to ensure that eligible voters could properly register. The problem originated from a software error involving the Texas department of public safety (DPS), according to a lawsuit filed last week. The glitch affected a website used for driver’s license applications that was also designed to allow Texans to register to vote. The lawsuit alleges that between October 2025 and February 2026, residents who selected “yes” when asked whether they wanted to register to vote were given receipts confirming their selections. However, their registration information was never actually recorded. The League of Women Voters of Texas and Move Texas Civic Fund, a non-profit dedicated to increasing civic participation among young Texans, brought the legal challenge against state officials. “Defendants have breached and continue to breach the contract by failing to maintain the procedures that ensure simultaneous online voter registration with driver license renewal or change of address transactions,” the lawsuit said. “DPS had failed to send almost 600,000 voter registrations to the SOS to distribute to local county registrars, with some delayed voter registrations stretching back as far as October 2025,” it added. “Unexpecting counties must now scramble to process this deluge of last-minute voter registrations ahead of the November 2026 election.” Among those named in the complaint are the Texas secretary of state, Robert Howden, the state’s top election official, and the DPS director, Freeman F Martin. The lawsuit demands that both agencies establish and maintain a working voter registration process. It also seeks records detailing registration failures and an order requiring officials to provide the court with evidence of compliance within one month. The registration breakdown is drawing national attention as Texas prepares for one of the country’s most closely contested US Senate elections this year. Donald Trump chose Texas’s attorney general, Ken Paxton, to run against James Talarico, a political newcomer who Democrats hope will be able to flip Texas’s longtime red Senate seat to blue. The California Democratic senator Alex Padilla, ranking member of the Senate rules committee, which has oversight of federal elections, demanded answers about the voting registration system from Texas leaders last month. In a letter addressed to the state governor, Greg Abbott, and Howden, Padilla pressed for an explanation of how the failure occurred and how many registrations were affected. The controversy comes as voting rights advocates continue to warn about what they describe as broader efforts by the Trump administration to suppress voter participation. Those concerns include bids to rig electoral maps and threats to deploy federal law enforcement at polling sites, among other actions.

title: Seven sailors missing after drones strike tankers near Romania’s Black Sea coast
summary: Nato source says drones came from Russia, while Romania’s president says attacking commercial ships ‘is unacceptable and has to stop’
text: Seven sailors are missing after drones struck two tankers near Romania’s Black Sea ⁠coast, setting them ablaze and raising ⁠fresh security concerns on a vital shipping route used by Ukraine. A Nato military source told Reuters the drones that had hit the Wine Trader and the Yara J came from Russia. “The drones that caused ⁠the fires on board two tankers inside Romanian territorial waters were of Russian origin,” the source said. Romania’s president, Nicușor Dan, described the situation in the Black Sea as serious. “Commercial ships are being attacked and sunk,” he wrote on X. “Seafarers killed, injured and missing very close to the shores of Romania and Bulgaria. This is unacceptable and it has to stop.” His statement followed a meeting with Bulgaria’s prime minister, Rumen Radev, and Nato’s secretary-general, Mark Rutte, on Thursday, where they agreed “to strengthen our defences in the Black Sea”, Dan said. Rutte said: “Nato will continue to work closely with our allies in the Black Sea, adjusting our deterrence and defence posture as needed.” A Nato official said the issue would be discussed at a meeting of the North Atlantic Council next week. The missing crew were from the Wine Trader, a San Marino-flagged tanker travelling from Tunisia to Romania. All crew on the Yara J, which was struck just inside Romanian waters late on Wednesday, were safe. Similar incidents in recent weeks have raised fears that the zone is becoming another front in Russia’s war on Ukraine. Dan said the two ships had been struck by drones, but declined to say whether Russia was responsible. Romania shares a 614km (381-mile) border with Ukraine, much of it along the Danube. The country has experienced frequent drone incursions since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, including a daytime encroachment last November that led Nato to scramble fighter jets. EU leaders were already concerned about drone strikes on merchant ships off the coast of Bulgaria. On Tuesday, drone strikes on two ships off the coast of Bulgaria prompted emergency rescue operations, with 11 crew member from the HS Dignity, a cargo ship sailing under a Guinea-Bissau flag, still missing. On another ship, the Ukrainian-operated Chelsea 3 sailing under a Maltese flag, rescuers evacuated all 15 crew members, with five receiving treatment for minor injuries. The crew reported that the ship’s deck and hull were hit by three aerial drones. “The results of this attack favour Russia. However, we don’t have any solid evidence that the drones are Russians,” Radev said after arriving in Brussels for an EU summit on Thursday. At least 23 sailors have been reported missing or killed after attacks on commercial shipping near the coasts of Bulgaria and Romania in the past 10 days, according to Reuters. Russia has stepped up its bombing campaign on Ukraine’s Black Sea infrastructure, forcing Kyiv to turn to Danube river ports and Black Sea routes off the coasts of Romania and Bulgaria to export its grain, sunflower oil and other products. According to a draft summit declaration, EU leaders will say that attacks against civilian shipping, including “member state-flagged vessels, such as the recent attacks in Bulgaria’s and Romania’s exclusive economic zones in the Black Sea, are unacceptable and constitute a serious violation of international and maritime law”.

title: Thames Water asks for £2.4bn more to avoid going bust this year or early 2027
summary: Water company tells creditors it will not survive long enough to agree refinancing deal without more money
text: Thames Water has asked its creditors for another £2.4bn as the embattled water company comes close to running out of cash. The UK’s largest water company said on Thursday it needed another short-term cash injection because it would be unable to reach a longer-term deal to sort out its giant debt pile before running out of cash by “the end of 2026 or the start of 2027”. Thames Water said in a statement to the stock market that it “does not expect to complete its recapitalisation process ahead of this date”, meaning it would run out of cash without creditors stumping up more. The utility company serves 16 million customers in London and the Thames valley. However, it has been on the brink of collapse for several years after it became overwhelmed by a debt pile that is now about £20bn. Its shareholders walked away, leaving the company under the effective control of its creditors while they work out a deal to avoid bankruptcy. The creditors gave Thames a £3bn lifeline in February last year to try to see it through negotiations on a deal to cut its debts and inject more money. The creditors, collectively called the London & Valley Water company, are led by a group of American hedge funds such as Elliott Management and Silver Point Capital, and institutional investors including BlackRock and M&G. However, those talks have dragged on, and the water company has now drawn down £2.65bn of the £3bn, leaving it perilously close to running out of cash even as it carries out a series of expensive repairs and upgrades. Thames said the extra cash would “extend […] liquidity into autumn 2027 and allow [it] to continue to deliver its capital programme and deliver improvements for customers and the environment”. Thames Water’s creditors have drawn up detailed proposals for a rescue plan that would involve them writing off £9.6bn in loans. However, that plan hinges on Ofwat agreeing to let the company pay set penalties for several years upfront, and effectively creating a special regime for the company. That prospect has proven politically unpalatable for the Labour government. Some Labour politicians and environmental campaigners called on Keir Starmer and then Andy Burnham to put Thames Water into special administration, a form of temporary government control while a new buyer is sought. Burnham has pledged more public control of the UK’s water industry, and has said that public ownership for Thames Water “is what should be done”. In addition, the change of prime minister has led to regulatory uncertainty for the broader water industry. Starmer’s government had committed to implementing recommendations on changes to the water system from the former Bank of England deputy governor Sir John Cunliffe, but Burnham’s government has not yet made clear what it plans to do. Thames Water said it “continues to work closely with stakeholders to secure a market-led solution”. Thames Water’s creditors are expected to vote on the proposals later in the month.

title: Woman resentenced to life in prison for death of Kansas City reporter
summary: Prosecutors say Adan Manzano was victim of Danette Colbert’s operation targeting New Orleans tourists
text: A woman involved in a New Orleans criminal enterprise that targeted tourists and led to the death of a reporter has been resentenced to life. On Wednesday, a Jefferson Parish judge resentenced 49-year old Danette Colbert to life in prison plus 75 years under Louisiana’s habitual offender law. In September, Colbert was sentenced to a total of 60 years in prison, 50 years for racketeering and a consecutive 10 years for negligent homicide in the death of Adan Manzano, a journalist for the Spanish-language news outlet Telemundo Kansas City. “The court is going to find that Ms Colbert is at least a fourth felony offender,” Judge Nancy Miller of the 24th judicial district court said during Colbert’s resentencing. Last February, Manzano had traveled to the New Orleans area to cover the Kansas City Chiefs’ Super Bowl clash with the Philadelphia Eagles. He was found dead in his hotel room in Kenner, Louisiana, days before the game. The Jefferson parish coroner’s office said Manzano died from positional asphyxiation. An autopsy found Xanax and alcohol in his system. Prosecutors said Manzano was among the victims of a years-long operation in which Colbert, her accomplice Rickey White, and a co-defendant who testified against them – Christian Anderson – targeted unsuspecting tourists in the city’s French Quarter. The group allegedly lured victims with the promise of sex before drugging and robbing them. Prosecutors said the criminal enterprise dated back to 2012. As prosecutors sought to enhance Colbert’s 10-year sentence, they cited six prior felony cases, including 2024 convictions in New Orleans for computer fraud and illegal money transfers that resulted in a 25-year sentence as a habitual offender. Her criminal record also includes convictions for fraud, stolen property, burglary, theft, battery and witness intimidation dating from 2013 to 2019. Fingerprint analysis by the Jefferson parish sheriff’s office confirmed Colbert’s identity in all six cases. Prosecutors needed to establish only three prior convictions to enhance her sentence. “We believe that sufficient evidence has been presented” to show Colbert was the person convicted in the previous cases, assistant district attorney Jenny Voss told Miller. Colbert’s life sentence will be served consecutively to her 50-year sentence for racketeering and a 25-year sentence for unrelated crimes in New Orleans, the Jefferson parish district attorney’s office said.

title: Matt Gaetz accused in suit of sex trafficking two women in Florida
summary: Jane Does allege ex-congressman and two others coordinated ‘payments, drugs and travel’ for sexual acts
text: The Republican former congressman Matt Gaetz has been accused of participating in the sex trafficking of two young women in a civil lawsuit filed on Thursday in district court in Florida. The allegations, which Gaetz denied in a statement to the Guardian, are the latest developments in a long-running sexual abuse scandal involving the politician who resigned from Congress in November 2024. In the 38-page lawsuit, filed in US district court for the middle district of Florida, the women identified as Jane Doe 1 and Jane Doe 2 claim Gaetz and two others “coordinated the recruitment, payments, drugs, and travel to obtain commercial sexual acts” from them “during 2017 through January 2019”. “The defendants collectively used their public office, power, and wealth to prey on the economic vulnerability of Plaintiffs to commit the acts,” according to the lawsuit. The lawsuit contends that the alleged victims “were recent high school graduates” at the time of the alleged misconduct. One of the defendants, Joel Micah Greenberg, a close associate of Gaetz, and the former tax collector of Seminole county, pleaded guilty in May 2021 to six federal offenses: sex trafficking of a child, illegally producing a false identification document, aggravated identity theft, wire fraud, stalking, and conspiracy. Greenberg was sentenced to 11 years in federal prison. Gaetz rejected the new lawsuit’s allegations in a statement to the Guardian. “I look forward to taking the plaintiffs’ depositions because much of the conduct alleged against me is false,” he wrote. “The lawsuit relies almost exclusively on a Congressional Committee Report that didn’t allow me to confront my accusers. Now I will finally have that chance.” Gaetz attached a photograph of three women in swimsuits from a social media post in September 2018 that appeared to show them on a beach in the Bahamas, with the caption: “#beers and #babes are all you ever need”. Gaetz added: “I don’t know if this is Jane Doe 1 and Jane Doe 2 or not. But if it is they seemed to portray their Bahamian trip differently on social media than in their lawsuit seeking money.” The congressional report Gaetz refers to was part of a bipartisan House ethics committee investigation into his alleged misconduct. That investigation was terminated when he resigned in November 2024 from his north Florida congressional seat shortly after being nominated by Donald Trump to become attorney general. Later that month, Gaetz withdrew from consideration to serve as attorney general amid intense scrutiny around the allegations of sex trafficking and drug use. He has repeatedly denied these accusations. Weeks later, in December 2024, the House ethics committee said its investigation found that Gaetz made payments totaling tens of thousands of dollars to women for sex and drugs on at least 20 occasions. It also found that in 2017, Gaetz “engaged in sexual activity with a 17-year-old girl”. Gaetz denied any wrongdoing. The complaint filed on Thursday alleges that Greenberg recruited the women through the website SeekingArrangement.com and “introduced them to Gaetz”. The lawsuit contends that Jane Doe 1 was 20 years old when she was first introduced to Gaetz in the summer of 2017 and that Jane Doe 2 was 22 years old when Greenberg first contacted her. “Gaetz was a sitting member of Congress, holding himself out to be one of President Donald J. Trump’s closest confidants and most loyal supporters,” the lawsuit states. Jane Doe 1 alleges that she had sex with Gaetz at a July 2017 party at the home of one of the other named defendants. She said she was invited by Greenberg and that Gaetz “introduced himself” to her before giving her “a tour of the upstairs”. The complaint claims that the tour “ended with Gaetz having sex with Jane Doe 1 in a guest bedroom”. Later that night, Jane Doe 1 alleges she saw Gaetz “having sex with ‘Victim A’,” who was “only 17 years old” at the time, and that Gaetz “gave Victim A $400 in cash that night, which Victim A understood to be payment for sex”. The complaint also alleges that three days after the party, Gaetz sent Jane Doe 1 $500 by PayPal, and that it was “the first of thirteen payments he would make to her”. “Between July 2017 and January 2019, Gaetz and Greenberg paid Jane Doe 1 on at least nineteen documented occasions,” the complaint reads, noting that “the payments ranged from $150 to $1,000”. Jane Doe 1 said she had “no meaningful savings and no stable income” and alleges that “they led her to believe they could solve her financial problems as long as she kept performing sexual acts for them and their associates”. Jane Doe 2 alleges that she first met Greenberg in 2017 and that he later invited her to a party at a rented house. “Greenberg promised Jane Doe 2 that she would be ‘well compensated’ for attending but gave her little details about what would be required from her,” the complaint claims. Jane Doe 2 alleges she met Gaetz that night, that “pressed MDMA pills” were “handed out” at the party, and that she took one with Greenberg. “Greenberg then had sex with Jane Doe 2, and Gaetz had sex with her afterward,” the complaint alleges. The lawsuit alleges that the “defendants arranged and funded travel for Plaintiffs, other victims, and other prominent political figures to Venice Beach, Miami, Las Vegas, the Florida Keys, the Bahamas, and New York City between December 2017 and January 2019. “These trips took Jane Doe 1 and Jane Doe 2 to places they had never been and into rooms with men they would never otherwise have met, and every part of that access, from the flights to the hotel rooms, was paid for by men, including the Defendants, who expected sex in return,” it reads.

title: Trump cancels plan to livestream execution after global condemnation
summary: Soldier who killed 13 people in 2009 will still be executed, but president said ‘people would rather not watch him die’
text: Donald Trump has shelved a widely condemned plan to livestream the execution of Nidal Malik Hasan, who was convicted of killing 13 people at a military base at Fort Hood in Texas in 2009. In a social media post on Thursday, Trump argued that broadcasting such an execution “might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan” but said that “many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die, through streaming, or through any other visual device”. “He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed,” Trump added. “That said, the execution may be viewed in person by the immediate families of the victims, if they so choose.” Hasan, who was left paralyzed from the waist down after being shot by law enforcement officers during the shooting at Fort Hood, now uses a wheelchair. The US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, said last week that the execution of Hasan would be a public event. Hasan’s sentence will be the first military execution in more than 60 years, and would have been the first in US history to be publicly broadcast. In a statement to the Guardian on Thursday, a spokesperson for the Pentagon said Trump and Hegseth “spoke about the decision to not livestream Hasan’s execution” before Trump’s statement. Hegesth “supports the President’s decision, and they are completely aligned”, they added. In an interview with Real America’s Voice last Thursday, Hegseth said he supported the public execution “because people need to understand that there’s serious consequences for these types of things”. But since then, the Trump administration has faced sweeping criticism, and comparisons to dictatorships in Iran and Afghanistan. Many US lawmakers, from across the political spectrum, have come out and condemned the announcement, and urged Hegseth to reconsider. Yassamin Ansari, the first Iranian American Democrat elected to the US Congress, wrote in a post on social media: “In Trump’s America, we’re doing public executions now. WTF. This is what happens under brutal dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan. It’s all part of Trump’s authoritarian takeover of the United States.” In another post, Lisa Murkowski, a Republican senator from Alaska, said that there was “no need to livestream any execution, including this one”, adding that she “would expect this from terrorists and dictators, but not here in America”. The representative Rob Bresnahan, a Republican from Pennsylvania, said in a post on social media that “an execution shouldn’t be a live-streamed spectacle”, adding that “the focus should be on justice for the victims and their families, not turning an execution into entertainment”. “Their pain deserves respect, not a public show,” he said. On Friday of last week, the United Nations’ office of the high commissioner for human rights warned that broadcasting the killing would amount to a public execution and “breach the absolute prohibition of torture”, and the president of the US Conference of Catholic Bishops also condemned the Pentagon’s plan, saying in a statement that “in no way can Hassan’s actions be condoned but this decision is a barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered”. “The public execution even of one who has done grave harm will only further undermine the moral fabric of our nation and be a blight on the conscience of its people,” the statement added. That same day, JD Vance appeared to cast doubt on whether the Pentagon would actually livestream the execution, telling reporters that “I don’t know that that’s actually going to happen” when asked about the plans. The vice-president also said that if it were livestreamed, “I’m not going to be watching it.” But over the weekend, Markwayne Mullin, who heads the Department of Homeland Security, stood behind the administration’s decision to livestream the execution. Speaking with CBS News, Mullin said that “no one has to watch it” and said: “I follow President Trump. He’s the commander in chief of the country, and he does a phenomenal job. He leads this country with a very, very, very direct, forward, straight hand, and he’s restoring American values.” Trump himself had made contrasting remarks in recent days on whether the live stream would happen. On Friday, he told reporters that he “absolutely” approved the plan to livestream the execution, but on Saturday he said that he had not yet made a final decision on whether to go through with it. “There are two thoughts: don’t show it and show it” he said. “’Cause you know, by showing it, maybe other people won’t be doing what he did. So I’ll make a decision ultimately. I know what the military would like to do, but I’ll make a decision.”

title: Eritrean aggression must not be overlooked | Letter
summary: Letter: Biruk Mekonnen, the Ethiopian ambassador, responds to an editorial on the war in Tigray
text: Your attention to Ethiopia is welcome, but your editorial (8 October) presents an incomplete account of the crisis, framing Ethiopia’s national interests as sources of regional instability while insufficiently examining the actions of other actors. The opening reference to the Nobel peace prize is particularly telling. By suggesting that the committee will hope its next choice “ages better than 2019’s”, the editorial invites readers to question Abiy Ahmed’s award because of the war that followed a year later. Yet the prime minister received the prize for his efforts to achieve peace with Eritrea. The subsequent war in Tigray does not erase that achievement or, by itself, establish that the award was undeserved. Describing the rapprochement with Eritrea as having “facilitated a war with the Tigray People’s Liberation Front” implies causation without adequately explaining the evidence. Likewise, claiming Mr Abiy’s coalition is “held together by his patronage” reduces political support to personal favours without establishing that this is what sustains it. More seriously, the editorial overlooks the broader context of Eritrean aggression. The current crisis must also be understood in the context of an Eritrean foreign policy that, from Ethiopia’s perspective, has treated a weak Ethiopia as serving Eritrea’s interests. The call for a truce also fails to address responsibility for renewed hostilities. Dialogue is welcome, but it must not reward armed aggression with political leverage or pressure Ethiopia into concessions. Ethiopia’s pursuit of Red Sea access and its right to develop the Nile’s resources should not be portrayed as threats simply because they challenge neighbouring states’ preferences. Whether or not Eritrea’s strategic value to Washington explains its approach, that should not eclipse the consequences of its actions for Ethiopia’s sovereignty and security. title: Endless fun with a legendary book of placenames | Letters
summary: Letters: Ian A Anderson reminds readers of The Meaning of Liff. Plus letters from Peter Lewis, John Davies, Penelope Fletcher, Phil Ivens and Chris Skelcher
text: Neither Adrian Chiles, in his column about placenames (7 October), nor the writers of the follow-up letters (9 October) mentioned Douglas Adams and John Lloyd’s legendary 1983 dictionary of placenames, The Meaning of Liff, still in print. Not so long ago, finding ourselves in Lincolnshire, we made a detour just to get a selfie with the village sign for Mavis Enderby (“the almost-completely-forgotten girlfriend from your distant past for whom your wife has a completely irrational jealousy and hatred”). The book is full of delightful definitions of placenames like Nempnett Thrubwell (“the feeling experienced when driving off for the first time on a brand new motorbike”) and Mellon Udrigle (“the ghastly sound made by traditional folk-singers”). Hours of endless pleasure. Ian A Anderson Cambridge • Friends and I in the Oxfordshire/Buckinghamshire area have long believed that the names of certain local villages could double as those of 1980s West Indies fast bowlers. Step forward the fearsome pace attack of Sutton Courtenay, Stanton Harcourt and Grendon Underwood. Peter Lewis Oxford • There also are, or have been, real people whose names should be Dorset villages. title: The UK must have digital sovereignty | Letters
summary: Letters: The government must stop allowing foreign companies to have access to our sensitive data, writes Ian White. Plus a letter from Bill Cawley
text: The UK cannot become dependent on foreign AI technology that can be switched off at short notice, says George Williamson, head of the Alan Turing Institute (Report, 10 October). The growing opposition to Palantir, an American company, having government contracts that give it access to sensitive data are all part of the same issue. The UK does not have digital sovereignty. This is not a theoretical problem. The US government imposed targeted sanctions on the international criminal court, stopping all digital services to certain individuals. This could happen to a country. Even if you use European email and cloud services, our computer operating systems require constant software updates. This is not just to add new features. There is a constant race between the good guys patching the software bugs and the bad guys trying to gain entry to your computer using those same software bugs. Recently, Holland and France took active steps to break the near monopoly of big Amercian tech by laying the foundations of a nationwide IT ecosystem that they would control. The UK needs to do the same. Ian White Cheltenham, Gloucestershire • The concern about the NHS’s dependence on Palantir (Palantir’s Tom Watson says ‘mob rule’ must not dictate awarding of government contracts, 9 October) is justified, but the £330m contract is a symptom of a wider habit. Whenever the government wants joined-up data, it buys one large platform from one supplier – and such projects have a long record of overrunning, costing far more than planned and locking the buyer in. There is a working example of the alternative: the world wide web. It does not require everyone’s data to sit in one place or run on one company’s software. It simply defines how data is requested and transferred. The NHS needs the same: an open specification for exchanging records, plus a registry of where each patient’s data is held. Any authorised clinician could then assemble the full picture of my treatment, while each hospital or practice chose its own software supplier. Specialist firms could still compete to analyse the data for planning and research – but none would own the plumbing. The NHS already has the beginnings of this in its interoperability standards. Why do the money and political attention go to a single proprietary platform rather than to making open standards mandatory? Bill Cawley Ludlow, Shropshire

title: Paxton v Talarico: tens of millions of dollars pour into closely watched Texas Senate race
summary: Elon Musk has spent $158m in a month to back Republicans in midterm races – with his efforts mostly focused on Texas
text: Tens of millions of dollars are pouring into Texas as Democrats stage an audacious bid to win a US Senate seat in the Republican stronghold. Elon Musk, the world’s richest person, is among those wading into the closely watched race as November’s midterm elections approach. In September alone, Musk gave $158m to the Senate Leadership Fund, the primary super political action committee (Pac) backing Republican Senate candidates, Axios first reported. The donation accounted for more than half of the Senate Leadership Fund’s fundraising in the third quarter. Separately, Musk donated $10m to Lone Star Liberty Pac, the committee dedicated to supporting Ken Paxton, the Republican candidate in Texas, after Alex Latcham, the president of the Senate Leadership Fund, requested the funding. A source familiar with the matter confirmed Axios’s reporting to the Guardian. The Guardian has also asked representatives for America Pac, the political operation founded by Musk, for comment. The donations came as Republicans were struggling to keep up with spending by Paxton’s Democratic opponent, James Talarico. Over the summer, Talarico released an ad painting Paxton negatively as a politician with a history of corruption. Talarico, a young, progressive candidate known for his faith-based messaging, made strides with liberal voters in Texas when he defeated an established Democrat for the Senate nomination earlier this year. Talarico raised $64m – the largest third-quarter fundraising of a Senate candidate in history, just this summer, Politico reported. “He’s fighting this battle basically alone while Elon Musk and the full weight of the GOP fundraising apparatus outspends him 2:1. This is still an uphill battle,” an unnamed Democratic strategist working in Texas told Politico. Polls have shown the two candidates are essentially tied, though some have Talarico polling narrowly ahead of Paxton. The Texas Senate race is one of the most competitive races in the country and was expected to cost millions of dollars because it’s an expensive state to run a campaign. The Senate Leadership Fund warned, months earlier, that supporting Paxton would cost anywhere from $150m to $200m. But Donald Trump chose Paxton himself to run against Talarico. When Musk’s team and the Senate Leadership Fund analyzed polling, they found Paxton’s chances of winning dwindling, leading Musk to step in, Axios reported. In the 2025-2026 election cycle, Musk has donated approximately $366m to federal committees, the New York Times reported earlier this week. That is significantly more than he did during the 2024 election cycle, when he gave about $290m to help Trump. The increase in spending contradicts a statement Musk made in May 2025 when he predicted: “I think, in terms of political spending, I’m going to do a lot less in the future.” Andrew Romeo, a spokesperson for America Pac, told the New York Times: “These robust investments have allowed the GOP apparatus to get its message out so Republicans can have a fighting chance to defy history. “If Democrats take control of Washington and win key gubernatorial and attorney general races this November, then America risks becoming a socialist, woke and borderless country,” Romeo added.

title: Eritrea accuses Shabana Mahmood of ‘political gimmick’ over visa ban threat
summary: Home secretary says she will block all Eritreans from UK unless a returns deal is agreed for rejected asylum seekers and criminals
text: Shabana Mahmood has been accused of launching a “perfunctory political gimmick” by the Eritrean government in a row over the return of rejected asylum seekers and criminals. After the home secretary threatened to block all Eritreans from entering the UK unless a returns deal was agreed, the country’s embassy claimed the UK had failed to engage in “meaningful and appropriate” dialogue. The spat began on Thursday morning when the Home Office claimed the east African country had abruptly withdrawn cooperation on the return of unwanted citizens earlier this year. From Thursday, diplomats from the east African country also face restrictions on their movement outside London and VIPs will be stripped of access to fast-track visas as preferential processing is scrapped. It prompted a statement from Eritrea’s north London embassy “categorically” rejecting Mahmood’s claims. “Despite Eritrea’s repeated requests for constructive discussion with relevant UK authorities on the dignified return of its citizens, the UK has shown no interest to engage in meaningful and appropriate dialogue,” it said. Describing the home secretary’s decision as regrettable, the statement added: “The act is nothing more than a perfunctory political gimmick. The fact is, the UK has not issued a single visa to an Eritrean official since 2023.” UK government officials denied this. They insisted a confirmed exemption from immigration control for an Eritrean official took place as recently as August 2026. Sources said Eritrea previously cooperated with the UK on returns between 2024 and March 2026, while the UK has repeatedly sought to engage with Eritrean authorities, including repeatedly offering to send a Home Office delegation to Asmara to discuss returns. A Home Office spokesperson said: “The Eritrean government’s press notice misrepresents the UK’s position and contains numerous factual inaccuracies.” Eritreans were the most common nationality arriving by small boat in the year ending June 2026. Returns arrangements are vital for removing people who have been refused asylum and foreign criminals. Mahmood said on Thursday morning: “Eritrea has had every chance to accept the return of criminals and those with no right to be in the UK. Unlike other countries, it has refused. “My message to the Eritrean government is simple: take back your nationals or face a complete ban on your citizens entering the UK. I will not hesitate to impose further measures on other countries refusing to cooperate.” The move followed similar threats of visa sanctions against Angola, Namibia and the Democratic Republic of the Congo in 2025. Angola and Namibia subsequently agreed to cooperate with demands on migrant returns, while the DRC faced visa restrictions before reaching an agreement with the UK in February. In March, ministers also placed an emergency brake on visas for nationals from four countries after the home secretary accused them of exploiting Britain’s generosity to claim asylum. Study visas for nationals from Afghanistan, Cameroon, Myanmar and Sudan were also halted, as were work visas for Afghans. Just over 100 refused asylum seekers from Eritrea have been deported – a figure comprising less than 4% of the 2,626 people whose claims were rejected in the past four years. Nearly 6,000 Eritreans have reached the UK across the Channel in the year to June, the highest number of any nationality. After the success of the previous sanction threats, Mahmood warned other countries that they faced similar visa restrictions if they continued to refuse to take back their criminals, illegal migrants and rejected asylum seekers. India, Pakistan, Nigeria, Bangladesh, Somalia, Egypt and Gabon have been identified as resistant to taking back illegal migrants and could face sanctions. Madeleine Sumption, the director of the Migration Observatory at Oxford University, said roughly 7,000 applications for asylum came from Eritreans, about 8% of the total. About 84% were successful on first application and more would be successful on appeal, she said. “There are different types of threats that can be made such as stopping student visas, or stopping visit visas. It will be interesting to see what kind of impact this has on the number of returns.” Reacting to Mahmood’s announcement, one Eritrean asylum seeker said any returnees would “be put in prison and may never be able to get out”. The advocacy group Justice for Eritreans condemned the announcement. “Many Eritreans have fled indefinite national service, arbitrary detention and severe human rights abuses,” it said. “These risks cannot be ignored for the sake of immigration targets. Refugee protection is a legal responsibility, not a political bargaining tool.” UN experts say the human rights situation in Eritrea continues to be dire. Mohamed Abdelsalam Babiker, the special rapporteur on human rights in Eritrea, said there were no signs of meaningful improvement in the country’s human rights situation. “There remain reasonable grounds to believe that crimes against humanity continue in Eritrea,” he said when launching a report this year into the human rights situation. “Regrettably, the core human rights issues that prompted the creation of this mandate 14 years ago remain mostly unresolved. “The ongoing systematic, and widespread enforced disappearance and prolonged incommunicado detention without charge or trial, torture, and the persecution of political opponents, journalists, and members of religious communities remain central features of governance in Eritrea.” Steve Valdez-Symonds, Amnesty International’s policy lead on refugee and migrant rights, said: “As Amnesty and others have documented, Eritrea has an appalling human rights record. “It has not become any less unsafe following the election in this country of a Labour government in 2024 or Shabana Mahmood beginning her term at the Home Office in 2025.” Jon Featonby, the chief policy analyst at the Refugee Council, said: “Severe political repression and widespread human rights abuses are the reason people are forced to flee Eritrea, and are, in the vast majority of cases, recognised by our government as in need of support. “It’s imperative that this policy only targets the Eritrean authorities, and does not undermine the UK’s moral and legal duty to provide protection to those who need it.”
