title: John Healey poised to raise taxes on banks in budget
summary: Exclusive: Chancellor to target sector in his first budget, to help offset Iran war’s damage to public finances
text: John Healey is poised to tax Britain’s banks in his 28 October budget, to help offset the damage inflicted on the public finances by war in the Middle East, the Guardian understands. The chancellor is in Bangkok, where the International Monetary Fund has praised the UK’s progress towards balancing the books, urging him to “stay the course”. To keep the Treasury’s deficit reduction plans on track in the face of rising government borrowing costs, the Guardian understands Healey has decided to tap the financial sector for additional revenue. One option understood to be under discussion – reversing cuts to the bank surcharge made by Jeremy Hunt – would raise upwards of £2bn a year. Lenders have been logging strong earnings on the back of rising interest rates, with the UK’s four largest lenders – HSBC, NatWest, Barclays and Lloyds Banking Group – alone having generated £200bn in pre-tax profits over the past five years. Thinktanks and trade unions have repeatedly urged Healey to tax Britain’s banks more heavily, an option considered but rejected by his predecessor Rachel Reeves, who was wary of deterring future investment. Paul Nowak, the general secretary of the Trades Union Congress (TUC), said: “Britain’s big four banks are making a billion pounds a week, while bonuses have hit a post-crash record. These are bumper profits, driven by high interest rates and households’ mortgage misery. It’s time to make sure banks pay their fair share.” Speaking to journalists in Bangkok, Healey praised the banks as crucial to supporting economic growth. “People too often see them as big, distant financial institutions, when they are hardwired into the economic fabric of this country and our future prospects,” he said. But he is nevertheless believed to be minded to increase the surcharge banks pay on their profits, over and above corporation tax. Industry figures believe that will probably mean raising the surcharge back to 8%, from 3% at present. The UK’s cost of borrowing has risen sharply in recent weeks, alongside that of other big economies, as bond markets have responded to the prospect of higher inflation as a result of the Middle East conflict. Analysts have suggested that could as much as halve the £24bn cushion Reeves had built up against Labour’s fiscal rules at the time of the spring forecast in March. Healey is understood to be willing to accept a narrower “headroom”, but is also keen to convince bond markets he is wedded to deficit reduction. Bank bosses have been lobbying intensively against tax rises since narrowly escaping higher levies during last year’s budget. UK bosses of lenders including HSBC, Lloyds, NatWest, Barclays and Santander met Healey last week but were given no reassurance that bank tax hikes had been ruled out. Their lobby groups – including UK Finance and TheCityUK – wrote to Healey days later, saying that on top of “weakening investors confidence and damaging UK attractiveness”, higher taxes would force them to move staff and business out of the country. That echoed warnings by the chief executive of JP Morgan, Jamie Dimon, who said in May he could scrap plans for a new £3bn London headquarters if the UK government became hostile towards banks. News of the tower – which will house more than half of the US investment bank’s 23,000 UK staff – came days after Reeves spared the sector further tax rises in her 2025 autumn budget. One industry source said banks were resigned to a rise in the surcharge. They believe Healey is minded to reverse Hunt’s cut – taking it back to 8% – but not go further. Such a move would raise £2.25bn a year, according to analysis by the TUC. Another industry source said they were caught off guard by the change in messaging, having come just hours after Healey hailed banks as a “jewel” in the crown of the British economy. “We’re surprised to see this following earlier comments which appeared to be more supportive of the sector.” When asked about how much the banking industry might be able to absorb in terms of tax rises, the head of policy at TheCityUK, John Godfrey, said banks “do not want to get into debating the menu of taxation. The fact is that we don’t want to eat in that restaurant.” Healey has also been “listening to representations” from specialist banks, including Revolut and Shawbrook, that want the profit threshold at which the surcharge kicks in to be raised from £100m to £500m. One government source said Labour was mindful of the UK needing to offer a positive environment for startup banks, especially the lending they offered to small businesses. The TUC has lobbied for a much more punitive increase, to 16%, saying that could raise £24bn in tax revenues over the next four years. Healey said he wanted his first budget as chancellor to give “breathing space” to both consumers and businesses in the face of rising energy prices. There will be little additional funding for other Whitehall departments, however, which he stressed would have to stick to the budgets Reeves set out at her spending review in June 2025. “It’s important that they do manage within what they’ve got, and it’s part of the job,” Healey said. “You have to reprioritise if you want to do fresh things, or more.” The Institute for Fiscal Studies has said Reeves’s plans could result in real-terms spending cuts for some departments in the later years of the spending review period. The Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, used a visit to a financial services firm in Edinburgh on Thursday to caution against further banking tax rises, saying the sector already faced a higher effective tax rate than in many other big global financial centres. Andrew Griffith, the shadow chancellor, said: “Britain needs growth. But a raid on the financial services sector will stifle it. Labour should be backing businesses and wealth-creators, not making their lives even harder. Rather than hiking taxes yet again, Labour should cut spending.” As well as an energy support package for households and businesses, Healey’s first budget is expected to set out more details of plans to devolve income tax to mayoralties, and explain how the government will fully fund the four-year defence investment plan announced by Keir Starmer before he stepped down as prime minister. Healey is expected to duck the longer-term question of when the UK will spend 3% of gross domestic product on defence, the issue over which he resigned as defence secretary in June, contributing to Starmer’s downfall.

title: How an accelerating Earth led experts to adopt the leap hour
summary: International delegates agree leap second no longer tenable, but first leap hour not likely to happen for thousands of years
text: After decades of discussion, quibbling and worrying about clocks in computer systems, the world’s official timekeepers have voted to replace what many viewed as a tiresome correction: the leap second. It’s time, they say, for the leap hour. Delegates from 69 countries cast their votes on Thursday at a conference in France of the International Bureau of Weights and Measures, which ensures the world sticks to the same standards of time, weight, distance and more. The decision to adopt the leap hour from next year aims to reduce the risk of computers and other technical systems tripping over as their software grapples with minutes lasting 61 seconds – and, worse, 59 seconds – instead of a round 60. “After 30 years of debate, the leap second is making way for the leap hour,” said Dr Setnam Shemar, principal scientist in the time and frequency department at the UK’s National Physical Laboratory (NPL). “This will reduce the risks to the systems and national infrastructure that depend on accurate time while still preserving the fundamental link between our global time system and the rotation of the Earth.” The vote at Versailles means that coordinated universal time (UTC) can drift up to an hour from astronomical time before a leap hour is needed, but that is unlikely to happen for thousands of years. “We already have daylight saving where we change by an hour and no one gets bothered about that, apart from losing sleep or getting an extra hour’s sleep,” said Shemar, who sat on the international timekeeping expert committee that proposed the leap hour. The more familiar leap year was introduced more than 2,000 years ago to ensure that the calendar year did not fall out of step with the time that the Earth takes to circle the sun. Adding a day to the end of February every four or so years does the job, because Earth orbits the sun every 365 and a quarter days. Leap seconds are a much more modern invention. In 1955, Louis Essen and Jack Parry at the NPL built the world’s first practical, high-precision caesium atomic clock. The device revolutionised timekeeping, and in 1967 the astronomical definition of a second, based on the rotation of the Earth, was abandoned. Ever since, the formal definition of one second has been 9,192,631,770 vibrations of the caesium atom. Atomic clocks are exceptionally stable and precise. Their timekeeping has become critical for modern computer systems, communications, satellites, trading systems and electricity grids. But the Earth’s rotation is far less reliable. Its spin is affected by the planet’s molten core, the shift of the oceans, global jet streams and other natural forces. Broadly, Earth’s rotation is slowing down: when an asteroid doomed the dinosaurs, a day lasted about 23 and a half hours. Because of this, officials have added 27 leap seconds since 1972 to ensure UTC is aligned with astronomical time. The strategy endured for more than 50 years until scientists spotted a fresh reason to fear technological mayhem. In the past decade, Earth’s rotation has sped up, meaning officials might have needed to add the first negative leap second, equivalent to lopping a second off UTC. The 30% probability of a negative leap second in the next decade brought the Versailles vote forward. “Leap seconds can be tricky enough to deal with,” said Shemar. Telecommunications, electricity grids and navigation systems used high-accuracy timing, he explained, but software updates could apply leap seconds at the wrong time, knocking networks out of sync. “After the leap second applied in 2012, there were some computer systems whose operating systems couldn’t cope with 61 seconds in a minute. The servers froze, they seized up. Systems went offline. And those are the sorts of failures that can happen with positive leap seconds,” Shemar said. Among the crashed websites were Reddit and LinkedIn. Separately, Qantas flights were hit with delays. Negative leap seconds come with even greater risks. “There could be software out there that hasn’t been tested on negative leap seconds because we’ve never had to apply one before,” Shemar said. To test all the computer systems that talk to one another around the world would cost companies a fortune. It was this concern that swung the vote. Historically, the UK has grumbled about canning leap seconds because of the link with Greenwich mean time. Russia has also opposed the move, citing concerns of the impact on its Glonass satellite navigation system. The IERS Earth Orientation Centre, in Paris, tracks changes in the Earth’s rotation and other movements that feed into UTC. The centre also issues notices when leap seconds must be added. Dr Christian Bizouard, the director of the centre, approved of the vote, but said it passed the decision to people far in the future. “It’s kind of a philosophical discussion, because if a leap hour happens, it won’t be for a very, very long time,” he said. “What we are doing is pushing back the decision.”

title: Pensioner pleads guilty to raping woman drugged by husband
summary: Graham Brougham, 74, was one of a number of men invited to sexually assault victim while she was unconscious
text: A man from Cheshire has pleaded guilty to the rape of a woman whose husband drugged her and invited other men to sexually assault her while she was unconscious. Graham Brougham, 74, pleaded guilty to rape at a hearing at Manchester Minshull Street crown court on Thursday afternoon. The husband, who cannot be named in order to protect the anonymity of his wife, has already admitted to more than 60 offences, and will be sentenced at a later date. The victim sat in the public gallery of the court as Brougham entered his guilty plea. She turned to watch him as he stood in the dock, while a relative sitting beside her held her hand throughout. Brougham, who was set to be the oldest defendant on trial, has been on bail throughout the proceedings, and Judge Greene again granted him bail before sentencing. However, addressing Brougham’s barrister, he said the defendant should not “be under any illusion”, as his “sentence will be custody, and a long time in custody”. Before his arrest Brougham, who lives in Northwich in Cheshire, had played in a 1970s tribute band and was a member of a walking football team. Two other men who were charged alongside the husband have also pleaded guilty at earlier hearings. Keith Fotheringham, 59, from Dundee, a former technician at the city’s university, admitted a number of offences earlier this year, and last month Sean Peers, 38, pleaded guilty to one count of assault by penetration. Ten men are due to stand trial at the same court, denying a range of offences including rape and attempted rape, which are alleged to have taken place between 2018 and November 2025. They are Philip Wild, 59, from Stockport; Jordan Wallace, 31, from Manchester; Alan Keelan, 42, from Manchester; Jonathan Kirk, 43, from Stockport; Robert Stewart, 70, from Stockport; Mohammed Sabir, 28, of no fixed abode; Richard Townsend, 37, from Heywood in Greater Manchester; Karl Lindsay, 55, from Taunton in Somerset; Daniel Rayner, 42, from Whitstable in Kent; and David Graves, 60, from Ilkeston in Derbyshire. A jury has already been sworn in, and the trial was due to get under way on Monday, but it has been delayed for legal reasons. The prosecution is now scheduled to begin its case in early November, with the trial set to conclude by the end of January next year.

title: Hegseth church allies backed plan for ‘public’ execution of Fort Hood shooter
summary: Leader of CREC church – whose pastors have advocated death penalty – says he ‘prefers public executions to private’
text: Donald Trump announced on Thursday he was cancelling Pete Hegseth’s recently announced plans to livestream a military execution – because “many very good and well-meaning people would rather not watch him die”. But there were some fans of Hegseth’s now-scotched idea: the rightwing religious figures who have long backed his career. Hegseth announced last week that the US public would be able to see the execution of Nidal Hasan, which is set for 3 December at Fort Hood, Texas. Hasan, a former army major and psychiatrist, killed 13 people and wounded 32 at Fort Hood in 2009. A military court sentenced him to death in August 2013. “We’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public,” Hegseth said. “It was a radical Islamist attack in uniform inside the ranks, and so he’s going to get a firing squad of soldiers – as it should be.” The de facto leader of Hegseth’s theocratic Communion of Reformed Evangelical Churches (CREC), Douglas Wilson, welcomed the announcement. Wilson, the Idaho pastor who co-founded CREC, has promoted capital punishment as biblically authorized for decades. Last Friday he told Religion News that he prefers “public executions to those conducted in the recesses of a prison somewhere in the middle of the night”, adding that “executions in the scriptures were public”. Wilson told the outlet that public executions can “turn into a circus”. Wilson told the Guardian that “I support the execution of Hasan, and prefer public executions to private”, adding: “I prefer the older forms, like a firing squad, as opposed to attempts to ‘medicalize’ it, as with the recent botched execution by injection in Tennessee.” He did stipulate that “the Pentagon has the responsibility to head off ghoulish behavior by some means”, but admitted: “That will be challenging with a live stream.” Wilson wrote that he had not spoken to Hegseth nor anyone in his department about the issue. Wilson and his religious allies are at odds with some other religious leaders, including Pope Leo and the archbishop to the US military, Timothy Broglio, both of whom have condemned Hegseth’s plans. But CREC pastors, whose church in Washington DC Hegseth attends, have for years advocated the death penalty for many perceived moral infractions including adultery, abortion and homosexuality, and a podcaster from Hegseth’s former church has repeatedly called for executions to be public. Several have expressed hostility to Muslims and Islam, with one calling Allah a “demon God”. “There was a consensus among the early Christian reconstructionists that the death penalty for certain crimes was part of the Old Testament that is still applicable, and that executions should be public,” said Julie Ingersoll, a professor of philosophy and religion at the University of North Florida, and the author of Building God’s Kingdom, a study of Christian reconstructionism, a movement with which Wilson has repeatedly identified. Ingersoll added: “I do think this is where Hegseth is getting this and, no, Wilson isn’t saying anything new.” The Guardian contacted the White House and the Pentagon for comment. An unidentified Department of Defense spokesperson wrote in an email response: “The secretary is correct. It will be livestreamed. Details will follow.” A ‘biblical republic’ Hegseth belongs to the CREC, and its senior pastors preach to his Washington congregation, Christ Kirk DC, as the Guardian reported in April. In a 2 March post on his blog, under the heading “A Proposal”, Wilson wrote: “The death penalty should be applied to violent criminals – murderers (Ex. 21:12), rapists and kidnappers (Ex. 21:16), abortionists (Ex. 21:22), and so on.” In his 2023 book Mere Christendom, Wilson wrote that when Moses “commanded a man to be executed for picking up sticks on the sabbath, that too was holy, righteous, and good”. He argued in the same book against letting modern governments execute blasphemers: “When you give the state power to punish a blasphemer, you are giving the state the power to blaspheme with impunity.” Wilson wrote about Hasan in the weeks after the shooting. In a 17 January 2010 post, he took up a military commentator’s view that Hasan’s statement that the Qur’an outranked the constitution was treason. The post affirmed that religious commands supersede the law of the state, but asserted that Hasan’s religion was mistaken. “Now of course, Hasan was mistaken, but this was a question of fact, not of principle,” Wilson wrote. “The word of God outranks Madison, et al, and if the Qur’an were the word of God, then the constitution should just sit down and listen for a minute.” CREC support Joshua Haymes hosts the Reformation Red Pill podcast, on which Hegseth has appeared, and was a pastoral intern at Hegseth’s former church in Tennessee. The Guardian reported in August 2025 that Haymes had proposed “death by a public firing squad wherein the accuser and witnesses partake in the firing”. He has returned to the subject since. In an episode dated 28 March, Haymes said of pornography producers: “Hang them in the streets. And I mean that. We need to bring back public executions.” In an episode uploaded last week, he said that “if we would just reinstitute public executions”, the number of killings in what he called high-density Black areas of major cities would “fall to the floor”. In an email response to a request for comment, Haymes reaffirmed all of these positions, saying that he supported the execution of Hasan, that “I do believe that child pornographers (those who produce and distribute child pornography) should be executed”, but that he “would stop short of capital punishment” for other pornographers. Asked about his comments on crime in “Black areas”, he wrote: “Right now, over 50% of homicides in America are committed by around 6% of the population. That is an astoundingly devastating statistic. And most of the violent crime is being done by a small subset of black Americans who are continually reoffending.” The Anti-Defamation League lists a similar claim in its hate symbols database, under the numeric codes “13/52” and “13/90”, which it calls “a shorthand reference to racist propaganda claims by white supremacists against African Americans to depict them as savage and criminal in nature”. According to the Southern Poverty Law Center, white supremacists “manipulate crime statistics in order to claim that nonwhite minorities, particularly African Americans, are far more crime-prone”, naming Jared Taylor of American Renaissance among the “white nationalist ideologues” who had “made considerable hay” from such figures. The Guardian reported in August 2025 that Haymes had endorsed Taylor’s views in a post on X. Taylor has long denied that he is a white supremacist, preferring to describe himself as a “race realist” or “white advocate”. In an emailed comment for prior Guardian reporting on his views, Haymes said: “I am not a white nationalist or white supremacist. My cousin is black, and my brother-in-law is Chinese, and I’m glad they’re here. I have no idea who that white nationalist is.” Hegseth’s announcement has stirred the wider Christian nationalist community. Last Friday, David Shannon, who as “Chocolate Knox” co-hosts CrossPolitic, a podcast the Guardian reported on in September 2025, reposted another user’s request for “all the Bible verses supporting public executions for capital crimes”. Ben Zornes told the Guardian that he is a pastor at Living Stones Reformed church, a church planted, or founded, by Christ Church Moscow. He wrote on 18 October 2018: “Rebellious sons, and unchaste daughters were a danger to covenantal faithfulness and thus were to be executed for the sake of the purity of the whole congregation.” He called efforts to abolish the death penalty “an example of us thinking we know better than God does”. Asked about the planned firing-squad execution of Hasan, Zornes wrote: “I do support the execution. I have concerns about making it a public spectacle, as I think public executions are for sober and mature societies, and ours is like a toddler.” He added: “A public execution should be solemn, and livestreaming it would compromise the gravity of the event, which is also why I am opposed to livestreaming church services.” But asked if he agreed with Douglas Wilson’s preference for public executions over private ones, Zornes replied: “I do.” Hegseth described Hasan as a “radical Islamist” when he announced the public execution, and CREC figures have frequently targeted the Islamic faith in their writings. Toby Sumpter, a CREC pastor in Moscow, Idaho, another co-host of CrossPolitic, wrote on 13 March 2025: “We can certainly begin by prohibiting public worship of false gods, legally suppressing Islam, Hinduism, etc.” On a 26 June 2025 episode of CrossPolitic titled “From 9/11 To a Muslim Mayor in NYC? The Rise of Islam in America”, Sumpter said Allah “is a real demon God”. On a 21 November 2025 episode he said Christians should “ask civil magistrates to outlaw mosques”. Haymes gave a 7 August episode the title “Christians MUST Support Banning Islam & Deporting Muslims”. In a 17 April debate with a Muslim man, he said: “No mosques, no calls to prayer, nothing like that.” Brooks Potteiger, the pastor of Christ Kirk DC and previously of Hegseth’s Tennessee church, said in a 30 August sermon that “the idols of Hinduism and Islam have rushed in to fill the void”. Sumpter, Shannon and Potteiger did not respond to requests for comment. ‘Turn death into a spectacle’ Experts say that, historically, executions were banned at least in part because they gave a platform for the executed to deliver any message they wanted. Michael Trotti is a professor of history at Ithaca College and the author of The End of Public Execution, a history of public executions in the American south. In an email, he said that in the north, executions were mostly moved inside prison walls from the mid-19th century due to “growing middle-class discomfort with the spectacles of death”, which “coarsened those who watched them” and “might even attract criminals rather than being something that would curb crime”. In the south, however, they remained popular until the end of the century. Eventually authorities “became convinced that these events were actually giving too much prominent, public authority to black condemned when they were asked if they had final words in front of massive mixed-race crowds, and to their pastors who were there to give final religious guidance and prayers/hymns”. “Public execution ended up being somewhat out of the control of any authority trying to enact it, for once the images are out there, they can serve many purposes. They can serve conservative purposes the state wants, but also radical purposes like the victims might want like being on a stage before a massive audience.” On Saturday, Pope Leo wrote on X that “the common good can be safeguarded and the requirements of justice can be met without recourse to capital punishment”. Leo did not mention Hasan, but the remarks were widely interpreted as being a response to Hegseth’s announcement. The previous evening the Vatican secretary of state, Cardinal Pietro Parolin, had said of the planned broadcast that it was “certainly unacceptable to turn death into a spectacle”. Archbishop Paul Coakley, the president of the US Conference of Catholic Bishops, reportedly called the plan “a barbaric promotion of a culture of death”. Walter Kim, the president of the National Association of Evangelicals, said a livestreamed execution “risks turning one of the state’s most solemn responsibilities into a public spectacle”.

title: Cost of balancing Great Britain’s power grid reaches nearly £50m a day
summary: Grid operator paying large sums to switch off windfarms in areas of excess electricity generation while turning on gas plants elsewhere
text: The cost of balancing Great Britain’s power grid has soared to near-record highs of almost £50m a day after windfarms were turned off because of bottlenecks in transmitting power around the country. The grid operator paid £47.9m on Wednesday to turn windfarms off in areas with an oversupply of electricity and turn gas plants on in areas where supplies were tight. The costs, which are levied on to household energy bills, included a £1.6m payment for one half-hour period, and were some of the highest recorded since the early months of the Ukraine crisis in 2022. They add to the increasing costs of balancing the grid, which reached a total of £505m in September alone, the highest monthly cost recorded, and are expected to reach £3.2bn over the next year. The costs underline the growing concerns over the pace of Great Britain’s £150bn power networks upgrade, which is failing to keep up with new renewable energy projects being connected to the grid. Overall, windfarms and hydropower plants with about 9 gigawatts of capacity were paid to not generate on Wednesday, according to the consultancy LCP Delta, enough to power more than 8m typical households. Instead, the grid operator was forced to pay for a string of gas and biomass plants to fire up and bought more electricity imports from Europe via high-voltage subsea power cables. The record costs have come to light days after the National Energy System Operator (Neso) was forced to call for “last resort” emergency assistance from its counterpart in France, which agreed to send last-minute power supplies to the UK on Monday and Friday last week. “The system overall wasn’t tight in terms of power supplies,” said Shivam Malhotra, the head of power trading at LCP Delta. “It’s the age-old story of a lack of infrastructure to transport power to where it’s needed, leading to lots of windfarms being turned off.” Typically, windfarms in Scotland are paid to turn off because there is not enough high-voltage cabling connecting the country to areas of growing electricity demand further south. “To resolve the energy needs in the south of the country Neso had to use one of their last resorts. It’s quite surprising for this time of year,” Malhotra said. During the summer Neso faced severe grid challenges when a high-pressure heat dome led to a drop in renewable energy output and surging electricity demand to power air conditioning and refrigerators. Neso was forced to bring in independent investigators to look into whistleblower claims that its staff were involved in a cover-up of a near-blackout during record high temperatures in late June. The accusations, which were raised in parliament last week by the shadow energy secretary, Claire Coutinho, included claims that senior bosses at Neso were “risking blackouts to protect Neso’s reputation”. Fintan Slye, Neso’s chief executive, told an industry conference on Wednesday that there would be “lessons to be learned” coming out of a review into that period by the industry regulator Ofgem. Asked how he thought Neso handled the situation, Slye said: “Through that period, no customers were disconnected [and] frequencies stayed within statutory limits. But undoubtedly, it was a really challenging period for the system and right across Europe we saw power systems … under strain. “I think the control room and teams that were in it did an absolutely superb job managing what was a really difficult situation through the week.” A Neso spokesperson said Great Britain’s energy supplies were “secure” during both calls for emergency assistance, and that the “separate incidents” were “not signs of a wider problem with Britain’s electricity system”. “In both cases, our control room responded quickly to changing conditions and used established tools to keep the system running securely,” they said. “While Neso continues to deliver savings through operational reforms and innovation, the single biggest opportunity to reduce balancing costs is the timely delivery of new infrastructure by transmission owners, which could halve balancing costs by the end of the decade.”

title: Repressive, secretive and highly militarised: Eritrea, the east African country facing UK visa ban threat
summary: Country has not had an election in 33 years and has withdrawn cooperation with UK on migrant returns
text: Eritrea, the east African country embroiled in a row with the UK over its refusal to accept the return of rejected asylum seekers and criminals, is considered one of world’s most secretive and repressive states, with reports of arbitrary detention and severe restrictions on freedom of expression, opinion and religion. Situated in the Horn of Africa and bordering Sudan, Ethiopia and Djibouti, it became a sovereign state after gaining independence from Ethiopia in 1993 following a 30-year war. The country is run by an authoritarian regime under Isaias Afwerki, who led separatist forces to defeat Ethiopian forces in 1991 and became president in 1993. He has served as president since independence and heads the People’s Front for Democracy and Justice, the country’s only legal political party. Eritrea has not held a national election since independence. A constitution that was ratified in 1997 by the constituent assembly has still not been implemented nearly three decades later. In 2001, the government shut down all independent newspapers after the publishing of an open letter by senior ruling party officials calling on the government to implement the constitution and hold elections. A highly militarised state, Eritrea runs a compulsory national service system that requires students to study at a military training centre in their final year of secondary school. They undergo military training and political education before working in either military units or civilian national service roles that can last decades. The repression and conscription has forced many Eritreans to risk harsh punishment for evading, deserting or escaping the military by fleeing the country. It is estimated that up to one-third of the Eritrean-born population lives abroad. Eritreans were the most common nationality arriving by small boat to the UK in the year ending June 2026. Earlier this year, Eritrea abruptly withdrew cooperation with the UK on migrant returns, and on Thursday the UK home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, said all Eritreans could be stopped from coming to the UK unless the country agreed to accept more rejected asylum seekers and criminals. Eritrea’s political, economic and social framework has been defined by a doctrine of economic self-reliance, with the country notably rejecting foreign aid. It was an Italian colony and parts of the country feature early to mid-20th-century Italian modernist architecture. The capital, Asmara, was inscribed as a world heritage site in 2017, with Unesco describing it as “an exceptional example of early modernist urbanism at the beginning of the 20th century and its application in an African context”. A multi-ethnic country, Eritrea is mainly made up of the Tigrinya people. Its extensive Red Sea coastline (1,388 miles) gives it a strategic position along the Red Sea corridor. The country has been in the spotlight in recent weeks because of fears of war with Ethiopia. Both countries have accused each other of aggression. Ethiopia has claimed Eritrean troops crossed up to 60km (37 miles) into Ethiopia’s northern Tigray region, while Eritrea has said the accusation is a fabrication to create a pretext for war. The escalation is linked to renewed fighting between Ethiopian government forces and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), an armed opposition group, in Tigray, which borders Eritrea. Ethiopia has accused Eritrea of supporting the TPLF, a claim that Eritrea has denied. On Tuesday, Ethiopian forces advanced to Zalambessa, a town on the border with Eritrea that was under Tigrayan rebel control.

title: Lisa Nandy ‘minded to intervene’ in Sky’s £1.6bn purchase of ITV
summary: Culture secretary’s move paves way for deeper scrutiny of deal that would create UK’s biggest commercial broadcaster
text: The culture secretary, Lisa Nandy, has said she is “minded to intervene” in Sky’s £1.6bn purchase of ITV, in a move that paves the way for deeper scrutiny of a deal that would create the UK’s biggest commercial broadcaster. Sky announced over the summer that it had reached a deal to buy ITV’s broadcasting and streaming arm, representing a big shift in the ownership of Britain’s public service media. Sky, which is owned by the US giant Comcast, sees the purchase as a chance to create a “UK-focused national streaming champion” that can survive in a media world dominated by Netflix, YouTube and Amazon Prime Video. Nandy said she was issuing her decision in relation to a series of “public interest considerations”. They included the need for free expression of opinion in news media, a “sufficient plurality of views” and a “sufficient plurality of persons with control of the media enterprises”. She said she also had to safeguard the availability of “a wide range of broadcasting, on-demand programmes or both, which … is of high quality and calculated to appeal to a wide variety of tastes and interests”. The move is a formal part of the takeover process. The companies now have five days to respond. Should Nandy decide to intervene in the process, it would trigger formal investigations into the deal by Ofcom, the media industry regulator, and the Competition and Markets Authority. With the TV industry under huge pressure as competition has increased from streamers, and audiences have switched to digital platforms such as YouTube, few in the industry believe the deal will be blocked. There have already been huge mergers across the media world as even big players believe they need greater scale to compete in a global marketplace. Netflix attempted to buy Warner Bros Discovery before it was eventually bought by Paramount in a mega $110bn (£85bn) acquisition. The new company, now called Skydance, will have David Ellison, the son of a billionaire tech mogul, at its helm. Nandy also threatened to intervene in that deal as the UK’s Channel 5 is also owned by Paramount. However, she eventually waved it through after securing significant concessions over its commitments to the UK and the content shown there. Under the UK guarantees, Paramount’s Channel 5 will continue to ‌operate as a public service broadcaster until the end of 2034. Channel 5 News will retain its editorial independence, remaining separate from other news operations covered by the merger – CBS News and CNN International.

title: Republican Susan Collins dismisses allegations of corruption as ‘completely false’
summary: Maine senator refutes claim from ex-Navatek CEO that he funded Collins’s Super Pac in exchange for naval contracts
text: Susan Collins, the US senator of Maine, has dismissed allegations that she traded federal contracts for campaign cash as “completely false” after it emerged the FBI examined the claims. Asked by a reporter about an ethics complaint filed last week by a Maine attorney, the Republican – currently campaigning to retain her seat ahead of November’s US midterm elections – said the allegations were recycled from 2020 and had been rejected by the Department of Justice, the FBI and the Federal Election Commission. “The allegations are completely false,” Collins said. She said the University of Maine, not the defense contractor Navatek, had asked her to back a research grant, and that she had never heard of the company. Its former chief executive, Martin Kao, she said, was “a crook” whom neither she, nor the university, knew about. “We have a picture of his meeting with me and with other people in my office that is many months before he ever made a single contribution,” she added. “He spun this story up again in the hopes that the judge would be lenient, or the prosecutor would be.” ProPublica reported in September that Kao, Navatek’s former president and CEO, told FBI agents and prosecutors that his company won millions in federal funding by bankrolling politicians, with Collins his most important patron. Kao, who is serving 87 months for fraud and campaign finance crimes, claimed the head of Collins’s Super Pac asked him for $500,000 in 2019. He claimed he then sent $150,000 through a shell company, and that Collins’s office later promised to secure $32m in naval contracts. ProPublica reported that the Senate allocated at least $10m that year based on Navatek’s proposals, funding Collins says she backed only because the University of Maine asked her to, but did not report that the full $32m was awarded. The outlet said it reviewed a trove of FBI evidence and thousands of pages of legal records, and interviewed dozens of people familiar with Navatek and the inquiry, and independently corroborated much of Kao’s account. Among the emails it cited was one in which the Super Pac chair, Scott Reed, replied “Very smart” to Kao’s shell company plan, and another asking for Kao’s phone number so Collins could thank him. ProPublica also reported that FBI agents sought to open a broader bribery investigation in 2024, which collapsed after Donald Trump returned to office and purged the bureau’s public corruption teams. No one in Collins’s orbit was charged. Kao declined to be interviewed, and Reed denied discussing Kao or Navatek with Collins or her staff. Pressed on why she would not welcome an ethics inquiry to clear her name, Collins said it was not up to her, and dismissed the complaint as the work of “partisan Democrats” and Valerie Adams, a lawyer in Maine “who lost her election” in the June primary to be district attorney. “I was never even interviewed because there was no evidence for it,” Collins said.

title: Top health official urged to recuse herself from private ADHD crackdown over ties to industry
summary: Exclusive: Four MPs raise conflict of interest concerns over Samantha Jones’s past links to a big provider of ADHD assessments
text: A senior civil servant should play no part in ministers’ crackdown on private attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and autism clinics because of her recent ties to the industry, MPs have said. Labour and Liberal Democrat MPs are demanding that Samantha Jones, the permanent secretary at the Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC), steps away from any role in plans to toughen regulation of the booming market in private neurodiversity assessments. They say Jones should not be involved because of her links to a company that is one of the biggest providers of NHS-funded neurodiversity assessments, which earned it £26m from the health service in England over the past six years. Ministers are drawing up plans for how to better regulate the “wild west” of private clinics offering assessment, diagnosis and treatment of ADHD and autism that has grown rapidly in recent years as people have struggled to access care via the NHS. The push comes after the government last week accepted the findings of a review by Prof Peter Fonagy, which raised concerns about the “consistency and quality” of assessments by private providers of neurodiversity services that had inbuilt “financial incentives” to diagnose and treat people. Jones is responsible for overseeing the implementation of government decisions on health policy. She would therefore be expected to advise ministers on how best to strengthen the regulation of private providers of ADHD and autism services. Yvette Cooper, the health secretary, has vowed to introduce a much tougher regime. Four MPs have called for Jones to recuse herself from any role in those decisions because of her previous ties to ADHD360, a provider of neurodiversity services. Her links to the private ADHD sector represent a serious conflict of interest, they claim. Jones was appointed as the permanent secretary on 22 April 2025. A month later, she was still the chair of and a director of and shareholder in the private care provider Keys Group when, on 16 May, it bought ADHD360, a clinic that has increased its NHS income considerably in recent years. At the time of the £22.5m purchase, Jones was also an operating partner in G Square Capital, the private equity company that owns Keys Group. She sold her shares in Keys Group and resigned her roles there and at G Square Capital before she started at the DHSC on 16 June. Jones has already recused herself from involvement in the department’s decision over whether to extend Palantir’s £330m, seven-year contract with the NHS because of her past work for the lobbyists Carnall Farrar, which advised Palantir regarding the contract. MPs believe her tenure at Keys Group could represent a conflict of interest. Ben Coleman, a Labour MP on the health and social care committee, said: “People will want to feel reassured that future regulation of private ADHD and autism assessments is beyond reproach. Given her recent close involvement with ADHD360, I would encourage Ms Jones to recuse herself from that work, as she has done over Palantir, to avoid any perception of a conflict of interest.” In June, Jones apologised after she was reprimanded by the Civil Service Commission for breaching lobbying rules by failing to ask the (now defunct) Advisory Committee on Business Appointments for prior approval before undertaking work for four healthcare companies. Helen Morgan, the Liberal Democrats’ health spokesperson, said: “Given Sam Jones oversaw the multimillion-pound acquisition of ADHD360 just weeks before entering the Department of Health, ministers must ensure she recuses herself immediately, just as she has over Palantir.” Jones, 55, was widely admired in the NHS when she ran West Hertfordshire NHS trust in 2013-15. After a role with NHS England, she began working in private healthcare. Boris Johnson as prime minister handed her a key role in Downing Street in 2021. She returned to private health in 2023 and by 2023-24 had paid roles or shareholdings in 13 health or consultancy organisations. Clive Lewis, the Labour MP for Norwich South, said Jones’s deep involvement in private healthcare meant she should not have been made DHSC permanent secretary in the first place, saying: “It just defies logic that anyone thought it was a good idea. Surely this must have come up during her recruitment process?” Jones did not answer questions put by the Guardian. The NHS has paid ADHD360 just over £26m for its services since 2020, according to figures supplied by the Tussell public expenditure database. “When it comes to the government’s response to the [Fonagy] review, there should be no suggestion that the top NHS official is being influenced by any past or current links to a major private provider of NHS ADHD services,” said Stella Creasy, the Labour MP for Walthamstow. “This issue is too sensitive and complex to permit any conflicts of interest. As a result the permanent secretary should recuse herself from this area of policy.” David Rowland, the director of the Centre for Health and the Public Interest thinktank, said: “The permanent secretary at the department which has responsibility for regulating private ADHD providers appears to have a conflict of interest in this area and so may struggle to remain impartial when it comes to implementing the recommendations made by Prof Fonagy.” A DHSC spokesperson said: “There is no conflict of interest. The permanent secretary has appropriately declared all interests, in this post and when she was a non-executive director [of the DHSC]. She resigned from all her private sector posts before taking on the permanent secretary role at the department.”

title: Just as Saint Nige thought it was safe to reappear, along comes pesky ITV | John Crace
summary: How dare the channel reveal more racism and bigotry within Reform just as he was planning a press conference?
text: Sometimes the world can be very unfair. As though life is just one cruel joke. How else to make sense of everything? For when the history books come to be written, Nigel Farage will go down as one of the century’s unluckiest politicians. Poor Nige. All he has ever wanted is a better Britain. A country united in a shared vision where everyone gets along with one another. Where people of all faiths and none look out for each other. Where men and women of all colours are treated as equals. Where Nige can teach the world to sing in perfect harmony. So why do so many bad things keep happening to such a good person? Where’s the justice in that? How come Nige has been given a lead role in the rewrite of Little Britain’s Book of Job. Nige as a latter day Old Testament prophet put on Earth to show us all the value of eternal suffering. Because Nige is a decent man. The very best of us. And yet time and again he is made to feel pain. No more so than in the last few months. First there was the money. Few would have batted an eyelid if he had been given £5m by the RNLI. For all he has done to support the work that unpaid volunteers do in rescuing all people in trouble on the sea. Let’s face it, a modern day ministry doesn’t pay for itself and no demigod-like politician can expect to get by on less than £1m a year. Those houses and bottles of champagne aren’t going to pay for themselves. Yet because the £5m came from a Thai crypto-billionaire, suddenly everyone was asking difficult questions. Anyone would think Reform might have crypto-friendly policies. Then there was the Channel 4 sting. And yet again our Messiah was the innocent victim of an establishment plot. Compared to Nige, Jesus had it easy in Holy Week. How could he be expected to realise that two associates whom he had barely known for years might allegedly be trying to secure an illegal donation from overseas? And what were the chances that Nige might be caught on camera giving considered responses as part of a conversation he hadn’t even been listening to? Some days you just can’t buy a break. On Thursday morning, Farage had been scheduled to host a press conference near Southend where we were promised he would spread goodwill to all men with yet another major policy announcement. Only for the event to be cancelled late on Wednesday evening. The official reason given was that Reform didn’t want to clash with the fifth anniversary of the murder of the former Southend MP David Amess. Yet more bad luck for Nige. Imagine only being given five years’ notice to plan your schedule. Or perhaps there was another reason for the cancellation. One related to another sting, this time by ITV, that had sent undercover journalists into the Reform operations room and uncovered the only bad apples in the entire organisation. Again, what were the chances of finding racists and misogynists attracted to a party that loved women and people of all colours? How could this ever have happened? The chances were slimmer than winning the EuroMillions lottery. And surely had nothing to do with Nige’s would-be chancellor, Honest Bob Jenrick, saying he would consider allowing soldiers to be able to blow up migrants in small boats in the Channel. What’s wrong with killing a few thousand people for the sake of a greater good? The country is just too woke for its own good sometimes. Then there’s the wannabe home secretary Zia Yusuf, who is on a one-man mission to round up all immigrants – even women and children – and send them back to countries where they may be killed. So again we are left with the question. Why are so many racists attracted to Reform? Let’s take Dean Miller. A vetted Reform councillor from Bromley who was filmed campaigning during the Makerfield byelection. Quite how extensive the vetting process was is anyone’s guess. “Tell us, Dean. Are you in any way prejudiced against people of colour?”. “Absolutely not. I just don’t want them anywhere near me.” “That’s great. Thanks Dean. Welcome to Reform.” Anyway, Dean was caught on camera saying that it was kill or be killed with illegal immigrants. “They’re all fucking black and they’re like animals,” he said. “I’m not a racist, but you know what I mean.” Yes, Dean. We know exactly what you mean. And he couldn’t have been clearer about his intentions towards the king. Charles was a Muslim and deserved to be beheaded. It’s a view. When Miller was asked for a comment before the film is aired this weekend, his defence was that he had been on heavy medication at the time. And suddenly that all made sense. Because I too am on regular medication both for my psyche and for my heart. So I chose to reread the common known side effects of one of my drugs. And there among the small print about causing faster breathing, fever, muscle stiffness and drowsiness, one thing stood out. “Never take in the presence of a black person or royalty. Can make you prone to racist outbursts and in extreme cases can provoke urges to kill the monarch.” I guess I must just have been extremely lucky so far. Miller was not the only one to have been caught out this way. Others – also apparently vetted – declared that all foreigners were parasites, that the UK should have a 1% limit on all immigrants and made disgusting comments about a female Reform councillor. Raymond Dunning said he was so far-far right it was unbelievable. Then there were those who thought it best to try to sound moderate until after they had been elected. Then the gloves would come off and they could give foreigners hell. And in the middle of all this we have the saintly Nige. Scratching his head and wondering why all this was happening to him again. He hadn’t come in to politics to stir grievance and division. He was the god of love, the man of peace. Others among the Reform elite knew exactly where the blame lay. And it wasn’t with the innocent men who had been caught saying the only racist and sexist words they had ever said. Dicky Tice and the former Tory MP Ben Bradley were pointing the finger at ITV for daring to do its job properly. It was outrageous they had recorded Reform councillors going about their everyday jobs. Every man and woman was entitled to be as racist as they like in the comfort of their workplace. For now, Nige was determined to rise above it. He would survive. He was doing God’s work. Just a shame that God didn’t seem to like him much.

title: ‘The valley has been left behind’: how one of California’s poorest areas became its toughest political battleground
summary: Rising costs and threatened healthcare benefits are testing voters’ loyalty to Trump as Democrat Randy Villegas challenges David Valadao
text: Vanessa Martinez used to work two jobs to make ends meet. Now she works three. In another era, the 26-year-old from California’s hardscrabble Central valley could have been a poster child for the American Dream, the sort of ambitious, up-by-her-bootstraps personality that politicians of both major parties like to highlight. Forced to fend for herself from the age of 18 and with no family money to fall back on, Martinez put herself through cosmetology school so she could work as a hairdresser. Now she’s studying again to qualify as a funeral director. When she’s not cutting hair, she has a job picking up bodies for a funeral home and another helping a large building company line up its subcontractors. Still, it is not enough, because the federal student grants she thought she could rely on have dried up and her government health insurance coverage is in danger of disappearing, too. Meanwhile, the price of day-to-day living – rent, groceries, fuel, and repayment of her student loans – keeps going up. “I’m making the most I’ve ever made, and I’m probably the brokest I’ve ever been,” she said. Martinez lives in one of the poorest and, this year, most competitive congressional districts in the country, California’s 22nd, and both parties have been courting voters like her aggressively. Her county, Tulare, voted for Donald Trump by a margin of 59% to 38% over Kamala Harris in 2024, thanks in part to the district’s majority Latino population, which shifted markedly to the right in the hope of seeing their economic fortunes improve. Polls now show that Trump’s popularity has fallen as dramatically locally as it has nationally – one, taken earlier this year, showed his approval ratings in the district underwater by 15 percentage points. Democrats in California have also redrawn the electoral map to tilt more in their direction. But that does not necessarily spell defeat for David Valadao, the incumbent Republican congressman, who has overcome a registration advantage for the Democrats in six of his last seven elections. Valadao likes to tell voters that he is a proud native son of the valley and an even-tempered pragmatist who works collegially with both parties to bring federal dollars to the district. Yes, he conceded in a candidates’ debate last week that the Iran war has caused a temporary, painful spike in prices, starting with the price of gas, which in Tulare now averages more than $6 a gallon. But he suggested that the war would be over soon, and argued that the surest way to bring prices down was through deregulatory measures that he and his fellow Republicans champion to increase the supply of food, oil and gas. Valadao’s Democratic challenger, Randy Villegas, has a dramatically different viewpoint, one that bucks the received wisdom that valley voters prefer their politicians moderate and soft-spoken. The entire political system is corrupted by corporate money, he says, and will never deliver for the agricultural, heavily working-class Central valley unless it is reformed from the ground up. “The valley has been left behind by both parties, in Sacramento and in Washington DC,” Villegas says. “We deserve better than the scraps these politicians give us.” Villegas is also a native son, who started out working in his family’s car repair shop in Bakersfield, the district’s biggest city, before pursuing an education and becoming a community college professor. He sees nothing moderate in Valadao’s recent voting record, which includes casting one of the decisive votes for Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act with its $1.1tn in tax cuts and steep reductions in government healthcare and other public assistance programs. “There’s nothing moderate about ripping health insurance from 70,000 of his constituents,” Villegas thundered at a crowded rally in Bakersfield last weekend, where he shared a stage with Bernie Sanders, the progressive Vermont senator. “There’s nothing moderate about voting six times to approve the war in Iran. There’s nothing moderate about tripling ICE’s budget …” Villegas’s fighting spirit resonates with Martinez, because she, like many valley residents, feels she has hit a breaking point. Her brother, who also works in the funeral business in Tulare, voted for Trump all three times that he ran for the White House. But she feels that was always asking for trouble. Voters who put their faith in Trump, she said, especially Latinos, were “licking the boot that will stomp them” and paying the price now. A few weeks ago, Martinez lost a federal Pell grant that previously paid for her community college classes. She is alarmed and demoralized by immigration enforcement raids that are breaking up families all over the district – an issue with particular resonance for her as her construction worker father was caught without papers and deported to Mexico in 2015. Now she is afraid of being kicked off Medi-Cal, California’s version of Medicaid, and having to pay out of pocket for the chronic diabetes she has lived with since she was 15. Type 2 diabetes is a widespread condition in the Central valley, especially among working-class Latinos, who often cannot afford the fresh fruit and vegetables grown in the region in great abundance. She lost her mother to the disease at 62. “I’m in the funeral industry, and I’ve seen the death certificates,” Martinez says. “There’s a lot of cancer, especially among farm workers exposed to pesticides. And a significant number have diabetes. You see it again and again in box 14, which lists underlying conditions … It’s cheaper to go to McDonald’s and eat a $5 meal than to make a salad at home.” Medi-Cal has hardly been a smooth ride for Martinez – she likened it to being served cereal without milk. She says she had to fight for two years before the program would reimburse her for needles for her insulin shots. She continues to fight for test strips to monitor her blood sugar. Now that she is in danger of losing her coverage altogether, she is stocking up on medication and getting her lab work up to date. It’s an approach that thousands of valley residents are taking as they remain unsure if they will keep or lose their coverage in the coming months. California’s 22nd has the highest percentage of Medicaid recipients of any congressional district in the country – close to two-thirds – and clinics report being inundated with appointment requests. Even doctors and health administrators say they have no idea who will stay covered – Villegas’s figure of 70,000 losing benefits is just one of many estimates. “There are a lot of unknowns,” said Raul Ayala, a medical director with the Adventist Health network of clinics. “These patients may be in cancer treatment or awaiting surgery … I’m pretty sure there are going to be exceptions, but I don’t know how that is going to turn out.” Ayala and other experts expect cuts to Medicaid to deter people from seeking mammograms, blood tests and other wellness checks in a district where doctors are already in short supply and preventive care is an area they have spent years fighting to improve. Hospitals now expect to see a lot more routine cases coming through their emergency rooms, which by law cannot turn away patients whether they have health insurance or not. “All of that puts a strain on patients, but also on the business side of healthcare,” said Jevon Price, who serves on the county healthcare board in Tulare. “We’re telling hospitals: prepare to not be funded for what we will be requiring you to do.” If Valadao does lose his seat, political observers say healthcare is likely to be the decisive issue in a year when Republicans are on the defensive all around. Villegas is certainly pushing the issue as hard as he can. “Nobody should have to fight cancer and their congressman at the same time,” he tells audiences. In response, Valadao’s campaign has sought to paint Villegas as a far-left candidate out of step with local sensibilities. When Mike Johnson, the speaker of the House, swung through the district late last month, he declared: “The Marxists are on the march to our institutions. And now the institution they have in their crosshairs is the United States Congress.” Such rhetoric works with Republican partisans, an outspoken and significant segment of the district electorate. “Villegas will tax you dry,” warns a homemade sign stapled to an electricity pole in Hanford, the town where Valadao grew up as a dairy farmer and still lives. Other, less ideological voters say the most immediate differences between the two candidates are in style and energy. Valadao, far from a natural public speaker, has not held an in-person town hall in over a decade and tends to prefer closed-door meetings with constituents and donors. Villegas, by contrast, has an easy touch with voters, whether he is knocking on their doors, as he often does between events, or addressing hundreds of them at once. His campaign knows turnout will be crucial in a district where many working-class voters are disengaged from politics – it’s more common, in smaller towns, to see a Jesus placard than a lawn sign for a congressional candidate – and need a reason to see this election differently. “Randy is the hardest-working candidate we have ever worked with,” said Jorge Contreras, state director of the Working Families party, which is championing Villegas and four other progressive congressional candidates in California in November’s general election. Villegas defines himself as a populist, not a leftist. He refuses to take corporate political action committee money, even if it means relying on individual donations averaging about $50 – or alienating the Democratic party establishment. Jasmeet Bains, his more conventionally centrist primary challenger who lost despite being championed by the party leadership in Washington, has yet to endorse him. “I’m running on the power of the many against the power of their money,” Villegas says. “The Democrats should be the party of the working class. And the only way we transform that is by electing leaders who stand up for the working class and for working people.” Villegas has Martinez’s vote, but she worries what might happen if he does end up in Washington. Valadao, she remembered, also campaigned as someone who would fight hard for the valley’s interests, only to succumb to pressure from his party to approve the war in Iran, trade tariffs, and other Trump policies linked to the sharply rising cost of living. “A lot of politicians get into this because they want to make a difference,” she said. “I don’t know what changes them.” Martinez is sanguine about what she can expect for her own future – a job with health insurance, perhaps, but not home ownership, which feels entirely out of reach now that coastal Californians stung by dizzyingly high housing costs in Los Angeles and San Francisco are moving inland and pushing prices higher in communities like hers. Her expectations of a member of Congress are similarly muted. “I want someone who can at least fake that he cares about us,” she says, only half joking. “My friends and I know what’s at stake … I’m really hoping Randy Villegas is the change we want.”

title: Milei adviser claims UK being ‘colonised by Islam’ as Falklands row grows
summary: Santiago Caputo cites election of Sagal Abdi-Wali as MP and calls UK a threat to the west in post shared by Argentina’s president
text: The chief adviser to Argentina’s president, Javier Milei, has cited the election of Sagal Abdi-Wali to the UK parliament as evidence of the Islamisation of Britain and further reason for Argentina to take sovereignty over the Falkland Islands. In a post on social media, Santiago Caputo, who is reportedly taking a key role in Argentina’s strategy over the Falklands, suggested that the taking of the south Atlantic islands was necessary to prevent the “interference of an Islamic state” in the region. Milei shared Caputo’s post on the social media platform X. The intervention from Buenos Aires comes at a moment of heightened tension between Argentina and the UK over the sovereignty of the British overseas territory, which is 300 miles off the South American coastline. Labour’s Abdi-Wali was elected as the MP for Holborn and St Pancras in London this month, seeing off a challenge from the Green party leader, Zack Polanski. She took her seat in parliament on Monday. Milei has sought to criminalise executives involved in the Falkland Islands’ nascent oil industry and has threatened to target the fishing sector on which the islands’ economy depends. Argentina has long sought sovereignty over the islands. The intensity of Argentinian pressure relating to the Falklands is at a level that UK officials say has not been seen since the war 44 years ago that followed the invasion ordered by the then Argentinian dictator, Gen Leopoldo Galtieri. The 74-day conflict in 1982 ended with the surrender of the Argentinian forces and cost the lives of 649 of their military personnel, 255 British military personnel and three Falkland Islanders. This week, Andy Burnham restated the UK’s position that it would respect the wish of the 3,600 islanders to remain British, and the government announced its intention to protect the interests of businesses working in the Falklands. The Guardian revealed that the Foreign Office had written to Interpol seeking assurance that the law enforcement agency would not respond favourably to requests for the detention of individuals working in the Falklands. In his statement on X, Caputo – who has worked for Milei since 2021 – wrote that the “United Kingdom was, in many ways, the cradle of modern western civilisation” but that it now posed a threat to the west. He wrote: “Seeing the United Kingdom being colonised by Islam is not only an imminent risk to the cause of the west as a whole, but also a historical tragedy for those of us who defend the ideas of liberty. “This is yet another reason why Argentina must firmly project itself toward the south Atlantic and reclaim the Las Malvinas [Argentina’s name for the Falklands]. Given the strategic geopolitical importance the south Atlantic will assume in the coming decades, the west cannot afford the encroachment of an Islamic state within that sphere of influence. Reclaiming the Malvinas is not merely a national cause, it is a cause for the west.” Caputo accompanied his post with an image of Abdi-Wali, a former child refugee from Somalia, being sworn into parliament. Under the image, Javier Negre, a rightwing Spanish journalist, commented: “Here is a Somali Muslim woman taking her oath of office on the Qur’an in the English parliament. She has taken the seat formerly held by Prime Minister Keir Starmer. Islam is steadily gaining more power in the country.” In a 2013 referendum, 99.8% of the Falkland Islands’ residents voted to remain a British territory, with only three votes against.

title: Neanderthal remains may be earliest human ancestor find killed by a spear
summary: Adult excavated in an Iraqi Kurdistan cave died more than 70,000 years ago and bears ‘kill shot’ shoulder wound
text: A smooth round hole in the shoulder blade of a Neanderthal who died more than 70,000 years ago may be the oldest evidence so far of a human ancestor being killed by a wooden spear. Archaeologists spotted the distinctive injury after excavating skeletal remains of the adult and other Neanderthals from under nearly 8 metres of rock and sediment in the Shanidar cave in Iraqi Kurdistan. At least five Neanderthals were buried at the same spot over several years, in a depression no larger than a fridge that ran behind a huge boulder near the entrance to the cave. Some of the bodies appear to have been laid on top of others that were still decomposing. “They’re coming back to the same spot to place bodies over a number of years or several decades and that’s really quite unusual in in the Neanderthal archaeological record,” said Dr Emma Pomeroy, a biological anthropologist at the University of Cambridge. “It suggests there’s some kind of meaningful behaviour in depositing the dead there.” Researchers found only partial remains of the injured Neanderthal, an adult aged about 45. The left shoulder blade that bears the wound was found with seven teeth, several ribs and fragments, and a near complete right hand that was leaning against the boulder. Close inspection of the shoulder blade revealed three fractures spreading out from the 1.5cm-wide hole and fragments of bone that filled the wound. The shards were probably punched out of the thin bone when the spear hit, the scientists said. The circular shape of the hole and the pattern of bone damage strongly suggest a wound inflicted by a wooden spear striking the body from the front.But whether it was a hunting accident or an intentional attack – a brutal jab from a foe, perhaps – is impossible to know. Pomeroy said the position of the wound and the force needed to push the spear through the chest, where it would have punctured the lung and probably severed arteries before punching out of the shoulder blade, pointed to a “kill shot” directed at the heart. “I don’t think that’s something you do accidentally,” she said. The spear wound was almost certainly lethal, but the individual was in bad shape before the fatal blow. Examination of the teeth revealed a lower incisor split vertically, leaving only half in place, its neighbours twisted inwards, according to details published in Scientific Reports. “You’d need quite a severe hit in the face to split a tooth like that and to rotate the others,” said Pomeroy. “They might well have needed help because they would have been in terrible pain.” The split tooth was caked in hardened plaque that would have taken at least a year to build up. Chris Hunt, the emeritus professor at Liverpool John Moores University, who co-authored the paper, said Neanderthals at Shanidar were taking ibex as their main prey and could have used wooden spears shaped like modern javelins to kill the animals. Because plant material decomposes so easily, very few wooden objects survive from prehistory, but timber spears from about 200,000 years ago have been discovered in Germany, preserved in waterlogged ground. The pointed end of a rounded wooden spear discovered in Clacton-on-Sea in 1911 is the oldest known at over 400,000 years old. Last week, scientists in Spain described hundreds of wooden imprints and artefacts that show Neanderthals embraced woodwork, making trays, plates, tripods, spears and other items. But proof of fatal skirmishes is harder to find in fossils: we may never know how the wounded Neanderthal at Shanidar died. “Conceivably it was a hunting accident,” Hunt said. “We can’t, however, rule out that purposeful interpersonal violence was involved.”

title: Holdout juror in Lindsay Clancy trial gives first interview since mistrial
summary: Michael Desronvil tells Fox News he never had reasonable doubt Clancy was guilty but didn’t back up his claims
text: Michael Desronvil, the sole holdout juror in the Lindsay Clancy trial has spoken in his first interview since a mistrial was declared. Desronvil spoke of “tense deliberations” in the jury room, and about how his strong Christian faith helped prepare him for those discussions. He also said he never had any reasonable doubt that Clancy was guilty of first-degree murder, adding there was “a lot of evidence to back up my claim”, although he refused to share it during an interview on Thursday on Fox News. “I made my decision, as far as with the case, based strictly on the evidence that was presented to me, and then the hearing, and paying attention, observing throughout the whole trial,” he said. “There were moments that were tense, as we were deliberating.” The jury of nine women and three men ultimately voted 11-1 to acquit Clancy after seven days of deliberations. The Massachusetts mother admitted strangling her three children, Cora, five; Dawson, three; and eight-month-old Callan, to death in January 2023, but pleaded not guilty by reason of insanity. Judge William Sullivan of Plymouth county superior court declared a mistrial on 4 September, and prosecutors have not yet announced if they will seek to try Clancy again. As the lone holdout, Desronvil became the subject of intense scrutiny after the trial, once his identity became known. Kevin Reddington, Clancy’s lead defense attorney, said he “stole seven weeks of the life of these other jurors”, and that his client was “robbed by this man”. Earlier this month Sullivan rejected Reddington’s motion to override the deadlocked jury’s vote and declare Clancy not guilty. Desronvil’s interview on Thursday, during which he read a Bible passage and maintained that “constantly praying” had guided him through 38 hours of jury deliberations, was his first since the trial. He previously released a statement in which he said he never had any doubt about Clancy’s guilt, and said he “kept getting cut off” as he tried to explain different possible theories as the jury mulled its verdict. The Fox host Kayleigh McEnany asked Desronvil if he felt “listened to” during the deliberations. “No,” he replied. “I definitely listened, but some moments in that deliberation room felt like that decisions were being swayed towards one way.” He said he was struck by “how methodical Lindsay was in the execution of the children, that was really big for me”, and that he was affected by the 911 call that Clancy’s husband Patrick made after he discovered their bodies in the couple’s home in Duxbury. The call was played to jurors but has not been publicly released. “It was surreal. You know, hearing the pain in his voice, hearing the desperation from that clip, it was surreal,” Desronvil said. He rejected claims made by Reddington after the trial, which included that Desronvil was biased against people with mental illness, and that he made a false statement under oath by providing untruthful answers in his jury questionnaire. “I answered the questionnaire truthfully,” he said. NBC 10 Boston reported that Desronvil was charged in 2021 with assaulting his then wife. The charge was later dismissed. “There was no physical abuse, emotional abuse, financial abuse.” Desronvil, who has a new partner and a young daughter, said he had been harassed at home by the media, and had surveillance footage of reporters rifling through his mail, and looking through his windows. He said police had to escort his fiancee home one night. “Of course I’ve been scared,” he said but added he had not received any threats of physical harm. He said he was not on social media, did not follow the news, and had “no idea” the Clancy case was as big as it was. The interview concluded with Desronvil accompanying McEnany to a memorial playground in Duxbury dedicated to the victims. “The focus has to be on the children,” he said. “People need to stand up for what’s right.”

title: Tech market sell-off deepens amid fears over US inflation and AI debt
summary: Chip makers and tech investors such as Samsung and SoftBank plunge as potential interest rate hikes spook markets
text: An accelerating sell-off of AI-linked shares has hit global markets, as fears over rising inflation and future interest rate hikes spooked traders already wary of the heavily indebted sector. South Korea’s benchmark Kospi 200 index, which is heavily skewed towards the companies that make memory chips, fell more than 8% overnight to a six-month closing low, triggering circuit breakers that brought trading to a halt at various points. Some of those semiconductor stocks, such as SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics, plunged nearly 11% and 9.5% respectively. The index closed at a six-month low, down 8.1%. Meanwhile, Japan’s Nikkei 225 dropped by 4.9% on Thursday, after an 11% slump in the memory chip maker Kioxia and a 10% drop in SoftBank, a big investor in the ChatGPT owner, OpenAI. The falls followed a slide on Wall Street during the previous day’s session, where the Nasdaq Composite fell by 1.9% and the S&P 500 dropped 1.1%, its worst performance since July. US stocks fell further when trading resumed on Thursday. The Nasdaq dropped another 1.4% at the start of trading, with Dell, which makes datacentre servers, and Coherent, which manufactures components for AI datacentres, leading the early fallers. The sell-off came after US data on Wednesday showed stateside inflation jumped to a higher-than-expected 3.7% in September, marking the fastest increase in prices since the consumer price index (CPI) rate hit a three-year peak of 4.2% in May. Fresh data on Thursday showing US producers increased their prices by 6.3% year on year in September – the sharpest rise since December 2022 – added to inflationary jitters. The figures have rattled investors who are now expecting fresh interest rate increases by the US Federal Reserve, with some punters pricing in another increase as soon as the end of the month. “Markets have just had an incredibly tumultuous 24 hours, as a strong US CPI print was then followed up with mounting fears around the AI trade,” Deutsche Bank analysts led by Jim Reid said. Worryingly, the figures showed this was not about fuel costs, which have been pushed up by geopolitical tensions including the ripple effects from the US war on Iran. Reid said: “This wasn’t just an energy surge driving prices higher, as there were broad-based moves across the consumer basket.” The sell-off follows warnings from the International Monetary Fund, which said this week that the threat of an AI share price crash rippling out across global markets was putting world financial stability at risk. “The consequences of an AI correction could be global,” the IMF said. Aside from the US, Asian markets would be most exposed, with the UK and eurozone potentially more insulated – although investors with US holdings would be hit. The latest jitters hit China, where the Shanghai Shenzhen CSI 300 slipped by as much as 2.4%, marking the lowest level since August 2025. In Taiwan, one of the world’s leading chip makers and Asia’s most valuable company, TSMC, fell 2% despite reporting its sixth straight quarter of profits. European stocks also came under pressure, with Germany’s DAX down 0.36% in afternoon trading and the Italian FTSE MIB dropping by 1.3%.
