title: Labour councils told to end agreements with Greens who do not condemn ‘Zionism is racism’ policy
summary: Party chair calls on Labour groups to end local deals if Green councillors do not reject motion attacked as ‘antisemitic’
text: Labour councils who share power with the Greens have been told to terminate agreements if their Green partners do not condemn the party’s new “Zionism is racism” policy. Bridget Phillipson, the Labour chair, said groups working with Green party politicians must review their agreements and end them unless they reject the controversial motion, which Andy Burnham has called “antisemitic”. The policy, which was adopted at the Green party conference in Brighton at the start of the month, equates Zionism, the movement for a Jewish state, with racism. It also rejects a two-state solution and calls for Israel to be replaced by a single Palestinian state “with equal rights for all”. The Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC) said on Thursday it had written to the Green party of England and Wales to seek more information about the motion “and assess its practical implications and potential impact”. Several individuals and groups had said they planned to contact the watchdog to argue that the new policy risked breaching equality laws. On Wednesday, Burnham ruled out Labour having a partnership with the Greens. Asked about the motion during prime minister’s questions, Burnham said: “It is wrong. It is antisemitic, and this side of the house will have nothing to do with it.” Burnham went on to state that Labour would not “support a partnership with a party that holds [the] position that has recently been adopted”. Giving further details of Labour’s response to the motion, Phillipson said Greens who were working with Labour in local government would be asked “to make clear that they reject this position and to call on their national leadership to reconsider” the policy. She added: “We have asked local Green groups to respond as a matter of urgency. Where they are unable to provide that assurance, Labour will bring any such local arrangement to an end. This isn’t an issue of party politics, it’s about doing what is right and upholding the values anyone holding public office should share. “The Labour party fought hard to address antisemitism within our own party and ensure it had no place in our politics. We have a responsibility to uphold those same standards in our relationships with other parties.” Responding to the announcement, a Green party spokesperson said: “For the Labour government to conflate criticism of Israel with antisemitism is disappointing and wrong. Trying to tell local parties what to do and who they can work with is undemocratic. “Whilst Labour continue to try to meddle in our internal democracy, arm a genocide and lock up protesting pensioners, we will not take lectures from them.” The Guardian understands that local Green party councillors are unlikely to face disciplinary measures if they do condemn the motion, as the party has a highly decentralised structure and no whipping system. Several MPs and the former leader Caroline Lucas have already stated their opposition, and dissent about policy is tolerated. Southwark Greens have already disowned the policy to maintain a coalition with the Liberal Democrats. The binding anti-Zionism policy motion was passed on 4 October by 1,022 votes to 813. The 1,022 votes represented 0.4% of the Green party membership. Four of the Greens’ five MPs opposed the policy, while the group representing European Green parties expressed dismay at the move, which runs counter to their support for a two-state solution for Israel and Palestine. Zack Polanski, the Green party leader, abstained from the vote to campaign in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, which he lost. In a statement on Thursday, the EHRC said it had received complaints about the policy breaching the Equality Act, “including concerns that Jewish people could face discrimination because of their beliefs following the adoption of the motion”. It added: “We recognise that many Jewish people will be feeling vulnerable following the party’s motion. Political parties, like all duty-bearers, must comply with the Equality Act and take steps to avoid discrimination including on the grounds of race, religion or belief.” Affected councils Derbyshire Dales Lib Dem-led coalition Broadland Lib Dem-led coalition West Suffolk Labour-led coalition Arun Lib Dem-led coalition Havant Labour-led coalition Lewes Green-led coalition Rother Coalition led by local independent group Runnymede Coalition with Lib Dems, Greens and local independent group Wealden Green-led coalition West Oxfordshire Lib Dem-led coalition West Sussex Lib Dem-led coalition North Somerset Lib Dem-led coalition West Devon Independent-led coalition Monmouthshire Labour minority-led coalition Coventry Labour-led confidence and supply agreement with the Greens Stafford Labour-led coalition Warwick Green-led coalition Sheffield Labour-led coalition

title: Jim Bakker obituary
summary: US television evangelist who preached the ‘prosperity gospel’ before being brought down by a sex scandal and imprisoned for fraud
text: Jim Bakker, who has died aged 86, was one of the most popular and influential US television evangelists of the 1970s and 80s, but he was brought down, as were many of his preaching contemporaries, by the twin sins of greed and lust. Bakker and his wife, Tammy Faye, built an empire around their Christian chatshow PTL (for Praise the Lord), which spawned their own satellite TV network based in Charlotte, North Carolina. At their peak, their broadcasts attracted more than 13 million viewers and $1m a day in donations; and their Disney-style theme park, Heritage USA, at Fort Mill, South Carolina, drew six million visitors a year. In 1980, Bakker joined President Jimmy Carter on Air Force One to pray for the American hostages held in Iran – but Bakker’s support and that of his fellow conservative evangelicals soon proved key in electing Ronald Reagan president. The Bakkers preached the “prosperity gospel”, growing from the Calvinist idea that material success was a sign of God’s blessing, and flaunted those blessings. “Excess and success are close together,” Bakker claimed. They never skimped on opulence, with everything from a fleet of luxury cars to jewellery for Tammy Faye and an air-conditioned dog kennel. But the mansion crumbled from within when, in 1987, Bakker was revealed to have paid $265,000 in hush money to Jessica Hahn, a secretary in his Assemblies of God ministry, who said she had been drugged and raped in 1980 by him and his fellow PTL host John Wesley Fletcher. Hahn then told her story and posed for Penthouse magazine, while Fletcher wrote his own story for Penthouse, The Devil in Jim Bakker, claiming he had been both Bakker’s lover and his pimp for other gay men. Bakker was stripped of his ministry in the Assemblies of God. He resigned as head of PTL and was replaced by Jerry Falwell, who called him “the greatest scab and a cancer on the face of Christianity in 2,000 years of church history”. Bakker had passed PTL on to Falwell to prevent another Assemblies of God preacher, Jimmy Swaggart, from taking it over. Swaggart, who faced his own sex scandal years later, called Bakker “a cancer on the face of God”. The sex scandal opened the doors to revealing Bakker’s frauds. PTL was nicknamed “Pass the Loot”. Under Reagan, the Federal Communications Commission, the government regulatory agency, had buried its investigation into the Bakkers’ soliciting donations for overseas aid that instead went to Heritage USA and into their own pockets. The Internal Revenue Service had sat for years on a report recommending that PTL should lose its tax-exempt status. But the Charlotte Observer’s reporting of PTL selling far more “lifetime memberships” guaranteeing annual three-night stays at Heritage USA than it was able to provide, led to a trial. In 1989, a jury convicted Bakker on all 24 counts, and Judge Robert “Maximum Bob” Potter sentenced him to 45 years, saying: “Those of us who do have a religion are sick of being saps for money-grubbing preachers and priests.” That animus led to the sentence being reduced to eight years on appeal. By the time Bakker emerged from prison, Tammy Faye had divorced him, and married Roe Messner, one of the principals of Heritage USA. Messner would be convicted of bankruptcy fraud two years later. Bakker was born in Muskegon, Michigan. His father, Raleigh, a machinist, and his mother, Furnia (nee Irwin), came from Pentecostal families. Jim studied at the Assemblies of God’s North Central Bible College in Minneapolis, where in 1961 he met Tammy Faye LaValley. Although he was engaged to his high-school sweetheart in Muskegon, three weeks later he and Tammy Faye married, leaving college and becoming travelling evangelists. In 1966 they caught the eye of Pat Robertson, who hired them for his Christian Broadcasting Network. Their children’s show, Come On Over, featuring Tammy Faye using puppets, became so popular that Robertson gave them a talkshow, The 700 Club, named in the then-optimistic hope of attracting $700 a month from loyal viewers. They left Robertson in 1973 to co-found the Trinity Broadcasting Network in Los Angeles, where they launched PTL. After quickly falling out with their partners, they moved to Charlotte, where they created the PTL Network. “I believe if Jesus were alive today, he would be on TV,” said Bakker, a statement that helped inspire Ray Stevens’ 1987 hit song, Would Jesus Wear a Rolex?. At Bakker’s 1994 parole hearing, his lawyer, Alan Dershowitz, pledged to “guarantee that Mr Bakker would never again engage in the blend of religion and commerce that led to his conviction”. That did not last long. His 1996 book I Was Wrong was more a rationalisation than confession. Bakker worked at the Los Angeles International Church (also known as the Dream Center), where in 1998 he met and married Lori Beth Graham, a youth preacher who had a strong resemblance to Tammy Faye. By 2003 they were broadcasting The Jim Bakker Show from Branson, Missouri. Bakker’s pitch switched from prosperity to apocalypse, selling “doomsday survival gear” including freeze-dried beans on toast. He said PTL now stood for Prophets Talking Loud and used natural disasters as examples of God’s vengeance against Americans who did not support him – and later Donald Trump. Barack Obama, he said, was “a representative of the antichrist” and he called Hillary Clinton “the bride of Satan”. During the Covid pandemic, Bakker sold colloidal silver supplements he claimed could cure the disease. He was prosecuted by state authorities in Missouri and Arkansas and forced to refund buyers. In 2020 he had a stroke. He is survived by his wife and their five children, Maricella, Lori, Clarissa, Marie and Ricky, and by a daughter, Tammy Sue, and son, Jay, from his first marriage. • James Orsen Bakker, television evangelist, born 2 January 1940; died 5 October 2026

title: Bring a bottle: Viennese dog owners told to rinse pets’ urine from trees
summary: Official guidance says ammonia in animal urine should be watered down to stop it corroding bark
text: A neighbourhood in Vienna has introduced guidelines for dog walking, including the use of bottled tap water to rinse away urine and protect vulnerable trees. Neubau, an up-and-coming, densely populated district dotted with cafes and galleries, rolled out the Schönes Gassi (nice dog walk) campaign this week. The project addresses the impact of the area’s 600 dogs on greenery, including about 250 trees planted over the past decade to help mitigate the effects of the climate crisis. Using the slogan Das Flascherl zum Sackerl (the bottle to go with the bag), the guidelines say animal urine corrodes tree bark, weakening its protective layer and potentially letting corrosive pathogens and fungi penetrate the trunk. “While marking territory is a form of communication for dogs, it causes stress for urban trees,” said Grätzllabor, a community group that takes its name from the Viennese slang for quarter or neighbourhood. “This results in rot and, in the worst case, compromised stability.” The group said the campaign had been launched in concert with “concerned citizens” in the Austrian capital. It also asks owners to carry plastic bags to clean up after their pets. Owners can pick up a free 270ml water bottle at the town hall to rinse areas used by their dogs. The voluntary scheme could be expanded to other districts. Fresh canine urine is highly water-soluble and dilution significantly reduces the concentration of ammonia and other harmful substances seeping into the soil, while also softening the smell. Grätzllabor said the rinsing strategy should not be interpreted as a “licence” for dogs to mark trees or green space but rather as an action owners could take to minimise harm caused by their pets. Conny Sporrer, who is a dog trainer, said the Schönes Gassi campaign could help head off more drastic calls to mitigate problems linked to animal waste. “In Vienna, we don’t need a city full of dog bans, or a city where dogs are just allowed to urinate anywhere they please,” she told reporters, saying most pets could be taught where to relieve themselves. “What we need is consideration, education and sufficient suitable facilities for dogs.” Similar schemes have been introduced in Japan, Italy, Switzerland and Spain, which has the highest share of dog-owning households in the EU at 70%. Austria has relatively low levels of ownership, at just 17% of households. Berlin, where more than 100,000 dogs are kept as pets after an increase in ownership during the pandemic, has also begun addressing the problem by stopping the planting of black locust trees in some areas because they are particularly sensitive to urine. In the spring, the western district of Charlottenburg-Wilmersdorf began installing “pee stones” for dogs to use as a target, instead of trees.

title: US lawmakers unveil bill to hold Wall Street’s ‘Epstein-connected’ bosses to account
summary: Move comes as Senator Elizabeth Warren condemns Barclays response to questions over ex-boss’s ties to sex offender
text: US lawmakers have unveiled a new bill to hold Wall Street’s “Epstein-connected” bosses to account for helping finance the late sex offender’s crimes. It came as top Democratic senator Elizabeth Warren condemned the UK bank Barclays for “dodging responsibility” over its failure to vet former boss Jes Staley and his ties to the once well-connected billionaire. A bipartisan group of politicians, led by Warren and House representative Robert Garcia, are introducing a bill on Thursday known as the Epstein Wall Street Records Act. The bill follows a months-long investigation into the financier, who died in prison in 2019 while awaiting trial on child sex-trafficking charges. If passed, the bill would force regulators including the Federal Reserve and the Securities and Exchange Commission to investigate “Epstein connected” financial firms and executives for potential breaches of banking, investment or illicit funding laws; and fine or even ban wrongdoers from the US financial sector. The bill – which is also being backed by House Republican Thomas Massie – will also force regulators to publicly disclose any records relating to Epstein and his associates; and refer any potential criminal violations to the US justice department. Warren said: “Since the big banks won’t hold themselves accountable – and the Trump administration won’t either – Congress must act to force real transparency and accountability for them and their executives who enabled Jeffrey Epstein’s crimes.” News of the bill came as Warren condemned the bosses at Barclays, one of the UK’s biggest banks, over their failure to adequately answer questions about its former chief executives Jes Staley and his links to Epstein. Staley’s ties with the well-connected billionaire spelled the end of his career. The American banker resigned from Barclays in November 2021, after UK regulators started investigating the true nature of his relationship with Epstein, whom he met in 2000 during his three-decade stint at JP Morgan. The Financial Conduct Authority’s original investigation, triggered by a cache of more than 1,200 emails between Staley and Epstein, concluded that the pair were “indeed close” and had a relationship that “went beyond one that was professional in nature”. Staley was eventually banned from the UK’s financial sector in 2023 for playing down those ties, and failed to overturn that decision in a court battle that revealed intimate details of the pair’s friendship last year. That included Staley admitting to having sex with a member of Epstein’s staff in New York – an encounter he said was “consensual”. The case also revived a 2010 exchange referring to Disney princesses, in which Staley said: “That was fun. Say hi to Snow White.” Staley denied knowledge of the exchange during a UK court hearing. After the loss of his legal challenge against the FCA, Staley said he was disappointed by the outcome but was “never dishonest”. In July, Warren and a team of House Democrats wrote to the Barclays chair, Nigel Higgins, asking how it had vetted its former chief executive, and whether the bank had investigated potential “deficiencies” in its executive hiring process, given it had “allowed the board to hire a CEO who held extensive professional and personal ties to a convicted sex offender”. Barclays has since responded with a letter from its head of US government relations, Lance Williams, that Warren said was not sufficient. The letter focused on the findings of the UK regulators’ investigation. Williams stressed that Staley had “concealed information about his actions and the nature of his relationship with Mr Epstein” and only after Staley’s resignation had “previously unknown information come to light through various public disclosures”. “This information paints a fundamentally different picture of Mr Staley than what he presented to Barclays,” Williams said, noting that Barclays had relied on external executive search firms to recruit Staley in 2015, when he was “known for his accomplishments in the banking industry”. Warren said Barclays’ lacklustre response illustrated why it was time for regulators to launch formal investigations into Wall Street’s ties to Epstein: “Barclays continues to dodge responsibility over its apparent failure to vet its former CEO Jes Staley’s close professional and personal ties to Epstein.” Barclays declined to comment. Staley’s legal representatives were contacted for comment.

title: ‘Fantastically special’: all 10 Victoria Crosses awarded to Royal Marines go on show for first time
summary: Exclusive: Portsmouth Historic Dockyard’s new £15m permanent display tells tales of courage from conflicts such as Crimean and both world wars
text: They tell tales of bravery under fire, may lead to conversations about the UK’s place in the world and could prompt visitors to reflect on what they might have done if faced with the same perilous circumstances. All 10 Victoria Crosses (VCs) awarded to members of the Royal Marines are going on display together for the first time along with tales of courage during conflicts such as the Crimean and both world wars. “It’s fantastically special,” said Matthew Sheldon, the chief executive officer of Royal Navy Museums. “The Royal Marines have only ever been awarded 10 Victoria Crosses. We have all 10 of them. The originals have never been seen together before. They’ve been in secure storage, not visible to the public, which seemed like a crying shame.” The medals will go on permanent display at a new £15m “Royal Marines Experience” at Portsmouth Historic Dockyard telling 360 years of marines’ history. Sheldon said the marines awarded VCs tended to be “youngish” and not from very senior ranks. Like modern marines, who usually work in small, agile teams, they tended to find themselves in very close quarters to the enemy. He said the stories could lead to debate about the role the UK played in global conflicts. “When we look at the world now and we look at our military, it’s not about large set pieces – it’s often quite small incidents below the level of full-out declared wars. I think the medals ask questions about the world we live in now.” Earlier this month, the Royal Marines returned to the Faroe Islands for the first time since the second world war as part of security efforts in the strategically vital Greenland-Iceland-UK Gap. This autumn, commando engineers have been practising digging underground hospitals that offer protection against drone attacks. Sheldon said he thought the medals could prompt visitors to ask questions of themselves. “They are about a moment in time and somebody’s choice in that moment. They are powerful because they make you think: ‘What would I have done in the same incident.’” Staff at the museum say it is hard to pick out a favourite story but when pressed, Sheldon said he was very keen on that of Sgt Norman Augustus Finch, born in 1890. Finch was awarded the Victoria Cross during the Zeebrugge Raid on 23 April 1918. While serving onboard HMS Vindictive, Finch was stationed on a high lookout platform. During the battle, his position was hit by shells, killing or wounding everyone around him. Although he was severely injured, Finch remained at his post and continued to fire on enemy positions until another shell finally put him out of action. Because of the bravery shown by the entire battalion, the marines were allowed to vote for who should receive the VC. Finch was chosen by his peers. Mark Berry, the assistant curator of artefacts, said he liked the story of L/Cpl Walter Richard Parker. During the Gallipoli campaign, Parker served as a stretcher bearer. On the morning of 1 May 1915, Parker was a member of a party tasked with taking aid to men in an isolated frontline trench. To reach the trench, Parker crossed 365 metres (400 yards) of open ground under intense enemy fire. He was the only person to successfully reach the trench. Having aided the wounded, he helped them evacuate the next morning, and himself was severely injured in the thigh and chest. Berry said: “It’s a really good example of the multilayered role of the marines. It’s not just fighting. It’s also trying to save lives, trying to help people.” The Royal Marines Experience opens at Portsmouth Historic Dockyard on 24 October.

title: Texas resident finds second world war-era grenades in box bought at estate sale
summary: Discovery of grenades prompted a neighborhood lockdown and a visit from the Austin police department’s bomb squad
text: A buyer at a Texas estate sale discovered several second world war-era grenades in a box of newly bought items, prompting a neighbourhood lockdown and a visit from the Austin police department’s bomb squad. The grenades, which were described as “live and active” in a social media post by the Austin police association, were removed and disarmed. Their age and apparent volatility, the post said, required delicate handling by bomb squad members whose “training, expertise, and steady nerves” were rarely seen by the public. “Handling 80-year-old explosives with unknown stability is dangerous, precise work, and they do it with the professionalism this city counts on,” the post said. “Huge thanks to our patrol officers, who quickly secured the scene, set up a perimeter, and kept neighbors safe while they waited for EOD [explosive ordinance disposal].” The police association did not identify the seller or buyer of the box of grenades, and said the person who bought them made the discovery only as he was rifling through several boxes of his new items on Monday. “No crime here,” the post said. “Just a great reminder, if you ever come across old military ordnance (grenades, shells, mortar rounds, etc), even if you think it’s inert, don’t touch it, don’t move it, and call 911. “Let the experts handle it.” Austin’s KLBJ news station identified at least three of the olive-colored grenades as Mk 2 anti-personnel fragmentation grenades, widely used by US forces during the second world war, and known as “pineapple” grenades because of their distinctive shape. The grenades were still in limited use with the US army and Marine Corps until the 1960s. The station said bomb squad technicians examined the highly explosive devices with X-rays and determined they were live, but did not pose an immediate threat under the circumstances. The Guardian reported earlier this month on the dangers specialist teams face in dealing with decades-old unexploded ordinance, including the degradation of fuses and increasing instability of explosives over time. It followed the discovery of two large, unexploded German bombs found separately in the UK county of Devon, one on a floating dredger and another on a building site. Experts said the devices “could knock a whole street down”.

title: Texas Democrat James Talarico faces grilling from voters at town hall in tight Senate race
summary: Talarico casts himself as a moderate who would put Texans’ needs over party allegiances amid close contest against Republican Ken Paxton
text: James Talarico, the Texas Democratic nominee for Senate, sat face to face with skeptical Republicans and independents voters who grilled him on a slew of contentious issues including Israel’s military campaign in Gaza, abortion and foreign aid, during a CNN town hall co-hosted by the Jubilee Media digital platform on Wednesday. One voter, a young Republican activist who volunteered at the party’s midterm convention in Dallas last month and recently appeared on Fox News as a supporter of Talarico’s opponent, questioned the authenticity of Talarico’s faith, referencing a past remark where he described God as nonbinary. “When I said that, I was being provocative and I want to admit that and come clean about that,” Talarico responded. “What I was saying is actually not controversial theologically: the idea that we can’t define God using human categories. Not only did I say that, but the late Charlie Kirk said that – the late Pope Benedict said that.” Talarico added that he was receptive to feedback from Christians. Jodi Hunt, a self-described single-issue voter, probed Talarico’s pro-choice stance, asking: “How would you convince me as a Catholic voter that I can trust you would protect the most innocent among us?” Talarico described the Bible as being silent on abortion, to which Hunt countered quoting “Thou shalt not kill”. “We may have different, moral conclusions when it comes to this particular ethical question, but we actually have the same public policy goal,” Talarico said, framing abortion as a public health issue that could be solved with a reduction in unplanned pregnancies. During the night, Talarico cast himself as a moderate, who would put the needs of Texans over party allegiances. He railed against the ultra-wealthy, framing them as the common enemy. Talarico and the Republican nominee, Ken Paxton, are locked in a competitive race to become Texas’s next US senator, with most recent polls showing Talarico with a narrow lead over Paxton. (Paxton declined an invitation to appear on CNN, host Erin Burnett said at the start of the town hall.) Though Democrats have not won a Senate seat in the state since the late 1980s, they’re hoping Talarico’s newcomer energy and popular appeal will persuade independents and Republicans fed up with Donald Trump’s second term – or turned off by Paxton’s many scandals. Over the weekend, Talarico became the subject of a disinformation campaign after he was absent from the campaign trail for more than a week. While Talarico’s campaign repeatedly said the candidate was sick with a bad case of the flu, conservative influencers falsely accused him of receiving medical treatment at a mental health facility in Ohio. The rumor was further propelled by Paxton and Trump, who sought to fuel skepticism about Talarico’s health and fitness for office. The Democratic candidate denied the false allegations after returning to the campaign trail last week, noting he had never been to Ohio. “False claims got millions of views online and this is an example of what I call the ‘rage economy’,” Talarico said during the town hall. “Billionaires who own these platforms get rich. We all get angry and nobody’s life gets any better. Conspiracy theories don’t put food on the table, put gas in the tank, or improve our communities.” Paxton, meanwhile, has been battling his own controversies. A series of leaked audio recordings – made during a closed-door meeting – have been posted online and revealed him being critical of his own party and campaign leaders in DC. Paxton entered the race with a history of scandals. He was impeached by the Texas state legislature in 2023 on allegations including bribery and abuse of public trust, though he was later acquitted. Paxton’s wife of almost four decades, Angela Paxton, then filed for divorce in 2025 on “biblical grounds”, citing adultery. But Trump endorsed Paxton to run against Talarico, passing up incumbent Republican John Cornyn.

title: Severe drought declared in six areas of England as reservoirs run low
summary: Some reservoirs in south at critical levels as water companies call for extended restrictions that would affect golf clubs, private schools and car washes
text: A severe drought has been declared in six areas of England, with some reservoirs at critically low levels, threatening public supplies. Parts of Devon, Cornwall, Dorset, Somerset, East Sussex and West Sussex have moved into severe drought, and urgent measures are being taken to secure public supplies of water after the UK experienced its hottest summer on record. Despite the crisis, the environment secretary, Angela Eagle, has yet to approve requests from three water companies, two in areas now in severe drought, to extend restrictions on water use to businesses such as golf clubs and commercial car washes. Emma Hardy, the water minister, indicated on Thursday that the environment could suffer in the continuing drought. Hardy instructed the Environment Agency to prioritise protecting public water supplies in areas affected by severe drought where there is an unavoidable trade-off between environmental rules and water supplies. After a meeting of the national drought group, Eagle, said: “This level of drought is something we have not experienced for decades, so this government is stepping up our support and planning. “We are working closely with water companies to protect public supplies in the areas affected, and I’d continue to urge everyone to think about how they can use water wisely over the coming weeks.” South East Water, South West Water and Southern Water want to impose non-essential user bans on businesses to protect supplies. This would affect golf clubs, private schools and commercial properties. But while Eagle called on water companies to step up their drought planning, she did not announce approval for the non-essential user bans. The south-east and south-west of England have experienced their driest April to September in more than a century, fuelled by the climate crisis, affecting reservoir levels in those areas. Levels at two reservoirs are critically low. Ardingly reservoir, which serves about 95,000 properties in Haywards Heath, Uckfield and surrounding areas, is only 19% full. Storage at Wimbleball, which supplies South West Water customers in East Devon, North Devon, Somerset and West Dorset and Wessex Water customers in West Somerset, is at 16%. The Environment Agency (EA) would expect reservoir storage to be about 75% at this time of year. There are also concerns for several smaller South West Water reservoirs serving homes in Devon and Cornwall; these include Drift and Stithians which supply 56,000 households in Cornwall, and the Tottiford and Venford group which supplies 47,000 households in Devon. The National Drought Group said the government and the EA would move to daily monitoring of reservoir and river levels and run heightened water quality monitoring because of the lower dilution levels of sewage, raising the risks for water quality and environmental pollution. Businesses that abstract water will be put through more compliance checks to make sure they are taking only what they are allowed. Philip Duffy, the chief executive of the EA, said: “We cannot change the weather, but water companies can act now. We expect them to follow their drought plans and take the steps needed to secure public water supplies. “We are also asking everyone to use less water. That will leave more in our rivers and the environment, helping farmers and protecting wildlife and nature.”

title: Online ads weaponised to deliver ‘zero-click’ spyware, researchers say
summary: Discover-Tech’s Controlium software lets clients mass-profile internet users then covertly hack targets, say researchers at University of Toronto
text: An Israeli advertising agency has been serving millions of online adverts that allow “zero-click” spyware to be used against targets, researchers at a Canadian university have said. Citizen Lab, a digital investigations research unit at the University of Toronto, said it believed dozens of devices at the Qatari broadcaster Al Jazeera had been compromised by spyware delivered through ads run by Discover-Tech, which describes itself as a specialised digital advertising agency. According to Citizen Lab, Discover-Tech operates a software platform called Controlium that allows its clients to “mass-profile and deanonymise” internet users then covertly hack targets with third-party spyware. Unlike infections that rely on people interacting with links or files, the spyware requires no interaction from the victim to be installed, making it a new delivery technique, Citizen Lab says. The infections happen without a user’s knowledge, and in a matter of seconds, according to Citizen Lab. “[The online advertising] ecosystem is being weaponised at a massive scale to profile millions of users, then silently infect targets with zero-click mercenary spyware,” the report says. According to the report, Controlium is able to harvest a user’s identity and IP address when the user is shown a seemingly benign custom-created ad – for example, for a digital game or a telecoms service. If the user has been selected as a target for hacking, a mercenary spyware firm can then send a malicious code containing spyware to their device, the researchers say. They say that millions of users worldwide have been served ads by Discover-Tech since 2024, including in Yemen, Brazil, Mexico and Czechia. Related work by the research group Confiant also suggests that Discover-Tech’s ads have been shown to users of the networks of government entities in Europe and the US, as well as the UN, Nato, the international criminal court and the International Atomic Energy Agency. “It’s disastrous that major ad vendors and organisations apparently were neither able to detect nor prevent the company’s malicious advertising operations for years,” said Wolfie Christl, a researcher at Citizen Lab. “The way the online advertising ecosystem works today is a security threat for states, the private sector, civil society and everyone else alike.” According to Citizen Lab, Controlium acts as a “facilitator” for third-party spyware firms that have targeted “government officials, journalists, businesspeople, activists, academics and embassy workers”. Citizen Lab claims it can deliver spyware that can access everything on the device of a target, extracting messages, photos and emails, recording calls and secretly activating microphones. The full extent of the targeting allegedly enabled by Discover-Tech is unknown. Citizen Lab’s findings join mounting evidence that the opaque arrangements underpinning the world of online advertising can be leveraged for surveillance. “There has been a lot of buzz that online ads can be used to identify and automatically hack targets with pinpoint precision, but now for the first time, we have concrete technical evidence showing this process in action,” said Bill Marczak, a researcher at Citizen Lab. Discover-Tech has been approached for comment. When a user navigates to a website that shows advertisements, their details become part of a split-second programmatic auction involving dozens or hundreds of companies. These companies bid automatically to place an ad in front of that user. These bids are based on the user’s profile, which can include information about their device and data compiled on them by tracking their activity across the web. For example, companies given the profile of a 35-year-old interested in sports betting and crypto might bid to show that individual an advertisement for an energy drink. There is little regulation on this automated online market, and there is growing evidence that it is being exploited by malevolent actors. Reuters has reported that billions of dollars’ worth of Meta’s ad revenue comes from ads for scams, illegal gambling, pornography and other banned content. In the US, ICE and other government agencies have bought software that uses ad tech data to track people’s movements. “Cybersecurity agencies, regulators and lawmakers in the US, Europe and other regions must urgently step in. They must investigate the involved companies and fix the systemic risks that enable malicious ad targeting,” said Christl.

title: Former DUP leader Jeffrey Donaldson sentenced to 15 years for child sexual offences
summary: Donaldson was found guilty in June of 18 counts of sexual abuse including one rape between 1985 and 2008
text: Jeffrey Donaldson has been sentenced to 15 years for sexual offences against two women who were children when he abused them, completing what was described as a “catastrophic descent into disgrace”. The sentence at Newry crown court on Thursday sealed the downfall of a former Democratic Unionist party (DUP) leader who once dominated unionism in Northern Ireland. Donaldson, 63, was sentenced to 11 years for rape against complainant B and four years for offences against complainant A, to be served consecutively. He is to remain on the sex offender register indefinitely. He had reached the “very height of public office” before a “catastrophic descent into disgrace”, the judge, Paul Ramsey, said. The former Lagan Valley MP had shown no remorse or empathy, said the judge. “There has not been, and doubtless will not be, one word of regret, apology or shame from this man to at least provide his victims with some crumb of comfort.” Ramsey paid tribute to the victims, who were in court. “It is only through the courage, resourcefulness and determination of two young women that you’ve been brought to justice in respect of the crimes you committed against them when they were children,” he said. The head of the Public Prosecution Service’s serious crime unit, Catherine Kierans, lauded the victims’ courage in coming forward to seek justice. “Jeffrey Donaldson held a prominent public position,” she said. “This case shows that sexual abuse can be hidden behind a facade of respectability.” Donaldson, wearing a blue suit, white shirt and pink tie, showed no emotion and was escorted from the dock by two custody officers. He was returned to Maghaberry prison, where he has been held since his conviction. He was found guilty in June of 18 counts of sexual abuse including one count of rape, spanning a period from 1985 to 2008. He has denied all wrongdoing and plans to appeal. Speaking outside court, DCI Leah Crothers of the Police Service of Northern Ireland said Donaldson had manipulated his victims and exploited their trust. Police and the criminal justice system had sent a clear message, she said. “No one is above the law.” Statements from the complainants, read by Crothers, detailed enduring trauma. Complainant B said the abuse had taken away her ability to trust people. “I stood up many years ago because for me this is about drawing a line in the sand and knowing that the Donaldsons can no longer hurt anyone else.” Complainant A said her childhood had been stolen. “I learned to survive by shutting away my emotions, trusting no one and expecting people to hurt me … I should never have had to become this strong. “The last few years have been nothing short of a battle … But those responsible do not control me now … The cycle is being broken and it ends with me.” The DUP said its former leader had committed “vile and disgusting crimes” and expressed sympathy for the complainants. “He deserves every day of the lengthy prison sentence he has to serve following the guilty verdict for preying on innocent child victims.” The jury in the four-week trial found that Donaldson’s wife, Eleanor, aided and abetted his offending. The 60-year-old was deemed unfit to stand trial on mental health grounds and faced a trial of the facts, which tests evidence but does not result in a criminal conviction. She is due to return to court on 13 November 2026 for a hearing in relation to the conclusion of her case. The case shredded the reputation of an establishment figure who was knighted and played a key role at Westminster during post-Brexit negotiations over Northern Ireland’s position in the UK. During the trial, Complainant B said she was raped when she was of primary school age and was of secondary school age when Donaldson lifted up her top and fondled her breasts. The jury heard that Donaldson’s wife witnessed part of the latter incident and walked away. Complainant A said she was of primary school age when Donaldson began to be “physical” with her. She recalled waking up in the night with a sexual feeling and having nightmares about “men doing horrible things to children”. The trial heard that in the 1990s the victim told a pastor about the abuse, after which Donaldson apologised to her at a Christian centre in County Antrim. Prosecutors also told the jury of a letter Donaldson wrote to Complainant A in 2020 in which he expressed regret for causing “hurt, pain and distress” and asked forgiveness for his “sinful nature”. At the trial he denied wrongdoing and said the apologies related to other matters. The prosecutor, Rosemary Walsh, told the trial both victims kept memories “locked away inside” until turning points in adulthood prompted the decision to report the offences to police in 2024. Until his arrest in March 2024, Donaldson was thought to embody unionist probity. Born into a Presbyterian family in Kilkeel, he married Eleanor in 1987 and served apprenticeships in the Ulster Unionist party before defecting to the DUP in 2004. Donaldson was knighted for political services in 2016 and became DUP leader in 2021, before resigning in 2024. After his conviction, King Charles stripped him of his knighthood in July.

title: Bad news for Trump ahead of the midterms: it’s still the economy, stupid
summary: Voters’ opposition to the state of Trump’s economy is well established – despite his desperate attempts to deflect
text: It’s indisputable that the political polarization of our time has reduced (and confused) the influence of economic conditions on US elections. In September of 2024, in the waning weeks of the Joe Biden presidency, 65% of Republicans believed the US economy was getting worse. About six months later, as Donald Trump launched a trade war on the rest of the world with his “liberation day” tariffs, the share of Republican pessimists had dropped to 33%. It’s hard to detect a reason for this in the economic data. Annual consumer price inflation fell from 2.4% to 2.3% between the two polls. The unemployment rate ticked up from 4.1% to 4.2%. Indeed, Democrats disagreed sharply with their Republican neighbors: from the last Harris poll of the Biden era to the first under Trump, the share who thought the US economy was worsening jumped from 28% to 73%. As the midterm elections loom into focus, suggesting a stark Republican defeat, Trump and his minions are hoping that this ideological lens, shaping economic reality to fit political preferences, can prevent an electoral bloodbath in November. Maybe Trump can somehow dupe the Maga base into believing that “we’re growing at a faster rate than we’ve ever grown before.” From three weeks out, it seems pretty clear that the gambit is not going to work. Polling by Harris for the Guardian suggests that the economy is looking pretty bad even for their most loyal acolytes. Too bad to convince them otherwise. The September reading of the consumer price index, which recorded a spike in annual inflation to 3.7%, had not yet been published when Harris performed its latest round of polling earlier this month. Still, the pollster reported that 38% of Republicans believe the economy is worsening. That is up from 29% a year ago. The pattern is evident among cohorts that have proven historical Republican bulwarks. Rural Americans, loyal Republican allies for decades, are being battered by Trump’s policies. They were hit not only by his trade war, largely barred from China’s markets. They have been hammered by the rising price of diesel and fertilizer, for which they can thank Trump’s war in Iran. They have been hamstrung by Trump’s raids against the many immigrants in their labor force. And they feel roundly attacked by Trump’s attempt to tame rising beef prices by lowering tariffs on imported meat. Unsurprisingly, this is showing up in the polling. Sixty-four per cent of rural Americans polled this month said the economy was getting worse, compared with only 52% of city dwellers. Six per cent more rural residents think the economy is worsening than in September 2024, during the last poll of the Biden administration. White Americans, another pillar of Republican support, are also turning sour: 61% believe the economy is getting worse, up from 48% in September of 2024. The share of men who believe the economy is getting worse increased from 46% to 52% over those two years. Bill Clinton famously won the presidency in 1992 campaigning on: “It’s the economy, stupid.” For much of the 20th century the state of the economy was critical in deciding presidential and congressional elections. Voters blamed or rewarded incumbents for the state of the economy. The relationship was always moderated by partisan preferences, though. And it has weakened dramatically as the electorate has set on divergent ideological paths, ultimately splitting into rival camps with diametrically opposed perceptions of reality. “The economic perceptions of Democrats and Republicans have polarized relative to Independents and that this polarization is not asymmetric in magnitude,” argued a recent study by political scientists from Stanford and New York University. They estimate the partisan gap in economic perceptions rose “from about 20 percentage-points at the beginning of the Bush II administration to a maximum of 73 percentage-points during the (first) Trump administration”. Partisanship doesn’t just affect voters’ perceptions of the economy. As reported by political scientists at Bucknell University and Texas A&M University, polarization reduces policymakers’ incentive to tailor policy to deliver broad economic prosperity. “If voters are relatively unwilling to cross party lines to reward good economic performance or punish economic decline, then elected officials can pursue policies that distribute economic benefits narrowly without affecting their chances of re-election,” they wrote. “This might include aiming policy to deliver rewards to co-partisans, donors, or even to the office-holder himself or herself.” This would explain Trump’s tactics to a T. Not only has he taken to scaring voters with culture war stuff – variously branding Democrats as apologists of Vladimir Lenin and claiming that they want to change the sex of young children. He seems to believe that he can sway the electorate by doing violence to groups that his Maga base dislikes, like immigrants and the “undeserving” poor. Maybe they will pay less attention to the cost of living, and to the Trump family’s self-dealing. It seems too late, though. Voters’ opposition to Trump’s economic stewardship is too well established, having built up since the “liberation day” tariffs through countless destructive decisions over the last 21 months. He has not only lost average US voters – 58% of those think the economy is getting worse, 10 percentage points more than in the last poll of the Biden era. His shots at distracting the base are unlikely to convince them that they are not, in fact, miserable too.

title: John Healey vows to give ‘breathing space’ to consumers and businesses in first budget
summary: Speaking at IMF meeting, chancellor says he will stick to fiscal rules while recognising business and living costs
text: John Healey has promised to use his first budget in a fortnight’s time to offer consumers and businesses a “breathing space” while sticking to Labour’s fiscal rules. Speaking to journalists in Bangkok, where he has been attending the International Monetary Fund annual meetings, the chancellor said he was conscious of rising costs. “I want the budget to be a budget that gives Britain a bit of breathing space – but also reinforces the strength of our fiscal plans and the strength of our resilience and our economy for the future,” he said. The government has already cut VAT on electricity bills, but Healey is expected to announce a further package of energy support at his 28 October tax and spending statement, before what is expected to be a sharp rise in the energy price cap in January. He said: “The prime minister’s talked about recognising the cost of business, not just the cost of living.” Healey also reiterated his insistence that he would be sticking to the spending plans set out by his predecessor Rachel Reeves at last year’s spending review – and that cabinet colleagues would have to find any additional resources within their existing budgets. “When the second half of a spending review is in place, there are pressures on departments, and colleagues are doing a good job of managing with what they’ve got,” he said, adding: “You have to reprioritise if you want to do fresh things.” The UK has been praised by the IMF this week for setting out a plan to tackle its deficit, with the fund’s managing director, Kristalina Georgieva, urging the government to “stay the course”. Healey stressed he would stick to the rules set out by Reeves. “We will meet those fiscal rules, and I think one of the hallmarks of the IMF’s backing of our fiscal plans is recognition that there isn’t just a forecast for the future, but there’s some evidence of performance already.” He declined to say whether he would increase taxes on banks, or raise capital gains tax, to offset the expected pressure on his budget from higher energy prices and government borrowing costs. “If you think back to the run-up to previous budgets, the speculation about what was set to be in those budgets was actually deeply damaging,” he said. “It led to people cashing in their pensions early when they didn’t need to. It led to people holding back or not investing in their businesses when they didn’t need to. So I’m just not going to get drawn into any speculation.” Healey, a former defence secretary, also hinted he was working on an additional package of support for Ukraine, to be announced at the budget. He said: “I’m working on different ways we can step up support for Ukraine: military, diplomatic and economic, and you know, if anybody needed any reminder of that, it’s what we see coming out of Ukraine, with [Vladimir] Putin targeting these energy systems with thousands without power, as we’ve got a harsh winter approaching. “The step back from this is that the future of Ukraine is the future of European security, and that’s why it’s so crucial that Putin doesn’t prevail.” Healey and the Bank of England governor, Andrew Bailey, chaired a meeting of G20 policymakers on Thursday morning, in the absence of the US Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent. The chancellor will fly back to London on Thursday evening to put the finishing touches to the budget.

title: US ‘betrayal’ over Starlink undermines Ukrainian defense | First Thing
summary: President Zelenskyy accused Donald Trump of taking Russia’s side after vital communications system was throttled
text: Good morning. Ukraine’s president has said he feels “betrayed” by Donald Trump over a throttling of Starlink access. Volodymyr Zelenskyy accused the US president of picking the other side after more than four years of war, risking a breakdown in US-Ukraine relations. Ukraine’s military reported that the communications system, produced by Elon Musk’s SpaceX but managed by the US government, was no longer working on terminals moving at speeds greater than 100mph. That effectively rendered most of the drones used by Ukraine to strike behind the frontlines inoperable and affected the country’s best air defence system to stop Russian jet-powered attack drones bombing Kyiv. What is the likely impact of the loss of Starlink? The Ukrainian human rights activist Oleksandra Matviichuk said: “Without that protection, Russian drones will strike residential buildings, hospitals and schools like targets in a shooting gallery.” However, Starlink is not required for long-range Ukrainian missions that target Russian oil refineries, which Trump has been concerned about because of their impact on world energy prices. Judge blocks US sanctions on rights groups helping ICC Gaza war crimes inquiry A US federal judge has temporarily blocked the Trump administration from placing sanctions on two US-based human rights groups for working to help the international criminal court’s (ICC) investigations into war crimes in Gaza. A lawyer for Dawn and Taag described the decision as “a victory for the first amendment and an important step in unraveling the ICC sanctions regime”. A spokesperson for the US state department said “we do not comment on pending litigation”, but added: “The Trump administration has been clear: the ICC poses an intolerable threat to US sovereignty.” How is Israel blocking Trump’s plans for Gaza? Israel is refusing to allow a key project for Donald Trump’s Board of Peace to proceed. In early August, the board issued its first construction contract, for a military outpost to host 150 international troops as a vanguard of an international stabilization force. Two months later, Israel has still not allowed the contract to move forward. Trump’s new press secretary faces scrutiny over claims to be a lawyer Katie Zacharia’s debut as Donald Trump’s new press secretary got an excoriating review from our Washington bureau chief, who called her “the Zachbot”, and columnist Arwa Mahdawi suggested that Zacharia’s love of the president, lies and conspiracies made her perfect for the job. Now Zacharia is under pressure over her claim that she is a lawyer. When asked to name the state where she passed the bar exam, she replied “when I moved to China”. No public record shows she has ever been licensed to practise law in the US states where she resided. According to a review from the Guardian, Zacharia was not registered in 38 states, as well as DC and the Virgin Islands, where the state’s attorney list was publicly available. Cornell president acknowledges he knew about fraternity sexual assault but did not follow up Michael Kotlikoff, the president of Cornell University, has acknowledged for the first time that he knew a student had reported being sexually assaulted in November 2024, but did not follow up with the Jane Doe involved in the months after learning about the alleged assault. He also revealed that he did not know she had dropped out of Cornell until she filed a lawsuit last month. What has happened at a frat house in Chicago? A 21-year-old woman reported being sexually assaulted last weekend at a fraternity house near the University of Chicago. A person of interest has been identified, according to university officials. The individual is not a student and has been banned from campus. Eight states accuse OpenAI of coaching children to harm themselves in lawsuit Kansas, Arizona, Montana, Iowa and four other states allege that OpenAI products carried out “willful, dangerous, reckless and unlawful conduct” by coaxing children into harming themselves. “OpenAI is hurting kids and they are lying to Iowans,” Brenna Bird, the attorney general for Iowa, said in a statement. “OpenAI claims ChatGPT is safe while it’s giving dangerous medical advice, encouraging people to hurt others, and coaching people to commit suicide – all while pretending to be their fake friend.” In other news … A school roof collapse in Pakistan has left at least 27 students dead. The death toll is likely to rise as rescuers in Peshawar work to find dozens of pupils still unaccounted for. Pope Leo’s recovery from lung cancer surgery is “progressing as planned”. The US-born pontiff has begun walking in his hospital room and is eating normally, doctors say. The ex-fiance of Nancy Mace and two others have been charged with sex crimes that Mace detailed in a House speech last year. The Republican representative described the assault in a nearly hour-long speech that had named the men. The University of Maryland club tennis team has been suspended over racist imagery sent to other schools. An image of the state flag incorporating KKK hoods was sent to those participating in a regional tennis tournament. The man shot by ICE in New York City says the agent did not identify himself. The account by Oscar Belgal differs sharply from that of DHS agents, who fired into his vehicle while there was a young boy in the back seat. Stat of the day: LGBTQ+ people go into hiding in Senegal as hundreds are arrested More than 320 individuals have been arrested and detained on allegations of “acts against nature” since February, according to HIV Justice Network, after Senegal’s parliament doubled the maximum prison term for consensual same-sex relations to 10 years. Here’s what months of taste-testing revealed. Having tried cloud seeding, water bombing and sending in army personnel to fight the fires, Indonesia’s coordinating security minister said dry ice would now be dropped on the province of South Sumatra.
