title: Revealed: Serbian ruler’s secret role in ‘illegal’ effort to help Trump business
summary: Exclusive: Aleksandar Vučić personally intervened to push plans for controversial $500m Trump Tower in Belgrade, which sparked protests and a criminal case
text: Serbia’s authoritarian ruler personally intervened to advance an allegedly illegal scheme to hand over a protected site in Belgrade for a Trump tower, the Guardian can reveal. Aleksandar Vučić summoned officials to a meeting at his presidential offices about the project, which has culminated in a landmark indictment of senior figures from his regime on charges of abuse of public office. The criminal case is believed to be the first resulting from the Trumps’ global moneymaking campaign, described by critics as a “pay to play” arrangement where everything from sanctions relief to cutting-edge chips is available to those who enrich the first family and their associates. The alleged scheme to override the protected status of a historic building in the Serbian capital looms over an election scheduled for 25 October, when Vučić will seek to extend his 12 years in power in the face of a mass protest movement spurred by government corruption. A nationalist former propaganda chief under Slobodan Milošević, Vučić hosted the US president’s son Donald Trump Jr and son-in-law Jared Kushner in Belgrade as they developed plans for a $500m hotel and residential tower to add to their global property portfolios. After the abuse of power charges were brought last December, Kushner’s company announced the project would not proceed “at this time”. Vučić threatened reprisals, calling the prosecutors “corrupt gangs” who “fabricated cases”. “We have lost an exceptional investment,” the Serbian president said. “I will personally ensure that everyone who participated in causing this damage is held accountable.” Vučić’s culture minister is among those charged with abuse of power. But a Guardian investigation, drawing on interviews and leaked documents, reveals that the Serbian president himself led the initial meeting where the alleged scheme was discussed. This crucial meeting is not mentioned in the indictment, raising questions about what information the prosecutors are holding back and why. Representatives of the Trumps and Kushner said they had no part in the removal of the building’s protected status and that it would be “false” to say the Belgrade project was part of a “pay to play” scheme. Vučić did not respond to requests for comment. His decision to call a snap election means that a hearing at which witnesses might reveal details of his involvement will not take place until after the vote. A free 99-year lease On 6 February 2024, Dubravka Đukanović, a Serbian conservation professor in her 60s, arrived for a meeting at the presidency, a domed former royal palace. For three years, she had been the director of the country’s institute for the protection of cultural monuments. The topic was the General Staff building, the former Yugoslav ministry of defence in central Belgrade. The building, an architectural gem seen as an emblem of resistance to the Nazis, was already cherished when Nato forces bombed it in 1999 during its campaign to force Milošević to withdraw from Kosovo, deepening its resonance. Vučić himself had reaffirmed the General Staff building’s legally protected status in 2016. Now, the president said he wanted Đukanović to rescind it, according to two people with knowledge of the meeting. Some unspecified “foreign investor” was keen on the site. Under Serbian law, stripping the General Staff building of its protected status was not in Đukanović’s gift. Her institute would have to commission an expert opinion, which would have to conclude that there were good reasons why protected status was no longer merited. But the president wanted it done. At 6ft 6in and intolerant of dissent, Vučić can be intimidating. His tone towards Đukanović and another heritage official present was unpleasant, the sources said. He told them they were lazy and incompetent. The message was clear: do what I want or resign. A plausible explanation for Vučić’s forceful intervention came the following month, when an agreement between the Serbian government and Kushner’s real estate company leaked. Married to Trump’s daughter Ivanka, Kushner had been an influential White House aide during his father-in-law’s first term. Since Joe Biden’s victory in the 2020 election, Kushner had been concentrating on his investment fund. By early 2024, Trump was storming to the Republican nomination and was favourite to win the coming election. If Trump took back the White House, Kushner would once more be one of the most influential people on the planet. The leaked agreement showed the Serbian authorities had granted Kushner’s company a 99-year lease over the General Staff site, free of charge. Kushner, whose spokesperson said he had been looking at the project since 2021, posted an image of the design on X, professing himself “excited”. The news was not universally welcomed in Belgrade. “Serbia is not a buffet, and Vučić is not a waiter,” said Aleksandar Jovanović Ćuta, an environmental activist who revealed the agreement. “This is not his private property.” Yet Vučić’s regime proceeded to sign a contract, dated 13 May 2024 and seen by the Guardian, undertaking that the “cultural heritage designation” of the site would be removed “to the satisfaction” of Kushner’s company. Comply or resign The week after the contract was signed, Đukanović was summoned to another meeting. The president was not there this time. Siniša Mali, his finance minister and right-hand man, took charge. Mali urged Đukanović and Olivera Vučković, Belgrade’s top heritage official, to cancel the General Staff site’s protected status, according to the indictment’s summary of testimony the two women would later give prosecutors. It makes no reference to the earlier meeting with the president but indicates that the subject had previously been broached. “Mali asked them if they had given it any thought,” the indictment says, “and if they would initiate the procedure to remove the building’s protected status.” The women refused, “believing that the legal conditions for it were not met”. In that case, Mali told them, repeating his boss’s ultimatum from February, they should resign. They did. In her resignation letter, which the Guardian has seen, Đukanović wrote that she could not agree “to inappropriate interventions that would permanently destroy all the values of the complex, which testifies to the highest achievements of contemporary Serbian architecture and is of incalculable importance for preserving enduring creative values, the education of future generations, and the strengthening of the cultural identity of the Serbian people”. Approached by the Guardian, Đukanović and Vučković confirmed the accuracy of this account. Đukanović added: “I prefer not to make any statement on this matter while the court proceedings are ongoing.” Little was heard of the General Staff plan for months. In November, Trump beat Kamala Harris to win re-election. Ten days later, Vučić’s government announced that the General Staff site had been stripped of its protected status. Keeping it in the family One of the first things Trump did upon regaining the presidency was to ditch the pledge he made in his first term that his family business would refrain from doing deals abroad while he was in office. “The scale of corruption will be orders of magnitude greater than what we saw in the first Trump administration,” Kathleen Clark, a government ethics lawyer at Washington University School of Law, warned at the time. Trump had made it much easier, she said, to buy his favour. The family business remained officially under the control of his two oldest sons, Don Jr and Eric. In January 2025, four days after their father’s inauguration, Eric spoke about some new projects. The Trumps and the Kushners, New York real estate families united by marriage, had decided to embark on their first venture together: Kushner’s Belgrade hotel and tower would bear the Trump name. “It’s going to be fun to bring the family together,” Eric told the New York Times. “Serbia is one of the fastest-growing countries in Europe, and we’re incredibly honoured to be there.” Kushner, who had travelled to Belgrade for what Vučić called an “inspiring” meeting with the Serbian leader, added: “Our research showed that the Trump brand would be the best for this market.” That brand has enjoyed a surge in demand around the world during Trump’s second term, accompanied by allegations that it comes with a quid pro quo. In Vietnam, Eric was showered with confetti at the groundbreaking ceremony for a £1.5bn golf resort, the permits for which were granted with unusual speed. Then Trump halved Vietnam’s tariffs. The Saudis poured money into Kushner’s fund, and plans emerged for a Trump plaza in Jeddah. Then Trump agreed to sell the kingdom new US fighter jets. A cryptocurrency baron’s company and senior Emiratis cut a lucrative transaction with World Liberty Financial, the digital currency venture Don Jr and Eric founded. Trump gave the crypto baron a pardon and the Emiratis access to restricted US chips. Asked about such deals last year, Kushner, now a presidential envoy to Russia, Israel and elsewhere, said: “What people call conflicts of interests … I call experience and trusted relationships that we have throughout the world.” Those who strike up “trusted relationships” with the Trumps, even if there is not an obvious quid pro quo, gain something less tangible but maybe still more valuable: the aura of friendship with a president who is happy to wield his superpower to make or break smaller nations and their leaders. Vučić has plenty in common with Trump. Both are friendly with Vladimir Putin and contemptuous of the EU – in Vučić’s case, despite his country having applied to join. A shared disdain for Nato may help explain why the one part of the General Staff building’s heritage that the redevelopment pledged to retain was a memorial to the alliance’s “aggression” against Serbia. And there is a lot that Vučić could use US help with, not least the fate of Kosovo, which he says is still part of Serbia. Not long after his father returned to office, Don Jr landed in Belgrade. Vučić said that during their meeting he “emphasised the importance of the economic and political relations between Serbia and the USA and stressed the importance of strategic cooperation between the two countries and joint projects in the years to come”. When Don Jr returned the following month, Vučić fed him a choice sucking-pig. For Vučić, the support of the first family was timely. Days before his regime stripped the General Staff site of its protection, the collapse of a canopy at Novi Sad railway station, which killed 16 people, triggered rolling protests against graft. The student organisers’ slogan has become “Serbia or mafia”. Don Jr’s visit came on the eve of the biggest demonstration in Serbia’s history. He invited Vučić on to his podcast, Triggered, and declared that the Serb ruler’s opponents were “weaponising” the Novi Sad disaster, just as Trump’s had done with the Capitol riots after his 2020 election defeat. But the protesters maintained their momentum, and began to rally against the Trump tower. In May 2025, Vučić went to the US, hoping to visit Trump at Mar-a-Lago, his Florida members’ club. He got to see Rudy Giuliani, Trump’s disgraced lawyer, but not the president. State media reported this was because Vučić fell ill. No sooner was Vučić home than police arrested Goran Vasić, the man who had been installed as head of the heritage institute to replace Dubravka Đukanović following her resignation. To achieve the cancellation of the General Staff building’s protected status, prosecutors said, Vasic had forged a supportive expert opinion. More arrests followed. In December 2025, Vučić’s culture minister was indicted for abuse of office for his alleged part in the General Staff scheme. Within days, Kushner’s company announced the project was off. Coup or cover-up? Vučić’s threat of reprisals was not idle. His allies attacked Đukanović, claiming that she had tried to profit personally from her time as a heritage official. Her deputy, who received a visit from the state security service after she went on television to denounce the cancellation of the General Staff building’s protection, has been accused of unrelated misconduct. The Serbian conservators’ industry body said this had “the obvious aim of discrediting her”. Both are expected to give evidence in the criminal proceedings. For the specialist unit of organised-crime prosecutors who brought the charges, this is a watershed case. Never before has a serving Serbian minister been indicted. Vučić accuses the prosecutors of staging a coup. Others, though, fear they are pulling their punches. That concern increased when Nikola Selaković, the indicted culture minister, used a court appearance in April to reveal that, while police were raiding his ministry, he was in his office sipping plum brandy and smoking cigarettes with Mladen Nenadić, the head of the organised-crime prosecutors’ unit. The unit’s spokesperson said there was “no discussion regarding the course of the case”. “In everything that happened regarding potential investments, I saw a chance for our country and citizens,” said Selaković, who faces three years in prison if convicted. Vučić has not been charged. Neither has his lieutenant, Mali. Both deny wrongdoing. The indictment refers to evidence from witnesses who were present at the Vučić meeting in February 2024 but does not mention it, raising questions about the apparent decision to omit what would appear to be a key part of the narrative. The spokesperson for the organised crime prosecutors’ unit said that it had evidence regarding Vučić’s February 2024 meeting with the heritage officials. Beyond those already indicted, prosecutors were “conducting pretrial proceedings in this case to determine potential criminal liability of other persons as well”, the spokesperson added. Vučić has stepped down and cannot seek another term but is expected to retain his control over the regime if he is elected prime minister on 25 October. In one of his last acts as president, he issued 49 pardons. Some of the recipients have not been identified and it is not clear whether they include defendants in the General Staff case. The White House referred questions to the Trumps’ company. Its representative said: “The Trump Organization has no plans to develop any project in Belgrade, was never, at any point, involved in any discussions or negotiations to acquire any site in Belgrade and denies any involvement in or knowledge of the alleged claims.” Kushner’s spokesperson said: “The suggestion that Jared Kushner pursued the Belgrade project as part of any political arrangement or ‘pay to play’ scheme is categorically false.” Rather, it was “an opportunity to transform a site associated with a painful chapter in Serbia’s history into a symbol of healing and reconciliation, while bringing substantial private investment, jobs and economic opportunity to Belgrade”. The spokesperson added: “Jared had no involvement in the Serbian government’s internal processes concerning the site’s protected status.” For all Vučić’s difficulties, the tale of the Trump Tower Belgrade does not appear to have put others off doing business with the first family. Trump retains stakes in dozens of his companies, even if his sons nominally run them. In July, he released his financial disclosure for his first year back at the White House. It showed he had made $2bn.

title: Cyril Hilsum obituary
summary: Government physicist whose radar research paved the way for flat-panel TV and computer screens based on liquid crystals
text: Cyril Hilsum’s research into stable liquid crystals and the devices in which they could be used paved the way for the flat-panel television and computer screens that are now ubiquitous in homes, offices and public spaces. Hilsum, who has died aged 101, was leading a Ministry of Defence team at the Royal Radar Establishment (RRE) in Malvern, Worcestershire, in the late 1960s when Harold Wilson’s Labour government, looking to develop a new generation of miniature radar systems, tasked him with creating flat displays to replace the bulky cathode-ray-tube screens used for traditional radar set-ups. Realising the key to flat-screen technology was the emerging science of liquid crystals, Hilsum organised a meeting of liquid crystal researchers – and soon realised there was only one person in the room who really understood anything about them: George Gray, from Hull University. Gray was immediately offered a contract, and began working with Hilsum and Peter Raynes, an optoelectronics expert at the RRE, on fulfilling the government’s brief. By 1972 the three of them had developed a mixture that was suitable for use in screens, made largely of cyanobiphenyls, compounds that remain stable even when heated or exposed to sunlight or ultraviolet light. This gave the resulting screens durability in real-world applications. Although originally designed to support the RRE’s nascent radar technology, the liquid crystal displays (or LCDs) that used the mixture soon found practical uses elsewhere. While the MoD retained the patents, Hilsum persuaded the chemicals company BDH to manufacture and sell the mixtures under licence, eventually netting the government more than £100m in royalties from their use in watches and calculators, and then later in laptops, tablets and phones. Hilsum was born in Stepney, east London, to Benjamin and Ada, who were street traders. A bright boy who had learned to read proficiently by the age of three and spent hours dismantling toys to see how they worked, he went to Raine’s Foundation school in Bethnal Green, after which, during the second world war, he won a scholarship to University College London, which had been evacuated to Bangor in north Wales. He graduated with a degree in physics in 1945 and later a PhD, meeting fellow student Betty Cooper at UCL and marrying her in 1947. He and Betty, who became a teacher, were keen Labour party supporters, and after the war would attend Winston Churchill’s meetings in order to heckle him. After an initial spell working for the MoD in central London immediately after the war, he moved in 1947 to the Admiralty Research Laboratory in Teddington, where he met Alan Turing, who worked at the nearby National Physical Laboratory, and whom he once beat at chess. By 1950, aged 25, he was leading a team studying military uses for infrared light, based at the Services Electronics Research Laboratory in Baldock, Hertfordshire. Hilsum joined the RRE in 1964 to carry out research into gallium arsenide, a semiconductor material that handles high-frequencies, and on the development of radar, transistors and light-emitting diodes (LEDs). In fact his work on semiconductors was as significant as that on LCDs, and included helping to develop infrared lasers that now underpin fibre optic telecommunications. He was also instrumental in developing the Gunn diode, a high-frequency oscillator that generates microwave signals used in motion detectors and proximity sensors, including police radar speed guns – sometimes to his disadvantage, given that he was a fast driver. In tandem, his work on developing miniature radar systems led to Claribel, a device for detecting the trajectory of a bullet, which was used to locate snipers in Northern Ireland during the Troubles. In 1974 Hilsum became the UK’s chief scientific officer, the highest rank for a scientist in the civil service and a position he held until in 1983 he accepted the role of chief scientist, and later research director, at the General Electrical Company’s Hirst Research Centre in Wembley, north-west London. Always a promoter of women in sciences, at GEC he insisted his department hire equal numbers of both sexes. Hilsum served as president of the Institute of Physics from 1988 to 1990, the year that he was appointed CBE. He retired from GEC in 1995. A fellow of the Royal Society, he won the Faraday Medal and in 2007 the Royal Society’s Royal Medal “for his many outstanding contributions and for continuing to use his prodigious talents on behalf of industry, government and academe”. The British Liquid Crystal Society awards the Cyril Hilsum Medal annually for the best contribution to liquid crystal technology. In later years Hilsum built a laboratory in his house in Pinner, Middlesex, where, aged 97, he came up with his final invention – an ink containing sensors to conduct electricity – earning him the last of more than 70 patents. He ascribed his longevity to red wine and chocolate, and was a lifelong reader of the Guardian. Betty died in 1987, and one of their daughters, Karen, also predeceased him, in 1997. Hilsum founded the Karen Burt award at the Women’s Engineering Society. He is survived by their other daughter, Lindsey, international editor for Channel 4 News, and a grandson, Alexander. • Cyril Hilsum, physicist and inventor, born 17 May 1925; died 23 September 2026

title: Food and fuel run low as besieged Yemeni city braces for Houthi breakthrough
summary: Speed of advance has left people rushing to buy food as basic supplies to city are cut off by fighting
text: Ali Abdulsamed spent all day waiting and walking. Like many people in the besieged Yemeni city of Taiz, he was searching for some food for his family of six. But each time he reached the end of the queue at the grocers, he was greeted with empty shelves. He would go on foot to the next shop, unable to afford the price of petrol, which more than doubled last week. After visiting more than a dozen stores, Abdulsamed managed to find a 25kg bag of wheat flour – sold at more than twice its usual price. It would have to do, he was lucky to find anything at all. As Iran-allied Houthi rebels advance and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces closes off routes into the city, conditions in Taiz have become increasingly difficult. Yemen’s third most populous city has found itself besieged from all sides, with its supplies of fuel, food and other basic goods cut off. The UN World Food Programme (WFP) warned on Monday that the fighting had denied vital assistance to 800,000 people in Taiz: a city of about 1 million, which already had some of the highest levels of food insecurity in the country. The speed of the Houthi advance gave people little time to prepare, prompting a sudden rush on stores and driving up the price of goods still left in the city. Crowds have been gathering around grocery stores and gas stations, trying to stock up on the essentials as fears of shortages spread. “I wasn’t aware that the situation would become difficult so suddenly and that shops would close, but since 3 October, almost all food items have disappeared,” said Abdulsamed, 48. “I don’t have savings to stock up on food for the family, so I resorted to selling my wife’s gold ring.” He, like many others in Taiz, has stopped driving or even taking buses as petrol and bus fares have become too expensive. To avoid paying, Abdulsamed sometimes walks up to 10km (6 miles) a day. Abdulsamed works in a mobile repair shop on one of the main streets in the heart of Taiz. Traffic outside used to be constant and the shop was visited by a steady flow of customers. Now, the street is almost empty, save for those few people in Taiz scrambling to find supplies before hurrying home. The sound of explosions and gunfire echoes throughout the day. Taiz has become the new frontline in the war between the Houthis and Yemeni government forces after the Houthis launched a military campaign last month to take Yemen’s Red Sea coast. The renewed offensive interrupted four years of relative calm in Yemen after a UN-brokered ceasefire froze frontlines in 2022. The Houthis have moved south at a blistering speed, seizing more than 1,000km of territory over the last month, which gives them control over the Bab al-Mandab strait: a vital shipping lane. They have traded strikes with Saudi Arabia, launching attacks on Riyadh airport, with rebel-controlled Sana’a being hit in return, as the Saudis try to support Yemeni government forces. Their offensive was halted at Taiz, a city that has never fallen out of Yemeni government control since the country’s civil war began in 2014, and has been a long-sought goal for the rebels. The city sits at the crossroads between the north and the south, and if it should fall to the Houthis, Aden, the seat of Yemen’s government, will be cut off. So far the Houthis have failed to capture the city. Its rugged terrain is defended by local fighters as well as reinvigorated government forces, who announced a counteroffensive two weeks ago to push back the Houthis. But those who live in Taiz fear the Houthis cannot be kept at bay for ever. Conversations at home, the mosque and at work are all dominated by the war. The latest news is shared at the dinner table, with out-of-school children asking their parents what will happen next. “Residents expect the war to reach the city soon, so everyone is stocking food at home, preparing to stay indoors for a long time and ensuring they have all their necessities,” said Abdulsamed. Life in the once-busy city ground to a halt as fighting drew closer last week. Schools, universities and many public institutions in Taiz closed on 4 October out of concern for the safety of students and employees. “This is not a time for studying. What we need now is to have enough food and water at home and wait until Taiz overcomes this crisis,” said Rawa, a 35-year-old schoolteacher, who asked to be identified only by her first name. Rawa spends almost all of her time at home, only leaving to scrounge for supplies. She used to spend her weekend afternoons at a nearby park, but on Sunday, arriving to find it completely deserted, she turned around and went back home. Even home offers little safety. Rawa’s house is located close to the frontlines in eastern Taiz and the sounds of explosions have been growing closer in recent days. In the past, she would have fled to her ancestral village south of Taiz, as she had done in the past. But now, the road is blocked. As fighting draws closer, she can do little more than make sure she feels prepared for a long siege. But, with each day, food and basic supplies grow more expensive. “We are just lucky we can afford [goods] and now have enough food and water at home,” said Rawa.

title: Trump’s ambassadors: the loyalists and allies at the center of controversy
summary: Kimberly Guilfoyle’s departure has renewed scrutiny of the president’s picks for diplomatic posts, from France to Jamaica
text: Donald Trump has appointed family members, friends and loyal political allies to represent the US on the world stage, dispatching an extraordinary array of characters to embassies across the world. While presidents of both parties have long rewarded donors and allies with plum ambassadorships, Trump has chosen loyalists willing to go to bat for him regardless of the implications for US-foreign relationships. The ousting of Kimberly Guilfoyle as US ambassador to Greece has renewed the spotlight on individuals appointed by the US president to such roles during his second term – from an election denier to a former auctioneer. She is just the latest Trump-era ambassador to become embroiled in scandal, and face resistance. Kimberly Guilfoyle Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle, a conservative personality and former politician, began serving as the ambassador to Greece in November 2025. She stepped down from her role in October after allegations of corruption. Guilfoyle was made ambassador to Greece shortly after the end of her engagement to Donald Trump Jr, the president’s son. She was accused of misconduct while serving as ambassador, such as promoting the business interests of one particular Greek construction and energy company, inviting Greek lobbyists to sit in on official diplomatic meetings, and asking an ally to pay off her $100,000 American Express card before her Senate confirmation hearing. Charles Kushner France Charles Kushner, the father-in-law of Ivanka Trump and father of Jared Kushner, began serving as ambassador to France and Monaco in July 2025. He is a former attorney and real estate developer, as well as a Trump donor. In February, Kushner was banned from a meeting with his counterparts after failing to show up for a summons regarding Kushner’s accusation that France allowed antisemitism and leftist extremism to run rampant. Kushner was convicted of tax evasion, making false statements to the Federal Election Commission and witness tampering. His conviction was later pardoned by Trump in 2020. Bill White Belgium Bill White is the former president of the Intrepid museum. He began serving as the ambassador to Belgium in November 2025, after being nominated by Trump. White has found himself in several public tiffs with Belgium’s foreign minister, Maxime Prévot. In February, the foreign minister admonished White for accusing Belgium of antisemitism. In August, the foreign minister scolded White for calling a Belgian official a “loser” on social media, though White denied doing so. Pete Hoekstra Canada Pete Hoekstra, a former Republican congressman from Michigan, began serving as the ambassador to Canada in April 2025. Trump’s contentious relationship with the US’s northern neighbor has put Hoekstra in the spotlight. Over the summer, more than 200,000 Canadians signed a petition to expel Hoekstra for normalizing Trump’s threats to make Canada the 51st state. Hoekstra has taken an openly critical stance toward Canada, most recently warning Canadians not to “meddle” in US politics before November’s US midterm elections. Billy Long Iceland William “Billy” Long, a former Republican congressman from Missouri and auctioneer, began serving as the ambassador to Iceland in August 2026. Long previously served briefly as the internal revenue commissioner but was removed, reportedly due to internal clashes with the treasury secretary, Scott Bessent. Earlier this year, Long was forced to apologize after joking that the US would make Iceland its 52nd state. Tom Rose Poland Tom Rose, a former conservative political commentator and adviser to Mike Pence, began serving as ambassador to Poland in November 2025. In February, Rose announced he would cut off communications with a Polish politician who serves as the speaker of the lower house in the Polish parliament over “insults” toward Trump. In return, Donald Tusk, the Polish prime minister, told Rose to “respect, not lecture” allies, which Rose rebuffed. Kari Lake Kari Lake, a longtime election denier and devout Trump ally, was tapped to serve as the ambassador to Jamaica in May 2026. Her nomination has not yet been confirmed. Lake has a long history of promoting false claims of election fraud, including in her own races that she lost. More recently, she served in the administration as the head of Voice of America, a federally funded news group. “Kari Lake is not the person for Jamaica,” Donald Tapia, who served as ambassador to Jamaica from 2019-2021, told the Miami Herald. Luis Moreno, the ambassador to Jamaica from 2014 until 2017, told the Miami Herald that Lake was “not really a policy person”. “It’s what we would call a lightweight appointment. I would expect lightweight efforts on her part, and what can I say? The Jamaican government will have to work with her because she’s an ambassador,” Moreno said. Other ambassador nominees with controversial histories have seen their nominations pulled or expired. The White House pulled its nomination of Nick Adams, a rightwing influencer known for his internet trolling, to become ambassador to Malaysia. Former officials in Muslim-majority Malaysia had criticized Trump’s decision to appoint Adams, calling it an insult to the country. Trump had tapped Amer Ghalib, a conservative Democrat who served as mayor of Hamtramck, Michigan, to serve as the ambassador to Kuwait. But Ghalib’s nomination stalled in the Senate after lawmakers accused him of engaging with antisemitic content on social media. While Trump has chosen various allies to serve in ambassadorship roles, more than half remain unfilled as of October. Just 92 of the 196 roles are filled, including for Cuba, where the US is exercising pressure and Ukraine, which is embroiled in a war with Russia.

title: US officials considering ad campaign to urge South African Afrikaners to emigrate
summary: Exclusive: Trump has falsely claimed Afrikaners are facing ‘white genocide’, but very few have applied to live in US
text: The US government could spend hundreds of thousands of dollars on a media campaign in South Africa to figure out why more white Afrikaners are not applying to become refugees to the US, as Donald Trump had hoped. State department officials, according to an August proposal seen by the Guardian, outlined a roughly $335,000 research and advertising effort after applications to the refugee program “trended lower than expected” since Afrikaners were allowed to apply directly online in November 2025. The document, written by the US mission in South Africa with a department research unit for the embassy in Pretoria, admits officials know little about why. “There’s currently little research about why Afrikaners are not applying to request referral into the US Refugee Admissions Program,” the proposal reads. The focus on Afrikaners flows from a February 2025 executive order directing officials to put Afrikaner resettlement first while the broader refugee program stayed suspended. Administration officials had said Afrikaners face racial discrimination and “white genocide”. The South African government has rejected the genocide claims, and experts have widely dismissed the idea that Afrikaners face targeted violence or genocide. Last year, the president restricted refugee admissions to 7,500, the lowest in US history, then raised it to 17,500 in May, with the added slots again going primarily to Afrikaners. The overall cap was 125,000 under Joe Biden. The US admitted 16,292 refugees in the fiscal year that ended 30 September, according to its most recent data reporting. The remaining five were Afghans: three from last November and two from September. A year earlier, South Africans made up 342 of 38,102 refugee admissions. The state department plan would proceed in three phases. The pitch suggests focus groups would be held in Pretoria and Krugersdorp in Gauteng, Bloemfontein and Kroonstad in Free State, Stellenbosch and Worcester in Western Cape and Kimberley and Orania in the Northern Cape, with the latter being an Afrikaner-only separatist community. Every location would host two age groups, 20 to 35 and 40 to 55, with participants grouped by urban or rural setting and household income. A survey of 1,000 Afrikaners, online and offline, would then test which messages work in which communities. The final phase is a six-month digital campaign, mostly in Afrikaans with possibly some English, aimed at Afrikaners “interested in migrating”. Because the community is hard to reach through conventional social and press channels, the proposal says, the department would hire an agency with local knowledge and use “trusted messengers”. In response, a spokesperson with the state department said “we continue to process and admit as refugees Afrikaners in South Africa who are escaping the threat of government-sponsored race-based discrimination”. “President Trump has been very clear that we are prioritizing the resettlement of Afrikaners in South Africa who are escaping government-sponsored race-based discrimination,” as part of US policy from the executive order, the spokesperson added. Trump’s 2025 order alleged “South Africa has taken aggressive positions towards the United States and its allies, including accusing Israel, not Hamas, of genocide in the International Court of Justice, and reinvigorating its relations with Iran to develop commercial, military, and nuclear arrangements.” This year’s Nobel peace prize went to Navi Pillay, the South African judge who chaired the UN commission that concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in Gaza, causing Trump to rave on Truth Social: “I know nothing about this woman, and neither does anyone else!” and that the prize should have gone to “the Great United States of America, whose Representative, ME, settled eight Wars, and many other things”. The South African government, for its part, has rejected the claim of genocide as unfounded and politically motivated. In New York last month, its foreign minister, Ronald Lamola, said “there is no evidence” for the genocide claim. Pretoria has also argued that few South Africans have taken up the offer, which it says shows the claims are false. The refugee program is one piece in a broader rupture. Trump announced last November that South Africa would not be invited to the 2026 G20 summit, which the US is hosting in Miami in mid-December, citing alleged abuses against white farmers. Washington has also cut aid and restricted visas over South Africa’s race and land policies. Last month, the US ambassador in Pretoria, Leo Brent Bozell III, wrote in an op-ed that his government was “shocked” by what it saw as Pretoria’s silence on a set of US requests. He cited concern over the country’s 2024 Expropriation Act and a push to make rural crime a priority. The administration is also putting money behind the cause. Just before funds expired, it moved to direct more than $175m from the state department’s Human Rights and Democracy Fund to 43 grants worth $176.9m, as the Guardian has reported. That is most of the $205m Congress appropriated for the fund, which bolsters rightwing causes abroad. One is a $1m grant meant for “advancing white Afrikaner rights” in South Africa and for collecting data on abuses against minorities. No recipient has been named. Sources with knowledge of the awards process told the Guardian that administration figures lobbied personally for the awards, reflecting the priorities of JD Vance on European cultural identity and Stephen Miller on immigration and support for white minorities. The bureau that runs refugee admissions has new leadership. Adam Zerbinopoulos, a career diplomat, became its senior official on 31 August.

title: Anatomy of a lie: James Talarico got the flu – sending rightwing midterm misinformation machine into overdrive
summary: Claims that James Talarico suffered a mental health crisis spread across rightwing media, offering a warning about disinformation ahead of the US midterm election
text: Where is James Talarico? The question ricocheted around rightwing echo chambers before metastasising into a conspiracy theory – and a reminder of the persistent danger of disinformation in the US midterm elections. The smear campaign began when Talarico, the Democratic candidate for the US Senate in Texas, was not seen in public for nine days. His campaign was slow to explain why. While nature abhors a vacuum, Donald Trump and social media seize on one and weaponise it. On 30 September, Talarico spoke at a Hispanic Business Council event by video. He had been diagnosed with the flu at an urgent care facility in Dallas after “starting to feel kind of under the weather a few days ago”, he said, and would not appear in person because he had a fever and was still contagious. On 7 October, the president held a rally in San Antonio, Texas, and claimed without evidence that “Tala-freako”, as he nicknames the Democrat, is vegan. Trump asserted: “He’s sick because he’s been forced to eat meat for political reasons and he’s throwing up all over the place.” On the same day, an X account with the username “Dan The Man, Always with a Plan” and a photo of “Trump 2028” cap tweeted without evidence: “He had a mental health crisis. That is what I heard from someone who would know inside information.” On 8 October, Steve Bannon, a former White House chief strategist, stirred the pot further on his influential War Room podcast in an interview with former Trump fundraiser Caroline Wren, who baselessly claimed: “I’m hearing that he checked himself into a mental institution – that he had a full-blown, like, mental breakdown.” On the same day, Ken Paxton, the Republican running against Talarico, weighed in with a social media post that showed Talarico on a “Wanted” poster and said: “Jimmy appears to be having a full-blown mental Tala-freak-out on the national stage. My campaign has a simple request: proof of life.” On 9 October, Spencer Pratt, a former candidate for mayor of Los Angeles, offered his take: “My sources are telling me Talarico is in a mental health facility. His campaign has stopped actively planning events in the vital homestretch of the campaign.” Rightwing media sites swung into action. RedState, the Daily Wire, the Right Scoop, Twitchy and PJ Media all amplified the false claims. Elon Musk, the world’s richest man, put more toxins in the bloodstream with posts such as: “The Talarico campaign is hiding something big that voters ought to know about.” Then, on 11 October, came the supposed coup de grâce. The conservative social media influencer Nick Sortor posted a 47-second audio clip on X that he said proved that Talarico had been discharged earlier in the week from Lindner Center of Hope, a mental health treatment centre in Mason, Ohio. The call was placed by Rhein Amacher, a self-described “right-wing provocateur”. In the clip, a woman whom Sorter claimed was an employee there says it looked like Talarico “was just discharged this evening”. The online Maga faithful were jubilant. But not for long. The Bulwark obtained the full phone call showing the purported employee had repeatedly denied any record of Talarico being at the centre. The timeline also did not add up. Amacher said he made the call to the mental health centre on Saturday evening, but Talarico was seen at the Austin City Limits music festival on Friday. On Saturday, he made an appearance at a Kacey Musgraves concert in Dallas. The Lindner Center of Hope wrote in an X post on Sunday that Talarico “has never received treatment” from the facility. Talarico replied to the post, saying, “I’ve never even been to Ohio.” He included a tears of joy emoji. JT Ennis, a spokesperson for Talarico, called Sorter’s claim “a lie designed to promote a pathetic conspiracy theory” in an X post and wrote that Talarico had been recovering from the flu at his home in Austin. Talarico has type 1 diabetes, placing him at higher risk for flu-related complications. Even Maga followers began to acknowledge that the claim had collapsed. But if the episode appeared absurd, its implications for the midterms were serious. Reed Galen, a former Republican strategist and co-founder of the Lincoln Project, an anti-Trump group, said: “It was a bit wild but a good reminder to all of us how sophisticated, effective and efficient the rightwing/ bot/Russian-generated misinformation-disinformation machine is. “This story came from some weirdos in Ohio or whatever but the point is that someone or something picked it up and amplified it to a point where – despite no evidence of reality – it became something that was an issue in the Texas Senate campaign.” Galen added: “Even if Talarico wins, that in and of itself was a win for the tactic. If you have the ability and the willingness to do this stuff, it’s not gonna work every time, but if you do it a lot, sometimes you’re gonna have success, and sometimes those successes might be strategic in nature, not just tactical.” Disinformation has been rampant in elections for at least a decade and 2026 is no different. NewsGuard, a company that tracks online misinformation, says it has identified and debunked 25 false claims about the midterms that have gone viral on social media platforms. Its list of false claims includes Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic candidate for US Senate in Michigan, having called for sharia law in the US during a 2022 speech; a Dominion Voting Systems whistleblower accusing US politicians of taking millions of dollars in bribes to rig the 2026 midterm elections; and Ken Paxton’s Senate campaign paying for a Texas billboard that says “Pedos Ain’t That Bad”. Another example related to an image that purportedly showed Rob Sand, a centrist Democratic candidate for governor of Iowa, campaigning with the progressives Ilhan Omar and Tim Walz. NewsGuard found it was generated by artificial intelligence (AI). Even as AI gives new tools to nefarious actors, defences have been weakened. Last year, the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, shut down the state department’s Counter Foreign Information Manipulation and Interference office, accusing it of censorship and wasting US taxpayer money. Major tech platforms – notably Musk’s X and Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta – have gutted trust, safety and factchecking teams, turning online spaces into a lawless wild west. Musk has spent a record $366m in ⁠the election cycle so far to help Republicans retain control of Congress. Richard Hasen, a professor at UCLA School of Law and election law expert, said: “When you’ve got Elon Musk owning one of the important social media platforms and being a vector for spreading the misinformation, and also when you’ve got the companies like Meta no longer doing the same kind of trust and safety work, it’s just an atmosphere where this kind of stuff can spread.” But there is another, more optimistic perspective. While the Talarico rumours spread like wildfire in corners of the internet, they did not penetrate the mainstream media, and fizzled out once the reality became clear. Hasen added: “The Talarico case shows the limits of being able to do this. This was something that was easily disproven and could have potentially even backfired, showing that the anti-Talarico forces are so desperate that they have to make up a false claim to try to boost a weak candidate. “Every election now we’re hearing it’s going to be ‘the AI election’ and voters are going to be tricked. What I think is happening in part is that everyone’s on their guard. We all know that we can’t necessarily believe our eyes or our ears and things that a politician might appear to say or do might not necessarily be true, so that’s a little bit of a natural check.” Hasen points out that candidates are better equipped to dismantle digital lies. To debunk the rumour, Talarico shared home security camera footage with the New York Times, establishing his presence at home. “Because we’re leaving digital footprints everywhere, that sometimes could be another way to debunk a rumour.” Tara Setmayer, a former Republican communications director on Capitol Hill, also believes that the conspiracy theories have lost their novelty value. “The voters have become hip to this game,” she said. “There are too many other negative things going on in everyday American lives, so I don’t think these types of cheap attacks are going to resonate at this point. “The difference between this election cycle and past election cycles is that, because it seems like we’ve been here before and we know how batshit crazy Maga can be, that mainstream media isn’t platforming the crazy as often,” said Setmayer. “They’re actually reporting it in a way with the healthy amount of scepticism that it deserves, so it’s dismissed off the top whereas in the past it was so novel.” Setmayer added: “At this point now it feels like Donald Trump and Maga’s greatest hits: we’re really in the fat Elvis period of the Maga election campaign tactics and it’s obvious to everyone. The absurdity is finally breaking through even with some Republican voters, evidenced by how terrible Donald Trump’s numbers are and Republicans writ large.”

title: ‘Like selling wolves from Yellowstone’: how protected US sharks are being sold off to foreign aquariums
summary: While anglers cannot take endangered sand tiger sharks, a loophole lets private firms catch the fish to sell abroad, profiting from Delaware Bay’s conservation success
text: Shortly after 12.45pm, what remains of a 300-metre line goes taut. Somewhere beneath the murky green surface of Delaware Bay, on the eastern US coast, a sand tiger shark has taken the bait of a mackerel chunk. Marine researchers at the University of Delaware haul the line towards a small boat as the shark’s grey-brown outline emerges. It is a large animal: 225cm (7ft) long with a 90cm girth. Its mouth hangs open, revealing rows of jagged teeth. The researchers work quickly, measuring the shark, recording its sex, and taking blood and muscle samples. A tag is then fastened beneath its dorsal fin, through its thick sandpapery skin. The mature male seems to watch them as they work. Then it is lowered back into the bay. With a powerful flick of its tail, it disappears almost as quickly as it arrived. Several thousand miles away, sand tiger sharks collected from these same waters circle tanks in Abu Dhabi, moving among artificial reefs and through blue-lit tunnels in the desert city’s aquariums, where visitors pay up to $100 (£75) for day passes. They will never return to Delaware Bay. Tagging sand tigers – a species of concern that is prohibited from being caught in US waters – offers clues about the lives of these fish, which are critically endangered globally. However, in recent years, the bay – a US habitat of particular concern between the states of Delaware and New Jersey – has become a hotspot for private collection of specimens for the global aquarium trade. A recent study by marine researchers from the University of Delaware, Delaware State University and the University of Rhode Island shows that, since 2018, the number of sand tiger sharks collected from Delaware Bay for public display has risen sharply, from two that year to 40 in 2023. In total, 80 of the sharks were taken from Delaware waters for aquariums between 2018 and 2024. The study, citing data from Delaware’s Department of Natural Resources and Environmental Control (DNREC) shows that nearly all the sand tiger sharks collected from Delaware Bay were sent overseas: the highest numbers went to China and the United Arab Emirates, while others went to South Korea and Thailand. Some were sent to other countries – including Turkey, Scotland, Israel, Italy, France and Uzbekistan – with a few remaining in the US. “This [private collecting of sand tiger sharks] is like going into Yellowstone [national park] and catching wolves and then selling them to zoos in France or in the Middle East,” says Brad Wetherbee, a shark researcher at University of Rhode Island who co-wrote the study. “[These countries] used to have sand tigers. They could just go out in their own waters and catch them and collect them, but their populations are so low they can’t do that any more.” The US has spent decades restricting the killing of sand tiger sharks, yet in recent years, through a regulatory maze of federal and state permits, private collecting companies can legally remove these protected sharks from the wild for public display. A shark that an angler would be required to release after catching can instead be transported thousands of miles and placed in a foreign aquarium, with private companies profiting from the trade. “How can we say these people [private collectors] can remove them and functionally harvest them, whereas these ones [recreational anglers] can’t?” says Aaron Carlisle, an associate professor from the University of Delaware’s school of marine science and another of the study’s authors. “If our concern is sustainability, we need to know what is the impact of removal.” Sand tigers, despite their fearsome appearance, are non-aggressive and docile. They have one of the lowest reproductive rates of any shark species, reaching sexual maturity at about six to 10 years old, depending on sex, and producing just one or two pups every two to three years. Once widespread across subtropical and temperate coastal waters, the species has declined across much of its range. Populations in parts of south-east Asia, west Africa and the Arabian Sea have fallen to critically low levels, largely because of overfishing, including bycatch, and habitat degradation. In some regions, they are believed to have been wiped out entirely. The north-west Atlantic is one of the few regions where the species’ populations are not critically endangered, largely due to federal and state protections. Yet the population has never had a formal assessment, and how healthy it actually is remains difficult to determine. One private company has accounted for most of the recent collection in Delaware Bay. Dynasty Marine, a Florida-based supplier of live marine animals to aquariums and research institutions worldwide that drew bipartisan outrage in Florida in 2025 after legally netting a manta ray for SeaWorld Abu Dhabi, began collecting sand tigers in Delaware in 2021. A spokesperson for Delaware state’s department of natural resources and environmental control (DNREC) says the company has “ramped up collection in the following years”. Records reviewed by the Guardian show that Dynasty Marine collected 71 sharks between 2022 and 2024. The study also records 35 sand tiger harvest requests in 2025, with most destined for China. Recipients of the sharks caught between 2022 and 2024 included SeaWorld Abu Dhabi, Dubai Aquarium and Underwater Zoo, Sea Life Busan in South Korea, Aquaria Phuket in Thailand and Guangzhou Ocean World in China. Dynasty Marine was asked to comment on the number of sand tigers it collects a year but did not respond. In a statement to the Guardian, it said: “Every collection we conduct is done in full compliance with all applicable federal and state permits and regulations. “The animals we collect are cared for to the highest standards and go on to live in human care, where they play a vital role in educating millions of people each year about marine life and the importance of ocean conservation.” The company says it supports “numerous marine conservation, science and education initiatives”, including shark research, manatee rehabilitation and coral restoration efforts. Private companies seeking to collect sand tigers for public display must first obtain an exempted fishing permit from the US National Marine Fisheries Service (known as Noaa Fisheries). If the collection takes place in Delaware waters, the permit holder must then obtain a scientific collecting permit from DNREC. Noaa Fisheries says it reviews applications for capture of the sharks on a “case-by-case basis”. “We have an overall scientifically based annual quota for all shark research and public display,” says John Chu, a Noaa Fisheries spokesperson. “We consider that overall quota when issuing public display permits.” The state follows the federal lead in granting permits. The DNREC says Noaa Fisheries’ approval is “evidence enough for the state to believe that removal of the permitted number of individual sharks is sustainable”. However, scientists argue that, without knowing the population’s size or trend, it is difficult to determine what impact removing sharks for display in an aquarium may have. The concern is heightened by the size of many sand tigers collected in Delaware. Many are large juveniles or near-mature adults that could soon reproduce if left in the wild. The DNREC says the recent increase in collections is “an emerging concern”, but says it would be up to the federal government to act on that. It says an assessment on the number of sand tiger sharks in the area would “lend context” to a permit request from a private collection company. This uncertainty extends to what happens to the sharks after they leave Delaware Bay. Neither the DNREC or Noaa Fisheries record the sharks’ final status, including whether those animals become sick or die, though the DNREC says it intends to change this. Dewayne Fox, an assistant fisheries professor at Delaware State University who also worked on the study, says the issue is not just whether the collections are sustainable, but also who benefits from a population protected in US waters. “We have protected the habitat and yet we are going to allow some out-of-state company to come in, catch these animals and then ship them all the way around the world and make money,” he says. “Everybody else is benefiting from our conservation success.”

title: Key US voters say economy is getting worse ahead of midterms, exclusive poll finds
summary: Nearly 61% believe country is in recession and 65% of independents say economy is worse, according to new Harris poll
text: With the midterm elections less than three weeks away, key voting groups including independents, rural voters and even some Republicans are increasingly disenchanted with Donald Trump’s economy, according to an exclusive Harris poll for the Guardian. The majority of those surveyed were pessimistic about the economy, with three-quarters of Americans saying they are concerned about a recession while 61% wrongly believe that the US is already experiencing one. By its typical definition, the US is not currently experiencing a recession. The poll shows growing weariness across the political spectrum over high prices. Republicans, fighting to keep control of Congress, are losing support with independent voters, who are expected to be the deciding factor in key swing races. Nearly two-thirds (65%) of independents said the economy was worse, up from 48% who said the same in September 2024 in the heat of the 2024 presidential election. Even within the Republican ranks, optimism has waned. In February 2025, just a few weeks after Trump was inaugurated, 39% of Republicans said the economy was getting better. By February 2026, just before the US launched attacks against Iran, that optimism was up to 49%. In the latest poll, just 28% of Republicans said the economy was getting better. Voters say the high prices they are seeing at gas stations and grocery stores will be a key factor when they cast their votes in November. Two-thirds of those polled said that gas prices and grocery prices are their most important issues heading into the election, followed by living expenses, healthcare costs and foreign affairs. Recent inflation data showed that annualized prices increased 3.7% in September, the highest reading before a midterm election, excluding the pandemic, since 1990. Energy prices have been especially high since the Iran war, with average gas prices at the pump crossing $1.20 more per gallon compared with a year ago. California drivers, who are experiencing the highest gas prices, are paying on average $6.20 per gallon, according to AAA. Democrats in swing races have spent much of the last few months framing their midterm battles as a fight, in part, against a growing affordability crisis. James Talarico, the Democratic candidate in a closely watched US Senate race in Texas, has a campaign ad of him holding a paper bag of groceries. “Too many Texans feel like they’re drowning, the cost of groceries, gas, healthcare,” he says in the video. “They say I can’t win because of my name,” Abdul El-Sayed, another Democratic candidate for a US Senate race in Michigan, said at a recent campaign event. “My name is not the reason your gas prices are through the roof. My name is not the reason you can’t afford your groceries.” In the new poll, a vast majority of Americans agreed that there was an affordability crisis, including 96% of Republicans. But Americans still remain divided over who has a solution. Democrats (71%) were more likely than Republicans (59%) to say that their own party had a solution. Republicans were more likely (26%) to say neither party had a solution compared with Democrats (17%) Half of independents said neither party had a solution, while 14% sided with Democrats and 10% with Republicans. Rural Americans, considered a core base for Trump, were more likely to believe that neither party has a solution (41%) compared with their suburban (35%) and urban (27%) counterparts. Four out of 10 of rural Americans said they were living in “survival mode”, where one surprise bill could sink them, compared with 35% of urban and 27% of suburban Americans. When asked what is most affecting today’s gas prices, 46% of rural Americans said the US government compared with 28% of Republicans who said the same. Republicans were the least likely of any group to blame the US government, instead spreading the blame across oil companies, the Iranian government and natural economic fluctuations. This survey was conducted online within the US by The Harris Poll from 24 September to 3 October 2026 among a nationally representative sample of 3,998 US adults.

title: UK economy unexpectedly grows in August despite fall in consumer spending
summary: Latest data showing surprise 0.1% growth is boost to John Healey a fortnight before his first budget
text: The UK economy unexpectedly continued to grow in August despite a fall in consumer spending before John Healey’s first budget as chancellor. Figures from the Office for National Statistics showed gross domestic product (GDP) rose by 0.1% that month, compared with 0.4% growth in July. That confounded a forecast by City economists of a 0.1% contraction. With less than a fortnight before Healey’s tax and spending announcement, the ONS reading represents a surprise boost given that the Middle East war is rattling the global economy and hitting British households and businesses with a surge in energy costs. After petrol and diesel prices rose and with higher energy bills hitting household spending, the ONS said the consumer-facing services sector fell by 0.3% on the month, after a decline of 0.1% in July. Despite the overall services sector showing no growth in August, the surprise headline improvement was driven by strength in manufacturing with 0.8% growth in the wider production sector, which includes manufacturing, mining and energy generation. Construction output fell by 0.2%. The largest negative contribution came from sports, amusement and recreation activities, alongside a slump in food and drink services. Analysts said the fall could be a sign of a reversal from an earlier boost from the World Cup and unusually hot weather, or could reflect households trimming their spending. The ONS said GDP over the wider three months to the end of August rose by 0.7%. On an annual basis, it said the economy had grown by 2.1%, the strongest growth rate since August 2022. It comes after the International Monetary Fund this week upgraded its growth forecasts for the UK this year but warned it expected a modest slowdown in 2027 as higher energy prices take their toll. Speaking from Bangkok, where he is attending the meetings of the IMF and World Bank, Healey welcomed the figures: “Despite conflicts in the Middle East and Europe hitting people across the world, today’s figures offer more proof of Britain’s resilience in the face of these global shocks. “This week the IMF have upgraded UK growth for 2026 and said that our fiscal discipline stands out with the lowest deficit in the G7 forecast by 2029 … my budget will build on this approach to drive good growth in every postcode.” Sanjay Raja, chief UK economist at Deutsche Bank, said: “Undoubtedly, there may be some hiccups to come in the runup to year-end, especially as energy prices continue to bite household incomes, and higher rates continue to drag on spending and investment. “The good news? The UK’s resilience story continues. It’s hard to overstate how strong the UK performance has been all year.” Against a volatile backdrop, the chancellor is under pressure to use his tax and spending address to the Commons on 28 October for a package of support to soften the blow for households, including help with rising energy bills. However, he will face a delicate balancing act amid a sharp increase in government borrowing costs. In recent months, Britain’s economy had shown more resilience than had been expected at the start of the Iran war after recording the strongest rate of growth in the G7 in the first half of 2026. Official figures suggested a strong expansion in AI-related business activity as one factor behind the surprise rise. Jake Finney, senior economist at PwC, said: “The UK’s growth performance has been a bright spot amid a less impressive run of economic news following events in the Middle East. Business investment has been an important driver, particularly spending on ICT hardware, likely linked to the build-out of AI infrastructure.” In a fillip for the chancellor, the IMF this week upgraded its UK growth forecasts for this year, but warned that it expected a modest slowdown in 2027 as higher energy prices take their toll. However, economists said momentum was likely to falter at the end of the year as households come under pressure from rising inflation. Financial markets now anticipate the Bank of England to raise interest rates next month from 3.75% to 4%, before four more quarter-point rate increases in 2027. Matt Swannell, the chief economic adviser to the Item Club, said: “We’re sceptical this strength can last … Some pullback looks inevitable. The impact of the conflict in the Middle East is also starting to be felt. Higher energy bills and petrol prices are pushing up inflation and hitting consumers’ spending power.”

title: No timeline for lifting Land Registry paywall as ownership remains opaque
summary: Defra promised in March to work towards free access to data on large plots in England and Wales
text: The government has refused to say when the public will be able to freely access information about who owns large plots of land across England and Wales. Emma Reynolds, the previous secretary of state for the environment, announced in March that the paywall protecting large amounts of the Land Registry would be partly lifted. Campaigners called for this change in order to make large landowners more accountable, particularly for key areas such as river catchments, grouse moors and peatland. But Reynolds did not put a date on when the paywall would be lifted, and the Land Registry is an “arm’s length body”, a non-ministerial government department that falls under the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government. In setting out the land use framework in March, the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) pledged only that it would “work with HM Land Registry this year to provide access to free, spatial land ownership data for larger properties covering the vast majority of England and Wales, excluding almost all homeowners”. This may require a further public consultation, in addition to the consultation that preceded the land use framework. In July, a spokesperson for the Land Registry said: “HM Land Registry is supportive of initiatives that promote the more effective use of land. However, our plans with regard to this are still at a very early stage, and a number of aspects will be subject to consultation before any firm decisions are made. As such, we are currently unable to comment on timelines, what may be released, the format, or any associated attributes. We anticipate being in a position to provide more of an update early next year.” In August, a Land Registry spokesperson said it was not clear which parts of the Land Registry data would be made public, nor who might be allowed to access the data and by what means. Guy Shrubsole, the environmental campaigner and author of Who Owns England?, said: “It’s ridiculous that in the 21st century the public are kept in the dark about who owns the land beneath our feet. This is data that will help councils build more homes, expose who’s polluting our rivers and help communities restore nature.” Andy Burnham, who took over as prime minister from Keir Starmer this summer, has made localism a key priority of his premiership. Shrubsole said allowing people to see data on the ownership of land should be part of that agenda. “Burnham has come to power promising place-first politics, and to bring unaccountable government agencies to heel,” he said. “Who owns our land underpins any politics of place, and it’s high time the Land Registry was made to reveal this profoundly important information.” A Defra spokesperson said: “We are improving the transparency of land ownership data, and will provide free access to land ownership data for the vast majority of England, as we committed to in our land use framework. We are taking forward this commitment and will share further details as this work continues.”

title: ‘I introduce myself to anyone who looks a bit jumpy’: a security guard’s take on anti-shoplifting fixes
summary: A professional reveals the most effective tricks of the trade, from a little bit of empathy to hi-tech cameras
text: I’ve run into volatile thieves for years – from opportunistic phone snatchers to people ripping computers off desks and biofuel bandits trying to steal vats of used cooking oil – and every time I file an incident report, I try to make a recommendation for preventive measures. It’s safer to try to avoid a situation where things get physical with a suspected criminal. I don’t want to let my employers down, but I also don’t want anyone to have to go to hospital – myself included. Greggs seems to be following a similar train of thought: earlier this year the chain phased out self-service cabinets in areas where shoplifting is rife and has installed safe pod “robocops” with 120-decibel sirens in some stores. But snatch thefts seem to be on the rise everywhere, from “steaming” (large groups overwhelming a store) in city centres to machinery being swiped from rural farm shops. The cost of this crime – in terms of lost merchandise and measures to tackle it – further erodes margins at a time when retailers are battling higher employment costs and increases to business rates. Customers, ever squeezed by rising energy bills, are becoming doubly impatient: those who are not tempted by grabbable goods are rightly affronted by measures such as sliding shields that seem to imply that everyone is a criminal. But is it possible to make a store thief proof and welcoming to law-abiding clientele? Discreet high technology is a happy medium. PTZ cameras (pan/tilt/zoom, which can be adjusted to track and focus on a single suspect) are one of the most-effective choices. They’re more efficient than fixed-camera CCTV, less controversial than AI surveillance and a serious upgrade on the convex mirror mounted at the end of the aisle in your local corner shop. PTZ camera manoeuvrability means high-quality facial images, a must-have when trying to build evidence. Freeze-frames can also be used to generate stills that some premises owners choose to turn into warning posters, or share on a chat group with other local businesses. My advice here is to be wary of GDPR regulations and remember that an incorrect time signature can render recordings inadmissible. As useful as movable cameras are, they still require a human operator. Hiring guards can feel like a tax on businesses – but one that goes unpaid at considerable risk. Ask anyone who lives in a village whether they’d prefer a CCTV camera or a “bobby on the beat” and the answer would be probably unanimously the latter. The sight of a uniformed officer can be a strong deterrent. However, it comes with an upper limit. For example: if a 3,000 sq metre supermarket can accommodate 40,000 goods and 4,000 daily customers, one guard will not be able to cover it all. It is also hard to identify which customers might be preparing to swipe something, especially given the rise of “middle-class shoplifting”. As someone whose job pays just above minimum wage, this is an interesting phenomenon. I get that inflation presses down on all of us, but people further up the pyramid than me should know it won’t be shareholders or bonus-receiving bosses taking the hit for goods being pinched: it will be prices. Higher costs will further imperil the most vulnerable people who walk on site, the ones who already cannot afford bread or baby formula. My best approach in these cases is empathy. I try to introduce myself to anyone who hangs around but looks jumpy; explain that every tap of my bank card makes me sweat too. I also try to build local knowledge of repeat offenders: insight that made the bobbies on the beat so valuable. I know it won’t work against content creators who film me for “lols” while I’m administering first aid, and who half of all young Brits apparently want to emulate. I honestly fear them more than I do getting punched, stabbed or spat on. But doing your revision pays off, especially when encountering an unsettled local resident with a penchant for threatening people with kitchen utensils. As the resident in question strode towards the premises one morning, my shiftmate quickly asked me whether I knew his name and address (I did). “Morning, Mr Beddlington,” said my colleague as the resident got level with us and before he could grab his first frying pan. “Everything OK at Thorn Court today? Anything we can help with?” The resident did an about-face and left the site. Loss prevention done low-cost and painlessly. • Names and addresses have been changed What the Bouncer Saw: Life on the Front Line of the Security Business by George Bass is published by Hachette.
