title: Burnham v Swinney: will the UK PM overshadow the SNP’s conference?
summary: Prime minister presents new kind of challenge for SNP, and his Scottish visit will loom large over its big event
text: This year, even Andy Burnham is invited to the Scottish National party conference. But by the time John Swinney stands up to address members on Saturday afternoon in Aberdeen to reinvigorate the case for a second independence referendum, his party may regret giving the UK prime minister so much prominence in the conference buildup. Burnham is expected to visit Scotland on Friday – the middle of the event – in a thinly veiled attempt to overshadow the SNP gathering. While he will be in a different venue, the former Manchester mayor’s presence in Scotland will loom large over the event. Since taking over at No 10 in July, Burnham has largely avoided direct confrontations with his political rivals, rarely attacking Nigel Farage or Kemi Badenoch. But he has taken a different approach with the Scottish first minister. The SNP leader was the only politician from a rival party, apart from Margaret Thatcher, that Burnham mentioned in his keynote address to the Labour party conference last month. He reflected on Swinney’s prediction that he would be the last prime minister of the UK at a meeting of separatist parties Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland to mark the first time all three devolved parliaments were governed by nationalists. Swinney inadvertently did so on the day Burnham’s father died. “I quote that not to seek sympathy,” Burnham said, holding back tears. “Nor to criticise John Swinney. I relay it because I want you to know how it made me feel. Utterly determined to prove him wrong.” Beyond ruling out a second independence referendum, recent British prime ministers have often paid little attention to Scottish internal affairs. Burnham has already said there is “no clear consensus” for another vote. But unlike his predecessors, he has decided to take on the SNP by loudly make the case for the union on Scottish soil. Burnham presents a new challenge for the SNP as they seek to re-energise the case for Scottish independence. Swinney has said he wants a new vote before 2031. The separatists have grown used to facing off against rightwing, pro-Brexit governments in London during two decades in power in Holyrood, making it easier to argue that Scotland’s interests have been dismissed. Burnham’s devolution agenda, openness to exploring a return to the European Union and £2 bus fares are harder to confront. Even among SNP voters, he is popular. Polling by PF Global found that 46% of Scots have a favourable view of Burnham, far higher than the Labour party itself, and double Keir Starmer’s when he left power. Only Swinney is more popular than the prime minister among SNP voters who supported yes in 2014, reaching a level not seen for a Labour leader since Jeremy Corbyn. Despite this, SNP figures have sought to capitalise on Burnham’s stance on the EU in their quest for a second independence vote. “We are in a situation where Andy Burnham is actively and unilaterally opening up the conversation about whether we are able to go back to results of referendums and relitigate those decisions while saying that that same democratic principle does not apply to the people of Scotland,” said Lara Bird, the MP for Arbroath and Broughty Ferry. “The idea that the union can continue to exist in its current form is absolutely farcical.” In Aberdeen, the SNP is hoping to draw a line under a bruising few years after Nicola Sturgeon’s resignation and the subsequent fraud conviction of her estranged husband and former SNP chief executive Peter Murrell, who is serving a five-year prison sentence for embezzling £400,000 from the party. A proceeds of crime case against Murrell is scheduled for early December. In May, the SNP won a fifth successive election, but only enough to form a minority government in Holyrood. Despite the victory, Sturgeon criticised a “lack of vision or big picture thinking” in the campaign in the opening to her memoir. Swinney has said they were still good friends. Some SNP figures wonder how much they owe to the unpopularity of Starmer. The party also faces challenges on multiple fronts: Reform has as many MSPs as Labour in Holyrood with 17, while the Scottish Greens won a record 15 seats. The Tories have showed that they can still win seats, defeating the SNP in Aberdeen South in June. Despite the potential for a standoff between Swinney and Burnham, there is growing appetite in Scotland for collaboration between Westminster and Holyrood. Since the May elections, there has been a sharp rise in Scots who support a closer working relationship between the UK and Scottish governments. Polling by Ipsos has found that 42% of Scots would feel happy about the SNP-led Scottish government working with London, up 12 points since Starmer was in charge in May. Just over half of Scots believe that the country is going in the wrong direction, up six points in the same time period. This conference, the SNP has invited speakers from other separatist and pro-independence parties. Sioned Williams, deputy first minister of Wales, will give a fraternal address on Friday. Gillian Mackay, a Scottish Green party MSP, will speak at a panel about the right pathway to independence on Saturday. “We understand, and members of the SNP know, that this is bigger than the SNP. Obviously, I fundamentally believe that the SNP will be the party who secures independence for Scotland. But that runs so much deeper throughout the Scottish population than just those who vote for the SNP. I do think that it is important at this moment to harness and to build on that support as broadly as we can,” said Bird. • This article was amended on 16 October 2026. Peter Murrell was the chief executive of the SNP, not the chair as an earlier version said.

title: Poland’s ascent from communist state to top 20 economy reverses the brain drain
summary: In the final part of our series on the country, Poles tell how wages have soared – along with the cost of living
text: Above the rain-soaked streets of Warsaw, the observation deck of the Varso tower overlooks Joseph Stalin’s gift to Poland that has divided opinion for decades. For some, the Soviet-era Palace of Culture and Science is a drunk confectioner’s nightmare; standing as a relic of oppression that should have been demolished. For others, it is an icon on the skyline and a monumental warning from history. For the managers of the Varso – completed four years ago, as the tallest building in the EU – with its 310m-high spire rising symbolically above its Stalinist neighbour, it is a waypoint on Poland’s rapid path to economic prosperity. “We look down on it,” says Cezary Błaszczyk, the managing director of HB Reavis in Poland, which owns the tower, gesturing at the palace opposite. A few months ago a slackline walker traversed the 500m gap between the buildings. “It was a symbolic walk from the past to the future,” says his colleague Natalia Kasperska. “Since we are higher and taller than the Palace of Culture, we treat it as: ‘We got over communism, and now we are a country with a strong economy,’” Błaszczyk says. Over the four decades since regaining its independence from Soviet-dominated rule, Poland has been transformed. Excluding oil-exporting states and financial hubs, incomes have converged with western levels at the fastest rate in the world; from 40% of the EU average in the mid-1990s to 81% last year. National income surpassed $1tn (£755bn) last year, ranking Poland among the world’s 20 largest economies. International Monetary Fund projections show income per capita will soon overtake Japan and Spain. “Four decades ago, we were in – excuse my English – deep, deep shit,” says Marcin Bosacki, the Polish deputy foreign minister. Stirring a cup of tea and lemon in his opulent Warsaw office, he recalls queueing after school in the 1980s for up to five hours to buy butter and meat as the communist government imposed martial law. However, the Gdańsk shipworkers’ Solidarność movement and Pope John Paul II’s 1979 pilgrimage to his home country paved the way for Poland’s transition to democracy in 1990 and an “economic miracle”. Integration with western institutions, including Nato in 1999 and EU accession in 2004, also helped. For years, many Poles chose to emigrate to earn more abroad, in a brain drain accelerated by EU membership. Polish plumbers became shorthand in Britain for foreign labour amid the political battles over EU freedom of movement before the Brexit vote. Now Britons are increasingly likely to have their taps fixed by Romanians and Bulgarians, after a surge in the number of Polish nationals leaving. In each year since 2021, when Brexit was enacted after a year-long transition period, twice as many Poles left the UK than arrived. Meanwhile, Germany recorded more non-Germans moving to Poland in 2024 than heading in the opposite direction for the first time on record. On the Varso’s 44th floor, in the Warsaw practice of Foster + Partners, Jedrzej Kolesinski and Krzysztof Gornicki are among those returnees. Both moved to London in their 20s to work in the British architecture firm’s head office – where they led the design team behind the tower they now occupy. Gornicki says Poland has changed dramatically in the years he was away. He always wanted to return to contribute to the country, and raising a family near his parents in a safe, green city that is more affordable than London also has its plus points. Now the pair are working to design Warsaw’s new airport – the biggest greenfield infrastructure project in Europe. “You can work globally from one location. In London we worked on projects from North America to Asia … right now, we’re doing the same thing, just from Warsaw.” On the streets below the Varso, the sights and sounds of progress are unmistakable. Modern electric trams glide past skyscrapers, there are cranes and construction work, giant advertising boards, and dockless e-scooters. The traditional working-class bar mleczny (milk bars) still do a roaring trade serving beetroot soup and Polish dumplings. But at the oldest, Prasowy, orders are taken on a digital touchscreen. Once an asphalt desert designed for columns of Soviet tanks, the old Parade Square surrounding the palace has had a green makeover. Further development is planned to bolster Warsaw’s bid for the 2040 summer Olympics. There are also growing pains. Just as the facades of Warsaw’s medieval old town – rebuilt from the rubble of the second world war – conceal 20th-century concrete, Poland’s stellar growth obscures tensions. The influx of global capital has driven up living costs, squeezing out poor Varsovians. Income inequality is among the highest in Europe, while growing political divisions set the stage for a fractious general election next year. Convergence with the west also presents a novel challenge for a country with a reputation as a low-cost hub within the EU. For years Poland’s cheap, skilled workforce attracted companies such as Volkswagen to build cars, Cadbury to make chocolate and banks such as JP Morgan to open global support centres. At €19.10 (£16.10) an hour, average labour costs (wages, taxes and other costs) are still half the level of Germany and France, but the gap is closing. Since 2004, the average monthly wage has more than tripled in nominal terms to 8,904 złoty (£1,723) last year. The net monthly salary in Warsaw has risen by 120% since 2016, according to Deutsche Bank, lifting it above Rome and Lisbon. A meal for two in the capital now costs more than in Tokyo and the price of a cappuccino has doubled. Rafał Brzoska, the billionaire founder of InPost, the pan-European parcel locker company started in Kraków, says Poles deserve their reputation as hard workers. But now the country must focus on working smarter, in higher-value-added manufacturing and knowledge-intensive services. “The next phase will depend less on catching up, and more on productivity. We don’t have labour cost advantage at all. We need to focus on productivity, technology, cheaper energy and better regulation.” He is, however, concerned about the tensions in Polish politics. Divisions between the nationalist president, Karol Nawrocki, and Donald Tusk’s liberal government have grown increasingly acrimonious. Meanwhile, fringe far-right parties together hold a fifth of public support. Poland is also investing heavily in defence and energy security – aiming to boost economic growth in the process – amid Europe’s response to Russian aggression and US disengagement. “People may put trust in someone else that has a magic remedy. [But] there is no magic remedy. We need to be super careful in terms of believing there is a secret sauce that will magically change things,” Brzoska says. “In my opinion – unfortunately for all of us – we still need to work hard.” As part of its growth plans, Poland is pushing to become a regional tech hub, bolstered by a $1bn investment fund backed by public and private capital to support tech startups and AI companies. The number of high-growth firms is rising, including ElevenLabs, an $11bn AI audio generation and voice cloning company named after 11 November – Poland’s national independence day. There are strong foundations for its ambition. The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development’s annual programme for international student assessment (Pisa) scores ranks Poland equal to the UK among the top countries in Europe and globally for maths, while a greater share of adults have higher education qualifications than in Germany. On the eastern side of the Vistula River in the gritty and creative working-class district of Praga, the campus of the games company CD Projekt Red shows the progress being made. As the developer behind the smash hit games series The Witcher and Cyberpunk 2077, the company started life in the 1990s as an importer of CD games made by US publishers. Michał Nowakowski, its co-chief executive, says this was about the limit of Polish ambition in the early days. Now he competes globally to attract coders, games developers and graphic designers. “In the late 90s and early 2000s I feel there was a massive inferiority complex. Among everybody who was young, you wanted to catch up with the west.” Growing up in the 1980s, his family were expelled from Poland in the period of martial law. He recalls visiting London aged 15 and being “blown away” by the Virgin megastore and British culture. “I could never imagine Poland being like it.” Within a generation, though, he says this attitude would be alien to his own children. “For young people now they have no inferiority complex. They don’t stop and think: ‘Can we be as good as Brits, French, Spanish?’ It’s not holding them back. “We have really good universities and skills teaching people. I think that can take us to unprecedented heights as a country. “We’re a proper-sized country. Not too small, not too big; no inferiority complex any more. There’s nothing holding us back.”

title: Thursday briefing: Thanks to an erratic Trump, peace in Ukraine is still far away
summary: In today’s newsletter: As Russia resists a ceasefire and Trump’s shifting priorities unsettle allies, an end to the conflict isn’t getting any closer
text: Good morning. In his usual asinine unconventional approach to international relations, Donald Trump announced on Sunday (via Truth Social, how else) an “ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine”, apparently without checking with either side. Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who said any such deal was “news to me”, nonetheless declared he was “ready and we will accept it”. Vladimir Putin responded by blowing up some Ukrainian power plants. This has been the tenor of much diplomacy during Trump’s tenure: false starts, U-turns, incoherent positions (and some playful flirting with Vlad). Meanwhile fighting continues, and America’s allies attempt to manage the fallout. Andy Burnham hosted Zelenskyy at Downing Street yesterday, stating the UK is doubling down on its support for Ukraine, and pointedly calling on others to “follow suit”. It’s a negotiator’s nightmare. So how are ambassadors, spooks and diplomats handling the chaos? Is an actual ceasefire or peace deal within their grasp? For today’s First Edition, I spoke to career diplomat and former ambassador Nigel Gould-Davies to find out. Before that, this morning’s headlines. Five big stories UK | Sally Rooney has said she is being forced to withdraw her books from sale in the UK because of her support for the banned organisation Palestine Action. Gaza | Israel is refusing to allow a key military outpost project for Donald Trump’s Board of Peace to proceed in Gaza, the Guardian has learned. EU | Britain will benefit from much closer trading relations with the EU even if that means giving up its ability to negotiate free trade agreements, the Scotland secretary has said. Ukraine | Ukraine’s military has suddenly had its access to Starlink satellite internet terminals restricted as the Trump administration has increased pressure on Ukraine to immediately halt long-range strikes on Russia’s oil industry. Vaccine | Guinea-Bissau has not approved the controversial hepatitis B study in newborns that would be funded by the US government and private partners, the African country’s minister of health said. In depth: ‘A peace agreement is only possible when both sides believe that it better serves their interests’ Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in early 2022, efforts to secure either a temporary ceasefire or a permanent peace deal have resolutely failed. Endless rounds of talks in Belarus, Turkey, Abu Dhabi and Geneva have all proved futile. To Nigel Gould-Davies, it’s obvious why. A former British diplomat, he was head of economics at the Foreign Office in Moscow before his stint as the UK’s ambassador to Belarus. Today, he is senior fellow for Russia and Eurasia at the International Institute for Strategic Studies. Gould-Davies tells me that there are established norms for negotiating during military conflicts. Diplomats look for the interests, needs and red lines that each side articulates, in pursuit of the elusive “win set”. “A peace agreement is only possible when both sides believe that it better serves their interests to end the fighting than to continue,” he says. “You have to find that overlap in the Venn diagram that leads to a defined set of conditions which, despite involving painful compromises, is ultimately judged to better serve each side than continuing to fight. “The problem with this situation is that Russia has no interest in ending the war,” he says. Tricky to find common ground, then. It is through this lens that we should view all Russia-Ukraine talks since Trump’s return to the presidency, Gould-Davies suggests. “They have not really been negotiations,” but “parallel efforts by Russia and Ukraine to persuade the White House it’s the other side’s fault” that a peace agreement (and, perhaps more importantly to Trump, that elusive Nobel peace prize) had failed to materialise. That said, the respective red lines aren’t difficult to identify. Ukraine has time and again said it is willing to accept an unconditional ceasefire. “Russia, by contrast, has repeatedly said publicly that it is not interested in a ceasefire,” says Gould-Davies, only in a full and final end to the war that, in Russian terms, means “decisive superiority and dominance over a severely weakened Ukraine”. That’s an outcome Ukraine can’t, and won’t, sign up for. *** The ‘non-standard president’ This is already a headache for UK, European and American diplomats, who most recently met in Miami at the end of last week. But there’s also the added Trump-shaped impediment to grapple with; what Gould-Davies diplomatically describes as the challenge of having “a non-standard president” in the White House. When Trump unilaterally declared an energy ceasefire, Gould-Davies says, it had “no basis whatsoever in reality”. Neither Moscow nor Kyiv was aware. “He simply made it up … a product of a fantasy.” The botched digital diplomacy aside, Trump’s interests also don’t appear aligned with Ukraine or traditional US allies. “[Trump’s] natural centre of gravity is to favour Russia,” says Gould-Davies, citing restrictions on US weapons supplies and past pauses in intelligence sharing. Yesterday, Zelenskyy accused Trump of restricting Ukrainian access to “military-grade” Starlink services, hampering Ukrainian drone strike missions and air defences. Granted, Trump has at times sided with the Ukrainian president: sanctioning Russian oil companies and helping Ukraine target Russian energy infrastructure. But for all Trump’s “lurching”, says Gould-Davies, his theory of ending the war involves concessions to Russia and coercion of Ukraine. *** The price of a deal After a period of relative quiet from Trump on the Russia-Ukraine front, this week Trump’s attention returned. With Americans facing soaring energy costs, he announced a plan to import Russian diesel in the hope of bringing down pump prices, much to the dismay not just of European leaders but a bipartisan group of US senators, too. Leave aside, for a second, suggestions that these imports could be illegal under American law and that quantities being discussed are seemingly too small to actually affect prices, even if the fuel could reach the US ahead of next month’s midterms, as Trump hopes. In some diplomatic circles, there are concerns that the diesel deal “is only the visible tip of the iceberg”, says Gould-Davies, with the White House privately pivoting towards a “much more substantial” pro-Russia tilt. Gould-Davies suspects that Trump could be, via Russia, seeking to get Iran to ease the blockade on the strait of Hormuz, in the hope of actually bringing down fuel prices before American voters head to the polls. Putin’s quid pro quo for brokering these efforts, Gould-Davies says, “could be an easing of America’s sanctions on Russia and an ending to America’s support for Ukraine”. It’s just a theory, he caveats, “but join the dots and it logically makes sense”. Either way, for diplomats it’s just further proof that Trump’s mercurial methods are more a hindrance than help. *** The quiet work behind the scenes Nonetheless, diplomatic back channels remain operational: secret, closed-door meetings and off-the-record communications between all sides. Not that Gould-Davies thinks they’re worth the effort. “There is a degree of collective delusion here,” he says: “A hope that Russia can somehow be persuaded” to change course, for which “there is literally no evidence for that whatsoever”. He worries that these informal discussions could even be “actively unhelpful, because they perpetuate the illusion that peace may be around the corner”. And, while Europe might traditionally have focused its diplomatic efforts in hostile territory, attention has now turned towards the US itself. There’s still hope that Trump’s whispers might pay further dividends. As Gould-Davies puts it, this “Avengers assemble” approach has seen European leaders and diplomats descend on Washington when Trump’s veered too far off course. For all the tumult, he says, this has proved effective in averting “the nightmare scenario” of Trump binning off America’s old transatlantic partners for good. But as fans of Netflix’s The Diplomat will know, even diplomacy between allies isn’t plain sailing. “Right now even ‘the White House’ is an abstraction,” says Gould-Davies. “It consists of many different players, plenty of whom have different views privately from President Trump.” Take John Ratcliffe, director of the CIA, who visited Moscow this summer. There is “reliable speculation”, says Gould-Davies, that he hoped to “warn Russia against escalation into Europe”. It’s a totally different note to those currently being struck by Trump. “There are people in positions of power and influence still in this administration who understand the problem of Russia in the right way,” says Gould-Davies. With that in mind, western diplomats will continue to try to shift the balance of influences within the White House, but they’re reliant on what he labels a White House Kremlinology – “trying to understand the different views and moods of those around Trump and who will be the last person to whisper in his ear.” What else we’ve been enjoying How We Win is a new Guardian newsletter series featuring writers like Naomi Klein, Mehdi Hasan and Bernie Sanders on defeating Trumpism. Read Robert Reich’s introduction to the project here, and then sign up here to get each week’s piece directly to your inbox. Charlie Lindlar, newsletters team Are you a Hannah, a Marnie, a Jess or a Shoshanna? Or did Lena Dunham’s Girls pass you by the first time round? If it did, then this excellent piece by Louis Staples (a Marnie) may well convince you to binge the whole thing in time for the recently announced five-episode revival. Lucinda Everett, newsletters team In another of our newsletters, The Long Wave, Micha Frazer-Carroll writes about taking up Jamaican Patois classes and what learning the language taught her about shame and her connection to her ancestry. Charlie I look forward to the Wildlife photographer of the year exhibition every year, and this year’s winning images didn’t disappoint. You can see a selection of them here, including my favourite: James Lewin’s dream-like shot of a young bull elephant giving a zebra an impromptu shower. Lucinda Rachel Dixon on our travel desk has pulled together this beautiful list of Britain’s best heated lidos to keep you swimming through winter. Move over WFH, and hello WFHL? Charlie Sport Champions League | Paris Saint-Germain romped to a 4-2 victory over Manchester City, while Bradley Barcola hit his first Liverpool goals with a hat-trick in a 6-3 win over Lask. Elsewhere, Aston Villa demolished Fenerbahce 6-0 at Villa Park. Fifa | Gianni Infantino will be questioned by Fifa council members over the aborted World Cup sell-off plan, the Folarin Balogun affair and awarding Donald Trump the Fifa peace prize at what is expected to be a heated meeting on Thursday. Formula One | Formula One has confirmed Rwanda will join its calendar, having concluded a 10-year agreement for the meeting on a purpose-built circuit, with the first race set for the early 2030s. The front pages The Guardian splashes on “Zelenskyy blames Trump for loss of protection from Russian raids”. The Times has “Zelensky: My people will die after Trump betrayal”, the Telegraph runs “More on benefits at age seven than age 50” and top story at the Financial Times is “Jump in US inflation deepens pain for voters ahead of key midterm elections”. Elsewhere, focus is on the Russell Brand trial. Brand denies all the charges and has pleaded not guilty. Reporting the prosecution’s opening statement, the Sun headlines with the quote “‘Ruthless calculated sexual predator’”, The i Paper also headlines with “Brand a ‘ruthless and calculated sexual predator’”, the Mail has “The ‘predator’ in sunglasses” and The Mirror leads with the quote “‘Predator’”. The Latest India’s Cockroach protesters defy Modi’s crackdown A fresh wave of protests by India’s youth-led Cockroach movement has been met with a brutal crackdown by Narendra Modi’s government and the closure of a historic protest site in Delhi. Two of the movement’s leaders have been imprisoned for five days for violating suppression measures. The protests, which began over frustration about education and unemployment, are now focused on voting rights. Modi’s government denies claims that it is seeking to disenfranchise millions of voters. But its treatment of protesters has been criticised by the UN and Amnesty International and raised concerns that the country is sliding further into autocracy. Lucy Hough speaks to the south Asia correspondent Hannah Ellis-Petersen – watch on YouTube Cartoon of the day | Nicola Jennings The Upside A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad On Copenhagen’s rooftops live 80 to 100 colonies of honeybees, tended by a collective of beekeepers called Bybi. Set up in 2010 with the aim of employing marginalised people, Bybi’s work has evolved into a response to the modern economic system. With the help of volunteers, from refugees to people on incapacity benefits, they produce between four and six tonnes of honey every year, which they sell (often letting people pay what they like) or give away, asking that people share it with loved ones and plant a flower to help the bees. They also run schools programmes, supported by sponsorships from universities and corporations. “Bybi is a constellation of time, work, money, community and connection,” says founder Oliver Maxwell, “asking an open question: what would it take for bees, people and communities to thrive?” Sign up here for a weekly roundup of The Upside, sent to you every Sunday Bored at work? title: UK households have paid extra £13,961 on bills since 2021 amid soaring inflation, TUC says
summary: Trades Union Congress urges chancellor to tackle rising additional living costs in this month’s budget
text: UK households have paid almost £14,000 on average in additional costs for mortgages, loans, energy and water bills over the past five years, according to a report urging the chancellor to tackle soaring living costs at the budget. With less than a fortnight before John Healey’s first budget as chancellor, the Trades Union Congress (TUC) said the cost of living crisis was weighing on the economy as hard-pressed households held back on spending. Urging the chancellor to support households through a series of measures in the budget, it said the UK had recorded the weakest growth in consumer spending in the G7 since before the pandemic. According to analysis of official figures by the union umbrella body, British households have forked out an additional £13,961 on bills on average since 2021 – an extra £2,792 a year – amid soaring inflation triggered by the exit from the Covid pandemic and wars in Ukraine and the Middle East. Paul Nowak, the TUC general secretary, said: “From austerity to the pandemic to energy shocks and Trumpflation, working people have borne the brunt of crisis after crisis. When the crackpots in the White House or the Kremlin launch an illegal war, everyone pays the price in their bills.” In his speech at Labour’s conference in Liverpool, Healey pledged to use his 28 October budget to give households “breathing space”. However, he warned that the government had limited resources to soften the global economic shock hitting Britain. Against a volatile backdrop, the Treasury has been preparing for a “tightly focused” budget to limit the potential for a market backlash provoked by large tax and spending measures. The International Monetary Fund this week urged Healey to “stay the course” to cut the budget deficit amid rising borrowing costs in global financial markets. The chancellor is however under growing pressure to take action to support households and businesses before the winter amid predictions that consumer energy bills could reach £2,000 a year from January for the typical household. After retail industry bosses pressed Healey for support in Downing Street meetings on Tuesday, the Confederation of British Industry said he should listen to calls for a cut in employer national insurance contributions to encourage firms to take on younger workers. The lobby group also called for cuts to business electricity costs, changes to business rates and measures to support private investment. In a separate report, the centre-left IPPR thinktank urged Healey to raise £16bn, mostly through a rise in capital gains tax that would be softened by a new entrepreneur “super exemption”. It was reported on Tuesday that Healey had rejected calls from Labour MPs and thinktanks to use the budget to equalise the rates at which capital gains and income from work are taxed. However, the IPPR said headroom against the chancellor’s fiscal rule was likely to have shrunk by between £7bn and £15bn since the spring amid the impact on government finances from the Middle East war. Calling for a cost of living package funded largely by higher taxes on wealth, it urged Healey to introduce a “rent stabilisation mechanism” to cap private rent increases, alongside a £2,000 cap on consumer energy bills, a freeze in fuel duty, and an increase in housing allowance benefits for households on universal credit. The TUC said Healey should launch a social energy tariff and take action to help poorer households and young people with rising living costs. It also called for a rise in capital gains tax and higher taxes on banks. Highlighting the costs from sticky inflation and higher interest rates, the analysis showed households with mortgages had spent on average £9,034 extra on repayments (£1,806 extra a year) since 2021. Those with loans had paid £1,911 extra in total (£382 extra a year). Average rental costs have risen at a higher rate than mortgages, suggesting mortgage costs are being passed on to renters. In the study of Office for National Statistics figures, it found households had spent on average £2,644 extra on electricity and gas bills since 2021 (£529 extra a year), and £372 extra on water bills (£74 extra a year). Meanwhile, growth figures show that consumer spending remains behind pre-pandemic levels, after a period of broadly flatlining growth in household disposable incomes since the 2008 financial crisis. Nowak said: “Eye-watering bill rises have hammered household budgets, squeezing consumer spending. That’s being felt on high streets up and down the country, holding our economy back. “The chancellor needs a serious plan to put working people at the heart of growth, raising living standards so Britain can afford to spend. That means shielding households from punishing energy spikes and putting more money in workers’ pockets.” The Treasury has been approached for comment.

title: Parents of Chloe Moffat want Treasury staff held to account over her death
summary: Exclusive: David and Anne Moffat to meet permanent secretary after coroner found Treasury ‘materially contributed’ to employee taking her own life
text: The parents of a woman who killed herself after facing disciplinary proceedings at the Treasury will call for anyone found to have contributed to their daughter’s death to be held to account. A coroner found in August that the Treasury had “materially contributed” to Chloe Moffat’s death after the 26-year-old personal assistant was called into a surprise disciplinary meeting about anonymous complaints alleging she had disclosed sensitive information at work, which she denied. The Treasury’s response to the coroner’s prevention of future deaths report, seen by the Guardian, acknowledges the department’s role in her death and commits to safeguards so this does not happen again. A review of the civil service by the Cabinet Office found that the conditions Moffat was subjected to had been replicated in other disciplinary meetings. “We have some tough questions to ask,” David Moffat, Chloe’s father, told the Guardian before a meeting with the Treasury’s permanent secretary, James Bowler. “We do want to know that staff have been held to account. The coroner didn’t ask for that, but obviously that is very important. Chloe was held to account; we need to know that the managers and HR staff are being held to account.” Moffat’s managers declined to allow her to bring a colleague to the meeting, did not give her any advance notice of it, and refused to tell her whether she was likely to lose her job. They also removed access to her director’s email and changed her work responsibilities. This was despite the meeting being described as “informal”. Moffat left the meeting “devastated” and convinced she would lose her job, the coroner found, and the next morning she took her own life. She had worked at the Treasury as a personal assistant for almost three years, “loved her job” and had an “exemplary employment record”, the coroner heard. During the inquest, Moffat’s line manager was asked if she would have done anything differently and told the court: “No, I think we did all we could at the time with the information and advice we were given.” Moffat’s parents have spent the year since she died fighting to get answers from the Treasury, which initially did not take any responsibility. “It has taken us a long time to get to this point, and they have not helped us in any form,” said Anne Moffat, Chloe’s mother. “Now we are also trying to think how we want lessons to be learned so no other young person suffers in the same way as Chloe suffered. So we are looking at Chloe’s legacy, to ensure that there is learning across all organisations in HR departments.” They say they have not had the chance to grieve properly yet and are thinking about holding a second celebration of life for Chloe. David said: “The funeral was in some ways uplifting as so many people chose to join us, but we didn’t really know what we knew now. We want to revisit it and have a more joyful time and celebrate Chloe as the person she was.” The prevention of future deaths report issued by the coroner found there was still a risk at the civil service due to its disciplinary procedures. The civil service has put in place multiple safeguards to address these issues. Documents seen by the Guardian read: “HM Treasury has accepted the findings in the report in full. In direct response to the inquest findings, HM Treasury immediately stopped using informal fact-finding meetings for allegations of potential serious or gross misconduct, introduced strengthened procedural and wellbeing safeguards, and issued urgent interim guidance.” This guidance includes allowing staff to have a supporter in disciplinary meetings, giving proper notice of any such meeting, and informing staff if a dismissal is not likely. The Treasury is also hiring an on-site occupational therapist to support staff wellbeing. Of this, David Moffat said: “We feel a lot better than we did about it going through the inquest. This is a step forward, but we still have some difficult questions to ask the permanent secretary.” The coroner heard that during the disciplinary meeting, Moffat repeatedly asked for her best friend at work to be allowed to come in for support. This was not felt by her managers to be “appropriate”, the court heard, despite the obvious distress the young woman was in. The department has now changed its policy. An email sent to staff at the Treasury last week, seen by the Guardian, reads: “Where concerns may amount to minor misconduct, these will continue to be handled informally. You will be able to ask to bring a colleague with you for personal support if you would like.” Anne Moffat hopes other young people will not be put in the same position as Chloe. “It is so avoidable what happened, and such a waste. I wish we had known the risks. As parents we are still taking a bit responsibility that we could have done things differently. And if we had, the result wouldn’t have been so catastrophic.” Chloe’s friends have been keeping her memory alive by running marathons for Shooting Stars Children’s Hospice, a charity for which her mother used to work, and volunteering for Samaritans. Her parents hope their experience can stop other families from going through the same tragic event. “We are hoping when we see the Treasury they will give us more reassurance and work with us on how Chloe is remembered,” Anne said. “We so miss having Chloe now. Our lives will never be the same again as we have lost her through something that was so preventable.” A HM Treasury spokesperson said: “The Treasury’s deepest sympathies continue to be with Chloe’s friends and family, and the department continues to mourn our colleague. Our response to the coroner’s prevention of future deaths report sets out the action we have taken following this tragic case. An independent review found staff acted in good faith and with a duty of care throughout.” In the UK and Ireland, Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org. In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found at befrienders.org

title: What is Starshield, SpaceX’s military-grade Starlink system, and how will its restriction affect Ukraine?
summary: Zelenskyy frames sudden shift as a betrayal by Trump, as spotlight turns on how Elon Musk’s SpaceX and the Pentagon control the crucial service
text: Volodymyr Zelenskyy has accused SpaceX of restricting access to its military-grade Starlink service, in effect hobbling Ukrainian drone strike missions and crucial air defences with a flick of the switch. The development – and its dire consequences for Ukraine – has put the spotlight on Starlink -SpaceX’s commercial satellite internet service – and Starshield, a powerful military version developed by Elon Musk’s company for the Pentagon. Here’s what we know about the two SpaceX systems, how they are controlled and why Zelenskyy has framed the shift as a betrayal by Donald Trump and the US. What has happened to Ukraine’s connection? On Tuesday night, Ukraine’s military reported the Starlink satellite communications system, produced by SpaceX but managed by the US government, was no longer working on terminals moving at speeds greater than 100mph (160km/h). Kyiv installs SpaceX Starlink receptors in many of its drones as part of an onboard guidance system. Kyiv said the change was imposed without any explanation from the US. How does the restriction affect Ukraine? The restriction had two immediate consequences: It effectively rendered most of the drones used by Ukraine to strike behind the frontlines inoperable and it hampered air defence systems that stop Russian drones bombarding Kyiv. Ukraine uses Starlink systems to direct many mid-range drones towards their targets – a critical frontline offensive capability. Russian Shaheds fly at speeds close to 200mph, so the new restriction means Ukrainian interceptor drones have no chance to chase them down. Starlink is not used for long-range Ukrainian missions that have successfully targeted Russian oil refineries in recent months. What is Starshield? Starshield is a SpaceX business unit that develops military and intelligence satellite systems for the Pentagon. Starshield’s service is separate from Starlink’s commercial broadband service, but the distinction is sometimes blurry. Starlink cannot be used for offensive military action, SpaceX says, only defensive activities or for use by civilian clients. Starshield, however, allows those capabilities and uses enhanced encryption to transmit sensitive information. In addition, Starshield provides users with the ability to integrate sensors on object like drones. Starshield’s secure communications rely on Starlink, the vast network of 11,000 satellites that Musk and SpaceX have sent into space since 2019. Who made the decision to restrict access, Musk or the Pentagon? Musk said the Ukrainian military was linked to Starshield, because Starlink is not licensed to clients who are using weapons. He added that any Starshield disruptions being experienced by Ukraine would be the responsibility of the US government, not SpaceX. “Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” Musk said, referring to Donald Trump. The White House has not confirmed or denied Musk’s assertion. But the Trump administration has been pressuring Ukraine to limit its strikes on energy targets inside Russia. What has the reaction been? Zelenskyy said he felt personally betrayed by Trump, in an interview with Piers Morgan, saying Kyiv was “losing a strong partner”. As for what it meant for Ukraine and its people, Zelenskyy said: “This decision will bring a lot of human losses … of course, people will die.” In the US, Democrats denounced the Trump administration. “Trump’s making a choice – and it directly aids Putin’s slaughter of Ukrainian civilians,” House Foreign Affairs Committee Democrats said in a post on X, describing the restrictions as “unconscionable”. Republican senator Tom Tillis voiced his concern on X: “Supporting Ukrainian sovereignty – or at the very least, allowing for it – should not be a gray area for the US government or for American corporations.” With Reuters and Agence France-Presse

title: Country diary: Thrilled by Darwin, and the wonder of worms | Lev Parikian
summary: Downe, Kent: It’s hard not to feel the earth move by a visit to the great man’s house. He truly valued these creatures of the dirt
text: The garden beds are moistened by steady rain, but the ground is still unyielding. A blackbird hops across bare soil. A dart, a jab, and up it comes – a wriggling tube of pink flesh. A simple catch. But when I rummage in the dirt, my only reward is loam under the fingernails. Perhaps I should have brought a bassoon. I’ve come to Down House. Here, Charles Darwin changed the world. And here he wrote his last book, its title usually shortened for convenience: Earthworms. “I know not whether it will interest any readers, but it has interested me,” he said. Quite the understatement. When a subject interested Darwin, no aspect of it escaped scrutiny, and earthworms had occupied his mind for decades. They were regarded by many as lowly creatures of the dirt, but he understood their worth. He tested their potential for intelligence, their sensitivity to atmospheric variations, their senses of taste, smell and hearing. The latter involved his son Frank attempting to stimulate them by tootling his bassoon. It’s no small wonder to stand in Darwin’s study, surrounded by his paraphernalia. All those years of painstaking labour and rigorous observation in the quest for truth… Crikey! Outside, a circular stone slab sits embedded in the grass. It’s the base for a “wormstone” – a wood-and-copper apparatus that measured the amount and rate of their soil displacement. A layer of about 2mm a year, it turned out. Darwin concluded that few animals “have played so important a part in the history of the world”. He wasn’t wrong – a modern estimate reckons that every 10 years, earthworms turn over the equivalent of all the soil on earth to a depth of one inch. I prod the ground. Still too hard. Away from the damp loam of the kitchen garden, they’ll be hard at work, aerating and mixing, grinding and digesting organic matter, their excretions converting unpromising clumps into fertile humus. Custodians of the soil. As I consider those worms, going about their business under my feet, I’m struck by a fanciful thought. Their ancestors were participants in the great man’s final project. Just for a moment, absurd though it is, the connection with something so special feels thrillingly tangible. • Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024, is available now at guardianbookshop.com

title: Indonesia fights fire with dry ice as toxic haze spreads across region
summary: Having tried cloud seeding and water bombing, one pilot project will see dry ice dispersed by plane across the province of South Sumatra
text: As fires ravage Indonesia, emitting a toxic smoke that has drawn the ire of regional neighbours, the government is testing an unusual new approach to tackle the haze: dry ice. Having tried cloud seeding, water bombing and sending in army personnel to fight the fires, Indonesia’s coordinating security minister said dry ice would be dropped on the province of South Sumatra on Thursday. “This trial of dry ice dispersal is being conducted under the president’s direct instruction to help tackle the haze in South Sumatra,” minister Dudung Abdurachman was quoted as saying by state news agency Antara. “We will first observe the results, and if effective, there is a possibility that this method could be implemented in other regions.” Since January, almost 900,000 hectares have been burned Indonesia-wide in the worst fire season in more than a decade, exacerbated by this year’s “godzilla” El-Nino and as the practice of “slash and burn” to clear land for crops such as palm oil persists. For months, millions of Indonesians have been subject to thick smoke and an apocalyptic tangerine haze, with criticism mounting of the government’s response, including a class action lawsuit filed last week accusing it of “gross negligence”. Tens of thousands of people have sought treatment for respiratory illness linked to the haze. Air quality has also plummeted in neighbouring countries, shuttering schools, grounding flights and driving a spike in respiratory illness. The haze has drifted into neighbouring Singapore, Malaysia and as far afield as the Philippines. Timor-Leste has said it would shut schools nationwide for three days from Thursday and urged families to keep children indoors or to use “respiratory protection” if going outside. Singapore rolled out subsidies for haze-related medical treatment starting on Monday, a measure last activated in 2015 when similar blazes occurred. The city-state has also begun distributing N95 masks to eligible residents. In the past week, the financial hub of Singapore was listed among the most polluted cities globally. Kuala Lumpur, also deeply affected, was at number two. On Thursday, a Cessna aircraft will reportedly disperse 1.5 tons of dry ice over the South Sumatran city of Palembang, a move the government hopes will ease the smoke and improve air quality and visibility. The technique was first deployed in the 1940s to promote ice formation in clouds, Bloomberg reported. But experts say the use of dry ice, or solid carbon dioxide, might only offer local, and limited relief. “It’s got some potential for local relief that might work for a while,” says Rick McRae, an adjunct professor from the University of New South Wales’ (UNSW) bushfire research group. “Weather systems are all moving from east to west. So if you’re in a town under that and you clear the smoke, there’s gonna be more blowing all the time,” he says, “So it’s a constant … It’s not going to be simple and it’s not going to be a permanent fix in any way.” In the Indonesian province of central Kalimantan on Wednesday, the ISPU air pollution index exceeded 1,200 – or four times the “hazardous” level of 300 – environment ministry data showed. Local news footage showed thick haze blanketing the provincial city of Palangka Raya, cutting visibility for motorists to a minimum. Indonesian president Prabowo Subianto has ordered firefighting efforts to be stepped up, and called for a crackdown on those suspected of starting fires. But the government has struggled to combat the fires, the worst of which occur in peatland areas, can burn for weeks underground, and are difficult to extinguish. “As time goes by and climate change kicks in, I think it could become a global problem, not just the fix that one country needs to find,” said McRae, of the widening regional issue. “There’s a lot of interconnectedness on a global scale.”

title: Unpolished, anti-Bibi, but evasive on peace: who is the Israeli opposition candidate Gadi Eisenkot?
summary: The ‘menschy’ former general contrasts with the current PM when it comes to style and character – yet on key policy points retains a studied ambiguity
text: He has been called the man who is everything the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, is not. Gadi Eisenkot, a former general and the main opposition candidate in Israel’s elections this month, is unpolished where Netanyahu is slick. To Israelis he is both menschy (decent) and schlumpy (unkempt), his crumpled appearance contrasting with Netanyahu’s hair rinse, makeup and obsessive need to control his media depiction. In the Israeli commentator Anshel Pfeffer’s framing, he is the anti-Bibi among a roster of wanna-Bibis. And in an era of Israeli politics that has been defined by betrayals, dirty tricks and public and private smears, Eisenkot’s brand is rectitude. He only entered politics four years ago, and the name of his party – Yashar – means “straight” or “honest”. But on key issues, an Israel under Eisenkot may not look very different, as he has been non-committal on crucial issues – including the two-state solution and Israeli settlement of the occupied West Bank. “He’s not sleek. He’s not corrupt. I think he’s going to be looking more inwards than outwards. Because he’s a military guy, he’s interested in calming the waters,” said Mairav Zonszein, a senior analyst for the International Crisis Group. “[But] he’s hedging a lot.” For many voters, Eisenkot’s appeal is less about ideology than the vibe around him. Key to his appeal, said Dahlia Scheindlin, an Israeli pollster and political analyst, is his “very modest background”. While Netanyahu is the son of a Polish-born academic, Eisenkot’s family were Mizrahi Jews from Morocco. He joined the army as an infantryman, and worked his way through the ranks to become the Israeli military’s chief of staff. “The fact that he’s from a working-class background, from a peripheral area, contributes to an overall sense that voters see in him somebody who is more with the people,” Scheindlin said. “He’s seen as empathetic. He’s seen as straightforward. That’s why I think they probably focus-tested the names of the party, and people probably thought he seemed very honest.” But if ideology remains an important predictor of how Israelis will vote, what precisely does Eisenkot believe in? On the domestic front, he is pushing for a full investigation of the intelligence failures that allowed Hamas’s deadly 7 October 2023 attack. More divisive is his support for the end of the military draft exemption for the ultra-Orthodox, long a source of friction in Israeli society. On the biggest issues, not least a two-state solution that would create a Palestinian state – he is ambiguous. “I’ve never said that the solution is two states for two peoples,” Eisenkot said on the campaign trail. “There is a very deep religious-national conflict here, and anyone who thinks an agreement can be reached now is gravely mistaken.” On the broader issue of Jewish settlements in the West Bank, Eisenkot is also evasive. He opposes the planned E1 settlement block that is seen as a potential obstacle to any future Palestinian state, but he supports settlement in general. Where Eisenkot separates himself from the current government, is over Netanyahu’s decision to place the far-right, pro-settler minister Bezalel Smotrich in charge of the occupied West Bank, where there has been a surge of settler violence, prompting widespread international condemnation and sanctions. Eisenkot has said he would immediately “reverse” that situation and put the army back in charge of the West Bank. Sceptics say Eisenkot and his allies are pushing for a return to an old, failed strategy: managing the conflict with the Palestinians – not solving it – with an aim of mitigating international pressure on Israel. “What Eisenkot and the rest are basically saying,” said Prof Yossi Mekelberg of the Chatham House thinktank, “is we’ll be better CEOs. We’ll manage the country better, not take it in a different direction … They are not really talking about the Palestinian issue.” Eisenkot is unequivocally not a dove in his views on the use of military force. As Israel’s northern front commander during the 2006 second Lebanon war, he was the architect of the notorious Dahiya doctrine, promising that Israel would wield “disproportionate power … and cause immense damage and destruction” – a policy that would see its fullest expression in the current Gaza war. On Gaza, he has been more of a military realist, insisting two years ago that Israel was unlikely to win “total victory” over Hamas, and calling for a strategy that prioritised the lives of hostages still held by Hamas. His son Gal Meir Eisenkot, 25, died of his wounds in late 2023 after an operation in Gaza to recover the bodies of Israeli hostages. Eisenkot’s philosophy governing the use of state violence is not the same as Netanyahu’s, who he criticised last year for saying that Israel needs to become a “super-Sparta” – a militarised state, feared by its neighbours. But while observers say an Eisenkot administration would be likely to crack down on settler violence in the West Bank, they wonder if it would go much further. “I think that is the low-hanging fruit and about half of Israeli society feels it would be good to crack down more [on violent settlers],” said Scheindlin. “It would help his foreign relations,” she added, but wondered whether there would be “a second step”. And even if Eisenkot wins sufficient votes to take the lead in putting together a coalition, there is question of how long such a government could survive – and what room he would have for making policies. “There will be a change if there is a different government,” said Mekelberg, “But I think it’s about managing expectations. “He would not be a prime minister who is facing corruption allegations [like Netanyahu]. I see it potentially as a government of containment, where there is an opportunity to build relations with the world again and not just [have ministers making] statements that lead you to the international court of justice and the international criminal court.” While Eisenkot has captured a moment for those who oppose Netanyahu, Scheindlin wondered how much is down to his character – and how much is projection. “I think Israel can get back to a normal path as long as there’s somebody who actually cares about the people. And people have projected on to him that he really cares about the people. “The more people see him, the more they project on to him the things that they want to see: he’s the one who will bring ‘professionalism’; he is the one who enjoys the aura of being ‘above politics’ because he comes from the army.” Shai Bazak, an Israeli former diplomat and communications figure and former adviser to Netanyahu, argued that Eisenkot’s main selling point may well be that he will not take dramatic action. “After a very charismatic and dominant leader, people deliberately choose someone less charismatic because they simply want peace and quiet,” he told Politico. “They do not want all the drama any more.”

title: Verse from the waste land: Rotterdam’s poetic bin lorries granted cultural status
summary: Lyrical lines printed on side of city’s fleet of rubbish trucks now recognised as one of Netherlands’ proud traditions
text: It is best known for its rich migration history and striking modern architecture. But now the Dutch city of Rotterdam is seeking recognition for a rather different characteristic: its tradition of printing poetry on bin trucks. Since a poetry festival first came up with the idea in 1988, lines of verse have been printed on all of the city’s waste vehicles. The practice was this week elevated to the status of intangible cultural heritage, with formal recognition from a Dutch body that guards the nation’s traditions. “Since 1988, poetry has been travelling through Rotterdam on our bin lorries,” said Joan Nunnely, the deputy mayor for culture, community and language. “You see it as you cycle to work or wait for a lorry to pass. Sometimes you read a line that stays with you for the rest of the day. What started as a quirky idea has become part of our city.” The programme is democratising as well as uplifting, say its proponents. “Sometimes people think about culture as something only for those with a theoretical education,” said Nunnely. “This is one way to bring poetry to all Rotterdammers.” For waste collection workers such as Paul Keijzer, who started driving Rotterdam litter trucks in 1988, the poetry gives an added connection to the city. He has even been inspired to write the odd line himself, he said, while the four trucks he has so far driven inspire all kinds of responses. “We get positive reactions that people have never seen anything like it,” he said. “But sometimes they say: I don’t understand that line!” His truck currently bears a verse from Neeltje Maria Min: Hoe langer ik terugkijk hoe Strakker de knoop in de tijd. Or: The longer I look back the Tighter the knot in time. Diana Chin-A-Fat, director of Poetry International, which came up with the initiative, said they and Rotterdam municipality had approached the heritage body with a plan to preserve this tradition. “It’s become so much a part of the city,” she said. “Every Rotterdammer recognises it. Every Rotterdammer reads it. It’s unique.” Poet and spoken word artist Derek Otte said it also demonstrated how Rotterdam was carving out a modern identity. “You can switch Amsterdam for Leiden or Delft and they are all beautiful – but Rotterdam is something else,” he said. “That initial idea was to combine something beautiful like poetry with something beautiful in a different way, like the garbage trucks. It’s a way to say the important things in life, in as few words as possible.” His own words have recently joined the fleet. In Dutch, they read: Van stenen gaat een stad de hoogte in De mensen geven diepte. Or: Stones build a city high. The people give it depth. In its inventory of more than 400 traditions, crafts, rituals and customs, the Dutch Centre for Intangible Cultural Heritage aims to document the Netherlands’ unique cultural characteristics. These range from the annual Pride Amsterdam festival and its parade of colourful boats along the capital’s canals to the 10 remaining shepherded flocks of sheep. Several Dutch traditions are recognised in Unesco’s international list, such as traditional irrigation and the craft of the miller operating windmills and watermills.

title: Brazil cuts work week to 40 hours in win for Lula ahead of runoff
summary: Congress approves constitutional amendment that bans six-day workweeks, which could affect up to 30 million
text: Brazil’s congress has approved a constitutional amendment to shorten the working week to a maximum of 40 hours, a move that could affect 30 million workers and that will hand a political victory to the leftist president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva ahead of the presidential runoff in under two weeks. In an attempt to overturn the first-round lead secured by his opponent, far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro, Lula has strongly championed the amendment, which will give some workers an extra day off each week. Bolsonaro, by contrast, spent months opposing the change but reversed course on Tuesday, saying “the majority of Brazilian workers” supported it. On Wednesday, he joined 75 senators who approved the reform, which passed the lower house in May. Only one senator voted against it: Hamilton Mourão, former vice-president to Jair Bolsonaro, Flávio’s father. The constitutional amendment bans six-day workweeks, currently worked by 16 million people, while cutting the maximum workweek from 44 to 40 hours for more than 30 million workers. The change is expected to affect mainly workers in retail, restaurants and hotels, most of them low-paid – one of the groups which Lula lost the most support from since the 2022 election, when he defeated Jair Bolsonaro. Lula celebrated the amendment’s passing, writing on social media “ending the 6x1 schedule is about more than changing working hours. It means more time to live, rest, be with family, watch your children grow up, look after yourself and enjoy life.” Victor Escobar, a researcher at the Laboratory of Parties, Elections and Comparative Politics, said the change “could indeed benefit Lula’s re-election campaign”. The proposal began as a TikTok movement called Life Beyond Work, founded by a pharmacy assistant who entered politics after its success and later was embraced by Lula. His party spent months pushing the senate to put the proposal to a vote and many believed that after the far right’s sweeping victory last week secured a broad congressional majority in 2027, the Senate would no longer vote on it. But Senate president Davi Alcolumbre, whose relationship with Lula has at times been rocky, put it to a vote. Flávio Bolsonaro’s party had considered blocking it, but polls showed the change had more than 70% of the general population behind it, and more than half of the senator’s voters. In May, Bolsonaro said the proposal could cause “mass unemployment”, an argument employers’ associations opposed to the change have repeatedly made. The senator voted remotely while campaigning in the country’s south. Even after changing his position, Bolsonaro said on Tuesday that he “supports something even better,” referring to an alternative proposal he had long advocated in which pay would be based on the hours actually worked. The Folha newspaper reported that he told business leaders that, if elected, he would review parts of the new amendment, a point several allied senators also made during Wednesday’s vote. Despite its approval, none of the changes will take effect before the runoff on 25 October. After the Senate president promulgates it, a 60-day period will follow before six-day workweeks are abolished and the maximum working week is reduced from 44 to 42 hours, then to 40 hours after a further 14 months. However, Escobar believes its approval could already benefit Lula: “It will speak to how voters feel economically when they cast their ballot; they can feel more relieved with a change in their working schedule”. Marilane Oliveira Teixeira, a professor and researcher at a study centre at the University of Campinas who has spent months examining the possible impacts of the change, said there was no shortage of evidence showing how harmful having only one day off is to workers. “People who work a 6x1 schedule are practically prevented from having even a minimum level of social life,” she said, adding that the negative effects could include illness, workplace risks and exhaustion, “especially for women, who still carry the burden of unpaid domestic work”. Lilian Cristo dos Santos, 50, has only one day off from her job as a saleswoman at a home appliances shop in Salvador, Bahia. “There’s no time to go to the doctor, to the beach, to the salon, to look after myself; I wanted to have time to study and I can’t. On my only day off, I have to clean the house and look after my family,” she said. Santos said she voted for Lula, but has colleagues who chose Bolsonaro. “They say he represents change – well, yes, but certainly for the worse.” Escobar is among many political scientists who believe that, despite Bolsonaro’s lead, Lula has gained momentum not only from the change to the working schedule, but also from demonstrations by his supporters that have drawn thousands across the country and an effort to build a stronger presence on social media. Lula also continued announcing benefits just days before the vote, including debt relief for microentrepreneurs, and published a letter to evangelical Christians – who have historically favoured Bolsonaro – stressing his commitment “to ensuring that everyone has two days off a week, because life is not just about work”. Escobar said: “Although most people have already decided their vote, there are some who are more responsive to political moves, and Lula has been trying very strongly to reach them. … The race still looks somewhat tangled, tied, with some degree of advantage for Bolsonaro, but it is still a very open election.”

title: Ukraine war briefing: UK pledges £17m to repair Chornobyl attack damage amid fears of slipping US support
summary: A Russian strike last year is estimated to have inflicted tens of millions worth of damage to the site of the nuclear power plant. What we know on day 1,695
text: Britain will provide £17m ($23m) to fund critical repairs to the Chornobyl power plant hit by a Russian drone attack, as Andy Burnham seeks to bolster support for Ukraine amid doubts about long-term US commitment. The UK will help restore its protective shelter and ventilation, which were damaged by an attack last year, amid concerns that corrosion could create longer-term environmental and safety risks, the chancellor and foreign secretary announced on Thursday. The pledge comes after Burnham hosted Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Downing Street, where he told the Ukrainian president the UK was “behind you and that will not change”. The meeting came during a period of strained relations between Kyiv and Washington after it emerged that Ukraine’s military has had its access to Elon Musk’s Starlink technology throttled in key areas, in effect rendering most of the drones used to strike behind the frontlines inoperable and reducing its air defences. Russia is already at war with Nato, a former top commander of the military alliance has said. Retired four-star general Curtis Scaparrotti, who served as Nato’s supreme allied commander Europe from 2016 to 2019, warned there was a long-term plan behind the Kremlin’s “spurious activities” against member countries and stressed the need to protect critical facilities. “If you looked at it from their spectrum, we’re at war with Russia today, within the alliance, because they’re taking actions that are intended to undermine individual countries’ capability to support warfare, undermine their civilians’ confidence in their own government or within Nato, and to break Nato,” he said in Washington. The US proposed European countries ⁠unfreeze some ⁠Russian sovereign assets and transfer them to ⁠a vehicle overseen by ‌Washington in ‌an attempt to ‌revive peace talks, the Financial Times reported on Wednesday. European delegates reportedly rebuffed the plan from US special envoy Steve Witkoff ⁠and Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner. Questions over the future of support in Europe for Ukraine were highlighted on Wednesday by surging far-right parties. France’s Marine Le ⁠Pen, who on current polling is predicted to win next year’s presidential ‌vote, said Paris ⁠cannot keep financing Ukraine due ⁠to the “perilous” ⁠state of the euro zone’s second-biggest ⁠economy. Germany’s far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) and the small leftist BSW party joined forces on ⁠Wednesday to pass ⁠a symbolic motion in the state parliament of Saxony-Anhalt calling for an end to Berlin’s military support for Ukraine. The motion has no practical effect, because state parliaments have no role in foreign ‌policy. Shares in European satellite operator Eutelsat have soared following news of Ukraine’s difficulties with Starlink technology, fuelled by investor bets that European providers could benefit from growing strains between Washington and Kyiv. But experts say Europe does not have a ready-made alternative that Ukrainian soldiers could attach to their drones. Christian Freiherr von der Ropp, an ‌independent satellite consultant, said Eutelsat’s OneWeb network was not well suited to wartime use and would require the replacement of thousands of Starlink terminals. European defence commissioner Andrius Kubilius said at a conference in Brussels on Wednesday that the continent was quite dependent on American space capabilities. “The answer to that situation is to develop our own capabilities,” he said.

title: Unemployment in Australia reaches 4.7%, its highest in nearly five years
summary: Financial markets trimmed the probability of an RBA interest rate rise on 3 November to below 20% following the latest figures
text: Unemployment has reached 4.7%, its highest rate in nearly five years, slashing the chance of another Reserve Bank interest rate hike as the economy unexpectedly shed jobs in September. The Australian Bureau of Statistics data showed the total number of employed Australians dropped by 39,300 jobs in the month, a surprise for economists who had expected employment to rise by 20,000. Brendan Rynne, the chief economist at KPMG, said the latest jobs report “reinforces the view that the Australian economy is losing momentum”. With Jim Chalmers, the treasurer, in Bangkok for meetings with G20 finance ministers, the shadow treasurer, Tim Wilson, attacked the government for its economic management. “The consequences of the Albanese economic model are now laid bare for everybody to see: higher unemployment, higher taxes, higher spending, higher inflation, and higher interest rates,” Wilson said. Anthony Albanese,argued Australia’s unemployment remained low by historical standards in parliament. “This government has the lowest unemployment rate of any government in 50 years,” he said. The ABS figures would have shown the jobless rate ticking higher last month had it not revised up the August figure from 4.6% to 4.7%. Unemployment started the year at 4.1%. Full-time employment increased by 34,400 in September, but this was more than offset by a sharp drop in part-time employment of 73,700. Signs that the labour market is deteriorating more quickly than anticipated lowered the chance of an RBA interest rate hike on Melbourne Cup day. Pricing in financial markets showed the probability of a rate rise on 3 November dropped to below 20% following the latest figures, from about 35% earlier this morning, according to Bloomberg. But economists were more circumspect, warning it was too early to rule out a fifth rate hike for the year. KPMG’s Rynne said he still believes the nation is heading for a Melbourne Cup day rise. “While today’s numbers show a slowing in the labour market, it is unlikely to be considered sufficient to take enough demand out of the economy to slow inflation and bring it back to the 2.5% target level anytime soon,” he said. Krishna Bhimavarapu, an economist at State Street Investment Management, said the “hurdle” for another rate hike had “risen materially” after the latest jobs numbers. “But we would not take further tightening off the table,” Bhimavarapu said. Underemployment, which includes those with jobs but trying to find more work, lifted to 6.3% in September, from 6.2%.
