title: English and Welsh water firms could be forced to return £107m via lower bills
summary: Yorkshire and Thames among providers facing penalties for missing performance targets, but bills could rise elsewhere
text: Thames Water, Yorkshire Water and other providers could be forced to cut tens of millions of pounds from household bills after the regulator said they had missed performance targets. Customer bills at Yorkshire Water could fall by £27 on average, while those at Thames could decrease by £7, according to estimates by Ofwat, the regulator of the privatised industry in England and Wales. The water industry has faced growing criticism in recent years amid rising bills, scrutiny over sewage pollution, high levels of debt and underinvestment in ageing infrastructure. As water customers cannot switch away from their provider if it underperforms, Ofwat instead has an “outcome delivery incentive” (ODI) system of automatic payments or penalties based on agreed targets. Yorkshire and Thames will have to return £75.1m and £45.8m, respectively, after missing targets in 2025-26, Ofwat said. The payments will add to the financial pressures on the companies, although Thames has been allowed to delay some of the penalties by a year. Yorkshire is among the companies subject to enhanced monitoring by Ofwat over its financial resilience, while the government is considering whether to bring Thames Water under public control after years-long negotiations to reduce its crippling debts. The other companies that must return money to customers include: Dŵr Cymru (or Welsh Water), at £16.7m; South West Water, at £16m; and United Utilities in north-west England, at £13.4m. However, some companies will receive a reward payment because they met their targets – covered by higher bills. Severn Trent, which serves the Midlands, south-west England and parts of Wales, and Northumbrian Water are in line to receive an extra £41.8m and £35.9m respectively, Ofwat said. Northumbrian customers’ bills could rise by an average of £21, the regulator said. Severn Trent customers could pay £8 more per year. Overall, the industry is expected to cut its bills by a net £240m for failures during 2025-26. Of this, £107m is expected to be returned to customers via lower bills in 2027-28. Ofwat said at this stage the figures were still at the draft stage and not every household would receive the same change. Bills are “affected by a range of factors and the effect will vary by company and customer type”, the regulator said. It will make its final decision on the payments by 15 December, which will take effect on bills from 1 April 2027. Ofwat recently announced that water companies could increase annual tariffs by an extra £3.4bn, on top of the 36% average rise agreed over five years to 2030. Customer bills are rising to pay for long-overdue investments to fix leaking pipes and treatment works, as well as to pay for new assets such as reservoirs. Andy Burnham last month said the government would pave the way for public ownership of water firms and promised a 10-year path to a “very different water system in the UK”. The comments suggested the prime minister might opt for a temporary nationalisation of debt-laden Thames Water as the government seeks to make a decision on a £10bn rescue takeover put forward by lenders for the UK’s biggest water supplier. Ofwat’s announcement came after Burnham said customers must not be “treated as a blank cheque” and after the regulator said in August it planned to allow yet more bill increases on top of those already agreed. A government spokesperson said: “This government won’t allow customers to be treated as a blank cheque, and we are committed to protecting households from cost-of-living pressures. We will always challenge water companies where they seek to pass unnecessary costs on to households. “We will deliver a strengthened water bill that puts people first, ensuring affordable access to clean water, driving down pollution, and strengthening public control.” A Yorkshire Water spokesperson said: “We recognise that our performance last year fell short of the standards we and our customers expect in some areas, and we remain focused on improving. “We are already delivering Yorkshire’s largest ever environmental investment programme and with the help of over 1,000 new colleagues, we’ve completed improvements at almost 300 locations across the county.” A Thames Water spokesperson said: “To help smooth customer bills, Ofwat has agreed to defer the timing of some ODI penalties by one year. This does not remove or reduce the penalties. Customers still receive the full benefit, and Thames Water does not gain financially. We recognise these penalties reflect areas where our performance fell short. The deferral will prevent sharp year-on-year bill movements, which research shows our customers want us to avoid.”

title: Is it really ‘madness’ to account for emissions from fossil fuels burned overseas? The Coalition sure thinks so | Temperature Check
summary: The emissions might occur elsewhere, but they generate global harm that scientists can now quantify
text: The Coalition has come up with the perfect solution to deal with the climate pollution from when Australian fossil fuels are burned overseas. We should either just pretend they don’t exist, or ignore the reason why people are concerned about them, even if those people include a majority of high court judges or the international court of justice. This week the Coalition said it wanted to roll back new rules that ask fossil fuel producers to disclose the greenhouse gas emissions that come from burning their products overseas. The step comes in response to a barrage of conservative outrage over a high court ruling last week that confirmed planners in New South Wales should have considered putting conditions on the overseas emissions from a coalmine. The high court’s decision was “absurd” and “madness”, the Coalition said, with the Nationals leader, Matt Canavan, calling it “net zero on steroids”. Fossil fuel groups called it “utter madness” and warned it could spark a wave of legal challenges. But none of those commentators tackle the reason why overseas emissions – known as scope 3 – are being counted and considered in the first place: they cause people harm. Rules are being phased in that require companies – the largest first, followed by smaller companies up to a threshold – to report annually on these emissions which they are indirectly responsible for. ‘The quiet part out loud’ The Coalition wants these requirements gone, describing them as “absurd”. Another way to look at them is that they help corporations and the public to understand the full impact of their activities on the climate. Sign up to get climate and environment editor Adam Morton’s Clear Air column as a free newsletter For fossil fuel exporters, these emissions make up the lion’s share of their climate impact. What sparked that announcement was a high court judgment last week that also concerned scope 3 emissions. The high court’s finding, by a majority of three judges to two, was clearly a victory for the retired NSW couple who had previously taken on the Mount Pleasant coalmine and won in the court of appeal. In the cold light of the judgment, all that the high court judges said was that the NSW Independent Planning Commission had not followed the state’s existing laws properly. “These requirements on the planning commission to consider scope 3 emissions have been part of the New South Wales planning system in one form or another for almost 20 years,” said Prof Jacqueline Peel, a leading international climate law expert at the University of Melbourne. “The high court has really just said the quiet part out loud. The majority of the court looked at the law and saw that the decision-maker didn’t follow it.” Peel said the provision that the high court had considered did not prevent the planning commission from approving a coal project. All that it did, she said, was say the commission had to consider whether to impose conditions in relation to scope 3 emissions. “Maybe [this decision] is construed as radical by some because if you do start to impose conditions on emissions generated overseas, then it could make coal production more expensive,” Peel said. “Whether you think that is good or bad depends on your views around climate change.” Wrongful act? The Coalition was angry with the decision because it said under the UN climate convention greenhouse gas emissions are assigned to the country where they are released. Being able to wave away responsibility for these emissions by suggesting it is just an entry on a carbon accounting spreadsheet in a foreign land ignores the reason why they are being counted in the first place. The emissions might occur somewhere else but they generate harms around the world that climate scientists are increasingly able to quantify. Those harms don’t stop at the NSW border. As one of the judges to side against the mining company on the issue, Justice James Edelman wrote the “natural and irresistible interpretation” of the planning commission’s reasoning was that it was “distracted by the accounting concepts of the scopes into which greenhouse gas emissions are divided”. What that meant, he wrote, was that the commission thought it didn’t need “to ensure that scope 3 greenhouse gas emissions are minimised to the greatest extent practicable.” The Coalition claimed the issue with scope 3 emissions “turns on the wording of NSW planning law” – ignoring the harms that emissions cause around the world. But the notion that a country should start mitigating scope 3 emissions has not appeared from out of the blue. As well as it sitting on the NSW state planning rules for more than a decade (rules which the Coalition is pushing to have rescinded), the international court of justice declared last year that a failure of a state to protect the climate from greenhouse gas emissions “including through fossil fuel production” may “constitute an internationally wrongful act”. At the UN, 141 countries voted to back the court’s opinion, against eight dissenters – Saudi Arabia, Russia, Israel, Iran, Yemen, Liberia, Belarus and, of course, the United States and its climate science-denying president. Rather than these growing calls to manage fossil fuel production being “net zero on steroids” they should more accurately be understood as an attempt to cut the steroids driving the planet’s climate to ever deadlier extremes. Graham Readfearn is Guardian Australia’s environment and climate correspondent

title: New York City moves to ban horse-drawn carriages
summary: Mamdani and city council leader agree on ban that would make it illegal to operate horse-drawn carriages in the city
text: Mayor Zohran Mamdani and the leader of the New York City council have agreed to ban horse-drawn carriages from the city, a popular tourist attraction that has faced widespread scrutiny. Mamdani has agreed to back a bill supported by Julie Menin, the speaker of the New York city council, that would make it illegal to operate horse-drawn carriages beginning in June 2028, Politico reported on Tuesday. The city council is expected to vote on the legislation next week. “The horse carriage industry is coming to an end in New York City. Our administration will make sure workers and owners are protected and the horses are safe,” Mamdani wrote on X on Tuesday. A person familiar with the mayor’s office confirmed a deal had been struck. While horse-drawn carriage rides are ubiquitous in Central Park, animal rights activists have long expressed concern over the treatment of horses. Multiple horses have died since 2020, occasionally collapsing in the middle of carriage rides. The push for a ban increased over the summer after an 18-year-old tourist, Romanch Mahajan, died after being thrown from a carriage. In a statement, Menin said horse-drawn carriages had “become a growing public safety liability”. “We can honor our city’s traditions while recognizing when it’s time to move forward in the interest of public safety, protecting workers, and strengthening our city’s economic vitality,” Menin said. A spokesperson for Menin said the city council speaker would bring up the legislation for a vote on 22 October. Though there has been broad support for a horse-drawn carriage ban, officials have struggled to push legislation forward because the Transport Workers Union, a New York transport union that advocates for carriage drivers, had raised concerns about the carriage drivers’ livelihoods. Mamdani had previously signaled he would support legislation banning horse-drawn carriages; however, he expressed concerns about the bill as written because it contained insufficient worker protections for carriage drivers. A copy of the bill, shared with the Guardian, includes language requiring the city to create a workforce transition program that provides carriage drivers with career counseling and referrals to other job opportunities in the private and public sector. The bill also requires the city to “consider” establishing a program to compensate the carriage owners for the value of their businesses. John Samuelsen, the international president of the Transport Workers Union, told Politico the bill gave “no meaningful economic relief for workers”. “This is disgraceful political opportunism, and Zohran should not simply go along with it, particularly when immigrant families’ livelihoods are being destroyed,” Samuelsen said. “This entire situation is reprehensible.” It is unclear if Mamdani plans to sign the bill as is or if there will be further changes. Sneha Choudhary, a city hall spokesperson, said in a statement, “We have been working closely with the city council, union partners, carriage drivers, animal welfare advocates, and community leaders to deliver a just transition that protects workers while ending horse-drawn carriages in Central Park once and for all.” The bill also requires the city to implement a program to assist drivers in getting rid of their horses humanely – prohibiting the horses from being sold or transported for slaughter or sold for horse-drawn carriage industries elsewhere.

title: Merry squishmas: £10 squeezy banana on list of top festive season toys
summary: Social media-driven craze puts ‘squishies’ up there with evergreen favourites such as Lego and Barbie, Hamleys says
text: A cartoonish banana so addictively squidgy that it is “really difficult to put down” is tipped to be among the must-have toys this Christmas, according to expert buyers at Hamleys. The £10 “slow-rise, squeezable, sensory” fruit taps into the “squishies” craze that is fuelling a high street boom in toy sales. In the coming weeks, Hamleys expects to sell thousands of the Big Squij toys, which come in a variety of food and animal shapes filled with a flour-based compound. Their popularity has been supercharged by social media and a growing army of child and adult collectors. There are more than 260,000 TikTok posts and more than 600,000 on Instagram tagged #squishies. The most popular official brand, NeeDoh, has 1.1m TikTok followers. Victoria Kay, the head of buying and merchandising at Hamleys, said the “squishy craze is only really just getting going”. “The demand is huge. There is a wonderful simplicity to their power whether you are a young child or an adult. Literally once you squeeze one, it’s really difficult to put it down.” Squishies are the biggest toy trend of the year, according to Andrew Murphy, who runs The Entertainer, the UK’s largest chain of toy shops. Some theories suggest their viral success is because of their stress-relieving powers or simplicity, but he suggests the “degree of fanaticism from kids under 10 for these products is not explainable in any rational way. It’s just a real, deep desire”. The squishies craze is good news for independent toy shops, he said: “It will be increasing sales in total by minimum of 30%. Most of their costs are fixed so they’ll probably be doubling the profit for the year.” The craze has been a shot in the arm for UK toy sales this year, which by the end of August were up 13% by value and 19% by volume, according the market research company Circana. Sales of toys that cost under £10 are growing fastest, with an extra £100m worth of these so-called “pocket money” items sold during the period thanks to the clamour for World Cup stickers and squishies. As for Christmas – still 72 days away – Hamleys says this week is when shopping for the festive season “officially” starts, according to a poll of consumers. With that in mind it has produced its annual shortlist of toys to please toddlers through to teenagers and older. At £10, the Big Squij toys are the cheapest. while the remote-controlled flying Thunder Unicorn” is the most expensive at £75. The list of 15 items includes evergreen favourites such as Lego, Barbie, Peppa Pig and PlayDoh. With the upcoming Marvel superhero extravaganza Avengers: Doomsday on the horizon it features two Doctor Doom toys – a £45 Lego bust and a £30 action figure. There is also something for J-Pop fans with a collectible figurine of the computer-generated pop-star Hatsune Miku. The 16-year-old vocaloid – her “voice” comes from music software – is playing London’s O2 arena next month. title: Closer EU trade ties greater prize for UK than making separate deals, minister says
summary: Exclusive: Douglas Alexander, on trade delegation to India, talks up economic benefits of joint trading arrangements with Europe
text: Britain will benefit from much closer trading relations with the EU even if that means giving up its ability to negotiate free trade agreements, the Scotland secretary has said. Douglas Alexander helped negotiate deals with India and the US when he was a trade minister under Keir Starmer. But he has told the Guardian he thinks joint trading arrangements with the EU – whether under a customs union or full membership – would be a bigger economic prize, not least because the EU has now negotiated its own similar deal with India. When Starmer was prime minister, ministers would argue against rejoining the EU because it would mean having to abandon trade agreements with other countries. Alexander’s comments show how much Starmer’s successor, Andy Burnham, who called this week for a “serious dialogue” on the UK’s relations with the EU, including possible re-entry, has shifted the government’s position. Speaking to the Guardian from a trade delegation to India, Alexander welcomed the progress made since the Indian agreement came into force earlier this year, since when the price of scotch whisky in India has fallen by 10-15%. But he said the economic benefits of trading agreements with the EU would be greater. “In trade policy, geography still matters,” he said. “The Channel is just 21 miles wide. Our largest trading partner is and will remain the European Union in the years to come. We trade almost twice the amount with the European Union that we do with the United States, the largest single-country trading partner.” He said: “It’s no secret that I was not a supporter of leaving the European Union, and I called out early as trade minister what I described as the ‘post-imperial delusions’ of the Brexiteers. Back in 2016, they promised a world of Britain as a buccaneering free trade nation in a world where barriers were coming down. Sadly, what we’ve witnessed in the year since is a more protectionist, more regionalised world in which barriers have been going up. “At the time we joined the Pacific trade grouping, the CPTPP [Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership] – which undoubtedly makes a lot of sense geopolitically for the UK – our own analysis made clear that the long-term boost to UK GDP from membership is less than a tenth of 1%. If you compare that with estimates of the structural damage to the UK economy from Brexit, you get a sense of just how important Europe remains to our future trade and prosperity. “We’re already paying a real economic price for putting up new barriers to our European neighbours who, with almost half of total UK trade, remain easily our largest trading partners.” Alexander was speaking in Mumbai, where he was joined by the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, and the environment secretary, Angela Eagle, as well as a group of mayors from northern England. He made it clear he did not support any particular method of achieving closer relations with the EU. The ministers spent much of their time in meetings with Indian officials as they attempt to iron out what they say have been “teething problems” with the early implementation, especially for smaller businesses. “There are always teething problems,” Alexander said. “We’re also having a conversation at the level of regulation to see how do we overcome non-tariff barriers that can prove to be an inhibitor to the kind of progress we want to see unless they’re addressed.” Many in the government say a bigger prize will be to reach an agreement at next month’s EU summit, where Burnham hopes to sign new trading deals for emissions, electricity and agricultural products. One hurdle to delivering that is the UK’s desire to discuss the protectionist “Made in Europe” policy, which British manufacturers fear will shut them out of a key market. EU leaders say they are willing to discuss British entry into that scheme, though they are also pushing for the UK to impose tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles, without which they fear the UK will become a back door into the European market. Reynolds told the Guardian this week he would not impose tariffs simply because of pressure from Brussels.

title: Excluding UK from ‘Made in Europe’ law will hurt entire EU car industry, Mercedes boss warns
summary: Ola Källenius says it will ‘weaken the industry on both sides’ ahead of act intended to counter non-EU competition
text: Locking the UK out of the EU’s flagship industrial “Made in Europe” legislation would amount to a “deliberate choice” by EU leaders to “hurt” the car industry across the bloc, the head of Mercedes-Benz has said. Speaking in his capacity as president of the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association (ACEA), Ola Källenius said such a move would “weaken the industry on both sides”. He was speaking just weeks before political leaders hope to reach agreement on the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA), potentially keeping the UK car industry out of key contracts in the EU. The act, known as the Made in Europe law, aims to protect local industry by countering competition from outside the EU. It is mainly aimed at China, which is now enjoying a £1bn a day trade surplus with the EU, but could cause problems for the EU’s close allies including the UK, Norway, Turkey and Switzerland. “It does not make any sense … We would hurt our industry in the UK and the EU. That would be a deliberate choice to worsen the competitiveness of your own [EU] industry,” Källenius said at an annual briefing in Brussels on the state of the car industry. “We are talking about how we industrialise more in Europe, how we build local supply chains, that is what the IAA is all about,” he added. Andy Burnham has been lobbying hard to get the UK included in the Made in Europe legislation but is hitting resistance, particularly from France. The prime minister intends to raise it at the UK-EU summit on 20 November and is hoping it is not too late, even though EU leaders are aiming for political agreement on the current text by December. Last month, the EU urged the UK to follow the bloc and impose tariffs on imported Chinese vehicles, which it introduced in 2024. It argued this would help the UK’s case to be included in Made in Europe as it would align more closely with the EU on key trading sectors. But the UK business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, said on a trip to India that this was not on the cards at the moment. The ACEA is also lobbying for an urgent suspension of plans to introduce 10% tariffs on UK electric vehicles (EVs) imported to the EU, and EU EVs exported to the UK. “We are getting very anxious about it. The deadline is in less than three months’ time. We have our feet to the fire in terms of the tariffs. All our manufacturers are worried,” said Jonathan O’Riordan, the ACEA’s international trade director. The tariff schedule is written into the post-Brexit Trade and Cooperation Agreement (TCA) as a way of incentivising the industry on both sides of the Channel to speed up the production of batteries, which can represent about 45% of the cost of a new car. Under the TCA, car exports on both sides are tariff-free if they are mainly made in Europe, but with the EU and the UK unable to produce sufficient electric batteries to compete with China, cars exported to each other’s market would be subject to a 10% tariff from next year. The tariff was originally due to come into force in 2024 but was suspended for three years to give the car industry more time. The car industry says it needs a further two- or three-year suspension urgently. Meanwhile, concern has intensified in the EU in the last three months over China’s trade surplus with the bloc, with a threat of trade barriers leading to an agreement on Friday between Beijing and Brussels to reduce sales of hybrid electric cars by half over four years. One official said the time to rebalance trade by increasing EU exports was gone. “No amount of champagne [exports] is going to revitalise the relationship [with China],” a senior EU official told a separate trade policy briefing in Brussels.

title: Texas prosecutor considering felony charges for ICE agent who ran over man
summary: A conviction on the possible charge of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon could mean up to 20 years in prison
text: A Texas prosecutor said he was considering felony assault charges for an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer who ran over a man following an attempted traffic stop and broke his leg in multiple places. Sean Teare, district attorney for Harris county, said video of the incident in west Houston on Saturday morning, in which the officer’s unmarked SUV is seen veering into the man as he runs away across an empty parking lot, could support a charge of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon. A conviction carries a possible prison sentence of up to 20 years. “It’s pretty obvious that this was an intentional striking and running over of the person by the vehicle,” Teare told NBC News, adding that his view was shared by “many other investigators” who had seen the footage. The injured man, Miguel Parra-Hernandez, remained under ICE supervision at a hospital in Houston on Wednesday with serious hip and leg injuries that his representatives said would require a series of future surgeries. ICE has conceded the 48-year-old was not the target of the traffic stop, but said he was in the country illegally. The video showed the officer pursuing Parra-Hernandez in his vehicle in apparent contravention of new guidelines for traffic stops implemented this month after a series of violent and fatal confrontations involving federal immigration officers over the summer. Teare is investigating the incident with the Harris county sheriff’s office, which said an ICE agent moved the pickup truck Parra-Hernandez and another unidentified person were riding in, then left the scene in the ICE vehicle before sheriff’s deputies arrived. The district attorney told NBC that ICE was refusing to cooperate, and had denied his investigators’ request for access to information from the vehicle’s data recorder. “Our office began drafting a search warrant that we were in the process of drafting when the ICE agent in question, the one that had been driving, we believed, at the time of the collision, jumped back into the car and drove it away from the scene,” Teare said. “In my 20-year career, I’ve never heard of anything like that. [You] put it on a flatbed trailer and you take it to forensically download it.” He said he believed two other persons from “an entirely different operation” were in custody in the back of the ICE vehicle when the driver began to pursue Parra-Hernandez, and that his office was working to ensure they remained in the country to provide evidence as material witnesses. “I’ve worked with law enforcement for 20 years. There is not a single agency in the US that would teach that once you put people in custody in your car, you then begin to pursue other people,” Teare said. “Every single person out there [was] in danger again.” His team, he added, had gathered evidence that “goes above” the surveillance video aired by multiple local media outlets, and set up a portal for videos or photographs of the incident that does not require witnesses to provide citizenship or immigration information. ICE did not respond to a request from the Guardian for comment. Over the weekend, an agency spokesperson said the target of the early-morning operation was another man, Jose Mendoza-Cervantes, an undocumented immigrant with multiple prior arrests and a final order of removal signed by a judge. At a press conference on Monday, Kim Bruno, Parra-Hernandez’s lawyer, and Cesar Espinosa, executive director of the immigrant advocacy group Fiel Houston, told reporters that he had never met Mendoza-Cervantes. Bruno said her client fled because he did not know who was in the dark-colored vehicle that was not using lights or a siren. He has no criminal record, and was on his way to work when ICE agents appeared, she said. NBC cited an ICE spokesperson who said allegations Parra-Hernandez was intentionally struck were “reckless and false” and “disgusting smears … peddled by the media”. “The men and women of ICE are entrusted with upholding the rule of law and are held to the highest standards of professionalism, integrity, and ethical conduct,” the spokesperson said.

title: Guinea-Bissau denies it has approved controversial vaccine trial in newborns
summary: Health minister says government ‘did not authorize’ Danish-led hepatitis B trial in babies backed by RFK Jr
text: Guinea-Bissau has not approved the controversial hepatitis B study in newborns that would be funded by the US government and private partners, the African country’s minister of health said on Tuesday. The study, which would not investigate the safety or effectiveness of vaccines but would instead track “nonspecific” health outcomes like overall mortality or neurodevelopmental conditions, has been championed by Robert F Kennedy Jr, secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and a longtime anti-vaccine activist. Members of a Danish research ethics committee were informed that officials in Guinea-Bissau had approved an updated design of the study, which influenced some committee members’ votes to proceed with the trial last week. But the health ministry never agreed to or authorized the trial, said Quinhin Nantote in Portuguese at a press briefing, where he referred to the study as “tests”. “The ministry did not authorize the tests under the terms presented in the publications currently in circulation,” the health minister said. He said officials in Guinea-Bissau were “surprised” to see media reports that the country had given approval to the study. “Any scientific research initiative involving human beings, particularly children, ‌must ⁠strictly comply with applicable national legislation, international ethical principles, competent evaluation and approval mechanisms,” Nantote said. He spoke after convening an emergency meeting in Guinea-Bissau with the Bandim Health Project, the local ethics committee, the National Institute of Public Health (Inasa) and the Expanded Vaccination Program (PAV). The Bandim Health Project is run by the Danish researchers Peter Aaby and Christine Stabell Benn, whose decades of research have been called into question in the past year. The claims made in nearly all of their papers are “highly misleading”, said Charlotte Strøm, a Danish researcher who has co-authored research showing that Aaby, Stabell Benn, and their co-authors had no significant findings in 24 out of 25 studies and that they’ve chosen not to publish research that may not support their viewpoints. “When researchers operate like this and abandon proper methodological rigor, they literally decide on the results themselves, and that is not science,” Strøm said, calling it “problematic, questionable [and] unethical”. She added: “I believe there is serious cause for concern.” Kennedy has repeatedly praised their work, which he says shows that after vaccination, “you can have mass injuries, and catastrophic injuries, and they’re hiding in plain sight”. Aaby, Stabell Benn and Frederik Schaltz-Buchholzer did not respond by press time to the Guardian’s questions about why the Danish ethics committee members were told the trial had been approved by local authorities and why it could not be held in Denmark. In Denmark, infants born to hepatitis B-negative parents do not receive the shot, there is widespread testing for and low incidence of the virus, and the robust healthcare system can track health outcomes and provide timely and comprehensive medical care – making it an ideal location for such a study. “It’s completely unethical that this trial is even proposed,” because a safe and effective vaccine has been available for decades, said BK Titanji, a researcher at Emory University. It’s “reassuring” to see Guinea-Bissau pushing back on the trial, Titanji said, adding: “A study like this one needs the highest level of ethical scrutiny. You are going to be conducting a study on the most vulnerable population, which is newborn babies, in a country that is resource-constrained.” When Titanji recently applied for approval of a collaborative study in Cameroon, she had to include extensive documentation in her application – and it was a survey, not medical research on human subjects, she said. “I can’t come to Emory’s [institutional review board] and just be like: ‘I got permission from Cameroon.’ I have to provide the document.” The researchers should release these documents and an updated protocol showing how the study would be conducted, she said. Experts have decried the African experiment as “horribly unethical and cruel”, “neocolonialist” and “damaging”. “For the government of Guinea-Bissau to stand up against the United States and Denmark exploiting its children is no small statement,” said Colette Delawalla, a researcher and founder and CEO of the non-profit Stand Up for Science. “We absolutely must respect their sovereignty as a nation.” It would cost approximately $13,200 to buy enough vaccines through Unicef and Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, to immunize all newborns in Guinea-Bissau each year, Delawalla pointed out. Everyone involved should work together to ensure that every baby in Guinea-Bissau receives the birth dose of the hepatitis B vaccination, she added. “This is not muddy water: we can use Black babies to further pseudoscience or we can save children’s lives with a 20-cent shot.” It is unclear whether the US plans to move forward with the study, even after reporting indicated that the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has again set aside $1.6m for funding for the trial this year, to be matched by private funding from the Pershing Square Foundation and the Bluebell Foundation. “The study has ⁠not been approved,” the HHS told Reuters in a statement. The agency has not responded to the Guardian’s questions about the trial. At least four members of the Danish committee resigned after approval for the trial was fast-tracked. The rules of the committee had to be changed because randomized controlled trials were outside of its purview. When committee members requested more information about the Guinea-Bissau approval, no further details were provided. The study would enroll 14,000 newborns in Guinea-Bissau, half of whom would be vaccinated at birth and half of whom would be denied the immunization for the first six weeks of life. Hepatitis B is widespread in the country, and infection in children can have serious lifelong effects. Guinea-Bissau, which currently has a transitional military government following a coup in November, requested in January a team of experts from the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) to help evaluate the study. In the meantime, Nantote said at the time, it was “canceled or suspended”. Other officials in Guinea-Bissau also pushed back on the research. “It’s not going to happen, period,” the foreign minister, João Bernardo Vieira, said in February. The World Health Organization (WHO) has offered support in rolling out the hepatitis B vaccine at birth to all newborns in Guinea-Bissau. “WHO stands ready to support Guinea‑Bissau as it considers its way forward and in accelerating the introduction of the birth dose and strengthening implementation,” the organization said in a February statement pushing back on the trial.

title: Uber begins self-driving robotaxi trial in Manchester
summary: Company hails first step in rolling out technology across UK as first autonomous vehicles take to city’s streets
text: Uber has begun a trial of autonomous vehicles on the streets of Manchester as it looks to bring robotaxis to cities around the UK. The first self-driving cars are operating, using the technology of its partner firms Pony and Verne, with whom Uber recently launched Europe’s first autonomous taxi service in the Croatian capital, Zagreb. Uber said it was “excited to take this first step toward making this technology accessible to people across the UK”. In social media posts, Verne said it had “started our autonomous vehicle testing in Manchester”, while Pony said there were “plans to bring robotaxis to the city” and that testing was under way. The tests involve the company mapping the streets of the city in north-west England with a safety driver behind the wheel and no passengers. Limited passenger services started last month in London, but with a safety driver in the front seat of cars supplied by Wayve under Transport for London’s licensing rules for private hire vehicles. The next steps are unclear. Opposition from Uber drivers, their unions and the capital’s politicians to the rollout of robotaxis is mounting. The GMB and ADCU unions have both said thousands of drivers jobs will be lost and have called for help for those affected. A critical report from London assembly’s transport committee this week called for the government to devolve authority over autonomous taxi services. It said there was “considerable uncertainty about many of the claimed benefits of autonomous passenger vehicles”, and fears over the impact on public transport and congestion, as well as safeguarding and accessibility for disabled passengers. There has been no official application to launch passenger services in Manchester so far. A spokesperson for Transport for Greater Manchester said it wanted the city’s taxis to be the safest in the country. “New technologies play an increasingly important role in the growth of our city region,” they said. “But they need to be introduced responsibly, safely and with real thought about what it means for our residents. “Although no applications have been made to operate driverless taxis in the Greater Manchester, we’re aware of potential interest from companies to do so. “Safety will always be our top priority, and we will need strong assurances that no vehicles will operate on our roads that pose any risk to residents.” Uber said it expected to offering robotaxi trips in as many as 15 cities worldwide by the end of 2026, mainly in the US and the Middle East.

title: French minister accuses Elon Musk of ‘online harassment campaigns’ against European leaders
summary: Jean-Noël Barrot criticises X owner in speech attacking foreign efforts to destabilise France before 2027 election
text: France’s foreign minister has accused Elon Musk of using his social media platform to orchestrate “massive online harassment campaigns” against European leaders as he took aim at foreign efforts to destabilise the country before next year’s presidential election. Speaking at an Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development conference on Tuesday, Jean-Noël Barrot pointed to the role that social media had come to play in the global battle over democracy. “The forces seeking to undermine democracy now dominate the information landscape, where they employ tactics designed to polarise public debate,” he said. The result was that “political movements with authoritarian aims”, which “play right into the hands of democracy’s declared enemies”, had been gaining ground in Europe and North America, he said. “They exacerbate the polarisation of our societies,” he added. “Their ultimate goal is clear: to seize power and then create the conditions to never relinquish it.” Barrot cited the 2027 presidential election in France, where the far-right leader Marine Le Pen is the frontrunner in the polls. “The enemies of democracy are doing everything they can to destabilise us,” he said. “They exploit our divisions and use immigration, secularism and the Israeli-Palestinian conflict to stoke hatred and tensions.” He listed several other examples, from an unnamed Israeli company accused of creating fake French social media accounts to influence perceptions of the Israel-Gaza war, to accusations that Azerbaijan stirred up tensions amid deadly riots in the French Pacific territory New Caledonia. Barrot also singled out Musk, the world’s richest man and owner of the social media platform X. “There are massive online harassment campaigns launched by Elon Musk against European leaders in order to influence debates by exploiting the virality of his social media platform.” Musk did not reply to a request for comment. Barrot also cited the protests that have rocked France in recent weeks, as schoolchildren, students and trade unionists blockaded schools and marched through cities. The events, said Barrot, had been exploited by “hostile narratives” from Russia, China and Iran, as well as those associated with the Maga movement in the US. Last week Musk and the US president, Donald Trump, weighed in on the protests in France, seeking to recast them through a lens of mass migration and brushing aside protesters’ demands for better school conditions. Barrot said his government was working to respond to a reality in which paid or commissioned influencers sought to explore the viral reach of digital platforms. “The Kremlin’s goal is explicitly stated: to put an end to our liberal democracies in favour of a new authoritarianism. Other actors are converging on this goal, seeking to dictate to Europe which democracies are ‘good’ and which are ‘bad’ based on whether they align with their own interests,” he said. The French minister’s remarks come days after the British prime minister, Andy Burnham, said it was “clear” that Russia had interfered in the Brexit referendum. Barrot said his government would work to counter these efforts by foreign entities. “We are uncompromising, because it is clear to us that they undermine the nation’s fundamental interests,” he said. “We do not tolerate any foreign interference, from wherever it may come. It is a matter of sovereignty.”

title: Family of man killed by tiger criticise online content after Trump reposts video
summary: Relatives of William Chapman say footage of attack shared online ‘deeply offensive’ and causing them ‘severe distress’
text: The family of a man killed by a tiger at a wildlife park in the UK have spoken about their “severe distress” at the circulation of online media after Donald Trump reposted a video of the incident. William Chapman, 23, was mauled to death after entering an enclosure at Yorkshire Wildlife Park, near Doncaster, on Saturday. His family described him as “bright, warm and engaging” and suffering from severe mental illness. They said online footage being shared was “deeply offensive” and causing them “severe distress”. One of those to circulate footage was the US president who posted a video clip of the tiger attack to 13 million followers on his Truth Social platform on Tuesday. The clip showed the tiger biting and clawing Chapman as he was sitting in the enclosure. At one point he wags his finger at the animal. Trump signed the footage with: “Don’t ever mess with nature! President DJT.” It did not show Chapman being killed. Later the president posted an AI-generated video of himself grinning and having fun by chasing and play fighting with the tiger. It is accompanied by the song The Lion Sleeps Tonight by The Tokens. It features Trump copying the pointing gesture made by Chapman and ends with him and the tiger hugging. Will Travers, the executive president of the Born Free Foundation, said the AI post was “not only incredibly insensitive”, but also reckless. “It increases the risk to the lives of humans and captive wild animals,” he said. “Such images and videos can encourage individuals to seek out direct, unrealistic and high-risk contact with captive wild animals.” Relatives of Chapman, in a statement released on Tuesday evening, said: “The family are utterly devastated by their loss and are struggling to come to terms with what has happened. The publication and circulation of deeply offensive media content is causing them severe distress at an exceptionally vulnerable time. We ask people to stop doing this. “The family are hopeful that the relevant authorities will do their upmost to get to the bottom of why our amazing son did what he did.” The statement continued: “William was a bright, warm and engaging young man whom his family dearly loved – and William loved them back. Sadly, William suffered from significant mental illness over a number of years and was consequently prescribed strong medication. “It will be for the coroner to decide what part this played in his death. “We would ask everybody to respect that process.” As a child, Chapman appeared in ITV’s 2009 comedy drama May Contain Nuts and in BBC Learning’s True Stories series, according to IMDb. He previously attended Jackie Palmer stage school in High Wycombe, Buckinghamshire, which paid tribute on Facebook and posted a picture of Chapman as a child student. The school said it was “deeply saddened” by Chapman’s death, adding: “We loved watching William grow, both as a person and as a performer. It was a privilege to be part of his journey and he will be remembered with great fondness by everyone who had the pleasure of knowing him. “William will be truly missed, and he will always hold a special place in our hearts. Rest in peace, William.” The wildlife park has said the Amur (Siberian) tiger called Altai, who was in the enclosure, will not be euthanised. The park has remained closed since the weekend and Doncaster city council, which is responsible for licensing the park, said it had started a health and safety investigation. An inquest is due to open into the death at Doncaster coroner’s court on Thursday morning.

title: ‘A big responsibility’: Clifton Suspension Bridge master hails £7.6m renovation
summary: Engineer Tristan Ralph describes task of maintaining and running Bristol structure without public money
text: The job does not give the holder age-old perks such as the right to drive sheep across the great structure, but the title “bridge master” does have a certain ring to it. “I don’t tend to say I’m the bridge master when I’m at a party,” said Tristan Ralph, the current holder of the title. “But people do seem to know and bring it up. It’s a job less ordinary, isn’t it? It’s a Victorian sounding title and people are really, really interested.” There is, however, nothing ceremonial about the title. Ralph is in charge of maintaining and running the Clifton Suspension Bridge, a UK feat of engineering, without any public money. “It does feel a big responsibility,” said Ralph. “When the chairman of the trustees rang to say we’d like you to do it, you suddenly feel the pressure. It’s so famous and people in Bristol, quite rightly, are proud and almost possessive of it. Bristolians think: ‘It’s our bridge.’” The bridge master – and the not-for-profit charity the Clifton Suspension Bridge Trust – have the task of maintaining the bridge “in perpetuity”. “I’m a temporary custodian,” Ralph said. “When I’m finished, I have to make sure it is handed on in just [as] good a condition or better than I inherited it.” Ralph, a bridge engineer by profession, was speaking to mark the conclusion of a large refurbishment project that has taken two and a half years and involved hand-painting more than 4,000 original iron chain links and installing an energy-efficient lighting system. It has cost about £7.5m. “It’s been a big job,” he said. “But it’s come pretty much bang on budget, which is rare these days.” That is important because, to many visitors’ surprise, the bridge does not receive public funding. “The upkeep of the bridge, the running of it, the salary costs and everything are all paid only by our toll money,” said Ralph. “People think that we might get something from local or central government. But, no, it’s just the toll money.” Motorised vehicles – including motorcycles – pay £1 to cross the bridge. There is no charge for pedestrians, cyclists or horse riders. As well as being a beautiful structure, it is also a vital part of Bristol and North Somerset’s transport system. Ralph said: “It draws the tourists in. We get visitors from hundreds of countries every year but primarily, it’s still a vital piece of local infrastructure. If the bridge wasn’t here, the difference it would make to Bristol traffic would be incredible. We average over 8,000 vehicles a day still. Maintaining it as a transport link is utterly vital.” The end of the refurbishment does not mean Ralph can rest on his laurels and spend more time hobnobbing with members of the Bridge Owners Forum. “In a few years, we’ll need to paint the underside of the bridge. The under-bridge gantry unit itself will be replaced over the coming years. So there’s always something. We need to keep on top of things. It’s like your house or your car. If you just ignore it, don’t do things for a couple of years, they start breaking down.” As in most walks of life, the climate emergency is a challenge Ralph and the trust are having to face. “We were monitoring the bridge daily in the summer with the very hot weather. And maybe if the bridge was being designed today, there would be a little bit more robustness around wind.” The prevailing south-west wind is not usually a problem and the bridge rarely has to close but if it blows directly through the Avon Gorge it can be more difficult. “We need to keep an eye at both the magnitude of any wind events but also their frequency,” Ralph said. The engineer admires the bridge’s designers, including Isambard Kingdom Brunel. “It’s remarkably advanced for its time.” And there is no sign that its days are numbered, largely because the Victorians did not skimp. Ralph said: “There are three layers of chains. The original Brunel design only had two, but because it went from a timber design to a cast-iron deck, they upped it to three. “There’s a little bit of comfort in there. Today there might be pressure to say, well, can you keep it to two, but in Victorian times they did like to add a little bit of meat on the bones. “It doesn’t have a finite life. There’s no end date in our plans. We all just keep it going in the highest standards as we can. It’s in really good condition as long as we keep doing what we need to do, keep our attention on it and don’t let things drift. Forever is a long time but there’s no reason why we have any need to worry at the moment.”

title: ‘From liabilities to goldmines’: refineries eye record profits from diesel shortage
summary: Firms turning crude oil into the ‘workhorse’ fuel stand to gain most despite economic fallout from record prices
text: Days after Donald Trump announced a deal to import Russian diesel into the US in an effort to lower soaring pump prices, the world’s energy watchdog has warned that the global fuel shortage will drag into 2027. Trump’s temporary sanctions reprieve was criticised for offering “too little, too late” to temper the sky high pump prices triggered by the shutdown of war-damaged refineries in the Middle East and Russia – once the world’s second-largest diesel exporter behind the US. The International Energy Agency said on Wednesday that the shortage would stretch into the new year despite plans to ease trade sanctions or release emergency stockpiles, in a blow to the global economy. “Record diesel prices are already having broad economic consequences by raising the cost of goods and impacting real incomes, economic activity, and inflation,” the IEA added. Yet amid this gathering economic gloom some of the western refineries that turn crude oil into fuels are preparing to have their day. The global shortage that has led to high prices on UK forecourts is poised to hand them record profits. “I prefer the world of disruption to the peaceful world,” the boss of the French energy company TotalEnergies, Patrick Pouyanné, mused last week. He said the energy crisis ignited by almost eight months of war in the Middle East had provided “plenty of opportunities if you’re able to capture them”. For Pouyanné, the key to reaping the benefits of a global fuel crisis lies in owning a string of refineries across Europe that stand ready to cash in by selling diesel into a starved market. Diesel accounts for 10% of the world’s energy consumption, and is known as a “workhorse” fuel for its role powering the equipment vital for sectors ranging from agriculture, mining and manufacturing to shipping and logistics. But by last month supplies into the global market had fallen by about 1m barrels a day from their 2025 level, owing to a combination of damage to refineries in the Gulf and Russia, and export restrictions from China. The soaring costs for businesses and consumers have economists worried. They are already piling pressure on areas of the global economy from US farmers in the midwest corn belt to local bus operators in England. Many fear a broader impact, as fuel prices raise the cost of food, goods and transport across the economy. However, for some of the companies that turn crude into diesel this is a very lucrative crisis. Refinery ‘goldmines’ “We’re doing really well by being integrated,” Pouyanné explained. “Integration means your refineries in Europe, which you thought were liabilities, are suddenly becoming goldmines.” These goldmines helped TotalEnergies to its strongest quarterly profits in three years this summer, after income from its refining and chemicals business more than quadrupled to $1.8bn (£1.35bn) between April and June. TotalEnergies is far from alone in its good fortune. The biggest windfalls are likely to come from refiners in the US, where exports of fuel products have climbed by more than 50% in the past year from about 1.25m barrels a day to an all-time high of 1.9m barrels a day over the summer, effectively offsetting the losses from Gulf refineries. The market value of three of the largest US oil refiners – Marathon Petroleum, Valero Energy and Phillips 66 – have more than doubled since the start of the crisis. The US listed stocks have climbed by a combined $215bn this year as their shares rose steadily to reach successive record highs. In the coming weeks these refineries are expected to reveal their largest-ever profits. Europe’s largest oil and gas company, Shell, told investors last week it expects to make record profits from each barrel of fuel produced over the last three months after it reported its second highest quarterly profit ever over the summer. Shell’s refining margins are forecast to nearly double to $42 for each barrel of refined product sold in the July to September period, up sharply from $24 a barrel in the second quarter. The companies are benefiting from the price difference between a barrel of crude oil and the barrel of refined fuel. The Brent crude benchmark price has eased back to oscillate around the $100 a barrel level in recent weeks, helped by an uptick in cargoes leaving the Gulf region, although given recent fears about the Middle East conflict escalating it is back above the $106 mark. . Meanwhile, fuel exports have remained constrained and global stockpiles of diesel, gasoline and jet fuel have continued to shrink. The supply squeeze means that while oil prices are lower than feared at this point, the cost of diesel is far higher. Fuel flex Refiners that produce diesel and jet fuel have fared best in the crisis. Some have been able to flex their capacity to produce more of the fuels in high demand; a strategy that has helped to ease the supply crunch and capture high revenues. “Think about the early days of the crisis,” the BP chief executive, Meg O’Neill, said last week. “If you go back to March and April, the first front of shortage risks was in Australia, where they were very worried about diesel and diesel availability; and you might have seen news coverage of petrol stations being out of diesel. Our team responded very quickly.” O’Neill, who officially stepped into the top job in April this year, told an industry conference in London that BP was able to ship diesel to its customers in Australia from its Rotterdam refinery in the Netherlands and its Cherry Point refinery on the US west coast. “Roll forward, the next wave of the crisis was jet fuel in Europe, and everybody was saying, ‘Can people go on their holidays? Maybe we shouldn’t travel.’ Our refineries were able to adapt their runs to produce 30% more jet [fuel] in May than they did before the conflict, again to make sure that the customer need was met,” she said. “Roll forward to even more recently, the diesel price pressures that we’re seeing around the world, and our refineries have adjusted back to try to max diesel.” However, not all refiners have been as able to adapt to benefit from the fuel supply squeeze. Many are shouldering the “crippling” cost of crude and fast-rising costs of hiring a supertanker while manufacturing products such as naphtha and gasoline (petrol) where prices are well below the highs seen for diesel and jet fuel, the IEA said. In north-west Europe, the profit margins for refineries – known as the “crack spread” – have fallen from $54 a barrel at the start of September to as low as -$11 a barrel earlier this month. Ultimately, the shift to diesel could lead to a surplus of the fuel by early next year, according to the IEA, while creating the conditions for the next fuel squeeze: gasoline. If refineries that produce the fuel were forced to lower their run rates to avoid spiralling losses, then petrol pumps could become the next frontier of the crisis.

title: Ken Paxton stirs vaccine skepticism to ingratiate himself with Maha movement
summary: Texas AG and US Senate hopeful announced inquiry into alleged conspiracy between pediatricians, vaccine makers and insurance firms
text: Ken Paxton, the attorney general of Texas and the Republican candidate for the US Senate, is aligning himself with the Make America Healthy Again (Maha) movement by investigating pediatricians for giving vaccines – actions that could further restrict access to vaccines as deadly outbreaks unfold. Paxton announced he would investigate an alleged conspiracy between pediatricians, vaccine makers and insurance companies in January, and at least one Texas pediatrician now says she is under investigation. Paxton linked his efforts to a campaign against vaccines from Donald Trump and Robert F Kennedy Jr, the secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), and directly referenced the Maha movement in his announcement. The president endorsed Paxton’s Senate run in May. Pointing to a sweeping collusion that “illegally incentivized” doctors to administer vaccines, Paxton alleges that the pharmaceutical and insurance industries were attempting to “bribe” medical providers. He also launched an investigation into the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP), accusing them in August of potentially recommending vaccines for financial gain – referencing a lawsuit the AAP filed earlier this year to halt sweeping changes to the childhood immunization scheduleand once again invoking Trump and Kennedy’s moves on vaccines. A new law in Texas makes it easier for parents to request school vaccine exemptions, as the rate of measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccination falls in the state. Only 93.3% of kindergarteners in Texas are now fully vaccinated against measles. Pediatricians are one of the lowest-paid medical specialties and “barely break even” on vaccines, said Marjan Linnell, a pediatrician and president-elect of the Texas Pediatric Society. But Kennedy has made millions suing vaccine makers. He has made at least $2.5m in referrals for lawsuits related to vaccine side-effects to the law firm Wisner Baum. He had a 10% contingency stake in a Gardasil vaccine lawsuit that reportedly settled for about $50m in June. In Kennedy’s confirmation hearing to become HHS secretary, Elizabeth Warren, a Democrat from Massachusetts, asked Kennedy about these potential conflicts of interest and whether he would continue receiving money from lawsuits while overseeing (and after leaving) HHS. Kennedy initially said he would stop profiting from vaccine lawsuits, but he later filed an amended ethics disclosure saying he would give the money to one of his sons. “I get reimbursed as little as $6 for giving a vaccine,” said Katherine Wells, director of Lubbock Public Health. Even when her health department receives vaccines free of charge from the state, it only receives about $13 for the costs of administering the vaccine. “That does not cover the time of a nurse to talk to the parents, review the shot record, draw up the vaccine, give the injection, provide the education. It’s way more than six bucks for me to do that in a health department, and I’m a low-cost, low-overhead entity.” Wells continued: “I’m taking a loss every time I give a vaccine, but it’s the right thing to do.” Primary care doctors have high levels of trust, as does the AAP – with both ranked as more trustworthy than federal health agencies in a February survey. “Pediatricians are beloved,” said Paul Offit, a vaccines expert at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia. “People see them as nice people trying to do the right thing.” Offit continued: “I just think this war on pediatricians is not a winner. Ken Paxton, I think, is desperate. He very well may lose to Talarico, and this is a stupid, desperate thing to do.” Despite their broad popularity, pediatricians have frequently been targeted by anti-vaccine activists – including recent claims from Children’s Health Defense that they have reported doctors in Lubbock to the Texas medical board for treating measles patients. The organization, which was previously led by Kennedy, also sued the AAP for racketeering on the same day that Paxton announced he would investigate pediatricians. Kennedy has frequently criticized the healthcare system in America, decrying what he says are doctors who make decisions based on a “financial bonus” and “hidden incentives that corrupt medical judgment”, according to a video he posted on X in August 2025. “Doctors are being paid to vaccinate, not evaluate,” Kennedy claimed, adding: “That’s not medicine. That’s coercion.” At least one pediatrician in Texas has received letters indicating they are being investigated by the attorney general’s consumer protection division about her records of vaccination, including “potential misleading or deceptive acts regarding incentives associated with the administration of childhood vaccines”, according to reporting from the New York Times. The investigators are requesting details on every “reward, financial benefit, bonus, discount, return, rebate or other consideration” from vaccine makers, prompting the pediatrician to spend thousands in legal fees, the Times reported. All pediatricians could be at risk of investigations, making the future of practicing pediatrics hazy. “Texas already has a shortage of primary care,” Linnell said. Actions like these could worsen the healthcare shortage, she added. “If you’re going to be potentially threatened with a lawsuit that could close your business down, it’s yet another reason for people to not go into primary care.” She worries about pediatricians at smaller practices who may be forced to choose between vaccinations and high legal and administrative fees. “If you have a fear that you’re going to have to spend a bunch of money – potentially stop your practice or really take a financial hit, having to defend a lawsuit – then it could be conceivable that you won’t be able to offer children vaccines,” Linnell said. Making it more challenging for children to get vaccinated will increase the risk of vaccine-preventable diseases such as measles, Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib), and others, Linnell said. These are diseases she had never seen before, and she had hoped never to see them in her entire career – but now they are spreading throughout the country, at the same time that the way to prevent them is being undermined. “Threats like this just feed into this fear,” Linnell said. The accusations of financial gain are particularly puzzling because vaccines are expensive and time-consuming to maintain and administer, Linnell said. Staff are trained on how to administer them; storage is complicated, with special freezers that can’t ever lose power. A couple of years ago, there was a freeze for five days, and the bridge to Linnell’s clinic was frozen, she said. Every vaccine in the freezer had to be thrown out. “All of those vaccines, our clinic had to pay out of pocket to replace,” Linnell said. With vaccination, “in some cases, we barely break even”, she said. “It’s not something we would do if we didn’t think they were so critically important and so safe.” She continued: “Vaccines are expensive, but they’re worth it. They are one of the best studied, safest things that we can do to keep kids in their communities, playing, going to school.”

title: UK government apologises for past burials of stillborn babies in mass graves
summary: Yvette Cooper acknowledges ‘unthinkable pain’ caused by practice between 1930s and 1980s after campaign by Wirral woman and others
text: The health secretary, Yvette Cooper, has issued a “profound apology” for the “unthinkable pain” caused to parents whose stillborn babies were buried in mass graves. Parents spent decades not knowing where their babies were buried, owing to a practice in which stillborn babies were taken from mothers at hospital and buried in communal graves. Over several decades between the 1930s and the early 1980s, many bereaved parents who lost babies in NHS hospitals were given no say in what would happen to their remains and no information about where they had been taken. More than 1,000 stillborn babies were interred in Wirral, at Frankby, Plymyard and Landican cemeteries, between 1935 and 1981. Another mass burial ground in Royton, Oldham, is believed to hold more than 270 babies. Gina Jacobs, from Wirral, whose son Robert was stillborn in 1969, did not know where he had been buried for 53 years. She has been among those campaigning for recognition from the government. Speaking in the House of Commons during a baby loss awareness debate, Cooper said: “On behalf of the government, I want to issue a profound apology to them.” She added: “I have issued that apology to Gina today, but to so many more like Gina who have sought answers over many years, I’m sorry for the unthinkable pain caused by those historic practices, because what happened to those parents should never have happened and we need to ensure it can never happen again.” Jacobs told ITV News: “It didn’t kind of sink in at first. I’ve wanted this, I’ve campaigned for this, I’ve begged for this, anyone who would listen, for four years now, and to actually have it said to me by the minister herself. “To me it’s like a lottery win because I have wanted this,” she added. “This brings dignity and respect to these babies, because they never got it at the time. And it brings it even to our missing babies.” In July, Liverpool city council passed a motion calling on the government to apologise in parliament to families affected by the practice. The motion, which was passed unanimously by all parties, said: “The historical handling of stillborn babies by public authorities was a cruel violation of human dignity that has caused decades of unresolved trauma, grief and anger for families across Liverpool.” In response to the government apology, the Liverpool councillor Kris Brown, who put forward the motion, said: “The government’s words of apology will go a long way. For many, just acknowledging that it happened will bring a sense of closure and justice. “However, this can’t just be words simply etched into Hansard. I hope that the secretary of state, along with the prime minister, issues a written apology and sets out a national framework on how families affected by the scandal can get support.” The council has urged the government to set aside national funding to retrieve burial records and has called for a comprehensive review into the mass burials, which took place under many successive governments. Brown welcomed the apology but said: “There is still far more to do for full justice.”

title: Nigel Farage says charities that help asylum seekers reach UK should be prosecuted
summary: Reform leader did not say who should be targeted but party figures have been critical of small boat rescues by RNLI
text: Charities and volunteers who help asylum seekers get to the UK should face potential criminal prosecution, Nigel Farage has said in an interview with a rightwing US podcaster. While the Reform UK leader did not specify which organisations should be targeted, he and other senior Reform figures have been heavily critical of the Royal National Lifeboat Institution (RNLI), which has faced a campaign of intimidation for its work in rescuing asylum seekers in the Channel. Speaking to Benny Johnson, a podcaster who has previously written for a series of rightwing US outlets, including Breitbart News, Farage discussed the arrival of asylum seekers on small boats, calling it “literally an invasion of people who could cause us enormous harm”. Johnson asked him: “Do you believe in criminal penalties for those who facilitated this invasion of the English Isles?” Farage replied: “Totally, totally. The role of the NGOs, the role of those that are sponsored by taxpayers’ money, because they’re nice, they’re good, they’re kind. They have actually aided and abetted criminality in absolutely every way. “These are people [who are] are deluded – deluded, hard-left socialist Marxists, who don’t believe in countries, don’t believe in borders, don’t believe in identities, are intent on destroying everything that exists.” Farage has previously described the RNLI, which rescues some asylum seekers, a small proportion of its lifesaving work, as a “migrant taxi service”, while other Reform figures have criticised the charity, including sharing footage of far-right protesters abusing RNLI crews bringing people ashore. Calling for charities and campaign groups to be prosecuted for their work has echoes of the efforts by the former Hungarian prime minister Viktor Orbán to try to cement his grip on power. A Reform spokesperson said Farage’s comments “speak for themselves”. In his conversation with Johnson, Farage repeatedly raised what he said was the issue of Muslim asylum seekers arriving in the UK, citing what the example of Michigan, the US state where rightwing agitators have sought to whip up anti-Muslim feeling. Farage said: “We are importing into our countries … people who will do us enormous harm, who will change, disrupt our lives in every way, in fact make our way of life potentially unrecognisable.” Saying that European countries such as the UK and France had a greater problem with migration than the US, Farage said if Donald Trump was followed in office by a “weak politician” who did not tackle migration and stand up for “American, English-speaking Christian values” then the consequences would be dire. Farage told Johnson: “If we don’t, this show of yours will be illegal in five or 10 years’ time. Literally, you’ll be banned for hate speech.” Elsewhere in the interview, Farage speculated that five UK nationals arrested near RAF Fairford late last month before being bailed had been undertaking “a dummy run for a proper terrorist attack on UK forces”. He added: “I’m deeply, deeply shocked that they’re out on bail whilst there are other people in this country who have said things that the establishment now thinks are racist, who are held inside behind bars without, frankly, proper charge. So it’s what we call here two-tier policing.” Farage has a habit of sometimes making his message more robust for rightwing US audiences. He has appeared several times on the web TV show hosted by the disgraced far-right pundit Alex Jones, who was sued by bereaved parents of the 2012 Sandy Hook school shooting, which Jones said had been a hoax. Farage was criticised by some Jewish groups for using these and other US interviews to discuss tropes and conspiracy theories associated with the far right and antisemitism.
