title: Immigration, climate, guns: key Trump policies to be tested at supreme court
summary: Conservative court asked to rule on several signature policies in 2026-27 term – will it rule in president’s favor?
text: Several of Donald Trump’s second-term policies will be tested at the supreme court in the coming months: it is being asked to rule on challenges to theadministration’s harsh immigration and deportation policies, along with a climate change lawsuit against energy companies and an attempt to loosen restrictions on assault-style rifles. The Roberts court is often split in favor of conservative issues 6-3, but it has also diverged from Trump on some key cases, leading the president at times to rage against some of the justices he nominated for the bench. Decisions are expected in or before June 2027. Here are some of the major supreme court cases in the 2026-27 term. Suncor Energy Inc v County Commissioners of Boulder County The case centers on a question raised in dozens of similar lawsuits: how can states, cities or counties hold energy companies accountable for contributing to climate change through fossil fuel burning. In 2018, officials in Boulder, Colorado, sued ExxonMobil and Suncor Energy, alleging damages to the state’s environment from burning fossil fuels. ExxonMobil and Suncor Energy argued the lawsuit was incorrectly brought in state court instead of federal court. Justices are being asked to decide if the lawsuit can move forward. The case could potentially end in a 4-4 split because Justice Samuel Alito recused himself, citing a conflict of interest. Rhoney v Barbosa da Cunha The case is a challenge to the Trump administration’s practice of indefinitely detaining immigrants who are arrested in the US and awaiting deportation. Previously, undocumented immigrants who had been living in the US could be released back into their communities on bond, as long as they did not pose a threat to safety nor were considered a flight risk. But last year, the administration reinterpreted the statute to mean any migrant who entered the US illegally should be held in detention while awaiting legal proceedings. The reinterpretation has led to a huge surge in the number of migrants held in detention centers and disputes in lower courts. Department of Homeland Security v DVD The case focuses on the Trump administration’s swift deportations of immigrants to “third countries”, or countries other than their own, without allowing them to contest their removals. The administration has entered into a series of agreements with other countries that have agreed to safely accept immigrants who cannot be deported to their home countries. But several immigrants say they were not given sufficient “notice and opportunity” to raise concerns about fear of torture or persecution in the countries where they are being sent. The supreme court will examine whether a lower court judge had the authority to pause the quick deportations and if the policy itself violates law, the constitution or international law. Already, the court handed Trump a victory in the dispute by allowing officials to temporarily deport immigrants to third countries while legal proceedings continue. St Mary Catholic Parish v Roy The case is the latest example of the clash between states’ anti-discrimination laws and religious organizations’ right to exercise their values. Two Catholic parishes say their preschools were precluded from participating in a state-funded universal pre-school program because it required them to sign a nondiscrimination agreement that prevented them from denying admission to families who do not align with Catholic values – such as same-sex couples. The Catholic parishes requested an exemption, which was denied. They say it violated their first amendment right because it excluded them from receiving state benefits that were “generally available”, and other pre-schools received exemptions, such as only admitting low-income families or children with disabilities. The conservative majority of the court has been largely sympathetic to plaintiffs in similar disputes, such as allowing a Colorado baker to refuse to create wedding cakes for same-sex couples. Viramontes v Cook County & Grant v Higgins The consolidated cases serve as a vehicle for justices to expand access to semi-automatic firearms, such as AR-15-style rifles, by striking down state or local bans on the types of weapons. Residents of Cook county, Illinois, challenged a county ordinance banning the sale, transfer or possession of any “assault weapon” – which AR-15-style rifles fall under. Separately, a group of Connecticut residents challenged a similar state law that was enacted after the Sandy Hook elementary school shooting. Lawyers in the cases argue that banning AR-15s is unconstitutional because they are common-use firearms. In recent years, the supreme court has expanded second amendment protections. In 2022, the court created a new test, requiring courts and legislators to determine whether a gun law conflicted with the United States’ “history and tradition” of firearm ownership. Republican National Committee v Mi Familia Vota The case centers on two Arizona laws, one requiring voter applicants to provide proof of citizenship, another allowing election officials to remove people believed to be noncitizens from voter rolls 90 days before an election. Voting advocacy groups argue the laws, enacted in 2022, violate the National Voter Registration Act. Donald Trump has long called for federal ID requirements and voter roll regulations to address his debunked claims of mass noncitizen fraud in elections. While a ruling in the case would not impact federal law, it could open the door for states to enact their own voter ID rules. Justices have yet to decide whether to take up several other major cases, including a dispute over providing gender-affirming care to transgender inmates, the administration’s ban on trans service members and a case challenging state laws requiring the Ten Commandments in classrooms, among others.

title: Pope Leo recovering from surgery after lung cancer diagnosis | First Thing
summary: Vatican says operation on US-born head of Roman Catholic church was ‘successful’
text: Good morning. Pope Leo XIV, the head of the 1.4 billion-strong Roman Catholic church, has been diagnosed with lung cancer. The Vatican made the announcement after Leo, 71, the first US-born leader to assume the role, underwent an operation and had the lower lobe of his right lung removed. A statement said the surgery was “successful, on schedule and as planned”. The Vatican said Leo had “now returned to his room” after the operation. All of his appointments have been cancelled until 20 October. The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, a practising Catholic who has met the pope, said he and his wife were “united in prayers” for Leo after the diagnosis. Setback for Trump as judge extends White House access to banned media outlets Donald Trump faced another setback in his battle over media coverage after a federal judge ordered that journalists from CNN, MS Now and Politico must still have access to the White House as the media coalition’s lawsuit against the administration plays out. In his ruling on Tuesday, Judge Kelly wrote that the plaintiffs “are likely to succeed not only on their due process claim, but also on their two first amendment claims”. While access to the White House is not guaranteed, court precedent dictates that once it is provided to journalists, it cannot be taken away for editorial or viewpoint-based reasons. What is the latest in Trump’s legal battle with the BBC? The BBC is asking a federal judge in Florida to force Donald Trump to sit for a deposition as part of the president’s $10bn defamation lawsuit against the British broadcaster. The president has so far declined to set a date to appear. “Plaintiff chose to file this lawsuit and, in doing so, he accepted the obligations of civil litigation,” the BBC’s motion reads. “The BBC therefore asks the court to compel plaintiff to confirm a date.” Kimberly Guilfoyle ousted as US ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle is stepping down as US ambassador to Greece after weeks of reports that she sought payment from a Donald Trump donor in exchange for access to administration officials. The decision ends the diplomatic career of one of the US president’s longest-standing political allies. The former fiancee of Donald Trump Jr, Guilfoyle confirmed her departure from the post which she described as the “honor of a lifetime”. She said she would “vigorously defend my name, my reputation and my integrity” and that “my commitment to President Trump, the America First movement, and the country I love will never end”. What were the allegations against Guilfoyle? The Wall Street Journal reported she used Signal messages to press the donor Eric Deters to pay a $100,000 credit card bill in exchange for official influence – a request Deters described as a quid pro quo. She was also accused of accepting improper gifts and promoting a private Greek firm during official business. Guilfoyle strongly contests all allegations and disputes the authenticity of the messages. Cornell suspends fraternity parties amid backlash over alleged sexual assault Cornell University has announced it is suspending parties and other social gatherings at fraternity houses for the rest of the academic year amid an intensifying backlash over its handling of allegations that a female student was sexually assaulted at a fraternity house in 2024. The university has also said it will involve New York state police in investigating alleged sex crimes on campus. Duane ‘Keffe D’ Davis sentenced to 40 years to life over Tupac Shakur’s murder Duane “Keffe D” Davis, the former California gang leader convicted of murder for orchestrating the 1996 fatal shooting of the rapper Tupac Shakur, has been sentenced to 40 years to life in prison. Judge Carli Kierny said as she delivered the sentence: “You don’t get to take a man from his family. You don’t get to take his very life, his whole future from him and just walk away from it.” On 7 September 1996, Shakur was gunned down near the Las Vegas strip shortly after a Mike Tyson boxing match. He succumbed to his injuries days later. In other news … Six deaths have been confirmed in Florida in the aftermath of Hurricane Isaias. The state’s governor praised Floridians and local officials for taking proper precautions, linking it to there being a lower death toll compared with previous storms. A sixth death has been announced in Pennsylvania’s measles outbreak, as new figures show cases in the state have risen above 1,100. An Iranian woman has been handed a death sentence for “blasphemy” in a social media post, as rights groups warn of Tehran’s increasing use of executions to suppress dissent, with at least 600 this year. Apple has unveiled new smart home devices that showcase an upgraded Siri AI. HomeView, an iPad-like device, acts as a hub for other smart home gadgets. Lena Dunham’s Girls is returning for a limited run at HBO. The creator and star will return along with other key cast members for a five-episode revival. Stat of the day: Elon Musk becomes biggest donor of US midterms cycle with $366m spent Musk’s midterm donations, mostly for rightwing candidates and causes, surpass his contributions to Trump in 2024. Meanwhile, Ukrainian soldiers in combat have suddenly had their access to Starlink satellite internet terminals restricted. Managed by Musk’s SpaceX, the terminals are a key component of Ukraine’s military operations, and the sudden restrictions led to the failure of several combat missions. Well Actually: They’re delicious, popular and versatile – but how healthy are berries? Experts say that if you’re eating any berry – strawberries, blackberries, currants, raspberries, blueberries – you’re benefiting. “All berries are good. We should eat a heck of a lot more than we do,” says Mary Ann Lila, a professor in the department of food, bioprocessing, and nutrition sciences at North Carolina State University. Don’t miss this: Could I make six figures from my couch? Influencers said yes – so I tried My colleague Vivian Ho has been looking to find out how realistic the promises of “passive income” schemes are, and whether she could actually make money from any of them. It’s a great read. Climate check: Scientists deploy a 24-armed secret weapon to save California’s kelp forests Off the coast of Monterey, California, a team of researchers is working to restore the sunflower sea star, as 95% of these key underwater ecosystems along the Pacific coast have been decimated in past decade. Last Thing: Joni Mitchell becomes US citizen Joni Mitchell has become a US citizen, after first moving to the country in the mid-1960s. The Canada-born singer-songwriter, 82, posted footage of her citizenship ceremony on her Instagram account, saying it was “a journey that began 62 years ago”. title: Nvidia, worth $5.5tn, donates $250m to UK for AI safety research
summary: Pledge spanning five years from world’s most valuable firm comes as concerns about AI agents have risen
text: The $5.5tn (£4.1tn) US chipmaker Nvidia is donating $250m worth of computing power to the UK to support AI safety research. The donation from the world’s most valuable company comes as the UK government confirmed its AI Security Institute (AISI), which tests advance AI models, will be able to examine cutting-edge technology developed by companies such as OpenAI, Anthropic and Google before they are released. Nvidia said the donation, which spans five years, would “support agentic safety and security research across the UK”. Safety concerns about AI agents – highly capable computer programs that are able to design and perform sequences of tasks autonomously – have risen since the summer, when OpenAI confirmed that a “swarm” of agents had attacked Hugging Face, a tech startup. Nvidia did not reference AISI in its statement but said most of the money would “support the wider UK AI safety and security research community”, with a proportion of the cash going to the British Open-Ended Learning and Discovery Lab, the Science of Fundamental AI Research Lab – run by the Edinburgh, Cambridge, Oxford and University College London universities – and Imperial College London. The computing power will be delivered via UK-based datacentres using Nvidia chips. “The UK brings world-class scientific rigour to this essential engineering challenge,” said Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s chief executive. “With this $250m commitment, Nvidia will put accelerated computing in the hands of UK researchers to develop, test and strengthen safeguards for increasingly powerful AI.” Kanishka Narayan, the UK’s AI minister, said the announcement was a “vote of confidence in our world-leading strength and expertise in AI research”. On Monday Narayan confirmed that AISI was conducting tests on US-developed AI models before they are released, after reports that the White House had restricted access. The AI minister also warned that the UK faces agentic attacks similar to the one carried out by OpenAI agents on Australia’s healthcare system this year. “It seems likely, if not inevitable, that our own cyber defences will be breached,” said Narayan. Anthropic, the developer of the Claude chatbot, warned of a new AI safety threat on Monday after it published a blogpost stating its models could soon become self-replicating. They find ways to infiltrate internet-connected devices such as smart ovens and lawnmowers, the company said. Under such a scenario the models could power themselves without datacentres, and instead could use a “botnet” of interconnected devices, Anthropic said, adding that the world should prepare for a future where such botnets were here to stay. “A replicator like this would be challenging to shut down since there’s no centralised point to shut off,” Anthropic’s researchers wrote.

title: ‘I wanted to change the stigma’: Nikita Hand on winning a civil rape case against Conor McGregor
summary: The popularity of Hand’s book Not the Perfect Victim is the latest twist in a story that puts the spotlight on how society responds to sexual assault allegations
text: Nikita Hand had a compelling reason to not pursue a civil rape case against Conor McGregor. She was, in her own view, an imperfect victim. The day of the assault, she had been partying with alcohol and cocaine before contacting McGregor, who took her to a Dublin hotel. Hours later, bruised and stunned, Hand made a report to police, but Irish authorities declined to pursue a criminal case against the mixed martial artist, saying there was no reasonable prospect of a conviction. That left the option of a civil case. But that would strip the hairdresser of anonymity, and pit her against a powerful celebrity who denied wrongdoing and had teams of lawyers and a vast online following. Hand went for it. “I’m not the perfect victim and I never portrayed myself to be,” she said in an interview in Dublin. “But I feel when victims are not perfect, they seem to get blamed. And I really wanted to try to change the stigma around people thinking you have to be a perfect victim to be believed or heard.” The cross-examination in the witness box at Dublin high court in 2024 felt like another violation, but Hand emerged victorious: the jury found that McGregor had assaulted her in 2018 and awarded nearly €250,000 in damages. “I felt vindicated. It was a really happy, special moment, but at the same time it was a really scary moment. It didn’t take away the fear and the anxiety – to this day I still live with the anxiety and the fear.” Hand, 37, has published a book, Not the Perfect Victim, that chronicles the assault and the aftermath of a case that continues to reverberate on both sides of the Atlantic. Jimmy Fallon triggered an outcry in June after hosting McGregor on The Tonight Show for a softball interview. Fallout from the case continued to play out on social media, said Hand. “I get so many beautiful messages online. And then I would get the odd hate message, from women and men, just calling me names, horrible names.” Hand’s appearance on the Irish bestseller list is the latest twist in a story that has put a spotlight on how the legal system, and popular culture, responds to allegations of sexual assault. Hand said she still struggled with being in the public eye, but was proud of the book. “I feel like I’m in control of my own story now, which I felt like I wasn’t for many years. The night of the assault, I wasn’t in control, another person was controlling my body.” Growing up in Drimnagh, a west Dublin suburb, Hand had acquaintances in common with McGregor, who was from nearby Crumlin. While he found fame and fortune in and out of the octagon, she worked in a salon as a colourist. In 2018 she had a partner, a five-year-old daughter and a new house. “Life was good. I was bubbly and loved going out with my friends.” At a Christmas work party she drank, took cocaine and, on a whim, messaged McGregor on Instagram, asking if he knew of any parties. He collected Hand and a friend on the morning of 9 December and took them to the Beacon hotel. Hand later testified that McGregor pinned her down on the bed, put her in a headlock and mock-choked her while raping her. Hand went to the home of her mother, who called an ambulance and insisted that Hand report the assault, regardless of McGregor’s status. “She didn’t care who it was. She just cared about her daughter. She’s seen the bruises on me, she’s seen the state I was in.” Hand was examined at a sexual assault treatment unit and gave a statement to police. When questioned, McGregor said the sex was consensual. In 2020 prosecutors decided to not press charges. After failing to reverse that decision Hand took a civil case. “I did want this person to go to jail for what he had done to me but I had no other option but to take up a civil case. Unfortunately, when you have a civil case and you win it, your perpetrator gets to walk free. But I knew I had to do everything in my power to get some sort of justice.” In June 2024, four months before the trial, three masked intruders broke into her home, smashed windows and stabbed her partner. Hand’s lawyers said they believed it was an attack by McGregor supporters, but that McGregor had nothing to do with it. The two-week trial in November 2024 drew intense media attention. The public gallery was packed and Hand was seated almost within touching distance of McGregor. The cross-examination was humiliating, she said. “I found it really degrading. I found it just as bad as the assault itself. Sometimes I feel like victims nearly are on trial rather than the perpetrators. That’s the way we’re kind of made to feel.” McGregor lost an appeal in July 2025. Last month a Dublin couple, Samantha O’Reilly and Steven Cummins, were charged with perjury after an investigation by police into evidence filed in McGregor’s appeal. Hand credits her mother, her partner and the Dublin Rape Crisis Centre with helping her to rebuild her life and to accept that the assault was not her fault. “The shame is leaving me but I do have my really bad days when I can’t leave my apartment. I have severe anxiety.” She is no longer a hairdresser. “I did try to go back to work and it just wasn’t the same. So it will be a complete career change for me. I’d love to work with victims and survivors and help them have a voice.” She wants her daughters – a teenager and a newborn – to grow up in a world where victims are not shamed or blamed. “It doesn’t matter what you wear or how much you drink or even take a drug. No means no and consent needs to be taken more seriously.” Hand said McGregor should not have been hosted at the White House in 2025 or on Fallon’s chatshow. “It’s really upsetting. I can’t understand how he’s still given such a huge platform.” She seldom mentions McGregor by name. “I don’t have any feelings for him. I don’t forgive him. I gave my evidence, he gave his and the jury made their decision. And that’s all there is to it.” • Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organisations. In the UK, Rape Crisis offers support on 0808 500 2222 in England and Wales, 0808 801 0302 in Scotland, or 0800 0246 991 in Northern Ireland. In the US, Rainn offers support on 800-656-4673. In Australia, support is available at 1800Respect (1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found at ibiblio.org/rcip/internl.html

title: ‘Like being in a vortex’: US report details extent of ‘devastating’ dating-app scams
summary: Congress calls for Match Group and others to do more to help victims like Mary, who lost $100,000 to app scammer
text: Mary met a man on the dating app Plenty of Fish in 2024. She told the Guardian she had been looking for a connection, but instead became the victim of a romance scam that cost her almost $100,000. “There was a lot of conversation, and then it started with the constant contact, pressure and repeated asks for money,” Mary, who asked that her last name be withheld, said in an interview on Tuesday. “It just escalated really, really quickly.” Mary was one of several people who spoke to staffers from the US Congress’s joint economic committee as part of an investigation by Senators Maggie Hassan, Democrat of New Hampshire, and Marsha Blackburn, Republican of Tennessee, into romance scams on dating platforms owned by Match Group. Match Group operates apps such as Tinder, Hinge, Plenty of Fish, Match (formerly Match.com) and others. “Romance scams, in which fraudsters form relationships to induce money or gifts from victims, have become a leading form of financial fraud in the United States and cost Americans at least $1.3bn annually,” the senators noted upon the investigation’s launch last September. On Tuesday, a report detailing the results of that investigation was published. Internal documents provided by Match Group showed that “as of the second half of 2025, Tinder had not updated most of its machine learning models in years” and “as a result, Tinder detected scammers and other bad actors less reliably and struggled to keep pace with emerging threats”, per the report. Data provided by Match Group also showed that through the third quarter of 2025 in the US, nearly 1.5m scammers or other bad actors on Tinder and Hinge had “matched with at least one other user”. The report also showed that nearly 500,000 of those accounts “exchanged contact information with another user”. Mary told the Guardian that she tried to establish whether the scammer she spoke with was real. He would contact her constantly, she said, and knew where she lived. She said that the man told her he needed money for work-related things and medical emergencies. “They never leave you alone,” she said. “I call it like being in a vortex. You don’t even realise what’s happening. You’re sending money, and it’s adding up, but each one of those times that you send money, it’s, like, not connected to the other times. But finally when I realized how much money I lost, I was like: ‘Whoa.’” In total, Mary said she sent the man about $100,000 in cryptocurrency payments. After realizing he was a scammer, she blocked his number. He would then switch phone numbers and contact her again. Mary has since sought to identify the people behind the fraud and discovered other Plenty of Fish profiles using the same photos as the man she had talked to. She has reported them to the platform. “If you knew me, you would say she would never do that,” Mary said, adding that she struggles to understand how it all happened, but believes it’s “really a lot about force of control”. Tuesday’s report noted that since the launch of the investigation last September, Match Group had “introduced and expanded important measures designed to combat scams” including a facial verification feature on the Tinder app across the US, “requiring all new Tinder users to complete a video selfie verification process”. In a news release on Tuesday, Hassan and committee Democrats added that Match Group also “instituted new efforts designed to remove harmful accounts more effectively” including in the first half of 2025, a “new AI model” that examines profiles and other information to detect scammers and other bad actors. “It is encouraging that following committee outreach, Match Group introduced new AI models,” the report states. However, those “changes came after a prolonged period during which scams continued to proliferate on Tinder”. In response to the report on Tuesday, Yoel Roth, Match Group’s senior vice-president of trust and safety said in a statement: “We’re grateful the committee recognized our significant advancements to protect our users against romance scams.” He said: “That said, the report mischaracterizes both the historical scale of our investment and the work already complete. Alongside our engagement with the Committee over the past year, we’ve made the largest safety advancements in Match Group’s history. Trust and safety is a foundational priority, and we intend to continue leading the industry in building tools that promote authentic, safe connections.” Much of the safety work, including face check, was already under way before the committee’s investigation, Match Group told NBC News. In June, Hassan introduced legislation alongside with the Republican senator Rick Scott, that would establish a central portal for Americans to report scams “and get the help they need from law enforcement and agencies”. Hassan, in a statement along with the release of the report on Tuesday, described romance scams as “devastating – both financially and emotionally – to people who are looking for connection and instead find themselves targeted and exploited by global criminal enterprises”. “During the course of our investigation, Match Group made progress in combating scammers – but it shouldn’t have taken so long, and there’s still more that Match needs to do,” she said. “As criminal networks use AI to supercharge their scams, dating apps and all companies must quickly and proactively keep their scam defenses up to date. Companies must stay vigilant and prioritize comprehensive scam prevention at every level to protect consumers and block fraudsters from infiltrating online platforms.”

title: Ukrainian soldier led team of divers sent to blow up Nord Stream gas pipelines, court hears
summary: Special forces officer Serhii Kuznetsov denies involvement in the 2022 blasts that left pipelines badly damaged
text: A Ukrainian soldier led a team of divers that, acting on the order of state authorities, laid explosives on the bed of the Baltic Sea to blow up the Nord Stream gas pipelines, a court has heard. On the opening day of his trial in the German city of Hamburg, Serhii Kuznetsov, who was a special forces officer with the Ukrainian military at the time of the pipeline attacks in 2022, was accused by prosecutors of being an accomplice to war crimes by attacking civilian infrastructure, causing an explosion, damaging property and disrupting public services. He appeared in court on Wednesday dressed in a grey suit, white shirt and black tie and flanked by his lawyers. Kuznetsov saluted as he entered the courtroom. He and his legal team listened in silence for 10 minutes as the federal prosecutor general read out the indictment, which was simultaneously translated into Ukrainian. Kuznetsov, 50, is alleged to have prepared and carried out the detonation of at least four incendiary devices of up to 27kg in weight at a depth of about 80 metres in the Baltic Sea close to the Danish island of Bornholm. He is believed to have had six accomplices – four deep-sea divers, an explosives expert and a ship’s captain – who are alleged to have used a rented yacht and timer-controlled explosives. Kuznetsov and his country deny any involvement in the attacks. Kuznetsov’s lawyers argued that the trial should not be taking place at all, telling the court that the defendant, who they said had been held almost entirely in solitary confinement for 11 months, was being treated “like a pawn on a chessboard”. They stressed his inability to defend himself in the conventional manner due to his role as an army officer, which they said forbade him from speaking. It meant he was having to defend himself “with his hands tied”. They also disputed the accusation that the attack was sabotage of civilian infrastructure, saying the pipelines were “a weapon in the hand of the Russians”. The explosions took place on 26 September 2022, badly damaging the pipelines which had been constructed to carry Russian natural gas between Vyborg in western Russia and Lubmin, near Greifswald in northern Germany. The blasts caused the Nord Stream 1 pipelines – Russia’s main gas supply route to Germany before Moscow cut the supplies in August 2022 – to burst. They also damaged Nord Stream 2, which was ready to carry gas but was never put into operation after Germany suspended its authorisation process just before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The attacks happened as European countries were seeking to transition away from Russian energy supplies in response to the Kremlin’s aggression. They exposed the dependence of Europe – and in particular Germany – on Russian gas as well as highlighting the murkiness of underground operations during wartime. Security observers initially blamed Moscow for the attack. Russia has denied involvement, in turn blaming the US, which has denied it just as forcefully. In July, German state prosecutors accused Ukrainian “state authorities” of ordering the attack, arguing: “The aim was to permanently halt gas supplies via the pipelines and prevent Russia from using the revenue from natural gas trade to finance its war effort.” The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, has denied his country was involved. Kuznetsov was arrested in August 2025 on a family holiday in Italy, with Italian police reporting that he surrendered without resistance. He had been travelling on a false passport. He was extradited to Germany last November after legal efforts to prevent this failed. Another suspect, Volodymyr Zhuravlyov, an air conditioner installer and hobby diver, was arrested on a European warrant in northern Croatia in August. He is fighting his extradition to Germany, having applied for asylum in Croatia. He denies any role in the sabotage. Aware of how potentially incendiary the trial could be, with Ukraine in effect in the dock for a crime committed against its ally – and one of its staunchest wartime supporters – the German government has declined to comment on the proceedings. On Wednesday, a group of protesters gathered outside the court holding Ukrainian flags and placards. One of them, a Ukrainian man in exile in Germany, said: “It’s a scandal that a Ukrainian is being accused of a war crime here today, when Russia is constantly committing war crimes in Ukraine.” The far-right populist, pro-Kremlin Alternative für Deutschland party, which is soaring in the polls, has seized on the Nord Stream plot to boost its argument that German aid for Ukraine must cease and the pipeline be reinstated so that cheap supplies of gas can help counter the cost of living crisis. The pro-Ukraine protesters who turned out on Wednesday were just a few feet away from a group of supporters of the far-left BSW party, which echoes the AfD’s stance on Russia and would also like to see the pipelines reinstated. They were holding placards demanding a parliamentary inquiry to investigate any political motives behind the Nord Stream attack. Nord Stream was already a controversial subject before the attack. Vladimir Putin and the then German chancellor, Gerhard Schröder, managed to bypass Ukraine as a transit country with Nord Stream 1. After Schröder left the chancellery, Putin appointed him as chair of the supervisory board of the company Nord Stream AG. Schröder was seen last week attending Putin’s birthday celebration. A request by the Russians to participate as co-plaintiffs in the Hamburg trial was rejected by the court. The company Gazprom, which owns the Nord Stream 2 pipeline, had argued its right to do so due to what it referred to as the severe economic consequences resulting from the attack. The court argued that while repair costs of the pipelines would be high, it would not be economically impossible to restore them. According to reports, Kuznetsov, whose military ID indicates he was in active service at the time the pipelines were blown up, is expected to maintain his right to remain silent during the trial. His legal team is expected to produce affidavits from two of his military superiors to support the argument that he is prohibited from revealing details of his actions as a soldier. He is reported to have allegedly taken his orders from a man who is considered to be the mastermind behind the attack and is one of those who have sworn in his favour. The trial will resume on 27 October. Sixteen trial days have been scheduled at Hamburg’s Hanseatic higher regional court up to and including 17 December, with further hearings likely in January.

title: Bank of England and IMF bosses warn of cyber threat to trust in financial system
summary: Kristalina Georgieva says online fraud could lead people to opt out of system and turn to ‘shoeboxes under their bed’
text: The heads of the Bank of England and the International Monetary Fund have issued a stark warning that rising cyber-attacks risk undermining trust in the financial system. Speaking on a panel about online fraud at the IMF and World Bank meetings in Bangkok, the governor of the Bank of England, Andrew Bailey, pointed to alarming headlines about self-replicating AI agents hijacking personal devices, and the French supermarket hack that heated fridges up to 50C. “If you try to say what’s at the heart of this debate about AI – for me, it’s about trust in technology and it’s about human control to achieve that trust in technology,” he said. Pointing to the key importance of technology in underpinning today’s financial system, he added: “If we don’t have trust in money, we don’t operate as a society.” Echoing his concerns, the IMF’s managing director, Kristalina Georgieva, said the toll of cyber-fraud was now so great that people could decide to opt out of the formal financial system altogether. “I was born and grew up on the other side of the iron curtain,” the Bulgarian economist said. “We didn’t trust the system. What did we do? I would have my dollars in a shoebox under my bed. “And I worry, today, that unless we figure out how to get ahead of this curve, given the speed, the scale and the cost of fraud growing up, we may end up with lots of people with shoeboxes under their beds.” She said this threat was particularly acute for people on the fringes of the financial system. “Imagine what would happen if trust disappears or is eroded to a point that people no more have the courage to be included,” she said. Her comments followed a warning from the IMF on Tuesday that the possibility of a big cyber-attack was one of the factors raising the global financial stability threat level to “elevated”, alongside higher borrowing costs and the risk of an AI share price crash. Bailey stressed that fraud was now frequently committed via social media platforms and apps, not just traditional financial channels – and urged big tech to take responsibility. He contrasted today’s environment with the legal status in the UK of outlets such as newspapers, which are responsible for the veracity of everything they publish. Instead, the governor said: “We’ve moved into quite an extreme position of, well, these platforms are open to everybody and there’s no real liability to the provision of the platform to what’s on it. Guess what? Everything’s on it. You know, the good, the bad and the incredibly ugly and downright criminal and terrible.” He added: “I don’t go around pointing the finger at people and saying: ‘You’re bad.’ What I have said is: ‘Look, there is responsibility all around.’ And we need to evolve to a world where everybody understands this responsibility, and everybody is then a part of addressing the problem.” He added: “We must get the social media companies involved because a lot of this fraud is transmitted through those channels.” Bailey called for the same tools that are being used by cybercriminals to be put to work protecting the financial system. “I’m going to use a sporting metaphor: this technology is arming the offence but it can also arm the defence, and it must do.” The panel event at which the pair were speaking was to launch a new set of international principles for avoiding cyber-fraud in financial institutions, called the Bangkok blueprint.

title: Minnesota professor linked to series of bizarre incidents involving urine at university
summary: Investigators determined professor responsible for urine found on a backpack, in trash cans and in water bottles
text: A former professor at Macalester College in the Minnesota city of St Paul is facing a felony charge for allegedly spilling his urine on a student’s backpack while he still worked at the school, costing more than $2,000 in damages, according to a state criminal court document. Paul Fischer, 55, is at the center of the bizarre, alleged workplace misconduct case that led to his being cited for first-degree damage to property – and linked to at least a half dozen such incidents involving urine at the liberal arts college over the course of a year. St Paul police homed in on Fischer after a student reported that she left her belongings unattended for about six minutes on 5 December in a common area near his office. Fischer was a biology professor at the time. The student told police that she found urine on her backpack when she returned to her belongings, according to the criminal court document obtained by the Guardian. The student reported the matter in February to St Paul police. Police learned that the college by then had also investigated her complaint – and determined there had been at least six such episodes involving urine at the school’s Olin-Rice science center during the span of about a year. Urine had been found in trash cans, individuals’ water bottles and inside professors’ decorations, the state criminal court document said. Investigators determined Fischer was responsible for the series of urine-related cases, and he resigned from Macalester College, where he had spent 25 years working. Authorities confronted Fischer before charging him, the court document said. He allegedly shared that “during the last one and a half to two years he developed a habit of urinating in a cup and disposing the contents in either trash cans or lab sinks around campus”, according to the document. The former professor allegedly claimed that he was emptying a container of urine into a trash can near his office on the day that the student who reported him said her backpack had been damaged. He said he believed that the cup of urine spilled on to the student’s belongings, the court document alleged. The urine on the student’s backpack resulted in damage to both the bag and her belongings inside, the document added. The student provided investigators with an itemized receipt for what was damaged that amounted to $2,070. Prosecutors for Ramsey county, Minnesota, whose jurisdiction includes St Paul, charged Fischer through a criminal complaint on 7 October. He could get up to five years in prison as well as a maximum fine of $10,000 if convicted as charged. A spokesperson for Macalester College on Tuesday said the school “is aware of the criminal charge against Paul Fischer” – and that his employment there ended during the 2025-2026 academic year. “As this is an ongoing legal matter involving a former employee, the college has no further comment,” the spokesperson said. Attempts to contact Fischer on Tuesday were not immediately successful. Commentary about the criminal complaint against Fischer made its way over to a page under his name on the RateMyProfessors.com platform. “So that explains the yellowish stain that appeared on my lab coat,” a comment posted on Tuesday read. The comment, which the Guardian could not authenticate, also said: “I don’t understand what motivates someone to do something like this, but avoid him at all costs.”

title: John Healey ‘targets tax crackdown on online marketplaces’ in first budget
summary: Move aimed at firms such as Amazon and eBay could raise up to £1bn more for Treasury, says report
text: A tax crackdown on online marketplaces such as Amazon and eBay that could raise up to £1bn more for the Treasury is reportedly being drawn up for John Healey’s first budget. The chancellor is said to be preparing to announce that online marketplaces will be made responsible for collecting tax owed by all retailers selling on their platforms. Marketplaces have been required to collect VAT for overseas businesses selling into the UK since 2021 but some foreign operators have posed as British retailers, using shell companies or other techniques to avoid this rule. Under the proposed change, websites would be made responsible for collecting VAT at source for retailers on their platform who have an annual turnover of more than £90,000, no matter where they are based. Healey is expected to announce this change will be made to fund cuts to business rates for high street shops, the Times reported. The government ran a consultation over the summer on changing the “deemed reseller” rules, saying “non-compliance persists among both overseas and UK-based businesses, distorting competition and disadvantaging compliant firms online and on the high street”. It consulted food delivery platforms as well as retail marketplaces, suggesting it was considering drawing them into the system. Amazon said it welcomed the prospect of a change to deemed reseller rules. “Closing this loophole will raise significant revenue for the exchequer and simplify compliance for both HMRC and legitimate sellers,” the UK’s biggest online marketplace said. The development comes as pressure continues to grow on Andy Burnham and Healey to relieve struggling small businesses on the high street before the budget on 28 October. Before he was elected in Makerfield, Burnham said he would increase the threshold for business rates so that 140,000 small high street retailers would not pay the tax. The government is facing calls from many factions to cut tax, with large retailers pushing for changes to national insurance to boost youth employment, for example. However, this week the Institute for Fiscal Studies warned Healey that his budget risks being a “work of fiction” unless he sets out plans to cover £35bn in spending pressures. The IFS said the damage from higher inflation meant the chancellor would need to either top up funds for his current government spending plans or impose deep real-terms cuts by the end of the decade. In a boost for the Treasury, this week the International Monetary Fund upgraded its GDP growth forecast for the UK this year to 1.3%, up 0.3 percentage points from its previous update in July. However, the IMF also cautioned that Healey should “stay the course” and continue repairing the UK’s public finances. Silvana Tenreyro, the IMF’s economic counsellor, said the UK “stands out” among G7 countries in having a plan to narrow its deficit. A spokesperson for the Treasury said: “As has always been the case, decisions on tax are a matter for the chancellor to set out at fiscal events rather than routinely commenting on rumour, speculation or proposals.”

title: Scale back on hake and coley, seafood charity tells shoppers
summary: Declining stocks and increased fishing pressure have led to lower sustainability ratings for two popular cod alternatives
text: UK shoppers have previously been urged to avoid UK-caught cod and to buy European hake or coley instead – but now these fish are in trouble, too. The Marine Conservation Society (MCS), an environmental charity, publishes its Good Fish Guide to help consumers and businesses make sustainable seafood choices. It uses a traffic-light system to rate seafood according to the health of fish stocks and environmental impact. On Wednesday, the MCS downgraded the ratings for European hake caught in the North Sea, Celtic Seas, or Bay of Biscay from green to amber owing to declining stocks and increased fishing pressure. Meanwhile, the rating on coley caught around the UK (North Sea, West of Scotland, Rockall and Skagerrak) has fallen from amber to red – the worst rating – meaning it is a “fish to avoid”. Of the 10 coley fisheries rated by the guide, two are still green while the other eight are amber. Kerry Lyne, the Good Fish Guide manager, said the “status of fish stocks are continuously changing” and a “fish that was a good choice a few years ago is not necessarily a good choice everywhere today”. Most of the seafood consumed in the UK is made up of just a few different species, known as the big five: cod, haddock, salmon, tuna and prawns. This puts a lot of pressure on a handful of wild stocks. Cod populations have been in decline since 2015. The main cause is overfishing, although changing sea temperatures and other ecosystem pressures have affected breeding and juvenile survival. “The best thing we can all do if we eat seafood is diversify our seafood choices and avoid those most under threat,” Lyne added. With that in mind, the charity has suggested wild-caught sea bass from around the UK as a more ocean-friendly alternative to cod. Similar to cod, sea bass is a mild white fish with a flaky texture that can be swapped like-for-like in any recipe. The guide is updated twice a year and of the 727 ratings, the latest review has 29 downgrades and 11 upgrades. On the good news front, UK Atlantic bluefin tuna, which has shown huge signs of a population recovery, has a brand new green rating. Chris Graham, the charity’s head of ocean regeneration and sustainable seafood, said one of the factors behind the resurgence was better fisheries management brought in more than 20 years ago. “We’re pleased to see a small, well-managed fishery in place, but caution must prevail, and this iconic species must be monitored closely so the health of the UK population can continue to improve,” Graham said. Lyme Bay “disco-pot” scallops were another new entry, with an amber rating. LED lights inside the pots to attract scallops mean the new technology has a much lower impact on the seabed than traditional dredging.

title: Pollinating insects flock to plants gardeners might think of as ‘weeds’
summary: Citizen scientists on UK Pollinator Monitoring Scheme recorded insect visits to flowers during 10-minute surveys
text: Ubiquitous urban plants often derided as “weeds” are the most attractive to pollinating insects. The autumn blooms of common ivy, rich in pollen and nectar, are the most visited by insects including bees and butterflies, according to an eight-year study. The next most popular are hogweed and bramble flowers, followed by non-native buddleia, which attracts four times as many butterflies and moths as other high-scoring flowers. The popularity and importance of plants for insects that many gardeners might dig up or cut down are revealed by the UK Pollinator Monitoring Scheme, in which citizen scientists have recorded insect visits to flowers during 10-minute surveys since 2017. Ivy received 22 visits by flying insects per 10-minute count with hogweed a close second (20) followed by buddleias, bramble, knapweeds and thistles, which received an average of 14 visits each. Jo Milborrow, the butterfly monitoring officer for Butterfly Conservation, one of the partners in the pollinator monitoring scheme, said: “We already recommend ivy as a great plant to grow because it is an important resource for breeding holly blue butterflies and nectaring commas and red admirals, so the fact that this easy-to-grow native species is also the number one plant for pollinating insect visits is a fantastic discovery – we would recommend people to start growing ivy today!” The survey, which is run by the UK Centre for Ecology & Hydrology (UKCEH) and the Joint Nature Conservation Committee (JNCC), found that hoverfly numbers had declined by about a third in both abundance and total number of species recorded across Britain over the past eight years. There was better news for solitary bees, which increased in one survey. Honeybees, beetles and flies excluding hoverflies all increased in the survey, which covered mostly gardens, suggesting that these could be providing an important refuge for some pollinators. Martin Harvey, a volunteer coordinator at UKCEH, said volunteers could contribute counts via the Pollinator Monitoring Scheme website next year between April and September. “Participants often say how much they have enjoyed spending time counting pollinators,” he said, “and it is always fascinating to observe the close association between insects and flowers”.
