title: Businesses could be barred from non-essential water use amid supply threat
summary: Golf clubs, private schools and car washes may face tighter rules from water companies as England’s drought continues
text: Three water companies are seeking to impose severe restrictions on businesses as the drought continues across most of England, putting rivers and wildlife under huge pressure. Golf clubs and private schools could be barred from using mains water to irrigate playing fields and courses, and commercial car washes stopped from operating, under “non-essential use bans” being sought by the companies. Eleven areas of England are still in drought, rivers are suffering from low flows, groundwater levels are declining and reservoir levels are at 54% – 21% below what is expected in the autumn. Yorkshire was the latest area to move into drought status on 9 October. Parts of Wales are experiencing the first signs of drought recovery after the whole country was declared in drought in July. Nineteen reservoirs or reservoir groups in England and Wales are less than 50% full, and eight are exceptionally low, up from five in August. The Met Office says above-average rainfall is needed over a sustained seven-month period to bring all areas out of drought. But last month England received about 65% of its typical September rainfall, with eastern and southern areas experiencing the greatest deficit. Businesses in drought-hit areas have been excluded from the hosepipe restrictions imposed on the public for the past three months. But South East, Southern and South West Water have applied to extend restrictions on water use to businesses via non-essential use bans in parts of their regions. If granted, water restrictions can be placed on golf clubs, private schools and commercial car washes to cut water use. Power hoses in car washes can use up to 25 litres of water per minute. Permission from the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) is required, but the government has yet to respond to the water companies’ requests. Pressure on wildlife and the environment from the drought is continuing. River flows in seven areas in England are exceptionally low, according to the latest Defra figures, affecting habitats, fish and wildlife. They include the River Derwent in the north-east, the rivers Yare and Ely Ouse in east England, and the River Tone and the Hampshire Avon catchments in south-west England. When river flows fall to low flow levels they can take years to recover, with potentially severe effects on fish spawning and river health. Mark Owen, the head of fisheries at the Angling Trust, said: “When rivers and fish are suffering from the ongoing effects of a severe drought, the Angling Trust supports further restrictions on non-essential water use, alongside urgent action to reduce huge leakage from water companies and unsustainable abstraction from rivers. “We must continue to reduce unnecessary demand for water. It makes little sense to ban people from washing cars at home while commercial car washes can continue operating.” In Hampshire, where the chalk aquifer is exceptionally low, Southern Water is seeking a drought order that would allow it to draw water from an internationally prized chalk stream and rare salmon habitat, even at levels below what is deemed ecologically safe. Southern said it was applying for the permit for the River Test owing to “a clear threat to supplies” in Hampshire and the Isle of Wight. The company is seeking a non-essential use ban on commercial premises and businesses to reduce demand as it seeks to draw more water from the Test at levels that were previously deemed unacceptable. As they seek permission to put restrictions on businesses’ water use, South East Water and South West Water have been allowed to alter the amount of water they draw from rivers to try to conserve water in their reservoirs. The Ardingly reservoir, near Haywards Heath in West Sussex, which serves 280,000 people, is exceptionally low, holding 1.05bn litres of water. Its total capacity is 5.2bn litres. In the south-west, Colliford reservoir on Bodmin Moor, which serves 255,000 households in Cornwall, is 37% full, holding 10.68bn litres against a total capacity of 28.5bn litres. Wimbleball in Somerset, which provides water for 390,000 people, is 18% full, with 3.8bn litres against a total capacity of 21.3bn litres. Sam Bottomley, South West Water’s director for drinking water services, said the region was entering a critical phase of an exceptionally prolonged drought. “Every day we continue to draw on our reservoirs to keep water flowing to homes, businesses and communities while river flows remain below the levels needed to support public water supply,” he said. “Many people understandably think a drought is over once it starts raining. In reality, recovery takes much longer. “Some rivers still remain at their lowest levels and with no significant rain forecast for the coming weeks, the immediate challenge is reducing demand and preserving enough stored water to maintain supplies until river flows and reservoir levels recover.”

title: Wednesday briefing: ​Why small boat crossings are here to stay ​
summary: In today’s newsletter: The ​collapse of the UK’s ‘one in, one out’ asylum deal with France exposes the limits of border enforcement that did little to stop crossings, and only made them more dangerous
text: Good morning. You’d be forgiven for missing it. Earlier this month, the government quietly scrapped its “one in, one out” deal with France. The partnership was supposed to eliminate small boat crossings by deterring asylum seekers from making the treacherous journey across the world’s busiest shipping channel. The deal, which lasted just 423 days, was beset with problems, had a negligible impact, and now joins a long list of policies that have tried and failed to address highly visible, often tragic small boat crossings. This morning, the Home Office announced that it would be doubling the number of riot police along the French coast in lieu of the deal. Although small boat arrivals have actually decreased over the last year, the far right continues to weaponise these crossings. In its annual threat briefing yesterday, the head of MI5 warned that extremists with anti-immigration opinions are increasingly considering carrying out terrorist attacks. Today’s newsletter speaks to specialist reporter Diane Taylor and Daniel Trilling, author of If We Tolerate This, to situate the deal’s collapse within the wider context of policies that have exacerbated the sense of disorder they’re supposed to resolve – and asks what comes next. That’s after the headlines. Five big stories UK news | Extremists holding anti-immigration opinions are becoming increasingly likely to consider carrying out terrorist attacks against immigration centres and asylum hotels, the head of MI5 has warned. UK politics | Nigel Farage has denied that a Reform UK government would authorise lethal force against small boat crossings in the Channel. Ukraine | Andy Burnham will host Volodymyr Zelenskyy at Downing Street on Wednesday as the UK seeks to further underline its support for the Ukrainian president, in contrast to his difficulties with Donald Trump. US politics | Kimberly Guilfoyle is stepping down as US ambassador to Greece after weeks of reports that she sought payment from a Trump donor in exchange for access to administration officials. Pope Leo XIV | Pope Leo has lung cancer, the Vatican said late on Tuesday. Leo, 71, underwent an operation and had the lower lobe of his right lung removed, with tests confirming a diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma, the Vatican said. In depth: ‘I’ve never seen as much suffering caused to refugees by government policy’ The one in, one out policy that was announced in a joint press conference between Keir Starmer and Emmanuel Macron in July last year was supposed to render small boat crossings pointless. A person arriving in a small boat to the UK could be forcibly returned to France in exchange for another person who would be brought legally to the UK. “In effect,” Diane Taylor wrote in a moving piece about the scheme in September, asylum seekers were “used as reluctant human shields to protect our borders from others in the same predicament.” The scheme was always limited in scale; of the 40,000 people who arrived in small boats while it was active, just 1,500 – roughly 4% – were returned to France. A report by British Future, a thinktank that championed the policy, recognised that it would have to be expanded twenty-fold to close down routes as a viable way to claim asylum. But it’s doubtful that, even at this far larger scale, it would have ever been effective. Diane reported in August that nearly 50 asylum seekers deported under the scheme returned to the UK a second time, and an unknown number arrived undetected. The government would have liked the scheme to continue, and its official explanation was that it was scrapped because it couldn’t be effectively scaled up. But it seems likely that political concerns in France also played a role. “At a time when immigration is going to be a major issue in the French presidential election, France doesn’t want to be seen to be taking in more unwanted people from the UK,” Rajeev Syal, the Guardian’s home affairs editor, tells me. *** The other side of one in, one out The deal was partially founded on a recognition of the need for safer routes to claim asylum in Britain. Starmer acknowledged when announcing it that “it is right that we offer a haven to those in most dire need”. But this flicker of humanitarianism was outweighed by the scheme’s arbitrary cruelty. Nearly 100 children were misidentified as adults and wrongly detained under the scheme, while some asylum seekers deported back to France were beaten by people smugglers. “I’ve been writing about asylum seekers for 25 years and I’ve never seen as much suffering caused to refugees by a UK government policy,” says Diane. It was also accompanied by the government’s fortification of security measures along the French border. To some extent, these security measures help to explain the drop in small boat crossings this year, together with an overall reduction in arrivals of asylum seekers to Europe. But they have also encouraged people to make even more unsafe crossings. The increased police presence in northern France has led to more trips in larger “mega-dinghies”, which became a subject of panicked headlines this summer, as smugglers attempt to transport more people in single crossings. Increased security has also encouraged people to take longer routes across the channel, sailing from Normandy and Belgium rather than Calais. Earlier this summer, far-right protests spread to Portsmouth, where people arriving on small boats had sailed from Normandy. “In effect, while the security measures seem on the surface to be working, they also contribute to boat journeys becoming far more dangerous, again adding to the sense of spectacle,” Daniel Trilling tells me. *** Why are so many people still crossing in small boats? The right frames small boat crossings as a failure to control immigration. Crucially, though, they’re a manifestation of ever-more draconian attempts to crack down on people trying to claim asylum in the UK. Before people crossed the channel in dinghies, they hid in lorries, or took flights to the UK using false passports. “When I first started reporting in Calais in 2014, it was still possible for refugees to stow themselves away on lorries without paying smugglers for access,” Daniel recalls. “But the more security that was placed around ports, the harder that became, and the more refugees had to rely on smugglers who could get access to secure lorry parks.” In 2020, when the pandemic temporarily grounded traffic between Calais and Britain, small boat crossings spiked dramatically. By the following year, these crossings had more than doubled. “There used to be really, really small numbers of boats arriving in Britain, and nobody paid attention to them,” Diane says. “And obviously, you didn’t get far-right influencers live-streaming arrivals at border control in Heathrow, or standing on the hard shoulder of the M25 waiting to film asylum seekers for their YouTube.” *** What happens next Part of the calculation behind the government’s latest decision to double the number of riot police in northern France is that, now the deal has ended, it has limited time in which to strengthen its partnership with the French government. If Marine Le Pen is elected in April next year, it’s plausible that her government could refuse to take any asylum seekers from Britain, further politicising the issue and causing a rise in crossings that would play into the hands of the far right here. Yet the decision is also yet another manifestation of the tendency to treat migration as a security issue rather than a reflection of an increasingly unstable world. No matter the increase in security or threats of deportation, people will keep trying to claim asylum. “As long as we have wars, instability and persecution, people will be displaced, and we need to work out ways to respond to that, rather than pretending that a policy tweak here or extra security measure there will simply make it disappear,” Daniel says. “At some point, you have to make a political argument for why asylum isn’t just an act of generosity, but a necessary response to the world as it is.” What else we’ve been enjoying This illuminating read explains how charity shops are facing a crisis as they compete with secondhand resale sites such as Vinted, a problem with unexpected consequences. Crucially, she outlines how we can all donate better. Craille Maguire Gillies, newsletters team Reading Morwenna Ferrier’s pest I’ll never forget made me reconsider the humble pigeon – which she describes as having encountered with such awe, aged 11. Poppy Noor, newsletters team Whatever side of the “will AI destroy society” debate you stand, read Leyland Cecco’s conversation with AI computer scientist turned sceptic Geoffrey Hinton: uncertainty, Hinton argues, is not a reason for complacency. Craille I loved our gallery of French photographer Jean-Pierre Laffont’s work – he spent two decades capturing protests, clashes and countercultural gatherings in America, and the images to come out are stunning and empowering. Poppy When species of birds decline, passing on the skill of singing becomes harder, even affecting their ability to breed. Rebecca Ratcliffe has this fascinating and warming look at how scientists are helping birds remember lost songs. Craille Sport Football | Pablo Barrios struck after 53 seconds and Leny Yoro was shown red as Atlético Madrid added to Manchester United’s woes with a 2-0 victory. Athletics | Ruth Chepngetich’s failed doping test, five months after she obliterated the record in 2024, left the sport deeply uneasy but powerless to act. Formula One | Formula One has confirmed Rwanda will join the calendar, with the first race set for the early 2030s. It will mark the first time F1 has raced in Africa since 1993. The front pages “M15 warns of rightwing shift from anti-migrant opinion to terrorism,” is the splash on the Guardian on Wednesday. “M15 chief: Russia did not sway Brexit vote,” says the Telegraph. “Putin’s Russia is biggest threat to Britain, M15 chief confirms,” says the i. “M15 chief: UK must not ‘play into hands’ of Putin,” has the Express, while the Mirror runs with: “Red Alert.” “Tax fears eased in Burnham’s ‘pro-business’ pitch to bosses,” is the lead story over at the FT. “Online tax crackdown to boost the high street,” says the Times. “4 out of 5 new jobs went to foreigners in the past decade,” has the Daily Mail, while the Metro goes with “Toxic water spills surge.” Finally, the Star with: “Tiger’s victim a child actor.” The Latest ‘I will not be silenced’: Trump critic Ilhan Omar defiant after home raided Democrats have described a raid on the home of Congresswoman Ilhan Omar as “deeply disturbing” and a “rogue abuse of power” by the Trump administration. The Democratic representative for Minnesota has long been a target of highly personal attacks by Donald Trump, who claims he was not involved in ordering the raid. Lucy Hough speaks to Guardian US political reporter Shrai Popat – watch on YouTube. Cartoon of the day | Ben Jennings The Upside A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad Peter Lloyd spent most of his life unable to read or write, despite repeated attempts to learn. He struggled in school, left with no qualifications, and developed coping strategies that enabled him to work successfully as a lorry driver. During the Covid lockdowns, he found that it had become an overwhelming issue, particularly when he could not help home-school his son. Encouraged by his wife, he contacted the charity Read Easy and began lessons with a volunteer tutor. Over three years, he learned to read and now Lloyd serves as a Read Easy ambassador. Lloyd says: “I think it’s important to encourage others in my situation to seek help, especially men who might be too ashamed. I have three books on the go at the moment – I can’t believe how beautiful reading is!” Sign up here for a weekly roundup of The Upside, sent to you every Sunday Bored at work? And finally, the Guardian’s puzzles are here to keep you entertained throughout the day. Until tomorrow. Quick crossword Cryptic crossword Wordiply

title: Trump urges Alaskans to vote for the ‘real’ Dan Sullivan in tight midterms battle
summary: Republican senator Dan S Sullivan is vying for re-election against Democrat Mary Peltola – and another candidate called Dan J Sullivan
text: Donald Trump has encouraged Alaskans to vote for the “real” Dan Sullivan, as he sought a breakthrough for the Republican incumbent senator in a tightly fought Senate race complicated by a rival candidate with a near-identical name. Sullivan’s re-election campaign this year against Democrat Mary Peltola, a former US House lawmaker, has turned into one of the most hotly contested battles of the midterm elections, in which Democrats are hoping to seize back control of Congress and hamper Trump for the final two years of his presidency. Though Alaska supported the president by a wide margin in the 2024 elections, recent polls have shown a close race between Peltola and Sullivan, who are joined on next month’s ballot by another candidate named Daniel Sullivan, a retired schoolteacher also running as a Republican. The incumbent has accused his similarly named challenger of colluding with Democrats to split the votes of his supporters to Peltola’s advantage. “On November 3, we’re going to send one of the best and most respected senators in DC Dan Sullivan, the real Dan Sullivan,” Trump told a packed auditorium on Tuesday in Wasilla, a city about 45 miles (72km) north of Anchorage. He urged the audience to reject “the fake Dan Sullivan”, whom he said was “put up by” the Democrats. “That’s just cheating. They’re terrible,” the president said. “They found a guy named Dan Sullivan, they put him up to get a little confused.” Noting the 2.5% of the vote that the challenger Sullivan received in the August primary election, Trump said: “That’s a lot, that’s too much. That could be the difference.” The incumbent senator will appear on the 3 November ballot with the words “(Registered Republican) Incumbent” next to his name. The election will be held under ranked-choice voting and Alaskans can rank up to five candidates. In his speech, Trump attacked the method approved by a 2020 voter referendum as “a scam”, and encouraged Alaskans to support a measure on this year’s ballot to repeal it. Speaking before Trump took the stage, Sullivan accused Peltola of planning to undermine Alaska’s oil and gas industry, which plays a major role in supporting the state’s economy even though production has declined since its peak in the late 1980s. “Joe Biden, [Chuck] Schumer, their Democratic allies came after Alaska with a barrage of executive orders to shut down our state, kill jobs, drive up the cost of energy, and my opponent, Mary Peltola, not only did nothing to stop it, she enabled it,” Sullivan said. In a statement, a spokesperson for Peltola’s campaign said the candidate “looks forward to working with President Trump to unleash Alaska energy and lower costs … when she’s elected to the United States Senate.” “While Dan Sullivan continues to feel the fallout of his failed policies and support for the war in Iran, Mary spent the day talking with Alaskans … about how she will fight to lower their costs (and) take on DC corruption,” the spokesperson said in reference to Peltola’s campaign visit on Tuesday to Kotzebue, in north-west Alaska. Peltola won a special election to the US House of Representatives in 2022 after the death of longtime Republican congressman Don Young, then a full term later that year. She was defeated in 2024 by Republican Nick Begich, who is seeking re-election this year. Recent polls have the candidates neck-and-neck in a state that has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 2008.

title: Leaders of India’s Cockroach party jailed for violating ban on protest site
summary: Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das will spend spend five days in prison for entering Delhi’s Jantar Mantar – a historic protest site that has been closed by authorities
text: Two leaders of India’s youth-led Cockroach movement have been sent to jail for five days for violating a ban on protests at a site in central Delhi. A court ordered that Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das, leaders of the Cockroach Janata party (CJP) movement, spend five days in Delhi’s Tihar prison for jumping over police barricades, holding up slogans and waving the Indian flag at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar. CJP leaders said the action was taken to demonstrate against the brutal crackdown on youth protesters in Delhi over the weekend and the decision by the Delhi police to shut-down Jantar Mantar – a stretch of road surrounding an observatory in central Delhi – as the capital’s designated protest site, a status it has held for more than 30 years. “You cannot denotify the resistance,” said Abhijit Dipke, the founder of the CJP, in a social media post which showed three of his fellow leaders entering Jantar Mantar, before they were tackled and detained by police on Tuesday. On Saturday, the CJP – a pressure group with a substantial following among India’s youth – called for a protest in Jantar Mantar to demand the resignation of the election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, who is accused of overseeing the mass disenfranchisement of millions of Indian voters. The CJP, alongside the opposition political parties and student groups, have accused Kumar of revising India’s electoral roll to advantage the ruling Narendra Modi government, a charge his Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) denies. The election commission has denied favouring any party and said wrongly deleted voters ‌can re-enrol. Police denied permission for the protest on Saturday to take place and instead imposed a sweeping security crackdown. About 30,000 police and paramilitary were deployed to prevent the demonstration in Jantar Mantar, which was blocked with barricades. More than 7,000 people were detained, including the CJP leaders who were kept overnight. In the aftermath, the police declared that protests would no longer be allowed at Jantar Mantar and instead proposed three alternative venues – all much further away from parliament – which provoked outrage among the CJP leaders. Prior to his arrest, Das posted: “Why is Narendra Modi scared of Jantar Mantar? Jantar Mantar belongs to the people of India.” Ranka and Das ‌were among about a dozen people who jumped the barricades on Tuesday to enter the grounds of the Jantar Mantar to wave flags and chant slogans. In response to their sentencing, CJP founder Dipke accused the Modi government of resorting to “cowardly tactics” to “crush dissent”. The jailed CJP leaders were also given the backing of opposition leader Rahul Gandhi, who said the people of India would “reclaim Jantar Mantar”. “Waving the tricolour at Jantar Mantar in a peaceful protest is not a crime. Jailing youth for it is an act of cowardice,” said Gandhi. The response by the Modi government to the protests that have erupted nationwide – including the mass detentions – has drawn criticism from the UN human rights commissioner and human rights groups such as Amnesty. The Indian government hit back at the UN statement on the protests, calling it “an unacceptable interference in the internal affairs of the country”. The crackdown was also met with concern by a UK political delegation visiting Delhi, led by trade minister Jonny Reynolds who confirmed he had raised it with the Indian government. Kiran Stacey contributed to this report

title: Birdwatch: the paradoxical puffin – a comical bird with a fighting spirit
summary: Despite their size and gentle appearance, puffins will fight to keep their catch of sand eels from an opportunistic gull
text: Few birds are as paradoxical as the puffin. It rivals the robin as Britain’s best-loved bird, yet most people have never seen one in the flesh. In spring and summer, they gather in large, noisy colonies to breed, but spend the autumn and winter far out to sea in the North Atlantic. And despite their small size, and gentle, clown-like appearance, puffins will fight to save their precious catch of sand eels from being seized by an opportunistic – and much larger – skua or gull. Puffins, like penguins, have a very human quality, too. When the late Bill Oddie and I filmed puffins at a colony on Shetland, he memorably described them as “looking like old men in dinner jackets, waiting to go into supper at the club”, while the bird’s scientific name, Fratercula arctica, translates as “little brother of the Arctic”. Their huge, colourful bill once earned them the name “sea parrot”, while “puffin” – meaning “fat” or “swollen” – was originally given to the young of another burrow-nesting seabird, the Manx shearwater. Confusingly, that species still retains the misleading scientific name Puffinus puffinus. Now, like so many seabirds, puffins are in trouble. The sand eels, on which they rely to feed themselves and their single chick, are shifting north because of the climate crisis. Puffins are also threatened by avian flu, pollution and disturbance – ironically often caused by visitors to their colonies, over-eager to get closeup photos of these charismatic little birds. The Puffin: A Biography, by Stephen Moss, is published on 15 October.

title: Global financial system is failing developing countries, says Ed Miliband
summary: UK foreign secretary will call for World Bank and others to help governments trapped by hefty borrowing costs
text: The foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, will claim the global financial system is failing developing countries, as he calls for a “new deal” for governments struggling under the burden of debt. Promising to throw the UK’s diplomatic weight behind urgent reform, he will evoke the example of the Gleneagles summit under the last Labour government in 2005 – the culmination of the Make Poverty History campaign. “The global financial system and indeed the global order is failing to serve developing countries on debt, on resilience and on climate. This is not just against our values but against our national interest,” Miliband is expected to say. “In the interconnected world we live in, more than ever, the opportunities and challenges we confront are collective.” Speaking in Bangkok on Wednesday, he will call for the World Bank and other multilateral development banks (MDBs) to use the resources they have available to lighten the load for governments trapped by hefty borrowing costs. “We need action on developing country debt through the MDBs,” he is expected to say. “Action that leverages the balance sheets of the international financial institutions to support these countries to repay over longer time horizons, and crucially, refinancing, with better rates, to give them precious fiscal space.” The foreign secretary will be in Bangkok to attend the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank annual meetings. He opted to take up the UK’s seat on the bank’s board himself instead of leaving it to the development minister, Kirsty McNeill. Labour’s manifesto in 2024 promised to restore the UK’s international reputation on development issues – but Keir Starmer subsequently slashed the aid budget to pay for defence. Campaigners have long claimed the high interest rates paid by many developing countries mean the repayments crowd out vital public spending – including on tackling the climate emergency. In sub-Saharan Africa, more than three times as much is spent on debt servicing as on education. Miliband will argue that making the global financial system work better for emerging economies will also help to attract more private investment – a key aim of the World Bank under the current president, Ajay Banga. The UK is due to take up the presidency of the G20 group of nations next year – a key global forum for discussing global financial issues, including sovereign debt, which includes emerging economies such as China, India, South Africa and Brazil. The chancellor, John Healey, will set out his own G20 priorities in Bangkok later this week, including mobilising more resources from the balance sheets of the IMF and the World Bank. When the UK held the chair of the narrower G8 group in 2005, at the leaders’ summit at the Gleneagles hotel the UK secured agreements that eventually resulted in more than 30 countries receiving large-scale debt write-downs. Miliband will say resources are now more constrained – but as well as debt refinancing for a large number of countries, he will demand an overhaul of the “common framework” for restructuring the debts of countries unable to pay. The framework is widely criticised as too slow and cumbersome. Among other reforms, the UK wants to see changes to ensure private creditors cannot hold up negotiations – as has happened in recent cases including that of Ethiopia. The foreign secretary will also call for overhauls to allow help to be made available more rapidly to countries in trouble. “We need finance teed up in advance of crises, so that governments get support in days, not months,” he will say. Miliband will be speaking at the launch of a report by the Rockefeller Foundation that calls for a “surge” in affordable financing from the IMF and the World Bank to debt-burdened countries. Tim Jones, the policy director of the campaign group Debt Justice, welcomed Miliband’s focus on the issue but said a litmus test of any plan would be whether private sector creditors bear some of the costs. “Action on debt relief is urgently needed. That must include private lenders sharing in the cost. Otherwise public money will just bail out private lenders rather than be used for investment.”

title: UK resists EU pressure to hit China with tariffs
summary: Exclusive: Business secretary says he will not change trade rules due to EU pressure and denies UK will become a ‘back door’ for cheap imports
text: The business secretary has hit back at European demands for British tariffs on Chinese imports, saying the government will not change its trade rules because of pressure from Brussels. Jonathan Reynolds warned that the government would not bow to calls from other countries for the UK to hit Chinese vehicles with import taxes, despite political pressure to align with the EU in exchange for deeper future economic ties. The EU imposed tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles in 2024 and last Friday agreed a 350,000 a year quota on Chinese hybrid cars amid fears cheaper alternatives are causing deindustrialisation and job losses. Reynolds conceded that levying sanctions on Chinese goods was an option in the future, but he dismissed concerns from Brussels that the UK could provide a back door to the European market. His comments highlight the divisions that remain between the UK and EU on trade and industrial policy, which could derail the prime minister’s attempts to move closer to Brussels. “I just want to be clear: when we make any trade decision in terms of trade defence tariffs in relation to the EU, that’s based on the UK interest – it’s not based on any other country asking for that,” said Reynolds during a trade trip to India. “In 2024, [we] looked at this issue carefully, and we keep it under review depending on what the needs of industry are … But it comes down to what is the fundamental nature of the UK automotive sector. It’s an export-led sector, so that’s what I’ve got to take into account.” With Europe having imposed tariffs of up to 45% on Chinese electric cars, some believe that the UK has opened an alternative route into the EU for Chinese companies setting up in the UK to sell into the bloc. Nissan, for instance, has agreed to look at building cars in northern England for the Chinese manufacturer Chery. Reynolds rebutted those accusations, however, saying: “The UK currently has no major Chinese manufacturer based in its automotive sector, so we’re not making vehicles here and sending them to the single market through some sort of back door.” His comments raise the stakes ahead of intense final weeks of negotiations before the long-awaited UK-EU summit, which Andy Burnham confirmed this week would be held in Brussels on 20 November. The prime minister told the Commons on Monday he wanted a “serious dialogue” over the UK’s place in Europe, as he framed the summit as a possible first step to EU membership. The new Made in Europe trade rules aim to protect European companies from subsidised Chinese imports, but British manufacturers worry they will also be shut out of supply chains. The issue will not formally be on the agenda at the November summit, but British officials are hoping to use those talks to shape the European legislation. Diplomats on both sides of the Channel say the summit will now be an early test of whether Burnham’s desire for a “real reset” in UK-EU relations is likely to bear fruit. One EU official said this week that the UK’s negotiating position would determine whether it was worth pursuing more fundamental changes such as British access to the single market, a new customs union or re-accession. Some in Brussels have been pushing for Britain to levy tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles in return for getting access to the European market under the new trade rules. Reynolds has previously dismissed such an option in part because of the risk that Beijing could hit the UK with reciprocal tariffs, damaging British companies such as Jaguar Land Rover. He said it would be to Europe’s detriment if it did not admit the UK into the scheme. “If you look at the impact analysis of such a policy, the consequences for the EU [of] excluding the UK are much more difficult,” he said. “This is not just in the UK’s interest; it’s not in the EU’s interest because obviously we have integrated supply chains.” Reynolds said the summit was an important milestone in EU-UK relations but also insisted that new trading terms for electricity, emissions and food and drink products would be a major achievement in themselves. Speaking from a two-day trade delegation to Delhi and Mumbai, he acknowledged that the landmark free trade agreement he helped strike last year with India would become defunct if Britain does rejoin the EU. “Obviously, if you enter those arrangements, you are doing things collectively. So there would be trade relationships with the UK that were based on Europe, the EU as a whole – that is how the European Union works in terms of its relationship. “That’s why obviously when we were part of it, we didn’t have these separate bespoke arrangements.” But he insisted that it remained worth continuing to push to broaden the scope of the agreement, as he unveiled a series of UK-India investments which officials say are worth over £1bn to the UK over the next 15 years. The deal has already begun to reduce the price of Scotch whisky in Indian shops, after tariffs were reduced from 150% to 75%. Now British officials are keen to free up trade in services as well as goods, for example, pushing for both countries to recognise each other’s legal qualifications. “There are some specific things regarding who can practice law and in which area,” Reynolds said. “I am confident over the medium to long term that this will improve over time.” He added: “We’ve got to be cognisant of this long-term position with the EU. But frankly, there’s a job to be done here and now, which we’re doing.”

title: Judge extends White House access to banned media outlets CNN, MS Now and Politico
summary: District court judge Timothy Kelly was ruling after Trump administration blocked access to three outlets last month
text: A federal judge ordered the White House on Tuesday to continue allowing journalists from CNN, MS Now and Politico to access the building as the media coalition’s lawsuit against the Trump administration plays out. Timothy Kelly, a district court judge, had on 24 September granted a 14-day reprieve for the news organizations, which six days earlier had been banned by the president in an extraordinary move from entering the White House grounds “as a result of their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS”. “Defendants (except for President Trump) and their agents, representatives, and all persons or entities acting in concert with them, shall not execute, implement, or enforce the September 18, 2026, decision to revoke the White House ‘hard pass’ press credentials held by employees of CNN, MS NOW, and POLITICO, thereby maintaining the status quo since the Court’s entry of a temporary restraining order on September 24, 2026,” the judge wrote in granting a preliminary injunction requested by the plaintiffs. The organizations filed a lawsuit on 21 September seeking to overturn the ban as a violation of their rights under the US constitution. But that temporary restraining order expired on Tuesday, bringing the media companies into court late last week to ask for a preliminary injunction that would lift the ban during the duration of the lawsuit, which could take months. During arguments at the E Barrett Prettyman federal courthouse in Washington, Kelly seemed inclined to lift the ban indefinitely, telling a lawyer for the federal government that his side had “a notice problem” that was “probably the biggest hurdle” they had to overcome. The Trump White House gave no advance notice to the media companies affected to say that they were at risk of losing their press badges, which the news organizations have said are essential to their ability to cover the administration. While the White House sent letters to the media companies informing them of the ban, they did so post-hoc, after building access had already been cut off, in violation of binding court precedent. In his ruling on Tuesday, Judge Kelly wrote that the plaintiffs “are likely to succeed not only on their due process claim, but also on their two First Amendment claims”. While access to the White House is not guaranteed, court precedent dictates that once it is provided to journalists, it cannot be taken away for editorial or viewpoint-based reasons. During arguments for a preliminary injunction on 8 October, media lawyer Theodore J Boutrous told the judge that Trump had offered a “confession” – in a Time magazine interview last week – that he was banning the media companies explicitly because of the content of their reporting, not because of any other considerations, such as national security. “The case has gotten stronger for the plaintiffs thanks to President Trump,” Boutrous told the judge. The judge seemed to agree. “President Trump’s own comments suggest that he intended the revocation of Plaintiffs’ hard passes to alter their reporting on him, bolstering the case that his action here is sufficient to deter a reporter of ordinary firmness from reporting in the same way she had before,” he wrote. Although the White House has largely adhered to the judge’s prior ruling restoring access on a temporary basis, journalists for CNN and Politico have on occasion been prevented from performing “pool duty” – covering the daily activities of the president – because the administration has interpreted the judge’s temporary restraining order to solely require access to the White House complex, not smaller spaces like Air Force One or the Oval Office. The judge required the media plaintiffs to post a bond of $1. In a statement, Boutrous said of the judge’s ruling: “When the President issued his ‘ban on the free press,’ he blatantly and explicitly violated due process and the First Amendment. Since then, the President has repeatedly, candidly, and consistently admitted in public that he banned our clients from the White House to punish reporting he doesn’t like and to try to force journalists to cover him in ways he prefers.” The court, he added, “was right to enjoin the White House from enforcing this ‘unconstitutional ban on the free press’ for the foreseeable future”.

title: Country diary: This is Dorset’s worst-located stone circle – but Nine Stones is well worth a visit | Sara Hudston
summary: Winterbourne Abbas: These bronze age megaliths have hosted rituals and seen off electricity pylons. Today they endure by the side of an A-road
text: The Nine Stones at Winterbourne Abbas have an inglorious setting. Hard by the A35, there are only slim iron railings and a small ditch to shield the circle from the heavy traffic rumbling west. And for about six months of the year the ditch flows with water (the winter bourne), often overspilling and flooding the road. Yet the surroundings used to be even less picturesque. Until a few years ago, a line of high‑voltage electricity pylons looped across the valley, humming and sizzling a few hundred metres from the monument. In 2022, the lines were buried out of sight. Today, the path to the circle crosses the underground cables, passing two small enclosures, each containing a pair of grey metal cabinets. Stern and mysterious, connected to hidden power, these modern installations echo the bronze age megaliths beyond. The circle itself sits in a wooded glade, which would be peaceful were it not for the lorries clattering by. The individual stones are markedly different from each other, varying in size from knee-high to 1.5m, some squat, some broad, and one like a tall, cloaked figure. An old beech tree stump, rotted and streaked with moss, acts as a tenth, more temporary, marker. From a distance, the monoliths look like typical sandstone sarsens found across southern chalk downland, grey and slightly bulbous. Viewed up close, a surprise reveals itself. The largest are made of a conglomerate of pebbles, flint and quartz held together with fine-grained sediment. It’s hard to believe that this mix – known locally as “puddingstone” – occurred naturally because it looks uncannily like a rough aggregate stirred into concrete. Some of the chunks of flint are flushed pink, an unusual effect caused by the presence of iron elements. The colour is diffused through layers of rock flakes, like strawberry juice frozen in ice. This oddity offers a clue about where the sarsens came from. Less than two miles away is the Valley of Stones, a scattering of large boulders left at the end of the last ice age, many of which contain the same rosy flint nodules. Material from there was used locally in other ritual settings from the Neolithic onwards. • Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024, is available now at guardianbookshop.com

title: Court overturns Tanya Plibersek’s protection order which stalled controversial NSW goldmine
summary: Federal court overrules decision by former environment minister for the McPhillamys goldmine development at Blayney
text: The federal court has overturned a rare protection order issued by former environment minister Tanya Plibersek under Indigenous heritage legislation, which the company said effectively blocked a goldmine in the central west of New South Wales. Regis Resources challenged the decision by the former minister to issue the order in 2024 under section 10 of the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Heritage Protection Act. The Wiradyuri Traditional Owners Central West Aboriginal Corporation asked the minister to protect the headwaters and the springs of the Belubula River as a site central to creation stories. The company said at the time the protection order, while affecting only part of the site and not the area intended to be mined, would make its McPhillamys goldmine development at Blayney unviable. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email The order blocked the company from building a tailings dam in the headwaters of the Belubula River. In a decision on Wednesday morning, Justice James Stellios ruled the order was invalid. The reasons for the court’s decision will be published on Friday. According to the ABC, Stellios said on Wednesday the court’s decision and his reasons “say nothing about the merits of the claim … whether it’s a significant area or under threat of injury or desecration … those are matters within the authority of the minister … not the jurisdiction of this court.” At a three-day hearing last year, Regis Resources argued it had been denied procedural fairness and the government made errors in the process it followed before issuing the protection order. The company’s lawyer, Perry Herzfeld SC, argued a blue-banded bee Dreaming story that influenced the government’s decision to protect the area was not raised until two years after the initial application for a section 10 order was made. In a statement, the company said it anticipated the current environment minister, Murray Watt, “will be required to redetermine the application for a Section 10 Declaration, having regard to the relevant findings made by Justice Stellios in the judgment”. “Today’s federal court judgment is a significant and welcome step forward for the McPhillamys Gold Project,” managing director Jim Beyer said. “The judgment finding that the Section 10 Declaration is legally invalid vindicates the position we have held since the Declaration was made in August 2024, and we are extremely pleased the Court has agreed.” Watt said the government respected the court’s decision. “I note the judge specifically made the point that his decision did not concern the merits of the minister’s decision. Instead, the court’s decision was based on an error in the process used to grant the declaration,” he said. He said the government was carefully considering the judgment and taking advice on next steps. “We understand this outcome will matter deeply to the Wiradyuri Elders who brought the application, as well as to the company and its workforce, and to the Blayney community. We’ll work through it as quickly as possible.” Regis Resources said because any process to redetermine the protection order application could be protracted and “or for the outcome not to be in Regis’ favour”, the company was still pursing an alternative approach to the development. The company said that plan would involve co-disposal of filtered processed ore and waste rock into a single facility – referred to as an Integrated Waste Landform – “and entirely avoids the area impacted by the declaration”. “After considerable delay and uncertainty, and more than two years of time lost, we are eager to move forward,” Beyer said. “We look forward to engaging constructively with the Department through the redetermination process, and to advance one of Australia’s largest undeveloped gold projects – one with the potential to deliver lasting economic and social benefits to the Central New South Wales region and our broader stakeholder community.” New South Wales premier, Chris Minns, said in 2024 he was disappointed the protection order was issued and believed the federal minister’s decision was an error. Before the court’s decision on Wednesday morning, Minns said he wanted the mine to proceed. “I want that mine to go ahead,” he said. “I understand that that’s not the view of the federal government, but we need the investment. “There are more people in mining jobs in New South Wales today than there were when we were elected in March of 2023. We’re proud of that. It’s a really important part of our economy.” Watt said the court’s findings were an example “how complex the current cultural heritage processes are for everyone involved”. “First Nations people, industry and State and Territory governments have been clear with us for some time that they feel the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Heritage Protection (ATSIHP) Act doesn’t give enough certainty,” he said. “We remain committed to working alongside them on a better system.” The Wiradyuri Traditional Owners Central West Aboriginal Corporation (WTOCWAC), which supported the heritage protection order application, said while it was disappointed by the court’s decision, it respected the judicial process. A spokesperson said the corporation would review the judgment “and its implications for Wiradyuri people, our cultural heritage, and the ongoing protection of Country”. “This case has always been about protecting places of profound cultural and spiritual significance to Wiradyuri people,” they said. “The areas covered by the protection declaration, including the headwaters of the Belubula River, remain deeply important to our community and to the continuation of cultural knowledge, practices, and responsibilities that have been maintained for countless generations. “The court’s decision does not diminish the cultural significance of these places, nor does it alter our obligation to speak for and care for Country.” with AAP

title: Ukraine is littered with landmines on a scale last seen in Vietnam. How can they be removed?
summary: Faced with deadlier threats, demining groups are coming up with new ways of working using drones and AI
text: Crouched over on her hands and knees in a field of weeds, Olena Kabanova is digging into the ground. With a shovel and a steady hand, the 58-year-old digs out a neat square around the spot where a mine detector has sensed a suspicious object. Four years ago, this field in eastern Ukraine was occupied by Russian soldiers. Now back under Ukrainian control, it is littered with landmines. Civilians such as Kabanova are trying to make the land usable again. Landmines are a scourge of conflict zones. Littered across contested territory, they leave land unusable for years after a war has ended. Removing them is an expensive and dangerous job. And the use of long-range drones in Ukraine, which is often described as the most mine-contaminated country in the world, is increasing the scale of the problem. “What we’re now seeing is the massive increase in the use of drone-delivered munitions,” says Paul Heslop, senior mine action adviser for the United Nations in Ukraine. “What already was a very high-intensity battle area is now potentially, through the use of drones on both sides, becoming a much wider area of contamination and a scale that we haven’t seen since the Americans were dropping cluster munitions on the Ho Chi Minh trail.” The task of clearing landmines from Ukraine is replete with challenges. Drone and missile attacks make working outdoors unsafe; humanitarian workers are sometimes directly targeted. And newer, deadlier threats are also appearing. They include the POM-3, a small cylindrical mine used by Russian forces that could be mistaken for an abandoned vacuum flask. It is detonated by the vibrations of approaching footsteps. POM-3 mines mean there are “specific villages that we just completely avoid”, says Anda Riza, a unit commander of the Halo Trust, the largest international humanitarian demining organisation in Ukraine, which employs Kabanova in the field in Kharkiv. The types of landmines are “constantly developing and evolving”, says Valeriia Shumska, Riza’s colleague. But the technological innovation that is emerging from the conflict is also helping deminers to come up with new ways of working, which they hope are quicker and safer than the traditional hands-and-knees approach. The advances are being supported by the $1.5bn funding that has poured into Ukraine’s demining sector since the start of the full-scale invasion. Take Kabanova’s job. Digging out a patch of land could take up to 45 minutes. But a new machine can do it in five. Called the DMR-7, it is a small, tank-like vehicle fitted with a hosepipe that shoots out jet flows of compressed air. The tank is operated by a human using a remote controller who stands at a safe distance away. The operator manoeuvres the tank into place and then, with a loud mechanical whirring and plumes of dirt billowing skywards, the DMR-7 uses the force of compressed air to blast away a small patch of soil. It is a bulky, expensive alternative to a shovel, but it’s one that deminers hope can make one of the most dangerous parts of the demining process quicker and safer. The DMR-7 is just one of a host of new pieces of kit that the Halo Trust is experimenting with in Ukraine. Other technologies include AI-powered image analysis, ground-penetrating radar and devices that can detect explosive material, not just metal. Just as drones have transformed the battlefield, they have also created new opportunities for humanitarians. Before 2022, much of Halo’s surveillance work – looking for signs of explosives – was done with binoculars and maps. Now it is done with drones, and satellite imagery, which can be analysed with the help of AI. But war has also led to innovations in anti-drone technology. Drone jamming systems, used by both Russian and Ukrainian forces, can interfere with humanitarian work. Halo has lost several drones to jamming and spoofing attacks. And the advances in new technology are not spread equally between providers. In a field adjacent to one that Kabanova is working in, staff from the state emergency services are also clearing mines. Under the glare of the late summer sun, Mykyta Shulzhenko, the head of the mechanised demining unit, says his colleagues have started using drones for surveillance. But they are not yet able to use AI to analyse the drone-captured imagery. “I really hope this kind of technology will be implemented soon in our work,” he says. The Halo Trust alone spent nearly £50m in Ukraine in the year to 31 March 2025, dwarfing the state’s annual budget of £28.6m for a programme to clear agricultural land of mines and unexploded ordnance. And there are dozens of other demining organisations with overlapping responsibilities and approaches. Responsibility for the sector is split across multiple government agencies. Attempts to reform the country’s mine action law to bring it in line with international standards have faltered. Ihor Bezkaravainyi, a deputy economy minister who leads the country’s work on demining, wants to streamline the policymaking process to create one cabinet-level office to oversee the whole sector. But progress has been slow. Asked why, he offers a weary shrug: “Because, people.” “When we’re talking about a new law, it will mean that some government bodies will lose responsibility, and, they think, power,” Bezkaravainyi says. One person who has worked in Ukraine’s demining sector puts it more bluntly: “The biggest barrier to demining Ukraine is the government of Ukraine.” Bezkaravainyi says: “When we’re talking about an ordinary situation with mine action … the conflict has ended, and the government does not exist … in Ukraine, it’s the opposite situation.” That leads to a host of regulatory and bureaucratic barriers. For example, deminers are often prevented from using vehicles that are driven directly by a person, with health and safety standards requiring that the vehicles are operated remotely. Riza says: “We know for a fact that doing it remotely is much slower than having a person in the cab. That continues to be our biggest challenge.” Heslop argues that the Ukrainian authorities are overly broad in their categorisation of land as being contaminated by mines, an approach that risks wasting time and money on clearing land that wasn’t dangerous in the first place. “Just because it was occupied by the Russians doesn’t necessarily mean it was contaminated,” he says. “Land is only contaminated if it’s got fucking explosives in it.” But deminers across the sector agree that technological advances will accelerate their ability to release Ukraine’s richly fertile land for civilian use at a much faster rate than has been possible in the past. “This is the cutting edge of technology,” says Heslop. “This is where the humanitarian mine action sector is going through the biggest pivot in the last 30 years.” Additional research by Illia Dyadik and Artem Mazhulin • This article was amended on 14 October 2026. Paul Heslop is senior mine action adviser for the United Nations in Ukraine, not programme manager for mine action at the UN Development Programme in Ukraine as an earlier version said.
