title: British and Irish governments ‘should negotiate paramilitary disbandment in Northern Ireland’
summary: Report finds ‘window of opportunity’ for formal process involving loyalist and republican groups
text: The British and Irish governments should engage with paramilitary groups in Northern Ireland to negotiate their disbandment, according to a report. A “window of opportunity” exists to establish a formal transition mechanism for loyalist and republican groups, provided certain conditions are met, it said. The Independent Report on Paramilitary Group Transition to Disbandment, commissioned by both governments and published on Tuesday, said groups should not receive financial rewards for engaging in the process. Fleur Ravensbergen, a Dutch conflict resolution expert who authored the report, said in Belfast: “I have concluded that there is sufficient merit in and support for a formal process of paramilitary group transition.” Ravensbergen said she found “significant willingness to engage” among paramilitaries during a year-long scoping exercise. She added: “There was limited support for the term ‘disbandment’ as the endpoint of a transition process. However, objections to disbandment appeared to be less about what transition should achieve and more about the wording.” Paramilitary groups were expected to fade after the 1998 Good Friday agreement, but some endured and evolved into lucrative enterprises involved in drug dealing, extortion and coercive control. Agreeing a transition process was more important than the terminology used to describe disbandment, said Ravensbergen, a lecturer in conflict resolution and governance at the University of Amsterdam. She said: “I believe that the risks of the persistence of paramilitary structures, continued drift and unmanaged fragmentation outweigh the risks associated with attempting a structured and time-bound transition process. Inaction is not a neutral option. My consultations suggest that a window of opportunity exists to pursue further progress, but that this may weaken over time.” Chris Bryant, the Northern Ireland secretary, thanked Ravensbergen and said the government was committed to ending paramilitarism. Bryant said: “While these groups may pose as protectors of their communities, they are largely engaged in criminality including drug dealing, extortion and intimidation, blighting the very communities they perversely claim to protect. Their continued influence is a stain on our collective conscience.” He said the government would consider the report and liaise with authorities in Dublin before responding to the proposed transition mechanism. He added: “It is evident from the report that the implementation of any process will face challenges and will need the support from across the political community in Northern Ireland.” Naomi Long, Northern Ireland’s justice minister and a member of the Alliance party, criticised Ravensbergen’s appointment as an interlocutor last year, saying engagement with paramilitaries and criminal gangs risked giving them a veneer of legitimacy. Long said at the time: “The idea that paramilitary groups can transition into law-abiding entities has long since moved beyond the point of credibility. They cannot continue to be treated as if they are genuinely committed to reform – that moment passed long ago.” The report did not identify individuals or specific organisations because discussions were held on a confidential basis. It said: “The nature, extent and impact of paramilitary influence vary considerably between paramilitary groups, communities and geographical areas. However, it is clear that residual paramilitary structures continue to cause harm in some communities.” Ravensbergen said a transition mechanism would need credible monitoring and verification of progress and robust law enforcement. She declined to comment on the recent standoff between the Orange Order and nationalist residents at Garvaghy Road in Portadown, saying it was outside the report’s remit. There is speculation that renewed tension over the Drumcree parade may boost paramilitary recruitment.

title: Texas man run over by ICE has never met the person agents were allegedly chasing
summary: Miguel Parra-Hernandez suffers from serious hip and leg injuries in Houston and remains in ICE custody, according to his representatives
text: A Texas man whose leg was broken in multiple places after being struck by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) vehicle during a weekend traffic stop has never met the person the federal agents were allegedly pursuing, according to his representatives. Miguel Parra-Hernandez, 48, suffered serious injuries including a shattered ankle and hip when he was run over in Houston, Texas, on Saturday by an SUV driven by an officer chasing two men who ran from a pickup truck. ICE, according to multiple media reports, said it was in pursuit of another man, Jose Mendoza-Cervantes, during an early-morning operation and attempted a vehicle stop before the occupants ran away. It said Parra-Hernandez was not its target – but he ran in front of the ICE vehicle and was struck. Video of the incident aired by ABC News affiliate KTRK, however, shows a dark-colored, unmarked SUV following Parra-Hernandez and veering towards him as he ran across empty spaces in the shopping center parking lot in Harris county, whose seat is Houston. Parra-Hernandez’s attorney, Kim Bruno, and Cesar Espinosa, executive director of the immigrant advocacy group FIEL Houston, told reporters at a news conference on Monday that Parra-Hernandez remained in ICE custody and faced more surgery as well as many weeks of recovery. Espinosa said Parra-Hernandez was hit “in a violent and brutal fashion”. Bruno said he told her that he fled because he did not know who was in the dark-colored vehicle. Neither he nor the other person in the car, whom he had picked up for work, knew Mendoza-Cervantes, she said. The ICE vehicle, she added, was not using a siren or displaying flashing lights. Earlier in October, ICE adopted new rules for traffic stops, including ensuring that vehicles are equipped with lights and sirens to let the public know they are law enforcement vehicles, although it did not mandate their use. The guidelines, in a memo written by Marcos Charles, executive associate director of ICE, and obtained by the Associated Press, state that ICE officers are no longer permitted to chase vehicles that refuse to stop. The memo came after a series of violent and fatal confrontations involving federal immigration officers over the summer. Espinosa said he and Bruno were able to meet briefly with Parra-Hernandez at the hospital on Monday morning. But their visit ended after about 15 minutes when ICE agents entered the room and began recording their conversation, and they were made to leave. “To add insult to injury, Mr Miguel is in the custody of the ICE agents who ran him down,” Espinosa said, as reported by NBC News. “This is so disheartening and so angering that Miguel has to face the people that brutally attacked them every single day, 24 hours a day.” The Guardian has contacted ICE for comment. Espinosa said Parra-Hernandez sustained hip and leg injuries, including a shattered ankle. Doctors have said he cannot put weight on his leg for at least six weeks, and Parra must wait for swelling to recede before reconstructive surgery can take place, Espinosa said. Parra was struck at about 7.30am on Saturday. Witnesses said he remained on the ground for at least seven minutes after he was struck. Bruno said Parra-Hernandez told her that the other person in the car was not Mendoza-Cervantes, who ICE has identified as an illegal immigrant with multiple previous arrests and a judicially issued final order of removal from the US. She said Parra-Hernandez had lived in the US for 34 years, having arrived at age 14, and has no criminal record. The Harris county district attorney, Sean Teare, said on Monday his office was investigating the Parra-Hernandez case. The Harris county sheriff’s office said in a statement that it was called by ICE after the crash, which occurred as the agency has been met with nationwide criticism throughout Donald Trump’s second presidency for its aggressive arrest, detention and deportation tactics. Footage from Saturday’s case appeared to show an ICE agent entering the pickup truck Parra was in and driving it into the parking lot, before driving off in an unmarked vehicle. Maj Anthony McConnell told the Texas news outlet KTRK that ICE personnel moved the truck before his officers arrived.

title: Chip stocks slide after Broadcom boss likens AI investing to ‘casino’
summary: Asian markets fall and Samsung shares tumble after its Chinese rival CXMT claims strong progress
text: Shares in semiconductor companies fell on Tuesday after the boss of Broadcom compared many AI investors to “casino” gamblers, and the Chinese memory chip maker CXMT said it had made good progress on a new chip architecture. South Korea’s benchmark Kospi index tumbled 6.25% as investors dumped chip stocks, while other Asian markets were also lower. Japan’s Nikkei fell 1.8% and the Taiwan exchange lost almost 2%, with the country’s chip maker TSMC down by a similar amount. Samsung Electronics shares dropped 7.4% on the South Korean exchange, while the memory chip maker SK Hynix was down 10%. In Japan, the chip equipment maker Tokyo Electron fell 7.15%, while SoftBank Group, an OpenAI investor, lost 8.5%. On Wall Street the tech-heavy Nasdaq fell more than 100 points, or 0.35%, to 30,556 after the open. Micron Technology slid 4.8%, Advanced Micro Devices dropped 1.4%, while Nvidia lost 0.8% and Broadcom slipped 0.2%. However, the Dow Jones industrial average, which tracks 30 large US companies, rose nearly 0.4% in early trading, while the FTSE 100 index in London hit a three-week high on the back of gains in ‌financial stocks, retreating oil prices and easing bond yields. The UK’s leading share index rose 0.73% to 10,762. Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, dropped 1.2% to $105.36 a barrel. AI shares have been on a rollercoaster in recent months amid concerns that companies are spending eye-watering amounts on AI infrastructure, funded by debt. The latest sell-off came after CXMT said it had made good progress on new Dram architecture that would boost memory density, with plans for a product rollout. Investors are worried that the company could challenge Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron, the world’s biggest memory chip makers. CXMT, which had an impressive debut on the Shanghai stock market in late July, makes Dram chips, which store the data that other AI chips draw on for their calculations. “The rout in chip stocks seems set to continue thanks once again to news from China,” said Chris Beauchamp, the chief market analyst at the investing and trading platform IG. “CXMT’s new developments remind investors of the huge competition in the sector. “While great for customers who can enjoy the white heat of technological improvement and get falling margins into the bargain, it is dangerous for high-flying tech stocks who have promised so much, and on whom the entire stock market rally seems to rest.” Hock Tan, the chief executive of the US chip maker Broadcom, said the AI boom had attracted investors who did not really understand what they were betting on. “A lot of investors have no clue what they are investing in,” he said at a conference in Singapore, in comments reported by Bloomberg. They “set very extreme expectations only to find out that it’s almost like they are in a casino”. AI companies such as the ChatGPT maker OpenAI are still lossmaking. Tan said OpenAI’s annualised revenues of $50bn (£38bn) at the end of September suggested a viable business model but offered little guarantee on long-term profitability. “For now it’s still losing money because they’re spending a lot on training,” Tan said. “So frankly, it doesn’t tell anything at this point except that there is a lot of potential revenue growth out of providing frontier generative AI models.” He noted that a sizeable portion of AI labs’ enterprise revenue came from pilot projects. “When you are a kid you go to a video arcade, you play,” he said. “Your parents give you $10 of tokens, you finish it in 10 minutes and you haven’t learned anything.”

title: You have politics questions. We answer them.
Britons travelling to EU countries told not to apply for delayed Etias visa waiver
summary: Abta advice comes as more than more than 150 websites offer service of securing entry to Schengen zone
text: Britons travelling to EU countries have been told not to apply for an Etias visa waiver, with more than 150 websites touting the service despite its introduction being delayed. Non-EU citizens, including UK travellers and those from other visa-exempt countries including the US, Australia and Canada, will soon need to pay €20 (£17) for an electronic waiver to enter the Schengen zone under the European travel information and authorisation system (Etias). The system was scheduled to be come into effect soon after the rollout of the EU’s parallel border scheme, the entry-exit system (EES). Both, however, have been repeatedly postponed, and the persistent problems after the introduction of EES, including the software at French entry points, have meant Etias remains suspended. The director of public affairs at the travel association Abta, Luke Petherbridge, said: “While Etias was due to come into force this year, it is now back on hold. Abta believes it shouldn’t be brought in until EES is fully operational and working properly. “This is particularly important when you consider that European authorities believe over 150 websites offering Etias already exist, but there is only one official site people should apply through when live.” Abta research found awareness was growing of the impending border requirements – up from 41% in 2024 to 56% now. The price to apply has risen from €7 to €20 – over-70s and under-18s do not need to pay – but no date has been set for launch. The pan-European border agency, Frontex, warned about the existence of scam websites long before Etias was to have been introduced. Commercial sites can legitimately apply for the waivers on behalf of clients, but the agency said the risk posed by third parties ranged from data protection and identity theft to extortionate fees. It found that some unofficial websites were also providing inaccurate information over who needed an Etias while mimicking the layout of the official website and using convincing domain names. “If you use one of these sites, not only will you lose money, you are also putting your personal data at risk as well,” Petherbridge said. “What I can’t stress is enough that you can’t – and shouldn’t - apply for an Etias now.” EES is in full operation, but border authorities have been told the EU will not enforce penalties if they continue to suspend the system at entry points when queues escalate. That flexibility has meant the worst fears of the travel industry have largely been avoided this summer. Abta surveys found only 46% of visitors to Europe reporting having full checks, with half of those people waiting less than 30 minutes, and only 13% queuing for an hour. * Gwyn Topham attended Abta’s convention in Madeira. His travel was provided by Abta

title: Russia did try to interfere in Brexit referendum, head of MI5 confirms
summary: Ken McCallum says Kremlin attempted to influence vote through social media and TV reports but had little impact
text: Russia did try to interfere in the Brexit referendum through social media and television reports, the head of MI5 said on Tuesday, but he added that did not mean the Kremlin had any impact on the result. Ken McCallum endorsed comments by Andy Burnham, who raised the issue over the past two days, though he said continuing to debate it risked giving the Kremlin a needless propaganda victory. During an annual threat update, the head of Britain’s domestic intelligence agency said the Russian-owned English-language broadcasters RT and Sputnik “came in pretty strongly around the time of the referendum” with biased anti-migration and anti-EU reports. He said there had also been “a second line of interference attempted through [internet] trolls”: an unspecified number of fake social media accounts, operating largely on X, that had sought to influence the result. Neither tactic was particularly sophisticated or successful, the spy chief said. There was a big difference between “what may have been attempted and what actually resulted”. Both interference attempts have been previously cited in studies released in the years after the Brexit vote. The digital campaign group 89up said RT and Sputnik had published 261 mostly misleading articles highlighting immigration and other anti-EU issues that achieved 134m potential page impressions. Other studies have reported on a “troll army” of state-linked Russian accounts tweeting about the referendum in the run-up to the vote, though estimates of numbers active have varied wildly from 54 to 150,000. Burnham had first returned to the issue on Sunday, during a podcast interview, though at first it was unclear whether the prime minister had been given new intelligence on a topic that had largely been considered forgotten. “I asked the question coming to Downing Street: ‘Was there interference in the 2016 referendum from Russia?’ And I’ve had the clear answer that yes, there was,” said the prime minister, implying he had a discussion or briefing on the issue. A day later, however, he backed off when challenged by the Conservatives on whether this meant he regarded the Brexit vote as illegitimate, and he did not supply any additional information in the Commons. On Tuesday Downing Street said it had been confirmed that Russia interfered in the 2019 general election and it was “inconceivable that they didn’t in 2016”. But the prime minister’s spokesperson added: “We don’t believe it was successful in the British referendum in 2016.” McCallum said it would be to Russia’s benefit if the issue was the subject of controversy for several more days. “It is up to us how far we allow our adversaries to divide us,” he said. Continued attention gave the impression that Kremlin disinformation attempts were more successful than they actually were, the MI5 chief added. “I’m a little bit worried that if we all stay in this debate for another few days, the Russian trolls who didn’t appear to do all that much at various points over the years, they’ll be delighted they are front-page news once again despite the comparative unimpressedness of what they do at all points along the journey,” he said.

title: Did Ukrainian strikes on Russian datacentres reduce online disinformation?
summary: While some viral online graphs suggest less bot activity, Zelenskyy’s claims of improved social media discourse do not entirely pass muster
text: Over the weekend, Ukraine carried out at least three airstrikes on datacentres belonging to the Russian search engine company Yandex. Reports suggest at least two of these datacentres took significant damage, with Telegram footage appearing to show one on fire. Yandex acknowledged the strikes, and Russian media reported that several websites appeared affected by the downed datacentres. On Monday, Volodymyr Zelenskyy suggested the strikes had dampened Russia’s massive disinformation operation, saying: “It suddenly became a little easier to breathe on many social platforms. There was less hate, less division and fewer provocations.” It is a commendable hope, but experts say the Ukrainian president may have overstated his case. Did Ukraine’s strikes lead to a decline in Russian disinformation? Probably not. While a few graphs went viral on social media suggesting there had been a big decline in activity from Yandex bots, those graphs are unrelated to Russian disinformation. “Our platforms are still monitoring Russian social networks across the world and there is no discernible change in their posting patterns,” said Amil Khan, the chief executive of Valent, a tech startup that tracks disinformation. Khan and his team track about 40 disinformation networks around the world, from the UK to Australia to Syria, and monitor what narratives they put out and how publics respond to them. They have seen no drop in the volume of posts from these networks, saying: “Yandex datacentres have no practical connection to social media bot farms.” So what exactly did happen? Yandex is a search engine which also hosts websites and bots. Data from Cloudflare, which monitors worldwide internet traffic, shows a marked decline in activity from bots associated with the Yandex network on 8 October and 11 October, corresponding to the dates of two of the strikes. The independent Russian news outlet Meduza reports that a number of websites in Russia are down: major banks, retailers, sports apps and Yandex’s services such as Yandex Go and Yandex Eats. It suggests the damage took out a large part of Yandex’s operation and could take months to fully repair. Some online commentators have mistaken the Cloudflare data to mean that the decline in bot activity has led to a major drop in disinformation on social media. But this is not what experts have noticed. What are these different kinds of bots? “The term ‘bot’ can mean many different things,” said Michał ‘Rysiek’ Woźniak, an internet infrastructure expert. “When Cloudflare data shows a precipitous drop in ‘bot’ traffic, that does not mean ‘automated social media troll accounts’, it means ‘software that makes automated web requests on a large scale.’” What Cloudflare picked up was a decline in activity from Yandex’s web crawlers. These are used by search engines to index websites and help users to find them, said Khan. State-sponsored disinformation networks – the kind of “bots” a lot of people misinterpreted this as – could still be affected by the strikes, said Woźniak. “But those effects are going to be much more indirect.” Those networks are far more distributed, and more resilient, said Ned Mendez, the head of research at Alliance4Europe. “Platforms will routinely flag traffic from datacentres as likely automated, so serious bot operations run more through distributed methods, such as residential connections and phone farms, that airstrikes can’t really knock out.” So how could Ukraine disrupt Russian disinformation in Europe? “We can’t simply bomb the bots out of existence, however appealing that might sound,” said Mendez. “They aren’t really a single set of buildings that can be switched off.” Khan said the Ukrainians could consider taking action against companies such as the Internet Research Agency, Yevgeny Prigozhin’s Wagner-linked troll farm that was engaged in influence operations until 2023. But another tactic could be to work with Europe to disrupt the supply chain and recruitment pipeline of private sector contractors used by the Kremlin. Another tactic could be to pressure big social media companies to moderate disinformation on their platforms. Khan’s team has successfully worked with Meta to tamp down on inflammatory content in Sudan. But, said Khan, the Trump administration would probably push back on this, hard. “I can see why blowing up datacentres is an easier option.”

title: ‘Shocking and sobering’: UK bird populations fall to lowest level on record
summary: Nearly half of species are in decline, with farmland birds and seabirds the worst hit, conservation bodies say
text: Wild bird populations in the UK have fallen to their lowest level since records began, figures show, with nearly half of species in decline. Figures produced by leading nature conservation bodies for the government show that average populations across 132 native breeding species fell by 19% between 1970 and 2025, with farmland birds and seabirds the worst hit in recent years. Prof Richard Gregory, the head of monitoring at the RSPB, called the overall findings “shocking and sobering”. “Birds are indicators of the way we’re looking after the countryside and the world around us,” he said. “We’re losing the birds that people are so emotionally connected to and want to protect.” Average populations of turtle doves have fallen by more than half in five years, showing no sign of the bird recovering from the brink of extinction. Tree sparrows, wood warblers and capercaillie were among the birds with the next biggest average annual decreases between 2019 and 2024. Swifts, whose arrival for many marks the beginning of summer, have declined by about 25% in five years, an average of nearly 6% a year across the UK. Bullfinches fell at a similar rate nationally, and by an average of 11% a year in England. Of the 132 native breeding species tracked, 45% have declined over the past five years, while just 27% have increased. In England, 55% of monitored species have declined. Seabirds are the worst hit group, down by more than a fifth over the past five years. Dr Ailidh Barnes, who helps build the index at the British Trust for Ornithology, said avian flu had “decimated” species such as Arctic skuas and terns. The disease spread quickly, she said, because seabirds nested shoulder to shoulder, and each year a different species appeared to suffer. “There’s a lag of data collection and then data analysis, and now we’re actually seeing that effect coming through,” she said. Farmland bird populations have decreased by 63% since 1970 and 12% since 2020. Defra attributes the long-term decline to changes in farming since the 1950s, including the loss of mixed farming (crops and livestock), increased pesticide and fertiliser use, and the removal of hedgerows. Gregory said if the trend continued, the songs of farm birds such as skylarks and yellowhammers would become only “memories” of what the countryside used to be like. “It’s a familiar story of declining farmland [birds],” he added. “That’s not showing any upturn. We need to do more there to get nature-friendly farming right and help support farmers.” Despite the general decline, some populations are booming. Red kite populations have risen by 48% since 2019, and firecrests are up 300% over the same period. Gregory also highlighted the number of cranes “really coming back from extinction in the UK”, rising to 87 pairs nationally. Gregory said these examples proved concerted efforts to save species worked. “We know the main drivers of change and we can bring about recovery, but we need to massively scale up our conservation intervention,” he said. “We need more funding to support these conservation measures and they need to be at a larger spatial scale.” A Defra spokesperson said: “We are committed to the recovery and protection of our native birds. There are multiple pressures on wild bird populations, including avian flu. We are acting to protect them, from supporting farmers to manage their land in a way that benefits farmland birds, to working with fishers to prevent the accidental catch of seabirds.”

title: Companies rushed in on AI. Now some are pulling back
summary: Rapid AI adoption left workers cleaning up a flood of errors and low-quality work
text: Employers around the globe are grappling with the fallout from rushing to adopt fast-changing artificial intelligence tools. Meta has scaled back plans to axe staff and use more AI agents after the company found employees were spending more and more time cleaning up technical and security errors, Reuters reported. And after thinning its workforce, especially middle managers, in a 2023 efficiency push, the company is expanding its managerial ranks again, LinkedIn posts from workers show. At Microsoft, which rolled out AI widely internally, executive vice-president Ryan Roslansky recently publicly lamented the prevalence of AI slop in his day-to-day work. After receiving “what was clearly an AI-generated doc” from a co-worker, he used his AI to summarize it and came away with no new thinking about the idea, he said. He warned his followers against falling into this potential “doom loop”, where AI does the reading and writing and leaves behind an “ocean of sameness”. Meanwhile, Walmart store and warehouse employees are being plagued by unreasonable expectations, errors and false alerts from AI tools that assign tasks, schedules and monitor performance, Business Insider reported. Employers are navigating a flood of errors and low-quality work that are sapping employee time, raising privacy and security risks and pushing up costs. Now, some businesses that started off fast and furious on AI are pumping the brakes, implementing restrictions where experimentation was once encouraged, bringing back experienced workers and upping training efforts. C-suite leaders say when it comes to AI, there’s a sense that “we’re driving the truck and building it at the same time, and that’s a problem,” said Johnny C Taylor Jr, president and CEO of the Society for Human Resource Management. “If we could all rewind … we would have introduced [this] in a more thoughtful, slow way.” Despite billions of dollars that firms around the globe have invested in AI over the past few years, major returns remain to be seen: 90% of executives say AI efforts have yet to translate to productivity gains at their companies, according to an Atlanta Federal Reserve working paper. And an Ernst & Young survey published last month found that 36% of senior AI executives at companies with at least $1bn in annual revenue reported an AI incident that led to issues including data loss, financial damage, brand damage or operational disruptions. Firms from Microsoft to McKinsey are limiting usage for employees, as the flood of new tools and rapacious consumption weighs on bottom lines. Others, such as Palantir, Booz Allen Hamilton and Nvidia, are restricting employee use over growing concerns about the security of their organizations’ data with AI companies, Reuters reported. Microsoft and Walmart declined to comment. Meta, Palantir, Nvidia and Booz Allen Hamilton did not respond to requests for comment. “We initially treated AI like a traditional technology rollout: deploy the tools, provide training, drive adoption,” Kathleen Hogan, Microsoft’s chief strategy and transformation officer, said in a recent blogpost about the company’s AI adoption journey. “We learned that access and usage do not equal transformation.” Expertise gaps and errors AI remains a mixed bag for managers and employees alike: more than half of employees said they “aren’t getting the AI training they need”, while most managers said they were outskilled in AI by their staff, according to an Indeed survey published in July. Just 45% of managers said they felt “equipped to effectively lead AI natives”. Many workers feel “like they’re being asked to make use of these tools without any guidance about how they best could be deployed”, said Zack Mabel, director of research at the Georgetown University Center on Education and the Workforce. Meanwhile, managers are balancing orders to “roll this out, find productivity gains and don’t compromise on quality”, he added. Companies are trying to address these perceived gaps by moving away from one-off webinars for broad swaths of staff and toward “sustained, role-specific training”, Taylor said. Microsoft found that “adding agents to a broken process still leaves a broken process” and “speeding up one step just creates a longer queue at the next”, Hogan’s blogpost reads. The company found that focusing on employee training, particularly pairing up early-career engineers with more seasoned employees, boosted productivity. One barrier to bigger AI-induced gains is the technology’s tendency to produce “plausible-looking output” with weaknesses or mistakes that are not immediately apparent, explained Jessica Reif, assistant professor of management at the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania. “This makes it more likely that an error propagates through a workflow instead of being immediately corrected,” which can cause problems to snowball, said Reif. Meanwhile, AI’s limited ability to assess human workers is still limited, which is creating tension at some companies. At Walmart, frustration is mounting among some rank-and-file store employees over inconsistent and inaccurate AI tools, Business Insider reported. Employees described bots that set unreasonable standards for human workers while introducing a host of their own inefficiencies and errors. AI tools plotted nonsensical routes for fulfilment workers that made it harder to fill orders quickly, pumped out useless safety alerts and set unrealistic schedules that left store employees cutting corners to keep up. These bots assume that workers are “going to be perfect every single time”, one manager told Business Insider. “We’re not going to hold people to these impossible standards.” Walmart declined to comment. Rising risks Neil Elan, attorney at Stubbs Alderton & Markiles LLP, said he had observed “a growing gap” between how his corporate clients think AI is being used and how it is actually being used, which is creating issues with confidentiality, intellectual property, efficiency and employee conduct. It’s also creating headaches for companies when workers’ use of ChatGPT spills into public view. The night before Will Moye was set to face 3M in court over a 2020 gas explosion at a Houston manufacturing plant that killed three and damaged hundreds of homes and businesses, the attorney received a report from the company’s independent expert witness. Skimming on his iPad, Moye noticed telltale signs of AI: strange formatting and fonts and time stamps showing that 14,500 pages were assembled in a matter of hours. Moye suspected that the author, Josh Autenrieth of Knighthawk Engineering, lacked expertise and had relied on ChatGPT, despite billing 3M $90,000 for a report arguing the company was not liable. Autenrieth’s chat logs, which Moye requested and shared in court, show he prompted ChatGPT, “What am I looking at?” after uploading a picture of the gas detector at the heart of the case. The jury found that 3M had failed to properly inspect the gas detection system and ordered the company to pay $61.5m to 24 homeowners. Moye said after the verdict, the jury “expressed a profound disbelief” that the company would hire an expert who would make claims “without any foundation”. “[3M] were trying to reset the narrative,” Moye said. “And they hired an expert who’d never touched the machine.” A 3M spokesperson said that “after independently reviewing the facts and reaching his own conclusions”, Autenrieth “used AI as a tool in preparing his report”. Autenrieth’s legal counsel Janina Wojtkowski said ChatGPT didn’t produce his opinions or replace his “professional judgment” but assisted in formatting, structuring and drafting amid “severe deadline constraints”. Performance boost? Not so much As companies and workers muddle through the unknowns of early AI adoption, costs are still coming into focus, while broad productivity gains remain elusive. In a study published in May, University of Pittsburgh researchers concluded that productivity didn’t rise after companies invested in AI and cut staff. Although executives have been overwhelmingly optimistic about AI’s potential impacts for years, “management optimism does not effectively translate into … better performance,” the paper states. More than 112,000 job cut announcements in the US so far in 2026 have mentioned AI, making it a top reason for layoffs, according to Challenger, Gray & Christmas. Earlier this year, Meta paused its practice of tracking employees’ computer activity to train its AI, according to Reuters. Meta also recently told employees that their adoption and usage of AI tools would no longer be part of performance reviews, the Information reported. Meta did not respond to a request for comment. Mark Ma, University of Pittsburgh professor and researcher on the AI layoff study, said leaders are focused on short-term performance, “which is why they tried to rush ahead by investing in AI and laying off workers”. But companies’ share prices tend to dip after they announce AI-related layoffs, he noted, suggesting that “the stock market also does not think these will work out.” “A lot of these mistakes could have been avoided,” Ma said. “Now I feel some managers have learned their lesson.”

title: Farage denies Reform would let troops shoot small boats after Jenrick’s ‘lethal force’ claim
summary: Farage’s intervention comes as Reform chair Zia Yusuf criticises ‘everybody’ in former Tory government that included Jenrick and Suella Braverman
text: Nigel Farage has denied that a Reform UK government would authorise lethal force against small boat crossings in the Channel, hours after one of his MPs said the Royal Marines should be permitted to fire on the boats. Farage overruled Robert Jenrick, a Reform UK MP who defected from the Conservatives, who had told TalkTV that the party would deploy the marines to take boats back to France. In a day of party splits where a poll showed the party had fallen to third place behind the Conservatives, the Reform UK chair, Zia Yusuf, also suggested he would not trust Conservative defectors such as Jenrick – and criticised another Reform MP, Suella Braverman, for her suggestions that she could not be considered English because of her ethnicity. The initial row was sparked by Jenrick saying his was the only party prepared to use force against people crossing in small boats. “What we are going to do, and we’re the only political party that has the courage to say this, is deploy the Royal Marines into the Channel. If they need to use lethal force, then they’ll be able to do so,” he said. But speaking on LBC, Farage said he would not authorise routine use of force, that it would be used only if soldiers were fired at, and that Jenrick was being “utterly misconstrued”. “Anybody wearing British military uniform who gets fired at has the right to respond. That’s what he was saying,” he said. “Remember, in these camps, every week there are shootings, there are stabbings. “We are dealing here with very, very serious international criminal organisations, and what we’re saying is, we will, if we win the next election, pick these people up and take them back to France. “There is a possibility that initially that might be met with some force. If it is, force will be met with force. But I tell you something: within two weeks of boats being taken back to France, the boats will stop coming.” Jenrick had said that allowing the use of force would mean the problem would end “in just a few days”. He said using force was “obviously not what we want to see happen”, adding: “We want to see these individuals picked up off the boats in a sensible and reasonable way, and taken straight back to France.” The defence minister Luke Pollard called the comments “disgusting and illegal”, and said the armed forces were not allowed to accept “an illegal order”. “We do not shoot unarmed civilians. We do not take military action against civilians,” Pollard told Times Radio. “The idea of this is a soundbite designed by Reform to distract from their sleaze and their scandal … it’s abhorrent to military values, it’s abhorrent to British values. “I don’t think anyone should give this any truck. We can all see what this is: an attempt to distract from Reform’s internal woes.” Yusuf, who himself has previously promised that “lethal force” would be used to stop migrants on boats reaching Britain, also rowed back on the comments on Tuesday. But he said on BBC Breakfast that it would only be used “in extremely limited circumstances where it is necessary to protect innocent life”. “In the event there are people on those boats with weapons, with firearms, who think nothing of shedding innocent life, throwing people overboard, we need to be ready to respond.” But Yusuf also opened up new splits with Jenrick and Braverman – a former Conservative home secretary – in interviews on Tuesday. Asked if he still considered them to be “quislings” because they had been part of a Tory cabinet, as he had once posted on X, Yusuf told Sky News: “Everybody in that Conservative government – that did things that were not only damaging to the country, but were literally the opposite of the things that they promised to do – need to take responsibility for that. “I was looking on, as the Tories claimed they were going to cut immigration to the tens of thousands and then did the complete opposite. And I do think there is collective responsibility for that.” He said he did not agree with controversial comments made by Braverman that her south Asian heritage meant she was not English. “In my view Ashley Cole is the best English fullback in history, and I won’t take any other position. So in my view, Ashley Cole is English. The argument that he’s not English doesn’t hold water with me,” he said. “I do think it is important that we listen to people who are worried about some of the demographics in this country. I think that there are some legitimate arguments that they can make about that. But I will also say … whether it’s [Bukayo] Saka, Ashley Cole, Rio Ferdinand, Nasser Hussain, who I grew up watching when I went to the cricket, the idea that those people aren’t English is an alien concept to me. I would respectfully disagree with people, who make the opposite argument.” A new poll for the Times on Tuesday showed Reform had dropped to third place behind Labour and the Tories, in a boost for Kemi Badenoch’s party, which has its highest rating since she became Tory leader.

title: US transport secretary’s war on ‘woke’ could make roads even deadlier, experts warn
summary: Sean Duffy targets bike lanes and immigrant truck drivers while steering funds away from addressing lethal US roads
text: Barbara McCann may have been the first person to notice that the Federal Highway Administration had removed several safety policies from public view. McCann worked on road safety policy at the US Department of Transportation (USDOT) for more than a decade across multiple administrations, retiring in January 2025 just before Donald Trump’s second term started. After Sean Duffy, the president’s ally and former Fox news host, took the wheel at USDOT, she became increasingly worried as the secretary appeared unmotivated to address pedestrian safety and regularly bashed bike infrastructure. It was typical bullying behavior, she thought. “You pick someone who’s vulnerable and attack them,” McCann said. “They decided that bicyclists are vulnerable and that they could use that as a political wedge. It didn’t seem to have anything to do with actual safety.” In a country where traffic deaths far surpass its international counterparts, that could be deadly. Shortly after he was confirmed to the post, TV personality turned politician Duffy signed orders last year to end what department officials called “woke policies” from the Biden administration and ensure that “all USDOT policies, grants, loans, and actions are based on sound economic principles, positive cost-benefit analyses, and pro-economic growth priorities”. “Remember when Biden and Boot-edge-edge used YOUR MONEY for DEI bike lanes and climate change? THAT’S OVER,” Duffy posted on X in July, saying he had diverted $1.73bn in USDOT grants “away from Biden-era DEI pet projects” and toward roads, bridges and ports. Amid that push, the department and its sub-agencies have been scrubbing information about safety measures from government websites that officials had deemed effective, and focused on building policy aligned with a rightwing, anti-immigrant agenda instead of research. The department removed five suggestions from a “proven safety countermeasures” list by the Federal Highway Administration: bike lanes; road diets, which involves reducing car lanes, often to make space for a bike or bus lane; plus three speed management tools, including automated camera enforcement and variable speed limits. Webpages that provided information about pedestrian and bicyclist safety have also been deleted. Improving safety is listed in one order as a benefit USDOT “may include” in decision-making “to the extent practicable”. Duffy has vowed that his agency is “committed to making our roadways safer and bringing down the number of fatalities”. “We’re taking a closer look because the Trump Administration supports transportation systems that benefit Americans, including the nearly 80% who rely on cars to get where they need to go safely and efficiently,” a USDOT spokesperson wrote in a statement. But transportation safety experts who spoke with the Guardian, including one former USDOT official, are raising concerns that federal officials are ignoring decades of science-based evidence to put a car-obsessed Maga ideology in the driver’s seat, which could make getting around more dangerous for everyone. Roads in the US demonstrate an unwelcome kind of American exceptionalism: they are deadlier for the millions who use them every day than those in dozens of other high-income countries. Duffy highlighted the scale of the problem in his department’s 2026 safety strategy. “Despite encouraging trends over the past few years, we estimate that 36,640 people died in motor vehicle crashes in 2025”, Duffy wrote in a letter leading the document. “Millions more were seriously injured.” But experts say the actions he has taken aren’t in line with the evidence of what keeps roads safe. After Duffy’s “DEI bike lanes” remark, McCann checked FHWA’s website and saw that several “proven safety countermeasures” had been deleted (an internet archive maintains the previous list here). For McCann, the purge of science-backed strategies to address speeding – a key factor in nearly a third of fatal crashes in the US each year – was “just gobsmacking”. One of those tools to manage speed, automated speed cameras, capture the license plate of a vehicle exceeding a posted speed limit by a significant amount and mail a citation to the registered owner. A growing number of communities are installing the technology on their streets – often in school zones – because they work, as FHWA’s website previously said. Jessica Cicchino, a senior vice-president of behavior and infrastructure research at the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety, a non-profit research organization, said it was concerning that speed cameras, which are “really effective at bringing down serious injuries and fatalities”, are no longer promoted by federal authorities. “If you really believe as an agency that your job is to make safety a priority, then we need to have those resources that tell states and cities the best ways to reduce fatalities on the roadway,” Cicchino said. The number of people killed by drivers while walking and biking has risen sharply in recent years, even before Duffy took over the agency. Pedestrian killings jumped 72% between 2009 and 2024, while cyclist deaths increased 73% from 2010 to 2024, according to federal data Cicchino’s organization gathered from USDOT. But she noted another issue that is troubling researchers: instances of federal databases disappearing with little explanation as to why. That includes the Highway Safety Information System (HSIS), which is maintained by the FHWA and features complex data on traffic crashes and roadway characteristics in several states. It was taken down last year and is still missing. In a statement provided to the Guardian, FHWA said the website hosting HSIS data “was down last year for a few months – while we updated guidebooks”, but remained “available upon request”. When the Guardian asked officials to share strategies aimed at fulfilling USDOT’s stated mission to build the safest transportation system in the world, a spokesperson pointed to Duffy’s “freedom to drive” initiative. The plan, launched in April, aims to reduce traffic congestion by “maximizing roadway capacities”. Duffy sent a letter to state governors calling on them to enact his plan. *** Duffy’s most publicized road-related campaign at USDOT is a crackdown on foreign-born truck drivers. Earlier this year, the department issued a new rule that disqualifies truck drivers without US citizenship or permanent residency from getting or renewing their commercial driver’s licenses (CDLs). The goal, according to Duffy, is to make the licensing process more stringent and subject to federal immigration enforcement to prevent alleged “dangerous foreign drivers” from operating large trucks on US roads. Critics say the effort has racist undertones and is guided by the Trump administration’s nationwide effort to target immigrants, not by data-based safety goals. “While DOT premised its rule on safety, its own data indicated that the CDL holders excluded by the rule (immigrant drivers) were involved in fatal collisions at a lower rate than CDL holders who are not excluded, meaning the rule would worsen, and not improve, safety,” the AFL-CIO, the largest federation of labor unions in the US, wrote in a March letter to Congress. To justify Duffy’s new road rules, department officials cited 17 fatal crashes in 2025 they claim were “caused by actions of non-domiciled CDL holders whose fitness could not be ensured”. Those collisions resulted in 30 deaths, 0.08% of USDOT’s estimated road deaths last year. “I think it’s just par for the course in looking at immigrants as a bogeyman”, said Jesus Barajas, an associate professor in the environmental science and policy department at University of California, Davis. Barajas studies transportation equity and mobility justice and said USDOT’s vehement rejection of “equity” as a factor in safety planning puts already vulnerable pedestrians and cyclists at greater risk. “We know that the safety problem is a problem of equity because it tends to be communities of color and low-income communities that are most affected,” he said. “When you’re shifting your investment dollars into prioritizing vehicles and eliminating barriers [so] that cars go faster, now you’re prioritizing only the vehicles at the expense of other people on the roadways.” McCann says she sees similarities in how Duffy’s USDOT is targeting both immigrant truck drivers and bike lanes, which she views as another way for the Trump administration “to express their dominance over vulnerable populations”. “That’s just a classic feature of the autocratic playbook,” she said. “They pick scapegoats and go after them. That has absolutely nothing to do with safety.” The downstream effects of Duffy’s hampering of speed management and bike and pedestrian safety infrastructure will come down to states and local governments, McCann said, since they actually build and maintain those projects. “The question is whether the states go along with this and cancel projects and submit to this ideology, or whether they keep following the science and the data and the facts,” she said. The impact is felt beyond the US. This July, the United Nations general assembly adopted a declaration that “preventable deaths and serious injuries are not an acceptable cost of mobility”. The resolution called on member nations to recommit to a goal of halving global road deaths by 2030 and work “to provide access to safe, affordable, accessible and sustainable transport systems for all”. The vote was 162-1, with the lone opposition from the US, whose delegate blasted the resolution as “a backdoor vehicle to enforce global climate pacts and top-down environmental restrictions on freedom of mobility”. *** Duffy has been trotting out figures to justify his approach. The department claims that traffic deaths “fell to record lows in 2025”, though the agency’s own historical data contradicts that. USDOT estimated 36,640 people were killed in collisions last year. That’s the fewest deaths since 2019, but far from the lowest number on record. Looking at the figures from 2010 to 2025, fatalities have increased 11%. Officials also touted the “second-lowest traffic fatality rate in recorded history at 1.10 fatalities per 100m vehicle miles traveled”. David Zipper, a transportation scholar, believes USDOT is counting the wrong way, arguing that deaths per capita (100,000 residents) provides the full scope of risk to the public. That metric also places the US death rate far higher than many peer nations. He noted another gap in the administration’s safety strategy: vehicles are getting larger and killing more people. Duffy’s safety roadmap includes broad goals of making vehicles safer by integrating new technology and supporting the “safe deployment” of autonomous vehicles, but does not mention any plans to look at regulating vehicle size. The USDOT under Duffy has not noted successful examples of the countermeasures it removed for alleged further review. Hoboken, a New Jersey city with about 60,000 residents, has not had a single person die in a crash on its streets in more than nine years after adding bike lanes, reducing space for cars and lowering speed limits on their local streets. And New York City last year marked the lowest death toll since it began keeping records in 1910, citing the city’s “dramatic expansion of protected bike lanes and newly pedestrianized space”, along with automated speed cameras, improved bus transit and focused police enforcement. In contrast, Duffy’s Department of Transportation has limited funding for speed camera and pedestrian safety projects and attacked the previous administration for its support of bike infrastructure, which the secretary dismissed as “crap” and “DEI pet projects” from Pete Buttigieg, his predecessor. “Biden and Buttigieg failed to thoroughly investigate the negative impact of bike lanes in their rush to achieve their radical social and climate goals,” a department spokesperson said in a statement, claiming roads redesigned to add bike lanes were “negatively impacting small businesses by eliminating parking, disproportionately hurting the elderly or disabled, and disrupting traffic flow”. That highlights the tradeoff at the core of the conflict over public roads: making them safer requires building them in a way that compels drivers to slow down. Duffy’s actions suggest it is not a tradeoff his department is willing to face. “What Duffy really reflects is this Maga idea of freedom,” said Zipper. “[It’s] all about: ‘Don’t tell me what to do. Whatever I want to do in my car, however I want to drive it or whatever kind of car I want to drive, the government and nobody else can get in the way of it.’”

title: The RBA keeps hiking interest rates – but are the rate rises actually working?
summary: With the cash rate at a 15-year high, consumer confidence has tanked – while household spending is still growing
text: Interest rates have risen to 15-year highs and are pushing up mortgage default risks – but household spending is still growing. Economists say the surprising result shows this year’s four rate hikes have not yet fully hit the economy and may be less effective at fighting inflation than they used to be. If true, that could mean more interest rate rises are on the way. So are interest rate hikes working? What is the RBA trying to achieve by increasing interest rates? The Reserve Bank has increased its key cash rate to cut household spending and discourage businesses and workers from seeking higher prices and wages. It aims to bring inflation back under 3%. Financial institutions now face higher funding costs and have responded by lifting the rates they charge for home loans, business loans or bonds for big companies. But eight months on from the year’s first rate rise in February, spending is not going backwards. Economic activity has slowed, businesses are less efficient and real wages are going backwards compared with a year ago as inflation rises. But Australian household spending has accelerated, up nearly 7% compared with a year ago, according to Australian Bureau of Statistics estimates. Part of the increase in spending is from higher prices for essentials such as fuel and food. But it also reflects strong demand for electric cars and non-essentials – particularly overseas travel. Inflation has risen to 4% as of August, both because of oil disruption and mass construction of big projects like datacentres and because local businesses are lifting their prices. When customers are willing to spend big, businesses find it easier to raise prices. Do higher mortgage rates cut household budgets? The cash rate’s most immediate effect is on household cashflow, taking money away from borrowers while giving more to debt-free savers. RBA data shows higher rates and prices have left 2% of borrowers unable to afford essential expenses but most people are meeting repayments. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Warren Hogan, the managing director of EQ Economics, says the emergence of mortgage offset accounts in the last decade has reduced rates’ effect on cashflow. Borrowers who have spare cash in offset accounts, often because they can afford to pay more than their minimum, now have “massive buffers”. Australians now hold nearly $350bn in total in offset balances. “You just didn’t have the same amount of capacity to pay off earlier and have offsets accounts and all that sort of thing,” Hogan says. Home ownership is in decline, meaning more Australians are renters whose spending is not directly hit by higher mortgage rates. One in three households own their home debt-free and benefit from higher interest on their savings. Commonwealth Bank data indicates older Australians and debt-free homeowners have steadily increased their spending this year. Will falling house prices discourage spending? The slide in house prices is a sign that interest rates and higher borrowing costs are directly restricting economic activity, according to David Bassanese, the chief economist at BetaShares. House price slides are also an indirect channel for hikes to slow spending as homeowners tend to cut back when falls in home values make them less wealthy than they had been. RBA research suggests a 10% fall in housing prices – which is expected by mid-2027 – will cut consumption by 1.5%. Bassanese says consumer spending does not appear to have slowed yet by as much as past RBA models would imply. “We’re probably not seeing a major effect yet, but in theory, it should be starting to happen,” he said. The “wealth effect” of interest rates is typically slower-moving than the cashflow effect. But most homeowners are also wealthier than they were two years ago, with the median national price back to where it was in September. What about exchange rates? The Reserve Bank says the most important effect of interest rate rises is through the exchange rate. Higher interest rates tend to push up demand to invest in Australia, lifting the Australian dollar, making imports cheaper. But the dollar has been fairly stable against other currencies because foreign central banks like the US Federal Reserve are also lifting their own interest rates. The Australian dollar rose from 65 US cents in November 2025 to 72 in May 2026, after the first three RBA rate rises but has fallen to 69 US cents. It has followed a similar path compared to an index of Australia’s trade partners, including China, Japan, Europe and South Korea. “We’re raising rates, but so is everybody else,” Bassanese says. “Our currency is not especially strong, although it has lifted somewhat over the past year.” How does higher unemployment stop inflation? Interest rate rises aim to push up unemployment but the hikes have had little effect this year. More jobseekers make it easier for businesses to find workers without lifting wages. Higher wages would be passed on as higher prices for customers, so more unemployment tends to mean less inflation. But the jobs market has been surprisingly strong. Health and care sectors have rapidly hired thanks to bigger demand and government subsidies while productivity is going backwards, forcing businesses to hire more workers to keep up production. The RBA governor, Michele Bullock, has said she wants to see a small increase in jobless rates so there is less pressure from wages on prices, drawing criticism from unions. Unemployment increasing from 4.6% to 5% would represent an extra 60,000 people out of work if the workforce stayed the same size. But Bullock said after September’s rate hike that she does not expect job losses, instead hoping job creation will slow and more people will look to join the workforce, leaving jobseekers searching for longer periods. Markets expect only one more rate rise and not until May 2027. But the Deutsche Bank strategist Lachlan Dynan warns rate rises’ weaker effects add to the risk of another hike. “The Australian household sector has been more resilient to hikes than many expected,” Dynan says. “Risks to RBA [rates] are back to being skewed to the upside in our view.”

title: Employees all over the world find themselves monitored by AI at work
summary: The latest example of workers under surveillance comes from Co-op, a British consumer cooperative that runs thousands of businesses
text: Hello, and welcome to TechScape. I’m Blake Montgomery, US tech editor at the Guardian, writing to you while moving laundry from the washer to the dryer, wishing a robot could do the task for me. Today in tech, we’re talking about workers and AI. Workers under surveillance Employees across the globe are increasingly finding themselves minutely monitored in their workplaces, with tiny changes in their behaviors resulting in negative performance evaluations. The latest example of workers under surveillance and bristling at it comes from Co-op, which operates supermarkets, undertakers, insurance and legal services companies in the UK. The company implemented an automated listening technology that rates every phone call some of them make to customers. In a system described as “oppressive and dystopian” by a whistleblower, Co-op Legal Services is using AI models to record, analyze and award a percentage score for interactions between agents and customers seeking advice about probate, wills and estates. “You are being watched,” said a Co-op worker who spoke to the Guardian on condition of anonymity. Read more: ‘Dystopian’: Co-op becomes latest firm to put staff under AI surveillance The Co-op said it did not recognize the criticism and said its probate advisers were highly engaged. Resentment of workers’ treatment is already translating into policy, a break from the sluggishness of most technology regulations. Across the Atlantic and the continental United States, Governor Gavin Newsom of California signed laws into effect last week that prohibit certain types of workplace surveillance. California’s laws aim to target workplace surveillance measures like heat maps that track employees’ movements, including how long they spend in the bathroom, or having their emotional states monitored. Amazon warehouse workers have previously complained about being timed on their bathroom breaks, for example. And at Kaiser Permanente, a California hospital chain, nurses have said automated systems rated their tone of voice in patient interactions. Read more: California’s new laws target workers’ biggest fear of AI taking their jobs *** Tell us: Are you being watched at work? Tell us: have you been monitored or assessed by AI at work? Silicon Valley on screen Artificial review – Luca Guadagnino takes on OpenAI in muddled tech satire The Social Reckoning review – Aaron Sorkin’s jittery sequel with all-new evil puppet Zuckerberg Whom does AI benefit? Two stories recently published in the Guardian’s Reworked series pose the question: who is AI enriching? The first story details how the AI boom is leaving women out of the single largest engine of growth in the US economy. One visible example: Donald Trump’s all-male summit of AI leaders last week: not a single woman in sight as the president preached the power of “superintelligence”. “We’re talking about who captures a major new source of economic mobility,” said Felicia Newhouse, founder of AI Powered Women, an organization that promotes women’s participation and leadership in AI. “The deepest risk is that a participation gap becomes a power gap.” Read more: The AI industry is booming. Women are getting left behind Across AI-related occupations, the median pay of men is $45,000 higher than that of women, partly due to the types of jobs men and women are more likely to have, according to research by LinkedIn: men are still typically hired for higher-paying roles in the AI industry. When pitching investors, one female co-founder of an AI startup said she had found through trial and error that she and her male co-founder are more likely to get an investment if he does the pitching. Another story in the series examines how dire working conditions can become under the pressures of AI and automation. Refugees in Kenya are completing tasks for foreign technology companies under bizarre and opaque conditions. The stories of desperate remote data workers used to highlight the low pay and horrid content they were exposed to. Today, workers who spoke to the Guardian say they aren’t even sure they will be paid, as their compensation is tied to a so-called “reward” system that decides whether they receive payment based on the quality of their work. Many of the workers called the system unfair but also said with dismay that they had few, if any, other options. Read more: ‘Someone else will do it for less’: refugees in Kenya are powering tech for dwindling pay The workers in Kenya also expressed a desperation to earn any money at these jobs before AI could carry out the rote tasks they were assigned. Contrast these stories of unequal benefit with Sam Altman’s recent remarks on a podcast: “We believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology.” Altman was referring to the consequences of AI like the hack of Hugging Face or the attempted creation of bioweapons by would-be terrorists. Bad, to be sure, but lacking the moral outrage of human consequences. title: Fewer Britons plan to ringfence money for holidays abroad next year, says travel industry
summary: Spain remains most popular destination as Britons book later in hope of better deals, Abta report finds
text: The UK’s cost of living squeeze means fewer people plan to ringfence money for holidays abroad next year, the travel industry has warned. Despite war, wildfires and EES border checks, the numbers of Britons taking holidays climbed back to pre-pandemic levels this year – but rising costs may mean the numbers have peaked, according to an annual travel industry report on Tuesday. Numbers taking holidays at home and abroad continued to rise, although late bookings and shorter city breaks have been an increasing feature of holidays through 2026. Confidence in travel dropped slightly year on year but rebounded as fears over jet fuel shortages and flight disruption faded since the start of the US-Israel war with Iran in February, according to research from the industry body Abta. Overall, 88% of Brits took a holiday this year, matching the 2019 pre-pandemic peak, with a new high of 74% in the UK and 62% abroad. However, Abta’s report found that almost one in three people were planning to spend less on travelling abroad next year, suggesting that the annual holiday is no longer sacrosanct. Fewer people now say they are willing to reduce spending on phones or other gadgets than the holiday abroad. Abta said the holiday business remained resilient, despite a dip in its travel confidence index to +50 – this measures the net proportion of people who felt secure in going abroad, compared with those who were worried. But it said that score had rebounded since disruption from the Middle East conflict and fears about fuel availability and the EU’s entry/exit system (EES). The Abta chief executive, Mark Tanzer, said it had been a tough year for the travel industry. But he added: “Demand has held up well despite a range of challenges this year, and that looks set to continue, as does the willingness to prioritise spending on travel over other discretionary items.” Speaking at the annual Abta travel convention in Madeira, Tanzer added: “It’s been a stop-start year but the market did come back in the summer. “We saw people switching their holiday plans and booking later, waiting and seeing – maybe hoping for better deals but also managing the uncertainty.” He said the industry would continue to lobby ministers hard to reduce aviation taxes and increase help in the switch to sustainable aviation fuels, to help cut costs and support an industry that contributed £57bn to the UK economy. Tanzer said the investment in tourism continued but he admitted: “The pressures of the last few months are not going to go away in the next 18 months.” Spain increased its dominance of the British outbound market. The number who said they visited Spain was up four percentage points to 36%, while Portugal moved up to sixth in popularity for holidays. Polling next year’s travel intentions, only 26% said they were planning to visit Spain, with places such as Japan and Norway cited in the top 10. However, previous surveys have underlined that, despite dreams of somewhere more exotic, Britons head resolutely back to Spain. Travel to the convention was provided by Abta

title: Miriam González Durántez launches new centrist party in Spain
summary: Wife of former British deputy PM Nick Clegg promises liberal alternative to the PP and Socialists before snap election
text: The Spanish lawyer Miriam González Durántez has launched a new liberal, centrist party, vowing to clean up politics and give voters an alternative to the dominant socialist and conservative parties as the country gears up for next month’s snap general election. González Durántez, an ex-EU adviser who is married to the former British deputy prime minister Nick Clegg, says her new party, Democracia21, will offer a modern, transparent kind of politics that “doesn’t feed on fear, insults or nostalgia”. Democracia21’s manifesto accuses both the ruling Spanish Socialist Workers’ party (PSOE) and the rightwing People’s party (PP) of squandering decades of government for short-term political ends. “In the meantime: housing became unaffordable, young people left, bureaucracy grew like a religion, and bickering took the place of governing,” it says. “Old-school politics turned every problem into a narrative – and every solution into an electoral threat.” Mindful of the corruption scandals that eventually toppled the last PP government – and the graft allegations enveloping the administration and inner circle of the socialist prime minister, Pedro Sánchez – the new party is promising “a radical political cleanup”, including far greater transparency for parties. González Durántez, who announced that Democracia21 will run in Madrid and Barcelona in the election on 29 November, has also positioned herself on two of the biggest issues facing voters: the housing crisis and immigration. The eviction last month of an 87-year-old woman in Madrid unleashed waves of demonstrations across Spain, led to the setting up of a protest camp in the centre of the capital and prompted Sánchez’s minority government to propose emergency measures to try to make the rental market more equitable. When those measures were voted down by rightwing and far-right parties at the beginning of October, the prime minister announced a snap general election. Speaking at her party’s launch over the weekend, González Durántez accused both the PSOE and the PP of ignoring the housing crisis. “One lot has been in government for eight years and the other controls 80% of Spain’s regional governments,” she said. “What’s going on here is that they only remember about housing when an election comes around and all the people are on the streets.” González Durántez proposed scrapping housing taxes for people under 35, and argued that a young person earning €1,300 (£1,098) a month should not be paying more than €350 a month in rent. She also defended the benefits of controlled immigration and of Spain’s place within the European project, which she described as “absolutely existential” for the country. “Immigration is an asset and an essential competitive advantage for Spain right now,” she said. “We need to get rid of all the xenophobic talk but the state needs to be in control of immigration. We need to decide who comes in; how they come in; when they come in and, if they have to leave, we will also decide when they leave. None of this is contradictory. We need to do all that while ensuring that Europe doesn’t fall into the traps of those political forces that haven’t come to reform Europe, but to break it.” Democracia21 is not the first centrist party to have tried to shake up the traditional socialist and conservative duopoly. The liberal Ciudadanos party, founded in 2006, briefly looked set to push past both the PSOE and the PP, but its decision to lurch to the right and its refusal to back the no-confidence motion that turfed the conservatives out of office in 2018 proved fatal. Ciudadanos’s support was so depleted by the last general election in July 2023 that it chose not to take part in the poll. Sánchez’s decision to call the snap election is another gamble from Spain’s pragmatic and unpredictable prime minister. Polls suggest the PP will comfortably beat the PSOE to win first place, but is unlikely to secure an absolute majority, forcing it to rely on Vox’s support to govern. Sánchez, meanwhile, will be hoping that the PP’s decision to side with Vox and the rightwing Catalan pro-independence Junts party to torpedo the housing proposals will mobilise leftwing and moderate voters. The prime minister, however, is already facing an electoral setback after Spain’s supreme court decided to maintain its suspension of the voting rights of tens of thousands of overseas voters who benefited from a law his government introduced in 2022 offering Spanish citizenship to the descendants of those exiled during the civil war and subsequent Franco dictatorship. The move has angered the PP and Vox, who have accused Sánchez of seeking to create more socialist voters beyond Spain’s borders. Although the suspension looks set to remain in place for the election, the court has said its ruling will not affect those who can prove that their parents or grandparents “suffered exile for political or ideological reasons, or for reasons of belief or sexual orientation”. The PSOE has denounced the political pressure behind the decision as an affront to democracy. “The grandchildren of the Franco regime will be able to vote, but not those of the exiles, just as the PP and Vox wanted,” the party’s organisational secretary, Rebeca Torró, posted on X. “Their fascist agenda has struck at the cornerstone of democracy: the right to vote. We will not stop denouncing this outrage.”
