title: Pennsylvania announces sixth death in measles outbreak as case numbers rise
summary: Latest fatality is unvaccinated woman, 39, with ‘underlying conditions’ but CDC still lists only two deaths nationwide
text: A sixth death has been announced in Pennsylvania’s measles outbreak, as new figures show cases in the state have risen above 1,100. The most recent fatality was reported in Franklin county on Monday in a statement posted to Facebook by its coroner. The victim was identified as a 39-year-old female who “had several underlying conditions, including a past diagnosis of measles with treatment”. The coroner, James Conner, said it was the first measles-related death in the county “for many years” – and that the patient’s recent diagnosis met the definition of the Pennsylvania health department for inclusion. Five other people have died after contracting measles since August in Pennsylvania, which state officials said on Monday had now recorded 1,137 cases and 219 hospitalizations. The outbreak began west of Philadelphia in April, with authorities blaming low vaccination rates. The federal Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), however, continues to list deaths nationally at two amid a dispute between the Trump administration’s health secretary, Robert F Kennedy, and Pennsylvania’s governor, Josh Shapiro, over the methodology for classifying measles-related fatalities. The CDC’s website, last updated on Friday, shows 4,080 confirmed measles infections across the US in 42 separate outbreaks, the highest figures in decades, and almost double the number of cases for the whole of 2025. Earlier in October, New York’s governor, Kathy Hochul, declared an emergency because of rising case numbers in her state; while Ohio, South Carolina, Texas and Utah have also seen significant increases. A spokesperson for the Pennsylvania health department told NBC News on Monday that it was aware of the Franklin county fatality – and was “conducting a thorough review of the reported death”. The coroner’s office told the outlet through a spokesperson that the woman’s “primary cause of death was a probable acute cardiac event due to possible complications of the measles”. The coroner’s office spokesperson said the woman was not vaccinated. Conner’s statement did not identify the woman to protect the privacy of the victim and relatives. “Families deserve the dignity to mourn in private,” that statement said. “We strongly encourage our medical community, first responders, and the public to follow the precautions set forth by” Pennsylvania state guidelines. Those state guidelines recommend two doses of the MMR (measles, mumps and rubella) vaccine, or a combined MMRV vaccine including varicella (chickenpox) protection for children 12 and older. The CDC website recommends the same vaccinations, but Kennedy – a longtime vaccine skeptic – has offered mixed messages. In March 2025, he questioned the effectiveness of the measles vaccine, saying people should be able “to make that choice for themselves” about whether to take it. And in September, he told anti-vaccine activists at a conference in Washington DC that they had “a strong and steadfast friend at the White House”, a month after telling US families in response to the rise in measles cases nationwide that parents “should get their children vaccinated”. The Pennsylvania outbreak has seen 157 new cases over the last week, state figures showed, and one-third of the overall number of infections have come in those 18 or under. Fewer than 1% of cases occurred in those who are fully vaccinated. The first two fatalities, reported in August, were infants, one whose mother had measles during her pregnancy, and the second a six-week-old who also had a rare genetic condition. The other Pennsylvania victims were women aged 40 and 20, and an 18-year-old, all of whom had coexisting health conditions.

title: How to escape our collective paralysis in ‘these uncertain times’
summary: Author Natasha Lennard discusses how to disrupt the ‘certainties’ that don’t serve us and how to fight back
text: At the onset of the Covid pandemic in 2020, journalist Natasha Lennard started noticing a constant thrum of collective apprehension, epitomized in the phrase “in these uncertain times”. The expression acknowledged we didn’t have solutions for many of society’s problems: a globally spreading virus, the rise of the far right and stark “haves v have-nots” inequalities. In the years since, that “uncertainty” hasn’t gone anywhere, risking enabling paralysis – not knowing where to start to fix things and therefore giving up before trying. In her new book, On Un/Certainty: The Uses of Doubt in Dangerous Times, Lennard, who also was an organizer in the 2011 Occupy Wall Street movement, deconstructs the problematic nature of giving in to uncertainty. She also uses the Austrian-British philosopher Ludwig Wittgenstein’s 1969 book On Certainty to question what is held as “certain” in today’s world, and who gets to make those calls. For example, why does the anti-trans movement get to define what makes a woman? Why do politicians run on the presumption that voters want “closed borders”, when just a few decades ago, neither party saw militarized borders as a foregone conclusion? Why do the tech billionaires who invested in AI want us to believe an AI “apocalypse” is inevitable? “Even though the book uses Wittgenstein, who was no activist, as a jumping-off point, it is definitely a book aimed at people who want to be thinking seriously about how we continue in this moment of fascist rule,” said Lennard. Below, Lennard discusses how this isn’t the first “uncertain” moment in history, how to disrupt the certainties that don’t serve us and how to fight back. Tell me why you think the phrase “these uncertain times” is reductive. “In these uncertain times” seems like a constant refrain from all sectors, be it political reporting or how we’re thinking about climate decimation, AI-driven futures or futures determined by authoritarian fascist rule. I think there’s something very true about this being an extraordinary time of grounded reasons for fear and doom, and indeed a lot of uncertainty about the shape of our collective futures. But also, I don’t necessarily agree that we are in a wholly uncertain time, because we, again and again, keep being in the midst of activities of certainty – things taken for granted, rather than proven. What are some certainties we take for granted? Certainties upheld around border regimes and the necessity of so-called border security. The certainty of anti-trans bigots on the far right and their complicit bedfellows in the center – and indeed in some of the left – who hold enforced gender binaries all too certain. Certainties around the frameworks of the crises that we are in – that they will be forever determined by capital and the drive for growth, and that we face a cascading so-called polycrisis, too complex for ordinary people to know how to respond or intervene. These certainties keep giving shape and direction to our fears and doubts. And it’s those certainties that I want to gesture toward as the very things we need to pay attention to if we really want to understand and demystify this moment of seemingly totalizing uncertainty. Thinking outside of paralysis means thinking about how movements and revolutionary histories have broken through what have seemed like political certainties in previous historical moments. In the book, you argue that we’ve seen some certainties ruptured in just the time since Occupy. Like what? We have seen certainties become unmoored. Paradigm shifts don’t happen all at once in some revolutionary spark moment, even though uprisings are often crucial catalysts. We might look at the 2020 George Floyd uprisings. There’s a temptation to say that was just a flash in the pan because it was so quickly repressed and didn’t immediately lead to the social change people wanted. But some of the networks that were most active against ICE in Minneapolis earlier this year – the neighborhood support networks, the ICE watchers, the militant blockades – were networks that developed around the George Floyd uprisings. Certainties of the Democratic party’s liberal-capitalist orientation – appealing to corporate interests and donors while failing to fight for programs like universal healthcare – have been challenged by the recent success of a number of DSA candidates and Zohran Mamdani’s campaign. We have seen what was considered to be a certainty about candidate electability ruptured through people organizing and door-knocking and meeting their neighbors and working around tenants’ rights. Part of the question of what we know requires engaging with how we know what we know, which is particularly challenging as higher education is under attack. How can we push back against these attacks? This moment directly echoes the destruction of records and histories during post-civil war Reconstruction, as WEB Du Bois points out in Black Reconstruction. The Trump regime is very purposely and specifically decimating higher education – as well as removing records of everything from Black history, LGBTQ history, health studies, and making us all, of course, dumber and less safe, accordingly. I don’t think we need to rebuild the university and college system into its pre-Trump, pre-enforced-AI status quo ante; it was already decimated and adjunct-ified and unaffordable. Higher education as a valued, free public good should not be beyond our horizon. It was closer to a reality just a few generations ago: in the UK, for example, there was free tuition until the late 1990s. Which is why the work of unions, and unions willing to be militant, in education is crucial now and will be crucial even when the Trump regime falls. You make clear that we don’t have the answers yet. But in the book, you argue there is still a lot of room left for movements to win. The book ends with me watching the last presidential election at the home of my friend Sarah Leonard, whom I’ve known since Occupy Wall Street. Trump won, and we hugged goodbye, and she said, “We’re not starting from scratch.” That we’re not starting from scratch is one of the key takeaways I want to be able to offer in this book. We might not have the formula for overthrowing capitalism, for overthrowing fascist regimes. We might not have the perfect recipe or solution for what needs to be done and what victory might really look like. But I don’t think that means it’s true that we don’t know how to go on, in better directions. Wittgenstein insists that we must go “back to the rough ground” of how we make meaning together in everyday, quotidian ways. I think it’s good advice. We see the activities of going on today, in sites of resistance and boycotts and mass strikes and mutual aid and protecting neighbors and strangers – people taking seriously that there must be ongoing practices of resistance and connections to build upon, and that have been built upon for years. Does that mean I know for a fact that we will win? No, but I do think we know how to go on. On Un/Certainty by Natasha Lennard is out now. Crouse is out now. title: Threat of AI share crash puts world financial stability at risk, says IMF
summary: High valuations and debt put sector in danger, while fund also warns on government borrowing and cyber-attacks
text: The threat of an AI share price crash rippling out across global markets is putting world financial stability at risk, the International Monetary fund has warned. In its twice-yearly Global Financial Stability Report, the IMF highlighted the sky-high valuations for AI companies along with their increasing debt pile as one reason that risks in the system are “elevated”. “The consequences of an AI correction could be global,” it warned. Aside from the US, Asian markets would be most exposed, and the UK and euro area potentially more insulated – though investors with US holdings would be hit. Athanasios Vamvakidis, the deputy director of the IMF’s monetary and capital department, launching the report, said: “The exposure of the rest of the world to US assets, particularly AI, is the highest it has ever been. So this is supporting the global economy through wealth effects today; but if we get a market correction it could have broad implications.” An AI crash was one of three “salient risks” to stability identified by the IMF, alongside rising government borrowing costs and the threat of a big cyber-attack. It called this trio of factors “plausible near-term catalysts for a sharp tightening of financial conditions and market turmoil”. The IMF’s analysis underlined the interconnected nature of big AI companies, and the high levels of borrowing being undertaken to fund investment in the sector. “Weaker or less durable investment and profitability in AI could trigger a correction in AI-related asset prices, exacerbated by rising leverage, concentrated exposures, and circular financing arrangements,” it said. Such a reassessment would then “sharply reduce investment, trigger equity market corrections, and tighten financial conditions, with global spillovers”. The “magnificent seven” big tech stocks – Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, Meta, Microsoft, Nvidia and Tesla – account for more than 35% of the S&P 500 share index in the US, up from 12% a decade ago, and their total market capitalisation has increased by more than 50% in the past two years. Yet the IMF warned of “growing evidence” that the successful rollout of AI “may not require investment on the massive scale being undertaken by ‘hyperscaler’ firms”, and “potential economic gains may not be as large as expected”. The hyperscalers are the companies building the underlying infrastructure for the AI rollout, including many vast datacentres. They include Amazon Web Services, Google, Meta and Oracle. Shares in semiconductor companies fell on Tuesday after the boss of Broadcom compared many AI investors to “casino” gamblers. Reports that the Chinese memory chip maker CXMT was making good progress on a new chip architecture also hit South Korean tech companies. The IMF also highlighted the growing leverage, or borrowing, that underpins the current boom and could amplify the effects of a crash. In particular, it identified soaring debts contracted by the companies themselves; hedge fund investment in the sector; and retail investors borrowing to speculate in AI stocks. In the event of an AI-led market downturn “these growing sources of leverage heighten the potential for forced selling and surges in equity volatility”, it said. It also pointed to the prevalence of “circular financing” deals, tying stronger AI companies to weaker partners in the same sector, and potentially exacerbating the impact of a share price correction. It identified $300bn (£227bn) worth of transactions between hyperscalers and “weaker AI firms” in just the past three years, supplemented by $650bn in debt, in exchange for $1.4tn in future financial commitments. In London, the chief executive of the UK’s Financial Conduct Authority, Nikhil Rathi, urged every small business across the financial sector to take out insurance to protect themselves against AI-related cybersecurity threats. He told MPs on the Commons Treasury committee that not all companies would have the resources to pay for access to “frontier” AI models such as Anthropic’s Mythos, which has been released on a restricted basis after it was said to be rapidly identifying gaps in government and corporate cybersecurity systems. “One message I’d give to every small business: you should consider making sure you are insured,” Rathi said.

title: Hobbs and Whistles owner investigates hack that may have exposed customer data
summary: Cyber-attack on TFG London comes less than a week after online fashion seller Asos was hit by hackers
text: The owner of Phase Eight, Hobbs and Whistles has said its websites and IT systems have been hit by a cyber-attack that may have compromised customers’ personal data. The South-African listed TFG London said it identified the “cybersecurity incident” at the three UK-based retail chains on Sunday. Its two other UK brands, Inside Story and White Stuff, are not affected. TFG said its stores had stayed open and trading but some of its IT systems “remain unavailable” and it had paused all online orders as a “precautionary measure”. An “investigation is ongoing, including establishing whether any personal or other sensitive information has been compromised,” the company said. If the investigation establishes that any personal information has been accessed by hackers, TFG said it would “notify affected individuals or organisations”. “Some of our brand’s website capabilities may not be available as the investigation continues. We apologise for any disruption and will provide additional updates to our customers as appropriate,” the company added. In an email to Whistles customers, the company said any orders placed on or after 11 October may be delayed. Orders placed before that date are being processed normally. Returns can only be made via stores at present and Whistles told customers it was “working on a solution for postal returns”. TFG has engaged external cybersecurity specialists to contain the incident, which has been reported to the relevant UK authorities. The group’s operations in Africa or Australia run on separate systems and are not affected. The attack on the three UK fashion brands comes less than a week after a cyber-attack affected the online fashion seller Asos, in which the names, addresses and recent search data of millions of customers was accessed. H&M said on Monday that it was also investigating claims that its systems had been attacked. However, the fast fashion retailer said: “We have not found any indications that our data environment has been compromised.” On Monday, it emerged that hackers had forced the temperature of many French supermarket fridges up to 50C overnight, in an “unprecedented” cyber-attack affecting several hundred stores. Several other British retailers, including Marks & Spencer, the Co-op and Harrods, were hit by damaging cyber incidents last year. M&S and the Co-op faced stock shortages and the former was forced to shut down its website for several weeks while it ensured its systems were clean. Marijus Briedis, the chief technology officer at the digital security firm NordVPN, said: “Coming so soon after the Asos incident, this latest attack on TFG London is another reminder that the retail sector is firmly in hackers’ sights. These attacks are becoming a recurring nightmare for businesses, and there’s every reason to believe we’ll see more of them. “Retailers are particularly attractive targets because they hold valuable customer information and rely on a sprawling network of payment systems, suppliers and third-party technology providers. Every connection is a potential weak point, and attackers are increasingly adept at exploiting stolen credentials, human error and gaps in security.”

title: Rightwing extremists increasingly likely to consider terrorist attacks, MI5 chief says
summary: Move from anti-immigration or anti-Muslim views to violence is ‘most marked trend’ in spy agency’s caseload over last year
text: Extremists with anti-migrant opinions are becoming increasingly likely to consider carrying out terrorist attacks against immigration centres and asylum hotels in the UK, the head of MI5 has warned. Ken McCallum said a shift from radicalised rightwing sentiment to violence was “the most marked trend” in the spy agency’s caseload over the past year, contributing to a rise in the overall UK terror threat level. The comments formed part of a wide-ranging annual threat update in which the spy chief indicated a more aggressive Iran had threatened other military bases in the UK, as well as being behind the incident at RAF Fairford late last month. He also warned of the potential use of AI by hostile states and terrorists, including to possibly develop a novel bioweapon – while adding that MI5 would create a new AI Threat Assessment Centre to distinguish fact from fiction. On the evolving extreme rightwing threat, McCallum said there had been an increase in cases where “extremist versions of anti-immigration and anti-Muslim grievance are tipping into terrorist intent”, such as planning attacks on migrants and Muslims. A number of aggressive anti-migrant protests have been held this autumn by the far-right Patriot Platform at Portsmouth and Dover, while racially and religiously motivated offences are running at record levels. McCallum said young people were particularly likely to gravitate towards extreme rightwing terrorism, and at one point this year the Security Service was “investigating a radicalised … 13-year-old in the UK”. A year ago, he added, a 16-year-old from Inverclyde received a 10-year prison sentence after he pleaded guilty to planning mass murder by firebombing a Muslim centre in Greenock. There was a “concerning trend of violence targeted at political figures, religious or community groups”, McCallum said, as demonstrated by the killing of the former minister and Reform UK spokesperson, Ann Widdecombe. Iran, he said, was trying to expand hostile activities in the UK and now had “ambitions to come at harder targets, like military sites”, including the RAF Fairford airbase in Gloucestershire. Five men from London drove to Whelford, a village next to a base used by the US air force, in three white vans shortly after midnight on 27 September. They were released on police bail a day later after no bombs or explosives were found. There was also a hint that Iran had sought to target other bases. “Fairford is not unique in the UK,” McCallum said, though he would not be drawn specifically on what other sites had been threatened, or the nature of the threat. However, allies said his comments were not a reference to RAF Molesworth in Cambridgeshire, where two Latvians were found by police at 2am inside the perimeter of a base used for US and Nato intelligence operations in Europe. They were subsequently released on police bail. Iran, though, still has a relatively low level of capability to match its ambitions. Tehran typically hired criminal proxies to carry out operations abroad, so any ability to target a military base “is really a function of the sophistication level of those criminals”. On Thursday, Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, is due to meet his US counterpart, Pete Hegseth, at the Pentagon for a discussion where the issue of base security in the UK is almost certain to be discussed. A week after the Fairford incident, the US withdrew 12 B-1 bombers from the RAF base, which had been used to attack Iran in the spring and early summer. MI5’s counter-Iran operation has led to more than 50 arrests in the UK in the past year, with much of Tehran’s increased aggression aimed at “British Jewish communities” including terrorist plots and arson attacks against synagogues, businesses and ambulances. In an unexpected observation, McCallum said he was “particularly focused” on the risk of hostile states or terrorists using AI to generate new, deadly bioweapons, particularly if guardrails introduced by software companies failed. Last month, Anthropic, the company behind Claude, warned that there were “five case studies of actors using our models in ways that could support biological weapons development” – and said misuse could have serious consequences. Liam Booth-Smith, head of Europe policy at Anthropic and a former chief of staff to Rishi Sunak, told the Commons business committee on Tuesday that there was a risk of real harm from the fast-developing technology. “Without appropriate mitigations, it’s possible that real harm could be caused in the space of helping people to create biological or chemical weapons,” Booth-Smith said. The MI5 chief added that AI could also be exploited by cyber hackers, to help terrorists refine their attack plans and even try to use “AI-enabled drones”, he said, and to easily produce “propaganda and radicalising material tailored to the individual”. In response, MI5 would create a new AI threat assessment centre to bring together expertise from across government to carefully distinguish the reality of the threats generated by the new technology and advise both government and the wider public to “separate the bluster from the realities”. Russia, the MI5 chief emphasised, remains “aggressor number one” as the Kremlin continues to lash out against the west with assassination plots, explosive threats and cyber-attacks that at times stop “not much short” of conventional warfare. Moscow tried to interfere in the 2016 Brexit referendum with anti-EU coverage on RT and Sputnik media, and via troll social media accounts, but there was a big difference between “what may have been attempted and what actually resulted”. The UK’s relationship with China was “multifaceted”, with MI5 focused on Beijing’s efforts to steal university research and intellectual property, and obtain political secrets about areas it was interested in. Overall, threats from hostile states had quadrupled in the last decade and now were running on par with MI5’s counter-terrorism mission. “We have again entered a new era of national security,” he said.

title: Burnham’s Your First Home scheme ‘could boost Bellway’s house output by 10%’
summary: Help-to-buy initiative for England could slow market while first-time buyers wait for launch, builder admits
text: The new Your First Home programme for first-time buyers could increase the number of houses British builder Bellway produces each year by 10%, its boss has said. Faced with a chronic shortage of homes, the government has made housing one of its top priorities and Andy Burnham’s surprise announcement of the YFH scheme a fortnight ago sent housebuilders’ shares soaring by more than 10%. Jason Honeyman, who has led Bellway since 2017, welcomed the new programme, which will be more targeted than previous help-to-buy initiatives. It features household income caps to exclude those with big salaries, and price caps to ensure people can only buy modest houses. Full details, including the launch date, are expected be announced by John Healey in his first budget as chancellor on 28 October. YFH applies only to England and is for prospective first-time buyers hoping to buy a new-build flat or house. They will be offered a government-backed equity loan worth 20% of the purchase price and the minimum deposit the buyer will have to put down will be just 2.5%. While the scheme has the potential to “provide significant support for first-time buyers”, it could weigh on the market in the near term, Honeyman said, as some will want to wait for the initiative to be launched. However, he added that it could drive Bellway’s annual completions back to 10,000 homes, in the 12-month period from next September at the earliest. “Based upon our past experience with help to buy, the new scheme has the potential to boost volumes by around 10%, and with a market recovery, provide a path back to at least 10,000 homes a year and a return on equity of 15%,” Honeyman said. Bellway is targeting between ⁠9,000 and 9,400 homes in the current year, down from 9,695 last year, ‌given a lower order book and “ongoing pressures on customer demand” coupled with higher construction costs, running at between 3% and 4%. It has a forward order book of 4,981 homes worth £1.4bn, compared with 5,285 homes with a value of £1.5bn a year earlier. Bellway also expects the average selling price to be flat over the coming year at about £325,000. The chief executive’s comments came after the company beat analysts’ expectations with revenue of £3.16bn for the year to 31 August, up 13% from the previous year. This lifted underlying profits before tax by 5.7% to £305.7m. Bellway shares rose 2% on Tuesday but are still down by more than a quarter so far this year. YFH is expected to give a shot in the arm to most big housebuilders, such as Persimmon, MJ Gleeson, Taylor Wimpey and Bellway. However, the upmarket builder Berkeley Group, which is focused on London, where prices are higher, and Vistry Group, which has pivoted towards building affordable and social homes, are not expected to get much help from the initiative.

title: Jury sworn in for Russell Brand trial on rape and sexual assault charges
summary: Prosecution expected to open its case on Wednesday after eight men and four women selected as jurors
text: Russell Brand has attended court for the second day of his rape and sexual assault trial and a jury has been selected in the case. The 51-year-old comedian faces three charges of rape, three of sexual assault and one of indecent assault against six women, in allegations spanning 10 years from 1999 to 2009. Brand denies all the charges. Jury selection at Southwark crown court began on Monday morning with a warning from the judge, Mr Justice Bennathan, to ignore past reporting about Brand and allegations of sexual misconduct. On Tuesday, eight men and four women were sworn in for the trial, which is expected to last six weeks. The jurors were sent away until Wednesday morning when the prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones KC is expected to open the case. One reserve juror was selected to sit through the prosecution opening. The judge told the jurors not to discuss the case or carry out any research. “Heaven knows what’s out there,” Bennathan said on Tuesday. “If you want to, you could go and have a look – but only once you have returned your verdicts.” Brand arrived at court just after 9.20am and said “blessed, thank you very much” in the direction of photographers and members of the press. He wore a double-breasted grey suit, an unbuttoned shirt with a long tie, brown boots and sunglasses. Flanked by his security guard, Brand looked at the cameras before taking off his sunglasses as he walked up the steps towards the central London courthouse. His wife, Laura Gallacher, who was by his side for the first day on Monday, did not accompany Brand on Tuesday morning. Brand became a British television personality in the 2000s, presenting shows and events such as the 2007 Brit awards, Comic Relief and the MTV video music awards. He also hosted his own show on BBC Radio 2. He made the move into Hollywood films with roles in the comedy Get Him to the Greek and the 2012 musical comedy Rock of Ages. He was married to the American pop singer Katy Perry from 2010 to 2012.

title: Is punishing the poor Trump’s last hand to play?
summary: The pre-midterm defenestration of ACA enrollees looks like political madness – but the president appears to believe hitting poor people might work for him
text: There is a manic quality to Donald Trump’s desperate dash to do something, anything, ahead of November’s midterm elections to convince beleaguered Americans that he can make the pressures his policies have imposed on their livelihoods go away. The US president offered to lower barriers against beef imports to limit surging meat prices, only to consider backtracking under pressure from the cow lobby. He offered to stop diesel exports, only to find oil companies were not interested. He weakened fuel efficiency standards, claiming this would trim the price of a new car (and forgetting to point out it will also raise spending on gas). In early October he started mailing $500 checks to nearly a million people touting his healthcare “wins”. Oh, and he promised adult Americans a $5,000 check if Republicans maintain control of Congress. That, too, will go nowhere. In the face of such setbacks, maybe Trump felt he had to demonstrate he still can get something done. Still, it is somewhat counterintuitive that the administration, in the shape of Vice-President JD Vance, decided to broadcast the one initiative it did manage to bring to fruition: ejecting more than 750,000 enrollees from the Affordable Care Act (ACA) health insurance marketplaces, on grounds that they are not entitled to federal subsidies. Trump could argue that the cuts fit within the administration’s promised commitment to restore fiscal discipline. But that part of the platform – which came as Scott Bessent, the treasury secretary, promised to trim the budget deficit to 3% of US gross domestic product – was never more than a rhetorical feint. The pre-midterm defenestration of ACA enrollees by Trump’s “fraud taskforce”, by contrast, looks a lot like political madness, given the persistent economic anxieties articulated by Democratic and Republican voters across the country. The savings from the ACA maneuver, estimated by the administration at $2.2bn per year, are chump change compared with the centerpiece of Trump’s fiscal policy – the One Big Beautiful Bill Act from 2025 that is expected to add $4.1tn to budget deficits over the next decade, largely due to tax cuts benefiting the most affluent Americans. Pace Bessent, the budget deficit is growing rapidly, expected to rise to some $2tn in the fiscal year of 2026, roughly 6% of GDP and about 18% more than in fiscal 2024, the last year of the Biden administration. Rather than stem budgetary red ink, it’s as if Trump’s objective is to spread misery beyond the 3 million Americans who had to drop their health insurance after the administration last year cancelled subsidies offered by the Biden administration. The effort is something out of the playbook of Elon Musk’s Doge. His promise to rid the government of “waste” and “fraud” probably caused the deaths of millions of children in the developing world after the dismantling of USAID, but proved largely irrelevant to the task of saving money for the government. It may serve as a masterclass in trolling. But it is not a vote-winner. Part of Trump’s brain seems to understand this. Trump paid in part for the “beautiful” bill’s colossal tax cut by cutting funding to Medicaid and the Snap food stamp program for low-income Americans. But he engineered most of the cuts to kick in after the midterms to minimize the political cost. The thinking was that lower-income Americans would happily vote for the Republicans out of gratitude for their somewhat bigger tax refund checks this year and tax breaks for overtime and tips (cleverly designed to expire at the end of Trump’s term) and not notice the cuts rushing down the pike on federal programs they relied on. But the new evictions from the ACA suggest that his brain’s darker side is winning. Indeed, it underscores Trump’s belief that hitting poor people might work for him. Rather than a commitment to sound fiscal policy, a helping hand for American families treading water or an economic platform of any kind, Trump’s latest exercise in “fraud prevention” points to a strategy revolving around punishing people he can define as “bad”. Deep underwater in the polls for his nutty stewardship of the economy, among other things, Trump seems to believe that his one remaining winning card is to do violence against constituencies that his base may not like. Top of the list are immigrants and low-income people. And so it is that ICE is also doubling down, announcing it will hire another 5,000 agents by the end of the year. The president is on to something. About two-thirds of Republicans believe giving more aid to the poor does more harm than good, according to surveys from the Pew Research Center. Despite the repeated instances of abuse by federal agents, only 19% of Republicans think the Trump administration is doing too much to deport immigrants illegally in the country. The most radical rightwing voters are all in for federal deportations and don’t think the federal government should be responsible for ensuring Americans’ healthcare. Perhaps Trump’s heart truly lies on the dark side. But doubling down on policies to please the most ardent fanatics in his base ultimately reveals the weakness of Trump’s position. Perhaps even he understands that he has lost the rest of the country. Punishing the poor and the foreign – alongside an unlikely $5,000 Hail Mary pass – is all he has left. Eduardo Porter is a journalist focused on economics and politics. He writes the newsletter Being There on Substack

title: Democratic leaders condemn federal raid on Ilhan Omar as she vows not to be silenced | First Thing
summary: Minnesota congresswoman criticized raid as attempt by Trump administration ‘to target political enemies and weaponize law enforcement’
text: Good morning. Ilhan Omar has said she will not be silenced after federal agents raided her home. In a social media post, the Minnesota congresswoman criticized the raid as an attempt by the Trump administration “to target political enemies and weaponize law enforcement”. Donald Trump and key allies have accused Omar of fraud related to her family’s immigration history, fantasizing openly about denaturalizing her and expelling her from the country. Omar said in her post: “This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation. I will not be silenced.” How have Ilhan Omar’s Democratic colleagues reacted to the raid? House Democratic leaders, including the minority leader, Hakeem Jeffries, the party whip, Katherine Clark and caucus chair, Pete Aguilar, issued a joint statement excoriating the president for the search, calling it “deeply disturbing”. The Democratic leaders vowed to “deliver full accountability for the rogue abuse of power” from the US Departments of Justice and Homeland Security. Mamdani says ICE agents who shot man in New York looked like ‘mass shooters’ The New York mayor, Zohran Mamdani, compared US Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s (ICE) recent shooting of a man in Manhattan to a mass shooting scene – and called for an end to the agency’s operations in his city. Oscar Belgal, 28, was struck in the neck during an enforcement operation while he was in his car with his five-year-old child also inside. Describing his perspective on videos of the shooting scene that have emerged since, Mamdani told MS NOW it was unclear even to the mayor that the agents in the footage were law enforcement personnel based on their being in plainclothes. Federal judge orders temporary halt to taxpayer-funded pro-Trump TV ads A federal judge has ordered Donald Trump’s administration to temporarily halt the broadcast of taxpayer-funded television ads promoting the president ahead of the 3 November midterm elections. A temporary restraining order aimed at the ads is meant to stay in effect for at least 14 days. The administration “shall not enter into, renew, or expand any agreement authorizing the development, creation, dissemination, placement, or airing of the … advertisements,” the judge said in her ruling. She also ordered the administration to cancel the remaining portion of a $20m advertising purchase, halting further spending on the campaign. Anti-vaxxers target Texas measles doctors to cast doubt on deaths amid outbreak Amid rising measles outbreaks and fatalities across the US, anti-vaccine activists – including figures such as the HHS secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr, and Children’s Health Defense – are actively working to dispute official death tolls and cast doubt on the virus’s severity. To deflect accountability for the resurgence of preventable disease, these groups are promoting claims that patient deaths stem from medical error and inappropriate treatment rather than measles complications, even filing formal medical board complaints against treating pediatricians. Public health experts and physicians warn that this playbook fuels distrust, vilifies frontline healthcare workers, and distracts from the core issue of declining vaccination rates Latin American organised crime ‘may operate in 16 European countries’ A four-month investigation by the Guardian has revealed that the surge in cocaine trafficking to Europe is directly linked to the expanding presence of Latin American criminal networks in Europe, where they have forged close ties with local mafia organisations. The investigation, utilising databases, police and intelligence agencies, along with interviews with judges, prosecutors and experts from eight countries, shows that cartels and factions from Colombia, Brazil, Ecuador, Venezuela, Mexico and the US are active in at least 12 European countries. The figure could be even higher, as it includes only groups officially identified in Europe and does not include gangs that lack a physical presence in Europe while working in “joint ventures” with European mafias. In other news … RJ Mitte, the actor best known for Breaking Bad, has died aged 34. title: UK shoppers seek deals as grocery price inflation rises again
summary: Price of chocolates falls in run-up to Halloween, while supermarkets use special offers to draw in sales
text: Grocery price inflation in the UK has picked up further, prompting shoppers to turn to special offers to keep their bills down – while the price of chocolates has fallen in the run-up to Halloween. Supermarket prices were 2.5% higher than last year in the four weeks to 4 October, up from 2.3% last month, according to data from the retail analysts Worldpanel by Numerator. Spending on promotions over the last month was more than £250m higher than a year ago, with many shoppers using special offers to keep their grocery bills in check or to make pricier items and larger packs more affordable, Worldpanel said. Fraser McKevitt, the head of retail and consumer insight at Worldpanel, said: “With the autumn budget fast approaching [on 28 October], the cost of living continues to weigh heavily on the minds of shoppers. And the cost of filling up a car is only adding to the pressure on household budgets. “More than half tell us they’re very or extremely worried about petrol prices, and almost one in three say it’s already taking a real toll on their finances. Until the chancellor sets out his plans, we expect that caution to carry on showing up at the till, with shoppers leaning more heavily on promotions to keep their grocery spend under control.” However, in some good news for households stocking up on trick or treat supplies for Halloween, chocolate confectionery prices are 3% lower than a year ago. About 1.2 million households bought a pumpkin over the latest four weeks, up 10% year on year, while more than 250,000 households treated themselves to a pumpkin spice coffee. McKevitt added: “Halloween and Christmas are two of the most important moments of the year for chocolate confectionery, so falling prices will be welcome news for shoppers and retailers alike. “After the double-digit increases of 2025, a 3% drop won’t fully reverse what consumers have paid in recent months, but it should help ease some of the pressure on household budgets as the festive season approaches.” While sales of hot chocolate and soup surged in September compared with August, by 41% and 35% respectively, they fell sharply when compared with last year, by 20% and 4% respectively. A separate report from NielsenIQ showed total till sales at major UK supermarkets grew 1.4% in the four weeks to 3 October, down from 1.8% growth in the previous month, as shoppers remain cautious about spending. Summer favourites remained popular as September was unusually warm this year, with strong sales of mineral water (+17.4%) and ice-cream (+11.7%). Asda was the only big grocer to report a drop in sales, of 0.5%, in the 12 weeks to 4 October, Worldpanel said. The German discounter Lidl led in market share gains and now controls 8.6%, on the back of a 7.1% increase in sales driven by fruit, vegetables and wine. Sales at the online grocer Ocado increased by 12.4%, outpacing online sales across the sector at 5.5%. Spending through the tills was 1% higher at Tesco and 1.3% higher at Sainsbury’s, with the two retailers holding 27.8% and 15.2% of the market respectively. Asda’s share now stands at 11.5%, while Aldi holds 10.5% of the market, with sales at the discounter up 0.4% year on year. Beyond the supermarkets, grocery sales at Marks & Spencer rose by 14.9%.

title: How a scandal engulfing Brazil’s top court could return the Bolsonaros to power
summary: The judge who helped convict Jair Bolsonaro is caught up in a crisis that could benefit his son and damage Lula
text: Thundering to a crowd of thousands of far-right supporters in São Paulo on 7 September, Brazil’s Independence Day, the senator Flávio Bolsonaro focused less on his opponent in the presidential election, the leftist president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, than on someone who is not running at all. “Whoever votes for Lula is voting for Alexandre de Moraes,” Bolsonaro shouted, referring to the shaven-headed supreme court justice once described as “Voldemort” by Elon Musk. Although Lula did not appoint Moraes to the court, Bolsonaro’s supporters have linked the two men ever since the judge oversaw the case in which the senator’s father, the former president Jair Bolsonaro, was sentenced to 27 years in prison for attempting a coup. Now, just days before the election runoff on 25 October, Moraes is once again at the centre of a presidential scandal – one that Lula believes may have helped Flávio Bolsonaro overtake him to emerge as the frontrunner. The justice once hailed as democracy’s “saviour” for containing Jair Bolsonaro may now have helped pave the way for the family’s return to power. The scandal began with a police investigation, which found that Moraes’s wife’s law firm had a contract worth about £20m with Daniel Vorcaro, the banker accused of orchestrating Brazil’s largest banking fraud. Text messages also emerged suggesting a close relationship between Moraes and Vorcaro, though the judge denies the messages are authentic. Investigations subsequently revealed that at least four other justices had links to the disgraced banker, meaning half of the court’s 10 current justices have been drawn into the scandal. The crisis peaked last month with a ferocious exchange of insults between Moraes and another justice during a televised court session. A series of rulings followed in which the pair – as well as other judges aligned with each side – overruled one another, dominating public debate for weeks. Lula, the day after losing the first round, blamed his poor result in part on having to “carry on his back … the promiscuity” of the supreme court, in what many political observers saw as an attempt by the president to distance himself from the crisis. His campaign coordinator, Edinho Silva, said that, “in the eyes of society … [Lula] paid the price for that institutional damage”. Although analysts point to a range of reasons for the far right’s lead, from household debt to a simple preference for Flávio Bolsonaro, many agree that the supreme court crisis played a decisive role, particularly among indecisive voters who, with the electorate generally divided between two similarly sized left and right blocs, are the ones who ultimately decide the election. “These are people who thought that, just as they see congress, the country’s highest court had become corrupt, too. That deepened apathy among some who might otherwise have voted for Lula and fuelled the anti-system sentiment that feeds the far right,” said Camila Rocha, a political scientist who studies Brazil’s new right and has spent recent months interviewing undecided voters. “We asked people about the court crisis, and they would say: ‘Everything is very confusing, but one thing we do know is that the big villain is Alexandre de Moraes,’” she said. “Precisely the judge who jailed Jair Bolsonaro now emerges, for these people, as the big corrupt figure and the main villain.” Conrado Hübner Mendes, a professor of constitutional law at the University of São Paulo and a leading scholar of the supreme court, said Moraes put himself in that position by “embracing the role of heroic protagonist”. The judge blocked some of Jair Bolsonaro’s moves during his government and drew the ire of far-right figures such as Musk and Donald Trump. The US went as far as to impose sanctions on him, in a move widely seen as an attempt to interfere in Jair’s trial. On Monday, Moraes authorised Flávio Bolsonaro to resume visiting his father after a 90-day ban imposed in July, when the senator read out a letter from his father that Moraes considered a breach of Jair Bolsonaro’s ban on using social media. Legal scholars and some on the Brazilian left, while acknowledging Moraes’s decisive role in the coup trial, have also criticised several of his other rulings as authoritarian. “He took on a huge responsibility, and now he has thrown that away in the most mediocre way possible, with this alleged corruption case,” said Mendes. While acknowledging the contract between the law firm run by his wife, Viviane Barci de Moraes, and the disgraced banker – who is worth an extraordinarily large sum by Brazilian law firm standards – Moraes denied any wrongdoing. He said he had never ruled on any case involving Vorcaro and that there was therefore no conflict of interest. Vorcaro has been behind bars since he was arrested in November as he prepared to board a private jet from São Paulo to Malta. He is accused of leading a scheme through his Banco Master involving aggressive fundraising, unrealistic returns and falsified balance sheets that left an estimated £9bn hole, much of it involving public money and pensioners’ savings. Text messages extracted from Vorcaro’s phone show that, two days before his arrest, the banker asked someone whom police later identified as Moraes: “Do you think … I need to get out [of the country]?” Moraes denies being the recipient and accuses a fellow justice, André Mendonça, appointed by Jair Bolsonaro, of using the police against him for electoral reasons, allegedly to benefit Flávio’s campaign. Mendonça is one of the four other justices suspected of having links to Vorcaro. An institute he created is said to have taken out an £800,000 loan from one of the banker’s associates, though he says it has already been repaid. In the other justices’ cases, investigators uncovered links ranging from a £64m contract to an alleged stake in a fund that received £5.2m from Vorcaro. All deny wrongdoing. No reports had linked Lula to the scandal until Friday, when Veja magazine reported that Vorcaro allegedly said he had paid £4.5m to finance a 2024 Oliver Stone documentary about the president. The federal police and the public prosecutor’s office, however, said the banker had neither made the allegation nor provided evidence to support it in his testimony. Lula denied receiving money from the banker. Flávio Bolsonaro is being investigated over what happened to the £20m he was caught on tape asking Vorcaro to provide for a biopic about his father. One suspicion is that the money helped cover living and travel expenses for his brother, the former congressman Eduardo Bolsonaro, during his self-imposed exile in the US, where he lobbied the Trump administration against Lula. The senator said all the money went towards sponsoring the film, which still has no release date. Besides Flávio Bolsonaro’s lead, the far right’s sweeping victory ensured an even more conservative congress in 2027, including the senate majority needed to impeach supreme court justices – a demand among his father’s supporters since the former president was convicted. “With the scandal, the justices handed Bolsonarismo something it still didn’t have: an impeachable offence that could justify their removal,” said Mendes. “A court that ignores conflicts of interest and immerses itself in relationships with political and economic power is a court that has already become corrupted.” Even if no justice is impeached, should Bolsonaro win, he could be entitled to fill four seats as justices retire during his term, leaving the court with at least six of its 11 members appointed by either him or his father. “We can expect a court completely servile to the government,” Mendes said, adding that the separation of powers would be at risk and that the justices themselves bear part of the responsibility. “The court ended up doing to itself the work an autocratic project needs – and brought itself down”.

title: ‘No one’s here, no one knows’: north-east Ohio is ground zero for ICE flights
summary: Away from the public eye, deportation planes at Youngstown-Warren and Akron-Canton airports carry hundreds of immigrants daily amid Trump’s ICE crackdown
text: Just after 10.30am on a recent weekday morning, a Bombardier CRJ200 Air Wisconsin aircraft landed at Youngstown-Warren regional airport. Having made the 75-minute flight from Milwaukee, the 50-seater came to a halt and its twin engines fired down next to another Air Wisconsin plane and a larger Eastern Air Express Boeing 737, planes that flew in the evening before from Alexandria, Louisiana. Together, the planes – which combined can handle about 300 passengers at a time – and this austere, quiet airport a few miles from the Ohio-Pennsylvania state line, represent the cornerstone of the Trump administration’s Great Lakes deportation campaign. Last year, the facility, which handles no commercial flights, saw 398 “shuffle” – ICE-contracted flights between US airports – and direct deportation flights. With about 300 flights from this and the neighboring Akron-Canton regional airport respectively recorded so far this year by ICE Flights Monitor, an advocacy group, these small, often empty airports have seen more enforcement flights between US cities than many bigger metro areas. In fact, only seven other US airports this year have seen more deportation shuffle flights than the two combined. Turning these small airports into a key cog of the Trump administration’s deportation campaign has angered many. “We have to fight for the rights of others because if they’re going to come for them, you know who’s next; they could knock on our doors next,” said Erin Bracken-Sanchez, a military veteran and resident of Massillon, Ohio, who has come to the Youngstown-Warren airport to monitor the activities of the planes contracted by ICE. “They’re [using these regional airports] to be more obscure, to be under the radar. Who’s here? No one’s here; no one knows.” Away from towns and cities and largely out of the public’s eye, every day a network of contracted planes carries hundreds of immigrants caught up in Trump’s anti-immigration campaign between Wisconsin, Michigan, Ohio and Massachusetts. The deportation shuffle flights in north-east Ohio’s airports typically take place in late morning, with immigrants held at jails across the region being bused to the airport and boarded on to planes that typically fly on to Alexandria, Louisiana, where ICE operates a swathe of detention facilities that have been pilloried for human rights abuses. From there, immigrants are flown overseas. Sometimes, detention flights from north-east Ohio have taken immigrants directly to a tiny airport outside the Mexican town of Tapachula that is situated close to the border with Guatemala. Now, flight safety among airlines contracted by the Trump administration has also come into focus. On 28 September, a plane operated by Eastern Air Express, a Kansas City-headquartered company and one of ICE’s main contracting airlines, struck the left horizontal stabilizer of a parked aircraft belonging to the same company at the Akron-Canton regional airport. “No injuries were reported, and other airfield operations were not impacted. [The airport’s] operations team responded immediately to the incident. Incident investigation is conducted by the Ohio state highway patrol,” said Lisa Dalpiaz, a representative for the Akron-Canton regional airport. “One of the planes has left, and the other is undergoing maintenance at the FBO [fixed base operator].” The incident has worried advocacy groups. “We’ve been very concerned on the safety of detained passengers on charter flights and followed the incident in Ohio,” said Savi Arvey of ICE Flight Monitor. A subsidiary of Eastern Air Holdings, Eastern Air Express has recently been in the spotlight for failing safety standards. In July, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) proposed a $65,000 fine for Eastern Air Express for allowing 26 employees including pilots to “perform safety-sensitive functions when they were not subject to required random drug and alcohol testing”. A representative of the FAA said, “the process remains open.” Emails sent by the Guardian to Eastern Air Express, which operates 19 aircraft, asking if the company plans to conduct its own investigation of the plane collision at Akron-Canton regional airport last month, were not responded to. Airlines are supposed to report incidents such as wing collisions to the National Transportation Safety Board but there is no record of the incident on the agency’s website. A spokesperson for the NTSB said it “is not investigating that event” due to the absence of “substantial damage or serious injuries”. However, the agency did exactly that with regard to an incident involving a commercial airliner in San Francisco on 6 October. The Department of Homeland Security and ICE didn’t directly respond to questions from the Guardian asking if the agencies plan to review their safety requirements for contracting airlines, considering the 28 September incident. In January, Maura Healey, the Massachusetts governor, demanded Eastern Air Express and GlobalX, another airline contracted by the Trump administration to ferry immigrants to deportation sites, end those flights. But as recently as last week, an Air Wisconsin plane contracted by ICE that took off from Youngstown-Canton regional airport landed at Massachusetts’ Hanscom Field. All the while, the ICE deportation flights have placed an additional cost burden on these small Ohio airports that have been struggling for years. Since last February, these and dozens of other airports around the country used by ICE have found themselves out potentially millions of dollars in landing fees that airlines typically pay to airports they use. “As of February 2026, landing fee waivers for Government operations were extended to cover contractors working on their behalf, so no landing fees are owed to the airport,” said Dalpiaz, of the Akron-Canton airport. In August, the month for which the most recent data is available, Akron-Canton airport saw 34 ICE flights over 27 days, a rate that has been sustained since late April. All this is happening at a time when these small regional airports are struggling with falling passenger numbers. Back at Youngstown-Warren airport, pilots flying the Air Wisconsin plane that arrived from Milwaukee remained on the aircraft for several hours after landing. Nearby, ground crew set up a barrier under the left wing of the Eastern Air Express plane before walking off the tarmac and into the terminal. For a moment, a man dressed in black appears on the roof of the terminal building to watch the Air Wisconsin plane taxi. Across four hours at the airport, no detainees are seen walking, though several of the plane’s window blinds are closed shut. Arvey said that last year, six deportation flights from Youngstown were flown directly to Honduras and Guatemala, with the most recent taking place in June 2026. Bracken-Sanchez, who served in the US army in Kuwait in the 1990s and is a member of the Buckeye Veterans Coalition, said her motivation for monitoring the ICE flights is her family – two of her children are Hispanic. While taking part in a protest outside the Akron-Canton airport recently, Bracken-Sanchez said she saw a bus belonging to the Butler county sheriff’s department in south-west Ohio, where dozens of Haitian nationals are being held, pass through on to the runway. “I did not expect to go to the Akron-Canton airport, to the back gate where I used to go 27 years ago to the Ohio national guard, and watch them bring in buses of immigrants shackled to deport them out of the country,” she said. “It doesn’t make sense to me in America, the country that I fought for.”

title: ‘It’s not glamorous’: the volunteers counting flushed wet wipes on the banks of the Thames
summary: A Thames21 charity citizen science project helps track plastic pollution in the capital’s river
text: On a pale-blue Sunday morning on the foreshore of the River Thames, 40 people are searching for what others have tried to lose. Dotted across a 250-metre stretch under Hammersmith Bridge, they are combing through layers of silt, seashells and dirty driftwood to find one of the river’s most stubborn problems: wet wipes. “People come and walk here and it looks just like mud, at a distance,” says the organiser, Dr Felicity Rhodes. “And then you get closer in and see.” The dig forms part a citizen science project that has tracked sanitary litter on the banks of the Thames for nearly a decade. Set up by the environmental charity Thames21, volunteers are recruited to help map out the amount of wipes that are flushed down the toilet and washed up along the river. Findings are added to a database that quantifies plastic pollution on the banks of the Thames. “It’s not glamorous,” says Rhodes, the programme manager at Thames21. “But through this data generation, we’ve created this dataset of really robust, accurate data that’s given us an understanding of the wet wipes here on the foreshore.” Hydrographic surveyors from the Port of London authority (PLA) are assisting the project, and are riverside before the volunteers arrive, having meticulously marked out channels of the foreshore based on where the last count took place. Volunteers lay quadrats, square frames, on the riverbed and drag metal sticks through the mud. One drag can pull up a clump of flushed wet wipes from what had appeared to be just silt to the naked eye; they are counted, recorded and deposited into a bucket for disposal, along with the plastic, vapes and other rubbish curios that come up. Jim Powell, an operations manager and hydrographic surveyor at the PLA, explains why Hammersmith is such a hotspot for grime. “You’re on the inside of a bend of the river so the water velocities are slower,” he says. Material builds up on the inside because the water flows faster on the outside. “As soon as you get bits of wood and tyres, they start to trap sediment and other things start getting caught, like plastic wipes. Then it just snowballs from there.” Elio Gregori, 66, has attended about 300 sessions since he retired. “You can look at a place like this and assume that it’s mostly nice and clean, but under the surface is a wet wipe,” he says, fishing a knot of rotten-brown wipes out of his bucket as an exhibit. “When it’s in the environment, you wouldn’t really recognise it as a wet wipe. If you look down, it opens your eyes to how much of this stuff is around.” Many wet wipes contain plastic fibres and are designed to stay intact when wet – even some marketed as biodegradable. When London’s wipes are flushed down the toilet, they can end up on the riverbanks, mostly through storm water overflow and sewage outfall. Thames Water estimates 3.8bn wipes are flushed into its network each year – enough to build more than 10 wet and stinking Big Bens. “Plastic here on the foreshore has the potential to make its way into the ocean and into our ocean food system as well,” says Rhodes. “We want to remove plastic here so that it doesn’t become microplastic in the ocean.” A young refugee from Sudan attended the count with the community centre West London Welcome. “It’s really a shame for people to throw bad things through toilets,” he said. “This waste is in this nice area … people should have to be more careful in the environment where these things ended up.” Some relief arrived last year when the delayed Thames Tideway Tunnel opened – the £4.6bn project designed to reduce sewage discharges into the river. Then diggers came to this part of the foreshore a few months later to remove the infamous “Wet Wipe Island”, the 180-tonne amalgamation of wipes that had grown so large it had begun to alter the shape of the river. Thames21 estimates the work removed 5m wipes that had congealed into a 250-metre island. Now, Thames21 is back to assess what the Tideway Tunnel – the “super sewer” – and removing Wet Wipe Island has done. “Will we see fewer wet wipes? Most likely,” says Rhodes. “Are they re-accumulating? We might be able to start to see any changes and that’s why it’s really important to keep monitoring.” Last December, the government announced that selling single-use wet wipes containing plastic will be illegal by May 2027. It was a win for Thames21, who had for years been banging the drum and sharing their data with Fleur Anderson, the MP for Putney, who campaigned on the issue in parliament. By the end of the weekend’s count, Thames21 said volunteers had found 733 wipes in 50 sampling squares, compared with 1,584 found in the same spots in April. It is a substantial drop in the recorded count, although the PLA says it is still early days, and two surveys cannot yet establish precisely how much of it is due to the cleanups, the Tideway tunnel or changing conditions on the river. But for now, Thames21 volunteers plan to keep counting. “We expect that they’ll still wash up on the river for a time,” says Rhodes. “What we’re doing here is tracking the ongoing change in that.”

title: Millions of Medicaid recipients to face draconian requirements as of 1 January
summary: Trump’s reform law that seeks to make coverage harder to get, and to keep, includes working 80 hours a month
text: It is a date keeping US healthcare providers up at night: 1 January 2027. As the midterm elections loom, everyone from hospital leaders and to patient advocates are focused on the New Year, when Republicans scheduled the most controversial elements of their healthcare reform law to go into effect. Millions of Medicaid beneficiaries will be required, though a maze of government paperwork, to show they are working 80 hours a month. And that’s just the marquee change. “The costs to the family – and society as a whole – cannot be overstated,” said the American Academy of Pediatrics president, Dr Andrew Racine. HR 1, also known as the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” and signed into law by Donald Trump on 4 July 2025, cut roughly $1tn in federal spending from the healthcare industry – the biggest clawback of federal health spending ever. Paired with Republicans’ refusal to extend subsidies for plans in Obamacare marketplaces, the cuts are expected to result in about 17 million newly uninsured individuals through 2034. Although the US has one of the most widely privatized healthcare systems in the world, nearly half of all health spending is paid for by government – whether federal, state or local, according to the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS). Nearly 40% of US health spending in 2024 was from just two programs: Medicare and Medicaid, the public health insurance programs for the ageing and low-income. To put the scale of the $1tn cut into context, Medicaid spent $937bn in 2024, according to the CMS. As a result, advocates, researchers, hospital leaders and doctors are all expecting more medical debt, more delayed care and more people losing coverage for which they technically qualify. “There couldn’t be a clearer link,” said Dr Luke Messac, an emergency physician at Mass General Brigham and a historian who has written about medical debt. “We saw that when Medicaid eligibility was expanded the flow of medical debt rapidly declined and sustained that decline. “The easiest way to reverse that trend – to make medical debt more of a problem – is to yank people off Medicaid and leave them uninsured and unprotected.” To understand Republicans’ new work requirements, you have to go all the way back to the Affordable Care Act (ACA) of 2010, when the Obama administration required states to expand Medicaid to cover people earning up to 138% of the federal poverty level, or about $16,000 for a single person today. Republicans hated this, and for the better part of a decade resisted the change through a supreme court case and dozens of Obamacare repeal votes. However, over fits and starts, 44 states opted in. The deal was too sweet to pass up: states could insure many of their poorest residents and help their hospitals survive, with the overwhelming majority of the cost paid by the federal government. Today, more than 82 million people rely on Medicaid for health insurance, or about 23% of the entire American public, according to the Kaiser Family Foundation (KFF), a health policy research organization. HR 1 is a direct assault on that system. Consider first: the effects on regular people. Work requirements that go into effect in January will apply only to people in the 44 states that “expanded” Medicaid, and then only to people in the “expansion population”. That’s about 20 million people, according to KFF. Those people will need to prove they are working, going to school or volunteering at least 80 hours or earning $580 per month. People will also need to re-certify eligibility every six months, instead of every year. In short, Medicaid will be harder to get and harder to keep. KFF has come up with some hypothetical scenarios to illustrate how even qualified people might be tripped up by these bureaucratic hurdles. Consider Jane, who has a depressive disorder that does not qualify for an exemption from work requirements. In May, she experiences a depressive episode that makes it impossible for her to work 80 hours. In June, when her work requirement verification is due, her hours mean she is no longer eligible for Medicaid, and she becomes uninsured. Without insurance, she can no longer get her medication, which results in another depressive episode. Or, consider John, who loses his job and is out of work in April and May. He gets a job in June, but his state requires people to satisfy three months of work before they are eligible for Medicaid. John does not satisfy this requirement, and is denied Medicaid. September 2026 will be the first month in a “look-back period” in some states. “The insistence on these Medicaid work requirements, which is really just a way to decrease the rolls – that was the intention – is really going to increase the number of people with medical debt and the amount of medical debt in the system, which is bad not just for patients but for providers,” said Messac. HR 1 has wrought other changes too. Come January, Medicaid coverage will be winnowed down from three months of retroactive coverage to two months – or one depending on the applicant and the state. Alongside those changes in January are others that already went into effect. For instance, HR 1 made some legal immigrants ineligible for Medicaid. In the future, HR 1 will cut some accounting mechanisms that benefit children’s hospitals. All of the different types of patients HR 1 will affect has created a long list of advocacy groups worried about the effects. Advocates for the elderly are worried some people won’t be able to get as much retroactive Medicaid coverage for nursing care, since the legislation shortened retroactive Medicaid benefits. (Elderly or unwell people often don’t file for Medicaid coverage for nursing care right away, either because they are too sick or falsely believe Medicare covers it.) Advocates for children are worried parents will lose health insurance and have “spillover” to children. “When parents lose their health insurance, children may lose their coverage, too, even if they remain eligible,” said Racine. Beyond the impacts on individuals: consider the systemic. One of the most common places to seek healthcare in the US is the hospital, for everything from births to cancer screenings. The Urban Institute estimates that HR 1 will cause $278bn in “uncompensated care” by 2034 – health industry parlance for unpaid bills. That puts hospitals in a bind, many of which operate on the thinnest imaginable margins. “There is a consensus that, particularly in rural healthcare, there is this deepening crisis,” said Dr John Osborne, a former doctor at the Veterans Affairs administration in Washington state, and one of the organizers of a grassroots declaration of a rural health crisis in October. “I would say what’s happening in rural America is a harbinger of things to come throughout healthcare in the US.” Although rural hospitals were a particular concern during passage – a closure can leave patients traveling hours for even routine care – new research shows both rural and urban hospitals are now closing at the same rate. “Loss of access for acute care in-patient hospitals is not just a rural problem – it’s a national problem,” said Dr Thomas Tsai, a health policy researcher and surgeon at Brigham and Women’s hospital in Massachusetts and an author of the research. That raises the possibility that even in urban cores, healthcare becomes inaccessible as patients from near and far crowd in to try to access care, including many newly uninsured people who will tend to use the emergency room more often. “The impact will be profound,” said Dr John McCarthy, assistant dean for rural programs at the University of Washington School of Medicine, about HR 1. “Unless you have something that’s obviously really impressive, you have a five-hour wait – if you’re lucky.”

title: Ex-Chicago detective identified as killing child in 65-year cold case
summary: Police used recently discovered DNA to pin murder of eight-year-old girl on Thomas McInerney, who died in 2006
text: Chicago police on Monday said they recently used newly discovered DNA evidence to tie the 1960 murder of an eight-year-old girl to one of its own former homicide detectives. Thomas McInerney had been dead for 20 years by the time authorities issued a statement identifying him as the killer of Gloria Kowalewicz – well after he retired from the Chicago police department (CPD) and two federal public defender’s offices in Nevada where he worked as an investigator. Nonetheless, the CPD’s statement expressed a hope that the news about McInerney “brings a measure of closure to all who knew Gloria and her story”. “McInerney should have never worn the CPD star,” the statement added. “And it is devastating to accept that he was never identified and held accountable while he was alive.” The Chicago Tribune was the first to report on the exposure of McInerney as Gloria’s murderer – recounting in a lengthy article on Sunday how the girl’s killing, which shocked the city, was solved more than six decades later by DNA evidence gathered from a genetic ancestry website. Gloria was last seen alive on the morning of 12 November 1960 as she walked from her family’s West Englewood neighborhood home to a mass at a nearby church. She never made it to the service. Someone abducted her on the way and fatally shot her, and within hours her body was found discarded in a ditch at a forest preserve south-west of Chicago, police said in their statement. Police said they secured various pieces of evidence at the scene where Kowalewicz had apparently been murdered – including a bullet, her coat and a white communion purse with a prayer book inside. “Investigators also lifted a fingerprint from the strap of Gloria’s purse,” police noted. Meanwhile, the Tribune reported that police – along with volunteers from the ranks of local firefighters, Boy Scouts and military veterans – mounted a large search for the girl’s killer. A police-headed taskforce interviewed about 1,300 people in connection with Gloria’s slaying, among them a dozen individuals who were given lie-detector tests while being questioned. Police said none of that allowed them to identify a suspect, however. Yet that changed when investigators eventually recovered traces of semen on Kowalewicz’s coat, according to the Tribune, which reported that the victim was not believed to have been sexually assaulted. DNA submitted to a family tree website earlier in 2026 then enabled the FBI to connect McInerney to the semen traces at the scene of Gloria’s murder, the Tribune reported. Further DNA, fingerprint and ballistic testing then established that McInerney had killed Gloria, the CPD said in its statement on Monday. McInerney joined the Chicago police force in 1959, said his obituary, which was published after his death on 30 August 2006. The US army veteran was about to turn 25 at the time of Gloria’s murder, and his parents lived around the corner from the girl. The obituary said McInerney was investigating homicides for the CPD when he retired from the agency in 1987. He then worked as investigator for the federal public defender’s offices in Las Vegas and Reno, Nevada, until his retirement in 2004. McInerney’s obituary also touted his receiving “numerous commendations during his years with the [CPD]” – as well as his being recognized as outstanding federal defender investigator in 2003. It described him as a husband, a father to two sons and three daughters, and a grandfather to a dozen children. The CPD statement on Monday made it a point to say that Gloria’s parents died without ever knowing who had murdered their daughter. The agency called McInerney’s crime “abhorrent”, saying it “not only took the life of an eight-year-old child – but left … all who knew and loved her shattered as they searched for answers”. Separately, the FBI said in a statement reported by NBC News that McInerney’s DNA had been entered into an agency database. The FBI’s statement added that it would check whether McInerney’s DNA matched any other unsolved cases. Gloria’s brother, Adam Kowalewicz, told the Tribune that it was a relief to learn his sister’s murderer had been identified. But he said to the outlet that he was frustrated McInerney had died at age 70 without ever being made to face justice. “He never paid his dues,” Adam Kowalewicz said to the Tribune. “You hope he’s going to pay his dues with the Good Lord.”
