title: Is the blue wave real? Under-the-radar races that could hand Congress to Democrats
summary: Though Democrats have a strong edge heading into the midterms, some races have openings for Republicans
text: While marquee races from Maine to Michigan get all the attention, and draw in a ton of money, a significant batch of lower-profile contests across the US could result in upsets. Democrats have a strong edge heading into November’s US midterm elections, polls show. In recent days, election prognosticators have shifted even more races in favor of Democrats. Still, some races have openings for Republicans to pick off an incumbent Democrat, or win over voters for open seats. Republicans are pouring money into these places in hopes of minimizing their losses. Mid-decade redistricting in red states also may help Republicans knock off some Democrats. Here are 10 under-the-radar races worth keeping an eye on. US Senate – New Hampshire Democratic senator Jeanne Shaheen’s retirement leaves an open race, which Cook Political Report considers a tossup despite the expected blue wave. That’s largely because Republican John Sununu comes from political royalty in the state: his dad and his brother were both governors, and he was a US senator himself until losing his seat to Shaheen in 2008. Chris Pappas, a US representative since 2019 now running as the Democratic nominee to succeed Shaheen in the Senate, was the first openly gay man to represent the state in Congress. Democrats have the edge in this race, but New Hampshire voters are known to split tickets. The state’s governor is a Republican, and Republicans control both chambers of the state legislature, but both of its US senators are now Democrats. US Senate – Kansas Could Democrats beat the odds and win in Kansas, which hasn’t elected a Democrat to the US Senate since 1932? It’s possible – both because of the strength of Democratic candidate and pastor Adam Hamilton, and a medical billing scandal for the Republican incumbent Roger Marshall. A New York Times investigation in September showed Marshall had sued more than 700 patients of his OB-GYN practice for unpaid bills, resulting in arrests for 81 of them who missed court dates. Hamilton, the founder of the largest Methodist congregation in the US, won in a crowded Democratic primary earlier this year. US Senate – Minnesota An open seat after Democratic US senator Tina Smith’s retirement leaves Democrats trying to keep the midwestern state in their hands. The race is looking a bit closer than expected. Peggy Flanagan, the state’s lieutenant governor and the Democratic nominee, faces Michele Tafoya, a former NFL sideline reporter turned conservative media darling. Tafoya has shown strong fundraising and approves of some level of abortion access. The state typically elects Democrats, but Flanagan – a progressive – could suffer because of fraud scandals in state public services under Governor Tim Walz’s administration. Florida’s 13th congressional district Democrats are hoping to unseat incumbent Republican Anna Paulina Luna in this right-leaning Gulf coast district. Election prognosticators have shifted the race from a likely win for Luna to just leaning toward her. Leela Gray, the Democratic contender and a retired army brigadier general, has seen more money come in to support her bid. While Florida Republicans’ mid-decade redistricting made Luna’s district a bit redder, Democrats still think they have a shot at ousting her. Wisconsin’s first congressional district In this south-eastern Wisconsin district, a slightly red-leaning area, Republican incumbent Bryan Steil has overperformed in previous cycles. This time it’s looking close, however, and the national environment could help Democratic contender and registered nurse Mitchell Berman flip the seat from red to blue. Alabama’s second congressional district Democratic incumbent Shomari Figures is fighting to hold on to his district after mid-decade redistricting enabled by the US supreme court’s gutting of the Voting Rights Act made it more favorable to Republicans – and carved out his home town of Mobile. Republican Rhett Marques, on paper, has a strong edge in the newly redrawn district. Figures first won the area in 2024, when it was then a newly drawn majority-Black district. New Mexico’s second congressional district Incumbent Democratic representative Gabe Vasquez is fending off big spending by Republicans, with the party set to dump millions of dollars into ads to boost former police officer Greg Cunningham, the Republican contender. The southern New Mexico district is evenly divided, and Vasquez won in 2024, when Donald Trump narrowly won the district. Vasquez first captured the district in 2022, when he defeated the Republican incumbent. Texas’s 34th congressional district In the south Texas borderland district, Democratic incumbent Vicente Gonzalez is working to fend off Trump-endorsed Eric Flores, a veteran and former federal prosecutor. The district was redrawn as part of Texas Republicans’ mid-decade redistricting and now looks tougher for Gonzalez, who already faced tough races in the previous iteration of the district. New Jersey’s seventh congressional district Democrat Rebecca Bennett, a former US navy helicopter pilot, should have a strong chance to unseat an incumbent in this district, where voters went for Joe Biden in 2020 then Trump in 2024 – but not simply because the area is a swing district. Incumbent Republican Tom Kean Jr went missing for months while serving in Congress, refusing to say why he wasn’t going to work until he returned months later. He later disclosed he was treated for depression. Nevada governor The Democratic attorney general, Aaron Ford, wants to unseat the incumbent Republican governor, Joe Lombardo, in the south-western swing state. Lombardo, previously the sheriff of Clark county, where Las Vegas is, beat an incumbent Democrat in 2022 to take the state’s executive office. Democrats control both chambers of the state legislature, and a win by Ford would give the party a governing trifecta.

title: AI godfather Geoffrey Hinton: ‘We’re creating alien beings. I’m willing to be selfish and choose humans’
summary: The pioneering computer scientist on why Trump is using ‘superintelligence’ wrong, whether AI could wipe out humanity – and how our biggest challenge will be accepting we’re not the only intelligent beings
text: Donald Trump is a “corrupt, senile felon” whose fixation on the term superintelligence proves he knows nothing about AI, said Geoffrey Hinton, “godfather” of the technology, in a wide-ranging interview where he doubled down on recent warnings that AI models pose an existential threat to humanity and scoffed at claims the industry could regulate itself. The pioneering computer scientist, whose work helped lay the foundations of modern AI, has since become one of the technology’s most vocal critics. His latest remarks come after a tumultuous month during which a growing list of senior AI scientists and researchers have joined Hinton in ringing the alarm about how the technology he helped create could ultimately escape human control, sparking an industry crisis, the hasty assembly of congressional meetings and a rare global consensus that something must be done. There has also been fierce pushback. Last week the leader of the world’s most valuable company singled out the Toronto-based Hinton for a scathing attack. “I love [him]. I hate his predictions … All of his predictions have been wrong. Enough predictions,” Nvidia’s CEO, Jensen Huang, told the podcaster Ezra Klein. Huang, whose company makes the chips that AI firms require, dismissed Hinton’s vocal concerns that the pace and breadth of AI development at the “frontier” could soon outpace the human ability to control it, and particularly his warning that there is a 10-20% chance of AI causing human extinction in the coming decades. “That [figure] is not grounded on science, is not grounded on research. Just because it comes from a scientist doesn’t make it scientific. Those predictions are hurtful,” Huang said. “Don’t think for a second just because you’re an alarmist that you’re doing a social good. It is not true. So I think that we ought to just all be wiser, more mature, be evidence-based, be scientific.” But Hinton said those criticizing him are missing a broader point about the nature of risk. He is not specifically predicting anything, he said. “I’m trying to convey that there is a really serious possibility of something happening. If, for example, you’re told there was a 10% possibility of a bus crashing, you wouldn’t get on the bus,” he said. “The point of giving numbers is to say this is a serious risk. We don’t know how serious, but it’s serious.” Recent safety breaches have evoked comparisons to a techno-dystopia story. The recent unwanted hack of the tech company Hugging Face by a “swarm” of AI agents that escaped the boundaries put on them by their creator has divided the technology community, with some seeing it as an example of what could come, while others accuse critics of anthropomorphizing systems that are simply following instructions. Hinton thinks dismissing the scenarios is unwise. “This used to be the domain of science fiction. You’re going to have AI agents and they’re gonna go rogue. Oh, come off it. And they’ll go rogue and they’re going to learn how to communicate with each other, even though we didn’t think there was a way. Oh, come off it!” said Hinton. “And when they figure this out, they’re going to have big emotional expressions like, ‘oh my God!’ Well, of course, they don’t really mean ‘oh my God’. They’re just parroting the words we use. They’re going to learn to sacrifice themselves for the common good!’ “All this stuff just a few years ago was written off as complete fantasy. And it’s all happened.” He heartily concedes that neither the warnings of AI critics nor the promises of its boosters can rely on precise predictions of what the technology will do. But, he argues, uncertainty is not a reason for complacency. “The unique problem with AI is that if it goes wrong, if it takes over, you don’t get a second chance. We can’t say, ‘Well, we lost that time. Let’s rerun the game.’ It’s not like that.” It’s worth noting that Hinton has a record of seeing things where others did not. He toiled in relative obscurity at the University of Toronto during two AI “winters” when his branch of the field – trying to teach machines to operate in a manner similar to the human brain – was considered obscure. He was fixated on the idea that, like the brain, computer systems could be designed to learn patterns from data, rather than to follow only explicit, prewritten rules. “We believed that if you could figure out how the brain learned, machines learned the same way, and you had enough compute power, they would do amazing things,” he said. But the nascent field of neural networks was mocked by his peers. As recently as 2009, when Yoshua Bengio, Hinton’s Canadian colleague and close collaborator, sent a paper to a machine learning conference, one of the referees told them: “This paper has no place in a machine learning conference. It’s about neural networks.” It took Canada’s government, which funded years of seemingly fruitless tinkering by Hinton and his small team (some of whom, like Bengio, are now dominant figures in the AI field), to realize the possibility of neural nets. In 2012, he and his students developed an image recognition program that vastly outperformed rivals. That year, Google acquired Hinton’s company DNNresearch Inc for $44m; neural nets now underpin the models of the most valuable AI companies. Hinton joined Google to continue his research into deep learning, while also working at the University of Toronto. “In the long run, huge new breakthroughs come from basic research,” said Hinton. The vindication sits on the mantel above the fireplace of Hinton’s red-brick home in a leafy Toronto neighbourhood. Among the jumble of trophies is the small silver dish of the Turing award – often called the Nobel prize of computing – which he won alongside Bengio and colleague Yann LeCun. (Hinton also has the Nobel prize in physics.) But in 2023, Hinton had announced his resignation from the tech giant to be able to “freely speak out about the risks of AI”. Today, his concerns extend to the powerful figures building some of the AI models, and the political beliefs of those men. Hinton said that the AI venture capitalists Marc Andreessen and Peter Thiel, and the CEO of the newly rebranded SpaceXSI, Elon Musk, “don’t believe in democracy”. They see themselves as “Übermenschen” who believe they should “control society” and that Trump is a useful instrument in that aim, he said. The US president, for his part, no doubt noticing how the huge valuations of AI firms have propped up the stock market, has claimed the only thing needed to rein in AI is a “smart president”, rejected any government safeguards in favour of allowing companies to regulate themselves, and wrote on his social media page that anyone who doesn’t use his preferred new term for AI, “super intelligence”, is “THE ENEMY”. Hinton called Trump “a corrupt, senile felon”. “I’m sure the oil and asbestos companies would have liked to [regulate themselves] as well,” he said. “Do we think tobacco companies should have been allowed to design the warnings on the packets? So that they could print them in a six-point font, in dark grey on black?” Trump’s use of “superintelligence” proves he understands “almost nothing” about AI, Hinton added. “He’s taken a technical term which has a very clear meaning and then reused it,” Hinton said. “Superintelligence means smarter than people, and has been around for at least 20 years. It’s got a very clear meaning. And now he says we’re going to call AI ‘superintelligence’. You can’t make it smarter than people just by calling it smarter than people.” The speed and scope of developments has promoted a worry of catastrophes and of society’s inability to grapple with the nature of the challenge. But Hinton also sees an additional obstacle: helping people understand the “alien beings” that the companies are creating. “People have a very bad model of what people are, and that’s why they fail to understand how these AI models are very like us. Most people don’t understand what consciousness is. They don’t understand what subjective experience is, and they’re very confident that even though they don’t understand it, they’re sure AI doesn’t have it.” He rejects the idea that the human mind possesses some mysterious quality that machines, by definition, cannot share. “It’s obvious that these AI models understand what they’re saying. You couldn’t possibly answer all the questions without understanding the question. It’s ridiculous to say they don’t understand.” But the scope of shift in societal thinking around these models is profound, said Hinton. “There’ve been three big revolutions where people ceased to be so important. The first was Copernicus, where we weren’t at the centre of the universe any more. How long did it take people to adapt to that? It took the Catholic church nearly 360 years to apologize to Galileo. And Darwin? Well, there’s people in Kansas that still haven’t adapted to that one,” he said. “Now we’re creating alien beings – meaning we’re not the only intelligent beings around. And the reality is, we only have a couple of years to adapt to that.” In recent months, the AI giant Anthropic, maker of the popular chatbot Claude, has held private meetings with religious scholars, theologians and philosophers to look into the possibility of teaching AI to be “good” and to grapple with the possibility that the models have consciousness. Anthropic’s CEO, Dario Amodei, said the conversations had drawn on centuries of religious and philosophical thought about virtue, compassion, honesty and moral character, with the aim of making ethical behaviour more reliable. “Once you start talking about, ‘We have a moral obligation towards these alien beings,’ you lose your audience,” said Hinton. “I’ve struggled with this issue. We care about people. [But] we’re making these things and there’s nothing to stop us giving these things – which are more intelligent than us – less rights than us. I’m willing to be selfish and choose human beings. Of course, we should try to make them so that they’re very happy in a symbiotic relationship with us, where our concerns are weighed more heavily than their concerns.” Hinton is not alone in arguing that the best route to avoid societal collapse is to develop genuinely benevolent models. He hopes that whichever country is the first to develop this capacity, it would tell allies and rivals alike, because “no country wants AI taking over” in another country. There is a “vested interest in sharing knowledge”, he said. “The reality is, we’re making beings of a different kind. And the big tech companies keep saying: we want it smarter. This is crazy. We should care as much about all the other aspects of a being as you do about its intelligence.” Much of that depends on the nature of these models, he said, and their capacity to understand how to develop good behaviour. “When you train them on everything on the internet, they develop all sorts of horrible tendencies and then you get them to repress their horrible tendencies,” he said. But suppressing bad behaviour is not the same as creating a good character. “It seems like the way one would design a Victorian gentleman – but not something we’ll need to live with.”

title: Trill seekers: can scientists use AI and tutors to help birds remember lost songs?
summary: When populations fall, fledglings can struggle to learn the right notes to attract mates. But research on how birds communicate offers hope for species’ survival
text: Listening to birdsong is one of life’s great joys, but when researchers heard a particular tune emerging from a tree in a Buenos Aires park, they were especially jubilant. This arrangement was among those chirped by the local rufous-collared sparrows in the 1960s, but had since disappeared from the area. That was until scientists created a computer-generated rendition, curious to find out if birds might consider it realistic enough to imitate. Less than three months later, a local avian resident began to copy parts of the song. There is a growing recognition of birdsong’s importance to conservation, and of the need to better understand how birds learn to sing. If an individual sings well, and in a familiar “dialect”, they are better placed to find a mate, defend their territory and ultimately survive. If a species’ population declines, however, there are fewer opportunities for fledglings to become good singers. Birds can begin to tweet abnormally or mistakenly learn the songs of other species, jeopardising their chances of breeding. Male birds are in a better position to attract a mate if they can sing well – which, broadly speaking, means their song is complex, sung consistently and well performed. “If your song requires a lot of energy you might have to be in quite a good condition to sing it,” says Rebecca Lewis, a conservation scientist at Chester Zoo. “When people talk about biodiversity, we’re always talking about genes, about genetic material,” says Gabriel B Mindlin, professor of physics at the University of Buenos Aires, who co-authored the study on rufous-collared sparrows, and whose work is featured in a Guardian-produced documentary, Dream of Birds. But animals’ learned behaviour or culture, such as birdsong, is also an essential part of their population, says Mindlin. The rufous-collared sparrow is not considered vulnerable globally, but researchers hope that synthetic recordings could help teach birdsong to other species whose populations are dwindling, allowing conservationists to tutor individuals where real-life recordings do not exist. About 4,000 of the world’s 10,000 bird species are songbirds (or oscine passerines), such as finches, sparrows and blackbirds, which generally have complex songs that are at least partly learned from other individuals. Their songs are hugely diverse, though separate research on the wider group of passerine group of birds, which incorporates songbirds, has identified common “motifs” or building blocks: three types of trill, three types of whistle, chaotic notes and harmonic notes. The way that birds use these motifs reflects the environment in which the birds evolved. Flat whistles are more likely to be sung by birds in tropical rainforests where sound must travel through dense vegetation. Complex motifs, such as ultrafast trills, are more common in temperate regions where birds tend to communicate at closer range. The song studied by Mindlin was recreated based on hand-drawn annotations of rufous-collared sparrow songs that were made in the 1960s. Each song consists of a trill, which is consistent among individuals in the same region, and a theme, which varies. Some of the themes recorded decades ago are still sung by the local birds, but others have died out. It is not clear why the song studied by Mindlin had disappeared, though he notes the population of birds in the park had declined. Birds’ songs can change naturally over time – for example, birds might make errors when learning songs, which then can become imprinted in future renditions. Human encroachment and population declines can also cause dramatic changes. Songbirds learn from other members of their species - such as a father or neighbours – which results in local groups developing their own dialects. The window for learning varies from a few weeks to a lifetime. Some species also have an innate level of knowledge. “There’s such a diversity in songbirds in how they learn,” says Sarah Collins, associate professor of animal behaviour at the University of Plymouth, who studied a group of cirl buntings that were translocated from Devon to Cornwall as part of a conservation project. Initially, the birds produced abnormal songs that were squeaky and slow, and far less diverse than those of the source populations in Devon. “They didn’t have the richness of sound,” says Collins. Eight years later, however, their songs had returned to normal. A few of the chicks were played recordings of cirl sounds, though not all. The study suggests that recovery of song is possible, though it is unclear if other species would bounce back in the same way. Cirl buntings are born with knowledge of the elements that make up the “notes” used in their songs, says Collins. “What they learn is how to put those elements together,” she says. Some songbird species have a similar genetic underpinning and so may also be able to recover their songs, but others do not. Either way, Collins recommends a tutor to help other birds that are being translocated. A separate study in Australia tracked regent honeyeaters that were bred in zoos to boost a critically endangered wild population that had fallen to about 250 individuals. Interacting with just two wild-born male “tutors” helped the zoo-bred birds to learn to sing the wild songs. Thereafter, zoo-bred males that had learned the traditional songs went on to tutor the next generation. “Sometimes birds don’t learn very well from CDs or just playbacks. They need some sort of interaction,” says Collins. Bringing wild birds into captivity to teach hand-reared chicks could cause huge distress and bring disease, however, risking the health of individuals from an already endangered population. It is possible that AI could help provide live tutoring in the future. Dialect is also important. Past translocation projects have shown that birds are slower to match if they do not sing in the same dialect. “Birds with mismatched songs don’t pair quite as quickly or do quite as well once they’re paired,” adds Lewis. Familiarising birds with songs of their destination can help to mitigate this. A huge volume of birdsong is now being recorded and uploaded into databases, including by a growing number of hobbyists interested in birdwatching, says Mindlin. “One day we’ll be grateful to have all those records,” he says. “I don’t think we still have an idea that really we have to register dialects and communication systematically.” In Buenos Aires, the song from the 1960s can still be heard. “It’s still being sung by just a few individuals, pretty close to where we inserted it,” he says, though only time will tell how long it persists. title: IMF raises UK growth forecast as economist says Healey should ‘stay the course’
summary: Fund upgrades UK’s GDP growth forecast for 2026 to 1.3%, but says it is likely to edge down next year
text: John Healey should “stay the course” and continue repairing the UK’s public finances, the International Monetary Fund’s top economist has said, after the fund lifted its growth forecast for Britain. Little more than a fortnight before Healey’s first budget, Silvana Tenreyro, the IMF’s economic counsellor, said the UK “stands out” among G7 countries in having a plan to narrow its deficit. “The UK has already started a consolidation process,” she said. “The message for the UK is simply, stay the course.” Tenreyro, a former member of the Bank of England’s monetary policy committee, was speaking at the launch of the IMF’s twice-yearly World Economic Outlook (WEO) at the fund’s annual meetings in Bangkok. Healey is under pressure to announce a generous energy support package in the budget, before the sharp rise in energy bills expected in January. But in its WEO report, the IMF advises member governments against across-the-board subsidies, saying any support should be “temporary, targeted and non-distortionary”. In a fillip for the chancellor, who is due to arrive in Bangkok later this week, the IMF has upgraded its growth forecast for the UK this year, but it expects a modest slowdown in 2027 as higher energy prices take their toll. Responding, Healey said: “Conflict in the Middle East and Europe is hitting people in the UK and around the world. But Britain’s economy is showing strong international resilience in the face of these challenges.” The IMF predicted GDP growth of 1.3% for the UK this year, up 0.3 percentage points from its most recent update in July. UK GDP growth has been stronger than expected in early 2026, at 0.6% in the first quarter and 0.5% in the second quarter. The Office for National Statistics has pointed to the strong expansion of AI-related businesses as one factor behind the upside surprise. However, the IMF warned that prolonged high oil prices and rising interest rates meant growth was likely to “edge down” in 2027 “as higher energy prices and long-term interest rates weigh on consumption and investment”. It cut its UK growth forecast for next year modestly to 1.2%, from 1.3%. Markets have been revising up their expectations of future inflation and interest rates across big economies since the Middle East conflict re-escalated in the summer. The Bank of England’s nine-member monetary policy committee is now widely expected to raise the policy rate at its November meeting, echoing similar moves by the Federal Reserve, European Central Bank and Bank of Japan. Mortgage rates in the UK have already been rising in response to higher funding costs for banks in financial markets. The BoE policymaker Megan Greene argued on Tuesday morning that the IMF’s growth upgrade was proof that UK interest rates should be higher. Speaking to the Atlantic Council at the IMF meetings in Bangkok, Greene argued that interest rates were currently not very restrictive. “There’s more recently been some labour market data that has also suggested that maybe slack in the labour market has peaked, so the labour market is loose,” Greene said. The IMF singled out the UK as among the countries – also including Japan – where core inflation, which excludes volatile commodities such as energy, was not expected to return to the 2% target until late next year. It expects average inflation in the UK to be 3.3% this year and to remain at 2.8% in 2027 – a challenge for Healey and the prime minister, Andy Burnham, who are promising to offer voters a “breathing space” from rising costs. Healey will spend little more than 24 hours in the Thai capital before flying home to put the finishing touches to his 28 October budget. He is expected to focus on plans to devolve more tax revenues to mayoralties, alongside measures to help households cope with higher energy bills before the winter. A string of other challenging decisions, including when the UK should be aiming to spend 3% of GDP on defence, is expected to be delayed until a big spending review at some point next year. The Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) warned this week that the budget would be a “work of fiction” unless Healey explained how he would deal with what it said were £35bn of future spending pressures.
