title: Andy Burnham promises ‘serious dialogue’ over UK’s relationship with EU
summary: PM hails next month’s ‘reset’ summit as first step to closer ties, but tensions over trade may prove problematic
text: Andy Burnham has promised a “serious dialogue” over the UK’s future place in Europe, saying the existing relationship is “not good enough” as he framed next month’s Brussels summit as a possible first step to EU membership. The prime minister said Britain must take a “clear-eyed rational look” at its long-term relationship with the bloc to boost economic growth and control immigration, which needed to go beyond Labour’s existing red lines. The next “reset” summit will take place on 20 November, ending months of uncertainty, with the two sides seeking to sign deals on food and drink, youth mobility and emissions trading, which Burnham hopes could provide a £10bn-a-year boost to the economy. One EU diplomat said a deal on the three “significant but modest” issues needed to be approved as a test of the UK’s good faith so both sides could get on with the “real reset” in the longer-term relationship. But the UK remains braced for a possible row over protectionist “Made in Europe” trade rules amid industry fears they could lock out UK manufacturers, prompting the prime minister to pledge he would raise concerns with his EU counterparts. Burnham was also forced to clarify that he did not think Russian interference in the 2016 Brexit campaign had affected the final result, after he raised questions about the legitimacy of the outcome in comments at the weekend. In a statement to MPs, the first since the party conference recess, an otherwise confident-sounding Burnham said it would be a “major dereliction of duty” for his government to turn away from exploring closer relations with the EU. “We should not turn our backs on this opportunity and I hope all sides of this house will get behind the government’s efforts to land a positive outcome,” he said. “I believe our chances of doing so will be enhanced by being open to a discussion about our relationship with the EU in the longer term. If we are serious about promoting growth, controlling immigration, upholding our values and security, it is a conversation we must have. “Sticking with the status quo is not good enough for Britain. Worse, it would be a major dereliction of duty to turn away. We need to take a calm, clear-eyed, rational look at the world as it is today to consider what is best for our country. “Our immediate priority is securing a successful outcome at the summit, and I believe we should then set up a serious dialogue about the different options for our relationship in the long term.” Burnham denied he was reopening the Brexit debate, insisting he respected the referendum result, but added that he wanted to take a “pragmatic approach” to boost economic growth and improve cooperation on migration. He was forced on to the back foot over his remarks on a podcast on Sunday that Russia had interfered over Brexit, rejecting suggestions from Kemi Badenoch, the Conservative leader, that he may have been loose with his language. “It is a matter of record that Russian actors sought to interfere in the 2019 general election, and we think it is inconceivable that this was the first time,” he said. Burnham had said on Sunday it was clear that Russia had interfered in the 2016 Brexit referendum after he sought answers when he arrived in No 10. He did not disclose who gave him the assessment, what evidence it was based on or, crucially, whether any interference had affected the result. Downing Street said the prime minister “absolutely” accepted the Brexit referendum result and believed it to be legitimate, while the foreign minister, Stephen Doughty, said it was clear Russia had attempted to interfere but had failed. In his statement, Burnham told MPs they were right to raise the question of the “loss of immigration control” that came with Brexit, as Labour grapples with continuing public concern over the issue, and suggested Brussels recognised this. The UK is excluded from Eurodac, a database that holds biometric and ID data to identify asylum seekers and irregular migrants, and exited the Dublin regulation, a legal mechanism to return refugees to the European country through which they had first entered or transited. But while the prime minister told MPs a return to free movement was “not on the table” in his discussions with the EU, and said he would honour Keir Starmer’s manifesto red lines, he was unable to rule it out for a post-election future. Sources on both sides believe they will be able to get other issues over the line at the summit next month, suggesting that a food and phytosanitary agreement would have been reached in July if the summit had gone ahead on its original date. Issues still to be resolved include a transition period for grains grown in the UK using recently approved fungicides not yet licensed in the EU. This would allow farmers harvesting this year to sell stockpiles next year even with the different regulations. The thorniest issue remains the youth mobility programme, allowing EU and British citizens under 30 to live, work or study in each other’s countries for up to three years. The two sides are at odds over the overall numbers, as well as the tuition fees students would pay at British universities. The biggest current risk to the UK of not aligning more fully with the EU is being locked out of the new Made in Europe initiative – aimed primarily at imports from China in strategic sectors such as renewable energy, nuclear and electric cars – which will block British-made components being used in EU supply chains. EU sources have insisted there can be no agreement on the issue with the UK at the summit, because the bloc is yet to agree its own position on the proposals. EU lawmakers hope to agree a position on a key proposal, the Industrial Accelerator Act, in December. But Brussels is, at least, open to discussing the issue, and it may be part of the summit statement – a joint text agreed by both sides. The UK has the support of the Netherlands, Poland and Italy for inclusion in the scheme, but France in particular has posed a stumbling block. Burnham acknowledged that Made in Europe presented “risks” to British manufacturing, perhaps in an attempt to address some concerns inside government that Downing Street hasn’t been prioritising the issue. He said: “It is important that we get to an arrangement here that works for both the UK and the EU. After all, we’re both trying to deal with the same issue, which is Chinese exports and the damaging effect that is having on our industry.”

title: After two tragic incidents in months does safety at English zoos need a rethink?
summary: Even though a man was mauled to death by a tiger and three-year-old was attacked in crocodile enclosure, experts say public protection is robust
text: On a busy Saturday afternoon at a zoo in Yorkshire, visitors looked on in horror as a man climbed into a tiger habitat, minutes after posing for a photograph beside it. Eyewitnesses said he scaled a metre-high viewing barrier, before dropping into the enclosure below, overpowering a woman who tried to pull him back. The resident 30-stone Siberian tiger, named Altai, was seen pawing at the man, who was dragged away, and later declared dead at the scene. Yorkshire Wildlife Park remained closed on Monday, while a City of Doncaster council spokesperson said the local authority had launched a health and safety investigation into the matter. It marked the second serious incident at a UK zoo in just a few months. In June, a three-year-old boy was seriously injured after being attacked by one or more crocodiles when he ended up in the enclosure at Johnsons of Old Hurst, near Huntingdon in Cambridgeshire. But experts have said that recent events do not reflect on zoo practices, and may instead point to issues with human behaviour, or mental health or support services. “These were two really terrible events, but rather than being about zoos themselves, I wonder whether they could reflect wider issues in society,” said Amy Dickman, professor of wildlife conservation and the director of WildCRU at the University of Oxford. “Given how many millions of zoo visits there are in a year, these are vanishingly rare instances, although of course that doesn’t negate how deeply tragic they are when they occur,” Dickman, an expert in big cat conservation, added. “I would not conclude that there was a major issue with zoo safety – the harsh reality is that it is virtually impossible for zoos to stop people who are very determined to breach safety measures.” In the Cambridgeshire incident, the boy was allegedly thrown into the crocodile enclosure. Police arrested a 30-year-old man from Norfolk on suspicion of attempted murder at the time of the incident, and police said he was “assessed as not being fit for interview”. This week, a spokesperson for Cambridgeshire police said the investigation was still under way and the suspect had been bailed until 17 December. “Two incidents have happened in the last few months, which is obviously really upsetting and distressing for the sector, but they are actually very, very rare,” Jo Judge, the chief executive at British and Irish Association of Zoos and Aquariums (BIAZA), said. There are hundreds of zoos, aquariums and animal attractions in the UK, and about 32 million people visit BIAZA member zoos and aquariums across Britain and Ireland every year. “The industry has already put in place so many safety measures that it is not being seen as a rising problem or something that we’re not doing enough about. These are just very unusual and very rare incidences,” she added. “It is unbelievable that these two incidents have happened so closely together.” Dickman said that because animals kept in enclosures do not come into contact with humans as those in the wild may do, “for someone to walk into that environment is probably far more dangerous, ironically, than if you were out in the wild with animals that were used to navigating those spaces alongside people.” She said she had “never visited a zoo in the UK and thought ‘this is dangerous’,” adding there was “layer upon layer of protection against people interacting with dangerous animals” and that “you do have to do it very intentionally”. All zoos in the UK must be licensed and follow strict safety procedures to protect their animals and human staff and visitors, with guidelines in place for zoo enclosures, including for sizing and perimeter fences. “There is no accidental falling into a category 1A dangerous animal enclosure, it just doesn’t happen – it’s not designed that way,” said Campbell Murn, a lecturer in conservation science at University of Reading, who until recently sat on Defra’s Zoos expert committee. Category 1A refers to a high-risk species kept in zoos that is capable of causing a human fatality, and includes rhinos, elephants, great apes and big cats. “In terms of preventing intentional entry to enclosures, there’s locks, there’s barriers,” he added. “But short of putting an electric fence [up], which of course has its own health and safety considerations, the protocol remains patrolling staff keeping an eye out for unusual behaviour. “It’s simply not possible though, at an attraction like Yorkshire Wildlife Park that gets hundreds of thousands – if not over a million – visitors a year to keep an eye on everybody all the time.” He said safety had to be balanced against visitor experience, so zoo-goers don’t get “a sense of walking into an electrified fence fortress where they can’t do anything other than look through heavy steel bars”, and used the analogy of “a determined thief”. “If a determined thief wants to get in your house, they’re going to get in your house,” he said. “You can mitigate risk to a certain point but there’s sometimes no stopping events from happening, unfortunately.” Paul Rose, a senior lecturer in psychology (animal behaviour) at the University of Exeter, also said that “public behaviour can be unpredictable, as we all know”. “There will be mitigation in place, such as high fencing, standoff barriers, signage and explanation and a code of conduct for how to behave at the zoo (and for visitors to take responsibility for their actions),” he said. “Risk assessments will also be undertaken regularly.” Following Saturday’s incident, he said he imagined that “lessons will be learned regarding how zoos try to manage the behaviour of the public and how they instruct visitors to conduct themselves in and around enclosures”. “The majority of visitors behave in a way respectful of the animal and environment at the zoo, but there is always a risk of rogue or unusual behaviour, and this will continue to be risk assessed and part of zoo personnel training,” he added. Experts did say they had some concerns about the role the internet and social media may play in encouraging people to interact with wild animals. Judge said: “We do unfortunately see on social media quite often videos of people, mostly in other countries, entering the enclosures with some of these animals, and that is something that we do not support at all.” “They are dangerous wild animals and they should be respected as such,” she added, but said it wasn’t something UK zoos are “hugely concerned about” as they “will make it very, very clear that these are dangerous animals”. But Dickman said that online content was definitely of concern. “Though it may not have been a factor here, it is worrying how many videos exist online of people playing around with tigers and lions,” she added. “AI has made that even worse, and the illusion that people should have those interactions with wild, dangerous animals can be really damaging.”

title: Mahmood orders urgent security review after killing of Ann Widdecombe
summary: Home secretary also expands police support ‘with immediate effect’ for high-profile public figures not currently MPs
text: Security arrangements for high-profile public figures including politicians and members of the royal family are to be urgently reviewed after the killing of Ann Widdecombe, the home secretary has said. Shabana Mahmood said former MPs, party leaders who are not MPs, peers, former members of devolved parliaments and party spokespeople will also be offered police support. The UK’s protective security system will be re-examined to combat the growing risks of terrorism, extremism and state threats, as well as harassment and intimidation, Mahmood said. The review will be carried out by Sir Stephen Lovegrove, a former UK national security adviser, who will look at whether current security arrangements ensure there is adequate protection for those most at risk. This includes high-profile individuals such as members of the royal family, government ministers, MPs, locally elected representatives and other prominent individuals in British politics. His review will not include an assessment of individual cases. Widdecombe, a former Conservative minister and Reform UK spokesperson, was found dead on 9 July at her home in Haytor, Devon, having sustained serious injuries. Joshua Kerry, 28, has been charged with Widdecombe’s murder. He is also accused of “online reconnaissance” of prominent people and institutions, travelling to Reform UK leader Nigel Farage’s home in south London on 19 April 2025 and trying to break into it 15 months before Widdecombe was killed. Addressing the Commons, Mahmood said that, regardless of the outcome of the investigation into an attempted break-in at Farage’s home, it is “clear there is insufficient protection for those who serve”. “I can therefore announce today that I will expand, with immediate effect, police support to political figures who are not currently members of parliament,” she said. “This will include former members of parliament, peers and party spokespeople, giving them access to a named police officer, as well as help with wider security measures. Mahmood added: “Today I also announce an independent root-and-branch review of the protective security provided by the state to those in public life. We can defeat those who mean us harm, but we are strongest when we act together. “In a more dangerous world, we are faced by threats from without and within that target our democracy and our way of life. In response, we are adapting and strengthening our defences. “As ever, I commend the work of the police and our security services, who labour in silence to keep us safe. And I’m sure the whole house joins me in offering thanks to them for that vital life-saving work.” Lovegrove will look at how existing security is provided, whether funding and other measures are being used effectively and proportionately, and how decision-making can be more consistent in response to threat and risk. Robert Buckland is conducting a separate review into the murder of Sir David Amess MP, which will consider the security of MPs in their constituencies. In May’s local elections the Electoral Commission found that 55% of all candidates experienced some form of harassment and intimidation, as did the same proportion of candidates at the 2024 general election.

title: Democrats rebuke federal raid of Ilhan Omar’s home: ‘rogue abuse of power’
summary: Top House Democrats question the ‘corrupt weaponization’ of federal government against Trump’s adversaries
text: Ilhan Omar’s Democratic colleagues have condemned federal agents’ search of the Minnesota congresswoman’s home on Monday morning, describing it as “deeply disturbing” and emblematic of the Trump administration’s “corrupt weaponization” of the US government. House Democratic leaders, including the minority leader, Hakeem Jeffries, party whip Katherine Clark and caucus chair Pete Aguilar, issued a joint statement excoriating the president for the search. “The Trump administration’s raid on Congresswoman Ilhan Omar’s home is deeply disturbing and raises serious questions about the continued corrupt weaponization of the federal government against [the president’s] adversaries,” their statement said. “For years, Donald Trump and far-right extremists have relentlessly targeted Congresswoman Omar with vile personal attacks and baseless accusations. Now, less than 30 days until the midterm election, his violent mass deportation machine has descended upon the home of a duly elected member of Congress and her family.” The Democratic leaders vowed to “deliver full accountability for the rogue abuse of power” from the US Departments of Justice and Homeland Security, the latter of which oversees immigration enforcement. Citing unnamed sources “close to the investigation”, Fox News – which is typically friendly with the Trump administration – reported that the search on Omar’s home pertained to a criminal fraud investigation concerning her immigration paperwork. Omar’s late father filled out that paperwork when Omar, a Somali-born, naturalized US citizen, was a child. The California representative Ro Khanna also condemned Monday’s search, saying: “It is simply chilling that they are targeting political opponents this way, and it is disturbing that they are targeting Muslim Americans and a Muslim American legislator. Any decent American needs to stand up and speak out.” Sydney Kamlager-Dove, Khanna’s fellow Democrat and California representative, called the search “fascism in the extreme”. “This is an unadulterated abuse of power,” Kamlager-Dove said. “Trump is weaponizing the federal government to escalate his racist attacks against [Representative] Omar, undermine her ahead of the midterms [on 3 November], and distract from his failures as president.” Pramila Jayapal, a Democratic House member from Washington state, similarly called the search of Omar’s home a “disgusting abuse of power from an out of control president” facing widespread public disapproval from high living costs amid the war in Iran that he helped start alongside Israel in February. “To use federal law enforcement resources to raid the home of a sitting Member of Congress weeks before an election is a dangerous sign of an authoritarian president who will stop at nothing to distract you from his deep unpopularity with the American people,” Jayapal added. Jayapal’s statement alluded to years of unsubstantiated rumors from Trump and others about Omar and her family, including the accusation that her ex-husband, Ahmed Nur Said Elmi, is in fact her brother – and that the marriage was part of an effort to earn him immigration status. Omar has denied those rumors. The Illinois representative Delia C Ramirez called for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to be dismantled. Omar “has not backed down, so now they are using DHS and the federal government to target and persecute her”, Ramirez said in a post on X. “This is an absolute abuse of power and unacceptable. We must strip them of their weapons. We must dismantle DHS.” Similarly, Greg Casar, a Democratic representative from Texas, wrote that the Trump administration was targeting Omar “because he thinks it’ll help his [Republican] party” during the midterms, when it is expected to lose seats in Congress. “Ilhan Omar stands up and won’t let Trump do whatever he wants to our country,” Casar said. “It’s up to us to do the same.” The Council on American-Islamic Relations (Cair), the US’s largest Muslim civil rights organization, also spoke out against the search of Omar’s home, saying: “We strongly condemn this unconscionable raid on her home for what it is: an obvious act of political persecution.” Criticizing the Trump administration’s handling of files pertaining to Jeffrey Epstein’s child sex-trafficking network as well as the president’s pardons for those who attacked the US Capitol in early 2021, Cair said the justice department “could clearly [not] care less about fighting crime and is instead focused on conducting a witch hunt”.

title: If Russia had interfered with the Brexit vote, Nige would have been the first to know | John Crace
summary: Burnham was lying, Farage told a press conference on Monday. This was clearly just another plot to undermine him
text: Let’s face it. The very idea that Russia may have tried to interfere with the Brexit referendum is clearly absurd. I mean, what could a hostile state hope to gain from sowing division between the UK and the EU? We all know that Vladimir Putin has nothing but the best interests of European democracies at heart. That’s why he invaded Ukraine. To help it become a bit more democratic. The sort of democracy which is so highly prized that 99% of its citizens vote for its leader. If only others could be more like Russia. If anything, Putin would have wanted the UK to remain within the EU and it was only his impartiality that prevented him from saying so. Besides which, why would the Russians want to get involved in anything so politically insignificant as the partial break-up of an organisation it considers an enemy. It just makes no sense. And it’s not as if Russia has any track record of clandestine foreign engagement. Next people will be suggesting Russia paid Reform’s former leader in Wales, Nathan Gill, at least £30,000 to make helpful speeches in the European parliament and recruit other MEPs. Andy Burnham sees it rather differently. Over the weekend he claimed that since he had become prime minister he had seen incontrovertible proof that the Russians had been involved in a misinformation campaign during the referendum. He didn’t say exactly what form the interference had taken. Merely that it was a reality. So it was no surprise that Nigel Farage was asked for his reaction during a Reform press conference in Kent on Monday morning. “The prime minister is a liar,” Nige snapped. “Yes, a liar.” Nige was beside himself with anger. He is getting more thin-skinned by the day. This was yet another myth fabricated by the Establishment. Another excuse to try to relitigate the result of the referendum. The whole thing was clearly a plot to undermine him. Everything that ever happens in the world somehow always becomes personal to Nige. His solipsism eclipses everything. We all only exist as satellites of his own imagination. When he dies, we will all die with him. If he hasn’t killed us first. It was like this. If Russia had tried to interfere with the referendum then he would have been the first to know about it. And frankly he had been deeply disappointed that no one had tried to buy him. Numerous punters had bought him for £80 a pop on Cameo. But despite having billions in petro-roubles, the Russians had blanked him. First the sound, then the fury. You can almost sense Nige’s desperation these days. It had all been going so well for so long. Reform had been 10 points clear in the polls for the best part of 18 months as Labour and the Tories flatlined. Nige was even being taken seriously as a possible next prime minister. Then along came the financial scandals and the election on the nod of Burnham and suddenly Farage found himself marginalised. His politics of grievance were no longer quite so attractive. Yet Nige can’t help himself. Logic would suggest that if the public mood was shifting more back to the centre ground of traditional two-party politics, then he would be better off heading in that direction himself. Instead, the Mr Nice Guy carapace – “I’m only saying what you’re all thinking” – is falling away. Nige is revealing himself to be a deeply unpleasant person all along. There is no longer the pretence of “let’s just have a pint and some bantz”. Everything has become actively nasty. Retreating to the safe ground of the 15% for whom nothing can ever be nasty enough. So much so that Nige is even back to sharing a platform with Zia Yusuf. A man who makes Honest Bob Jenrick look trustworthy. Almost cuddly. The Reform roadshow was in Kent to promote Nige and Zia’s war on immigrants. The UK had been invaded and everyone had to go. No exceptions for migrants with winning smiles or tragic backstories. There was no room for Afghan women and children. This was Toxicity Unfiltered. Prejudice 101. The Americans had removed their bombers from RAF Fairford because of the small boat crossings. He didn’t pause to wonder why the US president had kept some planes at other UK airbases. There would be tariffs on any countries that didn’t want their migrants back. Maybe even airstrikes. Asylum was just a scam, Zia insisted. He would starve the migrants in small boats. Refuse them medicines. Any civil servants who declined to activate the mass deportations would be lined up and shot in front of the white cliffs of Dover. Come the end we were treated to Nige’s stream of unconsciousness. Ukraine? Well, everyone had their limits and he was a bit fed up with Zelenskyy. You couldn’t go on supporting your allies indefinitely. And what had happened to the Sun? Not so long ago it would print any old bollox Nige told its reporters to write. Now they were daring to be nice to Kemi. It was an outrage. A stitch-up. Back in the Commons in the afternoon, you could almost feel the years peeling away in a return to the Brexit wars of a decade ago. And that’s without Burnham even suggesting the UK rejoins the EU. All he said was that he would try to reset the relationship in a way that worked for all parties and would grow the economy by £10bn a year. At all stages the British public would be boss. This was far too much for Kemi. Natch. She accused the prime minister of undermining the referendum result – for, er, speaking the truth – and that she would much rather the economy had zero growth than it came at the cost of closer ties with the EU. It was quite like old times. How I’ve missed them.

title: Man rescued from cave on Sardinia after being trapped by rockslide for 26 hours
summary: Luca Olmetto was trapped roughly 10 metres below ground in the Gorroppeddu cave in the Urzulei mountain range
text: A 31-year-old man has been pulled alive from a cave on the Italian island of Sardinia after being trapped roughly 10 metres below ground for 26 hours following a rockslide. In a huge and complex operation, rescuers worked non-stop after Luca Olmetto became trapped in the Gorroppeddu cave in the rugged Urzulei mountain range in central-eastern Sardinia on Sunday afternoon. He had been exploring the cave with his girlfriend, who was a few metres behind him and narrowly missed the collapse, which completely blocked the entrance to the cave. She managed to escape unharmed and immediately raised the alarm. Rescuers managed to reach Olmetto, who was conscious and responsive throughout the operation, by late Monday afternoon after manually removing rubble and earth blocking a narrow passage. They then proceeded with the delicate operation of removing the large amounts of debris that covered the caver before extracting him from the cavity. According to Rai News, Olmetto was brought to the surface just after 6pm CET and stabilised by medical staff before being airlifted to hospital. About 48 experts from Sardinia’s Alpine and Speleological Rescue Corps and 30 firefighters, as well as civil protection staff, were involved in the rescue operation. A helicopter also provided materials and equipment needed to make the site secure. In a message posted on social media, the council of Codrongianos, the town in north-west Sardinia where Olmetto is from, wrote that the past 24 hours were filled with “great anxiety for the entire community”. “We are closely monitoring the situation and are hoping for good news soon,” the council said. “Our thoughts are with Luca and his family, and we extend our deepest gratitude to all the rescuers working tirelessly to bring him to safety. Hang in there, Luca – all of Codrongianos is with you.” The Gorroppeddu cave is a largely unexplored natural cavity. In a similar incident in December 2024, another explorer, Ottavia Piana, 32, became trapped while exploring a cave in the Bueno Fonteno caves close to Bergamo in northern Italy. She remained underground at roughly 600 metres for 75 hours before being freed. Piana suffered injuries including fractured vertebrae, ribs and facial bones. Her high profile rescue involved 160 specialists.

title: Stellantis and Renault back UK to get EU car industry protection
summary: Bosses of Citroën owner and French carmaker also urge UK government to consider limiting imports from China
text: Stellantis and Renault have backed the UK car industry for inclusion in proposed rules to protect EU industry, but urged the British government to consider limiting imports of Chinese cars. Emanuele Cappellano, who leads Stellantis’s European brands including Fiat, Citroën, Opel and Vauxhall, and François Provost, the chief executive of France’s Renault, said the UK should effectively be counted as one of the EU’s 27 member states for the purposes of the proposed “Made in Europe” legislation. The new rules aim to ensure EU subsidies and government procurement benefits Europe’s industry, rather than helping manufacturers from other countries. The executives were speaking at the Paris motor show, which was attended on Monday by the French president, Emmanuel Macron. Brands including Li Auto, GAC and Chery were among a host of Chinese manufacturers exhibiting in Paris with ambitious European expansion plans. Europe’s car industry is under enormous pressure as it copes with lower demand than before the coronavirus pandemic, while also investing tens of billions of euros in shifting production to electric vehicles (EVs). At the same time, Chinese carmakers’ market share has soared as the transition to EVs opens the door to new entrants. The EU confirmed on Monday it would limit the number of hybrid electric vehicles imported from China to 350,000 cars a year. The EU expects that the quota, which will come into force in December, will halve China’s market share, which now stands at 6% in a landmark four-year agreement made in Beijing last week. The Made in Europe rules are another plank of the EU’s response to the rise of China in key manufacturing industries such as carmaking and chemicals. Under the proposed Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA), cars will have to be “made in Europe”, and contain enough European parts and materials, to continue to qualify for EV grants and to be bought by public bodies in the EU. However, automotive manufacturers and politicians are haggling over the details. If Brussels sticks to a strict definition of “European” as being only EU countries, Britain risks being left out – prompting intense lobbying from UK car industry and government to be included. Stellantis is among the manufacturers that still has a British factory, its facility in Ellesmere Port, Merseyside, which produces small vans. “I think that UK somehow needs to be equalised to the EU 27,” said Cappellano, referring to the bloc’s 27 member states. “We have a lot of relationship, we have footprint. Historically UK has been very close to the European market.” Europe’s main automotive lobby groups ACEA and Clepa have also put their weight behind the UK to be included. Some parts of European manufacturing, including France’s industry minister, had argued that the UK should be left out given Brexit. Provost said there was “no other choice” but a deal between the UK and EU. However, he said the UK would also have to stop allowing Chinese cars in without limits. “On your side, you have also to take decisions,” he said. “If the UK is willing to join the European ecosystem, this is to have an industrial ambition … to keep a strong automotive industry.” He said this would be an industry that “is not closed to Chinese competitors, but … if you want to operate in Europe, you have to deeply invest in the whole value chain, final manufacturing, suppliers, R&D, technologies.” Provost added: “I’m not here to demand whatsoever, but I think if UK is willing to join this ecosystem of IAA, there is some open question about the level of imports.” London has so far rejected pressure to impose its own tariffs on Chinese imports, but the UK business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, this month said that decision was under review. Cappellano also said the UK should consider imposing tariffs on Chinese imports. “It’s very important that the UK defines what is the priority,” he said. “It’s very difficult to defend industrial footprint and at the same time let the market completely open to import. Either one or the other.” He expressed scepticism over whether other countries beyond the EU such as Japan, Turkey and Morocco should be included in the rules. “We don’t necessarily need to have a larger definition of European scope,” he said, pointing to proposals that carmakers be allowed to source 30% of their materials from outside the EU. He also argued for more time until 2030 for manufacturers to source batteries from within Europe. China is dominant in the global supply of batteries and Cappellano said it would take longer to build up the European industry.

title: Iran’s Revolutionary Guards ‘almost certainly’ behind RAF Fairford threats, says Burnham
summary: UK to bring further sanctions against Tehran and IRGC after assessment Iran was likely to have coordinated incident
text: Andy Burnham said Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps were “almost certainly” behind threats to RAF Fairford, the firmest attribution of responsibility made so far by the UK after an incident late last month. The prime minister told MPs the UK would bring further sanctions against Tehran and the IRGC in the aftermath of an ambiguous episode that, despite over a fortnight of police investigation, has yet to lead to anybody being charged. Addressing parliament on Monday about events at RAF Fairford, Burnham said: “I can confirm our assessment that it is highly likely to have been coordinated in Iran, almost certainly directed by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards.” In a statement to the House of Commons, the home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, told MPs that the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, had summoned the Iranian ambassador over the Fairford incident and that the government had imposed sanctions on two individuals accused of spying in Europe and the US. “He [Miliband] will condemn Iran’s continued attempts to undermine our safety. We are also sanctioning two individuals involved in conducting espionage and attacks on behalf of the government of Iran in Europe and the US, and we will not hesitate to take further action to restrict Iran’s capacity to threaten international security,” she said. Five men from London drove to Whelford, a village next to a base used by the US air force, in three white vans shortly after midnight on 27 September. They were released on police bail a day later after no bombs or explosives were found. However, the incident was followed by the withdrawal of 12 B-1 bombers a week later, amid reports that the US was concerned about a possible drone attack on a base it had used to attack Iran during the Middle East war in the spring and summer. Burnham’s brief remarks were a step up from previous comments. The prime minister had said in the days after the incident that there were “strong indications” Iran had played a part – but now appeared confident enough to apportion responsibility. A joint statement from the UK, US and other European allies, released by the Foreign Office, added that the UK “has also concluded this event demonstrates the IRGC’s continued willingness to project hostile activity beyond its borders through covert networks and proxy actors”. However, despite his statement, it remains unclear what the authorities think happened at Fairford. Some experts have speculated it was a “feint” to demonstrate that Iran could in theory attack a relatively open site. British sources have repeatedly maintained that Iran lacks the capability to launch what would be a sophisticated drone attack, but the incident appears to have unnerved the US, which is worried about the security of its bases in Europe. The incident at Fairford comes after what the UK, in the joint statement, said was a recent campaign of attacks across Europe targeting Jewish communities, Iranian journalists and US interests, claimed by Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya (HAYI). Though the US has detained and indicted Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi, whom it accuses of being behind the HAYI group, there is evidence to suggest that Iran-linked attacks have continued. A week ago, two Iranian nationals, Salam Ahmadyan from Liverpool and Rahman Salehi from Salford, were charged with terror offences, accused of trying to target the Jewish community in Manchester with a homemade chlorine powder bomb. Prosecutors told a magistrates court the pair were in contact with a third party, believed to be in Iran, who directed them and sent them “instructions on how to prepare an explosive device”. A trial at the Old Bailey has been scheduled.

summary: Brief letters: Pete Hegseth | Pre-loved | Marlborough man | Canterbury tale | Newt kids on the block
text: Pete Hegseth, the US defence secretary, has authorised the livestreaming of an execution by firing squad (Report, 9 October). Morally this is no different from a terrorist group posting a video of a beheading. It marks yet another step in the brutalising of American society under the second Trump administration. Britain stopped holding public executions in 1868. John Boaler Calne, Wiltshire • I find nearly all the “pre-” expressions irritating, but the term pre-loved (Letters, 7 October) is, in this one instance, justifiable. title: How significant are Burnham’s remarks on Kremlin interference in Brexit vote?
summary: Prime minister has reopened the debate over whether Russia sought to influence the 2016 referendum
text: Andy Burnham unexpectedly reopened an old Brexit debate when he said he had been told after becoming prime minister that Russia had interfered in the 2016 EU referendum. It was a contentious issue in the second half of the previous decade, but one that had largely been forgotten about as the UK finally adjusted to the reality of leaving the EU. Now Burnham’s comments have given the topic a fresh impetus. What did the prime minister say, and why could it be significant? The Russia topic came up as part of a wide-ranging interview Burnham gave to The Rest is Politics, excerpts of which were released on Sunday, in which he appeared to suggest he had been given new information about the Brexit vote. “I asked the question coming to Downing Street: ‘Was there interference in the 2016 referendum from Russia?’ And I’ve had the clear answer that yes, there was,” he said. The prime minister did not say whom he had asked, or set out in detail what the answer was. But his comments suggest he had been given new information of some kind, although he then switched to talking about Russian disinformation in general. “These things are important now to put clearly on the record, and I believe, help voters in Germany and France understand that some of this politics is instigated via our enemies, namely Russia,” he said. What could Burnham have been told? It was hard to decipher from the interview. One possibility is that he was given a summary of a recent assessment by the UK’s intelligence agencies. Another is that it was a relatively informal conversation with officials, where opinions were exchanged. The difference is significant – if there was a fresh assessment it would run counter to the position established under a succession of Conservative governments in the aftermath of the Brexit vote. Later on Monday, in the Commons, Burnham did not share any extra information, saying instead: “It is a matter of record that Russia has sought to interfere in elections, the 2019 general election, and we think it is inconceivable that this was the first time.” What was the conclusion of previous inquiries? There were no serious official investigations into Russian interference attempts in 2016, not least because the Conservatives had no appetite to order them. As time passed, it became increasingly difficult to do so. The topic was addressed by parliament’s cross-party intelligence and security committee in its Russia report, published in July 2020, which took evidence in secret from the UK’s intelligence agencies before publishing a partly redacted report. It concluded that the government “had not seen or sought evidence of successful interference in UK democratic processes”. No formal post-referendum assessment had been made, the committee added, and the UK intelligence community was accused of taking its “eye off the ball” when it came to the Russian threat. What could have happened in 2016? This is an old controversy with three main elements. First, that a “troll army” of state-linked Russian accounts tweeted about the referendum in the run-up to the vote, though estimates of numbers have varied wildly from 54 to 150,000 (many of which were deleted). Second, that the Russian English-language media outlets RT and Sputnik published a large amount of anti-EU and pro-Brexit content, which had a wide reach. The digital campaign group 89up said the two broadcasters had published 261 articles that achieved 134m potential page impressions. The third aspect were claims that Arron Banks, a donor to the pro-Brexit campaigner Nigel Farage, had links to Russia. Leaked emails showed he met Alexander Yakovenko, then the Russian ambassador to the UK, three times – a figure he later revised up to four – and that he was offered the chance to participate in a goldmining deal in Russia. A subsequent investigation by the National Crime Agency into £8m of loans Banks provided to Brexit campaigns run by Farage concluded the money was legitimately his and there was no evidence of wrongdoing. But the EU referendum was also a complex, closely fought campaign in which many points of view were in play. The idea that one country, with an interest in weakening the UK and the EU, could have had a decisive influence in a vote of 33.5 million people is debatable. So what’s going on? The prime minister is making a broader argument that Britain needs to reconsider its relationship with the EU, arguing that Brexit has not delivered what was promised. Highlighting that there could have been Russian efforts to interfere with the vote raises questions about the outcome, though Downing Street insisted on Monday it regarded the result as legitimate. Burnham has also proposed creating a National Centre for Information Defence to detect, attribute and disrupt disinformation coming from overseas – and it appears that his comments about Russian interference were also intended to justify that. However, when he appeared in the Commons, Burnham was careful to limit his remarks. He emphasised that he had not said that Russia had altered the result of the Brexit referendum, only that the Kremlin had tried to interfere. But with little new to back up his initial statements about Russian interference, the prime minister risks being accused of exaggeration.

title: Zelenskyy vows to retaliate if Russian strikes on Ukraine’s power grid continue
summary: Ukrainian leader says he was surprised by Trump’s ‘energy ceasefire’ announcement, posted as Russian drones hit Kyiv
text: Volodymyr Zelenskyy has vowed to respond to Russia’s continuing attacks on the Ukrainian power grid as European leaders rally around Kyiv amid a feud with Donald Trump over Ukraine’s strikes on oil refineries. Speaking to a gathering of European security officials in Warsaw on Monday, the Ukrainian president said Kyiv would retaliate if strikes on its power grid continued: “If Russia does not agree to an energy ceasefire this winter, we will respond.” On Sunday, Trump announced an “energy ceasefire” between Kyiv and Moscow that Zelenskyy said neither side had agreed to. On Monday, Zelenskyy said he was “surprised” by the post, which went online while Kyiv was being attacked by Russian Shahed drones. Russia then launched a “targeted attack” on a Kharkiv power station hours later, as much of Kyiv was plunged into darkness. “It’s clear that Putin does not read Truth Social,” Zelenskyy said. Russia bombed six energy facilities on Monday, injuring 33 people, the Ukrainian president said. “It is becoming increasingly clear that Russia does not want to agree to the energy ceasefire proposed by the US and intends to continue its terrorist air attacks against our communities,” he added. Zelenskyy also suggested that Ukraine’s recent counter-strikes on datacentres belonging to the Russian technology company Yandex had reduced the number of bots posting messages in Europe and the US. “It suddenly became a little easier to breathe on many social platforms. There was less hate, less division and fewer provocations,” he said. The Kremlin refused to say on Monday whether it agreed with Trump’s Truth Social post, which claimed a ceasefire was “effective immediately”. It also rejected Zelenskyy’s proposal that Russia stop bombing for 60 days so Ukraine could hold a presidential election. Moscow wanted an overall peace deal first, it said, which, for the Kremlin, means Kyiv’s capitulation. The fast-moving row between Washington and Kyiv began on Friday, when Trump announced he was lifting sanctions on Russian diesel exports. He said the move would reduce global and domestic fuel prices before next month’s US midterm elections. Both Republican and Democratic politicians have criticised the move, pointing out that the deal violates a US law that blocks Russian energy imports. On Monday Trump defended it. “I made the right choice for the American People – ALWAYS, AMERICA FIRST!” he wrote in a social media post. Earlier a furious Zelenskyy called the decision “weak” and said it would generate “billions” in extra revenue for Putin, enabling him to wage war “even more intensely”. An equally irate Trump said Zelenskyy should “damn well stop” hitting Russian refineries. Ukraine needed a “new leader”, he said on Saturday. Ukraine has said it is ready to negotiate an energy ceasefire that would take the pressure off its electricity grid before the winter. European leaders have voiced support for Kyiv in its dispute with Washington, saying Russia was responsible for the continuing strikes on energy infrastructure in both countries. “We welcome the energy ceasefire when it holds,” the EU foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, said at a meeting of European foreign ministers on Monday. “We haven’t yet seen that also Russia will stick to it.” Ministers from the Baltic states criticised a US decision to lift sanctions on imports of Russian diesel, which had been blocked as part of punishment for Putin launching the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. “This deal doesn’t help, neither the crisis of the oil products, nor the unity within the transatlantic community when it concerns Russia,” said Lithuania’s foreign minister, Keʂtutis Budrys. “And it is not the European way. Our way is to increase pressure because we already see how it works.” Russia has increased its attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure, using jet-powered drones and ballistic missiles ahead of the cold winter months, leading to blackouts and water shortages far earlier in the season than has been usual during the war. Trump’s proposal was for both sides to halt strikes on oil refineries but Kallas said that deal favoured Russia, which has far more refineries. The US president has blamed the high price of diesel on Ukraine’s attacks, rather than the global shock to energy markets from the US war in Iran and the subsequent closure of the strait of Hormuz. According to the Financial Times, the US ⁠has threatened ⁠to stop the procurement ⁠system that provides ⁠Ukraine with ‌weapons, paid for by its European allies. The White House has also said it could turn off intelligence sharing unless Kyiv halts its ‌long-range strikes on Russian oil refineries. The Kyiv Independent newspaper said Ukraine’s commander in chief, Mykhailo Drapatyi, had received a call from the US telling him to stop bombing. “They called all the top military officials with threats,” a Ukrainian official told the newspaper. Ben Hodges, the former head of US forces in Europe, described the energy ceasefire “deal” as a fantasy and “a classic ‘Trumpian’ announcement of something not based on any facts.” “No one should be misled,” he said, adding that Russia “never adheres to any agreements unless forced to do so”. He urged Ukraine’s military to ignore Trump and “ramp up” their attacks on Russian oil and gas complexes. “Clearly, this is having a very significant effect. Otherwise, you wouldn’t be hearing all this pressure from the Kremlin on the White House demanding that it stop. Of course, it is having a huge impact.”

title: Did you solve it? The treacherous puzzle of the round table
summary: The solutions to today’s puzzles
text: Earlier today I set you these six puzzles. Here they are again with solutions. The round table Three people sit at a round table, facing inwards, towards the centre of the table. No two of them are the same age. Each of them says “I am younger than the person to my left.” 1. What is the greatest possible number of people telling the truth? 2. What is the smallest possible number of people telling the truth? Solution 1. The oldest person must be lying, so the maximum is 2. Here is an example with 2 people telling the truth: 30-40-20 (Ages as you go clockwise around the table) The answer is two. 2. The youngest person must be telling the truth, so the minimum is 1. Here is an example with 1 person telling the truth 40-30-20 The answer is one. Seven people sit at a different round table, facing inwards, towards the centre of the table. No two of them are the same age. Each of them says “I am younger than the person to my left, and I am younger than the person two places to my right”. 3. At this table, what is the greatest possible number of people telling the truth? 4. At this table, what is the smallest possible number of people telling the truth? Solution 3. The two oldest people must be lying, so the answer cannot be six or seven. It turns out that the answer cannot be five either. If five were telling the truth, the third oldest would be one of them, and so the three oldest people would have to be arranged in one of the two cases below (suppose the ages are 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70). * * * 60 * 50 70 (Ages as you go clockwise around the table) * * * 70 * 50 60 But now there is nowhere for the next oldest (the 40-year-old) to sit and be telling the truth. It is, however, possible for four people to be telling the truth: 10 20 40 70 30 50 60 The answer is four. 4. The youngest person must be telling the truth, so the answer cannot be zero. If you order everyone in descending order of ages, no one is telling the truth apart from the youngest: 70 60 50 40 30 20 10 The answer is one. 999 people sit at a third round table, facing inwards, towards the centre of the table. No two of them are the same age. Each of them says “I am younger than the person three places to my left, and older than the person three places to my right”. 5. At this table, what is the greatest possible number of people telling the truth? 6. At this table, what is the smallest possible number of people telling the truth? Solution 5. We might think about this by colouring the seats gold, silver and bronze in a repeating pattern, like so (in the illustration there are only 21 people, but the idea works for 999 people as well). It can now be seen that each person makes a statement about people sitting on seats with the same colour as them; in particular, the closest people on either side with the same colour seat. Consider those 333 people sitting in gold. The youngest and oldest of these must be lying, so there cannot be 333 or 332 gold truthtellers. But, as the example below helps to illustrate, it is possible for every other gold person to be telling the truth, by seating them with age increasing as we move clockwise around the table. Applying the same reasoning to those seated on silver or bronze, we can have all but six people telling the truth. The same idea with 999 people has 999-6=993 telling the truth. The answer is 993. 6. If the people are sat with age decreasing as we move clockwise around the table, then everybody is lying. The answer is 0. Thanks to Daniel Griller for today’s puzzles. He is the author of the excellent puzzle books Elastic Numbers and A Ring of Cats and Dogs, and Other Curious Puzzles. I’ll be back in two weeks. I’ve been setting a puzzle here on alternate Mondays since 2015. I’m always on the look-out for great puzzles. If you would like to suggest one, email me.

title: Saudi Arabia further suspends flights after latest deadly Houthi attack on airport
summary: Energy minister says ‘fear has no place in the Saudi lexicon’ as paramilitary group again breaches stretched defences
text: Saudi Arabia has been forced to suspend all flights to and from its main international airport in Riyadh until next Saturday after a further round of Houthi missile attacks caused more damage and left one person dead. Some airlines, including Gulf Air, had already said they were cancelling flights until next Saturday. More missiles were fired at Saudi Arabian cities by the Houthis on Monday, Saudi Arabian’s military spokesperson said. The Gulf nation announced it was suspending flights from Riyadh, its second busiest airport, after Houthi missiles killed 13 people on Saturday and left more than 300 injured. Saudi state TV broadcast CCTV footage that showed passengers deluged in smoke and falling masonry as they queued at the airport terminal to board a plane just as the Houthi missile struck. The country has pressed ahead with the 25th WPC Energy Conference in Riyadh, hoping to project an image of normality. But some senior oil executives did not attend or appeared virtually. The Saudi energy minister, Abdulaziz bin Salman, told the conference that “fear has no place in the Saudi lexicon”, emphasising the resilience of the kingdom’s energy system and the determination of its people to confront crises. Amin Nasser, the president and chief executive of Aramco, said Saudi Arabia had invested deeply in protecting its supplies, but “no nation, even one as capable and confident as ours, can safeguard them alone.” He added: “Markets can diversify suppliers. They cannot diversify geography […] when energy infrastructure in this region is targeted, the consequences reach economies everywhere.” An urgent review is under way as to how Houthi missiles are repeatedly penetrating badly stretched Saudi air defences. Schoolchildren and some office workers were advised to work from home. The Houthis have also targeted the city of Khamis Mushait, and the King Fahd international airport in Dammam. Interceptor missiles are needed to protect government buildings, oil facilities and infrastructure hubs across a wide geographic area. The Houthis have vowed to attack Saudi airports across the country. A Houthi official on Monday warned the US it would receive a “painful response” if it entered the war in Yemen, following Trump’s comments at the weekend that he was “going to look at” the possibility of joining Saudi strikes. “If the US becomes involved in the aggression against Yemen, we will not deliberate over the decision to respond, rather, there will be a swift and painful response targeting the US and all its interests in the region,” Houthi political bureau member Mohammed Al Bukhaiti told AFP in an interview. He also warned “all employees and workers at Saudi oil facilities and airports to stay away from these sites, as they have become legitimate targets”. Houthi attacks since last month have targeted fuel tanks at Riyadh airport and its affiliated warehouses, destroying a parked Airbus A320 passenger plane and damaging at least five other aircraft. The crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman, has not been seen in public since Tuesday last week, reflecting the pressure he is under to find a way out from a war that has intermittently dogged his leadership since 2014. Saudi Arabia badly needs stability to continue the slow diversification of its economy from oil dependence, but has not found a way to restore it in Yemen. Inside Yemen, fighting continued in and around Taiz, the third city, and the most populous governorate, with Saudi planes mounting eight separate strikes on any assembly of Houthi forces. As many as 60 fighters died on Sunday from both sides. The governor of Taiz, Nabil Shamsan, on Sunday issued an urgent call to lift the Houthi siege and warned a shortage of medicines meant the city would soon run out of emergency surgical and intensive care services. Overall the Houthis claimed the Saudis had mounted 124 raids on Sunday. The Saudis are seeking to locate Abdul-Malik al-Houthi, the reclusive leader of the Houthis, with rumours of his assassination repeatedly circulating, but Saudi Arabia does not seem to have contemporary intelligence on his precise whereabouts either in the capital Sana’a or in its stronghold of Saada. On the diplomatic front, Abbas Araghchi, the Iranian foreign minister, spoke to the Saudi foreign minister, Faisal bin Farhan, on Sunday to see if there was a way in which Iran could act as a mediator between the Saudis and the Houthis, a group that Iran has trained and armed. Mohammed al-Bukhaiti, a member of the Houthi Political Bureau claimed Saudi Arabia accepted the mediation offered by Iran and proposed first a one-month truce, and then a two week truce, but the Houthis had rejected both offers. He said “the battle this time is not like its predecessors; the arena is no longer the same arena, and the cards have changed. Therefore, a comprehensive settlement must be put in place between Riyadh and Sana’a, the Houthi capital because every day that passes in this battle will expand its scope and deepen its losses, and the settlement that is possible today may become difficult or impossible tomorrow”. A meeting of the UN security council in New York on Tuesday is expected to debate a resolution calling the Houthis a foreign terrorist organisation. The exiled leader of the Southern Transitional Council (STC), Aidarous al-Zubaidi, called for southern forces to fight on all fronts, and not just to defend the borders of the former South Yemen, in a move that is likely to be welcomed by Saudi Arabia as it supports the week-old call by the UN-recognised government to drive the Houthis out of the whole of Yemen, rather than just from the southern governorates. The STC has a vision of an independent South Yemen that would recreate the separate state that existed between 1967 and 1990. The reunification of Yemen at the end of the cold war proved fragile and many southerners nurse longstanding grievances about the distribution of resources in the unified state. The STC’s authority has been challenged by Abd al-Rahman al-Mahrami, the Salafist leader who commands the powerful Southern Giants Brigades. Despite Araghchi’s efforts to reach out to the Saudis, Mohsen Rezaei, the more hardline secretary of Iran’s supreme national security council, claimed Iran was hitting five or six small vessels in the strait of Hormuz every night, explaining the vessels were being used by the Emirati military to move oil through the strait to larger tankers, thus breaching the blockade that Iran is seeking to maintain to push up oil prices and weaken Donald Trump. Esmail Baghaei, the Iranian foreign ministry spokesperson, said Trump’s treatment of Volodymyr Zelenskyy, including his call for the Ukrainian president to stand aside showed the risks in dealing with Trump. He said: “Being an enemy of America can be dangerous, but being a friend of America is deadly. You can see for yourself what America’s friendship and enmity with its allies is like.”

title: Duel in the desert: US marine veteran aims to win back working-class voters for Democrats
summary: JoAnna Mendoza draws on unique biography to connect with voters in Arizona battleground – can she flip a key swing seat?
text: On a recent morning, Regina Romero knocked on a yellow door above a mat emblazoned with a cat’s silhouette and the words “go away, peasants”. A young man cracked the door open and stood there silently, a toothbrush dangling from his mouth. After giving him a moment to finish brushing his teeth, the Tucson mayor introduced herself and asked if the man had heard of JoAnna Mendoza, the Democrat running to unseat Republican congressman Juan Ciscomani. Romero handed him a pamphlet and rattled off her candidate’s virtues. The young man stood stone-faced, until she mentioned that Mendoza had served for nearly two decades as a US marine. His eyebrows raised as he looked over the brochure: “This is cool.” The man declined to disclose his voting intention or to be named in this story, citing privacy concerns. But the interaction, however brief, marked a victory for Romero. Democrats’ ambitions of retaking the House of Representatives in next month’s midterm elections will depend partly on Mendoza’s ability to sway voters like him. Congressional district six is a swing seat in a swing state, where voter identification is weak and more than a third of residents identify as independents. Located in south-eastern Arizona, the district tethers parts of liberal Tucson to a saguaro-dotted swath of more conservative countryside stretching toward New Mexico. In recent cycles, voters here have narrowly favored Republicans. But as the national mood turns sharply against Donald Trump amid soaring costs and an unpopular war with Iran, Democrats believe they have a real chance – and the right candidate – to tip the balance in this desert battleground. “Our political system is not designed for everyday working-class folks – and those are the voices that are needed,” Mendoza said in an interview. “Right now we have a Congress that’s very focused on themself and enriching themselves.” A first-time candidate in a federal race, Mendoza is drawing on her unique biography to connect with the working-class voters in a district that is roughly 20% Hispanic and home to a large population of military veterans. The daughter of farmworkers, she grew up in rural poverty, enlisted in the navy and served as a Marine Corps drill instructor. “That oath doesn’t expire,” Mendoza said. “I came back home and still felt this need to serve.” *** In an election that will be decided largely by kitchen-table issues, Mendoza is railing against Republicans for the myriad ways in which she says they’ve raised the cost of living since Trump’s re-election – the scattershot tariffs, the war in Iran, an “upside down” tax system that favors billionaires and corporations, and safety net cuts that left nearly half a million Arizonans without food assistance. While her campaign has a notably a populist tinge, she has not embraced leftwing causes such as Medicare for All. Playing to the political center is a commonsense strategy for running in purple Arizona, said University of Arizona political scientist Samara Klar. “The way Democrats usually win in Arizona is by conveying the most moderate image they possibly can,” Klar said. “Mendoza definitely seems like she’s following that playbook.” No one knows that better than her opponent, Juan Ciscomani, the telegenic, two-term Republican incumbent. With slicked-back silver hair and six children, Mexico-born Ciscomani made his immigrant story a part of his political identity during the past two elections, when he narrowly defeated the same Democratic challenger. But Ciscomani’s natural strengths as a candidate and bipartisan self-branding are now being tested by Trump’s increasingly extremist second term – most notably the president’s so-called “big, beautiful” spending bill, which cleaved healthcare and food assistance while showering tax cuts on the wealthy. Ciscomani led well-publicized efforts to soften the bill’s impact locally, but they ultimately failed. Like most Republicans in office these days, Ciscomani avoids publicly contradicting a notoriously vengeful White House. Ciscomani’s campaign did not respond to requests for an interview. That chain of events has left him the unenviable task of trying to sell the few elements of the president’s unpopular spending bill that benefit the working class, like eliminating federal taxes on tips. Compounding Ciscomani’s problems, the issues that elevated Trump to the presidency two years ago have lost their resonance with many voters. Trump’s immigration crackdown made border security a less urgent issue fo∫while the president’s violent mass deportation campaign has gone too far for many moderate voters. Meanwhile, Trump returned to the White House promising to hold back inflation, but prices have continued to climb, partly due to his rudderless war in Iran, which is costing Arizonans dearly at the pump. “Trump has a record-low approval in Arizona,” said Mike Noble, a non-partisan pollster. “His rating is actually below where it stood right after January 6. Put that in perspective. The only thing worse than storming the Capitol is apparently paying $4.50 a gallon for gas.” Facing such headwinds, Ciscomani is keeping a low profile, allowing the power of incumbency, name recognition and the conservative cultural tilt of much of his district to do the campaign’s heavy lifting. “Ciscomani is just invisible,” said Mo Goldman, a Democrat and Tucson immigration attorney who briefly ran for the House seat, before dropping out and endorsing Mendoza. “He keeps pounding the fact that he’s the most bipartisan representative in Arizona, but the people in his district have rarely seen him.” Activists from the left see Ciscomani’s limited public appearances as vulnerability to exploit. For months, they’ve staged protests outside his district office, urging him to hold a public event to discuss the spending bill’s cuts. The same morning Romero went canvassing, dozens of protesters had gathered again outside of his Tucson office. Standing on all four corners of a busy intersection, they waved signs with slogans that read “no more war” and “Ciscomani, stop raising our costs.” A woman walked up and down the sidewalk, beating a drum slung over her shoulder, as passing drivers honked in support. “Juan Ciscomani votes with Maga every time,” protester Norma Itule said. “He’s two-faced and insincere.” With both candidates fighting for the political middle, Ciscomani has focused his attacks on Mendoza’s alleged “wokeism”, highlighting pandemic-era comments she made criticizing ICE and police officers in the wake of high-profile officer-involved shootings. “She doesn’t have the ability to work across the aisle,” Ciscomani said at a televised debate in August. Mendoza brushed off the criticisms, saying that her words were taken out of context. She doesn’t support defunding the police, abolishing ICE or open borders, she said. “The truth is, I spent my life protecting our country, willing to die for American values,” she said. With the slightest opportunity, Mendoza resurfaced her military service, contrasting it against Ciscomani’s life as a civilian. (Ciscomani worked as a staffer for Doug Doucey, Arizona’s former Republican governor, before becoming a member of Congress.) Her most notable jab came as Ciscomani insisted that last year’s spending bill had not impacted Veterans Affairs medical centers. “As someone who actually gets my care at the VA, I can tell you that doctors were let go,” Mendoza, who deployed to Iraq and Afghanistan, shot back. With national small-donor money pouring into the race, Mendoza has so far out-fundraised Ciscomani. But the Mendoza campaign is hoping its edge will come from constantly connecting to individual voters however they can – TV ads, radio, public events and old-fashioned door-knocking. That’s why Romero, the Tucson mayor, was out walking the palm tree-lined streets of Tucson’s second ward, looking for voters in the midday heat. Almost no one answered as Romero wound her way through the courtyard apartments and bungalows, a broad-brimmed hat shading her face from the desert sun. But she said she loved the work all the same. Mendoza shares her enthusiasm, she said. The two met in 2019, when Mendoza joined Romero’s first mayoral campaign as a volunteer. Mendoza showed up three days a week, towing her then four-year-old son behind her on a stroller attached to a bike. “Ciscomani might have all the Elon Musk money in the world, but JoAnna has people power,” Romero said. “She has always been a public servant.” • This article was amended on 12 October 2026. An earlier version incorrectly referred to Regina Romero, instead of JoAnna Mendoza, in the subheading.

title: Is Wikipedia ‘deeply biased’? Sandi Toksvig says it is – so she’s backing a rival
summary: Just 19% of the online encyclopedia’s biographies are of women. Is this because it’s edited by ‘mostly white, middle-aged, European men’, as the comedian claims?
text: Name: Wikipedia. Age: 25. Appearance: Patronising and deeply biased. Is this because you haven’t got your own page? Well, yes. But these aren’t my words. They’re the words of Sandi Toksvig. But it has 65m articles across more than 300 languages! It’s the largest knowledge resource ever assembled! That may be, but it isn’t very good at women. According to Toksvig? Yes – and she’s very serious about it. As we speak, she is travelling the world trying to raise money to build something better. She is? Yes. Along with the University of Cambridge, she hopes that her Mappa Mundi project will be an “interactive digital atlas where we can find a home for the vast amount of knowledge that is currently sidelined or deleted”. And a lot of the sidelined or deleted knowledge is about women? It is. She cites the case of Donna Strickland, a Canadian physicist who repeatedly had her draft biographies rejected by Wikipedia, until she won a Nobel prize for her work. Awkward. But it goes broader. By the Wikimedia Foundation’s own estimate, only 19% of Wikipedia biographies concern women. Toksvig puts this down to the site being edited by “mostly white, middle-aged, European men who have both the time and the technology”, she told Cheltenham literature festival this weekend. I didn’t know that. Its content is weighted heavily towards wealthy countries. In 2013, for instance, the Oxford Internet Institute discovered that Wikipedia contained more coverage of Germany than of Africa and South America combined. Isn’t Wikipedia too leftwing anyway? Oh God, are you Elon Musk? This is a claim he has repeated for the last couple of years, to the extent of calling it “Wokepedia”. And what did he do about it? He started his own version – an AI-powered alternative called Grokipedia. And is it better? A paper published in November 2025 discovered that Grokipedia articles are 13 times more likely to contain a source blacklisted by the English Wikipedia community. What’s a blacklisted source? The paper pointed out that, at the time of its publication, Grokipedia included 42 citations for the banned neo-Nazi website Stormfront. Yeesh. Bring on Mappa Mundi! Indeed, Toksvig’s version has better intentions. If nothing else, hopefully it will update Wikipedia’s list of people who died on the toilet to include more women. Do say: “Wikipedia is systemically biased.” Don’t say: “At last, something Elon Musk and Sandi Toksvig can agree on.” • Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Federal judge orders temporary halt to taxpayer-funded pro-Trump TV ads
summary: New York judge also orders administration to cancel remaining portion of a $20m advertising purchase
text: A federal judge has ordered Donald Trump’s administration to temporarily halt the broadcast of taxpayer-funded television ads promoting the president ahead of the 3 November midterm elections. Effective as of 6.45pm ET on Sunday, US district judge Jennifer L Rochon of the southern district of New York issued a temporary restraining order aimed at the ads that is meant to stay in effect for at least 14 days. The administration “shall not enter into, renew, or expand any agreement authorizing the development, creation, dissemination, placement, or airing of the … advertisements,” Rochon said in her ruling. Rochon also ordered the administration to cancel the remaining portion of a $20m advertising purchase, halting further spending on the campaign. The judge’s ruling came amid a legal challenge filed by government watchdog Common Cause, Alabama state house Democratic candidate Robert Hunter, Service Employees International Union Local 32BJ, and the union’s political action committee, Empire State 32BJ SEIU PAC. In their lawsuit, the plaintiffs named the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) and the Executive Office of the President (EOP) as defendants. They argued that the administration was using public funds to influence elections, stating: “In short, lacking any legal basis, and in the face of explicit legal prohibitions, defendants are attempting to skew midterm and state elections by using taxpayer dollars to run publicity and propaganda.” The plaintiffs contended that the ads were a “blatant abuse of authority”. Rochon’s ruling on Sunday said that the plaintiffs “have demonstrated that they are likely to succeed on the merits, will suffer irreparable harm in the absence of an injunction, the balance of the equities tips in their favor, and an injunction serves the public interest”. The Guardian has reached out to DHS, OMB and the White House for comment. The White House referred to Trump’s 5 October post on his Truth Social platform in which he said he considered the ads “to be a positive promotion” for the US. He argued that “paying for them with [USA] money … is a rather standard thing to do” – but he claimed he would fund them himself with money raised by his Make America great again political movement. The plaintiffs responded to Rochon’s ruling with a statement that said: “We are pleased the court acted swiftly to prevent more taxpayer dollars from being used for such blatantly unlawful political propaganda. There is no legal justification – and no precedent – for the president to use the machinery of the government and funds set aside by Congress for other uses to influence electoral outcomes that further his own agenda.” The Democratic National Committee on 7 October filed a similar lawsuit against the Trump administration, asking a Washington DC judge to halt the president from using taxpayer money to promote himself. According to media tracking firm AdImpact, the ads have cost taxpayers more than $12m. They have also sparked bipartisan criticism. The lawsuit said the ads have aired on major networks such as ABC, CNN, NBC and Fox News. They have been shown during National Football League games as well as popular news and late-night shows, including Jimmy Kimmel Live, which Trump has previously criticized heavily. The suit also identifies eight unaired ads, including one celebrating UFC fights at the White House; a hymn praising Trump; and another showing a lion hunting while disparaging his political opponents, including former president Barack Obama.
