title: Children and women included in Reform plan to immediately deport 90,000 asylum seekers
summary: Farage’s party says it would ‘embed’ immigration enforcement in UK and use ‘aerial imaging’ to identify people
text: Children and mothers would not be exempt from plans by Reform UK to immediately deport 90,000 asylum seekers and impose a five-year ban on people being granted asylum. The party’s most hardline immigration policies to date were condemned by refugee charities and others as “unworkable” and an abandonment of Britain’s tradition of helping victims of war after they were announced by Nigel Farage on Monday. New claims ⁠would be automatically rejected and failed applicants would be returned either to their home countries or a safe third country while a Reform government would impose tariffs, visa bans or airspace restrictions on countries refusing to accept ‌the return of asylum ‌seekers. Asked if children would be exempt, Farage told a press conference in Kent: “If you allow Palestinian or Afghan women to come as well as children, that may well sound compassionate given the circumstances in that country. However, as soon as you do that you open the door to family reunions, to husbands coming, to partners coming, before you know it you have plenty of young men coming as well.” The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, said last month that approximately a quarter of arrivals under the reopened UK Resettlement Scheme (UKRS) will consist of Afghan women and girls fleeing Taliban rule and Palestinians who have fled Gaza. A Home Office source said Farage was mistaken in his claim as those coming under the scheme will not have reunion rights. Appearing in front of a replica of the type of inflatable boat that he said was now being used to cross the Channel, Farage said a Reform government would also review the status of anyone granted asylum since 2024. Those coming from countries deemed safe by a Reform home secretary would lose their permission to remain in the UK, while all legal resettlement routes would also be abolished, except for those set up for Ukrainians in the wake of the full-scale Russian invasion in 2022. A 17-page document published by the party on Monday envisages the “embedding” of immigration enforcement throughout the state, and effectively society, by including immigration checks in food safety, housing and licensing inspections. People targeted for deportation would be identified from data on water or electricity usage, “aerial imaging” and complaints from neighbours. Zia Yusuf, the party’s would-be home secretary, said Reform planned to deport “north of 1 million people” but insisted the party was “not in the business of sending people to be killed or tortured”, telling the press conference there would be “third-country options” for “edge cases”. However, the Refugee Council said that closing Britain’s asylum system would “cause chaos” and desperate people who would still arrive on the country’s shores would be driven underground instead of entering an orderly system. Jon Featonby, the chief policy analyst at the charity, said: “These unworkable proposals would see us abandon our proud tradition of offering safety to victims of war, which our ancestors established in response to the horrors of world war two.” The Labour party’s chair, Bridget Phillipson, said the Reform UK leader was “casting around for more and more extreme policies” as he faced questions about his own finances and the threat posed by rivals Restore Britain, which appeared to have cost his party the opportunity of finishing third in the St Pancras and Holborn byelection. Phillipson said that Labour could “control immigration and get numbers down with serious action, not by abandoning the asylum system altogether”. The new Reform policy was described by Luke Tryl, the UK director of More in Common, as an “eye-catching” move that was perhaps aimed at stemming the growth of Rupert Lowe’s Restore Britain party on Farage’s right. Tryl added that a policy to stop asylum entirely ran contrary to the desire of a majority of Reform voters, of whom only 14% wanted to see a cessation of Britain welcoming people fleeing persecution and war.

title: Indian opposition figures lead march to police barricades around supreme court
summary: Thousands join rally to deliver petition calling for resignation of election commissioner
text: Delhi police have again obstructed protests in India’s capital as thousands of people returned to the streets, led by opposition leaders, to demand the resignation of the election commissioner. After mass unrest in the capital over the weekend, when thousands were detained and harassed by police as they attempted to take part in a protest led by the gen Z Cockroach movement, on Monday the main opposition leaders led another procession through Delhi, this time to the supreme court. The leader of India’s opposition alliance, Rahul Gandhi, alongside other opposition figures and student groups, had declared their intention to march to the court and submit a petition calling for India’s chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, to step down. Kumar has become a deeply controversial figure for his role in an exercise to verify and “purify” India’s electoral rolls, which has led to more than 130m names – more than the population of Japan – being deleted from voter lists since last year. Opposition parties and civil society groups allege Kumar implemented this special intensive revision (SIR) to help entrench the power of Narendra Modi’s government and his Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata party (BJP). Muslim voters and other minorities who are traditionally not BJP voters have allegedly been disproportionately affected by the deletions. The election commission has denied favouring any party and said wrongly deleted ‌voters could re-enrol, while the BJP has accused its rivals of trying to undermine democracy by questioning legitimate electoral processes. Several metro stations were closed on Monday in central Delhi and police barricades prevented thousands of protesters getting within 600m of the supreme court, forcing them to turn back. However, lawyers confirmed they had submitted the petition on Gandhi’s behalf and by late evening, Gandhi had broken through the barricades and reached the court gates. In a press conference before the march, Gandhi reiterated his allegation that the Modi government was using the commission to commit “vote chori” (cheating) and accused Kumar of being a “thief”. Gandhi expressed support for the mass uprising of young people, led by the Cockroach Janta party (CJP) and student groups, who had tried to protest over the weekend but were met with police brutality and mass detentions. “Till the constitution is upheld, till the chief election commissioner is removed, till the system of elections is revamped, till justice is served for India, the youth won’t stop,” he said. The SIR and calls for Kumar’s resignation have galvanised support for beleaguered opposition parties, who are seen to have flailed in the face of the BJP’s electoral power. Gandhi was detained twice last week after the police refused to let him and other opposition leaders reach Jantar Mantar, the designated protest site in central Delhi. Mahua Moitra, an opposition MP who was marching after being detained last week, alleged that in her constituency in West Bengal more than 10,000 voters had been unjustly removed from the electoral rolls. “There’s no going back now. People know that their votes have been stolen and this government is finished,” Moitra said. “The police can detain us, they can use brute force and crack our skulls, but we are not going to get off the streets until Gyanesh Kumar resigns and this government is gone. If we don’t stand up to this, then there will be nothing left of our country.” Moitra accused the supreme court of helping to validate the SIR process and disenfranchise millions of Indians. “When the history of this dark chapter of India is written, the supreme court will be the most disgraced,” she said. “It was the supreme court who put a stamp of approval on every illegality of this government.” Gandhi has spent months accusing the BJP of fraudulently influencing elections, but his claims have been largely ignored. The issue exploded last month after the Indian Express newspaper reported multiple irregularities in the SIR process that had been pushed through by Kumar. The protests are likely to continue this week. On Monday, leaders of the CJP approached the Delhi police to seek a date to be allowed to hold a protest without obstruction. They said that if the police refused to comply, their supporters would take to the streets again.

title: Nobel Prize for economics awarded to Hall and Woodford for work on ‘smoothing’ crises
summary: US economists developed models that help central bankers and finance ministers to stabilise their economies
text: Two US economists have won the 2026 Nobel economics prize for their work developing models that help central bankers and finance ministers to stabilise their countries, avoiding long recessions and runaway inflation. Robert Hall of Stanford University, California, and Michael Woodford of Columbia University, New York, were recognised for developing the “microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation”, giving policymakers better tools to smooth out the peaks and troughs of their economies. The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences said it was recognising the pair for generating “a paradigm shift in stabilisation policy”, awarding them the prize worth a combined $1.2m (£900,000). “New Keynesian models, a result of their research, allow us to explain and quantify how stabilisation policy affects business cycles and are now used by central banks and finance ministries around the world,” the academy said. These models improved on John Maynard Keynes’s stabilisation models, which struggled to handle the impact of the oil shock in the 1970s, when countries suffered high inflation, weak growth and high unemployment at the same time. Hall and Woodford demonstrated how traditional models could be reconstructed, based on how individual households and businesses collectively affect an economy through their actions. Hall’s work was based on forward-looking consumer behaviour rather than the more mechanical rules of thumb used by Keynes, which linked key variables such as inflation, unemployment and gross domestic product (GDP). Woodford built on this work to create the New Keynesian model, a full macroeconomic stabilisation framework that is the main tool for policymakers now. This model was used after the 2008 financial crisis by policymakers as they steered the global economy away from the risk of a second great depression. “The laureates’ work has provided us with a stable theoretical foundation for the models that are now used by central banks and governments around the world. With them, we are better equipped to deal with shocks in the economy, such as energy crises or sudden changes in how much households consume,” John Hassler, the chair of the committee for the economics prize, said. Hall and Woodford’s work also led to the development of forward guidance, where central bankers communicate where they expect interest rates to be in the future. That became an important tool after the 2008 financial crisis, and the Covid pandemic, when interest rates were cut to record lows. Forward guidance has had its critics, though – the current chair of the US Federal Reserve, Kevin Warsh, has argued it should only have a “limited and circumscribed” role in normal times, to avoid “creating ambiguity in the name of clarity”. And in 2014, the then Bank of England governor, Mark Carney, was labelled an “unreliable boyfriend” for dropping hints over interest rate rises that never came to pass. Woodford said he was “elated”. “It’s a tremendous honour. It’s a surprise but I’m feeling very good about it,” he told reporters in Stockholm by phone after receiving the news. The Columbia University president, Jennifer L Mnookin, said: “I offer my deepest congratulations to Michael Woodford on this tremendous honour. “What a tribute to his groundbreaking work alongside Robert E Hall that has fundamentally reshaped the theoretical foundations of stabilisation policy and provided us with the tools to navigate economic upturns and downturns more effectively.” Hall is also known for coining the idea that US economists can be divided into freshwater and saltwater varieties. The fresh water group, who tend to be based at inland universities located near the Great Lakes, such as the University of Chicago, believe in free markets, neoclassical price theory, rational expectations and monetarism. Salt water economists, though, cluster at coastal universities, such as Harvard, MIT, UC Berkeley, Yale, Princeton, UCLA and Columbia. They tend to be Keynesians and New Keynesians, believing that governments and central banks can affect demand in their economies. The economics Nobel prize is not one of the five created by Alfred Nobel. Instead, it was invented by Sweden’s central bank, and is known as the Sveriges Riksbank prize in economic sciences in memory of Alfred Nobel.

title: Student lay in wait for housemate before stabbing him 30 times, Bristol court hears
summary: Zack Coughlan is accused of murdering Jamie Collins, with whom he studied at the University of the West of England
text: A university student lay in wait for his housemate to return home before stabbing him 30 times, a murder trial has been told. Zack Coughlan, 23, dressed in black and wore a mask and gloves to ambush Jamie Collins, 21, in the garden of their home near the University of West England in Bristol, where both were studying robotics. Collins was attacked shortly before 6pm on 8 April after returning from campus on his bike, Bristol crown court heard. Coughlan then allegedly cycled away on the bike, dumped it at a nearby retail park, bought a change of clothes and threw his bloodstained clothing into a pond. He returned to the house they shared in Filton, south Gloucestershire, at about 9pm, put a pizza in the oven and did some online gaming with friends, the court was told. Adam Vaitilingam KC, prosecuting, said: “A few hours later he decided it was time to call the police and pretend that he had just found his friend’s body in the garden. “At about 2am, eight hours later, the defendant called 999. He said that his friend had been stabbed. They told him to do CPR until paramedics arrived and he told them that he was.” He told police he had noticed the back gate was open, went outside and found Collins’s body. The court heard the attack was caught on CCTV installed at the house, which Coughlan showed officers, who initially treated him as a witness. Coughlan had injuries to his hands but he said he had hurt himself when he fell while climbing trees. Vaitilingam said that as the evidence against Coughlan mounted, he went from being a witness to a suspect. He now accepted he had killed Collins but denied murder. He said he “lost his self-control” when he carried out the attack, the barrister said. The jury was told that Coughlan and Collins were final-year students and lived together in a house owned by the defendant. Vaitilingam said there had been disagreements between the pair about rent and whether Coughlan was charging too much, but they appeared to have been resolved. “There was nothing that any friends were aware of that seemed to be a significant problem,” he said. “They hung out together, both in person and online, they did gaming together, they went out together; entirely normal student life.” The trial continues.

title: ‘BYD effect’: electric vehicle boom becomes unexpected tool to combat inflation
summary: More and more Australian consumers are expected to ‘unplug themselves from the oil shock’ with at least five EVs priced around or below $30,000
text: Electric vehicle sales are surging in Australia, powering a transition that goes beyond fuel savings to become an unexpected tool to combat high inflation. The abrupt shift away from petrol and diesel vehicles, accelerated by elevated fuel costs caused by the Iran conflict, is being supported by an influx of cheaper EVs that is reducing associated costs such as insurance. Chris Dickman, senior portfolio manager at fund manager Australian Ethical, describes the trend as the “BYD effect”, referring to the low-priced Chinese vehicles which he says are an unexpected disinflationary force. Dickman says that by helping drivers use less petrol, and bringing down the cost of new and used cars, EV uptake is blunting the impact of high oil prices across the economy. “There are more and more consumers who are trying to unplug themselves from the oil shock,” Dickman says. He says the rise of EVs is an example of how newer, cleaner technology eventually outcompetes incumbents on pure economics as they gain popularity and market size. Virtually all of the EV cost impediments of a few years ago – including high sticker prices, inadequate charging networks, elevated insurance premiums and expensive servicing, battery and parts replacements – are reversing as Australia’s market matures. NRMA’s car ownership report found that there are now at least five EVs priced around or below the $30,000 mark, all of which are Chinese brands. Fuelling the shift While EVs and hybrids have been gaining traction for years, the US-Israel war on Iran and subsequent oil price spike accelerated demand in March, and it has continued largely unabated. Battery EV sales now account for almost 25% of new vehicle sales, according to Federal Chamber of Automotive Industries data. About half of all new sales are either EVs or hybrids, and more EVs were sold last month than petrol-only cars. The EV-focused Chinese brands BYD, GWM, Chery and MG were all in the top 10 biggest selling automakers in Australia in September. Three years ago, only MG featured in that list. The American multinational Tesla delivered 5,654 vehicles in September, according to Electric Vehicle Council data, making it the sixth biggest seller. Adam Triggs, co-founder at economics consulting group Mandala Partners, said the next step towards protecting Australia from oil shocks was to electrify diesel-dependent freight networks. “When we look at light commercial vehicles, those are the little trucks that sort of fly around the streets, they already have a total cost of ownership that is very competitive against their fossil fuel counterparts, and we would expect those to be the first to go electric,” he says. Diesel prices have now surpassed $2.80 a litre at many petrol stations, while unleaded has pushed past $2.40/L in most state capital cities, according to Australian Institute of Petroleum data. The high fuel prices are rattling the Australian economy, elevating costs across nearly all goods and services and overshadowing the deflationary effect of the EV transition. Last month, the Reserve Bank lifted its key interest rate to 4.6%, its highest level since 2011, and warned of further hikes as the unending Iran conflict pushes prices “permanently higher”. Triggs says there’s a role for the government to help offset the upfront costs of electrifying Australia’s freight networks. “What’s happened over time is once you’ve got a critical mass, you end up seeing costs fall dramatically,” Triggs said. “It’s the same for trucks. There are some practical things for the government to do over the next five to 10 years to start getting the freight fleet electrified, and then the market will take over from there.” • This article was amended on 13 October 2026 to include Tesla in the table of top 10 vehicle brands sold.

title: Cyber-attack similar to OpenAI Medicare breach seems likely in UK, says minister
summary: Kanishka Narayan, concerned by Australian incident, says British cyber defences could be bypassed by artificial intelligence agent
text: An AI-driven cyber-attack similar to the OpenAI breach of Australia’s healthcare system is likely, “if not inevitable”, in the UK, according to a senior minister. Kanishka Narayan, the UK AI minister, indicated that the British government’s own cyber defences would be bypassed by a technology that has developed highly sophisticated skills in cybersecurity. In a speech Narayan said an incident in June when an OpenAI agent – a computer program acting autonomously – infiltrated Medicare, Australia’s universal healthcare system, could be repeated in the UK. “It concerns me,” he said. “It seems likely, if not inevitable, that our own cyber defences will be breached.” Narayan said the agent’s task was “benign” as it searched for information about public spending on medicines, but it nonetheless went after data that it was not authorised to have. “The Australian government has said that no personal medical records are known to have been accessed, and there is no evidence of wider compromise, but the incident should concern us,” he said. Speaking at a science and tech hub at Imperial College London, Narayan said the security minister, Dan Jarvis, would lead a government programme to strengthen against cyber-attacks, including from AI. The government will also consider using the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill as a vehicle for introducing AI safety regulations, including making it mandatory to report AI safety incidents. Narayan spoke before a parliamentary hearing on AI safety on Tuesday into the issue. Senior figures from OpenAI and Anthropic will be among those giving evidence to MPs on the business, innovation, science and trade committee. They will also be joined by the head of the UK’s AI Security Institute, Henry de Zoete. Narayan confirmed that the institute would gain access to advanced AI models before they were released, after the White House had reportedly placed restrictions on their availability. “I can confirm that AI scientists at the AI Security Institute are now conducting rigorous evaluations of the latest generations of models, including [Google’s] Gemini … to identify risks early to test robust safeguards to help keep people safe,” he said. The minister added that leading AI companies must “listen” to warnings of safety risks posed by their technology – and not release models if they carried a serious threat. “And to the companies developing the world’s most powerful AI systems, my message is: listen when your scientists warn of severe dangers; investigate unexpected behaviours; and if you can’t adequately control the risks, do not release the system,” he said. “I want the labs to be honest.” Narayan said the UK would “play its part” in coordinating an international response to AI safety by making the technology a “central focus” of Britain’s G20 presidency next year. “We know that these challenges cannot be addressed by a single country alone, but by virtue of our capability, by virtue of the foundations of our trust, Britain will play its part,” he said.

title: Revealed: Nigel Farage adviser had unpublicised role at polling firm
summary: Exclusive: Chris Bruni-Lowe used Redfield & Wilton Strategies role to develop potential campaign tactics, sources say
text: A close adviser to Nigel Farage had an influential role at a national polling company despite not being publicly associated with the firm, the Guardian can reveal. Chris Bruni-Lowe, Farage’s private pollster for many years, played an important role in the operations of Redfield & Wilton Strategies and used it to develop potential campaign strategies, according to several sources who have worked there. The firm, founded in 2020, is owned by Bruno Rodrigues, a lawyer. Its main public face was Philip van Scheltinga, a Harvard graduate. As the Covid pandemic grew and the UK entered lockdown, the company’s polls received increasing coverage, even while the source of the firm’s polling expertise was unclear. Former employees have now revealed the important role of Bruni-Lowe, who sometimes went by the name “Chris Redfield”, under which quotes were published by the Washington Post newspaper. As well as ordering UK and US voter intention polls, sources said Bruni-Lowe directed research on issues such as council spending, and appeared “obsessed” with producing a dossier which he suggested could be sold to political parties. Bruni-Lowe’s role at the company will amplify questions about transparency in the polling industry, given his longstanding association with Farage at a time of intense scrutiny over the party’s use of polls to shape its political narrative. The rules of the British Polling Council do not require pollsters to state any political affiliations, but they have strict guidelines on how they must declare who has commissioned and paid for any polling. In a statement, Rodrigues, the company’s sole director, said there had never been “an institutional, polling, research, commissioning or financial relationship” between Redfield & Wilton and Reform UK or Farage. He said Bruni-Lowe had worked as a “consultant” from mid-2020 until late 2022, and returned “voluntarily” in the summer of 2025 to train interns. Rodrigues added that Bruni-Lowe was “an important and highly valued member” of the team. Sources said Bruni-Lowe, who some employees said had been known as “Chris Redfield”, was heavily involved in the company’s polling operations. Rodrigues said the surname Redfield was used as an email account convention within the organisation, citing other examples of “Philip Redfield” and “Bruno Redfield”. He said: “It was not a device created specifically for Chris and it did not conceal his identity from people working within the company.” Nonetheless, the situation was confusing enough that at least one newspaper, the Washington Post, attributed quotes to that name, while notes taken by one former employee during an oral induction in the summer of 2021, and seen by the Guardian, described “boss – Chris Redfield is COO essentially”. Rodrigues said: “He was never presented to staff as the company’s chief operating officer and staff were never instructed to treat him as such.” He added that Van Scheltinga, as director of research, led the “day-to-day operation”. The Guardian can also reveal that Dan Jukes, then a senior adviser to Farage, sought to promote Redfield & Wilton’s work in 2020, looking to place exclusive polls in publications including the Guardian, which turned down the offer. Jukes stepped down as Farage’s chief of staff recently over a scandal in which undercover reporters posed as potential overseas donors to Reform UK. Footage published by Channel 4 News showed the co-founder of polling firm JL Partners, James Johnson, apparently acknowledging that Jukes had commissioned polling funded by an overseas donor. The polling had appeared in newspapers without any reference to the party, with JL Partners acknowledging “weaknesses” in its procedures. Jukes denies wrongdoing and Reform UK has said the party itself did not commission the work. On Wednesday, Reform announced that an internal inquiry had cleared the officials of breaking the law. The matter remains under police investigation. Redfield & Wilton started producing polls in 2020 with little information about the people behind the company. During its publicly active years before it became less visible in late 2024, its voter intention polls frequently appeared in politically influential newsletters from Politico, the Times, and the New Statesman. Bruni-Lowe ran Farage’s 2015 election campaign, helped test messaging for the formation of the Brexit party and advised on the 2019 local elections campaign, as well as having produced private polling for Farage since at least 2014, apart from during a brief period of working for Rishi Sunak before the 2024 election. In his book on political strategy, he writes of having worked for “organisations and candidates of all political persuasions”. He is considered to be part of Farage’s inner circle and was close enough to the Reform UK leader to have been present on a trip to party donor Christopher Harborne’s Thai wellness retreat at Christmas in 2022 to mark the crypto billionaire’s 60th birthday. Other guests photographed at the meeting include Farage’s unpaid aide and convicted fraudster George Cottrell. In May 2023, Van Scheltinga and Bruni-Lowe were photographed having drinks at a Mayfair restaurant with Farage, Cottrell and Richard Tice, the Reform UK deputy leader. Rodrigues said: “The existence of personal or social meetings involving individuals associated with the company does not establish a corporate relationship between Redfield & Wilton Strategies and Reform UK.” While much of Redfield & Wilton’s published polling related to voter intentions in the UK and the US, sources said Bruni-Lowe had its staff develop a “dossier” on local authority performance between autumn 2024 and spring 2025. One source said he suggested the firm’s work could be sold to political parties, and that Bruni-Lowe appeared “obsessed” with the dossier. Research by employees included freedom of information requests to councils to find expenditure on translation services. Rodrigues said the FOI project was a “commercial research project” and translation services were just one of “several dozen categories” examined by the company in a project led by Van Scheltinga. He added that none of the research was supplied to Reform or Farage. The company’s other work, sources said, included polling in Montenegro, Hungary, Hong Kong and the Bahamas, as well as research about attitudes in the UK to gold and cryptocurrencies. Employees were not always told exactly how their work would be used. According to one former employee, they were told their work on a foreign election would be for the Telegraph, but the polling never appeared in the newspaper. Another said they believed their work on cryptocurrencies was for a client. One unusual piece of work by the company was an October 2021 submission to an inquiry into central bank digital currencies (CBDCs) carried out by the House of Lords economic affairs committee. The company cited polling it said “was self-funded internally by Redfield & Wilton Strategies Ltd for the purpose of this submission”. The submission said the scepticism of the British public over the UK government’s capacity for innovation meant “it is strategically important that alternatives to a CBDC from the private sector, including those that are already in use, are also given the opportunity to be developed further”. According to a person who worked at the company at the time of the submission, “all of the crypto stuff came down from Chris [Bruni-Lowe]”. One online profile for Rodrigues, a solicitor based in London, refers to him holding a directorship of an “innovative market research firm”. However, according to former employees, he had a limited role in the day-to-day running of Redfield & Wilton. One source said that at a rare in-person meeting Rodrigues was “paraded around on a laptop on a Zoom call”. Van Scheltinga was frequently quoted giving analysis of the company’s polling and wrote columns for the Times and Telegraph. Van Scheltinga was the listed contact for the company with the British Polling Council, the trade body for pollsters, but one industry source said he never attended BPC meetings. This led to demands from the BPC for a representative of the group to appear before them: that was ultimately Rodrigues, the nominal director, who maintained “total silence”, according to the industry source. Bruni-Lowe declined to comment. Van Scheltinga did not respond to requests for comment.

title: Fire destroys Marché des Enfants Rouges, ‘coolest market in Paris’
summary: ‘A lot of sadness’ after 17th century landmark that escaped demolition in the 1980s goes up in flames
text: Fire has ravaged Paris’s oldest surviving covered food market, a popular street food venue dating back to the 17th century in the Marais district of the French capital that drew thousands of locals and tourists daily. Ariel Weil, the central Paris mayor, said the Marché des Enfants ‌Rouges had been “totally destroyed” in the blaze, which broke out soon after 3am. “The worst was avoided: the fire did not spread to the surrounding buildings,” he said. “But there is a lot of emotion. A lot of sadness.” The market was established in 1615 during the reign of Louis XIII and took its name from a nearby orphanage, the Hospice des Enfants Rouges – founded in 1536 by King Francis I and his sister Marguerite de Navarre – whose child residents were habitually dressed in red. The structure was listed as a historic monument in 1982 but narrowly escaped demolition shortly afterwards when Paris city hall, led by the then mayor, Jacques Chirac, approved radical redevelopment plans that would have replaced it with an underground car park, a council daycare facility and community centre. A determined campaign by local residents and neighbourhood associations, backed by intellectuals, writers and artists including film-makers and photographers such as Bertrand Tavernier and Willy Ronis, who captured its traders on camera, gathered tens of thousands of signatures in protest and the plans were eventually abandoned in the mid-1990s. Rather than demolish the building, the city undertook a six-year, 13m-franc (about €3m, or £2.5m today) renovation project, restoring the market’s historic wood and ironwork frame and glass roof. Les Enfants Rouges reopened as a food court in 2000. While still hosting some traditional stalls including a greengrocer, butcher, cheesemonger and fishmonger, the 1,000 sq m market was mostly given over to more than a dozen stands offering French, Lebanese, Moroccan, Japanese and other street food at the counter or at casual chairs and tables. The current Time Out tourist guide describes Les Enfants Rouges as “the coolest market in Paris”, while the authoritative US website Food&Wine ranked it fifth worldwide for street food this year after other food courts in London, Bangkok, Lyon and Mexico City. Lt Col Pierre de Bouvier of the Paris fire service said much of the metal structure of the market had fallen in, and most of the stalls had gone up in flames. More than 150 firefighters and 50 fire trucks battled the blaze after being alerted at 4.15am, he said, adding that the cause of the fire was not yet known.

title: Why are the Houthis attacking Saudi airports and how are the missiles getting through?
summary: Attacks by Iran-backed group come amid counteroffensive by Yemeni government supported by Riyadh
text: What happened over the weekend? On Saturday, a missile strike by the Houthis in Yemen hit Riyadh’s international airport, killing 13 people and wounding hundreds. On Sunday, another attack ‌killed one person and injured nearly a dozen others. CCTV footage showed people cowering at the moment of impact of Saturday’s attack. Footage filmed in the aftermath of showed damage inside one of the terminal buildings at the airport, which is located about 22 miles north of the Saudi Arabian capital. The attacks by the Houthis, an Iran-backed group, were the biggest escalation yet in their campaign ⁠against Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in recent weeks. Though the violence might appear at first sight to be restricted to the Arabian peninsula, it could have global consequences, pushing up fuel prices and so international inflation. Why now? The Houthis’ timing is partly opportunistic but also rooted in the dynamics of the conflicts across the Gulf. The Houthis initially stayed on the sidelines of the conflict launched by the US and Israel against Iran earlier this year. But last month, the Islamist militia movement seized control of key territory and gained virtual control of the Bab al-Mandab strait, which dominates the Red Sea, a critical shipping route for oil and gas exports from the region. The Yemeni government forces and local allies began a major counteroffensive last week to drive back the Houthis from the Bab al-Mandab and also hit other Houthi positions. Saudi Arabia is in the Houthis’ crosshairs because it supports Yemen’s UN-backed government and its forces. Their attacks on high-profile targets in the kingdom such as oil infrastructure and the capital’s airport – key symbols of its international integration and economic future – makes painfully obvious the costs of Riyadh’s strategic choices. Such attacks also benefit Iran, which has long supported the Houthis as part of its “axis of resistance”, a coalition of Islamist hardline movements that allows Tehran to project power and influence round the region. The new threat from the Houthis to the Red Sea and to Saudi Arabia highlights again the massive leverage Tehran and its allies can exert on global oil and gas supplies, countering recent US pressure in bold move on the conflict’s chessboard. How is this new territory for Saudi Arabia? The recent attacks on Saudi Arabia have been the deadliest to hit the kingdom in a decade. They also marked one of the most significant disruptions to Saudi civil aviation in years, forcing airlines across Europe and Asia to suspend services. Businesses in Riyadh’s financial hub have told employees to work remotely, authorities in Riyadh have asked schools to switch to online classes this week, and top energy executives were ⁠dropped from the schedule of a high-profile conference this week in the capital. Though Saudi Arabia has intervened indirectly in conflicts around the Middle East and beyond for decades, violence has rarely struck the kingdom itself. In recent months, the country has found itself on a frontline, something its rulers have long sought to avoid. Why couldn’t Riyadh stop the missiles? Saudi Arabia has invested enormous sums in its military – the kingdom is the world’s eighth biggest spender on weapons – but Houthi attacks are very hard to stop. “Saudi air defences have been able to intercept some Houthi missile and drone attacks, but Saudi Arabia is so large that it’s simply impossible for them to consistently defend themselves,” said Thomas Juneau, a security analyst at the University of Ottawa. Other analysts point out that even the vaunted Israeli air defence systems failed to stop a ballistic missile narrowly missing Ben Gurion international airport last year. Reprisals against the Houthis and efforts to pre-emptively destroy the movement’s offensive capabilities are not easy either. The US bombardment in 2025 showed how hard it is to destroy the militia’s capabilities, which have been much enhanced over recent years, in part through Iranian advice and investment. What might happen next? The Houthis say their actions were “guided by reciprocity” – suggesting they are responding to ongoing Saudi strikes on the territory they control in Yemen – but show no sign of stopping their attacks. “Unless the Saudi enemy stops its aggression and interference in Yemen, worse is yet to come, God willing,” official statements carried by the Houthi-run al-Masirah television channel said. It seems unlikely Saudi Arabia will halt its counterstrikes, and equally unlikely the kingdom will be able to find a way to block all incoming Houthi missiles, though it may improve its intelligence gathering and early warning to allow better defence of specific high-value targets. Nor is there any imminent prospect of an end to the hostilities between Iran and the US that are a major factor in the surge of the recent violence in Yemen. And though the Houthis are more a coalition of different factions than a coherent single movement, for the moment they appear unified behind hardline and ideologically committed leaders. Farea al-Muslimi, a specialist on Yemen and the Gulf at Chatham House in London, said the Houthis had been consistently underestimated over the years. “They have really upped their game and believe they can get something now which will reposition them within the region. They are very confident at the moment and feeling empowered …. But though they think they can control this [escalation], that may well be an illusion,” he said.

title: Is it a plane or a tree? Amelia Earhart expedition aims to solve mystery of disappearance
summary: Researchers will head to remote Pacific atoll, but sceptics say satellite images unlikely to be of her aircraft
text: A team of US researchers is approaching a remote Pacific atoll where they suspect the famed aviator Amelia Earhart crash-landed in 1937, in the latest attempt to crack one of the biggest mysteries of the 20th century. The 17-person expedition was inspired by satellite images taken over several years showing a submerged object in the uninhabited island’s sandy lagoon – evidence dismissed by other longtime Earhart sleuths who say it is probably a fallen tree. These researchers – led by archaeologists who raised funding from Earhart’s former benefactor, Purdue University – hope it will instead be revealed as the wreckage of her Lockheed Model 10-E Electra. Separate aerial footage of the area suggested the submerged object has a metallic glint, the team say. “Finding Amelia Earhart’s Electra aircraft would be the discovery of a lifetime,” said the expedition’s leader, Richard Pettigrew, before he set sail this month. “Confirming the plane wreckage there would be the smoking-gun proof.” Earhart and her navigator Fred Noonan vanished during their attempt to circumnavigate the globe at the equator. By that point, Earhart, 39, was already a celebrity and aviation pioneer, having broken several records including being the first woman to make a nonstop solo transatlantic flight. Locating the wreck of the twin-engine plane would confirm a long-held – but unproven – hypothesis that Earhart and Noonan ditched at the atoll of Nikumaroro, part of the archipelago country of Kiribati and about halfway between Australia and Hawaii. They were en route to Howland Island, about 400 miles north of Nikumaroro, when their plane ran low on fuel and disappeared. After a six-day sea voyage from Tarawa, the capital of Kiribati, the research group is expected to arrive on the uninhabited atoll on Tuesday local time and will spend several days searching for the “Taraia Object”, an elongated shape named after the part of the island where it was first noticed in a 2020 satellite image. The expedition says it has been lying there for several years, and is even visible in aerial photography dating back to 1938. Pettigrew, who heads the Archaeological Legacy Institute, a nonprofit organisation, raised funds for the mission with Purdue University in Indiana, where Earhart once taught and which funded her ill-fated final flight on the modified plane she called her “flying laboratory”. The university runs an airport and opened an Amelia Earhart Terminal last year. The expedition builds on an already large body of evidence pinpointing the atoll as the location where the aviators went down. Much of it was gathered during dozens of visits between 1989 and 2019 by teams from the US explorers group Tigher (The International Group for Historic Aircraft Recovery). Tighar’s co-founder – and perhaps Earhart’s most well-known explorer – Ric Gillespie, said the Taraia Object was likely a dead pandanus tree, which is native to the area, that washed into the lagoon. Gillespie, who is the author of One More Good Flight: The Amelia Earhart Tragedy, said he and other teams had visited the exact site where the object was located in 2001 and 2007 with metal detectors. “There’s nothing there, or we would have found it,” he said in an interview this year. “If they suddenly discover that Amelia Earhart’s wreckage is there, I’ll be very surprised, but I’d be the first one to congratulate them. But I don’t think they are going to find anything.” While Tighar agrees the Electra made an emergency landing on the atoll, they believe it was washed off a reef and now probably lies undiscovered and in pieces in deep water off the island’s western end. Tighar’s version of the mystery was that Earhart, and possibly Noonan, were marooned on Nikumaroro but survived for a while, drinking rainwater and eating small fish and turtles. This theory is based on signs of a castaway’s campsite and 1930s-era artefacts, such as a jar of what is believed to be cosmetics freckle cream. The pair’s disappearance led to a large US government search, including a flyover of Nikumaroro, then known as Gardner Island. The Purdue mission says the object may not have been found by previous expeditions as it could have been covered with sand.

title: Former Irish Olympic swimming coach and child abuser George Gibney jailed for 15 years
summary: Gibney, 78, has faced justice for abusing athletes in the 1970s and 80s after decades of effort to track and extradite him
text: More than half a century after he started sexually abusing children, and enjoyed prestige as Ireland’s Olympic swimming coach before fleeing to the United States, George Gibney has faced justice. The 78-year-old was sentenced to 15 and a half years in prison at the central criminal court in Dublin on Monday for abusing four young female athletes in the 1970s and 1980s. It was the culmination of a decades-long effort by victims, police, journalists and others to track down and extradite Gibney from the US. He was convicted in July of 39 counts of indecent assault and one count of attempted rape after a closely watched trial that detailed harrowing abuse. Judge Micheál P O’Higgin called Gibney a “manipulative predator” who had insinuated himself into the lives of children under his care. “It was predatory in nature and a gross breach of trust,” he said. “He used his coaching role to access and assault defenceless children under his care.” The judge said Gibney had once enjoyed a stellar reputation and that the sentence reflected the gravity of his offending. “From these heights he has fallen, and his reputation now lies in tatters.” The former coach, seated in a wheelchair, showed no emotion. Speaking to reporters outside the court, Orla Poole said she had spent “decades in silence” because of his actions. “I thought I was the only one, that somehow, I deserved what he did to me.” She said other survivors should know that they were not alone and could seek support. “The only guilt for what we went through lies with the convicted paedophile. When you are ready and able, unburden yourself by talking to someone from the Dublin Rape Crisis Centre, One In Four, a therapist, a trusted friend or even the gardaí.” Evin Daly, a child welfare advocate who helped to find Gibney in Florida, said the sentence was vindication for Gibney’s victims. “The abuse shaped some of their lives. The guy had no conscience, in my opinion.” Ireland had little international success in swimming in the 1980s but Gibney became a high-profile, respected figure for establishing the Trojan club in south Dublin and for coaching emerging talent at pools around the city. He was Ireland’s coach for the Olympic games in Los Angeles in 1984 and Seoul in 1988. Gibney urged his swimmers to “never give up” and to “hang in there”. After allegations emerged that he preyed on children at pools, in his car and other locations, he was charged with 27 counts of indecency and carnal knowledge, but in 1993 the supreme court ruled that he could not face trial because of the time that had elapsed since the alleged offences, a decision that stunned his victims. Free but infamous, Gibney moved to Scotland, then the US, where he obtained a visa and built a new life, living in Colorado, California and Florida and working mostly in low-level clerical jobs. Several journalists continued to dig into Gibney’s crimes, including Justine McCarthy of the Irish Times who wrote a 2009 book, Deep Deception. Daly, a forensic sociologist who was then the chief executive of a child protection advocacy group called One Child International, helped the media to locate and keep tabs on Gibney. “We provided data and resources,” said Daly, a Florida-based court consultant on child welfare cases. “At one point Gibney moved because his neighbours in the apartment complex got wind of the fact that he was an accused sex offender and they turned on him.” In 2020 a 10-part podcast series, commissioned by the BBC and presented by Mark Horgan, titled Where is George Gibney? revived attention and scrutiny. Four victims who were minors when they were abused made statements to Irish police between 2020 and 2022, leading to fresh charges, an extradition warrant and Gibney’s arrest and return to Ireland last year. After the conviction in July four victims told the court of the impact of the abuse. One said she retained “intensely personal and traumatic memories” and had harboured a “secret shame, hurt and bewilderment” for more than half a century. The abuse was a “frozen nightmare”, she said. Another victim, who was nine at the time of the assaults, told Gibney in court that he had abused his position of trust and that her burden of shame, guilt and embarrassment was now his. Gibney had presided over “the destruction of a previously happy and healthy child” who was powerless to verbalise her torment, she said. • In the UK, the NSPCC offers support to children on 0800 1111, and adults concerned about a child on 0808 800 5000. The National Association for People Abused in Childhood (Napac) offers support for adult survivors on 0808 801 0331. In the US, call or text the Childhelp abuse hotline on 800-422-4453. In Australia, children, young adults, parents and teachers can contact the Kids Helpline on 1800 55 1800, or Bravehearts on 1800 272 831, and adult survivors can contact Blue Knot Foundation on 1300 657 380. Other sources of help can be found at Child Helplines International

title: SAS personnel ‘refusing to answer’ questions about alleged extrajudicial killings in Afghanistan
summary: Judge leading inquiry says most operators using privilege against self-incrimination to refuse to provide information
text: Most SAS personnel approached by an inquiry into alleged extrajudicial killings in Afghanistan have refused to answer any questions, the judge leading the proceedings has said. Lord Justice Haddon-Cave is investigating allegations of more than 50 summary killings by UK special forces soldiers as well as claims of an alleged cover-up of illegal activity and inadequate investigations by the Royal Military Police. In a public hearing, Haddon-Cave said a number of rule 9 requests – written notices asking for information – had been sent to SAS operators who were linked to the deliberate detention operations (DDOs) at the centre of allegations. “The inquiry has identified numerous SAS personnel from whom it wishes to hear direct evidence as to the DDOs in question and has issued rule 9 requests for information to each of them,” he said. “A high proportion have indicated their intention to rely on their privilege against self-incrimination and have refused to answer any questions asked by the inquiry.” Ministers announced the statutory judge-led inquiry after allegations that 54 Afghans were killed in suspicious circumstances by one SAS unit in Helmand province between 2010 and 2011, and accusations that these amounted to war crimes. A high court case brought by the law firm Leigh Day on behalf of one man, Saifullah, alleged that his father, two brothers and a cousin were killed during an SAS raid on a compound in southern Afghanistan in February 2011. The inquiry is tasked with determining whether investigations conducted by the Royal Military Police were carried out properly and effectively, and whether there is credible information that “numerous” extrajudicial killings were carried out by British armed forces between 2010 and 2013. The judge said the three-year period “sufficiently captures the allegations currently being made”. The inquiry will also seek to determine whether the circumstances of the alleged killings were covered up at any stage and what lessons could be learned. During Monday’s hearing, Haddon-Cave revealed the inquiry had obtained about 10,000 high-resolution photos, taken in the course of the DDOs, which do not appear to have formed part of Royal Military Police inquiries. He said the inquiry was seeking evidence from Afghan families whose loved ones died during the detention operations, adding that the inquiry had heard “extensive” witness evidence regarding concerns and complaints raised by both UK special forces personnel and other individuals about the manner in which the SAS were conducting detention operations in Afghanistan during the period in question. Last week, during a high court hearing, the Ministry of Defence identified material that suggested UK special forces personnel deployed on some operations being considered by the inquiry may have committed serious offences under the Armed Forces Act 2006. The open hearings will continue throughout October and November. Separately, ministers announced a package of amendments to the Northern Ireland Troubles bill, intended to raise the bar before former soldiers can be prosecuted in cases dating back to the Troubles between 1969 and 1998, in an attempt to meet concerns raised by veterans groups. In future, prosecutions will have to be approved by the attorney general, and any evidence has to be “new and compelling” as well as essential to the case before veterans are called to court. Legislation would also emphasise there is no equivalence between soldiers and terrorists.

title: German minister quits after ‘indecent’ attacks intensify during bereavement
summary: Fragile coalition suffers another blow as labour minister and co-leader of SPD Bärbel Bas leaves both posts
text: Germany’s labour minister and co-leader of the centre-left ⁠Social Democrats (SPD), Bärbel Bas, has quit both posts, citing the death of her stepdaughter and subsequent political attacks against her, in a stinging blow to the fragile coalition government. “After my stepdaughter’s death, I realised that I need time to come to terms with my grief,” Bas said in a statement posted on Facebook, without giving further ⁠details. Explaining her departure from frontline politics, Bas explicitly blamed public broadsides against her as she grappled with the family tragedy, “unfortunately also from among the ranks of the coalition partner [Friedrich Merz’s conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU)]”. She said the attacks “continued to intensify during this difficult time for me personally”. Some CDU lawmakers had criticised Bas’s absences during a crunch phase of an economic reform drive seen as crucial to the teetering government’s survival, although it was widely known she had experienced a death in her immediate family. Bas’s co-leader at the SPD, Lars Klingbeil, who is also Merz’s vice-chancellor and finance minister, expressed regret at her departure and criticised the sniping against her while she was mourning as “indecent”. Klingbeil cancelled a planned trip to India to deal with the fallout from Bas’s resignation, and complained about a degradation of the national political discourse. “We are competitors, and we need a culture ‌of debate. But we also need a culture of mutual respect,” Klingbeil told reporters. Merz, who has been fighting for his political survival after three disastrous state elections for his CDU last month, thanked Bas for “cooperation based on trust” in government and offered his condolences. “As a father and grandfather, I can only imagine how deeply felt this loss is for you. I wish you and your family strength,” he wrote on X. Alice Weidel, co-leader of the far-right Alternative für Deutschland, also gave Bas her sympathies but said her angry words towards the CDU demonstrated that Merz’s coalition government “is at its end”. She added: “We need a fresh start for Germany.” The AfD, Germany’s biggest opposition party, is leading national opinion polls at about 30% after a strong showing in September’s regional elections, which also resulted in gains for the hard left. Bas, who will remain an MP for Duisburg in the former Ruhr mining region, is a former president of the Bundestag lower house of parliament and one of the most experienced members of the SPD. Her ministry oversees large parts of Germany’s costly social welfare system, which Merz has targeted for cuts. While a representative of the party’s left wing, Bas was widely seen as a constructive team player able to bridge the kind of implacable policy disputes that have plagued Merz’s government since its inception in May 2025. Her absence will now be keenly felt. The coalition is deeply divided over plans to revive the sputtering economy, the EU’s largest, with Merz spearheading a pro-business savings drive and the SPD insisting on maintaining protections of workers’ rights and benefits. The pension system is in particularly urgent need of reform as German society rapidly ages but plans to gradually lift the retirement age have met with angry resistance. Approval ratings for Merz and his government have plunged over the course of the year, with voters fearing further deindustrialisation in the face of Chinese competition and steep rises in the cost of living. Merz, a former corporate lawyer, is often perceived as haughty and out of touch, compounding his administration’s woes and giving rise to calls to replace him at the helm. He has vowed to stay in office and fight for his policy agenda, saying it was the only way to beat back the “poison of authoritarianism” with extremists on the march. The next general election is due in 2029 but five more state polls loom next year. One of Merz’s cabinet ministers, Karin Prien, sounded the alarm last week, publicly calling for a change of course in the CDU away from Merz’s harsher stances and rhetoric. “We bit our tongues for two or three years but that’s no longer an option,” the family affairs minister told Reuters ahead of a weekend party leadership meeting, referring to its centrist wing. “The ‘pure CDU’ approach (pursued by Merz) has failed.”

title: Time to tell US raider Saba Capital to get lost – again | Nils Pratley
summary: Boaz Weinstein’s hedge fund is waging an aggressive campaign against the FTSE 250’s Baillie Gifford US Growth Trust
text: Here we go again: another episode in the Saba saga, the story of a New York hedge fund causing havoc in the UK investment trust sector by taking big stakes in funds and then demanding change, often in only vague terms. The best that can be said about Saba Capital (and it’s not much) is that its belligerent boss, Boaz Weinstein, has disturbed the complacency that used to infect corners of the UK investment trust world, meaning companies that invest in other companies. It is now harder for a board to do nothing if the share price sits at a wide discount to the value of the underlying assets for long periods. Too often, though, Saba’s assaults look self-interested, short-termist or damaging for UK investors. The attack on Baillie Gifford US Growth Trust, a FTSE 250 constituent usually known by its USA ticker, is all three. Regular shareholders in USA have roundly told Saba to get lost twice in the past 18 months but they will have to do so again if they value what they own, which they should. The US raider, sitting on a near-30% stake, wants to install three of its nominees on the board via a vote at next week’s annual meeting. On a long view, USA’s performance has been excellent: an annualised return of 16.7% since launch in 2018, beating the S&P 500 over the period and within the top 10% of all UK investment companies. The only reason an opening, of a sort, has appeared for Saba is because the 16.7%-a-year returns haven’t happened in a straight line. The pop in AI valuations in late-2022 means USA’s five-year statistics are less impressive. But volatility is what investors accept when they buy into a strategy of backing high-growth US companies for the long-term. The portfolio is stuffed with stakes in big names in the AI world – Anthropic, Databricks, OpenAI, SpaceX and Stripe – that were acquired when the companies were smaller and sometimes still privately owned. A little bit of biodiversity in the UK investment landscape will be lost if USA falls under Saba’s control. What would a Saba-dominated board do? It’s hard to say definitively because this is all Saba says: “If our nominees are elected, we would urge them to offer all USA shareholders a 100% cash exit at or near NAV [net asset value] – providing a long-overdue liquidity event.” The absurdity of that proposal lies in the fact that the board of USA says it has already offered Saba what it supposedly wants – a chance to get out at a price nearly equivalent to the value of the assets. But the US hedge fund declined. The suspicion is that Saba’s nominees could try to appoint Saba itself as manager, or wrap USA into a Saba-managed vehicle. And, note, Saba’s main funds in the US now trade on far wider discounts to asset value than USA’s relatively modest 3%. Since Saba hasn’t spelled out much, all one can say is that its nominees cannot possibly be regarded as independent. One is a Saba employee; the other two are serial picks in Weinstein’s various campaigns. Here is broker Investec’s assessment: “Saba offers no credible plan. Shareholders are being asked to give its nominees potential board control on the strength of a conditional, non-binding liquidity proposal, with no roadmap for the future manager, strategy or governance: vote first, then find out later what you’ve voted for.” The choice, then, is between a known strategy that has been successful, with a few bumps, or a mystery ride under Saba’s tame directors. The analysis should not be hard: shareholders should stick with the existing board. Independence matters. Here’s the tricky bit, however. Saba’s near-30% holding, plus 7.7% in the hands of assumed sympathiser Sessa Capital, means USA shareholders need to act. “Not voting is a vote for Saba,” says broker Panmure Liberum. “Support the board, or suffer the consequences,” warns Investec. Sound advice. The annual meeting is on 23 October but, for anybody holding via an investment platform, the effective voting deadline can be as soon as this Wednesday. Those platforms – looking at Hargreaves Lansdown, AJ Bell and Interactive Investor – should be warning clients of deadlines right now. Preferably in red for danger.

title: Lebanon’s only church-bell maker on keeping a 300-year family tradition alive
summary: Naffah Naffah makes the bells in the mountains near Beirut. His sons will take over the foundry when he retires
text: The story of Lebanon’s last remaining church-bell maker begins with a rifle. In the 18th century, Youssef Gabriel, a local metalworker, was secretly making and equipping Arab revolutionaries with rifles to assist their revolt against the Ottoman empire, which controlled Lebanon at the time. Then, one day, a Russian engineer came to the Lebanese town of Beit Chabab to make a church bell. Gabriel, intrigued, shadowed the man and picked up the process on sight. Or, another story goes, the Maronite patriarch at the time, frustrated by the Ottoman empire blocking the import of church bells to Mount Lebanon, tasked Gabriel with making a bell. After several attempts he succeeded and decided to give up making arms, converting his gunsmithery into Lebanon’s first church-bell foundry. Where the stories converge is that the village, impressed with Gabriel’s handywork, rechristened him Youssef Naffah – naffah meaning useful or successful in Arabic. Three centuries later, the Naffah family is still making church bells in Beit Chabab. Once one of 10 bell foundries owned by the family, the workshop operated by the master bell-maker Naffah Naffah and his two sons is the last remaining production centre for church bells in Lebanon. It is also the sole source of church bells for much of the Middle East and even Lebanese diaspora communities in Europe, Australia and the US. Naffah, 57, said: “We have to pass it down to our kids, it’s been 300 years. I didn’t have any choice. My own father, he would come to the workshop when he could barely even walk.” The foundry sits under his home on the edge of a hill overlooking the red tiled roofs of Beit Chabab and the Lebanese coast that stretches beneath it. The picturesque town, in the Mount Lebanon range about a 30-minute drive from Beirut, offers an escape from the city’s chaos and a refuge from the violence of the country’s last two wars. The ceiling and walls of the foundry are blackened from decades of smoke that has belched from the furnace, and the floors are cluttered with bells in various stages of construction. Outside are mounds of white clay mixed with goat hair, each layer drying before the next is applied. The final product forms the interior mould that the molten metal is poured around. Inside the workshop, modern tools mix with the ancient, a hydraulic press sitting next to a well-worn anvil placed on top of a tree stump. Each bell takes about two months to make. It takes about 40 days to make the interior mould and another month to create the outer mould, with crosses, decoration and the workshop’s signature imprinted on the white clay as it hardens. The third and final stage is the quickest: a foundry is heated using burning wood, and a mixture of copper and tin is placed inside to be melted down over 24 hours. When the metal is ready, it is poured over the bell mould, hardening within three minutes. The workshop produces about 25 bells a year, about 20 of which go to churches in Lebanon. The cost of the bell depends mostly on the size, with every 100kg (220lbs) costing $8,000 (£6,000). A medium-size bell that is ready in the foundry and weighs about a tonne costs about $80,000. “I hate giving the bells away, it always makes me upset, like I’m giving away a child,” said Naffah. He pointed to a mould being worked on, imprints of crosses on its clay interior. “Look at this bell, it’s the work of my two hands. I’ve poured my heart and soul into it.” Each bell bears the names of those who worked on it. One bell ready to be installed has the name of Naffah, his son Charbel and the patron who commissioned it. Other bells in the shop for repairs – one from 1910, another from 1932 – bear the names of Naffah’s grandfathers. The family maps Lebanon by its churches, finding evidence of their ancestors up and down the small Mediterranean country. The earliest surviving bell that bears their name is in the town of Qalaat Sahyoun and was forged in 1725. The ringing of the bells is part of daily life in the villages that wind through Lebanon’s mountains and dot its sprawling coast; on a Sunday morning, the sound mingles with the chirping of the birds. During the Hezbollah-Israel war in Lebanon, which reignited in March, the Christian villages of south Lebanon were cut off from the rest of the country. Israel’s ground invasion, which bulldozed dozens of villages in south Lebanon, mostly spared the Christian villages, but it left them isolated. The church was a crucial source of comfort for the besieged Christians. It organised the distribution and transfer of aid in and out of towns and across frontlines when necessary. Naffah, Charbel and his other son Youssef are determined to preserve this Lebanese tradition and their place within it. Charbel will succeed his father as the master of the family workshop, and Youssef helps when he is not busy with his studies at medical school. Youssef said if Charbel ever decided he no longer wanted to make bells, he would leave medical school and take his place as master of the foundry. “We have six churches in the village [Beit Chabab]. If all of the bells played at the same time, I could distinguish between each one from their sound alone,” he said, surveying the village from the edge of the foundry. “Traditions are important to us. We are living and breathing tradition here in this workshop.”
