title: Melbourne Islamic leader rejects centre’s alleged Flydubai hijacker links after Facebook video
summary: MyCentre leader Samir Mohtadi, who also goes by Abu Hamza, says claims associating him with flyDubai pilot are unfounded
text: The leader of a Melbourne Islamic centre allegedly linked to the accused Flydubai hijacker has rejected any connection with the radicalised pilot, saying he never met the suspect, and condemned “violence in all its forms”. The UAE government has alleged that investigators had traced the ideological and professional background of the 29-year-old suspect, Omani national Hammam al-Hammami, and that his “drift towards extremism and terrorism” began while a student at RMIT University in Melbourne in 2017. The UAE’s attorney-general stated al-Hammami, had said that while studying in Melbourne he regularly attended a mosque affiliated with RMIT, and through those visits had become acquainted with people associated with a centre known as “MyCentre”. He allegedly said that the centre was managed by a man known as “Abu Hamza” but it was not stated whether the suspect had ever met Abu Hamza. There was no allegation that anyone at the centre was involved in radicalising al-Hammami or had kept in contact with him or had any knowledge of his intentions before the 30 September flight. In a statement issued late on Monday, Samir Mohtadi – who also goes by Abu Hamza – said al-Hammami was unknown to the Multicultural Youth Centre (MyCentre). “I have never met Al-Hammami, who has been referred to in recent media reports, and we have no record of him ever attending our centre. “I strongly reject any attempt to associate me or Multicultural Youth Centre with Al-Hammami. “Such claims are unfounded, misleading and risk unfairly damaging the reputation of an organisation that has served the wider Australian community for decades.” Mohtadi said MyCentre had provided community services, including education, gyms, sporting facilities, aquatic and medical centres, and spiritual support for the wider Melbourne community over decades. “Our doors are open to everyone, Muslims and non-Muslims alike, with hundreds of people visiting our facilities every day,” Mohtadi said. “Throughout my life, I have consistently preached peace, and both my work and the work of the centre have always focused on promoting peace, harmony, mutual respect and community wellbeing. We unequivocally reject violence in all its forms.” On Sunday night, Mohtadi appeared in a four-minute video released on the centre’s Facebook page. He referred to Islamic texts on the virtues of staying silent when being attacked by others but makes no reference in the video to the alleged Flydubai hijack attempt, the UAE attorney general’s statement or to al-Hammami Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email “You’ll find those who are righteous you’ll always find have been attacked, abused, accused, killed, imprisoned, and this is the way it is,” Mohtadi said in the video. “The best thing, sometimes, is not to say anything.” RMIT has confirmed al-Hammami had studied engineering at the university, but left Australia before completing the qualification. He subsequently underwent flight training in New Zealand and became a qualified commercial pilot. Passengers and crew on the 30 September flight, which had 182 people onboard, intervened to stop the alleged attempt to hijack the plane and crash it into Ben Gurion airport near Tel Aviv in a “premeditated terrorist plot”, according to the UAE attorney general’s statement. According to the statement, al-Hammami allegedly told prosecutors he adopted ideas advocating violence and terrorism and drew inspiration from the 9/11 terrorist attacks of 2001. “The idea of carrying out a similar operation using an aircraft became firmly established in his thinking,” the statement said. Al-Hammami allegedly prepared himself psychologically and physically to carry out the alleged terror plot by intensifying his exposure to material promoting terrorism and training in boxing under a private coach. Australian security agencies launched an investigation after it emerged al-Hammami spent about two years in the country, with New Zealand authorities also examining his time there between November 2018 and May 2019. On Sunday, Australia’s home affairs minister, Tony Burke, said the co-pilot was allegedly radicalised online. He also said the government wanted to properly screen people at the border and in online settings.

title: As US medical debt grows, AI will be used more to collect it
summary: The debt-collection ecosystem will change as AI takes notes in exam rooms, codes visits and sends billing messages
text: Medical debt is expected to grow in coming years as Republican-led health cuts come into force this winter. As it does, a changing world of medical billing and debt collection awaits patients: one where artificial intelligence increasingly listens, codes, bills and collects. Artificial intelligence takes notes in exam rooms, codes visits, sends out billing messages and powers AI agents who text patients in billing portals – all changing the debt-collection ecosystem. Medical debt will grow among “both the insured and uninsured, because of how we’re increasingly putting more costs onto individuals for those plans”, said April Kuehnhoff, a senior attorney at the National Consumer Law Center. “It’s people who lose their coverage because they can’t afford it, or they can’t meet these new stringent requirements. It’s people who maybe they can afford it but the plan they get isn’t as good, and they are asked to have a higher deductible, higher co-pay, so they just have a higher out-of-pocket [cost],” she said. A report released last Tuesday found that more than one in four US adults reported they owed a medical debt in 2025. The proportion was the same – about one in four – for people with health insurance, according to an analysis by the Urban Institute and the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation. AI company leaders, such as Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, have promised to cure all diseases in a decade. While scientists remain skeptical of those claims, financial analysts at JP Morgan have celebrated AI in coding, billing and collections as “early wins”. Artificial intelligence now helps medical debt collectors determine personalized discounts for settlements – an analogue of the personalized pricing criticized by the Federal Trade Commission – and helps medical debt-buying companies determine the price they should offer for debt portfolios. Companies offering AI-backed medical coding and billing services are finding new markets thanks to Republican-led health reforms. Donald Trump’s HR1, known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, cut roughly $1tn in federal spending from the healthcare industry. Paired with Republicans’ refusal to extend subsidies for plans in Obamacare marketplaces, those cuts are expected to result in about 17 million newly uninsured individuals through 2034. When rates of lack of insurance rise, something called “uncompensated care” tends to go up in tandem. This is health industry parlance for the doctor and hospital bills that go unpaid – from care that uninsured and under-insured people inevitably seek even when they can’t pay. The Urban Institute estimates that HR1 will cause $278bn in uncompensated care by 2034. The result will be cash-strapped hospitals seeking to improve collections, and thereby turning to increasingly high-tech collectors. That leads to openings for companies like Cedar, an AI-driven billing platform backed by venture capital firms such as Andreessen Horowitz and JP Morgan. The company screens patients for insurance, including Medicaid, through some decidedly low-tech questionnaires. That helps boost collections too – but is not a new practice by healthcare providers. Instead, Cedar’s innovation comes from data provided by hospitals and doctors to “train a machine learning model capable of predicting a patient’s propensity to pay”, according to the company’s website, and “[m]atch patients with Al-driven discounts”. The company also works to deflect calls to billing departments by deploying an AI chatbot named Kora to speak with patients about their bills, thereby containing labor costs. “We have been focused on uninsured and Medicaid-eligible patients for several years now,” said Dugan Winkie, chief strategy officer of Cedar, and an alum of McKinsey as well as Epic, the nation’s largest electronic health records company. “That’s where Cedar shines in my mind: our entire business is focused on ‘Patient A’, who is a single mother who has a $10,000 balance. We need to engage with you much differently than if you are a late-stage executive with a $50 copay,” said Winkie. Winkie said Cedar helps “get those more-difficult-to-collect-from patients who may not be digitally engaged aware of these offers”, such as zero-financing payment plans through providers. Use of artificial intelligence in coding – the scribes that listen to and translate bills – has attracted particular scrutiny. In spring 2026, the Blue Cross Blue Shield Association (BCBS), which represents state Blue Cross insurers, put out a white paper finding women in childbirth were increasingly being billed after severe blood loss during delivery even as the rate of blood transfusion rates remained steady. The paper was the latest salvo in the insurers-versus-providers feud – where sides have a long-running disagreement over who is to blame for sky-high healthcare costs. As the BCBS paper described, in-room scribes listened to conversations between patients and doctors and translated those conversations into “structured notes”. Then, an AI program used those notes and a patient’s electronic health record to suggest enhanced coding – and thereby billing – for the patient. In effect, researchers argued, AI was “boosting hospital billing”. This kind of coding is a selling point for AI scribing companies. One medical scribe company, also backed by Andreessen Horowitz, claimed in investor materials that its listening software created an additional $13,000 in revenue per clinician per year through greater “coding accuracy”. A second BCBS report from September claimed AI coding led to an additional $1bn in healthcare costs in a year. The American Hospital Association, an industry lobby, argued in a blog post that the analyses “raises concerns about coding trends, but it does not demonstrate that hospitals are coding patients inaccurately or that AI tools are driving inappropriate spending”. Importantly, insurers are also using AI, critics claim, to delay and deny care through inscrutable algorithms. Under Robert F Kennedy Jr’s health department, Medicare, the public health insurance for the elderly, also recently launched a program to use AI to issue prior authorization for some conditions, mirroring a tactic used by private insurers.

title: Anti-vaxxers target Texas measles doctors to cast doubt on deaths amid outbreak
summary: Children’s Health Defense and RFK Jr publicly dispute recent measles deaths to ‘distract’ from damage caused and question vaccines, experts say
text: The six-year-old girl at the children’s hospital in Lubbock, Texas, burned with fever and struggled to breathe. Doctors soon put her on a ventilator, snaking a thick tube down the child’s throat so a machine could breathe for her; they placed IVs to rehydrate her tiny body and they prescribed antibiotics for any bacterial infections that may have taken hold in the weeks she had spent at home battling measles. But it was too late. Within a day of being ventilated, the child went into shock, her blood pressure crashed and she went into cardiac arrest. She could not be resuscitated. Her family, and the nation, mourned: she was the first child to die of measles in the US in a decade. Yet some anti-vaccine activists soon began claiming that the girl died from medical malpractice, not measles, revealing a playbook that they are now running in Pennsylvania amid a growing outbreak – a message taken up by Robert F Kennedy Jr, secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and a longtime anti-vaccine activist, as he publicly disputes the rising death toll. The deaths in the US from measles – now numbering eight in less than two years – are a political minefield for Kennedy, centering him in a public backlash after years of his false claims about the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine. The deflection campaign is already having real-world consequences beyond the rising body count. Children’s Health Defense, the anti-vaccine group previously led by Kennedy, claims to have sparked malpractice investigations into the doctors who treated the two young unvaccinated girls who died from measles amid last year’s outbreak in west Texas, which infected at least 762 people. “At first they were going to throw out the complaints,” Brian Hooker, CHD’s chief scientific officer, announced in a recent video. “But they have, upon further review … decided that they’re going to let their own medical expert look at the records for those particular deaths. Because in each case, inappropriate antibiotics were prescribed, and that, I believe, led to both girls’ deaths.” Paul Offit, an infectious diseases pediatrician and internationally recognized vaccine expert, said “it’s not a good look” for Kennedy and other anti-vaxxers for so many cases and deaths to occur. “So they’re trying to say, ‘Well, it wasn’t measles.’” Katherine Wells, Lubbock Public Health’s director, agreed. “It’s their playbook,” she said. “It’s just another tactic by them to disrupt or to question vaccines and the safety of vaccines. The issue at hand is that we’re having these large measles outbreaks, and they’re not stopping.” It’s not just the deaths – it’s also the severe disease, Wells said. The “massive” outbreaks affect “families and communities and disrupt lives”, Wells said. About one in five unvaccinated measles patients are hospitalized. Measles erases immunity to all other illnesses for years, putting patients at risk of other serious infections. And survivors may years later develop severe measles complications such as subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE), which is fatal and untreatable. Last year, Hooker traveled to Texas to interview the deceased six-year-old’s parents, who said they still would not have vaccinated their children. A second child, aged eight, soon died from measles at the same hospital. Hooker asked to see the children’s medical records, and he shared them with Pierre Kory, a critical care physician with no pediatric training who lost his board certifications for promoting Covid misinformation, heavily promoted the anti-parasitic ivermectin as a Covid treatment, and claimed that polio paralysis is caused not by the virus but by pesticides. Kory, who himself escaped legal liability in a malpractice lawsuit brought by the estate of a Covid patient who died as a result of his treatment plan, concluded that the measles deaths were actually the result of medical error. Kory claimed the first child was prescribed “a completely inappropriate antibiotic” for a bacterial infection she developed because of measles, adding that “she did not die of measles by any stretch of the imagination,” but rather she died of pneumonia and medical mismanagement. He also attributed the second child’s death to “medical malpractice” because of her antibiotic regime. Secondary bacteria infections are very common with measles, which can create a cascade of deadly complications. Privately, Kory reportedly said that he suspected the two deaths in young girls in Texas were caused by a weaponized version of measles. Hooker and a colleague both submitted complaints to the Texas medical board alleging that the antibiotics were given improperly to the sick children. In the video, he said the medical board was reviewing the complaints. The Guardian and Important Context were unable to confirm Hooker’s claims. The identities of the doctors are not public. Anyone can file a complaint with a state medical board, and boards take complaints seriously. Several leading anti-vaccine figures have received medical board complaints about their own conduct. “The physicians went above and beyond, and the hospitals went above and beyond,” Wells said. Pediatricians in hospitals work with the sickest children, with high stress and relatively low pay. “It’s so hard to be told that you either wanted to hurt them or didn’t want to give the best care you could,” Wells said. Now, with the CHD accusations and possible medical board reports, “I think it’s in the back of everybody’s minds,” she said. Hooker’s remarks about the Texas complaints followed the measles deaths of two unvaccinated infants in Pennsylvania. Hooker vowed to “get boots on the ground” in the state to “make sure that if it was a hospital error that it doesn’t happen again”. Other anti-vaccine activists are helping to fuel the narrative. Peter McCullough, a former cardiologist whose board certification were revoked by the American Board of Internal Medicine, noted on X that there was “no mention of antivirals, antibiotics, or steroids” in the case of the third measles death in Pennsylvania, an unvaccinated 40-year-old woman. Yet the county coroner said the woman was not able to seek healthcare before she took a turn for the worse, so she would not have received medications for her illness. Kennedy has suggested that Pennsylvania’s governor, Josh Shapiro, made up the measles deaths for political reasons. The message was echoed by Jay Bhattacharya, director of the National Institutes of Health, who claimed in a Fox News interview that Shapiro was “playing this out over the airwaves for political purposes, just like what happened during Covid”, adding: “And this is why there’s such deep distrust in public health.” Mehmet Oz, administrator of the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, said in a Fox Business interview: “We don’t know if the children died from measles or had another condition that was already attacking them and they happened to get measles at the same time.” The CDC has also called the deaths into question, only listing two of the five deaths this year in Pennsylvania. Officials in Pennsylvania have been clear that the deaths were because of measles. Anti-vaxxers have long vilified and targeted physicians. In Texas, the attorney general, Ken Paxton, has launched investigations into doctors who vaccinate children, alleging a conspiracy with drug companies. And CHD has funded numerous lawsuits against pediatricians over alleged side-effects from vaccines. In January, the group launched a Rico suit against the American Academy of Pediatrics, which had sued Kennedy over changes to the vaccine schedule. Despite no longer leading CHD, Kennedy still appears to enjoy close ties to the organization. At their Washington DC conference in September, he said they had “a friend in the White House”. Advocates say the group appears to be running interference for Kennedy amid the ongoing resurgence of measles, which was previously declared eliminated in the US but has made a comeback with rising anti-vaccine sentiment. CHD and Kennedy have been top promoters of vaccine misinformation, according to a 2021 report by the Center for Countering Digital Hate. Kennedy has been “a very successful anti-vaccine activist”, which has resulted in the largest outbreak of measles in three decades as well as the resurgence of other preventable illnesses, Offit said. “Now we have more children dying of flu and measles and whooping cough – and Haemophilus influenzae type B meningitis is now coming back.” Anti-vaccine activists want to “distract, distract, distract” from the damage they have caused, Offit said. He believes the tactic will not be successful, pointing to pushback from leaders including Shapiro and from pediatricians. “I think pediatricians will continue to move forward as they have,” Offit said. When Kennedy attempted to slash vaccine recommendations in January, “pediatricians ignored him”, Offit said. “I think most people are ignoring him.” The efforts to spread misinformation and mistrust about pediatricians may take a toll, especially on people who already doubt vaccines, Wells said. “It just further divides us. It sticks with the people who want to believe that narrative, and I think it adds to the doubt that they have.” Yet when the outbreaks worsen, people who were previously vaccine-skeptical choose to get them, she said. “During our outbreak, all the parents that were hesitant came forward as soon as they heard there were cases,” Wells said, “and they got their kids vaccinated.” This article was written in partnership with Important Context

title: Zelenskyy blindsided after Trump announces ‘energy ceasefire’ in Ukraine war | First Thing
summary: Ukrainian president says the deal is ‘news to me’ and that Moscow is still attacking energy infrastructure
text: Good morning. The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, has said it was “news to me” after Donald Trump announced a partial ceasefire deal in the Ukraine war. The US president had posted to social media to say: “Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed.” There was no sign that the Kremlin was observing Trump’s ceasefire. According to Zelenskyy, Russian drones took to the sky “throughout the day” on Sunday and there were several airstrikes, including on energy infrastructure. He said Russia hit a power station in Kharkiv – the latest of more than 200 strikes during the past week against electricity generation and transmission facilities in Ukraine. How has the prospect of a deal been welcomed? Despite the unconventional nature of the announcement, the ceasefire appeared to garner support from Ukraine’s key western allies. The French president, Emmanuel Macron, said Paris supported a “real energy ceasefire” and the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, said a sustained energy ceasefire was “the best route to get energy and fuel back into world markets”. Will Trump’s deal with Putin bring down gas prices? The agreement to temporarily lift sanctions on US imports of Russian diesel will have little “meaningful” effect on motorists and businesses in the US and overseas, energy and foreign policy analysts have predicted. Abdul El-Sayed says Democrats must ‘win by massive numbers’ to fend off Trump election denial Democrats must “win by massive numbers” during November’s federal midterm elections because Donald Trump and his Republican allies are bound to try to sow doubt about the integrity of the results, the Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan said on Sunday. “Donald Trump has already threatened to do what he did in 2020, which is deny the outcomes of an election,” El-Sayed said. “So, yes, we have to win by massive numbers.” Riyadh airport hit again after deadly Houthi missile attack, Saudi authorities say A projectile hit a passenger terminal at the airport in Riyadh on Sunday, the day after a deadly missile attack on the facility carried out by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebel group killed 13 people. An unidentified projectile hit terminal 4 at King Khalid international airport, starting a fire, killing one person and injuring 11, according to Saudi civil aviation authorities. The escalating attacks threatened to draw more countries into the Yemen conflict and further widen the regional fallout of the US-Iran war, which has already spread to Lebanon and Iraq. AI less regulated than milk, Microsoft president says in warning over safety Artificial intelligence is less regulated than milk and washing machines, the president of Microsoft has said, as the tech industry warns over the safety of AI. Brad Smith said there should be more safety rules to govern the technology including a legal obligation to a “victim” if their system was breached by rogue AI agents. There are growing calls from experts, politicians and regulators for tougher rules to control AI, as well as warnings from Anthropic, Google DeepMind and OpenAI that the pace of the technology’s development should slow. Smith said AI could be a “tool and a weapon” that should be regulated urgently. US maternity wards face wave of closures as Medicaid cuts kick in Maternity wards across the US are facing a wave of closures as cuts to federal Medicaid funding take effect, experts have said. According to analysis by the nonprofit Protect Our Care, 52 maternity wards have closed since the HR1 bill was announced in July 2025, with a further eight having announced their upcoming closure. The legislation, which comes into full effect in the new year, will result in many adults covered through Medicaid having to meet new work requirements and being subject to more frequent eligibility checks, while there will be less federal funding for states for Medicaid. title: EU to limit Chinese hybrid vehicle imports to 350,000 a year
summary: Brussels uses WTO rules to quickly impose 350,000 vehicle-a-year quota, which will halve Chinese market share to 3%
text: The EU is to limit the number of hybrid electric vehicles imported from China to 350,000 cars a year, the European Commission has confirmed. Imports have been soaring in the past two years; about 800,000 battery and plug-in hybrids are likely to be sold this year. The EU expects that the quota, which will come into force in December, will halve China’s market share, which now stands at 6% in a landmark four-year agreement made in Beijing last week. The annual limit on imports of hybrids will be taken under the World Trade Organization safeguard measures, which mean it can be implemented swiftly without the type of investigations needed in anti-dumping measures. Any cars imported above the quota level will not be subject to tariffs, but will remain blocked in customs at docks in Europe. Chinese vehicles assembled within the EU, such as those made in Hungary or, in future, Spain, will not be subject to the quota, officials have confirmed, but EU companies making cars in China will. China’s exports of hybrids to the EU tripled to €6.7bn (£5.7bn) in the first half of this year, from €2.2bn a year earlier, according to Chinese customs data. As part of the deal, China has also agreed to drop some tariffs on auto parts and cut duties by half on footwear, olive oil and ice-cream from the EU. Officials stressed that the quota is fully supported by China, and further dialogue on cars and other imports including chemicals, renewable energy and furniture is continuing. “We will continue the dialogue on some products … this is by no means the end of the story,” an official said. Last month, the EU called for feedback on a new rule that could oblige companies to diversify their supply chains while the“Made in Europe” legislation would do the same in public procurement. On Thursday, EU leaders will discuss a French-German proposal for a “kill switch” or new instrument that would allow Brussels to block access to the single market for certain goods in the event of any harmful development, such as a ban on rare earths crucial for the tech and automotive industries. The deal on hybrid EVs comes amid mounting concern over the £1bn-a-day trade deficit the EU is now running with China. Up until recently, the EU’s strategy for tackling what it says is an “unsustainable” trade imbalance has been to seek to increase exports to China. Sources said there has been “a paradigm shift” with concerns of deindustrialisation and job losses in the industrial heartlands forcing a renewed focus on curbing imports rather than increasing exports. “We are closely surveilling, our imports. We know what’s coming in. We know where there’s a surge, and we know what hits the hardest in terms of our deindustrialisation,” said an official. Andrew Small, the director of the Asia programme at the European Council for Foreign Relations, said China was likely to “suck the EU into drawn-out negotiations” on other sectors but the mood had changed in the EU. “I think if China had offered a deal like this earlier in the year, say in spring, it would have been much easier to take the heat out. My sense is that things have now moved somewhat too far politically,” he said.

title: Why boarding schools must do more to tackle child-on-child sexual abuse
summary: Experts say children who live and learn in institutions away from their parents will always be more vulnerable
text: Benji* was in his early teens when a fellow pupil at one of the country’s most prestigious independent schools began a series of sexual assaults against him that went on for years. He had previously been happy at school, where he excelled at sport. Then one night he woke in his dormitory to find the other boy’s hand on his penis. “I just froze,” said Benji. The boy threatened to beat him up if he reported what had happened, and the abuse began to accelerate. He would forcibly masturbate Benji three or four times a week. From there he began to force Benji to engage in fellatio every two to three days. “It slowly got worse and worse,” said Benji. “He said he would beat the shit out of me. He claimed he had taken pictures of me when I was sleeping. He said he would put them up around the school and make this rumour up that I was gay.” Awareness and safeguarding have improved significantly in UK boarding schools after decades of shameful revelations about sexual abuse, but experts say children who live and learn in institutions away from their parents will always be more vulnerable. In the past, the focus has been on the appalling experiences of pupils who have been sexually abused by their teachers. Today, attention has also turned to the sexual violence perpetrated by one pupil on another – in boarding schools, as in other schools. Earlier this month, a Guardian investigation uncovered the horrifying scale of child-on-child sexual abuse in schools, with at least 1,700 sexual offences against under-13s, including multiple rapes, reported to police every year. It was not until more than a decade later that Benji felt able to disclose what he had suffered. “I was not in a place where I wanted to let out what happened to me. I was massively ashamed.” He abused alcohol and drugs and tried to kill himself. “I would do anything to blank it out. I was angry with the world.” After leaving school, he went abroad where he began to do seasonal work. “Until I was 26, I was running away from the darkness. I did not want to deal with it. I didn’t want to have to think or relive it.” After spiralling downwards, Benji finally told his mother. Horrified, she contacted the school. The police became involved, there was a trial and in September 2021 the perpetrator, Christopher Brewer, was convicted of 12 offences against Benji and one other pupil. Jailing Brewer for three years, the recorder of Bristol, Judge Peter Blair, said Brewer had “ruined” Benji’s life. “He felt a complete sense of powerlessness. This was not a very long way away from sex slave.” “I look back on that court case and that’s the proudest moment of my life,” Benji told the Guardian. “It’s the only time in my life when I’ve felt powerful. I had to do this for myself so I could move on, and could slowly become happier.” Following the criminal case, Benji pursued a civil negligence claim against the school. The school denied liability, and a compensation settlement was finally agreed. Now he feels compelled to speak up to support others. “If I can make a change to someone who is dealing with a similar situation, if I could change someone’s life for the better, it would make everything that happened worth it.” Andrew Lord, a partner in the abuse claims team at Leigh Day, represented Benji in his civil action. “I have advised several families whose children have been impacted by abuse in boarding schools, and a great number describe still feeling the impact many years later. “It is no longer credible for any school to plead ignorance on the shocking prevalence of sexual violence among pupils, nor is it acceptable to not have an immediate plan to investigate and mitigate these potential harms. “There has been a growing awareness of these issues for several years, and the idiosyncrasies of a boarding school setting can create additional flashpoints of concern. Schools ought to be aware and prepared for when a disclosure of abuse occurs.” Richard Scorer, who is head of abuse law at Slater & Gordon, said from his experience a “disproportionate” number of civil claims over child-on-child sexual abuse involve boarding schools. “Because, obviously, children are there more of the time and in circumstances where they might be dressing or undressing. “They’re living not just a school life, but their private lives as well. So there’s probably a bit more coming from boarding schools in terms of what we see.” Wealthier families may also be more likely to seek legal redress. Sam*, also represented by Lord, was a pupil at another renowned boarding school when an older student from a nearby dormitory got into his bed and sexually abused him. There were other incidents. Sam did not report the abuse immediately. He felt too embarrassed, and in the months that followed, he lived in a state of terror. “I could hear his door open. I was frozen in fear.” Eventually, Sam confided in a fellow pupil; it was reported to the housemaster, and he was asked to give a written statement. Yet, much to Sam’s alarm, in the days after disclosure, the boy was allowed to stay in the dormitory opposite. The incident was finally reported to the police by Sam’s family, but there were no charges. “Ultimately I think the school did not want any bad press,” said Sam. But the abuse had a devastating and lasting impact on Sam. Though he managed to secure a place at university, he had a “terrible” time. He hid in his room and left without completing his degree. “I think the assault and the aftermath did really change me. “What I really feel I lost was confidence. I lost confidence in the school, which was in a position of care and responsibility. And I lost my own self-confidence to do anything.” Sam brought a civil action against the school, claiming negligence and safeguarding failures. The school denied liability and a settlement was reached. Gabrielle Shaw, chief executive of the National Association for People Abused in Childhood (Napac), said awareness and safeguarding have improved, and there is greater recognition that children can be sexually abused by other children. “But policies alone do not keep children safe. Boarding schools have an especially high duty of care because children live as well as learn there and may be separated from trusted adults outside the institution. “Every pupil needs a safe route to speak out and a response that takes them seriously, protects and supports them, and acts appropriately. Crucially, it must be without reputation or institutional interests taking precedence. “Children in boarding schools are not inevitably vulnerable to abuse. The real test is whether they trust adults enough to tell them, and what those adults do next.” Robin Fletcher, chief executive of the Boarding Schools’ Association (BSA), said safeguarding young people is the top priority of every boarding school. “Over the past decade, BSA has worked to strengthen schools’ ability to recognise and respond to abuse through specialist training, conferences and safeguarding guidance. “That work addresses child-on-child abuse as well as abuse by adults, helping staff identify concerns and respond appropriately rather than waiting for a child to make a disclosure. “Any safeguarding incident reinforces the need for strong processes, training, support and a culture where abuse and abusers have no place in any school.” * Some names have been changed

title: This Georgia county is one of the US’s most diverse – and that could flip multiple elections
summary: Gwinnett county is home to many immigrants and other newcomers, and how it votes could be decisive for Congress
text: Johanna Park might just be an ambassador for Gwinnett county, Georgia, one of the 10 most ethnically diverse counties in the United States. Park owns Cafe Amico at Suwanee Town Center, one of her three Italian coffee shops in the area just north of Atlanta. She was born in Korea and lived much of her life in Argentina and Peru. She’s been in Gwinnett for more than 20 years, part of an early wave of Korean immigration that’s built Korean American car dealerships, banks, insurance agencies, supermarkets and restaurants like her own. It’s also a population that’s increasing in influence and not just numbers. In 2020, Gwinnett was 30.6% white, 27.8% Black, 23.7% Hispanic, 13.2% Asian, and 4.0% multiracial, according to the US census. About 28% of Gwinnett residents were born outside the United States. About half of those are US citizens. Extraordinary diversity is simply a fact of life here. According to the US census diversity index, there is an 84.9% chance that two randomly selected Gwinnett residents will belong to different racial or ethnic groups. Control of the Senate may come down to the results of Georgia’s contest between US senator Jon Ossoff and US congressman Mike Collins. And Georgia’s election may come down to a handful of places where turnout and partisan sentiment aren’t easily predicted. Gwinnett, with its surge in population, of both US-born newcomers and immigrants, may be one of those places. Park, who has generally voted for Democrats, has little good to say about the economy or the Trump administration. “They’re deporting all of the Hispanic people from here, left and right,” Park said. With little media fanfare, ICE began a “shadow surge” of arrests in August. Called “Operation Safe Community”, the agency detained more than 1,000 immigrants across metro Atlanta, disproportionately targeting immigrant-heavy communities along Buford Highway, Norcross and other parts of Gwinnett county. “And not only are they deporting them back to their country, but also they are deporting them to … to south[ern] Africa? I don’t know where … And who’s paying for all of this? You know, probably you and I, with the tax money. “Illegal immigration has always been a thing, but why are we are so adamant about kicking everybody out when they are the hardest-working people here, and they help overall with the economy?” she asked. Park noted that Gwinnett’s immigrant community tends to be politically split between Republicans and Democrats. While the county fields more Asian American Democratic elected officials such as Akbar Ali in Lilburn, others such as Buford’s Soo Hong have been elected as Republicans. The idea of “Asian Americans” as a single voting bloc ignores nuances. Vietnamese American voters tend to be more Republican, while Indian American voters tend to be more Democratic. But neither party owns their loyalty. Park thinks this divide “will remain, always. It’s deeply rooted. Especially the business owners are mostly pro-Republicans because of the benefits and the tax cuts and what not.” Their children, however, may be another matter. They are often splitting with their parents, driven left with the broader trend of highly educated Americans siding with Democrats. Elliot Kim, general manager of Suwanee Frame & Art, said: “I’m Korean. My parents live here as well, and typically that generation of Koreans and maybe a little bit younger than them stay pretty Republican and conservative because they stay close to the church. That’s what they relate to. But myself and my brother probably lean a little bit more to the left.” Immigration has been one driver of the county’s explosive growth. Its extraordinary school system is another. US News and World Report ranked the Gwinnett School of Mathematics, Science and Technology as the top high school in Georgia and seventh nationally. It is also far and away the largest school district in Georgia, with more than 180,000 students. Even as public school enrollment falls across America, parents around Atlanta have been voting with their feet by moving to Gwinnett. That growth – not the war, not gas prices, not even Trump – might be the key political issue for Gwinnett voters. Though housing starts have fallen since the early 2000s boom, the county has been absorbing more than 10,000 new residents a year since. Take Suwanee, on the purple fault line between football-obsessed Buford near the Mall of Georgia to its north and Duluth, where the storefront signs alternate between English, Spanish and Korean, to its south. Kim, a graduate of Gwinnett’s vaunted public schools, is concerned that the school system today isn’t rigorous enough for his daughter, taking issue with how little homework is assigned and how often students are permitted to retake tests. “I mean the principal was going on and on about how Roberts [elementary school] is award-winning, best in state, all this. And I’m like, how are these metrics even being formed here?” Kim said. “I am so unimpressed about what they’re learning, and maybe is that just me getting old and wanting my kids to have the amount of strife that I did going through school.” Thirty years ago, Suwanee’s town common was a cow pasture, a million-dollar home was a rumor and apartments were the punchline to a joke about Atlanta. Today, Suwanee’s town center is a model of suburban mixed-use development ringed with condominiums, and local property values are closer to Boston’s than Atlanta’s. Its population has increased fivefold since 1996. “My neighborhood is kind of in a bubble, I’m just going to say,” said Kristina Lindsey, a Democratic activist from Suwanee. “We have money. And so our neighborhood is not as concerned with what’s happening to maybe some people in southern Gwinnett, right? Or the gas prices or our grocery prices, right? … It does not affect us the same way it does someone who’s living paycheck to paycheck and doesn’t have an emergency fund.” She stood on the green at Suwanee with a group of about 20 people waving anti-Trump protest signs at a weekly demonstration. “I feel a moral obligation to be out here to be visible,” Lindsey said. “And so that other people who might share the same values as me see that we have the courage to be out here and make some noise.” For all of America’s focus on Georgia’s swing voters with the US Senate on the line, Gwinnett Democrats may be more motivated to flip control of the state legislature. Republicans have control of Georgia’s house chamber by a 10-vote margin. Gerrymandering protects some Republicans, but the vulnerable seats are in places like Gwinnett. Republican Matt Reeves represents part of Suwanee, along with some points north. He held on to his state house seat in 2024 by 621 votes on 29,003 ballots cast, and faces a rematch against Michelle Kang, an attorney and Korean American immigrant. There is little Republican red meat, culture war fodder, in his rhetoric. He talks about affordability – property tax relief, lowering insurance prices, and pushing for a statewide referendum for senior homestead tax exemptions. “Here’s the thing in Gwinnett county: we are the battleground. We have competitive seats,” Reeves said. “So I’ve brought my A-game every day for the last two years. And I’ve been saying affordability for at least the last two years, probably even before that, and I’m glad that the national conversation has caught up with that because we’ve got to deliver savings, for our people to have more money in their pocket.” State senator Adrienne White Carden heard much the same from voters as she knocked on doors. The longstanding Democratic political activist is married to a Gwinnett county commissioner and no stranger to retail campaigning. She won a special election by a 51-49 margin earlier this year in Gwinnett, serving in a temporary role until January. “I think people are still definitely concerned about the shenanigans that Trump is running, but at the same time, they’re more interested in what’s happening here at home,” Carden said. “You know, costs definitely came up, whether it be gas pump prices or, to be honest, as the wife of a county commissioner, those who knew I was his wife – which was many people – always had a message for Commissioner Kirkland Carden about property taxes.”

title: How immigration is molding the US midterms: ‘Trump has gone too far’
summary: From restaurants to farms to healthcare, the US president’s hardline policies have reshaped Americans’ daily lives
text: If there is one campaign promise that Donald Trump has kept, it is his pledge to deliver “mass deportations”. Two years later, voters are living uneasily with the consequences. Trump himself has called the midterm elections this November – which will decide which party controls each house of Congress – a referendum on his presidency. In many ways, they will also serve as a referendum of his hardline anti-immigration policies, and the multitudinous ways they have reshaped Americans’ daily lives. In Florida, restaurant and hotel owners have said that ICE’s presence is frightening away both workers and customers, and Republican congresswoman María Elvira Salazar, who is running for re-election, aired a Spanish-language ad breaking with the president, saying his immigration crackdown had “betrayed” Hispanic voters in her district. In Maine, the fatal ICE shooting of a 25-year-old asylum seeker has cast a pall over the campaign to re-elect the Republican senator Susan Collins, who supported Trump’s plans to supercharge immigration enforcement. In Kansas, cattle ranchers said ICE operations were having “a massive chilling effect on the legal, documented, skilled workers that put beef on the table” and warned that meat prices would spike as a result. At the same time, the Republican senator Roger Marshall – who had once vehemently backed Trump’s immigration agenda – started to grow uneasy in a tightening re-election race, and softened his hardline rhetoric. And in Texas, which has seen a slew of violent ICE arrests including a fatal shooting in July and a non-fatal shooting in September, the Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico appears to be gaining momentum against the state’s Trump-backed attorney general, Ken Paxton, with a message that Trump’s ICE has gone too far. Several national polls have shown voters’ growing distaste for the Trump administration’s militarized immigration enforcement operations. A Reuters/Ipsos poll released on 21 September found that only 36% of voters approved of Trump’s handling of immigration. According to Pew research, half of Americans see the administration’s immigration tactics as too aggressive. In Texas, a recent poll by the New York Times and Siena University found voters there evenly split on which Senate candidate they trusted more to handle immigration – a striking shift in a state that hasn’t elected a Democratic senator in almost 40 years. And while Latino voters, who swung toward Trump in 2024, still rank the economy as a top issue, a strong majority are viscerally opposed to the president’s immigration agenda. An October NBC News/Telemundo poll of registered Latino voters found that two-thirds believe his enforcement policies have gone “too far”. The issue is deeply felt, with more than one in four saying they know someone who had been deported or detained by ICE since Trump’s second term began, and 17% saying that they or someone close to them had considered not voting in person this year because of concerns about ICE. After the killing of two US citizens during immigration raids in Minneapolis sparked massive public backlash, the Trump administration signalled it would take a softer approach, and the new homeland security secretary, Markwayne Mullin, said his goal would be to keep ICE out of the news headlines. But immigration agents are still shooting people. And with enforcement operations across the US gaining momentum, and immigration arrests at a record high, voters are continuing to see a supercharged ICE at work. “It does cause quite a disruption in the community,” Scott Fischer, the Republican chair in Ford county, Kansas, told Politico. “We don’t want our community disrupted.” ‘It’s an issue across the economy’ Perhaps even more pertinently, voters – and the politicians vying for their support – are coming to the realization that even if immigration itself doesn’t rank in surveys as a top issue, Trump’s immigration policies have affected every other issue that matters to them. “Even if this isn’t a top concern for voters casting their ballots, it is a part of a general perception that the president’s policies have gone too far, and that they’re affecting people who are not immigrants,” said Matthew Grossman, a political scientist and professor of public policy at Michigan State University. Take, for instance, the cost of living – a consistently top-ranking issue for voters in midterm polls. Trump’s immigration raids, and his policies stripping legal work permits from thousands of workers, are causing disruptions not just in the cattle industry, but also across agriculture, food service, hospitality and construction. “So many industry segments are reliant on immigrants, so it’s an issue across the economy,” said Matt Teagarden, CEO of the Kansas Livestock Association. Dairy producers and ranchers have long lobbied the government to create more legal pathways for the immigrant workers who staff their enterprises. But now, the US cattle herd has shrunk to its lowest numbers in 75 years – and ranchers are struggling to keep up with consumer demand, Teagarden said, adding: “But they are not able to expand without the workforce.” Meanwhile, about two-thirds of farm workers are non-citizen immigrants. As the administration targets these workers, food producers could struggle to keep up operations, and prices are expected to increase steeply, according to a study by the thinktank Fwd.us. Many of the staff at chef Carlos Raba’s restaurant Clavel in Baltimore are Salvadorians who have lived and worked in the US for years while holding temporary protected status (TPS). Trump has already revoked TPS for thousands of Haitians and Syrians, and if the administration also revokes TPS protections for Salvadorians – as it is imminently expected to do – Raba could lose 80% of his staff, he said at a congressional hearing. “We could not operate the way that we operate today if they are all gone,” he said. “I think about the cooks, dishwashers, farmers, bakers, entrepreneurs that I work with,” he said. “They are my co-workers, my friends and my community.” The owner of a burger restaurant not far from Trump’s Mar-a-Lago golf course said the president’s policies and immigration raids had affected not only workers but also customers, who are scared to come out and eat due to the constant presence of ICE officers. “Our sales have dropped 70%. We spend hours empty,” said Katia Rios of Pipo Burgers. The same applies for healthcare, a top issue especially for rural voters, according to a KFF-AP poll. According to the Association of American Medical Colleges, a non-profit organization representing physicians in North America, nearly one in four doctors in the US was trained abroad – and these immigrant physicians have been key to addressing medical staff shortages especially in rural areas, where few American doctors want to move. Senior living and eldercare facilities – which are also heavily staffed with immigrant caregivers – have also been left in the lurch. Of the 330,000 Haitian TPS holders who suddenly lost their legal status this summer, about 13,000 work daily as nursing assistants, caring for 65,000 patients, according to the Boston Globe. Even voters who aren’t cattle ranchers or restaurateurs, who might not clearly see the impacts of immigration policies on their economic reality, are nonetheless feeling the effects, said Grossman, of Michigan State University. “Regardless of whether people connect the dots between the president’s policies and outcomes, if those policies have real effects, then that’s another channel by which people tend to move against the party in power,” he said. Lauren Gambino contributed reporting

title: Fraternities are the most likely place for unwanted sexual contact. Should they be shut down?
summary: As an alleged 2024 gang-rape at Cornell comes to light, universities are grappling with a choice: student safety or alumni donations
text: Daniel R Schwarz, an 85-year-old English literature emeritus professor, still works at Cornell University after 59 years because he loves teaching and “watching young people grow”, he said. Most of his students, he also said, have not been part of fraternities at Cornell in Ithaca, New York, where seven men allegedly gang-raped a woman in 2024. The incident, which has sparked national outrage, and other alleged wrongdoings at fraternities have prompted Schwarz and others to call for the abolition of “Greek life” at US colleges. In recent months, fraternities across the US have been implicated in multiple hazing cases; in Pennsylvania, one fraternity was even exposed as being at the center of a drug-dealing network. But even with a long history of scandal, critics of Greek life – so-called because of the letters of the Greek alphabet that make up most fraternity and sorority names – are uncertain that schools in the US will close them. At many colleges, they are a fixture of campus life, help students form friendships and can make institutions more attractive to high schoolers, a particular concern for university leaders as they grapple with a declining birth rate. In short, they argue, if students wish to pledge allegiance to fraternities and sororities, colleges won’t stop them. “All the Greek alumni would have pitchforks, and it would be a whole debacle rather than kind of letting this play out in the press and then just going back to business,” said Lucy Taylor, a University of Maryland graduate and the creator of the podcast Snapped about the sordid history of fraternities and sororities. In 1825 at Union College in Schenectady, New York, five seniors feeling “an aching void” after the dissolution of a military company at the school formed a secret society for “literary and social purposes”, according to The Company He Keeps: A History of White College Fraternities. It became Kappa Alpha Society, the country’s first social fraternity. Such groups opened at colleges across the country, and joining them became a rite of passage for some students. Comedy film classics like Animal House and Old School celebrated the shenanigans that occur at frat parties. Fraternities and sororities were also created at historically Black colleges, where they are often a vital part of campus life, providing crucial social support and post-college networks. But there has also always been a darker side to the organizations. The first hazing incidents were reported in the 1870s, and the first death at a fraternity house occurred in 1873 during an initiation at Cornell, according to a report, Fraternities in North America, in the Ebsco database. From 1838 to 2025, there has been an average of two hazing deaths reported annually, according to Hazinginfo.org, which tracks such incidents. This year, an 18-year-old at Northern Arizona University died from alcohol poisoning after he and three other Delta Tau Delta pledges passed around two bottles of vodka to ensure they vomited, the Associated Press reported. The fraternity’s national organization closed the chapter, and a 20-year-old pleaded guilty to felony hazing. Hazing has been an issue at Black fraternities, too. In 2025, at Southern University in Louisiana, a 20-year-old student died after allegedly being punched four times in the chest as part of a hazing ritual. The alleged perpetrator was charged with manslaughter and criminal hazing. At Penn State, 14 people were arrested in August for running a cocaine-trafficking ring out of two fraternities in which hazing allegedly played a role. In addition to abusing pledges, fraternity members have long been accused of encouraging women to drink so that they can take advantage of them. In a 2019 survey from the Association of American Universities, a quarter of undergraduate women reported experiencing nonconsensual sexual conduct. The setting where it was most likely to occur was a fraternity. In August, the University of Tennessee issued a safety notice to students after three reports of sexual assault, two of which included suspected drugging at fraternities, according to WBIR. In April at the University of Arkansas, a 19-year-old allegedly raped a woman at his fraternity, Kappa Sigma, months after another woman received a temporary order of protection against him, KNWA reported. At Cornell, the school suspended fraternity parties and social events in 2022 after reports that over the course of a weekend, one student was sexually assaulted and at least four others were drugged at residences affiliated with fraternities. Then, in 2024, the event allegedly occurred that has prompted a national reckoning with Greek culture: a 20-year-old female student, known as Jane Doe, said later that she had been drugged and raped by seven members of the Chi Phi fraternity. Despite concerns over toxic behavior at fraternities and sororities, students still join because they want community and friends, said Jennifer Freyd, professor emeritus of psychology at the University of Oregon, who has studied sexual assault on college campuses. A member of a different Cornell fraternity said he joined because he had a large friend group in high school but had not found the same connections on campus. “When I met the people in my fraternity, I felt that these were people that I felt would not only just be my friend, but be a support system,” including by giving career advice and connecting him with alumni, said the student, who asked not to be named for fear of being doxed. Students also join because family or friends encourage them and convey that the organizations “bring them power and status”, Freyd said. But to achieve that, some students often must engage in hazing rituals. During initiation rites, students “engage in humiliation, and there is a tradition in fraternities of objectifying women’s bodies and in sororities of complying with fraternities”, Freyd said. In September, police arrested two fraternity leaders at the University of Wisconsin-Madison after partially clothed pledges were discovered in the basement of the frat house covered in food, condiments and other liquids. Sorority leaders can also contribute to the unhealthy environment. New York magazine recently reported on the “Ozempidemic” at colleges. Students are taking GLP-1 drugs to get skinny enough to “get into the sisterhood of their dreams”. “The drug is new but the pressure isn’t. Sororities have always ranked women by how they look,” said Taylor, the podcast creator. She joined Alpha Phi as a freshman and was initially “feeling validated and excited about all my new friends”, she said. But after she posted a photo on social media of herself in a bikini, a fellow member commented, “SNAP”, which stood for “So Not Alpha Phi”, Taylor explained. A student then sent an email urging members to “keep the booties tucked away” and to use “SNAP if you think you see something that might not be the best image for our chapter”. Even after taking it down, Taylor felt ostracized from other members. While she was shamed for the photo, she also felt as though she were living in a “rape culture”. She said members were told not to leave a fraternity before midnight because “we don’t want to seem rude”. “It was just normal if someone didn’t remember hooking up with someone from the night before. Blacking out was totally normal,” said Taylor. She alleges she was raped by a fraternity member. She left the sorority after seven months. “The Greek system, in my judgment, supports alcoholism, sexual harassment, bullying under the guise of hazing, groupthink and, of course, the objectification of women,” said Schwarz, whose students have confided in him about sexual harassment. The Guardian asked the North American Interfraternity Conference, a trade association of fraternities, about the benefits of Greek life and concerns that fraternities are incubators of sexual assault. Hillary Brewer, the organization’s chief communications officer, did not respond to a question about whether sexual misconduct is pervasive at fraternities but stated in an email that they “are an accelerator for success in college and beyond. They create lifelong connections to the campus, community and friends.” Asked whether the alleged gang rape at Cornell was indicative of a larger problem, she stated: “Any fraternity man who commits or is complicit in sexual assault should be held accountable to the fullest extent of the law. The men involved in the incident at Cornell were immediately expelled from the fraternity and the chapter was disbanded. We will continue to call for necessary personal accountability when members neglect their fraternal obligations.” Despite concerns about Greek life, Schwarz said, university leaders haven’t stopped it out of fear that alumni will stop donating money. Colleges must grapple with the fact that their customer base will probably shrink because people are having fewer children. The United States is projected to experience a 13% decline in high school graduates from 2025 to 2041, according to the Western Interstate Commission for Higher Education. Michael Kotlikoff, Cornell’s president, said that the school would take “a serious look at the role of fraternities and sororities in campus life”, but officials are not considering ending Greek life, the Associated Press reported. On Wednesday, the Ithaca Common Council voted to stop issuing permits to Cornell student groups, including fraternities, WSYR reported. The Cornell fraternity member interviewed by the Guardian said the administration’s response to the alleged gang rape was “incredibly frustrating”. Two students were expelled and a third who graduated was barred from campus. Four others were given lighter punishments – including two suspensions – but allowed to remain at the school. Fraternities who “have too many people at an event, at a party, they get a far greater punishment than what seems to have happened to” the Chi Phi members, he said. He does not think the school should force fraternities to close. “When you get rid of Greek life, you get rid of some of the most passionate people that cared about the school, right? And so why would someone like that donate to the school if the school is eliminating something that was a key part of their time at Cornell?” he said. Schools like Bowdoin College, Middlebury College and Swarthmore College have, however, shut down Greek life and survived. This week, the University of Arizona dean initiated an “interim activities suspension” at its fraternities, the New York Times reported. “The alleged behaviors range from physical assault, drugs and alcohol, hazing and creating unsafe environments for our students,” the dean stated in a letter to fraternities and sororities. “Some cases are also under criminal investigation.” Freyd used to think Greek life could be reformed but changed her mind because leaders must “overcome the generations of tradition that are misogynist and bonding over humiliation. That is enormous work.” She thinks colleges should eliminate Greek life. “The colleges and universities that make change in this domain, it’s going to be hard, and it will take courage,” Freyd said. “But it will really be worth it.” • This article was amended on 12 October 2026 to correct a previous headline, which had stated that fraternities are the most likely place for campus rape. In fact, they are the most likely place for unwanted sexual contact on college and university campuses.

title: Balkan temperatures swing as heavy rain heads for Greece
summary: Clear skies bring warm days and cold nights to Montenegro, while a low-pressure system moves towards Aegean Sea
text: Temperatures fluctuated dramatically in the Balkans last week, with unusually large differences between daytime highs and overnight lows – known as the diurnal range. An area of high pressure over the region brought prolonged sunshine during the day, while clear skies at night allowed temperatures to drop rapidly as heat escaped into the atmosphere without cloud cover to slow the cooling. In Kosanica, Montenegro, the average maximum temperature in October is 15C (59F), while the average minimum is 4C. However, on 4 and 5 October the difference between daytime highs and overnight lows reached 30C, more than double the October average. Elsewhere in Europe, high pressure will build across the north and west over the coming week, pushing an area of low pressure southwards towards the Mediterranean. The low-pressure system will deepen as it crosses the Adriatic and Ionian seas before moving eastwards into the Aegean Sea by the middle of the week. Spells of heavy rain and strong winds are expected to sweep across Greece as a result. Forecast models suggest widespread rainfall of 50-150mm, with the highest totals expected around the island of Skiathos. Towards the end of the week, the system will continue eastwards, bringing showers to parts of Crete, which was hit by severe flooding a week earlier. Those storms swept some cars and trees into the sea. Meanwhile, Hurricane Simon, a category 4 storm, is moving close to Mexico’s Pacific coast, near the state of Jalisco. It is the latest of 21 named storms in the Pacific this season, 11 of which have reached hurricane strength. At the time of writing, Simon has a central pressure of 933mb and maximum sustained winds of nearly 150mph (241km/h). However, the hurricane is expected to weaken rapidly if its core moves onshore, cutting it off from the warm ocean waters that fuel it. Heavy rainfall is affecting south-western Mexico, where totals could reach 300-400mm across a wide area, rising to 400-500mm in the wettest locations.
