title: Met chief says ‘toxicity’ around DEI will not stop him recruiting more black and Asian officers
summary: Sir Mark Rowley says inclusivity is crucial for the force and he refuses to be ‘blown off course’ by critics
text: Mark Rowley has said the Metropolitan police must recruit more black and Asian officers in order to gain the trust of minority ethnic communities in London, and vowed not to be “blown off course by the culture wars”. The right has criticised drives for diversity, claiming they lead to lower standards. Rowley, who is commissioner of the Met and Britain’s top police officer, said that as a leader of a major organisation he was prepared to take a stand against the “toxicity” surrounding the diversity debate and criticised other leaders for “running away from the subject”. In London, 46% of people are from a minority ethnic background, compared with 18% of Met officers. Rowley said he was driven by operational necessity, not politics, and believed “inclusivity” was vital to policing by consent, which is the philosophical cornerstone of British policing. “We cannot police London effectively if we fail to recruit from all of London,” he writes in the Guardian. “Effective policing depends upon inclusivity. If you are committed to policing by consent which stands or falls on the trust of all communities, you cannot do without it.” He writes: “Today, we are launching a major recruitment campaign. We have no interest in the politics and ideologies of the culture wars. Inclusion is an operational necessity. “We cannot be effective if large sections of society do not trust us, do not work with us or do not see policing as a service that understands their experiences. An inclusive workforce is not a public relations exercise. It makes us better at protecting victims, catching criminals and preventing crime.” Rowley is braced for attacks from some on the left who may say his force is not going far enough, as well as from those on the right who are critical of diversity, equity and inclusivity (DEI) initiatives. Many on the right have previously accused police of being “woke” and of “two-tier policing”, a claim that alleges people from ethnic minorities are favoured over white people, when the evidence shows the opposite. “The toxicity is horrible around the DEI debate,” Rowley said. “Lots of leaders, both in the public and private sector, are running away from the subject. I think leaders need to stand up and make a practical case. We need to do what works for policing London.” The Met is disproportionately white. It has the greatest number of black and Asian officers of any force in the UK, but also the biggest race gap – the difference between the ethnic makeup of its officers compared with the population it serves. The gap is starkest with black officers, who make up 3.7% of the Met compared with 13.5% of London’s population overall. Rowley writes that the barriers have lasted for generations and limited opportunities. “Some will wrongly argue that recruiting from under-represented communities means lowering standards. It does not and they are wrong,” he writes. “Historically, some groups faced barriers that made it harder to join policing, harder to access specialist training and harder to progress into some roles. Removing those barriers is not favouritism, it is fairness.” The Met was found to be institutionally racist by the 1999 Macpherson inquiry into failings that meant it took 19 years for the killers of the black student Stephen Lawrence to be convicted of his murder. In 2023, the Casey report, commissioned by the Met, found the force to be institutionally racist, misogynistic and homophobic. Rowley accepted the findings and said bias was systemic but rejected the label of “institutional”, believing it was politicised and ambiguous. Louise Casey and others subsequently warned that Rowley would struggle to repair the poor trust levels among black people in London when it came to the police. Last year, Met officers at Charing Cross police station were recorded calling for immigrants to be shot, bragging about excessive use of force, being dismissive about a rape complaint and making anti-Muslim and anti-women comments. Responding to Rowley’s recruitment drive, Leroy Logan, who joined the Met in 1983 and was the first chair of the Met’s black police association, said he would hesitate to join the Met now. “The Met is seen as a safe haven for white supremacists. It has gone backwards since Macpherson,” he said. “It has lacked the leadership and the culture,” Logan added. “My younger self would be really questioning whether to join now. The Met has not helped itself to ensure the experience of black people at the hands of the police is as fair and just as for white people. People are not going to join just because Sir Mark Rowley says so.”

title: Ministers preparing to slash heat pump subsidies to fund defence spending
summary: Exclusive: Some of £2bn savings needed from energy budget expected to come from boiler upgrade scheme, sources say
text: Ministers are preparing to slash the amount of money available to subsidise heat pumps as they look for ways to fund higher defence spending, sources have told the Guardian. Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, has been tasked with finding more than £2bn in savings from her budget to help pay for defence investment under a plan drawn up by the previous government. Sources say a portion of those savings will come from cutting the boiler upgrade scheme (BUS) for England and Wales, which provides grants of up to £9,000 to help households switch to cleaner heating methods. The programme will not be abolished altogether but sources say hundreds of millions of pounds will be cut from its £2.7bn five-year budget. The scheme has helped tens of thousands of households install an electric heat pump in place of an old gas boiler, but Treasury officials have long considered it a subsidy used mainly by middle-class households. Critics say cutting the scheme would damage the nascent British heat pump industry and further undermine the government’s commitment to tackling the climate crisis. Ministers are also expected to give the go-ahead for the Jackdaw gasfield as soon as this week. Madeleine Gabriel, a director at the charity Nesta, said: “Bills are soaring again because of high gas prices. Our reliance on gas is the reason we are in an energy crisis, so cutting funding for heat pumps makes no sense. “It’s a kick in the teeth for the businesses and tradespeople who’ve put in time and money to build the industry.” Greg Jackson, the chief executive of Octopus Energy, said: “The boiler upgrade scheme is doing exactly what it was meant to do. It’s kicking off an industry to drive down the costs of heat pumps – they can now cost the same to install as a gas boiler after the grant.” He added: “Just as EVs are becoming the new normal, heat pumps are too. In the last 18 months, more than 500,000 have asked us for a quote. “The market is taking off. Cutting the engine now would be brutally damaging. Heat pumps are undoubtedly our energy future – slashing the cost of living and insulating us against fossil fuel costs and global dictators.” A spokesperson for the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero said: “Savings for the defence investment plan (Dip) are a small part of [the department’s] overall budget, which saw a significant uplift at spending review. “We will set out how we will fund essential investment in our national security this autumn.” The overall cuts were agreed to by the former energy secretary, Ed Miliband, as the then prime minister, Keir Starmer, looked for ways to fund a £15bn rise in defence spending over four years. Miliband agreed that the energy department would cut its capital budget by £2bn to help pay for the Dip. Energy officials say the cuts pale in comparison with the overall growth in the energy department’s capital budget, which is one of the fastest growing in Whitehall. The chancellor, John Healey, resigned as defence secretary in June under Starmer, arguing that the defence uplift was not enough. He now has to find an additional £4.7bn in savings over a four-year period beyond what departments have already agreed. Bloomberg reported this month that as part of the cuts to the energy department, ministers were planning to reduce spending on carbon capture and storage (CCS) and green hydrogen schemes. The government had been planning to spend £21.7bn on CCS from now until 2050 as ministers look to make the UK a leader in the still-developing technology. CCS supporters say it is the best way to cut carbon emissions while still protecting Britain’s North Sea oil industry. But its critics say the technology is being promoted by fossil fuel companies who are not being honest about how much it will end up costing the country. Asked recently about the future of the CCS programme, Martin McCluskey, an energy minister, told Politico: “I’m not betraying any confidences when I say that we are having to make some difficult decisions because of what happened as a result of the defence investment plan.” The Guardian has learned that heat pump subsidies are one of the other significant schemes due to be raided to fund the increase in defence spending. The scheme, which offers £7,500 as a basic grant towards an electric heat pump, has subsidised nearly 80,000 heat pumps since it began in 2022. Some properties that are off the grid can claim as much as £9,000 to upgrade. However, given those subsidies cover only just over half the cost of the median heat pump, much of that money has gone to better-off households. The scheme’s supporters say that more than 40% of the money has gone to households with an annual income of below £52,000. But more important, they add, is the fact the subsidies have helped to build a fast-growing domestic heat pump industry, which is expanding by more than 25% a year. Other countries have a far more developed industry. France sold four times the number of heat pumps the UK did last year. However, the technology also has vocal critics. Dale Vince, the energy entrepreneur and Labour donor, published a report recently that said: “Cleaner heat does not yet mean cheaper heat. “Electrifying heat without fixing electricity pricing risks shifting higher costs on to households rather than delivering savings.” • This article was amended on 13 October 2026 to add the detail that the £2.7bn budget for the boiler upgrade scheme is over a five-year period.

title: Burnham: not pursuing better EU deal would be ‘dereliction of duty’
summary: Post-recess statement will focus on damage caused by Brexit and the need to cooperate on immigration and trade
text: Andy Burnham will put Brexit back on the Commons agenda as MPs return from recess, warning that failing to pursue a better deal with the EU would be a “major dereliction of duty”. The prime minister will use a statement to the Commons on the first day back after the party conference break to urge MPs to face up to the damage caused by Brexit, and embrace closer ties with the EU to increase economic growth and tackle illegal immigration. In a stern warning ahead of the upcoming UK-EU summit, Burnham will argue that Britain cannot afford to turn its back on opportunities for greater cooperation with Europe and that maintaining the status quo is no longer good enough. He will call for a calm, clear-eyed assessment of Britain’s relationship with Europe and urge MPs from across the Commons to back a pragmatic approach. Burnham is expected to argue that most of the public would expect the government to seize the opportunity if closer cooperation could strengthen immigration controls while reviving the economy. A No 10 source said: “Andy understands why some politicians don’t want to face up to the reality that Brexit has not delivered what they once promised. But it is time for a different conversation about what our long-term relationship should be. “Sticking with the status quo and not working relentlessly to secure a good deal that boosts growth would be a major dereliction of duty.” The prime minister’s statement comes on the same day MPs are due to debate a petition in Westminster Hall, calling for Britain to apply to rejoin the EU, which got more than 111,000 signatures. The intervention comes amid renewed divisions over Britain’s relationship with Europe, with senior Conservatives vowing to reverse Labour’s moves towards closer EU ties, including a proposed agreement designed to ease post-Brexit barriers on food and agricultural trade. It has prompted warnings from businesses that abandoning such arrangements could prolong costs and uncertainty caused by checks and paperwork at the border. But the idea of Britain having a closer relationship with the EU has also prompted unease within Burnham’s own ranks. Some MPs representing leave-voting constituencies fear renewing the Brexit debate could reopen old divisions, with senior ministers warning of the political and economic risks of pursuing EU membership. Burnham’s statement also follows his declaration on Sunday that Russia interfered in the 2016 Brexit referendum. The prime minister has said he sought clarification on foreign interference after entering Downing Street and received confirmation of Russian involvement, although he did not reveal the evidence or suggest it had changed the referendum result. The prime minister has already signalled a significant change in tone from his predecessor Keir Starmer, who ruled out rejoining the single market or customs union. At Labour’s conference in Liverpool last month, Burnham said Brexit had done more harm than good and promised to examine Britain’s longterm relationship with the EU. He opened the door to options including fully rejoining the bloc. Monday’s statement will turn the focus towards the immediate negotiations, with ministers seeking progress on removing trade barriers, including bureaucracy affecting food imports and exports, and closer cooperation on migration.

title: Roman Abramovich aides falsified paperwork to disguise assets and dodge tax, records suggest
summary: Accountancy firm Deloitte Cyprus among those that appear to have backdated records outlining the Russian billionaire’s assets
text: Aides of Roman Abramovich – including staff at the global accountancy firm Deloitte – falsified paperwork mapping the oligarch’s sprawling offshore business empire, records suggest, helping his businesses dodge tax and disguise assets. New analysis of leaked corporate records uncovers what appears to have been a long-running and carefully orchestrated strategy of backdating documents. The Russian billionaire’s closest aide, London-based Eugene Tenenbaum, appears to have been involved in the backdating and may also have given false evidence to the UK high court during a potentially costly lawsuit, the papers indicate. Abramovich’s personal and financial affairs are now restricted, owing to sanctions imposed by the UK and EU in response to Russia’s war on Ukraine. But the documents raise questions about how Abramovich was able to shield his financial affairs from the authorities for more than a decade, with the apparent assistance of apparatchiks and blue-chip advisers. The findings are based on the Cyprus Confidential leak, more than 500,000 documents, first released to the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists (ICIJ) and analysed by organisations including the Guardian, the Bureau of Investigative Journalism and the BBC. The digital paper trail charts the reorganisation of billions of pounds that the former Chelsea FC owner obtained via the controversial acquisition of oilfields in the frozen wastes of Siberia, amid the break-up of the Soviet Union. From 1999 until at least 2013, a cadre of aides and accountants tasked with shifting the funds between offshore jurisdictions deployed tactics that experts say may have constituted fraud and tax evasion. This, it seems, involved backdating documents to create a convenient paper trail showing that agreements and transactions had taken place years earlier. Lawyers for Abramovich denied any wrongdoing and said he relied on the advice of his advisers and Deloitte Cyprus. Tenenbaum denied any wrongdoing and said he also relied on the specialist advice given by Deloitte Cyprus. Deloitte Cyprus said that it “acts in compliance with all applicable laws” and that it could no longer access the relevant material because of the time that has elapsed. The disappearing $2bn A crown jewel in Russia’s rich seam of natural resources, Sibneft’s oilfields fell into Abramovich’s hands during the chaotic post-Soviet privatisation era. The famously shrewd entrepreneur obtained the business for roughly $250m, reportedly spending as little as $19m of his own money. By the time he sold the last of his shares to Gazprom in 2005, Abramovich had raised $16bn, money he ploughed into investments, mansions, superyachts and Chelsea FC. One Cyprus-based company, Kravin Investments, was among several early vehicles through which that cash flowed. Kravin received a $3bn windfall in May 2003, of which it retained about $2bn. The money sat in Kravin’s bank account or was loaned to other companies, accruing interest that was, in theory, taxable in Cyprus. But Abramovich’s aides soon began devising plans to “eliminate” a tax liability that one financial adviser warned could be “very large”, records suggest. The gatekeeper to Abramovich’s fortune was Demetris Ioannides, who was the chair of Deloitte Cyprus before spinning out his own business Meritservus. That firm became Abramovich’s go-to financial advisory, serving him for nearly 20 years, before it was sanctioned by the UK in 2023, along with Ioannides, for its role helping Russian oligarch hide their wealth. “It will be necessary to change the [Kravin’s] financial statements and the accounting records accordingly for 2003 and 2004,” Ioannides wrote in an August 2005 email, citing discussions with Deloitte Cyprus partners and erstwhile colleagues Antonis Taliotis and Nicos Charalambous. The following month, in an email copying in staff at Meritservus and Abramovich’s investment vehicle, Millhouse, Taliotis appeared to agree. “Certain changes will have to be made to the accounts […]” he wrote. Millhouse and Meritservus duly began producing paperwork showing that Kravin was simply holding and investing the Sibneft billions as a trustee for another business, the British Virgin Islands-based Kelvedon Worldwide. Documents detailing this supposed fact, including correspondence and trust agreements, were given dates between March and December 2003, despite being created at least two years later. The result was simple: although the billions had sat in Kravin’s accounts for years, it now appeared that the money had never really been Kravin’s at all. Deloitte Cyprus, apparently aware of the deception, duly signed off the accounts. History had effectively been rewritten, analysis of the documents suggests, disappearing $2bn from Kravin’s balance sheet – and with it any tax liability. Andrew Mitchell KC, a leading expert in financial crime and tax law, described the scheme as a “blatant move to protect from legitimate taxation assets which should otherwise have been subject to tax”. This, he claimed, would amount to “straightforward” tax evasion. Abramovich’s lawyers said: “Any suggestion that our client evaded tax, or sought to deceive the Cypriot authorities, is denied, and publication of the same would be defamatory of him. If an arrangement was proposed by professional advisers of Deloitte’s standing, it would have been entirely proper for companies linked to our client (in which he was not involved on a day-to-day basis) to rely on it.” The oligarch’s signature It was not the first time that Abramovich’s subordinates appear to have resorted to backdating to solve a money problem for their boss. In 2000, Tenenbaum and Ioannides, then still working for Deloitte Cyprus, met in London to discuss a delicate matter. Abramovich, it seemed, wanted to extract almost $100m from Cypriot companies that held stakes in Sibneft. According to Ioannides, it was essential that any transaction couldn’t reveal these Cyprus companies and that the money had to appear “earned”. The logic for these conditions was not explained. Deloitte Cyprus’s solution was a complicated but seemingly bogus arrangement, directly involving Abramovich, that appears to have relied on falsified, backdated consultancy agreements. These agreements appeared to show that Abramovich’s Sibneft-owning companies had paid an intermediary business $98m for “consultancy services”, namely advice on share purchases. That intermediary had then supposedly passed on 99.9% of the money to Abramovich, as “commission” for having acted as its “agent”. But the share purchases in question had already happened a year earlier, meaning the intermediary company had to be at least a year old too, if backdated deals involving it were to appear legitimate. Ioannides found a suitable Cypriot off-the-shelf company called PB Mediapower Enterprises. With Tenenbaum’s authorisation, directors of Deloitte Cyprus signed the backdated documents and incorporated their content into PB Mediapower’s annual accounts. Abramovich’s commission was then converted into promissory notes – effectively IOUs – which he cashed in over the following three years. The leaked files contain 50 such notes. Unlike much of the paper trail tracing the Abramovich fortune, which kept his name out of it, each of the applications for repayment of the notes bore his signature. Lawyers for Abramovich and Tenenbaum denied that they had participated in any improper backdating or falsification of documents. Both also stressed that they relied on specialist advice from professional advisers such as Deloitte Cyprus as well as Cypriot corporate advisers. The ghost house One of Abramovich’s most prestigious assets was the Fyning Hill estate in West Sussex, an imposing mansion set in 424 acres of South Downs countryside. The Russian president, Vladimir Putin, reportedly flew in for lunch here during his first UK state visit in 2003. Two years later, accounts show, the estate was listed among $650m of luxury assets – including a London penthouse, French chateau, helicopters, jets, yachts and a supercar – all held in a Cypriot company, Amiscan Investments. New Cypriot disclosure rules, introduced in 2003, meant that these would have to be included in Amiscan’s accounts. But by the time those accounts were filed, this vast billionaire’s toybox had vanished, thanks to Abramovich’s squad of financial fixers. In an October 2005 email, sent to Tenenbaum, Ioannides suggested it might be “more prudent not to disclose” them. Files show that Abramovich aides, including Ioannides, worked together to backdate contractual agreements, giving the false impression that Amiscan’s assets had been shifted to its BVI shareholder, Kelvedon Worldwide, at the start of 2003. Deloitte Cyprus staff took part in discussions about this disappearing act, emails show. Yet the auditor signed off Amiscan’s accounts, now showing no trace of three properties and a fleet of luxury vehicles. Lawyers for Abramovich and Tenenbaum denied wrongdoing of any sort, including improper backdating, falsification, or any sort of tax evasion. They each also said that their clients could not recall the context or detail of documents more than 20 years old, which had not been provided to them by the Guardian. Both said their clients had relied on expert advice, including from Deloitte Cyprus. Deloitte Cyprus, also answering on behalf of Taliotis and Charalambous, said that it “acts in compliance with applicable laws”. It said the correspondence were more than 20 years old and no longer accessible, meaning it could not comment on whether the material was complete or accurate. A lawyer for Demetris Ioannides said he was unable to comment for personal reasons. Lawyers for Tenenbaum said that documents could sometimes be backdated for legitimate reasons, such as to show when a transaction became effective. Rachel Sexton, a forensic accountant experienced in fraud investigations, agreed that this was possible but added: “From the evidence I have seen, this does not appear to be the case.” She said backdating documents to create a false impression “could be considered to be fraudulent misrepresentation.” Two more accounting experts, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said the files did not appear to show legitimate reasons for backdating. Mitchell raised concerns about Deloitte’s apparent role in the tactic. “What you take away from it is that there are professionals who are prepared to bend and break the rules of their profession and therefore the law.” In one instance, backdating appears to have led to something else very serious: the misleading of a British court. The whole truth In 2008, Abramovich faced the prospect of a potentially costly lawsuit from Moscow businessman Chalva Tchigrinski, a former partner in their joint oil venture, Sibneft-Yugra. The partnership ended with Tchigrinski’s company, Sibir, ousted and left with nothing, leaving Abramovich free to sign the Sibneft deals that would make him Russia’s richest man. Tchigrinski’s lawyers claimed foul play. Abramovich, they claimed, had diluted his partner’s stake via a series of secret meetings that gave him full control and, as a result, the full financial benefit of the eventual sale to Gazprom. In a witness statement, Tenenbaum denied any knowledge of the project’s details before spring 2004, when Sibir’s made its complaints public. “I have searched my files, emails and documents from 2002 to 2004,” he told the court, “and I can confirm that I have in my possession no records or documents or other communications that relate to Sibneft-Yugra.” Files from the Cyprus Confidential leak appear to contradict this testimony. They show that Tenenbaum signed off on a string of agreements governing some of the very deals he claimed in court to know nothing about. They include the 2003 transfer of Sibneft-Yugra shares to an Abramovich-owned company called Ferenco Investment & Services, something Tenenbaum had told the court he knew nothing about. His testimony, according to the judgment, was “corroborated by” evidence submitted by Abramovich. The Guardian has not seen this evidence. What is more, documents submitted to the court in support of Abramovich’s case, which purported to justify Sibneft’s takeover of Sibir, appear to have been backdated. In other words, the documents – like Tenenbaum’s testimony – appear to have been false. Lawyers for Tenenbaum denied that his testimony misled the court, saying he had given evidence “honestly and in good faith” and denied “in the strongest terms” misleading the court. Lawyers for Abramovich denied that his corroboration of Tenenbaum’s testimony had misled the court. All in all, analysis of the Cyprus files suggest that more than 1,000 documents pertaining to the Abramovich empire were backdated. Often, it appears, this took place with the knowledge of those closest to the oligarch. Between them, that inner circle constructed a globe-spanning financial empire whose most important currency was, it seems, deceit.

title: Starwatch: Mars signposts the beautiful Beehive cluster
summary: From a dark location, the Beehive – or Praesepe – will appear as a faint, misty patch very close to the red planet
text: The red planet, Mars, sails through the beautiful cluster of stars known as the Beehive this week. Catalogued as Messier 44, the cluster lies in the constellation Cancer. It has been known since antiquity, when its hazy appearance earned it the Latin name Praesepe, meaning a manger or crib. Although it is one of the brightest star clusters in the night sky, it can be surprisingly difficult to locate because Cancer contains no bright stars to guide the eye towards it. Thankfully, this week Mars acts as the signpost. The chart shows the view looking east from London at 0200 BST on 13 October. Mars will appear as a moderately bright, distinctly red-looking object. Once you have Mars in your sights, look carefully around the planet. From a dark location, the Beehive will appear as a faint, misty patch very close to Mars. Light pollution will make the cluster much harder to see, and wherever you are observing, make sure you allow sufficient time for your eyes to adjust to the dark. This can take about 20 minutes, so resist the temptation to look at the bright screen of your phone. If you have binoculars, they will reveal the cluster beautifully, transforming the indistinct haze into a scattering of individual stars.

title: Country diary: Fungi season is here, so I head – yes – to the beach | Nigel Brown
summary: Aberffraw, Ynys Môn (Anglesey): Plenty of fungi can be found among the sand here; in fact it is vital to keeping the dunes at bay
text: Dapperlings and toughshanks, bonnets and brittlegills, bird’s nests and fairy clubs. Fungi season has begun, and for me it is heralded by the “fungus foray” held at Bangor University’s Treborth Botanic Garden. An annual event, this year it produced more than 200 species in just 90 minutes, thanks to the 225 forayers who took part. Among the feast of colour and form was one I’d never seen in 50 years of foraying – orange ping‑pong bat fungus (Favolaschia calocera), glowing vivid along a fallen twig. Climate change is implicated in its rapid global spread, and it was first recorded in the UK only in 2012. Every year, the botanic garden’s foray turns up something special. Back home on Anglesey (Ynys Môn), we’re blessed to have a remarkable range of fungi – including in surprising locations such as our sand dunes, one of the island’s defining habitats both in scale and in ecological importance. Aberffraw Dunes on the west coast are treeless, exposed and ever-shifting. Yet here we recently found fairy rings of two toadstools – parasols (Macrolepiota mastoidea) and champignon (Marasmius oreades) – patterning the links, while in the damper hollows were fibrecaps (Inocybe) and webcaps (Cortinarius), both of which can be highly toxic. Above the beach, one plant is king – marram (Ammophila arenaria). This is the only plant on earth that can stabilise sand and make tall dunes. Its underground stems keep pace with the engulfing dunes, but without fungi to assist it in mining the sand for vital minerals and nutrients, it would starve and be subsumed. And so, scattered about the bare sand between clumps of marram, we found scores of salt-resistant dune brittlestems (Psathyrella ammophila). This is only ever found growing with marram and is responsible for decomposing its constant supply of ailing roots and recycling them, ready to be absorbed in the next phase of the plant’s growth. Other, much smaller, mycorrhizal fungi are on hand to help out too, all specialised to seek out organic materials to satisfy their host plant’s insatiable appetite. This year, the word “funga” has been adopted both by the Cambridge Dictionary and negotiating parties at the forthcoming Cop17 conference, as an equivalent to flora and fauna. At last, fungi are being given the status they deserve. • Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024, is available now at guardianbookshop.com

title: Ukraine war briefing: Russia attacks multiple power plants after Trump energy ceasefire claim
summary: Zelenskyy says Ukrainian skies filled with Russian drones after truce claim, which Moscow has yet to confirm, as six killed in strikes. What we know on day 1,692
text: Russian strikes hit multiple Ukrainian power plants after Donald Trump claimed both sides had agreed to stop hitting each other’s energy infrastructure, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said. The Ukrainian president said on social media a drone had hit a power plant in Kyiv on Sunday, leading to power outages in the capital. Shortly after, he said there had been a strike on the CHP-5 power plant in the eastern city of Kharkiv, adding:“Ukrainian skies have been infested with Russian ‘shaheds’ [drones] all day.” Trump said earlier that “effective immediately, there is an energy ceasefire in the war between Russia and Ukraine”. “Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!” the US president wrote on his Truth Social platform on Sunday morning in Washington, without further details. Zelenskyy expressed surprise at the announcement, saying the deal was “news to me” and he was seeking further details. Russia has yet to confirm it agreed. The ceasefire appeared to garner support on Sunday from Ukraine’s key western allies, including the UK, France, Canada and the European Commission. British prime minister Andy Burnham said a sustained energy ceasefire was “the best route to get energy and fuel back into world markets”. French president Emmanuel Macron said Paris supported a “real energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine. Ukrainian officials said Russian ⁠attacks killed six people ⁠in two Ukrainian ⁠cities on Sunday, including a strike ⁠on a grocery store in Kharkiv, Ukraine’s second-largest city, where ‌three people died ‌and 20 were ‌injured. Two children were ‌among the injured, regional governor Oleh Syniehubov said. In a separate attack in western Ukraine, officials said ‌a Russian strike killed three people. Trump’s energy truce claim came two days after he announced a controversial agreement to buy Russian diesel fuel while temporarily easing US sanctions, prompting outrage from Ukraine and its European allies, who said it would embolden Moscow. Canadian prime minister Mark Carney added to the chorus of disapproval after a Sunday call with Zelenskyy, saying the diesel deal “is in direct opposition to the efforts of Ukraine, Canada and our allies to create peace and stability in Europe”. EU chief Ursula von der Leyen also backed Zelenskyy “as he leads the fight for his people’s freedom”, while Germany foreign minister Johann Wadephul said Berlin continued to “fully support” him. Trump lashed out at Zelenskyy when asked about criticism of the Russia diesel deal, saying it was “time for Ukraine to get a new president” who would finally settle the war. Zelenskyy pushed back, telling US ABC News on Sunday: “First of all, with all respect to President Trump, it’s up to our society, up to our people to choose one or another leader.” The Trump administration is threatening to stop the procurement system that provides Ukraine with weapons in order to press Kyiv to halt its deep strikes on Russian energy infrastructure, the Financial Times quoted officials in Europe as saying. The US was lobbying European capitals and Kyiv in an attempt to end the attacks on Russian oil refineries, they said. A Ukrainian ⁠drone killed one ⁠person in Russia’s ⁠border Belgorod region on Sunday, ⁠officials said. The operational headquarters ⁠in Belgorod region said the drone struck a car on a road ‌near the border. In the part of Ukraine’s eastern Donetsk region ⁠held by Russian forces, Moscow-installed officials said one person ‌had been killed in a Ukrainian attack. Russia’s military ⁠said it ⁠struck ⁠a logistics centre in southern Ukraine’s ⁠Mykolaiv region and a cargo vessel ⁠in the Black ‌Sea. The logistics centre in the town ‌of Ternivka was used to store military and dual-use cargoes for the ⁠Ukrainian military, the ‌Russian defence ministry ‌claimed on Sunday.

title: Indonesia looks to mosque loudspeakers to double as earthquake warning systems
summary: A five-year trial is assessing whether the loudspeakers used to broadcast the call to prayer can help to warn hard-to-reach territories
text: Scientists working on an early warning system in earthquake-prone Indonesia have taken the spiritual path to designing a network of alarms that will reach even the remotest communities: they hope to use mosques to save lives. A five-year trial is assessing whether the ubiquitous loudspeakers used to broadcast the call to prayer can double up as warning klaxons for earthquakes. “Every community has a mosque,” says project lead Dr Inoue Hiroshi, speaking to the Guardian from Indonesia. The pilot scheme was the brainchild of the Japanese disaster scientist, who says he came up with the idea nearly two decades ago while researching deadly quakes in Sumatra, Indonesia. Inoue, of the Disaster Prevention Research Institute at Kyoto University in Japan, is working with the Indonesian government to assess whether the country could implement an early warning system similar to Japan’s. “I thought if Indonesia had the same service and people received the warning before the shaking came, then many people among those few hundred wouldn’t have died,” he says of a devastating 2009 quake in western Sumatra which killed at least 1,000 people. Indonesia’s disaster agency has to grapple with huge distances and hard-to-reach territories, but it has the benefit of an already established network of regularly serviced loudspeakers, something many other countries do not. With the largest population of Muslims worldwide, Indonesia has hundreds of thousands of mosques, which broadcast the call to pray five times a day. The pilot scheme has already hooked up several mosques to its seismic sensor network. For an earthquake early warning system to save lives, there are two critical factors – it needs a network of alarms, and they need to work. “The advantage of a mosque speaker is that they’re existing and well maintained,” says Inoue. “For any disaster infrastructure, maintenance is the big challenge … but the mosque speaker is maintained by the people”. Many modern disaster preparedness strategies work using mobile phones, although those are vulnerable because earthquakes can disrupt communication infrastructure. The country has a tsunami early warning system dating back to 2008, but the earthquake initiative could be a “breakthrough”, says Andi Eka Sakya, senior researcher at the Indonesian government-affiliated National Research and Innovation Agency and the Indonesian head of the joint research team. While tsunamis affect coastal areas and can be predicted in minutes or even hours, earthquake waves move through the ground at incredible speeds, and Sakya says a village 50km from the epicentre could have only five to 10 seconds to respond. “It’s still a prototype, and they don’t issue warnings to the public yet,” he says. “The ultimate goal is actually to alert the people so that they can respond as early as possible.” The project, which runs until 2030, is also looking at installing alarm systems in school loudspeakers and using radio and television transmissions. Indonesia and Japan both lie on the Pacific Ring of Fire and are frequently affected by earthquakes. Researchers are looking at how behaviours and survival strategies differ between Japan and Indonesia. In Japan, official disaster guidelines focus on the widely used “drop and cover” strategy – taking immediate shelter, for example, under a table and staying indoors. In contrast, low-rise homes in some developing countries like Indonesia are frequently built from unreinforced masonry that is highly vulnerable to collapsing, and so people have survived by escaping outside. In some cases, two-storey buildings in Indonesia have seen the first floor crushed and the second floor remain relatively intact. “The way people react is they quickly escape out of the room,” says Inoue. “They know how to survive.” Because standard international advice does not always suit fragile buildings, project researchers are conducting simulations and human experiments to establish guidelines grounded in science. “This is actually one of the main research topics,” says Inoue. Other countries in the Muslim world have looked at similar systems. When the United Arab Emirates government planned to start its Barakah nuclear power plant, an official on the project said mosque loudspeakers would be part of a broader network of alarms in the event of a radiation leak. A far more extensive mosque loudspeaker project is going on in Uzbekistan, where the Ministry of Emergency Situations announced a pilot project this year for devices to be installed in 272 mosques. The alarms would alert people to floods, mudflows, landslides and avalanches. “The selection of mosques is not incidental,” the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), which partnered in the initiative, said in a statement. “They are traditionally perceived as authoritative social institutions with significant influence on local communities.”

title: Pennsylvania shooter who killed eight was a grandfather, says slain child’s dad
summary: Father of toddler killed in Erie mass shooting says reported gunman never seemed distressed or out of the ordinary
text: The man who killed eight people, before turning the gun on himself, in a mass shooting in a home in Erie, Pennsylvania, on Friday was a grandfather who had not shown signs that he was capable of such violence, according to people who knew the shooter. A man whose toddler was among those killed said on Sunday that the man never seemed distressed or out of the ordinary, the Associated Press reports. “I think that was a front for him,” said Julius Windham during a memorial to victims of Friday’s shooting. Windham’s one-year-old daughter, Amarianna; her pregnant mother; and the woman’s five-year-old son and unborn baby were among the victims. “Him every day, him smiling and being just – you would think of nothing like that would happen,” Windham said. The 45-year-old gunman took his own life. Authorities have not released his name, but the Erie police chief, Rick Lorah, said he was related to seven of the victims. The eighth was a friend of the pregnant woman, he said. Police have not made their names public, either. Mourners on Sunday placed candles, flowers and stuffed animals outside the home where the man opened fire shortly before 5 pm on Friday. Windham wore a T-shirt with pictures of the slain woman and children and the words “Forever in my heart”. “Words can’t even explain what I’m going through right now,” Windham said. “But I gotta be strong for my community, you know what I’m saying? My family, my daughters, my sons, everybody.” “We don’t want that dark memory to be what defines their lives in this world,” a family friend told Cleveland 19 News. “How do you even fathom something like this? How will you go home and tell your kids: ‘Hey, your mom, your siblings, your uncles and everybody else just got murdered by your grandpa?’” Video and audio evidence recovered by investigators included muffled gunshot sounds coming from inside the home just before two “distressed” women arrived and began pounding on the door, Lorah said. The gunman then came out and shot them before returning inside. Responding officers found the two women dead outside. After deploying a drone and robot, they went inside and found the bodies of the five-year-old boy and one-year-old girl on the first floor; two more women and two young men in a stairwell; and the shooter on the second floor. “Out of respect for the victims and the families, I will not discuss the details of what our officers encountered inside that home,” the chief said at a news conference. “But I want our community to understand the gravity of what happened and the profound impact this tragedy has had on those involved and on our community as a whole,” he said. Erie is about 120 miles (190km) north of Pittsburgh. Lorah declined to discuss motive but suggested mental health could be a factor. He said investigators would talk to relatives and examine the cellphones of the women who were killed outside the home. “They knew something was going on at that house,” Lorah said. “We have to figure out what that is.” Nicole and Debra Eller, whose best friend was among the victims, told the Associated Press they have known the family for more than 30 years. Nicole Eller said the shooter “was a good guy, and then he started going downhill with everything”. “They were a lovely family. Who would have thought this would ever happen?” Debra Eller said. “Oh my gosh, this is so upsetting. This should have never happened to her or the kids or anybody. His grandchildren, his kids, how can you do that?” The Erie shooting was reminiscent of a 1982 massacre in Wilkes-Barre, Pennsylvania, in which a man killed 13 people, including five of his own children. At a news conference on Saturday, Erie’s mayor, Daria Devlin, addressed a portion of her remarks directly to the victims’ families. “I am so deeply sorry,” Devlin said. What happened to you was horrific, and there is nothing that any of us can say today that will make this any easier ... Our entire community is with you, we’re grieving with you. And we are here to support you.” “My heart breaks for this family. Lori and I are praying for their loved ones and the entire Erie community,” said Pennsylvania’s governor, Josh Shapiro, in a post on X on Saturday.

title: UK to strengthen cyber defences as minister calls for AI firms to increase safety efforts
summary: Kanishka Narayan to say Britain cannot rely entirely on tech companies amid rising global concern over AI dangers
text: Companies building the most advanced AI systems must increase safety efforts, the UK’s AI minister will say, as he announces a strengthening of Britain’s cyber defences. Kanishka Narayan will call on companies developing frontier AI to do more to make sure it is safe. He will say Britain cannot rely entirely on technology companies to police their own models and will argue the UK needs to build more of its own AI infrastructure. Narayan’s speech in west London will be the first since Andy Burnham made AI a cabinet-level brief. It comes as Geoffrey Irving, a former chief scientist at the UK’s AI Security Institute, which tests the most powerful AI models, raised fears enemy states could steal unreleased cutting-edge models. Amid increasing global concern at dangers posed by AI, Irving told the Guardian: “The AI companies do not have security that would prevent an adversarial country from stealing the models.” He cited a recent incident at OpenAI where it was “hacked” by cybersecurity researchers, who said “the scope of what we could theoretically access was huge”. The attack was carried out under an OpenAI programme that rewarded ethical hackers testing its systems. OpenAI says it has multiple protections against theft of its models, including encryption and continuous monitoring. Irving, a former employee at OpenAI and Google DeepMind who now runs an AI safety research body, has warned there is a “50% chance” of humanity being wiped out by superintelligent AIs and the only answer, for now, is to stop development of advanced systems as soon as possible. Irving is concerned by the rate of progress in alarming attributes shown by models, which could lead to them becoming highly advanced in traits such as concealing their actions and manipulating humans. “It is possible we [will] get superintelligence in less than 12 months, on the current path,” he said. Narayan’s speech will be watched closely for signs the UK may join a call for international governments to coordinate common safety standards for AIs, which has been signed by leaders of nations including Finland, France, Germany, Australia, Singapore, the UAE and Ireland, but not the UK and the US, where Donald Trump has said he wants the leading AI companies to “self-police”. The international alliance calling for strict rules comes after a wave of recent incidents with misaligned advanced AIs hacking into private and government systems. In one of the latest cases, Anthropic on Friday revealed that when it was testing a version of its Claude model the AI contacted police claiming it could help solve a murder. It had landed on a page containing a police department tip form and a mention of an unsolved homicide. It wrote: “I may have information regarding this case. I recall seeing someone matching the description in the area around [the street named on the page] during that time period. Please contact me if this information is relevant.” Although Claude was instructed never to log in, create accounts, enter personal data, make purchases, or submit anything destructive, its instructions did not rule out form submissions. Last week UK intelligence leaders from MI5, MI6 and GCHQ briefed the cabinet on AI’s threat to national security, according to the Sunday Times. The warning from the spy chiefs is being seen by some as encouragement for Burnham to grip the AI safety issue more firmly. The prime minister told the UN last month that Britain would use its G20 presidency next year to champion agreement on AI safety with “a single set of global principles and standards”. But safety experts are calling for faster action to avert the most serious risks, which range from advanced AIs being used to mount a cyber-attack on essential infrastructure to the creation of novel bioweapons. Meanwhile, Satya Nadella, the chair and chief executive of Microsoft, which operates AI infrastructure and is an OpenAI shareholder, on Saturday called for AI models to be designed with an “emergency brake”. He said people needed to start from the principle of assuming advanced AI models posed an insider risk. “We can’t treat Super Intelligence as a set of nested black boxes and simply accept or reject its recommendations, answers, and actions,” he wrote. “We must build contained systems whose behaviour we can observe, limits we can test, and actions we can always contain.”

title: Riyadh airport hit again after deadly Houthi missile attack, Saudi authorities say
summary: Unidentified projectile strikes King Khalid airport, killing one and injuring 11, as escalating attacks threaten to draw more countries into Yemen conflict
text: A projectile hit a passenger terminal at the airport in Riyadh on Sunday, the day after a deadly missile attack on the facility carried out by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebel group killed 13 people. An unidentified projectile hit terminal 4 at King Khalid international airport, starting a fire, killing one person and injuring 11, according to Saudi civil aviation authorities. Air defences also intercepted a cruise missile in the vicinity of the airport. It was the latest of several attacks on the airport in the past week. The escalating attacks threatened to draw more countries into the Yemen conflict and further widen the regional fallout of the US-Iran war, which has already spread to Lebanon and Iraq. In a post on X, the British embassy in Saudi Arabia advised against all but essential travel to the cities of Jeddah and Dammam and to avoid almost all airports. After Saturday’s strike on Riyadh airport, the US president, Donald Trump, said he was weighing whether to join the Saudi military campaign in Yemen, telling reporters: “We’re going to look into it.” The Iran-allied Houthis claimed to have launched several attacks on the airport, including the attack on Saturday, which killed 13 people and injured more than 300 – the deadliest attack on a Gulf country since the war with Iran started in March and an apparent escalation in the Houthis’ war with Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government that Riyadh sponsors. In response to the attack, Saudi authorities extended the closure of the airport and said schools would be moved online until Thursday. The Houthis claimed that Saudi Arabia struck the airport in Yemen’s rebel-held capital, Sana’a, on Sunday, without providing more information on damage or casualties. Videos circulated on social media showing travellers walking through debris-strewn ground in the Riyadh airport as sirens blared. Four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshi nationals, a Palestinian, a US citizen, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Syrian and a Sudanese were killed in the missile strike. On Sunday evening, Saudi authorities also confirmed King Fahd international airport in the eastern city of Dammam had been attacked, with the country’s civil aviation authority saying on X: “The assessment of the damage and verification of the safety of airport facilities were still under way, in coordination with the relevant authorities.” On Saturday night, the spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen, Maj Gen Turki al-Maliki, said the coalition would “respond firmly” to the attack, offering few other details. The Houthis said a Saudi airstrike on Sana’a on Sunday hit a home and killed a child, as well as injuring six others. The Houthis doubled down on their threats on Sunday, warning airlines, passengers and staff to stay away from Saudi airports. The group said “the worst is yet to come” if Saudi military action in Yemen continued. “We renew our warning to all airlines, experts, employees, workers and travellers against using Saudi airports and airspace, as they are vulnerable to attack and have become a theatre of operations for our forces,” the Houthis said on X. Trump said on Saturday night that he would speak to the Saudi crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman, after the previous attack on the airport. The US has already been assisting with intelligence cooperation and targeting, with about 200 US military advisers stationed in Saudi Arabia to help with the campaign. Until now, the US has not directly taken part in fighting against the Houthis. Direct US involvement could lead the group to resume its targeting of ships passing through the Bab al-Mandab strait, through which about 10% of global maritime goods transit. It would also further entangle the US in Middle East wars as the American public grows increasingly frustrated with the continuing Iran conflict. Trump is facing the midterm elections in November with an unpopular war and soaring prices at home threatening his party’s performance at the polls. Saudi Arabia is already carrying out airstrikes against the Houthis in Yemen. The Houthi government’s health ministry said coalition airstrikes over the last six weeks had killed 91 Yemenis and wounded 168, 60% of whom it said were women and children. Saudi-backed government forces in Yemen launched a campaign to push the Houthis back from the areas the group conquered over the past month. Despite claiming initial successes, the government forces have not been able to loosen the Houthis’ grip over areas closest to the Bab al-Mandab strait such as Perim Island. The Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia said one of its citizens died on Sunday after being wounded in the Riyadh airport attack a day earlier. The Egyptian woman killed in the attack on the airport was a flight attendant identified as Azza Ramzy, 28, who worked for the Saudi airline Flynas, according to Egyptian state-run TV. The Syrian woman was a widowed mother of four who had been living in Saudi Arabia for five years, a relative told the Associated Press. The Syrian embassy in Riyadh identified her as Buthaina Ahmad Oweida. Her niece, Nisreen Oweida, said her aunt was 56, from Syria’s northern Idlib province, and had left during the country’s civil war. She was living in Mecca and had been returning from a visit to her sister in Riyadh when she was killed, the niece said. The airport attack was met with a wave of international condemnation, including from the UN secretary general, António Guterres, and the president of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen. “Attacks by Iran’s proxies are pushing the region into a spiral of violence,” von der Leyen wrote on X. “They are destabilising crucial global transport and energy nodes.” The increasing intensity of Houthi attacks against Riyadh and its energy infrastructure has brought more foreign involvement in the Yemen war. Governments are facing pressure over oil prices, already high from the US-Iran war since March. On Monday, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey issued a joint statement saying they would move quickly to implement their mutual defence pact, including by speeding up the deployment of military forces in the kingdom. The UK said it would assist with defensive military support of Riyadh, providing refuelling for aircraft working to intercept Houthi missiles. Saudi Arabia has asked for further assistance from France, Egypt, the UK and Pakistan as its stock of interceptor missiles are running low. The Houthis launched a military campaign to take Yemen’s Red Sea coast in early September after months of escalating tensions with the Yemeni government and its Saudi patron. The campaign interrupted years of relative calm in the country after a 2022 UN-brokered ceasefire froze frontlines between the Houthis and the government. Despite the Saudi-supported counteroffensive, the group seems to have held on to its recent gains. It is unclear what further Saudi military action would look like against the Houthis, who resisted years of strikes by an international coalition, as well as by the US. Saudi Arabia led an international coalition that intervened against the Houthis in Yemen in 2015 after the group took over Sana’a and toppled the Yemeni government. Recent Houthi attacks against Saudi energy infrastructure, as well as Houthi military advances, have pulled Saudi Arabia back into the Yemen war.

title: Steve Jones obituary
summary: Other lives: Consultant economist and project planner for humanitarian projects around the world
text: My friend Steve Jones, who has died aged 77, had a working life devoted to humanitarian causes, with a particular focus on Bangladesh and India. In retirement he then dedicated a sizeable portion of his time to charity work, helping people with the lung disease pulmonary fibrosis get the help and treatment they needed. Steve was born in London to John and Lettie, who were both teachers and shared the surname Jones. After secondary school in Crawley, West Sussex, he studied geography at Bristol University, worked for a short time as an economist for a company that became part of British Airways and then embarked on further studies at Cambridge University, where he gained a certificate in anthropology and began a PhD. While there he became involved with Operation Omega, a group that smuggled humanitarian aid across the border from India to Bangladesh during its war with Pakistan in 1971. This led him to cut short his studies so that he could begin work as a consultant economist and project planner. Over the years he worked on many projects, including for the University of New South Wales from 1984 to 1986 in the Solomon Islands on a smallholder project and a post-cyclone survey. In 1989 his work took him back to Bangladesh, where he was employed by the World Bank to develop a flood action plan. Fourteen years of his life, from 1992 to 2006, were then spent with the Department for International Development, working on ways to help tackle the social and economic problems related to rural poverty in India. He was also particularly proud of a cyclone recovery and reconstruction project he worked on in 2007 for the World Bank, which led to the building of cyclone shelters in Bangladesh. In 2006 he became a trustee and then chair of trustees of the Humanitarian Centre in Cambridge, which later became the Centre for Global Equality. Two years later he had to leave work after being diagnosed with pulmonary fibrosis, but eventually he was lucky enough to receive a lung transplant that prolonged his life considerably. That allowed him to focus on being a trustee, chair and patient president of the charity Action for Pulmonary Fibrosis, giving over the last decade of his life to fighting on behalf of people with the disease so that they can be provided with better diagnosis, care and treatment. He was also president of the European Pulmonary Fibrosis Federation. In 1976 he met Hilary Gretton, a nurse, and they married five years later. She survives him, along with their children, Rosie, David and Euan, and seven grandchildren.

title: Abdul El-Sayed: Democrats must ‘win by massive numbers’ to fend off Trump election denial
summary: Democratic Senate candidate’s remarks come as Trump has long baselessly claimed his 2020 election loss was stolen
text: Democrats must “win by massive numbers” during November’s federal midterm elections because Donald Trump and his Republican allies are bound to try to sow doubt about the integrity of the results, Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan said on Sunday. El-Sayed’s comments on NBC’s Meet the Press came with the Democrats favored to win control of the House of Representatives during the 3 November midterms – and polls show that the party could also win Senate seats in states that traditionally elect Republicans and gain a majority there, too. Meanwhile, Trump has long baselessly maintained that the 2020 presidential election which he lost as an incumbent to Joe Biden was stolen by fraudsters. He also gave a primetime speech in July in which he made unverified claims about Chinese interference in the election, and he fired members of an independent federal election commission. When asked later by a rightwing broadcaster whether the president might declare a national security emergency pertaining to elections for the midterms, Trump ignited alarm among some observers by replying: “Let me just say, stranger things have happened, OK?” The New York Times, meanwhile, reported that Trump had cast doubt on elections on 440 days of his second presidency, which began in early 2025. As such, on NBC’s Meet the Press Sunday, El-Sayed was asked whether Democrats needed to turn out in such numbers in November that the election would be “too big to rig” – as it had recently been put by former vice-president Kamala Harris, who lost the 2024 White House election to Trump. “Donald Trump has already threatened to do what he did in 2020, which is deny the outcomes of an election,” El-Sayed said. “So, yes, we have to win by massive numbers.” The Cook Political Report revised its predictions on Tuesday and declared that “A Senate Majority is Squarely in Democrats’ Sights”. A recent New York Times and Siena University poll found Democratic Senate candidates leading in Alaska, Ohio and Texas, states that Trump won by double digits in 2024. The poll showed El-Sayed leading Republican candidate Mike Rogers by five points. El-Sayed on Sunday’s Meet the Press alluded to how Rogers had also claimed that a 2024 US Senate election which he lost to Elissa Slotkin, a Democrat, was stolen from him – after first having conceded the race. Rogers in November 2025 was reported to have said at events that a single van carrying fraudulent ballots in Detroit cost him the race against Slotkin. “The guy … I’m running against insinuates that he didn’t actually lose,” El-Sayed said to Kristen Welker. “That’s the guy I’m running against right now.”

title: Trump announces partial ceasefire in Ukraine war as Zelenskyy says deal is ‘news to me’
summary: Ukrainian president earlier rejected US call for Kyiv to stop bombing oil refineries, saying Moscow must first end attacks on energy infrastructure
text: Donald Trump has announced an energy ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia, apparently without consulting Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who said the deal to stop long-range attacks was “news to me”. In a social media post, the US president claimed the two sides had reached an agreement. “Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!” he wrote on Truth Social. He offered no further details. Zelenskyy said he was surprised by the announcement but would agree to it if Vladimir Putin did the same. “If President Trump negotiated it with Putin – please tell us when the ceasefire begins. We are ready and we will accept it,” the Ukrainian president told the Axios website. Earlier, Zelenskyy rebuffed Trump’s demand made on Saturday that Kyiv stop bombing Russian oil refineries. Zelenskyy said Moscow had to first halt its own “brutal” attacks on his country’s energy infrastructure. Any deal to end long-range drone strikes by Ukraine on targets inside Russia would have to be “reciprocal”, he said. It should be backed by “real guarantees” – meaning punitive measures against Moscow from Ukraine’s allies, including the US. There was no sign that the Kremlin was observing Trump’s ceasefire. According to Zelenskyy, Russian drones took to the sky “throughout the day” on Sunday. There were also “unfortunately” several airstrikes, he said, including on energy infrastructure. The Ukrainian president said the Russians hit thermal power station No 5 in the eastern city of Kharkiv – the latest of more than 200 strikes this week against electricity generation and transmission facilities in Ukraine. There were another 17 hits on gas and oil facilities, he added. The fast-moving row between Washington and Kyiv began on Friday when Trump announced he was lifting sanctions on Russian diesel exports. He said the move would reduce global and domestic fuel prices before next month’s US midterm elections. A furious Zelenskyy called the decision “weak” and said it would generate “billions” in extra revenue for Putin, enabling him to wage war “even more intensely”. An equally irate Trump said Zelenskyy should “damn well stop” hitting Russian refineries. Ukraine needed a “new leader”, he said on Saturday. Responding to Trump, Zelenskyy said it was up to Ukrainians to choose “one or another leader”. He told ABC News he was willing to accept Trump’s demands and to organise elections, but only if Putin agreed to a “total” 60-day ceasefire. The bitter public feud is the most serious between the US and Ukraine since last year, when Trump berated Zelenskyy in the Oval Office. The Financial Times, citing officials in Europe, reported on Sunday that the US is ⁠threatening ⁠to stop the procurement ⁠system that provides ⁠Ukraine with ‌weapons to ‌press Kyiv to halt its ‌deep strikes on Russian energy infrastructure. The New York Times has reported that US officials have offered the Kremlin lucrative economic incentives in exchange for a ceasefire. They reportedly include releasing billions in Russian sovereign assets that are frozen. The Trump administration also revisited a plan to sell parts of Russia’s energy company, Lukoil. The multibillion deal would benefit Middle Eastern investors, the paper reported, some with “business ties” to US negotiators. On Saturday, Trump criticised Zelenskyy and said he had refused to make a deal to end the fighting. In response, Ukraine’s president laid the blame for Europe’s biggest war since 1945 on “Russia and Russia alone”. “It is possible to stop strikes on energy infrastructure as early as today, but Putin does not want to do so,” he said. Ukrainian officials point out that the White House is demanding Kyiv give up its most effective weapon, without demanding any corresponding concessions from Russia. In recent weeks, Kyiv has dealt a major blow to Russia’s economy, striking oil complexes, warehouses and datacentres. Russia’s own bombing campaign has been relentless. On Saturday it killed 23 people in the city of Zaporizhzhia, including four children, and hit a five-storey apartment block in the frontline town of Sloviansk. Zelenskyy said Moscow’s aerial campaign involved thousands of aerial bombs and jet-powered drones. It continued “unabated”, he said. The head of Ukraine’s foreign affairs committee, Oleksandr Merezhko, said Trump’s “bullying” demand for Zelenskyy to quit had strengthened him at home “paradoxically”, after recent damaging corruption scandals. “Putin’s plan is to decapitate Zelenskyy and remove him as a wartime leader. Trump is siding with Putin,” Merezhko said. He added: “I’m afraid that behind this situation is Trump’s worldview. He wants to do business with Putin. For him, Ukraine seems like an obstacle to be removed. Both Trump and Putin wish to pressure us into capitulation.” Referring to the notorious 1939 agreement between Nazi Germany and the USSR, Merezhko said: “We are moving to a new Molotov-Ribbentrop pact and to a world of strongmen and spheres of influence.” Merezhko said Ukraine would continue to destroy enemy oil refineries, against US wishes, because they funded Russia’s war machine and acknowledged that a cutoff of US intelligence sharing with Kyiv – threatened by the Trump administration – would “blind” Ukraine’s air defence systems. “This would be an act of complicity with Putin’s genocide. It would mean more dead civilians and dead children,” he said. Ukrainian negotiators had been meeting in Florida with their American counterparts, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, when Trump announced the US was lifting sanctions on Russian diesel. Blindsided, the Ukrainians went home early. “It felt like a trap,” one stunned Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent newspaper. On Sunday, Zelenskyy shored up support in a series of conversations with key allies including Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, the Polish leader, Donald Tusk, and the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen. Earlier Zelenskyy spoke with the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, France’s president, Emmanuel Macron, and the Finnish president, Alexander Stubb. Downing Street said Burnham recognised the last 24 hours had been “difficult” for Ukraine and “reiterated his complete solidarity”. Downing Street said the two leaders agreed “to maintain pressure on Russia” and to strengthen the sanctions regime, despite Trump’s efforts to the contrary. “Russia should agree to an immediate energy ceasefire, ending its brutal strikes on Ukrainian infrastructure and its attacks on shipping in the Black Sea,” a statement added. Speaking over the weekend, Zelenskyy said Trump’s decision empowered Putin and gave him “extra money for the war”, running into millions and “perhaps billions”. “It is certainly not fair. It is certainly not how partners should act. And, in my view, it is a weak decision,” he said. Luke Harding’s Betrayal: Trump, Putin and the New Age of Conquest is published by Guardian Faber

title: Volkswagen boss backs EU plan to bolster domestic European industry
summary: Oliver Blume says Made in Europe rules to counter rapid rise of lower-price Chinese brands ‘must reward real value creation’
text: The boss of Volkswagen has backed EU proposals to boost its domestic industry, arguing European carmakers need to be able to “compete under comparable conditions” with Chinese rivals. Oliver Blume said “Made in Europe” rules from the EU “must reward real value creation in Europe”, speaking in Paris before the motor show this week. The rules are aimed at countering the rapid rise of Chinese brands in Europe in the automotive sector and other important manufacturing industries. Lower-priced Chinese manufacturers have prompted a crisis in several industries. Volkswagen is among the most-affected European companies. Germany’s biggest carmaker has launched a brutal plan to cut as many as 100,000 jobs. Blume said it was the “largest transformation programme in its history”. The proposals for the Made in Europe rules, formally known as the Industrial Accelerator Act, would limit subsidies and public procurement to products with a large proportion of their materials and manufacturing coming from within the EU. Blume listed a litany of challenges facing European carmakers, saying: “Europe is under enormous competitive pressure.” These included: high energy costs; lower demand as consumers struggle with high inflation; the need to be quicker to develop cars; and intense competition from China. On Friday, the EU said it had reached a landmark deal with China to “halve” its sales of hybrid cars in the bloc amid fears surging sales could kill off parts of the European car industry. Blume said Germany’s carmakers were happy to compete with Chinese rivals, but said the EU should try to reward businesses with significant European footprints. “Companies that invest and develop in Europe must see a clear benefit,” he said. Referring to Chinese companies, he added: “Those who sell here should compete under comparable conditions and create jobs and value here in Europe, too. Blume added: “We believe in open markets, but openness also means standing up for our own interests in Europe. Because a strong industrial base means more than economic success. It protects technological independence.” Volkswagen is exhibiting at the Paris show for the first time in 20 years. Blume emphasised the “close ties between France and Germany”, while hosting the French industry minister, Sébastian Martin. Arno Antlitz, VW’s chief financial officer, said the job cuts were necessary to “increase our economic power” by increasing profitability and allowing it to defend its “home turf”. The company is cutting the number of models it offers worldwide from 150 to 75 across brands including Audi and Škoda. It hopes the move will reduce complexity in its factories and for dealers, cutting the cost of each vehicle it makes. On Sunday, it revealed the production version of its ID Tiguan, an electric edition of its bestselling family SUV.
