title: Trump’s deal with Putin will have little impact on US diesel prices, experts say
summary: Analysts say fuel will take weeks to ship and quantity is too small to affect prices, while full deal is unlikely to be met given damage to Russian refineries
text: Donald Trump’s deal with Vladimir Putin to temporarily lift sanctions on US imports of Russian diesel will have little “meaningful” effect on motorists and businesses in the US and overseas, energy and foreign policy analysts have predicted. The US president infuriated Volodymyr Zelenskyy when he announced the deal on Friday, writing on Truth Social that the agreement with his Russia counterpart to supply millions of tonnes of diesel was essential to reduce fuel prices in the US, which have soared after his decision to go to war against Iran. The package announced by Trump involves 300,000 tonnes of diesel released immediately “to the American and global marketplace” followed by 500,000 tonnes in November and a further 1m tonnes after that. The 300,000 figure equates to about three-quarters of what the US would use in a day, according to calculations using figures from the US Energy Information Administration. “Diesel prices for Americans and, indeed, the world, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST! Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my greatest priority,” Trump posted. However, experts suggested that the quantities involved – and the time it will take for the supplies to arrive in the US – is “too little, too late” to affect current high diesel prices, which observers have linked to challenging Republican party polling numbers before next month’s midterm elections. US prices have surged by almost 70% since the start of the Iran war, to about $6.30 a gallon, according to American Automobile Association. In the UK, the average price of diesel climbed to a record £2 a litre earlier in October, and sat just below that mark on Friday. Ashley Kelty, an energy analyst with the investment bank Panmure Liberum, said: “It is not going to have any impact on prices. The first amount [due to be shipped to the US] is so small. “They are going to have to charter vessels, load them and transport the cargo to the US. That will take about three weeks – so we are pretty much at the end of the month and about a week before the midterms.” The US Treasury secretary, Scott ⁠Bessent, said on Sunday: “This is good ‌for the American people … bringing these diesel prices down.” However, Kelty said the diesel shipments would also cause complications in a global supply chain, including multinational companies having to work out which of its supplies originated from Russia and therefore might breach sanctions in other jurisdictions, including Europe. The US Treasury suspended sanctions on Russian diesel exports until 7 April as part of the deal, while keeping in place other sanctions on Russian products. Zelenskyy described Trump’s deal as a “weak decision”, saying it would encourage Russia to keep attacking Ukraine, but Trump then blamed Kyiv’s strikes on Russian energy infrastructure for rising fuel prices. Trump said Ukraine neeeded “a new leader”. On Sunday, Zelenskyy said he would be ready to stop hitting Russian oil refineries if Russia curbed its attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure. Trump later posted on Truth Social: “Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it! Thank you for your attention to this matter.” Maximilian Hess, the founder of the political risk consultancy Enmetena Advisory and a fellow at the Foreign Policy Research Institute, said: “It will not have any meaningful domestic US effect or international effect given its full terms are highly unlikely to be met as a result of the impact of Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian refining which have limited its diesel output. “The whole point of the deal for Putin is that it fails, which he can blame on Ukraine and thus stoke tensions between Trump and Zelenskyy. Indeed, it’s already working.”

title: Feelgood factor of human interaction | Brief letters
summary: Brief letters: Happy hormones | Fuel costs | Drive-in parking | Guys and girls | Young or old? | Singapore pollution
text: Re your report (‘Pull the plug’: protesters resort to direct action against AI firms, 6 October), the US neuroscientist Ben Rein has shown that there is a fundamental difference in our cognitive response according to the type of interaction we have. In-person meetings and conversations show a dramatic increase in serotonin, oxytocin and dopamine – “feelgood” hormones – compared with online interactions. I have been encouraged to speak to people at bus stops. Judith Furner Eastbourne, East Sussex • Re easing winter fuel costs (Report, 6 October), it would benefit everyone if the outrageous daily standing charges were reduced or on a sliding scale based on usage. I can’t be the only person whose standing charges each month are half or more than the energy used. Judith Pearson Sheffield • To your tautology anthology (Letters, 5 October) should be added this sign at a farm shop in the Vale of Evesham: “Large drive-in car park.” Paul Gelling Prenton, Merseyside • Far worse than being called “young lady” (Letters, 7 October) is the ubiquitous use of “guys” in the hospitality industry. Stop it. Megan Parry Wallingford, Oxfordshire • At 91, I object to being addressed as “young man”, remembering that when I was actually a young man I was often called “old man”. Beverley Charles Rowe London • Irony corner: air pollution impairs F1 motor racing in Singapore (Report, 6 October). Martin Datta Lincoln • Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Please email us your letter and it will be considered for publication in our letters section.

title: Andy Burnham says it is clear Russia interfered in Brexit referendum
summary: PM says he asked question upon entering No 10 but does not reveal who gave him ‘clear answer’ Russia meddled
text: Andy Burnham has said it is clear Russia interfered in the Brexit referendum, after seeking answers on the Kremlin’s involvement in the 2016 vote when he entered Downing Street. Burnham said he had asked whether Moscow had attempted to influence the referendum and received a confirmation that it had. Speaking on the podcast The Rest is Politics, Burnham said: “I asked the question coming to Downing Street: well, was there interference in the 2016 referendum from Russia? I’ve had the clear answer that yes, there was.” Burnham’s comments mark a significant departure from the position taken by past Conservative governments, which insisted there was no evidence of successful interference by Russia in the referendum vote. The prime minister did not disclose who had given him the assessment, what evidence it was based on or whether any interference had affected the result of the vote. A report by parliament’s intelligence and security committee in 2020 criticised the government and intelligence agencies for failing to properly investigate potential Russian interference in the referendum. The cross-party committee found that ministers had failed to seek a full assessment of Moscow’s activities, despite evidence of attempts to influence British politics through Russian state-backed media outlets and social media accounts. It said the government had not provided any post-referendum assessment of Russian attempts at interference, in contrast to the investigation undertaken in the US after the 2016 presidential election. The committee also said that whether a hostile state had sought to influence a democratic process was important regardless of whether those efforts had succeeded. Burnham said Britain needed to be more open about attempts by hostile states to interfere in its politics, particularly as European leaders grapple with the rise of the far right. Last month the prime minister attacked Russian information warfare during a speech to the UN general assembly, saying there was evidence Moscow had tried to interfere with the 2019 general election. Burnham told the podcast: “These things are important now to put clearly on the record and I believe help voters in Germany and France understand that some of this politics is instigated via our enemies, namely Russia. “I think we’ve been too much on the back foot on that, actually, and we haven’t informed people sufficiently about the extent to which people are seeking to disrupt the political process from overseas.” He said he had discussed the threat posed by the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) with the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, on a visit to Berlin this week. Burnham said Merz raised concerns about the party’s links to Russia. “One thing I did say to Chancellor Merz … is we need to support you in taking on the threat that you face and particularly the type of politics that you’re facing,” he said. “You know, he was saying to me that the AfD are clearly linked to Russia – funded, I believe.” He added: “There is certainly misinformation, disinformation, that is emanating from Russia into German politics.” The UK is developing a new National Centre for Information Defence to detect and disrupt hostile state information campaigns aimed at undermining British democracy. Downing Street said it was working with Germany on a new partnership to counter hybrid threats, including hostile activities that threaten both countries’ security and prosperity. A spokesperson said: “National security is the first duty of any government – we are focused on ensuring our citizens and our institutions are protected from foreign powers and their proxies seeking to threaten lives and undermine our democratic values. “We are doing this by strengthening our powers through the National Security Act, strengthening the resilience of our institutions and critical national infrastructure, strengthening our borders, and strengthening our police and intelligence agencies. “We will continue to leave no stone unturned in our efforts to protect the UK from harm.” Last month Burnham opened the door to Britain eventually rejoining the EU, saying his government would examine all options for the country’s future relationship with Brussels.

title: Zack Polanski signals Green party overhaul after row over Zionism vote
summary: Rapid growth means structures need to change and give leaders greater control, Polanski says in Guardian article
text: Zack Polanski has signalled a potential overhaul of the Green party’s cherished grassroots democracy, calling for leaders to have greater control over strategic direction after a divisive vote equating Zionism with racism. The leader of the Green party of England and Wales has also questioned whether political parties should seek to define what members believe, in his strongest criticism yet of a motion that has provoked bitter divisions, international condemnation and calls for his resignation. Writing for the Guardian after his defeat in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, Polanski suggests the party’s focus on defining Zionism has been misguided, even though he agrees with the substance of the motion. Appearing to accept criticisms of his leadership over the issue, he admits his priority was “fighting a hugely consequential byelection for our party” and accepts that his own colleagues and members may feel “let down” by his decision to not make an intervention last week. He adds: “I put all my energy into the race in Holborn and St Pancras, despite Labour choosing the polling date so close to our conference, because I know that ultimately electoral success is how we drive change. I know, though, that some feel let down by that decision – and I hear that.” Polanski says the party’s rapid growth means its democratic structures need to change, including giving leaders more responsibility for setting its political direction. “Our party democracy must now evolve to meet that – creating wider engagement for members, giving leaders more responsibility to set the party’s strategic direction, and making our processes as robust and accessible as possible,” he writes. His intervention marks the clearest indication yet that he believes the party’s internal structures need reform, after senior Greens raised concerns that its system of policymaking gives disproportionate influence to a small minority of members. Under the Greens’ existing rules, policy is decided by members at party conference rather than by its leadership, a system that has increasingly come under scrutiny as membership surged. The controversy intensified last weekend when 1,022 members representing about 0.4% of the party’s total membership voted in favour of a motion declaring Zionism a form of racism and backing a single Palestinian state. The motion, which passed by 1,022 votes to 813, was opposed by four of the party’s five MPs and prompted criticism from the European Green party, whose position supports a two-state solution. Ellie Chowns, the Greens’ Westminster leader, said the party must not become vulnerable to capture by extremists and racists, arguing the vote demonstrated the urgent need to modernise its policymaking structures. Polanski, who is Jewish and grew up in a Zionist household, writes: “It has been difficult knowing how to approach this imperfect motion, because its substance chimes with my understanding of Zionism as the ideology that underpins the displacement and genocide of Palestinians. “This is something I share with many other Jewish people, including Stephen Kapos, the Holocaust survivor who was one of those supporting the motion. “At the same time, Zionism is not easily defined, and I know for many Jewish people it is bound up with identity, safety and belonging. In my view it’s not the job of a political party to tell people what to believe – and a narrow focus on definitions is neither desirable nor strategic. “There are also elements of the motion that I don’t agree with, such as dictating the future shape of a state in Israel and Palestine. While many people understandably see the idea of a two-state solution as standing in the way of concrete action to end the unbearable status quo, I believe it is not up to the British government – let alone the Green party – to decide the future for Israelis and Palestinians.” The comments go beyond Polanski’s previous objections to elements of the motion, which largely centred on its call for a single Palestinian state rather than leaving Palestinians to determine their own political future. The controversy exposed divisions within the Greens and raised questions about the party’s ability to manage its rapid expansion under Polanski’s leadership. The Guardian previously reported that senior Greens feared the existing structure allowed a small number of highly motivated activists to determine policy for the wider membership. Some argued members should set broad political priorities while smaller bodies developed detailed policies.

title: ICE agent strikes man with vehicle during pursuit in Texas, officials say
summary: Parra-Hernandez suffered a broken leg and taken to a hospital after being hit by car during an ICE operation
text: An Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent driving a vehicle struck a man on Saturday while trying to pursue him and someone else in the Houston area, according to authorities. The federal agency had been trying to pull over and arrest Jose Mendoza-Cervantes in north-west Harris county, Texas, when he and the victim, Miguel Parra-Hernandez, exited the vehicle, officials said. Surveillance footage showed the officer chase Parra-Hernandez and then hit him with his car. Parra-Hernandez suffered a broken leg and was taken to a hospital, the Harris county sheriff’s office said. In a statement, the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) that oversees ICE said the agency had been trying to arrest Mendoza-Cervantes after a judge had issued him a final order of removal from the United States. Mendoza-Cervantes had been arrested four times for driving under the influence and arrested for unlawful possession of a firearm, the DHS statement added. He remained at large as of Saturday morning. DHS did not address questions from the Guardian seeking the name of the officer who struck Parra-Hernandez and whether he was equipped with a body-worn camera, which ICE policy requires. Parra-Hernandez’s hospitalization came with ICE facing criticism throughout Donald Trump’s second presidency for the agency’s aggressive arrest, detention and deportation tactics. More than 30 people have died in 2026 during interactions with immigration officials, the Guardian reported in late September. On Friday morning, a 72-year-old man shot an off-duty ICE official who was “intoxicated and agitated” and was accused of attacking the man and his daughter on their property in Fresno, California. On Thursday, in New York City, an ICE agent shot a man who was in his vehicle with a five-year-old child, mayor Zohran Mamdani said in a statement. Markwayne Mullin, the Trump administration’s homeland security secretary, later said on CBS’s Face the Nation that ICE took the time to learn the “pattern of life” of the man shot in New York on Thursday – but “we didn’t know the five-year-old was in the vehicle”. The Harris county precinct 4 commissioner, Lesley Briones, alluded to those various other cases in a statement on Saturday, saying: “Under the Trump administration, ICE has brought chaos and destruction to communities across our country.” Briones described herself as “horrified” after Parra-Hernandez’s case on Saturday and called for ICE to release any relevant video to the sheriff’s office. DHS did not immediately respond to the Guardian when asked for comment on Sunday.

title: Over 100 Migrants Are Dead After Boat Capsizes Near Djibouti
summary: The shipwreck is among the deadliest ever recorded on the route to Yemen, the International Organization for Migration said. Dozens remain missing, and the bodies of 15 children were recovered.

title: Democrats Press Pentagon on Iran Civilian Deaths
summary: A new letter from 74 lawmakers suggests that civilian casualties will become a focus of investigation if Democrats take control of Congress.

title: At least 139 dead including children after migrant boat capsizes off Djibouti
summary: Eighty-four others still missing from vessel heading to Yemen with 305 people onboard, UN migration agency says
text: At least 139 people, including 15 children, have died after a boat carrying 305 migrants capsized off the coast of Djibouti, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) said. Another 84 people are still missing after the incident, which, according to survivors, happened near Guhere, north of the fishing town of Obock, during the night of 8-9 October when the boat was travelling from Djibouti to Yemen. Eighty-two people, all Ethiopian nationals, survived the capsizing, the UN agency said. It described the incident as one of the deadliest boat disasters recorded on a migration corridor between the Horn of Africa and the Arab peninsula known as the eastern route. “This is a devastating loss of life. Our thoughts are with the survivors and the families who have lost loved ones or remain without news of their relatives,” said Alexandre Coissac, the IOM’s chief of mission in Djibouti. The organisation is providing healthcare, psychosocial, food and other assistance to 64 survivors at its Obock migrant response centre. The IOM is working with local authorities to provide emergency assistance. Djiboutian authorities are continuing search and rescue operations, and local authorities are providing medical care to survivors and arranging burials for those who died. The eastern route is one of the busiest migration paths in the world. Hundreds of thousands of people a year, mostly Ethiopians and Somalis, use it to reach Gulf countries, mainly Saudi Arabia. Some have been forced out of their communities by conflict and natural disasters, and others move to seek work and other economic opportunities. The route accounts for most of the migratory movement from the Horn of Africa. The other main ones are the northern route to north Africa and Europe, and the southern route to southern Africa. The eastern route is also one of the most dangerous globally, with some people dying from walking long distances in searing heat and others from the capsizing of boats that smugglers have crammed them on to in the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden. Coissac said: “This tragedy is a stark reminder of the dangers faced by migrants along this migration corridor as they seek economic opportunities.” In 2025, more than 900 people died or went missing along the route, according to the IOM’s missing migrants project, while the number undertaking the journey increased by 18%. In March, nine people died and 45 went missing after a migrant boat capsized. This week’s tragedy shows the movement is happening despite fighting between the Iran-aligned Houthi rebel group and Saudi-backed government forces for control of strategic heights on the Red Sea coast. The violence has forced more than 3,800 people to cross to Djibouti to seek protection, according to the country’s office for assistance to refugees and disaster victims (Onars).

title: Wildlife park confirms tiger will not be euthanised after man mauled to death
summary: Ed Miliband, MP for nearby Doncaster North, offers ‘deepest condolences’ to family of visitor who entered enclosure on Saturday
text: A wildlife park in Yorkshire has confirmed the tiger that mauled to death a man who entered its enclosure will not be euthanised. A man, who has not yet been named, was seen entering a tiger enclosure at the Yorkshire Wildlife Park, near Doncaster, before police were called at 1.35pm on Saturday. South Yorkshire police said the tiger “subsequently attacked the man, resulting in serious injury” and despite the efforts of emergency services, the man was pronounced dead at the scene. In a statement on Sunday, the wildlife park thanked those who had expressed concern after the “tragic incident” and said their “thoughts and heartfelt sympathies” remained with the family of the man who lost his life. “The park will be closed today and the staff team who were deeply affected by events will receive specialist support,” the statement read. The park also confirmed that the tiger, named Altai, was “safe and well and will not be euthanised” after the incident. The foreign secretary and MP for Doncaster North, Ed Miliband, said he was “deeply saddened” and sent his “thoughts and deepest condolences to the family of the individual who died”. “I am very grateful to the emergency services and staff of the park who responded,” Miliband added. One visitor at the park, Marie Miller, wrote in a Facebook post that she had seen the man before the incident and he was “happily enjoying” his visit. Miller said the man had asked a stranger to take a picture of him. “The man who I saw on the bridge with his earpods in dancing was happily enjoying seeing the tiger,” the post read. “He asked a total stranger to take a picture of him with the tiger in the background.” Another visitor, who did not want to be identified, told the South West News Service that it was “frightening and confusing” when the park was evacuated after the incident. She said: “At first, we were all scared and confused because we had no idea what was going on. Different routes had been closed off, and staff were positioned around the park directing visitors where to go. “The scariest part was not knowing what was happening.” The visitor said she heard people saying the man was 22, but was unable to confirm this. “As we walked past the police near the tiger enclosure, we saw officers surrounding a young man in the tiger enclosure,” she said. “We saw an air ambulance outside the park, although, from what we observed, it didn’t take anyone away.” South Yorkshire police said the man’s family was made aware of the incident on Saturday and were being supported by specialist officers. The force has encouraged people not to share videos of the incident that have been circulating online. Yorkshire Wildlife Park opened in 2009, with the Land of the Tigers attraction opening in 2011. The attraction is on a purpose-built 2-acre reserve for Amur tigers, an endangered subspecies with about 500 left in the wild. • This article was amended on 12 October 2026. In an earlier version, a subheading incorrectly stated that the Yorkshire Wildlife Park was in Ed Miliband’s constituency.

title: Thousands without power in Florida and Alabama as Isaias moves north
summary: At least four deaths linked to storm amid warnings of flash flooding that could stretch into Appalachians
text: As what was left of Hurricane Isaias moved north on Sunday, bringing moderate to heavy rainfall across the central Appalachians and the mid-Atlantic region, nearly 396,000 customers across the Florida Panhandle and southern Alabama remained without power. Heavy rainfall associated with the storm could bring isolated flash flooding and strong wind gusts and remain a threat across the south-eastern US, especially near the southern Appalachians, according to the National Weather Service (NWS). That could bring scattered power outages and downed trees and power lines. Life-threatening surf and rip current conditions were expected to continue along the Gulf and south-eastern Atlantic coasts. According to the National Weather Service, parts of the Carolinas and Virginia, including Raleigh, Richmond and Washington DC were under threat of tornadoes on Sunday. At least four deaths were linked to the storm, including two people killed when trees fell on to homes in Florida and Alabama. Forecasters warned that flooding could stretch into the Appalachians. Isaias came ashore as a category 2 hurricane on Friday near Destin, Florida, a Gulf coast vacation spot filled with high-rises and tourist shops. This has been the first hurricane to make landfall in the continental US in two years, since Milton struck western Florida in October 2024. Despite warnings of storm surges ahead of the storm, several major routes along the coast were open by daybreak on Saturday and free of downed trees and power lines typically seen after major hurricanes. Hurricane-force winds in the Florida Panhandle blew the roof off a Pensacola hotel, and the city’s mayor said the airport “took some damage”. The storm flattened a boathouse in Destin and ripped away part of the facade of a high-rise in Panama City Beach. In Florida’s Escambia county, Sheriff Chip Simmons said a woman was killed when a tree fell on her home – and a man died of carbon monoxide fumes from a generator running in his garage. Four of the man’s family members, ranging in age from four to 72, were treated but were expected to survive, the sheriff said. The first hurricane of the Atlantic season, Isaias roared farther into Alabama with tropical-force winds. One person died when a tree fell on a house in Birmingham, the city’s fire chief, Cory Moon, said. A second storm-related death in Alabama was attributed to a motor vehicle crash involving a downed tree in Barbour county, said Josh Johnson of the state’s emergency management agency. Along Alabama’s Gulf coast, authorities in Mobile reported numerous downed trees and power lines. Donald Trump approved an emergency declaration for Georgia after the president did the same for Florida and Alabama, allowing for federal aid. The US energy department authorized emergency exchanges of crude oil from the nation’s strategic petroleum reserve to address disruptions in supply because of the storm. The NWS said parts of Georgia and the Carolinas could see heavy rain capable of causing flash floods. Meanwhile, in the Pacific, Simon strengthened to 155mph (250km/h), only just below the threshold for becoming a category 5 storm, as it approached Mexico’s coast. Simon was expected to bring heavy rainfall beginning on Sunday to parts of south-western Mexico with life-threatening flooding and mudslides. Forecasters say that conditions brought by Simon are spreading northward along a stretch of coastline that includes Puerto Vallarta. Rain could average 8-16in over sectors of south-western Mexico, with as much as 30in possible in places across Michoacán, Colima and Jalisco through Monday. A woman, a man and their dog in Burke county, North Carolina, were rescued on the Catawba River after their camping trip was overflown by the rising water brought by remnants of Simon that caught them off guard. Tropical Storm Rachel was also expected to bring heavy winds and rain to northern Mexico and southern California. The National Weather Service has issued a flash flood warning in parts of San Diego, Riverside and Imperial counties. Officials issued mandatory evacuation orders for some residents in the Long Beach peninsula through Tuesday. Eight buildings have been red-tagged, or deemed unsafe to enter, and one has been yellow-tagged amid conditions from Rachel. Long Beach officials have provided about 11,000 sandbags for the storm to protect homes from the rising tide.

title: Houthi attack on Riyadh airport forces swift rethink of Trump’s new strategy
summary: US president’s plan to park the wars in Iran and Yemen, while blaming Ukraine for diesel prices, looks unsustainable
text: The reckless missile attack on King Khalid international airport in Riyadh on Saturday did not just export the death and misery inside Yemen to Saudi Arabia, it also left Donald Trump forced to reconsider his diplomatic and political strategy designed to take him into the midterm elections next month. The US president’s plan had only been unveiled on Friday. He said it was the result of “a world problem” – spiralling diesel prices – which he blamed on Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s attacks on Russian oil refineries. He was going to keep the political temperature down on his war of choice in Iran and its spillover in Yemen until after the midterms. In pursuit of this strategy, he claimed the Iranian blockade in the strait of Hormuz was in effect broken, producing figures on daily oil barrel exports to assuage the markets. As a further insurance he also claimed it was impossible to negotiate with the Iranians since there was no single leadership in Tehran. Saudi Arabia, in conjunction with Turkey, and Pakistan, were largely to be left to sort out the Houthis along the Red Sea. The fate of Yemen, the poorest country in the world according to the International Monetary Fund, was not going to shift votes in Kansas or Alaska. Now, after the Riyadh airport attack, it is doubtful, for a basket of reasons, that this anyway threadbare strategy, largely born of desperation, can hold. For all the talk of the Gulf becoming responsible for its own security, it is doubtful that Saudi Arabia can be left to fend for itself after the carnage in Riyadh. One of the the 12 dead is an American and there may be more among the severely injured. Something is clearly wrong with Saudi defences since the Houthis are firing rockets from 500 miles away, and they are reaching their target too often. The US has had a unilateral ceasefire with the Houthis since 2025, and once the hostilities between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis recommenced in the summer, the pact was quietly renewed. Trump has twice rejected Saudi appeals for help. Can he spurn them three times? The pressure to act as allies are expected to may prove overwhelming. But “the blame Zelenskyy, trade with Russia” strategy is anyway unlikely to work. The amount of additional diesel Vladimir Putin will put on the market is not enough to bring down prices at the pump. Russia accounted for about 12% of global diesel shipped by sea. Exports have fallen by about a third, according to calculations by the Center for Research on Energy and Clean Air. The deal has also reawakened Europe’s worst fears about Trump’s relationship with Russia only weeks after Congress had passed a sanctions package against Moscow authorising Trump to penalise buyers of Russian energy. Europeans know full well that the inflation problem helping to drive populism is caused by the Iran war and not by Zelenskyy’s tactics. The only question is who will say so. The former UK Conservative prime minister Boris Johnson did not hold back, writing: “It is sickening that the USA is now lifting sanctions on Russian fuel, and transparently ridiculous to blame Ukraine for the spike in prices that obviously began with the closure of the strait of Hormuz. Putin is murdering innocent Ukrainian civilians every day. The Ukrainians are fighting for their lives. And yet the White House is apparently determined to force American drivers to bankroll Putin’s slaughter.” The German education minister and a member of the CDU, Karin Prien, said: “For a few litres of diesel. What moral bankruptcy.” Mark Rutte, the Nato secretary general and Trump ally, will this week travel to Estonia, one of the countries most supportive of Ukraine. He will have some explaining to do. Estonia’s foreign minister, Margus Tsahkna, vowed that EU foreign ministers on Monday will impose the biggest package of sanctions in its history, and he, along with Sweden, now wants to revisit using frozen Russian assets to help Ukraine. What is worse, it looks as if the political damage to the Republicans caused by the Iran war is irrecoverable. Polls show the ship has sailed. The war has already been weaponised as a pocketbook issue by every Democratic candidate in every TV debate. Republican candidates, challenged to disown the war, are scrambling for the relative safety of identity politics. The Iranians are also trying to maximise the damage they cause in the strait of Hormuz, countering the Trump narrative that the blockade has been broken. Scenes of tankers on fire are proliferating. So Trump post-Riyadh needs to rethink. He can rejoin the war against the Houthis, ending the unilateral US ceasefire, but, if so, he knows from experience this will be costly. The first three weeks of the war against Iran cost $1bn a day. Many of the US president’s advisers say he may as well also attack Iran, the Houthis’ backers, as Tehran expects him to do. The Iranian military nevertheless still believes it has escalation dominance, and what happened in Riyadh can be repeated across the Gulf. The alternative is that his team can negotiate discreetly and indirectly with Tehran as is occurring in Doha. Some Iranians are urging their leadership to seize the chance, arguing Trump is uniquely vulnerable in the run-up to the midterms. A deal could be done, including on uranium enrichment, but it would not be palatable for the US – or for the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu’s re-election chances. China and Russia are trying to sort out the Houthis diplomatically, but the Houthi objectives are broadening, while the south of Yemen is split about its future inside the country, a division that harms the country’s ability to be the ground component that Saudi Arabia needs to supplement its air-power dominance. Taiz, the third city of Yemen, is struggling to overcome a Houthi siege. The Saudis can deliver retribution, but retribution is not a solution to a decade-long civil war. So for the moment the twin Trump strategy – to park the Iran and Yemen conflicts while blaming Zelenskyy – is now so transparent, so morally craven, and in its own terms so ineffective, that it looks unsustainable. The only question is whether the strategy will be jettisoned by the president or instead just rejected by the American people at the ballot box.

title: ‘Cockroach’ party leaders say India is ‘at war with its citizens’ as protests enter second day
summary: CJP leaders say Modi’s government is creating ‘atmosphere of fear’ after they were among thousands detained on Saturday
text: The leaders of India’s Cockroach movement accused the Narendra Modi government of declaring “war with its own citizens” and vowed to continue with their protest after being released from police detention, as anti-government unrest rocked Delhi for a second day. The three leaders of the youth-led Cockroach Janta party (CJP) were taken into custody on Saturday when thousands were detained by police as authorities went to extreme lengths to prevent young people taking to the streets to protest. By Sunday morning, a magistrate had ordered that the three CJP leaders, Abhijit Dipke, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, be released on the condition that they would not “breach peace” for a year. In a social media post soon after his release, Dipke, CJP’s founder, pointed his criticism directly at the prime minister. “Modi, as PM, is an embarrassment to India. Never has this country seen a bigger coward and bully,” he said. Saturday’s protest was called by the CJP alongside student groups and civil society leaders to demand the resignation of India’s election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, who is accused of an “assault on democracy” by overseeing an exercise that has deleted 130 million names from India’s electoral roll. Kumar is accused of implementing the voter roll revision to help Modi’s ruling Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) entrench its power and to disenfranchise minority groups such as Muslims who are not traditionally part of the BJP’s voter base. Those who attempted to take part in Saturday’s demonstration were ruthlessly obstructed by a security crackdown, in which more than 25,000 police barricaded roads and the internet and public transport were shut down. More than 7,000 people were taken into police custody, many before they had even reached the protest site in the centre of the capital. Despite the heavy-handed police response, it was still an unprecedented display of dissent against the powerful Modi government, which has been notoriously intolerant of any political opposition or criticism over its 12 years in power. Several senior opposition leaders were among those who tried to protest and were detained. By Sunday, the centre of Delhi still resembled a high-security fortress, with roads blocked by barricades and tens of thousands of police and paramilitary still deployed. Supreme court judges have ruled that the government must restore internet and reopen the capital’s metro stations. Small groups of students and Cockroach supporters, many freshly released from police detention, again attempted to demonstrate in Delhi and were detained. Among those taken into custody for a second time was the student leader Neha Bora, whose repeated defiance in the face of the police crackdown has made them a figurehead of the movement. In a video they posted on social media after they were picked up by Delhi police, Bora showed a detention bus with metal grilles over its windows and four small “jail-like” compartments secured with latches. They said six to eight protesters were crammed into each of the compartments, leaving little room to breathe, and that male protesters were subjected to verbal abuse and physical violence. “So many troops, so much police presence, so much violence, abuses targeting mothers and sisters, caste-based slurs – why?” Bora said in the video. “Simply because you want to protect a thief, Gyanesh Kumar.” Marching alongside Bora was Surbi Yadav, 20, an undergraduate student at Delhi University, who said police detained her on Saturday morning. She accused police personnel of dragging her, injuring her arm and leg. “They treated us like animals. They pushed us into a bus and took us to a sports facility that had been turned into a detention centre,” Yadav said, while showing scars on her arms. “The police kept misbehaving with us on the way and warned us against taking part in the protests.” Yadav was released on Saturday evening. By Sunday afternoon, she was back on the streets with other students, holding a placard. She vowed to return the following day and keep protesting until their demands were met. “We are not afraid any more. The government and the police will have to understand that,” she said. “They can use as much force as they want to silence us, but it will be futile. In fact, it will only backfire. Every day, more people are turning against this government because of the way it is treating protesters.” At a press conference on Sunday afternoon, the CJP leaders Das and Ranka condemned the police and government for turning Delhi into a “war-like situation” and reiterated their message of defiance that “this fight is on”. They added that it was no longer just about Kumar but also targeted at Modi and his home minister, Amit Shah. “The state is at war with its own citizens,” Das said. “An atmosphere of fear has been created in country, it’s clearly being done to save one person. We want to ask Modi and Shah, why are you trying to save Gyanesh Kumar?” There was no response from Modi to the accusations by the protesters. However, the BJP’s spokesperson, Gaurav Bhatia, said earlier that the voter roll revision was a legitimate exercise to remove dead and illegal voters and refuted any political interference. “These are baseless allegations being levelled by an irresponsible opposition,” Bhatia said. “The claim that democracy is being destroyed and that the constitution is being undermined has no basis and not an iota of evidence.” The weekend’s protests had drawn support from the leader of India’s opposition alliance, Rahul Gandhi, who has accused the Modi government of “vote chauri” or vote cheating through the voter roll revision. Gandhi was detained twice last week as opposition parties attempted to hold a protest in central Delhi calling for Kumar to resign. “Mr Modi does not understand that the game is over,” Gandhi said on Saturday. “We will ensure that Modi pays for the crimes he has committed against the country.” • This article was amended on 13 October 2026 to correct the pronouns used by Neha Bora.

title: Fans hope to save ‘tartan fortress’ where Scotland football team first played
summary: Part of site of First Hampden in Glasgow is up for rent and campaigners want to turn it into a community hub
text: Fans of Scotland’s national football team may not have had many reasons to celebrate in recent years, but that hasn’t always been the case. Almost 150 years ago, in 1878, the team moved into their first home in a Glasgow ground known as First Hampden and promptly won every game they played there. As well as being celebrated as Scotland’s “tartan fortress”, First Hampden, about half a mile from where Hampden Park sits today in south Glasgow, is widely considered the world’s first purpose-built international football stadium. Many features now commonplace in grounds around the world – including season tickets, turnstiles and pavilions – have long been thought to have originated there. Now, a campaign has been launched to safeguard the site and turn it into a community hub and heritage space after it was put on the market when the previous tenant, a bowling club, closed its doors earlier this year. “We want to see it become a multifunctional community space,” says Calum Cameron, 37, one of the founding members of First Hampden community interest company (CIC). “Somewhere vibrant and usable for the community but that also upholds and develops this amazing footballing history through storytelling and heritage.” Before becoming the national ground, First Hampden was home to Queen’s Park FC, who are also credited with inventing many features of the modern game, including the passing style of play, as opposed to a more rugby-like kick-and-charge approach that was common at the time. A key generation of players nicknamed the “Scotch professors” went on to export the invention around the country and the world, including to nations such as Brazil that dominate the international game today. A striking black-and-white mural on the back of what was previously Hampden Bowling Club on the site commemorates a famous 5-1 victory over England in 1882 and depicts the then national team captain, Andrew Watson, the first Black international footballer. “There are all these little pieces of social history and I think there’s more to be uncovered,” Cameron says. “When you start talking to people about the site, there are so many stories and connections that come out – but a lot of people don’t know it is even here, which I hope will start to change as we do this work.” Today, there is little visible evidence of the original structure, but a 2021 excavation by Historic Environment Scotland uncovered remains of the pavilion, earning one part of the site, which now exists as a small public park, protected status as a national monument. The section up for rent, comprising the former bowling club building and lawn, sits on the other side of a fence and is not covered by the protection. The footprint of First Hampden is one of 21 historic footballing sites in the south of Glasgow that have been curated into Football’s Square Mile, a project set up to promote and celebrate the nation’s footballing heritage. While the legends of First Hampden have been passed down in folklore for generations, it was Football’s Square Mile’s engagement director, Graeme Brown, who proved its existence once and for all in 2017, through archival railway maps. “[First Hampden] is arguably the world’s most important football heritage site,” Brown says. “And you can just come and stand on it – you don’t need to go to a museum and pay an entry fee. You can come and stand on [what was] the pitch and say: ‘This is where Scotland played.’ “It always makes me tingle to walk around this area. You can kind of feel the ghosts of First Hampden all around you.” Attempts by First Hampden CIC to acquire the site have so far been unsuccessful, with a request for a community asset transfer rejected by the owners, City Property Glasgow, an arm’s-length company owned by the council. A spokesperson for the company said it was “obliged to obtain commercially reasonable terms for the sale and lease of our assets” and that the site was considered to have income-generating potential. They said there was no intention to sell for redevelopment and that bids would be assessed “on their individual merits, including but not limited to community benefits, heritage consideration, deliverability and financial value”. First Hampden CIC is exploring other options, Cameron says, including a full feasibility study and community consultation for its plans, and submitting an official bid through the lease process. So far, almost 1,000 people have signed up online to show their support. Cameron has become a bigger football fan since living in the area and learning more about its rich footballing history. But he says the campaign is about more than just sport. “Affordable, accessible public spaces are becoming fewer and further between in Glasgow and in general, and this is another that’s at risk of being lost,” he says. “We need places where people can come together. The city’s slogan is ‘people make Glasgow’, so let’s give those people places to go.”

title: There’s more to our music than Oasis, says Manchester mayor
summary: Bev Craig pledges £2m in funding to nurture local artists by improving access to rehearsal and production space
text: The Manchester mayor, Bev Craig, has said the city’s music scene is about more than just Oasis, as she announced funding to nurture a diverse range of local artists, be they “guitar bands or not”. Craig pledged the £2m investment funding in Greater Manchester, as the city region hosted a conference for the creative industries at MediaCity in Salford. She said there was a “real intentionality” to what Manchester was doing, in terms of growing its own music industry and attracting international events. Earlier this year, Manchester’s Co-op Live arena hosted the Brit awards and the Mobos, Europe’s biggest and most influential celebration of Black music and culture. “I wanted to have a major event that celebrated black music, culture and creativity,” Craig said, “and so that’s why we said, just after the Brits, we’d host their 30th anniversary, because we knew it would be the last one that the Mobos founder Kanya would be able to come to.” “I think there’s a real intentionality around what we’re doing with our music scene,” she added. “We’re known, I think, over the world for the influence that some of our indie guitar bands have had on Greater Manchester music, but there’s more to Greater Manchester’s music scene than just Oasis.” “I’m struck by the diversity, the creativity, the talent that we see,” Craig said. “And the job, as I see it, is making sure that that next generation of talent in an industry that’s becoming more and more middle-class, more and more London-centric, and a world where it’s more and more expensive to be able to break through, that we’re giving our local artists the hand up that they need to be able to be the next big thing, guitar band or not.” Addressing Beyond the Music’s creative industries AI summit on Friday, Craig set out her plan for diversifying opportunities in the music industry. She also outlined commitments to support AI literacy for music professionals, and to monitor the impact of new technologies on employment, income and diversity in Greater Manchester’s music sector. The festival that accompanied the summit featured performances from up-and-coming black and minority ethnic artists including Bawo, JayaHadADream and Alt Blk Era. The final day of the conference was convened by the prime minister, Andy Burnham, whose love of Manchester guitar bands is well known. The culture minister Ian Murray told the conference: “With a prime minister who picks up his guitar to murder Smiths tracks, we have a passion from the very top. He added, joking: “That’s probably a career-limiting sentence for me.” “We’re living and working at a time of considerable change, particularly with technology,” Murray said, “but the future of creativity will not be shaped by technology alone. It will be shaped by the choices we make today, and how we support talent, how we reward creativity and how we embrace that innovation.” The £2m of funding Craig has set out is in addition to the £4m Culture Fund investment announced earlier this month, which will fund music projects from grassroots venues to world-renowned institutions. The additional funding is aimed at improving access to rehearsal and production space across the city region, providing practical support and ensuring there are jobs for musicians in their communities. Although the Manchester music scene may be about more than Oasis, the newly elected Manchester mayor did say she would be going to see the band on their sellout tour next year, which includes 11 nights at Manchester City’s Etihad Stadium. “I will, and thankfully the price of pints are much too expensive and the clientele have aged [which] means that you’re not as cautious as to what’s travelling through the air as historically you once would [be],” she said. But she added that “as somebody who loves all forms of music” she was “as excited about seeing [Merseyside band] the Ks at Beyond the Music as I am about seeing Oasis”. “I’m a little bit more into my dance music than the previous mayor as well,” Craig added. “So maybe a bit more varied in my tastes, shall we say.”

title: Is there a different way to fix the small boats crisis?
summary: As ‘one in, one out’ scheme ends, refugees still want to cross the Channel despite French police aggression and hostile welcomes
text: The smuggler works quickly. Using a small shovel, he digs up a dinghy buried in a sand dune on a beach not far from Boulogne-sur-Mer, assembles it and affixes a motor in record time. “I never saw anyone work like this,” says Amad, from Iraq, one of a group of about 30 asylum seekers waiting to cross the Channel. “The UK government wants to stop the smugglers, but they are smart. They have plan A, plan B and plan C, so there is always a way for them to get people across this sea. For as long as asylum seekers will pay them, there is too much money involved for them to give up.” The wind has dropped, the waves are flat and there are no French police in sight. The conditions are perfect as the smuggler rushes everyone into the dinghy as it moves away from the shore. Amad is one of several asylum speakers who spoke to the Guardian this week from the area of northern France known as the Jungle. They were hoping to cross the Channel to the UK in the next few days. “This place is busier than ever,” says another asylum seeker, Omar, from Yemen. “So many refugees and so many smugglers are here. Everyone wants to cross.” Some who have already been forcibly removed from the UK are hoping to return. They were sent to France under the “one in, one out” scheme, where one small-boat arrival is forcibly returned to France in exchange for another asylum seeker brought legally to the UK. Now, after moving approximately 1,500 people in both directions across the Channel, the scheme has been brought to an end. Beset with problems, it could not be effectively scaled up, the British government concluded. NGOs working on the ground with asylum seekers in northern France were unsurprised by the outcome and say the end of “one in, one out” must prompt a wider discussion about how to deal with the crisis in the Channel. The UK government has shown little sign it is contemplating a radical shift in attitude. A Home Office spokesperson pointed the Guardian to an announcement about a refugee resettlement scheme that is likely to assist only a few hundred refugees a year and is highly unlikely to stop people crossing the Channel in small boats. The spokesperson said: “Just last week, the home secretary announced the reopening of the UK resettlement scheme for new referrals, providing genuine refugees with a safe and legal route to the UK.” The agencies calling for a different approach hope at least to expand the parameters of the debate. According to workers in the Jungle, living conditions there are appalling. Those at Utopia 56, which witnesses police interventions on French beaches where asylum seekers try to board dinghies, say that since the UK increased its funding to France earlier this year on a payment-by-results basis, police violence against migrants has increased significantly. Utopia 56 estimates a 40% increase in police violence from April to August 2026 compared with the same period the previous year. That coincided with an agreement for the UK to pay France £660m over three years to ramp up “stop the boats” initiatives. Sophie McCann, of Médecins Sans Frontières UK, said: “The government’s increasingly brutal efforts to stop people trying to reach the UK by boat are failing. MSF’s medical and mental health teams in Calais and Dunkirk witness the serious physical and psychological harm caused by violence and harassment meted out by French police, largely funded by the UK, on people who have already fled war, persecution and extreme hardship. “People will continue to risk their lives crossing the Channel in search of safety in the UK until the government provides safe and accessible routes.” The Public and Commercial Services (PCS) union, which has many Home Office staff among its members, has worked with the refugee charity Care4Calais to draw up a blueprint to introduce a refugee visa-to-travel scheme for asylum seekers to travel legally to the UK. The plan would still require asylum claims to be considered on merit and for those whose claims are rejected to be removed from the UK. But they say it would eliminate people smugglers from the equation and save lives. According to the UN’s International Organization for Migration (IOM), at least 225 people have died while trying to cross the Channel since 2018. The scheme would be unlikely to halt irregular arrivals entirely, but Care4Calais says it could dent the smugglers’ business in a way that other initiatives have failed to do. Charlotte Khan, of Care4Calais, said: “Consecutive governments have focused on border security measures that have only made Channel crossings more dangerous, resulting in a shocking number of lives lost, while completely ignoring the only solution that will work – safe routes.” The PCS general secretary, Fran Heathcote, called for safe routes to be significantly scaled up. “Our members deal with the human impact of the asylum system on a daily basis and their voices must be heard. The only way to truly undermine criminal smuggling gangs is to remove the demand through a Ukrainian-style visa system, allowing people fleeing war and persecution to travel safely and legally to claim asylum.” The Labour government has arguably made more efforts than any other to try to prevent asylum seekers from reaching the UK in small boats. Previously, people travelled less visibly, in the backs of lorries or on planes, and so attracted less public attention. Images of black dinghies overcrowded with people in orange lifejackets, monetised for social media clicks by far-right agitators, have generated mounting hostility from some who say they are evidence that the government has lost control of its borders. But desperate people continue to clamber into dinghies. In the six days between 2 and 7 October, 1,739 people arrived in 23 boats. Along with the now terminated “one in, one out” pilot, which government trumpeted as “groundbreaking” when it announced it in July 2025, the Home Office and the National Crime Agency make regular announcements about smugglers being intercepted and dinghies seized “upstream”. There has been a reduction of more than 40% in small boat arrivals so far this year compared with the same period last year, probably due to a combination of UK government initiatives, windy weather and a drop in irregular migration to Europe overall. According to data published by the IOM, there has been a 39% reduction this year in these arrivals to Europe – from 98,040 during the same period last year to approximately 60,000. Despite the reduction in arrivals, far-right agitators wearing masks and black paramilitary clothing continue to protest on the streets and try to block small boat arrivals. None of the policy roadblocks appear to have dented the resolve of asylum seekers who want to reach the UK. Sohrab, from Afghanistan, has been sleeping on the streets of Paris and is making his way to the Jungle. “I want to live and I will do anything to save my life from death,” he says. “I have already spent a bad day in jail in France after police caught me trying to get into a lorry heading for the UK. The smugglers are very violent, but there is no other way for me to reach the UK apart than to go to the Jungle.” Despite the failure of “one in, one out” to deter small boat crossings, Emily Graham, of the Future Governance Forum, believes it is the way forward. “The ‘one-in, one-out’ pilot proved cooperation based on responsibility-sharing is right in principle and has the potential to deliver results,” she said. “To reduce the number of people arriving by small boat, the government should build on the previous pilot and seek a new ‘routes for returns’ deal with European partners.” Amad has another idea. “We would much prefer to give our money to the UK government if they allowed us to come here legally, rather than to the smugglers,” he says. “No asylum seeker would pay smugglers who beat and exploit them, or risk our lives on a dinghy, if there was another way.”

title: Why a Chilean salt flat is a microcosm of the extractive frontiers of green capitalism
summary: In the Atacama desert, the extraction of lithium – so crucial to addressing the climate crisis – comes with escalating social and environmental costs
text: A high-altitude desert plateau traverses Argentina, Bolivia and Chile. I am on the Chilean side, sitting in a Jeep along with two other researchers. The afternoon air is thin and brisk but the sun is piercing – a combination I am familiar with from years of living and travelling in South America’s Andean range. The landscape is a study in contrasts and contours: broad basins suddenly cut off by sweeping curves; flat expanses sliced by near vertical ascents. The Licancabur volcano looms large above us. Vegetation and humidity levels change rapidly with the rising altitude, bringing cooler temperatures, wetter air and denser plant life. We are driving to the Salar de Atacama – the Atacama salt flats – the largest of several dozen salt flats in northern Chile, and the third largest in the world. The brilliant white flat lies in a high basin 7,500ft above sea level, enclosed by the even higher Andean mountains to the east and the Domeyko mountains to the west. This striking landscape – the salt flat, the flamingos, and the neighbouring Indigenous communities – is under threat from a counterintuitive source: our efforts to save the planet from catastrophic climate change. Just beneath my feet is nearly one-quarter of the world’s lithium reserves, suspended in water saltier than the ocean. Lithium is essential to addressing the climate crisis. It is a key ingredient in the rechargeable batteries that play a starring role in eliminating carbon emissions from transportation and energy – the two highest emitting sectors. But extracting this lithium will come at escalating social and environmental costs. It is this dilemma that has brought me to the salt flat. When it does rain in the Atacama, it’s hard to overstate the intensity of the floods. I once found myself caught in what is called invierno boliviano, or Bolivian winter, a paradoxical name for a weather phenomenon that occurs during the southern hemisphere’s summer months. These rainy fronts originate in the Amazon and travel up the steep slopes of the Andean mountains, where Bolivia’s high-altitude winds then drive them up and over the ridges, until their torrents drench the Chilean high plateau. The scientific term for closed basins like the Atacama is “endorheic” (etymologically, “inside” and “flow”), for water can flow down into the Atacama basin but it cannot leave – except by evaporation. And this is the key to Atacama’s extraordinary lithium brine. After deluges like the one I experienced, water pours down the surrounding mountains; during the long dry spells between storms, it trickles down ravines from the precious mountain springs. As it flows, the water leaches lithium from the volcanic rock, picks up wind-scoured lithium dust, and carries it down to the nucleus, or centre, of the salar. This pooled surface water can only escape through evaporation, and with every drop of water that evaporates, the concentration of lithium in the remaining brine increases. Without the parched and sun-blasted Atacama’s extraordinarily high evaporation rate, lithium concentrations would not reach the “economical” levels prized by mining companies. Yet further lithium enrichment takes place out of sight. Remaining water gradually seeps into the ground, creating underground wells of lithium-rich brine. These wells are linked to complex hydrothermal systems. Then the heat of magma, especially near the Andes’ active fault lines, drives circulations of subsurface brine through fissures and porous geological strata, dissolving even more lithium out of the subsurface rock. The resulting brine deposits anywhere from four to 200 feet below the Atacama’s salty crust represent a potential bonanza to corporations. The Atacama’s singular coincidence of climatic, geological, geothermal and hydrological conditions makes it one of the least expensive places on Earth to mine lithium. And at each step, the process of “mining water” is intimately related to the very environmental conditions that formed the valuable deposits in the first place: miners pump the underground brine to vast evaporation ponds on the surface, where natural evaporation concentrates the brine yet again, increasing its lithium levels 40-fold, from approximately 0.15% to a whopping 6%. One cycle of the process can take 10 to 24 months, depending on brine quality and weather conditions. But this relatively low-cost, low-tech and supposedly low-impact extractive process nonetheless imperils the species and communities that call the Atacama desert home. And it is a microcosm of a planetary phenomenon: the expanding extractive frontiers of green capitalism. Everywhere that mines are dug up to provide raw materials for the energy transition, global climate action comes into conflict with local environmental protection. Mining always transforms, in many ways irrevocably, the landscapes in which it occurs. In remaking the earth in the image of extractive capital, physically and chemically separating what is deemed valuable from often toxic waste, mining evokes the image of terraforming so central to science fiction. But if terraforming is supposed to make a lifeless planet as verdant as Earth, mining, to the contrary, often leaves parts of Earth itself uninhabitable. While the environmental impacts of mining brine are less obvious to the naked eye than, say, mountaintop removal, extracting the lithium-rich liquid does in fact threaten a fragile, desert water system, along with the ecosystems and people that depend on it. The world’s oldest, driest desert may appear bereft of life. Ecologists call it a “polyextreme” environment, given its altitude and high direct solar radiation, its intense aridity, its huge diurnal temperature swings and its densely saline lakes. Those who study such polyextreme environments alternately describe them as low-diversity, with relatively simple webs of life, or astonishing in their biodiversity. It all depends on perspective. Plants and animals have evolved to make do with less and saltier water and, above all, the abundant energy of relentless sun. Extremity stimulates nature’s creativity. Artemia, or brine shrimp, thrive in hypersaline lakes that would be intolerable to most species. These tiny creatures are a key node in the plateau’s food chain. The brine shrimp eat bacteria and phytoplankton (microscopic plants) and are, in turn, food for Chilean flamingos. The flamingos, too, have adapted to the saline lagoons, evolving a filter in their bills akin to the lamellar membranes of oysters or whales to strain the microscopic plants and animals from the brine. The flamingos are a barometer of wetland health. As the birds travel the salt flats in search of food and mates (attracted through a courtship ritual of synchronised dancing), they link together the saline lakes into a web of habitats. And as these habitats suffer, so do flamingo populations: all three of the Atacama salt flats’ endemic flamingo species are in decline. The distinct drivers of this population loss reveal the compounding harms afflicting this fragile environment. Warmer average temperatures due to climate change evaporate surface water faster, reducing the blue-green algae essential to flamingo and Artemia diets. And the noise and traffic associated with mining operations appear to directly disrupt the flamingos’ breeding. Researchers are struggling to predict the overall direction of the multiple processes changing the Atacama. Science can only play catchup, documenting the impacts long after the harm has occurred. Lithium extraction’s threat to the liquid supporting its ecosystem is a slow-motion disaster, with planetary causes and consequences. This fact raises existential questions for the planet’s zero-carbon future. In the Atacama, global supply chains intersect with local food chains, webs of economic production undermine webs of life, and colonisation and postcolonial state-building erase ancient histories of continuous Indigenous settlement. And these unexpected entanglements are just the beginning of the story. In more ways than I could have imagined when I first stepped foot on the Atacama salt flat on that blustery day, this extractive frontier is a portal into our planetary future. The task of achieving a globally just energy transition is daunting. But it is possible. Achieving it requires understanding supply chains in reverse, starting from what we produce and consume and working backwards to their material inputs and, further still, to the relentless scramble for new extractive frontiers. Policies that promote alternatives to car use, reduce sprawl, encourage more compact batteries and require recycling would all reduce the scale of mining needed for carbon-free transportation. We can start by demanding supply chains organised around justice for everyone they touch, rather than profits for just a few. Just as any workplace is simultaneously a site of exploitation and locus of worker power, and any mine is at once a setting for extraction and a potential scene of community resistance, the supply chains of green technologies are both a means of domination – of people and of nature – and fertile ground for making the world anew. This is an edited extract from Extraction: The Frontiers of Green Capitalism by Thea Riofrancos, published by Icon Books at £20 in the UK. title: US maternity wards face wave of closures as Medicaid cuts kick in
summary: Trump’s ‘big, beautiful bill’ spending cuts will be fully felt next year, but hospitals are already feeling the squeeze
text: Maternity wards across the United States are facing a wave of closures as cuts to federal Medicaid funding take effect, experts have warned. According to analysis by the non-profit Protect Our Care, 52 maternity wards have closed since the HR1 bill was announced in July 2025, with a further eight having announced their upcoming closure. The bill, which will fully come into effect in the new year, will result in many adults covered through Medicaid having to meet new work requirements and being subject to more frequent eligibility checks, while there will be less federal funding for states for Medicaid. Hospitals which have already permanently closed their maternity wards include the Centra Southside Community hospital in Virginia and St Mary’s Sacred Heart hospital in rural north-east Georgia, which both cited upcoming federal policy changes to Medicaid as a reason. Experts are expecting to see more closures of maternity units in the run-up to and after the federal changes to Medicaid come into effect in the new year. “We’re deeply concerned that these changes already have and will continue to worsen an already serious maternity care crisis,” said Erin Jones, senior director of legislative and strategic counsel of the non-profit March of Dimes. “Reduced funding and restrictions on how states finance Medicaid will put additional pressure on state budgets and hospitals, increasing the risk that communities lose essential maternity services and specialized providers close to home.” She added that the consequences for maternity care would be particularly devastating within rural communities. The non-profit has identified 31 at-risk rural hospitals with labor and delivery services, with their possible closure leaving 96 counties without a labor and delivery unit. “Losing these services means fewer places to deliver safely and fewer options for pregnancies requiring specialized care,” Jones added. About 40% of births in the US are paid for by Medicaid, while the country has one of the highest maternal mortality rates among high-income nations, at a rate of 17.9 deaths per 100,000 live births, according to the latest Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) figures. Benjamin Sommers, a professor of healthcare economics at the Harvard TH Chan School of Public Health, said the changes to Medicaid would “absolutely” affect women who are pregnant and specialist pregnancy organizations. “It’s not true that this law in any way protects Medicaid for pregnant mothers, for low-income parents. It adds financial strain to the providers and the insurance program that they rely on,” he said. Sommers, who was deputy assistant secretary for health policy under Joe Biden, said although the new work requirements for Medicaid are supposed to exempt pregnant women, his research has shown that many women are not enrolled in the Medicaid pregnancy pathway, meaning the state might not know that they’re pregnant. He added: “Someone could be enrolled through Medicaid expansion, they could get pregnant and they could mistakenly think – because they heard it on the news that this law doesn’t affect pregnant people – [they’re] fine, and it turns out the state doesn’t know they’re pregnant and they lose coverage.” Vaishu Jawahar, director of policy and programs at Protect Our Care, added: “When you’re cutting Medicaid by a trillion dollars, you’re cutting this money from hospitals. So these hospitals are going into the red and being forced to make hard decisions, which usually results in maternity wards being closed as they are extremely expensive to run.” Meanwhile, in early 2025, the entirety of the CDC’s pregnancy risk assessment monitoring system team, which oversees a population-based surveillance system collecting data on women’s experiences before, during and after pregnancy, was placed on administrative leave by the Trump administration. According to an upcoming report authored by academics and former CDC staff, seen by the Guardian, these actions by the federal government disrupted the collection and management of “one of the nation’s most important sources of population-based information on pre-pregnancy, pregnancy, postpartum experiences, and maternal and infant health” which has existed for over four decades. “There are no other datasets like it. Teams like mine used to have access to this data before the portal was shut down, and so now there’s no way to study the more recent trends in maternal and infant health,” said Rita Hamad, professor of social epidemiology and public policy at the Harvard TH Chan School of Public Health and co-author of the report. “Now we’re very worried that the cuts to US safety net policies or barriers that keep people able to access those programmes are going to have detrimental effects on maternal and infant health.” She added: “I think we’re going to see those geographical and maternal disparities widening. Or we’re not going to see it because we don’t have the data, but that’s what is going to happen. The Department for Health and Human Services has been contacted by the Guardian.

title: Physicians’ group calls for ban on raw milk – as it’s becoming increasingly popular in the US
summary: As raw milk industry experiences record growth, experts say it might contain pathogens that can sicken people
text: As raw milk becomes increasingly popular among Americans, there have been several recent disease outbreaks tied to the product, alarming public health officials. Last week, the American Academy of Pediatrics called for a ban on sales of unpasteurized milk in the United States. More people have started drinking raw milk, doctors say, because of influencers who have touted its health benefits; Robert F Kennedy Jr, the US health secretary, who until recently promoted it; and a lack of trust in government regulators. But there is no evidence for claims that it reduces lactose issues and can cure allergies and boost immunity, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and public health groups argue. And whereas raw milk producers say that pasteurization eliminates flavor and health benefits, public health officials say it keeps people safe. “I’m concerned about people consuming raw milk because while it isn’t a guarantee that you will get sick from it, there is a relatively high likelihood that you can get a pathogen, a bacteria that will make you sick,” said Petra Levin, a professor of biology at Washington University. US businesses started using pasteurization, a process in which milk is heated to destroy pathogens and bacteria, in the late 19th century. As more producers adopted the practice and regulators started requiring it, the country saw a dramatic decrease in the infant mortality rate. In 1987, the FDA banned the interstate sale and distribution of raw milk, but businesses were still allowed to sell it within their states, depending on their laws. During this century, more Americans started consuming raw milk and, over the last decade, many states have loosened their milk regulations. In 2024, raw milk sales increased by 17.6%, according to the market research firm Circana. Before becoming the health and human services secretary, Kennedy said on stage that he only drinks raw milk and vowed that the “FDA’s war on public health is about to end”, including its “aggressive suppression” of raw milk. Once in office, he took a shot of raw milk with Dr Paul Saladino, a psychiatrist and author of The Carnivore Code – but to the dismay of some in the industry, Kennedy has now apparently stopped advocating for it. The Trump administration now instead promotes whole milk. Ben Beichler “fell in love” with milk cows while farming and, eventually, he and his wife started their own operation, Creambrook Farm, in Virginia. They now milk 150 cows and legally sell raw milk through a “herd share” loophole that allows consumers to buy a share of a cow. He describes the Covid-19 pandemic as a “massive gamechanger” for his business because people started thinking more about how they could protect themselves from getting sick. Plus, “for better or worse, I think there is a skepticism in society that didn’t exist pre-Covid, and people are willing to question things more than they used to. So that has made people question a lot of their dietary needs,” Beichler said. “I’m not necessarily saying that skepticism has been a good thing.” Since 2020, his sales have increased between 30% and 50% annually, he said. As evidence of raw milk’s benefits, Beichler and others point to studies such as a 2011 report in the Clinical & Experimental Allergy journal which stated that “consumption of farm milk may offer protection against asthma and allergy”. But the FDA states that advocates have misused the findings because about half of the farm milk in the study was boiled. Also, the authors stated that they could not evaluate the “effect of pasteurized vs raw milk consumption because no objective confirmation of the raw milk status of the farm milk samples was available”. “At this stage, consumption of raw farm milk cannot be recommended as a preventive measure,” the study authors stated. To ensure his milk is safe, Beichler said, his farm tests every batch at its laboratory and then sends samples to a third-party lab. He declined to provide its name but said he would provide it to customers who ask for it. His farm has only five-star reviews on Google. “An honest and wholesome family who can provide safe and nutrient dense milk to the many people who are drinking raw milk these days,” one review stated. Despite his belief in raw milk, Beichler said that “the consumer has to be judicious” about “where they are getting” it. This summer, more than 100 people became sick after consuming raw milk, and 11 were hospitalized, according to National Public Radio. An E coli outbreak this year in California, Florida and Texas was also linked to cheese from the country’s largest raw milk distributor, Raw Farm. Most of those who fell ill were children ages three and younger. Dr Brian Dawes, an infectious disease specialist at Stanford University, said raw milk is especially dangerous for children because “they have weaker immune systems, less overall physiological reserves, so when they get these infections, they tend to get much sicker”. He supports a ban on raw milk. He said he also thinks public health leaders “have our work cut out for us to really regain public trust in the systems that have worked for milk for over 100 years, keeping people safe”.
