title: Families of 9/11 victims await key ruling in New York as truther conference is held nearby
summary: Families say Saudi Arabia provided aid to hijackers while conspiracist conference casts doubt on official narrative
text: “It’s shocking to me that we are still fighting for justice,” said Terry Strada, national chair of 9/11 Families United, whose husband, Tom, a bond broker at Cantor Fitzgerald, was killed in the north tower of the World Trade Center 25 years ago last month. Strada began her odyssey toward justice in 2004, but last week in New York she and dozens of family members of those lost in the 9/11 terrorist attacks sensed they were closer to a US court hearing their case that Islamists gained influence in Saudi Arabia’s government and provided aid to at least two of the 19 hijackers. Should the three Manhattan justices reject a Saudi appeal calling for the case to be dismissed on the basis of sovereign immunity and, citing the Justice Against Sponsors of Terrorism Act, uphold a 2005 ruling, the case could finally come to court in the next year. The merits of the claims have not been adjudicated. But the direction of the second circuit court of appeals judges’ questions, Strada said, had given the families hope. “It really was a good day for us,” she said afterward. “The judges asked really meaningful questions and hammered the Saudi attorneys and didn’t let up. They weren’t buying what the Saudis were selling.” The case centers on the role of Omar al-Bayoumi, a Saudi national who helped find and guarantee lodgings in San Diego for the hijackers Nawaf al-Hazmi and Khalid al-Mihdhar more than a year before attacks. Both died when they flew American Airlines flight 77 into the Pentagon. All 59 people onboard the flight were killed, and 125 people died on the ground. Neither of the two hijackers qualified as pilots, and, according to the 9/11 Commission Report, they “were ill-prepared for a mission in the United States … Neither had spent any substantial time in the west, and neither spoke much, if any, English.” But, it continued, it was plausible that the two men, or the 9/11 mastermind Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, would have tried to identify a friendly contact in the US, and it was unlikely they would have come “without arranging to receive assistance from one or more individuals informed in advance of their arrival”. In 2012, an FBI report named Fahad al-Thumairy, a Saudi Islamic affairs official and imam of a Saudi-built King Fahd mosque in Culver City, California, as having worked with al-Bayoumi. The report named another Saudi embassy official, Mussaed Ahmed al-Jarrah, who allegedly had ordered al-Bayoumi and al-Thumairy to assist the hijackers, according to the report. The report has long been criticized by the 9/11 families. The commission did not have access to videos seized by UK police in the days after 9/11 that showed al-Bayoumi in Washington DC in which he referenced a “plan” or a sketch of an airplane in blue ink and a mathematical equation for flight path descent rates or what lawyers for the 9/11 families call a “flight planning diagram”. The case, if it now comes to court, turns on whether the assistance the hijackers received from al-Bayoumi and others in California was part of the al-Qaida plot. This is denied by all those accused. “It has never been the policy of Saudi Arabia to attack its ally, the United States,” said attorney Greg Rapawy, who is representing the Gulf state kingdom. He pointed out that there was “no finding of direction and control” and the attacks had been “compartmentalized even within al-Qaida”. He pointed to the commission’s conclusion that it found “no evidence that the Saudi government as an institution or senior Saudi officials individually funded” al-Qaida. “Saudi did not support violent jihad, condemned terror and opposed al-Qaida,” Rapaway said in court. Last month, in a break with 9/11 commemoration tradition, Strada said successive US administrations had “withheld evidence … broke promises, both public and private. It’s been one betrayal after another.” She called on Donald Trump to confront the Saudis: “Tell them that if they want to be friends with the USA they cannot continue to deny all of this.” Over the same September weekend, a four-day conspiracist conference was being held uptown. Turning the Tide: 9/11 25 Years Later set out to examine inconsistencies in official accounts of the attack and assert longstanding theories that the twin towers could not have collapsed merely from the impact of jetliners loaded with fuel. Susie Bowham, whose father had worked on the towers’ elevator electrical systems, said those attending the conference were “on a journey to justice and accountability”. Roger Waters, one of the co-founders of the band Pink Floyd, said 9/11 was not “a mystery” and “the narrative we were all sold after 9/11 is a huge lie, obviously”, and called the 911 report “a complete whitewash and everybody with an IQ above room temperature knows it”. The 9/11 families and the 9/11 conspiracists arrived at approximately the same place from different directions. But they are certainly not friends. “It’s bullshit,” said Robert Kobus, who lost his sister Debbie on 9/11. “It’s what people want to think. We have identified who supported the act. The conspiracy is: what happened to the evidence that didn’t make it to the 9/11 commission? Not anything else.” Strada said. “Every word that comes out of the conspiracy theorists’ mouths is an insult to those murdered on 9/11.” A ruling that allows the case to proceed could open up discovery into other potential al-Qaida cells in Florida, New Jersey, Virginia, Phoenix and Minnesota before 9/11. “Once we go back to court, we’re going to be able to fully investigate what happened,” said Brett Eagleson, who lost his father in the attacks, outside the court. Asked how long that could take, he added: “We’ve fought for 25 years so we’re not stopping anytime soon.” Much depends on how the appeals panel interprets the Justice Against Sponsors of Terrorism Act. The law, which narrows the scope of sovereign immunity, was introduced by the outgoing Texas senator John Cornyn in 2015 and was vetoed by Obama, but became law after the veto was overridden by Congress. Another question is what the al-Bayoumi videos could prove if the case ever gets to court. The official had left the US for Birmingham in the UK a year before the attacks took place. The then FBI director, Robert Mueller, told a joint panel of the Senate and House intelligence committees in September 2002 that the hijackers “contacted no known terrorist sympathizers” in the US. As the three appeals court justices wrapped up their questioning last week, Judge William Nardini said: “It’s a difficult case and we will take it under advisement.”

title: Rapid showers and no flushing toilets: drought pushes Lundy island to the brink
summary: A dry summer has left the Bristol Channel island critically short of water, forcing visitor caps and talk of evacuating its 28 residents
text: Tom Carr was peering up at the clouds scudding around the island of Lundy, 10 miles off the coast of north Devon. “That one’s definitely got rain in it,” he said. “The mainland will be wet at the moment. And look over at Wales – it’s getting a real soaking just now.” But above Lundy the sky was, stubbornly, blue. No significant rain has fallen here since the start of May, leading to perilously low water levels. Restrictions have been put in place, visitor numbers limited and there has been talk of the island – home to 28 people – being evacuated. “It’s been a challenge,” said Carr, a conservation farmer who looks after sheep, cattle and ponies. He has been here more than 20 years and reckons the combination of the climate emergency and the topography of the granite outcrop, which soars out of the Bristol Channel, is the problem. “Climate change is here, it’s happening. We’re having hotter, drier summers. And when the rain clouds do come in, they tend to split as the approach the island and we stay dry.” The three-mile long island, famed for its puffins and its pirate past, relies on rainwater and five boreholes. The biggest rain catchment area is in the south. From there – when it does rain – water tumbles down to a collection tank near the harbour. It is then pumped up to an array of tanks and a purification plant near the old lighthouse. The island manager, Matt Scantlebury, said a fortnight ago the tanks were at 13% capacity – only enough water to keep the island going for about a week. Tonnes of water was being brought over in 1,000 litre containers on the island boat, the MS Oldenburg, to top up the supply. The campsite, which is popular with climbers once the cliff-nesting seabirds have gone, was shut. The toilets at the island pub, the Marisco Tavern, were closed. Bath plugs in holiday lets – up to 110 people can stay here – were taken away and people were asked to think twice before flushing toilets. Happily, on the day the water reached its low point, the island received confirmation that the water in one of its freshwater pools – called Pondsbury – was of a good enough quality to be used. About 12,000 litres of water has been taken from there every day since and the levels are back up to 22.5%. But now the pond is starting to run dry. “And still no proper rain is forecast,” said Scantlebury. “We know we have to find ways of future proofing ourselves.” To that end, a new 300,000-litre water tank has been ordered. The idea of a desalination plant – seawater is one thing the island is not short of – has been suggested but Scantlebury said it would be expensive and would probably need more energy than the island was capable of producing. Tristan Howes, the island’s engineer, said finding ways of conserving the little water Lundy had was crucial. “A dripping tap can lose a lot of water,” he said. A broken pipe would be a disaster. Staff have got used not only to having a rapid shower but catching the water they use in a bucket and using it to flush the toilet. “It’s about being as efficient as we can.” Luckily, visitors to Lundy, which is owned by the National Trust and managed by the Landmark Trust, tend to be the sort who don’t mind a little bit of hardship. Michelle Phillips, an animal lover keen to see the island’s ponies, and her husband, Fred Bullinaria, arrived for a day trip with 1.6 litres of water, four Lucozades and a tube of hydration tablets in their backpacks. “I think that will keep us going,” she said. Vick and Ed Crane were staying on Lundy for a few days to celebrate their 10th wedding anniversary. They had bought wet wipes to limit their water usage. “We don’t mind roughing it,” said Vick. “That’s part of the Lundy experience. It’s an adventure.” The residents are positive, always looking for the bright side. Tara McEvoy-Wilding, assistant warden on the island, said some creatures had done well from the hot summer. “It’s been a good year for butterflies and moths.” And it has also been a good summer for the Lundy cabbage, a primitive brassica that grows only on the island. “It’s quite a pioneering species and likes dry bare ground where there isn’t much vegetation,” said McEvoy-Wilding. “Hundreds of tiny cabbage plants have started to establish in areas where they wouldn’t normally. So that’s positive, at least.” McEvoy-Wilding said residents had become accustomed to using less water. “You’re more mindful – you only have a short shower and you don’t always flush the toilet. In a way it’s not a bad thing. It makes you think about how much water you could be saving every day by just making very small changes.” But that doesn’t mean that McEvoy-Wilding is not hoping for rain. “It’s amazing how little rain we’ve had. We had one day in August when it rained for an hour. Absolutely torrential. I was caught in it and got drenched but the ground was so dry it just poured off the island. “I’ve got an allotment and it’s been hard to keep my vegetables alive. The pumpkins aren’t anywhere near as big as normal. Some nice, steady rain would be perfect.”

title: Burnham faces questions over push to scrap photo ID voting requirement
summary: Ministers reportedly seeking to halve time for Lords scrutiny of voting and donations changes amid election speculation
text: Andy Burnham is facing questions over plans to speed up sweeping changes to Britain’s electoral system amid speculation that some of his closest advisers are pressing for an early general election. Ministers reportedly want to at least halve the time available for peers to scrutinise legislation that would make it possible to vote without photographic identification, lower the voting age to 16 and tighten restrictions on political donations. According to the Sunday Telegraph, the government is seeking to reduce scrutiny of the representation of the people bill in the House of Lords from an anticipated 10 days to fewer than five, despite plans for further substantial amendments. The reports come days after Labour’s victory over the leader of the Green party of England and Wales, Zack Polanski, in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, as well as Burnham’s own recent win in Makerfield, which have fuelled discussion within the party about whether Burnham should call a general election in pursuit of a fresh mandate. The prime minister does not need to call an election before 2029 and has repeatedly ruled out an early poll. The new voting legislation, first introduced under the former prime minister Keir Starmer, would allow voters to use bank cards without photographs as proof of identity at polling stations, easing restrictions introduced by the Tories in 2022. The proposals follow longstanding concerns that the requirement to show photo ID when voting disproportionately affects young people, those on lower incomes and minority ethnic communities. Polling published by the Guardian after the last general election suggested 6.5% of minority ethnic voters surveyed had been turned away from a polling station at least once, compared with 2.5% of white voters. The Electoral Commission separately estimated that about 16,000 people who attempted to vote in person were unable to do so because they lacked the required ID, and did not return. Burnham was among seven Labour mayors who criticised the restrictions in 2024, comparing them to voter suppression tactics used by Republicans in the US, and describing the changes as a “brazen assault on our democracy”. Although Labour opposed the introduction of compulsory photo ID for voting, Starmer’s government stopped short of abolishing the requirement after taking office, instead proposing to widen the forms of ID accepted at polling stations. However, the Electoral Commission has warned that accepting bank cards would make it harder for polling station staff to verify voters’ identities. The bill also forms part of the government’s efforts to tighten political funding rules amid growing concerns about foreign interference in British elections. The Guardian revealed that ministers were planning further restrictions on political donations that could retrospectively affect the £72m given to Reform UK by the crypto billionaires Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne. Labour MPs and trade unions have been calling for tougher safeguards against foreign donations, with some urging the government to go further by introducing limits on the amounts wealthy individuals can give to parties. A government spokesperson said: “The bill is going through the proper parliamentary process, giving MPs and peers the time and opportunity to examine and debate its measures. These reforms will strengthen our democracy and ensure the electoral system remains secure, fair and accessible.” The spokesperson added: “The PM has ruled out an early election.” Ministers argue the existing rules risk preventing legitimate voters from casting their ballots. Electoral Commission research found that about 4% of people who did not vote at the 2024 general election said the photo ID requirement had been a factor. But the watchdog also says Tory peers have accused ministers of attempting to rush through changes, while the Liberal Democrat peer Mark Pack warned about the risks of introducing significant amendments without sufficient scrutiny.

title: ‘Deeply concerning’: Democratic congressional candidate rebukes ICE’s presence in New York
summary: Darializa Avila Chevalier criticizes NYPD’s ‘inaction’ in protecting Marble Hill protesters after ICE shot a man
text: Democratic congressional candidate Darializa Avila Chevalier believes that the New York police departments’ conduct towards protesters after an ICE agent shot and wounded a man in the district she is running to represent violated “the spirit, if not the letter” of the city’s sanctuary laws. These rules ban local police from helping federal immigration authorities in civil immigration enforcement operations. Protests broke out in Manhattan’s Marble Hill neighborhood after a federal Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent shot Oscar Belgal, a 28-year-old Dominican man, while he was sitting in his car with a five-year-old in the backseat. The child was physically unharmed, and Belgal was taken to the hospital. He was reported as being in stable condition, before ICE reportedly took him into custody again. The Department of Homeland Security has said Belgal was undocumented. During Thursday night’s demonstration, which drew a few hundred New Yorkers, including Avila Chevalier, the NYPD set up barricades and clashed with protesters who were demanding ICE leave their neighborhood. Police had also helped carry Belgal to an unmarked car, where they laid him in the backseat while he was still handcuffed. Jessica Tisch, the New York City police commissioner, said during a Thursday press conference that the NYPD was not involved in the federal immigration operation prior to the shooting. Tisch said officers arrived for the purpose of preserving evidence. She also referred to Belgal’s previous criminal record during the event. Avila Chevalier said in a phone interview on Friday that the police commissioner’s mention of Belgal’s prior arrests unfairly villainized him and “showed that Tisch was more interested in peddling the narrative of the Trump administration than in upholding sanctuary policies”. The NYPD said in a statement that they always provide such information, and that many news outlets had asked about Belgal’s criminal history. Avila Chevalier also said the police’s “inaction” in protecting protesters was a failure to uphold the spirit of the city’s sanctuary laws. She wrote on X earlier on Friday: “The NYPD spent more time protecting a militia that just shot someone than protecting New Yorkers.” In the interview, Avila Chevalier appeared less concerned with the minutia of the city’s sanctuary law and more interested in getting rid of ICE entirely. “We wouldn’t need sanctuary policies if ICE didn’t exist,” she said. “The clearest solution here is the bold one: to demand that ICE be abolished.” Mayor Zohran Mamdani also reiterated calls to abolish ICE and has referred to Thursday’s shooting as “unconscionable”. But he is facing pressure from progressives over reforming the NYPD in the wake of anti-ICE protests. Many immigration advocates, including Avila Chevalier, are calling for Tisch to step down and for the disbanding of the strategic response group (SRG), a rapid response unit within the NYPD that has been criticized for cracking down harshly on protests. Mamdani has repeatedly promised to disband the SRG, although that has not yet happened. He has so far shown no indication that he would remove Tisch from her role. Avila Chevalier acknowledged her differences with the mayor on these issues but noted: “It is my duty as someone who was elected to represent this district to echo the demands of people in my district,” she said. “I would not be a good partner to [Mamdani] if I weren’t doing that.” The mayor’s office did not respond to a request for comment. However, in an interview with the New York Times on Friday, Mamdani affirmed that Tisch would remain in charge of his police force but condemned officers’ aggression towards Avila Chevalier: “I do not think it is acceptable to throw anyone to the ground in our city,” he said. “I believe that to be true when it applies to the congresswoman-elect and, frankly, any New Yorker.” Avila Chevalier was on the front lines of Thursday’s protest, and videos circling social media showed her being knocked to the ground by a police officer. She says she “felt a hand grab and then throw [her] down to the ground”. “At some point, I felt like my feet were not touching the ground. I felt like I flew,” she said, adding that she is “thankfully OK” but was “in some pain” the day earlier. Avila Chevalier had said she was trying to convince police that adding barricades was escalating the situation: “They were literally in a tug of war with people over these barricades,” she said. “People were being hurt and pushed back.” The police arrested five protesters and said demonstrators “agitated and pushed over barriers” and “repeatedly refused verbal commands to disperse”. The NYPD also said that Avila Chevalier was pushed back by officers in an attempt to prevent the crowd from trampling the captain. On Friday, Avila Chevalier was distraught that Belgal’s lawyers had not been able to locate him. “That is deeply concerning to me,” she said. Avila Chevalier is a longtime organizer, who was also present at Columbia University’s pro-Palestine encampments, but said she isn’t used to this level of police aggression. She remains a strong believer in the impact of protest. “So much of the power given to our electeds comes from the space that constituents and organizers give us to be bold and to make those demands,” she said. “To know I was there with my community – that is what made me feel not only that I can do this but that this is what my community is demanding of us.”

title: ‘A life-or-death race’: the volunteers protecting Kyiv’s skies from new jet-powered drones
summary: Russia’s latest weapons have left Ukraine’s civilian air defence teams frantically trying to adapt as winter approaches
text: Several hours into Kyiv’s nightly curfew, much of the capital lay dark and quiet. High above, on the roof of a grey tower block on the city’s outskirts, a small group of men in uniform stood beside two heavy machine guns, scanning the horizon. Soon, a drone appeared. Once, its unmistakable buzz would have sent the men scrambling towards their weapons. Now, the air defence unit will check speed and altitude on a monitor before taking a decision. The Mriya air defence crew on a rooftop in Kyiv. A Russian drone shot down over Kyiv. The Mriya air defence crew keep watch. This one flew too high and too fast. It was one of Russia’s new jet-powered attack drones, a weapon that has transformed the battle for the skies over Kyiv in just a few months. “They’re so fast, it’s extremely difficult to hit them. Our weapons simply can’t reach them. Often, we can hear them but can’t see them. It drives us crazy,” said the group’s commander, who goes by the call sign Sensei, looking over the city’s skyline. Over three days and nights, the Guardian accompanied Mriya, Kyiv’s largest volunteer air-defence formation, across its network of outposts around the capital, from high-rise rooftops to truck-mounted machine gun positions in deserted fields on the city’s outskirts. Since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion, Ukraine has relied on unpaid volunteers, often armed with Soviet-era weapons, as one layer of the air-defence network protecting its cities, homes and families. For years, they proved remarkably effective, emerging as a key part of the response to the Iranian-designed Shahed drones, which Russia calls Geran-2 and began launching en masse in late 2022. A ZPU-2 vehicle mounted with an American-made Browning M2, used for air defence, near Kyiv. A Browning M2’s sight on a ZPU-2 vehicle. “We live a double life. During the day, I deal with paperwork. At night, I shoot down drones,” said Oleksandr, a lawyer, standing beside his truck-mounted machine gun in a field outside Kyiv. “It’s a strange duality. With time you get used to it.” But warfare in Ukraine evolves at extraordinary speed and units such as Mriya are struggling to keep up. Since the summer, Russia has increasingly deployed jet-powered drones that crews say can travel at about 600km/h (373mph), much faster than the original propeller-driven Shaheds, and reach altitudes of up to 10km (6 miles), far beyond the range of the volunteers’ guns. Ukraine’s interception rate for the new drones is between 50% and 60%. “In 2023 and 2024, we were shooting them down in batches,” Artem, a 63-year-old military veteran, said proudly. On a good night, he added, a single crew could bring down three or four Shaheds. Now, his unit had managed to shoot down just one jet drone after it slowed enough to come within range of their guns. “There’s this feeling of helplessness,” he added. The problem, Artem explained, was that the guns’ sights were designed for slower targets. Jet drones fly so fast that gunners must aim beyond the sight to hit them. “The Shahed no longer fits inside our aiming grid,” he said. *** Ukraine’s air defences operate as a layered system, with different weapons matched to different threats. Volunteer machine gun teams work alongside interceptor drones to hunt slower, low-flying Shaheds. More sophisticated weapons, including the country’s scarce US-made Patriot batteries, are needed against cruise and ballistic missiles. Sensei rests between patrols near Kyiv. Ukraine relies on unpaid volunteers as one layer of the air-defence network protecting its cities. Ruslan having a break during a shift with Mriya air defence crew. Sensei during a rest break. For now, the main answer to the jet drones has been fighter aircraft, including F-16s, which are expensive to fly and put their pilots at risk. Russia’s introduction of new drones came at an especially acute moment for Ukraine. With its ground offensive making slow progress, Russia has sharply intensified its air campaign, striking Kyiv almost daily in an effort to make the capital unlivable as winter approaches. In the last week, jet-powered drones have repeatedly struck bridges across the Dnipro in Kyiv, prompting restrictions on several of the city’s main crossings. Russia launched another large-scale bombardment across Ukraine on Wednesday, firing dozens of missiles alongside drones and causing fresh disruption to electricity and water supplies in the capital. The attacks have upended daily life in a city that, for much of the war, was considered relatively safe compared with those nearer the front. Anti-drone netting, long a familiar sight in frontline towns, has begun to appear around Kyiv, and during the heaviest attacks some people have taken to sleeping in metro stations. Moscow has also begun sending waves of jet drones throughout the day, a break with years of assaults taking place mostly overnight. “Every hour, two or three come in,” said Oleksandr, the lawyer, who joined Mriya early last year. His mobile group once deployed from base as drones approached the city, but now spends hours at a time waiting in fields. “They’re fast and they keep our groups constantly moving. Some days, it feels like Russia has an endless supply of them,” he shrugged. Oleksandr prepares some tea during the night shift near Kyiv. Mriya’s volunteers are something of a mirror of Kyiv. The crews that the Guardian accompanied included in their ranks an advertising creative director, a man who repairs intercoms, a hand-to-hand combat coach and the former head of a design institute. The military supplies the units with heavy machine guns, including American-made Browning M2s and Soviet-era DShKs, both designed before the second world war. But the volunteers pay for their own vehicles, fuel and other equipment. What united them, they said, was that the stakes felt close to home. “If we let a drone through, that means it flies to the city and can kill our families,” said Ivan, a university professor in Kyiv. Ivan joined the unit after a Shahed struck the courtyard of his home about a year and a half ago. “It badly frightened my family and destroyed my property,” he said. “So I had a personal score to settle as well. I have two children. The more of this filth that is destroyed on the approach to Kyiv, the lower the chance that my children will be hurt.” When a shift runs into the morning, he teaches his class online from the position, on his phone. Others described volunteering as a way of reclaiming a measure of agency over a war that has left millions of Ukrainians feeling powerless. The volunteer soldiers training at a shooting range. The volunteers pay for their own vehicles, fuel and other equipment. “In the city you can’t do anything. People sit in basements, bomb shelters or apartments and wait: will you be lucky or not, will it hit or not?” Oleksandr said. Out on the position, he said, there was at least a chance of shooting one down. Help, though, may be on its way. Back in the field, Artem pulled out a tablet showing a live map of drones over Ukraine. Among the moving icons were ones the volunteers have begun to see more often: Ukraine’s new generation of high-speed interceptor drones, designed to hunt down their Russian counterparts. He pointed to two Ukrainian interceptors travelling at more than 600km/h. Moments later, each brought down a Russian drone and disappeared from the screen. Across the country, the Ukrainian government and private defence companies have been thrown into a race to build jet-powered interceptors that can match Russia’s latest drones. “We have to admit that we were caught sleeping by these jet-powered Shaheds,” said Stanislav Hryshyn, a co-founder of General Cherry, one of Ukraine’s largest drone manufacturers, which is developing the new interceptors. The biggest obstacle, he said, was a shortage of the small jet engines that power them, which Russia sources in bulk from China. Neither Ukraine nor Europe, Hryshyn said, had built the industrial capacity to make them in the quantities required. Hryshyn estimated it would take three to four months before Ukraine could produce enough interceptors to match Russia’s jet drones. Even if Ukraine fields thousands of new interceptors in the coming months, any advantage may prove short-lived. Russia has repeatedly adapted its drones, changing their speed, altitude and flight paths in response to Ukrainian defences, and Hryshyn said each new countermeasure invited another innovation. “It’s a constant race over who gets there first,” Hryshyn said. “A life-or-death race.”

title: ‘A living hell’: how Los Angeles got taken over by mosquitoes
summary: Heat and humidity have led to one of the worst mosquito years in recent history, with West Nile virus at a decade high
text: Los Angeles might be best known for blue skies, beaches and film premiers — but for the last several years it’s held another, unenviable distinction: the most mosquito-infested city in America. And this year has been especially nightmarish, thanks to a series of heatwaves and an extra-powerful El Niño. Locals have called it a summer of “living hell” as clouds of mosquitoes swarm backyards and leave diners at open air patios scratching their ankles. That double whammy of heat and humidity is making 2026 one of the worst mosquito years in recent history, causing a spike in cases of West Nile virus and raising fears that the nuisance bugs could spread other diseases including dengue, brought in by travelers. With moisture in this week’s forecast and overnight temperatures likely to stay above 50F (10C), there seems to be no end in sight for a problem that local authorities have struggled to contain for the last decade. “I’ve been here my whole life and the amount of mosquitoes I’ve seen this summer has been insane,” said one TikTok user in a video with more than 20,000 likes. “Everyone is talking about them … You can’t even go to your back yard. You can’t even sit in your car with the windows down. They’re infested everywhere.” Southern California residents have struggled all year to keep the winged bloodsuckers at bay. Some have resorted to sleeping in long sleeves after failing to kill off the mosquitoes that colonize their homes. Others have tried to seal off the cracks below their doors with towels. “It’s an absolute nightmare,” Truman Hedding, an El Segundo resident, told Fox 11 News earlier this year. “We invest a lot of money to live in a beautiful town like El Segundo. The last thing we want is to stay up all night fighting mosquitoes.” ‘A busy season’ Los Angeles county has documented more than 180 cases of West Nile virus this year, according to the county public health department – the highest number in nearly a decade. And mosquito season is still far from over. “This year in particular for our area has been higher mosquito activity and higher disease activity,” said Anais Medina Diaz, communications director for the San Gabriel mosquito and vector control district. “We can attribute that to some connection to the environment and how warm it’s been this year – particularly because we had a very warm winter. Mosquito activity plummets when temperatures approach 50F overnight. But this winter was exceptionally mild, with heatwaves in February and March that allowed mosquitoes to stay active. The unusually moist and humid summer made it easier for them to reproduce. The region has sweltered under a record-breaking heatwave since early October, although forecasts show relief on the way. But the temperatures won’t drop low enough in most places to halt mosquito activity entirely, while coming rains will give them new places to breed. Southern California hasn’t always been such a mosquito hotspot. The region’s most common endemic mosquito, the Culex quinquefasciatus – often referred to by the more easily pronounceable name “quinx” – prefers to target birds over humans. That preference exposes quinx to West Nile virus after biting birds, such as crows, known to host the disease. Infected quinx can then spread the disease to humans when they do bite them. The Orange county mosquito and vector control district monitors disease threats with a massive array of traps scattered throughout the area. So far, some 850 of them have tested positive for West Nile virus, according to the control district’s public information officer, Brian Brannon. “That doesn’t mean 850 mosquitoes – that means 850 traps full of mosquitoes with West Nile virus,” Brannon said. “We’ve had a pretty busy season.” The mosquito that southern Californians are most likely to notice, however, are those from the Aedes genus, which first showed up in the region back in 2014 and have proliferated ever since. Known locally as “ankle biters”, Aedes mosquitoes target humans. Because the mosquito is new to the area and people have had less exposure, Aedes bites can leave larger welts, according to Medina Diaz. “They like human blood,” she said. “They will bite you multiple times to get a full blood meal.” Aedes are not associated with West Nile virus, but they are known spreaders of diseases including dengue, chikungunya, Zika and yellow fever. This year’s moisture has especially helped the invasive Aedes thrive this year. Aedes mosquitoes can reproduce in pools of water as small as a tablespoon. Biting back While nowhere in southern California is truly safe from mosquitoes, the invasive Aedes is more common to suburban neighborhoods and the valleys, where people’s habits tend to create lots of small pools of water, such as saucers below potted plants or unattended water bowls for pets. One of the most effective ways to combat mosquitoes, and by far the cheapest, is to eliminate those stagnant puddles of water. Local authorities spend a lot of time doing just that, but suspicion from property owners can make it difficult to do a thorough job. “Not everyone wants us on their property, so it creates quite a hurdle,” said Angela Caranci, a scientific-technical manager with the greater Los Angeles county vector control district. “Half the battle is convincing people we’re not trying to sell them some subscription-service pest control.” For major problem areas, vector control districts also spray adulticide, an insecticide that targets adult mosquitoes, diluted to a concentration of about two tablespoons per acre. Pro-active spraying is one of the reasons that West Nile cases have not outpaced 2014 numbers, despite such a mosquito-infested year, according to Brannon. “It doesn’t take much, but what we want to do is knock down the adults that are flying around with West Nile,” he said. One of the most promising techniques deployed in recent years is to sterilize males using X-rays and then release them in targeted areas. Only female mosquitoes bite humans, using blood to nourish their eggs. With enough sterile males in the environment, local officials have beat back targeted mosquito populations by more than 80% at some experimental sites. It’s a strategy long used in agriculture to control insect pests that feed on valuable crops. But while promising, flooding the zone with sterile males remains a limited tool. It works best on the Aedes mosquitoes, who have small home ranges and whose annihilation poses little ethical concern because they’re a non-native invasive. But while at least three species of Aedes mosquitoes live in southern California, local authorities only have the ability to target the most prominent and best studied – the Aedes aegypti. It’s also very expensive. An experimental program in the San Gabriel Valley cost about $30,000 to cover just 25 acres (10 hectares), Medina Diaz said. Despite its success, property owners – particularly businesses – have shown reluctance to vote in favor of raising their taxes to foot the bill for mosquito reduction, according to the Los Angeles Times. Grab your zapper For the moment, southern California has little choice but to start getting used to the idea that mosquitoes are likely to become a bigger part of local life. The best ways to avoid bites, other than avoiding the outdoors entirely, are to cover your skin with long sleeves and pant legs, and to use a repellent with one of the four ingredients known to actually work: Deet, picaridin, IR3535, or oil of lemon and eucalyptus. “Most of our residents are used to not having mosquitoes, and that has now changed,” Medina Diaz said. “If you’re going to avoid mosquito bites, you’re going to have to make wearing repellent a part of your routine.” Because they can reproduce in such small splashes of water, Aedes mosquitoes have a knack for sneaking their way into people’s homes, where they can be difficult to remove. The first step toward clearing them out is removing all standing water, including saucers under plants. To deal with lingerers, Brannon suggests buying an electric fly swatter. “It looks like a tennis racket, and when you hit them, it zaps them,” he said. “It’s a very fulfilling activity. It brings a smile to my face.”

title: Did Trump get one thing right about Greenland?
summary: Threatening an ally is a terrible idea, but there’s no denying the Arctic’s increasing strategic importance
text: One of Donald Trump’s more diabolical talents is his ability to land on the right things in the wrong way. Since his first term, Trump has been obsessed with the Arctic – Greenland in particular – something that has puzzled and enraged many, particularly in Europe. He first brought up the idea of buying the icy landmass from Denmark in 2019. Right after re-election, he began ramping up his rhetoric about acquiring it “one way or another”, threatening the Nato alliance and the foundations of post-second world war security. Trump got his way – thankfully without military force – in September, when the US and Denmark signed an agreement that allowed for many more US troops on the island, albeit without the sort of takeover that the president enjoys “joking” about. “The United States will FOREVER have the complete ability to do what is necessary in Greenland,” Trump wrote on social media. “We will work with the people of Greenland in its development and construction.” Europeans could be forgiven for doubting that the US president would help any country in its development, let alone Greenland. But the truth is that there is something in Trump’s obsession with a place that has more reindeer than people, and he isn’t the first to suggest the US should own it; President Andrew Johnson floated the idea in 1867. The fact is that since the cold war, Greenland has played a crucial role in North American security, with airfields close to the eastern seaboard, vast mineral resources and a location perfectly suited to tracking Arctic weather (something crucial to military movements). More recently, it has become a pawn in the US-China geopolitical struggle. As Jeff Landry, the US special envoy to Greenland wrote in early 2026, greater American presence there would “facilitate deployment of advanced missile defense systems” and “crowd out hostile Chinese and Russian influence”. While there are no explicit Chinese or Russian security threats on the island now, many in the administration fear that if Greenland becomes independent – as it has said it wants to be by 2033 – it will be more open to Chinese or Russian influence campaigns. Whether you agree with them or not, the region is certainly becoming a geostrategic hotspot. Russia is upping energy transit there to avoid global choke points, and China declared itself a “near-Arctic state” in 2018. Security and military drills have been conducted by both countries close to US territorial waters near Alaska. All of this puts the US’s biggest adversaries squarely in its back yard, at a time when it’s unclear what the new, post-neoliberal world order will be, and how either Europe or Greenland will fit into it. Beyond geopolitics, there’s another reason for all the interest in the Arctic: climate change. When the seas at the top of the world were frozen solid, nobody cared much about what was happening there. But over the past few decades, global heating has opened the possibility of resource extraction (the Arctic seabed is filled with gas, oil and rare-earth minerals, most of which have yet to be mined or even claimed by individual nations). It has also made possible the passage by sea of energy supplies and goods – something that has been coveted by various powers for hundreds of years. In August, a Chinese shipping company, Sea Legend, started a weekly trans-polar commercial route across the Arctic, through Russian territorial waters. It claims that the voyage will cut the usual 40-day journey time between Europe and Asia in half, something that seems pretty attractive given the Houthi threat in the Red Sea. Of course, to take advantage of new pathways in the Arctic, you need ships, icebreakers in particular. The US, which has very little capacity in this area, has recently started trying to make them jointly with Finland, a project that was endorsed by both Joe Biden and Trump. But the lack of icebreakers is symptomatic of a larger problem. In 1975, the US shipbuilding industry was ranked No 1 in terms of global capacity, with more than 70 commercial ships on order for production domestically. Just over 50 years later, the US now produces less than 1% of the world’s commercial vessels. China, meanwhile, has tripled its production relative to the US over the past two decades, producing more than 1,000 ocean-going vessels last year, versus the US’s 10. The resulting asymmetry comes with commercial and military concerns for the US, but also for any country that depends on it for security. More than 90% of military equipment, supplies and fuel travels by sea. That goes to a larger point – conflict in the Arctic is happening against the backdrop of the end of the neoliberal era, which brought modern globalisation and great wealth, but also increased inequality and a sense that policymakers operating at a great height in the national interest were sometimes out of step with the economic reality of communities on the ground. The pendulum is now swinging back. In the US, Repubicans and Democrats alike are pushing industrial policy to restore industries such as shipbuilding and chip-making. While efforts are sometimes couched with xenophobic, anti-China rhetoric, the truth is that one country dominating any strategic industry isn’t in the interests of workers or nation states. It’s an issue that the EU, too, is now coming to terms with, as cheap Chinese electric cars, steel, lithium batteries and solar panels move from US markets to Europe. Trump’s focus on Greenland may not be as misplaced as it seems at first glance, then. But there’s a glaring flaw in his approach. In a world that will be dominated by new spheres of influence, the US needs friends. Europe does, too. Shared supply chains, security agreements and trade pathways can all be used to mutual advantage. But it will take careful statecraft of the kind that this administration isn’t exactly known for. Trump’s limbic brain knows that Greenland, and the Arctic at large, is important. What he doesn’t seem to understand is how to put aside his own ego and ambitions to make sure that the US can secure its own hemispheric back yard in ways that don’t destroy its existing alliances. Here’s hoping the next administration does better: the US’s future will depend on it. • Rana Foroohar is a columnist and associate editor at the FT and the author of Sea Change: America’s New Great Game in the Arctic Circle (Swift). Further reading Chokepoints by Edward Fishman (Elliott & Thompson, £10.99) The Next World War by Peter Apps (Wildfire, £12.99) Unfrozen by Mia Bennett and Klaus Dodds (Yale, £20).

title: US’s Reagan-era economic promises return as Trump’s AI-fueled growth fantasy
summary: ‘Even if AI supercharged the economy, its impact on the government’s finances would be muted’
text: Back through political history to the age of Ronald Reagan, Republicans have repeatedly promised the US public that tax cuts would pay for themselves, firing up economic growth and filling the government’s coffers. The promise never really panned out. From the Gipper’s day on, the Republicans’ tax cuts inevitably increased the budget deficit. Despite its failure, though, the promise is back, coated in a fine new layer of artificial intelligence pixie dust. It will fail again. The treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, is relying on an AI-laced economy when he promises to deliver annual economic growth of 3% – a rate that, except for the rebound from the Covid pandemic, has been achieved only twice this century. Dreams of AI inflect Donald Trump’s fantasy that “we’re growing at a faster rate than we’ve ever grown before,” which will allow the government to “take care of the 40 trillion” in federal debt “over a period of time”. Financial markets, however, are not buying. Last week, the yield on the 10-year treasury bond surged to its highest in almost a quarter century, more than a full percentage point higher than when Trump launched his misbegotten war against Iran. The war’s inflationary impact is the most immediate cause of rising bond yields. It already persuaded the Fed to raise short-term interest rates. But the treasury market is also being walloped by the US’s unbalanced finances. There is no realistic path for economic growth to generate the tax revenues needed to fix the US’s enormous and growing budget deficit. Investors are demanding more to cover the growing funding gap. Borrowing is likely to become more expensive still. Foreign central banks, which once reliably bought treasuries to build up foreign reserves and manage their exchange rates, have cut back on their exposure to US government debt. The treasury now relies largely on private investors seeking to turn a profit. It finds itself competing for their money with the very AI superscalers on which it is pinning its future hopes, which are borrowing hand over fist to fund the buildout of datacenters to train their agents. Indeed, the US’s finances find themselves in a bit of a negative spiral, as rising bond yields put additional pressure on the budget. Interest payments on the federal debt alone are consuming 3.3% of GDP, up from an average of 2.1% over the preceding 50 years. And Trump’s fiscal management – his One Big Beautiful Bill Act is estimated to add $4.7tn to the federal debt through 2035 – is not making the budget math easier. The deficit already hit 6% of GDP – twice the size Bessent once promised. The Congressional Budget Office projected it will close in on 7% of GDP by 2033. And that was before Trump promised a $5,000 “dividend” to every US adult if the GOP kept control of Congress in the midterms. There is no realistic amount of growth that can fill the fiscal hole that Trump keeps digging. The Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget (CRFPB) sketched out a few scenarios. Assuming the temporary tax cuts in Trump’s 2025 law are made permanent by a future Congress – an assumption that fits the historical pattern – and that the government does not recover the revenue lost when the supreme court struck down its national security tariffs, achieving a budget deficit of 3% of GDP by 2036 would require annual growth of 4.4% over the next decade. Achieving a balanced budget by then would require the economy to expand 7.2% per year. It is not impossible for AI to deliver this kind of growth. Some economists are willing to contemplate scenarios in which artificial intelligence boosts economic growth to 15% per year, by taking over much of the cognitive work usually performed by humans. But these scenarios do not appear likely. According to the CFRB, stabilizing the federal debt would require average growth in total factor productivity – a measure of how efficiently economic inputs are converted into goods and services – to hit 2.5% per year over the next decade. The US has only hit that once since 1959. And that is despite massive productivity gains over the period from electrification, the completion of the federal highway system, the telecommunications revolution and the first wave of IT and automation. Even if AI supercharged the economy, its impact on the government’s finances would be muted, for it would massively shift the fruits of growth from labor to capital, and the tax rate on capital today is only about half the tax rate on labor. Moreover, such a shift in the distribution of economic spoils would probably call for massive government spending to sustain the livelihoods of the many workers left behind. What can we expect from the AI-pixie dust? At the moment people seem particularly worried about AI agents slipping their enclosures and killing us all. But even short of that, it is not a given that their impact will be inevitably positive for the economy, not to say the government’s finances necessarily provide the money for the federal government to right its finances. For one, their massive debt-fuelled investments are pushing interest rates higher, complicating government financing. Their future promise, moreover, also comes with momentous risk. The Stanford economist Hanno Lustig estimates that for the owners of datacenters to break even on their massive investments in AI – estimated to reach $1.43tn this year – their revenue would have to grow by 45% on average every year for the next seven years. By 2032, it would amount to roughly 9.2% of GDP. A similar analysis by Jared Bernstein, former chair of Joe Biden’s Council of Economic Advisers, and Stanford economist Ryan Cummings, concluded that the nation’s six superscalers – Google, Meta, Microsoft, Oracle, SpaceX and Amazon – would need additional revenues of $13.1tn to $18.7tn over the next 10 years just to pay for their massive investments in AI. That is roughly the same as their total revenues over the last 10 years. It’s hard to forecast precisely what would happen to financial markets were these targets to be missed. But it’s safe to say that it might complicate the task of trimming the budget deficit and financing the US’s vast public debt. Eduardo Porter is a journalist focused on economics and politics. He writes the newsletter Being There on Substack

title: ‘I didn’t want to write about this’: the man who first saw chimps waging civil war
summary: John Mitani spent years studying a huge community of chimpanzees in Uganda. But then things took a dark turn – and his findings stunned the scientific world
text: John Mitani can still remember the first time he set foot in Uganda’s Kibale national park. The old-growth east African rainforest enveloped him, its canopy stretching to heights of 40 metres. Fruit trees bowed under the weight of African star apples and bountiful Ficus mucuso figs. And then there were the chimpanzees. Furry black blobs darted through the jungle, their raucous calls often deafening. It was the summer of 1995, and Mitani, a primatologist from northern California, had just come from working with the chimps living in the Mahale mountains of Tanzania. At the time, Mahale was home to the largest known population of chimps, with about 100 individuals. But there were rumours that this section of Kibale – only accessible via a 12-hour drive from the capital, Kampala – might host an even more unusual abundance of apes. “It only took a few days to realise that something weird was going on at this place,” Mitani, now 72, recalls. “There were chimps everywhere.” He was then a professor at the University of Michigan, and with his colleagues would eventually count nearly 200 chimpanzees living together peacefully in the forests of Ngogo, a research area in the central section of Kibale first established in the 1970s for the study of red colobus monkeys. Such a large chimp troop was then unheard of in primatology. Later that year, Mitani co-founded the Ngogo Chimpanzee Project with the Yale university primatologist David Watts, using a $500,000 (£380,000) award from the US National Science Foundation. Three decades on, the project is one of just 12 long-term studies worldwide of chimpanzees in their natural environment, and has transformed what we know about one of our closest relatives. It took years to build trust with the population, Mitani says. The chimps were not accustomed to human presence and were quick to run away whenever researchers approached. Days were spent chasing them over hills and down valleys. “It was fun, exciting and exhilarating. It was also a challenge.” The first ape to break the ice was a 25-year-old male with an easily identifiable cleft palate that Mitani would later name Hare. During his second year at Ngogo, Mitani was observing chimpanzees in a massive fig tree when Hare descended. Mitani assumed he would run away as he had done in the past. Instead, the chimp walked slowly toward the next fruit tree, permitting Mitani to follow. “When I realised what was happening, I almost started to cry. After working so hard for so long, it was tremendously gratifying to have gained Hare’s trust,” Mitani wrote in the 2022 anthology Chimpanzee Memoirs. Mitani estimates he has spent 85 months of his life hiking the forests of Ngogo, or approximately seven years. What began as a few basic structures and tents has grown into a large – albeit rustic – research camp that has housed the nearly 90 researchers who have worked with the Ngogo project over three decades. The findings that have emerged from Ngogo over the years have stunned the scientific world, similar to the discoveries first made at Gombe in Tanzania by Jane Goodall in the 1960s and 1970s. Mitani and his colleagues documented the lowest mortality ever recorded for a wild chimp population, suggesting that good habitat conditions could lengthen life expectancy to close to that of human hunter-gatherers. They found that unrelated males could form strong alliances and cooperate, moving beyond the accepted paradigm that only close kin would work together. Hunting and meat-eating (particularly munching on the red colobus monkeys) were found to be important for male social bonding, not just nutrition. But the most notable – and disturbing – finding of Ngogo began on a June day in 2015. Mitani and his fellow researchers were observing a cluster of the group when the chimps began to display nervous behaviour and scattered at the sounds of approaching group members. “All of a sudden, the individuals I was following just ran down the hill for no apparent reason,” Mitani says. “Chaos erupted. They started to run around and chase each other.” That moment, in retrospect, was the first sign of what would become a years-long bloody conflict – chronicled in the 2023 Netflix series Chimp Empire – between a once close-knit group of chimps. In a study published this April in the journal Science, Mitani and his colleagues describe what may be the first “civil war” among wild chimps. By 2018, two distinct chimp groups had formed in Ngogo. Nine males and 19 infants have been killed during the conflict. Scientists later found that the unexpected result of this lethal aggression was that female fertility doubled and offspring survival increased substantially at Ngogo. But for Mitani, who has spent much of his life among the Ngogo chimps, witnessing the split was far more personal. “I was in denial. I was still in this mindset that they were doing so well together as a big group,” he recalls. “It’s been hard to watch. In the first 20 years, going back to see the chimps was fun. I always looked forward to these visits. But it’s gotten to be increasingly difficult to go back and see this, to see these killings continue.” So much so, he adds, that it took him more than a decade to write the paper on the dark events they had borne witness to in the forests of Ngogo. “I think I was dragging my heels because maybe I didn’t really want to write about this.” Still, Mitani pushes back against the takeaway that the civil war says anything about humans’ evolutionary propensity for violence and in-fighting. This behaviour, he adds, has not been witnessed among bonobos, with whom we also share a common ancestor dating back approximately 8m years. “Many of us who study chimps emphasise the similarities, and for good reason,” Mitani says. “But when it comes to the behavioural similarities, sometimes I think my colleagues stretch things a bit too much. If there is one thing I’ve learned from studying chimps all these years, it is that they are not us.” Though the greatest threat the Ngogo chimps now face is, in a way, themselves, Mitani says the presence of researchers on the ground over many decades has helped to conserve these populations. Researchers work with the wildlife authority to remove snares for other wild game that occasionally trap a chimp by mistake, for example. But Mitani, who now lives between Michigan and Arizona, worries for the future of research at Ngogo. The project has received the bulk of its funding from the US National Science Foundation’s behavioural and cognitive sciences division. Under the Trump administration’s proposed 2027 budget, that funding is due to be eliminated. “The chimps there have many more important stories to tell us,” Mitani says. “This is one of the reasons I am so concerned about the war on science and truth in this country.” He will return again to Ngogo this month – and for as long as he is able. “The funny thing is that the hills at Ngogo get increasingly steeper every year. And the distance between the trails seems to get longer. But I feel blessed that I still can do it.” If there is any legacy to his life’s work, he hopes that being able to impart some knowledge of the complex lives of these animals will give people a better appreciation of the chimpanzees. That maybe that will inspire people to ensure we continue living on a planet alongside them. “That would be the grand, big hope.” Find more age of extinction coverage here, and follow biodiversity reporters Rebecca Ratcliffe, Phoebe Weston and Patrick Greenfield on the app for all the latest news and features.

title: ‘Some aren’t going to make it’: how pressure on farmers threatens UK food security
summary: Food producers are adding their voices to the chorus of warnings about the vulnerability of British supply chains
text: “There are so many decent, capable, productive, efficient arable farmers out there, asking how they are supposed to finance the crop they are meant to be putting in the ground,” Jamie Burrows says. Sitting in his tractor at his arable farm in Norfolk, Burrows is listing the multiple challenges facing him and other food producers. Crop growers such as Burrows are ploughing and cultivating their fields, preparing the ground – hardened and dried out during the long, hot summer – for their next crop. But machinery requires fuel, and the cost of red diesel – used for agricultural vehicles and machinery that is taxed at a lower rate than standard diesel – has almost doubled since the conflict in Iran began in late February. The cost of most fertilisers used to grow crops and feed for animals has also soared by about 20% over the same period. “Some of these businesses aren’t going to make it,” concludes Burrows, who is also the chair of the crops board at the National Farmers’ Union (NFU). “It is very, very difficult.” These are among the latest worries for Britain’s food producers, who also faced a succession of heatwaves and drought conditions during the UK’s hottest summer on record, which resulted in England’s worst recorded cereals harvest, according to official production estimates. Farmers, the first link in the food production chain, are adding their voices to the chorus of warnings about the vulnerability and precarity of the UK’s food supply. Food experts, academics, businesses and the public spending watchdog, the National Audit Office (NAO), have in recent weeks called on the government to work on making the UK’s food system more resilient. The climate crisis, this year’s huge El Niño weather pattern, geopolitical shocks, energy outages and cyber-attacks are all considered threats to food chain security. Amid calls for ministers to treat food as a national security issue, parliament’s influential public accounts committee is to begin a series of hearings on Monday as part of its inquiry into the resilience of the UK’s food supply. MPs on the committee will look at the NAO’s findings on the shortcomings of the last catastrophe planning exercise by the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra), which largely excluded food supply chain businesses. Britain produces about 60% of the food it needs to feed itself, but is more dependent on imports than many European peers. The government’s own research has shown Britons are less prepared for potential future emergencies than several European neighbours. Some in the food industry believe there are signs Andy Burnham’s government is beginning to take the threats to Britain’s food system more seriously. The Cabinet Office will launch a campaign telling households to stock up on tinned foods alongside preparations for possible future emergencies. The government’s Prepare website outlines steps it says people should take, which include storing items at home, including bottles of water and nonperishable food, such as tinned meat, fruit and vegetables that do not require cooking. Despite this, a recent warning from more than 150 food experts and academics accused ministers of being “complacent” about food security and not having a plan to feed people in an emergency. “Historically we have done pretty well coping with specific events such as Covid and we’ve managed to ride through them, but we’re moving into a period where we’re having multiple crises impact at the same time,” says Prof Paul Behrens of the Oxford Martin School, University of Oxford, who signed the letter. These include the worsening climate crisis and increased water scarcity in regions that now provide some of the fresh produce UK households rely on, including the Mediterranean and north Africa. Meanwhile, Behrens and other experts, including Prof Tim Lang of the Centre for Food Policy, City St George’s, University of London, have been warning for some time that the UK’s food distribution network is concentrated, leaving it exposed to potential disruption or targeting by bad actors. Lang has previously stated that the UK’s supermarket network is supplied by just 131 distribution hubs – serving 12,300 stores – while the industry body the Cold Chain Federation has warned that most of Britain’s food imports enter the country through four ports – Dover, Felixstowe, Southampton and London Gateway. The UK government wound up the strategic food stockpile that had been in place since the second world war in the 1990s. Behrens says other nations, particularly Scandinavian countries, now have “far greater national preparedness”. He says: “They’re looking at community responses and how much households can have on hand. They’re looking at their own local production and some countries have strategic stores of grain.” Mother of one Ana, 42, is one of a small but growing number of citizens who have been preparing for possible future emergencies for some time. Now living in south Wales, she is originally from eastern Europe and grew up in a family that grew food and preserved it for the colder months. She now shares tips on her YouTube channel, advising other households on resilience and how to build an emergency stockpile. “It’s just a normal way of life, basically safeguarding yourself and your family,” she says. Ana describes herself as a “prepper”, but wants to move away from its negative connotations, such as panic buying or being a survivalist. “The stereotype was … that preparedness is American, really weird, all camo and blokes in the bushes, hunting and eating squirrels and mushrooms,” she says. Instead she wants to help other citizens learn how they could cope for a few hours, days or even weeks without power, water or being able to get to the shops. “If the stereotype had been dispersed originally by the government, then people would look at preparedness as an everyday thing,” she says. Rob Haward, the chief executive of organic vegetable box delivery company Riverford, believes the UK’s food supply chain needs a “very complicated rethink and a different vision for future security”. Devon-based Riverford distributes about 65,000 boxes a week to customers and about 70% of the produce it sells is grown in the UK, although it also has long-term relationships with growers in Spain and Italy. While the UK is always going to import fruit such as bananas, which cannot be grown in large volumes domestically, Haward believes consumers can also play a role by returning to eating more seasonally. Haward says longer-term contracts can help farmers, giving them confidence to invest in their land and what they grow. He adds: “There are different ways we can try to create a food and farming sector different to now and much more resilient to the future world,” such as working to restore soils to better withstand the changing climate. He also wants government to “pull levers” such as offering lower business rates to greengrocers.

title: Labour has got the message – developing nations suffer most from bond market turmoil | Heather Stewart
summary: Just as Brown and Blair did in 2005, Andy Burnham aims to champion debt relief to help developing countries
text: From Washington to Paris, London to Tokyo, policymakers in every large economy have been counting the costs of bond market turmoil in recent weeks. But the brunt of the pain is being borne by heavily indebted developing countries that have little hope of influencing the whims of global investors, but pay the price regardless. Markets have responded to the war in the Middle East, and a spendthrift White House, by dumping government bonds – driving up borrowing costs just about everywhere. Finance ministers and central bankers gathering in Bangkok this week for the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank may be loth to point the finger at Donald Trump’s regime, but all are at least in part hostage to the US president’s war plans. That has made what was already a perilous situation even worse – just as the world is battling an energy crisis, and as developing countries urgently need to invest in adapting to the climate emergency. Even before the latest market gyrations, experts calculated that debt servicing costs absorbed 45% of government revenues in the global south, and 70% in low-income countries. That crowds out desperately needed spending on public services and investing for the future. There have been growing demands for reform of the framework for international debt in recent years, including from African Union heads of state, and under the G20 chairs of Brazil and South Africa. The G20 – the forum in which Gordon Brown coordinated a global fiscal stimulus package in the depths of the financial crisis in spring 2009 – is meant to be an important body for discussing international economic issues. With a much wider membership than the G7, it has coordinated previous efforts on debt, including establishing the IMF-administered Common Framework, to which struggling countries can apply, and suspending repayments for hard-hit borrowers during the Covid crisis. However, this year’s chair has been Trump’s US, which has placed much more emphasis on other aspects of the G20’s remit, including promoting global economic growth – somewhat ironically, given the main obstacle to achieving it is the war on Iran. Next year, the presidency falls to the UK, and Labour has made clear it will have different priorities. These will include seeking a global agreement on AI regulation, which seems a faint hope but is clearly worth pursuing. The UK also intends to put unsustainable debt on the agenda. The foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, who will be in Bangkok, told Labour conference delegates last month: “Friends, I promise this. We will use our G20 presidency next year to meet our responsibilities and mobilise the world, building on the great achievements on debt and development of the last Labour government.” He was referring to 2005, when Brown and Tony Blair rode the vociferous Make Poverty History movement to the Gleneagles G8 summit and beyond, securing significant debt relief for more than 30 countries. As the development minister, Kirsty McNeill, herself a veteran of that campaign, said recently, the circumstances now are very different, for two reasons. First, she said, “we’re now dealing with private creditors – the debt isn’t held by us. So that is quite a big shift.” And second, she suggested it was harder now to delineate a group of countries clearly deserving of support. “There isn’t this really clear demarcation between the very poor world and the very rich world that was true when I was starting out, and it was just a much starker and therefore more readily told story because the antagonists and the protagonists were just much clearer,” she told an event at the Labour conference. Yet she and other ministers have made clear they are open to proposals – and ready to throw the UK’s diplomatic weight behind making progress on this formidable challenge. One ambitious plan drawn up by the thinktank Development Finance International (DFI) and shared with the government would involve 27 of the most heavily burdened countries being given a 10-year “holiday” during which their debt service costs would be slashed to below 10% of their revenues. Implemented by cutting interest rates and extending loan terms rather than writing off debt altogether, the $13bn-a-year cost would fall primarily on private creditors – which might have to be coaxed, cajoled, perhaps even legislated into taking part, as in previous debt relief initiatives. The “hope initiative” also envisages potential relief for another six small island developing states that do not meet the threshold on the basis of their debt burden but are regularly battered by natural disasters. These could be offered a five-year “holiday” from the moment of the next extreme weather event they face, at the cost of a further $700m a year. An even more expansive version would embrace another five countries, including Pakistan and Angola. Crucially, because the international financial institutions – including the IMF and the World Bank – tend to be preferred creditors, only chipping in when other help is exhausted, the costs to them would be relatively low. Echoing Andy Burnham’s slogan – so far confined to the domestic sphere – Matthew Martin, DFI’s executive director and the author of the plan, says: “Let’s bring hope back to the poorest countries in the world, through an ambitious but financially and politically feasible initiative, which will free up $13bn for them to spend on their climate and development goals.” It remains to be seen how bold the government is prepared to be in setting its G20 agenda, but the groundwork is being done. Labour trashed its reputation as a champion for international development when Keir Starmer took the axe to aid spending to pay for defence. Perhaps 2027 could be the year Burnham starts to rebuild it.

title: Britain stands behind Zelenskyy, says Streeting after Trump’s call for new leader in Ukraine
summary: Defence secretary backs Ukrainian president and says priority is to maintain western unity over Russia conflict
text: Britain stands behind Volodymyr Zelenskyy, the defence secretary has said, after Donald Trump called for the Ukrainian president to be replaced and the US announced a controversial agreement to buy Russian diesel. Wes Streeting said Ukrainians alone should be able to decide who leads their country as he indicated Trump was facing domestic political pressure over fuel prices before next month’s midterm elections. Asked on the BBC’s Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme whether Britain supported Zelenskyy staying in office, Streeting said: “We are in no doubt that the aggressor here was Vladimir Putin. He is the person who chose to start this war. He is the person who could end this war tomorrow, and he chooses not to. So, we stand with Ukraine. We stand with President Zelenskyy.” Trump said on Saturday that Ukraine should get a new leader capable of reaching a peace agreement, accusing Zelenskyy of failing to end the war and blaming Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries for increasing American diesel prices. Zelenskyy condemned the diesel agreement as a gift to Putin, warning that increased Russian energy revenues would help finance the war against Ukraine. Trump has been facing rising political pressure over the economic fallout from the war with Iran, which has driven up global energy prices weeks before Americans vote in the midterm elections. Soaring fuel costs have hit Americans and added to wider inflation, damaging Trump’s standing with voters. The squeeze is felt particularly in agricultural states such as Iowa, Kansas, Texas and Ohio where farmers depend on diesel to operate machinery and transport their produce. These traditionally Republican-leaning states battling rising cost of living pressures will create a headache for Trump, whose party is trying to hold on to its majorities. Streeting told Sky News on Sunday: “Let’s be candid about this: midterms are coming up, cost of living is an issue. No doubt President Trump is feeling the same pressure that lots of leaders are facing in terms of wanting to ease cost of living pressures, energy prices. “I think it’s just a political reality, isn’t it? We would obviously prefer a stronger approach on sanctions.” Streeting sought to avoid a deeper public confrontation with Washington, insisting Britain’s priority was to maintain western unity. “Let’s not overstate the impact of President Trump’s decision on purchasing oil from Russia and let’s not also understate US support for Ukraine,” he said. In a phone call with Zelenskyy on Saturday, Andy Burnham, the prime minister, restated his “complete solidarity” with Ukraine. Downing Street said the leaders had agreed to meet in person in the coming days. Burnham has also pledged to strengthen sanctions against Russia, while both called for an immediate energy ceasefire. Gen Sir Richard Barrons, one of the authors of Britain’s strategic defence review, warned that Trump’s Russian diesel deal would lead to more Ukrainian deaths by helping Moscow fund its war. He told Sky News that money from Russian oil and gas was used to pay for the “missiles and drones that it fires at Ukraine”. Asked if the deal would mean more Ukrainians being killed, he said “for sure”, adding that security interests were being “sacrificed on the altar of an election”. Meanwhile, Streeting said Britain was not currently considering offensive military operations against the Houthis, after an attack on King Khalid international airport in Riyadh, Saudi’s capital, killed 12 people and injured more than 300 others. Streeting said he had been discussing further military assistance with Saudia Arabia, and he declined to categorically rule out future involvement. Asked on the BBC whether Britain could join US offensive operations, he said: “That’s not what we’re looking at, at this stage,” insisting there was no military solution to the conflict. The defence secretary described the overnight attack as a “shocking escalation” and said the UK was already providing air-to-air refuelling and ground-based air defence support. Streeting said he had spoken to his Saudi counterpart on several occasions in recent weeks about what further support Britain could provide. “I think there is clearly more to do, as evidenced by what we saw last night,” he said.

title: ‘When you look at the numbers, we win’: the prophetic Texas pastor poised to take Jasmine Crockett’s House seat
summary: Rev Dr Frederick Douglass Haynes III is reclaiming a faith-based politics to counter Trump-allied white evangelicals
text: It was that point in the evening: dinner plates were cleared; speeches had run long; people were chatting, milling or eyeing the exit. But then the Rev Dr Frederick Douglass Haynes III took the stage. Bald, bearded, bespectacled and dressed in black, he delivered a mix of fiery sermon and performance poetry. Soon the guests were back in their seats – rapt, listening, clapping and whooping. Haynes’s rolling cadence was evocative of the pulpit but the political message was far from kumbaya. Aiming to succeed Democratic star Jasmine Crockett in Texas’s 30th congressional district, he danced like a butterfly with references to the boxer Muhammad Ali and rapper Tupac Shakur. But he also stung like a bee, branding Donald Trump as “President Pickpocket” and Republicans as the authors of racist gerrymandering and voter suppression. “It’s not enough for us Democrats to diagnose the demolition,” Haynes, 65, thundered at last month’s Opal Lee empowerment gala, a Democratic fundraiser in Fort Worth, Texas. “We have to have the vision for a new reconstruction. You see, it’s one thing to talk about how sorry, trifling, cheating and tacky the Republicans are. That’s well known. It’s another thing to have our own vision of reconstructing what this nation should look like.” The speech reflected a growing trend of religious left candidates aiming to reclaim a faith-based politics they believe has been hijacked by white evangelicals allied with Trump.
