title: Ukraine war briefing: Trump and Zelenskyy’s public tussle over Russian fuel deal worsens
summary: Zelenskyy has ‘support of the people’, says Ukraine’s foreign minister after Trump calls for ‘new leader’. What we know on day 1,691
text: Ukraine’s foreign minister says Volodymyr Zelenskyy has the backing of the Ukrainian people and deserves support, after Donald Trump called for Zelenskyy to be replaced as president. “He has the support of the Ukrainian people, and they have the right to decide,” Andriy Sybiga said on Saturday. “Statements from abroad only confirm that he is doing his job well. He deserves support.” Earlier, Trump said Ukraine needed “a new leader” a day after the US president struck a deal allowing Russia to supply diesel to global markets, and as Moscow launched strikes on Ukrainian civilians, killing 20 people including three children. Trump on Saturday also called ⁠on Zelenskyy ⁠to stop hitting Russian ‌oil ‌refineries, saying: “He better damn ‌well stop.” Trump made the comments to reporters at the White House. Zelenskyy on Friday had reacted furiously to Trump’s deal with Putin, calling it “terrible” and “not fair and not honest”. Further ratcheting up the tension, Trump said Vladimir Putin would like to reach a deal on the war with Ukraine, and without evidence accused Zelenskyy of resisting a compromise. “Russia would like to make a deal … but for whatever reason, Zelenskyy does not want to make a deal,” Trump told reporters. “President Putin would like to see a settlement, strongly,” Trump said of a phone conversation he had with the Russian leader on Friday. The British prime minister, Andy Burnham, has moved to quickly back Zelenskyy, telling his Ukrainian counterpart they were in “complete solidarity”. In a call between the two leaders, Burnham told Zelenskyy he recognised that “the past 24 hours had been difficult for Ukraine and reiterated his complete solidarity”, according to a Downing Street readout. The leaders discussed “the importance of maintaining pressure on Russia”, with Burnham making it clear the UK “would continue to strengthen its sanctions on Russia and to take further action to constrain the Russian war machine”. They agreed to meet in person in the coming days, the readout added. US ⁠negotiators Steve ⁠Witkoff ⁠and Jared Kushner, who have ⁠spearheaded efforts to ⁠broker a ‌Ukraine peace ‌agreement, ‌may visit Moscow within the next ‌two weeks, Russian state news ⁠reported on Saturday, citing a source. A delegation of Ukrainian officials who visited Miami for talks on ending Russia’s war in Ukraine was on Saturday heading home, an aide to Zelenskyy said. “The groups are already on their way home,” Dmytro Lytvyn, an adviser to the president, told reporters. Vladimir Putin’s top economic negotiator on Saturday welcomed Trump’s call to replace Zelenskyy, describing his remarks as “historic”. “President Trump joins the many who believe that Ukraine needs leadership actually focused on peace,” Kirill Dmitriev, the Kremlin’s special envoy on economic cooperation, said in a post on X. Germany said Saturday it would continue to push for new EU sanctions against Russia despite Moscow’s agreement with Washington to release diesel to ease a fuel crunch. “The German government sticks to its measures sanctioning Russia and is working jointly with its European partners on new sanctions,” the government spokesperson, Stefan Kornelius, said in a statement. Germany’s “support for Ukraine in its struggle to defend itself remains unfailing,” he said. “Diplomatic efforts for a peaceful solution continue.” Russia’s defence ⁠ministry said its drones ⁠had ⁠struck a data-processing centre in ⁠Kyiv earlier on Saturday and a ⁠cargo ship ‌carrying military ‌supplies to ‌the Ukrainian port of Odesa. In a statement, the ministry said ‌the Kyiv facility was used by Ukraine’s armed forces to ⁠collect, process and store intelligence. The ⁠ministry ⁠also said ⁠its forces ⁠had captured ‌the ‌settlements of Lukashove ‌and Lobanivka in Ukraine’s ‌Kharkiv region, Russia’s Interfax news agency ⁠reported. Reuters could not independently verify the reports.

title: Five people shot and killed in apparent murder-suicide, Georgia police say
summary: Deceased were all members of the same family, officials say, and one of victims placed the initial emergency call
text: Five people were shot and killed in an apparent murder-suicide at a residence in Georgia on Friday, authorities say. The deceased were family members who lived at the home in Douglas, a city in south Georgia. Officers responded to reports of an active shooter later on Friday, Brannen Pruette, the Douglas police chief, said at a Saturday news conference. One of the victims placed the initial emergency call. Responding officers found four deceased adults inside the home. A fifth individual was transported to a hospital, where they were later pronounced dead. Details around how the tragedy unfolded remain unclear, including who opened fire. Hours before the deadly shooting, a female victim called police to complain that her husband was “killing her” with his smoking. EMS transported her to a local medical center. Police did not offer additional information, citing the ongoing investigation. “We recognize the profound impact this loss has on those closest to the victims in our community. We ask everyone to respect the privacy of the family and allow them the time and space they need to grieve,” Pruette said. Charlie Davis, the Douglas city manager, said it was the area’s second murder-suicide incident in three months. “Domestic violence doesn’t know race. It doesn’t know religion. It doesn’t know geographic location,” Davis said. “We encourage everyone to refrain from speculation and allow the family the space, dignity and compassion they deserve during this time.” In a similar episode of violence, a man in Pennsylvania fatally shot several family members on Friday, before killing himself. • In the US, you can call or text the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org. title: Twelve killed and hundreds injured in Houthi attack at Riyadh airport
summary: Donald Trump evaluating whether US should join Saudi strikes against the Iran-backed Yemeni rebels
text: The latest attack on the international airport in Saudi Arabia’s capital of Riyadh killed 12 people and injured more than 300 others, civil aviation authorities said early on Sunday, with some in a critical condition. A Saudi-led coalition blamed Iran-backed Houthi rebels in neighbouring Yemen. A missile struck a King Khalid international airport complex housing terminals 3 and 4 for domestic flights, a regional official said, speaking on condition of anonymity because they weren’t authorised to speak to the media. A Saudi statement said the dead included four Saudi citizens as well as two Bangladeshi nationals, a Palestinian, a US citizen, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Syrian and a Sudanese. It said the injured were being treated at several hospitals. The US president, Donald Trump, said he was evaluating whether the US should join Saudi strikes against the Iran-backed Houthi rebels in neighbouring Yemen. “We may. We’re going to look at it,” Trump said. “We just found out about the recent attack. So we’ll make a decision. We move very quickly.” The US secretary of ⁠state, Marco ⁠Rubio, called the attacks “reprehensible” and said “they must stop ‌now”. One witness at the Riyadh airport reported hearing an explosion while waiting to board a flight, and another said they saw a strike that left people wounded. “I was on gate 403,” at the domestic terminal, the witness told the Agence France-Presse news agency. “I saw [gate] 401 hit, I saw injured [people] in front of my eyes. Everyone was running.” The relative of one injured person said they had been wounded in the shoulders and arms by shattered glass and taken to hospital. A projectile also fell near the King Fahd international airport in Dammam, according to the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis. The Dammam airport has become an important alternative to Riyadh amid the recent spate of attacks. There was no immediate statement from the rebels, who earlier Saturday accused Saudi Arabia of striking Sana’a international airport in the Houthi-held Yemeni capital. Schools in Riyadh will move to remote learning for a week, according to the education ministry, following the deadly attack. Saturday’s incident comes amid an escalation of missile strikes by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis ⁠on the kingdom. The airport has already been attacked twice this week, leaving four people dead and ‌others wounded, and ‌badly damaging an aircraft. The Houthis have repeatedly attacked Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers after a truce in their long-running war with Yemen’s Riyadh-backed government unravelled in July. The attack came as forces allied to the UN-recognised government in Yemen claim to have mounted a successful offensive to retake the Bab al-Mandab strait from Houthi rebels, but accounts vary as to whether the push has been repelled. A Houthi spokesperson said forces from the Saudi-backed government based in Aden “were targeted with a large number of ballistic missiles, artillery support and heavy weapons, resulting in the destruction of more than 22 armoured vehicles and the killing and wounding of dozens, including a number of commanders. “More than 30 ambulances arrived in Aden to transport the dead and wounded from the Saudi enemy’s mobilisations.” By contrast, the Saudi ambassador to Yemen, Mohammed al-Jaber, said: “Blessed Friday and victory for every Yemeni and Arab. Bab al-Mandab has been cleared of the remnants of the Houthi terrorist militia.” The exposed 5 sq mile (13 sq km) Perim Island straddles the strait, acting as a lookout point for all traffic from the Red Sea into the Gulf of Aden and towards the Indian Ocean. Aidarous al-Zubaidi, the president of the Southern Transitional Council (STC), one of the main political forces in the south of Yemen, claimed the island and coastal area had been recaptured from Houthi hands. An official military spokesperson for the UN-recognised government forces qualified the claim, saying only half the area had been recaptured so far. Waddah al-Dabish said newly established Houthi defensive lines had been broken on the land next to the strait, leading to the death of thousands of Houthi fighters. It is thought that as many as 500 Houthi fighters are stationed on the island, and Saudi Arabia is desperate to be able to report that the strait has been reclaimed to show that the land counteroffensive it launched at the beginning of the week is advancing. The report came as the United Nations’ special envoy to Yemen, Hans Grundberg, admitted to the UN security council in New York that Yemen – one of the poorest countries in the world – had lapsed back into full-scale war and said the first victims would be women and children. The Houthis seized control of the strait two weeks ago and said no Saudi-linked commercial traffic would be permitted to go through the narrow waterway. The Houthis are waging a war to remove Saudi influence from Yemen, and have been mounting missile attacks on Riyadh in support of this objective. There have been previous premature reports of military breakthroughs by the Saudi-backed Yemeni government since it launched its counteroffensive at the start of the week, but the recapture of the land by the strait and Perim Island (also known as Mayyun Island) is a military prize western governments desperately need.

title: Nine people, including children, dead after mass shooting in Pennsylvania
summary: Authorities say suspect among dead in house after standoff with police in Erie and there is no ongoing threat
text: A man fatally shot eight people, including a pregnant woman and children, at a Pennsylvania residence on Friday before killing himself, police say. The victims have not been publicly identified, but seven relatives and a family friend died in the rampage. At a Saturday news conference, Erie’s police chief, Rick Lorah, said it was premature to speculate about the suspected gunman’s motive but noted mental health may have played a role. Police discovered the killings about 5pm Friday when officers were called to a residence following reports of gunfire. Witnesses told authorities that they had seen an attacker with a gun outside the property before making his way inside. Responding officers discovered two women lying dead in the street, both having suffered gunshot wounds. Inside the home, police said they made a devastating discovery, finding six additional victims, including a five-year-old boy and a one-year-old girl, as well as the suspected assailant. Investigators believe the attacker died from a self-inflicted gunshot wound. Video footage showed the women arriving in distress at the residence. They paced outside, pounded on the door and tried to alert neighbors. Authorities believe the suspected shooter came out of the residence, exchanged words with the women and then fired at them. “They knew something was going on at that house. We have to figure out what that is,” Lorah said on Saturday. The suspect had a history with law enforcement, but its nature remains unclear. At the news conference, Erie officials also addressed criticism that they were slow to share details of the shooting with the public. Some of the family members who also lived at the residence had been away, according to Erie’s mayor, Daria Devlin. “We could not allow this to be received on the news, numbers of people, before we had the opportunity to speak with them,” she said. Lorah previously spoke about the scale of the mass shooting, describing the scene as among the most distressing and heartbreaking he had witnessed. “The loss of life is devastating and the circumstances we are working through are deeply disturbing,” Lorah said. He added: “Our hearts are with the victims, their families and everyone affected by this tragedy. There are no words that can adequately express the magnitude of the loss of life here.” Figures from the Gun Violence Archive indicate that the killings in Erie marked at least the 19th mass murder of the year. Such cases are defined as ones in which four or more victims are murdered. Many of those mass murders have been what are considered family annihilations, in which an attacker kills multiple close family members. The nonpartisan archive also indicated that the killings in Erie were among more than 500 mass shootings across the US since the beginning of January. Mass shootings are defined as cases in which four or more victims are shot whether fatally or non-fatally. Mass shootings for years have remained a persistent problem in the US, often intensifying public demands for stronger gun control measures at the federal level. Despite those calls, Congress has not enacted such restrictions sought over the years. • In the US, you can call or text the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org. In the UK and Ireland, Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123. In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found at befrienders.org

title: Four dead as Isaias weakens to post-tropical cyclone after striking Florida panhandle
summary: Some of deaths came from falling trees as half a million people without power and rain and flooding still a concern
text: At least four people were reported dead on Saturday amid Isaias after it made landfall late on Friday on Florida’s panhandle as a category 2 hurricane, according to authorities. The storm also took down trees, knocked out electricity for hundreds of thousands and flooded highways – but as Saturday evening approached, the region was reopening. Despite warnings of storm surges ahead of the storm, several major routes along the coast were open by daybreak on Saturday and free of downed trees and power lines typically seen after major hurricanes. Two of the deaths reported during Isaias occurred in Escambia county, Florida, and two others were reported in Alabama, as the storm moved inland, local officials said. Of those deaths, one each occurred in Escambia and Birmingham, Alabama, when trees fell on homes. Another person whose death was linked to Isaias in Alabama was attributed to a motor vehicle crash involving a downed tree in Barbour county, said Josh Johnson of the state’s emergency management agency. Another death connected to the storm involved a person found in a closed garage with a running generator in Escambia county. Four members of that person’s family have been transported to the hospital with carbon monoxide poisoning, the Escambia sheriff’s office said. “Don’t run any generators inside your home, it can be very, very hazardous,” Florida governor Ron DeSantis said in a press conference. In Alabama, governor Kay Ivey said Isaias – predicted to dissipate on Sunday – “cannot clear fast enough”. Meanwhile, though it had weakened on Saturday to a post-tropical cyclone as it passed through central Alabama, Isaias still posed flooding and tornado threats as it moved inland, forecasters and officials warned. Hurricane-force winds in the Florida panhandle blew the roof off a Pensacola hotel, and the city’s mayor said the airport “took some damage”. The storm flattened a boathouse in Destin and ripped away part of the facade of a high-rise in Panama City Beach. A worker in a condominium parking lot swept piles of the building’s insulation while others put back beach chairs that had been tossed about. “Remember, there can still be flooding from rising rivers,” Jared W Perdue, the secretary of Florida’s state transportation department, said at a news conference. “I’m just going to remind all of you – please, if there’s standing water or flowing water on top of a road, please do not drive through it. “It does not have to be that deep, and it can wash away your car, it can wash away a human, it can become very dangerous very quickly.” Nearly 550,000 customers were still without power across Florida, Alabama and Georgia on Saturday afternoon as those in the path of the storm began the cleanup process, according to PowerOutage.us. Though still high, the number of outages was down from more than 900,000 earlier on Saturday. Storm surge and tropical storm warnings associated with Isaias by then had been discontinued, the National Hurricane Center (NHC) warned there would still likely be “considerable impacts” associated with Isaias across much of southern Alabama, Florida’s panhandle and south-western Georgia. “Flash, urban and river flooding is possible across the region,” the NHC said in a Saturday-morning advisory, adding that there was a considerable potential for flash flooding and landslides across the southern Appalachians. “A risk for tornadoes will persist … through [Saturday] afternoon across parts of the eastern Florida panhandle, Georgia and the Carolinas.” Isaias through Sunday is expected to produce rainfall amounts of 4-8in across southern Alabama, Florida’s panhandle and Big Bend regions, and south-west Georgia. Localized totals up to 15in are possible, particularly within rain bands across the Florida panhandle and Big Bend. Across much of the remainder of the south-east US, rainfall amounts of 2-5in are expected, and localized higher amounts up to 10in are possible, especially across the southern Appalachians and coastal Carolinas. The hurricane’s maximum sustained winds were 105mph (169km/h). That was intense enough to sound like “a train whistle”, Tim Mowry told the Associated Press after enduring the storm as his home in Pensacola, Florida. Mowry described losing power on Friday afternoon but said could rely on a generator. He said his son tried to drive to his home after his place about 15 minutes away lost power but had to turn around because downed trees and power lines blocked the road. All things considered, Mowry said he was “really fortunate” with respect to how he fared during Isaias. Along Alabama’s Gulf coast, authorities in Mobile reported numerous downed trees and power lines. Maranie Adams, who rode out the storm with her family and their chickens in Gulf Shores, Alabama, said the winds rocked their home, but it was nothing like Hurricane Sally, which left water under their elevated house. “I feel very much more relieved today,” she said. Donald Trump has allowed the Federal Emergency Management Agency (Fema) to provide resources to Georgia to help grapple with the ongoing storm, including possible tornadoes, the agency said on Saturday. Several roads have already been blocked by fallen trees around Atlanta, local outlets have reported. Trump previously approved emergency declarations for Florida and Alabama ahead of the landfall of Hurricane Isaias. While the stronger El Niño seemed to limit the number of hurricanes in the Atlantic for the year so far, Isaias forming in October with maximum sustained winds of 105mph marked a stark contrast from historical trends. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (Noaa) predicted a quiet year in terms of hurricanes at the beginning of a season that officially begins annually on 1 June. Noaa anticipated between three and six hurricanes, well below the average of seven. An August forecast from Noaa cut the expected number to between two and six. Isais is one of the two latest-forming Atlantic hurricanes on record, tying a record set on 8 October 1905. Otherwise, the second-latest date for the first Atlantic hurricane was 11 September – in 2002 and 2013. None of the eight previous named storms of the 2026 Atlantic season intensified above tropical storm status. The Associated Press contributed reporting

title: Skies across the UK illuminated by the northern lights
summary: Though mostly visible near the Arctic Circle, the natural phenomenon dazzled sky-gazers as far south Devon, Hampshire and Kent
text: The northern lights illuminated the skies across the UK on Friday and Saturday evening. Sky-gazers as far south as Devon, Hampshire and Kent were treated to the dazzling natural phenomenon, also known as the aurora borealis. The Met Office said sightings could continue during clear skies until Tuesday. Such occurrences are mostly visible near the Arctic Circle and northern Scotland. The aurora borealis is a natural light display in Earth’s sky, driven by solar activity and geomagnetic storms interacting with the upper atmosphere. Sightings will remain possible until Tuesday across Scotland and similar geomagnetic longitudes during clear skies, the Met Office said. Aurora displays occur when charged particles collide with gases in the Earth’s atmosphere around the magnetic poles. As they collide, light is emitted at various wavelengths, creating colourful displays in the sky. According to the Met Office, the sun emits charged particles known as solar wind, which travel at bout 1m mph. The forecaster said: “When these particles interact with Earth’s magnetic field – especially when the solar wind’s polarity is opposite to Earth’s – they are funnelled toward the magnetic poles. “As these energetic particles collide with gases in the upper atmosphere, they release energy in the form of light. Oxygen produces green and, at higher altitudes, rare red auroras, while nitrogen creates blue and purple hues.” Last year, experts said 2026 will be a peak year for aurora-spotting, as the sun has been in a heightened state of activity as part of its 11-year natural cycle.

title: Despair after 200-year-old ‘grandmother’ tree toppled for Trump’s border wall: ‘It crushes your heart’
summary: Protesters spent months occupying an ancient cottonwood. Then a tense standoff with US border patrol came to a head
text: A 200-year-old cottonwood tree near the US-Mexico border, known as the “grandmother”, has been destroyed to make way for the construction of Donald Trump’s border wall, despite a months-long effort by protesters trying to save it. In late July, land defenders began a tree-sit in the ghost town of Lochiel, Arizona, taking turns occupying a platform high in the tree’s canopy. The group remained there for more than 70 days. Then, on Monday at dawn, more than 80 federal agents swarmed the protesters’ camp, which is located on private land, making arrests and preventing people from reaching the cottonwood. Some agents in a steel basket on an extendable crane lift forcibly removed the person in the tree platform, according to videos and photos shared on social media and descriptions of people there at the time. Others were shoved and tackled as they tried to rush toward the tree to prevent its destruction, according to witnesses. Contractors with Fisher Sand & Gravel, a company building this section of wall, then used an excavator to push over the tree, which cracked and crashed to the earth. Land defenders shrieked, cried and yelled at the federal agents. “Seeing that – it crushes your heart,” said Erick Meza, the Sierra Club’s Borderlands coordinator who has been working to save the trees for months, beginning with a series of letters to US Customs and Border Protection (CBP). “That tree brought a lot of people together,” he said. Now, he added, “there’s a community response of outrage. People are pissed off.” The cottonwood’s toppling was filmed by a team from Turning Point USA, the far-right political group, who appeared to be embedded with border patrol and allowed free access to roam throughout the closed off public road. One of the land defenders had scaled another ancient cottonwood tree situated right on the border with Mexico. On Thursday, CBP and Mexican police, who have been present for several days and visibly working with American authorities, removed the tree-sitter’s platform, food and water supplies, according to Alex Chabbott, a land defender who has been present at the camp on and off for over a month. Late on Friday, the tree-sitter came down on their own volition after not being resupplied for several days. The agents involved include border patrol officers, part of CBP, and a special forces tactical unit called Bortac, whose self-described purpose is to “respond to terrorist threats”. The tree-sit began shortly after contractors knocked over and killed three other ancient cottonwood trees nearby on 27 July. Two 30ft-tall walls are being built throughout this area, known as the San Rafael valley, a remote and once idyllic high elevation prairie where the movie Oklahoma was filmed. The valley, and the Patagonia and Huachuca mountains on either side of it, form one of the most important regional wildlife corridors between the US and Mexico, providing passage to animals including jaguars, ocelots, bears and even beavers and porcupines in recent years. Already, government contractors have finished 88 miles (140km) of secondary wall, which is a second 30ft fence set at some distance from a primary wall of the same height. Another 444 miles of secondary wall are under construction, according to DHS, much of that in Arizona, using billions of dollars allocated by Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act. Protesters say that construction in the area is progressing rapidly, 24 hours a day. In recent days, Fisher Sand & Gravel has completed the secondary wall, which includes placing 30ft steel panels within a trench filled with rebar and cement, along a part of the private property where the camp is located, including up to the point where the tree stood. These trees, which depend on a regular supply of water underground, are a hallmark of riparian forests, an endangered ecotype throughout Arizona and the south-west, said Russ McSpadden, an advocate with the Center for Biological Diversity. The ecological importance of these trees is one of the animating factors behind the land defenders. Water use for wall construction has depleted wells throughout the south-west, threatening natural features such as Quitobaquito Springs. CBP does not say how much current construction uses, but in 2008 it estimated a smaller wall nearby could use up to 710,00 gallons per mile for construction; the current project likely uses more, as it is larger. ‘We are starting a movement’ Since Monday, dozens of land defenders have been arrested, many for entering the road between the private property and the border, which was ordered closed by federal authorities in late September due to wall construction. Protesters have been doing prayers in the road near the tree every morning. Some of those arrested were physically hit and came back with bruises and black eyes, Chabbott claimed. Several more people attempted to use nonviolent tactics to halt or delay construction, including one woman who locked herself to a cement truck on 7 August, according to videos shared on social media. The protester was sprayed in the face with mace and wrestled by several agents, and her limbs forced into painful positions, according to witnesses and social media videos. The truck was later driven away while the land defender was still attached, and cut from the vehicle later that evening, according to witnesses. She is now in custody, according to what authorities have told the land defenders’ lawyers. Julia Butterfly Hill, who spent two years living in a redwood in California’s Humboldt county in the late 1990s, said she was horrified to see how roughly border patrol treated this woman on a livestreamed video, she said. This land defender’s courage and commitment to nonviolent resistance in the face of brutality “brought tears to my eyes”, Butterfly Hill said. “She’s a hero of the highest order.” CBP did not respond to a request for comment about this and other clashes, but has previously said that walls in areas like this will help combat unauthorized immigration. The sheriff of Santa Cruz county, David Hathaway, who did not respond to a request for comment for this story, has previously said a wall in this area is senseless since this remote valley has no history of significant illegal activity. Fisher Sand & Gravel did not respond to a request for comment. In a press conference on 8 October, Adelita Grijalva, a congresswoman who represents the area, said she was “heartbroken” about the loss of the “grandmother” trees, and said she plans to try to introduce a bill that will revoke the DHS’s ability to waive any and all laws in building border infrastructure. The tree-sit began shortly after contractors knocked over and killed two other ancient cottonwood trees nearby on 27 July. In felling the tree, the contractors and federal agents “try to break us, but we are not broken”, said Kate Scott, one of the leaders of the tree-sit. “We are starting a movement, and we’re not going anywhere. We are rooted, like the grandmothers.”

title: Trump says Ukraine needs a new leader after diesel deal with Russia
summary: US president suggests Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, has not done enough to end war
text: Donald Trump has said Ukraine needs “a new leader”, a day after making a deal with Vladimir Putin to buy large quantities of Russian diesel. The US president suggested Volodymyr Zelenskyy has not done enough to end the war with Russia and blamed him for high diesel prices in the US. “I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal because he could have made many deals and for some reason he never does,” Trump said. Trump made the comments as Russia launched deadly strikes on civilians in Ukraine, which Zelenskyy said were a “thanks” to Trump for the diesel deal. The Ukrainian president has expressed outrage at the agreement announced by Trump on Friday, which the US president said was needed to reduce diesel prices, and comes ahead of November’s midterm elections in which fuel costs are a key voter issue. The deal, which appeared to blindside Kyiv as it was announced while Ukrainian negotiators were in Miami for peace talks, was described by Zelenskyy as a “gift” to Russia’s president. He said Russia would use the money it raised from the fuel sales to invest in its war and that “any easing of sanctions” would play into Russia’s hands, “allowing it to kill more, wage war for longer”. That prediction was realised hours later, when Ukrainian officials announced that a barrage of Russian strikes on the country’s south-east early on Saturday had killed 20 people, including three children. “Today, Russia expressed its thanks for the lifting of sanctions on diesel exports by dropping five glide bombs on residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia,” Zelenskyy said on social media on Saturday. “Last night confirmed once again that in Russia, they take any easing of pressure to mean they can keep fighting, to mean they can keep dropping bombs on cities. Different signals are needed,” he said. There were also “large-scale power outages” in the capital, Kyiv, the country’s largest private energy provider said. Andy Burnham reiterated his “complete solidarity” in a call with Volodymyr Zelenskyy and the leaders agreed to meet in person in the coming days to continue talks. The prime minister said he recognised the past day had been “difficult for Ukraine” and the two talked about the importance of keeping up pressure on Russia, No 10 said. In stark contrast to Zelenskyy’s open frustration with Trump, a Kremlin readout of Friday’s call between the US president and Putin was glowing, with the Russian ⁠news agency Interfax ⁠quoting an aide as saying it was “very substantive and friendly”. “Neither wanted to be the first to hang up,” the Kremlin foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov said of the two leaders. “They hung up simultaneously, literally at the same time.” Zelenskyy has previously said Putin is playing games with Trump. The diesel deal disrupts four years of western financial pressure on Moscow and leaves Kyiv’s allies in Europe and Nato scrambling to adapt their sanctions plan. The EU’s top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, said the diesel deal “provides Moscow with more revenues to wage war”. “This is not the time to ease pressure on Russia, and Europe won’t,” she said on Saturday. “On Monday, EU foreign ministers intend to approve the biggest set of sanctions listings targeting Russia’s war machine since the start of the war.” She was referring to plans to formally add 1,600 new individuals and entities to the EU’s sanctions blacklist. Major European governments have attempted to balance their diplomatic and trade relationships with a mercurial Trump and their support for Ukraine. The German government spokesperson Stefan Kornelius said Berlin “remains committed to the sanctions imposed on Russia and is working with its European partners on further sanctions”, adding that support for Ukraine “remains unwavering”. Ulf Kristersson, the Swedish prime minister, expressed “regret” at the US agreement, saying energy revenues were “a vital source of funding Russia’s war of aggression”. Zelenskyy said on Saturday that Russia “must feel its losses” and has promised to respond. In the Russian-occupied ‌Luhansk ‌region, Ukrainian attacks in the past 24 hours had killed four ⁠civilians and wounded ⁠five, the region’s ‌Russian-installed governor, Leonid Pasechnik, said on Saturday. Zelenskyy said that Ukraine was ready to take “de-escalatory steps” in the war but only if Russia did the same. Russia’s fuel production has become a key point of contention between Zelenskyy and Trump, who has attempted to stop Ukraine from bombing Russian refineries, which he says exacerbates a global diesel shortage. The Ukrainian leader has rejected such requests unless Russia stops attacking Ukraine’s energy infrastructure. The Financial Times reported that during the talks in Miami, Trump’s envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner raised the possibility that US intelligence sharing could be cut off if Kyiv did not halt the strikes.

title: US man shoots off-duty ICE agent who allegedly attacked him and daughter
summary: ICE official, who was sleeping on man’s lawn and appeared ‘intoxicated’, faces felony charges, California police say
text: A 72-year-old man shot an off-duty Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) official in California early on Friday morning after the “intoxicated and agitated” official assaulted him and his daughter on their property, local authorities allege. The Fresno police department said that the ICE official was receiving medical care after being shot in the midsection. The official, identified as David Gonzalez, is facing felony charges for assaulting the father-daughter duo, Fresno police said. It was not immediately clear for how long Gonzalez had been with ICE and what exactly he did for ICE. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees ICE, referred all questions about Gonzalez to Fresno police. According to Fresno police, at about 3am, a woman found Gonzalez sleeping on her and her father’s front lawn. She told her 72-year-old father, who was inside, and then attempted to shoo Gonzalez off their property. But when Gonzalez was awakened, “he appeared intoxicated and agitated” and physically assaulted the 72-year-old father, forcing him to the ground, police said. When the father’s daughter tried to intervene, Gonzalez physically attacked and took her to the ground as well, police said. The father feared for his and his daughter’s physical safety and shot Gonzalez once, police said. Shortly thereafter, the daughter’s boyfriend, an off-duty police officer, arrived and placed handcuffs on Gonzalez. “It is unknown at this time why Gonzalez was in the area at the time of the [shooting], but it has been confirmed he was off-duty and alone,” local authorities said. Fresno police on Friday said the investigation into the shooting was continuing while Gonzalez was in custody and receiving medical treatment. He was booked with battery likely to cause great bodily injury, felony vandalism and battery. The father and daughter were not booked with any crimes as they recovered from injuries of their own, police said. The confrontation that led to Gonzalez’s shooting is one of the latest cases in which federal ICE officials have fallen under scrutiny for alleged criminal behavior. ICE has also been met with nationwide criticism throughout Donald Trump’s second term for the agency’s aggressive arrest, detention and deportation tactics. Lawmakers have also criticized ICE’s hiring practices amid the agency’s rush to bring on more officials to carry out the Trump administration’s mass deportation agenda. In August 2025, an ICE supervisor filed a whistleblower complaint to the DHS office of inspector general alleging that the agency was skirting basic vetting and violating federal rules during its hiring spree. In July, an ICE officer shot and killed a Colombian immigrant in Biddeford, Maine. The ICE officer in question had reportedly been a recent hire by the agency despite an alleged history of violence and mental health problems. Meanwhile, in April, a longtime ICE officer in Cincinnati was arrested after allegedly lying to DHS about domestic violence allegations against him. Local news reports say police had been called more than 20 times in the past to years to the home he shared with his girlfriend. The Ohio Immigrant Alliance, a pro-immigrant group, released a report in August documenting more than 150 federal immigration officials accused of abuse and crimes. One of the latest entries in their report cited allegations that an ICE official reportedly broke into an ex-girlfriend’s apartment in south-east Louisiana.

title: Our place in the sun: Australia’s uptake of solar panels is already through the roof. How much higher could it get?
summary: Sunshine, government subsidies and high power prices are driving record solar installations
text: Zoom in on satellite pictures of the Melbourne postcode 3029 and one feature becomes glaringly obvious – there are lots and lots of solar panels on lots and lots of roofs. “If you walk along the streets, it’s actually hard to see a house without solar panels,” says Saajidh Nizam, a software engineer who lives in Tarneit with his wife, two children and a 6.6kWh solar system on the roof. This western Melbourne postcode has more rooftop solar than anywhere else in Australia. More than 28,000 systems have been installed there since 2001, according to Australia’s Clean Energy Regulator. Australia generates more electricity per person from solar panels than anywhere else in the world, making postcode 3029 the poster child for Australia’s residential solar sector. There are about 4m homes and small businesses with rooftop solar – about 36% of households have a system – and the country’s enthusiasm for the photovoltaic panels is only building with 2026 on track to be a record year of installations. But the copious amounts of sunshine hitting Australia compared with other countries isn’t the only reason solar is booming. For more than 20 years, the Australian government has been issuing certificates to homes and businesses that erect rooftop solar, cutting the upfront costs. The scheme has been extended this month to include larger systems on corporate premises. Tristan Edis, the director of analysis and advisory at research and analytics firm Green Energy Markets, says relatively high electricity prices together with less onerous regulations than other countries, in particular the US, are two reasons why Australians have adopted solar so enthusiastically. The other is the types of homes built around the country with “low-density housing and a lot of roof space, making [solar] easier to install,” Edis says. Sign up to get climate and environment editor Adam Morton’s Clear Air column as a free newsletter According to the Clean Energy Council, an industry group representing the renewables sector, in the second quarter of this year, records were broken in every Australian state for installations, with 102,234 systems installed on roofs – the highest quarter on record. Ten years ago, rooftop solar was generating less than 3% of the country’s electricity while coal supplied 75%. In the last 12 months, electricity from rooftops supplied almost 14%, while coal was down to 50%. “There are more rooftop solar systems in Australia than there are swimming pools in backyards,” said a spokesperson for the Australian Energy Market Operator. They said uptake of solar had “fundamentally changed the electricity system” and “given millions of consumers a more active role in how they produce and use electricity, and now store it with the influx of residential batteries”. Solar had led to demand for grid electricity falling and wholesale electricity prices reaching zero, or even going negative, in the middle of the day, they said. In winter, with fewer sunshine hours, rooftop solar still covered 10% of the electricity used in the national electricity market, which supplies more than 85% of the population. In the national market, rooftop solar now routinely supplies more than 40% of the electricity used during the middle of the day; on some days, it peaks above 60%. To cope with all of that solar power, new rules have been introduced requiring electricity retailers in most areas to offer customers three hours of free electricity every day. A report from the government’s corporate watchdog found households with solar and batteries had bills that were between 20% and 52% lower than regular electricity customers, and households who joined a virtual power plant – where the battery’s output can be linked with other households and controlled by a retailer – had bills 57% to 63% lower. Now, with the sudden arrival of home batteries – supported by a federal government program that has seen half a million installed since July last year – Edis says the traditional evening peak for electricity use is being flattened as solar-charged batteries kick into gear. “That is going to destroy the economics of fossil fuel generators,” Edis says. How much bigger? But how much bigger could Australia’s rooftop solar boom get? The government agency that operates the main electricity market produces a blueprint every two years for the most likely development of the electricity system. This blueprint forecasts that the capacity of rooftop solar systems will grow from its current level of 20GW to 87GW by 2050 – meaning 56% of homes would have rooftop solar systems, “driven by ever-falling costs”. Two-thirds of those homes would also have batteries. If that change materialised, the energy market operator said rooftop solar alone would be supplying about 27% of the country’s electricity. The challenge, the operator said, was “not simply accommodating more solar panels but making the most of the electricity they produce”. Edis’s own projections have suggested even higher amounts of rooftop solar could be possible. He says a typical 10kW solar system in Australia can produce more than enough electricity for an average household, even if they run an electric car. “Their demand for electricity is almost entirely taken care of by their solar and their battery. Residential electricity consumption disappears from the grid,” he says. A rising motivator for Australians buying solar systems, says Edis, is the advent of electric cars. “There’s a relationship developing between electric cars and solar. For a lot of Australians, charging up their car will be incredibly cheap,” he says. Some electricity system analysts, including Edis, point to commercial buildings and rental units as a “missing middle” where, with better rules, rooftop solar could grow even further. ‘A billion solar citizens’ This week in Fiji at a preparatory meeting before November’s UN global climate talks in Turkey, Australia became the first country to endorse a global voluntary pledge to double the number of homes with rooftop solar from 150m to 300m by 2030. “Rooftop solar is the sleeping giant of global climate diplomacy,” says Heidi Lee Douglas, the chief executive of Solar Citizens, an advocacy group representing more than 200,000 rooftop solar owners. “This is going to create a billion solar citizens,” says Douglas, who was in Fiji for the announcement. “[Rooftop solar] is politically popular, and it appeals to people because of the cost of living benefits and now, with energy security issues, governments are more motivated. “A lot of energy ministers are going to sit up and take notice of this. Rooftop solar has the potential to do so much good but it has been so underrated. We know it is safe and it is a known quantity, and it is easy to deliver quickly.” Solar Citizens was set up in Australia 16 years ago to advocate for solar owners and create a new political economy around rooftop systems. The charity is working with civil society groups in Japan, Taiwan, Pakistan, Vanuatu, Malaysia and Indonesia to set up “solar citizen movements” and build advocacy campaigns, says Douglas. In Australia, Douglas is pushing to triple the amount of rooftop solar connected to storage by 2030 and double the amount of rooftop solar capacity over the next eight years. Back in Tarneit, Saajidh Nizam says he is doing the sums on adding a battery to the solar system on his roof. “It’s a good idea,” he says, looking around his record-setting suburb. “We’re not putting as much pressure on the grid, and we’re trying to be a bit more self-sustaining and a bit less damaging on the environment. “We’re doing good on that front.”

title: Out of the rubble and on to the beach: Gaza’s junior surf lifesavers return to the waves after three years of war
summary: Just 15 of the program’s 45 Nippers have been found since the conflict disrupted it
text: As a group of smiling children in yellow and black rash vests bundled towards the beach near the Al-Shati refugee camp through concrete alleys lined with rubbish, rubble and the occasional bullet hole, Hassan Al-Habeel felt joy again. The Palestinian man, in his 40s, oversaw the return of Gaza Nippers, Palestine’s chapter of the popular Australian junior surf life saving program, last month after three years. The group of Gazan boys and girls spent the day catching waves, dancing and playing in the sand and sun, footage seen by Guardian Australia showed. But the return of Gaza’s Nippers program was a moment tinged with sadness for Al-Habeel, who trained at North Steyne Royal Surf Lifesaving Club in Sydney’s northern beaches over the 2019-20 summer. Of the 45 children involved in the original program, 15 have been found alive. The rest remain missing, uncontactable or have died as a result of the conflict. One of them was Ali, Al-Habeel’s 15-year-old son. Unable to access food and medicine due to blockades and bombings, Ali died in his father’s arms before he was able to reach the closest hospital. “I wanted to prepare [Ali] to be a lifeguard, so when he gets older, he would teach children how to swim on the shores of Gaza,” Al-Habeel said in the footage. “But unfortunately, the war took Ali from us as it took many children in Gaza. “And now I see children play without Ali, which is difficult for me, but what can we do? That’s the decree of God.” No safe place for children Devised on the shores of Sydney in 2017, the Gaza program was able to run its first summer season in mid-2023 after the pandemic set it back. But by October, it was indefinitely suspended as Israel began its invasion into Gaza after Hamas militants attacked southern Israel, killing 1,200 people, mostly civilians. Since then, Israel’s relentless military offensive has killed 73,000 Palestinians, mostly civilians, wounding many more and reducing swathes of Gaza to rubble. During the conflict, Al-Habeel and others coordinating the program tried to track down the children but some had fled south toward the Egyptian border, or couldn’t be reached. Shamikh Badra, the program’s co-founder who lives in Australia, says he worked tirelessly with Al-Habeel and others still in Gaza to confirm whether the children were still alive. Word of mouth from friends and family still in Gaza gave Badra clues as to their whereabouts – or worse. “We waited to make sure, if we found some of them were killed, we would confirm,” Badra tells Guardian Australia. “I can’t confirm anything without evidence because it’s not easy to declare something like that.” In the end, 15 were able to be contacted and were invited to again take to the waves. The original program targeted particularly disadvantaged kids who had been injured or lost family members in previous conflicts, but Badra says making the selection in the midst of the current war was even harder. “We said, ‘Let’s invite some children who have difficult circumstances like [before],’” he says. “Some of my friends told me all the children are suffering now, not like before … it’s no safe place.” There were other logistical challenges. Many of the rash vests, flags and flotation devices donated to them by the North Steyne RSLC had been lost, stolen or destroyed. The Northern Beaches Committee for Palestine raised funds to send to Al-Habeel so he could buy body boards, gold and black rash vests and other equipment. The final hurdle was safety. Badra says he and Al-Habeel spent months trying to find the right time to return without endangering the children. Even after the ceasefire was agreed to last October, intermittent bombings and increased tensions repeatedly forced the launch date back. Eventually, 25 September 2026 was marked in the calendar. As exciting as the moment was, thousands of miles away, Badra waited nervously to hear news of its success. “I was worried all this day. I was waiting, calling the team. I wanted to know, how are they? I wanted this day to be finished and people and children to return and come back to their home safe.” A ‘ray of hope’ in Gaza Christine Stewart Gibbs, the former North Steyne RSLC president and now a member of the Northern Beaches Committee for Palestine, says seeing the footage of happy children in Gaza was a “miracle”. “Here in the middle of war-torn Gaza – with buildings bombed out and a lot of rubble, and difficulty moving around, and still a lack of food and lack of healthcare – for Hassan to pull together the program with his helpers and bring the kids together was fantastic,” she says. “There’s no good news coming out of Gaza, and this felt like a ray of hope.” The plan is for the Gaza Nippers program to return again next summer. “To enjoy, to laugh, to swim … [is] something simple … but in Gaza, it’s so hard and difficult and dangerous,” Badra says. “If we surrender to the sadness and we be negative, we can’t help the people in Gaza. “This message is for the United Nations and all the world: these children need to live as all the children around the world. They need to live in peace. We should not leave them isolated under the pressure of occupation and siege and blockade.”

title: ‘We cannot accept foxes as part of our landscape’: the plan to save Australia’s threatened wildlife
summary: Draft national strategy accepts the wily invasive species can’t be eradicated but outlines steps to protect native animals most at risk
text: They dart across playgrounds on dainty paws, sneak into back yard coops to eat suburban chickens and kill more than a million native animals every day. The European red fox – a wily invasive species – is “one of the most impactful threats” for native mammals, says Sarah Legge, a professor at Charles Darwin University and author of a new draft plan to curb their predation. “Australia has the worst record of mammal extinctions of any country in the world – around 40 species – and the overwhelming cause for those extinctions has been predation by foxes and cats,” Legge says. If the federal environment department moves ahead with the plan, Australia would have its first updated national effort to halt the impact of foxes on native wildlife in nearly two decades. Legge says there have been dramatic advancements in understanding how to combat foxes since the last plan was released in 2008. Populations are hard to gauge, but estimates put the number about 1.7 million spread across the country, from central Queensland down through New South Wales to Victoria and South Australia. Populations are also thriving in Western Australia. All those foxes are hungry, with studies estimating foxes kill upwards of 367 million native mammals, 111 million birds, 88 million reptiles and “countless” invertebrates and frogs each year. The draft plan acknowledges that foxes are far too numerous to eradicate but steps can be taken to protect the species most at risk. These include increased funding for safe havens such as fox-free islands and fenced, predator-proof zones. The plan also calls for collaboration and “legislative harmony” between states and the federal government. “I’m not pretending that we can get rid of foxes from across the continent any time soon,” Legge says. “But we can definitely stop native wildlife population loss and extinction.” Rob Brewster, the rewilding manager at the Invasive Species Council, says ecologists have spent the past 18 years learning everything they can about foxes and the species they hunt. • Sign up to get climate and environment editor Adam Morton’s Clear Air column as a free newsletter A dozen key species have been identified as extremely susceptible to fox predation, including the critically endangered Gilbert’s potoroo; the endangered eastern quoll; endangered eastern barred and western barred bandicoots; and species of bettongs, hare-wallabies and the Tasmanian pademelon. Seven species of freshwater turtles are on the list, too. Researchers have said for nearly a decade that without urgent action, all face the threat of extinction. “It’s not climate change, it’s not habitat loss, those things are all bad … but the key driver of these extinctions is foxes and cats,” Brewster says. “And unfortunately the trajectory for a lot of our native mammals is still downward.” The Invasive Species Council is impressed with the long-term plan, which would roll out over the next three decades. But Brewster says it would need to build heavily on what, until this point, has been a scattershot approach more akin to “hurling baits out of car windows” than a nationally coordinated campaign. And that takes money. “We really like the bold, 30-year goal, which is a mission that is aimed at guaranteeing the long-term survival of all native species threatened by foxes,” he says. “But if there’s no dedicated funding streams … then this plan will not work.” The environment department estimates the total cost, if all actions are fully implemented, will be about $175m over the first five years, or about $35m annually. The spend on fox abatement now is only $5m to $7m. But, the plan notes, foxes are thought to cause about $190m in damage to Australian biodiversity every year, meaning the expense will more than pay for itself in environmental benefits. The department cites the 30-year nature of the plan as an essential timeline when asked about government support for such funding, saying the threat of invasive species requires “sustained action over many years to achieve measurable and lasting improvements in wildlife populations”. “Threat abatement plans play an important role in coordinating research, management and other actions necessary to reverse the decline of native species and prevent further extinctions,” a spokesperson says. Bronwyn Hradsky, a senior research fellow and ecologist at the University of Melbourne, agrees tackling invasive species requires comprehensive and lasting support. “If you’ve started fox control you’re basically committed to continuing it, and you’re looking at really substantial, long-term funding,” she says. “I think in parts of Australia we’ve got some of our amazing native species only because of our fox and cat control to date. “A plan like this that pulls it all together, and aims higher and further, is really valuable.” Matthew Rees, a research scientist at the CSIRO, says it’s not feasible to completely eradicate foxes on the mainland, but it is possible to reduce their negative impact on the ecosystem. “Threatened species can persist under fox predation and recent research has made strong progress in uncovering the factors which promote this,” he says. “Fox management has traditionally focused on lethal control usually through poison baiting, which continues to be important. But the draft plan broadens focus by also considering indirect control methods, which can be more feasible and cost-effective.” Brewster acknowledges that while foxes may be cute, researchers and the government need to retain the social licence to take the action needed to rein them in, for the benefit of wildlife populations that have been here long before they arrived. “It’s really scary because people are falling in love with the only thing they’re seeing, and they’re forgetting about native wildlife,” he says. “And if you don’t see your native wildlife because it’s all been eaten by foxes, then you’ll probably end up loving what killed them. “If we’re going to save our wildlife, we cannot have people out there who accept foxes as part of our landscape.”

title: Man dies after jumping into tiger enclosure at Yorkshire zoo
summary: Police say man was pronounced dead at the scene after being attacked by tiger
text: A man has died after being attacked by a tiger after jumping into its enclosure at a zoo in Yorkshire, police have said. Emergency services were contacted shortly after 1.30pm on Saturday when the man entered the enclosure at Yorkshire Wildlife Park, near Doncaster, and was set upon by the tiger. He was pronounced dead at the scene, South Yorkshire police said, adding his family had been informed. Videos circulating online appear to show a man being pawed at and grappled by a tiger in an enclosure. A police spokesperson said the tiger attacked the man and inflicted “serious injury”. “Emergency services attended and sadly, despite the best efforts of medical personnel, the man was pronounced dead at the scene,” they added. “Regarding rumours surrounding the condition of the tiger, the animal was uninjured and remained in the enclosure following the incident and there is no wider risk to the public.” The force urged people not to share “distressing” video footage of the attack, circulating on social media. Yorkshire Wildlife Park said a “serious incident” occurred inside the enclosure. It said in a statement: “Our emergency response procedures were immediately activated, and emergency services are currently attending the scene. “We are working closely with the authorities to ascertain exactly what happened.” It added that the “safety and wellbeing of visitors, staff and animals remain our highest priority”. Yorkshire Wildlife Park opened in 2009, with the Land of the Tigers attraction opening in 2011. The attraction is on a purpose-built two-acre reserve for Amur tigers, an endangered subspecies with about 500 left in the wild. Photos of the enclosure on the park’s website shows a high walkway for visitors and fencing above the section where the tigers can roam. A Yorkshire ambulance service spokesperson said it sent a number of resources to the scene including two ambulances, Yorkshire air ambulance and a doctor.

title: Christa Pike out of hospital and back in prison after botched execution attempt
summary: Pike’s lawyers said she is back in same prison she’s lived in for last 30 years and will continue to receive medical care
text: Christa Pike has been discharged from the hospital after surviving Tennessee’s botched 30 September attempt to execute her by lethal injection and is back in prison, her lawyers said on Saturday. Pike, 50, returned to the Deborah K Johnson rehabilitation center, where she has been imprisoned for the last three decades, her attorneys, Stephen Ferrell, Luke Ihnen, Randy Spivey and Kelly Gleason, said in a statement. “She is grateful to the first responders and her medical team for their care in these extraordinary circumstances,” Pike’s lawyers added. “She is continuing to receive medical care at the prison, and we will continue to track her recovery.” Saturday’s update about Pike came 10 days after the death row prisoner was given two doses of pentobarbital, a lethal injection drug, in what proved to be a failed execution attempt. She was hospitalized after surviving the botched execution and was declared brain dead on Monday. But in a shocking turnaround, on Thursday her lawyer said that she was “up and walking” – though she remained “somewhat foggy” and wasn’t able to use her arms very much. Pike said that her arms were burning during the failed execution and asked if it was supposed to feel that way. Witnesses present in the chamber said that “nothing was normal” while officials have maintained that they followed every step of Tennessee’s approved execution protocol. There has been no official explanation about why Pike survived the execution. Medical experts speculate that perhaps some or much of the drug missed her vein and went into surrounding tissue, that one of her veins blew, that the drug was faulty, or a combination of such factors. Her lawyers months earlier had flagged that Pike’s veins were problematic. Pike was convicted in 1995 for the torture and murder of Colleen Slemmer, then 18 and her classmate at Knoxville Job Corps. According to court filings, Pike, who was also 19 at the time, was worried Slemmer was trying to take her boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, then 17. Shipp and Pike were convicted of taking Slemmer into a wooded part of the University of Tennessee campus and murdering her. She was given the death penalty, and Shipp was sentenced to life in prison because he was younger than 18. After Slemmer’s murder, Pike was diagnosed with bipolar and post-traumatic stress disorders, her attorneys said. “It took me numerous years to even realize the gravity of what I’d done,” Pike said in an earlier petition for clemency. “Even more to accept how many lives I affected. I took the life of someone’s child, sister, friend. It sickens me now to think I had the ability to commit such a crime.” Pike’s survival of the botched execution has shocked many in the US and overseas and galvanized critics of the death penalty. Tennessee’s top prison official has announced his resignation. Meanwhile, the state’s governor, Bill Lee, has paused executions in Tennessee for the rest of the year. And Florida’s governor, Ron DeSantis, on Friday canceled a planned lethal injection execution in the state. But they continue elsewhere. For instance, the Pentagon confirmed on Thursday that it planned to livestream the execution by firing squad in December of former army psychiatrist Nidal Hassan, who killed 13 people at Texas’s Fort Hood, prompting condemnation from the United Nations. Donald Trump on Saturday said Hassan “was vicious – he was violent” and that he would “make a decision” about the plans to livestream his execution. “There are two thoughts: don’t show it and show,” the president remarked. “Because you know by showing it, maybe other people won’t be doing what he did. So I’ll make a decision ultimately. I know what the military would like to do, but we’ll make a decision.”

title: Thousands gather in London to express support for Palestinians after three years of ‘genocide’
summary: Twenty arrested in first march since Ed Miliband declared UK’s position was that Israel’s occupation of West Bank was unlawful
text: Thousands of people have gathered in central London to express their support for Palestinians after three years of “genocide” carried out against them by Israel. The demonstrators, many wearing keffiyehs and holding Palestine flags, gathered on the Embankment at midday on Saturday. Some carried placards reading “End the genocide” and “Free Palestine” as they marched towards parliament. A bride and groom appeared to be among those in attendance and a two-minute silence was held to reflect on the lives lost in Gaza. The Metropolitan police said 20 arrests had been made, including for criminal damage after demonstrators climbed on to the Battle of Britain memorial, having Palestine Action placards, making a Nazi salute and assaulting police as officers made arrests. Protesters were calling for the UK government to stop supplying arms to Israel, which various bodies – including the UN, Amnesty International, B’Tselem and Physicians for Human Rights, the latter two of which are Israeli-based – have said is committing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza. A ceasefire was declared a year ago but Israeli airstrikes have continued in Gaza. In the last year, the overall death toll has risen by a further 1,400 people. Settlers have also ramped up their attacks against Palestinians in the West Bank. According to UN figures, 230 Palestinians were killed in the West Bank by Israeli forces and settlers in 2025. Husam Zomlot, the Palestinian ambassador to the UK, shared a video from the march on social media. “Three years on, Israel’s atrocities in Gaza and the West Bank continue, and so does the solidarity of the British people. Louder, bigger and not going anywhere. Thank you all,” he said. By Saturday afternoon, organisers said 250,000 people were at the march. The Met have imposed conditions on the event – which is organised by the Palestine Coalition, which has organised more than 30 mass demonstrations since October 2023, with a counter-protest by Stop The Hate – to “minimise the risk of serious disruption to communities”. The Met posted on X saying: “The front of the procession has now entered Whitehall where a rally will take place. “Several arrests have been made so far including a woman and a man with placards declaring support for proscribed organisation Palestine Action. “We have also arrested a number of protesters on suspicion of criminal damage after they climbed on to the Battle of Britain memorial on Victoria Embankment.” The national march is the first held since the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, announced sweeping sanctions on trade with Israeli settlements and declared the UK government would take the official position that Israel’s occupation of the West Bank was unlawful in its entirety. He also told the Commons that settler terrorists supported by Benjamin Netanyahu’s government are committing ethnic cleansing in the West Bank. At Labour party conference last month, Miliband appeared to reference the marches, which at their peak regularly numbered hundreds and thousands of people, telling the audience in Liverpool: “I want to say to the millions of people in this country and indeed elsewhere who have been moved and outraged by the plight of the Palestinian people: we hear you, you were right.” Deputy assistant commissioner Carl Galvin said: “We know Saturday’s event, so close to the third anniversary of the terror attack on Israel, has the potential to have a greater impact on communities than the previous national marches.” Galvin, who is leading the policing operation this weekend, said the force’s presence on Saturday will be “significant”. “We will also be using powers under the Public Order Act requiring anyone in the protest area wearing face coverings to deliberately conceal their identity to remove them,” Galvin continued. The Met have imposed conditions on the march and require the group to travel via Westminster Bridge, York Road, Waterloo Bridge and The Strand on to Whitehall, with a rally concluding by 6.30pm. The force has said that any speeches and music must conclude by 5.30pm. A counter-protest by Stop The Hate is also taking place, with about 30 people gathered outside New Scotland Yard, some with flags. The force has also imposed conditions on the demonstration “to minimise the risk of serious disruption”. The demonstrators must remain within a designated area outside the Met’s headquarters, with the assembly concluding at 2.30pm. Last Saturday, on the third anniversary of the 7 October attacks, when Hamas militants broke across the Israeli border to launch a wave of attacks on kibbutzim, border towns, military bases and music festivals, killing at least 1,209 people, a small pro-Palestine student demonstration in central London was held. The Met publicly appealed to those behind the demonstration to “exercise [their] right to protest on a different date” and admitted that finding the organisers had been “frankly difficult”. In the end, it went ahead and about 100 people attended. Five people were arrested for breaching conditions imposed on the march. The Palestine Coalition organising the march includes Palestine Solidarity Campaign, Stop the War, CND, the Muslim Association of Britain, Friends of Al Aqsa and the Palestinian Forum in Britain.

title: A replica of Donald Trump’s Oval Office goes for the gold in Washington DC
summary: The tourist attraction just unveiled an elaborate, full-scale overhaul to match Trump’s second-term aesthetic
text: Sitting behind a replica Resolute Desk, nine-year-old Sydney Wright posed for the camera like a future US president. “I love it,” she smiled. And what about the dazzling gold appliqués, gold leaf and gold trim surrounding her? “It’s cool.” Sydney was among a steady stream of visitors on Thursday to The People’s House: A White House Experience, an interactive museum – with an orientation film narrated by The West Wing star Martin Sheen – at 1700 Pennsylvania Avenue, just 150 yards from the real thing. Run by the White House Historical Association, the tourist attraction has just unveiled an elaborate overhaul of its full-scale Oval Office to match Donald Trump’s second-term aesthetic, described by the New York Times as a “gilded rococo nightmare”. Gone is the understated, plain decor of Joe Biden and his predecessors. In its place is a spectacle of two dozen portraits in heavy carved frames, swirling wall onlays, gleaming brass vases and decorative knickknacks crowding nearly every available surface. Barack Obama had pictures of two former presidents on the wall; Biden put up a total of seven paintings. Trump has stacked the walls with historical figures including George Washington, Andrew Jackson and Benjamin Franklin. Ronald Reagan appears twice, while there is only one woman on display: former first lady Jackie Kennedy. A bust of former president Theodore Roosevelt by James Earle Fraser glowers from a bookshelf, flanked by bound volumes of the 26th president’s works. Other books on display include Hawthorne’s Works and Writings of Washington. There are two mirrors and a copy of the Declaration of Independence. But for all the detail, the people’s house cannot recreate the experience of former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt, who reportedly entered the Oval Office one day to find Trump in DIY mode, using superglue in an effort to stick gold ornaments to the fireplace. Still, for many tourists arriving in the nation’s capital, this is as close as they will get to the heart of presidential power, especially with the White House currently undergoing extensive demolition and construction work. Sydney’s father, Drew Wright, a 36-year-old firefighter from Athens, Georgia, said he viewed the room’s additions as “paying homage to the people who laid the pathway that we have to raise our children in this great nation”. Asked about the goldening, Wright, who voted for Trump twice, replied: “There’s always going to be critics. There’s always going to be haters. Just because they’re the loudest ones in the room doesn’t mean they’re right. I don’t know what it looked like before but I think it’s a pretty classic look.” Cheri Lujan Hamilton, 54, the chief clerk of the New Mexico state senate, also likes what Trump has done with the place. “I’m kind of in awe,” she said. “I was disappointed we couldn’t get into the White House for a tour so this is the next best thing.” Taking in all the gold, Hamilton remarked: “It’s grand. I like everything that’s grand. I do think all the gold around the doors is maybe a little too much. But I like it on the top.” Pedro Robles, 50, a police officer from Nashville, Tennessee, called the replica “pretty cool” and disputed the notion that the gilding crosses into bad taste. “I don’t think so,” he said. “I don’t think it looks tacky.” Such opinions would be music to the ears of Trump who, when asked by Time magazine what he would miss most about the White House after he leaves, answered: “This beautiful room that nobody should be allowed to rip down. The Oval Office.” A team of specialised designers visited Trump’s actual office while he was away to ensure authenticity. They used 3D scanning in Indianapolis and crafted hand-carved gold frames in California, while teams in Canada and Virginia worked on replicas of vases and other tabletop pieces. The replica transition took one week with more than 25 crew members onsite. They used laser levels and temporary adhesive to fix items to the walls, checking their work for accuracy against renderings of the actual office before nailing many adornments to the walls. Matthew Costello, chief education officer at the White House Historical Association, said in an email: “As we have seen throughout White House history, each president transitions the Oval Office according to his own tastes. It is our hope that through the evolutions of our Oval Office replica, people will be inspired to learn more about and even see themselves in White House history.” There is, however, one key difference between the real Oval Office and its imitator. While the actual workspace relies on gilded gold leaf, the museum opted for a specialised gold paint solution to protect against chipping or other wear and tear from visitors. The transformation provides a microcosm of an aggressive campaign by Trump to remake Washington DC in his own image. Beyond the Oval Office makeover, Trump knocked down the East Wing to build a $400m ballroom, paved over the Rose Garden’s traditional grass lawn to build a white stone patio reminiscent of his Mar-a-Lago resort in Florida, added a row of presidential portraits that replace Biden with an autopen and constructed a granite helipad on the south lawn. He also initiated a troubled overhaul of the Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool, proposed a towering 250ft triumphal arch near Arlington national cemetery and threatened to tear down the John F Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts if it does not bear his name. Washington purists and architecture critics have recoiled at Trump’s ostentatious tastes. But Carl Wilkerson, 73, a retired marine wearing a US Marine Corps T-shirt, offered an impassioned defense of presidential swagger, saying: “We need to have a little bling-bling, man. This is the United States of America. This is the greatest country on the planet, so we need to show it off.” Drawing on his time overseas, Wilkerson, from Hereford, Arizona, argued that US presidential architecture had fallen behind the competition, saying: “You go over there in the east. He’s walked in their palaces and it’s like, boom. It pops. Their palaces outdid the White House 10 to one. We need to step up our game a little bit. We are the greatest country on the planet. So you need to act like it – and look like it.”
