title: ‘People are leaving’: New York City’s EMS workers are struggling to make ends meet
summary: EMS workers, who make life-or-death decisions in emergencies, are the lowest paid first responders
text: After 31 years in New York City’s emergency medical services, Oren Barzilay has started giving young New Yorkers advice he never imagined giving when he began his EMS career. “Don’t come here,” he tells them. “You are only going to hurt yourself.” It is a striking reversal for Barzilay, the recently retired president of FDNY EMS Local 2507. What changed for Barzilay was not his view of work or the value of service. It was what he believes is the New York City failure to pay the people who put their lives at risk to save the lives of others. “After 31 years, I am stuck at $59,000,” he said. Barzilay’s reversal comes as New York City’s EMS workforces remain locked in a years-long fight over wages and pay parity. The fight has become an early test of a contradiction facing Mamdani’s young administration. As a candidate, Mamdani built his political identity in part around organized labor, affordability and demands that employers pay workers more. As mayor, he now sits on the other side of the bargaining table, responsible for a vast municipal workforce and a finite city budget. EMS workers’ years-long campaign for higher wages and pay parity – unfolding as his administration filed a lawsuit to stop $10,000 payments to public-school paraprofessionals in court – is forcing that tension into the open. For many EMS workers their job is a passionate calling. Natasha Villaruel, a paramedic, has about 20 seconds to make a life-saving decision. When the 36-year-old paramedic receives a 911 call for someone in respiratory distress, the routine begins almost automatically, with precision. “You respond with lights and sirens safely. You try to get there as fast as you can,” said Villaruel over the phone. By the time she and her fellow paramedic reach the doorway, she is already reading the patient’s vitals. “You assess the patient from the door to see how they’re breathing, to see the color of their skin,” she said. “The first thing you want to know is if they can speak, because now if they can’t speak, you know this is very, very urgent.” Villaruel, who was born in Jamaica and moved to Brooklyn at four, described the pressure of those first few seconds. “Within 20 seconds, you have to make a life decision.” More than 4,500 EMS workers such as Villaruel respond to over 1.9mmedical and fire emergencies each year across New York City’s five boroughs, making life-or-death decisions for a city of more than 8.58 million people. Yet the workers entrusted with those decisions are among the lowest-paid first responders in the city. An FDNY EMT starts at $39,386 a year, barely above New York City’s minimum wage. After five years, an EMT can earn roughly $59,534, but a firefighter with similar years of experience makes as much as $105,146 – nearly double what EMS and EMTs make. Many EMS workers are struggling to make ends meet. Villaruel said her own household is sustainable largely because her husband is a firefighter. But her colleagues, she said, have struggled far more. “We have people that live in shelters,” she said. “We have people that get vouchers. We have people that get food stamps.” Meanwhile, the ambulances are taking longer to reach New Yorkers facing life-threatening emergencies. The average ambulance response time rose from 11 minutes and 21 seconds in fiscal year 2025 to 13 minutes and 9 seconds in fiscal year 2026, according to the Mayor’s Management Report. The delay in emergency response comes as the city’s EMS system struggles to keep workers. According to New York State EMS workforce report, the number of active EMS responders fell 17.5% between 2019 and 2022 statewide. Union leaders said lower wages are driving an exodus of EMS workers. “We have a tremendous attrition problem. People are leaving,” said Anthony Almojera, an FDNY EMS paramedic lieutenant and vice president of Local 3621. Almojera said he remains frustrated with the city council and successive administrations. “I don’t know why, over the years, many administrations have decided they do not want to value us,” said Almojera For some patients, those minutes can be life-altering. “Time matters a lot,” said Dr Shreya Kashyap, second-year neurology resident at Mount Sinai. For patients suffering an acute stroke, she said, every delay can increase the risk of permanent damage to brain tissue. “There’s this phrase that’s very popular in neurology education,” Kashyap said. “It’s called ‘time is brain.’” The pay disparity is hardly new to city hall. Sandy Nurse, a Brooklyn councilmember, who has supported efforts to raise EMS compensation, said: “EMS workers, frontline emergency management workers, make very, very low wages.” In 2024, Nurse co-sponsored bills to establish a Department of Emergency Medical Services as its own standalone organization, ensuring better wages for service workers as well as mental healthcare. Her progressive caucus also has won $1m for an EMS mental health pilot program. Barzilay argues that the decades-long failure to achieve pay parity is not due to a lack of political support. He places much of the blame on city hall, particularly the offices responsible for negotiating labor contracts and determining what the city can afford. Nearly four years after the last contract, the Mamdani administration says negotiations are now underway but declined to disclose when bargaining sessions have taken place or where negotiations currently stand. “Contract negotiations are currently underway with the EMS union, and we remain fully committed to good-faith bargaining at the table,” Kenneth Londono, communications director for the mayor’s office of labor relations, said in a statement. “The Mamdani administration values the vital, life-saving work that our EMS members perform for New Yorkers every single day.” Londono said the administration hopes to reach a “fair and sustainable outcome” that supports EMS workers while “remaining fair to city taxpayers”. Barzilay remains skeptical. Asked whether he believed there are good-faith negotiations under the new administration, he said: “No. Not as of yet.” Almojera was more hopeful and believes the administration is making a good-faith effort to address the problems facing EMS. “Negotiations haven’t formally commenced,” Almojera said. “We’re just talking. You know, just talking back and forth.” For Almojera, Mamdani’s appointment of Lillian Bonsignore as fire commissioner was an encouraging sign. Bonsignore spent 31 years in FDNY EMS, beginning as an EMT before becoming a paramedic and eventually chief of EMS operations. “Making her commissioner is acknowledging that the Fire Department is mostly EMS,” Almojera said. “She knows exactly what we do. She’s one of us.” Villaruel was less optimistic: “I feel like politicians are politicians,” she said. “They tell you what you want to hear. And then when it’s time for the work to be put in, everyone is blind and deaf.” Bonsignore’s office did not respond to a request for comment. For Villaruel, who has spent more than a decade in EMS, the work itself is not what is pushing people away. “It’s not like they don’t like the job,” Villaruel said. “It’s the pay that’s the problem.” “Who doesn’t like saving people?” she asked.

title: United Auto Workers president Shawn Fain easily wins re-election
summary: Fain was dogged by investigation but still decisively beat challenger Rich Boyer, who received just 13% of vote
text: The president of the United Auto Workers, Shawn Fain, has easily won his re-election bid after an campaign period marred by accusations of corruption and election interference. The union’s election of leadership for a four-year term began with mail-in ballots being sent out in late August 2026, with vote tabulating commencing on 6 October. Fain won with over 68% of the vote as of Friday evening, with additional 13 candidates on his slate, United UAW, winning their elections. The closest opponent to Fain, Rich Boyer, received just over 13% of the vote. “The membership has spoken. UAW members are united and want us to keep fighting and building on what we’ve done,” said Shawn Fain in a statement on his re-election win, citing upcoming contract negotiations at John Deere, Volvo and General Dynamics Land Systems in 2027, and the big three automaker contracts expiring on May Day in 2028. “These results are about taking on corporate America and reversing the worst out-of-control wealth inequality in America’s history,” added Fain. “We are fighting for the entire working class, whether that’s at the bargaining table, organizing new members or in the political arena.” In July 2026, the Department of Justice announced it was investigating Fain over allegations he pressured Boyer, another union official, to provide benefits to his fiancee and sister and then retaliated against him when Broyer refused to cooperate. Fain denied the allegations and characterized them as an attempt to interfere in the election. Fain won his first election to serve as the union’s president as a reform candidate in March 2023. He has clashed with the union’s independent monitor, Neil Barofsky, claiming the monitor was weaponized by his re-election opponent. The monitor was also accused of pressuring Fain over the UAW’s passing of a resolution calling for a ceasefire in Gaza. Fain led the union during a roughly six-week strike in September 2023 through October 2023 at the big three automakers, General Motors, Ford and Stellantis, highlighting corporate greed through the strike and citing the companies’ stock buy-backs and record profits. Joe Biden joined the union on the picket line, the first sitting president to ever join a strike picket line.

title: New Orleans court deputy who handcuffed journalist disciplined – for violating etiquette
summary: Herschel Green handcuffed WWL producer and lawyer for not leaving public space, but was only punished for arguing about it with administrator
text: A New Orleans criminal court deputy who handcuffed a journalist covering July’s indictment of Louisiana’s state attorney general has been disciplined for breaching his employer’s professionalism policy – albeit for an argument with the facility’s judicial administrator that day, according to an internal agency report. New Orleans sheriff’s office deputy Herschel Green was ordered to undergo counseling for that argument after he and his colleague Diedra Rayfield placed both WWL Louisiana investigative producer Danny Monteverde as well as station attorney Elana Beiser in handcuffs, a 33-page agency report released on Friday said. The report also said that a sheriff’s office investigation into the chaotic circumstances surrounding Monteverde’s and Beiser’s handcuffings “revealed deficiencies involving operational planning, communication, training supervision, media management” and other factors. Those findings arrive after a prominent media rights advocacy organization – the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press – condemned Monteverde’s and Beiser’s handcuffings as “outrageous”. As the report recounted, Monteverde and Beiser were among “numerous” media and legal representatives present at New Orleans’ criminal courthouse for the handing up of an ultimately dismissed public intimidation indictment against the Louisiana attorney general, Liz Murrill. The judge overseeing the proceeding, Leon Roché, ordered his courtroom cleared before the handing up of the indictment, ostensibly to protect grand jurors’ identities. So the media, lawyers including Beiser, and other members of the public gathered in the hallway outside the courtroom, the report said. Deputies at that point ordered the crowd outside the courtroom to either move further down the hallway or leave the courthouse, according to the report, which attributed that information to conflicting witness statements. Monteverde responded by saying the courthouse was a public place and that he was not leaving the building entirely, the report said. The report said Green then handcuffed Monteverde, and Rayfield did the same to Beiser, who was there to help WWL object to the courtroom’s closure because state law requires indictments to be returned in open court. Courthouse construction work, meanwhile, triggered a fire alarm around that time, the report said. And, the report said, deputies maintained they couldn’t immediately rule out a genuine blaze, so they ordered an evacuation of the building to give the local fire department time to investigate. Whatever the case, Monteverde subsequently caught the attention of the courthouse’s judicial administrator, Robert Kazik, and showed him he had been handcuffed, according to the report. Kazik asked Green why he had handcuffed Monteverde, said the report, which contained statements to the sheriff’s office from all three men. And when it seemed to Kazik that Green intended to walk Monteverde out of the front courthouse entrance and down a set of steps there, where “local and national media outlets had gathered”, the judicial administrator “entered into a heated verbal exchange with the deputy and instructed him not to take” that route with the journalist. Green acknowledged to internal investigators that he had argued with Kazik – though he accused the judicial administrator of first approaching “in an aggressive manner”, questioning him about Monteverde’s handcuffing and threatening to call his commanders on him, according to the report. A sheriff’s office sergeant eventually arrived and successfully ordered Green to uncuff Monteverde, the report said. Rayfield, too, was instructed to uncuff Beiser. Both deputies said “that they acted independently” and had not been commanded to detain either Monteverde or Beiser, according to the report, supporting an earlier statement from Roché denying that he had ordered anyone to be handcuffed. The sheriff’s office’s investigation into the handcuffings later determined that Green’s argument with Kazik violated an agency policy requiring employees to “conduct themselves professionally with the utmost concern for the dignity of any individual with whom they are interacting”, according to the report. “Employees shall not demean or unnecessarily inconvenience any individual and shall not act in a manner that discredits the employee or the sheriff’s office,” the professionalism policy says. Green on 9 September signed a citation of disciplinary action requiring counseling for him, according to the report from the sheriff’s office’s internal affairs division. In conclusion, the report said courthouse deputies met that day’s events “without a documented operational plan or comprehensive briefing”. It recommended various corrective actions, among them “preparing a written plan for high-profile proceedings identifying the incident commander, chain of command, assignments, … media staging areas, access restrictions, … [and] detention protocols”. “Temporary handcuffing is a significant detention and should be supported by a clearly articulated legal basis, supervisory oversight and complete documentation,” the sheriff’s office report also said. “When the underlying conduct involves verbal disagreement or passive refusal, available de-escalation methods should be used before restraints unless immediate action is necessary for safety.” The Guardian has asked the sheriff’s office if it wanted to comment on the report. It did the same to WWL, a Guardian reporting partner. Green and Rayfield’s handcuffings of Monteverde and Beiser constituted one of two recent high-profile episodes pitting WWL – a CBS affiliate – against New Orleans’ criminal courthouse. The New Orleans criminal court judge Kimya Holmes filed a police report against WWL in September after investigative reporter David Hammer aired a politically unflattering segment examining a real estate transaction in which she was involved. Yet Holmes later conceded that she did not realize her complaint relied on a section of law prohibiting the dissemination of certain personal information that had been repealed at the beginning of August. And investigators concluded WWL had committed “no violation … or criminal offense”, a police report said.

title: Marina Silva on Flávio Bolsonaro: He will try to finish his father’s ‘perverse project’ to destroy the Amazon
summary: Exclusive: Former Brazilian environment minister warns of destruction as far-right scion favourite to become president
text: The former Brazilian environment minister Marina Silva has said that if Flávio Bolsonaro becomes president he will seek to finish the “perverse project” of rampant rainforest destruction initiated by his jailed far-right father. The Amazon was thrown into chaos during Jair Bolsonaro’s 2019-2022 presidency, when Brazil’s environment and Indigenous protection agencies were gutted and environmental criminals ran riot, causing surges in deforestation and violence. Despite that, Bolsonaro’s eldest son, Flávio, is the favourite to beat the leftwing incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, in the second round of the presidential election on 25 October. Flávio, 45, beat Lula, 80, by more than 2m votes in the first round last Sunday, amid a wave of anti-incumbency and anti-left sentiment that catapulted a record number of far-right politicians into an already conservative congress. Silva, a world-renowned environmentalist who was Lula’s environment minister until April, says a second Bolsonaro presidency will spell disaster for the globally crucial ecosystem, for its inhabitants and for the climate crisis. “I’ve no doubt that this time they will try to finish the perverse project they started with [Jair] Bolsonaro. If they are elected – and God, and the Brazilian people, willing they won’t be – they will use their time to try to speed up as much as possible all of the regressions they can, including to keep themselves in power,” says Silva, who was appointed after Lula beat Jair Bolsonaro in the 2022 election. “The vision they have for the Amazon is the same vision they have for everything. They are denialists. Their vision is that the forest must be removed for economic activities,” she adds. “They will again encourage illegal mining, the invasion of Indigenous lands, and violence against Indigenous and Quilombola communities.” Silva fears aggressive resource extraction could be turbocharged by Donald Trump’s designs on Latin America, exemplified by the US commandeering Venezuela’s huge oil reserves after the capture of Nicolás Maduro. The Bolsonaros are long-term allies of Trump, who has called Venezuela’s oil “the spoils” of his brief war. “Brazil cannot [be governed by] a political group that wants to turn itself into an American protectorate, as is the case with Venezuela today,” says Silva, who believes a Flávio Bolsonaro administration would be “subservient” to the US. Speaking from São Paulo, Silva recalls the “scorched earth” she encountered when she took over a defanged and dispirited environment ministry in January 2023 and set about trying to control soaring Amazon destruction. One of Lula’s first acts was to send troops to expel thousands of illegal miners from the country’s largest Indigenous territory. Silva says the “Herculean effort” of environmental and security forces has paid off. Amazon deforestation has fallen nearly 50% under Lula, with an estimated 2,600 sq km (1,004 sq miles) lost this year compared with almost 11,600 sq km during Jair Bolsonaro’s last year in office. Illegal miners and ranchers have been evicted from a succession of Indigenous territories. Tens of billions of dollars of international funding for rainforest protection have been restored after being frozen during Bolsonaro’s era of destruction. Now, Silva believes all those achievements are in jeopardy. “It’s deeply sad and troubling,” says the 68-year-old, who was born in the Amazon to a family of rubber tappers. The veteran activist pauses to compose herself as she considers the prospect that in just a few weeks all that work could be undone. “It’s just like the myth of Sisyphus. Rolling the boulder all the way up to the top and watching it fall back down. Except it won’t fall on open ground – it’s going to fall right on top of all of us,” Silva says of the consequences of allowing deforestation to again spiral out of control. “Paradoxically, just at the moment when we could be about to achieve the lowest rate of deforestation [in more than a decade] and hit a once unthinkable target of zero deforestation by 2030, we face the threat of a government which … would set all of this back to square one.” She adds: “It’s frightening, too, to think that [this is happening when] we’re living through a super El Niño, which will bring severe problems of drought and floods … during a government that has zero commitment to the prevention, adaptation and mitigation agenda.” Even if Flávio Bolsonaro loses, congress’s shift to the far right means the coming years are likely to prove dire for the environment in the world’s most biodiverse country. In the recent election, Bolsonaro’s Liberal party (PL) won 19 of the 54 seats up for grabs in the 81-seat senate and 121 seats of the 513 lower house seats, making it easier for lawmakers to remove environmental and Indigenous protections. Silva sought a seat in the senate but was beaten by a former special forces police officer and another Bolsonarista politician. “Even with the current makeup [of congress] we’ve witnessed numerous setbacks,” says Silva, who fears lawmakers will move to “uncreate” conservation units and Indigenous territories. “It’s a devastating process. I’m worried not just about the Amazon but about all of our biomes, like the Atlantic Forest, the Cerrado, the Pantanal, the Pampa. All of Brazil’s biomes are equally threatened by this Trumpist vision.” Silva’s fears are not confined to the environment. She believed countless social advances achieved during Lula’s three terms as president would also be reversed, including the eradication of hunger and dramatically increased access to higher education. She argues that Brazil’s democracy is at risk if the Bolsonaros reclaim power, with Jair, who is serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup after losing the 2022 election, expected to be released and made a minister. Those fears grew this week when Flávio Bolsonaro announced he would seek to “re-democratise” Brazil and change the constitution, possibly allowing longer presidential terms. “That is a very dangerous word, because to an authoritarian mindset, what does re-democratisation mean?” Silva says. “It means democracy for them to stay in power ad infinitum; riding roughshod over constitutional rules; interfering with the logic of the separation of powers; having the power to appoint supreme court justices to mould a supreme court in their own image and likeness. In reality, they are a sort of right-wing version of what was done in Venezuela [under Maduro].” “They are willing to erode our democracy from within,” she adds. Silva voices hope that Lula can bounce back in the second round. “I believe deeply that it’s possible,” she says, vowing to spend the coming days battling to convince the more than 30 million people who did not vote in the first round of the “incalculable damage” another Bolsonaro presidency could cause. On Thursday, a survey by the Datafolha polling institute gave Bolsonaro a 52% to 48% lead over Lula in the runoff. Silva, who has been defending the Amazon since the 80s, vows to fight on. “I draw my energy from insisting on living. I believe life means holding on, and the death impulse – strong as it may be – always loses to the life impulse. Look at us: we are here. Our parents and our grandparents are gone, but we made it. I truly believe this instinct to live will prevail. My hope is that it proves stronger right now, so Latin America isn’t consumed by this drive for death.”

title: Geordie Greep denies sexual assault allegations from stage in Vancouver
summary: While some heard the former Black Midi frontman out, others made for the exit as he addressed accusations
text: When Geordie Greep finally took to the stage in Vancouver this week, noticeably without his band, the crowd was hushed and the atmosphere tense. His lateness, however was the least of his problems. Greep, a Brit school graduate and the former frontman of Black Midi, had been accused of sexually assaulting a woman while on tour. Flyers had been handed out outside the venue spelling out the allegation against him. “Let him know what Vancouver thinks of rapists,” they read. What followed was an astonishing speech by Greep, who dealt with the accusations head on. While some of his fans inside the Pearl heard him out, others made for the exit. “This is a very serious matter that I must talk about,” he said. “Someone out front is handing out flyers saying I’m this, saying I’m that … and it needs to be talked about.” He added: “I would never rape a woman. I’m not a rapist. It’s not how that went down.” The flyers, which fans posted images of online, were detailed in their allegations. “You know what you did this morning Oct 8th,” it read, and: “He thinks he can do whatever he wants because he’s gone tomorrow.” Greep’s response was even more so. He said: “Essentially what happened last night … me and some of the band, we went out to some bars. We went around, we met people. And it ended up in a situation where really late at a house party I got the wrong end of the stick with someone that was there.” “I made a move and it didn’t come off,” he said, “and I really quickly of course apologised. It was a complete misunderstanding on my part. It felt extremely bad and I feel extremely sorry and extremely upset about the whole situation.” He added: “Basically I just wanted to be transparent with you about what happened. Very very sorry to someone … I made someone feel uncomfortable without meaning to. It’s not a good thing … and it’s not good.” Greep went on to explain the absence of his usual backing band, saying: “I didn’t want to force them to still play a show in the light of that happening. We were unsure what would, kind of, be the response in all of this. I can only tell you that it’s OK if people want a refund, if they want to leave it’s fine.” The 27-year-old added that proceeds from the evening’s event would be donated to a violence against women charity in British Columbia. Afterwards, Greep said that he would continue the show alone if the crowd wished. “It’s just gonna be me,” he said, “just like the old days.” Reports from fans online show that the musician continued with a solo set. Some members of the crowd could be heard cheering. Alex Lacidos witnessed the “jarring” speech. “The crowd was really confused, we had been waiting for more than two hours,” he said. “After his talk he started his performance by himself, the vibes were awful and it looked like he was about to burst into tears. “Many people left before it was over.” Reddit user wreeum – who recorded the concert – said he felt “conflicted” about the incident and that it was “a huge allegation to make on the same day it happened, especially to print out several dozen flyers”. He added: “Sexual assault shouldn’t be taken lightly.” Another fan who was present at the gig wrote on X: “Went to the Geordie Greep concert tonight, left after his little speech. I really don’t know what to think.” Greep is on tour in North America with his debut solo album, The New Sound. His previous band Black Midi released their album Schlagenheim in 2019, and it was shortlisted for the Mercury prize. After speculation around the band’s breakup, the group was disbanded in 2024 following a live-streamed announcement by Greep on Instagram. Greep and his current backing band were still down to play a show in Boise, Idaho on Friday as they continue a series of gigs in the US before a European leg in November. Greep’s team has been approached for comment.

title: Six men on how they plan to stand up against rape culture
summary: While most of the crowd at a Stop Sexual Violence rally in New York City was women, men of all ages were in attendance too
text: Tens of thousands of protesters gathered at city halls and college campuses across the country on Thursday to demand an end to sexual violence. The nationwide rallies followed weeks of public outcry over the mishandling of campus sexual assault cases at Cornell University and Louisiana State University. The protest organizers – including Women’s March, Feminist Generation and Me Too International – demanded justice for Jane Doe, who said she was drugged and gang-raped by seven students at a Cornell frat party; Kendall Francis, who said she was raped by an LSU football player; and all survivors harmed “from the frat house to the White House”. They also called for reform of Title IX, a set of protections for sexual misconduct victims and LGBTQ+ students that the Trump administration has slowly stripped away. The latest cases have outraged college students and their families over the pervasiveness of rape culture; 81% of women and 43% of men in the US said they have experienced sexual harassment or assault, according to the National Sexual Violence Resource Center. Parents online are questioning how to raise sons who will stand up to sexual violence instead of being bystanders. Women, survivors and longtime advocates say the onus has often been on them to use the momentum in moments like these to educate others and demand concrete change. While the demographic makeup of the crowd at the Stop Sexual Violence rally in New York City was majority women, men of all ages were there, too, holding “I Am Jane Doe” signs and yelling to end rape culture. We asked six of them how they are personally taking a stand against rape culture. Speak up against toxicity in the chat Kaif Gilani, 29 Too often, we see that after a big uproar and high-profile news, that the only people standing up and attending protests are women or female-identifying folks. It’s really important for men to step up and say: “Hey, I need to put an end to this in any way that I can in my day-to-day life.” We need to try to make a difference in our own communities, whether that’s speaking up against frat brothers who say something toxic or misogynistic in the chat, or going out and attending events like the Women’s March. Pass legislation for consent education Ben Tee, 42 There’s some really important legislation in the New York state legislature to make consent education a mandatory part of the school curriculum. I’m in Democratic party leadership, and we just passed a resolution last week supporting a framework for teaching consent. I actually think that’s the most important thing that we can do. People are talking about increasing penalties and closing the voluntary intoxication loophole, which is super important. But the reality is that we don’t get [sexual assault] convictions, the police don’t take [sexual assault] seriously and DAs do not prosecute. We need to be doing a lot more in prevention. After the assault is just too late. There have been really good studies that show that consent education can have a huge impact on reducing the rate of victimization and perpetration, and nobody talks about it at all. It’s a real, real shame. ‘Men need to do more teaching’ Peter Walsh, 64 I know from my own experiences as a man that many boys need to be taught what is appropriate, and when consent means consent. Men need to do more teaching. Be aware if someone is uncomfortable Nicola Francia, 21 It really starts with reconsidering your own position and understanding where it is near you, and in you. I’m from Italy, and there was a girl from my high school who was killed by her ex. In my home country, there has been a lot of mobilizing around this issue. It’s very evident that [rape culture] is near us, all across the country, in our society. There were cases in my social life where I wish I had been more present for the women I know. They have felt uncomfortable in social situations with guys being creepy when they were intoxicated. We all have to be very aware of whether someone is feeling uncomfortable or whether you are making someone uncomfortable. Take a stand against victim blaming Shalin Upadhyay, 27 I see rape culture as something that starts from little moments – how people talk, how women are treated. The language that we use when we talk to women or talk about them is objectifying. Those things are normalized, and then that’s what turns into something bigger, like rape. And when rape happens, it’s also not seriously considered. It always turns into victim-blaming. I’ve seen that, and I want to stand against that. When you see something happen, take action Daniel Olivier, 37 I grew up in the punk rock scene, and when things happened, we took action. You got your head kicked in if you did something bad. I wish that would happen more often. I know that’s not the right thing to say, and I don’t stand for violence. But the violence that [abusers] are doing to us is so much worse. In my current life, just being in New York, it’s constant. You can’t sit at a bar without overhearing people saying disgusting things about women. I worked in the music industry and the alcohol industry, and I’ve been surrounded by it my entire life. I’ve spent my whole life fighting against this stuff.

title: FDA may allow some toxic chemicals to be added to food without safety review. Experts are alarmed
summary: Regulator looks to expand loophole to allow dangerous compounds in food as long as they’re not carcinogenic
text: The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) is proposing to expand a controversial loophole to allow some of the world’s most toxic chemicals to be added directly to food without a safety review. The “threshold of regulation” (TOR) exemption currently allows dangerous compounds to be used without review in food contact materials, such as packaging or processing equipment, if they are not carcinogenic, and are added at levels below 0.5 parts per billion (ppb). But campaigners say many chemicals, especially hormone disruptors linked to brain damage and reproductive harm in children, are considered dangerous at levels far below 0.5ppb. Even in its limited form, the loophole has already raised alarm. One TOR exemption that allows the rocket fuel chemical perchlorate to be used in grain bags dramatically increased the amount of the compound found in kids’ cereal, which advocates say could cause brain damage. The new proposed TOR expansion would allow companies to use the chemicals as an ingredient added directly to food, as flavorings, preservatives, emulsifiers, processing aids, enzymes, stabilizers and binders, and for myriad other uses, in ultra-processing. The revelation comes after Robert F Kennedy Jr and the FDA claimed victory and declared “promises kept” in August for “closing” a different controversial regulatory loophole called “generally regarded as safe” (Gras), which over the decades was used to send ingredients to the market that campaigners said could sicken, injure or kill people. But Kennedy and the FDA did not mention in their public relations material that the proposed Gras rule submitted quietly to the Federal Register includes the TOR expansion, which public health advocates warn will also send alarming levels of toxic chemicals to grocery store shelves. Some advocates have accused Kennedy of deception. Regardless, the proposal represents a major win for big food, advocates say, and is based on flawed science. “The FDA and industry have this position that if there’s only a little bit of something in the diet, then it’s not going to be problematic, but that isn’t supported by science of any kind,” said Maricel Maffini, an independent food consultant who worked on TOR issues. “I don’t know how they’re going to square that circle because there are many ingredients that at very low levels also cause serious issues in the body,” Maffini added. The FDA said in a statement provided after publication that it can reject a TOR exemption application if it finds there is a risk. The proposed rule states that “any substance used in food (both directly or indirectly added) will be exempted from regulation as a food additive” if there is “no appreciable risk to human health”. Advocates say the problem lies in the definition of “appreciable risk”. Chemicals like perchlorate, some phthalates, some bisphenols, some Pfas “forever chemicals” and some flame retardants are not classified as carcinogenic, but they can cause harm at doses far lower than 0.5ppb. These could in theory be used as TOR ingredients, as could chemicals that are neurotoxic, cause brain damage, attack the immune system, harm the microbiota or give rise to any number of other adverse health impacts. Maffini said she was particularly concerned about flavorings because ultra-processed food companies use chemicals that “play around with the nervous system and receptors in your mouth to try to make us eat more and more of something”. Advocates say the rule also does not take into account cumulative effects – one small dose of a TOR-exempted chemical may not be harmful, but many small doses of multiple toxic chemicals could be a problem. It also creates a secondary loophole in allowing carcinogens if the substance is created as an impurity. Meanwhile, there is no way for consumers to know if a product contains a TOR-exempted chemical. “They’re widening another loophole, but trying to say they made our food safer,” said Maria Doa, a scientist with the Environmental Defense Fund (EDF) non-profit. “They did not make our food safer.” How TOR led to children eating rocket fuel chemicals The problems with perchlorate in kids’ cereal are a warning about TOR’s risks, advocates say. In 2005, German chemical giant BASF used TOR to exempt perchlorate from regulations for use in “super sacks”, which are one-ton polypropylene plastic storage bags used on farms to move grains, including rice, flour and oats. Perchlorate stops grains from sticking to super sacks. But the grains are loaded into and emptied from the sacks at high velocity, which can cause perchlorate and microplastics to break off. The FDA’s own data published in 2017 showed the number of samples of kids’ cereal with perchlorate increased after the 2005 TOR exemption. The agency similarly detailed a broad increase in the levels in each sample. Perchlorate reduces the thyroid gland’s ability to absorb iodine, which is a raw material needed to produce the hormone T4, an essential component of proper brain development. Very low levels of perchlorate exposure are linked to lower T4 production, and lower IQ scores for children. Still, six months after it published its data, the FDA reapproved perchlorate for use in super sacks. Advocates say the agency used flawed science and manipulated the data. The FDA wrote that there was no meaningful increase in perchlorate across all the 250 foods it measured. But critics countered that the problem was not in all the food – the problem was in kids’ cereal. The FDA largely ignored the cereal findings, and mostly does not consider endocrine system harms when developing regulations, said Tom Neltner, a former scientist with the EDF who is now director of the Unleaded Kids non-profit. He helped lead litigation over perchlorate, which was ultimately dismissed. “They put their blinders on and approved the exemption based on data that never considered the harms posed by endocrine disruptors,” Neltner said. Kennedy deceived on Gras? Kennedy leads the Make America Healthy Again (Maha) movement, of which eliminating toxic chemicals from food is a cornerstone. During the run-up to the 2024 US presidential election, he held up the Gras standard as an example of the broken regulatory system that he would take bold steps to fix as he stands up to big food and makes America healthy again. The loophole drew outrage because campaigners say it virtually eliminates regulatory oversight for new ingredients, chemicals and products, allowing food companies to self-certify that substances are safe without alerting the FDA. The Gras standard does require companies to demonstrate a new food product is safe by making “widely accepted” scientific evidence to support its claim publicly available. But some companies bury the “public” announcement deep in their websites, push the boundaries of “widely accepted” research or hire from a cottage industry of scientists who are paid to declare food products “safe”, advocates say. A 2026 review of FDA and other federal food records by Maffini and the Environmental Working Group non-profit found at least 111 food chemicals or substances exploited the Gras standard, and they are used across thousands of products. Upon his appointment to oversee Trump’s health agency, the FDA and Kennedy reiterated his promise to “close the loophole”, and in 2026 he appeared to make good on it. He and the FDA stated that they were “closing critical information gaps”. Critics warned the “closure” was at best a modest loophole tightening that effectively only requires voluntary compliance, and the quiet opening of the TOR exemption counteracted any gains. Either the White House or the office of management and budget were involved in the Gras rule negotiations, though it is unclear who added the TOR expansion. Regardless, the controversial exemption is consistent with the administration’s philosophy more broadly, Maffini said. “This administration is not keen on regulating anything,” she said. • This article was amended on 15 October 2026 to reflect a statement from the FDA that was received after publication.
