title: Greens must avoid ‘capture by extremists and racists’, says party MP
summary: Ellie Chowns says vote for ‘Zionism is racism’ policy by 0.4% of members shows party processes are not working
text: A Green Party MP has said she wants to make sure her party is not “vulnerable to capture by extremists and racists” amid the continuing fallout from the “Zionism is racism” vote. The party faces a political maelstrom over its policy decision last week to treat Zionism, the movement for a Jewish state, as any other form of racism, and to back a single Palestinian state over a two-state solution. The motion was passed at the annual party conference with just over 1,000 votes, approximately 0.4% of the total membership. Ellie Chowns, the party leader in the House of Commons, said the ability to pass such a “significant and damaging policy” in that way made it clear the party’s structures and policymaking processes were not working. “I don’t think that policy, ‘Zionism is racism’, represents the large majority of Green party members, nor of people in the country,” Chowns told BBC’s Radio 4 Today Programme on Saturday. “We don’t want to be in debates about the meaning of contested terms, we want to be united and focusing in contesting and criticising the horrific actions of the Israeli government,” said Chowns, who lost a co-leadership run against Zack Polanski in 2025. The debate over whether the Greens’ decentralised policymaking structures remain suitable for a party whose membership has expanded rapidly comes hours after the party’s leader for England and Wales was defeated by Labour in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection. Polanksi, who received just under 33% of the vote on Friday, insisted he intended to remain as Green leader, despite calls to stand down, including from the chair of the Jewish Greens. The party normally holds leadership elections every two years, meaning the next election would be in the summer of 2027. Chowns said Polanksi’s “clear” lack of leadership over the Zionisim motion was “disappointing”, but that he had an opportunity to unite the party, having recognised the flaws in the motion. Tensions were heightened between the UK and Israel after the Labour government imposed sanctions on illegal settlements in occupied Palestine, and Israel retaliated by trying to close the British consulate in Jerusalem. Research carried out before the motion was passed found that Jewish people who vote for the Greens felt their attachment to Israel had weakened, even as the percentage of British Jews who identified as Zionist rose more broadly between 2022 and 2025. When asked about extremism and racism within the party – not only in relation to the motion but comments made by the deputy leader, Mothin Ali, after the Hamas attacks on 7 October 2023 in which he called for an end to “white supremacist European settler colonialism” – Chowns stressed the importance of the party’s internal processes. “I don’t know if there are extremists and racists in my party but I want to make sure that my party isn’t vulnerable to capture by extremists and racists, I want to make sure my party’s policies represent the views of the majority of members of the Green party who absolutely are not that sort of person at all,” she said. “Of course its legitimate to have difference of opinions including on many of the matters that this motion covers,” she added. Polanski has been accused of abdicating leadership after he missed the debate and the vote at the conference to instead campaign in the byelection, and for giving no clear message about whether or not he backed it. In interviews after the byelection loss, Polanski said he would have voted against the motion had he attended, given that two amendments he supported, both saying any future structure of a Palestinian state should be decided by Palestinians rather than a one-state system being imposed, were voted down. On Friday, Vivien Lichtenstein, the chair of the Jewish Greens, said Polanski, who is Jewish, made a “big mistake” by avoiding the vote. Asked if he should continue in his role, she told Times Radio: “No, I think he should resign.” However, other members of Jewish Greens said Lichtenstein’s comments did not reflect the majority view in the group, and that a vote of no confidence in her had been tabled.

title: ‘Cockroach’ leader among thousands detained in Delhi protest crackdown
summary: Authorities impose strict lockdown in capital to try to stop rally against removal of 130m names from electoral roll
text: Indian authorities have placed Delhi under a severe lockdown and detained tens of thousands of people, including the leader of the youth-led “Cockroach” movement, in an attempt to stop an anti-government protest. Thousands of people from across India were blocked from attending the demonstration, which had been called by the “Cockroach Janata party” (CJP) to protest against an exercise that has stripped 130m names from India’s electoral roll. The Cockroach movement, as well as opposition parties, civil society and student groups, have alleged that the process of “purifying” India’s voter roll was done to entrench the power of Narendra Modi‘s government, and have called for India’s chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, who oversaw the exercise, to resign. Delhi police denied permission for the protest to take place in the centre of the capital, and in the days leading up to Saturday, officials began to barricade roads throughout Delhi. More than 25,000 police and security personnel were deployed across the city, many pulled from other states. Abhijeet Dipke, the founder and leader of the CJP, accused the government of being scared of the young people who were rising up in protest. “The mass crackdown on protesters and the shutdown of Delhi are not signs of strength but of a leader terrified of his own people,” said Dipke. On Saturday morning, police boarded Dipke’s plane as it landed at Delhi airport and detained him, alongside several other senior figures in the Cockroach movement. In a video recorded just before police detained him, Dipke said: “If you think you can stop us by threatening us with jail, then you have it wrong. Put us in jail if you want … but we will keep fighting to protect the democracy of this country.” Others in the CJP movement were detained across India, with arrests and detentions reported to be in the tens of thousands. One of India’s most popular YouTubers, Dhruv Rathee, who has 33m followers and has become a supporter of the CJP, was among those put under house arrest, while Delhi’s former chief minister Arvind Kejriwal was detained at the protest site. Student groups, who have also been calling for Kumar to resign, had described the march as India’s “second freedom struggle”, akin to Gandhi’s fight for independence. As police began mass detentions on Friday night, Neha Bora, a student leader at the forefront of the protests, said: “History is repeating itself. Just like in 1942, the arrest of leaders could not stop the Quit India movement; this movement will also not stop.” By Saturday afternoon, Bora had been detained. Over its 14 years in power, the Modi government has been rigidly intolerant of dissent. However, few protests have prompted such a draconian nationwide crackdown, signalling the government’s concern that this unrest could present a serious political challenge. In major disruption to travel, all trains arriving into Delhi’s two main stations on Saturday were cancelled for 10 hours and almost 50 metro stations were shut. Delhi’s schools and courtrooms were instructed to go online for the day and hotel owners were told to turn away customers. Traffic diversions were in place across Delhi and police checkpoints were set up along the main highways from neighbouring states into the capital, with passengers being stopped and interrogated about their final destination. Delhi police told Uber drivers not to drop people near the protest area and said they were “tracking and stopping” bulk orders on food delivery services to Jantar Mantar. In Mumbai, housing societies sent out mass WhatsApp messages, telling parents to “mind your kids” and make sure they didn’t attempt to travel to join the protest. Around Jantar Mantar, which had previously been Delhi’s designated protest site and where the Cockroach supporters had hoped to gather, most of the main thoroughfares were shuttered and barricaded, surrounded by police and paramilitary officers. Riot-control vehicles and trucks fitted with water cannon stood nearby. Buses were used to transport more than 6,000 people who were detained while attempting to reach Jantar Mantar. Paravin Singhal, a 75-year-old lawyer, said he had left home at 5am and shown his court identity card at checkpoints along the way, only to be stopped about 200 metres from Jantar Mantar. Singhal said he had come to stand with young people fighting to save the country from a “lawless regime playing with the constitution”. He accused Modi’s government and the election commission of using the revision of electoral rolls to influence future votes. After voting in elections for 50 years, he said, he had recently been told that his name had been removed from the rolls. “How can this happen to someone who has been voting for 50 years? What is even more disturbing is that the government is taking away our most fundamental right – the right to vote.” Singhal said he would stay put in the hope that more protesters would arrive. “The government is afraid because young people in this country are awake. They know their rights and are fighting for them. That is why the government is behaving like a dictatorship.” Amina Minnath, an undergraduate student at Delhi University, had also travelled to the area with friends. They had left before sunrise and navigated the checkpoints. The police barricading of Delhi, she said, had only strengthened her determination to protest. “These restrictions show that the government does not care about people’s rights,” she said. “This will not stop us. We may be detained, but we will come back in greater numbers. This will not end in a single day.” The revision of electoral rolls, in a process known as “special intensive revision (SIR), began last year and attracted criticism from civil society groups and the opposition alliance after it emerged that millions of names were being deleted. The backlash grew when SIR was held in the state of West Bengal and it became clear that Muslims and other minorities, who traditionally do not vote for Modi’s Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata party (BJP), were being disproportionately stripped of their vote. Yet it didn’t become an issue of national outrage until late last month, when the Indian Express newspaper published an investigation that exposed multiple irregularities in the SIR process, which had been flagged in more than a dozen internal objections but had been unilaterally overruled by Kumar. Opposition parties, the Cockroach movement and student groups began to call for the resignation of Kumar, who was appointed by a committee led by Modi. This week, India’s main opposition Congress party, also tried to reach Jantar Mantar to protest but were blocked by police, and the Congress leader, Rahul Gandhi, was detained twice. This week, the supreme court ordered the Modi government and the election commission to respond to the allegations. A BJP spokesperson said they had “no base, not an iota of evidence” and accused them of being driven by “an irresponsible, anarchist opposition”. Saturday’s protest follows the triumph of the Cockroach movement in July, when it led mass protests that forced the resignation of Modi’s education minister. Since then, India’s youth have proved more willing to criticise the Modi regime and have expressed mounting anger at the obstruction of their freedom to protest. By Saturday evening, young people continued to gather in central Delhi neighbourhoods as the police continued pick up protesters en masse. Many, such as Prakhar Vashishth, who is in his early 20s, remained defiant despite the aggression of Delhi police. He had recently been asked to submit additional documents to establish his eligibility to remain on the electoral rolls. “We are living in extraordinary times, and young people in this country must come out to defend their future,” he said, as he stood near the police barricades around Jantar Mantar. “This government will go to any lengths to stay in power, even changing election rules or removing people it believes will not vote for it. But they cannot keep us away for ever.”

title: Marcy Kaptur: longest-serving congresswoman’s bid for another House term roiled by anti-trans ad
summary: Democrat in Congress since 1983 rebuked over ‘dangerous’ campaign ad – will it harm her chances in tight Ohio race?
text: Last month, Marcy Kaptur, the longest-serving woman in congressional history, released a video advertisement in which she looks directly at the camera and says exactly what she thinks about one of the most divisive issues facing Democrats today. “Here’s the truth: I voted with Republicans to keep transgender ideology out of our schools because parents know what’s best for their kids,” Kaptur says, “and boys should not play in girls’ sports.” In the days that followed, two county Democratic parties in her north-west Ohio district called for Kaptur to take down the ad, the president of the largest LGBTQ+ rights group in the country told reporters it would not back her re-election campaign, and a former intern published an op-ed about how he was “embarrassed” to have worked for the congresswoman. For Kaptur, taking a stance at odds with much of her party may be a necessity as she navigates what could be the toughest re-election campaign she has ever faced, in a year where Democrats nationwide believe they are poised to win back the US House of Representatives and halt Donald Trump’s legislative agenda. In office since Ronald Reagan was in his first term as president, Kaptur easily won re-election for decades, until redistricting following the 2020 census increased the share of Republican voters in her area. She eked out a 22nd term against Republican challenger Derek Merrin in the 2024 presidential year, even as Trump won her district handily. Months later, the Ohio redistricting commission approved a legally mandated redraw of the state’s congressional map that shifted her district about four percentage points further to the right. Kaptur and Merrin are set for a rematch in the 3 November midterm election, and forecasters believe it could go either way, despite Republican candidates nationwide facing headwinds in the form of Trump’s public unpopularity and persistently high gas prices. In an interview, Kaptur said she felt it was important that voters knew precisely where she stood on the question of transgender rights, two years after Trump’s re-election campaign successfully weaponized the question against his Democratic opponent Kamala Harris. She also viewed it as inevitable that Merrin’s campaign would try to use the issue against her. “We knew what he was going to do, and they have done that to us in the past,” she said. A rebellious streak Kaptur is not the only Democrat facing a tough race this year to come out against equal access for transgender youth athletes, who have been targeted by a wave of bans in Republican-controlled states, including Ohio. In a ruling earlier this year, the US supreme court’s conservative supermajority upheld such laws. The Democratic gubernatorial candidate in Ohio, Amy Acton, opposes transgender participation in school sports, as does Rob Sand, the party’s nominee for governor of Iowa. This week, Annie Andrews, the Democratic Senate candidate in South Carolina released an ad saying she, too, supports the bans, while in May, eight Democrats in the US House – Kaptur included – broke with their party to vote for a bill that would require public schools receive parental consent before recognizing students as transgender. Some of the Democrats who supported that measure, which has not cleared the Senate, have been targeted by the mid-decade redistricting effort Trump encouraged Republicans to carry out, in hopes of stopping Democrats from taking the House this year. Kaptur has had a rebellious streak for much of her 43 years in Congress, which began when she unseated a Republican in 1982 after serving as a domestic policy adviser in Jimmy Carter’s administration. Representing a district centered on her hometown of Toledo that was navigating the fallout from manufacturing disinvestment and population loss, Kaptur opposed both the North American Free Trade Agreement and the bank bailouts of the 2008 financial crisis. She has made unsuccessful bids for leadership positions in the House Democratic Caucus, and complained openly that midwestern representatives like herself were being overlooked. In 1996, the late billionaire Ross Perot approached her to serve as his running mate when he made a third-party bid for the presidency, but Kaptur declined. Now 80, Kaptur still lives in her childhood home, and has no plans to retire, saying that since she is the top Democrat on a powerful, spending-focused House subcommittee, she feels a responsibility to use that leverage to help her community. “My ability to help them is a function of the positions I hold,” she said of her constituents. Though her job requires her presence in Washington many weeks, Kaptur may be the best known local politician in Toledo, simply because she manages to be around quite a bit. “Marcy’s here. I was just at an event, and I know it’s campaign time, but I was just at an event with her Saturday,” said Tony Totty, the president of the United Auto Workers’s political arm in the Toledo region. “That’s not just because it’s campaign time. Marcy is in her district, and, you know, these politicians fall in love with DC because it’s alluring, but Marcy’s been there too long to let that sway her.” Her career has coincided with a decline in Democrats’ fortunes in Ohio, a one-time swing state that’s now dominated by Republicans. As Kaptur’s re-election prospects have grown more competitive, she has repeatedly been among the first to publicly break with her party. “Joe Biden’s letting Ohio solar manufacturers be undercut by China, but Marcy Kaptur’s fighting back,” the narrator declared in an ad for her re-election bid in 2022, the first under Republican-friendly district lines. Kaptur wound up beating her opponent JR Majewski after it turned out he misrepresented his military service, a win that broke the record for length of service by a female lawmaker in the US Congress. ‘The public has to know where you stand’ In August, Kaptur and her campaign manager were injured when a hit-and-run driver slammed into their car on a rainy morning, as they were going to church. She had recovered well and was just returning to campaigning the following month when the ad on transgender rights debuted, and the backlash followed. Singling out her use of the term “transgender ideology”, the Democratic party in Lucas county, where Toledo lies, said: “This is the type of harmful ad we expect from Derek Merrin and the Republicans. We are disappointed and ashamed that the Kaptur campaign stooped to their level by using this incredibly dangerous anti-trans rhetoric.” In neighboring Wood county, the Democratic party said it was “disappointed and saddened that the Kaptur campaign is running ads that use hurtful language and dangerous anti-trans rhetoric”. The latest round of redistricting added three heavily Republican counties along the border with Indiana into Kaptur’s district. Sam Nelson, a political science professor at the University of Toledo, said the congresswoman’s path to victory this year requires getting her traditional support base in Toledo to turn out, while stemming her losses in those rural areas, perhaps by capitalizing on voter anxiety over issues like datacenters. “The anti-trans ad that she was running, that negates an attack line from the Merrin campaign, makes it harder for them to run ads painting her as supportive of trans issues. But at the same time, it potentially alienates not just LGBT supporters, but also people who support LGBT rights,” Nelson said. “How many people are in each of those buckets? That’s the calculation a campaign has to make.” Andrew Reising, a 36-year-old bartender in Toledo whose 14-year-old son is transgender, said the ads had worsened his perception of Kaptur. “Yes, I’m going to vote for Marcy Kaptur here in the fall. But I’m already talking to people in Toledo right now, talking about seeing if we can find somebody who will be able to primary her in two years. Those are conversations already happening with people disappointed in her,” he said. In an interview, Kaptur said she approved the ad because “the public has to know where you stand on something. I don’t think I’ve taken rights away from anybody.” She talked about how much she hated basketball growing up because other girls were taller than her, and how she wanted to figure skate but did not have the build for it. “Sports is essentially not fair to all people,” she said. “I have supported human rights for everyone, I have a good record. But on that particular issue, the people who should be giving us guidelines have no guidelines,” Kaptur continue. “So, I don’t feel like I’m the person to decide. I feel that I have to let people know I’ll protect their children, and … I do believe the responsibility is with the parents, with the schools, and with the leagues, especially after 18.” Michael Stwarka, a spokesman for Merrin’s campaign, noted the congresswoman voted against a measure House Republicans passed last year to bar transgender athletes from both women and girl’s sports. That bill has not advanced in the Senate. “For 43 years, Marcy has been able to talk out of both sides of her mouth to get elected, and now she is feeling the ground shifting beneath her. Northwest Ohio voters see through Marcy Kaptur and her lies,” Stwarka said. Perhaps a greater obstacle facing Kaptur is that for all her years of service, her name doesn’t carry as much weight in the Trump-friendly rural counties she will represent if she wins a 23rd term. “She is well received, I know, in Lucas county, but 40-plus years in the … House, to me, it’s time for change,” said Mike Weible, a Republican who chairs the board of commissioners in Paulding county, where Trump won more than 77% of the vote two years ago. Campaigning in Toledo on a recent Thursday, the congresswoman went from discussing rising costs with the proprietor of a beauty salon to buying a quart of paint for her deck at a hardware store where Kaptur was on a first-name basis with the staff. Then came a detour for pastries and coffee at Strachn Bakery, where 76-year-old retiree Glenn Taylor saw her walking up and said “I just want to hug you!” “You are doing fantastic job, I don’t care what nobody’s saying,” Taylor said after they embraced. “They’re going to say a lot, especially this last month,” Kaptur replied. “Can you tell me one thing?” Taylor asked. The election was 34 days off, and ads for Merrin and Kaptur were all over the airwaves in Toledo. “I see these TV ads,” Taylor said. “Are they … What are they?” “They’re paid for,” the congresswoman replied. “They’re paid for by people who don’t want us to win.”

title: ‘Our town is making jeans again’: meet the firm reviving jobs and skills in Wales
summary: In the first article in a series on high end British manufacturing, we visit the Hiut Denim factory in Cardigan
text: Worn on the streets of London’s Soho, San Francisco or Sydney, every pair of high-end jeans made by Hiut Denim comes from the rather unlikely location of a small coastal town in west Wales. Cardigan, with a population of just 4,200, has a proud history of denim production and was once home to Britain’s largest jeans factory, even if the town’s name recalls a different garment entirely. When jeans manufacturing in Wales was moved abroad at the start of the century, hundreds of local people lost their jobs and were forced to find work elsewhere. Hiut Denim was founded by David and Clare Hieatt in Cardigan in 2011. The couple, both originally from Wales, previously ran the ethical fashion brand Howies. They set up Hiut – the brand name blends their surname with the word utility – with the goal of reviving denim-making skills in the town and training up the next generation of skilled craftspeople. Elin Evans was one of those “grand masters”, as they are known in the company, with a lifetime’s experience of making jeans. Now 59, Evans is Hiut’s factory manager and has been in the trade since 1983, when she was 16. “I’ve done a full loop, because this is where I started,” she says, from her seat behind a sewing machine on the factory floor. Deftly handling the indigo fabric, she moves individual pieces through the machine and a pair of jeans begins to take shape. In its heyday, the Dewhirst factory in Cardigan where Evans once worked employed about 400 people, representing about 10% of the town’s population, and cranked out 35,000 pairs of jeans each week for Marks & Spencer. When Dewhirst decided to outsource production to Morocco, Evans was given the opportunity to move to Tangier. But the founding of Hiut led to her returning home to Wales and to a sewing machine. “I hoped it was like riding a bike,” she says, “but you never forget and the rest is history”. As Hiut took off, the company moved into what was once part of the Dewhirst factory, taking Evans back to the place she began her career. A slogan painted on the factory wall proclaims “Our town is making jeans again” and Welsh flag bunting flutters above the sewing machines, in celebration of the annual cultural festival, held this year in early August just a miles south of Cardigan. Evans and the other grand masters who joined Hiut have spent decades cutting pieces of fabric, creating pockets and stitching denim. The brand’s production levels are far removed from the mass manufacturing which previously took place in Cardigan – Hiut employs 20 people, who make 120 pairs a week. The company insists its product is no ordinary wardrobe staple. Each pair is made by hand from 17 pieces of fabric, with a “made in Wales” label inside the waistband and another label signed by the member of staff who stitched the jeans. Hiut also offers lifetime repairs. “The majority of the time, you know the name of the person that’s bought your jeans. You know your customer and the customer gets to know us as well,” says Evans. “We’re very proud of what we’re doing and the quality is top notch.” Indeed, online fashion reviews praise Hiut’s attention to detail, such as neat seams and how all of the rivets featuring the brand’s name or owl logo are added by hand to ensure they face the same way. Such premium jeans come with a suitably premium price tag – about 10 times higher than the cost of a high-street pair – starting at £245 for men’s and women’s slim-fit styles, made from organic cotton from Turkey, and rising to £350 for pairs made from premium Japanese selvedge. Hiut customers includes TV personalities Ant and Dec and the brand got a big boost when the Duchess of Sussex wore a pair during her first official visit to Wales in 2018, resulting in a three-month backlog of orders. Despite such endorsements, the company hit financial difficulties in the wake of the Covid pandemic, when the founders approached some of their top customers to ask if they wanted to invest in the company. One of these was the German von Loeper family. They initially became minority shareholders in late 2024, before taking over the company in September 2025. Johann von Loeper, 26, became the company’s chief executive, leaving a career in finance in London to move to Cardigan. He says his father, Philipp, was a loyal customer first, which prompted the family-owned investment group to take a stake in a firm beyond its usual investments in life sciences or agricultural companies. “We don’t do anything in retail or fashion really, this is more of a passion project,” von Loeper says. “My father sort of became obsessed with the product … I think he bought more than 30 pairs.” The family has committed to keeping the manufacturing in Cardigan, although von Loeper adds that the factory’s west Wales location creates logistical challenges when moving finished garments or bringing in photographers and models for photoshoots. He adds: “The thing that attracted all of us to Hiut was the purpose of making jeans again, and not just for the sake of making jeans, but to have the jobs, to have to craft, to have skills remain here.” Some high-profile visitors have tried out the craft. A framed photo and letter from Kensington palace hangs on the factory wall, commemorating the March visit of Catherine, the Princess of Wales, where she had a go on a sewing machine. Walking past huge rolls of fabric from some of the most prestigious denim mills in the world – in Japan, Italy and Turkey – von Loeper says he faced a big decision shortly after taking over running the company. A key Japanese denim supplier warned Hiut and other long-term customers that operational pressures meant it was about to close its order books until 2027. “We bought £100,000 worth of selvedge in my first few weeks here because I said ‘let’s get it now before we run out’ and that was one of the better things I did,” he says. When the von Loeper family took over, they said Hiut was “losing a lot of money every month”, but they believed that with investment and a new strategy, the brand could become profitable again. The new owners soon got to work updating the entire jeans collection, and are hoping to take on more staff so they can increase production. Von Loeper is aware that Evans and other grand masters are fast approaching retirement age and believes the company has a “five-year window” to hire and adequately train new employees. He also wants to broaden Hiut’s appeal, and as part of that has secured new stockists, including Liberty department store in London. “Our customer age group has always been 35-55,” says von Loeper. “Our jeans were worn to the office even before Covid, but we can definitely see that customers and what they are buying for has changed and we are trying to adapt to that.” At the shop located just metres away from where jeans are being made, customers come to try on different denims. One customer, Paul Tomlin, has made a purpose journey to Hiut during a visit to Wales to buy more of his favourite jeans. “I came to make sure I got the right fit. I tried on three pairs and found a style that suits me,” says Tomlin, holding a branded bag containing two new pairs. He says he likes the firm’s ethos as well as its clothing: “It’s a good story and has a good feel as a company”

title: ‘People are pissed’: union decries TSA’s removal of chairs for checkpoint staff
summary: Order for workers to remain standing to ‘reinforce professionalism’ draws rebuke amid plunging morale
text: Union officials have launched a campaign to allow airport security staff to sit once more after the Trump administration unilaterally removed all the chairs for Transportation Security Administration (TSA) staff at checkpoints. “People are pissed,” said Johnny Jones, secretary-treasurer of American Federation of Government Employees (AFGE) TSA council 100 and president of AFGE local 1040, which represents TSA workers in Dallas-Fort Worth. TSA officials ordered that chairs be removed from travel document check stations on September 25, arguing “maintaining a standing posture helps reinforce professionalism, attentiveness and active engagement with passengers” and that the policy change “reinforces both our security posture and our commitment to hospitality”. Jones said his members had been flooded with calls and messages about the agency removing chairs. “People are calling, members are mad, employees are upset because they literally started their day, everything was normal, and by halfway through their shift, they’re (TSA) taking all the chairs out and replacing them with inadequate mats,” said Jones. “The amount of phone calls I received is almost the same as if everybody got fired all at once, almost similar to when we have government shutdowns.” “Our officers screen millions of people a day and they do it right, sitting or standing,” said Hydrick Thomas, president of AFGE TSA council 100, in a statement. “Nobody who works a checkpoint asked for this. Nobody who flies asked for this.” Jones noted the TSA checkpoint podiums are one of two places where TSA officers can rest their legs while screening passengers. Chairs were not removed from x-ray machines because the manufacturers recommend sitting while operating the machines. Jones cited the union was not informed on the policy change and it was not negotiated, rather unilaterally implemented by the agency, and its unclear where it leaves TSA employees who require light duty accommodations. Following the policy change, TSA workers were also required to sign a pledge that promises to support “the well-being and morale of our colleagues,” according to the union. “They didn’t notify the union at all, obviously, nor the employees. They decided it would be a great idea to make their employees upset,” said Jones. He said he is unsure what is being done with the chairs in airports around the US. Jones explained the policy worsens the working conditions of TSA officers who no longer have the option of taking time off of their feet, and noted that border patrol officers and customs officers are still using chairs while screening travel documents. US Customs and Border Patrol said it has not adopted this policy. “A lot of people don’t have adequate footwear to need to stand up for that long,” Jones said. “The agency didn’t allow us to bargain any of these changes. They just implemented them. It’s very demoralizing, upsetting that the agency would do this to transportation security officers.” AFGE, the largest union representing federal workers and representing TSA employees, launched a letter-writing campaign calling on the public to tell TSA to “restore the chairs”. Union leaders criticized the policy change, TSA’s justification for it, and the agency requiring workers sign a morality pledge the same week the policy was unilaterally implemented. “Nobody who works a checkpoint asked for this. Nobody who flies asked for this,” said Thomas in a statement. “If TSA leadership truly believes standing makes people better at their jobs, I look forward to watching every manager in the building prove it for eight hours straight. We will bring the pledge. They can bring their own chair, if they are allowed one.” The policy change is just the latest issue to impact workers at TSA under the Trump administration, who are also currently facing possible pay freezes and significant increases to their health insurance premium costs. Under the Trump administration, the Department of Homeland Security has attempted twice to cancel the collective bargaining agreement between the agency and TSA unions, with a judge ruling in January to reinstate the contract, ruling the agency’s attempt to cancel it violated a court injunction. TSA workers also continued working during two government shutdowns without pay since Trump began his second presidential term, which included a government shutdown from 1 October to 12 November 2025, followed by a partial government shutdown that impacted TSA workers for 76 days from February to April this year. The Trump administration has also been expanding privatization of work done by TSA workers to private contractors through the TSA Gold+ program; however, following criticism of the plan, Tampa airport abandoned its plan to join the program. TSA did not respond to multiple requests for comment on the policy change and union’s criticisms of the policy and morale pledge. TSA still requires a chair must be available upon request for travelers. “This welcome change reinforces both our security posture and our commitment to hospitality by having these officers on their feet and alert,” a TSA spokesperson said in a statement to ABC News on the policy change, but did not cite why the agency did not negotiate the change with the union. “All officers must meet fitness for duty requirements to be capable of performing their vital national security function while simultaneously creating a welcoming and professional environment for travelers.”

title: Dozens injured and buildings damaged as tornadoes hit Sicily
summary: Marsala on island’s west coast badly affected after powerful storm approached from Mediterranean
text: Two tornadoes have struck the coastal town of Marsala in western Sicily, injuring dozens of people, damaging buildings including a school, and overturning cars. A series of videos began to circulate on Friday morning showing two waterspouts approaching the Sicilian town from the sea as people braced for their arrival. Dozens of people were reported injured, with at least 11 taken to hospital after being struck by flying debris and shattered glass. Among the most seriously injured was a 70-year-old man admitted to Mazara del Vallo hospital in a critical condition with several fractures. A school was also hit by the powerful winds, leaving six children with minor cuts and abrasions. At the time the tornado struck, 273 pupils were inside the building, all of whom were safely evacuated. Drone footage showing the aftermath revealed extensive damage to the school, with windows shattered and desks and chairs overturned. In recent years, people in southern Italy have been bracing for the arrival of a “medicane” – a rare Mediterranean storm with hurricane-like characteristics, capable of producing winds exceeding 60 miles an hour and waves reaching five metres in height. The weather system developed amid intense heat over north Africa and unusually warm Mediterranean waters. Scientists have warned that rising sea temperatures, driven by the climate emergency, can provide additional energy for powerful storms in the region. According to experts, record temperatures in the Mediterranean contributed to the freak storm that sank the Bayesian, a super yacht off the coast of Sicily, in August 2024, killing seven people including the tech tycoon Mike Lynch and his teenage daughter.

title: Zelenskyy furious as Trump announces deal to buy Russian diesel
summary: US president says agreement needed to lower fuel prices, but move likely to create fresh crisis with Ukraine and Nato allies
text: Donald Trump is on a fresh collision course with Volodymyr Zelenskyy and European allies after his stunning agreement to buy Russian diesel upended years of US and western pressure on the Kremlin to end its war against Ukraine. Zelenskyy reacted furiously to Trump’s announcement of the deal with Vladimir Putin on Friday, calling it “absolutely terrible” and “not fair and not honest”. The Ukrainian president said “back room deals” with the Russian leader would give Putin more chances on the battlefield. On Saturday morning, Ukrainian officials reported that a Russian attack had killed 12 people in the south-east, including three children, and Moscow claimed its troops were advancing in the east. In a move likely to create a fresh crisis with Washington’s Nato allies, Trump announced the deal with Putin on his Truth Social network, saying it was essential to reduce fuel prices in the US, which have soared as a result of his decision to go to war against Iran. “I have just concluded a highly successful discussion with President Vladimir Putin, of Russia,” he said, to deliver millions of tonnes of diesel fuel over the next few months. He added: “Diesel prices for Americans and, indeed, the world, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST! Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my greatest priority.” Fuel prices have soared since Iran closed the strait of Hormuz, a strategically sensitive choke point that was the passageway for 20% of global oil supplies before the war. While costs have risen for motorists – a gallon of regular fuel in the US is about $4.20 (£3.17) – it is the price of diesel, which last month hit a record high of $6.52, that has inflicted the most damage on Trump and the Republicans as November’s midterm elections approach. Diesel is the main supply chain fuel, and a rise in its costs feeds into consumer prices and also hurts US farmers, who need it to operate machinery. Democrats said the agreement undercut a law Trump signed last month allowing for a broad range of sanctions on Russian banks, officials and tankers, as well as directing him to impose steep tariffs on the top five importers of oil or natural gas from Russia. The law gave Trump wide discretion to make exceptions to its provisions. “This is what failure looks like. Failure for President Trump to live up to his promises to lower costs for Americans. Failure to protect America from its adversaries,” said a statement from the Senate Democratic leader, Chuck Schumer, Senator Jeanne Shaheen, who is the top Democrat on the foreign relations committee, and Senator Elizabeth Warren, the ranking Democrat on the banking committee. Some Republicans also criticised the agreement. “Propping up Putin’s war economy is morally wrong as he uses that money to bomb cities,” congressman Don Bacon, a Nebraska Republican, wrote on X. “The President’s policies towards Russia and Ukraine are failures. We need moral clarity not moral ambiguity.” Zelenskyy told Axios that it “looks like a happy birthday present for Putin. It looks absolutely terrible.” The Russian leader turned 74 this week. In a long social media post, Zelenskyy, who has had an uneasy relationship with Trump, said the deal amounted to “an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged”. Russia was likely to repay it with “further terror and perfidy”. “It plays into Russia’s hands – allowing it to kill more, wage war for longer, have even less respect for America, and inflict even greater losses and damage on the world,” he said. Referring on Saturday to the attack on the south-eastern city of Zaporizhzhia that killed 12 people, Zelenskyy wrote on X: “Today, Russia expressed its thanks for the lifting of sanctions on diesel exports by dropping five glide bombs on residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia. “Last night confirmed once again that in Russia, they take any easing of pressure to mean they can keep fighting, to mean they can keep dropping bombs on cities. Different signals are needed.” Separately, Russian media cited the defence ⁠ministry ⁠as saying its forces ⁠had captured ‌the ‌settlements of Lukashove ‌and Lobanivka in Ukraine’s eastern ‌Kharkiv region. Zelenskyy previously said Putin had been playing games with Trump, and on Saturday, a Kremlin spokesperson said the Russian leader had responded with “understanding” to Trump’s proposals to de-escalate the conflict. Trump announced the diesel deal as his envoys, Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner, met Ukrainian and European officials in Miami to discuss proposals to end the war. Zelenskyy, in a separate statement released by Ukraine’s embassy in Washington on Friday, said the Ukrainian negotiators had been “used as a smokescreen for the deal”, which he called “a weak decision by strong partners”. “That is certainly not fair. It is certainly not how partners should treat each other,” he said. Trump recently criticized Ukraine for attacking Russian diesel refineries, calling on Zelenskyy to choose alternative targets. The Ukrainian leader rejected the request unless Russia stopped attacking Ukraine’s energy infrastructure. Tensions have been rising between Russia and European Nato members amid speculation that Moscow might be preparing military action intended to test the alliance’s resolve. The latest development is likely to worsen Zelenskyy’s relationship with the Trump administration. He was infamously ambushed by Trump and the vice-president, JD Vance, last year in an explosive White House encounter when the president told him: “You don’t have the cards.” But Trump has since reportedly grown disenchanted with Putin, expressing disappointment at his failure to reach a peace deal. Trump’s willingness to reach a fuel agreement with Putin comes despite Russia’s support for Iran in its war with the US. Russia is believed to have given Iran satellite intelligence and overhead surveillance data detailing the locations of US forces, ships, aircraft and military bases. It has also provided drone components and ammunition.

title: UK must not be beholden to foreign AI, says head of Alan Turing Institute
summary: George Williamson says ‘national resilience’ is key focus of ATI amid US and China’s runaway leadership in field
text: The UK must not become dependent on foreign AI systems that can be switched off at short notice and must develop its own versions of the technology, according to the head of the Alan Turing Institute. The country needs a stronger domestic position in AI in response to the US and China’s runaway leadership in the field, with “national resilience” a key focus for ATI said George Williamson. The institute is the UK’s leading AI research body and is under new leadership after the government, its main source of funding, demanded a strategic shift. “As AI becomes more embedded in critical services, in domains like defence, national security, critical infrastructure and healthcare we shouldn’t depend solely on systems we can’t inspect or control, or that could be restricted or even switched off,” said Williamson. In June Washington temporarily blocked the release outside the US of Anthropic’s latest models, and has reportedly asked leading AI labs to withhold their models from being tested by the UK’s AI Security Institute until they have been examined by AISI’s US counterpart. “We’ve seen now that both political and commercial pressures mean we may not have access [to AI] in all the circumstances when we want it. That is not a place where a nation wants to be,” he said. Williamson added: “There’s a set of circumstances where it would be a good idea for us to have something that we don’t have to ask other people’s permission to use.” He said national resilience would be a focus of ATI’s work amid concern about the geopolitical situation and the risk posed by increasingly powerful AI systems. Those concerns were highlighted last month by the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, announcing a new national centre to tackle state-backed disinformation, and Anthropic predicting the technology had a greater than 10% chance of wiping out humanity by 2030. “It’s a moment when national resilience is definitely what the country needs and it’s definitely a thing I think the Turing institute can help with,” he said. “We are facing a more adversarial world, more frequent shocks to our critical infrastructure and now powerful AI amplifying these threats. To strengthen national resilience, the Turing will focus on securing critical systems against disruption, countering threats from AI itself and helping to shape the right strategic AI capability for the UK.” Williamson said the institute could assist in building such resilience by helping produce uses for AI “for the public good”, working on areas from weather forecasting to farming, as well as helping spot disinformation. Referring to state-led disinformation campaigns, he said: “It’s very dangerous for the state of democracy and it’s an area that we can monitor.” Williamson is the former head of His Majesty’s Government Communications Centre, a secretive government body that makes gadgets for UK spy agencies and counts Alan Turing – the second world war codebreaker and AI pioneer after which ATI is named – among its former staff. Williamson said it had become clear in recent months that the UK needed “more agency on access to technology” and a stronger sovereign position in AI. “It feels pretty uncomfortable if you don’t have some control or ability to use technologies when you want them, and also harder to imagine how you build an economy on the top of stuff that can disappear,” he said. In recent weeks Christine Lagarde, the president of the European Central Bank, and Ursula von der Leyen, the president of the European Commission, have urged Europe to be more self-sufficient in AI, with Lagarde speaking about the threat of being “cut off” from US and Chinese technology. Williamson cited China as another reason for boosting domestic AI, amid concerns that Chinese-made systems might not “coincide with our values”. He said: “Try asking some of these models about some events in the recent past in China and you’re not going to get an answer that’s particularly helpful if you’re doing GCSE history.” “This is the defining technology of our time. We want to be able to shape that technology … in a way that accords with who we are and our values,” he said, adding that while ATI and the UK probably could not match the financial resources of major AI labs, they could still produce “nationally owned IP” or smaller models that could be made available to startups. “We can be ambitious here without trying to copy what frontier labs are doing,” he said. Williamson said ATI, a registered charity, could be an “objective and helpful” arbiter of concerns about AI, including existential threat. “A national institute should be an active partner to government and the public more generally in helping to navigate some of this stuff.” He said there was a “a lot of stuff being tossed around” on the existential threat risk that “is not always well grounded in science”. Referring to the penchant among some in the sector for expressing the risk of AI-triggered extinction in percentage terms, he said: “I’m not sure it’s helpful trying to assign particular percentages to it because I have not seen anyone show me a convincing evidence of how they’ve arrived at the number they then start throwing around.” Williamson indicated that the focus on national resilience would enable ATI to keep doing work on the environment that Keir Starmer’s government had wanted to sideline. In 2025 the then technology secretary, Peter Kyle, wrote to ATI’s chair demanding the institute switch its main focus to defence and security. Williamson’s predecessor Jean Innes resigned soon afterwards. “For me climate is as much a national security issue as defence. For me, it [national resilience] is a frame that enables us to cover the range of threats and opportunities to the UK,” he said.

title: Don’t rebuild the dam: Ukrainian experts urge Unesco to protect site uncovered by Russian sabotage
summary: As archaeologists find treasure trove along new floodplain, conservationists say another Nova Kakhovka would be ecocide
text: On a warm September day, a group of underwater archaeologists and researchers were boiling water for tea on their campfire on the banks of the Dnipro River, tents pitched on the sandy shoreline. They were three weeks into an archaeological expedition of the waters around Khortytsia – a rocky island 12.5km long and 2.5km wide that lies just downstream of the city of Zaporizhzhia, in south-eastern Ukraine. High above the island, a Shahed drone whined on its way. A Ukrainian interceptor, and small-arms fire from the ground, tried, unsuccessfully, to bring it down. The archaeologists ignored it. This is life as normal, 28 miles (45km) from the combat zone in Russia’s war on Ukraine. Olena Dzneladze, senior research fellow at Ukraine’s national Institute of Archaeology, showed off their remarkable finds: a bronze-age deer antler, its tip shaped into a tool to press patterns into pottery or leather; a shard of ceramic most likely made by the Scythians, an ancient nomadic people of the steppe; a chunk of a Byzantine amphora; an 18th-century anchor. Most spectacular, though was an entire boat, hollowed out of a single tree trunk and beautifully preserved by a millennium’s river immersion – one of many remarkable vessels, including 18th-century warships, that have been discovered in this part of the Dnipro. The team was planning to lift it from the river the following day. With its neighbouring, smaller islands, Khortytsia comprises a natural and historical reserve – a place of profound symbolic importance to Ukraine’s national narrative as the first stronghold of the Zaporizhzhian Cossacks, and with traces of human life stretching back to the Mesolithic era. Khortytsia lies at the head of a vast landscape known as the “great meadow”. This 2,155 sq km area was, between the building of the Nova Kakhovka dam in the 1950s until 6 June 2023, covered by a reservoir. That was the day the 30-metre high, 3km-long structure was blown up – by the Russians, according to most analysts. Unchecked by the dam, the waters of the reservoir – 18 cubic km of it – drained out of its bed and roared downstream, creating an acute humanitarian crisis as its waters inundated towns and villages on both sides of the river, and both sides of the frontline. Now, however, a vocal group of historians, naturalists, ecologists and archaeologists want to see this territory of the “great meadow” protected as a Unesco world heritage site for its value as a natural and a cultural environment. The former reservoir bed has, with startling speed, regenerated itself into something like its pre-dam self: a habitat of wetlands, grassland and islands, richly populated with the traces of thousands of years of human life. The dam, say the experts, must never be rebuilt. Over 100 Ukrainian NGOs are formally supporting the bid. A letter of intent has been sent to Unesco, and cooperation sought from the Ukrainian government’s culture ministry. But other interests will want to see the dam replaced and the reservoir remade, to irrigate Ukraine’s southern farmlands. Soon after its destruction, the Ukrainian government set up a pilot project with the state-owned hydroelectric company Ukrhydroenergo to prepare the groundwork for its reconstruction after the end of the war. Valeriy Nefedov, leading the team of archaeologists on the island, is one of those pressing for the preservation of the “unique historical and natural environment” that has re-emerged. In 1999 the underwater archaeologist discovered an early-18th-century warship in these waters, now in the island’s Museum of Navigation. And, in the summer of 2023, he was one of the first to set foot on to the 2,155 sq kilometre territory revealed by the drained Kakhovka reservoir. Nefedov was serving in the army on 6 June 2023, in the Donetsk region, and quickly heard the news of the destruction of the Nova Kakhovka dam. For him, there was a certain irony: since the 1990s, he had been pressing for the dam’s gradual dismantling, the draining of the reservoir and the restitution of the “great meadow” with its mosaic of grassland ecosystems and marshes, reed beds, scrub and sandy mounds. But not like this, in one single, catastrophic event. “The first crime was building the dam in the first place,” he said. “The second was blowing it up.” Later that month, he was asked to join a newly formed military unit consisting of experts – historians, ecologists, scientists and other researchers – to investigate the reservoir bed. “Of course, I had some expectations about what I might see. But when we reached the area, it is impossible to describe the impressions and emotions I felt. The consequences were staggering: what had been a reservoir had, within a very short time, turned into the exposed bottom of the body of water. On the other hand, there was a sense of danger.” This was the grey zone, no man’s land, “extremely tense”, he said. There was constant shelling. Though Ukrainian reconnaissance units had been there ahead of them, Russian sabotage groups were also on the prowl. And they could see the occupied Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant, where the Russians were positioned. “It was a very strange feeling,” he said, “being between the positions of our Ukrainian forces and those of our Russian enemies.” It was more than that, though: a watery territory, that he knew intimately as a diver, was now dry land, and he was walking across it. “It felt like terra incognita, unknown land – as if we were the first people to set foot on it,” he said. “Everything we saw and found there made us feel like explorers or discoverers. “Very unusual, almost fantastical landscapes appeared before us. Ancient channels, straits and islands had been revealed. “We saw the remains of settlements, the foundations of houses, roads. We also found archaeological material lying directly on the surface, from the neolithic right through into the 20th century.” There were also toxic heavy metals revealed on the reservoir bed, which biologist Pavlo Oliinyk, one of the research team at Khortytsia, is involved in monitoring. But, he said, the rapid growth of vegetation in the drained “great meadow” area may provide a “green shield”. Trees, he said, had already grown up to as much as 7 metres high in the reservoir area, in just three years. “Building the dam was ecocide, destroying the dam was ecocide, and the third ecocide would be rebuilding it,” he said. The “great meadow”, this vast area of the Dnipro floodplain – which remains a grey zone between the opposing armies – has always had huge significance owing to its unique topography; its first surviving mention in the written record is by Herodotus, the fifth-century BCE Greek historian. This section of the Dnipro was the last easily navigable stretch of the river north of the Black Sea, before the rapids upstream at Zaporizhzhia rendered the river unmanageable by all but the most knowledgable. This protective geography created a safe haven for the Cossacks, who, fleeing persecution in the 16th century, established a free, quasi-democratic polity here. This Cossack state became a important reference for the 19th-century intellectuals, including national poet Taras Shevchenko, who led the modern Ukrainian national project. The area’s significance goes back even deeper. Also working on the island of Khortytsia in September was archaeologist Anatoliy Volkov, who, inland from the group of underwater archaeologists, was excavating one of a series of bronze-age stone enclosures. “We are in a frontline area,” he said of continuing his work during the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. “We are potentially threatened. There is always a chance a missile or rocket will land here, and so the more we research and preserve, the better.” The urgency of the research and monitoring was even more acute on the shoreline and riverbed, according to archaeologist Olena Dzneladze. After the blowing of the dam, she said, thousands of tons of sand started to move down the river, “with artefacts appearing in the moving sand”. Amid this volatile military and geographical situation, the Dnipro is settling into something like its old course, before the Nova Kakhovka dam was completed in 1956. Between Khortytsia and the next great dam upstream, at Zaporizhzhia, further rocky islands and sandy spits have been revealed as the water level has sunk 6-8 metres, transforming the landscape. Serhii Plokhii, Harvard’s professor of Ukrainian history, grew up in Zaporizhzhia hearing his grandfather’s stories of hunting in the wetlands of the “great meadow” before the dam was built. He recalled his emotions seeing the newly emerging landscape of the famous Zaporizhzhia rapids for the first time – though most of the rocky outcrops lie upstream, still submerged thanks to the Zaporizhzhia dam. “It was something that I read about and was part of history, but I had never seen before. And I thought: ‘Whatever happens with the Nova Kakhovka dam, whether they will rebuild it or not, I at least have had this chance to see this piece of history that was there, but was always invisible.’”

title: ‘We’re not asking for luxury’: school protesters in Paris suburb feel abandoned by French state
summary: Students say they are desperate to get back to class but conditions are so bad that the protests must continue
text: On a normal school day, Mohammed, 17, wakes at 6am, cares for his younger siblings to help his single mother who works as a security guard, then takes two crowded buses and a local train to get to his high school in Sevran, a low-income banlieue town in the suburbs north-east of Paris. “There aren’t enough chairs or desks to go round, so some students have to stand up,” Mohammed said. “Classes can be so packed you can’t interact with the teacher. In this year’s heatwaves, it felt like 40 degrees in overcrowded classrooms with no shade or curtains. It was so hot my brain couldn’t function.” The 17-year-old in his last year of high school wants to study management and digital communication at a Paris university. But he said conditions were so poor, he felt all odds were stacked against him and his classmates. “Some of us have to go months without teachers when absent staff aren’t replaced,” he said. “One class had no French teacher for several months just before the French baccalaureate, so they couldn’t even study all the set texts for their exam. Recently we needed a teacher for a subject taught through English, but when that teacher arrived they didn’t speak English.” The biggest youth protest movement in the country in decades brought hundreds of thousands on to the streets across France this week demonstrating against inequality in the French education system, decrepit schools, a lack of teachers and large class sizes. Hundreds of schools were blockaded, thousands of teenagers were arrested, and rights groups warned of alleged police brutality, with one child losing the use of eye and another losing a hand. Mohammed and his classmates, often supported by their parents and teachers, have been at the frontline, barricading their school, the Lycée Blaise-Cendrars, which is in one of mainland France’s poorest départements, Seine-Saint-Denis. They have voted to continue their protests next week, taking their grievances to the local mayor, elected officials and education representatives. Many local politicians have supported their demands. Even the French prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, conceded that teenagers had “legitimate” concerns. Photos on the Sevran students’ phones showed broken classroom chairs, holes in walls, holes in ceilings, mould, buckets to catch leaks, faulty lights. They said basic needs weren’t met, with some toilets broken, others with no doors and often no toilet paper or soap. Video projectors and science equipment were lacking. “We’re not asking for luxury, just the basics to learn in decent conditions,” Mohammed said. “And yet police on horseback charged us when we were gathered to protest outside our school, firing teargas at us and making arrests. It’s so dangerous to be charged by a horse, it could kill you. I just ran, I was trying to help my classmates.” The high schools of Seine-Saint-Denis, a suburban area nudging against northern Paris, have been a driving force in the protests. The area has the youngest population in mainland France, one of the highest birthrates and the among the lowest average income. Local high schools have a high turnover of young teachers. Despite co-hosting the 2024 Paris Olympics, and numerous government plans to try to combat long-running problems of inequality and poverty, the area north-east of Paris is still disadvantaged compared with the capital. In 2005, Seine-Saint-Denis was the starting point for weeks of unrest on housing estates across France, leading to a state of national emergency being declared, after the death of two young boys hiding from police in an electricity substation. This week’s protests have shown that inequality and discrimination has not been addressed in the Paris suburbs and the mistrust between young people and police persists. Sevran’s Lycée Blaise-Cendrars, with more than 1,000 pupils, has been at the heart of protests about school conditions before. In 2024, students and teachers made a viral video about the state of classrooms, toilets and equipment. The local Île de France region said it had put in place a major refurbishment project for high school buildings. But the teenagers said key issues had not been addressed. “We’re starting at an unfair advantage because our parents aren’t as rich as others, they can’t buy us books, they can’t take us to films,” said Ilian, 17, whose family has Moroccan roots and whose father is a traffic warden. “We’re missing school during these protests, we risk falling behind in an exam year, we’re desperate to get back into class to study, but the conditions we’re facing are so bad we can’t stop until the government promises action.” The education ministry this week promised 3,000 teachers to urgently fill gaps, but teachers’ unions expressed doubts and said longer-term plans and more funding was needed, even if the government argues there is little spare cash. Children’s mental health is also an issue in Seine-Saint-Denis. Ilian has been waiting to see a child psychiatrist for months. At the high school, there was no school nurse and a lack of support staff for children with disabilities, he said. “The police look down on us as if we’re animals”, Ilian said. “They talk to us with such cruelty.” He told local politicians that some teenagers alleged police had made racial insults against them during protests. Stéphane Troussel, the Socialist head of the Seine-Saint-Denis département council who met the pupils this week, said: “It’s intolerable that policing is causing part of the difficulties.” He called for the police to stop using a type of rubber-bullet launcher, after they suspended use of stun grenades following injuries. The French interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, has defended policing tactics. Stéphane Blanchet, the mayor of Sevran, said he supported the school protesters’ demands. He said many in his town of 52,000 people, with a higher than average poverty rate, felt “relegated” and forgotten by the state. Sarah, 17, who wanted to study at an elite Paris engineering faculty, and whose warehouse worker father was proud she was protesting and meeting the mayor, said teenagers in the banlieue “really feel abandoned”. She said: “We’ve been surprised and so appreciative of other teenagers in better-off places in France marching in the streets to support us this week. We know we’re disadvantaged and that we have to work 10 times as hard as others to escape discrimination against our postcode. But we can’t learn properly in these conditions when we’re not even guaranteed a chair to sit on in school.” Students’ names have been changed
