title: Recruitment boss accused of being behind ‘doxxing’ campaign against RNLI and anti-racism activists
summary: Tom Watson, of Worcester, alleged to be behind Big Time Charlie X account that created so-called Traitorbase
text: The owner of a recruitment firm has been accused of being at the centre of a so-called “doxxing” campaign against the Royal National Lifeboat Institution (RNLI), anti-racism activists and business executives who recruit black, Asian and minority ethnic workers. Tom Watson, from Worcester, is alleged to be behind an X account calling itself “Big Time Charlie”, which was deactivated shortly after he was named by the campaign group Hope Not Hate. The account had almost 50,000 followers and had become increasingly prominent in recent weeks as RNLI staff found themselves being harassed and attacked online as far-right activists targeted them over their involvement in rescuing people trying to cross the Channel in small boats. The account, which has a history of racist comments, appears to have been using AI to scrape data from LinkedIn and other sites to build a so-called Traitorbase. The Big Time Charlie account was removed almost immediately after Hope Not Hate alleged that Watson was behind it, and after the Guardian approached him for comment. Like the posts on Watson’s LinkedIn account, the X account has frequently praised the hard-right MP Rupert Lowe. It also claimed to have donated £2,500 to Lowe’s Restore Britain party and joined its “Cromwell Club” for those activists who pay a certain level of donation. Targets of doxxing by the Big Time Charlie account told the Guardian of the impact. They included Chantelle Lunt, a Green party councillor in Merseyside who has already been targeted by the far right, and who made a report to the police after details about her were published online by the account. She said: “Someone told me that I had been doxxed and when I went to look I saw that details about me appeared to be on a spreadsheet which included reference to other people who were involved in Stand Up to Racism. “The climate at the moment is horrendous and I’m no stranger to people targeting me and my family, but there’s a big concern when this information is actively put out there. You can see people engaging with it and actively encouraging each other.” A spokesperson for a charity that was targeted told the Guardian: “This is another example of a cynical attempt to spread misinformation that has unfortunately gone unchecked on social media platforms. “This is an attempt to sow discord and division among communities and prevent organisations trying to help the most vulnerable communities in this country from operating at their full potential. “Time spent combating misinformation and bigotry is a distraction from these organisations’ programme work here at home, which actually makes a difference in the ordinary lives of people in the UK. Social media companies, the media and politicians have a responsibility to clamp down on misinformation and the division it causes.” A number of businesses, big and small, were also doxxed on the account, which posted the photographs and names of executives who were said to have been involved in hiring minority ethnic staff. A businessperson who was also targeted described their doxxing by the account as “bizarre”. “Thankfully it doesn’t seem to have led to any problems, but it’s not something that you expect to have to contend with. It’s a pretty unpleasant thing to do, especially if it’s someone who is involved in their own business,” they added. Watson divides his time between the UK and US and founded the recruitment firm Futura Energy Group, which describes itself as “a specialist recruitment and build-with talent partner for companies operating across AI”. Archived online records show that the Big Time Charlie account originally bore the name Tom Watson, while a range of other evidence links him to it. That included regular references by the account to being in Puerto Rico, where Futura is based according to its LinkedIn account, and references to working in recruitment for technical roles. The Big Time Charlie account posted on 20 July that they were in Zurich and shared a photo taken in the grounds of the Vitznauerhof hotel. Two days later, Watson posted on his LinkedIn profile that he was in Switzerland and shared another image taken from the Vitznauerhof hotel. Watson was approached for comment.

title: ‘If voters aren’t better off by the next election, we’re screwed’: Labour insiders voice fears over budget
summary: Some say party risks ‘looking twee’ by focusing on small fixes amid growing nervousness that budget lacks ambition
text: In the days since Labour’s annual conference, party insiders have been sharing a word cloud produced by the pollsters More in Common, which shows the phrases voters most associate with Andy Burnham. Such polling is rarely flattering for politicians, and the prime minister’s version had its fair share of negatives. But one of the most prominent words in the cloud – and the one that has caught the imagination of Labour strategists – was “trying”. At a cabinet away day at Chequers on Monday and a meeting for special advisers on Thursday, the idea that the government was doing its best to improve people’s lives – despite the difficult economic backdrop – was a golden thread. “The public think the only person that can reach those levers is you,” said a government insider. “They justifiably ask, can you do it or not? And if not, they’ll look for an alternative. We have to avoid the sense of things being out of our control.” A party strategist said: “Voters don’t want us to put our hands up in despair; they want us to roll our sleeves up. They don’t want us to be helpless in the face of global stuff; they want answers.” But will this prime minister be able to provide them? At conference, Burnham set out his big vision for the future – on social care and the pensions triple lock, the EU and electoral reform. The party faithful lapped it up and polling suggested the “Burnham bounce” had continued. But while Labour MPs are relieved to have a leader with a clear political direction, many worry that offering big promises for after the next general election will not be enough to scratch the itch for dramatic change. Downing Street believes part of the answer is what it describes as “everyday fixes” – cost of living measures that might not, on their own, amount to very much, but added up can make a difference and show the government is trying. Overseen by the No 10 policy unit and the Cabinet Office’s cost of living taskforce, each department has “incubators” where proposals are dreamed up. Many are in the works, such as rules around car-parking apps and unbranded school uniforms. They might not grab the media headlines, but strategists say they pick up engagement online, with 85m views across all social platforms last week alone. There will be more announced in the two-and-a-bit weeks running up to John Healey’s first budget on 28 October. “We want to show we can tackle the everyday frustrations that people assume are part of life,” one adviser said. But several admitted they had some qualms about the drumbeat of small interventions. “We risk looking twee, frankly, if we aren’t successfully thinking about how to tie it to the bigger picture of structural change. Public control, tax, that is what we want to be able to point to as well as the everyday things.” Another added: “We need to tread carefully. We have very small interventions now and huge ambitions for three years’ time. We also need medium-scale changes in the medium term, and that is what is missing at the moment.” The government faces a difficult budget, with inflation and soaring borrowing costs as a result of the Iran war thought to have blown a £12bn hole in the public finances, forcing the chancellor to consider tax rises and spending cuts to fund plans to ease the cost of living. The statement, which is expected to be “low key”, will focus on fiscal devolution, with a household support package centred on cutting energy bills and more help for small businesses. Next year’s spending review would require more revenue, sources said, but details would have to wait. A No 10 aide said: “The budget is a moment of peak attention and potentially peak peril. We’re not able to do everything we want to, so we have to level with people and say we can’t fix everything all at once, but we’re trying.” But for some MPs, there is a growing nervousness at the low level of ambition at this budget, especially on cost of living measures, which the Burnham government has made its main test. One said: “If voters aren’t better off by the next election, we are screwed. As things stand, this looks like a Reeves budget with better vibes. I hope this isn’t all there is. But I really fear that actually it is.” Treasury insiders acknowledge the need to “kickstart” longer-term changes at the budget – and that a “low-key” statement with the big decisions put off until next year may not be enough for the public. “The budget will be our first punch in the face moment,” a government aide said. There was a “bit of friction” between the prime minister’s office and the Treasury over balancing fiscal responsibility with hope, the source added. “No 10 wants to signal intent: that we won’t get everything immediately, but we’ll get there.” There were lingering questions about “how this all adds up when we’re under grey skies”, another adviser added. “It’s impossible to see how anyone can square the additional spending we need given the tightness of the fiscal envelope.” Ministers and advisers are expecting a barrage of attacks from the Tories and Reform UK on welfare. But they believe the Milburn and Timms reviews, which will be published shortly after the budget – will help them fight back. Downing Street expects the days after the budget to be “bumpy” but is optimistic that Burnham’s communication skills will help to make the case, and that the public will continue – for now – to give him the benefit of the doubt. A source said: “We’ll take a bit of a hit over the budget. It’s going to be a tough couple of weeks. But then we have a run to the 10-year plan. If we get that right, we can potentially go into next year with people saying: ‘Yes, it’s difficult, but we trust this guy.’” At the cabinet away day, Burnham told ministers: “Politics has become too suffocating. We need greater ambition. The country is not where it should be and nothing simple gets us out of that. We need to show a journey and a longer-term plan.” Ministers were presented with polling that showed support for Labour’s social care policy, including adjusting the pensions triple lock, went up by a quarter after voters were shown a video of the prime minister explaining his plan. A party strategist told them: “On social care and the triple lock we need to continually make the case, time after time. When we make the case we have the power to persuade.” There is a political axiom that if you’re explaining, you’re losing. But Labour strategists are pushing back on that idea. The prevailing view inside government is that Burnham is the only one who can go out and make the case – on all of his big promises – to the country. Not everybody inside the party thinks it will work. “I don’t know how convinced I am about giving people essentially the same message as before: we want to do more but we’re constrained,” one insider said. But ministers hope that by focusing on policies which signal intent, they can get through these difficult months. “We need more time to lean into the big things we can do, like public control, but we need to be honest with voters. We set ourselves a target of tackling the cost of living, but so many things are out of our control.” No 10 insight work shows that people were still prepared to accept the Iran conflict as an explanation for why things are so tough, rather than viewing it as an excuse. At the away day, Healey told his colleagues: “We are recognising those pressures, being honest about what we can do and taking practical action wherever possible to give people some breathing space at the budget.” When parliament returns after conference recess on Monday, Burnham will give a statement, updating MPs on the past few weeks and taking questions. Throughout, he will aim to show the public he is on their side. But one senior Labour figure cautioned: “We all hope that he has a plan for what comes next. The sense that he gets it and that he’ll keep trying won’t last for ever.” On Tuesday 1 December, join John Crace and Pippa Crerar as they skewer the biggest stories from Westminster and beyond, as part of the Guardian’s year in review event. Joined by fellow Guardian writers, expect candid conversations, witty remarks and surprises as they look back on the year-defining stories of 2026. Book tickets here or at guardian.live

title: UK accused of giving people of Gaza false hope over new refugee safe route
summary: Only ‘very small number’ of people already in Lebanon or Jordan will be referred, says organisation running scheme
text: The Home Office is facing claims it gave false hope to the people of Gaza after it emerged that a new safe route for Palestinian refugees will only be open to those who have already escaped to Lebanon or Jordan. Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, announced the reopening of a resettlement scheme for refugees at Labour’s annual conference last month. A statement from her department said: “Around one in four referrals will be for Afghan women and girls and Palestinian refugees, fleeing war and persecution.” But the body administering the scheme has confirmed it would only refer “a very small number of extremely urgent cases”, all of which would be processed in Jordan and Lebanon. The umbrella alliance Communities for Palestinians (CFP) said this crucial detail was not in Mahmood’s speech or subsequent Home Office statements, giving people in Gaza and their supporters the belief that they could also apply. Vicky Moller, a co-founder of CFP, said: “The applause at Shabana’s announcement at conference was at the prospect of a resettlement scheme for Palestinians fleeing war and persecution. People understood that would mean rescuing people from Gaza.” The Home Office has pushed back at the claims, saying the UK resettlement scheme that Mahmood has reopened has always been for people from outside their country of origin. A Home Office spokesperson said: “To qualify for refugee status under international frameworks, individuals must be outside their country of origin. “Palestinians who remain in Gaza would not initially be in scope for these routes. However, Palestinians who have fled Gaza could be referred to the UK through the International Refugee Assistance Project [Irap].” Restrictions on eligibility for the scheme emerged after an exchange of emails between the CFP and Irap, which has been tasked with making referrals. According to Irap’s website, it will refer “a very small number of extremely urgent humanitarian cases to the UK for consideration for resettlement”, adding: “These cases will be referred to Irap by humanitarian organisations in Jordan and Lebanon and Irap will then hold interviews to determine if these cases can be referred to the UK government.” The programme focuses on “extremely vulnerable refugees whose lives have become unsustainable in Jordan or Lebanon”. The non-profit’s website added: “Irap does not know how many people the UK government will accept under the Palestinian resettlement programme. This is ultimately a decision for the UK government and depends on funding as well as local authorities’ capacity.” Other safe and legal routes administered by the UK have allowed small numbers of people to enter the UK from their country of origin, including previous schemes for Afghan refugees. Palestinian refugees fall outside the remit of the refugee convention and UNHCR. Unrwa was instead set up to serve Palestinian refugees who were defined as any person whose “normal place of residence was Palestine during the period 1 June 1946 to 15 May 1948 and who lost both home and means of livelihood as a result of the 1948 conflict”. As a result, Palestinian refugees live in what refugee charities and NGOs refer to as Palestine – in other words, the West Bank and the Gaza Strip – as well as second countries such as Syria, Lebanon and Jordan. Jon Featonby, the chief policy analyst at the Refugee Council, said ministers should recognise the particular circumstances that meant Palestinians could be refugees while living in their own country. “The government is right to commit to safe and legal routes. They provide a vital way for refugees to reach safety without having to put their lives in the hands of smuggling gangs,” he said. “But the warm words have to be accompanied by ambition, and that means supporting people in the thousands, not the hundreds. They must also recognise the particular circumstances of Palestinian refugees and be accessible to them no matter where they are in the world.” A renowned expert in asylum systems has said resettlement programmes are usually designed as a solution for people who have already left their own country. Dr Peter Walsh, a senior researcher at the Migration Observatory at the University of Oxford, said the UK government’s safe and legal route was always going to mean taking Palestinians from neighbouring states such as Egypt, Jordan or Lebanon. “The Syrian scheme worked the same way: the roughly 20,000 people resettled to the UK between 2014 and 2021 all came from countries around Syria, with nobody to my knowledge being flown directly from Syria,” he said. “Bringing people directly out of Gaza would be a different kind of programme, closer to an emergency evacuation … And crucially, such an emergency evacuation in Gaza would depend on Israel and Egypt letting people leave and on the Home Office finding a way to do security and biometric checks with no visa centre in Gaza.”

title: ‘Would I sit down with Tommy Robinson? It’s not a definite no’: lessons from people who fought the far right in the 70s, 80s and beyond
summary: Extremists are on the rise globally – but UK activists have seen them off in the past in everything from football, politics, music and more. How did they do it?
text: ‘If you’re not organised, you get picked on. When you’re organised, often they flee’ Tariq Mehmood encountered the far right early – at primary school. “When white children surround you in the playground and sing, ‘God made little black people, he made them in the night, he made them in a hurry, and forgot to paint them white’, and the school doesn’t clamp down on that, then you’re living within the far right. It’s not one organisation, it’s a mass movement.” I think it’s likely those kids used another word for “black people” but I can’t quite find the stomach to ask. Mehmood is speaking to me on a video call from Beirut, where he teaches at the American University. Now 70, he migrated, in 1967, from Pakistan to Bradford, where his grandfather and uncles worked in the textile mills, and immediately experienced racism. “The headmaster would tell us to be grateful to be in England, we were beaten up by white boys on the way to school, there was an intense violence and a feeling of helplessness.” Until he realised he wasn’t helpless, or alone. “We knew we couldn’t come to school on our own, so we assembled somewhere, got off the bus together and walked together to the classroom.” Later, when he was himself working in a mill in Otley in the late 70s, Mehmood was one of the founders of the Bradford Asian Youth Movement. The AYMs were a network of anti-racist groups demanding equal rights and a fairer world as well as defending their communities against attacks from groups such as the National Front (NF) and the British Movement (BM). Following disagreements within the AYM, Mehmood was part of a splinter group, the United Black Youth League, that broke away in 1981. “The police tried to paint that our split was because the UBYL wanted violence, but this is anything but the truth,” he says. “Some wanted to work within the system – one of the founders of the AYM became an MP, something I fundamentally disagreed with then as I do now.” There were frequent attacks on the south Asian community in Bradford. “Whenever the National Front had a demonstration, you could always bet that after the pubs closed they would attack us, groups of skinheads – five, six, seven of them in a car, going around, seeing what they could do.” So, as Mehmood had done at school, the UBYL organised themselves. “If you’re not organised, you get picked on. When you’re organised, often they will flee and you don’t have to fight. We couldn’t trust the police; either they were incapable, or they didn’t care, or they harassed us.” When they learned that a lot of fascists were planning to go to Bradford, they got ready. “We mobilised hundreds, many of them white, walking around, making sure people knew we were out, they didn’t have anything to fear. We said we’d arm ourselves if need be. Some of us made petrol bombs.” The petrol bombs require some context. “Remember, it was the year of the massacre of the teenagers in London,” he says, referring to the New Cross house fire in which 13 young black people died (even though it was never proved to have been a racist attack). “Members of the UBYL were blocking up their own letter boxes in case someone poured petrol in and set fire to their houses. That was a reality, and we said no, we will defend ourselves.” In summer 1981, 12 members of the UBYL, including Mehmood, were arrested after a police raid discovered 38 milk bottles filled with petrol. The Bradford 12, as they became known, were charged with conspiracy to cause explosions and endanger lives. They didn’t deny making the molotov cocktails, but said it was a precaution for self-defence. In jail, awaiting trial, Mehmood discovered another weapon: the pen. He wrote his first novel, Hand on the Sun, about a young immigrant experiencing racism. “Stories make us human. I wanted to share with future generations that we were proud industrial workers, we weren’t just going to have crumbs, we were politically conscious and had hope. I still have that hope.” After an active campaign and a lengthy trial, on 16 June 1982 Mehmood and the rest of the Bradford 12 – who had argued self-defence – were acquitted by a jury. The situation with the far right is no better today, he says. In fact, the opposite: “The atmosphere is more vicious than it was in the 80s, primarily because we were dealing with old-style racism born out of British colonial history. Today’s Islamophobia is a more violent, virulent form; it has always been there, under the surface, since the Crusades, but not at a scale you see today. The far right at that time were a few thousand demonstrators here and there, not 100,000, half a million. And they’re not just in Britain, but across Europe.” He sees it as a failure of the left, of the labour and trade union movements, to educate the white working class that “the real enemy is the billionaires at the top”. Plus, the loss of community organisations. Mehmood’s message about what to do about the far right today is to do as they did: organise and fight back. “The most important lesson is that if you believe there is an injustice, then fight against it.” Tariq Mehmood’s memoir, Rebellion: Self-defence and the Story of the Bradford 12, is published by Daraja Press. A documentary, also titled Rebellion and co-directed by Mehmood, premieres at the BFI London film festival on October 14 and 15 * * * ‘The idea was to harness music and politics together to fight fascism and racism’ It was half a century ago, the hot summer of 1976, but Red Saunders remembers it clearly. A photographer and at the time also a member of a radical theatre group, he was in a rehearsal at a studio in Soho, London. “Someone came in and said: ‘Have you seen this shit about Eric Clapton?’” An article in a music magazine said that at a concert in Birmingham, the musician had told his audience to vote for Enoch “rivers of blood” Powell in order to stop Britain from becoming “a black colony”, as well as chanting the NF slogan: Keep Britain White. “I was a Clapton fan, I’d been to his gigs, had the albums. I couldn’t believe it,” says Saunders, now 80 and talking to me from his Suffolk home. He wrote a letter to the music press, and got some of his like-minded friends, including Roger Huddle and Jo Wreford to sign it. The letter pointed out Clapton’s hypocrisy, that he was “rock music’s biggest colonialist” and that his own music had its roots in blues, R&B, reggae. And it concluded with a rallying call for musicians and fans to rise up: “Keep the faith, black and white unite and fight.” (Clapton later apologised and expressed deep shame for the ouburst.) With that letter, Rock Against Racism was born. “The idea was that if we harnessed music and politics together, it might be a powerful combination to fight fascism and racism.” Music was the key, to get the youth on board. The first event was a gig with jazz singer Carol Grimes at a pub in Forest Gate, east London. “We chose the Princess Alice because it was in an area where the National Front were getting substantial votes in local elections,” says Saunders. He admits they were anxious about getting attacked by the NF or the violent neo-Nazis of the British Movement, so they got a bunch of dockers in as security. In the end, it passed off without incident, apart from the usual disagreement with the pub over money. Rock Against Racism grew and grew from there, fighting racism through live music and putting black and white bands on stage throughout the country. Saunders remembers one gig especially, at the Polytechnic of Central London, featuring the reggae band Misty in Roots and the punk band Sham 69, a lot of whose fans were skinheads. In fact, Saunders says, although the band’s frontman Jimmy Pursey was strongly opposed to far-right politics, some people around the band were members of the British Movement. Saunders remembers the tension backstage. “Misty had a reading of the King James Bible, while getting into the mood of their music and culture. And they played dominoes, in the most theatrically aggressive way, slapping down the dominoes hard, all directed at these fascists and skinheads standing around watching. It was electric, I thought at any second it was going to kick off.” Somehow the gunslinger tactics defused the situation and the gig ended with the two bands on stage together in a show of solidarity. The gigs grew into full-scale carnivals, most famously one in London’s Victoria Park featuring the Clash, Steel Pulse, the Tom Robinson Band and more; it began as a march from Trafalgar Square and is thought to have been attended by 100,000 people. But the movement was just as much about small, grassroots responses around the country. Saunders remembers hearing from a kid in Aberystwyth. “She said she’d read my letter in the music press, and that one of her teachers was a Nazi, what could she do? I wrote back and said: ‘You are now Rock Against Racism Aberystwyth.’ When we next heard from her, she’d set up a club – all the local punk bands were playing.” Saunders says the far right today, with their black balaclava brigades, are more frightening than ever. “The hypocrisy – saying they’re looking after women and children, then we find out many have been reported to police for domestic abuse.” His rallying cry is to recognise the far right for what they want and who they are, and to call them out for it. “They’re looking to rid Britain of black and brown people. They’re flat-out, 100% racists.” * * * ‘Our football tournament was huge. Peter Cook came down and refereed’ You could say that in 1977 the NF and Tottenham Hotspur FC were heading in opposite directions. The NF, led by John Tyndall, was still on the rise, resurgent in elections for the Greater London Council. Spurs, meanwhile, were relegated to the old second division; the terraces at White Hart Lane weren’t a happy place. “When the team is doing bad, the community does bad,” says fan Richard Buckwell, who was in his mid-20s at the time, and is speaking to me today on a video call from Nottingham, where he now lives. The NF campaigned and recruited in and around football. “I suppose it’s historically the leading leisure activity of white men,” says Buckwell. When Spurs were back on the up and signed the Argentinians Ossie Ardiles and Ricky Villa, there was a lot animosity. Buckwell, who was active with the Anti Nazi League, and a few like-minded supporters, felt the opposite. “We handed out leaflets that said, ‘They’re welcome here’. And that’s what kicked off Spurs Against Nazis.” It was launched with a public meeting, attended by about 60 people. In October 1978, they organised a five-a-side football tournament. “It was a huge event – we got 47 teams entering. Aswad participated, Bill Oddie played, Peter Cook came down and refereed.” Having the comedian Cook, a high-profile Spurs supporter, involved was helpful when the club initially tried to stop the use of its cockerel logo. They printed T-shirts, made badges and banners, and handed out leaflets on match days, sometimes as the NF were doing the same. “I remember one day, leafleting outside the ground, suddenly seeing a load of youngsters running towards us. I thought, what on earth is happening? Is this the National Front?” But it was the opposite: they ran past to charge at and chase off the NF, who were campaigning behind. The message was getting across. And the Football Fans Against Nazis message spread to other clubs: Leyton Orient, West Brom, Everton, Swansea City, Norwich, Arsenal. In all, about 11 clubs formed grassroots anti-fascist groups to counter the far-right infiltration of fanbases. The message even travelled abroad. “Some of our T-shirts got sent to the freedom fighters against white minority rule in what was then Rhodesia.” Buckwell still has a Spurs Against Nazis T-shirt, “for memory’s sake”. We’re joined on the call not by a Zimbabwean freedom fighter but by Buckwell’s wife, Jane, holding up this last surviving shirt. Plus, a nice cartoon of a footballer kicking a skinhead wearing an NF shirt into touch. Buckwell remembers that when they saw NF graffiti, they used to alter it to read NF = No Fun. He says that anti-fascist campaigning – including by football fans – undoubtedly played a major part in the NF’s decline, though Tyndall and other members took its embers to ignite a new far-right flame in the British National party (BNP). Racism continued to rage, largely unchecked, through the football terraces, throughout the 80s. And to this day it hasn’t been totally extinguished. “One thing that made a difference recently was taking the knee, which many clubs continued for a long time. And [former England manager] Gareth Southgate had a tremendous influence.” But campaigns, such as Kick It Out and Show Racism the Red Card, are underfunded, and he would like to see more support, from government and – particularly – from the clubs themselves. “They pay lip service. The amount of money swilling around the big clubs, they could do a lot more.” At 74, Buckwell still fights the far right, working with Stand Up To Racism in Nottingham. He worries about Stephen Yaxley-Lennon (who goes by the name Tommy Robinson) and his lot. “It is frightening at the moment. But I went on the Together Alliance march, which was tremendous. Nottingham is very diverse and multicultural.” * * * ‘I was stood in the middle of this room watching this horrific violence – this wasn’t the change I wanted’ On a summer evening in 1989, at what became known as the Battle of Welling, Matthew Collins changed sides. As a “troubled and troublesome youth” growing up in south-east London, he’d joined the NF as a teenager. “I was horrendously and viciously racist. I didn’t like what I saw around me.” He became the NF’s south London organiser. In the mid-80s, the NF was becoming splintered and disorganised and Collins was also volunteering with the emerging BNP, rising to become its south London chair. The BNP opened a bookshop in Welling to distribute far-right material, and a group of concerned locals held a meeting at the library to discuss what to do about it. Forty neo-Nazis – including Collins – stormed the building and attacked them. It was, he remembers, a bloodbath. Nine people were hospitalised. Most people at the meeting were women, of south Asian heritage. “I was stood in the middle of this room watching this horrific violence, people assaulting women in a library, and realised I’d been looking in the wrong places – this wasn’t the change I wanted.” Sickened, the following day he phoned the anti-fascist magazine Searchlight, and told them who had been involved. Collins had flipped; he was now an informant. Over the next two and a half years or so, he continued his far-right activities but reported back to Searchlight, building up intelligence, warning of attacks, identifying people. It was incredibly stressful, and he would have been killed if he’d been found out, “particularly towards the end when Combat 18 [the security wing of the BNP] were around and it was all about shipping guns and drugs”. And he couldn’t tell anyone, not his family, not his girlfriend. “It was impossible, because you still have to live that life as a race hater.” Collins took part in a World In Action TV exposé of Combat 18, blacked out and with his voice replaced, but because of what he said it still placed him in the firing line. When he got a visit from special branch, telling him they had intel that there was a threat against him, it was time to get out. Collins went to Australia for 10 years, where he worked in the rag trade and got married. Now 54, Collins is back in the UK, working for Hope Not Hate, the advocacy group that campaigns against fascism and was an offshoot of Searchlight. He’s head of intelligence, meaning he now runs informants inside extreme organisations. He ran Robbie Mullen, the whistleblower who helped bring down extreme rightwing group National Action, a member of which was plotting to kill then Labour MP Rosie Cooper, and the subject of ITV drama The Walk-In (Stephen Graham played Collins). He’s not going to tell me all the tricks of the trade, but basically they identify people who are disappointed and disaffected. “They have constant schisms and fallouts because the far right in this country is now completely driven by drugs and alcohol. You just pick and choose and you find someone and you put pressure on them.” Collins wants to smash today’s far right. “Destroy, disorganise and disorientate. And one of the ways I do that is by finding the better-quality people and getting them out. We’re putting better-equipped and better-behaved people back into society.” He divides the misery caused by the far right into two: “The misery of being in hock to them, ideologically, socially, culturally. And the misery of the people who live in fear of them, because they might get their windows broken or get beaten up.” * * * ‘I was really proud of what we delivered, keeping them out, squashing them’ In the run-up to the 2010 general election, the far right were moving in on Jen Craft’s patch. “There were these, essentially, fascists not far from my home town and I wanted to do everything I could to stop them.” Fortunately, she was in a position to do so. Craft (pictured page 23), born and raised in Thurrock in Essex, was working for the Labour MP, now peer, Margaret Hodge at the time, in Barking. The BNP had targeted the east London constituency as somewhere they could win. They’d done well there in the 2005 general election, and gained 12 council seats the following year. Craft explains there was a lot of frustration in the area over lack of housing, drastically fewer jobs available with Ford in Dagenham, and rapid demographic change – from predominantly white working class to a significantly more mixed population. “It was a proper tinderbox.” A complacent local Labour party and council meant people “didn’t feel they had the ability to contact anyone or that politicians were on their side”. The BNP were cleverer than the NF before them. “The way they approached people, they didn’t knock on your door and say, ‘You don’t like all these so-and-so people moving in, do you?’ They’d say, ‘That playground in the park looks a bit rundown, we’ll come and paint it. I bet you’ve not seen a politician in years, tell us what’s worrying you.’” Craft, whose formative years had coincided with a Blair government and who saw herself as significantly left of him, knew what the BNP were all about. She believes they were targeting Hodge personally, “because she’s Jewish, and because she’d just lost her husband. They thought they could capitalise.” Craft, who was 25 in 2010, ran Hodge’s campaign. “If you’re going to throw everything at defeating the far right, that’s a good time to do it – when you’ve no real responsibilities and can spend 80 hours a week going for it.” How do you go about it? “If you knock on someone’s door and find they’re voting for the BNP and you say, ‘Did you know they’re a bunch of racists?’, what that person hears is you’re calling them a racist.” Nor did they begin with, “Hi, I’m from Labour … ” because, such was the mistrust, they would often end up with the door slammed in their faces. So they adopted tactics not unlike those of their opponents. “It was, ‘I’m out with your local team, what issues have you got, what can we fix? Not trying to convince them that our way of seeing the world is right, but just to open that door by saying, ‘We’re here, we’re listening, we’re on your side, how can we deliver for you?’” They organised coffee afternoons and street meetings to find out what it was people cared about. Later, there was a bit of “Do you know who the BNP are?” And that was the approach in recruiting volunteers and building a campaign team. “This is who they are, this is the threat they pose, come and help us, because if they do win here, where are they going to go next? They won’t stop … ” The BNP didn’t win. Though Labour lost nationally, in Barking Hodge increased her share of the vote, and the BNP were pushed into third place. It was a turning point for their support; the party fragmented, losing members to new parties emerging on the right, such as Ukip. “I was really proud of what we delivered, keeping them out, squashing them,” says Craft. After that, she became a civil servant, and took a break from politics for a while. In 2024, she stood for Labour in Thurrock, and won. Now an MP, we’re talking in her Westminster office. The incumbent Tory was beaten into third place, behind Reform’s candidate. The same issues – migration, economic uncertainty and insecurity, disaffection with politics – mean that “in my area, those far-right messages are taking hold again”. The difference now is social media. “In Barking, it was analogue – letters, leaflets. We just had to have a faster printer than theirs, more things to put through doors and more boots on the ground. But the advent of social media means people can spread untruths and distortions very, very quickly – like net migration is rising or there are more small boat crossings, when actually it’s the opposite.” Craft thinks that to fight the far right today, what’s mostly needed is more regulation of social media companies, and their owners. “Elon Musk wants us to turn against and fight one another. The fact we are not regulating against him is stepping away from our duty to keep this country safe.” That’s going to be more effective than some tactics she sees. “If you go with a placard and shout, ‘Nazis!’, you probably feel good about yourself, but you’ve done nothing to fight them where it counts, which is at the ballot box.” * * * ‘You’ve heard of the concept of breaking bread and the way to a man’s heart is through his stomach … ’ In the summer of 2024, after the murder of three girls at a dance class in Southport, misinformation and violence spread across the UK. Mobs smashed windows and cars, attempted to set fire to hotels housing asylum seekers and desecrated Muslim graves, while far-right keyboard warriors poured petrol on the flames from their sunloungers abroad. On the night of 2 August in Liverpool, an angry crowd gathered outside the Abdullah Quilliam mosque, the oldest in the country. Against police advice, Adam Kelwick, one of the imams, crossed the road to talk to them. He took food – burgers and chips – and drinks. “You’ve heard of the concept of breaking bread and the way to a man’s heart is through his stomach,” Kelwick says, on the phone from his Liverpool home. There is a famous picture of Kelwick talking to one man in particular. “I spoke to him for five minutes, we connected, built some kind of relationship, call it a friendship if you like, then I gave the guy a hug.” It takes two to hug. “So he had it inside him. After coming to the mosque to protest, he could reach out and hug me as well – the same people he was manifesting enmity towards.” Later, when it had quietened down and the cameras had gone, Kelwick sneaked him into the mosque. “I took him in, we walked around, and had an interesting conversation.” Kelwick thinks “the vast majority of people you see at these protests are just genuine, regular people who’ve been dragged into something they might not understand fully”. Which is why conversation is important. “You have to engage, otherwise you’ll go further apart, then it’s easy to hold enmity and hostility.” Since that time, Kelwick has been devoting energy to building these links. He tells me about a coach trip they had to north Wales soon afterwards – a bunch of families who’d attended the Liverpool Save Our Kids protest, which kicked off violently, along with families from the Muslim community. “We mixed everyone up together on two coaches; you should have seen the looks on the faces of the locals in north Wales when the doors opened and all these scousers got off along with some quite conservative-looking Muslim families. I think the academics call it contact theory – that you’re less likely to have negative feelings towards each other or uphold negative stereotypes if you have in-person interaction.” The paranoia cuts both ways. “A lot of people in the Muslim community think everyone at these protests wants to hang, draw and quarter them – so I’ve been working with both sides.” Kelwick travels a lot, and says the narrative – pushed and funded from above by far-right campaigns and individuals – is the same everywhere: “Immigration is bad, it’s an invasion of military-aged men, they don’t integrate, they’re committing all these crimes and raping our girls … it’s the same in the US, France, Germany, all across Europe.” But Kelwick has faith in people. “We’re all human, bleed the same blood, have the same issues in life. It doesn’t matter how many billions are pumped into this, if you can facilitate genuine interactions between people from different communities, that has the ability to make these hugely funded efforts irrelevant.” Would he sit down for a chat with Tommy Robinson himself, I wonder? “It’s not a definite no. I almost arranged to visit him when he was in prison. I think that would be the ideal meeting, without cameras, without anything to prove to anybody, just a genuine sit down where we don’t have to pull any publicity stunt – that would be beneficial.” Discussion rather than debate is the aim. “I don’t like to be the attacker; it pushes people away. The whole purpose of having this interaction is to come closer. When you strip things down to a human level, that’s where beautiful things can happen. You can do that with every single person – even Tommy Robinson.” Over to you, Mr Yaxley-Lennon, the invitation is there. There might even be a hug in it for you.

title: Country diary: The house martins are gone for another year. But they’re not forgotten | Ed Douglas
summary: Lockerbrook, Derbyshire: Last week they were here, now they are not. Yet the details of their epic migration are still a mystery to us
text: The sudden absence of something, even though you know it’s coming, can dent the heart a little. The Japanese, inevitably, have a phrase for it: mono no aware, the pathos of things – and by things, in this case, I mean house martins. Last week I had stood in the same spot, looking across the same valley. The weather then was much the same as it was today, low‑angled sunlight through patchy cloud lighting up the yellowing birch leaves and bronzing moors on the north-eastern slopes of Kinder Scout. It had picked out the spread wings of a buzzard a little below my eyeline, along with a haze of large insects, which in fact, I quickly realised, were house martins. Such fecundity was thrilling to see, especially as dwindling numbers have put house martins on the red list of threatened species. Dozens swooped and turned just in front of me, and as I looked through this cloud of acrobatic mayhem, dozens more were doing the same in the middle distance, gorging on insects before the long flight south. Today, though, they were gone, the sky empty save for a kestrel quartering her patch, head dropped between her shoulders like a jeweller over her loupe. I wondered where these brave little travellers were now and how many would survive to return. The mere fact of such migrations is astounding, made more so by the mystery that still surrounds them. These birds will winter somewhere in sub-Saharan Africa, but exactly where is unknown. Dutch researchers looked at isotopes in the feathers of their returning birds and could only narrow it down to west Africa. Researchers have also found microplastics trapped in house martin feathers, tiny fragments swept up into the air, where they linger among the martin’s insect food. We blunder through these gossamer systems, brushing them aside almost unseen with every turn around the sun. It’s revealing, too, how those who find it politically expedient to mention natural variation in climate are much less interested in discussing the evolved instinct of many species, including our own, to migrate for survival. • Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024, is available now at guardianbookshop.com

title: France’s dilemma: protesters demand spending as markets require fiscal restraint
summary: Waves of protests expose debt crisis faced by French government, but political wrangling is stalling an escape plan. Is there a way out?
text: Eight years have passed since rising fuel prices brought the gilets jaunes (yellow vest) demonstrators to the streets of France, prompting the first big crisis of Emmanuel Macron’s time in the Élysée Palace. As the French president contemplates his exit next year, turmoil has again gripped the streets in the form of student protests, but this time the financial markets are unhappy too. Investors are concerned about the government’s failure to bring spending under control and end a long period of “fiscal incontinence”. Financial markets are unnerved by similar trends in the UK, the US and more recently Italy, causing jitters in global bond markets. But it’s France that has become the biggest worry, hemmed in by debts across the public and private sectors, limiting their scope to dig the country out of a deepening hole. France’s debt-to-GDP stood at 115.6% in 2025, while its budget deficit was 5.1%, compared with 94.3% and 4.3% for the UK respectively. In Britain, the chancellor, John Healey, is on course to reduce the budget deficit this year and in 2027. His French counterpart, Roland Lescure, has promised to follow suit after a rise to 5.4% this year, but has yet to say how. ‘I am panicking’ One victim of the uncertainty is business investment. A survey by Medef, France’s largest employer federation, showed 82% of firms were pessimistic about the impact of the next government’s economic policy. In a warning to all politicians, 66% said their business would become vulnerable or even go bankrupt if economic policy remained deadlocked for the next five years. A rescue operation could be mounted by the European Central Bank (ECB), but France would demand unconditional support when the ECB’s rules say bailouts must come with strict conditions. Antonio Fatas, a professor of economics at Insead, the European business school, says the political and economic situation has pushed France to the edge of a financial collapse. “I am very worried about the economic situation because growth is low and it is difficult to see how the dynamics change. Then you have the debt numbers, which are bad, and the financial markets are thinking the government is not in control. “If I look at the political situation, I am panicking. That’s because too many political parties are saying let France burn. They want a crisis, believing it will improve their share of the vote.” There is much about the economic situation in France that mirrors what has happened in the UK and the US. A huge spending splurge during the Covid pandemic was followed by another round of subsidies to offset the worst side-effects from Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Investors have become wary of lending to all three countries, but the rise in interest rates is strongest in France. Last week, the yield, or interest rate, on ⁠10-year French bonds hit the highest level since July 2002, just short of 5%. Yields go up when bond prices go down. Japanese investors, typically strong supporters of France as a haven for their savings, have been instrumental in the panic after they found better returns on home turf, heaping further pain on the French treasury. Political turmoil According to many metrics, it is difficult to see why France should be so badly affected. The French economy has many things going for it, from relatively low electricity prices to better than average infrastructure. The schools that are the focus of recent protests are better funded than the OECD average. On the debit side of the ledger, Macron’s plan to raise the pension age from 62 to 64, saving tens of billions of euros from an almost entirely socialised retirement system, stalled at 62 and nine months after parliament was deadlocked after the 2024 snap election. This might have mattered less if the economy was growing, but Macron’s much-vaunted economic revival remains stuck in first gear. Laurent Warlouzet, a professor of history at the Sorbonne, says it is understandable that international investors are confused about France when Marine Le Pen, the frontrunner in presidential elections next year, says she will roll back the retirement age to 62 and at the same time introduce a “debt brake” via a referendum, restricting further borrowing. He said: “The far right used to be a spendthrift populist force, especially under Le Pen’s leadership, broadening the appeal of National Rally voters in the country’s rust belts. In 2016–17, she still wanted France to leave the eurozone, which she regarded as a straitjacket.” Warlouzet, the author of Liberty, Solidarity and Community: capitalism and European integration, 1945 to the present, added: “Nowadays, Le Pen has become an improbable fiscal hawk. How can she reconcile this with her voters’ demands for more nurses, teachers, police officers and judges?” ‘Too big to save’ Erik Britton, the director of Fathom Consulting, an international advisory firm, says the prospect of a runoff between Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the leader of the leftwing La France Insoumise (LFI), and Le Pen next April has spooked investors more than the failure to bring down the annual deficit. “What has changed is the likely runoff. In the second round, it now looks likely that Le Pen will contest the presidential election against Mélenchon from the far left. Le Pen’s election might mean a 20% risk of Frexit: Mélenchon’s election, though less likely on current polling, would have a much higher risk of Frexit.” Britton says the collapse of the centre ground would have implications far beyond its borders. “Where France goes, the euro area as a whole tends to follow. If it led to another test of the euro, all the considerations about debt and debt mutualisation would resurface, and bond yields would pop right across the euro area (perhaps with the exception of Germany) and beyond.” It may seem improbable for financial market traders to consider France’s exit from the euro when it has occupied a central position in the single currency since its inception. Yet it is understood several eurozone finance ministers and ECB officials have made representations to the French government, urging it to devise a budget formula that will gain a majority in parliament and a win over leading lenders. Without a budget, France may be left to fend for itself. And if that means traders boycott French bonds without a huge interest rate premium, the country may be forced to default on its debts. A bailout would also be expensive. As the US Nobel prize-winning economist Paul Krugman said recently: “If France does need to be bailed out, it would be extremely expensive. As the second largest economy in the eurozone, France may have crossed the line from too big to fail to too big to save” Dhaval Joshi, an independent City economist, said: “Ultimately therefore, France will have to make painful adjustments to bring its debt maths back under control. Just like Italy, Spain (and, of course, Greece) did a decade ago, from which these southern European economies have emerged much stronger. “The crucial question is how much political pain France must go through before it makes, or is forced to make, this adjustment.” The head of France’s central bank, Emmanuel ⁠Moulin, denied last week that France needed help from the ECB, but inflamed the situation by adding the rider, “not at this point”. Albert Edwards, a senior global strategist at Société Générale, said France may survive the onslaught from bonds market traders – some of them termed vigilantes for their habit of sniffing out weak nations – should another country begin to look vulnerable. “Although France has been in the crosshairs recently, the bond vigilantes’ focus is merely rolling from one market to another. Next month their attention might be back on Japan, the UK or indeed the US. “It is the way of the bond vigilantes to jab away and test each market to find out which is the weakest before launching an all-out attack,” he said.

title: Hurricane Isaias makes landfall in Florida and hammers Gulf coast
summary: Governors of Mississippi, Alabama and Florida declare states of emergency as a downsized Fema faces first major test
text: Hurricane Isaias crashed into the US Gulf coast on Friday as a dangerous category 2 storm, hammering communities in Alabama and the Florida panhandle with damaging winds, heavy rain, flooding and life-threatening storm surges. The first hurricane of the Atlantic season made landfall near Destin, Florida, the National Hurricane Center said. It had maximum sustained winds of 105 mph (169 kph). The storm weakened to just below major hurricane status before it came ashore. “The storm is here. Buckle down at this point. Don’t be getting out on the roads,” Florida’s governor, Ron DeSantis, said at a news conference, adding flash flooding would be a hazard “throughout the region”. In Pensacola, about 50 miles (80km) west of Destin an Agence France-Presse reporter witnessed howling winds rip the roofs from some homes and businesses, snapping tree branches as the power went out. “Things are flying really fast, and I’ve never seen wind this fast before, so it’s intense, it’s scary,” Jonathan Ramos, a 40-year-old government employee, said from his hotel in Pensacola, where the power went out. “I don’t recommend people coming down here for fun to do this.” President Donald Trump told reporters at the White House late Friday night: “We’re watching it very closely, the hurricane,” adding that it was “under control”. Forecasters had expected Isaias to weaken from its peak earlier on Friday as a major category 3 hurricane because of shifts in wind speed. But even as a weaker storm system, the NHC warned of a ‌life-threatening storm surge affecting the Gulf Coast as dangerous hurricane conditions and flash floods spread inland. The hurricane is expected to cross Alabama and into the Tennessee Valley on the weekend, the ‌agency added. Warnings included a storm surge of up to 7ft (2.1 meters) along the Alabama-Florida line, and powerful wind gusts reaching parts of northern Georgia. In the Florida Panhandle, Isaias’s early impacts also came into view. In Panama city beach, Noaa officials observed a water level 5.4 feet (1.64 meters) above average. About 125 miles west, at the Pensacola city hall, a wind gust up to 102 mph (164km/h) was recorded. Powerful gusts of wind and heavy rainfall appeared to down the canopy of a Crestview gas station on Friday evening, according to a video captured by meteorologist Nick Stewart. The tattered cover hung on top of a filling station. “The storm is here. Buckle down at this point. Don’t be getting out on the roads,” Florida governor Ron DeSantis said at a news conference, adding that flash flooding would be a hazard “throughout the region”. The governors of Mississippi, Alabama and Florida all declared states of emergency ahead of the storm’s arrival, urging some residents of coastal communities to evacuate and many more to prepare for the storm’s likely violent arrival. Alabama governor Kay Ivey announced shortly before the hurricane made landfall that Donald Trump had approved the emergency declaration for her state. “This will help cut tape for our federal partners to aid in any response,” Ivey said. The Mobile office of the National Weather Service warned parts of Florida could see “extremely dangerous” tornado-like winds. By Friday evening, nearly 500,000 customers had lost power across Alabama and Florida, according to PowerOutage.com. “Things are going to get really, really treacherous,” Jamie Rhome, deputy director for the National Hurricane Center, told the AP. Florida’s national guard deployed roughly 5,000 soldiers and airmen to aid with the response, the AP reported. Some prisons were also evacuating their incarcerated populations. Most flights were grounded at several airports in Florida’s Panhandle. The state guard has deployed about 400 soldiers to assess the hurricane’s damage and assist with route clearance, among other duties. The Florida fish and wildlife conservation commission has readied 10 airboats, 18 shallow-draft boats, nine ATVs and six larger platform vessels in the event of damage or flooding. Uber has also partnered with the state to offer free-round trips, up to $40 each way, to and from state-approved evacuation shelters. Isaias is notable as one of the two latest-forming Atlantic hurricanes on record, tying a record set on 8 October 1905. None of the eight previous named storms of the 2026 Atlantic season intensified above tropical storm status. Ahead of the storm, oil and gas producers shut down a significant share of offshore production in the Gulf, which accounts for almost 15% of crude pumped annually in the US. In a sign of how serious the warnings are, dozens of Waffle Houses in the Florida Panhandle were closed, according to the company’s website. The beloved Southern breakfast chain is known for staying open through severe weather and often is a measuring stick of a storm’s severity. Kelsei Frazier, a Florida native living in Pace who is no stranger to hurricanes, knows all about the Waffle House Index. “We joke because if Waffle House is still open, then you know it’s not a bad hurricane, but all the Waffle Houses that I know of within at least a normal range from us are closed,” said Frazier. “Which is a pretty big deal.” Associated Press contributed reporting.
