title: Climate crisis is coming to crush many of world’s best surf breaks, study warns
summary: Changing tide levels, shifting sands and hardened shorelines put waves at risk, affecting more than just surfers
text: The climate crisis is coming for some of the world’s greatest surf breaks, submerging some as sea level rises and wiping out others as classic breaks get crushed against coastal developments. Analysis of dozens of famous waves in world surfing reserves (WSR) found more than three-quarters were at high risk because of changing tide levels, hardened shorelines and shifting sands. The impacts matter not only to the surfers catching the waves but also to the communities that depend on the multibillion-dollar surf economy, often located in places with little else. The waves rated at most risk in the study include the “bombing barrels” of Croyde beach in north Devon, UK, the point breaks at Noosa in Australia and Oriente Salvaje, El Salvador, and Santa Cruz reefs of California such as Sewer Peak and Wind and Sea. The best surfing waves are created by intricate combinations of sea-floor shape, swell direction and tide. “Surf breaks are incredibly unique oceanographic phenomena – a confluence of all these factors that fit together just right to make the wave happen – and so those processes are really sensitive,” said Dan Reineman, an associate professor at California State University Channel Islands and a co-author of the study. Global heating is pushing up sea level and changing rainfall patterns that affect sediment movement, which can upset the delicate balance and destroy the wave. However, the researchers said the expert local knowledge of surfers could be tapped to help protect the waves. Trent Hodges, a co-author of the study and a senior programmes manager at Save the Waves Coalition, which launched the WSR programme in 2009, said: “Climate change will impact surf breaks all over the world in different ways, depending on their unique geographies. We learned directly from the local surfers how they are seeing their waves change. It’s a canary in the coalmine too – when a wave changes, that often means the beach is changing, and everybody enjoys the beach.” The study, published in the journal Climatic Change, concludes: “Climate change and coastal management both have significant negative implications for the future viability of multiple surf breaks of global significance and, therefore, the myriad distinct local communities, cultures and economies they support.” Almost 200 local experts analysed 57 surf breaks in all but two of the 13 WSRs, spread across eight countries. The researchers said thousands of other surf waves around the world faced similar peril. A key finding was that where coastlines were more natural, they could adapt better to the changes brought by the climate crisis, by shifting inland and relocating sediments. Development such as sea walls, jetties and groynes made the beaches and waves less resilient, Reineman said. Adam Hall, a co-founder of the North Devon WSR, was one of the local surfers who contributed to the study. He said: “North Devon is so special. We have Saunton Sands, a world-renowned longboarding wave with really long, mellow rides, and the UK’s best beach break at Croyde. We’ve got left- and right-hand point breaks and a sheltered spot for when it gets too windy and too big. Whatever you want to do, we’ve got it.” He said surfing was very important for the local economy, and not just in summer. “Surfers will come throughout the year. They fill up the pubs, restaurants and car parks when the swells are good in January, February and March, where if you go to any other tourist destination that doesn’t have surf, they’re dead on their knees.” The researchers want more local surfers to use the tools developed to assess their own breaks and work with local authorities and other groups to protect waves from coastal development and climate change. Some places already do this, such as the city of Gold Coast in Australia, which has put surf protection in planning law; New Zealand, which designates surf breaks of “national significance”; and Peru’s Ley de rompientes (law of the breakers) that protects listed surf breaks. “Surfing is a huge driver of local economies,” Hodges said. “So whether you’re a surfer or not, that money supports local businesses, hotels, lodgings and so on.” In Santa Cruz, surfing brings in about $200m (£151m) a year, he said. “In the east of El Salvador, you have some of the most perfect point break waves you will find, and the entire economy there is pretty much dependent on surfing,” Hodges added. • This article was amended on 12 October 2026. An earlier image was said to show Noosa on the Sunshine Coast, Australia, but showed the Superbank on the Gold Coast.

title: Trump fumes over Nobel peace prize snub and criticizes Norway
summary: President complains about not winning prize in year he started war with Iran and says: ‘We will not forget, Norway’
text: Donald Trump complained on Friday about not winning the Nobel peace prize for 2026, a year in which he started a war with Iran. At what was supposed to be a rally for other Republican candidates in Syracuse, New York, the US president devoted a long portion of his speech to airing his grievances with the Nobel committee. “The United States of America, represented by me as your president, should have received the Nobel peace prize, but didn’t. And this is an indelible stain on the country of Norway, and those people that made such a disgraceful and embarrassing decision,” Trump said. “The Nobel peace prize has been forever discredited by a handful of radical ideologues who are anti-democracy and really enemies of civilization,” Trump went on. “We will not forget, Norway, that you didn’t give this prize.” Trump also recited a list of wars he claims to have settled, some of which were not wars and some that are still not settled, before adding: “I’m about to settle or win two more: Iran and Russia-Ukraine.” Trump said he would be ending both wars “quickly”. “I will tell you what,” he added, darkly. “Iran will be very quick one way or the other: that they give us everything or they don’t exist any longer.” “Additionally, I stopped Iran from having a nuclear weapon and blowing up the entire Middle East and ultimately far beyond the Middle East, including Europe, perhaps the US and I saved more lives than anyone in history,” Trump claimed, despite the fact that US intelligence agencies reported to Congress in 2025 that Iran had actually suspended its pursuit of nuclear weapons in 2003. “Despite all of this and all of these unbelievable accomplishments, the Nobel prize was given out today to a liberal person who works at the United Nations, who nobody has ever heard of,” Trump said of Navi Pillay, the South African former UN human rights chief who chaired the UN commission that concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in Gaza. In Pillay’s first public comments after learning of the award, she joked to colleagues at a conference of human rights lawyers in Nuremberg, Germany, on Friday: “If you clap a little bit more, I may share this prize with Trump.” She then burst out laughing.

title: Ukraine war briefing: Kyiv blasts peace talks as just ‘smokescreen’ for Trump‘s Russian diesel deal
summary: Trump’s announcement a betrayal of Ukraine, Democrats say; Ukraine strikes major datacentre in Russia. What we know on day 1,690
text: Ukrainian peace negotiators in Miami have been used as a “smokescreen” for a “weak” decision by Donald Trump to lift diesel sanctions on Russia, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a furious response to the US president’s backflip on Russian sanctions. In a move likely to create a fresh crisis with Washington’s Nato allies, Trump announced the deal with Putin on his Truth Social network, saying it was essential to reduce fuel prices in the US, which have soared as a result of his decision to go to war with Iran. The Ukrainian president, who flew to Washington last month to plead with US lawmakers to pass tougher sanctions on Russia, said in a statement on Friday that it was “unfortunately, a weak decision by strong partners”. “I believe our team is simply being used as a smokescreen. And that is certainly not fair. It is certainly not how partners should treat each other.” Negotiators for the ⁠US, Ukraine and Europe ⁠held six ‌hours ‌of talks ‌in Miami on Friday with the aim ‌of reaching agreement on ending the war in Ukraine, a ‌source briefed on the talks said. They discussed a postwar economic package for Ukraine and potential new security architecture between Europe and Russia, the source said. President Trump announced the diesel deal as his envoy Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner were meeting with Ukrainian officials in Florida to discuss a peace plan. Trump’s announcement was a betrayal of Ukraine, the European allies and US national security, said Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer, top Democrat on the Foreign Relations Committee Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, and senior Democrat senator, Elizabeth Warren. “Enough is enough,” the senators wrote. “The President must end his war with Iran instead of funding Russia’s war machine.” A number of prominent Republicans joined Democrats on Friday to condemn Trump for lifting the diesel sanctions, including congressman Don Bacon, who said the majority of Americans supported Ukraine. “The President’s policies towards Russia and Ukraine are failures. We need moral clarity not moral ambiguity.” Ukraine struck and partly disabled a major datacentre operated by Russian technology company Yandex on Friday in the second such action in successive days. Yandex, which is heavily involved in Russia’s AI development, said its data centre in the Kaluga region south-west of Moscow had been struck by Ukrainian drones and partly put out of action. Ukrainian arms maker Firepoint said Kyiv had used its FP-1 one-way attack drones to mount the ⁠strike. Four Ukrainians were arrested in Vienna this week on ⁠suspicion of spying, Austrian interior minister, Gerhard Karner, said on Friday, with Ukrainska ⁠Pravda newspaper saying two ⁠of its team were among those detained. Three remain in custody, Karner said, declining ⁠to provide further details because the investigation was ongoing. Austrian news agency APA quoted a ⁠spokeswoman for the Ukrainian embassy in Vienna as saying it was awaiting ‌an explanation from the ‌Austrian authorities on the circumstances of and legal grounds ‌for the arrests. The embassy did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Russian ⁠forces struck three cargo vessels in and ⁠around Ukraine’s Black Sea ports on ⁠Friday, Russia’s defence ministry said. The ‌ministry said ‌one vessel was ‌hit in the port of Mykolaiv, another in the port of Chornomorsk and ‌a third, bound for Odesa, in the Black Sea. According to the ministry, all three vessels ⁠were being used to supply the Ukrainian military. Reuters could not ‌independently verify the report or the claim. Russian strikes killed three people and wounded at least eight across Ukraine, officials said Friday, as Ukraine struggles to counter escalating Russian bombardments that have killed more than 50 people over the past three days.

title: Flydubai co-pilot began radicalisation in Australia, UAE prosecutors say
summary: Hammam al-Hammami’s shift towards extremism began while he was a student in Melbourne, according to Emirati attorney general
text: The co-pilot who tried to seize control of a flydubai jet flying from Dubai to Tel Aviv last week had been radicalised while studying in Australia, prosecutors in the United Arab Emirates said on Friday. Passengers and crew on the 30 September flight, which had 182 people onboard, intervened to stop 29-year-old Omani national Hammam al-Hammami’s alleged attempt to hijack the plane on its way to Israel. Dr Hamad Saif al-Shamsi, attorney general of the UAE, said al-Hammami’s shift towards extremism and terrorism began while he was studying at RMIT University in Melbourne. During his time in Melbourne, he was influenced by the hardline takfiri ideology through reading extremist literature and online content glorifying terrorist organisations and suicide attacks, the attorney general said. The statement was shared on UAE government social media and first reported by the state-run Emirati news agency, known as WAM. According to the statement, al-Hammami allegedly told prosecutors he adopted ideas advocating violence and terrorism and drew inspiration from the 9/11 terrorist attacks of 2001. “The idea of carrying out a similar operation using an aircraft became firmly established in his thinking,” the statement said. Al-Hammami allegedly prepared himself both psychologically and physically to carry out the alleged terror plot by intensifying his exposure to material promoting terrorism and training in boxing under a private coach. Last weekend, Australian security agencies launched an investigation after it emerged al-Hammami spent about two years in the country as a student until 2017. On Monday, RMIT University confirmed that he had studied at its Melbourne campus, but “did not successfully complete an engineering qualification”. Contacted by Guardian Australia on Saturday, RMIT said it did not have any further comment to make while an investigation led by the Victorian joint counter-terrorism team was ongoing.

title: Three men found guilty of murders of Australian surfer brothers and US friend in Mexico
summary: Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, 30 and 33, and friend Carter Rhoad, 30, were killed on a surfing trip in 2024
text: The parents of Australian surfing brothers murdered in Mexico have said “no outcome can ever undo this tragedy” after three men were convicted of the 2024 killings. Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, aged 30 and 33 respectively, and their friend Carter Rhoad, 30, were on a surfing trip to Mexico’s Pacific coast when they were shot dead in Baja California state in a suspected robbery. The deaths of the trio sparked an outpouring of grief and condemnation in Australia and the United States. Jesus Gerardo – known as “El Kekas” – was accused of leading the attack. His surname has not been disclosed for legal reasons. He and two other defendants, Irineo Francisco and Angel Jesus, were found guilty on Friday local time. The judge ruled the three Mexican defendants acted with premeditation. Martin and Debra Robinson, the brothers’ parents, travelled from Australia to the port city of Ensenada for the trial, which began on 7 September. “They took our sons from our lives forever,” said Debra Robinson, who testified on the final day of the trial. “What hurts us most is that, in their final hours, they were treated with such cruelty.” She burst into tears when the guilty verdict was pronounced. Speaking outside the court after the verdict, Martin Robinson thanked family and friends for their support, and also thanked the judge, court staff, the Australian embassy in Mexico and the Australian federal police. He said: “No outcome can ever undo this tragedy, but we hope today marks an important step towards justice and allows us to continue honouring their lives and the extraordinary young men they were. They will never be forgotten.” Debra Robinson said: “I don’t feel any different today as I did yesterday or I will tomorrow, because … Callum and Jake are not here. A verdict is a good thing, but it doesn’t bring them back.” She said she had no feelings towards the three guilty men. “I have tried to hold on to the memory of my children, my sons, and I try really not to think about them. And I don’t actually want them to have any notoriety. We don’t actually really speak their names. They’re not part of our grief really.” Martin Robinson said a foundation in their sons’ names would carry on their legacy. The Callum and Jake Robinson Foundation aims to “help people live bigger, shine brighter and love harder in their honour”. Rhoad’s mother, Page, and his fiance, Natalie Weirtz, also participated in the hearing in a video call from the United States. “The accused are guilty and must be punished so that no other family suffers the same pain,” Weirtz said. “Since Carter’s death, I feel paranoid and isolated.” Sentencing is scheduled for 16 October. The prosecution requested 210 years’ imprisonment for each of the accused, though the maximum sentence in Baja California is 60 years. The surfers were camping in a remote beachside area when they were attacked in April 2024. Their bodies were found in a clifftop shaft, with gunshot wounds to their heads. In November 2025, Ary Gisell Silva, the then-girlfriend of the main defendant, was sentenced to two decades in prison after admitting that she instigated the robbery. Baja California is one of Mexico’s most violent states, plagued by organised crime and drug trafficking, although cartel activity does not usually affect tourists. Other foreign visitors have, however, been targeted in criminal attacks on Mexico’s Pacific coast. Two Australian surfers, Dean Lucas and Adam Coleman, were killed in 2015 while travelling through the north-western state of Sinaloa. Their bodies were later burned.

title: ‘Life-threatening storm surge’ headed to US Gulf coast as residents brace for Isaias
summary: Alabama, Florida and Mississippi declare emergencies, with preparations under way for ‘long-duration power outages’
text: Hurricane Isaias neared landfall Friday evening, barreling toward the US Gulf coast coast as a dangerous category 2 storm and prompting emergency declarations in Alabama, Florida and Mississippi. The hurricane, the first in the Atlantic in what has turned into a very late 2026 season, is expected to cause a “life-threatening storm surge”, officials said. Isaias is forecast to make landfall on Friday night, somewhere along the western Florida Panhandle, with surging seas up to about 7ft (2.1 meters) and waves as high as 30ft (9.1 meters). The National Weather Service issued a rare extreme wind warning Friday night for the western Florida Panhandle. “Treat these imminent extreme winds as if a tornado was approaching and move immediately to an interior room or shelter NOW!” the Mobile, Alabama, office for the National Weather Service wrote on social media Friday, calling the situation “extremely dangerous”. The National Oceanic Atmospheric Administration (Noaa) also warned that residents should “prepare for the possibility of long-duration power outages”. Noaa said a storm surge was expected from south-east Louisiana to Suwannee, in north-east Florida. Isaias could also dump up to 15in (380mm) of rain on coastal areas and even spawn tornadoes overnight on Friday into Saturday from Alabama to the Florida Panhandle and south-western Georgia. The hurricane is expected to quickly weaken after coming ashore. Heavy rain began falling along the coast on Friday morning and winds were picking up sharply, with tropical storm conditions expected by early afternoon. Isaias had maximum sustained winds of 110 mph on Friday evening, down from 120mph at mid-morning, according to the National Hurricane Center (NHC). The center also said that Isaias was about 45 miles south of Pensacola, Florida, and headed north at 18mph. The NHC said Dauphin Island, a barrier island off the Alabama coast, could see a 7ft (2.1-meter) storm surge, while Indian Pass, 200 miles to the east on the Florida coast, could see a 6ft surge. “Preparations should be rushed to completion as the weather will go downhill quickly today,” the NHC said. “While the storm is not expected to make landfall at peak intensity, it is likely that Isaias will still be a significant hurricane when it reaches the coast.” Alabama’s governor, Kay Ivey, ordered non-residents to immediately evacuate Dauphin Island, Gulf Shores and Orange Beach on Thursday, while officials encouraged voluntary evacuations for residents. Videos on social media showed traffic at a standstill on a highway leading out of Gulf Shores, where double red flags signaled that beaches were closed. Ivey has declared a state of emergency for 40 counties in Alabama, while Ron DeSantis, the governor of Florida, has declared a state of emergency in 27 counties. Several cities and counties in south Mississippi have done the same. DeSantis said 5,000 national guard troops were expected to mobilize in Florida, where at least four school districts cancelled late-week classes. The Atlantic hurricane season has been unusually quiet this year because of a strong El Niño, which disrupts storm formation over the Atlantic. The first hurricane of the season has not formed this late since 8 October 1905, which predates the satellite era of the 1960s for tracking hurricanes. Before the storm, oil and gas producers shut down a significant share of offshore production in the Gulf, which accounts for almost 15% of crude pumped annually in the US. As of Thursday, about 63% of the oil production in the region had been temporarily halted, taking nearly 1.3m barrels a day off the market, according to the Marine Minerals Administration. It said 121 of the Gulf’s 371 crewed oil platforms had been evacuated. The storm could be the first major test of the ability of the Federal Emergency Management Agency (Fema) to deploy a large workforce after the Trump administration’s sweeping cuts and restructuring of the agency, emergency management experts say. The Trump administration has said it wants to eliminate, or drastically downsize, Fema, putting more burden on states. More than 4,300 employees left the agency in fiscal year 2025, about 17% of the workforce, according to a recent US Government Accountability Office (GAO) report. The agency’s staffing reductions were not carried out systematically to ensure Fema could still meet its statutory obligations, said Chris Currie, director of homeland security and justice at the GAO. The Associated Press and Reuters contributed reporting

title: Powerful 7.7-magnitude earthquake strikes Panama and triggers panic in capital
summary: The quake caused buildings and roads to collapse but the country appeared to escape widespread destruction or deaths
text: A magnitude 7.7 earthquake struck southern Panama on Friday, damaging buildings and sending thousands into the streets, but the country appeared to escape widespread destruction or deaths. The US Geological Survey (USGS) said the ⁠earthquake hit at a depth of ⁠12.6km (7.8 miles), with an epicenter in a sparsely populated area about 200km (124 miles) from the capital, Panama City. It lasted about a minute. In Panama City, there were scenes of panic as people rushed to evacuate from the city’s emblematic skyscrapers. “I was scared because the shaking was very strong and prolonged. Heavy objects like dressers, the bed, and all the kitchen items were shaking,” Salomon Andion, 46, told Agence France-Presse after evacuating his 15-storey building. A video widely shared on social media showed water falling from the rooftop pool of a building over 20 storeys tall. Another showed a bridge over the Panama canal shaking violently but remaining upright as vehicles travelled across it. “We are facing a major disaster,” President Jose Raul Mulino said, adding that some roads had “completely collapsed”. Juana Alveo, a 38-year-old cashier at a store in the city of Penonome in central Cocle province, said: “It was horrible, like nothing we ever experienced. My daughter was trapped in school.” In the following hours, even as more than 40 aftershocks rattled the isthmus nation, the Panama canal and Cobre ⁠Panama copper mine reported normal operations and the Tocumen international airport lifted a suspension on flights. Office workers in the upmarket business hub of downtown Panama City fretted about how to get home in the snarl of traffic. Juan Sanchez, a 37-year-old economy ministry employee, waited for a bus he said he doubted would arrive. “They evacuated all of these buildings. Everyone is outside. Now the problem is, how do we get home?” An exposure report by the USGS estimated about 43,000 Panamanians lived in areas with at least severe exposure to the quake. In Panama City, Nestor Luque, director of the national geosciences institute, said he counted 40 seconds of vibrations, although other areas may have felt even longer tremors. Strong earthquakes are not common in Panama, and some elderly residents were in tears as they evacuated into the streets. The USGS estimated economic losses could amount to between 1% and 10% of Panama’s gross domestic product. Electricity provider Naturgy reported power outages in six provinces. Panama was due to hold a national evacuation drill on Monday next week to test the country’s emergency response. The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, wrote on social media that he was “closely monitoring reports” of the earthquake and the US was ready to help, if needed.

title: Women with PMOS should get subsidised weight-loss drugs, Australian advocates say
summary: With GLP-1s to treat the condition not specifically approved by the TGA, patients are being prescribed them off-label
text: Women living with a chronic hormonal condition should have access to taxpayer-funded weight-loss medications, advocates say. The Polyendrocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome Association of Australia (POSAA) is urging for GLP-1 drugs to be approved on the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme for people living with the condition. Formerly known as polycystic ovarian syndrome, PMOS affects one in eight women. Symptoms can include irregular periods, excess hair growth on the body and face, weight gain and hair thinning. The lifelong condition, for which there is no cure, can lead to an increased risk of type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease and endometrial cancer. While GLP-1s are not specifically approved by the Therapeutic Goods Administration to treat PMOS, patients are being prescribed the medications off-label. Half a million Australians are estimated to be using weight-loss medications regularly, a University of New South Wales study found in July. Lorna Berry, a spokesperson for the POSAA who was diagnosed with the condition at 32, said she would welcome GLP-1s being subsidised for patients diagnosed with PMOS, in addition to funding for evidence-based research. “It’s important for people to have access to medications, irrespective of where they live or where they were born … it’s really important that there’s equitable access,” she told the Guardian. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Berry said some women living with the condition were already missing out on being able to access the medications due to their high cost, which can set patients back several hundred dollars each month. Associate professor Magdalena Simonis, the women’s health spokesperson for the Royal Australasian College of Physicians, said the college did not currently have a position on whether GLP-1s were appropriate for the management of PMOS. “They’re not necessarily the only tool we have available to us, and that is important because long-term use is expensive, and it doesn’t look like these are going to be on the PBS anytime soon, and maybe not ever for conditions such as PMOS,” she said. “Because traditionally women’s conditions are not included in these changes.” Simonis, a GP with an expert interest in PMOS, said should research find the weight-loss medications more effective than existing treatments, a broader discussion about health equity would be needed. “That is a conversation that we’re having about obesity as a national issue,” she said. GLP-1 drugs – glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists – mimic a naturally occurring hormone which helps manage blood sugar levels and reduces hunger. Ozempic is listed by the PBS, but only for the treatment of diabetes. The Pharmaceutical Benefits Advisory Committee last November recommended Wegovy be subsidised for those with a body mass index above 35. The committee will meet next month when it will consider Novo Nordisk’s revised proposal to list Wegovy for obesity following protracted negotiations. The Danish pharmaceutical company produces both Ozempic and Wegovy. They contain the same active ingredient – semaglutide – but Wegovy has a higher dose. “Novo Nordisk is continuing to work constructively with the Department of Health to try to negotiate a solution for the PBS listing of Wegovy,” a company spokesperson said. “We remain committed to improving access for eligible Australians living with obesity.” QENDO, an organisation advocating for people affected by PMOS and other women’s health conditions, said it recognised “growing interest in GLP-1 medications for managing PMOS, particularly for people experiencing metabolic complications and challenges with weight management”. “While emerging evidence suggests potential benefits for some patients, further research is needed to establish their long-term effectiveness and safety specifically for PMOS,” QENDO’s acting chief executive, Kate Fisher, said.

title: One person killed and nine injured in chain-reaction crash in New York City
summary: Motorist, reportedly trying to beat a traffic light, barrels through busy intersection and slams into pedestrians
text: At least one person was killed and nine injured in New York City’s eastern Bronx when a motorist barreled through a busy intersection, slammed into pedestrians and triggered a chain-reaction crash involving several vehicles, according to authorities and media reports. The horrifying collision happened shortly after 2pm in the Bronx’s Allerton neighborhood, with the driver at the center of the crash reportedly saying he was trying to beat a traffic light. Sources told the New York Post that four women, ranging in age from 50 to 60, were walking through a crosswalk when the Mercedes struck them. The victims were transported to Jacobi medical center, where one woman was pronounced dead. Two others were reported to be in critical condition, while the fourth was expected to survive, according to the Post’s sources. The New York fire department (FDNY) said that emergency medical crews treated nine people in the aftermath of the crash, according to the local outlet News 12. Surveillance footage obtained by News 12 captured a white Mercedes-Benz hurtling through the intersection, striking a group of pedestrians in the crosswalk before crashing into multiple vehicles waiting at a traffic light. According to the NYPD’s preliminary findings, the Mercedes rear-ended two vehicles with such force that both cars were pushed into two additional vehicles. The driver, who suffered minor injuries and remained conscious and alert, reportedly told a witness that he had been attempting to beat the traffic light, the Post said.

title: Trump says he picked ‘devoted fan’ Katie Zacharia to be next press secretary
summary: Zacharia will replace Karoline Leavitt, who left the role at the end of August after giving birth to her second child
text: Donald Trump on Friday announced that he had picked Katie Zacharia to be the next White House press secretary, lining up a conservative commentator he called a “devoted fan” to be his most prominent spokesperson. Zacharia will replace Karoline Leavitt, who left the role at the end of August after the birth to her second child. “It is my Great Honor to have just appointed, as Press Secretary, Katie Zacharia,” the president wrote in a social media post on Truth Social. “She has an unblemished record of support, and has been a loyal and brilliant supporter, right from the beginning. She is, likewise, a devoted fan and member of MAGA!” Trump added. The New York Times was first to report that Zacharia has been selected for the role. The Guardian has reached out to Zacharia for comment. Zacharia’s selection puts her at the heart of the White House’s efforts to shape the public narrative around Trump’s second term, as his approval rating falls to record lows, and his party fights to maintain control of Congress in next month’s midterm elections. Trump has asked supporters to vote like his name is on the ballot, turning the election into a referendum on his presidency amid widespread economic discontent and an unpopular war with Iran. Zacharia previously worked as a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), and now serves as a communications adviser for the Trump Media and Technology Group, which owns Truth Social, the president’s social network, on which he made the announcement about her selection official. The appointment came as a something of a surprise in Washington, after weeks of building speculation about who the president might choose to replace Leavitt. Several reports suggested Scott Jennings, the conservative TV pundit was an “an early favorite” for the role, though skeptics noted that his past criticism of the president would likely be an issue. Zacharia, a California native, has been involved in Republican politics for years. She attended Pepperdine University and served as president of her school’s College Republican organization. She interned in the White House’s office of political affairs during the second Bush administration as well as at the Republican National Committee. She obtained her law degree from Pepperdine University in 2011. Prior to joining DHS, Zacharia worked as general counsel at Fix California, a conservative nonprofit focused on “election integrity”. The organization is headed up by Trump ally and diplomat Ric Grenell. Zacharia was a frequent join Fox News commentator, often promoting or defending the US president’s policies while harshly criticizing Democrats. She is married to film producer Tyler Zacharia. They have four children. In his Truth Social post, Trump praised Leavitt, who he said had done a “fantastic job” in the role. On Monday, Fox News announced that Leavitt would join the network as an on-air contributor. “I am confident that Katie will deliver strong results for our Country as the next White House Press Secretary, as she has the respect of, and will work fantastically with, the Media, the American People, and my Administration,” Trump wrote, adding: “Good luck Katie!”

title: New York City’s Marble Hill residents furious after ICE shooting: ‘Why do this?’
summary: Locals also express fear after man shot in the neck while his child was in the back of his car
text: Residents of Manhattan’s Marble Hill neighborhood were furious at federal Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) on Friday but also scared after an officer shot their neighbor who had his child in the back of his car. Orlando Perez had parked his car on the corner of 225th St and Marble Hill Avenue on Thursday night and witnessed ICE arresting Oscar Belgal, 28, after he had been shot in the neck, apparently with an assault-style rifle. “I thought I was going to get shot,” he said on Friday. The streets, now calm after protests had broken out the night before, were noticeably quieter than normal despite golden early October sunshine under blue skies. Perez said he did not notice that the agents targeting Belgal were wearing uniforms or identification badges showing that they belonged to ICE. However, footage of the aftermath of the shooting shows a man in a high visibility construction-type vest, possibly with a badge on a lanyard, and carrying an assault-style rifle. Bystanders can be heard on video asking each other: “Is it ICE or not?” The car that Belgal had driven appeared to have bullet holes in it, according to Perez. The homeland security secretary, Markwayne Mullin, said in a press conference in Washington DC on Friday morning that federal officers did not know there was a child in the target’s car. But Perez added that the car had only light tints on the windows and that ICE “had to see that the kid was inside”. Leading New York City and state politicians and officials have condemned ICE’s action, called for an investigation and demanded violent federal immigration enforcement cease. Zachary Miller said he heard six gun shots from his apartment on Thursday afternoon, when the shooting occurred around 4pm, just when children were streaming home from school. Federal and city law enforcement have listed prior convictions for Belgal and said he was on probation for felony offenses, with the Trump administration accusing him of having gang affiliations. Miller said he knew Belgal from being around the neighborhood and said: “He’s a nice kid. “I don’t see him doing something like this,” he said, referring to the accusations of gang ties and drugs and weapons crimes. Miller has lived in the Marble Hill neighborhood – which is geographically in the Bronx, but considered part of Manhattan – where the shooting occurred for 20 years and said he had never seen such a violent encounter with law enforcement. “I’m a little upset,” he said. “Why do this to this neighborhood?” Carlos Martinez, 18, said that he had heard five or six gunshots while he was eating in P & P Gourmet Deli, which sits on the corner directly across from where the shooting and arrest took place. “I thought the shots came from inside the store, so I was nervous,” he said. Coming from a Dominican family, like Belgal, and growing up in the Bronx, he said he no longer feels safe at home, despite he and all his family members being US citizens. “Over here we are all community, but personally I am uncomfortable,” he said. “They want to target the most innocent people.” The small three-way intersection where Belgal was shot is home to about five apartment complexes and some businesses. New York police on Friday afternoon took away street barricades but yellow crime scene tape was still visible around the scene. Another longtime resident, Carlos Rodriguez, said he felt “soiled” by ICE’s presence in his neighborhood. “I need to take a shower and clean off the filth that comes into my ambit of being,” he said. He said he wished that New York’s progressive Democratic mayor, Zohran Mamdani, would be more outspoken about ICE tensions in New York. “From my point of view, he can come out stronger and more often about this,” he said, adding that he wanted lawmakers to be more proactive against enforcement agents, especially where they are going to residents’ homes and demanding access to make checks or an arrest. Mamdani strongly condemned ICE at a hastily arranged press conference on Thursday night, as protesters can be heard chanting in the background, and called for the agency to be abolished. Meanwhile, several local residents said they had seen ICE officers and vehicles “camped out” in a parking lot nearby that serves a store belonging to the giant retail chain Target. Rodriguez said he suspected the agents were looking for Belgal. Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez late on Thursday criticized Target for accommodating ICE. At a hearing in federal court on Friday afternoon, Belgal’s attorneys said he still had a bullet in his body. A US justice department prosecutor said Belgal had been booked into the federal Metropolitan Detention Center, Brooklyn, which is newly being used to detain immigrants. He had been temporarily brought to a privately run ICE facility in New Jersey after the shooting, and a federal judge at the hearing on Friday ordered the agency to keep Belgal in the area after his attorneys filed emergency motions requesting his release. José Olivares contributed reporting

title: Northern Ireland secretary Chris Bryant bans Drumcree parade
summary: Prospect of contentious Orange Order march through Garvaghy Road in Portadown has led to a nearly two-week standoff
text: The Northern Ireland secretary of state has banned the Drumcree parade after a 13-day impasse between the Orange Order and nationalists. Chris Bryant announced on Friday night that it was “not in the public interest” for Orangemen to march the contested route through Garvaghy Road in Portadown, which Catholic residents had blocked. He said he took the decision after advice from Jon Boutcher, the chief constable of the Northern Ireland Police Service, that the parade “would carry an unacceptable risk of serious injury, disorder and a wider contagion effect” across Northern Ireland. The Parades Commission ruled two weeks ago that a small, circumscribed march could pass along Garvaghy Road – a reversal of 28 years of successive bans. But police prevented the Orangemen from marching after thousands of residents and supporters, including Sinn Féin leaders, blocked the road. Garvaghy Road residents welcomed the secretary of state’s decision, saying it brought relief and certainty after a tense standoff that revived memories of the 1990s, when Orangemen fought pitched battles with police in an attempt to march the route. It was the only “sensible, reasonable and logical outcome”, said Breandán Mac Cionnaith, of the Garvaghy Road Residents Coalition. The Sinn Féin leader, Mary Lou McDonald, and the party’s Northern Ireland first minister, Michelle O’Neill, said in a statement that residents had endured fear and anxiety. “There will be an enormous sense of relief within the community this evening.” The Irish government welcomed the decision and appealed to both sides to seek common ground. “This isn’t a time for triumphalism or claiming victories or anything like that,” said the taoiseach, Micheál Martin. “Those on the unionist, loyalist side will look at this through a different prism. We need to be conscious of that. We need to acknowledge that.” Gavin Robinson, the Democratic Unionist party (DUP) leader, accused Boutcher and Bryant of bowing to republican agitation and threats of potential violence. “These decisions are a mistake, and send profound signals that the country should be run on force of numbers and who shouts the loudest. The framework for both parading and protests now lies in tatters, and the rule of law has been fundamentally undermined.” Robinson asked the secretary to state to explain what the government will do to “restore confidence in the rule of law”. Earlier on Friday the chief constable asked Bryant to review the Parade Commission’s determination, made last month, that conditions in Portadown enabled the parade to go ahead. “I’ve looked at the changing situation in Portadown, the fact that it’s very difficult for that procession to proceed, and I’ve decided that it’s not in the public interest for it to proceed, and I’ve therefore banned the procession,” said Bryant. He thanked Portadown’s Orange Lodge for its “peaceful and law-abiding approach” and regretted that both sides could not reach a compromise, leading to a standoff. “With this in mind, I call for all protests, rallies and demonstrations to be stood down. There is no excuse for a continued ratcheting up of tensions.” Boutcher said the dispute had affected relationships within and between communities and the police. “It is in everyone’s interest that time and space is now created for conversations about finding long-term solutions to this complex and sensitive issue.” The dispute has fuelled angry exchanges at the Stormont assembly and destabilised the executive, with unionists demanding O’Neill step down as first minister for allegedly breaking the law at a Garvaghy Road protest. Earlier on Friday, the PSNI sent the Sinn Féin deputy leader a letter probing alleged criminal offences relating to her involvement in the protest. O’Neill said she will cooperate with the investigation.

title: ‘Abolish ICE’: Mamdani, AOC and other Democrats urge action after New York shooting
summary: Immigration officer shot man in car where five-year-old child was sitting, sparking fierce protests
text: Leading New York Democrats expressed anger and demanded curbs on Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) violence after a federal officer shot a man driving a car in which his five-year-old son was sitting, sparking fierce protests. At least seven shots were reportedly fired and the man was hit in the neck late on Thursday afternoon as children were coming home from school in the busy Marble Hill neighborhood of New York City. Marble Hill is considered part of Manhattan, but is physically located in the Bronx. Federal authorities on Friday morning identified Oscar Belgal as the man shot, saying he was undocumented, from the Dominican Republic and had a felony record and gang affiliations. Belgal was later booked into the Metropolitan Detention Center, Brooklyn, federal lockup, which is newly being used to detain immigrants, according to his attorneys and a US prosecutor who spoke during a hearing on Friday afternoon. He still has a “bullet in his body” and has not been able to communicate with his family, his attorneys said during the hearing. ICE took Belgal on Thursday from a New York hospital into New Jersey. He reportedly spent the night inside the Elizabeth Contract Detention Facility, a privately run ICE facility, before being brought back into New York and being booked into MDC Brooklyn. Meanwhile, Belgal was able to have only one phone call with lawyers on Friday, his attorney Paige Austin with Make the Road New York said. A New York federal judge on early Friday morning ordered ICE to keep Belgal in the area, after his attorneys filed emergency motions requesting his release. The justice department is likely to argue that Belgal’s transfer into New Jersey took place before the judge’s order, making the order requiring ICE to keep him in the area moot. And Belgal’s attorneys have indicated that they will continue challenging his detention. The Justice Department will likely argue that Bergal’s transfer into New Jersey took place before the New York judge’s order, which would make the judge’s order requiring ICE to keep him in the area moot. Bergal’s attorneys will continue to challenge his detention. Marcos Charles, a senior ‌ICE official, said Belgal refused to exit his car when approached by ‌federal officers who were trying to arrest him, and then accelerated, ‌struck two ICE vehicles and drove towards other officers. An ICE officer then shot Belgal and Charles said the wound was “superficial”. Footage showed a man in a high-visibility construction vest, possibly with a badge on a lanyard, carrying an assault-style rifle and standing close to Belgal, who is sat on the street, while another officer appears to hold a hand to his neck and shoulder area. New York police officers in uniform shortly afterwards carry the man to an unmarked car and lay him in the back seat, handcuffed behind his back. But Kathy Hochul, New York’s governor, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, a New York congresswoman, and Zohran Mamdani, the city’s mayor – all of whom are Democrats – led strong condemnation of ICE’s conduct. Darializa Avila Chevalier, the Democratic New York candidate, rushed to the protests and was knocked over in the chaos as local police and demonstrators clashed. The wounded man was conscious and hospitalized, authorities said. A joint statement from Bronx and Manhattan borough presidents Vanessa L Gibson and Brad Hoylman-Sigal, respectively, said their constituents “stand united in outrage” over Belgal’s shooting. “The frustration, pain, anger and trauma stoked by this incident extends far beyond an individual,” the statement said. Mamdani called the incident “unconscionable” and said on Thursday night that ICE, part of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), had “whisked him away” from the New York-Presbyterian Allen hospital in upper Manhattan. A similar incident occurred in Texas last month after a man was shot by an ICE officer in Austin and despite a bullet lodged in his back was taken by the federal authorities from a local hospital to ICE detention about 140 miles away. Ocasio-Cortez and Mamdani demanded ICE be abolished. Both Hochul and Mamdani spoke to Donald Trump and Markwayne Mullin, the homeland security secretary, by phone on Thursday night. “I have been on the phone with President Trump and Secretary Mullin negotiating ‌the release of the man ICE agents ‌shot. Those negotiations were unsuccessful,” Mamdani told a press conference. He demanded from the Trump ‌administration that ICE stop its enforcement actions in New York City. “ICE is rotten to its core,” he said. ICE has been stepping up arrests all year despite withdrawing massed militarized ranks from Minneapolis in January and adopting a more covert approach to enforcement. Both Hochul and Mamdani demanded that ICE cease enforcement operations in New York and the governor said she expressed outrage to the Trump administration on behalf of all New Yorkers. Hochul added that the incident could easily have ended in tragedy. “No child should ever have to experience the terror of gunfire,” she said. The child was being looked after by his family on Friday. The streets where the shooting and protests took place were calm on Friday morning but many residents remained shocked and angry. “Here’s an innocent child that was caught in the crossfire,” said Calvin Hayden, a south Bronx native. “That child could have been killed.” Hayden heard about the shooting the night before and said he was immediately disturbed. He came to Marble Hill, the northernmost part of Manhattan, to see the aftermath. “I don’t believe ICE has any reason or right to be in New York City,” he said, adding he thought New York was already equipped on its own to handle immigration disputes without ICE presence. “There’s a lot of individuals who are not committing crimes and they just want to make a better life for themselves,” he said. Some drivers on 225th Street yelled anti-ICE sentiments as they drove past the scene. Mullin said on Friday morning that the ICE officers involved in the shooting did not know there was a child in the vehicle and defended the agency’s actions. But he pointed out that Belgal would have obviously known the child was in his car when he drove it at officers. The exact sequence of events leading up to the shooting have not yet become clear. Mullin said that Hochul had asked the DHS for a pause on enforcement in New York. “No, we are not putting a pause on enforcement,” he said. Mullin criticized New York’s “sanctuary” policies, which restrict how much city agencies and police cooperate with immigration authoritie. Belgal, 28, has prior convictions, was serving five years of probation for felony grand larceny and was also arrested on drug charges in 2025, a case that is still pending, according to the New York police department. “What happened today was an outrage,” Mamdani said late on Thursday, adding: “When ICE agents opened fire, a five-year-old child – a five-year-old child! – was in the back seat of that car. Thank God that child is physically unharmed.” Witnesses told local media they heard the child yelling at the officers after the shooting. At least 20 people have been shot by federal immigration agents under the second Trump administration, as well as a rise in deaths in detention. “ICE is a rogue, lawless and paramilitary surveillance agency. It does not belong in New York City and it should not exist in the United States of America. Abolish ICE,” Ocasio-Cortez said in a statement. The representative also condemned the retail company Target for allowing federal enforcement teams to use its parking lots as staging areas from which to launch arrest operations. Protesters held signs saying:“Jail all killer ICE agents” and “Leave our neighbors alone.” “ICE, get the fuck out of our neighborhood,” shouted Gibson, the Bronx borough president. “I’m angry that we have to be here … We are a working-class community. We don’t deserve this type of treatment from the White House.” She encouraged the crowd to get involved in opposing ICE, saying: “There are more of us than there are of them. I want this to be a moment that we turn into a movement.” Protesters gathered at the hospital where Belgal was taken. The police set up barricades and protesters quickly clashed with officers in a chaotic scene. Demonstrators banged drums and shouted: “Shut it down,” and “ICE out!” as cars driving by honked in support. Standing outside the hospital, Murad Awawdeh, the president of the New York Immigration Coalition, said he wanted to see an independent investigation into the shooting led by New York officials. “The pain that you’re witnessing is people who are witnessing their neighbors, their family members, their friends being ripped away,” he said. ICE has arrested more than 19,500 people in New York and nearly 18,000 in New Jersey during the second Trump administration, mostly Latin American immigrant men without criminal histories, Gothamist reported earlier this week using government data, adding that those totals were more than double the number of such arrests in the last 18 months of the Biden administration. Lex McMenamin and Joanna Walters contributed reporting

title: Flydubai co-pilot planned suicide attack on Israeli airport, UAE prosecutors say
summary: Hammam al-Hammami is believed to have been targeting the passenger terminal at Ben Gurion airport near Tel Aviv
text: The co-pilot who tried to seize control of a passenger jet flying from Dubai to Tel Aviv last week was planning to launch a suicide attack targeting the passenger terminal at Israel’s international airport, prosecutors in the United Arab Emirates said on Friday. Hammam al-Hammami attacked the plane’s Indian pilot with an emergency axe, but failed to prevent his badly injured colleague from opening the cockpit’s security door to allow passengers to overpower his assailant. Passengers then tried to control the aircraft, which was safely landed in Saudi Arabia by a flydubai pilot who was among about 180 passengers. Dr Hamad Saif al-Shamsi, attorney-general of the UAE, said on Friday that al-Hammami, who is in Emirati custody, had admitted he had tried to execute a “premeditated terrorist plot to … launch a suicide attack targeting the passenger terminal at Ben Gurion airport near Tel Aviv, with the aim of causing the greatest possible loss of life”. The 29-year-old, who was hired by flydubai, a government-owned low-cost airline, began a process of radicalisation while studying in Australia when he was influenced by the hardline takfiri ideology through reading extremist literature and online content glorifying terrorist organisations and suicide attacks, al-Shamsi said in a statement. “[Al-Hammami] subsequently developed … ideas advocating violence and terrorism. He also drew inspiration from the 11 September 2001 attacks, and the idea of carrying out a similar operation using an aircraft became firmly established in his thinking. According to his confession, this was linked to his decision to pursue a career in aviation.” Over the weekend, Australian security agencies launched an investigation after it emerged al-Hammami spent about two years in the country as a student until 2017. He left the country without completing his engineering degree. New Zealand authorities have launched their own investigation after police confirmed al-Hammami underwent flight training there about a year after he abandoned a degree in Australia. There has been widespread concern about how al-Hammami was able to pass vetting and join a crew flying to Israel. An Omani national, he earned a distance-learning aviation management degree from Buckinghamshire New University in 2023 and was employed by Oman Air from 2020-24, joined Royal Air Maroc in early 2025 and worked there for several months before moving to flydubai in January 2026. Security officials have been keen to understand if al-Hammami was acting alone or had become involved with a group such as al-Qaida or Islamic State, which could suggest further such attacks might be planned. Emirate authorities believe this is not the case. “In the presence of his lawyer and with all legally prescribed safeguards ensured, the suspect provided a detailed confession outlining his motives and the stages of planning and execution. He admitted that he had acted alone, without the involvement of others, although investigations are continuing to verify this claim,” al-Shamsi said. Investigators have found al-Hammami had used two previous flights to Tel Aviv to “familiarise himself with the flight route ‌and the airport”, the Emirati state news agency WAM reported. The passengers on board the aircraft were overwhelmingly Israeli, with prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu hailing them and the pilot for their bravery after the foiled attack.

title: Prosecutors oppose Luigi Mangione’s push for dismissal of state charges
summary: Manhattan prosecutors say murder case over 2024 killing can proceed under ‘exception’ to state double jeopardy law
text: Manhattan prosecutors filed paperwork on Friday opposing Luigi Mangione’s arguments for dismissing his state-level case in the killing of the UnitedHealthcare executive Brian Thompson. Mangione on 14 August pleaded guilty to federal charges in Thompson’s 4 December 2024 killing outside a Midtown hotel – weeks before his scheduled 8 September New York state murder and weapons trial. The killing prompted an intense manhunt but also sparked an outpouring of rage against the practices of the for-profit US healthcare industry. Shortly after he entered his guilty plea to two federal stalking charges, Mangione’s legal team filed a motion to dismiss the state-level murder case against him. Judge Gregory Carro, who is overseeing Mangione’s state case, subsequently postponed these proceedings, scheduling the next court date for 10 December, according to a 17 August letter. Carro told prosecutors to respond to Mangione’s push for dismissal by 9 October and gave his defense a 30 October deadline to reply. Mangione’s defense has argued that New York state’s double jeopardy law prohibits him from being prosecuted by the Manhattan district attorney’s office. New York state law holds that “a person may not be twice prosecuted for the same offense” and “a person may not be separately prosecuted for two offenses based upon the same act or criminal transaction”. Manhattan prosecutors argued in their papers that Mangione’s murder case can proceed “under an exception” to the state double jeopardy law. They insist that elements of the federal stalking and state murder charges do not overlap in a way that would trigger double jeopardy protections. Mangione has claimed that Manhattan prosecutors cannot pursue weapons charges against him because he had previously faced federal weapons counts. But the federal court dismissed these counts, Manhattan state prosecutors noted. “Statutory double jeopardy applies only when a defendant has been ‘separately prosecuted’ for the same misconduct, and dismissed federal charges do not constitute a separate prosecution,” they argued. As for the murder charge, Manhattan prosecutors insist that the federal stalking charges Mangione pleaded guilty to are dramatically different from his state murder case.

title: Federal judge rules against Trump DoJ’s policy of collecting state voter rolls
summary: Judge says justice department policy of checking state voter rolls against a federal immigration database is unlawful
text: A federal judge ruled on Friday that the US justice department’s policy of collecting states’ unredacted voter rolls to check them against a federal immigration database is unlawful. The ruling, by the US district judge Sparkle Sooknanan, was a setback for Donald Trump, who has pushed his administration to ramp up investigations into non-citizen voting ahead of the November midterm elections, with control of Congress at stake. The department’s list maintenance policy, adopted to comply with the president’s election integrity executive order, violated privacy laws and risked disenfranchising voters, Sooknanan said. “The court vacates a policy that has removed United States citizens from the voter rolls in their home states and risks disenfranchising many more – a policy that flies in the face of duly enacted laws designed to protect Americans,” Sooknanan wrote in the 78-page ruling. Sooknanan said the policy not only violated federal laws, but also that the justice department did not have the authority to enact it because Congress gave the states, not the federal government, control over the maintenance of their voter rolls. “Behind all the window dressing, the challenged policy represents the federal government’s attempt to decide who gets to vote,” Sooknanan wrote. “But Congress has left that authority where our constitution has always placed it: with the states.” Sooknanan wrote that her ruling “does not prevent the federal government from taking lawful steps to support states’ efforts to maintain accurate voter rolls” and did not prevent states from maintaining their own. Sooknanan previously ruled against the administration in June, limiting the its ability to create a database of Americans’ information. The US supreme court later temporarily set aside her decision. The justice department did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The lawsuit, brought by the government watchdog group Common Cause, came after the justice department requested voter information from states in May. Roughly 18 states complied, handing over information that included voters’ full names, birth dates, residential addresses, and state driver’s license numbers or the last four digits of their social security numbers. Sooknanan said the department “improperly” disclosed and maintained records. The administration wanted voter roll information to compare with immigration data, to ensure non-citizens are not registered to vote. But Sooknanan said the justice department “failed to consider the risk that its use of citizenship records known to be unreliable would lead the civil rights division to demand that states remove US citizens from their voter rolls”. In her ruling, she cited two people who had been incorrectly removed from their state’s voter roll list because they had been wrongly identified as non-citizens. “This is a victory for voters and yet another loss for the Department of Justice. It’s time the Trump administration stop these desperate attempts to seize voters’ private data and take control of our elections,” said Virginia Kase Solomón, president and CEO of Common Cause.

title: I saw Iran execute a man in public. Is this what the US wants? | Robert Tait
summary: It is odd for the US defense secretary to be laying the groundwork for an event that could be organized by Tehran
text: Pete Hegseth’s plans to stage a public execution resemble a grotesque Iran-imitation game. Having failed over the past seven months to defeat the Tehran regime on the battlefield, the self-styled “secretary of war” now proposes to mirror its notorious practice of enforcing the death penalty as a grand public spectacle. “We’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public, because people need to understand there’s serious consequences for these types of things,” Hegseth, with barely concealed relish, told the rightwing Real America’s Voice network of the planned execution of Nidal Malik Hasan, a former army psychiatrist who killed 13 people at a military base at Fort Hood in Texas in 2009. The prospect conjures vivid flashbacks of my own experience witnessing such an event in Iran, days after arriving as a correspondent for the Guardian more than two decades ago. Then, the Iranian authorities hanged a convicted child serial killer, Muhammad Bijeh, from a crane – in contrast to the firing-squad execution Hegseth envisions – in the small town of Pakdasht, about 35 miles (56km) from Tehran. The resulting report was published by the paper in March 2005. It was the first I had filed for the Guardian. Reading it back now, almost 22 years later, my sparing, almost frugal, description barely does justice to the grim drama that unfolded – and its enduring effect on me. It was a searing and unforgettable experience that deeply imprinted on me, as a new arrival, the ruthlessly repressive nature of the Islamic republic. In many ways, that seemed the intention. For the locals, it was an exhibition they were encouraged to attend. I clearly recall police cars touring the streets as officers inside with loud-hailers summoned the local population to watch. I came to the authorities’ notice along with a BBC correspondent, who drew attention after sticking her microphone out of our car window to record the sound effects of the police summonses. After the police stopped us and learned we were foreign journalists, they took us to a municipal office, where a local court official – who seemed to be in charge of arrangements – appeared rather pleased to see us. What did I think of all this, he asked, as we looked out the window at the scene in a public square, where a makeshift gallows-like platform had been erected and a crowd was gathering. Unsure of myself, and mindful of Iran’s reputation for expelling aberrant foreign journalists, I hedged somewhat uncourageously, ignoring the whispered promptings of the BBC journalist – who had not been asked and, unlike me, was visiting the country on a short-term visa – to “tell him you think it’s awful”. How awful became gruesomely clear when we went outside. Before he was to be hanged, Bijeh, who had reportedly murdered 17 children and three adults, was to be subject to the Islamic punishment of 100 lashes. My report describes how officials took turns to administer them. My memory is of the condemned man’s muffled cries of agony as the blows inflicted bloody streaks on his bare back, prompting the feeling that this was an officially endorsed display of sadism. As Bijeh stood awaiting execution, a youth said to be brother of one of the child victims stormed the platform and stabbed him with a knife. The thirst for violence continued as he was hoisted from the crane. The crowd chanted “Allahu Akbar” (God is great) and “marg bar Bijeh” (death to Bijeh) while the father of one of the murdered children urged the crane operator to “turn him around, make him swing”. When the operator obliged, Bijeh’s shoes fell off, one after the other, leaving him barefoot as the life drained from him. I watched all this with rapt fascination, knowing I was witnessing a horror – yet also with a detachment that to this day gives me pause. I was working. As Bijeh’s limp and lifeless body hung high up above the town square, I took, for professional purposes, a photograph – asking myself inwardly whether it was morally the right thing to do. Now, I am sure it was not. The ignoble act was all my own, but perhaps also an illustration of the uglier impulses of the human psyche triggered by a public execution. As the dark carnival mood began to dissipate, the same court official who had canvassed my views earlier approached me to justify the scene. “Look at the way the emotions of the people have calmed down. We had to hold it in public,” he said. While I cannot recall my response, I was unconvinced. It was not the first execution I had reported on. I had been in Terre Haute, Indiana, in 2001 for the execution – by lethal injection – of Timothy McVeigh, the Oklahoma City bomber, who killed 168 people with a truck bomb outside a federal building in 1995. But that took place behind closed doors, in a federal prison. McVeigh’s high-profile crime accounted for the intense media and public interest in his death. In Iran, by contrast, officials had deliberately fanned voyeuristic impulses for what seemed like the purposes of flaunting authoritarian power. It amounted to a salutary first impression as I came to terms with life under an Iranian regime that took power after the 1979 Islamic revolution. It served as something of a moral compass as I reported on the regime’s actions, and tried to understand how – and why – its ideology seemed so at odds with the values proclaimed by the US and the west. How odd it now seems, therefore, for the US defense secretary to be proudly laying the groundwork for an event that feels as though it could be organized by the authorities in Tehran. It raises the question of whether, at least under Donald Trump, Washington and Tehran’s values are really so different after all.

title: Trump establishes committee to investigate Fed governor Lisa Cook
summary: US president renews his efforts to oust Cook despite supreme court ruling that her firing was unconstitutional
text: Donald Trump announced on Friday that he is establishing a committee to investigate Lisa Cook, the US Federal Reserve governor, over allegations that she committed mortgage fraud, renewing his efforts to oust her despite a June supreme court ruling that her earlier firing was unconstitutional. Trump said a committee will consult with justice department officials to decide whether there is “cause” for her removal. The White House will hold an in-person hearing on 5 November to consider the allegations against Cook, which will be closed to the public but transcribed and published. Cook will be able to submit a written statement to present her own evidence and will be subject to examination from White House and her own legal counsel. “As President, it is my job to ensure the laws are faithfully executed, including by firing subordinates who cannot be trusted to tell the truth and follow the law,” Trump said in a statement posted to the White House’s website. Her legal team has maintained that the White House is “cherrypicking” facts and any claims of fraud are based on unrelated clerical errors. In response to the announcement, Cook’s lawyers said that they had “grave doubts” that the White House hearing would be “a legitimate one that would conform to the law”. “But if it is anything close to objective,” they continued, “the conclusion will be that Governor Cook did not commit mortgage fraud, leaving no cause to remove her from the Federal Reserve Board.” They added that Cook “welcomes the opportunity to present the facts so she can clear her name and demonstrate there is no legal basis to fire her”. Cook was appointed by Joe Biden in 2022 to a 14-year term, becoming the Fed’s first Black governor. Before her tenure at the central bank, she taught at Harvard University and Stanford University and served on Barack Obama’s council of economic advisers. Cook’s battle with the White House began in August 2025 when she was abruptly fired after Trump said she committed mortgage fraud by listing two properties in Georgia and Michigan as her primary residence and failing to report rental income on her Atlanta property. Cook immediately sued the Trump administration, and the supreme court reinstated her after a 5-4 ruling that she could stay on as governor while fighting the fraud allegations. In June, the court ruled that Trump’s firing was unconstitutional because he did not follow proper procedure and give Cook an opportunity to dispute the allegations before she was fired. Cook was fired just as Trump was launching unprecedented attacks on the Fed’s chair, then Jerome Powell, in his blustering push to get the central bank to lower interest rates. Trump also launched a justice department investigation into Powell, which was dropped in April. Congress created the Fed to be an independent and non-partisan institution. Economists widely agree that a central bank unswayed by politics is essential for the stability of a country’s economy. Kevin Warsh, Powell’s successor, has repeatedly faced questions over how he will maintain the Fed’s independence. Before Trump picked him to lead the world’s most powerful central bank, he had echoed the president’s calls for cutting rates. But because of elevated inflation brought on by the war in the Middle East, the bank ultimately voted to raise rates in its last meeting, which drew the ire of the White House just more than a month before the crucial midterm elections.
