title: Pete Hegseth’s plan to livestream execution puts US in dubious company
summary: Only Iran and Afghanistan routinely carry out sentences in public, with Saudi Arabia appearing to have ended practice
text: If the US defence secretary, Pete Hegseth, goes ahead with plans to livestream the execution of a soldier radicalised to extremist Islam who killed 13 people at a military base in Texas, his country will join a motley assembly of lesser powers and rogue actors who have conducted public executions in recent years. Only two countries currently systematically carry out capital sentences in public: Iran and Afghanistan. In 2025, the Taliban authorities carried out six such killings and the regime in Tehran 11, according to Amnesty International. In April last year, the Taliban executed four men accused of murder in three different cities. All were shot dead in crowded public sports stadiums. Such events were common when the hardline Islamist militia movement was in power in the late 1990s. Then as now, the Taliban claimed a due court process had been followed. In July, two young men accused of killing police officers were hanged by Iranian authorities in the central square of Isfahan, Iran. Human rights monitors have reported about 30 public executions in the country in the last five years, with an intensification in recent months after massive popular unrest earlier this year and the war with the US and Israel. Historically, many hangings have been carried out using a crane as a makeshift gallows. Saudi Arabia appears to have ended the practice after decades of beheading convicted criminals in a square in the capital, Riyadh, and sometimes publicly in provincial cities. Legal experts and historians argue that public executions perform different functions. If the rule of law is shaky or there is doubt about the efficacy of the criminal justice system, they offer authorities seeking to win support a way of convincing the community that criminals will be punished. Such public spectacles can also be a way of cowing a population through terror. Armed militant groups have frequently resorted to public executions – often in an effort to assert their authority. Islamic State, which ruled a swath of Iraq and Syria between 2014 and 2019, conducted thousands of executions for alleged offences ranging from homosexuality to theft. Many of the executions took place in public or were videoed. A large number were deliberately choreographed to provide a spectacle for broadcast to terrorise enemies and potential dissidents as well as to radicalise IS supporters and attract new ones. In October 2025, as Hamas sought to reassert its control over the population of Gaza, it carried out a public execution of six men apparently accused of collaborating with Israel. In 2017, the group had executed three men accused of the same crime, partly livestreaming the event on Facebook. The execution of Maj Nidal Hasan, a former army psychiatrist, at Fort Hood in Texas would be the first public execution in the US in many decades. In the US, the practice of public executions was largely stopped in the 1930s, though in 2001, some survivors and victims’ relatives were allowed to watch the execution by lethal injection of Timothy McVeigh, convicted of the 1995 bombing of a government office in Oklahoma City. Hasan’s execution has been scheduled for 3 December. Hegseth, who has the authority to decide the conduct of the killing, has said that “of course” it would take place at the same time and in the same place as Hasan’s attack 17 years ago and would use firearms, as Hasan did. Hasan can launch appeals within the civilian federal court system that could delay the execution for many years. In 2025, Amnesty International recorded 2,707 executions, the highest total globally since 1981, and an increase of two-thirds on the previous year. The sharp rise was mainly due to more than 2,100 executions by Iran, its highest number of executions in decades. Amnesty said authorities had placed the death penalty “at the centre of flawed public security and ‘tough on crime’ narratives to assert control, project state power and score political points”. “This trend was strongest in countries where the authorities have tightened their grip on power by restricting civic space, silencing dissent and displaying disregard for protections established under international human rights law and standards,” the campaign group reported.

title: Democratic Senate candidate responds to anti-trans attacks pushed by Republicans
summary: Dr Annie Andrews voices opposition to ‘biological men … in women’s sports’ in response to Republican attacks
text: Dr Annie Andrews, a Democratic Senate candidate in South Carolina, has responded to persistent efforts by Republicans to make trans athletes in women’s sports a wedge issue in the race. In a restrained direct-to-camera statement, Andrews – a pediatrician – outlined her opposition to “biological men playing in women’s sports”, as her party pushes back against Republican attacks. “I want you to hear me loud and clear: I don’t support biological men playing in women’s sports, and I don’t support and haven’t ever performed gender surgery for minors,” Andrews said in a new ad. Andrews’ video, in which she wears a white lab coat with a stethoscope around her neck, was in response to recent attacks from Donald Trump and an aggressive ad, paid for by a super political action committee (Super Pac) supporting her Republican opponent in South Carolina, Darline Graham. The ad claims Andrews “is for they/them” and frames a transgender person as predatory toward a child. Republicans are using anti-trans issues, such as keeping trans women off women’s and girls’ sports teams, to try to thwart Democrats in the upcoming midterms. Trump has pushed the issue for years. A landmark supreme court ruling earlier this year handed Trump a key “culture war” victory by upholding laws in two conservative states excluding transgender girls and women from competing in female sports. Andrews, who has previously been vocal in her support of trans people, used her response ad to directly address Republican criticisms and claims as the party pushes anti-trans attacks against Democrats nationwide. Some Democrats running in competitive districts have shifted their tone on the issue of trans rights, particularly on the issue of trans athletes in women’s sports. Congresswoman Marcy Kaptur of Ohio, seeking re-election in a district that voted for Trump in 2024, recently aired an ad touting that she “voted with Republicans to keep transgender ideology out of our schools” and “boys should not play in girls’ sports”. Congressman Don Davis of North Carolina, running for re-election in a district that also backed the president in 2024, released an ad saying: “There’s real concerns about fairness and safety; that’s what I believe states should decide what’s right for protecting women and girls.” Blake Gendebien, the Democratic candidate running in a primarily Republican district in New York, released an ad stating that “boys shouldn’t play on girls’ sports teams” while also highlighting that the topic was a non-issue in the district. “The thing is, in 20 years raising a family here, I haven’t heard this issue come up. Not once,” Gendebien said. “But internet trolls like [the Republican candidate] Anthony Constantino use it to rile people up.” In 2024, pro-Trump groups seized on conservative opposition to the Biden administration’s trans inclusive policies to attack former vice-president Kamala Harris, the then Democratic presidential candidate. “Kamala’s agenda is they/them, not you,” a voiceover said in one widely seen pro-Trump ad. The ad attacking Andrews in South Carolina uses nearly identical language as the pro-Trump one two years ago. How Democrats should respond to Republicans’ anti-trans attacks has divided some. Equality Pac, the fundraising arm of the congressional equality caucus focusing on electing LGBTQ+ people, told Axios it disapproved of Kaptur’s handling of her response to the anti-trans attacks. The Pac called Kaptur’s language “unacceptable” and said it was “absolutely not supporting her campaign at this time”, referring to her ad in which she called transgender girls “boys”. Last month, the Human Rights Campaign – an LGBTQ+ advocacy group – wrote a Substack article to help guide Democrats on how to best respond to anti-trans rights attacks. “Turning on a vulnerable community is not a winning political strategy – and it’s exactly what Trump, [Elon] Musk, and MAGA want,” it wrote. “It legitimizes their side and weakens ours. And it harms transgender people.” The group pointed to the Ohio Senate candidate Sherrod Brown’s response to anti-trans attacks as a good example of how to handle those attacks. Brown released an ad last month featuring voters who dismiss the anti-trans issues, and instead redirected attention to affordability issues under Brown’s competitor, and the incumbent senator, Jon Husted. “With everything going on, that’s what they’re talking about?” one voter said in Brown’s advertisement. The Human Rights Campaign said Brown “didn’t play into MAGA’s hands” and “let voters do the talking” in the video.

title: EU ‘pulling out all stops’ with minerals projects as it tries to avert China trade war
summary: Commissioner Stéphane Séjourné says bloc will support 46 strategic projects including lithium and rare earths plants
text: The EU is “pulling out all the stops” to fend off an imminent potential trade crisis with China, the industry commissioner, Stéphane Séjourné, has said, as the bloc announced its backing for a string of critical materials projects. Séjourné said on Friday that the EU would support 46 new strategic projects to accelerate supplies of critical raw materials by 2030 across the bloc. “We could face a crisis in the coming months,” he said. “We may face trade tensions that could also trigger a crisis in a number of sectors. We need to be prepared for that. And we’re getting ready right now.” The new projects include plants for supplies of lithium, gallium and rare earths needed for the auto, defence and renewable energy industries, with a funding cost of €21bn (£17.8bn). They were unveiled just as the EU works to avert a trade war with China, with the trade commissioner, Maroš Šefčovič, continuing talks on Friday in Beijing aimed at reducing China’s “unsustainable” £1bn-a-day trade surplus with the bloc. “We’re pulling out all the stops to move as quickly as possible. The primary objective is the targets set by law, and beyond that, there’s a geopolitical challenge that could catch up with us very quickly,” said Séjourné. “Mines are opening, factories are being built, financing agreements are being signed, and a European value chain is emerging,” Séjourné added. Amid some scepticism over the EU’s ability to meet its 2030 targets to reduce dependencies on China, Séjourné cited three “emblematic” projects which have previously been identified as strategic, earmarking them for accelerated permits. These included a rare earths plant near Pau in south-western France. The Carester plant, which is expected to be up and running in late 2026, produces dysprosium and terbium, “two raw materials for which we are almost entirely dependent on China”, used in magnets for electric vehicles and offshore wind turbines. “This single project could account for about 15% of global production of these oxides. That is no small feat,” Séjourné said. He also name-checked a gallium plant in Greece which is already up and running. The third, Keliber, a lithium extraction and processing plant in Finland, is also operational after €150m support from the European Investment Bank. The 46 projects are the second batch of initiatives to receive flagship status since the Critical Raw Materials Act of 2024, which legally mandates the European Commission to reduce the bloc’s dependency on foreign countries. The EU hopes to follow in the footsteps of Japan, which has reduced dependency on China for rare earths to 60% from 90% since 2011, when Beijing prohibited exports of about 20 materials to Japan, claiming they were being used for military purposes. Although the flagship status does not bring the projects direct funds, it enables accelerated permitting, and help in mobilising funds. However, there has been criticism in industry within the EU that the scheme is not strong enough to deliver targets to mine 10%, process 40% and recycle 25% of the bloc’s needs by 2030. The French lithium refiner Viridian Lithium, which received EU strategic status in 2025, went into judicial liquidation in March this year. Earlier this year, a group of 23 of the 60 projects designated strategic in 2025 wrote to the European Commission calling for more action to “urgently unlock projects, particularly those working towards final investment decision which face acute liquidity and market pressure and immediate jeopardy”. Séjourné said member states had unlocked €1bn for six of the projects, with the European Investment Bank providing another €660m for eight projects.

title: Execution live stream could cause PTSD in viewers, say psychiatrists
summary: Warning follows Hegseth announcement that firing squad execution of Fort Hood killer will be public
text: Livestreaming an execution could cause post-traumatic stress disorder in the viewing public, mental health experts have said, after the US confirmed plans to broadcast the death by firing squad of a man who shot dead 13 unarmed soldiers. The US defence secretary, Pete Hegseth, said on Thursday that Nidal Hasan, a former army psychiatrist who killed 13 people at Fort Hood in 2009, would be executed by firing squad on 3 December. Officials later confirmed it would be livestreamed. It is believed it will be the first public execution in the US in almost a century. Hegseth said: “It was a radical Islamist attack in uniform inside the ranks, and so he’s going to get a firing squad of soldiers, as it should be, and we’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public, because people need to understand there’s serious consequences for these types of things.” Experts said watching the event could result in lasting harms for viewers. Dr Simon Duff, a forensic psychologist at the University of Nottingham in the UK, said that while there was not a lot of research into the impact of watching an execution, studies examining journalists’ experiences of witnessing violence suggested evidence of trauma response. “Certainly if people are not resilient they probably shouldn’t [watch], but if they have some underlying psychological driver towards viewing an execution they will likely do so regardless of the potential for harm,” Duff said. “Recent events suggest that executions do not always go to plan,” he said, referring to the failed execution by lethal injection of Christa Pike in the US. “That possibility needs to be acknowledged, and the likelihood that this would increase the trauma for viewers.” Neil Greenberg, a professor of defence mental health at the Institute of Psychiatry, Psychology and Neuroscience at King’s College London, said trigger warnings did not routinely lead to people avoiding media they may find distressing. “Instead they are likely to suffer anticipatory anxiety before the ‘trauma’ is shown and some people will then become distressed,” he said. “It is likely that people who have pre-existing mental health problems will be especially at risk of becoming distressed or experiencing a deterioration in their mental health. My advice would be not to watch the event at all and I would hope that mainstream media would not transmit highly traumatic images [or] sounds.” Public executions were once common around the world, including in the UK, but only two out of 17 countries that carried out executions last year did so publicly. Prof Rosalind Crone, a historian at the Open University in the UK, said: “Public execution in England and Wales was abolished in 1868 because of persistent and increasing concern about the effects of watching hangings on the crowd. It was clear that public execution did not have a deterrent effect, in fact, sometimes the opposite.” Crone said crowds were increasingly made up of people missing work to attend, and people who were drunk, rowdy and celebratory. “Charles Dickens sums up the increasing objections well in his letter to the Daily News in 1846: ‘No sorrow, no salutatory terror, no abhorrence, no seriousness, nothing but ribaldry, debauchery, levity, drunkenness and flouting vice in fifty other shapes,’” she said. “Public execution – and execution full stop – does not work as a deterrent,” Crone added. “If anything, the use of a medium like video broadcast will likely generate new, potentially more dangerous problems in managing crowd responses and reactions.”

title: Robert Jenrick launches scathing broadside against ‘Kensington Kemi’
summary: Reform UK shadow chancellor seeks to associate Tory leader with metropolitan elite as party relations sour further
text: Robert Jenrick has launched an extended attack on Kemi Badenoch, calling her part of a metropolitan elite and saying a coalition deal with the Tories would be like being “handcuffed to a zombie”. Reform UK’s economics spokesperson repeatedly called the Tory leader “Kensington Kemi” and claimed her party was for people who moaned about the decline of Mayfair clubs and complained that they could not find Ottolenghi recipe ingredients in the shops. He accused his former party of handing out “bungs for Belgravia” after the Conservatives said at their autumn conference that they would exempt property from inheritance tax and extend free childcare to higher earners if elected. Jenrick’s attack on Badenoch, whose approval ratings among the public have improved, come at a time of deteriorating relations between the Conservatives and Reform. Jenrick was the target of much mockery at the Conservative conference, where he was depicted in multiple places on a satirical Bayeux tapestry of the political landscape as a crying baby. He was kicked out of the Tories in January for planning to defect. In her conference speech, Badenoch firmly ruled out any move to “unite the right” with a deal between Reform and the Tories, questioning who would want to join with a party that made her British-born mixed-race children feel as though they were not English. The Reform leader, Nigel Farage, downplayed the idea of a post-election pact on Thursday, saying it was “extremely unlikely”. Jenrick took a tougher line against the Conservatives in his press conference on Friday, saying they were “nothing more than a metropolitan pressure group for the wealthiest” and likening a tie-up to being “handcuffed to a zombie”. “Kensington Kemi knows who her people are. Millionaires, not Mansfield,” Jenrick said. “The wealthy, not workers. She’s for people who complain that Mayfair clubs aren’t what they used to be. For people who struggle to find all the ingredients for that Ottolenghi recipe. And people whose lives have got almost nothing in common with my constituents in Newark.” Jenrick made the attacks on the Tories for having “retreated into the hinterland of Kensington and Chelsea” despite a number of senior Reform figures having lived in the area. Farage rented a house in Kensington and Chelsea during the Brexit years, paid for by the leave donor Arron Banks. Nick Candy, the party’s honorary treasurer and a property billionaire, sold his £275m Chelsea mansion this year. Last year, Farage announced a policy specifically designed to appeal to billionaires, offering them a flat £250,000 tax rate for non-dom status to attract the wealthy to London, and he bemoaned the “very rapid exodus” from central London and how it was “tough to sell a house” in Kensington and Chelsea. Farage is famously a member of an exclusive Mayfair club, 5 Hertford Street, while the party held its fundraiser at the trendy Oswald’s in Mayfair last year. Asked whether Reform was also the party of billionaires, Jenrick said it was focused on delivering tax cuts for 40 million middle earners. Jenrick also faced questions regarding the suggestion by Reform figures that Badenoch could not be English because of her Nigerian heritage. He said the debate was “pretty overblown” and that it was possible to distinguish ethnicity, cultural identity and citizenship. “Is there such a thing as the English ethnicity? Yes. Not always easy to define,” he said. “That is different from national identity. That is whether or not you ascribe to, you assimilate to, our heritage, our culture, our norms, our manners. And that is also different to whether or not you have a British passport in your bedroom drawer.” He said he was most concerned about people who had a British passport but “do not love our country”. Jenrick went on to defend his comments about the “Islamification” of the UK, which have now been reported to the police and the Prevent counter-radicalisation programme. He did not address the police reports, but he doubled down by saying there had been an increase in the use of sharia law, and in instances of young girls being forced to cover their faces, and churches being turned into mosques, which he said would not happen under a Reform government.

title: Tory tax break for banks has cost UK public purse £6bn, says TUC
summary: Exclusive: Chancellor urged to reverse Jeremy Hunt’s tax surcharge cuts to claw back billions in lost revenue
text: Tax cuts for big banks have deprived the UK government of £6bn in revenues, according to campaigners, who are calling on the chancellor, John Healey, to increase taxes and force lenders to pay their “fair share” in the budget. Calculations by the Trades Union Congress (TUC), which represents unions with more than 5.3 million members across England and Wales, shows that the public purse is billions of pounds worse off as a result of tax cuts introduced under the Tory chancellor Jeremy Hunt in 2023. The then government agreed to slash the bank surcharge – an additional levy on lenders’ profits – from 8% to 3% that year. The move was meant to offset a rise in corporation tax from 19% to 25%, after the industry argued higher taxes would put them at a competitive disadvantage compared with other big financial centres such as New York. However, the cuts came just as lenders started reaping handsome earnings, thanks to rising interest rates. The UK’s four largest lenders – HSBC, NatWest, Barclays, Lloyds Banking Group – have now generated £200bn in pre-tax profits over the past five years. The TUC says the 2023 cuts ultimately robbed the UK purse of tax revenues. Its analysis of HMRC corporate tax receipts shows the UK public lost out £2.3bn in 2023-24, a further £1.7bn in 2024-25, and £2bn in 2025-26 – totalling £6bn over three years. With banks pocketing record profits, the TUC said the surcharge should now be increased beyond its pre-2023 level at the 28 October budget. That could raise up to £60bn, which could be used to cover rising household bills as part of prime minister Andy Burnham’s drive to tackle the cost of living. “The Tories’ tax break for banks has cost the UK public purse £6bn and counting. It’s time to end it and to make sure banks pay their fair share,” the TUC’s general secretary, Paul Nowak, said. “At a time when families are struggling with soaring energy costs, taxing banks’ booming profits to cut bills is just plain common sense. There is a mountain of evidence to suggest that banks can afford to pay more tax – not least the record £25bn bonus pool they paid out last year. “This month’s budget is an opportunity to put things right.” Bank bosses have been lobbying intensively against bank tax rises, after narrowly escaping higher levies during last year’s budget. Jamie Dimon, chief executive of the largest US bank, JP Morgan, warned Burnham and Healey against further levies during a meeting last month, saying it could put investment and jobs at risk. Earlier this year, Dimon warned that he could scrap plans for a new £3bn London headquarters if the UK government became hostile to banks. The TUC has said raising the surcharge to 16% – double the rate prior to Conservative cuts – could raise £24bn in tax revenues over the next four years. Meanwhile, a 35% bank surcharge, which would match the windfall tax rate that Conservatives imposed on energy companies, would deliver £60bn over four years. Even reversing the surcharge cuts and setting it at 8% would raise £9bn over that same period, the union body said. “Reversing the last government’s tax cuts is the very least this government can do to claw back some of the lost billions it’s handed to banks in recent years,” said a spokesperson for campaign group Positive Money, which has also been pushing for bank tax rises at the budget. “Banks are making record profits without lifting a finger, thanks to the higher rates being paid to them, by both customers and the Bank of England.” David Postings, the chief executive of banking lobby group UK Finance said that a strong banking sector was essential for a strong UK economy and that profitable lenders would be able to invest in better services for customers, issue more loans, and deliver “returns” – such as shareholder dividends – that supported people’s savings and pensions. “Banks also make a major contribution to the public finances and already face a materially higher total tax rate in the UK than in other leading financial centres,” he said. “Further tax increases would weaken the UK’s competitiveness, discourage investment and job creation, and work against the government’s ambition to deliver growth in every postcode.” The Treasury was contacted for comment.

title: Chair of Jewish Greens calls for Zack Polanski to resign after byelection loss
summary: Vivien Lichtenstein urges party leader to quit over ‘Zionism is racism’ policy – but could face no-confidence motion herself
text: The chair of the Jewish Greens has called for Zack Polanski to step down as pressure increases on the Green leader to acknowledge anger within the party over a new policy that equates Zionism with racism and calls for the state of Israel to be abolished. The comments by Vivien Lichtenstein come after Caroline Lucas, the Greens’ former leader and first MP, criticised Polanski for a lack of leadership in missing the debate and vote at the weekend that resulted in the policy being passed. However, another member of Jewish Greens said Lichtenstein’s comments did not reflect the majority view in the group, and that a vote of no confidence in her had been tabled. Lichtenstein had said she was considering quitting the Green party of England and Wales following the vote at the party conference to adopt the policy, which states that Zionism is racism and calls for Israel to be replaced by a single Palestinian state. Polanski was not at the conference on Sunday when the motion was debated; instead he was campaigning in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, in which he finished second to Labour. In interviews after the byelection loss, Polanski, who is Jewish, said he would have voted against the motion had he attended. Two amendments he supported, both saying any future structure of a Palestinian state should be decided by Palestinians rather than a one-state system being imposed, were voted down. Lichtenstein, speaking to Times Radio, said that even though Polanski was campaigning, he should have spoken and voted for the amendments online, which was an option. “He should have done that. And I think that was a big mistake on his part.” She said she was surprised to hear Polanski say he had been working with Jewish members of the party, adding: “I don’t know which Jewish members of the party he’s been working with. It certainly hasn’t been with the Jewish Greens committee.” Asked if Polanski should continue in his role, she replied: “No, I think he should resign.” However, Annie Gottfried Cohen, who is communications officer of the Jewish Greens, said she and some other officers in the group disputed Lichtenstein’s claim that Polanski had not worked with Jewish members, saying he “held a long meeting with the Jewish Greens committee on this motion back in August”. She said: “Vivien’s views do not represent all or even the majority of Jewish Greens, many of whom have been campaigning for Zack all week, and some of whom, myself included, are furious that she has made this call in her capacity as chair of Jewish Greens. A motion of no confidence in the chair is being tabled as a result, asking her to step down.” A number of group members supported the motion and others were critical of only some parts of it, she said. But Lucas, who remains one of the Greens’ best-known and popular figures, said on Thursday that Polanski “should have been there and he should have voted”. Speaking to Newsnight, before the byelection result, she said: “I would have hoped that he would have really been a very strong critic of this motion, because the motion was flawed from top to bottom in my view. It’s dangerous, it’s divisive, it tries to have a singular definition of Zionism when we know that there are many.” Asked if Polanski should stand down, Lucas did not definitively say he should remain as leader: “I think let’s just see what happens in the … coming days and weeks. “Obviously he has been completely taken up with this byelection. I want him to speak now about what’s happened. I want him to show the leadership that was frankly missing on Sunday. I think the jury is out about whether or not he will do that, but I very much hope he will.” Jonathan Bartley, who was formerly the Green co-leader with Lucas and is now a councillor in Lambeth, south London, called on Polanski to “put his hands up” and apologise. “I think [the policy vote] was a failure of leadership from Zack and there is a certain toxicity now from the Green party,” he told the BBC. There is no formal mechanism for ejecting a leader of the Greens. However, they are re-elected every two years, meaning Polanski, who took over in September 2025, will have to go before party members again in less than a year. • This article was amended on 9 October 2026. An earlier version said one of Zack Polanski’s proposed amendments to the Green party motion was to call for a two-state solution rather than a single Palestinian state; in fact, the amendment was for the decision of Palestinian statehood to be decided by Palestinians. Also, Vivien Lichtenstein is the chair, not “leader”, of the Jewish Greens.

title: Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor faced £1.8m repair bill after leaving Royal Lodge
summary: Ex-prince was granted £302,000 in compensation for early end of lease and king has reportedly contributed to costs
text: Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor faced a £1.8m bill to cover repair and restoration of his former Royal Lodge home in Windsor after the lease was officially surrendered. But the former prince was granted £302,000 in compensation for giving up the lease early on the 98-acre property, meaning his total costs came to £1.5m. Recouping costs for dilapidations is a standard process when exiting a lease, and the Guardian understands the repairs covered the entire estate, which includes several properties, gardens and large outbuildings. Andrew was entitled to compensation because, as per the terms of his lease, he surrendered it within the first 25 years. The Times reported that King Charles had contributed to the repair costs. The crown estate spokesperson said: “The lease for Royal Lodge has ended and our focus now is firmly on its future use and the opportunities to generate additional financial value for the nation from its early return.” The former Duke of York moved out of the Windsor mansion this year as the US Department of Justice released files related to the child sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. He was forced to move into Marsh Farm on the king’s Sandringham estate in Norfolk amid public outcry about the rent he paid on the Royal Lodge. In June, a National Audit Office investigation revealed that the late queen’s second son received an unknown amount of private income from subletting three cottages on the Royal Lodge estate while paying a peppercorn rent – a small, symbolic payment – for more than two decades. The crown estate spokesperson said the property would now be marketed by two nationally recognised agents for its proposed future use. On Thursday, Mountbatten-Windsor won a legal challenge against Thames Valley police over search warrants used to raid his home. The former prince brought a judicial review of the legality of the force’s actions and those of the central criminal court, which granted the warrants. Mr Justice Hilliard, sitting at the high court in central London, said Thames Valley police (TVP) had conceded that it obtained the search powers under the wrong statutory provision and ruled that the warrants were unlawful. The episode is embarrassing for TVP but police believe it will not affect the success of the investigation. The arrest followed information that emerged from the Epstein files. It was alleged that when Mountbatten-Windsor was the UK’s trade envoy he shared sensitive information with Epstein. Police began searching the former duke’s residence on the Sandringham estate and the Royal Lodge on the same day as his arrest. Documentary material and electronic devices were seized. Late last year, King Charles stripped his brother of his right to be a prince and of his dukedom over his association with Epstein. Mountbatten-Windsor receives an annual stipend, the amount of which has not been disclosed, from King Charles’s private funds, but a palace source told reporters it had been made clear this should not be used to fund the judicial review.

title: Targeting Trump: how Democrats plan to investigate the president if they win Congress
summary: Control of Congress after the 2026 midterm elections would give Democrats power to subpoena documents and testimony
text: In August, Jamie Raskin renewed his demand that Jared Kushner hand over documents about the overlap between his informal role advising Donald Trump on foreign policy and the private equity firm he runs after an earlier request was ignored. Five of the 11 companies that Elizabeth Warren, Chuck Schumer and Ron Wyden wrote to about Donald Trump’s IRS settlement – including the Trump Organization and World Liberty Financial – never answered at all. Of course, none of them had to. That all changes if Democrats win the House and Senate in November. Control of the chamber would not only give Democrats the gavels, but they would be handed bigger staffs and the power to subpoena documents and testimony – and they have been unusually candid about how they plan to use it. Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the House oversight committee, has ranked his priorities in September: the Trump family’s businesses, the Epstein files, immigration enforcement, corporate profiteering and Robert F Kennedy Jr’s handling of vaccines. Raskin, the top Democrat on the House judiciary committee and its likely chair, calls the potential scope of the work “gargantuan”. Hakeem Jeffries, the House minority leader, has promised to “hold the crooks accountable”. Here are eight of the most consequential investigations, what Democrats have already demanded, and where they could hit a wall. The family business Garcia ranks Trump family corruption first on his list for the oversight committee, while Raskin has requested information on the business dealings of Kushner and Trump Jr. On 25 August, Raskin wrote to Kushner, renewing a demand for documents on his dual roles as an informal foreign policy adviser to Trump and the head of a private equity firm that does business with foreign governments. He has been chasing Kushner’s firm, Affinity Partners, since 2023, when he said it took $2bn from Saudi Arabia’s sovereign wealth fund after Kushner left the White House. There is also the $400m plane that Qatar gifted Trump, a Trump Jr wedding party that was partly funded by a Russian oligarch, and several multimillion-dollar defense contracts won by the extended Trump family that will draw more scrutiny. The IRS settlement In May, the Department of Justice settled the president’s $10bn lawsuit against the IRS with an order barring the agency from auditing past returns of Trump, his family and related companies. Richard Neal, the top Democrat on the House ways and means committee, and Raskin demanded documents on the negotiations, the roles of the justice department and treasury officials, and safeguards against fraud, with a 27 May deadline ahead of the appearance of the treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, before Neal’s committee. In the Senate, Ron Wyden, the top Democrat on the finance committee, and 12 other finance Democrats on 22 May called for a bipartisan investigation into the settlement and the administration’s decision to bar the IRS from auditing Trump, his family and businesses. At a hearing, Wyden pressed Bessent on whether the audit immunity remained in effect, which he declined to answer. On 7 July, Wyden, Warren and Schumer wrote to 11 companies, including Kalshi and Polymarket, asking whether they intend to rely on the settlement as protection against audits, given Trump Jr’s financial ties with the companies. Raskin and Garcia, meanwhile, demanded correspondence between Trump’s lawyers and the justice department over his reported $230m claim for past investigations. A federal judge has said the order conflicts with federal law, according to Warren’s office, and the legal fight is unresolved. Crypto and betting markets Richard Blumenthal, the top Democrat on the Senate’s permanent subcommittee on investigations, opened a preliminary inquiry and wrote to executives behind the $Trump memecoin and World Liberty Financial, asking about ownership and investment structure. Warren, the top Democrat on the Senate banking committee, asked the Office of Government Ethics to review a reported deal involving World Liberty, Binance and a UAE state-backed fund. Warren, Blumenthal, Gary Peters, Dick Durbin and Wyden demanded hearings after disclosures showed Trump earned more than $1.2bn from crypto ventures, including about $588m tied to World Liberty token sales. In the House, Maxine Waters, the top Democrat on the financial services committee, has called for legislation to “end the President’s crypto profiteering and recoup his ill-gotten gains”. On prediction markets, the July letter to Kalshi’s chief executive noted that Trump Jr was a “strategic advisor” to the company, and seven House Democrats asked the oversight chair, James Comer, to subpoena the markets over suspicious trades tied to the Iran war. This one has the most bipartisan appeal: the Republican senator John Curtis asked the Senate judiciary committee to subpoena Trump Jr over his Kalshi and Polymarket ties, and Comer opened his own insider-trading investigation. Epstein and the emails Thanks to a tag-team effort by representatives Ro Khanna and Thomas Massie, the Department of Justice was forced to release millions of files related to Jeffrey Epstein last year. But off the bat, the justice department blew the legally mandated deadline to disclose the files. Then it released only about 3.5m pages of the 6m in its possession; it said it has deemed the rest duplicates. And there has been bipartisan consternation about heavy redactions in some places, and the apparently accidental disclosure of the names of victims in other places. The justice department is now facing a lawsuit from journalist Katie Phang over many of these issues. Even under a Republican-controlled Congress, the oversight committee under its GOP chair, James Comer, has been a rare spot of bipartisan comity, with members of both sides routinely (but not always) acting in concert to subpoena witnesses and hold them in contempt when they don’t cooperate. Expect that to continue in any new Democratic Congress. The Pentagon and the wars Jason Crow, a Colorado congressman who sits on the armed services and intelligence committees and co-chairs the House end corruption caucus, says he will start with the Pentagon, citing reports of defense money steered toward companies linked to the Trump family. The sharpest look so far is a January letter from Warren, Blumenthal and Andy Kim. It lists companies backed by 1789 Capital, the venture firm Trump Jr joined as a partner: Cerberus ($45m), PsiQuantum ($10.8m), Firehawk Aerospace ($4.9m) and Vulcan Elements ($10m, plus a reported $620m loan). It also cites a $12.8m contract to Unusual Machines, a drone company in which Trump Jr holds a stake. The senators asked whether the Vulcan loan was competitive, which officials Trump Jr screened for Pentagon jobs, and for every contact between defense department officials and Trump Jr since 5 November 2024. A later Pentagon reply, they wrote, showed no safeguards against such conflicts. Vulcan and the Pentagon have denied Trump Jr had any involvement in the loan. On the war, Gregory Meeks, the top Democrat on the House foreign affairs committee, led his colleagues in demanding that Marco Rubio, Pete Hegseth, Steve Witkoff and Kushner testify on the Iran war, and forced a vote to subpoena them. He also demanded documents on Venezuelan oil revenue routed into a Qatar account. In 2025, Jack Reed, the top Democrat on the Senate armed services committee, pressed for an expanded inspector general investigation of the defense secretary’s use of Signal. He and Adam Smith, the top Democrat on the House armed services committee, objected to a Hegseth memo routing Pentagon communications with Congress through his office. Immigration enforcement and who profits In March, Raskin and Warren led 52 lawmakers in writing to six companies tied to ICE’s warehouse detention plan: CoreCivic, Geo Group, GardaWorld Federal, Gosin Group, KVG LLC and PNK Group. They asked for expected profit margins, lobbying efforts and donations to Trump’s campaign or cabinet officials, by 13 April. The plan carries a $38.3bn price tag and aims to hold nearly 100,000 people by November. The lawmakers flagged ICE paying $129m for a Georgia facility, nearly five times its assessed value, and a contracting official who came from Geo. Garcia’s oversight Democrats wrote separately to Geo about Corey Lewandowski’s dealings, after reports he sought personal payments from contractors. Peters, the retiring top Democrat on the Senate homeland security committee, led a letter seeking every DHS contract that the border czar, Tom Homan, may have influenced, after reports of a bribery investigation. Bennie Thompson, the top Democrat on the House homeland security committee, would take the matter up there. Warren’s Wall Street If Democrats flip the Senate, now-ranking member Elizabeth Warren would be positioned to chair the banking committee, and private credit is her likeliest target. On 13 May, she wrote to Bessent and the SEC chair, Paul Atkins, on how deregulation has increased private credit risks, with responses due by 26 May. In July 2025 she asked Bessent to run a stress test of the market, which he did not do. She has also written to ratings agencies including S&P, Moody’s and Fitch over reportedly inflated private credit ratings. When Blue Owl restricted withdrawals from a fund, she called for higher bank capital requirements for private credit exposures, transparent data from the firms and a stress test. The wildcard Impeachment hangs over all of it. Trump was impeached twice in his first term and acquitted both times. Jeffries says Democrats have ruled nothing in and nothing out, while the Republican House majority leader, Steve Scalise, predicts an attempt on “Day 1”. Even if Jeffries does not ultimately pursue impeachment, Trump could force his hand. Nancy Pelosi held off leftwing calls for impeachment for months after she became speaker of the House after the 2018 midterms, but when Trump tried to get Ukrainian leaders to pursue an investigation of Joe Biden – and then incited the January 6 attack on the Capitol – Pelosi relented and oversaw two different impeachments.

title: ‘This is not an anti-tech town’: backlash to datacenter in city once home to IBM
summary: Fight in East Fishkill, New York, part of a growing divide over whether AI benefits outweigh enormous downsides
text: For decades, East Fishkill helped build New York’s tech industry. The hamlet, located 70 miles north of New York City, was home to a 460-acre campus where IBM researched and manufactured semiconductor chips for nearly 50 years. So when the news broke in early 2026 that a real estate developer, Treetop Companies, was exploring plans for what could become one of the largest artificial intelligence (AI) datacenters in the country, a roughly 1-gigawatt campus spanning more than 1m sq ft across about 143 acres, it seemed the town would welcome a new phase in its technological evolution. Instead, a furious backlash erupted before even a single permit application was filed with the municipal government. Residents began attending town board meetings, organizing rallies and advocating for a temporary ban. Even before any plans for the facility were drawn up, East Fishkill’s existing zoning laws did not allow for the construction of large datacenters. The town issued a three-year moratorium on them anyway, a sign of the extreme ire against datacenters. The temporary ban, adopted unanimously in late June, forbids the town from considering new datacenters larger than 20 megawatts until July of 2029, while officials study their potential impacts on water resources and local ecosystems. The development company at the center of the controversy has appealed the measure. “I just think that we’re at this moment where things are happening very quickly, we need to get our ducks in a row and think about the various ways in which datacenters and new energy usage will affect our long-term community cohesiveness, environmental quality, and character,” said East Fishkill resident and professor Tanya Radford. The fight unfolding in East Fishkill is a single piece of a growing divide. Both rural towns and communities that once eagerly welcomed hi-tech development are increasingly questioning whether AI infrastructure adds enough local benefit to justify its enormous appetite for electricity, water and land. “This is not an anti-tech town,” said Radford. “I’m an educator. I use technology.” The proposal The saga began after Treetop Development purchased property in East Fishkill, initially pursuing approvals for a warehouse development. Residents later discovered that the company, through local property owner Donovan Drive Holdings, had entered the queue to have a project approved that would use approximately 1,000 megawatts of electrical service, an amount more consistent with a large-scale AI datacenter than a warehouse. This request for approval was not submitted to the town of East Fishkill. Rather, it was submitted to New York Independent System Operator (NYISO)’s interconnection queue. NYISO is an independent organization responsible for managing New York’s high-voltage power grid, meaning whenever a company wants to build a big new project, it must formally ask NYISO for permission to connect to the grid. For those that call East Fishkill home, the NYISO filing quickly raised concerns. The proposed datacenter would consume more electricity than the entire city of Buffalo, which has about 275,000 people. East Fishkill is home to just 30,000. “Residents have been speaking out against it to stop any application from coming into the town for the datacenter,” said Melissa Hoffmann, an East Fishkill resident and organizer with a local chapter of Food & Water Watch, an environmental advocacy non-profit. But because no formal application had been filed with East Fishkill, town officials repeatedly stressed that there was nothing before the planning board to review or reject. “There is no application before the Town. There has never been an application for a datacenter,” the East Fishkill supervisor Nick D’Alessandro wrote on Facebook in June. D’Alessandro later took down the post. His office did not respond to the Guardian’s request for comment. He stressed that standalone datacenters were “not even listed as a permissible use” under the town’s zoning laws. Nonetheless, in June the board banned their construction for three years “to give our community certainty and allow time for further study and discussion”. Hoffmann said months of public pressure ultimately convinced the town board to extend what had initially been discussed as a seven-month pause into a three-year moratorium. Tech town East Fishkill has often been described as an “innovation hub”, making opposition to the datacenter proposal remarkable precisely because the town has not been hostile towards new technology. International Business Machines Corporation, better known as IBM, transformed the town during the latter half of the 20th century into one of the nation’s leading semiconductor manufacturing centers, employing thousands of workers and laying the foundation for what is now iPark 84, home to mixed-use commercial and residential facilities. Former IBM facilities remain a defining part of the local economy, and iPark continues to house technology companies. One tenant is currently seeking to expand an existing datacenter by approximately 150 megawatts, far smaller than the facility proposed by Treetop. Residents have insisted that their opposition is not meant to hinder forward-looking tech, but is directed at the unprecedented scale of emerging AI infrastructure. “The pushback is really to the size,” resident Fran Caracappa, a candidate for county legislature, said. “The Treetop center would be 1,000 megawatts. People do not want to pay higher electricity rates because of a larger datacenter coming in and putting pressure on the grid.” Residents have also questioned whether the supposed economic benefits justify the costs. Hoffmann worried that the datacenter would “provide very few jobs”. Caracappa similarly expressed doubt that temporary construction jobs would lead to lasting employment for locals. “It’s not going to provide work to keep people here like the previous tech businesses did,” Caracappa said. “So what’s the benefit to the town?” Cozy hamlet rejects development The town’s skepticism toward a huge industrial project is also informed by the consequences of its past. IBM’s manufacturing operations helped establish the region’s tech-industrial identity, but groundwater contamination associated with semiconductor production left lasting scars. Several polluted Superfund sites remain in the area. In addition to groundwater protection, residents have raised concerns about noise, diesel backup generators, property values, wetlands and the area’s rural character. Radford, whose home sits near the Appalachian trail, said that the serene, woodsy landscape that currently surrounds the proposed site is one of the reasons she moved there. “My neighbors and I agree that additional development in the area could only negatively impact the quality of life here,” she said. Barely two weeks after the East Fishkill moratorium passed, New York became the first US state to enact a moratorium on new datacenters when Governor Kathy Hochul signed an executive order mandating a one-year statewide pause on so-called hyperscale datacenters. Donald Trump, an ally to tech billionaires and AI investors, responded with rage. He called the move “a terrible decision” on his Truth Social platform and accused Hochul of implementing the ban for purely political reasons. “One of the biggest Driving Forces in the Future for Jobs, are Data Centers. They are big, strong, bold, and Money Machines for the State in which they are built,” Trump wrote. Later in the summer, he called towns rejecting datacenters “backwards and poor”. Datacenter developer appeals Like Trump, Treetop did not take kindly to East Fishkill’s three-year ban. In a 17-page objection letter submitted to the town board and reviewed by the Guardian, attorneys for the company argued the three-year moratorium unlawfully targets the company’s property and effectively amounts to a permanent prohibition rather than a “legitimate temporary planning measure”. In the letter, the company said it spent years and significant resources advancing development plans for the site, including environmental reviews, wetlands investigations, traffic studies and utility coordination. Town officials have maintained that no datacenter application has ever been submitted and that the moratorium provides time to evaluate whether existing zoning properly addresses an entirely new class of industrial development. East Fishkill residents are claiming victory. “People are winning,” Hoffmann said. “Communities that fight these datacenters are winning.”

title: Cop31 host urges wealthy countries to spend ‘much more’ on climate than defence
summary: ‘The climate issue is the security issue,’ says Turkish minister at Pacific pre-Cop summit in Fiji
text: Wealthy countries should spend far more on dealing with the climate crisis than the 5% of GDP promised by Nato members for defence because “the climate issue is the security issue”, the host of the next UN summit has said. But, in comments that are likely to prove contentious, the Cop31 president-designate, Murat Kurum, hedged on whether countries should try to repeat a previous agreement to “transition away from fossil fuels” – the primary cause of the climate crisis – when they meet in Turkey next month. Kurum, the Turkish climate change minister, told the Guardian the world was “already in a transition” and suggested fossil fuel use could be addressed indirectly through other steps. Kurum was among national leaders and ministers, officials and civil society members in Fiji this week to prepare for Cop31, which will take place in the Turkish city of Antalya in November. Australia, which has the new role of “president of negotiations” at Cop31, had pushed to hold the pre-Cop meeting in the Pacific to bring attention to island nations. Geopolitical turmoil from war, a historic energy crisis and an unpredictable and climate-denying US administration – combined with the knowledge that many would be attending the main climate summit in a few weeks – meant only 13 national leaders joined Australia’s prime minister, Anthony Albanese, in the Fijian city of Nadi, and most were from the Pacific. But there were also about 30 ministers, including from India and European nations, representatives from the big emitters China and Saudi Arabia, the heads of global agencies and about 4,000 other attenders. On Tuesday, a delegation flew north to see Tuvalu, a low-lying atoll country of about 10,000 people that is among the most at risk from the climate crisis. They were shown a 20-hectare (49-acre) land reclamation project and heard stories of life in a country that is mostly only about 2 metres above sea level, and where rising waters, storm surges and intensifying extreme weather pose an accelerating threat to survival. In a powerful speech, Melelusi Sokotia, 13, told the visitors her friends’ dreams to be “teachers, doctors, builders” were being subsumed by the question of whether they could “grow safely here in Tuvalu”. Back in Nadi, Fiji’s climate minister, Lynda Tabuya, was moved to tears and received a standing ovation during her closing address. She urged delegates to “remember the people you met” and “carry something of the Pacific with you”. Tabuya said: “This pre-Cop draws to a close tonight. Our responsibility does not.” The governments of about 190 countries will head to Antalya with clear evidence that responsibility is not being met. A recent report by the UN environment programme warned that under the most optimistic future, global heating would reach at least 1.8C, well beyond the 1.5C ceiling of the Paris climate agreement. It called for immediate and sustained emissions cuts and said every fraction of a degree of heating avoided would save lives and reduce economic losses. Throughout the pre-Cop, Pacific leaders repeated their demands: that countries must act to “keep 1.5C alive”, that climate finance must be easily accessible for poor and vulnerable communities who have not caused the problem but are most at risk, and that the health of oceans must be prioritised. Australia’s climate change minister, Chris Bowen, said only 0.2% of global climate finance was spent helping small island developing countries adapt, and that the countries that needed it the most, such as Tuvalu, “get it the least”. “That has got to change,” he said. “It’s a key priority of Cop31.” Kurum said Nato countries should be much more focused on climate spending. He said they had promised to increase their defence budgets to 5% of GDP by 2035 as a result of “concerns for their own safety and security”, but had committed much less to addressing the climate crisis despite expressing concerns and it posing an even greater risk. Asked if he thought as much should be spent on climate as defence, he said: “Much more.” “The climate issue is the security issue itself,” Kurum told the Guardian through an interpreter. “If you don’t spend one unit of money prior to the disasters, then you are left in a position where you have to spend 10 units of money after the disaster. It’s cheaper pre-disaster.” Kurum and Bowen reiterated they would focus in Antalya on winning support for a global goal of 35% of the energy needed to run homes, businesses, factories and vehicles coming from electricity by 2035. Now it is about 21%. But the question of what direct action the global community should agree to take to phase out fossil fuels remains far more vexed. Both host countries backed a multi-country statement in Fiji that supported a global “transition away from fossil fuels”, echoing language adopted by the global community at Cop28 in Dubai three years ago. But both faced criticism, and accusations of hypocrisy, for continuing to back new coal and gas developments and being largely silent before the pre-Cop on the need to phase out fossil fuels. Bowen said the way to stop using fossil fuels was not to cut supply of the dirty fuel but to build enough renewable energy so there would be no need for fossil fuel power plants. Kurum said the world was “already in a transition” and suggested the focus at climate talks on wording about transitioning away from fossil fuels might not be productive as he did not think further progress could be made. Delegates from some countries, including Saudi Arabia, Russia and other oil-producing states, strongly opposed naming fossil fuels at Cop30 in Brazil. Dozens of countries frustrated with what they see as a UN stalemate on the issue met separately in Colombia this year to discuss a path away from fossil fuels. They are due to meet again next July in Tuvalu, and want the issue to be in an agreement in Antalya. Tzeporah Berman, the chair of the Fossil Fuel Non-Proliferation Treaty Initiative, said Pacific leaders had been clear in Nadi that there should be an urgent fossil fuel phaseout. “This means no new projects,” she said. “You can’t phase something out by building more of it.”

title: Trump immigrant purge could cut social security for Americans by $2,000 a year
summary: New report on economic cost of anti-immigration campaign projects 8.6% reduction in retirement payments by 2034
text: Elderly Americans can expect to lose an average of $2,152 in annual social security benefits each, a projected 8.6% reduction in their retirement payments, by 2034 and every year after as a direct consequence of the economic fallout from the Trump administration’s anti-immigration campaign, if that carries on, according to a new report shared exclusively with the Guardian. Already, US food prices are up, housing permits to build new homes are down – and even native-born Americans are losing out on potential jobs after the sudden exodus of 1.2 million foreign-born workers over the last two years as a result of Donald Trump’s policies, the report finds. “When the Trump administration says things, it’s not always data-driven. And we wanted to see what the data shows, and what other people have found the data shows,” said Michael Ettlinger, one of the report’s authors. “Turns out that refutes what the US president primarily is asserting.” The blowback on the economy from Donald Trump’s crackdown is wide-ranging, even as the federal government’s aggressive mass deportation campaign quietly ramps up further. “We are just beginning to see the harms in terms of what is happening here domestically. But the impacts of these policies, of these efforts, are going to be long-lasting. And I think that is by design,” Vanessa Cárdenas, executive director of the pro-immigration reform organization America’s Voice, told the Guardian. The report, Economic Impacts of Trump Administration Immigration Policy, was commissioned by America’s Voice and conducted by researchers at Economic Insights and Research Consulting, a firm focused on economic analysis. Its conclusions underscore how recent federal policies revoking immigrants’ legal protections or targeting them for enforcement have had dire effects on the nation’s affordability crisis and job market, especially in regions and industries that rely disproportionately on foreign-born workers. In the US agricultural sector, where 42% of crop workers are undocumented and 68% are foreign-born, farmers across the country are warning that the vast majority or in some cases all of their workforce has disappeared overnight, leaving produce to fall to, or rot in, the ground and go to waste. Food products heavily reliant on immigrant labor have experienced much sharper price increases than food overall since Trump retook the White House, according to the report. Examples of immigrant-reliant food price increases that have exceeded the average increase in grocery prices over the last 19 months, compared with the 19 months before Trump returned to office in January 2025, are: fresh whole milk up by 5.7%, canned vegetables up by 6.3%, and apples up by 7.2%, the report found. In that period before Trump’s inauguration, the vast majority of foods that principally depend on immigrant labor for production saw prices rise more slowly compared with other foods and some prices even fell outright, according to the report. “One thing that changed was the [immigration] policy. Before, the trend for all those goods was a lower inflation rate. And afterward, the trend was higher inflation. So the trend was reversed, and that was quite striking,” said Robert Lynch, one of the report’s authors. The construction industry, where foreign-born workers fill almost a third of all occupations, has also been severely affected. States more dependent on immigrant labor have seen costs for new single-family homes soar 10.9% in 2026, compared with the first eight months of 2024, bringing building projects’ monetary value from an average of $305,752 to $338,752. And the issuance of housing permits to build single-family homes has dropped 10.6% nationwide since January 2025, with higher declines in regions more reliant on foreign-born workers, the research found. Meanwhile, native-born Americans are missing out on potential income in hard-hit states like California, Nevada, New Jersey, Florida and New York, where construction employment is on the decline – because when there are no immigrant roofers to build a home, American electricians and plumbers lose that project, too. “It’s not like someone can go work in construction and just not have any skills. And we’re losing people who have been here for decades working in construction. That could be fixed, but it’s going to take time,” Ettlinger said. Other industries with soaring costs and severe labor shortages include healthcare, including home health care, nursing homes, adult daycare, lawn care, landscaping and groundskeeping, where immigrants have historically comprised a disproportionate share of the workforce and expertise. By September 2025, less than nine months into the second Trump administration, native-born workers had already lost an estimated 51,000 to 297,000 jobs because of changes to US immigration policy, the report said. The labor force shrunk by an estimated 919,000 people during the 18 months of Trump’s second term, while job growth has slowed to roughly a third of the rate it was before he retook office. The federal government risks losing a large segment of the $26bn in payroll taxes from unauthorized immigrants who help to support the US social security fund that pays out to American seniors – while not being able to access those benefits themselves. Now, social security trustees, including the treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, health and human services secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr, labor secretary, Keith Sonderling, and social security commissioner, Frank Bisignano, are warning that lower net immigration than expected is threatening worse finances for the flailing retirement benefits system, which could mean cuts to Americans’ entitlements. “The share of that annual loss due to the Trump immigration policy would be $2,152 [per person on average]. Thus, the Trump immigration policies, if continued, would reduce projected average annual Social Security benefits by 8.6% in 2034, and every year thereafter,” the report’s authors write. They told the Guardian that if the administration’s immigration agenda continues as expected, the implications for the US economy could get even worse. “We would expect higher prices,” Lynch said. “We would expect more job losses, slower economic growth and the affordability crisis getting worse – partly because prices are higher, partly because people are losing their jobs and their incomes and they can’t afford as much.”

title: Thieves make off with €5m haul from prestigious Italian winery
summary: Gang breaks into cellar of Marchesi Antinori in Cortona and loads two trucks with 30,000 bottles before getaway
text: Thousands of bottles of wine worth €5m (£4.2m) have been stolen from a prestigious winery in Tuscany in what is thought to be the biggest heist of its kind in Italy. A gang of at least seven masked individuals broke into the cellar of Marchesi Antinori, a family-owned winery dating back to the late 1300s, in Cortona after shutting off the alarms and surveillance cameras before using company forklifts to load two large trucks with 30,000 bottles of wine and making off. Among the bottles targeted were those most prized by wine collectors and consumers, including Solaia, Guado al Tasso and Tignanello, notable as one of the first red wines in the Tuscany region to be produced without white grapes. All the stolen bottles, ranging in price between €120 and €400 a bottle, are from the firm’s 2023 vintage. The theft occurred on Saturday as the company, based in the hilltop town of Cortona, prepared for a major shipment to buyers abroad. The robbery was discovered only when staff arrived for work on Monday morning. “The gang was very prepared,” Renzo Cotarella, chief executive of Marchesi Antinori, told Corriere della Sera. “A theft of this scale and value has never happened before in Italy.” He said he had “great confidence” that investigators would trace the stolen wine, which included 3,000 bottles, some of them magnum-sized, of Barolo Ginestra. “Two trucks full of merchandise can’t just disappear into thin air,” he added. “The Tuscan roads are full of cameras. Perhaps with a bit of luck we’ll be able to recover at least some of the bottles.” There have been several thefts at wineries in Italy in recent months, including one in Monforte d’Alba in the northern Piedmont region in mid-September. But Cotarella, who suspects the same gang could have been involved, never imagined a theft of such scale would happen to his company. Unfortunately, its insurance policy does not cover the robbery of wine at such huge value. “We had always considered the possibility of having a few cases of wine being stolen during their transportation, but certainly not that two trucks manage to enter the cellar and make off with such a huge haul,” he told Corriere. Such large wine robberies were usually meticulously prepared and would probably be carried out by those with an intimate knowledge of wine themselves, Corriere suggested, with the target destination possibly collectors, bars or restaurants. However, a sudden increase in the supply of such wines could raise suspicion. As the investigators continue their search, Cotarella said the company, which was established in 1385, has warned customers to be wary of any offers of its wine outside official channels. • This article was amended on 14 October 2026. A September wine theft occurred in the village of Monforte d’Alba, not the larger nearby town of Alba as an earlier version said.

title: Shein outsells British rival Asos as UK revenue hits £2.58bn
summary: Online retailer’s 26% jump sharpens focus on exemption letting cheap parcels into the country duty-free
text: Shein, the online fast-fashion retailer founded in China, increased sales in the UK by just over a quarter last year, overtaking its British rival Asos. The company, whose global parent group listed on the Hong Kong stock exchange valued at just over $26bn (£19.6bn) last month, increased sales at its UK division by 26% to £2.58bn, according to accounts filed at Companies House. Pre-tax profits rose 18% to £45.2m even as the number of people employed by the group in the UK, mostly in sales and marketing, rose to 113 from 91 a year before. The company paid £11.2m in current tax – understood to be mainly corporation tax – up from £9.6m a year before. Shein said sales had been helped by a marketing partnership with the Wireless and Creamfields music festivals, a pop-up shop on London’s Oxford Street and Christmas gift events in Edinburgh, Manchester and Liverpool as well as London. Asos’s sales were £2.47bn in the year to 31 August 2025 – although this figure includes revenues outside the UK, unlike Shein UK’s comparable statistic. Shein’s strong trading figures are likely to increase pressure on the government to bring forward action to change the “de minimis” rule that has underpinned the rise of the fast-growing online specialists Shein and Temu. Fears about China’s retailers and manufacturers dumping goods in the UK have grown since the US last year revoked its own de minimis exception for Chinese-made goods, crimping Shein’s expansion there. The retailer’s model is based on shipping orders of cheap clothes from Chinese factories to homes so that each order is low enough in value to avoid import duties. Under the US exemption, which was scrapped last year, parcels with a value of less than $800 (£600) shipped to individuals had been spared from import tax. The EU is also phasing out its exemption on customs duties for low-value parcels. It began in July by replacing the €150 de minimis relief with a flat €3 customs duty. The former UK chancellor Rachel Reeves said she would get rid of the UK’s rule, which allows overseas sellers to send goods valued at £135 or less direct to British shoppers without paying any customs duty, by 2028. However, major retail bosses have said the government should move sooner. Investors’ concerns about global government regulatory changes meant Shein’s value was far lower when it listed on the stock market than had been expected several years ago. It reached a valuation of $100bn in an April 2022 fundraising round, making it the third most valuable startup in the world, and then considered a £50bn ($66bn) float on the London Stock Exchange in 2024 before eventually launching in Hong Kong. Shein, founded by the entrepreneur Chris Xu, runs most of its operations from China but sells all its goods outside the country. It moved its headquarters to Singapore at the start of 2022 and has recently begun manufacturing in other countries including Turkey and Brazil. After forced labour concerns were raised, Shein said it had tightened its supplier policies, enforced through regular audits, with any child or forced labour violations becoming grounds for immediate termination of contract. Last week, Shein reported a 67% fall in group quarterly profits to £173m in its first results since the float, blaming higher oil prices and freight rates linked to the war in Iran.

title: Digested week: Don’t worry about the plague, go and read some Anne Carson | Emma Brockes
summary: The world may be going to hell in a handcart, but at least now I get to say I know a Nobel prize winner
text: Monday “Anyone worried about pneumonic plague?” This is a friend – a medic – texting me after reading reports at the weekend of the 28-year-old Russian woman who died while working at a “plague research lab” in Siberia. Relying on details from the famously open Russian state guaranteed the presence of a certain dark subtext to the tantalisingly short news item. Namely: lab-grown disease cultivated for reasons unknown and with a 100% mortality rate escapes Russian facility into general population, eight hours’ flying time from London. In other words, we’re all going to die. My first thought was: is this better or worse than the time that guy who’d been exposed to Ebola took the subway to go bowling in Brooklyn? The answer to which of course is that post-Covid, it’s worse: we know exactly how these things go, how they start small, with a news in brief buried 20 pages deep in the paper, moving glacially up the news list every few days until a lonely death in a Siberian laboratory leads, step by incremental step, to the zombie apocalypse. Meanwhile, the word “plague” remains outlandishly unrelaxing, despite the best efforts of the New York Times to contextualise it. Elucidating the various different types of plague that can kill you – pneumonic, septicemic and bubonic – I have to say my money would have been on bubonic as the worst, what with the Black Death and all. Apparently, however, the most virulent form of plague is the one in question, pneumonic, spread by a cough or a sneeze and causing “a severe rapid-onset lung infection” that can kill within a few days. Advice from my medic friend in New York: “Get antibiotics for everyone.” Alternatively, invest in a sense of proportion. Tuesday I did not have “let’s have more firing squads” on my bingo card of talking points this week, but that is the serious discussion under way in the US after the horrific, botched execution of Christa Pike, the convicted murderer on death row who regained consciousness and started talking on Tuesday after the state of Tennessee failed to kill her. This was the second botched execution by the state this year, and one of the apparently 7% of all executions in the US since 1972 that have not been effective, among the most common reasons cited being expired drugs and untrained executioners, but also malfunctioning electric chairs that set fire to their occupants. As a result, the single method of executing a prisoner in the US that has resulted in no failed attempts whatsoever is the firing squad, a phrase that raises images, incomprehensible in a supposedly modern world, of a semicircle of shooters, none bearing sole responsibility, firing in the direction of the condemned’s head. For the first time in the US military since 1945, one such execution is due to happen at Fort Hood, Texas, in December, which this week Pete Hegseth, the US defence secretary, promised to livestream in defiance of anything resembling normal human behaviour. Wednesday There’s likely a joke about the failure of the Tory party to lie down and accept its fate after so many lethal injections, but I can’t quite bring it home. Instead, at party conference this week in Birmingham, we saw a chipper-seeming Kemi Badenoch step out on stage to perform her pantomime version of common sense, smartly referring to the Reform party as “that” – as in “we are not uniting with that”. The Tory leader does an extremely good job of appearing to be a plain-spoken and regular human in contrast with Reform, on the one hand, and what might delicately be called the unusual makeup of the Greens on the other. It’s worth remembering what Badenoch looks like when the mask slips. If Boris Johnson’s real face was the rictus of an underbriefed, overconfident man white-knuckling his way through government while chuckling to himself like a toy in a horror movie, Badenoch strikes me as someone who is stuck on the gimlet-eyed setting of victory at all costs. Meanwhile, footage of Young Conservatives partying at conference never gets old, offering a strong rival for most embarrassing moment to the 30,000-word policy document the Tory leader – hide your face – has self-christened “Kemistry”. Someone tell her you can’t coin your own nicknames. Thursday Anne Carson has won the Nobel prize for literature and, forgive me, but very occasionally when life gives you the opportunity to be insufferable, you can’t not take it. So, in response to this news, I would like to say that when I went hiking with the Nobel prize winner Anne Carson in Iceland last year the thought struck me … There was no thought; I just wanted to get it on the table about the hike – OK, it was a short walk up a rocky incline – it was with the Nobel prize winner Anne Carson, who I have loved forever and have known since we met in Michigan many years ago. She is brilliant and funny and wise, and I could cite so many lines from her poetry but one of my favourites is this, from the poem Lines in her 2005 collection Decreation: “To my mother / love / of my life, I describe what I had for brunch.” I feel the same way about this line that Madonna used to say she felt about Frida Kahlo’s self-portrait, which is that if you don’t feel it vibrate through your system, I can’t ever really be your friend. (I’m aware most people would be fine with that.) Friday Sublime to ridiculous, Carson to Elon Musk, who is the subject of Alex Gibney’s four-hour documentary that launched this week and which I can’t wait to see. Pre-publicity has focused on the contributions to the film of Justine Wilson, Musk’s ex-wife, who along with MacKenzie Scott (formerly Bezos) is part of the tech titans’ first wives club via which one can measure the journey taken by very rich men from marriage to regular women to women with no apparent interior lives. “He was constantly remarking on the ways he found me lacking,” said Wilson, who also told Gibney her ex-husband once said to her: “If you were my employee, I would fire you.” No amount of money in the world, am I right? Digested week in pictures
