title: ‘Amazing piece of technology’: solar ‘traffic controller’ for apartments takes top Australian design award
summary: SolShare, enabling power produced by a shared rooftop solar system to be split among several apartments, also wins for sustainability
text: An unassuming white box that unlocks solar power for apartment dwellers has taken out the top honour at this year’s Australian Good Design awards. Melbourne-based Allume Energy won the 2026 Australian Good Design award of the year for its SolShare system. The product, which works like a “traffic controller for solar” enables power produced by a shared rooftop system to be split among several apartments without multiple installations, individual inverters and messy wiring. It also received the award for sustainability. Dr Brandon Gien, chair of Good Design Australia, said SolShare was not only “an amazing piece of technology” but also a beautifully designed solution to a complex problem. “Millions of people live in apartments, and many have had limited access to the benefits of rooftop solar. SolShare is a clever Australian design innovation that addresses that problem in a practical way, and it is already delivering benefits at significant scale.” Gien said the awards recognise design that is more than skin deep. Products need to be functional as well as aesthetically pleasing (a nice looking kettle is no good if it doesn’t boil water), with innovation and societal impact among the key criteria. First established in 1958, the event has a storied history as one of the world’s oldest design awards. Past top gongs have included the Cochlear hearing implant (2000), Marc Newson’s economy class seats for the Qantas A380 (2009), the Flow Hive beehive design (2016) and James Cameron’s Deepsea Challenger, a submersible designed and built by the Hollywood director and Ron Allum in collaboration with local designers Design+Industry (2012). This year, SolShare received the highest accolade among more than 1,000 entries from Australia and overseas. The awards, presented at a black tie ceremony at ICC Sydney on Friday night, recognised 13 disciplines in fields ranging from products and communication to digital and policy design, spanning more than 30 categories. Icons, a collection of animal-inspired climbable landmarks, was recognised for its product design. The structures – a cross between public art and recreation – designed by Industrial by Nature were a joint winner of the best in discipline for product design, alongside Allume. Some were already in use, like the custom-designed Rakali installed at Wilson Park playground in Perth. A ceremonial gathering space at Melbourne’s City Square received the award for best in discipline for the built environment. The space, designed by Greenshoot Consulting in collaboration with Wurundjeri elders, was created to welcome visitors to Country, sustain cultural knowledge and practices, make Woi-wurrung language visible and acknowledge First Peoples as the traditional custodians of the land. Sydney Children’s hospital’s placemaking and wayfinding project won best in discipline for communication design. Visiting a hospital and navigating the labyrinthine corridors could be a traumatic experience, for children as well as their parents and carers. Gien said the design by Frost*collective understood that “at a very deep and empathetic level”. Instead of neon lights and pale blue walls, the design reimagined what a hospital could be, with signs and artwork incorporating native animals and plants, grouped into three local environments: wetlands, sand dunes and sea cliffs. Bush Cradle by Xavier Earls, a modular habitat system for native animals, was recognised as the best in discipline for next gen designers (under 30s). Earls said he wanted to create a “universal system” that could meet the needs of different species. Bush Cradle’s four interchangeable pieces are able to be assembled into nest boxes or shelters. “One of the major threats to native animals in Australia is the loss of habitat, and this habitat like tree hollows, fallen logs, can’t be naturally replenished in a rate that is functional,” he said. “What I love about it is that it’s designing for a non-human, it’s designing for nature” Gien said. Many of the winners showcased designs supporting reuse, repair and alternatives to single-use plastics. Finnish company FabPatch topped the fashion and textiles discipline for its rub-on fabric repair system, while No Wrap, an Australian designed re-usable system for securing pallets, and Holy Carp, a plastic-free, compostable alternative to soy-sauce fish by Australian studio Heliograf, both won gold awards in different categories. The awards shone a light on good design that could “bring joy to our lives, but not at the expense of the environment”, Gien said. “Design is everywhere around us,” he said. “From the products that we use, the spaces that we work in, the homes that we live in, the services that we use, and the digital apps that consume us.”

title: ‘It could have been any one of us’: Black college students march for Nolan Wells
summary: Recent death of the student in Mississippi is just the latest in a long string of unsettling deaths of young Black people
text: On Wednesday afternoon, hundreds of students gathered on the Jackson State University (JSU) campus for a rally to call for transparency in the mysterious death of young Black people and to encourage student engagement in politics and the fight for voting rights. As the sun began to set, the students, many of whom wore black, marched through the historically Black university’s plaza chanting: “Nolan Wells, Trey Reed, Tasia Fortune, Kohen Wiley, Jaylen Lewis – Black Lives Matter!” All five were young Black Mississippians – the youngest, Wiley, was one-year-old while the eldest, Fortune, was 29 – who either died under suspicious circumstances or were killed by police. The students wound through the campus, with school police and others looking on, continuing their chants until they made it to the Cofo Civil Rights Education Center. The building was significant: it was the organizational home for the Mississippi Freedom Summer of 1964, a largely student-organized movement that aimed to increase Black voter participation during the Jim Crow era, and the statewide headquarters for the Council of Federated Organizations, a coalition of the Mississippi branches of the NAACP, the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee, the Congress for Racial Equality and the Southern Christian Leadership Conference. “This is the first step of advocacy,” Camrynn Wimberly, a JSU student and one of the organizers of the march, said. “This is the first step of collective action and political power. The more this spreads, the more we continuously advocate for the same thing and let them know that we will not stand idly by as rights are stripped from us, as parents grieve, as we wonder whether or not we will be next – that is the first step to something greater.” The students at JSU are part of a larger movement of students at historically Black colleges and universities (HBCUs) who are calling for justice and transparency in the cases of Nolan Wells, an 18-year-old Black student whose disappearance and death have received national scrutiny, and other young Black people who died in mysterious or suspicious circumstances. Also this week, students in the Atlanta University Center Consortium (AUC), which includes Spelman College, Clark Atlanta University (CAU) and Morehouse College, as well as Langston University, Prairie View A&M University and other schools, marched to demand answers about the cause and manner of Wells’s death, which remain undetermined, and other suspicious deaths of young Black people. ‘They look like me’ On 1 October, students in the AUC held a march in solidarity with Nolan Wells and his family. Thousands of students participated. “We’ve seen time and time again the mistreatment of cases involving young Black Americans,” Barhn Gadson, president of CAU’s chapter of the NAACP, said. “There’s not so much of an attention towards it until we do things like having to march and having to riot. We’ve gotten to a point where we are tired of having to fight for young Black males or young Black females or any Black individual for our lives to mean something.” A’Nija Hughley, president of Spelman’s NAACP chapter, said that it was important for all students, but specifically those at HBCUs, to speak up. “As HBCU students, we’re in a unique position where we are allowed to learn how to be critically conscious, and we learn how structures are built to work against us,” she said. “As students who are legacies of those who started the civil rights movement and the Atlanta student movement, it’s kind of our job to speak up and then also show our support for [Wells’] family.” Hughley said that the idea for a solidarity march came from a student in her chapter who wanted to know what they could do for Wells. Though the students are in Atlanta, they said that they marched in solidarity with Wells and other young Black people who have died in suspicious circumstances. “To us, it’s we either speak out or we just shut up,” Gadson said. “Just because we may not be in the same city or the same state doesn’t mean that we can’t speak out on it. And just because there is a ruling here doesn’t mean that we aren’t going to protest, doesn’t mean that we are not going to advocate for our community. I mean, we are the NAACP. This is what we’ve been doing for years.” Hughley said that, instead of a larger protest where they marched to the capitol building or otherwise engaged the larger community, she wanted to keep the march AUC-wide. “We cannot sit and look at injustice and not say anything about it,” she said. “It honestly could have been any one of us. This one hits close because he’s around our age. He looks like us.” Wells’s similarities to the students in age and appearance were also noted by the JSU students who rallied on Wednesday afternoon. As they made their way across the campus, they chanted: “Our lives matter. That could’ve been me. They look like me. Say their names!” Jakari Holland, an organizer of the rally and founder of the Mississippi Access Project, said that the school’s location in central Mississippi made it particularly important for students to speak out. “Multiple people have passed away inside Mississippi under suspicious circumstances,” Holland said. “Jackson State University, being a public institution and bringing in public funding, but also at the centerpiece inside the capital in Mississippi, we have to take a stance. We have to bring awareness and transparency in light of what’s happening. This could be any one of us. We’re young people inside Mississippi, and we’re seeing what’s going on in the backyard of our home. Like the students in Atlanta, Holland was keenly aware of the historical significance, not only of JSU, but of Jackson and Mississippi, in general. “Our HBCUs have a long history of people being advocates and standing against things,” he said. “The Greensboro Four, when they were at North Carolina A&T and sat down in Woolworth’s lunch counter. The Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee. The students at South Carolina State that were shot. The people that our Gibson-Green plaza is named for. It’s crazy to see that people love talking about and celebrating Black history, but when you’re living through it, that’s when the issue comes about because you don’t like people that challenge the societal norms.”

title: ‘People are feeling the real impacts’: influencers are targeting private equity with satire and rage
summary: The trillion-dollar industry has taken over social media, inspiring skits and parody raps with millions of views
text: Johnny Hilbrant Partridge kept getting stuck next to the same kind of finance guy at weddings – the one bragging about his family’s full-time nanny and lavish vacations while name-dropping elite club memberships and private schools. To Partridge, a former fitness instructor, their shameless knack for self-promotion felt ripe for comedy. Using a filter that puts an exaggerated sneer on his face, Partridge donned a puffer vest and created “The PE Guy”, a caricature of the men who work in the private equity industry. “All we did is acquire some youth hockey complexes, implement dynamic pricing and put some people on recurring revenue subscription models,” Partridge scoffed in a video after lawmakers introduced a bill this year to ban private equity from youth sports. “This country used to reward innovation, and suddenly it’s wrong to charge $11,000 for a development lacrosse weekend … give me a break.” Since he first debuted the character last year, “The PE Guy” has racked up millions of views on Instagram and TikTok, becoming the most popular player in a fast-growing ecosystem skewering private equity. The multitrillion-dollar industry has turned into a catch-all online for the ills of modern capitalism, inspiring “a day in the life” skits and parody rap music videos. For many viewers, the draw is the dark humor, something that even the finance guys are embracing. Partridge said he gets invited to speak at insurance and private equity conferences and finance companies’ annual meetings as comic relief. But it’s also been a way many Americans are learning how the industry, which often operates out of view and without the same oversight or regulation as publicly traded corporations, is affecting their lives. Every business has bad actors, Partridge said, but he chose to focus on private equity because it is changing everyday things like healthcare so radically that “people are feeling the real impacts from it”, he said. Private equity has found its way into everything from funeral homes to family dental offices. Once they were acquired by private equity firms, beloved chains such as JoAnn Fabrics and Toys “R” Us faced bankruptcies, and many name brands taken over by the industry have degraded in quality. “When people say private equity, they don’t just mean the exact technical term,” said Hojung Kim, whose August Instagram post on how private equity is changing veterinary care got a million views in just two days. The term has come to represent “leveraged buyouts, hard cost-cutting in order to ruthlessly profit-maximize and saddling the business with debt in order to self-enrich”. Struck by the response, Kim, co-founder of an affordable LSAT prep business, started a series on other industries changed by private equity and built Grass, an app that helps users find independent American businesses. “We hit a nerve. A lot of people were being affected by this rampant rise in costs and wanted to know what was behind it,” Kim said. “As it happens, private equity has changed a lot of industry landscapes.” TikTok and Instagram are awash in pro-business content too, of course, as companies overall have spent $37bn on influencer marketing in 2025, one advertising trade group estimates, and private equity companies are even buying up influencer tools like Uscreen. But the private equity criticism continues to grow. Journalist Pablo Torre and comedian Stavros Halkias have gotten hundreds of thousands of views on a YouTube video railing about Blackstone’s takeover of Jersey Mike’s Subs and financial investors in sports teams. “If they fucking destroy the Lakers, guys with Kobe [Bryant] back tattoos are going to start the proletariat revolution,” Halkias said on Torre’s podcast, going off news that the Los Angeles basketball team was acquired by Bob Iger and Josh Kushner for $12.5bn in August. “The closest we’re getting to class consciousness is fast food and sports teams.” Natalka Burian, owner of Elsa, a bar in Brooklyn, is among the food industry experts who are chronicling private equity’s takeover of restaurants and bakeries. They can pay outrageous rents and snatch up the best locations, she said, which drives out businesses like her own. “That’s money that should be going to local businesses,” Burian said. “I think there’s something about this blandness that takes away from our communities.”

title: Hegseth promises execution live stream as Trump appears to ‘pause’ war on Iran | First Thing
summary: US president says US will not attack Iran before midterms, while defense secretary says Nidal Hasan will face a firing squad next month
text: Good morning. The defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, has said the execution of Nidal Hasan by firing squad will be livestreamed next month, in a radical departure from the previous norm. Hegseth said: “We’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public, because people need to understand there’s serious consequences for these types of things.” Hasan opened fire at a medical processing center at Fort Hood, Texas, on 5 November 2009, killing 13 people and wounding dozens more. A military jury sentenced him to death in 2013 and he has been held at Fort Leavenworth in Kansas ever since. The last known case of a military firing squad in the US was in November 1945. A Reuters/Ipsos survey from late September found that only about a third of Americans approved of the strikes on Iran. The measure is being promoted amid a nationwide push by the Trump administration to restrict voting. California Republicans have long sought to advance a voter ID initiative in the state. Various out-of-state conservative donors have given millions of dollars in support. Why are some voters calling Missouri’s elections ‘dizzying and embarrassing’? CNN, MS Now and Politico were asking the judge to extend the temporary restraining order he issued on 24 September requiring the White House to lift the ban for 14 days. The district court judge Timothy Kelly – a Trump appointee – said he would extend it until next Tuesday. The project, which reportedly stars Danny Trejo and Harvey Keitel, follows an ICE agent’s effort to escape a mob seeking to free an immigrant he has detained, according to its logline. In one video of the shoot that surfaced online, a female actor portraying a protester can be seen driving a beat-up car into a flock of law enforcement agents, knocking one officer down as another fires his weapon. Then, the car abruptly lurches back. That scene drew backlash – and real protesters – over its resemblance to an ICE agent’s fatal shooting of Good in January. title: Isaias strengthens to become first Atlantic hurricane of 2026 season
summary: Storm expected to make landfall on US’s northern Gulf coast with risk of flash floods and isolated river flooding
text: Isaias has become the first Atlantic hurricane of the 2026 season, with wind speeds of 80mph and a minimum pressure of 975mb. It is expected to strengthen to a category 2 hurricane as it approaches the US’s northern Gulf coast on Friday, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA). As a result of the strong El Niño, it has been a notably quiet Atlantic hurricane season. The first hurricane of the season has not formed this late since 8 October 1905, which pre-dates the satellite era (1960s) for tracking hurricanes that has allowed for more non-landfall hurricanes to be discovered. Isaias is expected to make landfall on Friday evening local time, bringing an estimated 75-150mm (2.9-5.9in) of rainfall across the Gulf coast. There may be up to 250mm in places, with a possibility of flash flooding and isolated river flooding. The NOAA also said there was increasing likelihood of life-threatening storm surge along portions of the northern Gulf coast and damaging hurricane-force winds over portions of the Florida panhandle, southern Alabama and Mississippi. A hurricane warning has been issued and people have been told to prepare for long power outages and to obey any evacuation orders issued. In Zimbabwe, a state of disaster was declared in the south-east Masvingo province on Tuesday after a severe hailstorm caused widespread damage to homes and critical infrastructure. Preliminary assessments found the roofs had been torn off 8,500 homes. A further 15,300 people reported shattered windows, leaving many exposed to the elements as the rainy season begins. The country’s power infrastructure was badly affected, disrupting drainage and sewerage systems, raising concerns about public health. In Australia, a rare tornado hit the town of Ulladulla, about 140 miles (230km) south of Sydney, on 3 October. Tornadoes are relatively rare in Australia, where there are about 50 each year. This Ulladulla tornado damaged properties and felled trees.

title: Three Saudis killed in Riyadh airport attack claimed by Houthis
summary: Attack is deadliest in kingdom since it launched major military offensive with allies against Houthis in Yemen
text: Three Saudi citizens have been killed and several other people were wounded in attacks targeting Riyadh ⁠airport for which Yemen’s Houthis claimed responsibility, Saudi officials have said. The attack late on Thursday was the deadliest in Saudi Arabia since the kingdom and allied forces in neighbouring Yemen launched a major military offensive last weekend against the Iran-backed Houthis. It was also a significant escalation in the latest front in the Iran war, which has kept oil prices and markets jumpy. The first attack on Thursday afternoon targeted airport facilities, while the second struck aircraft, the Saudi statement said. It did not identify those responsible, though the Houthis claimed to have targeted the airport with a ballistic missile. Among the dead was Capt Hamoud Ali Alkalthami, the Saudia Group said in a statement. It appeared to be the first confirmed attack on the Saudi national carrier since the new offensive began. A separate Saudia Group statement said one of its aircraft was damaged while it was on the ground, with no passengers onboard. The aviation statement said the injuries to citizens and people of other nationalities “ranged from minor to serious”. The Saudia Group statement said operational activities at the airport returned to normal at 6pm on Thursday, hours after the attack. Meanwhile, the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said it had destroyed three rocket launch platforms used by the rebels to threaten regional security. The Houthis say they are targeting the kingdom over its support for government forces in Yemen’s reignited civil war. Saudi Arabia says it is backing an offensive by Yemen’s UN-recognised government to ‌take back territory from the Houthis. The Houthis have made a lightning advance across Yemen’s coastal plain over the last month, appearing to gain ground in the south-west on Wednesday as the group approached the city of Taiz. Independent observers said earlier this week there was danger the group was on course to capture Taiz, with some signs that forces linked to the government were pulling back to secure the major port city of Aden. Riyadh is due to host a meeting of energy policymakers, the WPC Energy Congress, this week.

title: ‘Self-imposed irrelevance’: why the EU is failing to act on growing public criticism of Israel
summary: While Israel’s actions against Palestinians intensify public anger, the bloc remains paralysed along familiar fault lines
text: When the British government announced sweeping sanctions on trade with illegal Israeli settlements and condemned “ethnic cleansing” in the West Bank by state-backed “settler terrorists”, some EU diplomats hoped this dramatic shift in UK government policy towards Israel would have a galvanising effect on the rest of Europe. So far, it has not. Although France and Canada joined the UK in pledging to ban goods from illegal settlements and impose sanctions on “those who facilitate them or profit from them”, there has not yet been a wider ripple effect. A meeting of EU foreign affairs ministers on Monday is likely to showcase the bloc’s stasis in policy towards Israel – a stalemate that is at odds with rising public criticism in Europe of Israel’s government. A survey of 10 European countries, including Spain, France and Sweden, found large majorities of people had a negative opinion of Israel. Views had become more negative compared with the previous year, according to the Pew Research Center, mostly after the start of the US-Israeli war on Iran, which unleashed a new crisis in the Middle East and a global economic shock. In Poland, negative views jumped eight points to 70% of respondents, in Italy they increased by nine points to 75% and in Germany they also rose by nine points to 73%. Israel is facing ever deeper isolation in the theatre of public opinion. Five countries chose to boycott the Eurovision song contest this year over Israel’s participation, after organisers declined to exclude it over its conduct in the Gaza war and rising violence in the West Bank. Organisers have now decided that broadcasters will no longer be eligible to host the song contest if their state is involved in an armed conflict or sensitive geopolitical situation. More than 74,000 people, including at least 21,200 children, have been killed in Gaza since Israel launched its war in retaliation for the Hamas attack of 7 October 2023, in which the terrorist group killed 1,209 people – including 36 children – and took 251 hostages, inflicting a nationwide trauma. Gaza remains a humanitarian catastrophe, with people facing acute shortages of water, nutritious food and medical equipment and medicines, while contending with disease, unemployment, economic collapse and the threat of death or injury. Israel’s airstrikes continue: the death toll includes 1,400 Palestinians killed since a ceasefire was declared a year ago. The EU talks on the Middle East will focus on the conflicts in Iran and Yemen, but ministers will also discuss the situation in Gaza and the West Bank in the context of elections in Israel on 27 October and the first legislative elections in Palestine in 20 years, which are expected by late November. The discussion is expected to expose familiar fault lines in the 27-member EU. One group of countries are vocal supporters of the Palestinian cause: Spain and Ireland were the first to call for a review of whether Israel’s conduct in the Gaza war was in breach of the human rights requirements of its association agreement with the EU, which covers the €68bn (£58bn) trade relationship, cooperation in research, environment and energy. A second group consistently opposes targeting Israel’s government: Germany and Austria are close allies for historical reasons, while Czechia and Italy are ideologically aligned with Benjamin Netanyahu’s administration. Among a third, larger group of countries in the middle are several, such as France and the Netherlands, that are increasingly critical of the Netanyahu government’s conduct in Gaza and its plans to build the vast E1 settlement, which threatens to critically damage the two-state solution. Martin Konečný, the director of the Brussels-based European Middle East Project, thinks the EU has a diplomatic role to play as Israel advances with the controversial E1 plan. However, he does not see any sign of action. “The EU is basically staying in its usual self-imposed irrelevance,” he said. This is not an isolated view. More than 500 former senior EU officials and diplomats issued a statement this week condemning the bloc’s failure to take action over Israel’s actions in Gaza and the West Bank. The signatories, which include former prime ministers of France, Italy and Sweden, as well as Josep Borrell, the EU’s former chief diplomat, singled out Germany and Italy for the first time in stark, uncompromising language. “Germany and Italy continue to systematically block the adoption of any EU measures, thus becoming de facto complicit in undermining both EU values and the two-state solution,” wrote the group, which includes a few dozen senior figures from those two countries. Given their size, Germany and Italy have been crucial in preventing the EU from forging a weighted majority to impose trade sanctions and ban commerce with illegal settlements. Michael Doyle, a former EU ambassador who co-organised the statement, told the Guardian the EU was not meeting the obligations of its treaties or international law. “Unfortunately our often-proclaimed EU values are set aside when it comes to the EU’s collective response to the dire plight of Palestinians,” he said. The widespread disquiet explained “why we get so many signatures from people who don’t normally sign such calls for action”. The statement was motivated by the absence of proposals from the European Commission, the guardian of EU law that initiates legislation for the 27-member bloc. The commission has declined to table proposals to ban trade with illegal settlements. The refusal to act has exasperated numerous lawyers and trade experts, who argue the ban is necessary for the EU to comply with a landmark advisory ruling from the international court of justice in 2024 on the illegality of the settlements. It told other countries to “take steps to prevent trade or investment relations that assists in the maintenance of the illegal situation created by Israel in the occupied Palestinian territory”. Ursula von der Leyen, the commission’s president and a German Christian Democrat who is not afraid to take political risks, has argued the EU cannot act when member states disagree. In her annual state of the union speech last month, she lamented: “When Europe is divided, it cannot change the course of events.” A year earlier she presented proposals to suspend preferential trade with Israel but never found sufficient support from member states. Advocates of the EU taking a stronger approach are not convinced she cannot act. Konečný said: “It is not guaranteed that the qualified majority would be reached. But once the commission tables the proposal [on banning trade with settlements], that changes the dynamic.” The blocking European governments may be lagging behind public opinion. Large majorities in Italy (88%) and Germany (83%) say they do not have confidence in Netanyahu “to do the right thing regarding world affairs”, according to the Pew Research Center’s study. Meanwhile, the question of Israel-Palestine continues to roil the left. This week the Green party of England and Wales adopted a motion equating Zionism with racism, drawing widespread criticism. The motion from a small political party in the UK was strongly condemned by the head of the Jewish Greens in England and Wales (“a very bad motion”) and the European Greens, which stressed the importance of being “absolutely unambiguous” in the fight against antisemitism. Peace campaigners think it makes their job harder. The motion “hands ammunition to those who want to paint pro-Palestinian activism as illegitimate”, wrote Yachad, an organisation that seeks to build support among British Jews for a political resolution to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict.

title: Hurricane Isaias ‘biggest test’ for Fema since Trump cuts, experts warn
summary: Gulf officials say they are ready for storm but concerns raised about restructured agency’s ability to respond effectively
text: Gulf state officials say they are prepared for Hurricane Isaias, but the storm could be the first major test of Fema’s ability to deploy a large surge workforce after the Trump administration’s sweeping cuts and restructuring of the agency, emergency management experts say. The Trump administration has said it wants to eliminate, or drastically downsize, Fema, putting more burden on states. More than 4,300 employees left the agency in fiscal year 2025, about 17% of the workforce, according to a recent US government accountability office (GAO) report. The agency’s staffing reductions were not carried out systematically to ensure Fema could still meet its statutory obligations, said Chris Currie, director of homeland security and justice at the GAO. “It’s not whether Fema is going to respond. They’re going to respond. It’s more about the depth,” Currie said. One of the ways that staff was reduced at the agency was through early retirement, meaning many of those who left were more experienced people. From January 2025 to January 2026, 58 senior executive service employees left Fema, according to the GAO report. In the previous three fiscal years, the agency reported about 13 senior executive service separations on average per year. Among the top officials who left the agency last year was the region four administrator, who oversees eight states, including Florida and Alabama, where Hurricane Isaias is expected to make landfall late Friday or early Saturday. Deanne Criswell, who led Fema under the Biden administration, said it was less about the number of people who left the agency and more about the loss of experience. “My biggest concerns are always the loss of institutional knowledge. You lose that knowledge. You lose the people who had been through these big disasters in the past,” she said. In a written statement, Fema said the agency was actively monitoring and preparing for Hurricane Isaias. “Under President Trump and Secretary Mullin’s leadership, the safety of the American people is DHS’s top priority,” the agency said. “Fema incident management assistance teams are deploying to Alabama and Florida, and Fema personnel are embedded in state emergency operations centers. Fema is also prepositioning emergency supplies at Maxwell air force base in Montgomery, Alabama, to supplement state resources if requested.” Governors of Florida, Georgia and Alabama have declared states of emergency for counties projected to be affected by Hurricane Isaias. State emergency management personnel in Louisiana and Mississippi said they had been in regular contact with Fema and received full support from the agency earlier this year during Tropical Storm Arthur, which brought flash flooding and tornadoes across the Gulf coast. At a news conference on Thursday, Jared Perdue, the Florida division of emergency management executive director, said the state had had very close coordination with their federal partners at Fema. But Currie warned that the agency could quickly find itself stretched thin if it has to respond to more than one natural disaster, a possibility that could become quickly consequential as El Niño strengthens and the agency heads into the fall and winter months. “The bigger risk is how big it is and a second disaster happening and their ability to staff those,” he said. For example, In 2024, Hurricanes Helene and Milton made landfall in Florida less than two weeks apart. In response, Fema deployed 13,500 employees, straining staff capacity. “Fema has struggled to have the right number of people with the right qualifications, even before these cuts,” Currie said. In June, Fema had active recovery efforts for over 1,000 open emergency disaster declarations. If the agency is forced to deploy personnel to multiple new disasters, as it did in 2024, Fema would probably have to marshal staff from these other active recovery efforts, putting those efforts on hold, Currie said. “Even though it’s been said that it’s been a quiet hurricane season, it could still be a busy disaster season,” he said. Last month, a federal judge ruled that the Trump administration’s plan to cut Fema staff by 50% was unlawful. The administration has been slow to approve major disaster funding this year, according to an analysis by the Texas Tribune. Most major disaster declarations by Fema in 2026 came a month after the initial request, about three times longer than average, according to the report. Ginny Goldman, the founder of Rebuild: the National Disaster Survivors Association, a member organization of climate disaster survivors, said those who went through the flooding in Texas Hill Country this summer still have not received Fema individual assistance. In a Truth Social post, Donald Trump said the federal government would send $50m for disaster recovery assistance. “Where is it at? What about the folks struggling to get back on their feet?” Goldman asked. Hurricane Isaias would be the “biggest test of Fema” since the Trump administration’s staffing cuts, she said. “And it’s coming at a challenging time because there are so many other compounding factors that are making life hard for people in America.” While Gulf state officials have not expressed concern that Fema’s staffing cuts could impact the agency’s ability to respond to Hurricane Isaias, Goldman said disaster survivors are likely to notice. “If you’re a disaster survivor that is trying to navigate a system that is already broken, versus a civil servant in a government agency that is used to navigating a broken system day-to-day, you will have a different perspective on whether it’s broken or not,” she said.

title: Bragging rights for Burnham, blues for Farage: conference season winners and losers
summary: While the Labour and Conservative leaders will be delighted with their showing, Nigel Farage, Ed Davey and Zack Polanski have less reason for cheer
text: Winners Andy Burnham Even his fiercest critics would struggle to argue that Andy Burnham’s first conference as Labour party leader was anything but a success. There was the requisite rapture among the Labour faithful after his deeply-personal speech, delivered without a tie or a lectern and, at times, with tears in his eyes. But even figures on the right, such as the broadcaster Piers Morgan, described it as “one of the best, and most powerfully delivered, by a British politician in a very long time”. The prime minister’s policy offering packed a punch too. He put forward radical progressive policies on social care, promising to “rip the plaster off” and make changes to the pensions triple lock, electoral reform and Europe. A YouGov poll after the conference showed that it had boosted the “Burnham bounce”, with Labour opening up a five-point lead over Reform UK in the polls. The upcoming budget, and next year’s spending review, will sorely test whether he can keep that momentum going and make good on his promises. Burnham’s success at the Labour conference was capped by a victory at the Holborn and St Pancras byelection a few days later seeing off a challenge by the leader of the Green party Zack Polanski. Kemi Badenoch This time last year, Kemi Badenoch was hanging on to her role as leader of the opposition by a thread. But in the past 12 months her personal favourability ratings have continued to improve, according to More in Common research. This was a conference where she tightened her grip over the Conservative party and leaned hard into her own brand, telling GB News’s Christopher Hope: “We are under new management. There’s a new captain, there’s a new coach, there’s a new owner, effectively, which is all me.” While Badenoch’s speech lacked the emotional firepower of Burnham’s, she was assured and disciplined in her focus on the economy – not mentioning small boats or other elements of the culture wars which have energised her in the past. Promised giveaways to wealthy individuals, such as free childcare for those earning more than £100,000 and abolishing inheritance tax on family homes for the 5% of households that pay it, were designed to appeal to the Conservative’s traditional base, one of the first indications of a resolve to win back the “blue wall”. The most powerful moment of the speech came as she drew a line in the sand between the Tories and Reform, thunderously telling her audience there would be no uniting the right: “I don’t want to live in a country run by people who threaten journalists, call veterans traitors and debate whether my mixed-race children are English.” Whether she will reject any deal with Reform if the electoral circumstances dictate remains to be seen. Online, all the time, communications Both the Conservative and Labour communications teams can congratulate themselves on a job vigorously done in the past few weeks. The coup of the conference season came in the guise of a 27-metre (88ft) graphical retelling of the past two years in British politics in the style of the Bayeux tapestry, as seen through Conservative eyes. Senior party figures and members alike enjoyed the “Birmingham tapestry”, for its pointed jabs at defector Robert Jenrick, but the canniest move was including depictions of high-profile journalists, most of whom duly posted images of the propaganda to their sizeable social media followings. The team at the Labour party conference successfully projected the “hopey-changey” vibes they had intended, mainly by producing as many posters and placards declaring there was “hope again” as there were participants at the conference. But special mention should also be given to the socials team at Labour HQ, whose snipes during their rivals’ conferences (“Who was less sure whether he’d finished, the shadow chancellor or the audience?”, they asked after Andrew Griffith’s less than assured end of speech exit) was a masterclass in side-eye. The battle of political ideas This conference season saw the most sharply defined battle lines between right and left in a generation. Burnham used his speech to attack neoliberalism, saying: “Britain has been on the wrong path for a long time. Deindustrialisation. Deregulation. Privatisation. Austerity. Brexit.” He was instantly accused by the Conservatives of indulging in a “socialist fever dream” of the 1970s. They went on to proclaim a love of Thatcher while simultaneously belting out the national anthem. In her speech, Badenoch pitched the fight against Labour as “a battle for the soul of this nation”, trotting out the well-worn Tory treatise that “what people earn belongs to them, not government”. Sidekicks with main character energy Ed Miliband lolloped through Liverpool’s conference centre with the ease of a man who appears to be very much enjoying his time as foreign secretary. In a lineup easily swallowed by the gravitational pull of the leader’s speech, Miliband delivered a deft piece of politics, telling assembled members they were “right” to be moved by the plight of the Palestinian people. Over at the Conservative conclave, the Conservatives’ candidate for mayor of London, James Cleverly, also had a jolly time away from the main stage. “[Kemi Badenoch] knows, as I do, that our best bet of getting her into No 10 is getting me into City Hall,” he told a panel convened by the Centre for Policy Studies (CPS). Losers Nigel Farage Reform UK billed its largest ever gathering at the National Exhibition Centre in Birmingham as “the most talked about event of 2026”. Its leader, Nigel Farage, wanted to use the conference to outline a series of policy pledges for a Reform government’s first 100 days in office. Instead the opening was overshadowed by the suspension of his close aides Dan Jukes and head of policy James Orr, after an undercover investigation by reporters from a group called Verbatim. Reform UK cleared them of breaking laws that ban foreign donations on Wednesday, but the matter remains under police investigation. Farage’s own speech was interrupted by protesters, who appeared to be roughed up as they were thrown out of the hall. A man was later given a police caution after footage appeared to show one woman having her hair pulled and being hit with a walking stick. Zack Polanski Zack Polanski started his run in to the Green party of England and Wales’s conference by asking, unsuccessfully, if it could be delayed so he could focus on campaigning in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection. He may now wish it had been cancelled altogether. The party’s gathering in Brighton was consumed by controversy, after members voted in favour of an official policy stating that Zionism, the movement for a Jewish state, is a type of racism. Polanski absented himself from the most toxic internal debate the party has faced for years, choosing instead to leave to campaign, and the party is still reeling from the fallout. Shortly after the Greens’ triumph in February’s Gorton and Denton byelection it was polling above 20%; it now stands on 11%. Ed Davey At first it seemed as if the Liberal Democrat leader, Ed Davey, had come through his party’s conference in Brighton relatively unscathed, despite going unexpectedly viral for a speech in which he enthusiastically, if not entirely successfully, attempted to rally a chant of “We care! We fight!”. But his opposition to Labour’s proposals to change the pension triple lock was met with opposition by senior and backbench Lib Dems, with one saying his defence of the current policy “gaslights an entire generation into believing it’s for our benefit”. John Healey The chancellor used the word hope 21 times in his personal conference speech that, while warmly welcomed by Labour party members, managed to say very little about actual policy over quite a long period of time. In the days that followed, senior Labour figures privately voiced unease about Healey’s approach to his crucial first budget this month, noting it lacked detail about policy on investment and growth or any pitch-rolling for possible tax rises. Andrew Griffith Among all the gaffes, the spills, the wrong names and forgotten policy details of this season of party conferences, one performance really did stand out. Griffith, the shadow chancellor, was described by Badenoch as having “more business experience than the entire Labour cabinet combined” – attenders at Conservative party conference were left wondering if any of it had involved public speaking. After an address variously described as “an historic clunker”, “curious” and “the worst speech ever heard”, Griffith’s speech appeared to simply peter out and the shadow chancellor wandering awkwardly off stage, leaving the audience not knowing whether to clap, or simply follow him out of the room.
