title: Labour fends off Green party to win Holborn and St Pancras byelection
summary: Victory by Sagal Abdi-Wali in north London seat will reassure Andy Burnham in high-stakes battle for left of British politics
text: Labour has seen off the Greens to win the Holborn and St Pancras byelection in a result that will reassure Andy Burnham and dent Zack Polanski’s position as a decisive power player on the left of British politics. The byelection, called after the former prime minister Keir Starmer resigned from the seat in September, was considered a two-horse race between the Labour candidate, Sagal Abdi-Wali, and the Green party leader, Polanski. Abdi-Wali received 12,292 votes, 45% of the vote, to Polanski’s 8,928, 33% of the vote. Turnout was 38.7%, the lowest for any byelection held in England during this parliament and 15.4 percentage points down from the 2024 general election. In an emotional victory speech, Abdi-Wali, a former child refugee who came to the UK from Somalia in the 1990s, hit out at “those who seek to divide us”, in what appeared to be a response to Reform UK’s Zia Yusuf, who suggested she was not British shortly after the byelection was called. “I hope this moment says something about who gets to belong,” she said. “For people who look like me. I hope they see themselves reflected in this place and know that their path too belongs here. This is Camden and this is Britain.” Labour’s victory provides assurance for Burnham in his first big electoral test as prime minister, and reinforces polling that shows he has recovered some public support lost by Starmer, his predecessor in Downing Street. However, the low turnout suggests Burnham still faces an uphill battle in urban areas, particularly in London where the Greens took control of three councils in May’s local elections. Bridget Phillipson, the Labour chair, insisted the win was a sign of progress for the party. She told Times Radio: “It demonstrates that Labour’s message of hope is really cutting through, that people don’t just want parties like Labour to talk about the progressive change this country needs, but they want to see it delivered in action.” Polanski’s loss caps a bruising week for his eco-populist party, which fell into turmoil after it voted at its conference on Sunday to adopt a policy declaring Zionism a form of racism, raising questions about his leadership. Shortly after polls closed in Holborn and St Pancras, Caroline Lucas, the former Green MP and party leader, refused to say whether Polanski should stand down. Speaking to BBC Newsnight, she said: “I want him to show the leadership that was frankly missing on Sunday [when the motion was voted on].” Polanski abstained and campaigned in the constituency instead. Speaking to the BBC after the result, Polanski insisted he would remain in his post. “Of course I can carry on as leader of the Green party,” he said. “We’re a party of 220,000 members. I’ve taken a loss tonight but our movement is so much bigger than one election or one motion and we’re going to grow.” In a later interview with Sky News, he said the result had been a good one for the Greens, and that “we are going to be more of an electoral threat to Labour than we ever have in our history”, noting that it had been the party’s second best byelection performance. The motion at the centre of the fallout said Zionism – the movement for a Jewish state – should be “treated as any other form of racism” and called for Israel to be replaced by a single Palestinian state. It was passed in a vote by Green members despite opposition from four of its five MPs. Polanski has faced criticism for not opposing or backing the motion, and for being absent from the debate and vote on Sunday so he could campaign in the byelection. He told Sky he would only have backed the motion if it had been amended to remove the call for a single Palestinian state. Asked if he backed it as passed, he said: “I would have supported the motion as amended. It wasn’t amended, so no.” Polanski defended himself against the criticism that he had not shown leadership by missing the vote. Campaigners in Holborn and St Pancras had “wanted to see me on the ground”, he said, adding: “They wanted to see me dealing with local issues. So I did exactly that.” Speaking to the Guardian after her win, Abdi-Wali said people at the school gates found the Greens motion “divisive”, adding: “It just speaks to the larger divisive discourse that set off and I don’t want to engage in that kind of thing.” On Labour’s stance on Palestine, she said: “The work Ed Miliband has been doing on Gaza, Palestine and Israel has resonated really well with local people. He’s been taking action and not just speaking.” The Greens’ standing in the polls, and Polanski’s personal approval ratings, had fallen in recent months after a peak in popularity last summer, exemplified by the party’s seismic win in the Gorton and Denton byelection in February. The Greens dispatched thousands of members to knock on doors in the north London constituency, even before Polanski was selected as their candidate. But the 8,928 votes cast for Polanski compared to the nearly 11,350 his party and the independent, pro-Gaza candidate Andrew Feinstein received combined in the seat in 2024 suggests the Greens have not significantly expanded their base of voters in the constituency. • This article was amended on 9 October 2026. Voter turnout was 15.4 percentage points down from the 2024 general election, not 15.4% as stated in an earlier version.

title: OpenAI projected to bring in $20bn less in revenue than expected
summary: Questions raised over AI growth as ChatGPT maker forecasts this year’s revenue at $50bn, way below the $70bn signalled before
text: OpenAI has revealed that it is making about $20bn less in projected revenue than it had recently indicated to investors, raising questions about the break-neck growth rate in demand for AI. The ChatGPT-maker company has told investors that its revenues for this year would reach $50bn (£37bn), a projection based on sales up to the end of September. However, this is significantly less than the $70bn that it had signalled in information provided to investors last month, which was widely reported. Forecasts of annualised revenues by the leading artificial intelligence players, including by OpenAI’s rival Anthropic, the maker of Claude, are closely watched by markets as an indicator of overall demand for a technology that is attracting huge investment. OpenAI is in early-stage talks to raise $30bn in a funding round that values the business at about $1.4tn. News of the $20bn gap buffeted US tech stocks on Thursday, with the tech-led Nasdaq closing down by 1.4%. Chip giant Nvidia fell 2.9%, Oracle was down 5.5% and Micron declined 4.8%. The discrepancy arose from attempts by OpenAI investors to provide a more direct comparison with how projected revenue is measured by Anthropic, which hit $65bn in forecast revenue by the end of July. Anthropic includes the revenue from sales via cloud partners, such as Amazon’s AWS and Google Cloud, while OpenAI does not. Last month, Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI, said that the company would not float on the stock market this year as had been expected, citing safety concerns over AI. Altman’s decision followed cases of AI agents going rogue to hack external systems and AI safety researchers quitting their companies concerned about the technology’s risks. Democrat and Republican politicians are calling for new rules to govern AI systems, after two researchers from Anthropic warned that the lightning pace of development of AI without safeguards could lead to the extinction of the human race. Anthropic is expected to push ahead with plans for an initial public offering (IPO) as soon as next month. OpenAI’s most recent fundraising was in March when it closed a $122bn round of finance at a valuation of $852bn. Two months later Anthropic announced it had raised $65bn, valuing the company at $965bn. On Friday, it emerged that Masayoshi Son, the founder of Japanese investment company SoftBank, is seeking to raise up to $100bn from Gulf states as he scales up his already mammoth investments in AI. SoftBank has aggressively pivoted towards AI, including making a $65bn investment in OpenAI, and discussions have been held with Gulf investors including the United Arab Emirates, the Financial Times reported. Last month, SoftBank raised $11.1bn in the largest high-yield corporate bond sale globally on record, paying investors yields as high as 9.75%, to fund its bets on AI and semiconductor assets.

title: Palantir’s Tom Watson says ‘mob rule’ must not dictate awarding of government contracts
summary: Former Labour deputy leader says tech firm would work with a Reform UK government on immigration crackdowns
text: Tom Watson, the former Labour deputy leader who recently joined Palantir, has warned against “mob rule” when it comes to awarding public contracts. Lord Watson, now a senior vice-president at the US tech corporation, said UK ministers could get themselves “in a lot of trouble” as he was questioned about concerns raised about the government working with his new employer. Palantir was co-founded by the Trump-supporting billionaire Peter Thiel and has provided AI-powered software to the Israeli military and the White House’s ICE immigration crackdown, leading to a public and political backlash against its deepening involvement in British public services. The prime minister, Andy Burnham, is under significant pressure from Labour MPs and unions to ditch Palantir from government contracts, including a £330m software deal with the NHS. The company is also fighting Sadiq Khan in court over the London mayor’s block on a £50m contract to use its AI in Metropolitan police investigations. It is seeking to win more public sector work in the UK, where it already has an annual turnover of £427m. Watson told the BBC podcast Political Thinking with Nick Robinson: “One of the things I’d say to my former colleagues is: do you want to let the rule of law lead procurement practice, or do you want mob rule to lead procurement practices? Because you get yourself in a lot of trouble if you go down on the latter one.” He added: “I think we are very targeted by the people that are targeting Israeli companies. We’re not an Israeli company, but because of our work in Israel we found ourselves in the middle of the row of the Gaza protests.” Watson told the podcast he would work with a Reform UK government on immigration crackdowns if the situation arose, saying: “We don’t actually work in that sector, but yes, of course we would.” He called Palantir “the most interesting company on the planet” as he announced his new role last month. The company said his job would be, in part, to “deepen the social and economic value its work creates through better British public services, jobs and skills”. Watson was a defence minister and a minister for digital engagement in Gordon Brown’s government. Since stepping down from parliament in 2019, he has been an adviser to the gambling and music industries and, since 2024, he has been a part-time adviser to Palantir. Palantir said Watson had taken a leave of absence from the House of Lords and had relinquished his parliamentary pass while he worked for the company in London. The Labour MP Chi Onwurah, who chairs the science, innovation and technology committee, which has raised concerns about Palantir, told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme: “Tom is not the first politician to be blinded by tech hype. The key issue is we can’t be so dependent on one company. It’s a US company, subject to US legislation regarding access to our data.”

title: Holborn and St Pancras byelection loss will disappoint Greens – but there may also be relief
summary: It may sound odd to think Zack Polanski would be happy with second place, but after his most challenging week in politics, it could have been worse
text: Parliamentary byelections can generate all sorts of emotional responses, often very strong ones. But for the main contenders in Holborn and St Pancras, the feeling this morning might be more prosaic: relief. For Labour, Sagal Abdi-Wali’s victory with just over 45% of the total vote was widely expected, but it allows the party to credibly claim Andy Burnham as a politician able to reach people in both Reform-leaning areas such as Makerfield and in Green-friendly inner cities. Retaining a constituency formerly held by your last leader, Keir Starmer, and which has been overwhelmingly Labour since it was created in 1983, is in normal political times not that notable an achievement, but these are not normal times. A low turnout of 38.7% and Abdi-Wali’s numerically modest 3,364 majority that resulted might not appear the greatest endorsement of the government, but it is also likely to have been in part due to the widespread assumption that Labour would win. And what of the Greens, and particularly Zack Polanski, the party’s leader in England and Wales, who decided to go for the high-profile seat himself? Again, it may sound curious to think he would be happy with second place, but after the most challenging week of his political life, it could have been worse. Polanski got just under 33% of the vote, well above anyone else apart from Abdi-Wali, a proportion which shows that in an another election, and up against a Labour party not enjoying a Burnham bounce, the Greens could still be highly competitive in seats like these. When Polanski said he wanted to stand, the hope was for another wave of enthusiasm and publicity of the sort that propelled Hannah Spencer to victory in February in another supposedly safe Labour seat, Gorton and Denton. He will nonetheless be quietly pleased that the result does not seem to have shown much of a shedding of Green votes after criticisms of, and deep divisions in, the party since it adopted a highly controversial policy on Zionism and Israel last weekend. The new policy, decided by members at the Greens’ annual conference, equates Zionism, the movement for a Jewish state, with racism, and calls for Israel to be replaced by a single Palestinian state. It is publicly opposed by four of the party’s five MPs, with numerous councillors distancing themselves as well and a handful resigning. Polanski’s decision to not take a side, and even to absent himself from Sunday’s debate so he could campaign in the byelection, has prompted deep unease among some Greens, who termed it a failure of leadership. It was notable that after the result, Polanski had to state that he intended to stay as Green leader. “Yes absolutely, that’s what leaders do,” he said. While some in the Greens had questioned Polanski’s decision to contest a seat in north London, rather than east London, where he lives, his allies make the point that Nigel Farage took eight tries to become an MP. Either way, the result has not made Polanski’s position any worse. Had the Green vote collapsed he would have been under very intense pressure. As it stands, he must try to reassure sceptics in the party before seeking re-election in a year from now, under the party’s policy of two-year terms for leaders. And what of the others? The Conservatives will be quietly happy with beating Reform UK to take third place, their 7.1% being almost exactly the same proportion of votes as they took in 2024. This might not seem like much of an achievement, but the party’s national poll ratings remain stubbornly below 2024 levels, and thus stasis will most likely be claimed as more evidence of a Badenoch bounce. Down in fifth place, the emotions are different. While they are byelection specialists, the Liberal Democrats were never going to win here, but they had put in at least some effort to boost their vote, with MPs going out this week to knock on doors. Coming behind Reform on just over 3% of the vote will be a disappointment. Amid the noisy debates over the leadership of Labour, the Tories and Greens, it can be easy to overlook the disquiet among some of Ed Davey’s MPs that the Lib Dems do not appear to be cutting through. He will not be feeling relief this morning.

title: Tories overstate net zero cost by nearly £500bn in apparent spreadsheet error
summary: Exclusive: Badenoch’s flagship conference policy document cites £957bn estimate, twice the total in climate advisers’ data
text: Kemi Badenoch’s flagship party conference policy document overestimated the cost of net zero by nearly £500bn, seemingly after someone accidentally double-counted figures on a spreadsheet. The apparent error appears in a chapter on net zero in The Right Way, a 100-page policy document produced for the Conservative conference in Birmingham. Badenoch repeatedly used the phrase in her main speech. Justifying the Conservatives’ decision to scrap the target of the UK reaching net zero emissions by 2050, introduced under Theresa May, the document says that estimates of how much this would cost the economy “have varied enormously”. It goes on: “In 2020, the Climate Change Committee (CCC) estimated that its route to net zero would cost £957bn.” It cites the Sixth Carbon Budget produced by the CCC, the government’s climate change advisers, saying the report put gross economic costs at £1.4tn, falling to £957bn when savings were taken into account. However, the figures in the report in fact total £478bn, half of what the Tory document said. The error appears to have arisen because a tally of all the costs in a CCC spreadsheet from the document also included the row showing totals for each individual column, thus doubling it. A CCC spokesperson said: “We don’t recognise this number. The committee has previously offered to meet with Ms Badenoch and talk her through our advice. That offer is, of course, still open.” The committee’s most recent analysis puts the expected cost of achieving net zero by 2050 at about £110bn, or about £4bn a year – 0.2% of GDP. The error was spotted by the publication Carbon Brief, which informed the Guardian. It is possible the Conservatives copied the figure without checking it. It appears to have been published in a report by the rightwing thinktank the Institute of Economic Affairs and also included in an article in the Spectator. The Conservative document says it is intended to be a precise diagnosis of the UK’s problems. It is modelled in part on The Right Approach, produced by Margaret Thatcher’s Tory party in 1976, which set out some of the economic ideas later used in the 1979 election. In a foreword, Badenoch notes that “as an engineer”, she is used to correctly diagnosing issues so they can be addressed. A later part of the report says: “To fix a problem we must first have an accurate understanding of what is causing it.” The Conservatives and Badenoch’s office were contacted for comment.

title: How California is bracing for a winter of floods, fires and extreme storms all at once
summary: The strongest El Niño recorded is expected to bring a cascade of hazards to a state still facing wildfire and heat risks, while budget cuts have weakened disaster response agencies
text: Before this year, the US National Weather Service had never issued a September coastal flood advisory for the San Francisco Bay Area. In the past month, it has had to issue two. As flood water swallowed intersections and eroded beaches up and down the California coast last week, scientists and emergency managers warned that this is just an early signal of a coming tumultuous winter as an already exceptional El Niño continues to strengthen. It’s been called everything from “super” to “Godzilla”, as forecasters hammer home the message that conditions brewing in the Pacific Ocean could soon climb off the charts, and fuel extreme weather around the world. Tens of millions could face food insecurity, and global food prices could be pushed higher. Climate scientists have projected that by February, more than 450,000 people around the world could succumb to spikes in temperature linked to the strong El Niño. Yet more deaths will be caused by floods and droughts, wildfires and rain. More on all this, after this week’s most important reads. Essential reads Comebacks for wild tigers, tuna and sea turtles prove nature loss can be reversed, scientists say Revealed: the methane mega-leaks from UN climate summit host Turkey To cull or not to cull: Greenland debates fate of world’s slowest shark In focus California is among the places most likely to be hit hard by the climate pattern. Models show a more than 90% chance that this El Niño will be “very strong”, with roughly a 75% chance that it will be historic, according to the latest forecast the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (Noaa). Severe storms, landslides and destructive high tides are on the menu – and they could happen all at once. The impacts will be a taste of what’s to come as the world warms. But the effects are also layering on top of conditions fuelled by the human-caused climate crisis. Officials hope that preparations already under way may ready the most vulnerable communities for a more extreme future. California’s governor, Gavin Newsom, issued a state of emergency on 21 September to mobilise efforts and resources, kicking off a flurry of activity. Preparations are already under way at all levels of government as officials work to secure vital infrastructure, preset response resources and inform the public of the incoming hazards. Some areas could see supercharged storms and relentless rains. Others face explosive surf, strong currents, and damage to marine ecosystems. The effects of El Niño will add an additional foot of sea level rise in California on top of the 8 to 12in of rise caused by climate change there over the last century, according to state climatologist Michael Anderson. In recent wildfire burn scars, including the slopes of Big Sur that burned this summer and neighbourhoods devastated by the 2025 firestorm in Los Angeles, there will be higher risks of debris flows. Officials said it typically takes five years for watersheds and hillsides to heal enough to withstand strong storms. Some adverse conditions fuelled by El Niño are already taking shape. Along with coastal flooding from elevated sea levels and high tides, powerful storms swirling through the Pacific have made for an unusually busy tropical cyclone season in areas unaccustomed to them. Hawaii is still recovering from a series of deluges and strong winds that flooded roads and buildings, unleashed landslides and toppled trees. Swaths of the Southern California coastline were hammered by massive waves that damaged homes and devoured beaches. Some spots already hit hard are now working to recover while they prepare for the next round of adverse weather. In Long Beach, just south of Los Angeles, the seawall has been lined with large sandbags to reinforce spots where strong surf has burst through. In Orange County, roughly 690,000 cubic yards (528,000 cubic metres) of sand is being pushed along the coastline. Workers are going door to door in San Diego’s flood zones to help small businesses ready their buildings. Los Angeles county public works director, Mark Pestrella, said flood control systems are ready and have been optimised during a recent briefing, but the systems are only designed to withstand a so-called “100-year event.” Those have a 1% chance of occurring in any given year, but El Niño could bump those chances higher. Meanwhile, LA’s office of emergency management director, Kevin McGowan, is juggling dangers on the other end of the hydrological spectrum: high heat and fire risks that are likely to linger into November. “We are in the middle of fire season and about to head into a significant heatwave,” McGowan said ahead of a scorching October weekend that smashed several records across Southern California. “People should continue to prepare not just for one hazard – but all hazards.” While local officials are rushing to get ready, the US is going into the high-risk winter with less capacity to respond or prepare for extreme events, due to cuts in staff and resources issued by the Trump administration, according to experts. From the beginning of his second term, the president has cracked down on climate science and gutted frontline federal agencies. Deep budget cuts and mass layoffs have reduced the capacity of emergency response agencies, including the Federal Emergency Management Agency (Fema), the agency tasked with coordinating national disaster responses, and the Noaa, considered a global crown jewel for climate science. “Agencies, particularly Noaa and Fema, were already stretched because we have been seeing more and more extreme weather events,” said Monica Medina, who served as the principal deputy administrator of Noaa during the Obama administration. It’s not yet clear where all the holes may be, but they will become more clear as the needs rise. “I worry about loss of life and about our inability to be protected at a time when you know we need our government the most,” she said. “If this is a real test,” she added, of a hotter, more precarious future, “we’re going to flunk.” Read more: • Landslides, flash floods and raging seas: is California ready for the ravages of El Niño? • What is El Niño, what causes it and can we reduce the risks? • A ‘Godzilla-level’ El Niño is causing extreme weather conditions around the world – your questions to our environment writers • To read the complete version of this newsletter – subscribe to receive Down to Earth in your inbox every Thursday.

title: Virgin unveils its future cross-Channel train as it gears up to take on Eurostar
summary: Group plans to launch services from London in 2030 and hopes to outshine competitor with design inspiration from its airline, cruise and hotel arms
text: Flash interiors, fancy food and maybe even a bar: Virgin has unveiled a mock-up of its future cross-Channel train, with a pledge to create “something genuinely new”. The group is planning to launch rail services from London to the continent in 2030, with Eurostar facing competition for the first time since the opening of the Channel tunnel. Virgin has ordered 12 high-speed trains from the manufacturer Alstom, matching Eurostar’s for speed at up to 190mph (300km/h) but aiming to outshine the incumbent on design and customer experience. While Virgin’s last stab at reimagining UK train travel may have peaked with the talking toilet seat on its intercity services in 2013, it has said the future trains will draw inspiration from its airline, cruise and hotel arms. Although details are being kept under wraps, it said it would draw on Virgin Atlantic’s airport lounges, or Clubhouses, for “pre-departure and onboard social spaces” with “more flexibility to work, relax or socialise in style”. Food will be influenced by its cruise line menu and the design by its Virgin Hotels brand. Virgin Trains is expecting to introduce 20 daily return services between London, Paris, Brussels and Amsterdam from 2030, adding almost 7.5m seats a year to the cross-Channel network, creating up to 1,000 new jobs. Josh Bayliss, the chief executive of Virgin Group, said: “Virgin has a proud history in UK rail. With our latest venture we are drawing on more than four decades of experience across travel and hospitality to create something genuinely new. “We’re confident that more journeys between the UK and Europe will be made by train. We’re adding capacity for millions more international rail journeys each year, growing the market as a whole. We’re looking forward to seeing our distinctive red and black trains travelling across Europe.” Virgin also hopes to connect its rail and airline networks, potentially bringing passengers from France for Virgin Atlantic flights. It will also wrap the train service into its loyalty platform so that passengers can earn points towards other types of Virgin travel. The Office of Rail and Road on Thursday published an agreement with Eurostar for Virgin to maintain its trains at the Temple Mills international depot near Stratford in east London, with track access in the UK confirmed until at least 2040. Italy’s state-owned Trenitalia is also expected to launch cross-Channel high-speed services. It already runs international trains as far as Paris and recently announced its own €2bn order for 19 new trains from Hitachi, some of which are expected to be based in France and run through the tunnel to London.

title: Friday briefing: Burnham​ passes first test as Labour heads off Green challenge
summary: In today’s newsletter: Holborn and St Pancras byelection defeat is a blow to Zack Polanski, who ‌has promised to draw support away from Labour
text: Good morning. Labour has won the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, heading off a challenge from the Greens and confirming prime minster Andy Burnham’s ability to consolidate vibes into votes. Labour candidate Sagal Abdi-Wali – who is currently leader of Camden council – won 12,292 votes while her closest rival and Green party leader, Zack Polanski, received 8,928 in a byelection that was called after former prime minister Keir Starmer resigned from his London seat last month. This was a comfortable win for Labour in a contest that also saw the Greens triple their vote share. The victory will probably be framed by Labour as another bound in the Burnham bounce, while a Greens spokesperson this morning insisted that Polanski winning 33% of the vote share to Abdi-Wali’s 45% “shows just how far we’ve come”. Some, of course, will be blaming that ill thought out Zionism motion for the loss. This morning’s newsletter takes you beyond the party spin lines with our correspondents who live and report in the constituency. But first the headlines. Five big stories Europe news | High school students in France again blockaded schools and marched through cities, in the tenth day of protests that have left hundreds injured. UK news | Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor has won his legal challenge against Thames Valley police over search warrants that led to his arrest, which have been ruled unlawful. US politics | Pete Hegseth has said the execution of the former army psychiatrist who killed 13 people at Fort Hood will be a public event. Ukraine | A Russian missile strike on a bus in the eastern city of Kramatorsk has killed at least 30 people, officials have said, in one of the worst attacks by Moscow on Ukrainian civilians this year. Business | Oil prices have risen sharply amid fears about escalating tensions in the Middle East and a squeeze on production from the threat of a hurricane off the US coast. In depth: Burnham shores up Labour’s left flank This vote was a test not just of Burnham’s bounce but also his breadth: after seeing off Reform in Makerfield in the victory that paved the way for him to become prime minister, Labour has shored up its left flank too after the prime minister delivered an unapologetically left wing prospectus to his party conference in Liverpool just a few weeks ago. Sagal Abdi-Walim, who arrived in the UK as a child refugee from Somalia, said her victory was “deeply personal”, telling supporters: “I hope this moment also says something about who gets to belong … I came here as a child and this place gave me so much.” Speaking to broadcasters after the declaration, Polanski stayed upbeat, insisting voters had been excited about Green policies, but conceding: “So many people on the doorstep told me they wanted to give Andy Burnham a chance – let’s see what he does with it.” Guardian reporter Sammy Gecsoyler, who was at the count in Camden council offices, described a fairly “low energy” affair, where it looked certain from early on in the night that Labour had come through. It’s worth reflecting that the turnout here was nothing like it was in Makerfield – or in Gorton and Denton in February, where the Green’s Hannah Spencer pushed Labour into third place. Turnout yesterday was 38.7%, the lowest for any byelection held in England during this parliament and 15.4% down from 2024. *** A constituency of contradictions The battle in Starmer’s former seat may have seemed fairly quiet from a distance, but not for those that live there. Guardian reporter Tobi Thomas, for example, estimates she’s had Green canvassers on her Camden doorstep four times a week since the start of September. She predicted a Labour win: “A lot of my neighbours are lifelong Labour supporters.” But she also observed the Greens were campaigning hard, “with talking points on the environment and Gaza.” As Tobi points out, Holborn and St Pancras is a wildly mixed constituency. It takes in everyone from media execs in their Primrose Hill mansions, to the Euston school leaders facing falling pupil numbers due to a lack of family council housing. Across the London constituency, 43% of people live in social housing, almost half are aged between 18 and 34, and around the same number were born abroad. Even before her selection as a candidate, Reform spokesperson for home affairs Zia Yusuf was keen to point out that Sagal Abdi-Wali happens to have been born in Somalia, in a dog whistle post on X that was later condemned as “straightforward racism” by Labour. While Reform has no foothold in the area, Guardian columnist Polly Toynbee – who lives in the constituency too – wondered if attacks like this might galvanise wavering Labour supporters otherwise tempted by the Greens. Polanski’s pitch has been that a vote for the Greens is a protest vote – but one with real power. According to analysis by Politico, the party has spent nearly £5,000 pushing Meta ads that promise a Green win would “keep the government in check”. Abdi-Wali, who says that she was spurred to join the Labour party in 2015 due to a the visible rise in homelessness in King’s Cross, has focused squarely on local issues in her campaign. But this local emphasis sits in tension with national scrutiny of the party. Out on the doorstep with Abdi-Wali in a social housing estate, Polly Toynbee described how warmly the Labour candidate was recognised for her community work. “She takes notes of people’s problems, from housing repairs to e-bikes blocking the road, her local campaign matching Burnham’s localism,” Polly wrote. “But we also meet a college lecturer, who had a run-in with their employer over Gaza, who will ‘never vote Labour again’.” *** Is Labour’s identity crisis over? It’s true that Gaza led many Labour voters to go Green in the English council elections earlier this year. Two years earlier, in Holborn and St Pancras, a constituency with a 20% Muslim population, Starmer’s majority fell from 27,763 to 11,572, and an independent candidate who described him as “terrible on Gaza” came in second with 18.9% of the vote. This morning’s results will now be scrutinised to assess the impact of Burnham’s significant shift of position. The new prime minister has apologised for Labour’s initial response to Israel’s military action in Gaza, saying that the UK was too slow to call for a ceasefire. More recently, foreign secretary Ed Miliband announced sanctions on trade with illegal Israeli settlements in the West Bank (but, Labour is still yet to act on the proscription of Palestine Action). Speaking on the BBC earlier this morning, polling expert John Curtice said that the result largely reflected shifts in national polls, with the Greens “notably weaker” than in the spring, when they were at an historic high of close to 20%. But he warned: “45% of the vote is four points down on what Keir Starmer got in 2024. Bear in mind that the vote for Starmer fell precipitously in 2024. And compared with what Labour was getting in this constituency in 2019 or 2017, Labour’s vote is still well down.” Curtice’s up-sum was that Labour are in a much better position than they were six months ago, but still not as popular as they were in 2024. Calling a general election now – which, to be fair, Burnham ruled out before Labour conference – would still be “an extremely risky project for them”, Curtice said. The results also show the Greens “are more significant players than they have ever been”, though they have lost a significant portion of the ground the gained during the early months of Polanski’s leadership. Meanwhile, the snap analysis from Peter Kellner, the former head of YouGov, was that Labour had defied its “truly dreadful record defending its own seats when it is in government and faces a by-election challenge from the left”. Most importantly, the result confirms Burnham’s ability to hold together Labour’s broad coalition: from the older, anti-immigration, Eurosceptic voters that made up a large proportion of voters in the Makerfield byelection, to the comparatively younger, more diverse and progressive left-leaning constituents of Holborn and St Pancras. Some might say this result cements a glorious union of north with south, but, I’ll say it for the umpteenth time: Makerfield is not in the north, it’s in the middle. *** Is the grass still Greener? At this point, it feels a bit rude to mention Gorton and Denton again. In politics-time, it might feel like a century ago now, but reporter Matthew Pearce tells me that the Greens were still celebrating it at their conference last weekend. It was a “sliding doors” moment for Labour, Matthew says, and many Green strategists see Polanski’s early success as a direct cause of Starmer’s downfall – and Burnham’s subsequent ascension. “It’s clear Polanski played a role,” says Matthew, “but the question now is whether that role will diminish because of Labour’s new direction.” Polanski has said from the outset of his campaign to be an MP that he would remain as Green party leader even if he lost – so take any early morning pundit speculation with a heavy salting. That said, former Green leader Caroline Lucas was quick out the traps shortly after the polls closed, saying he made a “mistake not to show leadership” over the Zionism policy vote. According to Matthew, the Greens are now focused on the impact of the New Labour prime minister. “In his conference speech, Burnham addressed so many issues that the Greens have been using to distinguish themselves from Labour,” he explains. When Polanski became leader he said many times he ultimately wanted the Greens to replace Labour. But in his speech at conference, he returned to a new phrasing: “Vote Green, watch Labour move”. “They know they have to adapt to the new political spectrum,” says Matthew. The move has been welcomed by senior European officials, including the French finance minister, who invited the UK ‘to come all the way back’ to the EU. With public polling now shifting against Brexit, is the door open for the UK to decide if it wants to rejoin? Lucy Hough speaks to Europe correspondent Jon Henley. Cartoon of the day | Ben Jennings The Upside A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad Can hope save the planet? Helen Pilcher ponders that question in this column centred on a new biodiversity report, The Science of Hope, which shows how 32 species of bird (including New Zealand’s kākāpō, pictured above) and 16 types of mammal have been saved from extinction since 1993. Pilcher writes that far from “hopium” (that is, misleading tales of false hope), the report shows the importance of telling the positive stories in the fight against climate change and habitat loss. “That’s the kind of hope we need: pragmatic, resilient and open to revision. We need our governments to be honest about the scale of the challenge we face. Because when they withhold information, they don’t just rob us of knowledge. They also rob us of hope,” she writes. title: Revealed: the ‘black box’ wastewater trade that rakes in millions for UK utility companies
summary: Exclusive: Firms made more than £340m last year from processing industrial and commercial wastewater at sewage works that are unable to remove many chemical pollutants
text: Water companies in the UK made more than £340m in revenue last year by pouring billions of litres of industrial and commercial wastewater into sewage treatment works that experts say are not designed to remove most chemicals, leaving pollutants to pass into rivers, seas and farmland. Water companies in England are required by law to take industrial wastewater and issue permits called “trade-effluent consents” that allow businesses to send it to sewage works, though water companies can refuse applications. However, no independent regulator oversees the trade-effluent process and there is no central register, so Watershed Investigations, the Guardian and the campaign group River Action compiled a database of 26,000 consents, providing the first ever national picture of the system. The investigation found an annual total of up to 608bn litres of industrial wastewater entering sewage works from sites such as power stations, pharmaceutical plants, food factories, hospitals, abattoirs and waste facilities. The permits are issued and enforced by the water companies themselves, with environmental regulators having no direct role. “It’s a bit of a black box,” one industry expert said. Most sewage works only have biological treatment facilities, which are not designed to remove industrial chemicals, including flame retardants, Pfas, solvents and pharmaceuticals. Some permits on the database feature chemicals such as cyanide, chromium, cadmium and mercury. Watershed has mapped every sewage treatment works and the industrial companies permitted to send waste to each one. Pollutants that survive treatment are discharged into rivers, lakes and seas as “treated effluent”, while those captured in sewage sludge are spread on farmland as fertiliser. The waste also adds to the overloading of sewer networks that triggers raw sewage spills, which have caused outrage, community protests and calls for the industry to be nationalised so that profits can be reinvested in improving the system rather than going to shareholders. United Utilities made the most revenue from industrial waste last year, at £61.6m, followed by Yorkshire Water at £48.8m. However, these companies included revenues from tankered waste in their figures, while some others did not. Dŵr Cymru Welsh Water, Scottish Water and Wessex Water said they routed commercial tankered waste through separate companies within their groups. Thames Water has the largest volume of permitted industrial sewage, at 113bn litres, followed by United Utilities at 105bn litres and Severn Trent Water at 79bn litres. Across the sector, revenues from receiving industrial and commercial wastewater have risen sharply in five years, with Anglian Water’s increasing by 62%. The industry expert said water companies had “a financial incentive to accept far more toxic material than they should”. The permit regime was very old and not fit for purpose, they added. “Currently the Environment Agency doesn’t know exactly how much of this waste is going into waterworks each year.” Waste handlers also drive tankers carrying industrial effluents, landfill leachate and other liquid wastes to sewage works. An Environment Agency (EA) officer said landfill leachate was its “greatest concern” because of the harmful chemical cocktail it can contain. Both the officer and the industry expert identified Davyhulme wastewater treatment works in Manchester, operated by United Utilities, and Avonmouth, operated by Wessex Water, as big receivers of tankered waste. “Carriers will drive [long distances] to dispose of their wastes here … You can see lines of tankers queueing outside Avonmouth,” the expert said. Checks by water companies across the sector can just involve taking a sample and carrying out basic pH and metals analysis, but even more advanced testing does not always pick up a wide range of potentially harmful substances, “and by the time you’ve identified [that] it had something nasty in it, it’s already gone”, the EA officer added. But “ignorance is no defence”, said the officer. “They should be seeking sufficient information from the producer of that waste to satisfy themselves so they can treat it properly.” The industry expert said the UK needed a dedicated liquid-waste treatment sector rather than relying on a “dilute and disperse” model. Amy Fairman, the head of campaigns at River Action, said: “Industrial pollution must not become a lucrative business for water companies … Polluters must be held to account and made to pay, rather than passing the costs and consequences down the line. “The public has a right to know what is being put into our sewage works and where those pollutants ultimately end up. The government has promised to clean up [England’s] rivers through the clean water bill – it must confront this hidden industrial wastewater trade and address the serious failures exposed by this investigation.” “Water companies should never profit from pollution,” said a spokesperson for the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs. “We know the water industry hasn’t been working in the public interest for far too long and that’s why we are reforming it, including how wastewater is disposed of.” An EA spokesperson said the trade-effluent framework was “developed over 30 years ago”, before many of today’s concerns about Pfas were fully understood, and that it was working to improve how contaminants in wastewater were managed. A spokesperson for the trade association Water UK said: “Water companies [in England] are legally obliged to accept trade effluent and charges are set by Ofwat. The Environment Agency sets the permit conditions, but they make no account of the fact that sewers are not designed to treat a range of toxic substances such as forever chemicals and mercury, which is still, sadly, used by many dentists. “That’s why we have long called for the government to ban these toxic substances and to force the manufacturers to pay the costs of removing them from the environment.” A United Utilities spokesperson said it had “strict consent and control processes” operating under “regulatory requirements designed to protect public health and the environment” and that it “assesses, monitors and treats wastewater”. It added that tankered waste, including landfill leachate, was accepted only at specifically permitted sites. NI Water said applications involving “priority substances” were referred to the Northern Ireland Environment Agency, and dedicated teams sampled sewer and tanker effluent to “oversee compliance”. Scottish Water said it assessed trade-effluent applications based on factors including sewer and treatment capacity, protection of infrastructure and staff, and compliance with environmental standards. All water companies included in this article were contacted for comment. Companies can also discharge industrial wastewater directly into rivers and seas, but this is subject to permits issued by the environmental regulators. In England, water companies are regulated by Ofwat and the Environment Agency, with policy set by Defra. Ofwat also covers Wales, but environmental regulation sits with Natural Resources Wales and policy with the Welsh government. Scotland and Northern Ireland have their own regulators and publicly owned water companies, with policy set by their devolved governments. • This article was amended on 9 October 2026 to add context on the policy and regulatory framework within the devolved administrations of the UK; to note that the cited figure of 608bn litres of trade effluent is a maximum annual total based on applied consents; and to clarify a reference to harmful substances that can be missed by most routine water analysis.

title: US midterms: key takeaways from Senate debates in Michigan, Georgia and Maine
summary: Candidates traded personal attacks, sparred over affordability, the economy and abortion win three closely watched US Senate debates on Thursday
text: With just weeks left in the contentious midterm election campaign, candidates in a trio of highly-competitive Senate races debated Thursday night, clashing over the economy, tariffs, the Iran war and abortion rights, with control of the upper chamber at stake. In Georgia, incumbent Democratic senator Jon Ossoff faced GOP representative Mike Collins. In Michigan, Democrat Abdul Al-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers debated over the state’s open Senate seat. And in Maine, longtime senator Susan Collins met Democratic challenger Troy Jackson. Democrats need to flip four Republican-held Senate seats to win the majority. Here are the key takeaways from the battleground state debates. Affordability, affordability, affordability Affordability was a major topic across all three debates on Thursday night, as voters consistently name the cost of goods, gas, housing and healthcare as their top concerns in this year’s midterms. “Can you afford your gas? Can you afford your groceries under this guy who’s going to rubber stamp everything Donald Trump tells him to rubber stamp?” El-Sayed asked during the Michigan debate, the first of two in one of this cycle’s most fiercely contested races. Both Rogers and El-Sayed said they support suspending a fuel tax to alleviate costs, while El-Sayed argued that the Iran war, which was driving up gas prices, needs to end. El-Sayed attacked Rogers for growing his personal wealth while in office as a US representative. Rogers called El-Sayed “bought off” by billionaire George Soros, Hamas and Hezbollah. “We cannot afford Abdul, and we cannot risk his ideology,” Rogers said. In Georgia, Ossoff repeatedly asked Collins to justify his support for Trump’s global tariff policies, which the senator said have “crushed Georgia families” and “strangled” economic growth. “Let’s see if he has the courage to explain his votes,” Ossoff said, adding later: “Still have not heard an explanation for the tariffs.” Collins, who is trying to cut into Ossoff’s lead, blamed inflation on Biden administration policies, singling out spending measures that his opponent had supported. Later in Maine, where polls show a tight race, Jackson focused his remarks on pocketbook issues, including the sharp spike in heating oil costs and high energy prices. Collins defended her record and argued that Maine had benefited from the $50bn rural health transformation fund that was appended to Trump’s signature tax cut and spending bill, the so-called Big Beautiful bill. It gets personal in Georgia In the Georgia debate, a question about data centers erupted into a pointed, personal exchange between Ossoff and Collins. “Mike Collins voted to take that money out of your pocket and out of your community and give it instead to data center developers,” Ossoff said. He then accused Collins of being a “bigot” who has “hired half the Third Reich” – a reference to the congressman’s history of employing staffers who have expressed white nationalist, antisemitic, and extremist views online. “If John Lewis were marching today from Selma to Montgomery,” Ossoff said of the late civil rights icon and long-serving Georgia congressman, “Mike Collins would be grabbing a billy club. His office has been in cahoots with some of the most notorious white supremacists on the country.” Collins was asked directly about his son-in-law’s social media posts promoting white nationalist and antisemitic views. “You know, Rick, that’s my family,” Collins replied. “That’s the craziness that Jon Ossoff has been spewing out there.” Collins noted that a New York man had recently been charged after threatening to kill him, and added: “I’ve condemned racism, antisemitism, hate; I don’t care where the source is. And I tell him that too, it’s wrong. We have no place in this world for that.” Collins, meanwhile, sought to cast Ossoff as “radical” and an “extremist” whose record in the Senate had left the state “less safe, more expensive and worse off”. Labatt and Red Wings in Michigan Tariffs were also a topic of heated debate in Michigan, which shares hundreds of miles of border with Canada. This week, Rogers publicly backtracked on previous support for Trump’s tariffs on the US’s northern neighbor, saying in a campaign ad that “Canada is not our enemy” and that the “tariff war” needed to end now. During Thursday night’s debate, Rogers said he had spoken to the commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, this week to advocate for a deal between the two countries. There are tariffs in place that are “too high and not helpful for us”, Rogers said. El-Sayed said he supports targeted, logical tariffs that protect Michigan manufacturing, but nothing like the “ham-fisted, chaotic, self-serving” tariffs Trump put in place. He called out Rogers for “flip-flopping” on the issue, saying he was only reversing his stance because of “sagging poll numbers”. “He’s doing an ad drinking a Labatt and talking about the Red Wings, pretending like he was not for this the entire time,” El-Sayed said. “Be serious, my guy.” Accusations fly in Maine In Maine, discussions about gas prices and the war in Iran raised notable tension in the second debate between Jackson and Collins, who is seeking a sixth term in her seat. “She’s the Chairman of Appropriations,” Jackson said. “Money has to come through them for these wars – she still can do something.” Collins, who plans to continue leading the Appropriations committee if re-elected, said she had repeatedly supported war powers resolutions to halt Trump’s military action in Iran. But Jackson pushed further, accusing the senator and her husband of profiting from the war. She could use her leverage to stop this war, but instead they’re making money,” he said, prompting a furious response from Collins, who called the allegation “absolutely outrageous”. “You owe me an apology,” she said. Reproductive rights under the spotlight in Maine In Maine, both candidates were also pressed to address inconsistencies in their positions on reproductive rights, a crucial issue for voters in the state. “Our records have changed,” Jackson said. “Mine has gotten better – hers has gotten worse.” He pointed to Collins’ vote to confirm supreme court justice Brett Kavanaugh, who helped overturn Roe v Wade in 2022. Collins, one of just two Republican senators who supports abortion rights, has said she does not regret her vote for Kavanaugh, even though she believed he had given her private assurances before his 2018 confirmation that he would not overturn the landmark ruling. Collins sought to turn the issue back on her opponent, noting his past stances on abortion that have left many voters wary. “From 2000 until he ran for the house seat in 2013 was very anti-choice,” she said, accusing Jackson of having held “extremist” views on abortion. “He was for a bill that would not allow abortion when the mother’s life was at risk.” She also pointed to legislation she helped write that sought to “codify Roe v Wade nationwide,” but the bill never made it passed the Senate. Mittens off in Michigan In Michigan, Rogers repeatedly attacked El-Sayed by attempting to tie him to Muslim terrorist groups, including Hamas, and suggested government surveillance would only bother someone if he or his family had something to hide. Rogers brought up El-Sayed’s mom and sister, prompting El-Sayed to say at one point that Rogers should just come out and say what he’s been dancing around all night, after Rogers’ repeated references to terrorist groups. “He wants this to be about anything but his own record,” El-Sayed said. Rogers claimed El-Sayed refused to condemn a terrorist attack in Michigan earlier this year and the 7 October Hamas terrorist attacks in Gaza, although El-Sayed said he had condemned both. But, El-Sayed added: “I’m not somebody who tries to make political theater out of other people’s pain.” He also retorted to Rogers: “Did you sell your yachts?” Rogers responded: “I never owned a yacht in Florida, brother.” After a 30-second commercial break, moderator Rick Albin said that in his 30 years of hosting debates, he’d never seen the sparring continue during the break, but tonight, it had.

title: Country diary: A passing osprey needs to eat – but the local terns won’t let it | Claire Stares
summary: Chichester harbour, Hampshire: I witness a battle of wills as this magnificent raptor attempts to fuel up on sea bass, before it heads south on migration
text: The autumnal sunlight gilded the sea as our boat drifted off Fowley Island, a small, uninhabited tidal saltmarsh between Thorney Island and Hayling Island. A colony of grey seals lay sprawled along the intertidal mudflats, their size and prominent, sloping Roman noses making them easily distinguishable from the more lithe, cat-faced common seals that also inhabit the harbour. Two sub-adults were tumbling and splashing in the shallows, play-fighting with the exuberance of puppies. They mouthed and nipped at each other’s heads and necks, lunging and rolling over one another before disappearing beneath the waves, only to pop up again in a spray of water and resume their boisterous tussle. These playful interactions are a form of social bonding, but they also serve as a rehearsal for future dominance contests. As we passed through the Sweare Deep tidal channel, the boat slowed to let us watch a flock of sandwich terns plunge‑diving for silvery bait fish driven to the surface by predatory sea bass. Glancing over my shoulder, I noticed a much larger bird approaching from the north. At a distance, it might have been mistaken for a black‑backed gull, but its long, crooked wings, bent at the “wrist” into a distinctive M shape, gave it away: an osprey, stopping off to fuel up on its migration. As I called out to alert my boatmates, the osprey dropped feetfirst towards the water to snatch a fish from the surface. Spotting the intruder, the terns intercepted, banking and diving to disrupt its flight path, and the fish escaped its talons. Their relentless harassment left the osprey little opportunity to hunt. It circled and tried again, but when a tern struck its back with its sharp bill, the raptor gave up, flapping away on slow, shallow wingbeats. Ospreys have made a remarkable recovery as a breeding species in Britain, but for this individual, the harbour was merely a brief pause on its journey south. As we puttered back to the marina, we passed an artificial nest platform installed in the hope of attracting these beautiful fish eaters to breed. I wondered whether, in some future spring, this osprey might return to establish a new breeding territory. • Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024, is available now at guardianbookshop.com

title: How a plant selfie in Colombian jungle led to ‘jaw dropping’ giant waterlily find
summary: Species with leaves large enough to be seen from space is already critically endangered – and plans are afoot to protect it
text: A chance social media encounter has led to the race-against-time discovery of a new species of giant waterlily that has until now been hidden in the depths of Colombia’s jungle. But the plant, which is so huge it is visible from space, is already considered critically endangered. Giant waterlilies, which can measure up to three metres across and carry the weight of a small child, are one of the oldest flowering plants in the world still alive today. They existed before the continents split apart and are present throughout culture, from the Egyptians to Monet. Three years ago, while scrolling through Instagram, Carlos Magdalena, a world-renowned waterlily expert at the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, came across a photo of someone swimming among several giant waterlilies in the Inírida River in Guainía, Colombia. Jeremiah Harris, who took the photo and who runs a carnivorous plant nursery in the US, was not aware of its significance, having mistakenly identified the waterlily as the more common Victoria amazonica. However, when Magdalena saw the photo, he “immediately suspected” something was unusual as the natural range of the Victoria amazonica does not extend to the Inírida River. He messaged Harris to track down the exact location and spent several years analysing satellite imagery and securing the funds and necessary permits to allow him to verify the presence of the waterlily for himself. Along with a team from the Jardín Botánico in Bogotá and members of the local indigenous reserves, Magdalena went on a five-day expedition deep into the rainforest. They spent several days exploring the flooded jungle with no luck, until, at the last moment, their driver advised them where to look. With only 10 hours left until their return flight, the team sailed overnight in total darkness to a small lake deep in the flooded rainforest, where they located a population of the waterlilies. “It was so emotional I shed a tear, it was one of those moments that will remain with me for life,” Magdalena said. “Coming across something like this is absolutely totally fascinating, it’s jaw dropping. “Giant waterlilies give away their secrets slowly,” he said. “It’s remarkable. We believe we know everything but the reality is we don’t, there’s lots of things still to be discovered and protected.” The team collected the material needed to begin a formal identification, with a paper published on Friday in the journal Phytotaxa confirming it as a new species to science. The waterlily has been given the official name Victoria colombiana. There are just three other known giant waterlilies. Harris, who is an author of the study, said his friends always teased him for taking selfies with plants, but the fact this one ended in the discovery of a new species was “incredible”. “I was just so excited, absolutely elated,” he said. Magdalena said: “This is one of those extraordinary stories where indigenous and horticultural knowledge with the help of social media and technology came together to uncover a truly extraordinary botanical achievement.” The team estimates there are between 30 and 50 of the Victoria colombiana waterlilies in the wild, making them extremely rare and at risk of extinction. Maarten Christenhusz, a plant taxonomist who analysed the sample, said new species were found all the time, but few were as “large, spectacular and emblematic as this one. This new giant waterlily can even be seen from space, which is a striking reminder of how much we still don’t know about life on our planet.” The team is working towards an official International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Red List designation. Efforts are also under way to support the long-term conservation of the waterlily, including the possibility of establishing a naturalised population in a more accessible lake within indigenous territory. The researchers hope to continue efforts to collect the plant’s seed, with the aim of cultivating it in Bogotá. If these efforts are successful, there is a chance the waterlily may be grown at Kew Gardens.
