title: Thousands march in Madrid after death of evicted pensioner Maricarmen
summary: Rally to remember woman, 87, whose rent battle with investment firm triggered nationwide protests over housing crisis
text: About 20,000 people took part in a march through the centre of Madrid on Thursday evening in memory of María del Carmen Abascal, the 87-year-old woman whose eviction from her flat in the capital a fortnight before her death triggered mass protests over Spain’s housing crisis. The pensioner, whose flat had been bought by an investment firm that sought to increase her rent by 230%, had become the public face of the crisis before her death in hospital on Wednesday night. Abascal’s eviction unleashed waves of demonstrations across Spain, led to the setting up of a protest camp in the centre of the capital, and prompted the socialist-led government to propose emergency measures to try to make the rental market more equitable. When those measures were voted down by rightwing and far-right parties last week, the prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, announced a snap general election, to be held on 29 November. Anger over the plight of the woman who had become known around the country as Maricarmen remained undimmed a few hours after her death. On the pavement across from the apartment building where she had lived for seven decades, a steady stream of people visited a small, steadily growing memorial. Some came to light candles or leave flowers, while others left handwritten messages such as, “You made history Maricarmen,” and “Thank you for changing Spain”. Sara, 41, who had come with her young son and a sign that read, “Maricarmen, we’ll fight for you”, said: “We’re here because I think Maricarmen’s death shows how institutions can kill a person by failing to care for them.” For many, the site was a reminder of all that Maricarmen had gone through as she tried to stay in her home, fending off three eviction attempts before the investment firm succeeded in forcing her out. “When people are protected less than investors, that leads to these kinds of things happening,” Sara added. “This woman could have died – if she had died of natural causes – she could have died peacefully in her home.” Jaime, 34, pointed to all that Maricarmen had come to represent, particularly in a country like Spain, where social rights are supposedly guaranteed. “She had become a symbol, albeit one she never wanted to be, of the fight for decent housing,” he said. “So I came here because I think it’s important to restore some of the respect that Spanish society took away from Maricarmen.” Visitors included some of the housing campaigners who had helped Maricarmen fight off previous eviction attempts. “This is really hard to take,” said Miguel, 59, fighting back tears as he added a red rose to the memorial. “When money is more powerful than people’s lives, it’s unbelievable.” He said he hoped Maricarmen’s death would mark a turning point in Spain. “At least now we’re talking about this and putting names to those who are being evicted,” he said. “Because until now, there were 44 people a day being forced out of their homes. To the people in power, those are just numbers – now at least we’ve started putting names to those going through this.” The Madrid tenants’ union announced a commemorative march at 8pm on Wednesday from the camp in the Puerta del Sol square to Abascal’s flat. “Farewell, Maricarmen!” the union said in a post on social media. “Tonight we’ll honour you with a march … to the place that was your home for 70 years, and where you just wanted to stay until the end.” Abascal’s ordeal has made housing a key issue in the forthcoming election, with Sánchez’s government seeking to push a redrafted package of measures through the council that operates when parliament has been dissolved. Meanwhile, the rightwing and far-right parties that opposed the legislation in congress last week have accused the prime minister of failing to act to address the housing crisis over the course of his eight years in office. Sánchez offered his condolences to Abascal’s family and friends on Wednesday night. “A hug also to everyone who’s feeling this loss today as their own,” he wrote on social media. “Rest in peace.” Alberto Núñez Feijóo, the leader of the conservative People’s party (PP), which voted against last week’s emergency measures, also offered his condolences. “No campaigning, no political parties, no partisan ends, no more bricks in the wall,” he wrote on social media. “When a person dies, there should be nothing but respect.” The following day, however, Feijóo accused the government of trying to “manipulate the emotions of the Spanish people” by focusing on one particular eviction when there had been countless others during Sánchez’s time in office. PP politicians also joined forces with the far right on Thursday to veto attempts to hold a minute’s silence for Maricarmen in Madrid’s regional parliament and the country’s senate. In Madrid’s municipal council, meanwhile, a rightwing attempt to block a minute’s silence was thwarted by opposition parties. Abascal’s death has prompted reflection on how she had been treated by politicians and the media. The far-right Vox party, which also voted down the new decrees, had falsely suggested that Maricarmen would have had a home had she been an immigrant from North Africa, while one commentator had opined that “Maricarmen was chosen during a casting call for people facing eviction” to become a leftwing saint. At least two far-right figures, including one of Vox’s MEPs, sought to sow doubt over the cause of Abascal’s death, with one even suggesting an autopsy should be carried out to determine whether the government had been involved. Another wrote: “Maricarmen was probably already made to send in her postal vote before they did her in. I expect anything from this scum.”

title: Trump donor accuses ‘grifter’ Kimberly Guilfoyle of $100,000 quid pro quo
summary: Eric Deters says US ambassador to Greece asked him to pay off American Express credit card bill in return for access
text: A Trump donor accused Kimberly Guilfoyle, the US ambassador to Greece and Trump family ally, of engaging in a “quid pro quo” by asking him to pay off her $100,000 debt in exchange for access to administration officials. Eric Deters, a former congressional candidate and lawyer, told MS Now on Thursday that Guilfoyle had “ambushed” him last year with an offer to provide access to government officials if he paid her American Express credit card bill, before her US Senate confirmation hearing as ambassador to Greece. “It absolutely was a quid pro quo,” Deters told the network in response to a Wall Street Journal report that she had pushed him for the money. “Kimberly Guilfoyle is a grifter,” he added. The Guardian has asked Guilfoyle’s lawyer for comment. Jesse Binnall, a lawyer for Guilfoyle, told the Wall Street Journal that Guilfoyle disputed the authenticity of the messages, but that she was “owed a balance” for travel and speaking at events before her nomination. Deters told the Journal that he did not owe Guilfoyle any balance. The report is the latest allegation about Guilfoyle’s conduct as a US official. Deters shared messages he and Guilfoyle exchanged in which the US ambassador to Greece promised him “ride or die” access to Trump administration officials if he wired American Express $100,000. Asked about the report during a press conference in Athens on Wednesday, Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, said he would not address the allegations. He reaffirmed his support for the US embassy in Greece adding, “Our ambassador has been a strong ambassador here.” Asked again about the reports on Thursday, Rubio refused to comment. The top Democrats on the House foreign affairs and Senate foreign relations committees have asked Rubio to open an investigation into Guilfoyle’s conduct as an ambassador. A spokesperson for the Democratic staff of the Senate foreign relations committee confirmed to the Guardian that they were requesting further information and continuing to investigate. JD Vance similarly expressed hesitation, similar to Rubio, on Thursday when asked to respond to a US ambassador offering access to government officials in exchange for money to pay off debts. “With that hypothetical, Jen, obviously I don’t love that,” the vice-president replied. “But I don’t know exactly who you’re talking about. I don’t know the full details. What I find with these stories is you never want to comment in a purely abstract way because a lot of times the details really matter,” he added. Concerns about Guilfoyle’s conduct were first raised in September when the Wall Street Journal reported she had used her position to invite Greek lobbyists to sit in on official diplomatic meetings and promoted the business interests of one particular Greek construction and energy company. Senator Jeanne Shaheen, the ranking Democrat on the Senate foreign relations committee, sent a letter to Rubio on Tuesday, asking him to look into the allegations against Guilfoyle. “Such actions do not serve US credibility overseas and risk undermining US diplomacy,” Shaheen wrote. “In advance of your upcoming travel to Greece, I request an immediate review of Ambassador Guilfoyle’s actions and a clarification of what steps have and will be taken to avoid undue influence and even the appearance of a conflict of interest.” Separately, Gregory Meeks, the ranking Democrat on the House foreign affairs committee, sent a letter to Rubio in September, requesting more information about Guilfoyle’s conduct, her relationship with the Greek construction and energy company and her relationship with the lobbyist. “If these reports are accurate, Ambassador Guilfoyle is unfit to represent the United States abroad and should be removed from her position,” Meeks wrote. Guilfoyle, 57, was once a member of the Trump family’s inner circle, having been engaged to Donald Trump Jr, the US president’s eldest son, for roughly three years. The couple ended their engagement in 2024, and shortly after taking office, Donald Trump nominated Guilfoyle to be ambassador to Greece. But now further allegations accuse Guilfoyle of promising a Trump donor, Eric Deters, access to the Trump administration in exchange for a $100,000 payment to American Express. Deters shared messages exchanged between himself and Guilfoyle with the Wall Street Journal in which she reportedly pleaded: “Honey please I need you to get this done for me today.” Deters said Guilfoyle had promised him thatshe would “be your Trump ride or die, forever and ever” if he made the American Express balance. Deters said he never made the payment. In other messages, Guilfoyle reportedly raised concerns about her communications with Deters becoming public and reprimanded him for not being discreet. “Eric, I really wish you would stop papering all these things. It’s really dangerous and not helpful to you or me while you could simply just call me on Signal,” she is said to have written in one message. “What a nightmare, you’ll literally cost me my ambassadorship stop writing,” Guilfoyle reportedly wrote in another message. A lawyer for Guilfoyle disputed the authenticity of messages Deters shared with the Wall Street Journal. It is unclear whether Shaheen or Meeks will ask Rubio for further information about the latest report. The Guardian has asked Meeks and Shaheen for comment.

title: A teen tried to navigate Canadian mountains with Claude. His trek ended in an emergency rescue
summary: The incident is the latest to raise questions about the growing reliance on digital maps for wilderness navigation
text: The route up the Widowmaker Arete, a 1,700ft wall in British Columbia, is deceptively described as “mostly easy slab climbing”, interspersed with “short steep sections that can include finger cracks” and “blocky face climbing”. It requires careful planning, and the right equipment. When 16-year-old Bryce Vincent Gowryluk found himself facing its sheer headwall last week, he had neither. He did, however, ask the AI chatbot Claude for directions. Last week, Gowryluk had to be rescued after those directions proved wildly incorrect, in the latest incident to raise questions about the growing reliance on digital maps for wilderness navigation. On Saturday morning, Gowryluk took a gondola up to the top of Grouse Mountain and, while ascending, asked Claude to plan a route to nearby Crown Mountain and back. After navigating scree and more than 2,000ft of elevation gain, the summit promises 360-degree panoramic views of Greater Vancouver, the Fraser valley and the Capilano watershed. Typically, the trek takes eight hours and hiking guides warn it is not for beginners. As Gowryluk, a keen indoor climber, navigated down the Crown Pass and up through Crater Slabs and into a boulder-strewn valley, the directions from Claude took him away from the planned course. He found himself at the final headwall of the Widowmaker Arete – a climb that requires ropes, cams and a clear plan for ascent. As he climbed, Gowryluk soon realized the terrain was far too steep and that he was stuck at the base of a cliff. He phoned his mother, then called emergency services for help. Police notified North Shore Rescue, which sent a helicopter, but Gowryluk was too close to the rock face for the rotors, so two members of the rescue team were hoisted down to lift him up. He was flown to the rescue base near the Cleveland Dam. In their debrief the rescue crew said Gowryluk was “far off” his intended route. While this is the first time North Shore Rescue had received a call from a hiker who has been lost because of AI, it is the latest in a string of mishaps in the mountainous region of south-western British Columbia, where hikers increasingly rely on imprecise mapping directions. In July, three people were rescued after they planned a route on the Howe Sound Crest Trail using Google Maps, which gave them wildly inaccurate time estimates, suggesting a route that often takes as long as 14 hours could be done in just over five. Search manager Paul Markey warned that mountaineers should not rely on the directions of artificial intelligence, and that proper preparation was key. “In this particular case, the boy had a headlamp. He had good clothing. He had a good pair of boots, spare battery and spare food. He was pretty well equipped for hiking and scrambling. But he was certainly not prepared or equipped for rock climbing,” Markey said. “Claude, in this particular situation, has never been in the area that this 16-year-old boy found himself in. Claude can only go so far with regard to describing what the area may be like. “There’s definitely a trend towards using electronic applications as opposed to map and compass skills. But it is really no substitute for good map and compass training and education.” He noted that in some cases apps give too much information. “We have found that some of the apps have identified trails in areas where, really, our preference as a rescue team would be that those trails or routes are not actually identified,” he said, adding that people see routes they think are good trails only to get into difficulty. “The main thing is: do not blindly rely on AI as a route planning tool. It can never substitute for good education, good training, a good experience, good decision making in the field.” • This article was amended on 9 October 2026. Owing to an error during the editing process, an earlier version said the climb for Widowmaker Arete requires “cameras”; this should have said cams, a protection device.

title: DoJ seeks to charge ex-Trump aide who gave key testimony on January 6 attack
summary: Cassidy Hutchinson told panel she had been told Trump lunged for wheel of SUV to try to join mob at Capitol
text: Prosecutors in the justice department’s civil rights division are seeking criminal charges against Cassidy Hutchinson, a former top Trump White House aide who gave explosive testimony to the committee that investigated the US attack on the Capitol, according to a person familiar with the matter. The potential charges involve lying to Congress, the person said. Hutchinson, a former top aide to the White House chief of staff Mark Meadows, told the panel among other things that the deputy chief of staff for operations told her that Trump did not want to return to the White House on January 6 and at one point grabbed the wheel of his SUV to try to join supporters at the Capitol. Republicans have long disputed this account. The justice department’s efforts to indict Hutchinson were first reported by Punchbowl News on Thursday. “The department does not confirm or deny the existence of investigations, or the lack thereof,” a department spokesperson said in a statement. In April, the New York Times reported that prosecutors in the justice department’s civil rights division, which handles investigations into civil rights crimes, had been tapped to investigate Hutchinson. It was seen as a highly unusual move at the time since the investigation would typically be handled by the US attorney for the district of Columbia. Hutchinson also said she was under investigation by the Department of Justice in filings in an unrelated case. The case is the latest example of how Trump has used the justice department to prosecute his enemies. Last year, the justice department indicted former FBI director James Comey on charges of lying to Congress and Letitia James on mortgage fraud. Both indictments were dismissed after a judge ruled the prosecutor overseeing them had been unlawfully appointed. The department has since filed a new indictment against Comey for posting a picture of seashells arranged in a formation that said “8647.” The Trump justice department has also filed charges against the non-profit Southern Poverty Law Center and the journalist Don Lemon.

title: Billionaires fund California ballot measure to make voters show ID at polls
summary: Various out-of-state conservative donors have given millions of dollars to support California’s Proposition 39
text: Billionaires across the US are spending vast sums to support California’s Proposition 39, a measure that would require voters to show identification before casting their ballots. The measure is being promoted as a way to “[increase] trust and confidence in our elections”, and comes amid a nationwide push by the Trump administration to restrict voting. California Republicans have long sought to advance a voter ID initiative in the state. The campaign has received more than $36m, according to a report from CalMatters, including $17m from Richard Uihlein, a prominent conservative donor and owner of a shipping supply company. Joe Gebbia, a co-founder of Airbnb and Trump administration official, has given $8m, and Cameron and Tyler Winklevoss and Nicole Shanahan have also made significant donations. The yes campaign has far outraised its opponents by as much as $13m, according to CalMatters. California voters do not currently have to show identification at the polls, but are required to provide a driver’s license or state identification number or their partial social security number when registering to vote. In addition to requiring ID at the polls, Prop 39 would also mandate that mail ballots include the last four digits of a government-issued ID number on an envelope. The Republican lawmaker Carl DeMaio authored the proposition after unsuccessfully fighting in California’s Democratic-dominated statehouse to advance legislation implementing voter ID requirements in response to a demand from Trump. He has argued the initiative could be a bright spot for Republicans in an election where the party is expected to see significant losses. “It’s not the same as the Trump Save Act. It is a more nuanced, balanced approach customized for California. It keeps mail-in ballots, but requires citizenship verification, requires voter ID,” DeMaio recently said. “This is a gamechanger.” The state Democratic party, the ACLU and the League of Women Voters oppose the measure. Supporters have said the proposition has bipartisan support. A recent poll from the UC Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies found that Prop 39 was losing some of the support it had attracted in late summer and was trailing by a 13-point margin. But other polls from late September showed it with a lead. A bilingual statewide survey of 600 Latino likely voters in early August found they were evenly divided on the measure.

title: Microsoft suspended from applying for green cards for H-1B workers, JD Vance says
summary: Vice-president also says Adobe is barred from visa program that allows high-skilled workers to apply for US residency
text: Microsoft is suspended from applying for permanent residency for workers employed through a US visa program for high-skilled workers, JD Vance announced on Thursday. The US vice-president accused the tech company of abusing the H-1B system, which allows those on the visa to work while they apply for and are in the process of obtaining a green card. “Our message to Microsoft is, you’re a great American company, but you’ve got to hire great American workers,” Vance said at a press conference announcing the suspension. “You cannot lay off American workers and then replace them with foreign indentured servants.” Microsoft said the vast majority of its workers were American and 80% of the H-1B applications it filed in the last year were for extensions or status changes for people who already worked for the company. “Microsoft only files H-1B petitions for those who meet the rigorous standards of this visa category,” the company wrote in a statement. “We pay our employees some of the highest compensation in the tech sector, and our wages are among the highest of all H-1B filings. We pay our H-1B employees the same as any other employees doing comparable work.” The US labor department also said Adobe had been similarly suspended. “We will not accept any new or process any pending permanent labor certification applications involving these companies,” said Keith Sonderling, the US labor secretary, in a statement. Microsoft applied for H-1B visas for nearly 3,700 workers in 2026, making it the fifth largest employer of workers on the visa. Tech companies are the biggest employers of H-1B workers across the industry. Amazon topped the list with more than 9,300 petitions this year. Sonderling said since 2009, Microsoft and Adobe had received about 230,000 approvals for H-1B visas and 100,000 “permanent labor certifications”, a step towards an employment-based green card. “If you do the math, for every worker that Microsoft laid off, they replaced that worker with one and a half foreign indentured servants,” Vance said. The Trump administration has set its sights on the H-1B program for some time, arguing that it is rife with abuse. Vance said that, on average, workers hired through the H-1B program were making $20,000 less than US workers in the same position. “So I’m sure that everybody here understands the game that is being played,” Vance said. “You bring in indentured servants from outside the country, you lay off American workers and, if you’re a corporation, you make a ton of money by undercutting the wages of American workers, replacing them with people who, frankly, shouldn’t be in the United States of America to begin with.” Immigration advocacy groups have long called for reforms for the H-1B program, though for different reasons. Those in the program are often beholden to their employer because their visas are tied to the company that applied for them, making it difficult to switch jobs if things aren’t going well or if they want to find a job with a higher salary. These groups, like the National Immigration Forum, largely disagree with Vance. They argue that competing for specialized talent from around the world benefits the US economy. “The United States has long benefited from its ability to attract talent from around the world, particularly in STEM, higher education, research, and innovation,” the National Immigration Forum wrote in a September 2026 blogpost discussing proposed changes to the H-1B program. “As countries increasingly compete for highly skilled workers, policies that make the United States less attractive could strengthen global competitors.”

title: Royal Navy sailor accused of spying for Russia appears in court
summary: Intelligence specialist Teddy Young, 24, alleged to have drafted message in Russian containing classified information
text: A junior Royal Navy intelligence specialist from Bedfordshire accused of trying to pass military secrets to Russia appeared in court on Thursday. Teddy Young, 24, was accused of abusing his high-level security clearance to access secret defence and intelligence data after being deployed on a warship. The navy rating was also said to have made efforts to contact Russian authorities directly, drafting a message in Russian containing classified information that he hoped to pass on. Young was arrested at his home in Bedfordshire on Tuesday after an investigation by Counter Terrorism Policing London (CTPL). He was charged with offences under the National Security Act, the Metropolitan police said. The intelligence specialist was first arrested in May last year. At that point he was suspended and relieved of his duties, and was on gardening leave until his latest arrest. He is the first member of the British armed forces to be charged under the National Security Act 2023. Young appeared at Westminster magistrates court wearing a grey navy tracksuit and spoke only to confirm his name, ate of birth and address in the village of Clapham, near Bedford. No application was made for bail, though the district judge made clear it would be denied. Annabel Pilling, presiding, told Young: “On the basis of the information I have already read, there are substantial grounds to believe that if granted bail you would not come back to court and that you would make efforts to avoid further court appearances and would commit further offences.” Young was remanded in custody to appear before a specialist judge at the Old Bailey on 16 October. The Crown Prosecution Service said between 26 November 2024 and 21 May 2025 Young had engaged in conduct in preparation for committing an offence of disclosing protected information. It is also alleged that in the same period he obtained, copied, recorded or retained protected information, intending the conduct to benefit a foreign power. Commander Helen Flanagan, the head of CTPL, said in a statement issued before the court appearance: “These are very serious charges against a serving member of the armed forces. “We have worked extremely closely with relevant operational colleagues within the Ministry of Defence as our investigation has progressed to ensure appropriate measures could be taken to mitigate any potential risks linked to this matter.” A Royal Navy spokesperson said: “A member of the Royal Navy has been charged with National Security Act offences following an investigation by Counter Terrorism Policing London. As legal proceedings are ongoing, it would be inappropriate to comment further at this stage.” The arrest and charges are not connected to the recent investigation into an incident at RAF Fairford.

title: Top bosses at Goldman Sachs to share bonus pot worth up to $500m
summary: Eye-watering sum, to be split between 20 bankers, is one of the biggest payouts in the bank’s history
text: Top bosses at Goldman Sachs are in line to share a bonus pot worth up to $500m (£378m) this year, marking one of the biggest payouts in the Wall Street bank’s history. The eye-watering sum will be shared between 20 bankers, with its chief executive, David Solomon, due to take about $100m (£75.6m) of the reward, which is made up of Goldman Sachs stock. That is more than double the value of the record $47m (£35.5m) annual pay packet he was granted last year. The $500m bonus pot is the culmination of a long-term investment plan first crafted by the bank in 2021. The final sum, which is due to be confirmed later this month, is tied to how high Goldman’s share price has climbed over the past five years, as well as how its stock price has performed compared with peers such as JP Morgan and Bank of America over that period. Goldman Sachs said the bonuses were meant to persuade bosses to stay at the bank “in an increasingly competitive market”. The bank’s president, John Waldron, who is widely expected to succeed Solomon as chief executive, is also in line for a payout, alongside other top bosses such as the co-heads of global banking and markets, Ashok Varadhan and Dan Dees. News of the bumper bonus, which was first reported by Bloomberg, comes days before Goldman is due to report third-quarter earnings on 13 October. The bonuses reflect the value of Goldman Sachs stock, which has surged roughly 146% over the past five years, and climbed about 300% since Solomon took the helm as chief executive. A spokesperson for the bank said: “The board created these awards to achieve three principal objectives: align compensation with rigorous performance thresholds, ensure leadership continuity and enhance retention of our top talent in an increasingly competitive market. It’s no secret our firm has performed exceptionally well in the years since.” The payouts are the latest in a string of large payouts for executives in the US, particularly on Wall Street. The US lender Citigroup announced earlier this year that its chief executive, Jane Fraser, had been paid a record $42m (£31.8m) for 2025. Meanwhile, JP Morgan’s chief executive, Jamie Dimon, took home a total pay package worth $43m (£32.5m) last year, up 10% from a year earlier. Dimon’s own long-term incentive award is worth about $270m (£204.1m), according to Bloomberg.

title: Nicolás Maduro and his wife indicted for alleged torture of US citizens
summary: Ousted Venezuelan president and Cilia Flores have been in jail in New York since early January
text: The deposed Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, have been indicted for alleged conspiracy to commit torture, according to Manhattan federal court papers unsealed on Thursday. The superseding indictment was unsealed shortly before Flores appeared at court in her ongoing push for pretrial release – which was denied by Judge Alvin Hellerstein. Maduro and Flores have been jailed in New York City since early January. They were captured by US special forces during a shocking predawn assault on Caracas and transported to New York to face “narcoterrorism”-related charges in a move that sparked widespread international outrage. Charging documents at the time alleged that Maduro spearheaded a “corrupt, illegitimate government that, for decades, has leveraged government power to protect and promote illegal activity, including drug trafficking”. Maduro and Flores have previously pleaded not guilty in the criminal case against them. CNN on Wednesday first reported that a new indictment was expected. The new charging document described how Maduro and his wife allegedly wielded untold horrors to suppress opposition and maintain their control. Maduro, Flores and other Venezuelan leaders “presided over a system of repression that relied on violence against political opposition, arbitrary detention, and the torture of detainees, including United States citizens”, the just-released charging document said. Maduro and Flores, the superseding indictment alleged, “sat atop that violent power structure”. They allegedly “developed and facilitated the systems which they and their co-conspirators used corruptly to amass immense wealth and power, rewarding allies with ill-gotten funds and terrorizing perceived opponents through persecution and violence”. Flores was integral to this effort, authorities claimed, saying she “helped develop this system of repression and ordered that individuals be tortured to protect her family members’ illegal activities”. The victims of their torture included US citizens “who were believed to pose a threat” to Maduro’s power. “One particular United States citizen was detained in Venezuela and subjected to, among other things, deprivation of food and water, simulated drowning, repeated beatings, electric shock to his testicles, and forced injections.” Maduro and Flores also put pressure on Venezuela’s judiciary to make legal decisions that supported their efforts to thwart opposition, charging papers alleged. When one official resisted, Venezuelan intelligence agents arrested and tortured their family members, charging papers stated. “For example, one family member … was forced to drink latrine water; assaulted with tear gas in Victim-1’s cell; threatened that Victim-1 would be killed at gunpoint; and placed in a cold room known as the ‘Freezer’ in which a bright light was left on at all times of day and night and music was blared on repeat,” the superseding indictment said. This official “ultimately … relented and blocked the opposition figures from running for political office”. During another alleged torture incident, authorities allegedly abused the friend of a suspected opponent by “asphyxiating him with a bag, applying electric shocks to his testicles and knees, and kicking and beating him with a blunt object”, court papers said. One torture victim, who was repeatedly interrogated, endured numerous threats “including that his daughter would be kidnapped and raped if he did not confess and name his supposed confederates”, court papers state. “On one occasion, interrogators produced women’s underwear, claiming it belonged to his daughter.” Shortly after this indictment surfaced, Flores’s attorneys argued for her release in an already scheduled proceeding, pitching house arrest guarded by 24-hour private security. In doing so, they invoked chronic health issues, including cardiac infirmities. Hellerstein pushed back on this claim, noting that Flores was refusing to have catheterization while detained in general population. “I’ve undergone it, so I know what it is,” Hellerstein said, noting that it was generally an outpatient procedure. “There’s no pain. There’s no general anesthesia.” Flores’s attorney then pointed to her high blood pressure. “It’s controllable by pills,” Hellerstein said. Her team also said in court that Flores dropped more than 25lbs and lost two teeth since her detention. “For whatever it’s worth, her appearance today is no worse than, and perhaps a little better, than when I first met with her [at] her arraignment,” Hellerstein said. Flores’s lawyer said that during her arraignment she was “still bandaged up” from her rough arrest. Flores wore dark jail scrubs during her court appearance. She listened to the proceedings with headphones through a Spanish-language interpreter. The US attorney’s office for the southern district of New York, which is prosecuting this case, opposed Flores’s now-failed bail request. Prosecutors have argued that Flores was a flight risk. Prosecutors also maintained that she had received appropriate medical care. Donald Trump has defended the controversial raid on Maduro, insisting it was a “surgical law enforcement operation”. At Maduro’s first US court appearance, he said: “I’m a kidnapped president – a prisoner of war!” After Maduro’s forced ouster, Trump worked swiftly to gain access to Venezuela’s expansive oil reserves. In August, Trump announced a new oil agreement with Venezuela – claiming that the US would have “majority” control over 65bn barrels of proven reserves. Venezuela boasts approximately 303bn barrels of proven oil reserves – the largest in the world. The White House has tried establishing a consistent flow of Venezuelan crude oil to US refineries while boosting US investment into the country’s flagging petroleum industry. Trump has faced mounting pressure over skyrocketing gas prices in advance of November’s midterm elections. Greater access to cheaper oil and broadened output could help lower costs. A Guardian investigation found, however, that Trump’s proclaimed “biggest oil deal in world history” is likely to fail due to legal and logistical problems.

title: Astronomers detect mysterious burst of energy from a galaxy far, far away
summary: Intense flash of radio waves is more than 10bn years old and has travelled through ‘approximately 80% of cosmic history’
text: A long time ago in a galaxy far, far away, a mysterious flash of energy was released into the universe. Astronomers have now detected that flash – a burst of radio waves which travelled for more than 10bn years before reaching Earth – what they believe to be the most distant fast radio burst (FRB) ever recorded. FRBs are intense bursts of radio waves that can emit as much energy in milliseconds as the sun does in months or years. These mysterious pulses were first discovered in 2007 and have puzzled scientists ever since, with speculation from some that they could have an alien origin. In a new study published in Science, researchers have detected an FRB that originated when the universe was only about 3bn years old, meaning it has travelled through “approximately 80% of cosmic history”. The burst, dubbed FRB 20240304B, is believed to be the farthest yet detected, more than double the previous distance record. The scientists detected the burst using the MeerKAT radio telescope in South Africa and subsequently identified its host galaxy using Nasa’s James Webb space telescope (JWST). Dr Themiya Nanayakkara of the University of Sydney, one of the lead researchers on the paper, said when the burst was produced, “there was no Earth, there was no sun”. Data from the JWST indicated that the burst originated from a “young, very small galaxy which is forming stars at a very high speed, with not many metals around it”. There are several theories as to what the source of FRBs is, including that they originate from magnetars, neutron stars with a very powerful magnetic field. “Whatever the mechanism that causes this radio burst has to account for that fact that it can be produced in … very young galaxies with very low amount of metals,” Nanayakkara said. More than 10,000 FRBs have been detected since 2007. Some repeat continuously, Nanayakkara said, while “some of them repeat for a while and then stop … and then there are some FRBs that only go once and we never see again”. Whether the new distant burst is a one-off flash or will yield recurrent signals remains to be seen. “[But] the fun thing about FRBs is that we don’t need to know what is causing them to do some of the science we are doing now,” Nanayakkara said. This particular burst “has been travelling for 80% of the age of the universe”, he said, adding that further detections of distant FRBs would enable scientists to map unseen matter in the distant universe. Prof Matthew Bailes of Swinburne University, one of the astrophysicists who first discovered FRBs, described the new paper as “a validation of how powerful the FRBs are for probing the universe”. Bailes described them as “a very fundamental way of counting how many atoms there are in the universe”. FRBs are affected by the particles they travel through, enabling scientists to quantify matter that cannot be seen through optical telescopes. Dr Sara Webb, an astrophysicist also at Swinburne University who was not involved in the research, said: “You can use them essentially as a line-of-sight count for how much matter they had to go through [to get to Earth].” The discovery suggests that “FRBs might have been very common in the early universe”, she added.

title: Trump promises not to attack Iran before November’s US midterms
summary: Statement outlines pause on protracted war US president has struggled to end after almost eight months
text: Donald Trump has promised not to attack Iran before November’s US midterm elections, outlining a pause on the protracted war he has struggled to end after almost eight months. In a Truth Social post on Thursday, the US president said Washington was “having productive discussions with the Islamic Republic of Iran”, which he claimed was “in very bad condition, both Economically and Militarily”. The strait of Hormuz, through which roughly a fifth of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas passed through before the war, was all but closed after the US and Israel struck Iran in late February. On Thursday, however, Trump suggested that oil was moving through the strait in record volumes: “22 Million Barrels, last night alone”, he claimed, “with not one barrel coming from, or going to, Iran”. The figure could not be independently verified. “We will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the Midterm Elections to be held in the United States on November 3rd,” Trump wrote. “IRAN WILL NOT HAVE A NUCLEAR WEAPON!” The US first imposed a blockade on the strait of Hormuz in April after talks in Islamabad collapsed, and reinstated it in July after a short-lived June deal to end the fighting. Fighting flared again in early September, when US forces struck rocket launchers on Iran’s Larak Island and Tehran responded with missiles aimed at American military bases in Jordan and the United Arab Emirates. Trump’s public position on the elections has shifted over the past month. On 2 September, as the US exchanged fire with Iran for the first time in weeks, he told reporters he was “not affected by the election”, adding that he was not on the ballot himself but intended to help his party. A week later, before heading to the Republican “midterm convention” in Dallas, he said he expected the war to end almost as soon as the voting was over, and accused Tehran of holding out in the hope that a change of power in Congress would leave it free to pursue a nuclear weapon. He also conceded that US oil prices were unlikely to fall before polling day. A Reuters/Ipsos survey from late September found that only about a third of Americans approved of the strikes on Iran, while more than four in five expected the conflict to last for an extended period, and that approval for Trump among Republicans had fallen from 82% to 73% in a week. Polling averages now show Democrats leading Republicans by roughly nine points on the generic congressional ballot, according to forecaster Nate Silver, the widest margin of this election cycle. The Wall Street Journal reported in September that JD Vance, the US vice-president, and secretary of state Marco Rubio had privately warned Trump the conflict could extend through the remainder of his presidency. Trump’s post did not say what the US would do after 3 November.

title: Israel promotes film that mimics NAZA documentary
summary: Embassies post links to hastily produced online film echoing style of real Guardian documentary about mass killings of Gaza civilians
text: The Israeli government is promoting an online film project that mimics the style of NAZA, the award-winning documentary that details Israel’s mass killings of civilians in Gaza, in an attempt to counter the real film’s findings. The real documentary, directed by the Oscar-winning film-makers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, and produced by the Guardian, is in cinemas and will be shown in more than 50 countries. The Israeli government has denounced the film and announced plans to strip Abraham and Szor of their citizenship, accusing them of treason. In recent days, Israeli embassies have been promoting a link to a hastily produced online film entitled NAZA: The Real Story. Mimicking some of the style of the real documentary, including the use of anonymised interviews shot on rooftops in Tel Aviv, it is hosted on a website called nazadocumentary.com. Ariel Averbuch, an Israeli attorney and army reservist who made the new documentary, described it as an “offensive move” intended to shift the world’s focus from allegations about the Israeli military’s killing of civilians. The film claims that Israel has the “most moral army in the world”. Another film-maker listed on the website for NAZA: The Real Story is Roi Danino, a candidate for the rightwing Israel First party. The website domain was registered on 16 September, six days after NAZA’s premiere at the Venice international film festival, where it won the special jury prize after receiving the longest ovation in the festival’s history. Initially, the website falsely presented itself as a promotional page for NAZA itself, naming Abraham and Szor as the directors, and listing film festivals where the documentary was due to be screened. “Shot at night on the rooftops of Tel Aviv, the film reveals in detail the systems behind Israel’s calculated mass killing of terrorists in Gaza,” it said, distorting the film’s official synopsis by removing the reference to the deaths of Palestinian civilians. That wording was removed from recent updates of the website, once the video for NAZA: The Real Story had been added to the page. It now appears as a platform for the rival film, with a counter that implausibly suggests the short film has been watched more than 42m times. (The film’s official YouTube page is listed as having just 30,000 views.) According to a technical analysis, the discrepancy suggested the viewer counter could have been driven by requests made to the website, by humans or bots, rather than the number of people who actually watched the video. When asked about the source of the 42m claim, Averbuch said he did not know and referred the questions to his tech team. The Israeli military has killed more than 73,000 Palestinians in Gaza since the Hamas attacks of 7 October 2023, in a military campaign that a United Nations commission has described as genocide. The 24 interviews with Israeli military insiders in the original film NAZA detail how an AI-assisted apparatus of mass surveillance was activated during the Gaza war, revealing the systems that were used to target Hamas operatives in the knowledge large numbers of Palestinian civilians would also die. The Israeli embassy to the US, which shared the new documentary on its social media, said the ministry of foreign affairs was not involved in producing the film, and that it had intended only to “amplify the message of its creators and expose wider audiences to arguments challenging and dismantling the blood libels and false allegations”. The Israeli government said on Thursday that it was awarding the film-makers with a certificate of appreciation “for their contribution to Israeli public diplomacy”, claiming the production had garnered tens of millions of views. A Guardian spokesperson said: “We are aware that the Israeli government has been promoting a film hosted on a website that initially – and falsely – claimed it was Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor’s documentary. “This was a brazen attempt to mislead audiences and distract from the urgent questions raised by NAZA.” As well as its global cinema releases, NAZA will be available free on the Guardian’s website from late November. Averbuch is the founder of an organisation that says it conducts “advocacy warfare”, including through the publication of scripts to help influencers criticise Abraham and Szor’s critically acclaimed previous film, No Other Land, which documents the destruction of the Palestinian village Masafer Yatta. The two Palestinian co-directors of No Other Land, Basel Adra and Hamdan Ballal, have been harassed or detained by the Israeli military since the film won an Oscar in 2025. Israeli government officials have scrambled to discredit NAZA’s content, while far-right activists have threatened to hunt down the directors. The Israel Defense Forces’ chief of staff, Eyal Zamir, has said they will use “every tool at our disposal” against the film, while the military has issued a 10-page response to the film, which was based on interviews with more than 100 sources with knowledge of the military systems used in the war. Within a week of NAZA’s premiere, Israel’s ministry of culture had announced a formal investigation into the documentary, calling for Abraham and Szor to be stripped of their citizenship. Demonstrators gathered outside the home of Szor’s parents, demanding that the she face the death penalty, and a mural depicting the film-makers through the sights of a gun appeared in the Israeli city of Ashdod. On Monday, the far-right Israeli activist Mordechai David announced he was fundraising in order to establish a team that would “chase” Abraham. “We’ll find him,” David said in a video posted to Instagram. Szor and Abraham addressed the backlash to their documentary at a Q&A after its New York premiere. “Our country is doing so much to hide these systems,” Szor told the audience. “It’s not a world that is open even to the Israeli public.” At the London film festival on Thursday, one of NAZA’s producers, James Wilson, said Israeli politicians’ “hysterical, vituperative, aggressive backlash” to the documentary had not been anticipated by the team behind it. Wilson said although Abraham and Szor had “anticipated displeasure … there wasn’t an anticipation of the level of aggression leading to these threats and the rabble-rousing aspect”. He added: “To have made a film, a documentary film and be threatened by the political elites of your home country, with charges of treason and defamation … it’s been very difficult and stressful and horrible and scary for them. “I try to look at the overwhelmingly positive reaction to the film in the majority of the world.” Additional reporting by Philip McMahon and Rachel Hall

title: What would make your life easier? Martin Lewis asks public for ‘small ideas’ to improve UK
summary: Finance expert launches Small Ideas Initiative to gather ‘practical, low-cost’ ideas to put before cross-party panel
text: Every day, people run into what the finance expert Martin Lewis calls “the life-potholes of unintended consequences” – clunky systems and poorly conceived rules that make life harder than it should be. His latest project, the Small Ideas Initiative, will attempt to address that, with a cross-party panel of politicians and policymakers crowdsourcing ideas for everyday fixes to take to government. The ideas could cover anything from health and schools to policing, tech and money. Lewis is encouraging people to submit ideas for “practical, low-cost, non-controversial ways to improve the UK” before 12 November. “If we can fix some of those frustration points, we can make people’s lives easier, save time and help everyone get on with work or the things they enjoy,” said Lewis. “There’s just a sense that there’s so many little things to fix,” said Polly Mackenzie, who worked with Lewis to come up with the idea. Mackenzie, who was director of policy to Nick Clegg during his deputy premiership, says the initiative could be an avenue to regaining trust in public institutions. “I think this is about rebuilding confidence in the idea that government can sort stuff out, rather than rebuilding confidence on any one political party having the right ideas,” she said. Mackenzie will sit on the panel, which will choose about 50 ideas to take to the government, councils and regulators. Alongside Lewis, the initiative is run by the innovation charity Nesta and the public participation charity Involve. The Reform MP Danny Kruger, the former Conservative MP Penny Mordaunt, and the Labour mayor of West Yorkshire, Tracy Brabin, are among those sitting on the panel alongside Mackenzie. She said the group had “a real interest and capability in getting involved and sweating the small stuff”. The ideas they are looking for will be “no-brainers” that are not party-political and would be easy fixes. Mackenzie said a good example was when she and Lewis first set up the Money and Mental Health Policy Institute and discovered through a survey that GPs had been charging to fill out debt and mental health evidence forms. “People in debt crisis were having to pay 80, 100, 150 quid to get forbearance for their debts, which is just wrong-headed,” she said. In 2019, two years after the Money and Mental Health Policy Institute started its campaign, the law changed. Before the initiative’s launch, people in north London shared the policies they would consider submitting. Clare, a railway worker, suggested the government should increase rubbish collections during heatwaves, saying her bins had been “a buffet for flies” this summer. Mark, who works on a market stall, said he would ask the government to put more bins in and around train stations. “There are no bins. I know it’s for security reasons, but I think they could find a way,” he said. Kwajo Tweneboa, a social housing campaigner who will also sit on the deciding panel, said relatively small changes could make a “massive difference”. “One small change I’d like to see is housing providers aiming to fix repairs properly, rather than repeatedly applying plaster fixes that don’t address the underlying problem and prolong the misery for tenants,” he says. “I’ve seen how something that should be a straightforward repair can drag on for months, with residents having to repeatedly chase their landlord while the problem gets worse. “It’s about listening to those everyday experiences and turning simple, practical ideas into policy that can make a tangible difference to people’s lives.”

title: A lake pilgrimage and a quiet car ride to the beach: last hours of sisters who took own lives in Brighton
summary: Inquest hears details of how three women spent their last days but why they ended their lives may never be known
text: Jane Adetoro and her younger sisters, Christina and Rebecca Walters, were “the closest sisters and the best friends”, according to their family. Devoted to their father, Joseph, whom they messaged every day, the adult siblings lived quiet lives in the flat they shared in west London and would do everything together. When they died in May this year, it was no different. Early in the morning of 13 May, the sisters’ bodies were recovered from the sea in Brighton, hours after a taxi had dropped the three women at the beachfront. On Thursday, an inquest in the city found that the women, who all drowned, died by suicide a day after making a pilgrimage together to the lake in Birmingham where their mother died by drowning 16 years earlier. In a statement, Joseph Jacobson told the inquest that the scale of his loss was indescribable. “There are no words that can adequately express the pain of losing a child. To lose all three of my precious daughters, Jane, Christina and Rebecca, is a heartbreak beyond anything I could ever have imagined.” Jacobson, who attended the inquest by video link, said he could not understand why their lives had ended so suddenly. “You were my daughters, you will always be my daughters and I will love you for the rest of my life. May your beautiful souls rest in perfect peace,” he said. Precisely why Jane, 36, Christina, known as Tina, 32, and 31-year-old Rebecca, or Becky, decided to end their lives may never be known, the senior coroner Penelope Schofield told the hearing at Woodvale coroner’s court in Brighton. “These three sisters lived very secluded lives. They were incredibly private. We don’t know why they took this course of action or indeed why they chose to do it in Brighton,” Schofield said. What police were able to establish, after initial public bafflement over the circumstances of the tragedy, is how the women spent the day before they died. On the night of 11 May, the sisters travelled by Uber from their home in Greenford, west London, to Birmingham, where they were dropped off at 11.36pm in Linton Walk, in the north of the city. This was the address where Jane and Rebecca, then 20 and 15, were living with their mother, Janice Adetoro, when she disappeared on 5 January 2010, prompting an anguished public appeal by family members. (Christina, then 16, was reportedly living with her father at the time.) Janice’s body was recovered a month later from Brookvale Park Lake, which runs to the end of Linton Walk. She was 43. Described as a doting mother, Janice had been suffering from “paranoid delusions”, the inquest into her death heard. She was sectioned and admitted to a psychiatric unit, the Sunday Times reported, but was discharged from a home treatment team weeks before her death. The tragedy of the sisters’ deaths “wasn’t a story that started in May”, their cousin Natalie Walters-Daniel told the newspaper last month. “It was a story that started long before.” DCI Mark Cullimore, of Sussex police, told the inquest there was no CCTV to show what the three sisters did in the time they were in Birmingham, but less than two hours after arriving, at 1.28am on 12 May, they were picked up by taxi and driven back to their London flat. The inquest heard that Christina, who had recently graduated from Brunel University of London and worked as an accountant, had experienced anxiety and depression since her mother’s death and made “extensive searches” about suicide in the days before her own death. Jane, who was also an accountant, had paid off a loan in full on 11 May. Described as “extremely intelligent”, Jane was said by family members to have taken on a maternal role after the death of her own mother. Rebecca, “the baby” to relatives, worked in HR. She was previously described as “mischievous” and “the lively one who was always cracking jokes”. The two younger sisters had changed their names to their mother’s maiden name after her death. “Their mother’s death was a hard thing to carry and bear,” their cousin said. “They held a certain level of their feelings to themselves … I believe it was their own coping mechanism.” On the evening on 12 May, the inquest heard, the three women caught a train to Brighton, arriving at 10.20pm, and then took a car to the beachfront near the marina. The Uber driver was struck by the lack of conversation between them, he later told police. Sussex police reviewed hundreds of hours of CCTV to establish that for at least four hours the women paced the seafront in the darkness. They were picked up periodically in snatches of footage, last being seen at 2.42am. It was a windy night and the sea was particularly rough, Cullimore told the inquest. Emergency services were called after a cyclist reported seeing a body on the beach shortly before 5.45am. Jane was brought to shore by an RNLI crew and declared dead at the scene. Christina’s body was also located by the lifeboat crew. Rebecca’s body was recovered from Brighton beach where it appeared to have been washed to shore. None of the women had been able to swim. Cullimore told the inquest he had “remained open-minded throughout and always considered whether there was third-party involvement” but he was now satisfied there had not been. There was no evidence that any of the sisters had used drugs or alcohol, and no indication of any violence. The coroner found that all three had intended to die. “I will record in respect for each of them that on 12 May they entered the sea at West Beach, Brighton, to end their lives,” she said. “They could not swim and the conditions were adverse.” In the UK and Ireland, Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org. In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found at befrienders.org

title: Harvey Nichols’ Birmingham store to close in January
summary: Closure will cost at least 60 jobs, while Leeds and Bristol outlets to be converted to Flannels brand
text: Harvey Nichols’ Birmingham store is to close in January, with the loss of at least 60 jobs, while its Leeds and Bristol outlets will be converted to the Flannels brand in a shake-up under Mike Ashley’s Frasers Group. The owner of Sports Direct bought the department store chain, whose headquarters are at the Knightsbridge site in London, for £43m on the day it was put into administration in mid-August. About 1,000 of the group’s 1,200 jobs and six UK stores were saved in that deal. Harvey Nichols’ Oxo Tower restaurant was sold to a separate buyer, saving 130 jobs. The chain’s branches in London, Edinburgh, Birmingham, Leeds and Manchester and Bristol are accompanied by outlets in Riyadh, Dubai, Doha, Kuwait and two in Hong Kong. A further store in Dublin was closed by administrators in September. The Harvey Nichols Group owed about £100m to unsecured creditors at the time of its administration, including dozens of brands from Canada Goose to Victoria Beckham. Ashley previously said he would keep Harvey Nichols’ Knightsbridge and Edinburgh stores, but rebrand the four other UK stores – in Birmingham, Leeds, Manchester and Bristol – as House of Fraser or Flannels. It has now emerged that Frasers plans to close the Birmingham store, which opened 25 years ago, with staff informed earlier this week, as first reported by the fashion trade journal Drapers. Frasers will rebrand Leeds and Bristol to Flannels, while the future for the Manchester, Edinburgh and London Harvey Nichols stores is unclear. Michael Murray, the chief executive of Frasers Group, recently said in a statement about the group’s luxury division: “Our ambition is clear: to continue scaling Frasers Group Luxury globally through organic expansion, acquisitions and strategic investments, creating long-term value for our brand partners, customers and the group.” Ashley has bought a series of struggling premium brands in recent years after starting out with a single sports shop. Frasers bought the House of Fraser department store chain out of administration in 2018 and has since closed about 40 of its 60 stores. It has been building its interests in luxury fashion with the Flannels chain and large stakes in brands such as the British handbag maker Mulberry. The group recently celebrated lifting its stake in the German label Hugo Boss to 48%, just short of taking full control, despite opposition from the company’s board. Frasers did not respond to a request for comment.

title: Israel’s downgrading of UK consulate aims to tighten its hold on Jerusalem
summary: Consulate targeted in sanctions spat has unusual diplomatic status that clashes with Israel’s ambitions to fully annex the city
text: Israel’s attempt to close the British consulate general in Jerusalem was primarily designed to deter London from imposing sanctions on settlements in occupied Palestine. But it also served the current government’s ambitions to fully annex Jerusalem as a national capital, diplomatic and legal experts said. The UK mission to the city has an unusual diplomatic status, which dates back to before the founding of the state of Israel, rooted in a vision of Jerusalem as a neutral enclave under international control. Unlike other consulates general around the world, it is not a satellite of the British embassy in Tel Aviv. Instead its diplomats are part of an independent team, who report directly to London. That is anathema to those in Israel who claim all of Jerusalem as their territory. Israeli forces occupied East Jerusalem in 1967, and the Knesset passed a law annexing the city in 1980, but that status has not been recognised by most of the world. Gideon Sa’ar, the Israeli foreign minister, threatened to close the consulate general a month ago in an attempt to deter the UK government from proceeding with plans to bar trade with West Bank settlements and put sanctions on companies that provide them with services including financing. The UK threatened to respond with a mass expulsion of diplomats but the two countries appear to have backed away from a full-blown diplomatic spat as Israel prepares for national elections, due on 27 October. Britain will rebrand its consulate general ⁠as a UK “mission” and reduce the number of diplomats, but it will remain independent of Tel Aviv in a compromise one source described as a temporary “ceasefire”. If Israel gets a new leader in three weeks, negotiations on the status of the consulate and its staff could resume. Maintaining a foothold in Jerusalem and the independent status of UK diplomats was important, said Daniel Seidemann, an Israeli lawyer and expert in the geopolitics of Jerusalem who has advised western diplomats including a British foreign secretary. “The arrangement that the UK arrived at with Israel was probably the optimal among a number of options that were even worse. So I’m not faulting anybody, but this is far from a victory,” he said. “The British presence in Jerusalem after almost a century and a half has been downgraded from one of the diplomatic mission to another office. And that is a stark qualitative change.” There are seven other consulates general in East Jerusalem, all opened before 1948, representing their nations’ interests in Jerusalem and occupied Palestine. Like the UK one, they are independent and report directly to their foreign ministries. They have long been a particular thorn in Israel’s side because of their unusual status, which reflects the designation of Jerusalem as “corpus separatum”, an independent body, under the UN’s 1947 partition plan for historic Palestine. Never implemented, it envisaged Jerusalem as a sort of Vatican-like independent enclave, under international administration. That clashes with Israel’s claim on the city, and Sa’ar’s attack on the consulate should be seen in that context, and not purely as a response to sanctions. “This is part of the overall attempt to establish the primacy of a very specific Jewish-Israeli Jerusalem,” Seidemann said. “Any diplomatic presence in Jerusalem that does not pay fealty to the government of Israel and Israel’s sole sovereignty is targeted.” Other countries have missions based in Ramallah to manage relations with Palestinians, but these are technically subsidiary to Tel Aviv embassies. The US had a consulate general but closed it after Donald Trump recognised Jerusalem as the capital of Israel during his first presidency. The UK sanctions plan represents the most consequential attempt by one of Israel’s allies to halt settlement expansion in the occupied West Bank. Israeli banks are rattled by a proposal they fear could affect their business, Haaretz reported on Thursday. An assessment by Israel’s Association of Banks laid out concerns that they could be affected, and they are refusing to say whether they will provide financial guarantees needed to underpin construction contracts for the E1 settlement in the West Bank. When Ed Miliband, the UK foreign secretary, announced his plans, he said the timing was driven partly by the Israeli government’s decision to put out tenders for this project. Israel’s finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, has boasted that it will “bury” the possibility of a Palestinian state by severing parts of the occupied West Bank. Ilan Baruch, a former Israeli ambassador to South Africa, left diplomatic service to advocate for a two-state solution, including pushing foreign governments to move beyond condemnations of Israeli policy to imposing a “meaningful price”. The threats to Britain’s Jerusalem consulate were a sign the UK had finally done that. “I was relieved [by Israel’s position], realising Miliband touched a nerve,” he said. Renaming the consulate while preserving its independent status indicated Israel had stepped back from confrontation, helped by Britain making smaller “face-saving” concessions, he said.

title: MoD has objected to four windfarms in past year over radar interference fears
summary: Complaints risks putting tdefence ministry on collision course with Department for Energy Security and Net Zero
text: The Ministry of Defence has objected to at least four planned windfarms in the past year over fears the spinning blades could cause “unacceptable interference” with radars used to detect military aircraft. MoD officials raised concerns in late June over plans for an onshore windfarm in County Durham that could result in aircraft “not being detected” within an RAF Low Flying Area, according to a letter to Britain’s planning authority. The objection to the planned Hope Moor project, which could see 23 turbines built to heights of 200m, is understood to be the latest of at least four objections made against a planned windfarm on national security grounds in the last year. The complaint risks putting the MoD on a collision course with the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ), which ended a decade-long block on onshore wind developments in England when Labour came to power in 2024 after it was put in place by the Conservatives almost 10 years earlier. The government aims to double the UK’s onshore wind power capacity by 2030, and has designated Hope Moor a nationally significant project whose fate will be decided upon by the energy secretary. The MoD has also warned against plans to build an onshore windfarm of six turbines at Burton Agnes, near Driffield in the East Yorkshire Wolds, and of the “unmanageable” risk of building a 13-turbine windfarm near the Scottish borders. Meanwhile, plans for a far larger offshore windfarm in the Irish Sea have also raised concern within the ministry on the grounds that the proposed 87-turbine array could interfere with aviation radar systems at the Warton Aerodrome base in Lancashire, on the west coast of the UK. The MoD has a long history of objecting to windfarm developments, but industry sources note that the precautionary concerns do not usually rule out development. The “well-trodden path to the negotiating table” usually leads to minor adjustments to the size or height of the turbines, which means they can move ahead, they said. However, the ministry’s “routine” interventions are often used by those opposed to windfarms to support their campaigns, the sources added. Hope Moor is one of four windfarms under fire from the “Not One Moor” campaign, led by former England cricketer Lord Botham. Others include the Scout Moor windfarm in Lancashire, the Walshaw Moor windfarm in West Yorkshire and Ray Fell windfarm in Northumberland. Angus Thompson, a Conservative councillor in North Yorkshire, said: “The MoD’s stark warning is the nail in the coffin for this scheme … This hopeless project should be abandoned without delay.” Alexandre Davies, the head of aviation at trade group Renewable UK, said the industry “works closely” to find solutions to radar issues, “and has done so for many years” to “deliver projects faster”. A DESNZ spokesperson said: “We work closely with the Ministry of Defence. All onshore wind projects are subject to a rigorous planning process in which defence and security, the views of the local community and impacts on the environment are considered.” The MoD was approached for comment.
