title: British consulate in East Jerusalem will stay open as UK mission, says Ed Miliband
summary: UK and Israel back away from full diplomatic confrontation, though British presence in Palestine will be much reduced
text: Israel and the UK have backed away from a full-scale diplomatic confrontation, with Britain announcing it is rebranding its consulate general ⁠building in ⁠East Jerusalem as a UK mission, a move that will result in UK diplomats leaving the region, with only seven to remain in the building. Among those leaving is the consul general, Helen Winterton. The change was forced on the UK by the Israeli government as punishment for the decision by the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, last month to ban trade with illegal settlements and introduce a tougher sanctions regime against those who aided the building of settlements. The UK is seeking to protect the two-state solution as the best means of ending the Israel-Palestine conflict. Miliband has also backed away from a threat to expel a parallel number of Israeli diplomats from London, as was once planned, arguing it would be unwise to do so during the Israeli election campaign. There has been a dispute within the UK government over whether taking tough measures against Israel at such a sensitive political moment could help the re-election chances of the prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, before polls on 27 October if they appear to boost his standing as a leader prepared to confront the nation’s critics. Israel had ordered the ‌British consulate ‌in East Jerusalem to shut on Thursday, and the foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, said that it had acted on its threat, describing the consulate as closed. The consulate is separate from the UK embassy, based in Tel Aviv, and has a distinct diplomatic role, covering East Jerusalem, the rest of the West Bank and Gaza, where it provides consular services to Palestinians. Miliband said in a statement: “The UK government reiterates its longstanding view that East Jerusalem is occupied territory.” Miliband said the mission remained independent, by which he meant it will continue to report directly to the UK Foreign Office in London rather than through the UK embassy in Tel Aviv. One former Foreign Office diplomat said: “Israel has always wanted to shut the consulates in Jerusalem […] Israel will come for the French next.” Sa’ar listed four actions to curtail UK activity in Israel, including the removal of British representatives from the International Gaza Support Center in Kiryat Gat and entry bans to Israel for 12 named individuals, including the former Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn. “We established a clear principle: It is not possible to act against Israel without Israel taking appropriate measures in response,” he said. “We did not want to reach this point, but the actions of the UK Labour government brought us here.” He also accused the UK government of “hostile rhetoric, including false accusations against Israel, such as accusations of ‘ethnic cleansing’”. Miliband, who is in Kyiv, said in a statement that, having ‌withdrawn a number of staff and families in recent weeks partly for security reasons, it would be possible to work to build up the staffing at the mission in future months. He said Britain would ⁠not take any reciprocal action against Israel while the two sides engaged in talks, in effect suspending discussions until a new Israeli government is formed. UK sources said Sa’ar had threatened to close the whole consulate, and that it was better for Britain to retain its reduced presence in the hope it could be restored and rebuilt, regardless of the imminent election outcome. The sources emphasised that the right to take reciprocal action remained, and the UK did not accept that Israel had the legal right to close the consulate, which has stood for 200 years and is in East Jerusalem on territory that Britain and international courts recognise as occupied territory. It was thought not feasible to defy Israel since the UK diplomats would have no security protection. Miliband said the UK mission would be independent, operational and still able to provide vital services to the Palestinian people. The value of that assertion will be tested by the small number of diplomats remaining and their reduced diplomatic status. The UK national security adviser, Jonathan Powell, travelled to Israel last week to negotiate a version of the deal. Vincent Fean, the UK consul general to Palestine between 2010 and 2014, said: “The term mission is a generic diplomatic term and does not of itself have any meaning … In terms of numbers, losing 20 staff is a big drop but it’s a better outcome than nothing. It leaves a space, a place and team to build up whatever the outcome of the Israeli election.” Diplomats from other western countries had been worried about any closure setting a precedent, and suggested Britain had to respond strongly to the Israeli move because it had implications beyond the immediate dispute. The ‌incident has highlighted growing frustration among Israel’s longtime allies over its settlements in the occupied West Bank, viewed by much of the world as illegal under international law. In his statement last month to the UK parliament, Miliband said settler terrorists, supported by Netanyahu’s government, were committing ethnic cleansing in the West Bank. Israel disputes this. The UK Foreign Office was advised informally by the former attorney general Dominic Grieve that Israel would be acting unlawfully if it closed the consulate on the basis it was sited in East Jerusalem, which is recognised by the UN and most of its members as being occupied Palestinian territory. Israel has also said it will revoke the credentials of Dutch diplomats from the country’s mission to Palestine in response to the Netherlands’ ban on imports from illegal Israeli settlements. France and Canada, which joined the UK in the settlement trade ban, have not had action taken against them. UK-Israeli relations have deteriorated steadily during the war in Gaza, prompted by Hamas’s 7 October 2023 attack on Israel, as Britain has become increasingly critical of the way in which Netanyahu seems prepared to tolerate the deaths of thousands of Palestinians in an effort to render Hamas inoperative, a task successive Westminster governments have thought is unachievable through his methods. The UK has rescinded a large number of arms export licences to Israel, and Miliband has spoken of evidence of war crimes in Gaza. He has declined to accuse Israel of genocide on the grounds he believed this a matter for international courts to determine.

title: Bank governor urges John Healey to use budget to allay market fears amid bond turmoil
summary: Andrew Bailey tells chancellor ‘whatever the stance of fiscal policy, it must be credible and be seen as such by financial markets’
text: The Bank of England governor, Andrew Bailey, has urged the chancellor, John Healey, to agree a budget that reassures financial markets after the UK’s medium-term borrowing costs hit a fresh 19-year high. With investors offloading government bonds previously considered safe havens amid fears of rising inflation, Bailey told all governments caught in the crosshairs of financial speculators that they needed to avoid market turmoil that raises the interest paid on debt. Recent dramatic moves in government bond markets have been driven by international factors, but will increase the pressure on Healey ahead of his tax and spending announcement on 28 October. The yield, or interest rate, on 10-year UK government bonds had risen 0.06 percentage points by lunchtime in London, to 5.515%. That was the highest level since July 2007, when the global financial crisis was starting to unfold. Yields on 20- and 30-year UK government bonds, which are known as gilts, also rose significantly, to their highest level since as long ago as 1998. Yields go up when bond prices go down. Yields later dropped back on a day of volatile trading, but analysts said further conflict in the Middle East would push them up again as concerns increased about inflation becoming embedded in many major economies. Meanwhile, the benchmark oil price rose by more than 5% to $105.3 a barrel amid escalating tensions in the Middle East and a squeeze on production from the threat of a hurricane off the US coast. Diesel prices at UK pumps hit £2 a litre last week, leading to concerns among central banks that inflation will surge over the coming months, leading to higher interest rates and burgeoning government debt financing costs. Speaking at a conference in Istanbul, Bailey said he would not meddle in government policy, but he had one observation for Healey after the recent bond rout dramatically increased UK borrowing costs. “Whatever the stance of fiscal policy, it must be credible and be seen as such by financial markets,” he said. Realistic commitments to rein in debt would help curb demands ‌for higher returns from investors who might sell when there were shocks like the outbreak of the Iran war, he said. “In other words, such commitments are needed more than ever when these negative shocks occur.” Economists believe rising borrowing costs and a weaker growth outlook are likely to have wiped out around half of the £24bn buffer against Labour’s fiscal rules that Healey’s predecessor, Rachel Reeves, built up at the time of her spring statement in March – perhaps significantly more. Healey is expected to raise taxes at the budget to partly rebuild that cushion, as well as paying for policy interventions including the six-month VAT cut on electricity bills and a modest energy support package for the poorest households. Some economists are warning the chancellor not to go too far in rebuilding the Treasury’s headroom, however. Andrew Wishart, of Berenberg Bank, said: “Raising taxes to keep the surplus close to the size it was in the March forecast (ie to ‘maintain the headroom’) would do unnecessary damage to economic incentives.” He argues that gilt yields are likely to come back down over the next year, with the Bank of England likely to make fewer rate rises than the four that investors currently expect. The Bank is widely expected to raise interest rates at its November meeting to tackle surging inflation, echoing moves already made by the European Central Bank, Federal Reserve and Bank of Japan. The bond selloff has intensified across big economies in recent days, as oil prices have soared, with no resolution of the Middle East conflict in sight. Investors appear to be anxious about higher inflation and runaway government spending. France has been hardest hit, as Paris battles to pass a budget, but the selloff has been widespread. Reuters reported that European Central Bank officials and eurozone finance ministers were preparing on Thursday to make representations to the French government to pass a 2027 budget to calm bond ⁠markets. Investors are worried about the country’s large budget deficit and 2027 presidential election. Its ⁠10-year bond yield has jumped nearly 80 basis points since the start of September and hit its highest level since July 2002, just short of 5%. An EU official said finance ministers were unlikely to make a public plea, but would call for a budget that brought down annual borrowing. “That’s kind of a no-brainer. So I would expect this to be the main message,” the official said. Kristalina Georgieva, managing director of the International Monetary Fund (IMF), has urged governments to tighten their belts in response to rising bond yields. “My message to the world’s economic policymakers will be this: we cannot keep delaying necessary policy action – you have the tools, now have the wisdom to use them,” she said, ahead of next week’s IMF annual meeting in Bangkok. Higher yields not only push up costs for indebted governments, but have knock-on effects for borrowers across the economy, including homeowners and businesses. The US Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, has tried to rein in yields on the US’s long-term debt by increasing buybacks of its government bonds, known as treasuries, but the policy appears to have had little impact. Yields on the 30-year treasuries targeted by Bessent’s policy were about 5.235% when he announced the doubling of buybacks in August, but have since surged above 5.7%.

title: Honouring Sylvia and Emmeline Pankhurst on stage and in political action | Letter
summary: Letter: As we approach the centenary of equal franchise in 2028, it is important to build on the rights that were won by the suffragettes, writes Helen Pankhurst
text: There was a proud Pankhurst in the audience in Leicester as Sylvia: A Musical Revolution began its national tour (Suffragette cities: blazing Sylvia Pankhurst musical hits the road – in pictures, 3 October). A blazing show indeed – and one that, 98 years after women gained the vote on equal terms with men, asks how much remains to be done, how to do it and how women can bridge their differences to advance their common cause. As Sylvia Pankhurst’s granddaughter and Emmeline Pankhurst’s great-granddaughter, I honour both women. Their political paths diverged. I seek to reconcile their legacies through Centenary Action, the cross-party coalition that I lead, in a shared cause: dismantling the barriers to women’s participation, selection and retention in politics. Also in the audience were Philippa, a relative of Emily Wilding Davison, and Peter, a relative of Alice Hawkins. The connections endure – and so does the activism. Remembering past sacrifices means protecting the rights won and building on those struggles as we approach the centenary of equal franchise in 2028. As Emmeline said: “You must make women count as much as men.” And as Sylvia said: “Great is the work that remains to be accomplished.” Helen Pankhurst Convener, Centenary Action • Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Please email us your letter and it will be considered for publication in our letters section.

title: Search warrants used in Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor raids were unlawful, court rules
summary: ‘Technical errors’ are embarrassing for Thames Valley police but unlikely to affect outcome of investigation
text: Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor has won his legal challenge against Thames Valley police over search warrants used to raid his home after they arrested him. The former prince brought a judicial review of the legality of the force’s actions and those of the central criminal court, which granted the warrants. On Thursday, Mr Justice Hilliard, sitting at the high court in central London, said Thames Valley police (TVP) had conceded that it obtained the search powers under the wrong statutory provision and ruled that the warrants were unlawful. The episode is embarrassing for TVP but police believe it will not affect the success of the investigation. The warrants were issued by an Old Bailey judge on 18 February and Mountbatten-Windsor was subsequently arrested the following day, on his 66th birthday, on suspicion of misconduct in public office. The arrest followed information that emerged from the Jeffrey Epstein files. It was alleged that when Mountbatten-Windsor was the UK’s trade envoy he shared sensitive information with Epstein, a convicted child sex offender. Police began searching the former Duke of York’s residence on the Sandringham estate and his former Windsor home, Royal Lodge, on the same day as his arrest. Documentary material and electronic devices were seized. Hilliard said the search warrants were quashed but police had made an application, which would be heard next year, to retain the seized property on the basis that it would have been lawful to take it under a different statutory provision. Mountbatten-Windsor opposes that application. The judge said: “The fact that the search warrants were quashed does not bring the investigation to an end or mean that the whole of the investigation is unlawful.” A senior police source said: “It’s not going to bring the investigation to a halt or affect the chances of success.” They added: “The news media might say the police messed up. But it was the judicial decision [to grant the warrant] that was incorrect.” TVP have been in discussions with lawyers from the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) about the strength of their case and what evidence they would need for a prosecution. A TVP spokesperson said: “The agreement that led to the quashing of the warrants relates specifically to a decision made by the court regarding the legal basis for these and is not a judgment on our ongoing investigation. “We ensured the court was presented with all the necessary information and paperwork to inform their decision, following the correct legal processes throughout. “We accept the position that the initial court’s decision to issue warrants under the specific piece of legislation used was incorrect and therefore these must be legally quashed.” Hilliard told the court that the grant of a search warrant under section eight of the Police and Criminal Evidence Act (Pace) 1984 was conditional on the issuing judge being satisfied there were reasonable grounds to suspect that the material sought did not include items subject to legal privilege or special procedure material. Special procedure material includes documents in possession of a person who acquired them in the course of any trade, business, profession or other occupation – for the purpose of any paid or unpaid office – who holds it subject to an express or implied undertaking to hold it in confidence. The judge said the presence of legally privileged material was expressly envisaged in the application for the search warrants and that material was likely to be in the possession of Mountbatten-Windsor “who had acquired or created it in circumstances which would make it special procedure material”. He concluded that a lawful warrant could only have been issued under section nine of Pace. Nick Vamos, the former head of special crime at the CPS, said: “Given the technical nature of the errors revealed today, I expect the crown court to rule in due course that the police can keep the material, or at least as much of it as they would have been entitled to seize in the first place, so they may not ultimately pay much of a price beyond today’s red faces.” Late last year, King Charles stripped his brother of his right to be a prince and of his dukedom over his association with Epstein. Mountbatten-Windsor receives an annual stipend, the amount of which has not been disclosed, from King Charles’s private funds, but a palace source told reporters it had been made clear this should not be used to fund the judicial review.

title: Ethiopia launches drone attack against Eritrean troops who crossed into Tigray
summary: Government forces’ attack raises risk of internal conflict in Ethiopia that could trigger regional war
text: Eritrean troops who crossed into Ethiopia’s Tigray region have come under drone attack from government forces, raising the risk that renewed internal conflict in Ethiopia could trigger an all-out regional war between the neighbouring countries. Military vehicles carrying soldiers drove across Eritrea’s southern border into Tigray on Wednesday, reaching the town of Adigrat 25 miles (40km) south, according to civilian witnesses, a militia commander and the conflict monitoring group Acled. Eritrean troops were then targeted by Ethiopian government drones on Wednesday evening and Thursday morning, Acled said. Eritrea has a historical enmity with the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), which launched an offensive against the Ethiopian government on 23 September, but that previous hostility has been superseded by Eritrea’s desire to head off a perceived risk of Ethiopia invading it, in order to access the Red Sea. In the last two weeks, the TPLF and six other armed groups in Ethiopia have fought the government in Tigray and the neighbouring regions Amhara and Afar. Ethiopia’s military pushed back and an allied militia, the Tigray Peace Force, took over Tigray’s regional capital, Mekelle, on 4 October after the TPLF withdrew from the city. Eritrea’s information minister, Yemane Ghebremeskel, said in a statement: “We are not in the business of refuting wild allegations or narratives.” He did not explicitly confirm or deny the presence of Eritrean troops in Ethiopia. Ethiopia’s foreign ministry said in a statement on Monday: “Ethiopia stands ready to defend its sovereignty, territorial integrity, and core national interests, while urging all regional actors to address shared challenges through constructive dialogue, partnership, and adherence to the principles of good neighbourliness rather than confrontation and zero-sum approaches.” The TPLF and Ethiopia’s government fought a brutal civil war from 2020 to 2022. Between 300,000 and 800,000 civilians died, according to British government estimates. Both sides and their allies were accused of war crimes. Eritrea intervened on the side of Ethiopia in that conflict, after a rapprochement between the two countries in 2018, which earned Ethiopia’s prime minister, Abiy Ahmed, the 2019 Nobel peace prize. Eritrea, which gained independence from Ethiopia in 1993, has a long enmity with the TPLF, which ruled Ethiopia from 1991 to 2018. The two countries fought a war from 1998 to 2000. Relations between the countries have deteriorated again in recent years. Abiy has said Ethiopia needs access to the Red Sea, and state media has claimed the country has historical rights to the Eritrean port of Assab. The US-Israeli war on Iran – leading Iran to limit shipping through the strait of Hormuz – has further raised the stakes of Red Sea access. In its statement on Monday, Ethiopia’s foreign ministry said: “Any serious discussion of regional maritime affairs and security architecture must account for Ethiopia’s legitimate interests and its enduring connection to the Red Sea.” Yemane said in a post on X on Wednesday that Ethiopia was “incessantly beating the drums of war and openly stating … that it will launch a war of aggression against Eritrea to acquire what it calls ‘sovereign access to the sea’ … In recent weeks, it has tried to repackage this war agenda in terms of ‘self-defence’ by fabricating various allegations against Eritrea.” Magnus Taylor, Horn of Africa deputy director at the Crisis Group thinktank, said: “The big worry is that [Abiy] might try to solve all his problems at the same time, by invading Eritrea, possibly a regime change move and also a land grab for the Red Sea port, and also solving his problem with Tigray at the same time. It’s a very ambitious military agenda, though.” While the full impact of the fighting on Tigrayan civilians is not clear, reports have emerged of the TPLF forcibly recruiting boys as young as 15 to fight. “The civilians in these three regions [Tigray, Amhara and Afar] didn’t get healed from the first round of violence that was halted by the peace agreement [in 2022],” said Acled Ethiopia analyst Jalale Getachew Birru. “They just started healing recently.” Associated Press contributed to this story

title: Florida judge allows lawsuit against Shah of Iran’s alleged ‘chief torturer’ to move forward
summary: Parviz Sabeti denies allegations he led Savak intelligence agency under shah and directed torture of thousands
text: The alleged “chief torturer” for the deposed Shah of Iran is a step closer to trial for human rights abuses after a Florida federal judge rejected his demand to halt a lawsuit brought by three former political prisoners. Parviz Sabeti, who was reported last year to have lived in a quiet upscale central Florida community, is accused of being the former head of Savak, the shah’s secret police and intelligence agency. The plaintiffs say they discovered his whereabouts only after a photo of Sabeti at a 2023 protest against the Iranian government was posted on social media by his daughter. He could now be made to answer as early as next year to civil claims under the Torture Victim Protection Act (TVPA) that he directed and took part in the detention and torture of thousands of the shah’s political opponents in jails in Tehran and elsewhere until the Islamic revolution swept the regime from power in 1979. Sabeti has denied allegations that that he was personally involved or that Savak tortured detainees, and claimed that he “always opposed torture”. Tuesday’s sealed order by the district court judge Gregory A Presnell rejected Sabeti’s argument that a statute of limitations on the allegations should be strictly enforced and a summary judgment issued in his favor. In August 2025, Presnell rejected a motion by Sabeti’s lawyers to dismiss the case outright, ordering the parties to conduct discovery on whether the TVPA claim was time-barred, and said he would listen to arguments about why the deadline should not be extended. Sabeti’s lawyers dispute that he was difficult to find and sue before 2023, filing dozens of documents which they said proved he had lived openly in Florida under his real name, including property records, media articles, and a photograph of Sabeti with George HW Bush and his son Jeb Bush, a former governor of Florida. In May, attorneys for the three Iranian plaintiffs filed a response presenting dozens of documents and articles of their own to try to bolster their argument that there were extraordinary circumstances in the case that warranted an extension of time to bring the claim. They included the Guardian’s September 2025 story that chronicled Sabeti’s departure from Iran and his low-profile new life in Florida, where the lawsuit asserts he “has spent the last four decades out of the public eye, concealing his whereabouts and identity”. As the Guardian reported last year, Sabeti was identified as a fiercely loyal ally of the shah, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, in a secret analysis by the US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) written in 1978, which was not released until 2018. According to the complaint, he was “widely recognized as one of the most powerful and feared men in the shah’s regime … with the authority to apprehend, interrogate and prosecute opponents throughout the country”. The plaintiffs, Iranian men living in California aged 68 to 85, claim they were among thousands of people rounded up as perceived opponents of the shah by Savak, Iran’s notoriously brutal internal security and intelligence agency, and subjected to abuses at Sabeti’s personal direction. Among their claims made under the TVPA are that their captors used rape, electric shocks, near-drownings and forced nail extraction against political prisoners. They say they were abducted by Savak in Tehran, beaten into giving false confessions and served prison time. The lawsuit details the alleged use of a torture device nicknamed Apollo, an electric chair named after the early US space program, which featured a metal helmet that amplified victims’ screams into their own ears. Sabeti has previously insisted he was not involved in the detention, torture or execution of prisoners. A 2023 report on the website of the People’s Mojahedin Organization of Iran, a dissident group, cited an interview Sabeti gave to the Persian channel Manoto in which he characterized his government employment as clerical work. Court papers list seven attorneys for Sabeti. None replied to the Guardian’s request for comment by the time of publication. Claret Vargas, senior staff attorney for the Center for Justice and Accountability, an advocacy group representing the three Iranian plaintiffs, welcomed Presnell’s ruling, which she said allows the case to move forward towards discovery on the TVPA allegations against Sabeti. The court previously dismissed the state law claims. “I’m very glad that our clients will be able to pursue justice after all these years, and everybody deserves justice for torture regardless of who was in charge, or the regime that tortured them,” she said. “Perpetrators of torture should not escape accountability simply because the survivors were forced to live with fear for decades. “We don’t yet know the specific legal basis for the court’s decision, but it’s a really important milestone for our clients to be able to bring forth this case and really address [their allegations].” Donald Trump’s war in Iran has brought new scrutiny of the resilience of the country’s hardline Islamic regime, and the strength of the opposition to it among a sizable Iranian expat community in the US. Washington DC-based Reza Pahlavi, the former shah’s son, has positioned himself as a possible new leader if the current regime falls, although questions remain over his level of popular support. In June, Pahlavi, 65, was forced to distance himself from far-right supporters who flew banners and wore shirts with the Savak emblem at rallies. Divisions between various opposition groups of Iranians in the US were highlighted by the killing in Canada earlier this year of the Iranian activist Masood Masjoody, a critic of the US-led war and the campaign to install Pahlavi as the country’s next leader. According to the Associated Press, Masjoody’s sudden disappearance in February was followed by a threatening post on X in Farsi directed at other activists by a since-deleted account named for Savak.

title: Trump says he is considering asking FBI to investigate the death of Nolan Wells
summary: Lawyers for Wells’s family have called for a federal investigation into 18-year-old’s disappearance and death
text: On Wednesday, Donald Trump said he was considering asking the FBI to investigate the death of Nolan Wells, a Black college freshman who was last seen alive on a 4 July boating trip with friends. Wells, 18, went missing while on Horn Island, a barrier island off the coast of Mississippi. His body was found on the island two days later. Wells’s cause and manner of death are still undetermined. His disappearance and subsequent death have become a flashpoint for racial animosity in the country, drawing national scrutiny. During the Jackson county investigation into the case, social media became rife with misinformation about Wells, his family and his friends. Wells’s mother, Christine Wells-Wonsley, started searching for him, leading to a photo of Wells with three white friends on a boat going viral. In the months between Wells’s body being found and a Jackson county grand jury declining to indict anyone in his case, many have suggested that the treatment Wells’s family has received by local officials would have been different if they were white. Wells’s family and Ben Crump, the civil rights lawyer who is representing the family, have called for a federal investigation into Wells’s disappearance and death, after a Jackson county grand jury’s decision to decline to indict anyone in the case. The Jackson county grand jury determined that Wells drowned. However, an independent autopsy conducted by the president of the Howard University hospital, Roger A Mitchell Jr, a forensic pathologist, determined there was no evidence of drowning due to the absence of water in Wells’s stomach, lungs and throat. That autopsy also noted bruising on Well’s head, back, left shoulder and buttocks. “We do not believe Nolan drowned, and the blunt force trauma to his head cannot be ignored or explained away,” Crump said in a statement. “Nolan’s family deserves the truth, and we will keep fighting until every question is answered and justice is served.” On Tuesday, Crump and Wells’s parents joined Cynthia Choi, Stop AAPI Hate’s executive director, in calling for a federal investigation into Wells’s death and disappearance. The California congresswoman Maxine Waters, the Florida congresswoman Frederica Wilson and others also sent a letter to Jessica Bowron, the acting director of the US National Park Service (NPS), noting that most of Horn Island is federally designated land and calling on the NPS’s investigative services branch to open a “prompt and exhaustive investigation” into Wells’s disappearance and death. “Today, I am asking the people whose job it is to serve and protect to keep their word to our family,” Elmore Wonsley, Wells’s father, said at the press conference. “Our son was found on federal land, and we are asking the FBI to step in and do a full investigation. We’re not asking for special treatment. We’re asking for what any father would do for his child, and that’s to find the truth about what happened to his child.” As he was leaving the White House, reporters asked Trump whether he planned to push the FBI to launch an independent investigation into Wells’s death. “Well, we’re looking at that,” he said. “Yes, we are.” “Sunday will mark 100 days since we have been looking into the death of Nolan Wells, so when President Trump responds to news reporters that ‘we’re looking into it’, we believe that carries more weight than the response given by the FBI,” Crump said in a statement. “Our team stands ready to work with the federal government to ensure Nolan’s death is investigated to the fullest extent.”

title: E.ON Next deal to buy Ovo Energy leaves UK with just ‘big three’ energy suppliers
summary: Competition watchdog clears takeover despite concerns that suppliers will have less incentive to lower bills
text: Almost three-quarters of households in Great Britain are now served by just three energy suppliers, after E.ON Next completed a deal to buy Ovo Energy despite fresh concerns about competition in the energy market. The takeover concluded on Thursday after Britain’s competition watchdog cleared it, despite concerns that the shrinking number of household energy suppliers could mean bill payers will have less choice and suppliers will have less incentive to lower bills. While there will be no immediate change for the 4 million households supplied by Ovo, the sale means that E.ON Next, which already supplies 5.6 million households, will hold 25% of the household energy market – or 13.45m gas and electricity accounts – and become Great Britain’s second-largest energy supplier. The supplier’s hold on the market is narrowly behind Octopus Energy, which holds a 26% share or 14.3m accounts, and ahead of legacy energy incumbent British Gas, which was once the top supplier but today serves about 23% of the market or 12.5m accounts. It also deals a blow to the decade-long efforts to dismantle the dominance of what were the “Big Six” energy suppliers to increase competition and lower energy prices. Tom Goswell, the energy supply lead at Cornwall Insight, a leading consultancy, said: “The big six have become the big three, and there have been questions raised over how this will impact household choice and the health of the market.” Those concerns were rebuffed by Chris Norbury, chief executive of E.ON UK, who described the market as “fiercely competitive” and said the company’s “flexibility and scale” would allow it to “deliver for customers now and to transform for the energy system to come”. The legacy big six suppliers – British Gas, EDF Energy, E.ON UK, SSE, Scottish Power and npower – dominated about 85% of the energy market in 2016 when a landmark investigation by the CMA warned that customers were overpaying by roughly £1.4bn to £1.7bn every year due to weak market competition. As a result of the E.ON deal, about 90% of Great Britain’s household energy supply market will be held by only five suppliers when including EDF Energy and Scottish Power alongside the big three. Although there was a surge in new energy start-ups after 2016 – led by Octopus, Ovo and Bulb Energy – the market began to shrink after SSE sold its household supply business to Ovo in 2019, and dozens of suppliers went bust during the 2021/22 energy crisis. Octopus became the biggest supplier in the market after taking on 1.5 million customers from Bulb, which became the biggest casualty when it went into administration in 2022. “Larger suppliers do bring with them a degree of stability, and after about 30 firms dropped out of the market, leaving customers wondering who would be sending their next bill, stability is not something to dismiss lightly,” Goswell said. “The concern with fewer suppliers is that the pressure to compete eases off, taking with it some of the incentive to keep prices low and offer something different. The big suppliers have the resources to give people real choice, and the test over the next few years will be whether households who shop around find a genuine range of deals waiting for them rather than three versions of the same thing,” he added.

title: ‘Entitled’ ex-police chief guilty of gross misconduct over affairs with junior officers
summary: Scott Chilton, who led Hampshire and the Isle of Wight police force, barred from becoming a police officer again
text: A former chief constable showed a sense of entitlement, dishonesty and lack of integrity by having sexual relationships with two subordinate officers, including engaging in sexual activity while on call to lead major incidents, a misconduct hearing has ruled. The panel found that the behaviour of Scott Chilton, 53, who retired as chief constable of Hampshire and the Isle of Wight before the hearing, amounted to gross misconduct. Chilton was found to have had “consensual sexual relations” when he was a chief inspector or superintendent with a woman identified as Officer A, including while he was on duty. When he applied to be chief constable – and during his tenure – he “repetitively and dishonestly” denied this relationship. The hearing in Eastleigh, Hampshire, was told that a consensual relationship with another woman, Officer B, began within weeks of Chilton becoming chief constable. He was found to have “abused his position for a sexual purpose” and should have declared the relationship. When it came to light, he “behaved inappropriately” to Officer B, putting pressure on her to conceal what had happened. Chairing the panel, Michelle Skeer of His Majesty’s Inspectorate of Constabulary and Fire & Rescue Services said Chilton’s behaviour showed “persistent dishonesty and lack of integrity”. She said his actions suggested he did not think the rules applied to him. “He was in the highest position of trust as the most senior officer in the constabulary and ought to have known the foreseeable risk of harm by having a covert relationship,” Skeer said. “He repeatedly lied by act and omission about both his relationships with Officer A and Officer B and he knew that this was wrong. His conduct was a serious, deliberate and sustained attempt to mislead … to subvert any negative impact on himself.” Skeer said Chilton had been privy to confidential and sensitive information on colleagues, security and national policing matters. “There was evidence that he was discussing issues which he shouldn’t have been discussing with Officer B during WhatsApp message exchanges.” She added that Chilton had attempted to bully Officer B into “keeping quiet” by asking her to “delete and double delete” their messages and not to go to events that his wife would attend, which showed the power imbalance between them. She said Chilton had engaged in sexual activity with Officer A while on duty and in silver command, which meant he would have been the officer in charge if a major incident had occurred. Skeer added that “his actions were driven by his own entitlement” and the “abuse of his position was for personal gain and ultimately his own sexual gratification”. She said Chilton had acted in a domineering fashion towards his colleagues in an attempt to “control the narrative” in relation to responding to press inquiries about the allegations. Attention also focused during the hearing on disciplinary proceedings against another prominent Hampshire police officer, the former DCI Roger Wood. In February 2025 a disciplinary hearing concluded Wood had inappropriate relations with two junior colleagues and would have been dismissed had he not already resigned. Before his case, Wood claimed to have “damaging information” about Chilton and during the proceedings stated that the chief had “had affairs”. John Beggs KC, who presented the case against the former chief constable, said Chilton had discussed using the force solicitor to prevent Wood from speaking to the press, adding: “He was trying to use his position as a chief constable to advance his own best interests.” Since Chilton became chief constable in February 2023, there have been about 20 misconduct cases in Hampshire in which officers were accused of various forms of sexual behaviour. About five of these have included behaviour against junior officers. Chilton retired in April 2025 after a career spanning 33 years that included acting as a lead for the National Police Chiefs’ Council on national investigation standards and coordination. At the start of the hearing, James Berry KC, representing Chilton, said his client would not be attending the hearing because of “medical issues”. Chilton said in a statement that he admitted the second relationship but not the first. He said he accepted that by not disclosing that relationship he fell short of the standards police officers were judged by. He added: “These were personal matters, rather than issues affecting policing or public safety, and at no point did this relationship influence policing decisions, operational matters or the discharge of professional responsibilities.” He said his “deepest regret” was for his family “for the hurt caused by my poor judgment and actions”. Chilton would have been dismissed if he had not resigned, the panel said. He has been placed on the College of Policing barred officers list, so he can never again become a police officer.

title: Former Labour MP cleared over role in fraudulent Covid-19 testing company
summary: Court hears former justice minister Shahid Malik had only ‘very limited’ role in business that made £6.67m in three weeks
text: A former Labour MP and justice minister has been found not guilty of charges around his role in a fraudulent Covid-19 testing company. Shahid Malik, 58, was MP for Dewsbury between 2005 and 2010 and served as a minister in three departments in Gordon Brown’s government. Malik was one of five people charged with offences relating to RT Diagnostics, a company that prosecutors said was a “cash cow” set up to take advantage of the UK government’s expanding test-and-trace system in March 2021. On Thursday, Malik was found not guilty of fraudulent trading, causing a public nuisance and money laundering in a trial at Bradford crown court, which was, unusually, conducted without a jury. The trial began in October last year and jurors were sent out to start their deliberations in March. In April, they were discharged by Judge Smith after an allegation of jury tampering. Smith took the decision to continue the trial without the jury, and that he would decide on the verdicts. The court heard that Malik started the business with the pharmacist and former Labour councillor Faisal Shoukat, 39, when the third national lockdown was ending in March 2021. Shoukat was found guilty of all three offences. Paul Moore, 57, who had a senior role in RT Diagnostics and was Malik’s office manager when he was an MP, was cleared of causing a public nuisance and of fraudulent trading. Lynn Connell, 64, a manager at the company, and Alexander Zarneh, 70, who was its clinical director, were also cleared of the same two offences. Prosecutors said RT Diagnostics, which made £6.67m in three weeks, was set up in “shoddy and inadequate premises” in Halifax and gave out false negative results to customers. The defence barrister, Jonathan Laidlaw KC, said Malik’s role in the business had been “very limited indeed” and he had acted as “a facilitator – putting the money up and making introductions”. Giving his closing speech to jurors in March, Laidlaw said Malik never went to the premises when it was in operation. He told the court that for most of the time the business was operating, Malik was out of the country and there was no evidence he was told about any of its issues while he was abroad. Laidlaw said the fact that the former MP had made money from RT Diagnostics “can’t possibly be the basis for a guilty verdict”. The court heard that as the third national lockdown was ending in March 2021, the government was looking to expand its test-and-trace system by increasing the number of laboratories offering PCR testing. The defendants were accused of “taking advantage” of that process with an “inadequate and non-compliant” testing company which, prosecutor Jonathan Sandiford KC said, “generated a suspiciously low number of positive results”. Sandiford said the Halifax laboratory was set up in inadequate premises with holes in the walls and ceilings, and rubbish strewn around. Jurors heard that the company employed “numerous young people who had little or no training in the handling of Covid-19 samples” and set them to work with no social distancing and no personal protective equipment. Malik and Sadiq Khan, now London mayor, were the first British-born Muslims to become MPs, and Malik was the first to become a government minister. He was appointed as an international development minister in 2007 and he later had ministerial jobs at the Department of Justice and the Department for Communities and Local Government.

title: Russian attack on bus kills at least 30 people near Ukraine frontline
summary: Zelenskyy says Kremlin deliberately targeted ‘ordinary public transport stop’ in Kramatorsk, with 18 wounded
text: A Russian missile strike on a bus in the eastern city of Kramatorsk has killed at least 30 people, officials have said, in one of the worst attacks by Moscow on Ukrainian civilians this year. The regional prosecutor’s office in the Donetsk region said on Thursday the vehicle had been hit at 10am by an aerial bomb. “As of now, the death toll from this morning’s attack has risen to 30. Eighteen people were wounded,” it said, adding that all local public transport had been suspended. Images posted by police ‌showed bodies ‌strewn across a street littered with debris, as well ‌as a charred shell of what appeared to be a bus. A second bus had also caught fire, officials said. The strike targeted an area next to a dental clinic on the city’s Yuvileina Street. Three people had also been killed by shelling in the village of Bilenke, outside Kramatorsk, they added. Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the Kremlin had deliberately targeted an “ordinary public transport stop”. Some of those killed could not be identified because of the severity of their injuries, Ukraine’s president added. He said the number of victims could “sadly rise”, as doctors fought to save the lives of those wounded. He said: “This strike will not go unanswered. Russia is trying to destroy all life in Donbas, and a response from the world is a must. A forceful response – exactly as the Russians deserve for all the deaths they have brought. May all those killed rest in peace.” The bombing follows a gruesome Russian strike on Wednesday on a five-storey block of flats in Pryluky in the northern Chernihiv region. The building collapsed, entombing those inside. At least 22 people were killed, including five children, aged between one and eight. Visiting the scene with Ed Miliband, the British foreign secretary, Zelenskyy urged the US to expand Starlink satellite internet coverage so that Ukraine could hit targets inside Russia such as launch sites. So far, Donald Trump and Elon Musk have refused Kyiv’s request. Miliband said there was “no clearer sign of Putin’s evil, evil intent and strategy in this conflict” than this week’s murderous attacks. He said: “Putin once said that he was going to win on the battlefield. He is trying to win by terrorising civilians.” Writing earlier on social media, Zelenskyy called on western allies to take “concrete steps” to boost Ukraine’s depleted air defences, amid a round-the-clock Russian onslaught in recent weeks featuring ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones. “Supplies of anti-ballistic capabilities, ammunition for our combat aircraft, and investments in interceptors – all of this is directly helping save lives every day. Important talks with our partners will take place today and tomorrow,” Zelenskyy said. Kramatorsk and neighbouring Sloviansk form part of a “fortress belt”. They are the last two big cities in northern Donetsk under full Ukrainian military control. Russia has been trying to capture them for more than a decade, after a brief period in which Russian forces occupied Sloviansk in 2014. The cities are home to thousands of civilians, as well as Ukrainian soldiers. In recent months, roads have been festooned with nets to protect traffic from marauding enemy drones. These defences offer little protection, however, against aerial bombs. “These are not ‘the consequences of war’, nor dry statistics. These are people killed by the Russian army,” the Donetsk regional governor, Vadym Filashkin, said ‌on Telegram after Thursday’s strike. “Russia comes to Ukrainian land with death.” He added: “The Russians are deliberately targeting civilians. For them, a bus full of passengers is an attractive target precisely because a single strike can kill as many people as possible. “Russia deliberately flouts every conceivable rule of warfare and the norms of international humanitarian law. It selects targets where it can inflict the greatest suffering on civilians.” There was criticism of the White House’s policy of engaging with Vladimir Putin, whom Donald Trump has invited to December’s G20 summit in Miami, Florida. The Kremlin has yet to say if Russia’s leader will take part. The former US ambassador to Moscow Michael McFaul said on social media that Russia was guilty of terrorism. “There is no other word for it. Putin is running a terrorist state. That officials from my country call this terrorist a nice guy is deeply embarrassing for me.” Putin has demanded Ukraine cede the rest of the eastern Donbas region still under its control. Kyiv refuses to hand over its territory, believing Russia will take any concessions and carry on fighting.

title: Asos says customers’ names, contact details and search histories hacked
summary: Experts say breadth of data accessed could help attackers devise “highly convincing” phishing scams
text: Asos hackers gained access to millions of customers’ recent search histories as well as names, addresses and phone numbers, the online fashion retailer has revealed. Terms typed in by customers such as “glamorous wide fit” and “Asos petite” were in the data accessed in the cyber-attack, which emerged on Tuesday after app users received a notification titled “Asos hacked” with a link to the Telegram messaging service. After carrying out a “detailed, 48-hour investigation” into the incident, Asos confirmed on Thursday that basic personal information had been accessed by an unidentified third party. This included delivery and email addresses, names and phone numbers. Experts said the extra information could help attackers devise “highly convincing” phishing scams targeted at customers. Hackers gained access to a database of one of Asos’s third-party service providers by impersonating a “trusted contact” to gain access to one of its employee’s accounts, the retailer said. Asos said they had also gained access to “certain non-personal account related information”, which are understood to include shoppers’ recent search history on the app, as first reported by the BBC which was contacted by the hackers. Payment card details and passwords had not been accessed, the retailer added. It said in a message to customers on Thursday: “We discovered that an unauthorised party gained access to an Asos employee account by impersonating a trusted contact to obtain login credentials. Those credentials were then used to access information on certain third-party platforms used by Asos. “The affected platforms were immediately locked down, ensuring that no further information could be accessed, and a full investigation was launched with the support of both internal and external cyber experts. We are also working with the relevant law enforcement and regulatory authorities.” Asos said its website and app continued to be safe to use, that customers did not need to take action and that it had “already taken additional steps to further strengthen security controls”. However, the company warned: “Please remain cautious of unexpected messages or calls claiming to be from Asos. We will never ask you to share passwords, security codes or payment details through an unsolicited message or call.” Charles Allen, an analyst at Bloomberg Intelligence, said the hack might “temporarily cap the pace” of Asos’s attempt to revive sales and profits, after the Covid pandemic led to a period of boom followed by a sharp drop in trade. “The loss of customer trust could weigh on efforts to rebuild its client base,” he said. Asos pledged to contact customers directly once its investigation was complete and “where we believe additional information, support or action may be required”. The Telegram channel operated by the purported hackers, who have named themselves the Xuanye Group, to which users were directed on Tuesday carried a message assuring Asos customers that “payment information is not affected”. Experts said they had not heard of the group before and that the push notification could have been an attempt to gain wider attention. Simon Phillips, the chief technology officer at the cybersecurity firm CybaVerse, said the admission that a wider array of customer information was accessed than previously thought could lead to more persuasive phishing attempts. “Given the information contained search data, and that Asos regularly sends customers reminder emails about the items they search for on the site, attackers could have used this data to send highly convincing scams which are disguised as the emails they typically receive from Asos,” he said. Lisa Barber, the tech editor for the consumer watchdog Which?, said: “Shoppers should be especially wary of unexpected phone calls, texts, messages and emails they receive in the coming weeks and months.” She said that if shoppers were unsure who they were speaking to, they should end the conversation and contact the company directly. It is possible to dial 159 to speak to your bank’s fraud team, or use the number on the back of your card. If you have been called by a possible fraudster, wait at least 15 minutes before calling or use a different phone to ensure the scammer is no longer connected to the call, she said. The hack comes after a number of British retailers, including Marks & Spencer, the Co-op and Harrods, suffered damaging cyber incidents last year. M&S and the Co-op experienced stock shortages, and the former was forced to shut down its website for several weeks while it ensured its systems were clean.

title: Italian opposition cries foul as Meloni’s electoral reform passed in secret ballot
summary: Parties vow to challenge law in court, arguing that extra reward for those with 42% of support distorts public representation
text: A controversial overhaul to electoral law that critics say is aimed at boosting Giorgia Meloni’s chances of clinging on to power in elections next year has been given final approval by the Italian parliament. Meloni, the Italian prime minister, says the new system, which introduces a fully proportional model, including bonus seats for any coalition that wins the most votes, will bring about greater political stability, while opposition parties argue that it mainly serves the interests of those in power. The change was passed in a secret ballot in the lower house with 227 MPs voting in favour and 164 against. There were protests from opposition politicians who held up signs decrying the law as a “scam” and a “con” when the result was announced. Opposition parties have vowed to challenge the changes in the constitutional court, arguing that the bonus seat element, which would be granted to any coalition that reaches a vote threshold of 42% of the vote, distorts voter representation. Another contentious requirement of the changes is that parties and alliances would be required lay out their government programme and name their candidate for prime minister well before a general election. Meloni, who leads the far-right Brothers of Italy, had made the vote a test for her ruling rightwing coalition, warning MPs from her allies, including Forza Italia and the League, that, if defeated, the government would face a crisis. While there are tensions within the coalition, which has suffered setbacks in recent months and is under threat from the rise of new far-right rival Roberto Vannacci, leader of Futuro Nazionale, it has put on a show of unity and has stability on its side after becoming Italy’s longest serving government since the second world war in early September. Whereas the broad leftwing alliance, led by the Democratic party, is highly fractious with no clear leader or programme. Meloni said the victory was a response to those who wanted to see her coalition divided. “Today we respond with action: we are united, cohesive and determined to fulfil the commitments made to citizens,” she wrote on social media. Elly Schlein, the leader of the Democratic party, said Meloni’s alliance sought to change the electoral system because it feared losing the next general election, which is officially due to be held before October 2027 but could be brought forward to April or May. According to a recent survey by Ipsos Doxa, the opposition coalition could reach the 42% threshold if it overcame internal divisions and managed to convince two small radical parties to join forces.

title: Three sisters who drowned in Brighton took their own lives, inquest finds
summary: Jane Adetoro, Christina Walters and Rebecca Walters from London visited late mother’s former home shortly before their deaths in May
text: Three sisters who drowned in the sea in Brighton collectively decided to end their own lives, a coroner has ruled. The bodies of Jane Adetoro, 36, Christina Walters, 32, and Rebecca Walters, 31, all from London, were recovered from the sea off Brighton in the early hours of 13 May. An inquest into their deaths heard on Thursday that in the days before they died, the three women made a trip together to Birmingham to visit the former home of their mother, who died by drowning in 2010. The inquest at Woodvale coroner’s court in Brighton heard that the sisters travelled by taxi to Birmingham on 11 May and were dropped off at 11.36pm at Linton Walk. The address is close to Brookvale Park Lake, where their mother, Janice Adetoro, died. They were picked up to return to the flat they lived in together in Greenford, west London, at 1.28am on 12 May. DCI Mark Cullimore, of Sussex police, told the hearing there was no CCTV to show what the women did in the time they were in Birmingham. On the evening of 12 May, they took a pre-booked taxi to Brighton and arrived near the seafront at 10.21pm. They are thought to have last been seen alive on CCTV from the beach at 2.42am on 13 May. The bodies of Jane Adetoro and Christina Walters were located by a RNLI lifeboat crew; Rebecca Walters’ body was recovered from the shoreline on Brighton beach. The senior coroner Penelope Schofield told the court on Thursday: “In hours of darkness, they entered the sea at Brighton, they could not swim and sea conditions were adverse.” A postmortem found all three women had drowned. There was no evidence of any drugs or alcohol in their bodies and no evidence to suggest they had been subjected to violence. The coroner concluded that the medical cause of death for all three women was drowning and that they had died by suicide. Schofield told the court: “These three sisters lived very secluded lives, they were incredibly private. We don’t know why they took this course of action or indeed why they chose to do it in Brighton. It is not for the court to speculate and sadly these reasons may never be known.” The inquest heard that Christina Walters had suffered from anxiety and depression since her mother’s death, but no such issues were recorded for her sister Rebecca. Adetoro was not registered with a doctor. The women’s father, Joseph Jacobson, who attended the hearing by video link, said in a written statement: “There are no words that can adequately express the pain of losing a child. To lose all three of my precious daughters, Jane, Christina and Rebecca, is a heartbreak beyond anything I could ever have imagined.” He said he could not understand why their lives had ended so suddenly, adding: “You were my daughters, you will always be my daughters and I will love you for the rest of my life. May your beautiful souls rest in perfect peace.” In the UK and Ireland, Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org. In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found at befrienders.org

title: Christa Pike is ‘up and walking’ for first time after failed execution, lawyer says
summary: Recovery marks a dramatic turnaround for Pike, who was declared brain dead after a botched execution in Tennessee
text: Christa Pike is “up and walking” in hospital, her lawyer said, just more than a week after she survived two lethal injections during a botched execution in Tennessee. The recovery marks a dramatic turnaround after Pike was declared brain dead on Monday, before waking up and beginning to speak on Tuesday. Her ordeal has shocked many in the US and overseas and galvanized critics of the death penalty. Stephen Ferrell, a lawyer on Pike’s legal team, told the BBC that she was able to walk, but remained mentally foggy. “What’s been described to me is that physically there’s quite a bit going on, that her arms are very injured and she’s not able to use them very much,” Ferrell said. “She is up and walking for the first time today, but just around the room, not very far,” he added. Pike, 50, was taken to hospital unconscious but alive from Tennessee’s execution chamber on 30 September, after receiving two doses of the barbiturate pentobarbital. After the botched execution attempt, one of her lawyers called the process “cruel and torturous”, adding that he had counted seven needles in Pike’s left arm, “one of which appeared to be bent when it was pulled from her”. Pike had lifted her head from the execution gurney to say her arms were burning as the drug was administered. Pike’s team is seeking psychological support for her, given that “clearly is necessary now”, Ferrell said. On Wednesday, Pike was described as “angry and confused” after regaining consciousness. Ferrell said of Pike’s mental state: “I think it’s kind of good and bad. Good that she is fairly with it, but she’s also somewhat foggy. She can lose her train of thought really easily and forgets where she’s going.” He said it remained to be seen whether Pike makes a full recovery. “I assume [Pike’s condition] will keep improving, but there could be some permanent damage. We don’t know that yet.” On Wednesday Randy Spivey, another attorney for Pike, said she was unable to move her arms and has pneumonia and a blood clot. Despite her condition, Pike was still being restrained, her team said, shackled to her hospital bed by her feet and right arm. Tennessee’s governor, Bill Lee, has paused executions in Tennessee for the rest of the year, but they continue elsewhere. On Wednesday, Texas executed Jamaal Howard by pentobarbital. He was convicted of murder in 2001 for fatally shooting convenience store clerk Vickie Swartout during a robbery. Howard’s lawyers argued the execution should be halted, given the issues the drug had caused with Pike, but a series of courts refused. Meanwhile Donald Trump this week approved the execution by firing squad of Nidal Hasan, who was sentenced to death for killing 13 people at Fort Hood in 2009. Hasan is due to be shot to death on 3 December; his execution is set to be the first carried out by the US military since 1961. Pike’s lawyers had warned before the execution that officials might struggle to locate veins and cause her suffering in the process, but the state had pushed to proceed and the US supreme court allowed the prison to move forward. There is speculation from medical experts that perhaps some or much of the drug missed her vein and went into surrounding tissue, that one of her veins – which were problematic, a fact flagged by her lawyers months earlier – blew, that the drug was faulty, or a combination of all these factors. Pike was 18 and her then boyfriend 17 at the time when they killed 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, one of their classmates at Knoxville Job Corps, in Tennessee in 1995. According to prosecutors, Pike was worried Slemmer was trying to take the boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, away from her. Together, they lured Slemmer into a wooded area, tortured and killed her. Shipp was convicted of first-degree murder in 1997 and was given a life sentence with the possibility of parole. Pike has never denied her involvement in Slemmer’s killing. She was later diagnosed with bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder but, because she was 18, she was sentenced to death and has been on death row, isolated, for 30 years. Pike’s attorneys have argued that her original legal team failed to present evidence about the sexual and physical abuse she suffered during childhood. Lee blocked Pike’s request for clemency. He has since ordered a “comprehensive, third-party review to determine exactly what occurred”.

title: First Thing: Trump endures protests in Texas as DNC sues over adverts
summary: The president was repeatedly interrupted at a rally, and faces a legal challenge over taxpayer-funded adverts. Plus Jonathan the giant tortoise, who may have the secret to longevity
text: Good morning. Donald Trump suffered a torrid night at a rally in Texas that was rocked by repeated protests. The US president briefly stepped away from the microphone after one protester appeared to approach the stage. At least half a dozen demonstrators interrupted Trump during his remarks in San Antonio, with some led away by police. One was physically assaulted by an older Trump supporter as he tried to leave the arena. What is the latest development in the saga over taxpayer-funded pro-Trump ads? The Democratic National Committee has sued the Trump administration in federal court, asking a judge in Washington to stop the president from using taxpayer funds to air a series of ads promoting himself. The ads have cost taxpayers more than $12m so far, according to the media tracking firm AdImpact. Why has Trump been forced to distance himself from two top aides? Trump claimed he did not have “any idea who else they work for” after it was reported that Chris LaCivita, the co-manager of his 2024 presidential campaign, and James Blair, a campaign adviser and White House deputy chief of staff on leave of absence, spent the weekend assisting the pro-Russia government in Republika Srpska in the Balkans. Trump said: “I will terminate them, immediately” if he determined there was a conflict of interest. Tanker attacked off Qatar as Ken Paxton admits Iran war and gas prices are plaguing Republicans A tanker sailing off the north coast of Qatar has been attacked, causing an unknown number of casualties. It came as Iran declared it would close a route in the strait of Hormuz being used to circumvent Tehran’s blockade of traffic. Ken Paxton, the Texas attorney general running as the Republican candidate in a competitive Senate race, admitted in a leaked audio recording that rising fuel prices as a result of Trump’s Iran war were hurting his party before the midterms. The Guardian has asked Paxton’s campaign for comment. What is the latest in the diplomatic dispute between the UK and Israel? Britain is rebranding its East Jerusalem consulate as a UK mission. The move was forced by the Israeli government as punishment for Britain’s decision to ban trade with illegal settlements. There has been some dispute within the UK government over whether taking tough measures at this time against Israel could help Benjamin Netanyahu’s re-election prospects this month. WHO says it does not have ‘full picture’ from Russia after suspected plague death The World Health Organization has said it does not have the “full picture” from Russia after the suspected death from plague last week of a 28-year-old laboratory worker in Siberia. Russian authorities have denied a connection with the anti-plague research institute and say Darya Shipilova died from “pneumonia of an unknown aetiology”. They insist there is no danger of a plague outbreak and have described the “sanitary and epidemiological” situation in the region as stable. What did the WHO director general say? At a press conference, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said: “We don’t yet have the full picture of this event. Timely, complete and transparent information-sharing is essential to clarify conflicting reports and enable an accurate assessment of potential public risks.” What action has Russia appeared to have taken? Officials have imposed sweeping quarantine restrictions at the lab where Shipilova worked and in nearby hospitals. Staff were locked down inside the institute for three days, sleeping on the floors and on chairs, while tests were conducted. Christa Pike ‘angry, confused’ and unable to move arms after failed execution, lawyers say Christa Pike had woken up “angry and confused” after surviving two lethal injections, her attorneys said. Pike remains hospitalized and shackled to her bed. She has pneumonia and a blood clot, and is unable to move either of her badly injured arms. Randy Spivey, one of her lawyers, said her first words were: “Where am I?”, adding: “I think she is angry and confused about everything right now.” A judge has ordered Tennessee state officials to preserve all evidence related to the failed execution. Pike was convicted for her part in the 1995 brutal murder of Colleen Slemmer. In other news … Margaret Hamilton, whose software powered the Apollo 11 moon landing, has died aged 90. Reflecting on the historic mission, she once said: “We were the luckiest people in the world; there was no choice but to be pioneers.” The FBI says it thwarted a terrorist attack on a Minnesota shopping mall by an 18-year-old it had supplied with an AK-47. An Arizona congressional candidate says she was raped while trying to repair a campaign sign. Bernadette Greene-Placentia says she is sharing her story to fight for victims of sexual assault. OpenAI’s release of mathematical findings has drawn concerns from experts, who say the company is not doing due diligence to vet results. María del Carmen Abascal, the 87-year-old whose eviction in Madrid set off a nationwide wave of protests against Spain’s housing crisis, has died. Stat of the day: Golden State Valkyries become first women’s sports team to top $100m in annual revenue The Golden State Valkyries are pursuing their first WNBA championship, but the second-year franchise has already achieved a historic financial milestone. The Filter Recommends: The first step of caring for your makeup is storing it right Lauren Gould speaks to three experts for their best advice on preserving the life of makeup and reducing the chance of it ending up in landfill. Don’t miss this: ‘Neither war nor peace’ – Palestinians in Gaza on existing amid disease, despair and ruins People tell Seham Tantesh in Gaza and Jason Burke, our international security correspondent, how their lives have been changed beyond recognition after the 7 October attacks by Hamas three years ago and the subsequent devastating Israeli offensive. … or this: Why Arturo Béjar left Meta – and blew the whistle Arturo Béjar’s daughter was 14 when she told him Instagram was failing to keep her safe, and he has subsequently testified repeatedly against his former employer Meta. Steve Rose interviews him. Climate check: Landslides, flash floods and raging seas – is California ready for the ravages of El Niño? A mix of natural disasters could all befall the state at once as it finds itself in the crosshairs of the climate phenomenon, as Gabrielle Canon reports. In other climate developments, the Indonesian government has been accused of “gross negligence” in a class action lawsuit over its handling of wildfires, and the Norwegian government has given a permit to a mining company to release waste into one of Norway’s most pristine fjords. Last Thing: Jonathan the giant tortoise, 194, offers up insight into secrets of longevity Alas, it is the animal’s DNA that has revealed a host of genetic variants in most of the biological pathways for ageing, not that he has learned to talk and started giving his opinion on things. title: An elderly woman’s death after eviction is rocking Spain. Will public outcry help its socialist PM stay in power?
summary: Recent death of 87-year-old woman likely to focus attention on crisis in run-up to election at end of November
text: Even before María del Carmen Abascal died on Wednesday night, a mere fortnight after her eviction from the Madrid flat where she had lived for most of her life, the frail 87-year-old woman had become the enduring face of Spain’s housing crisis. Her plight – and the wider issue it embodied – had led to street demonstrations, the creation of a protest camp in the middle of the Spanish capital, and spurred the socialist-led government to propose emergency measures to facilitate and protect access to housing. When rightwing and far-right parties voted down those measures in congress last week, the prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, responded by announcing a snap general election for the end of November. Abascal’s death now looks set to focus even more attention on housing in the run-up to that election and, in particular, on what her lawyer has called “the shameful violence of these types of evictions and the evident impact and consequences they can have on people’s health”. With more than 42% of Spaniards identifying access to housing as their main worry and with rents having risen by 80% over the past decade, the most pertinent question may be: why has it taken the eviction of an octogenarian and the accompanying protests to shake Spain’s political class into action? To which the answer could be that, despite years of protests against overtourism and gentrification, the tipping point had not been reached. Now, arguably, it has. On Thursday, Spain’s state centre for sociological research published polling that showed that 76.3% of those surveyed were in favour of the state intervening in the market “as much as necessary to guarantee everyone’s access to housing”, while 79% believed housing should be prioritised as a constitutional right. Sánchez’s socialist-led government is keen to persuade voters that it is the only political force that cares about rents and tenants’ rights – hence the emergency measures, which have been redrafted into two new decrees after their defeat in parliament last week. The 21 measures include facilitating renting or buying a new home; extending eviction protections for vulnerable residents; prohibiting speculative real estate purchases, and granting tax breaks to property owners and tenants who pay on time. “These are measures that, if I may say so, are a matter of simple common sense; a matter of humanity,” the prime minister said on Tuesday. “They unite small property owners and tenants while standing up to vulture funds, precisely because they target only those who view housing merely as a commodity for speculation.” The measures come almost three years after the prime minister promised to build 184,000 affordable public rental homes. His government has also sought to address soaring housing prices by introducing a law allowing authorities to cap “disproportionate” rent prices in some areas. Those who had voted down last week’s decrees, Sánchez said, had done so despite studies showing the measures enjoyed “cross-cutting support that transcends ideology”, adding that the public was in favour of regulating “a dysfunctional market”. He is now hoping that at least one of the decrees will be passed by congress’s permanent council, a special body that operates when parliament is not in session. Its approval could go some way to convincing voters that his administration is taking the housing issue seriously. Others disagree. Alberto Núñez Feijóo, the leader of the conservative People’s party, which voted down the measures last week, has said it is a bit late for Sánchez, who has been prime minister since 2018, to suddenly appoint himself Spain’s housing champion. “Housing has been the big failure of this government but will be the success story of the one that follows it,” he said on Monday. Feijóo, whose party is leading the polls, added: “When a prime minister has been in power for eight years, it’s hard to blame others for what he’s failed to do.” The PP has promised to address the crisis by building 200,000 homes a year, lowering taxes and cutting down on bureaucracy. However, the PP’s decision to side with the far-right Vox party and the rightwing Catalan pro-independence Junts party to fell the measures has left it looking less than committed to the issue of the day. Sánchez and his allies will be hoping that fact will not be lost on voters as the election campaign kicks off and as trade unions prepare a general strike over housing for 11 November. Mindful, perhaps, of the distance between his words and his party’s voting history in congress, Feijóo called for people not to manipulate Abascal’s death to suit their own purposes. “No campaigning, no political parties, no partisan ends, no more bricks in the wall,” he said on Wednesday night. “When a person dies there should be nothing but respect.” And yet, despite the primacy of housing as an issue, Feijóo opted to start his campaign in Spain’s North African territory of Ceuta, where at least 141 people died as tens of thousands tried to cross over from neighbouring Morocco at the end of July. The Spanish government’s handling of the mass crossing, which saw about 80,000 people enter Ceuta, has been criticised at home and abroad. Speaking in the territory on Wednesday, Feijóo promised that its safety would be at the “top of [the] in-tray” if he became prime minister. Vox, meanwhile, has responded to Absacal’s death by posting footage of a TV interview in which she said she held Sánchez responsible for what had happened to her. The far-right party accused the socialists of using “the suffering of an elderly person to stage a campaign to hide the government’s responsibility in the housing disaster”. It also suggested that Sánchez had visited “ruin and death” on Spain in the form of the floods that killed 230 people in Valencia two years ago, last year’s nationwide power cut, the deadly train crash in southern Spain in January, and recent events in Ceuta.
