title: UK’s military needs to focus spending on domestic defence, not overseas missions – report
summary: Exclusive: Thinktank says Britain’s drive towards global commitments is symptom of ‘outdated foreign policy’
text: The UK’s military is too focused on global commitments at the expense of domestic defence, meaning the government’s planned increase in defence spending is likely to result in even greater waste, a thinktank report has warned. According to an analysis by researchers at the Transition Security Project, Britain has the most overseas-oriented military among European nations, with almost a quarter of the defence budget spent on commitments across five continents. Calling this a symptom of a “destructive, outdated foreign policy” centred on overseas missions that have often made the world less safe, the report says ministers should prioritise changing their approach rather than immediately increasing spending, with resources shifted from overseas commitments to domestic defence. The government is committed to spending 3.5% of GDP on defence by 2035 and a defence investment plan (Dip) was unveiled in July at the tail end of Keir Starmer’s premiership. Starmer’s defence secretary John Healey resigned over a refusal to commit to reaching 3% by 2030, but now that Healey is chancellor that target has been shelved for now. It would involve a doubling of the defence budget in nominal terms from £70bn in 2026 to £151bn in 2035, according to the Transition Security Project, a research centre that was spun out of Common Wealth, a thinktank with close links to Andy Burnham. Using figures from 2024-25, the study estimated that about 23% of the military budget for that year was spent on overseas commitments, costing just over £14bn, with the real figure likely to be higher. About £2.8bn was spent on deployments used to project force outside Europe, including bases in places such as Cyprus, Kenya and Oman and elsewhere as “strategic hubs” for projecting UK military power. The report says this makes the UK the most overseas-committed military among European Nato members, even if France has more personnel posted abroad. The Dip seems unlikely to reverse this, talking about continuing commitments on other continents. The report questions whether more of the new money should be used for domestic defence, and whether the focus on overseas missions has made the UK safer. Since 2001, the study says, the UK has spent more than £51bn in modern terms on military interventions in Iraq, Afghanistan, Libya and elsewhere. “Britain’s decision to maintain a global network of military bases and force projection capabilities, combined with high levels of waste in the military procurement system, raise serious questions about how it is allocating public investment,” it says, urging the government to “review its military posture, prioritising defence over the global projection of military force”. Kevin Cashman, a researcher at the Transition Security Project who co-authored the report, said: “Britain should not pour more money into a bloated military sector geared towards alignment with the United States while Washington starts wars around the world that drive up our bills.” Khem Rogaly, a co-director of the organisation and also a co-author, said: “The billions of pounds Britain wastes on global military deployments every year symbolise its destructive, outdated foreign policy. Britain should end its support for these attempts at global policing. Instead, it should focus its military resources on defence and its public investment on health, housing and the climate emergency.” There is an awareness among defence officials of the importance of avoiding waste, including the risk that an arbitrary focus on reaching a certain level of spending could exacerbate this. The intention is to focus instead on what is necessary – primarily on preparing the UK for a possible war in Europe.

title: Oil prices jump 5% on Middle East tensions and US hurricane threat
summary: Global bond market sell-off continues and stocks fall amid reports White House has asked to see options for more strikes against Iran
text: Oil prices have risen sharply amid fears about escalating tensions in the Middle East and a squeeze on production from the threat of a hurricane off the US coast. Brent crude, the international benchmark, rose by 5% to $105.3 a barrel on Thursday, triggering a wave of selling in the global bond and stock markets. In the UK, the yield – or interest rate – on the 10-year government bond hit its highest level since July 2007, rising by six basis points to 5.515%. Investors appear concerned that rising oil prices could stoke higher inflation. The yield on the 30-year bond – the UK’s benchmark cost for its long-term borrowing – rose by three basis points to 6.0117%, after touching 6.036% on Wednesday, the highest since January 1998. The climbing cost of government borrowing places further pressure on John Healey, as he prepares to deliver his first budget, on 28 October. The market swings came after the Atlantic reported that the White House had asked the Pentagon to draw up options for strikes against Iran before the US midterm elections. The report cited unnamed officials in Donald Trump’s administration who said the size and targets of potential strikes, and whether they would go ahead, were still being debated. The report has weakened hopes that Trump will refrain from escalating the conflict with Iran before the midterm polls next month. A “limited operation” could be followed up with more substantial action after the midterms, it states. Another wave of strikes against Iran represents further risk to oil supply from the Middle East, with the US-Israeli war against Tehran now entering its eighth month. Attacks on tankers in the strait of Hormuz have reached their highest levels of ⁠the war, ⁠cutting traffic through the waterway and deepening fears about supply. The latest attack came ⁠on Wednesday, when a tanker was hit by projectiles off the north coast of Qatar, causing casualties, according to United Kingdom Maritime ‌Trade Operations. Oil prices also rose in response to a squeeze on production in the Gulf of Mexico, after Tropical Storm Isaias strengthened to become the first hurricane of the Atlantic season. Shell and Chevron said they were shutting down production as the storm approached the region, forecast to make landfall on Friday or Saturday. The Danish shipping group Maersk added to worries around rising energy prices on Thursday after it said it was increasing its emergency fuel surcharge on all its export collections and import deliveries. The rise in energy prices has fed fears about inflation, reinforcing expectations that central banks will have to raise their interest rates in order to control rising prices. A sell-off in global bond markets continued on Thursday. In France, which has been hit particularly hard over worries about its rising debt and growing spending, the 10-year yield rose by six basis points to 4.931%, just behind the 24-year high of 4.994% it hit last week. Yields rise when prices fall. The German 10-year yield, the benchmark for European debt, rose by two basis points to 3.504%. The yield on the US 10-year treasury, which is widely considered the best quality government debt on the market, rose by five basis points to 5.331%. Global stocks also fell, with Japan’s Nikkei share index falling 1.4% and the South Korean Kospi down 2.6%. In Europe, the Stoxx Europe 600, which tracks the biggest companies on the continent, dropped 0.9%. The UK’s FTSE 100 slipped by 0.4% in early trading on Thursday.

title: US infant defies bleak odds from rare congenital trait: ‘Don’t quit before your child quits’
summary: Wren Michelle Roberts was born with heterotaxy, a syndrome so rare a specialist could only find 15 similar cases
text: South-eastern Louisiana couple Nick and Savannah Roberts planned to bury their infant daughter the weekend after she was born in September with an exceedingly rare combination of birth defects that her doctors feared was unsurvivable. But an unforeseen congenital trait in Wren Michelle Roberts’ heart, combined with her parents’ dedication to her complex medical care, has allowed her to defy her bleak initial prognosis and meet weeks’ worth of milestones that each are a “miracle in [their] own way”, according to her doctor. As the one-month mark since her birth approached on Wednesday, Wren’s parents said they had been able to bring her to a high school football game, introducing her to one of their region’s timeless fall traditions. The Robertses, residents of the suburban New Orleans community of Montz, said they had also been able to bring their daughter to church. Wren is immunocompromised, and those outings saw the family observe myriad protective measures, from minimizing close contact with people outside their household to keeping a plastic covering over her bassinet, Nick said. Nonetheless, Nick said he, his wife and their supporters savored each activity as much as they did on the first occasions that Wren drank a bottle, took a pacifier, cried and cooed. “This is awesome,” Nick said. “Like this is just normal stuff – and she’s doing what she’s supposed to be doing, going with the flow.” Wren was born with what is known as heterotaxy syndrome, according to her physician, Dr Gabriella Bluett-Mills of New Orleans’ Ochsner children’s hospital. Generally, the organs of those with that congenital condition do not form in the positions that they should, Bluett-Mills said. And in Wren’s case, she was born with her stomach in her chest, no spleen to help fight infections, spina bifida and multiple heart defects. Bluett-Mills, a pediatric complex care specialist, said she and her team could only find 15 documented examples – across the whole of medical literature – of cases involving the same specific genetic mutation at the center of Wren’s case. The Robertses first realized Wren would be like few other babies after testing done 20 weeks into Savannah’s pregnancy. Nick, a chemical plant employee, recalled doctors advising him and Savannah, a nurse, to prepare for the reality that Wren would probably die before her birth given the substantial complications surrounding her syndrome. That prompted the Robertses to go so far as to plan for a funeral days after she was born. Yet Wren ultimately was able to outlive the worst-case scenario. And Bluett-Mills said all indications were that was because an abnormal blood vessel in Wren’s heart had attributes which turned out to be fortuitous in her case. Among the reasons the kind of vessel in question – known as a major aortopulmonary collateral artery, or Mapca – is problematic is that in many cases it is obstructed. But in Wren’s case it is not obstructed, her father said, citing what physicians have told him. Bluett-Mills furthermore said doctors had been able to determine that all of the blood from Wren’s heart is going into that one vessel before splitting off – with some going to her body to give her more oxygen and the rest going to her lungs to get more oxygen put into it. “Without that particular set-up – if one of those two things wasn’t happening – she would not be alive,” Bluett-Mills said. Not all of the milestones which that vessel has set the stage for have been as celebratory for Wren as going to mass or an evening under the lights of a Friday night high school football game for the first time. She had spinal surgery at one week old. And Bluett-Mills said there were more doctors’ appointments in her future than was likely to be typical for most of the babies around Wren, who stays nourished with the help of a feeding tube. But the Ochsner pediatric complex care specialist said Wren’s progress in her infancy had reminded her of physicians’ “need to look at the patient in front of us who is telling us that she is very much alive and wants to kind of hit some of these milestones, do these things that no one was expecting her to do, and we have to watch the baby in front of us to make the decision about what to do next.” “Every one of her milestones is something … all of us are celebrating as … its own miracle in its own way,” Bluett-Mills said. Meanwhile, Nick and Savannah Roberts have been documenting their and their daughter’s emotional journey on a Facebook page named Wren’s Warriors. The page had amassed a following of nearly 8,000 users which Wren’s parents say have rallied around their family as their baby grows. Nick told the Guardian he had already derived a poignant lesson on fatherhood from Wren: “Don’t quit [before] your child quits. … If they’re not giving up, then you can’t give up.” Savannah spoke to local news outlet WVUE about how her perspective as a nurse made it particularly difficult for her to learn that her pregnancy had complications. But she told the outlet that Wren inspired her to believe in the extraordinary. “You’re still fighting, you’re still here,” Wren’s mother later wrote to her daughter in a Facebook post. “Keep fighting, sweet girl.”

title: July 2026 was worst on record for wildfires in England, data shows
summary: Devastating blaze near Sizewell B nuclear power station in Suffolk among a record 624 wildfires in July this year
text: This July was the worst on record for wildfires in England, provisional data shows, with England experiencing a clear upward trend in the total number of wildfires recorded. This summer has been a stark reminder of the vulnerability of the UK to climate breakdown, after punishingly hot and dry weather turned large parts of the countryside into a tinderbox. Provisional government data reveals 1,354 wildfires have been recorded so far this year, with 624 of these in July alone, making 2026 the second worst year on record. July’s wildfires included a devastating fire that burned close to the Sizewell B nuclear power station in Suffolk and destroyed vast areas of a protected nature reserve. The summer of 2026 was the UK’s hottest on record, according to provisional data from the Met Office, with 40 days of temperatures above 30C (86F) recorded, smashing the previous record of 34 days. Scientists have said the record heat of 2026 has only been possible due to the climate crisis driven by fossil-fuel burning. This year also marks the first time in the data series, which runs from 2010–26, that a death has been recorded due to a wildfire. This incident involved the death of a 70-year-old man after a fire burned in fields behind Berrington Road and Castle Gardens in Chipping Campden, Gloucestershire. Last week, the Guardian revealed that the government quietly scrapped plans to prepare the countryside in England for wildfires. This was despite new data showing fire crews do not have the proper protective gear to tackle them. Alistair Carmichael, the Liberal Democrat MP for Orkney and Shetland and the chair of the Commons environment food and rural affairs committee, said this raised “serious questions” about whether this summer’s wildfires could have looked different with more resources on the ground. This year is the second worst year on record in terms of total number of wildfires, with the worst being 2022, when 1,592 were recorded. 2022 was also a record year for heat, with the UK recording temperatures of 40C for the first and only time. The 2026 data covers January to August only, whereas the 2022 data covers the full 12 months. Despite this, 2026 has already had a record number of woodland and forest fires, with 88 recorded. After a wildfire spread across an area including several homes in Stourbridge in the West Midlands in August, the prime minister, Andy Burnham, convened an emergency Cobra meeting and issued a temporary ban on the sale of disposable barbecues. The data shows a clear upward trend in the number of wildfires being recorded. Between 2010 and 2017, annual totals remained consistently under 750 (ranging between 310 and 721). In contrast, four out of the last nine years exceeded 950 incidents. The environmental author and campaigner Guy Shrubsole has accused respective governments of “fiddling whilst Britain burns”. He called on the prime minister’s upcoming Wildfire Summit to include “radical changes to how we fire-proof our landscapes – by restoring peat bogs, ponds and wetlands – and cut out the fossil fuels making wildfires worse”. A government spokesperson said this summer was one of the “most challenging wildfire seasons on record”. They added: “We have to make sure we are prepared for the threat of wildfires – which is why we have invested nearly £100m to upgrade national resilience assets and we are convening a summit with fire and rescue service partners to inform decision-making and make sure we have the right equipment and resources to be as resilient as possible.”

title: Supermarket shake-up: why Asda or Morrisons could vanish within a decade
summary: Talks between Sainsbury’s and Morrisons have set industry tongues wagging, with analysts saying the market is ripe for change
text: They may be two of the most recognisable brands in Britain, with a combined 188 years serving shoppers, but industry watchers agree that either Asda or Morrisons – or both – could disappear within a decade. This week, it emerged that Sainsbury’s and Morrisons – the UK’s second- and sixth-largest supermarket chains – had held merger talks between last November and February, before the larger player decided to walk away. News of the potential deal has relaunched speculation that the UK grocery market is now ripe for consolidation and revealed that the Sainsbury’s boss, Simon Roberts – who has been in post for six years – is at least willing to consider the possibility of buying one of his troubled rivals. Sainsbury’s, which has 600 supermarkets and almost 900 convenience stores, has until recently been seen as wary of trying to revive merger talks with its rivals after its bid to buy Asda for £7bn in 2019 was blocked. However, industry experts say Asda and Morrisons’ owners have held informal talks with each other – and both with Sainsbury’s team – and predict that talks could restart. “The three of them, one way or another, are talking to each other,” one said. He suggested that a combination of Asda and Morrisons could happen but was likely to be a weaker deal than a Sainsbury’s takeover of either, as both businesses struggle with costs and interest on debt piles. Competition fears ease The industry has undergone significant change since the collapse of the Sainsbury’s-Asda deal. While riding the wider retail trends towards online shopping and convenience stores, the supermarket groups have been jockeying for market share. Aldi is poised to overtake Asda to become the UK’s third-largest supermarket, with less than 1 percentage point separating them. Aldi is rapidly opening stores while Asda has struggled to find growth since a £6.8bn, debt-fuelled takeover in 2020 and heavy price competition from the discounters and from its bigger rivals Tesco and Sainsbury’s. Another big change could emerge this month when the UK’s competition watchdog is due to publish its final ruling on whether Aldi and Lidl should now officially be classified as “large grocery retailers” like Tesco, Sainsbury’s, Asda and Morrisons. In August, the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) said it had found provisionally that Aldi and Lidl no longer qualified as “limited assortment discounters” as they now carry a “full range” of groceries and operate stores larger than 1,000 sq m (10,700 sq ft) across the UK. The change means the German-owned discounters are now taken into account when assessing competition in different locations. This is the strongest hint yet that the CMA has changed its stance blocking the Sainsbury’s buyout of Asda on the basis that shoppers would be worse off. It also indicates that the CMA’s “balance of competition” – its estimation of the impact of a deal based on drive times for customers around stores – has shifted, meaning Sainsbury’s might have to dispose of dozens fewer stores to gain regulatory clearance for a merger. A figure of 150 was suggested when it tried to buy Asda. Clive Black, an analyst at Shore Capital and Sainsbury’s broker, says the CMA preliminary ruling indicates “the shape of the pitch has adjusted a little” and “the change encourages another chapter of consolidation”. It is a step-change from 2019 when analysts accused the singing former Sainsbury’s boss Mike Coupe and his board of directors of “arrogance” and “folly” for pursuing Asda. Now they say that consolidation is almost inevitable. That comes amid what is seen as a more welcoming regulatory environment backed by the UK government’s growth agenda combined with the appointment of Doug Gurr, a grocery industry veteran who has spent time at Asda and Amazon, to lead the CMA. Sainsbury’s holds the cards One analyst described Sainsbury’s as the “kingmaker” in any industry consolidation as it uniquely has the resources to snap up a rival without the market dominance to immediately prevent any deal. Analysts agree it is unlikely to face significant competition if it opts to buy Morrisons or Asda – Tesco is too big to buy a rival, while Marks & Spencer and Waitrose appear unlikely to have the financial firepower or desire to pursue such a deal. Amazon should not be ruled out as a player in consolidation, according to one analyst, who said the online specialist might be prompted into action by any of the supermarkets announcing plans to merge. “The last cards are coming on to the table,” he said, suggesting that Amazon might consider buying Asda, Morrisons or even Sainsbury’s, now that it had effectively disposed of Argos which may have caused competition concerns for Amazon. However, Amazon has not fared well with its dip into high street retail. Last year, it decided to close all 19 of its Fresh stores, with plans to convert five of them into shops under its Whole Foods Market brand. As analysts at Bernstein put it: “We believe that scale is the most important source of advantage in grocery retail, and the combined market share of Sainsbury’s and Morrisons would improve Sainsbury’s ability to take on Tesco.” The logic of a deal for Morrisons’ American private equity owner is clear. Clayton, Dubilier & Rice has few options for an exit, four years on from its £7bn acquisition of the Bradford-based chain. Private equity bidders are not likely to be lining up, as there is little room for a another debt-fuelled buyout, while pursuing a stock market flotation would require a compelling growth story to lure investors but which is now absent. The heavy debts taken on to fund CD&R’s acquisition in 2022 have left Morrisons struggling to compete as interest rates have risen, pushing up costs, while competition has toughened as pinched households look to save costs on their grocery bill. Clearly, the CD&R adviser and former Tesco boss Terry Leahy is unlikely to let Morrisons go cheaply – with price demands ultimately understood to have led Sainsbury’s Roberts to walk away from any deal. However, Morrisons has fallen back to be the UK’s sixth-largest supermarket with an 8.4% market share, just behind Lidl on 8.7%, according to the latest data from the industry analysts Worldpanel by Numerator. A ‘sweetheart deal’ Asda’s owners, led by the British investment firm TDR Capital, may also welcome a tidy exit although they are likely to be happier to wait, having largely made their money selling off various parts of the grocer’s assets, industry insiders say. Under the returning boss, Allan Leighton, there are nascent signs of a turnaround if the owners are willing to sit tight and he does not appear keen on reviving talks with Sainsbury’s. For Sainsbury’s, the appeal is cost-savings derived from larger scale. The combination of Sainsbury’s and Morrisons would hold 23.6% of the UK market and add 500 supermarkets and 1,600 convenience stores to its portfolio – taking it closer to Tesco’s 27.8% market share. Buying Asda would take it to about 26.7%. One industry expert said a combination with Asda was the “sweetheart deal” because it would not only bring larger scale but involve fewer stores serving the same customers in the south of the country. The main benefit of any deal would come from cost-savings garnered from combining central operations, such as buying and property management, and aligning supplier terms. Asda’s bigger supply chain brings greater potential savings and it is arguably a less complicated acquisition than Morrisons, which operates a large food processing business which Sainsbury’s would probably want to dispose of to a variety of specialist suppliers. One issue is that businesses cannot seek pre-approval for a deal from the CMA, so launching a formal takeover offer for either Morrisons or Asda would involve an element of risk – consuming management time, and costly fees for bankers and lawyers. As one industry expert says, “the critical argument is the role of the discounters” and the CMA’s rulings do not always follow the expected path. “It’s a lottery,” he said. Analysts at Bernstein also say that “despite the benefits of a possible deal, the risk of distraction for Sainsbury’s would be high”. The industry insider says: “Sainsbury’s is best served by being patient” as Asda and Morrisons are likely to continue to struggle. “There comes a point when the CMA has no choice but to let something happen as [Asda and Morrisons] can’t compete. You could argue that is already the case.” • This article was amended on 8 October 2026. An earlier version said that Sainsbury’s is unlikely to face significant competition if it opts to buy “Sainsbury’s or Asda”; that should have said Morrisons or Asda.

title: USS Abraham Lincoln to dock in San Diego after harrowing stretch at sea
summary: Deployment for nearly a year was marked by reports of supply shortages and deteriorating morale and mental health among crew
text: The USS Abraham Lincoln, the US aircraft carrier that has been deployed for nearly a year and has spent months supporting US military operations against Iran, is scheduled to dock in San Diego on Thursday afternoon. It marks the end of a deployment that has been described as “one of the most operationally intense and consequential of the modern era” and that became marked by a record-setting stretch at sea, repeated deployment extensions, and reports of supply shortages and deteriorating morale and mental health among some crew members. The Lincoln left San Diego last November, initially bound for the Pacific. But it was redirected to the Middle East after the US and Israel launched their war with Iran in late February. The carrier remained there until late August, when it was relieved by the USS George Washington and began its journey home. Earlier in August, the Lincoln’s deployment made headlines and faced scrutiny as reports began surfacing about poor living conditions onboard the ship, including shortages of supplies and water, plumbing problems, low morale and worsening mental health among the roughly 5,000 personnel on the carrier. Two leading military newspapers also reported that there had been two attempts by sailors to jump overboard, causing concern among families and military health experts. The reports prompted outrage from Democrats, while senior officials in the Trump administration pushed back. Pete Hegseth, the US defense secretary, called the reports “completely misrepresented”, and when reporters asked Donald Trump if he thought the deployment had gone on too long, he responded: “Not nearly long enough” – a comment that angered some naval families. In a statement at the time, Adm Brad Cooper, who heads US Central Command, claimed that of the US navy’s 11 active aircraft carriers, the Lincoln had “among the lowest number of cases related to mental health”. But he said that “this doesn’t mean that all is perfect”. Cooper said that a long deployment at sea “is uniquely challenging and tough, and every single one of us, including me, reacts to stressors in different ways”. Two weeks ago, as the Lincoln headed back to San Diego, Hung Cao, the acting navy secretary, acknowledged that eight service members from the Lincoln and its accompanying strike group attempted to take their own lives. Sara Jacobs, a Democrat representing California’s 51st district who visited the Lincoln in late September, said in a statement last week that while she is “relieved that the USS Abraham Lincoln will soon be back in San Diego” and “looking forward to welcoming them home”, her “demand for accountability won’t end when they make port”. “I will continue pushing for an [office of the inspector general] investigation into these conditions and a House armed services committee field hearing in San Diego to hear directly from these service members,” she said. “We need to prevent this crisis from happening ever again, and ultimately end the Iran war and bring all our service members home.” On Wednesday, Hegseth visited the Lincoln ahead of its return, and praised the crew. He acknowledged that their deployment had not been “easy”. “When you greet your families tomorrow, just pass my gratitude from the president and myself,” Hegseth said. “Let them know that their long wait, we believe, was in service of a righteous and historic mission.” During his remarks, Hegseth announced that those onboard the vessel would be awarded the presidential unit citation, which, according to the US military, is conferred on units of the armed forces “for extraordinary heroism in action against an armed enemy”. Ahead of the Lincoln’s arrival on Thursday afternoon, Blue Star Families, one of the largest US-based non-profit organizations supporting active military service members, veterans and their families, said in a statement that “every homecoming is an important moment for military families”. The organization said that it “welcomes home the sailors of USS Abraham Lincoln and wants every family to know they’re not alone as they reconnect”. In the weeks ahead, Blue Star Families said it will host appreciation days for Lincoln sailors and their families, including several events next month in San Diego.

title: ‘System is rigged’: Democrat Sherrod Brown puts datacenter danger at heart of populist Senate bid
summary: Ohio former senator attacks Republican rival as the ‘face of datacenters’ as he wraps AI concerns into pro-worker message
text: Sherrod Brown, the Democratic former senator from Ohio hoping to return to office in November’s midterm elections, has spent the past year traveling across his home state explaining to voters about all the ways the “system is rigged” against them. Recently, he’s been telling people about a trip he took across the north-west Ohio countryside. “You’re driving on what looks like really good farmland, driving past fields, driving past barns, driving past milking parlors, and you see, all of a sudden, you see these huge cranes and you see these trucks coming,” Brown told a crowd of dozens at a coffee shop in the city of Lima earlier this month. The construction site was for a datacenter, Brown said, a component of the AI boom in which Ohio is a national leader. Brown believes the massive installations that pop up without warning do little good for the people around them. “Nobody knows they’re there,” Brown, speaking in shirtsleeves and without notes, said in his gravelly voice, as the crowd murmurs in agreement. “They eat up our land. They swallow up our water … then once they’re built, our electricity prices go up.” It was the latest iteration of an argument that Brown has been making his whole political career: that the most powerful people in the United States do not have the interests of Ohioans at heart. That message helped him win seven terms in the US House of Representatives and then three in the Senate, even as Ohio grew increasingly dominated by Republicans, and the working-class voters Democrats once relied upon deserted the party. In 2024, Brown lost his bid for a fourth term in an election in which Ohio voters backed Trump by an 11-percentage-point margin. “It’s not, I promise you, the last time you’ll hear from me,” he said in his final speech on the Senate floor, and months later, he announced another run for the Senate. Now 73, Brown has made standing up to datacenter developers a centerpiece of this campaign, calling his Republican opponent, Senator Jon Husted, “the face of datacenters”. A report from Ohio’s chamber of commerce found the state gave $2.5bn in tax breaks for the facilities from 2017 to 2024, a period during which Husted was lieutenant governor. “John Husted, I mean, he’s the guy that – he’s talking like he didn’t know – but he’s the reason these datacenters are here – 200 of them,” Brown said. Whether the former senator’s message lands with voters is central to Democrats’ hopes of retaking the Senate and blunting Trump’s abilities to get bills passed and judges confirmed for the final two years of his presidency. Democrats must win at least four Senate seats to return to the majority, most of which will come from states that voted for Trump by double digits in 2024 – like Ohio. ‘The anchor hanging around Husted’s neck’ Brown has wrapped concerns over datacenters’ impacts into the broad message of affordability that many congressional Democrats are campaigning on nationwide. He peppers his speeches with references to the Iran war, tariffs, Medicaid cuts approved by the Republican Congress and rising prices for Affordable Care Act plans brought on by their inaction. Asked in Lima to name an idea to lowercosts if he wins, Brown proposed a new expansion of the child tax credit, which reduced the poverty rate among children during its single year of enactment under Joe Biden. As the election has drawn closer, Brown has intensified his efforts to tie datacenters to Husted, who the Republican governor, Mike DeWine, appointed in 2025 to the seat JD Vance vacated when he became vice-president. Whichever candidate wins will serve out the remainder of his term, which expires at the end of 2028. This week, Brown’s campaign announced a volley of billboards reading “See that datacenter? Jon Husted did that” and a website critical of the senator that offers voters a map of the facilities in the state. Amy Natoce, a campaign spokesperson for Husted, accused Brown of lying, saying that while serving as lieutenant governor under DeWine from 2019 to 2025, Husted “did not have the authority to grant tax breaks”. She also noted his championing of the Ratepayer Protection Act in the Senate, which would have required electric utilities to consider standards that would make datacenters pay for their impacts on the grid. Though it passed the House with wide, bipartisan support, Senate Democrats called the proposal ineffective, and last month blocked its advancement. “Sherrod Brown and his friends like to talk about affordability, but when the rubber meets the road, they’d rather play politics than actually lower Ohioans’ energy bills. It’s disgusting,” Natoce said. There’s evidence that Brown’s attacks could be effective. Last week, the New York Times and Siena University released polling that found voters believed Brown would do a better job than Husted would managing the development of datacenters, by an 11-percentage-point margin. The race otherwise remains tight, with the Democrat leading the incumbent by three percentage points, within the survey’s margin of error. In August, a memo emerged from the GOP’s Senate campaign arm, the National Republican Senatorial Committee, warning that the issue could sink Husted. “More than any other thing in this race, datacenters are the anchor hanging around Husted’s neck,” the memo read. “If he loses and datacenters get the blame, politicians across the country will take notice – and they will not go near the next one.” DeWine and his predecessor have sought to encourage the development of datacenters. But political winds have shifted rapidly on the issue – nearly 140 communities in the state have put moratoriums on new constructions, according to the Ohio Capital Journal, and in May, DeWine announced a pause on tax exemptions for the buildings. Last year, Democrats campaigned against datacenters to gain power in elections in Virginia, New Jersey and elsewhere, and are this year lumping their perceived impacts on electricity prices with the Iran war’s upward pressure on gas prices to argue that Republicans have failed to accomplish Trump’s promise of fighting inflation. “Husted has been involved in datacenters prior to this election year, and … he’s just more exposed,” said Dan Birdsong, a senior lecturer in political science at the University of Dayton. It also offers Brown a way to appeal to rural voters who typically do not vote for Democrats, but are sensitive to the possibility of the datacenters being built nearby. “He has a bipartisan voting base that he can appeal to with this issue that’s different than other issues in the state,” Birdson said of Brown. Powerful enemies An Ohio native who received a bachelor’s degree from Yale University, Brown had been in office almost without interruption from 1975 until he lost in 2024 to Republican Bernie Moreno. By the end of his time in the chamber, he was something of an outlier – the last Democrat holding statewide elected office in Ohio and still describing himself as a champion for workers even amid abundant evidence that they had soured on his party. Brown argues that he has the accomplishments to back up his record. As a House member, he voted against implementing the North American Free Trade Agreement, concerned about its impact on Ohio manufacturers, and one of his last votes in the Senate was to pass legislation that boosts social security payments to public employees. Brown has been in politics so long that when Bowling Green State University polled the Senate race last month, a quarter of respondents incorrectly thought Brown was the incumbent. He has long courted the alliance of unions, many of whom have backed his comeback attempt this year, though some who supported him in 2024 are now behind Husted. His stances have also earned him deep-pocketed enemies: as chair of the Senate banking committee, he was an adversary of cryptocurrency, and this year, Fairshake, a Super Pac linked to that industry, plans to spend $30m against him, after helping Moreno to victory in 2024. “We will be outspent for sure,” Brown acknowledged to reporters in Lima, echoing a reality for many Democratic campaigns in a year when Republicans are generally seen as having the fundraising advantage. His campaign against datacenters also runs up against their own benefits to building trade unions, for which they have provided significant employment opportunities. Lee Daher, the senior business representative at north-west Ohio’s Carpenters Local Union 351, said datacenters were “a really good source of employment for us”. “It means a lot of work for our members, not only today, tomorrow, but for the years to come,” he said. His local is backing Brown this year, as they did in 2024, and Daher said his comments about datacenters had not dampened that support. “They’re coming one way or another, and is there some regulation that’s needed? I think so, but I think big tech is hearing what is being asked of them,” he said. Asked to reconcile this tension, Brown insisted it was his emphasis on costs that would convince some of the same workers who turned their backs on him two years ago to give him another chance. “Those unions support me in large part because their members don’t like higher electric bills. Their members don’t like having no say on these datacenters coming to their towns,” Brown said. “I don’t think very many union members want the state to give these huge tax breaks to these out-of-state billionaires that are building these datacenters.”

title: New direct train services from London to Wrexham and Rochdale rejected
summary: Regulator also vetoes extra Blackpool service, citing lack of space on west coast mainline for new trains to capital
text: Plans to run direct train services to Wrexham and Rochdale from London have been rejected by the rail regulator because of “significant pressure” on the line. The Office of Rail and Road said that there was insufficient space on the crowded west coast mainline to introduce the two new separate train services. It also vetoed plans for additional London-Blackpool train services wanted by Avanti. The ORR had last year knocked back plans for a new independent open access service linking Wrexham and the capital put forward by the Wrexham, Shropshire & Midlands Railway Company (WSMR). WSMR had submitted plans for a slightly less frequent service but the ORR said the new routes would still put the reliability of the wider railway at risk. The new service could have allowed Wrexham to capitalise further on the town’s Hollywood-meets-football mini-boom, fuelled by the Wrexham AFC co-owners Ryan Reynolds and Rob McElhenney. Proposals for a new Lumo service between London and Rochdale, again slimmed down after being rejected in 2025, were once more rebuffed. The ORR also said Avanti could not add more Blackpool services from London. However, it did approve one extra London-Chester evening service from Avanti, which would otherwise have run as a “ghost train”, with crew and the rolling stock returning north to the depot overnight. The decision follows the outcry over the ORR’s initial ruling on a Manchester-London service which was barred from taking passengers last year. The regulator said its assessment, backed by external reviews, was that the “capacity and performance of the southern section of the west coast mainline has not materially changed since similar applications were rejected in 2025”. It said gaps in the current timetable were needed to provide important space for trains to recover when things went wrong, rather than escalating chaos. Stephanie Tobyn, ORR’s director of strategy, policy and reform, said: “New services, destinations and greater choice can bring real benefits for passengers and communities. But the west coast mainline is already under significant pressure, with performance reflecting limited resilience on a heavily used part of the rail network. “Our detailed analysis has shown that adding more trains to the current timetable would reduce the ability to recover when disruption occurs, increasing the risk of delays spreading and making reliability of the network worse for all passengers.” Private operators such as First Group, owners of Lumo, have been looking to increase open-access routes as Labour has renationalised major rail contracts in the transition to Great British Railways. London-Wrexham direct trains briefly ran from London Marylebone from 2008 to 2011 as an open-access service but stopped owing to financial losses.

title: ‘Dystopian’: Co-op becomes latest firm to put staff under AI surveillance
summary: Whistleblower says recording and analysis of all probate calls in Co-op Legal Services is oppressive
text: The Co-op has become the latest employer to place workers under AI surveillance with an automated listening technology that rates every phone call some of them make to customers. In a system described as “oppressive and dystopian” by a whistleblower, Co-op Legal Services is using AI models to record, analyse and award a percentage score for interactions between agents and customers seeking advice about probate, wills and estates. A model from OpenAI has been trained to assess more than 50 discrete aspects of each phone call and provide pass and fail scores to managers who use the data to analyse employee performance. One worker said the system can mean their work is monitored by AI for several hours a day as they handle inquiries often from recently bereaved customers. It comes after the Guardian last week revealed Euan Blair’s AI training company, Multiverse, has started using an AI for blanket monitoring of online classroom sessions, which teachers called “remorseless” and “unnerving”, while Multiverse said it was “using AI to improve the experience of learners and customers”. Experts have voiced fears that increasing AI monitoring of workers risks increasing stress. “You are being watched,” said a Co-op worker who spoke to the Guardian on condition of anonymity and said the AI created a sense of distrust. “It’s different from occasionally being listened to for compliance purposes. [You are] being monitored absolutely every word that you say and every time that you utter something … It just feels really dystopian. It’s the thin end of the wedge.” The Co-op, which operates supermarkets, undertakers, insurance and legal services companies, said it did not recognise the criticism and said its probate advisers were highly engaged. It said it supported colleagues with AI, which is a “key aspect of our quality assurance processes” and helps ensure “our clients consistently receive empathetic expert guidance”. The AI monitoring is understood to have been introduced in the last couple of months into the work of dozens of legal services staff. It is used in part to identify ways they can boost their sales performance. The Co-op said the AI is used solely as a support tool, is not a decision-maker, and helps leaders “support colleagues and continuously improve the experience we provide to clients”. Trade unions have begun pushing back against the spread of AI monitoring. In February Burger King in the US announced it would be using the technology to track restaurant workers’ customer interactions, and this summer, Meta paused tracking of employees’ computer keystrokes amid data privacy concerns and a staff backlash. “AI is sold as the solution to every problem, but examples like this make it clear that it can diminish sensible workplace practices and intensify working lives for no reason,” said John Chadfield, the national officer of the Communication Workers Union. “Unaccountable computer systems should not be people’s managers, and these hard-working employees demand far more respect.” “The office is becoming more like a factory now our performance feedback can be given in a more structured way,” said Hayfa Mohdzaini, a senior policy and practice adviser at the Chartered Institute of Professional Development. “Clearly some people have a problem with it. It will be interesting to see how it develops and how much managers need to adjust their approach.” This year, the International Labour Organization warned about the “psychosocial” risks of AI monitoring, including increasing work-related stress. “AI systems are being deployed in workplaces in the absence of a comprehensive regulatory framework,” it said. “Preventing the risk of harm by AI use and operation in this context may not be straightforward.” Caoilionn Hurley, the managing director of Co-op Life Services, which includes legal services, said: “The efficiency of AI over traditional methods allows us to review all customer conversations to ensure we consistently deliver high standards of service, while enabling more informed support, coaching and development for colleagues … Put simply, our goal is to provide expert support combined with empathy and understanding for every client at what can be a difficult time. AI helps us deliver that more consistently, while human judgment, accountability, care and kindness remain at the heart of every client relationship.”

title: Bullet and blast injuries … and a constant need for blood: inside South Sudan’s overwhelmed trauma wards
summary: Renewed fighting is bringing a flow of wounded to Juba’s military hospital, where medics never know what the next day will bring
text: By 11am on a recent Thursday, Dr Slobodan Mirosavljev had already seen two critically wounded patients at Juba military hospital. The day was barely halfway through, but the surgeon couldn’t say how long he would be at the facility. A patient shot in the abdomen, head or chest could arrive without warning. A helicopter could bring several critically wounded people from another part of South Sudan. A mass casualty incident could fill the wards within hours. For Mirosavljev and his colleagues, uncertainty has become part of the job at the hospital, where the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) supports surgeries for weapon-wounded victims of renewed fighting between the military, known as the South Sudan People’s Defence Forces (SSPDF), and the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-In Opposition (SPLM-IO), which is loyal to former vice-president Riek Machar, and allied groups. The conflict has increased the demand for surgical care, overwhelming an already fragile and under-resourced health system in the world’s youngest country. The fighting has intensified in the past year, particularly in Jonglei state, an opposition stronghold, amid a political crisis fuelled by the president, Salva Kiir, sidelining Machar. Machar and Kiir were members of the Sudan People’s Liberation Army, a guerrilla movement that fought for independence from Sudan, which it gained in 2011, with Kiir becoming president and Machar the first vice-president. South Sudan descended into a bloody civil war in 2013 after Kiir fired Machar and later accused him of planning a coup. Machar founded SPLM-IO, whose fight against the army in the ensuing civil war killed more than 400,000 people and displaced nearly half the country’s population. The fighting took place largely along ethnic lines, between Kiir’s majority Dinka community and Machar’s Nuer, the second largest ethnic group in the country. In 2018, Kiir and Machar signed a peace deal – ending the civil war, creating a unity government of the two parties and returning Machar to the vice-presidency. But implementation of the agreement has barely got off the ground, as the two parties are constantly at odds over power sharing. The renewed conflict was triggered by a deadly attack by the White Army, a rebel group that was allied to Machar during the civil war, on a government garrison in Nasir county in Upper Nile state in March 2025. It resulted in Machar being charged with murder, treason, crimes against humanity and other serious crimes in connection with the attack, and Kiir suspending him from his post. The actions have inflamed tensions in the country, with Machar’s supporters saying the charges against him are politically motivated and observers saying they risk jeopardising the peace agreement and plunging the country, where elections are due in December, into full-scale civil war. The events have also coincided with increased fighting between militias and government forces in parts of the country that has killed hundreds and displaced more than 200,000 people. Last month, the UN Commission on Human Rights in South Sudan expressed concern that the renewed violence and political tensions continued to place civilians at risk. “Visit after visit, we continue to hear from people who bear the consequences of violence, displacement, insecurity and the failures of those with political and security responsibilities to prevent and address those harms,” said the commission’s chairperson, Yasmin Sooka. *** At Juba military hospital, patients, medical workers and visitors moved between wards as the rainy season settled over the country. The sounds of footsteps, hospital trolleys and hurried conversations mixed with the steady hum of ceiling fans and the smell of disinfectant. Some patients recovering from gunshot wounds sat along covered walkways. Others waited on crutches, while patients further along in their recovery carried out morning rehabilitation exercises. As the fighting intensifies, the facility must be prepared to receive weapon-wounded victims at any time. For the surgical teams, that means there is no such thing as a predictable workday. Mirosavljev said that before midday they had had their morning meeting, received reports from the night shift team, seen critical patients in the high dependency unit, and started operating. The Serbian surgeon has been working at the hospital since August 2025. He operates on some of the most seriously wounded patients and supervises surgical teams. His day usually starts before 8am with a briefing, followed by ward rounds, consultations, emergency admissions and operations. Surgeries end in the early evening on typical days, but can go late into the night when critically wounded patients arrive. Besides victims of political violence, the patients arriving at the hospital include those wounded in communal fighting and cattle-related conflict. In the first six months of this year, the ICRC evacuated 266 injured people from conflict areas and brought them to the facility. Most cases at the hospital are gunshot wounds, and others include stab wounds, broken bones and explosive injuries. Mirosavljev estimated that one in 10 involve serious head injuries, including bullets entering the skull. For surgeons, the numbers translate into a daily struggle against blood loss, infection and damage to vital organs. Some patients require several operations. Every week, the medics receive at least two or three “very difficult” injuries from bullet or blast injuries to the chest and abdomen that need multiple surgeries, Mirosavljev said. For such patients, surgery is only the beginning. “They need a lot of blood; they need a lot of support,” he said. Blood is among the most critical resources in the trauma unit. The hospital may have about 15 units available, with capacity sometimes reaching 20. A single severely wounded patient can require half of that supply. Medical teams and hospital management work to find donors, sometimes relying on patients’ relatives and the national blood bank in Juba. But maintaining a reliable supply remains difficult. *** The consequences can be serious when several casualties arrive at once. Rose Ochieng, the ICRC’s health coordinator in South Sudan, said the surgical department at Giada military hospital was operating at more than 160% of its bed capacity at the most recent peak this year. She said: “We are doing what we can to keep pace: adding overflow beds and recruiting more physiotherapy staff. But demand is growing faster than the capacity of trauma services. And it is civilians caught up in the fighting who are paying the price.” For emergency room nurse Mubarak Jamal, uncertainty begins every morning. Jamal is from Central Equatoria state and has been working at the hospital since 2024. At the outpatient department, there are a limited number of beds. On a normal day, he said, the department sees about 30 patients. Between seven and 10 may be people suffering weapon-related injuries. Normal days, however, can disappear quickly, Jamal said, recalling that they received more than 93 patients in one day in the last mass casualty situation. His responsibility is to ensure the emergency department is prepared for whatever arrives overnight – restocking supplies, knowing who is working during the night, and how they will coordinate with the colleagues from the operating theatre and other departments. And survival is not the end of treatment. For physiotherapist Lotto Charles, the real measure of recovery is whether a patient can eventually return home and live independently. Charles, from Eastern Equatoria state, has worked at the hospital since 2016. His job includes rehabilitating the injured. Many of his patients are recovering from gunshot wounds. He lists others: “There are multiple fracture patients, patients with nerve injury, patients with lung collapse, and bedridden patients with extensive soft-tissue injuries who are not able to move.” His work can include casting broken limbs, managing patients on traction, and helping them regain muscle strength and movement. One day last month, he treated five patients. One needed to have a cast removed, modified and reapplied. Another required exercises to restore knee movement. A bedridden patient was assisted out of bed for the first time. For Charles, the reward comes when a patient who arrived on a stretcher walks out of the hospital. “That really motivates me a lot – that at least I’m doing something to help the community,” he said. For Mirosavljev, that makes the difficult days worthwhile. “It’s a good feeling when you do the job, and people survive … and they walk out,” he said.

title: French minister invites UK to ‘come all the way back’ to the EU
summary: Finance minister, Roland Lescure, welcomes Burnham’s pledge to explore closer ties with bloc
text: The French finance minister has invited the UK to “come all the way back” to the European Union after Andy Burnham raised the prospect of a new referendum to reverse Brexit. Roland Lescure was speaking after the prime minister used his Labour conference speech to pledge that the government would explore closer ties with the bloc at a summit later this year. He used subsequent interviews to spell out how wide-ranging his consideration of Britain’s future with Brussels could be because Brexit had caused “more harm than good”. Asked about Burnham’s comments, Lescure told the BBC: “British people decided, and that’s obviously their 100% right, and if they’re willing to come back, they will have to decide. But what I can tell them is: come back, anytime.” Lescure said he wanted Britain back in the union to face emerging global threats together. Burnham said last week that the government’s options included keeping the current arrangements in relation to the UK’s relationship with the EU, seeking a customs union, returning to the single market, or going “all the way” with full membership. He said ministers would examine “what is doable” and the “pros and cons” of each option. The prime minister is travelling to Germany for talks with the chancellor, Friedrich Merz, whose government has been supportive of Burnham’s suggestion that the UK could explore closer links with the EU. Burnham and Merz are expected to agree on a deal for closer security cooperation against cyber-attacks on European countries but the two will also discuss UK-EU relations. Lescure also responded to comments by Burnham that EU rules to help European manufacturers would damage the UK. British government sources warned days earlier that the “EU reset” summit would be delayed again unless the bloc agreed to discuss legislation that could lock British business out of parts of EU industry. “Come back, and you’ll be at the table, and we discuss all these things together,” Lescure said. Nigel Farage has claimed Burnham has given him “the biggest boost in my career” by reviving the Brexit debate, which the Reform UK leader said had reopened a “huge flank” to his party. Dismissing polls showing that as much as 59% of the public favoured rejoining the EU, Farage said: “Of course they do, until you tell them it’ll cost 25bn quid a year, until you tell him it’ll mean joining Schengen [the area of Europe that has open borders], until he tells them it will mean actually having to recommit to joining the euro.”

title: Britons kept in dark about scale of climate crisis, say viewers of ‘first-of-its-kind’ emergency briefing
summary: Nine out of 10 people felt motivated to act after watching film outlining threats to food security, economy and public health
text: The British government must be honest about the scale of the threat posed by climate and nature breakdown, researchers have said, after nine out of 10 people surveyed after watching a briefing on the issue felt more motivated to act. Last November, in the “first-of-its-kind national emergency briefing”, nine experts gave stark assessments in Central Hall in Westminster of the scale of the changes needed in the UK to adapt to the rapidly changing climate and ecological landscape. The team behind the event crowdfunded to produce the People’s Emergency Briefing, a film outlining the urgent threats that climate and nature breakdown pose to food security, the economy and public health. The film, which has so far been viewed by an estimated 185,000 people at more than 3,400 screenings, calls on the government to stage a primetime, televised emergency briefing on the climate and nature crisis. Of the 13,000 people surveyed, 87% said watching the film made them more motivated to act. Watching the film is associated with a “substantial shift” in environmental understanding and concern. Furthermore, 89% of people said the government should respond to the crisis with emergency-level mobilisation, similar to the Covid-19 pandemic or the second world war. Prof Mike Berners-Lee, the chair of the National Emergency Briefing, said the threat from Covid-19 was easy for the public to understand when they were trusted with the facts. The team is calling for a similar united emergency response delivered by independent experts and fronted by the prime minister. In addition, 93% of those surveyed said the public was not being fully informed about the climate crisis and nature loss. The government has previously been accused of hiding the truth from the public after refusing to publish a report from UK intelligence officers warning of the catastrophic impacts on national security from the collapse of vital ecosystems around the world. Prof Lorraine Whitmarsh, from the University of Bath who led the research, said while most people were aware of some of the risks associated with the climate crisis, the “second-order risks” around national security, food supplies and impacts on the NHS were not so obvious. She said: “Once somebody has sat through the film, I think they understandably feel everybody should know about these risks as these are going to be things that impact everybody on a day-to-day level, and so they support that greater education of the public.” The National Emergency Briefing team is calling on Andy Burnham to be honest about the scale of the threat posed by climate and nature breakdown. “In doing that, he will send out a message that he speaks the truth, however comfortable or uncomfortable,” said Berners-Lee. John Swinney, the first minister of Scotland, recently attended a screening of the film at the Scottish parliament. The UK government did not respond to a request for comment on whether it will screen the film but said it “welcomes any campaign that keeps our action against climate change and nature loss in the public discussion”. • This article was amended on 8 October 2026. An earlier version said last year’s national emergency briefing took place in Westminster Hall; in fact, the location was Central Hall, Westminster.
