title: Tesco predicts a low-alcohol ‘healthier’ Christmas
summary: First-half sales rise 2% to £33.8bn, helped by strong trade online, as retailer says it is making more delivery slots available
text: Tesco has raised its profit outlook as it expects households to splash out this Christmas – despite buying less alcohol – as they shrug off “uncertainty” over the Iran war. The UK’s biggest grocer said sales rose just 2% to £33.8bn in the 26 weeks to 29 August, but underlying profit was up 6.5% to £1.8bn. Ken Murphy, the chief executive of Tesco, said growth had been helped by strong online sales, which were up 8%, and a 9% jump in revenue from its premium own-label Finest range. He said: “Consumers in the UK have been pretty resilient in an uncertain environment and there is a sense that customers want to enjoy Christmas, given everything that is going on in the world.” The retailer had bought more stock of “key Christmas lines”, understood to be foods such as turkey and mince pies, and added 10% more delivery slots for its online grocery business. It is also ramping up its in-house rapid delivery service, Whoosh, and has signed new partnerships, including with Deliveroo. Murphy said he expected Britons to seek out a “marginally healthier Christmas” with higher sales of low-alcohol and no-alcohol drinks, including ready-mixed mocktails, but that families would still treat themselves as “customers do love to indulge”. He said he was not expecting food supplies to be hit by this summer’s drought. Tesco had also hedged its energy costs into next year and was making savings across the business to help keep prices down for shoppers. He said the business still had room for growth despite being almost twice the size of its nearest rival, Sainsbury’s, with a 28% market share, and that he did not “dwell too much” on the possibility of its closest rival acquiring another leading supermarket. Sainsbury’s is understood to have walked away from merger talks in January with the UK’s sixth-biggest supermarket, Morrisons, prompting consolidation chatter across the industry. “Whatever happens in the market we will respond to it,” Murphy said. While Tesco is expanding its reach with financial services and more fashion, he said its strategy “begins and ends in winning in food”. The company added: “While consumer confidence has remained relatively resilient in the first half of the year, ongoing geopolitical tensions continue to create uncertainty and we remain focused on helping customers get the best possible value.” Earlier this year, Tesco warned that profits could fall in the year ahead, citing increased uncertainty caused by the conflict in Iran, which began in late February. However, some economic indicators have suggested that the war has not yet had a significant impact. Last week, official estimates for UK growth in the second quarter were upgraded. The company said it now expected to make underlying annual profits of between £3.15bn and £3.3bn. That represents an upgrade from its previous expectation of at least £3bn in profits but the bottom end of the range would still mark a fall from a year earlier. Sales at established UK Tesco stores were up 1.5% as food sales motored, but the group’s Booker wholesale arm continued to struggle, with sales falling 2.6%. The supermarket said it was increasingly using artificial intelligence across the business, including in a meal-planning assistant that was tested from April with 280,000 staff before being launched for customers in September. It said AI was also helping to cut costs by making in-store stock replenishment more efficient and improving energy efficiency in its supermarkets. Tesco shares rose 4% on Thursday morning.

title: Voting opens in high-stakes Holborn and St Pancras byelection
summary: Zack Polanski has led energetic campaign for the Greens, while Labour will hope to hold on to Starmer’s old seat
text: Voting has opened in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, a contest seen as a key gauge of Andy Burnham’s ability to energise voters and whether Zack Polanski’s Greens can still peel off support from Labour’s left. Polanski, who leads the Greens in England and Wales, is standing for his party in the north London constituency, previously held by Keir Starmer before he stood down as an MP shortly after resigning as prime minister. The seat is, under normal circumstances, a Labour stronghold. Starmer won it with a majority of 11,500 at the 2024 general election despite strong challenges from the Greens and a leftwing independent candidate, who is not standing again and has endorsed Polanski. In 2019, Starmer won by nearly 28,000 votes. Polanski has run a highly energetic campaign. He has mobilised a large numbers of supporters to knock on doors, mimicking February’s Gorton and Denton byelection where the Greens overcame an even bigger Labour majority to take the seat. However, the political landscape has changed. Shortly after Gorton and Denton, YouGov polling put the Greens briefly above Labour, on a peak of 21%. The most recent equivalent had Polanksi’s party on 11%, 16 points behind Labour. Burnham, who succeeded Starmer as prime minister in July, is seen as having revitalised Labour, and used his speech at the party’s annual conference last month to set out a more ambitious and left-leaning collection of policies. Polanski’s fortunes in contrast appear to have declined, especially since last weekend’s Green party conference where a vote by members to adopt a policy equating Zionism with racism and calling for Israel to be replaced by a single Palestinian state prompted condemnation and splits in the party. Four out of the five Green MPs have condemned the policy, while councillors and others have distanced themselves from it or in some cases left the party. While policy is decided by Green members in direct votes, Polanski has been criticised for not saying whether or not he backed the motion and leaving the conference before the vote took place to resume campaigning. The stakes are also high for Burnham. Failure to win the seat by a reasonable margin could end his honeymoon period and bring renewed doubts about Labour’s ability to protect inner-city seats from the Greens, who won several London councils in May’s local elections. Holborn and St Pancras could be promising ground for the Greens, with a young and diverse population that includes many students. About 45% of constituents were born overseas and 48% are aged between 18 and 34. Labour has campaigned hard, fielding as its candidate Sagal Abdi-Wali, the 42-year-old leader of Camden council who arrived in London in the early 90s, speaking no English, after fleeing war in Somalia with her four brothers and her mother, who trained as a lawyer in Somalia. In a pre-poll message to voters, Burnham said: “This area gave Sagal a home when she arrived here as a refugee in the 1990s. Camden gave Sagal and her family hope. Now she wants to give that back to the communities that have always been there for her. It’s hard to think of someone more committed to their local area and the care of people than Sagal.” In his own statement, Polanski said the result was “looking close”, and that voters should choose him to pressure Labour. He said: “We already have a Labour government, a Labour council and a Labour [London] mayor. Isn’t it time for a Green voice for Camden to push Labour to do better on issues like rent controls and to put Thames Water into public ownership – issues where they’ve been backtracking?”

title: Thursday briefing: Why young people are taking to the streets across France
summary: In today’s newsletter: A youth-led movement is protesting crumbling school buildings and teacher shortages while turning adult focus onto wider educational inequalities
text: Good morning. In my experience, at any protest, the most memorable and encapsulating slogans are always the ones written by hand with marker pen on cardboard placards. “School is a right, not a privilege,” read one such sign held aloft by a student in Paris, where huge youth protests over the state of high school education have brought tens of thousands of young people and adults on to the streets, with further strikes planned today. “A state that gasses high school students is a weak state,” another sign said, referencing growing public anger at alleged police brutality towards young protesters. Tens of thousands of young people have also taken to Spanish streets in recent weeks to protest against the country’s deepening housing crisis. And outside the Labour conference in Liverpool last week, a crowd of jobless young people protested against what they saw as their bleak employment prospects. From Paris to the north of England, a similar thread runs through it all: a generation who feel betrayed by the absence of basic economic security and the erosion of public services that older generations took for granted. I spoke to our Paris correspondent Angelique Chrisafis who has been reporting from the centre of the French protests. But first, the headlines. Five big stories UK politics | Kemi Badenoch has announced that the Conservatives would abolish inheritance tax on family homes if elected, prompting criticism that she is prioritising cutting taxes for the rich. Education | Labour’s flagship changes to special education in England are at risk of unravelling because parents are rushing to secure support for their children before the system changes, new analysis has found. Spain | María del Carmen Abascal, the 87-year-old whose eviction set off a nationwide wave of protests against Spain’s housing crisis, has died. Science | A type of gene therapy based on Nobel prize-winning science is safe and can partly restore sight in blind people, researchers have revealed. Epstein | British billionaire Sir James Goldsmith warned that Jeffrey Epstein was a “sexual deviant” decades before the FBI closed in on the abuser, a Guardian investigation has found. In depth: Why have young people taken to the streets? The most significant youth movement to emerge across France in recent decades started on 17 September. Pupils returning to the Lycée Saint-Exupéry in Créteil, southwest of Paris, after the summer holidays, discovered they couldn’t continue their studies because of the extent of staff absences. The 15- to 18-year-olds blockaded their high school in protest. After negotiations with the education ministry, those staffing gaps were filled, but the impassioned complaints about crumbling buildings, overcrowded classrooms, and long school days – alongside a wider sense of inequality in the education system – resonated in the suburbs. “This movement grew from the ground up, from teenagers speaking to others outside their lycées. And over a couple of weeks, it has spread to hundreds of schools across France,” Angelique tells me. There’s a tendency to mythologise youth protest, especially in France – my uncle Joss was in Paris in 1968, and I lapped up his tales of pulling up cobblestones with his bare hands to build barricades. But youth activism is often diminished. When I reported on the schoolchildren who protested against the war in Iraq in 2003, and those who took part in climate strikes more than a decade later, adults repeatedly questioned whether they were swayed by older provocateurs or just wanted an excuse to dodge school and indulge in petty vandalism. (In my experience: no, no and no.) So it is in France this past month. “This is very much a youth movement,” says Angelique, comparing it to similar protests in 2006 over an unpopular youth employment contract, which were organised by students’ unions. “High schoolers are organising themselves without a centralised system or even spokesperson. That’s historic, and it’s taken the government by surprise.” *** Who are the teenagers on the streets? This week, the sociologist Fabien Truong, who has written widely on youth protest culture, praised the “maturity and coherence” of the protesters. He pointed to a “social media effect” whereby teenagers in wealthier areas were sharing videos of scurrying rats, gaping ceilings and leaking toilets in poorer schools. “It’s beautiful, this solidarity with students from more privileged backgrounds fighting for others and more equality.” This is precisely what Angelique has witnessed on the streets of Paris in recent days, where some of the most elite state schools have also been barricaded. She spoke to one teacher outside a school in a richer inner-city area, who was proud of her pupils. “She said there was a feeling of solidarity and generosity between teenagers, and how it flies in the face of the idea that they’re part of a social media generation who are selfish and narcissistic.” “I spent a long time speaking to teenage girls at one of the barricades in the centre of the city,” Angelique says,“who were sitting on top of a pile of bins and shopping trolleys. They told me: ‘We’re told in France that state education is a great leveller, but that’s not the case. We are being taught our lessons, but we’re getting out on to the street because we can’t bear to know that other students in poorer areas are in buildings that are crumbling’.” *** What’s wrong with French schools? As Angelique sets out in this helpful explainer, the pupils’ grievances are backed up by evidence – and the prime minister himself has described them as “legitimate”. Thousands of French schools at all levels, both primary and secondary, are in need of repair. Class sizes are bigger on average, and school days are longer, than in other comparable countries, while about 10% of teaching hours across the year are not delivered because of absent teachers. And yet France’s expenditure on high schools is 28% higher than the OECD average. What’s going on? The high spend can be explained in various ways, Angelique tells me. France has a lot more high school buildings to maintain than other countries, and many more vocational courses that cost more to teach. At the same time, more spending is desperately needed on staff. Teacher shortages are linked to very low pay progression through the profession, while there are severe difficulties in finding teachers to work in deprived areas. There’s also a shortfall in other crucial roles, including school nurses and support staff for pupils with disabilities. *** How have adults responded? Angelique tells me that what has defined how adults are responding to this burgeoning movement is the behaviour of politicians and police. Initially, the French government “had its head in the sand”, she says, distracted by public anger at rising fuel costs and a difficult budget process. “And when it suddenly woke up, the reaction was not a political one, it was a police crackdown.” Eighteen investigations into possible police brutality are already under way after injuries allegedly involving the use of police weapons, including a 15-year-old who lost his hand after contact with a stun grenade and a 14-year-old whose jaw was shattered after police allegedly beat him and fired a form of rubber-bullet launcher. Yesterday, the French interior minister suspended the use of stun grenades but rejected accusations of police brutality, saying riot officers only intervened when protesters turned violent. Dozens of teachers have also been injured in clashes, and a small number of schools burned or ransacked, but Angelique tells me that most protests have been peaceful. The injuries, however, have prompted outrage, with parents and teachers angry at the “disproportionate police response” now joining young people at the barricades. An Elabe poll for BFMTV, published on Wednesday, found that 72% of French people thought the student’s demands were legitimate – although 55% of of those surveyed also thought the protests should come to an end. The movement has also brought to the fore a debate about the wider state of public services ahead of next year’s presidential election. The radical left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon, backed for president by 47% of voters under 35, is loudly supporting the protesters, while far-right candidate Marine Le Pen has blamed the current government for chaos and called for an anti-riot law. The sheer scale of the marches in cities across France this week was unexpected, Angelique says. “There were hundreds of thousands of parents, grandparents and teachers. There is a lot of support for these young people’s demands and an understanding that the problems they are raising reflect wider worries about public services.” What else we’ve been enjoying As a 90s sitcom fan, I ate up Hollie Richardson’s interview with Jane Leeves and David Hyde Pierce, who played will-they-won’t-they couple Niles and Daphne in the Cheers spin-off, Frasier. Micha Frazer-Carroll, newsletters team At a time when English football is caught in a brutal off-field legal battle, Barney Ronay’s celebration of Harry Kane’s on-field genius is a reminder of what the sport should be about. Dipo Faloyin, newsletters team If you’re one for forbidden experiments, you’ll be fascinated by this article on the second world war generation who grew up on sugar rations, and saw lower rates of type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure and even anxiety in later life. Micha I really enjoyed Chibuzo Emmanuel’s much-needed piece on the damage that is being done by flattening of the wide variety of music genres across Africa into the simple bucket “Afrobeats”. Dipo This piece on the US’ first public nature library expanded my understanding of what a library can achieve – parents, children and other members of the local Colorado community can borrow hammocks, night vision binoculars and cameras for wildlife photography. Micha Sport Football | Southampton’s manager, Tonda Eckert, has been given a six-week suspended ban by the Football Association for his part in the Spygate scandal that landed the club with a four-point penalty and expulsion from last season’s Championship playoffs. Golf | Confirmation that Jon Rahm will play no part in LIV Golf in its post-Saudi Arabian form is likely to be only the start of a mass exodus from the breakaway circuit. Football | The Women’s Super League will face major disruption next season due to the Club World Cup, with Arsenal and Chelsea likely to be absent from domestic competition for up to a month. The front pages The Guardian splashes with “Special education overhaul under threat amid surge in applications”. Reporting on Kemi Badenoch’s party conference speech, the Mail leads with “Kemi’s family home pledge”, the Times says “Tories ‘will make you better off’”, and the Telegraph goes with “We’re ready for the fight”. The top story for the Financial Times is “Iran war blows £12bn hole in Healey’s room for manoeuvre”, while the Sun has “Dinghy pervert given free home” and the Mirror runs with “Reform not dodgy, says Reform”. The i Paper leads with “Young people should get ADHD help even without diagnosis, major report will say”. The Latest Christa Pike awake and speaking after botched execution: what happens now? Christa Pike, a death row inmate who survived the state of Tennessee’s attempt to execute her last week, is conscious and speaking. The 50-year-old is recovering in hospital after surviving two lethal injections in a case that has shocked many in the US and prompted a debate about the death penalty. She was due to be the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years. Michael Safi speaks to the chief reporter for Guardian US, Ed Pilkington. Cartoon of the day | Ella Baron The Upside A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad At 65 years old, Luis Gómez was still hawking vegetables at the market he had worked at since the age of eight. Now at 80, Gomes, or JM as he is popularly known, has become a musical sensation, selling out venues across Chile, as well as in Mexico, the UK, Argentina and France. He is the frontman of Los Crack del Puerto, who in May released their fourth record, Lo Mucho Que Nos Queda (So Much Yet to Come), as a cassette – to great acclaim. It’s a long way from his early life in the city of Valparaíso; the youngest of five children, he was three when his father died, and 10 when he lost his mother. For a time, he slept on the street between parked cars. JM would eventually form a musical double act with his cousin, Juan Navarro, and the two entertained crowds in Valparaíso’s bars. The pair would find fame well into their 70s after forming the band in 2017. “I never planned any of this, and I’d be happy still working at the market,” JM says. “But I suppose it’s never too late to give something a try.” Sign up here for a weekly roundup of The Upside, sent to you every Sunday Bored at work? And finally, the Guardian’s puzzles are here to keep you entertained throughout the day. Until tomorrow. Quick crossword Cryptic crossword Wordiply

title: ‘I feel perfectly safe’: white Lutonians on the town’s supposed no-go zones
summary: Little if any sign Bury Park is a place where any group might fear to tread, despite Tory MP’s comments to the contrary
text: From behind the counter of his chippie, Tanner Ahmed is wrestling with the notion that the regular stop-off point for fans attending Luton Town’s nearby football ground could be in a “no-go zone” for white people. “The whole point of setting up was to cater for thousands who were coming through here every week, especially in the first year when the club was in the Premier League,” said Ahmed, affectionately known as Mr T, in the Bury Park area, a predominantly Asian district of Luton. Outside, on the day after a shadow Conservative Home Office minister had claimed there were “no-go zones” for white people in Luton, there was a hum of activity on Dunstable Road, a thoroughfare lined with restaurants, jewellery stores and shops selling pakoras and other snacks. Further along, shoppers of different races trundled trolleys through the car parks of Sainsbury’s and Lidl. Blake Stephenson, the MP for Mid Bedfordshire, who lives in a village 15 minutes away from Luton, had claimed at the Tory party conference on Monday that the town was “a very dangerous place” where some communities “live in ghettoes”. “There are parts where white people won’t go,” he said. “They are like no-go zones.” His comments have been roundly condemned in Luton, but they echo the longer-term far-right framing of the English town as a poster child for the supposed dangers of Islamism and multiculturalism. As the home town of the far-right activist Tommy Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, it is also where the English Defence League (EDL), the street movement he used as a springboard to semi-celebrity status in likeminded circles, was launched. International far-right figures have eagerly seized on his depiction of the town. The Australian senator Pauline Hanson joined him there in July for a walkabout filmed by a major Australian TV network. The 2021 census found that 54.8% of Luton’s population were non-white, making it one of four places outside London at that time where the majority of the population was from minority groups. A day after Stephenson’s comments, there was little sign if any that Bury Park was a place where any group might fear to tread – even those giving out parking tickets. Among a smattering of white faces on Dunstable Road was a traffic warden, who declined to give their name but said: “I’ve always felt perfectly safe, and if ever there has been a minor incident, generally a member of the public or a shopkeeper has come to my aid.” Joshua Bozier, 36, a homeless man, said: “To be honest, I feel safer here in Bury Park than in the town centre. I know everybody here, whereas I’ve been spat at and urinated on in the centre. I’ve lived all over and Luton’s not what it’s made out to be.” He said Robinson “spilled a lot of shit”, but he did point to the past conduct of some Islamist activists in the area, who in 2009 demonstrated against the Royal Anglian regiment’s homecoming parade from Afghanistan. Only a tiny proportion of the town’s Muslim community were involved, but the incident became a useful symbol for the far right. Dr William Allchorn, an associate professor at Richmond American University and an expert on the far right, said the relationship between the EDL and the Islamist activists “was mutually reinforcing and for people looking for a European example of the supposed consequences of multiculturalism, Luton came with an unusually ready-made set of images, personalities and stories. “A series of confrontations occurred at exactly the moment when a new anti-Muslim form of street politics was developing, and an unusually effective political entrepreneur in Tommy Robinson was able to turn those local events into a national and eventually international story.” Sarah Owen, the Labour MP for Luton North, accused Stephenson of pushing the same “rightwing nonsense” as Robinson. The police and crime commissioner for Bedfordshire, Labour’s John Tizard, wrote to the Tory MP to say: “These statements are not supported by evidence and bear a troubling resemblance to far-right agitators seeking to divide communities.” Luton’s independent mayor, Javed Hussain, said he was baffled by Stephenson’s claims as he strolled through Bury Park, pointing out Christian, Sikh and Muslim places of worship and emphasising local regeneration. “I’m at a loss to know why he is saying this because Luton is a very multicultural, diverse town, as well as very vibrant one, so it’s disheartening,” he said. “Yes, in this area there may be a large number of people from an Asian background, but people from all over do travel here for all sorts of reasons, whether to shop or eat.” Research by the council has also found that cohesion was strong enough for the town to avoid the fractures that led to violence in other English towns in the past, though there were warnings that more needed to be done, such as broadening cultural experiences for school pupils. Not unsurprisingly, community relations are never far from the lips of local policymakers. While proud of the aspirational ethos among second- and third-generation British Asians in Luton, including his own family, Hussain said: “Look, if there was something I wish we could do more of, it would be to support children from council estates that are predominantly white. There is always more to do.”

title: South Korea threatens legal action if fuel shipments to Russia found to have broken law
summary: Responding to a Guardian report that revealed thousands of tonnes of fuel was transported to Russia, Seoul said it was investigating the cases
text: South Korea will take legal action if it finds that shipments of fuel from its ports to Russia broke domestic law, the government has said, responding to a Guardian report on the trade. The government, in a statement issued by the foreign and trade ministries and the customs service, said that it is “checking additional information concerning the loading cases reported by the Guardian” and “if the verification establishes that our laws and regulations have been violated, it plans to act in accordance with the law”. Guardian analysis of port records and ship-tracking data found that in July and August over 176,000 tonnes of fuel, mostly diesel, was loaded at several South Korean ports on to seven tankers that made 14 voyages to Russia’s far east. Three of the tankers were under UK and EU sanctions. One of them took on about 26,000 tonnes through a ship-to-ship transfer at an anchorage off the southern port of Yeosu. Isaac Levi, an analyst at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), a Finnish thinktank, said the trade “undermines the sanctions regime and South Korea’s support for Ukraine.” Russia’s capacity to refine oil has been severely disrupted by Ukrainian drone strikes. Its refinery throughput fell in June to its lowest level in more than 20 years, and diesel output is down nearly 30% on last year, according to the International Energy Agency. Thursday’s statement from Seoul said the refined petroleum products involved were not covered by South Korea’s export controls on Russia, which apply mainly to industrial machinery, electronics and vehicles. “As reported by the Guardian, the loading of refined petroleum products at our ports does not constitute a violation of our domestic law”, it said. The government said whether fuel of South Korean origin, such as diesel, had been exported “has not been confirmed”, adding that no diesel, aviation fuel or motor petrol had been “exported” from South Korea to Russia through customs clearance. It is unclear who owned or sold the fuel, which South Korean port records do not show publicly. The government also cautioned that the “mere fact that a vessel did not proceed directly to the final destination country stated on its declaration and instead moved to another country makes it difficult to conclude that there is a suspicion of false declaration of destination”. It said it would examine the tankers’ actual routes, any divergence from their declared destinations and the reasons for them, before judging whether the law had been broken. The three sanctioned tankers told South Korean authorities they were bound for Japan or Singapore before sailing to Vladivostok. The Russian-flagged Aram Khachaturian, which is not under western sanctions, loaded at Ulsan three times in July and August and on each occasion gave a destination other than Russia before sailing there. An adviser to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said this week that the shipments stood in “sharp contrast” to South Korea’s sanctions policies. On Wednesday South Korea’s presidential office said those remarks were “contrary to fact and inappropriate”, and asked Ukraine to refrain from public comment that could damage South Korea’s international credibility. Ukraine’s foreign ministry reportedly said on Wednesday that it had raised the fuel shipments with Seoul through closed diplomatic channels and asked for an explanation. Its spokesperson, Heorhii Tykhyi, said Kyiv also had “our own data on such activity”. Seoul, which has also been at loggerheads with Ukraine since Zelenskyy disclosed the transfer of North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea, on Thursday it will recall its ambassador to Kyiv. “The government has decided to recall its ambassador to Ukraine,” the foreign ministry said in a statement. “The government hopes that all outstanding issues between the two countries will be resolved amicably and will continue consultations with the Ukrainian side to that end.”

title: Country diary: The changing face of stubble fields, those shortcuts of my youth | Nicola Chester
summary: Linkenholt, Hampshire and Wexcombe, Wiltshire: Even to the untrained eye, traditional ones and modern, regenerative ones look very different
text: Stubble fields, those post-harvest acres of short straws, seem to be lasting longer into the season, as farmers respond to changing practices. I have a wistful attachment to stubble fields: for so long a kind of temporary commons where, for a few redundant weeks before autumn or winter ploughing, you could shortcut across them, the dew-filled straws flicking water up the inside of your legs. But today, stubble fields aren’t all equal. Below Cleve Hill Down, a tractor is drilling winter wheat directly into bare seedbed between the stubble. Regularly sprayed with herbicide, it is free of weeds or any green – a pale-gold spread of machine-knitted tweed. A hundred years ago, the stubble would be left, full of weeds, birds and insects, until midwinter ploughing, allowing frosts to break down the clods. The next field over, on another traditional farm, is another piece of arable history. Just over 30 years ago, it was the last stubble field to be burned in Berkshire; burning killed pernicious weeds, but a lot else besides. Many farmers had already given up the polluting practice when it was banned in 1993. Today, the stubble here remains while a cash crop of winter wheat begins to germinate – better for soil structure than ploughing. But, being otherwise bare, it’s at risk of erosion from wind and rain, having already been baked to death, and holds no value for wildlife. Over the hill at Wexcombe, the Hosier family are farming regeneratively to improve soil health rather than deplete it. Even to the untrained eye, their stubble looks different, the standing straws almost lost among the lush, green leaves – it’s a rarity in this landscape. George Hosier takes time to explain that the stubble was drilled with a cover crop – fodder radish, phacelia, buckwheat, clover, vetches – in August while the combine was still in the field, harvesting wheat planted last winter. It’s what he delightfully calls a “five-minute fallow field”. Some of those cover crops are beginning to flower now, their roots feeding, covering and protecting the soil. Wexcombe’s outdoor-living cows will graze some over winter (fodder they might dream about) before spring barley is planted around April. All that time, the soil – a living, complex resource – will be replenishing, and providing shelter and food for wildlife. • Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024, is available now at guardianbookshop.com

title: Next UK banknotes to feature barn owls, bumblebees, puffins and hedgehogs
summary: Four native species selected after consultation, but which one adorns which note is yet to be decided
text: Bees, barn owls, puffins and hedgehogs have been picked to feature on the next generation of banknotes, the Bank of England has announced. The quartet of creatures were selected after a large-scale consultation settled on wild animals as the theme, with members of the public then asked to pick their favourites out of 18 options divided into three categories. The buff-tailed bumblebee got the most votes in the insects, fish and amphibian group; the barn owl won the bird division; and the European hedgehog was named top mammal. The Atlantic puffin was added to celebrate Britain’s coastline, the Bank said. It is as yet undecided which species will adorn which banknote. An image of King Charles will continue to be represented on the other side of the £5, £10, £20 and £50 notes, which are expected to take several years to design. Victoria Cleland, the Bank’s chief cashier, said: “I am delighted that nearly half-a-million people responded to our wildlife imagery consultation, showing that cash still matters.” She said the public had chosen “four distinct and inspiring animals” that not only showcased the great variety of wildlife in the UK but would “also enhance the security of our banknotes”. Among the species losing out were the basking shark, the common frog and the red fox – the last celebrated in David Attenborough’s recent Wild London documentary, but seen as a pest by some. Atlantic puffins, with their distinctive multicoloured beaks, spend much of their lives at sea, coming ashore in summer to nest in burrows on clifftops on the coast including on the Farne Islands and Lundy. With their numbers declining, the bird is classified as “vulnerable” on the International Union for Conservation of Nature’s red list of threatened species. The decision to replace the historical figures on the banknotes – including Winston Churchill and Jane Austen – prompted a backlash when first announced in March, with the Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, accusing the Bank of “erasing our history”. Badenoch called it “a silly thing to do”, adding: “I absolutely do not support it.” Her Reform UK counterpart, Nigel Farage, described the move as “absolutely crackers”. The Liberal Democrat leader, Ed Davey, joined in, issuing a social media video in which he brandished a fiver and claimed that Churchill deserved “better than being replaced by a badger”. The badger was not among the 18-strong shortlist of animals eventually published by the Bank in June. That selection prompted the RSPCA to complain about the choice of animals on offer, calling for less obviously cute creatures to be included. “Gulls, badgers, rats and pigeons all divide opinion, but this would have been a great opportunity to discuss these fantastic animals,” it said. • This article was amended on 8 October 2026. An earlier version said that Atlantic puffins came ashore in summer to nest in burrows on islands off the coast; in fact, they also nest on clifftops around the UK’s coast.

title: Sardinian village where more women reach 100 may be new centenarian ‘blue zone’
summary: In Bolotana, 70 miles from island’s original blue zone, 13% of women who reach 70 will live on to a century
text: The secret to longevity is being a woman – specifically, a woman in one part of Sardinia. At least, that is the conclusion of a study on centenarians in a tiny mountain village on the Italian island. Sardinia became known as a haven for longevity, especially for long-lived men, in 1999 when a cluster of remote villages nestled in the slopes of its central and eastern provinces were classified among the world’s five “blue zones” – geographic areas with high concentrations of centenarians. Now Bolotana, located in the Margine area of central Sardinia about 70 miles (110km) from the island’s original blue zone, has emerged as a new potential candidate, researchers say, generating centenarians every year in a trend driven by women. A study by professors at Sardinia’s University of Sassari and the University of Alabama at Birmingham in the US, published in the scientific journal Frontiers in Aging, found that 13.8% of women in the village who reach the age of 70 will live to 100 – placing it second in the world for female longevity after Hong Kong. In Italy, where the number of centenarians has more than doubled since 2009, 3.5% of women who make it to 70 will achieve the milestone. The researchers analysed records of people born in Bolotana between 1900 and 1925 and found that 38 had lived beyond 100, putting their longevity rate at 57% higher than the Italian national average. The study began in 2024 and as of last year there were 12 centenarians among a population of 2,266 in Bolotana – roughly 12 times the Sardinian average. Six have since died and the six who are left are all women, the two eldest being 102. More residents are expected to reach the milestone age by the end of this year and during 2027. The findings also showed that, compared with the world’s other four blue zones – Okinawa in Japan, the Nicoya peninsula in Costa Rica, Ikaria in Greece and Loma Linda in California in the US – Sardinia’s zone was expanding. “The important thing is that, for the first time in more than 25 years, we have found a place for longevity outside of the conventional blue zone [in Sardinia],” Giovanni Mario Pes, the study’s lead scientist and a co-creator of the blue zone concept, told the Guardian. “But while Bolotana shares the same characteristics, it is even more exceptional. Whereas the original zone had an unusual balance between the two sexes, here female longevity prevails.” Pes said that while it was already well established that women lived longer for biological reasons, “the extraordinary thing is that the longevity of the women in Bolotana is three times higher than that of most western women”. Pes, a Sardinian whose great-grandfather lived to 110 and whose mother is 101, declined to be drawn into hypothesising over the secrets to the village’s longevity, saying the study was “limited to pointing out the existence of the phenomenon”. However, after spending time with sprightly centenarian women there, he said what struck him most were the “very intense and very real social relations” maintained throughout their lives. He gave the example of Giovanna Marras, 101, who lives with her sister. “They live together, they cook together, they talk to each other easily,” said Pes. “There was absolutely no sign of cognitive decline.” Francesco Manconi, the mayor of Bolotana, offered some theories. “I’m not a scientist but it’s probably a mix of things,” he told Corriere della Sera, citing a clean, fresh diet, although he said nobody renounced seada, a traditional local pastry filled with cheese, or mustazzolus, a spiced biscuit often eaten at breakfast. The “uncontaminated nature” surrounding the village could also play a role, Manconi added, as well as physical activity, despite Bolotana not having a gym. “Elderly people have always walked a lot … as much as 20km [a] day. And I would say they were mostly women.” As of November 2025, official statistics showed there were 23,548 residents in Italy who were aged 100 or over, up 2,000 from the previous year. Of those eclipsing a century last year, 82.6% were women. Women also take the lead among Italy’s 724 semi-supercentenarians, who people aged 105 and over – and among the 19 supercentenarians, those in the 110-plus age bracket.

title: This is one of Norway’s most pristine fjords. So why is it being used as a dumping site for mine waste?
summary: The Norwegian government has given a permit to a mining company to release waste into Førde fjord despite a 17-year battle by campaigners and a supreme court ruling against it
text: Shortly after the Norwegian stock market closed on 17 June 2026, a few dozen local people from the small west coast town of Vevring crowded around a laptop in a school. Surrounded by children’s drawings and windows looking out over Førde fjord, they listened as news arrived from Oslo. Norway’s supreme court had ruled against its government: a permit to release mining waste directly into the fjord two miles upstream was illegal, the court said. The moment marked the end of a 17-year fight, one of Norway’s most protracted environmental battles in living memory. In Oslo, Ingvild Fonn Asmervik, the project leader for Naturvernforbundet (Friends of the Earth Norway), compared the joy she felt to giving birth to her child. For Anne-Line Thingnes Førsund, a third-generation fisher living on the banks of the fjord in Vevring and a volunteer for the charity’s local branch, it was more of a relief. Like a mountain lifting off her shoulders, she said. These feelings of elation were short-lived. While Førsund and others celebrated, a government lawyer appeared on a television debate show to set out plans for a new temporary permit, and to allow the mine to continue to release waste directly into the fjord in the meantime. Four days later, the mine applied for fresh permission, and in late September, it was granted by Norway’s climate and environment ministry. “When we heard the pollution would continue, it was like they snatched the carpet from under us,” says Førsund. “We have answered every letter, commented on every consultation, complained whenever we could. We have been knocked down so many times and this could have been the opportunity for change.” While the government insists that it is acting lawfully, critics say the dumping threatens to foul one of Norway’s most pristine fjords. Others worry that the decision heralds a new wave of permits to pollute Norway’s fjords in the race to secure critical minerals. “This is not only about the fjord and us and our lives,” says Førsund. “This is about principles. When you have a government that doesn’t respect the supreme court you’re changing the system itself.” The move comes just as a wider spotlight is being shone on the issue of polluted waters in Norway. A recent report showed that Norwegian fish farms are filling fjords and other coastal waters with nutrient pollution equivalent to the raw sewage of tens of millions of people each year. Meanwhile, populations of Atlantic salmon are at a historic low in the country – 155 of Norway’s 450 or so salmon rivers were closed to fishing at the start of the season this year. Submarine tailings deposition (STD) – known colloquially by Norwegian critics as “fjord dumping” – is the process of pumping crushed rocks and chemical waste into the sea through pipelines hundreds of metres underwater. Proposed as an alternative to disposing of waste on land, the Norwegian government’s own Institute of Marine Research (IMR) warns that STD releases fine particles of toxic waste that can accumulate in smaller sea life and disrupt ecosystems at large. STD is outlawed in all of North America, Australia, Russia, Brazil, China and most of Europe. The few countries that still permit the practice include Papua New Guinea, Indonesia and Turkey. The Engebø titanium mine, on Førde fjord near Vevring, was first proposed by Nordic Mining in 2006 and the government awarded a permit to release waste into the fjord less than 10 years later. In response, Friends of the Earth Norway launched legal challenges that worked their way up the country’s legal system, arriving at a week-long supreme court hearing in spring 2026. Meanwhile, the mine came online and began releasing waste late in 2024. Nordic Mining is financed by investors including Japan’s Iwatani Corporation and the British offices of the international banks Morgan Stanley, UBS and Goldman Sachs. Other banks, including Standard Chartered and Citigroup, explicitly ban financing projects using STD. Nordic Mining did not respond to repeated requests for comment from the Guardian, but said in a social media post shortly after the supreme court decision that it would continue with how it disposed of waste, with the encouragement of Norwegian officials. “It has been said that our operation is illegal, that we have to close, that our work must stop. That is not the situation,” Nordic Mining said, adding that it was continuing “with the ambition to act responsibly, with respect for the fjords and mountains, and for the local community around us”. Legal wrangling over the permit came to focus on the EU’s water framework directive (WFD), which applies to Norway as a member of the European Economic Area. The WFD allows industrial activities to pollute water bodies only when there is an “overriding public interest”. The supreme court ruled that the reasons given when the permit was first awarded were not strong enough. However, the government argues they have grown stronger since the EU added titanium to its list of “critical minerals” in 2020. “The Norwegian government considers the Engebø project to be of significant importance for Norway and Europe,” a ministry spokesperson said, because “the Engebø mountain contains one of the world’s largest known deposits of rutile, a titanium-bearing mineral. Within Europe, Norway and Ukraine are the only countries with significant resources of this kind.” Legal scholars have questioned this logic. “That’s wrong. A permit exists or it doesn’t, and the supreme court decision is quite clear: the permit is illegal,” says Tarjei Ellingsen Røsvoll, associate professor of administrative and constitutional law at the University of Inland Norway. “The government is then openly allowing a company to dump a bunch of stuff in a fjord illegally. That is unprecedented; it damages trust and undermines a fundamental structure of constitutional and administrative law. They should take responsibility for having made an invalid and illegal decision, morally and legally.” While Nordic Mining awaited its new three-year permit, it continued to dispose of waste into Førde fjord. Økokrim, Norway’s central office for white collar and environmental crime, is now considering whether to investigate the dumping for illegality. While there have been few comprehensive studies of the impact of STD on marine ecosystems, scientists have linked heavy metal pollution now present in some fjords to STD decades earlier. The impact is particularly damaging when the waste is milled into small pieces, according to Terje van der Meeren, a research professor at the IMR, who co-authored the institute’s response to the Engebø mine application and testified during the supreme court hearings. “It’s like flour,” says Van der Meeren, adding that waste from Engebø includes a chemical that degrades into carbon disulphide, a neurotoxin. “Our concern is that this fine dust will pass into the rest of the fjord. What will happen with the [fish] spawning in this fjord? We don’t know.” In 2016, Van der Meeren and other IMR researchers travelled to the Arctic Repparfjord, in Hammerfest in the far north of the country, where a copper mine dumped waste for six years in the 1970s. Decades later, they found haddock with higher levels of lead, arsenic and chromium in their muscles than those in nearby waters, according to research published this year. Other Norwegian studies have found historic STD contamination in plankton, crabs and fish eggs. Back in Vevring, Førsund and other campaigners are now preparing for a fresh legal battle over the temporary waste permit – though dumping is likely to continue for as long as it takes for a new decision to be reached. She looks back on the first protests against the mine with nostalgia. In one photograph, taken more than a decade ago, protesters gathered for a meal on the banks of the fjord; Førsund’s daughter, now an architect, was only a child. “So many of these people are dead now,” she says. “The fjord is bigger than us. It has given us food and income and meaning and music and fish and birds for thousands of years. Now it gives us the energy to keep fighting.”

title: Japan beer giants raided over suspicions they colluded to set the price of beverages
summary: Investigators probe Asahi, Kirin, Suntory and Sapporo breweries – which together control more than 90% of Japan’s beer market
text: Japanese authorities have raided the country’s four biggest breweries over suspicions they colluded to set the price of beer and other beverages – a practice media reports said could have forced drinkers to pay over the odds. Officials from the Fair Trade Commission this week searched the offices of Asahi Breweries, Kirin Brewery, Suntory Beer and Sapporo Breweries – which together control more than 90% of the domestic market. The quartet are suspected of violating the anti-monopoly law. The commission’s secretary general, Hiroo Iwanari, confirmed an investigation had begun, but declined to give details. The companies said they would cooperate with authorities. The commission is understood to have launched the investigation given the potential effect the alleged cartel has had on prices after wholesalers sell their products on to supermarkets, convenience stores, bars and restaurants, the Mainichi Shimbun said. Japanese media quoted sources as saying that sales managers and other executives from the breweries were suspected of meeting secretly over a prolonged period to coordinate on the timing and scale of retail price increases, which ranged from several yen to several dozen yen a time. Prices for beer and a low-malt version called happoshu have risen multiple times to reflect the rising cost of raw materials and logistics. The commission suspects the breweries bypassed proper pricing competition and collaborated to ensure they made a profit, the Mainichi said. Alcohol consumption in Japan has declined in recent decades as a result of depopulation and changes in drinking habits among younger people. But sales still reached ¥3.8tn ($24.3bn) in 2024, with beer accounting for 30% of the total, followed by happoshu and third-category beer, which contains little or no malt, with a combined 11.9% The four breweries have all raised their prices at the same time, most recently in April last year, citing the rising cost of materials and distribution. Prices also rose in October 2022 and October 2023. Shares in Asahi, Kirin, Suntory and Sapporo fell after Wednesday’s raids – the first investigation of its kind involving the food and beverage industry. Japanese media quoted sources as saying the commission had judged the case to be particularly serious given its potential impact on consumers, adding that the probe could result in a criminal complaint. The probe comes three months after the commission raided six Japanese ice-cream makers over allegations of operating a cartel.

title: Indonesia accused of ‘gross negligence’ in wildfires lawsuit as haze tests region
summary: NGOs in Indonesian Borneo file class action lawsuit calling for government to better manage annual fires
text: The Indonesian government has been accused of “gross negligence” in a class action lawsuit over its handling of wildfires that have cloaked large parts of South-east Asia in a toxic haze, shuttered schools and caused a spike in respiratory illnesses. The lawsuit, filed by indigenous and civil society groups in the Indonesian part of Borneo, named President Prabowo Subianto and the governor of West Kalimantan among 10 defendants. The case seeks comprehensive recovery and rehabilitation measures that would include covering the healthcare costs of residents. None of those named in the lawsuit attended the opening day of court in West Kalimantan’s provincial capital Pontianak on Wednesday, leading judges to adjourn the hearing until 21 October. “We feel sad and regretful about their absence … But on the other hand, we also understand that perhaps this haze condition caused them to be unable to land in Pontianak,” the plaintiffs’ lawyer, Glorio Sanen, told reporters. Sanen said the case was “a step to address the problem” of wildfires that flare up annually in Indonesia, where they are often lit as a cheap way to clear land for oil palm planting. Indonesia, the world’s largest producer of palm oil, has been accused of not doing enough to stop the so-called “slash and burn” land clearances, although the government has vowed a crackdown and deployed the military to fight the fires. The blazes hit a crisis point this year due to an unusually intense El Niño weather phenomenon, which has created drier-than-usual conditions, sending a putrid smog to Malaysia, Brunei and Singapore, and even the Philippines. The transboundary haze has angered Indonesia’s neighbours. Schools in the Malaysian state of Johor, just north of Singapore, were to be closed on Thursday and Friday due to deteriorating air quality, local authorities said. The four plaintiffs in the West Kalimantan lawsuit, which was filed last month, include a chapter of Indigenous NGO AMAN and the local branch of Catholic Youth. Yakobus Kumis, a plaintiff representing a Dayak ethnic group, indigenous to the island of Borneo, expressed disappointment that government representatives did not attend this week’s hearing, saying it was a “way of the central government teaching the people that violating the law is OK.” He said the government ignored warning signs ahead of the fires breaking out, and called for the smoke crisis to be classified as a national disaster. A similar lawsuit filed last year at a court in South Sumatra was dismissed. The presidential office did not immediately ⁠respond to a request for comment. Agence France-Presse and Reuters contributed to this report

title: Tanker attacked off Qatar as Iran claims route transporting oil through strait of Hormuz will be ‘closed’
summary: Oil rises above $100 as attacks on ships hit new high, amid reports Trump is discussing launching strikes before the US midterms
text: A tanker sailing off the north coast of Qatar has been attacked, causing an unknown number of casualties, a British maritime security agency said. The attack came as Iran declared it would close a route in the strait of Hormuz being used to circumvent Tehran’s blockade of traffic. The vessel was in the Gulf, about 500km (300 miles) west of the strait of Hormuz, when it reported being struck “by multiple projectiles”, the UK Maritime Trade Operations said on Wednesday. The UK authority did not specify the origin of the ship. Wednesday’s attack comes as strikes on tankers sailing through the strait of Hormuz hit their ⁠highest weekly level since the Iran war began, according to maritime security firms, as oil prices climbed above $100 per barrel. In the ‌week to 5 October, there were at least 12 attacks ‌on oil, liquefied natural gas and liquefied petroleum gas tankers around the strait, according to data from three security sources. On Tuesday, India’s foreign ministry said 12 crew members were injured after an attack on a Panama-flagged oil tanker passing through the strait of Hormuz. Attacks, attempted attacks and harassment activity including drone overflights and surveillanceby Iran’s Revolutionary ⁠Guards have persisted in the strait, a US Navy-led agency said on Sunday. “These actions ⁠continue to demonstrate Iran’s intent to assert presence along key transit lanes and maintain pressure on transiting vessels,” ‌the Joint Maritime Information Center said. Ships in the Gulf and those attempting to transit the strait, the only way in or out of the oil-rich region for vessels, have come under repeated attack since the US and Israel attacked Iran on 28 February. On Wednesday, Tehran said it would further choke Hormuz, declaring transit routes in the strait deemed illegal by Iran ⁠would soon be closed, in reference to a southern pathway hugging Oman’s coast. Mohammadreza Naqdi, an adviser to the Revolutionary Guards’ Commander, said these “few routes” had been created by blasting and damaging ⁠some of the rocky passages and were used by “small boats smuggling oil and transferring ⁠it to tankers”, despite evidence Gulf oil exports are regaining prewar levels. “The strait of ‌Hormuz is closed, ‌and the armed forces of the Islamic Republic of Iran have ‌full control over it,” he told the Fars news agency. The IRGC has consistently denied that seaborne crude flows in the strait are rebounding thanks to US Navy help. IRGC adviser Majid Mirahmadi said on ⁠Thursday that a daily average of 10 ships were transiting the waterway against an average of 125 before the war. The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, disputed that account on Wednesday, saying Iran had “lost complete control” of the strait. “There’s almost as much oil flowing out now as there was before this conflict began.” Amid mixed messaging and supply concerns, the price of oil rose on Wednesday, with Brent crude topping $100 per barrel. The continuing stalemate in the war is heaping pressure on Donald Trump. On Thursday, the US president announced he would not attack Iran before the midterm elections, contrary to recent reports in US media that he was considering resuming military operations against Iran in the coming weeks. On social media he wrote that “while Iran is in very bad condition, both Economically and Militarily, and while the Blockade will remain in full force and effect, with Oil flowing in Record Numbers of Barrels through the Hormuz Strait (22 Million Barrels, last night alone, with not one barrel coming from, or going to, Iran!), we will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the Midterm Elections”. Last week, a third US aircraft carrier set sail for the region. It could mean that three carriers are in the region as early as the end of October. As a result of Trump’s war with Iran, Americans have been grappling with high gas prices and soaring diesel costs. The US has set up its own counter blockade of Iranian ports and occasionally fires on vessels linked to Tehran. It has also bombed Iranian targets in retaliation for Tehran’s attacks on ships, although there have been no such reported strikes since 1 September. Hormuz is vital to the world economy, with around a fifth of the planet’s oil and liquefied natural gas passing through the strait before the war began. With Reuters and Agence France-Presse

title: Donald Trump’s Texas rally rocked by repeated protests
summary: Trump briefly stepped away from the microphone after one protester appeared to approach the stage
text: Donald Trump’s latest campaign rally was rocked by repeated protests on Wednesday as the US president urged Texas voters to back the embattled Senate candidate Ken Paxton. At least half a dozen demonstrators interrupted the US president during his remarks in San Antonio, with some led away by police. One was physically assaulted by an older Trump supporter as he tried to leave the arena. Trump briefly stepped away from the microphone after one protester appeared to approach the stage. “He’s going back home to mom,” the president said after the man was removed. “But what he doesn’t know is his mom voted for Trump.” Supporters waving cowboy hats and chanting “USA” drowned out some of the protesters, while Trump told demonstrators to “get the hell out of here”. He mocked their appearance and claimed without evidence that “they’re paid by enemies of our nation”. The president also used Wednesday’s rally to address recent comments in which he appeared to suggest that Iran could destroy Los Angeles or San Diego, earning widespread condemnation from Democrats. In remarks that were again less than crystal clear, Trump said: “I said it the other day, let them hit a missile into San Diego or Los Angeles on the way. Let them hit – you want to see a horror show? You want to see problems? Let them hit San Diego. Let them hit Los Angeles and you want to see some bad things happen. “You want to see a country that would be in freefall. We’re not going to let that happen. We protect our cities, we protect our country, we’re not letting that happen. And they’d use it, too. They’d use it.” Trump was making his third trip to Texas in less than a month as Republicans pour money into races they had expected to win comfortably in November’s midterm elections. Paxton, whom Trump endorsed during the Republican primary after turning against the incumbent senator John Cornyn, was called on stage by the president and thanked him for his support. “Mr President, I want to thank you for coming for me, for coming for us, and for coming for Texas,” Paxton said. “We are going to win this race.” Trump described Paxton as “perhaps the greatest attorney general in the United States of America”, and said: “He was tough and he was with us all the way. He’s a fantastic man.” The Republican campaign to maintain control of the Senate has become increasingly focused on Texas, where Democrat James Talarico has emerged as a serious threat. A New York Times/Siena College poll released last weekend showed Talarico leading Paxton 51% to 45% among likely voters. Texas has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1988. Trump won the state by almost 14 percentage points in 2024, but his approval rating has fallen sharply. A Reuters/Ipsos poll completed on Monday put his approval rating at 32%, while registered voters preferred Democrats to Republicans 44%-37%. Trump’s relationship with Paxton has sometimes appeared uneasy. Trump called Paxton “a pain in the ass sometimes” last week, but on Wednesday did not discuss a leaked recording of Paxton in which the Senate candidate reportedly complained about the war in Iran, rising fuel prices and the way his campaign was being run. Instead he spent much of the rally attacking Talarico, whom he repeatedly referred to as “Tala-freako”. He claimed without evidence that Talarico is vegan and recently disappeared: “He’s sick because he’s been forced to eat meat for political reasons and he’s throwing up all over the place.” Trump insisted: “The people of Texas are not going to let weak, gutless, self-hating, transgender-promoting freak shows destroy everything that we’ve built.” The president’s political difficulties in Texas were underlined by the absence of the Republican governor, Greg Abbott, a close Trump ally who is himself facing a competitive re-election race against the Democratic state representative Gina Hinojosa. Abbott was instead due to attend the dedication of a hospital about 330 miles away. Democrats seized on his decision not to appear with Trump. Republicans have now devoted more than $300m to elections in Texas, according to the Associated Press, while Trump’s broader 32-day campaign blitz has taken him through several Republican-leaning states, including Oklahoma, Alabama, Ohio and Nebraska.

title: Ukraine war briefing: Zelenskyy condemns ‘vile’ attacks from Russia that killed 20 in one apartment
summary: Death toll from latest attack wave on Ukraine climbs to 28; Moscow says it ​hit military cargo vessel and port infrastructure. What we know on day 1,688
text: The death toll from Russia’s latest attack on Ukraine has climbed to 28, its interior minister, Ivan Vyhivskyi, has said. Russia pounded Ukraine with waves of missiles and drones on Wednesday. The heaviest losses were in ⁠Pryluky, in Ukraine’s northern Chernihiv region, where a Russian missile obliterated a five-storey residential building. Twenty people died in the attack, including five children, said Pryluky’s regional governor, Vyacheslav Chaus. On Wednesday evening, prosecutors in Kyiv said falling debris from a drone killed two people in a suburb of the capital. In ‌Pryluky, an excavator and dozens of rescuers with ‌shovels sifted through rubble at the site where several sections of the apartment block had collapsed. Emergency workers used ladders to get to the upper floors of what remained of the building, and as they worked their way down brought out ‌15 survivors. About 55 people were wounded in the town, regional officials said. Volodymyr Zelenskyy called the Pryluky attack one of Russia’s “most vile”. “The Russians wanted to strike painfully and demonstratively,” the Ukrainian president said. “This was one of the most vile strikes.” Russia’s ⁠defence ministry has said ⁠its ⁠forces struck a ⁠vessel heading ⁠to the Ukrainian ‌Black ‌seaport of ‌Odesa with cargo for the Ukrainian military. The ‌statement on Telegram on Wednesday gave no further details of the strike. The ⁠ministry also said Russian drones had hit infrastructure in ‌Ukrainian ports, without elaborating. Bulgarian president Iliana Yotova blamed Russia’s war in Ukraine for worsening security in the Black Sea on Wednesday. Early on Tuesday, two ⁠ships were hit in a drone attack in Bulgaria’s Black Sea exclusive economic zone, with one sinking and the other damaged. The crew of the damaged ship were rescued but the crew of the ⁠sunken one remain missing. Yotova did not directly blame Russia, but said on Wednesday that the war had led to “a significant deterioration” in security for commercial vessels in the region. Bulgaria has halted its search for the missing ⁠crew. European Union envoys approved 1,646 new designations under the bloc’s sanctions regime for Russia, with most focused ⁠on the country’s military industrial complex, three EU diplomats said on Wednesday. More than half of the newly added entities and individuals are involved in the ⁠chain of production of Russia’s ballistic missiles.

title: Texas kills man in first US execution since botched lethal injection of Christa Pike
summary: Jamaal Howard, 46, executed by fatal dose of pentobarbital after lawyers’ bid for stay had been denied
text: A Texas man was put to death on Wednesday in the first US execution since the botched lethal injection of Christa Pike in Tennessee last week. Jamaal Howard, 46, was pronounced dead at 8.03pm after receiving a fatal dose of pentobarbital, a sedative, at the state prison in Huntsville. Howard’s lawyers sought to halt the execution, arguing to the Texas court of criminal appeals there were similar risks of executing Howard using the same lethal injection drug that was used on Pike. Pike survived two doses of pentobarbital and had complained her arms felt like they were going to explode as she was given the drug. “Texas should not be eager to follow in Tennessee’s footsteps,” Howard’s attorneys argued. The court denied the request for a stay and later denied a second attempt to stop the execution over the drug. The court denied both without elaboration. The US supreme court also denied a late appeal on Wednesday evening without comment. Texas has executed six people so far this year, with two more lethal injections scheduled after Howard. He is the 30th person executed nationwide in 2026. Howard was found guilty of capital murder in 2001 for robbing a convenience store in Silsbee, a town north of Beaumont, and fatally shooting 42-year-old clerk Vickie Swartout. Asked by the warden if he had a final statement, Howard apologized profusely to members of his victim’s family, who watched through a viewing window just feet from the death chamber. “I wish that you accept my apology and I wish for your forgiveness,” he said, shortly before the injection got under way. “I’m sorry for what happened. I wish you can learn to forgive me one of these days.” His legal team argued that, at the time of the crime, Howard was intellectually disabled and thus ineligible for the death penalty, as the supreme court ruled in 2002. Pike regained consciousness on Tuesday. Her lawyers say she has pneumonia and is unable to move her arms. Pike’s was the second botched execution in Tennessee this year, and Governor Bill Lee has barred any further lethal injections for the rest of the year. He has also ordered an investigation into why Pike’s execution failed. Pike’s lawyers had previously argued her blood disorder would make a lethal injection painful. Speculation has also swirled over the quality of the pentobarbital. “There is a similar risk,” Howard’s attorneys wrote in the Wednesday motion filed with Texas’s court of criminal appeals, “that Texas’s execution drugs are likewise degraded, as they are far past the original beyond-use dates that the pharmacopeia allows for drugs of this kind.” Last week, the fifth circuit court of appeals declined a request to stop Howard’s execution. Texas officials did not immediately return a request for comment on Wednesday morning. The Associated Press contributed reporting

title: Margaret Hamilton, trailblazer whose software powered Apollo 11 moon landing, dies aged 90
summary: MIT computer scientist led development of software for moon mission and earned Presidential Medal of Freedom
text: Margaret Hamilton, the computer pioneer whose software powered the first moon landing, has died, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) announced on Wednesday. She was 90. In an era before titles such as software engineer and computer scientist became mainstream, Hamilton, who died on 30 September, learned to program under the tutelage of a renowned MIT meteorologist. She continued to perfect the craft in an MIT laboratory, writing software that could detect enemy aircraft. When the institute received a Nasa contract to develop the Apollo onboard flight software, she jumped at the opportunity. “I was attracted both by the sheer idea and the fact that it had never been done before. I was the first programmer to join and the first woman they hired,” she told the Guardian in 2019. In 1969, minutes before the Apollo 11 spacecraft was set to make history by landing on the lunar surface, an onboard computer’s alarm rang, indicating an emergency. Faced with a decision of whether to abort the mission, the spacecraft continued on. The software was working just as Hamilton and her team intended. “It quickly became clear the software was not only informing everyone that there was a hardware-related problem but was compensating for it – restarting and re-establishing the highest priority tasks. The error detection and recovery mechanisms had come to the rescue,” Hamilton said. Barack Obama referenced the incident when he presented her with the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2016. “Our astronauts didn’t have much time, but thankfully they had Margaret Hamilton,” he said. Hamilton is survived by her daughter, a son-in-law, two grandsons and four great-grandchildren, according to MIT. Reflecting on the mission, in a 2009 interview with MIT News, Hamilton said: “Looking back, we were the luckiest people in the world; there was no choice but to be pioneers; no time to be beginners.”
