title: ‘People are scared of her, to be honest’: Kemi Badenoch remakes Tories in her image
summary: At Conservative conference, some worry about becoming a one-woman party, while others say party should thank their lucky stars they have her
text: Kemi Badenoch has long said that the Conservatives were “under new management”, but in a TV interview to mark the end of a party conference at which she has been front and centre of more or less everything, she took the analogy further. “Your viewers will know that sometimes you have a football team that’s disappointing,” the Tory leader told GB News. “There’s a new captain, there’s a new coach, there’s a new owner, effectively – which is all me.” These are bold words even for a politician known to possess an iron-clad self-confidence. But they are no exaggeration. Badenoch is not only outperforming her party in polling terms, she is busy remaking it in her own image. The broad ideological direction was already set, with Badenoch saying explicitly at the start of this year that centrist ideas were no longer wanted. Some more moderate figures remain in her shadow cabinet, but they are signed up to a right-leaning agenda, including opposition to net zero and a bonfire of human rights protections. Those around Badenoch say, however, that her control goes further, with policy decisions such as the move to grant free childcare to people with incomes above £100,000, announced on the eve of the conference, made simply because she believes they are the right thing to do. “With policies it’s not about chasing certain groups of voters,” one shadow cabinet minister said. “She focuses on what she thinks needs to be fixed, what she feels is wrong.” Talking her out of a policy decision, they said, was a tall order: “It’s not going to happen – it’s tablets of stone. She’s not going to change her mind. She knows what the policies have to be.” Many political parties are, to a greater or less extent, a cult based around the leader, but this is particularly the case for the 2026-period Conservatives, where MPs say Badenoch is talked about on the doorsteps with an admiration and respect not accorded to their party more widely. MPs recount how her name is raised unprompted. One said: “She’s brought up in a positive way. Crucially, in a world where most people couldn’t name more than a handful of politicians, they know who she is.” This starring role was obvious throughout the Conservatives’ conference in Birmingham, not least Badenoch’s arrival, which saw her greeted by a flag-waving crowd of activists chanting: “Kemi, Kemi.” Inside the venue, Badenoch was the heroic centrepiece of the party’s “Birmingham tapestry”, shown in mocked-up 12th-century form doing everything from chastising Wes Streeting to sitting in the turret of a tank. Such veneration is not just wishful thinking by a party eager to move on from a revolving door of previous leaders. While last year’s conference was viewed as make-or-break for Badenoch, even with her party still bumping along at 20% or so in the polls her position is now seen as secure, with the Conservatives more unified than they have been for years. This is in part the result of some serial malcontents leaving for Reform UK, especially Robert Jenrick, as well as the party’s diminished size in the Commons, which as one shadow cabinet minister notes, is too small for factions: “We could just about fill a corner table in Pizza Express.” There are still private doubts, including Badenoch’s instinct to lean into culture wars rather than focus on the economy, which those around her believe is the party’s strongest electoral card. Some party figures also wonder if Badenoch is thinking about election strategy at all with her very personal suite of policy choices, which in Birmingham mainly consisted of giving tax breaks to wealthier people. This was capped in her end-of-conference speech with the announcement that a Badenoch-led government would exempt people’s homes from inheritance tax, an idea which, given that the levy only begins on property worth more than £500,000, is a largely theoretical idea outside London and the south-east of England. While such policies could be appealing to prosperous home counties voters who defected to the Liberal Democrats in 2024, this does not seem to be the plan. During another TV interview, Badenoch chided her questioner for suggesting her tax cuts were aimed at bringing back such support. “I’m very sad that you’re looking at this in crude electoral terms,” she said. “That’s how we’ve all got into this problem where we keep thinking about winning elections rather than thinking about what works.” One former Tory strategist said there was a risk of incoherence: “I can’t understand what is being achieved with these announcements. Forget lots of the small ones, just use the money and do a big tax cut for middle earners.” There was, they added, little chance things would change: “People are scared of her, to be honest. I think a lot of her team don’t know how to say no to her.” However, much like football, politics is not a one-person game, and a star player or manager will only get you so far. And while Badenoch was at pains to praise colleagues in her speech, it is fair to say that the rest of the shadow cabinet is lagging. Andrew Griffith, Badenoch’s new shadow chancellor, was feted by his boss for his private sector business expertise. But on Monday he gave a speech widely seen as one of the worst delivered to any conference in years. It is a matter of profile as well as ability. While Badenoch is recognised by 90% of voters, according to YouGov polling, only 22% say they know who Griffith is. A number of his colleagues are on similar ratings, with pollsters saying even these are likely to be inflated by people who don’t want to admit ignorance. The experienced Tom Tugendhat, now in the foreign affairs brief, does slightly better, on 46%. Laura Trott, the shadow education secretary, hits 50%, but this is because some people mistake her for the Olympic cyclist, now Laura Kenny, formerly of the same name. There was some unease in Birmingham about Badenoch blotting out everyone else. “Isn’t there a danger we are becoming a one-woman party?” one activist asked a fringe of shadow cabinet members. Others disagree. “It’s a normal dynamic for an opposition party that is unpopular,” said Nick Timothy, the shadow justice secretary. “It needs a strong popular leader that can pull it up and we should thank our lucky stars that we have her.” Either way, most Conservatives now accept that, for now, it is up to Badenoch to chart the Conservatives’ course, whatever it involves. One ally said: “We win elections on the economy but there’s no point telling Kemi not to do anything.”

title: George Galloway contests London byelection without setting foot in UK
summary: Veteran leftwinger has been ‘in exile in the east’ in Russia and not been to Holborn and St Pancras constituency since campaign began
text: George Galloway has been elected seven times to parliament, but his attempt to succeed for an eighth this week, in the London seat formerly held by Keir Starmer, is undoubtedly his most curious effort yet. Since the byelection campaign began, the leader of the Workers party of Britain has yet to set foot in the UK, let alone the Holborn and St Pancras constituency, because he is in what he describes as “self-exile” after being questioned by counter-terrorism police at Gatwick airport a year ago. Prolific social media feeds show that the veteran leftwinger has spent the past few weeks on a speaking tour in South Africa, with his most recent public appearance on Saturday at a pro-Palestine rally in Cape Town, though posts in the last 24 hours suggest he is in Shanghai, China. Prior to that he was in Moscow, repeatedly making his hostility to Ukraine and Nato as explicit as his support for Palestine and opposition to apartheid. “The biggest issue in the H&StP byelection is the path leading us to WW3 in Ukraine,” Galloway wrote on X in the middle of September, an argument that has not gained much traction with voters, though he has chosen to repeat it online – the only way he can reach voters personally before Thursday’s byelection. Meanwhile, social media feeds show handfuls of Workers party activists campaigning in the constituency without their candidate, fighting a peripheral campaign in a byelection considered to be a battle between Labour’s Sagal Abdi-Wali and Zack Polanski, standing for the Greens. “Sincere gratitude to my campaigners who are performing miracles on the ground in my enforced absence. Salute to the supporters they are encountering every day. We can win this. And me and my family can come home. Thank you,” Galloway posted at the end of September. The campaign highlights an anomaly with Britain’s electoral law. Any British, Irish or qualifying Commonwealth citizen over 18 may stand for parliament – as long as they are not bankrupt or members of the police, armed forces, civil servants or judges. There is no requirement to be a registered elector or other residency requirement, according to the Electoral Commission. Last month, Galloway also revealed he had been “debanked” – his bank accounts suddenly closed – by the Lloyds-owned Bank of Scotland. “Thirty-nine years ago I opened a personal bank account with Bank of Scotland in Byres Rd Glasgow. Yesterday without explanation or notice they closed my accounts,” he posted on 4 September, threatening Lloyds with legal action. The bank said it would not comment on individual cases, though account closures are rare. A Bank of Scotland spokesperson added: “Our policy is not to close a customer’s account based on political or personal beliefs and we make customers aware if we make the decision to close an account.” Galloway chose to leave the UK after he and his wife, Putri Gayatri Pertiwi, were stopped for what he said was “a total of 11 hours” in September last year by “five armed police officers” after returning from the Russian city of Nizhny Novgorod and attending a World Youth Festival assembly. Last month, the former MP said the first question police asked him was: “Why do you admire Mr Lavrov?” They were referring to Russia’s long-serving foreign minister, Sergey Lavrov. Posting on X, Galloway attached a photo of Lavrov smoking and added: “I could have just shown him this picture!” Galloway told the broadcaster RT, the former Russia Today, in an interview in March this year that officers “took all our stuff and copied everything on our phones”, forcing them to miss a public meeting in London at which, his wife said in a post on Instagram, “the Chinese ambassador [was] waiting for us”. Neither Galloway nor his wife were subject to any further legal action in a stop that took place under schedule 3 of the Counter-Terrorism and Border Security Act 2019. This allows police to detain people to determine if they have been engaged in hostile activity, considered by investigators to be a low bar. The former MP had appeared on a discussion panel with Lavrov in Moscow in June 2025, at the Forum of the Future, an event described as “far-right” by the Moscow Times, where Elon Musk’s father, Errol, and Alex Jones, the rightwing founder of Infowars, were also speaking. In Galloway’s March interview with RT, where he had hosted a talkshow for nine years until Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, he said he was “now in exile in the east, and I must say that Moscow in the spring is quite the place to be”. He was in Moscow in late April, speaking at the inaugural conference of Sovintern, an international pro-Soviet socialist network led by the opposition A Just Russia party, where a welcome address from the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, was read out. In early September, Galloway released a video promoting his online talkshow, filmed from Moscow’s Red Square where he also said he would appear at a roundtable event on security at the city’s “prestigious university”. On 13 September he participated in a public Sovintern discussion with Zakhar Prilepin, a leading pro-war author and propagandist who has fought in Ukraine and called for “the return of Kyiv to Russia”. A day later, Galloway was selected as the Workers party candidate, and he shortly afterwards went to South Africa for a speaking and fundraising tour with the leftwing activist and former journalist Yvonne Ridley. He continued to post on social media from South Africa, frequently on international affairs. He places a particular emphasis on Russia and Ukraine. Earlier this month Galloway posted an anti-Andy Burnham image, with the prime minister dressed in blue and yellow, the colours of Ukraine. “I want you to die for Ukraine. Conscription coming soon!” the caption read. Particular criticism has also been reserved for Polanski, his most obvious rival for political support. On 25 September, Galloway posted: “I am with Russia Zack is with NATO. I am with an end to the war in Ukraine Zack is with Zelensky and risking WW3.” Galloway and the Workers party were approached for comment.

title: Trump administration sued over plans to send election monitors to voting sites
summary: NAACP files lawsuit after head of DoJ’s civil rights division says she hopes to send election monitors to polls
text: The Trump administration has been sued over its plans to deploy “a historic number” of election monitors to polling stations during next month’s midterm elections. The bid “stands to jeopardize” the elections and could “interfere with the right of voters to participate in the election free from intimidation”, according to the NAACP, which filed a lawsuit against Harmeet Dhillon, head of the justice department’s civil rights division, who has said she hopes to send 1,000 monitors to midterm polling sites in November. “To be clear, there is no federal statute that gives the US Department of Justice [DoJ] the right to send their so-called ‘election monitors’ to polling sites across the country, and this administration has made clear its intent to disrupt and interfere with the way elections are run in our country,” said Kristen Clarke, the NAACP’s general counsel, who served in Dhillon’s role under Joe Biden. The NAACP lawsuit seeks to force the Trump administration to release records regarding the deployment of the monitors. The NAACP said it requested such records under the Freedom of Information Act on 1 September, but said the Department of Justice had failed to comply. “The timely release of these documents is critical to protecting voter rights and ensuring election integrity,” the NAACP said in a statement. On Sunday Todd Blanche, the attorney general, confirmed that election monitors will be sent to all 50 states. Speaking to Fox News, however, he downplayed the role of the monitors. “Since the 60s, the Department of Justice has monitored elections. Every single election’s been monitored,” Blanche said. “This administration, President Trump, is doing the same thing that every single administration has done in our generation, multiple generations.” In a statement a justice department spokesperson said: “Department election monitors comply with all legal and ethical requirements, including the requirement that they not interfere with the voting process, and their work is consistent with longstanding department practice of monitoring elections for compliance with federal law.” The monitors have raised concerns, however, from within the Republican party. In August Mark Gordon, the Republican governor of Wyoming, criticized the behavior of two election monitors who he said arrived at a polling station during the state’s primaries earlier this year without notice, and attempted to examine voting machines. “It was aggressive, unexpected, disruptive – certainly didn’t seem to show respect for the state,” Gordon told the New York Times. “We’re going to get to the bottom of it as best we can.” The justice department spokesperson said: “AAG Dhillon had a cordial meeting with Gov Gordon, the Wyoming Attorney General, and the county clerk for Laramie County. We disagree with the public framing that the two monitors we sent were ‘aggressive’ or did anything improper. The discussion with the Governor and his team was helpful and we look forward to having a presence in Wyoming in the general election.” “During the primary season, we saw monitors deployed with no notice to the public or jurisdiction, and no clear evidence that they were there for a legitimate civil rights purpose,” Clarke said. “Americans deserve to know whether the justice department is abusing its law enforcement powers to the detriment of voters and the election officials tasked with running our elections. Americans deserve transparency on the justice department’s increasingly evolving and unwieldy plans. With election day just weeks away, the NAACP is seeking judicial intervention to ensure transparency and to safeguard the fundamental right to vote.”

title: Satellite images show attack jets at Chinese military facility in Laos
summary: New ‘support and training centre’ prompts concern in region but China says it is ‘not directed at any third party’
text: Satellite images show attack jets stationed at a new Chinese military facility in Laos, which opened last week and gives Beijing’s air force its first foothold in mainland south-east Asia. Images provided by the commercial satellite provider Vantor show eight light attack aircraft positioned at Ban Keun airport alongside what appear to be more than a dozen military vehicles lined up in rows. The planes’ shape matches that of the Chinese-made Hongdu JL-8 jet, a two-seat trainer that can be deployed in combat to carry bombs. Laos is reported to have four such aircraft, according to the London-based International Institute for Strategic Studies. In a rare example of Beijing’s overseas military expansion, China opened what it said was a joint “support and training centre” at Ban Keun on 29 September. The airport, about ⁠30 miles (50km) north of Vientiane, the capital of Laos, has been significantly expanded over the past year. Satellite images taken months ago show farmland and dirt paths where there are now new buildings and a paved runway. Aside from its island bases in the South China Sea, Beijing does not have a significant network of military outposts in other countries, and the Laos airbase would be its first facility in another country capable of handling fighter jets. The new satellite images, taken a day after the announcement and first reported by Reuters, show extensive construction work that appears to be focused on a future runway extension, which could make the airport capable of handling larger planes such as bombers. In its announcement last week, China’s defence ministry said the new centre would “help Laos strengthen the training of its air force pilots” and was not “directed against any third party”. Governments will be watching closely for signs of deployments or the installation of defence equipment that may serve wider military ambitions. After the announcement, the Singapore-based security analyst Collin Koh said it “may not be wrong to conclude this is the first full-fledged PLA [People’s Liberation Army] overseas base in south-east Asia”. Over the past two decades, China has built up an extensive network of outposts on islands in the disputed South China Sea, including airbases with air defence installations. Otherwise, its navy’s sole overseas military base is a logistics base in Djibouti, on the coast of the Horn of Africa. The Laos agreement follows a similar programme established in Cambodia, at the Ream naval base on the Gulf of Thailand, although that facility has no runway. After years of speculation and denials, China announced in April last year that it had created the “joint logistics and training” facility in Cambodia. It said the centre would support the two militaries in “conducting regional counter-terrorism, disaster prevention and mitigation, humanitarian assistance, joint training and other operations”. US forces are believed to have used Ban Keun airport in Laos during covert military operations at the height of the Vietnam war in the 1960s and 1970s. Its development will be monitored by Vietnam, which maintains disputes with China over the South China Sea, and Thailand, which shares a border with Laos. After the announcement last week, Thailand’s defence ministry spokesperson said Bangkok considered itself a close partner of both Laos and China and saw it as Vientiane’s sovereign right to decide whether to grant permission for a Chinese base. “Nevertheless, Thailand will continue to closely monitor developments and how the matter proceeds, particularly with regard to building mutual trust,” said R Adm Surasant Kongsiri. China’s government did not mention sending aircraft to Laos in its initial announcement, while the government of Laos has not commented on the project. The US-based Institute for the Study of War has described the Laos base as the “first PLA overseas military facility focused on air power”. In its assessment, the thinktank said the base was “not yet equipped to provide the PLA with the ability to execute major combat operations, unlike US military bases”. It said the base would give the Chinese military alternate routes to access to the South China Sea and strategic air routes. Reuters contributed to this report

title: Could the UK really rejoin the EU?
summary: The big question facing ​A​ndy Burnham is not whether Brexit has harmed Britain, but if a rapidly changing Europe will keep the door open​ if the UK decides it wants back in
text: It was lobbed into the national conversation without fanfare or warning, almost a footnote in the UK prime minister’s first speech as leader to his governing Labour party’s annual conference last week. But Andy Burnham has kicked off a quiet U-turn on Brexit. By stating bluntly that the decision to leave Europe’s core political community had done “more harm than good”, Burnham broke a taboo in his own party, in effect, discarding his predecessor’s paralysing ‘red lines’ on Europe, and signalling he will not be bound by these constraints after the next British election. Over the coming six weeks Burnham will gauge public support before setting out options for the UK’s long term relationship with the UK’s largest market. Rejoining the 27-nation bloc will be one of them. Burnham is opening the door to Britain reversing Brexit. The famous red lines, or non-negotiables, enshrined by Keir Starmer in Labour’s 2024 election manifesto, were meant to reassure Brexit-supporting voters that under Labour there would be no return to a single market, customs union or the free movement of people. But these pledges left Starmer with little room for manoeuvre with Europe, beyond warm words. The evidence that Brexit has stunted the British economy is not new. Estimates for the damage quitting the single market has already done range from 6% of 8% of GDP. What is new is a prime ministerial readiness to publicly acknowledge that harm and conclude that an ambitious new path is required. “This is the first time that a UK politician in power has been willing to stand up and say that Brexit is a failure that we must address or redress in some fundamental way,” Joël Reland, an analyst with the UK In a Changing Europe thinktank, told me. “Keir Starmer’s public message was that we will be sticking with Boris Johnson’s [2019] Brexit deal, but we’re going to improve it to make Brexit work. Burnham is saying Brexit doesn’t work and that we need a different form of deal. That has never been said before.” Burnham is not yet committing himself to fighting the next election on a particular course of action. Much will depend on the response he gets. But all options – Lisa O’Carroll details them here – are on the table, from a customs union to re-joining the single market and becoming, like Norway, a rule-taker, to “going all the way”. But crucially, Burnham has already departed from the orthodoxy that makes questioning Brexit a heresy. Instead of shutting down the topic to limit his exposure to Eurosceptic attacks, the prime minister is meeting it head-on, Reland said. “Burnham could have done what every other leader before him has done since the 2016 referendum, and take a clear red-lines position against Brexit, but he didn’t. And I don’t see why you would do that unless you wanted to take on the political argument”. Why would Burnham choose this juncture and risk drawing down what Rafael Behr calls the Brexit curse? The economic rationale is the obvious one. “Burnham’s ten year domestic agenda promises radical reform of such things as the social care system, and somebody is going to have to pay for that,” argues Reland. “One of the ways you can get economic growth is by rejoining your largest and closest trading partner.” The modest ‘re-set’ agenda launched by Starmer in May 2025 is stuck, bogged down in disputes, such as that over fees for EU students in the UK. A pencilled-in 20 November summit is still up in the air. Britain’s big impediment from outside the club is its lack of bargaining power. A cherrypicking attempt to coax the EU into a selective single market for goods only (without free movement of people) was firmly rebuffed by Brussels in May. And even if this reset were fully delivered, the government’s own figures estimate it would add at most, 0.3% to GDP by 2040. Labour meanwhile has lost votes to its left, particularly to the Greens, so a more progressive offer on Europe might be a gamble worth taking. New polling, as Pippa Crerar and Rowena Mason revealed at the weekend, shows that if Burnham’s preference is for rejoining the EU, almost half of the country already agrees. Gaby Hinsliff noted that among Burnham’s opponents the only one to react to the surprise move with “unfettered glee” was Nigel Farage. Yet, she suggested, the Conservatives, also obsessed with economic growth, may not side with Farage given that most voters think Brexit has made them economically worse off. “It’s not in Tory long-term interests to strangle this at birth” wrote Hinsliff. *** A warm welcome? Events in Europe are also dictating the pace. “Welcome back!” was the French president Emmanuel Macron’s possibly tongue-in-cheek response to Burnham’s remarks. But it is a French-led project called “Made in Europe” that is both concentrating the PM’s mind and could ultimately undermine his ambition. Made in Europe is a highly protectionist idea for turning the EU into an industrial powerhouse, able to withstand competition from China. UK-made goods, if legally classified as non-European under the law, would be locked out, spelling trade devastation for the British car industry. France, facing its own domestic upheaval and crunch elections next April, is being hardline about Britain’s exclusion: Macron’s ministers insist that if you’re not paying the costs of the internal market you don’t get to claim the benefits. Made in Europe is emerging as a symbol, Reland explained, of how geopolitics is driving the EU’s agenda, and widening its range of competencies to such areas as industrial policy, AI and tech sovereignty. “It is no longer just food and environment policy that is set at EU level but the big, strategic, hard security decisions too,” he said. The more that EU countries strategically pool sovereignty to respond to shocks such as US trade aantagonism or Russian hybrid warfare, and the more aggressively they protect that cooperation, the steeper the costs of being outside the club become. With Norway and Switzerland, both non-EU members with single market access, now also facing the Made in Europe battle, it’s no wonder Burnham is mulling the full rejoin option. But, as Mujtaba Rahman’s prescient column advised, the coming debate will need to go beyond the question of whether Britain could contemplate rejoining, to an honest assessment of what Europe has become in the years since it left. To receive the complete version of This Is Europe in your inbox every Wednesday, please subscribe here.

title: ‘Like an earthquake’: El Niño is coming for California – is the state ready?
summary: A mix of natural disasters could all befall the state at once as it finds itself in the crosshairs of the climate phenomenon
text: On a cloudless autumn afternoon, sunlight sparkled on the water that had quietly swallowed a busy intersection to the north of San Francisco, as the surrounding rush-hour traffic slowed to a painful crawl. There were no crashing waves or storm surges to blame for the flood. Marin county was one of many areas up and down the California coast affected by high tides last week, as parts of the Pacific swelled with excess warmth. The submerged streets stood as an early signal of California’s vulnerabilities as it braces for what could be a tumultuous winter. “If you think this is bad, just wait until December,” a state worker grumbled as he directed swarms of cars past the choke point toward a sidestreet. Experts have warned that a potentially historic El Niño is brewing, with the power to unleash extreme weather around the world. The climate phenomenon, characterized by warmer than average equatorial sea surface temperatures, is already under way, according to federal forecasters, and it is expected to strengthen through the northern hemisphere’s autumn and winter. California is poised to be in its crosshairs. Landslides, flash floods and encroaching sea levels are all on the menu – and they could all happen at once. “What we’re really looking at is the compounding element,” Nick Brubaker, the chief resilience officer for the office of emergency management in Marin county said. The biggest concern isn’t just rising tides. It’s the way everything could collide. Dangerous spikes in temperature are likely. Some areas could see supercharged storms and relentless rains. Others face explosive surf, strong currents and devastated marine ecosystems. The effects of El Niño will add an additional foot of sea level rise in California on top of the 8in to 12in caused by the climate crisis there over the last century, according to Michael Anderson, a state climatologist. And in recent wildfire burn scars, including the slopes of Big Sur that burned this summer and neighborhoods devastated by the 2025 firestorm in Los Angeles, there will be higher chances of debris flows. The risks are but a taste of what’s to come as the world warms. Preparations are already under way at all levels of government as officials work to secure vital infrastructure, preset response resources and inform the public of the incoming hazards. “We are trying to make sure that people are aware that this may be one of the most significant El Niño years that we’ve seen,” Brubaker said. Preparing for a hot fall and a wet winter California stretches across roughly 770 miles (1,240km), and its regions are likely to experience El Niño very differently. Southern California typically sees wetter winters in El Niño years, but that’s not necessarily the case further north. While the stage may be set for violent weather, it’s impossible to forecast what will unfold. “What the science supports is elevated risk,” said Dr Ariel Cohen, a meteorologist for the National Weather Service, during a recent briefing held in Los Angeles. “A strong El Niño shifts the probabilities – it does not determine exact outcomes.” With the potential for dangerous conditions already rising, emergency managers are planning for the worst. Gavin Newsom, California’s governor, issued a state of emergency on 21 September to mobilize efforts and resources, kicking off a flurry of activity. Adverse conditions fueled by El Niño are already taking shape. A mass of warm water known as a “Kelvin” wave is crawling up the California coastline with the ability to raise sea levels by up to a foot. Along with coastal flooding from elevated sea levels and high tides, powerful storms swirling through the Pacific have made for an unusually busy tropical cyclone season. Hawaii is still recovering from a series of deluges and strong winds that flooded roads and buildings, unleashed landslides and toppled trees. Swathes of the southern California coastline were hammered by massive waves that damaged homes and devoured beaches. Areas already hit hard are working to recover – and build resilience. In Long Beach, just south of Los Angeles, the seawall has been lined with large sandbags to reinforce spots where strong surf has burst through. In Orange county, roughly 690,000 cubic yards of sand is being pushed along the coastline. Workers are going door-to-door in San Diego’s flood zones to help small businesses ready their buildings. The Los Angeles county public works department has been assessing risks over the last six months, according to Mark Pestrella, its director, who said flood control systems are ready and optimized during a recent briefing. Channels and debris have been cleared from drainages, 14 dams were tested and reservoirs prepared. These systems, he clarified, are designed to withstand a so-called “100-year event”, which he said had a roughly 1% chance of occurring in any given year. But El Niño could bump those chances higher. “We are assuming it is going to rain and with El Niño we assume it is going to rain with high intensity,” Pestrella said. Of particular concern, he added, were the areas still in recovery from the devastating wildfires that swept across LA county in January 2025, consuming more than 16,000 structures. In Pacific Palisades and Altadena, the communities that were most intensely affected, homes and buildings are still being rebuilt. Pestrella said it takes five years for watersheds and hillsides to heal enough to withstand strong rains. Along LA county’s 23 miles of coastline, large berms and sand dune systems are being built on beaches to fight against erosion, according to Gary Jones, the director of Beaches and Harbors. That effort happens every year, but officials are starting a month and a half earlier than usual. “This El Niño won’t be the last one and unfortunately erosion at our beaches is becoming more and more common,” Jones said. Meanwhile, LA’s office of emergency management director, Kevin McGowan, is juggling dangers on the other end of the hydrological spectrum: high heat and fire risks that are likely to linger into November. “We are in the middle of fire season and about to head into a significant heatwave,” McGowan said before a sweltering October weekend that smashed several records across southern California, noting that fire conditions can still peak through the winter months. “People should continue to prepare not just for one hazard – but all hazards.” ‘The sandbags are ready’ For Mary Ellen Carroll, the executive director of the San Francisco department of emergency management, the good news is there is still time to prepare. “It feels like I’m planning for an earthquake, but I’ve gotten two months’ notice,” she said. Along with elevated flood risks around the port and the Embarcadero on the Bay side, and dangerous ocean conditions along the beaches, there could be long power outages during storms. For people that are more vulnerable – older people and folks that are medically dependent – “it can get very dangerous quickly”, she said. While El Niño doesn’t as directly produce more moisture-laden storms in this part of the state, elevated sea levels will continue to be a concern. Record high-tides are likely between December and February next year. California king tides – when surf is highest – will occur during the week of Thanksgiving, the week of Christmas, and on the Martin Luther King Jr long weekend, making for a potentially dangerous holiday season. Back in Marin, where low-lying areas flood even without the added influence from El Niño, Brubaker said the county was rushing to clear drains and culverts, and installing temporary flood barriers. They have also expanded their supplies of free pre-filled sandbags and generated detailed online interactives so residents and visitors can more easily visualize their risks. About 70 miles south, in the beachside tourist town of Santa Cruz, the emergency services manager, Meredith Albert, said this year’s preparations fall in line with the challenges coastal communities have long faced. “We are building on what we all know have been our risks and hazards all along – for better or worse, they aren’t a surprise,” she said of the atmospheric river events, coastal erosion and flooding that can wreak havoc in any year. Santa Cruz has seen its fair share of extreme weather. In 2024, a parade of storms and violent surf knocked out the city’s beloved pier, which only recently reopened. While there’s careful consideration of overstating messages and emergency alert fatigue, Albert added that “the public messaging is ready to go. The sandbags are ready.” But the biggest priority is to ensure preparedness starts at individual and neighborhood levels “and grows outward from there”, Albert said. In Santa Cruz, they have planned neighborhood workshops where city staff will meet with small groups to discuss the dangers, what the city will be able to do and how people can help one another. The goal is not to make Santa Cruz invulnerable. But building resilience in communities will be the key to navigating the uncertainties of when and how calamity could strike. “Those community connections are the difference between a disaster being something you can’t come back from and something you can learn from.” It’s a sentiment being echoed across the state. “We are never going to have enough resources at the onset of a disaster to support every single person,” McGowan cautioned in Los Angeles. “Our communities are the fabric that gets us through these disasters – neighbors helping neighbors saves lives.”

title: Whistle-Blower Says I.R.S. Leaked His Tax Records in Retaliation
summary: Brian J. Visalli, a veteran investigator of tax fraud, said in a lawsuit that the agency had sent his personal and tax information to federal prosecutors.

title: South West Water owner taps investors to fix infrastructure after sewage spills
summary: Pennon slashes dividend and launches £550m cash call ‘to drive improved outcomes for customers and communities’
text: The owner of embattled South West Water has slashed its dividend and launched a cash call to investors as it attempts to fund infrastructure investment, days after it was hit by a record £7.9m fine for hundreds of sewage spills. London-listed Pennon said on Wednesday it would tap investors for £550m, as part of a £1bn investment “to drive improved outcomes for customers and communities”. Shares in the utility company, which supplies water to about 3.5 million customers across the south-west of England, as well as 380,000 business customers around the UK, tumbled in response to the announcement, making Pennon the biggest faller on the FTSE 250 index. Pennon’s new chief executive, Keith Haslett, who was appointed in April, said he had conducted a comprehensive review of the business and had identified areas for improvement, including customer service and the company’s environmental performance. Last month, a judge issued South West Water with the largest fine for environmental offences in the region, at nearly £8m, and said the company’s conduct amounted to reckless failures in management systems and response to known risks. The fine will be paid by shareholders rather than through bill increases. The company was fined after hundreds of sewage spills during a six-year period at popular bathing spots including the coastal village of Harlyn in north Cornwall and in sensitive habitats, such as the River Camel, which is home to otters and Atlantic salmon and popular with birdwatchers and sailors. In June, South West Water was fined £1.85m by a judge in a separate case. The company pleaded guilty to the criminal offence of supplying water unfit for human consumption, after a 2024 parasite outbreak in Brixham, Devon, made hundreds of people sick and forced thousands of households to boil their water. Pennon said on Wednesday it would also slash its shareholder dividend by about 30%, including the impact of the equity raise, as part of its “operational reset”. Shares in Pennon, which also owns Bristol Water and SES Water, slumped by as much as 22% on Wednesday after the company’s announcement, named “project Proteus”, after a sea god in Greek mythology. Haslett told reporters the reaction to the company’s plans had been mixed, saying: “Investment is needed to achieve improvements – we’re funding the plans in the right way.” He added this would not be funded by further increases to customers’ bills and said he was also bringing some critical roles back in-house, including leakage teams that were previously outsourced. In its recent results for the year to 31 March, Pennon revealed it had incurred outcome delivery incentives from the water regulator for England and Wales, Ofwat, of about £42m for its water and wastewater performance. It said it had faced operational pressures from “exceptional storms and sustained rainfall coupled with a step up in targets and penalty rates”. The company anticipates it will continue to incur the penalties until 2030 but is aiming to reduce them by at least 50% a year. On Tuesday, South West Water applied for a ban on non-essential water use for some businesses across parts of Devon and west Dorset, after a lack of significant rainfall after the hot, dry summer. The proposed ban would restrict activities such as vehicle washing, the cleaning of buildings and the filling of non-domestic swimming pools and ponds. Customers of South West Water are already seeing their bills rise to fuel £2.5bn of investment in infrastructure in the years to 2030. The number of customer complaints received by South West Water more than doubled over the past year, according to the latest figures from a consumer watchdog. The Consumer Council for Water found complaints to the company soared by 153%, and rated South West Water and Thames Water “poor” for the number of complaints received and how they handled them. In recent weeks, Andy Burnham has come under further pressure from a cross-party group of MPs to take control of indebted Thames Water. The MPs are calling for ministers to break off talks with the US hedge funds that are effectively running the company and to consider emergency legislation to take charge of Thames’ financial affairs. However, the environment secretary, Angela Eagle, has previously suggested a special administration regime – effectively temporary public control – could not be triggered for Thames Water and would require a change in the law.

title: Australia is building a lot of new homes. But is the datacentre boom holding us back? | Greg Jericho
summary: Housing construction is at its strongest level since 2016, but it’s AI that is sucking up resources for builders
text: The latest series of data on housing and building activity has been released, showing residential building is growing strongly but also that the datacentre boom is massive and ongoing. As political parties look to keep housing on the agenda, the massive resources devoted to building datacentres is going to hit anyone wishing to increase housing supply. For a government wanting a good story, it has one in the form of housing. Not only are house prices finally showing some semblance of reality, housing construction is also doing well. In the year to June, the volume of residential building rose 8.7% – the strongest since 2016. The increase of total building was even stronger – up 10% on the year, the best since the GFC stimulus years: Click here if this graph does not display The government would also be extremely satisfied to see the number of new private sector house commencements rose 11.6% to 31,707 dwellings. That number is the highest recorded since 1994, excluding the boost during the Covid “homebuilder” surge and the abnormal number of commencements in March 2000 designed to beat the introduction of the GST. Click here if this graph does not display The government will suggest this is a sign that investors are shifting to new housing construction, given that still gives them the 50% capital gains tax discount. As the June quarter includes time before and after the budget, we will need to wait for the September quarter to get a better sense of whether or not this is a blip or a more sustained increase. But there is decidedly no blip for public sector housing, which has – for over 30 years now – been barely part of the housing equation. Click here if this graph does not display This was a key aspect of a report released last week by the Senate’s select committee on intergenerational housing inequality, Locked Out: The Growing Generational Housing Divide. The committee, chaired by the Greens senator Barbara Pocock and at which I gave evidence, made numerous findings of a pretty general nature. The first was unanimous across all members of the multiparty committee: “It is an indisputable fact, universally agreed by the committee, that Australia is in a housing crisis. This crisis has been long in the making.” The report highlights that while the changes to the CGT discount and negative gearing were vital to improve the housing crisis, there remains still much to be done. Public housing is a key part of that. The committee found “the dominant message from submitters [including myself] was the need to build significantly more affordable and social housing at scale through long-term government investment and clear delivery targets”. While the committee itself made no specific recommendations, due to its multiparty nature, Senator Pocock proposed “that the Australian government commit to a national target to increase public and community housing to at least 10% of Australia’s housing stock over the next decade”. This would mark a significant shift. From 1955 to 1985, public and social housing accounted for, on average, 13% of all new residential buildings. By contrast, over the past 30 years (aside from the GFC stimulus period), public and social housing has never accounted for more than 4%. In the year to June, it was just 2.3%: Click here if this graph does not display The report also noted the issue of rents, and Pocock also proposed a cap on annual rent increases at the lesser of 2% or the inflation rate. The issue of rents is rather hot at the moment as the opposition tries to blame rents going up on the changes to the CGT and negative gearing (which is laughable, given anyone renting a place before May is grandfathered), and One Nation are claiming their cuts to migration will deliver falls in rents. In reality, rents essentially follow interest rates: Click here if this graph does not display But all housing policy around new builds always needs to deal with the issue of the available number of builders to actually do the work. And this is where the datacentre boom is truly becoming an issue, because that is accounting for stonks of work. Datacentres are covered in the Australian Bureau of Statistics survey under the “commercial building not elsewhere classified (n.e.c)” category. Usually that makes up about 1% of the value of non-residential building commencements. But in the year to June, it was 20%: Click here if this graph does not display So big has the surge of datacentre building been that it was worth just under three-quarters of the increase in non-residential building commencements over the past year. We are putting a heck of a lot of eggs into the datacentre basket, hoping like hell it delivers benefits to someone other than AI companies selling hopes and dreams. Usually almost double is spent building factories compared with the buildings in the “commercial n.e.c” category. But in the past year, more than 17 times the amount of money was spent building datacentres than factories: Click here if this graph does not display That’s a lot of resources devoted to something that, unlike a factory, will not employ many people after it is built, and unlike a house will not provide a place for people to live for the next 40 years. Right now building construction is doing well. But the question is whether we will look back and see a waste of money and work on buildings that didn’t deliver what was promised, instead of money spent building homes for people to live in or places for people to work. Greg Jericho is a Guardian columnist and chief economist at the Australia Institute

title: Overseas, Albanese sees ‘the very definition of climate injustice’ – but at home, he still wants coal
summary: It isn’t hard to see a contradiction between the PM’s message in Fiji and his opposition to legal action to stop a NSW coalmine
text: There are unlikely to be many bigger moments in Australian community action on the climate crisis this year than a judgment by the high court on Wednesday. In what may prove a historic victory, the court sided with a handful of community members in the Hunter Valley to overturn a state regulator’s approval of a coalmine expansion that allowed it to operate until 2048. This doesn’t happen every day, and the judgment could have ramifications for other coal developments in New South Wales. If comments he made in May are taken at face value, the decision won’t please Anthony Albanese. Speaking on 2HD radio in Newcastle, the prime minister said the renewable transition was needed, but the government supported “existing industries” – that is, coal. He hoped the community group would lose as the Mount Pleasant mine expansion had “been through appropriate approvals”. Well, not according to the high court. Critics were quick to note the contrast between Albanese’s language opposing legal action to stop a coalmine and the message he delivered over the past three days at a climate conference in Fiji in preparation for the Cop31 summit in Turkey next month. With Pacific island counterparts, the prime minister helped lead a delegation of about 50 dignitaries to the atoll and reef island nation of Tuvalu. Remote and tiny doesn’t do Tuvalu justice. It is described as the least visited country on the planet. Its land totals just 26 sq km, mostly narrow strips less than 2 metres above sea level. And the distance between the ocean and where most of its people live is getting smaller. Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here The rate of sea level rise around Tuvalu is about twice the global average, according to Nasa researchers. It means the edges of the nation are being eroded. The delegation was given a presentation illustrating the escalating threat of floods and storm surges washing through homes and infrastructure in the years ahead. They also saw an example of what the country is doing to give itself the best chance to survive, visiting a land reclamation project on the main atoll of Funafuti that is mostly funded by the Australian government. Sand and gravel dredged from the lagoon is being used to create more than 20 hectares of new, higher ground. It is a project of hope, and a way to buy time. Possibly the most powerful moment on the quick trip came when the delegation was addressed by a 13-year-old, Melelusi Sokotia, who spoke powerfully about how her friends’ aspirations to be “teachers, doctors, builders” was being overridden by the basic question of whether they could “grow safely here in Tuvalu”. Melelusi made a plea: “Please work together to protect small islands like ours.” Later, back in Fiji, a leaders’ plenary heard from the Nepali foreign affairs minister, Shisir Khanal, who travelled for the pre-Cop meeting while his country staggers under the fallout from devastating flooding in August. While the Pacific confronts a crisis of rising tides and more fierce cyclones, Khanal said Nepal was threatened by melting mountain ice bringing havoc from above. He pointed out the two threats were linked. Melting glaciers ultimately add to rising seas. The minister said Nepal and the Pacific had something else in common. Neither contributes much at all to the global emissions causing these catastrophes. “Yet our people pay with their lives and development gains for a crisis they had no hand in creating,” he said. “This is the very definition of climate injustice.” Albanese didn’t ignore this. He took Khanal’s message on enough to repeat part of it – that Nepal faced “extraordinarily traumatic” climate events despite running entirely on hydroelectricity – in a speech before flying out on Wednesday. He described other examples of extreme events becoming less predictable and more intense as “the science told us would occur”. Climate change wasn’t an abstract future challenge, but “a daily reality that communities are dealing with”. “We saw that first-hand yesterday in Tuvalu,” Albanese said. The point of Albanese’s speech was to argue for more international investment in the Pacific Resilience Facility, a fund designed to help people in the region cope and live that has received A$100m in Australian government support. He didn’t mention coal. But when held up against his commentary about the high court judgment, it wasn’t hard to see a screaming internal contradiction – a case of a leader sending conflicting messages to different audiences. Does Albanese disagree with the high court judgment and still support coal expansion, given its contribution to the crisis he has accurately identified? There was no chance to test this on Wednesday. He left pre-Cop without taking questions from journalists. None of this is to dismiss the work being done in Fiji. Despite the focus in Australia on the number of leaders who flew to Nadi and Funafuti for the meeting, there is little sense on the ground of it being the failure some have described. Pre-Cop meetings usually barely make a blip on the public radar. They’re not meant to. They’re a chance for diplomats and bureaucrats to gather before the big end-of-year UN climate summit to lay groundwork and hopefully give it some chance of success. This year is something else entirely. It is being held in the Pacific in an attempt to bring focus to the plight and needs of its peoples. In that, it has had at least some success. Ministers and their representatives from about 50 governments, including India and European nations, attended. So did thousands of diplomats and civil society members. They talked about Pacific needs. The trip to Tuvalu included only two national leaders from outside the region – but the EU climate commissioner and the heads of the Asian Development Bank, the Green Climate Fund and the UN climate secretariat were on board. They saw and heard things people doing their jobs should see and hear. Pacific national and community leaders are not uniform in their views, but they have largely applauded the focus and Australia’s support. Some are also critical, and cynical, about what they see as Australia’s hypocrisy on fossil fuels. That issue isn’t going away. The ultimate test of this week’s success is whether it helps Cop31 pull off a meaningful agreement on issues to limit climate catastrophe and better direct finance to those that need it to survive, including in the Pacific. To describe that as a challenge in the current geopolitical climate is a spectacular understatement. One upside of this week has been that the two men responsible for trying to pull that off – the president of the formal negotiations, Australia’s Chris Bowen, and the Turkish Cop31 president, Murat Kurum – have had a few days together to build their relationship and consider how they might do that. And they have had a consistent and forceful reminder from those around them of why it matters. Adam Morton is Guardian Australia’s climate and environment editor and writes the Clear Air newsletter

title: Nobel prize in chemistry awarded for work on mirror-image molecules
summary: Henri B Kagan and Kensō Soai awarded prize for discovery that has aided understanding of how medicines work in the body
text: The Nobel prize in chemistry 2026 has been awarded to two scientists for discoveries that showed how chemical reactions can produce an overwhelming excess of one of two mirror image forms of a molecule. Henri B Kagan at Paris-Sud University in France and Kensō Soai at Tokyo University of Science in Japan have been awarded the prize “for the discovery of nonlinear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis”. The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced the winners in Stockholm, Sweden, on Wednesday. They will each receive an equal share of a prize of 12m Swedish kronor (about £900,000). Many molecules, including amino acids that form the building blocks of proteins, can exist in two forms that contain the same atoms, but are mirror images of one another, much like a person’s left and right hands. This property is known as chirality. However, the chemistry underpinning life is surprisingly “homochiral”, or same-handed. Proteins are built almost exclusively from L-amino acids, while the sugars that form the backbone of DNA and RNA have the opposite D- configuration. How this homochirality could have emerged when chemical reactions in the laboratory typically produce equal quantities of both forms had long puzzled scientists. The question also had practical consequences: “Although these molecules look very similar, they can behave very differently when they interact with other molecules,” said Prof Andre Cobb, an organic chemist at King’s College London. “This matters enormously for medicines because many of the molecules in our bodies, including proteins that drugs target, are themselves chiral. So the ‘left-handed’ and ‘right-handed’ versions of a drug can interact with the body in different ways which can lead to different or weakened drug effects.” The drug thalidomide provides a potent example. During the early 1960s, thousands of children were affected by birth defects after their mothers were prescribed it to combat morning sickness during pregnancy. Researchers subsequently found differences in the biological effects of the drug’s two mirror image forms. Manufacturers wanted a way of steering reactions towards particular forms of the molecules that they produced, and Kagan and Soai eventually provided a solution. It began in 1986, when Kagan discovered that a relatively small imbalance between left- and right-handed forms of a catalyst could create a greater excess of one of the mirror image products than the other. Soai took the idea further, developing a reaction in which the molecules produced themselves acted as catalysts for making more of themselves, a process known as autocatalysis. “You have to be aware, this is probably the coolest experiment in organic chemistry ever,” said Prof Peter Somfai, an organic chemist at Lund University and a member of the Nobel committee for chemistry. In 2003, Soai demonstrated a reaction that produced almost exclusively one mirror-image form, reproducing the kind of molecular one-handedness found in living organisms for the first time. Speaking by telephone at Wednesday’s announcement, Soai, 76, said he was “very proud” of the experiment as it offered a potential explanation for how the molecular one-handedness of life could have arisen. He described hearing the news about the prize as “one of the most exciting days of my life”. Taken together, Kagan and Soai’s discoveries had “reshaped our understanding of molecular chirality, how it is created, amplified and transmitted”, Somfai said. These insights have since become embedded in the development of catalysts that steer chemical reactions towards producing a particular mirror image form across different industries. “It is in the backsides of our heads all the time,” said Somfai. “It might be difficult to say that this drug or that drug was developed using this. I would say all of them because we use this as a tool. We use this as an understanding of how to develop catalysts and how they function.”
