title: ‘Now is the moment’: housing activists at Madrid encampment pin wary hopes on Spain’s early election
summary: Campaigners set up in more than 1,200 tents in Puerto del Sol square say challenge now is to translate a groundswell of public support into concrete change
text: At a makeshift lunch counter tucked within a maze of tents at a housing protest camp in Madrid, Sélpide San Luis pointed to the dizzying pace of change. “We built a city in a week,” said the 26-year-old, whose videos documenting day-to-day life at the encampment have attracted tens of thousands of views on social media, as she pointed to the more than 1,200 tents set up in the central Puerta del Sol square. “We have urban planning, the streets have names and we’ve put surveillance systems in place. And thanks to what we’re doing here, media have not stopped talking about the issue of housing – something that we’ve been trying to get on the agenda for so long.” This week marked another significant moment for the impromptu movement. After days of protests and encampments that have sprouted up across the country after the eviction from of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal from her home, the Socialist prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, announced a snap general election in response to rightwing parties torpedoing emergency legislation to tackle the housing crisis. Housing campaigners vowed to keep up the pressure. “The power of the people has ushered in a new era,” said Alicia del Río, of the Madrid Tenants’ Union, as she floated plans for a general strike in November. “An election campaign is now beginning that will be deeply shaped by the housing issue. So we ask the members of parliament, are you going to introduce the measures that people are demanding – ones demanded by the majority of voters across all parties – or are you going to continue to be the lackeys of the rentier economy?” The election, which did not have to held until August 2027, is a high-stakes gamble for Sánchez. Polls suggest the most likely outcome will be a rightwing coalition between the People’s party and the far-right, anti-immigration Vox party. But as anger seethes over rents that have surged 80% in a decade and housing costs that have risen by 63%, the protests also present Sánchez with an opportunity to keep his leftwing coalition in power. “Bringing forward the elections is risky. But there’s also a feeling of ‘now is the moment’,” said Antonio Prieto, 36, as he and other volunteers transformed the steady stream of food donations into lunch for those at the Madrid camp. “If we had waited until 2027, the right and far right would have crushed us. And now, at least with this momentum, putting the focus on housing, we can have a tiny bit of hope.” Prieto is among the many closely watching the parties to the left of the Socialists, hoping they will unite to form a broad front before the election. “I’m hopeful that what we’re doing has really got through, so that parties on the left realise that this is a big issue and they start working on real solutions,” he said. The eviction of Abascal, a wheelchair user who was carried from the home she had lived in for more than seven decades on a stretcher, catapulted the long-simmering frustration over the deepening housing crisis into public view. It cast a spotlight on the intense competition for housing across Spain, one that pits local people against tourists lets, investment funds and short-term rentals. As a wave of outrage swept the country, the investment firm that bought Abascal’s home said she could return home without paying the 230% rent hike it had reportedly demanded. But the protests and encampments have continued to gain strength as people demand change. Prieto described them as a “moral duty”, given that the Spanish constitution recognises the right to “decent and adequate housing” for all. “What we’re seeing is a systematic violation of the constitution … So we have to be here,” he said. The growing tent city has had visitors too – some to snap photos, others to ask questions and some to provoke. But the vast majority express their support, said Juan Vázquez, of the Housing Union of Carabanchel, a district in the south of Madrid. “People of all ages have stopped by to wish us strength, bring us water and food, and tell us to keep going,” he said. The challenge now is to translate the groundswell of support into concrete change. “On the one hand we have a right wing that pursues policies of misery and directly attacks the working class,” Vázquez said. “But on the other hand, Sánchez and his government have not gone after the profits that speculative rentiers make from our misery.” He described the coming weeks, as people across Spain prepare to vote, as crucial. “Basically, what we want is to channel all this energy so that it doesn’t just remain a footnote in a week-long encampment – to organise, apply pressure and secure our rights. We know that the organisation of the working class is the only means of looking after our interests.” Jorge Rubio, 27, said the scale of the protests had hopefully made it clear to everyone just what was at stake. “If you don’t vote, the impact could be huge. You could end up without a place to live,” he said, citing rooms for rent that had surged from €180 to €700 (£150 to £600) a month in six years. “It’s crazy. It’s not viable. We’re all affected by this,” he said. He was among the many hoping the movement would go further. “Housing is not just a problem here, it’s a European problem. The revolution needs to reach them too.”

title: Electric-shock gloves ICE plans to use inflicted intense pain in army study
summary: Immigration enforcement agency has signed $16.7m deal for devices that induced ‘excessive’ fear in military subjects
text: The electric-shock gloves immigration agents could soon use to control detainees and protesters worked so powerfully during a military exercise that participants felt intense pain, stopped fighting immediately and feared additional exposures, according to a previously unreleased army study. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) leaders were aware of the findings before signing a $16.7m contract in August to purchase 6,000 pairs of shock gloves, according to records obtained by the watchdog group American Oversight and shared with the Associated Press. The shocks had a profound impact on army employees who played the role of combative prisoners during the exercise, which took place at the military prison at Fort Leavenworth in Kansas in October 2024 – as the Biden administration was in its final months. The participants, several of whom were large-statured men, stopped resisting seconds after officers applied shocks by touching the gloves to their skin, and were left with “fatigue, soreness and excessive apprehensiveness to being shocked again”, the study found. The gloves carry the brand name G.L.O.V.E., which stands for Generated Low Output Voltage Emitter, and are manufactured by Compliant Technologies, a company owned by military veterans and based in Lexington, Kentucky. When it emerged that the second Trump administration was ordering the devices for ICE, amid a hardline anti-immigration crackdown and record arrests and detention of immigrants the government wants to deport, experts expressed alarm and pointed to some high-profile lawsuits over their use in local correctional facilities. In one extreme case, a 43-year-old man died after allegedly being shocked 40 times by officers with a combination of the gloves and a Taser in a county jail in Kentucky, and the man’s widow is suing authorities. In the previous military exercise, the authors of the study shared with AP said: “After experiencing the effects of the GLOVE … participants stated just seeing the GLOVE was enough to make them want to comply.” ICE has called the gloves “distraction and de-escalation devices” that will be safer than other non-lethal options to subdue targets for arrest and deportation and protesters who create civil disturbances. The agency has argued the rapid compliance they cause will keep officers safer and prevent incidents from requiring potentially lethal force. But critics have warned the gloves will give ICE another weapon to intimidate and brutalize people even as the agency is under fire for excessive force that has left a trail of deaths and injuries across the nation. “The military assessment in ICE’s own files shows that these gloves can cause ‘intense pain’ and force compliance. It does not establish that they are safe,” said Chioma Chukwu, executive director of American Oversight. “Everyone should be alarmed that ICE is preparing to deploy a tool designed to inflict, at best, intense pain, without showing that it is safe for the people who will be subjected to it.” ICE released the study and other documents to American Oversight as part of the group’s Freedom of Information Act lawsuit against the agency seeking records related to its use of force. The military prison study assessed whether the gloves could be used effectively to forcibly remove combative prisoners from their cells, to respond to disturbances in common areas and to transport uncooperative inmates. Role-playing employees conducted several scenarios with and without the gloves to test their impact, including violent encounters in which inmates were to fight as hard as they could. The study found that using the gloves “increased the efficiency” of teams carrying out forced cell extractions and responding to disturbances by reducing the length of physical encounters, keeping guards from becoming exhausted and preventing injuries. They did not “significantly change” the time it took to control inmates during escorts but required less effort. “GLOVE provides a boost in confidence to smaller or less trained members,” the study found. “Inmate compliance was immediate” compared with other methods, it added. The electric jolt does not cause the body to freeze like a Taser shock does, but instead “works by overloading the peripheral nerve endings” of the skin to cause pain, the study said. Participants who were wet or had oil on their skin described even more powerful shocks, with one reporting discomfort for 30 minutes afterward. ICE’s contract requires the manufacturer to deliver the gloves within six months. The company owner, Jeff Niklaus, declined to make himself available for an interview. The White House border czar, Tom Homan, has said it could “be a while” before the gloves are in the field because ICE is still ironing out training and policy issues. A statement released on Tuesday by ICE did not address questions about the study and the status of the rollout, but said “officers are highly trained in de-escalation tactics”. Senator Catherine Cortez Masto of Nevada said ICE had not responded to a 27 August letter in which she and 15 other Democratic Senate colleagues called for ICE to abandon its plan to buy the gloves or explain how they would be used and managed to avoid abuse. She said she still wanted answers. “Without ICE’s responses to legitimate questions from 16 United States senators, the American public is being left in the dark about how these electric-shock gloves are being deployed and what, if any, training the agents who use them have received,” she said.

title: The Jaguar Type 01: a £150k gargantuan getaway vehicle utterly useless in the city
summary: Too costly for most, too large for UK car parks, and wheels bigger than a warlord’s pickup truck. But it does come in ‘London red’
text: The cutting-edge car du jour, even while very few will ever buy one, is a good index of what the world’s coming to. It’s a dress-for-the-job-you-want principle, on wheels: drive for the world you want to inhabit. That’s why when Tesla launched the Model X with a bioweapon defence mode (2016!), we should have been much more worried than we were, and it’s why the Jaguar Type 01 Grand Tourer EV has a lot to say. “A new era,” the heritage carmaker calls it, and it’s not wrong. But having test-driven the era (just with my eyes and imagination, rather than the car itself), I would like to return it to the showroom and choose pretty much any other era. Its gigantic size alone makes it look as if it wants to wage war on the future. The whole point of the electrification revolution in motoring was that we could wean ourselves off energy profligacy and on to elegant sufficiency. If you counteract all that with a car too wide (2 metres) and too long (5.2 metres) to fit into any UK car parking space, whatever advances you’ve made with aerodynamics cannot overcome the fact that you are hulking around something that looks more like a tank than a car, the atmospherics underscored by the glassless tailgate and 23-inch wheels. To unpack that a bit, you can’t see into the back at all, the preference for all the other glass is blackout, and the wheels on a Toyota Hilux, the Chad warlord’s vehicle of choice, are between 16 and 18 inches. All the aluminium in the world (73% of the car’s makeup) can’t put a dent in the 2.5-plus-tonne weight, and they’ve bust their own balls to reduce the drag coefficient only to arrive at one (0.23) easily bested by any average electric saloon (0.21). The look it’s going for, according to the literature, is “monolithic”, but it’s a thin line, isn’t it, between an immutable colossus and a menace, so attempts have clearly been made in the design to introduce a note of friendliness. It comes in peace, the Jaguar 01 GT; you can tell by the rounded nose, and the body design creating the visual illusion of a front-to-back taper. If it were in a cartoon, it would be driven by the heroes not the villains, but they’d be heroes with no domestic life who knew how to handle themselves. They wouldn’t be The Incredibles. Traditionally, the Jaguar was driven by a guy in his 50s, wanting to signal to the world that he could afford a car that cost roughly half his salary. That’s what the company is now trying to steer away from, preferring buyers who are “rich, urban, very design literate, very technology literate”, according to Rawdon Glover, Jaguar’s MD. Some texture on that 50-year-old of yesteryear, whose type I knew well: my uncle had a Jaguar. Its paintwork was maroon, its interior a buttery leather, which meant we all knew he was earning a tidy packet, and we weren’t allowed to bring our dog for Christmas in case he scratched it. That, in a nutshell, was the personality type, which – I posit – was bad enough. Jag Persona #0.1 is different: he doesn’t want your social admiration, he wants you to jump out of your skin and get your children indoors at his approach, which you’ll see before you hear and only fleetingly, as he races from 62mph to 112mph in four seconds. He wants you to know he has 150 grand in spare change (ticket price is £120,000 but the extras make that unlikely), and “urban” my aunt Fanny, there is no city situation in which this is a useful car. Regular city driving would be unbearable, given its width, and its standout features of power and agility (three engines, one at the front, one on each rear wheel) are best conceived for a getaway vehicle. Considering its gargantuan size, it doesn’t even have much space – only four seats and boot space that a Skoda Octavia would look at and laugh. And yet, on the plus side, it comes in “London red”, inspired by our mansion blocks and doubledecker buses, our postboxes and room 32 of the National Gallery. These are all different reds, by the way, but then so are red trousers, yet their message is always the same: “I am the kind of person who would wear red trousers.” So if you see one, just think of that person and make them worse, times a thousand.

title: Detained immigrants at Georgia ICE facility launch mass hunger strike
summary: At least 73 people estimated to have joined protest against prolonged detention and Folkston facility’s ‘violations’
text: A group of people detained inside a privately run Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) jail in Georgia have launched a mass hunger strike this week to protest against their prolonged detention and the facility’s conditions, according to advocates and family members. Advocates estimate at least 73 detained immigrants are participating in the hunger strike inside the Folkston D Ray James ICE processing center in south-east Georgia. The Folkston facility, a former state prison, is run by the private prison company GEO Group under a contract with ICE. Some of the men participating in the hunger strike released a video and an open letter, requesting they be released while they continue pursuing their asylum and immigration cases. Two Russian asylum seekers detained in Folkston also released a document they wrote, outlining what they claim to be “violations” inside, including allegations of substandard medical care, threats by GEO Group guards, moldy food and a lack of due process. “Many of us have been separated from our families,” reads the open letter, which was signed this summer by 45 detained immigrants and published this week, as dozens joined in to stage the hunger strike. “We have missed births, funerals, years of our lives while sitting behind fences without having committed any crime.” The hunger strike appears to transcend nationality, language and race, according to the detainees’ video, letter and report. The majority of the men who signed the letter are asylum seekers from a wide range of countries, including Russia, China, Sudan, Afghanistan, Nepal and others. One of the lead organizers of the hunger strike, a Russian asylum seeker named Idris Makhmudov, has reportedly been placed in solitary confinement this week, according to Monica Whatley, an organizer in Georgia from the Campaign to Shut Down the Folkston ICE processing center. The letter further reads: “We come from different countries, races, believes [sic], and background, but we share one thing in common: we came to the United States seeking protection and have been detained since then.” The men say in their letter that they have been locked up for a long time, between 16 months and almost three years, from the moment each arrived in the US “yet have never been accused of any crime”. They argue they should be free while their legal cases go through the immigration court system. “Many of us have tried every available legal path to seek release from detention” but without success, they say, adding that their letter is for those who believe in “fairness and human dignity”. “Innocent people can remain in detention for very long periods, without any individualized finding that they are dangerous or likely to flee,” the signatories complain. One of the men participating in the hunger strike is an asylum seeker from Yemen who is suffering from lung cancer and has a US citizen child, advocates told the Guardian. The reports of the hunger strike at the Folkston facility represent the latest protest inside an ICE detention center, as the Trump administration continues with its aggressive anti-immigrant crackdown. GEO Group referred all questions to ICE. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS), ICE’s parent agency, did not respond to detailed questions about the allegations or requests for comment. ICE, along with other federal agencies and local officials deputized to carry out immigration arrests, have been quietly increasing their arrests nationwide. As a result, rising numbers of immigrants and asylum seekers are detained in federal facilities like Folkston. The Folkston facility opened in 1997 but began detaining people in ICE custody in 2018. Last year, the Florida-based, for-profit company GEO Group extended its contract with ICE to expand the facility’s capacity. The latest ICE data from July of this year shows there were about 2,200 people detained there. The majority of the detainees in Folkston who signed the letter are requesting asylum. The open letter includes the names, government-issued alien numbers, countries of origin and time in detention for the 45 men who signed it. All have been in ICE detention for at least one year. A Chinese man named Liang Sonji, who signed the letter, came to the US and requested asylum in October 2023 and has been detained since. “We understand that temporary detention may sometimes be necessary to verify identity or conduct background checks,” the open letter, drafted by Makhmudov, reads. “But detention lasting one year, two years, or longer without a clear individual justification raises serious questions about fairness and reasonableness.” The two Russian men who also sent out a document about conditions – Alexei Kovalko and Alexander Borovkov – accused an unnamed medical staffer at the facility of telling one of them: “I have no obligation to treat you; the only thing that matters to me is that you don’t drop dead.” Kovalko and Borovkov also write describing moldy food, foul-smelling water, and other allegedly deficient conditions in the detention center, including leaky ceilings and problems with plumbing. The document also says that some GEO Group employees at the Folkston facility are “xenophobic” and rude, and frequently threaten detained immigrants with solitary confinement. GEO Group and ICE did not respond to questions about these allegations. There have been a series of hunger strikes inside ICE detention centers since the Trump administration took office again last year, some of which have received widespread attention. Earlier this year, a group of detainees inside the Delaney Hall facility in New Jersey, which is also operated by GEO Group, launched a hunger strike. Protesters outside the facility, demonstrating in solidarity with the hunger strikers, were met with force by ICE and local officials, making international headlines. Similarly, the Guardian has reported on individual cases of hunger strikes throughout the ICE detention network and the secretive response by ICE officials, including finding that ICE has quietly sought court orders to provide “involuntary medical procedures” on 19 hunger strikers since January 2025, including force feeding, a practice widely seen as torture.

title: Israel marks third anniversary of 7 October Hamas attacks | First Thing
summary: Site of the Nova music festival near Re’im one of the locations where grieving relatives have gathered
text: Good morning. Israel is holding ceremonies and gatherings to mark the third anniversary of the 7 October attack by Hamas, in which about 1,200 people were killed and another 251 taken captive to Gaza. Israeli communities shattered by the massacres, torn between rebuilding their lives and remembering lost friends and relatives, have spoken to Emma Graham-Harrison about their experiences of that day and the days since. The Guardian is marking the day with a live blog, featuring the latest images of events taking place in Israel and around the world. Israel’s government responded to the attack by launching a devastating war on Gaza, during which at least 74,243 people have been killed, according to the territory’s health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN. What is happening with the flydubai attack investigation? New Zealand authorities have launched their own investigation into the flydubai co-pilot who allegedly tried to hijack an Israel-bound plane, after police confirmed he underwent flight training there about a year after he abandoned a degree in Australia. Disaster was narrowly averted on 30 September when passengers and crew intervened to stop the alleged attempt to take control of a flight to Tel Aviv with 182 people onboard. What it is the latest settler violence? Armed Israeli settlers beat a photographer in the presence of Israeli soldiers, hospitalising him, as he covered worsening settler violence against olive farmers in the occupied West Bank. Jaafar Ashtiyeh, a 58-year-old veteran photographer for Agence France-Presse in Palestine, was beaten with the butts of rifles, despite him being marked as press, in view of about a dozen armed Israeli soldiers. US justice department moves to strip citizenship of 40 naturalized citizens The justice department has moved to strip the citizenship of 40 naturalized citizens accused of crimes in what authorities describe as “the largest” such initiative over a single period. Officials announced the filing of “denaturalization actions” against more than three dozen people alleged to have committed such offenses as “acting as an agent for a foreign government, committing voluntary manslaughter, and aggravated sodomy against a special‑needs man.” A statement attributed to the US attorney general, Todd Blanche, maintained that those at the center of Monday’s announcement “concealed critical facts from the US government and represent serious criminal offenders.” Who is the latest person taking legal action against the administration’s immigration enforcement? Marimar Martinez, a US citizen who was shot one year ago by a Customs and Border Protection agent during a sweeping immigration crackdown in Chicago, has filed a lawsuit against the federal government, alleging the agent lied about the shooting and fired into her vehicle from behind. What has a whistleblower said about FBI investigations into LA anti-ICE protesters? Alex Padilla, a Democratic senator who represents California and serves on the Senate judiciary committee, said his office had received a copy of a complaint from a whistleblower that makes sweeping allegations about the Trump administration’s response to protests in LA in early 2025, claiming the president himself ordered the FBI to investigate protesters. Riot police fire teargas as 250,000 people take part in schools protests across France Police fired teargas at ⁠protesters as more than 250,000 pupils, teachers and parents demonstrated across France on the biggest day yet of a campaign for better high school conditions that has been marred by often violent clashes with police. The French prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, said at least 215 teenagers and 85 school staff had been injured since the protests began more than a fortnight ago. Nearly 500 people were arrested and authorities said 43 police officers were injured. Why are there such large protests over French schools? School students say the education system is riven with inequality, that many buildings are in disrepair, class sizes are too big, and there are not enough teachers or funding. Lecornu has promised to address what he called “legitimate” complaints, including on class sizes, long hours, dilapidated buildings and teacher provisions. Christa Pike is conscious and speaking after botched execution attempt, lawyers say Christa Pike is awake and speaking as she receives treatment at a hospital, her attorneys said Tuesday. Pike, 50, survived two doses of pentobarbital, a sedative, as Tennessee officials attempted to put her to death last Wednesday, in a case that shocked many in America and created headlines around the world. Pike and her boyfriend killed 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, one of their classmates, in 1995. The case garnered nationwide attention due to the young ages of those involved and the brutality of the murder. In other news … An oil tanker off Russia’s Black Sea coast was struck by a naval drone, causing a huge fire and a black smoke cloud that blanketed parts of the resort city of Sochi, Russia’s transport ministry has said. Paramount has completed the $111bn acquisition of Warner Bros to form a new media empire, Skydance. Donald Trump said his administration was considering suspending the federal gasoline tax. Pump prices have stayed high since the US-Israeli war on Iran raised them sharply earlier this year. The New York governor, Kathy Hochul, has declared a state of emergency in response to a dramatic rise in measles cases in the state. There have been 108 confirmed cases in New York so far this year. There was just one reported case in 2023. A former senior CIA official pleaded guilty to a charge that he abused his position and government funds to enrich himself by acquiring Florida real estate and hundreds of gold bars. Stat of the day: California couple charged with child abuse in surrogacy scheme involving at least 21 children Silvia Zhang and her husband, Guojun Xuan, are expected to face conspiracy to commit child abuse charges. Fifteen children were removed from the couple’s opulent home in Arcadia last year after an allegation of abuse, and another six living elsewhere were also located. Well Actually: Experts on how to get more comfortable with death Madeleine Aggeler explores how we live in, as one expert puts it, “grief-illiterate and grief-phobic societies” despite us all knowing that we will die one day. It is a very thought-provoking piece. Don’t miss this: Who owns ‘brain rot’? Inside the international legal drama over a beloved meme Kari Paul reports on the extraordinary legal tussle over Tung Tung Tung Sahur, also known as Triple T. There is a huge question about who gets to profit from the OpenAI image-generated character, created in 2025 by an Indonesian teen who goes by the username Noxa. title: The 80-year-old market trader who became a Chilean music star
summary: Born and raised in Valparaíso, JM is seen as one of the last of a golden generation after a late foray
text: At a concert hall in the Chilean capital, Santiago, an 80-year-old man edges unsteadily down a steep staircase. With one hand he grips the metal bannister, in the other he carries a mug of hot water with a slice of lemon, as if heading to bed. But when the red stage curtain is pulled aside for him, Luis Gómez, or JM as he is universally known, transforms in an instant. He skips on to the stage to a roar from the crowd and launches into a bolero, punctuated by hip thrusts and shuffling two-steps. JM is the frontman of Los Crack del Puerto, and one of the last remaining voices of a golden generation. Born and raised in Valparaíso, Chile’s vibrant second city, JM’s late foray into music has taken him all around the country, as well as to Mexico, the UK, Argentina and France. But things could – and probably should – have worked out very differently. At 65, he was still hawking vegetables at the market he had worked at since the age of eight. This May, Los Crack del Puerto released their fourth record, Lo Mucho Que Nos Queda (So Much Yet to Come), as a cassette – to great acclaim. “Singing has always been my release,” JM says in a wavering voice, in contrast to his confident onstage vocals. The father of two speaks with captivating enthusiasm about his life, often leaping to his feet to re-enact minor scenes. Scattered with bursts of song, most conversations return to his mostly tongue-in-cheek fear of his wife of 55 years, his penchant for sports clothing, or the market on Avenida Argentina in Valparaíso. JM was born in the O’Higgins neighbourhood of Valparaíso in 1945, the youngest of five children. He was three years old when his father died, and 10 when he lost his mother. For a time, he would sleep out on the street between parked cars, until his aunt and uncle took him in and laid down the law, insisting that he was home by 10pm each night. “JM” was a cheeky nickname bestowed upon him by the family – the initials of a childhood friend, Juan Muñoz, with whom they said he spent too much time. The moniker has long since replaced his full name. Valparaíso then, as it is now, was defined by its music. As in many ports, cultures and ideas have long arrived in the city and been woven into its fabric; but the musical styles of its 20th-century heyday, from boleros to waltzes, tango to cueca, Chile’s official national dance, have barely changed in generations. “The same songs that were sung before are still the ones they sing now,” says JM decisively. Many now form Los Crack del Puerto’s repertoire. One of his cousins, Juan Navarro, known simply as Juanín, would bring friends home and play his guitar for them, and the younger JM would come sing along. The cousins remained lifelong friends while Juanín pursued a career in the police and JM sold vegetables at the market. “That’s still what I am – a market trader,” he says. Through middle age, the self-taught double act entertained crowds in Valparaíso’s bars – JM the entertaining foil to his more serious older cousin, who would perch on a stool to play his guitar, always in an immaculate pressed suit. “Sometimes Juanín would just invent chords,” says Los Crack del Puerto’s manager, Juan Nuñez. “The rest of the band would stop and ask him what chord he’d just played, and he’d just shrug.” “JM was the entertainer, he can make anyone laugh,” Nuñez adds. But the dynamic worked. In 2017, JM and Juanín began taking their music more seriously, forming the band with a group of talented local musicians. “That generation is an intangible cultural heritage. They’re a living legacy,” says 33-year-old musician Felipe Riveros, who has played with JM as a guitarist. “He’s charismatic. People go mad when he comes on stage. He and Juanín are the archetypes of the old porteño.” Juanín died in 2025 at the age of 87. “For three or four months, I missed him so much, I couldn’t bring myself to get back on stage,” says JM of his cousin. “People would request Juanín’s songs, but they were his, I didn’t feel like we could play them.” Now, as JM approaches his 81st birthday, the royalty cheques that supplement his miserly state pension are of little consequence to him. “I never planned any of this, and I’d be happy still working at the market,” he says quietly during a break between songs at the Quinta de los Nuñez, a hillside restaurant where he sings every Sunday for an adoring crowd. “But I suppose it’s never too late to give something a try.”

title: Husband of Norfolk GP found dead at home appears in court charged with her murder
summary: Mark Cain, 45, charged on Tuesday after Hannah Cain was found dead in Fern Hill, Dersingham, on Sunday night
text: The husband of a GP has appeared in court charged with her murder. Dr Hannah Cain, 45, was found dead at her home in the village of Dersingham, near the Sandringham estate in Norfolk, on Sunday 4 October. Mark Cain, 45, of the same address, was arrested and charged with the GP’s murder on Tuesday afternoon, Norfolk police said. He appeared before Norwich magistrates court on Wednesday, where he was not asked to enter a plea, and was remanded in custody. Prosecutor Jacqui Hanlon told the court that Hannah Cain was attended by paramedics in the early hours of Sunday and “found in an upstairs bedroom not breathing, not conscious”. The ambulance service contacted the police at 2:25am, the court was told. Children were present in the property at the time, the prosecutor said. District judge Matthew Bone said the case would be sent to King’s Lynn crown court, where Mark Cain will appear on Thursday morning. After the hearing, Hannah Cain’s family described her as a “beloved” mother and daughter, and asked for privacy “at this difficult time”. In a statement released by Norfolk police on Wednesday, the family said: “We are devastated by the loss of our beautiful Hannah. “She was kind, generous and loving; a beloved mother, daughter, sister, auntie, daughter-in-law and friend. “We are incredibly proud of the woman she was and of the great care she took of all her patients, who knew her as Dr Terry.” Hannah Cain was listed as a member of the practice team at Grimston medical centre. According to the Sun, she served in a pool of doctors who were regularly on call for members of the royal family nearby. The medical centre announced its temporary closure on Monday. “We are sorry to let patients know that Grimston medical centre, including the dispensary, is temporarily closed due to extremely difficult circumstances affecting our practice team,” a Facebook post said. “We apologise for the disruption and appreciate your patience and understanding at what is a very difficult time for our colleagues.” Norfolk police said on Tuesday that specialist officers were continuing to support Hannah Cain’s family.

title: Royal Mail to cut up to 2,500 jobs amid restructure and fall in letter deliveries
summary: Postal service says cuts will focus on head office and ‘support function roles’
text: Royal Mail is to cut up to 2,500 jobs as the embattled company seeks to restructure its business amid intense competition and the continuing decline in letter deliveries. The postal service, which has been fined a total of £37m since 2023 for missing delivery targets set by the regulator Ofcom, said the job cuts would focus on head office and “support function roles” with the restructure to be completed by the end of next year. Pointing out that the volume of letter deliveries had declined more than 70% since their peak in the mid-00s, Royal Mail said the cuts would be achieved through “natural attrition” and a voluntary exit programme with no compulsory redundancies. The company said there would be no reduction in operational frontline roles in delivery and processing, including the number of postal workers and drivers it employs. The cuts amount to less than 2% of Royal Mail’s workforce of more than 131,000. However, the Communications Workers Union (CWU), which represents frontline staff, said about 200 members with jobs in administration and revenue protection would be affected. “We will be meeting management to discuss this announcement, which is further evidence of a company that is demoralising staff and failing to deliver for customers and the wider community,” said Martin Walsh, a deputy general secretary of the CWU. “We urge the government to confront the reality of a collapsing Royal Mail and intervene to save this national institution.” The cuts are the first to be made since the completion of the £3.6bn takeover of Royal Mail’s parent company, International Distribution Services, by the Czech billionaire Daniel Křetínský’s EP Group last year. Royal Mail last made a big round of cuts in 2022 when it said it was looking to eliminate up to 10,000 roles, including 6,000 full-time frontline jobs. “We have been working hard to reduce costs and simplify processes across all areas of the business as we transform to win in a very competitive market,” said Alistair Cochrane, the chief executive of Royal Mail. “These proposed changes remove duplication and allow us to invest further in the service we deliver for our customers. “The proposed changes will not be easy, but they are an important part of building a stronger, simpler and future-ready Royal Mail for our customers and colleagues.” The union Unite said further job cuts were likely unless the government and the regulator Ofcom addressed a number of issues facing Royal Mail, most notably high competition from rivals that operated “gig economy postal services”. “These devastating job losses have been directly caused by years of inaction, without urgent action, this will happen again,” said Sharon Graham, Unite’s general secretary. “More jobs will be lost, employment standards will continue to fall and customers will continue to be let down. “The answer cannot simply be another round of job cuts. Unite is now supporting our affected members at Royal Mail during this very difficult time and is committed to fighting this decision every step of the way.” Last week, the company announced it was to hire 22,000 temporary workers – in roles including sorting, delivery and collection and HGV and MGV drivers – to cover the seasonal jump in mail volumes, including online purchases over Black Friday and Cyber Monday in November, and Christmas deliveries. In June, the postal regulator launched an investigation into Royal Mail for once again missing its annual delivery targets, with almost a quarter of first-class mail arriving late. Royal Mail has not hit its Ofcom-mandated delivery target for first-class post since 2017, or for second-class mail since 2020. In April, Royal Mail faced criticism for raising the price of a first-class stamp by 10p, or 6%, to £1.80. The cost of a first-class stamp has more than doubled since 2020. The cost of the second-class service rose by 4p, or 5%, to 91p. Royal Mail blamed the need for price increases on the “continued rise in the cost of delivery for every letter”. Last July, Ofcom gave IDS permission to loosen Royal Mail’s universal service obligation, ending second-class post on Saturdays and reducing the service to alternate weekdays from Monday to Friday. A decade ago Royal Mail was delivering 20bn letters a year, but that has shrunk to 6.7bn and could drop to 4bn within four years. Over the same timeframe the number of addresses it serves has risen by 4m.

title: Millionaire tax no more? Rightwing groups lead effort to repeal Washington state law
summary: An initiative on November’s ballot aims to overturn the 9.9% tax on earnings above $1m – who’s winning the fight?
text: Voters in Washington state will soon decide the fate of the state’s so-called “millionaire tax” – a 9.9% income tax on earnings above $1m that was signed into law in March and is now facing a conservative-backed effort to repeal it. An initiative on November’s ballot aims to overturn the tax, claiming that the tax represents a slippery slope, and would eventually result in taxes for more than just millionaires. A coalition of advocacy groups and unions opposing the initiative say taxing the state’s 20,000 highest-earning households could raise approximately $3.5bn in necessary annual revenue to fund core priorities like education and healthcare, and expand tax credits and sales tax exemptions. Facing dwindling federal funds under the Trump administration yet home to substantial tech-industry wealth, including prominent billionaires such as Bill Gates, Steve Ballmer and, until recently, Jeff Bezos, Washington has joined other states and municipalities by turning to its wealthiest earners as a source of revenue. Massachusetts, Maine and New York already impose a unique tax rate on millionaires, and Hawaii passed a similar measure in May. California, whose resident billionaires possess a collective net worth hovering above $2tn, will see voters decide on a proposed one-time, 5% tax on billionaires’ wealth. The measure is opposed by most billionaires as well as Gavin Newsom, the governor; some progressive groups also question the long-term benefits of the one-off tax. Washington’s governor, Bob Ferguson, has said he would veto any effort to expand the millionaire tax to encompass lower-earning households. And, after decades of voter-rejected efforts to reform the state’s tax structure, which has historically lacked an income tax and instead levied sales taxes, property taxes and fees, Washingtonians in recent years have approved new progressive revenue streams, including a capital gains tax. Advocates claim that the millionaire tax is part of a clear mandate to better align the state’s largely regressive tax code with its progressive values. *** The statewide fight over an income tax really began in the 1930s, according to the Washington state senate majority leader, Jamie Pedersen, an architect of the millionaire tax. Nearly 100 years ago, the state’s supreme court ruled that income taxes constituted a property tax, hamstringing efforts to diversify beyond flat-rate excises. By 2002, a state commission led by Bill Gates Sr concluded that Washington’s tax code was uniquely regressive, and called for a state-level income tax. But, in 2010, voters still voted by wide margins against a proposed tax for those earning above $200,000; Steve Ballmer, Microsoft’s then CEO, was the leading contributor to the campaign opposing the tax, and the Amazon founder, Jeff Bezos, ranked fourth. A reliance on sales, property and other taxes leaves the state with “the second-worst tax code in the nation when it comes to who actually pays as a share of their income”, said Emily Vyhnanek of the Washington State Budget and Policy Center, a non-partisan research group. Those in the lowest-earning quintile spend up to 13.8% of their annual income on state taxes, while those in the top 1% currently spend about 4%, they said. In 2021, lawmakers passed a 7% tax on capital gains above $250,000, which survived a constitutional challenge and a conservative-led ballot initiative aiming to overturn it in 2024. The initiative’s resounding defeat was “some indication that voters were willing to vote for something that the opponents labeled as an income tax”, Pedersen said. By 2025, facing a nearly $15bn shortfall over the ensuing four years, Democratic lawmakers debated new ways to tackle the state’s structural budget problem, and landed on the high earners’ income tax. Lawmakers had “99.9% certainty” that conservative groups would challenge the tax through a ballot initiative, Pedersen said. *** Brian Heywood, a conservative hedge fund executive and the founder of Let’s Go Washington, a political action committee, has helped spearhead and fund initiative 645, the ballot initiative to overturn the millionaire tax. Heywood and his business moved from California to Washington state in 2010, in part drawn by the state’s lack of capital gains and income taxes. Voicing concerns about a slippery slope, Heywood said the new income tax and ensuing capital flight risked compromising Washington’s “golden goose” economy, which features Microsoft, Amazon, Boeing and others. “I can’t tell you how many people have left the state,” he said. “My business partner moved to Arizona. I probably know 50 people that are deca- or centi-millionaires that have left the state.” Academic research suggests about 2% of residents affected by the millionaire tax might leave Washington, according to Rian Watt of the Seattle-based thinktank Economic Opportunity Institute. Since Let’s Go Washington’s founding in 2022, Heywood has spent at least $11m of his own money on 20 proposals, including a campaign to repeal Washington’s carbon market. More than 60% of voters rejected that effort in 2024, and the campaign opposing Heywood was partially funded by Gates and Ballmer. In September, several business owners in Washington confronted public outcry and boycotts after public disclosure forms revealed they had donated to Let’s Go Washington; in both cases, business owners claimed they solely supported Let’s Go Washington’s efforts to overturn the millionaire tax, and not its other initiatives on the 2026 ballot. Let’s Go Washington is behind two other proposals, including a campaign to ban trans girls from participating in girls’ sports at school. Opponents have expressed alarm at the initiative and have dubbed it “the most extreme proposal of its kind”, as it would require girls to undergo “verification of biological sex” during sports physicals, potentially through genital exams. Heywood claimed Democratic lawmakers, and the state’s election-finance watchdog, have strategically tried to isolate him and Let’s Go Washington, and “try to make me toxic, somehow” in the eyes of donors. A separate campaign backing the millionaire tax repeal was launched in July, and selected former Republican congresswoman Jaime Herrera Beutler as its spokesperson. That campaign did not return the Guardian’s request for comment. Pedersen suggested that advocates interested in overturning the millionaire tax may “have figured out Brian Heywood” and may be “trying to distance themselves from his pretty toxic brand”. The state supreme court is also slated to hear a legal challenge to the tax early next year, which will test the validity of the new income tax against state-constitutional and legal precedent. ••• Recent polling suggests that the initiative is likely to fail. In a survey of Washington residents, research firm DHM found 57% of respondents opposed repealing the tax. Kara Krnacik, who helped lead the survey, said Washington residents may be growing more open to an income tax below the million-dollar threshold: 41% of respondents said they were in favor of an income tax that might eventually extend to those making $100,000 or more, up from 36% in November 2025. But if the tax is overturned, lawmakers face a “very stark reality”, Pedersen said, and may have to find revenue through “inferior alternatives” such as hiking the sales tax rate, or enacting a statewide payroll tax. Meanwhile, if the tax survives, Pedersen said lawmakers may begin to scrap or reform other regressive taxes in Washington, including its business taxes. “I think it’s really significant that you do not see almost any major business that is aligning itself with the initiative 645 folks,” Pedersen said. Public disclosure records suggest the initiative’s opponents have outspent its supporters by more than 50%; and major labor unions in the state have contributed more than $6m to the campaign defending the tax. In addition to new legal challenges, Heywood said he had begun to consider ways to circumscribe how unions receive and disburse funds in the state.

title: Separatists win in Quebec – but does that bring separation from Canada any closer?
summary: Lack of majority for Parti Québécois puts any referendum in doubt, especially amid bruising trade war with Trump
text: The victory of the Parti Québécois in Monday’s election in Quebec might seem to bring its signature goal, of separating the French-speaking province from Canada, much closer – but Canadian unity may not be nearly as threatened as may first seem. The PQ’s victory was both impressive and disappointing. The party added 56 seats to its roster and more than doubled its vote share compared with the 2022 election, giving it its first taste of power in 14 years. Crucially, however, it was left five seats short of a majority, making its promise to hold a referendum after Donald Trump leaves office in 2028 nearly impossible. It also won with barely 28% of the popular vote, the lowest percentage for any government in Canada’s electoral history, according to the polling analyst Philippe Fournier. The vast majority of Quebecers voted for parties that want nothing to do with a referendum. It’s a reflection of the province’s 30-year aversion to another bruising debate about Quebec’s place in Canada – particularly in the wake of Trump’s tariffs and threats against the country. The result not only puts another referendum in doubt, but a raft of other PQ initiatives too, including abolishing the monarchy and applying Quebec’s strict language laws to the province’s colleges. The new government will also face stiff opposition to its plans to reduce immigration levels, which have angered farmers and the business community. Meanwhile, the most popular politician in the province remains far and away the Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, in large part because of his resistance to Trump. That has left the PQ leader, Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, in an awkward situation for a separatist: he can’t be seen as a threat to Canadian unity. He essentially acknowledged this in his victory speech, pledging to be a “good-faith collaborator” with the rest of the country, and even addressing the crowd in English; then attempted to court the other side of the debate by announcing on Tuesday he would prevent the lieutenant governor, who represents the British crown, from swearing in his new government. “Seventy per cent of Quebecers don’t want a referendum,” said John Parisella, who served as chief of staff to two Quebec premiers and the province’s delegate general in New York and Washington. “And every time they see Trump’s picture on the screen at night, it does nothing to improve a desire for separation. For a lot of Quebecers, the link with Canada is absolutely crucial, even if it isn’t necessarily emotional.” The vote, in fact, may have less to do with embracing separatism and more about punishing the current government. The election saw the total collapse of the governing Coalition Avenir Québec (CAQ), which has been in power since 2018. An alliance of federalists and separatists (the party describes itself as nationalist), it didn’t win a single seat, and harvested just a third of its vote share compared to 2022. Its leader, Christine Fréchette, lost her own riding to the Parti Québécois, and on Tuesday afternoon she resigned. In a province whose political discourse has focused on the federalist-separatist divide, the election also suggested a return to normalcy of sorts – with separatists returning to the PQ’s fold, while the federalist vote dispersed to the opposition Liberal party and the upstart Parti Conservateur du Québec (PCQ). The PCQ feasted on the CAQ’s support in the election, winning 19 ridings in the hinterland and in the Quebec City area, where leader Éric Duhaime won his seat for the first time. Founded in 2009, the populist party counts a prominent anti-vaxxer and a rage-bating anti-woke radio host as two of its winning candidates. The party was able to break through in part because of its promise to build an underground highway linking Quebec City to its suburbs across the St Lawrence, despite government reports saying the endeavor would cost as much as C$9.3bn (US$6.5bn) and do little to alleviate traffic. Montreal, meanwhile, went decidedly Liberal red, with leader Charles Milliard regaining seats on the island and in the traditionally English redoubt of the Eastern Townships. The staunchly federalist Liberals, who are unaffiliated with Carney’s federal Liberals, will serve as Quebec’s official opposition. Governing with but a handful of seats in the province’s biggest metropolis will be challenging enough for the PQ; as history has shown, winning a referendum without it is somewhere near impossible. Canada faces another potential menace to its sovereignty in a little less than two weeks, when Alberta in the west holds a “referendum on a referendum” on secession. Happily for Carney, and unfortunately for Trump, polls suggest Albertans are as averse to dalliances with separation as their Quebecer brethren have now become to the east – no matter the party they just chose to govern.

title: McDonald’s sued for allegedly using AI tool to determine pricing for franchises
summary: Suit says AI tool allows independently owned franchises to exchange nonpublic price and sales information
text: McDonald’s is facing a lawsuit in federal court over its alleged use of an AI tool to determine pricing across independent franchises, which prosecutors say violates antitrust laws and has unfairly inflated menu prices for Americans. The vast majority of McDonald’s US stores are independently owned and are said to individually decide on prices under company policy. Antitrust laws require businesses to set prices independently from their competitors, as coordinating prices can stifle market competition and push up costs for consumers. The lawsuit, filed on 2 October in a federal Chicago courtroom, alleges that McDonald’s AI tool is illegal because it amounts to independent franchise locations exchanging nonpublic price and sales data. “This case is about McDonald’s bringing ‘optimization’ to America’s largest fast food chain,” the complaint says. “McDonald’s has built and for years deployed its own information-sharing pricing platform, which draws on data from its millions of daily transactions to set menu prices across thousands of US restaurants. The result is algorithmic price-fixing aimed at customers who are already stretched thin.” In response to the lawsuit, a spokesperson for the McDonald’s corporation said that the “complaint is filled with inaccuracies and we will vigorously defend against this lawsuit”. “AI does not set menu prices at McDonald’s restaurants – McDonald’s franchisees do,” it said. “Optional tools are available to franchisees to help them make the best decisions for their businesses and customers, but these tools do not automate, coordinate or fix pricing in any way.” A recent Reuters investigation reported that some McDonald’s franchise owners have been pressured by the company to use the AI pricing tools and record their deviations from the tool’s recommendations. McDonald’s contested that characterization, calling the Reuters reporting “speculative and uninformed”. The litigation, which has been proposed as a nationwide class-action lawsuit, was first brought forward by an Illinois man named Michael Thomas. Thomas, a McDonald’s regular who is described as “price conscious”, found that the cost of his usual order – a Quarter Pounder with cheese, fries and a Coke – varied even within his neighborhood in DeKalb, Illinois. The attorney listed as representing Thomas did not immediately reply to a request for comment. Thomas does not appear to be alone in his experience. At a McDonald’s in Manhattan’s financial district, Chukwama Okeke, 43, was finishing a mango-pineapple smoothie that he bought as part of a value meal that cost about $15 – something he only gets about once a month. Okeke said that when he orders the same meal at a McDonald’s in Brooklyn’s Crown Heights neighborhood, he ends up paying closer to $9. “McDonald’s in Manhattan is much more expensive than those in Brooklyn,” he said. “I’ve notice in some areas if they have a lot of like foot traffic, the prices tend to get higher.” Beatriz Milander, 27, who ordered a snack wrap, a small fries and an iced coffee for $11.51, hadn’t noticed a huge difference between what she pays in the financial district and what she pays in her Bronx neighborhood, but said prices overall had inched up. “In the last few months, I’ve seen them do more deals or like lower-priced things,” she said. “But it definitely was pricing up for a little bit there.” Experts say that companies using AI to set or alter pricing could exacerbate the country’s affordability crisis and make it harder for Americans to bear everyday costs. So far this year, at least 90 pieces of legislation have been filed across the country to push back against algorithmic price-fixing, according to Lindsay Owens, the head of the left-leaning thinktank Groundwork Collaborative, who recently authored a book on the topic. McDonald’s acquired an AI company, Dynamic Yield, in 2019, but has firmly denied using AI in setting menu prices. In a statement released on 1 October, the day before the lawsuit was filed, the chain denied using dynamic pricing and described its pricing tool as simply providing information that franchises are free to decide whether to adopt. The fast-food chain has been scrutinized over recent years for its elevated prices, and went viral in 2023 over an $18 Big Mac meal at a Connecticut McDonald’s. The franchise’s owner filed a lawsuit alleging that it was the AI pricing tool that suggested the $18 price to the franchise. According to a fact sheet the chain published in 2024, the average price of a McDonald’s menu item increased about 40% between 2019 and 2024.

title: Tents, night-vision goggles and bear tracking kits: America’s first nature library opens
summary: As well as books, the new facility in Colorado offers equipment to help connect people with the natural world. We asked five of the first visitors what they thought of it
text: Mark Fink knows exactly why he opened the first public nature library in the US. “There are a lot of barriers for people to access nature here. We want people to learn about the birds and the plants in their own back yard and to appreciate that you don’t need a three-day camping trip in the mountains to experience nature.” The library offers people in Colorado’s Adams county the opportunity to borrow books and equipment to help them to engage with the natural world – for free. While most of the 40,000 items in the library’s collection are books, members can also check out 850 nature-focused “try it” kits – anything from birdwatching equipment, gardening tools and wildlife cameras to hiking gear, microscopes and hammocks. “In the US, as more information has come out about climate change and global warming, there’s been a lot of pushback on those scientific studies and their validity,” says Fink. He is executive director of Anythink Libraries, which opened the Nature Library in August and is funded by a local property tax levy. “We want to let people make up their own minds. We want to provide opportunities for them to learn more about the climate, the human impact on the Earth and how we can help reduce climate change and make our environment more sustainable,” he says, adding that spending even 20 minutes in nature has physical and mental health benefits.In addition, research suggests that people who have more experience with nature are more likely to be inspired to help protect it. Built using local stone, the library has 370 solar panels on the roof and a sustainable geothermal heating and cooling system. It sits on a 6-hectare (15-acre) site – a former ranch – with a hiking trail and eight different types of garden, including sensory and pollinator gardens, and two focusing on plants that thrive in Colorado and the nearby Rocky Mountains. Inside, children can play in a boulder field made up of rocks from a local quarry, plus there are free workshops to help people build their confidence in activities such as birdwatching, gardening and hiking. We asked five of the first people to visit the library what they thought of it. Paula Jensen, 64, visiting with her mother, Jeanette, 88 I heard about the library on Facebook. I decided to take my mom. It’s hard for an 88-year-old to go up to the mountains and connect with nature. I work full-time – I’m a pharmaceutical shipping specialist – and although my mom’s pretty independent, she mostly stays home when I’m at work. There was a peaceful little rock garden outside, and she was able to walk around in there with her walker. At her age, it’s very important to get out of the house and do that. Then we sat down by the mud pit. That was really cute to see – all these little children running through it and making mudcakes. My mom loves reading and doing puzzles, and she was surprised to discover she could borrow a wooden puzzle and a Danielle Steel book. She told me it would be too expensive. I said: “Mom, it’s a library.” It was such an impressive building and she couldn’t quite believe that everything was free. It made her so happy. We’re having a water shortage in Colorado, so when I go back, I’m planning to borrow a book about how to design a drought-friendly garden, like the one I saw there. Anna Amici, 36, visited with her husband, Prashant, and daughter Asha, two I’m a scientist for a science education company – I write curriculum for college students, for labs. I love nature and I love libraries and thought a nature library sounded like a cool place to go, especially with a child. Asha is growing up in a world where we have to care about and protect our environment. And with the current people in power, it feels like we’re going backwards, and that’s scary. I think she’s going to be forced into making tough decisions to protect the natural world – I think we all are – and I would rather she do that from a love of nature than a sense of doom. What’s exciting about the library is that it makes nature more accessible to her. She can touch it and interact with it in ways that she can’t when we’re out elsewhere. Also, when I’ve had a stressful week, I want to be able to go outside where I can hear birds and touch grass. We’re thinking of replacing our lawn, which died over the summer, with plants that can support pollinators, so we borrowed a pollinator-garden planning kit and a couple of bird guides from the library. We live near a lake that the birds of the Rocky Mountains visit – if I can learn to identify them, I can teach Asha their names. The next time we go, I’d like to borrow a stargazing kit so we can take Asha up into the mountains and look at the stars together. During our visit, Asha had a great time climbing on the boulders and playing in the mud pit. It was such a fun way for her to connect with nature on a very physical, sensory level and it made me realise that she doesn’t get many opportunities to actually touch some dirt in her everyday life. We’ve since created a little mud patch in our own garden, which she has really enjoyed playing in. Being in the library has made me recognise that this kind of activity is a good experience for her, it’s building the love of the natural world that I want to foster and nurture in her. It’s worth the mess. Nataliya Zasadko, 40, who visited with her son Marko, seven I’m a freelance photographer, videographer and content creator, focusing on outdoor family adventures, so the Nature Library sparked my interest. Camping gear can be expensive and a lot of people don’t know if they want to invest in it. Having tents and hammocks available to borrow is a phenomenal idea. We borrowed an outdoor camera with a macro lens, which encouraged my son to go out in nature and photograph bumblebees and flowers, and a GPS gadget. We used that to go on an adventure along a very scenic alpine trail, Santa Fe Peak. I didn’t have to convince my son to come with me – he was excited to go because of this gadget. He was able to use it to plan our route and guide me. We picked a spot we had never been to before and explored. It was a perfect all-day adventure. That gadget would have cost me $300 or $400, and the camera $500, so to be able to check them out without buying was brilliant. We also borrowed a digital wind-speed meter, and talked about that, too. We watched a whole YouTube series about windmills and wind-power plants, and how the energy is produced and stored. I think visiting a nature library is a good way to teach children about nature and encourage them to care about the environment and wildlife. Whether my son was climbing on the boulders or playing in the mud pit, time flew by. The trail around the library is also very beautiful and I noticed that in the garden, they have hoses so children can water the plants. We’ve gone back twice because there’s so much to do, and I’m excited for the winter when I’m thinking of borrowing some snowshoes and micro spikes, and going on hikes to test them out. In this economy, with families struggling, I love that people are able to go to this library for a few hours and share community resources that can help us build a better future and learn to explore the great outdoors. Alex Bueno, 30, visited with his wife, Monse, and their son Edgar, six We live in Nebraska and decided to go to the library while we were on a trip to the Rocky Mountains. My wife is an architecture designer, so she wanted to see the building and I love the idea of a nature library. The countryside in the US is beautiful. But I’m from Cuba and when you go into nature there, there is a feeling that it is wild and untouched. There are so many trees and so much wildlife. Here, by comparison, it is quite built up. My son and I are interested in books about bugs at the moment and enjoyed reading about insects at the library, what they do, how they live and why they are important. We get a lot of insects in Nebraska and my son doesn’t always realise they aren’t dangerous, especially if they are big and buzzing around. Like every kid, sometimes he gets scared. I think if he knew more, he would probably just say “oh look at this”. I grew up much closer to nature in Cuba than he is growing up. I’d like to encourage him to go out and do more. I wish there was a nature library near us in Nebraska. Ricarose Roque, 42, visited with her son Miles, seven I’m a professor at the University of Colorado in Boulder – I study kids, learning and technology. I do a lot of community engagement work with libraries and I decided to visit because I was curious about what it meant to have a nature library. I also grew up visiting libraries and want my son to do that. When we arrived, Miles gravitated towards the “try it” equipment and the natural disasters section – he has been interested in tornadoes, tsunamis, earthquakes and wildfires since he was about three. He grabbed a book on wildfires and decided to borrow a fire sensor. He thought it could sense fire, but actually it’s a tool that measures humidity, temperature and wind velocity and direction, so you can understand if there’s a risk of a wildfire nearby. But we decided that next time we will try to borrow night-vision binoculars and hike one of our favourite trails at twilight. We also borrowed a bird-watching book and a brochure about animals, insects and trees that can be seen here in Colorado. I was born in the Philippines, and emigrated to Los Angeles when I was young. I don’t know much about the wildlife of Colorado, although I’ve lived here for 10 years. Until we borrowed that book, I didn’t know what a Steller’s jay was. But because of that book, we were talking about it – and today I saw one. I can’t wait to tell Miles. We’re not a very outdoorsy family and as someone who grew up in a big city, I feel a bit intimidated by the idea of camping in the mountains. But Miles is always asking to go, and being able to borrow camping equipment from the library makes it easier for us to try it. I hope going to the library can help me and other transplants to Boulder to feel that the wild open spaces of Colorado are ours, too – that they are there for everyone and we all need to take care of them. Find more age of extinction coverage here, and follow the biodiversity reporters Rebecca Ratcliffe, Phoebe Weston and Patrick Greenfield in the Guardian app for more nature coverage.

title: IMF chief urges governments to tighten belts as global debt levels soar
summary: Kristalina Georgieva says big economies will have to make ‘very touch choices’ as soaring bond yields hit budgets
text: The head of the International Monetary Fund has called on governments across big economies to tighten their belts as soaring bond yields hit budgets. Speaking in Singapore, the IMF’s managing director, Kristalina Georgieva, said global debt-to-GDP ratios were at their highest level since the second world war and on course to hit 100% in the coming years. She said governments could not rely on rapid economic growth to lift the burden of debt – and instead would have to make “very tough political choices”. Georgieva was speaking before the IMF and World Bank annual meetings, which are to be held in Bangkok next week. “My message to the world’s economic policymakers will be this: we cannot keep delaying necessary policy action – you have the tools, now have the wisdom to use them. “And yet we don’t see decisive action in the high-debt advanced economies where the need of the hour is for credible medium-term fiscal consolidation plans, supported in some cases by upfront fiscal measures,” she said. Bond yields – effectively the interest rate on the debt – have jumped in recent weeks, raising the cost of borrowing for many governments to multi-decade highs as markets adjust to the prospect of higher inflation as a result of the war in the Middle East. “Elevated yields are inflating the interest bill at a time of tight budget constraints and competing spending priorities, including defence,” Georgieva said, calling for “an urgent and comprehensive set of policy responses”. The Bulgarian economist suggested central banks should be prepared to raise interest rates to see off resurgent inflation. The ECB, US Federal Reserve and Bank of Japan have already tightened policy in the face of rising inflation – moves Georgieva said were “highly appropriate” – but the Bank of England has so far left rates on hold at 3.75%. “Now may be a good time for a prudently hawkish bias in many countries’ monetary policy,” Georgieva said, suggesting central banks might want to err on the side of caution. She also stressed the importance of tackling some of the risks of AI, which has buoyed the US stock market but raised fears of mass layoffs. She highlighted IMF research predicting that the adoption of AI could add half a percentage point to global economic growth if carried out effectively. However, she urged policymakers to “help manage AI’s substantial perils, including large-scale labour market fallout, serious cyber and stability risks and frontier models threatening to escape human control and run amok”. The Bank of England governor, Andrew Bailey, who is also chair of the Financial Stability Forum that brings together the world’s central banks, recently warned of the “real and significant” risks posed by frontier AI models and called for the “right to intervene”. In the UK the chancellor, John Healey, has said he will stick with his predecessor Rachel Reeves’s plans to balance day-to-day spending with tax revenues – borrowing only to invest – and bring the debt-to-GDP ratio down over time.
