title: Yemen civil war: what sparked latest escalation and who is involved?
summary: Conflict between UN-recognised government and Iran-backed Houthis has impacts far beyond country’s borders
text: Yemen has been plunged into a civil war that has extended to one of the world’s most vital maritime choke points and to Saudi Arabian oil sites. What was the spark? The semi-dormant conflict over Yemen’s future reawakened in the summer, when Saudi Arabia bombed the runway of the airport in the Houthi-controlled capital, Sana’a, in an attempt to prevent an Iranian plane carrying Yemenis who had attended the funeral of Iran’s supreme leader from landing. Saudi Arabia said a charter plane could land, but not an Iranian-owned one. The plane eventually flew to the port of Hodeidah on the Red Sea coast. The Houthis described the bombing as part of a Saudi siege of Houthi-controlled Yemen, and vowed “a siege for a siege”. The Houthis announced a naval blockade of Saudi Arabia and sent missiles towards the country’s oil facilities. The Saudi-Houthi ceasefire in place since 2022 was over. After months of failing to help their ally Iran in its war with the US, the Houthis had opened a new front. What did the Houthis do next? The Houthis have sporadically used their strategic position on the coast of the Red Sea to disrupt commercial traffic, mainly linked to Israel. But its leadership decided in mid-September to escalate and to try to tighten its grip on the waterways by pushing south down the coast to the narrowest part of the waterway, the Bab al-Mandab strait. It succeeded within days. By 16 September, they had captured the coastal town of Mocha and small islands in the strait, as well as an airport. The battle then moved into the al-Waz’yah district and the high mountain chains overlooking the strait and towards Taiz governorate, including Taiz itself, Yemen’s third city and the home town of the president of the UN-recognised government, Rashad al-Alimi. Why did the Houthi advance succeed? Some have blamed betrayal by Tareq Saleh, the nephew of Yemen’s former president and leader of the National Resistance Forces in the region, but others say the forces of the UN-recognised government are divided, suffer from poor command and control networks, and lack the military intelligence the Houthis possess. The Houthis also had Iranian support; by saying they would block Saudi oil from the port of Yanbu, they were aligning themselves with the Iranian war effort. But the Houthis are not pure proxies of Tehran. Their hostility to the Saudi presence in Yemen is self-standing and has religious as well as political roots. How did the Saudis respond to the shock of the Houthi advance? It took three weeks, but over the weekend Alimi announced a broad counteroffensive called Operation Yemen Dawn, designed to end the “Houthi coup”. It saw 100 Saudi jets fly in support of Yemen ground forces driving towards Bab al-Mandab. Fighting is happening across at least three fronts, including in the mountains west of Taiz, in Marib and in Sana’a. The Houthis have sent missiles towards at least five Saudi cities. The scale of the Houthi reverse has probably been exaggerated. What is the relationship between the legitimate UN-recognised government and Riyadh? The two countries share a 1,200km-long contested border, secured only after the 1934 Saudi-Yemen war. Since the British departure in 1967, Yemen has come to rely heavily on Saudi Arabia to remain an economically viable state. There are officially 2 million Yemenis working as migrants in Saudi Arabia. Many send money home and are just now being given legal status. Riyadh regularly provides grants to the Yemeni government to prevent its collapse (up to $12.6bn in the last 14 years). This heavily shapes its choice of leaders. Indeed so much of Yemen’s leadership resides in Riyadh’s hotels, instead of Aden, that critics call the administration the hotel legitimacy. Are the anti-Houthi forces inside Yemen aligned? No. Yemen is a maze of tribes, governorates and religious beliefs, which is reflected in its politics and militia armies. A dispute over which force can take credit for leading the counteroffensive also reflects political rivalries, but the southern forces are prominent, even though they are fighting to dislodge the Houthis from land that would not form part of a separate southern state. The separatist political wing, the Southern Transitional Council, will test its latent support with a popular mobilisation on 23 October and this may determine whether its leader, Aidarous al-Zubeidi, can risk returning from exile. He has been charged by the legitimate government with high treason for trying to set up a secessionist state in January. Fearing arrest by the Saudis, he fled to the UAE. His aides fear his one-time military ally Abu Zara has aligned himself with Riyadh. What is the role of the United Arab Emirates? The UAE joined the 2015 Gulf coalition to dislodge the Houthis from Sana’a but, as Saudi methods became ever more unpopular, the UAE distanced itself. It had its own anti-Muslim Brotherhood agenda and regarded the Islah party – strong in the Yemeni government – as an offshoot of the Brotherhood. It slowly aligned itself with the southern separatists, largely as a way of gaining leverage inside Yemen, just as Saudi Arabia ironically did during the 1994 Yemen civil war. They trained the STC and National Resistance Forces. The UAE left Yemen in January 2026. It remains wary of Saudi intentions. Why is the US so reluctant to intervene? It has its hands full and its munitions stocks are empty due to the war in Iran. Ahead of the midterms, Donald Trump does not want to launch another forever war. After bombing the Houthis for 50 days in spring 2025, he struck a bilateral ceasefire with the Houthis – a deal that excluded Israel. He has twice rejected Saudi pleas that the fate of the strait is a matter for the world. Is anyone else involved? Yes. European countries, including the UK, are providing some air refuelling for Saudi jets. More importantly, rumours swirl around the new Mecca joint defence agreement, signed on 7 August 2026, by Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan. Its purpose is clear: filling the Gulf security vacuum exposed by the US-Israeli war on Iran, but its relevance to Yemen is sketchy. There are reports Pakistan is sending weaponry to Aden. Who will win? Many doubt Saudi Arabia has the staying power to reach Sana’a. Saudi energy infrastructure is vulnerable. The attack on the Saudi east-west pipeline on 11 September from Iraqi territory showed how a broader regional confrontation could open multiple fronts for Riyadh. Over nearly two decades the Houthis have shown themselves to be the masters of ground combat. But Yemen is now part of an international conflict and so many assumptions are up for review.

title: EU negotiators head to China hoping to curb cheap imports of hybrid electric cars
summary: Mood in trade talks said to have changed as EU member states harden demands for protection against Chinese imports
text: EU trade negotiators are heading to China for two days of crunch talks aimed at sealing a breakthrough deal tackling Beijing’s record £1bn-a-day trade surplus by curbing its exports of cheap hybrid electric cars into Europe. Trade commissioner Maroš Šefčovič and his team fly out on Wednesday and will be negotiating up to the wire in talks scheduled to start the following day and continue late into Friday. Sources say they hope to achieve “tangible, meaningful and measurable” results before the meeting of EU leaders in Brussels on Thursday next week, where China is high on the agenda. The main focus is on what has been described as a “proof of concept” pilot agreement involving one sector, which is expected to be cars, which could be scaled up for other sectors in the coming months. Diplomatic efforts to avert a full-scale trade war started at the end of June, albeit with little hope that China could curb exports to the EU given its historic ability to pivot quickly any time trade barriers are put in its path. For example, after the EU imposed tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles in October 2024 there was a boom in exports of hybrid cars, which were not subject to tariffs. Last month, the EU asked China to voluntarily restrict hybrid exports to address soaring sales, warning that if they did not restrict them, safeguards – which could include quotas – could be enacted. It is not known what China’s response was. But sources say the mood in talks has changed as EU member states have hardened demands for protection against Chinese imports that threaten their own industries. On Monday, Germany’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz, agreed a “historic U-turn” on its policy on China by siding with the French president, Emmanuel Macron, in authorising effective permission for EU leaders to approve a new instrument to allow them to defend trade by cutting access to the single market at short notice. In a joint paper with Emmanuel Macron, the two countries spoke of “a massive industrial shock … affecting sectors at the heart of the European industrial model and of systemic relevance [pharmaceuticals, aerospace, automotive, machine tools, chemicals, etc.]”. The paper called for the use of all existing trade defence tools, but also for a new diversification instrument and “possible additional” new measures to allow the bloc to react when “third countries seek to undermine the restoration of a level playing field”. Andrew Small, a former EU adviser on China, said Šefčovič’s talks will test the resolve of both Beijing and Brussels and will “determine whether China is willing to put sufficiently serious offers on the table”. Small, who is the Asia director at the European Council on Foreign Relations in Berlin, warned: “China’s most effective tactic may be to draw Europe into a ‘process trap’ offering just enough to delay action, without addressing the forces driving European deindustrialisation.” Sources say the Franco-German proposals for a new instrument, dubbed a “kill switch”, were born out of frustration, particularly in Paris, that a so-called “trade bazooka” available to Brussels, officially known as the anti-coercion instrument, has never been used. Paris pushed for the use of the ACI following Trump’s threat of tariffs last year but it never gained traction from others as it could take up to a year to implement. Handlesblatt, the Germany business newspaper, described Monday’s change in policy as “nothing less than an economic turning point”, with chief political reporter Martin Greive concluding in a hard-hitting column that Merz was “putting an end to years of naiveté towards Beijing”. “Merz has recognised in recent months that Germany is the epicentre of the China shock 2.0; that there might not be much left of German industry if Germany continues to stand by and watch as China gains enormous export advantages through trillions in subsidies, the unilateral siphoning off of knowhow, and a – to put it mildly – questionable monetary policy,” he wrote.

title: Poland’s ‘solidarity’ push for EU energy resilience in face of Russian aggression
summary: In the second article in a series on the Polish economy, we look at how the country is forging closer ties with its neighbours
text: Two miles off the coast of Gdańsk, the white steel piles of Poland’s first offshore gas terminal rise from the slate-grey Baltic. Installed at a height eight metres above the waves, the floating cranes and construction vessels here are on the frontline of Europe’s push for energy security. Since the taps were turned off on Russian gas after Vladimir Putin’s invasion of Ukraine four years ago, Poland has turned to the global energy market for supplies. But while conditions are far from ideal as the Middle East war drives oil and gas prices to stratospheric levels, strengthening the diversity of the country’s energy mix remains a top priority for Poland, its Baltic neighbours, and the EU at large. Looking out to sea from the windswept beach backed by pine forest, Maciej Wawrzkowicz, the offshore project manager at the national gas company Gaz-System, and the construction manager Krzysztof Polatynski say the Baltic is not an easy place to build. Before work could start, Polish navy minesweepers were called in to torpedo unexploded mines and bombs from the second world war. Construction is halted by storms, while the sea froze over last winter. But speed is important in this project of international significance. “Every quay that’s available right now in the area that has some prefabrication workshop space, a contractor is occupying them. And you are seeking for more. Gdańsk harbour is a significant construction place right now.” Poland used to import more than half of its gas from Russia but refused to pay in rubles in 2022 as the Kremlin became a pariah in the west over Putin’s war on Ukraine. A Norwegian pipeline under the Baltic and liquefied natural gas (LNG) terminal at Świnoujście, close to the border with Germany, helped to keep most homes warm and the fires of industry burning. At Gdańsk the construction of the floating storage and regasification unit (FSRU) – a specialised marine vessel used to store and convert LNG – is planned to further bolster Poland’s booming economy. But it will also increase the country’s capacity beyond domestic needs – turning it into a hub for eastern Europe and its Baltic neighbours. Poland has LNG regasification capacity of 8.3bn cubic metres a year. Once the FRSU is operational in early 2028, that will add 6.1bn cubic metres a year of additional capacity. A second vessel at the Gdańsk FRSU is also planned for 2030 to lift total capacity to more than 20bn cubic metres a year. In an age of geopolitical challenges, the FSRU vessel also has a symbolic name: “Solidarity”, in a nod to its home port’s history, and Poland’s drive to strengthen EU ties in the face of Russian aggression. In the 1980s, as the Soviet Union crumbled, strikes at Lenin shipyard in Gdańsk over communist rule launched Poland’s Solidarność (Solidarity) movement. Led by Lech Wałęsa, it paved the way for independence and the transition to a free-market economy. Living standards have shot up since, from 40% of the EU average in the mid-1990s to 81% last year. Agnieszka Ozga, the director of the energy transition division, and her deputy, Paweł Sęk, say Poland has been working to diversify energy supplies for decades, with the 2014 annexation of Crimea by Russia accelerating the process. But 2022 was a “gamechanger,” says Sęk. “After the war started, we knew what was going on and we knew many countries in our region would end up with no gas flows coming from Russia”. Since then the Gdańsk FSRU has grown in importance, says Ozga. “Not only for Poland. But also Slovakia; central and eastern Europe countries; the Baltic states. It is also very, very important for the European Commission: to end the isolation of the Baltic states, because they were fully dependent on inflows of gas from Russia.” However, there is also plenty of evidence in Gdańsk highlighting the energy challenges Poland must still confront. On the edges of the old town’s narrow cobbled streets, the red and white-banded chimney stacks of a Soviet-era coal-fired power plant belch out thick plumes of smoke. Tourist boats ferrying visitors to the Westerplatte peninsula – where the first shots of the second world war were fired – must also pass through the jet-black mountains of a coal dock. Coal accounts for more than half of electricity generation in Poland, significantly above the EU average. The legacy of Soviet fossil-fuel infrastructure and centuries of domestic production in this resource-rich country mean it remains key for the economy. More than 80,000 people still work in coalmines, mainly in the south around the industrial city of Katowice – once called Stalinogród – as one of the few remaining coalmining regions still digging among EU countries fully committed to decarbonisation. However, cutting out coal in favour of LNG, renewables and nuclear power is seen as critical for Poland’s future sovereignty and prosperity. Relying on heavily polluting and costly fossil fuels, the country’s average wholesale electricity prices are the ninth highest in the EU – holding back growth in a country accustomed to powering ahead. As wages and living standards catch up to western European levels, Polish manufacturing is beginning to lose its competitive edge from cheap labour – a factor that had long attracted multinationals such as Volkswagen and Toyota to locate factories in the country. As a result, keeping down other production costs – such as energy – is growing in importance. Rafał Brzoska, the billionaire founder of InPost, the pan-European parcel locker company started in Krakow, is among Poland’s concerned entrepreneurs. “The competitive cost of energy is not our big advantage. So we need to somehow change and reshape and focus on those elements of our economy that we can compete against, let’s say, France, that has the cheapest cost of energy. We cannot compete on the most cost-driven industries.” Warsaw has pushed in recent years to decarbonise with a strategy up to 2040. However, critics warn that it still puts the country on a path to being the last EU economy to be producing the most of its power from fossil fuels by 2030, endangering economic security and prosperity. It will also require vast levels of public investment, at a time when the national debt is piling up and borrowing costs are rising. There are also political challenges in the run-up to a general election next year, with rightwing opponents of Donald Tusk’s liberal government pushing to rally Eurosceptic voters by weaponising the green transition. The government is also investing in nuclear, building a plant on the Baltic coast. However, critics highlight an eye-watering price tag of more than €42bn (£35.6bn), for a facility that will not come online until the late 2030s. Poland’s deputy foreign minister Marcin Bosacki says EU membership is, however, aiding a transition that will strengthen the economy. “We inherited from communist times the worst electricity or power mix of all EU members. It is changing – maybe not fast enough – but it is changing quite fast.” Poland has secured €54.7bn in funding through the EU’s post-Covid recovery and resilience facility, with 40% going primarily to energy-related objectives. It is also the largest beneficiary of a Brussels fund intended to support the introduction of the EU’s emissions trading system carbon-pricing scheme. “Poles are the world champions in getting EU funds,” Bosacki says. Since joining the bloc in 2004 he estimates more than €300bn has flowed to Warsaw, supporting road building, railways and other critical infrastructure to power its economic boom. “We calculate the growth of Polish GDP would be half of what actually happened in the last 20 years if Poland was not a member of the EU. Almost a half.” After annual output surpassed $1tn (£756bn) last year – ranking Poland as the sixth largest economy in the EU, ahead of countries including Belgium, Sweden and Austria – the flow of catchup funds from Brussels is, however, likely to dwindle. Mateusz Urban, a Warsaw-based economist at Oxford Economics, says changing the energy system by 2040 will be tough. But ditching its status as a laggard in the green transition is vital – for the climate, for energy independence, and economic security. In the past, Poland has come under pressure from the Kremlin using its gas supplies for political ends, including attempts in 2010 to extract punishing terms from Warsaw that would have stitched up the Polish gas market in Russia’s favour. “If you have one big supplier through a pipeline you have no power,” Urban says. With the closure of the strait of Hormuz and as Donald Trump rattles the global energy market by threatening to limit diesel exports, risks remain. Large volumes of the LNG imported by sea to Poland are from the US and Qatar. But Polish energy officials are sanguine, suggesting that other markets could still be utilised, and argue widening horizons beyond Russian imports remains critical. Urban agrees that diversifying energy supplies, while renewable power generation takes time to develop, could help strengthen Poland’s hand. “We need it for geopolitical security. Moving away from Russian gas, and coal, is a huge step forward. If you have a diverse supply, then you’re more insulated from trouble in each region.”

title: Japan PM leads outcry after US Marine arrested over alleged killing of woman on Okinawa
summary: Crimes involving US troops on Okinawa have been a constant source of tension between Tokyo and Washington
text: Japan’s prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, has led public outcry over crimes committed by US servicemen after a marine suspected of killing a woman on Okinawa was arrested on Saturday. In a speech in parliament, Takaichi described the alleged crime as “heinous” and urged US military authorities to enforce discipline among American servicemen stationed on Okinawa, an island 1,000 miles south of Tokyo. Police said Devin Ballard, a 20-year-old lance corporal, had been arrested on suspicion of strangling Anna Yagi, 39, at a hotel in Okinawan capital Naha early on Saturday. He is also suspected of stealing her wallet and backpack. Ballard denied the allegations, police said. If convicted, Ballard could face life in prison or the death penalty. The US military has paused all operations on the Japanese island for two days, following Ballard’s arrest. Lt. Gen. Benjamin Watson, commander of III Marine Expeditionary Force, said in a letter posted on social media that incidents allegedly involving service members “demand we pause for reflection”. During the two-day operational pause, which was due to begin at noon on Wednesday, military personnel will receive training on standards and discipline, and “our responsibilities as members of the Okinawan community”, Watson said. Off-base liberties will be cancelled during the period, including a blanket ban on alcohol. The US military will also impose a monthlong curfew from midnight to 5am starting Friday, the Kyodo news agency reported. The alleged crime has sparked an outcry on Okinawa, which hosts tens of thousands of American troops and dozens of bases. Crimes and accidents involving US troops on Okinawa have been a constant source of tension between Tokyo and Washington and the target of protests among local people. The island hosts most of the 50,000 US troops in Japan and 70% of the country’s military facilities there. Ballard’s arrest triggered anger in Okinawa days after voters elected Genta Koja, a pro-US base governor backed by Takaichi’s Liberal Democratic party, ending the eight-year-tenure of Denny Tamaki, a critic of the US military presence on the island. Koja’s election had raised hopes that the US and Japan might finally make progress on the planned transfer of a marine corps base from a densely populated city to a remote off-shore location. The relocation of Futenma air station, where Ballard is stationed, has been held up for decades amid opposition from people living near the alternative site and local politicians who want US military facilities moved off the island altogether. Koja said the arrest had dealt a “major shock” to the island and “raises fears among Okinawans who have already been forced to live next to US bases”. He added: “It is absolutely unforgivable, and we are outraged.” He said the case proved that US attempts to improve discipline among its troops had failed. “I’m enraged by the loss of a precious life of an Okinawan resident,” he told Lt Gen Benjamin Watson, commander of III Marine Expeditionary Force, and the US consul general in Naha, Andrew Ou, after Ballard’s arrest. Watson said he recognised that the incident had caused “significant concern and anxiety among the residents of Okinawa, our neighbours”. He added: “We are committed to being good neighbours … and earning the trust of the Okinawan people.” Anti-US sentiment on Okinawa intensified after the 1995 rape of a 12-year-old girl by three American servicemen. A year later, Tokyo and Washington agreed to reduce the US military footprint by closing Futenma and relocating its functions to the quiet fishing village of Henoko on the north-east coast. Anger erupted again over the rape of a teenage girl by a US service member in 2024 and the delayed disclosure of the crime. Crimes involving US troops on Okinawa have risen in recent years, from about 40 in 2020 to 101 last year, according to the prefectural police. Okinawa plays a central role in regional tensions. Japan’s government insists US bases on the island act as a deterrent amid Chinese claims over disputed parts of the East and South China Seas and the emergence of a nuclear-armed North Korea. Under the Japan-US status of forces agreement, Ballard, who was arrested in a civilian district while he was off duty, will remain in the custody of the Japanese authorities. Security footage showed him entering the hotel with Yagi and later leaving alone. Yagi’s family said they were “devastated” by her death. Her brother said in a statement: “Our parents are especially exhausted with grief after losing their daughter.”

title: Friends of Nolan Wells sue NFL Hall of Famer Terrell Owens for defamation
summary: Owens sued over September Instagram post that suggested trio tampered with evidence in death of Mississippi teen
text: Three friends of Nolan Wells, a Mississippi teen who died after a July boating trip, have sued NFL Hall of Famer Terrell Owens for defamation. On 26 September, Owens shared an Instagram video that suggested Wells’s friends Warren Hudson, Jax Pitalo and Morgan Seymour had deleted evidence from Wells’s phone after his death, which the three men denied in their lawsuit. “Arrest them immediately!! Like yesterday,” Owens captioned the post. In a Monday complaint filed in a Mississippi district court, the fathers of the three young men, who are also named in the complaint as plaintiffs because they are deemed minors under state law, accuse Owens of harming their reputation and endangering their physical safety with the post. “Due to the conduct of Owens and many other less-famous individuals, these completely innocent young men have been subjected to thousands of death threats, face-to-face harassment, and daily fear and ridicule from complete strangers. They’ve even been refused service at public establishments. Their lives, and the lives of their family members, will never be the same,” the complaint alleges. Owens could not be immediately reached for comment. The friends’ counsel also indicated they intend to take legal action against other public figures who have been vocal about Wells’s death including Al Sharpton and The View’s Sunny Hostin. On 4 July, Wells and his friends sailed for a Mississippi island. He was last seen that afternoon. Two days later, his body was found on the island. The circumstances of his death have fueled public suspicion. Wells, who was African American, had been partying with a mostly white friend group – a detail that gained traction online as some referenced Mississippi’s past with racial violence. In late September, a Mississippi grand jury declined to file criminal charges, finding Wells’s death to appear “consistent with drowning”. Jackson county district attorney Angel Myers McIlrath has said Wells’s death was not racially motivated. Wells’s parents and civil rights lawyer Ben Crump continue to call for further investigations, citing the state’s autopsy report, which said Wells’s airways and stomach were empty. His family has said the lack of water found undermines the drowning determination. “I cannot take that ruling, and I cannot move on with my life,” Christine Wonsley, Wells’s mother, reportedly said, referring to the grand jury’s findings at a Monday press conference. “We have been left with more questions and heartbreak than any answers.”

title: Privacy watchdog launches investigation into China-based company behind Kmart ‘pervert glasses’ app
summary: Commissioner says Shenzhen Qingcheng, the app maker behind the HeyCyan app in the smartglasses, failed to respond to her inquiries
text: The Australian privacy regulator has opened an investigation into the China-based software company behind the HeyCyan app in Kmart’s $89 smartglasses, following public outrage over the covert use of the devices. In August, Guardian Australia reported Kmart had sold out of the Anko-branded discount version of Meta’s smartglasses that can capture images and record high-definition video, which led to widespread concern and calls to ban or restrict their use. The glasses were removed from Kmart’s website as of Wednesday. The retailer has been approached for comment. A GetUp petition has had more than 55,000 signatures calling to restrict the use of what has been labelled as “pervert glasses”, and councils around the country have looked to ban the glasses in public spaces such as swimming pools. The federal government is also considering a restriction on use in government workplaces. The Australian privacy commissioner, Carly Kind, was asked by the attorney general to assess the privacy implications of the glasses at the time. Kind wrote to Kmart and BDI Technology, retailers for the glasses, as well as Shenzhen Qingcheng, the app maker behind the HeyCyan app in the glasses. She also wrote to Meta – for its Ray-Bans glasses – and Google which is planning its own smartglasses. In a blog post on Wednesday, Kind announced an investigation has been opened into Shenzhen Qingcheng after it failed to respond to inquiries, “as well as concerns arising from third party analysis of the technology itself as well as the entity’s privacy policy” None of the other companies will be investigated as part of this process, Kind said. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email The privacy commissioner also highlighted the difficulty in applying privacy law to individuals who may use the devices given the privacy act only applies to companies and Commonwealth agencies – not individuals. “Retailers that sell smart glasses – for example on an e-commerce website – or companies that manufacture them, may not have any Privacy Act obligations if they do not collect any personal information with respect to those devices,” Kind said. “Instead, the entity providing the software at use in the device is likely to be the entity that collects and holds the information for the purpose of privacy law.” Kind said that potential changes to the privacy act proposed by the government would strengthen how privacy law would apply to surveillance wearables such as smartglasses. “The most substantial change will be the replacement of the ‘reasonably necessary for an entity’s functions and activities’ test with a ‘fair and reasonable’ test,” she said. “The new test will require an entity to look at a range of factors, including the extent to which an individual had genuine choice in the collection of their personal information, as well as the best interests of the child where children are involved.” Kind said she hoped the community would “find comfort” in the proposed reforms as it would raise the bar over what personal information smartglasses can collect. “These reforms are likely to become increasingly necessary as we face subsequent generations of surveillance wearables and connected devices, from personal assistant gadgets to ambient recording badges.” Researchers at the University of Sydney in August analysed 350 publicly-available Instagram videos shot on smartglasses from around the world during 2023 to 2026, showing what they said was “a shift to discreet, point-of-view recording that is difficult for bystanders to detect”. In a subset of these videos, about 60% of interactions could be classified as potential harassment, with subjects visibly uneasy or attempting to disengage. Canterbury-Bankstown and Sydney City are among the councils in Sydney to have banned the glasses from some venues, as well as Brisbane in Queensland, and Yarra city council in Melbourne. Shenzhen Qingcheng was approached for comment.

title: ‘Not exactly his favorite senator’: Susan Collins distances herself from Trump in Maine debate
summary: Republican challenged by Democrat Troy Jackson in critical Senate race says she opposes Iran war and Canada tariffs
text: Susan Collins, the Republican senator for Maine, pointedly distanced herself from Donald Trump in a televised debate with Democratic challenger Troy Jackson on Tuesday, as she sought to present an image of independence in a state that has voted against Trump three times. Proclaiming herself as not the US president’s “favorite senator”, Collins made the highly unusual boast for a Republican that she had voted with Joe Biden, a Democrat, more than 90% of the time when he was president. She also emphasized her differences with her fellow Republicans, saying she voted against her own party more than any other senator. Collins’s defensiveness came amid a determined onslaught from Jackson, 58, a veteran former state legislator who was getting his first chance to present himself to a broad audience since replacing Graham Platner as the Democratic candidate in a contest that could be vital to the party’s hopes of winning the Senate. Platner, a former harbor master, was forced to withdraw from the race in July after facing sexual assault allegations, which he denied, leaving Democrats racing against the clock to replace a candidate who had built up momentum campaigning on a populist progressive platform. Jackson painted Collins as a Trump loyalist, saying she voted with the president 96% of the time. He also doggedly focused on her 2018 vote for the conservative supreme court justice Brett Kavanaugh, tying it to the court’s subsequent overturning of Roe v Wade, which had for half a century guaranteed the national right to abortion. “Tonight is about who you stand with when it matters,” Jackson said in a pithy opening statement. “Eight years ago today, Maine women went to DC and begged Senator Collins not to confirm Brett Kavanaugh, but she did it anyways. “He helped overturn Roe v Wade, and today she says she has no regrets. Would you trust her to pick the next supreme court justice?” Collins, 73, who has been a senator since 1996, has frequently presented herself as a moderate who stands against more radical trends in her own party. The posture is in line with Maine’s profile as a more Democratic-leaning state, which Trump has not won in any of his three presidential campaigns and which has voted for Democratic presidential candidates in every election since 1992. Nevertheless, Collins went to unusual lengths to differentiate herself from Trump on a range of issues, including the war with Iran, which she said she voted to end nine times, calling it “not well thought out”. Collins reacted with something close to alarm when the moderator, Gregg Lagerquist, said Trump had suggested that the president might pay a campaign visit to Maine. “I don’t think that President Trump is going to come to Maine,” she said. “He’s talking about going to a lot of different states. I’ve heard nothing from his office, and I’m not exactly his favorite senator.” Collins stressed her differences with the president on specific issues pertinent to the Maine economy, including rural healthcare and tariffs against Canada, with which the state shares a border. “I have been the most outspoken opponent of the tariffs on Canada,” she said. “Canada is not China. It’s our neighbor and our friends.” Polls show the two candidates running neck and neck.

title: Ukraine war briefing: Zelenskyy blames Russia for attack on Bulgarian vessels in Black Sea as investigation launched
summary: Bulgarian authorities investigating origin of drone attack on two vessels in Nato member’s exclusive economic zone. What we know on day 1,687
text: Bulgaria’s prime minister said that two commercial vessels were struck by drones on Tuesday in the first attack on shipping in the Nato member’s exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea. Bulgarian authorities said the origin of the drones was under investigation, but Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, blamed Russia for the drone strikes. “This is an unacceptable attack in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone. It is a blatant violation of international law and maritime law,” Rumen Radev said. Explosions rang out in Kyiv on Wednesday, news agencies reported, after the military warned a ballistic missile was heading toward the Ukrainian capital. Zelenskyy warned in his nightly address on Tuesday that Russia was planning a “massive strike”. “Ukrainian services and our air force ‌are ready ‌to respond to the extent permitted by ‌our available means of defence,” he said. Ukraine struck an oil tanker off the southern Russian coast on Tuesday evening, Russia’s transport ministry said. The ministry said the Liberian-flagged tanker had been attacked by “naval drones” and that “crude oil was burning openly in the waters of the Black Sea”, triggering a huge fire and black smoke cloud that blanketed parts of the resort city of Sochi. Russian air defenses intercepted nearly 900 Ukrainian drones overnight on Monday into Tuesday over multiple regions of the country, as well as the occupied Crimean Peninsula and the Sea of Azov, Russia’s defence ministry said Tuesday. Unconfirmed media reports said a major fuel depot in the Moscow region was on fire after the attack that killed two people. A Ukrainian drone attack on a minibus in the Russian-occupied part of the Ukrainian Zaporizhzhia region killed three people on Tuesday, Moscow-installed authorities said. Kremlin-appointed official Yevgeny Balitsky said on Telegram that a Ukrainian drone hit the bus near a frontline village, killing “three people, including the driver” and wounding “three passengers with various degrees of severity”. The ⁠Kremlin dismissed on Tuesday comments ⁠by ⁠Germany’s head of foreign intelligence about Berlin ⁠being at risk of ⁠entering a violent conflict ‌with ‌Russia, describing them as ‌baseless and a ploy to justify defence spending. On Monday, intelligence ‌chief Martin Jaeger said the risk of a direct conflict was rising ⁠and accused Russia of stepping up an increasingly aggressive “shadow war” ‌against European democracies. EU envoys are ⁠expected to approve about 1,650 new designations on Wednesday under ⁠the bloc’s sanctions ⁠regime for Russia, with the majority focused on the country’s military ⁠industrial complex, EU diplomats said on Tuesday. The package, proposed by the EU’s ⁠foreign policy arm, will be the single largest ‌set of ‌designations since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine ‌in 2022. Ukraine on Tuesday said oil supplies to Russia through South Korea helped Moscow offset losses in refining capacity caused by recent strikes on its fuel facilities. The Guardian reported that 176,000 tonnes of oil products were shipped through South Korea in July and August, citing port records and ship-tracking data. Zelenskyy’s adviser on sanctions, Vladyslav Vlasiuk, said the shipments were “in sharp contrast” to South Korea’s sanctions policy. Ukraine’s national grid operator has ordered rolling blackouts in the capital Kyiv, the country’s largest private energy provider said Tuesday, after Russian attacks on energy infrastructure. The power outages were to begin at 3pm local time (1200 GMT) and last until the end of the day, the provider said in a statement. • This article was amended on 7 October 2026. An earlier version described Volodymyr Zelenskyy as Ukraine’s prime minister, rather than president.

title: Jaguar targets young Americans with Type 01 EV – but it’s too long for UK parking spaces
summary: Latest model is launching in New York to target rich US buyers – and is more than 5.2 metres long and 2 metres wide
text: It has no rear window, will not fit into a UK parking space and – starting at £130,000 – ($172,000) is aimed squarely at rich tech industry buyers driving the wide open roads of America. Jaguar’s electric car, the Type 01, was launched in New York on Tuesday night and marks the culmination of a two-year rebrand that has been one of the most scrutinised in automotive history. Bosses hope the vehicle will appeal to a younger, richer audience than the manufacturer’s previous “shrinking and ageing” customer base of “men in their 50s”, said Rawdon Glover, 58, Jaguar’s managing director. With an ultra-long bonnet, low roof and muscular design, the Type 01 is a sharp departure from its predecessor, the F-Type. It is also double the F-Type’s starting price of about £62,000. Buyers are likely to be rich, “urban” and “very design literate, very technology literate”, Glover said. “The person making this purchase will be choosing the car because it’s a bold choice.” A senior JLR executive close to the Type 01 project put it more bluntly: “It’s the type of car that you park up and everybody stops and says: ‘Fucking hell, what have you just turned up in?’” The launch comes at a critical juncture for parent company Jaguar Land Rover (JLR), which has grappled with falling sales as cheaper Chinese rivals eat into its UK market share. It is still recovering from a massive cyber-attack last year that cost the economy an estimated £1.9bn. JLR recently announced 4,000 job cuts in an attempt to save £1.7bn over two years, citing “intense competition and ongoing geopolitical uncertainty”. The Guardian understands Jaguar employees working on the Type 01 programme were offered voluntary redundancy along with the rest of JLR’s non-manufacturing workforce. The car will go on sale in early 2027, with the first deliveries anticipated in the second half of the year. “It’s really important that we put Jaguar back on a more solid financial footing,” Glover said. Asked if doubling prices would be effective, he said it was better than “to toil away as we have done for the last two decades in the volume premium space”. Range Rover also unveiled its first fully electric model in September with a starting price of £154,070 compared with £107,530 for its combustion engine predecessor. Waning demand in China, a key market for luxury cars, has also hit Jaguar hard. Glover revealed that the Type 01 will not launch in the country for “a couple of years. We’ve decided just to hold off on that.” However, he added that China would eventually be “an important part of the equation … it’s very difficult for any car manufacturer to exclude the single largest car market in the world”. PB Balaji, the JLR chief executive, has said the parent company will pivot towards North America and target more sales to millionaires and billionaires to turn its fortunes around. Glover admitted that while the Type 01’s launch was in New York, it “absolutely” could have been in Silicon Valley instead, reflecting the type of buyer Jaguar is targeting. He recently took a prototype to the offices of Nvidia, the California-based AI company, whose boss, Jensen Huang, had a ride and “loved it”. The car has no rear window, instead using a rear-facing camera feeding a screen where a traditional mirror would be. The car produces more than 1,000 horsepower and Jaguar says it will travel up to 400 miles on a single charge. It follows a controversial rebrand that started with an ad in late 2024 featuring stern-faced models without a car in sight. The ad prompted a backlash online and was followed by the Type 00 concept car that was unveiled in “Miami pink”, which Donald Trump described it as “woke” while Nigel Farage said Jaguar deserved to go bust. Glover admitted the backlash “wasn’t always easy” but added: “The reality is we will need to attract a new audience.” It is just as well: at 2 metres (6ft 7in) wide the Type 01 will hog the British country lanes frequented by Jaguar’s old customer base, while at more than 5.2 metres in length it will not fit in a standard 4.8 metre UK parking space. “There are long cars out there on the market,” Glover argued, adding that a Land Rover Defender with a wheel on the back is longer than the Type 01, which he claimed had the “turning circle of a Fiat 500” with its all-wheel steering. “It is incredibly manoeuvrable.” The business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, said: “Jaguar’s new EV is a crucial step in JLR’s plans to invest over £15bn in the UK, and another big vote of confidence in our world-class automotive industry. “This cutting-edge new model being designed, engineered and built in Britain will support thousands of jobs across the West Midlands and North West, and builds on over £1bn of UK automotive investment secured just last month – marking another step forward in our mission to reindustrialise Britain.” • This article was amended on 13 October 2026. 2 metres converts to 6ft 7in, not 6ft 5in as an earlier version said.

title: LA and San Diego residents ‘horrified’ by Trump suggesting Iran bomb them
summary: As Angelenos bemoan ‘sad situation’, those in San Diego say remark a ‘disservice’ to town with multiple naval bases
text: Donald Trump’s extraordinary implication that Iran could “take out” Los Angeles and San Diego have sparked condemnation across the political spectrum. As residents of the two major west coast cities awoke on Tuesday to another sweltering day in a record-breaking heatwave, the president’s comments sent blood boiling even higher. Jessica, a 28-year-old Los Angeles hair stylist, was scrolling through social media early on Tuesday morning and was shocked to see that Trump had just suggested Iran should decimate her home town. For Jessica, who declined to be identified by her full name because she fears for the safety of her Mexican-born parents, the comments marked a new low for a president who had already spent years attacking immigrant families like hers. “I was just thinking what the fuck is wrong with him?” she said while waiting for a Waymo outside grocery store in LA’s Koreatown neighborhood. “He hates us. He hates LA. He hates any Democratic state ... It’s just a really sad situation.” In southern California, Trump’s unprecedented musing before a cheering crowd at a Nebraska rally on Monday night – that perhaps a foreign power should decimate two of the country’s best-known cities – has been met with reactions ranging from deep hostility to dismissive incredulity. Gavin Newsom, the state’s governor, called the remarks “dangerous – if not treasonous – putting a target on two of our biggest cities and one of America’s largest naval hubs”. Perhaps most of all, California residents see it as a sign of the president’s fixation on tearing down west coast progressivism and diversity, most visibly through the deployment of national guard troops in Los Angeles during a series of brutal ICE raids in 2025. During a bustling lunch service at Grand Central Market, a food hall in downtown LA, tourists and residents milled between taco stands and dumpling stalls. Many had yet to hear of the president’s threats, until asked by a reporter. One of those who had was Jens Midthun, a downtown resident who often stops at the market for coffee. “Trump has tried to paint Los Angeles as a dystopia despite it being a wonderful place,” said Midthun, sipping an iced coffee under a shaded outdoor table as the temperature approached the triple digits. (Midthun serves as the president of the downtown LA neighborhood council, but was speaking in a personal capacity.) “It reminded me that the president is obsessed with us – obsessed with California, obsessed with Los Angeles,” Midthun said. “We try not to think about him and yet, here he is with Los Angeles’s name right there in his mouth.” Trump’s remarks have sparked a particularly strong reaction in San Diego, which is home to roughly a quarter-million veterans and has one of the largest concentrations of military personnel in the US. “His statement was so irrational, it’s hard to explain exactly what he was saying, but it sounded like he was willing to give us up,” said Gil Field, communications director for San Diego Veterans for Peace, a group that opposes the war. “It’s horrible and we’re horrified.” The military supports nearly 357,000 local jobs in the region, representing $61.3bn of San Diego county’s economy, according to a report released last year. Defense spending accounts for 22% of San Diego’s gross regional product and the area is home to multiple naval bases and Marine Corps stations, with one out of four active-duty marines based in San Diego. “This is a military town, so you’ve got bipartisan objections to his comments,” said Field, who noted that there were always concerns that San Diego could be targeted in war due to the heavy military presence. “So for him to say this about San Diego is particularly galling. He did San Diego a disservice.” Jim Desmond, a Republican naval veteran running for a congressional seat in San Diego, also offered a pointed rebuke. “I served to protect Americans, not write off American cities as an acceptable price of war. Our job is to keep Americans safe, stand up to our enemies, and make sure a threat like that never becomes reality,” Desmond said on X. “No American city is expendable, and no American family should ever be treated as collateral damage.” Back in Los Angeles, far from the negative fantasies that Trump spins in his speeches, Midthun sees an economic powerhouse and vibrant cultural center sandwiched between the beach and the mountains, and enriched by some of the largest diaspora communities from across the world – South Korea, Mexico, El Salvador, Armenia and even Iran. “The president keeps talking about us, and talking about us,” Midthun said. “He’s got a lot of issues to solve. He should work on those issues instead of obsessing over the beautiful, great people of Los Angeles.”

title: ‘Rip it open’: Big Girls Don’t Cry director explores wounds of early love in film festival hit
summary: Director Paloma Schneideman explores issues of consent and queerness in coming-of-age film set in New Zealand
text: In Big Girls Don’t Cry, the New Zealand coming-of-age film quietly devastating film festivals, there is a scene on a moonlit beach. It features the main character, Sid, played by Ani Palmer, and one of the cool older city boys who has come to the small, golden-sand town of Ōmaha for the summer. It is a deeply relatable, deeply uncomfortable watch; reliving the teenage negotiation – or not – of consent feels unsettling and validating. “Yeah, an 18-year-old at the screening last night said, ‘I feel so seen and exposed,” director and writer Paloma Schneideman, 34, says. “I was like, whoa, that’s quite an astute way to think about it. One is cathartic and healing, and the other is quite confronting.” Schneideman says she wanted to tell a story about the place “between consent and non-consent, where it was just something we felt we had to do”. “It’s such a tricky space, and I don’t think we see it a lot. How do we make amends with the scars of that time?” The global response to Schneideman’s debut film, which also explores desire, queerness and finding your way – in this case, through small-town New Zealand in the early millennium – suggests the need to feel empathy for our teenage selves is universally felt. Since its debut at the Sundance film festival in February, the film has won the Nouvelle Vagues film festival’s Grand Prix – actor Kristen Stewart said it “unpacks the early 2000s, and subliminal trespass, and pain and strength … with such an astounding touch” – and has been shown at major festivals from South by Southwest to London’s BFI Flare. Variety called it a “gentle, rigorous, queer coming of age story”, while the Hollywood Reporter said it “pulses with a powerful sense of place and terrifically charged scenes of chaotic intimacy”. Ahead of its general release in New Zealand and the US on 8 and 9 October, Schneideman is feeling grateful for the way it’s connected with audiences. “The most amazing part is seeing how many people take such ownership over the film, they think it’s for them. And it is.” ‘Sleepless nights’ The film’s protagonist, 14-year-old Sid, negotiates adolescence at a time of fledgling dial-up internet and brick phones, where options for connecting with like-minded people or exploring sexuality included booting up MSN messenger or flicking through satellite TV to covertly watch Red Shoe Diaries. It wasn’t a particularly safe moment to be queer, or a teenage girl in New Zealand. “I found the one queer person in [high school] and they very quickly became my best friend,” Schneideman says. “There was a boy in the First XV [rugby team] who people found out had two mums, and it was the point of gossip and bullying.” Schneideman developed Big Girls Don’t Cry while at Wave in the Ocean, the prestigious film school set up by Oscar-award winning director Jane Campion (The Piano, Power of the Dog) as part of its first 10-person intake in 2022. It’s the first feature film to be released by a graduate, and is supported by the New Zealand Film Commission. “We were sort of these guinea pigs and we just had the best time, learning from the best practitioners in the country and if we weren’t doing that we were watching and shooting films and having mental breakdowns together,” Schneideman says. The script she began writing in 2019 kept evolving, even as it got into the hands of Palmer, Australian actor Noah Taylor, and American Rain Spencer in the 25 days it was shot between Ōmaha and Auckland early last year. “They’re all master improvisers, they meet me in this middle space between the script and the screen. Some of their best lines were theirs.” Campion, named as an executive producer on Big Girls Don’t Cry, encouraged creativity – including a daily movement practice – and listening to intuition, Schneideman says. “She was very much ‘the precedents you set for yourself in your first film will stay with you for the rest of your career,’ so lead how you want to lead.” As a result, Schneideman developed what she calls a “body gauge” during Big Girls Don’t Cry to help her discern if a shot, a performance, or a cut wasn’t right. ‘When the work’s not there, when the performance is not there, it actually just makes me feel quite sick. I can’t tell you how many sleepless nights I had, staring up at the wall being like – how do we blow that up and start it again and fix it?” she says. “My whole thing as a film-maker is to try and make you not notice any of the work, so as soon as something pulls you out, we’ve failed.” She’s got a whirlwind of international release dates ahead of her, but Schneideman is already looking ahead. On a taxi-ride recently to LAX, she found herself running through scenes for the next film she wants to make, which she describes as an “anti romance,” exploring the wounds of lost love. Will this be a hallmark of her career? “Yeah. Rip it open. Then when I finally feel healed, just rip it open again. We don’t want a film that’s just happy, and everything goes right. I think that would be deeply dissatisfying.” • This article was amended on 12 October 2026 to correct some misspellings of Paloma Schneideman’s surname.

title: Plague epidemic risk in Russia low after death of lab technician, WHO says
summary: World Health Organization detects no sign of further outbreak since Darya Shipilova died last week
text: The World Health Organization has said the risk of an epidemic in Russia is low after the sudden death of a lab technician who worked at a plague research institute in Siberia. Darya Shipilova, who was 28, died last week, two days after falling ill. Russian media reports suggested she may have become infected after an accident at her workplace, where dangerous pathogens are kept and studied. Russian authorities have downplayed the incident and say Shipilova died of “pneumonia of an unknown aetiology”. Strict quarantine measures have been imposed at the research centre in the city of Irkutsk and in several neighbouring hospitals. Christian Lindmeier, a WHO spokesperson, said on Tuesday that there was no sign of a wider outbreak. “All ‌of the patients’ contacts have reportedly been identified and are being monitored for ‌illness, and none to date have shown symptoms of illness,” he said. Russian ⁠officials were still investigating whether viral pneumonic plague caused Shipilova’s death but the WHO had assessed the health risk as “moderate to low” for Irkutsk, “low” for the rest of Russia and “very low” for Europe, he said. WHO chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus urged Russia on Tuesday to be transparent about Shipilova’s death. “Timely, complete and transparent information sharing under the International Health Regulations is essential to clarify conflicting reports and enable an accurate assessment of potential public health risks,” he wrote on X. According to Russian media, 60 of Shipilova’s colleagues have been locked in the institute where she worked since Friday, sleeping on the floors and chairs while tests are carried out. Similar measures have been imposed in five hospitals, with relatives forbidden to see patients. The Kremlin’s spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, urged people on Tuesday not to listen to rumours but to rely on statements from Russia’s health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor. It said the situation in Irkutsk was stable, with no new infectious disease cases reported among institute employees. Washington has been watching developments closely. The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, called on Moscow on Tuesday to release more details about the case. “I think it’s incumbent upon ⁠Russia to obviously share more information with the world,” he said. “We’re watching it very closely, hour ‌by hour.” The Wall Street Journal reported that the US state department had sent Russia a confidential diplomatic communication known as a demarche warning Moscow that failure to disclose details runs counter to its international health obligations. Trump said on Tuesday that he was due to speak shortly with Russian president Vladimir Putin about the technician’s death. “I have a call scheduled, yes,” Trump told reporters at the White House when asked if he had spoken to Putin on the issue yet, adding that it would happen “very soon”. Trump had said earlier that his administration was willing to offer assistance. “I hate to see them having it. We’ll help. Everybody who has that kind of a problem, we’ll always help,” he told reporters. In an apparent mirror response, Rospotrebnadzor announced that Russia was prepared to assist the US in combating its own outbreaks of infectious diseases. “The situation regarding dangerous infectious diseases remains unstable,” it said, highlighting a “significantly worsened” measles situation in three US states and a “fatal case of plague” recorded in New Mexico in June. *With Agence France-Presse

title: New Zealand greenhouse gas levels hit record highs threatening catastrophic glacier melts
summary: Government report finds the country could be hit with more frequent and intense heatwaves, as well as damaging storms and cyclones
text: New Zealand could be hit with more frequent and intense heatwaves and catastrophic glacier melts in the near future, as greenhouse gas levels hit record highs, a new report about the nation’s climate has revealed. Released on Wednesday, the Our Atmosphere and Climate 2026 report shows New Zealand is experiencing mounting climate pressures, which will have wide-reaching implications for the environment, native species and communities. “The signal is just becoming clearer … there are multiple indicators that are showing increased warming and the likelihood of climate change,” Dr Alison Collins, chief science adviser for the ministry for cities, environment, regions and transport (Mcert) told the Guardian. New Zealand’s annual average temperature has risen by 1.36C since records began in 1909, and seven of the 10 warmest years on record occurred in the last decade, the report said. “Whilst it sounds like a small amount … it is a significant baseline shift that’s having ramifications through nature, through our communities, and through businesses and industry,” Collins said. The report finds that as the climate heats, glaciers are shrinking. New Zealand has roughly 3000 glaciers, and they have shrunk in volume from 56 cubic kilometres in 1997 to 30 cubic kilometres in 2023, the report said. Modelling of glacier retreat shows a high risk of further decline on the horizon. Under the “low climate scenario” – which assumes low emissions – glaciers will very likely lose between 14 and 86% of their volume by 2100. Under the “high climate scenario”, that figure rises to between 69 and 100% of their volume. “We’re talking about substantial loss,” Collins said. Greenhouse gases have increased to record levels in New Zealand’s atmosphere, the report shows. There was a 30% increase in carbon dioxide since monitoring began in New Zealand in 1972. Methane levels had also slightly increased in 2025 to their highest concentration ever. “That additional heat is showing up in rising temperatures, warming oceans, rising seas, shifting rainfall patterns and more intense extremes,” the report said. Among those extremes were heatwaves, which the report said were “very likely” to increase in frequency, length and intensity across the country. The number of days hitting more than 25C was also “very likely” to increase by 2050, which will expose people to heat-related health risks, including physical illness, disease and psychological distress. Marine heatwaves are also becoming more pronounced and affecting some native species, the report said. In 2025, the series revealed New Zealand’s oceans were warming 34% faster than the global average which has been linked to mass sea sponge bleaching, die-offs of southern bull kelp, large scale fish standings and penguin deaths. The three-yearly update from Mcert and Stats NZ collates statistics, data and research across five domains – air, atmosphere and climate, freshwater, land, and marine – to paint a picture of the state of New Zealand’s environment. The report outlined a myriad of issues that will stem from continued warming, including damaging storms and cyclones that pose a risk to life, droughts affecting species and agricultural industries, sea level rise eroding infrastructure and housing and Māori communities having reduced access to culturally significant places. Severe storms, including Cyclone Gabrielle and the Auckland floods in 2023, have battered New Zealand in recent years, causing deaths, widespread devastation and billions of dollars in costs. New Zealand was built and developed around a relatively stable set of climate conditions and the report examines what happens when those conditions begin to change, Collins said. “Climate change is not just an environmental issue. It’s a human story. It’s an economic story.”

title: Ikea to pilot online buyback service for secondhand furniture
summary: Service to be tested in Spain and Portugal this year, with a UK rollout if successful, as pre-loved markets boom
text: Ikea is to test an online version of its buy-back service where the retailer offers vouchers for unwanted secondhand furniture. The service will be tested in Spain and Portugal before the end of December and will be launched in the UK if it proves successful. Ikea already offers buy-back in stores, including in the UK. The online version will extend it to a much wider audience, with Ikea predicting pre-owned goods are likely to grab 16% of the UK homewares market by next year The new plan emerged as the world’s largest furniture retailer takes on Vinted and eBay with its own secondhand online marketplace which launches in the UK this week. The platform, which is already online in other countries including Spain and Portugal with bestsellers including the Kallax shelving system and Malm chest of drawers, will enable shoppers signed up to the Swedish company’s membership scheme to connect directly to one another to buy and sell pre-owned Ikea items locally. The UK service will be free initially, but a “buyer protection fee” of about 5% of an item’s price will be introduced in time. At launch, buyers and sellers will arrange collection or delivery directly with one another through the marketplace. Ikea said it is exploring ways to make delivery easier in future. “The secondhand market is growing and growing. It is now really significant,” said Greg Lucas, sustainability manager at Ikea’s UK & Irish division. “Secondhand browsing and shopping is now mainstream. “The way people furnish their homes has changed. Whether they are moving, redecorating or looking for a particular piece, more customers are considering pre-owned furniture alongside new and are actively searching for items that can help create a home that feels personal to them.” The secondhand home products market is now worth more than £4.5bn in the UK and is growing at about 6.5% annually. Ikea said its products accounted for about 9% of furniture sold on secondhand marketplaces in the UK. Ikea said it was making the sale of used versions of its products easier by providing pre-filled product descriptions and price suggestions. The company also offers sellers 15% extra on the price of the item sold if they agree to be paid in the form of an Ikea gift card. The change is part of a revolution in retail, where shoppers of all ages are now prepared to consider secondhand items. In 2025, 63% of UK consumers bought products through reselling platforms, up from 51% in 2024. The trend has boosted sales at Vinted, which began as a clothing resale site but is now expanding into homewares and electronics, as well as at Facebook Marketplace, Gumtree and smaller, more upmarket sites such as Vinterior. The US secondhand site eBay recently bought UK fashion seller Depop for $1.2bn (£900m). Preloved items now make up about a 10th of global fashion sales. There is heavy competition for the secondhand market, with the electrical goods retailers Currys and AO, for example, both selling pre-owned items. AO expanded its secondhand position after acquiring MusicMagpie, which sells refurbished electronics and secondhand video games, in 2024. It recently also bought camera specialist Jessops, which controls the Camera Jungle secondhand site.

title: Record high temperatures as southern California swelters under heatwave
summary: Several cities shatter temperatures for time of year as extreme heat warnings in place along California coast
text: An unprecedented heatwave has gripped southern California, boosting temperatures 15 to 20 degrees above normal for autumn. Monday was a notably sweltering day for several cities. Downtown Los Angeles saw a record high of 104F (40C), breaking the previous 5 October record of 101F in 1953, according to the National Weather Service (NWS). About 30 miles south of Los Angeles, residents of Santa Ana experienced a record 106F day, up from the past daily high of 103F in 1953, the agency also reported. Extreme heat warnings were in place along the coast from Santa Barbara to San Diego through Thursday, as health authorities advise the region’s millions of residents to limit their outdoor activity and stay hydrated. The NWS has attributed the blistering spell to a ridge of high pressure, when hot air is trapped over a region. In San Diego and Los Angeles, the NWS has forecast overnight temperatures hovering in the mid to upper 70s, which the agency noted provides only little relief. The unusual spell of extreme heat has set records not only for its sweltering temperatures, but also its prolonged length. This past week, Los Angeles recorded four consecutive days of 100F or more, marking the longest streak of triple-digit temperatures in October. California’s coastal areas are expected to cool starting on Thursday with rain in the forecast for next week, according to the NWS. The state’s interior regions may also see cooler temperatures on Friday and Saturday.

title: Tropical depression in Gulf predicted to be Atlantic season’s first hurricane
summary: First hurricane of the season has not formed this late since 1905 as scientists say possible US landfall on Saturday
text: Tropical Depression Nine has been predicted to be the Atlantic season’s first hurricane and potentially the latest first hurricane to develop in over a century. The system was located on Tuesday afternoon about 630 miles south-west of the mouth of the Mississippi River, with maximum sustained winds of 35mph (56km/h), according to the US National Hurricane Center. The NHC expects the depression to grow into a tropical storm by Wednesday before potentially becoming a hurricane on Thursday as it moves across the Gulf of Mexico. If it becomes a hurricane, the storm would be the first of the 2026 Atlantic season. The first hurricane of the season has not formed this late since 8 October 1905, the Associated Press reported. “Our forecast track has the storm avoiding the strongest wind shear, which should foster strengthening, until the end of the week when it approaches the central Gulf coast, at which point it should start to lose wind intensity,” AccuWeather hurricane expert Alex DaSilva said. The storm is expected to turn north-east and approach the central Gulf coast late this week, with a possible US landfall early Saturday, AccuWeather said. The most likely area stretches from south-eastern Louisiana to the Florida Panhandle, it added. The system is expected to bring 3-6in of rain across parts of the central US from Friday through the weekend, with some areas potentially receiving as much as 10in (25cm), according to the NHC. Flash and urban flooding, in addition to isolated river flooding, will be also possible. Strong winds, dangerous surf and rip currents are also expected. If the system reaches hurricane strength, gusts of 60-80mph could occur near the center, with stronger gusts possible, AccuWeather reported. Meanwhile, heavy rainfall from a separate tropical wave has already triggered flooding and landslides in St Vincent and the Grenadines, where schools were closed on Tuesday, according to the Associated Press. The current, extremely strong El Niño climate pattern is a factor in the quieter Atlantic hurricane season. While it warms sea surface temperatures in the Pacific, and there has been greater storm activity there, it also increases wind shear over the Atlantic, which can reduce the likelihood tropical storms grow into hurricanes.
