title: Labour figures rule out working with Greens after ‘Zionism is racism’ vote
summary: Minister says they could not see parties cooperating, while official says coalition should be formally ruled out
text: Senior Labour party figures said it was very unlikely their party would cooperate with the Greens in the future after they adopted a policy treating Zionism as a form of racism. One Labour minister said they could not foresee how the two parties could work together, while a government official said Labour should formally rule out a future coalition or other arrangement. There is also pressure within the Liberal Democrats for them to end existing arrangements with Zack Polanski’s party, with some senior Lib Dems calling on the party to end its coalition with the Greens in Southwark, south London. Green members from England and Wales voted at the party’s conference on Sunday to adopt a binding policy that says Zionism should be treated by the party as racism, and which calls for a single Palestinian state in place of Israel. After the vote, Bridget Phillipson, the Labour chair, called the move “shameful”, saying it highlighted how vital it had been for her party to tackle antisemitism under the leadership of Jeremy Corbyn. While Phillipson’s statement was backed by her fellow ministers, there was debate as to whether Labour should go further and formally rule out any ties with the Greens, for example if a future general election delivered a hung parliament. A source linked to the Jewish labour movement said Labour should “absolutely” rule out governing with the Greens, arguing the policy raised serious questions about whether its treatment of Jewish members could breach equality law. It follows months of speculation of possible cooperation between the parties. Polanski said earlier this year that the Greens could consider an electoral pact with Labour under Andy Burnham or Angela Rayner, while ruling out one under the former prime minister Keir Starmer. Labour views the Zionism motion, and the criticism that has followed, as a means to simplify its political argument against the Greens at a time when Polanski’s party has increasingly sought to attract disillusioned Labour voters on the party’s left. A big test of this will come on Thursday, with voting in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, where Polanski is seeking to win Starmer’s former seat from Labour. The Greens have poured huge resources into the contest, with Polanski telling the Guardian that it is “really on a knife-edge”. Despite the Greens’ campaigning efforts, helped by their massively increased membership, Labour is considered the favourite to win. The Lib Dems and Greens already govern together in Southwark after May’s local elections, with the Greens as the senior partner. Following the Zionism motion, both Southwark parties released a “joint administration statement against antisemitism”. Without mentioning the new Green policy, it said they would “continue to work with Jewish community organisations to make sure they know they have a place in Southwark”. It brought a scathing response from some senior Lib Dems. Tagging Victor Chamberlain, the Lib Dem deputy leader of Southwark, Sarah Ludford, a peer and former MEP for the party, wrote on X that she did not understand “how you think this greenwash is an adequate response to the Greens’ antisemitic ‘Zionism is racism’ motion, from which I believe you should entirely distance yourselves”. Chamberlain condemned the motion on X, saying he was reassured by discussions with Green party colleagues and that “we must never allow events in the Middle East to divide our communities here at home.” Another Lib Dem peer, Lynne Featherstone, who was formerly an MP, replied to say: “I would ditch them. Grow a pair!” The policy was adopted at the Green party conference in Brighton on Sunday by 1,022 votes to 813, despite being opposed by four of the party’s five MPs. Polanski, who left the Green conference early on Friday to campaign, stopped short of endorsing or criticising the motion. In a statement on Monday night after the European Greens and German Greens distanced themselves from the policy, Polanski said antisemitism and criticism of the Israeli state “are and must always be completely distinct”. Polanski said he remained proud of the party’s stance on Palestinian rights.

title: British man arrested over suspected RAF Fairford terrorism plot
summary: Counter-terrorism police say 22-year-old detained in London on suspicion of terrorism offences
text: A seventh man has been arrested in London on suspicion of terrorism offences as part of the investigation related to threats to RAF Fairford, police have said. The 22-year-old British national was arrested in Westminster, central London, on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts under section 5 of the Terrorism Act 2006, counter-terrorism police said. Police are continuing to investigate a so far unexplained incident on 27 September, when five men from London driving three white vans were arrested in the small hours in a village outside the Gloucestershire airbase used by bombers from the US air force. A week later, on Sunday, the US decided to hastily withdraw all 12 of the B-1 Lancer bombers that had been based at Fairford back to the US. Some had only arrived at the base a week earlier, and refuelling aircraft had to be scrambled in order to complete the evacuation. There remains speculation that Iran wants to target the base, which was used for US bombing runs on the country earlier this year, but the US and UK appear to have divergent views about the security situation and level of threat. UK sources question whether Iran would have the capability to launch a Ukraine-style drone attack on military aircraft at the base, given the complexity of such an operation. On Monday, Downing Street said the base was safe. But some reports suggested the US feared a drone strike along the lines of Ukraine’s Operation Spiderweb attack on Russian airbases last year, and so did not want to leave its bombers stationed at Fairford. On Monday night Donald Trump, the US president, said the aircraft had been moved because “there were some threats, and rather than tempting the enemy – we’ll capture the enemy and beat the enemy, but why should we leave them there?” So far there has been no breakthrough in the investigation by counter-terror police. The five men detained in Whelford on 27 September were released on police bail a day later, without charge. No explosive devices were found in their vans, though a barrel of petrol was recovered. One of the five had also called 999, and their intentions remain publicly unexplained. On Thursday, a 25-year-old dual UK-Iranian national was arrested in Westminster on suspicion of terrorism offences. He was also released on bail on Saturday. Speaking on Tuesday, the senior national coordinator for counter-terrorism policing, Vicki Evans, said: “This remains a live investigation and our specialist teams continue to pursue multiple lines of inquiry into the circumstances surrounding events near RAF Fairford. “Once again, I’d like to thank the public for their continued support and patience whilst we work through this highly complex investigation. “We’re acutely aware of the public interest in this investigation, and we are working around the clock, and at pace, to identify the motivation behind events in Gloucestershire. We remain committed to investigating all possible angles.” The 22-year-old is being held under rules that allow detectives to bail him, just like the other six men who have been arrested on a terrorism charge. People arrested for terrorism offences can be held under two legal schedules which dictate how long they can be detained without charge. Under the terrorism schedule a suspect can be held for up to 14 days, but cannot be bailed, meaning police have a fortnight to charge or release them. The 22-year-old arrested for alleged preparatory acts is being held under the Police and Criminal Evidence Act, a spokesperson for counter-terrorism police said on Tuesday. That means he could be released under investigation on bail, but detectives have much less time to hold him. The five men arrested close to RAF Fairford were held under the same act before being bailed the next day, to the surprise of some. Tensions have been high at RAF Fairford since Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said in July that the base was a legitimate target. Iran’s embassy in London has denied any involvement in the events of the past few days. Ministers have been briefed that Iran has various reasons for hiring proxies, who sometimes are unwitting, to carry out acts that aim to eat up resources and create chaos. The Iranian embassy in London has said it “categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations” of Iranian involvement. Senior US politicians, including the president, Donald Trump, have expressed surprise that the suspects were released on bail. Counter-terrorism police last week defended the move. “I understand why this development will have come as a surprise to many, but I’d like to reiterate that it was an investigative decision, and one which is grounded in experience and careful consideration of policing powers,” Britain’s head of counter-terrorism police said.

title: Morrisons is not a must-do deal for Sainsbury’s
summary: Odds are good the CMA would approve of a supermarket merger. But does Sainsbury’s need Morrisons?
text: Would competition regulators really smile upon a combination of Sainsbury’s and Morrisons? One must assume the two companies believed the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) would give a thumbs up if asked, otherwise they would not have initiated their now-aborted merger talks. It’s easy to list the arguments the duo could make. First, the combined market share of Sainsbury’s (15.2%, on the latest numbers from Worldpanel analysts) and Morrisons (8.4%) would still be less than that of mighty Tesco (27.8%). It would not be a case of leap-frogging the market leader, which was Sainsbury’s big idea back in 2018 when Asda was in its sights. Second, Aldi and Lidl are a stronger force in the land. Together, the German discounters represent almost a fifth of the UK market and, since they’re backed by serious international buying muscle, their role as the country’s grocery price police might not be affected one jot. Third, since Morrisons has already sold its petrol stations, the CMA needn’t worry about the touchy issue of fuel. Fourth, at a push, Sainsbury’s and Morrisons could argue that the UK’s food security (a growing political worry) would improve if the latter’s 18 food-processing factories were housed within a stronger company that could boost local production. So, yes, one would probably bet that the CMA would ultimately approve some version of a deal. But what version? How many store disposals would be demanded? The CMA, as in 2018, would presumably conduct a site-by-site analysis of drive-times to judge local competition. The regulatory instinct, one suspects, would be to err on the side of intervention in light of the overall national picture. Never mind Tesco’s size, it would still not be a simple decision for a competition regulator to sanction a supermarket setup in which half the trade, or thereabouts, would be in the hands of just two companies. Would a deal still make sense after the CMA’s remedies? It’s impossible for Sainsbury’s and Morrisons to know until they go through the process. That’s the distraction factor for Sainsbury’s. Does its chief executive, Simon Roberts, really want to spend a year bogged down in regulatory back-and-forth? In the Asda episode, the effort sucked the life out of his predecessor’s reign. It’s not as if Sainsbury’s is struggling today. The group is winning market share, profit margins are stable, there’s enough spare cash for share buy-backs and the strategic headaches of its bank and Argos have been solved by selling both. While it would be preferable to square up to Tesco’s buyers on more equal terms, life ain’t bad. Round at private equity-owned Morrisons, the calculation will be different. Five years after buying the chain for £7bn, owners Clayton, Dubilier & Rice’s thoughts will be turning to how to exit a tricky investment. A disposal will surely look easier than a stock market flotation and the list of potential suitors is short: Sainsbury’s is indeed the obvious candidate. All of which says Sainsbury’s can afford to do nothing, or wait for the terms of any deal to improve. It was the party that walked away from the talks, reported the FT. That’s not a surprise. If a relative bargain is possible, the hassle of a CMA process might be worthwhile. But this is not a must-do deal for Sainsbury’s.

title: Google told to halt work on datacentres in Finland over environmental concerns
summary: Order on two construction sites comes after Google failed to carry out environmental impact assessments
text: Google has been ordered to temporarily stop work on two datacentres in Finland after failing to carry out the necessary environmental impact assessments on its construction sites. The planned datacentres in Muhos and Kajaani are part of a €13bn (£11bn) project across multiple sites in northern Finland by the technology company amid huge demand for space to house online infrastructure. It comes after it emerged that Tuike Finland Oy, the company representing Google, had felled 330 hectares (815 acres) of forest in Muhos without completing an environmental impact assessment (EIA). In Kajaani, the company has reportedly been logging across just under 200 hectares (494 acres) of land. The Finnish Association for Nature Conservation said the sites had been reduced to “sand”, blaming the oversights on the “overheated” market for new datacentres. On Tuesday, the Finnish Licensing and Supervision Authority (LVV) said it had issued a notice to the company to “immediately suspend” – by 23 October at the latest – “preparatory measures that significantly change the environment” of the two sites until the environmental impact assessment had been completed. Google has until next Wednesday to submit a written explanation. The EIA is ongoing and expected to be completed later this year. But Google has gone ahead with “extensive preparatory measures”, including removing trees, stripping topsoil and constructing site roads, LVV said. Tommi Muilu, the head of the environmental department at LVV, said: “In our opinion, the measures in question will change the environment and cause impacts, the identification and assessment of which are among the key objectives of the EIA procedure.” If Google does not comply, LVV said it would consider enforcement proceedings and a fine. In response, Google said in a statement “we understand the concerns” and that it had “fallen short of our own high standards”. The company added: “We will study the LVV’s findings and follow their guidance. We acted in good faith under the Forestry Act, and ran nature surveys and put in place measures to protect high-value areas. As we continue our long-term work in the region, we are advancing our landscaping and biodiversity plans, which include tree planting across 130 hectares (321 acres) at Muhos.” Tapani Veistola, the chief operating officer at the Finnish Association for Nature Conservation, said the malpractice across two sites appeared to be a “systemic problem”. The site at Muhos, he said, was “not a forest any more. It is a sand area.” One of the reasons behind it, he said, was the enormous demand to build datacentres in Finland, which is leading companies to work as fast as possible and overwhelming small municipalities. “The main reason behind everything is the overheated market situation that makes companies speed up processes so much. Also a lack of expertise in municipalities.” • This article was amended on 16 October 2026 to correct a misspelling of the town of Kajaani.

title: Asos warns customer data may be compromised after ‘unauthorised’ app access
summary: Shares in fashion company fall nearly 10% after its app systems are accessed by ‘unidentified third party’
text: Asos is investigating unauthorised access to its app system after shoppers received a notification claiming hackers had “fully compromised” its data. The online fashion retailer said basic personal information including name and contact details might have been accessed by an unidentified third party but it did not believe payment card records or passwords had been compromised. It said in a statement: “We are investigating unauthorised activity involving third-party platforms that we use to communicate with customers. We took immediate action to restrict access to the notification platforms and are working with our internal and external specialist advisers, as well as all relevant authorities. “Our website and app are operating as normal, with no current disruption to any aspects of our operations. Customer trust is incredibly important to us, and if the situation changes an update will be provided as appropriate.” It later apologised directly to customers, saying: “We’re sorry that you may have received an unauthorised push notification from us earlier today. Please disregard the notification and do not click or engage with the external third-party link it contained.” The value of Asos’s shares on the London Stock Exchange dived more than 14% after thousands of customers received a notification titled “Asos hacked” with a link that sent them to the Telegram messaging service. Shares closed down by 9.56% after Asos announced it had cybersecurity insurance with a large global provider, including business continuity insurance. However, the company added: “It is too early to quantify any potential impact on trading.” The message sent out to customers said: “Dear Asos DPO [data protection officer] and IT, we have fully compromised the Snowflake instance.” Snowflake is a cloud platform used to store, process and analyse data including transactions and demographic information such as clothing sizes and body measurements. It also enables push notifications to phones. The Telegram channel operated by the purported hackers, who have named themselves the Xuanye Group, carried a message assuring Asos customers that “payment information is not affected” and a further post stating “the app is safe to use”. Indicating that Asos had been set some form of deadline, the post added: “The incident involves customer information, it is safe on our server, and it will not be touched for a designated period.” The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), part of the government’s GCHQ intelligence agency, is offering assistance to Asos. The NCSC chief executive, Dr Richard Horne, said: “The unauthorised notification sent out to Asos customers has brought into the light how cyber incidents do not simply affect big business but can have repercussions for individuals much more widely too.” Dray Agha, the senior manager of security operations at Huntress, an online security firm, said: “Sending a ransom demand directly to consumer devices is an aggressive extortion tactic designed to force the business into a quick negotiation. I strongly advise shoppers to watch out for targeted phishing attempts while we wait for official confirmation of a data breach.” The link directed Asos customers to a Telegram channel apparently operated by the Xuanye Group. Cyber experts said they had not heard of the group before and the push notification could be an attempt to grab wider attention. “It’s not unusual to see new groups emerge, and often they wait until they have what they see as a significant opportunity before they announce themselves so as to enter the ecosystem with ‘credibility’,” said Aiden Sinnott, the principal threat researcher at the cybersecurity firm Sophos. Xuanye had not been mentioned before on hacker forums or other Telegram channels, Sophos added. Marijus Briedis, the chief technology officer at the online service provider NordVPN, said: “High-profile cyber incidents create ideal conditions for phishing attacks. Criminals may exploit the publicity by sending emails and texts claiming to be from Asos, perhaps asking customers to reset a password, confirm payment details, check an order or claim a refund.” The potential hack comes after a string of British retailers, including Marks & Spencer, the Co-op and Harrods, suffered cyber incidents last year. M&S and the Co-op experienced stock shortages and the former was forced to close its website for several weeks as it battled to ensure its systems were clean.

title: Riot police fire teargas as 250,000 take part in schools protests across France
summary: Officers also carry out baton charges as students, staff and parents march in cities including Paris, Marseille and Lyon
text: Police have fired teargas at ⁠protesters as more than 250,000 pupils, teachers and parents demonstrated across France on the biggest day yet of a campaign for better high school conditions that has been marred by often violent clashes with police. The French prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, said at least 215 teenagers and 85 school staff had been injured since the protests began more than a fortnight ago, calling the figures “the heaviest ⁠toll in decades paid by the school system”. The country’s president, Emmanuel Macron, called key ministers to the Élysée Palace for talks on Tuesday night, French media reported. The interior ministry said 200,000 people had taken part in mainly peaceful marches in cities including Marseille, Nantes ⁠and Lyon on Tuesday, with 56,000 more joining the biggest demonstration in Paris. Organisers put the total at 450,000. Most passed off without serious incident, but some – including in Paris – ended in sporadic vandalism and running skirmishes with riot police, with officers firing teargas and carrying out baton charges to disperse protesters. Nearly 500 people were arrested on Tuesday, according to figures from the Interior Ministry reported by newspaper Liberation. The ministry also said 43 police officers were injured. Trade unions and rights groups have accused the police of using unnecessary force against the young protesters in recent days, with Amnesty International saying French authorities should “put an end to the disproportionate police repression”. But interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, said the police response had been proportionate in “almost all cases” and that the protests had at times turned into riots, requiring police intervention. At Tuesday’s demonstration in Paris, students held aloft smoke flares and placards with slogans including “under our text books, anger” – a nod to a celebrated “under the paving stones, the beach” slogan from the May 1968 student riots. Other slogans included “schools with no money = country with no future”. One student, Anna, told reporters at the capital’s Place de la Nation: “Our demands are simple: better study conditions, enough teachers, decent school buildings. The authorities’ response has been catastrophic. There’s enough violence already.” Tuesday’s marches came after two weeks of protests that ⁠began in the northern suburbs of Paris and have snowballed nationwide. Besides the injuries to protesters and staff, 715 police officers have been wounded in the clashes, Lecornu’s office said. Demonstrators have set dustbins on fire outside their schools, destroyed bus shelters and hurled projectiles at riot police, who have responded with batons, teargas and riot-control rounds. Twenty-four schools have been burned or ransacked since mid-September, while more than 6,100 people have been arrested, almost all of them minors. More than 1,800 are being prosecuted, nearly 1,500 of them under 18, the justice ministry said. The education ministry said more than 900 of the country’s 3,700 high schools were blockaded or had been closed for the day on Tuesday, although student groups put the number at 1,800. Some local education authorities moved classes ‌online. Océanne, 18, was among the marchers in Marseille. “We just want to save our education and be educated,” she said, adding that she had suffered from absent teachers who were replaced either by “pointless substitutes” or not at all. Many teachers were also demonstrating. In the western city of Rennes, Romain Dubourg said he and “about 30 colleagues” had “talked about the police brutality that we’ve witnessed, and decided to be there for our students if they need us”. Trade unionists were also on the marches, with the head of the CGT union, Sophie Binet, urging members to “protect high school students”. The Green party leader, Marine Tondelier, urged local officials and parents to wear white and “go and protect our children during demonstrations”. Anne Savinel-Barras, the president of Amnesty France, said: “The images and testimonies widely circulated over the past week raise alarming concerns about the dangerous use of teargas, batons and policing techniques by the police.” Nuñez, said police had launched 10 internal investigations into allegations of brutality since the protests started. On Monday, a 15-year-old’s hand was blown off as protesters battled riot police in northern France. A 16-year-old lost the use of his right eye after he was seriously injured in the head on Wednesday during the blockade of a high school in Tours. The local prosecutor, Catherine Sorita-Minard, said the wounds were “compatible with the impact of a defensive bullet of the blast ball type”. In another incident, a 14-year-old lost most of his teeth on Monday when a police officer appeared to fire a grenade at him at close range during a protest north-west of Paris. “His jaw is sealed shut, he can no longer speak and he eats through a straw,” his mother told reporters. Lecornu has ordered his ministers to tackle the students’ core demands, which include ensuring absent teachers are replaced, reviewing the length of the 8am to 6pm school day and repairing ‌ageing buildings. He denied accusations of routine excess force by police, saying officers had mostly acted proportionately. He told MPs on Tuesday that “extreme violence” had come “knocking on high-school doors, and must be condemned”. “Setting fire to a school will not help repair it. Attacking a teacher will not help replace missing staff,” he said. The protests, seven months before crucial presidential elections to choose a successor to Macron, have piled pressure on a government trying to reduce a ballooning budget deficit amid mounting investor concern over France’s mountainous debt and weak economic growth. The government has accused the radical-left La France Insoumise party of encouraging and even orchestrating the movement after numerous LFI MPs attended school blockades. The party’s veteran leader and presidential candidate, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, has strongly supported the protests, while urging non-violence. • This article was amended on 7 October 2026. A caption in an earlier version said a picture showed protesters in Paris. In fact they were near the Porte d’Aix, in Marseille.

title: Alleged Iranian spies planned ‘serious violence’ against UK journalists, court hears
summary: Mostafa Sepahvand, Farhad Javadi Manesh and Shapoor Qalehali Khani Noori did not dispute they surveilled their targets
text: Three alleged Iranian spies carried out surveillance and reconnaissance to target journalists in the UK as part of a plan to commit “serious violence”, a court heard on Tuesday. Mostafa Sepahvand, 41, Farhad Javadi Manesh, 46, and Shapoor Qalehali Khani Noori, 57, are charged with offences under the National Security Act. Their “subjects” included Mojtaba Pourmohsen and Kambiz Hosseini, journalists for London-based Persian broadcaster Iran International, as well as a founder member of UK Lawyers for Israel, Jonathan Turner, the court was told. The prosecution alleges Sepahvand intended to physically carry out a “violent attack” against at least one of the targets, while Manesh and Noori assisted in planning. Sepahvand claims he was threatened into conducting surveillance against his will, but the prosecution described this as an “entirely bogus claim”, telling jurors he did it to get paid and have his theft conviction in Iran “fixed”. In a voice note read out to Woolwich crown court in London, Sepahvand told an associate he would “finish off” a target if he was paid £150,000. “They made me a promise and said: ‘We’ll sort out your matter/court case, and we’ll give you £150,000 as well. Finish the job. We’ll show you him/her (the target),’” he said. “This is an illegal job. It’s something that constitutes a criminal offence, and it carries a heavy prison sentence. At the absolute minimum, they should transfer £10,000 for now. “Wherever they tell me, I’ll go there and stand there. If the person (the target) is inside, they pay the £150,000, and I’ll finish him/her off.” The defendants were said to have visited addresses linked to their targets, taken photos and videos and used platforms such as ChatGPT to research them online between August 2024 and March last year. There was no dispute that the three defendants conducted the surveillance and reconnaissance, the jury was told. Sepahvand accepts he was doing so for the benefit of the Iranian regime but claims he was threatened or bullied into doing it, and that he “deliberately did a bad job of it”, the prosecution said. The crown added that Manesh and Noori claimed they did not know they were carrying out the surveillance to assist the Iranian intelligence service. The defendants are charged with engaging in conduct likely to assist a foreign intelligence service. Sepahvand, of St John’s Wood, north London, is also charged with engaging in surveillance, reconnaissance and open-source research with the intention to commit serious violence against a person in the UK. Manesh, of Brent, and Noori, of Ealing, are also charged with engaging in surveillance and reconnaissance, with the intention that serious violence against a person in the UK would be committed by others. The three men, who deny all the charges, were assisted by interpreters in the dock. The trial continues.

title: Three men jailed for raping teenage girl before fleeing UK in back of lorry
summary: Trio and 17-year-old boy convicted of rape after they persuaded girl to travel into Bristol alone and got her drunk
text: Three men who raped a 17-year-old girl before escaping from the UK to France in the back of a lorry have been sentenced to a total of 33 years in detention. Mehrab Safi, 21, Salman Habibkheil and Awal Ahmadzai, both 19, and a 17-year-old boy plied the girl with alcohol after she had been persuaded to travel into Bristol alone, and all four raped her at a house in the city. Safi was found guilty of two counts of rape, and Habibkheil of one. Both were convicted of arranging or facilitating the travel of a female with a view to exploitation. Ahmadzai was found guilty of one count of rape and one of sexual assault. The 17-year-old was convicted of one count of rape. Safi was jailed for 15 years while Habibkheil and Ahmadzai were each sentenced to nine years in a youth detention centre. The 17-year-old was sentenced to two years and seven months in youth detention. The victim had met Safi in Bristol during a trip she made in November 2025 to do some Christmas shopping with a friend – her first trip to the city from her home in Somerset, Bristol crown court heard. Immediately after they left, Safi began messaging the girl. He told her he loved her and asked her to send indecent images. Four days later, Safi, in collaboration with Habibkheil, arranged for her to be collected by a taxi and brought into Bristol. She was taken to his house where she was raped over several hours. The victim’s mother reported her missing and police found her and the 17-year-old boy at Safi’s house. As officers arrived, the three men fled, eventually managing to make their way across the Channel in the back of lorry carrying frozen goods. Footage from Safi’s mobile phone showed the men laughing and gesticulating in the back of the lorry, which the prosecution suggested showed they thought they had escaped. But they were swiftly arrested in France and returned to the UK. The girl had been raped five times by the four offenders. In a victim personal statement, the girl said she felt like a different person now and could not leave her home alone. She had put on hold her dreams of going to college and working with children. Bristol crown court was told the four were born in Afghanistan and displaced as young people by the “brutality” of the Taliban regime. Habibkheil had lost his father to the Taliban and was instructed by relatives to travel to England. Ahmadzai had ambitions of being a mechanic when he arrived in the UK but was unable to as an asylum seeker. He is believed to have post-traumatic stress disorder and was terrified of being deported to Afghanistan. The 17-year-old offender lost his parents in Afghanistan and fled to the UK aged 11. The court heard he suffered “horrendous abuse” en route to England, arriving aged 12. He had flashbacks and nightmares. But Judge Cullum said their experiences did not excuse the serious psychological harm they had caused to a “vulnerable” girl who had been “groomed and trapped”. DS Jo Babbage, of Avon and Somerset police, praised the girl’s bravery in telling police her story and being questioned in court. “It’s impossible to overstate the courage she has shown,” she said. Babbage said: “We do understand there is going to be anxiety in communities, but we need to be clear that this is not about a culture, a community, any religious belief. This is about deep-rooted misogyny and criminal behaviour in individuals.”

title: Lord Archer of Weston-super-Mare obituary
summary: Bestselling author and Conservative politician whose scandal-ridden career ended with a prison sentence
text: Jeffrey Archer, who has died aged 86, was irrepressible, though not necessarily in a good way. Ordinary humans would be sunk by the allegations of lies, thefts, frauds, gussied-up CVs, expenses fiddles, charity swindles, plagiarisms, insider trading deals, funding illicit coups and – perhaps most unforgivable of all – unpleasantness to underlings that dogged Archer’s life. But Lord Archer of Weston-super-Mare – bestselling novelist, disgraced politician, one-time athlete and convicted liar – was not ordinary: he was what the Titanic was designed to be, unsinkable. One morning in September 2000, for instance, Archer emerged from Wimbledon police station. He had just been charged with perjury for persuading a friend to lie for him during his 1987 libel action against the Daily Star newspaper, which had claimed he had paid a sex worker to buy her silence. That morning, Archer’s life had started to unravel: the following July he would be jailed at the Old Bailey for this crime. But instead of returning to his sumptuous Thameside apartment overlooking parliament to consult with lawyers or have a good cry, he smiled for the media, climbed into a chauffeur-driven BMW and went on to his next appointment. The Archer show had to go on. That evening he made his senior stage debut in a production of his own play at the Theatre Royal, Windsor. The Accused was, if nothing else, strikingly topical. In it, Archer played Patrick Sherwood, a GP accused of poisoning his wife. Posters for the play read: “See You in Court”. The stage was a simulacrum of the Old Bailey courtroom where he would later stand in the dock. Critics noted that it was a good job Agatha Christie was no longer alive to add the charge of plagiarism to the list he was soon to face. The Accused, they pointed out, bore a striking resemblance to her play Witness for the Prosecution. This was not the first time he faced allegations of plagiarism: Archer once judged a short story competition and duplicated many of the features of the winning entry in one of his own. The theatre audience was the jury, giving their verdict on keypad. Most nights, Archer got off. In the real world, he was not so fortunate. But Archer’s comeuppance was not fatal. In jail, he wrote the three-volume memoir A Prison Diary and was regularly visited there by literary editors, eager to work up the raw copy of Britain’s most bankable novelist into publishable form in time to capitalise on the Christmas market. Born in London, two weeks later Jeffrey moved with his family to Weston-super-Mare, in Somerset. He was the third child of Lola (nee Cook) and William Archer. The first two of Lola’s children, including another Jeffrey, were born outside marriage and given up for adoption. His father, a convicted fraudster and bigamist who was 64 when Archer was born, left the family home not long after and died in 1956, when his son was 15. His doting mother spoiled him in compensation for that loss. She wrote a column for the local paper called Over the Teacups, about her scamp of a son who featured as “Tuppence”. He attended Wellington school, in Somerset – though he later implied he had attended the grander Wellington college, in Berkshire – where weedy Jeffrey was nicknamed The Pune, for his puny skin-and-bones physique, and bullied. He took up bodybuilding and athletics in response and was so successful at the latter that he became a blue at Oxford and later ran for Britain. He left school with three O-levels (English literature, art and history), trained for the army and the police, and then found a niche at private schools as that rare thing, a popular PE teacher. Then he went to Oxford, where he studied for three years at Brasenose College, though he was never registered there as an undergraduate. Rather, he studied for a teaching qualification on a course based at the college. At Oxford, Archer also raised money for Oxfam, and succeeded in inviting the Beatles to visit Brasenose to sign a cheque and mingle with the dons in the senior common room. During that February 1963 soiree, undergraduate Sheridan Morley and Beatles drummer Ringo Starr found themselves at adjacent urinals. “[Ringo] asked if I knew this Jeffrey Archer bloke,” theatre critic Morley later told the Guardian. “I said everyone in Oxford was trying to work out who he was. Ringo said: ‘He strikes me as a nice enough fella, but he’s the kind of bloke who would bottle your piss and sell it.’” While at Oxford, Archer wooed the student Mary Weeden, who in 1966 became his wife and later a chemistry lecturer at Cambridge University. Despite her husband’s shaming bankruptcies and his reported infidelities, Mary Archer justified standing by her man with more imaginative verve than, say, Tammy Wynette. She said much later: “I think I would find it a little monochrome, a little grey, to have a sort of a more conventional life with a more conventional husband.” After leaving Oxford, he continued as a charity fundraiser, working for a medical charity and for the United Nations Association, whose chairman, the former Conservative MP Humphry Berkeley, alleged that Archer fiddled his expenses. He also served as a Conservative councillor on the Greater London council from 1967 to 1970, during which time he was accused of fiddling other councillors’ expenses. Despite these allegations, and despite Berkeley striving to convince Conservative central office that Archer was an unsuitable parliamentary candidate, he beat the future Tory minister Ian Gow to become Conservative candidate for Louth in Lincolnshire. He took the seat in a byelection on 4 December 1969, becoming – or so his book blurbs repeatedly claimed – the youngest MP in the House of Commons, aged 29. In fact, as Michael Crick points out in his biography, there were four younger MPs already in the Commons. In 1974, he became one of the youngest MPs to relinquish his seat. That year, as a result of a complicated speculation he was involved in, Archer lost £500,000 in a fraudulent Canadian company called Aquablast. At the edge of bankruptcy, he resigned from parliament. In terms of fulfilling his ambitions, he may have been prudent: “I realised there would never be a career for me there,” he said of the Commons later. Facing bankruptcy, he told his wife, then pregnant with their second child: “The only way I can get out of this is to write my way out of it.” Friends were sceptical that Archer could make capital from novel writing, having failed to do so from property deals. “Jeffrey, you can barely spell,” his friend Adrian Metcalfe told him, “let alone write.” “No, but I can tell stories,” Archer is said to have replied. He was right. His first novel, Not a Penny More, Not a Penny Less, published in 1976, became a bestseller, as did many of the more than 50 novels, prison journals, children’s books and short story collections that followed. That fictional debut was something of a roman a clef, since it told the story of four men swindled out of $1m – roughly what Archer lost in business deals. The novel’s denouement though, in which the men revenge themselves on their swindlers, was part wish fulfilment and partly cribbed from the then popular movie, The Sting. His wife reportedly helped him edit it, correcting his spelling and grammar. Later, teams of editors worked on making his novels publishable. They were impressed by his capacity for work: he would address the task in blocks of two hours at a time, then wrote as many as 17 further drafts at their behest. Jonathan Coleman, one of four editors who worked on Archer’s international bestseller Kane and Abel (1979), said that, though the book was heavily edited, “he did the rewriting ... I mean, he wasn’t trying to write a literary masterpiece.” He was, rather, trying to make money – and he did. Much came from TV adaptations, but he was a publishing phenomenon whose books were bought at the rate of 25,000 a month at the peak of his literary bankability, resulting in overall sales of around 300m copies. By the mid-70s, then, the disgraced ex-MP was back. Yes, there was a report that he had stolen some suits from a Toronto store when he was giving evidence at the Aquablast trial in Canada in 1977, but that was never proved. And yes, some did complain that he trod on the little people as he rose again (“The sales people at HarperCollins loathed him – absolutely loathed him – because he was so awful to booksellers,” one company manager told Crick, referring to the sales rep as a “waste of space, being very abusive and unpleasant”), but none of this would stop him becoming rich and famous. In 1979, Archer bought the Old Vicarage, Grantchester, a house associated with the poet Rupert Brooke. He also began to hold shepherd’s pie and Krug parties for politicians, business people and even journalists at his Thames-side apartment. He loved to give directions to the toilet: “Past the Picasso and left at the Matisse.” He even returned to politics. Margaret Thatcher made him Conservative deputy chairman in 1985 – despite the misgivings of the senior Tories Norman Tebbit, Edward Heath and Willie Whitelaw – partly in gratitude for the sums he had funnelled into Tory party coffers. The political return was shortlived. The following year he resigned because of newspaper allegations that he had paid Monica Coghlan, a sex worker, £2,000 through an intermediary at Victoria station to go abroad. In 1987, he sued the Daily Star for claiming he had slept with her. In one of the case’s more memorable moments, Mr Justice Caulfield spoke to the jury: “Remember Mary Archer in the witness box. Your vision of her probably will never disappear. Has she elegance? Has she fragrance? Would she have, without the strain of this trial, radiance? How would she appeal? Has she had a happy married life? Has she been able to enjoy, rather than endure, her husband Jeffrey?” He said of Jeffrey Archer, “Is he in need of cold, unloving, rubber-insulated sex in a seedy hotel round about quarter to one on a Tuesday morning after an evening at the Caprice?” The judge’s questions, counterintuitively, were rhetorical. Archer won and was awarded £500,000 damages. In 1992, thanks to the prime minister, John Major, Archer was politically rehabilitated again. Major made him a life peer, Lord Archer of Weston-super-Mare, chiefly because of his role in the previous year’s fundraising concert for Kurds. Archer, with the Red Cross, set up the charity Simple Truth. But once more his philanthropy was questioned. Archer had claimed to have raised more than £57m for Kurdish refugees. Kurdish disaster relief groups claimed only £250,000 had been received by groups in Iraq. Years later, Scotland Yard investigated these discrepancies, but Archer was never prosecuted. In 1994, Archer was back in trouble over alleged insider dealing involving shares in Anglian Television, of which his wife was a director. An inquiry by the Department of Trade and Industry concluded that Archer would not be prosecuted. In 1999, aged 59, Archer was poised to fulfil one of his ambitions – to hold high political office – when he was selected as Conservative candidate for the London mayoral election of 2000. But that ambition was thwarted when the News of the World reported that he had perjured himself in the 1987 libel case. His former friend, the TV producer Ted Francis, and his former personal assistant, Angela Peppiatt, decided to reveal that he fabricated an alibi at the trial because they thought he was an unsuitable mayoral candidate. He withdrew his candidacy the next day and was, in February 2000, expelled from the Conservative party for five years. The then party leader William Hague, who had hailed Archer’s “probity and integrity”, said: “This is the end of politics for Jeffrey Archer. I will not tolerate such behaviour in my party.” Archer’s trial for perjury began in May 2001. Once more, his wife Mary gave evidence. Archer did not, though he had to hear his former secretary, Peppiatt, detail alleged marital infidelities with a former employee. During the judge’s summing up, his mother died. As a result, she missed seeing her son sentenced to four years’ imprisonment by Mr Justice Potts. He served only two years in jail and retained his life peerage. Archer’s scandals were not over yet. A year after his release, he was accused by Equatorial Guinea’s government of co-financing the failed 2004 coup d’etat attempt. He continued writing after his release. In 2007, he collaborated with the Catholic scholar Francis J Moloney in a book entitled The Gospel According to Judas. In this version of the story, Judas did not betray Jesus. The treatment of the story must have appealed to the disgraced peer, since in it he rehabilitated Judas. Perhaps in his mind, Archer – similarly maligned though more fairly – hoped for a similar rehabiliation. Archer’s life was lived, if not told, in heroic denial of what he was. “He will dive over a cliff and then be amazed that he’s falling,” said his college friend Morley who, like many politicians in the party that Archer disgraced, remained supportive. “He thinks he’s Peter Pan, that he’ll never die. Everything he does he thinks is going to be all right in the end.” In fiction, if not reality, Archer was rehabilitated. The maligned Judas became a national hero when in 2002 the writer Guy Jenkin wrote a TV comedy called Jeffrey Archer: The Truth. It told the version of the Archer story that never gets told (least of all in the newspapers) – about a misunderstood man who took the blame selflessly, suffered abuse, disgrace and imprisonment for the nation’s good. “My Jeffrey Archer is the man who has frequently saved Britain over the last 30 years,” said Jenkin. “He’s beloved of all women he comes across, all men, all dogs – he’s a superhero.” If only the real Jeffrey Archer had been like that. But his life did not imitate art because it could not: it was rather, in the title of Crick’s biography, Stranger Than Fiction. Archer retired from the Lords in 2024, and said that his final novel would be Adam and Eve. His death came unexpectedly, on the day before its publication. He is survived by Mary, and his sons, William and James. • Jeffrey Howard Archer, Lord Archer of Weston-super-Mare, author and politician, born 15 April 1940; died 5 October 2026

title: Why a PR voting system is the best bet for Britain | Letters
summary: Letters: Tom Walker responds to a letter that said first past the post is the lesser of two evils for voters. Plus letters from Susanna Dammann and Steve Smart
text: It is common in the argument against proportional representation (PR) to reach for Italy as a cautionary tale, as Gian Lorenzo Spisso does in his letter (A proportional representation voting system could spell disaster for Labour, 30 September). The irony is that Italy does not actually have a proportional system: it has a mixed system. If we want to assess PR, we should look at countries that actually use it – Germany, Sweden, the Netherlands, Denmark – hardly synonymous with political instability. Also, small parties or weak local representation are not unique to PR. The tiny Democratic Unionist party held the balance of power at Westminster less than a decade ago under first past the post (FPTP), while the Scottish National party and Plaid Cymru wield influence disproportionate to their UK-wide vote because their support is geographically concentrated. Germany limits fragmentation with a minimum electoral threshold. And systems such as Germany’s combine PR with constituency MPs, while Ireland’s single transferable vote system retains a strong geographical link between voters and representatives. Gian’s letter does raise a more interesting point: FPTP encourages major parties to contain competing tendencies within broad internal coalitions rather than allowing them to form separate parties. But is it preferable for those coalitions to be internal and opaque, forcing voters into tactical choices, rather than external and explicit, requiring parties to negotiate and find common ground? The fundamental problem with FPTP is that millions of votes have little bearing on parliament. If your preferred candidate has no realistic chance of winning, voting for them does not translate into representation. In 2024, Labour won 33.7% of votes cast but 63.2% of the seats. That distortion is not a minor technical flaw. Who wields power depends heavily on where votes are cast rather than who people vote for. This disconnect is precisely why Britain needs electoral reform. The question isn’t whether PR is perfect, but whether we can design a system in which parliament reflects the votes people actually cast. Other stable democracies do so. Britain can too. Tom Walker London • Re Gian Lorenzo Spisso’s letter and Zoe Williams’ article (Electoral reform could be a gamble too far for Burnham, 30 September), there are several reasons for the UK to adopt a more proportional voting system of which the most important is the moral one: it’s fairer. In the last general election, the current system gave us a government that only about 20% of the electorate had voted for. No wonder the public has been hostile since the start of this administration: almost 80% of us didn’t vote for it. There are other, more pragmatic reasons, particularly for those of us on the centre/soft left: if we are anxious to avoid having an extreme party in power, we need to ditch first past the post – and fast. Reform UK may be lagging a little in the polls at the moment, but with £76m behind them, they may be able to mount a campaign of mis- and disinformation that could persuade 30% of the electorate to vote for them – and they might win. If we don’t want an extreme right (or left) party in power, we need a way to elect MPs that reflects that view. We need proportional representation. Of course, not all PR systems are the same. Italy uses a mixed system similar to the one used in Scotland for elections to Holyrood. However, as a report published by Make Votes Matter on possible future electoral systems points out, the Italian system “tilts the playing field rather than levelling it”. Its results do not reflect the views of the Italian population accurately. The crucial effect of any proportional system that meets the criteria of the “good systems agreement” (which sets out the standards that a system should meet to be considered by the proposed national commission) is to encourage cross-party collaboration and cooperation. It undermines the tit-for-tat squabbling so typical of our House of Commons and reduces the policy flip-flop of right-left-right administrations that makes it so hard for businesses, and individuals, to plan long term. It is precisely that collaborative, creative approach to policy that would encourage the stability and prosperity our people are longing for. Susanna Dammann London • Gian Lorenzo Spisso’s letter arguing against proportional representation voting in the UK is superficial and wrong-headed. Up and down the country there are huge numbers of voters like me whose entire lifetime has been spent thoroughly fed up with our unfair system. I am 79 now, and my vote has never elected an MP since I lived in an urban area private rental in my early 20s. As a middle-class, left-leaning voter living in mainly middle-class towns and suburbs, my vote has been wasted in a succession of places. Of course PR could elect a rightwing government; it could also lock the right wing out of power for a long time, and as a democratic socialist I would be happy to live with the prospect of a long-term progressive coalition. PR would also give the Greens the scale of representation in parliament that their increasing national support deserves. Steve Smart Malvern, Worcestershire • Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Please email us your letter and it will be considered for publication in our letters section.

title: Is regulation enough to stop AI systems killing us all? | Letters
summary: Letter: Martyn Thomas wonders how any rational person can argue that independent oversight and regulation will be sufficient
text: Once again a frontier AI model has been withdrawn because it fails safety tests (OpenAI scraps release of new model over safety concerns in internal testing, 28 September). There is the usual call for “independent oversight and regulation”, though never any explanation of how this would work or, most importantly, what evidence should persuade a regulator that an AI system is adequately safe. There is a long engineering tradition of regulating safety-critical software systems, such as those controlling aircraft or nuclear power stations; international standards require “safety cases” – rigorous analyses that show that the possible hazards have been identified and controlled and that the probability of an accident is extremely low. Typically, the safety case should show, with a probability of at least 99%, that an accident that could cause multiple fatalities will not occur more often than once in 1,000 years. It is extremely hard to provide evidence for such low probabilities, even for aircraft that at worst might kill 1,000 people in a single accident. The developers of frontier AI systems tell us that their systems might kill the whole of humanity, yet they have provided no detailed risk analyses, no safety cases that could be independently assessed, and no evidence that such safety cases could ever be produced for frontier AI systems. How, then, can any rational person argue that independent oversight and regulation will be sufficient? Policy must be based on rigorous analysis of the facts, not on fantasy. Martyn Thomas Fellow and emeritus professor of IT, Gresham College • Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Unemployment and the rise of the Nazis | Letter
summary: Letter: John Plowright reflects on how unemployment was viewed by Germans and the fear the KPD sparked
text: Philipp Ruch believes that the impact of the 1929 Wall Street crash cannot explain the Nazi breakthrough at the 1930 Reichstag election, as the full effects of Black Thursday “didn’t fully arrive in Germany until July 1931” (‘Hitler was a lazy criminal who slept in until noon’: why most of what we think we know about the rise of the Nazis is wrong, 1 October). But unemployment more than doubled between 1928 and the 1930 election, and that fact alone might be thought sufficient to explain the change in Nazi fortunes. Not so, says Ruch, for “in regions where unemployment was high, the Nazi party performed relatively poorly. If anything, unemployment was a factor contributing to anti-fascist resilience.” This, however, marks a failure to appreciate how rising unemployment was seen by most Germans at the time. Not only did they see it as signifying one aspect of the failure of the coalition parties in government to manage the economy competently, but they also rightly regarded it as fuelling the rise of the Communist party of Germany (KPD) – with it being the other great political beneficiary of the Wall Street crash along with the National Socialist German Workers’ party. As the KPD grew, so the Nazi party grew – as it was perceived as the only party with the resolve and the numbers (thanks to the brownshirts) to stop the communists seizing power on the streets. The fact that the KPD proved a damp squib should not blind us to the fact that the party once inspired genuine, strong and very widespread fear. John Plowright Repton, Derbyshire • Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Please email us your letter and it will be considered for publication in our letters section.

title: Plant trees – and make sure they are watered | Brief letters
summary: Brief letters: Saving saplings | A proper referendum | Smartglasses | Showing guests the door
text: I am delighted to hear Angela Eagle has pledged that half a million trees will be planted in the next three years (Report, 30 September). However, it is really important that there is a system for regular watering until they become established. Across the country there are swathes of newly planted saplings where about 80% have died due to lack of appropriate management. The resulting impact on climate, shade and water storage is also reduced by 80%. Diana Lowry Epping, Essex • If Andy Burnham does promise a referendum on rejoining the EU (Report, 3 October), I hope he will have courage enough to say that, for this constitutional issue, the threshold for victory will be at least 60%, rather than a simple majority, as should have been the case in the 2016 referendum. I shall be very disappointed not to be able to visit Oslo next year in my rather fetching Garrett Leight varifocals. title: Outcry in Trinidad and Tobago after passing of police bill that could threaten press freedom
summary: Journalists call for urgent amendment to special operations bill, which increases police search and seizure powers
text: Journalists in Trinidad and Tobago have called for an urgent amendment to a sweeping new bill that increases police powers of search and seizure, which they argue threatens the country’s much-vaunted freedom of the press. The government says the special operations bill 2026, passed on 24 September, is designed to tackle alarmingly high crime and murder rates in the Caribbean nation. The country has spent more than a year in an almost perpetual state of emergency, with police empowered to bypass normal constitutional rights around arrest, detention, and search and seizure. But journalists in Trinidad and Tobago have called for explicit exemptions in the new legislation to prevent police from searching and seizing their notebooks, phones and laptops. In the past, journalists have been forced to challenge warrants empowering police to raid their homes and offices. Although the country prides itself in honouring freedom of speech, ranking 19 out of 180 countries in the 2025 Reporters Without Borders press freedom index, this year it fell 13 places to 32, and journalists say they are deeply concerned about whether they can protect whistleblowers and vulnerable sources who share information on the understanding that they will be protected. The president of the Media Association of Trinidad and Tobago (MATT), Prior Beharry, said the organisation had called for clause 15 of the bill to be urgently amended “to explicitly shield our devices and materials … and confidential source information from standard police seizure”. Clause 15 prevents police from seizing “a tool of a lawful trade or business” or material protected by legal professional privilege. But MATT says journalism is not explicitly recognised as a protected trade, nor does the bill establish a procedure for handling confidential journalistic material discovered during searches. It wants the clause changed to “expressly name journalism as a protected lawful trade and safeguard journalists’ devices, materials and confidential sources”. Beharry said the bill’s search‑and‑seizure powers were particularly worrying in a digital era where “the tools of a journalist is … usually [a] cell phone”. Though he said journalists had not been directly threatened under recent states of emergency, he warned that other restrictions were worsening. “One of the issues we are having is the access to the government, the executive, including the prime minister, who has not had an official press conference for more than a year,” he said. “Ministries use state resources and we are not invited, but state media is invited.” The independent journalist Pearce Robinson said the combination of surveillance capability, expanded search powers – without explicit protection for journalistic practice – and declining access to government ministers created a “concrete” threat to press freedom, with a particularly significant impact on investigative reporting. “If your phone, your laptop and your notes can be searched or seized without explicit protection for journalistic material, that raises serious constitutional concerns,” he said. “Investigative journalism depends on people being able to speak confidentially.” He also raised concerns about phone tapping and surveillance, pointing to an investigation by the Trinidad and Tobago Guardian which said that “judges approved 314 warrants to intercept communications in Trinidad and Tobago between 2020 and May 2026”. “My concern is not that press freedom has disappeared,” he said. “It is that several of these pressures … are accumulating at the same time.” Pedro Cárdenas, of the press freedom and human rights organisation Article 19, expressed concern about the clause in the new bill. “It empowers law enforcement officers to seize any vehicle, article or document deemed likely to be of substantial value. We find this clause particularly problematic because it is vague and opens up to discussion what is substantial value or not,” he said. He added that it “might directly counter” existing international human rights laws. The office of the prime minister did not respond to a request for comment. Stuart Young, Trinidad and Tobago’s former prime minister, labelled the bill “unconstitutional and very dangerous”, adding that it “breaches fundamental and entrenched constitutional rights” and was passed “without a required constitutional majority in highly questionable circumstances”. He said the government’s past use of emergency powers – including detaining citizens without charge – showed “the real likelihood of abuse” under the new legislation.

title: Election deniers stoke Trump-driven ballot security fears before midterms
summary: Former and current officials who bolstered claims of voter fraud in 2020 make fresh allegations of vulnerabilities
text: Prominent election deniers have spent recent weeks stoking fears over US election security before next month’s midterms, echoing claims pushed by Donald Trump to justify asserting more control over voting. On conservative-friendly media outlets, former or current officials who tried to bolster the US president’s false claims of mass voter fraud in 2020 have in recent weeks made fresh allegations of election vulnerabilities. Cleta Mitchell, a former politician who tried to help Trump overturn the 2020 election results, capitalized on recent reports that voting machines in Georgia had a privacy vulnerability to assert the state was not doing enough to secure voters’ ballots. “The problem in Georgia is that they use a version of these machines where … the machine doesn’t count the choices. The machine actually counts a QR code,” Mitchell told the conservative strategist and longtime ally Steve Bannon in an interview on Friday. Ed Martin, the controversial former US pardon attorney, repeated claims from top administration officials that voting machines, which used parts manufactured in China and other countries, were “compromised”. Other election deniers have planted seeds of doubt about the predicted outcome of the 2026 midterm elections. Kevin Roberts, president of the Heritage Foundation, which established and published Project 2025, told Fox Business in September that predictions Democrats could flip the Senate were “a psyop” – a term popularized by online theorists to describe something they believe authorities are doing to influence people covertly. “I think that this prognosticating is a psyop by so many of these polling firms. In order to do what? To depress conservative turnout,” Roberts said. In conducting media hits about election integrity, some prominent election deniers also revealed that the Trump administration was continuing its effort to assert greater power over states, which are responsible for running elections. Martin told Eric Bolling of Real America’s Voice on Monday that Trump had met with Tina Peters, a politician convicted of crimes related to her efforts to interfere with 2020 election results. “Just hours ago, maybe two hours ago, Tina Peters, you know, from Colorado, was in the Oval Office meeting with the president on election integrity, and they were talking about the plans,” Martin said. “The president is taking it seriously. If the Congress won’t pass the Save America Act, and they won’t, then the president’s going to have to do what he’s going to do,” Martin added. Trump has sought to undermine public confidence in US elections by promoting false claims of election fraud and making unverified claims of election insecurity. Earlier this year, the president tried to heighten those claims in a prime-time address. The president has attempted to crack down on voting, ostensibly to secure elections – despite experts assuring voters that elections are already secure. That includes directing his administration to implement new rules to restrict mail-in ballot voting, a method of voting Trump has criticized despite using it himself, create a federal database of eligible citizens, and force voters to provide proof of citizenship when voting in federal elections. Most of those actions have been stalled by court challenges. The supreme court has allowed the administration to move forward with compiling a federal database of eligible voters. Mitchell told Bannon she had “on good authority, from some of the highest levels in the Trump administration”, that the justice department was inquiring with the Georgia secretary of state about voter data it shares with two non-profit groups. She accused the states, including Georgia, of being “hypocrites” for refusing to share voter data with the federal government.

title: Don’t mention the Iron Dome: comedy genius Kemi on warpath at Tory conference | John Crace
summary: ‘It’s a Britannia Shield’ announcement proves no one does farcical improv better than the Conservative leader
text: Just another day in Crapland. It’s amazing what you can get used to. You can’t say the Tories haven’t put a lot of thought into their party conference. It takes some programming skill to make every day even more dismal than the last. You come expecting very little and get even less. Schopenhauer would be in dreamland. The very act of being has never felt so inconsequential. Yet there’s something very comforting about this. You leave the Birmingham theme park attraction feeling better about yourself than when you arrived. Who knew abject failure could be so much fun? You find yourself congratulating some members on being able to dress themselves. A curious hybrid of an endangered species and care in the community? You might find yourself wondering if you are being gaslit. Small pockets of people roaming around aimlessly with a smile on their face, insisting that it is very heaven in this dawn to be alive and repeatedly crossing themselves before images of the beatific Kemi Badenoch. But then you realise that the people the Tories are really gaslighting are themselves. It’s almost painful to watch. Almost. But mostly it’s like a remake of The Truman Show. Everyone waking up each day and believing they are engaged in something meaningful. When the reality is nothing is happening. They are living in a Potemkin village. A series of distractions designed to look like a party conference. The breakout star is, of course, Kemi. She is the Tories’ chosen one. KULT KEMI. The leader who has rescued them from one black hole and is plunging them straight back into another. I’ve come to realise I’ve got Kemi wrong. Sure, she’s short-tempered and can’t tolerate dissent. But she’s actually a supremely gifted entertainer. A comedy genius. A woman whose one-liners often get mistaken for serious comment. A female Jack Dee. She would be far more successful taking her show to the Edinburgh fringe than Birmingham. Kemi’s act on the morning media round was one of her best yet. No one does improv better. Understandably, every interviewer wanted to ask her about the Tories’ overnight announcement of a £10bn Iron Dome to rival the Israelis’ that would protect the UK from any kind of drone or missile attack. Like, how did she imagine she was going to build the Iron Dome for about a tenth of the money that all the experts said it would cost? And wasn’t this just some bullshit nonsense designed to make the front pages of the Tory press that wouldn’t stand contact with reality? “Stop calling it an Iron Dome,” Kemi dead-panned. She really is a comedy pro. Even at 8.10am she’s still in role. “It isn’t an Iron Dome. I’ve never called it an Iron Dome. It’s a Britannia Shield.” Genius. She couldn’t think for the life of her why everyone was calling it an Iron Dome. Mmm. It might have been something to do with the Tory press office releasing a statement calling it an Iron Dome? And the opinion piece in the Sun, written by Kemi herself, calling it an Iron Dome? There are clearly a lot of replicant Kemis rushing around pretending to be the real one. OK, OK, we’ll call it a Britannia Shield, said the radio and TV presenters. Sometimes it’s easier to humour a guest. So when was it going to be operational, what would it look like and how much of the UK would it cover? Kemi laughed. She hadn’t a clue. She was just the one with the ideas. The details she left for others. But it definitely would be up and running before Penny Mordaunt returned to parliament to reprise her role in Sky’s The War Game. As for the shield itself, that would be a few Sopwith Camel biplanes and barrage balloons that could be diverted to Scotland at a fortnight’s notice if required. Are you really just a one-woman band? Anna Foster asked on the Today programme. Your personal polls are higher than your party’s. A polite way of saying the Tories are tanking in third place. Not at all, Kemi ad-libbed. Even Jeffrey Archer would have struggled to lie quite so shamelessly. Everyone knows who my shadow cabinet is. Er. I’m not sure I could name them all. I’m not even sure the shadow cabinet could. Just an array of nodding dogs on a dashboard. But maybe we’ve underestimated the public. They do know exactly who the shadow cabinet is. And that’s why the Tories are still bottom-lining. Back in the conference centre, those members who were still alive were struggling to find something to do. The morning’s entertainment was centred around the “Main Hall”, AKA the converted cupboard. For Laura Trott, the shadow education secretary, there were about 15 people in the room. The rest of the audience had disguised themselves as seats again. Still, not all bad news. Eight people were watching online. A figure that soon went down to one. For a while I wondered who this one poor sod was. Then I realised it was me. Laura looked close to tears by the time the session was over. She was met beside the stage by someone who I hope was a therapist. Quite where everyone else had got to was a mystery. There was also no one to hear Rebecca Paul – me neither – talk about £50k handbags with a woman called Plum. Self-selecting, I guess. Maybe there’s a separate hall for those experiencing extreme catatonia. By the afternoon we lucky few were stretched out into the much-reduced Symphony Hall to prepare for war with a Shahed drone hanging above our heads. First up was the shadow foreign secretary, Tom Tugendhat, a man who has sold his one-nation soul for a job in Kemi’s Kabinet. “I am coming back to serve,” SuperTug announced, matching the oratory skills of Andrew Griffith. He is a man who wakes up every day, and seems disappointed not to find himself at war. He rather died on his arse. Then we got the special guest. The rightwing historian Niall Ferguson. A more swivel-eyed, deranged Dr Strangelove. He had come to tell everyone that he too fancied a war, even if you didn’t want one. “A world war is coming,” he said, trying not to show if he had become sexually aroused. “And there is nothing we can do about it.” All of which made the later speeches of Kemi-come-latelies Helen Whately and James Cartlidge somewhat redundant. There’s no need to starve benefits claimants or build an Iron Dome when the apocalypse is upon us. Suddenly the Tory conference made sense. It wasn’t just a place where hope came to die. It was a place where we all came to die.
