title: Ofcom investigates Meta over Instagram Instants safety checks
summary: Watchdog examining whether company carried out adequate risk assessment as required by Online Safety Act
text: Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta is under investigation for a potential breach of the UK’s digital safety laws after launching a Snapchat-style feature on Instagram. The communications watchdog, Ofcom, is investigating whether the $1.9tn (£1.4tn) company infringed the Online Safety Act (OSA) by failing to carry out adequate checks on whether its Instagram Instants product could show illegal content or be accessed by children. Social media companies are required to carry out risk assessments before making significant changes to their service’s design or operation. Breaching the OSA carries a range of potential actions, from a formal warning to a fine of up to 10% of global revenue. George Lusty, the director of enforcement at Ofcom, said risk assessments were a vital step in keeping tech platforms safe for users. “You wouldn’t launch a new car without testing it properly, and it’s the same for online services,” he said. “Safety by design must be built in, not bolted on, and today’s investigation shows we’ll take action where we have concerns that providers are failing to comply.” Instagram’s Instants feature allows users to send images that disappear after viewing. The company said it had conducted a risk analysis of Instants and talked to Ofcom on a number of occasions before launching it. It said the feature carried protections such as blocking forwarding and included all the safeguards under its teen account settings, the default mode for under-18s on Instagram, Facebook and Messenger. “We will of course cooperate with Ofcom during this investigation,” a Meta spokesperson said. The Molly Rose Foundation, a charity established by the family of Molly Russell, a teenager who took her own life after viewing harmful content on Instagram, said it was crucial that Meta was “held to account for their failures under the Online Safety Act”. Ofcom is already investigating whether Meta breached the law by failing to comply with a request for information related to its WhatsApp platform. Zuckerberg’s company is challenging Ofcom in court over the OSA. It is suing the regulator in the high court over how it charges tech firms fees to cover its operating costs and, in a further case, it is challenging Ofcom for placing WhatsApp and Instagram in a new category under the act that subjects it to additional duties. Meta has also joined TikTok and Elon Musk’s X in a court challenge over the amount of information Ofcom is demanding they provide under the online safety regime.

title: New York governor declares state of emergency after spike in measles cases
summary: The deadly outbreak in Pennsylvania is its largest in more than three decades, and confirmed cases in New York are up
text: The New York governor, Kathy Hochul, declared a state of emergency on Monday in response to a dramatic spike in measles cases in the state. Hochul’s administration said the emergency declaration was in response to a “growing number of measles cases across rural areas of New York and neighboring states”, including Pennsylvania, which has been grappling with a deadly outbreak that is its largest in more than three decades. The declaration expands the pool of people who can administer vaccines against measles and allows more individuals to order testing. It comes as there have been 108 confirmed cases of measles in New York so far for the year, up from just one reported case in 2023. In Pennsylvania, which neighbors New York, five people have died after contracting the disease, and there have been 198 hospitalizations. The state surpassed 1,000 measles cases on Monday while Ohio has also seen an increase. New York, Pennsylvania and Ohio have sizable Amish populations, which tend to be undervaccinated. And undervaccination has been a driving factor in measles spreading after its domestic US spread had been eliminated in 2000 by high vaccination rates. “After reviewing the latest data on measles cases in New York state, I am declaring a State Disaster Emergency to strengthen our ongoing efforts to confront this disease,” Hochul said. “No one should get seriously ill or die from a vaccine-preventable disease. That is why I have taken steps to increase the number of health professionals who can vaccinate and test. These emergency measures will protect New Yorkers and support our community partners as they work tirelessly to address the spread of this disease.” The US is experiencing its worst year for measles since 1991, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, with nearly 3,900 cases reported. Of New York’s 108 measles cases, 101 have been reported outside of New York City, the state said. Since 15 July, 92 cases have been reported in underimmunized rural communities. It is a stark increase from previous years. Beside the one reported case in 2023, there were only 15 in 2024 – and in 2025, there were a total of 48 measles cases. The Trump administration health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr, has been criticized for his response to the measles outbreak. Before his appointment as health secretary, he was best known as an anti-vaccine activist. Kennedy headlined an anti-vaccine conference in Washington DC in mid-September, as measles cases surged. He told the crowd there that they had a “strong and steadfast friend at the White House”. Meanwhile, the Pennsylvania governor, Josh Shapiro, has called Kennedy “incompetent”, and the two men have clashed over how to classify measles-related deaths. “The concerning rise in measles cases is due to a decrease in childhood vaccines driven by misinformation and is causing a public health emergency,” said state senator Gustavo Rivera, who chairs the senate’s health committee. At least 95% of a community must be vaccinated against measles to prevent outbreaks.

title: Jailed Lego collector’s insurance scam highlights UK’s £1.3bn fraud problem
summary: Industry leaders say bogus claims rose 14% last year, pushing up premiums for all customers
text: An insurance fraudster who pocketed more than £14,000 for the supposed theft of Lego sets, fishing gear and gaming consoles was behind one of last year’s most high-profile bogus claims. Investigators uncovered £1.34bn of fraud in 2025, a 14% increase on the year before, according to the Association of British Insurers (ABI). The Lego fraudster, Matthew Johnson, was sentenced to 28 months in prison last December after an investigation by the City of London police’s insurance fraud enforcement department. Johnson, of Misterton in Nottinghamshire, submitted false claims to Axa Insurance between May 2021 and January 2022, relating to alleged burglaries at properties in Shetland and Goole, East Yorkshire. He claimed that high-value items had been stolen, including MacBooks, televisions, gaming consoles, fishing equipment and large quantities of collectible Lego sets. Johnson received more than £14,000 in insurance payouts across four claims. He was ordered by Nottingham crown court to repay the money. Axa raised concerns after inconsistencies were identified in the documentation provided by Johnson, including repeated use of the same receipts across different claims and invoices that appeared to have been altered to match the policy address. The ABI and police warned that insurance fraud pushed up the cost of premiums for all customers. Mark Allen, head of fraud and financial crime at the association, said: “Anyone considering committing insurance fraud should be under no illusion – it’s a serious crime with serious consequences, including a criminal conviction and imprisonment.” While the number of detected fraudulent claims fell by 2.7% to 93,900 cases last year, the value of scams rose sharply. The ABI said this was a sign of its growing scale and sophistication. The average value of a fraudulent claim reached £14,300 last year – the second-highest figure on record, just below the peak of £14,600 in 2022. Motor insurance was again the area with the most fraud, accounting for 55% of all cases. With 51,900 fraudulent motor claims worth £625m uncovered last year, the figures point to fewer but more costly cases. The average value rose to £12,000, the second-highest figure since 2015. A fraudster who staged motor collisions using women he met online was sentenced for the “crash for cash” scheme designed to generate fraudulent insurance claims, the ABI said. Aviva discovered bogus insurance claims worth £233m last year, it said in June. Scammers tried new tricks including using artificial intelligence to fake car accident scenes and documents. Simon Klust, who heads the City of London police fraud team, said more than 250 bogus claims were detected each day but this was “likely to be just the tip of the iceberg”. The travel sector had the sharpest rise in the number of bogus claims. Investigators uncovered a £300,000 insurance scam that used multiple fake identities, fabricated medical documents and bogus websites to support false medical emergency claims. Exaggerated loss remains the most common type of fraud, with 26,900 cases identified. This is when someone deliberately increases the cost of a claim beyond its true value. Ursula Jallow of the Insurance Fraud Bureau, which is funded by insurers, said: “Insurance fraud is devastating. It costs honest consumers when times are already tough.”

title: Veteran conservative lawyer quits Trump’s interior department and warns of ‘assault on the rule of law’
summary: John Murdock had been working for the agency for 18 years and his resignation comes during an exodus of longtime federal workers and scientists
text: An 18-year veteran of the US Department of the Interior has resigned in protest from the sprawling federal agency, denouncing “a deeply troubling assault on the rule of the law” that took place at the department under Donald Trump. John Murdock, an attorney and self-described conservative Christian, began working for the agency’s legal office in 2002. In his resignation letter, first sent to his supervisor earlier this year and obtained exclusively by the Guardian and Public Domain, Murdock cites “glaring legal flaws” he witnessed within the agency during the course of the Trump administration, as well as concerns over offshore oil and gas drilling, the aggressive push to expand fossil fuels and the flouting of environmental regulation. “We are headed in the wrong direction,” wrote Murdock, who officially stepped down on 30 September. Murdock’s resignation and public comments come amid an exodus of longtime government workers and scientists within federal agencies, including at the interior department, which has lost thousands of employees ever since Elon Musk’s so-called “department of government efficiency” (Doge) began its controversial efforts to slash government employment last year. “Sadly, I am but one of many civil servants who have departed the government under less than ideal circumstances in recent years. If my story helps others or in some small way assists in preserving the rule of law, I am willing to share it,” Murdock said. In his resignation letter, Murdock said he grew especially concerned about the actions of a top official at the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management, or BOEM, an interior department agency that oversees offshore oil and gas drilling. His decision to resign in protest stemmed, in particular, from an incident that occurred last December, when Matt Giacona, the acting director of BOEM, appeared on stage at a gathering in New Orleans to announce the results of an oil and gas lease sale in the Gulf of Mexico. The lease sale received bids from 30 companies, including BP, Chevron and Shell, totaling more than $370m. During his speech, Giacona extolled the Trump administration’s pro-drilling agenda. He then claimed that the administration was “upholding the highest environmental standards”. The lease sale in question, however, has been mired in legal controversy. Environmental groups and other critics contend the Trump administration explicitly bypassed numerous federal environmental laws, including provisions of the Endangered Species Act (ESA) and the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), while carrying out the sale. Known as BBG1, the lease sale was mandated by Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act. In a memo published shortly before the sale took place, BOEM’s Giacona, in coordination with the interior department’s legal office, determined that NEPA, a key provision of the ESA, and several other environmental safeguards “are not applicable at the lease sale stage of” BBG1 and similar sales. Environmental groups quickly filed a lawsuit challenging the legality of the administration’s actions. “The Trump administration has no basis for exempting these massive drilling lease sales from the bedrock laws that Congress passed decades ago after destructive oil spills off our coasts,” said George Torgun, a senior attorney at Earthjustice, one of the environmental groups involved in the ongoing lawsuits against BBG1 and similar lease sales. “This illegal action is a payback to oil and gas drillers. Gulf communities – and the marine ecosystems that we all depend on – will pay the price.” The administration pushed back on such arguments in a legal filing earlier this year. Because the lease sale was mandated by Congress, the agency says it did not have “sufficient discretion to alter the scope or terms of the lease sale in ways that could affect environmental outcomes”. When Murdock heard Giacona claim that the administration was upholding the highest environmental standards, he decided he needed to resign. “I felt an ethical obligation to highlight the glaring legal flaws I saw,” he wrote of his actions leading up to his resignation. An interior department spokesperson, in a statement, said that “one former employee’s personal disagreement with the Department’s policies does not transform lawful policy decisions into an ‘assault on the rule of law,’ nor does his inflammatory rhetoric make his opinion accurate. The Department stands firmly behind its work to implement President Trump’s agenda consistent with federal law.” Among other troubling policies Murdock witnessed while at the Department of the Interior was the Trump administration’s decision this year to exempt oil and gas operations in the Gulf of Mexico from the Endangered Species Act. “Whether technically legal or not, it is a repugnant policy that I in no way support,” Murdock wrote in his letter. “That repugnancy is especially true with one of the most imperiled species of marine mammals, the Rice’s whale, calling the Gulf home.” Murdock’s work at the interior department included efforts “to help clean up a mess that BP had made” during the Deepwater Horizon oil spill. “I do not want to now be part of creating an even greater disaster,” he wrote. Murdock also protested against the administration’s continuing political attack on offshore wind energy. Under the current Trump administration’s energy policies, he wrote, an “all of the above” energy strategy has morphed into “one of the above”, solely focused on fossil fuels. “The recent decisions to shutter nearly complete offshore wind projects and to pay Total Energies hundreds of millions of dollars to renounce wind leases are an assault on logic and the American taxpayer,” he added, referencing the administration’s announcement earlier this year that it would reimburse a French energy company nearly $1bn to forgo plans to build windfarms off the US east coast. He denounced too “the weekly propaganda video, Inside Interior, sent to every employee’s inbox. Though some version of a self-congratulatory update has long existed, the change in tone to something approaching cultish worship has been jarring.” A recent Inside Interior video, for instance, described “the fearless leadership of President Donald J. Trump, who reminds us everyday what true patriotism looks like as he works tirelessly to make America great again”. In resigning, Murdock, who now lives in Texas, acknowledged that he will probably pay a personal price. “I walk away from the stable salary and benefits of a government job and my retirement likely becomes less lucrative and more complicated,” he wrote. “Yet, I will gain much – including a deeper admiration for those who have made much greater sacrifices – and I will preserve my integrity.” BOEM’s Giacona, meanwhile, departed the agency in September to go work for oil services giant Halliburton. The Guardian and Public Domain reached out to Halliburton seeking comment from Giacona, but did not receive a response before publication. This article was co-published with Public Domain, an investigative newsroom covering public lands, the interior department and wildlife.

title: Trump 2.0 is targeting US protesters with ‘antifa’ charges. Activists started a union to fight back
summary: NSPM-7 Defendants Union plans to offer legal clinics, media training and more to people facing prosecution for protest
text: Darío Sánchez is facing state charges related to a protest he did not attend. Indictments against the 33-year-old Texas middle school teacher have changed three times. He has also been arrested and released three times, most recently for an online search for how to replace an old Game Boy battery; police alleged he was seeking information on explosives. “I’ve seen my case as one manifestation of all the different ways the Trump administration is going after people – regardless of if you’ve even been to a protest,” Sánchez said. “The reality is, as long as you disagree with the government, you’re a target.” Sánchez’s charges of “tampering with physical evidence” and “hindering the prosecution of terrorism” stem from allegedly removing someone from a Discord group and a Signal chat related to a protest at an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention facility on 4 July 2025. Nine of the other 21 people arrested in the Prairieland, Texas, protest have received unusually harsh sentences of up to 100 years in federal prison. Now, Sánchez is one of the first members of a project called the NSPM-7 Defendants Union, scheduled to launch today. The union plans to offer access to legal clinics, media training, and support for people facing state or federal prosecution under the president’s NSPM-7 memorandum, which directs the FBI to investigate “violent and terroristic activities” associated with “anti-fascism”. One of the union’s goals is to dismantle this government notion of “antifa”, a label applied to many of the protesters charged by the administration, even though it is not a formal organization. “Antifa’s not a real thing,” said Alex, an organizer of the project who used a pseudonym for his safety. “The only one who benefits from this is the government, because they can convince people what it is, and a fake organization can’t rebut what the government says.” Instead, organizers want to connect defendants’ cases and the causes they are fighting for. Early union members include anti-ICE protesters arrested in Minnesota, New Jersey and Texas, and protesters in solidarity with Palestine arrested in Michigan during the second Trump administration, as well as others from the movement against the Atlanta police training center known as Cop City. But the group also hopes to include those who have taken part in protests across a range of other issues, including Tesla Takedowns against Elon Musk and his company, against the construction of datacenters and in solidarity with Palestine. It also welcomes anyone who publicly opposes “the Trump agenda and want[s] to support those facing repression for doing the same”, according to the union’s website. “There are things we can learn from each other,” said Sánchez. The defendants union may be the first effort of its kind in the modern history of political protest in the US, said movement historian Dan Berger, author of the upcoming book Prison: Incarceration and the History of America. “It fits in with the genealogy of people facing repression trying to find solidarity with other people facing repression,” said Berger, pointing to efforts such as the Jericho movement, formed by former Black Panther party members and others in 1998 to support political prisoners. By calling itself a “union”, the project shows how collective organizing can respond to the federal government’s expanding surveillance, arrests and court cases aimed at protesters, said Alex. “When the police or the FBI show up at your door, it feels isolating, like it’s happening only to you,” he said. “But the problems people are facing are shared; we want to help de-individualize the experience and create collective leverage – like in a union.” Unlike a typical union, however, the project will not maintain membership rolls or charge dues. It is centered around taking a pledge to follow a handful of the project’s practices, such as not cooperating with law enforcement, adopting collective legal strategies when there are multiple defendants in a case and, when possible, sharing information learned in discovery. Another defendant who has joined the project is Isaac Sant, a 36-year-old nursing assistant from St Paul, Minnesota, arrested in June and charged with “conspiracy to impede or injure a federal officer” as part of the community response to the city’s ICE surge last winter. Sant’s arrest was trumpeted in a White House press release that called him and the 14 others arrested “antifa operatives”. The federal surveillance leading up to the arrests included spying on unions, churches and libraries – what Sant called “an attack on all of Minnesota’s civil society”. And yet this attack isn’t contained to one city or state, Sant said. He named other high-profile cases linked to protest: the Broadview Six case in Illinois, in which six people protesting outside an ICE facility were charged with “conspiracy to impede a federal officer”, only to have the federal government drop the case amid allegations of prosecutorial misconduct; and the Michigan Eight, a group of students and others who face multiple charges, including “conspiracy to transmit threats in interstate and foreign commerce”, for protesting against Israel’s ongoing assault on Gaza. Organizers of the union expect to be met with the same repression as protesters, including hacking and other digital threats. The group delayed its launch by several weeks to troubleshoot against possible insecurities after the Intercept reported on Pentagon-related hacks of leftwing websites. But as a member of SEIU – a national union with 2 million members – Sant sees the spirit of unions as positive for the project: “The federal government would prefer prosecuting each defendant – but at the very least, we should compare notes, come together to increase leverage and create strategies in a more sophisticated way. “This is new and bold,” added Sant. “That’s one reason I’m hopeful about it.” Berger, the historian, said that what makes the project exciting is that it centers on being a defendant. “But it’s also a tragic commentary on where we’re at, with a large swath of people and politics under attack right now,” he said. “We’re all defendants.” • This article was amended on 6 October 2026. Isaac Sant is 36 years old, not 31 as an earlier version stated.

title: Making scents: could AI help perfumers take pressure off endangered plants?
summary: Firms working on reproducing compounds without need for repeated harvesting but conservationists are sceptical
text: Many of the world’s most expensive perfumes begin with a wounded tree. When some Aquilaria trees are damaged, they produce a dark, fragrant resin that becomes agarwood, or oudh – an ingredient so valuable that wild trees have been illegally felled in its pursuit. The result has devastated wild Aquilaria populations. But what if perfumers could create the smell without cutting down the tree? With the help of AI, scientists are learning to predict how molecules that have never been made will smell, reconstructing scent-producing genes from flowers believed to be extinct. Others have collected microbes from clouds and used them as a starting point for new perfumes. Now scientists and biotechnology companies say advances could soon allow the fragrance industry to reproduce scents and compounds from endangered plants without repeatedly harvesting them. “Being able to recreate the scent of an endangered plant would be a huge win for both the environment but also the brands,” said Alex Wiltschko, the founder of Osmo, a Google Brain spin-off that has raised $130m to develop artificial intelligence capable of predicting and recreating smells. Osmo has recreated the scent of a rare tree from a piece of bark “the size of a finger”, Wiltschko said. A spectrometer analysed the sample, its AI reconstructed the chemical formula and the scent was reproduced in its laboratory. BioHarvest Sciences says it has created a stable cell culture from an endangered south-east Asian fragrance plant, allowing its valuable compounds to be produced without cultivating or harvesting the original plant. The plant has not been named for commercial reasons but BioHarvest has announced an agreement anticipating production of 20 tonnes of the fragrance composition, with limited production potentially beginning next year. “The challenge is that human demand can be effectively unlimited while biological supply is not,” said BioHarvest’s chief executive, Zaki Rakib. “We believe biotechnology can help close that gap, not by replacing nature but by allowing us to use what nature has given us without continually putting the source under pressure.” But conservationists and perfumers say such claims risk giving advances in fragrance technology an environmental gloss they have not yet earned. “Calling this conservation is greenwashing,” said Mandy Aftel, the pioneering natural perfumer, author and founder of the Aftel Archive of Curious Scents. “Making a synthetic version of an endangered plant’s smell doesn’t save the plant.” She said producing a substitute did not stop people buying the original – or address other causes of a species’ decline. Rhian Smith, of the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, agreed. She pointed to the Aquilaria tree. AI could help design an alternative to oudh, she said, but wild-sourced material remained highly prized. “It doesn’t completely take the pressure off wild plant populations,” she said. There is also the question of motivation. Wiltschko admitted that conservation was not “an explicit priority” for Osmo’s work. Synthetic perfume itself is nothing new: the industry has relied heavily on synthetic ingredients for more than a century, and machines have long been able to identify molecules in a scent. “What’s changed is what happens after the data comes off the machine,” Wiltschko said. “What’s new is prediction.” He claimed Osmo had trained its AI on more than 5m human responses to smells. “That means it can predict how combinations of molecules will be perceived,” he said. Elsewhere, AI is claimed to be changing the whole world in which perfumers work. Christina Agapakis is not a perfumer, but her work reconstructing genes from preserved flowers has produced fragrance compounds that perfumers can use to create new scents. Another perfumer, Future Society, has gone into the clouds, making two flights in a small plane to collect living microbes. Thirteen were identified, producing 57 scent molecules, which became the starting point for Cloud Reverie, a perfume launched this year. Even AI has its limits: a flower’s scent can contain hundreds of molecules and change according to which part of the plant they come from and the conditions in which it grows. It is still not enough for the purists. “The smell we got was this ghostly fragment of what had been lost,” Agapakis said of her project. She could not recreate the living organism, or the soil, climate, season and ecology that produced its scent, she said. “What we have to remember is, ultimately, however powerful AI is, a smell is not simply a formula or dataset.”

title: Kenya confirms first Ebola case as virus ‘surges’ in DR Congo province
summary: Health minister says 28 contacts identified after death of citizen who arrived from DRC on Saturday
text: Kenya has reported its first-ever Ebola death, the health minister announced on Tuesday, as the disease continues to spread rapidly through the north-east of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), where the outbreak was announced in May. This is the 17th outbreak of the highly infectious, often deadly disease in the DRC. As of 2 October, 4,082 people had died out of 8,463 confirmed cases in the country since the emergence of the Bundibugyo strain of the Ebola virus, for which there is still no vaccine nor specific treatment. A Kenyan man who had been living in the DRC for seven years died after returning to Kenya, the Kenyan health minister Aden Duale told reporters. The man, who has not been named, had been treated in the DRC after falling ill about a month ago. He then travelled overland to the Ugandan capital, Kampala, before flying to Nairobi on 3 October. Kenya has previously never reported a case of Ebola, but neighbouring Uganda recorded 20 – almost all people who had travelled from the DRC – and two deaths, before being declared Ebola-free in August. Duale said the man was taken by a relative and a friend from Nairobi’s international airport to Nairobi hospital, where he was immediately isolated, suffering from “fever, chills, intense fatigue, weakness, muscle pain, painful swallowing, sore throat and bleeding under the skin at the injection sites”. He said the man was subsequently screened and confirmed positive for the virus, but “regrettably passed on last night at around 1130” in the evening (2030 GMT). Duale said officials had listed 28 contacts of the deceased, including family members and healthcare workers, but that so far “only one test has turned positive and is the one that we have just discussed”. He added that authorities were looking for another 23 passengers and four crew members who were on the same flight with the man and that “arrangements” for quarantine for those at risk had been prepared. “I wish to assure the public not to panic, as all systems are in place to mitigate the spread of the disease,” he said. Duale said a “safe and dignified burial” of the man had been planned for later in the day, in line with public health standards, but did not give further details. Kenyans reacted furiously to government plans earlier this year to allow the US to set up an Ebola facility at Laikipia airbase, about 125 miles from Nairobi. After starting in the DRC’s north-eastern Ituri province, the current outbreak has spread to seven provinces in the country’s north and east. The response to the virus in the vast central African country has been hindered by instability, including clashes between armed groups, mistrust of authorities – which has led to violence against health workers and other officials – and a lack of resources amid huge cuts in international aid. The medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières warned on Monday of an “alarming surge” in cases in eastern North Kivu province, which borders Uganda. The province now accounts for 40% of all new Ebola cases, compared with 24% at the end of August, the NGO said. “It is like fighting a megafire,” said Stephanie Hoffmann, coordinator at MSF’s Ebola treatment centre in the city of Butembo. “Multiple outbreaks are developing at the same time, with varying intensity and in different locations.” The wider Butembo health zone is home to around 2 million people and only has four Ebola treatment centres, two of which only opened recently, MSF said. Hoffman said: “Because there are not enough beds available, we are sometimes forced to refer confirmed Ebola patients elsewhere, despite the significant risk this poses to the wider community. In addition, standards of care in some peripheral facilities do not always meet the requirements for Ebola treatment.” North Kivu is particularly affected by conflict, with 134 violent incidents there in the past month, according to tracking group Armed Conflict Location and Event Data, more than any other province. Agence France-Presse contributed to this report

title: ‘Deranged’ and ‘dangerous’ Trump calls for Iran to strike US cities amid historic ratings low | First Thing
summary: California’s leaders attack president after he suggests Iran could ‘take out’ Los Angeles or San Diego
text: Good morning. Donald Trump has suggested Iran could “take out” Los Angeles and San Diego, in comments described as “reckless” and “deranged” by California officials. At a rally in Nebraska on Monday, the crowd applauded when the US president said high prices owing to the war with Iran were a “small price to pay for keeping the world safe – keeping our country safe”. He added: “They can take out a city. Let them take out Los Angeles. Let them take out San Diego.” Gavin Newsom, the governor of California and a Democrat who has repeatedly clashed with Trump during his two terms, said from his press office account: “Let’s be clear: the president is advocating for an attack on 10+ million US residents in two of America’s largest cities. This is not normal … He is deranged and dangerous.” What is happening with Trump’s approval rating? A new Reuters/Ipsos poll shows Trump’s approval rating at a record low of 32% and the president losing support among independent voters and Latinos, who had backed him in 2024. The dip comes before the crucial midterm elections in November that will determine control of Congress. What is the latest with taxpayer-funded Trump ads? After repeated criticism, Trump said on Monday he would pay for the hitherto taxpayer-funded ads from Maga Inc, his political war chest. He provided no details on reimbursing taxpayers for ads that had already aired, nor how he would go about having his political organization pay for such advertising. Saudi-backed forces recapture key areas around strait from Houthis in Yemen Forces of the Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen have recaptured several key areas around the Bab al-Mandab strait from Iran-backed Houthi rebels, Yemeni officials said. The push by Yemen’s internationally recognized government was part of a large offensive launched early Monday under an air cover by a Saudi military coalition, which aimed to retake all territory held by the Houthis. Asked if the Saudi-led coalition coordinated the action with the United States, Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, said Saudi Arabia and the US had a defense agreement but would not give more details. Why has Iran’s oil minister resigned? Mohsen Paknejad has resigned days after allegations that an intermediary trust selling Iranian oil abroad owed millions of dollars-worth of export receipts to the state. Iran is grappling with a dire economic situation, including inflation running at 85%. What is behind the latest disagreement between Israel and the UK? It stems from the UK’s decision to ban trade with illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank – a move that Gideon Sa’ar, Israel’s foreign minister, labelled “morally distorted”. Israel has threatened to close the British consulate in East Jerusalem, prompting the UK to warn it will expel one Israeli diplomat for every British diplomat forced out. Why has the Green party in England and Wales been condemned over its Zionism policy? The English and Welsh Greens are facing international ostracism after adopting a policy declaring Zionism as a form of racism, which has drawn dismay from the group representing European Greens. The co-leader of the German Greens separately said the policy was “intolerable and unacceptable”. Student protests erupt at Cornell over mishandling of gang-rape allegations Mass protests erupted at Cornell University on Monday, with students criticising officials’ handling of gang-rape allegations, demanding the president’s resignation and painting “SMASH THE PATRIARCHY” on an administration building. Thousands of students and faculty gathered for a demonstration over the high-profile case of a former student known as Jane Doe, who said in a recent lawsuit that she was plied with drugs and raped at a fraternity house in 2024. US supreme court hears big oil’s attempt to block climate damage lawsuits The US supreme court began its new nine-month term hearing arguments on Monday in a major case in which big oil companies attempted to strike a fatal blow against lawsuits seeking to hold them accountable for the climate crisis. In Suncor Energy Inc v County Commissioners of Boulder County, local officials in Boulder are suing Suncor Energy and ExxonMobil in state court to force the companies to share a portion of the costs that the climate crisis has imposed on local taxpayers. However, Exxon and Suncor, which is based in Canada, are arguing that federal law prevents state courts from hearing Boulder’s climate change lawsuit. In other news … Televangelist Jim Bakker has died aged 86. He built a multimillion-dollar empire and lived ⁠in opulence before being disgraced by a sex scandal and a conviction for defrauding followers. title: US, Israeli and European far-right figures to gather for conference in Israel
summary: Trump’s counter-terrorism ‘czar’, Sebastian Gorka, was scheduled to speak at conference but White House says he will no longer attend
text: A National Conservatism (NatCon) conference beginning today in Jerusalem advertises a talk from the Trump administration’s anti-terrorism czar alongside speeches from far-right Israeli politicians, European figures who have faced disciplinary action over alleged antisemitism, and Christian nationalist and far-right figures from the United States. The Jerusalem event is perhaps the most significant recent gathering to feature large contingents of Israeli nationalists alongside Christian nationalists and far-right European nationalists from a milieu sometimes shadowed by accusations of antisemitism. Sebastian Gorka, a senior White House official whose May anti-terrorism strategy promised to target and neutralise groups “whose ideology is anti-American, radically pro-transgender, and anarchist”, was scheduled to speak at the Jerusalem event, and his presence is still advertised on the website. But when the Guardian contacted the White House for comment on Gorka’s attendance at the conference, a spokesperson advised that he would no longer be attending due to a scheduling conflict, and that he had condemned Hamas’s 7 October attack on Israel. From Israel, the program lists Bezalel Smotrich, the finance minister, self-declared “fascist homophobe” and internationally sanctioned extremist, and Rabbi Shmuel Eliyahu, who in 2023 called for an atom bomb to be dropped on Gaza and was earlier ordered to face disciplinary proceedings for racist incitement against Palestinians. The Guardian contacted both men for comment. From Europe come Hans-Georg Maaßen, who once led Germany’s domestic intelligence agency but in 2023 faced an expulsion attempt by his then party, the CDU, for “statements in the language of the milieu of antisemites and conspiracy ideologues”, and Austria’s Harald Vilimsky, whose far-right Freedom party has been subject to a policy of non-engagement by Israel’s own government. According to Israeli media reports, Vilimsky has played a key role in building a rapprochement between the Freedom party – whose first two leaders after its founding in 1956 were former SS officers – and Tel Aviv. He has visited the country repeatedly and in January reportedly led a European delegation to the country that was received by Benjamin Netanyahu, the Israeli prime minister, despite criticism from Austria’s own Jewish community. In a statement, Maaßen wrote: “I firmly reject the claim that I made ‘statements in the language of the milieu of antisemites and conspiracy ideologues’. This deliberately vague wording was never a concrete accusation but a politically motivated label, designed to damage my reputation and to discredit critics of the political mainstream of the time,” Vilimsky was also contacted for comment. The American contingent includes William Wolfe, a self-described Christian nationalist who has called for “mass deportations, denaturalizations, and remigration” to preserve a white Christian majority, and Jonathan Keeperman, the publisher unmasked by the Guardian in 2024 as the man behind the far-right internet persona “L0m3z”. Keeperman did not address questions sent to him when asked for comment. Wolfe did not respond directly to questions on his attendance at NatCon, instead sending personal insults. Dr Brendan McGeever, co-director of Birkbeck University’s Institute for the Study of Antisemitism, said: “Many attendees at NatCon view Israel not just as an ally but as an embodiment of the exclusionary ethnostate they wish to establish. National Conservatism sees in Israel a blueprint for the realization of a white, Christian nation built on racialized exclusion, while far-right Israeli attenders at NatCon often argue that partnering with white Christian nationalists is the best way to protect Israel. It is racism that binds these forces together.” Attenders will also share a stage with high-profile conservatives including the Heritage Foundation president, Kevin Roberts, and former deputy national security adviser Victoria Coates, who is now vice-president at Heritage’s Davis Institute for National Security and Foreign Policy. The Guardian contacted Heritage with questions about their attendance at NatCon. Last October Roberts defended Tucker Carlson after the broadcaster gave a friendly interview to the white nationalist and Holocaust denier Nick Fuentes, saying in a video that “the venomous coalition attacking him are sowing division”. He later called the phrase “a terrible choice of words”, and said he and Heritage would speak out against antisemitism. In July a Heritage spokesperson said the thinktank’s “record opposing antisemitism is long, consistent and public”. In May, Heritage elected the Israeli nationalist and rightwing intellectual Yoram Hazony to its board. Roberts and Wolfe are among the NatCon Jerusalem attenders singled out last month by the evangelical conservative commentator Erick Erickson, in a broadside against “a group of white guys” who “have subtly inserted themselves into conservative institutions and church organizations” and who “to varying degrees … embrace white nationalism, antisemitism”. Erickson’s principal target was the shampoo tycoon and would-be “warlord” Charles Haywood, the subject of extensive previous reporting in the Guardian, but he also singled out Heritage fellow Scott Yenor, another Jerusalem speaker. He was supported in his efforts by other NatCon attenders, including the writer Rod Dreher. The Guardian contacted Haywood and Erickson for comment. Matthew Taylor, a senior visiting fellow at the Georgetown Center for Faith and Justice and author of the new book Defying Tyrants, said: “I think they were trying to find a way to kind of carve out a version of Christian nationalism that could synchronize with kind of European and Israeli politics … and I think what they’re discovering is kind of the impossibility of that.” He added: “[Hazony is] running up against the limits of that project because the reality is that you can’t simply stir up abstract Christian nationalism. One side of the Christian nationalist coalition is very aligned with Israel, is very Christian Zionist, the other side is leaning hard into this antisemitic impulse.” The gathering is the latest in a series of NatCon conferences held in the United States and abroad since 2019 by the Edmund Burke Foundation, whose founder is Hazony. The conferences are high-profile gatherings of the international national conservative movement, which scholars describe as the most influential strand of an anti-liberal “New Right”. Past NatCons have featured JD Vance, Viktor Orbán, Giorgia Meloni and Nigel Farage, and have drawn accusations of racism and extremism since a speaker at the first Washington conference argued for an immigration policy of “more whites and fewer nonwhites”. Conference organizer Hazony, reportedly said at that time that the speaker’s views were “legitimate and should be heard and debated”. In 2024 a Brussels mayor ordered police to shut the event down before a court overturned him. The Guardian contacted Hazony for comment. Gorka is listed for a 7 October plenary titled “The Meaning of October 7”, alongside Israel’s diaspora affairs minister, Amichai Chikli, and the former Polish president Andrzej Duda. The Guardian previously reported on a video in which Gorka offered Israeli leaders advice on Hamas: “Kill every single one of them. God bless Israel. God bless Judeo-Christian civilisation.” In August 2024 Smotrich said of Gaza: “Nobody will let us cause 2 million civilians to die of hunger, even though it might be justified and moral, until our hostages are returned.” Britain sanctioned him on 10 June 2025, acting with Australia, Canada, New Zealand and Norway. It held him responsible for “inciting, promoting and/or supporting” abuses, “in particular acts of aggression and violence against Palestinian individuals in the West Bank”. Rabbi Eliyahu, who for decades has served as chief rabbi of Safed, a public office in Israel, remarked of Palestinians in Gaza in a lecture his office posted to YouTube in November 2023, “Drop an atom [bomb] on them? It’s an option,” he said. The disciplinary hearing Israel’s high court ordered in 2020 was reportedly not held until June 2024, and its outcome kept from the public. The conference’s co-sponsors include the Sovereignty Movement and Regavim, the organisation Smotrich founded. The ultranationalist Israeli television news outlet Channel 14 says it is producing the event with Hazony’s foundation and his Herzl Institute. The conference website does not currently list the channel as a partner. The Guardian contacted Channel 14 for comment. One panel is titled “Immigration and Cultural Replacement”. Maaßen’s talk is billed as “Why Elites Embrace Mass Migration as a Tool of Cultural, Racial, and Political Transformation”. A fellow panelist, Nathan Pinkoski of the Center for Renewing America, wrote the introduction to a 2025 edition of The Camp of the Saints, a novel Dreher at one time called “racist”. Dreher appears to have since softened that view. The Guardian contacted Pinkoski for comment. Vilimsky reportedly told a Budapest conference in April 2024: “We do not want Mohammed to become the most common name in our countries.” He is listed for a NatCon plenary on 7 October. Gideon Sa’ar, the foreign minister, who last month welcomed a speech by the FPÖ leader, Herbert Kickl, at a Strasbourg event Vilimsky organised with Likud, as making possible “a substantive, open and sincere dialogue” despite the ongoing disengagement, is listed for the conference dinner on 6 October. Wolfe told a Texas audience in February: “My boys all look like me. And I want my children to grow up in a country where they’re not minorities.” He has called Erickson’s essay “a call for the assassination of a group of conservative Christians”. His conference bio says he served at the state department and the Pentagon in the first Trump administration. As previously reported in the Guardian Haywood’s private foundation gave the Edmund Burke Foundation, which organizes the NatCon conferences, $25,000 for “general operations” in the year to June 2023, its tax filing shows. Hazony’s former communications director was among the Jewish conservatives who criticised him in January, after he blamed an “antisemitism-industrial complex” for failing to make the case against Tucker Carlson. He has since refused Carlson a speaking slot in Jerusalem, and on 28 September called the broadcaster’s show “the leading clearinghouse for antisemitism on the political Right in America”. Taylor, the religion scholar, said: “[Hazony is] still trying to play an older game of drawing boundary lines and saying, oh, there is an antisemitic far right that is the fringe that we have to cut off … But Tucker Carlson is not [fringe]. Tucker Carlson is about as mainstream today in rightwing politics as you can get.” The Guardian contacted the Carlson Network’s press office for comment. McGeever, the antisemitism scholar, wrote: “Yoram Hazony may express bewilderment about this surge of antisemitism, but it is baked into the very political alliances he has forged. His allies have repeatedly promoted ideas about ‘globalist elites’ and ‘secret cabals’ which utilize the same structural logic of antisemitic conspiracy theories.” The conference runs from 6 to 8 October at Jerusalem’s International Convention Center.

title: Germany arrests former intelligence chief over alleged spying
summary: August Hanning served as president of Federal Intelligence Service from 1998 to 2005
text: A former head of Germany’s foreign intelligence service has been arrested on suspicion of treason and spying on behalf of an overseas intelligence agency, in what prosecutors suspect could be the most egregious national security breach since the cold war. August Hanning, 80, was head of the federal intelligence service (BND) – which operates outside Germany to gather information across the fields of political, economic and military intelligence – between 1998 and 2005. He was arrested at his home in Nordwalde near Münster early on Tuesday. His former chief of staff, identified only as Manfred D, was arrested at the same time in Bavaria, on suspicion of “aiding and abetting attempted treason and treasonous espionage”, according to a prosecutor’s statement. Media pictures showed Hanning, dressed in an open-necked white shirt, being taken from his redbrick house to a bullet-proof vehicle by masked officers. Manfred D, who continued to work for Hanning’s successors at the BND after Hanning’s departure until the present day, is accused of using his role to gain access to classified information which he then handed to Hanning “in exchange for payment”, the prosecutors’ statement continued. “The current findings suggest that, over the years, Manfred D provided Hanning with approximately 2,000 documents, many of which contained classified information to be used exclusively by the federal intelligence service for internal purposes, particularly for executive intelligence briefings,” the statement said. Prosecutors believe that Hanning intended to resell the documents as part of a paid consulting role he had built up after leaving the BND, prosecutors added. To what extent and to whom he disseminated them remains part of an ongoing investigation. He is accused of using the information to “draft an analysis for an officer of a foreign intelligence service”, prosecutors said. It was unclear if this information had reached its intended recipient, they added. Over several years, Hanning is also believed to have passed on potentially sensitive political information, in part based on information passed to him by Manfred D, to a close contact representing a separate foreign intelligence service. Hanning and his legal team denied the allegations following his arrest. There was no immediate response from Manfred D. or his legal representatives. Several properties connected to both men were searched simultaneously on Tuesday, including in Berlin. Manfred D is due to appear before judges at the federal court of justice in Karlsruhe later on Tuesday, while Hanning is scheduled to appear on Wednesday. The allegations prompted shock in German political and intelligence circles, where memories resurfaced of historic espionage scandals. Hanning is thought to be the most prominent person to be accused of treason in Germany since Günter Guillaume, one of Willy Brandt’s personal aides, was exposed as a long-term Stasi agent in 1974. The “Guillaume affair” brought an abrupt end to Nobel peace prize-winning Brandt’s career, as he swiftly resigned as chancellor of West Germany. Marc Henrichmann, chair of the Bundestag’s intelligence oversight committee, said in a statement to AFP: “Whoever allies themselves with the enemies of our liberal democracy will be found out.” If proven to be true, Hanning’s alleged behaviour would represent “trampling his official duties underfoot”, he added. Konstantin von Notz of the Greens, a prominent member of the same committee, urged the federal government to establish as soon as possible the “potential intelligence-related damage” that might have been done by Hanning’s alleged betrayal of Germany’s official secrets. “This is a truly outrageous and deeply disturbing story,” he told Der Spiegel. Suspicions over Hanning’s activities emerged as a result of an investigation into the kidnappings of the children from a prominent Hamburg business family, which is the focus of a major trial in the north German port city. Investigators were led to Hanning over allegations, which he denies, that he helped Christina Block, the heiress of a steak restaurant dynasty, to organise the violent cross-border seizure in Denmark of her children from her estranged husband who has custody of two of their children. Block denies the charges. After he left the BND, Hanning worked as a global consultant in the fields of security and business, based on his credentials as former intelligence chief. He is considered to have been well connected with government and business sectors in Russia and China, and also had contacts with top-ranking intelligence authorities in Israel. Hanning was an officer stationed at the embassy-equivalent organisation for West Germany in communist East Berlin. After his role as president of the BND ended in 2005, he became the highest-ranking official in Germany’s security sector as the head of all security agencies under the federal interior minister Wolfgang Schäuble.

title: Argentina will stop Falklands exploiting offshore oilfields, foreign minister says
summary: Pablo Quirno says move is part of Argentinian government’s strategy to peacefully assert sovereignty over the islands
text: Argentina’s foreign minister has told an audience that included the British ambassador that his government would stop the Falkland Islands from exploiting its offshore oilfields as part of a strategy to take sovereignty. During a speech at a thinktank event in the Argentinian capital, Pablo Quirno condemned the British government for failing to open negotiations over the islands and facilitating a significant offshore oil project in its waters. Among those in the audience was David Cairns, the UK’s ambassador to Argentina. Cairns, who was photographed listening to Quirno, left the event shortly after the foreign minister returned to his seat. Quirno told the audience at the event organised by the Argentine Council for International Relations that his country’s president, Javier Milei, had a strategy for the “peaceful” assertion of Argentinian sovereignty. He said: “The British government not only refuses to enter into negotiations to resolve the sovereignty dispute, but is also taking unilateral measures regarding the exploitation of natural resources in the maritime areas that are part of the controversy. “Preventing the exploitation of our resources from consolidating the British occupation is part of a strategy to recover, through peaceful means, the full exercise of our sovereignty.” Last month, Milei told the UN general assembly in New York that the international organisation had failed his country as he condemned the Sea Lion project, an oil development in the North Falkland Basin, as an “unlawful act”. Argentina has accused the UK of flouting a 1976 UN resolution ordering both parties to desist from unilateral action on the islands. On 28 September, Milei gave the UK a two-week deadline stop the oil project or face arbitration and a binding decision under annex VII of the UN convention on the law of the sea (UNCLOS) at the international tribunal for the law of the sea. The UN does not officially recognise British or Argentinian sovereignty and maintains that the archipelago’s status remains a disputed matter that must be resolved through bilateral negotiations. It has repeatedly invited both governments to find a peaceful solution to the dispute that erupted into conflict in 1982 after an invasion by Argentinian forces. The 74-day war ended with the surrender of the Argentinian forces. It cost the lives of 649 Argentinian military personnel, 255 British military personnel and three Falkland islanders. The UK government has said that the islands, known as Las Malvinas in Argentina and which are home to approximately 3,600 people, will remain a British overseas territory for as long as it is the wish of those who live there. In a referendum in 2013, on a turnout of 92%, 99.8% voted to remain a British territory, with only three votes against. In a statement issued last week, the Argentinian government rejected “the manipulation of the principle of self-determination of peoples that the United Kingdom seeks to impose upon it”. In his speech on Monday night, Quirno also warned third parties that they should not assist Falkland islanders in the exploitation of the natural resources. A new shipping link is due to be opened between Chile and the Falkland Islands by the end of the year. Quirno said: “Whoever contributes, directly or indirectly, to the illegitimate exploration or exploitation of resources that belong to all Argentinians will hardly be able to aspire to share in the benefits of our country’s growth.”

title: Australia faces summer of extreme weather, Anthony Albanese warns at pre-Cop
summary: Prime minister tells delegates in Tuvalu and Fiji that ‘super El Niño’ brewing in the Pacific shows climate change is ‘here right now’
text: Anthony Albanese has warned Australia faces a hazardous summer, likely including floods, cyclones and extreme heat, due to the immediate threat of climate breakdown and a rising “super El Niño”. Speaking alongside national leaders at a climate summit in Fiji, the prime minister said the expected nasty summer and the demonstrated impact on Pacific island countries – including low-lying Tuvalu – showed the world could not afford to let the goal of limiting global heating to 1.5C “just slip from our grasp”. “Climate change is not a problem for the future. It is here right now, and we know that sea levels here in the western Pacific are rising at more than twice the global average. We know also that the forecast of super El Niño may test us all,” he said “In Australia, we are expecting a summer of floods, of cyclones, of extreme heat, and extreme behaviour … The science told us that if we didn’t act to address global emissions this is precisely what would occur, and tragically that is playing out.” Albanese’s comments came after a delegation of national and global agency leaders visited Tuvalu to see the impact of the climate crisis on one of the countries most at risk. A collection of three reef islands and six atolls, Tuvalu is home to about 10,000 people and sits mostly less than 2 metres above sea level. The visit was promised by the Albanese government last year as part of a compromise deal when it missed out on hosting the Cop31 climate conference. Cop31 will be in Turkey next month; Fiji and Tuvalu are hosting a preparatory meeting. Tuvalu was wet and grey for the visit, and the capital of Funafuti – spectacular from the air on a clear day – was visible only in strips between heavy rain clouds during descent. After a cultural welcome and a tour of a climate resilience project, leaders held a sautalaga meeting – an exchange of views – where they expressed support for the country and urged more rapid action to cut emissions and provide island states with the money needed to adapt. The delegation heard from Melelusi Sokotia, a 13-year-old local student, who said her friends dreamed of “becoming teachers, doctors, builders” but spent their lives wondering if their island would survive into their adult lives. “We all have one single dream: to grow safely here in Tuvalu,” she said. “We are not asking for peace. We are asking for help and partnership. Please work together to protect small islands like ours.” Tuvalu’s prime minister, Feleti Teo, stressed island states needed faster access to global climate finance to deal with worsening extreme events. “Why should countries like Tuvalu take on more debt to protect ourselves from a climate crisis we did so little to cause? We should not have to borrow our way out of a crisis.” The Fijian prime minister, Sitiveni Rabuka, said the world was on the brink of overshooting the goal of limiting global heating to 1.5C – agreed in the 2015 Paris agreement – and must bring forward plans to cut emissions. “That is not radical. It is in line with our agreement, our obligation, and the scientific reality,” he said. “The transition away from fossil fuels was agreed to by all of us in Dubai [at the Cop28 summit in 2023]. It is not a new ask, and it is not open for renegotiation.” Australia has faced criticism at the talks for arguing for greater climate action while continuing to new expanded coal and gas developments. An Australian state regulator last week approved a major coalmine development that would be the largest in New South Wales’ history if it receives federal approval. Albanese, attending his first UN climate conference as prime minister since his election in 2022, said a message from the Tuvalu trip was that “climate change must be understood as being something more than about science or targets”. “It must be understood that effectively it’s about people,” he said. The delegation, which include former Australian prime minister Julia Gillard, now the chair of health charity Wellcome, were shown a land reclamation project to extend the atoll by about 20 hectares using sand and gravel dredged from its lagoon. Tuvalu’s director of climate change, Jamie Ovia, told the visitors sea level rise was projected to increase the annual cost of damage from flooding and storm surges to US$34m a year by 2050 and $63m – more than Tuvalu’s GDP – by 2100. He said the coastal fishing catch could be reduced by 16% and tuna stocks worth $4m a year could be lost as seas warmed. “We need time to adapt,” Ovia said. “Tuvalu is doing our part. Will you act with Tuvalu, and will you act in time?”

title: Former UN food agency official claims he was fired for highlighting hunger in Gaza
summary: Benjamin Davis appealing against dismissal from FAO, after being accused by director general of playing ‘political games’
text: A former senior UN food agency official has alleged he was fired last week for his work highlighting hunger in Gaza, and has launched an appeal against his dismissal. Benjamin Davis said the leadership of the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) had refused to renew his contract as director of its rural transformation and gender equality division because his team had published a brief on hunger in Gaza and held a seminar on the subject last year, and because he had taken part in weekly “moment of silence” vigils on FAO grounds for those killed. The seminar on hunger in Gaza last September triggered a complaint from the Israeli mission to the FAO, which also sent a diplomat to take pictures of staff taking part a moment of silence gathering last October, according to a FAO staff report filed at the time. Davis, 62 and a Spanish-American dual citizen, left the FAO last week after 26 years of service. Video of the event shows FAO staff standing and applauding him as he left the Rome headquarters for the last time. “It’s a nice feeling that I’m not alone, that other people are behind me in this,” Davis said. “I was stopped constantly in the hallways by people, even those that I didn’t know, just to shake my hand or just to thank me or just to say that they supported me or that they were upset.” The FAO did not respond to the Guardian’s request for comment on Monday, but the organisation’s director general, Qu Dongyu, appeared to refer to Davis’s dismissal in public remarks last Tuesday, in which he threatened to fire more people for what he deemed to be political activism. “We are not going to allow you to play the game here of human rights,” said Qu, a veteran Chinese agronomist. “Of course human rights are very important, but they have a human rights agency in Geneva. If you want to take care [of human rights], go there.” “Thats why [when] some senior members play political games here, I fire him,” he said, suggesting that Davis had violated staff regulations. “I’m a very soft person. I didn’t fire that many. I’m going to use my last year … to fire more if they’re against the law.” Davis said he and fellow FAO staff members had been stunned by Qu’s remarks. “Even more than the threat about firing people was just what he said about human rights. I think that really shocked people because it undermined the foundations of why we’re here basically, or why FAO is part of the United Nations and why the United Nations exists,” he said. “We’re surely an organisation which is based on human rights, right?” Davis added, pointing to the FAO slogan: “Leave no one behind.” The official letter informing Davis that his contract would not be renewed said that Qu was “no longer confident in your ability to discharge your obligations in the manner required of a senior international civil servant”. The letter cited paragraphs in the official code of conduct for international civil servants regarding “honesty, truthfulness, impartiality and incorruptibility” and limits on public expression of personal views on “controversial matters”. In his written response, Davis said that approach taken by FAO leadership was “simply wrong”. “Silence in the face of suffering and injustice is not neutrality, it is complicity,” he wrote. “Shutting down discussion on the starvation of the Palestinian people weakens the reputation of the organisation and the legitimacy of our mandate. Being true to our mandate calls for a frank and open discussion around starvation, famine, and genocide in Palestine and elsewhere.” Davis said that FAO leadership had previously criticised him for a briefing paper published by his team in May last year describing the level of hunger in Gaza and setting it in the context of international humanitarian law. “The current conditions in the Gaza Strip … reflect a gross violation of the right to food and the unlawful obstruction of humanitarian assistance,” the report said. It was removed from the FAO website a few weeks later on the orders of its leadership. Davis led a seminar on the same subject in September 2025, which led to a complaint from the Israeli mission to the FAO and other Rome-based international agencies. Davis said he had also been criticised for taking part in moment of silence gatherings held by concerned staff in the FAO car park every Thursday, in remembrance of those in Gaza who had died of hunger. There was an altercation there on 23 October when a woman identifying herself as an Israeli diplomat appeared and took photographs of those attending. “The person explained she was the permanent representative of Israel, and asked if we were allowed to do these events, and asked specifically who says we could not take photographs,” a report by a FAO witness on the day of the incident said. On being told she could not take photographs, the woman complained to FAO security that she was being harassed, the report said. The Israeli embassy in Rome said it had no comment on the report. Davis said that the Gaza briefing paper, the associated seminar, and the weekly moments of silence had all been approved by FAO management, and he had not been told at the time that they represented violations of the code of conduct. He said he had lodged a formal appeal against his dismissal. “I filed the appeal mostly as a matter of principle, not because I’m looking for or expecting any monetary compensation or anything like that,” Davis said. “I have requested to be reinstated, and also for them to take back the accusations that they made against me.”

title: Nobel prize in physics goes to Francis Halzen for south pole work on neutrinos
summary: Belgian physicist praised for work on the IceCube detector that observes the ghost-like particles in Antarctica
text: The Nobel prize in physics 2026 has been awarded to a researcher who turned an enormous block of ice at the south pole into a detector for ghostly particles called neutrinos that reach Earth from outer space. Prof Francis Halzen, a Belgian particle physicist at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, led work on the IceCube neutrino observatory, which made the first detection of high-energy extraterrestrial neutrinos in 2013, soon after it was switched on. To build the observatory, scientists, technicians and engineers embedded thousands of basketball-sized light detectors into a cubic kilometre of ice to detect faint flashes of light that can result when neutrinos from space crash into atomic nuclei. Announcing the prize on Tuesday, the Nobel committee said Halzen won “for decisive contributions to the IceCube neutrino observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin”. He receives a prize of 12m Swedish kronor (about £900,000). “It feels strange,” Halzen told a press briefing on winning the prize. “I hope it reflects on the really courageous people who joined me in the beginning of this project when no really respectable, conservative physicist would have joined me, but many talented people did.” Neutrinos are mysterious particles that are as elusive as they are ubiquitous. They pass through almost everything they encounter, from people to planets. Every second, billions of neutrinos from the sun pass unnoticed through the body. But every now and then, a neutrino will interact with the nucleus of an atom in a collision that can be picked up by a sensitive detector. Halzen realised that brief flickers of light from neutrino collisions could be detected in clear, glacial ice and in 1988 put forward a plan to convert a chunk of the south pole into a neutrino observatory. The detector uses Earth to shield against the background noise of cosmic rays, and has downwards-facing light sensors to detect neutrinos passing through the planet from the northern hemisphere. Apart from a hostile environment for the team, the site benefited from being far from sources of interference and the risk of vibrations from earthquakes. After the first detection of high-energy extraterrestrial neutrinos in 2013, scientists working on IceCube identified the first cosmic source of neutrinos 3.7bn light years away. The observatory has paved the way for a new kind of astronomy. Until now, researchers have learned about the cosmos from light, other electromagnetic radiation, and gravitational waves. Neutrinos are considered messengers from the cosmos and provide fresh clues as to how the universe evolved. Halzen, who received the news while travelling in Italy, said he was working on a new proposal and hoped that winning the prize would help in getting it approved. Dr Patrick Dunne at Imperial College London welcomed the prize. “For all of human history the only way we’ve been able to understand things outside our solar system is with light. Detecting neutrinos from astrophysical sources opens up a new lens, so it isn’t overstating things to liken this to when Galileo first pointed a telescope at the stars,” he said. “Neutrinos are the most abundant massive particles and their ability to pass through matter much more easily than light makes them ideal for observing distant phenomena or the inside of extreme phenomena like those seen by IceCube,” he added. Other experiments to understand neutrinos include the Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (Dune) in the US and the Hyper-Kamiokande detector in Japan. The observations of cosmic neutrinos have led some scientists to speculate that the ghostly particles could be used by alien civilisations to send messages across the universe. Asked what he made of the idea, Halzen said: “I don’t think I’ll go there. We have enough realistic problems to deal with right now [to] make neutrino astronomy a reality rather than worry about this.” But he added that when astronomers have opened new windows on the universe, they often make unexpected discoveries. “I’m sure this will be true for neutrinos 50 years from now,” he said. On Monday, three scientists won the Nobel prize in medicine for optogenetics, a powerful technique that has allowed researchers to shed unprecedented light on the workings of the brain. The Nobel prize in chemistry is announced on Wednesday.
