title: Misuse of AI is brands’ top reputational threat, new survey says
summary: The findings come after warnings from tech leaders that AI placed in the wrong hands could trigger larger threats such as nuclear war or bioweaponry destruction
text: Misusing artificial intelligence (AI) is the top threat to companies’ reputations – more so than being accused of putting children in the way of mental, emotional or physical harm and issues exposed by the US-Israel war on Iran, among other brand risks, according to a new survey of more than 150 public affairs leaders. Those findings in the new edition of the quarterly Reputation Risk Index, released on Tuesday, came on the heels of other perhaps more dire warnings from leading tech figures that AI in the wrong hands could precipitate existential threats on a mass scale such as nuclear war or destruction by bioweaponry. The index’s publisher, the Global Risk Advisory Council, acknowledged that misuse of AI is not a particularly new concern in its area of focus, having been identified as a top worry repeatedly since the first edition of the survey in April 2025. But the council said what was new was its attaching an advisory to its latest survey advising business leaders to “take immediate and decisive action to mitigate potential long-term brand damage” with respect to AI, as the technology has “become a clear and present danger to public confidence for many corporations”. “As AI is rapidly deployed for productivity gains, we have also seen diminishing public trust in the technology, elevating the need for businesses to take measures to protect their brands,” council chair Isabel Casillas Guzman said in a statement. “In this environment, AI use or overuse can quickly damage a company’s standing with customers, investors, or other key stakeholders, making it essential for companies to deploy preventive tactics now.” The creators of the council and the Reputation Risk Index – the Washington DC-based public affairs firm Global Situation Room – said such tactics include removing or reducing the use of AI content and relying on humans for customer service. The Global Situation Room said that the Reputation Risk Index released on Tuesday surveyed former heads of state, government ministers and senior executives from more than 20 countries in five continents who were invited to participate after establishing their credentials in responding to crises. Respondents to that survey collectively perceived the technology to have shown great promise in creating “organizational efficiency” – while simultaneously “accelerating safety and data concerns, hacks, fraud, straining privacy protections, upending the workforce, and dragging companies into court as lawsuits increasingly link AI products to real-world harm”. Meanwhile, actions or accusations of putting children at risk of mental, emotional or physical harm also ranked highly behind misused AI – along with infringing individuals’ sensitive information, according to the index results published on Tuesday. Unethical or illegal behavior used to gain a strategic advantage or profit and, separately, poor strategic or operational decisions resulting in reduced financial or public standing rounded out the top five, according to the index. The index noted that its preceding edition released in July identified supply chain issues, divisive political stances and other factors associated with the war that the Trump’s administration started in Iran alongside Israel as the leading risk to companies’ reputations. But those surveyed indicated that those anxieties had eased as the conflict dragged out – and perhaps despite it remaining unresolved since it was launched in February. “The geopolitical shock … hasn’t gone away, but its first, sharpest reputational blow has faded, and the conflict has slipped out of the top tier [of concerns] even as it grinds on,” Guzman said in a “message from the chair” included in the index. Guzman put out her message two days after Donald Trump’s administration named a new AI czar: the director of national intelligence, Jay Clayton. The president said in a social media post that Clayton would oversee an entity coordinating “the federal government’s engagement with consumers, public interest groups, religious organizations, critical infrastructure providers, and” AI tech companies. Clayton had previously told federal lawmakers that AI was a “gamechanger” but also posed “a threat”.

title: Democrats upbeat as unpopular Trump imperils Republican midterm hopes
summary: Polls show GOP candidates trailing Democrats in Senate races, and Republicans also struggling in House contests
text: Thirty days remain until the midterm elections, and Donald Trump and his Republican allies are pulling out all the stops to maintain control of Congress. Super Pacs aligned with the GOP have already spent hundreds of millions of dollars on advertising and voter outreach in races expected to decide the majorities in the Senate and House of Representatives, and plan to spend even more before the election is over. The president, Vice-President JD Vance, and other top Republicans are fanning out across the country to stump for vulnerable lawmakers. So far, there are no signs the money or the rallies have improved what appears to be a grim state of affairs for Republicans, less than two years after their resounding victories in the 2024 election. Recently released polls continue to show the party’s candidates trailing their Democratic challengers in the Senate races that will decide the majority and control of the chamber. “Candidate quality is beating gobs of Republican money,” the Senate’s Democratic minority leader, Chuck Schumer, quipped over the weekend, when the New York Times released the latest in a series of closely watched polls that confirmed the momentum behind their bid to retake the Senate. The surveys, conducted with Siena University, found Democratic Senate candidates leading in Alaska, Ohio and Texas – all states Trump won by double digits two years ago. In Kansas, which has not elected a Democrat to the Senate in 94 years, the party’s candidate Adam Hamilton was neck-and-neck with the Republican senator Roger Marshall, while in Iowa, Democrat Josh Turek is narrowly trailing the Republican candidate, Ashley Hinson. Democratic candidates for governor were also leading in many traditionally Republican states, the Times and Siena found. “If the election were held tomorrow, all state wide races [would] go blue,” Briscoe Cain, a Republican state representative in Texas wrote on X Monday. The Democrats’ Senate candidate James Talarico and gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa were both leading in the Times and Siena survey. “Republican voters feel too comfortable and are not as intense about this election as they should be. We have more voters than the left in Texas, but we have to vote,” Cain added. Last Friday, the news outlet Semafor reported that the Senate Leadership Fund, a major GOP Super Pac, planned to pull money from the campaign of its candidate Michael Whatley in North Carolina, in favor of upping support for Marshall in Kansas. No Democrat has won a US Senate election in North Carolina since 2008, but Whatley has trailed in polls for months. Democrats need to win at least four seats in the chamber to regain the majority they lost in the 2024 election. The situation for Democrats appears to be similarly positive in their campaign to retake the House, which Republicans control only narrowly. A CBS News and YouGov poll released on Sunday found Democrats with a nine percentage point lead on the generic ballot, an important indicator of voter intention in congressional races. A Reuters/Ipsos poll released on Monday found Trump’s approval ratings remained at the lowest point of his career, with only 32% of adult respondents approving of his performance as president. Independent voters – whose views often make the difference in close races – planned to back Democrats by a 16-percentage-point margin, though many remained undecided. The president’s poor marks are believed to be a major cause of the Republican candidates’ struggles nationwide, but are far from the only one. Discontent over the state of the economy – particularly the price of gasoline and other consumer staples – is another reason, as is the on-again, off-again conflict with Iran, and concern over Trump’s hardline approach to enforcing immigration laws. Republicans maintain they have avenues to victory in both chambers of Congress. Eight House Republicans represent districts that voted for Kamala Harris in 2024, as opposed to 22 House Democrats representing districts Trump won – a number that has grown larger thanks to the unprecedented redistricting war Trump instigated. Many polls show voters have an unfavorable perception of the Democratic party, though views of Republicans are similarly negative. And despite strong fundraising by some Democratic candidates, Republicans and groups allied with their agenda have an edge in cash to spend on this election. It may not be enough to halt the disintegration that appears to be occurring in the coalition that elected Trump two years ago. Only 26% of Hispanic voters – who swung towards Trump after years of leaning Democratic – plan to vote for Republicans this year, while 52% prefer the Democrats, the Reuters/Ipsos poll found. “We’ve been seeing among Latino voters, as we’ve been seeing kind of in the electorate as a whole, a real strong rejection of the Trump administration, and that has inflated into an increase in support for Democratic candidates,” said Maria Isabel Di Franco Quinonez, a senior research director at Equis Research, a progressive firm that focuses on the community. Should the trend hold, it could bode well for Democrats’ hopes in states and districts with large Latino populations. The effect may be pronounced in Texas, where the Republican leaders drew new congressional maps to favor their candidates, but only if Latino voters continue voting the way they did in 2024. “If we see those levels continue to rise and see those districts look more like the kinds of support levels for Democrats that we had seen back in 2018, then that would result in maybe Republicans get one more seat after redrawing all the lines, as opposed to getting four or five more seats,” Quinonez said.

title: Drax datacentre could create nearly twice the yearly emissions of all Gatwick flights
summary: Exclusive: Campaign group’s analysis of North Yorkshire plans finds datacentre would have to burn 4.9m tonnes of wood a year
text: Drax’s planned datacentre could produce nearly double the emissions of all flights out of Gatwick airport each year by burning 4.9m tonnes of wood annually, an analysis has shown. Campaigners say this would make it “one of the dirtiest datacentres out there”. Last year, the energy company Drax unveiled plans to convert part of its biomass power plant in North Yorkshire into a datacentre in response to the increase in demand for AI capability. AI datacentres use a massive amount of electricity to power servers and cooling equipment, and to run facility systems. There are 315 datacentres in the queue to connect to the UK’s electricity grid, representing 73GW of demand. This is almost double the peak winter energy demand for the entire UK. In public documents, Drax says it is developing options for a 1.2GW datacentre, with 100MW of this energy coming from the electricity grid and the rest from its own power station. The Drax power station currently burns millions of tonnes of imported wood to create energy. This has been touted as a clean way of producing energy that could even result in “negative emissions”, as replacement forests take up CO2 from the air when they are grown. However, scientists and environmental experts strongly contest this accounting approach, with researchers finding such systems could take 150 years to be “carbon negative”. Based on information in Drax’s 2025 annual report, the Natural Resources Defense Council (NRDC) estimated that if built, Drax’s datacentre will require 4.9m tonnes of wood each year. The campaign group calculated the total emissions from this to be 8.6m tonnes of CO2 a year. This is based on an assumption that the datacentre would run at a constant rate for all hours of the year. This is nearly double the total CO2 emissions of all flights from Gatwick airport, which measured 4.79m tonnes in 2024. Matt Williams, a senior advocate for NRDC, said this would make it “one of the dirtiest datacentres out there”. Oliver Hayes, head of policy at the campaign group Global Action Plan, said, “Burning millions of trees to power server farms is indefensible.” The datacentre has not yet entered the formal planning process but Drax said it could be fully operational from 2031 if secured the necessary consents. “The government must urgently set minimum standards for datacentres and rule out dirty energy generation like burning trees,” Williams said. There is growing pressure for more transparency over how these energy intensive datacentres will align with the government’s legally binding net zero targets. In response to previous reports that just two planned datacentres in Buckinghamshire and Bedfordshire will have higher UK carbon emissions than ExxonMobil, Toby Perkins, a Labour MP and chair of the Commons environmental audit committee, said: “Without the right measures in place, datacentres could represent a serious threat to the environment and to our legally binding climate goals.” Hayes said the absence of coordinated government policy was a “dereliction of duty”. “The only sensible solution at this point is a moratorium on datacentres until very basic questions about how many we need, what for, where, and how pollution will be avoided are answered satisfactorily by the government,” he added. The government has previously ruled out issuing a moratorium on datacentres, stating that doing so would send investment and good jobs abroad. In Scotland, MPs voted in September to pause all new datacentre planning applications for up to a year until a national strategy can be developed. A Drax spokesperson said: “The potential plans for datacentres at Drax Power Station can support UK economic growth as well as helping meet the government’s ambitions for industrial renewal, in places like North Yorkshire, as well as AI sovereignty. “NRDC are a longstanding anti-biomass campaign group and have no positive vision for our Selby site. Their inaccurate assertions are not independently verified and are rooted in basic errors regarding the international standards for GHG accounting of biomass and bioenergy and on the potential datacentres’ power mix.”

title: New Jersey congresswoman faces deadline in Trump case days after giving birth
summary: LaMonica McIver is only the 15th member of Congress have a baby while serving, and also the only member indicted for visiting ICE facility
text: A US congresswoman who just gave birth to a baby girl faces a deadline this week on whether to seek a rehearing of a federal case against her by the Trump administration after an oversight visit to an immigration detention facility. LaMonica McIver, 40, represents New Jersey’s 10th congressional district. She gave birth to her second child last Thursday – a rarity for a sitting member of Congress. She is only the 15th member of Congress to give birth while serving and part of a small subset of congresswomen who have school-age children. McIver first won her seat during a special election in mid-2024, then won a full term later that year. She is also running for re-election this year. In announcing the birth of her second child after publicly discussing fertility struggles, McIver called being a mom “one of the greatest joys of my life”. “Getting the chance to raise a family is a priority and a delight for me, something I hope everyone who wants to, gets the chance to do,” she said in a statement last week. “Bringing a child into the world is a reminder not only of why we fight for maternal healthcare and reproductive rights, but of why we fight for the rights and freedoms of our most vulnerable – they are someone’s babies too.” In late August, a federal appeals court declined to dismiss criminal charges against McIver, who is charged with interfering with an arrest in May 2025 outside Delaney Hall, an immigration detention facility that has drawn protests over poor conditions inside. She is the only member of Congress whom the Department of Justice has indicted, and the charges carry a potential 17 years in prison. She has pleaded not guilty to the charges and sought to get them dismissed, arguing that she is immune from prosecution under the US constitution’s speech and debate clause because she was doing her job and that she has been selectively prosecuted by the Trump administration. McIver and her legal team will need to decide by 9 October whether to seek a rehearing or en banc hearing before the third circuit court of appeals in New Jersey in the case, basically a further review of the case by the full appellate court. She could also ask the US supreme court to consider the appellate court’s decision, or let the case go to trial. McIver previously told the Guardian that the case against her was part of a pattern of intimidation and retaliation by the Trump administration against those who disagree with the president or try to hold him accountable. “This is about intimidation. It’s about bullying,” McIver said last year. “It’s about trying to stop our level of government from having oversight and holding this administration accountable.” Charging documents in the case noted that people, including members of Congress, surrounded the Newark mayor, Ras Baraka, outside Delaney Hall to prevent his arrest and alleged that McIver shouted “hell no” repeatedly. The Washington Post, after analyzing video from many angles, said McIver “made contact with at least two agents” in the scuffle, but that it was “difficult to discern the force of the contact and to what extent it was intentional or the result of the chaotic moment”. In a radio interview in September, McIver described the situation outside Delaney Hall that day as “very chaotic, very scary”, noting that armed federal agents were surrounding her and her congressional colleagues. She called the charges “dangerous for all members of Congress on both sides of the aisle, not just for me”. McIver has spoken about the challenge of doing her job, managing the case and fundraising to pay for legal fees as a relatively new member of Congress, especially while pregnant and caring for her older daughter, who is 10. In a profile with Elle magazine, McIver said that she “couldn’t put the world on pause” while contending with her legal case and her dream of another child. “Now, instead of just running for reelection – which, to be fair, I am also doing – I spend my days writing bills about bringing down energy costs and protecting food stamps, and my nights talking to lawyers about how to keep standing up to ICE without being sent to prison,” she told Elle. Members of Congress do not get paid parental leave, McIver noted in her announcement, adding that she plans to return to voting in November after taking October to heal and spend time with her new baby.

title: ‘Using the presidency to line his pockets’: could claims of corruption fuel backlash against Trump?
summary: Experts say president is vulnerable amid discontent over rising prices
text: In Donald Trump’s telling, he’s a model of incorruptible self-sacrifice. “I’m the only president that donated his salary,” he told a group of cheering supporters at a Hispanic heritage month celebration in the White House last week, before conceding that George Washington – “a very wealthy person” – might have beaten him to the punch. “They pay me $550,000 a year, and in my first term, I donated it,” he continued. “In my second term I donated it too. I donated it to fixing the White House. I donated the salary into the White House preservation.” Trump’s ethical self-depiction was undercut in startling fashion a day later when the crypto company that runs his memecoin offered “the most exclusive dinner in the world” at the president’s members-only Trump National club in Washington. “Join three legends and featured speaker Donald J Trump,” gushed the invite to the 185 biggest investors in the Trump coin. The top 29 buyers were promised an invitation to an additional “VIP reception with your favourite president and one of the legends”. For the top four donors, a Trump 18-karat gold watch lay in store. The aim appeared to be to boost sales of the memecoin – called $Trump – over the next two months. Trump personally profits from the coin, and disclosures show he made about $636m from it last year. With just over a month to go before November’s midterm elections, Democrats seized on the dinner invitation as a political gift as they try to convert concerns over Trump’s perceived corruption into a groundswell of outrage. They theorize it will power a “blue wave” that could enable the party to retake control of the House of Representatives and the Senate on 3 November. “Donald Trump is vying to become the most corrupt person to ever walk the face of the earth,” posted Chuck Schumer, the Democrats’ leader in the US Senate. With the US president’s approval ratings already at record lows amid discontent over rising living costs fueled by the unpopular war with Iran, ethics experts say “unprecedented” levels of corruption engaged in by Trump, his family and close associates are sufficiently serious to make him vulnerable to a popular backlash. The question is whether the myriad of accusations – many of them technical in nature – are straightforward enough to carry popular resonance. The administration vigorously rejects the assertions, which a White House spokesman, Davis Ingle, called “irresponsible” and likely to “reinforce the public’s distrust in what they read”. “President Trump only acts in the best interests of the American public – which is why they overwhelmingly re-elected him to this office, despite years of lies and false accusations against him and his businesses,” he said in a statement. “There are no conflicts of interest. “The only special interest guiding President Trump’s decision-making is the best interest of the American people. President Trump has taken on a broad swath of entrenched special interests: negotiating most-favored-nation pricing deals with major pharmaceutical companies, launching TrumpRx.gov to lower drug prices, ending unfair trade practices that international corporations have exploited to offshore jobs, and implementing schedule F to fire unelected bureaucrats who actively subvert a democratically-elected president’s agenda. “Through these actions, President Trump is delivering on his promise to empower the forgotten men and women of our country by finally putting their interests first.” Recent surveys, however, indicate American voters are more concerned than ever before about government corruption. A Gallup poll published in September recorded 89% of both all adults as saying the problem was widespread. Only Lebanon, Peru, Ghana and Nigeria have registered higher levels of public concern in the past three years. Analysts insist the US public has ample cause for complaint. “We’re facing an ethics crisis which starts and ends with a president who is constantly using his office to find new ways to personally profit,” said Jordan Libowitz, communications vice-president with Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, a non-partisan watchdog. “With a new story every day about Donald Trump using the presidency to line his pockets, it’s no surprise that Americans are losing faith in their government.” Trump’s own filings show he earned $2.2bn from his various business dealings in his first year back in the White House – including $1.4bn from his family’s cryptocurrency enterprise, World Liberty Financial. Observers identify at least three main areas of potential abuse; crypto, a venture which Trump denounced as a “fraud” just five years ago; stock trading by government officials, including the president himself; and the predictions markets, represented by companies such as Kalshi and Polymarket, both of which have links to Donald Trump Jr, and which have raised concerns about well-connected figures profiting through putting bets on government decisions and the content of official speeches. There are also concerns about the growth of “pay to play” practices that have seen wealthy donors being granted special access and favorable decisions, including dropped criminal investigations, in exchange for donations to Trump’s campaign and political Super Pac. Presidential pardons and sentence commutations have been doled out to those who have contributed to the president’s re-election effort. As Schumer’s post indicates, Democrats have increasingly tried to make corruption a campaign issue. A 30-second advertisement from Chris Pappas, a New Hampshire representative running for re-election, reflects a more widespread mood in favor of putting it center stage. The question is whether the message on rampant graft is cutting through with an electorate that may find inflation and higher living costs easier issues to grapple with. Dylan Hedtler-Gaudette, director of government affairs at the Project on Government Oversight, another watchdog group, acknowledged that many voters were confused by the complexity of the accusations leveled at Trump. “Support for the Trump administration and for President Trump himself is declining pretty rapidly,” he said. “But it’s hard to disentangle. Is it about the corruption? Or is it about the affordability crisis continuing and in some ways getting worse? “Corruption tends to be in the eye of the beholder. And if you ask different people about the word corruption, they say, ‘Yeah, it’s a problem.’ But if you ask them to define what they mean by corruption, it can diverge wildly depending on how they affiliate and how they identify in terms of their partisanship and their political identity.” Brendan Fischer, director of strategic investigation at the Campaign Legal Center, said the public had been overwhelmed and “numbed” by a “fire hose” of corruption emanating from Trump’s second presidency which, experts agree, has greatly exceeded that of his first administration. “It can become overwhelming trying to keep up with each of the latest examples,” said Fischer. “I think the Trump’s crypto dealings are incredibly concerning. His investments in the crypto industry open up new avenues for wealthy special interests to channel money to the president. But It’s potentially harder for the public to grasp. So it hasn’t broken through in the way that it that it probably should.” Easier to grasp, he believed, was Trump’s acceptance of a $400m plane from Qatar, which the president has said he will use in place of the existing Air Force One. The scale and brazenness of Trump’s cavalier disregard for ethical considerations creates a danger of apathy among voters, who may feel they are powerless to change the situation as they grapple with more quotidian cost issues. “It’s easy to just throw your hands up and say, ‘Everybody’s corrupt, nobody’s representing my interests, and my life is just not getting any better,’” Fischer said. “That is a dangerous situation for democracy. We need voters to cast their ballots and then remain engaged in the political process to make sure our elected officials are representing the interests of voters and not just their own or the interests of their donors.” Richard Painter, a former White House ethics lawyer under George W Bush, said Trump’s decision to go war with Iran opened up further corruption avenues – citing reports that both Donald Trump Jr and his brother, Eric Trump, have invested in drone manufacturers that have secured government contracts. “Whenever there’s a war, there’s an enormous amount of money to be made. People say there are those who die in a war, and those who become millionaires, or maybe in this case billionaires,” said Painter, now a corporate law professor at the University of Minnesota. “This is what President Eisenhower talked about with the military-industrial complex back in 1961, but we’ve never had a president whose family actually made money from the military-industrial complex.” Painter predicted that conditions were ripe for “an enormous public backlash” but said the Democrats had to adopt a credible anti-corruption message after losing the public’s confidence by failing to speak out against Hunter Biden’s attempts to leverage his White House access when his father Joe Biden was president. “The Democrats had their chance in 2021 when Biden took office, when we should have had our reawakening on ethics, and they failed,” he said. “If they want to win races not only in 2026, but in 2028, they’d better get their act together and focus on ethics.” One historical model, Painter suggested, was the anti-corruption crusade championed by Jimmy Carter in his successful 1976 presidential campaign, which took place amid lingering anger at Richard Nixon over the Watergate scandal that drove him from office and his failure to quickly end the war in Vietnam. Democrats have invoked a more recent inspiration: Hungary’s recently elected prime minister, Peter Magyar, who mobilized rising resentment over government corruption in April this year to unseat the incumbent, Viktor Orbán – a close ally of Trump – in an election landslide. Steven Levitsky, a political scientist at Harvard University and co-author, with Daniel Ziblatt, of How Democracies Die, said the key similarity between the US and Hungarian circumstances was the sense of corruption further undermining an already failing government. “Orbán was successful in part because the economy was pretty good for much of his period in office,” Levitsky said. “But eventually it slowed down, and corruption became a major factor. “It’s sad but true that in many, many cases in democracies around the world, if incumbents are perceived to be delivering – if the economy is going well, if they brought down inflation, etc – voters will turn a blind eye to corruption. It’s only when you combine poor performance with corruption that it becomes salient. “Unfortunately, in the United States, one of the things that’s benefited Trump is the perception that all of politics is corrupt, mainly because of the extraordinarily outsized role of money in politics. “There are a lot of reasons why Trump is unpopular now. Corruption is one of them but I don’t think it’s the principal one.”

title: US households pay 62% more for water than they did a decade ago, study finds
summary: For-profit water corporations, federal cuts and climate crisis are ‘supercharging water rate hikes’, study co-author says
text: US households are paying 62% more for drinking water than they did a decade ago – outpacing inflation, grocery prices and household incomes, according to a new study. Food & Water Watch, a Washington DC-based non-profit, analyzed 2025 billing data from the 500 largest community water systems in the US, which together serve about 155 million people, or 45% of the country’s population. The analysis compared current rates with data from a similar Food & Water Watch survey conducted in 2015. The study does not include wastewater or storm water charges, which are often billed separately from drinking water service. In 2025, the average household using 60,000 gallons of water paid $531 for drinking water service, according to the study. However, costs varied widely, with annual bills ranging from $133 at the cheapest system to $1,416 at the most expensive. Water prices rose 1.6 times faster than overall inflation between 2015 and 2025. Consumer prices increased 39% during that period, compared with a 62% jump in water bills, according to the study. Water costs also rose more than twice as fast as groceries, which increased 30%, and eggs, which rose 28%. Water bills also rose faster than household incomes, increasing 19% more than the national median household income between 2014 and 2024, the study found. Mary Grant, Food & Water Watch’s water program director and a co-author of the study, said: “Water bills are increasing much faster than many households can keep up with and these escalating water costs impact every corner of the country. Low-income households are being hit the hardest. “Corporate water abuses, federal disinvestment and climate change are supercharging water rate hikes across the country.” The increases were particularly severe in some states. Water bills in New Hampshire jumped 177% over the decade, followed by Oregon at 114% and West Virginia at 95%. In Louisiana, Maryland and West Virginia, water bills grew at roughly twice the rate of state median household incomes, while in New Hampshire water bills increased nearly five times faster. The study also found a major disparity between publicly owned and for-profit water systems. Corporate-owned utilities charged the average household $823 a year, compared with $494 for publicly owned systems – a difference of $329, or 67%. Corporate systems accounted for just 11% of the 500 systems the study analyzed but represented 44% of the 25 most expensive systems. The study added that 70% of the top 10 were owned by for-profit corporations. California accounted for 52% of the 25 most expensive water systems. By contrast, all 25 of the least expensive systems were publicly owned. About 60% of the least expensive systems were in the south, including many in Florida and Georgia, the study found. Water was even less affordable for low-income households, according to the study. Water bills exceeded the study’s affordability threshold in 93% of systems, costing more than 1.5% of income for the poorest fifth of households. Only Idaho and Utah stayed below the threshold. West Virginia and Puerto Rico faced the heaviest financial burdens, the study found. Water bills consumed about 11% of income for low-income households in West Virginia and roughly 20% in Puerto Rico, which the study described as “simply unaffordable by any metric”. Grant of Food & Water Watch said water systems must make updates to repair “ageing water lines and help clean up toxic contamination from lead pipes, Pfas forever chemicals, nitrate pollution from industrial agriculture, the list goes on”. She added: “Corporate control of water systems exacerbates this affordability crisis, as big water monopolies take away local control, prioritize profit and hike water prices even higher.” Grant said communities could face increasingly difficult choices as they struggle to secure additional public investment. “Without real solutions to hold polluters accountable, establish local affordability programs and expand federal support, systems serving vulnerable communities could face the impossible choice: forgo an urgent water safety project or price many out of water service,” she said. In a separate statement, the American Water Works Association (AWWA), a non-profit whose membership includes more than 4,300 utilities supplying roughly 80% of North America’s drinking water and treating nearly half its wastewater, pointed to infrastructure renewal, resilience and regulatory requirements as key cost drivers threatening drinking water affordability. “If communities rely exclusively on revenue from water bills to address these needs, average annual household drinking water bills would rise from $429 in 2025 to $969 by 2050 (2025 dollars) – more than doubling in real terms,” Greg Kail, an AWWA spokesperson, said. “That would mean an estimated 30.4m households – or 21.5% – would spend more than 2.5% of their income on drinking water, and 53.5m households – 37.8% – would exceed a 1.5% income threshold. An estimated $13.6bn per year in assistance would be needed by 2050 to keep water bills below commonly understood affordability benchmarks,” Kail added. Meanwhile, the National Association of Water Companies (NAWC), a trade association representing privately owned water and wastewater utilities, said it had not reviewed the Food & Water Watch study but emphasized the growing costs of maintaining water systems. “Affordability is a legitimate challenge for many households and one that NAWC and its members take seriously,” an NAWC spokesperson, Jenn Kocher, said, citing costs tied to ageing infrastructure, Pfasand lead regulations, cybersecurity and severe weather. Kocher also highlighted customer-assistance programs offered by private water companies, saying: “Many regulated, private water companies offer robust assistance programs that help low-income customers maintain service and manage bills. These programs are often overlooked in rate comparisons. “By comparison, many government-owned utilities face legal or other restrictions on cross-subsidizing customers, which can limit the types of assistance programs they are able to provide,” she added. “Evaluating affordability based solely on published rate schedules can produce a misleading picture of what many customers actually pay after assistance and conservation programs are taken into account,” Kocher continued.

title: ‘Spit on our sacrifice’: Canadian veterans fume after Trump and allies take jibes at military
summary: Military families say Trump officials ‘owe us an apology’ after disparaging remarks by JD Vance, Pete Hegseth and others
text: On the morning of 11 September 2001, Perry Chalmers was running drills for the Royal Canadian Regiment’s specialised mortar platoon in New Brunswick when he heard the news: America was under attack. Word quickly spread across the base. “I went inside to watch the news,” the former corporal recalls. “And there was a huge feeling of – and you’re going to have to excuse me – holy shit. What the fuck just happened?” Chalmers called his wife, who informed him that, just before 10.30am, the second of the World Trade Center towers had fallen. With that, his battalion was put on notice: dispatched to nearby airports to assist in the forced landings of commercial aircraft after the shutdown of North American airspace. The Canadian troops went to retrieve their rucksacks and any other necessities, should they need to spring into action at a moment’s notice. As Chalmers recalls: “Things started to happen really quickly.” Chalmers would deploy to Afghanistan, on a nine-month tour of combat duty, where he saw combat alongside US troops. He put his mortar platoon training to good use, as a counter-IED engineer, dealing with the threat of improvised explosives in conjunction with the US army’s 10th Mountain Division. He was one of more than 40,000 members of the Canadian armed forces who served in Afghanistan, supporting US and Nato operations. The Canadians lost 158 lives. In 2007, a stretch of Ontario’s highway 401 was rechristened the “Highway of Heroes” to commemorate the convoys of fallen soldiers ferried between the military base in Trenton, Ontario, and the coroner’s office in Toronto. This response to 9/11 was consistent with the longer history of Canadian-US military cooperation. About 14,000 Canadians landed on Juno Beach in Normandy on D-day during the second world war. More than 26,000 Canadians served in the Korean war. While Canada did not officially participate in the Vietnam war, an estimated 30,000 Canadians headed across the border to volunteer for the US military. Over the course of the war in Afghanistan, Chalmers can count 35 fellow Canadian troops who lost their lives. But he never really brooked any regrets, or bad feelings, about his role in the US-led war. “My experience was that we were participating in an operation to help our brothers and sisters in the United States,” he says. “None of them ever snubbed their noses at us. We were treated as equals, and respected, for what we brought to the table.” But no longer. While calling Canada “a state”, the US vice-president, JD Vance, recently commented that it “had underinvested in its military that quite literally would get invaded by a foreign country were it not for the umbrella of protection provided by the United States of America”. Going one step further, Donald Trump’s transportation secretary, Sean Duffy, told Fox News that Canada “doesn’t have a military”. Self-styled “secretary of war” Pete Hegseth has spent time on X, mocking Canadian cadets and criticising a Canadian coast guard detachment for taking part in a Pride celebration. Trump himself was criticised earlier this year for claiming that Canadian and other Nato forces in Afghanistan were “never needed”, claiming these allies “stayed a little back, a little off the frontlines”. The remarks have been condemned at the highest level of the Canadian government. The defence minister, David McGuinty, described Hegseth’s social media posts as “below the dignity of the office he holds”. Amid a serious diplomatic dispute between the two countries, the prime minister, Mark Carney, accused Trump and Hegseth of “doing memes”. “It’s disrespect and betrayal,” Chalmers says. “It makes me very angry.” “It’s really hard to hear how ungrateful they are, especially Vance, who served,” said Chris Banks, a retired Canadian army sergeant with nearly two decades of experience. “To hear him spit on our sacrifice is insulting, it’s hurtful, and it’s disrespectful to the dead. On the other hand, these men have proven themselves nothing more than children. So when I heard JD Vance say it, it’s like, ‘Oh, good. Dumbass said something else.’” Banks deployed to Afghanistan in 2008, where he was part of a Canadian platoon that laid down cover fire for Americans under attack from the Taliban. To this day, he still has vivid memories of taking cover in a ditch near Pashmul, alongside an American platoon, looking up as the trees overhead were shredded by shrapnel. He says he was proud to serve. But when he came home to Ontario in 2009, he felt something had changed. He began drinking heavily – sometimes as much as a litre of vodka a day – and struggling with suicidal thoughts. All hallmarks of PTSD. He received treatment, and now advocates for the mental health and wellbeing of other Canadian veterans. Still, a tinge of bitterness remains, when he thinks back on fighting on behalf of the US. “I lost a part of myself,” he says. “In that war we fought, for them.” *** Nancy Payne still remembers exactly where she was when she found out her son had died. Cpl Randy Payne served with a military police unit, stationed in Wainwright, Alberta. He was part of a specialised close protection team, charged with safeguarding high-ranking officers, government officials and other VIPs, in war zones. On 22 April 2006, an armoured vehicle triggered a roadside bomb outside Kandahar airbase, killing Payne and three other Canadian soldiers. It was the deadliest attack on Canadian forces since 2002 – when four Canadian soldiers were killed by a US bomb after a disastrous friendly fire incident at the Tarnak Farms training facility in Afghanistan. Nancy was at home, alone, when the phone rang in the dead of the night. It was her son’s commanding officer. “When you get a call at three in the morning from Randy’s boss, you know it’s not good news,” she recalls, speaking over the phone from her home in Lansdowne, Ontario. “I just kept saying ‘Not my Randy … not my Randy’.” In 2025, the Canadian government awarded Nancy a Silver Cross, a commendation for Canadian military mothers. She laid a wreath at the national war memorial during the Remembrance Day ceremony in Ottawa. More locally, she has commemorated her son with a prize – “the Captain’s Award” – bestowed to students who distinguish themselves in athletics and leadership at his former high school. She, too, is unnerved by the US attacks on the Canadian military and veterans like her son. “What they’re saying is not right,” she says. “We were neighbours for so long. That’s all changed, now.” Nancy is not the only military mother who feels this way. Earlier this year, Jane McKay, mother of deceased Master Cpl Tim Wilson, penned an op-ed for the Toronto Sun newspaper taking aim at the Trump administration. “Trump has no respect for any soldier – American, or Canadian, or those from the Nato alliance,” she wrote. “He owes them all an apology.” Some US politicians have tried to make amends. On 1 September, the Arizona Democratic senator Ruben Gallego travelled to Ottawa on an official congressional trip. The goal was to strengthen the weakening trade relations between the two countries. But Gallego made a point of singling out Hegseth’s anti-Canadian military tweets as “deeply disrespectful to the men and women of Canada that have died fighting with us”. For veterans like Chalmers, such words may be too little, too late. He used to play tabletop strategy games with a group of civilian friends in the US, via the online social platform Discord. That all ended when they laughed off his concerns about Trump’s talk of Canada becoming the “51st state”. Banks used to routinely take his family across the border for vacations and stateside shopping trips. No more. “I loved working with Americans, I loved training with them,” he says. “But now it’s hard to have that same level of empathy.” Would he eagerly enlist to help the US again? “What would happen if there was another hypothetical 9/11?” he says. “I hate to say it, but why would any nation, ever again, partner with the United States, if this is how they treat their closest neighbour and ally?” • This article was amended on 7 October 2026. The Silver Cross is awarded by the Canadian government, not by the Royal Canadian Legion.

title: Loss of green space could be issue that decides Holborn and St Pancras byelection
summary: Labour could pay price for disappearance of parks and playgrounds around Euston station
text: When HS2 construction began around London’s Euston station in 2017 and people living nearby watched parks and playgrounds give way to diggers and rubble, they were promised that the lost green space would be replaced. “They have to give it all back,” said Dorothea Hackman. “But they are destroying it – so there’s nothing to give back.” As the dust from the political party conference season begins to settle, disappearing green spaces and housing developments have become central issues in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection. On Thursday, Labour and the Green party will contest the seismic seat vacated by the former prime minster Keir Starmer. Planning documents show that the high-speed railway project and surrounding developments will permanently swallow 14,404 sq metres of green space and playgrounds from the constituency, with more closed off as work takes place. The work forms part of the Euston section of HS2. The government estimates that the full high-speed railway between London and Birmingham will open between May 2040 and December 2043. The biggest park under threat is St James’s Gardens, an 18th-century burial ground designated as a site of importance for nature conservation. While HS2 Ltd originally committed to replacing the gardens by building a new park on a concrete deck above the railway tracks north of the station, government cost-cutting redesigns have dropped that replacement park from the scheme entirely. Responsibility for the surrounding site now sits between public planners and private developers. While HS2 was approved directly by parliament, the private developer Lendlease is drawing up plans for commercial space and homes across the site. Camden council is assessing Lendlease’s plan, with a decision expected next year. Alice Brown, a cofounder of Climate Emergency Camden, said it was vital that green space was retained for people to take a break from the bustle of the station. “Otherwise it’s just going to be the site of the massive office building.” For people living around Euston, the development of their neighbourhood encompasses more than just the parks. The issue is about housing, frustrations with the council and a broader question of who London is for. “They say this is all in order to be able to provide some affordable housing, but it’s a very small amount of affordable housing for the loss that’s being suffered,” Brown said of the construction sites. “By affordable, they mean 80% of current cost – they don’t mean social housing.” Lendlease has said the scheme will provide up to 1,500 homes, but neither the final number or the amount that will be affordable has been determined. Hackman is a governor at Netley primary school, a stone’s throw from Euston. She is worried about what the new buildings will mean for the area’s falling pupil numbers. “Camden’s policy of failing to provide family-size housing means that all our families with children are driven out of the borough,” she said. “It’s very difficult to see how the social-cleansing consequences of what they’re doing can be of any benefit to our community.” For some, the byelection will be a chance to shock Labour’s grip on the council and the constituency. The party has dominated control of the council since the 1960s and represented Holborn and St Pancras since the constituency was created in 1983. Frustrations with the council could spill into a vote against Labour. “So much that Camden Labour are doing is seen to be not in the best interests of people who live here,” said Brown. “It’s either performative or it’s money generating. Every development, every bit that they sell off is to the detriment of the local residents.” At Labour’s conference, the party’s deputy leader, Lucy Powell, said she thought it was “unlikely” that Zack Polanski, the Green party leader standing in the constituency, would win the seat. Brown is not so sure. “I think he’d really roll his sleeves up and get involved in what’s happening here,” she said. “And that would include trying to get the council to perform better.” A Camden council spokesperson said: “The Euston area plan sets out the council’s vision for future development at Euston until 2051.” They said the plan is being submitted to the Planning Inspectorate for public examination after a consultation this year. A spokesperson for Lendlease said: “Working with our partners, we’re developing proposals that could deliver up to 1,500 new homes, including affordable ones, as well as public spaces, improved connections and places for businesses and communities to thrive.”

title: UK events firm that hosts arms fairs and comic shows sold to rival for £2bn
summary: FTSE 100 firm Informa to buy Clarion from private equity group Blackstone
text: A British events business that hosts arms fairs and conventions for comic book fans has been snapped up by a FTSE 100 rival for more than £2bn. Informa has struck a £2.24bn deal to buy the London-based events organiser Clarion from the private equity group Blackstone The takeover will add more than 100 events to Informa’s portfolio – from the defence and security exhibit DSEI held at London’s ExCel, to the comic book and pop culture themed Awesome Con in Washington. DSEI, which is held every two years in London as well as in Germany and Japan, has also attracted protests. Last year, hundreds demonstrated outside the four-day fair in London in protest against Israel’s three biggest arms companies present at the event. Elbit Systems, Rafael and Israel Aerospace Industries have supplied the Israel Defense Forces; the latter two are state-owned. Clarion’s portfolio also spans travel shows, classic car meet-ups and events for the technology, gaming, design and technology industries. Its Classic Motor Show event in Birmingham next month is billed as the “world’s largest vehicle club gathering”. Stephen Carter, the Informa chief executive, said the company was “accelerating the focus” on its core live events business, as it also laid out plans to spin off its academic publishing arm, Taylor & Francis. Informa, which is headquartered in London and employs 14,000 people, hosts big industry events around the world, including London Tech Week and the Cannes Lions International Festival of Creativity. However the FTSE 100 group’s shares have been flat so far this year as it was forced to reschedule several events in the Middle East because of the conflict in the region. Last year Carter, who has led the group since 2013, moved his residency from the UK to the UAE and retired from the House of Lords. Informa makes more than a third of its revenue in India, the Middle East and Asia. The academic publishing business made about $1bn (£760m) last year. Informa said that it had launched a formal process to separate Taylor & Francis, and that it would “review all options”. The outcome of the review will be reported alongside its full-year results in March next year. Taylor & Francis, which was founded in London in 1852, joined Informa in 2004. It publishes journals and books about science, medicine, technology and engineering. Informa told investors on Tuesday that in order to fund the Clarion deal, it will raise £940m through a share placing, which will include an offer for armchair investors through the broker RetailBook. The takeover is expected to accelerate Informa’s growth and bolster its earnings per share from 2027, the company said. Shares in the business, which is listed on the London Stock Exchange, rose by 1.4% in early trading on Tuesday.

title: Trump suggests Iran could ‘take out’ Los Angeles or San Diego
summary: Gavin Newsom calls comments ‘deranged and dangerous’ after president tells Nebraska rally: ‘They can take out a city’
text: Leaders in California have denounced Donald Trump as “reckless” and “deranged” after the US president suggested Iran could “take out” Los Angeles and San Diego – two liberal cities in the blue state that has been a frequent target of his administration. At a rally in ruby red Nebraska on Monday night, Trump told supporters that he hoped to see a “tremendous victory” in the fast-approaching November midterm elections. He then suggested high prices due to the war with Iran were a “small price to pay for keeping the world safe – keeping our country safe”. “They can take out a city,” Trump said in Grand Island. “Let them take out Los Angeles. Let them take out San Diego.” The crowd applauded. “It’ll be over very soon,” Trump said of the war. The governor and the cities’ mayors quickly condemned the comments. “After sending the National Guard and Marines to occupy California, Donald Trump is now saying our foreign enemies should ‘take out’ Los Angeles and San Diego,” the California governor, Gavin Newsom, said on X. “He is deranged and dangerous.” Newsom, a Democrat who has repeatedly clashed with Trump over his two terms, said from his press office account: “Let’s be clear: The President is advocating for an attack on 10+ million U.S. residents in two of America’s largest cities. This is not normal. None of this is. And we will continue to remind folks of that every day.” Karen Bass, the mayor of Los Angeles, assailed the president for making what she called “irresponsible threats” that “could potentially compromise” the safety of America’s second-largest city. “The role of a president is to protect the country, not to actively threaten it and encourage attacks on American lives,” she said in a statement. Todd Gloria, the mayor of San Diego, said his city was “not collateral damage” in the president’s war. “We are not expendable. And we are never a “small price to pay,” he wrote on X “Keep our city out of your reckless war talk.” San Diego, the nation’s eighth-largest city, is home to critical US military infrastructure. Online, the comments – part of a rambling, nearly hour-and-a-half speech – set off a debate about what the president actually meant. Was it a crude joke about two blue cities or had he, accidentally perhaps, disclosed confidential intelligence about potential Iranian targets? Some conservative activists argued that Trump, in his elliptical way of speaking, was referring to high gas prices when he argued that it was a “small price to pay”, and not the capacity of Iran to “take out” a US city. The White House on Tuesday sought to downplay the remark, calling the backlash a “media freakout” and “not rooted in reality”. In a social media post, the White House communications director, Steven Cheung, said the president was “clearly stating US cities would have been threatened if a nuclear Iran hadn’t been stopped”. “America is safer because of the President,” he added. “Iran has no nuclear, no navy, no air force, and no money.” US defence officials have previously stated that Iran currently lacks the capability to launch a direct missile attack on the US mainland. Trump has argued in previous speeches that allowing Iran to develop a nuclear weapon would threaten US cities. In his last state of the union speech he claimed that Iran was working to build missiles that would “soon” reach US soil. In Nebraska, where an unexpectedly close Senate race has rattled Republicans, Trump insisted that he was “doing great” and urged supporters to pretend like his name was on the ballot when they vote in November. But in California, where Steve Hilton, the Republican gubernatorial candidate endorsed by Trump, is seeking an upset, the president’s comments were met with furious denunciations. “Thirteen million Californians call LA and San Diego counties home,” said Xavier Becerra, the Democratic nominee for governor who has sought to take up the anti-Trump mantle carried by the outgoing Newsom. “Their lives are not a ‘small price to pay’ or a punchline for Donald Trump.” • This article was amended on 6 October 2026. Trump suggested that Iran could “take out” the two cities, but did not suggest that it do so, as the original headline indicated.

title: Flávio’s surprise first-round election win highlights rapid rise of Brazil’s House of Bolsonaro
summary: Four members of disgraced ex-president Jair Bolsonaro’s family have been elected to office, most notably his wife and son Flávio, who won the first round of voting to be Brazil’s new president
text: The weekend’s elections in Brazil not only put Jair Bolsonaro’s eldest son, Flávio Bolsonaro, in the lead in the presidential race, but also underscored how far the former president has come in building a political dynasty. As his far-right senator son heads into a runoff against the leftist incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, a sweeping far-right victory in congressional races also secured seats for Jair Bolsonaro’s wife, two of his sons and one of his brothers. Few in the family have spent much time working outside politics since the patriarch led the way four decades ago, but the offices they now hold have had a significant upgrade. Former first lady Michelle Bolsonaro, 44, who divided her campaign with caring for her husband as he serves a sentence under house arrest for attempting a coup, ran for public office for the first time and was elected senator. Bolsonaro’s second son, Carlos Bolsonaro, 43, regarded as the most radical of the siblings – he ran his father’s social media accounts and was indicted by federal police for leading a so-called hate cabinet that spread fake news and attacks on opponents – was also elected senator for the first time. His previous political career amounted to 25 years as a city councillor in Rio de Janeiro – starting at the age of 17, when his father put him up for a seat against his own mother, Rogéria Bolsonaro, who had divorced Jair. Carlos won. (Rogéria also ran last Sunday for a seat in the state legislature, still using the Bolsonaro surname, but lost.) The patriarch’s fourth son, Jair Renan Valle Bolsonaro, 28, who dropped his two middle names on the ballot to run simply as Jair Bolsonaro, jumped from city councillor to federal congressman. Of Bolsonaro’s five children, only his 15-year-old daughter has never held political office. Even the former president’s younger brother, Renato Bolsonaro, 62, nicknamed the “brother who can’t win” after losing seven consecutive elections for lower-level offices, was elected. He went from fewer than 10,000 votes in a mayoral race two years ago to 380,000 votes for congress. During the campaign, Renato caused some friction within the family by saying that “Flávio is not Jair. He doesn’t draw crowds”. At the polls, however, Flávio ended up winning more votes than his father did in 2018 and 2022, although the result is seen by some as more of an anti-Lula vote than a strong preference for the senator. The number of Bolsonaros in office could have been even higher had “son 03”, Eduardo Bolsonaro, 42, not abandoned his seat in congress and gone into self-imposed exile in the US, where for more than a year he has lobbied for what Lula and many others see as Donald Trump’s attempts to interfere in Brazil’s elections. Although Michelle is the most recent member of the family to enter politics, it is she who is often considered to be the leading figure among the Bolsonaros. In a July poll, she was named the most powerful woman in Brazilian politics, well ahead of the current first lady, Janja Lula da Silva, in addition to a supreme court justice and many members of congress. “She is a phenomenon,” said Camila Rocha, a researcher at the Brazilian Center for Analysis and Planning, who has interviewed voters and studied the Brazilian right for a decade. “Even Bolsonaro voters don’t like his sons very much, but many of them like Michelle, who is very charismatic.” The daughter of a housewife and a retired bus driver from the metropolitan region around Brasília, Michelle was working as a parliamentary secretary for another politician when, at 25, she met Bolsonaro, then a 52-year-old congressman. She is his third wife. When he took office as president in 2019, Michelle made history by becoming the first and only Brazilian first lady to deliver a speech at an inauguration. She did so in Brazilian Sign Language, which she had mastered while working as an interpreter at evangelical church services – her religiosity is seen as one of the main assets behind Bolsonaro’s close relationship with evangelical voters. Despite playing by Bolsonaro’s party’s rules, Michelle was at the centre of one of the most contentious moments of Flávio Bolsonaro’s campaign, when she said that she had been “humiliated”, “disrespected” and “mistreated” by the senator. Reports of friction between her and her stepsons are frequent. Given her popularity, Flávio had to apologise publicly – although Michelle accepted it, the two did not campaign together. Polls suggested Bolsonaro supporters would have preferred the former first lady as the presidential candidate, but the patriarch opted for his eldest son, and gave her the senate mission instead. “That was the mission my husband entrusted to me, and I will represent him, God willing,” she said in August. Michelle and Bolsonaro’s sons were also widely seen as helping secure victories for other far-right candidates from Bolsonaro’s party, which will have by far the largest bloc in the next congress. “Although the family has been in politics for a long time, many voters still see the Bolsonaros as representing ‘renewal’ and an anti-system vote,” said Rocha. “So, to change everything, these voters want to throw a ‘bomb’ that blows up congress and Lula. And that bomb is the Bolsonaro family,” she added.

title: Buckingham Palace says it will not fund Andrew’s legal action against police
summary: Former Duke of York is attempting to quash search warrants that led to his arrest in February
text: Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor has been warned not to use the king’s private money to fund his legal action against Thames Valley police. The former Duke of York is attempting to quash search warrants that led to his arrest, with a private high court hearing due to take place on Thursday. Mountbatten-Windsor receives an annual stipend – the amount of which has not been disclosed – provided by King Charles from his private funds, but a palace source told reporters it had been made clear this should not be used to fund the judicial review. The source is reported to have said Mountbatten-Windsor’s legal defence was a matter for him and his lawyers, and Buckingham Palace had no role in determining its strategy or actions. The late queen’s second son was arrested on his 66th birthday earlier this year on suspicion of misconduct in public office, after allegations he had shared sensitive information with Jeffrey Epstein during his time as the UK’s trade envoy. The Telegraph previously reported that Mountbatten-Windsor had been granted permission to challenge whether Thames Valley police acted lawfully over the searches relating to his arrest in February. A judge at the Old Bailey issued warrants that allowed police to raid his residence on the Sandringham estate and his former Windsor home, Royal Lodge. On Monday, a judicial spokesperson confirmed that a hearing in Mountbatten-Windsor’s legal claim was due to take place at 2pm on Thursday at the high court, before Mr Justice Hilliard. When Andrew was arrested on 19 February, the king issued a written statement saying “the law must take its course”. The former duke, who now lives on the king’s private Sandringham estate in Norfolk, was interviewed under caution before being released under investigation. Police began their searches of the properties on the same day, with the force confirming on 24 February that they had ended. The judicial spokesperson said the hearing would concern an attempt by Thames Valley police to restrict access to court documents, with the hearing to begin in private. It is not known whether Andrew will attend the hearing. A Thames Valley police spokesperson said: “Whilst our investigation into misconduct in public office continues, we are engaged in legal proceedings in relation to warrants previously obtained from the central criminal court. “As these legal proceedings are currently ongoing, it would be inappropriate for us to comment further.”
