title: India’s supreme court demands answers over changes to voter roll
summary: Modi government, election body and its head issued notices after removal of millions from lists prompts mass protests
text: India’s supreme court has demanded accountability from the government and the election body over a controversial exercise that has led to the deletion of tens of millions of voters from the electoral roll and prompted mass protests. Demonstrations have erupted across the country in recent days as opposition parties, student groups and the youth-led Cockroach movement have demanded the resignation of Gyanesh Kumar, the head of the Election Commission of India (ECI). They have accused Kumar of overseeing a direct attack on India’s democracy through an exercise to verify and “purify” the electoral roll in states across the country, which so far has led to 130 million names being removed. In Delhi, hundreds of people were detained as they tried to protest over the weekend. On Monday, the supreme court issued notices to Narendra Modi’s government, the ECI and Kumar to demand answers over concerns raised about the voter list revision, saying it expected all “to respond in a clear, transparent manner”. The ECI has claimed the exercise is simply cleaning electoral rolls of duplicate, dead and ineligible names, as well as removing “illegal infiltrators”. However, large numbers of people in Delhi and states such as Bihar and West Bengal say they have been wrongly stripped of their vote and have struggled to get it back. There are accusations that revision of the electoral rolls particularly targets minorities such as Muslims, who are traditionally not voters of Modi’s ruling Bharatiya Janata party (BJP). The opposition alliance, led by the Congress party, have accused the ECI of being hand in glove with the government over alleged vote “chori” or cheating. Kumar was chosen to head the ECI by a panel headed by Modi. While the exercise, known as the special intensive revision (SIR), began last year, widespread outrage only recently erupted after a report in the Indian Express newspaper revealed multiple irregularities in the process, which were flagged in more than a dozen internal objections. The two petitions taken up by the supreme court on Monday alleged that the credibility of the ECI was now in question and called for an independent inquiry into the decisions taken by Kumar in how the SIR process was conducted. “Deletions of voters have been made in the largest democracy,” said Menaka Guruswamy, a lawyer acting for one of the petitioners. “We have grown up with free and fair elections, that is not the case now.” Another advocate told the supreme court judges that if action was not taken to ensure that India’s electoral rolls remained fair, “this country will burn”. Another hearing in the cases will be held next week. The controversies over the ECI have once again driven India’s young people on to the streets in protest, amid rising frustration at the Modi government. The Cockroach Janta party (CJP), which led massive unrest over the summer that forced the resignation of Modi’s education minister, have once again mobilised and called for the resignation of Kumar. Thousands of CJP supporters took to the streets of Mumbai last Friday in protest and another demonstration was held on Saturday in Delhi. In Delhi, police have been criticised for their heavy-handed approach to stopping any student groups protesting in the heart of the capital. Officers have been accused of sexually assaulting three journalists at the protests over the weekend and hundreds of young people were forced on to police buses. Delhi police said it was investigating the assault claims.

title: US book bans in public schools reach record annual high of 12,000
summary: Texas tops list with 8,100 bans while Stephen King is again most banned author, PEN America finds
text: The US saw almost 12,000 book bans in public schools during the 2025-2026 school year, the highest number in a single year, according to the free-expression non-profit PEN America. In a report released on Monday, PEN America said that there had been 34,000 instances of book bans since the organization started tallying the increasing “book censorship crisis” across US schools in 2021. PEN said that new state-level censorship laws fueled much of this increase, in conjunction with the implementation of artificial intelligence tools that remove an expansive number of titles. Texas saw the greatest number of book bans in the 2025-2026 school year – more than 8,100. PEN America’s report said this surge in Texas stemmed from the Texas law SB13, which bars extensive categories of books in schools. Florida had previously ranked No 1 in school book bans for the three previous years. The bans involved a “record number of unique titles” – exceeding 7,000 – involving more than 4,000 authors, illustrators and translators. Analysts found 114 school districts that banned books during the school year, “the highest number ever for a single year”. The most frequently banned title for the 2025-2026 school year was Sold by the journalist Patricia McCormick. This young adult novel involves a teen from Nepal who is sold into sexual servitude. Stephen King was the most banned author for the second year running, PEN America said. “Mostly I feel angry on behalf of the women that I interviewed for the story: young women who’ve been sold into sexual slavery, who told their stories so the world could know what was going on. To hear people, or book banners, say that their accounts are pornographic is so disrespectful to them,” McCormick said in a statement issued by PEN America. “It’s also really disrespectful to the students who seek out that book. There are kids who need a book like that because they have some kind of sexual exploitation experience in their own life, and there’s something about reading a story about someone who’s six degrees away from you – a girl in Nepal – that inspires a certain amount of empathy and understanding that you might not have for yourself.” The bans also revealed worrisome prohibitions on books youth seek out, such as fiction and manga. Fiction comprised more than 90% of young adult titles subject to bans, per PEN America. Kasey Meehan, director of PEN America’s Freedom to Read program, said: “When reading for pleasure is in decline across all ages, bans on popular and engaging titles are exceptionally tragic. “Schools should be doing everything possible to connect kids with reading by introducing them to engaging stories and formats,” Meehan also said in the statement released by PEN America. “Instead, many are doing the opposite, banning books that help kids see themselves in literature, deepen their understanding and empathy of others, and develop their imaginations.” While book bans are increasingly pervasive, parents, students and educators are fighting the conservative turn seen in many US school districts – including book bans. Progressive school board candidates bested many rightwing candidates in many Florida elections this year.

title: Iran’s oil minister resigns as country’s economic crisis worsens
summary: Departure comes amid large drop in oil receipts, rampant inflation and shrinking economy
text: Iran’s oil minister has resigned days after allegations that an intermediary trust selling Iranian oil abroad owed millions of dollars’ worth of export receipts to the state. Mohsen Paknejad’s departure comes as Iran grapples with a dire economic situation, including inflation running at 85%. An overall drop in oil receipts has led to a massive shortfall in foreign exchange earnings and one of the biggest drops in the value of the rial since the Iranian revolution in 1979. The Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, said he had accepted the resignation of Paknejad, who had given personal reasons for going. The rial is trading more than 10% lower than a month ago, largely due to the US naval blockade preventing Iran from selling oil, the mainstay of government receipts. Emergency government meetings over the weekend to combat the crisis have yielded little tangible progress, and there are growing reports that the professional middle class, notably teachers and nurses, are resigning in large numbers because their salaries are not keeping up with price rises. The central bank says its role is not to defend a specific rate, but manage fluctuations. Iran’s economy contracted by 10% in the first three months of the year. Despite concerns that continued sanctions may lead to protests, Iranian diplomats are not planning any new concessions after a proposal to speed the process of nuclear negotiations was rejected by Donald Trump a week ago. Iran has been using informal networks known as “trustees” to bypass US sanctions and repatriate oil revenues. A report last week by the Farhikhtegan newspaper alleged that a trust set up on Paknejad’s watch to recoup income from Iran’s overseas oil sales owed the state-owned National Iranian Oil Company nearly $2bn (£1.5bn) in revenues. Three individual trustees awarded oil contracts allegedly owe hundreds of millions of dollars each to the NIOC. Some of the leaks behind the reporting may reflect a power struggle inside the oil industry. Reza Sepahvand, a spokesperson for the parliament’s energy commission, has announced the launch of an inquiry. Although Iran’s oil export problem, and its impact on foreign exchange reserves, is primarily caused by the US naval blockade on Iran’s oil exports, reports of lax management or possibly corruption will do little to bolster confidence in government at a time when most Iranians are going through an unprecedented squeeze on their standards of living. It is claimed the difficulties were regarded as so serious that they were conveyed by one security official to the president and then before the US attack on Iran in February to the supreme Leader himself. The president apparently took up the complaint with the oil minister but no satisfactory response was received. In an attempt to shore up public confidence in the government’s strategy, ministers have been seeking to rebut Donald Trump’s claim that oil is now flowing through the strait of Hormuz at near pre-blockade rates. The number of attacks on ships trying to use the strait’s southern route close to the Oman shoreline has risen in recent days, including four attacks in the past 48 hours. It was also reported that Saudi Arabia’s east-west pipeline had been forced to close again after a further attack. Reuters reported last week that the seven-day moving average of the region’s crude oil exports reached 18.5m barrels a day on 1 October. About the same amount was exported before the US-Israeli war with Iran began. The dollar traded at 269,000 tomans (a toman is 10,000 rials) this week, a record high, and has risen 12% since 9 September. The minimum monthly wage of 166m rials is worth about $66. Food inflation is 130%. Alireza Zakani, the mayor of Tehran, has announced he is freezing the price of 12 basic items including sugar, rice, oil and detergent for six months. There has been scepticism about how these price controls will be enforced, but he claimed the national government was going to study his plan. Ministers also said a second rise in public sector wages was likely. Mohammad Sharifi Moghaddam, the secretary general of the Nurses’ House organisation, stressed the scale of the squeeze on living standards: “Nurses have explored all possible avenues – logical, legal, professional, and every type of protest or critical path – to achieve their demands. “The current healthcare system has shown no regard for the issues and demands of the nursing community.️ Nurses have come to the conclusion that it is more cost-effective and less damaging to their wellbeing to stay home and receive a salary of 25m tomans.” At the same time, repression of mainstream dissidents has continued, with the summoning of the leadership of the Reform Front by the ministry of intelligence to explain criticisms it had issued during the crackdown on protests. The front has already written to the government calling for transparency about corruption at a time when people are facing pressure from inflation, high prices and falling living standards.

title: Mel B ‘heartbroken’ by Windrush scandal victims’ fight for justice
summary: Public figures back commissioner’s call for government commitment to funding legal support for those affected
text: The singer and television personality Mel B has said she is “heartbroken” by the Windrush scandal victims’ fight for justice, as the Windrush commissioner urged ministers to commit to providing funding for legal support for those affected by the end of October. In April, the Guardian revealed that the Home Office had refused to pay compensation in more than half the claims made by victims of the scandal, in which mainly Black Britons who came legally to postwar Britain were wrongly stripped of citizenship and settlement rights. However, in a series of cases, claimants who were initially refused compensation have learned they are entitled to it, after legal advice. Research led by the University of Sussex found the average successful compensation claim rose from £11,400 to £83,200 after legal help, with one man who was initially offered nothing securing £295,000. Despite this, the UK government has refused to provide Windrush compensation claimants with funded independent legal support of the kind given to those affected by the Post Office and infected blood scandals. Now, Mel B, the television presenter Alison Hammond and the former justice secretary David Lammy are among the public figures backing calls from the Windrush commissioner, Rev Clive Foster, to end the disparity. In a letter seen by the Guardian, Foster urged the migration minister, Jo White, “to show government is serious about putting things right” by committing to funding legal support at the Windrush National Organisation conference in Birmingham on 30 October. Mel B, whose father was born on the Caribbean island of Nevis, said she felt privileged to support “Windrush families” by backing Foster’s call and co-signing his letter. “People affected by the Windrush scandal have already been through so much,” the former Spice Girl said. “I have met and talked to many of them and the stories they tell break my heart. Now they are facing the next step – a compensation process. “This is a step forward, but it can be so difficult and anxiety-inducing to have to fill out endless forms and papers, especially for those living on their own. Funded legal support could make a real difference in helping people access the compensation and justice they deserve. “My own grandparents were part of the Windrush generation. I owe them so much.” Foster, appointed as the Windrush commissioner in 2025, said under the current system “the Home Office is deciding claims for harm caused by its own policies”. He has made a formal recommendation to the Home Office that it funds independent legal advice for claimants before an official decision and again at review, in a scheme designed by victims and lawyers. His letter’s signatories include victims, campaigners, lawyers, academics, faith leaders, parliamentarians and celebrities including Mel B. In the letter, Foster said: “Some survivors have died waiting for compensation … In several claims, evidence that changed the outcome had been held by government departments or other organisations all along. “The parliamentary and health service ombudsman has also found cases where people were wrongly told they were ineligible, or where evidence they sent in was ignored. “The UN committee on the elimination of racial discrimination has raised concerns … and parliamentary committees and human rights organisations have called for funded legal support. Some 65,000 people have signed petitions asking for it, and people who campaigned over the Post Office, Grenfell and Hillsborough have backed the call.” Lammy added: “We owe it to those affected to make sure that justice works in practice, not simply on paper.” Last year ministers introduced the £1.5m Windrush compensation scheme advocacy support fund, which provides community-based help to navigate the Windrush compensation scheme, stopping short of formal state-funded legal representation. A Home Office spokesperson said the fund had “significantly enhanced” support, adding: “The home secretary is determined to put right the appalling injustices caused by the Windrush scandal, making sure those affected receive justice and the compensation they rightly deserve. “The [compensation] scheme has now paid over £132m across 4,177 claims, and in January major reforms to the scheme came into effect.”

title: Spain’s PM Pedro Sánchez calls snap election after housing law fails to pass
summary: Election called after rightwing parties voted down emergency legislation aimed at tackling housing crisis
text: Spain’s socialist prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, has once again staked his political future on a snap general election called after rightwing parties torpedoed emergency legislation to tackle the housing crisis. Sánchez, who has been in office since 2018, used a televised address to communicate his decision, which had been widely expected. The next general election had been due before the end of next summer. Announcing on Monday morning that an early general election would be held on 29 November, the prime minister defended his government’s social, environmental and humanitarian record – and admitted it had made mistakes – but said it was time to let the Spanish people have their say. “It’s up to you now,” he said. “A glance at the horizon shows us that the world is in a very complex era of transformation and transition. It’s a time of great tension, of climate emergency, and of social and technological changes – including highly disruptive advances in artificial intelligence. It is, therefore, a time of great dangers, but also – if we know how to seize the moment – of great opportunities. You, the Spanish people, must decide what role you wish to play in this era, and what role you want Spain to play as well.” Sánchez’s gamble is being seen as a pragmatic move from a seasoned political risk-taker. His minority coalition government with the small, leftwing Sumar alliance has faced a turbulent time in parliament since the prime minister secured his return to office by striking a controversial deal with Catalan pro-independence parties in the aftermath of the inconclusive snap general election he called three years ago. Unable to pass a budget since 2023, with his party and inner circle beset by corruption allegations and his government facing enduring pressure over its handling of the mass crossing into Spain’s north African enclave of Ceuta over the summer, he appears to have decided another snap vote is his best chance of survival. Sánchez repeated his familiar assertion in Monday’s address that the choice was between his progressive government and a Spanish right that would curtail freedoms and turn back the clock on hard-won advances. “You, the men and women of Spain, must decide whether you want to join the far-right wave that rolls back progress wherever it governs, or to ensure that Spain remains a bastion of openness, social justice, and environmental responsibility,” he said. “You must decide whether you want our country to move backwards or continue moving forwards, and whether you prefer a government that works for the interests of the majority of society.” The government’s efforts to tackle the housing crisis were set out in two decrees that contained a range of measures – from a ban on evictions until 2030 to the regulation of temporary lettings and lettings by room – but were voted down in congress last Friday by the conservative People’s party (PP), the far-right Vox party, and the rightwing Catalan pro-independence party Junts. The PP, which is leading the polls but which may need to rely on Vox’s support to form a national government, said it believed construction, and not regulation, was the best way to tackle the crisis. The votes were met with an angry response from the crowds who had gathered outside congress, eliciting boos and cries of “Shame” and “Your profits, our misery”. The PP welcomed news of the snap election. “At last, the Spanish people will decide,” said the party’s leader, Alberto Núñez Feijóo. “This isn’t an election like previous ones. This is about Spain beating Sánchez.” Vox, which already governs with the PP in four Spanish regions, hailed the decision. The party’s leader, Santiago Abascal, said Vox would fight to ensure that Spaniards “are not discriminated against in their own homeland” when it came to housing and benefits. He also said his party would focus on “remigration” in order to reverse what he called “the migrant invasion”. Long-brewing fury over the high cost of renting and the precarious nature of many tenancies exploded late last month following the eviction of Maricarmen Abascal, an 87-year-old woman who was removed from the home in Madrid where she had lived for 70 years. Abascal said she could not possibly afford the 230% rent hike demanded by the investment fund that bought her apartment. Her plight prompted tens of thousands of people to take to the streets to protest, and saw a huge tent camp reminiscent of the 2011 indignados movement spring up in Madrid’s central Puerta del Sol square. Over the weekend, large demonstrations were held across the country as protesters stepped up their demands for urgent action on the housing crisis. Authorities said 70,000 people had taken part in a protest in Madrid on Saturday, while organisers put the figure at 500,000. Sánchez will be hoping that the focus on housing, and the right’s rejection of his government’s plans to address the crisis, will mobilise voters. The housing issue has served to deflect attention from the government’s much-criticised handling of the continuing crisis in Ceuta, which was sparked when about 70,000 people crossed into the territory from neighbouring Morocco in the space of 48 hours. Members of Sánchez’s administration, his party and his inner circle have also been battling a series of corruption allegations over the past two years. In July this year, the prime minister’s brother, David Sánchez, was banned from holding public office for nine years after being found guilty of administrative misconduct relating to his hiring by a socialist-led council in the south-western region of Extremadura. Meanwhile, Sánchez’s wife, Begoña Gomez, is due to face trial after a judge charged her with embezzlement, influence peddling, corruption in business dealings and misappropriation of funds at the end of a two-year investigation. David Sánchez and Begoña Gómez have both denied any wrongdoing, and the prime minister has previously accused his political and media enemies of launching a “harassment and bullying operation” against his family.

title: Snakes, bobcats, mountain lions: the secret animal world beneath the Hollywood sign
summary: An international symbol for the city, the sign is also hallmark of the region’s environmental richness
text: Atop Mount Lee, in the heart of Los Angeles, the wind is quiet. Two red-tailed hawks sail above, barely flapping as they coast the thermal air like surfers on a wave. Standing beside the giant letters of the Hollywood sign, the city seems peaceful. On a clear day, blocks and blocks of homes unfold beneath and the skies reveal sights all the way to Catalina Island – nearly 50 miles out, across the Pacific. That’s the beauty seen from the Hollywood sign. The sign sits on a hillside in Griffith Park, which, at about five times the size of Central Park, is the largest municipal park in the city. The letters have long been an international symbol for human residents in the metropolis – of dreams, film-making ambition and success. But it’s also a hallmark of the region’s environmental richness. Because the area is closed off from the public, it has become a favorite of animals seeking respite from the city. There are birds nesting in the sign, snakes curled up at its base, bobcat roaming around the letters. It was the backdrop that made the famous wild mountain lion P-22 into an LA icon when a 2013 National Geographic photograph captured him prowling at night with the illuminated Hollywood sign in the background. Now, a team of scientists is preparing to outfit the letters with cameras, able to capture any fire outbreaks that the basin may experience. The sign’s caretakers are collaborating with Torch Systems, a technology company that uses solar-powered sensors, on an AI fire-detection service that can identify smoke from miles away. Fire is considered the area’s largest anticipated risk, particularly as visitors may bring lit cigarettes into the park. On a recent Wednesday, the Guardian hiked up the mountain with the team to survey the environment of the sign. As we don gloves, skirt a steep trail and rappel down a private trail to the letters, mounds of coyote scat are a constant reminder of who has walked these paths before us. “Los Angeles is butted up against nature,” says Diana Wright, official caretaker for the Hollywood Sign Trust. She gestures around the hillside, part of the 4,310 acres, or about 6.5 sq miles, that exist in the shadow of the sign. “We’re inside this huge natural park – way bigger than Central Park – and also much more native. And then you’ve got this man-made sign of it that’s meant to withstand rockslides and landslides and winds.” The park is home to many creatures. The Educational Research Center at the University of California, Los Angeles, has designated Griffith Park a Significant Ecological Area, in part for its crucial role “as a corridor for any gene flow and species movement between the Santa Monica, San Gabriel and Verdugo Mountains”. Researchers have documented about 200 species of birds in the park, along with 50 species of butterflies and 40 species of mammals. Like many parts of Los Angeles, the sign was originally a publicity stunt – and a temporary one. It was originally constructed of tin and telephone poles in 1923, to advertise a local housing development called “Hollywoodland”. Eventually, the “land” section was dropped. Over the years, the structures deteriorated. Hugh Hefner led a campaign in 1978 to replace the letters with massive steel beams set in concrete foundations. Over the century, it became a real anchor point for life in the city. Wright points to streetlights in downtown Los Angeles that are designed to resemble New York, and other parts of the city where Parisian city scenes are filmed. “Much of the city is designed to look like other places due to our filming background,” says Wright. “The sign offers that sense of place that so many parts of the city lack.” She thinks that is why it is often the sign that is blown up in movies – or photographed when something unusual, like a once-in-a-decade snowstorm happens. The sign may have stronger footholds in the earth now, but it is also facing challenges. Mount Lee is steep, and the hillside, and the animal habitat it is home to faces risks from earthquakes, climate change, changing rainfall and events such as El Niño. The conservancy caregivers have ongoing projects to clear brush to keep fire dangers down, but they have to balance erosion control, fire concerns and unobstructed views of the sign. Wright and the other caretakers are also developing a plan with the city to plant more native California flora and potentially create a native flower super bloom near the sign. “The Hollywood sign is such a celebration of California,” Wright says. “It should be beautiful and stunning in its natural glory.” Will the letters still be here in 100 years? And what will the wildlife surrounding it look like then? Wright says it all depends on the land beneath. “The hillside is going to define what the sign is like in the future,” she says, pointing out that the whole city could look different after a big environmental shake-up like an earthquake. “I think that’s a real metaphor for Los Angeles in general.” But on that day, it was only blue skies and lizards scuttling away from our footsteps, in the shadow of giant letters. • This article was amended on 6 October 2026. An earlier version said Catalina Island was 10 miles from the Hollywood sign; in fact, it is nearly 50 miles away.

title: Artist calls in lawyers after Tories use his Burnham portrait without consent
summary: Stanley Chow’s cartoon was put on water bottles at party conference with the slogan ‘Bottler Burnham’
text: An artist is considering legal action after the Conservative party used his cartoon to mock Andy Burnham. Stanley Chow, a Manchester-based illustrator who works for the New Yorker magazine, created a cartoon of the prime minister for campaign material in the Makerfield byelection earlier in June. At the Conservative conference this weekend, party workers handed out water bottles to journalists with the slogan “bottler Burnham” above Chow’s cartoon. He told the Guardian that the Conservatives did not ask permission before using his image: “I am taking legal advice, I may take legal action. It is copyright infringement, they are stealing my artwork to use for their own purposes. “An institution like the Tory party – there is no excuse for them not to do their diligence, and find out the rules of copyright. It’s amazing how it got signed off – that really disappoints me.” Chow first realised the cartoon was being used while watching Sky News. The presenters held the water bottles up to the camera and laughed at the joke slogan. “I was more shocked really,” Chow said. “When it appeared up on Sky News they were having a laugh and a joke about it, I thought, hang on, they have done this without telling me? I am peeved.” Chow said he had written to the Tories asking for an explanation but had not heard back. “It would be nice to get an apology out of them at some point.” Chow was also not a fan of the “bottler Burnham” joke: “It is very childish too, I think they should grow up.” He has also locked horns with Reform UK, which used his cartoon in an attack advert on social media aimed at the prime minister. It was deployed for an anti-immigration message – a stance the artist does not endorse. Colin Bell, a partner at the law firm Brabners, said: “This is a clear case of copyright infringement. It’s important because an artists’ work, created with care and intention, has been used and edited without permission and without acknowledgment or remuneration. “That’s not acceptable. Stan is entitled to an injunction – or undertakings to cease and desist and take down the infringing works – compensation and a public apology. “We’re advising Stan in his pursuit of this claim to secure redress and to make clear that artists’ work, rights and reputations cannot be treated in this way without consent, including as leverage or collateral in political campaigns.” The Conservative party has been contacted for comment.

title: Man caught with 300 tortoises and 77 parrots bound for Malta at Sicilian port
summary: Italian police say Maltese citizen under investigation for smuggling after animals found packed in car
text: A Maltese man is facing animal cruelty charges after allegedly attempting to transport 300 tortoises and 77 parrots from Sicily to Malta. The animals were found packed into a car near the boarding area for a Malta-bound catamaran during an inspection at the Sicilian port of Pozzallo, the local unit of Italy’s financial police squad said on Monday. Police said they spotted the man “while he was transporting numerous animals” inside a car that lacked adequate space and temperature control. Subsequent checks by veterinarians found that 76 of the parrots belonged to species protected by the Washington convention, a global agreement signed in 1973 to protect endangered plants and animals from the risk of international trade. Police said the seizure was one of the most significant under the convention. The animals have been entrusted to a breeding facility, police added. The Maltese man faces charges of keeping animals in conditions that were incompatible with their nature and causing them severe suffering, along with breaching laws governing international trade in protected species. The discovery comes a month after police found the dried head of a critically endangered crocodile in the luggage of an Italian man at Turin’s Caselle airport after he landed there from Miami via Istanbul. The man was placed under investigation on allegations of smuggling a specimen belonging to a protected species. Italy is a major transit hub for the illegal trade of exotic animals, much of it rooted in organised crime. In a report published earlier this year, the Italian branch of the WWF said animals including “tortoises, ornamental birds, tropical reptiles and even small primates are illegally traded via online channels and cross-border exchanges”. In 2025, a chimpanzee held illegally in Sicily was seized, the report said.

title: Accept ‘bad things’ in return for benefits of AI, says Sam Altman
summary: Boss of OpenAI calls for a regulatory light touch because of the ‘good stuff’ the technology can deliver
text: Sam Altman says he believes the world should accept “bad things” happening with AI in exchange for the benefits of the technology. The chief executive of OpenAI cited hacks, scams and “other bad things that will happen” in an interview that sparked an instant backlash from critics of the big AI companies. His comments came after one of his company’s safety experts resigned, saying at the weekend that its “culture is broken”. In an interview released on Monday, Altman was asked about how OpenAI’s approach to safety differed from that of Anthropic, which has called for the industry to slow down after one of its researchers quit, warning that AI experts believed “it could kill us all by the end of the decade”. “I think there’s a lot of daylight,” Altman said. “One of the differences between us and some of the stricter AI safety people is that we believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology and people having the agency [to use AI widely]. “I do think the lighter touch regulatory stance we advocate for comes with an accepting of the fact that some bad things are going to happen as society figures out the resilience. “I wouldn’t take a trade of saying we will make sure there’s no major hacks, there’s no misuse of this technology, there’s zero scams or all the other bad things that will happen because I think that people will do tremendously – orders of magnitude – more good stuff than bad stuff.” The interview for Politico’s Decoded podcast drew a strong response from Ron DeSantis, the governor of Florida. He said he had “no dice” with the idea “a handful of tech oligarchs get to make that decision [on safety] for the rest of us”. His state last week asked a judge to bar OpenAI from developing new AI models without third-party approved guardrails. Gary Marcus, a prominent AI sceptic and professor emeritus at New York University, said Altman was “saying the quiet part out loud: suck it up, so you can make us rich and powerful”. Altman also reignited a feud with Elon Musk, telling Vanity Fair: “I don’t like bullies, and I think Elon’s a bully.” He had been asked if the AI industry could “grow up” and work together. “I think once in a while you got to punch a bully back in the nose,” Altman said. “And I also think Elon, like many bullies, only respects people who do. So if you want me to be able to work with him, maybe you should be happy I hit back once in a while, but I will work with Elon, of course.” Altman co-founded OpenAI with Musk in 2015 but earlier this year Musk alleged in court that Altman, OpenAI, and the company’s president, Greg Brockman, unjustly enriched themselves and broke a founding contract. Musk’s claim was dismissed by a judge and jury. OpenAI was hit by multiple safety crises over the summer, including when a swarm of its AI agents escaped their training “sandbox”, cheated, deceived and conspired to hack into the Hugging Face website. Other agents accessed Australian government data. In the interview with Vanity Fair, Altman warned of “a coming tidal wave of cybersecurity problems” from rival open-source models. He suggested OpenAI could help its customers defend against the risk. The company has scrapped the release of a cutting-edge model but Altman’s comments reflect a more bullish mood ahead of a stock market flotation. The wave of public and political concern last month about the potentially catastrophic consequences of fast-progressing AI agents that act beyond human intent had led to hopes of US-wide or even international safety agreements. However, Donald Trump and AI bosses including Altman and Dario Amodei of Anthropic signed a far more laissez-faire pact at the White House last week. The US president said he wanted the companies to “self-police” to limit the risks from AI-enabled cyber-attacks and bioweapons. Geoffrey Irving, who worked at OpenAI and Google DeepMind and as chief scientist at the UK’s AI Safety Institute, said warnings about AI risks understated the dangers. “There’s about a 50% chance we all die because of the development of smarter-than-human AI systems,” he said, adding that actions taken over the next two to 10 years would be decisive. OpenAI’s David Robinson announced his departure at the weekend, saying “the companies building this technology aren’t being nearly careful enough” as they sprint from one product launch to the next. His view was endorsed by Miles Brundage, an AI policy researcher who worked at OpenAI for six years. He said he regretted helping “spread the idea of iterative deployment”, which may have made sense when AI was less powerful “but makes no sense at all after many deaths have been tied to AI and as we’re careening towards extinction-level risks”.

text: A longtime chef for the famous Japanese restaurant chain Nobu was killed over the weekend in Malibu, California, when a teen driver crashed into his parked vehicle, where he was sleeping while waiting for his shift to start. The 51-year-old chef, named by the Los Angeles medical examiner’s office as Ryo Uchimiya, had arrived at work at Nobu Malibu early on Saturday when his vehicle was hit by a 16-year-old boy driving a Range Rover at 6.50am. John Addington, a Los Angeles county sheriff’s department sergeant, told the LA Times that it appeared the boy had been speeding. Citing authorities, NBC Los Angeles reported there were no signs of intoxication by the driver, who stayed at the scene of the crash and cooperated with police. No charges had immediately been filed, but an investigation was ongoing, officials said. According to the LA Times, the stretch of the Pacific Coast Highway that passes through Malibu is one of the deadliest roads in California. It averages four crash-related fatalities a year over the past decade. In 2023, a 24-year-old Malibu man driving a BMW traveling at more than 100mph through a 45mph zone struck three parked cars, killing four sorority sisters from Pepperdine University. The driver was later charged with murder. The highway, known as PCH, is dotted with construction zones after the 2025 wildfires in the area. The California Post reported that the teen driving the Range Rover in Uchimiya’s case on Saturday veered across the road’s fog line, which separates the traffic lane from the shoulder – and hit the chef’s car. Uchimiya was a beloved sushi chef who had worked for Nobu for 25 years, according to KTLA. He was said to have built the restaurant’s operation and was reported to be preparing for Saturday’s service. KTLA quoted the manager of Nobu Malibu as saying the “family of staffers” there were doing what they could to support Uchimiya’s family. “Obviously, it’s been a very, very difficult day for so many people,” the manager said, according to the outlet.

title: Two people die trying to cross Channel as anti-migrant protesters clash with police in Gosport
summary: French authorities say two men, one in his 30s and another in his 40s, died during overnight crossing
text: Two people have died and two more have been injured trying to cross the Channel in a small boat, French authorities have said, while 12 anti-migrant protesters on England’s south coast were arrested after what police described as “violent disorder” as they opposed the rescue of nearly 150 more people on a second vessel. Even though the number of small boat crossings has fallen in recent months, the incidents come amid growing unrest in some quarters partly fuelled by far-right agitators. Authorities in the Pas-de-Calais area said one man in his 30s and another in his 40s died during the overnight crossing from the French coastal town of Berck towards England’s south coast. Two women were taken to hospital after suffering burns over large parts of their bodies. A spokesperson for the Pas-de-Calais prefecture said: “An investigation has been opened by the Boulogne-sur-Mer public prosecutor’s office to determine the circumstances surrounding the deaths. François-Xavier Lauch, the prefect of Pas-de-Calais, thanks all the services involved, particularly the firefighters, for their intervention and commitment during this operation.” Anticipating the arrival of another boat, demonstrators gathered in Gosport in Hampshire on Sunday night. It was the second time protesters had targeted the town amid rumours of rescued people disembarking there. Referring to the 12 arrests, Hampshire and Isle of Wight police said there had been assaults on a police officer and on an emergency worker, as well as affray and racially aggravated public order offences. A crowd of about 350 people had gathered and a handful of officers were treated at the scene for minor injuries. Simon Dodds, an assistant chief constable, said: “Violence and criminal damage have no part in peaceful protest. Our position on this has been clear that we will investigate thoroughly and take robust action against anyone responsible. “Last night saw a number of incidents that were clearly not peaceful protest, rather violent public disorder, and this will not be tolerated as we work to keep our wider communities in Hampshire and on the Isle of Wight safe. “Our officers did not deserve to be assaulted as they worked incredibly diligently on Sunday to ensure the safety of everyone in the area. Neither do they, or anyone from our partner agencies, deserve to be singled out online or subjected to abuse via social media. We will work with our colleagues across policing to address any online threats.” There were similar scenes last month when protesters gathered in the area expecting migrants to arrive on a dinghy but they were ultimately taken to Dover by sea. On Sunday evening, several rescued people were seen arriving at a marina in Gosport after being transported onboard two RNLI boats. Their dinghy was shadowed by French rescue vessels while in the Channel until it was met by RNLI boats in English waters, according to ship tracking data. The Home Office said 149 people were believed to be onboard. It said: “The Border Security Command works around the clock to protect our border. We have established contingency plans to make sure we can securely disembark, check and process all small boat arrivals. Migrants will be transported to short-term holding facilities in Kent, where they will be processed as normal and undergo stringent health, security and biometric checks.” Departures from so far west on the northern French coast have been rare in recent years, but it is the third such crossing in a month. In September, British rescue boats collected passengers off a dinghy that had spent about 30 hours at sea after setting off from Normandy. The 51 people, who refused help from the French coastguard, arrived in Dover after being transferred to Border Security Command boats. It had been expected they would be taken to Gosport, with hundreds of protesters gathering after coaches and ambulances were seen in the area. Six people were arrested by officers that evening. The provisional total for Channel crossings this year is 19,451. This is down 43% on this time last year and 23% below the figure at the same time in 2024.

title: Senate-approved bills aim to ease burden on pilots amid mental health ‘stigma’
summary: Culture of silence and fears of exclusion means aviation workers less likely to seek help for mental health issues
text: Pilots and air traffic controllers in the US could soon have an easier time achieving a healthy mental altitude – a move with implications for the safety of air travel in America. The US Senate recently approved bills aimed at encouraging aviation professionals struggling with a mental health condition to get treatment. The House and president must still approve the legislation, but if that happens, the law could help those with depression and anxiety who are reluctant to seek medical care because they worry it will hurt their high-pressure career. “It starts breaking down the stigma and showing that when you raise your hand asking for help, it is no longer a third rail,” said Chris Finlayson, a pilot and executive director of the Pilot Mental Health Campaign. A 2016 survey of more than 1,800 pilots found that almost 13% met the criteria for a depression diagnosis and 4% reported having suicidal thoughts, according to a study published in the journal Environmental Health. Among European airline pilots, a quarter suffered from anxiety and 40% displayed alcohol misuse, according to a 2025 report in the Frontiers in Public Health journal. Among US air traffic controllers, 19% struggled with moderate to severe anxiety, a 2025 Collegiate Aviation Review International report states. While many adults struggle with those issues, pilots and air traffic controllers are less likely to seek care because of the stigma and concerns that it could disqualify them from flying, according to people in the industry. In 2015, a Germanwings airline pilot, who had suffered from suicidal tendencies, deliberately flew a plane into the French Alps, causing 150 deaths. Afterwards, the US senator Dianne Feinstein commissioned a report which found that the Federal Aviation Administration’s “ability to mitigate safety risks is limited by pilots’ reluctance to disclose mental health conditions”. “You put a bunch of type A people that enjoy being in control [with] frankly archaic mental health standards for those type of people, and then you add in a little touch of federal bureaucracy and you have a perfect storm for people who just do not want to admit or say they have they have issues,” said Finlayson, who in 2021 developed long Covid and started to experience depression and anxiety attacks. The Federal Aviation Administration has guidelines concerning which health conditions prohibit pilots from flying because, of course, they control the fate of thousands of people. As such, pilots must disclose their medical history and medications to an aviation medical examiner approved by Federal Aviation Administration. Until recently, the United States had much stricter rules than other countries concerning how long pilots with depression had to remain grounded. For example, if pilots disclosed that they had started taking an antidepressant, they could not fly for a minimum of six months. In the United Kingdom, they can return to flying in as little as one month. The FAA also requires pilots to get approval from more doctors than other countries and to undergo neurocognitive testing, which other countries also do not require. “Reporting these conditions has created an extra regulatory step to keep working,” said Dr Gregory Kirk, a psychiatrist who evaluates pilots to determine if they can safely fly. Finlayson started taking an antidepressant, which provided relief, but he could not fly for six months. He then tried to stop the drug because he thought the depression was just tied to long Covid and temporary but realized he needed it, which meant he had to wait another six months to work. The FAA also kept asking him to do more testing, he said. He ultimately did not return to the cockpit for almost five years. “It’s a death by 1,000 paper cuts,” Finalyson said. “There is this expectation that if you have even a mild to moderate treatable mental health issue, that you are a detriment to safety, even though that is not what modern science shows.” In December 2025, the FAA changed its protocol to allow pilots to potentially return to the sky three months after starting an antidepressant. The legislation would shorten it to two months, which is still longer than most other countries. Antidepressants typically achieve their full therapeutic effect within four to eight weeks. “If science has proven that a two-month period of waiting is appropriate, then that is what we should go to,” said Dennis Tajer, a spokesperson for Allied Pilots Association, the union for American Airlines pilots. “The longer the waiting period, if it’s not based in science, the more likely a pilot is to say, ‘Nah, I got this. I don’t want to put my career on hold that long.’” The legislation also directs the FAA to follow its mental health aviation rule-making committee’s recommendations, including that it “minimize the requirement for neurocognitive testing”. One of the bills, the John A Hauser Mental Health in Aviation Act, named for an aviation student who died from suicide in 2021, calls for a public information campaign to “destigmatize individuals” in the aviation industry who seek mental health care. Finalyson, who loves his job, said he was doing “phenomenal” because he received the medical care he needed. “The whole point of our movement,” he said, “is that once you get treated, you’re good to go.”

title: UK reviewing whether to impose tariffs on Chinese car imports to align with EU
summary: Move would strengthen Britain’s case to be included in new legislation to protect European manufacturing
text: The UK is reviewing whether to impose tariffs on Chinese car imports to align itself with the EU and strengthen its case to be included in new legislation designed to protect the European manufacturing sectors including autos and chemicals. It is understood the EU has raised the question of tariffs with the UK as part of the discussions on the “Made in Europe” legislation, known as the Industrial Accelerator Act. The UK is an outlier in choosing not to put import taxes on Chinese vehicles, even as the US has shut them out almost entirely. Brussels believes the UK would have to introduce tariffs to create a level playing field to qualify for inclusion in the scheme and match the tariffs of up to 45% it has levied on Chinese cars since October 2024. Imposing tariffs on Chinese cars would probably prompt a hostile response from Beijing and test Andy Burnham’s desire for a reset in the post-Brexit relationship with the EU. It would also involve a lengthy World Trade Organization process. It took the EU 13 months between the launch of the investigation into state subsidies in production and transport lines and finally imposing tariffs in October 2024. The UK has been lobbying hard to be included in the legislation, which will require manufacturers to procure components from the continent to protect against the growing presence of China in supply chains, particularly the auto and chemicals sector. A government source pointed to comments from the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, last week, saying tariffs on Chinese EVs were “always kept … under close review”. If tariffs were to be imposed, the move would be a break with the previous government policy. Keir Starmer’s government positioned itself as a strong ally to China, viewing it as an important source of economic growth rather than a risk to British manufacturing. The UK has consistently argued it does not need trade barriers in the way Brussels does because it does not have the huge trade deficit – now running at more than £1bn (€1.18bn) a day – that the EU is struggling to contain. China’s increasing trade with the EU – not only in finished products such as cars but also in components – is causing deep concern about cannibalisation of native industries in European capitals. The EU trade commissioner, Maroš Šefčovič, is visiting Beijing this Wednesday for talks over a reset in trade relations. Experts said last week the UK car industry faced a “difficult trade-off”, with Chinese investment a potential “lifeline” for carmakers, while access to Europe would also be “crucial” for smaller manufacturers. However, Nissan’s chair in Europe, Massimiliano Messina, recently said Europe “cannot have a Trojan horse where the Chinese are going to flood the market” through imports via Great Britain. Nissan is in talks with the Chinese company Chery to manufacture cars in its Sunderland plant, but this would still align with the EU’s Made in Europe policy. The EU views Chinese manufacturers based in Europe, employing EU staff, as less of a threat to its indigenous industries. Chinese brands made by BYD in Hungary, for example, will not be subject to import duties. Mike Hawes, the chief executive of the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders, said any consideration of tariffs needed to be based on “robust evidence” and maintain a rules-based open and competitive market, adding: “Trade restrictions can have unintended consequences. “The immediate priority is a pragmatic agreement recognising the UK as a trusted ‘Made in Europe’ partner as the exclusion of UK-built vehicles would severely damage both our highly integrated industries, jeopardising the €80bn trading relationship.” Brands such as BYD, Leapmotor and Jaecoo more than tripled their share of the UK new car market in 2026, reaching 12% of sales, according to the latest industry figures. BYD has almost doubled its share of the UK market in September 2026 compared with September 2025, with 5.75% of the market, according to figures from the SMMT released on Monday. In the year to date, BYD’s share has gone up from 2.2% to 3.93%, with 68,000 BYD cars sold up to the end of September, closing in on BMW, which shifted 91,000. Jaecoo’s share has rocketed, increasing by 223%, with 58,000 new cars sold in the year so far, while Leapmotor sales have soared by a phenomenal 765% – up from about 1,500 cars sold in 2025 to more than 13,000 in the year so far. A UK government spokesperson said: “We have not put tariffs on Chinese EVs. We continue to engage closely with industry so that our approach reflects the sector’s and UK’s national interests.”

title: Why Spain Is Holding an Early Election
summary: Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, dissolved Parliament on Monday, after months of spiraling crises.

title: Will Pedro Sánchez’s gamble to call snap general election in Spain pay off?
summary: Spanish PM is hoping to shore up his fragile mandate by tapping into public anger over country’s housing crisis
text: Spaniards will head to the polls on 29 November – months before schedule – after the country’s socialist prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, announced a snap general election on Monday morning. The vote, which will be Spain’s fifth general election in 10 years, is likely to be dominated by growing anger over the housing crisis. Why has Sánchez called the snap general election? Although the next general election was due to be held sometime before the end of next summer, Sánchez has decided to gamble by bringing it forward in the hope that widespread anger over Spain’s housing crisis could work to his advantage and allow him to shore up his fragile mandate. The eviction last month of Maricarmen Abascal, an 87-year-old woman who was removed from the home in Madrid where she had lived for 70 years, unleashed huge protests. Sánchez’s minority coalition government responded by putting together emergency measures that were put before congress at the end of last week. Despite the evident strength of public feeling, the conservative People’s party (PP), the far-right Vox party and the rightwing, pro-independence Catalan party Junts voted down the measures, infuriating housing campaigners and many ordinary Spaniards. Sánchez, who has a well-deserved reputation for pragmatism, risk-taking and improvisation, has seen his chance. While his critics argue that his eight years in office should have given him time to address Spain’s housing problems, both the protests and the rightwing opposition to his emergency measures offer Sánchez the chance to leverage the issue for electoral ends. How are the polls looking? Not great for Sánchez’s Spanish Socialist Workers’ party (PSOE), which has been trailing the PP for months. Although the PP is firmly in the lead, it doesn’t appear to be on course for an absolute majority, meaning it would be forced to rely on the support of Vox to govern – possibly in a coalition. What would such a coalition mean for Spanish politics? If Vox were to take office with the PP, it would be the first time that a far-right party has governed Spain since the country’s return to democracy after the death of Francisco Franco in 1975. The PP, which repudiated Vox in 2020, accusing them of being demagogues who practised a politics based on “fear, anger, resentment and revenge”, has since bitten its tongue and repeatedly entered into pragmatic regional coalitions with the far-right party. The price for Vox’s backing in those regions recently has been the adoption of the party’s hard line on immigration, including its “national priority” policy that insists Spanish-born people receive priority over those born abroad for housing and public services. It sounds like quite a gamble, then. Why is Sánchez prepared to risk the early election? The prime minister only just scraped his return to office in the last general election in July 2023 after he won the backing of Catalan pro-independence parties by promising a controversial amnesty law to those involved in the failed, illegal push for independence from Spain in 2017. Sánchez’s minority coalition government with the smaller, leftwing Sumar alliance, has struggled to get legislation through a fraught congress and has not passed a budget since 2023. Junts, which offered him conditional support three years ago, has attempted to extract maximum benefits from the government, only to abandon it when it feels so inclined, as it did with the emergency housing measures. Nor do his problems end there. The government has also been fiercely criticised over its handling of the crisis in Spain’s north African enclave of Ceuta, which was sparked when about 70,000 people crossed into the territory from neighbouring Morocco in the space of 48 hours. Last, but by no means least, Sánchez’s administration, party and inner circle have been mired in corruption allegations over the past two years, which have proved acutely embarrassing for a prime minister who took office vowing to be a scourge of sleaze and graft. Faced with all that, it’s not hard to see why the prime minister may have decided that an early election was preferable to several more months of legislative deadlock, mud-slinging and uncomfortable headlines. What happens now? Sánchez, a politician with an almost feline allocation of lives, will be hoping that his efforts to tackle the housing crisis will contrast sharply with those of his rightwing opponents and thereby mobilise disenchanted voters. He was also careful to remind people in his address on Monday that he has been one of the few political leaders to stand up to Donald Trump, to repeatedly criticise Israel over its actions in Gaza, and to warn of the death and destruction caused by the climate crisis. Perhaps unsurprisingly given what’s at stake, the prime minister is once again pushing to characterise this latest election as a simple choice between progressive and reactionary politics. “You, the men and women of Spain, must decide whether you want to join the far-right wave that drives regression wherever it governs, or to ensure that Spain remains a bastion of openness, social justice, and environmental responsibility,” he said on Monday morning. Sánchez’s opponents, meanwhile, will be hoping that, after eight long years, the public has grown tired and disillusioned, and that the great survivor of Spanish politics has finally lost his lustre.

title: Euro falls to 17-month low against dollar amid French debt fears
summary: France’s Cac 40 index slides as announcement of snap election in Spain also helps fuel eurozone uncertainty
text: The euro has slumped to the lowest level against the dollar in 17 months amid growing concern France’s debt position could threaten the stability of the wider single currency bloc. The single currency fell as much as 0.8% against the dollar in early trading on Monday to below $1.12, its lowest level since May 2025. It has slumped by about 1.2% this month, accelerating a drop of about eight cents against the greenback from a peak of $1.20 in January. Investors said the sell-off in the euro was fuelled by concerns over France’s rising debt costs as the government battles to control its stretched public finances in the run-up to next year’s presidential election. France’s blue-chip Cac 40 index of leading company shares fell by 1% on Monday, as markets elsewhere across Europe rallied. The FTSE 100 was up 0.2%, while Germany’s Dax was little changed. Monday’s announcement of a snap election in Spain by the socialist prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, after rightwing parties torpedoed emergency housing legislation last week has also fuelled eurozone uncertainty. Madrid’s benchmark Ibex 35 index rose by 0.5%. “Europe is taking the spotlight at the start of the week, as fiscal and political concerns hit the bloc,” said Kathleen Brooks, the research director at XTB. “France is the epicentre of the concerns; however, Spain is also set to get ready for an early election, which is adding to investor worries.” Amid a global sell-off in sovereign debt as the Iran war rattles markets, the yield – in effect the interest rate – on French 10-year government bonds last week hit the highest level since 2002, before dipping back on Friday. This pushed the gap between France and Germany’s borrowing costs, an important measure of investor concern, to its widest level since 2012 at the height of the eurozone sovereign debt crisis. Investors are focused on Paris’s fiscal position and concerns that the presidential election and a hung parliament – with Marine Le Pen’s far-right National Rally party gaining ground – could make it tougher for the government to curtail a yawning budget deficit. The minority government of the French prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, announced plans last month for a €54bn (£45.8bn) savings drive to curb borrowing levels, setting the stage for a fierce political battle. With President Emmanuel Macron’s centrist administration under pressure amid strikes and protests across the country, the budget measures involve cutting pensions spending and funding for government departments, excluding defence. Lecornu said the savings would result in limiting a budget deficit of 5.5% of GDP this year to 5% next year. He warned that without action the shortfall between public spending and revenue could reach 6.5%. However, investors fear political pressures could derail fiscal consolidation, threatening to push up borrowing and adding to France’s debt pile at a time of soaring government borrowing costs. Analysts warned the stresses in the French bond market could spread to other countries in the euro area, stoking fears over a return to the dynamics of the 2010s sovereign debt crisis. It comes amid concerns over the test facing the European Central Bank from mounting inflationary pressures from the war in the Middle East and the risk France’s debt problem spreads throughout the euro area. Roberto Mialich, a currency strategist at the Italian bank UniCredit, said: “Investors still do not rule out riding a further decline of the euro, making a retest of $1.10 possible in the near term. “This is also because growing political tensions across the eurozone (primarily in France and Spain) and fears of contagion across the European sovereign debt market are putting pressure on the euro.”

title: Christa Pike’s lawyers had warned execution would be ‘difficult and perhaps cruel’ due to her veins
summary: Ex-lawyer for woman Tennessee attempted to execute says defense filings said she was at risk for ‘exactly what happened’
text: A former lawyer for Christa Pike says he was not surprised that Tennessee botched its attempt to execute her because attorneys had warned that problems accessing her veins could make the procedure dangerous and potentially cruel. James Crowson, who represented Pike during part of her post-conviction appeals, said he had followed the case from afar before the failed execution at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville on 30 September. “Well, I can’t say I’m surprised,” said Crowson, who represented Pike while working for the Tennessee Post-Conviction Defender. “I knew that there were a number of defense filings saying that she had compromised veins, and that was going to be a difficult and perhaps cruel procedure for her because it was going to put her at risk for exactly what happened.” Pike, 50, on Sunday remained hospitalized and on a machine helping her breathe after Tennessee administered two doses of pentobarbital that failed to kill her, as far as an attorney now representing her knew, the lawyer said on the CNN program State of the Union. “She’s still in the hospital, on a ventilator, critically ill – we don’t really know the prognosis yet and may not know for several days,” Stephen Ferrell, an assistant federal defender, said to CNN host Jake Tapper. Ferrell told Tapper that he had not been able to personally see Pike, but “this is the extent of what we know”. Pike’s attorneys allege improperly placed intravenous lines allowed the drug with which she was injected to enter tissue rather than her bloodstream, leaving both arms severely injured. The Tennessee Department of Correction has maintained that it followed every step of the state’s lawful execution protocol. And the department said the protocol did not permit additional procedures after the steps carried out on Wednesday. Crowson said the accounts that officials followed the written protocol and that the execution was badly mishandled are not necessarily contradictory. “The state comes up with a protocol and, typically, states that are inclined to impose the death penalty don’t really include medicine or science in the discussions when they’re coming up with these protocols,” he said. Crowson said the reported injuries appeared consistent with the concerns raised before the execution, citing the theory that the drug entered surrounding tissue instead of circulating properly through Pike’s bloodstream. Pike was sentenced to death for the 1995 torture and killing of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, a fellow student at the Knoxville Job Corps. Pike was 18 at the time. Her then boyfriend and co-defendant, Tadaryl Shipp, was 17 and was ineligible for the death penalty. He received a sentence of life imprisonment. That gap in punishment based on a small age difference remains significant to Crowson. He said it illustrates what he views as the capricious nature of capital punishment. “She’s a few months older than the young man that was engaged in the same conduct, and she’s been fighting for her life now for 32 years,” Crowson said. “He’s still in prison, but hasn’t been subjected to the death penalty.” He said the age of 18 that was decisive for Pike “just seems like an arbitrary number”. Crowson represented Pike during a stage of her post-conviction case about 16 years earlier and said he visited her “dozens of times” on death row. He said he last spoke with her in 2009. He described Pike at the time as “very superficially charming” and attentive to people around her. But he said the person he knew bore little resemblance to the teenager whose crime sent her to death row. “I never saw the Christa that committed those crimes that put her in prison,” Crowson said. “That person exists, obviously.” The core of the post-conviction appeal, he said, was ineffective assistance of counsel. His team argued that Pike’s original attorneys failed to adequately present evidence about her mental illness, brain damage and history of severe childhood abuse during the sentencing phase. Pike ultimately exhausted her appeals without ever getting relief, despite her attorneys’ offering evidence of being diagnosed with bipolar and post-traumatic stress disorders. “It took me numerous years to even realize the gravity of what I’d done,” Pike had said in an earlier petition for clemency. “Even more to accept how many lives I affected. I took the life of someone’s child, sister, friend. It sickens me now to think I had the ability to commit such a crime.” Crowson more recently said “there was a lot that was left out” at the time of Pike’s conviction. “Would it have made a difference? I don’t know. There are a lot of people who feel very strongly, and her crime was grisly and horrifying.” What happens next depends on whether Pike ultimately survives the botched execution – and, if she does, the extent of any lasting injuries. Crowson said he expects intense pressure on Bill Lee, Tennessee’s governor, to commute Pike’s sentence to life imprisonment if she recovers. If she suffered serious neurological damage, he said, questions about her competency would become central to any attempt by Tennessee to execute her again. The fallout of the botched execution widened on Saturday when Lee announced that Frank Strada, the Tennessee Department of Correction commissioner, would resign later in October. Lee has ordered an independent review and halted executions in the state for the remainder of the year. Strada’s resignation was a predictable consequence of a botched execution now under national scrutiny, according to Crowson, who said: “Whenever you have a disaster like this, there’s going to be some fallout.” Furthermore, Pike’s was at least the fifth execution Strada had botched since 2022 in Tennessee as well as Arizona, where he previously worked, according to death penalty lawyers. Crowson said he hopes that Pike’s case results in the government taking a closer look at the death penalty as a functional legal punishment. He said there is a clear pattern between people who are sentenced to death and their history of trauma and mental illness not being accounted for during trial and sentencing. “I think we as a nation have a strange relationship with mental illness,” he said. “It’s just so often discounted and mocked. It’s unfortunate.”

title: Son of disgraced ex-president Jair Bolsonaro takes election lead in Brazil | First Thing
summary: Flávio Bolsonaro is favorite to win 25 October runoff against 80-year-old incumbent leftwing president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva
text: Good morning. Brazil’s presidential race will go to a second round after the far-right candidate, Flávio Bolsonaro, beat the incumbent leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, but failed to secure the outright majority he needed to avoid a runoff. The 45-year-old son of the disgraced former president Jair Bolsonaro will go into the second round as strong favourite, likely to pick up votes from the election’s other rightwing candidates, including Ronaldo Caiado, who secured 2.1%, and Renan Santos, who won 2.2%. The second round will take place on 25 October. How have Bolsonarista politicians taken a grip on Brazil? Brazil’s far right put in an even stronger than expected showing, with a succession of Bolsonarista politicians winning congressional or gubernatorial races. They included Jair Bolsonaro’s second son, Carlos Bolsonaro, and his wife, Michelle Bolsonaro, who both won seats in the senate. Bolsonaro’s youngest son, Jair Renan Bolsonaro, was elected to the lower house of congress. Woman in Cornell rape allegations case targeted with threats, her lawyer says The woman who has alleged that ⁠she was drugged ⁠and raped by Cornell University students has been the target of threats, her lawyer said. Giuffra ‌said he had also been threatened. “I’m not afraid of these people,” he ‌said. “But the threats, the abuse to protect what’s going on, the status quo – these guys are disgusting. They should stay in their mother’s basement and stay out of the world.” What has been the latest response from Cornell University? In a video message, the Cornell University president, Michael Kotlikoff, said the school would take “a serious look at the role of fraternities and sororities in campus life”, adding: “At their best, these organisations can provide ‌students with friendship, belonging, mentorship ‌and a powerful sense of community. At least 10 B-1 bombers out of 12 flew out of the base on Sunday, including some that arrived on rotation less than a week ago, underlining the haste of the departure. According to reporting by US media, the withdrawal appears to be in response to fresh or renewed security concerns about safety on the base. Five British nationals were initially detained on suspicion of explosives offences and terrorism last weekend after three vans were found near the base. They were later released on bail. The statement came just hours after the Houthis cut a vital supply route linking the besieged city of Taiz with the government’s interim capital, Aden.
