title: Lidl GB’s sales soar by over 10%, helped by price cuts and Deluxe range
summary: German-owned supermarket beats Morrisons to become fifth largest grocer in Great Britain
text: Lidl’s sales in Great Britain jumped 10% to more than £13bn this year, as shoppers sought out cheaper fresh meat, fruit and vegetables and snapped up its Deluxe range. Pre-tax profit at the German-owned supermarket’s arm in Great Britain grew by 30% to £245.5m in the year ended in February, up from £156.8m in the previous year. Shoppers have flocked to discounters such as Lidl amid rising food inflation, with in-store prices stepping up to an annual rate of 1.5% in August, up from 0.9% in July. Inflation for fresh produce remained high at 3%. Lidl said it had spent £315m on price cuts and promotions such as its “pick of the week” product, while increasing numbers of shoppers were choosing its Deluxe upmarket food range. “Deluxe sales are up 12% as more households dine in rather than eat out,” the Lidl GB chief executive, Ryan McDonnell, said. “Customers are looking to trade up and treat themselves at home.” This year Lidl beat Morrisons to become the fifth largest grocer in Great Britain, with its market share hitting 8.6% in the 12 weeks to 17 May, according to figures from the market analysts Worldpanel by Numerator. That compared with an 8.3% share for Morrisons, which increased its sales by just 1.3% compared with a year earlier. Aldi and Lidl have grown rapidly, thanks partly to slowing performance at Asda and Morrisons after both were acquired in debt-fuelled private equity deals. However, Aldi’s growth has slowed recently as Tesco and Sainsbury’s have offered more savings via their loyalty schemes and ranges that match the German discounter on price. Lidl said performance at its loyalty programme Lidl Plus had been particularly strong, with a 23% rise in participants this year. The analyst Clive Black, the vice-chair at the broker Shore Capital, said that was in contrast to Aldi “where management has a clear strategy to deride such programmes”. Aldi is the only big supermarket chain in the UK that does not operate a loyalty scheme. This month the boss of Aldi UK, Giles Hurley, criticised some loyalty discounts that he said tricked customers by starting with “unrealistically high prices” that then dropped. He told BBC News that discounts were helpful “when they’re real and when they show realistic reductions”, but criticised what he described as unrealistic reductions which “dupe customers”. The UK’s competition watchdog investigated loyalty pricing schemes at supermarkets in 2024 and found that shoppers “almost always make a genuine saving”.

title: BT to buy broadband supplier TalkTalk in £400m rescue deal, saving 900 jobs
summary: Virgin Media O2 complains of ‘stitch-up’ over rival provider, which has 1.5m customers
text: BT has agreed to buy the broadband supplier TalkTalk out of administration in a £400m rescue deal that will save 900 jobs. The company said it had struck a deal to acquire TalkTalk and its wholesale business PlatformX Communications (PXC) on a debt-free basis, in a move that is expected to cost it £400m. The deal, which will add a further 1.5 million UK retail broadband customers to BT, will trigger a regulatory review by the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA). But the secretary for digital, culture, media and sport, Lisa Nandy, intervened ⁠on ⁠Monday after the acquisition ⁠was confirmed, invoking a public interest intervention notice “to ensure that impacts on public health, critical national infrastructure and supply to vulnerable customers are fully considered as part of this process”. TalkTalk has about 250,000 vulnerable customers, thousands of whom are disabled or elderly and rely on wearable pendants, known as telecare devices, which are connected to the old copper network and trigger alerts in a medical emergency. In 2023, two vulnerable people died when their devices failed during a switch from copper to digital landlines. TalkTalk’s PXC arm has about 1 million wholesale customers including critical nationalinfrastructure providers across health, emergency services, defence, education, transport, banking and government. Nandy said her department was acting under Enterprise ‌Act powers, allowing her to consider the wider public interest once the CMA has reported back by 19 October on any competition concerns raised by the tie-up. Virgin Media O2 (VMO2), which had also looked at buying TalkTalk and also operates as a rival to BT’s Openreach, reacted angrily to the deal, calling it a “stitch-up” that would further boost BT’s dominant position. Last week, the UK competition watchdog cited “substantial” concerns over nexfibre, the joint venture between VMO2’s owners Liberty Global and Telefónica and InfraVia, attempting to push through a £2bn deal to buy its rival Netomnia. “This has all the characteristics of a stitch-up masked as a rescue deal in the public interest,” said a spokesperson for the company. “Just days after the competition regulator proposed potentially blocking a logical deal between nexfibre and Netomnia … it now appears that rules might be watered down so [that Openreach] can roll its tanks over competition and further tighten its grip on the market. We don’t believe rules should be thrown out the window to allow TalkTalk to fall into BT’s lap without a proper process and we will be raising our concerns directly with government and regulators.” BT is the biggest broadband provider in the UK, with a market share of about 30%, according to estimates by Enders Analysis. Openreach, the broadband network owned by BT, is also TalkTalk’s biggest supplier. BT, whose shares rose almost 2% after the deal was announced, said it expected to report a £400m cash hit from the takeover in its current financial year. This is comprised of transaction and administration costs and working capital, as well as a £60m trading loss and £100m in uncollected Openreach revenue. Allison Kirkby, the BT chief executive, said it was “a genuinely unprecedented situation, where millions of citizens and businesses were at risk if TalkTalk had collapsed”. She said: “Our immediate priority is to stabilise the business and provide a safety net for the households and businesses who rely on TalkTalk.” She said Nandy’s intervention reflected the “critical nature of the services that this industry provides and the scale of impact TalkTalk would have had if it had gone into liquidation and failed as an entity. It was BT that stepped in as we became aware that all other alternatives were no longer an option for the [TalkTalk] directors to consider.” Melanie Dawes, the chief executive of the telecoms regulator, Ofcom, said that she welcomed a commercial deal to protect customers and critical communications services, but had also written to BT to “underline our expectations”. “The transaction will now be subject to the appropriate clearances and we will be working closely with the government and the CMA during that process,” she said. Existing regulatory obligations will continue to apply. We will keep a close eye on the transition to protect consumers and competition.” Kirkby said it was “too early to conclude” whether BT would maintain the TalkTalk brand, but that for now nothing would change for customers of the UK’s fourth-biggest broadband company and there was “nothing they need to do differently”. TalkTalk has struggled in a highly competitive telecoms market, with its retail customer numbers dwindling from 4 million in 2019 to about 1.5 million this year. Its founder, Charles Dunstone, engineered a £1.1bn deal with the London-based hedge fund Toscafund in 2021 to take the company private, which saddled the business with about £1.5bn in total debt. Since then it has, in effect, been under the control of its lenders, led by the US private credit group Ares Management. The deal with BT ends Dunstone’s prolonged efforts to sell TalkTalk. Administrators at Alvarez & Marsal Europe said the sale would transfer all 900 employees at TalkTalk’s consumer and broadband business and PXC to BT. The companies would operate separately and continue to compete until the regulatory review is over, BT said in a statement. TalkTalk, which is headquartered in Salford, reported revenues of about £1.2bn over the past 12 months and was loss-making, BT said. The UK’s fourth-largest broadband company was founded in 2003 by Dunstone as a subsidiary of Carphone Warehouse.

title: Catholic priest given life sentence for sexual assault in Texas found to have neglected daughter
summary: Child of Anthony Odiong, born in 2023, did not have car seat while cleric spent $20,000 on phone calls from jail
text: A Roman Catholic priest who was sentenced in June to life imprisonment for criminal clergy sexual assault in Texas was making a Louisiana parishioner with whom he had a daughter raise their child “as a single mother”, according to those who prosecuted him. Anthony Odiong’s daughter, born in 2023, and her mother “were living without the support a [biological] father would normally provide” even before authorities successfully pursued a case leading to his conviction on charges that he exploited his status as a clergyman to sexually assault two other women, prosecutors Ryan Calvert and Liz Buice of the McLennan county district attorney’s office wrote in a lengthy article in the September-October issue of the Texas District & County Attorneys Association’s official journal. Perhaps the most striking indication of Odiong’s treatment of his daughter – whom he fathered despite having made the standard clerical promise of sexual celibacy – and her mother was the fact that investigators noticed the girl lacked “a proper car seat”, Calvert and Buice wrote in The Texas Prosecutor. She finally got one because police detectives Bradley DeLange and Zach Koenig in Waco, Texas, joined victim assistance coordinator Melissa Beseda to buy one with their own money, according to the article. Meanwhile, Calvert and Buice wrote, there was evidence establishing that Odiong, 58, had spent more than $20,000 just on telephone calls while in jail in the roughly two years that he awaited the outcome of the case against him in custody. Odiong’s daughter’s mother, identified in court proceedings by the pseudonym Presley Jones, nonetheless eluded authorities’ attempts to get her to testify against him at his trial. Calvert and Buice said she apologized after Odiong’s conviction and “emotionally thanked” them for holding him accountable “with obvious relief” in her voice. The Texas Prosecutor article served as a postscript of sorts to the Odiong case, a rare instance of a cleric being held criminally liable for illegally using his religious office to sexually abuse adults. It also provided the most details yet of how Odiong fathered a child with one of his congregants in the New Orleans suburb of Luling, Louisiana, where he had been the pastor of St Anthony of Padua church beginning in 2015 after a prior stint working in the Waco area. As Calvert and Buice put it in their article, titled “Faith was his weapon”, Jones told investigators that Odiong first kissed her as she confessed her sins to him at church. “Things progressed to a sexual relationship, and Presley became pregnant, giving birth to their daughter in 2023” initially in secret, the prosecutors wrote. The detectives who later investigated Odiong realized that his cellphone contained pictures of him wearing his priestly vestments and baptizing his own daughter into the Catholic faith, with Jones and other members of her family looking on. DNA samples investigators took of Presley, her daughter and Odiong established that he was the girl’s father. That DNA eventually became evidence of a broader pattern of pursuing sex with female parishioners whom he met through his ministry. Odiong’s path to prison began in earnest with his likening members of the LGBTQ+ community to “monkeys and chimpanzees” while preaching to St Anthony congregants at a Sunday mass in November 2023. Soon after, New Orleans’s Catholic archdiocese announced it was suspending Odiong from ministering locally, mainly due to complaints of misconduct with multiple women that it had known about by then for five years. The archdiocese said the inflammatory, anti-LGBTQ+ comments also hurt his standing, and that it had asked church officials to recall him to his native Nigeria. One of those complainants subsequently spoke with the Guardian and its reporting partner WWL Louisiana. That spurred a previously unknown accuser, eventually referred to in court proceedings as Jane Doe, to speak to the Guardian and recount how Odiong positioned himself as her spiritual counselor in Waco, where he had also worked for several years beginning in 2006. Odiong, a naturalized US citizen, persuaded Jane Doe to have a form of intercourse with another man to which she did not legally consent, as she later testified in court. That persuasion, from a religious cleric, qualifies as sexual assault under Texas law. Jane Doe’s account ultimately caught the attention of a woman whose son had seen her having sex with Odiong in 2011. Later adopting the pseudonym Mary Doe, she reported Odiong to Waco authorities in March 2024 under Texas’s criminal clergy abuse law. Mary Doe’s report kicked off a criminal investigation that identified several more women who reported Odiong for behavior that met the definition of criminal clergy sexual abuse. Even though not all yielded charges that were considered by the jury seated for his trial, testimony from or about them supported prosecutors’ case against him with respect to Mary Doe and Jane Doe. On 29 May, the jury found Odiong guilty of having sexually assaulted Mary Doe and Jane Doe. Four days later, that same panel sentenced him to life imprisonment. Odiong has since been sent to a maximum-security prison in Abilene, Texas, according to state criminal justice department records. He filed an appeal, which remained pending at the time of Calvert and Buice’s article. He was at least the fifth New Orleans archdiocese clergyman to be convicted of or plead guilty to sexually violent crimes after the organization filed for federal bankruptcy protection in 2020 amid the financial fallout of the Catholic church’s worldwide, decades-old clergy abuse scandal. The archdiocese and its insurers in December agreed to pay $305m to hundreds of abuse survivors, though the individual payout process had not been completed as of Monday. Neither the New Orleans archdiocese nor the diocese of Austin, Texas – which supervised Odiong during his tenure in Waco – immediately responded to requests for comment. His attorney, Gerald Villarial, said on Sunday: “I didn’t take the time to read the [journal] article, although it does have a catchy title. The case is now working its way through the appellate process, and I’ll reserve comment while [it] is being appealed.” A Guardian investigation after Odiong’s conviction determined that Catholic church officials in New Orleans and Austin had internal documents clearly showing several women had accused him of sexual misconduct or unwanted advances while ministering to them years before he was removed from his role as pastor of Luling’s St Anthony of Padua church.

title: Nobel prize in medicine 2026 awarded for research into mysteries of brain
summary: Three scientists to share 12m Swedish kronor prize for their work on ‘light-gated ion channels and optogenetics’
text: The Nobel prize in physiology or medicine 2026 has been awarded to three scientists for their work investigating the mysteries of the brain. Karl Deisseroth of the Howard Hughes Medical Institute and Stanford University, Peter Hegemann of the Humboldt University of Berlin and Georg Nagel of the University of Würzburg have been awarded the prize “for their discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics”. The Nobel assembly at the Karolinska Institute in Stockholm, Sweden, announced the winners on Monday. They will each receive an equal share of a prize of 12m Swedish kronor (about £900,000). The 2026 award is the 117th time the prize has been given. Of the 235 laureates – including the latest winners – only 14 have been women and none have been awarded to black scientists. In a nutshell the trio’s research led to the development of a light-sensitive switch that can be used to control nerve cells in the living brain, switching them on or off. Jonathan Levin, the president of Stanford University, said the subsequent discoveries by Deisseroth, along with those of his fellow laureates, have deepened understanding of neural circuits and how they shape feelings, behaviour, and more. “Their implications are profound, not only for understanding the human brain, but for opening possibilities into new treatments for neurological and psychiatric disorders,” he said. The work had its origins in research by Hegemann, who wanted to explore how a green alga called Chlamydomonas swam towards light. “He discovered that its eye spot contains a light-sensitive protein that converts light almost instantly into an electrical signal, allowing the alga to move,” said Abdel El Manira, a professor of neuroscience at the Karolinska Institute and member of the Nobel assembly. Nagel and Hegemann identified the proteins, called channelrhodopsins, and working with frog egg cells they revealed that when the proteins were exposed to blue light, they allowed charged particles – or ions – to flow into the cell, producing an electrical impulse. Further work by the pair revealed that when the genetic instructions for one of the proteins were inserted into human or mouse kidney cells, those cells became light sensitive. Deisseroth took the discovery even further, using rats to demonstrate that by introducing the gene for a channelrhodopsin into nerve cells, it was possible to produce electrical signals in them using light. He and his colleagues later applied the approach to nerve cells in the motor cortex of the brains of mice, allowing them to use light – delivered by tiny optic fibres passed through their skull – to trigger movement in the rodent’s whiskers. Subsequent work in mice showed the approach could also be used to investigate which networks of nerve cells were involved in the formation of particular memories, including fear. While rooted in basic science, the team’s work has already had real-world implications, opening up a field of medicine known as optogenetic therapy. In one trial it was used to partially restore the sight of a man who went blind as a result of retinitis pigmentosa, a condition that results in damage to light-sensitive cells in the retina. In that case, the genetic instructions for making a channelrhodopsin were delivered by means of a harmless virus into retinal ganglion cells in the man’s eyes. He was then kitted out with light-stimulating goggles that captured pictures of the world around him and converted them into single-wavelength images that were projected on to his retina using pulses of light. Prof Botond Roska, the director of the Institute of Molecular and Clinical Ophthalmology Basel who co-led the study, welcomed the announcement of the Nobel laureates. “This is truly wonderful news. I hope this helps to boost all efforts on optogenetic vision restoration to bring back vision to blind patients,” he said. Anna Wedell, a professor at Karolinska Institute and a member of the Nobel committee for physiology or medicine, said the laureates’ work had provided new possibilities to map which cells were responsible for which functions, and which cells communicated with each other, opening up a new understanding of the function of the brain. “We’ve had anatomical maps and correlations, but now we have a tool that can provide cause-and-effect relationships so we can get a functional map of the brain, exactly pinpoint which cells do what, which cells are responsible for creating behaviours or even emotions and memories in the brain,” she said. Wedell said that by studying animals to understand how a normal, healthy brain worked, it was then possible to explore what happened when thing went wrong – for example in the case of diseases such as dementia, epilepsy and addiction. “By understanding which cells are active in these diseases in the mouse, we can also understand where to look in the human,” she said.

title: Mixed start for pre-Cop as just two non-Pacific leaders accept Australian invitation to climate summit
summary: Anthony Albanese joins about 4,000 people in Fiji for preparatory meeting for year-ending Cop31 UN climate summit
text: The Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, has declared it is “important that Pacific voices are heard” after landing in Fiji on Monday to attend his first UN climate summit since becoming prime minister more than four years ago. Albanese joined about 4,000 people in Nadi for a preparatory meeting for the year-ending Cop31 UN climate summit in Turkey while facing criticism from his political opponents at home. Pre-Cop meetings are usually small and bureaucratic affairs, but this meeting has a double purpose: it is being held in the Pacific after Australia and regional leaders argued it would help bring global attention to the plight of countries most at risk from the climate crisis. Sign up to get climate and environment editor Adam Morton’s Clear Air column as a free newsletter In achieving the latter goal, the meeting has been a mixed success. The Australian government invited national leaders to visit the low-lying atoll nation of Tuvalu, but distance, geopolitical ruptures and the expectation that leaders would prioritise a trip to the Turkish Mediterranean resort city of Antalya for more significant climate talks in a matter of weeks made that a difficult sell. After declining to comment for days, the Australian government acknowledged on Monday that only 14 national leaders would make the trip to Tuvalu on Tuesday, and just two of those – Timor-Leste’s José Ramos-Horta and Mauritius’ Dharam Gokhool – have travelled from beyond the Pacific. The climate change minister, Chris Bowen, said they would be joined by EU climate commissioner, Wopke Hoekstra; the heads of the Asian Development Bank and the Green Climate Fund; UN climate chief, Simon Stiell; the incoming Cop president, Turkey’s Murat Kurum; and international journalists. Australian opposition energy and emissions reduction spokesperson, Dan Tehan, said the number of leaders attending showed the Fiji conference was a waste of taxpayers’ money, a “farce” and Bowen’s “vanity project”. Albanese said it would be an important meeting leading up to the Cop31 summit. “It is important that Pacific voices are heard, because the Pacific is the frontline of action on climate change,” he said. “For many of the nations represented by leaders here it is literally a threat to their very existence, which is why the world must act.” At a welcome event on Monday night, the Fijian prime minister, Sitiveni Rabuka, said it was important that Pacific stories were told. He said the Pacific Ocean covered about a third of the Earth and “was the engine room of the world’s weather”. When the water was warm and an El Niño was gathering, it could cause “havoc in every country”. “I’m not asking you to look at the Pacific with your sympathy,” Rabuka said. “I’m asking you to look at us as a bellwether, indicating the scale of the challenges that will come.” The Australian government has faced criticism for approving large new coal and gas developments, and calls for it to reject the largest coalmine development in New South Wales history after it received state approval last week. Bowen told journalists on Monday the path transitioning away from fossil fuels was “to build more renewable energy to replace the need for fossil fuels”, and gave a speech arguing for greater electrification. Fiji’s environment minister, Lynda Tabuya, said the country’s aim this week and at Cop31 was to keep the goal of limiting global heating 1.5C within reach, unlocking “faster, fairer” access to climate finance for developing countries and making ocean health a focus of climate action. The UN Environment Programme warned last month the world would overshoot the 1.5C global heating goal included in the Paris agreement, and said every fraction of a degree of temperature rise would intensify destructive extreme weather, glacier melt, ecosystem loss, and coastal submersion.

title: Quebec poised to elect separatists to power for first time in more than a decade
summary: Parti Québécois promises to hold an independence referendum in Canada’s French-speaking region by 2028
text: Voters in Quebec are going to the polls in provincial elections which will probably result in victory for a party that has promised to hold a referendum on independence from Canada within the next two years. If polls are correct, the Parti Québécois (PQ) will form the government of the province of roughly nine million, the first time that the separatist movement will have gained power in the French-speaking region for more than a decade. A PQ victory in Monday’s election would also be likely to trigger a return to pitched battles over questions of language and identity between Quebec and the federal government. Long considered a declining force in Quebec politics, the PQ owes its resurgence to party leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon. The 49-year-old Oxford-educated lawyer and polyglot has positioned himself as a TikToking gen-X rebuttal to François Legault, Quebec’s long-serving Premier until he resigned early this year. Analysts say that St-Pierre Plamondon’s electoral success is not because he is a separatist – the majority of voters do not support an independent Quebec – but because of his rightwing take on red-meat identity issues. He has blamed immigrants for Quebec’s overflowing schools, increased crime and skyrocketing housing prices, while promising to slash immigration levels and ban “conspicuous” religious symbols from the bodies of teachers and their students. He has derided his critics from the leftist Quebec Solidaire party as “woke”, and has taken to repeating the talking points of hard-right columnists. Many in the province agree with St-Pierre Plamondon’s rhetoric, even though it strays from PQ’s social democratic roots, according to radio host Patrick Lagacé. “Most Quebecers traditionally see themselves as being on the left. Increasingly, though, they are on the right when it comes to social issues like systemic racism and accommodation of religious behaviour. They’ve hardened on these issues, and don’t see themselves in the left’s recent fixation on identity issues,” Lagacé said. The biggest drag on St-Pierre Plamondon’s popularity has been his oft-repeated promise to hold a referendum during the first mandate of a PQ government. An overwhelming majority of Quebecers don’t want such a thing any time soon – particularly with Canada locked in a trade war with the US. The province mostly voted for Liberal leader Mark Carney over the separatist Bloc Québécois in last year’s federal election, expressly because of Carney’s “elbows up” posturing against the Trump administration. But for the PQ, Donald Trump was at first a curse, then a gift. Early in the campaign, St-Pierre Plamondon said he wouldn’t hold a referendum as long as Trump was in power, defusing the issue and allowing St-Pierre Plamondon to concentrate on attacking immigration and immigrants. The party has also benefited from a four-way race for the right-leaning nationalist vote beyond the reliably Liberal fiefdom of Montreal – particularly around Quebec city, where the upstart Parti Conservateur du Québec has made significant inroads. “The Parti Québécois is benefiting from a massive vote split because those who don’t like the PQ don’t agree on who to vote for,” said poll analyst Philippe Fournier. Though the PQ will probably form the next provincial government, it remains unclear what sort of mandate it will have. Polls have the party hovering at roughly 30%, somewhat below the likely threshold for a majority government. In any case, St-Pierre Plamondon is laying the groundwork for confrontation with the federal government. He has mused about defunding the office of Quebec’s lieutenant-governor (the British Crown’s representative in the province) and promised to introduce a law to abolish the province’s ties with the monarchy, which separatists see as the ultimate symbol of oppression of Canada’s French minority. St-Pierre Plamondon also tore into Carney, after the prime minister said the government will probably increase immigration rates in the country. Doing so, St-Pierre Plamondon said, was an “abuse of power” that would have further nefarious effects on French-language services in Quebec. For a man who trades on his relative youthfulness, St-Pierre Plamondon’s attacks on the monarchy have the whiff of anachronism – the kind of thing the PQ did in its 1970-era heyday. Attacking the federal government is similarly outdated, and potentially risky for St-Pierre Plamondon. Carney remains popular in Quebec, and is likely to remain so, at least until the existential threat of Trump recedes.

title: Coach services could be cut due to record diesel prices, UK operators warn
summary: Rising fuel costs are pushing hundreds of firms out of business, threatening school transport, firms say
text: Coach operators have said record diesel prices could force cuts to services including school transport, as hauliers warn rising fuel costs are pushing hundreds of firms out of business. The average price of diesel on UK forecourts hit a fresh record of more than £2 a litre last week, as the war in the Middle East continues to disrupt global fuel supplies. Alison Edwards, the director of policy at the Confederation of Passenger Transport (CPT), said the cost of fuel had “surged this year to unsustainable levels, pushing coach operators’ already tight margins to breaking point”. “It is time for urgent action,” she said. “Without intervention, soaring prices will mean difficult decisions on the availability of services, including home-to-school transport, and the viability of businesses.” Edwards said 85% of independent coach operators are family businesses, and called on the government to provide temporary support with the cost of diesel, adding that the industry “needs help”. Local bus operators in England have already received help with fuel costs via subsidies to help cover running costs. Coach companies, which say they carry out a similar role, have received no equivalent support. Richard Smith, the managing director of the Road Haulage Association (RHA), said the haulage sector was under similar strain. “Businesses in our sector operate on slim profit margins, typically about 2%, so the continuing high fuel costs are a huge challenge for us,” he said. He said hauliers were now paying an extra £350 a week for each truck compared with before the Iran war. “It’s just unsustainable,” he said. “If haulage, coach and van operators can’t pass these costs on, they struggle, and we’ve seen hundreds of transport businesses going bust already this year.” Hauliers are calling for a pause on planned fuel duty rises, and a rebate to help offset the cost of diesel. The RAC motoring organisation has called for the government to expand its 5p cut in fuel duty, which has already been extended until the end of the year. Rhys Hackling, the managing director of Direct Connect Logistics, said the impact on his own business had been “absolutely enormous”. The company runs 22 lorries out of Oxfordshire, Northamptonshire and Warrington, transporting goods ranging from supermarket products to live events equipment. He said the company was spending much more on fuel compared with last year: “We normally spend about £50,000 a month on fuel … it’s now knocking on £65,000.” Many hauliers work on fixed contracts with customers, Hackling said, meaning rising fuel costs squeeze or wipe out their margins entirely. “If these events continue, then it’s going to put a lot of haulage firms out of business,” he said. “There’s less confidence in the market, so there are fewer jobs, and that means the work dries up very, very quickly. Somebody somewhere is having to pay for this, whether it’s the haulage firm or whether it’s the consumer.” In a move offering some hope that fuel prices might ease, leaders of G7 nations said on Friday that they would release up to 100m barrels of their emergency diesel and crude oil stockpiles. The announcement was partly in response to Donald Trump suggesting he might introduce a ban on diesel exports after the rise in sales to overseas buyers pushed US prices to record highs. It appears to have averted the threat, which could have pushed diesel prices even higher in the UK, since Britain relies on the US for about a third of its diesel imports and does not refine enough to meet demand on its own. The transport minister, Keir Mather, has said the UK’s fuel supply is “inherently resilient” and that people “shouldn’t be concerned about shortages”.

title: Head of Jewish Greens says she may leave party over ‘Zionism is racism’ vote
summary: Vivien Lichtenstein says she believes motion is unhelpful as anger grows over Zack Polanski’s absence for vote
text: The head of the Jewish Greens has said she may leave the party after it voted to adopt a policy that equates Zionism with racism and calls for Israel to be replaced by a single Palestinian state. Vivien Lichtenstein said that while opinion among Jewish members of the party was split on the motion passed at its annual conference in Brighton on Sunday, she said she believed it was unhelpful and it was “possible” she might quit. It comes as anger grows among some in the party about the decision of Zack Polanski, the leader of the Greens in England and Wales, to miss the vote and to encourage supporters to do the same so they could instead campaign for him in Holborn and St Pancras before the parliamentary byelection for the seat next week. Polanski sought to have the conference postponed so the party could focus on his efforts to win Keir Starmer’s former seat. When the Greens’ executive committee refused this, the party contacted members, encouraging them to get refunds on their conference tickets to campaign. Sunday’s binding policy motion was passed by 1,022 votes to 813, and some Greens say more effort by Polanski could have stopped it. One long-standing member said: “There’s so much anger at his disinterest in such a critical issue. You can’t run a party on vibes alone.” The motion was opposed by four of the Greens’ five MPs, and is expected to face a legal challenge under equality laws. Polanski did not take a side but justified the motion’s broad argument by pointing to the death toll in Gaza. Speaking on BBC Radio 4’s Today programme, Lichtenstein condemned the motion: “I don’t think it’s helpful, and it doesn’t make any difference whatsoever to Palestinians.” Asked if she would remain in the party, she said: “I haven’t decided yet. Certainly it’s quite possible that I will leave the party, and I’m giving it a little time, and to talk with colleagues.” The motion says Zionism – the movement for a Jewish state – should be “treated as any other form of racism”. It calls for Israel to be replaced by a single Palestinian state “with equal rights for all”. Some Jewish Greens have expressed concern that this will mean they could face disciplinary action for belonging to Jewish organisations that officially support Zionism, even synagogues. Supporters of the motion, which was led by a group called Greens for Palestine, have said this would not happen. Asked about this issue, Lichtenstein said she was less worried about being personally targeted than about the potential impact on organisations. She said: “I’m not concerned about people accusing me of supporting Israel’s right to exist, and therefore, I’m a racist, which of course is not the case. I’m just concerned that this is a very bad motion … “What concerns me is that the party might accuse UK organisations, Jewish organisations, and also Israeli-Jewish and joint Arab-Jewish organisations, of being Zionist and therefore racist. I support an awful lot of those sorts of organisations that are working against the occupation, and even go out on the ground to assist Palestinians.” The idea of calling for a single Palestinian state was not an issue for all Jewish Greens, Lichtenstein said, but party policy had been that it should be “up to Israelis and Palestinians to choose their future, one state or two”. The chief rabbi, Ephraim Mirvis, described the motion as “poisonous antisemitism” and a “threat to British Jews and to Britain”. He said he was “appalled” by the motion, claiming the Green party had resurrected a “discredited and dangerous slander” first promoted by the Soviet Union. “All decent people will see this for what it is: poisonous antisemitism, a threat to British Jews and to Britain,” he said. Israel barred Polanski from entering the country in retaliation for the motion, which the Israeli foreign ministry said “constitute[d] a clear antisemitic text”. It is understood some Green members are consulting lawyers over whether the policy could be challenged for breaching equalities legislation. Adam Wagner KC, the barrister who led a case that concluded Jeremy Corbyn’s Labour party broke equalities laws over antisemitism, said such a case would have a good chance of success. “I think there is a strong risk that the motion as passed contravenes the Equality Act 2010, which applies to political parties, as it will discriminate against and harass people who hold Zionist beliefs and Jewish people more generally,” he said.

title: Extreme heat warnings issued for parts of southern California
summary: Temperatures in US state forecast to hit high 30s this week, while parts of Indonesia grapple with wildfires
text: The National Weather Service in the US has issued extreme heat warnings for parts of southern California, including Los Angeles, until Thursday, as temperatures are expected to hit the high 30s celsius. Burbank, a suburb north of Los Angeles, recorded 39C on Saturday, a few degrees shy of the October record for the region set in 1987. A persistent area of high pressure will remain in place this week, leading to further hazardous hot weather and increased fire risk. Parts of Indonesia are in the midst of an extreme wildfire season, which has peaked over the past month. Western Kalimantan (Borneo) and southern Sumatra have been particularly badly affected. The lack of rainfall has dried the usually water-logged tropical soils, meaning that fires have been able to spread quickly, above and below the surface. Indonesia’s soils are also extremely rich in peat, meaning that the smoke produced from the fires contain higher levels of toxic gases such as sulphur dioxide and carbon monoxide. Cities in surrounding areas and as far as Malaysia and Singapore have experienced reduced air quality in recent weeks as a result. Drought and wildfires are more common in this part of the world during El Niño events owing to suppressed thunderstorm activity. On the flip side, El Niño is contributing to an extremely active period for tropical cyclones in the Pacific Ocean. After recent hurricanes in the eastern half of the basin, Super Typhoon Choi-Wan is now active and a category 4 typhoon to the south-east of Japan, while on a strengthening trend. After developing on 30 September, Choi-Wan moved through the Northern Mariana Islands as a tropical storm, causing power outages on the island of Tinian, forcing the closure of schools and government offices. Choi-Wan underwent rapid intensification after clearing the islands on Sunday, and as of Sunday night has sustained winds of 150mph, and gusts of up to 180mph. The system is expected to curve away from mainland Japan and areas affected by Typhoon Dujuan last month, while steadily weakening over the coming week.

title: Apple iPhone 18 Pro review: big changes for small differences
summary: Longer battery life, better screen, upgraded Siri and new variable aperture camera in refreshed design from last year’s model
text: Apple’s smaller Pro iPhone gets the best kind of spec bump for 2026: longer battery life, faster chips and a fancy new variable aperture for the main camera. The iPhone 18 Pro is one of a pair of slab phones launched alongside Apple’s first folding phone, the iPhone Duo, and is the cheapest of the new phones, with a regular iPhone 18 yet to be announced. It isn’t exactly low cost, priced from £1,199 (€1,449/$1,199/A$2,099), with a £100 or equivalent rise over previous models courtesy of RAMageddon. Having fully revamped the design of the body for the iPhone 17 Pro, the new model is a modest refinement. It is 7g heavier and the back glass now matches the colour of the aluminium body, which is available in a handful of new shades. Apple has shrunk the amount of the screen taken up by the Face ID camera, allowing the dynamic island to show three continuing tasks, up from two on previous devices. It also now shows the 3/4/5G indicator next to the signal level when playing music, which is a most appreciated feature for public transport commuters sorely missed on previous models. Otherwise, the 6.3in screen is one of the very best on a phone: super bright, crisp and smooth, while being big enough without making the phone enormous. An anti-glare coating makes it much easier to see outside, too. Specifications Screen: 6.3in Super Retina XDR (120Hz OLED) (460ppi) Processor: Apple A20 Pro RAM: 12GB Storage: 256GB, 512GB or 1TB Operating system: iOS 27 Camera: 48MP + 48MP UW + 48MP 4x, 18MP front-facing Connectivity: 5G, wifi 7, NFC, Bluetooth 6, Thread, USB-C, Satellite, UWB and GNSS Water resistance: IP68 (6 metres for 30 mins) Dimensions: 150 x 71.9 x 8.75mm Weight: 211g Faster chip and longer battery life The 18 Pro has Apple’s new A20 Pro chip, which is about 27% faster than the A19 Pro in last year’s model, with about 45% faster graphics performance. Since the A19 Pro was no slouch, that’s quite the leap and puts it miles ahead of the competition, ready to handle anything. The phone has a redesigned cooling system for longer peak performance, too, which is especially useful for running games on top settings. The battery lasts a solid six hours longer than the iPhone 17 Pro, managing to stretch to about two days between charges with more than six hours of active screen use across apps, browsing, messaging and photos. Even with the heaviest of use while out and about, the 18 Pro managed to end the day with 40% left in the tank. Most people will only need to charge it every other day. iOS 27 with new Siri The 18 Pro ships running iOS 27, which was released for the rest of the iPhone line on 14 September. It refines the relatively controversial Liquid Glass redesign from last year and speeds up the system, including app launches. But the big new addition is Apple’s revamped Siri, backed by Google’s AI technologies. Siri AI, as the new system is called, is significantly more capable of understanding and answering questions than previous iterations. It is a chatbot like most other AI assistants, but it is less chatty and sycophantic than others, being more likely to just get the job done. As well as a choice of voices, there are sliders to control how fast it talks and how expressive its responses are. It has its own app where you can review previous interactions, but it is accessible anywhere on the phone via the side button, is built into Spotlight search and can see what’s on your screen, including when using the camera. It can also offer suggestions, such as adding an event to your calendar from the messages or mail apps, and attempts to display relevant information from your emails in the phone app when you call a business. But Siri can only do so if you use Apple’s apps, so if you use WhatsApp for texting and Gmail for your email, none of it works. Sustainability The battery will last more than 1,000 full-charge cycles with at least 80% of its original capacity and can be replaced for £119. Out-of-warranty screen repairs cost £349. The specialists iFixit awarded the phone a seven out of 10 for repairability. It contains more than 40% recycled material. The company breaks down the phone’s environmental impact in its report. Apple offers trade-in and free recycling schemes, including for non-Apple products. Camera The 18 Pro has a similar camera system to last year’s 17 Pro with one big addition, a variable aperture for the main camera. That means it has a very good 18MP centre stage selfie camera on the front and three 48MP cameras on the rear: main, 0.5x ultrawide and 4x telephoto. The ultrawide is one of the best on a phone, handy for landscapes and group shots. The 4x telephoto is very good too, full of detail and manages lower light settings well. It shoots excellent photos with a crop zoom to reach 8x before digital zoom is required, which is a little behind rivals with 5x/10x telephoto zooms. The variable aperture on the main camera can be left on automatic or controlled manually. It allows the camera to open wider than previous models for better low light performance, speeding up night mode shots and reducing unwanted motion blur. But it also enables a number of creative uses, such as making starbursts by narrowing the aperture when shooting lights, which is very fun, or controlling the depth of field in your photo. However, because the iPhone’s camera is tiny compared with an APS-C or full-frame camera, the difference in depth of field – where the foreground and background of the image are either in focus or blown out for a nice bokeh effect – is pretty minor. When shooting something up close, manually closing the aperture to f/4.0 can bring things in the foreground or background into focus, but otherwise the difference for most shots is small. The 18 Pro’s camera has a number of other useful upgrades. My favourite is AI-powered focus tracking that keeps a subject in focus as it moves about or into and out of the frame, which has been one of the best features of a Pixel camera for years and is extremely handy for fast-moving children or pets. Apple has also added texture and grain control to its Photographic Styles feature to customise how the camera shoots photos beyond what was introduced with the iPhone 16 Pro, including film simulation. Finally, the new Apple Reference Image feature can sign an image for authenticity, on a per pixel level directly on the sensor, to help later prove a shot is not AI-generated, similar to a digital negative. The camera shoots some of the very best video on a phone, too. New for this year is the ability to convert a regular video to a cinematic one after the fact, a bit like the excellent automatic portrait mode for photos. Price The iPhone 18 Pro costs from £1,199 (€1,449/$1,199/A$2,099). For comparison, the iPhone 17 costs £899, the iPhone Air costs £1,099, the iPhone 18 Pro Max costs £1,299, the Google Pixel 11 Pro costs £1,079 and the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra costs £1,359. Verdict The iPhone 18 Pro is an iterative upgrade on an already great device from last year. Inside, it has some quite big changes, but their impact is fairly minor on the whole experience. The new A20 Pro chip is super fast, but you can’t really notice the difference day to day, as previous iPhone chips have already been very quick. The extended battery life is great, but most people will still have to charge it every other day. The smaller camera cutout in the dynamic island now shows three continuing activities instead of two. Even the variable aperture in the main camera makes only a small difference to image quality unless you’re really trying to get creative. The screen is fantastic and big enough. The aluminium body feels great to hold. The cameras are some of the best on a phone and even Siri is better now. All of these things add up. The 18 Pro is without doubt the best iPhone ever made and at this size is one of the very best smaller phones available. It’s just not a transformative change unless you’re upgrading from a much older model and it now costs even more thanks to RAMageddon. Pros: relatively compact, great screen, better dynamic island, longer battery life, great cameras, variable aperture, USB-C, top performance, long software support, Face ID, better AI. Cons: small upgrade on last year, expensive, heavier than previous model, AI tools still lag behind top competitors.

title: Alleged flydubai attacker left Australia without finishing engineering course, university says
summary: RMIT confirms co-pilot was a student as Australian authorities examine his time in country between 2015 and 2017
text: An Australian university has confirmed a flydubai co-pilot who allegedly tried to hijack an Israel-bound flight studied at its Melbourne campus, but left before completing his qualification. Disaster was narrowly averted on 30 September when passengers and crew intervened to stop the alleged attempt of the co-pilot, identified by media outlets as Hammam al-Hammami, to take control of a flight to Tel Aviv with 182 people onboard. The United ⁠Arab Emirates’ prosecutor general said the co-pilot allegedly used a crash axe in the attempted “terrorist attack”, in which the pilot was stabbed mid-air. Numerous media outlets have named the co-pilot al-Hammami, an Omani national. On Monday, the RMIT university in Melbourne said in a statement that it “is aware of media reporting of a former student alleged to be involved in the Flydubai flight incident”. “The individual was enrolled at RMIT but did not successfully complete an engineering qualification,” the university said. “As this is an ongoing investigation, the University is unable to provide further comment.” Former RMIT engineering students contacted by Guardian Australia said they did not remember al-Hammami. RMIT university’s confirmation came after the Australian federal police (AFP) on Sunday said agencies were investigating the man’s time in the country. A source familiar with the case, but not authorised to speak publicly, has said the man was granted an Australian student visa in 2014, before arriving in the country to commence a university course the next year. He left Australia in 2017, and his visa was cancelled in 2019 after authorities confirmed he was no longer enrolled in the course, the source said. The AFP on Sunday said multiple agencies – including the Australian Security Intelligence Organisation (Asio) – were probing the man’s connections to the country. “The Victorian Joint Counter Terrorism Team (VIC JCTT), comprising the AFP, Victoria Police and ASIO, can confirm it is investigating the man’s links to Australia,” an AFP spokesperson said. “An update will be provided at an appropriate time.” Court records and previous media reporting show that a number of Australians charged with terror offences or suspected of Islamic extremism studied at RMIT around the same time as al-Hammami, but there was no indication he knew any of these individuals. A British university, Buckinghamshire New University, has confirmed a student named Hamam al-Hammami had “previously completed a distance-learning course in aviation management”. It added: “He did not undertake any pilot training at the university.” A flydubai spokesperson on Saturday said the circumstances surrounding the incident were still ‌under investigation and the airline was not in a position to comment further. The airline’s flights between Dubai and Tel Aviv were suspended after the attack. The Omani co-pilot and the flight’s Indian captain, Smit Machchhar, were taken to the UAE, as it leads the investigation. Officials have said a number of countries including Israel are participating. The Wall Street Journal has reported that the co-pilot had been barred from flying by Oman over concerns he had adopted extremist views. He was then moved to an administrative job at Oman Air, according to the official, before being hired by the UAE-based budget airline flydubai.

title: Monday briefing: You asked, we answered – how will the US midterms go?
summary: In today’s newsletter: As Americans get ready to vote on whether the Republican party remains in control of Congress, our Washington editor talks about the disconnect between Trump and his supporters
text: Good morning. Later today, Donald Trump will be in the state of Nebraska to rev up supporters as he kicks off a campaign blitz of rallies ahead of the midterm elections on 3 November. If his early speeches are anything to go by, cornhuskers can anticipate poll denial, accusations of veganism and an expletive ratio that my nine-year-old would love. And Nebraskans may love it, too: aside from one “blue dot” district in Omaha, Republicans argue their support is steady in the state that has easily backed Trump three times. This campaign is set against the president’s plummeting approval ratings, the unravelling of his Maga movement and an affordability crisis escalated by his unpopular war on Iran. But Trump supporters are also among the most motivated to vote, and Republicans have far deeper coffers to mobilise their base. I asked First Edition readers what you really want to know about the US midterms. Today, in a happy exercise in newsletter cross-pollination, I put your questions to our Washington editor Ankita Rao, who runs our US elections newsletter The Stakes. First, the headlines. Weekend roundup UK politics | The Greens in England and Wales have formally adopted a policy that equates Zionism with racism and calls for Israel to be replaced by a single Palestinian state. Schools | Lawyers and campaigners have condemned the “horrifying” scale of child-on-child sexual abuse in schools after a Guardian investigation revealed thousands of sexual offences against under-13s are reported to police each year. Brazil | Brazil’s presidential race will go to a second round after the far-right candidate, Flávio Bolsonaro, beat the incumbent leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, but failed to secure the outright majority he needed to avoid a runoff. Environment | A study of Europe’s summer paints a grim picture for the future, with doctors and climate scientists calling on governments to stop burning fossil fuels, shade buildings, green cities, and install air conditioning in hospitals, schools and care homes. US military | The US Air Force has pulled its bombers from RAF Fairford following an investigation into an alleged planned terror attack at the base. In depth: ‘We are prepared for anything’ You’d be forgiven, readers, if the state of US politics is perplexing you. On the one hand, there are voters who have little faith in the president’s war in the Middle East and are increasingly angry about his inability to make daily life more affordable at home. On the other, Trump has promised a “big surprise” come 3 November – and polls have predicted the wrong results for previous elections. As Ankita Rao set out in The Stakes in September, her team of reporters across the US are hearing the same things in almost every community they’ve spent time in: • Americans feel their lives are dictated by an elite class that goes beyond political parties – best summed up by Democratic senator Jon Ossoff’s use of the term “Epstein class”. • People are exhausted by an ongoing crisis in affordability of childcare, healthcare, food and gas. • Many have lost trust in institutions, from hospitals to schools. With this deep knowledge of the mood of the country, she is the woman to answer your questions. Over to you. *** Who still believes in Donald Trump? Johanne, Quebec, Canada Ankita’s short answer is that it might be the other way around: a lot of Americans don’t feel they’ve been presented with a better option yet. This was evident during primary season, when both Democrats and Republicans went for candidates “who they felt would actually stick it to the man”, says Ankita, rather than regurgitating established party platforms. After all, that was what so many hoped to get with Trump – but those voters who had flocked to him as the anti-establishment leader, or the man who represented something beyond the two-party system, now see him aligning himself with big tech and other corporate interests, particularly this last term in office. There’s a serious disconnect between Trump and his supporters, Ankita tells me. His previously impressive political instincts have faltered “partly because he can’t see beyond his own fixations” – be that his ballroom, the war in Iran, or the unfettered growth of AI. As one Ohio voter told us at the weekend: “I’m sorry, but I don’t give a shit whose name is on the Kennedy Center.” *** Has Trump got a decisive ‘dirty trick’ up his sleeve? Bron Purkiss, England A big concern for First Edition readers is election interference: how Trump has already restricted voting and what dirty tricks he might still try. Will he try to ignore the election results – and how would the Guardian report that? Ankita joined Guardian US seven years ago as voting rights editor, launching our multiyear democracy project. “We had four reporters on that, but now they’re part of the larger politics team, and election integrity has become essential to our coverage,” she says. In the months leading up to the midterms, Trump signed executive orders seeking to assert more control over voting methods, and in a Time magazine interview last week, he refused to rule out declaring a national emergency around elections to implement them. “So we are prepared for anything,” says Ankita. Legal challenges in individual races are “almost inevitable”, she says. “We know the states where the election systems are fully controlled by Republicans, and we’re ready to move everybody there if we see anything strange happening”. Fear of election rigging is high in the communities Guardian reporters are visiting. “We hear this a lot from Democrats who are worried about making sure their vote counts, and more nervous about using mail-in ballots.” This September edition of The Stakes covers Trump’s attempts to restrict postal voting – which is how almost one-third of Americans vote. Ankita suggests this could result in higher turnout. Early data in the deeply red state of Florida, for example, showed voter registration among Democrats already very high. “There’s a sense that ‘we need to go out in droves and make sure that all of these wins are very decisive, so that nobody can question them’.” *** Would Republican losses limit Trump’s excesses? Peter Alexander, England Ankita tells me she doesn’t make predictions any more – a lot can change in a few short weeks – but if an election was called tomorrow “it looks as if the Democrats will absolutely win the House and most likely win the Senate”. The mechanics of voting mean that it will take a decisive majority in both chambers to act as a genuine bulwark against Trump, says Ankita, before adding the weighty caveat that Trump sidestepped congressional authorisation altogether ahead of the Iran war. Nonetheless, she anticipates a slew of investigations after the midterms, launched in the House and then requiring the Senate to move them forward. For example, there are already calls for an investigation into revelations that a Russian oligarch bankrolled part of Donald Trump Jr’s recent wedding in the Bahamas. *** How will democratic socialists influence policy decisions after the midterms? Feride Hekimgil, Turkey This is a “huge question”, Ankita agrees, as progressive candidates capture the enthusiasm of voters desperate for radical change. While the number of Democratic Socialists actually elected is likely to only be a handful, it could become a “very vocal group”. What’s not clear yet is how they will act once in the Congress. Ankita points to Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, one of the country’s most prominent democratic socialists: “She was very clear about her affiliation when she ran, but she hasn’t been that type of lawmaker where she exists to stop the party from doing certain things. She has been much more strategic and collaborative with establishment Democrats.” It remains to be seen whether an augmented group after 3 November takes a similar route or choses a more hardline stance, in particular on Israel’s decimation of Gaza, which has already created gaping divisions in the Democratic party. *** One more thing In an early edition of The Stakes, Ankita described her morning bike ride to the Guardian’s Washington office, navigating National Guard trucks and reflecting on the militarisation of her city since the last election. I wanted to ask her, as a citizen as well as a journalist, how that influences the way she approaches this election. It can’t be overstated, she tells me, how it changes your day-to-day life: “It adds a layer of subtle fear. I’m not actively scared about walking around DC, but it feels as if things could escalate really quickly.” Will it hold people back from voting, or at least displaying their preferences? Quite the opposite, she tells me. “Places where we see this military presence – in Minneapolis, or LA, or DC – are such vocal, largely Democratic cities that people are undeterred.” “There are double the number of lawn signs,” she says. “It’s defiant.” • For more from Ankita and the Guardian US politics in the run-up to the midterms, sign up to The Stakes 2026 here The week to come Tuesday | ABC News is suing the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) over its licence review, and on Thursday its hearing will take place. The broadcaster claims the review, ordered by Donald Trump in April over comedian Jimmy Kimmel’s comments about the US president, is a “retaliatory campaign” in violation of its first amendment rights. Wednesday | Kemi Badenoch is to speak at the Conservative party conference in Birmingham. This day also marks the third anniversary of the 7 October attacks by Hamas. In London, the Met are asking organisers of a pro-Palestinian student march to move the event. Thursday | Holborn and St Pancras will hold its byelection. The seat belongs to former prime minister and Labour party leader Keir Starmer, who held it from 2015 until his resignation in September. What else we’ve been enjoying Helena Horton’s sweeping interview with the Royal Horticultural Society boss Clare Matterson is an absorbing conversation about everything from her high hopes for Andy Burnham, the roles of gardens in public health and the RHS’s £2.3m roadworks compensation. “Who is gardening for in the 21st century?” Matterson asks. “Is it for a small elite band of people, or is it for everybody?” Craille Maguire Gillies, newsletters team If you didn’t catch it yesterday, our interview with the actor John Boyega, recounting the impact of seeing his close friend Damilola Taylor die when he was a child, is deeply moving. Poppy Noor, newsletters team Who doesn’t love images of funny animals? This photo gallery of laughing bears, a sexy mantis and a truly angry bird is worth a look and chuckle. Craille Sport Football | Manchester City came from behind on two occasions to beat Arsenal 4-2 ⁠in the Women’s Super League on Sunday, keeping the champions top of the table. Racing | Formula One drivers have issued a damning condemnation of the sport’s engine regulations that caused the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia to open with scenes of cars stopping on track and unable to accelerate because of software problems. Max Verstappen got his first win of the season at the chaotic race. Football | The Republic of Ireland’s manager Heimir Hallgrímsson has called on Uefa to keep his side away from Israel in future draws after a pair of fixtures he admitted “has been tough on us all”. The front pages The Guardian leads with “Horryfying scale of child-on-child sexual abuse in schools revealed”. The Times splashes with “Badenoch to pledge a bonfire of green laws” and the Mail has “Kemi’s common sense blueprint”. The Mirror, on Badenoch’s pledges to cut benefits, goes with “Bad to the future”. The Telegraph has “Andrew takes police to court over arrest” and The Financial Times says “Hopes for record year in dealmaking punctured by interest rate increases”. The i Paper runs with “Man City owners’ link to Burnham’s No 10 North site after ‘sweetheart deal’ with UAE firm”. And the Sun leads with a story on the romance between Mark Chapman and Kelly Cates, headlined “Love match of the day”. Today in Focus Colonialism for clicks? The influencers targeting uncontacted tribes Features writer Elle Hunt and Indigenous activist María José Andrade Cerda on the growing phenomenon of influencers around the world trying to reach uncontacted tribes. Cartoon of the day | Tom Gauld The Upside A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad Five years ago, Barbara Scully sat in her car crying. Trying to find work after taking time to raise her children, she found herself facing closed doors. “I presume it was the fact that I was 50 and had a 10-year gap where my career used to live [while she was raising children],” she says. “I sat in the car on the driveway in tears, thinking: that’s it, I’m washed up, I’m done.” Then something changed. “Once I pulled myself together, I thought: OK, if this were one of my kids, what would I tell them? … Look at what it is you enjoy doing and try to make that work for you.” Scully relaunched her career for the sixth time, as a broadcaster and comedian, and feels happier than ever. “I am on a mission to try to tell women in particular not to fear getting older; to embrace it, to push back against all the bullshit about how you should be fighting ageing,” she says. Sign up here for a weekly roundup of The Upside, sent to you every Sunday Bored at work? And finally, the Guardian’s puzzles are here to keep you entertained throughout the day. Until tomorrow.
