title: ‘The future is bright’: breeding programme brings world’s heaviest insect back from the brink
summary: Wētāpunga can weigh as much as a mouse and its numbers dwindled across New Zealand due to predators and habitat loss
text: The population of New Zealand’s endemic wētāpunga – believed to be the world’s heaviest insect – is officially “increasing” thanks to a groundbreaking breeding programme that has overseen the release of 11,000 insects into the wild. “The future of wētāpunga is looking bright,” said Dr Chris Green, an honorary researcher at the department of conservation, who documented the success of the project for the New Zealand Journal of Zoology. Green co-authored a report released on 2 October that outlines the success of the breeding programme. “Eleven thousand individuals for release is extraordinary and outstanding.” A female wētāpunga can weigh as much as a mouse. Its body can grow up to 10cm long (nearly 4in) and its leg span can be as wide as 20cm. It is the largest of 70 wētā species and was once found across parts of the North Island before predation from introduced species and habitat loss contributed to their decline. By the 1990s, they were considered “endangered” and are now presumed extinct in the wild on New Zealand’s mainland. The insects reside primarily on a smattering of predator-free islands in Auckland’s Hauraki Gulf and off the coast of Northland. But their fortune is starting to change. Over the past 15 years, tens of thousands of wētāpunga have been bred at Butterfly Creek, a wildlife facility, and Auckland zoo, enabling the release of wētāpunga across new predator-free islands and some mainland reserves north of Auckland. Butterfly Creek and Auckland zoo established husbandry techniques that, over time, have been scaled up to rear large numbers of wētāpunga in communal creches. The young wētāpunga – or nymphs – are fed a three-part diet of fresh foliage, fish flake protein and leaf litter. The protein is “critical” to the survival of the youngest nymphs, Green said. Once big enough to protect themselves, the insects are transferred to their new habitat. The efforts have led to 45 separate translocations to wild habitats, which is “a very high number in any recovery of a species”, Green said. Monitoring on two islands has shown wētāpunga have established self-sustaining populations, with fourth and fifth generations born there, in what Green said was a marker of success. As a result, the species’ conservation status has improved from “nationally endangered” to “nationally increasing”. “It’s so exciting, because we are unable to report that for so many of our other threatened species,” Green said. New Zealand is particularly vulnerable to species decline because of its high rates of endemism and problems with introduced pests. Green said the country was at the forefront of invertebrate recovery work and he was not aware of any other examples of breeding programmes working to this scale, or with such success. By documenting the project’s work, he hopes other institutions will feel encouraged to develop their own programmes. “That’s the extraordinary aspect of it – that we’ve been successful,” he said. “If other institutions can get into that sort of position, then there can be huge benefit for threatened species in New Zealand.” • This article was amended on 6 October 2026. Owing to an error in supplied information, an earlier version said the wētāpunga’s conservation status had improved to “nationally recovering”; in fact, its status is now “nationally increasing”.

title: Authorities issue shark warning over whale that swam 11km upstream in Clarence River and later died
summary: Juvenile humpback was spotted near Bundjalung national park in what experts say is a rare but not unprecedented event
text: While the case of a whale found 11km upstream in a New South Wales river this weekend was unusual, it was not unprecedented, experts say. The juvenile humpback, which swam into the Clarence River on the state’s mid-north coast and later died, was towed out to sea on Sunday, according to NSW authorities. Members of the public first reported a sick whale swimming into the river near Bundjalung national park on Saturday afternoon. “The whale subsequently swam on to a sandbar and became grounded in shallow water, and within 30 minutes observers indicated the whale had died,” a spokesperson for NSW National Parks and Wildlife Service said. Increased shark activity in the surrounding area had been reported, with beachgoers advised to avoid surfing, swimming, or diving at surrounding beaches, SharkSmart NSW said in a post to social media. Whale scientist Dr Vanessa Pirotta said while the circumstances were rare, whales were known to explore rivers and estuaries from “time to time”. This could be the result of “misadventure” or “curiosity”, or due to ill health, as appeared likely for the animal in Clarence River, which looked “extremely unwell”. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Most whales wouldn’t be aiming for the river at this time of year, she said. “Right now the main bulk of the east and the west coast populations are heading south to Antarctica. They’re on their way back for their summertime extended Christmas dinner where they’ll be going to Antarctica to feed on krill.” Earlier this year, in April, another whale became stranded on a sandbar in Wallis Lake on the NSW coast after swimming under the Forster Tuncurry Bridge. Last year, two humpbacks swam under Melbourne’s West Gate Bridge and into the mouth of the Yarra River. In 2020, three humpback whales entered the East Alligator River in Kakadu national park, with one travelling 30km upstream. All three eventually made their way back out to sea. While these air-breathing mammals could survive in freshwater environments, it probably wasn’t good for their skin, Pirotta said. Anyone spotting a whale in an unusual location such as a river, or an animal that appeared to be in distress, should alert environmental authorities, she said. A spokesperson for Orrca, the cetacean rescue organisation, said while it was unusual for a whale to travel several kilometres into a river system, it was not unprecedented. “Humpback whales regularly travel close to the NSW coastline and may enter bays, harbours and estuarine environments temporarily during their annual migration.” Based on the large number of barnacles and other organisms on its skin, the juvenile in the Clarence River could have been experiencing a chronic illness, injury or another underlying health issue, the spokesperson said. “However, the cause of death cannot be determined from imagery alone,” they noted. “Each year, approximately 50,000 humpback whales migrate along Australia’s east coast. Across a population of this size, it is unfortunately not uncommon for a small proportion of animals to be observed in poor body condition or displaying other signs of illness, injury or compromised health.” The unusual event occurred less than a week after a humpback whale carcass washed ashore at Perth city beach, attracting multiple sharks before the body was removed on Thursday. “As with any deceased marine animal, people should avoid entering the water close to the location of the whale carcass, including surrounding beaches, and follow any local warnings or closures that may be in place. Whale carcasses can attract scavengers, including sharks,” the Orrca spokesperson said.

title: BBC morale dented by gradual ‘bloodletting’ after weeks of job cuts
summary: Plans to shed as many as 2,000 employees have been announced in stages, and staff fear further cuts in 2027
text: Morale at the BBC has been severely dented by a gradual “bloodletting” that has seen plans to shed as many as 2,000 staff slowly announced over several weeks, members of the corporation’s staff have warned. More internal meetings have been called for this week to discuss further details of the cuts, which aim to save £500m. Some staff already fear that further waves of cuts will follow soon after in the new year. It is expected that BBC Scotland and BBC Three will both be made online-only channels as part of a bid to save money, the Guardian understands. The BBC is having to make the cuts as a result of its serious financial challenges, which have seen its cash revenues fall at an alarming rate over the last year. Matt Brittin, the BBC’s director general, has said he was not fully aware of the pressures when he took the job. The drawn-out process of announcing the cuts comes as a result of the BBC’s decision to tell the teams affected as soon as possible, department by department. However, many acknowledge the result has been a “drip, drip” of announcements that has added to the low morale at New Broadcasting House. “We have our problems, but we seem to be creating new ones,” said one insider. Referring to yet another internal announcement on further job losses, another BBC figure said: “The bloodletting continues.” Closing the linear channels for BBC Three and BBC Scotland will be one of the most difficult moments in the latest savings programme. Insiders said the viewing numbers could not justify keeping them on the air. Brittin has made a series of comments suggesting the corporation has too many linear channels, when viewing habits have switched to catchup viewing on the BBC’s iPlayer platform. Sweeping redundancy plans have been announced across the BBC, from the news division to local radio and its relatively new media tech division, where 110 compulsory redundancies will be made, with 280 roles closing in the division in total. Redundancy pay terms are also being reviewed. The BBC has already announced a reduction in local news correspondents, as well as making existing correspondents carry out general reporting duties. Local radio will also be made more regional. While children’s television has been protected, with the BBC touting its children’s programming as a high-quality antidote to online slop, even staff in that division have been asked to come forward should they wish to take voluntary redundancy. Gallows humour has already gripped some BBC staff. Managers had to chastise staff after one online call about cuts last week, after it was flooded with disapproving emojis. Meanwhile, some presenters have begun to refer to the cuts on air. BBC Look North’s Peter Levy joked last week that the “BBC cuts are starting” after a weather presenter could be heard but not seen by viewers during an update. Some staff are now asking when the cuts will end, given some have been told cost savings have been divided into “waves” and more could be coming next year. One staffer feared a “doom spiral” of weaker output and an increase in the number of people unwilling to pay the licence fee. “The challenge is real but the reality playing out over weeks and weeks … is likely to make that challenge worse and not better anytime soon,” they said. Any future plans will be shaped by weekly talks taking place between the BBC and the government over its future funding model, which could see the licence fee widened to include anyone who watches a streaming service. Currently, only those who watch live television on any platform, or watch the iPlayer, have to pay the fee.

title: Internet Watch Foundation reports huge rise in AI child sexual abuse material
summary: Abuse material monitor says number of AI images assessed this year is already 40% higher than last year’s total
text: AI-generated child sexual abuse material is proliferating online, with the amount of illegal material investigated this year already exceeding the total for 2025. Analysts at the Internet Watch Foundation have found more photorealistic child sexual abuse material in the first half of 2026 than for the whole of the prior year. The UK-based IWF, which monitors abuse material globally, said it had assessed 6,310 AI images that met the legal definition of child sexual abuse, 40% higher than last year’s total of more than 4,500. Instances of AI-made child sexual abuse material have been rising for several years, with a huge surge in videos in particular, although the latest IWF figures refer to still images only. The majority of the images seen by analysts were of girls, and of children aged seven to 13. The IWF said the figures underlined the need for new statutory regulation on AI. Andy Burnham’s government has not signalled that a new bill focused on the technology is imminent. Kanishka Narayan, the UK’s AI minister, has said “nothing is off the table” in terms of fresh regulation, but that the test for any legislative proposal will be: “Will it make the British people safer?” Hannah Swirsky, the head of policy at the IWF, said she backed calls from parliamentarians for “binding legislation on AI” to compel companies to build safer models. “It is incumbent on tech companies to build tools which cannot be abused this way,” she said. This problem has been created by technology, and if companies won’t build tools which are safe by design.” AI-generated child sexual abuse material is illegal in the UK and the government has also made it illegal to adapt an AI model to create abuse material or to distribute such models to others. Developing a model designed to produce hyper-realistic child sexual abuse material carries a criminal sentence of up to five years. A government spokesperson said: “UK law is clear that child sexual abuse material is illegal, regardless of whether it is AI-generated or not. We are going further by banning AI models that are used to create this type of abuse material and produce sickening, hyper-realistic imagery that often contains the likeness of real children.” AI has also enabled online predators to create explicit images of children. The Report Remove service, which blocks intimate images from appearing online, has received 420 reports from children concerning images of themselves that they believed had been faked or manipulated to appear explicit. The number has already exceeded its 2025 total of 397. The use of AI tools to create abuse tools has led to the National Crime Agency and IWF encouraging parents and guardians to keep pictures of their children off social media. The guidance suggests making social media accounts private or sharing pictures of children through a “close friends” group only.

title: Revealed: the methane mega-leaks from UN climate summit host Turkey
summary: Exclusive: Cop31 leader calling for global curbs on climate-heating gas has landfills producing some of world’s worst plumes
text: Two or three nights each week, the smell descends. Residents of villages on the rural outskirts of Istanbul don’t know what the smell is, but they have been plagued by it for years: a smell so bad they have to sleep with their windows closed even during hot summer nights. They know the source, too: the huge Silivri municipal waste dump a few miles away that is belching out stinking gases as food and other organic waste rots. “The smell is not subtle. It suffocates you,” said Kemalettin Özenç, sitting outside a tea shop in the village of Yolçatı. “It’s worse when the air is still: sometimes families linger until midnight out here. Even when you go inside it’s inescapable.” These gases are more than a local problem. They include methane, a potent climate-heating gas, pouring out of the site in such vast quantities that the plume is visible from space. Satellite surveillance shows that the Silivri landfill is Turkey’s worst super-emitting waste site. In fact, its average emission rate of 7.4 tonnes an hour makes it one of the worst identified anywhere in the world by a team of expert researchers at the University of California (UCLA). The planet-warming impact of this single leak is equivalent to 1.5m gas-guzzling SUVs gunning their engines and there are more super-emitting dumps across Turkey. They stretch from İzmir in the west, to Ankara in the centre and Antalya in the south, many with “mind bogglingly large” leaks, the UCLA researchers said. The revelation that Turkey has some of the world’s worst landfill methane leaks comes at an awkward time: in November, the country will host the next UN global climate summit, Cop31, and has put cutting methane emissions at the top of the action agenda it wants all nations to agree on. Turkey’s first lady, Emine Erdoğan, has been a prominent campaigner for zero waste and methane cuts on the global stage – despite the super-plumes now revealed at home – and the president, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, said waste management was a priority in a speech he made in June. ‘They have the power’ On the ground, the problem has festered for some time. Özenç and a growing crowd of disgruntled people in his town and others around the Silivri landfill have spent years looking for someone to intervene, but the notion of contacting the Istanbul municipality who operate the facility did not cross their minds. Some took to the internet to leave outraged messages about the smell underneath the dump’s listing on Google maps, while Özenç tried to rally people to sign a petition intended for the forestries ministry which oversees several nearby mines. But in the end, too many were afraid to sign. “They have the power and can say whatever they want,” he said, in a sweeping reference to the authorities. Turkey’s most notorious maximum security prison looms 30 minutes from Yolçatı: the mayor of Istanbul, Ekrem İmamoğlu, was accused of corruption and detained there in 2025. Özenç and others in the community feared what might happen to them if they were seen to complain too publicly. Staff from the Istanbul metropolitan municipality’s waste management division, İstaç, at the site in Silivri appeared surprised when shown satellite images of the massive gas leak emanating from a spot visible from their office windows. Methane, also known as natural or fossil gas, is transparent, and so the plume coming from the site is invisible to the naked eye. Fatih Arslan of İstaç cleared his throat while staring intently at the satellite images presented to him by the Guardian. “Well there’s not much to say,” he said, initially blaming the emissions on areas of the waste site not yet covered with clay after the dumping process. “It’s inevitable that this is happening … of course we have to make improvements,” he ventured. Their priority, he explained, was to cover exposed areas of the dump as quickly as possible and trap the methane produced by the rubbish for use as fuel. An on-site facility extracts 6,000 cubic metres of methane an hour from the landfill to burn for energy: letting methane leak into the atmosphere, he said, is therefore a waste. For the head of the facility, Ebu Bekir Ikinci, the current situation is actually a vast improvement on the past. He showed newspaper headlines from Istanbul in the 1990s, when the streets were piled high with rubbish and, in 1993, methane trapped at a dump exploded, killing 39 people. A year later, Erdoğan became the mayor of the city with a promise to bring in better waste management. “The baseline scenario we use for emissions from waste is what would happen if the waste was not stored at all,” said Arslan, pointing to the deadly scenario from the 1990s. “Compared to that, the emissions now are way better. This is actually very good.” ‘Mind-bogglingly large’ rates Silivri is the largest landfill in Turkey, processing 10,000 tonnes of waste every day. Another waste dump in outer Istanbul, on the other side of the city in Şile, is also a source of huge methane leaks, pouring 4 tonnes of methane into the atmosphere every hour, the global heating equivalent of about 800,000 SUVs. The UCLA team used satellite data from the Carbon Mapper portal to identify the 10 highest-emitting landfill sites across Turkey. “Many of these sites have mind-bogglingly large methane emission rates, even in a global context,” said Cara Horowitz, who leads the UCLA Stop Methane project, which carried out the analysis, and is executive director at the Emmett Institute on Climate Change and the Environment. “These are huge leaks, some of the largest single manmade sources of methane emissions in the world,” she added. Methane emissions cause a quarter of all global heating and there has been a “scary” surge since 2007 that risks triggering catastrophic climate tipping points, scientists have said. However, cutting methane emissions is often relatively easy to do and has a rapid impact because the gas is naturally removed from the atmosphere far faster than carbon dioxide. Some experts call cutting methane the climate “emergency brake”. Turkey says that as the Cop31 host, zero waste and methane reduction are the highest priority on its action agenda. Murat Kurum, Turkey’s environment minister and the Cop31 president-designate, wrote to the 196 nations due to attend the summit in Antalya, saying: “Reducing methane emissions is among the fastest and most effective strategies for slowing near-term temperature rise. The waste sector therefore represents a critical opportunity for delivering immediate climate benefits.” However, Turkey’s environment ministry declined to comment when contacted by the Guardian about the nation’s methane super-emitters. The Istanbul municipality also declined to answer questions about the methane emissions at Silivri and refused permission to photograph the site. Reducing emissions from waste disposal has also been described as the “personal project” of Emine Erdoğan, who is the honorary president of Turkey’s Zero Waste Foundation and chair of the UN Advisory Board on Zero Waste. While opening a “zero waste forum” in June, she noted that some landfills in the world were filled with discarded food while people went hungry, and that food waste causes enormous methane emissions. However, Turkey is not among the 159 countries to have signed the Global Methane Pledge to achieve a 30% reduction in these emissions by 2030. Waste opportunity Turkey could become a global leader in cutting methane emissions, Horowitz said, if it managed to clean up its many polluting landfill sites. A suite of tried-and-tested solutions exists across the world, ready for adoption, which start with being aware of the leaks. “Landfills are a significant proportion of the top global methane super-emitters, so just making sure we’re accurately understanding the scale of these emissions is an important first step,” she said. The official record of greenhouse gas emissions submitted to the UN by Turkey acknowledges that a major contributor to its emissions from the waste sector “is the uncontrolled release of methane gas from landfills into the atmosphere”, and that such gases are meant to be monitored by the environment ministry. However, legislation enacted last August – intended to launch a monitoring mechanism for emissions from select Turkish private interests – only monitors carbon dioxide emissions, and excludes any facilities “using biomass” like landfill. Methane gas coming off landfills can be captured and used as fuel, as at Silivri. However, Dr Tia Scarpelli, waste sector lead at Carbon Mapper, said: “Not all sites that have gas collection are created equal. It does come down to the design and efficiency of the system and day-to day management practices.” Causes of major leaks can include poor maintenance, failure to keep flares alight when burning off excess methane, or collecting only good quality gas and venting the rest. A more foolproof way of halting methane leaks is to stop organic waste going into the landfill and rotting in the first place. In South Korea, close to 100% of the country’s food waste is now recycled. “Getting at the real source of the problem is an even better opportunity to reduce methane leaks,” Horowitz said. Stopping the massive methane leaks in Turkey is a climate imperative, but may yet fall victim to politics: Istanbul, Ankara, İzmir and several other big cities remain under municipal opposition control, despite a prolonged crackdown on Turkey’s largest opposition party. Imamoğlu and hundreds of other former employees from the Istanbul municipality are on trial on corruption charges, and the government in Ankara is eager to claim the opposition are incapable of running Turkey’s largest city, including its waste management. After his petition went nowhere, Özenç said he and other communities in Silivri living with the unbearable smell feared another instance of what he saw as a “cover up”. “It’s not like we have a say anyway,” he added. “What can you do? The moment you talk about this, there is silence.” • This article was amended on 5 October 2026 to remove an incorrect reference to Istanbul as Turkey’s capital.

title: From hotel suites to virtual reality, museums turn to licensing deals as costs rise
summary: Natural History Museum and British Museum among cultural institutions leveraging collections and exhibitions
text: They are often free to visit but museums are bolstering their finances by putting their stamp on everything from upmarket hotel suites to trendy jumpsuits and virtual reality experiences. Forget buying a T-shirt. If you can afford the “from £724” price tag, you can spend the night in the Natural History Museum family suite at the Park Plaza London Riverbank hotel, which has an interior inspired by the museum’s founder, Sir Richard Owen, complete with Tyrannosaurus rex bunk beds. Deals such as this are becoming more commonplace as cultural institutions look to leverage their renowned collections and trusted brands in the face of funding cuts and rising costs. Data shows that overall UK sales of licensed merchandise and services grew 7% to $19.2bn (£14.5bn) last year, according to the industry trade body Licensing International. A breakdown of the UK market figures shows that the “art property” category, which includes museums, grew by more than 8%, while “attractions and promotions” (which includes immersive experiences at museums and art galleries) soared by 53%. “Our licensing programme continues to grow consistently at about 15% year on year,” said Louisa Skevington, the licensing manager at the Natural History Museum, who added that “experiences” were becoming an increasingly important part of that. “It’s about finding creative ways to bring the museum and its stories to people wherever they are, while continuing to grow the reach and impact of the programme.” The Natural History Museum’s previous deals include a Farrow & Ball paint range inspired by Werner’s Nomenclature of Colours and a collection with the fashion brand Lucy & Yak featuring dinosaur-print jumpsuits and dungarees, aimed at millennials and gen Z. More recently it worked with the virtual reality experience company Sandbox on the prehistoric adventure Age of Dinosaurs. The importance of licensing means a growing number of museums, galleries and heritage organisations are exhibiting at this week’s Brand Licensing Europe conference in London. New attenders include the National Gallery, the National Trust for Scotland, the Ashmolean Museum in Oxford and Tate Enterprises. They join the British Museum, the Natural History Museum, the Victoria and Albert Museum and the Imperial War Museum. The competition is stiff, however, as the agenda includes talks on the “Bluey effect” and the new Harry Potter TV series. The huge demand for Bayeux tapestry tickets “demonstrates the appetite for major cultural moments, and the opportunity to build on that interest beyond a visit to the museum”, says Craig Bendle, the manager of product licensing at the British Museum. Indeed, the Bayeux tapestry merchandise created by its separate retail team, which includes a collaboration with the London department store Liberty, made it into Vogue. Bendle reports growing interest from brands that want to create something “genuinely distinctive”, with the museum’s collection of more than 8m objects an “extraordinary source of inspiration”, he says. The V&A is also looking for novel ways to draw on its 2.8m objects. It launched 63 product ranges in 2025, which demonstrates the “growing role licensing plays in taking the V&A beyond our museum walls”, said Jen Maude-Roxby, its head of licensing and business development. That programme includes William Morris-inspired phone cases with the tech accessories brand CASETiFY, and pictures for the art store of Samsung’s “the Frame” TV, which displays artworks when the TV is off, transforming the blank monitor into a picture.

title: Starwatch: how to spot Saturn as it makes it closest approach to Earth this year
summary: The planet looks like a moderately bright, creamy-white object and is easily visible to the naked eye
text: This week offers an excellent opportunity to track down Saturn. The giant planet, situated about 10 times further from the sun than the Earth, reached opposition on 4 October. In this configuration, Earth is passing almost directly between the planet and the sun. This makes opposition an excellent time to see a planet: the distant world rises as the sun sets, remains visible throughout the night and sets around sunrise. It is also at about its closest point to Earth for the year. Saturn is easily visible to the naked eye, looking like a moderately bright, creamy-white object. Unlike most stars, however, its light remains steady rather than noticeably twinkling. The chart shows the view looking east- south-east from London at 2100 BST on 5 October. By this time, Saturn is already well clear of the horizon and will continue climbing higher as the evening progresses. It lies beneath the Great Square of Pegasus, which provides a distinctive signpost to the planet. Saturn is currently shining at about magnitude +0.3. Once you have identified it, try returning to it on subsequent evenings. Unlike the surrounding stars, Saturn slowly changes position as it travels against the background constellations. Although the planet itself is an easy naked-eye target, you will need a small telescope to see its famous rings. From the southern hemisphere, Saturn is even better placed, climbing higher into the sky.

title: Country diary: Lave net fishing is a tradition in trouble | Gwyneth Lewis
summary: Portskewett, Monmouthshire: For hundreds of years this has been a method of catching salmon in the Severn’s churning waters. I visit one of the few fishermen still going
text: Every time I cross the new Severn Bridge leaving Wales, I check the state of the tide, using a buoy in the middle of the channel. I learned to sail in these cocoa-coloured waters of the Bristol Channel, with its ferocious tidal range (the distance between low and high water) the second highest in the world. You can’t work against these currents, you can only cooperate. Today I get down to sea level itself, to meet Martin Morgan. He’s secretary of the Black Rock Lave Net Fishery, started by his great-grandfather over 100 years ago, and has known these grounds between the two Severn crossings since childhood. He’s fished the Grandstand, the Hole and the Gruggy, all using a traditional method of netting salmon – lave nets. Outside the fishery’s fascinating museum, Martin shows me one of these wonderful contraptions. It’s a foldable Y-shaped frame, with a horseshoe-shaped net strung between the arms. The fisherman uses the rock staff (handle) to feel his way into the channel, then, using a yoke made of pine, opens the arms (or rimes), constructed from pollarded willow. Putting the net down into the ebbing tide, the fisherman threads his fingers into the mesh, feeling for vibrations of trapped mullet, flounder or salmon. The season finished in August and Martin, one of only a few remaining lave net fishermen, is despondent about the fishery’s future. They are, he says, “hanging on to this ancient fishery and all it represents with our fingertips”. The craft has been practised here since the 1600s, but with declining stocks, tightening legislation and a lack of young people to take skills forward, it has dropped 80% since 2020. No salmon have been caught since 2019. Martin feels that increasingly severe Natural Resources Wales regulation is throttling a sustainable practice, and is aimed at the wrong target. He adds that salmon numbers here won’t rebound “until our rivers become a place where these fish can thrive”. Out on the Severn, the silt from time to time reveals putchers, cones woven from hazel and willow – remnants of how salmon used to be caught. We look over the churning waters as the traffic roars above. Martin’s sadness at this ending is painful to witness. • Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024, is available now at guardianbookshop.com
