title: Trump names intelligence chief Jay Clayton as new White House AI czar
summary: Clayton had said AI was a ‘gamechanger’ but also posed ‘a threat’ during his confirmation hearing
text: Donald Trump on Sunday named Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence, to also serve as the new White House AI czar. Clayton, who leads the US’s 18 intelligence agencies, previously served as the top federal prosecutor in Manhattan and led the Securities and Exchange Commission during Trump’s first term. During his Senate confirmation hearing, Clayton said AI was a “gamechanger” but it also posed “a threat”. “When something’s both an opportunity and a threat, you better get your arms around it,” Clayton told lawmakers when asked about AI. CBS News was the first to report that Clayton would be appointed White House AI czar. In a social media post on Sunday, Trump announced that Clayton would lead what the US president called “the Super Intelligence Force (SIF)”. Trump’s post also said the SIF would “coordinate the federal government’s engagement with consumers, public interest groups, religious organizations, critical infrastructure providers, and super intelligence companies”. Among those reacting on Sunday to Trump’s invoking the term “super intelligence” was the SpaceX chief, Elon Musk. Musk said on his social media platform X that SI was “better” than AI – and that he was renaming his aerospace company’s AI unit from SpaceXAI to SpaceXSI. Senator Mark Warner, a Virginia Democrat who is vice-chair of the Senate select committee on intelligence, cautiously welcomed the appointment of Clayton, while noting that “the administration has resisted meaningful safeguards without offering a serious alternative for addressing the national security risks posed by increasingly powerful AI systems”. “I look forward to working with Director Clayton on ensuring the United States stays ahead of China and other adversaries, strengthening the security and resilience of our most advanced AI systems, and establishing rigorous testing and safeguards so that increasingly powerful systems remain secure, reliable, and under human control,” Warner added. In September, Trump announced he was creating an “AI Force” and a czar to oversee the technology’s growth and monitor for “bad” development. The announcement came after tech industry leaders warned that AI was developing too rapidly to control and that it could harm humans. The president has largely brushed aside concerns about AI development and the construction of datacenters, which power the technology. Trump has insisted continued development is paramount to defeating China in the global AI race. But to address concerns, the president created an advisory committee in addition to the czar – whom he previously promised would be led by a “high IQ” individual. Trump also recently met with AI industry leaders to discuss concerns. On Tuesday, Trump and six executives signed an AI accord at the White House, promising to create internal and external monitors to ensure the technology is used as intended and any safety issues are addressed. Trump had initially created the AI and cryptocurrency czar position when he returned to the White House in January 2025. David Sacks, the venture capitalist and tech businessman, served as the administration’s AI and cryptocurrency czar until March 2026, when he reached his employment limit under his designation as a “special government employee”. Sacks still co-chairs the President’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology. Trump previously floated Clayton’s name as a potential AI czar, telling Axios in September that Clayton was “a good man” and the prospect of appointing him was “a good idea”.

title: Green party votes to adopt policy that equates Zionism with racism
summary: Motion calling for single Palestinian state, which is opposed by most Green MPs and expected to be challenged, passes by 1,022 votes to 813
text: The Greens have formally adopted a policy that equates Zionism with racism and calls for Israel to be replaced by a single Palestinian state, a move opposed by the bulk of the party’s MPs and which is expected to face legal challenge. Zack Polanski, who heads the Greens in England and Wales and missed the vote at the party’s conference in Brighton to campaign in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, has faced criticism for a perceived lack of leadership on a hugely divisive issue. There have also been concerns that the policy change was pushed largely by newcomers who have little interest in the rest of the party’s platform. Four of the party’s five MPs opposed the motion. Adrian Ramsay and Ellie Chowns said they were “deeply saddened” while Siân Berry and Carla Denyer said they would support any Jewish members who believed they were being targeted as a result of the policy change. The binding policy motion, passed by 1,022 votes to 813, says Zionism – the movement for a Jewish state – should be “treated as any other form of racism”. It calls for Israel to be replaced by a single Palestinian state “with equal rights for all”. Israel’s foreign ministry said the resolution “constitutes a clear antisemitic text according to the IHRA (International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance) definition, as it denies the Jewish people’s right to self-determination”. Foreign minister Gideon Sa’ar decided to declare Green party leader Zack Polanski barred from entering Israel, the ministry said, adding the decision had been coordinated with the relevant authorities. While opinion among Jewish Green members is split, some have expressed worry that this will mean they could face disciplinary action for belonging to Jewish organisations that officially support Zionism, even synagogues. After the vote, one backer of the motion, Salma Yaqoob, a former member of George Galloway’s Respect party who is now a Green, insisted this would not happen, saying: “Nobody will be removed, challenged, disciplined, suspended because they put forward or articulate their belief in Zionism.” However, an amendment put forward saying the motion should not be used to “pressure, proscribe or discipline members based on affiliation with Jewish community institutions” was voted down. It is understood that some Green members are consulting lawyers over whether the policy could be challenged for breaching equalities legislation. Adam Wagner KC, the barrister who led a case that concluded Jeremy Corbyn’s Labour broke equalities laws over antisemitism, said such a case would have a good chance of success. “I think there is a strong risk that the motion as passed contravenes the Equality Act 2010, which applies to political parties, as it will discriminate against and harass people who hold Zionist beliefs and Jewish people more generally,” he said. Zionism when defined in the broad sense of supporting a Jewish nation state “is likely to be a protected belief” under the act, he said. The motion argues that Zionism is necessarily racist as it “privileges one ethnic group on the basis of the subjugation of others”. It adds: “This motion is aimed at the political ideology and practice of Zionism, as defined, and not at the religious or ethnic background of those who may identify as Zionists. Not all Jews are Zionists and not all Zionists are Jews … “Zionism, as defined above, will be treated as any other form of racism, and this motion will be implemented by the anti-racism policy working group as appropriate and in accordance with its ordinary practice.” According to the Institute for Jewish Policy Research, about two-thirds of British Jews consider themselves Zionists. During the lengthy debate, which was for members only, Chowns and Caroline Lucas, the former leader who was the Greens’ first MP, argued against the plan. The motion had been pushed by a group called Greens for Palestine, which encouraged non-party members to sign up to the party to make sure the policy was debated and adopted. After it was passed, supporters came to the front of the hall to hug and cheer. One member who opposed the motion said: “There are now two Green parties – the everyday members, and those who have joined for just one reason, Palestine, and who have no interest in anything else.” There is considerable disquiet among some senior Greens who feel that Polanski, who is Jewish, could have taken a stronger stance on the issue. The party leader has justified the motion’s broad argument by pointing to the death toll in Gaza during Israel’s assault on the territory. Asked on Saturday if he believed Zionism was racist, Polanski told the BBC: “Well, in the motion, it is defined as the displacement and genocide of the Palestinian people. I think that is clearly racism.” After the vote, the party’s five MPs, plus Polanski and his two co-deputy leaders, released a joint statement saying the party “will never tolerate any form of discrimination or harassment”, adding: “We know there is no conflict between supporting the rights of Palestinians and the rights of Jewish people.” However, Ramsay, Chowns, Berry and Denyer all posted this on social media with messages noting their opposition to the motion. The Movement for Progressive Judaism, one of the main Jewish denominations in the UK, condemned the vote, saying: “The motion is antisemitic in its formulation and intention. By adopting it, the Green party has made antisemitism party policy and become a racist party. “Jewish self-determination is a right. Declaring it racist is an attack on Jews. The Green party has chosen to brand Jews who hold this belief as racists and make their equal participation in the party conditional on renouncing it.” Adam Langleben, who coordinated complaints from the Jewish Labour Movement to the Equality and Human Rights Commission, said: “This is without doubt the most antisemitic and racist motion brought before a mainstream political party in my lifetime. It is Corbynism on steroids, and would seem even more open to legal challenge.”

title: After a deadly paper mill explosion, a community in Washington state looks to a key House race
summary: In a district shaken by the deaths of 11 workers, Democrat Marie Gluesenkamp Perez faces a stiff challenge to keep her seat
text: On a misty morning in May in south-west Washington state, Laura Oltmann, a 41-year-old dietitian, had barely clocked in when an unfamiliar overhead announcement echoed through the hospital. “We get overhead pages for different types of emergencies. But this one, we don’t get very often,” recalled Oltmann. Doctors, nurses and staff began guessing what could have happened. Perhaps it was a train derailment. Maybe a major highway crash. As the speculation grew, so did the uncertainty. Staff started calling one another. The answer shook them all. “Someone mentioned there had been an explosion at this plant, and that we were probably going to be getting some patients from there,” Oltmann said. Forty miles south, in the port city of Longview, residents had awakened to a thunderous boom. At approximately 7.18am, as workers changed shifts at a paper mill company, Nippon Dynawave Packaging, a tank of white liquor, a caustic chemical used in the paper-making process, imploded. Hours passed with no explanation of what had caused it or how it could have happened at all, and suspicion began to brew. With roughly a thousand people working at the mill, thousands more were waiting for a phone call. Parents called children. Wives called husbands. Grandparents called grandchildren. “For those that did not get that response,” said Jeff Wilson, a Republican state senator representing Longview, who also sits as the port commissioner, “all they got was silence.” In the end, 11 people were killed in one of Washington state’s deadliest industrial accidents in nearly a century. Nowhere was that impact felt more deeply than in Longview itself, a working-class city of about 38,000 people whose economy and identity have long been tied to the paper industry, shipping and logging. For generations, families have depended on the mills for their livelihoods. The disaster struck at something the city had long regarded as permanent: the mills where generations had gone to work, and helped many send their children to college or put down a down payment on a home. The implosion rippled through nearly every corner of a community affected by mill closures and economic change. Those concerns will probably have an impact at the ballot box. As summer turned toward fall and the leaves along the Columbia River began to turn yellow, memorial services gave way to campaign rallies. The same communities that had gathered around grieving families were preparing for one of the country’s most closely watched House races in November. Nearly two months after the implosion, on 8 July, Wilson still spoke first about the workers, the funerals he had attended, the families and the co-workers who ran toward danger looking for one another. He recalled brothers Tyler and Brad Covington, 27 and 29; he said: “They went to work together. And then they died together.” Before entering politics, Wilson spent more than 23 years cleaning tanks at the Nippon Dynawave mill. In the aftermath of the tragedy, he worked routinely with Democratic congresswoman Marie Gluesenkamp Perez’s office as local, state and federal officials responded to the disaster, his role in Olympia intersecting with hers in Washington. Though he declined to endorse her re-election, Wilson credited the Democratic congresswoman with being “present and accountable” and praised her for asking questions rather than “rubber-stamping anything”. For a community divided by many of the same political forces pulling at the rest of the country, the disaster briefly created a sense of togetherness, as the whole community grieved the deaths of many of their neighbors and family members. “Natural disasters will tend to bring people together,” said Mark Alan Smith, a political science professor at the University of Washington who studies American politics and religion. “It’s something people can unify around … across race and class and other divisions.” *** On 4 August, Gluesenkamp Perez and the Republican state senator John Braun advanced from a field of nine to face off for the district’s congressional seat in November. Braun finished first with about 39.7% of the vote to Gluesenkamp Perez’s 36.4%. Brent Hennrich, the progressive Democrat who argued that Gluesenkamp Perez no longer represented many of her party’s voters, took 16.7%. The results exposed the competing pressures facing Gluesenkamp Perez heading into the general election. Braun, who netted a Trump endorsement in April and millions in pro-Trump money, finished ahead of the incumbent. Meanwhile, Hennrich’s showing demonstrated the size of the progressive bloc she will have to contend with in November. Many of those voters remain angry over parts of her vote on the Safeguard American Voter Eligibility (Save) Act (which would require proof of citizenship to vote), ICE funding, and a bill restricting how public schools address gender identity. When asked about those direct criticisms of the congresswoman – whom many on the left feel has drifted from the party – her campaign responded with a written statement to the Guardian that cast her independence as the reason south-west Washington should return her to office. “DC has enough career politicians following national agendas,” said her campaign manager, Timothy Gowen. “Southwest Washington deserves an independent representative who delivers real results. Marie will always be loyal to her district first.” The statement did not address questions about her voting record or the primary result. The race stretches far beyond Longview and the nearby city of Battle Ground. Washington’s third congressional district runs from the Pacific coast through the timber towns of the lower Columbia and inland farm country to Vancouver and the fast-growing suburbs north of Portland. Logging, paper mills, agriculture, shipping and manufacturing still shape daily life across much of it, while its politics pull hard in opposite directions. That geography has forced Gluesenkamp Perez to build an unusual coalition. Her political survival has depended partly on voters who do not ordinarily identify with Democrats, including moderates and conservatives drawn to her emphasis on the trades, guns and independence from her party. But that same positioning has alienated Democrats who believe she has moved too far from them. “Two years ago, people reported having to hold their nose and vote for her, because she was better than [former opponent and one-time counter-intelligence official] Joe Kent,” said LaDonna Kirkpatrick, chair of the 18th Legislative District Democrats, speaking in a personal capacity. “But now we’re in a situation where I’m hearing from so many people that even if she wins the primary, they will not vote for her. And the frustration is real. I’m feeling that personally.” Thea Zaine, chair of the 20th Legislative District Democrats, speaks for the bloc of progressive Democrats whose discontent showed up in the primary returns. Her organization was the only Democratic party body in the district to endorse Hennrich. “We believe in protecting immigrants. She’s voted to give more money to ICE,” Zaine said. “She voted to give funding to wars in Iran. And she takes money from Aipac, and she’s voted to fund the genocide in Gaza.” Gluesenkamp Perez’s record on Iran, however, is more complicated than Zaine suggested. The Democratic representative voted for war powers resolutions directing the removal of US forces from the unauthorized war with Iran, while also breaking with most Democrats to support the broader $1.15tn National Defense Authorization Act. For Zaine, those votes have made the choice straightforward. But not every young, left-leaning voter who shares her frustration has reached the same conclusion. Tanner Manley, 25, an incoming law student who lives near Vancouver and describes himself as left-leaning, shares much of the critique. He plans to vote for Gluesenkamp Perez anyway. “Of course, I wish more progressive candidates were viable here, and that Marie would take a clear moral stand on Israel and reject Aipac funding the way she refuses corporate Pac money,” he said. “In another race with different options, I’d likely support a different candidate.” What keeps Manley with her is closer to home. After the Longview disaster, the US Chemical Safety and Hazard Investigation Board, the independent federal agency investigating the tank failure at the Longview paper plant, faced elimination under the administration’s proposed budget. In June, Gluesenkamp Perez backed an amendment restoring $14m for the agency, which passed the House appropriations committee with Republican support. “That might not satisfy progressives watching from the other side of the country,” Manley said, “but try telling people in this district that that kind of fight in Congress doesn’t matter.” Neither candidate’s campaign has made the Longview tragedy a centerpiece of the race. A recent poll underscores how little room both candidates have: the survey, conducted by DHM Research for Oregon Public Broadcasting, found Braun at 48% and Gluesenkamp Perez at 47% after undecided voters were asked which candidate they leaned toward, with 5% still undecided. Smith, of the University of Washington, said events that bring communities together can be difficult to translate into partisan advantage. “In order for something like that to affect how people vote, somebody has to channel it,” Smith said. “It’s hard to channel anything where everybody agrees.” That could change, he said, “if you can somehow link your opponent to some negative aspect” of the event. So far, neither campaign has done so. And Wilson praised Gluesenkamp Perez’s handling of the disaster. “She’s been representing, you know, from the federal angle, well on this,” he said. The response also fit the political identity Gluesenkamp Perez has cultivated in south-west Washington, where she has emphasized the trades and the economic pressures facing rural and working-class communities. In an interview with OPB, she described watching the decline of industries that have long sustained towns across the region. “Mill after mill closed in our region,” she said. “It’s just got people really at high anxiety levels.” About three miles north of Nippon Dynawave, at the Pentecostal church where Ron Peterson is pastor, the disaster remains part of the community’s memory. For Peterson, 38, the tragedy had briefly brought together people who otherwise disagreed about much else. But when I asked him about politics, he drew a distinction. “We don’t win politically,” he said. “We win spiritually.” A few miles south, and across a district where the divisions are not only political, Chydell Armijo, 35, mother of two, was thinking about something more immediate. She had little enthusiasm for either political party. What worried her was whether people like her could still build a stable life: whether a small business could survive, whether her children could find opportunity and whether working people could still move up. “I honestly feel like everybody is struggling,” Armijo said. “There is no such thing as middle class any more.” For all the attention on which party will control this congressional seat after November, Armijo saw a divide that would remain regardless of who won. “Our economic system has become difficult, in many ways, for us to climb,” she said.

title: For Kemi, being the Nasty party is not toxic but a badge of honour | John Crace
summary: The Tory leader says the party’s plans to cut people’s benefits are no more than ‘common sense’
text: It’s a thought. A bold one. Possibly a career-ending one. But a thought nonetheless. When Theresa May told the Tory conference in 2002 that under Iain Duncan Smith the Conservatives had become “the Nasty party”, many members took that to mean they had become undesirable. Within a few years, David Cameron had moved the Tories closer to the “hug a husky” centre and by 2010 he was prime minister. Kemi Badenoch takes a rather different view. For her, being the Nasty party is a badge of honour. An aspiration. People had had it far too good with austerity, Brexit, Covid and the Liz Truss mini-budget. The country needed a reality check; a return to old-fashioned unpleasantness. A taste of genuine hardship. People had got far too used to getting something for nothing. Especially the physically and mentally ill. What they needed was a short sharp shock of intense labour from 8am to 8pm. That would make them feel better. And anyone found skiving would be banged up for a short time in prison. Say 10 years. And take a bow, her cheerleader-in-chief. The man whose sycophancy consistently goes above and beyond the call of duty. We’re talking, of course, of the shadow home secretary, Chris Philp. He had chosen to mark the beginning of Tory conference with an interview to the Sun in which he had identified himself as a one-man vigilante force. For the next four days, he had personally guaranteed that Birmingham would be a crime-free zone. The Philpster would be on guard night and day to arrest all shoplifters and to check up on people who hadn’t paid their TV licence. From now on he would be a superhero. BatTwat. For Kemi, the beginning of conference was marked with the traditional BBC interview with Laura Kuenssberg. One where she would try to be the cosiest version of herself. The nasty leader with the heart of gold. A woman who could say in all honesty that “this was hurting her more than it was hurting you” as she removed someone’s benefits. This was Kemi returning in triumph. A year ago, her position as leader had looked ropey. Now the Tories have had a long, hard look around and concluded there actually isn’t anyone better. “Is this a return to the nasty party?” asked Kuenssberg. Kemi was trying not to phrase it in precisely those terms. Nasty was only a word to be implied. Rather, she would prefer it if we could use the words “commonsense” party. Common sense, as in it was plain to everyone that something had to be done. And that something was to pick on the poorest and most vulnerable people in society. For years now, these parasites had been lounging around and getting fat on benefits. Asking themselves not what they could do for the Tory party but what the Tory party could do for them. To illustrate her point, Kemi proudly drew Laura’s attention to her rather desperate pamphlet The Right Way, which the Tories have published as their new credo. Six principles of Conservatism to get them through the bad times. To remind them they are right even when the country thinks they are unelectable. Kemi’s Kemistry, as she hopes we will call it. The first rule is that Kemi never makes mistakes. Asked to name anything she has changed her mind about, she comes up with nothing. The laws of physics will change long before Kemi. She wants us to think of The Right Way as her foundational document that will be spoken of in hushed tones for decades to come. It will be lucky to survive until tomorrow. We then moved on to Kemi’s latest big idea: to give everyone who makes more than £100,000 a year unlimited free childcare. The case was unarguable, said Kemi. Free childcare was totally wasted on people on the minimum wage because they couldn’t be trusted to spend the money wisely. It would probably all be wasted on Happy Meals at McDonald’s or a Sky subscription. Let’s face it, it was just chucking good money after bad. Most working-class kids were bound to end up on benefits anyway, so why encourage them from the moment they were born? It’s time they learned to be self-sufficient. What a contrast with the top 5% of the country. They could at least spend their benefits on something worthwhile. Like baby yoga. Kemi was also keen to keep pensioners happy. We will retain the triple lock, she said. Even though half the shadow cabinet know it’s completely unaffordable. Old people definitely had to be kept sweet, as they were about the last section of the country who actually voted Tory. Not that this was any factor in shaping current policy. Because Kemi had just published The Right Way, in which she had declared that her principles were whatever she wanted them to be on the day. And, by the way, this would all be paid for by cutting benefits for the 10 million scroungers who were cheating the system. Could you verify that figure? Laura asked. Kemi shook her head. It was just a well-known fact that she had made up. So no need. After going on to say she would be building 50,000 more prison spaces for all the criminals BatTwat arrested in the next four days, the interview meandered to a close. In the studio, Penny Mordaunt declared it to be the best interview a Tory leader had ever given. Penny is beside herself with joy at having passed the test to be admitted to the MPs’ candidate list. Answering yes to questions such as: “Are you mad?” and “Are you happy to trash the Good Friday agreement?” It was Penny’s performance in the Sky reality show The War Game that swung it. As defence secretary she couldn’t wait to start a nuclear apocalypse. Come friendly bombs. Over in the conference centre, the complex was strangely quiet. Maybe the news that everything is going swimmingly for the Tories hasn’t yet filtered down to MPs and members. Even the main hall wasn’t full, and there was nothing going on elsewhere. But those who were there seemed happy enough. Perhaps they are genuinely delighted that things aren’t going even worse. That they are still only four points in the polls off their disastrous 2024 election result. That it doesn’t matter that the so-called Keminaissance exists largely in their imaginations. But on we go. A party the country still regards as toxic is determined to double down on its toxicity. Desperate to track ever further to the right and abandon its centre right to Labour and the Lib Dems. It feels like madness. But this conference is all about Kult Kemi. There is even an AI slop, sub-Beano reproduction of the Bayeux tapestry. A series of tableaux leading to the moment Kemi saves the world. She looks on beatifically as several easily identified journalists take dictation. Curiously, I’m not one of them.

title: Labour offers too litte, too late for Afghan women and girls | Letter
summary: Letter: The home secretary’s language of ‘compassion’ and ‘international obligations’ is at odds with the party’s record in protecting vulnerable migrants, writes Eleanor Luxton
text: Regarding your article (UK to open new refugee resettlement routes for Afghan women and Palestinians, 27 September), rather than focusing on whether or not Shabana Mahmood’s policy change will deter small boat arrivals (which it won’t), shouldn’t we be in uproar over her use of the language of “compassion” and “international obligations”? Considering Ed Miliband’s admission at the Labour conference that the party has not done enough to support the Palestinian people – and the abrupt closure of the Afghan Relocations and Assistance Policy and Afghan Citizens Resettlement Scheme with almost no notice on 1 July 2025, again under Labour leadership – is this not a case of too little, too late? Mine and others’ research with Afghan women living in so-called “refugee hotels” throws Mahmood’s sudden concern for “vulnerable women and girls” into sharp focus. A significant proportion of Afghan women and girls who arrived in British hotels after the so-called fall of Kabul in August 2021 experienced violence, were isolated from essential support services and were evicted by the Home Office with guidance to seek permanent accommodation on Rightmove. In a time when the far right is increasingly weaponising the discourse of “protecting vulnerable women and girls” from what they consider to be violent male migrants, Mahmood should reflect carefully on Labour’s rediscovered sense of duty towards Afghan women, and the effect on Afghan women and girls caused by the government’s own policies. The government would do well to consider the research of academics such as Louise Ryan, Caroline Oliver and their team of Afghan peer researchers who use evidence-based approaches to understanding the experiences of migrants and refugees in the UK. Eleanor Luxton London • Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Please email us your letter and it will be considered for publication in our letters section.

title: Let’s build a better future for female scaffolders | Letter
summary: Letter: Emma Claassen responds to an article by Adrian Chiles on the recruitment crisis in scaffolding
text: Adrian Chiles is right: scaffolding is hard work (Britain’s scaffolding should be a source of national pride – instead we’re struggling to recruit workers, 1 October). It demands physical resilience, skill, judgment and proper training. That will naturally mean it is not a job for everyone – men or women. Which is why the conversation about the skills shortage should be less about who traditionally became a scaffolder, and more about who is willing and able to learn the trade and meet the same standards. As the industry is already facing the significant shortfall that Chiles describes, we need to widen the pool of people who can see scaffolding as a genuine career. That includes women, but the bigger issue is attracting capable people into the trade, training them properly and keeping standards high. That is part of what the Women in Scaffolding Association (WiSA) is trying to do. We support women already working on the tools, make them visible and connected, and show women and girls that scaffolding is a genuine skilled career. We also work to bring more people into construction generally. Nobody is suggesting lowering the bar. Scaffolding requires strength, but also technique, teamwork, training and considerable skill. The standards should remain the standards. Chiles also makes an important point about AI. Scaffolding is practical, skilled work that cannot simply be automated away. Britain still needs people who can build, solve problems and work safely with their hands. If scaffolders are becoming a dying breed, perhaps the answer is to look more widely for the next generation. Some of them will be women. Emma Claassen Founder, WiSA

title: Time to move the UN away from Donald Trump’s grasp | Brief letters
summary: Brief letters: UN headquarters | A third Stephen Moss? | Overstaying guests | Cutting cafe sign | Haircut patience | Pre-loved ridiculousness
text: Nesrine Malik rightly questions the effectiveness of the current United Nations (War, power games and impunity. I watched the farce that is the UN general assembly: what a tragedy, what a mess, 1 October). Why has there been so little outcry about Donald Trump’s blocking of visas for Palestinians and Sudanese (or any other accredited members) to attend the UN in New York? Despite the cost and upheaval, it is time to call Trump’s bluff and relocate the UN, preferably to Switzerland. title: Russia strikes Kyiv bridge as German chancellor visits Ukraine in show of support
summary: Attack shortly after Friedrich Merz arrived on unannounced visit intended to underline Germany’s backing
text: Russia has struck another major bridge in Kyiv as the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, arrived in the capital in a show of support for Ukraine. A Russian drone hit Kyiv’s key Northern Bridge over the Dnipro River, marking the fourth consecutive day that Russia has targeted bridges used by tens of thousands of residents commuting between the city’s two banks. Video footage showed cars driving across the bridge as the drone plunged into the roadway and exploded in a burst of fire. Two people were injured in the strike, said Kyiv’s mayor, Vitali Klitschko. The attack came shortly after Merz arrived in the city on an unannounced visit intended to underline Germany’s backing of Ukraine, as the country enters one of the most precarious periods since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022. Germany has become Ukraine’s biggest provider of military aid since Merz entered office in May 2025, surpassing the US as American support has declined. Kyiv has come under near-constant attack from Russia’s new jet-powered drones in recent weeks, as an intensifying strike campaign increasingly disrupts everyday life in the capital and threatens to leave the city without power this winter. On his visit, Merz announced that Germany would fund the joint production of drones designed to intercept Russia’s jet-powered drones, adding that “significant technical breakthroughs” in recent weeks were speeding up production. “This will quickly and tangibly strengthen Ukraine’s air defence,” he said. “And this strengthening is urgently needed.” The German leader got a taste of the new reality of daily life in the Ukrainian capital. Air-raid sirens sounded repeatedly during his visit, including as Volodymyr Zelenskyy showed him the badly damaged National Academy of Sciences building, where a Russian drone strike killed two people last week. The Ukrainian president told Merz that people in Kyiv were suffering “terrible nights and days” from the relentless attacks, and called Ukraine’s Russian adversaries “absolute barbarians”. “We can see the entire pointlessness of this war at this place,” said Merz, adding as he arrived that Ukraine “needs all our support in the coming weeks”. “If Russia is not stopped, its war machine will sooner or later turn against us,” he said. Russia had already damaged Kyiv’s Northern Bridge and repeatedly struck its Southern Bridge. Although the crossings remain standing, repeated attacks and the threat of further strikes have prompted the city’s authorities to restrict or suspend traffic on five of the city’s six road bridges over the Dnipro, causing temporary closures and large traffic jams. If Moscow succeeds in seriously damaging Kyiv’s bridges, it could create a logistical nightmare for the city of 3 million people, whose crossings over the Dnipro were last destroyed on a large scale as Nazi German forces retreated in 1943. More than a third of residents live on the left bank while much of the city’s employment and infrastructure is concentrated on the right. The attacks form part of a broader Russian campaign against civilian and industrial infrastructure inside Ukraine. In recent weeks, strikes have hit logistics hubs, railway lines, datacentres, medical storage facilities and steel plants, alongside a sustained assault on the country’s energy system that is expected to intensify over the winter. “He [Putin] is counting on constant escalation. He wants this very much,” Zelenskyy said at a press conference alongside Merz. “This is an answer to everyone – to those who believe that all you have to do is simply ask Putin and he will end the war for real. It won’t happen, simply.” Russia’s foreign ministry on Saturday warned foreign nationals and diplomatic staff against remaining in or travelling to Ukraine. “Responsibility for any possible adverse consequences lies entirely with those who choose to disregard this warning,” the ministry said. A number of foreign ambassadors, including Germany’s, responded on social media that they intended to remain in Kyiv. “The EU delegation is staying,” the European Union ambassador, Katarína Mathernová, wrote on X on Sunday. “Threatening us will not stop Europe’s support for Ukraine. It only reminds us why that support matters.” In Moscow, some pro-war commenters noted with glee that the Russian strikes had continued despite Merz’s arrival. “Russia used to pause strikes on Kyiv during visits by European politicians. Not any more,” wrote Sergei Markov, a prominent pro-war commentator. The trip is Merz’s second to Ukraine since becoming chancellor. He has been among Kyiv’s most outspoken supporters in Europe and a leading voice warning about Russia’s hybrid campaign against other nations. Last month, Germany formally accused Moscow of being behind a suspected plot targeting Leipzig/Halle airport, a key logistics hub for western military aid to Ukraine. But Merz is also facing growing discontent at home over his support for Ukraine, as his approval ratings fall. Germany’s far left and far right are sceptical of support for Ukraine and want Berlin to scale back aid. The pressure has intensified as the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) has made big electoral gains. Alice Weidel, the AfD’s co-leader, wrote in a social media post: “Merz is travelling to Ukraine on Germany’s national holiday and promising further billions in German taxpayer money that is missing from the pension and health insurance funds, while Germany is mired in its worst energy crisis.”

title: Mass shootings leave two people dead in Georgia and 12-year-old girl dead in Baltimore
summary: At least 25 injured at block party shooting in Georgia and three wounded in Baltimore park shooting, officials say
text: Two people were killed and at least 25 others injured when a shooting erupted at a homecoming block party in Vienna, Georgia, early on Sunday, according to authorities. In another high-profile mass shooting in the US over the weekend, a 12-year-old girl was shot and killed and three other people were wounded after gunfire evidently broke out over a parking spot in a Baltimore park on Saturday, officials said. The violence in Georgia occurred at a gathering of more than 1,000 people, local sheriff Craig Peavy told area news outlet WMAZ. Shots were fired at about 50 people in two locations about a block apart just after 1am on Sunday, Peavy told WMAZ. The pair killed at the scene were not immediately identified. The identity of the suspects, or a possible motive for the gunfire, also were not immediately identified. Peavy added that about 25 people were taken to the hospital, as many as 35 people may have been wounded, and deputies were monitoring the crowd at the time of the shooting. Meanwhile, with respect to the shooting in Baltimore, police commissioner Richard Worley said two suspects were being sought after two different types of gun cartridges were found at the scene of the violence near a youth football event at Leon Day Park. “What we know is that there was some type of argument between two cowards, and of course they both opened fire on each other,” Worley said at a Saturday night news conference. “The dispute most likely occurred from a stupid parking spot, and they get into a fight, and the two cowards pull guns on each other.” Worley said the 12-year-old girl who was killed in that case was a bystander at a nearby field, who was hit when one of the shooters “fired multiple rounds down range”. A 25-year-old woman with the girl was shot, too. So were two men, aged 23 and 28, according to police. None of the three wounded victims were believed to have life-threatening injuries, police said. The 12-year-old girl was pronounced dead at the scene, and paramedics took the woman to the hospital. The two other victims walked into a nearby hospital with injuries. “Two grown men got into an argument, and now a 12-year-old is gone,” the Baltimore mayor, Brandon Scott, said to reporters. “What happened out here today, is one of the most disgusting things I’ve ever seen in my life because that baby was just out here, at homecoming for this youth football league is out here every single day, trying to keep young people safe, trying to keep young men and young women on the right path.” There had been at least 355 mass shootings reported in the US so far for the year as of Sunday, which was the 277th day of 2026, according to the Gun Violence Archive. The archive, a nonpartisan reference resource, defines mass shootings as cases in which at least four victims are killed or wounded. The US perennially has high rates of such shootings, fueling calls from some quarters for more substantial federal gun control. But Congress has not passed such measures over the years.

title: Knox Chitiyo obituary
summary: Other lives: Expert on Zimbabwean political and economic affairs who became head of the Royal United Services Institute’s Africa programme
text: My friend and former colleague Knox Chitiyo, who has died aged 65 of bowel cancer, was a Zimbabwean academic and later an important voice in Britain on his homeland and its future. He was regularly consulted by diplomats, business people, journalists, academics and activists. From 1992 to 2003 he was a senior lecturer in war studies and military history at the University of Zimbabwe, where he co-founded the Centre for Defence Studies, serving as its deputy director. He also taught on the joint command and staff course at Zimbabwe’s National Army Staff College and at the Gweru Military Academy, helping shape the strategic thinking of a generation of officers. As intellectual space in Zimbabwe tightened under Robert Mugabe, Knox moved to the UK in 2005. He joined the Royal United Services Institute, eventually becoming head of its Africa programme (2007-11), and developed an international reputation for his work on Zimbabwe, defence and security. In 2012 he became an associate fellow at Chatham House – a position he retained until his death. Knox was born in Salisbury (now Harare) in Southern Rhodesia, then part of the Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland, to Wynona (nee Chieza), a nurse, and McLeod Chitiyo, a pathologist. Growing up through the turbulent final decades of white minority rule in Southern Rhodesia, he attended a private, racially mixed secondary school, St George’s, which was run by Jesuits in Salisbury, an unusual experience that shaped his interest in race, identity and political change. After school he gained a general degree at the University of Zimbabwe, where he then built his academic career, completing a PhD and lecturing in history and war studies before simultaneously becoming deputy director of the university’s Centre for Defence Studies from 1995 and then leaving for Britain a decade later. Knox was particularly passionate about ensuring that Zimbabweans in the diaspora had a voice in policy debate in the UK. Beyond his role at Chatham House, he was president of the Britain Zimbabwe Society and served on the board of the Business Council for Africa, including as acting chair. He was also a fellow of the Brenthurst Foundation, an thinktank on African economics and politics, and became a trustee of the Mines Advisory Group, a charity devoted to finding and destroying landmines in places affected by conflict. He brought warmth, humour and humanity to serious subjects, and moved easily between academics, soldiers, diplomats and politicians without losing either his independence or his kindness. In his spare time he wrote poetry and short stories and played the saxophone, including, he once told me, at Ronnie Scott’s in London. Knox is survived by his wife, Nhamburiko, a midwife, whom he married in 2002, and their son, Kyle, and his sister Cathy. • This article was amended on 6 October 2026 to correct some personal details.

title: Egyptian journalist faces terrorism charges after entire newsroom detained
summary: Calls for release of six Matsadaash staff after one is charged, while whereabouts of other five remain unknown
text: An Egyptian journalist has been charged with joining a terrorist group, days after an entire newsroom was detained in what rights groups have said is a crackdown on press freedoms. Last week, authorities arrested six journalists from the independent fact-checking and investigative platform Matsadaash – literally meaning “don’t believe” – accusing them in a statement of being unlicensed and publishing false news on behalf of the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood. The outlet’s six journalists, Abdallah Qadri, Mohamed Ashraf, Mohamed Adel, Islam Barakat, Mohamed Mahmoud and Omar Helal, were arrested by security forces over the course of two days. On Sunday, Egyptian authorities charged Ashraf with joining a terrorist group and spreading false news, according to a statement by the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights, a NGO. The charges came after an interrogation that lasted from 10pm to 8am and focused exclusively on material published by Matsadaash, the rights group said. Ashraf was to be held for 15 days, pending investigation, while the whereabouts of the other five journalists were still unknown. Abdelrahman Mansour, the co-founder of the platform, denied having any association with the Muslim Brotherhood, a transnational movement that was designated a terrorist organisation by Egypt in 2013 after the former president Mohamed Morsi, a senior Brotherhood figure, was ousted in a coup. Mansour called the arrests “one of the gravest attacks on journalism in Egypt’s modern history”. “My colleagues were doing what journalists should do: asking difficult questions, uncovering facts, and reporting on issues that affect people’s lives. They deserve recognition for their work. Instead, their homes were raided, and all six were taken away,” he said. “The government must answer this question: why have you arrested six journalists? What have they done beyond doing their jobs?” The Guardian contacted the Egyptian State Information Service for a comment but did not receive a reply by the time of publishing. Dozens of journalists staged a sit-in outside the Egyptian Journalists Syndicate (EJS) in Cairo on Saturday, demanding the release of the Matsadaash staff. Members said they would keep the sit-in open ended until the journalists were released, and the EJS said it would convene an emergency meeting on Monday. The EJS had filed a request with the ministry of interior and public prosecutor for the release of the journalists, as well as for information on their whereabouts. More than 80 rights groups, including Human Rights Watch and the Committee to Protect Journalists, condemned the arrests as a violation of freedoms, and demanded the immediate release of the Matsadaash staff. The arrests came little over a week after the US government waived its human rights conditions on $320m (£242m) in military aid to Egypt, citing Cairo’s “helpful role” to US national security after the US-Iran war. The US gives about $1.3bn in aid to Egypt annually, but a portion is contingent upon the Egyptian government meeting certain human rights and democracy-related requirements. The US has withheld portions of aid several times since the 2013 coup owing to Egypt’s poor human rights record, but has largely kept funds flowing. This year, Washington waived the human rights requirement in total, as doing so was “essential for the US-Egypt relationship and US national security priorities”, according to a state department memo revealed by Reuters. While saying that he was unsure whether the arrests were linked to the recent waiver, Mansour said: “The use of the national security waiver on human rights conditions by the US by many years, a willingness by other states to look the other way on Egypt’s human rights record … certainly enables violations like this to occur more easily.” Cairo has for years faced criticism for its human rights abuses, with the rights monitor Freedom House saying Egyptian security forces “engage in human rights abuses and extrajudicial killing with impunity”. Since the Egyptian president Abdel Fatah al-Sisi took power in the coup that ousted Morsi, civil liberties have been curbed and domestic political opposition has been violently crushed. Egypt ranks 169th out of 180 countries on the Reporters Without Borders Press freedom index. Freedom of the press is tightly restricted in the country and independent platforms such as Matsadaash are rare. About 26 journalists are held in Egyptian prisons, according to the EJS.

title: More than 400 schools in France to be closed on Monday as more protests planned
summary: Education minister says 24 schools have been burnt or ransacked and 78 staff members injured since student unrest began last month
text: More than 400 schools in France will be closed or partly closed on Monday as authorities brace for another week of student protests. Lessons will be totally or partly suspended in 400 to 500 schools because security conditions “have not been fulfilled”, the education minister, Édouard Geffray, said on Sunday. The minister said 24 schools had been burnt or ransacked and 78 education staff members injured. The number of school closures on Monday would be comparable to Friday’s but the government envisaged a “partial, progressive return to lessons”, said Geffray. Thousands of teenagers staged widespread demonstrations and erected barricades last week to protest against what they said was underfunding and neglect of the education system. Clashes with riot police left hundreds of people injured, led to more than 5,000 arrests, mostly of minors, and jolted President Emmanuel Macron’s centrist administration. There was a lull at the weekend, but protest organisers called for renewed demonstrations on Tuesday because the government had failed to produce “concrete measures”. Authorities say political agitators have infiltrated the protest, which started at a Paris school on 17 September and spread across the capital and the rest of France. “There are activists – particularly from the far left – who have infiltrated the high school student movement, hijacked it from the students themselves, and engaged in extreme violence,” said Geffray. “Clearly, this poses a risk to both our staff and our students.” The injured education staff members were deliberately targeted, “something we have never seen before”, said Geffray. The protests caught the government by surprise and confronted Macron with his worst crisis in months. Images of burning barricades and police using teargas, batons and other methods to disperse protests have dominated TV news. Student grievances include overcrowded classes of up to 40 children in crumbling buildings, poor teacher pay, staff absences and an unequal system in which social background determined success. Other factors are an opaque and difficult online system for university applications as well as the sweltering temperatures in classrooms during heatwaves. Protesters have accused the state of disengaging from secondary education and cited difficult conditions such as leaks, cockroaches, collapsed ceilings and decayed buildings. Others have complained about excessively long school days and a lack of teaching staff. The government said the grievances were legitimate but condemned what it called “urban violence”. On Sunday, police detained a 16-year-old in relation to an assault of a teacher in La Ciotat, a town on the southern coast between Marseille and Toulon. The teacher, 59, was doused with gasoline and struck during a protest on Friday. The government is also under pressure from trade unions that called a day of strikes last week to compel the new prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, to rethink budget cuts and consider a form of wealth tax on the super-rich. The CGT trade union exhorted workers to sustain the pressure with demonstrations this week.

title: Nigel Farage questioned by standards commissioner over £5m gift
summary: Reform UK leader was interviewed for half an hour last month over money from crypto billionaire
text: Nigel Farage has been interviewed by the standards commissioner for an investigation into whether he should have declared a £5m gift from the crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne. The Reform UK leader spent about half an hour being questioned over the money, the Sunday Times reported. Farage maintains the gift was for his personal security. The interview conducted last month is a sign the process is nearing a conclusion, although Reform UK is not believed to have been informed that the report is finished. An MP under investigation is usually notified before the conclusion of the process. If the commissioner finds that there has been a serious breach of the rules, the matter is passed to the standards committee of MPs and lay members, which can ask for further evidence. The committee can recommend a sanction or override the report. If it suggests more than a 10-day suspension from the Commons – and parliament agrees – the Reform UK leader could find himself facing a recall petition and second byelection in his Clacton constituency. Farage has been under investigation over the gift since shortly after the Guardian revealed in May that Harborne had given him £5m just before the last election in 2024. The Reform leader has said it was a personal matter, not political, and the money did not need to be declared. The rules state that financial support related to an MP’s job needs to be registered if given in the 12 months before they enter parliament. After a slide in the polls over the summer, Reform is about to embark on a major reorganisation at its headquarters to try to revive its fortunes. Insiders said it would involve a big shake-up of staffing, in addition to the suspensions of James Orr, the party’s head of policy, and Dan Jukes, Farage’s close aide. The pair are facing an internal investigation into whether they encouraged illegal foreign donations during an undercover investigation by reporters from Verbatim. The inquiry is being carried out by lawyers who are expected to reach their conclusions soon. The matter is also the subject of a police inquiry. The party is working out how to spend £72m in donations from Harborne and another crypto billionaire, Ben Delo. The huge sums have prompted calls from political rivals for a donation cap. A possible use of the money is the relaunch of a TV channel that produces Reform-related video coverage and a show fronted by Farage. Farage told the Sunday Times he thought the reaction to the donations would be “far worse” but had produced “some grudging respect – the fact that I managed to pull off a coup of that magnitude, I think people were quite impressed”. It is not clear whether the donations fall within the rules because the government is putting forward legislation to ban overseas donors from giving more than £100,000 in a calendar year – backdated to March this year. Harborne joined the UK electoral register only this summer and Delo has been largely based in Hong Kong, although on the register for some years. If the donations are ruled impermissible, Reform could have to hand them back, a prospect that is likely to lead to court action.
