title: Andrew Rutter obituary
summary: Other lives: Conservation officer in Winchester responsible for protecting the city’s old buildings and landscapes
text: My father, Andrew Rutter, who has died aged 93, was a trained architect and worked in planning for Hampshire county council. He became Winchester’s first conservation officer responsible for championing the city’s old buildings and landscapes. His great gift in that role, which he held from 1974 until his retirement in 1998, was his ability to visualise the effect of planning applications and then to make councillors aware of potential consequences before coming to their decisions. Among other things, he and his team had to face the major challenges presented by a re-routing in the early 1990s of the M3 motorway through a small chalk valley near Winchester; he helped to reduce most of the possible destructive environmental impacts of the original plan, apart from the notorious cutting through Twyford Down. Andrew was born in Shaftesbury, Dorset, the youngest of the five children of William, a solicitor, and Hester (nee Fox), who were both Quakers. At Sidcot boarding school in Winscombe, Somerset, he showed artistic talent and an early interest in architecture. He then went to the Architectural Association School of Architecture in London and gained a diploma in architecture. National service was due to follow, but as a conscientious objector Andrew was allowed to do architectural-related work for the charity International Voluntary Service for Peace instead, first in Germany and then in newly independent Ghana. In 1959 he met Margery Haygarth at a work camp hostel in the East End of London, and they married in 1960. The following year they moved to Ghana, where Andrew was employed by the United Nations at the Technical University in Kumasi, training planning assistants. In 1969 he and his young family moved to the UK so he could take up his post with Hampshire county council, where he became a forward planning officer. It was after an internal re-organisation in 1974 that he was appointed as Winchester’s first conservation officer. In retirement he spent some of his time writing a book, Winchester, Heart of a City (2009), which recorded the distinctive features of the buildings and surroundings of Winchester’s conservation area. Having been involved in establishing Winchester’s first permanent Quaker Meeting house in 1973, he was also a well-known character at vigils and peace demonstrations around the area and was a long time supporter of a local Quaker initiative, Friends of the Family, which helped many vulnerable people. Margery died in 2022. Andrew is survived by their sons, Mark and me, and grandchildren Toby, Hannah and Theo.

title: JD Vance flexing Maha connections as he eyes 2028 election
summary: Considered Republican frontrunner for presidential election, Vance is cozying up to the movement – as it splits
text: JD Vance, widely considered to be the Republican frontrunner for the presidential election in 2028, is aligning himself with the Make America Healthy Again (Maha) movement as some say it is shedding its grassroots supporters in favor of political and corporate interests. The US vice-president has positioned himself as the inheritor of Make America Great Again (Maga), and attaching himself to Maha, which many in the Trump administration believe helped to win the 2024 election, signals a greater overlap between the two movements as the administration’s popularity plummets amid the war in Iran and rising prices. More than two-thirds (68%) of rural Maha supporters said that Trump’s health policies have “had a negative effect or no impact on the health of people where they live”, according in a new AP-KFF survey that highlights the disconnect between the sprawling political project and its grassroots support, especially in rural areas that overwhelmingly supported Trump in the 2024 election. More Americans view the president and vice-president unfavorably than favorably, according to a January survey by Pew Research. At the Maha summit in Washington DC on Tuesday, Vance traded jokes about memes and the “carnivore” diet of meat and fermented foods with Robert F Kennedy Jr, the secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and the leader of Maha. But Vance also highlighted his role in identifying what he says is fraud in Medicaid, Medicare and the Affordable Care Act marketplace – blaming it on immigrants, especially undocumented immigrants. “We’ve found close to $250bn in fraud just since I’ve been leading the anti-fraud task force,” Vance claimed, though the administration has released scant details on who has been unenrolled from these programs and why the activity was considered fraudulent. Vance said that “the states that administer the programs don’t enforce them at all”, claiming that undocumented people were receiving Medicare benefits, though there is no documentation that this is occurring. “Cut that shit out and be honest about your intentions. It’s about giving benefits to illegal aliens,” Vance said to applause. Kennedy alluded to the more cost-efficient health systems of Europe, which have universal healthcare, to speak about the inefficiencies of the health system in the US, where costs have been “allowed to get out of control”. Vance seemed to point to the need for stronger regulation of the health system, saying that programs like Medicaid and Medicare are stronger when fraud can be detected – though the Trump administration has largely focused on deregulation. Speaking at the event, Vance underlined “the politics that Maha is stirring up”, said Art Caplan, professor emeritus at the NYU Grossman School of Medicine. “I think Vance was there making a calculation. He wants to replicate what Trump did, get the Maha devotees on his side, not Rubio’s.” Vance poked fun at secretary of state Marco Rubio, his closest political rival, saying Rubio “doesn’t have a great poker face”, which makes for “absolutely incredible” meme material. “Bobby and I are on a text chain with a bunch of the cabinet secretaries, where we’re basically beating social media to the memes,” Vance said, describing one image of Marco in a blonde wig after Dolly Parton died. The second annual summit showcased the fracturing of the Maha movement, which has often been an uneasy alliance among environmental, nutrition and anti-vaccine activists, and political and corporate actors. The event appeared to eschew the former and prioritize the latter, featuring companies like UnitedHealth, Walmart and Anthropic, including companies with active business before the US government. Grail, an experimental cancer-treatment company whose approval is currently before the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA), was a top sponsor. Companies that paid $300,000 were given the option of speaker slots, as well as a private dinner with Kennedy and Mehmet Oz, the administrator for the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS), according to reporting by Bloomberg. The Maha Center, which organized the event, is one of many Maha-affiliated endeavors headed by Tony Lyons, a longtime vaccine critic, who has paid Kennedy $4m in the past year. Tickets were available for “Maha members” who pay $6,000 a year to Maha Holdings, whose sole board member is Finn Kennedy, Kennedy’s 29-year-old son. “The Maha summit, I thought, was a giant conflict of interest,” said Caplan, adding that the “ethically disturbing” event appeared to be “pay to play” to access high-ranking officials in the Trump administration. Speakers included Oz; Brooke Rollins, secretary of the US Department of Agriculture; and Stefanie Spear, a top Kennedy aide. “Normally, you don’t get a chance to cozy up to FDA officials. That’s troubling,” Caplan added. While Maha appears to be fracturing in favor of corporations, it could still prove a powerful movement for Vance, Caplan said: “If he can get half of what Trump got, even if there’s a split, he’s doing well.” The strong focus on corporations was not lost on Maha activists. “Why are they excluding our voices?” Mary Talley Bowden, a doctor who opposes Covid vaccines and was reprimanded for stealthily providing unproven Covid treatments, said on X. The lineup did not “reflect the issues that birthed the original Maha movement and drove voters, especially women, to show up and vote for this coalition”, said Kelly Ryerson, also known as the Glyphosate Girl. Some of the speakers “could not be less Maha”, she added. Maha has been “captured” by the very corporate interests it sought to fight, Robert Malone, a conspiracy theorist who voted to restrict vaccines while he was a member of the now-halted vaccines advisory committee, wrote on his Substack – decrying the “incestuous nature” of Maha, where “conflicts of interest seem to multiply by the day”. Kennedy, who has long railed against corporate influences affecting Americans’ health and wellbeing, was notably quiet about corporate power at the event. Instead, he praised companies like OpenAI, which has millions of dollars in US government contracts. “Today, it would be malpractice for a doctor to make a diagnosis or to make a prescription without at least checking AI,” he said, attributing the quote to OpenAI’s Sam Altman. Kennedy added that large language models “can give you a second opinion that is much better informed than any doctor in the country”. About a third (32%) of Americans consult AI for medical information and advice, though AI chatbots are inaccurate about 25% of the time. “We’re never, ever again going to be able to be dominated by public officials who tell us ‘trust the experts’,” Kennedy said. “If somebody tells you ‘masks work, trust the experts’, AI may tell you otherwise. If somebody tells you ‘social distancing works, trust the experts’, AI may correct that. And if somebody tells you that ‘a vaccine will prevent transmission and infection, so you need to take it to protect your grandmother’, AI may say ‘it actually doesn’t do that’, So it really has the capacity to dominate us and free us from medical tyranny,” Kennedy said. His “fringy science agenda was on full display”, Caplan said. If Kennedy aligns himself with Vance and Vance wins the election, “it gives him power to pursue some things that he cares about”. Vance has long seen Kennedy’s faction as essential for Trump’s success, and he also spoke at the Maha summit in 2025. But fewer than one in four Americans (23%) view Kennedy favorably, according to a new survey from the Annenberg Public Policy Center.

title: Australia and Turkey criticised for hosting UN climate conference while embracing coal
summary: Global campaign group 350.org urges Cop31 hosts to announce a coal phase-out date and national roadmaps to get off fossil fuels
text: The hosts of the next major United Nations climate conference, Turkey and Australia, are facing criticism for being partners in a coal supply chain while remaining near silent on the need for a global deal to rapidly get off fossil fuels. With the Cop31 summit in the Turkish Mediterranean city of Antalya just a month away, the two countries running the fortnight-long talks have been accused by activists of a “vacuum of action” on plans for a transition away from coal, gas and oil – a key goal of many nations at the talks. Preparations for Cop31 will kick up a gear this week with a small group of national leaders, including the Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, expected to join representatives of more than 50 countries for a preparatory meeting in Fiji and Tuvalu. Pre-summit meetings are typically bureaucratic gatherings, but expectations for his year’s event were elevated after Australia – which has the new role of “president of negotiations” at Cop31 – pushed to hold it in the Pacific, and invited leaders to attend, arguing it would highlight the plight of low-lying island nations. Few leaders from outside the region accepted. The Fijian government named five expected attenders – from Thailand, Antigua and Barbuda, Cape Verde, the Maldives and Timor-Leste – but some have since cancelled. They include the Thai prime minister, Anutin Charnvirakul, as Bangkok suffered severe flooding. Sign up to get climate and environment editor Adam Morton’s Clear Air column as a free newsletter The meeting is being held just days after a New South Wales regulator approved the largest coalmine expansion in the Australian state’s history. Joint owners Yancoal and Glencore estimate the 19-year life extension for the Hunter Valley Operations thermal coalmine could lead to 809m tonnes of heat-trapping carbon dioxide emissions if it wins federal approval. A report, by campaign group 350.org, cited UN Comtrade data suggesting the supply of coking and thermal coal from Australia to Turkey had been responsible for more than 75m tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions since the signing of the landmark Paris climate agreement in 2015. It said the countries were now expanding their trade in liquified natural gas (LNG). The organisation said this had continued while the Cop31 presidents largely ignored fossil fuels – the primary cause of the climate crisis – in public comments before the summit. Three letters to countries setting out the mission and expectations for the summit, two from the Turkish government and one joint letter with the Australians, did not mention fossil fuels. Albanese also did not mention fossil fuels in a keynote speech at Climate Week in New York two weeks ago. Andreas Sieber, 350.org’s head of political strategy, said the hosts should be following the previous host, Brazil, in working on a roadmap to accelerate a transition away from dirty fuels. He said both countries should announce coal phase-out dates as a first step. “Amidst the biggest energy crisis in history, it is extraordinary that the Cop31 presidency continues to ignore the central issue of fossil fuels,” Sieber said. “Rather than leading the transition away, both countries are still expanding fossil fuels at extreme rates.” Australia has accelerated its clean energy expansion at home, but remains one of the world’s biggest exporters of coal and LNG, with shipments this year expected to be worth more than A$140bn. The 350.org report said Turkey was Europe’s biggest coal-power generator and it had signalled it could expand its coal and gas power capacity by about 30% by 2035. Australian climate change minister, Chris Bowen, has argued at previous summits that the world needs to move away from dirty fuels, including declaring at the Cop28 conference in Dubai that “the age of fossil fuels will end”. He told the Guardian on Sunday that Australia was a fossil fuel-exporting country, but acting on climate change was in its national, economic and strategic interest. He said Treasury analysis had found Australia could have an impact on global emissions by becoming a renewable energy exporter. “Our trading partners are pursuing their own energy transitions. We want to help them do that, so we remain a reliable trading nation,” Bowen said. Turkey and Australia are sharing hosting duties at Cop31 in a unique agreement struck after a protracted standoff. Turkey has ultimate responsibility, including running a massive green trade fair, but Bowen has been appointed “president of negotiations” for the formal talks between nearly 200 nations. The Cop30 summit in Brazil last year avoided collapse, but could manage only a voluntary agreement to begin discussions on a roadmap to phase out fossil fuels after oil-producing countries opposed stronger wording. Frustration over the impasse prompted 57 national governments to hold a separate conference on how to transition away from fossil fuels in Colombia in April. Turkey and Australia were represented at the Colombia meeting by senior officials. Vanuatu’s climate change minister, Ralph Regenvanu, said it would be “deeply disappointing” for Pacific countries if Australia extended the life of a major coalmine as it led the Cop31 negotiations. “This decision sends the wrong signal at a critical time,” he said, Bill Hare, the chief executive of the Climate Analytics, a science and policy institute, said it would be “interesting to see” if Turkey and Australia could set aside their “addiction to fossil fuels”. He said the Australia Labor government had approved 37 fossil fuel developments for export since its election in 2022, while Turkey under president Recep Tayyip Erdoğan seemed “fixated on prioritising digging up and burning coal … and establishing itself as a regional fossil gas hub”. Cop31 will be held amid rising concern about the impact of what has been described as a “super El Niño” weather pattern, and after the UN Environment Programme warned the world would breach the 1.5C global heating goal included in the Paris agreement. The UN agency said every fraction of a degree of temperature rise would intensify destructive extreme weather, glacier melt, ecosystem loss, and island and coastal city submersion, and called for immediate and sustained cuts in emissions.

title: Retailers are making returns harder. A carpet seller taught me why that’s a mistake | Gene Marks
summary: A standard business practice offsets future costs by funding a reserve for returns – but many small businesses don’t do it
text: In my 30-plus years of being an accountant I have learned many business lessons from people who were much smarter than me. Jerry Crawford was one of those people. Jerry taught me about product returns. Jerry – who sadly passed away a decade ago – sold carpets wholesale from a nondescript little building in south Jersey. He employed about 50 people and counted many local and national carpet retailers as his customers. When I reviewed Jerry’s books, I noticed a large reserve for “returns”. “They’re a part of every business,” he told me. A “reserve” is something businesses create for potential future costs. Some reserve for bad debts. Others reserve for inventory that grows old and will need to be disposed of. And plenty of businesses – like Jerry’s – reserve for the potential costs that will be incurred if a customer returns their product. Returns are just a normal part of business. Plenty of small business owners like Jerry go to great lengths to make the process as easy as possible. Some big companies, such as Amazon, do the same. “There’s a cost to do this,” Jerry said. “So I make sure to build a reserve for that cost.” Makes sense. And yet, it seems that many businesses still haven’t learned this lesson. According to the Wall Street Journal, many Americans are complaining that it’s getting harder to return things. They’re seeing “surprise fees, shorter return windows and more questions about their reasons for sending products back”. Some, according to the report, are “getting warnings that they won’t get a refund on their next return”. Jerry would be shaking his head at this. To him, it wouldn’t make sense. And it doesn’t make sense to me either. Yes, there are a few bad actors that will take advantage of the practice. And yes, accepting returns adds costs for a business. But, like credit card fees, health insurance and overtime, this is a cost that can easily be recouped. All you need to do is capture those costs over a year or so, build a history, estimate what the next year’s cost will be and then factor those costs into your overhead. Your overhead is then factored into your pricing. In Jerry’s case, he reserved one-half of 1% on each of his sales as a returns allowance based on his history of returns. He built up this reserve throughout the year, then charged returned products against it. A 0.5% reserve meant that instead of charging $1,000 for a roll of carpet, he charged $1,005. His customers didn’t notice the $5 difference. Would you? The difference is negligible. But for a business, those costs add up and, by doing this, those costs are covered. You’d think that, after thousands of years of business practice and the knowledge of some of the finest institutions, pundits, academics and experts, our business leaders today would understand this concept. So why don’t retailers realize this? It’s a mystery to me. They must see that creating obstacles and charging their customers for returns only creates animosity, ruins their loyalty and results in unfavorable press coverage. It’s shocking to me how businesses continue to make the same mistakes over and over again, despite the lessons of history. You can keep your customers happy, build loyalty and grow your business by not nickel-and-diming them. Jerry Crawford, a small business owner with a high school education who profitably sold carpets for decades, understood this.

title: Medicare for All remains key pressure point for Democrats before midterms
summary: The idea of universal health coverage in the US is embraced by party’s left but often considered a liability by centrists
text: Last week, 1,500 unionized nurses gathered in a large conference room at the Marriott Marquis in San Francisco to cheer for a cause they’ve championed for years: Medicare for All. Considered a radical and even fringe idea for decades, interest in sweeping healthcare reform has surged as progressive Democrats have won a series of primary victories before November’s crucial midterm elections. Most prominent among its advocates is Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic US Senate nominee from Michigan, who took the lectern before the nurses. “Medicare for who?” asked El-Sayed. “All!” the crowd shouted back. El-Sayed went on to describe why he wrote a book about Medicare for All: to answer questions about “the very simple idea that in the richest, most powerful country in the world you should not have to suffer for your healthcare”. As progressive candidates like El-Sayed prevail in primaries, and the Democratic party stresses unity in the face of its midterm challenge to Republicans, Medicare for All remains a pressure point – embraced by the party’s left but often considered a liability by centrists. “There’s too many unnecessary illnesses and unnecessary costs,” said Michelle Gutierrez Vo, president of the California Nurses Association, the National Nurses Organizing Committee and vice-president of National Nurses United – all unions that represent nurses attending the San Francisco conference. “What are we doing?” These unions have advocated for Medicare for All for years, and watched interest swell as candidates like El-Sayed picked up steam. By contrast, centrist Democrat groups, such as Third Way, consider Medicare for All an unattainable albatross. “Medicare for All has a lot of political and substantive issues,” said Gabe Horwitz, senior vice-president for the economic program at Third Way. The party is unanimous in opposition to the $1tn in healthcare cuts made by Donald Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which Democrats have taken to calling the “big, ugly bill”. The legislation is expected to result in an additional 16 million people becoming uninsured by 2034. “We want to get everyone insured, we want to lower costs and want to make care easier to use,” said Horwitz, who also said the party acknowledges that it needs to make reforms for people struggling to afford employer-sponsored health insurance. “I don’t know if there’s one Democrat in the party who wouldn’t agree with that. “There is unanimity in the goals – the ends – there’s just not necessarily unanimity in the means to get there,” said Horwitz. This divide was most recently evident in an 84-page memo sent to Hakeem Jeffries, the House minority leader, from the cost-of-living healthcare working group. “Members of the Democratic Caucus hold a diversity of views on how to achieve universal coverage,” the memo read, “including Medicare for All” and a wide range of other more incremental policies. Centrist Democrats have sought to answer the gnawing question of what to do about soaring healthcare costs and reviled insurance company practices by proposing incremental reform – a strategy that builds off the Affordable Care Act (ACA) passed by the Obama administration. A healthcare bill of rights, more government subsidies to health insurance companies to offset costs to consumers, and some version of a “public option”, or a government-sponsored health insurance plan that people could buy into. For years, the party’s left has offered a proposition at once seen as radical by US standards and typical by many of the world’s industrialized democracies: a single-payer health system sponsored by the government. “All Democrats from 1948 on have been in favor of universal healthcare – that’s been in every democratic platform since literally Harry Truman,” said Elaine Kamarck, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, whose recent analysis of primary victories across the political spectrum found mainstream candidates continue to win. “That’s not the issue – the issue is how do you do it.” What’s more, said Kamarck, the issue is one likely to simmer long past the primaries. US health reform is a virtual nonstarter while Republicans hold the Oval Office. But if Democrats won a “trifecta” in 2028, “then this is going to be a really big issue”. At present, the US health system is a patchwork of different insurers, or “payers”, all of which are subsidized by US taxpayers. Four large programs dominate the mix: employer-sponsored health insurance covers almost half of Americans (48% of the population), Medicare covers people older than 65 (14.8%), Medicaid covers low-income and disabled people (20.4%) and Obamacare allows people to buy private insurance as individuals (6.6%), all according to Kaiser Family Foundation. About 27 million people (8.2%) lack insurance entirely. About one in four Americans are “underinsured”, or have high health costs relative to their incomes. Across these various programs, the US government plans to spend $33.6tn through 2034. This includes subsidies for the private insurance Americans get through their jobs, for which employers receive a tax break. That is equal to 7.4% of gross domestic product. As a point of reference, the United Kingdom spends about 11.9% of GDP to insure everyone in the country, according to the Commonwealth Fund. Total US health spending is 18% of GDP – far more than comparable countries. Although the slogan Medicare for All has a somewhat loose definition, a bill repeatedly introduced in Congress provides for a Medicare-style single-payer system, with universal health coverage. Private insurers would be barred from duplicating services. Because healthcare as an industry represents 18% of US gross domestic product (GDP), and such a dramatic transition would inevitably disrupt thousands of jobs, the bill also provides for temporary worker compensation. But for advocates of Medicare for All, such as Gutierrez Vo, anything else is, “a patch-up – it’s not a fix”. “Just like nurses take care of the whole patient– that’s like taking care of a leg and letting the rest be ill,” he said. “That’s silly.”

title: Debris found as US Coast Guard search for missing medical plane carrying six people
summary: Six passengers and crew onboard still unaccounted for after medical plane vanishes off coast of Massachusetts
text: Researches found debris from a medical transport plane that was carrying six people when it vanished over the Atlantic early on Saturday during a flight from Bermuda to Boston, the US Coast Guard said. A statement from the coast guard issued on Saturday evening said crews searching off the coast of the Massachusetts island Nantucket “located a debris field confirmed to be from the aircraft”, described as an air ambulance. Six passengers and crew on board were still unaccounted for at the time of the debris field’s discovery, a spokesperson for the coast guard said. Boats, planes and helicopters were launched after flight controllers lost contact with the air ambulance. Air traffic controllers had difficulty communicating with the flight in its final moments. “You’re coming in blind? Is that what you said?” a controller asked the pilot at about 12.46am. “Are you declaring an emergency, or no?” According to a recording captured by LiveATC.net, the pilot’s response was not audible. The air ambulance – a Gulfstream G100 – took off from Bermuda late on Saturday, carrying a patient, a family member and a four-person crew. The patient and family member were identified as citizens of Bermuda. The crew was identified as Canadian citizens, though the names of the people onboard the flight were not immediately released. As it neared Nantucket, the plane reported electrical failures, according to radio transmissions. Data from the website FlightAware shows the plane descended thousands of feet within three minutes and disappeared from radar shortly after about 1am local time. The coast guard said on Saturday evening that its William Sparling cutter boat would continue searching for those onboard the air ambulance through the night. The agency reported that its crews searched roughtly 1,644 sq miles (4,258 sq km) for the aircraft in about 27 hours. Bermudian government officials said they had been in touch with the passengers’ families. “My thoughts are with everyone on board and their families during this deeply worrying time,” Bermuda premier David Burt in a statement. “We are praying that all six people will be found safe, and we thank the search and rescue crews for their continuing efforts.”

title: Polls close in first round of Brazil’s high-stakes presidential election
summary: Leftwing incumbent Lula trying to fight off close rival Flávio Bolsonaro, far-right son of jailed ex-president
text: The polls have closed in the first round of Brazil’s highly polarised and high-stakes presidential election that could change not only the direction of Latin America’s largest country but that of the entire region. The election pits the leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who is seeking a fourth non-consecutive term, against the far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro, an ally of Donald Trump and the son of the former president Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving a 27-year sentence for attempting a coup after his failed 2022 re-election attempt. Late on Sunday Bolsonaro was leading Lula in partial results. With results in from almost 65% of the country, Bolsonaro had 49.8% to Lula’s 42.25%, while several other candidates stood in the single digits. Lula and Bolsonaro have alternated as frontrunners in the final stretch, making the outcome unpredictable. In recent days both have focused on persuading undecided voters in hopes of reaching 50% plus one vote; if neither does, there will be a runoff on 25 October. Brazil is one of the few Latin American countries that still has a leftwing government after a wave of rightwing and far-right electoral victories across the region and the US takeover of Venezuela after the capture of Nicolás Maduro. The 80-year-old Lula has positioned himself as one of the last regional leaders still willing to say no to Trump, and has recently accused the US president of trying to interfere in Brazil’s election in Bolsonaro’s favour. Like his father, who was Brazil’s president during Trump’s first term, Flávio Bolsonaro, 45, frequently praises the US president and has pledged to join the US-led anti-drug-cartel coalition that has killed dozens of people in airstrikes and carried out military operations across the region. Voting on Sunday morning in São Bernardo do Campo, the industrial city where his political career began nearly half a century ago, Lula said: “People will have to choose between strengthening democracy and barbarism.” The incumbent played down polls released on Saturday that showed the race was wide open – they suggested either candidate could finish ahead and force a runoff, or even win outright on Sunday. “The poll that matters will be carried out today,” he said. Flávio Bolsonaro, who voted in Rio de Janeiro’s north zone, urged supporters of other rightwing candidates to switch to him in a “protest vote”. “Our internal polls show people who would have voted for other candidates, who are also against Lula, already voting for Flávio Bolsonaro … I hope it’s enough to give us victory in the first round,” he said. Claudinei Ferreira Viana, 45, a workshop manager in Pinhais in Paraná state, is one of the senator’s supporters. “My first choice would be Jair Bolsonaro but, since he is under house arrest and there is no other rightwing candidate strong enough to take on the current president, I’m going with Flávio,” he said. At the beginning of the year, polls suggested Bolsonaro voters would have preferred a ticket led by the São Paulo governor, Tarcísio de Freitas, or the former first lady Michelle Bolsonaro. But the former president chose his eldest son. The campaign was also marked by a scandal in which the senator was caught on tape asking a banker accused of corruption for $26.8m (£20m) to fund a film about his father, as well as speculation that Bolsonaro might strip the country’s widely cherished patron saint of her status, but he has nevertheless remained highly competitive. For many analysts, that reflects a combination of a straightforward transfer of his father’s voter base – Jair Bolsonaro lost to Lula by less than two percentage points in 2022 – and an anti-Lula vote, with the president still facing high rejection rates despite strong social and economic indicators. The incumbent’s campaign has also been hit by corruption allegations – still under investigation – involving his son and a former aide, as well as a scandal involving supreme court justices, which, despite having no connection to Lula, is seen as fuelling an “anti-system” vote and by extension an anti-incumbent one. Brazilians will also elect 27 state governors, members of state legislatures, all 513 federal congress members and 54 of the country’s 81 senators in Sunday’s vote. AMC, 40, who asked to be identified only by her initials because she fears reprisals from the local conservative government where she works in the interior of Amazonas state, will vote for Lula on Sunday “because of the many programmes he created to support the most vulnerable groups”. “Jair Bolsonaro weakened protections for Indigenous peoples, and everything Lula has done over the past four years to strengthen those protections and protect the Amazon would be seriously threatened if his son came to power,” she said.

title: Oat of this world: cooks descend on Scotland for ultimate porridge making contest
summary: Technical mishaps and plenty of whisky as competitors from as far afield as US and Australia vie for Golden Spurtle
text: There are many varieties of spurtle. The traditional Scottish cooking implement, designed for stirring porridge without forming lumps, comes in a range of sizes, can be formed from cherry wood, beech, or maple, and might be topped with a decorative finial or smoothed out at its end for a more modern finish. But on Saturday in Carrbridge, in the Scottish Highlands, only one spurtle mattered: the Golden Spurtle, awarded annually to the winner of the World Porridge Making championship, which have been hosted here since 1994. The sun shone on the picturesque village as almost 40 competitors lined up in the village hall for six heats across the day. Tasked with producing a traditional porridge – made only from untreated oatmeal, water and salt – and a speciality dish where additional ingredients and flourishes were permitted, entrants had travelled from across Scotland and as far afield as Australia and the US for a shot at the Golden Spurtle. As the first heat kicked off, technical difficulties beset some contestants when the provided induction hobs, new this year after a long tradition of gas, failed to heat. But the reigning champion, Norway’s Sven Seljom, was unaffected, serenely stirring Norwegian mutton into oats and filtered water he had brought with him especially for the competition. He had planned to bring Norwegian cheese, too, he said, but import rules meant he had to make do with something more local. A sizeable entourage watched on in traditional Scandinavian dress as he measured, stirred and tasted, boisterous chants of “SVEN, SVEN, SVEN” breaking out at each mention of his name. The first of the day’s many whisky breaks came 10 minutes into proceedings at 10.40am, with shots of a lowland malt distributed throughout the exuberant crowd as competitors did well to retain their focus. The drams’ effects meant nobody seemed to mind too much when the crucial timer was accidentally reset just moments from the heat’s tense final countdown. Any initial teething problems were quickly ironed out as the day settled into a well-oiled rhythm. In a separate “judging chamber”, a trio of judges from Scotland’s culinary scene blind-tasted each batch, assessing primarily for taste, texture and colour. Among the speciality porridges on offer throughout the day were a “Granola Espanola”, a porridge cannoli from the Australian national champion, Robert Reid, and a recipe featuring soft-boiled quail eggs. “The first thing I did was burn my oats,” lamented Switzerland’s Jeremy McTeague after a heat that didn’t quite go to plan. But he remained upbeat: “It gave them a distinctive toastiness – maybe the judges will like it.” Hundreds of spectators showed up for the day’s spectacle, from Carrbridge residents who turn out each year to support the community-powered event, to tourists such as Joe, 43, and Tina, 39, who were visiting from England and had overheard a conversation about the championship in a local pub the previous night. “We looked it up and decided straight away we’d be here,” said Joe. “It’s Scotland, it’s porridge, someone said there would be whisky … it was a no-brainer.” The pair said they were making a beeline for the tasting room to sample the produce left over from judging. The event proved so popular that the village hall had to operate a one-in, one-out policy. Those who couldn’t fit inside were decanted into a merch tent bursting with oats, spurtles and “always stir clockwise” tote bags, while local cafes and tourist centres screened a live stream of the competition. There was plenty of action to be found around the village, from competitors spotted calming their nerves with pints in the local hotel, to an American visitor who accidentally caused controversy by dressing as a box of Scott’s Porage Oats – rolled oats of the kind not allowed in competition, and a rival to the event’s sponsors, Hamlyns. By the afternoon, the hall was full of cooking aromas and the crowd full of whisky and porridge as they took their seats once more to see who would walk away victorious. There was a minor upset when the reigning champion, Seljom, missed out on the final, but a surprise win for McTeague saw him through to the cook-off despite his earlier woes. Once the top six had taken to the hob one last time, though, it was the Netherlands national champion, Gina Saarberg, who emerged victorious in the traditional competition, with the speciality prize going to Reid for his cannoli. “I’m at a loss for words,” Saarberg said as she clutched her Golden Spurtle. “To be here was already such a win in the first place. This is a beautiful community, so of course I’m very happy I won, but it’s also just a pleasure to be here.”

title: Manhattan ‘mole’ mystery: rumors of lost gold spur clandestine excursions into New York sewers
summary: A recent arrest suggests that underground invaders of city’s sewer system are lured by the promise of lost valuables
text: There’s been one thing in particular that has been intriguing New Yorkers this summer: the existence, and whereabouts, of so-called “mole people” – a mysterious group of individuals who spend at least some of their time wading about in the city’s sewers. New Yorkers learned a bit more about the phenomenon this week, when two men were caught red – or perhaps another color – handed, after allegedly emerging from a tunnel in Manhattan. Their arrests have shed some light on a slew of instances where people have been witnessed lifting manhole covers and clambering underground. Samuel Reveron and Kevin Rodriguez were apprehended in Queens after police tracked them down through video footage. The pair were allegedly spotted entering the sewers with four other people, who have yet to be identified. Both were charged with criminal trespassing, but it is the reason the men gave for their adventure that has proved particularly fascinating. “We go into the sewer and look for valuables that get stuck in the storm drains and sewers, gold, anything of value,” Reveron, 25, reportedly told police after his arrest. The gang’s quest fits an apparently misguided pattern of people thinking New York’s sewers are paved with gold. Last year, three men were arrested after they were allegedly seen emerging from a sewer in Brooklyn, one of them telling police: “The reason we went down there is that people lose their gold down there. We got to get it and sell it to make money.” Despite that vaulting ambition, there is little evidence that sewer foraging is a lucrative trade. Steve Duncan, a former urban explorer who has spent a lot of time in New York’s sewers and subway tunnels, told the New York Times that in more than 100 sewer trips, the most valuable thing he found was an expired credit card. Still, the penchant for sewer exploration continues. In May this year there were three separate reported incidents of people climbing down into sewers, two of which were captured on video. In footage of the first incident, three people, wearing dungaree-style hip waders and carrying flashlights, walk into the middle of the road in Astoria, Queens. They haul a circular man cover aside, and descend into the darkness of the sewer. “Three random guys walking around in a strange suit. Open the sewer, go in like the Ninja Turtles,” eyewitness Aki Jakupovic told NBC New York at the time. Jakupovic isn’t the first to make the comparison to the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles, a fictional group of human-turtle hybrids who, across a comic book, cartoon TV show and feature film, are depicted as living in the sewers. Per canon, the turtles mutated into humanoids after being exposed to a toxic green goo. They are subsequently trained in martial arts by a large rat. The turtles, who are brothers, fight crime, frequently crossing paths with a man called Shredder and his accomplices Bebop, who is a mutant warthog, and Rocksteady, who is a sort of rhino. They also encounter Krang, an alien blob-thing who lives in a robot. While there appears to have been an increase in sewer incidents this year, this isn’t a new phenomenon. In 2015, a trainee at the New York department of environmental protection was arrested after being caught in the sewers, and last year three men were arrested after entering the sewer system in Brooklyn, allegedly in an attempt to find gold. “God knows what they were looking for. I know for damn sure I wouldn’t be crawling through the sewers of New York, but these three were evidently looking for something,” the then New York police commissioner, Bill Bratton, told journalists at the time. Reveron and Rodriguez’s September sojourn might have been written off as a bit of a hoot, but police were seemingly extra interested because it coincided with world leaders gathering at the UN, some of them staying at swanky hotels close to where the two men went underground. Brian Kennedy, an attorney for Reveron, dismissed those concerns when he spoke to NBC News. “It seems like not much of a case,” Kennedy told NBC News. “I understand that it is strange that it’s alleged he went [into the sewer]. But there’s no connection to the UN or the appearance of Netanyahu or any other kind of nefarious scheme.” It’s both strange and dangerous, Rob Wolejsza, a spokesperson for New York’s department of environmental protection, previously told the Guardian. Wolejsza said it was “both illegal and extremely dangerous” to go into the sewers, adding: “Sewers can contain numerous hazards, including noxious and potentially deadly gases, unstable surfaces, flooding risks and confined spaces. For these reasons, members of the public should never enter a pipe, drain, catch basin, manhole or outfall.” Whether people will listen remains to be seen. On the same day Reveron and Rodriguez were arrested, another three men were spotted climbing out of a sewer at 4.30am in Bensonhurst, south Brooklyn. ABC7NY reported that police found a shovel in the sewer, but the men got away.
