title: Court quashes block on mothers and children in Gaza joining families in UK
summary: Immigration court judge finds ‘unsafe journeys’ policy was applied unlawfully to two families
text: A decision by the Home Office to block mothers and children in Gaza from joining their families in the UK has been quashed by a court. Families abroad who have had their applications approved to reunite with loved ones in the UK usually have to undergo biometric checks, including fingerprinting and facial images at a visa application centre. But the VAC in Gaza has been closed since October 2023 and it is difficult to get out of the territory. The government has an unsafe journeys policy that offers some flexibility in this kind of situation, but has taken a more strict approach to families – often mothers with very young children – in Gaza who are hoping to reunite with husbands and fathers granted refugee status in the UK. A judge in the immigration court known as the upper tribunal has found the home secretary acted unlawfully in the way the policy was applied to two families and has quashed the decision to block them. Both are young mothers with five children between them aged seven and under, hoping to reunite with their husbands who have been granted refugee status in the UK. Both families are living in dire straits in tents in Gaza with insufficient food, no access to clean water, rodents, mosquitoes, bedbugs and the risk of snipers. The Home Office says it is looking to appeal against the decision. An estimated 250-300 people in Gaza who want to reunite with immediate family members who have been granted refugee status in the UK are similarly stranded. The Home Office says biometrics should be obtained before families travel. The Foreign Office has said it is willing to evacuate some of these families from Gaza so they can obtain biometrics in Jordan. In her judgment, the judge, Fiona Lindsley, said the families were living in vulnerable structures in a war zone, malnourished, unwell and struggling psychologically with anxiety from their husbands and fathers in the UK that they would not survive much longer if they remained in Gaza. “The best interests of these children should be the primary consideration, and it cannot be in their best interests to be afraid, undernourished and suffering from diseases of poverty and insanitary conditions without their fathers and no end in sight to that separation,” she said. Decla Palmer, a solicitor at Greater Manchester Immigration Aid Unit who represents the families, said: “The Home Office is doing everything possible to delay and to defend its unlawful decisions, taking a policy position that blocks people in Gaza who are eligible to come to the UK from being able to do so. “These families are completely broken – it is difficult to put into words the trauma they have faced and continue to endure. The mothers and children, trapped in Gaza, are suffering each and every day. The fathers, in the UK, are facing the prospect that they may never hold their children again. The Home Office is actively keeping these families apart, leaving them stranded in Gaza in grave danger.” On Monday, the Home Office announced refugee resettlement routes including for Palestinian refugees and women from Afghanistan. However, this scheme processes only a few hundred applications each year. It is not known when the much larger refugee family reunion scheme will restart, after it was suspended in September 2025. The Refugee Council estimates that since then approximately 20,000 people have been denied family reunion. Initially, the government indicated that new refugee family reunion rules would be introduced in the spring of 2025, but the scheme remains suspended. Home Office sources have indicated that no further details will be announced about this safe and legal lifeline for refugees to reach the UK until 2027. A Home Office spokesperson said: “We will be looking to appeal this decision. Biometrics, including fingerprints and facial images, are a core part of the UK’s immigration system, and their enrolment at a UK overseas visa application centre is a standard requirement when making a visa application to come to the UK. “The enrolment of biometrics enables comprehensive checks against UK and international immigration and criminal records to identify individuals who may pose a threat to national security, public safety or immigration controls, or who are likely to breach UK laws if admitted.”

title: Trump sets off on midterm blitz – are his trademark rallies a liability for Republicans?
summary: Rallies have been mainstay of president’s brand but even some in his own party fear voters are sick of the sight of him
text: “Get your asses in that car.” That was Donald Trump’s order, he later recalled, to his motorcade after foul weather grounded Air Force One in Texas on Thursday. The 85-mile dash to Oklahoma at nearly 100mph was proof that nothing can keep Trump from a Trump rally. Which might not be the good news for Republicans it once was. As the US president embarked on a 32-day campaign blitz aimed at helping them defend narrow congressional majorities in next month’s midterms, some fear that he is driving them towards an electoral wipeout. Trump’s approval rating is at an all-time low. Voters are angry about the cost of living, the Iran war and excessive immigration crackdowns. Some Republicans are moving to distance themselves from a man they now see as more liability than asset. Wherever he turns, the outlook is grim as he sets off on an expected schedule of five to seven rallies a week. “They’ve been a mainstay of his brand, but they’re also the engine of his doom,” Steve Schmidt, a political strategist, said of Trump’s signature campaign rallies. “Everybody knows the obvious, which is that his presence hurts every Republican candidate on the ballot because the race is fundamentally about Trump and the American people are sick and tired of him.” Schmidt added: “He’s surrounded by people who tell him that he’s beloved and that the answer to his problem is to keep talking, to keep performing, to keep doing the rallies, that the answer is more, not less. These rallies have become his lead weight, his proverbial anchor that’s going to drown them all.” Even in a hyper-digital age, Trump’s rallies have shown the enduring power of live performance. The atmosphere, somewhere between cult worship, rock concert and partisan sports event, offers his followers a sense of belonging. Since launching his bid for president in 2015 he has held roughly a thousand of them, though definitions of what counts as a full “rally” can vary. Blake Marnell, a rally regular in a brick-patterned suit resembling Trump’s border wall, was in Oklahoma on Thursday night. He said: “Getting in the motorcade, driving 100 miles an hour to Durant – he’s not gonna let stuff get in his way. He enjoys the rallies. They’re energising for the crowd and for him. It’s a way for him to connect with the grassroots.” Once in Durant, Trump again basked in the adulation of the rally crowd. Having spotted two diehard supporters being interviewed by TV crews outside the venue, he replayed the clip and summoned them on to the main stage. “You can’t miss big, strong, handsome Oklahoma studs,” he said. “Where are you? Come up here!” The pair were white, male and elderly. One, wearing a green Trump cap and grey Trump T-shirt, stepped up to the microphone and said: “Thank you, President Trump, for all you do. Every day you work harder than any American I know.” The other, wearing a red Make America Great Again cap and red T-shirt, said: “Absolute honour of a lifetime to be with the greatest president this country has ever had!” Marnell, from San Diego, California, loved this example of Trump showmanship and dismissed the notion that his rallies are hurting rather than helping Republicans. “That’s ridiculous. How many years now have we heard critics saying that Trump is done, the end is near, the walls are closing in, this is the beginning of the end, he can’t possibly win. “They’ve written him off so many times, I don’t know why people listen when they say things like that. It makes no sense to me. This election is, to an extent larger than normal, going to be swayed by turnout and so turnout is the goal of these rallies.” Yet beneath the carnival atmosphere in Oklahoma lay an undercurrent of anxiety and a new vulnerability. At one point Trump entreated the audience, “Pretend I’m running, please,” and begged them to contact friends and relatives. He openly admitted the Republican party’s precarious footing across the national map. “We’re worried about Michigan, we’re worried about Texas, we’re worried about a few states.” He has cause to be worried. A recent survey by the Associated Press-Norc Center for Public Affairs Research found that just 17% of US adults approve of Trump’s handling of the cost of living, while 26% approve of his handling of the economy – a new low. Only about three in 10 approve of how he is handling his job as president. In a striking sign of trouble, a major Republican political action committee has reportedly pulled back its spending in North Carolina, the only battleground state Trump won in all three of his presidential bids, diverting its resources instead to ruby red Kansas. Even among dedicated fans who have followed him around the country and become known as “front-row Joes” at his rallies, doubts are creeping in. Trisha Hope, a “front-row Joe” who once bought an RV and published a book of Trump’s tweets to fund her travel, recently declared him a “fraud and liar”. Speaking to Politico, Hope cited Trump’s abrupt dismissal of the Jeffrey Epstein investigation during a cabinet meeting, as well as his unfulfilled promises regarding the war in Iran. “If we do lose the midterms and he is impeached again, I will be walking the halls of Congress in support of that impeachment,” she said. But when confronted with the negative numbers, the president has sounded like a man in denial, preferring to discuss his architectural projects in Washington including a new White House ballroom. At his stop in Denton, north-west of Dallas, Texas, earlier on Thursday, he insisted that inflation was entirely the fault of Joe Biden as he dismissed concerns about everyday living costs. “We have the greatest numbers of any president in the history of our country, and I can’t get the word out,” Trump lamented to workers at a truck factory. “Maybe we’re doing a bad job selling it.” John Zogby, an author and pollster, said: “It looks as if he’s very out of touch with the reality of most Americans. Of course, he has spent a lifetime being out of touch and creating that kind of lifestyle for himself.” The 80-year-old’s rally performances have noticeably deteriorated, Zogby argues, marked by rambling digressions that fail to speak to the immediate anxieties of ordinary voters. “Number one, he is tending to digress. He’s not on his best form. But secondly, when he does address affordability, it’s, ‘Wait and see, just a little longer, the war will be over.’ It’s not connecting.” The strain between Trump and Republicans was highlighted this week by a secret audio recording from a high-dollar fundraiser. On the tape, obtained by the New York Times, the Texas attorney general, Ken Paxton – whose Senate campaign has been floundering under the weight of scandals – was overheard candidly admitting to donors that Trump’s midterm convention in Dallas damaged Republican prospects. Paxton admitted: “When we did that convention, it dropped our numbers; everybody’s numbers dropped. Right now? Yeah. It’s not good. I wish there was something we could do to turn that around, but obviously nothing.” At the event in Denton, Trump praised Paxton as one of his “most loyal people”, while jokingly adding: “I have to always remember that because he can be a pain in the ass sometimes, I’ll be honest. Is he here, by the way? Oh, there he is – good. I didn’t even know if he’s here. I don’t care!” The president also insisted: “My heart is in it like never before.” Yet his early campaign schedule has raised eyebrows. He is spending the first five days of October in Texas, Oklahoma, Alabama, Ohio and Nebraska, all reliable Republican strongholds in recent years. Critics say it shows that he is on the defensive. Schmidt, who worked for Republicans George W Bush and John McCain, observed: “The BS stops on the map. When you’re campaigning in October as a Republican in those states, not only does it mean you’re losing, it means you’re losing in a biblical sense, an end-times sense. The reality is that there’s no safe Republican anywhere in the country. That’s why he’s there.” Generic congressional polls show Democrats holding a lead approaching double digits, raising the spectre of a “blue wave” that could sweep away Republican majorities in the House of Representatives and Senate. A Republican official said: “We’re not going to send Potus to areas where it would be hurtful to our candidates.” For Democrats, Trump’s tour through safe conservative territory is an open admission of weakness. Michelle Lujan Grisham, the governor of New Mexico, suggested that reminding voters of Trump’s presidency in the final weeks of the campaign is a strategic blunder on his part. “In those places, I would hope that it hurts,” she said. “People are angry and you shouldn’t be reminding them. So, I’m going to say go ahead. Maybe he should spend some more time in Texas.” Lujan Grisham criticised Trump’s second term, pointing to what she described as a litany of broken promises, economic mismanagement and foreign policy overreach. “He promised to deliver for Americans and he did none of the above. He’s in a war that nobody wants in Iran that he can’t get out of. He’s doing nothing for inflation; he’s making it worse. And he certainly isn’t addressing affordability.” She singled out the administration’s aggressive policies under Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), which she described as a major moral and political liability for the White House. “ICE of course is a huge liability for the White House and this administration, just given they continue to detain both lawfully present individuals and Americans. We’ve had Americans lose their lives, and we’ve devastated whole communities and families. He’s in real trouble.” Trump hopes the campaign rallies that featured so prominently in his victories in 2016 and 2024 will do the trick again on behalf of Republicans in 2026. They will also feed his appetite for the cheering faithful that have become central to his political identity. Schmidt sees a parallel with the faded Hollywood star from one of Trump’s favourite films, Sunset Boulevard. “He needs attention like Norma Desmond and that’s who he’s become here at the nadir of his presidency as he moves from king of the hill into decrepit lame duck. All of the Führer rallies in the red states don’t change the fact. There’s no amount of money that could be spent on his behalf, no amount of rallies, nothing that can save him from the judgment that’s coming down on his head.”

title: Republicans say they hate communists. So why do they like Donald Trump?
summary: Trump supporters may be surprised to learn the state takeover of means of production is not driven by the left
text: Americans will never accept the Democratic party’s slide to the left, or so desperate Republicans are hoping. With the midterm elections fast upon us, Zohran Mamdani’s promise of a few city-run bodegas in New York City will scare the bejeezus out of middle America. Disgust over the democratic socialists’ unicorn-and-puppy promises of a world without capitalism will keep the Republicans in power. Leading the charge against the new reds-under-the-bed is Donald Trump. “Together, we will defeat communism,” Trump promised in his recent TV ads. Trump’s supporters might be surprised to discover that the United States is, indeed, sliding in the direction of a command and control economy. But the state takeover of the means of production is not being driven by the left. The grab for the US’s productive resources is the project of none other than Trump – who, it’s a fair guess, has never read Lenin. The latest evidence comes in data crunched by the V-Dem project in Sweden, which measures the erosion of democracy around the world. It built a scale to gauge “state ownership of the economy”. As noted by Cullen Hendrix from the Peterson Institute for International Economics, from 2002 to 2024, the US ranked among the four countries with the least state control. In 2025, the first year of Trump’s second term, it dropped from second place to 16th. By November of last year, the Trump administration had spent more than $10bn taking stakes in companies he deemed essential for national security, from Intel to a range of ventures mining for critical minerals. It also acquired an option to take a stake in Westinghouse, which makes nuclear reactors. And it blackmailed Nippon Steel into granting Trump’s Washington a “golden share” in exchange for the go-ahead to purchase US Steel. To be fair, Trump’s acquisitiveness notwithstanding, the US is not even close to flirting with the flavor of socialism favored by the Soviet Union and its satellites in the second half of the 20th century. By the V-Dem accounting, Washington’s stake in the economy is still smaller than in 163 countries. Government-run companies are a standard feature in many market economies. The Norwegian government has a majority stake in its massive oil company, which puts the country in 18th place. Even “communist” countries are pretty capitalist: private companies contribute 60% of China’s GDP. And in a geopolitical landscape shaped by competition with China, there is a reasonable case to be made for Washington to take equity stakes in industries that are critical for American leadership and security, and which might not develop autonomously in competition with rivals heavily subsidized by Beijing. Yet Trump’s wanton lunge for private assets lacks the discipline required for this kind of strategic positioning. The president’s statist leanings mark a dramatic break with the market-focused presidencies of his recent predecessors, Democrat and Republican. The question is, what motivates him? His appetites are embedded in a body of thought that is skeptical, if not outright hostile, towards essential building blocks of the global market economy. He has pushed back against globalization since his first term in office, seemingly drawn to the Marxist-inspired dependency theory, which washed across Latin America in the 1960s and 1970s proposing protectionism and state industrial policy as a path to economic development. His lust to control the economy is there for all to see. Though the supreme court already slapped down his attempt to take over trade policy from Congress, he is still threatening to “STOP TRADING WITH COUNTRIES WITH WHICH WE HAVE A DEFICIT”. His promise to give $5,000 to every American if Republicans maintain control of Congress in November’s elections underscores how he views the state’s coffers as his private piggy bank. Even his commie-bashing ads were paid for by taxpayer dollars. Still, he clearly has no interest in the dictatorship of the proletariat, caring little if at all for the fate of the downtrodden. His preferred flavor of redistribution takes from those on the bottom to give to those on the top. If anything, Trump reminds us that socialism is not the only ideological justification for state projects to take control over resources and wealth. Watching the US president bow to Xi Jinping last week, it’s tempting to think that Trump wants to emulate China’s leader. Xi gets to rule unimpeded over more than one billion Chinese. He gets to shape China’s society and economy at will – purging this rival, raising that sycophant to power. But Xi’s China is too disciplined for Trump. The Chinese leader still relies on hordes of technocrats to execute a coherent strategy aimed to achieve technological superiority. The US president doesn’t have the attention span for this kind of thing. Rather, Trump’s model might be Vladimir Putin, who rules Russia like a fiefdom. Or maybe one of those dictators the US used to support in Latin America during the cold war: Haiti’s Papa Doc Duvalier or Anastasio Somoza in Nicaragua, who saw government as a tool to enrich their families and cement dynasties in power. If nothing else, Trump’s dealings with crypto suggest he views his administration as a road to family riches. Karl Marx may not be Trump’s guiding light. But his writings can help understand Trump’s place in history. Marx proposes that his tome The 18th Brumaire of Louis Bonaparte, about the 1851 coup that brought Louis-Napoléon Bonaparte to power in France, was meant to “demonstrate how the class struggle in France created circumstances and relationships that made it possible for a grotesque mediocrity to play a hero’s part”. Americans may be grateful that their most recent class struggles didn’t produce a homegrown Lenin. But they did deliver Donald Trump. Perhaps this does not condemn the US to an autocratic future. Hendrix points out that while Trump “clearly wants to be king”, the US’s political economy may not let him. Putin managed to establish autocratic rule over a fairly primitive, oil-based economy. This kind of control “is much harder to achieve in a modern complex economy” such as that of the United States, Hendrix noted. You can’t simply seize the oil to run the place. Though Trump may fail, Americans’ acquiescence as he grabs for power raises a question for those who freak out over Mamdani’s city-run bodegas: why is Trump’s lurch to take over the American economy any better than what they hear from the Democratic Socialists of America? Eduardo Porter is a journalist focused on economics and politics. He writes the newsletter Being There on Substack

title: Do humans really have a ‘lizard brain’ lurking beneath our rational minds?
summary: It’s a powerful analogy that captured the popular imagination, but the biological reality is quite different
text: Humans have a cognitive quirk for the number three. Think of the many stories that use it, from The Three Little Pigs to Goldilocks and the Three Bears and The Three Musketeers. Public information and political campaigns use it for impact and ease of recall (“Stop, look and listen”; “See it. Say it. Sorted”; “Reduce, reuse, recycle”). And then there are psychological or philosophical frameworks: Freud with his id, ego and superego; Plato’s three parts of the human soul; the Holy Trinity. Well, it turns out neuroscience isn’t immune from tri-mania. In 1959 Paul D MacLean set out a new way of thinking about the evolution and function of the brain, which he christened the “triune” – three-in-one – model. It quickly became one of best known and most enduring concepts in human biology. His idea was that a trio of distinct brains are layered inside our skulls, one on top of the other, all fighting to generate our feelings and thoughts. Deep inside, at the centre, lurks the primitive lizard brain, retained from an ancestor we share with reptiles. This contains ancient regions responsible for survival, helping us to hunt and forage, and driving our sexual impulses so that we reproduce. A second layer sits wrapped around the first, the so-called mammalian brain. It contains the limbic system, deemed to be the seat of our emotions. It enabled mammals to play, care for and nurse their young and communicate in some crude way. The third and final layer, sheathing all of this and making humans in particular a cut above, is the “neomammalian” brain: the eminently rational cortex. This, it was proposed, provides us with our superior intellect, capacity for language and ability to reason. According to MacLean, it helped to keep in check our primitive, lizard-like impulses and rudimentary emotional reactions. Human behaviour was thought to be a result of interactions between all three layers of the triune brain. Frayed tempers, impulsive acts and short termism were signs of the lizard brain winning out. The notion of reptilian impulses “breaking through” proved so popular it found its way into the worlds of pop psychology, business and self-help, and has proved remarkably tenacious. A mini-industry of books, talks and training grew up around the idea that you could draw on the power of the neomammalian brain to keep basic, unhelpful or destructive emotions in check. The underpinning analogy – of an onion-like brain made up of different strata – is now considered deeply misleading by neurobiologists. It’s easy to grasp, sure, and tells a compelling story. But evolution just doesn’t bolt-on neatly divisible mental capacities in this way. MacLean conducted dissections of living creatures to try to prove his theory, but the results, and his interpretations of them, have since been largely discredited. For example, it’s now accepted that many reptiles do actually possess the “mammalian” limbic system, while all mammals exhibit “neomammalian” features previously thought to be unique to “higher” ones like us. Alongside these anatomical observations, there’s the behavioural data too, with many “lower” animals good at problem solving, responding and learning via emotion, and communicating in complex ways. As Guy Leschziner, consultant neurologist at London’s Guy’s and St Thomas’ hospital put it to me: “the concept of different parts of the brain having different functions is extremely well established. However, to portray humans as having different brain layers, for example a ‘lizard brain’ underlying basic physiological functions, is not borne out by evolutionary or physiological evidence. For a start, mammals and reptiles split early in evolutionary terms. Whilst it is true that more primitive functions in our brains evolved earlier in the course of life on Earth, this view of three separate brain systems driving our basic instincts, emotions and logic respectively does not stack up.” Lisa Feldman Barrett, professor of psychology at Northeastern University is another contemporary voice actively debunking the lizard brain myth. In her view, rather than operating as a battleground between ancient instinct, raw emotion and sophisticated logic, the brain is a dynamic, integrated system, whose aim is to keep us alive by predicting and budgeting our energy requirements. Neuroanatomically and behaviourally, if not yet in the popular consciousness, the idea that we all have a lizard brain has been thoroughly discredited. Yet despite the mounting evidence, and the success of more recent frameworks, the triune brain endures. Shockingly, it is still being widely taught in introductory psychology textbooks (as one journal article mischievously titled “Your Brain Is Not an Onion With a Tiny Reptile Inside” showed). The study also highlighted some of the pitfalls of allowing the hypothesis to go unchallenged, which include giving students a false sense of how evolution unfolds, and promoting the idea that human beings have a monopoly on “rational” actions such as deferring gratification – sacrificing a short-term reward for a longer-term gain. So, what is it about MacLean’s model that we just can’t seem to let go of? Well, as we’ve seen, people really do seem to love threes. But perhaps there’s more to it than that. The triune brain tells us an ego-stroking story about our place in the world: that we really are the pinnacle of evolution, standing apart from other species. It reaffirms heady ideas about our sovereignty over nature, and tells a reassuring story about our logical, orderly, almost computational abilities. We are storytelling creatures, of course, but this is a story that needs updating – to one about how much in common we have with other animals, and how simplistic assumptions about the way our minds work are almost never true. • Dr Hannah Critchlow is a neuroscientist and author of The 21st Century Brain (Torva). Further reading Seven Deadly Sins by Guy Leschziner (William Collins,£20) How Emotions are Made by Lisa Feldman Barrett (Pan, £12.99) Our Brains, Our Selves by Masud Husain (Canongate, £20)

title: A cargo ship, 20 crew, and a huge stash of cocaine: the seafarer imprisoned for smuggling – on no evidence
summary: After Turkish police found drugs on board the Phoenician M, the ship’s chief mate, Ali Albokhari, was sentenced to 30 years in prison. His wife is still fighting to free him
text: In the early hours of 6 October 2023, Elena Albokhari was woken by a text message from her husband. Ali Albokhari, 42, a Finnish-Syrian with dark hair and cherubic features, was chief mate on a cargo ship named the Phoenician M and had been at sea since June. The 180-metre bulk carrier had docked at Ereğli in the Turkish Black Sea a few days earlier and Ali was due to return home to Helsinki soon, but instead of feeling excitement, Elena was growing increasingly worried about his welfare. She’d had a similar feeling of unease a month earlier, when the ship had arrived at Barranquilla, Colombia. Ali had called in a panic to report that drugs had been found; Armada Nacional officers had marched onboard and uncovered holdalls stuffed with 137kg cocaine. Labels on the packages – the crest of Turkish football club Kayserispor – hinted at their destination: Turkey was the next port of call. “I never want to work as a seaman again,” Ali told Elena. “We are having big problems.” For two days, the ship was held at the port. Elena, 39, a tour guide from Russia, was so anxious, she could barely sleep. Then she received a photo from Ali of the crew happily drinking beer in a restaurant – the drugs had been removed and, after a meeting with the harbourmaster, the ship cleared to depart. “So will you go on working as a seaman?” Elena asked. “Yeah,” Ali said. “Sometimes it happens … so it’s OK.” Yet when the Phoenician M arrived at Ereğli on 2 October, loaded with coal, it was targeted by Turkish narcotics officers. The ship’s captain, Marko Bekavac, 63, a steely Croatian with three decades’ experience as a seafarer, had already informed the ship’s management company about the incident in Colombia, and when Turkish authorities boarded, he immediately declared that drugs had previously been found on the ship. Despite this, officers delivered a statement: should anything be found onboard, he would be accountable. The 20 crew members, including citizens of Russia, Ukraine, Poland and the Philippines, were ordered to remain in the ship’s mess room as the police continued to investigate. Nothing was found in an initial search but days later, as the coal was unloaded, suspicious bags were reportedly found buried in the cargo hold. They were packed with more cocaine. The captain and other crew were escorted from the ship. Ali, who was second in command, remained onboard as unloading continued. He had managed to keep hold of his phone and was sending Elena updates. These had done little to allay her fears. Now, in the middle of the night, a text message confirmed the worst: “They are going to arrest us.” * * * Unless we are related to a seafarer, or live near a major port, most of us don’t encounter the people who work in shipping. Yet without them our lives would grind to a halt. Oceanic trade routes are the thread that weaves the world together. Merchant shipping – often described as the “lifeblood of the global economy” – is responsible for the movement of 90% of trade; every year, 11bn tonnes of goods, from coffee to fuel to fashion, are transported by ship. The scale of the maritime infrastructure is staggering, but the 2.57 million seafarers who operate within it remain largely invisible, as do many of the challenges they face. Elena never thought of Ali’s work as inherently risky, and the life of a merchant seaman can seem mundane. Cargo ships travel at around 15 knots (17mph). A boat like the Phoenician M can take more than two weeks to traverse the Atlantic. The routine involves inspections, maintenance checks, paperwork and long stretches at sea. But seafarers have become vulnerable to rapidly shifting conflicts – from the Russian invasion of Ukraine to the battle around the strait of Hormuz – as well as poor regulatory oversight, abandonment by shipowners and abuse by port authorities. Seafarers’ rights are frequently neglected and they are too easily scapegoated for events outside their control. When an incident occurs, it is often far easier for authorities to pursue crew members than the shipping companies that employ them, who have an incentive to let the blame fall on individuals, and the P&I (protection and indemnity) clubs that insure them are there to serve the company, not individual crew members. The very nature of the job means voyaging to far-flung destinations, so if things do go wrong, seafarers can be forced to navigate unfamiliar judicial systems, with discretionary legal support, and face long periods of detention in a foreign country. Data on the scale of the problem is limited, but one 2018 survey by Nautilus International, the maritime professionals’ union, found that 90% of seafarers feared criminalisation above anything else. A recent survey by InterManager, the ship management association, has compiled 118 known cases over the past three decades, with a peak of 23 cases in 2023. Senior officers are most at risk; in 63% of cases, the captain was imprisoned. Cases of seafarer criminalisation range from fuel smuggling allegations to collisions, but of particular concern is the global drug trade. Much like any other commodity, the vast majority of cocaine is transported by sea. Ports in Colombia are key export hubs. Cargo ships are up to 400 metres long and usually have just a couple of dozen crew; it’s not hard to find a place to hide something on them. In 2019, Capt Andrzej Lasota, a Polish seafarer, spent two years in prison in Mexico after 240kg of cocaine – planted on the ship at Barranquilla – was uncovered during unloading at Altamira. He was charged with “negligence” for failing to be aware of the drugs buried under coal in the cargo hold. The case was widely condemned, and resonates with that of the Phoenician M. Ali is now the only crew member who remains imprisoned, three years after his arrest. The International Maritime Organization has said the case “demonstrates how vulnerable seafarers are when they fall victim to organised international crime”. The International Transport Workers’ Federation (ITF), a union that represents seafarers, described it as a “gross abuse” of human rights. * * * As a seafarer’s wife, Elena was used to spending time apart from her husband. But now Ali – whom she would speak to by phone or message almost daily – was no longer contactable, she felt truly alone. When she called the German crewing agency, Team Ship, desperate for answers, it was still unaware of the incident. A number she had for the company responsible for the crew and the ship, Iskenderun Ship Management, a Turkish operator, went unanswered. She waited for a call from some sort of official body, explaining what was going on, but none came. Elena frantically tried to make contact with anyone who might know what had happened. After she posted on online chat groups for seafarers, she was messaged by the wife of a crew member who had not been among those taken by the police. Only after calling him was she able to piece together what was happening. Ali, along with Bekavac and eight other crew members, had been arrested on suspicion of drug smuggling. Another week or so passed. Elena had another call with the crewing agency, which said lawyers would be provided by Iskenderun at no cost. “Don’t worry, they are in the police station, they are being questioned, then they will be released,” Elena recalls an agent telling her. “You just need to wait.” So she waited. But instead, the men were detained and charged. During those first days, Elena says, the crew had no legal representation. When shipping incidents occur, a lawyer is usually appointed by a local P&I club “correspondent”, an independent adviser who can act on behalf of the shipowner and the club. When a lawyer was appointed, the crew said they were encouraged to accept the charges and sign what they described as arrest warrants, written in Turkish. “So we did,” one told Human Rights at Sea, an NGO. “We were detained.” UK P&I, the club that provided insurance for the Phoenician M, said all appointments in this case, “including legal representation and the P&I correspondent”, were made by the shipowner, not them. They added that while they were not bound to do so, they provided support for the crew’s “significant” defence costs. Days turned to weeks, then months. The men were moved from a local detention centre to a maximum security prison. Ali was one of many now isolated from their families, terrified about what would happen next. “Every day I was crying inside of that cell,” one Filipino crew member told me, adding that for a long time he didn’t know why he was being held. As for Elena, six months passed before she was finally able to speak with her husband. He put on a brave face, telling her he was OK, but asked her to send money: “If nobody sends you money in prison, you can’t buy food, you can’t buy anything.” Elena sent money and clothes, and waited for the men to stand trial. Another six months passed. Finally, on 16 September 2024, following a number of hearings at Karadeniz Ereğli high criminal court, a verdict was due. Elena was sure Ali would be released. While he sat in the courtroom, she spent the day at home, anxiously awaiting the outcome. Then she received a brief message from the Finnish embassy. “I’m so sorry ... ” it said. While the eight other crew members had been acquitted, Ali and Bekavac had been found guilty on the basis of “command responsibility” and sentenced to 30 years’ imprisonment. Elena was stunned. Eventually she replied, “What should I do now?” * * * Ali and Elena’s home is a one-bedroom flat in a modern housing estate not far from Helsinki’s airport. When I visit in September, Elena, true to her profession as a tour guide, has laid out a spread of local treats: pancakes, blueberry juice, grilled cheese with cloudberry jam. Ali’s suitcase, which she was able to retrieve after his sentence, is still slumped near the balcony door. She tries to remain optimistic for his return. Every week, she buys fresh flowers. On the wall above it she has pinned a banner: “Welcome Home”. If the maritime industry is emblematic of the power of globalisation, Ali and Elena’s relationship is a story of what it means to live on its faultlines. Ali was born in Damascus, Syria. His mother raised him and his three siblings, together with his stepfather, who ran a shoe business. When Ali reached college age, his options for further education were limited – as were the countries he could travel to – so his family decided he should attend the maritime university in St Petersburg, Russia, which was the most affordable option. He graduated in 2011, just as Syria descended into civil war, meaning he could neither remain in Russia nor safely return home. He applied for asylum in Finland and was accepted, continuing his studies at the Novia University in Turku. In 2017, Ali was granted full citizenship. Elena was born in Moscow. Her mother was a language teacher, her father an electrician. As she got older, she, too, was eager to build a life beyond her homeland and spent time as a student in Spain. She met Ali on a dating app in 2021. At the time, Elena, who had been working as a Spanish-language interpreter and tour guide in Russia, was hoping to continue her studies in Finland. If she managed to get accepted to a Finnish-language programme, the education would be free, and she was eager to practise with native speakers. When Ali struck up a conversation, she was intrigued by this Middle Eastern man who spoke her native Russian. He was at sea at the time, but they began speaking regularly over phone and video call. When Elena travelled to Finland to take her Finnish-language test, he met her at the airport. She passed her test and they married in January 2022. A month later, Russia invaded Ukraine. They had all these plans, Elena says, but Ali struggled to find a job. For the past decade he had primarily worked on Russian ships; now Russia was at war and he struggled to find work with Finnish companies, which Elena believes was due to his Syrian heritage. Ali eventually secured a nine-month contract with a Russian shipping company, and Elena returned to Moscow to visit her mother. She was able to meet him briefly, when his ship stopped at Murmansk, but when Ali returned to Finland at the end of his contract, Elena became stranded in Russia for a further three months while she awaited the paperwork needed to leave. It was December 2022 when they finally reunited in Helsinki. For the first year of their marriage, they were like ships in the night. It took months for Ali to secure his next contract: not just a job but a promotion, too. “I remember when he received the call,” Elena says. “He was so happy.” In May 2023 he was packing his bags, preparing to head to London to join the existing crew as they finished their rotation. The ship he was heading for was the Clipper Palma. In June, under the new management of Iskenderun, it was renamed: the Phoenician M. Looking back, there were things about the job that seemed a bit off to Elena. Ali, who was appointed as the ship’s security officer, described the vessel as very old. He was also critical of the attitude of Iskenderun. When the crew made requests they would be unresponsive; some of these requests would prove critical to the case. When Bekavac noted Barranquilla was on the list of destinations, he requested additional security personnel, as well as cameras and locks for doors and hatches, due to the high risk of interference from drug cartels. Iskenderun did not respond. Elena says the lawyer appointed to Ali by Iskenderun visited him in prison rarely and did not seem to be prioritising his interests. “They were saying, ‘Don’t say a single word about the company … otherwise he will spend a long time there.’” Since Ali was sentenced, Elena has been lobbying for his release while trying to keep her own life afloat. When he was arrested, she was still a relative newcomer to Finland, with no support network and no job, as she was still studying. Sanctions on Russia meant their credit cards did not work: “I was left without money, without help.” Elena was dismayed by the lack of support from the Finnish government. While its consular service has visited Ali in prison a number of times since late 2024, statements on the case have been scarce, and it is notably absent from Finnish media. One reason may be that Finland and Turkey have not had the easiest relations in recent years. Ankara put up resistance to Finland’s application to join Nato in 2022; since then it has made a growing number of extradition requests for political dissidents, which Finland has largely rejected. For Elena, the apparent indifference to Ali’s plight has been underlined by Bekavac’s experience. The Croatian prime minister and foreign minister spoke out against the verdict, and his then wife, Katja, received support to arrange prison visits without delay. When Elena went to Ankara, she attended the Palace of Justice with her lawyer and without consular assistance. It took all day to navigate the bureaucracy of the building and, after submitting documents and photos, she had to wait a further two weeks before a prison visit was approved. Katja, Elena says, was able to meet the captain without a barrier between them, but when she finally made it through the prison gates, after the humiliation of a strip-search, she had to speak with Ali through a glass pane. “Psychologically, it was very difficult,” she says. During that first meeting, Elena was shocked by how much he had changed. “I have never seen my husband sad,” she says. “He’s always laughing, singing, dancing, but this time I didn’t recognise him. He was very thin, depressed and with grey hair.” The hardest thing was to contain her emotions: “When I’m alone here I can cry, I can tell my friends everything is very bad … but I can’t say such things to him. I have to support him.” She told him they had a new lawyer. That his mother was well. That they would be waiting for him. That they’d fight for him. After 40 minutes, their time was up. As Elena continued to battle for diplomatic support, travelling to Turkey to visit Ali every month, she became aware the Croatian authorities were working behind the scenes. In August 2025, Ali watched from his cell as Bekavac was collected from the prison by a Croatian diplomat and flown home. In Croatia, there has been speculation that his release was negotiated as part of a prisoner swap with Mustafa Yiğit Zeren, a Turkish billionaire and close friend of President Erdoğan who was wanted by the Russians over alleged embezzlement of €600m. When Elena heard the news she felt hopeful for Ali, but soon this turned to dismay. “I was absolutely sure that after that Finland would change their attitude … but nothing. Every time they say, ‘We don’t know what happened, we do not know why the captain was released.’” It was as if her husband did not exist. When I spoke to Jussi Tanner, Finland’s director general for consular services, he told me he cannot comment on the details of the case but described it as “concerning and troubling”. Finland, he says, continues to engage with the Turkish authorities and, particularly since Bekavac’s release, has been seeking clarification regarding Ali’s prolonged detention. “Everything I know about the case seems to indicate that it makes no sense that he’s still in custody,” Tanner says. Elena says she spends all her spare time investigating the case herself, poring over the details as she grows increasingly suspicious of the motivations of all the parties involved. She pulls out a black folder of documents relating to Ali’s employment records. She also shows me her diary, a white book with a gold heart on the cover filled with neat handwriting. Its pages are full of memories, but from October 2023 they are blank. * * * As the case of Phoenician M has lingered on, it has drawn attention to the protections afforded to seafarers and the need for these to be reaffirmed. There are numerous international agreements designed to protect their rights, such as the International Labour Organisation Guidelines on Fair Treatment of Seafarers and the Maritime Labour Convention – often described as the “seafarers’ bill of rights” – but in practice they are at the beck and call of whichever jurisdiction they happen to sail into. “It’s aspirational, but not very concrete,” is how James Turner KC, who specialises in shipping law, summarises it to me. Maritime organisations have also expressed growing concern at the extent to which supply chains are being exploited by organised crime. In 2019, MSC, the world’s largest ocean carrier, came under intense scrutiny after 20 tonnes of cocaine with a value of $1bn was discovered by US authorities on the MSC Gayane at Philadelphia. Large cocaine shipments were also found on three other MSC ships that year. An investigation by Bloomberg alleged the company had been infiltrated by members of a Balkan cartel. Eight Gayane crew members pleaded guilty of involvement in the drug-smuggling operation. Criminal actors clearly do exist in the industry, but innocent seafarers are also being caught in the net. Keith Svendsen, an executive at Danish group Maersk, told the Financial Times shipping companies were now dealing with “some of the most dangerous people in the world” and cited crew members coerced into helping smuggling gangs. Fabrizio Barcellona, a coordinator at the ITF, says the issue is not with countries taking a strong stance against drug trafficking, but that seafarers are being scapegoated. “It’s not good enough just to put them in jail without clear evidence,” he says. Over the past decade, Turkey has become a significant hub for the importation of cocaine to Europe, and there is growing pressure to address the issue. Erdoğan’s government has been accused of allowing organised crime to proliferate, and high-ranking political figures have been accused of involvement in drug trafficking. Imdat Öner, a former Turkish diplomat turned public policy analyst, told me that instead of effectively pursuing organised crime networks, the authorities are focusing on low-volume trafficking of the sort found on the Phoenician M. “It allows the government, the police, to save face internationally,” he says. David Hammond, a former military seafarer, qualified barrister and founder of Human Rights at Sea, has published a review of Ali’s case which calls it a “grave miscarriage of justice” and questions the prosecution’s integrity and motivations. Court papers state that the investigation was triggered by intelligence from Kayseri province police narcotics department, and the conviction based on evidence gathered following the seizure. But according to Hammond, Turkish police failed to request documentation relating to the Colombian incident, key witnesses were not interviewed, and no forensic evidence linking crew members to the drugs was presented. It is unclear why, of 20 crew onboard, only 10 were arrested. The prosecution seems to have rested solely on the rank and responsibilities of the crew. The conviction, as Ali’s lawyer argued, “rests on speculation rather than proof”. There appears to be some awareness of these weaknesses within the Turkish judiciary. In April 2025, the chief public prosecutor referred the case to the supreme court of appeal, which in March 2026 upheld Ali’s conviction by a 3-2 majority. However, the opinions of the two dissenting judges pointed to many of the issues raised by Ali’s defence. They agreed the investigation was incomplete, there was not proper communication with the Colombian authorities, and police did not pursue an investigation in regard to the source intelligence that led them to the drugs on the ship in the first place. In July, Ali and Bekavac (who remains convicted as far as Turkish law is concerned) had their sentences increased to 33 years, due to a failure to pay a £3,000 fine that was part of their original sentence. Bekavac may now be at home with his family, but he remains incensed about the case and is outraged at the suggestion that he could have been involved in a drug-smuggling operation. He told me he was made aware of the destination list for the Phoenician M only three days before it arrived in Barranquilla and the responsibility for loading cargo fell on the stevedores working at the port. The cocaine reportedly found in Turkey was buried 5 metres deep within the coal, he adds, so could only have been concealed while the ship was being loaded in Barranquilla, not during the journey, as alleged by the prosecution. Bekavac, like the other crew, believed that, having been cleared by the Colombian harbourmaster, they would have no further issues. The captain also told me he documented his email correspondence relating to the incident on a USB drive. This was confiscated by Turkish police and not presented as evidence in the case. When it was returned to him, the drive had been wiped (he was later able to recover the data). In an interview with Slobodna Dalmacija, a Croatian newspaper, Bekavac said the lawyer provided to him by the company told him not to mention the stamps on the packages or talk about the company. As Hammond sees it, there is evidence that gestures to serious organised crime – as well as the possible knowledge of state authorities – yet Turkish police appear not to have pursued lines of inquiry that might shed light on this. The cargo’s recipient, for example, does not seem to have been scrutinised, nor were any representatives from Iskenderun called as witnesses. If the crew can be held liable due to “command responsibility”, then the shipping company should, at the very least, have to answer as to whether it did all it could to address the risk of drug trafficking on its vessel. Hammond believes the case should be a wake-up call for everyone who has a moral duty to the welfare of seafarers – from P&I clubs to shipping companies to unions – and is appalled that a sector responsible for trillions of dollars of trade cannot guarantee the protection of its workers. Seafarers, he tells me, are simply treated as “disposable assets”. Iskenderun did not respond to requests for comment. However, the company appears to now be operating as Phoenician Shipping & Crewing, which has the same office address and is listed as the owner of the Phoenician M. Emails to Phoenician Shipping bounced, and the telephone number dialled to Orontes Shipping, another Turkish company established in 2024, which also lists the ship in its fleet. Emails and calls to this company also went unanswered. The Turkish Ministry of Justice did not respond to requests for comment. * * * In January, Elena returned to Ankara to visit Ali. He always has presents for her, she says, holding up an intricately beaded cushion by way of illustration, but this time he told her there was a box waiting for her to take home. “The guards will give it to you,” he said. When she left, she collected it. Inside were two budgerigars. One boy, one girl. “A couple.” Ali has always loved birds, Elena says. There were budgies and parrots in the prison, and Ali began breeding them. Dozens of his fellow prisoners have a bird now and Ali wanted her to have some, too. Transferring them to Finland was not straightforward, though compared with the other challenges in her life, it was, at least, achievable. Panjo and Lucy now live in a cage above the kitchen counter, chirping loudly. Elena opens the cage and they flutter around the room before landing happily on her outstretched finger. Along with the cat, Koko, they join the list of those waiting for Ali to return home. Ali’s lawyer has petitioned the chief public prosecutor – who appears to believe there are questions over Ali’s conviction – to file an objection to the supreme court of appeal’s decision, which would prompt a further review of the case. While Elena awaited further news, she was distraught to receive a call from Ali telling her he was being moved to a unit for prisoners whose convictions are considered final. Then, in August, the prosecutor agreed to submit the objection to the court. No date for a decision has been set, so again Elena waits. She says Ali is coming under intense pressure from the Turkish authorities to accept a transfer to Finland, but to do so could disrupt attempts to overturn his conviction – and risk him remaining in prison on his return. For now, both their lives remain suspended. Elena takes care of the cat and birds, and continues to make a living as a guide in Helsinki. She avoids talking too much about herself to holidaymakers. To do so would probably tarnish the theme of the tour: “The happiest country in the world.” • This article was amended on 5 October 2026. An earlier version referred to Human Rights at Sea International, rather than its sister organisation Human Rights at Sea.

title: Jacob Rees-Mogg accuses Tucker Carlson of ‘verging on defending Hitler’
summary: Former Tory minister defends UK decision to enter war in podcast with US rightwinger and Putin sympathiser
text: The former Tory minister Jacob Rees-Mogg has found himself defending Britain’s decision to fight against Adolf Hitler after inviting the US rightwinger and Vladimir Putin sympathiser Tucker Carlson into his home for an interview. During the encounter, Carlson repeatedly suggested the west was to blame for inviting aggression from Russia and said of the prospect that Britain could have lost to Hitler: “Who cares?” Rees-Mogg, who lost his parliamentary seat in 2024, appears to have agreed to host Carlson’s podcast show after carving out a post-politics career as a commentator. Carlson set up the show after leaving Fox News and losing faith with Donald Trump, largely citing the US president’s willingness to get involved in foreign wars. Carlson has interviewed Putin and taken a sympathetic position towards Russia over Ukraine. In the lengthy debate on foreign policy and global tensions, the US commentator repeatedly goaded Rees-Mogg over the smallness of the UK armed forces and suggested Russia was more powerful. Rees-Mogg explained that the UK economy was bigger and made the case that Britain and western allies had to support Ukraine and deter Russian aggression. Carlson went on to question why Britain bothered entering the second world war and claimed Germany had a legitimate claim over parts of Poland. Rees-Mogg said: “Otherwise we’d be speaking German.” Carlson replied: “Who cares? There are a lot of people in Britain who can’t speak English. So it would be nice to have at least a European language spoken in your country.” During the interview, Rees-Mogg said he was very surprised that Carlson was “verging on defending Hitler”, adding: “I think this is not really what you want to be doing.” Carlson replied: “Yeah, I guess I’m just a secret Nazi. I’m actually not a secret Nazi … and hardly a public Nazi.” Rees-Mogg responded that he was reassured, before saying that “Germany would have invaded us” if the UK had not gone to war. The interview has raised eyebrows in the US as well as Britain, with the Republican Mike Huckabee, the US ambassador to Israel, posting on X: “When it seemed impossible for Toxic Tucker to descend deeper into the sewer here he goes opining that UK should have let Nazis take over. Forget that Hitler murdered 11 million people? I thought Tucker was against killing? He needs help. Serious help.”
