title: Lack of inspections at fish slaughterhouses a ‘disgrace’, says Animal Equality UK
summary: Charity calls for faster progress on humane slaughter laws for farmed fish in England and Wales
text: Up to 77m fish are slaughtered each year in the UK but there are no routine or mandatory inspections of fish slaughterhouses in England and Wales, it can be revealed. Concerns within government about the way fish are slaughtered date back decades but all of the official bodies responsible for animal welfare and food standards in England and Wales said they do not undertake regular inspections. When Animal Equality UK contacted the Animal and Plant Health Agency (APHA), it referred the charity to the Fish Health Inspectorate (FHI). In response to a previous inquiry, the APHA had said it does not carry out mandatory inspections of fish slaughterhouses and suggested contacting the Food Standards Agency (FSA). Both the FSA and the FHI told Animal Equality UK that they did not carry out routine or mandatory inspections. Abigail Penny, the executive director of Animal Equality UK, said: “Fish are thinking, feeling beings, capable of pain. It is a disgrace that not a single government agency will take responsibility for checking on their welfare at slaughter. This is a huge blindspot, and it leaves these animals all the more vulnerable behind closed doors.” In 1996, the government’s expert advisory body, the Farm Animal Welfare Council – now called the Animal Welfare Committee – suggested there should be legislation governing the slaughter of farmed fish. The committee returned to the issue in 2014 and again in 2024. On the latter occasion it urged governments across the UK to legislate for fish to be stunned before slaughter, and for inspection systems to be put in place to enforce those standards. In its Animal Welfare Strategy for England, published in December 2025, the government committed to introducing humane slaughter requirements for farmed fish but draft legislation has yet to be published. Penny said: “For 30 years, people in power have known that farmed fish need legal protection when they are slaughtered, yet for 30 years decisionmakers have failed to act.” She added: “The government promised to change the law, and we welcome that promise, but promises don’t protect animals. Every month of delay leaves millions of fish at risk of prolonged, painful deaths. Ministers must bring forward species-specific slaughter legislation now, backed by a proper inspection regime, so that what happens to these animals is no longer left to chance. It’s the least they deserve.” Animal Equality UK estimates that about 7,742 tonnes of trout a year are killed in England and Wales. The British Trout Association says the UK has almost 290 trout farms, including hatcheries, concentrated in northern England, southern England and southern Scotland. An APHA spokesperson said: “It is incorrect to suggest fish farms aren’t regulated or inspected by government bodies. APHA investigates reports of suspected cases of poor welfare at fish farms, and the Fish Health Inspectorate inspects them on behalf of the government. We do not hesitate to take further action if we find evidence of cruelty or neglect.”

title: OpenAI safety leader quits, warning AI company’s culture is ‘broken’
summary: David Robinson joins other insiders in urging industry to take more care over rapidly developing technology
text: A safety leader at OpenAI has quit the company, warning that its culture was broken and that AI firms were not “being nearly careful enough” about developing the technology. David Robinson, who led the writing of safety reports that accompanied the ChatGPT developer’s product releases, explained his resignation in an essay headlined: “I quit OpenAI because its culture is broken.” Robinson wrote that a cultural overhaul was needed at cutting-edge AI firms and incidents such as a “swarm” of OpenAI agents – AI programmes operating autonomously without human oversight – attacking the AI startup Hugging Face were “typical of the industry, given the speed and flexibility with which people operate”. Writing in the Atlantic magazine, Robinson wrote: “I agree with other recently departed staff that the companies building this technology aren’t being nearly careful enough. But I believe that we need to look deeper than specific rules or new laws. We need to talk about culture.” Referring to OpenAI’s pace of development, he wrote: “As the company sprints from one launch to the next, it is failing to achieve the level of care that I believe is needed.” OpenAI has shown signs of caution in recent weeks, after the Hugging Face incident and the revelation that it has notified more than 100 organisations about rogue agent activity. This week it announced it was scrapping the release of a next-generation ⁠AI model after researchers raised safety concerns ⁠during internal testing. OpenAI has also paused training of its most advanced models. Geoffrey Irving, who worked at OpenAI and was chief scientist at the UK government’s AI Safety Institute before joining the AI safety researchcompany Resolution, also issued a warning on AI on Saturday. Writing in Time, he said: “Recent warnings about the potential destructive power of AI are understating the severity of the situation. I believe there’s about a 50% chance we all die because of the development of smarter-than-human AI systems, and that our actions over the next two to 10 years will determine the outcome.” The warnings follow the resignation of Jacob Coxon, a researcher at the OpenAI rival Anthropic, who quit the Claude chatbot developer last month. He said he believed AI “could kill us all by the end of the decade” – and was backed up by an Anthropic employee warning there was a more than 10% chance AI would wipe out humanity within the next decade. Critics of such warnings have cautioned, however, that they are unscientific because they cannot be verified or falsified. Robinson wrote that Silicon Valley lacked an awareness of “how to handle dangerous technology” and “what it means to care for people”. Warning that OpenAI had “unimpeded optimism” about solving problems as they arose, he wrote that this internal culture meant safety failures would only grow as systems became more capable. “Imagine ‘rogue’ agents that work like teams of hackers (for example, holding hospital computer systems for ransom) but never need to sleep,” wrote Robinson. Robinson called for two safety changes: that AI firms rely on safety expertise in other fields such as nuclear and aviation, and that they develop “new science” that ensures powerful systems in the future are capable of being reined in when they are operating autonomously. “Given today’s risks, frontier labs need to run like nuclear power plants or busy airports, with layers of redundancy and careful, time-consuming planning, so that the occasional and inevitable human error does not open a door to disaster,” he wrote. An OpenAI spokesperson said the company was continuing to “strengthen our safety and security practices to address the risks we see today”, while working on dealing with the risks that might be created by future AI breakthroughs. “We’re making sure our models don’t become more capable than we can safely manage and secure, and we pause training or hold back models when we need to slow down,” said the spokesperson.

title: Revealed: Government quietly dropped plan to prepare England for wildfires
summary: FOI request shows wildfire risk scheme scrapped, as data highlights many fire services lack proper protective gear
text: The government quietly scrapped plans to prepare the countryside in England for wildfires, it has been revealed. This was despite new data showing fire crews do not have the proper protective gear to tackle them. This summer has been a potent reminder of the scale of the threat posed by the climate crisis, with the UK experiencing record-breaking wildfires after punishingly hot and dry weather turned large parts of the countryside into a tinderbox. In the third national climate adaptation programme, published in July 2023, the Conservative government, then headed by Rishi Sunak, said it would run a wildfire risk programme in England from 2023 to 2027 so land management would be adapted for the risk. However, it has now emerged the programme was never implemented, with the current government stating the commitment “was made by the previous government but was not brought into effect”. The environmental campaigner and author Guy Shrubsole, who obtained the information via a freedom of information request, said it was “appalling” the government “couldn’t be bothered to pay attention to wildfire risks until jolted into doing so by Britain burning this summer”. After a wildfire spread across an area including several homes in Stourbridge in the West Midlands in August, the prime minister, Andy Burnham, convened an emergency Cobra meeting and issued a temporary ban on the sale of disposable barbecues, criticised as being too little too late. “Successive governments have been asleep at the wheel in preparing us for the impacts of the climate crisis,” Shrubsole said. Alistair Carmichael, a Scottish Liberal Democrat MP and the chair of the Commons environment food and rural affairs committee, said it was alarming that ministers had not prioritised work to adapt land for wildfire risk. “It begs further serious questions about whether this summer’s wildfires could have looked different with more resources on the ground,” he added. Shrubsole said the government must agree a plan to re-wet the UK’s peat bogs, restore lost ponds in farmers’ fields, and stop grouse moor owners setting fire to moorland. New data obtained by the Country Land and Business Association has also revealed that more than half of the 29 fire services that responded to requests for information had no wildfire personal protective equipment (PPE). They included the Suffolk fire and rescue service, which had to deal with an “apocalyptic” wildfire earlier this summer that burned close to the Sizewell B nuclear power station and destroyed vast areas of a protected nature reserve. Standard particle-filtering respirators do not protect against dangerous gases such as carbon monoxide, which are heavily present in wildfire smoke. Standard PPE can also be too hot and heavy for wildfire conditions. This can cause crews to overheat, or remove their PPE altogether, exposing them to greater danger from heat, smoke and radiation. The data also revealed that training for wildfires was limited. For example, in Cleveland just five staff (1.2%) were qualified to give tactical advice or command wildfires, and in Cheshire just 8.62% of employees were trained to undertake wildfire operations. In response to these findings, the Fire Brigades Union is calling for correct PPE to be provided to all members combating wildfires, alongside adequate training programmes. Steve Wright, the union’s general secretary, said: “It is vital for our country’s wildfire resilience to have better land management, stronger public awareness campaigns and long-term prevention measures. Only by proper investment and a wildfire strategy can we make the country more resilient.” A government spokesperson said: “We have made wildfire preparedness a government priority and, following incidents this summer, we are convening a summit with fire and rescue service partners to make sure we are as resilient as possible. This includes making sure services have the right equipment and resources, building on the £100m we previously gave to upgrade our national resilience assets. “Land management and landscape adaptation play an important part in this, and we work closely with land managers and experts to support the restoration of peatlands, the creation of firebreaks and other adaptations that help to prevent fires from starting or from spreading as quickly during incidents.”

title: Return of the nasty party? Badenoch walks tightrope with ‘punch down’ policies
summary: Shadow minister says Tories have ‘outsourced our toxicity to Reform’, but others doubt leader can spark lasting revival
text: The forthcoming Conservative conference will be, almost everyone in the party agrees, notably more upbeat and unified than last year. There is a similar consensus that Kemi Badenoch is doing well as party leader. That is, however, not the whole story. “The mood is better but the facts are still very poor,” one Conservative MP said. “We are still a distant third in the polls, and if there was an election tomorrow we would lose, and badly. That means the mood is overhyped.” This is the inescapable shadow over the Tory gathering in Birmingham, which begins on Sunday. Almost two years since Badenoch was elected leader, her party is still polling lower than it did in 2024, when it suffered a catastrophically poor election result. There is, of course, context behind her MPs’ patience, not least the fracturing of the political landscape and the rise of a new competitor on the right in Reform UK. But while Badenoch’s future is secure for now, there is concern among some Tories that her dogged focus on winning back support from Nigel Farage’s party, with little on offer to more centrist voters, poses both political and reputational risks. “We need to be attracting as many voters who left us for the Lib Dems as Reform, and I don’t personally think we have got the balance right,” a shadow minister said. “There is an economic offering, but they don’t want us to be so intolerant on social issues. The way we are going, we risk being seen as the nasty party again.” The phrase “nasty party” was coined by Theresa May in 2002, when the then party chair warned activists against focusing on too narrow a voter base and targeting other parts of society with punitive policies. Even if Badenoch has learned to prioritise core policy and walk away from culture war arguments, it seems she has not fully absorbed May’s lessons about not punching down. In recent weeks, the Tories have pledged to bar non-Britons from social housing, strip UK citizenship from dual nationals convicted of serious crimes, and cut some benefits payments to a “subsistence” level, with restrictions preventing the money being used to buy alcohol or tobacco. The main pre-conference policy offering was in a similar vein: a pledge to slash overseas aid to pay for 50,000 new prison places. There are plenty of Conservative MPs who don’t view this as a problem. “I’ve not heard any colleagues say they were worried about the nasty party stuff,” one said. “In contrast, a lot of constituents say they are very worried about welfare costs.” One of the paradoxes of Badenoch’s tenure is the relative lack of open dissent, even on totemic ideas such as the commitment to leave the European convention on human rights (ECHR) to enact more rigorous deportation policies. This is, in part, because many of her MPs respect the way Badenoch has taken time over decisions and sought to make her case, with the ECHR plan prefaced by a 185-page report by David Wolfson, the shadow attorney general. But its is also a function of the apparent lack of appetite for a fight from centrist Conservatives such as the One Nation group, most of whom are either outside parliament, lying low on the backbenches or co-opted into the Badenoch project, as with Tom Tugendhat, made shadow foreign secretary in a recent mini-reshuffle. “The thing about the One Nation group is that we never actually did anything,” one centrist MP said. “We got together and metaphorically held hands from time to time, but that was about it. “Either way, everybody seems to be pulling together now. It’s not quite yet the Blues Brothers on a mission from God, but there’s a real sense of purpose. There are no factions, no five families. The arguments have stopped.” This end of the arguments – at least for now – is in part down to Badenoch’s improved performance. While last year’s party conference was widely seen as make or break for a leader who had started shakily, she is now feted by Tory MPs for her performances in the Commons. Her personal poll ratings are also on the rise, even if this is a relative achievement – Badenoch’s net favourability score with YouGov has gone up by 20 points, but remains at a lowly minus 15. Similarly, when voters are asked to describe her, common epithets include not just “strong” but also “mean” and “cold”. Last year’s conference was also overshadowed by comments from Robert Jenrick, the then shadow justice secretary, who was accused of amplifying toxic nationalism after he complained about “not seeing another white face” in a part of Birmingham where the event was taking place. There is no risk of this happening again, given Jenrick defected to Reform three months later, having been sacked by Badenoch for plotting against her. “We are very unified, and a lot of that coincided with Jenrick going. We have outsourced our toxicity to Reform,” a shadow minister said. “But there is more to it than that. This time last year, Reform and Keir Starmer were both talking about us as being dead or irrelevant, and we’re not. Kemi has had a lot of cut-through.” What public dissent does exist often comes from Prosper UK, a centrist grouping launched earlier this year by Andy Street, the ex-West Midlands mayor, and Ruth Davidson, who formerly led the Scottish Conservatives. Among its vice-chairs is David Gauke, the May-era cabinet minister, who says Badenoch must pay more attention to “politically homeless” moderate Tories who helped the Liberal Democrats win dozens of seats in southern England in 2024. “There’s a set of the electorate that don’t feel the party has spoken to them for at least 10 years, and Conservatives need to start doing that,” he said. “There is no route to a Conservative majority that does not involve winning back seats in Oxfordshire and Surrey and other parts of the home counties.” Badenoch’s calculation, according to Tim Bale, professor of politics at Queen Mary, University of London, seemed to be to try to stop Reform running riot, and then hoping Reform implodes and Andy Burnham’s government slumps. “It is a risk, but what else have they got?” he said. “But I can’t see how it’s going to work for them and where the votes are going to come from. “They seem to be overstating the extent to which voters think even Badenoch is a good thing. She’s still in negative territory. They have gone from a situation in which they got 24% of the vote in 2024 and they’re now, at best, on just over 20%. If this is what success looks like, I’d love to know what failure is.”

title: Ministers explore how to stop regional leaders misusing planned new spending powers
summary: Labour wants to make sure mayors and council chiefs in England can be held to account for extra revenues devolved to them
text: Ministers are mulling over how to ensure that England’s regional leaders do not misuse their newfound spending muscle, as Whitehall prepares to devolve more revenue to local levels. Ideas under consideration include a new select committee in Westminster, enhanced reporting rules and a new audit body focused on local and regional government. The Guardian understands the idea has even been mooted of allowing spendthrift mayors to be recalled by the electorate, as can happen to rule-breaking MPs. The government will publish a white paper on “rewiring the state” later this month, setting out detailed plans to hand over more income tax revenue to regional mayors. Rachel Reeves suggested the idea in her Mais lecture earlier this year, and it has been adopted by Andy Burnham’s government, which sees devolution as a big part of its growth policy. However, officials are concerned about how to ensure local leaders are fully accountable for what they do with the additional cash – including in between elections. Meg Hillier, the chair of the Treasury select committee, said she believed hers would be the right body to scrutinise the use of the additional spending powers. “It’s clear that one of the prime minister’s key ambitions is to take spending power out of Westminster and hand it to local leaders,” the Labour MP said. “It is absolutely critical, though, that strong, clear scrutiny structures are established which match this move to localism. It would be reckless to hand out new powers without ensuring there are transparent mechanisms to hold mayors to account for their decisions.” Hillier added: “One way to do this is to establish clear lines of authority running through departments and up to ministers, which will allow existing select committees to judge this work. “A core role of a select committee, particularly the Treasury committee which I chair, is to ensure politicians are publicly held to account for how they decide to spend taxpayers’ money. That is just important at a local level as it is on a national scale.” The Audit Commission, which had the specific task of overseeing local government spending, was abolished in 2015, with its role split across several other bodies. As well as shoring up accountability, it is understood there have been lengthy discussions in government about how to balance the need to incentivise local leaders to encourage economic growth, with the imperative to ensure funding is stable over time. The Institute for Fiscal Studies said last week that the government should use “equalisation payments” to prevent the funding of areas with the highest share of income tax, such as London, pulling ahead of other regions. David Phillips, the IFS’s devolution expert, said: “With more skin in the game of economic growth, mayors will be more incentivised and empowered to support growth through local policies and investments. But careful design will be needed to prevent richer areas’ funding unfairly pulling ahead. “The government must also decide how big a gap in funding it is willing to see between ‘winners’ and ‘losers’ in the years ahead.” Burnham has made clear his intention of accelerating devolution, with his new No 10 North office focusing on the regional aspects of growth policy.

title: Polish activists launch abortion pill locker to bypass near-total ban
summary: ‘AbortOmat’ in Warsaw offers novel way to challenge country’s restrictions and allow women swift and anonymous access to pill
text: They call it the “world’s first parcel locker for abortion pills”. Polish campaigners have launched a new means of distribution as part of their ongoing effort to skirt the country’s near-total ban on abortion. Painted pink and framed by zebra-striped curtains, the 22-compartment “AbortOmat” in Warsaw allows women to access the pills swiftly and anonymously using a six-digit code. The service was envisaged for those who cannot or do not want to wait days for mail delivery due to a missed miscarriage or health complications, or who worry about receiving the pills at home. “And why not?” said Kinga Jelinska, the director of the Women Help Women foundation and co-founder of the Abortion Dream Team, the two groups behind last week’s launch. “You can order underwear, cosmetics, mascara, whatever and receive it practically the same or next day,” she said. “Why not abortion pills, where in some cases there might be more urgency?” The innovation comes six years after people across Poland took to the streets to protest against the tightening of abortion laws that already ranked among the strictest in Europe, setting off the country’s largest demonstrations since the fall of communism. In 2023, the protests were credited with helping to propel Donald Tusk, and his promises to overhaul the laws within 100 days, into power. Since then, political stagnation has set in, said Jelinska, citing comments made last year by Tusk in which the prime minister said there was “simply no majority” to change the laws to allow abortions until the 12th week of pregnancy. Tusk instead hinted that his government was intent on doing things differently, telling reporters that it would not prosecute those who helped to facilitate abortions. While the possession or ingestion of abortion pills is not outlawed in Poland, provision of the medication or helping someone to obtain it is considered a crime punishable by up to three years in prison. The locker offers a novel way to challenge these restrictions, said Jelinska. “It’s a little bit of a hack on the law,” she said. “The law is about directly giving to someone. So here we have a machine in between, which makes the legality of everything much more vague.” The locker sits inside the abortion centre that was opened in March 2025 by the Abortion Dream Team. Described as the first of its kind in democratic Poland, it offers a safe space for people to consult on abortion options or receive support while they take the pill. Symbolically located across the street from the Polish parliament, the centre has allowed campaigners to shine a spotlight on the continued need for abortion access in Poland while also providing services to a wide array of people, said Jelinska. “It has exceeded our expectations.” But it had also laid bare how few in power were willing to stand up for them, she said. “The one thing that has surprised us, and it speaks to the political situation, is that there are protests in front of the centre; three, sometimes four times a week.” While usually less than a dozen people turn up, the protesters regularly use sirens and vuvuzelas to make their point, leaving campaigners worried that the noise levels would eventually result in neighbours asking the centre to relocate. “Neither the city or the police have reacted. So that has been a big disappointment to us,” said Jelinska. It was a glimpse of how these organisations had increasingly felt abandoned by politicians, even as about 50,000 people in Poland contacted the wider network of pro-choice organisations last year seeking help, said Jelinska. “I think in Poland, abortion access won’t be solved by politics but by women and communities,” she said. “We cannot trust politicians with our own bodies.”

title: Star Wars actor John Boyega on the day his 10-year-old school friend Damilola Taylor was killed: ‘It kept me up at night because I was just with the guy’
summary: The star was just eight when his friend was stabbed. Decades on, he’s ready to talk about that day – how it shaped him, and how, as he becomes a father himself, it will shape him as a dad
text: “I feel a bit nervous,” confesses John Boyega, as he sits down in front of the camera. “Speaking about it could possibly help. I haven’t revisited this in a long time. Yeah, my heart is just beating.” The Attack the Block and Star Wars actor is talking in the opening scene of a new BBC Two documentary about the killing of 10-year-old schoolboy Damilola Taylor. On 27 November 2000, Damilola was stabbed in the leg with a broken bottle and left to die in a concrete stairwell, attacked as he walked home from an after-school club at Peckham library in south London. It took six years and three separate trials at the Old Bailey, costing a total of £16m, to secure a manslaughter conviction. His death shocked the nation not only because he was so young, but because all the suspects were also children. Boyega was one of the last people to see Damilola alive. The pair had enjoyed a close friendship since Damilola’s move to the UK from Nigeria in August of that year. Watching the film at a Bafta screening a few weeks before its premiere, it’s striking how young and vulnerable the 34-year-old actor looks as he talks about the death of his friend. Boyega is more often seen looking assured and confident, be that his impassioned, impromptu address to thousands of people at a Black Lives Matter protest in Hyde Park, posing for the Pirelli calendar, or portraying an African king in a Hollywood movie. Usually he stands tall, with broad shoulders supported by a proud stance. But in revisiting the memories of that day, it feels as if he has almost reverted to the eight-year-old child he was nearly 26 years ago when he found out his friend had died. A couple of hours later I reconvene with him at BBC New Broadcasting House to discuss the show. In person, Boyega is unassuming, with a calm demeanour and a welcoming smile. He has just returned from a trip to New York fashion week and looks surprisingly fresh-faced for somebody who has not long stepped off a transatlantic flight. Boyega is sitting comfortably with his father Samson, his mother Abigail and an older cousin. It’s a lively space – Boyega lives in Los Angeles now and I get the impression that everybody is excited to snatch a bit of time with him while he’s in London. We immediately get into a five-way conversation about the criminal proceedings around Damilola’s death. Everybody is talking at once. The first trial collapsed after the judge ruled that the prosecution’s key witness was unreliable and there was controversy about items of crucial evidence that were excluded from the proceedings. The family closely followed all three trials – in the second, the jury failed to reach a verdict for two of the three defendants on a charge of murder – and there is a sense of frustration at the opportunities missed when it came to bringing the killers to justice. “You would have thought the influence of the Stephen Lawrence case would have been way stronger, if they had actually learned something. It didn’t come across like that,” Boyega sighs. The police investigation was heavily criticised after it was found to have made a number of significant mistakes. The whole Boyega family knew Damilola; but the actor has previously said very little about him in public. Boyega has worked consistently since his 2011 debut in sci-fi cult classic Attack The Block, including a gamechanging role as a lead in Disney’s Star Wars franchise. His most recent projects, The Woman King (2022) and They Cloned Tyrone (2023), were both critically acclaimed. He has said that his professional success is in no small part due to being inspired by the way Damilola lived his short life. He has been deeply involved in the documentary. “The first time I watched a rough cut I was in my living room and it was bright out. Since then, we’ve been watching daily edits, y’know, on a phone, on a laptop, on a little TV. But viewing it in the cinematic setup hits different – it was an emotional hill to get over, seeing the film like that. I feel really impacted by it.” Throughout the 75-minute screening, crying and sniffling could be heard around the room. “It’s one of those films I wouldn’t watch multiple times because of my personal relationship to it, but it’s definitely a film I will refer to – when my child comes of age I will show him this film. You need to know the realities of your lineage.” * * * On Damilola Taylor’s first day at Oliver Goldsmith primary school in Peckham, shortly after his arrival in the UK, a teacher assigned Boyega’s sister Grace to be his chaperone. She says in the documentary: “My teacher was like, ‘Grace, there’s a new guy and he’s from Nigeria and obviously you’re Nigerian so you understand the language – you can show him around.’” They became a trio, because Boyega and his sister were inseparable at the time. “The only reason I was around him a lot was because I was always with my sister – I inherited Damilola,” Boyega tells me, laughing. “I stayed because I found him hilarious.” His father chimes in with a poignant memory: “John don’t have many friends – at least not boys. John had girls surrounding him. And I remember asking, ‘John, why are you hanging around girls?’ and he said, ‘Dad, boys are dangerous – they’ll beat me up.’” At lunchtimes, the three of them would run around the playground together. Boyega describes the day Damilola died as a transformational moment for him. “The psychological impact is something that definitely stayed with me, but now it’s expressed through appreciation. Every time I wake up and I’m here, I appreciate it.” He smiles as he says of talking to his friends: “I’ll tell my boys, ‘Hey, a bullet don’t look at you and be like, “You’ve done movies before,” and swerve you!’” As a child, though, his thoughts were less positive. “When I would hear that anybody had been stabbed or whatever, it just felt like it was getting closer and closer and that awareness became part of day-to-day life. I was very scared of that.” Boyega was eight when Damilola was killed; he had previously thought that death “only happened to old people”. He was bewildered by it – “like when babies fall and everyone goes, ‘Oh my gosh!’ and then the baby [seeing the response] decides to cry? It was like that.” As the news sank in, he found it difficult to comprehend that bad things could happen to good people. “I was trying to compute what that meant. I thought about the practicality of it. The last breath. Does it hurt? I remember with Grace we would have conversations where I’d be like, ‘Do you think death is sleep?’ or, ‘Maybe they go for 20 years and then, they come back?’ It kept me up at night because I was just with the guy, y’know?” In the aftermath of Damilola’s death, Boyega spent a lot of time at home in his bedroom. Sometimes friends would knock for him and he would tell his mother to relay the message that he didn’t want to go out. “The hand of death is influencing kids to kill kids. I’m like, ‘Damn, I’m a kid, let me stay where I feel the most safe.’ I had a home that granted extreme safety and my parents didn’t shy away from showing concern.” This played out in many ways, including their choice for his secondary school. Instead of the options in their home borough, he was sent to Westminster City School – almost an hour away by bus. Was getting out of the area a response to Damilola’s death? Boyega’s father answers: “Before John says anything, I went to his teacher when he was going to secondary school and he said to me, ‘Mr Boyega, why do you have to choose Westminster?’ And I never said to him what I saw: that the environment here will corrupt this guy,” he says, pointing at his son. “I saw what was coming, that in the future this environment is going to be very, very dangerous.” This was in 2003. By the end of the decade, 188 teenagers had been murdered on the streets of London. I direct the conversation back to Boyega. Did he have therapy back then? He lowers his chin and looks at me with a furrowed brow. What he appears to be conveying is there’s no such thing as therapy in an African household – especially not a 1990s African household. We both laugh. At this point I am conscious that my question could easily be construed as a criticism of his parents, who are sitting on the sofa opposite us in the suddenly quite claustrophobic room. We quickly move on. Over the years there have been numerous documentaries focusing on various aspects of Damilola’s killing, from a 2002 BBC Panorama special to most recently one fronted by broadcaster Yinka Bokinni to mark the 20th anniversary of Damilola’s death. This latest project focuses much of the narrative on the 24 hours leading up to his killing. We hear from a number of people who were critical to the investigation in its early stages, including the estate maintenance worker who first found Damilola as he lay bleeding in the stairwell. There were several months of discussions between Boyega and the director, Alex Thomas – who also directed the award-winning Sky Original documentary Bibaa and Nicole: Murder in the Park, about the 2020 killings of Bibaa Henry and Nicole Smallman. “It fell to me to decide who was coming from my world to sit down and talk,” says Boyega. “That’s when I decided that Grace would be more appropriate to discuss Damilola than me because that was her direct friend – they were around the same age. And I think her perspective on it was quite important.” That was the easy part. More difficult was deciding how to address the ecosystem of bullying and fear on the streets of Peckham that led up to and ultimately underpinned Damilola’s killing. In the final edit, much of this element of the storytelling is omitted. It doesn’t go unnoticed. During a Q&A after the screening, a Bafta member in the audience queries the lack of backstory included about the lives of the two boys convicted of Damilola’s manslaughter. In August 2006, brothers Danny and Ricky Preddie were each sentenced to eight years in youth custody after the third trial. The questioner pointed out that the brothers appeared at the Old Bailey unattended by any family. “I’d love to know why you left that out,” they said, referring to the brothers’ troubled childhoods. It was well known that their single mother struggled immensely while raising them. The pair were eventually placed in a local authority children’s care home. “We did look at the option of interviewing the two brothers,” said Boyega, who explained a general concern within the team that it might be viewed as being too empathetic to the perpetrators. In the end, the decision was made not to approach them. But Boyega agrees that some elements of their backstory do have a place in the narrative, in particular when it comes to the debate about how to end youth violence. “Family. Discipline,” he says decisively. “The fact that you don’t have an adult at home that holds you accountable is a very important thing, especially for boys. Especially for boys.” He repeats the last sentence a little slower to emphasise its importance. “But y’know, you could have two parents at home and the child still goes out and does what they need to do, so there’s obviously a more nuanced conversation. Even in the sense that someone showed you that they loved you, that they cared about what you did or whether or not you made a mistake. What that person [in the screening Q&A] said made me think about what it meant – that they didn’t have that. Not even a social worker.” There’s an extended silence when I ask Boyega what was difficult about making the documentary. “Poverty,” he replies, eventually. He means it brought back memories of the poverty he experienced as a child. Growing up, he lived in a small flat on Sceaux Gardens estate just off Peckham Road, with both his parents and his elder sisters – Grace, who appears in the documentary, and Blessing, who generally keeps a much lower profile. His mother was a care worker and his father a Pentecostal minister. “I didn’t know I was poor until I was in year 7. When you’re super-young, you’re not really thinking about that. And then when you get to school, you start to see where you are in the food chain of life, and that’s when you start to compare yourself with other children and other kids.” The process of filming the documentary brought that world back into focus. Boyega recalls being keen not to stand out for the wrong reasons in his first year at Westminster City School, and begging his mother to buy him a pair of Kickers. She took him to Barrie Howard, a shoe shop on East Street in Walworth – a strategic rite of passage for any south Londoner who hoped to survive the brutal transition from primary to secondary. But once he had the shoes he felt bad, because he could tell how much it cost her. “I never asked for Kickers from my mum again – I wore Clarks for the rest of school.” Recounting these memories, plus seeing the archive footage of Peckham and the burgundy Oliver Goldsmith school sweater, brought back the distinct feeling that he had so much less than many of his peers. “I did work hard to get out of that. In making this film I had to revisit who I used to be, and that bothered me.” The interviews took place while he was on location in the Isle of Skye making a supernatural horror movie, The Punishing, in which he stars alongside Cara Delevingne (it is currently in post-production). The surroundings served as a physical reminder of how far he’s come in life. Boyega had some reservations about being involved in the project. His main concern was that he wanted to make sure that Damilola’s brother – Tunde Taylor, chair of the Damilola Taylor Trust – was happy with the way Damilola’s life is portrayed. “I’ve been in the public eye for a minute now and from my experience, you have to be very careful, because you don’t know which journalist is being stressed by an editor. You don’t know which person wants to grab a story and not use it with the right intentions. You don’t know if they’re gonna be respectful to the people who are really involved.” But he was reassured by meeting producer Nelson Adeosun, a childhood family friend, and fellow contributor Leroy Logan. Logan is a founder and former chairman of the Black Police Association, whom Boyega portrayed in the film Red, White and Blue, from Steve McQueen’s 2020 anthology series, Small Axe. The performance won him a Golden Globe award. Settling down thousands of miles away from Peckham has inevitably changed Boyega’s relationship with the place that made him who he is. “South is still familiar, but if I go now, people have to guide me … it’s so, so different,” he says, referring to the gentrification of the area. For him, though, the heart of the place is in the people who remember what it was like when he was growing up. We do a little reminiscing about which legendary hangouts have survived. He is pleased to note that Bagel King is on the list. Somebody pokes their head round the door to tell us we need to wrap up. Boyega’s on a tight schedule. I ask a final question. Tell me about your jewellery, I say, indicating towards his left hand. “Oh yeah, this is my wedding ring,” he says casually. “I’ve been married for coming up to two years now.” He doesn’t give any detail about his wife, but does say they had a small ceremony, joking that he got married the way Braveheart did, while miming the action of planting a sword in the ground. He continues by reaching to the deepest depth of his vocal range and bellowing, “Will you come with me?” His eldest sister has now joined us and the room has erupted into a chorus of unrestrained laughter. I note that the ring he is wearing is different from the one he wears in the documentary. “Yeah, this is our very sentimental ring,” he says of the two-toned band. “This is the one we decided to pick up spontaneously because I just wanted the ring on my finger, so we went to Walmart to get this. It was a lovely trip to Walmart. Shout out, Walmart Canoga Park!” he laughs. I am surprised to learn that he didn’t have a traditional Nigerian ceremony. “I would love to have a wedding celebration. We both like the idea of celebrating something established, rather than celebrating the entry. And by then, we’ll have to shut Nigeria down!” It occurs to me that the child he mentioned earlier in the conversation may not be hypothetical. Are you about to hard launch a baby, I inquire tentatively. “My baby’s on the way. We got a baby cooking.” And you said my son earlier – is that because you’re having a boy? He confirms this and that he also has a young stepson. “So, you know, my life is completely, completely fulfilled in terms of family. It’s been so nice with the timing.” Getting used to the new dynamic away from the public eye has obviously served him well – and perhaps this is why he is now ready to speak publicly about his friendship with Damilola. “I do think it’s important to reach back and tell people the grounded realities of your origins, because it wasn’t until I knew the grounded realities of other people’s origins that I decided to pursue something more.” When thinking about the kind of father he wants to be, it’s all still sinking in. “Us being parents is funny! I just want to make sure I’m present, I’m consistent and full of love.” These personal milestones explain why he’s been less visible in recent years. “I’ve tried to as much as possible – especially following periods when I’ve worked a lot – to de-centre my career. There have been certain moments when I’ve known that this is a time for family. Y’know, there’s stuff to do.” In this moment he’s clear that his purpose is to love his wife and sons and invest in the support system that he knows he is lucky to have had. • Damilola: The Untold Story is on BBC Two and iPlayer from 5 October

title: UK car industry faces ‘difficult trade-off’ between Chinese and EU markets
summary: Britain under pressure to put tariffs on cheap Chinese vehicle imports ahead of protectionist trade measures
text: Britain’s car industry is grappling with a “difficult trade-off” between China and Europe, as manufacturers struggle to balance the benefits of both markets ahead of looming trade measures that could restrict UK exports to the EU. The UK is an outlier in choosing not to put import taxes on Chinese vehicles, even as the US has shut them out almost entirely, and the EU imposes duties of up to 45%. EU officials reportedly warned Andy Burnham last month that the UK must put tariffs on cheap Chinese vehicles otherwise Brussels would impose protectionist “made in Europe” barriers on British exports to the bloc, hitting British carmakers in their largest market. Ministers have so far resisted such calls, with Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, arguing any levies would “probably be reciprocated” – costing UK manufacturers sales in China. Tariffs would also raise prices for British drivers, who have flocked to cheaper Chinese models, and could deter brands such as Chery, which is in talks to build cars at Nissan’s Sunderland plant, from investing further in the UK. “There is a difficult trade-off,” said Emily Sawicz, of the consultancy RSM UK, adding that the UK “cannot afford to drift between the two indefinitely”. Chinese investment could be a “lifeline” for carmakers, while access to Europe would also be “crucial” for smaller manufacturers. “Being excluded risks UK suppliers becoming increasingly shut out of those European opportunities,” she added. “Manufacturers need clarity on which direction the government intends to take so they can make long-term investment decisions.” Ian Plummer, commercial director at Autotrader, said competition from Chinese brands had made cars more affordable and “is encouraging more people to go and buy a new car”. Brands such as BYD, Omoda and Jaecoo more than tripled their share of the UK new car market in the first eight months of 2026, reaching 12% of sales, according to industry figures. Figures released on Friday showed that British new car ⁠registrations rose 12% in the year to September, the best month for annual growth since 2017. The preliminary data from the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders (SMMT) showed the boom was powered by a demand for electric vehicles and Chinese brands, with the Jaecoo 7 and BYD’s Sealion ‌7 among the top sellers. The trade body said on Wednesday that the European Commission’s made in Europe rules, which restrict subsidies, tax breaks and public procurement contracts to vehicles built within the EU, pose an existential threat to British car production. The EU accounted for 58% of UK car exports in the first half of the year, compared with about 4% for China. Mike Hawes, the SMMT’s chief executive, said: “The UK and EU automotive industries are deeply integrated, so effectively excluding British-produced vehicles from their largest market would assure mutual damage.” . Massimiliano Messina, Nissan’s chair in Europe, said last month: “Europe cannot have a Trojan horse where the Chinese are going to flood the market through the UK.” Victor Zhang, the deputy UK chief of Chery, which owns the Jaecoo and Omoda brands, rejected that claim, saying: “Most of what we sell are super-hybrids, not the cars that those tariffs are about, and the cars we sell here stay here.” He added: “Tariffs can come and go, but we won’t change our ongoing investment in the UK.” Brussels raised its own tariffs on Chinese EVs in 2024, triggering a decline in what was then an accelerating sales trajectory. It is now facing calls for fresh barriers to be imposed on importing hybrid electric vehicles, potentially quotas or price floors. Imports of plug-in and battery hybrid cars rocketed after the EU tariffs were imposed on EVs, underlining China’s ability to pivot its export efforts when hit by trade barriers. Others in the industry believe tariffs could help protect the UK’s manufacturers, whose market share in Britain continues to be eroded Chinese firms. Tim Tozer, a former chair of Vauxhall, said that tariffs were “vital” to stop Britain’s car sector “atrophying”. He said: “We are at last knockings now, trying to save the industry.” He added that Reynolds was “whistling in the wind” with hopes of continuing to export to China en masse, arguing the market had become “fiercely nationalistic,” with buyers increasingly loyal to domestic brands “because they’re bloody good”.

title: Ukraine war briefing: Kyiv to increase oil refinery attacks because of Moscow’s winter strategy, Zelenskyy says
summary: Kyiv working on better jamming capabilities, interceptors for Shahed drones and ballistic missiles that can reach Moscow. What we know on day 1,684
text: Ukraine will increase its attacks on Russian oil refineries, but won’t target civilians, because of a new policy of airstrikes by Moscow designed to force people to abandon Kyiv and other cities, Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said. Ukraine’s intelligence service has obtained documents showing the Russian ruler, Vladimir Putin, has issued a new doctrine of military attacks on a much broader range of civilian targets ahead of winter, ⁠Ukraine’s president told Reuters. “We saw documents and we know that they ⁠allow them to attack infrastructure, logistics, and especially to attack in the cities, in the villages, everywhere, roads, schools, hospitals,” he said. “To pressure people to leave the capital, leave different cities: this is the goal of the operation.” “We have to respond in any way [we can]. With their attacks on our energy, we have to respond on their energy. First of all, oil refiners: what gives money to them for this war,” Zelenskyy said. “But we will not respond, of course … on any civilian objects.” Russian attacks on Saturday in Ukraine killed at least six people and damaged Kyiv’s Northern Bridge, disrupting traffic for a third day in Moscow’s latest effort to complicate life in the Ukrainian capital. Previously, it has hit apartment blocks, supermarket warehouses, gas stations, datacentres and other civilian targets. A continuing Ukrainian counteroffensive dubbed Vivaldi had recaptured about 140 sq km (54 sq miles) of Ukraine’s eastern Donbas region, Zelenskyy told Reuters. It is a setback for Putin who wants Russia to completely control the Donbas before agreeing to any peace deal. Zelenskyy said Ukraine was working to offset low supplies of ammunition for its fighter aircraft – F-16s and MiGs – that bring down about 60% of the Russian jet-powered drones. He said Ukraine was working to boost its jamming capabilities; and in the second half of October it would receive a first shipment of small, cheap air defence missiles capable of hitting new jet-powered Shahed drones. Ukraine had begun to deploy its own domestically made ballistic missile – the FP-7, which has a range of about 250km (155 miles), said Zelenskyy. It hoped to have a longer-range model, the FP-9, ready by autumn. Germany’s chancellor, ⁠Friedrich Merz, arrived in Kyiv on Sunday ⁠accompanied ⁠by CEOs from German defence companies in a ⁠show of support for Volodymyr Zelenskyy ⁠amid increased Russian attacks on ‌Ukrainian ‌cities. “I travelled to Kyiv ‌today because Ukraine needs all our support in the coming weeks,” Merz said, saying ‌that Russian forces were bombings towns, residential buildings and heating plants. “If Russia is not stopped, sooner or later ⁠its war machine will turn against us … I will tell President Zelenskyy today: you ‌can continue to count on our help.” Exit polls from Latvia’s parliamentary election published on Saturday night favoured prime minister Andris Kulbergs’s centrist, pro-Ukraine United List party, suggesting the country will maintain its pro-European and pro-Ukrainian course. But populist parties also had a good night after an election campaign dominated by fears about neighbouring Russia and the cost of living at home. With 72% of ballots counted, United List was on 36.5%, followed by the populist, Maga-style Latvia First on 13.0%. Kulbergs told journalists his party would not cooperate with any parties that were pro-Russian: “Our strong position is that any economic ties with Russia makes us weak; Russia would exploit this.” Baltic countries have warned for months that Russia is mounting sabotage, cyber and other hybrid ⁠attacks across Europe to erode support for Ukraine and sow fear, although some western officials doubt it is capable of launching a direct assault on Nato, of which Latvia is ‌a member. Throughout his campaign, Kulbergs promised more anti-drone capabilities for Latvia and to maintain defence spending at 5% of gross domestic product, one of the highest levels in Nato. His pro-Kremlin rivals said Latvia should stop any aid to Ukraine and instead focus more on cost-of-living issues, particularly among the country’s Russian-speaking minority.

title: ‘We are in a kind of war’: row over viral Amsterdam chip shop lands in court
summary: Neighbours say crowds drawn to Fabel Friet are clogging the picturesque canal street and attracting litter, gulls and rats
text: People living in one of Amsterdam’s most exclusive neighbourhoods have taken the city to court for licensing a chip shop that has gone viral on TikTok. On busy days, the queue for Fabel Friet on Runstraat stretches across a bridge on the Keizersgracht – one of Amsterdam’s most famous canals – a court was told last week. The narrow street itself is crowded by tourists waiting for their orders seven days a week. And loitering with intent – on parked cars, on the street itself, and on steps and porches – gulls wait to swoop. “We are in a kind of war where a very unwelcome chip shop has polluted the whole area,” said Thomas van Leeuwen, who lives nearby. “Eating in the street is a shameful behaviour. It gets filthy food on our doorsteps and mayonnaise in the beautiful stone. The herring gulls have moved in as residents, and the worst thing is the rat infestation.” Nineteen neighbours have formally protested against the business licence for Fabel Friet, whose signature product is fries topped with parmesan cheese and truffle mayonnaise. Niek van der Heijden, the lead plaintiff, said the problem was the takeaway’s small size. “What we call the ‘TikTok queue’ for Fabel Friet causes the most nuisance,” he said. “The business takes place on the street: waiting to order, waiting to be served, eating. We want Fabel to go to a place where there is enough room to have clients inside.” In a packed courtroom on Tuesday morning, a lawyer for Amsterdam city council acknowledged that the city’s mayor, Femke Halsema, can refuse a licence to operate if the “residential and living environment” is negatively affected by a business. While the chip shop, she said, sticks to its licence obligations to manage the queue and clear litter “it has been going on for a long time, the impact remains severe, and you have to ask: how long can we tolerate this?” For the current licence, she said, the city would be guided by the court’s ruling. The shop’s owners, Abel Klatser and Floris Feilzer, said they employed a cleaning service seven days a week, four times a day, and that year-on-year visitor numbers had dropped by 23% this August after they opened four new locations. “A few neighbours have experienced nuisance, but other people enjoy eating chips,” said Gertjan Teeuwen, their lawyer. “It can be busy, but there are peaks and troughs.” Klatser and Feilzer said in a public statement that they felt unfairly attacked while doing their best to be good neighbours. “Fabel Friet is our child, and we have put our heart and soul into it,” they said. “It is painful if people talk about our business negatively.” The case goes beyond irritations about so-called performative tourism, where tourists flock to a place to post images on social media. “The tiny streets might be charming, but actually the space is not designed for so many people,” said Lisa-Bobbie Kamp, a lawyer for the neighbours. “This is a question of taking space, who owns the place and whether you can just use public space.” Marije Peute, a PhD student at the University of Amsterdam, has studied the effects of “viral urbanism” in the neighbourhood. “The municipality should really think about how they want to act, because this is about the public space. A lot of much older retail spaces have lost their local clients because they don’t want to go there any more,” she said. Rogier Havelaar, a councillor from the Christian Democratic Appeal party, said that, while Fabel Friet should probably be offered a “flagship store” licence in a more suitable location, the benefits of tourism to the city should not be overlooked. “Amsterdam would never have as many museums, restaurants, going-out spots and theatres if they were only for the residents,” he said. “And tourism provides 70,000 jobs. Amsterdam would have a gigantic financial problem if tourism went away.” Standing on the bridge over the Keizersgracht, some German laboratory apprentices drawn by TikTok were enjoying their chips. Natalie Stübben said crowd managers had just asked them to move away from people’s houses. “It’s pretty hard to get through here with a car or just by walking,” she said. “I don’t think we were thinking about annoying the neighbours, but it makes sense.” Some of those neighbours will be pleased if the business location has had its chips after the court verdict on 12 November. “There’s something very alarming about the fact that these people are all led by their higher power – influencers – and call themselves followers,” said van Leeuwen. “It’s Orwellian. This court case is part of the parasitic industry that lives on tourists.”

title: Chalmers says global economic turmoil will drive budget cuts, but Australia should avoid recession
summary: Treasurer says ‘very substantial and intensifying pressure’ on federal budget as he points finger at private sector for driving up inflation amid Middle East conflict
text: Jim Chalmers has warned of “very substantial and intensifying” economic pressures on the horizon but insists he’s not planning for a recession, as he prepares to find new ways to cut the budget ahead of its mid-year update. The treasurer on Sunday called on critics of government spending to name the services that should be cut, as he points the finger at the private sector for driving up inflation in Australia amid the protracted conflict in the Middle East. Chalmers said the US-led eight-month war against Iran, which has severely curtailed global oil supplies from the region, has been “disastrous” for cost-of-living pressures. He also said there was “very substantial and intensifying pressure” on the federal budget. “No serious observer of what’s going on right now would conclude anything other than [that],” he told ABC’s Insiders. “The longer this thing drags out, the bigger the impact on the global economy and on the Australian economy, whether it’s … on inflation or downward pressure on growth. “We’re not anticipating [a recession] here in Australia, but certainly it is weighing on global growth, and we’re not immune from that.” Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Inflation has jumped to 4% in the year to August, from 3.5%, while the Reserve Bank lifted its key interest rate to 4.6%, the highest figure since 2011. Chalmers said the government was working on finding further savings to the budget in the mid-year economic and fiscal outlook, due in December, after cuts of $44.9bn over four years were identified in the May budget. The treasurer said cuts to government spending weren’t the only factor driving up inflation in the economy, and cutting larger sums would impact essential services. “If people don’t want us to strengthen Medicare, for example, or cut income taxes, or provide cost-of-living relief in other ways, then they should nominate where that should be cut,” he said on Sunday. Beyond the war’s impact on driving up prices in Australia, Chalmers said the private sector was partly to blame. “For every $5 of demand in our economy, $1 is public, $4 is private,” he said. “Budget settings are not the primary driver of prices in our economy. There’s a whole bunch of other things going on.” But the shadow treasurer, Tim Wilson, said Chalmers should be sacked, claiming his decisions have increased inflation to generate tax windfalls. “He’s actively stoked inflation, and he’s fundamentally undermined the success of this country, and now he’s announced today he’s on a sort of Argo-style salvation trip for investment, because he’s created a problem of sovereign risk,” he told News24. The assistant science and digital technology minister, Andrew Charlton, said the consequences of having a recession, which would ease inflation, would be devastating. “If you have a recession, you throw hundreds of thousands of people on to the unemployment queues, and that pulls a huge amount of demand out of the economy,” he told News24. “It’s pretty easy to have low interest rates and low inflation if your economy goes through a recession. “As a Labor government, that is a big priority for us to make sure that we don’t go into a recession that drives a lot of people into unemployment.” Chalmers will travel to Japan for meetings with business leaders and the country’s finance minister, in an effort to boost investment and improve fuel security.

title: Flydubai co-pilot’s time in Australia being investigated by security agencies after alleged cockpit attack
summary: Police confirm investigation into period the man reportedly spent in Australia before alleged attempted terrorist attack
text: Australian security agencies have launched an investigation after it emerged that the flydubai co-pilot who allegedly tried to hijack an Israel-bound flight spent about two years in the country as a student. Disaster was narrowly averted on Wednesday when passengers and crew intervened to stop the co-pilot’s attempt to take control of the flydubai flight to Tel Aviv, which had 182 people onboard and plunged 16,625 feet (5,067 metres) in just over 30 seconds. The United ⁠Arab Emirates’ prosecutor general has said the co-pilot had used a crash axe in the attempted “terrorist attack”, in which the pilot was stabbed mid-air. Numerous media outlets have named the co-pilot as Hammam al-Hammami, an Omani national. A source familiar with the case, but not authorised to speak publicly, said the man was granted an Australian student visa in 2014, before arriving in the country to commence a university course the following year. He left Australia in 2017, and his visa was cancelled in 2019 after authorities confirmed he was no longer enrolled in the course, the source said. The Australian federal police (AFP) on Sunday said multiple agencies – including the Australian Security Intelligence Organisation (Asio) – were probing the man’s connections to the country. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email “The Victorian Joint Counter Terrorism Team (VIC JCTT), comprising the AFP, Victoria Police and ASIO, can confirm it is investigating the man’s links to Australia,” an AFP spokesperson said. “An update will be provided at an appropriate time.” US media outlets, including CNN, reported that a now-deleted LinkedIn profile said al-Hammami had studied engineering at an Australian university. Guardian Australia has not verified which university the co-pilot attended. It came after a British university, Buckinghamshire New University, said a student named Hamam al-Hammami had “previously completed a distance-learning course in aviation management” at the institution. It added: “He did not undertake any pilot training at the university.” A flydubai spokesperson on Saturday said the circumstances surrounding the incident were still ‌under investigation and the airline was not in a position to comment further. The airline’s flights between Dubai and Tel Aviv have been suspended until further notice after the attack. The Omani co-pilot and the flight’s Indian captain, Smit Machchhar, were taken to the UAE, as it leads the investigation. Officials have said a number of countries including Israel are participating. The Wall Street Journal has reported that the co-pilot had been barred from flying by Oman over concerns he had adopted extremist views. He was then moved to an administrative job at Oman Air, according to the official, before being hired by the UAE-based budget airline flydubai.

text: A murder investigation has been launched after a 40-year-old man was shot dead in a “senseless act of violence” during a memorial service in west London, police have said. Police were called on Friday at 7.47pm after multiple shots were heard in East Acton. Officers attended alongside the London ambulance service. The victim was treated at the scene on the junction of Braybrook Street and Erconwald Street, however, he was pronounced dead. The Metropolitan police said about 40 to 50 people were at the scene, including children. The man’s family have been informed and are being supported by specialist officers. A postmortem examination is scheduled to establish the cause of death, but the victim is believed to have sustained a gunshot wound, the force added. No arrests have been made. DCI Brian Howie, who is leading the investigation, said: “Our thoughts are with the family and friends of a man whose life was taken in a senseless act of violence. “We understand a large number of people had gathered for a memorial service and what should have been a time to come together in remembrance has instead left a family devastated. “We believe between 40 and 50 people, including children, were present when this incident occurred. Someone knows what happened and we need them to come forward. “If you were around Erconwald Street, Braybrook Street, the surrounding roads or Wormwood Scrubs playground between 6pm and 8pm, please think carefully about what you saw. Did you see anyone carrying or concealing weapons, people on bicycles acting suspiciously or vehicles being driven at speed? “We also want to hear from anyone with photographs, video, dashcam, doorbell or mobile phone footage or who has seen anything relevant on social media.”

title: Tories would expand free childcare to high earners, Badenoch says
summary: Kemi Badenoch says those earning more than £100,000 should not be discouraged from working more
text: The Conservatives have unveiled a proposed £700m childcare giveaway for high earners ahead of their annual conference, saying they would end the “cliff edge” where free entitlement ends at salaries above £100,000. The plan, set out the day before the event begins in Birmingham, follows the earlier proposal by Kemi Badenoch’s party to abolish most stamp duty, another change to taxation that would disproportionately benefit wealthier people. Under the current system, put in place under Rishi Sunak’s government, families with young children in England are eligible for 30 hours a week of free childcare, but this cuts off if one parent earns more than £100,000, irrespective of another parent’s salary. Under the Conservative plans, this limit would be abolished, with all parents working 16 or more hours a week able to claim the childcare. The party says it would cost aabout £700m a year, which it says would be paid for by cutting jobs at organisations such as Arts Council England and the Environment Agency. In comments released to promote the idea, Badenoch said the current system was “absurd” and a disincentive to work more. She said: “Conservatives believe that you shouldn’t be punished for working more, but this childcare cliff edge does exactly that. “I’m a mum-of-three and I’ve had to make the same choices many families have had to make on work and childcare. Those choices are difficult already, government should not be making them harder. “No one should be turning down a promotion or a pay rise because they literally cannot afford to earn more. “It is often women who end up carrying more of the childcare responsibility so a system that makes it harder for them to progress in their careers is not helping families, it is not helping women and it is definitely not helping the economy.” A Labour spokesperson said: “It tells you everything you need to know about the Tories that the first of their own tax policies they want to unpick is one helping higher earners. They clearly don’t want to admit that they set the thresholds in the first place.” The idea of abolishing stamp duty on people’s primary residences in England and Northern Ireland was unveiled by Badenoch at last year’s conference, costing an estimated £9bn a year. While some economists have argued that stamp duty can have a drag on the housing market and even the economy, as it disincentivises moving, scrapping it rather than reforming the tax would disproportionately benefit better-off people and those in London and south-east England. The other main policy set out ahead of the conference was a plan to build 50,000 new prison spaces in England and Wales, a 50% expansion in capacity. This would be paid for in part by slashing overseas aid to £1bn a year, a 90% cut on current plans. Under Keir Starmer, Labour said they would reduce aid from 0.5% of GDP to 0.3% by 2027, but even that lower proportion would still amount to £9bn a year. When Reform UK announced plans to cut aid to £1bn a year, aid groups warned that this would not cover existing contributions to global bodies such as the UN and World Bank, shredding Britain’s international influence.

title: Whales on Australia’s ‘humpback highway’ are at growing risk of injury from boat and propeller strikes
summary: Exclusive: Images show deep cuts and damage to tails and fins, as experts warn the migrating species often aren’t able to avoid a collision
text: Gruesome images of adult and juvenile humpback whales along Australia’s east coast with slash and gouge injuries from boat and propeller strikes highlight what experts say is a growing problem, as the population booms 60 years after the ban on whaling. Missing tail parts, deep red lacerations and shocking injuries to the spine of a whale calf can be clearly seen on the images, gathered by WWF Australia and shared with the Guardian. One image of fresh and broad cuts on the back of a calf was taken last month in Hervey Bay in Queensland, where many mothers choose to bring their calves for rest and shelter on the long migration down to Antarctica. The atmosphere on the town’s whale-watching boats is often one of heightened excitement and elation, as the majestic mammals come to the surface, says Isabel Taylor, a senior naturalist with the Pacific Whale Foundation’s whale-watching tours. Last month, Taylor saw two mothers with calves come to the surface, but all was not well with one pair. “The others were very surface active and putting on a show, but this other mum and calf were more reserved,” she says. Clearly visible on the calf’s back were slash marks from a boat propeller. “The mood on the boat changed a bit,” says Taylor. “We get people from all over the world and some say it’s the best day of their lives. So to have this on the other end of the spectrum was quite profound.” Another image taken in June by drone off Sydney’s Bondi beach shows a humpback with lacerations and exposed red flesh that appear to have been caused by repeated sweeps of a propeller blade. An image from 2024 shows a female humpback off the coast of southern New South Wales that has become known as “bladerunner” because of a highly distinctive sequence of deep slashes from a propeller blade on her back and tail thought to have been sustained more than 20 years ago. “These images really bring home the physical and direct impact we’re having on these animals, especially on animals that size,” says Dr Raphael Mayaud, a marine ecologist at Griffith University and a member of an expert group advising the International Whaling Commission (IWC) on vessel strikes. Rebecca Dunlop, an associate professor and humpback expert at the University of Queensland, says most of the images showed injuries to the back and rear of the whales, “suggesting they are surfacing as the boat propeller goes past and over their back”. “When migrating humpbacks travel and surface like clockwork they don’t seem to be able to change their dive and travel behaviour to avoid an intercept pathway – this could be due to a boat approaching the intercept point at speed where they just don’t have the time to make an avoidance decision,” Dunlop says Conservation success story The IWC banned humpback whaling in the southern hemisphere in 1963 – after numbers had already crashed. Soviet whalers continued to hunt them in the Southern Ocean until the early 1970s. Estimates from the 1960s put their numbers off the east coast of Australia at less than 300. But as the threat of the harpoon was progressively removed, the population rebounded. One study based on observations of whales suggested that by 2004 the east coast humpbacks numbered 7,800. It is seen by many conservationists as one of the planet’s great wildlife recovery stories. By 2015, their numbers had more than trebled to 25,500. Estimates now suggest between 40,000 and 50,000 whales are migrating up and down the coast each year. Some modelling has suggested numbers will peak and plateau this year. Dunlop and Mayaud both observe that, as populations have increased alongside the rise in popularity of boating and water recreation, the numbers of vessel strikes have also likely increased. One in 10 Australians have a boat licence and of the more than 970,000 registered boats, more than half a million are in Queensland and New South Wales. But it is difficult to know how many collisions there are with both large and smaller boats, experts say. The IWC says that globally, “most collisions go unseen and unreported”. On Friday, it passed a resolution to work with all parties around the world to reduce “vessel strikes” which, the meeting agreed, was a “priority concern” for the commission. Chris Johnson, the WWF’s global lead on initiatives to protect whales, who was at the meeting, says it is an important step for the IWC. “Humpbacks have been one of the great conservation success stories. But along Australia’s humpback highway, there’s growing risk for them to be hit by vessels,” he says. “Those strikes [in the images] would have been incredibly painful. We can see the evidence, but we have a black hole of information.” Experts say cutting speed limits for all vessels moving along migration routes, and making boats and ships more aware of the riskiest places and times of the year, would help. In California, for example, Johnson says shipping companies compete with each other to win high grades on public scorecards that assess how well they stick to speed limits during high-risk periods for whale strikes. In San Francisco Bay, AI-assisted whale-spotting cameras are being trialled to give captains more notice about whales in their path. While Australian law in theory requires that collisions with protected species like humpbacks be reported, Mayaud says most are either undetected or are never documented. “The big thing is that a strike doesn’t have to kill a whale to have a serious impact,” he says. “If a whale loses part of its fluke [tail] it may still survive, but swimming is likely to become less efficient and more energetically costly. That can then have knock-on effects on things like migration, feeding, body condition and potentially reproduction. “There’s also the immediate trauma – the pain, blood loss, infection – and then the possibility the animal is carrying the effects of that injury for years afterwards. “So I think the welfare issue is really about both the initial injury and the longer-term energetic and physical consequences for animals that survive.”
