title: Tennessee’s top prison official resigning after botched execution of Christa Pike
summary: Frank Strada leaving position as state launches independent investigation into what went wrong
text: Tennessee’s top prison official is stepping down in the aftermath of the failed execution of death row prisoner Christa Pike, the state’s governor Bill Lee announced Saturday. Frank Strada, the department of correction commissioner, will leave his position later in October as the state launches an independent investigation into what went wrong during Wednesday’s botched execution of Pike, according to Lee. Strada for his part said his resignation would allow that review to move forward in the best interests of Tennessee. “Serving as commissioner of the Tennessee department of correction has been a great honor, and I continue to believe the department carried out its responsibilities in accordance with the established protocol,” Strada said in his resignation statement. “Even so, stepping aside is in the best interest of Tennesseans as the independent review moves forward,” he said. “I believe this review is entirely appropriate and necessary, and I look forward to doing everything I can to help determine exactly what occurred.” Strada handed in his resignation amid intensifying scrutiny of Tennessee’s closely guarded execution procedures after Pike was injected with lethal drugs on Wednesday but survived. She became the first death row prisoner in the US to undergo such an execution attempt and live. Pike’s attorney Randy Spivey, who witnessed the procedure from inside the death chamber, described what happened as “cruel and torturous”. He said he personally counted seven needles inserted into Pike’s left arm, “one of which appeared to be bent when it was pulled from her”. Attorneys have alleged that Pike’s failed lethal injection was the fifth “botched” execution carried out under Strada’s leadership in two states since 2022, as the Guardian reported on Saturday, hours before his resignation was announced. Pike remained unconscious and on a ventilator at a hospital as of Friday, according to a court filing submitted by her attorneys. Her lawyers said hospital personnel were trying to save her life and, as of late Thursday, were working to clear the two doses of the execution drug from her system. Wednesday’s extraordinary breakdown inside Tennessee’s execution chamber has triggered demands for an explanation from people on both sides of the death penalty debate. Besides ordering the independent review into case, Lee has paused the scheduling of executions in Tennessee. Pike’s attorneys said they believe complications involving intravenous lines caused pentobarbital to enter her body rather than her bloodstream. “Frank Strada’s resignation does not change the fact that Tennessee is shrouding its executions in secrecy,” Kit Thomas, a death row attorney in the federal public defender’s office in Nashville, said in a statement. “When Governor Lee hired Strada to fix execution problems in Tennessee his problematic history of executions in Arizona was well known. Strada then oversaw the implementation of a new protocol that ignored the recommendations of the independent investigation and weakened protections leading to a string of problems in Tennessee, including this week’s horrific botched execution attempt and another one in May. Until there is transparency and accountability, botched executions will keep happening.” Laura Porter, the executive director of the US Campaign to End the Death Penalty, said in a statement: “Hopefully this is the beginning of accountability and an end to secrecy that enables these debacles.” “Attorneys and community leaders across Tennessee have been trying for some time to get the Governor and the administration to take seriously the huge problems with the competency of the state’s execution process,” Porter’s statement continued. “They were ignored.” Pike, 50, was sentenced to death for the 1995 killing of teenage classmate Colleen Slemmer. Pike and her then boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, killed Slemmer at a job training camp in Knoxville. A pentagram had been carved into Slemmer’s chest. After the murder, Pike was diagnosed with bipolar and post-traumatic stress disorders, her attorneys said. “It took me numerous years to even realize the gravity of what I’d done,” Pike had said in an earlier petition for clemency. “Even more to accept how many lives I affected. I took the life of someone’s child, sister, friend. It sickens me now to think I had the ability to commit such a crime.” Had her execution that day succeeded, Pike on Wednesday would have been the first woman put to death in Tennessee in more than 200 years. The Associated Press contributed reporting

title: Florida jury finds ex-sheriff’s deputy not guilty in shooting death of Black air force airman
summary: Roger Fortson was shot by deputy when he opened door with gun in hand after a false domestic disturbance call
text: A Florida jury recently found former sheriff’s deputy Eddie Duran not guilty of manslaughter with a firearm in the fatal shooting of Roger Fortson, a Black US air force airman who was killed inside his apartment after authorities responded to an unfounded report of a domestic disturbance. An Okaloosa county jury acquitted Duran, 38, on Thursday after about two hours of deliberations. He had faced up to 30 years in prison if convicted. Duran, who is Hispanic, was an Okaloosa county sheriff’s deputy in May 2024 when he was sent to Fortson’s apartment in Fort Walton Beach where Fortson – originally from Atlanta – was stationed. Authorities have said Duran was directed to the apartment after a report of a domestic disturbance that turned out to be false. After Duran repeatedly knocked on the door, Fortson answered while holding a handgun at his side with the weapon pointed toward the ground. Authorities say Duran fired multiple times before telling Fortson to drop the gun. The encounter was captured on the deputy’s body camera. Thursday’s verdict came after a four-day trial. One day after Duran was acquitted, civil rights attorney Ben Crump said that Fortson’s family would continue its legal fight and vowed to “seek accountability” through the civil court system for the 2024 shooting. While the criminal prosecution has ended with Duran’s acquittal, a federal civil rights lawsuit filed by Fortson’s family remains pending. “Roger’s life and his service will always matter,” Crump said in a statement on Friday. “His family will keep fighting for him, and we will stand with them as they pursue their civil rights case in federal court and seek accountability for the tragic loss of his life.” Duran was fired from the Okaloosa sheriff’s office after killing Fortson. His defense attorney argued that the former deputy was “doing his job” and said Fortson would still be alive if he had not armed himself before answering the door. Fortson’s mother, Chantemekki Fortson, told the Atlanta news outlet WXIA she was unsurprised by the verdict, citing the speed of the jury’s deliberations. “They went to deliberate for just two hours,” she said. “So, again, I wasn’t surprised.” She also said the trial forced her to face details surrounding her son’s death that she had spent the previous two years trying to avoid. “Now I can’t do that,” she told WXIA. “Like he’s really gone. “He’s never coming back. He’s never gonna say, ‘Mom, what you doing? Mom, you wanna go get something to eat? Mom, you need do your hair.’ Like I’m never going to hear my baby’s voice no more.”

title: Women given free cycling shorts to prevent upskirting on Oktoberfest amusement ride
summary: Investigation revealed thousands of voyeuristic videos taken on Munich beer festival’s Teufelsrad, or Devil’s Wheel
text: Women have been given free cycling shorts to prevent upskirting on a famous amusement ride at the Oktoberfest in Munich, after an investigation revealed tens of thousands of voyeuristic videos circulating online. The Teufelsrad, or Devil’s Wheel, which rapidly spins around while people try to sit on it for as long as they can, is one of the beer festival’s oldest rides. But many of the videos discovered by German journalists focus on women whose traditional dirndl dresses have ridden up, often showing their underwear. The findings have revived concerns about upskirting – secretly filming or taking photos under someone’s skirt without consent, which has been illegal in Germany since 2020. It is punishable by a fine or up to two years in prison. But some women’s rights advocates have said the law is not enough to stop the abuse. According to the research by the Munich daily newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung, more than 32,000 videos linked to the Teufelsrad were found on Meta platforms alone, some of them with millions of views. The operator of the ride, Elisabeth Polaczy, told the BBC she has been handing out free cycling shorts to women and girls wearing dresses to protect them from people filming them. She has given out more than 100 pairs during this Oktoberfest, which finishes on Sunday. “I want to do everything I can to make people feel secure,” she said. There are signs and police posters in German and English around the tent where the Teufelsrad is located that warn against filming under people’s skirts. But Polaczy, 80, said it was difficult to control everyone filming with smartphones. A spokesperson for the Bavarian police told the BBC they have put up posters at the Oktoberfest warning against upskirting since 2025. Police arrested a 45-year-old Swiss man for filming under a German woman’s dirndl at this year’s festival. In 2025 there were 10 arrests for upskirting and seven in 2024.

title: Burnham must remember: more regulation is not the best way to improve public services | Phillip Inman
summary: In the NHS as in the private sector, the measure of success should be customer satisfaction and not just box-ticking
text: Andy Burnham said he wanted to “rewire” the economy. Then he seemed to slam on the brakes, kicking most reforms into the 2030s. Local government reorganisation is on hold, along with an overhaul of the much-maligned water industry. Social care and significant welfare reform are matters to be resolved by the next government. A delay is understandable when the issues are knotty and plans on the left to replace the word “rewire” with “renationalise”, stir up accusations of taking Britain back to the 1970s. And yet delay is unnecessary when the knowledge is available now to get on with the kind of changes that rebuild public trust in time for a 2029 election. There are oblique ways of achieving success, and the measure of success should be customer satisfaction. Without this aim, the hopes of reform are lost. The economist Sir John Kay, a fellow of St John’s College, Oxford and former head of the Institute for Fiscal Studies, is a keen advocate of organisations that remember for whose benefit they exist. That means their primary aim should be to achieve customer satisfaction. In the private sector, profits will follow. In the public sector, there will be savings. In his book Obliquity, Kay shows how those companies that pursued shareholder value as their primary aim failed. And those that wanted to produce the best product secured long-term success. Just as a devotion to shareholder value – a financial metric of the benefit to investors -proved a blind alley for thousands of now-deceased companies, so the reliance on protocols in the public sector as a substitute for understanding the task in hand leads to failed outcomes and wasted money. You can see it now in the NHS, where satisfaction levels are rising in relation to GP and hospital visits. The new system for booking appointments has its drawbacks, but people are finding doctors are available more quickly, especially for GP and outpatient appointments. You can see the failures in the NHS from the cover-ups by maternity unit managers of rising mortality rates. Neither the success nor the failure can be attributed to the regulation of the health service. Regulation is an extra layer of cost that has, time after time, been shown to undermine productive behaviour, either because private providers and managers find they can game the system or it stifles innovation. Another example can be found in two unconnected government agencies. Last week, the Environment Agency said it would fund the planting of half a million trees, giving funds to councils and mayors and other government bodies to carry out the work. Surely this is a good thing? On the other hand, you might think it a complete waste of time and money when National Highways, the main road builder in England, planted 850,000 saplings in 2020 along a widened stretch of the A14 north of Cambridge, only to report three years later, in an internal review, that three-quarters of them had died. These failures are about the way public sector departments and agencies go about their work. Regulation only adds to a tick-box culture that asks: “Did you follow the protocol? If so, everything’s fine.” Eminent figures in Whitehall, from the former mandarin and Bank of England deputy governor Sir Jon Cunliffe to the House of Lords industry and regulators committee believe the answer is more intensive oversight. Kay has many examples of companies that grew because the boardroom was dominated by people who were more obsessed about delivering the best service or product than rewarding their shareholders as the chief metric. Profits and improvements in things such as market share were not the dominant metrics in companies that expanded. The aircraft maker Boeing succeeded before it lost its way chasing quarterly profit targets. ICI, once the UK’s largest industrial company, was broken up and faded away after a higher stock market value became the main target. The management consultant John Seddon, whose Vanguard consulting firm has adapted the Toyota systems method, supports Kay’s studiously well-informed analysis of what it takes to make a successful organisation. Seddon puts flesh on the bones with the kind of practical systems approach that has helped Portsmouth city council’s housing department win international awards for its repairs service. He has seen many new initiatives in public sector management from grand strategies to more prosaic schemes for benchmarking services against the private sector. All have failed to improve services. Seddon is not in favour of ditching regulation altogether. Regulation based on how well an organisation achieves the purpose will, he says, avoid the persistent problem of regulation “running behind events, shutting the stable door after another horse has bolted”. He adds: “Having a clear statement of purpose will enable regulators to apply sanctions immediately if and when an organisation is found to be undermining its allotted purpose. “It is time to liberate public servants from the prison of suspicion and distrust that our current method of regulation locks them in, demeaning their professionalism and casting them as part of the problem rather than as active creators of solutions.” Burnham’s staff should avoid letting the debate about ownership dominate – ignoring a maxim that says “private bad, public good.”. They should work more closely on how public sector organisations achieve better outcomes. The evidence is available. They don’t need to look very far.

title: Tories plan to extend cuts beyond £47bn previously pledged, leak reveals
summary: Exclusive: Shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith told party members last year he had discussed making further savings if they win next election
text: The Conservatives are planning to make sweeping cuts beyond the £47bn announced last year if they win the next election, according to leaked comments by the shadow chancellor. Speaking last year when he was shadow business secretary, Andrew Griffith told Conservative members he and fellow shadow cabinet ministers had discussed making further cuts in “every part of government”. The comments, which have emerged on the eve of the Tory party conference in Birmingham, suggested that the Conservatives are planning to make cuts similar in scale to those made during the austerity years should they take power. Last October, Griffith said: “There are decisions made and signed up to by everybody to deliver that £47bn. Last week at the shadow cabinet, we talked about [how] we will need to go further. “The rate at which the economy is deteriorating, as well as our ambition to cut more taxes, means that we will have to find further savings, and I’m up for that in my department. I know there are areas that we can make savings, and that’s true of every every part of government.” He added: “There is a moral mission to get our economy growing, give people opportunity, as well as let people keep more of what they earn. It’s pretty simple. We’re Conservative, this is what we stand for.” A Tory spokesperson acknowledged the party was seeking to make cuts beyond what it had already announced. “Under Kemi Badenoch’s leadership, the Conservatives have consistently advocated for a smaller state and a government that does fewer things but better,” the spokesperson said. “In Birmingham, we will go further, setting out further savings to Labour’s bloated welfare bill and cracking down on wasteful spending as part of our plans to build a stronger economy and a stronger country.” Kemi Badenoch has previously outlined how the government would cut government spending by £47bn, mainly by cutting welfare spending for all non-British or EU citizens. The plans would also save £8bn by cutting 132,000 civil service jobs, another £1.6bn by scrapping almost all of Labour’s clean energy scheme and more than £7bn by cutting international aid. In August she promoted Griffith, who previously worked as chief operating officer for Sky, from his role as shadow business secretary. In government, Griffith worked in the Treasury under Kwasi Kwarteng and was one of the ministers tasked with defending the mini-budget even as the markets tanked in response. On Friday Badenoch promised another £4bn of spending reductions, including taking another £2.5bn out of the aid budget – leaving it with just £1bn as year – as well as reducing the budget of the Department for Culture, Media and Sport by £1bn. The Tory leader said she would use half of those savings to pay for an additional 50,000 prison places. She has previously promised to use half of any cuts she makes to reduce the deficit. Griffiths’ leaked comments come as the Tories prepare to gather in Birmingham for their annual conference, with Badenoch seeking to make a virtue of the growing distance between Labour’s plans for government and her own. The prime minister, Andy Burnham, has promised a series of potentially expensive interventions, including a new national care service and public control over utility companies, as he seeks to end what he calls “40 years of neoliberalism”. However, Badenoch, who has called Margaret Thatcher her hero, is attempting to gain an electoral advantage with her vision of lower taxes and a significantly smaller state. “[Thatcher] is somebody who brought a lot of wealth and prosperity to this country,” the Tory leader told ITV Meridian on Friday. “Privatisation was a success … I don’t think that Andy Burnham running the water companies is the answer to those problems.” The Tories remain in third place in the polls, behind Labour and Reform UK, although Badenoch’s personal ratings have rallied over the last 12 months.

title: Greece returns priceless relics – and suggests UK should follow suit with Parthenon marbles
summary: Greek PM hopes handover of Tsar Samuel to Bulgaria will persuade Britain that time has come for ‘truth, reason, justice and morality’
text: In a ceremony replete with the sort of fanfare usually reserved for great events, Greece and Bulgaria have formally exchanged “a treasury” of relics and bones, sealing a cultural deal negotiated over decades. The handover involved priceless religious objects removed from Greece at the height of the first world war, as well as remains thought to belong to Tsar Samuel, Bulgaria’s revered medieval warrior ruler. Greece hailed the exchange as emblematic of the headway countries could make in similar repatriation disputes, with the prime minister, Kyriakos Mitsotakis, saying he hoped the accord would bolster Athens’ campaign to retrieve the Parthenon sculptures and send a clear message to Britain. “The global community is essentially re-evaluating its longstanding stance on protecting cultural heritage,” he told a crowd gathered for the ceremony in Thessaloniki on Saturday. “This shift is embodied by today’s initiative, which rests on the obvious principle that monuments and historical heirlooms cannot be treated as spoils of war, nor as the result of circumstances subsequent to their creation.” The Greek-Bulgarian deal, reached after 50 years of intense cultural diplomacy between the two neighbours, was also an example of the “political will” needed to settle the west’s longest running cultural row, Mitsotakis said, referring to the fifth century BC Parthenon marbles. “It took time, and above all, political will and determination to overcome the obstacles of the past,” he added. Under the agreement, 48 relics, including icons, crosses and ornate ecclesiastical vessels, pillaged by Bulgarian troops from churches and monasteries in northern Greece during the first world war, will be returned to Athens. In the more than 100 intervening years, they had been safeguarded at the National History Museum in Bulgaria. Meanwhile, the remains of Tsar Samuel, regarded as a national hero for his role in battling to preserve his country’s independence from the Byzantine empire, were discovered by archaeologists more than 60 years ago in a border area of Greece. Authorities arranged a homecoming with full state honours, with the tsar’s bones flown to Sofia, the Bulgarian capital, on a military aircraft accompanied by an escort of jet fighters and a 21-gun salute upon arrival. Free transport had been organised for pilgrims to pay their respects. In his own address at the handover, Bulgaria’s prime minister, Rumen Radev, a former air force officer, said: “These are items that belong to both our peoples; they constitute our memory and our bond, and our compatriots and future generations deserve, and must have, the opportunity to pay tribute to their ancestor. If in the past Tsar Samuel divided us, I can say that today he unites us. He strengthens our strategic cooperation and makes the historical relations between our states and peoples even stronger.” Mitsotakis emphasised that Greece’s campaign to win back the Parthenon marbles was neither “dictated by a vague national claim, nor does it call into question the mission of museums worldwide”. Athens remained committed to repatriating the sculptures, he said, because it would allow viewers to fully enjoy what has long been seen as the high point of classical art if the masterpieces were reunited. “It is precisely this same principle – the principle of the integrity of a monument – that underpins our continuous efforts to reunite the Parthenon sculptures. The Parthenon constitutes a unique and singular case,” he said of the building that is the predominant temple on the Acropolis of Athens. “[The campaign] is about the restoration of a universal monument that remains violently dismembered. My country will not accept arrangements that imply recognition of foreign sovereignty or the supposed borrowing of its own treasures. On the contrary, it now believes that the time has come for truth, for reason, for justice and morality.” The fifth century BC carvings were sawn from the Parthenon on the order of Lord Elgin, Britain’s then ambassador to the Sublime Porte, in what have since become highly contentious circumstances. They were acquired by the British Museum in 1816 after the bankrupt peer was forced to sell them and have been on display there ever since.

title: ‘This can’t go on’: tens of thousands protest against housing crisis in Spain
summary: Demonstrators take to the streets of Madrid ⁠and other Spanish cities ⁠after ​new legislation fails to pass
text: Tens of thousands of people have taken to the streets of Madrid ⁠and other Spanish cities as they step up demands for action to tackle ⁠a mounting housing crisis ⁠after government measures were struck down by the opposition. Demonstrators on Saturday waved posters calling for a general strike ⁠after the measures drawn up to address mass anger over the eviction of an 87-year-old woman in ⁠Madrid, and other housing issues, were rejected in parliament on Friday. Authorities said 70,000 people were protesting. Organisers put the figure at 500,000. “It’s a shame,” Nando ‌de Anguulo, 26, ‌who joined the protest in Madrid, told Reuters. “It only proves that it ‌is us, the people, who have to adapt to the political parties, and not the politicians to what the people want, and this can’t go on like that.” Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, may call a snap election for November after the ‌legislation failed to pass, Spanish media reported on Friday, and would be watching the strength of Saturday’s protests before making a decision. The demonstrations have dominated the national conversation, breathing new life into Sánchez’s beleaguered government and shifting attention away from the lingering impact of recent events in Ceuta. Protests on Saturday were peaceful in 50 Spanish cities. In the south-eastern city of Valencia, demonstrators clashed with police who fired rubber bullets and teargas ⁠to break up the protests. About 30 people managed to get inside the City of Arts and Sciences, a landmark cultural building in the city, before they were ousted by ‌police. One protester in Madrid, Marcos Sainz, a librarian, 26, said he used to rent a two-bedroom apartment with friends for a monthly rent of 900 euros ($1,000) but that a one-bedroom flat often now cost 1,000 euros – or half the median monthly salary in the capital. He told AFP he would protest rental spikes “until someone dares to regulate it all, as (otherwise) we’ll all have to leave Madrid and that would be a shame as I am from Madrid”. Javier, 31, a solar panel installer, said: “We are demanding a fundamental right: decent housing, stability and conditions allowing us to construct a decent life project.” He added: “I spend half of my salary on a tiny room.” “What we are feeling in the streets is a new energy that we haven’t seen in a long time, an energy that is showing that eight days of people power can achieve more than eight years of progressive government,” Valeria Racu, one of the spokespeople of the Tenants’ Union organising the protest, said in a statement. “Now begins real politics – politics which has always belonged to the people and which will return once and for all to the streets,” she said. Late on Saturday groups of far-right protesters, some of them performing Nazi salutes, tried to get to the camp in Madrid but were blocked by police. One video posted on the website of Spanish daily El País showed police chasing some members of the group through the streets and the newspaper also reported that officers had made three arrests. On Friday, Sánchez’s Socialist-led coalition put forward two decrees that included a range of measures aimed at improving access to housing, from a ban on evictions until 2030 to the regulation of temporary lettings and lettings by room. Despite the anger of the protesters outside parliament, the conservative People’s party, the far-right Vox and the Catalan pro-independence party Junts voted against both decrees. The People’s party said it had voted in line with its belief that building, rather than regulating, was the best way to address the crisis. “Housing doesn’t become more affordable through decrees; it becomes more affordable by building more homes,” said the lawmaker Juan Bravo. News of the package’s rejection was met with boos and cries of “shame” outside. “Your profits, our misery,” the protesters chanted. The long-simmering anger at soaring housing costs boiled over late last month, when 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal, who uses a wheelchair, was evicted from the home she had lived in for 70 years. The octogenarian said she was unable to afford the 230% rent hike demanded by the investment fund that bought her apartment. Reuters and AFP contributed to this report.

title: Michigan state police rule out claim that Larry Nassar was removed from sex offender registry
summary: Eaton county prosecuting attorney’s office had said court ruling forced removal of Nassar’s name – but he wasn’t on list because he was imprisoned out of state
text: Michigan has removed more than 20,000 entries from its sex offender registry, but convicted serial abuser Larry Nassar is not one of them – the former Michigan State University and USA Gymnastics doctor was not in that system, as a local prosecutor’s office claimed, because he was serving an out-of-state federal prison sentence, according to state police. On 9 September, the Michigan supreme court ruled that the state’s Sex Offender Registration Act (Sora) cannot be applied retroactively to cases involving offenses committed before the law’s relevant date. Michigan’s state police, as a result, removed more than 20,000 people whose offenses occurred before 1 July 2011 from the agency’s online sex offender database. One of the agencies to prosecute Nassar, the Eaton county prosecuting attorney’s office, asserted that he was among those removed from the Michigan state police sex offender registry. The office – helmed by Republican Michigan state attorney general candidate Doug Lloyd – even shared a screenshot showing a search for his name returning zero results. The office also published a statement that read: “The Michigan supreme court’s decision to eliminate Sora requirements for these offenders is deeply concerning.” The statement, which was widely reported on by the news media, including the Guardian, continued: “Our community, along with the victims of these crimes, expected the registry to provide a measure of protection and awareness – assurances that have now been removed by the court’s ruling.” But on Friday, Michigan state police released their own statement saying: “Information suggesting that convicted sex offender Nassar was removed from the sex offender registry by the Michigan state police because of the Smith decision is incorrect.” US Bureau of Prisons records show Nassar has been imprisoned at Pennsylvania’s Lewisburg federal correctional institute – and “offenders not currently domiciled, temporarily residing, working, incarcerated or going to school in Michigan do not have the duty to register in Michigan under [Sora], and would not be visible on Michigan’s public sex offender registry”, the state police statement said. “Should the offender later domicile (including being incarcerated), temporarily reside, work or go to school in Michigan, they would be expected to register and be placed on Michigan’s public [sex offender registry] if still required under Sora at that time.” The Eaton county prosecuting attorney’s office on Friday issued a statement, too, saying: “We must correct our earlier social media post about removal of convicted sex offenders from the Michigan sex offender registry … We never contemplated that one of the most notorious sex offenders in the history of the state would not have been registered despite the law requiring otherwise.” The office noted that offenses for which Nassar was convicted in Eaton county and neighboring Ingham county had 2009 and 1998 dates associated with them, which “fall within the time frame [of] the recent supreme court order”. At the time he was sentenced for those offenses in 2018, he was incarcerated in Michigan and would have been required to be registered as a sex offender in the state until being transferred into federal custody out of state, according to the Eaton prosecuting attorney’s office’s statement. “We apologize for the confusion,” the office’s statement said. But the statement also said: “As prosecutors, we have a responsibility to provide information to victims and survivors of sexual assault.” Michigan lawmakers do not have the authority to reverse the state supreme court’s decision. However, the legislature could pass new legislation that would place the affected offenders back in the database. Nassar was sentenced in 2018 to as many as 175 years in state and federal prison after being convicted of sexually abusing women and girls for decades while working at Michigan State University and serving as a doctor for Team USA Gymnastics. As of Friday, Nassar’s projected earliest release date for his federal prison sentence was in 2068, when he would be 104. More than 150 women and girls have accused Nassar of assault. His accusers include Olympic gold medal-winning gymnasts Aly Raisman, Simone Biles, McKayla Maroney and Gabby Douglas. Nassar pleaded guilty in November 2017 to multiple counts of first-degree criminal sexual conduct. He survived being stabbed multiple times in July 2023 while imprisoned. During his sentencing hearing, his accusers delivered impact statements describing the shame and trauma they said they experienced because of Nassar. Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organizations. In the US, Rainn offers support on 800-656-4673. In the UK, Rape Crisis offers support on 0808 500 2222. In Australia, support is available at 1800Respect (1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found at ibiblio.org/rcip/internl.html • The headline, subheading and main text of this article were amended on 3 October 2026. Based on information provided, an earlier version said that Larry Nassar had been removed from the Michigan sex offender registry. As the revised version makes clear, he was not in fact on that registry because he was serving an out-of-state federal prison sentence.

title: California’s new laws target workers’ biggest fear of AI taking their jobs
summary: The state, which is home to many AI companies, is one of the first to roll out workplace regulations targeting the technology
text: California’s laws aimed at protecting workers from the impacts of artificial intelligence could pave the way for broader workplace safeguards across the US as calls for regulating the technology mount. As the federal government goes hands-off on AI, California is taking the reins to address workers’ biggest fears. On Thursday, California governor Gavin Newsom signed a suite of new laws that ban bosses from relying entirely on AI to decide whether to fire workers, using it to predict employees’ emotional states or collecting neural data, meaning the information from electrical signals of someone’s brain or nerves. They also require companies to notify workers if layoffs were caused by AI and prohibit AI surveillance in workplace bathrooms. The new laws come as workers increasingly worry whether AI will take their jobs, lead to discrimination and increase workplace surveillance. Unions, worker advocates and even some lawmakers pushed for the new rules, a regulatory shift for a technology that has largely developed unchecked. California, home to many of the leading companies developing AI, represents one of the first states to roll out a sweeping set of workplace regulations targeting the technology. “It’s a turning point,” said Lorena Gonzalez, president of the California Federation of Labor Unions, AFL-CIO, who’s been helping leaders across the country write regulations. “It’s really the first time we’re seeing California workers showing the country that we don’t have to accept [this].” Other states that have recently passed individual laws aimed at AI’s use in the workplace include Colorado, Connecticut, Illinois and Texas, narrower in scope than California’s. And more bills across the county are being lined up for consideration, Gonzalez said. California’s laws aim to target workplace surveillance measures like heat maps that track employees’ movements, including how long they spend in the bathroom, or having their emotional states monitored. Amazon warehouse workers have previously complained about being timed on their bathroom breaks, for example. And at Kaiser Permanente, nurses have said automated systems rated their tone of voice in patient interactions. But the laws could also prevent future unexpected harms. “We don’t know all the places companies are using AI, and that is and should be scary,” Gonzalez said. Part of the strategy for worker advocates and union groups like the California Federation has been following AI companies’ latest products. “If it’s being sold, that’s a good indication” it could be in use, Gonzales said. The federation also plans to use the momentum to revive issues like requiring employers to disclose when they’re using AI in the workplace, which was a bill that died in the state’s assembly appropriations committee this year. California’s new laws are a key step in gaining regulatory ground for worker advocates, said Robin Feldman, director and founder of AI Law & Innovation Institute at The University of California College of the Law, San Francisco. Still, the statutes are somewhat limited in how they are implemented. “The bills have no private enforcement,” Feldman said. “In other words: workers can’t sue. Only the government can enforce the laws.” The new regulations come amid a backdrop of record AI spending at big tech companies along with massive job cuts. But workers have started pushing back. In June, Meta paused a program that tracked workers’ computer activities to train its AI models. And one month later, dozens of employees filed a lawsuit claiming the tech company’s AI tools targeted those with disability accommodations or on medical or parental leaves for layoffs. Meanwhile, safety concerns, including fears that AI could destroy humanity, have been garnering more attention from lawmakers across the country and prompted OpenAI and Anthropic to call for slowing the pace of development. “Workers are increasingly part of that movement, speaking up about the fear of job loss and the dehumanizing experience of being surveilled and controlled by an algorithm,” said Annette Bernhardt, senior tech policy adviser at UC Berkeley Labor Center. While the new laws “have teeth”, according to Danielle Ochs, shareholder at employment law firm Ogletree Deakins’ San Francisco office, it’s unclear how sweeping the change will be. Ochs said employers generally aren’t grappling with the AI uses outlined in the new regulations and instead are more interested in how to responsibly implement AI across their systems. “Having 10 hoops you have to jump through per tool is not reflective of reality,” she said. It would be better to have “guardrails that are more aligned” with employers’ wider use of AI rather than focused on specific tools or uses. She says opponents worry that the new rules could unexpectedly prohibit helpful AI that might, for example, ensure truckers don’t fall asleep at the wheel. While it’s too soon to gauge how effective the laws will be, worker advocates believe the momentum is moving in a positive direction. Gonzalez said the measures are only the beginning of addressing AI’s potential impacts. “We have so much work to do,” she said. “But this should give us all hope we can win … against the tech lobby, against big corporations, because we are the majority.”

title: Southern California swelters as late-season heatwave smothers region
summary: Temperatures expected to hover around 100F in downtown LA and even hotter inland, raising concerns about wildfires
text: Southern California faced scorching heatwaves this summer that made locals wonder what happened to their famed Mediterranean climate. Now, the fall is bringing heatwaves too. Friday kicked off a new round of long-duration heatwave advisories from the National Weather Service (NWS), which expects unseasonably high temperatures to linger for at least a week. Temperatures are expected to hover near 100F in downtown Los Angeles, and spike well into the triple digits farther inland, raising the risk of both heat-related illness and wildfires. “We’re expecting temperatures will run some 15-20 degrees above normal – that’s pretty significant,” said Richard Bann, a meteorologist with the NWS’s Weather Prediction Center. “Stay cool. Stay hydrated. Limit exposure to the sun.” October heatwaves are not uncommon in southern California. They’re caused by ridges of high air pressure that park themselves above the region. This year, they’re also influenced by an ongoing marine heatwave that, in turn, is driving a strong El Niño – a year of above-average surface-water temperature in the Pacific Ocean. But experts say the severity and duration of this year’s fall heatwave is extreme, and likely to become more common in the future as the climate crisis nudges global temperatures higher. “The extremely hot temperature Friday is rare,” said V Kelly Turner, a professor of geography and urban planning at UCLA. “Nearly 7F hotter than the hottest October 2 ever and about 30 degrees higher than historical averages around 75F.” If there’s a silver lining for southern California, it’s that current forecasts do not call for strong winds that would threaten to fuel and spread wildfires – though the increased heat and low soil moisture still makes them more likely. It’s difficult for scientists to point to a specific event and describe it as an effect of climate change, said David Neelin, an atmospheric physicist who researches climate change at UCLA. But research is showing that with every half-degree of global warming, heatwaves become both more likely and longer lasting. “Overall, it’s hard to escape that a warmer climate adds to the strength of heatwaves,” Neelin said. “It adds to the probability of heatwaves and the likelihood of getting longer-duration heatwaves.” This week’s heatwave will coincide with major outdoor events in the region, including the first game of the National League division series between the LA Dodgers and the Atlanta Braves on Saturday, noted Edith de Guzman, a researcher who studies climate change and heat adaptation at UCLA. She urged political governments to invest in heat adaptation now to make the region more livable in the future. Providing more shade is the most “most effective way to keep people safe”, she wrote in a text message. “Climate change is making longer-duration heatwaves possible, while simultaneously increasing their frequency and intensity,” De Guzman wrote. “So we should prepare for more of this in the future.”

title: Badenoch returns to Conservative conference much stronger than a year ago
summary: Approval ratings for Tory leader and her party have crept up as she has asserted her style and authority but big challenges lie ahead
text: A year ago, Tory MPs were braced for the prospect of yet another leadership battle to topple Kemi Badenoch as the party sunk to historic lows of 14-16% in the polls. At the time, the word “November” was uttered in hushed tones – this being the decisive month when rebels would be able to mount a challenge, Badenoch having served 12 months in office. But times appear to have changed and – against the odds – the Tories have undergone what has been termed a “Keminisation”, with the leader asserting her style and authority on the party, despite its wider poor performance in the polls. “Right now, Kemi is the only thing that’s holding them up,” says Luke Tryl, the director of the More in Common thinktank, which conducts focus groups and polling. “If they ditched her, I think they’d be certain for electoral oblivion.” Badenoch is running a party still discounted as toxic and incompetent by much of the electorate, but polling numbers and focus groups suggest some of them have recently begun to give her more of a hearing. The party has crept up from the teens to the low 20s – occasionally edging ahead of Reform UK for the first time in almost two years. “It’s not great for them, but it’s a lot better,” says Tryl. “The problem is the party brand. She is now in our approval ratings net neutral and has been net 1 or net 2. She was in the minus 30s and now only her and Burnham have positive approval. “Progressives don’t like her, but when you come to those who might conceivably be Tory voters there’s a lot of ‘like her, don’t like the party, she tells it like it is, wish she was in another party’. I do think the Kemi bounce is real. People talk about her having improved and they have seen her PMQs clips.” Data from the other pollsters backs up the idea that the public is more open to Badenoch than before. James Crouch, the head of policy and public affairs at Opinium, said Badenoch’s approval rating had been rising since May 2025, when she was at -27, to -3 in its latest poll. He said that among 2024 Conservative voters she had the approval of 64%, compared with just 8% who did not approve, while of those who voted Conservative in 2019, 56% approved of her, while 16% did not. Further research from YouGov this week found four in 10 people used at least one negative term to describe the Tory leader, one of the most common themes being a perceived unpleasantness. But three in 10 included one or more positive terms in their description, strong and intelligent being the main compliments. Some Tory MPs attribute Badenoch’s improvement over the last year to a willingness to learn and take advice on her performance. This is in spite of her having the preternatural public self-confidence to claim to the FT this weekend that she couldn’t think of any mistakes she had made, saying everyone makes them but “nothing comes to mind”. But insiders say she has listened to people warning she needs to focus more on the economy and less on culture war talking points, with the party’s conference slogan set as “Stronger economy, stronger country”. She has also improved her prime minister’s questions appearances, partly with help on preparation from Conservative grandees such as David Cameron. Tory MPs believe a turning point for Badenoch was the defection of Robert Jenrick and Suella Braverman to Reform – because their departure removed a source of destabilisation on the right, and it gave her an opportunity to show decisiveness in pushing Jenrick before he jumped. She has also been aided by the increasing questions over Nigel Farage and Reform UK’s finances, with the party’s dominance in the polls slipping. However, the arrival of Andy Burnham on the scene for Labour has changed things. Giles Kenningham, the former Conservative director of communications who now leads the Trafalgar Strategy advisory firm, says Burnham “raises the bar … he’s a great communicator and comfortable in his own skin”. “It’s a harder ask now. Starmer was not a great orator or someone who electrified voters … Burnham has had a great conference but all eyes are now on the budget, so her conference needs to be on the economy and welfare. John Healey’s speech didn’t say anything, and there is an opportunity for Badenoch to put pressure on them and drive the agenda.” Badenoch’s star has also risen further with the membership of the party, the most recent ConservativeHome poll showing she has a 87% net satisfaction rating with the party faithful. Despite this, a number of Conservative aides and insiders believe that Badenoch’s future is still not totally secure if the party does not start to creep above Reform UK on a sustained basis. One pointed to the Tory selection races – excluding some high-profile former MPs from standing – as a sign of perceived weakness that those around Badenoch are worried about her being challenged. “She is not alone among politicians in not liking tall poppies,” said one Conservative strategist. “Ultimately, she is not immune from a challenge,” said another. “The shelf life of politicians is getting shorter and shorter. Leaders are much more exposed and the job is precarious. The thing most in her favour is that there are currently no other obvious contenders.”

title: Two Iranian men identified Manchester synagogue as site for alleged bomb plot, court hears
summary: Rahman Salehi, 34, and Salam Ahmadyan, 36, were charged with preparing attacks on city’s Jewish community, including Heaton Park synagogue
text: Two Iranian men identified a Manchester synagogue previously subjected to a fatal terrorist attack as a target for an alleged homemade bomb plot, a court has heard. Rahman Salehi, 34, from Salford, and Salam Ahmadyan, 36, from Liverpool were charged with preparing to commit an act of terrorism or assisting another to commit an act of terrorism on Friday. The two men appeared in Westminster magistrates court on Saturday morning. They wore grey overalls in the dock while and, through a Kurdish interpreter, spoke to confirm their names, dates of birth and addresses. The pair were alleged to have carried out “hostile reconnaissance” within Manchester’s Jewish community and identified a number of potential targets including the city’s Jewish museum and Heaton Park synagogue. The court heard the pair came to the UK illegally via small boats. Salehi arrived in 2020 before being granted leave to remain in 2023. Ahmadyan came in 2023 and has an outstanding asylum claim. They were in contact with a third party, believed to be operating from within Iran, who “directed and coordinated” the planned attack and sent them “instructions on how to prepare an explosive device”. Prosecutor Mark Luckett told the court: “Both defendants are accused of preparing acts of terrorism targeting the Jewish community in Manchester through the use of a homemade explosive device. “The defendants were observed carrying out, what the prosecution say, is a hostile reconnaissance within Manchester’s Jewish community, identifying attempted targets such as the Jewish Museum and Heaton Park synagogue.” “They were in contact with a third party who is alleged to have directed and coordinated the planned attack and provided instructions on how to assemble a homemade explosive device,” he said. “It is assessed this individual is also an Iranian national and most likely operating from within Iran.” The two men were arrested on 20 September 2026 in broad daylight, just before the festival of Yom Kippur, widely regarded as the holiest day in the Jewish calendar. Before coming to the UK, Salehi lived in Germany for five years. The men are accused of acquiring a document entitled Steps for Making [a] Powder Chlorine and Car Brake Oil/Fluid Bomb and video material on how to manufacture or assemble an improvised explosive device. They are also accused of acquiring liquids, components and equipment required in order to manufacture or assemble an improvised explosive device. They are also accused of using the internet to identify and research potential targets, acquiring images, plans and maps of potential targets and conducting reconnaissance of potential locations for attack. District judge Nina Tempia remanded the two men into custody to appear at the Old Bailey on 23 October
