title: Soaring diesel prices take their toll on US farmers in midwest corn belt
summary: Fuel costs are biting for crop growers, trucking firms and a host of other industries as Iran war stokes record prices
text: Joe Hamilton farms corn and soybeans on 2,500 acres in Indiana’s Delaware county. Next week, when his soybean harvest kicks off, four tractors, two combine harvesters and five semi-trucks will roar to life. And with that, a record bill for about 9,000 gallons of diesel awaits him. “During harvest, we use about 300 gallons of diesel fuel per day, and we have around 30 harvest days in a typical fall,” he says. With diesel-guzzling combine machines now entering fields across the eastern corn belt for the beginning of the soybean harvest, crop growers, trucking companies and a host of other industries that rely on the fuel are dealing with record-high prices. An estimated 20bn bushels of soybeans and corn (522m metric tons) are set to be harvested in the midwest between now and the end of November. Estimates suggest that the war with Iran, damaged refineries in Russia and regional diesel supply disruptions could add an additional $12,500 in fuel costs for every 1,000 acres of crops harvested. “Farmers are price takers. It’s not just fuel – it’s chemicals, it’s seed, it’s the cost of equipment,” laments Hamilton. “Everything has increased along with the commodity prices.” As well as farmers, manufacturers, trucking companies and store owners in the midst of ramping up orders for the holiday buying season are facing the fallout of higher diesel costs. Four of the five states with the highest weekly diesel price increases in the country in September were in the midwest (Illinois, Michigan, Ohio and Indiana), with the fuel jumping by more than $3 per gallon compared with a year ago. On top of the war on Iran, regional issues are playing a role. A power outage and flooding last month at an ExxonMobil refinery in Joliet, Illinois, saw it shut down for more than a week, taking more than 80m gallons of diesel and gas offline. An ongoing six-month dispute between union members and BP at one of the largest refineries in the country in Whiting, Indiana, has also fueled a surge in prices regionally. “The midwest is different form the coasts or even the Gulf, primarily in the [lower] number of oil refineries and how it can respond in times of crisis. If you have water access you can bring tankers in with additional oil,” says Kurt Lykins, a lecturer at Otterbein University. “So, it’s hard for the midwest to respond.” Lykins adds that he’s concerned about the Strategic Oil Reserve – the 714m-barrel-capacity reserve held in salt caverns in Texas and Louisiana that today is lower than at any time in the past 43 years. “We’ve drawn down 172m barrels. Although the prices for gasoline and diesel have been rising, drawing down from the reserve has given some stability to prices,” he says. But that could soon change, he notes. “The issue is when we are no longer able to do that, the stability will no longer be there. We’re getting ready to go into a high diesel demand season in winter.” Amid the rising prices, large consumers of diesel fuel across the region are moving to reduce expenses where they can. In Ohio, 15,000 school buses that overwhelmingly run on diesel are charged with getting about 800,000 grade school students to and from their homes every school day. The Columbus school district, already facing a potential $157m financial deficit by 2031, has recently had to cut nearly 300 jobs, close four schools and limit bussing for students. The diesel issue, say administrators at the largest public school system in the state, is front of mind. “I believe we are contracted through 2027, so no major changes [are being put in place] at this time,” says Michael S Brown of the Columbus school district. “That said, we are constantly looking at bussing as a budget issue, at more than $70m total cost per year. I expect there will be transportation changes to the system in the next budget.” Almost 40% of school districts that participated in a national survey published in May say they are consolidating bus routes to help reduce diesel fuel expenses. But that means longer commutes and working hours for students and drivers alike and 20% of those surveyed said they had cut “non-required trips” such as field trips. “Any school district that’s using last year’s budget needs to refine that upwards,” warns Lykins. “The sad thing is that this increase is not the same across school districts – rural districts are going to be even more impacted because they transport more students over further distances.” Back on the farm, crop growers such as Hamilton are looking to cut down on fuel costs by using no-till and cover crop farming methods, which reduce the number of times he has to put diesel-guzzling machinery in the field. Now, he uses between two and four gallons per acre in a typical year. “It’s much less than we used when we were a full tillage operation,” he says. But in order to get his crops to market this fall, there’s no getting around paying elevated prices for machinery fuel. Hamilton says that limited fuel storage capacity at his farm means he will be forced to buy more diesel in the coming weeks to cover the back end of the 2026 harvest, and with nearly half of his harvesting fleet consisting of semi-trucks that use the more expensive on-road diesel (by contrast, red dyed or agricultural diesel typically has no federal fuel tax), uncertainty remains. “Fuel is $3 more expensive than it was 12 months ago. Soybeans right now are $12.88 per bushel, last year they were $10.14 but corn is $5.23 now versus $4.22 a year ago,” he says. Observers say that the high prices aren’t going away anytime soon. “Let’s say everything goes back to normal – we still need to build up the [Strategic Oil] Reserve and that’s going to slow the drop in prices for consumers,” says Lykins. “That’s the best-case [scenario].” What’s more, a report issued by the Government Accountability Office in May found that several of the Reserve caverns in Louisiana may see their capacity reduced due to stability concerns in a neighboring cavern that was recently decommissioned.

title: ‘Trump? I think he’s a disaster’: Ohio voters aggrieved as president prepares to visit
summary: President’s popularity has plummeted in solidly Republican state – will his presence at midterm rallies help or hinder?
text: Kelly Savage-Radich grew up in a Republican-supporting Ohio family and voted for Donald Trump in 2016 and 2020. But today the mother of three, who lives in a Montgomery county suburb of Dayton, is facing the prospect of having to sell one of her family’s vehicles due to the high cost of gas. Her grocery bill has gone up about $100 a week. She lays the blame squarely at the Trump administration’s door. “He wants his name on everything,” she said. “I’m sorry, but I don’t give a shit whose name is on the Kennedy Center.” That wasn’t the only matter on her list of grievances – Savage-Radich also brought up the killing of Renee Good in Minneapolis earlier this year. She said: “The shooting of an American citizen dead in the street, and no one was held accountable? I have two daughters, and I’m trying to teach them all the freedoms this country has, but it feels like our freedoms are being taken. “For people that always claim, ‘Don’t tread on me,’ they sure have no problem now.” On Saturday, Trump will visit Montgomery county, which he only barely lost in 2024, to rally for two Republicans struggling in key Ohio election races: incumbent US senator Jon Husted, and Vivek Ramaswamy, the candidate for Ohio governor. Ohio has been solidly Republican for more than a decade. Trump won Ohio by handy margins in the past three presidential elections, and the state has not voted for a Democratic president since Barack Obama in 2012. The Republican party holds a supermajority in the state’s legislature. But the president’s popularity in the industrial midwestern state has plummeted during his second term, and his presence may be more of a hindrance than a help. A Marist poll of nearly 1,300 registered Ohio voters conducted late last month found that 56% of participants disapprove of the job Trump is doing as president. In two important primaries held earlier this year, turnout for Republicans in Montgomery county was just two-thirds of that for Democrats. In last May’s Republican gubernatorial primary, turnout was down 33% or 362,000 votes compared to the previous primary, held in 2022. In a US Senate race that could help decide which party controls the national political landscape, Husted is polling behind his Democratic challenger Sherrod Brown. Despite Ohio electing Republican governors in six out of the past seven elections, Ramaswamy, a billionaire former Republican presidential candidate who until recently was one of Trump’s most vocal supporters, is also polling behind Amy Acton, the Democratic candidate. Other prominent Ohio Republicans have been in the headlines recently for all the wrong reasons. Representative Max Miller, who until domestic and child abuse allegations against him emerged last summer enjoyed close ties with Trump, faces stiff opposition to retain his congressional seat from a union ironworker. (Miller has denied all of the allegations, and has not faced criminal charges. The House ethics committee is investigating the allegations.) Montgomery county, a mix of urban, suburban and rural communities, has been a swing county for decades: in the presidential election two years ago, Trump lost it by just 1,201 votes, one of just seven of 88 counties in Ohio to fall Democratic nominee Kamala Harris’s way. With the midterms just a month away, the county’s leading Republicans admit that they’re in a fight. “You know, it’s been slower [than in previous election cycles], but it’s picking up. Honestly, I haven’t seen much energy on either side, but we’re getting more interest, people are getting engaged,” said Phil Plummer, the chair of the Montgomery county Republican party and a member of the Ohio house of representatives. “Obviously our candidates knocking on doors are hearing about the affordability issues. But we tell them: we didn’t create that, the Democrats did, and it’s hard to fix it in two years.” Plummer said that during the Biden administration too much money was printed in the form of hundreds of billions of dollars in federal tax breaks and investment spending, which has fueled higher costs today. Democrats say Biden’s spending surge was to combat the economic recession caused by the 2020 pandemic and point to Trump’s war on Iran costing Americans more than $44bn. “Obviously, the war [on Iran] hasn’t helped as far as oil prices, but Ohio has been deemed the number one state to do business in the nation. We’re moving the ball in Ohio; we’ve lowered property tax and cut income tax,” he said. “So we’re doing the best we can.” Few residents care to talk politics in the neighborhoods of Dayton, Montgomery county’s largest city. “Trump? I think he’s a disaster,” said a woman who declined to give her name as she stood outside a tattoo parlor in the Old North district, a working-class area north of downtown Dayton. Caring for his invalid mother on the porch of his home, Bill, a former nurse and Republican voter who asked not to be fully identified in order to speak freely, disagreed, and said the wider focus on rising gas prices was misplaced. “It’s always been crazy high, and people will buy a whole lot of gas at $2.99 but act like it’s out of control when it’s $3,” he says, adding that he has not decided whether he will vote in the midterms yet. “It seems like everybody is making more money, even with the most menial jobs.” Independents are set to play a major role in deciding Ohio’s next governor and the senate race between Husted and Brown. Nearly 38% of Ohio voters, or 2.9 million people, are independents, according to the Independent Voter Project. Running as an independent candidate for US house of representatives, Sandeep Dixit has knocked on hundreds of doors and met thousands of Ohioans on the campaign trail in north-east Ohio’s 13th district. He says the biggest issue voters are talking about is the hate-filled language coming from the political class. “People understand that if we continue with extreme positions the country’s going to get torn apart,” he said. “That’s the number one issue.” Dixit wouldn’t say for which parties he voted in the past but believes that Ohio Republicans have done well on the rule of law. However, “when it comes to being empathetic to people and understanding what people need, there is a complete extreme ideology” among Republicans, he said. For Savage-Radich, there have never been clearer choices. “I would never vote for Ramaswamy, I don’t believe anything he says – I don’t believe anything any Republican says right now because every time I fact-check something, they’re lying,” she said. “And now we’re like buddies with China? It’s all crazy. I thought Republicans were the party that was so against China?” She said she doesn’t know a lot about Acton, the Democratic candidate. Republicans have attacked her for enacting Covid-related restrictions during the pandemic, but Savage-Radich noted she was working as the director of the Ohio department of health under a Republican governor. “She didn’t do anything that Mike DeWine didn’t have her do, and that’s a Republican governor,” she said. “To be honest, I think I’m going to vote Democrat all the way down, for everything. Because I want it not to be this way.”

title: The DSA has a believability problem with older Black voters. But young people want to take more risks
summary: Black voters reveal a generational divide, with younger voters drawn to the Democratic Socialists of America, and older voters focused on what can realistically be achieved
text: One of the most heated debates in the Democratic party is how left it should go – especially after a year that has seen several democratic socialists win their primary races. Moderate Democrats worry that left-wing candidates will struggle to win general elections, while progressive voters want fresh solutions to healthcare and the rising cost of living. But largely left out of this debate is one of the most critical bases of the party: Black voters. A Pew Research Center study found that among Democrats, only 21% of Black voters are likely to positively view candidates who align with democratic socialists, compared to 40% of white, 30% of Asian, and 20% of Hispanic voters. To better understand this gap, the Guardian spoke to nearly a dozen Black voters about their perceptions of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) – the largest socialist organization in the country, which mostly operates within the Democratic party. The group advocates for a working-class democracy with publicly funded education, as well as housing and healthcare paid through excessive taxes on the rich and corporations. What emerged from the interviews was a clear theme: a generational divide exists between older voters who back establishment Democrats and young people who seek to push the Democratic party more to the left. The trend follows a long tradition of young organizers fueling progressive movements. *** In late August, Claire Valdez, the New York seventh congressional district Democratic nominee and longtime DSA leader, won 59.6% of the young Black vote, while only garnering 39.9% of the Black voters over 50 years old (according to a breakdown from the political analyst Michael Lange). Darializa Avila Chevalier, New York’s 13th congressional district Democratic nominee, won 52.8% of Black voters under 50 years old, while receiving 46.4% of votes from older Black constituents. In the aftermath of these wins, political analysts question who the DSA represents, and whether most Black voters feel connected to a socialist message. Sid Carlson White became involved in the DSA as an undergrad at Yale University in 2017, and officially became a member of the organization five years later. “I realized that DSA was really one of the only places where a regular person could get involved and have real Democratic control over an organization and carry out our goals collectively,” Carlson White said. He thinks the idea that the DSA isn’t reaching Black constituents is outdated. A member of DSA’s national political committee based in Jersey City, New Jersey, Carlson White, who’s 27, has served in the organization’s nearly 2,000-member Afrosocialists and Socialists of Color caucus, which holds discussions on race and political education. Over the past six years, he said he and other Black and brown members have pushed the organization to improve their outreach to Black communities. Reading circles and group discussions have also helped educate white members on causes such as ending mass incarceration. “We want people to understand that these issues around racial justice, economic equality, job discrimination, police brutality, democracy for Black America are things that we fight for and things that we can deliver on many levels of politics,” Carlson White said. Two years ago, when Carlson White campaigned for Eon Huntley – a Black DSA-endorsed socialist running for New York state assembly – he noticed a class divide. Huntley’s call for universal rent stabilization resonated with Black renters, while his message fell flat for older and more financially stable Black homeowners. Carlson White drummed up support from tenant organizers fighting against displacement in Black neighborhoods. Though Huntley didn’t win in 2024, he defeated incumbent Stefani Zinerman in the Democratic primary in June 2026. According to Huntley’s campaign, his vote share in majority-Black precincts rose from 44.9% in 2024 to 57.8% in 2026. “Black Brooklynites understand the threat posed by Big Real Estate better than anyone, because we’ve watched our friends and family being displaced year after year,” Huntley said in a statement to the Guardian. “I believe the voters chose a democratic socialist because they want to remain here, to thrive here, and to pass this community and its culture along to the next generation.” *** Founded in Detroit, Michigan, in 1982, the DSA was born from a merger of two leftist groups, the Democratic Socialist Organizing Committee and the New American Movement. The anti-capitalist organization functions as a member-driven network with national leadership and local chapters in every state. Unlike the Democratic party, which operates within established political institutions, the DSA proposes abolishing the Senate and the electoral college. Ending economic and military aid to Israel is another key tenet, which continues to split establishment Democrats. The DSA often backs leftist candidates in electoral campaigns, and members participate in grassroots organizing. Interest in the political group has surged in the past decade, after the 2016 presidential campaign of Senator Bernie Sanders, who describes himself as a democratic socialist. The group also grew in popularity when the New York-based DSA member Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez won a House of Representatives seat in 2018. The New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani’s election in late 2025 marked the organization’s largest electoral victory. Between July 2017 and July 2026, DSA membership grew from 24,000 to more than 120,000. Over the past year, young Black voters have increasingly supported progressive candidates, diverging from their elders’ endorsements of established Democratic politicians. While Mamdani only garnered 26% support in precincts with at least a 70% Black population, he appealed to young Black voters through social media posts about affordability as well as appearing on radio shows and podcasts such as The Breakfast Club and Ebro in the Morning. According to a DSA survey shared with the Guardian, among DSA dues-paying members who have joined within the past two years, 66% were white, while about 11% were Latino, 6% were Black, and 4.6% were Asian. As for registered Democrats, 56% were white, 18% were Black, 16% were Latino, and 6% were Asian, according to a 2023 Pew Research Center study. Many older Black voters question the pragmatism of the DSA. While Shirley Sowell, a 66-year-old congregant of Philadelphia’s Salt and Light church, agreed with some DSA policy points such as free childcare, she said she was unsure if she’d vote for a DSA candidate. More progressive members of Congress would be at loggerheads with the Republican party, she said, which would preclude them from accomplishing their lofty goals. “The socialists – they’re out here to help people and to get things that need to be done,” such as lowering housing costs for low-income people, Sowell said. “In today’s time, it’s kind of hard trying to get all that stuff. You’re battling back and forth with the other party.” But some DSA wins this year have also shown that the group’s message can draw Black voters of all ages – even if the candidate’s connection to the organization is tenuous. In August, Black DSA member Angie Nixon secured votes in counties with the most Black residents by 30 points over retired Lt Col Alexander Vindman in the Florida Democratic primary for US Senate. Nixon, who worked as a community and union organizer for decades, only joined the group in June and was not endorsed by it. And after she became the first DSA member to win a statewide primary, she stated that she doesn’t identify as a socialist. Nixon’s campaign manager, Eunic Epstein-Ortiz, said in a statement to the Guardian: “As she has consistently said, she doesn’t align with any group 100%.” Pennsylvania state representative Chris Rabb, a Black DSA member, secured the Democratic primary for Pennsylvania’s majority Black third congressional district in May 2026. “Average voters appear to be more enthused about anti-establishment/anti-corruption candidates who don’t frame problems and solutions with left/right labels, but offer bold platforms that acknowledge & address people’s daily struggles,” Rabb said through text message. The DSA’s advantage has been “its organizing strength that focuses on engaging and educating young, disaffected and/or anti-establishment voters toward mobilizing grassroots efforts to get out the vote in Democratic primaries where conventional campaigns and party apparatuses have chosen not to”. ‘Where else would you go?’ Millennial and gen Z members within the DSA said that the historically white organization is drawing more Black voters than ever before. The DSA struggled with diversity in the past, said member John Lewis, due to a suppression of Black political power throughout national history, which precedes the organization’s formation. Lewis, a 34-year-old Black man from Louisiana who serves on DSA’s national political committee, didn’t become aware of socialism until he was an adult, after several years of organizing. “There’s been a 100-year-long campaign to disorganize Black people and communities of color, and we know from COINTELPRO [an FBI covert operation] we know this from … white domestic terrorism after the civil war,” Lewis said. “I’ve seen the most conversation and the most interest and curiosity among Black people in DSA this summer than ever.” Marcus Board, an associate professor of political science at Howard University and a democracy visiting fellow at Harvard’s Kennedy School, said that there is a long tradition of young people driving socialist movements, which is now reflected in the generational divide seen in Black voters’ support of the DSA. Socialism has “always been youth-based and youth-driven”, Board said. “A lot of the Black Panther movement was invested in socialist politics. The SNCC [Student Nonviolence Coordinating Committee] was invested in socialist politics. Fred Hampton very famously talked about promoting socialism before he was killed at 21 years old in Chicago.” During the civil rights movement, Black activists and their allies fought to regain political agency that was taken away after the Reconstruction period after the civil war. Black elected officials grew from roughly 1,500 in 1970 to about 4,900 in 1980. Shirley Chisholm’s 1972 run for president, followed by Jesse Jackson’s presidential bids in 1984 and 1988, further solidified Black political power within the Democratic party. But during that same period, more young Black organizers were interested in starting their own revolutionary movements, rather than falling in line with existing power structures. Now young people are working within the Democratic party to push it to the left, Board said, and are supporting the progressive political movement, the Working Families Party. Barack Obama’s presidential election may be another reason that young Black voters are more interested in pushing the Democratic party to the left, Board said. “Obama’s presidency has in fact impacted gen Z by making it clear that just because you have a Black president does not mean that you have progressive politics,” Board said. Older Black voters, on the other hand, “are incredibly pragmatic, and so they’re thinking not just about the future, but also historically and what they believe is actually possible”, said Ranada Robinson at the progressive funding coalition Georgia Alliance for Progress. As the senior director of research and strategy, Robinson studies Black and brown voter behavior through focus groups and statewide surveys in Georgia. “A lot of times when you hear older Black voters talking, they’re weighing the balance between who they want in office and who they think can actually win.” Lewis, an engineer, learned about socialism for the first time from a Wikipedia page in 2020. “My family comes from both sides of the Mississippi River in Mississippi and Louisiana, living in rural poverty and in urban poverty in Atlanta,” Lewis said. “Seeing those things, you recognize poverty is the correlation between so many of these evils when you talk about health outcomes and crime.” He saw socialism as a solution to some of the systemic injustices he witnessed, Lewis said: “Democratic control for workers, trying to eliminate poverty, trying to make sure people are cared for.” A few months later, Lewis helped found the first Baton Rouge DSA chapter recognized by the organization. Initially, Lewis was the only Black person in the chapter, joined by three white members. But within about a year, the group grew to 15 members, with half of them being Black. Just as young Black people are helping push the Democratic party left, they have also helped expand the DSA’s racial justice platform. Recently, the DSA recognized the historical injustices that Black and Indigenous people have faced by calling for a recognition of tribal sovereignty, honoring treaties and reparations for enslavement. “Calling for reparations and calling for finishing Reconstruction in the DSA national program didn’t come from nowhere,” Lewis said. “That came from many Black folks and white folks who were like, ‘Hey, this is a priority for me politically. This is something I care about.’” When Black voters ask Carlson White why they should join the DSA, he tells them that it’s one of the only spaces where a working-class Black person can advocate for economic equality within a democracy. “Where else would you go?” Carlson White said. “DSA really is the only functional home for any sort of radical Black politics that is capable of winning a majority within a mass party.”

title: ‘He feels more relatable’: Burnham’s conference speech wins praise from drifting Labour voters
summary: The UK prime minister has earned his party a rehearing but the battle of public opinion is not yet won
text: “He’s offering what no other politician has offered for a long, long time. He actually feels like he’s one of us,” was how Neil, a geography teacher, described Andy Burnham in our focus group on Thursday night. Neil wasn’t alone in his praise: this group of Labour 2024 voters – some of whom had drifted to Reform, the Tories and Greens during the Starmer era – provided the most positive reception for a politician since Boris Johnson at the height of his Covid-vaccine bounce. Talent manager Megan said: “He feels more relatable to people from a working–class background.” Simran, another teacher, added: “He’s obviously better than the others in the short timeframe that he’s been in his position.” Linda, who works in banking, went further, saying: “He actually sounds like a person that’s there, not just for himself, but for all of us, which none of the others prior to him came across that way.” That praise for Burnham stood in stark contrast to his predecessor Keir Starmer who was, as contracts manager Craig put it, “just a shambles from the moment they won the election up until he left”. None of the group felt it would have been better to keep the former PM in place. Labour’s conference also seemed to have cut through the noise of the attention economy. Most had picked up at least something from the prime minister’s speech and liked what they had heard. After seeing the clip where Burnham spoke emotionally about the death of his father, the group, in contrast to some online criticism, appreciated a politician willing to show his human side. But what about two of the substantive proposals in the speech? On Burnham’s pledge to revisit the UK’s relationship with the EU there was an overwhelming feeling Brexit had been a disaster. Most in this group had voted to remain, but even those like Darren, a field manager at a utility company who had voted Leave, felt cheated: “The amount we got told we were putting into the EU, I thought we could stand on our own two feet … we got told quite a few things, and it didn’t quite happen.” Interestingly, for most of the group it was less the economic impact of Brexit that worried them but instead the sense of isolation in an increasingly dangerous world and a less reliable US. But, and here is the caveat, once it came to the specifics of what rejoining may involve the group were far more cautious. Many felt if Britain could rejoin on its old terms it would be a “no brainer”. But the participants now worried that Britain would end up with a worse deal as punishment. Neil said: “I voted remain, but we’ll get utterly shafted if we rejoin … what do they gain?” Others described feeling 50/50 and nervous about where we’d end up. If this group is anything to go by, Burnham’s biggest fight won’t be in the principle but the details. What about Burnham’s other, more controversial, pledge that the triple lock would be reformed to pay for social care? The discussion here revealed two things. First the rise in wages is less salient to people than other bits of the lock; most of the group felt as if their wages had not kept up with inflation for a long time anyway, so pensioners would not really lose out. As Linda put it: “My salary has not been increasing that greatly.” Second, reforming care is a real priority. For Tariq, who works in the pharmaceutical industry, this was an example that “sometimes you need to take hard decisions”. But the mood definitely shifted when the group were played a clip from Unite leader, Sharon Graham, opposing the move. Suddenly some participants worried this was “taking off pensioners” while others asked “couldn’t the highest earners fund it instead”. And the group were even more negative when they read former Institute for Fiscal Studies chief Paul Johnson’s analysis that triple lock reform wouldn’t pay for a national care service in the near term and so taxes would have to rise. None of the group were willing to pay more taxes, personally, for care. Simran said: “If the income tax increases any more, you’re going to find people are going to migrate.” Joanne, who works in dentistry, added: “I feel rather selfish about it because I don’t want to pay any more tax ... people just can’t afford to live a decent life at the moment.” This led to a wider discussion about the budget and people’s worries that, while Burnham had done some “small things”, was it just going to be, as Linda put it, “robbing Peter and paying Paul”. If this group is anything to go by, Burnham is impressing the voters who put Labour into office in 2024, and has earned his party a rehearing that Starmer simply could not. But beyond the top line, big questions remain on the details. The Labour leader can be happy with the reception for Tuesday’s speech but definitely cannot afford to rest on a post-conference glow in the battle for public opinion on his plans. (Participants’ names have been changed) • Luke Tryl is the UK director of the research group More in Common

title: Flydubai co-pilot used crash axe to attack captain, says UAE
summary: Attorney general says ‘terrorist attack’ was attempted by suspect who is said to have been barred from flying by Oman because of extremist views
text: The co-pilot of flydubai flight FZ1073 used an axe to attempt to carry out a “terrorist attack” during the Israel-bound flight, the United ⁠Arab Emirates prosecutor general has said. Disaster was narrowly averted on Wednesday when passengers and crew intervened to stop the co-pilot’s attempt to take control of the plane, which had 182 people onboard and plunged 16,625ft in just over 30 seconds. The descent was so extreme that part of the rudder was ripped off. Investigators have been trying to establish how the alleged attacker, who was seen by witnesses repeatedly stabbing the pilot in the cockpit, managed to smuggle a weapon onboard. But on Saturday, Gen Hamad ‌Saif Al Shamsi, a UAE prosecutor, said the co-pilot had used a crash axe to mount the attack, an implement typically kept inside the cockpit to use in emergencies, such as crashes or fires, and which would not have needed to be brought onboard covertly. “Investigations into the incident involving flydubai flight FZ1073 found that the co-pilot had attempted to carry out a terrorist attack,” Al Shamsi was quoted as saying by the state news agency WAM. Media outlets have named the co-pilot as Hammam al-Hammami, an Omani national. Speaking to the Associated Press, a Gulf diplomat said investigations were under way to establish whether he acted as a “lone wolf or had any connection with any extremist groups”. The Wall Street Journal reported that the co-pilot had been barred from flying by Oman over concerns he had adopted extremist views. He was then moved to an administrative job at Oman Air, according to the official, before being hired by the UAE-based budget airline flydubai. It was not immediately clear to what extent he was vetted when he was hired. A British university, Buckinghamshire New University, said a student named Hamam al-Hammami had “previously completed a distance-learning course in aviation management” at the institution. It added: “He did not undertake any pilot training at the university.” A flydubai spokesperson on Saturday said the circumstances surrounding the incident were still ‌under investigation and the airline was not in a position to comment further. The airline’s flights between Dubai and Tel Aviv have been suspended until further notice following the attack. A former flydubai crew member told the Wall Street Journal that all its pilots were subject to security screening before flights, as well as medical checks at least once a year. How the co-pilot managed to be working in the cockpit on Wednesday morning is a central question for investigators. It also raises serious concerns about background checks in aviation recruitment. Israel says it has agreements with foreign carriers to keep pilots out of its airspace who come from nations with which it does not maintain diplomatic relations. Israel and Oman do not have formal diplomatic relations. Security agencies from four regional countries were working to establish the co-pilot’s motives, aided by the US and other western governments, an official said, speaking on condition of anonymity to discuss details of the investigation. On Friday, Anwar Gargash, a senior adviser to the UAE president, called the attack a “dangerous terrorist act”. The incident is a test for the UAE government, which has earned a reputation for effective measures against extremist activities but has also bristled in the past over criticism of security lapses. Little else was immediately known about the co-pilot’s background. His Instagram account was active until the day of the flight and then deleted. The Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, said on Friday that the co-pilot had undergone “Islamist radicalisation” but provided no evidence. He added that Israel was looking into whether the co-pilot had acted under anyone’s direction and warned that anyone involved would pay a “heavy price”. Most of the passengers onboard were Israeli nationals. The Indian captain, Smit Machchhar, who had multiple stab wounds, has been praised for his bravery. He said he used his remaining energy while being stabbed to unlock the cockpit door, allowing people who had noticed loud noises to come in, tackle the co-pilot and stabilise the plane. In a video call with the Indian prime minister, Narendra Modi, Machchhar said: “I was lying on the floor injured but I told myself to go for one last push to open the door from inside. “Others came in and also played a role [in controlling the situation]. I was of course fighting for my own life, but at the same time I knew I was not going to let others die. After passengers restrained the attacker, two reserve pilots, who were onboard, safely landed the plane at Tabuk airport in north-western Saudi Arabia at 06.58 local time. The captain and co-pilot were taken to the UAE, as it leads the investigation. Officials have said a number of countries including Israel are participating. Netanyahu on Saturday said he wanted to invite Machchhar and Modi to light a flame at a national ceremony for Israel’s Independence Day next May, saying the role was usually reserved for Israeli citizens. In a video his office released of his telephone conversation with the hospitalised captain, he said: “You are a true hero of the brave peoples of India and Israel and you are a hero of the entire world.” With Associated Press and Reuters • This article was amended on 5 October 2026. An earlier version included a picture caption that could not be verified. This description has been changed.

title: They embraced the Fiat 500, the Vespa, even tuk-tuks. But will Romans draw the line at the golf cart?
summary: Authorities crack down on trade they says risks spiralling out of control – but operators say they are being targeted unfairly
text: On the edge of Piazza Navona, one of the grandest squares in central Rome, Barry and Linda, visitors from Texas in the US, stepped out of a golf cart. They planned to cross the square on foot, perhaps stopping to admire Lorenzo Bernini’s 17th-century Fountain of the Four Rivers, before being picked up by their driver at the opposite end. The couple had already done a walking tour on day one of their trip, and had been so exasperated by a stifling three-hour shuffle along a corridor towards the Sistine Chapel on day two that by the third day they wanted to give their tired feet a rest. “When I first heard you could do golf cart tours in Rome, I thought to myself: that sounds a little weird,” said Barry. “But then we decided to try it out.” He said the most enjoyable thing about the experience was “feeling the breeze”. Rome is a difficult city to navigate, noted Linda, especially its ancient narrow streets in the centre. “There are no sidewalks,” she said. “Our feet were hurting and we needed a break.” For visitors, golf cart tours offer respite from the heat, crowds and cobbles. For residents, however, their proliferation in recent years has become another source of frustration in a city already wrestling with traffic and overtourism. Taxi drivers are especially incensed, accusing golf cart operators of stealing their business, while one local newspaper said the city had been “taken hostage” by the vehicles. Now Rome authorities are cracking down on the burgeoning trade. Police intensified checks this week after the news agency Adnkronos reported that 90% of the roughly 500 golf carts circulating in the city were operating without authorisation. In recent days, police stopped 131 carts around Piazza Navona, the Pantheon, Circo Massimo and the Spanish Steps, issuing €38,000 of fines for offences ranging from unlicensed driving to illegal parking. Rome’s leaders are pushing for regionwide measures to properly regulate an activity that “risks spiralling out of control”, Eugenio Patanè, a councillor for mobility, told the news agency Adnkronos. Prices vary based on the type of tour and duration, but the cost per person can start at €100 and exceed €400 for a half-day trip. Barry and Linda paid €310 for their three-hour ride. “But it’s worth it,” said Barry. Rome’s traffic problem is hardly new. Julius Caesar tried to tackle the issue more than 2,000 years ago by banning private vehicles and commercial carts from the city’s streets during the day. Today, pedestrians, cars, scooters, delivery vans and the occasional rogue horse-drawn carriage all jostle for space. Tourists can also take tours in Fiat 500s, on Vespas with sidecars, and even in tuk-tuks. But the golf carts seem to have drawn a special kind of wrath. “There are too many of them,” said Nora Fahmi, who works at Trevimage, an art photography shop behind the Pantheon. “We’ve had this shop for 13 years and have seen all sorts of things, but the golf cart situation is kind of wild.” Nearby, two teenagers from Israel were taking a rest on a parked cart. “We just want a lift to the Colosseum but you have to book online,” said their mother, Miri. “Rome is too crowded and it’s difficult to walk.” Elisa Isacco, who lives in the Monti area, spares no sympathy for the weary tourists. “What do they actually see or learn about Rome when they are on one of these things?” she said. “I find myself having to dodge them all the time – Rome is chaotic, it’s like a jungle.” Amid the clampdown, several golf cart tour operators have banned staff from speaking to the press. But Leo Pavoncello, a driver for an operator in the Jewish Ghetto area, was happy to publicly defend the trade. “Golf carts are silent and eco-friendly,” he said. “Rome is not an easy city to visit but these vehicles allow people with disabilities and families with children to see the sites in a comfortable way. On top of that, they provide jobs for young people.” Pavoncello, who was subjected to the police checks and was found to be operating fully legitimately, argued that a few rotten apples were giving the business a bad name. “I don’t understand why they are targeting us,” he said, although he suspects “taxi lobbies” are piling on the pressure. “But Rome is a touristic city that has always been full of traffic, and the golf carts are simply another mode of transport.”

title: ‘It’s enraging’: lawmakers call for action after Guardian investigation into convenience store overcharges
summary: Congress members say pricing practices at 7-Eleven and Circle K stores underscore everyday Americans’ affordability struggles
text: Five US House members have called out pricing practices at the US’s two largest convenience store chains in response to an investigation by the Guardian. The Guardian found that 7-Eleven and Circle K stores frequently charge customers more at the register or pump for snacks, gas and other items than the prices they promise on the shelf or on outdoor fuel signs. “It’s enraging that these massive companies are now essentially forcing us to fact-check every price tag and receipt just to make sure we’re not getting ripped off,” the representative Becca Balint, a Democrat from Vermont, said in a statement. “7-Eleven and Circle K have a responsibility to make sure the price we see on the shelf is the price we pay at the register.” She called on the Federal Trade Commission to “investigate this trend and hold these companies accountable if they’re deliberately misleading customers”. “This story is disturbing,” added the California representative Nanette Barragán, whose congressional district covers a swath of Los Angeles county. “Americans work hard to feed their families. As Trump and Republicans continue to skyrocket the cost of food and other basic necessities, businesses need to keep their prices transparent and fair.” Balint and Barragán are part of a growing wave of politicians who have made inflation and affordability centerpieces of their pitches to voters. Others include New York’s mayor, Zohran Mamdani; the Texas Democratic US Senate candidate James Talarico; and Rick Fazio, a Republican state legislator who is running for governor in Connecticut. Donald Trump has dismissed affordability concerns as a “hoax” and “con job” perpetrated by Democrats. An AP-NORC poll released on Thursday found that just 17% of Americans approve of the president’s handling of the cost of living. The Guardian’s convenience store investigation included a review of customer complaints and state and local price-accuracy inspections. Between 2023 and 2025, for example, 7-Eleven failed 41% of its price inspections in Arizona and 47% of price inspections in both Colorado and Utah. Over the same span, Circle K failed 35% of its inspections in Florida, 39% in Arizona and 62% in North Carolina. The two chains did not answer detailed lists of questions from the Guardian. In brief statements, 7-Eleven said it takes pricing accuracy “very seriously” and Circle K said it is “committed to complying with all applicable laws and regulations”. Convenience stores are not the only retail outlets where customers often pay more at checkout than what shelf tags declare. The Guardian reported in December that the nation’s two largest dollar store chains, Dollar General and Family Dollar, had repeatedly failed to honor their shelf prices, charging more at checkout for everything from frying pans to Frosted Flakes. Both chains told the Guardian they were committed to pricing accuracy. In response to the findings, 30 US House members signed a letter demanding answers from the two dollar store chains about their pricing practices. The lead author of the letter, the Illinois representative Nikki Budzinski, said the Guardian’s new reporting on convenience stores “shows the problem goes even deeper … We will not let up on federal oversight until these chains fix this glaring issue and treat consumers with the fairness and respect they deserve.” In response to the new reporting on convenience stores, the Illinois representative Delia Ramirez said she is concerned about people in her district who are vulnerable to unfair practices in the marketplace. “Through price gouging, price fixing, predatory algorithms and corporate monopolies, corporations have put profits and production over people, and our government has allowed it,” Ramirez said. “People in my district are tired. Our communities want their representative to put an end to corporate greed” and to fight for lower prices and higher wages. In Los Angeles county – where 7-Eleven stores failed 37% of their price-accuracy inspections between 2023 and 2025 – the Democratic representative Laura Friedman said the “last thing” families already paying high prices for gas and groceries need is to be charged more at checkout than what is promised on the shelf. “California law says you must charge the price on the sign, so these reports of overcharging, including in our own communities, are deeply concerning,” said Friedman, whose district includes West Hollywood and Burbank. “State and local officials should investigate, and any store found breaking the law needs to be held accountable.” Experts told the Guardian that one of the challenges to solving the problem is a lack of inspection and enforcement resources across much of the country. When state and local agencies do take action, modest fines and even large settlements often do not stop deep-pocketed retail chains from charging customers more than their posted prices. “If the goal is to prevent stores from ripping off their customers by posting phony prices on their shelves, this can be done by imposing serious fines,” Dean Baker, senior economist at the Center for Economic and Policy Research, wrote in an article about the Guardian’s investigation. “If a store had to pay a $50 fine for every instance where they overcharged someone 10 or 20 cents on a pound of apples, they would very quickly figure out how to get their shelf prices to agree with their cash register prices.”

title: Outgoing prison chief in Christa Pike case oversaw five ‘botched’ executions, lawyers say
summary: Frank Strada will leave role next month after uproar over execution attempt, which sent Pike to hospital in critical condition
text: Tennessee’s prison chief is resigning after the failed execution of Christa Pike, which lawyers say was the fifth “botched” execution under his leadership across two states since 2022. Frank Strada, the commissioner of the Tennessee department of correction, has faced mounting questions about the state’s highly secretive death penalty protocols since Wednesday evening when Pike became the first death row prisoner in the US to to be injected with lethal drugs and survive. Witnesses said Pike, 50, was heard choking and struggling an hour after receiving the first injection of pentobarbital, a sedative, and after a second dose failed to kill her she was hospitalized in critical condition. The scrutiny on Strada comes as Pike’s failed execution has sparked international outrage, with lawyers and advocates calling for a national halt on executions in the US. Pike’s lawyers have called the process “cruel and torturous”, and one death penalty expert said it was the worst botched execution in modern history. Bill Lee, Tennessee’s Republican governor, on Saturday announced that Strada would step down from his role this month, the Associated Press reported. Lee also suspended executions in the state until the end of the year and ordered an independent inquiry. Strada said in a statement that stepping aside would “be in the best interests” of the state as the independent review was carried out to determine why Pike’s execution failed on Wednesday. Lee called the case “deeply disturbing”, but when a reporter asked him about Strada’s leadership on Friday, Lee responded: “So far as we know, the department of correction followed exactly the protocol that was outlined.” The journalist was pressing the governor on Strada’s history, which includes another failed execution in May of this year, when Tennessee officials struggled for more than an hour to locate Tony Carruthers’ vein, prompting the procedure to be called off. And when Strada was a deputy prison director in Arizona in 2022, the state carried out three executions that experts and attorneys said were prolonged and “botched”. Death penalty lawyers said there were common threads in the five problematic executions under Strada, including the prisoners’ protracted suffering and questionable injection procedures, and argued that Lee should never have appointed Strada given his Arizona record. Tennessee department of correction spokespeople declined to answer questions about Strada’s record on Friday and said the commissioner was unavailable for an interview. A spokesperson for Lee did not respond to inquiries. ‘Botched’ executions in Arizona After joining Arizona’s corrections department in 2020, Strada oversaw executions, which included forming the teams that carried out the procedures, monitoring the practices and obtaining lethal injection drugs, he said in a deposition. In the May 2022 execution of Clarence Dixon in Arizona, a media witness said the execution team struggled to place IVs to administer the lethal drugs, ultimately requiring them to make an incision by his groin to insert the IV. That process, according to his attorneys, took roughly 40 minutes. In June 2022, a witness said Frank Atwood, a death row prisoner, had to help executioners find a vein after officials repeatedly struggled to kill the 66-year-old, who had a degenerative spinal condition. And in November 2022, Arizona officials struggled to find a vein in Murray Hooper, forcing them to insert a catheter into his groin. The Death Penalty Information Center, a non-profit organization that studies capital punishment, classified all three Arizona executions as “botched”, based on researchers’ analysis. “Botched” is not a legal term, but the group says executions can be botched when there is a breakdown in protocol or unexpected problems or delays that cause needless suffering. Dale Baich, who represented Arizona death row prisoners during Strada’s tenure, said the fact that execution officials’ struggled to find veins suggested they were not qualified: “If your job is to access veins, you should be able to do that ... to me, it indicated the department of corrections did not properly vet those team members.” In a 2023 declaration in a court case, Arizona’s corrections director said his review of execution procedures identified “several critical issues”, including “inadequate knowledge and expertise” of the people involved in executions, concerns about the IV team’s procedures, and concerns about the efficacy of the drugs. Trouble in Tennessee Despite reports of three botched Arizona executions, Lee appointed Strada to head Tennessee’s prisons in early 2023. That appointment came while Tennessee was grappling with its own scandals around lethal injections, with a 2022 state-commissioned independent report finding that Tennessee had failed to follow protocol in several executions, not properly tested drugs and had a “tunnel-vision, result-oriented” approach to executions. Death row attorneys have argued that Strada has failed to address the problems raised in that report. Under Strada, Tennessee removed a key training requirement for people involved in lethal injections, according to Kit Thomas, a death row attorney. Before Strada joined, execution team members were directed to practice catheterization with saline, records show. But training guidelines put in place under Strada eliminated that requirement, saying: “No IV is inserted into the person playing the role of the inmate.” “He reduced the training requirements and we’ve seen disastrous results,” said Thomas. “He oversaw executions in Arizona which involved prolonged, torturous attempts to establish IV lines, and he brought a similar practice here.” After Strada left Arizona, corrections officials made changes to the state’s lethal injection process, including increasing the number of people on the IV team responsible for injections and requiring more rigorous training, records show. But Strada has not overseen similar changes in Tennessee, instead implementing a protocol that mirrored the older Arizona policy of requiring only two people on the IV team that does injections, Thomas noted. Thomas also provided excerpts of a November 2025 deposition where Strada was questioned by death row attorneys. When Strada was asked what he considered to be a successful execution, he responded: “The condemned is put to death.” When a lawyer followed up, asking: “Anything else?”, Strada replied: “No.” Thomas said Strada’s response suggested he had “no regard for the experience of the individual being executed other than that they end up dead”. The response, she added, echoed the same “tunnel-vision” approach to executions that investigators had called out in the Tennessee-commissioned report in 2022. In the 2025 deposition, Strada further acknowledged he had not followed some of the recommendations of the 2022 report, including failing to hire a full-time employee or consultant with a pharmaceutical background to provide guidance on the lethal injection process and failing to hire a full-time employee or consultant to assist with locating lethal injection sources. “What good is an independent investigation if those investigators provide recommendations that are ignored?” said Thomas. Questions mount over lethal drugs Questions about how the state acquires, maintains and administers lethal injection drugs are critical following the botched killing of Pike, who was sentenced to death in 1996 at age 20 for the murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer. Pike’s lawyers said Friday that she remained unconscious and on a ventilator. Prison officials have not addressed questions of what might have gone wrong, but some outside experts have questioned whether the pentobarbital could have been degraded or may have failed to properly enter her bloodstream and instead seeped into surrounding tissue. Tennessee keeps secret the identities of people involved in executions and basic facts about the drugs it uses in executions. Thomas pointed to a number of questions that Strada previously declined to answer, including whether he was using the same drug supplier he used in Arizona, whether Tennessee’s supplier had complied with Food and Drug Administration rules and regulations, and whether he had any procedures or checklists to ensure the lethal injection chemicals had not been adulterated. Stephen Ferrell, federal defender and one of Pike’s attorneys, expressed skepticism about the governor’s call for another independent inquiry, noting the last independent investigation on the state’s death penalty system resulted in continued secrecy. “We are kept in the dark,” he said in a press conference Thursday, noting that reporters who served as witnesses to Pike’s botched killing also raised concerns about the secrecy surrounding the execution procedure: “Our predictions are downplayed, and yet they continue to come true. Tennessee should not be torturing its citizens in the name of justice.” As the governor sidestepped questions about Strada, candidates running to replace Lee said they would not keep Strada in the job if they were elected in the November midterms. Robin Maher, executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center, said Tennessee officials should answer questions about Strada’s involvement in multiple botched executions. She also raised concerns about the lack of transparency or accountability after Carruthers’ botched execution in May: “We saw no information about why this had gone wrong and no explanation or corrective action to ensure that wouldn’t happen another time.” “Governor Lee should urge his officials to be forthcoming about all the mistakes that may have been made and to accept responsibility for whatever went wrong with these executions,” she continued. Ed Pilkington contributed reporting

title: Can anything politicians say at Sunday’s election stop young people from leaving Bosnia?
summary: They are the support base for non-nationalist parties but are voting with their feet and not on ballot papers
text: On a perfect October morning in Sarajevo, the motivation for young people to be leaving Bosnia and Herzegovina in droves is not immediately apparent. The country’s capital is basking in the autumn sunshine and the pavement cafes in the shadow of the Sacred Heart Cathedral are packed. People lingering over coffee and cigarettes mix peacefully with the Swedish football fans in town for their team’s Nations League match. But Sarajevo’s many charms have not been enough to keep young people in Bosnia. One local organisation that tracks emigration estimated that more than 600,000 people had left the country in the decade after the 2013 census, when the official population was 3.5 million. “If I weren’t optimistic, maybe I would also move out,” said Timur Vilić, a 28-year-old municipal councillor in Sarajevo, who is standing on Sunday for election to the cantonal government. He represents Our Party – a multi-ethnic, non-nationalist, liberal movement that he admits faces a struggle to appeal to voters in a country dominated by ethnonationalist parties. “People are not ready for a significant change,” he said. “They’re afraid of uncertainty. I think there needs to be a new generation which doesn’t understand why people are willing to put up with this situation and who are willing to maybe vote for us to try something different.” The problem for Our Party – and other non-nationalist movements – is that the young people who make up their support base are voting with their feet, rather than making their mark on ballot papers. In theory, Sunday’s vote should be one of the great European festivals of democracy, with the election of no fewer than 14 prime ministers and five presidents. But the plethora of posts on offer reflects a fiendishly complicated system of governance. The Dayton agreement’s creation of two powerful regional “entities” – with a weaker central government – was intended as a stopgap to ensure peace after the ruinous conflict of the 1990s. Instead, it has perpetuated the divisions in the country. Most Serbs live in the Republika Srpska (RS), while the Federation is home to most of Bosnia’s Croats and Bosniak Muslims. There is no incentive for the ethnonationalist leaders to change that situation – or to appeal to young people who see a brighter future outside the country. “They don’t want young people to be interested, and young people are not interested in politics,” said Sarah Ćato, gesturing over her shoulder to a banner of the unsmiling leader of the Bosniak SDA party looming over the cafe tables in central Sarajevo. The 19-year-old student of political science and international relations is eligible to vote on Sunday for the first time – but she says that her age group feels unseen by the political mainstream. “Young people don’t know how to vote or who to vote for because nobody’s standing for us,” she said, adding that the reluctance to engage in politics reflects its status as a “taboo subject” after the end of the conflict in 1995. “I think educating youth from middle school on how to be a good citizen should be mandatory.” But there seems little chance of that happening, given that Bosnian children learn different versions of their country’s recent history depending on whether they are Serbs, Bosniaks or Croats. Indeed, the curriculum in the RS now celebrates Radovan Karadzic and the late Ratko Mladić – both convicted of genocide by an international tribunal in The Hague – as “national heroes”. East Sarajevo is just a short drive from the centre of the capital – but it is on the other side of the “entity line” that divides the Federation from the RS. The road signs are written in Serbian Cyrillic, and young people grow up “surrounded by murals of war criminals”, as 23-year-old local resident Dijana Papaz put it. She worked on an exhibition with Sarah Ćato called What If the Border Is Within You?, looking at the divisions between Sarajevo and East Sarajevo – and how young people overcome them. Papaz rejects ethnic labels, referring to herself as “Bosnian”, but she concedes that the glorification of Mladić following his death in August reflects both enduring divisions and the need for change. “We need to do something about our constitution, because Dayton wasn’t supposed to last 30 years,” she said. “It was supposed to be a temporary thing after the war while we made the country better, but that never happened.” People born since 1995 may have no memories of the conflict or its causes, but they do hear plenty about it from family members. And Ajna Mešić from the Youth Initiative for Human Rights says the continuing exodus of Bosnia’s brightest prospects can also be put down to pressure at home. “Our parents tell us to go,” she said. “Growing up, my destiny was to be a lawyer in Germany. Then somewhere in high school, I remembered I have free will. But a lot of parents will tell you that they fought the war for nothing and they don’t want us also to live here.” Young faces were thin on the ground at a pre-election rally for the non-nationalist Social Democratic party (SDP) opposite Sarajevo’s historic city hall, with red flares reflecting off the Miljacka River as party activists put on a show. But 23-year-old Benjamin Ahmedbegovic, the vice-president of the local branch of the SDP’s youth forum, admitted he did not expect the polls to change the country’s situation – or the propensity of its young people to leave. “Political instability has been one of the main drivers of migration from Bosnia and Herzegovina,” he said, pointing to the phenomenon of people “voting for their own” as an aggravating factor. “Everyone just wants someone who has the same ethnic label to be in power, rather than judging whether they do something well or not.” That means the elections are unlikely to bring any surprises – or any reasons to make young Bosnians who are thinking of leaving change their minds. They may, as Vilić puts it, “miss the coffee”. But they certainly will not feel the same way about the divisive politics that leave their country stuck in the past.
