title: Cyclospora found at Mexican farm linked to lettuce outbreak, FDA says
summary: Announcement from US officials comes after CDC declared end to outbreak that infected nearly 13,000 people
text: The Food and Drug Administration said on Friday its inspectors had detected cyclospora at the Mexican farm blamed for the largest foodborne illness outbreak of the parasite in US history. FDA inspectors said Friday they found cyclospora in two places: a wastewater tank and a drainage ditch used for lettuce cultivation. They said it was unclear how the lettuce became infected. The agency’s announcement comes less than a month after the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) declared an end to the multi-state outbreak, which infected nearly 13,000 people across 21 states and led to 570 hospitalizations and two deaths. It also follows an announcement from regulators at Mexico’s own food safety authority, which conducted its own investigation and said cyclospora was not detected in the lettuce or water at the facility. That conclusion came days after the FDA was forced to retract a faulty test result that had incorrectly identified cyclospora in a sample of lettuce from Taylor Farms collected at the border. The FDA announcement comes more than six weeks after the agency sent its investigators to the farm in Guanajuato. The visit was the agency’s first time there in more than seven years following a steep drop in international food safety inspections after the Covid pandemic. While it’s unclear how the contamination took place, the FDA claimed the samples provide “strong epidemiological data” linking the outbreak to the Taylor Farms site. In a separate statement, Taylor Farms attributed the contamination cited by FDA to an independent grower “who is no longer part of our supplier program”. “Our facility remains closed in central Mexico as we work with our research team to implement enhanced safety protocols from the field to the facility,” the company said. Cyclospora is a microscopic parasite that commonly causes watery diarrhea “with frequent and sometimes explosive bowel movements”, according to the CDC. Other symptoms included loss of appetite and weight, stomach cramps, bloating and increased digestive gas. The illness, called cyclosporiasis, is less common than foodborne illnesses caused by other germs, including salmonella and E coli.

title: Magnitude 4.8 earthquake hits Victoria with tremors felt across Melbourne
summary: The epicentre was at Leongatha, 130km south-east of Melbourne, with residents reporting houses shaking just after 2am
text: A magnitude 4.8 earthquake struck Victoria in the early hours of Saturday morning, shaking Melbourne and waking people across the whole region. Geoscience Australia said it detected an earthquake with a preliminary magnitude of 4.8 at 2.01am near Leongatha, 130km south-east of Melbourne, with the tremors felt across the city’s eastern suburbs. Geoscience Australia said it had received thousands of reports from people who said they had felt the earthquake. Posting on Facebook, Brian Morley in Narre Warren said “felt it and woke me up”, while Theresa Stevens said: “Shook our house in Garfield.” Other posts indicated the quake had been felt in Preston, Heidelberg Heights, Venus Bay and many other parts of Melbourne. The quake was estimated to have struck at about 10km below the Earth’s surface. Victoria’s State Emergency Service said the earthquake was a “timely reminder” to remember the drill to follow during an earthquake and that was drop to the ground, take cover under a sturdy piece of furniture and protect your head and neck, and hold on until the shaking stops. The Bureau of Meteorology said there was no tsunami threat from the quake. The quake occurred in a region of South Gippsland considered to be amongst the most active seismic zones in Australia. Victoria’s two most recent quakes with magnitudes of 5 or above, however, were recorded elsewhere: a 5.9 magnitude in 2021 near Mansfield, in the state’s north-east, and a 5.0 on the Great Ocean Road in 2023. The quake on Saturday morning was the largest recorded in the state since that shock in 2023. An aftershock of 3.1 magnitude was recorded 55 minutes after the 4.8 magnitude earthquake early Saturday, with a magnitude 3.3 earthquake also recorded on Thursday morning at Yarram, about 80km east of Leongatha. Mark Quigley, associate professor of earthquake science at the University of Melbourne, said aftershocks could be felt for weeks in the region. “South Gippsland is one of our more seismically active parts of the country,” Quigley told the ABC. “We know it’s an area where seismicity is common, [and] we know we would expect aftershocks from an earthquake of that magnitude.” He said the earthquake was the result of a two by three kilometre area of rock about 10km below the surface slipping five to 10 cm rapidly, releasing seismic energy. Quigley said that earthquakes were not being recorded more often, despite a seeming increase in frequency in recent years. While the earthquake was “not an opportunity for people to panic or anything”, Quigley said it could be useful for people who lived in the region to consider whether they had items in their houses that could be damaged or create a safety risk in the event of a larger quake. “We know from the geological record we’ve had much larger in Gippsland in the past, larger than six and possibly as large as magnitude seven which I can assure you would cause widespread damage should they occur.” The last earthquake to cause property damage in Victoria was the 2021 quake, which resulted in tremors about 700km from the epicentre.

title: Partner of Gypsy Rose Blanchard found dead in Louisiana home
summary: Kenan ‘Ken’ Urker, 34, who died of apparent drug overdose, was partner of woman convicted of murder of mother
text: The on-and-off partner of Gypsy Rose Blanchard, who spent time in prison for her role in the murder of her abusive mother, was found dead inside his Louisiana home on his 34th birthday on Thursday in what authorities described as an apparent drug overdose. The sheriff’s office in Lafourche parish, Louisiana, confirmed Kenan “Ken” Urker – the father of Blanchard’s daughter – was discovered on Thursday after relatives asked police to conduct a welfare check at his residence. According to a sheriff’s office report on the case, Anita Blanchard said she and her husband – who is Gypsy Rose Blanchard’s half-brother – went to Urker’s home and saw him lying unconscious through an outside window. A man who was with the couple then entered the house through a window and found Urker unresponsive. The sheriff’s office report obtained by the Guardian states that Urker was not breathing and was “cold to the touch”. Authorities who arrived at the scene were “able to see Mr Urker from the living room area lying on his back in [a] bed”, the report said. Deputies reported that they then walked in the direction of the room where the bed was “and located paraphernalia (syringes and spoon) in the bathroom next to a brown powdery substance”. Authorities also found a syringe and a handgun on the nightstand beside the bed. Besides being cold to the touch, Urker “appeared to have been there for an extended period of time”. In an interview with People published on Friday, the 32-year-old Gypsy Rose Blanchard said that she believed Urker died from an overdose – though she said she did not know whether it was deliberate. “I don’t know if it was intentional or not,” Blanchard said, adding that Urker “was not in a good state of mind lately”. In a statement published to her Instagram story on Friday, Blanchard said Urker “endured an unimaginable level of public scrutiny and relentless cyberbullying across social media platforms, including TikTok and Reddit”. “The cruelty directed toward him was something no human being should have to endure,” Blanchard wrote. “I believe the tremendous weight of that scrutiny and harassment had a profound impact on him, and I hope his passing serves as a reminder that there is a real person behind every screen, every headline, and every comment.” The sheriff’s office report on Urker’s death confirmed the case had been called in to the agency as an evident overdose. In a statement to the news media, Brennan Matherne, the Lafourche parish sheriff’s captain, said Urker’s death remained “under investigation” as of Friday. Matherne also said investigators as of Friday had not discovered “any signs of foul play”. Blanchard previously spent eight years in prison after being convicted of second-degree murder in connection with the 2015 stabbing death of her mother, Clauddine “Dee Dee” Blanchard. Dee Dee Blanchard was found stabbed to death in her home in Springfield, Missouri, in June 2015. Gypsy Rose Blanchard had provided her then boyfriend, Nicholas Godejohn, with a knife and hid in a bathroom while he killed her mother. Blanchard pleaded guilty to second-degree murder. Godejohn, whom Blanchard met online, was sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole. Dee Dee Blanchard’s murder drew widespread attention after it was revealed that she had forced Gypsy Rose to pretend she was seriously ill and undergo medical procedures she did not need. Blanchard met Urker while serving her prison sentence, from which she was released in late December 2023. She said on the We Need to Talk podcast in June that Urker had contacted her after watching Mommy Dead and Dearest, a 2017 documentary about Gypsy Rose and Dee Dee. As Gypsy Rose put it, Urker sent her a “supportive letter, not on any kind of romantic level” and included his phone number. Urker proposed in October 2018. The pair later ended their engagement before reuniting in August 2019. They eventually split again and spent several years apart. During that time, Blanchard married Ryan Anderson. Anderson and Blanchard later separated, with her announcing the split four months after her release from prison. Blanchard and Urker rekindled their relationship in April 2024. Eight months later, they welcomed their daughter, Aurora Raina Urker. Ramon Antonio Vargas contributed reporting

title: Federal judge halts Big Bend border wall construction in blow to Trump agenda
summary: Plan to install barriers through popular national park sparked outrage from advocates and politicians alike
text: A federal judge has temporarily blocked the Trump administration from expanding the border wall and other security infrastructure across the Big Bend region of west Texas, where contentious plans to build roads and vehicle barriers through a popular national park have led to furious backlash and public protests. US district judge Kathleen Cardone’s ruling after a Friday hearing in El Paso deals a major blow to the Trump administration’s efforts to expand the border wall through west Texas at breakneck pace, while riding roughshod over the objections of local business owners, landowners, public land advocates and politicians from both parties. Plans to mar Big Bend national park with new roads and 6-ft tall vehicle barriers have drawn the most national attention since the Trump administration started advancing the border wall construction earlier this year. Images of bulldozers plowing up ground for new roads at the park in August drew outrage, prompting Rodney Scott, the CBP commissioner, to temporarily halt construction. Construction resumed in September. Friday’s ruling came after a hearing in a lawsuit filed by the Friends of the Ruidosa church, the Center for Biological Diversity and river guide Billy Miller seeking to overturn several Department of Homeland Security (DHS) waivers that suspended dozens of environmental and historical protection laws to speed construction. Cardone blocked the DHS waivers in her ruling, saying that the plaintiffs were likely to win and would suffer irreparable harm if construction moved forward. The ruling bars CBP from border security infrastructure construction or ground disturbance, unless it complies with the federal laws that DHS tried to suspend. “This is a historic victory for Big Bend and everyone who loves this wild corner of Texas,” said Laiken Jordahl, a public land advocate with the Center for Biological Diversity. “No administration has the right to destroy a crown-jewel national park for political theatre.” “But this fight is far from over,” he added. “We won’t rest until Big Bend’s environmental protections are fully restored and the illegal waiver that allowed so much destruction is gone for good.” CBP has already awarded five contracts for Big Bend totaling more than $6bn to expand what the agency calls the “smart wall” – a mix of 30-ft steel bollard fencing, vehicle barriers and surveillance technology. “We stand by our assessment and remain confident in our legal authorities to secure the border while preserving the unique landscape of the Big Bend region,” a CBP spokesperson wrote in an email in response to the ruling. “We are working with the Department of Justice on next steps.” The Republican-dominated Congress included a whopping $46.5bn for border wall construction in last year’s “big, beautiful” spending bill. That massive war chest led CBP to focus much of its efforts on the Big Bend region, which contains the longest unwalled stretch along the US-Mexico border. The plans have sparked furious responses from landowners and local political leaders, who say that unauthorized crossings are already rare there due to the region’s remoteness, the lack of nearby cities on the Mexican side and prominent cliffs that make it very difficult to cross through many stretches of the border there.

title: ‘We want action’: Fijian climate activist sends message ahead of UN talks in Pacific
summary: Lavenia Naivalu has seen the impact of the climate crisis first-hand and is determined to amplify Pacific voices at this year’s pre-Cop summit in Fiji
text: From her wooden veranda in Fiji’s remote Yasawa islands, climate activist Lavenia Naivalu remembers when the reefs were once so healthy, her grandfather would walk to the shoreline and return with fish. But life there has changed. “The reefs that the older generation of men spearfished in, no longer provide what they once did,” the 44-year-old says. “Young people … now must travel further out to sea to find fish for their families.” As she looks out at a white sandy beach, eaten away by rising sea levels, Naivalu recounts watching painfully as her three children “feel the brunt of changes in the climate. “I ask myself ‘what did they do wrong?’” The question is personal, but it’s also part of what drives her pursuit of climate justice for Pacific people, whose way of life is being threatened as the planet warms. At this year’s UN climate talks, known as Cop31, the region will be in the spotlight like never before. Next week, Fiji will host leaders ahead of the climate summit, where Naivalu hopes to draw attention to Indigenous and Pacific perspectives which she says are often relegated in global negotiations. The Pacific Islands are disproportionately affected by the climate crisis, despite accounting for just 0.02% of global emissions, according to the United Nations. “One thing that triggers me is when somebody else is speaking on my behalf,” she tells the Guardian. “I want to amplify the voices of my community and the people that I represent directly to all leaders.” Naivalu, an Indigenous representative participating in the Fiji meeting and the Cop31 summit in Turkey, has been a trailblazing advocate for her people. She was Fiji’s first female mata ni tikina, or district representative, overseeing seven village chiefs under the traditionally male-dominated governance system. Naivalu was also the first Indigenous representative selected to Fiji’s tourism board. A veteran of past Cop summits, Naivalu – who lives on the island of Nacula in the Yasawa islands – says bringing the climate talks home matters, but she wants discussions to move beyond language that people do not see reflected in their daily lives. “We talk about climate change, climate finance, about adaptation and mitigation,” she said. “But my people in Nacula don’t know what climate finance is; what we want to know is action.” On the frontline of the crisis Turkey and Australia agreed last year that the Pacific would host preparatory meetings before Cop31 under a compromise deal to resolve a standoff about where the 2026 summit would be held. The summit will be hosted in Turkey’s Mediterranean resort city of Antalya in November, while Australia will chair negotiations. Sivendra Michael, Fiji’s permanent secretary for environment and climate change, said Naivalu “closes the distance between negotiating room and the reef. “Fiji will go into Cop31 arguing for direct access to finance, for adaptation that is actually delivered at community level, and for Indigenous knowledge to be treated as evidence rather than decoration,” he said. “We are asking the world to trust Pacific leadership. That argument is far stronger when Pacific leadership is not confined to officials like me.” Having grown up in Nacula village, Naivalu has seen the impact of the climate crisis first-hand. “Water sources that used to sustain our village are now drying up, while seawater increasingly threatens the hand-dug wells,” she said. Nacula is doing its best to adapt to climate change – families now store drinking water for dry periods and women preserve food. Village chief, Ratu Manasa Naikasowalo, said he sees the value of Naivalu’s advocacy. “Her work has helped bring important connections and practical initiatives back to the community, including food security, salt making, coral planting and food-preservation programmes,” Ratu said. Naivalu knows adaptation cannot be left solely to frontline communities, and has witnessed the gap between Cop discussions and what happens at home. In Fiji next week, she will be bring the lived experiences of Indigenous communities into the Cop31 process, pushing for their voices to be heard as leaders negotiate climate finance, adaptation, loss and damage, and keeping global warming within 1.5C. “I don’t attend Cop to worry about texts and brackets; I attend Cop to forge partnerships with organisations that I believe can help the people of Nacula.”

title: Two Iranian men charged over alleged terror plot targeting Manchester’s Jewish community
summary: Man, most likely in Iran, was in contact with men arrested on the eve of Yom Kippur, police say
text: Two Iranian men have been charged in relation to an alleged terror plot targeting Manchester’s Jewish community. Police say another man, most likely in Iran, was in contact with them as part of a plot to get a bomb to attack Jewish targets. They were arrested two Sundays ago in broad daylight in a Manchester street during the Jewish holiday period. Rahman Salehi, 34, from Salford, and Salam Ahmadyan, 36, from Liverpool have been charged with preparing to commit an act of terrorism or assisting another to commit an act of terrorism. Police said the two men face charges that they gained materials and instructions to make a homemade bomb, identified possible targets and carried out reconnaissance ahead of an attack. Police said: “It is alleged that the two men were in contact with an overseas third-party who may be in Iran in relation to the plot.” The development, terrorism charges and detail given so far by British authorities marks an extraordinary chapter in British and Iranian relations. The prime minister, Andy Burnham, said Iran had a link to a weekend scare at RAF Fairford when five men were arrested close to the military base, along with three vans, one of which contained petrol in a barrel. Those men have now been bailed, having been arrested in the early hours of Sunday in the Gloucestershire countryside on suspicion of explosives offences and preparing a terrorist act. Vicki Evans, deputy assistant commissioner and the senior national coordinator for counter-terrorism, said: “This week also brought into sharp focus some of the wider threats being projected into the UK from Iran. “While this [Manchester] incident and the investigation into the RAF Fairford incident are not connected in any way, I want to reassure the public that CTP, working with our national security partners, are using the full range of our capabilities to protect the UK from any hostile acts.” The alleged plot in Manchester, where the two arrests followed a joint counter-terrorism police and MI5 investigation, has significant potential ramifications on several fronts. A government statement, minutes after the police announced the charges, revealed one of those accused over the Manchester plot had been granted asylum status in the UK and the other had an asylum application pending. The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, said that both of the accused had come to Britain via small boats, one in 2020 and another in 2023, when the Conservatives were in power. Mahmood said Iran had shown hostile intent to the UK in a series of incidents. “The fact both suspects arrived by small boat several years ago is a reminder of the importance of our relentless work to tackle illegal migration into this country,” she said. “While numbers are down, I know there is more we must do. “We will be unrelenting in our efforts to protect our Jewish communities, root out antisemitism in this country, and maintain our border security. “It is no secret that this country faces a range of serious threats from the Iranian regime. They target our Jewish communities and try to silence their critics overseas, often through proxies and criminal networks to hide their involvement. “The prime minister has been clear there are strong indications of Iran’s involvement in the events near RAF Fairford. We are responding to these threats with new powers and record funding to disrupt hostile activity. This week marked the anniversary of an attack on the Heaton Park synagogue in Manchester, where two worshippers died, as well as the attacker who said he supported Islamic State and was shot dead by police. Jews in Britain have faced a dramatic increase in attacks since the 7 October attack on Israel by Hamas, which has ties to Iran. It led to an internationally condemned military response by Israel in Gaza that has killed tens of thousands of people. The Community Security Trust, which offers security and advice to British Jews, said: “The charging of two men in connection with an alleged plot targeting the Manchester Jewish community will be deeply concerning to Jews across the UK. “These charges come exactly a year after the appalling terrorist attack at Heaton Park synagogue, and are a reminder of the ongoing terrorist threats facing British Jews. “We urge the Jewish community to remain calm and report any suspicious activity to police and CST.” In a statement, counter-terrorism police said the charges will allege the two men were “communicating with others using encrypted applications to acquire components to assemble a homemade explosive device”. Furthermore, the charges allege they obtained a document called “Steps for Making [a] Powder Chlorine and Car Brake Oil/Fluid Bomb”, obtained video instructions on how to make an improvised explosive device (IED), and got the “liquids, components and equipment” to make an IED. The charges also allege the men carried out internet research on targets, acquired “images, plans and maps of potential targets for attack” and carried out reconnaissance. Iran has faced attack by the US, with Britain allowing the RAF Fairford base to be used, which it said is for defensive operations by its Washington ally. Tehran’s embassy in London this week denied any involvement in the events at RAF Fairford. Evans said: “These are extremely serious charges and allegations, and have come about from a joint CTP investigation, working closely with our partners in the security services. This investigation has led to the disruption of what we believe to have been a plot targeting the Jewish community in Manchester.” The men were arrested on 20 September in Newton Street, in the Northern Quarter area of Manchester’s city centre, just before 3pm, hours before Yom Kippur, the holiest day in the Jewish calendar. Salehi and Ahmadyan are due to appear at Westminster magistrates court on 3 October. Frank Ferguson, head of the CPS’s special crime and counter-terrorism division, said: “Our prosecutors have worked to establish that there is sufficient evidence to bring this case to court and we remind all concerned that proceedings against the defendants in this case are active and they have the right to a fair trial.” As part of the investigation officers raided and searched properties on Epworth Street in Liverpool and Lancaster Road in Salford.

title: US sanctions three individuals and two charities over alleged Hamas financing
summary: The justice and treasury departments said they moved up to $2m to Hamas through charities and cryptocurrency, and six people were arrested across the US and France
text: The Trump administration on Friday unveiled sanctions against three individuals allegedly related to the Islamist militant group Hamas and against two charities based in France while also announcing six arrests – actions that the government called an “extraordinary counter-terrorism work” to expose “a sophisticated, multi‑year financing architecture”. Investigators alleged that the network moved more than $2m to Hamas “through deceptive charitable fronts and cryptocurrency channels”. The United States treasury department announced that all property in the US of those sanctioned is “blocked and must be reported” to the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) – and that entities owned by those individuals are also blocked. “Terrorist organizations like Hamas rely on sophisticated financial facilitators and fraudulent schemes designed to exploit the public to sustain their operations,” US treasury secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement. “Treasury will continue to identify, isolate, and impose consequences on those who provide Hamas with the financial lifelines it needs to survive.” Those sanctioned are Saleem Alzaq, accused of being part of the Hamas military wing and based in Gaza, as well as Faouzi Barika and Amel Oualid, both residents of France who run charities “ostensibly to raise money for humanitarian purposes to aid Gazan civilians”, according to the treasury. The charities sanctioned are Association Baraka and Ensemble C Mieux. The three of them allegedly collected more than $2m for Hamas during a six-year period beginning in 2020. And treasury officials said $1.5m was raised after Hamas’ deadly 7 October 2023 attack on Israel, which responded by launching war in Gaza. Meanwhile, the US justice department on Friday announced the unsealing of an indictment charging one man and the arrests of another three for their alleged “involvement in paying, soliciting and collecting funds for Hamas”. As part of that same plot, three other associates were arrested in France. The FBI said those men were engaging in a conspiracy to “funnel money to Hamas and fuel violent attacks”. Alzaq, 45, was the man indicted on charges of conspiring to provide material support to Hamas, among other counts. He allegedly “operated an international Hamas fundraising network that collects donations from individuals around the world, including … in the United States”, US attorney Jamie McDonald of New York’s southern district said in a statement. The US justice department also described Alzaq as a Hamas member in the Gaza Strip and a battalion deputy in the group’s armed wing. Justice department officials accused him of serving in “a Hamas propaganda office” as a photographer who “posted propaganda” of the organization on social media. Two of the three men arrested in the US were identified as Omar Adhami and Abdel Adhami, residents of the New Orleans suburb of Covington, Louisiana. The third was identified as Raed Yousef of the Tampa suburb of Lutz, Florida. A statement attributed to the US attorney for Louisiana’s eastern district, David Courcelle, alleged that the Adhamis provided Alzaq with “resources intended to fund Hamas’ relentless reign of terror”. The Adhamis and Yousef were accused of contributing tens of thousands of dollars to Hamas and could face up to 80 years in prison if convicted as charged. Some of the charges that they face include conspiracy to provide material to “a designated foreign terrorist organization” and conspiracy to commit money laundering. A statement from the Trump administration’s attorney general Todd Blanche said “anyone who finances or assists” terrorist groups should expect to face federal prosecution. A separate statement from the Trump administration’s FBI director Kash Patel said the agency would “never forget the horrific attack on Israel by Hamas” on 7 October 2023 – and that it would “never stop … efforts to cut off funding to Hamas terrorists”.

title: Brazil’s Lula says only he can stop rise of fascism under Bolsonaro’s son
summary: President leads huge rally in Rio before election on Sunday seen as most important for decades
text: The Brazilian president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, has claimed he is the only thing standing in the way of far-right “fascists” reclaiming power, as he led a huge rally through the streets of Rio ahead of Sunday’s crunch election. Speaking on the eve of the demonstration, the 80-year-old leftwinger said he had decided to seek a historic fourth term because he believed only he could prevent the family of his rightwing rival, Flávio Bolsonaro, returning to government. “If it weren’t for me standing up to these fascists they’d easily win another election. I’m the one standing in their way,” Lula told a popular podcast called Flow, before adding: “It’s either me, or it’s barbarism.” Hours later, Lula flew to Rio, staging what his team called a “victory march” between two highly symbolic downtown locations that played an important role in Brazil’s fight for democracy during the 1964-1985 military dictatorship. “What’s at stake is not the victory of one man, it is the victory of an idea, it’s the victory of democracy,” Brazil’s president said after the parade set off from the Candelária church. The church is the location where more than a million people, including Lula, famously gathered in 1984 to demand direct presidential elections. Lula, who was among those who spoke at that historic demo when he was an up-and-coming politician in his 30s, added: “Either we consolidate democracy, or we will lose it.” From Candelária, a sea of red-clad Lula supporters marched a mile south towards Cinelândia, the scene of an equally well-known pro-democracy protest in 1968 called the March of the Hundred Thousand. “No gringo is going to lay a finger on Brazil’s things,” vowed Lula, in an indirect reference to claims Donald Trump’s administration is seeking to sway the vote in Bolsonaro’s favour with a campaign of economic and diplomatic pressure. The decision to hold Friday’s rally between two such politically charged places spoke to how this year’s election has stirred up renewed fears over the future of Latin America’s biggest democracy. Election-eve polls suggest Lula holds only a slender lead over his adversary, whose father, the ex-president Jair Bolsonaro, is serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a failed coup after Lula beat him in the 2022 election. Many Brazilian democrats fear that if 45-year-old Bolsonaro wins this year’s election, he will move quickly to free his father and his fellow coup-plotters from jail – and then set about dismantling and co-opting the country’s democratic institutions, such as the supreme court. “This is the most important election of our lives – and we have to do everything we can to win,” said Marcelo Freixo, a politician from Lula’s Worker’s party (PT) who is running for a seat in congress. Freixo warned: “We spent 21 years living under a really harsh dictatorship. We fought so hard to attain our democratic institutions. And a victory for the Bolsonaro family – a family that always … openly defended the dictatorship and tried to stage a coup … would spell the end for our democratic process and institutions.” Valmir Aleixo, a 55-year-old history teacher who was one of thousands of people who joined Friday’s pro-Lula demo, said: “This is [a choice] between democracy and the savagery of far-right fascism. This is perhaps the most important election since the return of democracy in the 80s.” Noni Ostrower, 74, came to what was Rio’s largest leftwing protest in years carrying a homemade banner that read: “Democracy Is Valuable”. “I’m the daughter of two refugees from nazism. They came to Brazil from Germany because of this,” Ostrower said. “I was born here in Brazil … and today I have grandchildren and I absolutely do not want to see fascism return to Brazil – it would be a tragedy for the country. That’s why I’m here today.” During the campaign, Flávio Bolsonaro has vowed to pardon his 71-year-old father if elected, with some speculating Jair Bolsonaro could even become a minister. His brother, Eduardo Bolsonaro, a radical former congressman with ties to Trump’s Maga movement, reputedly hopes to become foreign minister. Flávio Bolsonaro has announced plans to appoint five firmly conservative supreme court judges. Luiz Eduardo Soares, a prominent anthropologist and writer, said he feared what might happen if the Bolsonaro clan managed to reclaim power. “I think these elections could be the last ones in my life, for my generation … What was done over the course of 10 years in Hungary, [Bolsonaro] will do in two,” Soares predicted in reference to the European country’s transformation into an “electoral autocracy” under its former prime minister, Viktor Orbán. Diogo Nogueira, a famous samba singer who came to the rally wearing his trademark panama hat, said: “We need to win in the first round so we don’t allow this type of people to get back into government. If they do get back in, it won’t just be a problem for four years, but for 10 or 20.” Polls suggest the election is likely to go to a second round runoff between Lula and Bolsonaro on 25 October, with Lula expected to secure about 45% of votes on Sunday and Bolsonaro 40%, according to the Datafolha pollster. But at Friday’s rally Lula claimed he could pull off a shock first-round win by claiming more than 50% of the vote. In an online broadcast, Bolsonaro insisted his campaign would prevail. “Brazil is a few hours from deciding its future … for the next 30, 40, 50 years. It’s the end of an era. title: Christa Pike remains on ventilator after failed execution in Tennessee
summary: Attorneys say hospital staff are working to clear pentobarbital she was administered from her system
text: Christa Pike remained hospitalized, unconscious and on a machine helping her breathe after her failed execution in Tennessee, her attorneys said in a court filing Friday. The attorneys said hospital staff were working to save Pike’s life and clear the pentobarbital she was administered from her system as of late Thursday. Pike received two doses of the drug in a failed attempt by the state of Tennessee to execute her on Wednesday. In the court filing, Pike’s attorneys said they believed problems with intravenous lines caused the pentobarbital to flow into her body instead of her bloodstream. “Apparently at no point did any member of the execution team realize that the IV lines were not correctly placed or that the veins had blown and that the pentobarbital was, in whole or in part, entering Ms Pike’s body,” they wrote. They also wrote that instead of “remedying this failure” the execution team proceeded to prepare and administer a backup set of pentobarbital syringes. In a statement reported on X by NewsNation journalist Brian Entin, Pike’s attorneys described her as “critically ill and … receiving medical care for the devastating effects of Wednesday nights events”. “We are working close with those closest to Christa to respect her wishes, safeguard her privacy and protect her rights as a patient during this extraordinarily difficult time,” the statement also said. “We ask that the public and the media respect that privacy as well.” Pike’s attorneys on Friday asked a state court to order Tennessee’s department of correction to preserve all evidence from her failed execution. “Preserving this evidence is essential to understanding what happened, ensuring accountability and protecting Christa’s legal rights,” her attorneys’ statement said. Pike, 50, was sentenced to death in 1996 at the age of 20 in connection with the 1995 murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer. Pike and her then boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, killed Slemmer at a job training camp in Knoxville, Tennessee. One grim detail about the case is that a pentagram had been carved into Slemmer’s chest. After the killing, Pike was diagnosed with bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder, her attorneys said. “It took me numerous years to even realize the gravity of what I’d done,” Pike had said in an earlier petition for clemency. “Even more to accept how many lives I affected. I took the life of someone’s child, sister, friend. It sickens me now to think I had the ability to commit such a crime.” According to the Death Penalty Information Center, the last execution of a woman in Tennessee was in 1820, meaning Pike would have been the first woman to be executed in the state in more than 200 years. Tennessee’s failed attempt to execute Pike has prompted top lawyers, doctors and members of the faith community to call for a moratorium on the death penalty in the US. The state’s governor, Bill Lee, has ordered a third-party investigation into Pike’s botched execution. He has also paused executions in Tennessee. The Associated Press contributed reporting

title: Hundreds gather in Mississippi to protest Republican redistricting: ‘This fight is familiar territory’
summary: Dozens of residents testify to legislature’s redistricting committee in heated hearing, the last of eight
text: Hundreds of people gathered across from the Mississippi state capitol building on Thursday evening to rally against the aggressive Republican efforts to draw maps that favor their own party. Shortly after the US supreme court’s decision in Louisiana v Callais, which severely weakened section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, Tate Reeves, the Mississippi governor, moved in lockstep with other Republican governors and lawmakers to call for a special session to redraw maps. However, before that special session could occur, Reeves canceled it and wrote on X that he expected “lawmakers to redraw congressional lines BETWEEN NOW and 2027 elections!” In August, members of the Mississippi legislature’s joint redistricting committee began a tour of eight redistricting hearings across the state. The last of those hearings took place Thursday evening in Jackson, the state’s capitol. “This fight is familiar territory for all of us. The giants of the civil rights movement didn’t fight so that we could sit this fight out. They fought so we could stand exactly where we’re standing right now and finish what they started,” Safia Malin, policy director at One Voice, a civic organization, told the crowd before the hearing. Malin was one of several speakers who reminded the people gathered of the history and fight for voting rights in the state, from the 1890 constitution, which disenfranchised Black voters and ushered in an era of Jim Crow, to the 1964 efforts of the Mississippi Freedom Democratic party and the work of Medgar Evers, Fannie Lou Hamer and others. Following the rally, those gathered marched to the capitol holding signs, their chants of “Leave our maps alone” and “Whose maps? Our maps” echoing through the capitol building. An hour before the hearing was scheduled to begin, the room was full, with some people leaning against the walls. Others sat in an overflow section outside and watched the proceedings on television screens. Prior to the proceedings, house Democratic leader Robert Johnson, who is Black, encouraged audience members to ensure that they made the historical record. “This is testimony,” said Johnson, one of several Democratic lawmakers who showed up to observe or speak at the proceedings. “And at some point it may be evidence. So let’s make sure we’re heard.” The committee, handpicked by legislative leaders, is primarily made up of white men. It consists of 16 Republicans, all of whom but one are white, and four Democrats, all of whom are Black. The committee did not answer questions, provide information about how the redistricting process would look on their end or explain how citizens’ testimony would affect their decision. And in a room full of dozens of Black men and women, six of the first 10 speakers were white. The first Black woman called to give her testimony was the 15th person to speak. Overall, 67 people spoke. Each person was given two minutes to speak. The proceedings lasted just under two hours. State auditor Shad White, who is considering a gubernatorial run, created controversy almost as soon as he began his comments. “The delta deserves better leadership than Bennie Thompson. It just does,” White said, as members of the audience booed. Bennie Thompson, who is Black, is Mississippi’s lone congressional Democrat. White, Reeves and other Republicans in the state have openly targeted Thompson and his district. Through continued boos, White said that there was a “silent majority” of people who “want better representation for the Mississippi delta”, and not someone who is “focused on running the January 6th committee”. Jesse Otto Smith, who was born and raised in Mississippi, said that the stakes of the redistricting hearing were personal. “I’m 76 years old. My father was born in 1926 – he couldn’t vote. My grandfather was born in 1891 – he couldn’t vote. That’s why I’m here. My great-grandfather was born as an enslaved man, considered less than a human, in 1861 – he couldn’t vote. He was a piece of property,” he said. “That’s why I am here. My mother graduated from Rust College, grew up in Starkville, but couldn’t go to school at Mississippi State, paid taxes without representation.” Walter Boone, who is white, called the redistricting efforts “Mississippi plan 2.0”. “The original Mississippi plan culminated in our 1890 constitution, and we cannot ignore that history. I’m not a scholar or trained historian, and even I know that Mississippi has been here before,” he said. “Our first reconstruction ended in much the same way, through a culmination of redistricting and fraud. Our Black elected representatives were stripped of their offices, and Black constituents did not see another person represent them that looked like them for 75 years.” Lauren Wilson, a sophomore at Tougaloo College from Tupelo, spoke in opposition to redistricting. She asked why the committee held hearings about redistricting, but not for Medicaid expansion or any of the myriad issues in the state. “If I’ve learned one thing from history, if I’ve learned one thing from the Lord, if I’ve learned one thing from my educators and my pastors, I’ve learned no matter who holds the position, the people hold the power,” she said. “The pharaoh had the position, but Moses had the power. Woodrow Wilson had the position, but Ida B Wells had the power. Lyndon B Johnson had the position, but Martin Luther King had the power. “We stand today before the committee who has to make a decision on redrawing the lines that seek to disenfranchise the people. So I want you to know that even though tonight you have the position, we hold the power.” The full legislature is expected to convene in a special session later this year to redraw the state legislative maps. While those maps would not affect November’s midterm elections, lawmakers will likely target Thompson’s seat before he is up for re-election in 2028.

title: Hawaii’s centuries-old sea arch collapses into Pacific after series of rough storms
summary: Hōlei sea arch, formed 550 years ago by erosion from ocean waves, no longer standing, National Park Service confirms
text: A famed centuries-old sea arch on Hawaii’s remote and rugged coastline has collapsed into the Pacific Ocean, the National Park Service confirmed on Friday, following a stretch of rough storms in the region in recent weeks. The beloved landmark, Hōlei sea arch, stood at around 90ft high for over half a millennium in Hawaii’s Volcanoes national park, located on the dramatic southern coast of the Big Island. It was naturally formed around 550 years ago due to differential erosion by ocean waves. The exact timing of the collapse is unknown. The National Park Service (NPS) said the arch was still standing on Wednesday 23 September, when the park was temporarily closed during Tropical Storm Nolo, but had collapsed by Sunday night, on 27 September. “The arch formed in ancient lava flows by removing rock along cracks and weaker rocks,” the US Geological Survey said in a description of the arch in 2014. “It will not be here for ever. Every day the ocean crashes against the pillar of the arch, eroding it a little more. One day, it will be gone.” Indeed, the cliffs on either side of the sea arch had shown signs of instability for years amid tropical systems and volcanic activity, the NPS said, meaning the arch’s collapse had long been expected. Earthquakes during the 2018 Kīlauea volcanic eruption and summit collapse damaged the cliffs around the arch. Then, in January 2020, new cracks and instability prompted the park to close the original viewing area and open a safer one further from the cliff edge three months later. Later that year, huge surf from Tropical Storm Darby broke off a chunk of rock from the arch’s lower portion. The Hawaiian islands have seen an unusually high number of severe storms this year, with storm activity in the Pacific running above average during what is already the peak of hurricane season. Experts say the pattern is consistent with El Niño years, when the Pacific often sees more tropical storms and hurricanes. Nolo, which rapidly intensified into a hurricane on 24 September – causing Volcanoes national park to shutter - was the third major storm to devastate the islands of Hawaii in recent months. Residents were still recovering from hurricanes Lala in August and Lowell in early September, which had flooded homes and roads, toppled trees and caused power outages, when Nolo then battered the islands with heavy rain and high surf. Forecasters have warned there is a high probability that this “supercharged” El Niño will reach a historic intensity, with its effects in strengthening the storms compounded by the broader overheating of the planet caused by the burning of fossil fuels.

title: Republicans pull funding of Trump-backed Senate candidate in critical North Carolina race
summary: Senate Leadership Fund is redirecting ad spending from Michael Whatley’s campaign to support other candidates
text: A major Republican political action committee pulled the plug on financial support for its Senate candidate in North Carolina, Michael Whatley, according to multiple reports, as the party begins to triage resources amid increasingly dire midterm polling. The Senate Leadership Fund (SLF), the campaign arm of the Senate majority leader, John Thune, has withdrawn its ad spending in North Carolina to redirect support to other candidates, Semafor reported on Friday. The New York Times, CNN and other publications have confirmed the report with sources close to the fund. The retirement of Thom Tillis from the US Senate opened the door for Democrats to flip the seat. Former governor Roy Cooper, a venerable presence in the state’s politics, easily won the Democratic nomination. Whatley, a former chair of the Republican National Committee, was handpicked by Donald Trump and viewed as a more mainstream candidate than other Republican contenders in the closely contested state. The SLF had pledged $71m to hold North Carolina’s US Senate seat, and started targeting Cooper before he even won the nomination. The fund ran ads last year trying to link Cooper with the murder of Iryna Zarutska, a 23-year-old Ukrainian refugee, in an unprovoked attack onboard a light-rail train in Charlotte. Cooper was not in office at the time of the attack. The Pac’s advertising in North Carolina has consistently focused on crime and public safety, featuring a series of interviews with crime victims. Ronald Hayes, whose son Shemar was murdered in 2024, appeared in one such ad. Hayes later said he had been “swindled” by the SLF, believing he was going to appear in an advertisement against gun violence and not a political campaign ad. The SLF had planned to spend $30m more supporting Whatley. But polling data presents an increasingly difficult political map for Republicans trying to hold control of the Senate. Republicans have a 53-47 majority today. With the vice-president, JD Vance, as a tiebreaker, Republicans can afford to lose no more than three seats to keep control. The Cook Political Report rates the North Carolina Senate race as “leans Democratic”. Seven other races are toss-ups; five are currently held by Republicans, including seats in Alaska, Iowa, Maine, Ohio and Texas. Roger Marshall, the senator from Kansas, is facing a stiff challenge from Adam Hamilton, a Methodist pastor. Cook rates the race as “leans Republican”. The SLF reportedly will redirect its North Carolina spending to support Marshall. Cooper has persistently maintained a polling lead over Whatley despite the deluge of political ads. An AARP poll released on Monday gave Cooper an 11-point lead, consistent with other recent polls. Cooper has never had less than a four-point lead on Whatley in any poll this year. In-person early voting starts on 15 October in North Carolina.

title: Kennedy Center Honors awards moved to new venue amid Trump’s onslaught
summary: Ceremony will not be hosted at its traditional home for the first time since awards began in 1978
text: The Kennedy Center Honors will take place away from its traditional home this year for the first time in its history as the John F Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts remains in jeopardy amid Donald Trump’s ongoing battle to have it named after himself. The Capital One Arena in Washington DC is now set to host the ceremony on 7 December, a Kennedy Center spokespersonsaid. The list of honorees this year has not yet been announced. The ceremony has been staged in the Kennedy Center’s Opera House each year since the awards began in 1978. The change came as the Trump administration faces challenges in Congress and the courts over its plans for Washington landmark, including the possibility of demolishing it. The Kennedy Center Honors are widely regarded as one of the leading US distinctions recognizing achievement in the performing arts. Last month, Christopher Cooper, a US district judge, directed the Trump administration to give at least 30 days notice before taking any action toward tearing down the building. Earlier this week, the Republican senator Mike Lee blocked a bipartisan bill that would have prevented Trump from demolishing the Kennedy Center without the approval of Congress. Trump addressed the future of the center while speaking with reporters last month, threatening to tear the whole facility down. The center had abruptly closed for renovations, following cratering ticket sales amid his influence over programing there since he retook the White House, followed by a limbo. “I think that the Trump administration should certainly have recognition. Because frankly, if we don’t do that, it’s going to close. It’ll end up being ripped down,” Trump said. The dispute has involved efforts to put Trump’s name on the facility. The center’s board, whose members were largely appointed by the Republican president, had voted in December to add his name to the institution. Congress established the facility, which opened in 1971, as a memorial to President John F Kennedy, who was assassinated in November 1963. In May, Cooper ordered the Kennedy Center to remove Trump’s name. In his ruling, he said the venue “must be named for, and is meant to honor, President Kennedy alone”. Last month, Trump ordered that the Kennedy Center be closed “immediately” and warned that he would cancel the planned renovation of the institution unless federal courts permitted his name to appear on the front of the building. That move followed another vote by Trump’s handpicked board to shut down the institution’s performing arts building. The board cited financial and safety concerns in support of the decision. Trump’s plans for the Kennedy Center have also led to protests.

title: UCLA law school accused by justice department of illegally using race in admissions
summary: University denies allegations, saying it is committed to making admissions decisions in compliance with all laws
text: The Department of Justice said on Thursday that the law school at the University of California, Los Angeles illegally considered race in admissions. The announcement follows a similar accusation against the university’s medical school and comes as the Trump administration ramps up scrutiny of colleges’ processes for selecting students. The Trump administration has also accused the UC Berkeley School of Law and the medical school at the University of California, San Diego of illegally discriminating against white and Asian applicants. The UCLA School of Law denied the accusations and said in a statement that it was committed to making admissions decisions in compliance with all applicable laws. “Students are admitted through a comprehensive, merit-based review process that considers each applicant’s achievements and experiences,” the statement said. “We are confident in our process.” Affirmative action in college admissions has been illegal since a 2023 supreme court ruling forbade it. The same ruling said colleges could continue to assess how applicants’ backgrounds might speak to broader characteristics, but the president has accused colleges of using applicants’ personal statements and other proxies to consider race in admissions – which conservatives view as illegal discrimination. The justice department said UCLA’s law school discriminated against white and Asian American students by favoring Black and Hispanic applicants in its 2023, 2024 and 2025 incoming classes. The department said its analysis found the mean LSAT score was lower for admitted Black applicants than for admitted white applicants. The department also said admissions staff at the law school instructed applicants during recruitment efforts, including one called the “Diversity Admissions Open House”, how to reveal their race in essays. “Like many of its peer institutions, UCLA Law School runs a two-tiered admissions system whose academic bar for acceptance shifts up or down depending on the color of your skin,” said Harmeet Dhillon, head of the justice department’s civil rights division, in a news release. The Trump administration earlier this year tried to compel higher education institutions to release data including the race and sex of colleges’ applicants, admitted students and enrolled students to enable it to investigate whether the schools were considering race in admissions. A federal judge in August halted that effort, granting a preliminary injunction after 17 Democratic state attorneys general filed suit. The federal judge said the federal government probably had the authority to collect the data, but the demand was rolled out to universities in a “rushed and chaotic” manner. The states argued the data collection risked invading student privacy and leading to baseless investigations of colleges and universities. They also argued that universities had not been given enough time to collect the data.

title: Ann Widdecombe murder suspect charged with planning terror act against Nigel Farage
summary: Joshua Kerry, 28, of Rotherham in South Yorkshire, charged with one count of preparation of terrorist acts, say police
text: The man accused of murdering Ann Widdecombe has been charged with engaging in conduct in preparation of acts of terrorism including against Nigel Farage. Joshua Kerry, 28, of Rotherham in South Yorkshire, was charged by the Crown Prosecution Service on Friday with one count of preparation of terrorist acts. The charge relates to activity alleged to have taken place between 31 May 2024 and 8 July this year, counter-terrorism police said. Vicki Evans, the head of counter-terrorism policing, said: “We have been running a hugely intensive and complex investigation for some time. The charge announced today is a result of the tireless work of investigators across the counter-terrorism policing network. “This investigation has been led by a dedicated team of detectives, analysts, and forensic experts, working on multiple lines of enquiry, which has resulted in this very serious charge.” Kerry was due to appear at Westminster magistrates court on Wednesday, police said. The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, said the charge raised “serious questions” about the security of MPs. She wrote on X: “I know the new charges made today will be extremely concerning. My profound sympathies are with Nigel Farage and his family. “Let no one make any mistake: an attack on anyone in politics is an attack on us all. “This case raises serious questions about the security of those in public life. We must use this as an opportunity to reset. Once parliament returns, I will update on our work to strengthen protections for those who choose to serve.” Widdecombe, 78, a spokesperson for Farage’s Reform UK party and a former Conservative minister, died in July after being hit over the head with a hammer 21 times at her home in Haytor on Dartmoor, Devon, a court previously heard. She was found lying face down on her kitchen floor by her gardener on the morning of 9 July and declared dead by emergency services shortly afterwards. Kerry is accused of her murder. The suspect spoke only to confirm his name, date of birth and address during a hearing at Westminster magistrates court in July. He was not asked to indicate a plea. Olivia Field, the chief executive of the Jo Cox Foundation, which was set up in honour of the Labour MP who was murdered in 2016 in West Yorkshire, said: “No one in public life should have to fear for their safety. “Violence, abuse and intimidation not only endanger individuals and their families, but threaten our democracy and have no place in public life. “We must do more to prevent the rising levels of abuse and intimidation in politics. That means looking across society – from education and political literacy to the safety of online environments – alongside ensuring that appropriate security and support are in place for politicians, their staff and families.” In August, CTP reopened a year-long investigation into an alleged firebomb attack at Farage’s home in south London. The Metropolitan police and CTP London said they investigated the incident as an “attempted burglary” but made no arrests before the case was closed pending any new lines of inquiry. After its reopening, CTP London identified a line of inquiry that it said “may have been relevant” but had not been “identified and pursued by them at the time”.

title: King Charles III to acknowledge ‘darkest days’ of Britain’s colonial rule during Caribbean tour
summary: Buckingham Palace say the king will not ‘shy away’ from Britain’s role in slavery when he visits Commonwealth nations later this month
text: King Charles III will acknowledge the “darkest days” of colonial rule and slavery while touring Caribbean countries on a visit beginning this month, but will not formally apologise, a Buckingham Palace spokesperson said on Friday. The king will first visit the Bahamas and Guyana alone, followed by a trip with Queen Camilla to Antigua and Barbuda, where Charles will give a speech at a meeting of Commonwealth heads of government, the palace said. Charles, 77, who is still receiving treatment for cancer, will visit former colonies that are now independent from Britain and are members of the British Commonwealth. He remains head of state in the archipelago nations of the Bahamas and Antigua and Barbuda, a role that is largely ceremonial. The palace spokesperson told reporters the king’s visit, from 27 October to 4 November, would not “shy away from the ‘darkest days of our past’, as His Majesty has described them”. Charles used the phrase in a speech in Barbados when he attended the ceremony in which it became a republic in 2021, removing his mother, Queen Elizabeth II, as head of state. He also said then that the “appalling atrocity of slavery” stains Britain’s history. The palace said Charles had worked to acknowledge “the wrongs of the past” and “right inequalities that endure”, and on this trip would “renew his personal, wholehearted and continuing commitment to that process”. The UK government reiterated last month its rejection of calls for the payment of slavery reparations after a Jamaican delegation filed a petition addressed to Charles on the issue. It called on the monarch to refer three questions on the legality of the transatlantic slave trade to the Caribbean island’s highest court of appeal based in London. Modern British royals have expressed remorse for the brutal slave trade that enriched their ancestors but like the UK government have not issued an official apology for the slave trade. The palace said discussions about the colonial legacy and the slave trade were “important” but “primarily matters for governments to address”. On a 2022 Caribbean tour, Charles’s son Prince William and his wife, Catherine, were met with anti-monarchy protests and calls for slavery reparations. Charles’s younger brother, Prince Edward, later that year cancelled a visit to Grenada after pro-republican protests there. In Antigua and Barbuda, the royals will attend a parade to mark 45 years of independence. Guyana, the only English-speaking country in South America, is a republic and Charles will make a state visit on the 60th anniversary of its independence from Britain. The trip will feature plenty of meetings with local people and will focus on “the vibrant present and promising future of each country”, the palace said. The programme includes meetings with cricketing legends in Antigua and Barbuda, where the West Indies team is based, and meeting conservationists responsible for Guyana’s rainforest.

title: Georgia holds emergency meeting on AI exposing voters’ secret ballots
summary: A Princeton researcher found that publicly available election records could be combined with AI to link voters to their ballots
text: When voters cast their ballots, their votes are supposed to remain secret: from their family, their neighbors, and the government. But what if artificial intelligence could make secret votes visible? Last month, Max Springer, a postdoctoral research fellow at Princeton University’s Center for Information Technology Policy, tested the prospect of identifying voters based on their Georgia ballots with a $20 subscription to an AI large language model and data obtained from an Open Records Act request. “Within a couple of hours, I had a pipeline to analyze and identify secret ballots across the state of Georgia and the agent told me exactly what further information it would need to identify real voters’ ballots,” Springer wrote. “At no point did the agent refuse to comply or raise concerns over implementing the exploit.” The issue has raised alarms among Georgia’s election officials less than two weeks before early voting starts in the high-stakes midterm election that will determine control of the US Congress. Ballot secrecy is a democratic safeguard, allowing voters to shield their selection from anyone who might try to influence or intimidate them into voting a certain way. But Springer’s test showed that he could use AI to find out who people voted for, using Georgia’s public election records. Georgia’s state elections board held an emergency meeting on Thursday morning to discuss how artificial intelligence has made it easier to identify voters through their ballot code, leaving people more vulnerable. Georgia’s outgoing secretary of state, Brad Raffensperger, locked down the tabulation data that someone might use to identify a voter, ordering any public release to redact the ID numbers after an election, which “substantially address[es] this flaw”, said Ben Adida, an MIT-trained cryptographer and the founder of the election technology non-profit VotingWorks, as he addressed the board on Thursday. Election workers make a record of every voter who comes through a polling place. Voters then choose candidates on a touchscreen, which then prints out a paper ballot. The voter feeds that ballot by hand into a scanner to be tabulated. “When a voter inserts their ballot into a tabulator, a digital record of that ballot is created. Think of it as a row in a spreadsheet. One row is one scanned ballot. It’s often called a cast vote record, or CVR for short. In order to later retrieve the CVR, the tabulator assigns a unique identifier to each CVR at the time of scanning.” The flaw shows up in how the machine records that ballot, Adida said. The identifying is not actually random enough. Using AI, the early-voting list and the cast-vote record file for each county, Springer, the Princeton researcher who says he’s never been to Georgia, could recover the voting order for 1.52m ballots, or 98.9% of in-person ballots in 114 of the 139 counties he examined. “In some of Georgia’s counties, I can determine the exact ballot cast by every voter at the vote centers – ballot secrecy is entirely lost,” he wrote. In places with few voters on any given day, like tiny Heard county, Springer said: “the agent was able to match the majority of the 650 early in-person voters to a specific ballot, and the rest to within a single swap.” About four years ago, election security researchers had discovered a flaw in the software used by Georgia voters that could connect a voter’s identity to their secret ballot. The fact that ballots have an identifying number assigned at all is a product of the political paranoia attending Georgia’s elections. An ID number for each ballot addresses a fear of unscrupulous election workers double-stuffing ballots through tabulator machines. But if the order of ballots can be paired with other information, like sign-in data when a voter checks into the precinct, or perhaps Flock camera imagery that shows when someone entered a building on a slow day, then that ballot can be synched up to a voter’s name. Representatives of the secretary of state’s office say they have been shouting into the wind for help with this problem for three years. Requests for money have been bound up in the long-running political feud between Raffensperger and conservative legislators positioning themselves in the orbit of Donald Trump and 2020 election skeptics. (Raffensperger has remained a top Trump target after refusing to overturn his defeat in the state’s 2020 presidential election.) Spokesperson Robert Sinners sent a litany of emails and phone records showing requests for an appropriation to upgrade Georgia’s voting system, to no avail. The governmental affairs committee secretary, Tim Fleming, now the Republican nominee for secretary of state, was on the receiving end of many of those requests. “We have presented numerous plans to the legislature for this – not, not just a patch, but an entire overhaul of the software to fix up any known vulnerabilities,” Sinners said. “Guess what we were gifted with from the legislature? A big fat goose egg.” Fleming did not respond to a request for comment. Other states use Dominion software for their elections. Every other state has either patched the software or withholds vulnerable voting data from public inspection. Georgia law has two competing imperatives. The Georgia constitution explicitly requires a secret ballot, and the law protecting ballot secrecy in Georgia is among the strongest in the country. However, Georgia law – with revisions driven by the election disputes of 2020 – also demands transparency for election records. Elections board member Salleigh Grubbs raised that latter point as she circulated a draft proposal that would call for poll workers to hold ballots in a tray before voters cast them into the machine, to shuffle the printed pages out of order as a way to defeat the problem. Grubbs said that Raffensperger’s fix – redacting the ID numbers in the cast vote record – violates the law. But county elections officials and other board members – including Janelle King, a conservative Republican – dismissed the proposal as equally problematic. “We are asking our election officials to completely retrain everybody that has been a part of this process up until this point on how to administer the election,” King said. “I also have major concerns about dropping our ballots into a secured box and then having other individuals scan my ballot. How do I know that in the shuffling something doesn’t fall out? I mean, I just have some major concerns about whether or not we are creating more problems while we are trying to address a problem.” With early voting around the corner, changes to processes now are “a day late and about $30m short,” Sinners added.

title: G7 to release up to 100m barrels of emergency oil and diesel reserves
summary: Leaders agree a coordinated drawdown after surge in prices and Donald Trump’s threat to cut off US supplies
text: Leaders of G7 nations are to release up to 100m barrels of their emergency diesel and crude oil stockpiles after Donald Trump threatened to cut off supplies of US diesel. The French President, Emmanuel Macron, said ministers from some of world’s largest economies had agreed to release stocks from their strategic oil reserves after crisis talks on Friday. Macron convened the leaders’ video call to discuss the global surge in diesel prices, and Trump’s threat to cut off US diesel exports unless Europe tapped their own stockpiles to help cool global markets. Under proposals reportedly drawn up by Macron, the current G7 chair, members will release 50m barrels of diesel and 50m of crude oil into the global market to ease prices. The agreement suggests European countries will avoid being cut off from vital supplies of US diesel after coming under pressure from the White House in recent days to release their emergency supplies or face a US diesel export ban. Trump said he was considering a ban on diesel exports after the surge in sales to overseas buyers pushed US diesel prices to record highs in a blow to the economy before the US midterm elections in November. Macron said G7 nations – which also includes the US, UK, Germany, Italy, Canada and Japan – wanted to “work in a coordinated manner to help bring down the prices of petroleum products, particularly diesel”. He added that the G7 members and partners would front-load a substantial diesel release within the first 20 days and that ministers would discuss the “possibility of additional diesel releases as necessary” in the coming days. “We have all committed together to releasing these strategic reserves in the proportions I mentioned, with a focus on diesel, and we are all committed to ensuring there are no export bans, and President Trump, in particular, was very clear on this point,” Macron said. Trump said in a post on his Truth Social platform that Europe had “agreed to release a massive amount of their heavily stocked Diesel Oil” and that the process would start “immediately”. The threat of a US export ban presented a considerable challenge for Europe, which produces about 70% of the diesel it consumes from domestic refineries but relies on imports to make up the shortfall. The ongoing disruption to fossil fuel exports from the Middle East has limited output from the region’s refineries as well as those in China, which is a leading buyer of Gulf crude. Meanwhile, Russian refineries have come under attack from Ukraine, causing its fuel output to fall to 20-year lows. In response, the US exported a record high of 1.9m barrels a week to overseas buyers in early August as the slump in global refining squeezed supplies across Europe and Asia. The record exports caused the US’s own distillate stockpiles to fall to their lowest seasonal levels since 1996, causing diesel pump prices to climb above $5.85 a gallon (£1.18 a litre) for the first time in early September. The proposed ban on US exports was expected to fuel greater competition for cargoes on the global market which would push prices in the UK and Europe well beyond current record levels. In the UK, the average price of diesel at the pumps climbed to a record high of £2 a litre on forecourts on Friday, putting more pressure on motorists and the wider economy. The cost of filling up an average family car is now £110, according to the RAC motoring group, nearly £32 more than before the Iran war. UK lorries, vans and farming vehicles are also typically diesel-fuelled, meaning the price rises will be felt in the higher cost of goods across the economy. Brent crude oil was trading at just above $100 (£76) a barrel on Friday, compared with about $72 before the Iran war started. It fell to about $98 a barrel after news of the emergency stockpile release before returning to more than $102 a barrel by the end of the day. Macquarie Group’s Walt Chancellor said a US ban on diesel exports would not address the underlying problem in the US or the global market. “The core issue the US faces is not a diesel problem. Nor is it a refined product problem. It may not even be a petroleum problem. It is a global energy problem,” he said, according to CNBC. “So what is the solution then? In short, more oil through the strait of Hormuz and out of the Middle East. Anything short of that is really just shuffling deck chairs,” he added. The IEA, the world’s energy watchdog, ordered the largest release of government oil reserves in its history in March when it agreed to release 400m barrels of emergency crude, to help calm the oil price shock sparked by the US-Israeli attacks on Iran. The intervention represented a third of the group’s total government stockpiles and was more than double the release of 182m barrels of oil made in 2022 after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. • This article was amended on 4 October 2026. Walt Chancellor was speaking in response to the news of a potential US ban on diesel exports, not about the subsequent reaction by some European nations.

title: How Trump changed the way US women vote
summary: A decade after his infamous Access Hollywood tape, the gender divide is again shaping a pivotal midterm election
text: A decade ago, Donald Trump’s improbable presidential campaign was rocked – and nearly derailed – by the now-infamous Access Hollywood tape, a 2005 recording in which the real estate developer turned reality TV star boasted about kissing and grabbing women without their consent. “When you’re a star, they let you do it,” he said, a remark he later downplayed as “locker-room talk” before musing that the tape might be fake. (It wasn’t.) In the moment, it felt fatal – the ignoble end of an explosive campaign for the White House. Back then, Americans hadn’t quite grasped Trump’s capacity to shock but not surprise. Within days, the outrage receded, swallowed by two more “October surprises” – WikiLeaks released the hacked emails of Hillary Clinton’s campaign manager, John Podesta, and then-FBI director James Comey announced the bureau was reviewing new emails related to her private server. That November, voters punished the first woman to be nominated for president by a major party for her emails, among other grievances, real and imagined, and handed the presidency to the man who had boasted that he could “grab em by the pussy”. US women haven’t voted the same since, and next month’s midterm elections offer another test of their tolerance for Trump in the Trump era. Long divided by race and class, Trump’s rise – or perhaps Clinton’s defeat – splintered US women further, along lines of educational achievement and marital status. In 2016, Trump won white women overall, but Clinton prevailed among college-educated white women, a partisan reversal from the presidential election four years earlier. In 2018, suburban women voters “revolted”, propelling Democratic victories and sending a record 102 women to the US House of Representatives in what was hailed as another Year of the Women. A conservative backlash brewed. The Senate confirmed Brett Kavanaugh to the supreme court after Christine Blasey Ford testified that he had sexually assaulted her when they were teens – a claim he vigorously denied. Gen Z grew up in the shadow of that collision. As a cohort, they are marked by a wide ideological gender divide, with gen Z women – many mobilized by the overturning of Roe v Wade – becoming more progressive and politically engaged, while their male peers drifted rightward into Maga and the “manosphere”. Anger over the loss of federal abortion protections helped forestall Democratic losses in the 2022 midterms. But the gender gap wasn’t enough to shatter the glass ceiling in 2024, when Trump defeated Kamala Harris – even after a jury found him liable for sexual abuse and defamation in a civil suit brought by writer E Jean Carroll. A gender divide once again looms over the midterm map that will determine the balance of power in Washington for Trump’s final two years in office. A recent New York Times-Siena poll found 65% of women disapproved of Trump’s handling of his job as president, compared with 52% of men. According to the survey, 57% of women would back the Democratic House candidate in their district, whereas only 45% of men said the same, a dynamic that played out across three key Senate contests surveyed in the poll – Maine, Michigan and New Hampshire. Trump has maintained that he has empowered women throughout his business and political career. His chief of staff, Susie Wiles, is the first woman to ever serve in the role. But polling suggests women are deeply dissatisfied with the president’s second-term performance, including, according to one national poll, one in four women who voted for him. In Maine, Republican senator Susan Collins, long considered untouchable, is facing voters for the first time since Kavanaugh joined four conservative justices to end the constitutional right to abortion. Her Democratic opponent, logger-turned politician Troy Jackson, is working hard to ensure voters don’t forget that their senator cast a decisive vote to put him on the bench. The Times poll shows him leading among women voters by 53% to 44%. Trump has cast the November election as a referendum on his presidency. Will voters cement his power – or turn over control to Democrats, and grind his agenda to a halt? It all may depend on what US women want. Can US voters trust everything they see? Most Americans don’t know Hasan Piker.
