This is the decline. As powerful and transgressive as he’s been, the country does not have a positive outlook right now. In fact, the negativity and pessimism among voters has reached a point that is unparalleled since Jimmy Carter,” Rick Wilson, a longtime Republican strategist, said about Trump’s final years in office. Read more: ‘The weaker he gets, the more dangerous he gets’: Trump lashes out as his power wanes Watch this race: A Hobbs’ Choice in Arizona A “unity ticket”? In these partisan times? Katie Hobbs, the Democratic governor of Arizona, and John Giles, a former Republican mayor of Mesa, a populous Phoenix suburb, are giving bipartisanship a whirl in the battleground state. Facing a tough re-election, Hobbs tapped Giles – a vocal Trump critic who formally left his party in May to become an independent after endorsing Kamala Harris in 2024 – to be her running mate. Hobbs’ choice of Giles is an overture to the independents and moderate Republicans she will likely need to secure a second term. Once a reliably Republican stronghold, Arizona has elected a string of Democrats statewide since Trump was first elected. In 2020, voters there narrowly backed Joe Biden for president before swinging back to Trump in 2024. This year is the first time Arizonans will elect a lieutenant governor, after voters approved the second-in-command role in 2022. Hobbs faces Republican congressman Andy Biggs, a staunch Trump ally who played a prominent role in the effort to overturn Biden’s 2020 victory. Biggs has chosen Sine Kerr, a dairy farmer and former state senator as his running mate. In an age of political tribalism and populist rage, is the center a viable path to power for the unassuming Hobbs-Giles ticket? *** The US politics team is hosting a series of reader Q&As leading up to the midterms. title: Sir William Heseltine obituary
summary: Australian private secretary to Queen Elizabeth II, a moderniser who helped open up the royal household to public and press
text: Sir William Heseltine, who has died aged 96, has a strong claim to have been one of the most consequential royal courtiers during the reign of Queen Elizabeth II, and was perhaps her favourite. Not only was he the first Australian to enter the tweedy aristocratic atmosphere of the royal household, but during his 27 years at the palace, rising from an assistant information officer to being the queen’s private secretary (1986-90), he initiated changes that have shaped public perceptions of the family firm ever since. In the words of the royal biographer Ben Pimlott, whereas Heseltine’s predecessors had done everything to keep the press out, he “saw it as his job wherever and whenever possible to let them in”. Heseltine, said Pimlott, “was the first press secretary who recognised a need to sell royalty to the public and, if necessary, to shape its behaviour accordingly”. It was he who suggested and organised the groundbreaking 1969 Royal Family documentary, watched by an estimated 68% of the British public and many millions abroad. He also instigated the concept of the first royal walkabouts on public visits. And he might have persuaded the royals to pay income tax well before they chose to do so in 1993, if his support for the idea had not been deemed a step too far at the time. Heseltine said later: “While it was not the business of the monarchy to be too avant garde, it could not afford to be too far behind the times either.” He was born in Fremantle, Western Australia, the elder son of Louise (nee Payne) and Henry Heseltine, who were both teachers and both from families long settled in the country – he claimed his ancestors arrived on convict ships. Part of his childhood was spent in the small town of Wyalkatchem deep in the bush, 100 miles east of Perth, where his father was a headteacher. Later William was educated at Christ Church grammar school in the Perth suburb of Claremont, before obtaining a first-class history degree at the University of Western Australia. As a young high flyer he began his civil service career in the private office of the conservative prime minister and arch-royalist Sir Robert Menzies, and it was from there in 1960 that he was seconded for two years to Australia House in London, then to Buckingham Palace as a junior press officer. It was a surprise posting as far as Heseltine was concerned: “I have never had anything to do with the press,” he told the recruiting officer, who replied: “They will probably consider that an advantage.” Indeed, at that time the palace press office was under the command of Cmdr Richard Colville, who was anything but welcoming to the media. Colville, known to correspondents as the Abominable No Man, had been in post since 1947 and saw little need to transmit any information to journalists whatsoever. Even some members of the royal family had begun to notice the need for change. After a two-year posting, Heseltine returned to Australia as official secretary to the governor general, but within four years he was called back to become assistant press secretary to Queen Elizabeth II. Possibly apocryphally, when he put his new job description in his passport he was told bluntly by an immigration officer at Sydney airport: “Mate, there’s no T in courier.” With a more informal Aussie style, Heseltine actually liked journalists and also transmitted that informality in his dealings with the monarch. He even got on well with Colville. One member of the entourage on a trip to South America in 1968 told Pimlott: “Bill had such an easy manner with the queen. He would come up from the back of the plane and plonk himself down to go over the newspapers with her. But he was never disrespectful.” The queen rather approved, especially as she had not got on particularly well with his civil service predecessor, Philip Moore, seen by colleagues as “stuffy”. It was an era of innovative royal stunts, such as the knighting of the around-the-world yachtsman Francis Chichester by the queen in public at Greenwich in 1967, with the same sword Elizabeth I had used to knight Sir Francis Drake in 1581. Two years later came the ersatz inauguration of Prince Charles as Prince of Wales at Caernarfon Castle. Heseltine became press secretary following Colville’s retirement in 1968 and was one of the instigators of the Royal Family documentary that depicted the royals semi-informally at breakfast, cooking a barbecue by a Scottish loch during their annual holiday at Balmoral and chatting to dignitaries. Heseltine told the author Valentine Low: “I shall set modesty aside here and make the claim to have been essentially the person who came up with the idea and brought it into being.” Another innovation was the royal walkabout, which originated during a tour of New Zealand in 1970, when the queen and Prince Philip left their official car and met the waiting crowds. It was an idea now commonplace on royal visits but revolutionary then: it has certainly helped to boost the numbers of enthusiastic spectators at royal public appearances. Heseltine progressed up the court hierarchy: assistant private secretary for five years from 1972, then deputy private secretary for nine and finally private secretary for four years until his retirement in 1990. Although he missed the royal upheavals of the 1990s, his own period had its ups and downs, notably the sacking of the Australian Labor prime minister Gough Whitlam by Sir John Kerr, the queen’s representative as governor general, in 1975 – an event that took Heseltine and the palace by surprise and which gave one of the most significant boosts to Aussie republicanism. Heseltine later said that he would not have advised it, and rebutted allegations that it was a stitch-up by the queen’s advisers. Shortly after becoming private secretary in 1986, Heseltine was confronted by a Sunday Times story claiming that the queen was out of sympathy with the hardline policies of Margaret Thatcher, especially during the miners’ strike. The story was the result of a lunch between a journalist from the paper and the then press officer Michael Shea. It forced a denial from Heseltine, unusually through the letters column of the Times, in which he wrote that any suggestions the queen had suddenly departed from “34 years unvarying adherence to constitutional principles” were “preposterous”. Some indiscretions were beyond the pale, though, and Shea was effectively sacked a few months later without the customary knighthood. It was, Heseltine said, the worst problem he had to deal with at the palace: “It carried a threat to our relationship with No 10,” he told Low. The report that he compiled in the 80s suggesting the queen should pay income tax proved to be a plan too toxic to be considered, until a decade later in the wake of the Windsor Castle fire, which caused a public furore when taxpayers were expected to pay for the repairs. Heseltine retired to Western Australia after nearly three decades working for the queen, though he always dropped in for tea at the palace with her on subsequent visits to London. He was made a Knight of the Order of the Bath (KCB) in 1986 (later advanced to GCB), to add to an earlier appointment as Knight of the Royal Victorian Order (KCVO) in 1982 (later advanced to GCVO). His first two wives, Ann (nee Turner) and Audrey (nee Nolan), predeceased him, in 1957 and 2013 respectively. He is survived by his third wife, Diana (nee Loftus), whom he married in 2016, and two children, John and Sophy, from his second marriage. • William Frederick Payne Heseltine, courtier, born 17 July 1930; died 2 October 2026

title: At Brighton, Polanski raised his arms in triumph. It felt more like a wave goodbye | John Crace
summary: The Greens’ leader seems long on agitprop but short on ideas – and one byelection away from losing his job
text: The Chronicle of a Death Foretold. It must be weird to realise that you have in effect made yourself obsolete inside a year. Worse, that you have actively accelerated your demise. Even AI doesn’t work at that speed. But that’s precisely what it looks as if Zack Polanski has done. Maybe he should just look on the bright side. He’s managed eight Liz Trusses. Not to be sneezed at. Polanski is partly a victim of his own success. A cautionary tale of being careful what you wish for. Like Nigel Farage, the leader of the Green party was one of Keir Starmer’s fiercest critics. Andy Burnham and Wes Streeting excepted. Keir wasn’t radical enough. Did not care enough about Gaza. Was too dull. And under Zack’s leadership, voters swarmed from Labour to the Greens. The party climbed to a record high of 18% in the polls and won the Gorton and Denton byelection against the staggeringly dim Matt Goodwin. But then Keir was airbrushed out of history and Labour chose a prime minister that a lot of people in the country actually liked. Someone who could communicate. Even if they weren’t in love with Andy, voters were willing to give him a chance. Ever since, the Greens have tanked. Now they are down to 11%. Zack’s net approval rating’s almost as bad as Nige’s. Not content with this, Zack has almost certainly fatally holed his credibility by standing in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, which he is very likely to lose. Shares in brand Polanski have never been lower. The Green party conference in Brighton could not have come at a worse time. Zack didn’t want it to go ahead because he wanted to concentrate on his byelection campaign. Senior members of the leadership were briefing that the whole conference was pointless. But the conference did go ahead, and on Friday lunchtime it began with the local MP, Siân Berry, and Gorton and Denton MP, Hannah Spencer, doing their best impressions of a Duracell bunny. High energy, hyperactive enthusiasm. Like Blue Peter presenters on amphetamines. Everything was great. Never better. “Come on, everybody,” said Siân. “We think the best of everyone.” We’ll reserve judgment on that till Sunday when some of the more toxic issues are aired. Hannah was also rushing on her run. “We have forced the government to change course,” she said. Mmm. And that’s sort of the problem. Siân and Hannah were just the warm-up acts for the main event. And with the arrival of Polanski to give his leader’s speech, almost all the excitement was sucked out of the room. The packed hall became like a dead zone. The slogan on the back of the stage said “real hope” but all you could feel was desperation. The sense that the Greens had had a fleeting moment in the sun and the long nights were drawing in. It is customary for a leader’s speech to be punctuated with standing ovations. That’s the whole point of them. Even if the leader is talking pure bollocks. Zack got two. One for saying Palestine and the other for “green revolution”. In Brighton, everyone gets a standing ovation for saying Palestine and green revolution. It’s written in the city’s DNA. Zack looked down from the start. Normally he’s an animated speaker, but today he just looked defeated. As if he was trying and failing to will himself to care. It was just too big an ask. And maybe you couldn’t blame him. His team had chosen this day to brief the media that if they could persuade 30% of Labour voters in Holborn and St Pancras to vote for Zack, he would lose by only four points. That’s a bit like walking into A&E and being told by the doctors they can give you a heart and lung transplant but you are going to die regardless. “What a year,” he began. Indeed. Though maybe he didn’t need to spell it out so clearly. From fringe party to something more mainstream and back again. All over in a heartbeat. Zack couldn’t disguise the look of regret in his eyes. From time to time his head bobbed up and down, as if trying to get his brain to agree with him, but his body language spoke of an inner despair. Rather than the leader of a national political party, he came across as a rather shouty undergraduate student. Long on agitprop and soundbites. Short on genuine argument. Sure, there were nods to taxing the rich more, imposing rent controls, Free Palestine and environmentalism. But these were just words to try to please the crowds. There was no sense of how much this would cost, how it would be done or where the money would come from. “I say to government, ‘Slogans aren’t enough’,” he said without a hint of self-awareness. You could only put it down as a man who knows his political career could be as good as over by this time next week. There was something rather sad about it all. The Greens had wanted so much more than this. They had believed they had elected a man of substance – someone less polite and deferential than previous leaders such as Caroline Lucas and Carla Denyer – who would go toe to toe with the other mainstream parties. But he had turned out to be a chimera. Just another hollow man. Long on slogans, short on ideas. A leader who had briefly burned brightly but had fizzled out. A victim of his own success. A one-year wonder destined to become a man of absence. Losing the byelection would only hasten the end. Most leader’s speeches last about an hour. Zack was done and dusted in just over half that. Even then, it felt far too fluffy, far too long. Come the end, Hannah and Sian came on stage to raise his arms aloft in triumph. It felt more like a long wave goodbye.

title: Palestine Action activists used whips and hammers to threaten guards at arms factory, court hears
summary: Five defendants accused of being part of ‘black team’ tasked with overcoming security at Israel-linked firm Elbit near Bristol
text: Palestine Action activists brandished whips, hammers and kebab skewers to intimidate security guards and keep them at bay during a break-in at an Israel-linked arms factory, a court has heard. Five defendants are accused by prosecutors of being part of a “black team”, wearing black jumpsuits, whose role was to overwhelm security guards, so that a “red team”, wearing red jumpsuits, could break into the Elbit systems factory in Filton, near Bristol, and smash up equipment including drones. Qesser Zuhrah, 21, Zahra Farooque, 26, Kamran Ahmed, 29, Heba Muraisi, 31, and Liam Mullany, 34, went on trial at Woolwich crown court on Friday charged with criminal damage and violent disorder over the raid during the early hours of 6 August 2024. They deny the charges. The prosecutor Deanna Heer KC told the jury that an alleged plan of the raid, discovered by police, said: “Shut Elbit Down. This is our primary objective as Palestine Action. We can do that by sticking together and ensuring its destruction with our brains and muscle.” Jurors were told that a security guard, Nigel Shaw, who had struck a member of the black team across the back of his legs with an umbrella, suffered a 4cm laceration to his head after being attacked. Heer said: “The role of the black team was to overwhelm the security guards so that the red team could break into the factory. They did so by threatening, intimidating and, if necessary, assaulting the guards, by throwing fireworks at them and brandishing weapons, such as whips and hammers and large kebab skewers. “When one of the black team was detained by a security guard, other members of the group attacked him, hitting him until he released their colleague, leaving the security guard with a laceration to his head.” She told the court the break-in was carefully planned and a prison van, driven by a member of the red team, crashed through the first perimeter fence surrounding Elbit’s factory at about 3.30am. The black team followed on foot shouting slogans including “Free Palestine” as the van was driven through a second perimeter fence at the site of the firm, whose parent company is based in Israel. Heer said: “The footage shows that the black team used or threatened violence against the security guards that night. It is clear, the prosecution submit, that Nigel Shaw was physically attacked and [was] caused injury but violence was also used or threatened by the black team before then when they threw fireworks or smoke grenades or cracked whips and brandished skewers in order to intimidate the security guards and keep them away.” She said the idea was for the red team to destroy “as much property as possible” before the police arrived and they used fire extinguishers filled with red paint to spray the walls and floor, crowbars and sledgehammers to smash apart computer equipment and drones and also damaged a disabled toilet. The court was told that the plan for the break-in described the black team, who had their faces covered, as “coverts” because the intention was “to get away without being caught”, unlike the red team who were labelled “overts”. The trial continues.

title: Drumcree march standoff: protesters and Orange Order both vow to stay ‘as long as it takes’
summary: As members of Orange Lodge No 1 gather and residents occupy Garvaghy Road, each side speaks of grievances that go back decades and centuries
text: Half a mile of countryside separates Drumcree parish church and Garvaghy Road. You can walk it in 15 minutes, listening to birdsong. The protesters gathered at each end, however, speak of grievances that go back decades and centuries to explain why a dispute once thought settled has returned to torment Northern Ireland. Up on the hill at Drumcree this week, Paul, a 64-year-old Orangeman who declined to give his surname, said for too long he and his brethren had been denied the right to parade along a traditional route that would honour Protestant forefathers who fell at the Battle of the Boyne in 1690 and the Somme in 1916. “The people of Garvaghy have nothing to fear from 35 mostly elderly gentlemen. We’re not out to cause fear or offence to anybody. We just want the rule of law to be applied.” It was a shame, he said, that Garvaghy’s Catholic residents were beholden to “militant voices”. Fellow members of Portadown district Orange Lodge No 1 – once labelled the “Vatican of Orangeism” – take turns staffing a tent filled with supplies. Some wear union jack stickers. How long will they stay? “As long as it takes,” said Paul. The mood at Garvaghy Road, also bedecked with tents, was equally determined. “It’s not about 35 men walking down this road, it’s about what they represent – sectarian domination and triumphalism,” said Tomás Óg McKinney, 57. “How long will we stay? As long as it takes. We’ll be having our Christmas dinner here if we have to – turkey sandwiches.” Dessie Trainor, 65, said the road, bedecked with Irish flags and republican symbols, must remain free of Orangemen. “Loyalists murdered my mother in 1975. That’s the history of this place and they want to march through it, and through us.” Breandán Mac Cionnaith, the head of the Garvaghy Road Residents’ Coalition, is a former IRA bomber with a reputation for stubbornness. Talks to end the dispute foundered on Friday, raising the spectre of a prolonged crisis that has already poisoned public discourse and put a question mark over power sharing at Stormont between the Democratic Unionist party and Sinn Féin. Earlier in the week, the secretary of state for Northern Ireland, Chris Bryant, spoke of a “tantalisingly close deal” between residents and the Orange Order, an expression of optimism at odds with the dispute’s history of entrenched positions and refusal to compromise. On Friday, Bryant said deadlock remained. “We’ve discussed a wide range of options, including mediation, including an option where the right to march was respected but wasn’t exercised, including an option where there was a final march and no further applications for marches into the future, and we’ve not managed to come to agreement on any of all that.” The situation, he said, was between a “rock and a hard place”. Police, meanwhile, launched what they called a “large-scale investigation” into events last Sunday when Sinn Féin’s first minister, Michelle O’Neill, and the party leader, Mary Lou McDonald, joined throngs of residents and supporters and urged them to block a legally sanctioned parade. O’Neill said she understood the law but chose to “stand in solidarity” with residents. Gavin Robinson, the DUP leader, said there must be consequences for “people who are law makers who are acting as law breakers”. Some analysts say the crisis contains electoral calculation – that the DUP and Sinn Féin hope a rallying call will distract voters from party scandals and failures in office – and that the result will be another collapse of the executive which cripples devolved government. However, in recent days both parties dialled down the rhetoric in a dispute that has left many in Northern Ireland anxious and bewildered. On Friday, 480 people from a Protestant background signed a joint letter calling for an end to the impasse. Each side at Drumcree insists it is the victim of the other’s intolerance. Orangemen marched through the area since the early 1800s before houses with Catholics started lining parts of the route, said Nigel Dawson, the Orange Order’s district master. “Garvaghy is not a toll road or a motorway where people can say go down it or do not go down it. All roads in Northern Ireland are open to all citizens. The tradition has to be respected and the law has to be enforced.” The rule of law and this corner of County Armagh parted ways in the mid-1990s when the annual Orange Lodge march in July turned into a showdown with Garvaghy Road’s Catholic residents, triggering pitched battles between loyalists and police that fanned sectarian violence. Police eventually established authority in 1998 – months after the Good Friday agreement – by blocking the parade in accordance with a ruling from a nascent Parades Commission, which was set up to adjudicate on marches. The Orange Order acquiesced to subsequent prohibitions and staged only symbolic protests each July, a 28-year limbo that led most people in Northern Ireland to conclude the issue was settled even though the Orangemen continued to make regular petitions to march, some with the help of the loyalist activist Jamie Bryson. Procedural blunders by the Parades Commission and a series of legal rulings released the genie last week by granting permission for a scaled-down march. Police stopped the march to avert clashes with those blocking the road. The chief constable of the Police Service of Northern Ireland, Jon Boutcher, must not let nationalists flout the law, said Dawson. “For 52 Sundays, for 28 years, he has vigorously policed a negative determination. And the one time there’s a positive determination, he’s not vigorously policing it.” A legal bid by residents to overturn the Parade Commission decision will be heard on Monday. Regardless of what happens in court, there must be no parade, said McKinney. “OK we’re breaking the law, but for now it’s our only option. We’re a peaceful community standing on our own road.” Another protester, Grainne Milligan, said loyalist paramilitaries murdered her cousin, Michael McGoldrick, a taxi driver, in 1998. “Everyone here is doing their bit,” she said. “I don’t want that trauma to be passed down to another generation.”

title: The Rev Ian Gregory obituary
summary: Other lives: Minister and former journalist who launched a campaign to bring back courtesy
text: There was a point in the 1980s when the Rev Ian Gregory, a former journalist and church minister, who has died aged 93, was himself making the news. In the time of Margaret Thatcher, the yuppy and union battles, Ian, my father-in-law, launched a campaign to bring back courtesy. Ever with an eye for a good headline, he called his campaign group the Polite Society. The landline in his Staffordshire house lit up with calls from newspapers and broadcasters around the world. The Los Angeles Times quoted Ian as saying that Britain had rebutted many enemies in the past 80 years, but “in 1986, the British people face national defeat at the hands of a sinister foe: our ignorant and ill-mannered selves”. During this heyday there was a warm seat for Ian on breakfast TV sofas, often side-by-side with pop stars – Rick Parfitt of Status Quo wore a Polite Society badge on his leather jacket for years after they met. Although the Polite Society may have had a conservative, nostalgic whiff about it, Ian was a radical in his Christian ministry. Ordained in 1983, he was a much-loved minister at King Street Congregational church, Newcastle-under-Lyme, who was not afraid to question faith, and invited people to think rather than accept. He was one of few ministers who would marry divorced people. He blessed babies in pubs – because he believed in meeting people where they felt comfortable – and he held Christmas services for licensees. A pub chain asked him to train staff in the importance of courtesy, and this led to a hostelry in his home town being named after him: the Polite Vicar. Born in Bolton to Gabriel Gregory, a Congregational minister, and Lilian (nee Unsworth), a teacher, Ian went to Silcoates, Wakefield, a boarding school for the sons of Congregational ministers, then Peartree secondary school in Derby. In 1953 he went to Lancashire Independent College, a theological institution in Whalley Range, Manchester, where his father had also studied. Ian became a journalist after leaving college following a “scandal” when a bottle of ginger wine was found in his room there. He said what made him a good journalist – getting things done by deadline and “being impatient with wafflers” – did not sit well with being a church minister, so the ministry had to wait. He knocked on the editor’s door of the Stockport Advertiser in 1954, was given a reporting job, and was told that all journalists wore a trilby hat. Ian took to it, and a trilby became a wardrobe staple. Ian was one of the first journalists to work at BBC Radio Derby when it launched in 1971; his combative interviews with the then Derbyshire county council leader, David Bookbinder, were well known. He retired in 2003. He continued questioning up to his death, reading theology and science books, and writing pamphlets from his garden shed office. Ian is survived by his wife, Trisha (nee Donaldson), whom he met in 1960 and married five years later, their children, Russell (my husband), Rachel and Jamie, four grandchildren and two great-grandchildren.

title: Burnham plans to pass law scrapping pension triple lock before next election
summary: Guarantee will remain until 2030 but MPs will vote on changes during this parliament, government says
text: Andy Burnham plans to pass legislation to scrap the state pension triple lock in this parliament, even though the guarantee will remain until 2030, the government has said. The prime minister used his conference speech to announce a change to the policy, which guarantees that the state pension rises by the highest of 2.5%, inflation or earnings growth. In future, the earnings element will be adjusted to avoid much larger pension increases in years when wages spike. In his speech, Burnham said the triple lock would remain in place until 2030 – after the next election – keeping Labour’s manifesto promise to retain the guarantee. However, guidance published alongside the speech shows that the government intends to legislate before then, requiring MPs to vote on the changes. It means parties will go into the next election setting out in their manifestos whether to retain Labour’s changes or repeal them if they win power. The guidance also shows that the government estimates that the adjustment to the triple lock would reduce state pension spending by £15bn a year by the end of the 2030s and by £50bn a year by 2050. However, the Resolution Foundation said on Friday that it was extremely difficult to estimate the savings, with figures ranging from nothing to about £24bn a year depending on which recent decade was used as a model. Ruth Curtice, the thinktank’s chief executive, wrote on Friday: “The adjusted triple lock saves most in a volatile world, and so saves nothing in the 90s or 00s, and £24bn in the 10s. “Over the longer term, which will most likely deliver some mixture of all of these economic realities, the new mechanism should trend closer to earnings. “If real earnings growth permanently disappoints then even the protections in the new mechanism could prove expensive. A new, if not the main, reason to fight to avoid stagnant wages.” Since it was announced, the policy has been criticised by the Conservatives, Reform UK and the Liberal Democrats – although some Tory and Lib Dem MPs are unhappy with their leaders for campaigning to retain a policy they believe is too costly. Sharon Graham, the Unite general secretary, said earlier this week that getting rid of the pension triple lock to help fund social care changes would be “electoral suicide”. However, YouGov has published polling suggesting voters support Burnham’s plan by 48% to 28%. In his conference speech, Burnham confirmed he would end the pension triple lock and use the savings to fund a national care service in England that would be free at the point of use. He said his changes would still leave millions of pensioners better off and that they would benefit from the new care system, which is expected to follow the Scottish system by covering care costs but not accommodation. Burnham also promised to exempt lower-income pensioners from income tax during this parliament.

title: Spanish right wing votes down housing crisis plans as protest movement grows
summary: Opposition lawmakers join forces to defeat proposals made by Socialist-led coalition after eviction of 87-year-old
text: Rightwing lawmakers in Spain have rejected emergency measures put forward to tackle the country’s housing crisis, pitting a fractured parliament against the widespread protest movement that has swelled in recent days. On Friday Pedro Sánchez’s Socialist-led coalition put forward two decrees that included a range of measures aimed at improving access to housing, from a ban on evictions until 2030 to the regulation of temporary lettings and lettings by room. As hundreds of protesters outside the parliament building in Madrid held up homemade signs bearing images of vultures, the conservative People’s party, the far-right Vox and the Catalan pro-independence party Junts voted against both decrees. The People’s party said it had voted in line with its belief that building, rather than regulating, was the best way to address the crisis. “Housing doesn’t become more affordable through decrees; it becomes more affordable by building more homes,” said the lawmaker Juan Bravo. News of the package’s rejection was met with boos and cries of “shame” outside. “Your profits, our misery,” the protesters chanted. The long-simmering anger at soaring housing costs boiled over late last month, when 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal, who uses a wheelchair, was evicted from the home she had lived in for 70 years. The octogenarian said she was unable to afford the 230% rent hike demanded by the investment fund that bought her apartment. Tens of thousands of people heeded the call by housing campaigners to take to the streets, while encampments protesting against the housing crisis sprung up in cities across Spain. The demonstrations have dominated the national conversation, breathing new life into Sánchez’s beleaguered government and shifting attention away from the lingering impact of recent events in Ceuta. On Friday, as a poll suggested that two-thirds of people in Spain supported the idea of government intervention in the housing market to limit prices, sources told the news site Eldiario.es that the Socialists were mulling whether to bring forward next year’s elections, potentially to this November. After news broke that several rightwing parties were planning to vote against the proposed measures, Sánchez said the parliamentary vote would go ahead as planned. “You’re with the social majority or with speculators,” the Spanish prime minister said on social media, adding that the vote would reveal the “true colours” of the rightwing parties. Following five hours of parliamentary debate on Friday, Sánchez made a last ditch appeal to lawmakers to back the measures. “What is behind these decrees is the desire to instil order and a sense of humanity in a market that – if we do not rein it in – will destroy our society,” he said. “Do the right thing, or history will judge you, and sooner than you think.” Across Spain, where rents have surged 80% within a decade and the cost of homes climbed by 63%, the issue of housing has long ranked as one of people’s biggest concerns. Earlier this year, the Youth Council of Spain said the average rent in Spain had climbed to €1,176 ($1,323) a month – an amount equivalent to 98.7% of the average salary for under-30s. The figures help to explain why the protests that began with Abascal’s eviction have continued even after the investment firm that bought her apartment said it had struck a deal that would allow her to return to her home, with her rent returning to a level closer to that she had paid in the past. The government decrees presented in parliament on Friday were intended to quell some of this public uproar. As they were rejected, campaigners vowed to continue their push to improve access to housing. “They’re not going to stop us,” the Confederation of Tenants’ Unions said in a statement, as it called on people across the country to take to the streets this weekend. “In the face of a parliament that is out of touch, the answer is more organisation and mobilisation. The next step: a general strike.” Saturday will mark one week since a small group of protesters, intent on making their demands heard, set up 10 tents in Madrid’s central Puerta del Sol plaza, a short walk from parliament. Since then, the encampment had swelled to more than 1,200 tents – a peaceful settlement in the heart of the capital with its own street names, a medical centre and even a co-working space. As news of the vote reached the camp on Friday, some said it was not what they had expected. “People here are disappointed,” said Marta García. “We had thought that at least one of the decrees would be approved.”

title: Woman in alleged Cornell gang-rape case was ‘failed’ by system, New York governor says
summary: Kathy Hochul briefs journalists with state attorney general Letitia James, who will be taking over the entire case
text: Kathy Hochul, New York’s governor, said on Friday that she would “ensure” that all the facts of the alleged gang-rape at a fraternity house at Cornell University “are brought into the light”, while harshly criticizing the elite institution for how it handled the 2024 case. Hochul, a Democrat, said the woman in the case, was “failed” by people obligated to protect her, including the police and the county prosecutor. “I’m deeply disturbed at Cornell University’s police and how they handled this,” Hochul said of the Ivy League university in Ithaca in upstate New York. In a rare legal development, Hochul late on Thursday announced that the state attorney general, Letitia James, was taking over the entire case as a special prosecutor. “I will not allow anyone to sweep this case under the rug,” Hochul said in a press conference on Friday morning alongside James. “Every New Yorker deserves to know that when they report a crime, they will be investigated fully and fairly. That they will be seen and heard. I stand ready to lead a process guided by the facts and the law,” James said. James will oversee the investigation and, if warranted, present evidence to a grand jury in a process that could lead to criminal charges. Hochul sharply criticized the investigation that began in 2024 after the woman in the case went to the police. “In what world would the police learn from a victim that she’d been literally gang-raped while intoxicated by five men in a fraternity house, and not elevate those allegations to the district attorney?” Hochul said, of the alleged assaults. The governor also criticized what she called “a gap in state law” that makes it very difficult to bring charges relating to accusations of sexual crimes when the alleged victim was voluntarily intoxicated. She said: “If someone is too intoxicated to consent, it should not matter whether they chose to use drugs or alcohol. Voluntary intoxication is not a license for sexual assault or gang-rape. Period.” Hochul said on Thursday she was appointing James after she “lost faith” in the ability of the local Tompkins county district attorney, Matthew Van Houten, to oversee the case after he decided not to prosecute the case in 2024, among other reasons. Prior to James’s appointment this week, Van Houten had reopened the investigation. A former Cornell University student, who identifies by the pseudonym Jane Doe, filed a civil lawsuit in September alleging she was gang-raped at a fraternity in 2024, when she was 20. She said she was drugged and repeatedly raped over the course of seven hours. The case has sparked national outrage, roiled the campus and raised questions about why no criminal case was brought. Thomas Giuffra, a lawyer for Jane Doe, told CNN on Friday morning that his client was “not doing well” amid the uproar and that they feel as though “a cover-up was going on” in order to protect the university and its reputation. He added that he had “a real issue” with the district attorney and accused him of trying to “throw” his client “under the bus”. On Friday, Cornell University said it supported Hochul, including her effort to pass legislation to update the relevant law. “We fully support the appointment of a special prosecutor and efforts to change New York State’s rape law and are committed to an independent external review of all aspects of how Cornell has handled this case,” a spokesperson said. Two members of the Chi Phi fraternity at Cornell were expelled, but none of the seven were arrested nor faced any legal consequences. Some were made to write essays, attend workshops or serve short suspensions. Now, Doe is suing the seven men whom she said perpetrated the assault, and also the university itself, the fraternity and others. Some in the group argue that sexual contact was consensual, others deny such participation. On Monday, Van Houten said the allegations presented in the lawsuit were “dramatically different” from the statement the alleged victim gave the police two years ago. He said the woman’s first testimony did not include allegations that she was drugged, incapacitated beyond the ability to consent or forced into sex. However, he later told CBS News he had never seen her detailed account, but relied on a statement written by a campus police officer. Hochul further said on Friday that Van Houten had said that Doe’s statement “did not establish that a crime had occurred” – but that new reporting raises serious questions about the information his office relied upon when it made that decision. Now, she demanded that James conduct a “fresh and thorough review of all the facts” and “go wherever it leads”. Hochul said: “Every parent who sends their child off to college expects them to be safe, and if something terrible happens, the student deserves to know that the people they turn to will listen to them, protect them, and fight for them. That is the bare minimum.” James said her first priority was the criminal investigation into the alleged rape. “At this time we will not be focusing on the actions of the district attorney,” she said. Cornell, which is a private sector elite university, has suspended the Chi Phi fraternity indefinitely. A fraternity is a selective, traditionally all-male club at a university in which some male undergraduate members may live together in residential fraternity houses on or near campus. Cornell agreed on Wednesday to bring in outside lawyers to independently investigate how it handled the woman’s allegations. • Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organizations. In the US, Rainn offers support on 800-656-4673. In the UK, Rape Crisis offers support on 0808 500 2222. In Australia, support is available at 1800Respect (1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found at ibiblio.org/rcip/internl.html

title: Peter Thiel revealed as secret buyer of Bel Air mansion that sold for $130m
summary: The 1938 mansion, Casa Encantada, once belonged to Conrad Hilton and was sold at foreclosure auction
text: The tech billionaire Peter Thiel has been revealed as the new owner of a storied Bel-Air estate that quietly sold in July for a staggering $130m. The 1938 mansion, Casa Encantada, was sold at an open-air foreclosure auction in Pomona, with the name of the buyer kept under wraps for months. The winning bid is now revealed to have come from a limited liability company linked to the venture capitalist and PayPal and Palantir co-founder, according to the Wall Street Journal, which first reported the buyer’s identity. The sale of the 40,000sq ft estate is the most expensive in Los Angeles so far this year, though it is far less than the previous asking price. The former owner, late telecom mogul Gary Winnick, wanted $225m for the property in 2019 and $250m in 2023, making it the priciest home in the US at the time. Winnick died in 2023 amid a mountain of debt. Set on about 8.4 acres of land, the stately property overlooks the Bel-Air Country Club and boasts grand Deco-Hollywood interiors with seven bedrooms, 20 bathrooms, multiple dining rooms and lounges, a walnut-paneled library, a tennis court, terraced gardens, a 60ft tiled swimming pool and a two-storey guesthouse. Other previous owners include the hotel magnate Conrad Hilton, who bought it in 1950, and billionaire David Murdock, who purchased it in 1980 for a record $12.4m. It set a second price record in 2000 when it sold to Winnick for $94m. According to the Journal’s report, Thiel had been considering the mega-mansion for months before the auction, though he does not plan to live there. Rather he sees the property as an investment and plans to upgrade it. The purchase adds to his sprawling real estate portfolio that spans three continents, including compounds in Hawaii and New Zealand, homes in Miami and Washington DC, and a recently acquired mansion in the most exclusive neighbourhood in Buenos Aires. He reportedly relocated his primary residence from California to south Florida last year amid a wealth tax debate in the Golden state.

title: Englishness is not defined by ethnicity | Letters
summary: Letters: Maariyah Seedat wonders at what point does her family become ‘English’ enough, Mark James Slater has always regarded himself as British and not English. Plus letters from Dr Richard Seabrook and Alan Baker
text: Jason Okundaye’s piece on defining Englishness mirrored my own experiences as a member of an ethnic minority (Of course you can be English if you’re not white. So why can’t the right leave the question alone?, 26 September). As a child, growing up in multicultural Leicester in the 1990s and 2000s, I was “corrected” by adults in positions of authority – the vast majority of whom were white – for wanting to call myself English. It was a descriptor that I could not claim and, implicitly, was not my right because of my skin colour. I learned very quickly that referring to myself as British was the better, less objectionable option. It always rubbed me up the wrong way. At what point does my family become “English” enough? How many generations later? I love my country of birth, and when I am abroad my Englishness is never brought into question, so why can my country not accept me as I am? I believe that lived experiences like mine indicate why ethnic-minority adults “prefer an identification with Britishness”: a potent mix of historically being put in one’s place, and a desire to avoid exhausting circular arguments with those who cannot see beyond the colour of one’s skin. Maariyah Seedat Toronto, Canada • Given that my grandparents’ family names are a mixture of Norman French, Dutch and Huguenot French, and we have probably lived within the borders of England from arrival to today, and that I was born in London, is it strange that I have always regarded myself as British and not English? My understanding of being English is either the staid and stuffy upper classes residing in rural isolation or having some background role in an embassy or assurance office or living in a working-class community of very similar people in the terraced streets around a (former) factory. That isn’t me. I am as invested in the other British cultures of Scotland, Wales, Ireland, Cornwall, the West Indies, Pakistan, Australia, India, Bangladesh, New Zealand, Canada, Africa and the US, not to mention western Europe and more recently eastern Europe. Simply being English is such a restrictive definition, and I am proud to be counted as British as any of my neighbours. Mark James Slater Helston, Cornwall • Jason Okundaye asks “Can you be English and non-white?” The answer is no, according to the government’s own system of coding ethnicities for the 2021 census. English appears as a subcategory of white, and not elsewhere. Thus it is not possible using this coding scheme to describe oneself as, for example, Black English, whereas you can choose to declare yourself Black British. So the racist implications of “Englishness” are baked into the coding scheme until such time as “English” is moved out of its colour category and treated as a cultural identity (whatever that is) rather than as a consequence of DNA. Dr Richard Seabrook Beckenham, London • While Jason Okundaye claims as a simple truth that “there is no single, historically fixed population from which today’s ‘English’ have descended”, he misses a more important general point. While I am able to claim to be a personally responsible agent as a grandfather, father, husband, researcher and writer, I am unable to claim responsibility for the fundamental structure within which I have acted and continue to act. I was born in Canterbury, Kent and thus I am English. My birth certificate, dated 20 October 1938, records my “sex” as “boy”. I am simply not responsible for my nationality or gender. I am accordingly neither proud nor ashamed to be an Englishman: that is just a matter of fact. And this in turn means that I cannot either adulate or castigate others of different nationality or gender on the grounds of those characteristics alone. The right’s fixation based on bloodlines and biological inheritance has no foundation: it is baseless and crass. Alan Baker Cambridge • Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Please email us your letter and it will be considered for publication in our letters section.

title: Utilities are public services – and should not be run as businesses | Letters
summary: Letters: Readers respond to an article by Will Hutton and Andy Haldane suggesting that they could be run for the public benefit
text: Will Hutton and Andy Haldane advocate “turning [utilities] into public-benefit companies with a primary, constitutional objective of delivering high-quality services, with profitability subordinate to that broader aim” (Andy Burnham talks about ‘public control’ of the utilities but it’s a minefield. We can lead him through it, 25 September). So still companies, but with a public interest rather than a profit motive. This is still the wrong approach. Utilities should not be run as businesses but as essential public services. They do not function in isolation, and business models are unsuited to their functioning in the public interest. They have social and environmental as well as economic responsibilities that have to be met. For 20 years, prior to the advent of the Scottish parliament, local government functioned well in Scotland within a framework of regions and districts. The regions had powers and responsibilities for the wide range of functions that had to be coordinated and operated strategically at the regional level. They included water and sewerage. The present government appears to be edging sideways, through metro mayors and joint working, towards governance for city regions. This should be formalised and given a full portfolio of responsibilities, powers and resources for strategic planning, economic development, education, health, transportation, infrastructure and the environment. Infrastructure should include water and sewerage. As an example, urban rainwater needs to be collected and recycled for cooling, which was normal practice for thousands of years in southern Europe. Such practice should be moving north to include water reserves for wildfire control. How could such provisions, urban cooling and wildfire control ever be met through the profit motive? If the present water companies in England have liabilities that exceed the value of their assets, and cannot meet their legal responsibilities, then it is difficult to see why they should be rescued and maintained through public expenditure. Roger Read Former secretary general, Metrex • Will Hutton and Andy Haldane put forward a poor argument for maintaining private ownership of utilities. Instead of comparing the present situation with how things were when the water utilities were publicly owned – surely the fairest comparison – they cite spurious examples of the alleged failings of other nationalised industries. We are alone in the world (apart from Chile) in having a wholly privatised water industry; is everyone else out of step? Sally Thompson Cardiff • Will Hutton and Andy Haldane give some interesting thoughts on the public control of utilities. These could also apply across the complete essential services sector, from water companies to dental practices. Few who experienced the performance of the old postwar nationalised industries would wish a return to this failed model. However, why not just keep it simple and legislate to force all essential-services operators to list as companies on the London Stock Exchange? For each sector, further legislation could set maximums for yields and permitted borrowing: two key indicators of company activity. The public would then be more inclined to invest in the companies, just as they do at present with National Grid. Ian Graham Port Carlisle, Cumbria • Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Please email us your letter and it will be considered for publication in our letters section.

title: Andy Burnham’s ultimate test will be whether people’s lives improve | Letters
summary: Measures of wellbeing should carry real weight in decisions about tax, spending and public services, says Sarah Davidson
text: Re your editorial on Andy Burnham’s conference speech (29 September), the outcome that all governments should seek is a real improvement to people’s lives, particularly for those with the least, and without storing up problems for future generations. But that requires ministers to measure what matters and use that evidence to guide decisions. The good news for the prime minister and his colleagues is that the Office for National Statistics already collects robust evidence about our lives through its UK Measures of National Well-being Dashboard. Yet there is little suggestion that this sort of data has been driving policy, including tax and spending plans. If improving lives is the goal, measures of wellbeing should carry real weight in decisions about tax, spending and public services. Sarah Davidson Chief executive, Carnegie UK • Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: A Democratic upset is brewing in Alaska’s governor’s race as Trump’s popularity craters
summary: Support for 37-year-old Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins could upend the governor’s race in the heavily Republican state
text: This July, Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins spent four days and 450 miles (725km) wending his way down the Yukon River in a 24ft Alweld skiff, a flat-bottomed aluminum boat built for shallow Alaska rivers. Starting in Koyukon Athabascan country, he passed through Indigenous Deg Hit’an communities like Anvik, before ending among the Yup’ik villages of the lower river, Russian Mission and Pilot Station among them. The boat carried him through 11 villages – some only reachable by water or small plane, and most with fewer than 300 residents, and fewer still who could recall the last time they had seen a candidate for Alaska governor, Republican, Democrat or independent. The 37-year-old former state representative is hopping on snowmachines – only people in the lower 48 call them snowmobiles – as well as boats and floatplanes to accomplish what Alaska Democrats have failed to do for nearly a generation: win the governor’s office. “Alaskans are hungry for change,” Kreiss-Tomkins said. “We’ve been running the same campaign since we launched in February, and I don’t take anyone’s vote for granted.” Just two years after Donald Trump carried Alaska by 13 points, his approval rating there has collapsed – a net 21- to 22-point swing, among the steepest drops in any reliably Republican state he won. In August, Kreiss-Tomkins came in first ahead of his Democratic and Republican rivals in the state’s non-partisan primary. Now, “JKT”, as he’s known in his home town of Sitka, is betting that an old-fashioned exercise in retail politics – traveling the vast expanse of a state larger than Texas, California and Montana combined and asking voters for their support in person – will help him do it again in November. But a question looms over the race: how much of his strength is a reflection of the changing national political environment, and Americans’ broad dissatisfaction with Trump, and how much is particular to the candidates, personalities and particular electoral system of the last frontier? Unlike nearly every other US state, Alaska no longer holds a traditional party primary followed by a winner-take-all general election. Under the ranked-choice voting system adopted by voters in 2020, the top four candidates from an open primary advance to the general election. Voters then rank candidates in order of preference, and votes can transfer to their next-ranked candidate as lower-placed contenders are eliminated. Though reliably Republican, the state has a long independent streak. The outgoing governor, Mike Dunleavy, an early supporter of Trump, leaves office deeply unpopular, largely for his unfulfilled promise to increase the amount of oil-dividend money Alaskans are given each year; in 2026, every eligible Alaskan received $1,000, with an additional $200 energy relief payment. This localized frustration coupled with Trump’s sagging approval ratings, particularly on the economy, has created a potential opening for Democrats. A recent bipartisan AARP poll found Kreiss-Tomkins winning 40% of first-choice preferences, compared with a combined 41% for his three Republican opponents, Bernadette Wilson, Dave Bronson and Treg Taylor, all of whom will appear on Alaska’s general election ballot. *** Kreiss-Tomkins grew up in Sitka, a fishing town of 8,500 where compromise is required. It’s wedged among the spruce and hemlock of the Tongass national forest and the open swell of the north Pacific, where you can’t escape political opponents in a town with just 14 miles of coastal road, accessible only by water or air. He entered politics in 2012, at the age of 22, winning a statehouse seat by defeating the Republican incumbent by 32 votes. “JKT is the clear frontrunner for governor not because of anything Trump did, but because he’s running a good campaign,” said Larry Persily, who has watched Alaska politics since the 1970s, first as the owner of the Wrangell Sentinel newspaper and later as an editorial page editor at the Anchorage Daily News. “He’s energized a lot of young people. His Republican opponents are just a sorry lot. The Republicans just put up a bunch of political losers.” Wilson, the top-finishing Republican candidate, would disagree. The Anchorage garbage-hauling entrepreneur, who finished third in August’s primary, is a former competitive figure skater and the great-niece of the late Republican governor Wally Hickel. She has secured endorsements from the Arkansas governor, Sarah Huckabee Sanders, one of Trump’s press secretaries during his first term, and Alaska’s own Republican congressman, Nick Begich – along with Byron Donalds, the Florida congressman running to succeed Ron DeSantis as governor there. Wilson casts Kreiss-Tomkins’s decade in elected office, and his elite educational background – he dropped out of Yale University in 2011, one credit short of graduating – as liabilities. “Alaskans are looking for fresh leadership from the private sector,” she said in an emailed statement. “Not another ‘experienced’ politician who will wreck our energy economy, raise taxes, continue to fail us on the PFD [permanent fund dividend], and sell out Alaska to advance their career.” Wilson’s relationship with one of her Republican rivals is tangled: she chaired Bronson’s 2020 campaign for Anchorage mayor. He won, arrived in office as a political newcomer, then spent his single term fighting the assembly over homelessness – at one point floating one-way plane tickets to the lower 48 for people living on the street – before losing re-election to the independent Suzanne LaFrance in 2024. Republican candidate Taylor’s route to the ballot has been stranger still. The former state attorney general was elevated to the final slot after Tom Begich withdrew and endorsed Kreiss-Tomkins, only to be disqualified four days later over an undeclared rental income disclosure; briefly replaced by his own running mate; then reinstated after a department of law review – conducted by the office he used to run – found trivial but, he claimed, similar issues among dozens of other candidates. The three Republicans’ competing campaigns have prompted efforts to consolidate conservative support behind Wilson. Alaska’s electoral history offers a precedent. In 1994, Democrat Tony Knowles won the governorship by just 536 votes after the conservative vote split between Republican nominee Jim Campbell and Jack Coghill, the sitting lieutenant governor, who ran on the Alaskan independence party ticket. Knowles, the last Democrat elected to the office, went on to serve two terms. *** The governor’s race is unfolding against a national backdrop of declining approval for Trump. A Reuters/Ipsos poll published in September put his approval at 32%, with dissatisfaction over living costs among the principal concerns. But national figures alone cannot explain what is happening in Alaska, where the statewide candidates are also confronting distinctly local issues. Electing a Democrat here is not as surprising as it is in some other red states, said Tom Kizzia, a longtime Anchorage Daily News reporter and Alaska historian. “It’s that Alaska iconoclasm that kicks in – the simmering resentment of big business ripping off our resources.” The common thread, in Kizzia’s telling, is not a particular political party, but rather a distrust of whoever is currently perceived as extracting Alaska’s wealth without giving enough back – a role historically filled by outside oil and mining interests, and one conservatives have often redirected toward the federal government instead. That history helps explain why Trump’s brand of politics has not translated into durable support for his allies on this year’s ballot. “Dunleavy hitched himself to the Maga wagon, which contained elements of that iconoclasm,” Kizzia says. “But Trump was mostly about non-Alaska things that don’t register strongly with Alaska voters.” What does register, he argues, is Dunleavy’s failure to deliver on a hefty permanent fund check, the annual payment that Alaskans receive from the state’s oil-wealth savings each October. Dunleavy promised to up the amount of these checks, and even to pay Alaskans retroactively. None of this has come to pass. This same unresolved grievance now faces all three Republicans running to succeed him. Kreiss-Tomkins argues for a dividend payment that can be maintained without destabilizing the budget. “I want a permanent fund dividend that is meaningful and sustainable. We don’t need an election-year promise that blows a hole in the budget and is mathematically impossible,” he said. His campaign blends the Alaska tradition of “visiting” with people, sometimes onboard his skiff retrofitted with a three-quarter-ply cabin with the amber varnish flaking off, with a volunteer operation nicknamed “Superpod”, built on the premise that someone responding to a campaign text should reach an actual human being rather than a bot. That emphasis on personal contact was apparent to Debbie Moderow, who operates sled dog kennels near Denali national park and in Anchorage. At a meet-and-greet in Anchorage attended by about 30 people, she watched Kreiss-Tomkins climb on to a folding chair to address the crowd. “He was brimming with energy and wisdom, young and bright-eyed, and it was obvious that he had been obsessed with government in a geeky way for a long time,” she said. “I immediately thought, this guy has a vision, and a way to chart the way forward at a time when our state desperately needs it.” Persily, the newspaper publisher, who keeps his 100-year-old Underwood manual typewriter atop a restored lead-type cabinet and pops in CDs for music, sees the campaign’s emphasis on face-to-face campaigning as significant. “Elections are determined by turnout,” he said. “If you can turn out people who wouldn’t otherwise vote, that will make the difference. The public in the state is looking for someone who is going to excite people who wouldn’t otherwise get engaged. On a boat, on a snowmachine, what have you – Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, from what I can see, is making that happen.” It hasn’t been without hiccups. Kreiss-Tomkins’s campaign has attracted criticism over its finances. He outraised the entire field during the primary, drawing substantial contributions from outside Alaska, including six-figure sums from employees of artificial intelligence companies. He has responded by emphasizing his proposed moratorium on new Alaska datacenters and his support for regulations intended to protect Alaskans from harms associated with AI. His position is that the donations reflect support for his proposals rather than an effort to influence them. Asked about his priorities in office, Kreiss-Tomkins returns to two concerns familiar to Alaskans: education and the cost of living. “Our top-of-mind campaign issues are supporting our schools and lowering everyday costs for Alaskans,” he said. Whether dissatisfaction with Trump translates into votes for Democratic candidates remains a separate question from whether Kreiss-Tomkins can assemble a coalition of his own. The governor’s race will test both possibilities, alongside the ability of Alaska’s ranked-choice system to accommodate three Republican candidates competing for many of the same voters. For Moderow, Kreiss-Tomkins’s relative youth is less significant than his years of experience in Juneau. “People frame it as giving a young guy a chance,” she said. “For me, it’s the opposite. It’s giving a professional an opportunity when Alaska needs a leader.”
