title: Polanski says he does not need to win ‘50/50’ byelection to stay Green leader
summary: Exclusive: Party leader says outcome of ‘knife-edge’ vote in Keir Starmer’s former seat will not affect his position
text: Zack Polanski has said his authority as leader of the Green party of England and Wales does not depend on winning next week’s Holborn and St Pancras byelection, amid suggestions the party’s popularity may have peaked. Polanski, who is trying to take Keir Starmer’s former seat from Labour, described the contest as “probably 50/50 right now” and “really on a knife edge”. Asked in an interview with the Guardian how much his position as leader depended on victory, Polanski said: “It doesn’t depend on it whatsoever.” He said the election had ramifications for politics nationally but “not for my leadership”. “I’ll be completely honest, it won’t surprise you to know that I want to win the seat,” Polanski said. “I think the seat is winnable, and I think it’s probably 50/50 right now. It’s really, really on a knife edge.” Senior Green party figures privately fear a defeat in Holborn and St Pancras could severely damage Polanski’s leadership, amid concerns the party’s rapid rise in membership and polling has not translated into campaigning strength on the ground. Attempts to concentrate resources on the byelection have caused internal friction, with the Guardian revealing last month that Polanski wanted the Greens’ annual conference postponed so the party could focus on the contest. That proposal was rejected by its executive. Polanski, who has never been an MP, maintained there were “still advantages to being a leader outside Westminster”, while also arguing that entering parliament would offer another way of putting pressure on the Labour government. Polanski is facing a separate test of his leadership at the Green party’s annual conference, where members are due to debate a deeply contentious motion declaring “Zionism is racism” on Saturday. Asked about criticism from senior Greens who believe he has failed to provide leadership over the issue, he said: “Leadership is about priorities, and this motion isn’t my priority. My priority is the cost of living. My priority is nationalising Thames Water. My priority is ending the genocide that’s happening in Gaza and freeing Palestine.” Caroline Lucas, the former leader of the Greens, Adrian Ramsay, the former co-leader, and Rachel Millward, a current co-deputy leader, have distanced themselves from the motion, warning it could be “divisive”. Some Jewish Greens have raised concerns about what the motion could mean for their place within the party. Asked whether he could guarantee that a Jewish member would not face disciplinary action simply for attending a synagogue that identified as Zionist, Polanski said: “I can guarantee that this motion has absolutely nothing to do with disciplinary action against anyone.” The byelection has become an early test of whether Labour under Andy Burnham can reclaim progressive voters who have moved towards the Greens, and the result may inform the government’s decisions over expanding North Sea oil and gas drilling. “I see this election as high-stakes for people in Holborn and St Pancras and high-stakes for the climate crisis,” Polanski said. “We know that … a decision on [drilling projects Rosebank and Jackdaw] has been delayed until after this byelection, because Andy Burnham literally wants to see whether he can get away with drilling for new North Sea oil and gas.” The Guardian has reported that the Jackdaw decision is likely to be held until after the byelection, while a decision on Rosebank is still pending. Burnham has promised a more “pragmatic” approach to North Sea oil and gas than his predecessor, as the government balances its climate commitments against pressure over energy security and jobs. Both projects already hold licences granted under the Conservatives, meaning approval by Labour would not amount to issuing new exploration licences. Asked whether Burnham’s surge could win back younger and progressive voters from the Greens, Polanski said there were two possibilities. One was that Burnham “means what he’s saying right now” and would actually “implement action today and not tomorrow, and not after the next general election”. In this case, Polanski said, the country would improve as a result of pressure from the Greens and others. The other, which Polanski called “the more likely scenario”, was that “what we’re getting is talk”. He said Burnham was “promising things after the next general election, but soon we’re going to have a budget that he’s already warning is going to be a difficult budget”. In this case, he said, “more and more people will start to question why would you vote for the Labour party or get involved with the Labour party when the Green party has been growing for over a year now”. He added: “You don’t have to accept the half-fat version. You can join the Green party and actually make sure we have the country that Andy Burnham’s talking about, but not taking the action on.” Arguing that Labour’s climate policy had a gap between rhetoric and actions, Polanski asked: “Does Andy Burnham just not care about the climate crisis? It just feels like such a glaring gap in everything that he’s talked about, not just because of Rosebank and Jackdaw, but in the need to invest in renewables, the need for a clean green revolution, the need for new jobs, and it just feels like this vision is just not there.” He added: “When are we going to see difficult choices for the super rich and the very, very wealthy? Instead, he’s talking about difficult choices for pensioners. So already the action is not meeting his ‘hope’ rhetoric, and I think people are already starting to ask questions.” Referring to arrests of Palestine Action supporters outside the Labour party conference, Polanski said: “Those people on the doorstep, they can see that Ed Miliband stood on stage and told many of us that we were right on Palestine, but just behind him, outside the conference hall, pensioners were still being dragged off, being arrested for holding signs up saying ‘I support Palestine Action’.” Polanski used his conference speech to introduce new Green party policy, calling for a “three-year emergency brake on private rents”. He said: “No rent rises above CPI wage growth or 2%, whichever is lower. No sudden hikes. No evictions under the guise of rent rises. No more uncertainty, no more fear.” He went further on Palestine Action on Friday, calling for the group to be deproscribed, which led to chants of “free, free Palestine” from Green party members in the hall in Brighton.

title: Bosses of three firms that supply trains to UK railways made £3.5m last year
summary: Rolling stock companies, which also paid out nearly £400m to shareholders, accused of profiting at passengers’ expense
text: The chief executives of three firms that rent out trains to Britain’s railways were paid a combined £3.5m last year as they passed on almost £400m to shareholders in dividends. Rail unions accused the rolling stock companies (Roscos) of raking in profits at passengers’ expense. The figures emerged in accounts published this week after ministers announced a new rolling stock strategy for Britain’s railways. The government is considering direct ownership of trains through the public body Great British Railways rather than leasing them from the private sector. The latest figures show Porterbrook Holdings paid £80m in dividends and increased the pay of its chief executive, Mary Grant, by more than 10% to £1.44m. Eversholt Rail paid out £200m in 2025 shortly before it was sold by CK Hutchison to Beacon Rail, with its departing CEO, Mary Kenny, paid £1.33m. Angel Trains paid £111m in dividends and a relatively modest £700,000 to its boss, Malcolm Brown. Their pay far outstrips the highest salaries elsewhere on the railway, including the bosses of Network Rail and HS2. The RMT union called for a levy on Roscos after highlighting the dividend payments and salaries. It said the three biggest Roscos had paid out £2.4bn over the last 10 years in dividends. The general secretary of the RMT, Eddie Dempsey, said: “The government’s commitment to explore publicly owned rolling stock for the new trains in the future is welcome but in a cost of living crisis we need action now. “We are calling on the government to use this month’s budget to introduce a ‘cost of travel’ levy on profits to fund a 3.4% fare cut, rather than watching the cash being salted away.” The transport secretary, Heidi Alexander, told the Labour conference on Monday that if Great British Railways owning trains would best serve taxpayers and passengers, then we should do it”. According to the rail regulator, operators last year spent more than £4bn leasing trains from the Roscos, whose net profit margin was 18.5%. A spokesperson for Porterbrook said it had “deployed over £1bn of capital in new trains, fleet upgrades, traction innovation and rail infrastructure since 2020, and we are actively looking to invest a further £1bn in the years ahead”. They said the group’s companies were UK tax resident, and had paid £82m in the past three years, adding: “It is because of the funding that our shareholders provide that we can make substantial investments in the railway.” Angel Trains is incorporated in Jersey and within the realm of UK taxes. A spokesperson said: “We believe decisions on future fleets should be focused on securing the best outcomes for passengers, while maintaining the conditions and opportunities needed to attract future investment into the railway. We look forward to continuing to work constructively with government and Great British Railways.” Eversholt and its new owner, Beacon Rail, were approached for comment.

title: ‘Stand on the right side of history’: Starbucks urged to close stores in China’s Xinjiang
summary: US lawmakers say operating in region where Muslim minorities face mass detention is ‘morally bankrupt’
text: US lawmakers have urged Starbucks to close newly opened outlets in China’s Xinjiang, saying it was a “morally bankrupt decision” to operate in a region where Beijing has been accused of widespread human rights abuses against Muslim minorities. The coffeehouse chain, which last year sold a controlling stake in its China retail business to the Hong Kong-based investment firm Boyu Capital, opened two stores in the region on Tuesday. Videos on Chinese social media showed long queues for the flagship store in Urumqi’s Grand Bazaar tourist area, with influencers showing off special edition drinks including “milk-skin-flavoured salty milk tea”. But John Moolenaar, the chair of the US House of Representatives’ select committee on China, called the move “morally bankrupt”. “There is no justifiable reason for an American company to do business in a region where the Chinese Communist party has detained more than a million Uyghurs and is stripping them of their faith, language and culture,” he said. “Every cup sold in these stores ties an iconic American brand to the CCP’s brutal campaign against the Uyghurs.” Washington is among several governments and rights groups that have accused China of genocide in Xinjiang, which Beijing has categorically denied. The United Nations has warned of possible crimes against humanity, including the detention of more than a million Uyghurs and other Muslim minorities in camps. China says these were “education” camps and that crackdowns were necessary to combat terrorism. The World Uyghur Congress advocacy group called on Starbucks to “stand on the right side of history”. “The presence of Starbucks in Xinjiang’s streets … fits in the party state’s narrative, that there’s nothing wrong about the region,” said Human Rights Watch’s deputy Asia director, Maya Wang. Responding to the US comments, the Chinese foreign ministry told Reuters that allegations of repression were “naked lies” and that Xinjiang enjoyed a “stable society, economic growth, racial unity and religious harmony”. The Guardian has contacted Starbucks and Boyu Capital for comment. China has poured resources into developing Xinjiang as a tourism destination in recent years. Starbucks is far from alone in seeing the commercial appeal there: other major western brands such as Hilton and InterContinental Hotels Group have been criticised for their operations too. Critics have characterised Xinjiang’s development as “Disneyfication” – commodifying the region’s heritage even as its inhabitants’ ability to practise their culture on their own terms has been restricted. On Chinese social media, excited visitors posted pictures of Starbucks-branded merchandise, including patterned flasks and teddy bears in outfits based on local ethnic dress. When the deal with Boyu Capital was announced, Starbucks said it would bring “deep local expertise”, with analysts noting the US behemoth had been losing ground to domestic competitors for some time. The move by Starbucks makes “commercial sense”, said Yaling Jiang, the founder of the research and strategy consultancy ApertureChina. “What is politically correct in China is not necessarily politically correct in the rest of the world, and this is a prime example,” she said. “Starbucks in China is now operating from a Chinese perspective rather than a US perspective, and that is ultimately how they can win in China.”

title: Letter: Paul Brown obituary
summary: Sean Ryan writes: The Guardian environment correspondent knew how to deal with Brazilian muggers
text: In 1992, the Guardian environment correspondent Paul Brown and I were walking along Copacabana beach during the Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. Paul was mugged at my side by two women, who ran off with his wallet. “Just ignore them,” he said. A seasoned traveller, he had put an empty plastic wallet in his pocket for precisely the purpose of getting through a mugging unscathed. Cool guy!

title: Suicide by plane or terrorism? Speculation over motive in flight 1073 attack
summary: Experts sceptical flydubai co-pilot’s only motivation was to end his own life and say key question is means of radicalisation
text: At about 9.30 on Wednesday morning local time, Tali Manes was taking her six-year-old daughter, Nina, to the toilet on the regular flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv when she heard a series of heavy blows against the cockpit door. Manes, an Israeli bank executive, immediately told a flight attendant seated nearby that something was wrong. When he did not react, she shouted at him: “Something is happening in there!” Seconds later, the man “simply went to the [cockpit] door and opened it”, Manes told Israel’s Channel 12 TV. Inside, the scene was the stuff of travellers’ nightmares: blood spattered over the cockpit walls and a brutal struggle in progress between the badly injured pilot and the co-pilot, who was armed with some kind of sharp weapon. There was no one at the controls of the Boeing 737. Manes shouted again: “He’s stabbing the pilot, he’s stabbing the pilot, come help!” Many of the details of what happened on flight FZ 1073 are still unclear, but what happened next is well documented by witness testimony and videos. As the plane went into a steep dive, losing 16,000ft of altitude in about a minute, most of the 182 passengers screamed, prayed and tried desperately to reassure panicking children. But a small group rushed to the cockpit and overpowered the co-pilot. One, a plumber, copied an action seen on TV documentaries about plane crashes to pull the aircraft out of its dive. Two off-duty pilots on the flight, both among the handful of non-Israeli passengers, then took over the controls of the now almost rudderless aircraft to guide it eventually to a landing 90 minutes later in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia. In the meantime, Manes had helped truss the co-pilot with a telephone cord while a dentist treated the injured Indian pilot, Smit Machchhar. It was a “great miracle”, Manes said on eventually reaching Tel Aviv on an emergency flight 10 hours later. In a video call with Narendra Modi, the Indian prime minister, broadcast live by TV networks, Machchhar, who is recovering in an Abu Dhabi hospital, said he had been “fighting for my life”. The pilot successfully sent an alarm to air traffic control signalling the attack and then, as his strength ebbed, managed to unlock the cockpit security door. “I had so many wounds. I had fallen down,” Machhchar said. “At one point, I realised that if I didn’t get up … then passengers would lose their lives.” For the moment, the identity of the co-pilot who attacked Machchhar is unknown, though regional sources said he was an Omani national who had joined flydubai – which is owned by the United Arab Emirates (UAE) government – between five and nine months ago. The co-pilot was barred from flying in Oman over concerns he had adopted extremist views, the Associated Press quoted a source as saying on Saturday, and was subsequently hired by flydubai. In Israel, there is little doubt about the co-pilot’s intentions. “The co-pilot is a terrorist who tried either to hijack the plane or bring it down as a suicide. The worst scenario is he was trying to get into Israel,” said Arik Arad, the chair of the aviation cybersecurity consultancy Cyviation and El Al’s former head of security at Ben Gurion airport Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel’s prime minister, has claimed the co-pilot was exposed to “Islamist radical indoctrination”, saying Israeli investigators had found evidence on social media accounts that he wanted to “kill Jews”. “The attacker, he calls out to the aircrew: ‘Kill me, kill me,’” Netanyahu told Fox News, adding it was “clear he was suicidal”. Experts said there have been only a handful of instances of suicide by plane – cases where the pilot’s motivation is primarily to kill him or herself by crashing the plane, rather than using the plane as a weapon, as in the 9/11 attacks. In 2015, the co-pilot of a low-cost German airline flight who had hidden evidence of psychiatric illness from his employers deliberately crashed, killing himself and 150 others. Suggestions that the crash of an AirIndia 787 in Ahmedabad last year was the result of a pilot deliberately cutting fuel to engines have been fiercely disputed. Terrorism experts are sceptical that the flydubai co-pilot’s only motivation was to end his own life. “The odds that a pilot would decide to commit suicide and just happen to be flying a plane full of Israelis are pretty low,” said Colin Clarke, a terrorism expert at the respected Soufan Center in New York. “Netanyahu has a big interest in this being terrorism, but the best explanation is probably the most obvious one [ie terrorism],” he said. “The question … is: was [the co-pilot] recruited by a group or an organisation … or was he radicalised alone? In which case, what was hyping him up, given he was flying a planeload of Israelis? Could that be Gaza?” Security services have been warning of a wave of radicalisation across the Middle East prompted by the war in Gaza, which came to an inconclusive halt with a fragile ceasefire a year ago. But there has been limited evidence as yet that any violent Islamist extremist groups have gained support as a consequence of the conflict. Terrorism experts said the most obvious group that might be involved in such an attack would be al-Qaida in the Arabian Peninsula (AQAP), which is based in Yemen and has a history of efforts to bring down planes. They said AQAP had recently sought to launch or inspire violence internationally. “Aviation remains the classic propaganda by deed,” Clarke said. “It’s been said that terrorism is theatre, and nothing is more theatrical than taking down an airplane. You get a body count, media coverage, you get your message across, and this makes a plane the ultimate spectacular terrorist attack.” There are now many questions for aviation security. Changes made to plane design after 9/11, which allowed pilots to lock cockpit doors from the inside, have long been controversial among experts. If Machchhar’s desperate efforts to allow access to the flight deck had been unsuccessful, there is little doubt all onboard FZ 1073 would have died. There are also questions about screening of pilots. This can be expensive for airlines and could deprive them of valuable crew if too many fail more rigorous efforts to expose psychiatric illness or extremist views. Pilots may be reluctant to fly routes where they undergo greater screening, and some may hide physical or psychological problems for fear of being grounded. Arad said: “The important issue … is that obviously pilots are not being screened enough. Lots needs to be done.” Dubai international airport, the world’s busiest airport for international passenger traffic, has built some of its appeal on a reputation for safety in a volatile region, said Philip Baum, a visiting professor of aviation security at Coventry University in England. “They are very conscious of the fact – a little bit like Israel in many respects – that they cannot afford to have a terrorist attack happening on a flight out of there,” he said. The UAE has ordered investigators to “collect information and evidence to determine the truth of the incident, its circumstances, details and motives, and to verify the extent of its connection to any terrorist activity or purpose, or the existence of prior planning or direction for it,” its attorney general, Hamad Saif al-Shamsi, said on Thursday. Arad foresees growing threats to civilian aviation from cyber-attacks and the malevolent use of AI, which could allow the targeting multiple planes simultaneously. But other experts pointed out there was no need for such sophistication to pose a threat. Clarke said: “Whether or not it involves an attacker who was self-radicalised or part of a group, keeping things simple is always the best way to carry out an attack, and this came pretty damn close.”

title: Welsh first minister calls on Burnham to deliver ‘new deal’ on devolution
summary: Rhun ap Iorwerth tells Plaid Cymru conference he asked PM to ‘put Wales on equal footing with Scotland as bare minimum’
text: The Welsh first minister has formally called on Andy Burnham to deliver a “new deal” in his first address to a Plaid Cymru annual conference since taking office. Rhun ap Iorwerth told party members during a keynote speech in Llandudno on Friday that his government had a “clear mandate” for devolving more powers from Westminster. The first minister, who beat Labour to lead his nationalist party to a first victory in Senedd elections in May, said he had written to Burnham on Thursday to ask the prime minister for “a new deal to redress the historic unfairness of our fiscal and constitutional settlement and to put Wales on an equal footing with Scotland as a bare minimum”. After being greeted by delegates with a standing ovation, ap Iorwerth said: “A new deal – the first of its kind – whereby a Welsh first minister invites the UK government to genuinely treat Wales not as a region of England but as a nation in its own right. A new deal to secure powers … not as an end in themselves but as a means of growing our economy and improving outcomes for everyone.” The 2,000-word letter to Burnham made the case for transferring powers over policing and justice, rail infrastructure and the crown estate. Ap Iorwerth recently told the Guardian he had been encouraged by warm initial discussions with Burnham – a stark contrast to his interactions with Keir Starmer. However, the Welsh wing of the Labour party in Westminster is generally sceptical of devolving more powers to Cardiff, especially now Labour no longer controls the Senedd. The first minister said on Friday: “I do believe the new prime minister and I both want to have a constructive and positive relationship. I’ve looked him in the eyes and said do not undermine Wales as a nation … do not bypass our Senedd, and he looked me in the eyes and promised he would not. I will hold him to that.” Since becoming prime minister, Burnham has made much of his support for regional devolution of power and resources in England, but his approach to the existing devolved administrations in Belfast, Cardiff and Edinburgh is still forming. Plaid Cymru’s Welsh election win ended 100 years of Labour dominance in Wales and blocked the momentum of Nigel Farage’s Reform UK. Welsh Labour had governed in Wales since devolution began in 1999 but won just nine of the 96 seats in the new Senedd. Support for the party had been ebbing for years, driven by frustration about the management of public services, which have fallen behind the other UK nations on many metrics. Ap Iorwerth’s win also put nationalist parties in government simultaneously in Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland for the first time, although Plaid Cymru has ruled out an independence referendum during its first term. The party’s last autumn conference in Swansea had been full of excitement as members sensed the tide turning in Welsh politics. Its first as a party of government remained more relaxed and homely than those of rivals with deeper pockets and more seats in Westminster. The first minister’s demands for a “new deal” came a few weeks after a landmark summit of Plaid Cymru, Sinn Féin and Scottish National party leaders during which they affirmed their respective countries’ right to seek independence from the UK. Support for independence in Scotland has hovered between 45% and 50% since the 2014 referendum. Data suggests it is rising in Wales and Northern Ireland, and stands at 32% and 36% respectively. Burnham is expected to meet the three first ministers of the Celtic nations at the end of October. A UK government spokesperson said: “This government is committed to building a stronger and fairer Wales in a stronger and fairer United Kingdom. “That’s why our focus is now on working with the Welsh government to empower local leaders and communities to deliver good growth and jobs in every postcode.”

title: Throwback to 2011: why it feels different to the last time interest rates were this high in Australia
summary: From the supermarket checkout to the petrol pump, the way price rises ripple through the economy has changed dramatically
text: Mortgage holders are facing the highest cash rate in 15 years, but interest rates are only half the story of how the economic picture has changed since they last reached these heights. While indebted households bear the direct weight of Reserve Bank of Australia decisions, the broader cost-of-living squeeze is hitting everyday budgets through compounding price rises on just about everything. From the supermarket checkout to the petrol pump, the way price increases ripple across the economy has shifted dramatically since 2011. Sticker shock There are some costs most people can’t avoid such as groceries and petrol, and they are hitting households hard. The competition regulator found last year that between 2018 and late 2021, grocery prices increased largely in line with wages, before escalating quickly. By the end of 2022, grocery prices were increasing at more than twice the rate of wage growth. There are different views on why this has occurred, but it is notable that Australia’s heavily concentrated supermarket sector, led by Coles and Woolworths, has consistently expanded profit margins during inflationary surges. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email One of the fastest rising food prices has been beef, a kitchen staple for many Australian homes, with the relevant meat category up 95% since 2011, Australian Bureau of Statistics data shows. Wages rose 45% in total in that time. Beef mince at Coles, for example, has more than doubled in price. A 2011 catalogue prices regular mince at $6 a kilogram. Today it costs about $15 a kilo. The relentless price increases mean Australians have been living in a near constant state of “sticker shock” for the past five years. Petrol prices are another significant cost that has been an increasing burden. In 2011, the average unleaded price over the course of the year was just under $1.50 a litre, according to the Australian Institute of Petroleum, which was considered high at the time. They are now close to $2.40 a litre due to the US and Israel war on Iran, as well as fallout from the Russian invasion of Ukraine, and the related disruptions to global oil supplies. AMP’s chief economist, Shane Oliver, has warned petrol prices could surpass $2.70 a litre in what would be an inflation trigger given high fuel prices drive up costs across most goods and services. Another household cost, insurance premiums, has more than doubled since 2011, with the vast majority of that surge hitting policyholders since 2023, ABS data shows. Insurers attribute the recent bump to higher costs for tradespeople and materials required to do the same work. As climate-charged disasters become increasingly common, more Australians have been left paying more for inferior coverage. Mortgage pain The RBA lifted the official cash rate to 4.6% on Tuesday, its highest level since 2011, and warned of further hikes as the enduring US war on Iran rattles the global economy. Although the cash rate, which informs mortgage rates, has reached these levels before, property price rises have run far ahead of wage increases over the past 15 years, resulting in larger repayments. In 2011, the average house price was about $487,000, according to Loan Market, compared to more than $912,000 in 2026. Monthly repayments would have typically been a bit over $2,500 in 2011, almost half today’s level, according to the broker network. One upside, however, is that mortgage rates are generally closer to the official cash rate than they used to be, according to Canstar analysis, because lenders are fighting harder for customers. Canstar expects the average lowest variable mortgage rate to settle under 6.3% in response to the official cash rate rising to 4.6%. When the cash rate was last near this level in late 2011, the typical low rate was close to 7%. Now showing Sometimes, comparing prices of an item in 2011 to 2026 doesn’t tell the whole story because buying habits change. Cinema ticket prices were about $13 in 2011, according to data from Screen Australia, and hovered around that mark for years. When venues sought to stay competitive against the rise of streaming platforms like Netflix – which launched in Australia in 2015 – movie prices effectively froze. However, that strategy shifted during the pandemic when cinemas began leaning heavily into luxury offerings, such as recliners and in-seat catering, to lure viewers back to the big screen. That upgrade came at a cost, with average ticket prices jumping by a third in just a few years to about $18. Varis Desai, industry analyst at IBISWorld, says the pivot was designed to drive higher spending among affluent moviegoers, which has been successful at some premium venues. Meanwhile, the change in the price of takeaway coffee varies widely according to location. Almost 15 years ago, coffee prices were so high in Perth, the then BHP Billiton boss Marius Kloppers made media headlines when he complained about paying $5.50 for a takeaway. Western Australia was at the tail end of the iron ore boom at the time, which had filtered through the state economy, driving up wages and inflating operating costs for everyday businesses. The boom subsided, and prices started to normalise, making it possible to still find a $5.50 coffee in Perth 15 years later, although it’s probably a smaller size and not from a specialty roaster.

title: India’s Cockroach movement launches new protests over changes to voter roll
summary: Thousands gather in Mumbai with heavy police presence as concerns mount that millions will be denied voting rights
text: India’s youth-led Cockroach movement kicked off more nationwide protests on Friday as thousands of people gathered in Mumbai, amid mounting concerns that millions of citizens are being unfairly stripped of their vote. The movement, which calls itself the Cockroach Janta party (CJP) and has massive support among the country’s gen Zs, returned to the streets to demand the resignation of the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar. Kumar has become a highly contentious figure after a report in the Indian Express newspaper alleged irregularities and internal concerns about a process to revise and “purify” India’s electoral register, called the Special Intensive Revision (SIR). SIR, which was overseen by Kumar, has resulted in tens of millions of people being deleted from the electoral register. Large numbers are challenging their removal. Opposition politicians and civil society groups have alleged SIR is part of a widespread manipulation of India’s electoral system to benefit the ruling Bharatiya Janata party (BJP). The CJP began as online satire but grew into a powerful manifestation of youth power and an unexpected challenge to the Narendra Modi government. There were protests for weeks in the heart of Delhi and the education minister was eventually pressured into resigning in July. In the aftermath, the group declared it would remain active as a “pressure group” to hold the government to account on issues of education and democracy. Last week, after the revelations about the election commission, the CJP’s founder, Abhijeet Dipke, announced that if Kumar did not resign over the controversy, the “Cockroaches” would resume their agitation until he stepped down. Dipke said the Mumbai protest would kick off a nationwide movement, with more protests planned in Delhi, Goa, Kolkata and Bengaluru. The authorities denied permission for the group to hold their protest at Mumbai’s Shivaji park but Dipke had vowed to go ahead regardless. “We are fighting against those in power,” he said at a press conference. “We all remember Mahatma Gandhi, who fought against the Britishers. Did the British ever permit him to agitate?” Hundreds of people assembled in Mumbai on Friday afternoon, amid a heavy police presence, including many young people who said they were there to fight for India’s democracy. “Voting is the most basic right of any citizen, but because of the actions of Kumar and the election commission, that right is under attack,” said Deesha, 22, a student activist. “So many millions of people have lost their votes and aren’t even recognised as citizens of India any more. This attack on our democracy must stop. The first important step is to get Gyanesh Kumar to resign, and then SIR must be reversed.” Janvi Upadhyay, 18, said the Cockroach movement had awoken the young people of India “and if they think they can just come and take away votes and cheat the elections, we will show them just how wrong they are”. “We already forced the education minister to resign. Gyanesh Kumar should be very worried right now because he is definitely next,” she said. The election commission has denied wrongdoing in the SIR but in a move that appeared aimed at easing tensions, officials were directed to expedite the process to register newly eligible voters and those who claimed to have been wrongly omitted from electoral rolls. Anger at Kumar and the election commission also erupted in Delhi on Friday, even as the police took draconian measures to try to stop people from protesting. Thousands of police were deployed to the Jantar Mantar protest site in Delhi – which was the epicentre of the last Cockroach agitation in July – a dozen metro stations in the surrounding area were closed and an internet shutdown was imposed. Hundreds of those who turned out to Jantar Mantar were immediately forced into police buses. The mass detentions of at least 700 people, including civil society leaders and opposition politicians, prompted outrage, with protesters leaning out of the bus windows to accuse police officers of depriving them of their fundamental democratic rights. Opposition parties said they would also start a nationwide protest movement to demand Kumar’s resignation. All opposition lawmakers plan to march to the election commission office in Delhi next week.

title: Fires, fury and hundreds of arrests as France gripped by student protests
summary: Government struggling to deal with worst crisis in months after being taken by surprise by massive demonstrations
text: As dozens of school pupils sat on top of a pile of wheelie bins blocking a high school entrance in north-eastern Paris, Sophia, 17, was on the frontline of the barricade, when she would normally have been attending Spanish class. “We hope this grows into a massive youth protest movement,” said the final year baccalaureate student at Paris’s Lycée Voltaire, who did not want her real name published. She was on her second day of blocking the school entrance along with hundreds of others, ensuring all lessons were cancelled. “We just want to be listened to by the government. We’d rather stand here doing this than have to learn in poor conditions. It’s the only way to make ourselves heard.” “School is a right, not a privilege,” read a cardboard sign as Sophia listed the grievances of teenagers across France: a lack of state investment in education, overcrowded classes of up to 40 children in crumbling buildings, poor teacher pay, staff absences and an unequal system in which social background determined success. Other reasons for the protest included the opaque and difficult online system for university applications as well as the unbearable temperatures in classrooms during the heatwaves in May and June. “The education budget is being cut to shreds while so much extra funding is being put into the army,” said Sophia, who wanted to go on to study art and work in animation. She said she hoped the demonstrations and blockades would continue into next week. Several teachers stood by the barricades in support. The French government is struggling to deal with its worst crisis in months after it was taken by surprise by the thousands of teenagers demonstrating outside schools across the country this week. Students’ unions say the education system is underfunded and neglected. Hundreds of high schools were closed or barricaded on Friday, and hundreds of young people have been arrested as the movement threatens to roll on into next week. Many school students protesting have accused the state of disengaging from secondary education, describing difficult conditions in classrooms with ceilings partially collapsing during class, leaks, cockroaches and buildings in disrepair. Others have spoken of excessively long school days and a lack of teaching staff. The government said the grievances were legitimate but condemned what it called “urban violence”. Students have accused police of using excessive force and causing injuries by regularly firing teargas canisters to disperse the protests. In Paris on Friday morning, fire damaged the entrances of two high schools – Léonard de Vinci in the south of the city and Gaston-Bachelard in the south-east. Several students have been injured in the protests, while the education ministry said 65 education staff were injured, including 40 school principals. An investigation is under way after a 14-year-old boy in Val d’Oise suffered serious injuries to his mouth and jaw after police allegedly beat him and fired a form of rubber-bullet launcher. The family’s lawyer said the boy had thought he was “going to die”. Outside Lycée Voltaire, riot police stood guard on Friday amid the quiet demonstration by hundreds of children. “We’re totally pacifist,” said Yves, a 17-year-old final year pupil who did not want his name published. He would normally have been in history class but said he had the full support of his parents to be on the barricade. He wanted to study catering next year. “The atmosphere on this barricade is generally very calm,” he said. “But there have been other people from outside school who have come past and tried to set fire to things, so we’ve tried to move the bins to stop that.” On Friday morning, loud bangs rang out as some people further away from the school let off firework mortars. Yves said: “Yesterday I heard bangs going off every two minutes, it’s loud and scary when things are being fired horizontally and not up into the air. There were people provoking running battles with police but it wasn’t pupils from our school.” Camille, 18, who said he wanted to become a teacher, said pupils were also protesting over the French government’s lack of engagement over poor results in international education rankings. “France has disastrous results and yet we’re one of the countries with the longest school days,” he said. “The government refuses to see that it’s about quality, not the number of teaching hours.” Farther east, on the barricade outside the Lycée Hélène Boucher, students were singing and holding cardboard signs of support for people in Gaza, as well as banners against the far-right presidential candidate, Marine Le Pen, who is riding high in the polls. Sofiane, 19, who was studying literature, said students feared the government would scrap its special €1 meals for struggling students and reduce welfare aid for housing. “We’re also protesting about the conditions in the heatwave,” he said. “It was unbearable sitting exams in 35C-40C heat, even the teachers said those were impossible conditions.” He said the demonstrations were likely to continue. “Young people just want to study and learn in decent conditions. The French state seems surprised about worsening school results, but they’re doing nothing to remedy that.”

title: US added just 29,000 jobs in September in sharp drop from last month’s gains
summary: Final jobs report before the midterm elections also shows the US unemployment rate rose slightly to 4.2%
text: US employers added just 29,000 jobs in September, a sharp drop from last month’s gains, and unemployment rose slightly to 4.2%, a sign of a cooling labor market in the final jobs report before the midterm election. The numbers were under half of economists’ expectations of just under 70,000 new jobs. Most job gains were concentrated in the healthcare industry, which added 17,000 new jobs, while the information, financial and professional industries saw losses, according to the latest data from the US Bureau of Labor Statistics. Earlier jobs figures were also revised down: Initial reports from July and August altogether dropped by 60,000. The labor market contracted by 10,000 jobs in July after revisions, while August saw 133,000 jobs added. Growth in average hourly earnings slumped to 3%, the lowest rate in over five years. The unemployment rate has remained relatively steady since last year, when it hit 4.5% in November. US jobless claims also inched lower for the fourth week in a row, the labor department said on Thursday. But a closer look at the data also reveals how not all Americans are experiencing the same labor market. Unemployment among Black Americans grew an entire percentage point to 7%, double the rate of white Americans. Though job growth slumped over the summer – the labor market unexpectedly contracted in July and figures in June and May were revised sharply down from initial reports – 162,000 jobs were added in August, the highest since March. Job openings and the number of hires have also remained little changed in August, according to the recent data from the labor department, as the “slow-hire, slow-fire” job market continues. Data from private employers released by the payroll firm, ADP, earlier this week had painted a much rosier picture of the labor market. It found that private sector hiring accelerated last month for the first time since May, carried by growth in the healthcare, education and hospitality industries, and private employers added 90,000 new jobs. The labor market has remained largely strong this year even as the US-Israel war on Iran has upped inflation, especially energy prices. Last month, the Federal Reserve raised interest rates for the first time in three years, citing higher prices. At the time, the Fed chair, Kevin Warsh, emphasized the strength of the US labor market, which “is basically running consistent with full employment”, but he noted that “inflation is too high and has been for too long”. Though the data still reflects an overall solid jobs market, the September release cools expectations for the US Federal Reserve to increase rates again in its final meeting before the 3 November midterms. Most central bank officials penciled in at least one more rate hike before the year’s end, which is now more likely to come at the Fed’s December conference. But higher prices continue to be the biggest economic pain point for Americans. Mortgage rates accelerated to their highest level in three years on Thursday from 7% to 7.28%, the largest weekly jump since 2022. The 10-year treasury yield, which underpins mortgages and other loans, also reached a 24-year high as the recent global bond sell-off continued. Meanwhile, higher oil prices have cost Americans an estimated $936 per household.

title: Palestine Action crowdfunder for UK supreme court challenge blocked due to US sanctions
summary: Exclusive: CrowdJustice platform says US firm Stripe, its payment processor, ‘cannot support accounts or transactions’ linked to group
text: An online crowdfunder to raise money for the UK supreme court challenge to the ban on Palestine Action has been blocked as a result of US sanctions against the direct action group. CrowdJustice, a UK company, has declined to host a fundraiser for legal fees to fight proscription because the platform uses the US company Stripe as its payment processor. In an email seen by the Guardian, CrowdJustice said Stripe had confirmed “that it cannot support accounts or transactions linked to, or for the benefit of, Palestine Action. This includes circumstances where funds are being raised for legal proceedings.” The US sanctions were imposed last month by Donald Trump, using powers introduced by President George W Bush in 2001 shortly after the 9/11 attacks by al-Qaida on the twin towers in New York. Huda Ammori, a co-founder of Palestine Action, who has brought the legal challenge against the UK ban, said: “Due to CrowdJustice’s and other platforms’ reliance on US services, we are unable to fundraise for legal fees needed for our supreme court challenge. “On the other hand, the state continues to spend millions of pounds to cover their legal costs to defend the disproportionate and draconian ban, which has led to more than 3,700 arrests for holding signs [allegedly supporting a proscribed organisation]. The British government and the US are putting every possible obstacle in our way, in order to stack the odds against us.” The Home Office has spent £700,000 defending proscription in the high court, according to the Independent. The total amount spent by the government will be far higher as the case has since been heard by the court of appeal, which overturned the high court’s decision that the ban was unlawful, and moves to the UK’s highest court in November. When the then home secretary, Yvette Cooper, announced her intention to ban Palestine Action under UK law in June last year, placing the group alongside the likes of Islamic State and Boko Haram, a CrowdJustice fundraiser for legal fees to fund a high court challenge raised more than £300,000 within days. Ammori said: “Clearly, the powerful have banded together against citizens acting on their conscience against the Israeli war machine and ethnic cleansing of Palestine. It is extremely clear that Palestine Action faces harsher sanctions than Israel. “The supreme court case is extremely important for our rights to free speech in Britain, but also for the people of Palestine. If we are successful, all prosecutions of protesters who held signs will be rightfully quashed. If not, we will witness thousands of people facing jail for holding placards.” The former British diplomat Craig Murray, who is separately challenging the legality of the ban on Palestine Action in Scotland, had his own CrowdJustice fundraiser for legal fees taken down after the US designated the group as a global terrorist organisation. “It’s really disgraceful,” Murray said. “Not only do you have draconian legislation with the proscription of Palestine Action affecting freedom of speech but you’ve then got moves to cripple our ability to fight it legally through the courts, which is just adding injustice to injustice.” Stripe said it did not comment on individual users. CrowdJustice was also approached for comment.

title: John Maynard Keynes: the cultured economist who governments turn to in a crisis
summary: A new play about the art-loving Bloomsbury Group member speaks of the enduring battle of ideas with his free-market rival Friedrich Hayek
text: The sound of guns from the advancing German armies could be heard clearly by John Maynard Keynes as his train trundled across northern France in the spring of 1918. The evidence of the struggle on the western front was everywhere but Keynes, then a Treasury official, was not heading to Paris on war business; he was off to buy some art. Keynes made the risky trip to attend an auction of the studio of Edgar Degas, who had died the previous year. The man who would become the foremost economist of the 20th century returned to London with some impressionist treasures for the National Gallery, having successfully petitioned the chancellor of the exchequer to spend £20,000 at the sale. This story reveals much about Keynes. His skill in lobbying officialdom for funds at a time when the country was involved in a costly war. His love of art, which culminated in him being instrumental in setting up the Arts Council. His conviction that economics mattered less than the good things in life. All of which makes the title of James Graham’s new play about Keynes, The Standard of Living, wholly appropriate. Keynes pored over statistics but was much more than a number cruncher. He had firm views about why the economy was malfunctioning in the 1920s and 1930s, but was just as interested in discussing philosophy with Bertrand Russell and Ludwig Wittgenstein. He believed a growing economy should provide the opportunity for more leisure time rather than the accumulation of monetary wealth. He revolutionised economics without having a revolutionary bone in his body. Born into a well-off academic family, Keynes went to Eton before studying maths at Cambridge. His circle of friends after university was the Bloomsbury Group, painters and writers who included Virginia Woolf, and two of his lovers, Lytton Strachey and Duncan Grant. This was a group that prided itself on being unconventional, on not accepting the status quo. Bloomsbury helped satisfy Keynes’s cultural needs but also helped shape his economic thinking. He did not see growth as an end in itself but rather as a means to live the good life or – as he put it – to live like the “lilies in the field”. In Economic Possibilities for Our Grandchildren he foresaw a time when the economic problem had been solved, when the working week would be considerably shorter and “when the accumulation of wealth was no longer of high social importance”. His willingness to challenge the orthodoxy was demonstrated in an early book, The Economic Consequences of the Peace, which correctly predicted that the punitive terms imposed by the treaty of Versailles in 1919 would result in a humiliated Germany remaining bitter and vengeful. To the surprise of his Bloomsbury friends, Keynes later fell in love with a Russian ballet dancer, Lydia Lopokova, and the couple married in 1925 when he was 42. While forthright and confident when expressing his opinions, Keynes was self-conscious about his appearance, considering himself repulsive. Others agreed. Virginia Woolf once described him as like “a gorged seal, double chin, ledge of red lip, little eyes, sensual, brutal, unimaginative”. One of the central themes of the play is the battle of ideas between Keynes and the Austrian economist Friedrich Hayek. The latter believed that left to their own devices, free markets provided the best economic outcomes and that over the long term crises would be resolved without the need for state intervention. Keynes took the opposite view, summed up by perhaps his most famous quote: “In the long run we are all dead. Economists set themselves too easy, too useless a task if in tempestuous seasons they can only tell us that when the storm is long past the ocean is flat again.” By this he meant that the economy had no natural tendency towards full employment. Rather, high unemployment could last indefinitely unless the government was prepared to step in and stimulate demand. This argument formed the centrepiece of his most famous book, The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money. The General Theory, as it is commonly known, challenged conventional economic thinking and had a profound influence on policymakers in the decades after the second world war, when it was seen as the responsibility of governments to manage demand to secure full employment. Keynes saw the many flaws in the capitalist system but was no Marxist. As an unashamed elitist, he saw it as his mission to save capitalism from itself, if only because he saw it as the best way to safeguard civilised values. “He is contemptuous of common men, especially when gathered together in herds,” the social reformer Beatrice Webb once observed. “He dislikes the human herd and has no desire to enlist the human herd on his side.” Unsurprisingly, the hard left have their suspicions about Keynes. As his biographer Robert Skidelsky wrote: “Marxists have long argued that Keynes’s ideas were taken up because they served the interests of the bourgeoisie in the 1930s and were dropped when they started to endanger capitalist profits in the 1970s.” It is certainly true that Keynes and his ideas fell out of fashion by the mid-1970s, a period when western economies were afflicted by rising inflation and weak growth at the same time. Postwar Keynesian economists were baffled by the appearance of high inflation and high unemployment at the same time, and the new right – spearheaded politically by Margaret Thatcher and Ronald Reagan – emerged victorious from this era of “stagflation”. Inspired by Hayek’s ideas, it set about dismantling the postwar settlement based on full employment, state ownership, strong trade unions and generous welfare spending. The 2008 global financial crisis saw the new right model come to grief. A belief that markets could never be wrong meant the dangers of excessive speculation were ignored and ultimately left the global banking system teetering on the point of collapse. For the first time since the 1930s there was a real risk of a full-scale depression and in those circumstances policymakers dusted down their copies of The General Theory in the search for a response. Keynes would have sensed a financial crisis was coming. He speculated on the financial markets, not always successfully. In 1920, he created what would be today called a heavily leveraged hedge fund using money provided by his Bloomsbury friends – taking bets on currency movements – only to see his syndicate’s capital wiped out when the pound unexpectedly fell. Even so, he was aware of the risks. “Speculators may do no harm as bubbles on a steady stream of enterprise,” he said. “But the position is serious when enterprise becomes the bubble on a whirlpool of speculation. When the capital development of a country becomes the byproduct of the activities of a casino, the job is likely to be ill done.” Today, Keynes and Hayek are still revered by their followers on the political left and right respectively. Yet, the past two decades have showed the enduring nature of Keynes’s insights, first in 2008 and then during the global pandemic of 2020. Faced with a crisis, belief in free markets goes out of the window as governments use every policy tool at their disposal to boost growth and prevent unemployment from rising. Or as the arch-critic of Keynes – the Nobel prize-winning economist Robert Lucas – put it in 2008: “I guess everyone is a Keynesian in a foxhole.” The Standard of Living is at Theatre Royal Haymarket, London, until 12 December.

title: Tesco is first supermarket to offer paid ‘safe leave’ for victims of domestic abuse
summary: Exclusive: Britain’s largest private-sector employer has also trained managers to spot signs of domestic abuse
text: Tesco has become the first supermarket to introduce paid “safe leave” for victims of domestic abuse, giving staff dedicated time to access support, secure their safety and take steps to move on with their lives. The UK’s largest private-sector employer is offering up to three days of paid leave which can be taken flexibly for activities such as attending court hearings, arranging emergency accommodation, changing locks, securing childcare or separating finances. Managers across the business, which employs 300,000 people, have also been trained to spot the signs of domestic abuse, support those affected and flag them to specialist services. Under the new policy, which was developed in partnership with the shopworkers’ union Usdaw, Tesco will not ask those suffering abuse to provide formal evidence to gain access to the special leave. Tesco is thought to be the first big British retailer to introduce safe leave, but similar policies, such as protected paid leave, emergency accommodation and training staff to spot the signs of domestic abuse, have been enacted at other UK companies, including BP and Vodafone, as well as some local councils. Daniel Adams, an Usdaw national officer, said domestic violence and abuse affected the lives of at least one in five women, and he urged other employers to introduce similar support. “Usdaw has long campaigned for support at work for survivors of domestic abuse and we are pleased to have successfully negotiated this new policy with Tesco. Domestic abuse often has an impact on the working lives of survivors, and it is important that employers understand this and the actions they can take to support and protect them,” he said. “Historically violence against women, and domestic violence in particular, has been hidden, excused and ignored. That needs to change.” Emma Taylor, the chief people officer at Tesco, said: “We believe we have a responsibility to support colleagues in what are likely to be some of the most challenging moments in their lives. “That’s why we’re introducing guaranteed safe leave, ensuring colleagues can access practical support and the time they need without worrying about taking unpaid leave or explaining deeply personal circumstances. “We’re proud to be taking this step and want it to help drive wider action from employers across the UK. No one should have to choose between their job and their safety.” More than 3 million people suffered some form of domestic abuse in England and Wales last year, most of whom were women, according to the campaign group SafeLives. It says eight women a month are killed by a current or former partner in England and Wales, based on 2023 data. There was a sharp increase in abuse incidents during the pandemic lockdowns as victims were trapped at home with perpetrators. The permanent shift to working from home since then is seen to have made some people more vulnerable. The Domestic Abuse Act, which became law in April 2021, includes workplace protection for domestic abuse victims, who can see their place of work as somewhere to seek help and support. A private member’s bill currently before parliament proposes granting 10 days of paid leave for domestic abuse victims in England and Wales to give them time to deal with the practical and emotional steps. In 2020, Northern Ireland passed legislation guaranteeing domestic abuse victims 10 days’ paid leave, and similar laws exist in Australia, New Zealand and the Philippines.

title: Reform UK-run council boycotts reporter after row over potholes
summary: Derbyshire county council accused of ‘worst kind of double speak’ as it denies banning local democracy journalist but says it will ignore his inquiries
text: Rows over potholes and a viral story about a garden gate have led to Reform UK’s latest confrontation with local media, after one of its councils announced it would refuse to engage with a reporter behind the stories. Reform-run Derbyshire county council has been accused of setting a “dangerous precedent” after withdrawing all cooperation with Eddie Bisknell, a Derbyshire Live journalist who is publicly funded to cover local democracy. Stephen Reed, the Reform council’s deputy leader, said the reporter would now have to work “twice as hard” to do his job after confirming that Bisknell’s inquiries would be ignored. It comes after a neighbouring Reform council last year banned journalists from a major local newspaper. Nottinghamshire county council eventually ended its ban on the Nottingham Post and its website, Nottinghamshire Live, after being threatened with legal action. In the Derbyshire case, Reform said its decision had been made after a “prolonged period of concerns”, which culminated in a story about potholes. Councillors had hoped to produce positive headlines with a press release stating that the number of potholes in the county had been slashed from 12,000 in April to less than 700 – a figure it described as the lowest recorded in over a year. However, an article by Bisknell, one of a group of local democracy reporters funded by the BBC, reported that questions had been raised about statistics used in the release. The block on engaging with Bisknell emerged as the council took issue with another story about how a fence panel had been cemented across a gap in a wall between an 81-year-old woman’s garden and a council car park. The work had been initiated by the previous Conservative-led administration. However, Reed said the decision to block the reporter had been made before the latest story about the fence appeared. He denied an outright ban had been imposed, saying Bisknell was still able to write about the council and attend public council events – a right enshrined in law. However, he confirmed the council would ignore his requests for information. “I want to be very clear: non-engagement is not a ban,” he said. “He can still write whatever he wants. What we’ve chosen to do as an administration and as a council is just not respond to his inquiries. “We don’t think it’s fair to other good working reporters and journalists who actually hold us to account. We want to be scrutinised. We want people to challenge what we’ve done. We want to get good news stories out and we accept that we’re going to have criticism, but it needs to be fair and balanced.” Natalie Fahy, editor-in-chief for London and the east of England for Reach, which owns Derbyshire Live, said Reform’s decision was plainly a ban. “We have covered some awful situations at many different councils over the years, and we don’t always expect our relationships with councils to be cosy, but we do expect there to be an open dialogue,” she said. “To say this isn’t a ban is the worst kind of double speak and something we should all be on guard for, if you consider a free press essential to a functioning democracy.” Dawn Alford, chief executive of the Society of Editors, called for the decision to be reversed. “Refusing to engage with a journalist because you object to their reporting sets a dangerous precedent,” she said. “A council cannot simply choose which reporters deserve answers. Transparency is a responsibility, not a favour. “This matters far beyond one journalist or one story. When a public body shuts out a reporter, it is the public who lose access to answers about decisions taken in their name and money spent on their behalf.” Laura Davison, the NUJ’s general secretary, called on the council to “get off its high horse and respect the democratic norms voters and local communities they represent expect”.

title: A small Texas town stopped Trump’s border wall construction – for now
summary: As they had in the past, San Ygnacio residents banded together to stop a development threatening their town
text: This story was co-published and supported by the journalism non-profit the Economic Hardship Reporting Project. Joel Ruiz pointed his cane toward a long piece of metal lying in the dirt. Unwanted construction crews had left it behind on his riverfront property where he has lived and run a small fishing business for decades in San Ygnacio, Texas. At 90, Ruiz still tends the land. But in July, heavy machinery gouged the earth where mesquite and dense brush once grew. A steel barricade of 30ft-high bars was erected across the riverfront, including on his property just across the Rio Grande from Mexico. For months, Ruiz and a handful of other San Ygnacio residents have been trying to halt the construction of a federal border wall in their Mexican American town of roughly 400 people. They’ve blocked bulldozers, been arrested, unearthed 75-year-old land records and filed lawsuits challenging the federal government’s authority to build here. Even though residents say nearly all the riverfront land in the county is privately owned, the government is building on it anyway, claiming a decades-old right. While they have stopped construction on the disputed land for now – a verbal concession, not a court order – the reprieve is precarious: the lawsuits are unresolved, the federal money set aside for construction remains in place and residents know the crews could be back. But they are drawing on the memory of a town that rose up against the government once before. “This little spot is all we have,” said Elsa Hull, who owns property downriver with her two daughters. “But [residents] fought the federal government before and won – and we can do it again.” ‘Life or death for us’ Founded along the Rio Grande in 1830, San Ygnacio grew from a cluster of ranches into a small border town. Today, its plaza is still lined with homes made of sandstone quarried from the riverbank. The town sits in Zapata county, where roughly 38% of residents live below the poverty line and the median household income is about $39,000. Many work in healthcare, schools, food service and ranching. The border patrol is a major regional employer: its sector in Laredo employs about 3,025 people. The construction is part of the Trump administration’s renewed border-wall push – a roughly $46.5bn expansion funded by what is known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. San Ygnacio is located in one of the stretches where that money is now hitting the ground – and it’s going up as the number of border apprehensions is dropping drastically. Ruiz said he rarely sees anyone crossing this stretch of river any more. The Rio Grande is also San Ygnacio’s sole source of drinking water, and the wall is being built in its floodplain. To expedite construction, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) waived 30 federal laws – among them the Clean Water Act and the National Environmental Policy Act, eliminating the environmental review that would normally accompany a project of this scale. (The DHS did not respond to the Guardian’s request for comment.) To fill that gap, the Laredo-based Rio Grande International Study Center (RGISC) commissioned its own. The assessment warned that the wall and buoy system along and in the Rio Grande would worsen flooding – and, in places, fail outright. “This is life or death for us,” said Tricia Cortez, the center’s executive director. A breach of the wall system, she warned, would be sudden and catastrophic – homes destroyed, lives endangered. “The wall will straitjacket the river, forcing flood waters to rise and move faster.” Construction in San Ygnacio had begun without notice. Residents watched what they called a “man camp” rise at its edge and sensed something was coming. At a June community meeting to discuss other business, word began spreading through the back of the room: contractors were clearing land along the riverbank. Several residents hurried down and confronted the equipment operators, telling them they were on private property. Hull spent 25 years as an environmental investigator for the Texas commission on environmental quality. She recalled how she would watch deer, bobcats, coyotes and sunsets over the river from a bench beneath a tree on the bluff. Border construction has since knocked the tree down and smashed the bench. “Every part of my life is intertwined with the Rio Grande,” Hull said. “To me this river is sacred.” When contractors arrived near Ruiz’s home and RV park in June, he invited Hull and her friend to see the damage done. Crews had razed trees and severed an irrigation line. Before leaving for an appointment, Ruiz signed a paper authorizing Hull and her friend to stay and watch the property. Two contractor trucks slipped through the gate. Hull said one worker repeatedly flashed a card marked “CBP” – presumably Customs and Border Protection. Then she noticed Southwest Valley Constructors identification on his vest. “You’re not CBP,” Hull recalled telling him. When another truck approached, Hull drove her car across the entrance. More trucks arrived, followed by sheriff’s deputies, state troopers and border patrol agents. “We were just surrounded by all these men,” Hull said. Hull pulled up the county appraisal map and argued the crews were on Ruiz’s property. A deputy insisted the land was federal. Finally, Hull put her water bottle on the hood of her car and sat down. “Fuck it,” she said. “Arrest me.” They did. On 14 August, Hull returned, carrying a flag that read “Keep Our River Free” on one side and “Walls and Buoys Kill” on the other. When a sheriff’s deputy called to her from across a fence, she thought he wanted to talk. Instead, she was handcuffed and arrested again. A win from the past San Ygnacio had fought the federal government for this land once before – and won. When government contractors insisted the land was federal, Frank “Chip” Briscoe, an architectural conservator, started digging through county records. The trail led back to the early 1950s, when the government built the Falcon dam. Its reservoir submerged historic ranch communities and Indigenous sites along the river, and San Ygnacio was scheduled to be condemned and cleared for the reservoir, too. But residents refused to accept it. In 1951, more than 200 people signed a petition, organized by local veterans and civic leaders, opposing the measure. It worked: the government carved San Ygnacio out of the condemnation, the one stretch along the river bend spared from the reservoir. Seventy years later, the town is invoking that same exclusion again. Briscoe and attorney Ricardo de Anda searched subsequent property records and still found no evidence that the federal government had later acquired the excluded land. The documents gave De Anda something concrete to act on. In mid-June, he met with the US army corps of engineers on Ruiz’s behalf, arguing the crews had no legal grounds to build on the disputed property. When construction continued, De Anda sent a warning letter and filed two lawsuits against the federal government, alleging it took private property in violation of the fifth amendment. Two more landowners are preparing to sue, and De Anda plans to sue the contractor, Southwest Valley Constructors, in state court. Landowners filed criminal trespass complaints, while about a dozen residents pressed local officials to intervene. About a month later, according to De Anda, the county attorney arranged a meeting with contractors and federal officials. “They agreed to stop,” he said, and the crews pulled back – for now. For De Anda, stopping construction is only part of the plan. “Our strategy is to affect the national consciousness,” he said. The rest is a matter of time. Every day they hold the line – with their bodies, their deeds, their lawsuits – buys more of it. They are looking toward the midterms, hoping a change in Congress could give them another opening. They are betting they can outlast it. At San Ygnacio’s Grito de Septiembre festival, enlarged copies of the 1951 petition and its signature pages were displayed in the plaza. Residents gathered around them, searching for the names of their ancestors. Back on Ruiz’s land, people have stopped coming to fish for white bass and alligator gar; when construction began, it blocked his boat ramp access. The small fishing business he ran here is now, in his words, “kaput”. Still, Ruiz keeps coming to the river. In 1973, he helped establish a bird sanctuary beside his property. “My baby,” he called it. “I built it.” When asked whether his daily walks down to the river had become a way of watching for the crews to return – their equipment still sitting idle on the land – he shook his head. He was here “just to be here”, he said.
