title: Man shot by ICE in Texas has surgery to remove bullet lodged in his back
summary: Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez remains in custody after surgery to remove bullet supporters say was stuck close to his spine
text: The Venezuelan delivery driver who was shot and wounded by a federal immigration agent in Texas last month had surgery on Thursday to remove the bullet that had been lodged in his back for nearly two weeks. Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez, 28, had appeared in court in a wheelchair on Wednesday, wearing a sling on his arm. He remains in custody on charges that he assaulted an officer while trying to evade arrest. Supporters and representatives had been lobbying for him to be given the chance of surgery, asserting that there was a risk he would lose feeling on the left side of his body because of the bullet being stuck so close to his spine. He had been taken from a hospital where he was being treated after being shot by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer in Austin and put in detention at a facility about 140 miles away the same day. The authorities said Garcés Pérez struck an officer with his side mirror on 20 September while trying to drive away after a traffic stop and questioning. The federal officer who shot Garcés Pérez, and who allegedly was hit by the side mirror of the car, was not wearing a body camera. Garcés Pérez faces up to 20 years in prison if convicted on the assault charge. He was also facing deportation when he was stopped while driving on a DoorDash delivery in Austin last month, with some of the incident caught on bystander footage, including how ICE officers called an ambulance and then stood by as the wounded man sat in his car and then was given first aid by local police when they arrived. The bullet was successfully removed during surgery, and Garcés Pérez is recovering in the custody of the US Marshals, said Fabiana Meléndez Ruiz, a spokesperson for his legal team. His case has sparked outrage and protests in the Texas capital city against Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown, including federal officers’ conduct. It was the latest shooting by ICE officers. Garcés Pérez said he was struck by a law enforcement SUV and his car spun around before he was shot. Federal officers told investigators, however, that Garcés Pérez attempted to strike an officer with his car at the end of the chase before the officer fired his weapon. The Associated Press contributed reporting

title: Does Philadelphia’s ‘house of horrors’ hold the key to seven missing women?
summary: City on edge as police comb home of Raymond Horsch, pornographer who died last year, in grisly case involving disturbing pictures and film
text: A dilapidated house, burned out above the second story, may hold clues to dark tales and – potentially – the darkest of endings as the FBI and police in Philadelphia try to unpick what took place at 417 West Chew Avenue for more than three decades. Last week, homicide investigators shifted their focus from examining an archive of a million photographs and film recovered from what is known locally as the “house of horrors” to excavating what is in or under the home of Raymond “RC” Horsch, a career criminal, local artist, author and snuff photographer who died last year aged 82, and his son Eugene, 44. So far, at least seven missing women have been linked to the home in the Olney section of the city, originally a German American neighborhood but now largely African American, Hispanic and Asian. Investigators believe five are dead. Fifty-eight women seen on film and in photographs recovered from the trash-strewn property have been identified. Of those, 25 have been located but not yet interviewed; 19 have spoken with detectives but declined to cooperate. Investigators are faced with a difficult task: how to discern from images whether Horsch’s subjects are posing, and what is real and what is staged. Such is the grim nature of snuff photography and the murky exchanges that lie beneath. Investigators have said that the five women appear unconscious, lifeless or injured, but with no bodies the medical examiner cannot issue death certificates. “We’re going slow and methodical,” a police source said. “Do we think people were killed in the house? Sure. It’s a tough investigation because the guy who had the house was a violent pornographer. Is it art or is it reality?” Deputy police commissioner Frank Vanore said at a news conference on 10 September: “Some of this is play-acting. Some of it we believe could be real, but we’re not there yet.” The five women who police believed to be dead are Blair Tonzelli, 35, missing since 2023; Nicole Fusaro and Maribel Fresses, both 27, who disappeared in 2018; Amy McHale, who disappeared in June 2016 and had been married to Horsch; and Gabrielle Amarando, 22, who disappeared in 2012. Four miles from the Olney home lies Philadelphia’s Kensington neighborhood, an area notorious for its open-air drug use, prostitution and homelessness, and as a place where people simply disappear from life. Many women in the community last week recalled some of those identified by investigators. One had connections to the Olney house – her driver’s license was registered there – but declined to discuss the case. Others said they recalled Horsch’s son, Eugene, currently in custody pending federal gun and drug charges, cruising the block in a black BMW. One remembered Fresses as an “Italian princess – sweet and kind”. Ashley, making her way from a woman’s shelter with a plastic bag of candies, syringes, and a glass bowl for smoking fentanyl or meth, said bleakly: “A lot of girls go missing here. You get dope sick, it makes you crazy, and then you make bad decisions.” Not all the women who passed through the Olney home were connected to Kensington. Media reports suggest that some met Horsch in Camden, New Jersey, 20 miles away. A woman from the area told ABC Philadelphia she had gone to the Olney home, blacked out from the drugs Raymond Horsch gave her, and woke up with him standing over her, taking pictures. Police first raided the home in June after Eugene Horsch was stopped in a car in Philadelphia’s Old City neighborhood. Horsch was carrying fake ID indicating he was federal law enforcement and DEA agent. A female passenger was carrying Tonzelli’s identification. Two handguns and approximately $8,000 worth of illegal drugs were found in the vehicle. According to court documents, Eugene Horsch allegedly said Tonzelli would “never be seen again”. A search of the home turned up an additional illegal firearm, a marijuana grow operation, a fake FBI badge and five urns containing cremated remains. The arrest of the younger Horsch, who had not been charged in connection with the missing women, shone a spotlight on his father, who was never charged in connection with the disappearances of any of the five identified women. The city’s medical examiner’s office has advised that if images of at least three women recovered from the home “are authentic and have not been altered, the women depicted appear to be deceased”. Court records show that Raymond Horsch was convicted in 2009 for attempting to lure a nine-year-old girl into his car in Kensington. “Come here, in my car, sexy girl,” Horsch said to her, according to an arrest report. Horsch was found guilty, sentenced to two and a half to five years in prison, and required to register as a sex offender. But his lawyers sought a new trial and the case collapsed because the girl was too afraid to testify a second time, according to the Philadelphia Inquirer. Horsch’s conviction was expunged and the records placed under seal. A judge has ordered them to be preserved. According to a 1985 psychological examination obtained by the Inquirer, Horsch was a manipulative criminal who was “consumed by anger … grandiose, mistrustful, suspicious, and excessively controlling”. The profile was commissioned as part of a federal drug manufacturing case. Horsch fled the US with his second wife, Myroslawa Anna Ferkuniak. He was arrested in New Zealand, where he’d been living under the name of Stanley Stokowski, a real California chemist who had a Stanford doctorate. According to the profile, he spoke in the third person, as if describing “events from someone else’s life”. Michael Yoder, a retired FBI special agent, told the outlet that, judging from the report, “I would say you have a potential serial killer on your hands.” For a time, Horsch and his young son lived in Pennsylvania’s Berks county, where he opened a barbecue restaurant while also pursuing a career as a fetishistic or “snuff” photographer. In 2009, he was arrested after a marijuana grow operation was discovered in his basement, and he was sentenced to five years in prison. Raymond Horsch had been offering cash and drugs to women in Kensington in exchange for participating in his violent pornographic films since the early 2000s. He also had access to to a crematorium connected to Kensington’s Garzone funeral home to photograph corpses. In 2007, the business was shut down for selling body parts on the black market. Horsch wasn’t hiding his access to the morgue – a video exhibited at a “Transgressions” art show in 2014 featured a body being loaded into an incinerator. The exhibition asked visitors to consider if Horsch’s “often transgressive images can possibly be art? Or, as many critics and philosophers claim, are art and pornography completely and forever mutually exclusive?” Horsch was not reticent about his obsession with women in addiction. He uploaded photos of his subjects to his website featuring women “imagining and acting their own deaths” juxtaposed with real photos of overdose victims. A handwritten note found in the home describes hurting people and makes reference to serial killer Ted Bundy. Horsch’s films included a documentary, Whore!, and films including Deleted Scenes: A Serial Killer’s Video Journal and Slaves. He starred in and directed Lovers, which was produced by a feminist porn studio. He produced The Erotic Memoirs of a Male Chauvinist Pig, featuring Georgina Spelvin, the star of The Devil in Miss Jones. He published a two-volume photo book called Eroto~ To the Prurient Interest, showing a woman he referred to as “Anna” in staged “deaths”. 2014’s Empathy included a chapter about dissolving a murdered woman’s body with chemicals. The home is already a tourist attraction even as investigators still search for evidence. “It was creepy vibes. He’d be out front staring at women, or he’d be in his yard doing some kind of chemist stuff,” recalled Jessica Diaz, 37. A neighbor living opposite the home said he recalled young women coming and going from the home. On occasion, ambulances were called. “They need to tear that house down,” he opined. With Raymond Horsch dead, and his son Eugene under investigation, it remains possible that no charges will be brought and the best the families of the missing can hope for is a police report. “We have a duty to those families who are all concerned about whether their loved one lost their lives in that house or maybe somewhere else,” said the Philadelphia police commissioner, Kevin Bethel. But the story of Raymond Horsch is already entering the annals of Philadelphia horror lore. Edgar Allan Poe and Bram Stoker both wrote in the city, and it’s had serial murderers in the past. In the 1980s, Gary Heidnik, an inspiration for the fictional character Buffalo Bill in The Silence of the Lambs, imprisoned six vulnerable women in a pit in his basement with the goal of creating a “baby farm”. Josh Hitchens, a writer and historian known locally as a prominent “purveyor of the macabre”, said that in each case, it was people preying on the vulnerable. “These are often not the people that law enforcement pays much attention to. That’s one of the horrifying things about what’s unfolding now – what Raymond Horsch was doing was apparently known and talked about within the community.” Hitchens said Horsch is likely to become a point on the horror map of Philadelphia, achieving a measure of recognition in death that his films and writings failed to secure in his life. “I hope that within that we’re not just talking about Raymond and Eugene Horsch, but the lives of the women are also remembered and given the respect they deserve.”

title: ‘A persistent crisis’: the 16 children removed from an Ohio family are part of a statewide issue
summary: The case of the Siders family illustrates major shortcomings among Ohio’s political and administrative authorities
text: In June 2025, Jody Walker stood in front of Ohio lawmakers at a senate finance committee meeting in Columbus. As the head of South Central Ohio Job and Family Services, he was desperate for help. “I have been a county director since 1999, yet I have not seen such a challenging time in the child welfare system as I do today,” he said, “specifically in terms of the needs of our children.” His agency, which oversees three rural counties in southern Ohio, frequently saw children sleeping at the organization’s office because they had no other safe place to go. Twelve months later, Walker’s fears were realized right in his own backyard. On 30 June, 16 children were found in a dilapidated home in Hamden, a short drive from where Walker works. Several were found near death; two children were flown to a level one trauma medical facility, where one was placed in an intensive care unit, according to reports. Gary Siders and Christina Siders, the children’s grandparents, and Gary Siders II and Elizabeth Siders, their parents, were charged with 16 counts of child endangerment. In August, Gary Siders II and Elizabeth Siders were additionally charged on separate counts of sexual battery and unlawful sexual conduct with a minor, who was not their own child. All four have pleaded not guilty to the charges. The Siders case illustrates major shortcomings among Ohio’s political and administrative authorities when it comes to supporting the most at-risk in society, say experts. “Our biggest challenge is a persistent crisis in identifying appropriate, affordable and accessible placements … Paid placement costs have increased 41% since 2020, far outpacing inflation, with the cost for residential and group home care skyrocketing by more than 65%,” said Angela Sausser of the Public Children Services Association of Ohio, which represents public children services agencies in the state. “While the state share [of spending on children services] has been rising over the last eight years, from 10% to 20%, it still falls below the national average of 42%.” Today, the family services department in Vinton county is drowning in the estimated $200 per child per day expense of caring for the 16 Siders children, who are now in foster care; six of the children are twins aged four or younger. A rural region with fewer than 13,000 residents, Vinton county is the least populous county in Ohio. Property tax levies in the area fail to come close to covering the costs of caring for at-risk children, which for South Central Ohio Job and Family Services rose from less than $4m in 2015 to more than $10m in 2024. In fact, the conditions facing the children were discovered by accident. Law enforcement officers went to the property to serve arrest warrants on Gary Siders II and Elizabeth Siders on charges unrelated to the neglect of their children. “County leaders should not have to choose among services for vulnerable children, public safety, seniors and those with behavioral health needs or developmental disabilities,” said Sausser. For more than 30 years, Republicans have broadly controlled governing and lawmaking in Ohio, regularly holding a supermajority in the state legislature. According to the Annie E Casey Foundation, a private philanthropic organization focusing on children’s needs, while the percentage of children in Ohio living in high-poverty areas has fallen in recent years, figures for child deaths, children without health insurance and children aged three and four who are not in school all have risen. Financial disclosure information from the Siders family published by Los Angeles magazine found that Elizabeth Siders had no income and her husband’s salary amounted to $1,500 per month in 2021. Ohio isn’t alone in struggling to fund care for vulnerable children. Nationally, a swathe of cuts including supports such as food benefits for 1 million children are under way. For the 2027 federal budget, the Trump administration is proposing cuts to nutrition programs for women and children, home energy assistance for low-income families, a $6bn cut to the budget of the National Institutes of Health and the elimination of a federal preschool development grant program. Data and research overwhelmingly show that children in states governed by Republican leadership face higher risk factors than those run by Democrats or members of both parties. The infant mortality rates in Tennessee, Mississippi and Arkansas are more than 50% higher than in states such as New York and California. In Ohio, a case worker reported in 2020 that the Siders children suffered from high levels of lead; last year, Republican lawmakers in Ohio cut funding for a lead abatement program from $7.5m to $250,000 a year. The office of Andy Wilson, Ohio’s Republican attorney general, declined to comment on questions from the Guardian asking, among other things, whether he believed the state of Ohio had failed the Siders children. Search warrant materials have been sealed by a judge, and a gag order has been issued by another, meaning attorneys for the accused and others involved, including law enforcement officials, cannot speak publicly on the matter. Wilson has claimed that the adults in the Siders household “[w]ere pretty adept at keeping these kids out of sight and out of the eyes of investigators” and called the family members responsible for the abuse “pure evil”. State authorities through the Ohio department of children and youth have initiated a review of the Siders case, “to determine how the county public children services agency followed federal and state requirements and to provide technical assistance on best practice”, said Jodi Norton Trimble of the Ohio DCY. However, reports show that child and family services at the county and regional levels made significant efforts to highlight the conditions the Siders children faced. When the family lived in neighboring Gallia county in 2020, a staff member from its department of jobs and family services visiting the children reported finding them living in desperate conditions, prompting court-ordered protective supervision for the children. But by May 2021, the supervision requirement was terminated and the family moved out of Gallia county. The same year, school officials in Gallia county filed a complaint in a juvenile court reporting that several of the Siders children had become habitually truant. But local authorities were unable to keep up with the family’s movements. “I believe the school made contact with the appropriate school district where the family was living in West Virginia. However, before authorities could take action, the family moved again,” a representative of Gallia juvenile court said. At 34 years old, Elizabeth Siders, the mother of all 16 children, was pregnant every 15 months. She was 15 years old when she was married in West Virginia, (before 2023, a child of any age in the state could legally be married with permission of a judge) and, shortly after, gave birth to her first child at the Holzer health system outside Gallipolis, Ohio. She would give birth to nine children at the facility, according to reports. Her attorneys have called for a mental health evaluation to see whether she is competent to stand trial. The Ohio department of children and youth report on the incident is expected to be completed by the end of the year, “but it must be conducted without interfering with the criminal investigations that are ongoing”, said Norton Trimble.

title: Christa Pike left in ‘critical condition’ as Tennessee halts all executions | First Thing
summary: Failed attempt to execute 50-year-old prompts review of state’s execution practices amid distressing witness accounts
text: Good morning. Tennessee’s governor has suspended executions as Christa Pike’s lawyer says the state’s failed lethal injection execution attempt has left her in a critical condition. Bill Lee, the Republican state governor, has suspended all executions in the state until at least the end of the year and ordered an independent inquiry. Leading voices on the death penalty in the US have told the Guardian that the failed execution was such a violation of the constitutional prohibition on “cruel and unusual punishment” that all judicial killings should be halted nationwide. What have Pike’s lawyers said about her condition? Randy Spivey, one of her attorneys, said: “We don’t have a sense of her prognosis or much update on her health at the moment, but we do know that she is alive right now and receiving life-saving medical care. She is in a critical condition.” What did witnesses say took place during the execution attempt? Catherine Sweeney, a reporter at the Nashville Public Radio WPLN, said: “They went through two rounds, and she was still breathing at the end. She was very ragged. She lifted her head up and was looking around. At one point, she said … there was a spot that was burning and hurting, and asked if that was normal. None of it was normal.” What was Pike convicted of? She was convicted of the brutal 1995 killing of Colleen Slemmer, alongside her then boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp. Lee said he had not yet spoken to Slemmer’s family after the failed execution. In the lawsuits, Good’s partner, Becca Good, and her brother, Brent Ganger, alleged wrongful death and other violations of federal law, according to a press release issued by their lawyers. Why has the DNC issued a lawsuit against the administration? The Trump administration broke the law when it pushed through a last-minute change to the form overseas citizens use to register and request absentee ballots, the Democratic National Committee (DNC) said in a lawsuit filed on Thursday. “Trump and Republicans are so desperate to hang on to power that they are trying to eliminate the way some American citizens abroad register to vote and request mail ballots,” said Ken Martin, the chair of the DNC. Which states are leading the resistance to the Trump EPA’s repeal of emissions rules? Twenty-one states, led by New York, are challenging the Environmental Protection Agency’s power plant rule. The New York attorney general, Letitia James, said the federal government was showing “callous disregard” for Americans’ health and the environment, and future generations would pay the price. Power plants that burn fossil fuels are a major source of planet-warming pollution. California’s attorney general, meanwhile, has issued an investigative subpoena to OpenAI over reports of rogue agents’ hacking. SpaceX launched a crew to the ISS successfully, with Jessica Watkins, the first Black woman to lead a crew to orbit, making her second trip to the space station. Lawmakers have called for action on what they say are “plainly illegal” taxpayer-funded ads to promote Donald Trump in the run-up to the midterms. The judge in the Lindsay Clancy murder case on Thursday refused to declare her not guilty, turning down a defense motion. Kanye West’s sold-out Russia concerts have been cancelled, organisers have confirmed. title: Digested week: My heart sank at seeing Labour’s ‘Hope Again’ conference slogan. But then came Andy Burnham | John Crace
summary: The prime minister gave far and away the most powerful, emotional and gamechanging leader’s speech of the century
text: Monday Words I thought I’d never write. We owe a huge debt of gratitude to the Tory party. Look, I know we ended up with Theresa May and Boris Johnson in the Conservative party leadership contests of 2016 and 2019 – and they were shockers, both of them – but at least the Tory MPs twice ensured we dodged the bullet of Michael Gove. Last week, Sky broadcast The War Game, a reality show for superannuated politicians and former senior civil servants and military officers. The setup was that the Russians had engineered an attack on a British warship in the North Sea and over the course of four episodes set in the Cobra emergency situation room, the assembled cast had to figure how to respond. We were left hanging at the final credits, but a nuclear apocalypse felt like the most likely outcome. And for that we have The Govester to thank. He was playing the prime minister and – to be blunt – he had an absolute shocker. For the first two episodes he seemed to be in a coma. All he could manage was to repeat back what the last person had said to him and then shout “asap”. But that was far more preferable to the Gove that turned up for the last two episodes. Despite frequently being warned about the dangers of escalation and the inadequacy of the UK war machine, Mikey kept on taking the option that would get the most people killed. Why bomb one Russian city when you can bomb two? The game ended with what were almost certainly nuclear warheads minutes away from destroying a major city in the UK. Still, Gove wasn’t the only deadbeat. Nicola Sturgeon, acting the deputy prime minister, was as hopeless as you would expect of someone who failed to notice her kitchen filling up with new appliances. It was terrifying TV. Not so much in the premise. What was really scary was the knowledge that our politicians were even more clueless than the rest of us. Tuesday Pep Guardiola timed his departure well. Perhaps he had an inkling of what was coming down the road. The top bods at Manchester City have predictably responded to being found guilty of 114 charges of financial misconduct by insisting they will appeal and drag out proceedings. No doubt hoping that either the charges will go away or they can reduce the potential penalties. I wouldn’t bet against it. My main reaction when the news broke that City had been found guilty was surprise. Not that I thought they were innocent – there wasn’t a football fan who didn’t think they were bang to rights – but that the Premier League finally got round to doing something about it. The earliest charges date back 17 years and it just felt as if nothing was ever going to happen. What happens next is anyone’s guess. Obviously any fine would be more or less meaningless as the City owners have bottomless pockets. Removing titles is equally pointless. Who would turn up for an open-topped bus ride for a cup won years ago? The issue of compensation is more nuanced. Because where does it all end? Can I file a claim for mental distress, not to mention the travel and ticket costs, for having paid to see countless matches which had been financially rigged against Spurs that are now null and void? There again, I have had two of my best nights ever at the Etihad. When Spurs secured a Champions League place for the first time and when we won a Champions League quarter-final thanks to City having an injury time goal disallowed by VAR. There has also been talk of a 50-point deduction. Probably not enough to ensure they finish behind Spurs. We’re only five games into the season and already 13 points adrift. Wednesday By a very rough calculation, I reckon I’ve spent the best part of six months of my life at party conferences. And yes, I am a lucky man to be doing a job I love, but it is sometimes hard not to feel a wee bit jaded during the conference season. Living out of a suitcase and listening to a series of speeches from politicians who can often barely hold their own attention let alone an audience’s, can make the days feel very long. And I was prepared for more of the same when I arrived in Liverpool for this week’s Labour conference. My heart sank when I saw banners, mugs and T-shirts with the slogan “Hope Again” everywhere. There’s nothing more guaranteed to see me sliding into despair then people loudly instructing me to look on the bright side. To make it worse, I had to endure the chancellor, John Healey, lie through his teeth and say “I am an optimist”. You’re fooling no one, John. He had clearly been told to be upbeat and dropped the H-word about 20 times. But on every occasion he gasped “Hope” it looked like a dagger had been plunged into his heart. Come the end, the whole audience was signing up to Dignitas. But then, Andy Burnham. By far and away the most powerful, emotional and gamechanging leader’s speech of the century. I can’t tell you how rare it is for a politician to hold an audience in his hands for an hour and say exactly what he thinks, feels and believes. Only Nigel Farage comes close, though what he offers is only anger, grievance and division. Burnham was offering something else. I may not have agreed with the details of all of it and most of it may never happen, but this was a world of social care, closer ties to the EU and electoral reform to which most in the socially progressive world could sign up. It was as though the sun had come out. Thursday When I turned 50, friends used to assure me that 50 was the new 40. That felt almost true. I can remember my Dad’s 50th birthday and he looked ancient to me. For my 60th birthday, those same friends were confident that 60 was the new 50. There was the slight drawback that I had already had a knee replacement, but I still went to the gym four times a week and my career was in good shape. Next week I will be 70. No one has even tentatively suggested that 70 might be the new 60. Seventy is unequivocally old. Some might even say that 70 is the new 80. I am now undeniably at the business end of life. My children are both in their 30s and have gone on to live their best lives. Much of my work as a parent is done. I had a heart attack two and a half years ago and am doing my best to avoid another one. My wife is being treated for cancer. Yes, I still enjoy my work and go to the gym four times a week but, as the great Leonard Cohen so exquisitely put it, “I ache in the places where I used to play”. It’s been weird watching the series 70 Up. I’ve always felt a kinship with the men and women in the documentary because I’ve followed them since I was 14 when they were the same age and felt grateful that my own life had not been part of the social experiment. But now we hear that 70 is to be the end point of the series. As though the lives have come to a meaningful end. I’m not quite so ready to go quietly into the night. I plan to keep going for a while yet. And for those of you who would like to join me trying to make sense of the world, there are still tickets available for my shows at the Komedia in Brighton on 18 October and at the MAC in Birmingham on 31 October. Friday My happy place. The Celebrity Traitors is back and all is more or less well with the world. The first episode may not have quite lived up to the hype but as a scene setter it was more than good enough. The side missions increasingly feel pointless – we all know everyone is in it for their ego and career rather than the charity cash – and in any case the celebs always need time to bed in and show their true colours. Though not Ross Kemp, who was showing worrying levels of paranoia from the off. Who will be the Alan Carr, a true star of the series? Who will be the Stephen Fry, all affected diffidence? And who will be the David Olusoga, the one who tried to work things through with careful intelligence yet always comes to the wrong conclusion? The first to show his face was actor Michael Sheen who declared that he didn’t know what he was letting himself in for and then said “I’m a huge fan of the game”. Hmm. Maybe he’s been watching with his eyes closed. The rest of the celebs trooped in one by one and we were up and running. Things soon hotted up when Claudia nominated Maya – never heard of her – and Richard E Grant as traitors. Richard was so thrilled – he had been desperate to be a traitor – that he promptly blew the show wide open by telling all the other celebs that he was a traitor. A move that may prove to be utterly inspired or catastrophically dim. Given a night to sleep on it, Richard was inclined to believe it might have been the latter and spent the rest of the day trying to persuade everyone it was a bluff. Sit back and enjoy the next five weeks.

title: Minister denies UK faces diesel shortage after Trump threatens to ban exports
summary: In effort to avoid panic at pumps, Keir Mather insists supply of fuel to Britain is ‘inherently resilient’
text: The government has sought to avert panic at the pumps, insisting that the UK is not facing a diesel shortage after Donald Trump threatened to cut off US supplies of the fuel. The transport minister Keir Mather said on Friday that the UK has a wide range of sources of the fuel and is in talks with other European countries over the potential release of emergency diesel stockpiles. “I want to reassure people that they can still go to the pump and fill up with diesel because the supply we have to the UK is inherently resilient,” he said on ITV’s Good Morning Britain. “The flows of diesel into the UK come from a variety of sources, and that is resilient. “The government’s obligation now is to work really closely with our partners [in Europe] and officials in the US administration to re-stress how important it is to have flows of diesel into the UK. People shouldn’t be concerned about shortages because of the inherent resilience that is built into that system.” The UK relies on the US for about 30% of its diesel, with the vast majority coming from mainland Europe, and has reserve supplies for 42 days. Earlier this week it emerged that the UK’s biggest refinery, Fawley in Hampshire, is set to shut for up to 10 weeks for planned maintenance. The UK had 18 refineries in the 1980s but now has only four. On Thursday the UK opened talks with European allies over releasing emergency diesel supplies, after the Trump administration told Germany and France to release their stockpiles to help ease soaring prices or face a US supply ban. The average price of a litre of diesel in the UK hit a record high on Friday, breaking the £2 mark for the first time, according to the motoring body the RAC. “This is a pump price threshold that no one wanted to cross,” said Simon Williams, the head of policy at the RAC. “The average price of a litre of diesel has risen to a record 200.01p and is showing no signs of slowing, heaping more misery on to motorists.” The government has extended the 5p cut in fuel duty until the end of the year. Earlier this week the RAC called on the government to extend the freeze into spring. “We need to give people support where we can,” Mather said on GMB. “The government is not powerless. That is why we have a fuel duty freeze in place at the moment. The chancellor will set out the future of that at the budget, but is very aware of the impact that [high prices] are having on people.” On Friday, Dan Jørgensen, the EU commissioner for energy, said Europe was discussing the question of whether to release emergency reserves of diesel with all members of the International Energy Agency, not only the US. “This ‌is one of the opportunities that we have; we ⁠have used it before, and it is likely that ‌we would use it again,” he told Euronews.

title: OpenAI disclose another hack on government department in Australia
summary: Attack accessing historical data on bushfires occurred in June but not disclosed by the tech company until Thursday
text: Artificial intelligence company OpenAI has disclosed another unauthorised hack on a government department in Australia. In June, an OpenAI agent hacked into a New South Wales state government department and accessed historical non-public data on bushfires without authorisation. The breach, which comes weeks after news of a similar hack on a federal government department involving Medicare data, was not reported by the US based company until Thursday. The NSW Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water is now working with the state’s cyber security agency to investigate the breach. The Australian Signals Directorate has also been informed of the hack on the NSW national parks and wildlife service. OpenAI told the NSW government that its agent had operated beyond its intended use and the statistics it obtained were not publicly available. The company first became aware of the breach on Tuesday and conducted a 48 hours review to determine its scope before informing the NSW premier’s office. “The results we reviewed do not show that the model retrieved any personal information,” an OpenAI spokesperson said. This latest breach has added to calls for tougher regulation of AI companies and for bolstered cyber security defences. “We simply cannot trust these companies. They have no respect for the sovereignty of our governments, of our way of life,” Greens MP Abigail Boyd said. Boyd said it was damning that the breach occurred in June but the government was not notified until this week. “We clearly cannot rely on these multinational big tech companies to comply with even the most minimal of social obligations such as notifying when, or even taking enough care to notice if, their products are hacking government systems,” Boyd said. On Wednesday, the department of home affairs on Wednesday told federal departments to examine their older software and ensure cyber security was up to date. The prime minister expressed his “extreme concern” about at an OpenAI agent hacking Australian Institute of Health and Welfare in June. The Victorian Department of Health and the New South Wales Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research were also compromised by an OpenAI agent. An artificial intelligence agent is a system that autonomously solves problems, makes decisions, plans and performs complex tasks on behalf of another user or system, using all available tools. • AAP contributed to this report

title: Kinky dating app Feeld’s founders share in record £3.8m dividend after sales jump
summary: UK app ‘for the curious’ says users outside the UK account for nearly 90% of its revenues
text: Feeld, a UK-based dating app aimed at non-monogamous, queer and kinky users, has reported strong sales growth and paid its largest-ever dividend as it attracts users from more “vanilla” rivals. Revenues jumped by 32% to £64m following a surge in interest from what it called “open-minded people exploring love, desire, and alternative relationships in a safe, inclusive space”. Pre-tax profits grew from £9.3m to £11.4m, and the company’s shareholders – including the couple who founded it – shared in a dividend of £3.8m. Ana Kirova and her partner, Dimo Trifonov, started the business under the name 3nder (pronounced Thrinder), initially targeting couples and singles looking for threesomes. They were forced to change the company’s name to Feeld owing to a lawsuit from Tinder but it has since experienced rapid growth even as larger rivals have faltered. Match Group, which owns Tinder and other dating apps such as Hinge and OK Cupid, reported a 5% decline in user numbers earlier this year, amid reports of fatigue with the experience of seeking romance or sex via an app. But Feeld, which calls itself a dating app “for the curious”, appears to be scooping up some of those users. While this has prompted reports that its edgy image has been watered down by an influx of people with more conventional or monogamous sensibilities, Feeld’s president, Kyle Brennan, said it reflected changing tastes. “These numbers speak to something bigger than the growth of our business,” said Brennan. “They reflect a broader shift in how people are thinking about connection, with greater openness, curiosity and agency to do things differently.” Accounts filed at Companies House said rising sales reflected “strong global user growth”, particularly outside the UK, with the rest of the world accounting for £56m of its total £64m in revenues, nearly 90%. Mexico and Spain were Feeld’s fastest-growing regions, while New York, Toronto and Paris led the way among cities, each recording an uplift in user numbers of more than 20%, the company said. Feeld makes money via the sale of its Majestic memberships, which give users features such as unlimited opportunities to “like” other members, the ability to see who has liked them, and advanced filters to tailor specifications for a potential partner. It also sells members extra “pings”, a feature that allows members to express interest in someone and send them a message, without having matched with them first. In 2024, it emerged that some of these features were temporarily vulnerable to manipulation due to security “vulnerabilities” exposed by cybersecurity experts. Research by the London-based cybersecurity firm Fortbridge found that users could have had sensitive data including messages, private photos and details of their sexuality accessed or even edited. At the time, Feeld said it had investigated the problems brought to its attention by Fortbridge on 3 March and fixed them by 28 May that year. It said there was no evidence that any customer data had been accessed. It has invested £10.5m in technological upgrades in the past year. The largest dividend reported in Feeld’s previous accounts was £600,000 in 2024. As well as its dating platform, Feeld runs in-person social events including a “kinky trivia” night and a “pitch your mate” event, at which guests take to the stage to wax lyrical about why people should date their friends.

title: Drumcree talks break up without agreement on fifth day of standoff
summary: Dispute over march will go to legal appeal on Monday after talks hosted by Northern Ireland secretary end
text: Talks aimed at resolving the Drumcree parade dispute have broken up without agreement, with the Northern Ireland secretary, Chris Bryant, describing the situation as being between a “rock and a hard place”. Speaking on Thursday night after the latest talks with the Orange Order and residents of Garvaghy Road broke up, Bryant said: “I think this is the end of these conversations. We haven’t come to a settled agreement, and it’s a shame, but my door remains open.” Last Friday’s Parades Commission decision to grant the Orange Order the right to hold a procession down the nationalist Garvaghy Road plunged Northern Ireland into one of its most perilous periods since the 1998 peace deal. A legal appeal by the Garvaghy Road Residents’ Coalition originally scheduled for Friday has been pushed back to Monday to facilitate any further talks. “Obviously we’ll have to see how that plays out,” Bryant said, indicating he would not be intervening unilaterally. “I would say that the law, in the end, is the law.” Five days of talks ended in deadlock, he said, outlining the compromises on the table for the first time. “We’ve discussed a wide range of options, including mediation, including an option where the right to march was respected but wasn’t exercised, including an option where there was a final march and no further applications for marches into the future, and we’ve not managed to come to agreement on any of all that.” Earlier in the week, reports suggested one option was a “one and done” parade involving just a dozen people without insignia in October. This would have been on condition the Orange Order would never apply for permit for that parade route again. Breandán Mac Cionnaith, of the Garvaghy Road Residents’ Coalition said “the reality is” there was “no such thing as half a march”. “There’s a march or there’s not a march – simply that,” he said. Jamie Bryson, a legal adviser to the Orange Order, who earlier this week said he would “not surrender” said he would accept Monday’s ruling. “The challenge that we would put down to the Garvaghy Road residents – they’re going to the court of appeal on Monday – if the court of appeal upholds this determination, commit to accepting the law and walk away, and we’ll do the same,” he said. “Abide by the law, and if the court of appeal upholds the determination, get off the road, stop breaking the law and allow the parade to go ahead. If we lose, we’ll accept that.” The dispute began last week after the march along the mainly nationalist Garvaghy Road was given the go-ahead by the Parades Commission for the first time since 1998, a decision denounced by Sinn Féin as “madness” and by the taoiseach as “incomprehensible and wrong”. The dispute, which threatened to collapse Stormont and has returned Northern Ireland to bleak days of the past, has also revived the interest of key US Democrats. Richie Neal, the US representative for Massachussetts’ 1st congressional district, described the parade as “needlessly provocative”. The Congressional Friends of Ireland Caucus, which Neal sits on, wrote to Bryant urging him to use his powers to reverse the Parades Commission decision. “Over the last three decades, the progress made on the island of Ireland has been nothing short of extraordinary. Twenty-eight years have passed since the signing of the Good Friday agreement, and a generation has grown without a single memory of the Troubles,” the lawmakers wrote. “Without decisive action, we risk reopening one of the most painful chapters of Northern Ireland’s history and undermining nearly three decades of peace, stability and reconciliation made possible by the Good Friday agreement.” The Northern Ireland Policing Board has been told that the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) operation around the parading dispute has topped £3m.

title: Calls grow for US death penalty halt after ‘torturous’ botched execution of Christa Pike
summary: Pike alive but in critical condition as experts call ordeal that unfolded in Tennessee ‘unimaginably barbaric’
text: Top lawyers, doctors and members of the faith community are calling for a moratorium on the US death penalty after Tennessee’s failed attempt to execute Christa Pike left the prisoner alive but in critical condition and receiving life-saving medical care. The recent spate of harrowingly botched executions across US death penalty states reached a new low late on Wednesday when Tennessee’s governor, Bill Lee, called off the procedure after Pike had been injected with two full syringes of pentobarbital. She is the only person to have survived being administered 5g of the sedative – a massive dose that under normal circumstances is considered fatal. An hour after the first injection was given, she was overheard by eyewitnesses to be still breathing, choking and struggling, and was found to have a heartbeat. Her lawyers said that her current condition, and the degree to which she may have been brain-damaged through oxygen deprivation, were as yet unknown. Sandra Babcock, a death penalty scholar at Cornell law school who advises Pike’s legal team, told the Guardian that the events that unfolded were “unimaginably barbaric. They demand accountability.” She added that at a minimum Lee must now “commute Christa Pike’s death sentence to life imprisonment”. Another of Pike’s lawyers, Randy Spivey, who was present in the death chamber, called Pike’s ordeal “cruel and torturous”. He said he had personally counted seven needles stuck in Pike’s left arm alone, “one of which appeared to be bent when it was pulled from her”. Pike, 50, was sentenced to death for the brutal 1995 killing of a teenage classmate, Colleen Slemmer. She was set to be the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years. Leading voices on the death penalty in America told the Guardian that the failed execution was such a violation of the constitutional prohibition on “cruel and unusual punishment” that all judicial killings had to be halted. Bryan Stevenson, an internationally renowned death penalty lawyer and founder of the Equal Justice Initiative in Montgomery, Alabama, said that many warnings had been made in recent months that US executions were flawed and unreliable. “Nearly a dozen botched executions in recent years should have suspended executions long before now,” he said. Stevenson said it was time to turn around the threshold question. Instead of asking whether a prisoner deserved to die for the crime committed, the question should be: “Do our governments which tolerate inequality, unreliability and bias deserve to kill?” He added: “Last night’s tragedy makes clear we should stop the misguided policy of killing people to show that killing is wrong.” Wednesday night was the second time in five months that Tennessee had failed to carry out an execution. In May, Tony Carruthers survived the death chamber after the execution team were unable to set up an IV line. He has been given a new execution date for next May. That followed Alabama, which also failed to execute two death row prisoners, Alan Miller and Kenneth Smith, having been unable to find a vein. The spectacle of prisoners being sent to their deaths, only to have the executions called off as a result of basic failures in IV procedures, has sent death penalty states scrambling to find alternatives to lethal injections. In turn, those alternative procedures have become mired in complications and disputes. Miller and Smith were both eventually killed by Alabama using an experimental procedure, nitrogen gas, that veterinarians have banned as inhumane for the euthanasia of cats and dogs. In June, a federal judge blocked Alabama’s use of nitrogen in executions, ruling it cruel and unusual punishment. Other states have opted for the firing squad. But recent firing squad executions have been troubled by bullets missing the heart, to the extent that the suggestion has been raised that some of the mis-targeted shots may have been intentional. Helen Prejean, a Catholic nun who is perhaps the best-known advocate for abolition of the death penalty in America after her book Dead Man Walking was turned into a film of the same name, told the Guardian that the events on Wednesday night were the definition of cruelty. “This is the essence of cruelty. Take a conscious, imaginative human being, give her a date for her death, have her anticipate it over and over again, and then take her out and try and kill her. She was rendered defenceless as they deliberately attempted to kill her – what greater mental torture for a human being is there?” Prejean added that she hoped the agony Pike had endured “would be redemptive for others, and help to wake up the nation”. As the number of gruesome botched lethal injections rapidly mounts, the central premise that has been held up by supporters – that it is a humane, medicalised and scientific way to kill a person – has come under fire. Joel Zivot, a professor of anesthesiology in Atlanta, Georgia, who has reviewed hundreds of autopsies of executed people in the US, said that lethal injections would never deserve the label of medicine. “This is the impersonation of a medical act. It is the theft of a medical act. So when it goes awry, that is not at all surprising to me.” Zivot was invited to present as an expert witness at a hearing convened in August by a special master in the Pike case. He warned the senior judge that Pike had a blood condition in which her blood platelets were elevated that rendered her vulnerable to blood clots. Zivot told the hearing that Pike, as a small woman who had been in solitary confinement on death row for almost 30 years, probably had veins that were of poor quality, small in caliber, and hard to find. “I told them. I warned them,” he said. The special master rejected almost all the evidence presented to him. The last time that the US saw a moratorium on executions was in 1972 when the supreme court ruled in Furman v Georgia that capital punishment was capricious and arbitrary in its rendition. The ban was lifted four years later. Paradoxically, calls for a renewed nationwide pause are reaching fever pitch at precisely the time that pressure to carry out executions is also peaking. Donald Trump has repeatedly exhorted death penalty states and the federal Department of Justice to speed up judicial killings, and his orders are having an effect. Last year saw the highest number of US executions – 47 across 12 states – in 16 years. Prejean said that the answer to the growing determination of Trump and the death penalty states to carry out executions was to bring the American people closer to the action. She pointed to Gallup’s findings tracking popular sentiment towards capital punishment. In 1993, when her book came out, 80% of Americans supported the death penalty for convicted murderers. Now that figure is 52%. “That’s progress, though not enough. People have good hearts, but they are too removed from the process that is secret and hidden. We have got to bring this to the people, bring them into the execution chamber, so that they too become a witness.”

title: Christa Pike survived her execution attempt. Tennessee must not try again | Austin Sarat
summary: What happened to Pike was gruesome. No one deserves what she went through, not even those who commit horrible crimes
text: Botched executions are nothing new in US history. In the era when hangings were common, some condemned people were decapitated. Later, when the electric chair was in vogue, every now and again, someone would catch fire during an electrocution. And nitrogen hypoxia, the US’s newest execution method, has already proven notoriously unreliable. But, of all of the ways we have tried to execute people, lethal injection has the worst track record. More than 8% of all lethal injection executions have been botched. Most of them resulted when those charged with carrying them out could not find a usable vein. Last night, we entered uncharted territory when Christa Pike survived Tennessee’s effort to execute her with lethal doses of pentobarbital. It was the first time someone received a drug intended to kill them but did not die. Robin Maher, the executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center, told the New York Times: “This event is the worst we’ve seen and unlike any other botched execution in the modern era … There is no precedent.” Moreover, there is almost no precedent for what should happen next. Whatever fate awaits Christa Pike, one thing is clear. The state of Tennessee should not be allowed to try to execute her again. Beyond that, it is time to give up on the fantasy that this country will ever be able to find an execution technology that is safe, reliable and humane. We have not found one yet, and we never will. What happened to Pike was gruesome. No one deserves what she went through, not even those who commit horrible crimes. Pike was sent to death row for one such crime. The Tennessean describes her crime this way. “Pike lured Slemmer to a wooded area near the University of Tennessee’s Agricultural Campus with the promise of marijuana. With the help of … [her boyfriend], Pike tortured Slemmer before beating her to death with a chunk of asphalt. A pentagram was also carved into her body.” Pike was barely 18 years old at the time. She was herself the victim of violence and abuse throughout her life. As the date of her execution drew near, Pike claimed that it should not go forward, because using lethal injection on her would be cruel. Little did she know what would be in store for her. As allowed by its execution protocol, state officials in Tennessee administered two doses of pentobarbital that were supposed to be enough to end her life. However, as NBC notes, instead of killing her, it left her “snoring” and complaining about pain, as well as “kicking her feet so often that she knocked off the sheets laid on her”. After the Tennessee governor, Bill Lee, was contacted, he authorized the execution team to stand down, and Pike was taken to a hospital. This is not the first time that Lee has received a call about an execution gone awry. In May, he had also agreed to stop the execution of Tony Carruthers when officials couldn’t find a vein for a backup IV. Lee granted him a one-year reprieve. Now he and his colleagues in Tennessee will have to decide what to do about Pike. So far, he has only called a halt to the one other execution scheduled in the state this year and ordered a review of what happened during Pike’s execution. That is not enough. The last time someone survived when a method of execution that was supposed to kill them failed to do so was in 1946, when Louisiana tried to put a man named Willie Francis to death in the electric chair. Francis survived because the electric chair malfunctioned and the current wasn’t strong enough to kill him. He sued the state to prevent it from trying again. But to no avail. The United States supreme court allowed Louisiana to put him in the electric chair again. Writing for the court, Justice Stanley Reed said: “Even the fact that petitioner has already been subjected to a current of electricity does not make his subsequent execution any more cruel in the constitutional sense than any other execution … The fact that an unforeseeable accident prevented the prompt consummation of the sentence cannot, it seems to us, add an element of cruelty to a subsequent execution.” Francis was executed soon after. Since then, many other executions have been botched, but few have lived to tell about them. Between 1946 and today, that has happened only nine other times, including with Pike. Four of those execution survivors were killed by a second execution attempt, while others escaped that fate. Some died on death row. In another case, the state agreed not to try to execute the person a second time, and now three of them are still alive. Tennessee had its chance to execute Christa Pike. It shouldn’t get to try again. To do so would be a form of double jeopardy that is prohibited by the constitution. And it would be cruel. Justice Harold Burton, who dissented in the Francis case, got it right when he said that no one should be subject to a second execution. “The intent of the executioner,” Burton wrote, “cannot lessen the torture or excuse the result.” In his view, when the state seeks to execute someone, they have a duty “to make sure that there … [is] no failure”. It doesn’t get a do-over. In the end, this is not just a matter of what the law says. It is a matter of simple human decency. Austin Sarat, associate dean of the faculty and William Nelson Cromwell professor of jurisprudence and political science at Amherst College, is the author of Gruesome Spectacles: Botched Executions and America’s Death Penalty
