title: Eastern Spain braces for torrential rain and flooding
summary: Up to 300mm of rain could fall in places, while extreme downpours bring landslides and deaths in Nepal
text: Torrential rain and potentially damaging flooding are forecast in eastern Spain over the coming days, as cold upper air moves over the warm, humid surface air of the Mediterranean Sea, fuelling violent, slow-moving thunderstorms near Spain’s east coast. The weather pattern, known as a Dana, occurs most often in autumn. Models show more than 100mm of rain could fall across the region on Friday, with 200-300mm possible in some areas. Cities including Valencia and Castelló de la Plana, are most at risk. Valencia has experienced several damaging floods in recent years. Catalonia has now put three towns under lockdown and Valencia has shut schools for nearly half a million children. Meanwhile, heavy rainfall in Nepal last week resulted in 542 disaster incidents and left 27 people dead between 24 and 27 September, according to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority. Of the recorded incidents, 304 were related to landslides while 87 were linked to flooding. During this extremely wet period, 186 meteorological sites recorded more than 100mm of rainfall, with Dedhgaun, in Lumbini province, recording 544.2mm. Nearly a million people received SMS flood warnings, and 2,000 people living in high-risk areas were relocated. This heavy rainfall also affected the Gandak River in Bihar, north-east India, which reached a record water level of 91.25 metres on Tuesday, 0.35m metres above the previous record, set only in 2024, according to the water resources department. So far, 169 seepage points along the embankments have been repaired, with teams deployed across several sites along the river as the embankments continue to face heavy water pressure. Strong winds, heavy rainfall and coastal flooding have hit the north-east US as a very deep area of low pressure developed into a nor’easter on Saturday. Such storms are named due to the north-easterly winds typically affecting coastal areas. This was the first nor’easter of the autumn and winter season, bringing gusts of up to 74mph (119km/h) and waves rising to 3 metres. The storm left approximately 200,000 people without power, inundated the streets of New York City and killed one person when a tree fell in Brooklyn. However, the storm also uncovered a piece of history as the wreckage from the Warren Sawyer, a three-masted ship destroyed in 1884, washed ashore on Nantucket, off Cape Cod in Massachusetts.

title: Recent lobbyist for Palantir had key role in helping Andy Burnham become PM
summary: Exclusive: Martha Dalton worked closely with Burnham’s team on byelection that secured his return to parliament
text: A recent lobbyist for the controversial $450bn US tech company Palantir played a senior role in helping Andy Burnham become prime minister, it has emerged. Martha Dalton, whose company Lodestone worked for Palantir in 2024 and 2025, campaigned for Burnham in the Makerfield byelection that secured his return to parliament. She worked closely with his team on strategic communications and rebuttals, and was among supporters who clapped him into Downing Street in July. Lodestone, which Dalton co-founded, worked for Palantir on projects including promoting its software at events in parliament where its engineers demonstrated AI-powered systems for use in British public services to MPs. Dalton previously worked on the autumn 2025 deputy leadership campaign for the current education secretary, Lucy Powell, a few months after Lodestone stopped working for Palantir. Her role emerged as Palantir fights to retain its £330m contract with NHS England to run the federated data platform, a national medical data system. Burnham’s government is under pressure to scrap the deal. Campaigners are angry about Palantir’s work for the Israeli military in Gaza and Donald Trump’s ICE immigration crackdown. They have also raised concerns, acknowledged by NHS England’s chief executive, Jim Mackey, that the benefits to public health may not be as significant as has been claimed. Lodestone’s work for Palantir and Dalton’s subsequent role with Burnham is the latest link between Labour and the tech firm, which also works for the US and UK militaries and was co-founded by the Trump-supporting tech billionaire Peter Thiel. The Labour peer Tom Watson took a full-time job lobbying for Palantir earlier this month after a period as a member of Lodestone’s “strategic advisory council”. Palantir previously employed Peter Mandelson’s lobbying firm, Global Counsel, before it collapsed over the former Labour trade secretary’s links to Jeffrey Epstein. Dalton wrote on her LinkedIn account that it had been “an absolute honour to work on Andy Burnham’s campaign to become Labour leader and prime minister”. She took six weeks’ unpaid leave from Lodestone to spend time in Makerfield “supporting on strategic comms and rebuttals”. A spokesperson for Lodestone said: “She had no contact with clients during that time and did so because she believes Andy Burnham is the best person to lead the Labour party and the country. Lodestone had previously worked with Palantir on various projects – all focused on helping them to explain their technology to those who rightly hold them to account.” Health workers who want ministers to scrap Palantir’s NHS deal protested at the Labour party conference in Liverpool on Tuesday. Labour members had earlier tabled a motion calling for the deal to be axed, claiming Palantir was “facing numerous allegations of involvement in serious breaches of human rights”, citing its development of technology for Israel’s military. Palantir’s executive vice-president for the UK and Europe, Louis Mosley, has said its technology was used to locate hostages but not to identify military targets in Gaza. That appears to contradict an earlier statement by the firm’s chief executive, Alex Karp, who was challenged last year by a protester alleging “Palantir kills Palestinians” in Gaza. He replied: “Mostly terrorists, that’s true.” Palantir’s fortunes in the UK are intertwined with the Labour government. A break clause in the NHS England contract looms in February 2027. The Labour mayor of London, Sadiq Khan, is also in a legal battle with Palantir after he blocked the Metropolitan police from awarding it a £50m contract to supply AI tools to assist criminal investigations. The firm also has a £240m contract with the Ministry of Defence and has been selling its services to other police forces and councils. Mosley recently said that people who don’t recognise the positive impact the firm’s technology has on cutting treatment waiting times and speeding up hospital discharges were suffering from “Palantir derangement syndrome”. Tom Brake, the chief executive of Unlock Democracy, a not-for-profit campaign group, said candidates should observe Cabinet Office advice on secondments before adding volunteers or secondees to their campaign teams. “This requires successful secondees to declare relevant outside interests, clarify that potential conflicts will be explored and ensure appropriate mitigations are put in place,” he said. A Labour spokesperson said: “There are robust rules and procedures to manage any potential conflicts, whether that be in government or in campaigns, and those were followed.” A Palantir spokesperson said: “Lodestone has worked with us on a range of projects to explain how our software is used to deliver public services – for example parliamentary events that enable MPs to see demonstrations of our software and ask our engineers questions around data privacy and security.”

title: ‘I was fighting for my life’: Indian pilot hailed as hero recalls flydubai cockpit attack
summary: Smit Machchhar says in video call with Indian PM that he realised if he did not get up ‘passengers would lose their lives’
text: The Indian pilot who helped thwart an apparent attempt to crash a flydubai flight to Tel Aviv said his faith and his desire to save his passengers allowed him to make a “last push” to open the cockpit door as he fought for his life. Capt Smit Machchhar, who was recovering in an Abu Dhabi hospital, described to India’s prime minister, Narendra Modi, how he helped save the plane and its more than 170 passengers. “I had suffered so many injuries that I had collapsed. At that time, I could feel that the aircraft was going down. I knew this was the last push,” Machchhar told Modi in a video call on Friday. “I was fighting for my life. At one point, I realised that if I didn’t get up … then passengers would lose their lives.” His Omani co-pilot apparently stabbed him and set the plane on a steep descent, with the aircraft plummeting about 17,000 feet in the span of a minute. While still being attacked, Machchhar managed to open the cockpit door, allowing passengers to enter, subdue the attacker and ultimately stabilise the plane. The full circumstances of the attack are still under investigation, but a relief crew on the flight helped land the plane safely in Tabouk, north-west Saudi Arabia. Saudi authorities arrested the co-pilot and have since interrogated him. Machchhar, a father of two, was seriously injured during the attack, but credited his 17 years of aviation experience with giving him the wherewithal to understand the gravity of the situation. Modi praised the captain for his actions, which he said helped prevent a “great tragedy.” “You have done such a great thing that people across the country and around the world are eager to see you and speak to you,” Modi told him. “You have truly made the whole country proud.” The motives and affiliation of the apparent attacker are still unknown, but Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, said that an initial background investigation indicated he had undergone “Islamic radical indoctrination”. The attacker is to be sent back to the United Arab Emirates, where Emirati investigators will work to establish any links with terror organisations. Netanyahu said Israel would cooperate with the UAE on the investigation. Machchhar was hailed as a hero by world leaders, who said his actions had helped prevent a great disaster and save many lives. The pilot said that during the difficult moments he recited the Hanuman Chalisa, a devotional hymn dedicated to the Hindu deity Hanuman and traditionally recited as a prayer for strength and courage. “Lord Hanuman gave me courage,” Machchhar told Modi. He added that he felt proud of himself for the first time since the attack. “I am feeling very proud right now. I had not felt proud of myself until now,” he told Modi. “I am not thinking of it as a wound, I am thinking of it as a journey,” he said, while covered in bandages. “And it will take time, but I am very, very confident that I will recover.”

title: Almost half of Fayed abuse accusers are potential trafficking victims, MPs told
summary: Exclusive: Met police say 70 women’s accounts have hallmarks of trafficking, suggesting case numbers could rise
text: Almost half of the women who reported allegations of sexual abuse by Mohamed Al Fayed to the Metropolitan police are potential victims of human trafficking, MPs have been told. In a briefing for the all-party parliamentary group (APPG) for the survivors of Fayed and Harrods in July, senior Met officers said a review earlier this year found 70 survivors’ accounts bore the hallmarks of trafficking. The Home Office has confirmed that at least five survivors were victims of international and domestic trafficking. The Met’s figures suggested the number of confirmed cases could climb much higher, said the Liberal Democrat MP Wendy Chamberlain, a co-chair of the APPG. “I can’t believe that wouldn’t increase,” said Chamberlain, who also compared the scale of Fayed’s abuse to Jimmy Savile’s. The Labour MP Dave Robertson, the APPG’s other co-chair, said: “The number of women who were trafficked by Mohammed Fayed and his trafficking ring is certainly much higher.” Some women were trafficked from Harrods to Fayed’s private offices and residence in Park Lane while others were taken out of the UK and abused overseas, senior police officers running the Met’s investigation, Operation Cornpoppy, told the APPG. But several survivors told the Guardian that the Home Office had not recognised them as victims of trafficking because they now live abroad. Amy, who lives in Italy, said she was trafficked from Harrods, where she initially worked on the shop floor, and her home to Fayed’s other properties. She said she was transferred to a PA role in his private residence and office at 60 Park Lane in London, where he allegedly sexually abused her, including groping her breasts and forced kissing. She said Fayed also took her in his private car and helicopter to his estate in Oxted, Surrey, where she was sexually assaulted in a lagoon-style swimming pool located behind a concealed door. “I would be removed from my home in Hammersmith and then be changed into clothes like Lacoste polo shirts and Bermuda shorts and boat shoes, which I absolutely hated,” said Amy. “That was robbing me of my actual identity. Whoever saw me leave my bedsit would say that’s not her. That’s a strong component of what trafficking is and was very calculating.” In a letter sent in June to the then minister for safeguarding and violence against women and girls, Natalie Fleet, Amy raised concerns about the apparent exclusion of survivors living outside the UK from the Home Office assessment of potential trafficking victims, the National Referral Mechanism (NRM). She received a response from the Home Office in August, which said there was not a requirement that a potential victim be resident in the UK before being referred to the NRM by the police, or another first responder organisation. But last month Amy was informed by her contact officer at the Met that the Home Office had confirmed it would reject any referrals made for international residents. KP Law (KPL), which represents Amy and 277 other alleged survivors of Fayed’s abuse, said nearly a quarter of those women now lived overseas. Lucy Traynor, a senior associate at KPL, criticised the apparently inconsistent advice as to who was eligible to be recognised as a victim of trafficking. The lawyer said: “We are still seeing individuals whose experiences meet the threshold for trafficking struggling to secure recognition through these systems which are designed to identify and protect victims. Amy’s case is a stark example. Despite the nature of what she experienced, she continues to face barriers to recognition outside the UK. That disconnect between what the Home Office has committed to and what survivors experience in practice is simply not acceptable.” First responders including police forces and some charities can refer someone to the NRM if they suspect they are a victim of human trafficking. The Home Oﬃce then makes an initial “reasonable grounds” decision if it believes a crime may have occurred before investigating further and making a final “conclusive grounds” decision. So far it has confirmed that five women allegedly abused by Fayed were trafficking victims. Eleanor Lyons, the independent anti-slavery commissioner, said the Home Office’s statutory guidance explicitly stated that people needed to be in the UK to be referred to the NRM. Lyons said this was because the process involved getting access to support including a safe house and counselling, which officials believed would be difficult to provide to people who do not live in the UK. But she called on the Home Office to reconsider the requirement because many affected people she spoke to just wanted to be recognised as trafficking victims, adding that the situation was causing deep distress for alleged survivors of Fayed’s abuse. “The government should be doing everything it can to make it easier to identify these women and recognise them as potential victims of modern slavery,” Lyons said. “They’re doing directly the opposite right now, which is causing further harm to the survivors.” Survivors’ groups say more than 500 women have come forward about abuse that allegedly took place at Harrods, Park Lane, Fulham football club, the Ritz hotel in Paris, and other places owned by Fayed. The Met is investigating 165 victims who have contacted the force directly. A Met police spokesperson said: “We were previously making referrals to the Home Office for victims living in the UK and abroad, but those relating to victims living abroad were being rejected. As a result, we have paused any further such referrals. Should the Home Office position change, we will restart those submissions. Our support to victims continues, regardless of where they live.” A Home Office spokesperson paid tribute to “the incredible bravery” of survivors of Fayed’s alleged abuse. They added: “We are ensuring modern slavery survivors get the support they need to recover and move on with their lives.” A Harrods spokesperson said it “supports all survivors in their pursuit of justice and continues to work closely with the Met police on its investigation”.

title: Friday briefing: How we covered the flydubai incident as it unfolded
summary: In today’s newsletter: When a passenger plane plunges 17,000ft amid claims of terrorism, hijacking and geopolitical intrigue, Guardian journalists have to try and separate fact from fiction in real time
text: Good morning. Shocking news of a cockpit stabbing. Graphic footage of bloodied crew members. Mid-air testimony from terrified passengers. This was the tenor of the heart-in-mouth reporting as the horrifying events unfolded onboard flight FZ 1073 to Tel Aviv: the early morning budget flight that plummeted 17,000ft in under two minutes before the courageous intervention of passengers and crew averted an apparent hijacking, potentially saving the lives of not just the 170+ passengers and crew on board, but many more. This morning, speculation and conflicting reports are continuing to emerge about this dramatic incident in the sky above the most geopolitically sensitive region in the world. So how does the Guardian report a swiftly developing story engulfed in misinformation, as accurately and responsibility as possible? I spoke to the reporters, bloggers and editors involved to find out. But first, this morning’s headlines. Five big stories UK politics | Ministers are working up sweeping plans for welfare changes including scrapping a key disability benefit for under-25s and replacing it with a multibillion-pound package of support to get into work. Northern Ireland | Talks aimed at resolving the Drumcree parade dispute have broken up without agreement, with Northern Ireland secretary Chris Bryant describing the situation as being between a “rock and a hard place”. US news | Tennessee’s governor has suspended all executions in the state and ordered an independent inquiry after a botched attempt to put a condemned inmate to death on Wednesday night. AI | When prompted, AI chat bots will edit images to remove the hijabs from Muslim women, a violation of one of the world’s most common and visible expressions of faith. Europe news | A fast-growing protest by high-school students over long hours, teacher shortages and decaying facilities has escalated into “urban violence”, the French government has warned. In depth: ‘It was very, very tricky to untangle what was happening’ International leaders have rushed to praise Smit Machchhar, the captain of flight FZ 1073. Bleeding heavily from multiple stab wounds, he somehow managed to release his cockpit door, allowing passengers and crew to gain entry and overpower his co-pilot turned assailant, an Omani national, who had attacked Machchhar in an apparent attempt to crash the plane. Other crew members were able to stabilise the flight and, just before 11am local time on Wednesday, the Boeing 737 Max made a safe emergency landing in Saudi Arabia. All 174 passengers on board escaped serious injury. Yesterday, as internationally coordinated investigations continued, the attacker’s motives remained unknown. Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu told Fox News it was “too early to say” if there was any Iranian involvement, while claiming the co-pilot had previously undergone radical Islamist indoctrination and was suicidal. Other senior Israeli figures have been more vehement, with ambassador to the UN, Danny Danon, describing the incident as a “terror attack”. Two Israeli security sources later told Reuters that they had not yet found Iranian involvement. Saudi investigators detained the co-pilot upon landing and are cooperating with the United Arab Emirates, the US, Oman and Israel to determine his reasons and potential affiliations. William Christou, a Beirut-based reporter with the Guardian, tells me: “They’re examining whether it’s a terror attack, whether it had any previous planning or prior direction, and if it could be a lone wolf attacker, who was perhaps motivated by anti-Israel hate, but wasn’t necessarily linked to any larger organisation or state.” *** ‘The story changed moment to moment’ William began drafting his initial report as soon as he woke up to news alerts about a potential hijacking. The Israeli government originally minimised the incident, describing it as a fight between pilots, while another early report suggested the plane had to land because of a fight between Ukrainian and Russian co-pilots. “I was sifting through so much misinformation,” he says. “The story changed very quickly, and moment to moment.” Back in the UK, Oliver Holmes was looking at flight trackers. Now based at Guardian HQ, Oliver has reported extensively across the Middle East. What I didn’t know until we spoke is that he once trained as a pilot, which has left him with an enduring interest in aerospace and aviation. Flight tracking websites have transformed how we report in-air incidents, he tells me. “Before any government has made an announcement, these platforms can tell you something seriously wrong has happened.” Flight tracking website Flightradar24 recorded the aircraft rapidly descending from its cruising altitude of about 34,000ft to 17,000ft in less than two minutes, just as it reached to the Saudi-Jordanian border. Oliver suggests that investigators will look at whether this sudden and ferocious plunge was why the plane eventually landed with part of its tail missing. Oliver sent what he could interpret from the tracking data to his international desk editors, who asked him to work on a tick-tock piece – not, for once, a reference to social media, but an old-school print term for an article that sets out the hour-by-hour narrative of an unfolding news story. “It was very, very tricky to untangle what was happening,” says Oliver. Eventually there came a flood of footage purporting to show images from inside the plane – but was it real? Each clip that the Guardian incorporated into our reporting had to be verified, particularly given the potential for AI-generated fakes. (The Guardian’s head of photography Fiona Shields is fascinating here on how we assess AI images.) *** ‘Netanyahu was trying to present himself as Mr. Security’ But this wasn’t just an aviation disaster. “It was taking place in this hugely sensitive geopolitical situation,” says Oliver. “The plane landed in Saudi Arabia which does not officially have diplomatic relations with Israel.” The budget airline itself, flydubai, had by now suspended all its flights to and from Israel, but warned against “premature speculation” while multiple governments, and Israeli officials in particular, were doing just that. This incident has occurred at a moment of extreme instability across the region, with the strait of Hormuz still closed as a result of the US-Israel assault on Iran and the resurgence of conflict in Yemen. It is also weeks ahead of knife-edge Israeli elections, with polls showing Netanyahu’s current coalition unlikely to meet the threshold needed to form a government but no clear path to power for his rivals. Just days ago, Netanyahu warned Israel faced an unspecified attack risk during the election period – an assertion greeted with cynicism by political opponents. The Israeli military subsequently confirmed they had no specific intelligence of an anticipated attack. “Most people interpreted that as Netanyahu trying to stir up his base by presenting himself as Mr. Security,” says William. Nevertheless, Netanyahu’s supporters consider him vindicated. On Thursday, William tells me, the Israeli foreign ministry started briefing diplomats that the flydubai incident was an attempt to drive a further wedge between the UAE and Israel, a relationship already strained after leaks suggesting Netanyahu was personally alerted to the 7 October attacks by the UAE president a week before it took place, something the president has denounced as “an absolute lie”. *** ‘These stories can be incredibly powerful’ It’s a challenging time to report a story like this, says Taz Ali, who led our live blog which covered the incident unfolding in real-time on Wednesday. “Readers are making connections with what’s happening in the Middle East in general, and you’re trying to answer their questions, first with very scant detail and later with a deluge of information, much of which is proved to be inaccurate.” Taz, who has a decade of experience in reporting on global events, knows the human drama of a potential hijacking immediately grabs reader’s attention. “Often those stories can be incredibly powerful, involve emergency landings, and sometimes they end in great tragedies”. And with the recent 25th anniversary of 9/11, the incident had an even deeper resonance. “Especially with the anniversary happening so recently, those memories would have been so raw in people’s minds when they came to this story.” What else we’ve been enjoying A new Taschen book of images from the National Geographic’s archives charts a century of dramatic change. And this fantastic gallery shows a tantalising selection, from the burlesque clubs of Baltimore to a blimp crossing New York Harbour. Lucinda Everett, newsletters team I loved our piece on when book clubs get dramatic, featuring werewolf smut, bad book choices, and infuriation when people don’t actually read the book. Poppy Elle Hunt’s piece about the evolution and cultural significance of human hair tackles many questions I never knew I needed answering. Case in point: what on earth is the purpose of pubic hair? Lucinda Guardian contributor Katherine Rowland went to Chicago for the United Astrology Conference and tells a captivating story about the battle over who gets to interpret the stars and how they should do it. Poppy Philip Oltermann’s interview with German artist and writer Philipp Ruch is a fascinating read. Ruch argues that “most of the theories we have to explain the rise of the Nazis don’t make sense – the data tells a far darker story”, one that could help us understand the rise of right-wing extremists today. Lucinda Sport Football | Wales ended their long wait for a Nations League win by beating Norway 2-1 in Cardiff, while Portugal maintained their perfect start with a 4-2 victory over Denmark in Copenhagen. Football | The United States is poised to host the first Women’s Club World Cup in January 2028, becoming the latest in a series of major Fifa tournaments staged in North America. Football | Andy Burnham’s intervention in the Manchester City debate has revived tensions between the Premier League and the prime minister. Something for the weekend Our critics’ roundup of the best things to watch, read, play and listen to right now TV Blue Lights (BBC One) | ★★★★☆ This Northern Ireland-set police drama has always been modern but never explicitly topical. Until now. Race riots, organised crime and institutional politics bring it bang up to date. Read Jack Seale’s full review. Music Meshell Ndegeocello: Synonym | ★★★★☆ In the jazz-soul singer’s ‘expression of queer liberation’, stars from Chaka Khan to Bill Callahan to Cynthia Erivo duet on equally varied songs from Cher to the Human League and beyond. Read Alexis Petridis’s full review. Film Knife: The Attempted Murder of Salman Rushdie (in cinemas now) | ★★★★☆ Alex Gibney’s documentary follows the celebrated author’s life up to and after the attack, but what shines through is Rushdie’s remarkable courage. Read Peter Bradshaw’s full review. Art Renoir and Love (National Gallery, London, from tomorrow) | ★★★★★ Grab your straw boater – and revel in the Impressionist’s light-as-souffle masterpieces that celebrate life’s pleasures, from picnics to dances to frolics in the bushes. Read Jonathan Jones’s full review. The front pages The Guardian splashes with “Welfare changes may axe disability benefit for young”. The Times leads with “Emergency diesel talks after Trump ultimatum” and the Telegraph says “Trump tells Europe to release diesel”. The Mail runs with “Labour frees first of 10 tidal waves of convicts”, while The i Paper has “Burnham leaving the door open to snap general election in 2027”. The Sun, on Andy Burnham’s Manchester City comments, says “Own goal”. The Financial Times goes with “Global bond sell-off leaves US trapped in vicious loop”, and the Mirror leads on an interview with a survivor of the Manchester synagogue attack, saying “He stabbed me 3 times but I had to stop him”. The Latest US woman on death row survives two lethal injections in Tennessee A woman convicted of murdering a schoolmate 30 years ago has been taken to hospital after surviving two rounds of lethal injections in Tennessee. Christa Pike would have been the first woman to be executed in the state in 200 years. Pike, 50, has spent three decades on death row after she was convicted of the murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer in 1995. A last-minute appeal to stop the lethal injection was overturned by the supreme court, but the state governor, Bill Lee, has suspended executions in Tennessee for the rest of the year. Lucy Hough speaks to the attorney and anti-capital punishment campaigner Clive Stafford Smith. Cartoon of the day | Ben Jennings The Upside A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad Eleven-year-old Bodhana Sivanandan has become the youngest ever ‘woman grandmaster’ at the Chess Olympiad in Uzbekistan – while playing on a car booster seat so she could reach the board. Sivanandan, who lives in Harrow, was taught to play by her father when she was five. Within a year, she was beating him and by eight she had beaten the former British champion Peter Lee. If she reaches a rating of 2,500 in the next 11 months, she will become the world’s youngest ever outright grandmaster. She fits her chess career around school, but takes everything in her stride. “Now that I’m in secondary school there might be more homework,” she says, “but I should be able to manage”. Her ultimate ambition, she says, is simply to be the best chess player in the world. Sign up here for a weekly roundup of The Upside, sent to you every Sunday Bored at work? title: Increased air pollution linked to more night-time coughing, UK-led study finds
summary: ‘Day-to-day’ symptom of harmful emissions, which in turn can disrupt sleep, can be overlooked, say researchers
text: New research has found that increased air pollution is associated with more night-time coughing, leading to disturbed sleep. Most air pollution research looks at symptoms that are severe enough for people to seek medical help, but day-to-day symptoms can be overlooked. Prof Cecilia Mascolo, who led the study from the University of Cambridge, said: “I come from an area in Italy with very high pollution and I am very aware of its not-talked-about effects.” Many more of us are using apps to monitor our sleep patterns. A recent survey of 18- to 30-year-olds in the UK found that 37% used sleep apps, while data from 2025 suggested that more than 40% of UK adults used tech to track their sleep. The researchers looked at data from a commonly used sleep app. For 18 months they collected anonymised data from 32 cities in 12 countries, an average of 98,000 people a night. As well as tracking sleep, the app also counted how many times people coughed. About half of the people coughed during the night, with 1% coughing more than 10 times. The greatest frequency of coughing was recorded in Milan and around Monza, both cities in north Italy’s Po Valley, one of the most polluted areas in western Europe. A look at the data for Los Angeles and London shows that people cough more in cold weather and there are more coughs recorded when flu is circulating. Mascolo said: “The hardest part was understanding if what we were seeing in the cough peaks was really affected by pollution or rather by viruses/flu trends as well as weather.” Dr Tong Xia, part of the research team and now at Tsinghua University, added: “I thought that adding in the confounding factor of flu season would make the link in the data disappear, but it didn’t.” High daily particle pollution was consistently associated with increased night-time coughing, but effects could also be seen at lower concentrations, well below the World Health Organization’s (WHO) air pollution guidelines. Mascolo said: “Even in cities with relatively low levels of air pollution, such as Melbourne and Sydney, we observed positive associations between particle pollution and increased coughing. “The LA wildfires were the clearest and most severe pollution spike in our study window.” Night-time coughing increased by 13 % during the wildfire smoke, and some people experienced effects that were delayed by several days. Mascolo and Tong also found increased coughing in the London data around the time of Guy Fawkes fireworks and bonfires: “During the first week of November 2025, when influenza activity remained low, days with PM2.5 [particulate matter of less than 2.5 micrometres in diameter] concentrations exceeding the WHO guideline became more frequent, accompanied by a noticeably higher cough rate than previous months. “Emission sources, such as firework displays, may have contributed to episodic air pollution and subsequent airway irritation, although source-specific data are needed to substantiate this.” Rather than stopping action on air pollution once legal limits are met, we should be continuing to reduce air pollution. Mascolo added: “These findings underscore the global health relevance of air pollution and suggest that the potential chronic health effects of long-term exposure to low concentrations of particle pollution warrant attention, even in comparatively less polluted cities.”

title: Would a gambling tax rise in the budget really shut shops and cost jobs?
summary: Most of the betting industry is urging the chancellor not to double slot machine duty to raise up to £460m more a year
text: Gambling industry kingpins are fuming about reports that the chancellor, John Healey, is considering increasing taxes on high-street slot machines in his first budget. The influential Social Market Foundation thinktank, the most vocal advocate for a rise in machine games duty (MGD), from 20% to 40%, thinks the measure could raise between £275m and £460m annually, on top of the roughly £610m collected last year. Its proposal is likely to meet with sympathy from Andy Burnham, a vocal and repeated critic of slot machines, who has already moved to tighten licensing laws so that gambling firms find it harder to open up new shops. The billionaire owner of Betfred, Fred Done, is among industry bosses who say such a policy would force shop closures, cost jobs and ultimately fail in its objective, depriving the Treasury of taxes. But not every figure in the gambling world agrees. Stewart Kenny, the co-founder of Paddy Power who has become a critic of his erstwhile industry, accused Done of “scaremongering”. So who’s right? It’s complicated … What does the industry say? Bookies might be best known for bets on horses or football but they make big money from slot machines. The Betting and Gaming Council, an industry lobby group, commissioned a report from the accounting firm EY that estimated a duty rise to 40% could close up to 1,470 betting shops (nearly a third of the total 5,617), resulting in 15,900 job losses and a net loss to the exchequer of about £120m. Horse racing, which receives a levy from bookies’ profits, would also take a hit. Done said he alone would be forced to close about 495 betting shops, nearly half of Betfred’s estate, with the loss of 2,475 jobs and £67m in taxes. Entain, the owner of Ladbrokes and Coral, has written to Burnham saying it would have to make job cuts across its nationwide estate of 2,300 shops, were the policy to go ahead. Casinos and bingo halls are in the firing line too. Rank Group, which owns Mecca Bingo and Grosvenor Casinos, cautioned that a third of its venues could close, affecting 2,000 staff. Are they crying wolf? When dealing with bookmakers, it is wise to be sceptical. Back in 2019, Betfred had about 1,620 shops. Since then, the company has threatened to close nearly 1,000 in response to tougher regulation or taxes. While most of the policies it objected to have come to pass, the number of shops has decreased by only about 330. Some of that is down to a broader shift to the web that has led to soaring online gambling revenues. In one Betfred TV ad, Done encourages punters to “come and see me”. In your neighbourhood bookies? No, at Betfred.com. Meanwhile, the Done family has taken out tens of millions of pounds in dividends, including £50m in 2022 alone. Any other examples? Bet365 does not have high street shops, operating only online. But it recently cited an increase in gambling duties in the former chancellor Rachel Reeves’s budget last year as it announced plans to cut about 300 jobs at its Stoke-on-Trent headquarters. What it failed to mention is that it has been increasing its use of AI within the business since well before the tax rise. Some staff at Bet365’s Stoke HQ are understood to feel that government policy is a convenient smokescreen for good old-fashioned corporate cost-cutting. A spokesperson said Bet365 was responding to a “highly competitive trading environment, plus increased regulatory and tax-related costs”. So it’s all a bluff? Well, no. The UK’s biggest gambling companies, including Betfred, Entain, Flutter and more, have all announced cuts since Reeves’s duty rise. It is impossible to say how much of this retrenchment might have happened anyway, given economic worries and structural shifts within the sector. However, it makes sense that any further increase in costs, in the form of higher taxes on slot machines, will negatively affect the gambling sector. Simon Thomas, the chief executive of the Hippodrome Casino in London, says that fear of the tax is already hurting investment. “We have a £6m rooftop expansion plan with full planning permission, ready to go. With MGD up in the air, we’ve had to shelve it,” he said, adding that if MGD goes up to 40%, a third of bingo halls and a third of casinos could close. Does the government want a smaller gambling sector? Burnham has already moved to limit the opening of new gambling premises. He has voiced particular concerns about 24-hour adult gaming centres (AGCs), high street venues packed with the sort of machines that would be more heavily taxed by an MGD increase. The rise of these “slot farms” is understood to be the main driver for any such move. But there are question marks over whether AGCs would actually take the hit. They already have much lower overheads and looser regulation than casinos and bingo halls, which have experienced negligible growth. Last year, AGCs managed to increase their takings from £528m to £613m by packing more machines into larger venues. So if slot machines taxes go up, in theory AGCs are best placed to survive the impact. The AGC operator Merkur has already offered to buy some of the 132 shops that Betfred put up for sale, indicating it is unruffled by the prospect of a tax rise. If others follow suit, just as bookies retrench, an MGD rise could simply lead to bookies being replaced by 24-hour slot farms. As Treasury officials weigh up duty rises, they will have to consider the law of unintended consequences.

title: Country diary: A TB scare is still hanging over the farm | Andrea Meanwell
summary: Tebay, Cumbria: I’ve had a stroke of luck with applying for government funding, but some bad vet results are overshadowing things once more
text: Last week was an important one as the government’s sustainable farming incentive opened for this year. Thankfully, I was working on my laptop when the email came through, so I submitted an application for us to become an organic farm. Others were not so lucky – the funding ran out after a few hours, and WhatsApp became a catalogue of despair among farmers who missed out and now don’t know how their farm businesses will survive. It’s clear that the government needs to provide more money to support sustainable farming. Meanwhile, it’s been a difficult period since June as we’ve been “shut down” with TB. We’ve been waiting to test again so we can hopefully sell our bullocks, bull and breeding heifers. The wait has been extended because of my son’s wedding, and we had to find a new vet after our previous vet stopped taking farm animals as it was uneconomical for them. I’ve been unable to sleep. Another shutdown would again impact us financially. Before the new test, it took a day for us to get the 67 cows home from the fells, and they were heavily in calf. One decided to calve en route, on the side of a fell at about 1,200ft. We phoned our new vet, who said they all had to come in, so we walked the other cows home and went back for the cow and calf. It was a job getting the quad and trailer close, but we managed to get the calf in the trailer. The cow then set off for home at top speed; I followed, and my son took the calf home. Thankfully, they were reunited happily and spent the night in the farm garden. The cows receive two injections on day one, and if any lumps develop by day four, they have to be assessed. By day four it was going well, but then one cow developed a 3mm lump – an “inconclusive reactor”. She had to be isolated and will be tested again in 60 days. In the meantime, we are shut down again and cannot sell any breeding cows, only direct to slaughter. We need to think carefully about what we do next, for the sake of the cows, and ourselves. • Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024, is available now at guardianbookshop.com

title: Tennessee suspends executions as Christa Pike’s lawyer says failed lethal injection leaves her in critical condition
summary: Independent inquiry ordered after failed execution of Pike, who was convicted of 1994 murder
text: Tennessee’s governor on Thursday said it was “deeply disturbing” that his state botched the execution of a death row prisoner who remained alive and snoring 40 minutes after receiving a double dose of the lethal drug that should have quickly killed her. Bill Lee, a Republican, has suspended all executions in the state until at least the end of the year and ordered an independent inquiry after Wednesday night’s failed attempt to put to death Christa Pike, who was convicted of murder, at the execution chamber in Nashville. Meanwhile, Pike, 50, remained in the hospital on Thursday afternoon. “We don’t have a sense of her prognosis or much update on her health at the moment, but we do know that she is alive right now and receiving life-saving medical care,” Randy Spivey, one of her attorneys, said at an afternoon press conference. “She is in critical condition receiving life-saving care. That is the extent of what we have at the moment.” Spivey, of the office of the post-conviction defender, condemned Tennessee authorities for the manner in which the failed attempt unfolded. He said officials used seven needles, one of which became bent as it was removed from Pike’s arm. “Last night was not just inefficient, it was cruel and it was torturous. It was also predictable,” he said, adding that he saw no life-saving care given after the execution attempt was abandoned at about 8.25pm. Speaking to reporters on Thursday morning, Lee said he had spoken with Frank Strada, secretary of the Tennessee department of correction, but did not have an update on the condition of Pike, who was taken to an off-site medical facility after surviving two doses of pentobarbital. “This is a tragedy,” Lee said, adding that he had not yet spoken to the families of Pike or the teenager she killed in 1995. “There is no one that wanted what happened last night to happen. It shouldn’t have happened. “It’s the most difficult of circumstances as it relates to the sentence that should have been carried out by the state. It’s a tragedy, and it’s deeply disturbing that that has happened in this state. The people deserve better than that.” Lee added, in comments reported by the Tennessean, that he had not yet chosen an investigator to lead a “comprehensive, third party review” he announced in a statement late on Wednesday. “There are a lot of questions,” he said. “The people of our state deserve to have those questions answered. I’m highly disappointed, along with Tennesseans, about what happened.” Cameron Sexton, the Republican speaker of Tennessee’s house of representatives, said on Thursday in a social media post that he and other lawmakers would also be investigating what went wrong with the attempted execution. He added that they would look at other ways to prevent executions from failing. “We will look at all options – expanding the alternatives, and changing the current medications to include potassium chloride,” he said. “Thirty years is too long for justice.” Robin Maher, executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center, said her group was aware of seven other people that had survived medical problems due to an execution team’s failure to access a vein to administer lethal injection drugs, but nobody had remained alive after receiving the drugs used in such executions. “This failed attempt is the worst we’ve ever seen and unlike any other botched execution in the modern era,” she said in a statement. “What happened to Christa Pike can be attributed to the extreme secrecy Tennessee officials have maintained about their execution procedures, their refusal to answer reasonable questions and their unwillingness to accept responsibility for their mistakes.” In May, Tennessee officials called off the lethal injection of Tony Carruthers, another convicted murderer, after failing for more than an hour to place an intravenous line into his arm. On Thursday, Donald Trump was questioned on how an execution like Pike’s could fail, but told reporters they would have to speak to Tennessee officials about that. When someone he was travelling with said, “It should be easy to do,” Trump reiterated his words, saying, “it shouldn’t be very difficult.” Pike, who was sentenced to death for the brutal 1994 killing of a teenage classmate, was set to be the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years. The execution attempt was allowed to proceed only after the US supreme court intervened late on Wednesday to lift a federal court stay issued earlier in the day, a delay it said was necessary to assess whether Pike’s allegations of childhood sexual abuse were fully considered at her 1996 sentencing. Lawyers for Pike filed an emergency motion to the Tennessee supreme court after the second pentobarbital dose was administered asking to halt and stay the execution, saying she was in “unnecessary agony”, and that the state was violating her right to be executed free of cruel and unusual punishment. A representative of the state corrections department defended its handling of the unsuccessful execution attempt. “The Tennessee Department of Correction followed every step of the State’s lawful, established execution protocol approved by the Attorney General’s Office,” the spokesperson, Dorinda Carter, said in a statement. “The lethal injection chemical in the protocol has consistently been effective, and the protocol does not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried out this evening. Christa Pike has been transported to an off-site medical facility.” According to the AP, Tennessee’s execution protocol calls for a secondary set of drug syringes to be administered “if the inmate is not deceased” after the first set. It does not spell out what happens if the subject is alive after the second set. Seven journalists who were present at the Riverbend maximum security institution as witnesses described what they saw during a live stream hosted by WVLT television station soon after curtains in the execution chamber were lowered for the final time. They said Pike was snoring as corrections officials escorted them out. John North, of ABC News affiliate WBIR, said: “It appears this did not go how this was supposed to go. When we left the building, so far as we knew, she was probably still alive.” Pike and her boyfriend Tadaryl Shipp were 18 and 17 when they and another female friend tortured and killed 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, one of their classmates at Knoxville Job Corps, in January 1995, using boxcutters and a rock. The case garnered nationwide headlines due to the ages of those involved and the brutality of the murder, in which Shipp carved a pentagram into their victim’s chest and Pike later showed a friend a fragment of her skull. Pike never denied the killing, and was later diagnosed with mental health disorders. “I was a mentally ill 18-year-old kid. It took me numerous years to even realize the gravity of what I’d done,” she said in a clemency petition that Lee and the US supreme court denied. Lee’s suspension order affects the only other execution set in Tennessee this year. Gary Wayne Sutton has been on death row since 1996 for the murder of a friend, and was scheduled to be put to death on 3 December. The Associated Press contributed reporting

title: ‘No one disrespects Our Lady’: fears for Brazil’s patron saint grip country ahead of election
summary: Speculation that Flávio Bolsonaro will try to strip Our Lady of Aparecida of position could become deciding factor in run-up to Sunday
text: A row of Biblical proportions has erupted in the run-up to Brazil’s presidential election, with the country’s patron saint, Our Lady of Aparecida, emerging as an unlikely kingmaker in the deadlocked race. Ahead of Sunday’s vote, the two frontrunners – the leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, and his far-right challenger, Flávio Bolsonaro – are level in the polls. But in recent days, speculation that Bolsonaro – son of the former president Jair Bolsonaro – might strip the widely cherished patroness of her position have caused a nationwide outcry, leaving some to question if it could tip the knife-edge election in favour of Lula, who is Catholic. “It could sway things one way or the other,” said Thomas Traumann, a political analyst who has been tracking the unusual election row. It remains unclear precisely how the commotion began, but debate over the issue exploded last week when a remark by Bolsonaro, whose movement includes many evangelical Christians, went viral online. In a recent broadcast, the former senator said one of his first acts as president would be to “decree that Brazil belongs to the Lord Jesus Christ”. Some Catholics took that as a sign that the Protestant politician planned to unseat Our Lady of Aparecida, although only the Vatican – which declared her Brazil’s patroness in 1930 – has the authority to do so. Those suspicions were reinforced by Bolsonaro’s reported links to JB Carvalho, an evangelical leader who has previously called for the patroness’s removal. In 2007, another Bolsonaro ally tried to introduce legislation to the same effect, although the bill was dropped. Bolsonaro has called claims he plans to unseat Our Lady of Aparecida “fake news”. He alleged the rumours were being spread by Lula supporters, as well as members of the Episcopal Conference of Brazil, a Catholic bishops’ organisation. The conference rejected the charge. Lula’s leftwing movement has taken advantage of the furore, keenly aware it could hurt the far-right candidate’s chances in a country where nearly 57% of the population is Catholic. With the result expected to be even tighter than the last one – when Lula beat Jair Bolsonaro by less than 2% – even a small number of votes could mean the difference between victory and defeat. Lula has appeared on the campaign trail holding statuettes of the Virgin Mary while his wife, Janja da Silva, has worn a pendant honouring Our Lady of Aparecida. “As long as I’m president, no one will disrespect Our Lady of Aparecida. No one. People need to learn to respect all religions,” Lula told a rally in the Amazon. Lula’s vice-president and running mate, a devout Catholic called Geraldo Alckmin, published a video describing how he had received messages from Catholics “worried about the direction of the country and the terrible news that has been circulating”. Alckmin assured voters he and Lula would preserve and protect “religious traditions, so sacred to Brazilian families”. The row speaks to the rivalry and tensions between Brazil’s once dominant Catholic church and the evangelical movement, which has grown rapidly since the 80s. Traumann said: “It touched a raw nerve, which is the growing power of the evangelicals. Evangelicals make up about 30% of the population, but their political power is much greater than 30% – and within Bolsonarismo it is even more significant”. Traumann believed that, irrespective of whether Bolsonaro really did intend to remove the patroness, the furore had tapped into “a genuine fear among Catholics of being pushed outside the system”. “I have no doubt that this is going to be important [in the election]. [Flávio Bolsonaro] knows it has landed badly,” he added. Luiz Antônio Simas, a historian and author of the book So Many Marys: Our Lady in Popular Culture, said the outcry “was a symptom of the popularity that Aparecida and the Virgin Mary in general have in the formation of our culture”. “For Brazilian popular culture, Our Lady of Aparecida transcends altars … She is extremely powerful as a defining element of what we envision Brazilian popular culture to be,” Simas said, noting how Brazil’s “Black Madonna” was present in samba parades, football culture and Afro-Brazilian faiths. While the debate flared up on the eve of the election, Simas said Our Lady of Aparecida was a long-running point of tension between Catholics and evangelicals, who oppose the Catholic veneration of saints and images. He recalled a major outcry in 1995 when a neo-Pentecostal pastor kicked a statue of Our Lady of Aparecida on TV. Simas believed religious racism was at the heart of the outcry, given that Our Lady of Aparecida was a black representation of the Virgin Mary. “When all of this comes into contact with a turbulent political context, in a country experiencing the tensions of a highly contested pre-election scenario, all these controversies come to the surface,” Simas added.

title: ‘Like caring for a pet’: the app that lets you know if your neighbourhood tree is thirsty
summary: Gieß den Kiez app shows trees in critical need of watering and can be adopted by other heat-stressed cities around the world
text: Amanda Gläser-Bligh sometimes attracts puzzled looks when she goes to water the eight-year-old street tree she has adopted outside her door in Charlottenburg, Berlin. “I named her Linda the linden,” she says. “Berliners are not always known for being super friendly but most people react really positively when they find out what I’m doing.” As summer heatwaves intensify across the city, Gläser-Bligh carries about 20 litres of water to Linda once a week during the hotter months. It takes a couple of trips up and down stairs with a watering can to finish the job, but she has noticed the tree is no longer wilting in the summer heat. Linden trees are a hallmark of Berlin, even lending their name to Unter den Linden boulevard. Their mature, dense canopies offer essential street cooling, while their blooms provide vital nectar for local bees. Gläser-Bligh adopted the tree through CityLAB Berlin’s Gieß den Kiez project, which translates to “water your neighbourhood”. An interactive map tracks more than 900,000 trees across Berlin and calculates the water needs of each one based on its age, species and local rainfall. This real-time watering data is what separates the Gieß den Kiez project from other tree maps around the world and allows volunteers to coordinate on a city-wide level. You can see the last time a tree was watered, log a watering, and colour-coding indicates trees in critical need. For instance, saplings lack the mature root networks of older trees and require more frequent watering to survive. Gieß den Kiez also offers advice on the correct watering technique, collecting rainwater and the location of Berlin’s water pumps. “It feels very fun, almost like a video game,” Gläser-Bligh says. “I think many people may want to water the trees, but they might feel weird about doing it or they’re not sure if it’s their responsibility. But, if you have this app encouraging you, you know it’s the right thing to do.” The Gieß den Kiez project has been running since 2020 and currently 12,000 registered volunteers are using the platform. Their efforts complement those of the district street and green space authorities, which are already watering thousands of trees but cannot always keep up during Berlin’s increasingly hot summers. “I was really surprised at just how deeply people care about trees – for many people it’s almost like caring for a pet,” says Anna Mehrländer, who has been leading the Gieß den Kiez project for more than a year. “Climate change is happening on our doorsteps. But watering a tree is a small action that helps your neighbourhood cope as summers get hotter. It also creates community at a time when people are increasingly working from home and on their phones all day.” Indeed, the biggest annual peak in tree waterings when nearly half a million litres were poured came just after the platform was launched in 2020 at the start of the Covid pandemic. Anna believes this was because watering trees gave people a reason to get back outside and connect with people and nature again. Seasonally, the waterings tend to rise during heatwaves. For instance, on 27 June, when Berlin experienced an all-time record high of 39.9C (103.8F), people poured 8,000 litres of water over trees across the city. There is a growing body of evidence showing the myriad benefits of street trees to counter the effects of the climate crisis. Studies show trees cool the air and break up urban heat islands during heatwaves, while reducing the risk of flooding during downpours. They also increase biodiversity, reduce air pollution and can improve mental health. Urban forestry expert Dr Cecil Konijnendijk has proposed a 3:30:300 rule of thumb for greening in cities: every citizen should be able to see at least three trees from their home, have 30% tree-canopy cover in their neighbourhood, and not live more than 300 metres from a park or green space. “In the past, trees were thought of as a nice aesthetic element in cities,” Cecil says. “But now we’re starting to see them as critical infrastructure.” He supports citizen initiatives like Gieß den Kiez that complement city efforts to care for trees. Aside from watering, Konijnendijk also highlights the importance of soil volume and underground space to ensure trees can grow a healthy root system. “The question I always ask is ‘how do you take care of your existing trees?’” he says. “It takes 30 to 40 years before a new tree starts delivering the ecosystem services of a mature one… But a lot of trees are now being pushed to their limits during increasingly hot summers – drought is a big issue.” Cecil says that AI and new technologies could help us monitor and maintain the health of city trees better than ever before. He points to increased use of soil sensors and city-wide scanning of tree canopies using lidar, with cities like Malmo and Singapore at the forefront of innovative urban forestry. The open-source nature of Gieß den Kiez means the map can be adopted by any city in the world. Already residents in Potsdam, Leipzig, Magdeburg, and the 17th arrondissement of Paris have launched their own versions of the platform to coordinate tree watering. “Anyone can copy the code and set up their own Gieß den Kiez,” Anna says. “The main requirement is a data set of all the trees in your city. It’s possible to replicate anywhere, from China to the UK.” Back in Charlottenburg, Gläser-Bligh recently spotted someone else using the map to water a tree on the other side of her local park – a promising sign that word is spreading about Gieß den Kiez. “It’s a small step, a very small step,” she says. “But it has a direct climate impact.”

title: May heatwaves, deaths, ruined harvests: study of Europe’s summer paints grim picture for the future
summary: EU Copernicus report shows surface air temperatures from June to August were 2.5C above decadal average
text: The scorching heat that persistently baked western Europe this summer was the worst on record, a report has found, with more than half the continent seared by “very strong” heat stress that felt hotter than 38C. Surface air temperatures in western Europe from June to August were 2.5C above the recent decadal average, according to an update from the EU’s Copernicus climate monitoring service on Friday, while milder but still deadly heat across the rest of the continent made the summer Europe’s third hottest on record. The finding comes as a swelling El Niño of unprecedented strength raises global temperatures and supercharges violent weather from South America to Australia. The natural sea warming pattern, which has broken the temperature record months before its expected peak at the end of the year, is expected to cause almost half a million extra heat-related deaths by February. In Europe, where El Niño’s effects are felt mostly indirectly – for instance, through higher food prices and inflation – the intense heat experienced this summer is the result of fossil fuel pollution clogging the atmosphere. The report found at least 60% of western Europe suffered through temperatures above 30C on 17 days this summer. In 2003, a year also marked by ferocious heat, this was observed on 11 days, and in 2025 on just seven. The high heat led to a record-breaking 13 days of “very strong” heat stress across western Europe. Europe saw an abnormally early start to summer-like weather when a powerful heatwave boggled climate scientists in late May, and high heat continued even through September, the report found. Recurring heatwaves, made hotter and more common by climate breakdown, killed tens of thousands of people across the continent while ruining harvests and shutting power plants. “The consequences extended far beyond temperature records – affecting water availability, energy systems, transport, ecosystems and human health,” said Samantha Burgess, a climate scientist at the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts. “As the climate continues to warm, events like these underscore the importance of building resilience to increasingly interconnected climate risks.” Compounding extremes of heat, drought and fire proved particularly damaging. European sea surface temperatures this summer also broke records, the report found, while the continent’s rivers experienced their lowest summer flows in more than 30 years. Hot weather and widespread drought helped wildfires run rampant. The severity of fire weather conditions in 2026 was the worst that scientists have ever recorded, data published by the European Forest Fire Information System on Wednesday showed. By the end of September, the 680,000 hectares that were burned made it the third-worst on record, behind the million hectares burned by this time of year in 2025 and the 768,000 hectares burned in 2022. Smoke, one of the greatest environmental threats to human health, spewed 30% more fine particulate matter into the air than the average over the last two decades. “Frankly, after the summer we’ve just had, there’s little new to say,” said Xavier Rodó, who leads the climate and health programme at ISGlobal, a Spanish research institute, who was not involved in the report. “This surge in the number and intensity of extreme weather events is clearly indicative of unprecedented changes in the European climate, as many records have been broken, not only locally, but also regionally and continentally.” To stave off the heat, doctors and climate scientists have called on governments to stop burning fossil fuels, shade buildings, green cities, and install air conditioning in hospitals, schools and care homes.

title: Ukraine war briefing: Zelenskyy says new ballistic missile used in combat
summary: Volodymyr Zelenskyy hails use of FP-7 tactical ballistic missile, which manufacturer says is being developed as an interceptor. What we know on day 1,682
text: Ukraine used its FP-7 tactical ballistic missile in combat for ⁠the first time, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said. Writing on Telegram on Thursday, the Ukrainian president said: “First combat use. Thank you for ⁠the result. Next – production.” He did not say where or how the FP-7 had been used. The missile’s manufacturer, Fire Point, says it is being developed as a ballistic interceptor within the European missile defence programme, called Freyja, launched this year. Ukrainian military analysts describe the FP-7 as a short-range missile with a range of about 200km (125 miles), likening it to the US army Tactical Missile System but much cheaper. Ukraine – whose missile production is well behind Russia’s – has viewed development of its own tactical ballistic missiles as an important element of its response to Russia’s frequent use of them in its attacks. Russian drones smashed into a school in Kyiv and an important bridge over the Dnipro River on Thursday, triggering fires ⁠in the capital, officials said. The ⁠school was struck early in the morning, but all the students were in a shelter and no injuries were reported, city authorities said. As Russian forces engaged in almost non-stop attacks on the city, Mayor Vitali ⁠Klitschko said two drones hit the Southern Bridge around noon. A new strike late in the evening damaged a support, part of the road surface and protective structures around the metro crossing the bridge. On Wednesday, Russian forces unleashed what Ukrainian officials described as the start of a cold-weather strike campaign against Ukraine’s power grid. Meanwhile, Ukraine is pressing on with strikes on Russian oil refineries, defying Donald Trump, who blames the attacks for exacerbating a global diesel shortage and pushing up fuel prices. Kyiv struck an oil facility in Russia’s southern Samara region overnight, Zelenskyy said on Thursday in a statement on social media. He added that a Russian vessel in the Black Sea was hit, as well as a launch and storage site for attack drones in the Oryol region. Ukraine ⁠also attacked the ⁠Russian ⁠city of Volgograd, home to a ⁠large oil refinery, with ⁠drones targeting industrial ‌facilities, ‌Governor Andrei Bocharov ‌said on Telegram on Friday. Ukraine’s campaign in recent months has knocked out more than 45% of Russia’s refining capacity, according to Ukrainian estimates, prompting fuel rationing in some regions and long queues at petrol stations. Europe has become increasingly dependent ‌on US fuel after banning Russian imports because of the war and after the US-Israeli war against Iran disrupted supplies from the Middle East. The Trump administration has told Germany and France to draw down emergency diesel inventories to help ease soaring ⁠global fuel prices or face a ⁠potential US diesel export ban, according to three people close to the discussions. At a Group of 20 meeting this week, trade ministers agreed it was “not acceptable” for countries to target food supplies in conflicts, France’s minister delegate for international trade, Nicolas Forissier said on Thursday, adding that European leaders took aim at Russia on the issue. Forissier’s comments come as trade ministers from the G20 met for a second day in the midwestern US city of Milwaukee, where European officials criticised Russia’s attacks on Ukraine’s grain sector. Forissier said European leaders’ comments against “the aggression of Russia in Ukraine” on food exports merely constituted “the truth”. Moscow warned Nato that it would not hesitate to use nuclear weapons to defend Kaliningrad, a Russian exclave and seaport located on the Baltic Sea, should any members of the military alliance try to cut it off. Several Russian embassies in Europe this week issued statements that said Moscow has “information that Nato is preparing [an] air and naval blockade of Kaliningrad and [the] Kaliningrad region”. Asked on Thursday whether Russia was on the cusp of a war with Nato or whether both were trying to intimidate each other, Putin said: “It’s not intimidation, it’s a response to an attempt to intimidate us.” Putin said also on Thursday Russian assets of western companies that Moscow had seized could be returned in a “favourable scenario”. Last month, the Russian president ordered the seizure of businesses and assets of Swiss food giant Nestlé, French retailer Auchan, the former Leroy Merlin DIY chain and German wholesaler and food retailer Metro. He also said Russia ⁠would prefer to ⁠end the conflict ‌in ‌Ukraine through ‌talks and wanted Ukraine to be ‌a neutral country after the end of hostilities.

title: California outlaws child marriage, joining 17 other US states
summary: Advocacy group that pushed for the legislation says 9,000 children are married in California every year
text: California has outlawed child marriage, joining 17 other US states where the taboo practice is also banned. Under past state law, minors of any age could obtain a court order for marriage with the consent of their parents. Assembly bill 1267, which Governor Gavin Newsom signed on Wednesday, prohibits minors from being issued a marriage license or establishing a domestic partnership (an arrangement that provides spousal protections). The law has no exceptions. “This is a long-overdue measure to protect young Californians and minors. Today, California kids are safer than ever before,” Newsom said in a statement. He was joined on Wednesday by activist Courtney Stodden, who was thrust into the public eye in 2011 when at 16 she married 51-year-old actor Doug Hutchison in Las Vegas, a union she has since reflected on with deep regret. “Governor Newsom’s action today made clear to me and to survivors of child marriage everywhere that we should never have been expected to carry this burden,” Stodden said in a statement. “I’m deeply grateful to Unchained at Last and every survivor who fought to make this possible – California is a victory, but I’m not stopping here. I will keep fighting until children are protected from marriage in all 50 states.” Unchained at Last, the advocacy group that pushed for the legislation, says 9,000 children are married in California every year.

title: Swing-and-a-miss: MLB rescinds idea to host baseball game in national park after backlash
summary: Officials in Wyoming had called notion to host game in Grand Teton national park ‘deeply unwelcome’
text: Major League Baseball (MLB) leadership is no longer considering holding a game inside a national park, according to a letter the commissioner, Robert Manfred, sent to officials in Teton county, Wyoming, on Thursday in what could be the league’s biggest swing-and-a-miss off the diamond. On 26 September, the Washington Post reported that MLB had reached out to the White House about staging a one-day game at Grand Teton national park in Wyoming. Teton county describes itself as a “a year-round resort community” and sits within the Jackson Hole valley. It’s also a habitat for grizzly bears, osprey, bison and more. News of MLB’s outreach to the federal government quickly sparked concern about the impact that erecting a field and the infrastructure to hold spectators could have on the natural landscape and habitat of scores of wildlife that call the 310,000-acre (125,500-hectare) park home. In the letter, Manfred noted that MLB had held games at places like the Fort Bragg military base in North Carolina and the nation’s oldest Negro Leagues stadium in Birmingham, Alabama. He added that MLB staff had been doing their due diligence to see whether a game at Grand Teton was possible and to evaluate the potential environmental impact. “Since the story was reported, it has become clear that the local community does not want us to continue Grand Teton national park as a potential site,” Manfred wrote. The outrage over the possible MLB game comes as national parks across the US struggle under funding cuts, staffing shortages and consistent overcrowding. A Teton county commissioner, Luther Propst, who described the potential game as an “incomprehensible and deeply unwelcome notion”, celebrated the MLB’s decision in a post on Facebook. “Ever since I got a call from the Washington Post about [MLB] scouting a ballfield in Grand Teton National Park, I have been hoping this idea would die a quick death – and today it did!” he wrote. “This is what can happen when we stand up firmly together, and I am proud to have played my part.” In a statement to the Guardian, a White House spokesperson said that it was approached by the MLB about the possibility of hosting the game but the National Park Service had not granted any permits to do so and the game is not a White House directive. Neither MLB nor the National Park Service immediately responded to the Guardian’s request for comment.

title: Letitia James appointed special prosecutor in alleged gang-rape at Cornell
summary: New York attorney general brought in by governor after recent questions raised over university’s 2024 investigation
text: Kathy Hochul, the New York governor, said on Thursday she was appointing Letitia James, the state’s attorney general, as special prosecutor to investigate the alleged gang-rape at Cornell University. “The young woman at the center of this case deserves to know that every fact will be examined and justice pursued,” Hochul said in a statement. “This action will ensure that the matter is fully and thoroughly investigated without conflict or bias, and handled independently with the rigor that this matter demands.” In her statement, Hochul said the decision by Matthew Van Houten, the Tompkins county ⁠district attorney, not to prosecute the 2024 case, and the questions raised in recent days over the Cornell police department’s investigation of the allegations, have “undercut my faith, and the public’s faith, in the district attorney’s ability to effectively investigate and prosecute the case at this time”. Hochul said James would oversee the investigation and, if warranted, present evidence to a grand jury. The former Cornell University student who alleges she was gang-raped at a fraternity in 2024 filed a lawsuit in September, in a case that has sparked national outrage, roiled the Ivy League campus and raised questions about why no criminal case was brought. Van Houten declined at the time of the alleged assault to bring criminal charges, but this week said he would reopen the investigation based on new information in the woman’s lawsuit, which identifies her only by the pseudonym Jane Doe. He has maintained that the woman’s first account to police did not include allegations that she was drugged, incapacitated beyond the ability to consent or forced into sex. After CBS News this week revealed details from the police interview transcript, he told the network he had never seen her detailed account and had relied instead on a statement written by a campus police officer and signed by the accuser. She is suing seven men whom she said perpetrated the assault, as well as the university, the fraternity and others. Lawyers for two of the men she is suing have denied they perpetrated a sexual assault. One said his client had not touched the woman or engaged in any drug use. Cornell has said it suspended the Chi Phi fraternity indefinitely and disciplined or expelled some students, but the university has declined to provide specifics, citing student privacy rules. Under pressure from the public and politicians, including Hochul, Cornell, a private university, agreed on Wednesday to bring in outside lawyers to independently investigate how it handled the woman’s allegations. • Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organizations. In the US, Rainn offers support on 800-656-4673. In the UK, Rape Crisis offers support on 0808 500 2222. In Australia, support is available at 1800Respect (1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found at ibiblio.org/rcip/internl.html
