title: Falling glass and ‘decapitated’ plants: the race to protect Edinburgh botanic garden’s plants
summary: After five years of work, 5,750 panels of toughened glass will help keep hundred of plants safe from Scottish winters – but more work needs to be done
text: In the early autumn sunlight, Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh’s extensive plant collection appears safe in their glass enclosures. But danger lurks from above for the tropical ferns, cycads and rare alpine heathers. Soon the September sunshine will give way to the storms and gales of the Scottish winter, which can bring hundreds of glass panels crashing to the greenhouse floor on the windiest days. Nobody is allowed inside when the wind is above 30mph. “We’ve had plants that have essentially been decapitated by falling bits of glass,” says Sadie Barber, the glasshouse curator at RBGE. “You go into one of these tropical spaces in winter and there’s icy air coming in. It’s traumatic for those of us who put decades into caring for these plants. A storm can literally just wipe them out.” But this week, change is in the air for the creaking infrastructure at the 356-year-old botanic garden, the second oldest in Britain after Oxford. On Friday, the palm houses are reopening after five years of painstaking restoration work, complete with 5,750 panels of toughened glass to keep out the elements. Before they closed for renovation works, the horticultural team had installed a net in case panels fell from the weathered structure. The new ones are not bulletproof – but they are strong enough to resist a bird strike. Part-Georgian, part-Victorian, the £23.5m refurbishment has kept nearly all of the original sandstone and wrought iron shell. Inside, more than 600 temperate plants have returned to the building. The air is clean and crisp, purified by ferns that naturally remove toxins from the air. Its temperature and humidity is still controlled by the original pulleys and winches. “We have made it one vast cathedral-like space for temperate plants,” says Prof Julia Knights, the garden’s regius Keeper and the royally appointed chief executive. She points out her favourite tree fern, which comes from Tasmania and has a Scottish liverwort growing on its woody stem. “They can grow outside in our botanic garden in Logan on the west coast of Scotland because of the oceanic climate,” she says. Founded by two physicians in 1670 to teach doctors about medicinal plants, RBGE has morphed into one of the most important collections of plant biodiversity in the world. Its research glasshouses are stuffed with rare ginger species, bananas, blueberries and dozens of begonias. It is a global authority on rhododendrons and ferns, houses rare plant species that have gone extinct in the wild, and its scientists have helped pioneer new technology, such as DNA barcoding which is used to identify plant species. Arthur Conan Doyle studied here, infusing Sherlock Holmes novels with his botanical knowledge. Today, conservation is its primary focus. “Our conservation collections are so important to have. The threats are extreme in the wild,” said Prof Pete Hollingsworth, RBGE’s director of science. “The driver[s] for environmental damage are so strong, so having these ex situ safe sites is really important,” he said. But the restored palm houses aside, many of the glasshouses used to care for the plants are decades past their originally intended lifespan and are waiting for upgrades. Leaks from Scottish rain rot the rootstock of plants, sometimes killing them. Last year, horticulturalists were not allowed inside the greenhouses for 20 days due to high winds. In 2026, they have been shut out 15 times. When they return, they have often worn hard hats and safety gear to pick out the broken glass. “The glasshouses are the one thing we don’t want to break. It’s the plants inside that suffer,” said Barber. “I was looking at one of our records the other day of a plant we lost in the lowland tropical house. It just had ‘storm’ written next to it. It had either suffered from the cold, or even been cut by falling glass.”

title: New Washington DC law bans landlords from imposing dog breed restrictions
summary: Landlords can no longer refuse pit bulls, rottweilers, dobermans or other breeds considered ‘scary’
text: Landlords in Washington DC will no longer be able to refuse a tenant’s dog based on its breed, size or weight, nor can they impose special charges related to these factors. At least, that’s what a new law that took effect on Thursday aims to achieve. Animal welfare organizations and animal shelters applauded the legislation, emphasizing the benefits of reducing barriers to pet ownership in the US capital. Dog breeds considered “scary” used to face restrictions, especially pit bulls, rottweilers and dobermans. Property owners could ban certain breeds, regardless of their behavior. With these restrictions, landlords tried to avoid incidents with aggressive dogs that could damage property or harm other tenants or pets. However, animal groups challenged this claim, explaining that breed bans penalize responsible dog owners and that in the vast majority of cases, aggressive behavior is linked to owner management and control, and not to the dog’s breed. Also, they warned that exorbitant pet fees and breed restrictions were putting housing out of reach for people. What takes effect this Thursday is the last part of the Pets in Housing Amendment Act, or “Roscoe’s Law”, brought forward by councilmember Robert White in honor of his dog. The first part has been partially in effect since 2025. It included caps on pet-related fees: under that first part of the legislation, pet security deposits cannot exceed 15% of a tenant’s monthly rent, pet rent is capped at 1% of the monthly rent, and all other non-refundable fees are prohibited. While organizations like the DC Landlord Association acknowledged the law’s intent “to help keep families together and prevent the separation of pets from their owners due to restrictive housing policies”, they expressed concerns. In May, they worried that the security deposits and rent caps included in the law might not cover the costs associated with pet-related damages, and called for “adequate” deposits and rent. Although breed and weight restrictions are prohibited in all residential leases beginning after 1 October 2026, immediate changes may not be evident. Real estate websites commonly include pet restrictions on their property listings. In a quick search on Zillow on Thursday, many “pet-friendly” DC listings included a “pet essentials” section where it stated if the property allowed cats or dogs and their weight limit, and it was sometimes set at a maximum of 75lb.

title: Former Dallas police officer convicted of murdering Black neighbor given early parole
summary: Amber Guyger, who has served seven of 10-year sentence, had said she had walked into Botham Jean’s home thinking it was her own when she shot him
text: A former Dallas police officer convicted of murdering her Black neighbor after walking into his apartment thinking it was her own was granted early parole on Thursday after serving seven years of her 10-year sentence. Amber Guyger, 38, who is white, was convicted of murdering 26-year-old Botham Jean, an accountant from St Lucia. Jean was eating ice-cream and watching television when Guyger mistakenly entered his home and shot him on 6 September 2018. Guyger was arrested three days after the shooting and was fired before her murder trial. She had faced up to life in prison or as little as two years. Prosecutors initially asked the jury for a minimum sentence of 28 years, a symbolic reference to the age Jean would have been at the time. Guyger was in the end given 10 years behind bars. The Texas board of pardons and parole rejected Guyger’s initial parole request in 2024, but approved her case over the objections of Jean’s family the first time she was eligible to ask again. The shooting drew widespread national attention because of the unusual circumstances and inflamed racial tensions as one in a string of shootings in the US of Black men by white police officers. Jean’s mother, Allison, pondered days after his death: “If it was a white man would it have been different? Would she have reacted differently?” Guyger’s sentencing hearing also included stunning courtroom scenes when, after the sentence was handed down, Jean’s younger brother, Brandt, offered Guyger his forgiveness. “I forgive you, and I know if you go to God and ask him, he will forgive you. I’m speaking for myself, not my family, but I love you just like anyone else,” Brandt told Guyger. He then asked the judge’s permission to hug Guyger and the two embraced for about a minute. The Black judge, Tammy Kemp, also embraced Guyger, whom she gave a Bible after the trial had ended. Kemp said Guyger had asked her if she thought God would forgive her, to which Kemp replied: “Yes, God can forgive you and has.” She rejected criticism, saying after the trial: “I could not refuse that woman a hug.” At trial, Guyger testified that after a long shift at work and still in uniform, she had walked up to Jean’s apartment – which was on the fourth floor, directly above hers on the third – and found the door unlocked. She said she mistook the apartment for her own and thought that Jean was an intruder when she drew her service weapon and entered. Jean family attorneys Lisa Blue and Bhavani Raveendran issued a statement on Thursday saying their clients had celebrated what had been Botham’s birthday two days earlier. The statement requested privacy for the Jean family “as they process these developments and continue to process”, adding: “To all of the many well-wishers who have continued to say Botham’s name and carry his memory, they wish to give their thanks for the continuing support.” In 2024, a jury ordered Guyger to pay Jean’s family nearly $100m in damages in a federal civil trial. The jury found that she had used excessive force and violated Jean’s constitutional rights when she shot him. In granting Guyger’s parole on Thursday, the board said the panel conducted “a thorough review and consideration of a plethora of information”. Her record did not include a documented pattern of violent arrests or convictions and she had “maintained a satisfactory institutional adjustment” and completed programs in her prison treatment plan to obtain and keep a job when she is released, it said. It is unclear when Guyger will be released. The board said the state prison system would determine that timeline. Dallas police said in a statement to NBC News Dallas-Fort Worth that the department played no role in Guyger’s request for parole or the decision to release her. “The Dallas Police Department understands this decision may bring renewed attention and emotion surrounding the tragic death of Botham Jean. Our thoughts remain with the Jean family and all those impacted by his loss,” the department said. The Associated Press contributed reporting • This article was amended on 3 October 2026. A quotation from Lee Merritt, who was misidentified as the Jean family’s lawyer, was removed, and a statement from the family’s lawyers was added.

title: UK airlines to be banned from charging parents to sit with children
summary: Planned rule change forms part of Burnham’s bid to crack down on the ‘little charges that add up’
text: Airlines will be blocked from charging parents extra to sit with their children on planes, according to government plans. The new rule would require airlines to seat passengers aged under 14 next to their parents or an accompanying adult free of charge. Passengers will also no longer need to pay to tweak the name on their flight booking if they need to correct a mistake. It is understood that ministers will try to introduce the changes before the start of next year’s summer holidays. The prime minister, Andy Burnham, has said the rule changes are part of a crackdown on the “little charges that add up” when families plan their holidays. MPs are in the process of debating a new set of rules for travel companies, as the civil aviation (consumer protection and regulatory reform) bill makes its way through parliament. The proposed law will give ministers flexible power to set out passenger rights and the duties of airlines and airports. Burnham said: “Charging parents just to sit with their children is a rip-off, plain and simple. And being hit with a hefty fee for a simple spelling mistake on a booking form isn’t right either. “People are fed up with these little charges that add up, so I’m putting a stop to them. This is what our everyday fixes are all about – giving people room to breathe by tackling the small irritations that catch people out, waste their time and cost them money.” An arrangement to sit together can currently cost a parent and child up to £104 on a return journey, according to the Department for Transport. Rory Boland, editor of consumer magazine Which? Travel, said: “It’s clearly unfair to force parents and children as young as three to pay an extra fee just to sit together. Airlines that have separated families are putting profit ahead of passenger peace of mind.” Earlier this year, Ryanair adjusted its family seating policy after an investigation was launched into the company charging parents to sit with their children on flights. The Irish operator previously required parents travelling with children aged between two and 11 to pay to reserve what was referred to as a mandatory family seat. Children were then allocated seats next to or near parents free of charge. The fee for a mandatory family seat was typically about £8 each way, the UK Competition and Markets Authority watchdog found. Under the new policy, parents will still have the option of paying to reserve a seat of their choosing and have their children alongside them free of charge. The transport secretary, Heidi Alexander, has also announced a crackdown on bad behaviour by passengers on aircraft, with the government, airlines and trade unions working on a new system for sharing information about disruptive passengers. Airlines logged more than 1,000 serious disruptive passenger incidents in 2025, government figures show, including what it described as a mid-air brawl that caused a flight to be diverted. Using the new system, airlines could choose to ban persistently disruptive passengers from their aircraft.

title: Alan Ferguson obituary
summary: Other lives: Academic who became an aid agency worker in Kenya after lecturing at Nairobi University
text: My brother, Alan Ferguson, who has died aged 79, was a Scotsman who began his working life as a geography lecturer at Nairobi University in Kenya, before working with aid agencies in that country. Alan joined the university in 1972, but left after a couple of years to teach in Britain at Cambridge University, and then in the US at NorthEastern University in Chicago. However, Kenya had got a hold on him, and he returned to work there, first for Amref, a Dutch organisation, and then GTZ, a German body, mainly in family planning and public health. Eventually he went freelance, helping various aid agencies with their work in Kenya, until a serious accident incapacitated him, forcing him to retire to Scotland. Born in Glasgow, Alan was the son of Bill, an analytical chemist, and Jessie (nee Moncrieff), a shorthand typist. At the local Angus Oval primary school his hair was permanently unruly and his mum decided one day to plaster it with Brylcreem into a cow’s lick. Alan came back from school in a huff; clearly comments had been made. “But Prince Charles has a cow’s lick,” mum pointed out. “Prince Charles doesnae go to Angus Oval,” was the terse reply. After Queen’s Park senior secondary, Glasgow – where he and some friends formed a band, the V5, which played gigs around the west of Scotland – he moved on to Strathclyde University to study geography (1965-69) before completing a PhD at Bristol University. Alan went straight on to Nairobi University but eventually left after a disagreement over student grading, and decided to go back to the UK. Once he returned to Kenya, his work with aid agencies took him to remote rural parts of the country where he was often the first white man many of the locals had seen in the flesh, and where his hairy legs were a great novelty. He was different from many other foreign workers in that he spoke Swahili, integrated with the people and was curious about their lives. His attachment to Kenya was strengthened when he met a local registered nurse, Florence Miyawa, whom he married in 1982. They settled happily in Nairobi, where they had three daughters, Janice, Lynne and Iona. Sundays were an important day for Alan in Kenya, as the airmail edition of the Observer would be delivered to him. He would quickly settle down to tackle the cryptic crossword and would then wing his completed answers back to the UK, often winning the weekly prize. Having turned freelance, he was about to embark on a new project with the global health management consultancy Constella Futures in 2009 when he was knocked down by a bus while he was out jogging, sustaining serious head injuries that meant he was unable to drive or continue working. In 2014, fed up at having to renew his visa every few months as he did not have a job, he returned home to Glasgow with Florence. He is survived by Florence, their daughters, granddaughter Rowena, and by me.

title: Supreme court to hear case challenging Trump’s immigration detention policy
summary: Court will review practice of indefinite detention for undocumented immigrants living in the US
text: The US supreme court agreed on Thursday to take up a case challenging the Trump administration’s practice of indefinite detention for undocumented immigrants living in the US and awaiting deportation proceedings. At the center of the immigration case is a dispute over Donald Trump’s reinterpretation of a longstanding policy that has led to a huge surge in the number of migrants held in detention centers. For years, undocumented immigrants, who had been living in the US could be released back into their communities on bond, so long as they did not pose a threat to safety or were considered a flight risk. But last year, administration officials reinterpreted the statute to mean any migrant who entered the US illegally should be held in detention while awaiting legal proceedings. The case was the latest Trump-era immigration policy to be added to the high court’s docket this term. This week, justices said they would hear arguments in a case challenging the administration’s “third-country” deportations, which allow immigrants to be sent to a country other than their own. The challenger to the Trump administration’s reinterpreted policy denying bond hearings is Ricardo Aparecido Barbosa da Cunha, a Brazilian citizen who has been living in the US for more than 20 years. Authorities say Barbosa da Cunha entered the US illegally in or around 2005. He owns a home in Massachusetts, runs a small construction company, has a wife and two US-born children, and has never been charged with a crime. He was arrested by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents last year while driving to work and moved to an immigration detention facility in Buffalo, New York. Barbosa da Cunha had requested a bond hearing but was denied. A district court sided with Barbosa da Cunha, ordering the government to give him a bond hearing. An appeals court affirmed that decision after the administration appealed. But now lawyers for the government are asking the supreme court to intervene. The dispute is not unique to Barbosa da Cunha; lower courts have been split on the Trump administration’s policy reinterpretation in other immigration cases as well. More than 500 district court judges and nine of the 11 federal appeals courts who have heard similar cases have rejected the Trump administration’s new interpretation, according to the New York Times. Judges have largely agreed that the statute the Trump administration is using to indefinitely detain undocumented immigrants only applies to those who have been apprehended at a port of entry, such as the US-Mexico border.

title: Lyft agrees to pay California $272.5m in largest-ever wage theft settlement
summary: More than $237m will be distributed to drivers over firm labeling them independent contractors and not employees
text: Lyft agreed to pay the state of California $272.5m on Thursday to ⁠settle claims that it stole drivers’ wages by mislabeling them as independent contractors rather than employees. Rob Bonta, California’s attorney general, called the agreement a “landmark win for workers” and said it was the largest settlement involving wage theft claims in the state’s history. “Rideshare companies like Lyft have enjoyed massive growth and profits on the backs of drivers over the past decade, many of whom are from immigrant communities and communities of color,” Bonta said. “Lyft’s success would not be possible without the drivers Lyft sought to unfairly short-change.” The settlement, subject to court approval, covers alleged violations between April 2016 and December 2020. Once approved, more than $237m will be distributed to the thousands of Lyft drivers who were involved in the suit. Lyft said in a statement that drivers have always been properly classified under the law and “we’re glad to put this case behind us”. The debate over driver classification has raged in California for more than a decade. As independent contractors, Lyft and Uber drivers don’t get benefits including social security, health insurance, paid sick days and overtime. Minimum wage laws and other labor protections under federal and state governments also do not apply to independent contractors. California’s lawsuit against Lyft was first brought in 2020, and the cities of Los Angeles, San Francisco and San Diego subsequently joined on. Afterwards, the case was merged with other suits brought on behalf of thousands of Lyft drivers. As the litigation was under way, Lyft joined Uber and other gig companies in putting forward a state ballot measure, Proposition 22, to exempt ride-share drivers from California’s law. In a win for the companies, that proposition passed in November 2020, leading to several appeals in the state’s case against Lyft. The attorney general’s office said it remained steadfast in its demands for getting drivers wages and protections, which ultimately led to Thursday’s settlement agreement. A near-identical lawsuit against Uber is still continuing. “This settlement is about the workers who came forward and spoke up,” said Lilia García-Brower, California’s labor commissioner. “Their voices made this outcome possible.” In 2023, both Uber and Lyft jointly agreed to pay $328m to settle similar claims by New York’s attorney general.

title: Trump doesn’t rule out declaring state of emergency before midterm elections
summary: President also dismissed low poll ratings as ‘fake numbers’ and deflected responsibility for Iran war in Time interview
text: Donald Trump deflected responsibility for misleading Americans about the length of the Iran war, dismissed low poll ratings as “fake numbers” and refused to rule out the possibility of declaring a state of emergency before the midterms, in a wide-ranging interview with Time magazine. When confronted with questions about the length of the Iran war, the US president blamed the media for reporting his remarks in which he said the conflict was projected to last “four to five weeks”, in March. “ … I think the press fed it to them,” Trump told Time when asked whether Americans misunderstood him. At the end of March, Trump had told Americans he planned to wind down the Iran war over the next “two to three weeks”. In May, Trump insisted that a peace deal with Iran was nearly finalized. The US president said that he could have ended the Iran conflict whenever but chose to extend it “because I wanted to go further”. For more than seven months, Americans have been grappling with higher everyday costs as a result of Trump’s war with Iran – from gas prices surpassing $4 per gallon to stubborn inflation hovering at 3.4%. Economic concerns, fueled by Trump’s conflict, have angered voters, most of whom say they are unhappy with the president’s handling of the economy and his job overall. Just 26% of adults said they approve of the economy under the Republican president, according to an Associated Press/NORC Center for Public Affairs Research poll. Overall, just 31% of people said they approve of Trump’s handling of his job as president. But when asked about his low approval rating during his interview with Time, Trump dismissed concerns. “They’re fake numbers,” Trump said. “I would beat anybody running today by 20 points. Your numbers, that you have, are fake. The pollsters are corrupt. They’re almost as corrupt as the writers.” The US president added: “See, I’m doing very well. I think I am. Look, we have the strongest economy.” Despite Trump’s assertion, Americans do not feel the same way. Approximately 74% of Americans told AP/NORC that the economy was leaning poorly. Another 65% of survey respondents said they blame Trump’s policies directly for higher costs. Voters’ frustrations with Trump could affect Republican candidates in the upcoming midterm elections, particularly those closely aligned with the US president. Polls show many Democratic candidates making progress with voters, even in historically conservative states such as Texas. Trump brushed aside the likelihood of Democrats winning, telling Time magazine that, so long as he campaigns with candidates, Republicans could perform well. Some Democratic lawmakers have raised concerns that Trump will again make allegations of election fraud if Democratic candidates outperform Republicans in the November elections. Trump refused to concede the 2020 presidential election after losing to Joe Biden. In the months leading up to the midterms, Trump has claimed US elections are insecure and signed executive orders seeking to assert more control over voting methods – such as restricting mail-in ballot voting and requiring ID. He has previously refused to rule out declaring a national emergency around elections to implement his desired regulations. Other administration leaders, such as the FBI director, Kash Patel, have not ruled out the possibility of deploying federal law enforcement officers to polling locations, which is against the law. When asked whether he would declare a state of emergency before the midterms, Trump told Time magazine: “I don’t rule anything out or in. We’ll see.” Trump further specified that while he’s never invoked the Insurrection Act, a 19th-century law that allows the president to deploy military troops domestically under specific circumstances, he “could use it”. “A lot of people think I should use it sometimes,” Trump said. Among other topics the president discussed with Time magazine, he responded affirmatively when asked whether he regretted appointing supreme court justices Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett. “What can I do? I put them in. They voted against me too often. I was very – I gave them the position of a lifetime, and they voted against me often,” Trump said. The supreme court often votes in favor of the Trump administration but it has ruled against the president – such as in the case challenging his sweeping tariffs and his efforts to roll back birthright citizenship.

title: How success of Manchester City helped put Andy Burnham in power
summary: PM has praised Abu Dhabi group as ‘huge partner’ in reshaping Manchester, but critics say this ignores public cost of city’s transformation
text: In July 2016, the Manchester City player Yaya Touré ambled into a small bar near Beijing’s Workers’ Stadium and offered a bemused smile as dozens of Chinese fans rushed towards him. Manchester City had just won their sixth trophy under the big-spending ownership of Sheikh Mansour’s Abu Dhabi United Group and the blues were international megastars. They were also magnets for investment. On a trade mission led by Sir Howard Bernstein, the architect of modern Manchester, civic leaders rolled out club legends such as Mike Summerbee and Sun Jihai in a charm offensive to football-mad Chinese businessmen who saw that the club and the city were on the rise. A decade on, Manchester is transformed. Estate agents advertise £15,000-a-month penthouses in a city-region growing faster economically than any other in Britain, while the success of “Manchesterism” has powered its mayor, Andy Burnham, to Downing Street. Yet the city’s close ties with Abu Dhabi United Group are now facing fresh scrutiny, after Manchester City’s owners were found guilty of more than 100 breaches of Premier League financial rules. In a surprising intervention on Wednesday, Burnham praised Abu Dhabi United Group as “such a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester” and said he would be “really concerned” to lose them as the club’s owners. The prime minister went on to say that he would not get involved in the Premier League’s disciplinary process, but appeared to express some sympathy for City’s plight by referring to a similar investigation into Everton, the club he supports. “I remember people proclaiming Everton guilty at the time and, with hindsight, I think more people would say that wasn’t fair the way that was handled,” he said. Burnham’s comments raised eyebrows given the continuing disciplinary process – the Premier League is considering a range of sanctions – and because it turned the spotlight on to Abu Dhabi United Group’s wider investments in Greater Manchester, where he was mayor from 2017 until June this year. One Burnham ally said it was “absolutely mad” for the prime minister to comment and risk being seen to be influencing a disciplinary process, describing it as his “biggest mistake so far”. In an attempt to clarify the prime minister’s remarks on Thursday, a No 10 spokesperson said: “As the prime minister made clear, the initial judgment is serious and there can’t be any suggestion that anyone is above the rules. He also stressed that it is an ongoing independent process. “It is essential that it is allowed to run its course and the outcome respected. Wherever wrongdoing is established, those responsible should face the appropriate consequences.” When Mansour’s Abu Dhabi group took over Manchester City in 2008, the grounds for success had already been laid. The club had a gleaming new stadium, built with taxpayers’ money for the Commonwealth games just six years earlier, and council bosses were eager for a reliable long-term investor in a city battling the financial crash. In 2014, Manchester city council announced a “£1bn deal” with Mansour, one of the world’s richest men, to transform a large stretch of land between the stadium and the edge of the city centre. Richard Leese, then the council leader, promised it to be “a world-class exemplar of regeneration”. The partnership between the council and Manchester City’s owner, which was called Manchester Life, included more than 1,000 private rented apartments and 395 built-for-sale homes – but not one social or affordable home. In a sharply critical assessment of the Manchester Life partnership published in 2024, researchers at the University of Sheffield said it appeared that the council had leased the land to Abu Dhabi at a much cheaper rate than many comparable developments – they had “sold the family silver too cheaply”, the academics said – and did not appear to be receiving any rental income or revenue from the property sales. All of the property, with an estimated worth of £350m, is controlled by Jersey-domiciled subsidiaries and ultimately owned by Abu Dhabi interests, the researchers found. They described it as a “transfer of public wealth to private hands that is difficult to justify as prudent”. Dr Richard Goulding, who co-authored the University of Sheffield research, said on Thursday that the Manchester Life development raised “questions about what type of Britain we’re trying to build and who the type of Manchester that we’ve built works for”. He added: “On the one hand, [the Abu Dhabi deal] was bringing money in. On the other hand, a lot of that money was flowing into flats whose rents, according to our research, are being taken offshore.” In July, Manchester city council published a review of its deals with private developers. It found that while these agreements had delivered “significant benefits”, there were “weaknesses in documentation, monitoring and assurance”, particularly around the profit-sharing nature of these deals. A Manchester city council spokesperson said: “We do not recognise the criticisms linked to the disposal of public land and the idea that there is no financial benefit to the council through this partnership. “The tired claim that working in partnership with Manchester City FC’s owners has not been a good deal for the council or the city has been debunked repeatedly. It is a one-sided perspective that fails to take into account the positive impact of investment in Ancoats and New Islington as well as the wider east Manchester area.” The council added: “Claims that some land was sold too cheaply to Manchester Life ignore the fact that there was zero market interest at the time of the sale, that the land is worth more now precisely because of Manchester Life’s investment and the significant financial return the council is receiving through profit-sharing arrangements.” Gleaming skyscrapers have transformed Manchester’s skyline over the past decade, as the city’s population has grown by nearly 100,000 people and become one of Europe’s most attractive destinations for foreign money. Yet born-and-bred Mancunians have felt increasingly pushed out. A report published earlier this year by Greater Manchester combined authority, which Burnham led until June, revealed that of the 10,974 homes built across the region in the nine years to 2024, only 679 (6%) were classed as affordable. Hayley Flynn, an anti-gentrification campaigner who leads tours of Manchester, said development of luxury flats in Ancoats, the home of the Manchester Life project, had not benefited the area’s existing community. “What provisions have we got for them? They’re not going to spend £7 on a loaf of bread in Pollen [a trendy bakery], but that’s their nearest bakery,” she said. “All these apartments for influencers – it’s quite a forceful erosion that’s just pushing the community out.” Tim Heatley, a co-founder of the Manchester developer Capital & Centric, said the city had benefited from Abu Dhabi’s riches and that the success of City had “put Manchester on the map internationally”. Under the ownership of Mansour, Manchester City won eight Premier League titles, four FA Cups, seven League Cups and one Champions League, becoming one of the world’s elite clubs. The club, which continues to deny any wrongdoing, won eight trophies, including three Premier League titles between 2009 and 2018, the period under investigation. Heatley said Abu Dhabi had had “a major impact on that particular area of the city” between the Etihad Stadium and Manchester city centre, but that he believed the region’s economic upturn would have happened without the football investment.

title: Key disability benefit for young people may be axed under major welfare changes
summary: Exclusive: Plan under discussion involves intensive support to help young people into employment
text: Ministers are working up sweeping plans for welfare changes including scrapping a key disability benefit for under-25s and replacing it with a multibillion-pound package of support to get into work, the Guardian has learned. Whitehall sources said the package of changes under debate was much bigger than previously thought, as Andy Burnham’s government hopes to persuade more people on benefits back into work. The move could be fraught with political danger after last year’s dramatic welfare rebellion by Labour MPs. But ministers have spent weeks trying to persuade them the plans are about reform, and feel confident opposition has waned. The plans are still awaiting the conclusions of reviews by Alan Milburn, who is looking at young people’s employment, and the Timms panel, which is examining the personal independence payment (Pip), a non-means-tested benefit that helps sick and disabled people with support costs. However, a central option under consideration for young people is removing the health element of universal credit for claimants under 25, which has already been almost halved to £217 a month, and offering intensive support for people to get into work. The possibility of removing it for existing claimants – not just new ones – is being looked at. The extra support will include subsidised jobs for younger people, more targeted “back to work” schemes and support with mental health, as part of a drive to help more of the nation’s one million 16 to 24-year-olds not in education, employment or training (Neets) back into the workplace. As part of the same package, officials are looking at a new system to replace the Pip, which is claimed by 4 million people, after attempts to change existing eligibility criteria were rejected by MPs last year. One possible plan is for a separate regime to apply to the under-25 agegroup, with reduced or withdrawn entitlements – although those with the most severe and debilitating disabilities would not lose any money. More broadly, officials are working up plans under the replacement system for a new set of eligibility criteria and assessments for the extra costs of disability, and looking at whether this would apply to all claimants of working age, or those below a cut-off point such as 50 or 60. Again, those with the most severe conditions would not lose money or be reassessed. Officials have also been returning to the idea of cuts to the Motability scheme at a future budget, after axing tax breaks worth £300m. The scheme allows disabled people to use their Pip benefit to lease new cars for three years. One Whitehall source said removing or further cutting the health element of universal credit for those older than 25 had been considered, but government sources said this was not on the table. Officials have looked at systems in other countries, such as Denmark, which restricts access to its “disability pension” for under-40s, who instead are given help with flexible jobs and training unless they have no ability permanently to work. A government source said: “We will be bringing forward a comprehensive package of support and reform to tackle the scandal of a million young people not in education, employment or training. The details are yet to be decided, but we are committed to enabling work and opportunity, while always protecting those unable to work.” The significant changes would need legislation, with ministers and officials looking at a bill encompassing the replacement for Pip and changes to the under-25 system to be presented in the next session of parliament next year. Pat McFadden, the work and pensions secretary, used his conference speech this week to describe changing the welfare system as a “moral crusade”, saying too many younger people were stuck claiming benefits for too long. However, the scale of the plans could reignite concerns among Labour MPs about the impact on the cost of living for disabled people, particularly when Pip is a non-means-tested benefit that is unrelated to a person’s employment status. Kemi Badenoch, the Conservative leader, has gone further by saying she would ban young people from signing straight on to the benefits system if her party won the next election, as part of a plan to cut £23bn from the welfare bill. Under-25s with less than six months of continuous employment would no longer be able to claim universal credit and would instead have to undergo intensive job coaching. Reform UK plans to cut the overall welfare bill by £50bn, with Pip replaced by another cash benefit that would be restricted to only the “gravely ill and severely challenged”, while “lower level conditions” would get support overseen by local authorities. Polling suggests that while the public favours cutting the welfare bill overall, they believe that tackling the root causes of joblessness instead of cutting benefits is the best way to do it. Burnham has said he wanted to avoid “crude cuts”, and used his party conference speech to signal an overhaul of the welfare system to pay for an expansion of youth jobs and training support. UK welfare spending has reached £333bn this year, with pensioners receiving roughly 55% of the budget, and young people including Neets – but not children – about 2.5%. Milburn said it was “shameful” the government spent 25 times as much on benefits for them than it did on supporting them into work. More than 40 of the UK’s leading charities warned ministers earlier this year against imposing tougher benefit sanctions or cuts on disabled young people. In their joint letter to Milburn and McFadden, they said cutting support or bringing in sanctions risked pushing thousands of vulnerable youngsters deeper into poverty and further away from employment. The disability charity Scope has estimated about half of households with an under-22 receiving the universal credit health element are already in poverty, which it said could rise to more than nine in 10 if support was removed. Campaigners warned that any move to cut benefits or increase conditionality rules was likely to drive many youngsters further away from the jobs market. Lucy Schonegevel, the director of impact at Action for Children, said: “We are deeply concerned by reports that disability benefits for under-25s could be cut. If confirmed, that would be at odds with the prime minister’s recent warning against ‘crude cuts’ … Serious investment in high quality, tailored employment support is vital, but employment support alone cannot overcome a lack of jobs.” A DWP spokesperson said: “The Milburn and Timms reviews, due in the autumn, will lay the foundation for sustainable reform, and we will not pre-empt their findings. “We are already changing the system through the youth guarantee, narrowing the gap between universal credit standard and health rates, restoring face-to-face assessments, and investing a record £3.5bn in employment support for disabled people and those with long-term conditions. We will always ensure there is a safety net for the most vulnerable and those who are unable to work.” Milburn has said that too few young people who moved on to disability benefits received help into work. Many became “trapped” on benefits, with evidence showing half were not in work 15 years later, an outcome he called a “catastrophic failure”. He appeared to hint at the potential political risks of cuts to benefits at a Labour party conference fringe meeting on youth employment on Monday, saying “when it comes to benefit cuts it will be tricky” – but added that not acting would be financially unsustainable and worse for young people. About 184,000 young people in the UK aged 16-24 receive the universal credit health element. The government has already cut this benefit, having previously announced a 50% reduction to £217 a month for most new claimants from April. • This article was amended on 2 October 2026. An earlier version suggested that the universal credit health element for young people would be cut by 50% to £217 a month in April 2027; in fact, this cut came into effect in April 2026.

title: Welcome to the new Reform roadshow. Same as the last but more desperate | John Crace
summary: Nige is not rattled that the UK likes its new PM. Or that Reform is second in the polls. Oh no. Because Nige believes in Nige
text: Nearly 10 years ago, Nigel Farage told LBC he would leave the country if Brexit were not a stunning success. For reasons that no one can quite fathom, he is still here. Could it be that he is a man who can’t be trusted to keep his word? Surely not. Nige wants you to know he’s very much still around. He might have been a bit quiet over the past few weeks, as Reform had to deal with one or two unfortunate investigations into their funding, but now he’s very much back. And he’s definitely not rattled that Labour has a prime minister the country likes. Nor is he at all rattled that Reform has tumbled into second place in the polls. Oh, no. Because Nige believes in Nige. Now more than ever. The last creepy-crawly after the apocalypse. Lying on its back, gasping for air. But still breathing. The dream still alive. Welcome to the new Reform roadshow. Much the same as the last Reform roadshow, only with added desperation. You can almost sense the jeopardy. A dream receding into the distance. Supporters clinging just that bit tighter to each other in the echo chamber. The cheers just a bit too forced. The performance ever more contrived. Just a rehash of all the old lines with a flashing light show thrown in. We are promised one a week from now until the next general election. It’s going to be a long three years. Even Nige might be sick of Nige by then. For the first outing of The Rolling Grievance Tour, Reform had taken over a room at Doncaster racecourse. But we were made to wait for Nige. The Reform leader goes nowhere these days without a couple of charisma-free fluffers as his warm-up acts. Men whose sole job is to make Nige look good. Men who are guaranteed to have the audience begging to be let out within minutes. First up was Matt Goodwin, the candidate who failed to get elected in Gorton and Denton. Someone who everyone seems to dislike on sight. Because it saves time that way. His sole function appears to be to make Nige look a little less unpleasant. Then we had Richard Tice. Dicky would travel the length of the country if he was told there was going to be an audience of two. He is the very definition of needy. He is also spectacularly dim in the way that only posh boys can be. On the self-awareness scale he drops below zero. He has no idea people are laughing at him, not with him. His attempts to be down with the little people were met with collective despair. “My first job was digging trenches,” he said, desperate to ingratiate himself with an audience he openly despises. Mate, you became director of that multimillion-pound property empire because your grandfather owned it. In a fairer world, you would still be a complete nobody. At best, you would be a low-achieving middle manager somewhere. Instead, Dicky thinks he is eyeing up a cabinet post in the next government. “If I fail to deliver in 100 days, I will resign,” he promised. Why not just call it quits now? Then a video of Nige saying he couldn’t be bought. Except he can. With a £70 cameo video or what looked like a £5m inducement from a Thai crypto-billionaire to lure him out of retirement. Then the man himself. Looking tired. Struggling to find his usual energy as he went through his familiar numbers. All this hate must be exhausting. But it was worth it, when he was a novelty. No one asked too many questions. He could pretend to be an insurgent. The anti-establishment choice. Except he will never be anything but the establishment. He began by insulting his audience. First by claiming the St Leger was the first classic of the season when it is the last – if you’re going to try to ingratiate yourself, you should at least get some basic facts right – then by rubbishing Doncaster itself. It was a shithole. He couldn’t imagine why anyone still lived there. If what the residents did could actually be called living. Still, he was doing them a favour by granting them an hour in his presence. So they did have that. “Ed Miliband is never seen in Doncaster,” he declared. Yup. And you’re never seen in Clacton. So that evens things up. At least he’s in the cabinet. Time to talk about foreigners coming over in small boats. They were all a security risk. As the incident at Fairford proved (not). I’m sure the police will be thrilled to have Nige commenting on a live investigation. He had earlier even suggested that the men had deliberately got themselves arrested so they could time the police response. Even Matt the Twat isn’t that half-witted. On and on Nige went. Same old lines. Same old grievances. Nothing positive to say other than that he would miraculously cure the entire country in 100 days. A task that may take other politicians decades. It goes without saying he didn’t say how. Just believe. A man of his brilliance can do anything. Moral decline, he said sadly. We are a Judeo-Christian country. Foreigners had been put on warning. Yawn. Inevitably, we got to Andy Burnham’s promise to reset the country’s relationship with the EU. Nige was certain it would be a disaster. Because Brexit had been a tremendous success and Burnham was seeking division. The irony meter had ramped up several notches. No one does division quite like Nige. It’s his USP. Though weirdly he has achieved some consensus. Thanks to him, most of the country now thinks Brexit was an idiotic idea. Quite the achievement. He also went on to accuse Andy of smashing the pensioners by removing the triple lock. He may want to tell Thick Dick that. Dicky is on record as saying the triple lock had to go. “I am different,” he said in conclusion. He wasn’t in politics for rank or status. He had enough money to do what he liked. He was getting on a bit. In fact, he wasn’t sure why he was doing this. Other than the fact he is a raging narcissist who craves constant attention and affirmation. As if to prove the point he insisted that people kept begging him to save them. In his mind, he is the Messiah. The second coming. He didn’t want to change the electoral system, he wanted to abolish it. After him, there would be no need for elections. The thousand year Reich. Nirvana. All he wanted was just a normal far-right country. A place where England was for the English. Once we had deported all foreign criminals there would be no need for prisons because white people would stop breaking the law. Foreigners were dragging us down. Spiritually, financially, morally. We had lost our way like lost sheep. All we had to do was believe in Nige. An act of faith. Only not even Nige believes in Nige any more.

title: Brazil attorney general says meddling ‘cannot be tolerated’ after Trump funding plans revealed
summary: Jorge Messias calls Guardian report ‘an important alert for Brazilian sovereignty’ as nation prepares to go to polls
text: Brazil’s attorney general has said foreign meddling in his country’s institutions and democracy “cannot be tolerated” after a Guardian report revealed how the Trump administration was pushing to direct funds to a campaign against the Brazilian supreme court. Writing on X, Jorge Messias called the report “an important alert for Brazilian sovereignty”. “The information is especially serious in light of Brazil’s electoral process and the recent episodes of external pressure on our institutions,” Messias added. Brazil is three days away from its presidential election – the outcome of which Washington has been accused of trying to influence – where the leftwing incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, will face off against his far-right rival, the Trump ally Flávio Bolsonaro. The pair are neck and neck in the polls. According to the Brazilian television network GloboNews, the attorney general’s office on Thursday filed a criminal complaint to investigate potential wrongdoing, in response to the Guardian story. Last year, the Trump administration used a campaign of sanctions and tariffs in a failed attempt to pressure Lula’s government and the supreme court over the coup trial of Bolsonaro’s father, the ex-president Jair Bolsonaro. Trump called Bolsonaro’s prosecution a “witch-hunt”, but he was convicted and handed a 27-year sentence for trying to seize power after losing the 2022 election to Lula. In recent months, the Trump administration has again been accused of meddling in Brazilian affairs by using tariffs and the designation of two Brazilian organised crime groups as foreign terrorist organisations to boost Flávio Bolsonaro’s campaign and weaken Lula. Writing on Thursday, Messias said: “Disagreements between governments are inherent to international relations. What cannot be tolerated is for foreign political interests to seek to interfere in the functioning of Brazilian institutions or to influence, directly or indirectly, choices that belong exclusively to the Brazilian people.” Messias added: “It is the right of each generation of Brazilians to freely decide their destiny, protect their institutions, and hand over to their children a country that does not accept decisions about Brazil being made outside of Brazil. Our democracy belongs to Brazilians. And so it must remain.” The attorney general’s comments came in response to a report that the Trump administration was pushing to direct more than $175m of the state department’s flagship human rights fund to a slate of awards that includes a $40m grant for an anti-communism fund, support for a group advancing white Afrikaner rights in South Africa and the campaign against Brazil’s supreme court. A $1m award titled “Countering lawfare and censorship in Brazil” would fund civil society groups opposing what it calls judicial overreach and censorship by Brazil’s supreme court. Bolsonaro’s far-right movement considers the supreme court – and in particular justice Alexandre de Moraes, who oversaw Jair Bolsonaro’s trial – its greatest foe. Moraes is widely seen to have played a key role in thwarting Jair Bolsonaro’s authoritarian plot, which culminated in the 8 January 2023 riots in Brasília, despite concerns about the judge overstepping his constitutional authority in his crusade to protect democracy. During the rightwing riots, hardcore Bolsonaro supporters trashed the presidential palace, congress and supreme court. The court sustained the most severe damage. Bolsonaro supporters continue to claim their leader’s imprisonment is unjust and that he is the victim of a politically motivated sham driven by a corrupt “judicial dictatorship”. Their criticism of Moraes and the supreme court has been bolstered by a recent scandal linking several judges, including him, to Daniel Vorcaro, the playboy banker at the centre of Brazil’s biggest banking scandal. Vorcaro has also been linked to the Bolsonaro family. The banker reportedly gave the family more than £9m, supposedly to produce a biopic about Jair Bolsonaro starring Jim Caviezel, who played Jesus in Mel Gibson’s film The Passion of the Christ. On the eve of Vorcaro’s arrest last November, Flávio Bolsonaro messaged him to say: “Brother, I’ll always be with you.” Vorcaro is being held in federal police custody in Brasília. His legal team has consistently denied wrongdoing. On Wednesday, his lawyers said he was not involved in “any kind of illicit activity or criminal practice”.

title: Labour figures uneasy about Healey’s ‘underpowered’ approach to budget
summary: Chancellor faces global volatility and soaring energy costs as some insiders worry lack of clarity could trigger fresh market shock
text: Senior Labour figures are privately voicing unease about John Healey’s approach to his crucial first budget this month, against the backdrop of volatile global markets and soaring energy costs. The chancellor’s work has been made significantly harder by the global bond sell-off, which continues to raise the cost of government borrowing, and ever increasing energy prices as Donald Trump continues the US war with Iran. The yield – in effect the interest rate – on 30-year UK government bonds hit 6% on Thursday for the first time since 1998. Barclays raised some of its mortgage rates for the second time in a week, underlining the impact of these market moves on UK borrowers. The chancellor’s party conference speech, which centred on the theme of reindustrialisation, was warmly received by Labour members in Liverpool. But government insiders and other Labour figures cast doubt over the lack of detail about policy on investment and growth or any pitch-rolling for possible tax rises. One senior Labour politician said: “I missed any real sense of growth and investment, which Rachel [Reeves, the former chancellor] often emphasised, despite her faults – when business leaders speak to me, that’s what they were waiting to hear, and we got nothing.” A Labour MP lamented the fact that on tax and spending Healey had gone little further than reiterating the fiscal rules. “It was Rachel’s speech delivered by John,” they said. One senior Labour insider said they believed the chancellor was risking a fresh market shock on 28 October if he was not willing to be clearer about his approach to taxation, headroom and spending. Market moves since the spring are expected to have wiped out at least half of the £24bn “headroom”, or buffer, Reeves had built up against Labour’s fiscal rules. Healey is believed to be minded to accept a slimmer margin, but he gave no indication of his likely approach in his speech, aside from repeatedly stressing the need for discipline. Rebuilding the headroom in full could require significant tax increases or spending cuts. Prof Arun Advani, the director of the centre for the analysis of taxation at the University of Warwick, said: “The chancellor didn’t give us a sense of how he’s thinking about these issues. It was a speech where at the end of it we didn’t come away understanding more about the direction of policy, or what he wants to do with the Treasury.” There are concerns, too, about how Healey will tough out demands to say when the UK will spend 3% of GDP on defence – having resigned as defence secretary three months ago over the issue. Treasury sources stressed that Healey was intimately involved in some of Andy Burnham’s significant conference announcements, with 40 officials working at the department through the weekend on the details of the triple lock pension changes. They also pointed out that the chancellor opened the door to a renewed attempt to overhaul welfare for the young unemployed – a fraught issue for Labour – and stressed his determination to present an optimistic picture of the UK economy. Healey’s team are committed to avoiding the rollercoaster of leaks that happened in the run-up to Reeves’s budgets, particularly last year. The Treasury team have initiated military-style “black boxes” – learned from Healey’s time in the Ministry of Defence – for different teams to work within to avoid accidental leaks. They also remain committed to what one called a “tightly focused” budget, though they concede that offering voters more “breathing space” on energy costs had become more urgent. The narrow focus of the statement is expected to rule out radical changes to property and capital gains taxes previously mooted by Burnham supporters including the first secretary, Louise Haigh; though reports that Healey is calling in bank bosses next week has reignited speculation of a windfall tax on the sector. Labour MPs fear that failing to take more drastic action, particularly on surging energy prices, could leave voters nonplussed. One MP said: “The budget is only a few weeks away. He may want it to be low key but it will send a massive signal of our intent.” Others are concerned that Burnham’s focus on long-term issues such as social care and public ownership of utilities will suck up political airtime without helping with the immediate crisis. Alfie Stirling, the director of policy and insight at the Joseph Rowntree Foundation, said: “The focus on ‘room to breathe’ now, alongside the focus on taking greater control over the costs of essentials over the longer term, is the right strategy for government. But families are currently facing the worst parliament on modern record for real incomes and they simply cannot wait three years for government to grip this in the here and now.” Several Labour figures pointed to Burnham’s last-minute decision to appoint Healey as one factor making the chancellor’s job harder, giving him little time to build up an effective team before the budget. Rav Athwal, an economist and the author of Labour’s 2024 manifesto, has only just joined Healey as a senior special adviser. Reeves’s chief economic adviser, Neil Amin-Smith, was poached by No 10. One Treasury insider said: “He’s slow to get through his boxes and it’s hard to get meetings in the diary because he needs time to prepare before each one. It all feels a bit underpowered.” But another Labour figure defended him: “John got virtually no notice he was getting this job. He’s not an economist. He didn’t have two years in opposition to prepare. It’s early days and the Treasury is there to support him. He’s very capable – just give him time.”

title: The Guardian view on the death penalty: Christa Pike’s execution was botched, but cruelty is inherent | Editorial
summary: Editorial: Three-quarters of nations have rightly abolished capital punishment in law or practice, but killing by the state has surged in the US
text: What is the kindest way to kill? That’s the question being asked once more following Tennessee’s failed attempts to execute Christa Pike for the brutal murder of a classmate, Colleen Slemmer, when she was 18. The 50-year-old was taken to a medical facility, her condition unknown, with witnesses describing her snoring loudly around 40 minutes after receiving two injections of pentobarbital on Wednesday. It is the second botched killing in months, prompting Tennessee’s governor to order a halt to executions. Lethal injection was supposed to be the humane alternative to firing squads and electric chairs. They in turn were seen as an improvement on hanging, which looked much like lynching in a system disproportionately handing the death penalty to black men. The age and ill health of those executed, and the ethical refusal of most medical staff to be involved, may contribute to botched injections. But analysis of autopsy results has provided compelling evidence that suffering is inherent; injections – especially those involving paralytic drugs – have merely disguised it. What is described as safeguarding the dignity of prisoners is really about reducing the discomfort of witnesses who would otherwise see their suffering. Pressure from campaigners on pharmaceutical companies has curbed the supply of lethal drugs, but it has not stopped executions. Donald Trump’s enthusiasm for the death penalty has spurred on state officials, with the highest number of executions for 16 years in 2025. Some states have found alternative drugs, which may increase the suffering of those killed. Others are using different techniques. In June, the supreme court stopped Alabama from executing a prisoner with nitrogen gas, which it has used in other cases. The use of firing squads has resurged. Experts say such deaths can be “excruciating”, especially where marksmen miss the heart of the condemned, with allegations that some executions could even have been deliberately botched. The US is in a shameful minority. Three-quarters of countries have got rid of capital punishment in law or practice – with Lebanon this year becoming the first Middle Eastern country to abolish it. Only 17 countries executed prisoners last year, though the total number killed rose to more than 2,700 – the highest since 1984. (The figures do not include China, believed to carry out the most executions.) But while Mr Trump and others champion capital punishment, the American public are turning away from it. In 1994, 80% supported it; by last year that had fallen to 52%. A majority of younger people oppose it. High-profile miscarriages of justice have contributed to growing disquiet. So have cases such as Pike’s. She endured sexual abuse and rape by three perpetrators in childhood, as well as beatings and neglect – yet her experiences and age were not adequately put forward by lawyers at her trial. Her bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder were diagnosed only afterwards. Sandra Babcock, an expert on the death penalty who has acted on Pike’s behalf, argued that her execution would confirm that it was reserved “not for the worst of the worst, but for the most damaged and vulnerable among us”. The ultimate problem, however, is not that the wrong people are being executed, but that anyone is being executed. The search for a humane way to kill is inherently preposterous. It is not just lethal injection, the firing squad or electrocution that should be rejected – but the death penalty itself. Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: ‘Total class act’: Marie-France van Heel is poised to be a very different PM’s wife
summary: The former marketing executive is expected to play a big role in promoting the UK and could be the most influential spouse in No 10 in years
text: Sarah Brown called Gordon her hero, Samantha Cameron insisted David was “incredibly funny”, while Akshata Murty said Rishi was her best friend. When Marie-France van Heel spoke about her husband, Andy Burnham, in a rare public interview a decade ago, she joked that she had noticed his “good looks … and monobrow”. The spousal humanising of a party leader is a well-worn political tool, but van Heel is likely to be a very different prime ministerial partner. The former senior marketing executive is poised to play a more significant role in promoting Britain than any other spouse in the last two decades, stepping up her political engagements after stepping back from her own corporate career. Van Heel has chosen a political adviser to help her navigate the role at home and promote the UK’s interests overseas, the Guardian understands. She has shifted her role at Be.EV, an electric vehicle-charging network based in Manchester, quitting her job as chief customer officer to give her schedule more flexibility, while remaining on the company’s board. While it is standard for the partners of prime ministers to have taxpayer-funded office support, van Heel has taken on a former special adviser to a cabinet member and is expected to play a more significant role behind the scenes than the previous prime minister Keir Starmer’s wife, Victoria, who continued her work in occupational health for the NHS throughout her husband’s tenure. Last week, she travelled with Burnham to the UN general assembly in New York, attending a lunch hosted by the US first lady, Melania Trump, as well as holding meetings with Ukraine’s first lady, Olena Zelenska, and the Canadian prime minister’s wife, Diana Fox Carney. The UK is holding the G20 presidency next year and the G7 presidency the year after, and van Heel is seen as a valuable addition to the UK’s diplomatic vanguard. At the Labour party conference this week, she posed for photos with the Labour Asians Society and attended a fringe event on apprenticeships. One gushing corporate communicator later wrote that she had spent half an hour making apprentices “feel like the most important people in the room”, adding that she was “a total class act”. Van Heel and her team are now speaking to charities and leaders and weighing up how to make best use of her “impressive” personality and professional experience to champion causes. They will be lucky to have her, said Rose Caldwell, the chief executive of Plan International UK, where van Heel was a trustee until July. “She brought valuable insight and unwavering commitment to the role,” she said. “She really made a lasting contribution to our mission of advancing equality for girls.” Born in Roslyn, Pennsylvania, to Dutch parents, van Heel grew up in the Netherlands and Belgium and met Burnham on her first day as a student at the University of Cambridge. In a campaign video for his mayoral campaign, she asked the future PM if he remembered his response to her question about what he wanted to do with his life. “You said you wanted to be an MP,” she said. “Yeah. And I left the room at that point.” After almost a decade in Manchester, van Heel is something of an unknown quantity in Westminster, but insiders say she has already impressed staff behind the scenes. “She’s incredibly cool,” said one source. “She’s very nice, very smart … she just gets it.” The clearest picture of the prime minister’s partner has come from Burnham himself. Speaking to Elizabeth Day for the How to Fail podcast, he said that his wife of 26 years was “forthright” when she thought he had got something wrong. “She’s Dutch, and they don’t hold back,” he said. “They’re pretty plain speaking, and yeah, I’ve been on the receiving end of a lot of that over the years.” Burnham has recalled finishing an interview when he was an MP and seeing a text from his wife exhorting him to “ANSWER THE F***ING QUESTION”. When he told van Heel he was planning to run to be Labour leader earlier this year, after failed bids in 2010 and 2015, she did not hold back. “She was like, ‘Oh, not again! They’ve told you twice. They don’t want you. Why again?’” Burnham said. “She took some persuading, to be honest, because I guess she didn’t want to see me go through it all again […] But she gives me good advice.” But there are earlier hints, too. Much has been written of van Heel’s appearance on the Cilla Black TV show Blind Date in 1992, when she punctured the private school hubris of “Will from Surrey” – otherwise known as Will Harris, who later became the marketing director for the Conservative party. But a full viewing of the video – in which van Heel flicks Harris’s wandering hand off her knee, before smacking her unfortunate date with a cushion when he calls her a “fridge” – gives a sense of her blunt confidence and quick wit. When Harris says his “interests were honourable”, she retorts: “I didn’t have any interest at all.” Officially, Downing Street will say only that van Heel, who has three adult children with Burnham, is supporting her husband and “advancing UK interests” as spouses have done before. Where van Heel’s energy will be directed now that her husband has reached No 10 is still being mapped out, but it is likely that she will be the most active – and potentially influential – prime minister’s wife since Sarah Brown at the start of the century. Brown’s diaries from Downing Street note there is “no formal spouse job to step into […] no permanent office, no salary, no allowance, no pre-set duties or official role, not even an official title” for the prime minister’s wife. It is a job that van Heel did not ask for, and may not even want – but it looks likely she will make it her own.

title: US borrowing costs hit 24-year high as global bond sell-off intensifies
summary: Fears that US deficit is unsustainable also drive UK 30-year bond yields briefly above 6% for first time since 1998
text: The global bond sell-off intensified on Thursday, driving 10-year US government borrowing costs to their highest level in 24 years in a frantic day’s trading. The threat of a renewed round of inflation from the persistently high cost of oil has spooked investors on both sides of the Atlantic, with central banks expected to raise interest rates in the coming months to prevent price increases from becoming embedded. The sell-off drove the yield, or interest rate, on 10-year US Treasuries to 5.34% – the highest level since 2002. In the UK, where surging borrowing costs are increasing the pressure on the chancellor, John Healey, before his first budget later this month, the yield on 30-year bonds hit 6% for the first time since 1998, before easing slightly later in the day. Yields on five- and 10-year UK bonds were also up. Stock market investors sold heavily too, knocking almost 1.7% off the FTSE 100 in London – its worst daily fall since May. Bourses in other parts of Europe were also hit, with Germany’s DAX falling 1% and France’s CAC 40 losing 1.6%. “There is carnage in the bond market, which is hitting stocks hard,” said Neil Wilson, the investor strategist at Saxo UK. “It looks like the relentless rout in the bond market is sending investors running for cover.” The bond sell-off around the world is being driven by fears of high inflation, as the Middle East conflict continues to restrict oil supplies from the region. Japan’s 10-year yield rose towards the 30-year high set last month. US bonds weakened despite inflation data on Wednesday coming in lower than forecast, which was expected to calm investors’ nerves about the prospect of further increases in the cost of borrowing by the US Federal Reserve. Traders remain anxious that the Fed will continue to raise interest rates to fight inflation, mainly in response to the strength of the US economy and the prospect of workers bidding up their wages. Mohit Kumar, an economist at Jefferies, said there was growing concern at the amount of debt being issued to fund government deficits, as well as inflation concerns. “Inflation, deficit and issuance concerns continue to weigh on the bond market,” he said. “There is also a buyers’ strike as investors do not want to step in till we get some form of stability. Hedge funds have suffered in the latest round of sell-off and do not have the risk appetite to fade the move. Real money potentially has the risk appetite, but won’t step in till we get some stability.” Axel Rudolph, the chief technical analyst at the investing and trading platform IG, said: “While the latest data has reduced expectations of an October Fed rate hike, investors remain wary that persistent inflation and higher oil prices could keep rates elevated for longer. “The dollar is benefiting from that caution, climbing to a three-month high, while the prospect of a December rate increase keeps pressure on bond markets.” Oil prices rose again on Thursday, despite analysis that showed exports of crude from the strait of Hormuz have largely returned to levels seen before the outbreak of the Iran war, as oil producers and the shipping industry have found alternative ways of transporting crucial fuel out of the Middle East. Brent crude rose 3% to about $101 a barrel. The price of crude remained at elevated levels as traders balanced the recovery in some Middle East exports with uncertainty over a long-term solution to the conflict and reopening of the strait. Eurozone countries were also caught up in the wave of selling, with France in particular in investors’ sights. Ten-year yields on French government bonds hit 4.96%, the highest level since 2002. The spread over German yields – an indicator of the additional risk France is believed to face – has jumped to its highest level in more than a decade.

title: France school protests escalate into ‘urban violence’ as PM calls crisis cabinet meeting
summary: About 900 demonstrations, blockades and related incidents under way outside high schools around the country
text: A fast-growing protest by high-school students over long hours, teacher shortages and decaying facilities has escalated into “urban violence”, the French government has warned, as it said many schools would switch to online classes to protect teachers and pupils. The prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, called a crisis cabinet meeting on Thursday and told ministers to cancel travel plans to deal with the demonstrations, which erupted in the Paris region last week but have snowballed across the country. Lecornu’s office said: “This upsurge in violence makes it virtually impossible to maintain the continuity of public education and is exposing staff and students to danger.” The education minister, Édouard Geffray, is to meet pupil representatives on Friday. About 900 demonstrations, blockades and related incidents were under way outside high schools around the country, police said, with more than 160 shut down as a result. Access was also blocked to about 30 university campuses on Thursday, including in Paris and Marseille. Nearly 3,000 lycée students – aged between 15 and 18 – have been detained since the start of the protests, including 1,949 on Thursday alone, the interior ministry said. More than 300 police and dozens of firefighters, teachers and pupils have been injured. The pupils’ grievances range from overloaded timetables and overcrowded classes to insufficient teachers and unbearable temperatures during heatwaves earlier this year. Riot police have been deployed to confront the increasingly violent protests. Injuries have mainly been from hurled objects but also from police-fired riot-control projectiles, with the interior ministry announcing an internal police investigation after accusations of excessive force and brutality by officers against three pupils. Rubbish bins have been set on fire outside many schools and more serious arson attempts have been reported inside some buildings. Fire damage in one school in Nantes in the north-west was so extensive that it will stay closed for a month, authorities said. In the northern city of Caen, 16-year-old Maelle said she wished those setting bins on fire would protest “with words”. Students were protesting “against this government that doesn’t invest in heating, air conditioning, or teachers’ salaries”, she told AFP. In Strasbourg in the north-east, tram services were temporarily suspended to “restrict the movements of rioters and demonstrators”, the regional prefect said, after protesting students obstructed the tracks with crowd control barriers. “There are 35 of us per classroom,” one 17-year-old Strasbourg student said. “There aren’t enough toilets, and there are water leaks in some rooms. The building is falling apart, the cafeteria is too small. There’s zero budget, zero resources.” Several bin fires were also reported in the southern city of Toulouse; while in Lille, young people wearing black hoodies destroyed a bus stop. In Marseille, there were attempts to light fires inside two schools. In one, a teacher was splashed with petrol. While many teachers and several headteachers have reported being physically threatened and sometimes attacked, some support their pupils. Juliette Estiville, a high-school Spanish teacher in Paris, said that the police response had disgusted her. “I’m actually here just to provide protection, to form a barrier between the police and the students,” she said. “Today went well, it’s going well, but I think that the teachers who come to the blockades are really there to protect our young people.” The government has accused the radical left La France Insoumise (LFI) party of encouraging the protests, with several LFI MPs and mayors, including Bally Bagayoko, the LFI mayor of the Paris suburb of Saint-Denis, cheered at demonstrations. The party’s candidate for the 2027 presidential election, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, insisted on Thursday that LFI backed “non-violent methods of struggle” and added that his “greatest worry is an unbearable level of police violence against these young people”.
