title: DNC sues Trump administration over last-minute changes to overseas voting form
summary: DNC accuses Pentagon of pushing through changes to how voters abroad request absentee ballots ahead of midterms
text: The Trump administration broke the law when it pushed through a last-minute change to the form overseas citizens use to register and request absentee ballots, the Democratic National Committee (DNC) said in a lawsuit filed on Thursday. Until recently, the form, the Federal Post Card Application (FPCA), gave overseas voters four options to choose from when describing their geographic location. Voters could say they needed an overseas ballot because they were on active military service, living outside the US with an intent to return, or living outside the US and uncertain about their return. The form also allowed voters to check a box if they were a US citizen who had never lived in the country (38 states and the District of Columbia allow citizens born abroad to vote in at least some elections even if they have never lived in the country). In August, as the deadline to send out overseas ballots approached, the Pentagon – the agency that oversees the form – submitted two emergency requests to modify the form. Among the changes, the Pentagon sought to eliminate the option allowing voters to say they were citizens who never lived in the US. The requests were quickly approved by the office of management and budget (OMB). NPR first reported the changes earlier this week. “Trump and Republicans are so desperate to hang on to power that they are trying to eliminate the way some American citizens abroad register to vote and request mail ballots. They know that Americans, both at home and abroad, are going to reject their destructive agenda, and they are scrambling to disenfranchise as much of the electorate as possible by any means necessary,” said Ken Martin, the chair of the DNC. A Pentagon spokesperson said: “The Department is committed to ensuring all Service members, their families, and overseas citizens have seamless access to the tools and resources to successfully exercise their right to vote from anywhere in the world. “To actively protect voting rights and eliminate voter confusion, FVAP.gov is routinely updated to ensure all online tools, federally-prescribed forms, and state-specific guidance remain streamlined, legally compliant, and simple to navigate. This includes updated online guidance on August 31 that clarifies instructions and voter eligibility requirements regarding the Federal Post Card Application and Federal Write-In Absentee Ballot,” the spokesperson said. The changes could confuse and discourage US citizens who have never lived in the country from registering and casting a ballot, experts said. “The Uniformed and Overseas Citizens Absentee Voting Act guarantees US citizens abroad, along with service members and their families, the right to vote, and nothing in it requires a plan to return. Changing the form does not change that right. It changes whether a voter recognizes themselves on it,” said Susan Dzieduszycka-Suinat, president and CEO of the US Vote Foundation, which works on helping overseas Americans vote. “If an overseas voter goes on to the FPCA website, goes to get their Federal Postcard Application to request their ballot, they’re going to see this form and they have to sign it under penalty of perjury,” said a DNC official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to candidly discuss the lawsuit. “They’re going to see that there is no longer the checkbox they’re used to checking. And the other options may not fit them accurately and they may not be able to comfortably or confidently sign that form and request their mail ballot.” In an August letter to the OMB, Sean O’Keefe, the deputy undersecretary of defense for personnel and readiness, said the department had recently become aware of the option on the form for citizens who had never lived in the US. The changes were necessary, he said, because the existing versions “may confuse voters about the information they are required to provide under federal law”. He added that the changes could not go through a normal process because the election was less than 90 days away, and therefore had to be rushed. Lawyers for the DNC said in its lawsuit that justification was pretextual and implausible. The government “has at least 15 years of experience issuing guidance to US citizens born and remaining abroad, reviewing public comments concerning use of the FPCA by these applicants, and modifying the FPCA to best serve these eligible voters”, they wrote. By rushing through the changes, the government violated the Administrative Procedure Act, a federal law that requires government agencies to carefully weigh the impact of rules changes before implementing them. The OMB also did not follow proper procedure by not allowing for public comment in the federal register. The lawsuit, filed in federal court in Washington DC, asks a judge to declare the government violated the APA and to set aside the government’s changes to the form. There are an estimated 2.2 million US citizens living abroad who are eligible to vote, according to the Federal Voting Assistance Program (the highest number of eligible citizens are living in Canada and the UK). About 11% of eligible US citizens living abroad voted in 2024. It’s not immediately clear how many US citizens live abroad but have never lived in the country. A 2016 government report estimated there were about 11,590, though lawyers for the DNC believe the number has increased since then. The Pentagon changed the form as the Republican National Committee (RNC) has pushed to prevent US citizens who have never lived in the country from having their votes counted. Republicans have sued in nine states challenging the policy of counting ballots for these types of voters. While one North Carolina court agreed with Republicans, several other courts have rejected their arguments while other lawsuits remain pending. In August, around the time the Trump administration rushed through the change, the RNC put out a statement saying it was “leading the fight to shut down a loophole that allows certain people who have never lived in a state to vote in its elections. As the case heads to the Nebraska supreme court, the RNC is pushing to protect residency requirements and stop the spread of ‘never-resident’ voting nationwide.” “The RNC strongly agrees that every eligible US citizen should be able to vote. The difference is the DNC wants to extend voting rights to people who aren’t eligible. Enforcing citizenship and residency requirements isn’t disenfranchisement – it’s following the law,” Ally Triolo, the RNC’s communications director for election integrity issues, said in a statement. “Regardless of the number of people at issue, as the DNC, we want to defend the rights of Americans to vote – of eligible US citizens to vote at home and abroad,” the DNC official said. “It is simply offensive that the RNC is trying to outright disenfranchise eligible US citizens. And it is offensive that [the Pentagon] would be joining that campaign just before the election.”

title: Hegseth puts the future of warfare in the hands of major Maga donors
summary: Installing tech billionaires Elon Musk and Palmer Luckey to Pentago defense board raises conflict-of-interest concerns
text: By installing the tech billionaires Elon Musk and Palmer Luckey to advisory roles in a Pentagon project about the future of warfare, the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, bestowed extraordinary influence on two of Maga’s most significant campaign donors – and both men own companies that benefit from federal defense contracting. The new project, which Hegseth dubbed “Project Meridian” in an event in Quantico, Virginia, on Wednesday, will be led by Pentagon official Emil Michael, a former Uber executive. As the Guardian has reported, Michael made millions in profits off non-public Musk company AI stock while in federal office – and while guiding the Department of Defense’s artificial intelligence efforts. Along with Luckey and Musk, Project Meridian will also include the Trump loyalist and former speaker of the House Newt Gingrich. Musk was one of the chief financiers of Trump’s 2024 victory, spending over a quarter of a billion dollars in the run-up to the election. Recent campaign records show he is still a major force in the coming midterms. His America Pac spent $3.4m attacking the Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan’s Senate race, for example. In the hotly contested Texas Senate race, America Pac spent $6.4m to oppose Democrat James Talarico and $1m to support the Trump-endorsed Ken Paxton. Musk’s SpaceX has been a crucial contractor for US space programs since 2018, and in the second Trump administration his company has emerged as key player in Trump’s pet Golden Dome ballistic missile defense project, a phenomenally expensive effort that could cost as much as $1.2tn. Musk dwarfs Luckey in resources and fame, but Luckey has achieved immense celebrity in the defense contracting and world. Initially a young celebrity in the tech world for inventing a virtual reality headset, Luckey later founded Anduril, a defense contracting company that has already won significant federal contracts. Luckey has also become of the most important “bundlers” for Republican candidates on the west coast, as the Guardian reported in August. One of the sources called him the “godfather of Republican fundraising on the west coast”. Invitations to political fundraisers obtained by the Guardian show Luckey hosted and co-hosted events for candidates from Trump himself to Ken Calvert, Rick Scott, Mehmet Oz, Ted Cruz and others. The most recent event was on 22 August, where he and his wife co-hosted a $50,000-a-head effort to “Keep the Senate”, and listing guests John Thune of South Dakota, Mike Rogers of Michigan, Dan Sullivan of Alaska and Jon Husted of Ohio. It is not necessarily a mystery what Musk and Luckey think about warfare’s future. The 34-year-old Palmer, whose company is backed by Joshua Kushner’s equity fund, has acquired manufacturers of underwater drones, UAVs, and space technology, has been already been voluble about his philosophy on warfare. Earlier this year, for example, he said he thought warfare in the second half of this century would involve “subterranean” conflict, with vehicles that can “move through he crust of the earth the same way that submarines move through the water”. He has claimed that his company has “working prototypes of subterranean systems”. “Bringing major industry players into these types of positions at the Pentagon is not something new, but what feels different now is the substantial financial support these two have, and continue to, deliver for the Republican party,” said Brendan Glavin of Open Secrets, a non-partisan group that tracks campaign spending. The Pentagon did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

title: UK-Iran national arrested under Terrorism Act over RAF Fairford incident
summary: Counter-terrorism police arrest 25-year-old in Westminster and search two properties in central London
text: Detectives have arrested a dual UK-Iranian national on suspicion of terrorism offences as part of an investigation into a suspected plot near RAF Fairford. Counter-terrorism police said the 25-year-old man was arrested on Thursday in Westminster on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts under section 5 of the Terrorism Act 2006. Five men in their 20s were arrested in the village of Whelford, Gloucestershire, outside the RAF base in the early hours of Sunday after police were alerted to suspicious vans in the area. They were released on police bail. Announcing the most recent arrest, Vicki Evans, the senior national coordinator for counter-terrorism police, said: “As we’ve made clear, we’re looking at all possible angles – including possible foreign state involvement.” Counter-terrorism police said two properties had been searched in Westminster, London. Evans added: “The investigation into circumstances surrounding events in Gloucestershire is hugely complex, and our specialist teams are interrogating multiple lines of inquiry.” An Iranian link to the events in the Gloucestershire countryside over the weekend is considered increasingly likely, as the police and security services’ investigation continues. Senior US politicians, including the president, Donald Trump, have expressed surprise that the suspects were released on bail. It was revealed on Sunday that a farmer driving home from a party at about 1am on Sunday had spotted the men and vans and called 999. But on Tuesday it emerged that one of the five men arrested near the base called the police to report the incident. The mounting view among investigators that Iran was likely involved was a key reason for Andy Burnham’s decision to call a meeting of Cobra, the government’s crisis committee, on Monday, which was attended by senior police and security officials. Tensions have been high at RAF Fairford since Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said in July that the base was a legitimate target. Iran’s embassy in London has denied any involvement in the events of the past few days. Ministers have been briefed that Iran has various reasons for hiring proxies, who sometimes are unwitting, to carry out acts that aim to eat up resources and create chaos. The suspects were first arrested on explosives charges and then later for preparing acts of terrorism. The decision on Monday to bail the men came after an examination of what was found in the vans, and searches of addresses linked to them across London, all of which found no evidence of a viable device. Counter-terrorism police are leading the investigation, which is trying to establish why the five men, all British nationals from London, were in the Gloucestershire countryside, close to a sensitive site in the middle of the night. The vans were marked with the logo of a legitimate fuel transit company that later denied ownership of the vehicles. People detained for terrorism offences can be detained under two legal schedules that dictate how long they can be held without charge. Under the terrorism schedule, a suspect can be held for up to 14 days but cannot be bailed. The 25-year-old man arrested on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts is being held under the Police and Criminal Evidence Act (Pace), a spokesperson for CTP said. That means he could be released on bail under investigation, but detectives have much less time to hold him. The five men arrested early on Sunday in the Gloucestershire countryside were held under Pace before being bailed the next day. The Iranian embassy in London has said it “categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations” of Iranian involvement. Eighty-five households were forced to decamp to a leisure centre on Sunday as the bomb squad and counter-terror police descended on Whelford. Some of the evacuated residents were able to stay with families, about 60 people received support from a Cotswold district council rest centre in Cirencester, and 28 people were accommodated overnight in hotels.

title: Britain in talks with European allies over release of emergency diesel stockpiles amid Trump pressure
summary: Ministers discuss drawing down EU countries’ reserves after Donald Trump threatens to cut off US supplies
text: Britain is in talks with European allies over releasing emergency diesel stockpiles after Donald Trump threatened to cut off US supplies of the fuel. Ministers held calls with counterparts from the European Commission (EC), Germany, France, Italy and Ireland on Thursday to discuss whether to draw down reserves after the Trump administration told Germany and France to release their stockpiles to help ease soaring global energy prices or face a US export ban. The warning marks an escalation of pressure on Europe as Trump considers a potential wider ban to help lower domestic fuel prices before the US midterm elections in November. Trump said Washington could ask its European allies to release strategic diesel reserves. “We may do that. They have some diesel,” Trump told reporters on a midterm elections campaign trip to Texas, shortly after the Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, urged Europe to “immediately” release its reserves. Bessent flagged the potential diesel cuts in a social media post, writing: “Our European partners should accelerate delivery on their existing commitments and make additional supplies immediately available to address ongoing disruptions.” Martin McCluskey, the UK minister for local energy, was reportedly on the call with EU countries on Thursday. The Trump administration has been frustrated with France and Germany for what it considers their not following through on commitments to release oil and petrol stocks. Fuel stations across Europe are unlikely to run dry, because Europe produces about 70% of the diesel it consumes from domestic refineries. It also stores fuels in reserve. But experts fear that competing for cargoes on the global market would lead to higher market prices. It was unclear whether the UK would be included in such a ban, but the loss of US supply would drive prices up sharply at the pumps because the UK does not refine enough diesel to meet domestic demand. About a third of UK diesel imports last year came from the US. The average price of a litre of diesel in the UK hit a new all-time high on Wednesday of 199.72p, according to the motoring body the RAC. John Healey, the chancellor, admitted earlier this week that UK diesel prices were “extreme” and said the government was in discussion with the US over trying to stop a ban. EC commission spokesperson Anna Kaisa Itkonen confirmed that EU member states will hold urgent talks with the commission on Friday to discuss a coordinated response. “The commission … is closely coordinating with EU member states to take stock of the situation and examine appropriate measures to tackle these high prices,” Itkonen added. Discussions will also involve the International Energy Agency. The US energy secretary Chris Wright said he was “highly confident” Europe could help ease soaring global fuel ⁠prices by drawing down its emergency diesel inventories. “This is a time for a coordinated release of diesel stores as we go ⁠into to harvest season and we go into winter heating oil season,” he told Fox ⁠News. “Now’s the time to bring more ‌diesel to the market, and that diesel is available.” Miatta Fahnbulleh, the UK energy secretary, has been in contact with Wright to raise concerns. Earlier, a US official told reporters it was “in Europe’s best interest” to ⁠work with the US as it pursues options to boost the supply of refined products and lower costs for consumers. The US war in Iran has disrupted energy supplies via the strait of Hormuz and sent the price of oil soaring. Before the war, in February, Brent crude – the international benchmark for oil prices – traded at about $72 a barrel. It was above $101 on Thursday. Releasing more stocks would represent a problem for European countries, which need to balance the need to bring down domestic fuel prices with keeping high stocks for a potential worsening energy crisis over the winter if the Iran war continues. “The UK continues to need fuels – from transport to chemicals, agriculture and defence,” said Elizabeth de Jong, the chief executive of the trade group Fuels Industry UK. The latest US threat showed the UK “cannot solely rely on overseas production for domestic energy security”, she added. Trump has said he was “very seriously” considering a US diesel export ban to try to curb soaring prices, and has urged Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, to pause strikes on Russian oil refineries over concerns that they could further push up prices. Russia had already extended its ban on diesel exports until the end of October after Ukrainian attacks on refining companies. A government spokesperson said: “We have a diverse and resilient supply. We continue to engage with our international partners and the UK fuel industry.”

title: How poor public transport policy is putting the brake on cities | Letters
summary: Letters: David Andrews suggests a tram network could be the answer to London’s clogged streets, while V Narayanan says unused cycle lanes are a waste of valuable road space
text: Your analysis of slowing buses in global cities sets out the mechanism exactly, and the remedy follows from it (London buses in decline? Why public transport in global cities is slowing to a crawl – visualised, 23 September). Transport for London’s own calculation that a 10% fall in speed costs 6% of demand and Imperial College London’s finding of the same decline across 15 cities show what happens to buses as the traffic thickens around them. Retiming the lights will not reverse it, and London is already trying. The phrase to notice in the article is one used by TfL: signals will give more buses priority “where possible”. There lies the difficulty. On a route running a bus every two minutes, the signals are asked to intervene 30 times an hour in each direction, and the junction cannot recover between calls before the next bus arrives. Bristol city council’s engineers found precisely this when they reviewed their bus priority: in the most congested parts of the city, priority delivered no journey-time saving at all. This is a bigger brake on the economy than it looks. What holds a city back is the plain difficulty of getting across it to work, to customers, to the shops. A firm can recruit from a smaller area, a worker can reach fewer jobs, and a high street can be reached by fewer people. Much of the decline of the high street is a decline in how easily people can get to it. The cure is to carry the same people in fewer vehicles. One tram carries as many people as three or four buses, so it can be given priority junction after junction, and the crossing traffic still gets its turn. About 30 French cities have put trams through their centres since Nantes started in 1985, and they rebuilt those centres around them. Their central streets are visibly busier for it. Sheffield’s trams share a shopping street with cars and vans, and run to the same timetable in the peak as at midday. David Andrews Chair, Light Rail Transit Association; lead author, Bristol Area Bus and Tram Business Case • Your article on London buses in decline highlights poor transport policy in London, which is guided by publicity rather than practicality. Buses have slowed down as dedicated bus lanes have been largely replaced by a poor choice of cycle lanes. London is an old city with narrow lanes and, with individual cycle transport given priority over mass public transport, it’s no wonder that buses have slowed and become erratic in service. One only needs to observe the utilisation of cycle lanes that are empty except during the peak hours of 7.30am-9am and 4pm-5pm on weekdays. That is a gross waste of valuable road space that could be used by buses. Having a dedicated bus lane instead of a cycle lane would speed up buses and make them more reliable. The bus lane could be shared by cycles and during peak times be dedicated to them, while being free for buses rest of the day. Sadly, politicians rarely look beyond elections, and fail to prioritise buses over bicycles. The authorities have wasted millions on cycle lanes while failing spectacularly to improve mass public transportation. V Narayanan London • Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Please email us your letter and it will be considered for publication in our letters section.

title: Family of Renee Good sues ICE agent and top Trump officials
summary: Wife and brother of Minneapolis woman killed in immigration crackdown allege wrongful death
text: The family of Renee Good, the woman killed by immigration agents in January in Minneapolis, filed two federal lawsuits against the agent who shot her and several top officials in the Trump administration on Thursday. In the lawsuits, Good’s partner, Becca Good, and her brother, Brent Ganger, alleged wrongful death and other violations of federal law, according to a press release issued by their lawyers. Good was a US citizen and mother of three who, on 7 January, joined her wife in protesting against the deployment of thousands of ICE agents in their city as part of the Trump administration’s mass deportation policy. The 37-year-old woman was shot and killed in her car by an agent who claimed he acted in self-defense, and the Department of Homeland Security claimed that she had engaged in “an act of domestic terrorism”. Multiple video clips of the encounter, however, show that Good was steering her vehicle away from the agent as she tried to drive away. Her death and that of Alex Pretti, an American nurse who was also shot and killed by an immigration agent during Minneapolis protests two weeks later, sparked outrage and a wave of anger across the country. Shortly after Good’s killing, Todd Blanche, then the deputy US attorney general, said he saw no grounds for opening a civil rights investigation. Days later, the justice department opened an investigation into the relationship between Becca Good, the deceased’s partner, and protest groups. At least 10 prosecutors resigned following the fatal shootings. Now these lawsuits have become some of the first major civil litigation actions filed against Trump’s deportation campaign in Minnesota. In one of them, the attorneys for Good’s wife and brother allege wrongful death and seek to recover – receive damages – for the “immense suffering Renee endured in the final moments of her life and for the profound and permanent losses that her death has inflicted upon her family”. “The complaint also seeks to recover for Becca Good, who was standing feet from the couple’s vehicle when Ross fired three rounds into it, and she watched her partner die,” the complaint says. “Peaceful assembly, speech and even dissent are protected rights. However, the government has distorted the exercise of these rights as violence against our republic and acted with extreme and unconstitutional force, causing egregious harm. Many of these illegal uses of force resulted in death – including the death of an American mother of three, Renee Good … Today’s legal actions demand accountability for countless violations of the law, the constitution and the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) own rules governing the use of force,” the lawsuit says. The other lawsuit alleges a conspiracy to interfere with civil rights by senior federal officials and federal immigration enforcement agents, and names Jonathan Ross, the immigration officer who shot Good, the former homeland security secretary Kristi Noem, the White House deputy chief of staff and architect of hardline US immigration policies, Stephen Miller, and former US border patrol officer Gregory Bovino, among others, for their “roles in Renee Good’s death”. Backlash against Trump’s anti-immigration campaign following the deaths in January led the president to withdraw agents from Minnesota, and there has been no other deployment of that kind to a major US city since then. However, investigations such as the one by the Guardian are showing that ICE is arresting more people than ever, while the administration shifted its tactics from “siege” to “soft feet”.

title: Judge dismisses DC reflecting pool damage case against former Olympian
summary: Judge barred further charges against David Hearn, whom Trump blamed for damage caused by flawed installation
text: Federal prosecutors in Washington DC can never again charge the former Olympic canoeist David Hearn over damage to the Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool, a judge ruled on Thursday, closing a case the US attorney’s office had already conceded it should not have brought. Judge Todd Edelman, of the DC superior court, dismissed the case with prejudice, siding with Hearn’s lawyers over the office of the US attorney Jeanine Pirro, which had wanted to keep the option of refiling. Pirro, a Donald Trump ally, publicized the charges at a press conference in July. Later that month her office moved to drop the case, conceding that the damage resulted from flawed installation rather than anything Hearn did. Trump, who had pressed for the prosecution, told reporters in the Oval Office on 3 August that Pirro had “choked” in abandoning the vandalism charges, and “folded like an umbrella”. Edelman agreed to the dismissal in August but left open whether it would be with or without prejudice. Prosecutors argued for the latter, which would have allowed a future revival. Hearn’s lawyers countered that the case was politically driven and lacked factual support, and warned of a risk of “harassment and bad faith” if the door stayed open. At a hearing last month, Edelman pressed a prosecutor on the point. “What future prosecution could even occur?” he asked. Michael Spence, a career official in the US attorney’s office, said he did not know, though he stressed there was no active investigation of Hearn “as of this second”. The court heard that the section of the pool Hearn allegedly touched was already damaged, and that prosecutors could not prove losses beyond $1,000, which would make a new felony case unworkable. Edelman also asked how he should regard Trump’s public calls for a prosecution that Pirro’s office itself accepted had no merit. Trump’s statements, Spence replied, “speak for themselves”. Steve Levin, one of Hearn’s attorneys, accused the government of rushing to indict in order to please the president and of misleading a grand jury. Spence maintained that prosecutors had acted in good faith. Norm Eisen, another of Hearn’s lawyers, called the ruling “a victory for the rule of law and for an innocent American seeking justice”. “This case never should have been brought in the first place,” he said.

title: Co-pilot in flight stabbing had ‘Islamic radical indoctrination’, says Netanyahu
summary: Alleged flydubai attacker interrogated by Saudi security services as investigation into apparent crash attempt opens
text: The Omani co-pilot who stabbed his captain in an apparent attempt to crash an Israel-bound flight from Dubai had previously undergone radical Islamist indoctrination and was suicidal, Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has claimed. Israeli passengers intervened to stop the attack on Wednesday, restraining the co-pilot, while a reserve crew in the plane was able to stabilise the plummeting plane and ultimately land it safely in Saudi Arabia. The plane had more than 170 people onboard and Israeli officials praised the bravery of those who intervened, announcing that four of the Israeli passengers would receive a “heroism” award for preventing a potential disaster. Netanyahu told Fox News: “We know that he underwent Islamic radical indoctrination. That appears to be something we are gathering from his personal information.” The co-pilot, whose identity is still not known, was being interrogated by Saudi security services, which arrested him on the plane’s arrival in Tabuk, in the north-west of the country. Saudi investigators were cooperating with the United Arab Emirates, the US, Oman and Israel to try to determine the attacker’s motive, a regional official familiar with the investigation said. “All possible scenarios, from terrorism to mental disorders, are being looked into. Nothing is ruled out for now,” they told the Associated Press. Two Israeli security officials said that Israel’s initial assessment was that the co-pilot was probably acting alone, Reuters reported. Netanyahu said that the co-pilot was probably suicidal, citing preliminary “indications”. “It looks very likely that he was going to down the plane … The Islamist tendencies, that radicalisation that are found in his background, I think that’s a pretty good clue,” he said, emphasising that final conclusions had yet to be made. Netanyahu had previously said it was “too early to say” if there was any state backing – namely Iranian – of the attack. Two Israeli security sources told Reuters that they had not yet found Iranian involvement. The attack came just days after Netanyahu warned of an unspecified security threat to Israel that could come during its October election. The Israeli military had said before the incident it had no specific intelligence of an imminent threat and the opposition leader Yair Lapid said that a security briefing on Tuesday night included no mention of a related threat. Other Israeli officials, including the defence minister, Israel Katz, and the ambassador to the UN, Danny Danon, suggested the incident was a “terror attack”, with the Israeli foreign ministry briefing its diplomats that the attack was against Israel and its relationship with the UAE. Donald Trump suggested the co-pilot was “perhaps a terrorist or perhaps a whack job”, and told reporters at the White House that he and Netanyahu had spoken at length. Netanyahu also spoke to the president of the UAE, Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, who agreed to Israel’s involvement in the investigation. Flydubai said its flights to and from Israel would be suspended while the investigation took place and urged all parties “to refrain from premature speculation while authorities gather the facts”. The UAE announced on Thursday that it would conduct its own investigation into the incident, which started about two and a half hours after takeoff from Dubai. It said its investigators had begun to look into the attacker’s motive and if he had any links to any “terrorist purpose”. Passengers said they saw a knife-wielding man – apparently the Omani co-pilot – putting the captain of the plane on the floor, after which the plane began to plummet. The wounded pilot, Smit Machchhar, an Indian national, managed to send out an emergency signal and open the cockpit door, allowing passengers to enter and stop the plane’s descent. A video shared by the prime minister’s office showed one passenger, Yaniv Hayoun, a plumber, speaking to Netanyahu at length about how the events onboard had played out. Hayoun told the prime minister he and other passengers heard screaming and felt the air pressure change as the plane dived before they forced their way into the cockpit and found the attacker at the instrument panel. “I grabbed the attacker, put him in a chokehold, and dragged him out first,” Hayoun said during the meeting with Netanyahu after the plane had landed safely and the passengers were flown to Israel. Machchhar was widely praised for his bravery, with Netanyahu and the Indian prime minister, Narendra Modi, hailing him as a hero. India’s ambassador to the UAE met the wounded captain’s family and briefed them on his recovery, the Indian consulate in the UAE said. Machchhar was being treated in a hospital in Tabuk, but was in good health and recovering well, according to the Indian embassy in the UAE, which said the ambassador had visited the pilot. “Captain Smit Machchhar is a HERO,” Modi said, in a post on social media. “In the face of the gravest danger and despite being seriously injured, he showed immense courage and an unwavering resolve to protect the lives of others.”

title: Crude oil exports from strait of Hormuz largely return to pre-war levels
summary: Alternative ways being used to move fuel out of Gulf region, but flows of refined products such as diesel still constrained
text: Exports of crude from the strait of Hormuz have largely returned to levels seen before the outbreak of the Iran war, as oil producers and the shipping industry have found alternative ways of transporting crucial fuel out of the Middle East. Pipeline exports and ship-to-ship transfers are among the methods being used, according to analysts tracking the situation, while the US military continues to escort some vessels. However, flows of refined products such as diesel remain constrained, pushing prices higher. At least 16.5m barrels per day (bpd) left the region in September, according to figures from the global trade intelligence firm Kpler, equalling the pre-war average, excluding Iran. The figure is 10.5m bpd higher than the monthly average for March, during the first weeks of the Iran war. Since the conflict began on 28 February with US and Israeli strikes on Iran, Tehran has sought to exert its authority on the strait of Hormuz and has at times even declared the strategic waterway closed. However, Iran’s control appears to have declined in recent weeks, as oil exporters have found workarounds to address the disruption. About 40% of the region’s crude is now transported without transiting the strait, compared with just 17% before the war, through Saudi and Emirati pipelines, according to Kpler analysis. Saudi Arabia was able to restart operations on its east-west pipeline in late September, after it was damaged during drone attacks, allowing exports from resume from the Red Sea port of Yanbu. In a sign of the other adaptations, the majority of crude transported through the strait of Hormuz is carried on a shuttle fleet mostly comprising very large crude carriers, sailing with their satellite transponders turned off. The cargo is moved on to different tankers in open water, usually off the coast of Oman or Fujairah in the United Arab Emirates. More than 70% of the crude that passed through the strait in August changed tankers, whereas before the war almost no Gulf crude changed ships in the Gulf of Oman. However, the recovery in exports from the region remains unbalanced, and supplies of refined products remain constrained. This poses a problem for businesses and households that depend on refined products such as diesel to run their cars, vans and lorries. The average diesel price in the UK hit an all-time high of 199.18p a litre on Monday, with many motorists already reporting prices above £2 on some forecourts. “Diesel carries the sharpest risk,” said Kpler analysts, who found that less than 20% of pre-war levels of refined products shipped through Hormuz were being transported. They recorded a seven-day average of 677,000 bpd of refined products as of Monday, compared with 3.6m before the conflict. Even as oil exports from the region have increased, the level of threat to ships operating around the strait of Hormuz has not disappeared. “New routes emerge, cargos are rerouted, risk is priced in and absorbed. The danger is assuming that resilience equals security. It doesn’t,” said Richard Meade, the editor in chief of shipping publication Lloyd’s List. “Oil flows have recovered because the market participants have accepted greater operational complexity and higher costs. The underlying threat remains.” The danger to vessels and their crew was highlighted on Tuesday, when three Liberian-flagged tankers were hit by projectiles while transiting the strait. The price of crude remains at elevated levels and moved higher again on Thursday, as traders balanced the recovery in some Middle East exports with uncertainty over a long-term solution to the conflict and reopening of the strait. The price of Brent crude briefly was back above $100 a barrel on Thursday, up 3% to $101. The rise came after reports that China had suspended exports of oil products to regions beyond Hong Kong and Macau, a move that would add further pressure to oil markets. Oil analysts said China’s decision could suggest it was concerned about the availability of domestic products.

title: Burnham’s reopening of Brexit debate is ‘biggest boost in my career’, says Farage
summary: Reform UK leader tells supporters PM’s move has ‘opened up a huge flank to us’
text: Nigel Farage has claimed that Andy Burnham has given him “the biggest boost in my career” by reviving the Brexit debate, which the Reform UK leader said had reopened a “huge flank” to his party. The prime minister’s pledges to the Labour conference and admission on Wednesday that rejoining the EU was among options the government would look at had put “put me back into the debate”, he said. Looking tanned and relaxed before his party’s first major rally since its conference last month, Farage indicated to reporters that he was relishing a return to the playbook that he and others deployed during the 2016 referendum. Dismissing polls showing that as much as 59% of the public favoured rejoining the EU, Farage told the Guardian: “Of course they do, until you tell them it’ll cost 25bn quid a year, until you tell him it’ll mean joining Schengen [the area of Europe that has open borders], until he tells them it will mean actually having to recommit to joining the euro. “Remember that the leavers haven’t made their arguments since 2016. The ‘remoaners’ have made their arguments every single week. I mean, do you know what? I actually think that Burnham has made a very big political mistake here.” Farage was speaking before a rally in the South Yorkshire city of Doncaster, the first of a series Reform is holding around Britain on the theme of what the party would do in its first 100 days of government. While the Reform UK leader said he believed Burnham had calculated that new language on the EU might help win back voters from the Greens in big cities, Farage added: “Here in Doncaster and across the ‘red wall’ in the north and Midlands, I think he’s opened up a huge flank to us.” To cheers from hundreds of Reform supporters who gathered inside an event space at Doncaster racecourse, Farage said: “Today I’m back on the road and today is when our general election campaign starts.” There were even bigger cheers when Farage said he would relish – “Bring it on, I say” – the prospect of fighting Burnham in red wall areas such as Doncaster on the issue of rejoining the EU. “He might just have given me the biggest boost in my career I’ve ever had. Thank you, Andy, if you’re watching.” The focus of the rally – “100 days to save Britain” – had been planned before Burnham’s announcement about UK-EU relations. However, Reform sources claim that the prime minister’s intervention has energised them and that specific donors are already discussing how they can fund a rerun of the 2016 campaign. Meanwhile, Farage strongly hinted that Reform’s internal inquiry into the donations controversy that has overshadowed the party this year would absolve two key aides and that legal action would be launched against journalists involved. Indicating that he had already seen the report and knew its conclusions, Farage said its release was “imminent”. “It’s been done. It’ll be out in public very soon and I think some of your co-conspirators might find themselves with one or two legal challenges,” he told a Channel 4 journalist among reporters who questioned him. Reform was rocked on the eve of its party conference after some of Farage’s team were filmed appearing to plot to avoid electoral laws on foreign donations in an undercover investigation broadcast by Channel 4 News. A group of investigative journalists called Verbatim, founded by the Centre for Climate Reporting, posed as a potential Reform supporter and his wealthy American father, an impermissible donor, who paid for £30,000 of polling commissioned by Reform and which benefited the party. In Channel 4 News’s investigation, footage showed that the fake UK-based supporter also had conversations with Reform’s head of policy, James Orr, who talked about commissioning polling that would be paid for by the US-based father. In footage of another meeting, a senior adviser to Farage, Dan Jukes, appeared to suggest to the fake UK-based supporter that his US-based father could make a substantial donation by channelling it through the son. Jukes has denied “any wrongdoing” while Orr has said he would cooperate with the party’s internal investigation “fully”. The Metropolitan police are carrying out a criminal investigation into Reform over allegations it broke foreign funding laws.

title: Lawmakers call for action on ‘plainly illegal’ taxpayer-funded ads to promote Trump
summary: House Democrats say officials may have illegally misused public funds to pay for president’s ‘narcissistic ego trips’
text: The Trump administration is facing growing questions over whether it illegally used taxpayer money to air television ads promoting Donald Trump five weeks before the US midterm elections. Two congressional Democrats, Jamie Raskin of Maryland and George Whitesides of California, have asked federal watchdogs to investigate the ads. Raskin, the top Democrat on the judiciary committee of the House of Representatives, and Whitesides wrote to the Government Accountability Office (GAO) and the office of special counsel (OSC) on Wednesday, describing the commercials as “desperate pre-election propaganda”. The first ad was initially broadcast on 23 September. It shows dozens of images of Trump as a singer repeats “love me”, and the UFC president, Dana White, praises the president. A second ad, which aired days later, pairs footage of Trump with audio from a rally criticizing the “deep state”. Both end with fine print saying they were paid for by the US government. “President Trump is obviously desperate for the American people to ‘love’ him, a problem that goes beyond your jurisdiction,” Raskin and Whitesides wrote in their letter. “But stealing taxpayer dollars to pay for Mr Trump’s narcissistic ego trips is plainly illegal.” The lawmakers asked the GAO to identify the source and total amount of money used, and to issue a legal decision on whether the ads broke the law. They asked the OSC to investigate and determine who should be held accountable. The lawmakers say the ads may violate four sets of laws, and cited a provision in this year’s spending act that bars funds for “publicity or propaganda”, along with the Anti-Deficiency Act, federal criminal statutes on misusing public money and the Hatch Act. The Hatch Act exempts the president but covers executive branch staff, and the lawmakers argue that employees must have helped produce the ads. Raskin and Whitesides reject the White House’s description of the ads as public service announcements. They say nearly every claim in them is false, and that they are virtually identical to Trump’s 2024 campaign ads. In one example, they say an ad credits Trump with reviving manufacturing, though the US has lost tens of thousands of manufacturing jobs in his second term, according to a February report from Congress’s joint economic committee. They also challenge the White House’s argument that the ads are not political because Trump is not on the ballot, though at an August rally he urged supporters to “pretend, please, that I’m on the ballot”. A White House spokesperson has called the ads “educational and unapologetically patriotic”. Trump said on Wednesday that he would “gladly pay the money” if the ads were found to be improper. Some Republicans have also raised concerns. The Senate majority leader, John Thune, and the senators Mike Rounds, John Kennedy and Thom Tillis have questioned the use of public money, while the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) chair, Brendan Carr, a Trump appointee, said the ads were appropriate. The ads are not the first administration advertising spending to draw scrutiny. Last year the Department of Homeland Security under Kristi Noem spent more than $200m on ads promoting her and Trump’s immigration policies. In March, Noem testified that Trump had approved the campaign (which the president denied to Reuters), and he then removed her from the secretary role, relegating her to special envoy of the “Shield of the Americas”.

title: Christa Pike: what we know so far about Tennessee woman’s failed execution
summary: Pike, sentenced to death for a 1995 murder, has survived two lethal injections and was taken to a hospital after
text: The convicted murderer Christa Pike, sentenced to death, has survived two lethal injections – we take a look at the situation and what might happen next. Why was Christa Pike on death row? Pike, now 50, was sentenced to death in 1996 at the age of 20 over the murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer in 1995. Pike and her then boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, killed Slemmer at a job training camp in Knoxville, Tennessee. In a grim revelation it emerged that a satanic symbol had been carved into Slemmer’s chest. According to the Death Penalty Information Center, the last execution of a woman in Tennessee was in 1820, meaning Pike would have been the first woman to be executed in the state in more than 200 years. Campaigners have long argued that Pike should be taken off death row, with Amnesty International noting Pike endured rape, sexual and physical violence, abuse and neglect during her childhood. “The state failed to protect her as a child despite having knowledge of what she was facing. Her court-appointed lawyers then failed her at her trial, presenting little of the mitigating evidence of this abuse or its psychological consequences,” the organisation has said. Earlier this week Tennessee’s governor, Bill Lee, denied Pike’s request for clemency. On Wednesday, the execution was temporarily blocked by judges on the sixth circuit court of appeals. However, the US supreme court subsequently stepped in to overturn the stay, allowing the execution to proceed. Did the execution go ahead? Pike was given two lethal injections late on Wednesday, but she survived both, with witnesses reporting she was still breathing after the second attempt, and some stating she was heard to snore. Pike has now been taken to the hospital. The Tennessee department of correction said in a statement: “The lethal ⁠injection chemical in the protocol has consistently been effective, and the protocol does not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried ‌out this evening.” What’s in a lethal injection? The substances used in lethal injections vary by state. Most states either use a protocol involving three different drugs – one to sedate the prisoner, one to paralyse their muscles and one to stop their heart – or a single drug. Tennessee takes the latter approach, using an injection of a barbiturate called pentobarbital. “Pentobarbital usually takes effect within seconds to minutes of injection,” said Richard Levy, a professor of anesthesiology and pediatrics at the Stanford University School of Medicine. “The intended goal of pentobarbital injection is to render the inmate unconscious and then to induce apnea – cessation of breathing. It is the cessation of breathing that then results in hypoxia – lack of adequate oxygen. Ultimately the heart stops and the prisoner dies,” he said. “However, pentobarbital may not always induce apnea – if dose is not high enough or injection is not successfully injected into a vein – and the inmate may not stop breathing. Without apnea, the injection will likely not result in death.” All lethal injections have been the subject of controversy, as is the death penalty itself. However, pentobarbital was removed from the federal protocol by the Biden administration over concerns that it could cause unnecessary pain and suffering. It was later reauthorised by the Trump administration. How could Pike have survived two doses of pentobarbital? No official explanation has been provided. The Tennessee department of correction said in a statement that they “followed every step of the State’s lawful, established execution protocol approved by the Attorney General’s Office”. Clive Stafford Smith, founder of Reprieve, who has spent 25 years working on behalf of those on death row in the US, told Al Jazeera there were two probable explanations. One, he said, is that the drugs could have been out of date – something he said could arise due to difficulties in acquiring them – while the other is that there may have been difficulties in administering the lethal injections, adding doctors are not involved in the process. Levy said the case was another botched execution and further evidence that the process of lethal injection needs to be re-evaluated. “The fact that two injections failed indicates that either the doses were too low or they were not injected into her veins,” he said. What happens next? At present it is unclear what will happen to Pike, and whether she will be executed at a future date. Lee has halted the state’s remaining executions for the rest of the year and has ordered a “comprehensive, third-party review to determine exactly what occurred”. “Carrying out a lawfully imposed sentence is among the State’s most serious responsibilities, and the people of Tennessee expect it to be done in a manner that is not only legal and constitutional, but is effective,” Lee said in a statement. Levy said policy needs to change. “Either eliminate lethal injection entirely or engage medical experts to guarantee the product,” he said.

title: Why is the UK-France ‘one in, one out’ migration deal being scrapped?
summary: Agreement expected to end on Thursday after running for 423 days, during which it has been beset by problems
text: The UK government’s “one in, one out” deal with France, which was supposed to help deter small boat arrivals, is expected to expire on Thursday, government sources have said. What was one in, one out? The deal involved returning to France one asylum seeker who had arrived in the UK in a small boat, in exchange for another brought legally to the UK from France. It lasted 423 days – from 10 July 2025 until 1 October 2026. Why didn’t it work out? The UK’s official explanation was that it had not been able to scale up the numbers of asylum seekers involved as much as it would have liked to. However, the scheme was beset with problems. Scores returned to the UK during the scheme because they felt unsafe in France. Some were returned to France a second time while others were allowed to remain in the UK to have their claims processed here. Many were believed to have vanished after being returned to France. Asylum seekers said they were threatened by smugglers because they owed them money and feared being sent back to their home countries or to another European country they had passed through on their journey. How many people were sent back under it and how many returned to the UK? Approximately 1,500 asylum seekers were returned to France, with a similar number brought legally from France to the UK. The numbers removed under the scheme were fewer than the total who arrived in small boats over seven days in the second half of last month. More than 40,000 have arrived in Britain in small boats during the period the deal has been in place. What do the French say about the scheme? It is understood France wanted to end the deal because it did not want to carry the weight of accepting small boat arrivals back from the UK alone and instead wanted the rest of Europe to also get involved. Other European countries have so far not agreed to join the scheme. “Why do we have to manage this border on our own?” the French interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, said at a parliamentary hearing this year. “We believe that France should not have to bear the burden alone, and that it would be better to incorporate it into an agreement between the European Union and the United Kingdom.” What do the British say? The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, said at a recent session of the Commons home affairs committee that it was difficult to pinpoint exactly why there had been a reduction of more than 40% in the number of people crossing the Channel so far this year compared with the same period last year. Others say that lower levels of irregular migration into the UK from France in the first five months of this year compared with the same period last year are likely at least partially to be due to a drop in arrivals of irregular migrants to Europe overall. The Home Office said it would continue to remove as many small boat arrivals as possible. But it is not possible to forcibly remove people to unsafe countries such as Iran, Eritrea, Sudan and others, where many on small boats come from. What do critics of the scheme say? NGOs such as Medical Justice have condemned the trauma they have documented due to the detention of this group, many of whom are survivors of trafficking or torture. Force was used against one in 10 of 224 asylum seekers during their removal to France in the first three months of this year, according to Home Office freedom of information data. Both the NGO Médecins Sans Frontières and the French health organisation Samusocial, which provides treatment for returnees to France, documented physical and psychological injuries. At the home affairs committee the home secretary suggested these injuries may have been self-inflicted. The Labour MP and committee member Bell Ribeiro-Addy accused the home secretary of “victim blaming” and said there was independent evidence of injuries sustained as a result of use of force. What could the UK government do now? Successive prime ministers and home secretaries have vowed to stop small boats crossing the Channel. So far none have succeeded. For as long as people flee war and conflict a percentage of them are likely to turn up in the UK by one means or another. The use of return hubs in third countries is under discussion by some European countries although no details have been confirmed. How do asylum seekers feel about the end of one in, one out? In a word, overjoyed. “Thank God. You gave me the best news,” said one asylum seeker forcibly returned to France, after hearing the news. He is now considering returning to the UK. Another who is also hoping to return said: “That’s good news. We just hope the UK doesn’t make a worse agreement with a new country.”

title: Finnish PM says suspected break-ins at MPs’ homes could be work of foreign power

text: The Finnish prime minister, Petteri Orpo, has said a foreign power could be responsible for a series of suspected break-ins at the homes of several members of parliament. Police said on Thursday they were investigating multiple reports of MPs’ homes being broken into in the Helsinki area in the last year in which nothing was stolen but subtle signs of breaking and entering were left. When asked by a reporter if a foreign power could be behind the alleged intrusions, Orpo said: “It is very possible. Quite possible in this day and age. “If someone tries to destabilise Finland, our sense of security, or our support for example for Ukraine, it has the opposite effect. It strengthens our unity.” He said the incidents would be investigated by police and within government and would be “taken very seriously”. With the Finnish parliamentary elections just six months away, Orpo said the risk of election interference must be taken seriously. “We see in several European countries that Russia has sought to influence elections,” he said. Finland shares a long border with Russia that has been closed for years amid a rapid deterioration of relations since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine and Finland joining Nato. The Finnish president, Alexander Stubb, said when asked about the suspected incidents: “An attack on a member of parliament is an attack on democracy. “It should not be allowed or accepted in any form … I stand in support of every member of parliament.” At a press conference in parliament, the speaker, Jussi Halla-aho, said he did not have an exact number of suspected cases but that it was “significant”. He said it was the kind of behaviour associated with state actors. “It is known that state actors sometimes engage in activities that resemble suspected cases, but we have no information to comment on at this time and there is no point in speculating,” Halla-aho said. Observations had been made “drop by drop”, he said. “It is possible that the marks were left visible on purpose.” According to the broadcaster Yle, suspected cases include doors being left open to homes and lights being left on. Helsinki police said they had received information from parliament about suspected intrusions at the homes of MPs and had begun a preliminary inquiry. The force said in a statement: “The Helsinki police department is working closely with the national bureau of investigation in clarifying the matter. The inquiry is at an early stage, and the police have nothing further to comment on at this time.”

title: Witnesses detail horror of Tennessee woman’s botched execution: ‘None of it was normal’
summary: Witnesses in the chamber said Christa Pike was still breathing despite receiving injections intended to kill her
text: When the prison warden asked Christa Pike if she had any last words, she said she was going to leave this world “with love” for those on her side and also the ones angry with her. What followed was the second botched execution in Tennessee this year, after two doses of the lethal injection failed to produce the desired effect. Witnesses present in the chamber said Pike was still breathing despite the injections intended to kill her late on Wednesday, that nothing about the failed execution was normal and that it was unprecedented. For their part, officials said they followed every step of the approved protocol. Pike was finally taken to the hospital after surviving the two attempts to execute her. The current status of the woman convicted of murdering a classmate in 1995 is unknown. John North, an investigative producer at WBIR television in Knoxville and also a witness at the Riverbend maximum security institution in Nashville, said when he left the building she was “probably still alive”. “This event is the worst we’ve seen and unlike any other botched execution in the modern era. There is no precedent,” said Robin Maher, the executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center, according to the New York Times. “Nothing about today was normal, typical, at all,” said Tori Gessner, a reporter and anchor at WKRN of Nashville and one of the members of the media who served as witnesses in the execution, according to NBC. “They went through two rounds, and she was still breathing at the end. She was very ragged,” said Catherine Sweeney, a reporter at the Nashville Public Radio WPLN, at a news conference after the execution attempt. “She lifted her head up and was looking around. At one point, she said … there was a spot that was burning and hurting, and asked if that was normal. None of it was normal.” Gessner also said Pike was heard saying: “My arm feels like it’s about to burst open. Does this happen like that?” Gessner described the victim as “inconsistently going in and out of snores and silence” after the injections. “When the curtains closed the final time at 8.05, we could consistently hear her snoring, and then it kind of developed into a snore squeak, and then a snore. And even at 8.53, when the microphone was cut off, we could still hear snoring.” Pike, 50, was convicted of killing Colleen Slemmer, her 19-year-old classmate at Knoxville Job Corps. She had been scheduled for execution on Wednesday and would have been the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years. An appeals court stopped the lethal injection just an hour before it was to start, but hours later the US supreme court overturned that stay. Slemmer’s mother, May Martinez, described the failed execution attempt in a phone interview with NBC News on Thursday. “It was a mess,” she said. The Tennessee governor, Bill Lee, said he was suspending all executions this year and ordered “a comprehensive, third-party review to determine exactly what occurred”. In a statement, the department of correction said the state “followed every step of the State’s lawful, established execution protocol approved by the Attorney General’s Office” and that “the lethal injection chemical in the protocol has consistently been effective.” In May, Tennessee also aborted attempts to execute a man convicted of murders after failing to find a suitable vein for his lethal injection.

title: Trump and his allies credit deportations with record low crime. Experts disagree
summary: Administration says increased immigration enforcement led to fewer homicides, but they have been on the decline since Joe Biden’s term
text: Over the last year and a half, the US has seen a historic drop in homicides. Researchers and reporters are still puzzling through the complex set of reasons why - from the easing of pandemic-era stressors and the Biden administration’s investments in community-based violence prevention to policing and other factors. But for the Trump administration, there’s one easy explanation: increased immigration enforcement. As the midterm elections approach, the White House has been doubling down on this message, saying its crackdown against immigrants is why US crime rates are now falling. “We have the most secure border in the world, nobody comes in, unless they’re invited. Unless they have permission,” Trump said during a speech to the UN general assembly last week. “As a result, last year we achieved the largest drop in violent crime ever recorded.” JD Vance, the vice-president, made a similar claim at a rally in Iowa the week prior. “When you get the violent criminals out of your country you see the largest drop in violent crime in the history of the United States of America,” he said. “Murder rates, because we got the bad guys out.” But experts say this simply isn’t true. There’s no data that proves mass deportations or enhanced immigration enforcement leads to lower crime rates, and the research that does exist shows there is no relationship between immigrants – documented or not – and homicide rates in the US, experts say. “It’s a specious claim if you’ve never attempted to verify anything with actual facts and are willing to believe what the administration will tell you,” said Pratheepan Gulasekaram, a law professor at the University of Colorado, Boulder. “If you live in a fact-free world this is the type of nonsensical data you’re willing to imbibe.” In addition, the plummeting homicide rate the US is experiencing now didn’t start during Trump’s second term. It started in 2023, when Biden was president, researchers say. Even though there’s no evidence to back up the Trump administration’s claims, Gulasekaram said xenophobia is one reason why they resonate with many Americans. “There’s an intuitive appeal to that claim if you start with the premise that foreigners are so different from us and are the source of economic and social ills,” he said. “That feeds into that underlying sentiment and it becomes extremely sticky.” Other conservatives are echoing the White House’s unsubstantiated claims by making the same link between immigrants and crime. In a May Instagram video, Erich Pratt, vice-president of Gun Owners of America argued that Americans are “enjoying unprecedented safety”, because of the Trump administration’s aggressive approach to immigration enforcement. “It didn’t come from new gun restrictions,” he said in an email to the Guardian of the plummeting homicide rates across the US. “It came from a shift in priorities. President Trump implemented measures aimed at deporting violent gang members, ending catch-and-release policies for illegal aliens, and getting repeat offenders off the streets.” A Guardian analysis published in February showed that more than 75% of people who entered deportation proceedings for the first time had no criminal convictions. Only 34 of more than 18,400 people arrested by ICE between 2025 and June this year were convicted of killing someone, according to DHS data. The most common convictions were for illegal re-entry, driving under the influence and a category marked as “other”. It’s unclear how many undocumented migrants are currently in prison for murder convictions or have been convicted for killing someone since Trump took office. State prisons track demographic information such as age, race and type of conviction but, with the exception of Texas, immigration status is not one of them. And by the federal government’s own acknowledgment, there is no comprehensive or centralized data on the citizenship status of people incarcerated in local jails and state prisons, the government accountability office said in a 28 September report. Still, Trump has spent a decade claiming, without evidence, that undocumented migrants pose a safety threat to US citizens. In his 2016 presidential run, he repeatedly talked about the killing of Kate Steinle, a 32-year-old woman who had been killed in San Francisco the year before. The man accused of killing her was undocumented, but he was eventually acquitted. And during his 2024 run, he often spoke of Laken Riley, a nursing student who was killed while she was jogging. Her killer was an undocumented immigrant, and was sentenced to life in prison. Researchers say that stories like these have long been used to push for tougher immigration policies and more deportations. “The argument in their tragic cases is that they should have never been at risk because this person should have never been able to commit these crimes,” said Michael Light, a sociology professor at the University of Wisconsin-Madison. “But that’s more of a political disagreement than an empirical one.” Leaning on these kinds of anecdotes to determine immigration policy, and then claiming that they have led to public safety can cause misunderstandings of why homicides and other crimes have decreased, Light said. “There’s no question that they’ve increased enforcement and we’ve seen a historic decrease in homicides,” he said. “But the idea that immigration policy is the only thing that’s changed is problematic. And if we misdiagnose what’s actually driving the homicide decline, that’s going to lead to bad public policy.” This week, the Department of Justice announced a new $25m grant program to support people whose loved ones were killed or injured by undocumented migrants and fund law enforcement efforts to prevent future deaths. The Guardian approached the DHS and the White House to request any data or research that can prove a causal relationship between immigration enforcement and the declining homicide rate. Both agencies reiterated their claims that deportations are the reason homicides are down, but did not supply any evidence.

title: British Sikh activist released from Delhi jail after nine-year detention
summary: Indian government issued with warning it would be in contempt of court if it failed to release Jagtar Singh Johal
text: The British Sikh activist Jagtar Singh Johal has been released from a Delhi prison after the Indian high court warned the government it would be found in contempt of court if it continued to attempt to keep him in jail despite an 18 September court order releasing him on bail. Johal has been incarcerated for nine years without any full trial. The court order was issued after Johal’s lawyers issued a writ of habeas corpus alleging he was being detained against the express direction of the court. Johal’s nine-year detention on alleged terrorist offences, has been a cause of diplomatic tension between the UK and India, but campaigners have claimed the British government has not been active enough to secure his release or, alternatively, a full trial. The campaign group Reprieve says his case has never come to full trial largely because of the inability of the Indian government to assemble credible witnesses to back their claim that Johal transported £3,000 to France to fund a multinational extremist plot involving targeted killings in the Punjab in 2016-17. On Thursday morning, the high court in Delhi instructed the Indian government to release Johal by 2.30pm Indian time, giving government officials three hours to comply or find themselves risking contempt proceedings. In the end, he was released in the late afternoon wearing a red T-shirt to be greeted by friends, family and flowers. Documents shown to the court by Johal’s lawyers on behalf of his father-in-law as petitioner revealed that messages from the prison to the Ministry of Home Affairs seeking permission for his release had been left unanswered. His lawyers in their petition stated he had met all the bail conditions yet “the detainee has nevertheless not been released, and is being held in custody without the authority of any court, pending a ‘clarification’ sought by the jail from the Ministry of Home Affairs”. The petition added that no clarification from the ministry had been forthcoming, explaining: “Every day of such detention is a continuing violation of the detainee’s fundamental rights under article 21 of the constitution of India.” Johal has been detained by Indian authorities since 4 November 2017. He is facing eight charges of terrorism in the federal court, but had been cleared of largely similar charges by a Punjab court. He claims any initial confessions he gave were extracted under torture. The bail terms last week imposed 11 conditions, including surrender of passport, a personal bond of 500,000 Indian rupees (£3,930) with two sureties, fortnightly reporting to the investigating officer, prior intimation of any change of residence and a ban on travelling to the Punjab. He was also restricted from talking to media about the case directly or indirectly. The Indian government has alleged the Khalistan Liberation Force undertook the killings and Johal had “complete knowledge of the conspiracy” and was a KLF member. His Dumbarton-based brother Gurpreet Singh Johal said: “There have been so many setbacks and disappointments in the last nine years that I didn’t dare to believe it until I saw Jagtar walking out of the prison gates with my own eyes. The last two weeks have been torture – knowing that Jagtar had been granted bail, but the authorities were refusing to let him out. I’ll sleep well tonight, knowing that he’s not behind bars. “Tomorrow morning, the fight continues, because he’s still on trial and facing the death penalty for something he didn’t do, trapped in a sham legal process designed to punish him for standing up for human rights”. Reprieve’s deputy executive director, Dan Dolan, said: “While tonight is the first night in almost nine years that Jagtar Singh Johal is not caged in a prison cell, he still has the threat of a death sentence hanging over him. It should also be noted that, despite bail being ordered, the prison refused to release Jagtar until his family brought a habeas corpus petition and a judge warned the jail they’d be found in contempt of court”. The UK Foreign Office is understood to have been supporting recent calls for his release on bail after last week’s court order, as have two campaign groups in the UK Redress and Reprieve.

title: Travelodge guests are still at risk, finds review launched after sexual assault
summary: Report finds complaints of room intrusions at nearly one in 10 hotels, after woman attacked by man given a copy of her key
text: An independent review into Travelodge after a serious sexual assault has found that guests are still at risk, with room intrusions reported at nearly one in 10 of its hotels this summer. The damning findings were published in a 70-page report on Thursday, which was commissioned earlier this year after a man was convicted of a serious sexual assault against a Travelodge guest in Maidenhead in 2022. The perpetrator was handed a copy of the victim’s room key, having falsely claimed to be her boyfriend, and sexually assaulted her in her hotel bed. The victim – referred to as “Lily” in the report – was later offered what she described as an “insulting” £30 refund. The incident prompted further reports of security failings at the hotel chain, eventually leading to the resignation of Joanna Boydell as chief executive in August. Paul Greaney KC, the barrister who led the review, said Lily “was treated by Travelodge in a way that was inappropriate and unfair; indeed, it was disgraceful” He said the hotel’s response to her complaint “was driven by a desire to get rid of the complaint as quickly and cheaply as possible”. The report said: “Travelodge’s treatment of Lily, following her complaint in writing, fell short of every standard the public would expect of an organisation such as Travelodge. It was simply appalling. “Overall, these failings are extremely serious and rest principally with the organisation, rather than with any individual [member of staff].” Greaney acknowledged that Travelodge had been trying to improve its room security policies and training since March. However, he said not enough had yet been done to ensure guests were safe. Despite Travelodge strengthening its key security policy, Greaney found it was “not being applied with anything like sufficient consistency on the ground. In other words, it has not sufficiently embedded.” “Even in this period of strong improvement, there were reports by guests of room intrusion across nearly one in 10 of Travelodge hotels, which represents around 60 hotels,” the report said. “I am not satisfied that enough has yet occurred to make guests as safe as they should be when staying in a Travelodge,” Greaney added. Although the review was focused on the budget chain’s failings, the KC said guests were suffering unacceptable security breaches in hotels across the country and room intrusions “are a problem across the hotel sector”. The review put forward a series of recommendations, including: Creating a new policy to address violence against women and girls. Improving safety policies for staff working alone. Introducing body cameras for all reception staff. Installing consistent CCTV systems across all its hotels. Introducing mystery shoppers to test its key security policy. Travelodge said it welcomed the report’s recommendations, had put together a new board committee to ensure they were implemented and planned to track their progress over the next six to 12 months. In a statement released alongside the review, Travelodge’s interim chief executive, Ray Reidy, said: “I apologise unreservedly on behalf of Travelodge to all guests where we have failed, and particularly to Lily. We have made significant progress in preventing and addressing these issues over the past six months, and we recognise we still have further to go. “We are working hard to transform our customer service so we respond appropriately when things don’t go right. We will continue to improve so customers get the right level of support and empathy when they need it most.”
