title: Bedford rail crash: train sped up after red light warning, say investigators
summary: Driver of East Midlands train, who died in June crash, received automatic warning after passing red light but train continued to accelerate
text: The train that ran into the back of another in the Bedford rail crash sped up after the driver received a warning he had passed a red light, rail investigators have reported. The driver of the East Midlands train, who died in the crash in June, acknowledged the automatic warning but did not appear to act after passing a danger signal that was rarely ever red. According to an updated report by the Rail Accident Investigation Branch, the train continued to accelerate before the driver applied the emergency brakes when the stationary train in front came into view. The train, a southbound Luton airport express from Corby, could not stop in time, and the collision killed the driver, 60-year-old Shaun Burton, who was described by his employers as a “dedicated railway professional”. Investigators had been seeking to establish if the automatic warning system (AWS) had worked properly, after an initial report found the train had passed a red signal. The latest interim report published on Thursday concluded that the driver had acknowledged the warning, which had not previously displayed a red light during all of 2026, but continued to accelerate to 76mph. After braking, the train slowed to 49mph before it collided with a stationary Nottingham-London train on the same track. The first train had stopped after braking when an AWS warning incorrectly sounded after passing a green signal. The train was a new Aurora class 810 model built by Hitachi, brought into service within the past six months on East Midlands Railway. In a cab with an unfamiliar layout, when no warning signal was expected, the RAIB report said that “neither the driver nor driving instructor recognised this sound as being an AWS warning indication”. Without an acknowledgment in 2.7 seconds, the system applies an emergency brake. The accident inspectors reported that in the weeks after the crash, another class 810 train had also incorrectly received an AWS warning indication at the same signal on green. The RAIB said it would continue to seek to understand why the Corby train had passed a red light, and whether its safety systems had been functioning correctly, as well as the reason why the first Nottingham train had come to a halt. The report said 160 people had also been injured in the crash, which happened at about 5.13pm on 19 June. It was the fourth involving passenger trains on the UK railway since 2020, after more than a decade without any similar serious incident.

title: Ukraine persists with Russian oil refinery strikes in defiance of Trump
summary: US president blames attacks for driving up fuel prices before midterms, though analysts say his Iran war is main cause
text: Ukraine is pressing on with strikes on Russian oil refineries, defying Donald Trump, who blames the attacks for exacerbating a global diesel shortage and pushing up fuel prices. Kyiv struck an oil facility in Russia’s southern Samara region overnight, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Thursday in a statement on social media. The Ukrainian president added that a Russian vessel in the Black Sea was hit, as well as a launch and storage site for attack drones in the Oryol region. Trump has urged Zelenskyy in a private phone call to halt attacks on Russian refineries and repeatedly suggested in public that Ukraine’s strikes are to blame for the squeeze on global fuel supplies. “Diesel is really hurt much more, not by the Middle East, but by what’s going on in Russia, because those diesel refineries are being knocked out at a pretty alarming rate,” Trump said on Wednesday. Diesel prices in the US have risen to record highs in recent weeks, adding to cost of living pressures that have helped push Trump’s approval ratings to a career low before next month’s crucial midterm elections. Energy analysts, however, have pointed to the war in Iran and wider disruption to global oil markets as the leading drivers of the price increases. Ukraine’s long-range strikes on Russian refineries have nevertheless emerged as an additional headache for Trump, with the attacks also contributing to tighter diesel supplies at a politically sensitive moment for the US president. Ukraine’s campaign in recent months has knocked out more than 45% of Russia’s refining capacity, according to Ukrainian estimates, prompting fuel rationing in some regions and long queues at petrol stations. The Ukrainian president on Thursday also said the FP-7 tactical ballistic missile, which has a range of 200km and was developed by the Ukrainian defence firm FirePoint, had been deployed for the first time. Zelenskyy accompanied the statement with footage of a missile launch, but did not disclose when or where the weapon had been used. Speaking at the Valdai discussion club, Vladimir Putin on Thursday acknowledged that Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries had cost the country roughly 1% of its GDP. Earlier this week, Russia – traditionally the world’s second-largest diesel exporter – extended its ban on diesel exports until the end of October, adding further pressure to a global supply crunch. Mykola Bielieskov, a military analyst at Ukraine’s government-run National Institute for Strategic Studies, said it was unlikely Kyiv would stop targeting Russian oil infrastructure as long as Moscow continued its daily attacks on Ukraine. “There is no rationale for Ukraine to continue exercising restraint while it is being bombarded and major urban areas are under constant attack,” he said. “We need to deprive Russia of revenue,” he added. Zelenskyy has been pushing for a US-brokered energy ceasefire with Russia, but Putin has shown little interest in the proposal, instead vowing to intensify strikes on Ukraine. At Valdai, Putin called “absurd” a proposal he said was be discussed, under which Russia would stop striking Ukrainian vessels if Ukraine halted attacks on Russian oil refineries. In wide-ranging comments at the forum, Putin said Moscow was not on the verge of attacking foreign factories producing weapons for Ukraine, but that such facilities were something Russia’s military and intelligence services needed to monitor closely. He also ramped up his nuclear rhetoric, warning that Russia would consider using “all types of weapons” if its exclave of Kaliningrad was attacked, while insisting that Moscow had “no intention of attacking anyone”. Tensions over the exclave have risen this week, with Russia previously sending a letter to Nato warning it would be ready to resort to using nuclear weapons if the western alliance attempted to cut off Kaliningrad. Meanwhile, Russia has continued its deadly missile and drone strikes on Ukrainian cities, targeting energy infrastructure, commercial warehouses and other businesses in an apparent effort to cripple the country’s economy and render Kyiv increasingly uninhabitable. A Russian drone struck a school in Kyiv on Thursday morning, but no one was injured because the children were sheltering in the basement, mayor Vitali Klitschko said. A key bridge in the Ukrainian capital was also hit, forcing authorities to suspend metro services and other public transport. Kyiv has experienced near round-the-clock Russian attacks in recent weeks, at times increasingly resembling a frontline city in what many see as the most challenging period for the capital since the early days of the full-scale invasion. Russia’s newer jet-powered drones have proved particularly difficult for Ukrainian air defences to intercept, with success rates significantly lower than for the slower Shahed-type drones. The sustained attacks have revived fears of another winter with prolonged power and heating outages, after similar strikes last year left parts of Ukraine without electricity during temperatures that fell as low as -20C (-4F).

title: White House airs new taxpayer-funded ad praising Trump’s war on Iran
summary: New ad features audio from Trump’s declaration of war and Pete Hegseth saying ‘if you kill Americans … we will kill you’
text: The latest in a series of pro-Trump television ads aired using taxpayer funds in the run-up to the the midterm elections is a one-minute spot that celebrates Donald Trump’s decision to go to war with Iran. The ad aired during a commercial break on Fox News on Wednesday night, according video posted online by MeidasTouch, a leftwing outlet. A copy of the new ad posted on social media by Medium Buying, a company that purchases airtime for Republican candidates, features audio taken from the president’s 28 February declaration that the United States military had begun major combat operations in Iran. “This regime will soon learn that no one should challenge the strength and might of the United States armed forces,” Trump can be heard saying over images of combat, some of which appear to be dramatizations or computer-generated. A cover version of John Lee Hooker’s Boom Boom provides the soundtrack. The audio then switches to comments made by Pete Hegseth, the US defense secretary, in a briefing on the third day of the war. “He reminded the world, as he has time and time again, being an American means something unbreakable,” Hegseth says over slow-motion images of Trump walking down a corridor. “If you kill Americans, if you threaten Americans anywhere on Earth, we will hunt you down without apology and without hesitation and we will kill you,” Hegseth says. “We didn’t start this war, but under President Trump, we are finishing it. Their war on Americans has become our retribution against their ayatollah.” As the words “Paid for by the US Government” appear at the bottom of the screen, the ad’s audio switches back to Trump’s call for regime change in Iran in his announcement of the war in February. “To the great proud people of Iran, I say tonight that the hour of your freedom is at hand,” Trump can be heard saying, against a backdrop of dramatic music and images of Iranian Americans in New York celebrating the US strikes on 1 March. “When we are finished, take over your government. It will be yours to take.” The images of Iranian Americans demonstrating in support of Trump’s war in New York City, marching down 42nd Street and holding signs that read “Thank you President Trump”, were all previously included in a White House video posted on YouTube on 4 March. The focus of the ad on speeches and images of celebration that all came in the first three days of the war, when it looked like Iran’s government could collapse, raises questions about why the administration is releasing it as the war enters its seventh month and continues to alienate many of Trump’s supporters.

title: Should cockpits stay locked from the inside? Flydubai stabbing raises flight security questions
summary: Co-pilot who attacked captain in apparent attempt to crash flight casts doubt over locked-door policy
text: Cockpit security on planes will come under renewed scrutiny after passengers and one wounded pilot joined forces to prevent flydubai flight FZ 1073 from crashing. With more than 170 people, mostly Israeli, on board the jet heading from Dubai to Tel Aviv, some have spoken of averting “Israel’s 9/11”. However, the changes made to plane design after the terrorist hijackings in the US a quarter of a century ago, locking cockpit doors from the inside, have divided expert opinion. Wednesday’s events, during which one pilot stabbed another and apparently tried to crash the plane, again raises the question of where the biggest threat lies. “We have as an industry lost more lives on commercial aircraft as a result of aircraft-assisted suicide since 9/11 than we have due to terrorism,” says Philip Baum, an international aviation security expert. “And in most of those cases, it was because we had created a fortress that could not be broken into by the good guys who were outside the flight deck to neutralise the rogue individuals – usually pilots inside the cockpit.” On the flydubai flight, despite being stabbed, the captain Smit Machchhar managed to resist his attacker, the unnamed Omani co-pilot. Crucially, Machchhar was also able to ensure help reached him from the cabin by making sure the doors could be breached. Two pilots are normally required on deck under safety rules – primarily discussed for if one gets sick, rather than goes rogue. Since 9/11, commercial aircraft have also had locked doors in place where the pilot effectively holds the key. The configuration of locks can vary and while crew have access codes for emergencies, the pilot can normally override attempts to gain access – a system designed with hijackers in mind. The crash of Germanwings flight 4U9525 in 2015 was, perhaps until this week, the most incontrovertible demonstration of the danger it posed: the captain locked out by a suicidal co-pilot who deliberately crashed the plane in the Alps, killing 150 people. It had been preceded by a smaller and less reported Mozambique Airlines plane crash in 2013, killing 33, that was judged by investigators to have been suicide by pilot, with the co-pilot apparently locked out. Questions also remain over the role of pilot intent in major disasters whose causes have yet to be proved – not least the mystery of Malaysia Airilnes flight MH370, as well as the Air India crash in Ahmedabad in 2025, or China Eastern in 2022. Without malign intent, doors can be opened in incidents of “pilot incapacitation”, such as heart attacks. A Lufthansa plane flew for 10 minutes over Spain in 2024 with no one at the controls when the captain went to the bathroom and was locked out of the cabin after the co-pilot blacked out. The captain reached the deck to land the plane using an emergency entry door code – but a conscious attacker could have blocked the request. On the balance of risks, Baum argues, there needs to be some kind of override system for the cockpit doors – whether timed, or from the ground. But preserving security begins well before the cockpit doors: “The primary method is to ensure that the people that you are employing have gone through extensive background checks, gone through medicals, psychological appraisals – and that that process doesn’t stop once employment commences.” With the motives of the Omani co-pilot in the latest attack still as yet unknown, Israel is introducing measures to do greater background screening of pilots, while flydubai has cancelled further Tel Aviv flights and British ministers have said they will “be looking at” the safety of flights to Israel. Pilots may be reluctant to fly routes where they undergo greater screening – or indeed officially admit to mental health issues, a much more common threat than radicalisation. The UK pilots’ union Balpa said it would “caution against premature speculation and urge all parties to allow the relevant authorities to investigate without interference”. The full facts of the co-pilot’s actions are yet to be established, but, says Baum: “Whatever happened yesterday, we know that that cockpit barrier can impede a rescue attempt if there are rogue pilots.”

title: Mamdani’s nuanced plan offers a roadmap to tackle antisemitism – and reignites criticism of the mayor
summary: Critics noted that the plan does not discuss Israel; others praised it for not conflating Jews with the state of Israel
text: When the New York City mayor, Zohran Mamdani, announced the city’s first-ever municipal strategy to address antisemitism – a nuanced, multi-pronged approach ranging from greater security measures for synagogues to an increased focus on Jewish history in public school education – critics were quick to note what the 33-page document does not mention at all: Israel. Israel has played an outsized role in Mamdani’s campaign and since his election, with the mayor standing by his years-long support for Palestinians, and frequently describing Israel’s actions in Gaza as genocide and it’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, as a war criminal. His positions have split New York’s Jewish communities, and earned him frequent accusations that he is fomenting the very antisemitism he has pledged to fight. At the United Nations general assembly last week, Netanyahu – who is wanted for war crimes and crimes against humanity by the international criminal court (ICC) and whom Mamdani had at one point pledged to arrest – called him “the antisemitic mayor of New York”. Mamdani has gone to great lengths to engage with representatives of New York’s many Jewish communities and the antisemitism strategy, several of them said, reflects those conversations and the mayor’s willingness to listen to those communities’ concerns. “This strategy is an important intervention that reflects the voices of the hundreds of Jewish New Yorkers consulted throughout the process, that celebrates the diversity and vibrancy of Jewish New Yorkers, and that commits real city resources to fighting antisemitism wherever it appears,” Rabbi Jill Jacobs, chief executive of T’ruah: The Rabbinic Call for Human Rights, said in a statement. Still, many of the critiques hinge on an absence: Mamdani’s strategy does not endorse a specific definition of antisemitism, the subject of many disputes largely stemming from the centrality of Israel to Jewishness. Instead it mentions three different ones while noting that “New York City can and will leverage all of the tools at its disposal to combat antisemitism effectively without needing to adopt a definition for this specific form of hate.” Federal hate crimes statutes, the strategy notes, also do not adopt a standalone definition of discrimination. Instead, the strategy, which was announced on Tuesday, cites extensive polling capturing how Jewish Americans feel about safety and antisemitism and notes the diversity of ways in which they experience antisemitism. “These experiences are shaped by individual perception, context and a person’s sense of safety, and may vary from person to person while still reflecting real concerns felt more broadly across communities,” the strategy notes. The document adds that New York police have reported a “notable increase” of anti-Jewish crimes in the three years since the 7 October Hamas attacks in Israel and its subsequent war in Gaza, and references a string of antisemitic incidents across the country going back years, including the attack on the Tree of Life Synagogue in Pittsburgh, which killed 11 people in 2018. While Jews make up 12% of the city’s population, antisemitic crimes make up more than half of all hate crimes, the mayor said in a video introducing the strategy. “This is not only unacceptable, it’s something we all have an obligation to change,” Mamdani said. The plan has reignited criticism of the mayor – from both pro-Israel and pro-Palestine camps. A coalition of Jewish organizations and the New York board of rabbis wrote in a joint statement that the strategy “fails to address a central issue that the Mayor himself has perpetuated: rhetoric that demonizes and delegitimizes Israel inevitably leads to the targeting of Jewish New Yorkers”. Meanwhile, some of the left have also been unhappy with the plan. “One loud camp is (predictably) saying that Mamdani’s antisemitism plan is not Zionist enough, while another is claiming it’s (somehow) too Zionist,” noted Ben Lorber, an analyst who researches antisemitism. “Of course, the issue of antisemitism is overdetermined today by Israel/Palestine. But at root this is a municipal hate crimes prevention strategy. Nobody benefits by obsessively reading it through the [Israel/Palestine] prism.” Those who praised the plan saw the omission of Israel as a welcome and deliberate effort to separate what has so often been conflated: antisemitism and criticism of Israel, which can veer into antisemitism but is not that by default. Mamdani’s plan “makes it really clear that Israel is not a synonym for Jew”, Lila Corwin Berman, director of the center for American Jewish history at New York University, said. “Jews are not the same as Israel. “In a very material way it is resisting what I think is a vector of antisemitism, which is the conflation of Jews with the state of Israel, which tends to produce some awfully antisemitic kinds of actions.” She added: “If there is a sort of downside to it, I think it might be that it takes some critical thinking skills to understand why they’re approaching the topic in the way they did and not foregrounding Israel and Zionism.” Still, she said: “Some people, they feel as if Mamdani’s views on Israel are disqualifying.” Mamdani’s plan came just a day after the US commission on civil rights, a bipartisan federal agency tasked with monitoring civil rights enforcement, issued a 220-page report on campus antisemitism. The report analyzed how anti-discrimination protections enshrined in the Civil Rights Act apply to campus antisemitism and drew a distinction – collapsed by both the Trump administration and many universities – between conduct “motivated by hostility toward people of Jewish ancestry as such” and speech criticizing “ideas or institutions” such as Israel or Zionism. “The report makes clear that the former can constitute discrimination under the Civil Rights Act, while the latter generally cannot,” said Amanda Shanor, a law professor at the University of Pennsylvania who has written about the Trump administration’s instrumenatlization of antisemitism charges. “The report explains that rallies, chants and protests directed at a campus community as a whole also generally do not constitute the type of targeted discrimination or harassment that is actionable under civil rights laws.” Mamdani’s plan offers a roadmap for municipal efforts to tackle antisemitism, and the commission’s report offers a legal framework for universities addressing campus antisemitism while respecting free expression, freedom of assembly, and academic freedom. But the two documents offer nuanced interventions, informed by a diversity of perspectives, in a debate that has been largely flattened amid heated political rhetoric, said Jonathan Jacoby, the president of the Nexus Project, a Jewish group dedicated to combating antisemitism and upholding free speech. “Some institutions and individuals are going to just see it as an opportunity to continue to bash Mamdani for reasons that have to do more with their own opinions about Israel than they have to do with antisemitism,” he added. “Mamdani’s strategy respects the complexity of the issue, and there are those who will try to dumb down the issue and flatten the complexity.”

title: ‘Page one of repressive playbook’: critics warn of Trump’s conspiratorial attacks
summary: President’s outlandish and extensive conspiracy theories endanger US freedoms, health and science, experts say
text: Since the start of his second presidency, Donald Trump has often launched outlandish conspiratorial attacks on critics and foes that mock them and label their views as hoaxes, prompting scholars and legal experts to say Trump’s attacks endanger US freedoms, public health and science. Trump’s extensive use of conspiracy theories is the hallmark of an authoritarian leader that has weakened trust in the coming midterm elections, dangerously ignored scientific evidence, and often pushed for prosecutions of his political enemies in ways that seriously erode civil liberties, say critics. Trump’s conspiratorial and authoritarian-style tactics are palpable say critics, in his false claim that the US faces a “crisis of election security” to bolster his radical push for new curbs on voting rights, and his labeling of climate change as a “hoax” despite extensive scientific evidence that it’s a reality. To some scholars, Trump-backed conspiratorial claims have had a damaging impact on all levels of US society and democracy and are emblematic of how authoritarian leaders use conspiracies to justify repression. Steven Levitsky, the Harvard professor of government and the co-author of How Democracies Die, said: “Conspiracies are page one of the repressive playbook,” noting that Mao, Stalin, Putin and other authoritarian leaders have historically launched attacks on enemies by floating conspiracies. “They’re almost always used to justify repression,” Levitsky added noting that authoritarian leaders can simply allege conspiracies without providing any or only minimal “evidence”. In a notable twist, Trump charged in mid-September that some AI leaders and experts were engaging in a big “conspiracy” and perpetrating a “HOAX”, by urging strong safeguards to protect against potential extinction-level threats to humanity from this powerful new technology. Similarly, Trump without evidence disparaged critics of datacenters as people who “want to end up being backwards and poor”, and asserted he was the best “guardrail” to protect society from threats that unregulated AI pose. Scholars and former federal officials say that Trump’s tarring foes in conspiratorial attacks endangers democracy and recall the tactics of the infamous rightwing lawyer Roy Cohn, a key promoter of the “red scare” in the 1950s who Trump had close ties with in the 1980s during his early New York real estate career. “Trump, mentored by Roy Cohn, learned that baseless allegations about shady forces working against him could serve to mobilize and lead the public to see him as a victim rather than a wrongdoer,” said the Princeton historian Julian Zelizer. “Whenever faced with criticism, such as from the media or about his AI policies, his instinct is to throw out charges of a vast conspiracy that is out to get him.” Zelizer stressed: “Trump’s frequent use of conspiracies to attack critics has a damaging impact on all levels of society and democracy, from weakening confidence in elections to hurting our ability to deal with serious problems involving the AI industry.” Trump’s penchant to paint critics in conspiratorial tones as dangerous enemies was palpable in his attacks last week on three news outlets – CNN, Politico and MS Now – barring them from White House access which prompted them to jointly file a lawsuit on 21 September challenging his moves on First Amendment and due process grounds. In a Truth Social post on 21 September, Trump boasted that the White House “is instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS, something that has grown like Cancer in our beloved United States of America. It is corrupt, purposeful, pervasive, fully coordinated, and totally out of control. It is a threat to our National Security, and must be stopped, NOW!” A federal judge in DC ruled on 23 September that the administration should immediately return the press passes to the three outlets and its punitive action against them was probably unconstitutional. Former federal prosecutor Ty Cobb who was a special counsel in the White House during Trump’s first term, warned that “Trump denies, denigrates and demeans his foes by painting them as part of a conspiracy … He resorts to abject fabrications in response to any criticism or resistance.” This year Trump and his justice department have devoted sizable resources to bolster his conspiratorial claims that his 2020 loss to Joe Biden was due to fraud, and that the current voting system is riddled with fraud, notwithstanding overwhelming evidence to the contrary. Trump has repeatedly pushed bogus claims laced with conspiracies as he did in a nationally televised speech on 16 July, when he urged tough new measures to curb voting by mail and investigate non-citizen voting ostensibly to make elections more secure. In the TV speech, Trump made the factually inaccurate claim that non-citizen voting, which is illegal and historically negligible, poses a “crisis of election security”. Trump’s obsession with painting non-citizen voting as a crisis is badly undercut by data from the conservative Heritage Foundation that cites just 100 cases over a 25-year period. Critics see these moves by Trump to raise bogus fears about election safety and dark forces bent on voter fraud as a tool to “undermine public confidence” in the elections. “It seems that the Trump administration is grooming the electorate to believe that the fall election will abound with fraud,” said Barbara McQuade, a former US attorney who teaches law at the University of Michigan. “It is difficult to know if this effort is a pretext for seizing voting equipment, a strategy to intimidate some likely Democratic voters from showing up at the polls, or a campaign to undermine public confidence in the outcome, but all of it is harmful to democracy.” On another front, Trump’s justice department has struggled for almost a year to find evidence to bring charges in an investigation looking at a “grand conspiracy” against Trump involving the so called “deep state” going back to President Barack Obama and inquiries into Russia’s efforts to influence the 2016 election. The investigation, which Trump has cheered on, has issued subpoenas to several former national security and law enforcement officials including ex-CIA director John Brennan and ex-FBI director James Comey. This sprawling inquiry has tapped some key Trump-allied election denialists for top posts. Notably, Trump recruited 81-year-old Joe diGenova, a former prosecutor who led the effort until he abruptly announced his departure on 10 September, and ex-White House lawyer Kurt Olsen. Both lawyers had worked to discredit the 2020 election results and Joe Biden’s win. The sudden move by diGenova to resign – after only five months on the job – raised questions about its direction and credibility. DiGenova’s departure followed that of another top prosecutor who was heading the investigation; Maria Medetis Long, a veteran national security prosecutor, resigned in April after reportedly voicing concerns about its direction. “The so-called Grand Conspiracy investigation turns prosecutorial practice on its head,” said ex-justice department inspector general Michael Bromwich who has represented ex-FBI deputy director Andrew McCabe in the inquiry. “It starts with designated targets, the president’s perceived enemies, and then searches for facts and bends the law to support the theory. Joe diGenova found that it was easier to be an outside propagandist cheering the theory from the sidelines than have the responsibility to build such a case with actual facts.” In other energy and environmental matters, Trump and his top officials have deployed bogus conspiracies and specious information to counter growing evidence of the risks posed by climate change from rising temperatures to dangerous storms worldwide. The Trump administration has moved hard to kill energy and environmental regulations aimed at fighting climate change, and simultaneously have promoted greater usage of coal, which Trump has lauded erroneously as “clean and beautiful”, and other fossil fuels that worsen climate change. Late last year, Trump energy officials issued emergency orders to keep open five ageing coal plants in Michigan and four other states that were scheduled to shut down, spurring some states to challenge the costly moves. In mid-September, a federal judge ruled that the energy department had exceeded its authority by ordering the Michigan plant to stay open past its retirement. Further, after years of conspiratorial attacks on wind energy by Trump, his administration in December announced it was pausing leases on five offshore wind projects on the east coast in a big blow to the industry. The five windfarms were slated to power over 2.5m homes and create 10,000 jobs. A federal judge in February issued a preliminary injunction allowing one of the five to stay open. “Trump’s decisions make no sense from either the perspective of environmental protection or the cost of energy,” Naomi Oreskes, a Harvard University science historian and professor of earth and planetary sciences, told the Guardian earlier this year. Oreskes added that “by blocking wind projects that [were] just about ready to go on line, and reviving dangerous and uneconomic coal-powered plants, this administration is raising both the direct costs of energy for the American people, and the indirect costs we suffer through polluted air and climate damage.” Significantly, the Trump administration in February revoked a major scientific finding that climate change endangers public health, an idea that Trump has derided as “a scam”, despite numerous scientific studies saying it’s a well quantifiable harm. Dr Howard Frumkin, a professor emeritus of public health at the University of Washington told PBS: “It boggles the mind that the administration is rescinding the endangerment finding; it’s akin to insisting that the world is flat or denying that gravity is a thing.” In healthcare too, Trump and Robert F Kennedy Jr, the secretary of health and human services (HHS) who has a long history of making factually erroneous claims about vaccine safety, have indulged in flawed and conspiratorial claims about vaccines. Trump declared flatly in August that the combined MMR vaccine for children could be “quite lethal”, but failed to offer scientific evidence to back his claim. Trump too has advocated breaking up longstanding immunizations into three separate shots that currently are not available in the United States. Even as the death toll from the worst outbreak of measles in decades rises, Kennedy on 16 September starred at a Washington DC conference of the anti-vaccine organization Children’s Health Defense, which he spearheaded for almost two decades. “Let me be clear. You have a strong and steadfast friend at the White House,” Kennedy told the gathering in an almost 90-minute talk. “You have friends in the White House, and we are doing this one day at a time.” According to recent polls about one-quarter of Americans now have doubts about the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccines in the wake of multi-year campaigns against immunizations by groups that once were fringe figures. From a historical perspective, Zelizer noted that conspiracy theories in American politics have a long history, but that before Trump “the role of presidents and other high-level elected officials had been to push back against this part of politics, rather than to amplify these ideas.”

title: Trump the environmentalist? How his Iran war exposed the fragility of dirty energy
summary: Gavin Newsom says Trump is a ‘gift’ to the climate cause for dispelling notions of fossil fuel energy security
text: Of all the epithets hurled at Donald Trump since he became US president, perhaps the most unusual was delivered last week – that he is, in fact, some sort of environmentalist. Trump is the “greatest gift” to the environmental movement, argued Gavin Newsom, California’s governor, due to the fallout from the US-Israel war on Iran. “He’s woken the world up to how vulnerable we are to petro-dictatorships, how vulnerable we are to disruptions in the Middle East,” Newsom told the Guardian during Climate Week in New York. “This war has completely gutted any sort of romantic notions of energy security and it’s compelled folks to think differently. It’s accelerating investments and clean energy and renewables.” If Trump has been an accidental environmentalist, it’s been in the international sphere. The strait of Hormuz, where a fifth of the world’s oil and gas exports usually flow, is now starting to open up but has been routinely snarled since the Iran war began in February, causing the cost of these fossil fuels to soar around the world. Countries reacted by scrambling to cut their oil and gas use while turning to cleaner forms of energy such as solar and wind (although there’s also been a small rise in coal, the dirtiest of fossil fuels). The overall consequence has been a positive one for our shared climate, with global fossil fuel emissions set to drop by 0.5% this year due to the crisis, Carbon Brief has estimated. The peak in oil consumption may have been sped up enough to arrive this year, rather than the previous estimate of 2029, according to the International Energy Agency. By launching the war, Trump is set to achieve something only dreamed about by climate advocates and not seen outside global economic crashes or the Covid pandemic – an annual reduction in the emissions that are overheating our planet. The president’s imposition of tariffs and importation of foreign ground beef, meanwhile, may also end up hurting the US cattle industry, another major source of greenhouse gas emissions. “It’s a curious thing to say, but I believe it,” Newsom, a potential contender for the Democratic presidential nomination, said of Trump as a sort of unintentional biophile. “This moment will mark how we can’t go back to our original form.” Yet the idea of Trump as an environmentalist, even an accidental one, can still appear faintly absurd. His administration has eviscerated pollution limits on cars, trucks and power plants, funnelled taxpayer cash and favors to the fossil fuel industry and set about unilaterally cancelling renewable energy projects. Trump, who has never by available evidence ever set a Florsheimed foot in any of the US’s national parks, has called environmentalists “terrorists”, the climate crisis “a hoax” and has slashed conservation rules to the extent you can now kill a protected species as long as it wasn’t provably intentional. Perhaps tellingly, when asked during the 2024 election campaign about his environmental credentials, Trump cited his Florida golf course getting awards for “the way I built it, for the water, the way I use the water, the sand, the mixing of the sand and the water”. Critics say this record overshadows any embrace of clean energy by other countries spooked by an oil price that has hovered about $100 a barrel for months but should, at some point in the interminable Iran conflict, drop well below this. The impetus for quitting fossil fuels could wither when it does so. “Trump’s illegal attack on Iran may hasten clean energy in some countries, but he has gutted green tech in the United States and set us back decades,” said Rob Jackson, a climate scientist at Stanford University who said Newsom was guilty of “tunnel vision” in his framing of Trump. “The notion that he is an accidental environmentalist is wishful thinking.” The conflict may have rocked the oil and gas industry but it has also enriched it, netting eight of the largest companies more than $90bn in just the first three months of the war, with even pro-oil Trump complaining that the major fossil fuel firms are “making too much money”. There is little sign big oil fears a looming obsolescence when this bonanza ends. Last month, Exxon forecast that while the world will reduce its emissions, it will still use 105m barrels of oil a day in 2050, up from 100m barrels last year. Two-thirds of the global energy mix will stubbornly remain composed of oil, gas and coal at the midpoint of the century, the oil company estimated. “All of the oil that is produced will be burned – if they produce more, more will be used,” said Juan Carlos Navarro, environment minister of Panama. “The people who predict that there will be a reduction in the emission of greenhouse gases are simply lying or blind.” The only hope is that the world “can cap consumption and production at levels similar to the ones we have right now”, Navarro added, citing the enormous energy demand of artificial intelligence datacenters, which are largely being run on gas-fired power. However, climate advocates maintain the Iran conflict will accelerate trends that are already swinging behind clean energy. Investment in renewables globally is now double that of fossil fuels, almost all new power being added to grids comes from clean sources and last year one in four cars sold was electric. Unlike previous oil shocks, the world now has a viable alternative to fossil fuels, even if it’s unclear how lasting an impact Trump’s military and trade actions will have in pushing countries towards them. “There is one thing that all these events are making clear,” Ursula von der Leyen, president of the European Commission said in April. “We are paying a very high price for our over-dependency on fossil fuels.” Countries from the UK to India to Thailand have sought to speed up the transition to renewables as the price of fossil fuel dependency has spiraled, saving billions. Electric vehicle sales have surged, although not in the US. Trump has urged other countries to reject the “scam” of clean energy but the market is increasingly favoring cheap wind, solar and batteries that have plummeted in cost in recent years, including in the US. “Demand has massively spiked for solar and for battery storage,” said Sonia Dunlop, chief executive of the Global Solar Council. “We’re seeing that all over the world – the Philippines, across Europe, across south-east Asia, Australia and beyond.” “This Iran crisis, which was, in effect, started by President Trump, has led to a massive surge in demand for our technology … but actually it’s just building on a trend that was already there,” she added. Political and business leaders can mull the fact that the wind does not funnel through the strait of Hormuz and the sun doesn’t only shine on a foreign autocrat’s lands. The Iran war may not prove a fatal blow to fossil fuels, but it has starkly highlighted their inherent volatility. The case for renewables has become obvious at a grassroots level in developing countries, too, where rooftops increasingly glitter with cheap Chinese-made solar panels that are helping negate soaring power bills. “The price of solar has come down so quickly that there are now 100,000 solar panels installed every day in Africa,” Al Gore, the former US vice-president, said last week. “In parts of Pakistan, a common bride’s dowry is now three panels and an inverter, instead of 10 or 12 goats. It’s beginning to kick into gear.” This momentum won’t stop once the conflict around the Persian Gulf ends, Dunlop insisted. “I don’t think the world is just going to go back to business-as-usual demand of fossil fuels once this crisis ends,” she said. “Once someone decides to step off the fossil fuel rollercoaster, they’re off it.” So does all this, then, make Trump an environmentalist? “I wouldn’t say that,” Dunlop demurred. “He certainly has his own ideas.”

title: First Thing: Details remain unclear after ‘terror attack’ on Dubai-Israel flight
summary: Netanyahu says it is too early to tell who was behind the apparent attempt to crash flight after pilot stabbed
text: Good morning. Benjamin Netanyahu has said it is too early to tell who was behind the apparent attempt to crash a ⁠Tel Aviv-bound flydubai flight, even as Israel’s ambassador to the UN called the incident a “terror attack”. Flydubai said its flights to and from Israel would be suspended while an investigation takes place. What is believed to have taken place in the cockpit? Pilot Smit Machchhar, an Indian citizen from Mumbai, has been hailed as a hero after releasing the cockpit door to allow passengers in to wrestle back control of the plane, after his co-pilot – reportedly an Omani national – stabbed him and ⁠sent the jet plunging nearly 14,000ft (4,267 metres) in less than 30 seconds. What happened next? One passenger said: “There were two spare pilots who were supposed to operate the next flight. The relief pilots … entered [the cockpit] and pulled the aircraft up, pulled the yoke, stabilised the plane and landed us in Saudi Arabia.” How has Donald Trump responded? The president said: “It seems as though the co-pilot was perhaps a terrorist, or perhaps a whack-job, and he stabbed the pilot.” Woman taken to hospital after surviving two lethal injections in botched execution Tennessee officials were unable to carry out the execution of Christa Pike despite her being administered two doses of a lethal injection drug, her lawyers said, adding that she had been taken to hospital in an ambulance. The Tennessee department of correction later confirmed that Pike had survived the state’s effort to execute her. Pike, 50, had been scheduled for execution at 10am Wednesday, and would have been the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years. In 1995 she and her then boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, brutally beat and murdered an acquaintance, Colleen Slemmer, 19. Why has the death sentence for Pike been so controversial? As Ed Pilkington reported for the Guardian last month, at the time of the crime she was 18, and her co-accused was 17. That age difference meant he was spared the death penalty. Pike, at that age, had already been subjected to serious abuse, including multiple rapes by three separate men and beatings by numerous relatives. Hegseth confirms plan to cut 20% of US top military brass amid outburst at ‘weirdos’ The US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, has confirmed plans to cut 20% of generals and admirals and declared “no beardos, no weirdos, no wimps” would be tolerated inside the country’s military. He also dismissed claims of low morale within the US armed forces as “false”. What were Hegseth’s words? Addressing lower-ranking troops at the Marine Corps Base, the defense secretary said: “The complainers, the ideologues and the poor performers are no longer in the driver’s seat. It’s worth saying again, so the fake news understands it. We are no longer the woke department or the weak department. Simple translation of that: no fatties, no trannies, no beardos, no weirdos, no wimps, no radicals. Just warriors.” What did Hegseth announce about Elon Musk? Musk will co-lead a government project to study the future of warfare, called Project Meridian, with a goal of “identifying the capabilities required to achieve absolute technological dominance on the next-generation battlefield”. The project will run for 120 days and culminate in an unclassified public report of its recommendations. US trade regulator opens investigation into AI giants including Anthropic and OpenAI The US’s main trade regulator is conducting an industry-wide investigation ⁠into Anthropic, OpenAI and other ⁠AI labs to uncover the potential dangers their technology poses to consumers. The investigation by the federal trade commission is the first official US enforcement ⁠action that delves into rogue AI agents. How has AI embarrassed Donald Trump this week? The president launched America.gov, an AI platform which includes a chatbot that is rather inconveniently quoting official government statistics which frequently debunk or contradict some of the president’s most notorious false claims. In other news … Former homeland security secretary Kristi Noem is divorcing her husband, Bryon Noem, after 34 years of marriage, citing “irreconcilable differences”. The US Department of Justice has indicted another 10 individuals on noncitizen voting-related charges in Minnesota. Administration officials have sought to support Trump’s longstanding unsubstantiated claims of widespread voter fraud in US elections. A 40-year-old man has been arrested on suspicion of plotting to attack the Texas state capitol, authorities said. The US Senate has blocked a Republican bill restricting stock trading by members of Congress. The parents of a Detroit-area toddler who pulled a loaded pistol out of his backpack at a daycare will face charges, police said. Pennsylvania has reported its fifth measles-associated death of 2026 as the state’s outbreak climbs to 943 confirmed cases across 39 counties. Stat of the day: Catholic clergy sexually abused nearly 1,000 Massachusetts children over decades More than 270 Catholic clerics sexually abused nearly 1,000 children across three Massachusetts dioceses over several decades, according to a report released by the state’s attorney general’s office. Don’t miss this: New Google Maps images reveal massive scale of devastation in Gaza An update to Google Maps has revealed the extent of devastation during the three-year Gaza war and the severity of the continuing humanitarian crisis faced by the territory’s 2.3 million inhabitants. … or this: From mass raids to quiet crackdown – a timeline of Trump’s strategic ICE pivot After switching tactics, federal agents are detaining and deporting record numbers of people from the US. Here is how the change has unfolded during the year. Climate check: 20% of Swiss glaciers lost in five years Alpine regions in Europe are experiencing extreme glacier collapse due to the heat-trapping effects of fossil fuel pollution. Scientists have not yet compiled a formal tally of lost glaciers this year but said they had witnessed the death of a number of small ones. title: Democratic senators accuse Trump administration of worsening childcare crisis
summary: Six lawmakers demand information on childcare center closures, cost changes, Head Start and government grants
text: Democratic senators have accused Donald Trump’s administration of worsening the country’s childcare crisis, warning that rising costs and daycare closures are leaving families with fewer affordable options. In a letter seen by the Guardian and addressed to Alex Adams, assistant secretary of the Administration for Children and Families (ACF), senators led by Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts argue that federal cuts and changes to childcare programs like Head Start are destabilising an already fragile system. Childcare costs rose faster than overall inflation in 2025, the letter notes, while the cost of daycare and preschool increased by 3.5% in the year to May 2026. “American families face skyrocketing child care costs,” the senators write, asserting that rising prices for food, supplies, insurance, rent and utilities are forcing providers to choose between increasing tuition fees and closing. The letter says more than 400 daycare centres have closed in Oklahoma since November, while more than 300 programmes have shut in Indiana since September last year. The senators also criticise the administration’s handling of Head Start, the federal programme providing early education and other services to low-income children. “The Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) unlawfully froze program funding for grantees mere weeks after President Trump took office – which forced some Head Start programs to temporarily close and left thousands of the country’s most vulnerable families’ child care with uncertainty – and withheld funding from grantees until they complied with the administration’s rigid requirements,” the letter says. The letter also highlights an ACF decision in January to freeze $2.4bn in Child Care and Development Fund grants for five states. The freeze was subsequently rescinded after legal challenges, but the senators warned that a similar move could happen again. The senators say regulatory changes could also increase costs for families. In May, the ACF finalised a rule rescinding Joe Biden-era requirements including a federal requirement that states cap eligible families’ childcare co-payments at 7% of income and provisions requiring states to pay providers based on enrollment. The senators say the changes risk making childcare more expensive and could push providers out of business. They also raise concerns about proposed changes to Head Start, including loosening or eliminating rules governing child-to-teacher ratios and rolling back wage and benefits requirements for staff. The letter says such changes risk worsening staff turnover and reducing access to high-quality, affordable care. The senators ask ACF to provide information by 14 October on the number of childcare centers that closed since January 2025 and changes in average childcare costs. They also request monthly data on Head Start and Child Care and Development Fund grants, details of support for centers facing closure and analysis of how the latest regulatory changes could affect costs and the number of childcare providers. The group asks specifically whether ACF had calculated how much families’ costs would increase following the removal of the 7% co-payment cap, and how many centres could close as a result of the changes. The letter is signed by Warren and six other Democratic senators: Raphael Warnock, Jeffrey Merkley, Andy Kim, Peter Welch, Ben Ray Luján and Angela Alsobrooks.

title: Tech in cars can be used to snoop on you, Dutch spy chiefs warn
summary: Hostile states could access cameras, microphones or GPS, says intelligence agency amid concerns over Chinese imports
text: Drivers have been warned that the smart features built into modern cars such as microphones, cameras and GPS trackers could be used by hostile states to spy on them. The Dutch General Intelligence and Security Service (AIVD) called for “awareness of espionage risks around modern vehicles”, including microphones that can by switched on remotely to listen to conversations. It did not mention an individual country, but the warning will add to concerns around a recent boom in Chinese car imports into the UK. In a translated document released on Wednesday, the AIVD said cars were becoming “increasingly smart” with digital systems that collected data and connected to the internet. “On the one hand this offers practical benefits, but on the other hand these systems collect a great deal of data about occupants, the vehicle itself, and about objects and people in the vicinity. Various parties, including state actors, can gain access to this data,” it added. The alert follows reports last year that British defence firms working for the UK government had cautioned staff against connecting or pairing their phones with Chinese-made electric cars, owing to fears that Beijing could extract sensitive data from the devices. Chinese-owned brands now account for 15% of all new cars registered in the UK, according to the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders, almost 175,000 vehicles in the first half of 2026 and more than double the same period last year. Models by MG, BYD and Jaecoo, whose parent company Chery is part-owned by the Chinese state, have led the surge, popular for their low price and in-car technology. The Jaecoo 7 was the UK’s bestselling car in March. MPs have raised concerns that China’s national intelligence law requires its companies to assist the state’s intelligence services when requested. The UK Ministry of Defence has said it is working with other government departments “to understand and mitigate any potential threats to national security” from vehicles. This year, the MoD reportedly banned cars with Chinese parts from sensitive military sites, including RAF Wyton in Cambridgeshire and the Dorset headquarters of Britain’s maritime special forces, the SBS. The AIVD said it was “technically possible to activate” microphones and cameras remotely in some cars, allowing malicious actors to “eavesdrop on conversations” and “make recordings in and around the vehicle”. The agency added that drivers should “not hold confidential conversations in or around the vehicle”, or “use a vehicle with an external camera when travelling to a sensitive location”. It also said connecting phones and other devices, either via Bluetooth, wifi or charging systems could allow malicious actors to “extract data from connected devices via the vehicle”. The AIVD suggested systems such as GPS navigation systems, telematics modules and charging stations could all be used to gather and send data about the car and drivers’ whereabouts elsewhere. On Wednesday, MI5 issued a rare public warning to UK universities to stop working with the China General Technology Research Institute, which it said was being used as a front by Beijing’s intelligence service to pay for research by UK academics and steal the secrets of hi-tech projects. The Chinese embassy in London issued a strongly worded rebuttal, describing the accusations as “imaginary and purely fabricated”.
