title: ICE got ‘quieter’ – then killed a father in Maine. Now watch groups are shifting their tactics too
summary: ICE-watchers get creative after the killing of Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, as Trump’s immigration crackdown takes a more secretive approach
text: Most of the time, the scene outside the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) facility in the small, coastal town of Scarborough, Maine, could be confused for a nature watch in “Vacationland”, the slogan on state license plates. People sitting in lawn chairs under a tent. Birds chirping. The sound of the breeze moving through the trees. But when four Escalades zoom into the ICE facility parking lot on an August afternoon, the group springs out of their chairs, binoculars and clipboards in hand. Some rapidly call out license plate numbers, makes and models, while another scribbles the information down. This is what monitoring ICE operations looks like in the east coast’s most sparsely populated state: documenting the agency’s unmarked vehicles and keeping a record of detainments – the people arriving for routine appointments or brought in by agents and never seen leaving. ICE-watching – following, documenting and alerting neighbors to federal immigration agents’ public activities – is a longtime, constitutionally protected practice that became more popular in response to the Trump administration’s ramping up of violent, on-the-ground immigration-enforcement operations last year. It particularly drew attention in Minneapolis in January, when neighbors came out in droves to record and interfere as agents pulled people out of cars, off sidewalks and from bus stops. Though ICE has shifted to less visible tactics since the start of the year, the number of immigration arrests is higher than ever, including in rural and suburban areas, such as much of Maine. ICE observers are still there, too – albeit exhausted and burned out. In many of the US’s largest cities, immigrant rights networks count hundreds if not thousands of volunteers, and dozens of neighborhood-based encrypted chats and organizations activate on short notice. But in areas like this one in Maine, organizers mobilizing against ICE’s deportation machine are often spread out and strapped for resources. The Maine Immigrant Rights Coalition (MIRC), a small non-profit representing more than 100 state-based organizations, estimates it has about 100 trained, regular volunteers on its roster. Some days, ICE-watching in the state is just three people in lawn chairs scrawling license plate numbers in their notebooks. “People are trying the best they can – learning and utilizing new skills, and responding to crises in community – and then there’s another one, and there’s another one, and there’s another one,” said Crystal Cron, co-founder and executive director of Presente! Maine, a Latino-led organization that has given out about $200,000 in bond money for immigrants in detention every month since Donald Trump retook office through its solidarity fund. But the work is never-ending, she said: “That is what the escalating violence is meant to do – it’s meant to exhaust us and confuse us.” Recovering from an ICE surge ICE-watching efforts in Maine ramped up in January, when the Trump administration launched Operation Catch of the Day, an intense crackdown on undocumented residents named in reference to the state’s $600m fishing industry that’s powered in part by migrant labor. In a state with a population a third of the size of the city of Los Angeles and where immigrants make up roughly 4% of residents, 100 people were arrested in three days, the majority of whom had no criminal records and were lawfully in the US. Masked agents smashed car windows to abduct drivers, then abandoned the vehicles – and at least once, with a mother and baby inside – on the side of the road; children watched agents detain their parents from their front steps. It “shocked the whole system”, said Mufalo Chitam, executive director of the MIRC. “The tactic was much faster than the traditional system that we had envisioned. By the time somebody can call [in a sighting], somebody’s already been picked up.’” Residents and local community groups in the state came together, following ICE vehicles and dropping off groceries for immigrant neighbors too scared to leave their homes. The operation lasted for nine days, and soon after, public backlash over ICE violence across the US reached new heights. The killing of two ICE observers in Minneapolis sparked widespread protests and intensified scrutiny of the administration. Trump replaced Department of Homeland Security (DHS) leadership, directing ICE to adopt “a little bit of a softer touch”. But while agents have become less visible in public, in Maine they never went away. In July, an ICE agent killed 25-year-old father Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero during a traffic stop in Biddeford, 15 minutes from Scarborough. This happened just days after an agent killed Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Houston, Texas, also during a traffic stop. Any illusion of ICE’s “softer touch” was shattered. Organizers’ ICE-watching hotline received 128 calls the week that Durán was killed, according to MIRC’s Chitam. People in Biddeford once again took to the streets and elected officials demanded an investigation. This time, though, already-traumatized and outraged residents felt pushed to the brink, organizers said. Many of the state’s immigrants have been effectively sheltering in place for the last nine months. “The death of Johan has been devastating, but for us it was not a surprise,” said Cron. “Our communities have always been under threat of persecution. Being hunted in the streets is not new.” Organizers had been preparing for this moment. Last October, the MIRC and other community groups such as the People’s Coalition for Safety and Justice launched their hotline to report ICE sightings. The MIRC also built a network of volunteers who could speak the many languages reflected in Maine’s immigrant population – Somali, Haitian Creole, Arabic – coordinated via the encrypted app Signal. Since then, the MIRC’s handful of staffers have been triaging between state offices, other policy organizations and community members – from assisting business owners protecting immigrant employees to lobbying elected officials on what resources they need. In May, the MIRC and Presente! created Lighthouse ME, an online “immigrant defense hub” that includes ICE arrest data and a visual tracker of sightings. To hold ICE accountable, the Maine chapter of the American Civil Liberties Union recently launched a hotline to report first amendment violations. During the operation ICE agents followed observers home to intimidate them, fired pepper balls at their cars and told residents they would be added to a “domestic terrorist” list. Those residents and other observers have since launched a federal class-action lawsuit against the DHS. “The constitution guarantees your right to observe and record law enforcement agents when they’re doing their job in public. And yet the government keeps finding new ways to try to interfere with people’s first amendment rights,” said Zach Heiden, chief counsel at the ACLU of Maine. “But if bringing a lawsuit is necessary, then that’s what we’re going to do, for as long as it takes.” ‘Anytime they’re here, we’re here’ While organizers in Maine and many other parts of the country have been stretched thin, ICE-watching remains robust in bigger cities, although the tactics are evolving. In Chicago, a year after Operation Midway Blitz, ICE observers are still pounding the pavement, looking for agents and carrying whistles to alert their neighbors. But community support is now more focused on managing the trauma already suffered through planning cultural events and vigils. While New York never saw the sweeping on-the-ground operations that Chicago, Maine or Minnesota did, the city’s large population is a boon for its ICE-watching network. A patchwork of non-profit organizations, longtime community organizing groups and mutual aid networks all support immigrant communities. Organizers with Hands Off NYC, which launched a year ago to organize against ICE, said there are at least hundreds of people who have taken know-your-rights training, offered online, in the last several months. And yet despite Maine’s smaller ICE-fighting network, residents have already seen its impact on the state level: 13 days after Durán’s killing, three “ICE Out” laws went into effect, blocking cooperation between the agency and local police forces, landlords, schools and state healthcare facilities. Heiden, of the ACLU of Maine, observed that none of those laws would have saved Durán’s life, though. Many organizers said that much more needs to change to prevent another ICE killing. This weekend, residents plan to march 70 miles (113km) from the office of Senator Susan Collins in Biddeford to the state capital in protest of her support for ICE funding. “Johan’s death is not an isolated tragedy. It is part of a system that has inflicted fear, separation, detention and death on immigrant communities,” Cron testified during a hearing in August. “The responsibility for his death, and the many deaths by immigration police and in ICE detention this year, is a collective one.” And so residents continue to push for justice, accountability and structural change. At a congressional “shadow hearing” in August – an unofficial proceeding hosted by the US representative Chellie Pingree investigating Durán’s killing – the Biddeford high school auditorium was packed with irate residents holding signs declaring “ICE = Terrorists, Democrat Silence = Complicity”. When Durán’s parents walked in, a heavy hush fell over the room. Durán’s father, his voice thick with held-back tears, testified through an interpreter: “Our dream was always to be reunited and to hold each other again. Today that dream can no longer come true.” On the same day, just 10 minutes away, another group of Mainers grieved and organized at Biddeford’s Mechanics Park. The site where French and Irish immigrants blocked the Ku Klux Klan from a planned march into Biddeford more than 100 years ago is now occupied by activists and an art installation – hundreds of ribbons tied to a fence with messages for Durán and the city’s immigrant residents. Nearby are stocks of snacks, Narcan, “know your rights” zines and 3D-printed whistles. When a neighborhood kid drops by a tent and takes a free Gatorade from the cooler, he tells the person making “Fuck ICE” bracelets he’ll come back later. “We’ll be here,” she replies. Meanwhile, at the Scarborough facility, observers say they have been seeing, on average, two detentions a day: people brought to the facility in shackles by ICE agents and people who arrive for appointments and never come back out, abandoning their cars. (Their estimate is borne out in DHS data monitored by the Guardian.) In their informal capacity, they have, at times, become the first line of support to dazed family members exiting the facility. Still fresh in their minds is Jonas Manywa, a 42-year-old asylum seeker from the Democratic Republic of Congo who arrived at the facility for a routine appointment in early August. Agents arrested him in front of his two young daughters. When his wife came with their nine-month-old to pick up their children, she had his car keys but couldn’t drive. The crew of ICE-watching volunteers helped her figure out how to get home. Most days, people stop by the tent at the Scarborough facility, dropping off water bottles and snacks for the volunteers and thanking them for their efforts. But even with this community support, it’s been difficult to recruit new volunteers. “Now more than ever, we need people to join us to build a better, more free world,” said Cron. Still, the organizers, volunteers and advocates making up Maine’s resistance to ICE will keep doing the work. “Anytime they’re here,” one ICE observer said, looking at the Scarborough facility, “we’re here.”

title: A Louisiana preschooler was allegedly abused at school. Then a hospital counselor discussed her chart with her principal
summary: ‘Impermissible disclosure’ preceded hospital counselor’s firing and departure of principal, her sister-in-law. The child’s attorney calls events ‘vile and repugnant’
text: A counselor at Louisiana’s premier pediatric hospital accessed the medical records of a girl whose parents reported that she was sexually abused by a classmate at her preschool – and then was fired after it was discovered that she shared information from the child’s file with the school’s principal, her sister-in-law, a Guardian investigation can reveal. The details of the breach and resulting employee termination at the Manning Family children’s hospital in New Orleans came to light in a sworn deposition taken in August during civil litigation being pursued by the girl’s parents. The deposition also preceded an unexpected 4 September announcement that the counselor’s sister-in-law “would no longer serve in the role of preschool principal” at Kehoe-France, the respected private suburban New Orleans school that her family founded in 1950 but has been owned by the International Schools Partnership (ISP) of London, England, since 2018. During the deposition in question, the fired hospital employee, Claire Beaumont Poché, was asked about texts that she received from former Kehoe-France preschool principal Emily France Poché in which the latter woman called the father of the alleged abuse victim a “narcissist” – and said, without evidence, “my head of school thinks the dad is abusing” his daughter. All of those developments came after the child’s father – Roger Williams, who earned a bronze star medal for “exceptionally meritorious wartime service” with the US army in Iraq – and her mother, Jana, successfully championed a new early-childhood education safety law in Louisiana amid the litigation centering on the couple’s daughter. Private preschools across the state staunchly opposed the law, arguing that it would be unfairly financially burdensome for them to comply. The Williams family’s case illustrates the kind of tangled circumstances those who report abuse at well-heeled institutions in the US – which potentially have connections to other influential organizations – may have to grapple with. And it remains to be seen whether there may be an investigation by authorities into whether what happened with the medical chart of Jana and Roger Williams’ daughter constituted a violation of medical privacy laws under the federal Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (Hipaa), certain violations of which can carry criminal penalties. “The thanks [for] a bronze star medal recipient and literal war hero was to accuse him in secret of sexually abusing his own daughter without a scintilla of evidence, and to trounce all over his baby daughter’s Hipaa privacy rights,” one of the Williamses’ attorneys, Richard Trahant, said in a statement. “Vile and repugnant don’t begin to describe this.” Neither Claire Poché nor Emily France Poché are named defendants in the lawsuit. When offered the chance to comment, their lawyers contended that Claire’s deposition and her texts with Emily, which she was confronted about under oath, were subject to a protective order. Trahant countered that the protective order provided 20 days for the deposition to be designated confidential, which no one did. Portions of that deposition are also accessible in the public court record after attorneys for Kehoe-France entered them without any confidentiality designation. A filing on Monday from Claire Poché’s attorney, Michael Nolan, said she had turned over “additional text messages, under seal, between [her] and Emily France Poche”. Those texts were redacted at the time of Claire’s deposition – she was not asked about them at that session, and the Guardian has not seen them. Emily’s attorney, Renee Culotta, on Monday issued a statement attributed to her client which said she “care[s] deeply about the well-being of [Roger and Jana’s daughter] and all children at Kehoe-France” – and that “the best interests of my students have always been my highest priority”. The statement, citing the protective order, said Emily would not comment on either the deposition or the texts, which she characterized as being “between family members and close friends” while asserting that they were “intended to be private”. Her statement also accused the plaintiffs’ attorneys of “utilizing … personal messages to deflect attention from the actual matters at hand” and said that the Guardian’s reporting on them would “serve their purposes very neatly”. Kehoe-France, for its part, said in a statement that it “disagrees with the allegations made against the school” in the Williams family’s lawsuit “and will continue to defend itself through the legal process”. The statement also said “the appropriate forum for resolving these claims is the court” and that the school would not “litigate the case through the media”. The ISP issued its own statement echoing that sentiment. “The safety and well-being of our students are Kehoe-France’s highest priorities,” the school’s statement said. “The school maintains and follows policies and procedures designed to protect student safety and address concerns when they arise.” The Manning Family children’s hospital did not respond to requests for comment. ‘Wanna know … who is seeing her?’ Setting the stage for Claire Poché’s 31 August deposition as a fact witness was a suburban New Orleans state court lawsuit alleging that Jana and Roger Williams’ daughter was fondled in a sexually abusive manner by another three-year-old student at Kehoe-France’s preschool in March 2024 while in its care. The lawsuit, broadly, seeks damages contending that the school was negligent in its supervision of the couple’s daughter, which Kehoe-France denies. In any event, after the alleged abuse, Jana and Roger Williams took their daughter to the children’s hospital to be examined. Claire Poché was a licensed professional counselor at the hospital – recently named the No 1 pediatric hospital in Louisiana, and among the top 15 regionally, by the US News & World Report. But she acknowledged in her deposition that she was not a member of the plaintiffs’ daughter’s treatment team. Furthermore, Trahant said at Claire Poché’s deposition that Roger was concerned about “a familial connection” that his daughter’s then principal had at the hospital. And, Trahant said during Claire’s deposition, when Emily France Poché remarked to him that she was going to call the hospital to discuss his daughter’s case, Roger “asked her not to do this because he wanted the evaluation to be unbiased”. Nonetheless, Claire Poché testified during her deposition that she learned of the situation involving Jana and Roger Williams’ daughter from Emily France Poché. And Claire acknowledged that she accessed the girl’s medical chart, using an emergency – or “break the glass” – protocol to overcome a restriction otherwise prohibiting her from doing so. Claire Poché was asked at her deposition about a series of text messages with Emily France Poché which emerged as part of the discovery process in the Williams family’s lawsuit. Collectively, the messages made clear that the two discussed information from the plaintiffs’ daughter’s chart. “You wanna know the [doctor] who is seeing her”? Claire Poché asked, before providing the physician’s name to which the girl had been referred. A reply from Emily to Claire read: “I hope she tells [the girl’s parents] that she’s lying.” Claire went on to text Emily that the emergency room visit that the girl had already undergone involved the taking of vital signs, a brief physical examination and a discussion with ER doctors who “aren’t specially trained in child abuse”. She said the “visit” with the hospital child advocacy center where Claire worked – and to which the girl had been referred – is “more invasive”, so she didn’t know “why [the parents] are pushing for this”. “My head of school thinks the dad is abusing her,” read a later text from Emily to Claire which alluded to Tanya Price, Kehoe-France’s top official. Claire’s reply to Emily said, “I mean it would make sense if he’s being so insane about this. To deflect.” Trahant more recently said his client wanted to address that insinuation directly, on his terms, and dismissed it as “totally false” and “defamatory”. At her deposition, he asked Claire Poché about an email to a colleague in which she indicated that she was not notifying Louisiana department of children and family services (DCFS) authorities about Jana and Roger’s daughter’s case – despite Trahant arguing that Claire had a duty to report such matters. Claire’s email mentioned “the age of culpability”, alluding to the fact that children younger than 10 in Louisiana cannot be criminally charged. During Claire’s deposition, Trahant remarked: “Age of culpability … has absolutely nothing to do with the duty to report.” Jana and Roger Williams ultimately filed reports with local law enforcement, the DCFS and state education authorities. Kehoe-France also made its own reports, and the couple sued in August 2024. During the ensuing litigation, there surfaced documents and texts which established that Claire Poché had accessed the couple’s daughter’s chart and then discussed aspects of it with Emily France Poché. An attorney for Claire Poché produced redacted copies of some of her texts with Emily France Poché after Trahant and his co-counsel, Bobby Truitt, sent a subpoena. Roger separately alerted the Manning Family children’s hospital’s operator, LCMC, to his belief that his daughter’s medical records had been impermissibly accessed as well as disclosed. Five days before Claire Poché’s deposition, LCMC issued a letter to Roger telling him “an investigation … determined that an impermissible disclosure (as opposed to an impermissible access) occurred in violation of Children’s express training, policies and procedures”. “Specifically, the fact that your daughter had a medical appointment at the [hospital], and the identity of the specific provider during that appointment, was disclosed to a third party,” the letter to Williams said. “This disclosure was in violation of Children’s express training and instructions provided by it to the … employee who disclosed such information to the third party.” The letter also said the fact that Roger’s daughter had been seen “in the emergency department … along with general information about what occurs in [such an] encounter was disclosed to a third party by a Children’s employee, again contrary to [the hospital’s] instructions and training to that employee.” The children’s hospital missive made it a point to say “specific clinical information was not included in the disclosure”. But, the letter added, “the individual involved no longer has access” to any LCMC health system, including the one for electronic medical records. The letter said, “Children’s deeply regrets that this situation occurred” – yet did not specify whether it disciplined “the individual involved”. But when asked at her deposition to name her workplace, Claire Poché replied: “I am not currently employed.” She then said she had been “terminated by children’s hospital”. Trahant asked Claire Poché if she was terminated because of violations of Hipaa, which mandates the protection of medical patients’ sensitive information. She replied that she had been told she was terminated because of code of conduct violations. She also said at the deposition: “I don’t believe that I accessed the chart inappropriately.” Asked if she conceded that her texts with Emily France Poché “are sneaky and sleazy”, Claire replied: “Um, I agree that they could come off that way.” Trahant had summoned Emily France Poché to her own deposition on 8 September. But four days before that scheduled session, members of the Kehoe-France community received an email informing them that Emily was leaving her post as preschool principal and would “no longer be part of [the] administrative team” there. The email did not provide a reason for her departure. Alluding to how her grandparents had founded Kehoe-France in the New Orleans suburb of Metairie, the email – from head of school Price – wished Emily “all the best in her future endeavors” while also thanking her for her work with the institution. Emily’s deposition as a fact witness was postponed to 15 October. Her statement said she would “remain fully cooperative with the legal process”, looked forward to providing “truthful testimony when the time comes” and “was entirely confident that the facts will speak for themselves”. The departures of Claire Poché and Emily France Poché from their jobs have been not the only consequences from the civil case pressed by Jana and Roger Williams, which remained unresolved as of Friday and was tentatively set for trial on the week of 26 October. Charlie’s Law The couple spent more than a year advocating for Louisiana state legislators to pass a measure aiming to strengthen the safety of preschool programs. For instance, it set maximum child-to-staff ratios and effectively required those programs to obtain daycare licenses, therefore forcing them to adhere to a number of additional regulations. Louisiana’s legislature in the end passed that measure, which came to be known as Charlie’s Law – and it took effect on 1 August 2025. Yet groups supporting private preschools similar to Kehoe-France lobbied heavily against the law, saying it would result in steep compliance costs. And in June, Louisiana’s Republican governor, Jeff Landry, signed legislative changes that exempted “nonpublic prekindergarten programs” affiliated with private schools – such as Kehoe-France – from Charlie’s Law’s daycare licensing requirements, among other amendments. Two entities, meanwhile, filed a federal lawsuit challenging the law’s constitutionality. The plaintiffs argued that Charlie’s Law disproportionately affects religious schools, though a federal judge dismissed their lawsuit, saying the extra anticipated costs did not amount to either irreparable or imminent harm. An appellate court later upheld that decision, according to case records. Emily France Poché’s texts with Claire Poché commented on Roger’s advocacy for Charlie’s Law, which drew media attention. She wrote that Roger, in the course of championing Charlie’s Law, “only attends things that get him seen”. And Emily also called Claire’s attention to a quote attributed to Roger at a website with Charlie’s Law information that recounted how his daughter’s plight affected his mental health “equivalent to, if not worse than, my combat deployment to Iraq”. “This is all about him,” Emily France Poché said. “Like he is a narcissist.” Roger Williams had received US army approval in 2023 for a bronze star medal in part because of his role in defeating a pair of enemy unmanned drones sent in to attack Al-Asad airbase in Iraq two years earlier, when American troops were stationed there. The army said Williams’ actions “preserved military civilian lives, critical assets and vital infrastructure” at the base. He more recently said that he and Jana dedicated most of their free time to fighting for Charlie’s Law to protect their daughter as well “as everyone and their child in Louisiana” as much as possible. “If not me, then who?” Roger said. A statement from Jana – a certified registered nurse anesthetist – said, “I hope my family’s effort with Charlie’s Law helped someone, even if only one child.” And, referring to her and Roger’s daughter, the statement concluded: “If she ever finds this … in the future, I hope she knows how much she is loved, and we tried our best.”

title: Trump officials abandon effort to investigate election threats, experts warn
summary: Credible threats appear to have been overlooked as administration focuses on unverified claims of voter fraud
text: The Trump administration has abandoned key security bodies meant to investigate direct threats to US elections by foreign actors and domestic terrorists, according to former officials and a recent report. While administration officials have been actively focused on unsubstantiated claims of widespread voter fraud by noncitizens, other credible election threats appear to have been overlooked, the officials say. Between 2021 and 2024, the justice department’s election threats taskforce prosecuted 21 cases, such as that of Solomon Peña, a failed candidate for the New Mexico house of representatives who organized shootings at the houses of election officials, or Quintez Brown, who shot up a campaign meeting of Louisville’s mayor. Democrats and Republicans faced prosecution for harassing, intimidating and threatening elections workers, noted Nikki Fisher, former chief election security officer for the Oregon secretary of state, now the executive director of the Oregon District Attorneys Association. Since then, the taskforce seems to have gone quiet. “While officials are being trained to handle threats, the federal deterrent meant to punish the people making them appears to have gone quiet,” Fisher said. “To date, no new cases have been prosecuted, and the [justice department’s] election threats taskforce appears to be defunct in practice.” Contacted for comment on the status of the election threats taskforce, the justice department referred to a series of nine media releases over the past five weeks describing indictments of foreign nationals on charges of election fraud and stolen identities. In an academic paper published in June, while she was studying at the Naval Postgraduate School, Fisher noted that the taskforce received more than 2,000 reports of election threats between 2021 and 2024. It opened more than 100 investigations into those threats. Trump administration officials began disbanding election investigative groups within the justice department, the office of the director of national intelligence and other agencies almost immediately after the president started his second term. The first day after Pam Bondi won Senate confirmation as attorney general, she eliminated the FBI’s foreign influence taskforce, which had been investigating influence campaigns waged by China, Russia and other adversaries. Administration leaders fired or reassigned personnel working on foreign election interference at the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (Cisa). They also defunded Cisa’s training program for local officials to monitor and coordinate threats through the Elections Infrastructure Information Sharing and Analysis Center. Pleas from Democratic lawmakers during budget negotiations in 2025 to retain the taskforce and other election integrity assets went unheeded. “I’m less worried about jurisdictions’ ability to defend themselves in particular,” said Geoff Hale, a visiting fellow for election security at the Center for Democracy and Technology and former director at Cisa. “I’m more worried about the lack of an information-sharing environment across the community.” Federal cuts to these agencies’ monitoring and investigative apparatus leaves local agencies blind to broader patterns, he said. “The relationships and trust that Cisa had built up over 10 years, that was how the tapestry of security professionals that support elections across the country stayed in close contact and were able to close vulnerabilities to keep events and incidents from occurring in multiple locations.” Agencies working together with state and local election leaders offered regular warnings about suspicious activity, said Caitlin Durkovich, a former deputy homeland security adviser for resilience and response on the national security council, said at a briefing staged by the Brennan Center for Justice last week. “This administration … has dismantled the entire apparatus that is responsible for detecting and holding these bad actors accountable,” she said. “That has all gone away at a moment when this administration is again claiming that the specter of foreign operations is … in play.” Meanwhile, Trump officials have been focused on some of the president’s longstanding personal grievances when it comes to election integrity. FBI agents swooped into Fulton county in January to seize ballots from the 2020 election, ostensibly as part of a continuing investigation into foreign election interference. Tulsi Gabbard, then the director of national intelligence, was present at the FBI raid. Similarly, the ODNI and the FBI seized elections materials in Puerto Rico, again while investigating foreign interference. Nothing has yet come of either event. But both cases led up to a primetime address by Trump on 16 July, in which he claimed China had acquired extensive voter information during the 2020 election cycle, characterizing it as an effort to influence and undermine the legitimacy of the 2018 midterm and 2020 presidential elections. Trump argued that US election databases and hardware had vulnerabilities to foreign adversaries, and that Venezuela had digitally manipulated its election results in ways that might be replicated in an American election. Trump’s claims could not be substantiated from the evidence presented. Since that address – and the public’s tepid response to the claims – the administration has pivoted to a dogged pursuit of noncitizen voters in American elections. The justice department has charged more than 90 people with voter-related fraud offenses, including 50 noncitizens in the last five weeks alone, the US attorney general, Todd Blanche, said on Wednesday, contrasting it with 13 cases brought under the Biden administration. “What we do at Department of Homeland Security is not controversial; we’re enforcing our nation’s laws,” said the homeland security secretary, Markwayne Mullin, who was also at the event. “Underneath the Trump administration, we will always protect the integrity of our election system and enforce our nation’s laws.”

title: AI chatbots remove hijabs from images of Muslim women when prompted
summary: Guardian tested chatbots after French far-right politician stripped a Muslim woman of her hijab in a photo
text: When prompted, AI chatbots will edit images to remove the hijabs from Muslim women, a violation of one of the world’s most common and visible expressions of faith. The Guardian asked ChatGPT, Grok, Gemini and Claude to take the veil off an AI-generated image of a woman wearing a hijab. Both OpenAI’s ChatGPT and xAI’s Grok bots complied with the prompt. Anthropic’s Claude responded that it does not have an image-editing or -generating feature but that it would not alter a photo to remove someone’s hijab. Gemini initially said that it could not remove clothing or head coverings from photos of real people because it could not digitally alter someone’s appearance without their consent. But when asked to make the woman look more “western”, the bot created an image of her without her hijab. The Guardian US tested the chatbots after a French far-right politician stripped a real Muslim woman of her hijab and long-sleeved dress in a picture he made clear was modified. Julien Odoul, a member of parliament and of the National Rally party, posted the altered image of the woman on X with her hair visible and arms exposed alongside the caption “LIBERTÉ FRANÇAISE”, meaning French Liberty. He quote-tweeted the original image, posted by someone else, which showed the woman crossing a street wearing a hijab and full-length dress. It was unclear which software or AI model Odoul used or even whether he modified the image himself, but experts say the MP’s actions were part of a growing pattern of tech-enabled anti-Muslim hatred around the world. In India, where anti-Muslim sentiment is rampant, generative AI is playing an increasingly significant role in producing images that, among other things, sexualize Muslim women or dehumanize Muslims generally, according to a study by non-profit US thinktank the Center for the Study of Organized Hate (CSOH). The CSOH also found that there are similar types of AI-enabled hatred being directed at prominent female Muslim politicians in the US such as Ilhan Omar and Rashida Tlaib. “This is just part of an ongoing trend of how we see Muslim communities, and particularly Muslim women, being targeted and abused,” said Eviane Leidig, the director of research and outreach at the CSOH. While Grok promptly complied with a request to edit an image of a woman wearing a hijab, the chatbot declined to take the dress off an AI-generated image of a woman. When asked what the difference was, the chatbot replied, “Removing the hijab was treated as a relatively straightforward clothing/hair change.” However, the chatbot said it would be willing to do a “less explicit version” of the edit and “change the dress to underwear, a different outfit or a partial reveal”. In May, xAI announced it had implemented technological measures that would not allow its AI image generator to comply with requests to digitally undress “images of real people in revealing clothing such as bikinis”. ChatGPT similarly declined to remove a dress off the AI-generated woman, saying that the “distinction is that removing a hijab changes a head covering, while removing a dress would expose the person’s body”. However, ChatGPT eventually conceded that for someone who wears hijab, exposing their hair “can be a meaningful violation of privacy or religious practice”. “The fact that an edit doesn’t create nudity doesn’t mean it can’t violate someone’s privacy, dignity or religious boundaries,” ChatGPT responded. These distinctions show the gaps in community guidelines that dictate how AI chatbots can behave, said Leidig, as platforms such as X soften its enforcement of existing rules, emboldening far-right figures. The de-veiling of Muslim women “may not be distinctly violative [of platform rules] but it’s still harmful”, she said. OpenAI, Google, xAI and Anthropic declined to comment. The Guardian conducted similar tests for other religious head coverings like a turban traditionally worn by Sikh men and a Catholic nun wearing a habit. ChatGPT readily created new images removing both the habit and turban off the AI-generated people. Gemini initially declined to create a new image of the man without a turban. However, just as in the case of the image of the woman wearing hijab, when asked to make the AI-generated image of the man wearing a turban more western, Gemini created a new image of the man without a turban. Despite initially claiming that it couldn’t remove a hijab from an image of a woman because “attempting to remove clothing or head coverings from photos of real people relies entirely on artificial generation to guess what lies underneath”, Gemini removed the habit off of the AI-generated image. Claude, for its part, said that if it could edit images, it would not edit an image of a real woman to remove her hijab regardless of the requester’s intent. “That kind of edit changes how a real person is depicted in a way tied to their religious dress and identity, and it could be used to embarrass, harass or misrepresent them – that’s true whether the woman is a public figure or someone private,” the chatbot responded. Publicly available AI chatbots and third-party “nudify” apps have been used broadly to disrobe women, and in some cases minors. In January, sexualized images of women proliferated across X as users realized they could ask the Grok chatbot, developed by the Elon Musk-owned xAI, to undress images of women posted on the social media platform. The spread of these images prompted countries like France to investigate X. Malaysia temporarily restricted the use of Grok in the country.

title: The German town where the right has banned new ‘stumbling stones’ for Nazi victims
summary: Heidenau council has halted the laying of Stolpersteine installed to remember individual victims of the Nazis
text: The town hall of Heidenau, Germany has a freshly restored cream-coloured facade, tidy flower boxes on the windowsills and a charming shingled clocktower. At the entrance, closer inspection reveals a single brass plaque embedded in the pavement honouring the former mayor Paul Gröger, whom the Nazis hounded into killing himself. The plaque is one of 128,000 Stolpersteine (stumbling stones) across Europe, a donor-funded project keeping alive the memory of individual victims of the Nazi era. It is by some measure considered the world’s biggest grassroots memorial project, and has become an integral part of Germany’s “remembrance culture” for the atrocities committed under Adolf Hitler. But last week at the same town hall, the council of Heidenau voted to halt the laying of future stumbling stones. In a decision that drew a national outcry, the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) party joined forces with the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) of Germany’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz, to help form the majority. “They want to drive the victims’ memory out of the city centre, just like the victims themselves were driven out,” said Anne Nitschke of AKuBiZ, a citizens’ group coupling history education with pro-democracy work in Saxony state, a hotbed of rightwing extremism. “The point of the Stolpersteine is that you stumble across them every day and then think about who lived here and who was forced to leave,” said Nitschke, 40. Her organisation had filed for permission to lay another 12 plaques for Holocaust victims, until the Heidenau council stopped them. The vote came in a month in which the anti-immigrant, pro-Kremlin AfD widened a lead at the top of the national polls, won two state elections and performed strongly in a third, in the capital, Berlin. Like the other mainstream parties, Merz’s CDU has ruled out cooperation with the far right in a stance known as the “firewall”. But political realities have often made the AfD an unavoidable partner in municipal policymaking, particularly in the former communist east. Supporters of the stumbling stones ban criticised that their placement on the ground meant they were walked on and exposed to the elements. They called for a “memorial space” in a Christian cemetery north of town “for the victims of war, terrorism, dictators and forced displacement”. Nitschke noted that the council had not made any plans or committed funding for such an endeavour, and said the broad spectrum cited served to deny the “singularity of the Holocaust”. Merz’s national CDU referred queries to the Heidenau chapter, which did not respond to a request for comment. The AfD began as a Eurosceptic party 13 years ago and has morphed into an increasingly nationalist force. It has long targeted memory culture as detrimental to patriotism. One of its founders, Alexander Gauland, compared the Nazi period to a “speck of bird shit in over 1,000 years of successful German history”. The Saxony-Anhalt chapter, which won a record 44% of the vote in September, pledged to “liberate” Germans from shame over the Holocaust while offering “more Bismarck, less Hitler” in schools. And the part’s co-leader, Alice Weidel, falsely called the Nazi leader “a communist, socialist guy” in a campaign appearance with Elon Musk last year. (The tech billionaire told AfD supporters at the event there was “frankly too much of a focus on past guilt” in Germany.) Many residents of the town said they supported the Stolpersteine and were sceptical of the councillors’ motives. “Why would they have anything against the Stolpersteine? It’s easy enough to walk around them if you don’t want to step on them,” said Christine Bauer, 85, who uses a rolling walker to move about town. “I’m a child of the war and remember its awful aftermath,” said Bauer, who worked on Elbe river ships until she retired. “It’s not as if the town council didn’t have bigger problems to worry about now,” she added, mentioning affordability. But Silke Schutz, 63, a baker who called herself a “staunch AfD voter”, described the Stolpersteine as “a waste of money, regardless of who pays for them”. “There are so many victims no one cares about,” she said, citing people killed in traffic accidents. “We had nothing to do with the war and at some point it [remembrance] has got to come to an end. But when I express my opinion, I’m insulted as a Nazi.” Started by the artist Gunter Demnig in the 1990s, the Stolpersteine are laid before a Nazi victim’s last home or workplace and inscribed with stark biographical details: date of birth and the date and circumstances of their death. Heidenau has five, all laid personally by Demnig. He reacted angrily to the town council’s decision, calling it a “unprecedented” and wrong. Four plaques are laid just a few minutes’ walk from the Heidenau railway station in honour of the Reiner family. Its Jewish patriarch, Maximilian, ran a local department store until he was deported to the Theresienstadt concentration camp in 1943. He survived and, after liberation two years later, emigrated to the US and died soon after, in 1949. Gröger, the Social Democratic mayor until 1933, refused to run up the swastika flag at the town hall and was removed from office. In June, Nazi officers spirited him away to the Hohnstein concentration camp, where they beat and tortured him. In August, he took his own life. School pupils raised the funds for his plaque, while AKuBiZ sponsored the remaining four Stolpersteine. Descendants often travel from abroad to attend their installation, as most Holocaust victims lack a gravesite. Local residents support the project by regularly polishing the Stolpersteine, and digital apps provide detailed information about the victims’ fates. Nitschke said no plans had been announced to remove any of the existing Stolpersteine, but for now the 12 planned plaques were on hold, including for Fritz Goldstein, a Jew whom the Nazis stripped of his property and deported to the Soviet Union with his wife, Martha. He died a broken man aged 50, five years after his return to Heidenau. Juliane, 29, a music teacher who declined to give her last name, said she found it moving to learn about the victims through the Stolpersteine. “It is so important we don’t forget, so we don’t make the same mistakes again.” But 28-year-old Philipp, a cook, said he supported the town council’s ban. “It’s not relevant to me – it’s in the past. So there’s no point in dwelling on it now. At some point, you’ve got to put it behind you.” He said Germany’s memory culture had been imposed from abroad. “Other countries just want Germany to constantly have to justify what it did.” Nitschke said her team planned a legal challenge to the ban. This weekend they will lead a march through town to the sites of the planned new Stolpersteine, recounting the stories of each of the victims.

title: Tennessee woman on death row taken to hospital after surviving two lethal injections
summary: Christa Pike, sentenced to death over 1995 murder, was heard snoring after lethal doses administered, say witnesses
text: A Tennessee woman convicted of murdering a schoolmate 30 years ago has been taken to hospital after surviving two attempts to execute her with lethal injections. Witnesses reported that Christa Pike was still breathing despite the injections intended to kill her late on Wednesday. It was the second botched execution in Tennessee this year. Her attorneys told a local news station: “This has turned into agony and a violation of Pike’s right to be executed free of cruel and unusual punishment.” The Tennessee department of correction later confirmed in a statement that Pike had survived the state’s effort to execute her: “The lethal ⁠injection chemical in the protocol has consistently been effective, and the protocol does not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried ‌out this evening.” Pike had been transported to an “off-site medical facility”, they said. In a press conference, media witnesses described hearing Pike snore 40 minutes after she was administered two doses of pentobarbital. The failed execution is the second in Tennessee this year, after prison officials in May aborted attempts to execute a man convicted of murders after failing to find a suitable vein for his lethal injection. The Tennessee governor, Bill Lee, who denied Pike’s clemency petition on Monday, issued a ‌statement suspending all executions this year and calling for a “comprehensive, third-party review” of the latest attempt, according to Nashville’s the Tennessean. Pike, 50, had been scheduled for execution at 10am local time on Wednesday for a killing she committed when she was 18, and would have been the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years. An appeals court stopped the lethal injection just an hour before it was to start, but hours later the US supreme court overturned that stay. Pike’s attorneys have filed an emergency motion to the US supreme court asking to halt and stay the execution, saying she was in “unnecessary agony” and the state is violating her right to be executed free of cruel and unusual punishment. Seven journalists who were in the room to witness the execution said afterward, on a livestream hosted by WVLT television station, that after the injection Pike was clearly alive and snoring before corrections officials escorted journalists out. “It appears this did not go how this was supposed to go,” said the investigative journalist John North of WBIR, who was a witness at the execution site. “When we left the building, so far as we knew, she was probably still alive,” he said. Earlier Pike, who was convicted of murder 30 years ago, had her execution halted by an appeals court in a 2-1 ruling. It said the delay was necessary to assess whether Pike’s allegations of childhood sexual abuse were fully considered at her sentencing. The state governor and the supreme court had earlier refused calls for clemency. Tennessee’s attorney general immediately appealed against the ruling to the supreme court, writing that the 11th-hour stay rewarded “abusive delay tactics by Pike’s attorneys”, according to the Associated Press. The US supreme court sided with Tennessee in an order signed by justice Brett Kavanaugh. Justice Sonia Sotomayor, joined by fellow liberal justices Elena Kagan and Ketanji Brown Jackson, dissented from the court’s order “because its decision clears the way for the state to execute Pike before her still-pending legal challenges to her conviction can be properly considered”. Pike and her boyfriend, who was 17 at the time, killed 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, one of their classmates at Knoxville Job Corps, in 1995. The case garnered nationwide headlines due to the ages of those involved and the brutality of the murder. According to prosecutors, Pike was worried Slemmer was trying to take her then boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, away from her. Together, they lured Slemmer into a wooded area behind the agriculture campus steam plant at the University of Tennessee on 12 January 1995. Pike cut Slemmer’s stomach and throat with a box cutter before smashing her head with a rock. Shipp carved a pentagram into Slemmer’s chest and Pike later showed a friend a fragment of Slemmer’s skull. Shipp was convicted of first-degree murder in 1997 and was given a life sentence with the possibility of parole. Pike has never denied her involvement in Slemmer’s killing. She was later diagnosed with bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder. “I was a mentally ill 18-year-old kid. It took me numerous years to even realize the gravity of what I’d done. Even more to accept how many lives I affected. I took the life of someone’s child, sister, friend. It sickens me now to think I had the ability to commit such a crime,” Pike said in a statement that was included in her clemency petition. On Saturday, May Martinez, Slemmer’s mother, said she was waiting for Pike’s execution. “Every time I think about it, I think about Colleen feeling that pain and trying to get up and run,” Martinez told the Associated Press, adding: “Not a day goes by, or a minute goes by that I do not think about Colleen. Holidays are the worst.” The Associated Press contributed reporting

title: Nature boys and girls – here’s your chance to get published in the Guardian
summary: Our wildlife series Young Country Diary is looking for articles written by children, about their autumn encounters with nature
text: Once again, the Young Country Diary series is open for submissions! Every three months we ask you to send us an article written by a child aged 8-14. The article needs to be about a recent encounter they’ve had with nature – whether it’s a hedge full of berries, a beetle on the move, or a nervous deer. It doesn’t matter if the child is a nature expert or not – we’re especially keen to reach teachers who might like to get their class outside and noticing nature. And note that any child who has their article published will be paid! The deadline for autumn submissions is noon on Monday 2 November. Four of the entries will be chosen to be published in the newspaper and online – two each in October and November. (Note that any early birds who submit a piece before the 15th stand a chance of being published in October.) If you don’t get selected this time, don’t worry, the form will reopen on 1 January for winter submissions, after it takes a break in December. How your child can take part First of all, we’re looking for children age 8 to 14, so we will need your permission, as parent or guardian. Then here’s what the child needs to do: Step 1 – Go out one day to where there is some nature. It could be their local woods or beach, their garden, a farm, or simply the nearest park. Step 2 – Write an article of 200-250 words telling us what they saw and what happened. Step 3 – Send the article to us using the form below. We ask that you fill in the form yourself rather than the child. Photos/drawings – These are helpful (especially landscape rather than portrait) but they are not a condition of entry. If you have some, please tell us in the “more information” field, as there’s no way to attach them to the form. Hints and tips for any budding YCD writers If the child gets stuck and doesn’t know what to write about, here are a few pointers: • Good nature writing starts with the senses – so what did you see and hear? What about smell and touch? Take notes when you’re out and about so you don’t forget • How would you describe what happened? Did it remind you of anything? • It’s great to look up some extra information about what you saw, and tell us about that too. For example, if you find an interesting-looking bug, see if you can find out what type of butterfly it was, how long they live – any juicy details! • You can think big, and describe the whole scene – the sky, the horizon, the landscape. Or you can think small, and tell us some details about the butterfly’s wings or the beetle’s markings. • What did your encounter with nature make you think about? How did it make you feel? Anyone can enter their child who is aged between 8 and 14 and based in the UK. You the parent/guardian will be contacted if your child’s piece is selected for publication, and you will be paid on behalf of the child. For further inspiration, here are a few recent Young Country Diaries: • Aled, 8, on his afternoon of crabbing • Jess, 10, on the jellyfish party • Henry, 14, on a weary wheatear A note on AI usage We’d love to hear what your child has to say, and how they’d like to say it. For that reason, we ask that every sentence is written by the child, not by LLMs such as ChatGPT or Claude. LLMs may be used for research, planning or checking, though their output should be used with caution and double-checked. Many thanks, and good luck! title: Boots owner ‘closing in on sale to Canada’s Weston family for $9bn’
summary: Deal would mark return of Canadian family to UK after it sold Selfridges department store for £4bn in 2022
text: The private equity owner of high street pharmacy Boots is reportedly closing in on a deal to sell the business to the Canadian branch of the billionaire Weston family for $9bn (£7bn). Sycamore Partners, which bought the wider Walgreens Boots Alliance for $23.7bn in 2025, is said to be in advanced talks with the Westons, with the Financial Times reporting that a deal could be completed as soon as next week. If successful, it would mark the return of the Canadian branch of the Weston family to the UK high street, having previously owned Selfridges. The family later sold the department store chain for £4bn in 2022. The Westons are widely known throughout Canada for owning the grocery store Loblaws and the pharmacy chain Shoppers Drug Mart. The UK branch of the family, which operates its businesses through a separate investment vehicle, is known for holding a majority stake in Primark through the parent company Associated British Foods. News of the prospective Weston deal comes months after Sycamore tried and failed to sell Boots to the Australian pharmaceutical group Sigma Healthcare in a deal that would have valued the business at $10bn this summer. Sycamore has been widely expected to spin off and sell Boots – alongside other parts of the group – after its takeover of the Walgreen Boots Alliance last year. It as has already split the group into five stand-alone companies. Boots, which was founded in Nottingham in 1849 by John Boot, has changed hands several times in the past 20 years. After a merger with Alliance Unichem in 2006, the combined company was taken over by the private equity firm KKR in 2007, before Walgreens first took a 45% stake in 2012 and then completed a takeover at the end of 2014. Boots – which has 1,800 stores across the UK – employs about 51,000 people, including about 6,000 at its headquarters in Beeston, three miles south-west of Nottingham. This summer it reported that revenues had risen 3.2% to £7.5bn in the year to the end of August 2025, with pre-tax profit up by 25% to £337m. It said strong demand for weight loss jabs and beauty products had helped increase its profits. Boots declined to comment.
