title: Group encouraging people to join Green party to back ‘Zionism is racism’ agenda
summary: Exclusive: Greens for Palestine group has links to activists who say pro-Israel ‘infiltrators’ must be rooted out of UK
text: An organisation pushing the Green party to equate Zionism with racism has encouraged people to join the party specifically to support that agenda, and has links to activists who say that pro-Israel “infiltrators” must be rooted out of the UK, the Guardian has learned. Some Green members are increasingly concerned that the party risks being manipulated by extremist outsiders over a motion to be voted on at the party’s annual conference this weekend, which states that “Zionism is racism”. Some Jewish members have said privately they fear it will be difficult for them to remain in the party if the policy passes. Zack Polanski, who leads the Green party in England and Wales, has come under pressure to take a definitive stance on the motion amid worries the controversy will harm the party in next week’s key Holborn and St Pancras byelection, where Polanski is seeking to win Keir Starmer’s former seat. The motion came top of a members’ ballot of policy issues to be debated at the event in Brighton. It calls for a single Palestinian state and, if passed, it would mean members who support Zionism – the movement for a Jewish state – could be disciplined for racism. The controversy reflects a longstanding debate about the definition of Zionism, the political movement whose supporters see it as the necessary struggle for a Jewish homeland, and whose critics see it as a colonial project that has inevitably led to the dispossession of Palestinians. The term Zionist is, meanwhile, sometimes used as a synonym for Jew by antisemites. Efforts to push the policy have been led by Greens for Palestine (GfP), a group not formally affiliated with the party. In repeated social media posts over recent months, GfP has urged backers of the idea to sign up as Green members specifically to get the motion debated at the conference and then adopted. Polanski last week declared he was anti-Zionist, adding that Zionism was a form of racism because it involved the displacement and genocide of Palestinians. But he has supported amendments to tone down the motion. Lubna Speitan, a leading member of GfP who co-authored the motion, has rejected the amendments. “It doesn’t matter what the leadership thinks,” Speitan said in a recent video, adding: “We are certainly not here to negotiate the terms of our liberation or oppression with any of our oppressors.” GfP and Speitan have links to a group called the Anti-Zionist Movement (AZM), a more militant campaign group that argues that the “so-called Jewish state” should be dismantled, along with “Zionist organisations” in the UK and elsewhere. A key member of AZM is David Miller, a former academic who was sacked by Bristol University over his criticisms of Israel, and subsequently won a tribunal case after it ruled he had been discriminated against because of his anti-Zionist views. He now presents a show for Press TV, the Iranian state channel. In social media posts, Miller has argued that Zionists have, as “infiltrators and subversives”, gained access to not just all UK political parties but also “the media, entertainment industries, the law, financial institutions, sports and all sorts of apparently obscure parts of the UK”. GfP and AZM have collaborated on a series of social media posts, and Speitan attended an AZM meeting in London this year. In a video posted by AZM about the meeting, Speitan said it was important for anti-Zionist groups to collaborate. Speaking in the same video, Miller said his aim was to “dismantle Zionist organisations wherever they are in the world, including the 3,000 or 4,000 Zionist organisations in this country”. Some senior Greens say they are deeply worried about the links. One said: “I just don’t understand why Zack hasn’t provided any leadership on this, especially when we have such a crucial byelection just days later.” A spokesperson for the Greens said: “The Green party is a democratic party and membership has grown as more people join to support our full policy platform. The vast majority of members joined prior to a specific attempt at mobilisation.” They added: “The Green party does not support the views of the AZM.” A spokesperson for GfP cited Miller’s employment tribunal, saying it “concluded that anti-Zionist beliefs constitute a protected belief”, adding: “We reject all conflations of anti-Zionism with antisemitism, just as we reject the settler colonial project in occupied Palestine.” Asked about the links to AZM, they added: “We welcome the adoption of our motion by all anti-racist organisations, political parties and unions.” GfP, the statement added, “affirms the Palestinian people’s inalienable right to self-determination, including the right of the Palestinian people to resistance and liberation from Israeli occupation, domination and subjugation” via any means under international law.

title: ‘It’s utter surrealism’: Venezuela’s Chavistas lament government’s embrace of Trump
summary: Diehard Hugo Chávez supporters struggle to comprehend ideological U-turn being executed by Delcy Rodríguez’s interim administration
text: He was one of the most passionate propagandists for Hugo Chávez’s Bolivarian revolution: a feisty leftist TV personality who spent more than two decades singing the movement’s praises on his state-funded show, The Razorblade. Mario Silva’s devotion was such that he often hosted his programme with Chávez’s portrait behind him and he had El Comandante’s curly signature tattooed on to his left wrist. But nine months after Venezuela’s political landscape was scrambled by Donald Trump’s abduction of Chávez’s heir, Nicolás Maduro, Silva’s show has been cancelled, and its host is livid about the revolution’s direction under Maduro’s former deputy, Delcy Rodríguez. “[I feel] a lot of disappointment – depressed … and sometimes I wake up and feel like the world is collapsing around me,” the 66-year-old said during a rare interview at his home studio in the mountains outside the capital, Caracas. Silva has spent recent weeks railing against Rodríguez’s interim administration on YouTube, his home since his programme on state TV was axed, berating those he blames for Venezuela’s “shameful and utterly illegitimate surrender” to the US. Since January, a parade of high-ranking US officials – including the head of the CIA, the chair of the joint chiefs of staff and the energy secretary, Chris Wright – have visited Caracas, while Trump recently trumpeted striking “the biggest oil deal in world history” with Rodríguez’s regime. Last week, Rodríguez and Trump met on the sidelines of the UN general assembly, posing for a smiley photograph that left diehard Chavistas such as Silva aghast. “I thought it [the photo] was artificial intelligence or something like that. But it’s surrealism, utter surrealism … It’s impossible to understand,” Silva fumed on YouTube as a red flag emblazoned with the faces of Karl Marx, Friedrich Engels and Vladimir Lenin hung behind him. “They have surrendered this country and surrendered it the most vile and despicable way,” Silva went on. “Honestly, they are dragging the country’s name through the mud. They are dragging Chávez’s name through the mud.” In another broadcast, Silva seethed about the cosy post-Maduro relationship that has developed between one-time anti-imperialist flagbearers in Caracas and Trump officials: “Traitors and lackeys, you will have to answer for this!” Silva is not the only Chavista loyalist struggling to comprehend the ideological U-turn being executed by Rodríguez, who was Maduro’s vice-president but has engineered a historic rapprochement with the US since his rendition on 3 January. Elías Jaua, a vice-president and foreign minister under Chávez, is also up in arms, and claims the feeling is widely shared. “What I hear from comrades across the country is bewilderment, disagreement and indignation,” said Jaua, who believes Trump’s oil deal “amounts to an act of pillage against an entire nation”. Juan Barreto, a former member of the ruling Socialist party (PSUV) and mayor of Caracas, said such an agreement would have been unimaginable when the Bolivarian revolution began after Chávez’s 1998 election. He said Chavistas, who had once vowed “Not a drop of oil to the empire if Venezuela is attacked!”, were now in effect saying: “All of the oil reserves [for the US], for as long as you want!” “The current situation is one of tutelage,” Barreto said. Rodríguez has defended the deal, claiming it will create more than $209bn (£158bn) in revenues that will help improve healthcare and education. “We are thinking of Venezuela’s future,” she said in a recent TV broadcast. Héctor Rodríguez, another prominent Chavista politician, has sought to deflect criticism of Venezuela’s interim government by recalling how Chávez was forced to make a tactical retreat after his failed coup attempt in 1992. “No one can tell me Chávez was a coward. He understood that the balance of power had shifted … and decided to take a step backwards,” Rodríguez said recently. Last week as Delcy Rodríguez met Trump in New York, thousands of people joined a pro-government rally in Caracas, where supporters parroted the slogan “Delcy avanza, tú tienes mi confianza!” (“Move forward, Delcy. I trust in you!”). “No matter how much they kick and scream, there’s nothing they can do to try to cover up the success of President Delcy Rodríguez’s visit to New York,” her interior minister, Diosdado Cabello, told the crowd. Unlike at previous marches, there was scant mention of Maduro and few calls for him to be released. The depth and potential consequences of Chavista anger over Rodríguez’s embrace of Venezuela’s longtime foes in Washington remain unclear. Orlando Pérez, a Latin America expert from the University of North Texas at Dallas, recognised there was indignation at what some considered a sellout of their anti-imperialist ideals. “There are Chavistas that are pissed off, there’s no question about it,” he said. “There are Chavistas who see this as a betrayal of Hugo Chávez and the betrayal of the movement.” But Pérez believed that for many Chavistas who had remained in power after Trump’s invasion, the “pragmatic reality” was that working with Washington was “a necessary evil” if it meant keeping Venezuela’s opposition out of power. “If that means negotiating with Trump, if that means dealing with the CIA etc, it’s fine,” he said. “Beyond whatever ideological position they might have … I suspect most of them are gritting their teeth and just going along with this process as long as they can stay in power and keep their jobs. I think for most it’s as simple as that: it’s about their material wellbeing.” However, Pérez believed Rodríguez’s government would need to demonstrate to supporters “tangible benefits to the cooperation” with the US in order to avoid a backlash. “They’re going to have to show that these things have a material consequence to the lives of their social base … if you don’t deliver, then it is going to get very volatile,” he warned. So far there has been no sign of significant resistance from outraged supporters of Chavismo. But Silva claimed the government’s new direction and economic policies could eventually trigger a social uprising and protests. “Worsening economic conditions will degrade [people’s] quality of life, and that pressure is bound to explode. It has to explode – it’s not just wishful thinking. This isn’t a prediction born of desire, it’s an inevitability,” said the broadcaster, who has claimed he is facing investigation for alleged acts of “aggravated defamation and slander against the interim government”. Silva lit one cigarette after another as he recalled the early hours of 3 January 2026 when, as US troops swept into Venezuela’s capital, he realised the revolution he had spent more than 20 years defending was not going to defend itself. The Chavista broadcaster said he moved from one strategic point to another across Caracas before finally calling the commander at his assigned post. “I said: ‘Hey, what happened? Where are the weapons?’” Silva recalled, his face settling into a sad grin as he remembered the answer. “Go to sleep, Mario,” he was told. Silva pauses. “You have no idea how disappointed I was.”

title: Australian couple on plane diverted after flydubai co-pilot’s alleged attack on pilot
summary: Two people from Sydney were on board flight to Tel Aviv that was dramatically diverted to Saudi Arabia after one pilot allegedly stabbed the other
text: Two Australian citizens onboard a flight to Tel Aviv that was diverted after one of the pilots allegedly stabbed the other in an attack are “safe,” the foreign minister confirmed. The passengers are a Jewish couple from Sydney, the Israeli embassy in Australia confirmed to the Guardian on Thursday. No further details were provided. The flydubai aircraft was travelling from the United Arab Emirates to Israel when it was forced to make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia. In a post on social media, Penny Wong thanked the “heroes” for thwarting the attack. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email “Relieved to confirm at least two Australians who were on the Flydubai flight to Israel are safe – thanks to the heroes who thwarted the attack and helped bring the passengers to safety,” she wrote. “We’re thinking of those injured and hope for their full recovery.” One of the pilots, whom Israeli officials said was an Omani citizen, is accused of stabbing his fellow pilot. During the alleged attack, the plane plunged about 17,000 feet in just two minutes. Passenger Yaniv Hayoun later recounted how he and other passengers heard screaming and felt pressure as the plane dived before forcing their way into the cockpit and finding the attacker at the instrument panel. “I grabbed the attacker, put him in a chokehold, and dragged him out first,” Hayoun said during a meeting with Netanyahu after the plane had landed safely and the passengers were flown to Israel. “He was trying to destroy the instruments to disable the plane.” Israel’s ambassador to Australia, Hillel Newman, said the incident reminded him of the 11 September attacks. “You have here a very special incident, and due to the real heroism of some people on board, they were saved.” Newman said heightened security alerts had been issued after the attack. “It just shows that … those that hate Israel also hate the peace. “It’s an attempt to hit at the peace itself, at the Abraham Accords, and the relationships which Israel does have with Arab and Muslim countries.” The Abraham Accords normalised relations between the UAE and Israel in 2020. Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, said it was too early to tell who was ultimately behind the incident. There are about 12,000 Australian citizens living in Israel and 25,000 in the UAE. • The headline of this article was amended on 1 October 2026 to clarify that the alleged attack was by the co-pilot towards the pilot.

title: ‘Where illegal ebikes go to die’: first bikes seized under new laws in NSW crushed
summary: Major Sydney hospital also warns recent injuries from ebikes include fractures, internal bleeding, as well as ‘perforation of certain organs’
text: The first illegal ebikes seized under new laws have been crushed in New South Wales, as a major Sydney hospital has warned of a spike in trauma injuries driven by those riding under the influence. The NSW government crushed 23 ebikes at a wrecking yard in western Sydney on Thursday, turning them into scrap metal. NSW police are assessing applications for the return of an additional 13 bikes seized during a joint operation with Transport for NSW in the northern beaches in September. The NSW transport minister, John Graham, told reporters onsite on Thursday “this isn’t a scene from Mad Max. This is where illegal ebikes go to die.” Graham said tough new laws were necessary “because of some of the bad behaviour we’ve seen … on our state’s streets, on the golf courses in Sydney suburbs, even on the Sydney Harbour Bridge”. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email On the same day, St Vincent’s hospital released figures that showed a 22% spike in legal and illegal ebike injuries, with 42% of those injuries triggering a trauma response and the majority being injured while riding under the influence of alcohol or drugs, riding too fast or without a helmet. It found 361 patients presented to the hospital for ebike injuries between January and July, compared with 296 presentations during the same period last year. Dr Ed Lewis, acting head of rehabilitation medicine, told reporters injuries included fractures, internal bleeding, as well as the “perforation of certain organs”. He said they often included brain injuries from severe head trauma, “as well as milder knocks, like a concussion, which can still have long-term repercussions for patients”. Lewis told Guardian Australia that those contemplating riding an ebike home while intoxicated “need to have a plan B or a backup solution”. “The message that we want to say to people is: enjoy using ebikes, but respect what they are. Respect that they are fast. Wear a helmet and just don’t ride impaired.” Graham said the government was concerned by the number of injuries, but it was “important to keep it in context”. “The number of ebike injuries is still low compared to cars … but is rising,” he said. “If you’re not wearing a helmet, you are dicing with danger.” He stepped aside to allow a giant metal claw pick up a tangle of ebikes, cracking frames in half and popping tyres. They were loaded into a conveyor belt before being crushed and shredded. Graham said batteries had been removed for safe disposal and recycling beforehand. Under powers which came into effect in August, police and transport officers can seize bikes not restricted to 25km/h, whose maximum speed while not pedalling exceeds 6km/h, and maximum continuous power of 500 watts, due to reduce to 250 watts in March 2029. The government says the bikes crushed include one capable of speeds of more than 90km/h seized from a 14-year-old, a food delivery bike, and bikes with speed restriction settings that had been tampered with. The 36 ebikes seized so far represent a fraction of the estimated 760,000 in the state. The changes were prompted by a surge in injuries and high-profile incidents, including one in which about 40 ebikes swarmed the Sydney Harbour Bridge in February. An expert review on implementing an age limit of between 12 and 16 was due to report back to the government in June. The NSW premier, Chris Minns, appearing on the debut of Kyle Sandilands Live in August, said the government was “examining an … age limit of 12”, but hadn’t finalised the details. On Thursday, Graham would not say if the premier had revealed the planned age limit. “I want to discuss this with my colleagues and also with the public,” he said. • This article was amended on 2 October 2026. An earlier version said bikes whose maximum speed does not exceed 6km/h while not pedalling can be seized; this should have said bikes whose speed does exceed 6km/h.

title: Daredevil Jaan Roose completes slackline walk high above central Seoul
summary: Estonian completed first of two attempts to navigate narrow ribbon, 160 metres long and 120 metres high, near the city’s famous Gyeongbokgung palace on Thursday
text: The lunchtime crowds drifted slowly back to their offices along central Seoul’s main boulevard, heads up and phones raised to the sky. High above, a narrow ribbon ran between the Koreana hotel and the Dong-A Media Center, a few hundred metres from the capital’s famous Gyeongbokgung palace and Gwanghwamun square. A countdown ticked down on a big screen, and at 1pm, a figure stepped off the roof of the Koreana and out over the drop. Jaan Roose, an Estonian aerial athlete and three-time slackline world champion, was in Seoul to cross a 160-metre long highline suspended 120 metres above the city, in what organisers called South Korea’s first high-altitude slackline performance. The 34-year-old has made a name for himself slacklining dramatic urban environments, such as his 185-metre high feat between Qatar’s Katara towers. In 2024, he became the first person to slackline the strait of Messina between mainland Italy and Sicily, completing the 3.6km traverse despite a fall near the end, caught by his safety harness. Last month, he covered 14.7km over 12 hours on a line above the Danube in Bratislava, Slovakia. Below Roose, the Seoul traffic kept moving and the crowd held its breath each time he wobbled. “Just looking at him makes my legs go weak,” said Kim Young-sook, an office worker. “I can’t imagine how he can do that without being scared. It’s incredible.” Midway across, Roose sat cross-legged on the line, then lay flat on his back, drawing gasps from below, before the daredevil rose and continued. “I’m worried he might fall”, said Choi Eun-jung, who came out to see Roose. “I know he’s a professional, but it’s still a little frightening to watch.” On reaching Dong-A Media Center, he turned around, and started his return to the hotel rooftop. At the halfway point, he again dropped down and waved at the crowd. But this time he hung from the line with one arm and then dangled by his feet. When he finished his performance, the crowds clapped, some clearly relieved. At nearby Cheonggye plaza, people tried out their skills on slacklines, but these were set a mere 30cm and 50cm off the ground. Roose was scheduled for a second performance at 4pm. Roose said a visit in 2022 to South Korea inspired his Gwanghwamun walk. On that trip, Roose encountered jultagi, Korea’s traditional tightrope walking, which Unesco added to its list of intangible cultural heritage in 2011. Unlike tightrope walking elsewhere, jultagi is as much comedy as acrobatics. The walker sings, jokes and dances on the rope, trading banter with a clown on the ground as musicians play.

title: ‘Hitler was a lazy criminal who slept in until noon’: why most of what we think we know about the rise of the Nazis is wrong
summary: In a new book, German artist and writer Philipp Ruch argues that viewing the ascent of Hitler’s NSDAP through the prism of the Third Reich has distorted our understanding of fascism’s electoral breakthrough
text: With your art collective Centre for Political Beauty you famously built a replica of the Holocaust memorial on a property next to the home of an AfD politician. Now you’ve written a history book about the Nazis’ rise to power. Don’t we already know everything there is to know about the 1932 elections, the Reichstag fire and the Enabling Act of 1933? About three years ago I became interested in how Hitler’s National Socialist German Workers’ party (NSDAP) rose to prominence when Germany was still a democracy, because I hoped it could tell us something about the success of rightwing extremist movements today. From looking at historical sources, I realised that the Reichstag elections of 14 September 1930 were in many ways more important than what happened in 1932 and 1933. And I expected it to be an open-and-shut case. But the more I looked into it, the more I realised that most of the theories we have to explain the rise of the Nazis don’t make sense – the data tells a completely different, far darker story. Why were the 1930 elections so important? The numbers behind the vote were astonishing. In 1928, the NSDAP got 800,000 votes and 12 seats in the Reichstag. A few weeks before the 1930 election, Hitler’s propaganda chief Joseph Goebbels, history’s grand master of exaggeration, still thought they had a chance of going up to 50 to 60 seats at best. Yet on the night, the Nazis got 6.4 million votes and 107 seats. That’s a ninefold increase over the space of two years. In one night, a small splinter party from the political fringes overtook the three established parties of the right – the Centre Party, the DVP and the DNVP – coming in second place behind the Social Democrats. It was an enormous shock. It was the moment at which a racist sect of loudmouths and club-wielders, a party of absolute cranks, came to be politically legitimised. You call the NSDAP a “party of cranks”. Didn’t Hitler have a certain dark charisma? Among German historians, this has long been the dominant theory to explain the Nazi party’s success: that Hitler had an irresistible inner aura that captured the masses. There’s a second theory that is very similar, the führerkult idea. It argues that the NSDAP was so irresistible because it had a leader that spoke to Germans’ yearning for authoritarianism. The problem is: I couldn’t find any evidence before the 1930 vote to support those theories. Because in 1930, every party was practising a star cult around their own political leader, even the Social Democrats. The Nazi party didn’t have a USP in that respect. And the Nazis didn’t even seem to be wholly on board with the führer principle themselves at this stage. Several people in the party complained about the “Byzantine” star cult around Hitler, which is also why the campaign wasn’t really tailored around him as a personality. Let’s remember that in 1930 Hitler wasn’t even on the ballot, because he wasn’t a German citizen: he was a foreigner who had a criminal record for trying to mount a coup and was at risk of being deported. I had grown up seeing Hitler as a monster, but one with a certain political talent. And after 1930, that’s not entirely untrue. But when you focus on 1928 to 1930, even his biographer Ian Kershaw concludes that the NSDAP’s success had very little to do with Hitler. He was going through an absolute dip in form. He only held 29 speeches in 1929, half of what was customary, and 21 of them were all in Bavaria. In 1930 Goebbels spent half the year complaining about Hitler’s prevaricating: when he travelled to Munich to track down the NSDAP leader, he didn’t even bother looking at the party headquarters. “The Reich leadership is at [Hitler’s favourite coffeehouse] Café Heck or the cinema,” Goebbels wrote sarcastically. In 1930, Hitler wasn’t a political genius. He was a lazy criminal who slept in until noon. If not Hitler, was propaganda chief Goebbels the key figure behind the rise of the Nazis? One explanation being revisited these days is that political crises tend to go hand-in-hand with media crises: that the Nazis pounced expertly on new forms of media like illustrated news, radio and film. When we talk about the Nazis, everyone has these images in their head that point to this slick propaganda machine: the Nuremberg rally, the cathedral of light, all these awe-inspiring spectacles. And it’s true that pre-1930 Goebbels invested a lot of effort into building up propaganda newspapers inspired by American formats, such as Der Angriff, Völkischer Beobachter and Illustrierter Beobachter. But early Nazi propaganda was an embarrassing, amateurish joke. I’ve looked through every edition of Illustrierter Beobachter, and the images they presented to the reader were laughable, such as SA men dressed as advertising pillars. It just wasn’t professional. The sales figures were pathetic: nobody was reading these newspapers. Compare it to the means that the other parties had at their disposal: they put up neon signs on street corners and hired planes for aerial advertising. Propaganda just doesn’t explain the NSDAP’s success. What about the economy? The stock market on Wall Street had crashed a year beforehand, German exports were collapsing and unemployment was on the rise. It’s always tempting to fall back on economic factors when explaining the rise of fascist movements. We are hearing it again in Germany now: the economy is crumbling, the trains aren’t running on time, so people are going to fall for the fascists again. But if I look at historical sources from the run-up to 1930, I come away thinking that voters weren’t that stupid. Take the unemployed. Over the last 30 years, historians have established a pretty good picture of who voted for the NSDAP. And we can say with certainty that in regions where unemployment was high, the Nazi party performed relatively poorly. If anything, unemployment was a factor contributing to anti-fascist resilience. And as to the idea that the Nazis managed to attract young first-time voters, the same applies: the NSDAP also performed badly in areas with high rates of first-time voters. The young were also running away from this party. The global economic crisis may explain why the NSDAP managed to double its support in 1932 and attain 37.3% of the vote. But as an explanation for the ninefold boost in 1930, it falls short. Wall Street’s Black Thursday didn’t fully arrive in Germany until July 1931, when several major banks collapsed – 10 months after the Nazis got 107 seats in the Reichstag. The Weimar Republic’s GDP went into a tailspin, with a 36.6% collapse, only over the course of the two years that followed – by the end of 1930, it had merely shrunk by 7.1%, and we don’t know how much of that was as a result of the election outcome. There’s a risk here of confusing cause and effect. What if we look at the democratic parties instead? One of the central tenets of the Nazi party’s campaign was the alleged corruption of the established parties, but there is very little evidence that this was actually the case. The most striking – and also the most puzzling – thing I learned was that all of the three big rightwing parties of the Weimar Republic had put political hardliners in charge between 1928 and 1929. If voters had really been desperate for tough rightwing policies, they could have voted for the Catholic Centre party, the nationalist liberal DVP or the monarchist DNVP – all parties in a pole position to turn their promises into practice. Didn’t they just experience what many conservative parties are finding out now: that when they copy the positions of the far right, voters tend to prefer the original? I think that’s a platitude that simply isn’t true. Because in 1930 Hitler wasn’t the original, he was a washed-out copy of what was offered by the DVP or the DNVP. The DNVP ran a more antisemitic campaign than Hitler, and yet it was the biggest loser of the election, shedding 7.3% of the vote. What strikes me as much more important is credibility. In 1930, the nationalist-liberal DVP was attacked by its own party newspapers for betraying the legacy of its former leader Gustav Stresemann, who had died a year earlier. It’s not unlike the situation we now have with Germany’s Christian Democrats: a party that under Merkel was absolutely centrist and managed to retain loyal voters but then picked a figure from its right wing as their new leader in Friedrich Merz. And voters are switching to the AfD. The central lesson to me is that conservative parties can only win from the centre. You say credibility is key. Then why do corruption scandals barely seem to hurt the modern far-right parties railing loudest against ‘the system’? It’s true that the NSDAP in 1930 was absolutely riddled with scandals: back-stabbing, power struggles, corruption, the whole spectrum. And many German journalists at the time believed they were just one more scandal away from complete collapse. There were some excellent and brave journalists leading some really good investigations. But it didn’t work. I look at far-right parties across Europe now, and I see undercover reporters revealing the AfD’s remigration plans, leading to the biggest protests in postwar German history. And these kinds of investigations are extremely important. But fascist or rightwing extremist parties seem to be immune to this kind of stuff. They are like lightning rods: the scandal is a flash of energy that passes straight through them into the ground and then it’s gone. A corruption scandal might temporarily damage a party, like the “Ibiza affair” did to the Austrian Freedom party, but five years later they are back at double their strength. So why did the Nazis perform so strongly in 1930? As paradoxical as it sounds, it might be for the same reason that voters turned away from the Nazis in 1928: its propensity to violence. Ever since Hitler had been in the NSDAP, he had talked about one thing: executing his political opponents. And the Nazi party remained absolutely consistent in that respect. In the run-up to the 1930 vote, it didn’t talk about social policy, it didn’t talk about building the autobahn. It just had murder plots. How does that help us understand the rise of fascist or rightwing extremist movements today? It’s hard to admit this from a modern perspective, but historical fascism’s lust for violence didn’t make it repulsive but extremely attractive to a lot of German voters. And we are seeing similar things with the AfD today, where fantasies of violent retribution seem to be integral to campaign events on market squares. We are witnessing the poisoning of an entire society, and as a democracy we should ask ourselves whether criminal law shouldn’t apply when political parties communicate that way. Communication is one thing, political plans are another. The NSDAP had both. But we know that the AfD is a radical party that seems to want to ethnically cleanse Germany. If the AfD is voted into power, one of the most highly advanced economies in the world could experience something similar to what happened in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Philipp Ruch’s Der Rückfall (The Relapse) is published by Penguin

title: Thursday briefing: The long, long wait for a male contraceptive pill may soon be over
summary: In today’s newsletter: Reversible male hormonal contraception could reach the market within five to 10 years. But why has this development been so slow?
text: Good morning. Since the first vasectomy was performed in the 1890s (imagine being that volunteer), the male contraceptive armoury has barely advanced. The last reversible method was added to this repertoire centuries ago: while rubber condoms hit the mass market in the 1850s, earlier versions date back beyond ancient Egypt. This looks on the cusp of change. In a landmark announcement last week, the World Health Organization said it expects reversible male contraceptives to be available on the market within five to 10 years. But no major medical breakthrough has just been announced - the fundamentals of male hormonal contraceptives have been known for decades. So what is the science, how does it work and why has it taken so long to get here? That’s the subject of today’s First Edition. Before that, this morning’s headlines. Five big stories Politics | Senior Downing Street officials have been reaching out to thinktanks and pollsters as they look to test public support for the UK rejoining the EU. Middle East | One of the pilots of a plane flying from the United Arab Emirates to Israel stabbed his co-pilot and appeared to try to crash the aircraft, Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said, as Israeli officials said they were investigating whether the incident was an attempted terror attack on Israelis. UK news | There are “strong indications” that Iran played a role in events in which five men were arrested near RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire as part of a terror investigation, Andy Burnham has said. Immigration and asylum | The UK government’s “one in one out” deal with France, which was supposed to help deter small boat arrivals, is expected to expire on Thursday, as talks stall over French demands for an EU-wide scheme. Television | Esther Rantzen, the Bafta-winning TV presenter and founder of Childline, has died aged 86. In a statement, her family paid tribute to “the most wonderful mother” and “cherished grandmother”. In depth: The ‘agonisingly slow’ wait for male contraceptives It’s estimated that 70% of women in the UK have used the contraceptive pill at some point in their lives, having first been introduced here in 1961 (for married women only). The pace at which the pill proliferated is remarkable - the first trials of hormonal contraception for women began in the United States in the 1950s: by 1960 it was available, and within two years, 1.2 million American women were using it. Despite the pill’s wide uptake and high efficacy, the need for further effective methods of reversible contraception has remained consistent. Nearly half of all global pregnancies are unintended, with many resulting in unsafe abortions. An array of options have been developed for women to use - coils both hormonal and metal; implants, injections, patches, pills and vaginal rings. Men have condoms, and, well, coitus interruptus. Even with these limited options, about 30% of couples already rely on a male method. Male hormonal contraception targets sperm, which are constantly produced. “This requires continuous, steady suppression, suppression all day, every day,” Richard Anderson tells me, “but it is proven to work”. Anderson is a professor of clinical reproductive science at Edinburgh University, and has spent decades in the field. It’s close to 50 years since the first hormonal contraceptives were tested on men, but their development has since been “agonisingly slow,” says Anderson. It’s not that scientific successes weren’t there. “While there have been refinements focused on optimal drug formulations, the fundamentals have remained the same.” *** How do male hormonal contraceptives work? While some research looks to target either sperm function or transport, most male contraceptive science today focuses on sperm production. A testosterone-based treatment can trick the brain into switching sperm creation off, while ensuring bodily hormones remain at a healthy level. In the late 1980s, proof-of-concept clinical trials were conducted by the WHO with weekly testosterone injections. “In the first trial, over 60% of men achieved a zero sperm count and successfully used it as their sole contraceptive for a year,” says Anderson. He was involved in a subsequent trial of 450 couples which confirmed hormonal suppression is “highly effective” in reducing sperm count. By the 1990s, the science was further fine-tuned. With the addition of progestin (a synthetic hormone also widely used in hormone replacement therapy), these male hormonal contraceptives became far more effective, with a success rate equivalent to female hormonal methods. The quantity of testosterone required also decreased with this new formulation, potentially improving long-term patient safety. More recently, the US National Institutes of Health funded a major international study of a testosterone/progestogen gel, with participants rubbing it into their shoulders daily. Trials have been conducted across North and South America, Africa and Europe (Anderson has overseen Edinburgh’s 40–couple cohort), with “surprisingly effective” early results and an “extremely low” pregnancy rate. The global findings are still being reviewed, but Anderson’s patients recorded zero pregnancies. As with any hormonal interventions, side effects such as mood shifts can occur. But worldwide, in this study “participant dropouts due to side effects were extremely low at only a few per cent,” says Anderson. And in Edinburgh, at least, “participants tolerated it exceptionally well, with female partners often thrilled to take a break from birth control.” Crucially, this suppression of fertility proved reversible. “Across all trial follow-ups (typically after up to 18 months of use), sperm counts returned to normal, and many couples have subsequently conceived healthy children.” *** The unequal burden of contraception In her brilliant (and surprisingly funny) new documentary It’s Different For Girls film-maker Billie J D Porter explores the sluggish evolution of hormonal male contraception. Years of filming confirmed what gut instinct told her on day one: “It boils down to corporate greed and systemic misogyny.” After experiencing a series of severe contraception side effects herself, Porter started questioning why there have never been widely available male equivalents. She looked at how business, medicine and culture approached hormonal contraception over decades. “There is a deep-rooted reluctance to tinker with male bodies,” she says, a concern that’s not afforded to women. The WHO classifies combined oral contraceptives for women as a group 1 carcinogen; during 1970s US congressional hearings on the safety of women’s birth control pills, not a single woman who had taken the pill was invited to testify. Powerful male execs have also long projected their own reluctance to take hormonal contraceptives into the market. Take German pharma giant Bayer: despite having run a trial that had proved to be “efficient, with a tolerable side-effect profile”, the multinational cut all funding to male contraceptive research in the early 2000s, because bosses felt that for men, taking the medication would be “inconvenient”. “The physical trauma, health risks, and burden of contraception have been forced entirely onto women’s bodies, while protecting male bodies from potential discomfort,” says Porter. Plus, the female hormonal contraceptive market is worth billions globally, and forecast to hit nearly $30bn by 2034. Male birth control represents disruption and risk. Major clinical trials have therefore historically been run by public health bodies on tight budgets. *** What could change? There’s a nuanced picture here. Women’s bodily autonomy was - and continues to be - hard fought for across the world. Despite the risks and complications women’s contraceptives can create, an alternative timeline, in which men kept a tight grip of the contraceptive keys, isn’t necessarily an ideal outcome. It’s a question of equity and increasing options for everyone. Social attitudes shifted, even if big pharma didn’t. A recent WHO study found nearly 75% (72.3% male, 76.2% female) of respondents across a diverse range of countries reported willingness to use new male contraceptives, with more than 85% of women saying they would trust their male partners to take responsibility for contraception. “Men today are increasingly open to gender equality and sharing contraceptive responsibility,” Dr James Kiarie, who heads up contraception and fertility care at the WHO, tells me. “Concerns about side effects are the leading reason women discontinue birth control,” he says. “Soon, if one partner experiences side effects, the other will be able to try.” The biggest obstacle remains “limited research financing,” says Kiarie. “We urgently call on funders to invest in this area… it is a gamechanger for public health and human relationships.” This couldn’t come at a more opportune time. Globally, 40% of women live in countries with restrictive abortion laws. After overturning Roe v. Wade in 2022, the US supreme court ended the constitutional protection for abortion, with millions of Americans now unable to access safe and legal abortion services and living in contraceptive deserts. In the US, interest in male contraceptives increased from 39% to 49% after the supreme court’s decision. Still, in the era of antivaxers, peptide-injections and crackpot conspiracy theories emanating from the US’s uppermost political echelons, what effect actual scientific evidence will have on uptake if and when male contraceptives reach the market is another question. “The rise of hyper-masculine ‘red pill’ subcultures obsessed with testosterone and sperm retention” is a real concern in the sector, Porter says. During filming, Porter spent time with couples who’d been on recent trials. “The male contraceptive option transformed their relationships,” she says. “It fostered deep mutual respect, relief, and shared responsibility. It offers men a meaningful way to share a burden that women have historically carried alone under immense social judgment.” What else we’ve been enjoying After writing about romantasy for First Edition, I’m super-interested in the expectation-busting that goes on within the genre and these thoughtful reflections from men who read about love. Libby In this week’s Long Wave newsletter (sign up here!), Nesrine Malik has written a loving ode to the “long, long diaspora phone call” at once about “nothing and everything”. Charlie Lindlar, newsletters team If you want to understand why Andy Burnham has yet to convince Scottish Labour colleagues that he gets the scale of his challenge north of the border, read Herald deputy political editor Rebecca McCurdy’s excellent analysis (£). Libby England coach Sarina Wiegman dropped heroes Chloe Kelly and Ella Toone from her next World Cup qualifying squad – Tom Garry has an excellent analysis of why it could be a managerial masterstroke for all involved. Charlie I’ve suffered a serious allergy to coorie (Scots: snuggle, nestle, cuddle) culture for a decade now, so I was intrigued by Lucy Knight’s more forgiving take on the interior decor obsession with Highland cows. Libby Sport Football | The Premier League will face pressure from Manchester City’s rivals to push for a sanction that will result in a prolonged absence from the top flight after the club was found guilty of more than 100 charges of financial rule-breaking. Football | Chelsea claimed a valuable point against OL Lyonnes as they played out a goalless draw in the Women’s Champions League, while Arsenal threw away a two-goal lead to draw 2-2 with Paris FC. Rugby | In a candid and absorbing interview, Irish former professional rugby union player Peter O’Mahony speaks with Donald McRae about allowing his own feelings after excelling in “a game of hard men”. The front pages The Guardian leads with “Pilot attacker tried to crash plane, says Netanyahu”. The Times splashes with “Passengers storm cockpit to head off Israel’s 9/11”, while the Telegraph goes with the “Hero who stopped Israel’s 9/11”, and The i Paper says “Hero passengers storm cockpit to save Israel flight from disaster”. The Daily Mail runs with “Kemi to stop school leavers going straight on the dole” and the Financial Times has “‘Strong indications’ Iran was involved in Fairford incident, warns Burnham”. In tributes to TV presenter Esther Rantzen, the Mirror leads with “Esther: See you on the other side” and the Sun: “That was a great life, Esther.” The Latest Mid-air panic as pilot attacked on Israel-bound flight A commercial flight travelling from Dubai to Israel was forced to make an emergency landing after an apparent brawl between its pilots. The flight was in Jordanian airspace when it diverted to Saudi Arabia, after the plane fell 16,000ft in two minutes during the incident, which raised fears of an attempted hijacking. Authorities are investigating a number of lines of inquiry including a hijacking attempt or a mental health incident. Lucy Hough speaks to the Middle East correspondent Will Christou. Cartoon of the day | Ben Jennings The Upside A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad The coastline of Achiltibuie, a string of hamlets and villages in Scotland’s Summer Isles, is dotted with beds of maerl – a 9,000-year-old pink seaweed whose coral-like skeleton provide nurseries for scallops and fish. Ten years ago, this biodiverse habitat was being devastated by scallop dredging, until a group of locals successfully fought to have the practice banned in a 600 sq km (150,000 acre) zone – now the biggest protected area in the world for maerl. They have since seen a dramatic revival of marine life, including the recovery of scallop populations and increased sightings of whales, porpoises and dolphins. Sara Nason, founder of Sea Change (later BHA), one of the groups that led the campaign, says the protection of the maerl beds is “beyond priceless … We’ve achieved recovery of the whole ecosystem.” To read more from Karen on how the battle for the maerl beds was won, sign up for Down to Earth, our climate newsletter, before noon today Sign up here for a weekly roundup of The Upside, sent to you every Sunday Bored at work? title: The zero-bills home: how one family is beating the energy price hikes
summary: The Naylors’ four-bedroom home in Milton Keynes acts like a mini-power station after retrofitting solar panels, a battery and a heat pump
text: Clare Naylor paid close attention to how much energy she and her family were using last winter, filling hot-water bottles and bringing out extra blankets to ensure they didn’t go over budget. This year, she won’t have to worry as she is guaranteed not to receive a bill. While millions of British households face the highest energy charges in three years from this week after a 4% rise in the price cap, and predictions of a 16% increase in January, upgrades to Naylor’s home mean she will not have to pay a thing. The four-bedroom detached home in Milton Keynes was recently fitted with a heat pump and 17 solar panels, and a large battery was installed in the garage to manage the energy generated. The new technology, as well as four new radiators, means the house can use an energy tariff which guarantees she will not pay any bills for five years. In effect, the house behaves like a mini-power station which feeds excess energy back to the grid. As long as the Naylor family stay within a “fair usage” limit, Octopus Energy guarantees they will not be billed for heating, lighting or any of the devices that a family, with three children under 10, use. “We were always fairly careful,” says Naylor. “Our heating was only ever set to 18 degrees although we might boost it if the family were coming around. Otherwise it was slippers, hot-water bottle, jumpers – that’s how you got through.” This year, she says she will heat the house before the children come home from school, something that did not use to happen. The family’s energy bills were relatively low – she says they were about £130 a month, a sum they now plan to spend on holidays. The house, which was built in the 1980s, was retrofitted for free by Santander as part of a project to examine how to fund homes towards better energy efficiency. If she had to pay, the solar panels, heat pump and battery would have come to just under £20,000 after a government grant was applied. The Octopus “Zero Bills” tariff is operating in hundreds of new-build homes around the country since it was launched five years ago. The company is now testing how it works in houses, such as Naylor’s, that are older and need to be retrofitted. Properties have to have good insulation, solar panels, a heat pump and a battery so that they can generate more energy than is being used. “Typically, the homes generate slightly more energy over a year than we’d expect them to use,” says Nigel Banks, technical director of Zero Bills at Octopus Energy. “One of the fundamental requirements is we need to make enough revenues from selling power back to the grid.” To qualify for the tariff, homes must have no gas, even for cooking, so the Naylors had to have their gas boiler removed. The zero-bill promise does not cover charging electric vehicles (EVs). Typically, the best candidates for the retrofitting work are homes built in the last 10 years with good insulation levels, says Banks. The usage cap will be different for each house and is set depending on how much energy they would normally use, with a margin on top. Santander is working on how to offer financing for households who need to borrow money to fund retrofitting projects. In the meantime, using its home improvement loan, at a 6.4% interest rate over five years, would mean repaying £389 a month for a £20,000 project. Mick Taylor from Santander adds: “We’ve got a big challenge. We’ve got 1.5m mortgage accounts, and the vast majority of those are paying monthly energy bills. “Consumers are concerned that energy bills are only going one way – they’re probably the second- or third-biggest outgoing for most households,” he says. “What can we do to help the country move towards net zero with such a big mortgage portfolio? We’ve obviously got a role to play.” Naylor says that she will try to keep the home at a constant warm temperature during the coming winter. “And then train my children to keep the door shut, which will be fun,” she says.

title: Country diary: Which tree sounds the best in the wind? Take a bough, the poplar | Derek Niemann
summary: Frome, Somerset: With a sway and a swoosh, we’re entering the season to enjoy psithurism – the aural quality of the breeze in the trees
text: The wind-catchers along the bottom of the valley miss nothing. Even the lightest breath has them whispering. And when the wind strengthens, they do a good imitation of the river streaming over boulders below their feet. Truly, when it blows, it pours. Pass a poplar and you are enjoying the best example of psithurism, the sound of wind in trees. All this growing season, I have listened politely to oaks, alders and willows, but if I rocked up in a pub looking for chatty company, I’d want a poplar as the bar stool next to me. The name psithurism seems to have been conjured up from Greek roots as recently as the 19th century, yet the practice is as old as humanity. It exposes a curious and inescapable fact – wind itself has no voice. The explorer‑conservationist John Muir tramped many a mile through America’s wild lands, observing that “winds are advertisements of what they touch”. He may well have been thinking of talkative, animated aspens, but all members of the poplar clan are physiologically equipped to shoot the breeze with a wide range of sound and movement. Every broad leaf, shaped like an ace of spades, is well separated from its neighbour on a long stem. Every leaf is therefore washing on a line. Blow, wind, blow. Right now, conditions are what meteorologists call a fresh breeze, enough to bring out a sway and a swoosh, the noise a tide over fine pebbles, the sight upper trunks tilting back and forth to the rhythm. The top boughs are visible evidence of wind as wave, for each sprig springs to life in turn, hundreds of leaves twirling at once. The overall effect is something akin to a host of green glitterballs. Close up, each leaf appears to be spinning in agony or ecstasy, desperate to break free or stay attached. Photosynthesis must be quite a giddy wonder, for how do rotating cells catch the sun? Over the coming weeks, these wind chimes will break, their leaves raining down. And up above, in the so-tall trees, there will be a new percussion, the click-clack creak of branch on branch, the incoming drumbeat of winter. • Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024, is available now at guardianbookshop.com
