title: Steve Hilton, Xavier Becerra clash in testy California governor’s race debate
summary: The candidates running to replace Gavin Newsom sparred over taxes, immigration and regulating AI
text: Xavier Becerra and Steve Hilton, the candidates running to be California’s next governor, clashed on Wednesday over taxes, immigration and regulating artificial intelligence in a testy debate held days before voters begin receiving their ballots in the heavily Democratic state. Hilton, the former Fox News host endorsed by Donald Trump, used the hourlong matchup, hosted by CNN in its studio in Burbank, California, to argue that Becerra, a former congressman who served as the US health and human services secretary during the Biden administration, was not actively campaigning and instead taking voters for granted. “He wasn’t even supposed to be the candidate,” Hilton, 57, said, referring to Becerra’s unexpected success after an unusually wild primary campaign. “I just want to ask every Californian: aren’t you tired of that?” Becerra, 68, pitched his experience as an asset, vowing to tackle the state’s punishing cost of living crisis while being a bulwark against the Trump administration’s policies. He accused Hilton of owing loyalty to Trump – and not the state that roundly rejected the president in each of the last three presidential elections. “If you listen closely, you can hear Donald Trump in that response,” Becerra said of Hilton’s reply to a question about regulating the development of AI. Hilton’s bid to succeed California’s term-limited governor, Gavin Newsom, is aimed at voter discontent with the political status quo in a state that hasn’t elected a Republican governor in two decades. But his pitch is complicated by his party identification and the president who has backed him. Though most Californians say the state is headed in the wrong direction, fewer than a quarter of likely voters approve of the president’s job performance, notably lower than the national average, and many cite “fight against Trump administration policies” as a priority. Recent polls show Becerra with a significant lead over Hilton, suggesting the onus was on the Republican hopeful to persuade voters partisan change was needed in Sacramento. The debate, the only scheduled face-to-face debate before the 3 November general election, comes just days before voters begin receiving their ballots by mail. Both candidates said they would oppose the so-called billionaire tax proposal, a November ballot measure that would levy a one-time 5% tax on any California resident worth more than $1bn. Becerra’s opposition puts him at odds with progressives, including Senator Bernie Sanders, who will campaign for the measure in California this weekend. But they were at odds on Proposition 39, a ballot measure that would require voters to show a government-issued ID to vote in person. Like other Democratic leaders in the state, Becerra said he opposed the measure, calling it an initiative “backed by Donald Trump” that would make it harder for Californians to vote. Hilton said he supported the proposal, but insisted he had confidence in the state’s voting system despite Trump’s unsubstantiated claims of fraud. “I’ve got confidence in what we saw in the primary and in this process,” Hilton said. Without distancing himself significantly from Trump, whose Maga base he cannot afford to alienate, Hilton sought to draw subtle differences: “My whole aim here would be to lower the temperature.” An exchange over immigration policy became personal, when Becerra, the son of Mexican immigrants, accused Hilton, who grew up in England and was an adviser to the former UK prime minister David Cameron, of appearing to support measures that would “welcome immigrants who look like you” while wanting to “deport immigrants who look like me”. “What a disgraceful remark that was,” Hilton shot back. Becerra’s path to the general election was winding. After languishing in the low single digits for much of the race, he was catapulted to the front of the pack after the implosion of Eric Swalwell’s campaign amid a slew of sexual misconduct and assault allegations – claims the now former congressman denied. Becerra ultimately advanced first in the June primary, overcoming fierce opposition from his more progressive rival, the billionaire activist Tom Steyer. Hilton came in second, with Trump’s endorsement helping to consolidate conservative support and avert the risk of a Democratic lockout in the state’s non-partisan primary. But the president’s support risks being a liability in the general election as the unresolved war with Iran has spiked oil prices and kept US inflation stubbornly high. Since reaching the general election, Becerra has maintained a low profile, while Hilton has blitzed the state as he seeks to make inroads with voters who disapprove of Trump. “Thank you to CNN for bringing Xavier out of hiding,” Hilton said, slamming his opponent as a “career politician” who was the product of the “machine in Sacramento”. Becerra pushed back, arguing that the challenges facing the state and country were too great to risk rolling the dice on a political newcomer. “There aren’t training wheels in the governor’s office,” Becerra said, repeating a line he deployed in the primary. “You have to know how to do the job, and that’s why I’m asking California voters to vote for me for governor of state of California.”

title: Israelis divided as vote that could oust Netanyahu only weeks away
summary: Some on streets of Jerusalem pledge their support to prime minister while others hope for change
text: On the streets of Jerusalem, crowded with secular and ultra-Orthodox Jews, religious nationalists, settlers, Palestinians, and soldiers returning from deployments, uncertainty hangs over an election less than a month away that could mark a turning point for a country profoundly changed after the Hamas attacks of 7 October 2023 and nearly three years of war in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran. The political battle remains on a knife-edge. For over two years most polls have predicted that the coalition of parties led by prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu will collectively slip below the 61-seat threshold needed to form a government. But there is no clear path to power for his main opponent, Gadi Eisenkot, the former chief of staff of the Israel Defense Forces, even if he maintains current levels of support, because he has ruled out going into coalition with any of the parties led by Palestinian citizens of Israel, who are projected to claim a critical 12 seats. For Netanyahu to stay in power, he would have to either put together a different coalition or pull off an unprecedented election night surprise. Another deeply fragmented Knesset seems likely, in which neither side is close to securing a majority. The latest Channel 13 poll, published last week, captured that deadlock: Jewish Israeli parties opposed to Netanyahu were projected to win 52 seats, against 51 for the prime minister’s bloc, with both falling short of the 61 required for a majority. Eisenkot’s Yashar party topped the poll with 22 seats, while Netanyahu’s Likud was projected to take 18. The lack of clarity over the next government – with both main blocs on the right – is fuelling unease among Israelis, some of whom believe little will change whoever becomes prime minister. “I’m not going to vote because I don’t trust anyone,” said Rachel, 42, an Israeli citizen living in West Jerusalem. “I used to vote for Yair Lapid,” she added, referring to the leader of the centrist Yesh Atid party. “The party’s name means ‘there is a future’. But today, I don’t see any future for this country.” Average public trust across the eight Israeli institutions measured consistently by the Israel Democracy Institute, a statistics body, stood at 34% in 2025, compared with 61% in 2012. An atmosphere of pessimism and indecision is palpable in Jerusalem, where tensions between Palestinians in occupied East Jerusalem – the majority of whom cannot vote in Israeli national elections – and rightwing Jewish Israelis have deepened since 7 October. The Hamas attack is likely to weigh heavily on the ballot: a recent poll by the Israel Democracy Institute found that 68% of Jewish respondents said 7 October would be a central factor in deciding how they voted. “After 7 October, everyone in this government has to take the blame,” said Ilda, who owns a clothing shop on Jaffa Street, one of Jerusalem’s oldest and busiest thoroughfares. Referring to a Haaretz investigation claiming Netanyahu had been warned about the possibility of a major Hamas attack, which he denies, she said: “After journalists exposed what happened, look what they did: they attacked the journalists instead of taking responsibility.” West Jerusalem has long been considered fertile ground for Netanyahu and the Israeli right. Yet Israel’s growing diplomatic isolation and the prospect of seemingly endless conflict on multiple fronts are beginning to worry voters even here, a few steps from the bustling Mahane Yehuda market, where giant election posters for Itamar Ben-Gvir, the far-right national security minister known for his anti-Palestinian rhetoric and championing a racist death penalty law that in practice applies only to Palestinians, loom over the streets. “This country needs radical change. I think I’ll vote for Naftali Bennett,” said Yosef, 26, a religious Israeli, referring to the rightwing former prime minister who now leads the B’Yachad alliance and is one of Netanyahu’s main political rivals. On one side are tens of thousands of Netanyahu supporters – called “Bibi-ists” in reference to the prime minister’s nickname – as well as backers of the far-right ministers Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, who want to return the current coalition to power to “finish the job” in Gaza, Iran, Lebanon and the West Bank. On the other are tens of thousands of voters who believe Israel is losing its standing in the world and needs a change of direction – something many see as embodied by the centre-right Eisenkot. His supporters argue that he would place greater emphasis on education, social policy and the economy, areas they say have been neglected by the current government. “I’ll vote for anyone but the prime minister of 7 October,” said Turgeman as he enjoyed a coffee with his wife at a cafe in Jaffa during the Jewish high holiday season. “I’ve never voted Likud in my life, and I’m certainly not going to start now. I’ll vote for Eisenkot. We need a normal prime minister – someone who also cares about the economy and about prices, which have soared because of the war.” Food prices in Israel have reached record highs amid the regional conflict and supply chain disruption, with food inflation outpacing the broader consumer price index. The cost of food, including fresh fruit and vegetables, has risen by 9.5% over the past two years. “They think about wars, while nobody is dealing with the economic crisis,” Turgeman said. “And what has Netanyahu done? He has continued to provide financial support that benefits the Haredi [ultra-Orthodox] community.” Since 7 October, Israel’s ultra-Orthodox community has been at the centre of a bitter dispute over military conscription. While most Jewish Israelis serve, Haredi men studying in religious seminaries have long been largely exempt. In 2024, amid war and growing pressure on reservists, the supreme court ruled there was no legal basis to continue the exemption, fuelling anti-draft protests, roadblocks and clashes with police. Haredi parties have blamed Netanyahu for failing to pass legislation to protect the exemption. Ultra-Orthodox Jews, who make up about 14% of Israel’s population, have traditionally voted for parties backed by their rabbis, including the two main Haredi parties in Netanyahu’s coalition. But anger among younger Haredim over conscription and the policing of protests could lead some to defy their religious leaders this time. “All the options in this election are junk, but I think I will vote for Eisenkot,” said Pinchas, 24, an ultra-Orthodox student who recently completed his military service. “I have the impression that this time people my age won’t vote according to what the rabbis tell them. Many are angry about the way Netanyahu handled the conscription law, and especially about the crackdown on those who protested against it.” As the Guardian conducted interviews near Jerusalem’s central bus station, an elderly passerby called out: “There is only one prime minister – Bibi!” It was a reminder that, despite the uncertainty and the opposition’s narrow lead in the polls, the Israeli leader retains a loyal base. “I’m sure Netanyahu will win,” said Avraham Levy, 76, a Likud supporter and fruit seller at Mahane Yehuda market. “We’ll have the majority. We need to support Netanyahu because he has to finish the job. If he doesn’t, who will?” he said, referring to Israel’s wars on several fronts. Among those still backing Netanyahu’s coalition partners are supporters of the far right, including Jakub, 23, who was due to begin his military service soon. “I’ll vote for Moshe Feiglin,” he said, referring to an extreme far-right former Israeli Knesset member who declared in 2025 that the conflict in Gaza was not against Hamas but against every child and baby in the territory, and is now running jointly with the far-right Religious Zionist party. “Because he represents my values, and he has never changed his principles,” Jakub said. The field is wide open and the divide is also generational: by 2019, support for a Palestinian state stood at about 20%-30% among the youngest Jewish Israeli cohorts, compared with roughly 40%-55% among older generations, reflecting a longer-term shift towards more hawkish attitudes. No more recent comparable data was available. The difficulty for the anti-Netanyahu camp is that it remains fragmented and has struggled to agree on a coherent political platform or a common strategy capable of uniting its different factions. Parties representing Palestinian citizens, known as Arab parties inside Israel, could push Eisenkot’s coalition over the 61-seat threshold, but amid a campaign of racism and Islamophobia, he has ruled out going into government with them. They could potentially support a minority government. But last week, the Central Elections Committee voted to bar Ra’am and the Joint List, the country’s two main Palestinian parties, from the election, after the far-right Otzma Yehudit party filed a petition arguing that they support terrorism and deny the existence of Israel as a Jewish and democratic state. The opposition Democrats party filed a similar petition arguing for Otzma Yehudit to be banned for incitement to racism and negating the existence of Israel as a democratic state, because of racist policies pursued in power under its leader Itamar Ben Gvir. That was not upheld. The decision is being challenged in the supreme court, which has overturned similar bans in past elections. If allowed to run in the elections, the Arab parties will be crucial to the opposition’s prospects of forming a government and to Eisenkot’s chances of replacing Netanyahu. Tensions between Palestinian citizens of Israel and the state have deepened since 7 October amid arrests, interrogations and other legal action against Arab citizens, often over protests or social media posts. For these reasons, Palestinian citizens of Israel are often reluctant to express their voting preferences. In the 2025 Israeli Democracy Index survey, 70% said they preferred to remain silent about their political views in the presence of strangers, up from 45% in 2016 and compared with 53% of Jewish respondents. But Palestinian citizens of Israel remain divided over how best to respond, with many pessimistic that any future government will defend rights they say have too often been denied. The Joint List has maintained a more oppositional stance, signalling it could support an anti-Netanyahu minority government from outside while stopping short of joining a coalition, although it has done so in the past. “These elections are about our strength as an Arab community and our ability to have an influential political voice,” said Amir, 34, from Mashhad in northern Israel, who plans to vote for the Joint List. “We need strong, united Arab representation on equality, discrimination and the Palestinian cause, while cooperating when it benefits our community.” Ra’am, led by Mansour Abbas, has instead made political pragmatism its defining strategy. In 2021 it became the first independent Arab party to join an Israeli governing coalition, seeking budgets, services and greater influence for Palestinian citizens of Israel. “Arab society is being torn apart by crime and violence, while relations with Jewish Israelis are becoming more hostile,” said Abu Mahmoud, 33, from Kafr Kanna, also in the north of the country. “That’s why I’ll vote for Ra’am: negotiate, secure budgets and work with Jewish Israelis where possible.” He added: “I want politics that can actually improve people’s lives.” Jamal Risheq contributed to this report

title: ‘They raped our country’: documentary follows Kenyans’ fight for restitution over stolen land
summary: Multinational tea companies still occupy ancestral highlands of communities displaced during British colonial era
text: For British colonialists, the fertile and cool uplands of central Kenya were the “White Highlands”, to be reserved exclusively for European settlers. Local communities were forced from the land, which was turned into plantations for tea and other crops. In recent decades, descendants of the displaced have fought to reclaim their ancestral land, some of which is now occupied by multinational tea companies and other large corporations. The fight for restitution is the subject of Kikuyu Land, a documentary film directed by the Kenyan film-maker Bea Wangondu and her American counterpart Andrew H Brown that is being released in the UK on Friday. “Colonial structures didn’t just shape land and labour in Kenya. They created patterns of power that thrive today globally,” said Brown. “This isn’t just a Kenyan story. This could be told sadly in almost every part of the world.” In 1902, under Sir Charles Eliot, then commissioner of the East Africa Protectorate (present-day Kenya), a law was passed making vast tracts of fertile ancestral land “Crown land”, allowing the government to sell and lease land to white settlers to encourage their settlement and farming, ignoring African communal land ownership systems. The policy attracted settlers and led to the violent displacement of local communities to marginalised, crowded and less-productive “native reserves”. In 1962, a year before independence, the colonial administration initiated a redistribution programme to transfer farms in the highlands from departing white settlers to landless Kenyans. The programme was aimed at purchasing land in the highlands from willing white settlers and reselling it to Kenyans on credit. By the time it ended in 1971, about 1.15m acres of land had been bought from 780 white farmers and sold to approximately 35,000 Kenyan families. But much of the land remained with the political elite and foreign corporate interests, including companies that held huge plantations. The idea of the film was inspired by Wangondu’s curiosity since childhood about why her grandfather had disproportionately vast land, compared with his neighbours. With answers unforthcoming from her family, she decided to dig deep into colonial history. Having worked for international film companies and news organisations for years, Wangondu wanted to tell her own story, asking questions that have shaped her perception of herself and her family. “It’s time for us to tell our stories in our own voices and in our own understanding,” she said. She discussed the idea with Brown in 2021 after they met while working on a National Geographic production, and they pursued it. Kikuyu Land follows Wangondu’s search for answers about her family’s land, interspersed with a wider investigation into tea plantations and the story of the pursuit by one man, Mungai, to reclaim his family’s ancestral land. “They raped our country, they displaced us, they took our land and they did the unfairness they did to us,” Mungai tells Wangondu in the film. Wangondu and Mungai’s journeys in the documentary expose colonial legacies, buried histories and family pains that the two struggle to face up to. In one scene, Mungai crouches under a tree and grieves after his aunt shows him a spot, now inside the fence of the tea farm whose land his family is claiming, where their patriarch was buried. Kenya was under British rule from 1895 to 1963, first as a protectorate then as a colony. The period was characterised by racial discrimination, forced displacement and labour, and brutal suppression of resistance. Members of the Kipsigis and Talai communities have made calls for redress in recent years over the violent eviction of their ancestors from their lands in the Rift Valley to make way for tea plantations owned by white settlers. In 2021, UN special rapporteurs expressed concern about the British government’s failure to provide “effective remedies and reparations” to the two communities. Kikuyu Land premiered at the Sundance film festival in the US in January and had its UK festival premiere in June at the Sheffield DocFest. It will screen at the NBO film festival in Nairobi in October. Joseph Njenga, one of its producers, said hearing stories while making the film of people who suffered pain and atrocities caused by the colonial administration had left an emotional imprint. “My head could not contextualise and process the pain that was brought upon us – and for no reason,” he said. • Kikuyu Land is in UK cinemas from 2 October

title: New Google Maps images reveal massive scale of devastation in Gaza
summary: Satellite imagery shows further destruction of homes, businesses and places of worship since fragile ceasefire
text: An update to Google Maps has revealed the extent of devastation during the three-year Gaza war and the severity of the continuing humanitarian crisis faced by the territory’s 2.3 million inhabitants. The images were taken in June this year and show further destruction of homes, businesses, places of worship and infrastructure since a fragile ceasefire came into effect almost 12 months ago. They show huge tented camps lining much of the shoreline, often within a few metres of the sea. Gaza’s once busy main port, now badly damaged and empty of fishing boats, is surrounded by makeshift accommodation. Any available open space in Gaza City is packed with shacks, tents and huts. The images also show massive damage to northern towns such as Beit Hanoun, as well as the destruction of places of worship such as the Istiqlal mosque in Khan Younis. Major neighbourhoods in Gaza City such as Jabaliya and Shuja’iya, which were targeted in repeated Israeli offensives, are clearly now uninhabitable. Swaths of rubble are visible in the south of Gaza, where a wide strip appears to have been cleared by Israeli forces along the border with Egypt. The town of Rafah appears to have been almost entirely reduced to rubble and Tel al-Sultan razed to the ground. More than 2.1 million displaced people are living in tents and temporary shelters in Gaza, where about 82% of structures – roughly 200,000 buildings – have been damaged, with about two-thirds of those destroyed, according to the UN agency for Palestinian refugees, Unrwa. A recent UN assessment estimated that the number of destroyed structures across Gaza had increased by 9% since the declaration of a ceasefire in October 2025. “The estimate of the total amount of rubble in Gaza is 61m tonnes. It is approximately 20 times the amount of rubble generated in all wars across the world over the last 18 years,” Jaco Cilliers, the UN Development Programme’s special representative in Palestine told the Guardian last month. The presence of human remains still buried under the rubble remains one of the most urgent humanitarian problems. More than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza since the start of the war, mostly civilians. The conflict was triggered by a surprise attack by Hamas into Israel in October 2023, in which militants killed about 1,200 people, mostly civilians, and took 251 others hostage. • This article was amended on 5 October 2026 to remove satellite images of Beit Lahiya. While Google Maps dates the more recent photo to 2026, data from Google Earth has the date as December 2024.

title: ‘Explosion of melt rates’: 20% of Swiss glaciers lost in five years
summary: Alpine regions in Europe experiencing extreme glacier collapse due to heat-trapping effects of fossil fuel pollution
text: Switzerland has lost almost one-fifth of its ice in just five years, research has found, in a dramatic reshaping of the Alpine country whose big white glaciers have been reduced to moonlike rock deserts, scientists say. Swiss glaciers shrank by 5.5% in the first eight months of 2026, according to an annual monitoring report, after a summer of scorching heatwaves that followed a winter with little snow. The reduction in ice volume falls just shy of the record set in 2022 and brings the total loss of glacier ice since 2021 to 19.4%. Matthias Huss, a glaciologist at ETH Zürich and lead author of the report, said many people do not realise how fast glaciers are retreating, or that just one generation ago some now-barren sites used to sit beneath hundreds of metres of ice. The scientists have not yet compiled a formal tally of lost glaciers this year but said they had witnessed the death of a number of small ones. “I visited one last week and it’s so impressive to stand in this moonlike landscape where there was a big layer of ice – an extensive glacier – just a few years ago,” said Huss. “And now it’s a rock desert where there’s some scattered blocks of old ice still lying around and melting on the hot rocks.” The report, a collaboration between the Swiss Glacier Monitoring Network and the Swiss Commission for Cryosphere Observation, found the mean thickness of individual glaciers fell by between 2.5 metres and 4 metres in 2026. Huss said scientists were increasingly seeing glaciers collapse from the inside – the result of internal streams beneath the ice that excavate caverns – rather than simply retreating from surface heat. “You have huge holes like cheese in the middle of the ice that have collapsing roofs,” said Huss. “These are processes that tear the glaciers apart and make them retreat even faster.” Europe is warming twice as fast as the global average from the heat-trapping effects of fossil fuel pollution and the destruction of nature, with Alpine regions experiencing some of the most dramatic changes. Analysis published by MeteoSwiss on Tuesday found the summer half-year from April to September was the hottest and driest it had been since records began in 1864. In that time, humanity has filled the atmosphere with 1.8tn tons of carbon dioxide and heated the planet by about 1.4C. The heat this summer was worse than in 2022 but Swiss ice loss just missed the record-breaking levels set that year. The scientists attributed this to limited deposits of Saharan dust, which foul the snow and prevent it from reflecting sunlight, as well as slightly greater snow cover at the end of winter and more sunlight in the summer. Huss visited the former Plattalvafirn, or Griess glacier, in September, which used to cover a mountain flank but lost 99% of its area in just 20 years. The glacier was the subject of some of the most detailed monitoring in the world in the 1950s and Huss worked with its data when he was a PhD student. “What was different at that time, is that the rates of retreat were still kind of at a normal level,” said Huss. “What we are seeing now is a complete explosion of these melt rates, leading to the disintegration of glaciers. They’re really just falling apart.”

title: It was the most welcoming town in Britain. Why has Crowborough become so divided?
summary: In 2022, they opened their arms to Ukrainian refugees. But this year, the arrival of more than 300 asylum seekers has split the community. Can the rift be healed?
text: It’s Sunday morning and in the East Sussex town of Crowborough a few dozen anti-migrant activists are waving union jacks outside a travel agent. Their sound system is blasting out a song about “lefty lemons”. A few yards away, a similar number of protesters are supporting the asylum seekers being housed at a nearby military camp. Their signs read “Humanity has no borders” and “Civilisation fails when hatred prevails”; they’re playing classics about love and peace by Bob Marley, the Beatles and Aretha Franklin. The arrival of more than 300 asylum seekers in Crowborough Training Camp in early 2026 has split this town of 22,000 people. Depending on who you speak to, the asylum seekers, who are all men, are either a marauding threat to women and girls, or the loveliest human beings you could wish to meet. There is one thing that unites Crowborough, however: everyone criticises the Home Office for its failure to consult them about its plans. “It’s shocking to see Home Office incompetence up close,” says Rachel Millward, deputy leader of the Green party, and leader of Wealden district council, which covers Crowborough. “Failing to inform, never mind consult, local authorities and residents has created a communications vacuum, and a petri dish for an organised, well-funded far-right hate campaign.” Holly Jeffery, 36, has come out to support the asylum seekers. She is wearing earrings shaped like lemon slices, saying she has decided to “lean into” the song about her and others she is standing alongside. The full chorus is: “Lefty lemons haven’t got a clue, standing on street corners with their fellow crew, always on the left, none of them are right.” While the groups are within touching distance, they are separated by a path that leads to the Waitrose car park. A few police officers form a relaxed human buffer. Since the first asylum seekers arrived, there has been a weekly anti-migrant march through the town, organised by groups including Crowborough Says No! and Crowborough Shield. The demonstrators are not all local, but many describe themselves as “concerned residents”. Today, they have decided to stage a static protest, occupying the spot where the pro-asylum seeker group usually holds a vigil. The two groups look at each other. There is no overt hostility. One protester is dressed in black paramilitary gear, a mask covering most of his face, the initials on his uniform identifying him as a member of a “community safety” group called the British Security Project. That aside, a casual passerby might interpret the scene as neighbours having a polite disagreement. Because the numbers are small, the music is blaring and the weather is mild, the atmosphere is relatively laid-back. But since the Home Office dropped the bombshell late last year that asylum seekers were moving in, the mood in town has been increasingly dark. The people of Crowborough never used to be divided in this way. The town is not one that politicians describe as “left behind”. It is relatively affluent, with low levels of unemployment; it celebrates its most famous former resident, the author Arthur Conan Doyle, and takes pride in nearby Ashdown Forest, where AA Milne set the Winnie-the-Pooh stories. In 2022, the Guardian hailed Crowborough as one of the most welcoming towns in the UK to Ukrainian refugees. Today, however, some residents stress the fact that the Ukrainians came to the UK legally. It is also legal under international law to claim asylum, although in 2022 the government introduced the offence of “illegal arrival” to deter people from entering the country without authorisation – on small boats, for example. Some residents are also unhappy that the people on the military base are all men, most of them young. According to Anna, who has lived in Crowborough since she was a child, and has come out today to support the camp’s residents, the town used to be “boring”. “Nothing ever happened here,” she says. “There was never any excitement.” But the arrival of the asylum seekers has changed all that. High-profile figures on the far right have visited and whipped up fear and hatred. When Ukip leader Nick Tenconi spoke at one of the protests, he started a chant of: “Send them home!” and declared: “It is time for patriotic rage and holy fury … No one asked for uncontrolled illegal migration.” When Katie Hopkins came, she said she understood that “you are fed up of being treated as second-class citizens in your own country”. She added: “When people who have no right to be in this country get put at the front of the line, that is not OK.” The town’s divisions have also featured in a Channel 4 documentary, England ’Til I Die, which centred on Liam Tomsett, a local utilities manager turned anti-immigration activist. “Those who are hostile towards the asylum seekers predicted there would be a crime spree from the day they arrived,” says Anna, who, like most people interviewed for this piece, asked to use a pseudonym. “But it hasn’t happened. A lot of this is based on people’s fears rather than their actual experience.” Signs prohibiting urinating, defecating and spitting have been fixed to the fence surrounding the military base, tapping into racist tropes about asylum seekers. The Home Office has confirmed that neither it nor Wealden district council erected them. According to Sussex Police, there have been just three criminal charges related to Crowborough since the camp opened in January, one involving an asylum seeker who was inside it at the time of the alleged offence. The others involve two anti-migrant protesters, both with addresses outside the town. But that scarcely seems to matter. “They haven’t done anything wrong so far – but should we have to wait for that to happen, because it’s going to?” one man holding a union jack asks. Others talk of migrants defecating in gardens and groping a girl, but are unable to provide details. One woman complains about men from the camp buying alcohol in town, then drinking on the streets. “They’ve got no morals. What sort of people are they to sit down outside Lidl after buying alcohol? And we taxpayers are paying for it. While our children are struggling to make ends meet, they’re getting everything for free.” “These idiots talking about love and peace with their unicorns and rainbows, a lot of them are mentally retarded,” adds another woman, repeating claims that asylum seekers “spit and poo in people’s gardens”. She goes on to praise Daniel Thomas, known as Danny Tommo, a far-right agitator recently charged with offences connected to allegedly slashing a dinghy in the Channel. Apart from Holly Jeffery and Caroline Coxon, 71, both supporting the asylum seekers, nobody on either side wants to be identified. A local organisation, Samas (Supporting Arriving Migrants and Asylum Seekers), has more than 200 volunteers who help the base’s residents with everything from English classes to clothes and growing plants and food. But most are afraid to show their faces at the weekly vigil, or even to announce their support, for fear of being abused as “migrant babysitters” or “boat shaggers”, or having their personal information circulated and used to harass them. Some far-right “auditors” have been filming volunteers as they go in and out of the camp, as well as recording their car number plates, sometimes streaming footage to their own YouTube channels. “Some people are disguising themselves when they go into Crowborough town,” says Pam, who supports the asylum seekers. “I go out wearing a hat and sunglasses and change the colour of my hair every time I go to the hairdresser.” “What have we become?” asks Don, a retired teacher. “I would love to go out there loud and proud, but the reality is you are putting your whole life and family on the line if you do that.” He was giving out leaflets telling a more positive story about asylum seekers than the rapist invader narrative when he was told: “Don’t give me one. I want to see them all die in the Channel.” “I find this deeply disturbing,” Don says. When he speaks about meeting the new arrivals recently at a social event, he starts crying. “I found the asylum seekers to be incredible people, normal people. The fact that they got here at all is a miracle,” he says. “They have fled terrible things and they just want to get on with their lives here.” Anna helps source clothing from local charity shops. “I’m never sure, when I pay for 14 T-shirts or something like that, if I can say to the person behind the counter: ‘I’m buying these for the asylum seekers,’ or if it’s better just to keep quiet,” she says. Most of those protesting against the camp would not want to harm the asylum seekers or their supporters. But a dossier compiled by local residents and passed to the police claims that some have gone further than marches or vigils. On Facebook and other platforms, people who are known to support the asylum seekers have been threatened with acid attacks, petrol bombs and rape. The dossier, which has been seen by the Guardian, also claims that several local businesses have been threatened by far-right agitators, along with a church where some asylum seekers worship. One man was punched in the throat after he held up a “Love Thy Neighbour” sign, while an elderly couple were falsely accused of supporting sex offenders. In yet another case, a 92-year-old church volunteer was reportedly woken at 3am for two nights in a row by a man standing outside her home, shining a torch through her window and shouting abuse. Jeffery and Coxon say they thought long and hard about going public, given the hostile climate that pervades their home town. Both have been the subject of unflattering cartoons online. “The far right discovered who I was and where I live,” says Coxon. “I was quite scared. I decided I could do one of two things. Either I could hide away or I could stand up and be counted. I’m proud of what we’re doing. I’m more determined than ever to speak up for what I believe in. I will not let them stamp on me.” “I’ve been targeted on Facebook,” says Jeffery. “Seeing all the scaremongering and misinformation on social media, I thought: ‘Enough is enough. I can’t let this go unchallenged.’ Those who shout loudest aren’t necessarily in the majority.” She is hopeful that Crowborough may yet be able to heal from the damage the Home Office decision has caused. But she isn’t holding her breath. “Crowborough is still a town divided,” she says. The Home Office defends its decision to accommodate asylum seekers in Crowborough. A spokesperson said: “The government is working on a fairer distribution of asylum accommodation across the country, with over £1bn saved in costs since the election. This includes closing all asylum hotels and moving to alternative accommodation, including former military sites. These are designed to be self-contained, with 24-hour security and CCTV, to reduce the impact on local communities.” Back at the protests, the anti-migrant group is first to drift away. The pro-asylum seeker group move into the space they have vacated and start singing and dancing to the Black Eyed Peas: “Whatever happened to the values of humanity? … Lack of understanding leading us away from unity … Where is the love? Where is the love?” • Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Kyiv Independent editor: ‘Our readers want Russia to suffer but we can’t be propagandists’
summary: Olga Rudenko says news site has duty to report on Russian military gains and Ukrainian corruption even if subjects are not so well read
text: Readers of Ukraine’s leading English news site “really want Russia to suffer” but that should not lead the title to downplay the military and political problems facing Kyiv, its editor-in-chief has said. Speaking to the Guardian before an event in London, Olga Rudenko said many of the Kyiv Independent’s most-read stories described Ukrainian deep strike attacks into Russia, potentially distorting its coverage. The Kyiv Independent, however, cannot afford to become propagandistic, she argued, and marginalise Russian military successes or reduce reporting on Ukrainian corruption because the subjects are not so well read. “We had a conversation in the newsroom when somebody raised that our website, in the mornings, is all about Ukrainian attacks on Russian Wildberries warehouses and so on,” Rudenko said. “But it’s misrepresenting the full picture when you don’t balance it out with enough stories about attacks on Ukraine, which are, by the way, far less popular with our readers.” The challenge is that “people really want Russia to suffer”, and read about “something going boom” but it was the Kyiv Independent’s duty to “not just to feed them more of what they like”. The “core idea of the Kyiv Independent is that we’re not Ukrainian propaganda, we’re not affiliated with the government, we’re not Ukraine’s PR service,” the editor said. Rudenko said she had “no expectation” that the war would end any time soon, with Russia stepping up its bombing of Kyiv before winter and Ukrainian strikes denting its neighbour’s economy while diplomacy is stalled. It is a feeling that has hung over journalists at the site for some time. This year employees did not bother planning for a peacetime scenario in their annual strategy session. “It was the first time when this question wasn’t really arising,” Rudenko said. On Friday, Rudenko will host a “live story-telling event” in London where reporters, including the frontline correspondent Francis Farrell, will give their personal experience of Ukraine in the midst of the biggest war in Europe since 1945. The title relies on readers to make monthly contributions for its revenue, an idea also used by the Guardian, and London was chosen as a venue because it “is probably the biggest city in terms of membership”, the editor said. Media freedom in Ukraine has not worsened under Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Rudenko said, but added: “I would struggle to say it has gotten better.” Reporters can write freely without “fearing some immediate consequences” but the editor said that a concentration of power around the president remains. Zelenskyy has not held a press conference for independent Ukrainian media since February 2025, and there is still a bitter legacy from the president’s attempt a few months later to neutralise Ukraine’s two anti-corruption agencies, which had to be reversed in the light of public protests. “We’ve been casting a critical look at Zelenskyy and his government for a while now, she said, highlighting an editorial written in July 2025 at the height of crisis, headlined “Zelenskyy just betrayed Ukraine’s democracy”. The president and his allies, Rudenko said, had “brazenly and stupidly” sought to take away a central achievement of the Ukrainian revolution of 2014, after which the independence of Ukraine’s anti-corruption bodies was introduced. Despite this, she said, “a critical mass of Ukrainians” do not think it is time to hold a presidential election, as called for by the former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov in August. Elections have been suspended under martial law, though Zelenskyy’s term expired more than two years ago. The Kyiv Independent has not come out in support of elections, Rudenko said, partly because support for holding them is running at about 15%. Protests this summer against Fedorov’s firing by Zelenskyy were “of the size that the president can still afford to ignore”, she added. The Kyiv Independent was founded three months before the full-scale Russian invasion by journalists who had lost their jobs when the rival Kyiv Post was temporarily closed by its owner. Launched with a $100,000 grant, it rapidly became an essential English language news sources for Ukraine as the country was attacked and the war with Russia became global news. The number of contributing readers, or members, most of whom pay $5 a month, has risen from 14,000 at the beginning of 2025 to 25,500 a year later and to 36,000 now, allowing staff numbers to grow to 99 and the title to move to bigger offices.

title: Cornell’s Jane Doe Said She Was Given Ketamine. Here’s How the Drug Works.
summary: Ketamine is a short-acting anesthetic that can have hallucinogenic effects. It is becoming more easily available, and some experts fear misuse is increasing.

title: ‘The toll is huge’: El Niño-driven wildfires overwhelm Indonesia’s orangutan population
summary: The global climate phenomenon has triggered devastating infernos in the ape’s Indonesian heartlands, with long-term effects on the animals still unknown
text: The mother’s hands were peeling from walking on the torched ground. Her eight-month-old baby, which clung to her side, was dehydrated and thin. The pair, named Mama Abu and Abu (“ash” in Indonesian), were found in an oil palm subsidiary estate, rescuers say. The orangutan pair were saved last month from wildfires that are devouring Indonesia’s forests and peatland, unleashing thick smog, and destroying the habitat of some of the planet’s most vulnerable species. Primate specialists from the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) have called for urgent international assistance to help control the fires, warning this week that thousands of orangutans could be killed, injured or displaced. Wildfires happen every year in Indonesia, where fire is often used to clear land to make way for palm or pulp plantations. But the arrival of a supercharged El Niño has brought especially dry conditions, causing blazes to spread rapidly across parts of Sumatra, Kalimantan (the Indonesian part of Borneo) and Papua. The fires have also taken hold across peatland, which is extremely hard to extinguish as it smoulders underground. In its natural state, it should be waterlogged, but over recent decades, vast areas have been drained by industrial agriculture, leaving it highly flammable. Habitat containing 52% of the total Bornean orangutan population is now affected by the fires, according to a statement from the IUCN’s primate specialists. They are not the only animals affected, however. Blazes have also spread into the habitats of five gibbon species, all of which are listed as endangered on the IUCN Red List. Geopix, an environmental NGO, warned earlier this month that 4,500 fires had been detected across 21 Sumatran elephant habitats over recent months. “I believe that the toll on wild animals being burned, dead, because of the fires is huge,” says Dr Karmele Llano Sanchez, a veterinarian and co-founder and CEO of Yiari, a non-profit focused on primate and habitat conservation, which rescues orangutans and other species from torched forests. Even animals that survive the catastrophe can face long-term consequences. Food availability falls in the aftermath of fires as forests struggle to recover, and the risk of conflict between animals can rise if they are displaced and forced to live closer to each other. Experts believe that, as with humans, there will also be health impacts for animals that have lived with months of dense smog. So far, more than 20 orangutans, as well as other species such as pangolin, have been evacuated from the fires by Yiari, which is working alongside West Kalimantan’s Natural Resources Conservation Agency, searching the forests for animals in need and responding to reports from the public. One of the rescued orangutans died, probably due to smoke inhalation. Others have been found with burns on their hands after touching the scorching ground, or are hungry and dehydrated. “It hasn’t rained in 80 days here, and everything is dried and burned,” says Sanchez. “[There are] no leaves and no fruits – nothing they can eat.” Animals that are evacuated are given sedatives through a dart, which can be fired as high as 30 metres into the trees. A team of about 10 people will hold a net to catch the animal as it tumbles from the branches. An adult male orangutan can weigh about 70kg. If a mother is carrying very young offspring, they usually fall together, with the baby clinging to its mother. Such evacuations are a last resort, says Sanchez, undertaken when the area of forest is destroyed: “Otherwise they will for sure die.” There are many animals in peril that simply can’t be reached: proboscis monkeys, which are endangered, Sunda pangolin and snakes – including a python and king cobra – have all been found dead, according to local media reports. Forestry minister Raja Juli Antoni told media the wildfires could continue until early November, with the rainy season expected to arrive late. An estimated 600,000 hectares (1.4 million acres) were damaged by fire in August, according to the environmental group YKAN. Researchers have observed that large fire events have been followed by unusually high litterfall, where leaves and small branches drop from trees. This is probably because smog has blocked sunlight, preventing photosynthesis, says Dr Susan Cheyne, co-director of Borneo Nature Foundation International, which has conducted studies on the trend. “Even though the fires are out at this point there is still a knock-on effect on food,” says Cheyne, who is also vice-chair for the International Union for Conservation of Nature primate specialist group section on small apes. Such die-offs of leaves occur just as dry season returns, just when species such as orangutan need to eat more, as they rely on flowers and leaves rather than the sugary fruits and pulp that are abundant during the rainy season. Erin Vogel, professor at Rutgers University in New Jersey, says the forest can take years to recover, with trees producing less fruit afterwards, possibly due to a decline in pollinators. In the longer term, tree diversity across burned peat forests can remain suppressed even 12 years on, research has shown. If fires recur, this risks trapping forests in a permanently degraded state. The full extent of the long-term impact of the fires on surviving orangutans’ health is unknown. During smoky periods orangutans show ketosis, a sign of increased fat breakdown. It’s believed this is because the smoke raises energy demands, probably by forcing the immune system to work harder. Research published after the 2015 fires found orangutans called less in heavy smoke, and that they had reduced vocal quality. Most vocal changes persisted for two months after the smoke had cleared and probably signalled changes in health, researchers concluded. Gibbons, which rely on song to attract mates, cement bonds and defend territory, have also been found to sing less when exposed to heavy smoke. “We know how [smog] impacts humans in the long term – it can lead to medical problems, breathing problems, asthma, cancer, infections, future lung capacity issues,” says Vogel. “So, I think, there’s no reason to predict that it wouldn’t affect them the same way.” Further studies are needed, but for now, research sites themselves are threatened by the flames. Both the Tuanan orangutan research station in Central Kalimantan, and Rangkong research station in West Kalimantan, have been threatened by fires in recent weeks. Staff and local people have worked to halt the spread, setting up improvised sprinkler systems and clearing the ground cover. Localised rains have brought some relief at Rangkong, though staff fear this may only be temporary. At Tuanan, where there is still no rain, the fire fighting continues day and night. Decades of research are at risk, says Vogel, who is co-director of the Tuanan orangutan research programme. Academics there have studied the same trees, 2,500 in total, and the same individual orangutans for 23 years, accumulating a crucial body of long-term data. The IUCN says “urgent technical and financial support” are needed, but that the emergency response must be followed by greater investment in re-wetting peatland, addressing deforestation, and ensuring burned forests are restored, not converted into plantations. For now, rescuers continue to search the forests for wildlife at risk. The mother and baby rescued last week are now being held at a quarantine centre run by Yiari. When it is safe, they will be released in a new location – one with enough food and no other orangutan populations that might compete with them for territory. “We need to look for a location that is safe, that is a good forest,” says Sanchez. “It is not easy. But we are trying to do our best to find a place that is suitable for them.” Find more age of extinction coverage here, and follow biodiversity reporters Rebecca Ratcliffe, Phoebe Weston and Patrick Greenfield on the app for all the latest news and features

title: ‘Hero’ pilot, plumber and dentist among those who saved flydubai flight to Israel
summary: Swift actions of Smit Machchhar allowed passengers and off-duty pilots to subdue attacker and land plane safely
text: Smit Machchhar was lying on the floor of the flydubai flight deck, covered in blood, when he managed to click the release to open the cockpit door, allowing passengers and crew to gain entry, overpower his attacker and save 174 passengers onboard. Moments earlier, Machchhar’s fellow pilot had stabbed him, in an apparent effort to crash the plane, which was travelling from Dubai to Tel Aviv. Machchhar, from Mumbai, is being treated in a hospital in Saudi Arabia’s north-western city of Tabuk, where the plane landed safely. The Indian prime minister, Narendra Modi, lauded Machchhar as a hero in a post on X early on Thursday. “In the face of the gravest danger and despite being seriously ‌injured, he showed immense courage and an unwavering resolve to protect the lives of others. His valour helped save hundreds of lives and avert a great tragedy,” he wrote. The Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, was equally impressed with Machchhar’s actions. “Despite being stabbed and seriously injured, he fought back, resisted, opened the cockpit door and enabled passengers and crew to overpower the attacker,” he said. Machchhar is one of several people hailed as heroes for managing to wrest control of the plane from the attacker who apparently attempted to crash it, according to Israeli officials who also provided much of the detail on how events played out inside the plane. The incident began with a struggle, when Machchhar’s fellow pilot – reportedly an Omani national – stabbed him and ⁠sent the jet plunging nearly 14,000ft (4,300 metres) in less than 30 seconds. Several passengers were able to enter the cockpit soon after to help subdue the attacker. “What made it difficult for us was [Machchhar] himself,” said Yaniv Hayoun, who was among those in the cockpit and whom Netanyahu described as a plumber. “He had been stabbed and was on the other side of the door.” Hayoun later told Netanyahu that as people wrestled with the attacker “I jumped back, grabbed the controls, and started pulling back the handles”, the way he had seen on television shows. Then other crew members took over. Dr Shota Musaev, a dentist, was also among those who ran to the cockpit. He told CNN they found the attacker on the floor on top of the pilot, stabbing him. He then rushed to help Machchhar, “terrified” he was going to die. “He was covered in cuts – his head, his hands – they were practically sliced open, almost severed in two … he had lost a lot of blood and was in bad shape. “I think that if we had waited even a few more moments, we would have lost him. His blood pressure had plummeted, he suddenly lost consciousness, and there was blood everywhere,” he said. Musaev said he had also helped subdue the attacker by tying him up with headphone cords and plastic zip-ties. Other crew members then stabilised the plane’s descent of the plane and landed it safely. Among those who intervened was an off-duty British pilot, according to a passenger, Almog Itali, who said the plane was carrying a pair of relief pilots who were meant to fly the next flight. “The relief pilots are European, one of them British, who entered [the cockpit] and pulled the aircraft up, pulled the yoke, stabilised the plane and landed us in Saudi Arabia,” Itali said in a clip posted by the BBC. Other reports suggested the off-duty pilots were from South Africa or New Zealand. Indian officials confirmed that Machchhar had undergone surgery in Saudi Arabia and was in a stable condition. They said they had been in touch with his wife and two children, aged seven and two. Neighbours from the Mumbai community where Machchhar was born, and where his parents still live, spoke of their pride at his bravery. Janit Shah, a neighbour who has known Machchhar for years, said: “We were initially very concerned when we heard about the incident. We know him as a very jubilant and kind person. It is incredible to hear about his brave act.” Another neighbour, who said she was a friend of Machchhar’s mother but asked not to be named, described the pilot as a warm and active member of the community. “We are elated with joy and so proud of him,” she said. Aviation experts have expressed surprise the plane did not crash after a descent so rapid that most of the rudder was torn off the tail. One passenger described the moment of the nosedive as like “massive turbulence … for 20 or 30 seconds”. Steve Arroyo, a former United Airlines pilot and aviation safety expert, said: “That was a serious descent and strong aerodynamic forces on that rudder for that to happen. I’m just amazed the aircraft didn’t come apart.” Jeff Guzzetti, another aviation expert, said: “What saved them is there was enough altitude left for them to recover.” It may not have been possible for the plane to level out if it had fallen below 10,000 feet, he said. The fact Machchhar was able to unlock the cockpit door no doubt saved all the passengers onboard. Philip Kean, the chief executive of Mainland Air in New Zealand – where Machchhar trained for 18 months in 2008 and 2009 – said the pilot had shown leadership after being attacked. Speaking on a podcast last year, Machchhar said he had not originally intended to become a pilot, and had initially trained to go into his family’s textile business, before coming across an aviation seminar aged 19. “That’s where the aviation bug, in a way, bit me,” he said. He had never left India before he took his first commercial flight as a pilot in training, and said his mother had been very scared about him becoming a pilot. He hailed pilots’ training to deal with all sorts of emergency scenarios. “When we are up there and if something happens, you know who’s going to save you,” he said on the podcast. Pilots “can save your life, you know”.

title: How AI could ‘supercharge’ election risks across south-east Asia
summary: Some experts fear AI could be weaponised in south-east Asia, home to nations with predominately young and hyper-connected populations
text: Years ago it would have been an elaborate operation involving an army of cyber troops creating fake news websites, social media accounts and forged dossiers, all deployed to spread disinformation en masse. Now, all you need is AI. In a worrying sign of how AI could “supercharge” fake news, Anthropic recently revealed how Claude AI was used in a political influence operation in Malaysia. It created a commercial election manipulation platform, utilising a network of about 1,000 X accounts, a fake news outlet called “Malaysia Pulse” and a series of fabricated documents. The operation appeared designed to target voters in recent state elections, pulling in census and electoral data to exploit sensitive political and social fractures, including race, religion, and royalty across all 222 Malaysian parliamentary constituencies. The experiment was ultimately ineffective once Anthropic stepped in but has sparked alarm about how AI could be weaponised in future elections in south-east Asia, a region already deeply vulnerable to fake news. Katie Harbath, who formerly worked on public policy for global elections at Meta, says the case is an example of how AI brings a new level of sophistication and ease to the disinformation landscape. “AI can supercharge it in terms of you can make a lot more content that’s more personalised, quicker and cheaper,” says Harbath, who now heads the tech consultancy company Anchor Change. “But you still need a distribution mechanism, and at the moment, that’s still your more social media type platforms.” Anthropic detailed the Malaysia election operation in its latest threat assessment, released in September. The report revealed how actors used Claude to build networks of fake social media profiles and news websites that targeted audiences on six continents. Anthropic said the actors included “governments, state-aligned propaganda institutions and state media, as well as private firms selling influence”. ‘Flood the zone’ South-east Asia is no stranger to disinformation. In recent years Nobel laureate and Filipino journalist Maria Ressa has likened the Philippines to a “petri dish” for the weaponisation of disinformation and fake news, with techniques tried and tested in the south-east Asian nation later successfully replicated in the west. But AI makes it all much easier. “Basically AI is just mimicking what we would have, I guess, termed a few years ago, a troll factory,” says Rossine Fallorina of Sigla, a Philippine thinktank that researches AI. “Mostly because it speeds up the production process. So you don’t need 10 people to create a narrative or a story. You can just prompt it and then have it propagated.” Last year OpenAI banned accounts using AI to generate comments about Philippine politics and public officials across social platforms, with many fictitious comments generated in support of President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr. Across south-east Asia, home to nations with predominately young and hyper connected populations, some fear the divisive potential of AI on social media. “It feeds political polarisation and it feeds on divisions,” says Bridget Welsh, from the University of Nottingham Asia Research Institute Malaysia. “That’s really what’s concerning about the fragmented nature of what’s happening in Malaysia.” Malaysia’s general election could be called for late 2027, while the Philippines and Cambodia have polls in 2028, and Indonesia the following year. Already in the region, AI has been effective. In Indonesia, an AI-generated cartoon image of now-president Prabowo Subianto that helped soften his strongman image became wildly popular in the 2024 election. It has also been used to inflame tensions, such as inciting hatred toward ethnic Rohingya refugees who fled to Malaysia from Myanmar during the civil war, says Dr Ben Loh, a media lecturer at Monash University Malaysia. “It’s come to the point where people already have this deep-seated hate in their minds and when they see the content like this, even though it’s AI-generated to them, it’s merely reinforcing what they believe is already true,” says Loh. The Anthropic report notes that the fake news outlet scraped legitimate Malaysian reporting and had the model rewrite it several times before republishing it under fabricated bylines. It also republished articles from Russian and Chinese state-aligned foreign outlets, including TV BRICS, Xinhua, Sputnik/RIA, and CGTN, stripping them of attribution. Anthropic said in its threat assessment that in each case of identified political influence the company “disrupted the activity, used what we learned to strengthen our safeguards, and shared intelligence with authorities and industry partners, where appropriate”. In future, Harbath says AI could be used to “flood the zone” in an attempt to influence the large language models (LLMs) from which AI models draw their information. “If there’s any sort of news drought, or if you have a place where there’s mostly government-sponsored media,” she says, “It wouldn’t take very much money to kind of flood the zone.”

title: Man arrested over alleged plot to attack Texas state capitol
summary: Suspect Benny Caldera Jr in custody as officials say they received ‘credible’ information about Austin threat
text: A 40-year-old man was arrested early on Wednesday on suspicion of plotting to attack the Texas state capitol, authorities said. The Texas department of public safety said in a statement that it received “credible information about an individual planning a violent attack” for Thursday in Austin. Benny Caldera Jr told a friend, “I am going to the capitol and I am going to shoot it up,” according to an arrest warrant affidavit obtained by NBC 5 DFW. “I love you, if you don’t see me again,” Caldera allegedly told the friend, police wrote in the arrest documents. Caldera had expressed anger over the American Israeli Public Affairs Committee (Aipac), NBC 5 DFW reported. “These people have to be exterminated,” Caldera allegedly said. The tip came in on Tuesday evening, and Swat officers arrested Caldera around 3am on Wednesday at a residence in Converse, Texas, near San Antonio. Caldera has been charged with felony terroristic threat against a public servant, court records show. On Wednesday afternoon, the public records indicated Caldera had been released after posting a $75,000 bond. The Texas department of public safety (DPS) clarified later that evening in an X post that Caldera was not out on bond. He has been released from a local jail into federal custody. “At this time, there is no reason to believe there is an ongoing threat to the Texas State Capitol. DPS will continue an increased posture at the Texas Capitol and encourages ALL Texans to remain vigilant,” the agency wrote in its update. Messages were left seeking comment from an attorney listed for Caldera. Public safety officials notified state lawmakers about the threat and arrest early on Wednesday. The capitol remained open during regular operating hours. The Texas senate secretary, Patsy Spaw, said in a notice that there will be increased security at the state capitol during the investigation. The governor, Greg Abbott, said the DPS was assisted by the FBI in making the arrest. “Texas will NOT tolerate threats of violence against our Capitol,” the governor said in a statement on social media.

title: Ukraine war briefing: Russia pounds power grid with seven killed in biggest energy attack in months
summary: Emergency power cuts imposed in Kyiv for first time since spring after airstrikes across at least 10 regions ahead of winter. What we know on day 1,681
text: Russia has unleashed a widely anticipated air campaign against Ukraine’s energy grid, hitting power facilities and infrastructure ⁠around Kyiv and other regions in the ⁠heaviest combined attack on energy sites in months. The strikes on Wednesday, in which Ukrainian officials said seven people were killed, came after days of intensifying drone barrages primarily on the capital, a prelude to what many Ukrainians expect to be a winter of attacks intended to plunge cities into cold and darkness while Ukraine is short ⁠of air defences. State power grid operator Ukrenergo said it had imposed emergency power cuts as a result of the attack in Kyiv and three surrounding regions – the first time such a measure had been imposed in the capital since the spring. “Russia has escalated to massive ‌strikes on energy infrastructure,” the prime minister, Sergii Koretskyi, said ‌on X after the overnight attacks. A child was among the seven dead across Ukraine, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said, with critical infrastructure coming under attack in five regions. Further damage was reported in another five regions, the Ukrainian president added. Forecasters say they expect freezing temperatures at night in Kyiv in coming days. Zelenskyy visited a military command post near the town of Lyman near the eastern frontline and praised what he said were gains against Russian forces ‌during a counteroffensive. Ukrainian forces had recaptured 176 sq km (29.3 sq miles) of territory since the start of the operation, he said. “A serious ‌operation, important in many ways for our ‌defence overall and in Donbas in particular,” Zelenskyy wrote, referring to eastern Ukraine’s Donbas region, which Russia aims to capture in its entirety. Zelenskyy said the operation had ‌prevented Russian forces from breaking through the rear of defensive lines around Sloviansk and Kramatorsk, part of the network of “fortress cities” Ukrainian forces are defending. Ukraine is urging the US to impose sanctions on several Russian entities it says are helping develop Moscow’s Rassvet satellite network as a domestic alternative to SpaceX’s Starlink, its acting ⁠ambassador said. Denys Sienik, ⁠deputy chief of mission at the Ukrainian embassy in Washington, said Russia was rapidly expanding the Rassvet satellite network and that its goal to start operations in 2027 would pose grave risks to Ukraine. Kyiv planned to issue its own national sanctions against the entities linked to the network, Sienik said, adding: “If these entities are not sanctioned, it ‌will actually make this program possible for ‌Russia and that will be a gamechanger.” Papal envoy Cardinal Matteo Zuppi discussed humanitarian issues in the Ukraine war in ⁠talks with Russian officials and visited Ukrainian prisoners of war, Russia’s foreign ministry said. Zuppi’s three ⁠days of talks ⁠coincided with an appeal by Pope Leo to Russia and Ukraine to sit down and discuss how to ⁠end the four-and-a-half-year war. The pontiff also decried national leaders who he said were “beginning to speak about nuclear weapons ⁠and wars that are becoming ever more destructive”. The foreign ministry said on Wednesday that Zuppi also discussed conditions in the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky in Ukraine’s Kherson region, where Ukrainian officials said Kyiv’s military used drones last weekend to deliver ‌food and medicine to civilians.

summary: Noem cites irreconcilable differences in filing that comes after husband Bryon Noem involved in tabloid scandal
text: Kristi Noem, who was fired by Donald Trump after a rumbustious stint as homeland security secretary, is divorcing her husband, Bryon Noem, after 34 years of marriage, citing “irreconcilable differences”. The divorce claim “for settlement purposes only” was disclosed in court records filed in Hamlin county, South Dakota, the state of which Noem was previously governor. The document was signed by Noem’s lawyer, Michael Sabers, on 6 April – just over a week after the Daily Mail published pictures of her husband wearing inflated fake breasts under a spandex shirt. At the time, Noem issued a statement saying she was “devastated” by the images, adding that “the family have been blindsided by this”. The papers were only filed in court this week, according to the New York Times. Sabers confirmed that Kristi Noem had filed for divorce and said she would reserve further comments for the legal process. Tim Bottum, Bryon Noem’s attorney, said his client was “saddened that the marriage is ending” and would welcome the opportunity to share his perspective if court proceedings were necessary. “Bryon’s priority is to protect the family and move forward as loving parents and grandparents,” Bottum said in a statement. The revelations came weeks after Noem had lost her job at the department of homeland security. The state of her marriage had already been subject of speculation amid rumors that Noem was in a relationship with her aide at the department, Corey Lewandowski. In a Capitol Hill on 4 March, a Democratic member of Congress asked her openly whether she had sexual relations with Lewandowski. Answering under oath, Noem – who was accompanied to the hearing by her husband – dismissed the question as “tabloid garbage” but did not say no. She was fired the following day after Trump was reportedly angered by her answers to questions about a taxpayer-funded publicity campaign that promoted Noem’s image. Noem told the committee that Trump had signed off on the spending. Noem was replaced by Markwayne Mullin as homeland security secretary after a controversial period that had included the shooting deaths of protesters Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis during an immigration enforcement surge. Noem came under intense criticism after calling Good and Pretti “domestic terrorists”. Noem, 54, married Bryon Noem, 56, in 1992. They have three adult children.

title: Floating scarecrows: how Cornish fishers are stopping seabirds drowning in their nets
summary: Simple deterrents can slash the number of razorbills and guillemots being trapped underwater, two-year study shows
text: Bird-shaped kites and a floating scarecrow are being tested to try to stop endangered seabirds drowning in fishing nets. Every year an estimated 95,000 diving birds, including razorbills and guillemots, are accidentally caught in nets off European coasts. But simple deterrents tested by Cornish fishers and devised by scientists and the RSPB have been shown to reduce the toll by about two-thirds. The scarecrow – or more properly a looming-eyes buoy – has a spinning head with two large eyes that scare diving birds away from gillnets, walls of netting which hang vertically beneath the surface. The LEB was tested alongside a commercially available scarybird kite. Ten Cornish fishers and Fishtek Marine, which created the LEB, fitted cameras to boats to monitor the effect of the devices on seabird behaviour. The results of the two-year trial, which was analysed by scientists from the University of Exeter and published in the journal Conservation Letters, showed that the chance of seabirds being caught in gillnets fell by 59% using LEBs and by 71% using kites. The research revealed that in Cornwall most seabirds were caught in winter, which will help target the use of the devices by season. Tom Horton, lead author of the University of Exeter research, said: “This study provides some of the strongest evidence to date that simple, practical deterrents can substantially reduce seabird bycatch in gillnet fisheries. “By also identifying when and where bycatch risk is highest, we now have a clear opportunity to target mitigation measures where they can deliver the greatest conservation benefit for vulnerable seabird populations and encourage sustainable fishing practices.” Yann Rouxel, bycatch programme manager at the RSPB, said: “After over a decade of research into gillnet bycatch and its solutions, it’s great to see this work moving towards real-world implementation. “The performance of the LEB and kite, as evidenced in this study, is a major milestone in the effort to reduce seabird bycatch without impeding gillnet fishers while at sea.”

title: ‘Hugely exciting’ finds on tiny Scottish island shed light on spread of Christianity
summary: Community-funded archaeological excavations of ‘really important’ sixth-century monastery also rewrite story of Lismore
text: To the residents of the Scottish island of Lismore, population 190, history is never very far away. The tiny island near Oban in Argyll has no row of shops or even a pub – if islanders want to meet for a coffee, the only place to do so is in the lively Gaelic heritage centre that records the many centuries of community life on the island. This quiet place, documentary evidence records, was home to a monastic settlement in the sixth century AD, when missionaries from Ireland were first moving into northern Britain to spread Christianity. But apart from a few fragments of an early carved cross, there was almost nothing to see from this period of history. A group of local people from the island’s historical society were determined to look a bit harder, however. After scraping together funding from grants, donations and legacies of locals and a crowdfunding campaign, they commissioned a professional archaeologist, Dr Clare Ellis of Argyll Archaeology, to lead a group of islanders and other volunteers in an excavation on the site of a much later medieval cathedral. Their “hugely exciting” findings have not only rewritten the story of the island but cast new light on the spread of Christianity in the period, according to archaeologists. What the islanders discovered were extensive burial grounds, decorated stonework and early buildings – all the features belonging to a major sixth-century monastery, comparable to the much better known site of Iona a little to the south-west. In addition, the excavations uncovered rare evidence of slightly later high-status craftworking, including huge numbers of crucibles which had been used to cast gold and silver. The finds have shown that rather than being a small island church in an overlooked backwater, the monastery of Lios Mór, founded by Saint Mo Luóc or Moluag, was a high-ranking site of international importance, experts say. To Robert Hay, a retired plant scientist who moved to the island in 2001 and who coordinated the fundraising and volunteer efforts, the experience was thrilling. “We were [excavating] in this really unfavourable, boggy area. To be digging out the best small crucibles ever found in Scotland – it’s extraordinary,” he said. “The most exciting moment for me was when they were doing the post-excavation analysis and they found that they had been melting gold, copper, silver, and they were making jewellery on our little island in the seventh century.” While plenty of islanders have an idle interest in its history, a “dynamic minority” of mostly older people had mustered the volunteers and funds to carry out the digs, said Hay. Raising the low five-figure sum needed to pay for it all had been “just a business of getting down to it and organising and so on”, he said. “It was actually a lot easier than what my previous job used to be.” Gordon Noble, a professor of archaeology at the University of Aberdeen, said the finds were highly significant. “We know about sites like Iona having these very famous monastic sites from this early medieval world. But apart from the association with Moluag and a piece of sculpture from this site, we knew practically nothing really about Lismore. So it was hugely exciting to see the results emerging through the local group’s work with Clare [Ellis] … This was clearly a really important early Christian establishment.” While professional archaeologists often worked with local people, Noble said, “it’s not always the community themselves coming up with the ideas. Here, it was very much a bottom-up approach of the heritage society coming up with a plan, working with professionals – and lo and behold, what a great series of discoveries they’ve made at the site.” Hay said he hoped the finds would go some way to restoring the reputation of Moluag, who has long been overshadowed by the more celebrated Saint Columba, the founder of Iona and the subject of an influential ninth-century biography. “Unfortunately, Moluag never had a hagiographer, so his contribution to the evangelisation of Scotland has been very much underestimated,” he said. “So finding his monastic site and [the evidence of metalworking] – it’s all about recalibrating the situation. I think Moluag had a very big impact on the evangelising of Scotland, but unfortunately, he didn’t get his PR right.” The results of the community excavations will be published in the forthcoming edition of Antiquity.
