title: US immigration judge allows cold war-era law to deport Wisconsin mosque’s president
summary: When one track failed, Trump administration rushed immigration case of Palestine rights advocate Salah Sarsour
text: An immigration judge has ruled that the president of Wisconsin’s largest mosque can be deported under a controversial, cold-war era law the Trump administration has sought to wield against foreign nationals who have been outspoken about Palestinian rights. Salah Sarsour, a US permanent resident for nearly three decades, was detained by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement in March. He was released after a federal judge found he had probably been detained in retaliation of his advocacy for Palestinian rights, which the federal judge said would render his detention unlawful. Despite that ruling, the administration pressed forward and fast-tracked Sarsour’s immigration case – a separate legal track – and on Tuesday night an immigration judge ruled he is “removable”. Judge Jayme Salinardi, who was brought in from out of state to oversee the case, announced he would be retiring shortly after issuing the decision. In a statement, Sarsour’s attorneys called the ruling “a setback for free speech rights”. “The case we presented compels only one conclusion, which is that Salah is not deportable, he has done nothing wrong,” Patrick Taurel, one of Sarsour’s attorneys, said during a press conference shortly after the hearing. “He should be given back his green card with an apology for what’s been done to him.” The Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to a request for comment, but claimed before that Sarsour was “suspected of funding terror organizations and lying on immigration forms”. He has denied both claims. In a statement issued shortly after his arrest, the DHS cited Sarsour’s decades-old military court convictions in Israel for, it said, “throwing a Molotov cocktail at the homes of Israeli armed forces and illegally attempting to possess weapons and ammunition”. Sarsour said those accusations stemmed from an arrest as a teenager by Israeli soldiers in 1989, during the first intifada. He also says he was forced, under torture and threat of rape, to sign documents in Hebrew without understanding them. He ultimately spent two years in an Israeli prison after being convicted in a military court system that has a conviction rate of over 96% for Palestinians. Sarsour was again detained by Israeli authorities for nearly three months when he last visited Palestine in 1995. His lawyers detailed those facts over four immigration court hearings, during which they noted that the government had for years known about Sarsour’s arrests in Israel. In addition to his involvement with several local organizations, Sarsour is a board member of American Muslims for Palestine (AMP), a national advocacy group that Trump administration officials have accused of countering US foreign policy interests. “They’re retaliating against him for speaking out about Palestinian human rights,” said Luna Droubi, another attorney. “That should terrify all of us.” “It’s a principle of this country that people should feel that they can speak freely, and that’s being eradicated”. In a statement, Sarsour, who has six children and nine grandchildren, all US citizens, called the decision “deeply disappointing” but vowed to “continue fighting”. “We have a mission: let’s continue to make our voice clear, to protect the first amendment, to support justice,” he told the Guardian in July. “I’ll continue with that message whether I’m inside or outside.”

title: Federal Reserve watchdog finds no criminal violations for building renovation cost overruns
summary: Trump criticized $2.4bn rehab amid attempts to pressure then Fed chair Jerome Powell into lowering interest rates
text: An internal watchdog said the Federal Reserve mismanaged costs associated with a $2.4bn renovation of its Washington DC headquarters, but noted that no criminal violations occurred, according to a report released on Wednesday. For over a year, Donald Trump has centered his attacks against the Fed and former chair Jerome Powell around the renovations, including a months-long Department of Justice criminal investigation that was dropped in April. The report said that the Fed’s board of governors “has not effectively managed” the construction project and “repeatedly deviated from its cost-management provisions”, but noted that the mismanagement was not criminal and that it did not find any administrative misconduct in its evaluation. “At no point during our evaluation did we find reasonable grounds to believe that a violation of federal criminal law had occurred,” the report said. Over the course of renovations, construction costs have gone from an initially budgeted $921m in February 2020 to $2.018bn by December 2024. Construction was supposed to be completed in mid-2024 but is not slated to go until December 2027. The renovations have been a key part of the tension between the White House and the Fed, which by law is supposed to be non-partisan and independent. Trump has long been trying to pressure the Fed into lowering interest rates, to no avail. Trump latched on to the Fed’s ongoing renovations as an attack point against Powell in June 2025, suggesting that it amounted to corruption. He suggested that renovations included elaborate features including a VIP dining room and a garden terrace. In response, the Fed posted a video tour of the ongoing construction, noting that two buildings have not undergone renovations since the 1930s. Trump visited the Fed’s headquarters to highlight the expenses that July. Donning hardhats in the bowels of the construction site, Trump and Powell had a spat over budget figures. “It looks like it’s about $3.1bn,” Trump said at the time. “It went up a little bit or a lot.” The typically reserved Powell became visibly annoyed. “I am not aware of that,” he said. Soon after, Trump turned his Fed fight toward Fed governor Lisa Cook, whom he tried to fire over mortgage fraud. The supreme court ruled earlier this summer that the firing was unconstitutional because the White House did not follow proper procedure. In January, Powell released a stunning video statement announcing that the Department of Justice was investigating the renovations as part of a criminal investigation, noting that the investigation was “pretext” for the Fed not lowering interest rates. “This is about whether the Fed will be able to continue to set interest rates based on evidence and economic conditions – or whether instead monetary policy will be directed by political pressure or intimidation,” Powell said at the time. The justice department investigation would end up stalling the confirmation of current Fed chair Kevin Warsh, after a key Republican senator said he would be a holdout until the department ended its investigation. In April, the justice department closed the investigation. Trump and his economic advisers have continued to call for the Fed to lower interest rates, though the Fed most recently hiked rates, citing high inflation.

title: Senate Democrats block datacenter energy bill, saying ‘toothless’ legislation ‘misses the mark’
summary: Republicans supported legislation although Democrats said it wouldn’t effectively address energy consumption
text: Senate Democrats on Wednesday blocked legislation intended to offset the impact of datacenters on consumer electricity bills, calling it a “toothless” attempt to address a top voter concern ahead of November’s midterm elections. The Ratepayer Protection Act failed by a 57-to-43 vote, falling just shy of the 60 votes necessary to advance through the Republican-controlled chamber. Four Democrats – Maggie Hassan of New Hampshire, Amy Klobuchar of Minnesota and both Georgia senators, Jon Ossoff and Raphael Warnock – joined Republicans in support of the measure. “Americans are calling for real solutions, real guardrails, real solutions on AI. Republicans’ toothless datacenter bill completely misses the mark,” the Senate Democratic leader, Chuck Schumer, said in a floor speech before the vote. Schumer assailed Trump for a meeting with top tech executives on Tuesday that the president said yielded a “morally binding” agreement to put controls on artificial intelligence. “Relying on ‘self-regulation’ is how we got into this mess,” Schumer added. Earlier this month, the House of Representatives had approved the bill by an almost unanimous vote. Datacenter construction and electricity consumption has grown in recent years amid advances in AI and other technologies, and with it has come increasing anxiety among voters about the facilities’ impacts on their energy bills. The bipartisan legislation is an attempt by Congress to address those anxieties, and would have required electric utilities to consider adopting new standards so that datacenters pick up the costs of any necessary upgrades to transmission, generation and distribution, which can otherwise be transferred to households and businesses. It was proposed ahead of the 3 November midterm elections in which Democrats are campaigning on lowering the cost of living in their bid to regain control of the Senate and House. Its sponsor in the lower chamber was Gabe Evans, a Colorado Republican who is a top target of Democrats, while the Ohio Republican Jon Husted championed the bill through the Senate. “It’s clear that big tech should be paying their own way, not passing the cost on to local communities and states – and this bill does that,” Husted said in a floor speech on Wednesday, urging Democrats to back the bill that the president had indicated he would sign. Though Ohio voted for Trump by an 11-point margin two years ago, recent polls have shown Husted trailing his opponent, the Democratic former senator Sherrod Brown, who has accused the incumbent of bowing to the demands of the datacenter industry. While the proposal was seen as an attempt by Republicans Senate leaders to bolster Husted’s re-election chances, it also presented a quandary for the chamber’s Democrats, since voting it down could be seen as running counter to their pledges of lowering electricity bills. Nonetheless, the party’s leaders opted to oppose the measure, saying it would have been ineffective at actually addressing datacenters’ electricity consumption. The vote was one of the last the Senate is expected to take before the midterms. The chamber is scheduled to conclude its work on Friday, after which senators will return to their states to campaign.

title: ‘Whoever is hearing me, we need help’: how flight 1073 survived its 17,000ft plunge
summary: On morning service from Dubai to Tel Aviv, 150 passengers witnessed a horrific cockpit assault and a daring rescue
text: As flight FZ 1073 soared west over the waters of the Gulf towards Israel, its passengers may have bemoaned a 20-minute delay at takeoff. For a low-cost airline route, flydubai’s daily service to Tel Aviv is usually convenient and reliable. The nonstop flight takes about three and a half hours and departs early enough from Dubai that it usually lands at Ben Gurion airport at about 9am local time. That was not the case for Wednesday’s catastrophic flight. The passenger jet never made it to its scheduled destination. Instead, it dropped thousands of feet in seconds before limping down to make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia – perhaps miraculously, since photos suggested a large part of the tail of the aircraft was missing. Passengers evacuated, some covered in blood, with stories to share of a pilot-on-pilot stabbing, and footage posted online from inside the fuselage showed the aftermath of violence. In one video, two men lie on the floor with breathing masks on their faces as passengers stand over them in the cramped gangway. One wears a white shirt soaked red with blood, and the distinctive pilot stripes on his shoulders. He appears almost unresponsive. The other man blinks slowly, with blood smeared on the wall next to him. A person off camera appears to encourage the injured man to remain conscious: “No sleep,” he says. More footage, apparently from a seat further back, shows passengers screaming and weeping in distress as the Boeing 737 Max shakes. Israeli media reported that the plane was carrying about 150 Israeli passengers. Accounts from the airline, passenger testimony, flight trackers and Israeli officials describe a series of horrific events starting about two and a half hours after takeoff. The flight tracking website Flightradar24 recorded the aircraft abruptly descending from its cruising altitude of about 34,000ft to 17,000ft in less than two minutes. Investigators will look at whether such a sudden and ferocious movement was the reason for damage to the aircraft’s rudder. Minutes later, the plane sent out a series of emergency transponder signals in the form of “squawk codes”. These four-digit codes are normally used by pilots to broadcast their position but can be used in an emergency situation, even if pilots are in radio contact with air traffic control. Aircraft trackers at Flightradar24 said the flydubai plane transmitted emergency and hijack signals. The aircraft made an erratic circle close to the Jordanian border before turning around and heading south. In one video, a passenger with blood dripping from an open wound on his head pleads for assistance and says the jet is descending into Saudi Arabia. “Whoever is hearing me, we need help,” the man says in Hebrew. “We are in the Tabuk area of Saudi Arabia, which we don’t know. All the passengers are OK except for the pilot. We need help.” What was happening during these critical minutes is still being investigated, but early unconfirmed reports pointed to a cockpit fight, followed by passengers storming up the aisle, and then either one or more pilots who were travelling as passengers wresting control of the plane to avert a disaster. The Israeli newspaper Haaretz cited a passenger as saying that the plane lost control and began to dive. Dalia Shpigel was quoted as saying that “suddenly there were terrible screams throughout the plane” before “three to five guys burst into the cockpit” and subdued the alleged assailant and began treating an injured pilot. “We realised that the situation was stabilising and continued the flight. Gradually, information began to emerge about what had happened in the cockpit,” Shpigel told Haaretz. Her fellow passenger Miryam Shira Ohayon said the “co-pilot tried to murder the pilot and basically carry out a suicide attack on the plane”. Speaking to reporters via speakerphone held up by her mother, who was waiting at Ben Gurion airport, she said the plane “was really on the way to crashing, and it was simply the resourcefulness of many people who took control of the co-pilot and neutralised him”. “There was also a doctor who gave first aid, and people who treated both of them … but the bigger fear was really a crash, which is exactly what he was trying to do,” she said. The Emirati carrier, in a statement later on Wednesday, said the aircraft was “successfully secured by on-duty flydubai crew travelling on the flight”, who diverted and landed the aircraft safely at Tabuk airport. Airlines often move pilots around different airports as passengers, and it is possible it was these pilots who sent the emergency codes. One passenger, Almog Itali, was quoted by the BBC as saying that one of the pilots onboard who stabilised the plane was British. “There were two spare pilots who were supposed to operate the next flight,” he said. “The relief pilots are European, one of them British, who entered [the cockpit] and pulled the aircraft up, pulled the yoke, stabilised the plane and landed us in Saudi Arabia.” Stanislav Bukhman, the head of risk at Osprey Flight Solutions, an aviation security firm based in the UK, said investigators were likely to focus on a few key areas, including how pilots were vetted, and crew screening at the departure airport. On how the flight deck might have been accessed, he said cabin crew could request entry to the cockpit using an emergency access code. “This exists for situations where the pilots are incapacitated. There is a safeguard built in, though. If the pilots are conscious and operating normally, they can deny that request and keep the door locked. This is designed to protect the flight deck in a hijacking or hostage situation,” he said. “At this stage there isn’t enough information to say how the flight deck on FZ 1073 was accessed. The door may have been opened by the captain, who reportedly resisted the co-pilot’s attempt to take control, or by cabin crew using the emergency procedure.” The Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, announced that one of the pilots had planned to crash and kill its mostly Israeli passengers, who stopped a “major disaster” with their actions. The alleged assailant was arrested after the plane landed, Netanyahu ‌said. “During the flight, as they approached the country, one of the pilots stabbed the other pilot and apparently tried to crash the plane with everyone onboard,” Netanyahu said in a video message, calling the passengers “heroes”. All the passengers were accounted for and safe. Flydubai, however, said an “altercation” occurred in the flight deck of flight FZ 1073, and it warned against drawing conclusions about the motive. “At this early stage, the underlying reasons and motives behind this event are unknown and remain subject to a formal investigation,” a flydubai spokesperson said in a statement. “We urge all parties to refrain from premature speculation while authorities gather the facts.” Agence France-Presse contributed to this report

title: Grenfell police hand files on 20 organisations and 54 people to CPS
summary: Met calls move ‘milestone’ moment that paves way for ‘very best possible evidence for charging decisions’
text: Police investigating the Grenfell Tower fire have asked prosecutors to consider charges including manslaughter and fraud against a range of companies and individuals. The Metropolitan police announced they had given prosecutors evidence relating to 20 companies and organisations and 54 individuals ahead of charging decisions, in what the force described as a “milestone moment”. Andy Burnham joined survivors’ groups in saying it had “taken too long”, but he pledged to support Grenfell families “to ensure they get the justice and accountability that they deserve”. Potential charges include corporate manslaughter, gross negligence manslaughter, health and safety offences, fraud and fraud-related offences and misconduct in public office. The housing secretary, Angela Rayner, said on Wednesday that the files passed to prosecutors by police included one relating to her department. The Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) would review whether the department, which police began investigating in 2023, had potentially breached the Health and Safety at Work Act. “I recognise the significance and gravity of this development, and we will respond with the appropriate and necessary diligence and care,” she said. The Guardian has learned that a leading prosecutor has been appointed to head any possible court cases. The fire in North Kensington, west London, on 14 June 2017, led to the deaths of 72 people and was found by a public inquiry to have been avoidable. It was the result of “decades of failure” by central government to stop the spread of combustible cladding, combined with the “systematic dishonesty” of multimillion-pound companies whose products spread the fire, a public inquiry found in 2024. The CPS has said charging decisions will be made before the 10th anniversary of the disaster, which falls on 14 June 2027. Kevin Southworth, a deputy assistant commissioner at the Met, said: “This is a milestone moment in the police investigation into this devastating tragedy which took the lives of 72 people. “We appreciate, of course, it has taken nine years to get to this point. As we have said before, this is one of the most complex investigations ever undertaken by any UK law enforcement agency – the scale is truly enormous. “While we know this has had a significant impact on those waiting for answers, it has necessarily taken this long to ensure our investigation is meticulous and presents the very best possible evidence to the CPS for charging decisions.” Investigators have looked at the role of more than 15,000 people and 700 organisations as part of the inquiry, and have submitted 12,600 pages of evidence to the CPS. A total of 14,700 statements have been taken and more than 27,000 exhibits, including cladding, insulation, doors, windows and other parts of the building – down to screws, nuts and bolts – are stored in a secure warehouse. Scale replica parts of the tower are being built at a cost of £2m in anticipation of potential court proceedings. Grenfell United, which represents some bereaved families and survivors, said: “We expect the Met and the CPS to do everything in their power to make sure this case moves forward without further unnecessary delay. Our families have waited long enough. “We want those responsible to face justice. If people are found guilty of crimes that cost our loved ones their lives, we want to see them behind bars. Only then will people see that there are real consequences for what happened at Grenfell.” Burnham told Channel 5 News: “It has taken too long, but at least [the evidence] has been submitted. To be fair to the Metropolitan police, it has been a complex and wide-ranging investigation and they’ve had to do it in a forensic way, dealing with multiple, multiple organisations.” He cited the role of the Hillsborough law, which he was involved in campaigning for, and which imposes a duty of candour on public authorities to prevent cover-ups. “It’s intended to speed up situations like this so we can get the truth and justice much more quickly. And accountability, that’s the piece that’s often lacking. There must be accountability for Grenfell,” he said. Frank Ferguson, the head of the CPS’s special crime and counter-terrorism division, said the service remained confident that it would complete the process and make charging decisions before the 10th anniversary of the fire next year.

title: Scottish screen sector boom brings questions over jobs and overtourism
summary: The Traitors and big film shoots help boost economy but some highlight lack of opportunities for local talent
text: Scotland’s striking Ardross Castle, the oldest star of The Celebrity Traitors, which kicks off on Thursday night, is just one of the stops on the Scottish tourist board’s “screen tourism” trail. From Outlander and The Odyssey filming in the Highlands and islands, to Glasgow city centre standing in for New York and Gotham City in the latest instalments of Indiana Jones and Batman respectively, film and TV is increasingly big business in Scotland. The country’s screen sector, growing year on year, is projected to be worth £1bn to the economy by 2030. But while some have celebrated the upsides of a booming production sector, others highlight a lack of opportunities for Scottish talent and the challenges of excessive tourism in areas featured on screen. After last year’s Celebrity Traitors finale, the BBC announced that the show had added £21.8m to the Scottish economy since 2022 through employment, supply chain spend and screen tourism, where visitors travel specifically to see on-screen sites in real life. But research last year by Peter Strachan, a documentary film-maker and academic who set up the campaign group Standing Up For Scotland’s Screen Talent, found that only about 6% of production staff on series three of The Traitors were Scottish, despite the production counting towards Ofcom quotas stating that the BBC must use 8% of network hours and expenditure in Scotland. “This is the tip of the iceberg,” Strachan wrote at the time. “We have found many other supposedly Scottish productions are failing to create jobs for broadcast freelancers in Scotland.” The BBC reiterated that The Traitors was a Scottish production, and Studio Lambert, which makes the show, said Scottish representation was increasing behind the scenes each year. Earlier this month, Strachan also called for Sony Pictures to release a breakdown of the local crew hired in Glasgow for Spider-Man: Brand New Day, which filmed in the city in 2025. “Local hiring is not necessarily the same thing as employing Scotland’s established screen-sector workforce,” he said. “Someone can be locally hired to work on a film without normally working in film and television – a Glasgow carpenter brought in for a few weeks of set construction, for example.” David Smith, the interim executive director of Screen Scotland, the national body for the country’s film and TV industry, said Scotland had benefited from its growing screen sector, but that there had been a “consistent decline” in the number of shows commissioned by public service broadcasters from Scottish production companies. “We think this needs to change,” Smith said. “Ultimately, we want to see a sustainable mix of film and TV projects made across genres, broadcasts and platforms.” Even for those not directly involved in the industry, its effects are still being felt. Glenfinnan, in Lochaber in the Highlands, is home to only about 150 people – as well as a majestic viaduct made world-famous when it doubled as the Hogwarts Express railway bridge in the Harry Potter films. In the years since, the tiny hamlet has become so overrun with film tourists that Police Scotland last month issued a warning to visitors over dangerous parking and antisocial behaviour. Gillian Shields, 54, lives in Inverness, close to the village of Culloden where the Clan Fraser stone has become a major tourist attraction for fans of historical fantasy series Outlander. In 2023, the site was temporarily closed after deterioration caused by excessive visitor numbers. “People here are welcoming, and most of the visitors are lovely and respectful,” she said. “We’re not trying to turn anyone away, it’s just we see more and more every single year and it’s a worry whether our beautiful area can keep up with it.” Culloden battlefield, which features heavily in Outlander, saw a 43% increase in visitor numbers last year, according to data from Glasgow Caledonian University and the Association of Scottish Visitor Attractions. Jenni Steele, the film and creative industries manager at VisitScotland, said the benefits of film tourism “are worth millions to the economy, bringing jobs and opportunities, and are felt long after the film or TV series is released”. But she said: “We know that success can bring with it challenges in certain locations. Film and TV fans will be drawn to them regardless. That’s why we work with partners and local bodies to understand the challenges so we can educate and inform visitors of where and when they should visit and encourage them to act responsibly and explore beyond the on-screen locations.” Many Scots, though, are in full support of the country’s booming screen sector. Matthew, 42, lives in Glasgow city centre and has watched on in recent years as the streets around his home have been transformed into everything from 1960s New York (Indiana Jones and the Dial of Destiny) to dystopian America (The Running Man) and Soviet-era Moscow (Tetris). “Some people moan about road closures and parking, but it’s great to see the city buzzing with excitement when a new show comes to town,” he said, noting that local residents he knew had been employed as extras, and nearby restaurants as on-set catering suppliers. “The city needs those jobs and that money – and, to be frank, a bit of fun and glamour never hurt a Glaswegian either.”

title: Andy Burnham’s social care plans could be much more radical | Letter
summary: Letters: Readers respond to the Labour leader’s conference speech and plans for changes to social care and the state pension triple lock
text: In the aftermath of Andy Burnham’s speech to the Labour conference, media discussions are focusing on how to define social care and estimate its cost (How will Burnham’s national care service work – and how will it be funded?, 29 September). Most arguments assume that any new system will look like the existing one, with services outsourced to large companies, using contracts without scope for innovation, with rigidly defined targets, often delivered using poorly rewarded, precariously employed migrant workers. The reality is that many of the services needed by elderly and incapacitated people – such as cleaning, meal preparation, transport to medical appointments, household repairs and personal services such as podiatry, hair care, physiotherapy, counselling or therapeutic massage – are also required by others and are already freely available in local markets. The trouble is that they are most often supplied by online platforms such as Uber, Deliveroo or Housekeep with no commercial incentive to address social need. One solution would be to set up local platforms that supply these services to anyone, regardless of age or disability. If these platforms made sure that all staff were suitably trained, qualified and security-checked, and their vehicles suitably adapted, they could be attractive to all local residents, whose commercial use of them would help subsidise their costs. Social care recipients could be provided with access to them using a voucher system that would be much cheaper than setting up such services from scratch or bundling them in with huge outsourcing contracts. With suitable public oversight, using platform technology for public good would also bring other benefits to the local economy. Services would be better for all. Workers could upgrade their skills and gain job security. And, instead of being siphoned off to tax havens, any profits could remain, as Burnham might put it, “in every postcode”. Ursula Huws London • Andy Burnham’s commitment to a national care service brings welcome clarity to a debate that has too often avoided difficult choices. But before deciding how to pay for care, we must answer a prior question: what should people be able to count on? Reports that the proposed service may follow Scotland’s model of free personal care raise an important distinction. Removing charges for help with washing, dressing and eating could make a substantial difference. But social care is about much more than these tasks. When we in the coalition government developed the Care Act, we placed wellbeing at its heart. Its purpose extends to dignity, independence, relationships, participation and people’s control over their own lives. There is a risk that defining a national care service primarily through free personal care narrows our understanding of what social care is for. The two need not be in conflict. Free personal care could form part of a wider national guarantee, grounded in the Care Act’s wellbeing principle and applying to people across adulthood. The Casey commission has an important opportunity to help establish that wider promise. The question is whether the new service will simply change what people pay, or also strengthen the care and support that they can rely on to live their lives. Paul Burstow Former minister of state for care services, 2010-12 • Andy Burnham’s decision that proposals for social care reform will not happen until after the next election is the latest instalment in almost two-decade saga of delays. Since a Labour government first committed to social care reform in 2007, we have seen a succession of unfulfilled promises: the discarded Personal Care at Home Act 2010, David Cameron’s part-implemented Care Act 2014, Theresa May’s failed 2017 proposals, and Boris Johnson’s 2019 pledge on the steps of Downing Street to fix social care – delayed under Rishi Sunak, then scrapped by Rachel Reeves in 2024. In the years since this saga of broken promises began, both of my parents were diagnosed with Alzheimer’s disease. One of them survives, and our family continues to wait for any meaningful help. Families living through the reality of the social care crisis do not have the luxury of waiting for another election cycle. Mr Burnham needs to get a move on. Dr Ruth Charles Swavesey, Cambridgeshire • As a 69-year-old in receipt of 20 years’ teacher’s pension and a full state pension, I say by all means take money from pensioners. Scrap national insurance (a retrogressive tax) and increase income tax. Scrap all age-related tax benefits/exemptions. But please don’t hit the triple lock until the state pension reaches parity with most European states (Will pensioners be poorer as a result of Burnham scrapping the triple lock?, 29 September). It is mainly women who rely solely on this inadequate pension, and many of them live alone in rented accommodation. They are the last people who should be asked to make sacrifices. Sarah James Monmouth • As an 86-year-old, I’m sure I am not alone in having anxiety about paying for a care home if the need arises, and am delighted that Andy Burnham is determined to sort out the system at last. While the triple-lock pension increases are very welcome, I’d happily accept their change into simply keeping up with prices as a trade-off for never having to worry about paying for social care. Michael Miller Sheffield • Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Please email us your letter and it will be considered for publication in our letters section.

title: A proportional representation voting system could spell disaster for Labour | Letters
summary: Letter: Gian Lorenzo Spisso says his knowledge of Italian voting systems and British politics leads him to the view that first past the post is the lesser of two evils
text: Reading that Andy Burnham wants to push electoral reform forward and move the UK towards proportional representation (Report, 29 September), I found myself shouting at the screen. I come from Italy, where I have seen proportional systems at work. They drive a wedge between MPs and their constituents. They reward tribalism (yes, even more than here). They leave large parts of the electorate hostage to the whims of tiny parties, and force parties into ragtag coalitions that produce unstable, ineffective governments. And for all that, people do not seem to feel any better represented. Having lived in the UK since 2014 and watched its parties with an outsider’s eyes, I still see first past the post as the lesser of two evils. Brexit exposed a complete lack of leadership in David Cameron’s Conservative party, and it was an act of unprecedented self-harm that we are all still paying for, quite literally. But it also showed that parties outside the big two can exert enough pressure to force the party in power to adapt and, alas, to listen to voters. Labour, meanwhile, has reinvented itself remarkably: from Ed Miliband’s soft left to Jeremy Corbyn’s more radical programme, and back again when that proved ineffective. Would a major party put itself through so much self-scrutiny without the incentives of first past the post? Or would it have split into several streams, perhaps more representative but far less effective, squandering its history as so many parties of the Italian left have done? As a settled-status resident who expects to become a citizen this year, and is hoping to vote for Labour at the next general election, I can only say: please don’t do this. Gian Lorenzo Spisso Bristol • Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Please email us your letter and it will be considered for publication in our letters section.

title: Macron says ‘welcome back’ to Burnham suggestion UK could rejoin EU
summary: French president, speaking alongside Spanish counterpart Pedro Sánchez, says EU bid would be good news for UK and Europeans
text: The French president, Emmanuel Macron, has reacted warmly to Andy Burnham’s suggestion that the UK could rejoin the EU. “Welcome back,” the French leader said in English with a smile at a news conference in Madrid on Wednesday. Macron continued in French: “If the British want to come back and if the prime minister is moving in that direction, I think that is very good news, both for his country and for the Europeans.” Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, said his country would open its arms to any bid from the UK to rejoin the EU. The two leaders were responding to the British prime minister’s speech at the Labour party conference in which Burnham said Britain would not have a clear path “until we decide on a long-term relationship with what is still our largest market” and that Brexit had “done more harm than good”. In a series of interviews on Wednesday, Burnham said the government could maintain the status quo, seek a customs union, return to the single market or “go all the way” for full EU membership. Macron said the British had “always been useful in helping us simplify things” when the UK was part of the EU and were “demanding partners”. Burnham “is right to have this boldness”, he added. Earlier, Macron, who has frequently accused the proponents of Brexit of misleading the public, said Brexit had been “the biggest lie of the last 30 years”, pointing to shortfalls in promised economic growth and trade opportunities. Sandro Gozi, an Italian Social Democrat, told the Guardian: “Burnham has finally swept away the so-called red lines that have constrained the debate on Britain’s relationship with Europe. That is a welcome and important step.” The MEP, who co-chairs the EU-UK parliamentary partnership assembly, added: “Europe should respond with the same openness. We should be ready to turn the page and build a new EU-UK partnership, removing unnecessary barriers and restoring much closer economic and political cooperation.” EU officials welcomed the change in tone but said it was up to the UK to define what it wanted from the future relationship. They have told their British counterparts that the UK is welcome to join the customs union or single market via membership of the European Economic Area. In recent weeks Brussels has again mooted British membership of the customs union as an answer to the bloc’s Made in Europe policy, which could exclude British clean technology and electric vehicles from valuable European subsidy programmes and public contracts. But EU officials also stress that joining the customs union would require full alignment with EU trade policy and tariffs. Single market membership means accepting free movement of people, alongside free movement of goods, services and capital. More than 10 years after the Brexit vote, the EU remains attached to its red lines. A recent proposal from the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, that Canada should become the EU’s first-ever associate member, is not seen as a serious option for the UK (or even Canada). The idea is widely regarded by EU insiders as an ill-defined symbolic gesture with no legal basis. The EU and UK are due to hold a summit in Brussels, with a date in the second half of November expected to be announced in the coming days. The annual gathering was postponed after the resignation of Keir Starmer. The Burnham government has made resolving Britain’s exclusion from Made in Europe a top priority, but several EU sources say the issue will not be settled at the summit as the EU is yet to agree its internal position on key legislative texts. France is the staunchest opponent of opening Made in Europe to countries outside the EU, including the UK. Macron pointed to the limits of the UK seeking close ties with the EU while remaining outside. “You cannot choose between the freedoms of the union, nor can you decide to take what suits you and leave the rest,” he said. “So, come back.” A European Commission spokesperson said: “The UK is a close and valued partner of the European Union. It is for the UK government to set out how it wishes to develop its relationship with the EU going forward. We remain open to engaging on the options it may put forward.”

title: New UK gas and oil projects are a ‘no-brainer’, says EDF boss
summary: Developing North Sea fields does not contradict net zero goals, according to Simone Rossi
text: New oil and gas projects are a “no-brainer” that pose “no contradiction” to the net zero agenda, according to the head of EDF Energy. Simone Rossi has joined a string of renewables leaders in making the case for more North Sea production as the government prepares to decide on two projects there. He said ministers should give the Rosebank and Jackdaw fields the green light, while accelerating support for heat pumps and electric vehicles. “It will take decades to wean off from that dependency,” Rossi said in an interview with the BBC. “So while this is happening we should use the resources that we’ve got rather than importing them from afar. For me, it’s really a no-brainer. It is not in contradiction.” New North Sea developments would help to create jobs and increase government tax receipts that could be used to support households struggling to pay energy bills, according to Rossi. He said locally produced fossil fuels had lower emissions than imports because they do not need to transported over long distances. “In the UK the only way we can reduce emissions is to genuinely reduce the usage of fossil fuels at the point of use,” he said. “Over time, the only solution is electricity.” The boss of EDF Energy, which generates about a fifth of the UK’s low-carbon electricity, has become the latest high-profile advocate of climate action to also make a case for more North Sea production. Others include: Greg Jackson, the founder of Octopus Energy; Jürgen Maier, the former boss of GB Energy; and Tara Singh, the boss of RenewableUK. EDF Energy, which is owned by EDF of France, has about 8 gigawatts of low-carbon generation capacity in the UK, including eight nuclear power plants with a combined capacity of 6GW and 2GW of wind, solar and battery storage. It is building the much-delayed Hinkley Point C nuclear power station in Somerset. Politicians to have spoken out in favour of more North Sea production include: the former chancellor Rachel Reeves; the defence secretary, Wes Streeting; former Scottish Labour leader Anas Sarwar; Liberal Democrat leader and former energy secretary, Ed Davey; and the leaders of the largest trade unions. Support on the left aligns with the Labour party’s election manifesto, which ruled out granting exploration licences while still allowing for some new streams of North Sea oil and gas. This was provided they came from already licensed areas or fields adjacent to existing projects, which can use the same infrastructure. Ministers have come under pressure from environmental groups as well as from Zack Polanski, the Green party leader in England and Wales, to deny final consent to Rosebank and Jackdaw after a summer of heatwaves caused by the intensifying climate crisis, and increased volatility in oil and gas prices. Both projects already have licences – granted under the Conservative government – which means they could be given final approval without breaching the manifesto. Andy Burnham promised to take a “pragmatic approach” to the North Sea after Donald Trump used one of his first conversations with the new prime minister to urge him to “open up” more drilling. The government is expected to decide on Rosebank and Jackdaw within weeks. The decision was reportedly delayed until after the 8 October Holborn and St Pancras byelection – in which Polanski plans to stand. The oil and gas proposals were put to the government earlier this year after a court ordered the developers to resubmit their applications with additional consideration for the climate impact of burning their fossil fuels.

title: ‘President of the Unites States’: White House’s AI accord includes spelling error
summary: Donald Trump and six tech executives voluntarily signed the document, which included a misspelling, committing to safely developing AI
text: The White House misspelled “United States” under the signature of Donald Trump on an accord he signed with AI executives on Tuesday. At the bottom of the accord on “Super Intelligence”, the term Trump has used to rebrand artificial intelligence, the president’s signature appeared as “President of the Unites States”. It is unclear how the misspelling occurred or whether it will appear in the Federal Register, the database that contains official presidential actions and other government documents. Trump and six tech executives signed the document voluntarily committing to safely developing AI to address widespread concerns, sparked by industry leaders who warned the technology is evolving too rapidly to control. Trump has largely brushed aside concerns about AI harming humans and called for companies to continue developing the technology so the US can become the global leader in AI. Even while signing the accord on safety, the US president praised the business executives for growth. Trump posted the document containing the misspelling on Truth Social, and the White House Communications Team emailed it out shortly after it was signed. The Bloomberg News correspondent David Gura appeared to be the first to notice the spelling error. The Guardian has asked the White House for comment The accord on artificial intelligence outlined four layers of “controls and audits” that companies will implement to ensure AI capabilities operate as intended. That includes “robust” internal controls and partnering with an “independent external auditor or evaluator”. Potential internal controls could include empowering a team to monitor and detect that AI is operating correctly and creating monitors to ensure AI technologies will not hack or access technical systems in cybersecurity, biosecurity and chemical threats. External monitors would also check to make sure the AI is operating as intended and companies could designate a committee of the board of directors to oversee reports from teams operating the controls of the AI. The accord is the first step in addressing concerns, raised by industry experts in mid-September. Americans have become increasingly skeptical of AI. A recent New York Times/Siena College poll found that 61% of voters opposed the construction of datacenters, while an SSRS/CNN poll found that 71% of Americans believed the government wasn’t doing enough to regulate the growth and development of AI. While Tuesday’s document is only an accord, it left open the possibility of codifying the framework into formal regulations or laws – something Trump has repeatedly rejected. “I think I’m seeing tremendous self-policing,” Trump told reporters outside the White House on Tuesday. “And they understand that they have to self-police.” The six executives who signed the accord are Dario Amodei from Anthropic; Elon Musk from SpaceXAI; Greg Brockman from OpenAI; Jensen Huang from Nvidia; Mark Zuckerberg from Meta; and Sundar Pichai from Google.

title: ‘Strong indications’ that Iran played role in RAF Fairford incident, says Burnham
summary: PM also defends decision to release suspects on bail and expresses ‘complete confidence’ in security services
text: There are “strong indications” that Iran played a role in events in which five men were arrested near RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire as part of a terror investigation, Andy Burnham has said. Speaking to the media at the end of the Labour party conference in Liverpool, Burnham said he could not give any more details amid a police investigation, but that Iran was believed to be involved. On Tuesday, Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, said Washington believed “a foreign actor” was involved in the events on Sunday night at the airbase, which has been used by US planes for missions against Iran. In an interview with BBC News, Burnham said: “There are strong indications that Iran played a part in what happened over the weekend at RAF Fairford, but of course it remains an ongoing, complex, and serious police investigation. “And of course, we are working closely with our colleagues in the United States of America. So it’s ongoing.” Noting that he had held a meeting of the government’s Cobra emergency committee while in Liverpool, Burnham said: “We are on top of it in every possible way imaginable.” He added: “We will say more in due course, but we can confirm our belief that we believe Iran to have played a part.” Asked why he believed this, Burnham replied: “Well I can’t go into all of those details, but obviously I wouldn’t say it lightly.” In a separate interview with Sky News, Burnham was asked if he needed to recall parliament, which is in recess for the party conference season. He replied: “At this stage there is not an urgent need to do that, but should that arise, of course, I wouldn’t hesitate.” The five men, all in their 20s and from London, were arrested in the Gloucestershire countryside near the airbase after a local woman driving home saw a series of vans and men in masks, and called police. They were first arrested on explosives charges and then later for preparing acts of terrorism. All five were released on police bail on Monday after an examination of what was found in the vans, and searches of addresses linked to them across London. On Tuesday the Guardian reported increasing confidence of an Iranian link to the weekend’s events. The decision to release the men has prompted criticism from the Trump administration, with Rubio saying he was “disturbed” by it. Questioned by the BBC about US criticism of the bail decision, Burnham said this had happened only with very strict conditions. He said: “I think people need to understand that when it says released, that isn’t as people might think. It’s obviously with the strictest possible bail conditions. We’ve been talking to counterparts in the United States all week to explain what is happening here, how things are being done. I have complete confidence in the way British security services are handling this.” It emerged on Tuesday that one of the five men arrested called the police to report the incident. The local woman who also phoned police subsequently told newspapers that she was alarmed the men had been allowed to get so close to the airbase without apparently being noticed. However, UK officials and Wes Streeting, the UK defence secretary, have indicated that security services were aware in advance of what was happening. A statement from Britain’s head of counter-terrorism police hinted that officers swooped on the rural location for several reasons. Assistant commissioner Laurence Taylor said: “A police response was activated in the early hours of Sunday morning due to a range of information received, including a call from a member of the public about several vehicles acting suspiciously close to RAF Fairford.”

title: French court jails six men for manslaughter over mass drowning in Channel
summary: Seven others found guilty of lesser charges in connection to incident in 2021 when inflatable dinghy sank killing at least 27 people with four more still missing
text: A Paris court has jailed six ⁠men for manslaughter over the deaths of at least 27 people in the worst mass drowning on record from a small-boat crossing in the Channel. Seven other men were ⁠found guilty of lesser smuggling charges with varying degrees of seriousness, including facilitating illegal immigration as part of ⁠an organised gang and criminal conspiracy. Five years on, another four people are still missing. The court heard that the sinking of an inflatable dinghy in November 2021 was caused by “individuals driven by greed, with utter disregard for human life”. Prosecutors said the convicted men helped launch a “substandard small boat, uncertified, unfit for navigation on the open sea, overcrowded and lacking appropriate lifejackets”. Emmanuel Daoud, a lawyer for one victim’s family, called the proceedings a “trial of greed, cynicism and inhumanity”. Twenty-seven people were confirmed dead when their inflatable dinghy sank in the early hours of 24 November 2021. Four people remain unaccounted for. The victims were mostly Iraqi Kurds, but also included people who were Afghan, Ethiopian, Iranian, Somali, Vietnamese and Egyptian. The youngest known victim was a seven-year-old girl. The confirmed dead included 15 men, seven women and two teenagers. Sentences for the six men found guilty of manslaughter ranged ‌from six to 10 years in prison. For others, sentences ranged from six months suspended to four years in prison. The court heard that the men were linked to Afghan and Iraqi-Kurdish smuggling networks ⁠that organised the migrants’ passage to Britain from camps near Grande-Synthe and Calais in northern France. One man was found innocent. According to testimony from the two survivors, the flimsy boat, which had attempted to cross one of the world’s busiest shipping lanes between the northern French coast and Kent in southern England began to deflate and take on water after several hours at sea. Passengers fell overboard and drowned one after another, despite making about a dozen desperate calls for help to French and British rescue services. Only two men survived. For the people onboard the sinking boat, despite several distress calls, it was nearly 12 hours after the first pleas for help before the dinghy was finally found by a French fishing vessel. A separate investigation is continuing in France into seven French military personnel – five members at a maritime rescue coordination centre, and two sailors onboard a patrol vessel. They have been under investigation since 2023 for failing to help a person in danger. They deny the allegations. Zana Mahmand Mohammed travelled from Erbil in Iraqi Kurdistan to address the court about his younger brother, Twana, 18, who drowned in the disaster but whose body has never been found. He said: “We’ve been waiting for our brother’s body for five years. I live with the uncertainty of ever finding out what happened. We lost a member of our family. He had a project for another future to live … ” The family had tried to dissuade Twana from leaving home, but he had wanted to find a job and develop his sporting success as a black belt in taekwondo and escape the violence and insecurity of his region. Mohammed said every time he read in the media about other small boats in difficulty, he relived the tragedy. “Destruction is being repeated,” he said.

title: ‘We want justice’: series of rapes trigger mass protests at Indian universities
summary: Women say nothing has changed since Delhi’s infamous Nirbhaya bus rape case 14 years ago
text: The posters, just like the women holding them, were taking no prisoners. “Girls don’t need curfews, rapists need consequences,” read one. “Lock your dicks rather than your women at home,” read another. As hundreds of women walked from the gates of their university campus into the streets of Delhi – where sexual harassment, assault, catcalling and molestation are a constant, daily threat – they shouted together in a chorus of rage and defiance: “We want justice.” The fury that has erupted on India’s university campuses over the past week has been double-edged. The trigger was a series of brutal rapes that have taken place in Delhi in recent weeks, including the alleged gang-rape of a 17-year-old in a public park close to Delhi University by three men who posed as police officers. Just a week earlier, another 17-year-old was gang-raped and murdered in Delhi’s Swaroop Nagar neighbourhood after she went to meet friends. The accused allegedly raped her, stabbed her to death and dumped her body in a field, where it was discovered days later half eaten by dogs. Rapes of an 11-year-old and a six-year-old were reported in the same month. Last month, a 16-year-old was allegedly raped by a bus driver and conductor after she boarded a sleeper bus in Delhi. Women who have taken part in protests on Delhi university campuses have condemned these alleged violent rapes on minors as disgusting and unforgivable – but they have also been at pains to emphasise that they are not out of the ordinary. Fourteen years have passed since Delhi’s infamous Nirbhaya rape case, when a woman was gang-raped on a bus and died from her injuries. But while it provoked international outrage and a slew of legislation and government promises, women say nothing has changed; for them, India’s streets, particularly in Delhi, remain as unsafe as ever. According to statistics, a women is raped in India every 20 minutes – though the real scale is believed to be far worse due to chronic under-reporting. This week, the supreme court said the five successive rape cases “starkly underlined a systematic failure” and it could not help but “draw painful parallels to the Nirbhaya incident of 2012”. Vaishnavi Dhruw, 21, a history student at Delhi University, was among the female protesters at the “smash the patriarchy” protest march on Wednesday afternoon. “I don’t know a single woman who lives in this city and feels safe,” she said. While some of the key demands of the protest have been better lighting and policing, Dhruw emphasised that for anything to change, the country required a deep societal shift where men no longer felt they had ownership over women’s bodies. “We are not marching for safety, we are here to protest for our freedom, for the most basic right to walk in our own streets,” she said. “Again and again, women are told to stay indoors, to not go out at night, to cover ourselves, to protect ourselves. When will society tell men in our country not to rape?” Much of the anger driving the protests has also been prompted by the response by the authorities to the rapes, which women say once again has only been to police their freedoms. Women in Delhi were told to stay out of parks at night, and classes were temporarily halted at one of Delhi’s most prestigious female colleges. Many hostels where female students stay impose strict curfews preventing them from going out at night. “Instead of going after criminals, you’re going to tell women to sit at home,” said Aranya Rathore, 25, a student at Delhi University. “A demand for more surveillance is not a solution. In fact, it’s going to curtail our freedom more.” Female students say a lot of their time is taken up by safety logistics – from wearing modest clothes to reorganising their days to ensure they do not travel alone or at night and always having a trackable live location on their phones. There is widespread awareness that should anything happen, the onus of blame – both within the family home and more widely in society – tends to fall on women. As one poster at Wednesday’s march pointed out, “no one ever asks what the rapist was wearing”. Yet despite their best efforts, many women said it was almost impossible to avoid harassment. Aanya Wig, a 26-year-old graduate of Delhi University and the founder of Her Haq, a gender equality initiative, said she had experienced harassment both around university campuses and in public spaces. She recounted an incident where a driver rolled down his car window and began masturbating as she and female friends got off a rickshaw and walked through the college gates. “This wasn’t at night, it was in the middle of the day,” she said. “I’ve always lived in Delhi and the city has not changed.” The protests have brought into focus a dilemma faced by many Indian women, who are being educated in greater numbers than any time in the country’s history and have better job opportunities than ever before, but still have to navigate the constant debilitating threats to their safety and the conservative pressures from their families. “I know so many girls, not just 10 years ago but even today, who end up choosing educational institutions and jobs and other employment opportunities depending on how close they are from their home,” said Wig. “Not on the basis of their marks, not on the basis of their aspirations, but simply, ‘OK, the shorter the distance is, the more likely it is that I will be safe’.” Many of the Delhi University students who took part in the marches said that sexual harassment had become prevalent on campus, and have demanded better accountability mechanisms for reporting assault. The university has not responded. Devyani Sarkar, 24, who is studying for a master’s in English, said: “Delhi University is one of the most prestigious universities in India right now but there are various cases of women being assaulted by professors, sometimes unfortunately also for grades. It’s despicable, but it’s also a living truth.” Many on the marches said it was no coincidence that they were taking place in the aftermath of India’s “cockroach” movement, in which hundreds of thousands of young Gen Z Indians took to the streets over education reform. “My generation is not afraid to stand up and protest. We know that society has to change,” said 17-year-old Subhani. “The days of women being silent is over.”

title: Sweden must apologise for harm done to Sami people, says state-backed report
summary: Truth commission accuses country of failing Indigenous people, amid rising tensions over land rights
text: An independent commission set up by the Swedish state has called on the country’s government to apologise for the “harm and injustice inflicted upon the Sami people” and to start a national process for “redress and reconciliation”. The Truth Commission for the Sami People also called for a special apology to be issued urgently to elderly Sami people who were forced as children to attend segregated so-called “nomad school” and other boarding schools where they were “subjected to violations or abuse”. The commission’s report, published on Wednesday, is the outcome of a four-year investigation and hundreds of interviews with Sami people across Sweden. It was due to be presented to a government representative at a ceremony featuring readings from the text, but with no government yet in place after the election earlier this month, it went instead to Parisa Liljestrand, the last government’s culture minister. The commission’s chair, Lena Nyberg, told her: “We hand over a big responsibility.” Liljestrand thanked the members of the commission and those who were interviewed for the report, saying it had been a “historic process”. There have been similar truth commissions into the treatment of Sami people – Europe’s only recognised Indigenous people – in Norway and Finland. Norway has issued an official apology and discussions in Finland are ongoing. The new report accuses Sweden of failing to meet its domestic and international human rights obligations and says that as a “direct consequence” of mistreatment, the Sami people today face “major challenges” in preserving and developing their culture. It coincides with rising anti-Sami rhetoric in Sweden, including from political leaders, amid clashes over land used for grazing by Sami reindeer herders for hundreds of years, which the state wants to mine for rare-earth minerals. The report says issues with the handling of Sami land rights in Sweden have been “reinforced and aggravated” by an ideology that Sami people are “an inferior people and therefore neither deserving of nor capable of exercising the same rights and responsibilities as other citizens”. It adds that the Swedish state has failed to implement the United Nations declaration on the rights of Indigenous peoples. The commission’s 71-point call to action recommends an official apology for the harm and injustice inflicted upon the Sami people, as well as financial compensation and completing the process of ratifying the International Labour Organization’s convention on Indigenous and tribal peoples. It calls for the establishment of a national centre for redress and reconciliation, and for authorities to recognise that the Swedish nation was founded on lands belonging to two peoples – the Sámi and the Swedes – and that parts of the land have Sami names and are part of Sami cultural heritage. It also urges recognition that Sápmi, the region traditionally inhabited by the Sami people, extends across present national borders; an end to racial discrimination against Sami people; and better provision for children to learn Sami languages. It adds that the Swedish government must uphold the Sami people’s right to practise reindeer husbandry and other cultural practices on their traditional lands. The report concludes that the state, including the Swedish parliament, government and public authorities, and in some cases the Church of Sweden, must “bear responsibility” for policies and decisions that led to the violation of Sami rights. It says: “Accepting responsibility also requires the state to work towards providing redress for the harm inflicted on the Sami people and individual Sami, while pursuing policies that do not repeat these historical injustices.”

title: Good news in US inflation report boosts chances Fed won’t hike rates
summary: Traders see about a 35% chance of an October rate hike, down from ​about 45% following White House pressure
text: Good economic news boosted Wall Street’s main indexes on Wednesday, as a softer-than-anticipated inflation reading buoyed up hopes that the Federal Reserve might not hike rates as soon ⁠as next month. A commerce department report ⁠showed the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index stood at 3.4% on an annual basis in August against estimates of 3.7%, per economists polled by Reuters. Separately, second-quarter GDP data – the broadest measure of the economy’s health – showed that the US economy grew at a solid clip, driven ⁠by robust consumer spending and business investment related to the buildout of AI infrastructure. “The market had been tracing out a bullish formation, meaning the price pattern suggested that any positive catalyst could trigger a move higher and that’s exactly ⁠what happened,” said Sam Stovall, chief investment strategist at CFRA Research. Traders now see a roughly 35% chance of an October rate hike, down from about a 45% chance, according to data ‌compiled by LSEG. The Federal Reserve is under pressure to cut rates from the White House after raising them earlier this month for the first time since 2023. Inflation has emerged as the top issue for voters in the run-up to the midterm elections with Donald Trump receiving poor marks for his handling of the economy. US stock markets rose in early trading, but the S&P ended the day down 0.25% and the Dow fell 0.86%. The Nasdaq ended the day up 0.24%. Despite weakness in September, driven by bond market volatility and elevated oil prices amid the US-Iran conflict, the benchmark S&P 500 and the ‌Nasdaq were on pace for a second straight quarterly advance, if gains hold. On Wednesday, the yield on the 10-year treasury bond held steady at 5.246%, a day after hitting its highest since June 2007. Crude oil prices rose on the day, with the December contract for Brent crude futures moving higher. There was also positive news from the jobs market. ADP, the US’s largest payroll supplier, said private employers added 90,000 jobs in September, higher than expected and up from 36,000 in August. On Friday, the labor department will release its latest monthly jobs tally, which is expected to show a gain of 84,000 for September, down from 162,000 in the prior month. Reuters contributed reporting

title: ‘He persuaded us’: Labour ministers moved by Andy Burnham’s emotional conference speech
summary: Prime minister’s pure political argument marks new era for party as he sets out his plans and priorities
text: The hottest ticket at Labour conference – after Andy Burnham’s speech – was an afterparty in Liverpool’s Baltic Triangle, headlined with a set by the noughties girlband Sugababes. As Labour activists and ministers belted out the lyrics under pink spotlights, it was hard not to draw some parallels with the party’s recent history. There have been painful lineup changes and a lot of internal division, but this week onstage in Liverpool the originals are back together and they only played the hits. The fans can’t get enough. Burnham’s own show on the main stage had the conference hall in raptures not because of Brexit or social care but because of the display of raw emotion after the tightly choreographed repression of the last six years. He may as well have walked across the stage with his feet crunching over the debris of shattered Ming vases. The speech combined plans that had been forming inside Burnham’s head for the last decade as well as seat-of-his-pants political instinct. On the morning of the conference, the prime minister took off early for a morning jog and then returned to make final amendments. Even moments before he went on stage, he was still rewriting, aides said. About a quarter of the speech was entirely ad-libbed. When Burnham was rehearsing the speech, aides said, he knew he was going to cry when he got to the paragraph about his late father – he never managed to get through any of the practice runs without tears. But the long pause as he composed himself was the most emotional he had been. Several ministers said they themselves had been moved to tears, including Ed Miliband, who had recently lost his mother, as well as Louise Haigh and Anneliese Midgley, who are Burnham’s closest friends in government and the architects of his ascendancy. After his speech, Burnham gathered all his ministers for a private pep talk. He said he knew they would not agree with everything, but – with the aura of a general sending his troops into battle – he told them to “get out there” and fight for it. He said he would not send them out with “a pea-shooter” – they needed proper weapons for the fight ahead and he promised he would provide them. In the hallway outside the conference hall, minister after minister spoke with voices quivering with emotion. “This is all I have ever wanted,” one said. The bar for speeches from political leaders has been low for the past decade or more. It is rare for clips to be anything more than a soundbite for social media and then a long shopping list of statistics and achievements. Burnham’s was the first time many MPs can recall a speech that was pure political argument. And there was much in the speech that in normal times would have been a recipe for rebellion: Brexit, the triple lock, electoral reform and the lingering question marks over growth and defence. “I found parts of the speech challenging, if I’m honest,” one cabinet minister admitted. “It contained things I had always thought we should never touch or an argument about public control which I would previously have said was too backward-looking. But in the room I agreed with every word because he persuaded us, he made an argument and made me question myself. It was a quite extraordinary thing.” Even within the cabinet, there are those who grimace at the idea of electoral reform. “But you know, he believes in it, and I’m going to swallow it,” said one. Burnham called his cabinet ministers in for a last-minute meeting just before the speech, where he laid out his private arguments and took their comments and feedback. “I feel almost embarrassed admitting this, but that has never happened before with any other leader,” one said. On the sidelines of the conference, when cabinet ministers are at their most candid, they sometimes talk as if they have been through a kind of collective trauma – and the Burnham ascendancy has given them the release they need to confess how hard they have found the last two years. There are close new friendships and alliances forged in the coup, which defy previous factional lines. “There’s the management-speak slogan: ‘Culture eats strategy for breakfast.’ Well, this is proof positive,” one cabinet minister said. “The past two years were utterly miserable, almost every single thing we achieved was poisoned by petty fighting. Every meeting was a choreographed exercise in pointlessness. Now we are discussing ideas and politics among colleagues who respect and like each other. I look back and I am so overwhelmed with relief that we did this.” Another cabinet minister said: “I wasted so much of my own bandwidth fighting over the most puerile things, or defending my own staff who were being made miserable. Keir [Starmer] never dared to take it on.” Even veterans of the Starmer years said they found themselves persuaded despite themselves. “Feels like there’s something quite psychologically profound about daring to take on the triple lock and finding that the planes don’t fall from the skies,” Starmer’s former strategy director Paul Ovenden posted. Darren Jones, the ousted chief secretary who has made himself the face of the awkward squad, was also quick to lavish praise. “[The speech] told the story of his politics and the type of Britain he wants to build,” he said. “He told us we’d be in no doubt what his priorities are for the country, and he was right.” Burnham will not welcome the comparison, but the closest recent one is how it felt at the Conservative party conference in the pre-disgrace Boris Johnson years: an electric electoral prospect who can genuinely reach across the political spectrum, hypnotising his doubters by the sheer force of his personality. But this prime minister has no hint of the sleaze or incompetence that was always in the shadows for Johnson. If it comes, Burnham’s downfall will probably be his own voracious appetite for political risk – but that could also be the making of his premiership.

title: We need ‘right to intervene’ in AI amid growing threat, says Bank of England boss
summary: Andrew Bailey’s comments come as fears grow that rogue models could take financial system hostage
text: The governor of the Bank of England has called for the “right to intervene” in the AI industry amid growing fears that rogue models could take the financial system hostage. Andrew Bailey said the risks posed by frontier AI models – a number of which have gone rogue in recent months – were “real and increasingly significant”. Meanwhile, it was becoming harder for the public to have proper oversight of powerful AI models that were “functioning within a self-reinforcing loop”. That is putting financial stability at risk, with the new technology having increased the “scale and sophistication of cyber threats to the financial system”, he said. The governor warned it could threaten daily card payments, bank transactions, and stock and bond trading across financial markets. The comments came as the Bank’s financial policy committee (FPC) said the growing mountain of AI debt was increasing financial stability risks. The potential benefits of AI “are immense”, Bailey said but he added that authorities needed to be ready to step in. In an opinion piece penned for the Bank of England’s Insight series, he said: “If we are to realise those benefits safely, we must answer one critical question. Should society retain the ability to intervene, to establish the boundaries within which these systems operate and to revise those boundaries as the technology evolves? To my mind, the answer is unequivocally yes.” But Bailey said authorities needed to figure out why they might be forced to step in. He said a “sensible starting point” would be rigorous testing of new AI models to understand how they behave and identify “credible points” where authorities could intervene. “In time, that understanding could be codified into a set of standards which will help to ensure consistency in approach across the financial system, and perhaps more broadly across the economy,” he said. However, the governor stopped short of calling for a regulatory clampdown, saying it was “not, in my view, the right place to start. In the excitement surrounding AI development, there is a risk that we move too quickly to debates about regulatory architecture before establishing where the failure exists in the first place.” A growing number of lawmakers, AI researchers and even some AI companies have called for more government oversight of artificial intelligence in recent weeks. However, hopes for international cooperation faded after Donald Trump broadly rejected calls for more regulation of AI technology – most of which is being developed in the US – warning it could hurt efforts to compete with China and threaten economic growth. But Bailey said a set of standards could help safeguard the financial system from harmful AI, which may end up operating outside well-established “shared norms, obligations and responsibilities”. “Central banks have a responsibility to safeguard the stability of the system as a whole,” Bailey said. “We cannot stand aside and assume that technological progress will resolve these questions on its own. The public interest requires that we engage with them now, before the risks become more difficult to contain.” Warning of the ballooning AI debt pile, the FPC said large players in the sector had taken on $450bn (£339bn) worth of debt between January and September this year, already overtaking the $333bn worth of gilts due to be issued by the UK government for the whole of 2026. That has tied investors – including hedge funds, asset managers and private credit firms – to the fortunes of AI companies at a time when those tech businesses have yet to turn a profit. “The rapid increase in artificial intelligence-related debt issuance broadens the exposure of capital markets to development in AI,” minutes of the recent FPC meeting on 25 September said. “The committee underscores the importance of timely and careful management of these intensifying, interconnected risks.”
