title: Hedge fund CEO gives $3bn to Carnegie Mellon University in historic donation
summary: Unprecedented university donation from Citadel CEO Ken Griffin will go toward building a new Miami campus
text: Carnegie Mellon University will receive an unprecedented $3bn donation from the billionaire investor Ken Griffin, making it the largest single donation in the history of US education. Griffin, 57, is the founder and CEO of Citadel, described as the most profitable hedge fund in history. The money is going toward a new Miami campus as well as big investments at the university’s longtime home in Pittsburgh. Part of the funding will be used to develop Carnegie Mellon’s presence in Miami, Florida, where Griffin lives and where Citadel is now headquartered. The rest will support priorities in Pittsburgh, including recruiting prominent academics and making attendance more affordable for students. The Miami campus will support more than 3,500 undergraduate, master’s and PhD students, nearly 300 faculty and more than 600 staff members, with construction slated to begin in 2027. $1bn will go toward Carnegie Mellon’s computer science school and other priorities, including financial aid, Griffin and the university president, Farnam Jahanian, said. The school will be renamed the Kenneth C Griffin School of Computer Science. “Throughout our history, CMU has anticipated moments of profound technological change and responded with new ways of thinking and solving problems,” Jahanian said in a statement. “Artificial intelligence represents one of the defining intellectual developments of our time, and it demands that we rethink how we educate students, conduct research and partner with others.” Founded by the industrialist Andrew Carnegie, Carnegie Mellon is particularly known for computer science, artificial intelligence, robotics and the performing arts. Its School of Computer Science is ranked as the top undergraduate computer science program in the US. The planned Miami campus will take a different approach from the traditional academic-major model. According to the university, education there will instead be structured around “societal challenges”. The campus will concentrate on “challenge areas spanning human health and biological discovery; national security and strategic capabilities; energy and climate resilience; and advanced manufacturing and industrial transformation”. The expansion also reflects Griffin’s continuing investment in Miami and south Florida. Citadel moved its headquarters from Chicago to Miami in 2022, and Griffin has since increased his commitments to the region to about $2.4bn, according to Reuters. Those contributions include support for a Miami charter school network, the University of Miami, Miami Dade College, public schools and math tutoring. Griffin, whose net worth Forbes estimated at about $58bn, will also become a member of Carnegie Mellon’s board of trustees. The board already includes hedge fund billionaire David Tepper, a Carnegie Mellon graduate and donor. The announcement comes one week after Nike co-founder Phil Knight donated $1bn to establish an engineering college at the University of Oregon. Universities are increasingly seeking wealthy donors to expand science and tech programs as artificial intelligence drives economic changes. These large donations have generated concerns about how much influence the wealthy class has over higher education. Griffin has publicly criticized the use of political power for personal enrichment, emerging as one of the most vocal critics of Donald Trump and his administration on Wall Street. Earlier this year, he condemned how the president’s family appear to have made financial gain from their proximity to the White House.

title: What we know so far about alleged stabbing of pilot by co-pilot on flight to Israel
summary: Plane made emergency landing after pilot tried to crash aircraft, Israeli PM says, as officials investigate whether it was an attempted terror attack
text: One of the pilots of a plane flying from the UAE to Israel stabbed his co-pilot and appeared to try to crash the plane, the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, said, as Israeli officials said they were investigating whether the incident was an attempted terror attack on Israelis. Here is what we know so far: A commercial plane travelling from Dubai in the United Arab Emirates to Israel was forced to make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia, after an apparent brawl between its pilots prompted distress signals that briefly raised fears of an attempted hijacking. The flydubai flight was over Jordan when it diverted to Saudi Arabia, transmitting three emergency signals, one of which indicated a possible unlawful interference. The plane dipped dramatically during the reported fight, descending about 16,000ft in just two minutes. Israeli officials scrambled fighter jets, fearful of a possible hijacking attempt on a plane containing dozens of Israelis, and the plane landed at Tabuk airport in north-western Saudi Arabia. Netanyahu said one of the flydubai pilots stabbed his co-pilot and appeared to be intending to crash the plane. He added that a passenger managed to break into the cockpit with one of the crew members, and together they “neutralised” the attacking pilot. Netanyahu described it as “an extremely severe security incident”. Other officials, including the defence minister, Israel Katz, have called it an attempted terrorist attack. Netanyahu thanked the passengers and crew who helped to stop the attack, saying they “showed exceptional resourcefulness and courage”. An Israeli official has identified the attacker as an Omani national, Reuters reported. The Boeing 737 plane, which Israeli officials said had between 160 and 180 passengers onboard, transmitted a general emergency signal about two and a half hours after leaving Dubai, according to the flight-tracking website Flightradar24. A passenger on the flight, Miryam Shira Ohayon, said the plane was “pretty much out of control” when the alleged stabbing took place. “The co-pilot tried to murder the pilot and basically carry out a suicide attack on the plane,” she told reporters, on speakerphone held up by her mother, who was waiting at Ben Gurion airport near Tel Aviv. The plane transmitted the initial general emergency signal again before landing at Saudi Arabia’s Tabuk airport. The airport said the plane landed at 9.45am local time and both pilots were taken to hospital after sustaining injuries. A second flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv landed safely at its destination. Flightradar24 initially showed flight FZ1081 diverting back towards the UAE but it was later shown to be on its way to Israel, where it landed in Tel Aviv on Wednesday afternoon.

title: If turbocharged petrol prices are driving up inflation, then why are Australia’s unemployed on the line? | Greg Jericho
summary: Avoiding a rise in unemployment is important for the RBA – but apparently not a dealbreaker
text: And here we are again. Hello darkness my old friend. Interest rates up again and talk of a recession if needed. The Reserve Bank’s enacting legislation gives it a dual mandate – “price stability [ie stable inflation] and the maintenance of full employment in Australia”. But in reality the RBA seems to ignore the “full employment” aspect overall and we now need to worry about a recession. It’s not just me who noticed this. After the RBA governor, Michele Bullock, held a press conference where she announced that the cash rate was being raised to 4.6%, the ABC’s Alan Kohler (enjoy your retirement, Alan!) told Afternoon Briefing: “She defines ‘full employment’ in terms of inflation. There’s really only one mandate that means – the mandate is inflation. That’s it.” The market also understands this. After the RBA’s July meeting, the markets predicted no rate rise this month and maybe no more to come. Now a rise to 4.85% is priced in before March next year: If the graph does not display click here They predict this even though without the increase in petrol prices driven by the war on Iran, inflation in August would have fallen (which is why core inflation remained steady at 3.6%): If the graph does not display click here When thinking about petrol prices, recall that Ampol’s interim profit this year rose 376%, and its share price has risen so much since the war on Iran began that Woodside and Santos seem like the poor cousins: If the graph does not display click here Apparently, companies are not to blame for raising prices. Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here Never mind that household spending in August fell once you took away the increase due to petrol prices: If the graph does not display click here No, forget all that, the RBA is devoted to getting inflation under 3% regardless of what is causing that inflation. Bullock said the RBA was not failing to deliver full employment because “the full employment target is the unemployment rate, if you like, or the level of employment which is consistent with low and stable inflation. And what we’re saying at the moment is that the rate of unemployment or the employment, is actually a bit tight, and it’s not consistent, we don’t think, with low and stable inflation.” Truly Humpty Dumpty language territory. If you are not angry now, you should be. But just wait. With inflation at 4.0% mainly driven by petrol prices due to a war in Iran and a massive boom in datacentres (which are not delivering any productivity benefits yet), the RBA is worried we might think this clearly abnormal period is normal and that inflation will always be above 3%. God spare us. The governor was asked if she could see a situation “where you do actually need to put the economy into recession in order to get what you desperately hope for which is basically the mid-point of 2.5%? Can you see a scenario where that would be needed?” Now for me that is a pretty easy question to answer; something along the lines of “No! Are you crazy? There is no way lowering core inflation from 3.6% to under 3% would justify a recession.” Instead, Bullock replied: “Well, I hope it’s not needed. Are there scenarios in which it might have to happen that way? I guess possibly. And the scenario that I’m thinking of there is if inflation expectations get away from us. If inflation expectations start – if people start saying, ‘You know what, three point something is fine or four is fine,’ and you do hear some of that, if that gets away, then that is a circumstance in which I think you might need to have quite a dramatic slowdown in the economy to – and that’s our worry.” [My italics] Just think on that – the central bank thinking if people would start considering that inflation between 3% and 4% is OK, then a recession could be on the table, even if it wasn’t their “central base case at this moment”. Bullock once again on Tuesday told journalists that rising unemployment “doesn’t mean job losses. What it often means is that people might be taking longer to find a job.” She’s technically right but for her to say that “we’ll do what we have to do to get inflation down because we need to”, shows the skewed priorities. Sure, she went on to say, “but if we can avoid massive job losses and a massive increase in the unemployment rate, that is a really important thing to be able to try and do”. Avoiding massive increases in unemployment is important but, for the RBA, apparently not a dealbreaker. Recessions are horrible things and many a central bank has come a gutser thinking they can just lower rates and get things going again. During Covid the percentage of adults with a job fell by as much as during the 1990s recession but it was due to lockdowns, not economic conditions, so the recovery was very quick. The GFC was almost a recession but the percentage of adults with a job fell much less than in the 1990s recession. In the 1990s recession, not only was there a massive loss of jobs, it took a decade to recover: If the graph does not display click here Recessions over the past 55 years have seen the level of men in full-time work fall and never recover. Never: If the graph does not display click here But that, it seems, might be the price we have to pay to lower inflationary expectations from 3.5% to 2.5%. • Greg Jericho is a Guardian columnist and chief economist at the Australia Institute

title: All of a flutter: how butterflies avoid being a predator’s lunch
summary: Their whirring wings and bright patterns help keep them safe from birds, British study finds
text: Naturalists have long wondered how brightly coloured butterflies manage to evade the attention of birds that make a meal of other insects. New research from British ecologists suggests it is not simply a matter of good luck but instead a visual illusion created by their fluttering wings. The study by researchers from the universities of Exeter and Essex concluded that the spots and stripes found on many butterfly wings – combined with their dancing flight – scramble a predator’s sense of the insects’ speed and direction. George Hancock, of the University of Exeter’s Centre for Ecology and Conservation in Cornwall, said very few European butterflies were toxic or unpalatable and they were relatively easy to spot in flight, so they needed something special to stay out of harm’s way. “The illusions interfere with the predator’s most basic visual targeting system and disrupt the final ballistic attack,” Hancock said. “As a result, birds and other predators often miss.” Jolyon Troscianko, also of the University of Exeter, said: “Butterfly wings deform as they fly, clapping together on the upstroke and peeling apart on the downstroke, so their stripes shift angle and point in different directions as they flap. “Combined with their unpredictable flight paths, this patterning creates misleading motion illusions, causing a predator to miss entirely or to strike a less vulnerable part of the wing, such as the hindwing or tail.” The experts compared the mechanism to the “barber pole illusion” – the red and white stripes appear to travel upwards even though the pole is only spinning in place. The breakthrough came when Troscianko put a slow-motion video of a butterfly flying upwards through a “bird-vision” computer model. It seemed to indicate – wrongly – that the butterfly was moving downwards. Troscianko said: “First I checked this wasn’t a coding error, that I’d swapped up and down somehow, but then it dawned on me that this would be a perfect way to confuse attacking predators.” The team looked at hundreds of types of European butterflies and found different patterns created different effects. Swallowtail butterflies were found to be among the best at using motion confusion. Troscianko said: “They are also thought to be closest to the ancestral butterflies, suggesting motion confusion might have been around right at the point when butterflies evolved away from night-flying moths. “Swallowtails have little tails trailing from their hindwings that help increase their levels of motion confusion. They are frequently found with their tails missing and beak-shaped holes cut from their wing edges by failed bird attacks. This fits with our modelling that shows how the wing markings should deflect attacks sideways and behind the butterfly’s vital body and inner wing sections.” The team used a high-speed camera to film butterflies taking off to capture how their patterns behave in flight. To test how patterns might affect attacks, 100 human volunteers acted as “predators”, trying to catch virtual butterflies on a touchscreen. They struggled. The study found that largely white butterflies also managed to dodge predators. The researchers believe that when in flight they appear to move more quickly than they actually do because of the stark contrast they make with their background – which may put out the timing of strikes from predators. Troscianko said the discovery could be used to begin to explain how other animals used motion confusion. “We think it is likely to be far more widespread in nature than previously realised, from the flapping wings of birds to the flicking tails of lizards and fish. It opens up an exciting new research avenue.” The study – Butterfly wing patterns in flight create powerful illusory motion cues – is published in the journal Nature.

title: Trump ally urges administration to ‘step back’ and rethink immigration agenda
summary: Republican senator Jim Justice of West Virginia criticizes immigration crackdown as ranchers’ associations condemn ICE activity
text: A close political ally of Donald Trump has broken from the administration’s aggressive immigration enforcement agenda and recommended it “step back” to evaluate what it could do better. “To get better, the first thing you got to do is admit you’re doing something wrong,” Jim Justice, a Republican senator of West Virginia, told Politico. “And in this situation, with all that’s going on and all the stuff, we probably got to step back from it and say: ‘Maybe we’re doing something wrong here or there,’ and then adjust to that.” Justice, who also sits on the Senate agriculture committee, made his comments after three rancher associations condemned Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) activity for negatively affecting agricultural communities. But his comments also come after an ACLU of West Virginia investigation found that about three-quarters of the more than 593 arrested by ICE in the state during “Operation Country Roads” in January had no criminal record. “Before you know it, you get people that get carried away in their job and whatever it may be, and all of a sudden, then you’re dragging people away that have lived on your street corner for 15 years, and I don’t know that we need to be doing that stuff,” Justice told Politico. Trump’s immigration enforcement agenda is a signature policy of his administration. Many voters indicated they wanted stricter immigration policies, but the intense tactics of federal agents have sparked anger nationwide. For ranchers in rural communities, ICE operations have had “a massive chilling effect on the legal, documented, skilled workers” who assist in beef production and the cattle supply chain, the Kansas Livestock Association, Oklahoma Cattlemen’s Association and Texas Cattle Feeders Association said in a statement released last week. Dairy farmers have also recently raised concerns that ICE operations in rural areas could soon hurt their industries. “If we had a concerted effort to have enforcement activities within agriculture, you could really harm our ability to produce food to feed ourselves,” Rick Naerebout, the CEO of the Idaho Dairymen’s Association, told NPR. West Virginia is home to more than 22,700 ranchers, most of which are family-owned. Justice’s criticisms make him the latest Republican to distance himself from Trump in the lead-up to the midterm elections. Maria Elvira Salazar, a Republican congresswoman from Florida, recently ran a campaign advertisement telling Trump his “immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far”. The Guardian has asked the White House for a response.

title: More than 44,000 file legal objections to Palantir NHS platform handling their data
summary: Exclusive: Campaign comes amid backlash against tech company’s involvement with Israeli military and Trump’s ICE crackdown
text: Tens of thousands of people have formally demanded NHS England blocks the Palantir-powered national medical data platform from handling their personal information. More than 44,000 people have filed legal objections to their health data being shared with, stored in or used by the nationwide Federated Data Platform (FDP) operated using the US company’s AI technology. The coordinated campaign utilises rights enshrined in data protection laws and means the NHS must stop using the data unless it can provide a “compelling reason” to continue. Hundreds of thousands of people have signed petitions demanding the government cancels its £330m deal with Palantir, and Andy Burnham will be required to make a decision to back or axe Palantir within months. Campaigners have voiced anger at Palantir’s work for the Israeli military and Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown, and two House of Commons select committees have called for Labour to exercise a break clause in the seven-year deal which comes into force in February 2027. David Murray, a retired IBM systems engineer and one of those requesting the data block, said: “I am a believer in the NHS having really good data on their patients, but I want it to be something you can really trust to be used for the right purposes. I am not happy about Palantir’s involvement with the IDF in Gaza and ICE in America.” On Wednesday, the human rights group Amnesty International and patient campaign group, Just Treatment, parked a van styled like a shot-up Palestinian ambulance outside Palantir’s London HQ in a stunt that asked: “Why should a company linked to Israel’s destruction of Gaza’s healthcare system have any place in ours?” Protesters have also raised concerns, acknowledged by the NHS England chief executive, Jim Mackey, that the benefits to public health from the Palantir-powered platform may not be as significant as has been claimed. Palantir says the FDP, which is designed to connect sprawling health service data on topics ranging from surgery schedules to discharge planning, is helping to cut waiting lists and frees up beds. Louis Mosley, the company’s executive vice-president for UK and Europe, has accused people who disagree with that assessment of suffering from “Palantir derangement syndrome”. A spokesperson said: “Palantir software is helping to deliver better care, with trusts using it recording 117,000 additional operations, a 14.3% reduction in discharge delays for long-stay patients and a 5.6% improvement in the number of people finding out whether or not they have cancer within 28 days.” Mosley has said its technology was used for locating hostages, not military targeting, in Gaza, although when challenged last year by a protester alleging “Palantir kills Palestinians” in Gaza, the company’s chief executive, Alex Karp, replied: “Mostly terrorists, that’s true.” The formal objections to the FDP using personal data cite article 21 of the UK General Data Protection Regulation and express concern that “the involvement of Palantir undermines my personal trust in NHS data confidentiality”. Palantir said its patient data could only be handled according to the NHS’s instructions and remained in the UK. Veronica Hawking, the campaigns director at 38 Degrees, a not-for-profit that coordinated the data objections, said: “The scale of this public backlash should be a huge wake-up call for the government.” A spokesperson for NHS England said: “All NHS organisations remain in control of their data within the FDP, with suppliers unable to access it for their own purposes, and we will respond to the objection requests in line with data protection law.” The 44,000 objectors have also asked that the NHS halts processing of their data through the Palantir platform while their main request is assessed.

title: How Europe’s housing crisis is fuelling a new movement
summary: As soaring rents and house prices across Europe​ feed into the political discourse, campaigners believe they have a rare opportunity to force housing to the top of the agenda
text: It was billed as one of the largest real-estate events in Europe, attracting as many as 15,000 people ranging from investment firms to developers. But as the District trade show and summit got under way last week in Madrid, housing campaigners from 140 organisations across the globe turned up, intent on holding their own “counter-summit” to push back against the idea of housing as a financial asset. Many of the campaigners arrived in the Spanish capital as Maricarmen Abascal, an 87-year-old woman who uses a wheelchair, was being evicted from the apartment where she had lived for seven decades. As anger over the eviction gave way to days of protests and an encampment in the heart of Madrid, the presence of campaigners from Italy to Ireland was a poignant reminder of the global dimension of the crisis. The eviction underscored how brutal access to housing had become for so many around the world, said Teresa Mamede, a housing campaigner from Lisbon who travelled to Madrid for the counter-summit. “Nobody among us is safe from having this happen to them.” The Guardian has long reported on the depth of the housing crisis across Europe. Within the EU, prices soared by 53% between 2010 and 2024, according to Eurostat, while rents increased 25% over the same period. Not all countries have been hit equally; while Vienna remains a bright spot for its ample stock of public housing that has tempered rental costs, Estonia has seen rents surge 208% in the same time period, while Ireland and Hungary have seen increases of more than 100%. Some of the soaring costs can be chalked up to the “ever-intensifying social experiment” playing out in Europe, research fellow Tim White noted last year, as officials see whether the machinations of finance capitalism can deliver on the fundamental need for housing. “The evidence now seems overwhelming: no.” Instead, vulnerable people and minorities have been disproportionately affected by the market’s shortcomings, while others warn that the crisis could drive voters into the arms of the far right. “We cannot remain stuck in the rhetoric of defending democracy, inclusive societies and equal opportunities if people’s standard of living is getting worse,” Jaume Collboni, the mayor of Barcelona, told me last year. Voters in Berlin, however, recently opted for another path. In a city where rents had climbed nearly 70% in the past decade, a quarter of voters backed the leftwing party Die Linke in this month’s state elections, making it Berlin’s strongest party. The strategy behind their success was far from rocket science, said Guardian Europe columnist Fatma Aydemir. “Because, more than any other party in this campaign, Die Linke made this issue [of housing] unmistakably its own: the question of who gets to live in Berlin, and at what price.” *** ‘This is just getting started’ Some have sought shared solutions to the shared crisis. At the Madrid counter-summit, campaigners launched a pan-European alliance to demand indefinite rental contracts and rent control across the continent. Earlier this month, dozens of organisations launched the European Citizens’ Initiative, calling on people to sign their petition for EU-level measures to protect tenants, curb speculation and convert empty buildings into homes. “In every European country, in every major survey, and across all age groups, housing emerges as the number one concern of citizens,” the initiative notes. “We see and feel it every day: workers who can no longer afford the city they build, young people who cannot leave their parents’ home, tenants pushed out of their neighbourhoods after renovation, empty buildings while people sleep on the street.” In Spain, where the days-long encampment in Madrid has led to similar camps in cities such as Barcelona, Seville and Palma de Mallorca, the protests have already begun to have an impact. Maricarmen, the evicted octogenarian, will be allowed to return to her apartment, it was confirmed on Tuesday. Her rent will remain around the €500 a month she had paid for years – significantly less than the €2,650 the investment firm that owns her apartment had initially demanded. This week the Spanish government also said it had approved two housing decrees that include reforms such as a ban on evictions until 2030, and the regulation of temporary lettings and lettings by room. But these measures will now have to win approval in the country’s fractured parliament. What exactly comes next for the housing movement that has gripped Spain in recent days is anyone’s guess. With the spectre of general elections looming and the Socialist-led coalition scrambling to shore up its base of progressive voters, campaigners have spotted a singular opportunity to tackle an issue that Spaniards have long ranked as one of the country’s biggest problems. “The coming days will be crucial,” the Madrid Tenants’ Union said on Tuesday as it called for further protests this weekend. “A historic window of opportunity has opened to reverse decades of the commodification of housing. That is why we need to step up the pressure.” Or, as the Málaga Tenants’ Union put it in an online post: “This is just getting started.” To receive the complete version of This Is Europe in your inbox every Wednesday, please subscribe here.

title: Grooming gangs inquiry to investigate offending in Wales and Birmingham
summary: National inquiry will conduct local investigations and look at wider picture of sexual abuse and exploitation of children
text: Birmingham and Wales will be investigated as part of an independent inquiry into grooming gangs, it was announced on Wednesday. The inquiry, chaired by the former children’s commissioner Anne Longfield, will have the power to compel witnesses and obtain documents to interrogate what individuals and agencies “did or did not do to protect children from being sexually abused”. The problem has blighted Britain for decades, with thousands of girls being raped, beaten and drugged by groups of adult men. The offending has been linked to the deaths of several teenagers. The government faced a backlash last year – including from Elon Musk, the owner of X – when it initially refused to fund a statutory inquiry into abuse in Oldham, Greater Manchester. It eventually agreed to hold a national inquiry after a recommendation by the crossbench peer Louise Casey, who carried out an audit. The inquiry will conduct local investigations and look at the national picture and the response of agencies such as the police, NHS and local and central government. The Welsh strand will focus on offending across the country, rather than one town or city. There has been cross-party backing in the Senedd for such an investigation. A number of police operations have targeted grooming gangs in Wales. Last week, four men were jailed for abusing teenage girls in Rhyl, Denbighshire, between 2022 and 2024, in relation to exploitation centred on a coffee house. Amy Clowrey, a director at Switalskis solicitors, which represents a number of Welsh survivors, said: “It’s not just an English problem. The survivors I represent, and have represented, have always felt [Wales] has been overlooked in the national conversation.” The inquiry said its Welsh investigation “will provide an important opportunity to examine safeguarding and multi-agency responses, the operation of devolved arrangements, and cross-border working between organisations in Wales and England”. Longfield said: “Victims and survivors in Wales have waited too long for answers. This work is about establishing the truth, delivering accountability, and setting out clearly what must change so children are better protected in the future.” Grooming gangs have also been known to operate extensively in Birmingham. In 2010, police documents uncovered by the Birmingham Mail revealed that offenders were targeting children at schools and children’s homes. A large proportion were from the city’s Pakistani-heritage community. Four years later, Birmingham city council went to court to secure landmark injunctions against a number of men in an attempt to stop them approaching underage girls. Victims from other parts of the West Midlands have been trafficked into Birmingham to be abused. A previous inquiry into child sexual exploitation in Telford, Shropshire, was told that concerns were raised about this problem as far back as the 1990s. The inquiry said the investigation “will focus initially on Birmingham but may extend to surrounding, connected or satellite areas where the evidence supports it”. In June, the inquiry announced its first dedicated investigations, focusing on Oldham, London, Bradford and Keighley. It will also examine whether agencies in areas that have previously held inquiries into grooming gangs – such as Telford, Rochdale, Oxford and Rotherham – have adequately addressed the recommendations made. A central theme across the investigations will be the role played by “ethnicity, religion and culture” in gang-based exploitation. Lady Casey found that men from “Asian ethnic backgrounds” were overrepresented in recent police investigations into grooming gangs in parts of the north of England. However, she said it had been difficult to paint an accurate national picture due to a lack of data. She said: “More effort is required to identify the nature of group-based child sexual exploitation and why it appears men of Asian and Pakistani ethnicity are disproportionately represented in some areas, in order to understand it better and to tackle it more effectively.” Many survivors of group-based sexual exploitation have said they were targeted by “street grooming” gangs, particularly those operating from takeaways and taxi companies. Others say they were introduced to offenders by their peers or family members. Frontline workers say that as social media platforms have developed, children are increasingly being targeted by networks of perpetrators online. The national inquiry will look at the evolving nature of exploitation by grooming gangs and the potential role played by technology. It will run parallel to Operation Beaconport, an investigation being carried out by the National Crime Agency. It will also operate a “national listening project” so victims and their families can outline the impact of the abuse. In the UK, the NSPCC offers support to children on 0800 1111, and adults concerned about a child on 0808 800 5000. The National Association for People Abused in Childhood (Napac) offers support for adult survivors on 0808 801 0331. In the US, call or text the Childhelp abuse hotline on 800-422-4453. In Australia, children, young adults, parents and teachers can contact the Kids Helpline on 1800 55 1800, or Bravehearts on 1800 272 831, and adult survivors can contact Blue Knot Foundation on 1300 657 380. Other sources of help can be found at Child Helplines International

title: South African leader urges men to speak up on gender-based violence after series of killings
summary: President announces measures amid anger at authorities over recent murders of women
text: South Africa’s president has called on men to take more responsibility for violence against women as he announced measures to tackle the problem, amid anger at authorities over a recent wave of murders. Cyril Ramaphosa acknowledged that not enough had been done to protect women. He said police would be reviewing unsolved murders, attempted murders and serious sexual offences against women and children, as well as producing a funded plan to reduce the forensic backlog for such cases, both within 60 days. In a televised speech on Tuesday night, the president said local governments would have five months to address issues that compromised women’s safety, from broken streetlights to overgrown public spaces and abandoned buildings. He added that he had tasked five ministers to come up with a plan within 60 days to reduce alcohol-fuelled violence. “Alcohol does not cause gender-based violence and it can never excuse it. Responsibility always lies with the perpetrator,” Ramaphosa said. “But harmful alcohol use is a significant aggravating factor in interpersonal violence and it must be addressed as part of our wider prevention effort. “Women should not have to live in fear because government has failed to repair a light, clear a public space, process evidence or enforce a law.” South Africa has been gripped by grief and fury after the discovery of 11 women’s bodies dumped across Ekurhuleni, the municipality adjoining Johannesburg to the east, since 15 July. Eight of the women were found in the last three weeks, including Elizabeth “Tsontso” Moselakgomo, who was discovered on 12 September after she went missing when she went for a run after work. Ramaphosa said suspects had been arrested in connection with three of the killings and that the other cases would not be left to go cold. He added that police had not found evidence that a serial killer was responsible for all 11 killings, but that all possibilities were still being investigated. He directly addressed South African men, urging them to challenge relatives, friends and colleagues who harassed, humiliated or abused women. “It is time for good men to stop being silent men,” he said. “For too long, gender-based violence has been treated as a woman’s problem to solve. Women march, the women of our country organise, they speak out, they protest, they confront and they comfort survivors,” Ramaphosa said. “Women change their routes home. Avoid going out at night and warn one another about dangerous places and dangerous men. We have placed the burden of male violence on women. That must change.” Activists expressed their frustration that solid policy actions had not been taken years ago and scepticism that the measures Ramaphosa had announced would work. Shenilla Mohamed, the executive director of Amnesty International South Africa, said: “These are not new issues and as a country we have been talking about ways to tackle the high numbers of [gender-based violence and femicide], especially since 2019 when women took to the streets to protest, and yet here we are again in the face of continued attacks against women. “Amnesty International South Africa also notes the timelines put in place by the president, but this will only mean something if it results in action, and if there are consequences for inaction.” Mpiwa Mangwiro-Tsanga and Bafana Khumalo, of Sonke Gender Justice, an NGO, said: “Our concern … is that the response remains heavily weighted towards what happens after violence has already occurred.” They added: “Investigating unresolved cases, processing forensic evidence and repairing unsafe public spaces are necessary, but they do not constitute a comprehensive prevention strategy. It is concerning that the president is asking municipalities to do what is actually their mandate and yet they do not deliver on these.”

title: UK income growth revised upwards as markets hail ‘resilient’ economy
summary: Boost for John Healey before budget as GDP figure shows UK economy grew faster than first estimated in second quarter
text: UK household income grew at a stronger pace than previously estimated during the first six months of the year, according to revisions of official data. The rise in income per head to 1.1% between January and June followed an increase in the level of economic growth that illustrated the resilience of the UK economy since the outbreak of hostilities in the Middle East more than seven months ago. The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said gross domestic product (GDP) increased by 0.5% rather than the previously estimated 0.4% in the April to June quarter, showing that the UK economy grew at the same pace as the US in the first six months of the year. The economy grew 0.6% in the first quarter. Analysts said a “Burnham bounce” in confidence could have been a factor, as the Makerfield byelection announced in May paved the way for the former mayor of Manchester to become prime minister. The ONS said households were also able to put some of the rise in incomes into savings accounts. The savings rate increased from 8.6% in the first three months to 8.8% in the three months to the end of June. Thomas Watts, a fund manager at the private bank Julius Baer, said the figures were “yet more positive news for the new administration” after previous data had shown the resilience of the UK economy since the start of the US-Israel war on Iran in February. The upgrade is a boost for the chancellor, John Healey, as he prepares to give his first budget next month. The sharp increase in GDP per head in the first half of the year put the UK near the top of the G7 leader board, ahead of Germany, France and the US and just behind Canada, which topped the poll with a growth rate of 1.3% in the first and second quarters. Businesses also kept spending, especially on investment. The ONS said business investment increased by 1.8% in the second quarter and was estimated to be 5.2% higher compared with the same quarter a year ago. Kathleen Brooks, the research director at XTB, said the markets were in an “upbeat mood” after the revisions, which “suggest that the UK economy was resilient to the effects of the Iran war, the energy price surge and the rise in borrowing costs”. She said: “Stronger services growth and rising household spending boosted the figure. This is fairly typical of the UK economy, which is service based; the real surprise was the strength of business investment and an improvement in the trade figures, which showed a boost in exports.” Currency markets reacted positively to the figures. Traders speculated that the UK’s strong growth rate may persuade the Bank of England that the economy is “running hot” and needs higher interest rates to calm it down, especially when inflation at 3.1% is above the central bank’s 2% target. Sterling hit a six-week high against the euro and edged higher against the US dollar, up 0.4% to a one-week high of $1.3292. Against the euro, sterling was at its highest since mid-August, with the euro down nearly 0.3% at 85.43p. UK government bond yields, which provide a measure of the interest rate paid on UK debt, eased on the stronger economic data and lower global oil prices. Two-year UK bond yields were down 0.05 of a percentage point at 4.86%, while 10-year UK bond yields were four basis points lower at 5.356% on Wednesday. Oil and gas prices have surged since the conflict first started. After a ceasefire in the summer, traders have lost confidence in efforts to secure a peace deal and sent Brent crude prices back above $100 a barrel, though they have eased in recent days.

title: Do parents make the politician? Find out on the Today programme’s psychotherapy couch | John Crace
summary: Dad’s the word for Andy Burnham, so maybe all party leaders should be seen afresh through a Freudian lens
text: Is this the sketch my father would have wanted? Not something I have previously given much thought to. He died 15 years before I even started this job. But my guess is that it is. He was the loveliest of men who only ever wanted for me what I wanted for me. He was stupidly proud of even my most forgettable successes. I still see him in my dreams, cheering me on. He’d almost certainly be embarrassed, but secretly pleased, to find himself in the first paragraph. But that’s enough about my father issues. Time now to talk about Andy Burnham’s. In his emotional and gamechanging leader’s speech on Tuesday – I can’t tell you how refreshing it is to have a politician other than Nigel Farage say exactly what he thinks and believes – Andy told us he wanted to build the country his father would have wanted. It was almost a debt of honour. Burnham was very precise. This was not his vision. This wasn’t the country he wanted to build. It was the one his dad had wanted. Andy was merely a conduit, channelling Roy, who died earlier this month. So come Wednesday morning, on the traditional post-speech media round, the BBC’s Nick Robinson had clearly designated himself a latter-day Sigmund Freud for Burnham’s Today programme interview. You get the picture: Andy on the couch, Nick sitting just behind his right shoulder, firmly out of view. Never let the therapist get in the way of the subconscious. Only Robinson can’t take the silences. Some analysts pride themselves on a 50-minute session where nothing is said. That’s when the real psychotherapeutic work gets done. Apparently. A nice earner if you can get it. There was no time to bother with the niceties. Nick specialises more in speed therapy. Done and dusted inside 20 minutes. From nought to catharsis. There was no “How are you feeling? Is there anything you need to talk about today?” Instead, he cut straight to the chase. And why not? Everyone knows that all patients are merely mainlining their parents. Everything can be traced back to childhood. Andy clearly doesn’t hold with the Philip Larkin “They fuck you up” doctrine. He only got good stuff from his dad. Or maybe the good stuff is all that he cares to remember. Siggy Robbo missed a trick there. Surely your father would be telling you not to be so nostalgic, he said, but Burnham was adamant. Roy would have stuck to his roots of quiet patriotism. Nick tried another tack. The funeral was taking place on Friday. Was he on an emotional rollercoaster? Andy conceded that he could be. But rollercoasters were his happy place. This could be habit-forming. Maybe it’s an approach we should take with all our party leaders. Rather than seeing them as players on a global stage with the capacity to make our lives infinitely worse, we should be more understanding. Treat them as patients in need of treatment. After all, you’ve surely got to be a dangerously unbalanced narcissist to even imagine you can run a country. Desire for office should act as a disqualification on health grounds. Some politicians would probably get an automatic upgrade from narcissist to sociopath. Donald Trump and Boris Johnson come immediately to mind. Think also of Keir Starmer, Nigel Farage and Kemi Badenoch. Keir clearly had a tricky relationship with his dad. One where there was a lot that went unsaid. So maybe we shouldn’t blame him for never being able to articulate what he felt. Then there’s Nige. Has he inherited a hatred for all immigrants, or is he reacting against his parents? Maybe they took in refugees and forced the seven-year-old Nige to play with them against his will. And where did he get his pathological need for money, no matter how questionable the source? Did his parents squander his inheritance on gifts to charity? As for Kemi, where to start? I’ve never seen a politician so full of loathing. Could that be down to a Larkin-like childhood? With the therapy over, Siggy briefly turned to the substance of the speech. All the big-ticket policies were for after the next election. What was going to happen in the next three years? Andy shrugged. He was a straight-talking guy. There wasn’t much he could do. Energy bills were going up faster than he could offer rebates. He couldn’t stop the wars around the world. The cost of debt was out of his hands. The Tories could say they would cut welfare, but nothing much would change. We needed to be patient. Things would get better. Just so long as Labour won in 2029. Social care, the triple lock, Brexit and electoral reform. These were the real engines that would transform the country and reconnect voters with politics. Instruments of trust. How that would happen would be for others to decide. Single market, customs union, rejoin. All were on the table. Let’s just hope the far right haven’t taken over the EU by the time it happens. A national care service. Not ideal – some people would still lose their homes – but better than what was currently on offer. Just don’t forget: Andy was merely a channel of peace. In a rare turnabout, Nick thanked Burnham for the therapy session. The bank transfer would follow. Over in the main hall, the conference proper was dying on its arse. You could hear the exhibition stands being dismantled as Yvette Cooper, Lucy Powell and others made the last few speeches to polite applause. We ended as all Labour conferences ended – with renditions of The Red Flag and Jerusalem – and then it was a dash for the exits. Not that there was a scrum. Most people had already left. But it was always going to be this way when the main event had taken place the previous afternoon. This had been the Andy Burnham show. And delegates couldn’t have been happier. The Labour party had rediscovered its soul. Its belief. A leader who could go toe-to-toe with the other parties. Maybe this was also the sketch that Andy Burnham’s father would have wanted.

title: Two million people in England unaware their properties are at risk of flooding
summary: Environment Agency warns residents of 6m at-risk properties to prepare for wet and windy three months ahead
text: More than two million people in England are unaware their properties are at risk of flooding, as the UK braces for a wet and stormy start to the winter, according to the Environment Agency. Experts say the next three months are more likely than usual to be wet and windy – due to a combination of large-scale weather patterns and the “subtle” impact of a supercharged El Niño – increasing the risk of flooding. However, the EA warned on Wednesday that people in a third of the six million properties most at risk of flooding are unaware of the threat they face. Caroline Douglass, the director for flood and coastal risk management at the Environment Agency, said: “We know with the 6m properties at risk [in England] … we know that one-third of people who are at risk don’t think they are at risk.” She urged people to check on the government website whether their properties were at risk, and to take measures to prepare. “We want the public to make sure they know what their risk is, so check on gov.uk. We need them to sign up for flood warnings … and if they are at risk, to have a flood plan so they know what they need to do.” Flooding caused havoc across the UK last year and the Met Office said that, after a summer of droughts, extreme heat and wildfires, the UK was facing a wet and stormy start to winter. Will Lang, the chief meteorologist with the Met Office, said its three-month outlook indicated there was an increased likelihood that October, November and December would be wet and windy, adding there were early indications of drier, colder and calmer conditions later in the winter. “There is an increasing likelihood of it being wet overall, windier than normal and milder than usual as well,” said Lang. He said El Niño – which is bringing devastation to other parts of the world – increased the likelihood of wetter and windier conditions in the UK but was only one of several factors influencing the UK’s weather. “This is just a subtle shift in the odds of it being wetter and windier,” he said. But he added that would lead to “a heightened potential for flooding”. The Met Office said that although flooding was likely in the months ahead, drought conditions would remain in large parts of the UK until reservoirs returned to their normal water levels, adding that would require above-average rainfall over the winter.

title: Backpack edges past Dancing Queen to win Alaska’s Fat Bear Week title
summary: Bear known for sitting in solitude won tournament celebrating the animals’ ability to eat large amounts of fish
text: A chunky ursine called Backpack has out-gobbled a challenge from an outsized female nicknamed the Dancing Queen to waltz – or rather waddle – off with the Fat Bear Week title at Alaska’s Katmai national park. Backpack, a 20-year-old quiet giant known for sitting in solitude for long periods on his rock on the Brooks River, won by barely 5,000 votes in the public tournament celebrating the brown bears’ ability to eat as many fish as possible, Alaska rangers announced. More than 2.3m online votes were cast this year overall, and more than 200,000 votes in the final round alone. The contest has become a popular annual tradition bringing attention to the park’s population of almost 2,000 bears as they gorge on wild salmon to fatten up ahead of their winter hibernation. Backpack’s triumph comes seven years after his mother, Holly, more familiar to fans as the Queen of Corpulence, landed the crown in a landslide in the fifth year of the competition. Holly was on course to win again in 2022 until it was discovered that virtual ballot boxes, rather like the bears themselves, had been (dishonestly) stuffed. Despite that vote-rigging scandal, public participation has grown every year in the tournament that pits 16 of the park’s heftiest bruins against each other in a head-to-head knockout bracket. After Backpack’s win was confirmed on Tuesday, the US Department of the Interior posted on X its congratulations to the newly anointed “lord of lard, earl of girth”. According to Sarah Bruce, a Katmai park ranger, Backpack, whose formal name is Bear 89 and weighs an estimated 1,200lb (544kg), benefited from a large loyal fanbase to emerge as the champion. “He’s one of the bears that we’ve been able to watch on the live cams since the live cams were put in in 2012,” Bruce told Alaska Public Media. “He’s a familiar bear. People have watched him his whole life.” She said Backpack was commonly found fishing for salmon and contemplating life on his favorite rock in the river. He had also overcome challenges, she said, including a serious leg injury in 2007. The runner-up, Bear 910, has no formal name like Backpack, but is known to fans as Dancing Queen because of the way she moves her head while fishing. Her mother is also a previous winner. Bruce said the ultimate proof of success was the amount of weight the competitors had been able to pack on over the summer months, as shown in their before and after photographs. “They have already won in the fact that they are set to survive another winter hibernation,” she said. “They win all of the love.”

title: MI5 warns UK universities over ‘theft of tech secrets by Chinese front company’
summary: Security service says academics should stop working with and taking grants from firm backed by Chinese intelligence
text: MI5 has issued a rare public warning to UK universities that China’s intelligence service is using a front company to pay for research by UK academics and steal the secrets of hi-tech projects. Britain’s domestic security service said researchers and academics should cease work with the China General Technology Research Institute (CGTRI), sometimes also known as the China Academy of General Technology (CAGT). MI5 believes the body poses a “significant threat” and is now prepared to say publicly that the CGTRI is a front for Chinese intelligence, namely the Chinese ministry of state security (MSS). It said continued collaboration by UK academics could be prosecuted under the National Security Act 2023. The Chinese organisation has funded 100 or more academics at a string of universities across the UK, in return for access to the research, which it is alleged found its way back to China’s intelligence service. On Wednesday, the Chinese embassy in London issued a strongly worded rebuttal, describing the accusations as “imaginary and purely fabricated”. A spokesperson said: “We firmly oppose such baseless allegations and have lodged solemn representations with the UK side. “Exchanges and collaboration between UK universities and China have always been conducted on a voluntary basis and in compliance with laws and regulations. Such exchanges and collaboration are mutually beneficial.” The MI5 warning sent a shock wave through the UK university sector, with staff reviewing the implications for existing or future partnerships with China, and experts raising concerns about the rigour of the vetting process in sensitive research collaborations. Areas of research targeted include AI, cybersecurity, covert communications and steganography – the embedding of secret data in seemingly innocuous files. MI5 believes it has clear evidence of sensitive information being passed back to Chinese intelligence, and the Guardian understands that some British-based academics were given honours and awards by the Chinese as well as research money. Successive British governments have courted Chinese investment and encouraged academic cooperation. Sam Dunning, the director of the UK-China Transparency group, said: “It is reasonably obvious from the internet that CGTRI was focused on areas of high interest to the military and intelligence services. “Granted, CGTRI used various aliases and have certainly obscured some funding streams, but as for the UK universities or academics who knew they were dealing with CGTRI, open-source research made clear that CGTRI had military or intelligence links.” Vice-chancellors who spoke to the Guardian said they were not aware of receiving any funding from the Chinese institute, but warned that individual academics working on joint projects with other universities or third parties may not know the original sources of funding. Prof Peter Mathieson, vice-chancellor of the University of Edinburgh and the lead for international security for Universities UK, which represents 142 institutions across the UK, said MI5’s warning meant that future collaborations with the CGTRI would be illegal. “They are saying that anyone who has a link to this institute up until now has not committed any kind of offence, because it’s not previously been said this was a high-risk activity. “Now that they have said it, we have to sit up and take notice. It’s very much a forward-looking directive. He added: “I can’t speak for MI5, but I think what they are attempting to say is that people may not realise that the institute they are working with is connected to the security services of the Beijing government. And there’s no reason why anyone should have realised that, because it’s a new piece of information that MI5 has discovered.” In the alert issued on Wednesday, the Security Service said: “MI5 has identified that the primary purpose of CGTRI is to fund academic research that directly improves MSS technical capability for espionage.” It said that CGTRI had “very strong ties to the … MSS, China’s civilian intelligence and security service”. The alert continued: “Many academic institutions and individuals will to date have engaged with CGTRI in good faith given CGTRI’s obfuscated links to MSS. “UK academic institutions are strongly advised to immediately review any ongoing or planned collaboration with CGTRI. This is to ensure MSS derives no further benefit from UK universities or research institutions. Further, academics are advised to establish the ultimate funding source when conducting any research collaboration with Chinese institutions, to ensure CGTRI is not involved.” That MI5 has decided on a public alert as a deterrence strategy, rather than trying to pursue every single case, demonstrates the scale of Chinese state espionage targeting the UK. It hopes universities will heed the warning and immediately cease their work with CGTRI. The Guardian understands that cutting-edge British research on scraping social media (gathering large amounts of information from social sites and apps) is among the data to which MI5 believes Chinese intelligence gained access. The security minister, Dan Jarvis, demanded universities end ties to the CGTRI. He said: “This alert exposes attempts by Chinese intelligence to covertly benefit from the expertise and research of our academics, undermining our national security and that of our allies. “I have written to all university vice-chancellors to ensure they support their staff to end all arrangements with this company, preventing further benefit to the Chinese intelligence services and ensuring compliance with the National Security Act.” Responding to the MI5 alert, Vivienne Stern, the chief executive of Universities UK, said universities took their responsibilities around research security and national security extremely seriously. “The sector has made significant investments in recent years to strengthen due diligence, risk assessment and research security processes, while continuing to support the international collaboration that is essential to world-leading research and innovation,” she said. Chinese government filings suggest that CAGT is connected to the China General Technology Group, a major state-owned conglomerate administered directly by the government of China that is also known as Genertec. The Genertec brand has a UK presence, with a company called Genertec (UK) Ltd, appearing to be owned by the Chinese state. The British company, which has been registered in the UK for a decade and is based in a shared office address on Southwark Bridge Road, had £5.6m in the bank according to accounts to the end of 2024 – cash that seems to have come exclusively from a single property transaction. Additional reporting by Helena Horton

title: UK-France ‘one in, one out’ deal to expire on Thursday, say sources
summary: Deal aimed at deterring small boat arrivals set to end as talks stall over French demand for EU-wide scheme
text: The UK government’s “one in, one out” deal with France, which was supposed to help deter small boat arrivals, is expected to expire on Thursday, government sources have said. Negotiations to extend the deal have stalled over French demands for a Europe-wide deal instead, and a reluctance to scale up the numbers of people exchanged between the two countries. Flights that remove people who have been already detained under the scheme will continue, but they are expected to end within weeks. A UK government source confirmed that the expectation was that the deal would be formally drawn to a close on Thursday. “We would like to see the deal continue. But it’s not the end of the world if it doesn’t because it never got to the scale where it would have been a proper deterrent to people coming to the UK in small boats,” the source said. The French interior ministry told French media on Wednesday: “We are discussing with the British the terms of exiting the agreement.” Negotiations in Paris over how best to tie up the deal are continuing between Home Office staff and their French counterparts. More than 1,400 people who have arrived in the UK via small boats have been sent back to France under the deal. As of the end of June 2026, 1,117 people with links to the UK had been sent to the UK from France. The deal had been set to expire in April but was extended to 1 October to help counter the anticipated increase in attempted crossings during the summer. The scheme was announced by Keir Starmer and the French president, Emmanuel Macron, in July 2025 and the first flights took off in September that year. At the time, Starmer described the deal as “groundbreaking” because it would help to deter the number of people crossing the Channel illegally. “There is no silver bullet here, but with a united effort, new tactics and a new level of intent, we can finally turn the tables,” he said. Many of the detainees deported to France under the deal have become homeless in the French capital. Others have returned to the camps around Calais and Dunkirk, and some have made the Channel crossing back to the UK. In June, France’s interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, lauded the scheme as a potential deterrent but said France was not prepared to go it alone with Britain. “According to information from the UN high commissioner for refugees, word of the scheme is beginning to spread, which is prompting a number of migrants to abandon their plans to make the crossing,” Nuñez told a parliamentary commission. “The value of this scheme is therefore clear. Nevertheless, we consider that France should not bear the burden alone and that it would be better to incorporate it into an agreement between the EU and the UK. “I have therefore already made it clear to my counterpart that this pilot agreement, which we signed in August 2025, was not intended to be extended beyond 1 October 2026.” An EU-wide returns deal known as the Dublin agreement existed before the UK left the EU. Attempts to continue the returns deal post-Brexit have been rejected by EU leaders. Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, disclosed to MPs this month that the deal cost about £56,000 for every person sent back to France. She dismissed suggestions that an EU-wide system would be a “silver bullet” for the Channel crisis. She said: “It is a real mistake to think that that pact is the future. And if we were in that, this problem would go away, because I promise you it would not.” She added that the government’s scheme had struggled to scale up to larger numbers of returns and it had been “operationally difficult” to increase removals because of constraints such as detention space. “It’s not been without its challenges. Obviously, the numbers are still relatively small,” she said. Between January and 27 September, 19,135 people crossed the Channel by small boat from France. This was down by 42% on the same period the previous year.
