title: Ranulph Fiennes’s stepson says he is in contact with police about explorer’s wellbeing
summary: Exclusive: Alexander Millington-Cotes says call from police has given him hope concerns are being taken seriously
text: The stepson of Sir Ranulph Fiennes has been contacted by police and says he intends to speak to them this week over his concerns about the explorer’’s wellbeing. Alexander Millington-Cotes – who is estranged from his mother, Louise, Fiennes’s second and current wife – said an officer from Cheshire police had called him in recent days. The call, he said, had given him hope that the concerns of Fiennes’s friends and family were being taken seriously, adding that the officer appeared interested in what he had observed. “That’s the one bit of hope,” Millington-Cotes told the Guardian. Questions have been raised in recent months about the welfare of Fiennes, who has Parkinson’s and is in the care of his wife, who has power of attorney. Among those who have raised issues is his relative Joseph Fiennes, the actor, who wrote in January to the Office of the Public Guardian, setting out concerns about Ranulph being cut off from friends and family. He has not been seen in public for two years. Millington-Cotes, 31, said he had been disappointed by the response of the authorities so far. Cheshire police issued a statement on Monday in which they said they did not have “safeguarding concerns” regarding the 82-year-old. It said officers were “satisfied that Sir Ranulph Fiennes is living in an appropriate setting with suitable care and professional oversight”. Millington-Cotes said a wide group of friends were concerned the police did not have the full picture. It is claimed that the explorer has spent more than a year living under assumed names in a succession of care homes and that even attempts by the king to check on him had been rebuffed by Fiennes’s wife. Millington-Cotes said: “I might have possibly one more avenue with the police. I just got a call the other day from a detective who wanted to speak to me, which was interesting and encouraging. They kind of wanted to get my perspective on things and the sort of things that I’ve observed and things like that, and what I believe to be the truth.” Cheshire police said: “Yes, we’re in touch with him. Our original statement still stands.” Millington-Cotes, an aerospace engineer, described the initial police statement as “slapdash” and “really disappointing”. He is crowdfunding a legal application in an attempt to wrest power of attorney over Fiennes away from his mother. Among the last people to see Fiennes was Arabella Pepper, the younger sister of Ranulph’s late first wife, Ginny, who claimed visitors were asked to sign non-disclosure agreements. She claimed Fiennes appeared “incredibly relieved” to see her and that he had spoken of “longing” to see friends. Michael Kobold, a friend who has been among those questioning Fiennes’s treatment, said he was concerned the explorer’s isolation had since become “even more draconian”, including during his time in a care home in Wales, where staff were given strict instructions on his day to day activities. When the arrangements at that home were raised as an issue of concern by the owner with the regulator, the Care Inspectorate Wales confirmed in an email that the correct protocols were not in place. They wrote: “Currently [Sir Ranulph] is being deprived of his liberty unlawfully as there is no authorised deprivation in place which reflects the current residence and restrictions in place.” Kobold said: “This was reported to me by the owner of the care home in Wales, from where Louise moved Ran after the owner raised concerns with the relevant authorities.” Fiennes’s current whereabouts is not known. Louise Millington-Cotes was contacted for comment.

title: ‘Oozing everyman charm’: what the papers say about Andy Burnham’s speech
summary: PM’s oratory at least as good as Blair’s, says Andrew Marr, while Mail asks who pays for Honest Andy’s ‘New Jerusalem’
text: When assessing British political speeches, even many critics of the New Labour years measure success against Tony Blair, a leader whose podium appearances are regarded as the peak of oratory. On that measure, Andrew Marr, the former BBC political editor and now the New Statesman’s chief political commentator, reached for the ultimate accolade. “Rather to my surprise, I have to report Andy Burnham is at least as good a platform speaker” as Blair, he said. “Perhaps better.” Piers Morgan, the former News of the World editor, concluded that Burnham’s speech to the Labour party conference on Tuesday was “one of the best, and most powerfully delivered, by a British politician in a very long time”. Burnham’s onstage performance was also praised by Tim Shipman, the right-of-centre Spectator magazine’s political editor. He concluded it was sub-Blair but “as good as anything we’ve seen since”. Shipman wrote: “I’ve been attending party conferences since 2001 and in that time I’ve heard about 70 leaders’ speeches from all the parties. This was one of the most important and defining – I expect it will remain among the half-dozen most memorable.” Patrick Maguire, the Times’s chronicler of Labour’s inner workings, agreed. “The Labour party will talk about this speech for years and it will be remembered, as so few speeches are, as a formative, watershed moment in the history of this young century, for better or worse,” he said. The praise was not universal, however. Quentin Letts, the Mail’s sketch writer, said the speech was so saccharine in its plea for unity that “I got diabetic twinges”. While there was both fulsome and grudging praise for Burnham’s delivery – the Daily Mail’s highly critical editorial on the speech said the “PM’s performance was slick, oozing everyman charm” – its radical nature placed it squarely in the crosshairs of the right-leaning media. A new Brexit deal, the prospect of a proportional voting system and his social care and housing plans were all targeted. The Mail’s front page described the “triple shock” of Burnham’s pension changes, care plans and Brexit rethink. It regarded the speech as the “most leftwing speech by a PM since [the] 1970s”. The Telegraph said it was a “road back to a failed past”. The Sun, which has a difficult relationship with Burnham amid claims that he will not give any interviews or opinion pieces to the once dominant red top, did not hold back. It labelled the speech the “locky horror show”, a reference to Burnham’s pledge to end the pensions triple lock that guarantees big increases in the state pension. “The British vote system ‘rigged’,” it said. “Government to seize private homes,” it claimed, a reference to Burnham’s plan to remove homes from bad landlords. Trevor Kavanagh, the Sun’s veteran political commentator, was damning. He described the address as “the most divisive speech I’ve heard from any prime minister”. He even described the prime minister’s emotional reference to his late father as “a blatant pitch for sympathy from voters who might otherwise have been shocked by what we can all now see as Burnham’s truly socialist revolution”. The Sun’s editorial column lamented Burnham’s lack of action on cutting the “ballooning welfare bill”. Attacks on Burnham’s lack of attention to the welfare bill –a theme for both the Conservatives and Reform UK – was reflected across the rightwing media. “Who pays for PM’s New Jerusalem,” asked the Mail’s editorial column, suggesting the speech would have pleased Labour supporters in the hall but concerned the general voter. It also took the chance to put the boot into Burnham’s predecessor, Keir Starmer. “There’s no question he is an oratorical improvement on his incorrigibly wooden predecessor, a strong candidate for worst public speaker in political history,” it jibed. “[Burnham] knew his audience, enthralling them with his northern working-class boy made good life story. The truth is that Middle England is about to be deluged with new tax rises, but ‘Honest Andy’ is too craven to admit it.” The Daily Express’s front-page headline decried the speech as a “crying shame for our nation”. Despite praising the delivery, the Spectator’s Shipman cited “room for improvement” in the speech’s content, citing potential flaws in his plan for a national care service and the limited early savings from ditching the pensions triple lock. He argued Burnham had “no plan for growth” – the issue that has plagued prime ministers of both main parties. Shipman concluded that the speech amounted to “the most partisan leftwing set of priorities we have seen since the days of Harold Wilson”. What united coverage was a conclusion that unlike Starmer, Burnham had produced a clear statement of intent about who he was and what he wanted to achieve – for better or worse. The Times’s Maguire concluded: “There will be a hell of a row before we know whether it’s an epoch-defining Thatcherism of the left or Truss with charisma. But for the first time in recent history, the leader of the Labour party wants that argument and is making his own.” The Times’s editorial column, however, reflected the political right’s early verdict on Burnham’s address – an appeal based in Labour’s comfort zone. “Mr Burnham’s speech was in some ways a curious throwback,” it stated. “Labour is becoming more middle class by the year, in composition and support, yet he imagines it as a vehicle dedicated to the working class of his memory. What exactly are wealth creators supposed to make of this charming man?”

title: Wildlife arrives on time at rewilded chalk grasslands built along HS2 route
summary: The trains may be running late, but the Western Slopes project is already attracting birds and insects on lands around the high-speed railway
text: The air is scented with the sweet tang of ladies bedstraw and made musical by skylark and blackcap song. An abundance of marbled white butterflies, small skippers and common blue damselflies dart over the flowering knapweed, yarrow and wild carrot. That the largest chalk grassland in the Chilterns is full of wildlife may not surprise you. But the fact that it is completely artificial, only four years old and has been built by the much-maligned HS2, may do. The Western Slopes “rewilding” project is due to open to the public next year on land beside the high-speed railway as it dives under the M25 and into a 10-mile tunnel beneath the Chilterns. The trains may be running late, but the wildlife has already arrived. A decade ago, this area was a vast wheatfield with precious little biodiversity. Today, as the construction effort winds down, more and more of the 127-hectare site is being turned into wildlife-rich grasslands, wet meadows, ponds and small woods. It is now one of the largest wildlife habitat creation projects in south-east England, and has already witnessed the arrival of hedgehog clover, which hasn’t been recorded in Hertfordshire since 1878, alongside water voles, lesser emperor dragonflies and pyramidal orchids. The transformation began when Matt Hobbs, lead ecologist at Jacobs, was invited to take a look at the huge planned HS2 works around the south entrance to the Chilterns tunnel. “I asked the engineer: ‘What’s coming out of the tunnel?’ When he said ‘chalk’, it was like a lightbulb moment. I thought, I know what I’d like to do with that chalk,” said Hobbs, who has designed and overseen the Western Slopes project for HS2. Chalk grassland is one of the most wildlife-rich habitats in southern England because a wide range of wildflowers flourish on its thin, nutrient-poor alkaline soils, alongside an array of associated invertebrates, including rare moths and bees. According to Hobbs, the valley slopes could have been expensively restored to arable land by HS2, as much of the land temporarily taken for the huge construction effort will be. “We saw the opportunity to do something different,” he said. “This project is unique. The whole landscape was predicated on what’s the best thing to do with the earthworks and soils. We’re not moving any soils or material off site. Any concrete waste from this site is crushed and used as aggregate under the grasslands.” Reusing 10m cubic metres of chalk, topsoil and subsoils from the construction effort in the immediate vicinity of the tunnel mouth has also drastically reduced CO2 emissions, and the construction traffic that dumping it elsewhere would have entailed. According to HS2’s calculations, the wildlife grasslands here could sequester 7% of the carbon impact of the whole high-speed line’s construction, because grassland is much better at storing carbon than regularly-ploughed arable land, which releases carbon every time it is ploughed. Over the past four years, all the chalk excavated from the tunnel has been sculpted into rolling “downs” on the land above the Colne Valley, creating varying topsoils and a future mosaic of grassland, scrub, woodland and ponds and wet areas. It took the ecologists a bit of effort to retrain the digger drivers who were spreading the chalk over the site. Groundworks teams are trained to leave everything beautifully smooth and neat, whereas the ecologists were seeking topographical variation, with dips, hollows and “untidy” rough areas. The future vision is a “wood pasture” landscape, inspired by rewilding sites such as Knepp in West Sussex, where a mixture of scrub and wildflower glades are grazed by herbivores. Four cattle-grids have been installed on roads – believed to be the first in Hertfordshire – to enable free-roaming cattle to graze within four separate compartments. “They were really key to the project. We wanted to have that Knepp rewilding technique where you have cattle that can move anywhere they want within the site – it’s brilliant for soil health, soil carbon and dung beetles,” said Hobbs. Luke Craner, a senior landscape clerk of works for the HS2 contractor Align, said: “I’m really keen to get livestock grazing sooner rather than later so we can kickstart biological processes. We’ve already got a really good grassy sward establishing. We want natural regeneration to occur, because it’s always much more beneficial for wildlife. We’ve already got loads of hawthorn and quite a few oaks coming up. It’s already going out nicely.” Later this summer, green hay from other calcareous grassland in the local area will be spread on the Western Slopes to bring in more invertebrates. As ant populations develop, rare butterflies including the Adonis, chalkhill and small blue are likely to arrive, with these species interacting with ant colonies. There is also a mammal shelf built into a culvert beneath the railway, enabling badgers, stoats and other mammals to safely cross the high-speed line. Some footpaths through the site are set to be opened up in the next 18 months, although the western portion of the site is likely to remain protected from public access to boost the ground-nesting birds – from skylarks to little ringed plover – that have quickly colonised the land. While HS2 is still under construction, the forthcoming track-building and electrics phase will require a much smaller construction footprint, enabling the nature areas to be expanded. At the bottom of the slopes, beside the River Colne, nearly five hectares of new wetlands have been established. These pretty ponds have been rapidly colonised by club-rush, water mint and sneezewort, as well as breeding reed warbler and lesser emperor dragonfly. “We’ve definitely extended the population of kingfishers,” said Craner, who has also recorded new sightings of water vole on a tributary of the Colne. “Water voles are a massively declining species because of habitat loss – we’ve put in habitat that’s good for water voles. They’ve colonised it immediately.” What Craner has noticed is the changing soundscape. While the roar of the M25 and the clank of ongoing construction is never far away, in certain glades the human din is now overwhelmed by birdsong and insect hum. “We didn’t have this harmony last year and all of a sudden it’s never silent,” said Craner. “This is our hidden gem.” • This article was amended on 30 September 2026. In an earlier version we misidentified the pictured damselfly as a dragonfly.

title: ‘So much uncertainty’: Michigan’s Arab American businesses navigate Trump’s Canada trade war
summary: Arab communities on both sides of the border grapple with ongoing tensions as US-Canada relations continue to sour
text: In Dearborn, Michigan, home to the largest community of Arab Americans in the US, one industry has risen above all others in recent years: Yemeni cafes. At the forefront is Qahwah House, a powerhouse in the burgeoning Yemeni cafe world with 32 branches open across the country. Three of those are here in Dearborn, with more on the way, and they attract people from near and far. “We estimate that around 10% of our Dearborn business comes from Canadian customers,” says Mohamed Ahmed, marketing director at Qahwah House. But the recent downturn in relations between the Trump administration and Canada has caused it to pause a planned expansion north. The company was hoping to open a branch in Toronto, Canada’s biggest city that’s home to thousands of residents of Arab descent, until Donald Trump, who has repeatedly suggested that Canada become a US state, announced 50% tariffs on Canadian imports in July. “Where it does affect us is that we are trying to expand into Canada. We have our registrations, license, everything in place to open up in Canada. For now, we’re holding off just to make sure it’s a feasible move to expand,” says Ahmed. “There are a lot of super recent changes, so we’ll see how that plays out.” Canada is Michigan’s largest trading partner, and for immigrant communities such as Arab Americans in Dearborn, situated a five-minute drive from the nearest border crossing, Canadians represent an important slice of their business. Dearborn’s Arab restaurants were so popular north of the border that a decade ago, the Toronto Star dedicated an article to highlighting the suburb’s best eating spots, despite it being a four-hour drive from the Canadian city. Last year, during the initial round of tariff disputes with Canada, Detroit businesses reported a huge fall in income from Canadian visitors. “Since early 2025, Canadian visitation to the Detroit region is down about 30%, and remains at that level,” says Brett McWethy of Visit Detroit. Ottawa announced reciprocal sanctions on US imports that came into effect on 8 September. Talks last month failed to resolve differences between the two countries. Home to about 25,000 people of Arab descent, the city of Windsor on the eastern shore of the Detroit River in Ontario has for decades provided a strong source of customers for the fleet of Arab restaurants and cafes across Dearborn. For dozens of families in the Ontario city, Friday and Saturday evenings were once spent lounging in Lebanese cafes after a quick jaunt across the border. “We are south [of] Detroit [in Windsor]. I can see the river from my house – I am 1 mile from the center of Detroit,” says Robert Nelson, a professor of history at the University of Windsor who has written extensively on food and its cross-border dynamics. He says informal surveys he has conducted have found demographic variances between Canadians in Windsor who are continuing to visit Dearborn and wider Detroit, and those who are staying put in symbolic opposition to the Trump administration. “Those who go to Arabic restaurants in Dearborn are overwhelmingly Arab Canadians. Dearborn is where it’s at; there’s so much Arabic being spoken around you. Before [the trade problems] Arab Canadians would go to Dearborn restaurants,” he says. “Now, if you have family or work [in Dearborn] you’re not stopping crossing the border because of politics. But there are members of the Arab community in Windsor who are traveling less, who speak about supporting local.” One of Michigan’s biggest companies, Ford Motor Company, employs thousands of workers at its Rouge plant in Dearborn. It and a host of other automotive manufacturers have been hit by the tariffs war with Canada. However, communities on both sides of the border are demonstrating renewed resiliency amid the politics. For Khader Masri, who has been running Masri Sweets on Dearborn’s Schaefer Road for more than 35 years, the customers he knows who are Canadian have for the most part remained loyal. “There are five or six families who come over here that I know of – one came from London, Ontario, last weekend. They are still coming,” he says. “They are not thinking of any of that [political] commotion.” It’s a sentiment echoed by Nelson in Windsor. “Our lives are so intertwined with greater Detroit that it is no simple political act to say: ‘I’m not going to cross the border any more,’” he says. “To punish the small business owners who rely so heavily on Canadian customers because of the current administration also strikes me as a very difficult argument to make.” In a sign of the deep ties between communities on both sides of the border, an NFL game held in Buffalo, New York, on 17 September made headlines when the Canadian national anthem was sung on field by the Canadian group the Barenaked Ladies, to the ire of rightwing media in the US. “I think the Canadians are smart enough to disassociate whatever president [Trump] says versus not coming here to visit the states for work or leisure. I think Canadians do a good job of understanding that,” says Ahmed. Dearborn’s chamber of commerce said it hadn’t received any reports from businesses struggling as a consequence of seeing fewer visitors from Canada. However, several restaurant owners declined to comment due to the political aspect of the trade dispute and the Trump administration’s wider targeting of immigrant communities. Others interviewed said that they didn’t track whom among their customers travel from Canada. Still, challenges among the wider food industry in Michigan are pointing to growing struggles. A report from April by the Michigan Restaurant and Lodging Association found that more than half of businesses in the state reported declining sales. That’s far higher than the national level, which was reported to be 39%. For his part, Ahmed says the decline of the political relationship between Canada and the US has led to his company holding off on buying furniture from a Canadian supplier. “There’s just been too much uncertainty,” he says.

title: UK banks are Europe’s biggest coal financiers, report finds
summary: Study says UK-based banks provided $8.3bn in coal financing in four years, with Barclays and HSBC leading rise
text: UK banks are Europe’s biggest financial backers of the global coal industry, providing billions of pounds in funding for the climate-wrecking fossil fuel in the past four years, according to a report. The study found UK-based banks had provided $8.3bn (£6.2bn) in coal financing since Cop26 in Glasgow in 2021, when global leaders pledged to “phase down” coal use. This compared with $4.9bn from German banks and $3.4bn from French banks over the same period. The sums provided by UK banks were largely driven by Barclays and HSBC, which both increased their coal financing between 2022 and 2025 despite high-profile climate and net zero commitments, according to the research. It found Barclays’ coal financing increased by 34%, from approximately $1.2bn in 2022 to $1.6bn in 2025, while HSBC’s more than doubled from $200m to $414m. The research was carried out by Urgewald, a Germany-based environmental and human rights organisation. It tracked loans and underwriting from 744 commercial banks around the world to companies operating across the “coal value chain” – those organisations involved in every aspect of the industry, from mines and power generation to logistics, exploration and trading organisations. Heffa Schücking, the director of Urgewald, said: “Barclays and HSBC should explain why their financing is moving in the opposite direction to the rest of Europe.” A spokesperson for HSBC said the bank had committed to phasing out financing “for thermal coal-fired power and thermal coal mining” by 2030 in EU and OECD markets and by 2040 in other markets. They added: “These commitments support our ambition to align the financed emissions in our portfolio with net zero by 2050. As reported in our 2025 annual report and accounts, financed emissions from thermal coal mining fell by 94% between 2020 and 2024, while reported thermal coal financing exposures, calculated on the basis set out in our disclosures, fell from approximately $1bn to approximately $0.5bn over the same period.” A spokesperson for Barclays said many of the companies named in the report were “diversified energy or mining companies”. They said Barclays did not provide financing to companies that generated “more than 30% of revenues from thermal coal mining or power generation”. “Barclays is financing an energy sector in transition, providing finance to meet current energy needs and also financing the scaling of clean energy,” the spokesperson said. “Over the past three years we have facilitated more than $300bn of sustainable and transition finance, including billions to cleaner energy projects, and invested millions into climate tech.” Urgewald defended its definition of companies in the “coal value chain”, saying it was widely accepted by many financial institutions. Its report found that although some UK banks had reduced their coal financing, the overall financial flows from Britain-based banks to the “coal value chain” grew by 17% over the period. This compares with a 46% reduction overall from EU banks. Globally, Urgewald found that between 2022 and 2025 bank financing for coal remained broadly flat, averaging about $117bn a year, despite the commitment made at Cop26 in Glasgow. However, researchers said the headline figure concealed a growing divide within the banking industry, with Chinese and US banks increasing their funding. The study found Chinese banks accounted for 62% of global coal financing, providing $289bn, an 8% rise over the four-year period. US banks provided $67bn, a rise of 23%, while Indonesian banks increased their coal financing by 64%, from $1.4bn in 2022 to $2.3bn. By contrast, banks in the EU, Taiwan, Malaysia and Thailand significantly reduced their coal financing. Schücking, welcomed the decrease, saying it showed that a clear coal policy could “disrupt the flow of money to the industry”. But she cautioned that this progress was “being swallowed up” by rising coal finance elsewhere. “Banks still funding coal cannot hide behind distant climate promises. They need policies that rule out new coal and bring their financing down now,” she said.

title: ‘Third country’ deportation can resume, US supreme court rules | First Thing
summary: Trump administration can deport immigrants to countries other than their homeland
text: Good morning. The supreme court has ruled the Trump administration can resume deporting immigrants to “third countries”, or countries other than their homeland, without giving them any opportunity to contest their removals. The six-justice conservative majority of the high court temporarily lifted a decision by a lower court that required the administration to provide immigrants sufficient notice and the opportunity to claim fear of torture or persecution in the countries where they were being sent. What has the administration asked the supreme court to rule on about trans prisoners? The administration asked the justices to allow it to deny gender-affirming care to transgender people in federal prisons. The solicitor general, D John Sauer, wrote that gender-reassignment surgeries, hormone therapy and social accommodations such as undergarments, makeup, padding and wigs “could no longer be justified.” Why is the EPA union suing the administration? The union, which represents more than 8,000 workers at the Environmental Protection Agency, has filed a lawsuit against the EPA and the agency’s administrator, Lee Zeldin, alleging it illegally terminated a collective bargaining agreement. Which legal battle has Trump appeared to have conceded? title: AI tool that copied actor’s ‘lustrous’ voice violated his rights, Tokyo court rules
summary: Kenjiro Tsuda secures partial victory against TikTok account in landmark Japanese verdict to protect publicity rights
text: A court in Japan has ruled that the human voice has legal protection after a landmark case involving a well-known actor and a TikTok account that he claimed had cloned his “lustrous” baritone voice in its AI-generated videos. Tokyo district court said on Wednesday that voices should enjoy the same protection as publicity rights, at the end of a closely watched legal action brought against TikTok by Kenjiro Tsuda – best known for voicing the character Kento Nanami in the anime Jujutsu Kaisen. But the court dismissed Tsuda’s request that the operator of TikTok remove the videos, noting that the user had deleted them soon after the suit was filed last November. “The unauthorised use of a performer’s voice … can be considered an infringement on publicity rights,” said the presiding judge, Aya Takahashi. The lawsuit is believed to be the first in Japan seeking to defend an individual’s vocal identity against AI-generated copies. Japan’s voice actors, many of whom achieve star status through their “appearances” in anime, are increasingly worried that AI mimicry is threatening their livelihoods and the industry as a whole. An actor’s voice “is the result of years of rigorous training and apprenticeship”, Yuko Sasaki, executive director of the Japan Actors Union said ahead of the ruling. Tsuda, 55, claimed that the 188 TikTok videos uploaded on an anonymous account between July 2024 and September last year had been narrated by a “deep” and “lustrous” voice that could only be his. In response, the platform argued that the videos contained a “generic male voice” and that any perceived similarities to Tsuda’s voice were highly subjective. The verdict is the first in which a Japanese court has declared that the human voice is protected under publicity rights, a reference to the ability to control and profit from aspects of an individual’s identity, in Tsuda’s case his distinctive voice. The protection applies “if the purpose of using the voice is exclusively to take advantage of its commercial appeal”, Takahashi said, describing a voice to be “as symbolic of one’s personality as portraits are”. The TikTok account, whose picture resembled Tsuda’s Jujutsu Kaisen character, combined images and AI-generated speech about urban legends, the occult and conspiracy theories. At one point, the account had more than 200,000 subscribers and, according to the legal complaint, the clips would have earned its owner between ¥500,000 (£2,395) and ¥75,000 in monthly revenue, the Kyodo news agency said. Describing the content as “sordid”, Tsuda’s legal team claimed the account had only attracted attention because it had cloned the “attractive voice of a popular actor”. TikTok said in a statement it would “respect the court’s judgment while considering what steps to take after scrutinising [the ruling’s] details”. It added: “We will continue to sincerely work on the balance between technology development and rights protection.” In 2024, actors in Japan launched a campaign called “No More” to oppose the unauthorised use of their faces and voices in AI-generated content. With reporting by Agence France-Presse • The subheading of this article was amended on 6 October 2026 to better reflect the verdict of the court.

title: California rushes to prepare for massive ‘Kelvin’ wave and predicted sea level rise
summary: Wave nearing southern California expected to reach San Francisco Bay Area by October as it crawls toward Alaska
text: Communities across California are rushing to prepare for the imminent arrival of the so-called “Kelvin wave”, a massive underwater band of warm water threatening to inundate swaths of the vast North American shoreline. The wave is nearing southern California and expected to reach the San Francisco Bay Area by early October, as it crawls toward Alaska. Waters could rise by a foot along the California coast, according to scientists, who have warned that this could dramatically double the 8-12in rise in sea levels already caused by climate change over the last century. The Kelvin wave doesn’t climb and crash like a typical ocean wave; rather, it swells the tides from beneath the surface. It’s effectively a massive slosh of warm water, driven by El Niño conditions, that moves across the Pacific before colliding with the South American coastline and surging north. It also won’t transport water in the way a tsunami might, but creates conditions that enable higher sea levels to linger. On their own, Kelvin waves aren’t always hazardous, according to Mike Jacox, a research oceanographer with the National Marine Fisheries Service, though they can reduce the growth of phytoplankton that form the base of the marine food web. “But when there are very high tides or storm surges, their effects can be amplified,” he said. If the rising waters coincide with other climatic events, such as rainstorms and high tides, the phenomenon could swallow beaches, chew away bluffs and coastlines, and submerge streets, homes and businesses. “This coming Kelvin wave is just the beginning,” said Dr Jonathan Warrick, a research geologist at the US Geological Survey. “The thing to look out for is what will happen in January, February and March – that’s when we get the biggest storms, we get our largest waves and we have some very large tides.” If these events align, their effects will compound, setting the stage for a tumultuous winter. Together, Warrick said, the systems will pack a far bigger punch. “When it comes to these storms and the tides,” he said, “we really are kind of rolling the dice.” Excess warmth in the ocean, caused by the human-caused climate crisis, has already turned up the dial, supercharging weather events around the world. But a “super” El Niño that’s brewing in the Pacific – which could become the most severe ever recorded – has layered on top of that warming, and increased the likelihood that the higher sea levels will overlap with severe storms. The climate pattern characterized by high sea surface temperatures in the central and eastern tropical Pacific is already spurring extreme weather around the world, fueling destructive storms in Hawaii and unleashing Pacific hurricanes that have hammered beach towns. California will probably see the worst effects this winter when the state could get pummeled by moisture. Storms do damage on their own, but the most destructive occur alongside high tides, according to a recent memo from the California Coastal Commission – and the “super” El Nino will increase the severity of both. The highest tides of the year in areas of California will occur in November and December, further increasing water levels during the months when the state tends to be hit by wet weather. “Coastal flooding is at this point practically certain,” climate scientist Daniel Swain said in an interview with Inside Climate News. He added that a wetter-than-average winter would also bring increased inland flooding risk. “Both of these in some places can combine where you have freshwater outflows and saltwater inflows mingling,” he said. “The damage can be devastating.” Swain pointed to the winter of 1997-1998, which exhibited similar hazards. Heavy storms caused massive coastal erosion, as enormous landslides ruptured and buried highways, and huge waves swept into harbors across Santa Cruz and the San Francisco Bay Area. Levees failed north of Sacramento and seawalls were overwhelmed, while relentless rains tore into thousands of homes and businesses. Twenty-one of California’s 58 counties were declared disaster areas. It’s impossible to predict how exactly the season will unfold, but the El Niño forming now is swirling off the charts. Surface temperatures in the Pacific Ocean are warmer now than they were before the onslaught in 1997. Several areas are already feeling the effects. “Just the first few inches of elevation in southern California have already caused enough erosion to close the Amtrak line along the coast, and this is just the beginning,” Swain said. He noted that the San Francisco Bay Area was particularly vulnerable, due to the critical transportation arteries, population centers and big tech firms at risk of flooding, saying: “There’s a huge amount of people and infrastructure within 6ft of sea level there.” Across the Bay Area, sandbags are already being supplied as emergency managers and local governments work to secure infrastructure and inform businesses and residents about the incoming dangers. Nick Brubaker, the chief resilience officer for the office of emergency management in Marin county, just north of San Francisco, said preparations were already under way for El Niño when they received reports about how high sea levels will rise. “It certainly changes our baseline assumptions on how we’re going to be planning for impact,” he said, noting that in January of this year, there was flooding from high tides without the added effects from the Kelvin wave. Engorged creeks and streams will be less able to drain out in the face of rising sea levels. “We could see some significant flooding,” Brubaker said. There has also been work done to clear drains and culverts, evaluate infrastructure and rush through temporary mitigation measures, including securing flood barriers. Checklists have been issued, and emergency alert signups encouraged. Similar strategies are unfolding in cities up and down the coast, as teams brace for what’s an all-but-guaranteed rise in the risks, but a lot of uncertainty over what exactly will unfold. “We’re using all of the data that we can, but we don’t have a perfect measure,” Brubaker said. He’s been focused on outreach and communication, “to make sure that people are aware that this may be one of the most significant El Niño years that we’ve seen”.
