title: Mediation over Drumcree parade is ‘dead in the water’, say nationalists
summary: Northern Ireland secretary holding talks with both sides as Garvaghy Road group launches fresh legal challenge
text: Talks to break the deadlock over the controversial Drumcree parade will continue with the Northern Ireland secretary, Chris Bryant, on Wednesday as nationalist protesters declare the prospect of mediation with unionists “dead in the water”. The nationalist Garvaghy Road Residents’ Coalition has at the same time launched a fresh legal challenge to reimpose the almost 30-year ban on the Orange Order marching down their road, mounting fresh arguments that the Parades Commission has “materially misdirected itself”. Breandán Mac Cionnaith, the leader of the group, said his goal was “no parade, just no parade, that is what our community wants, that’s what nearly 4,000 people living in our community wants … that’s our mandate”. After his meeting with Bryant on Tuesday he told residents at the local pastoral centre that mediation was “dead in the water”. Members of the Portadown Orange Order left Drumcree church, the start point for the parade, overnight on Tuesday for the first time since the dispute over their march erupted on Sunday morning. They made a further attempt to walk the route down the nationalist Garvaghy Road just after 10pm on Tuesday night, accompanied by the DUP MP Carla Lockhart, and returned to the church on Wednesday morning having vowed to remain there until the police allowed them to complete the march. The Orange Order Portadown district master, Nigel Dawson, said he had “constructive” talks after his meeting with the Northern Ireland secretary over the possibility of a mediator on Tuesday night. “We look forward to the law being applied to the parade,” he added. The two groups will have further talks with Bryant on Wednesday and the Garvaghy Road court hearing is scheduled for Friday, but there is little sign of a breakthrough. The high court at a special sitting on Saturday heard that the documentation around the decision to allow the parade showed past risk assessments of disorder in relation to parade requests but none looking to the future. Under a heading on a form listing any risk of public disorder or damage to property, the commission’s information was “directed to the past”, their barrister, Denise Kiley KC, told the judge. “Nowhere do we see any assessment of future risk,” she said adding that it was “not clear who had provided this template” to the Parades Commission. Efforts to end the dispute, which has heightened sectarian divisions in Northern Ireland, were also brought to Dublin where Sinn Féin’s leader, Mary Lou McDonald, and the Northern Ireland first minister, Michelle O’Neill, met Micheál Martin and Simon Harris, the leader and deputy leader of the Irish government. Martin has described the Parades Commission decision to allow the parade march down Garvaghy Road for the first time in almost 30 years as “incomprehensible and wrong”. McDonald said people were “gobsmacked” by the decision as it had “the potential to drag that community and society back to a very bad and very bleak days”. O’Neill has faced criticism from unionists after she and senior colleagues were among a large crowd that blockaded the road in the predominantly nationalist Garvaghy Road area on Sunday to prevent the parade from passing the route. Under parading laws in Northern Ireland, protests must be notified to, and approved by, the Parades Commission adjudication body and the gathering at the head of Garvaghy Road, that continues on Wednesday, has not yet been notified. However, police have not tried to break up the protest, fearing it could trigger violence. Bertie Ahern, the former taoiseach and co-architect of the 1998 peace deal that led to republicans and loyalists laying down their arms after 30 years of violence, warned of the dangers of returning to the “tribal past”.

title: Insects play critical role in ecosystems beyond just providing food, new research shows
summary: Insects provide protection, sanitation and even shelter to vertebrates, making them a priority for conservation efforts
text: For many vertebrates, insects are more than a food source. As “little things that run the world”, insects provide critical functions such as protection, sanitation and shelter across ecosystems, according to a new study. The study, published in Nature Reviews Biodiversity on Wednesday, sheds light on the various ways insects support vertebrates, ranging from birds and bats to reptiles, amphibians and mammals. Nearly three-quarters of terrestrial and freshwater vertebrates eat invertebrates, according to the paper, with insects frequently making up a large portion of their diets. However, their relationship goes beyond predator and prey. The paper, led by Eliza Grames, an assistant professor of biological sciences at Binghamton University, State University of New York, documents dozens of less obvious ways vertebrates depend on the estimated 14m to 30m species of insects found around the world. Chimpanzees, for example, have been recorded applying insects to treat open wounds, while more than 200 bird species use ants to remove parasites or maintain feathers. Other birds build nests near wasps or other stinging insects, in a likely effort to gain protection from predators. Insects also provide shelter, the study notes. Birds, reptiles and mammals use termite mounds and ant nests, which can offer stable temperatures and humidity. White-throated round-eared bats, for instance, excavate cavities in termite mounds and use them as roosts. Other insects act as sanitation workers. Dung beetles remove animal waste and can make dung drier and more aerated, in turn reducing parasite survival, according to the study. Meanwhile, moths living in some bird nests consume feces, feathers and other debris. The review notes that insects have performed similar functions for millions of years, citing evidence of beetles feeding on feathers in dinosaur nests during the Cretaceous period, which lasted from about 145m to 66m years ago. Other insect-vertebrate relationships include beetles removing ectoparasites from rodents and snakes feeding on firefly larvae to obtain defensive toxins, as well as antbirds using live crickets during courtship. Mutually beneficial relationships also occur across the insect-vertebrate realm, with sloths relying on moths to deposit nitrogen in their fur and spur algal growth, which the sloths then eat. Sloths then descend from trees once a month to defecate on the ground, providing substrate in which moths lay eggs. According to the study, such overlooked relationships could become increasingly important as insect communities evolve. Although the extent of insect declines varies across habitats and regions, the review says that “widespread and considerable disruption” of insect communities is “inevitable” as land use changes. Grames called the study a “wake-up call for anyone concerned about the biodiversity crisis”. “We need to pay attention to insects and make their conservation a top priority, because conserving insects will benefit all the other species that rely on them. Insects are so much more than just food for vertebrates like birds and bats – they create and maintain habitat, provide protection to other species, help with reducing diseases and removing waste, and so many other ecosystem services that we, and other species, rely on. They really are the unsung heroes of the natural world,” she added. Grames also pointed to the critical role insects play in addressing the climate crisis, saying: “About 12% of the global carbon forest stock is leaf litter and dead wood, and insects are responsible for decomposing about 30% of it. So even though insects are small, their activities influence global carbon cycles. Insects also help with forest regeneration by dispersing seeds into areas where other, large – seed dispersers have disappeared. Pollination and seed dispersal, both of which are done by insects, are two of the biggest limitations in forest regeneration.” Similarly, Rob Cooke, senior ecologist at the UK Centre for Ecology and Hydrology and a co-author of the study, highlighted the broader ecological implications of insect declines, saying: “Widespread insect declines globally are likely to have far-reaching effects on wildlife. Beyond reducing an essential food source, losses of insects risk changing ecosystems, disrupting pollination and seed dispersal, weakening sanitation, and altering the many interactions that help ecosystems function.” The consequences for vertebrates remain difficult to predict due to the lack of studies on insect-vertebrate relationships. The study notes that “the lack of systematic descriptions of trophic and non-trophic interactions, hampered by an ongoing decline of natural history research”, makes it difficult to understand how changes in insect biodiversity affect other species. For co-author Chris Elphick, a professor of ecology and evolutionary biology at the University of Connecticut, understanding the diverse roles that insects play across vertebrates’ lives is essential for designing effective conservation strategies. “If you want to have vertebrates, then you’ve got to be thinking about insect conservation, and we don’t do that nearly enough,” Elphick said.

title: From mass raids to quiet crackdown: a timeline of Trump’s strategic ICE pivot
summary: After switching tactics, federal agents are detaining and deporting record numbers of people from the US
text: When federal agents fatally shot the US citizen protesters Alex Pretti and Renee Good in Minneapolis in January during the nation’s largest immigration enforcement operation ever, it marked a turning point for the second Trump administration’s mass deportation campaign. Donald Trump in his second term had sparked outrage and huge protests with federal immigration officers descending en masse on one Democratic-run city after another in what some leaders called militarized “invasions”. Los Angeles, Chicago, Charlotte, New Orleans, then Minneapolis saw lines of masked and armored officers swaggering into town to conduct street arrests, ambushes of day workers waiting in Home Depot car parks for hire, and neighborhood sweeps. Adults and kids were whisked off to detention and protests met with aggressive deployment of chemical spray, teargas, fists and batons. The killings in Minneapolis were the culmination of what appeared to many to be a federal shock force increasingly out of control while being defended by federal leaders – and public opinion broadly turned against this violence. There was a change of personnel and the administration flagged a switch to a “quieter” approach to immigration enforcement. But while large-scale theatrics on the streets waned, less visible enforcement is no less aggressive on the ground today and continues to ramp up in multiple ways. Here’s a timeline of how the administration’s anti-immigration campaign has evolved in recent months as Trump races to remove millions of people from the US. 2026 26 January Minneapolis madness leads to a changing of the guard Two days after Pretti was killed by Customs and Border Protection (CBP) officers and 19 days after Good had been shot dead by an ICE agent, the US president announces that his “border czar”, Tom Homan, an immigration enforcement veteran, will deploy to Minnesota, while Gregory Bovino, the border patrol’s confrontational commander-at-large, suddenly stands aside. Bovino was the face and voice on the street of federal aggression; Good, Pretti and ICE watchers were the symbols of the resistance; and Liam Ramos was the image of collateral harm. 5 March Secretary of homeland security fired Kristi Noem becomes the first cabinet secretary fired during the second Trump administration when she loses her leading role at the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). Noem was tainted with scandals over her close relationship with senior adviser Cory Lewandowski and a $220m advertising campaign starring herself and using a firm with connections to her former staffer. She had also repeated a false narrative that Pretti “brandished” a gun at federal agents and called Renee Good a domestic terrorist. Weeks later, Bovino retires and tells the New York Times: “I wish I’d caught even more illegal aliens.” 24 March New face, new approach Markwayne Mullin, formerly a first-term senator from Oklahoma with “mixed martial arts fighter” on his résumé, is confirmed by the US Senate as the new DHS secretary. At his confirmation hearing, he says about immigration-enforcement officials: “My goal in six months is that we’re not in the lead story every single day.” Spring Empowering local police on the streets The DHS, in its own words, has “supercharged” efforts to work with local and state law enforcement via so-called 287(g) agreements. From January 2025 these deals mushroomed nationwide, from 142 to 2,315, with most modeled as a “taskforce”. They deputize local and state officials to actively enforce immigration laws during regular police work – normally under federal jurisdiction. By spring, this collaboration acts as a force multiplier for arrests, while allowing federal agents to avoid the spotlight as local cops take on more frontline duties. It also makes immigration enforcement harder to spot for protesters. May Pressure from the courts Attorneys and researchers start noticing immigration court dates being scheduled for unusually large groups of people with little to no notice, in what they say is a tactic to increase the number of deportation orders without ever giving someone an individualized hearing. These mass court dates balloon in June, affecting many thousands of people. Many more applicants struggle to find attorneys and prepare their now-rushed cases. Children are a particular target, too, being rushed through hearings as due process is undermined. 9 June Money, money, money After the longest DHS shutdown ever, congressional Republicans use a partisan process to provide the department with an additional $70bn, funding it for the rest of Trump’s second term in a move that critics say undermines accountability. All told, the DHS has received roughly a quarter of a trillion dollars in funding since Trump retook the White House. 25 June Scotus The US supreme court rules in favor of the Trump administration’s bid to strip temporary protected status (TPS) from hundreds of thousands of Haitians and Syrians who were legally in the US and protected from deportation. When Trump took office, 17 countries had active TPS designations, which allowed roughly 1.3 million people who were already in the US to live and work legally while it was unsafe for them to return home. But under his second administration, more than a million people who are generally law-abiding and often contribute economically to essential industries with significant labor shortages have already lost their TPS permissions. Now they face imminent risk of deportation to countries as dangerous as Afghanistan, Haiti and South Sudan if they do not qualify or cannot afford to apply for another immigration status. “We’re going after them right now,” Mullin has said of Haitians. “These individuals can either self-deport or we’ll arrest you and send you back. It’s that simple.” Summer 2026 Airport hazards ICE significantly increases its collaboration with the Transportation Security Administration (TSA) to detain immigrants with expired visas – many of whom have pending applications for green cards, asylum, employment-based visas, etc – at airports, sometimes near public spaces such as ticket counters or gates. However, the vast majority of arrests continue to occur where they are far less easy to detect and record on camera, such as in people’s homes and cars. July 2026 All paying off for ICE The DHS reports 49,571 immigration arrests, which sets a new monthly record for the second Trump administration, after previously doing so in June. A majority of the people arrested in July have no criminal history. Detentions also increase, with about 66,000 people in custody by the end of the month. Preliminary reports suggest immigration arrests in August have kept pace with July. 13 July Deadly days An ICE officer kills Joan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, 26, in Biddeford, Maine, during a vehicle stop in which Durán was not the intended target, making him the 11th person fatally shot by federal immigration officials both on and off duty during Trump’s second term. The shooting comes days after federal agents similarly killed another immigrant father, Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, in Houston while he was driving his building crew to their job. The DHS briefly pauses most ICE traffic stops until Trump intervenes, posting online: “We CANNOT give up one of I.C.E.’s most important and effective Crime Fighting tools, THE TRAFFIC STOP!” In one 24-hour period, 13 to 14 July, three people die in ICE-involved incidents. August Even more local cops do ICE’s bidding Federal officials reach the milestone of 1,000 new 287(g) agreements since 26 January, expanding collaborations with local law enforcement agencies at an even faster clip than during the second Trump administration’s first year in office. August Visa applications All visas for people applying to immigrate to the US are paused for an unknown amount of time while officials undergo training around the new “public charge” policies. 1 September Big footprint in the Big Apple Mullin retroactively announces Operation Rotten Apple, which from 27 July to 29 August quietly rounded up nearly 2,200 immigrants across New York state. The operation is a case study in how aggressive immigration enforcement continues, including in Democratic-led “sanctuary” cities, without the previous theatrics. Summer into fall Suffer the children On August 1 the federal government ends its contract providing more than 20,000 unaccompanied immigrant children with legal representation. At the same time, attorneys report that immigration judges are taking a “deport at all costs” approach to their young clients, who suddenly are not receiving the time they need for their pending applications to be adjudicated by other agencies before they are ordered removed from the US. Many of these kids qualify for a green card or other immigration status because they have been abused, abandoned, neglected, trafficked or otherwise severely mistreated, but their applications are often subject to backlogs and quotas that cause delays. In September, the Guardian reveals that Stephen Miller, White House deputy chief of staff, has been leading an unprecedented drive across several government departments to accelerate the removal of undocumented immigrant children from the US, using tactics that critics say are cruel and racist, and, in some cases, flout federal law. Taken together, these policy changes are less showy but they have ramped up arrests, detentions and the number of people forced to leave the United States – and put millions more at immediate risk of the same. Many of these people have legal status or ongoing cases for winning or upgrading their legal status, or years of crime-free, honorable life in the US, but are being rounded up, often with little access to due process or attorneys who can help. This latest iteration of Trump’s mass deportation campaign is no longer defined by federal agents patrolling cities with smoke canisters in hand. It’s much more insidious but also more ruthless and effective – and it’s happening everywhere.

title: A ‘freaked out’ US food industry is hitting back at Maha – with social media influencers
summary: Cross-partisan support in Washington on issues like pesticides and food additives pose a threat to the industry’s bottom line
text: Some of the biggest food and agriculture corporations in the US are funding a campaign that pays social media influencers to combat elements of Robert F Kennedy Jr’s Make America Healthy Again platform, according to an investigation by the Guardian and Documented, an investigative watchdog and journalism project. The ascension of RFK Jr to secretary of health and human services has boosted his putative campaign to end chronic illness in the US, which he believes is primarily caused by processed foods and dyes, exposure to certain chemicals, and poor farming practices, along with an overuse of what he falsely claims are dangerous vaccines. The “Maha” movement blends long-running mainstream concerns about food and farm safety with conspiracy theories about everything from medicine to milk. A Maha “summit” in Washington this week will feature JD Vance and several members of Trump’s cabinet. A KFF poll from May 2026 reveals that some Maha themes resonate with a broad segment of US adults. About four in 10 say they support the Maha movement, while a majority of the public say there is not enough regulation of pesticides used in agriculture (64%) or of chemical food additives (75%). Cross-partisan support in Washington on some of these issues poses a threat to the food industry’s bottom line – though the Trump administration has largely stopped short of enacting new regulations. But several large corporations are fighting back. An effort by the Center for Food Integrity, an industry-funded non-profit, tracks public sentiment around key issues central to Maha and suggests ways that agricultural interests can counter those narratives by appealing to emotion or scientific reasoning. They call it Gaha: Growing a Healthier America. Documents show the coordinated effort is tracking Maha closely and researching ways to respond to the movement’s claims without alienating its supporters. They are focused on several key areas: seed oils, pesticides, high-fructose corn syrup, regenerative agriculture, organic farming, raw milk/dairy and “big ag”, internal documents obtained by the Guardian and Documented show. The campaign involves deploying social media influencers with significant reach online in an effort to rebuild trust in the industries that the Maha movement has made their target. The Gaha influencer campaign officially launched late last year. In February, CFI compiled a report listing dozens of sponsored posts on platforms such as online blogs, Facebook, TikTok and Instagram about key Gaha subjects. So far, at least six influencers have signed on to the Gaha campaign, reaching a total audience of more than 2.6 million viewers. Influencers who participated in the paid campaign said they saw it as a way to counter misinformation that comes from Maha proponents, many of whom are paid to promote products in the wellness space. Some of the paid posts involved talking to farmers about pesticides or regenerative agriculture, which is the practice of restoring soil health, or explaining what seed oils are to counter claims that they cause a host of health problems. In one July 2025 training video uncovered by the Guardian and Documented, the center explained the goal was to create an “echo chamber” among the food and agriculture industry groups, aligning them behind “the same ultimate message”. “Without this coordinated response, that misinformation [from Maha] risks undermining consumer trust, fueling new regulations and eroding confidence in agriculture as a whole,” said Kelly Leighton, the center’s executive director, in the video. The Center for Food Integrity, formed in 2007, conducts research and public relations campaigns on behalf of the food and agricultural sectors. The board consists of corporate executives from top brands: Bryan Malenius, CFI’s board president, also serves as the director of reputation strategy for public affairs at Chick-fil-A, while other members hold senior positions at companies such as Cargill, Dairy Farmers of America and the National Pork Board. Its members, whose dues pay to keep CFI operating, include groups such as the American Farm Bureau Federation and several state farm bureaus, CropLife America and the National Restaurant Association. CFI created the Gaha campaign in partnership with its member organizations in the farming, agribusiness and food industries, in a bid to re-establish credibility with the public after Maha gained popularity. The American Farm Bureau Federation was also an important driver of the effort: the group’s president, Zippy Duvall, took credit for bringing industry groups together to form the Gaha coalition during a speech in January 2026. Critiques of the food system, from pesticides to processed foods, have long been the purview of Democrats. With Maha, and Trump’s embrace of Robert F Kennedy Jr, the views have taken hold with many Republicans as well, presenting a broader threat to the agricultural industry. “That surely freaks the industry out,” said Tom Philpott, senior research associate at the Center for a Livable Future at Johns Hopkins University. “For the industry, they are very concerned about, for want of a better word, a vibe shift.” The Center for Food Integrity declined an interview request, saying in a statement: “At the Center for Food Integrity we recognize the critical link between diet and health. Growing a Healthier America supports an informed dialogue about how the food system can work together to assure a healthy affordable food supply and strong rural communities.” The farm bureau also declined to comment, saying questions should be referred to CFI as it was their project. Inside Gaha messaging In mid-2025, the Gaha campaign began taking shape: CFI released a variety of resources for industry groups to use as a framework for their communications strategies moving forward. The Guardian and Documented uncovered dozens of pages of internal materials related to this effort, including a “Say This, Not That” guide. It provided highly specific advice about language on key Maha topics, and included an influencer campaign creation guide. Since last May, CFI has also released regular insight briefs, which identify Maha narratives gaining traction in the news and on social media, allowing industry to understand public sentiment shifts and adjust their messaging accordingly. In a brief covering February and March, for example, the summary of online activity about processed foods noted that childhood obesity had reached a new high, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, and cited a Canadian study linking ultra-processed foods in early childhood to “adverse behavioral and emotional changes” in children. On the following page, CFI pointed members to new resources to “support” their communications work specifically on the issue of processed foods. CFI’s consumer research also directly informs who gets hired to deliver their messaging. An influencer campaign guide outlined preferred messengers for each consumer segment: for audiences who value authenticity, local farmers and wellness enthusiasts were best; for rationalists, scientists and dietitians; and for comfort seekers, CFI suggested lifestyle creators or faith-based voices. Industry donors were invited to contribute hundreds of thousands of dollars to the Gaha campaign. An internal flyer revealed the perks for those who opt to contribute: supporters who pledge up to $50,000 receive regular updates, donors of up to $100,000 participate in quarterly meetings and provide strategic input, and contributors of more than $100,000 earn a seat on the leadership council, with the opportunity to review and approve strategy as well as help secure funding from others. Why influencers got involved According to a 12 August brief by the center, the campaign has had impact: Gaha has generated 13.2m impressions online, with more than 1.1m engagements and an 8.74% engagement rate. Influencers who participated in the campaign posted about key topic areas the center wanted to target: raw milk, seed oils, agriculture. Some featured farmers talking about their work and how they balance using pesticides. Slade Wentworth, who has more than 1 million followers on thedadbriefs, his Instagram account, said he participated in the campaign as part of a series he does that helps families “think critically through political and cultural noise”. “In my opinion, many of the loudest voices in the Maha movement and in the food/wellness spaces in general tend to push anti- and pseudo-scientific claims,” Wentworth said via email. “To me, engaging with CFI was an opportunity to present a balanced discussion on topics that overlap with what I’d typically cover” in the series. One of the topics he covered, on the raw milk movement, resonated well with his audience, he said. The comments he received on the work he did for the campaign were “varied and substantive”, a sign that the content “struck a good balance, enabling folks to lean into their perspectives thoughtfully”. The anonymous creator of hydroxide.foodscience, which has more than 300,000 followers on Instagram, made posts about regenerative agriculture, ultra-processed foods and seed oils as part of the paid program. They decided to participate because it was a “uniquely positive spin on food and agriculture”. “It can be difficult for people to sort through the weeds of food and food science and agriculture to really get the facts, so I think that was like a big reason why this campaign resonated with me,” they said. They do not disclose their name on their accounts. Jessica Steier, the CEO of Unbiased Science, interviewed a farmer as part of the campaign to show what modern farming looks like. Unbiased Science received “a modest fee” for the campaign, but kept full editorial and scientific control, Steier said in an emailed statement. The center didn’t script the post or tell them what to say, which would have been a dealbreaker for Unbiased Science, she said. The work was not about defending industry, but about giving people information to make their own decisions, she said. Much of the information amplified by Maha, Steier noted, falls under a “wave of chemophobia”, where people are told they’re being harmed without much evidence. Unbiased Science wanted to counter the fear by showing why farmers use pesticides, that the goal is to use the minimum amounts necessary and what regulations are in place, she said. Hearing it directly from a farmer “does something a fact sheet can’t”, she said. “If anything, the financial incentives are far stronger on the other side of this,” Steier said. “The wellness economy that profits from fear about food and ‘toxins’ is enormously lucrative. Explaining why a preservative is safe is not where the money is. The people being richly rewarded for shaping what Americans believe about their food are not the ones defending the evidence.” Other influencers the center included in its campaign were Happy Strong Healthy, Dietitian Hannah and Veggies and Chocolate. These accounts did not respond to emailed requests for comment. Maha as ‘existential threat’ Jerold Mande, a nutritionist who served as deputy undersecretary for food safety at the US Department of Agriculture under Barack Obama, said the campaign sounds like “crisis management”. He has worked for decades to make food policy a priority, but thinks Maha, with its cross-partisan appeal, represents the biggest threat to the food industry that he’s seen. Using influencers to counter Maha, which is in essence a loose grouping of influencers itself, makes sense. “They realize now that they’re facing an existential threat, and their whole business model over the last decades has evolved around, you know, how do we make money?” Mande said. Still, he said, as Maha has charted some wins and made food policy a political priority, it has failed to install regulations that would create meaningful changes. “You’re not going to make progress if you don’t use government’s two powerful levers: funding and rules,” Mande said. Marion Nestle, a molecular biologist and nutritionist who has studied and written about food politics, said food and agriculture groups are always working to protect their industries, so a campaign like this is “nothing new”, especially when Republicans are now talking about agrochemicals. “Of course, they’re going to lobby, and they’re going to do it in absolutely every way they can,” Nestle said. Using an outright attack on Maha influencers, many of whom are moms whom Nestle believes “really care about their kids”, would not be a good idea, she said, leading to softer and more behind-the-scenes methods to sway opinion. Maha isn’t “getting anywhere” with major changes to the food system, given the refusal to regulate coming from Kennedy and the Trump administration, she said. “Food companies have license to do all the lobbying they want, and they can say whatever they want,” she said. “They don’t have to do anything. Nobody’s making them do anything. Nobody’s holding them accountable for anything.” This article was produced in partnership with Documented, an investigative watchdog and journalism project. Riley Messer is a senior researcher at Documented.

title: Trump campaign ads paid with public money violate federal law, critics say
summary: White House has labeled ads ‘public service announcements’ and has responded defiantly to criticism
text: Federal regulators have been urged to stop the broadcast of White House advertisements promoting Donald Trump that critics say amount to government propaganda and violate laws against using public money to promote partisan causes. Public Citizen, an advocacy group, called on the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) and the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) to intervene and block further airing of three ads it said were “designed to boost the image and character of Donald Trump” as part of the Republicans’ campaign for November’s midterm elections. “Federal law explicitly prohibits using appropriated public funds for government propaganda, self-aggrandizement, or partisan political advertising,” the organization wrote. “Yet, that is exactly the nature of Trump’s recent campaign ads.” Broadcast stations cannot reject ads from legally qualified political candidates – but Trump is not technically a candidate, although he has urged voters to imagine that he is, on the November ballot. “Public Citizen strongly urges the Federal Communications Commission and Federal Trade Commission to direct broadcasters to stop broadcasting these apparently illegal campaign advertisements and calls on individual broadcasters to cease airing the campaign advertisements,” the group wrote in a letter addressed to both agencies. “It is the greater responsibility of both the FCC [and] FTC and individual broadcasters to keep the airwaves fair and honest and operate in the ‘public interest, convenience, and necessity’.” The White House has labeled the ads – which began airing last week – “public service announcements” and has responded defiantly to criticism. It has established a webpage arguing for their use. Axios reported that more ads are set to broadcast, with Trump personally choosing which to use during the campaign for November’s midterms, which most polls suggest the Republicans are on course to lose. “This is just the beginning,” an administration official told Axios, which reported that the ads are being produced inside the White House. One is a rerun of a commercial aired by the Trump campaign before the 2024 presidential election and features black-and-white footage of him walking while his voice announces “the final battle”. He pledges to “throw off the sick political class that hates our country” and “rout the fake news media”. The only difference from the 2024 ad are the words “paid for the US government”. Another shows images of the president at various events while he is heard declaring “America will never be a communist country.” It takes place against the soundtrack of a choir signing the song Love Me. A third advertisement shows images of Mount Rushmore and has Trump declaring that “the United States of America is the most successful, most accomplished, most exceptional nation ever to exist in human history.” The Wall Street Journal reported that the commercials were funded by US Customs and Border Protection (CBP), which is responsible for immigration enforcement and is part of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). The DHS came under scrutiny early this year after a $200m advertising campaign that boosted Kristi Noem, then the homeland security secretary. Noem told a congressional committee that Trump had “signed off on the ads”. Her testimony reportedly infuriated Trump, who subsequently fired her. The latest Trump ads had aired more than 90 times across nationwide channels, including Fox, Newsmax, MS Now and CBS by Sunday evening, the Journal reported. They were run during Saturday Night Live, Fox News Sunday and during several college and NFL football games. Public Citizen said the cost of the three ads already broadcast was estimated at more than $1m. “Donald Trump is not a candidate for any elective office. The FCC and broadcasters are not constrained by the special rule protecting candidate advertisements. “Although the White House contends these ads are ‘public service announcements’, and therefore may be paid for with taxpayer dollars, [they do not] meet the standard of a public service announcement. They do not refer to any specific governmental program and they do not serve the purpose of informing the public about any specific governmental program.” On its website, the White House denounced the criticism as “highly dishonest” and likened the ads to previous public service announcements by previous presidents, dating back to Woodrow Wilson and Franklin D Roosevelt in the first and second world wars, and including the more recent administrations of George W Bush, Barack Obama and Joe Biden. “The announcements are very clearly not campaign ads; President Trump is not on the ballot and there is no call to action,” says the statement, under the headline “Presidential public service announcements are nothing new.” “Instead, the announcements are a reminder for Americans to love their country and know why it’s worth defending – at home, at the border, and abroad.” The Guardian contacted the FCC and FTC for comment. Brendan Carr, the FCC chair and a close Trump ally, said on Wednesday that the ads fell “within standard practice” without raising “red flags” and did not require the commission’s intervention.

title: ‘Beyond priceless’: how a halt to dredging saved the seas of Scotland’s Summer Isles
summary: Fish and shellfish populations were falling rapidly as scallop dredgers devastated the seabed, but local activists and small-scale fishers battled hard to protect their coastline
text: Inside a bothy overlooking the Summer Isles, in the north-west of Scotland, the lilting tones of a traditional Gaelic duo fill a room full of musicians, storytellers, artists, local people and revellers, hung with fish-shaped lanterns and “Happy Birthday” signs. It’s no ordinary birthday. The people in the small cabin have come together, on a windy night in Achiltibuie, a string of coastal hamlets and villages north of Ullapool, to celebrate an important milestone in the community’s history: a hard-won battle to protect their waters from the ravages of scallop dredging. The coastline here, a metallic grey seen through the bothy’s windows, is dotted with beds of one of the UK’s most biodiverse and carbon-rich habitats, a 9,000-year-old pink seaweed called maerl, two of which are a mile long. This rare, fragile and threatened seaweed produces hard, chalky, coral-like skeletons that provide nurseries for scallops and fish. Now, 10 years after local people, divers, activists and creel fishers ran a successful campaign to have scallop dredging banned by law in a 600 sq km (150,000 acre) zone now designated a marine protected area (MPA), they say they have already witnessed a dramatic revival of marine life. The transformation of a seabed damaged by decades of dredging has allowed the recovery of scallop populations and ended the fractious territorial battles between the industrial dredge fishing boats and the smaller, more sustainable creel boats, local people say. The community rowing club and nearby tour operators report increased sightings of whales, porpoises and dolphins. A large spawning ground for herring, once plentiful here but since overfished, has been spotted nearby and in prawn and lobster creels, or pots, which are laid on the seabed. Diyanne Ross, 65, the local artist who made the lanterns, is part of the Blue Hope Alliance (BHA), a coalition of groups using citizen science to protect marine ecosystems in the north-west Highlands. She says the community’s achievements in protecting underwater habitats was the “most amazing thing to happen to the Summer Isles. It is an archipelago that is made in heaven for breeding fish.” As a child, Ross remembers going out to sea for “boxes” of haddock, ling, pollack and cod – before populations declined. But she has seen recent signs of recovery. “There is more variety of fish being caught here than before,” she says. – anglers are catching haddock and cod.” Outside on the pier, a hardy angler on holiday from Glasgow who has braved the wind to catch what he can, is rewarded by three fresh mackerel. The recovery of scallop stocks, says Alasdair Hughson, a scallop diver, Scottish Creel Fishermen’s Federation (SCFF) chair and one of the BHA’s founders, has been “massive” and the seabed transformation like “night to day”. A decade ago, a boat supplying hand-dived scallops to his company, Keltic Seafare, would spend just two weeks in the Summer Isles. Hughson, whose firm supplies shellfish to UK restaurants, admits his business stands to gain from the dredge ban, but says hand-diving is more sustainable, a claim backed up by research from Open Seas. The marine conservation organisation found low-impact fishing methods, such as diving and creeling, are not only more sustainable than dredging or trawling but that more of the revenue generated stays in the local economy. Now, the Donna Marie creel boat, skippered by Ullapool-based Gary Lewis, runs to the Summer Isles almost all year. Lewis, who used to have to travel farther, to Skye and the Western Isles, before the dredge ban, says: “It’s not just the catch that’s improved, but the general health of the seabed.” Central to the weekend-long Maerl-Herring festival celebrations, which includes storytelling, artworks and film, is the public launch of a BHA report spanning a decade of citizen science studies. Jason Hall-Spencer, a professor of marine biology at Cyprus University of Technology, who wrote the report, says it shows the dredge ban in Wester Ross’s MPA, set up to protect the slow-growing maerl habitats and other marine features, has done its job. It has “protected the maerl to a massive extent” he says. Author of the Conservation Status of Maerl Habitats in north-west Scotland, partly funded by NatureScot, Hall-Spencer has carbon dated the maerl in the bay as 9,000 years old. “If scallop dredgers had spent the last 10 years going up and down here, the habitat would be obliterated,” he says. A single pass of heavy towed gear such as that used by scallop dredgers can crush or bury up to 70% of maerl. “The seabed is now incredibly rich. Maerl is a very important habitat, chock full of bivalves which provide food for skates and rays.” Peter Drake, 73, a retired prawn fisherman from Polbain, a hamlet that is part of Achiltibuie, was part of Sea Change Wester Ross, a campaign group supported by SCFF, which grew into BHA. “It’s good to remember what we have achieved here” says Drake. “There’s already an improvement in fish populations, but it will take time.” Orfhlaith McDevitt, 25, who has lived here for two-and-a-half years and runs Coigach Community rowing club, says: “People from the club say they see more minke whales, dolphins and porpoises than they did 10 years ago.” Years before Ocean, David Attenborough’s documentary, sparked outrage by showing footage of scallop dredgers bulldozing the seabed, causing damage that could be seen from space, Sea Change and the SCFF compiled a body of evidence of the devastation scallop dredgers were doing to fishing grounds and seabeds in Wester Ross. The dossier was presented to Scottish ministers in parliament. In 2016, despite fierce opposition by the dredging lobby, scallop dredging was forbidden by law in the Wester Ross MPA, now the biggest protected area in the world for maerl. Prawn trawling is permitted in designated areas, while hand-diving for scallops and creel fishing by local boats under 150 gross tons, is also permitted. The maerl’s three-dimensional structure allows high levels of oxygen, essential to scallops, and emits a chemical that attracts them. But threats to the ecosystem remain: the BHA surveys, also highlighted damaged maerl in some locations – from illegal dredgers and from invasive algal growth that scientists believe could be caused by nutrients from salmon farms. “We know that salmon farms put more nutrients into the water,” says Sara Nason, a journalist and documentary maker who founded Sea Change, which later became the BHA and organised the Maerl-Herring festival. The BHA has now launched a three-year project with more than £153,000 of support from the National Lottery Heritage Fund and additional funding from members of the North & West District Salmon Fishery Board, to continue its work. Elsehere, the battle for Scotland’s sea rages on. The Scottish government, which was criticised in June by the independent watchdog Environmental Standards Scotland for not fulfilling its legal duty to restore and protect the seabed, has launched a public consultation on improving protections for marine habitats and species inside and outside the MPA network. Theresa Ross, who runs Achiltibuie Stores for the community of about 250 people living along this stretch of coastline, says the MPA is “fully supported” by local people as it “ensures fishing is more sustainable”. But for a rural coastal community, where the sea supports livelihoods and few jobs exist, there are competing concerns, she says. “There are more people working on the fish farm here than fishermen,” says Ross, whose husband is one of about six fishers in the village, while her son is one of 10 working on the farms. “I support the status quo. But the fish farms are full-time jobs, guaranteed employment and well paid,” she says. “They are not weather dependent, like fishing.” Nevertheless, Nason is one of many who are delighted that the end to dredging has been such a success, describing the protection of the maerl beds as “beyond priceless … We’ve achieved recovery of the whole ecosystem.”

title: A fake image of a Georgia mayor kissing a person went viral. Can US voters trust everything they see?
summary: Deepfakes and misinformation driven by artificial intelligence have become a point of deep concern for legislators, advocates and the public
text: An image of Bianca Motley Broom, the mayor of College Park, Georgia, kissing a man who was not her husband in a bar spread far and wide on Facebook. The fact that it was fake is spreading faster, now, but only after it had been seen by thousands of people. “I think this is a sad commentary about where we are in our democracy, and where we are in our political discourse,” Motley Broom said. “It also seeks to reinforce really tired stereotypes about women in leadership.” Six years ago, when Motley Broom first took office in the Atlanta suburb, a political enemy might have needed at least rudimentary skill with image-editing software to forge an image of a politician in a compromising position. Today, all that is required is a computer and a prompt for an AI image generator. The threat of deepfakes and misinformation driven by artificial intelligence has become a point of deep concern for legislators, advocates and the public. A poll taken in mid-June by Rad Campaign, a digital marketing agency, and Women Who Tech, an advocacy organization for female entrepreneurs, showed that about 71% of respondents worry about AI-generated deepfakes and disinformation affecting elections, while two in three respondents said they were concerned about AI being used to sexualize women. “The findings show that Americans are more concerned about AI’s use in deepfakes, election disinformation, and the sexualization of women and children than its impact on jobs or the economy,” said Allyson Kapin, founder of the Rad Campaign and co-founder of Women Who Tech. The Trump administration has a penchant for deploying AI imagery. In January, the White House’s official account on the social media platform X posted a digitally altered image of Nekima Levy Armstrong, who had been arrested in connection with a demonstration that disrupted church services in St Paul, Minnesota. A picture of her calmly being escorted by a DHS agent was altered so that she appeared to be crying, and her skin had been darkened. Kaelan Dorr, the White House deputy communications director, later described the image as a “meme”. Fake images of Zohran Mamdami, New York’s mayor, also began circulating from a “parody” account on X in February, falsely depicting him and his mother in the company of the disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein. Using Google’s SynthID tool, Reuters debunked the images, but not before other accounts had recirculated them as authentic, fueling conspiracy theories. Despite significant apprehension around the potential economic consequences of AI, concern about deepfake images being used to sexualize women or children, or to influence elections, outstrips concern about AI affecting jobs by about three to one, Kapin said. “The public is deeply concerned,” she said. Fact from fiction Raphael Warnock, a Georgia Democratic senator, said in a video posted to Facebook that deepfake images had been circulating online falsely depicting him with health problems, with an armful of grandchildren he does not have – and with a full head of hair, which he said was funny, if problematic. “As these tools become increasingly powerful, it will get harder and harder to distinguish fact from fiction, and there are already bad actors out there, who are doing everything they can to divide us and confuse us,” Warnock said. “This has huge implications for our democracy. What if hours before an election, someone created a page with AI-generated images, fake stories about the candidates – how will voters know what’s true, and what’s not true?” Warnock is among a group of Senate Democrats who have been war-gaming political responses to possible election interference scenarios. Chief among those scenarios: disinformation driven by fabricated images or videos circulated through social media. The outgoing US senator John Kennedy, a Louisiana Republican, offered a bill last week requiring AI firms to install a “kill switch” for rogue AI. Senator Rand Paul of Kentucky blocked Kennedy’s bill, describing the effort as premature without additional industry input. Hakeem Jeffries, the Democratic House minority leader, said in an interview earlier this month on SiriusXM that government should move “urgently” on AI regulations, broadly, calling for “guardrails to protect the American people from bad actors and bad behavior”, adding: “It should be a high priority.” Jeffries noted that Republicans attempted to pass legislation pre-empting states from regulating AI last year, as part of the omnibus One Big Beautiful Bill. The amendment failed on a 99-1 vote in the Senate. State legislatures are also wrestling with AI regulation amid a widespread, bipartisan public backlash. Some states have legislation like Tennessee’s Ensuring Likeness Voice and Image Security Act – the Elvis Act – which protects politicians and residents alike from AI voice cloning and digital likeness replication, using the state’s robust right-of-publicity protections that are a product of Nashville’s recording industry. Clear disclaimers are legally required in most states when a political campaign uses AI to manipulate the speeches, appearances or actions of officials or candidates. Georgia is not one of them. While legislators in Georgia began debating deepfake protections in bills proposed in 2024 and 2025, they have not yet enacted legislation. Motley Broom said she believed she was targeted by political opponents who objected to her role as a past president of the Georgia Municipal Association. “I have worked for my city to try to be the best advocate I can be on behalf of College Park,” Motley Broom said. “And I certainly won’t be deterred by internet trolls who think this carries weight.” While she could consider legal action under existing defamation law in Georgia, Motley Broom paused for a moment when asked what legislators should be doing about this. The first amendment protection for speech has to be considered, she said. “These types of attacks should not be without consequences,” she said. “I hope that lawmakers can address this in a way that balances not only first amendment protections, but the right of an individual not to have completely false accusations being levied. And I’m really hopeful that … lawmakers on the state and federal level can think about that and think about it carefully, because this is the tip of the iceberg.”

title: Greggs announces plans to shut four UK factories that could cost 740 jobs
summary: Bakery chain, whose sales are up 7.7%, says move is necessary to provide growth in ‘most cost-efficient manner’
text: Greggs has announced plans to close four of its factories, in a move that could result in 740 job losses over the next two and a half years. The bakery chain said it was consulting on the closures, which would initially cost £60m when including disruption costs and redundancy payments but then could create £20m of savings each year by 2028. The proposed cuts come as Greggs reported stronger sales growth in its most recent quarter at 7.7%, up from 7.2% in the first half of the year. The company said the closures, “while difficult, are necessary” to ensure it can grow in the “most cost-efficient manner”. It said: “Our immediate priority is to minimise the impact on our people where possible. We will enter into a consultation period shortly to work with trade unions and employee representatives of those affected to refine and develop these proposals.” The closures could affect factories in Enfield, north London, Penrith in Cumbria, Kelso in Roxburghshire, Scotland, and Seaham in County Durham. It will continue to run distribution operations from Enfield. The proposals could also affect manufacturing operations at its Treforest site in Wales, but this will continue as a distribution centre for business. Greggs has grown to become Britain’s biggest fast-food business thanks to the popularity of its low-cost pastries, cakes and hot drinks. It has expanded rapidly this year, with 57 net new openings, as part of its plan to open between 100 and 110 shops by the end of 2026. Iced matcha lattes and a bigger range of salads and chicken rolls also helped to boost sales over the summer, the company said. However, Greggs told investors on Wednesday that while stronger sales had “modestly improved” its outlook for this year, “there are signs of greater inflationary pressures in 2027”. Alex Pugh, an analyst at the investment broker Freetrade, said that while the bakery chain “has survived a heatwave and a cost of living crisis … a £1.50 sausage roll could be a real test of loyalty”. Earlier this year the company raised the cost of its bestseller sausage roll by 5p, taking it to £1.35 in most shops. It also increased the price of a latte by 10p, taking it to £2.25, as it looked for ways to combat rising wage, energy and packaging costs. Shares in Greggs rose by 7.3% in early trading on Wednesday morning, making it the best performer across the mid-cap FTSE 250 index and taking its year-to-date rise to 17%. Greggs, which is headquartered in Newcastle, employs more than 33,000 people around the UK.

title: New Orleans judge files police complaint against CBS affiliate over reporting
summary: Kimya Holmes’s police report over a news segment on a real-estate transaction invokes law that no longer exists
text: A New Orleans state court judge filed a police complaint against a local CBS affiliate after it aired a segment scrutinizing a real-estate transaction in which she was involved, with the jurist invoking a section of law that no longer carries criminal penalties, according to the journalist who reported the story. The situation centering on New Orleans criminal court judge Kimya Holmes and investigative reporter David Hammer was only the latest in a series of high-profile matters pitting Louisiana journalists against members of the state’s court system. Deputies at the New Orleans criminal courthouse handcuffed Hammer’s WWL Louisiana colleague, investigative producer Danny Monteverde, and an attorney for their station – Elana Beiser – in early July while the outlet covered an indictment filed against the state’s attorney general, which was ultimately dismissed. And in August, a state court jury awarded a $300,000 verdict to the Louisiana supreme court justice Jeff Hughes, who sued the Advocate newspaper for libel over an editorial – an outcome some US press freedom defenders fear could weaken the “actual malice” legal standard which has long governed such cases. Hammer, whose channel is a Guardian reporting partner, published a 24 August story exploring how a $765,000 home was donated to Holmes in 2025 by a man to whom she was engaged at the time. Holmes’s then fiance, accountant Arthur Allen, had been criminally charged weeks earlier with fraudulently collecting more than $712,000 in Covid-19 pandemic relief that was taxpayer-funded. The judge told Hammer she didn’t start dating or become engaged to Allen until four years after he had committed the crime for which he was charged. She maintained she didn’t learn about his charges until close to the time he pleaded guilty in April – after the couple had broken up. Hammer’s report on Holmes, Allen and the gated community home he donated to her – in which she continued to live while he paid the mortgage – arrived as she prepared for a tough 3 November re-election race against a fellow judge whose section of court was eliminated by a new law. And on 10 September, a little more than two weeks after Hammer’s story, the New Orleans criminal courthouse’s judicial administrator sent WWL a letter demanding it remove a public record showing the address of the house Allen gave Holmes, the outlet reported on Tuesday. Judicial administrator Robert Kazik’s letter furthermore demanded that WWL remove images of the license plate number of a Corvette leased by Allen that had been photographed by a station source while it was parked in the courthouse garage in August. Kazik’s letter also requested that WWL reveal who photographed the Corvette. Kazik’s letter cited a Louisiana law that gave “third parties” including the news media three days to unpublish certain kinds of personal information about a judge once a judicial administrator requested it. It also made violations of that law a misdemeanor crime punishable by up to 90 days’ imprisonment and a $1,000 fine. Yet the Louisiana legislature repealed both the portions of the law requiring news outlets to remove published information and making it a misdemeanor if they don’t do so. Those repeals took effect on 1 August – before Hammer’s reporting on Holmes’s donated house as well as Kazik’s letter. Hammer reported on Tuesday that WWL reacted to Kazik’s letter by having videos with the information that the judicial administrator mentioned taken offline on the morning of 11 September. The outlet reposted them later with the address and license plate numbers blurred. Nonetheless, WWL said it refused to disclose who photographed the Corvette. And on 11 September, Holmes filed a criminal complaint with the New Orleans police department (NOPD) against WWL for allegedly “revealing her home address and vehicle information”. The outlet sought comment on the police complaint from New Orleans media lawyer Scott Sternberg, who lobbied for the repeals that took effect in the beginning of August. Sternberg, who represented the Advocate newspaper against the state supreme court justice Hughes, said he believed the repeals were necessary because those portions were “wildly unconstitutional”, with press freedom being a fundamental US right. “I can’t imagine a public official filing a criminal complaint in response to reporting that, based on my own opinion of it, seems to be accurate,” Sternberg remarked. “I mean – it was a real estate transaction.” Hammer confirmed that the accuracy of his reporting on Holmes and Allen was never challenged, prompting Sternberg to say “it wouldn’t warrant a criminal complaint” even if it had been inaccurate. Sternberg added that neither Kazik’s letter nor the police complaint “had any force or effect and that’s probably why … NOPD isn’t coming down here to arrest you – because there hasn’t been a crime”. Hammer said WWL asked Holmes’s campaign spokesperson what the legal basis of the criminal complaint against the station was. The outlet also asked if Holmes knew that her complaint relied on a section of law that was no longer on the books. The spokesperson replied with an email forwarded by Holmes that in part had an out-of-date version of the relevant law attached to it. That version of the law – still carrying the criminal penalties – came from Louisiana’s legislative website which had not been updated according to records from the state legislature’s most recent session. A state legislature spokesperson told WWL that updating laws on the legislative website can take “many months”. The spokesperson also pointed to a website disclaimer which made “no guarantee … to its accuracy” – and said “these provisions and annotations have not been edited for publication and are not official or authoritative”. The email which Holmes forwarded originally came from state appellate court judge Tiffany Gautier Chase on 26 August, two days after Hammer’s report on the house donated by Allen. Chase’s email notified judges of “protections against the dissemination of certain personal information”. WWL reported that its attorney, Mary Ellen Roy, wrote to the NOPD to make sure the detective assigned to Holmes’s complaint was aware of the updated law. Roy also wrote to the NOPD that WWL expected the detective’s investigation into the judge’s complaint “to be closed, forthwith”. The NOPD said on Tuesday that its investigation into WWL was continuing.
