title: Country diary: The land here is scarred from a year of hard weather – now what will winter hold? | Alexandra Pearce-Broomhead
summary: Camborne, Cornwall: There will be more storms like Goretti and more fires next summer, but we can make the landscape more resilient
text: A grey wagtail flits at the stream’s edge, its flaxen underbelly matching the woodland’s autumn swatch. A few months ago, this bird may have struggled to catch a midge or water snail here, after the streambed nearly ran dry. Sitting by the water now, it’s easy to forget the damage this area suffered this year. But the land remembers. Many months on from Storm Goretti, the entrance to these woods is still a battlefield of fallen trees, Scots pines and ageing oaks torn ungainly from the ground. Just over a mile away, a gorse break is still scarred from a late-summer wildfire that blackened the coastline. I stopped by the other day; the western gorse should have been blooming, delicate coconut notes luring in late pollinators. Instead, their petrified remains jutted lifelessly out towards the sea. The common denominator in all this is the climate crisis, and yet, in our severely nature-depleted country, the natural world itself can help minimise the damage, if we give it half a chance. Just over the border in Devon, the Dartmoor Headwaters Project has shown how native woodland increases water infiltration compared with nearby grazed pasture, and how restoring peatland can improve water storage; both have helped to slow runoff during heavy rainfall. At Woodland Valley Farm, near Truro, the introduction of beavers has also helped with water storage and absorption into the floodplain. Farther north, in Tywi Forest, up in the Cambrian mountains, rewetted peatlands have proved resilient to fires, thanks in part to sphagnum moss. And the mix of hazel and sweet chestnut canopies rustling above me, in high heat, will offer just the sort of cover that cools the air, provided we preserve and plant them. All this just scratches the surface of what can be done. Looking at this stream now, I wonder what the future holds. One intense winter storm could bring yet more damage, and next summer the threat of wildfires will arrive once more. We know it’s coming, but while we cannot control the weather, we can influence how the land copes with it. The grey wagtail disappears, leaving the stream to purl steadily on. • Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024, is available now at guardianbookshop.com

title: Tokyo succumbs to ‘rain fatigue’ after a record 35 consecutive days of showers
summary: The record rainfall has been blamed on a combination of climate change and El Niño, which has created a prolonged high pressure front in the Pacific
text: Residents of Tokyo awoke to a familiar sound on Wednesday: raindrops splashing against windows and balcony floors. The Japanese capital has seen a record 35 consecutive days of rain that experts blame on a combination of climate change and El Niño, which has created a prolonged front of high pressure in the Pacific Ocean. The record rainfall has triggered a sharp rise in the price of vegetables, cast a shadow over tourism and left millions of Tokyoites wondering if they will see sunshine again. Central Tokyo has been drenched by 629mm (24.8 inches) of rain between the start of September through to Monday this week, nearly three times the normal level, according to the agency. It experienced just 45.8 hours of sunshine over the same period, the second lowest on record, the Mainichi Shimbun said, while on 14 days the sun did not appear at all. The weather is affecting people’s physical and mental health, according to Hiromichi Ito, a doctor and director of a clinic in the capital, who told the Sankei Shimbun newspaper that prolonged rain, low atmospheric pressure and high humidity can lead to headaches, dizziness and other symptoms. While the rain had turned to a light drizzle by late Wednesday morning, more could be on the way, as this year’s El Niño warms the Pacific Ocean, intensifying extreme weather patterns triggered by the climate crisis. “Autumn rain fronts are staying longer than usual,” Masayuki Kyoda, an official at the Japan meteorological agency (JMA), told Agence France-Presse. Tokyo’s rainy season usually occurs in June, but there have been regular downpours throughout the summer, causing heavy flooding in parts of the region. Earlier this month, Typhoon Dujuan caused flooding and landslides in neighbouring Chiba prefecture, killing eight people and destroying dozens of homes. This week, meteorological officials said another typhoon, the 26th of the season, was moving in a north-easterly direction and could brush the Kanto region, where Tokyo is located. While Kyoda said it was difficult to establish a direct link between climate change and the streak of wet weather in Tokyo – the longest since records began in 1886 – the agency said in a recent report that “global warming was affecting Japan’s weather long-term, including through more precipitation”. The previous longest period of consecutive rain in Tokyo lasted 33 days between 27 June and 29 July 2019. The prolonged rainfall has triggered a rise in the price of vegetables, particularly leafy greens, as a result of crop damage in agricultural regions near Tokyo, media reports said, with one supermarket worker in the capital quoted as saying that price of a head of lettuce had more than doubled to ¥450 (£2.17). Residents also complained of not being able to dry their washing, forcing them to make trips to the local launderette. The news that the city has not enjoyed a single dry day since 27 August prompted many take to social media to complain of “rain fatigue”. “This endless rain must be to blame for my low mood,” said one X user. “If you’re feeling worn out, it’s not your fault.” Yojiro Noda, the lead singer of the band Radwimps, posted to his 1.1 million followers: “Tokyo, a lifetime of rain.” Another wondered if the city would match the 40 days and 40 nights of rain referenced in the Old Testament. • This article was amended on 30 September 2026. An earlier version said that central Tokyo experienced just “45.8 hours of daylight” between the start of September and 28 September; that should have said 45.8 hours of sunshine.

title: Economic growth and democratic decline: the ‘cotton king’ who reshaped Benin
summary: Patrice Talon has transformed the west African country’s economy and infrastructure at the expense of political freedom
text: In recent years, a building boom has reshaped Benin’s largest city, Cotonou, and a shiny new coastal road has reduced journey times to Ouidah, the west African country’s spiritual and cultural capital. In the last decade, Benin’s annual GDP has grown from 3% to 6%, a regional high, and an industrial zone has been launched north-west of Cotonou to help industrialise the relatively small nation’s largely informal economy. “Benin is now looking like a paradise,” said Savossou Stanislas, a 40-year-old tyre repairer in the official capital, Porto-Novo. The rapid infrastructural development has been overseen by Patrice Talon, the president from 2016 till this May. For years, Benin was so content being in the shadow of Nigeria, a neighbour about eight times its size and with about 16 times its population, that Talon’s predecessor, Thomas Boni Yayi, once quipped during a visit to Abuja that “Benin is the 37th state of Nigeria”. Talon, who also enjoys good relations with Nigeria and called on it to help quell an attempted coup d’etat in December, chose a different path: to engineer enough growth for Benin to be recognised in its own right. The Kagame model Widely believed to be Benin’s richest person, Talon, known as “the cotton king”, made his name in agriculture but diversified into banking and hospitality. Before becoming president, he had financed the campaigns of Yayi and Yayi’s predecessor, Mathieu Kérékou. Critics say his development agenda has come at a severe cost: once held up as a poster child for democratic transition in west Africa, Benin has also undergone democratic decline since Talon took power. In many respects, Talon modelled his governance style on the leader of another relatively small African country: Paul Kagame. The archetypal “benevolent strongman”, Rwanda’s de facto leader since 1994 has also combined repression with policies aimed at economic and social transformation. In time, the two men became allies and Talon even appointed two former Rwandan officials to head sensitive Beninese government agencies. Benin has also sought the east African nation’s help in countering a growing insurgency along the border with Nigeria. By the end of Talon’s first term, strict new election laws and heavy registration fees had purged a lot of the opposition from parliament. In 2019, the government shut down the internet during a parliamentary election as people protested against the changes. The judiciary was co-opted to muzzle dissent, resulting in the targeting of several dozen former allies and dissidents, including the opposition leader Reckya Madougou, who is in prison on charges of “undermining the state”, and the journalist Hugues Comlan Sossoukpé. In April 2021, a month after Madougou’s arrest, Essowé Batamoussi, a judge at the court for the repression of economic offences and terrorism, resigned his post and fled to France to seek asylum. “There was no justice in her [Madougou’s] case,” Batamoussi said. “We received an empty file and a threat: if we did not put her in jail, we were in danger.” Last November, it became apparent how deeply Talon had control of every major aspect of life in Benin. A controversial constitutional amendment, the second of his tenure, elongated the presidential term from five years to seven and introduced thresholds that kept opposition parties outside parliament. It also created a new senate, whose members are all appointed by government rather than elected. Within a month of parliament approving the amendment, mutineers led by a former commander of the national guard attempted a coup, citing Talon’s authoritarianism and inability to tackle rising insecurity. Only one opposition candidate was approved to stand in April’s presidential election, which was won by Talon’s hand-picked successor, Romuald Wadagni, with more than 94% of the vote. In August, Talon himself returned to centre stage as president of the senate. Morgan Assogba, a Cotonou-based geopolitical analyst, described Talon as a “gigantic political actor with a good understanding of how politics works in Benin”, who had reshaped the political arena to suit his economic development drive. For Guillaume Moumouni, a professor of political science and international relations at the University of Abomey-Calavi, Talon’s dual policies of constitutional change and development constituted a “carrot and stick” approach to governing, aimed at ensuring the political environment did not jeopardise his economic objectives. In time, however, he added, there was “less carrot and more stick” as freedoms were increasingly suppressed. What price progress? During his campaign for the April election, Wadagni vowed to tackle extreme poverty, a tacit admission that economic growth had not been to the benefit of all Beninese. The minimum monthly wage increased from 40,000 CFA francs to 52,000 CFA francs (£52-£68) in January 2023, but many still earn far less. In recent years, rent and electricity tariffs have also risen by at least 15%, while the price of fuel has almost doubled. “With the upcoming school term, we don’t know how we’ll manage,” said Stanislas, the tyre repairer, who has four children of school age. Most of the development has been in Cotonou and Ouidah, Talon’s home town. Opposition figures have said there has been a lack of transparency in some of those projects, while civil society groups said some were awarded to entities linked to Talon’s political allies and business network. According to a 2023 report by Amnesty International, four development projects resulted in mass forced evictions that affected at least 6,000 people. The communication ministry was approached for comment. Moumouni said economically Talon’s vision had brought net progress. “People are not gaining or enjoying much more in terms of cash, but they are enjoying [progress] in terms of social infrastructure,” he said. “There’s room for improvement for sure but compared to 10 or 15 years ago, there is quite a huge difference.” Eugène Azatassou, the vice-president of the opposition Democrats party, feels differently. “Development cannot be limited to roads and buildings,” he said. “It must also be measured by the quality of democracy, purchasing power, employment, security, improvement of living conditions … when a power continuously modifies political and electoral rules in order to conserve control of institutions, we have the right to ask ourselves if we are facing [only] a facade of development.”

title: Tern turnaround: colonies in England show signs of recovery after decline
summary: National Trust says latest figures encouraging – with numbers of birds on the rise – but work still to be done
text: England’s most important tern colonies are showing signs of recovery after being hit by years of bird flu, flooding and increasingly unpredictable weather, new figures from the National Trust reveal. The trust reported record numbers of little terns at Long Nanny in Northumberland, one of the UK’s most important breeding sites for what is the country’s second-rarest breeding seabird. Numbers are also slightly up for arctic terns, the long distance superstars of the avian world that annually breed in places such as Northumberland before making the incredible journey south to Antarctica. In Norfolk, more than 1,100 pairs of sandwich terns returned to breed at Blakeney Point after a two-year absence. Ben McCarthy, the trust’s head of nature conservation, stressed there was no room for complacency. But he said the figures showed “what can be achieved when internationally important breeding sites are carefully protected and managed. “These results are particularly encouraging given the challenges seabirds have faced in recent years – from avian flu and extreme weather to wider pressures on the marine environment.” The trust said there had been a “remarkable turnaround” for little terns at Long Nanny with at least 126 pairs nesting – doubling the previous site record. At least 82 chicks are known to have fledged with the final total potentially exceeding 100 birds, rangers said. Little terns are a particularly sensitive and vulnerable species that migrate from west Africa to breed, making nests, known as scrapes, on open sandy beaches. The species had experienced “significant long-term declines nationally, making this year’s record breeding season especially significant”, the trust said. The arctic tern colony at Long Nanny consisted of at least 730 breeding pairs this year with nests containing 1,346 eggs. That was slightly up and a sign of numbers “holding steady” after a torrid past few years for the species. In 2023, Long Nanny’s arctic tern colony was devastated by avian flu, when rangers found more than 600 dead chicks. In recent seasons nests have been lost to high spring tides and extreme weather, the trust said. James Porteus, the trust’s lead ranger for the Northumberland coast, said it was “incredibly encouraging” to see little terns doing so well, calling it an “exceptional season” after several years “dominated by bird flu outbreaks, flooded nests and concerns about declining numbers”. He added: “To more than double the previous site record for breeding pairs is a remarkable achievement and a testament to the dedication of staff, volunteers and partner organisations who help protect the colony each year. “It’s especially exciting to see so many chicks hatching and fledging. Little terns face huge challenges throughout their migration and breeding cycle, so every successful nesting attempt matters.” Rangers in Northumberland also reported the return, for the seventh consecutive breeding season, of a black tern they have called Nigella. Black terns are not normally found breeding in the UK. The trust stressed that the picture for breeding seabirds was “not universally positive”, pointing to a 27% fall in arctic tern numbers on the Farne Islands, Northumberland. Also there were no common terns there this year compared with five last year while sandwich tern numbers remained unchanged at two breeding pairs.

title: ‘I just saw this furry brown bottom disappear!’ In search of Samba – the fearless fugitive capybara
summary: Six months ago, Samba made a brave, unprecedented escape from Marwell zoo. Her life on the lam continues today. We join the team hunting desperately to find her in the Hampshire countryside
text: Samba the capybara is still at large. Along with her older sister, Tango, the intrepid rodent made her escape from Marwell zoo in Winchester in March. Tango all but gave herself up on day two; Samba broke for the marshy wetlands of the River Itchen. Word spread and within days the fugitive was an international social media star. But despite an intense search, the dense Hampshire countryside has afforded her a haven. Six months on, Samba remains elusive. Marwell’s staff still aren’t sure how the capybaras escaped, although they have their suspicions. Tango and Samba were born on Jimmy’s Farm and Wildlife Park in Suffolk in the summer of 2025. They arrived at Marwell zoo on Monday 16 March, to great excitement. “They were a little bit shy when they got here, as you would expect,” says Laura Read, the chief executive of Marwell Wildlife. “But they were fine.” They were immediately placed in a quarantined habitat, as is standard procedure for new arrivals. The plan was to keep them there for 30 days. The next day, the vet and zookeepers did their morning checks and everything was fine. But when they returned that afternoon, Samba and Tango had vanished. “There was no sign of them digging out – they don’t dig – and there was no sign of them chewing their way out,” says Darren Ives, a senior zookeeper who has been at Marwell for 15 years. He’s a member of the hoofstock team, who are responsible for “horses, equids, that kind of stuff … basically anything that’s big and shits a lot”. That includes capybaras – which are native to most of South America – although rather than hooves they have partly webbed toes. “We think they really squeezed under a tiny gap in a gate,” says Read. “That’s the only explanation we have.” After 30 minutes of searching the enclosure, the alarm was raised. “In a situation like this, we are really well versed and have set drills that we practise regularly around animal escape.” When an animal escapes at Marwell, a call identifying the species and type of emergency is sent out over the zoo’s radio network. Staff then send out searchers, contact the relevant authorities (Natural England, Winchester city council, the police) and mobilise drone support (provided by the University of Southampton, which Marwell already works with on population mapping conservation projects). Every species has its own emergency procedure, which includes determining whether a firearm response is required. Despite being the world’s largest rodents, capybaras do not demand a firearm response. The search was initially confined to Marwell zoo’s 57 hectares (140 acres). By the evening, staff had located two warm bodies inside a dense section of tree and bush clippings used for composting. Neither was reachable. As dusk turned to night, staff did their best to secure the perimeter, laid out some food and left. The next morning, Tango left the compost pile and was captured with throwing nets (“without trying to stress her out too much,” says Read). Samba, however, had vanished. Later that day, Marwell heard that Samba, who is about the size of a spaniel, had been spotted near the Ship Inn pub in Owslebury, nearly 2 miles away. A convoy of Land Rovers set off with transport crates and nets, while farmers were contacted to ask for permission to cross their land. Or, as Ives puts it: “In about five minutes, someone in Marwell uniform will be walking across – don’t shoot them.” Read convened a crisis meeting, which looked at the threats to Samba’s wellbeing. “It was cars,” she says. “She’s got no natural predators here. She’s too big. We knew she’d probably seek out water as well, and they’re fantastic swimmers. Water would be her sanctuary.” The decision was made to go public. Was there any hesitation? “That was the quickest way to find her and secure her welfare, so no. Our PR, you know, in terms of: ‘We’ve lost an animal,’ came second.” Local people poured out to look for Samba, including a woman with a trained search dog. “But, in hindsight, did all that activity drive her further away from our direct locality?” Read wonders. By Friday, the local press was taking an interest, then social media, with waves of AI capybara memes appearing. Soon, the story was being reported as far away as the US and Australia. Glenn Moores also joined the search after seeing the hunt on social media. “I had a bunch of drones and a skill set that could help.” He runs Digital Fauna, a company that conducts wildlife surveys with drones, mostly counting deer (“there’s far more deer than anyone even estimated,” he says). Moores’ involvement has been pivotal, says Ives. “It meant that he could search areas and go: ‘Don’t bother looking there.’” Staff would have to respond to every credible sighting, but “until we had him, we were literally just on foot … walking like a police search when they’re looking for a lost person.” Such was the quality of Moore’s thermal imaging that he was able to detect rats. “We were going out at six in the morning, we were going out at night, we were walking the fields around the river,” says Moores. “It’s amazing that nobody saw Samba in that time.” Is he surprised how hard it has been to find her? “I’m used to counting deer at night, so we’re not strangers to finding animals about the size of a capybara with thermal imaging. That’s what we do. But finding one specific animal in an entire landscape is very different.” How long has he spent hunting for Samba? “My goodness. Days, days and days. Probably about three weeks’ worth of evenings.” His selflessness is not lost on the Marwell team. “All of his time has been given for free!” says Read, appreciatively. (Moores says he wants a free pass to the zoo.) On Sunday morning, five days after Samba vanished from her enclosure, a member of the public was walking along the bank of the Itchen in Twyford when she spotted a capybara sunning herself. Then her dog, Growler, chased Samba into the river. The video she took of the incident found its way to Marwell and the focus of the search shifted: staff donned waders and mounted paddleboards. On land, they looked for tracks, droppings, a body. They flushed out barn owls, deer, a pheasant, but no capybara. Read is convinced she caught a flash of her. “I just saw this brown furry bottom disappear into the river.” For the next week, the search was constant: at least six people a day, mornings and nights. “Everything went really quiet,” says Read. “We just couldn’t find any trace of her.” *** Six months later, my own trip to Marwell begins with a capybara hunt. Peering into their enclosure – a mixed wetland habitat they share with two swamp-dwelling antelopes called sitatungas – I can’t spot Tango or her new companion, Ripple, a seven-year-old male. “They’re in there, definitely. Don’t worry,” says Read, who has just come from proofreading a press release about a monkey vasectomy performed at the zoo. It’s easy to see how Samba has evaded capture: “Try that in acres and acres and acres of an SSSI [site of special scientific interest] along the Itchen.” Ten minutes later, Tango and Ripple waddle out to the grazing area. Ripple was brought in from a zoo in Blackpool a few months after the escape – partly to breed with Tango, but mostly to keep her company. Capybaras are sociable animals, Ives says, used to living in packs of between 10 and 20. Ripple is calmer and much bigger than Tango – the size of a small sheep, he weighs about 40kg. Capybaras can start breeding once they are about a year old and Tango has already started showing signs that she is in the mood to do so. “When you put the two of them together, they seem to complement each other,” says Ives. So, how has Samba evaded capture for so long? For one, her biology. Capybaras are quick. “The things that would hunt these guys [in their native habitat] are jaguars. They need to be able to outrun them,” says Ives. Capybaras are quite angular, he says, making them streamlined when running – it’s an explosive speed, rather than one sustained over long distances. When chased, they head towards water and dive, barely breaking the water’s surface as they do so. Submerged, they can hold their breath for up to five minutes, or furtively breach the surface revealing just their eyes, ears and nose. “They’re designed to be quite stealthy. They’re very good at hiding in the undergrowth.” Is Samba a danger to the public? “They’ve got a cracking set of teeth,” says Ives. “If she were to bite you, she’d probably take your finger off. But also if you get that close – I mean you’re doing better than us! – she would just run away. She would see you, smell you, hear you way before you see her.” As Read says, capybaras have “a reputation, shall we say, for being quite slippery customers in the zoo world”. Also in Samba’s favour is her likeness to local wildlife, particularly muntjac deer. Marwell set up a hotline for sightings. “We had everything from: ‘We’ve seen her dead on the side of the M3,’ to: ‘She’s in my back garden,’” says Read. “We had one man who was absolutely adamant that she was in his back garden and was behaving weirdly. And we were like: ‘Right!’ We went down there … and it was a hedgehog.” Some calls came from as far away as Stonehenge, about 40 miles away. More frustrating were the prank calls from drunk people in the middle of the night. “You very quickly got the gist of who was serious,” Read says. (If you think you have seen Samba, take a picture, record your exact location and send it to the zoo.) In August, Marwell received an image of a rodent-like creature from a camera trap used to spot poachers. The zoo set up its own cameras and a week later received unmistakable proof of life. The first image: a hairy, rotund animal bottom. The second: Samba. “Without a doubt, that’s our girl looking fat and healthy,” says Read. She was two to three miles away from the zoo, near where she had been chased by Growler. “It’s an ideal location for her to stay and disappear,” says Ives. The plan now is to make Samba feel comfortable in that area, allowing the keepers to narrow their search. They want to tempt her back to the same spot repeatedly with food (sweet potato and honeydew melons, apparently). They have laid more camera traps and put down bedding used by Tango and Ripple to see if she is enticed by their scent. Read and her team insist they are doing everything they can, but interest in Samba has brought with it criticism of the zoo. “It’s been really upsetting for me and for the team, because we know how hard we’re working, still, on bringing Samba back,” says Read. “A lot of what we’re doing isn’t necessarily publicly visible, because it is things like drone flights at 6am, it’s camera traps, it’s someone sitting at a desk reviewing camera-trap footage hour after hour. It’s scientifically grid-mapping where we’re camera-trapping. We know that loads of boots on the ground will just drive her further away.” She dismisses accusations of carelessness. “We’ve been here for 50 years. Our record speaks for itself. We’re award-winning for our animal welfare. No one did this because of carelessness. No one did this because they couldn’t be bothered or didn’t do their job properly. This happened because an animal did something that we could not have foreseen it doing.” As for whether Marwell should have capybaras in the first place: “Just because the capybara itself is not an endangered species doesn’t mean that the ecosystems and the habitats that they occupy aren’t under threat,” says Read. The Amazon and Pantanal – the capybaras’ native habitats – are under threat and Read believes capybaras could be used to tell that story, not least because they are trendy and draw a crowd. “With the caveat that their welfare needs to be exceptionally well met,” says Read. “Yes, they’re here for conservation, for breeding programmes, for insurance and all the rest of it, but also they’re here to tell a story and to inspire people.” Samba’s story will help with that, she hopes. “We are a conservation charity first and foremost,” says Read. “We are hands-on with our conservation work. We don’t just make donations to NGOs. We have teams in the field doing the work. We want to be really famous for the great work that we do and if Samba is one way of us doing that, then great. We’d like to shine a light on that as well as ‘we’ve lost a capybara’.” She pauses. “Although we did. We own that.” Winter could prove crucial: with less vegetation, Samba may be easier to spot, but capybaras are not built for harsh weather. Is it a race against time? “If we got a really cold snap, we’d all be pretty worried,” says Read. If, on the other hand, it’s just “wet and windy, she’ll be fine with that. It’s more that we have no control over her welfare out in the world, whereas here we can give her everything she needs, including socialisation.” Are they confident they’ll find her? “Well, technically, we’ve already found her!” says Ives. “We’ve seen her on the camera-trap footage. She’s very chunky. She’s very healthy.” If they do catch her, a reunion with her sister beckons. “But when – when, not if – we get her back, it’s going to be a very slow process to mix them, because she’s now a wild animal.” How much longer she stays that way remains to be seen. For Samba, the net is closing in. • Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Can a mushroom make music? Devon exhibition explores ‘cultural world’ of fungi
summary: Exeter museum to host DJ’s ‘collaboration’ with woodland fungi and artist’s map of her own body’s mycobiome
text: For one of the installations, a musician spent hours in woodland “collaborating” with fungi to create a soundscape inspired by the electricity they emit. Another is a kinetic sculpture of an extinct fungus that honours Beatrix Potter not for her tales of mischievous rabbits but for her lesser-known skills as a mycologist – a fungi expert. These are just two of the exhibits playing starring roles in a rather extraordinary contemporary art show called Living Labyrinths, at the Royal Albert Memorial Museum & Art Gallery (RAMM) in Exeter, aiming to celebrate the “cultural world” of fungi. Lara Goodband, the contemporary art curator at the RAMM, said it had been five years in the making. She suggested the south-west England was a good place to focus on fungi. “We have great weather for it, warm and damp,” Goodband said. “But also, I think people here have a special affinity for fungi.” She said a wide range of people in the south-west were fungi fans, from the ecologists who study the role they play in soil health to the ravers who enjoy the hallucinogenic properties of some mushrooms and the storytellers who work with the fairytale associations of toadstools. RAMM is also an excellent place for this deep dive because of its Victorian collections of fungi. Specimens of stinkhorn and bird’s nest fungi appear alongside the modern pieces. Goodband said interest in fungi had risen sharply over the past few years, partly after the success of Merlin Sheldrake’s book Entangled Life, which argued fungi provided a key understanding to the planet. “I think we’ve hit a moment,” said Goodband. Among the highlights is a sound installation by the musician, composer and DJ Jason Singh, who spent hours hunkered down in two Devon woods, Fingle and Yarner, for his piece, The Intelligence Below. He said he used biofeedback sensors to measure the electricity coming from mycelium – the rootlike networks of fungi – and translated these into sound. Singh said: “So all the notes that you are hearing are translations of voltage being emitted from the living thing. This is music being generated by the living system of the mushroom. “I’m interested in this idea that all living things generate and vibrate. This is a way for us to try to tune into and connect with other living things.” Singh said he did get some odd looks from passersby when he was out in the woods collaborating with fungi. “But it’s magical being in a space recording mushrooms.” Visitors to the exhibition will also be able to see watercolour studies by Beatrix Potter loaned by the Victoria and Albert Museum. Her work was overlooked in her lifetime but is recognised by modern mycologists. Near them is a recent work called In Balance by the artist Jo Pearl based on a fungus called Potteromyces asteroxylicola, named after Potter in 2023 when it was identified in the collections of the Natural History Museum. Another new piece is by Gemma Anderson-Tempini, who worked with scientists from the University of Exeter’s MRC Centre for Medical Mycology to create a map of her own mycobiome, the fungi dwelling within the human body. Like Singh, Anderson-Tempini ventured out into the Devon landscape to gather material for her piece, Myco-Mother, 2026. She collected pieces of red sandstone from Exmouth and chocolate-brown soil from Killerton, which she ground up to create the watercolours she used. Anderson-Tempini believes her work is a first. “Every one of us is carrying a fungal ecology and until now nobody had drawn it,” she said. “Fungi is fashionable but Sheldrake and the rest stayed outside the body in forests and soil. This work turns it inward.” Living Labyrinths opens on 3 October and runs until 21 February. • This article was amended on 30 September 2026. An earlier version said that Lara Goodband was head curator at the Royal Albert Memorial Museum & Art Gallery; she is contemporary art curator.

title: Ukraine war briefing: Nato condemns Moscow’s ‘irresponsible nuclear rhetoric’ as strikes on Kyiv intensify
summary: Comments come after Moscow warned it would ‘deploy its entire arsenal’ if Kaliningrad was threatened.
text: Nato on Tuesday condemned “irresponsible nuclear rhetoric” by Russia, after Moscow warned it would “deploy its entire arsenal” if the alliance threatens its exclave Kaliningrad. “I can confirm that Russia sent a non-paper to Nato and that we have sent a response, noting that Nato is a defensive Alliance and none of our activities or exercises pose a risk to any part of Russia,” Allison Hart, a Nato spokesperson, said. “We strongly denounce the threat of force, including any irresponsible nuclear rhetoric. We call on Russia to end its unprovoked war in Ukraine.” Russia has intensified daytime strikes on Kyiv using jet-powered drones that Ukrainian forces are struggling to intercept. Russia fired ballistic missiles and dozens of jet-powered drones at Kyiv, Ukraine’s air force said Tuesday, as Moscow seeks to make Ukraine buckle under the pressure of day-and-night bombardment of its capital and other cities. Russia has used new jet-powered drones that fly too fast and too high for Ukrainian ground-based air defenses to shoot down. Russia struck ⁠two datacentres ⁠in Kyiv overnight, a military-linked ⁠cargo vessel in the Black Sea, and ⁠another vessel with military ‌cargo ‌in the Ukrainian port ‌of Odesa, the Russian defence ministry said on Tuesday. In a later evening statement, ‌the ministry said its forces had launched a drone strike on a ship in ⁠the Black Sea which it said was carrying cargo intended for ‌the Ukrainian armed forces. Ukraine’s top university on Tuesday said it was ordering students to stay home as it switched to remote classes due to the surge in Russian daytime drone attacks on the capital. Kyiv’s Taras Shevchenko National University said it would “switch to a remote format of work” until at least 16 October, “due to the deteriorating security situation in Kyiv”. The university’s main campus is close to the National Academy of Sciences, which was hit by a drone strike, killing one person, on Monday. Russian glide bombs ⁠struck a school in the northern ⁠Ukrainian ⁠city of Sumy on Tuesday, killing ⁠two people and injuring six, the regional ⁠governor said. The city’s governor, Oleh Hryhorov, said three children ‌were among the injured. He said teachers and school officials had managed to ‌evacuate 100 people. Russia’s foreign investment envoy, Kirill Dmitriev, met US officials in Washington for talks about future US-Russia energy projects planned after Moscow’s war against Ukraine, a US government official told AFP. Dmitriev and US officials held “constructive discussions on a peaceful resolution to the Russia-Ukraine conflict and possible US-Russia energy initiatives after the war ends” on Monday, the official said on Tuesday. “The visit follows special envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner’s recent meeting with president Putin in Moscow and their discussions last week with Ukrainian officials in NYC,” said the official, speaking anonymously. The US president, Donald Trump, favours a proposal under which the US would lift some sanctions if Russia released a number of political prisoners, according to a report in the Atlantic. The White House did not comment directly on the report. When asked about the article, a US official told AFP that Trump was “committed to continuing to play a constructive role in ending the war between Russia and Ukraine, and he remains optimistic that we’ll ultimately get a peace deal done”. Russia will cut funding for welfare, education and healthcare in next year’s state budget to help cover soaring military spending, fiscal documents obtained by Reuters showed. Russia plans to spend 17.1tn ⁠roubles (US$202.58bn) on defence in ⁠2027, about 27% more than the 13.5tn roubles originally budgeted and the highest figure since the start of the war in Ukraine in ⁠2022. Funding for social policy, which covers items such as state pensions, payments to war veterans and maternity benefits, will shrink by 7%, while education funding will fall by 6% and healthcare by 6.8%. Belgium will transfer three F-16 fighter jets to Ukraine by the end ⁠of the ⁠year to help in its war with Russia, Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said on Tuesday. Zelenskyy said Ukraine had already received “urgent deliveries” of F-16 ‌ammunition from Belgium and Spain, among other countries. Zelenskyy later said later Ukraine had received a “very good” assistance package the day before of a NASAMS air defence system, ‌developed jointly in the US and Norway. A Russian nuclear-capable strategic bomber crashed Tuesday on a training mission in the country’s far east, killing six members of its crew, its defence ministry said. The ministry said in a statement that the Tu-95 bomber went down in an unpopulated area in the Amur region, adding that one crew member survived the crash and was hospitalised with injuries.

title: Judge ends federal oversight of Oakland police department after 23 years
summary: Group of officers known as ‘riders’ in 2000s prompted longest arrangement of its kind in US history
text: After 23 years, a district judge has released the Oakland police department (OPD) from federal oversight, marking the end of the longest arrangement of this kind in US history. In the early 2000s, a group of police officers known as the “riders” were exposed for offenses like planting evidence, falsifying reports and using excessive force against primarily young Black men. These actions led victims to file more than 100 civil lawsuits against the department. In 2003, as a part of the settlement of these cases, the OPD was put on a federal court-ordered reform program. The OPD was given more than 50 tasks to complete including collecting and analyzing data on racial profiling, dealing with complaints against officers more quickly and updating their community policing practices. Despite this, issues remained and the department’s reforms were put under the direct control of a federal judge in 2012. Since then, the department has still had its share of scandals including allegations that several OPD officers sex-trafficked a teenage girl; nearly a dozen officers were either fired or suspended. The investigation into the trafficking of the teenager began in 2015 and the OPD issued her a nearly $1m settlement in 2017. For organizers against police misconduct and brutality, the decision to end the federal oversight scheme does not mean that the department should be free of scrutiny. “Police cannot police themselves. Oakland’s history has already taught us that lesson,” the Anti Police-Terror Project (APTP) said in a statement following the judge’s decision. “The end of federal oversight does not mean the end of police misconduct. It does not erase the history that brought OPD under federal supervision. And it certainly does not mean Oakland should simply trust OPD to hold itself accountable.”

title: An EV sold every 100 seconds: Australian demand for electric cars more than doubles
summary: A record 157,957 new EVs were sold nationally between January and June, according to the Electric Vehicle Council
text: Australians are buying electric vehicles at record levels, with sales more than doubling year on year and occurring at a rate equivalent to one EV sold every 100 seconds. A record 157,957 EV sales occurred between January and June – an 117% increase on the same period last year, according to a new report released by the Electric Vehicle Council. Comparatively, petrol and diesel vehicle sales decreased by 14% year on year, according to the council’s chief executive, Julie Delvecchio. EVs accounted for one in four new vehicles sold in the first half of the year, up 12.1% from the first six months of 2025, the state of EVs report said. “EVs are being taken up as a cost-of-living measure by households across Australia,” Delvecchio said of the rise, noting that the ongoing fuel crisis was an accelerating factor but was “not the starting gun”. “It exposed the value of the policy work that had already been done – and made the lower running costs and energy security benefits of EVs much more immediate for Australian households,” she said. The new figures include about 104,000 battery electric vehicles and 54,000 plug-in hybrids. As of June, there were 612,000 EVs in the national vehicle fleet. “We are well on track to hit the target of 1 million EVs on Australian roads by next year,” said Aman Gaur, the head of policy and advocacy at the EV Council. The Australian Capital Territory, where 44% of new cars registered are electric, retained its crown as the nation’s EV capital. Tarneit, in Melbourne’s west, was the individual postcode with the highest uptake. A key driver of the growing uptake has been the national vehicle efficiency standard, which requires carmakers to supply new vehicles that meet an average per-kilometre emissions target. The standard had “substantially increased the options and the price competitiveness of EVs”, with nearly 200 EV models available in 2026, Gaur said. The council is pushing for the federal government to extend the standard beyond 2029, to align with the government’s 2035 emissions reduction target. Subdued take up of electric trucks Charging infrastructure had largely kept pace with growing EV demand, the report found, with the number of public charging locations growing to 4,268 across the country. While Australia was no longer a global laggard compared with other electric car markets, buses and cars were “roaring ahead” of electric trucks and vans, for which sales continued to be less than 1% of their respective markets, Gaur said. “Every truck that is electric is an upgrade to Australia’s energy security,” Delvecchio said. “We’ve barely touched the sides on that transition.” The report also found the federal, ACT and NSW governments’ EV policies were “top of the class, while South Australia, Queensland, Tasmania and Northern Territory have gone backwards”. “Queensland and the Northern Territory are … moving to back to fossil fuels rather than trying to electrify their transport systems,” Gaur said. “The most disappointing example of this was when the Queensland government recently invested in 630 diesel buses. “The diesel buses will be on Queensland roads until the end of the next decade, and they will certainly be polluting the air in Brisbane when the Olympics are held.”

title: A tight election looms in New Zealand. This time, overseas voters could be bad news for the big parties
summary: More than 100,000 have enrolled to vote from abroad in the November poll, and many are unhappy with how things look back home
text: New Zealander Kris Taute has lived in Australia for 15 years, but his head and heart are turning towards his home country and a looming general election that could be influenced by a large block of overseas voters. From across the Tasman Sea, Taute has felt growing frustration at New Zealand’s centre-right coalition government, and analysts believe large numbers of New Zealanders who have left the country since they came to power in 2023 may be poised to vent their grievances at the ballot box in November. “I see a lot of poverty among families and friends, and inequality … stuff that needs to be addressed,” Taute, who is Māori, tells the Guardian. He says the government’s removal of “quite a lot of Māori rights” troubles him deeply, and is why he’s more motivated to vote in this election. Akhil Donthireddy moved to Melbourne last year after struggling to secure a job in New Zealand. The 29-year-old says voting enables him to shape a future he wants to see, and he plans to vote for the Green party. “If the outlook for the future is hopeful, then I would consider moving back”, he says. Polls show the right- and left-leaning coalition blocs will fight one of the tightest elections in years, so votes from New Zealanders abroad like Taute – who plans to vote for Labour or Te Pāti Māori (the Māori party) – could help shape the outcome on 7 November. Stats NZ estimates there are about one million New Zealanders living overseas. Offshore voter enrolments are rising – currently 104,164 – up a whopping 60% compared to the same point in the 2023 election cycle, according to the latest electoral commission data. The commission told the Guardian this is the “highest number” of enrolments it has seen in recent elections. New Zealand’s overseas votes form part of a larger group called “special votes”. Special votes typically favour leftwing minor parties, says Lara Greaves, a political scientist at Victoria University of Wellington. In 2023, special votes resulted in Te Pāti Māori and the Greens gaining three seats between them. “If I had to guess where the overseas vote would go this election … it will go to the minor parties, because they are all offering alternative visions for New Zealand,” Greaves says, adding “a lot of them” would be left-leaning. “That’s been the conventional wisdom and I can see an argument for that this time around”, she says. That would place the current government in a danger zone. The latest 1News Verian poll shows support for the two major parties at 28% each, and the Greens surging to their highest ever result of 16%. Other minor parties are polling above the 5% threshold of seats needed to enter parliament under New Zealand’s mixed member proportional (MMP) system. If major parties do not get enough votes to form a government, minor parties can become “kingmakers”, with the power to decide who will govern. Tracey Lee runs Every Kiwi Vote Counts, a non-partisan initiative to encourage overseas voting. With the polls so close, Lee believes overseas votes can “legitimately have an impact” and “a fraction of a percentage point can become a decider,” she says. In a sign of how important that growing overseas voting bloc is, leaders of the prominent political parties will speak to offshore New Zealanders directly in a virtual town hall next month – a first for the country. Record exodus Australia is home to the biggest NZ diaspora. Those numbers have surged in recent years as NZ experienced record high departures of its citizens across the Tasman, many escaping a weak labour market, sluggish economy and high living costs. About 74,000 chose to move to Australia since the 2023 election adding to the roughly 600,000 New Zealanders already living there. Some left because it seemed to be “the only option available to them to find work and experience”, Lee says. “They’d love to come home and voting is a way to ensure they’re part of making it a place they can come home to.” Greaves says there is a disgruntled bloc of voters who left the country because they could not see a future for themselves. “There is a possibility that a good chunk of that bigger group that have now moved overseas are quite oppositional or quite opposed to what the government has been doing and do feel a level of spite.” Australian-based voters told the Guardian of their desire to retain their voice in New Zealand’s election – either to help their families, or to shape the country for their possible return. Onkar Singh has lived in Melbourne for more than 20 years and while he has no plans to return to New Zealand, he wants to keep the option open. Singh did not wish to disclose who he would vote for but said members of his New Zealand-Punjabi community “were happy with the current government”. Most of those the Guardian spoke with, however, would be voting for change. For Melbourne-based lawyer, Joseph Nunweek, a move back to New Zealand is likely. Despite living in Australia since 2014, he feels a responsibility to vote for policies that would support his family and community back home, particularly in healthcare, renewable energy and foreign policy. “Washing your hands of [the election] is not really an option,” he says. Lee argues the “mega-electorate” living abroad should no longer be ignored. “We’ve had the right to vote [overseas] since 1956, but it’s slightly frowned upon: ‘you left, it’s not your business’ is the unwritten rule,” she says. “But … democracy only works if we are all part of it.”

title: US Senate blocks resolution demanding accountability over Israeli violence in West Bank
summary: Nine American citizens have been killed by Israeli settlers or security forces in occupied West Bank since 2022
text: The US Senate on Tuesday evening rejected along mostly party lines a Democratic resolution that would have forced the state department to report to Congress on violence in the occupied West Bank, including the killings of nine American citizens by Israeli settlers or security forces over the last few years. The resolution, led by the Maryland Democrat Chris Van Hollen, would have given the state department 30 days to report to Congress on those deaths and on wider human rights conditions in the territory, including Israel’s detention of Palestinian children. The resolution failed to advance by a vote of 47 to 51. Pennsylvania senator John Fetterman, a Democrat, joined Republicans in voting against the resolution, while Kentucky Republican Rand Paul voted in favor. Van Hollen was able to force the vote under section 502B of the Foreign Assistance Act, a law that lets senators demand human rights reports on countries receiving US military aid. The measure drew 24 Democratic sponsors, including Bernie Sanders of Vermont, Tim Kaine of Virginia and Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, the top Democrat on the foreign relations committee. “While I was pleased that so many of my Democratic colleagues joined this effort, it’s clear the United States must do more,” Van Hollen said in a statement after the vote. “It is our responsibility to ensure recipients of US taxpayer dollars act in line with our laws and our values – this resolution was an opportunity to shed light on a reality that flies in the face of that principle.” Nine Americans have been killed in the occupied West Bank since 2022. The most recent include Sayfollah Musallet, a 20-year-old from Tampa, Florida, who was beaten to death by Israeli settlers in July 2025 while visiting family in the village of Sinjil. His family said the settlers surrounded him for more than three hours and blocked an ambulance from reaching him as he tried to protect their land. Weeks later, Khamis Ayyad, a 40-year-old father of five from Cicero, Illinois, died of smoke inhalation after settlers set fire to cars and homes in the village of Silwad. Two other Americans, both 17, Tawfic Abdel Jabbar and Mohammad Khdour, were shot dead in separate incidents in early 2024. Ayşenur Ezgi Eygi, a 26-year-old raised in Seattle, was shot in the head by Israeli troops, and Amer Rabee, a 14-year-old from New Jersey, was shot 11 times, according to Van Hollen. The victim list also includes the journalist Shireen Abu Akleh, killed in 2022, and Omar Assad, an elderly man who died after Israeli soldiers bound and gagged him. Van Hollen said none of the cases has ended in accountability, from either the Israeli or US government, and he places the blame largely on Republican senators who continue to vote against it. “If the killing of nine Americans does not justify a report from our own state department, I would ask my colleagues: what would?” the Maryland Democrat said in a floor speech. “How many more Americans must be killed before the executive branch does its job? These families deserve answers.” In August, 45 Democratic senators signed a letter to Benjamin Netanyahu urging him to act to protect Americans in the West Bank. The vote comes amid what human rights groups describe as rising settler violence. Human Rights Watch in August reported that settler attacks, together with a rapid expansion of settlements, had fully or partly displaced 107 Palestinian communities, about 5,900 people, since January 2023. The group cited UN figures showing more Palestinians were displaced in the first four months of 2026 than in all of 2025. A UN report from March covering the 12 months up to October 2025 documented 1,732 settler attacks causing injuries or property damage, and determined that Israel’s settlement expansion had forced more than 36,000 Palestinians from their homes. Many of the Democrats, who have historically been in lockstep with Israel, have now shifted over the last few years. When Sanders first forced a Senate vote on blocking arms sales to Israel in November 2024, 18 senators backed him. Then, in April of this year, 40 of the 47 Democrats voted to block a $295m sale of bulldozers to Israel, which Sanders argued would be used to demolish homes in the West Bank, Gaza and Lebanon. Another 36 voted to block a $152m sale of 1,000lb bombs. The measures failed because every Republican voted against them.

title: Antarctic winter sea ice falls to third-lowest level on record as scientists warn of ‘now problem’
summary: Coverage levels fall a million square kilometres short of the long-term average, with global heating likely driving losses
text: Antarctica’s winter sea ice has peaked at its third-lowest level on record, falling a million square kilometres – or almost 400,000 square miles – short of the long-term average, scientists have confirmed. Confirmation of the peak meant the four lowest years on record for the continent’s sea ice – a vital component of the planet’s climate and critical for marine life – had all occurred in the past four years. Satellites have been watching the continent’s sea ice since 1979, and this year data showed the sea ice peaked on 14 September at 17.59m square kilometres, about a million square kilometres short of the average maximum or an area roughly twice the size of Spain. Dr Walt Meier, a senior scientist at the National Snow and Ice Data Center at the University of Colorado, said the centre had held off in declaring the maximum because there was a “lot of potential variability” at this stage in the continent’s sea ice cycle. But the levels of sea ice had been falling since 14 September and he now thought “the maximum has been reached”. Antarctica’s sea ice goes through an enormous annual swing, melting through summer to below 2m sq km in recent Februaries and then growing through winter reaching above 17m sq km in September. But recent years have seen records broken for low sea ice in both winter and summer, raising concerns that global heating could be driving the losses. “The past four winters have had the lowest sea ice maximum on record – that’s a very clear indication of a system that has changed,” said Dr Ariaan Purich, a Southern Ocean expert at Monash University in Melbourne. “This is not a one-off event any more. The sea ice is no longer covering the same extent of ocean that it used to. We are seeing low winter after low winter and that suggests the sea ice is behaving differently because we have warmed our climate. “This is not a future problem. It’s a now problem.” In June, the Antarctic peninsula saw a heatwave with temperatures 20C above normal while scientists pointed to a France-sized area of open ocean where ice should have been. In early August when sea ice should be steadily expanding, a large area of the Amundsen Sea to the south of the Pacific lost ice. Purich said changes in winds associated with the El Niño climate pattern in the tropical Pacific had likely played a role in reducing the sea ice in that region. Dr Phil Reid, who monitors Antarctic conditions at Australia’s Bureau of Meteorology, said El Niño tended to change the movement of storm systems around Antarctica leading some to be held in the same place, churning up the sea ice below. But he said even without an El Niño, “I think we would still be in a similar position … and that is a bit disconcerting”. “The atmosphere will play around a bit, but in the end thermodynamics wins. If the water is too warm, you won’t have as much sea ice.” Purich said as Antarctica now emerged from its “polar night”, sea ice reflects the sun’s energy during the day. But less sea ice meant the Southern Ocean could take up more heat. Loss of sea ice does not directly affect sea levels as it was already floating, but it can expose ice shelves to buffeting ocean extremes and weaken them. Ice shelves slow down the advance of glaciers and the continent’s vast ice sheet that has the potential to push up global sea levels by many metres if it reaches the ocean. As well as providing habitats for algae and krill – critical elements of the continent’s food web – unstable sea ice has raised concerns for other species, including emperor penguins, that use the ice to breed and raise young. Dr Will Hobbs, Antarctic sea ice expert at the University of Tasmania, said since reaching its peak earlier this month, Antarctic sea ice had been dropping “faster than usual”. “We could be looking at another low summer and that’s when things get really worrying,” he said, pointing to concerns about impacts on ice shelves. “How sensitive is the global climate system to this loss of sea ice? We are still working to put numbers on that. But the system is changing faster than we are understanding it.”

title: ‘He’s unbearable’: bear that went viral for living under LA home is back
summary: ‘Yellow 2120’ has been driven out of other Altadena neighborhood crawlspaces, but he just keeps coming back
text: He’s back: the 550lb bear made famous after he took up residence under an Altadena home in November 2025 is wandering the Los Angeles neighborhood again after he moved in and out of the crawlspace of another home. “Yellow 2120”, as the black bear has been tagged, was spotted in the crawlspace of a home on Minoru Drive on Monday. Steve Clark, whose in-laws live in the house, told NBC LA that they monitored their new neighbor through security cameras, and tried to scare him away by playing loud music and turning on a leaf blower. “I didn’t even realize that the bear could get all the way back to that access point. He has to rip out ductwork and do a bunch of damage to get there,” Clark said. Although those attempts to oust “Yellow 2120” from his adopted den failed, the bear later left on his own. While the homeowners have sealed up their crawlspace, their neighbors are on alert in case the bear decides to move in with them next. “Yellow 2120” made headlines last year when he took up residence under another Altadena home for two months. In November 2025, homeowner Ken Johnson noticed the bear leaving the crawlspace and later contacted California’s department of fish and wildlife for assistance removing it from under his home. Despite sweet-scented lures and ammonia-doused towels, “Yellow 2120” remained in place until January – when Johnson sought assistance from members of the Bear League, a volunteer organization that aims to help humans live in “harmony” with the animals, that was able to force the bear out with paintball guns. “He’s a nuisance and he’s living under my house rent-free,” Johnson told the Orange County Register at the time. “We call him … unbearable, but he’s so cute. Once he gets out, we’ll call him bearable, but for now it’s unbearable.” After the Eaton wildfire tore through the Angeles national forest and scorched parts of Altadena in January 2025, wildlife – including several bears – sought shelter in the community. In the weeks following the fire, at least two 500-plus-pound black bears sought refuge in homes evacuated during the wildfire. Although it’s unclear whether “Yellow 2120” was one of them, he had previously taken up residence under another Altadena home, said Cort Klopping, a fish and wildlife spokesperson. As cities encroach closer on bear habitats, bear sightings are growing more common. In 2017, California registered 28 bear sightings in Los Angeles county. In 2023, that number rose to 455. This month Alex Heeran, a research scientist at the California department of fish and wildlife who studies the human dimensions of wildlife encounters, told the Guardian that human and bear interactions generally peak every year in late summer and early fall as black bears finish up their pre-hibernation feeding period. This year is on track to be record setting when it comes to reported bear encounters, Heeran said. Black bears – the only species of bear living in California – are largely non-confrontational, having killed only one person in the state in recorded history. The population is estimated to be between 49,000 and 71,000, with 50% living in the north coast and Cascade regions, and 40% in the Sierra Nevada.

title: Trump AI deal rebrands ‘artificial intelligence’ as ‘superintelligence’
summary: The US president announces vague ‘morally binding’ AI agreement among tech CEOs for ‘tremendous self-policing’
text: Donald Trump announced on Tuesday that the heads of the largest US tech and AI companies had signed a “morally binding” agreement to put controls on artificial intelligence. He announced the deal, called the Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities, following a White House luncheon with top tech executives. “It’s almost like a constitution in a way, and the biggest people in the world signed that, and I signed it as president, and it really ⁠is a form of protection,” Trump said. Trump also signed an executive order renaming artificial intelligence as “superintelligence”, similar to a declaration he made at the United Nations last week. “The Order directs all departments and agencies to use the terms ‘Super Intelligence’ and ‘SI’ in official correspondence, public communications, policy documents, and non-statutory documents within the executive branch and to no longer acknowledge the terms ‘Artificial Intelligence’ or ‘AI’,” the order declared. The agreement, which Trump suggested would allow the companies to perform “tremendous self-policing” of their products and technologies, outlines a vague framework for how AI firms would establish safety standards as they test out new products. The tech industry has faced increased public scrutiny following a series of incidents in which major AI companies’ products hacked into outside organizations during safety tests. While lawmakers, AI researchers and even some AI companies have called for more government oversight of artificial intelligence, Trump has broadly rejected calls for more regulation of the technology – citing competition with China and threats to economic growth. The joint commitment that Trump posted to his Truth Social account on Tuesday appears to carry no enforcement mechanisms or legal implications and is instead a voluntary commitment. The document outlines four “layers of controls and audits” for AI companies. The first involves implementing internal safety monitoring during training – something that already exists at major labs and has failed to prevent testing failures thus far. The second calls for empowering an internal team to make sure the first layer of monitoring is operating correctly, while the third agrees to give an external auditor the ability to independently assess safety controls. Finally, the agreement calls for companies to designate an independent board to review reports about those safety controls. None of the controls listed in the agreement involve government regulators or include a commitment to publicly detail the findings of independent evaluations. The agreement also appears to allow companies to pick their own evaluators, appoint their own oversight boards and decide whether to publish their results. Trump made the remarks after holding a luncheon with tech leaders including Elon Musk, the SpaceX CEO; Mark Zuckerberg, the Meta CEO; Jensen Huang, the CEO of Nvidia; Dario Amodei, the Anthropic CEO; and other top industry executives. The tech industry, which has largely aligned itself with the Trump administration, has lobbied against strict regulatory oversight, arguing that it would stifle the economy. Zuckerberg, flanked by Trump and other tech moguls, told a press conference after the lunch that he was proud of the agreement and said that it was created to assure the American public that their technology was trustworthy. “This is a start and an accord that the whole industry could come to,” Zuckerberg said. “It was sort of a historic conversation.”
