title: Burnham’s emotional solo act had Labour in raptures – but his promises will take time to come good
summary: PM’s speech, written almost entirely alone, was full of radicalism but his biggest plans will have to wait until after the next election
text: Hope Again is the conference slogan. But what felt even more apt was Try Again. Just forget about the last two years, after the party won a historic majority but where the mood never matched the achievement. Now, as conference delegates and MPs filed out of the hall after Andy Burnham’s first speech as prime minister, it was close to euphoria. Where the hell have you been all our lives? What have we been doing – when you were right there all along? That feeling rarely lasts: Burnham himself warned he would make choices that would be a harsh comedown from this Labour high. But the “people pleaser” prime minister said he was prepared to weather the worst political pain to change the country. In his sights are some of the most untouchable topics in British politics: social care, the triple lock, Brexit, public control of water and council homes and changing the voting system. Burnham wrote the speech almost entirely alone, working on it until the very last minute. Cabinet ministers have been full of tales of how often meetings overrun with the new prime minister, clearing their diaries for the extra half an hour, because of his desire to chew the fat, to understand, to argue, to persuade. Close friends saw the speech just the night before, as Burnham reworked it. But strategists in No 10 were very clear that the new prime minister did need to introduce himself, his story, to the country that barely knows him. Each judicious choice of an anecdote from his past drew on his personal history to explain his desire to make fundamental change. The home in Old Roan in Merseyside bought by his grandmother Kitty, which gave his family security that the younger generation cannot now experience: sold, he explained, to pay for Kitty’s care, which he will promise future generations will never happen under a new national care service. The care of his dad, Roy, who died two weeks ago, and his promise to his care workers that he would elevate their profession. Burnham was overcome with emotion at the moment he spoke about his father, pausing for so long it caused one member of the audience to cry out: “You can do it Andy.” They want to back him, they want to believe. Unusually for a conference speech, Burnham did not use the speech to attack his opponents. There were no reference to either Kemi Badenoch or Nigel Farage. But one of the loudest cheers came from the crowd as Burnham drew the dividing line with the right in the starkest terms on public ownership. “The British right talk about ‘taking back control’. Never let them forget, they are the ones that gave it away in the first place,” he said, the reddest of red meat to a jubilant Labour crowd. So, was it Burnham – and Labour – unleashed? No, because the prime minister is still constrained by his own party manifesto and the state of the public finances. “I would love to go quicker,” he said. “But I have to be honest about what the country can afford.” His most radical promises are promises deferred. The party will overhaul the triple lock by 2030, the national care service can only be paid for if the party ditches its tax pledges, it can only explore a customs union, the single market, even rejoining, outside the manifesto’s “red lines”. Even at this most united Labour conference the party has seen in two decades, there remains a proud Labour tradition – pessimism. And there are causes for concern, which creep in when cabinet minsters are at their most candid. The first is the impatience of the country for change – and that being told to wait will not be enough. People, they say, are suffering now. The budget will need to show that any sparse funds that remain must be delivered to giving people relief from everyday costs. “People need to start feeling actual benefits next year. We have got less time than we might think,” one cabinet minister said. The second is a fear that Labour is not speaking to a broad enough base, no matter the elevation in Liverpool. Though there has been a discernible “Burnham bounce”, the polls are volatile. A YouGov poll on the eve of Burnham’s speech put Reform UK back in first place by a tiny margin. Labour is reuniting a progressive coalition with a divided right, which is an advantage but which is unlikely to put them in majority territory. There are few cabinet ministers who are so frustrated with the constraints of their own legacy manifesto that they want to swap that for the constraints of a Lib Dem manifesto. There is no sign of revival yet in Wales or Scotland, so crucial to a Labour majority government. When the dust clears and Labour strategists pick over the bodies of the sacred cows that Burnham promised to slay in his speech, many will probably wonder why he didn’t choose an easier life. But perhaps now Burnham has waited this long to be prime minister – and watched so many others squander the office – he knows he has no choice but to tool up for the fight.

title: Barclays softens return-to-office plans for UK staff after backlash
summary: Bank allows employees to delay being in workplace at least three days a week until 2027, if permission granted
text: Barclays has watered down its return-to-office plans after a major staff backlash, with the bank allowing some employees to wait until next year before having to be in at least three days a week. The bank this summer announced the attendance requirement would come in for its 45,000 UK staff from 5 October, with more senior employees expected to come in for at least four days. That compares with current rules requiring staff to come in for two days. Now Barclays has offered a reprieve after thousands of bank staff signed an open letter drafted by the Unite union, calling for payouts to help cover travel costs and an exemption for those living more than 40 minutes from work. The bank will allow staff to delay complying with the order until 2027. However, they will need to ask and receive permission to do so from their line manager by the end of this week. In a memo emailed to staff, Barclays’ executive committee announced: “We are extending the implementation period for UK colleagues to ensure colleagues have the right support as we move through the transition … We are also reviewing our flexible working policy.” The extension, first reported by the Financial Times, could give unions more time to request further concessions. Barclays and Unite said they would continue discussions on the issue, which has become a flashpoint across the banking sector. Banks ranging from JP Morgan to Revolut have clamped down on remote working after the Covid pandemic, arguing it harms the training of younger staff. Unite have said that while they recognise face-to-face working can support collaboration, team development and relationship building: “We do not accept that this requires a blanket, one-size-fits-all increase in mandatory office attendance.” The union has requested a series of concessions, including: Automatic exemptions of in-office attendance rules during school holidays and Christmas. Capping in-office requirements at one day a week for any carers or people with disabilities. Flexible start and finish times to allow for cheaper off-peak travel costs and to accommodate school pickup and drop-offs. Subsidised onsite meal costs. A single, consolidated payment made to all staff to make up for the costs of coming into the office, before March 2027. A spokesperson said: “Unite is continuing to engage with Barclays on its proposals relating to colleagues’ working arrangements.” In an emailed statement, a Barclays spokesperson said: “Our updated onsite working arrangements will take effect as planned. “We have continued to listen to colleague feedback to ensure colleagues have the right support while enabling us to deliver the benefits of working together in person. This includes transitional measures for those whose personal circumstances currently prevent them from meeting the new arrangements.”

title: CDC reports second measles death in US while excluding Pennsylvania deaths
summary: Pennsylvania has reported over 900 measles cases and four deaths as governor and health chief RFK Jr spar over data
text: A second measles death in the US has been announced on Tuesday by the federal Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), as the country grapples with an outbreak affecting 47 states. As of 24 September, a total of 3,659 measles cases have been confirmed by the CDC, with the two deaths having been confirmed on Tuesday. The confirmation did not specify in which states the deaths had occurred. Although Pennsylvania is the hardest-hit state, having reported more than 900 cases and four deaths from measles, the CDC is not including the deaths there in its national data. Differences in the federal measles death figures compared with those from Pennsylvania’s department of health is part of an ongoing dispute between Pennsylvania’s governor, Josh Shapiro, and the US health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr. The CDC, which used to collect data from states, has now shifted to using mortality data from the National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) for its national measles death count. Pennsylvania also reported 114 new cases of measles in the last seven days, with a third of these being children aged under 18. The state has also reported 176 hospitalizations, and less than 1% of the total number of measles cases involve people who have been fully vaccinated against the disease. Pennsylvania’s health department said: “While daily numbers fluctuate, tracking these trends provides Pennsylvanians and health care providers with visibility into community transmission across the [state] and helps inform the department’s ongoing response.” The US has now recorded more measles cases this year than any other since 1991. The disease was declared to be eliminated by the US government in 2000. Measles is a highly contagious virus that can cause serious health complications. And although rare, deaths from measles occur in approximately one to three patients per 1,000 cases The announcement also comes as the CDC has faced a dramatic reduction in its work force, with the Trump administration laying off 18% of its staff in 2025. According to the American Federation of Government Employees (AFGE), the largest federal employee union representing 82,000 workers, there are 3,810 fewer civil service employees within the CDC in the past year, a total reduction of a third. Measles symptoms usually begin seven to 14 days after infection, according to the CDC. These symptoms can include high fever, cough, runny nose and red, watery eyes, followed by a rash that spreads down the body. The CDC advises that two doses of the MMR vaccine “provide the best protection against measles”.

title: Saudi Arabia urged to reconcile with UAE to drive back Houthi separatists in Yemen
summary: Relations between two countries soured in January when a UAE-backed force was defeated by Saudis
text: Saudi Arabia is being urged to reconcile with the United Arab Emirates over Yemen as the price Riyadh must pay to form a military alliance capable of driving the Houthis back. Relations between the UAE and Saudi Arabia in Yemen, where both had backed anti-Houthi forces, plummeted in January this year when a force with which the UAE had been aligned – the separatist Southern Transitional Council (STC) – was attacked and defeated by Saudi Arabia in a move intended to squash its attempt to recreate a separate southern state. The UAE subsequently in effect quit Yemen. But the unexpected success in mid September of the Iran-aligned Houthis’ drive to the narrow Bab al-Mandab strait against pro-government forces has transformed the geopolitics of the region again. The push south defeated the previously UAE-backed National Resistance Forces led by Tareq Saleh, whose front rapidly collapsed. The future role of the UAE in Yemen was discussed at a meeting in Abu Dhabi on Sunday attended by the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, the UAE president, Sheikh Mohammed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, and a group of other Arab states, including representatives of Saudi Arabia. Netanyahu reportedly offered to help Saudi Arabia defeat the Houthis, an offer that Riyadh would probably find near impossible to accept, even though Donald Trump has failed to answer the Saudi call for US help in Yemen. A further meeting to discuss Yemen took place on Tuesday in Riyadh between Prince Khalid bin Salman Al Saud, the Saudi defence minister, and Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan, the UAE vice-president. It is part of a range of signs from the two sides suggesting they may want to find a path to reconciliation, even if only on energy. Following the Houthis’ push to the Bab al-Mandab strait, a chokepoint on Saudi oil exports, their forces are now trying to consolidate their gains and take the south-western city of Taiz. “The Houthi forces are mounting simultaneous waves of attacks on the city, trying to exhaust the Taiz Axis force defending the city,” said Baraa Shiban, a Gulf and Yemen specialist at the defence thinktank Rusi who has just spent a week in Taiz. “The Houthis are pushed back, but then the next day they come again on a different front. “Efforts are being made to try to end the rift between Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates and there may be some confidence-building measures. But the UAE has left Yemen, and it is unlikely that Riyadh would let them back in since they are aligned with the STC, and that would spell trouble … the UAE and Saudi Arabia are fundamentally on opposite sides.” The STC leader, Aidarous al-Zubaidi, fled into exile after the Saudi attack on its forces and the movement became marginalised as a political force. The former Yemen foreign minister and STC supporter Khaled Alyemany told the Guardian that Saudi Arabia may have to reconsider its political approach to the southern issue since the Giant Brigades, the UAE-trained southern forces once associated with the STC, provided some of the most reliable, well-equipped forces on the ground to stem the Houthi advance. The STC has urged the Giant Brigades to resist merging with Yemen government forces, arguing to do so will set back the separatist cause. “We cannot fight and wage wars in the north against the Houthis if we do not have a horizon for our independence,” Alyemany said. “The UN-recognised government … operating from exile in Riyadh, insists that southerners fight to retake the capital, Sana’a, on its behalf, but without any promise of the south’s right to self-determination,” he said. “The problem is, so long as the Yemen government derives its legitimacy from its Saudi funders rather than its people, the outcome is not Saudi Arabia’s stated goal of security along its southern borders.” The White House has been privately urging the UAE and the Saudi to bury their differences and allow a unified military command including the Southern Giants Brigades to challenge the Houthi advance. An additional proposal is to use Israeli intelligence and hire Israeli private security firms, something the UAE has done in the past in Yemen, sometimes to brutal effect. Saudi Arabia, reluctant to be seen cooperating with Israel, has always resisted helping the southern separatists since division of the country might entrench Houthi rule in the north along its border. The Houthis have used drones and missiles to attack Saudi energy installations. Despite Saudi air cover and support, the current battle to prevent the Houthis consolidating their gains is such that the parliament of the UN-recognised government has sanctioned a general mobilisation of the Yemeni people to fight the Houthis. The World Health Organization said 838 people had been killed and 3,643 others injured due to the escalation in Yemen from 6 August last year until 26 September this year. The Houthis insist they are not seeking to block general commercial shipping in the strait but only that linked to Saudi Arabia. On Monday they published figures showing commercial shipping was flowing as normal. The Houthis claim Saudi Arabia is in effect a colonial power and the UN-recognised government based in Aden is a creature of Riyadh with no independent ability to govern the country. April Longley Alley, a senior fellow at Washington Institute, told an International Crisis Group seminar that the war was existential for the Saudis, but the Houthis were not going to compromise. “We will have to see if they hold these territories, but what the Houthis learned from the Iran war is that Saudi under pressure and attack will seek de-escalation,” she said. “The Houthis are demanding a victor’s peace.”

title: Labour has its own role in this climate of hate and racism | Letters
summary: Letters: Readers react to a piece by Polly Toynbee in which she argues that Andy Burnham is the person to lead Britain out of its cohesion crisis
text: In her article, Polly Toynbee mentions the rise of racism globally, citing Donald Trump and the usual suspects (There is a racism and cohesion crisis in Britain, and someone needs to lead us out of it. His name is Andy Burnham, 22 September). She fails to mention that the Labour party has also indulged in overt and dog-whistle racist rhetoric. Keir Starmer spoke about Britain becoming “an island of strangers”. He later retracted it, but the message was out there. Wes Streeting, when health secretary, agreed with Katie Lam on the problem of foreign doctors (rather than the real problem of disastrous NHS restructures, poor management and underfunding). More recently, the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, said that a video clip where Zack Polanski says a few sentences in Urdu makes him “uncomfortable”. In refusing to call out Labour’s role in creating a climate of hate, Toynbee fails to address the seriousness of the problem. Labour politicians indulging in or endorsing racist rhetoric does far more to normalise racism than when it comes from Trump and his supporters. And if we choose not to identify the real problem, we have no hope of making it better. Name and address supplied • History clearly confirms Polly Toynbee’s main point that the rise of divisive scapegoating politics in a time of economic pressures ultimately represents a genuine threat to everyone’s basic rights. Immigration policy issues cannot be separated from turning this tide, since they are central to the lure of today’s far-right populism. A sizeable minority of Reform UK voters cannot be persuaded to change their allegiance as they now feel part of a wider “community of grievance”. Its myths and symbols seemingly explain current predicaments, revive old prejudices and suggest simple solutions. But many others have simply not heard these anti-immigrant notions being challenged. Too many mainstream politicians have echoed them instead, giving the far right control of the agenda and greater legitimacy. The majority of Britain’s voters share a traditional milder patriotism and can understand the need for immigration to grow our economy, in a country with an ageing population and labour shortages, and the need to avoid splitting communities. That case has to be made, before the poison spreads. John Chowcat Bridge, Kent • The rising tide of grievance that is powering Reform and rightwing sentiment is threatening the whole idea of democratic politics here and abroad. It must be confronted. It appals me that so-called responsible commentators argue that it is “understandable” because politics doesn’t deliver what people want. When what people want is defined by those with the most money and influence and involves selfish, discriminatory, reactionary and violent attitudes and behaviour it is the antithesis of democratic politics because that has to be founded on the principles of equity and justice. Without that, we are lost. Responsible politicians must lead the fight against that or the very ground on which they stand will be taken from under their feet. That slide into chaos already has far too much momentum. Neil Blackshaw Alnwick, Northumberland • Polly Toynbee’s powerful plea to defeat anti-migration fascism reminded me of the words of the nurse Edith Cavell before she was executed by the Germans in the first world war. “Patriotism is not enough. I must have no hatred or bitterness towards anyone.” E Douglas Lawson Cheltenham, Gloucestershire • Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Even George Osborne might be a nimby if an AI datacentre was built next to his home | Letters
summary: Letters: The quality of life for people living next to one would be destroyed, writes Moira Brewer; plus a letter from Mark Davis
text: So, George Osborne thinks people who don’t want an AI datacentre on their doorstep are nimbys (OpenAI’s George Osborne says datacentre nimbys holding back Britain, 22 September). He ought to come and visit our small town in Devon, where there are plans to build one of the largest datacentres in Europe, along with a battery energy storage system, on 850 acres of farmland. The size of this proposed development is quite out of proportion to its location – larger than the town itself – and accessed by narrow lanes. It would be a huge blot on a beautiful rural landscape that is enjoyed by holidaymakers who are vital to the local economy. It would destroy local residents’ quality of life, with its noise, lights and greed for energy and water, and we will not accept the imposition of this monstrosity on our doorstep without a fight (‘People are standing up and fighting back’: the north Devon revolt against a vast AI datacentre, 27 September). title: Don’t knock Palantir – it provides highly skilled, well-paid British jobs | Letter
summary: Letters: Tom Watson responds to an article by Clive Lewis about the former Labour deputy leader’s new job at the technology company
text: Clive Lewis is, unusually, right about one thing in his recent article: there is a danger of rot setting in (Tom Watson’s move to Palantir is the latest sign of how far the rot has spread in UK politics, 24 September). But I think he is looking in the wrong place. Attack me if you want, Clive. I’ve been around long enough to take it. But don’t malign the nearly 1,000 people I now have the privilege of working alongside. We are predominantly a young workforce. Our average age is under 30. We are engineers, software developers and people who have chosen to build their careers here in Britain. We help nurses and doctors improve public services. We help our armed forces and police keep us safe. And we are proud of what we do. Nearly one in five of Palantir’s global workforce is based here in the UK. These are highly skilled, well-paid British jobs that most countries would welcome. There is a respectable argument to be had about technology, power and accountability. But a politics that treats the people building Britain’s technological future as part of the problem is unlikely to leave us with much of a technological future. title: Team of skydivers drop in to help survivors of a plane crash in Wisconsin
summary: Recreational jumpers used their training as paramedics to treat crash victims before ground crews arrived
text: A team of experienced skydivers recently dropped in to help at a plane crash they happened to witness in Wisconsin – and used their training as paramedics to treat a seriously injured victim before ground-based rescue crews arrived. The single-engine plane carrying four people crashed in a cornfield near East Troy on Sunday, watched by the occupants of a Skydive Milwaukee aircraft who were preparing for an afternoon of recreational jumping. “He kind of banked up and then he disappeared behind the trees, and we were all waiting for him to show back up,” John Bechtel, one of several veteran skydivers on board, told Wisconsin ABC News affiliate WISN. “We all looked at each other and said, ‘Did we just see a plane crash?’” Bechtel, who has more than 30 years of skydiving experience, said he and two colleagues decided to jump straight to the site of the crash after calling in what they saw to authorities on the ground. One of the jumpers, who like Bechtel is also a former paramedic, helped a woman with a serious head injury until an EMT crew arrived by ambulance. “The timing couldn’t have been any better. Had we left five minutes earlier, we wouldn’t have seen it. If we left 15 minutes later, we wouldn’t have been able to get there to assist,” Bechtel said. “I’m just glad that we were able to do what we could and get in and help.” Officials in Walworth county said three passengers in the crashed plane were taken to hospital and the fourth was treated at the scene. All are expected to survive. Aerial footage on the WISN website showed the aircraft, a Beechcraft 35-A33 Debonair manufactured in 1961, upright on the ground with one of its wings detached. Jonah Johnston, the pilot of the jump plane, told air traffic controllers in an emergency call: “I have a plane crash, just south of East Troy. He’s in a field. I can drop a load of skydivers right over them to potentially help aid.” Kevin Flynn, another of the skydivers, told Milwaukee news outlet WDJT that he and Bechtel started calling out as soon as they hit the ground because they couldn’t see the plane through the tall corn. “I got in there and started doing the Marco Polo game to get a response,” he said. “People started yelling at me so I could dial in where I was going. “It could’ve been a lot worse for those poor people in that crash, no fatalities. I know it’s a terrible thing to happen, but I think it’s a wonderful outcome.” In a statement, Skydive Milwaukee said: “A few members of our skydiving community who are trained [emergency medical technicians] were already airborne in our jump plane and jumped out to assist at the scene, which was difficult to access from the road. “We’re grateful they were able to help when they were needed.” The identities of the victims have not been released. The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) opened an inquiry into the cause of the crash and an investigator arrived at the site on Sunday afternoon.

title: Conference laps up Andy unplugged as he offers chance to take road less travelled | John Crace
summary: Nothing was off the table and by the end no one could be in any doubt about what Burnham believed
text: You’ve got to hand it to Andy Burnham. He left nothing out on the pitch. It would have been so easy to play it safe. To deliver a traditional leader’s speech to a home crowd. One we’ve been seeing from leaders of all parties for more than 15 years. Something warm, a feelgood vibes word salad with the odd minor spending announcement thrown in. Hell, the Labour conference would have probably settled for it. They already had all the hope that they had come for. The hope that they were back in with a fighting chance of winning the next election. They wouldn’t have even dared think that three months ago. But Andy did it differently. Just as he had promised. He had said he was a different kind of politician and he duly made good on that. Hope came with honesty, he said. And honesty was what we got. Nothing was redacted. No coded hints. Come the end of his hour-long speech, no one could be in any doubt about what he thought. More than that, what he believed. Not so much a speech, more an article of faith. This was Andy unplugged. Unmediated. That most elusive of hybrids. The career politician who can still make the political personal and deliver it fearlessly. Keir Starmer could never have done this, even if he had wanted to. He was just too naturally cautious. A man one step removed from himself. Andy was running on pure emotion. Some things you can’t fake. At one point, just as he was about to talk about his dad, he choked up. Unable to speak. It became a moment of communion. Burnham was not going to die wondering. He knew he might be delivering one of the longest suicide notes in history, but he did it anyway. Because he couldn’t not do it. Better to go down remaining true to his principles than being slowly airbrushed out of history like the previous six prime ministers. Failures all. Andy was prepared to burn through all his political capital right there in Liverpool, right then. Not just for his own legacy but for a country he wanted to rebuild. It was the only way he could look himself in the mirror. Honour his parents. It goes without saying that Andy was received with a long series of near rapturous standing ovations throughout the speech. The audience was only too happy to be a pushover. Even the physicist Brian Cox. He was up and down like a yo-yo. If there were any black holes in the sums, he was far too polite to point them out. Not that this was a speech where anything so grubby as actual numbers were spelled out. This was all big-picture stuff. A reimagined vision of the future. Where the country didn’t feel permanently broke and broken. “All together now,” Burnham began. That would be his rallying cry. And he put his money where his mouth was. So many politicians use their conference speeches to trash the other parties. Many of the cabinet have done just that this week. But Andy didn’t once namecheck his rivals or use them to score points. The closest he got was to say we would all have failed if we voted in a divisive party on a vote of less than 30%. He would rather work with opposition parties for the common good. Fat chance. This is never going to happen. The idea of getting Nigel Farage and Kemi Badenoch round a table and agreeing to a unified sense of purpose was never going to happen. Kemi is unable to even agree with herself. But it sounded good. On message with brand Burnham. And Andy is no fool. That’s why most of the changes were ones that would be up for grabs at the next election. He wasn’t about to rat out on the manifesto that Labour had campaigned and won on. That would be a breach of trust. Not the Burnham way. This was a line in the sand. A chance for the country to take the road less travelled. It was up to voters whether they wanted to follow Burnham or stick with a decade of failure. That included Keir. Andy did give his predecessor a passing nod of thanks for winning the election but his heart wasn’t really in it. Later in the speech, he talked of the key moments in Labour history. 1945. 1964. 1997. And now. Not 2024. Keir was a has-been. A leader in the school of failure. Nothing was off the table. Social care. Bring it on. Other politicians of all parties had been content to ignore it on the grounds that it was just too difficult to sort out. Far better that old people should die of dementia in their own piss and shit than politicians be forced to make decisions that might cost them a general election. Just keep calm, tinker around the edges and carry on. The triple lock. For years, most economists have been saying the triple lock is financially unsustainable and has redressed the imbalance in pensions for which it was introduced. But no party had dared touch it. Terrified that old people would take their revenge at the ballot box. So politicians had pretended to be able to fix the problem with telepathy. Just think pure thoughts and the problem would go away. Andy was prepared to rip it up and replace it with a double lock. Electoral reform. Even the Lib Dems had gone a bit quiet on that one after they won more than 70 seats in 2024. Burnham was all for it. People were fed up with feeling that their vote didn’t count. He didn’t say what form of voting should replace first past the post, but even the most anodyne form of proportional representation would have left Labour short of a majority at the last election. Not all Labour MPs will have been pleased to hear that one. They are going to have to get used to it for the next three years at least. Andy wasn’t finished. There was still Brexit to go. It had been an unmitigated failure and it was time for a radical reset. Anything was on the table. It was like listening to a stream of consciousness. A private therapy session in which everything that had been bothering Burnham about the way the country didn’t work was laid out for public consumption. And Liverpool loved it. Loved Andy. He was one of them. It would have been no surprise if he had ended by ascending into heaven. As it was, he walked among the faithful. They were his people and he was one of them. Let’s hope it lasts.

title: From Brexit to electoral reform: key takeaways from Andy Burnham’s conference speech
summary: Ending the pensions triple lock, creating a national care service and making changes to leaseholds were all announced by the PM in Liverpool
text: Andy Burnham’s first speech to a Labour conference as prime minister was not only quite long, at over an hour, but unusually dense with policy. Here are some of the things he set out: Ending the pensions triple lock One of Burnham’s most concrete promises was to end the triple lock as we know it. For the last 15 years, the state pension has increased by whichever is the highest out of earnings, inflation or 2.5%. From 2030, if Burnham is still prime minister, it will instead rise by the highest out of inflation or 2.5%, meaning that for the first time since 2011, pensions will be allowed to increase by less than earnings. There is a backstop however – in years where earnings are higher than inflation or 2.5%, the government will guarantee that the state pension will be at least 30% of average earnings. This change to the earnings element of the policy sounds technical, but officials say it could save about £15bn a year by 2040. National care service Burnham repeated his promise to create a national care service, saying it would be a system to which everyone contributes and from which everyone can benefit, free at the point of use. The universal, NHS-style system will be funded in part by the change to the triple lock. But such an expansive system is likely to require more funding than that. Burnham’s promise of a system where everyone contributes suggests Labour will go into the next election promising a tax rise to pay for it. Electoral reform “We will all have failed in our public duties if we carry on as we are and open the door of No 10 to a divisive government on less than 30% of the vote,” Burnham said as he argued passionately against the first-past-the-post electoral system. Under the prime minister’s proposed solution, however, there will be at least one more election under the old system. Burnham announced a national commission to report on voting options, with the recommendations to be included in Labour’s next manifesto. Whatever option Burnham picks, it will not be purely proportional – officials clarified on Tuesday that the PM sees the link between MPs and their constituencies as vital. Changes to Brexit Burnham’s rhetoric here was blunt. “Brexit has done more harm than good,” he told the conference, citing depressed economic growth and a lack of the promised control over immigration. What followed was vague, however, with the PM saying only that he would use an upcoming summit with the EU to “lay out to the country what I believe the different options are for Britain’s long-term relationship with our European partners” and to “see if we can find consensus around one”. Aides say Burnham is hoping to build a political consensus, but the chances of Labour and Reform agreeing a path on integration with the EU seem slim. Changes to leasehold and new controls on landlords Reforms to the leasehold property system were promised under Keir Starmer but delayed. Burnham said a bill on the matter would come to parliament before Christmas. He also said there would be new powers so that landlords who rent out poor-quality homes would be ordered to improve them – and if they did not, it would be much easier for councils to compulsorily purchase the properties. Legislation on the public control of water In a plan that feels more symbolic than anything, Burnham said the environment secretary, Angela Eagle, would present a changed water bill to parliament, the “centrepiece” of which would be “the repeal of Margaret Thatcher’s ideological ban on public ownership of water companies”. Such a move, however, fails to tackle the main problem with taking public control of private companies – how to compensate existing shareholders. Ministers are talking about changing insolvency law to make it easier to take a company into administration, but this was not part of Burnham’s speech. Measures on housing In a speech that repeatedly referenced the houses in which his grandparents and parents lived, and the need for a secure family base, Burnham said the right to buy council properties would be removed for any new social homes built – but not for existing properties. He also set out an already-announced plan to help first-time buyers with a 20% equity loan to help them buy a new-build home, with an initial interest-free period.

title: EPA union sues Trump administration to restore collective bargaining contract
summary: Federal workers’ union alleges EPA illegally terminated agreement with the goal of repressing political dissent
text: The union representing more than 8,000 workers at the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) filed a lawsuit against the agency and administrator Lee Zeldin on Tuesday alleging the agency illegally terminated the union’s collective bargaining agreement. The lawsuit, filed by two local unions of the American Federation of Government Employees (AFGE), claims the agency failed to justify the contract’s termination and was motivated by a desire to repress political dissent, a violation of the employees’ first amendment rights. “While the dedicated civil servants … are working hard every day to advance the Agency’s mission to protect human health and the environment, the Agency has turned its back on them, unlawfully eliminating their workplace protections and stifling their free speech rights,” the lawsuit said. The EPA terminated the collective bargaining agreement in August 2025, citing Donald Trump’s executive order earlier that year that sought to eliminate collective bargaining agreements for more than 1 million federal workers. The union is asking a court to restore the union contract. The contract went into effect in June 2024 and was supposed to last through June 2028. It included a scientific integrity provision aimed to protect workers at the agency from retaliation. Justin Chen, president of AFGE Council 238, said the union’s members work as civil servants because they believe in the agency’s mission and in serving the public. “They believe in the kind of work that they do,” Chen said. “When they’re gagged and have no rights, they’re unable to serve the American public, they can’t do their jobs and they can’t serve the agency’s mission.” The EPA declined to comment, citing a longstanding practice on not commenting on pending litigation. Earlier this month, an arbitrator ruled in favor of EPA workers in a separate local union, AFGE Local 704, over the EPA’s disciplining of 139 workers who signed an open dissent letter, in violation of the union’s collective bargaining agreement. The EPA disciplined the workers despite emails revealing a top EPA attorney warned the agency about its legal risk. The arbitrator ordered the agency to wipe the workers’ records, provide them with back pay and cover the union’s attorney fees. Since Trump took office in January 2025, about 4,000 workers have left the EPA through resignations, early retirements and layoffs, reducing the agency’s workforce to about 12,700 employees. “The protection of my members is incredibly important and paramount, quite frankly, to an effective civil service [and for] protecting the American public,” Chen said.

title: New York man killed after bag caught in subway train doors, police say
summary: Man, 57, was reportedly leaving A train at Utica Avenue station when stuck bag dragged him back and on to tracks
text: A man in Brooklyn, New York, died after his bag got caught between the doors of a subway train which then dragged him down. On Monday, a man was leaving a Manhattan-bound A train at the Utica Avenue station in Brooklyn’s Bedford-Stuyvesant neighborhood when his shopping bag became caught between the subway’s doors. The man was subsequently dragged backward, pulled between train cars and on to the tracks, ABC7 reports, citing investigators. New York police, who received a 911 call about the accident at about 6.05pm ET on Monday, have identified the man as Yaw Boahene from Brooklyn. “Upon arrival, officers were informed that a 57-year-old male was discovered unconscious and unresponsive, on the roadbed of the northbound ‘A’ train. EMS responded and pronounced [the man] deceased [at the] scene. The New York City Office of Chief Medical Examiner will determine the cause of death, and the investigation is ongoing,” New York police said in a statement. Speaking to ABC7, a witness said she was returning home from school when the incident unfolded, prompting people on the subway platform to panic. While subway accidents are rare, in 2022 a 20-year-old man was killed after his clothes were caught between the doors of a 1 train at Columbus Circle station in Manhattan during rush hour. According to the Metropolitan Transportation Authority, which oversees New York City’s transit system, subway customer accidents increased slightly in 2025 by 2%. However, the MTA noted, “ridership grew at a greater rate than accidents,” adding: “As a result, the 12-month rate decreased by 4.7%.”

title: Trump administration asks supreme court to block gender-affirming care for trans prisoners
summary: Trans prisoners have sued administration over the policy and, so far, two lower courts have blocked implementation
text: The Trump administration asked the US supreme court, on Monday, to allow it to deny gender-affirming care to transgender people in federal prisons, while litigation over the matter continues in lower courts. In its latest emergency request to the high court, the solicitor general, D John Sauer, wrote that certain care, including sex-trait-modification surgeries, hormone therapy and social accommodations – such as undergarments, makeup, padding and wigs – “could no longer be justified as treatment for gender dysphoria”. Sauer asked that justices intervene in a legal dispute over Donald Trump’s executive order from January 2025 that directed the Bureau of Prisons to “ensure that no Federal funds are expended for any medical procedure, treatment, or drug for the purpose of conforming an inmate’s appearance to that of the opposite sex”. The order prohibited trans prisoners from receiving certain gender transition medical care and ordered trans women prisoners to be housed in men’s facilities. Trans prisoners sued the administration over the policy and, so far, two lower courts have blocked officials from implementing the order as the larger lawsuit over the executive order continues. In his second term, Trump has sought to restrict trans rights by rescinding Biden-era policies that allowed trans women and girls to participate on athletic teams that align with their gender identity, trans service members to serve in the military and trans minors to receive gender-affirming care. The administration has leaned heavily on the conservative-majority supreme court to assist it in implementing anti-trans policies, often in the form of emergency requests. In Monday’s request, Sauer argued the government had suffered harm by not being permitted to deny gender-affirming care to trans prisoners because “prison administrators have determined is necessary to maintain institutional security”. He cites conclusions from the Bureau of Prisons that found providing greater gender-affirming care access “raise fairness concerns” and “breed resentment among other inmates”, among other concerns. Justices are asking lawyers for the trans prisoners to respond to the government’s request by 8 October. So far, the court has been sympathetic toward the administration’s policies. It has allowed the state department to remove preferred gender markers on passports for nonbinary or trans Americans and the Department of Defense to enforce a ban on trans service members. Last term, the justices also upheld state-level bans on providing gender-affirming care for trans minors and banning trans women and girls athletes from participating on sports teams.

title: South West Water fined £8m for hundreds of sewage spills in Cornwall and Devon
summary: District judge orders record fine for region and says incidents of pollution cannot be tolerated
text: A water company has been ordered to pay a record fine of almost £8m for hundreds of sewage spills at popular bathing spots and sensitive habitats in Cornwall and Devon. On one occasion, untreated sewage gushed through a harbour wall on a bank holiday weekend but South West Water (SWW) engineers took 10 hours to attend. Sewage was also discharged into the River Camel, which is home to otter and Atlantic salmon and is popular with birdwatchers and sailors. Fining SWW £7,867,733 at Plymouth magistrates court – the largest fine for environmental offences in the region – District Judge Matson said incidents of pollution could not be tolerated. The judge repeatedly found the company’s conduct amounted to reckless failures in management systems and response to known risks. In August 2019, untreated sewage gushed through the harbour wall on a bank holiday weekend at Polperro harbour on the south coast of Cornwall. Between January 2016 and July 2021, there were 231 illegal sewage discharges at Harlyn on the north coast of Cornwall, not far from the foodie hotspot of Padstow. In another case, SWW failed to provide a permanent fix for a sewer that entered a creek in Plymouth, despite multiple formal warnings from the Environment Agency over several years. The company pleaded guilty to 18 charges, 17 for illegal water discharge activities and one for failing to take reasonable remedial measures after a failure at a pumping station. Matson described the offences as “horrendous, very significant incidents of pollution” and said they should never happen again. Despite the company pleading guilty, the judge found that SWW had tried to minimise its role in the offending rather than being remorseful and accepting full responsibility. Clarissa Newell, area environment manager at the Environment Agency, which led the prosecution, said: “Hundreds of pollution incidents occurred at some of the most scenic locations in Cornwall and Devon, including bathing waters, a designated special area of conservation and a priority habitat. We hope this record fine will influence a new approach for South West Water.” The fine came as the prime minister, Andy Burnham, described water as a symbol of what had gone wrong with Britain and promised to reverse Margaret Thatcher’s “ideological ban” on the public ownership of water companies Responding to the fine, the environment secretary, Angela Eagle, said: “For six years, South West Water repeatedly broke the law. That’s why we’re overhauling the water system to give the public control, with tougher regulation, stronger enforcement and greater accountability, so water companies deliver for customers and the environment.” The Liberal Democrat MP for North Cornwall, Ben Maguire, criticised the punishment. He said: “Yet again, the response is essentially another slap on the wrist fine, which a company of this size can absorb as simply the cost of doing business. The hard-working South West Water technicians and other staff I meet are being completely let down by rotten executives. “I strongly believe we urgently need much tougher penalties for repeat offenders, including prison sentences for those responsible for overseeing serious and illegal sewage dumping.” SWW described the offences as “historic” and said: “The majority of the charges concerned the use of overflows in storm conditions. We’re investing £760m to tackle storm overflows and have reduced spills by 17% in the last year alone, with spill duration down by 25%. Significant improvements have been made across the sites concerned. We apologise for what happened in the past, and we remain focused on the future as we deliver record levels of investment.” The water company was ordered to pay £329,993 costs.

title: National Rally’s Jordan Bardella rails at ‘war’ on party after antisemitism claims
summary: President of Marine Le Pen’s far-right party faces calls to resign over comments he allegedly wrote as a teenager
text: Jordan Bardella, the head of Marine Le Pen’s far-right National Rally (RN), has claimed a “total war” is being waged against his party as he faces a political storm after the publication of antisemitic comments he allegedly wrote as a young party member. Bardella, who is facing calls from political opponents to resign, said on Tuesday that the report by the investigative website Mediapart was false. To a standing ovation from his party’s lawmakers and senators at a meeting in parliament, he said the report was an attempt to damage his party as Le Pen tops the polls before the 2027 presidential election. “We are seeing the beginnings of a total war, an attempt to destabilise the presidential campaign,” Bardella said. He accused Mediapart of wanting “to kill my political career” and said he would take legal action for defamation. Le Pen, at Bardella’s side, said she had “absolute confidence” in him. Journalists at Mediapart said they had independently authenticated the comments allegedly written between 2013 and 2015, including in email groups and on messaging services. Bardella was aged 17 to 18 at the time and was a member of the party that was then called the Front National. The alleged comments included “the Jew has to dominate other peoples, crush them, and rob them; a Zionist is necessarily a Jew, and fundamentally so”. He is also alleged to have written “all the banks are owned by Jews”. Mediapart’s investigation has shaken Le Pen’s presidential campaign. Since Le Pen took over the party leadership in 2011, she has sought to detoxify the party image and move it away from its antisemitic past in order to increase its electoral reach. When Le Pen’s father, Jean-Marie Le Pen, co-founded the party in 1972, its ranks included former members of a Waffen SS military unit under Nazi command during the second world war. Pierre Bousquet, a former member of the Waffen SS Charlemagne division, was the party’s treasurer for its first nine years. Another early member had been in the paramilitary militia under Philippe Pétain, the leader of the puppet Vichy regime that collaborated with the Nazis and ensured the deportation of one-quarter of France’s Jewish population to concentration camps, about 76,000 people. In 1987, Jean-Marie Le Pen described the Holocaust as a “mere detail” of the second world war. In the decades that followed he was convicted more than 15 times for hate speech and contesting crimes against humanity as he repeated negationist comments, including saying the Nazi occupation was “not particularly inhumane”. Marine Le Pen, who expelled her father from the party in 2015 after he repeated antisemitic comments, has in recent years directly appealed to French Jewish voters. She said her party would protect them, describing the RN as “the best shield for our fellow French citizens of Jewish faith”. Bardella made an unprecedented visit to Israel in 2025, the first by a French far-right leader, in an attempt to demonstrate the RN’s new credentials. In 2023, Bardella told a TV interviewer he did not think Jean-Marie Le Pen was antisemitic, before backtracking on his comments after criticism. The French foreign minister, Jean-Noël Barrot, responding to the Mediapart investigation, wrote on social media: “To all those with a short memory: antisemitism isn’t an accident in the RN, it’s that party’s history. That’s the real face of the far right.” Aurore Bergé, the minister for equality and against discrimination, said the “antisemitic and conspiracy theory” content of the alleged messages “reminds those who might have forgotten the nature of the far right”. Raphaël Glucksmann, a candidate in the Socialist presidential primary, wrote on social media that no public relations exercise would fundamentally change the RN. “Let us never forget that they all joined a party founded by antisemitic fanatics and out-and-out racists,” he said. Yonathan Arfi, of the CRIF, the umbrella group of French Jewish organisations, told France Culture radio he was “stupefied by the virulence of the antisemitic comments” allegedly made by Bardella. He said that if true, the comments undermined the RN’s claims to have detoxified its image. He asked: “How could a political party leader, having made such sickening comments, reach such a high position in a party that claims to have changed and now fights against the hatred of Jews?” The Green leader, Marine Tondelier, said Bardella, an MEP, should resign from all his political positions. She said: “The man who presents himself today as the biggest defender of Jews … is in reality an obsessional antisemite.”

title: Body of newborn baby found on Welsh shoreline, prompting search for mother
summary: Police and medics fear mother could be ‘extremely vulnerable’ after discovery in Bangor close to Menai strait on Sunday
text: Police are searching for the mother of a newborn baby whose body was found on a Welsh shoreline, fearing she may be ill or vulnerable. A member of the public found the body of the child, whose age and sex have not been disclosed, close to the Menai strait in north Wales. Fiona Giraud, director of midwifery and women’s services for Betsi Cadwaladr University health board, said there were “real concerns” for the mother’s health. She said: “We recognise that she is likely to be extremely vulnerable. She may be fearful of seeking the support she needs through fear of identifying herself.” Making a direct appeal to the mother, she added: “Our immediate concern is for your health, safety and wellbeing. We recognise that you may be feeling frightened, overwhelmed or unsure about what to do next. Please do not feel that you have to face this alone. “We don’t yet know all the circumstances surrounding your baby’s death but what is important right now is that we find you, make sure you are safe and ensure you receive any medical attention and support you may need. You can speak to a healthcare professional, approach a police officer or attend a police station.” North Wales police said the baby’s body had been found in Bangor shortly before 5pm on Sunday. DS Kelly Wynne said: “We are concerned the baby’s mother may not be in a position to reach out for support, so we are appealing directly to her, the father and those who may have knowledge, such as friends, family, neighbours or colleagues. “If you have any information regarding a woman or girl you think may have been pregnant or whose behaviour has been unusual or out of character over the past few months including withdrawing from friends, family or social ties, please contact us. “The mother desperately needs help. Anyone with information, we need you to do the right thing to ensure this mother gets the health support she needs. “All names received will be treated with the utmost discretion and can be eliminated as the mother without delay.” The force said a postmortem examination was due to take place on Wednesday.

title: ‘Every moth is precious’: why are there so many bogong moths, and how can you safely remove them from your home?
summary: Bogong numbers dropped up to 99.5% between 2017 and 2019, but wetter and cooler conditions are thought to be behind the recent surge
text: Skies over parts of New South Wales have been aflutter in recent days as swarms of bogong moths begin their annual migration, travelling up to 1,000 km from their breeding grounds in different parts of the country to a small number of cool caves in the Australian Alps. Sightings of the endangered moth have increased over the last two years, but reports to the citizen science program Moth Tracker this September alone have exceeded 2025’s total figures, according to Zoos Victoria, which runs the platform. What do the burgeoning insect numbers mean for their recovery, and what should you do if you find bogongs inside your home? Why am I seeing so many bogong moths? Spring marks the beginning of an annual migration: huge numbers of the bogong moths migrate to the Australian Alps, where they spend the summer escaping the heat. “They breed and then migrate from their breeding grounds, which are in southern Queensland, in NSW, the ACT, even western Victoria and into South Australia,” said Dr Marissa Parrott, a reproductive biologist at Zoos Victoria. The moths play a critical role as pollinators and also a key food source for the critically endangered mountain pygmy possum. An estimated 4 billion moths used to arrive in the Alps each year, until a catastrophic sudden population collapse – numbers dropped up to 99.5% between 2017 and 2019 – which was thought to have resulted from severe drought in the breeding grounds. Favourable conditions this year – wetter, cooler weather – are thought to be behind the surge in sightings in NSW, in addition to strong winds which have blown the insects from their more typical inland migration routes towards major cities including Sydney and Canberra. Linnea Emneby, project manager of the citizen science project Bogong Watch, run by Invertebrates Australia, said there were no certain estimates of their recent population, but “it does look like they’re on their way to recovery”. The sightings are a promising hearkening back to pre-crash days, when bogongs descended en masse upon Parliament House in Canberra, and interrupted the 2000 Sydney Olympics closing ceremony. “I think people just quickly forget what’s normal and think of this as an extreme occurrence rather than something that is just part of the Australian way,” Emneby said. Newspaper articles from the early and mid-1900s include reports of lighthouse lights being obscured and trains being stopped or delayed by bogong moths, “whose oily bodies were crushed on the rails in thousands”. Bogongs “are a boom and bust species to some extent but climate change makes it worse with prolonged drought seasons for several years, and bushfires where there didn’t used to be bushfires,” Emneby said. Their relative absence in recent years was “as far as we know, not normal”. What do I do if I find bogong moths in my home or workplace? If you encounter bogong moths on their migration, experts urge people to refrain from insecticide use and to upload sightings to the Moth Tracker or Bogong Watch platforms. “Turn off unnecessary outdoor lights, then they won’t be as drawn to buildings, to homes, to businesses,” Parrott said. “If you can shut your vents that’s good … shake your laundry before you bring it in,” Emneby added. For moths already inside buildings, she suggests turning off indoor lights and attracting them back out with one outdoor light. “If they’re close to a window, you can … wave your hand to herd them towards the open window,” Emneby said. “They’re quite skittish.” Another method is to put a glass or container over the moth, sliding a piece of paper underneath to contain them. “Just help them on their way by popping them outside in the safe location, turning off outside lights and they’ll move on,” Parrott said. “Every moth is precious, and we want to help them on their migration.” How do the moths know where to go? How long do they travel for? Young bogongs live underground, “coming up to feed on broad leaf plants before pupating and metamorphosing into the beautiful moths that we know,” Parrott said. “On Moth Tracker we get [verified] reports coming in from almost every state and territory,” she said, adding that the Northern Territory was the only region without verified sightings. The moths’ first migration occurs months after their parents have died, to mountainous caves in the Australian Alps where they have never travelled before. The nocturnal travellers use the Milky Way to guide their way – the only invertebrates known to use celestial navigation – as well as the Earth’s magnetic field. “It could be days to weeks that the moths are migrating to get up to the Alps, but they do come in waves – they will likely be emerging at different times,” Parrott said. “During things like storms and rain, they likely seek shelter, so they’ll be less visible, or they may have been able to move on, sensing its approach. We don’t know exactly how they do that – there’s a lot left that we still need to discover.” After spending the summer months in the alpine caves, in autumn the moths return to their breeding grounds to reproduce and die.

title: Soho House launches investigation after out-of-date food mislabelled in kitchen
summary: Private members’ club apologises after former employee exposes issue at its Shoreditch House venue
text: The Soho House private members’ club has launched an investigation after out-of-date food was mislabelled in one of its kitchens. The club, which charges up to £4,500 a year for membership, has apologised after a former employee made a video on TikTok exposing the issue. “Two days ago I was fired from Soho House, the one at Shoreditch,” the unnamed employee claimed on an account named “Soho House Opp”. “I was fired after I complained about people changing labels and selling out-of-date food to customers.” A Soho House spokesperson said the employee’s contract had been terminated for reasons unrelated to his complaint. The club chain is popular with celebrities, with Kate Moss, Kendall Jenner and Ellie Goulding among those spotted in its venues. The Duke and Duchess of Sussex, Harry and Meghan, met on a blind date in 2016 at its 76 Dean Street house in London, and Meghan has been seen drinking coffee at its Cotswolds location, Soho Farmhouse, since her move to London. A Hackney council spokesperson said it had received, and was reviewing, a health and safety complaint relating to Shoreditch House, one of the club’s 10 London locations. The spokesperson said: “We have received a report about food safety and hygiene at Shoreditch House and have opened an investigation.” The employee claimed he had been “pressured” to change labels to mask out-of-date food. He said he had first made an internal complaint and then, when he did not feel sufficient action was taken, submitted a complaint to the council. He says that shortly after this, he was fired. It is illegal to sell food past its “use-by” date, but food can be sold after its “best before” date as long as it is of acceptable quality. Restaurants and other commercial kitchens have a strict legal duty to ensure all food served to customers is safe and fit for human consumption. A Soho House spokesperson apologised for the mislabelling incident, and said it was an isolated occurrence but that they had launched an investigation. They added: “We’re really sorry that this isolated food labelling incident took place at one of our kitchens. This is not how we expect our Houses to operate and it is not company policy. We have taken immediate action, including our director of health and safety together with an external independent consultant conducting an investigation as a matter of priority.” The spokesperson said the location takes food hygiene seriously, adding: “Delivering the highest level of food safety for our members and guests is incredibly important to us. Shoreditch House has consistently achieved the highest food hygiene rating score of 5 from environmental health inspections – including the most recent in March this year – and also performed strongly in an independent and unannounced external audit last week.” Soho House was founded in 1995 with a single club in the central London area from which it takes its name. It has 10 locations in London, and 48 that are either open or planned around the world, ranging from Paris and Istanbul to Bangkok and Mumbai. It has four clubs in Los Angeles and three in New York. The club chain has had some financial issues in recent years, with members complaining it is no longer as exclusive as it used to be. The owners have attempted to turn its fortunes around by opening a more “exclusive” location in Mayfair and launching mini two-sip cocktails, as well as IV drips, to attract younger members.
