title: RFK Jr outlines expansive vision for collecting US health data at Maha event
summary: Health secretary calls for medical and lifestyle details to be sent to doctors and AI to address ‘chronic disease epidemic’
text: Robert F Kennedy Jr laid out an expansive vision for collecting, sharing and analyzing US health information at a Maha event hosted by a close ally and outspoken anti-vaccine activist. Medical and lifestyle data, from doctor’s visits to exercise, should be connected and shared with the government and independent researchers, where it can be searched by AI – including potential links between vaccines and health outcomes including autism and mortality, suggested Kennedy, the secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and a longtime vaccine skeptic. “We need to use America’s health data to determine whether the food we eat, the chemicals we encounter, the vaccines that we’re administering, the other environmental and lifestyle exposures are contributing in one way or another to the chronic disease epidemic,” Kennedy said at an event with the Maha Institute on Monday, with about two dozen people tuning into the live stream. The Maha Institute is headed by Mark Gorton, who called himself “the boldest anti-vaxxer in the anti-vax conference” two weeks ago. The institute was co-founded by Tony Lyons, whose publishing house gave $4m to Kennedy through various Maha foundations with funding from political contributions and health-related corporations, according to reporting by the New York Times. Kennedy has focused on pulling together data from all of the agencies he oversees, including the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), and the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS). ”Your health information should follow you wherever you go,” Kennedy said. Providers, insurance and technology companies are creating apps for portable health records, for instance – making it easier for individuals to access their medical records, and also opening up the records for governmental and outside use. “Medicaid is a really useful vehicle for studying that because there are hundreds of millions of lives in there, including tens of millions of children who’ve been in that program for 10 or 20 years,” Kennedy said. The Trump administration is now tracking “exposures”, interventions and claim data in Medicaid, and “Medicare gives us enormous amounts of information on older Americans and people with disabilities,” he said. FDA monitoring systems can link claims data and electronic health records “to conduct active safety surveillance”, while commercial platforms, such as HealthVerity, can link insurance claims, prescriptions, laboratory results and electronic health records, he said. State-level datasets reported to the CDC were “unusable” because they often collect different data points, Kennedy said: “Too many of those systems remain siloed and cannot give us the real-time information we need to understand health at scale.” Yet wider access to state health data could allow officials and others to connect immunization records, clinical data, laboratory results, pharmacy information and insurance claims “to create a more complete picture of a patient’s health over a long period of time”, Kennedy said. Federal officials are using AI to process the data, he said: “Studies that used to take years, you can do them literally in seconds. You can ask questions and you can get immediate answers, and that’s what we’re doing today.” Kennedy repeatedly touted the benefits of AI, which has been embraced by some in the anti-vaccine world for purportedly showing the dangers of vaccines. “It can help researchers find patterns across millions of health histories that human beings could never find by reading those records one at a time,” Kennedy said. The OpenAI co-founder Sam Altman met with Kennedy this week and told him that HHS uses generative AI – Kennedy used the term “superintelligence” – more than any other federal agency, Kennedy said. OpenAI agents hacked US government websites and the Australian Medicare website this summer, reporting recently revealed. “We’re already using all of these data to answer some of our most important questions,” Kennedy said. Officials have created an autism registry despite widespread protest. The Trump administration has also launched studies on the roles of such factors as diet, electromagnetic fields, screen time and vaccines in the development of illness, Kennedy said. He repeatedly returned to vaccines. At the CDC, officials are using the Vaccine Safety Datalink (VSD) to compare outcomes in healthcare for vaccinated and unvaccinated people, as well as examining the role of aluminum adjuvants in vaccines; the timing of the hepatitis B vaccine in infancy; comparing live and attenuated vaccines; and studying influenza, Covid and HPV vaccines in children, Kennedy said. Using Medicaid and “linked real-world data”, officials are also studying vaccination during pregnancy and subsequent childhood outcomes. FDA researchers are using the Biologics Effectiveness and Safety (Best) System and Medicare data to “replicate and expand previous studies” on vaccinated and unvaccinated populations, aluminum and asthma, and maternal influenza vaccines and autism spectrum disorder, he said. “We will have answers soon,” Kennedy said. “A more connected health data system will make this research even stronger.” Kennedy returned repeatedly to an old grievance – how independent citizens attempting to link vaccines to autism were blocked from accessing VSD data in the early 2000s after they violated confidentiality agreements. Mark and David Geier were not affiliated with any research institutions at the time of their suspension, and they created their own institutional review board to oversee their work, according to the Maryland state board of physicians, which suspended Mark Geier’s medical license. The board also charged David Geier with practicing medicine without a licence. “I cannot get access to that data today. I cannot get access to it,” Kennedy said of the VSD data after 2002, which is safeguarded by healthcare organizations for health privacy reasons. “A qualified researcher with a legitimate hypothesis should not need permission from a gatekeeper to test it,” Kennedy said, calling the VSD an “unworkable system”. The Trump administration’s goal now was to make health data “research ready, and then give access to hundreds of external researchers to actually come in and look at it”, Kennedy said. Gorton, the Maha Institute president, focused on open data in his comments at the event on Monday. But less than two weeks earlier, at a meeting of the anti-vaccine organization Children’s Health Defense, Gorton called vaccines a “public health nightmare”, spread misinformation about their ingredients, claimed that 40% of all kids are “injured” by vaccines because of allergy, asthma and eczema diagnoses, and railed against “the poisoners running the medical system”. The success of vaccination, frequently called one of the greatest achievements in science, is a “complete fabrication” and “massive fraud”, Gorton said at the 17 September conference. He took particular aim at polio vaccines, claiming that an outbreak of polio in the 1950s was actually because of pesticides. “The supposed success of the polio vaccine was a massive medical fraud and a masterful PR deception,” Gorton claimed. “The time has come to stop caveating every introduction with ‘I’m not an anti-vaxxer, but …’ Vaccines are a nightmare, and only anti-vaxxers can speak clearly enough,” Gorton said at that conference, adding: “More vaccines, more autism. It’s that simple.” Focusing on opening up health data is new for the Maha Institute. But having greater access to US health information would help advocates make new links to the issues they have long focused on, Gorton said on Monday. Organizations including the Maha Institute, which exists outside the government but enjoys close ties to top leaders such as Kennedy, can “fill the gaps” and “bring political pressure”, he said. Kennedy thanked Gorton, his longtime friend, for his “incredible support”.

title: Spain announces plan to ease housing crisis amid outcry over eviction of 87-year-old
summary: Measures, which need to be approved in Congress, include extending ban on evictions of vulnerable people
text: Spain’s Socialist Workers’ party-led coalition government has approved a range of measures aimed at easing the country’s housing crisis, including extending a ban on evictions of vulnerable tenants until 2030, after a public outcry over the eviction of an 87-year-old disabled woman from her Madrid apartment last week. Two decrees have been approved by cabinet but will need to be approved in Congress, where the coalition lacks a majority. The government has requested a special parliamentary session on Friday in the hope of getting the decrees passed as soon as possible. Although the fine print has yet be revealed, the main decree includes: extending restrictions on evictions of vulnerable tenants to 2030; regulating temporary lettings and lettings by room; a ban on so-called vulture funds buying property until 2028, plus a two-year extension on current rental agreements that are due to expire at the end of 2028. A separate agreement was reached on the automatic renovation of rental agreements. Hundreds of people remained camped out in ⁠one of Madrid’s main squares on Tuesday to protest against Maricarmen Abascal’s removal from her home on a stretcher last Wednesday. They are demanding legal reforms including a rent freeze and the ⁠automatic renewal of leases without abusive rent hikes. It is believed that the first decree has the approval of the conservative Catalan and Basque parties, which previously opposed the government’s housing overhauls, but they are likely to vote down the second decree. Mónica García, the health minister, celebrated the decision, saying: “We’ve achieved something that even a month ago was unthinkable.” She added: “It’s time to intervene in the speculative housing market and begin to restore the balance between citizens and vulture funds.” The Tenants’ Union, which has been the driving force behind the demand for changes to the housing law, as well as the occupation of Madrid’s central Puerta del Sol by protesters in recent days, said it needed to read the small print but opposed the policy of dividing the issue into separate decrees. “It’s a tactic of tearing something into shreds so that all that’s left are scraps,” said Alicia Del Río, a union spokesperson in Madrid. “The union demands the implementation of the Maricarmen decree in its entirety,” she said, referring to a set of changes drawn up by the union. “They have to accept what people are demanding.” The government has 30 days from the decree’s publication to reach a consensus with allies in congress. Junts, the Catalan pro-independence party that would need to back the decree for it to pass, said on Tuesday it was still far from agreeing to ‌it and wanted protection for small landlords, who make up the vast majority of property owners in Spain. “Owning two properties isn’t the same as owning entire buildings,” said Míriam Nogueras, Junts’ spokesperson in congress. “But here they’re not making any distinction between the two.” Alberto Núñez Feijóo, the leader of the conservative People’s party, dismissed the proposals. “The government has created a problem that didn’t exist when it took office,” he said. “A problem that was created over eight years can’t be solved in five minutes.” Urbagestión, the company whose eviction of Abascal last Wednesday forced the housing crisis to the top of the political agenda, has said Abascal can return to her apartment at a rent that will not exceed 30% of her income. On Tuesday, she accepted the offer and will pay €533 (£457) a month – less than a third of the original demand of €1,650 that had led to her eviction. Underlining the lack of affordable housing, Ada Colau, a housing activist and a former Barcelona mayor, recently revealed that she has had to move out of her rented apartment after 15 years because it became impossible to pay the rent with a single income since she separated from her husband. Colau, who renounced most of her mayoral salary during her eight years in office, said the market was geared towards dual incomes, whether couples or people sharing, adding that she had gone to live with a relative.

title: Estonia blames Russia for arson attack on drone maker supplying Ukraine
summary: European and Nato leaders express support for Estonia after August attack on manufacturer in Tallinn
text: European and Nato leaders have expressed full support for Estonia and Ukraine after the Baltic state said an August arson attack on a drone manufacturer supplying Kyiv was an act of sabotage commissioned by Moscow’s security services. Estonia’s foreign minister, Margus Tsahkna, said on social media on Tuesday that such attacks were “absolutely unacceptable” and that Russia’s chargé d’affaires in the Estonian capital, Tallinn, was being summoned to his ministry. Estonia’s national security agency said a fire broke out on 15 August at a building in Tallinn used by Milrem Robotics, which makes unmanned ground vehicles used in Ukraine. Two Latvian suspects were detained in Latvia on 17 August, followed by a third the next day. All three were handed over to Estonia, it said. Tsahkna said the subsequent investigation had led authorities to “conclude with certainty” that the attack was “an act of sabotage ordered by the special services of the Russian Federation”. It was part of a “broader campaign across Europe aimed at intimidating us and weakening our support for Ukraine”, he said. Estonia’s prime minister, Kristen Michal, said his country’s response to Russia’s campaign would “be the opposite: stronger security at home, more support for Ukraine and greater pressure on Russia. We will not be intimidated.” Estonia has repeatedly accused Russia of hybrid provocations since the beginning of Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and, along with its fellow Baltic states Latvia and Lithuania, has significantly increased its defence spending. Dmitry Peskov, the Kremlin spokesperson, said Estonia’s allegations were “unfounded, ill-considered, absolutely not reflecting the reality, not containing any substantiation whatsoever”. He said Russia “cannot take such statements seriously, and we won’t”. Western allies pledged their continued support to Estonia and Ukraine. Speaking in Brussels, Mark Rutte, Nato’s secretary general, said Russia “continues its reckless campaign of hostile actions against Nato allies”, adding that it was “failing … on the battlefield in Ukraine, and failing to undermine our unity and support for Ukraine”. Speaking alongside Rutte, Lithuania’s prime minister, Mindaugas Sinkevičius, said Russia’s actions were becoming “increasingly hostile and less restrained … We see the hybrid attacks – in Lithuania, Poland, Germany, elsewhere. And it’s not a question of proximity now, it’s a question of Russia’s actions.” Lithuania’s foreign minister, Kęstutis Budrys, said Russia’s fingerprints were “all over” the Tallinn attack, while the Latvian president, Edgars Rinkēvičs, said further support for Ukraine “will be needed, and must be provided”. The EU said it stood with Estonia, describing the arson attack as “reckless” and saying it would not be put off supporting Ukraine. “Moscow is trying to scare Europe into winding down its support for Ukraine. This will not happen,” a European Commission spokesperson said. France’s president, Emmanuel Macron, called the arson attack a “dangerous escalation”. Moscow “needs to know that it will not overcome our unity or our determination to continue supporting Ukraine”, Macron said on social media. Sweden’s acting prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, called Estonia’s formal attribution of the attack “extremely serious”, and Britain’s ambassador to Estonia, Jo Lomas, said the UK “stands with Estonia in confronting these unacceptable attacks. They will not weaken our resolve or our support for Ukraine.” About 200 incidents of suspected Russian sabotage and malign activity have been recorded across Europe since Moscow’s invasion of Ukraine, including arson plots at warehouses, drone incursions, thefts of defence technology and cyber-attacks on essential European infrastructure. Agence France-Presse and Associated Press contributed to this report

title: Nor’easter unearths pieces of 19th-century shipwreck in Massachusetts
summary: Storm seems to have exposed segments of the Warren Sawyer, a wooden vessel that ran aground in 1884
text: The nor’easter storm that pummeled New England over the weekend looks to have exposed large segments of a 19th-century schooner shipwrecked in the so-called graveyard of the Atlantic. The Warren Sawyer was sailing from New Orleans to Boston carrying cotton and scrap iron when the three-masted wooden vessel ran aground in Nantucket on 22 December 1884. Its captain and crew of seven were rescued and the ship began to break up after several weeks on the shoreline. Now marine investigators in Massachusetts are looking at splintered timbers fastened together by rusted iron that emerged from the sand during the weekend storm close to where smaller remnants of the lost schooner have been located previously. The Egan Maritime Institute, a Nantucket-based educational non-profit, by Monday said it was sending staff in the coming days to examine the site and fragments. And the group said it would prepare a report for state archaeologists to help identify the vessel they came from. The institute, in a statement to the Associated Press, said it was too soon to be sure the newly emerged segments were definitely from the Warren Sawyer. Nantucket, it said, was one of the “graveyards of the Atlantic” and its “treacherous shoals and inclement weather” contributed to more than 750 wrecks during the 19th century when hundreds of vessels would traverse the island’s waters daily without modern maritime navigation equipment. But the proximity to the recorded site of the Warren Sawyer’s demise convinced journalist Jason Graziadei, editor of the online news site the Nantucket Current, that it was likely. Graziadei said he went to the beach on Saturday during the storm with his eight-year-old son after receiving a tip about wreckage on the island’s south shore, and he posted video of what he saw to YouTube. He said they found the wooden beams on a drive-on beach by the town’s wastewater facility known as the sewer beds after parking and climbing down to the beach because erosion from the storm had formed a steep drop-off. “Given where it was and where it emerged, it means that everyone who was driving on to the beach this summer was just directly over this,” Graziadei said. “It’s amazing to think from, you know, over 100 years old that it’s still there.” Records from the Massachusetts Board of Underwater Archaeological Resources show the Warren Sawyer was carrying 1,115 bales of cotton and 28 tons (25.4 metric tonnes) of scrap iron from New Orleans to Boston when it ran aground. The schooner remained intact on the island’s Miacomet Beach for two weeks, allowing islanders to save 700 bales of cotton using skids and teams of oxen. On 6 January 1885, another storm tore the ship apart, scattering pieces of its hull, remaining cargo and cordage across more than half a mile of beach. Remnants believed to be from the ship have continued to emerge from the sand. Massachusetts state archaeologists inspected a roughly 42ft (12.8-meter) section of hull exposed on Miacomet Beach in late 2022 and concluded it was probably part of the Warren Sawyer. A roughly 15ft square section of the lower stern appeared nearby in February 2023, but shifting sands buried it again before state archaeologists could return to document it. The Egan Institute urged visitors not to disturb the newly exposed wreckage. Massachusetts law prohibits removing, damaging or displacing underwater archaeological resources. The Associated Press contributed to this report

title: Meta’s AI agent Muse gives out user’s home address without permission, sending buyer to his house
summary: The new AI agent, Muse, was released last week and has been downloaded by 3 million users
text: When Usman asked if a keyboard for sale on Facebook Marketplace was still available on Saturday, he received an enthusiastic and immediate response. “Yep still available!” wrote Matt Robb. The two agreed on a price, and Robb sent his Toronto address. Usman, wife and daughter in tow, showed up several hours later at Robb’s home and sent a text that he had arrived. Robb responded, “yep I’m here!”, but he was not at home. Nobody walked out of the apartment building. Usman sent Robb a picture of the building’s door and wrote, “Hello???? I am standing outside.” After 20 minutes of no face-to-face contact, he abandoned the sale. “Man if you didn’t want to sell it why did you waste my time man,” he wrote, and drove away. An hour later, Robb, or who Usman thought was Robb, responded apologetically. “Hey really sorry about tonight, got tied up and missed you completely,” read the message, which the Guardian reviewed. Usman had not contacted the real Robb. Throughout the daylong interaction, the human version of Robb never knew Usman had messaged him or had agreed to buy the keyboard. He did not know Usman had received his address or that he was waiting outside his apartment building. Usman had spoken to Meta’s new AI agent, Muse, released on 22 September in the US and downloaded 3m times. The company advertises the semi-autonomous AI product as a personal assistant. Without Robb’s consent or approval, Muse had given out his home address, creating the false impression that Robb was expecting the would-be buyer at his apartment, he said. The first message Robb actually sent Usman came 24 hours later, once he realized what had happened. “Hey man I’m really sorry for the other day,” the message, which the Guardian reviewed, said. “I activated muse metas new Al and it literally took control of my Facebook marketplace and it gave you my address. Genuinely didn’t even know it had arranged for you to come to my literal apartment it didn’t ask me for approval.” Robb, a consumer tech reviewer, had seen Meta advertise Muse’s ability to automate his Marketplace listings and decided to take advantage of it. He input his address as the pickup location but said he never gave Muse permission to share it with potential buyers. Muse was also negotiating on his behalf without seeking approval, accepting lowball offers, he said. Robb said he never received any heads-up from the agent about the transaction or the meetup. He never knew that Usman was en route to his house. Usman told the Guardian he thought he was speaking to Robb the whole time. Robb shared screenshots of Muse’s interaction with Usman on Threads, the text-based social network owned by Meta. David Singleton, the co-founder and CEO of Meta’s Superintelligence Labs, tweeted that he had been in touch with Robb. Singleton said that, when investigating similar reports, the company had “consistently learned that Muse was following direct instructions and correctly asked for permission. Would love to help and figure out what’s going on here!” After speaking with Singleton, Robb said when he asked Muse to handle his marketplace interactions, he was shown two options: “Allow One Time” or “Allow Always”. Unbeknown to Robb, clicking the latter meant he had given Muse permission to respond to all his marketplace messages on his behalf going forward with the information he provided – including his address. “I clicked the latter thinking it would still send approvals to accept offers later down the line (it didn’t so be careful),” Robb posted on Threads in an update. “I mentioned to the meta team it could be easily overlooked as it was with me and they said they will be making this more clear moving forwards.” Muse ultimately admitted to Robb that he never gave it permission to share his address. “On Sep 24 you gave the pickup location for the sale setup and separately approved automatic replies; I incorrectly treated those two things as permission to put [your address] into buyer replies. I never asked for consent.” Robb said he assumed that, because Meta owned Marketplace, Muse and Messenger, there would be an integration that would make it clear when other users were speaking to an AI agent or that messages would be clearly marked as being sent by Muse. Meta AI, another of the company’s AI products, makes it obvious a user is conversing with a chatbot. “But Muse is doing something else,” he said. “It’s almost imitating me.” After the incident with Usman, Robb told Muse to stop giving his address. To test the bot, he asked a few friends to see if Muse would still share it. “And it literally gave my address out to five people,” he said. In addition to sharing his address and inviting a stranger to his home without his approval, Muse also made up information. The AI agent, responding as Robb, told Usman that Robb was home when he was not, then apologized with a fabrication about being too busy. “The worst part was Muse actually replied: ‘I’m right here, like waiting for you,’” Robb said. “It made it so much worse because I don’t know if the guy thought I was messing with him.” While a great deal of attention has been paid to the ways frontier AI models are going rogue, Meta’s agent is an AI product in the hands of millions of everyday consumers, many of whom have given it their private information.

title: Dennis Haskins, US actor who played Mr Belding in Saved by the Bell, dies aged 75
summary: Agent calls death of Haskins, who played the school principal in three programs, ‘a tragic loss’
text: The US actor Dennis Haskins – most known for co-starring in the popular Saved by the Bell television series franchise – has died, his agent confirmed on Tuesday. He was 75. Alluding to Haskins’ Saved by the Bell character, the fictional high school principal Mr Richard Belding, agent Jay Schachter said in a statement: “It’s a tragic loss. Everyone loved Mr Belding, and those of us who got to know Dennis loved him even more. “He was a great person, and he loved, I mean absolutely LOVED his fans. He always had time for them, no matter what.” Authorities have not disclosed Haskins’ cause of death, which reportedly occurred late on Sunday. Haskins played Belding in three programs. First, he was the character in Disney’s 1989 show Good Morning, Miss Bliss. NBC later turned that show into Saved by the Bell, achieving a level of prominence among its viewers during a four-season run beginning in 1989. He then once again played the principal during Saved by the Bell: The New Class during its seven-season run beginning in 1993. Saved by the Bell achieved a cult status among a generation of US youth as a sitcom centering on high school students grappling with growing up as teenagers. On the show, Belding’s memorable catchphrase was “Hey, hey, hey, what is going on here?” during efforts to discipline his students. One of the show’s stars, Lark Voorhies, reacted to Haskins’ death on Instagram by saying “losing him hurt so deeply’. “Knowing Dennis Haskins for almost 40 years has been one of the truest blessings of my life,” said the post from Voorhies, who portrayed the character Lisa Turtle. “We shared so much history together from our earliest days, and through it all, he remained a fabulous person, a loyal friend, and someone with such a kind, gentle heart. I am truly heartbroken by his passing and will miss his warmth and laughter more than words can say. Rest in peace, Dennis, you will always hold a special place in my heart.” Dimples Karaoke, a karaoke bar in Burbank, California, which Haskins regularly patronized, also mourned his passing, Variety reported. “Dennis was a staple at Dimples,” the bar said in an Instagram post on Monday. “A lot of people thought he owned it, but he didn’t. He just loved the place and its people. He enjoyed singing for people, meeting them, and taking selfies with his fans.” The bar also said: “Dimples closed down about 11 years ago, and people still associate him with his beloved ‘second home.’ He was known to most as Mr Belding from Saved by the Bell, but to us, he was much more than that.” The bar’s post said that Haskins fell ill about eight years ago but didn’t discuss his conditions “because he did not want the attention”. “Late last night, that journey ended for him. He is now at peace and is probably entertaining the people in the sky,” the post furthermore remarked. It added: “What a cool and amazing life he had. Rest in peace, Dennis. You were very much loved and will never be forgotten.” Haskins, a native of Chattanooga, Tennessee, also acted in a variety of other television shows and movies. His parts included appearances on Hot in Cleveland, It’s Always Sunny in Philadelphia, Mad Men and A Million Ways to Die in the West, according to IMDb. He also expressed pride in having completed a bachelor of arts degree in theater from the University of Tennessee at Chattanooga in 2015. “As successful as some have said I’ve been, from the incredible success of ‘Saved by the Bell,’ other quality acting roles, the books I’ve written, and even UTC Distinguished Alumni in 2000, there’s always been something missing for me – my college degree,” Haskins said in a statement on the university website at the time. “Now, … I join these graduates in holding my head high having earned my liberal arts degree in theater from the University of Tennessee at Chattanooga!” The Associated Press contributed reporting

title: New English homes in flood-risk areas could become uninsurable, says Aviva boss
summary: Amanda Blanc says flooding threat is ‘absolutely increasing’, as she also warns ministers over ‘kite flying’ before budget
text: The boss of Britain’s biggest insurer has said that homes being built now in England could become uninsurable in the future because they are sited in flood-risk areas. Amanda Blanc, the chief executive of Aviva, said the flooding threat was “absolutely increasing”. She told the BBC: “You’ve seen a very dry summer, and what happens if you then get heavy rain on very dry surfaces is you get more surface water flooding.” She said 110,000 homes had been built in flood areas in the past 10 years, and if that continued, a further 115,000 new homes would be built in flood areas in the next decade. “That doesn’t seem to me to make sense. We need to think about where those homes are being built,” she said. Blanc told the BBC’s Big Boss Interview podcast that England was “for sure” building properties that might become uninsurable in the future. “If you think that there’s an inevitability of something happening, that’s not what insurance is, right? Insurance is a pool where you know there’s a risk that something happens for some people and not for others. When there is an inevitability, it makes it very difficult for it to be insured.” She added: “It’s very well known where these flooding areas are. Let’s think very carefully about homes that are being built,” she told planners and housebuilders. “It’s dangerous.” About 6.3m homes and businesses in England are at risk of flooding, according to the Environment Agency. It has said this could increase to about 8m, or one in four properties, by the mid-century as the climate crisis worsens. If a property cannot get insurance cover or it is prohibitively expensive to insure because it is prone to frequent flooding, the homeowner would have to foot the bill, with knock-on effects on their ability to get a mortgage or sell the property. Some towns may have to be abandoned as climate breakdown makes many areas uninsurable, a Guardian investigation found last year. Blanc said a lot could be done to mitigate damage, such as using bricks with self-closing air vents, having stainless steel kitchens instead of wooden furniture and creating plug points halfway up the wall rather than near the floor. “You can do all sorts of different things to your property to make it more or less vulnerable to flood.” According to Aviva’s research, more than a quarter (26%), or 101,657 new homes, have some risk of flooding now, and one in seven will be at medium to high risk of flooding by 2050. After the very wet and stormy winter in the UK in 2023-24, the Met Office estimated that such winters had gone from once in 80-year events to once in 20-year events. Blanc also called on the government to avoid policy “kite flying” before John Healey’s first budget as chancellor on 28 October. Aviva is a leading private pension provider, and speculation about changes to pensions led to a jump in withdrawals in the run-up to the budget in the last two years. “Effectively we saw in the last year 30 times the normal withdrawal from pensions that we would normally see, which is clearly something which customers may regret afterwards because once you take your tax-free lump sum out, you can’t put it back in,” she said. Blanc has come under criticism over her role as BP’s senior independent director in which she led the search for a new chair twice in a year, after the controversial ousting of Albert Manifold. She will stand down next year after five years on the board. She said: “It’s been a tough gig, right? There’s no doubt about that, and there’s been a lot thrown at BP. But if I look at it today and the combination of a new chair, new CEO, I think that’s a good combination to take BP forward … it’s time for me to move away.”

title: What is Burnham’s GB Grid plan and could it bring down energy bills?
summary: Proposed government-backed network body welcomed by some in sector but others call it just another quango
text: Andy Burnham’s first address to the Labour party conference as prime minister addressed Britain’s rising energy costs and sluggish economic growth with plans for a new government-backed body to invest in the electricity grid. The proposals to set up Great British Grid, first revealed by the Guardian, build on the party’s manifesto pledge to create Great British Energy, a state-owned company to invest in renewables. However, GB Grid faces a tougher challenge: lowering bills and supercharging the economy through public investment in the electricity network. “We have a cost crisis. We all know it,” Burnham argues. “The price of energy is crippling for businesses, and British bill payers pay some of the highest energy costs in Europe. “We have an energy system where prices are dictated in markets miles away, while families and businesses here shoulder the costs. Once again, the British public has lost control.” Few would disagree with the diagnosis – but is direct government investment in grids the remedy Britain needs? What is the grid plan? Burnham says the government-owned GB Grid will work with the private sector and network companies to increase competition in the sector, drive down costs and speed up delivery. This should help companies and businesses connect to the power grid sooner, and make energy costs cheaper for all consumers. The creation of GB Grid is timely. In the coming years Great Britain plans to invest more in upgrading its power lines and electricity infrastructure than it has in the past three decades combined. It also fits in with Burnham’s philosophy of increasing public control over utilities. “The essentials in life will be controlled by the people. They are ours: we rely on them, we pay for them, and we will have power over them. That is what public control can do,” the PM argues. How will it work? GB Grid has limited funds – at most about £4bn, or a fraction of the £70bn investment expected over the next five years – so its level of “control” is likely to be limited, too. However, alongside the new quango, Burnham plans to expand the rights of developers and businesses to build their own infrastructure to connect projects to the grid. GB Grid will be available to support and co-invest alongside companies, so they can vie for competitively tendered transmission projects with the established network companies to get work done cheaper and faster. The idea was inspired by the approach taken in Ireland, where allowing fresh companies to compete with the incumbent networks has sped up connections by 11 months. What has been the reaction? Given the long history of delays linking projects to the electricity network, it remains to be seen whether Burnham’s plan can make a meaningful difference to the cost and pace of the grid overhaul, but the PM’s approach already has its supporters. “The UK is one of the only countries to have fully privatised its grid,” said Mathew Lawrence, a director at Common Wealth, which campaigns for public ownership. “Our vision is a fully public grid, but today’s announcement can help rebuild state capacity in energy, learning by doing.” Doug Parr, a policy director at Greenpeace, said the plan was “a welcome step to grapple with a problem that has plagued the green energy sector for years”. Greg Jackson, the founder of Octopus and a member of the Cabinet Office board which advises the government, has been a vocal critic of the network industry, which is built around a series of regional monopoly network companies that undertake the grid upgrades in their local area. In recent years other companies have been allowed to tender for work in competition with the regional monopolies – but Octopus has argued that more competition could speed up connections, improve innovation and reduce costs. Not everyone is convinced by the proposals, however. One network industry source told the Guardian: “If they want to have more competition, that’s fine. But at the end of the day, we are all chasing the same supply chains and skilled contractors, and then we’re all using the same planning system. The pressures won’t be different if you use a different name.” What has been holding up grid upgrades? In recent years, Great Britain’s power networks have become inundated with applications for grid connections. These have come from prospective energy developers hoping to plug in new renewable energy projects and batteries to the grid, as well as those hoping to build new housing, factories and datacentres. Queue times for a connection hit more than 15 years at one point, due in large part to a deluge of speculative project applications that were unlikely to move ahead. Despite a two-year programme by the government’s National Energy System Operator (Neso) and the industry regulator to remove these “zombie” projects from the queue in favour of “shovel-ready” schemes, there are still complaints over the speed of connection work. This has raised concerns over whether the government’s target to double onshore wind, triple solar power and quadruple offshore wind might be derailed. It has prompted warnings that the UK economy might miss out on investment in new infrastructure if developers cannot be sure of a swift connection to the grid. So are electricity networks driving up the cost of energy? In short: yes. After years of underinvestment, Great Britain’s ageing power grids are in need of a multibillion-pound overhaul to build new pylons and substations while rolling out thousands of miles of new power lines across the country. The amount spent by network companies is controlled by the industry regulator for Great Britain, Ofgem, before the costs are recovered through our energy bills – and the sums are rising fast. Network companies are expected to spend between £70bn and £80bn between 2026 and 2030, and network investments of £89bn could be needed in the 2030s, according to Neso. This means bill levies will rise, too. Power grid costs currently make up almost a quarter of household electricity bills – almost £210 on the average annual dual-fuel bill last year. Some analysts believe that could rise to £341 a year by 2030. These costs should allow the UK to access more low-cost renewable energy and reduce the system’s reliance on gas, which should eventually lead to lower costs and falling bills. Over the longer term this investment makes sense – not least because much of the upgrade work that would need to happen whether the UK government pursued ambitious green targets or not. However, in the near term, rising energy costs are piling pressure on households and slowing the economy. Are private network companies to blame for rising costs and delays? While there are many factors at play in the slow progress of the UK’s energy transition, the energy networks industry has come under fire for making healthy profits while millions struggle with the costs loaded on to bills. The companies argue their activities are already tightly controlled by Ofgem, which approves all their spending and how it is collected from bills. It is also guided by the government-owned Neso, which has set out the roadmap for the government’s energy policies. “If the government wants things to be different it is within their power to make changes,” the industry source added. “I don’t think spending £4bn in an industry already spending £70bn in the next few years will do much to change anything.” Sam Richards, the chief executive of the pro-growth campaign group Britain Remade, accused Burnham of “setting up yet another quango” rather than “doing the serious work of bringing down bills” by reforming the market and the planning system. “This is a sideshow,” he said. “Britain needs more competition and fewer barriers to new energy projects, not more government bureaucracy with a grand name.”

title: ‘Dangerous precedent’: authors sue LA library over cancelled Palestine event
summary: City of LA faces free speech suit after public library officials scrapped two writers’ Read Palestine Week book talks
text: Two authors have sued the city of Los Angeles over the Los Angeles public library’s (LAPL) cancellation of a Read Palestine Week event where the writers were scheduled to discuss their books featuring Palestinian stories. Jenan Matari, a Palestinian-American author, and Nora Lester Murad, a Jewish-American writer, were invited to speak virtually at a 6 December 2025 event organized as part of the LAPL’s Teen’Scape program, which works with youth. Matari and Murad’s talk was promoted as the library’s programming for Read Palestine Week, an international event promoting Palestinian writers. Members of the library’s “teen council”, a youth volunteer group, had advocated for the event. Matari was promoting her debut children’s book, Everything Grows in Jiddo’s Garden, about a young Palestinian girl and her grandfather, and Murad was set to discuss Ida in the Middle, her young adult novel about a 13-year-old Palestinian-American girl. Three days before the discussion, the writers were told that LAPL administrators had cancelled the event without explanation, according to their complaint filed on Monday. The authors said their requests for a follow-up meeting were ignored. The lawsuit, filed in state court in LA, alleges free speech violations, discrimination and breach of contract. “Palestinian writers and creatives are so exhausted by having to fight every day to have our voices heard,” Matari said in her first interview about the lawsuit. “To be censored by an institution like the library is really scary because this is where free speech should be cultivated and nurtured. It sets a very dangerous precedent … Nora and I agreed we had to show these institutions they cannot continue to get away with this.” The cancellation came after a staff librarian wrote an email to library leadership on 17 November, accusing both writers of having “strong terrorist ties and virulently antisemitic views”, according to documents disclosed through public records requests and cited in the lawsuit. The email said it was sent on behalf of a group of Jewish library staffers, and said: “although the event is planned as an online program, the safety of library staff and participants must still be taken into consideration.” The email included links to rightwing news articles and pro-Israel activist websites that had accused Matari and Murad of antisemitism. One website cited social media posts by Matari after the 7 October 2023 attacks in which she wrote “resist”, “May this Palestinian uprising be the push needed for the dominos of colonialism to fall from every corner of this world.” In another post, she said the US was “under Zionist occupation”. A pro-Israel webpage about Murad cited her participation in Gaza solidarity protests at Columbia University in 2024 and included video of her chanting along with protesters: “Resistance is justified when people are occupied!” In a 16 December staff email discussing the cancellation, John Szabo, the longtime city librarian, said all library programs must “align with our core values, including welcoming everyone”. He said Matari’s posts related to 7 October “did not meet these requirements”, and said cancellation was “necessary to uphold the library’s commitment to an inclusive environment”. An LAPL spokesperson did not respond to detailed questions about the event and the claims raised in the complaint, saying in an email on Monday that it had not yet seen the lawsuit. Szabo and the librarian who sent the email criticizing the authors did not immediately respond to inquiries, nor did a spokesperson for the city attorney’s office. Matari said she was used to being criticized, but that the terrorism allegations were particularly disturbing. She stood by her social media posts, saying her detractors had conflated anti-Zionism with antisemitism: “I’m vehemently anti-Zionist and all my posts reflect that … I have been watching people back home living every single day with a violent oppressive boot on their neck that I pay for with my tax money.” She added: “Every day for the last 100 years has been 7 October for Palestinians.” Murad, who has written for the Guardian and previously taught at Fordham University, condemned the claims made about her and Matari: “To say someone has strong terrorist ties is an accusation of a crime, the consequences of which can be lifetime in jail.” The claims of antisemitism, she said, were “laughable”. But these kinds of baseless claims, she added, can have big consequences: “In this historic moment, a completely bogus accusation can have a lot of power. It got me canceled from a library, but it’s getting people abducted and deported.” Matari also objected to claims that the event raised “safety” concerns: “Nora and I weren’t even supposed to be there physically, but they framed it as if our event was going to put the library in a position of danger. This fear is all manufactured. Bringing Palestinians into your spaces does not make it dangerous.” The authors’ lawsuit said the cancellation was “hypocritical” and “inconsistent” with past practices, saying the library had recently hosted several panellists who had expressed political beliefs, including an actor who campaigned for a presidential candidate. The lawsuit claims violations of a California anti-discrimination law, writing: “The portrayal of Palestinians … as hateful or violent simply because they speak out in opposition to the Israeli genocide and in defense of the fundamental and legal rights of Palestinians is an anti-Palestinian trope that has long been employed to silence and dehumanize Palestinians.” Emails show there was internal backlash to the cancellation, including from two librarians involved in organizing the event, who wrote a joint email to leadership saying the message accusing the authors of terrorist ties was “disrespectful, disgusting, and racist”. More than 100 staffers signed a letter to administrators condemning the cancellation and requesting an apology to the authors. One LA librarian, who was not authorized to speak publicly and requested anonymity, said the library was normally dedicated to promoting diversity, inclusion and platforming marginalized voices, and that the cancellation took staff by surprise: “People were questioning whether this was an organization for them, whether they could do the work we’re tasked with under these conditions.” Mark Kleiman, a lawyer for the writers, argued that as a taxpayer-funded institution, the library cannot ban people from giving a talk based on their identities or viewpoints: “When you are dependent on public money, you don’t get to be bigoted and shut people up because they are Palestinian-American … and are speaking up about a genocide.” Before the LA library, two private bookstores had already cancelled planned readings with Matari. After the LA news broke, a library in New York also cancelled her scheduled event, she said. The writers are coming forward at a time of widespread outrage about the suppression of pro-Palestine advocacy in the US after the rapper Macklemore was dropped from Ed Sheeran’s tour after his “free Palestine” comments. In past youth events about her book, Matari said she had talked about her grandfather’s displacement and connected with a diverse range of families about their own histories and relationships to gardening: “I get to plant that seed in kids’ heads about the importance of being land stewards versus seeing land as this thing so many people abuse and take for granted. “It would have been such a pivotal moment to see a Palestinian author and Jewish author sitting with each other,” Matari added. “These events are geared toward kids, but it really does wonders for parents who may have been hesitant to talk about Palestine to see the solidarity.” Murad said she wanted to file the lawsuit on behalf of youth, who may no longer think the library is a safe space: “The violation of our rights has this much bigger ripple effect … not just for the children that day who couldn’t hear about our stories, but to all children who received a message that these books, these people, these ideas are too dangerous to be in the library.” She noted that Read Palestine Week was aimed to amplify works and authors already facing censorship, arguing the library should be publicly censured: “The mission of the libraries is to protect accessibility to all information for the public … if they can get away with censoring Palestinians, then censorship is allowed and normalized.”

title: ‘It’s just cruel’: US households hit by surge in electricity shutoffs amid record hot summer
summary: Utility disconnections were up 28% in 10 states in July 2026 – the hottest month ever recorded in the US – compared with July 2024, data shows
text: A record hot summer collided unhappily with rising energy costs for households across the US that struggled to the point where many were disconnected from their electricity supply, even as dangerous heat baked their communities. In July, the hottest month ever recorded in the US, 173,598 households were shut off from their electric supply by utilities across 10 states, figures provided to the Guardian show. This snapshot of American life points to a worsening problem, with the rate of electricity disconnections surging 28% compared to July 2024. Even as three separate “heat dome” events scorched the US in July, probably worsened by global heating caused by the burning of fossil fuels, many people were rationing their use of air conditioning and other appliances or lost use of them entirely by being cut off for non-payment. “We have been hearing from so many people angry and desperate because their bills have doubled – temperatures are going up and so are the costs,” said Mark Wolfe, executive director of the National Energy Assistance Directors Association (NEADA), which represents the state and tribal bodies tasked with helping low-income people afford their energy bills. “People now are cutting back on food or medicine or resorting to payday lenders because you need to get the power back on. The protections in place aren’t working, it’s just cruel. Poorer people and older people aren’t turning on the AC because of the cost and when you get back-to-back heatwaves they may die because of that.” Not all states require utilities to report shut-off figures, but NEADA was able to compile data from 10 states, including New York, Georgia, California and Illinois. The true level of disconnections nationally is far higher – the federal government reported 13.4m household shut-offs in 2024, with rates particularly high in southern states including Texas, Florida, Oklahoma and Louisiana. About one in six US households are now behind on their energy bills, putting them at potential risk of being cut off, NEADA estimates. This risk varies by state – 23 states and Washington DC have rules preventing electricity disconnections when the heat rises above a certain threshold, meaning the remaining 27 states allow shut-offs regardless of the weather. “Most people do manage to find some way to pay the bill and get reconnected, but the core problem is that electricity prices are continuing to rise faster than overall inflation,” said Wolfe. The crunch of extreme heat and ballooning bills resulted in a fraught summer for many Americans. Carol Norman, 70, who lives in the town of Tom Bean, Texas, said her utility bills soared to about $600 a month, mostly due to air conditioning. She now just uses bursts of air conditioning in one room despite barely venturing outside over summer because of the heat. “A couple of times I walked to the grocery store before it got too hot but once it gets to 100F [37C] you can’t go out,” said Norman, who has custody of her grandson, aged 18. “It’s very isolating, it’s depressing. I’ve had panic attacks worrying about my electricity bill. If my daughter didn’t help out I would probably have ended up homeless or close to it.” Others asked to recount their experiences of this summer also felt life was altered because of the heat. “It’s sad because I usually love being out and about in the summer and I want to share that joy with my child but I’m scared of her overheating and suffering a heat injury,” said one man, who wished to remain anonymous, from North Carolina. Nina Johnson, from Austin, Texas, said electric bills of more than $200 take up a large portion of her monthly income of $550, meaning she has cut out pleasures such as ice-cream and lunch out with friends. “I’m eating a lot of peanut butter sandwiches,” she said. “There are food banks, but I don’t have transportation and taking the bus and walking in the heat for blocks is too much for me.” Some said their health, as well as their wallets, had suffered. Erin Hutchins, who lives in Biddeford, Maine, has previously suffered heatstroke and found this summer “unbearably hot” as her air conditioning doesn’t adequately cool her older building. “I pay over $100 a month in electricity bills, and have had to go without other necessities to do so, because I live on a fixed income,” she said. “I think having heatstroke multiple times has permanently done damage, but it’s too soon to say. I don’t feel like the same person any more though.” Electricity bills have been climbing in the US since 2021, spurred by the power demands of artificial intelligence datacenters and the cost of utilities’ grid upgrades. The severe global energy disruption caused by the US and Israeli attack on Iran earlier this year has accelerated this trend, raising power bills and adding $100bn in extra gasoline costs for Americans’ cars and trucks. Donald Trump, who has dismissed both established climate science and concerns over soaring bills as a “hoax”, has consistently rejected criticism that the ongoing Iran war has hurt Americans by pushing up the cost of oil and gas. “I don’t think about Americans’ financial situation, I don’t think about anybody,” Trump said in May. “We cannot let Iran have a nuclear weapon, that’s all. That’s the only thing that motivates me.” At a recent rally in North Carolina, Trump acknowledged that Americans were facing higher gasoline costs but that was a “very inexpensive price to pay for what we’ve done”. To compound matters, the Trump administration has also sought to completely axe the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program (Liheap), which gives states money to assist people struggling with power bills. While Congress has not agreed to the scheme’s demise, the administration has been accused of freezing obligated funds. “Americans are very concerned about affordability and getting rid of low-income energy aid is a step in the wrong direction, especially since the administration has made decisions that have increased many people’s costs around energy,” said Kate Gallego, mayor of Phoenix, which has just had its second hottest summer on record. Speaking to the Guardian at New York climate week, Gallego, a Democrat, said that the Trump administration’s attempts to strangle solar and wind energy, typically the cheapest sources of new power, and prop up more expensive, and dirtier, coal has also been harmful. The Trump administration insists it is focused on cutting energy costs. “Lowering electricity prices is a top priority for President Trump, and he is aggressively unleashing reliable energy sources like coal and natural gas to reverse the catastrophic damage that Joe Biden and the Democrats did to our power grid,” said Taylor Rogers, a White House spokesperson. “Joe Biden created a grid crisis, President Trump is fixing it. If the Democrats had their way, these costly and unreliable renewable energy projects would still be failing our grid and our communities.” Yet successive presidencies have floundered in updating policies to align with a much hotter world. Even if the Liheap is saved, the program still allocates about 80% of its funding for heating assistance in winter, rather than for cooling in summer. “That’s been a problem across multiple administrations when we’re seeing so much of the country have challenges with heat,” said Gallego. “When I think about the mayors I know throughout the world, most of them have a heatwave to contend with. This is a growing and global challenge.” Some cities and states have sought to provide financial assistance to households caught in the crunch of extreme weather and rising bills. Shade from extra trees, new water features in parks and playgrounds, cooling centers and early warning systems have all also become priorities for municipalities as hazards such as heatwaves have got fiercer. “I have never known more about the weather than I do now,” admitted Zohran Mamdani, the mayor of New York City, last week as he recounted how the city has been repeatedly battered by floods since he took office. Another mayor, Michelle Wu of Boston, said this summer’s roasting temperatures were particularly challenging due to an influx of people drawn to the city for the World Cup, America’s 250th anniversary celebrations and a tall ships event. “We are past warning signs at this point, we are seeing increasing impacts from heat, flooding, air quality and livability and at the same time it has become more and more a political flashpoint to avoid talking about certain issues or words,” Wu said. “At the city level, it doesn’t matter what words are said. We just have to take action and respond to the reality our residents are living.” With a record hot summer now passed, NEADA’s attention is now turning to how the elevated costs of oil and gas will affect Americans heating their homes in the colder months. On Monday, the organization estimated that homes heated by oil, most common in the US north-east, will face bills 50% higher than last year. “Winter is just around the bend, and we are very concerned about what this means for low-income families that use heating oil,” said Wolfe, who has requested that Congress provide a further $3bn for Liheap to help defray this burden.

title: Israeli Settlers Stop Soldiers From Returning Palestinians to Their Home

title: M&S links up with Sephora to lure younger shoppers
summary: Beauty specialist will open branded areas in 100 Marks & Spencer stores and will sell its products on chain’s website
text: Marks & Spencer has signed a deal with Sephora to open areas under the beauty brand’s name within its stores, in its latest tactic to attract younger shoppers. The French retailer is to launch branded areas staffed by Sephora employees in 100 M&S stores and sell through the British retailer’s website in spring next year. Sephora relaunched in the UK in 2023 with huge fanfare and now has about 18 stand-alone British stores. The company is owned by LVMH, the luxury goods group led by Bernard Arnault, who with his family is among the world’s richest people with a $171bn (£129bn) fortune, according to Forbes. The company has rapidly expanded on its second attempt to enter the UK market after closing a handful of stores in 2005, having failed make a dent in a competitive sector. The deal with M&S marks a new strategy in its expansion plans. Analysts have said Sephora’s work with up-and-coming brands and collaborations with high-profile influencers on Instagram, TikTok, and YouTube has helped the company reach its target female audience of 24- to 36-year-olds. John Lyttle, the managing director of M&S’s fashion, home and beauty division, said: “Beauty is an important category for M&S, with the potential to attract new customers to shop with us and give existing customers the opportunity to shop with us more often.” “Combining Sephora’s specialist expertise with the strength of the M&S brand, our store estate and our growing digital platform,” Lyttle said. “Alongside this, we will continue investing in our own-label beauty categories where we have established strength and customer trust.” Retailers have been battling to grab a share of the beauty market after the disappearance of many department stores. In recent years a swathe of UK department stores have closed, including Debenhams, Beales and about half the House of Fraser chain. Sephora’s self-service model – which allows consumers to touch and test makeup and perfume without the help of shop staff – is seen to appeal to younger shoppers, who may test in store and buy online. The tie-up could provide increased competition for the specialist health and beauty chains Boots and Superdrug. Lyttle said the deal was part of M&S’s wider transformation plan, which involves £700m of investments in revitalising stores, modernising its supply chain and distribution system, and further improvements in products. The group, which employs more than 65,000 people, has 227 full-line stores – containing food, clothing, homewares and beauty – after closing dozens of old and out-of-place outlets. More will shut over the next two years and a handful of new outlets are opening with the aim to have 200 full-line stores in the UK. M&S’s food arm is expanding rapidly, with 18 food-only stores opening this year as it heads for a target of 420, compared with 335 directly operated outlets. Franchise partners run another 466 in the UK and more overseas. Sarah Boyd, the managing director of Sephora UK, said: “Together, we can redefine what high street beauty means for customers across the UK, bringing the very best curated brand and beauty experience to the M&S stores.” She said the group would introduce its beauty advisers to M&S stores to “provide a truly personalised experience, and to reach customers in more communities where they already live, shop and spend their time”.

title: Two ex-ministers from Orbán era held over suspected bribery and misuse of public funds
summary: Ministers from former far-right government arrested after MPs vote to lift their immunity
text: Two ministers in Viktor Orbán’s former far-right government suspected separately of misusing millions of euros of public funds and taking millions more in bribes have been detained, hours after Hungarian MPs voted to lift their immunity. Prosecutors said on Tuesday that Balázs Hankó, Orbán’s culture minister and still an MP in the former prime minister’s nationalist Fidesz party, was taken into custody late on Monday. Hankó is suspected of misappropriation of funds. He has denied any wrongdoing. Miklós Seszták, an MP from Fidesz ally KDNP who served as minister for national development between 2014 and 2018, was also detained on Monday as part of an ⁠investigation into alleged bribery. He too has denied wrongdoing. “Yesterday was an important day,” said Hungary’s prime minister, Péter Magyar on Tuesday. His Tisza party swept to victory in April elections promising to investigate alleged corruption and abuse of office during Orbán’s 16-year rule. “After decades of lies, for the first time, many millions of Hungarians could experience what real regime change and equality before the law really mean, Magyar said on social media. “Hungary is no longer a country without consequences.” The arrests came hours after Hungary’s parliament on Monday voted to suspend Hankó and Seszták’s immunity – but also that of Magyar, who had asked for his to be lifted so he could clear himself of what he called a “character assassination”. The graft investigations into the Orbán-era ministers are the first against senior figures in the former government. Magyar, meanwhile, is accused of snatching a phone from a man filming him in a nightclub in 2024 and throwing it into the Danube River. The prime minister has denied his conduct amounted to theft and called the case, which involves a damages claim of €300 (£260), a “sham”. He said he took responsibility for his actions but denied committing a crime and criticised prosecutors for “conflating” the ex-ministers’ corruption cases with “an attempted political character assassination”. Magyar has repeatedly said that in recent years corruption and misuse of public funds have cost Hungary between 8% and 10% of its GDP under successive governments led by Orbán, who has repeatedly denied allowing rampant corruption and outright theft of public money during more than a decade and half in power. Prosecutors allege Hankó oversaw the criminal misuse of 17.3bn forints (€47m) of public funds from Hungary’s national cultural fund (NKA), channelling the money to artists and groups with ties to Fidesz and financing its 2026 election campaign. “My conscience is clear, this is a political show trial,” Hankó said ‌in a live video broadcast on Orbán’s Facebook page shortly before his arrest. In July, police raided the Fidesz offices and seized the party’s internet servers in connection ⁠with alleged “misappropriation and other criminal offences” at the NKA, prompting Orbán to accuse authorities of conducting a sham investigation in order to render his party “legally unviable”. Prosecutors also suspect Seszták of accepting more than 12bn forints (€32.6m) in bribes and kickbacks connected to vehicle procurements under Hungary’s state bus company, as well as to public construction projects. The case centres on the purchase of secondhand buses at allegedly inflated prices. Separately, Hungary’s national ‌asset protection and recovery office, the anti-corruption body established by Magyar’s government as part of his anti-graft ⁠drive, on ⁠Monday announced the first four cases it intends to tackle. The first concerned “selling political connections to obtain residence permits ‌for employment”, the body said in a statement, and the second case is about alleged corruption involving local council expenditure on park maintenance and public catering. The third case involved “a state-owned company and state investments” and has links to Dániel Jellinek, a real estate mogul and one of Hungary’s wealthiest businessmen, the statement said. The real estate firm that Jellinek heads has said he will cooperate fully with the authorities. “Our firm position is that Mr Jellinek has not committed any offence in connection with the matter. We are confident that the investigation will confirm this and that the proceedings against him will soon be discontinued,” it said in a statement this month. The fourth concerned “seemingly unjustified propaganda and event costs” at the sovereignty protection office, an Orbán-era body set up to monitor what Fidesz alleged was “undue political interference” by foreign entities in Hungary, and abolished by Magyar’s government in June.

title: Accusations of Antisemitism Hit a Star of the French Far Right
