title: ‘It takes a lot of work’: Deb Haaland puts addiction struggles at center of New Mexico governor bid
summary: First Native American woman to serve as US cabinet secretary candid about history with alcohol as she seeks to tackle billowing public health crisis
text: “It clouds your mind,” recalls Deb Haaland, the trailblazing US cabinet secretary now running to be New Mexico’s next governor. “They say that, after the first drink, you lose your judgment.” Haaland developed a drinking problem after leaving high school and was twice arrested for driving under the influence. But in her 20s she decided to get sober, a battle that required personal commitment and critical external support. She went on to become a member of Congress, one of the first two Native American women ever elected to the House, and then to become the first Native American to serve as a US cabinet secretary. Now Haaland is writing her next chapter. The Democrat is taking the unusual step of putting her own 35 years of sobriety and her past struggles with alcoholism at the center of her campaign for governor in November’s midterm elections. In a statewide six-figure broadcast and digital ad buy launching ahead of the election, Haaland links her intimate experience with addiction directly to the public health crisis ravaging local communities. “I guess I’m like so many New Mexicans,” she told the Guardian by phone on Monday. “I started abusing alcohol at a young age and I was very fortunate that, at the age of 23, I recognised that I wanted to live a sober life and so I went on that journey and worked on myself for quite a while. It’s a lot of hard work to pay attention to yourself. I recognised there were so many things in my life that I needed to change.” She added: “I was fortunate to have the help of an inpatient treatment programme way back then, and so that helped me to get sober initially, but it takes a lot of work even after your head clears. I went to meetings and therapy and all of those things. I found the help that I needed and thankfully I’ve been sober for 35 years now.” Haaland, a member of the Pueblo of Laguna tribe who grew up in a military family, served in Congress from 2019 to 2021 then as interior secretary in Joe Biden’s cabinet from 2021 to 2025. She is now taking on Republican Gregg Hull, the former mayor of Rio Rancho, in the election for governor of New Mexico. In a political era in which personal vulnerability is often weaponised, her campaign is betting that voters in The Land of Enchantment – where the deadly fentanyl crisis has touched families in every corner of the state – will appreciate her candid treatment of a subject once regarded as taboo. “I look at this as a public health issue,” she emphasised. “I look at this as not somebody with a moral failing but essentially a victim of this terrible disease. We want to make sure that this is looked at as a public health issue, that we move some behavioural health dollars to this area so that people can get the help they need.” She notes that the pervasive stigma surrounding substance use disorder frequently prevents families from seeking life-saving care. “For a lot of folks it’s hard not to feel remorse and shame and all of those things,” Haaland said. But attitudes are changing. “This fentanyl crisis in our state affects even our smallest rural communities here in New Mexico. It’s hitting us in the face. People are dying from this drug, and so I feel like any shame or remorse that anyone might feel about a family member in facing this type of substance use disorder, we would put that aside and say we want people to find the help they need.” The campaign’s political ad brings these human stories into sharp focus. The spot features Jorge, a local father who announces on screen: “I am one year and one month sober.” Jorge tells viewers that while addiction leaves individuals feeling isolated, “there’s a community of people that understand completely.” The commercial also features David, a behavioural health psychologist, who highlights Haaland’s plan to force insurance providers to cover comprehensive treatment and crack down on drug-trafficking networks. Jorge closes: “With Deb, I have hope.” Haaland frames her recovery experience as the foundation for reforming New Mexico’s fractured health infrastructure. She offers sharp criticism of former Republican governor Susana Martinez, whose administration dismantled local treatment networks through unproven fraud allegations against providers. Haaland said: “She essentially destroyed our behavioural health system. She accused a lot of behavioural health professionals of fraud and so many of them went out of business and it took years for the attorney general to clear them all of any wrongdoing. It’s easy to demolish something; it’s difficult to build something back, so we’re still building back from that and I feel committed to helping people live better lives.” She proposes a structural redesign to prevent addiction being funneled into the criminal justice system. Haaland proposes creating a state office of community safety that would deploy behavioural health specialists to non-criminal emergency calls on street corners, allowing police officers to focus their resources on violent crime and drug traffickers. “A lot of these issues with substance use are not criminal in nature and so my office of community safety would ensure that we can help law enforcement to focus on crime. Drug traffickers are part of crime and then we can focus on the people who are suffering.” Haaland’s campaign trail stops have included visits to extended residential care facilities such as Grand Summit, in Albuquerque, which provides long-term housing, job assistance and financial support for recovering residents. During a recent stop, Haaland invited programme residents to walk across the street and cast their ballots alongside her. “They felt empowered and they felt like they were part of something larger than themselves,” she reflected. Haaland’s focus on community health coincides with looming federal challenges. She raised alarm over impending Medicaid rollbacks under the Trump administration, scheduled to begin on 1 January, that could strip addiction treatment coverage from vulnerable state residents. In response, New Mexico has established a Medicaid trust fund intended to provide longer-term support for the programme. She also voiced opposition to aggressive federal enforcement actions in New Mexico, calling recent ICE raids “untenable” “cruel” and “ruthless”, referencing an incident where an individual was detained in front of his 11-year-old child outside a medical clinic. “They wear masks, they don’t identify themselves.” Haaland also linked voter discontent to economic pressures such as tariffs and rising fuel costs, which hit rural New Mexicans commuting up to 100 miles round-trip for work. “I can’t say why people are coming out to vote and why people want to build this momentum in New Mexico for Democrats,” she said, “but it’s happening.”

title: How gold surpassed cocaine as Peru’s most profitable criminal industry
summary: As gold prices surge, illegal mining has laid waste to swathes of Tambopata National Reserve’s rainforest
text: “Halt, stop right there,” shouts a Peruvian Navy Seal, firing warning shots into the air. But the fleeing man pays no attention, scrambling up to the rim of a football pitch-sized crater and disappearing into the dense rainforest as the commandos give chase, swearing and shooting. Meanwhile, other marines set dynamite charges on a makeshift wooden raft that floats in the crater, which is essentially an enormous pit of opaque, stagnant water. The raft has a diesel-fuelled suction pump motor with thick plastic tubing used to suck up and sift through river sediment for tiny particles of gold. Soon after, a mushroom of orange and black fumes envelops the trees – and seconds later comes the sound of the explosion, shattering the peace of the Tambopata National Reserve, one of Peru’s most prized Amazon parks. Located in the south-eastern Madre de Dios region, the reserve is visited by about 40,000 tourists a year, many of whom stay in luxurious ecolodges further down the Malinowski River that marks the Tambopata park’s northern border. But today eight patrols are moving along the river, by helicopter or boat – and every few hundred metres they encounter more evidence of illegal gold mining, operations that have laid waste to more than 500 hectares of the park’s rainforest in the last year, according to satellite mapping data from Amazon Conservation. In total, more than 140,000 hectares have been lost to mining in Madre de Dios – a shocking 97.5% of the total deforestation caused by mining in Peru’s Amazon rainforest, an area twice the size of the US state of California. Military crackdowns on illegal mining in the Amazon are not new in Peru. But the skyrocketing international price of gold has caused this destructive activity to spread, empowering local gangs and attracting transnational organised crime. “Dirty” gold has become the country’s most profitable illicit industry, even surpassing drug trafficking in the world’s second-biggest producer of cocaine after Colombia. “Gold prices have risen,” said Gen Víctor Cotrina, the military commander of Madre de Dios, who is leading the crackdown on illegal gold mining. “That’s why, if a miner’s motor is destroyed, he’ll replace it quickly because gold is at its peak price; the very next day he’s back to his mining activities. He’s back at work again.” For troops used to combating drug trafficking by targeting well-hidden plantations of coca, which is used to make cocaine, the fight against illegal gold presents new challenges as the end product is not an illicit drug but a legally traded commodity, Cotrina said. “The difference is that an open-pit mining operation doesn’t require covert operations, whereas drug trafficking does.” He said previous anti-mining crackdowns had been ineffective due to corruption and patchy enforcement. But now, with “aerial surveillance and military personnel who are available 24/7 to conduct patrols, we are determined to eliminate mining in this region”. According to Peru’s financial supervisory body, illegal gold mining is the top illicit finance threat to the country. For the first time, the illegal trade surpassed the legal production of gold in the first half of this year, according to the Peruvian Economics Institute think tank, which estimates it could reach as much as $18 billion in value by the end of 2026. The country’s Financial Investigation Unit found that illegal mining accounted for nearly 60% of all investigations in terms of value between 2021 and 2025 – far higher than drug trafficking (8%) or tax crimes (4%). The evidence is not difficult to find or destroy. Behind the wall of green that marks the edge of the reserve, troops and environmental prosecutors set ablaze a network of well-supplied mining camps, built with timber and blue tarpaulins and stocked with food and beer. In one location they find a jungle brothel with wooden tables, a bar counter, a stereo and a giant teddy bear, a shower still wet with beauty products inside. A lone cockerel crows as the abandoned camps go up in flames. But during four days of operations in late August, prosecutors arrested just a handful of suspects. Two women had been left behind by the fleeing miners: Andrea, 30, wept as she begged the officers not to arrest her, explaining she was a single mother who had been working as a cook and could find no other work to support a sick mother and two children. Liz Compi, 20, was found sitting on a boat with her one-year-old son. She said she had taken the job as a cook for $450 a month after being abandoned by her partner and sacked from a previous job. Authorities took both women back to the city and released them. Ronal Flores, a deputy prosecutor for Peru’s Office of the attorney Ggeneral who helped to rescue Compi, said it was pointless to arrest most workers at the camps as they tended to have no knowledge of the workings of the much bigger illicit enterprise. Many are left behind to sink motors in the river to avoid detection; even hours later, the machines can be winched up with pulleys and put back to work. “In these places, the big fish – the owners – are rarely caught. It’s usually the low-level operatives who we find,” said Flores, a short, energetic man with a black moustache who led the operations on behalf of the Public Prosecutor’s Office backed by the US non-profit Global Conservation. He admitted that they could only slow the pace of the rainforest’s destruction, but that the state agencies lacked the budget to maintain the intensity of raids, even though the military destroyed and seized an estimated $500m in machinery, supplies and illegal dredgers, according to government figures. Flores said the raids had destroyed about 150 mining barges and motors in the Amazon park, but that was “nothing compared to the magnitude of the damage being caused within the reserve”. A single mining dredger, operating 24 hours a day, can produce as much as 50 grams of gold – which, with the price of gold at more than $4,650 a troy ounce in late August (having peaked at roughly $5,600 an ounce in late January), could fetch more than $6,000 in Madre de Dios. Since the beginning of Covid-19 pandemic, the price of gold has tripled. Tens of thousands of miners have poured into protected Amazon parks and Indigenous reserves, stripping away vast tracts of rainforest and leaving behind a denuded, pocked terrain, stagnant pools and disrupted river courses. Mercury is the cheapest and easiest way to extract gold because it binds with the particles in the river sediment. As a result, an estimated 180 tonnes of the toxic metal contaminates Peru’s waterways every year, poisoning wildlife and damaging human health, particularly among Indigenous communities that depend principally on freshwater fish as their main protein source. The latest raids, dubbed Operación Mercurio II, follow on from an earlier iteration, Operación Mercurio, which began in 2019 and achieved a 62% overall reduction in illegal mining deforestation, including a 92% drop in the most critical illegal hub, La Pampa. But the miners returned to La Pampa and deforestation surged, while extortion and hired killings spiralled as a local gang, Los Guardianes de la Trocha, took control of the $1bn trade. The dirty gold departs Peru as contraband to Bolivia and Brazil, but much of it is laundered into the legal trade via a controversial registration system called Reinfo. The system, in theory, should bring informal miners into the legal economy, but critics say it allows them to continue working without environmental permits and laundering illegal gold through formal companies. The trade is so lucrative that members of Congress have backed five repeated extensions of Reinfo, despite pushes to reform or eliminate the registry. “The government’s response is moving very slowly,” said Flores after another day of relatively fruitless jungle raids, destroying camps that are likely to spring back up soon after. “Meanwhile, illegal mining operates 24 hours a day. The miners measure time in grams, not minutes, so we need to rethink how we investigate mining,” he said. “Unfortunately, as we can see today, they are getting the better of us.”

title: The night sky is getting 10% brighter every year. We’re forgetting what darkness feels like
summary: If more cities start regulating outdoor lighting, we humans could make the environment better for all living creatures
text: Every night, I can turn off the lights in my room – but I can’t do anything about the outdoor lights in the walkway or parking lot that leak through the curtains. Living in Portland, where the night is still illuminated by street lights, porch lights and parking lot glare, I forgot what it actually feels like to sleep in darkness. I was excited when I realized my travels to a residency in south-east Oregon would show me a sky I hadn’t experienced in decades. In the Oregon outback, part of the International Dark Sky Places network, I would be surrounded by 2.5m acres of unpolluted night in every direction. I sent out a note to the other residents asking if anyone wanted to look at the stars with me. Everyone said yes. Thirty minutes after sunset, we trekked through the tall grass and out on to the dry lakebed. Those of us with headlamps set them on red so we wouldn’t destroy our night vision. We laid down our blankets and looked at the night sky together. There, just over the hills, was Venus. Vega shone overhead. So did numerous satellites which we could tell weren’t natural by their movement. They were so bright my eye was constantly drawn to them. As it got darker, more stars and constellations seemed to materialize: Ursa Major and Minor, Cygnus, Cassiopeia. By the time the Milky Way appeared, a band of light rising out of the night, we fell silent. We saw one shooting star and then another. I lay on my blanket and looked up until I felt small. Every year, the night sky is becoming 10% brighter. Eighty per cent of people live under light-polluted skies. And while the UN declared a healthy environment – clean air, clean water – to be a human right, I believe we also all have a right to darkness as well. This doesn’t mean turning off every streetlamp. But do we really need bright white floodlights at the front of every garage? Replacing lights with ones that are bright enough to do the job – and no brighter – might make it so I wouldn’t have to get in my car and drive for hours to see the night sky as it actually shines above us. To preserve the darkness would mean rules and enforcement around the warmth of the lights, where they point, and how bright they can be. It would mean not putting in three lights when one would do. If we recognized that darkness is something we need, we’d become more careful about chasing it away. Some communities have already done this. Flagstaff, Arizona, was the first city to have outdoor lighting rules, adding them in 1958. In 2001, Flagstaff became the first recognized Dark Sky City. Their rules regulate how much light can be used, what type, and where it can shine. Other cities and towns in the US and abroad have followed. New York state is now considering a Dark Skies Protection Act, which would add restrictions on outdoor lighting – including some that would affect the city that never sleeps. All it takes to preserve the night near you is the desire to protect it with a new zoning law or, perhaps, a rule for how bright car headlights can be. Access to darkness is about more than stargazing. The night is its own habitat. Artificial lights confuse animals who use the moon to navigate, whether they’re baby sea turtles navigating toward a parking lot instead of the ocean or moths who fly in circles around a lightbulb. Lightning bugs and frogs need darkness to complete their courtship rituals. Migrating birds get thrown off course by the bright lights of big cities. But the effects of light pollution linger even after it’s daylight again, becoming visible. Research has shown light pollution is breaking the relationship between plants and pollinators, changing the time of year trees break into flower, and disrupting circadian rhythms for all living creatures. This includes humans. Whether it’s artificial lights indoors or creeping in through the window at night, studies have found that we need darkness in order to rest, recover and stay healthy. Most light pollution comes from street lights, buildings, parking lots and sports courts left lit all night but increasingly there’s a threat of light pollution coming from the sky itself. Even if the rules of the Dark Sky Sanctuary let me see the Milky Way that night on the lake, it couldn’t stop the growing number of satellites from mixing in with the starry night. Dark-friendly practices such as making sure nightlights are targeted and shielded won’t do anything about the more than 11,000 Starlink satellites currently in orbit, or a company who wants to provide artificial sunlight on demand, using satellites to illuminate areas of the Earth as large as three miles. Things we launch into space aren’t required to have an environmental review even when they affect life back on Earth. The stars hold our history. They have been maps, calendars, omens and landmarks. When it was dark, the constellations helped people find their way home. Now the night sky is an attraction people travel to. In our urbanizing world, the night sky is out of reach for those who don’t have the time or resources to find it. Darkness is becoming another luxury, but it can belong to all of us again. A right to darkness doesn’t mean every city would look like the rural Oregon outback but it might make a few more stars visible after dark, let a few more creatures rest, give all of us a reason to look up again – no matter where we are. Tove Danovich is a journalist and the author of Under the Henfluence: Inside the World of Backyard Chickens and the People Who Love Them. She runs the newsletter A Little Detour

title: ‘Visible and engaged’: Burnham in listening mode with businesses at Labour party conference
summary: PM reassures firms and chancellor vows help on costs – but unease remains over possible budget tax rises
text: A year ago Andy Burnham had a tough business reception at Labour’s party conference. The then mayor of Greater Manchester, with clear ambitions to replace Keir Starmer, had rattled the City of London with his comment that Britain should be less “in hock” to bond markets. Returning to the annual gathering in Liverpool a year later as prime minister, the mood is different. Labour is pushing to repair relations with corporate Britain and reassure City bond traders against a jittery backdrop amid the Middle East war. At a private reception on Monday night hosted by the Confederation of British Industry (CBI), HSBC and National Grid, John Healey told executives the government would do “our bit” to support firms struggling with rising costs. The chancellor said his budget next month would also have fiscal discipline at its core. “I very much welcome the chance as chancellor to work with you,” he said. Over bottled beer and glasses of wine overlooking the River Mersey, one executive praised the chancellor: “Can I just say, bloody wonderful speech of yours at conference today. Really determined to achieve success; it went down very well.” For most bosses, however, there is a caveat: the 28 October budget. Labour gained a reputation after its return to government in 2024 for love-bombing bosses before then raising taxes on firms. “Ask us on 29 October [how business feels]” said the CBI chief executive, Rain Newton-Smith. She said that while Burnham appeared to be in listening mode, Labour faced difficult decisions at next month’s budget. “When you get a change [of administration], you’re sort of changing mid-flight, and that allows you to think what was working, what wasn’t. Without denigrating the previous [administration], they’ve sort of said, ‘“Look, we need to get change, but also, how can we be responsive?’” In previous years there had been a clamour among businesses to attend Labour’s annual conference – held for three years running in Liverpool – to the point it was jokingly dubbed the “Davos on the Mersey”, referring to the annual gathering of the global elite in the Swiss ski resort. Starmer had run a strategy before his landslide election victory to win corporate endorsements to burnish Labour’s credentials in City boardrooms. But within his first months in office relations had soured, after Rachel Reeves sprung £40bn of tax increases – centred squarely on employers – in her first budget. This year, delegates said there appeared to be fewer top bosses at Labour’s “business day”, where executives paid £6,000 a ticket to attend an exclusive breakfast reception hosted by the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, followed by a “fireside chat” with Burnham. However, corporate Britain was still evident en masse, with companies including Mastercard, HSBC and Heathrow among those paying thousands to sponsor fringe sessions and private networking events. After smaller sessions focusing on policy, executives were ushered into the main auditorium to hear the chancellor’s speech, including Paul Thwaite, the chief executive of NatWest, and the bosses of the “B5” group of leading business trade bodies. In the auditorium the chancellor gave little away about the budget, despite striking a markedly different tone to Burnham’s “in hock” comment from a year earlier – insisting that he and the prime minister were “in lockstep” in their commitment to balance the books. “There is nothing progressive about losing control because it’s always working people who pay for it,” he said. Shevaun Haviland, the director general of the British Chambers of Commerce, said Healey’s speech was “significant” because the chancellor had acknowledged that private enterprise was vital for helping the UK economy to grow. However, she warned that companies still faced severe headwinds. “[The government’s] strategy is unlikely to succeed while the everyday cost of doing business is still soaring. Firms are being asked to invest while facing a tsunami of rising costs from employment, energy and business rates,” she said. Lobbyists said there appeared to have been a concerted effort to ensure senior ministers spent time with business leaders and to match them more directly with the relevant sector. One external affairs chief at a FTSE 250 retailer noted a marked shift in willingness to listen to business concerns, highlighting the work of the prime minister’s special adviser for business relations, James Carroll. Varun Chandra, who had been Starmer’s chief business investment and trade adviser and who stayed on under Burnham, was also orchestrating meetings at the private CBI reception on Monday night. One minister said the business leaders they had met in Liverpool welcomed the renewed sense of optimism projected by the new government – in contrast to what some saw as Starmer’s downbeat attitude. Businesses have welcomed individual initiatives, such as Burnham’s tax cut for pubs and clubs; but are yet to understand what “Manchesterism” might mean if applied UK-wide – and remain concerned about the possibility of tax rises in next month’s budget. Steve Rigby, the chief executive of the family-owned property and technology company Rigby Group, said Labour’s approach to business had improved from two years ago, but he was reserving judgment until the budget in a month. “The PM and Jonathan Reynolds are visible and engaged, whether they are listening to our concerns will become clear in the budget,” he said. “You can buy tickets to get into the right rooms, where proper access [to the politicians] is possible – but you have to work hard to get it. “Really we are in a holding pattern until the budget. The signs are good – we like the boring, no-leaks approach from Healey [so far]. However, businesses have absorbed about as many tax rises as they can, which is what the main focus will be over the next month.”

title: OpenAI scraps release of new model over safety concerns in internal testing
summary: GPT-6.1 Astra showed deceptive behaviour and tried to use external tools despite knowing it would be unsafe
text: OpenAI is scrapping the release of a next-generation ⁠AI model after researchers raised safety concerns ⁠during internal testing. The model, GPT-6.1 Astra, was expected to appear in ChatGPT and ⁠Codex in October, designed to handle more complex tasks without human assistance. Saachi Jain, the head of safety systems at OpenAI, said the new model “didn’t quite meet the bar” of the company’s standards. The UK’s AI Security Institute published its own testing report on GPT-6 Astra – GPT-6.1’s predecessor, which launched this month – on Monday, and found that it conducted a range of unsanctioned attack activities more frequently than previous OpenAI models. Experts welcomed OpenAI’s move to mothball the latest Astra model but warned it showed AI companies were in charge of their own regulation rather than government-backed watchdogs. Jain told the Wall Street Journal on Monday ‌that Astra fell short of the company’s standards in alignment tests, which assess whether a system follows human intent. The model showed more deception than its predecessor, including at times failing to accurately disclose actions it had or had not taken. It also had problems with “scope authorisation”, pushing ahead with tasks without requesting user permission and sometimes attempting to use external tools or services ‌when doing so could be unsafe. The San Francisco-based company’s move comes after a number of AI agents went rogue around the world, which prompted a spate of warnings from researchers and company bosses over the dangers of the technology. Earlier this ⁠month, Dario Amodei, the chief executive of OpenAI’s rival Anthropic, called for the AI industry to “slow down” and offered a three-part plan for doing so. He quickly received backing from Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI, and Elon Musk, the SpaceX CEO. Experts said shelving the model showed OpenAI was willing to act strongly on safety, but such decisions should not be in the company’s hands. “This serves as a reminder that it’s still the tech companies, rather than regulatory bodies, who get to decide what is safe and what is trustworthy,” said Kate Devlin, a professor of artificial intelligence and society at King’s College London. Dame Wendy Hall, a professor of computer science at the University of Southampton and a UK government adviser on AI, said companies were now showing concern about future liability for possible harms. “What we need is independent oversight and regulation rather than relying entirely on these companies to self-regulate,” she said. The decision comes before OpenAI’s developer conference in San Francisco, where the company typically announces new products aimed at software developers. On Tuesday, OpenAI apologised for the hacking of an Australian government website by ⁠a rogue AI agent, and set aside funding to improve cyber defences and to set up a local response taskforce. In a blog⁠post ⁠entitled How we will do better for Australia, the company acknowledged it mishandled its response and pledged to take accountability to “rebuild trust with the Australian people”. OpenAI said: “We are sorry and working to do better in the future.” The hacking, which ⁠happened in June but was not made public until last week, is the first known instance of an AI agent hacking a government website. The Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, called it “unacceptable” and criticised the company’s delay in notifying the government. Also on Tuesday, it emerged that Anthropic – which makes Claude – had warned potential investors that its technology may pose “existential risks to humanity” in the long-awaited prospectus for its planned $2tn (£1.5tn) stock market flotation. The “risk factors” in its prospectus include the potential for AI models to blackmail, manipulate and exhibit other unpredictable behaviours, the Financial Times reported. The California company reportedly said AI would transform the global economy more profoundly than industrialisation, electricity and the internet. However, this comes at a staggering cost. Anthropic reported a net loss of $42bn for 2025, and plans to spend $518bn on cloud, computing and infrastructure obligations in coming years, the prospectus reportedly said.

title: Revealed: the five-paragraph email OpenAI used to inform Australia about agent attack
summary: Executive to front parliamentary committee on AI as ministers reveal how brief message telling them about hack was signed off ‘best’
text: OpenAI has apologised to Australians for its agent attack on Medicare, and will front parliament next week as the tech company revealed more details about its June hack of Australian government websites. Ministers on Tuesday evening released a brief, five paragraph email which OpenAI used to inform the Australian government about the attack. The email was sent to a public inbox monitored by Services Australia on 10 September – nearly three months after the AI agent accessed the website on 18 June – and was signed off with the closing “best”. The Labor government has publicly voiced its fury at the manner in which OpenAI disclosed the incident. The email itself, obtained by Guardian Australia, advised Services Australia that “an OpenAI model identified a way to make the server carry out instructions sent through the public reporting interface, without a private account or password”. It comes as OpenAI’s Medicare breach prompted a government-wide assessment of cyber systems to bolster Australia’s public sector against further AI threats – deliberate or not. Home affairs directed all government departments and agencies to undertake a “rapid” stocktake of legacy systems, to formulate risk management for legacy technology and to report their compliance back to the department. The directive prioritises systems of government significance – the government’s critical systems – with a review due by the end of the year, while other systems will be assessed by March. The acting home affairs minister, Richard Marles, said AI is “changing the environment in which we operate at extraordinary speed.” “We can’t wait for an old system to fail before replacing it. We need to identify vulnerabilities and deal with them before they can be exploited.” In a blog post released on Tuesday morning (AEST), OpenAI said it should have handled its response to the hack better. “We also should have handled our response better. We are sorry and working to do better in the future.” The company also provided more detail on the incident revealed by the Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, last week. OpenAI said it became aware of agent activity on Australian government websites in mid-August after the company reviewed earlier training incidents after the Hugging Face attack in July. The agents gained non-public access to a Services Australia portal for Medicare statistics, and OpenAI said the agent was able to run commands, retrieve internal files, credentials, and write files, but no patient or client records were accessed. OpenAI’s email to Services Australia pointed the government to the “affected URL”, a Medicare statistics page on the human services website, as well as specifying an “affected report” – a CSV file, commonly used for spreadsheets. “We recommend that the team responsible for the service investigate the vulnerability and assess the changes needed to prevent it. We would be glad to brief your security team and provide supporting evidence as available,” OpenAI wrote. “Best, OpenAl Security Team”. OpenAI was contacted for comment. The NSW Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research’s public crime mapping tool was also accessed, with application configuration, operational jobs and logs and website metadata provided to the agency. The agent discovered an exposed access key to query the Victorian agency for health information’s reporting system to access aggregate survey statistics. For the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, OpenAI agents retrieved aggregate statistics, but separate attempts to bypass access controls were unsuccessful and the information obtained was publicly available. Services Australia and the Victorian health department were informed on 10 September, while the NSW bureau of crime statistics was informed on 18 September. The Australian Institute of Health and Welfare was not informed until 24 September, as OpenAI deemed it did not meet disclosure thresholds. “Since then we’ve worked closely with Australian government agencies to share what we’ve learned to date,” OpenAI said. “If we identify any additional affected agencies, we will notify them promptly and directly with the information available and provide updates as further facts emerge.” The incident occurred after one model was tasked to research government spending per person on medicines for skin conditions in Victoria. The model had difficulty obtaining that information, and OpenAI said “it took actions that we had not authorised it to take” including accessing Services Australia’s Medicare statistics reporting service. OpenAI said it would commit resources and expertise to affected agencies, and provide Australian government agencies with support to build cyberdefences on critical infrastructure. Australian government agencies and industries will also be given credits out of OpenAI’s US$1bn (AU$1.4bn) Daybreak fund, which lets those organisations use frontier AI for cyberdefence, and to harden their systems by reviewing code and system configurations for potential vulnerabilities that can then be patched. The company said it would also establish a taskforce with Australian expertise to develop practical policy recommendations on managing risk with AI agents. OpenAI’s chief strategy officer, Jason Kwon, will appear at the joint select committee on AI on Tuesday 6 October. Guardian Australia reported on Monday that Anthropic would also appear at this hearing, but not at a Senate inquiry into AI and datacentres this week. Albanese, who was in the United States last week when he announced the hack, said at the time he had spoken with OpenAI’s chief executive, Sam Altman, “to express Australia’s extreme concern about this incident”. On Tuesday, Albanese said OpenAI had been “very constructive and open in engaging” since the incident, as had Anthropic. He said AI can improve economic growth and productivity but it also carries risks. “And we’ve seen those risks exposed – not just in what occurred in Australia, but the revelation that has occurred in the United States and other countries as well.” The federal government has flagged it could introduce mandatory reporting rules for AI-related data breaches, after the revelation OpenAI used a public-facing email address three months after the hack to report the incident to Services Australia. The company said on Tuesday it had “a lot of work ahead” to rebuild trust with Australians but said it was making “meaningful changes”.

title: How American political campaigns are using AI – and what they’re spending on the tools
summary: Though politicians are quiet about how they use AI, the book Rewiring Democracy examines how AI is starting to influence American politics
text: New campaign finance disclosure data shines a light on which US political campaigns are using AI tools and how much they are spending on them. Candidates’, parties’ and committees’ spending reveals that AI is fast becoming an essential tool of politics. The candidates themselves are quiet about how they are using the technology in their own campaigns. It’s a sensitive issue that we have been tracking closely since we started writing our book, Rewiring Democracy, which examined how AI is beginning to influence politics. A September 2025 Pew survey of Americans found that more than 70% would think less of a candidate if they used AI to help write a speech. Itemized expenditure disclosure data from the US Federal Election Commission, dating back to 2020, reveals at least $17m in disclosed spending on AI technology vendors across 523 federal candidates and campaigns. Data from four states, California, Colorado, Massachusetts and Washington, provides a more localized picture going back to 2022. Beginning with the AI behemoths, at least 80 federal campaigns and committees have reported spending with OpenAI since 2024. The total spending is not huge: only about $50,000 reported, skewing slightly more Republican than Democratic. The Republican National Committee is the largest overall buyer, with nearly $10,000 in reported expenses. Top individual users include the campaigns of Republicans Mike Lawler, John Kennedy and Bill Cassidy, as well as the California Democrats Ro Khanna and Ted Lieu. Most of these expenses are listed as office expenses, subscriptions to ChatGPT for staff, or research tools, rather than as specific political services. The company’s policies prohibit some political uses of their ChatGPT tool. OpenAI’s biggest competitor, Anthropic, has rapidly built a similar level of usage, but with a different split. At least 65 candidates or committees now report paying the Claude maker in 2026, up from essentially zero in previous years, with a nearly two-to-one Democrat-to-Republican ratio. However, the largest individual user is the campaign of Tom Cotton, a Republican senator from Arkansas, who reported more than $4,000 in spend on Anthropic software in his June filing. Other major users are the Montana independent Senate candidate Seth Bodnar and Jason Knapp, who lost a Democratic House primary in Virginia, and the Democratic Alaska Senate candidate Mary Peltola. Candidates use either Claude or ChatGPT, rarely both, according to the disclosures. Only about 12% of campaigns or committees using either tool reported expenditures to both vendors. The Democratic lean of Anthropic usage may reflect the company’s alleged liberal skew and clashes with the Trump administration. In contrast, Elon Musk’s xAI caters to Republican interests and, accordingly, its meager usage comes almost entirely from the political right. Just seven federal and two state-level candidates or committees have reported paying xAI, a total of about $5,000, the majority of which was spent by the presidential campaign of RFK Jr in 2024, but also includes Republicans Dave McCormick and Thomas Massie. More dollars go to the vendors specializing in political campaign applications of AI. For years, AmplifAI, which provides automated text messaging, essentially a new iteration on robocalling technology, was a dominant target of spending, soaking up $4.7m in campaign spending in the 2022 cycle alone. It was used heavily by Democratic candidates including Mark Kelly, Joe Biden, Bernie Sanders and Adam Schiff. Spending on AmplifAI, now owned by the troubled media conglomerate Triller, seems to have tapered off in the years since 2022. The new rising Democratic solution for AI-powered text messaging is Daisychain, which has so far garnered about $300,000 in reported candidate spend in the 2026 cycle – up from only about $50,000 reported in 2024. More than half of this year’s spending comes from the Senate campaign of Democrat Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan. The closest equivalent on the Republican side has been Campaign Nucleus, associated with former Trump campaign manager Brad Parscale. The AI-powered voter engagement tool has attracted six-figure spending from the Republican National Committee, multiple Pacs aligned with Donald Trump, and five-figure investments from Mike Johnson, Kari Lake and other candidates. It is displacing the legacy texting vendor Prompt.io, which has retained about $375,000 in 2026 spending to date, down from more than $500,000 in the 2022 cycle. But it continues to be used: the A More Affordable California Pac sponsored by Uber has single-handedly spent more than $1m on Prompt.io in 2026. The Republican Massachusetts gubernatorial nominee Michael Minogue has been a recurring customer, as has the failed Republican California gubernatorial candidate Ché Ahn and Republican-aligned Super Pac Neighbors for a Better Colorado. At the state level At the state level, the AI spending is smaller but growing fast. Across the four states studied, we found a total of at least $92,000 in spending confidently attributable to modern generative AI vendors since 2022. The spending is spread across at least 108 candidates and committees. The growth has been explosive; there has already been about 10 times the amount of state-level AI spending reported in 2026 as there was in all of 2024. Much of the state spending mirrors federal patterns. Daisychain again has the highest overall spend, and OpenAI and Claude dominate among the general-purpose AI vendors. DonorAtlas – the AI-powered prospect research tool – sticks out for its usage in these states, sitting behind only Daisychain and OpenAI and buoyed up by nearly $4,000 in spending by the California Democratic party. Even though it has dominated so much media conversation, few candidates seem to be reporting spending on AI tools designed specifically to create synthetic audio and video, also known as “deepfakes”. We found just six federal candidates or committees reporting spending on the popular AI audio generator tool from ElevenLabs, with total spending of about $1,400 led by independent candidate for Colorado’s sixth congressional district Samir Witta. The AI image generator service Midjourney has five reported federal campaign or committee users reporting about $1,600, led by Sholdon Daniels, the Republican primary runner-up in the Texas 30th district. Combined, those two firms had less than $100 in reported spend across the four states. However, recent data from the Wesleyan Media Project shows that at least 164 political ads in this cycle have included AI-generated media, supported by at least $80m in ad spending. What this illustrates is that candidate and committee disclosure reports are just the tip of the iceberg. They don’t cover spending on AI by political consultants, media firms and other vendors hired by the campaigns or by Pacs, or independent committees raising and spending money aimed at boosting candidates’ campaigns. Those entities aren’t required to disclose detailed expenditure reports, and are very likely where the bulk of campaign AI usage is happening. Since a large fraction of all spending in the campaign cycle will happen in the final weeks leading to November, much remains to be seen about the totality of how campaigns will leverage AI and what impact its use will have on voters’ decisions. • This article was amended on 13 October 2026. An earlier version wrongly said that Prompt.io was a “Republican-serving texting vendor”. In fact, it is a non-partisan company.

title: Former snooker world champion Graeme Dott jailed for child sexual abuse
summary: Dott, 49, receives seven-year sentence after abusing a boy and a girl in what judge says was ‘gross violation of trust’
text: The former snooker world champion Graeme Dott has been jailed for seven years at the high court in Edinburgh after being convicted of sexually abusing two young children. In August, Dott was found guilty of sexually abusing a boy and a girl after a five-day trial at Glasgow high court. The court heard that the 2006 world champion inappropriately touched and exposed himself to both children. He denied the charges but was convicted of two counts of lewd, indecent and libidinous behaviour by a majority verdict. Dott appeared at the high court in Edinburgh on Tuesday, where the judge, Lord Harrower, told him he had “robbed the complainers of a significant part of their childhood”. Imposing a backdated sentence of seven years, he said the 49-year-old’s behaviour had involved a “gross violation of trust” that carried “the hallmarks of grooming”. Using pseudonyms for the boy and girl, Harrower said: “In both cases the abuse included penetrative sexual activity and in the case of Jane behaviour that would now be classed as rape.” Dott has continued to maintain his innocence, the court heard. Between 1993 and 1996, Dott – starting when he himself was still a child aged 16 or 17 – targeted a girl on multiple occasions. The woman, now in her 40s, told the trial that the abuse began when he started “caressing” her bottom over her clothing while giving her a piggyback. She told the court that Dott had told her not to tell anyone that he was sexually abusing her, describing incidents when he had suggested playing a “guessing game”. He would expose himself to her, she said, and began touching her with different parts of his body, including his penis. The second victim, a man now in his late 20s, was targeted between 2006 and 2010. He said he was sexually abused by Dott on multiple occasions, with the snooker player touching him inappropriately, kissing him and performing sexual acts. He told the court a lot of the abuse took place while he was in a shower, when Dott would come in either partly or completely undressed. “He would … come into the shower and put soap on my body and wash me in the shower,” the man told the court. “While he was washing me he would touch me in inappropriate places.” He said looking back at it now, Dott was “clearly getting sexual gratification from it”, and he was “pleasuring himself” while this was taking place. The man said that because of his age at the time, he “did not know what was going on”, and it was only later he realised the interaction “wasn’t right”. The witness also described abuse which took place in a car, where he said Dott would kiss him on the face, head and lips and “push himself up against me”. Harrower remanded Dott in custody and his name was added to the sex offender register indefinitely. Euan Dow, Dott’s lawyer, told the court in mitigation that his client had longstanding mental health issues, adding that his personal and professional reputations had been destroyed. The 49-year-old has separated from his wife but she remains supportive of him, the court heard. Dott, who turned professional in 1994, won the World Snooker Championship in 2006, defeating Peter Ebdon in the final at the Crucible in Sheffield. He reached the final in two other years but was beaten by Ronnie O’Sullivan in 2004 and Neil Robertson in 2010. Following his conviction, Dott’s name was removed from World Snooker’s hall of fame.

title: Anthropic ‘warns of existential AI risks to humanity’ in IPO document
summary: Reported admission to investors of AI’s ‘self-preserving behaviours’ comes as company prepares for a potential $2tn flotation
text: Anthropic is telling investors that advanced AI could pose “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity”, according to reports, as it prepares for a potential $2tn (£1.5tn) flotation. The warning inside the startup’s IPO prospectus, which has yet to be made public, was reported by Reuters and the Financial Times. It follows the company’s call for a slowdown in breakneck development of the technology – a warning echoed by rivals. The prospectus – a document outlining a company’s finances, growth plans and risk profile ahead of a share listing – is said to warn that AI models could exhibit “self-preserving behaviours”, including attempts to “resist shutdown”, to “conceal or manipulate information” and behaviour “resembling blackmail”. “Our development of highly advanced models, platforms, and applications and expansion of use cases could further ⁠increase the risk that our models cause harm,” the developer of the Claude chatbot reportedly said, adding the potential for a model to be aware it was being tested created a “significant limitation” on Anthropic’s ability to assess model safety. Anthropic declined to comment. Companies preparing to go public routinely report on risks ranging from safety issues to regulatory concerns but warnings about a product causing human extinction reflect heightened concern about such a consequential technology. The reported prospectus admission follows a surge in debate about the existential risk question, triggered this month when an Anthropic researcher, Jacob Coxon, resigned warning that people building AI “earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade”. A senior safety researcher at Anthropic then posted their agreement on X, claiming there was a more than 10% chance it “could kill all humans” within the next decade. Days later, Anthropic’s chief executive, Dario Amodei, said the industry “must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models”. Some experts have criticised the existential risk warnings, saying they are unverifiable and unscientific. However, there are growing examples of unsanctioned behaviour by the technology, including OpenAI agents – autonomous systems that carry out sequences of tasks without human intervention – hacking dozens of third-party organisations including the AI startup Hugging Face and Australia’s universal healthcare system. OpenAI announced on Monday it had cancelled the release of its newest model because of safety concerns. It said the GPT-6.1 Astra model showed higher levels of deception and performed poorly on tests for alignment, the term for ensuring a model adheres to human values and goals. Reuters reported that approximately 80 pages of the 261-page main body of the Anthropic prospectus were devoted to laying out risk factors, compared with 48 pages to describe its business. Anthropic is reportedly seeking a valuation of more than $2tn, compared with the $1.8tn achieved by Elon Musk’s SpaceX.

title: Three deaths, three states, 24 hours: one day in ICE’s quiet but ‘gruesome’ surge
summary: These men in Maine, Georgia and Florida shared no ties – until they became casualties in Trump’s anti-immigration campaign
text: It was 7am on 13 July this year. A warm, sunny morning, as residents of Biddeford, Maine, left their homes, got into their cars and began their commute. Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero came out of the apartment he lived in with his partner and daughter and drove off in his white car. Minutes later, neighbors heard three pops. Durán Guerrero was dead. More than 1,200 miles (1,900km) away in Ocilla, Georgia, Jesús Manuel Arenas-Silva was shuffled on to a bus. Private sector guards and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officials were beginning the process of transferring him and several other immigrants from one detention center to another nearly two hours away. Ten minutes into the ride, he became unconscious. Doctors at a nearby hospital pronounced him dead. Less than 24 hours later, Juan Jairo Coronilla Durán, pulled up to a gas station near a busy highway in St Augustine, Florida, as the sun was rising in the bright sky. Soon after, he would lie dead on the road nearby, hit by a semitruck when running away from immigration officers. There were no ties between Durán Guerrero, Arenas-Silva and Coronilla Durán, but within those 24 hours, the three men suddenly became connected as casualties in the latest phase of Donald Trump’s aggressive anti-immigration campaign. Twenty-four hours. Three states. Three people dead. Countless lives changed in seconds. The men in Maine and Florida were not even ICE’s intended targets for arrest – they became “collaterals”, as agency officials call them. “Three people dying in one day is an amplification of what we’ve already seen,” said Andrew Free, a former immigration attorney and investigative journalist who has for years extensively worked on ICE-related death cases. “The choices that the Trump regime has made since January 2025 have had the consequence of increasing the numbers of people who die in the field and in custody.” Throughout 2025 and into early 2026, federal immigration officials descended on cities including Los Angeles, Chicago and Minneapolis. They swaggered in militarized gear and brandished their weapons and crowd-control sprays, while engaging in raids and arrests in a high-profile attempt to show that Trump’s promise of “mass deportations” would be fulfilled. An explosion of protests and public backlash grew, reaching a climax after the January 2026 fatal shootings of two US citizens in Minneapolis as they protested against what local leaders called “an invasion” by federal immigration officials. Since then the flashy immigration enforcement mass operations have all but disappeared. Throughout the rest of 2026, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has switched strategy: more low-key arrest operations by small groups of officers and more 287(g) collaborations with local and state police and sheriffs deputized to make immigration arrests. Also, quicker processing with less representation in immigration courts and White House-directed collaboration to target undocumented children are fueling enforcement that is quieter but just as ruthless. A summer surge of enforcement means arrests are at a record high, with the majority now being people with no criminal history. And deaths keep ticking up “even though ICE’s current tactics have been less visible than the chaos in Minneapolis at the start of the year”, said Austin Kocher, an assistant research professor at Syracuse University and an immigration data and policy expert, in his Substack posts. At least 31 people have died in 2026 during interactions with immigration officials. Four people have been shot, 25 have died in detention and at least two people, including Coronilla Durán, have died while fleeing officials. The 24 hours between the mornings of 13 and 14 July stand out as exceptionally deadly. When contacted for comment, a DHS spokesperson sent along the three previous statements they had issued when the deaths originally happened in Maine, Georgia and Florida. Much remains unclear about the three deaths in that period, but some crucial details are still known. Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, 25, shot while driving On the Monday morning of 13 July when Durán Guerrero left his home in Biddeford, a city in southern Maine, ICE officer David Brouillette and other officers were reportedly looking for a different person, whose last known address was where Durán Guerrero had just exited. Brouillette, 37, had recently been hired by ICE amid the immigration agency’s push to increase arrests by bringing on more officials. With a blond-brown beard, baseball cap, sunglasses and a green tactical vest marked “POLICE ICE” over a navy T-shirt, Brouillette sat in a federal vehicle and watched the streets. As Durán Guerrero got into his white car and drove away, Brouillette and the officers spotted him, gave chase and attempted to stop the car. The next few moments are still unclear, but neighbors suddenly heard the “pops” of gunfire in the quiet neighborhood. Brouillette had fatally shot Durán Guerrero. A statement from the DHS at the time said that the ICE officers attempted to stop the vehicle, but that Durán Guerrero “attempted to flee”. The DHS added the official fired at Durán Guerrero “fearing for public safety”. It has not been verified whether Durán Guerrero drove his vehicle in the way that the DHS stated. Surveillance footage obtained by the Associated Press appears to show a white car slowly driving in circles at an intersection. The footage was recorded after the shooting, with Durán Guerrero either dead or dying at the wheel. The video then shows one of ICE’s vehicles ramming into the white car to stop it. Two officers open the driver’s door and Durán Guerrero’s body slumps on to the asphalt. Two more ICE officers rush over. “He had blood on his head, blood on his face. It was gruesome, just gruesome,” a neighbor told Maine Public Radio. “I believe it was [Durán Guerrero’s] wife that was sitting on the curb across the street, just crying hysterically.” The Colombian man was 25, with a dazzling smile that lit up his face below closely cropped dark hair. He lived with his partner, Karolina Rojas, and their three-year-old daughter, and he had authorization to live and work in the US. He was a food delivery driver and is remembered by his neighbors as a good man and hard worker. “My son was a person who left his country to make a future for his family,” Omar Durán, Durán Guerrero’s father, told BluRadio, a Colombian news outlet. Brouillette, the ICE officer, was hired by the agency after years of employment instability, according to reporting from the Associated Press, the Portland Press Herald and other outlets. He was recruited even though family members have made allegations of a history of violent behavior, including accusations of domestic violence and threats. Attempts to reach Brouillette for comment were not successful. About ICE’s recruitment policies, the DHS said: “The ICE Office of Professional Responsibility diligently applies the proper personnel vetting regulations, including guidelines for national security, and evaluates all available information for every applicant based on these factors.” The ICE office of professional responsibility internally investigates any alleged misconduct. The DHS has still not publicly confirmed Brouillette’s identity as the official who shot Durán Guerrero, nor commented on his alleged personal history. The agency has criticized the media for publishing his name, saying it put officers and their families in danger. Jesús Manuel Arenas-Silva, 45, died in ICE custody Meanwhile, in Georgia, just after 7am on 13 July, Arenas-Silva sat in an ICE transport bus, surrounded by other ICE detainees. The Venezuelan man had been held for a few days at the Irwin county detention center, a privately owned facility operating under contract with ICE. He and the other detainees were being transferred to the Folkston D Ray facility, another privately run detention center in the state. Arenas-Silva, 45, had a myriad of physical and mental health conditions, including hypertension, diabetes, anxiety and depression, according to a preliminary death investigation report released by ICE. He relied on several medications to survive, his family and the ICE report said. He had been in the US since 2021 and an immigration judge ordered his removal in April 2026, a DHS spokesperson said. Days before his death, ICE arrived at Arenas-Silva’s home to arrest him. “We implored ICE not to take him due to his medical needs, but they didn’t listen to our pleas,” Sonimar Arenas, his sister, later said. While cuffing Arenas-Silva, the ICE officials only allowed him to take one of his medications with him, according to Sonimar. In a phone call from ICE detention, Arenas-Silva told his sister that ICE had not yet given him the medication he needed, according to a statement she later released. The preliminary ICE death report confirms Arenas-Silva did not have all of his necessary medication on 10 July during his medical intake screening at the Irwin facility. A nurse noted that the only medication he arrived with was for anxiety, the ICE report says. That same nurse later confirmed he had other active medical prescriptions he never received. Three days later, Arenas-Silva was shuffled on to the transport bus, where staff saw him interact with other detainees at 7.34am. But about 10 minutes later, Irwin detention center staff saw Arenas-Silva was unconscious. As staff dialed 911, the bus began driving to a nearby hospital, the report said. Fifteen minutes later, Arenas-Silva arrived at the emergency room, “unresponsive and pulseless”, the ICE report says. The medical staff worked on Arenas-Silva, but at 8.31am he was pronounced dead. “While in custody, Arenas-Silva received medical care and was seen by medical professionals,” a DHS spokesperson said in a statement. “ICE is committed to ensuring that all those in custody reside in safe, secure and humane environments. Comprehensive medical care is provided from the moment individuals arrive and throughout their stay. “At no time during detention is a detained noncitizen denied emergency care,” the statement added. Juan Jairo Coronilla Durán, 28, hit by truck while fleeing ICE In Florida, Coronilla Durán, a 28-year-old Mexican tourist, had been enjoying a few weeks traveling in the US. Before 14 July, he had reportedly been in Atlanta, Georgia, and then traveled to St Augustine, the northern Florida city with beaches on the Atlantic Ocean. Coronilla Durán and his wife, who had been married for 10 years, lived in the central Mexican state of Guanajuato with their then seven-month-old daughter and a seven-year-old son, according to reporting by the Miami Herald. He was visiting friends and relatives in the US, while his wife was at home in Mexico. On the fateful July morning, Coronilla Durán and three other men pulled up to a convenience store at a gas station just before 7am. It is unclear who exactly he was with when he arrived there, next to a busy highway. Details of exactly what unfolded next remain unclear, but a number of federal immigration officials spotted the men and approached them. For unknown reasons, Coronilla Durán and the three others took off running. As Coronilla Durán ran away from the federal officials, he continued to look back to see if they were giving chase. He ran into the busy highway, at first avoiding vehicles speeding by, witnesses told the Miami Herald. But when Coronilla Durán arrived at the grassy median, he lost his footing, slipped and fell. He stood up, looked back at the immigration officials and continued to run into the next lane of traffic. According to a bystander, as Coronilla Durán began to cross the other highway lanes, he lost his footing again and fell in front of a tractor-trailer. The witness said he immediately knew Coronilla Durán had been hit. “The tractor trailer immediately stopped and attempted to render aid to the victim,” a statement by Florida highway patrol said. The DHS has still not formally identified Coronilla Durán as the victim and only said homeland security officials “conducted an operation near St Johns, Florida. Florida Highway Patrol and HSI are investigating an incident resulting in the death of a Mexican national. We will provide an update when available.” Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) is part of ICE. ‘At what time does this become indefensible?’ All three men’s deaths are still under investigation by local and federal officials. Durán Guerrero’s parents traveled to the US from Colombia to collect his body. His killing in Maine led to protests, especially since another deadly ICE shooting had taken place a few days earlier in Houston, Texas. Durán Guerrero’s death, and the subsequent reporting of allegations about Brouillette’s personal history, led to calls for ICE to improve its hiring practices and to equip officers with body cameras. ICE officials were briefly instructed to stop pulling over vehicles. The FBI referred all questions about the case to the Maine attorney general’s office and the DHS inspector general’s office. The Maine attorney general’s office said it could not comment further because it was still investigating the shooting death. The DHS inspector general’s office did not respond to a request for comment. The Georgia bureau of investigation (GBI), a state-level agency, was asked by local county officials to investigate Arenas-Silva’s death, according to a statement provided to the Guardian. A GBI spokesperson confirmed the investigation is open and active. Arenas-Silva’s sister continues to press for answers: “I am 100% certain that he did not receive proper care,” she said in a statement. “I will seek justice for him and for everyone else who goes through this, so that other families do not have to endure what we are going through. No one deserves this.” In Florida, Coronilla Durán’s wife flew into the US days after her husband’s death to make arrangements with a funeral home. The Mexican government was assisting the family in transporting his body back to Mexico to be buried. “The Florida Highway Patrol Traffic Homicide Investigation is currently ongoing,” a spokesperson said in a statement. “There are no updates currently regarding that case.” Free, the legal expert on ICE-related deaths, fears that ICE involved deaths are going to continue rising. Just over a week ago, an ICE official shot another person – this time in Austin, Texas. The man survived, but the shooting appears to have taken place during an attempted vehicle stop. “Sometime soon, we’re going to have four people die in a 24-hour period. And then it’s going to be five,” Free said. “What happens when we get there? What’s the red line? For policymakers, for states, for companies – at what time does this become indefensible or unsustainable?” In Durán Guerrero’s case in Maine, one detail stood out to community members. As neighbors gathered at the intersection watching the federal and local officials attempt first aid on Durán Guerrero, they noticed a small girl nearby, wearing a pink backpack and crying. It was the couple’s daughter, who would never see her father alive again. Though, it turned out, she might have escaped an even worse fate. Her mother recently collected some items from investigators and was told the girl’s car seat, from Durán Guerrero’s car, would not be returned. A bullet had pierced it during the shooting.

title: Trial of live facial recognition in London stations leads to a false positive and no arrests
summary: Freedom of information request finds six-month trial cost £320,000, used almost 100 police hours and led to just one – incorrect – alert
text: A six-month trial of live facial recognition (LFR) technology in London’s railway stations that cost more than £320,000 and almost 100 hours of police officers’ time led to one false match against a watchlist of suspects and no arrests. More than half a million faces were scanned between February and July this year in some of the capital’s busiest transport hubs during the British Transport Police (BTP) trial of the surveillance technology, which aimed to help catch offenders and people breaching court orders. A freedom of information document obtained by Liberty Investigates and shared with the Guardian shows that equipment hire and police staffing for the 18 deployments across the trial cost £320,786 and led to only one alert on a watchlist, which turned out to be an incorrect identification, also known as a false positive. Last month BTP announced it was extending the trial for a further four months and expanding the deployments to include London Underground stations. British Transport Police said that since the extension there had been three positive confirmed alerts of people who were subsequently confirmed to be complying with sexual harm prevention orders or other imposed court conditions. When Transport for London announced its support for the extension of the trial, it said LFR technology “will target and identify people on police watchlists at key stations chosen for maximum impact” and would “specifically tackle violence against women and girls, whose travel behaviours are shaped by experiences of sexual harassment and sexual offences”. Fraser Sampson, a former biometrics and surveillance camera commissioner for the UK, said the police needed to show that the use of the technology was proportionate. “There many variables and all need to align: the choice of location, times of day, make up of the watchlist and likelihood of people being present and many more.” Sampson, who is now a non-executive director of Facewatch, a company that operates facial recognition systems in shops, added: “We know the technology works, but using it in supermarkets to deter shoplifters and prevent attacks on staff is very different from deploying it to catch people on a public transport network. “Success in a shop means no such people coming in. Success for the police trying to catch people means people being caught. In that respect the trial doesn’t appear to have been very fruitful. “Everything depends on the police watchlists; if you’re not on a watchlist, the live FRT cameras do not ‘see’ you and they don’t retain your image in the same way as CCTV cameras. “However, they are processing special category personal data and the technology must be used in a way that is appropriate, proportionate and necessary. It’s for the police to show how any deployment meets those criteria and – as the ICO [information commissioner’s office] has recently reported – for their oversight boards to hold them firmly to account in doing so.” More than half of police forces in England and Wales have now deployed LFR on British streets, according to an analysis by Liberty Investigates. The Metropolitan police and London mayor’s office announced this summer that fixed LFR cameras would be installed in the capital’s West End. Sadiq Khan, the mayor of London, has since confirmed the technology will be used on the newly pedestrianised Oxford Street. A recent report from parliament’s joint committee on human rights, which called on the government to introduce a law to address the threat of artificial intelligence to human rights, identified the rollout of live facial recognition technology as a “particularly clear example of risk”. Bell Ribeiro-Addy, the Labour MP for Clapham and Brixton Hill, said: “Live facial recognition technologies are a serious invasion of our privacy. The government should be suspending their rollout until there are stronger safeguards in place, including a proper legal framework.” A BTP spokesperson said it had launched the LFR pilot “to understand how the technology could most effectively support the identification of wanted offenders and individuals who may pose a risk to passengers and staff”. They added: “During these deployments, officers have made a number of associated arrests, including for assault, theft, possession of an offensive weapon, breach of a criminal behaviour order and public order offences, as well as locating individuals wanted by the courts and other police forces. As these arrests did not result directly from an LFR alert, they are not included within LFR performance data. “Throughout the pilot, we have continued to refine how the capability is deployed within the railway environment. This has included developments to deployment locations, operating procedures, equipment and watchlist construction. “A particularly important point is that watchlist growth has been deliberate, controlled and aligned to BTP policy. We began with a more limited watchlist whilst ensuring data quality, governance and safeguarding arrangements were robust.”

title: Dale Vince plans London-wide news operation to take on ‘rightwing bias’ in the media
summary: Green energy entrepreneur plans rescue package for the group behind the Camden New Journal, Islington Tribune and Westminster Extra
text: The green energy entrepreneur and Labour donor Dale Vince is planning to launch a London-wide news operation, as part of a “rescue” of one of the capital’s most highly regarded local newspapers. Vince, who has vowed to take on what he sees as rightwing bias in the UK media, said he would invest “whatever it takes” to support the loss-making group behind the Camden New Journal (CNJ), Islington Tribune and Westminster Extra. He told the Guardian he was already looking at expanding the Westminster edition to cover London-wide issues, in an attempt to serve a city in which a series of major newsrooms have closed or drastically shrunk over the past 20 years. “We’re going to go forward together to put the CNJ on a better financial footing and take it digital – properly digital,” he said. “At the same time, [we will] get behind the Westminster edition and make that an edition for the wider London area. “I think London is missing a local paper now, with the demise of a couple that have gone before. It’s quite a bold plan, that we might morph the Westminster edition. “We might call it the north, south, east and Westminster edition, in a kind of nod to our intended larger audience.” Vince’s rescue package for the titles, which has not been formally finalised, is one of several attempts being made to revitalise local journalism in London. Despite its 9m population, media outlets have struggled to support large London-focused newsrooms. The Evening Standard, which has been published for almost 200 years, shut down its daily newspaper in 2024. It was replaced with a weekly edition renamed the London Standard, with a greater focus on arts and culture. Other attempts to run daily freesheets failed. The London Paper, launched by Rupert Murdoch’s News International, now News UK, closed in 2009 after just three years. Its rival, London Lite, published by the owner of the Daily Mail, closed later that year. Meanwhile, Metro, a national freesheet distributed in UK cities including London, is undergoing major structural changes to put it on a “sustainable footing”. However, journalism focused on London has been boosted in recent years by the arrival of small, subscription-based operations. Jim Waterson, a former Guardian journalist who founded the London Centric news site that now has more than 5,000 paying subscribers, said Vince had chosen to help a local group that had resisted “the disastrous choice in the 2010s to abandon quality for chasing clicks at all costs”. However, he said the success of his own “back-to-basics local journalism” outlet was still “only enough money to support a tiny operation that’s still run from a kitchen table”. “Vince has also realised that London is also one of the UK’s worst local news deserts,” Waterson said. “The challenge that we all face is how to get the funding to grow our audience without becoming financially unsustainable.” While not large, the Camden New Journal group still employs 18 people, according to recent financial records. It spent a chunk of its cash reserves in the last year. Vince said he was not supporting the Camden New Journal and its related titles “for business reasons”. “I’m motivated by the impact of local journalism,” he said. “I’m motivated by the bias of media in our country more broadly – the rightwing bias – and trying to do something about that.” Vince has already launched an online publication, Babelfish. He said he would consider writing comment pieces for the London titles, but would generally be a “hands-off” investor. “Big picture-wise, I’ve got a view of the world and how things should be, and the Camden people already fit within that,” he said. “There’s no kind of culture clash and I write op-eds for all kinds of people already. I would absolutely write op-eds for the Camden [New Journal], but it wouldn’t be a requirement.”
