title: Fayed survivors say GMC let abuse continue by refusing to investigate doctors
summary: Women say inquiry should look at medical regulator after it dismissed request to scrutinise medic accused of sharing results of intrusive sexual health examinations with tycoon
text: Victims of Mohamed Al Fayed have accused the medical regulator of allowing his sexual abuse to continue unchecked by refusing to investigate allegations that doctors were complicit in his crimes. Survivors of Fayed’s abuse have called for the General Medical Council (GMC) to be investigated after it dismissed a request in 2017 to scrutinise a doctor accused of subjecting a woman to intrusive sexual health examinations and sharing the results with Fayed. Almost a decade after complaints were first made to the GMC about Dr Wendy Snell, who died in 2022, the doctors’ regulator has now taken action against two other surviving doctors who are also accused of passing sexual health information to Fayed about women who he later abused. Fayed, the former owner of Harrods died in 2023 a year before hundreds of women went public with accusations of sexual assault by Fayed over the previous decades. Pelham Spong complained to the GMC in 2017 about Snell, a doctor employed by Fayed who subjected her to sexual health tests in 2008 as part of an interview process for a job with the former Harrods owner. The same day Fayed grabbed her face and forcibly kissed her, Spong alleged. Fayed also quizzed Spong about a sexually transmitted disease that Snell had assured her would be kept confidential along with all her results, she claimed. Her complaint, seen by the Guardian, said: “I know that there are other women who have similar stories involving both Fayed, and doctors and improper health screenings at Harrods. In fact, the recruiter who sent me on this interview had previously sent another candidate.” It added: “I felt humiliated, ashamed, and embarrassed that this potential employer knew the most intimate details of my body.” The GMC told Spong it was not in the “greater public interest” to investigate Snell. It added: “We have no powers to investigate, resolve or comment on whether a gynaecological examination should have formed part of your recruitment process.” Spong, who was 23 at the time of the abuse, told the Guardian: “It’s shocking that the GMC received intelligence like mine in 2017 and did nothing. They have been sitting on this for almost 10 years and let my abusers escape. There was an alarming lack of curiosity by the GMC which begs all sorts of questions. I was reporting trafficking.” In October 2017 Spong also reported her ordeal to the Metropolitan police, which obtained a copy of her complaint to the GMC as part of its initial inquiries, before taking no further action. She said: “Fayed continued abusing women until he died. So the fact that the Met and the GMC didn’t do their job in 2017 means more women were harmed. That’s on them, so absolutely they should be investigated.” Spong is backing calls for a public inquiry into Fayed’s crimes that would include failures by the Met and the GMC. Joan* alleges she was raped in the 1990s by Fayed’s brother Salah Fayed after a sexual health examination by Dr Ann Coxon. She alleges that before she was raped, Salah Fayed, who died in 2010, phoned Coxon in her presence and put her on speaker. She alleges Coxon then told him the results of her sexual health tests over the call. Joan said: “I heard it first-hand and I’ve got it all written up in an affidavit that I made at the time. I have also got the test that she refers to.” Joan said: “If the GMC had acted when the first complaints were made in 2017, Fayed could have been stopped and held to account. If they were hearing reports about malpractice they should have escalated it to the police. But instead the GMC, very begrudgingly, very slowly, after massive political pressure, are only now finally starting to take action. This is just the wrong way around. What is the GMC for?” A third victim Judith*, says she was groped by Mohamed Al Fayed after a humiliating sexual health examination by Snell as part of a recruitment process for a job working for the family. She said the examination occurred after Fayed sold Harrods in 2010. Judith said: “I had a full gynaecological test with sexually transmitted disease testing as well. I was really shocked and traumatised that this was needed and I felt so much shame. As a result, I have really struggled with having smear tests since. So the whole episode has really put my life at risk.” She said: “I don’t want an apology from the GMC and a promise that this will never happen again. Instead there has to be clear legislation in place to ensure private doctors are monitored. At the moment there seems to be no oversight at all. “A public inquiry needs to be started as soon as possible and that the GMC should be part of that.” Coxon told the Guardian she could not comment but has previously denied carrying out sexual health tests on Harrods staff. The GMC has imposed restrictions on her ability to practise, and that of another doctor, pending a full investigation. Emma Jones, a solicitor at Leigh Day who is representing several of Fayed’s victims, said: “The GMC is finally taking things seriously, because they’ve imposed interim conditions on these doctors which isn’t always a standard step in these investigations. This is far too little, far too late. “When the complaints were first made to the GMC it should have reported them to the police. It beggars belief why they were not investigated earlier – they were such serious allegations they were conducting sexual health examinations and reporting back to Fayed without permission of the patient. “The failings of the GMC is one of the crucial areas that needs to be investigated, and the only way to do that properly is through a public inquiry.” A GMC spokesperson said: “The reports of sexual abuse carried out by Mohamed Al Fayed are horrifying and shocking. “We are investigating doctors employed by Mr Al Fayed, and have written to the parties involved to provide an update on our investigations. We are taking these concerns very seriously and remain in contact with relevant authorities, including the Metropolitan police. “We will take the appropriate action if we identify any potential fitness to practise concerns about individual doctors, but cannot provide information about individual investigations.” * Names have been changed

title: Andy Burnham expected to say he will push ahead with electoral reform plans
summary: Exclusive: Labour conference speech will kick off process that could replace current system with proportional representation
text: Andy Burnham is expected to announce that he will push ahead with plans for electoral reform in his first conference speech as Labour leader, in the latest sign that he intends to radically transform the UK’s political system. The prime minister, a longtime advocate of reform, will kick off a process that could eventually lead to ditching the first-past-the-post system in favour of proportional representation. Government sources told the Guardian that Burnham would set out his plans in “broad strokes” in the speech, underlining his commitment to drawing up proposals before the next general election. Along with social care changes and closer ties with the EU, the plans – which would represent the most significant shake-up of the electoral system since 1918 – would then be put in Labour’s manifesto to get public backing. One option open to Burnham is to set up a new national commission for electoral reform, an idea he endorsed at last year’s party conference as Greater Manchester mayor. At the time, he said there should be “a manifesto commitment to a system of proportional representation to be introduced into Westminster elections in the next parliament”. Almost 100 Labour MPs supported the plan when the representation of the people bill went through parliament earlier this month. The minister leading the bill, Florence Eshalomi, told MPs that Burnham “remains committed to electoral reform”, while warning it was “premature to legislate now for one approach”. Polling of MPs by YouGov suggests the change is supported by a majority in the Commons. Of those polled, 53% of MPs said they supported a review into first past the post. In May, before he returned to parliament, Burnham told the Guardian that sweeping changes to the electoral system to make politics “less point-scoring, more problem-solving” would be needed if he became prime minister. Critics of proportional representation have said it would lead to a more chaotic form of government, with unstable coalitions and an inability to pass legislation. Yet Burnham has long argued that Britain has suffered from an overcentralised, London-centric form of government in which two parties dominate at the expense of many of the UK’s nations and regions.

title: Police dog’s heatstroke death prompts criminal investigation in Tennessee
summary: Dog’s handler resigned from sheriff’s office after it emerged Bart had died due to severe dehydration in nearly 101F heat
text: The recent death of a Tennessee sheriff’s office dog after being left in an outdoor kennel without water for a day and a half in excessive heat has prompted the animal’s handler to resign amid administrative and criminal investigations, according to authorities. Bart had been a patrol dog specializing in suspect apprehension, tracking, searches and drug detection before his handler found him dead inside his outdoor kennel on 19 September, Julian Wiser, the Madison county sheriff, said in a social media video announcement. A veterinary necropsy of the two-and-a-half-year-old German shepherd found that he had died of heatstroke due to severe dehydration, with investigators learning Bart’s handler at the Madison sheriff’s office had not been home for about 36 hours while temperatures climbed to 101F (38.3C) and water was inaccessible to the canine. In his video addressing the case, Wiser called Bart’s death “unfortunate and preventable”, and the sheriff also described himself as a former canine unit supervisor. “This is … very sad and unfortunate,” Wiser said in the video on Friday. “We depend on our canines to help keep our community safe and our law enforcement officers, but our canines depend on us to take care of them.” Bart’s handler was neither immediately identified by Wiser’s office nor formally charged with a crime. Wiser said the deputy resigned after being placed on administrative leave. The sheriff added that his office had also served search warrants in connection with simultaneous internal and criminal investigations into Bart’s death. Wiser said resulting findings would be forwarded to prosecutors. A survey published in the Police Practice and Research Journal found heatstroke to be the second-leading cause of death for police dogs in the line of duty, behind only gunfire. In fact, heatstroke was responsible for one in five such deaths, according to the survey. “Being left unattended and mechanical failures overwhelmingly (70.6%) characterized these heatstroke deaths,” said an abstract of the survey, which studied information on more than 400 canine deaths listed on the Officer Down Memorial Page website. According to the survey’s abstract, “Summer months were also significantly implicated in increasing the odds of line-of-duty heatstroke deaths.”

title: Burnham to signal willingness to look at scrapping pension triple lock to fund social care
summary: PM to tell Labour conference he is prepared to make difficult arguments and have ‘honest conversation’
text: Andy Burnham will signal he is prepared to look at scrapping the pensions triple lock to fund a national care service, telling the Labour conference he will be willing to make difficult arguments to tackle the UK’s intractable issues such as social care. Government sources have suggested the prime minister will signal his willingness to review the policy but stop short of a pledge to scrap it altogether. The Unite general secretary, Sharon Graham, said the move would be “electoral suicide”, with an end to the triple lock likely to be attacked by the Conservaties and Reform. In his speech, he will promise “an honest conversation” with the public, saying: “Hope comes from honesty and from saying the things politicians usually avoid.” Graham said Burnham had not committed to scrapping the policy, which ensures the state pension increases annually by either inflation, average wage growth or 2.5% – whichever is highest. “When we met with Andy this week, it certainly wasn’t mentioned,” she told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme. “But I do think that it’s important that Labour make sure that working-class people know that they’re on their side, and this would be a direction of travel that would say the opposite to that.” Asked whether the lock should be overhauled to fund social care, Graham said: “What I understood the national care service to be was a universal benefit: everybody paid in and everybody gets out, and that is what actually the principle of that is. “Going to a group of people who are getting around £12,500 a year in order to pay for it, to take away their security, is wrong. I think it’s morally wrong.” Labour’s deputy leader, Lucy Powell, said the party remained committed to the triple lock, which was in its manifesto. “The triple lock has really delivered for pensioners, in this country, over the course of this parliament,” she told Sky News. “I think we’re going to see [the] state pension rising by about £2,000 a year, significantly, and that’s really important so pensioners … can know that their income is secure and will continue to rise over the course of this parliament. “I don’t know what Andy’s going to say about that today, but I know that what he’s talking about is this big conversation about solving these big problems, but being really honest with people that they come at a cost. “They do come at a cost. You can’t just solve the social care crisis without having the big conversations about how you’re going to do this.” The housing secretary Angela Rayner said Burham would start a “brave” conversation on the funding of social care. “I think he’s absolutely right to start the conversation,” Rayner told Sky. “We’ve got a prime minister who said, I am okay with burning through all my political capital to the point where it might finish me off, on the basis of my legacy will be something better and different.” Having ousted Keir Starmer from office, Burnham has spent much of his first few weeks promising a radical shift in tone and policy. He will tell the conference on Tuesday: “We can’t carry on as we are. Politics as usual has taken Britain backwards. More of the same isn’t good enough and isn’t going to get us where we need to be.” Though the conference has been upbeat, Burnham will tell Labour delegates he wants to strike a serious tone with his speech and address some of the most intractable issues in British politics, such as social care, energy costs and youth inactivity. In the speech, the prime minister will say that he will resist “the usual tub-thumping conference speech … the patriot in me tells me something very different is needed”. He will say “everyone wants less drift and more direction” and that he will “answer that call” today. His offer – expected to contain a number of new policies – will be “a more serious prospectus for Britain than people have been offered in a generation”. “I accept people will not agree with every part of it, but I believe it can turn Britain around,” he will say.

title: RBA interest rates: Reserve Bank raises cash rate to highest level in 15 years and warns of more hikes ‘if needed’
summary: Michele Bullock says board knows decision will hit some people hard but hopefully in the next few years ‘this will all have been worth it’
text: The Reserve Bank of Australia has lifted its key interest rate to 4.6%, its highest level since 2011, and warned of further hikes as the unending US war on Iran pushes prices “permanently higher”. The widely expected fourth increase to the cash rate this year will add to repayment costs for millions of mortgage holders. Before Tuesday’s meeting, it sat at 4.35%. The RBA governor, Michele Bullock, said inflation had been too high for most of the last six years but she was confident higher rates would bring it back down. “We knew that this was going to hit some people pretty hard,” Bullock told reporters in Sydney. “Hopefully, in the next couple of years, when we get inflation back down, this will all have been worth it.” The RBA board said it voted unanimously for a hike in response to higher prices from the AI investment boom and amid fears that firms would begin passing on rising costs to consumers. Bullock singled out the US war on Iran, saying it could disrupt oil supply longer than expected. “It’s lasted, and there doesn’t seem to be any end to it,” she said. “That means that fuel prices, fertiliser prices, transport prices, all these things now are permanently higher.” Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Data to be released on Wednesday is expected to show underlying inflation rising at an annual pace of 3.6% for the third month running in August, well ahead of the RBA’s target range of 2% to 3%. The board in a statement accompanying the decision to hike rates said the economy was slowing as expected but that it would still lift interest rates “if needed”. Bullock said the RBA did not expect a recession but may have to create one if households began to assume inflation would stay at its current level. “If people start saying, ‘you know what, three-point-something [inflation] is fine or [4%] is fine … you might need to have quite a dramatic slowdown in the economy,” she said. But the governor said she wanted to avoid a “massive” increase in unemployment and didn’t “like the idea” of job losses, adding: “maybe there doesn’t need to be any more interest rate rises.” Markets interpreted her remarks as a sign the RBA would avoid multiple rate rises. Another increase was still expected by February or earlier but traders dropped their bets on a further hike next year, putting it at now just a 50% chance. Analysts at top bank ANZ and wealth manager UBS stood by their predictions of a hike as soon as November. My Bui, an AMP economist, said Bullock had offered a balanced view of the risks and predicted rates would stay on hold. Commonwealth Bank and NAB also reaffirmed their forecasts for rates to stay put. The Coalition leader, Angus Taylor, said federal government spending was to blame for Tuesday’s hike but would not be restrained by higher interest rates. “This is a dark day, a tough day for hardworking Australian families with a mortgage, those in small businesses,” Taylor said. The treasurer, Jim Chalmers, said the government took responsibility for “our part of the fight” against inflation but was managing the budget responsibly, blaming the US war on Iran for inflation. “Australians are paying a very hefty price for that war in the Middle East and today that price became a bit steeper with this decision from the independent Reserve Bank,” Chalmers said.

title: ‘Jaw-dropping’ play based on Pelicot rape trial comes to London for one night
summary: Four-hour production featuring star-studded cast will be performed at London County Hall
text: A play based on the trial of the men who drugged and raped Gisèle Pelicot will come to London for one night only this November – and promises to feature a star-studded cast. The four-hour production of The Pelicot Trial: Tribute to Gisèle Pelicot has been performed around the world, including in New York City and Avignon, the city in France where the trial took place. This autumn, it is coming to London County Hall, the home of Agatha Christie’s Witness for the Prosecution. “I saw it in French originally – all four hours of it. It was jaw-dropping, harrowing, really emotional,” said Nadia Fall, artistic director and co-chief executive of the Young Vic, which is putting on the performance. “It was the act of witnessing that really got me: it is long-form and testimonial in form.” Fall expects the show to sell out immediately. “Because it’s one night only, what we are able to do is ring our best actors, people you will know ‘off the telly’ as well,” Fall said. The full cast will be announced before tickets go on sale in the coming weeks. Fall added: “The ensemble rehearses together just once. That allows you to call up the best of people who are available for a short commitment. I really can’t wait to announce the company. It is, I think, 27 actors all in all.” The play was created by Milo Rau and Servane Dècle. The Swiss director and playwright Rau is known for adapting court cases for the stage, including the Moscow trial of the Russian punks Pussy Riot and the trial of the Romanian despot Nicolae Ceaușescu. Pelicot became internationally recognised after she waived her right to anonymity to ensure a public trial of her ex-husband, Dominique Pelicot, who, for almost a decade from 2011, drugged her unconscious and invited dozens of men from an internet forum to rape her. Her husband was sentenced to 20 years in prison in December 2024 and guilty verdicts were returned for all 51 accused men. She wanted the story to be public, saying “shame must change sides”. “We do it one time only in each city,” said Rau. “It is more of a political act really, than a play.” “It is a harsh watch,” said Dècle, “but people stay for the whole time. We let them come in and out if they want, but very few do. Even Gisèle Pelicot herself came to watch in New York. That was amazing. She said, ‘The actress was doing better than I did on trial.’” Journalists covering the trial gave Rau and Dècle thousands of pages of their notebooks, and the play is based on what was said in court. “Everyone wanted to share with us,” said Rau. “It became a trial of our society, of the patriarchy. And we have toured it in at least 15 different countries, in different languages, some I barely understand myself, and the audience still understands the play. Sadly it is a universal experience. It would be better for humanity if this was just a French experience.” “It isn’t scenes and costumes in a set like a traditional piece of theatre. It is the facts. It just floors you,” said Fall. The large majority of the audience has been female, Dècle said. “I wish more men would see it. The very interesting thing about this whole affair is you can really dive into who these male perpetrators were.” Fall said: “Pelicot represents so much for everybody, especially women; resilience and courage and a radical joy for me that she triumphed and lives on. She’s in love and lives her life. That is two fingers up to the patriarchy and I think that is really empowering for us women. This piece and her story is not just about the specifics about her story and sexual assault.” She agreed to the play, the writers said, because she wanted to keep the conversation that was started by her trial going. “We always say she opened the door, and we just keep it open,” said Rau.

title: Large shark stuck in South Korean city canal draws 600,000 visitors
summary: Port city of Busan inundated with tourists keen to see the 3.5-metre animal close up
text: A large shark has become an unlikely tourist attraction after getting trapped in a narrow city canal in South Korea for more than a week. More than 600,000 people are estimated to have visited a waterfront park in the southern port city of Busan since the 3.5-metre shark – nicknamed Bukang-i after the name of Busan’s North Port – was first spotted in its waterway on 18 September. Experts believe it to be a bronze whaler shark that followed prey from the sea into the canal and could not find its way out. The coastguard in the city about 200 miles (325km) south-east of Seoul tried to drive it out on the day it appeared but suspended the operation six hours later, on the advice of scientists who warned that forcing the animal could harm it or make it aggressive. On Tuesday morning coastguard boats sprayed jets of water behind the shark to push it towards the canal’s mouth, a method officials said was modelled on the rescue of a great white shark that became trapped in shallow water off Massachusetts in 2004. The first attempt failed, after the shark slipped past the boats and swam back into the canal, the Herald Business reported. The national institute of fisheries science said the shark was stable, but officials said its ability to feed and move was restricted, which could weaken it the longer it stayed. On Tuesday afternoon the operation was suspended again because the shark wouldn’t leave the waterway. Sharks are not unknown in South Korean waters. The fisheries institute recorded 46 large sharks off the east coast in the first half of this year, nearly four times as many as a year earlier, which it attributed to warmer seas and more of the fish that are the sharks’ prey. The North Port Waterfront Park, which usually draws about 2,000 people a day on holidays, recorded 607,000 visits between 19 and 28 September, according to the city. On Tuesday Kim Jung-sook, 62, came to say goodbye to the shark, telling the Maeil Shinmun newspaper: “I’ve grown attached to it after seeing it here for a few days … I feel a bit sad.” Busan’s mayor, Chun Jae-soo, is a fan too. “It really has star quality. It comes up every five to 10 minutes,” he told CBS radio. “It’s just so pretty.” The city has named the shark an honorary publicity ambassador, giving it the title “Shafluencer”, after 91% of respondents to a city Instagram poll backed the idea. Boogi, the city’s mascot, is to accept the certificate on its behalf. Lee Do-yoon, eight, who came with his father to see it off, was not worried that it appeared to be time to see it off. “It’s OK,” he said. “Bukang-i is going to meet its friends.”

title: Rubio says foreign actor was ‘clearly’ behind suspected RAF Fairford plot
summary: US secretary of state, who offered no evidence for claims, also says many people ‘disturbed’ that five suspects released on bail
text: A counter-terrorism operation near RAF Fairford in the UK was mired in confusion on Tuesday after police released five suspects on bail, prompting concern and surprise from the US president and secretary of state. Five British nationals from London were detained on suspicion of explosives offences and terrorism after three suspicious vans were reported to police in the early hours of Sunday, outside the base in the village of Whelford, Gloucestershire. A rapid and significant security response was triggered, with the village locked down, residents evacuated for 36 hours and bomb disposal robots dispatched to the scene. However, on Monday, the head of counter-terrorism policing in the UK announced all five men had been released on bail. Sources said their release suggested detectives believed it unlikely they had been on the brink of a mass casualty attack by exploding a bomb close to the base. Donald Trump later told reporters at the White House that he would not have released the suspects on bail. “We know everything about them. We would not have released them.” Asked whether the case was linked to Iran, Trump said: “It might be.” Pressed to give details, he said: “I’d rather not. I mean, I know the answer, I could be very specific, but I’d rather not say. I would not have released them.” Likewise, Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, said a lot of people were “disturbed that some of these people [being investigated] have been released on bail”. “What could have happened in the UK over the weekend is a ‌very serious situation,” Rubio said in an interview with Fox News on Monday evening, adding that it “clearly involves the hands ‌of a foreign actor”. Rubio provided no evidence for his claims. Tensions have been high at RAF Fairford since Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said in July that the base was a legitimate target. Iran’s embassy in London has denied any involvement in the events of the past few days. Adding to the sense of confusion on Sunday, Trump suggested the plot was known to the US authorities, while British sources were suggesting the specific activities of the men were unknown. MPs and councillors representing the local area said the messaging was inconsistent. Tristan Wilkinson, a councillor representing the ward, said: “It seems insane that this appears to have been a tipoff from a member of the public, and the security services are claiming that there was a level of intelligence involved as well. I don’t see how those two things can both come through at the same time.” The head of UK counter-terrorism policing, the assistant commissioner Laurence Taylor, said the release of the men on bail did not mean the investigation was over and that they were subject to “stringent conditions”. He said: “I know there is significant interest in whether the current geopolitical context has a bearing on this incident. At counter-terrorism policing we are working within this context every day, and at this stage we are keeping an open mind in this investigation … “But be assured, we are considering this from every possible angle. Including, that this may be activity committed by proxies, or individuals either knowingly or unknowingly working on behalf of a foreign state.” An initial examination of the vans led police to suspect they carried explosive materials, with assessments made as to whether they were viable improvised explosive devices. After the suspects’ release it emerged that no explosive material had been found. Iran is suspected of using proxies in the UK, in incidents ranging from alleged arson attacks against Jewish targets to men flying a basic drone near the Israeli embassy.

title: ‘This is terrorism’: daytime Russian strike hits science academy in Kyiv
summary: Jet-powered drones are increasingly targeting Ukraine’s capital, with medical centre also hit
text: A Russian drone hit the National Academy of Sciences in central Kyiv on Monday, killing at least one person, in the latest daytime attack on Ukraine’s capital. Flames tore through the historic building as people clambered out of first- and second-floor windows to escape, in dramatic scenes increasingly familiar in the heavily bombarded city. At least one person was killed and three others were wounded, according to Kyiv’s mayor, Vitali Klitschko, who said the injured had been taken to hospital. The 19th-century building stands close to the German embassy, the National Opera, St Volodymyr’s Cathedral and several government buildings. Anatoliy Zagorodny, the president of the national academy, said the blast struck while many staff members were inside. Standing outside the burning building, he said he did not know why Russia had targeted a leading centre of scientific research. “We are not connected with the military. This is an attack on science. It is terrorism,” he said. He feared some of his colleagues could still be trapped inside the academy. While the sciences building is a civilian scientific institution, it has longstanding ties to Ukraine’s defence sector. Among those injured in Monday’s strike was Volodymyr Horbulin, the academy’s first vice-president and a former high-ranking security official. Another Russian drone struck a nearby private medical centre, killing at least one person. Ukraine’s foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, accused Russia of cynicism for targeting a scientific institution during the working day. “Russia is deliberately expanding the boundaries of what it believes the world will tolerate. Every attack left without a strong response only encourages the next one,” he said. Russian strikes over the past week involving missiles and increasingly sophisticated jet-powered drones have hit apartment blocks, offices, warehouses and datacentres across the capital, killing and wounding civilians almost daily and giving Kyiv an increasingly frontline feel as it faces some of its most sustained bombardment since the early stages of Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022. The drone and missile campaign is designed to grind down public resilience and damage the economy. Monday’s double strike is likely to raise fresh concerns over Ukraine’s ability to protect even the most heavily guarded parts of the capital. The newer jet-powered drones fly faster and are harder to intercept than the older Shahed or Geran-2 models that were the backbone of Moscow’s air campaign. Ukraine is racing to develop and manufacture interceptors capable of bringing them down. Moscow has also changed its tactics, launching more attacks in daylight hours so that residents in major cities have to spend more of the day under air raid alerts. Buildings hit during daytime strikes are often occupied because many Ukrainians work through drone alerts rather than spend hours in shelters. Meanwhile, a Russian jet-powered drone struck western Ukraine near the border crossing with Poland, prompting Warsaw to issue an alert warning of a possible air attack and urging residents in the eastern Lublin region to seek shelter. Russian forces have increasingly targeted Ukrainian border crossings with Poland and Moldova, leading Kyiv to consider relocating joint customs checkpoints to the territory of neighbouring countries. “It’s again a threat very close to our border,” said Lt Col Jacek Goryszewski, speaking to Poland’s broadcaster TVN24. Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, called on western countries to intensify their pressure on Russia. “Every Russian terrorist attack is a loss of life that could have been prevented if pressure on Russia had finally become total,” he wrote on X on Monday. “The world must understand that terrorists will go further if they are not stopped here, in Ukraine. And we cannot turn a blind eye to such brutal strikes.” Russia has signalled that its attacks on Ukraine could intensify, and US-brokered efforts to end the war show little sign of progress. “Ukraine will have to pay a price for the actions that have taken place in recent months,” the Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, told reporters on Monday, referring to Ukrainian strikes deep inside Russian territory. “That is happening right now.”

title: UN warns of ‘narrowing window’ to restore world’s forests
summary: Food and Agriculture Organization urges governments to make forest restoration a national priority
text: The world faces a “narrowing window” to restore forests essential for food security and resistance to the climate emergency, a United Nations report has warned. More than 489m hectares (1.2bn acres) of forests have been cleared since 1990, while an even greater area is degraded, the world body said in a call for governments to make forest restoration a national priority. The State of the World’s Forests report acknowledges recent steps forward in protection and tree planting around the globe but says action has not kept pace with commitments. Over the past two decades, national, regional and global initiatives have promised to place more than 1bn hectares of land under restoration, but barely a fifth of that is actually being restored, the report by the UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) notes, saying: “Progress is uneven, and it is insufficient to meet growing global needs.” Forests, which cover 4.14bn hectares (about a third of Earth’s land surface), store 714 gigatonnes of carbon and host up to 80% of the world’s terrestrial biodiversity. They also play an important role in regulating rainfall and in reducing hunger, with nearly one-third of the global population depending on them for livelihoods. Threats are intensifying. Every year, about 127m hectares of forest are affected by fires, with further damage caused by insects, diseases and severe weather events. This is making forests ever more vulnerable, as it comes on top of pressure from farm expansion, the climate crisis, pollution and the extraction of fossil fuels and other resources. “This widening gap between demand and sustainable supply highlights a structural imbalance that threatens both ecological integrity and the long-term viability of forest-based economies,” the report states. It says remedial action on forests and other degraded ecosystems would benefit people, food security and the economy – with restoration of 1bn hectares estimated to generate $1.8tn in benefits each year. Qu Dongyu, the FAO director general, said the report “makes clear that forest and landscape restoration is more than an environmental priority – it is a strategic investment in resilient agrifood systems and rural development”. He said: “The window for action is narrowing, and delayed or poorly designed restoration will increase long-term costs, exacerbate inequalities and risk locking landscapes into unsustainable trajectories. Given the continued loss and degradation of forest ecosystems, as well as growing global demand for land-based products and services, there is an urgent need to scale up effective restoration.”

title: Mac mini M6 review: truly mighty but now more pricey
summary: Apple’s cheapest desktop computer is no longer a bargain but its newest, fastest chip makes it a pocket powerhouse
text: Apple’s latest Mac mini brings real speed and power for far more than everyday tasks in a practically pocketable form you can fit almost anywhere. The impressive new desktop machine is the first to receive an update to Apple’s latest M6 chip while remaining smaller than a headphones box. It is the cheapest computer Apple sells with an M-series chip, but like every other memory-containing piece of electronics, it has been hit by RAMageddon, driving up the starting price to £899 (€1,049/$899/A$1,449) from the £599 or equivalent of its M4 predecessor. Apple introduced the Mac mini’s dainty form with 2024’s M4 model, which remains the same for the new M6 version. A lot has changed since the M2 Mac mini, which was pretty compact. The current mini measures just 12.7cm square and 5cm thick, with rounded corners and a solid aluminium body. It’s happy to sit on a desk, but is small and light enough to mount behind a monitor to turn any screen into a DIY iMac. The machine is fairly minimalist. A small LED on the front shows you when it’s on. The back has three Thunderbolt 4 (USB4) ports, a 2.5Gb ethernet socket, an HDMI 2.1 port, and a figure-eight power cable. It lacks any USB-A ports, but adapters are readily available for legacy devices not yet converted to USB-C, such as flash drives or printers. It has basic speakers built in, which are good enough for macOS’s notification sounds. The mini runs the latest macOS 27 Golden Gate, which brings welcome refinements to Apple’s Liquid Glass design that was introduced last year. But the big update is a relaunch of Apple’s Siri assistant and AI tools. Siri AI, as it is now known, is vastly superior at understanding and performing tasks, such as finding information on your Mac or the web, and has a dedicated app to see previous interactions. It can read what’s on your screen, so you can ask it to track parcels from just a code in your email or find an object from an image with the CMD+Shift+Space keyboard shortcut. Siri is integrated into Spotlight search, which is handy but sometimes results in it trying to search the web instead of launching an app or a file on your Mac if you mistype, which can be frustrating. Apple Intelligence is smarter too. Writing, proofing and summarising tools are built in and accessible from most apps, along with a collection of other features. The most surprisingly useful tool I found was file and folder naming suggestions, which made matching long file-naming schemes a doddle. Boring but very useful. Specifications Processor: Apple M6 RAM: 16, 24 or 32GB Storage: 256, 512GB, 1 or 2TB SSD Operating system: macOS 27 Golden Gate Ports back: 3x Thunderbolt/USB 4, HDMI 2.1, 2.5Gb Ethernet Ports front: 2x USB-C (USB3), headphones Connectivity: wifi 7, Bluetooth 6, Thread Dimensions: 127 x 127 x 50mm Weight: 670g Serious M6 speed The Mac mini is offered with the newest Apple Silicon chip, the M6 (as tested) or with an M5 Pro, which has greater performance in multicore or graphics applications. For most people the M6 is more than enough, with the fastest single core performance of any of Apple’s chips by about 8.5% in testing. That means it absolutely flies along with apps launching near instantly and tasks just flying by. Compared with the previous generation M4 Mac mini, the new machine is about 25% faster in single core tasks, 50% faster in multicore tasks with graphics performance about 75% faster. That makes it a giant leap over older machines coming to the end of their useful lives. The machine is also power efficient and runs silently unless pushed to the limit, and even then is very quiet. Sustainability The Mac mini is made with 50% recycled materials. Apple breaks down the computer’s environmental impact in its report. Apple offers trade-in and free recycling schemes, including for non-Apple products. Price The Mac mini M6 costs from £899 (€1,049/$899/A$1,449) with 16GB of RAM and 256GB of storage. For comparison, the A18 Pro MacBook Neo costs from £699, the M5 MacBook Air starts at £1,299, the M4 iMac starts at £1,499 and the Mac Studio costs from £2,499. Verdict The Mac mini is a fantastic general computer squeezed into a tiny box that fits just about anywhere. The new M6 chip has buckets of power and performance for practically anything. If you know you need more graphics performance the M5 Pro chip is also available, but at a significant cost. The port selection is very good for a machine of this size, only lacking traditional USB-A ports of those commonly needed. With three Thunderbolt 4 (USB4) ports it’s easy to add a dock or hub if you really need more connectivity. The only downside is the RAMageddon-linked price hike that makes the Mac mini M6 slightly less of an instant recommendation than its predecessor. At £899 (€1,049/$899/A$1,449), it is still a lot of Mac for the money, just not the total bargain the M4 version used to be. Pros: very fast M6 chip, quiet and cool running, plenty of ports, headphones socket, 2.5GbE, wifi 7, Bluetooth 6 and Thread support. Cons: price hike, no expandable/replaceable storage or memory, no USB-A ports, no SD card slot, only 256GB of storage in base model, power button on base is difficult to reach.

title: Tuesday briefing: Inside the suspected bomb plot at RAF Fairford
summary: In today’s newsletter: New details suggest there is a counter-narrative to how events unfolded at the airbase used by the US
text: Good morning. Vehicles suspected of carrying explosives zipping across Britain, entirely unbeknownst to authorities, is a disconcerting prospect. Initially, it seemed precisely this had occurred in Gloucestershire early on Sunday. A major attack on RAF Fairford appeared to have been scuppered by “pure luck”, a local farmer said, after she noticed suspicious vans and masked men on an otherwise deserted country lane. Had she not tipped off police, the vigilant villager believes the five men arrested on terror offences would not have been apprehended. That account prompted questions about whether police and security services had been caught off guard. Bu new details emerging suggest there are competing, if not conflicting, versions of how events unfolded in the Cotswolds this weekend. So what exactly happened in the early hours of Sunday morning? In today’s First Edition, we’ll explore this, and some other unanswered questions, with the help of Guardian international security correspondent Jason Burke. Before that, this morning’s headlines. Five big stories Energy | Andy Burnham will take his first major step to putting Britain’s utility companies into public control when, at the Labour conference, he announces a new government-backed body to invest in the electricity grid. Immigration | Home secretary Shabana Mahmood has signalled she is considering watering down her plans to make it harder for foreign workers to claim permanent residence in the UK, amid growing demands for a U-turn from cabinet colleagues and unions. AI | Two of the “godfathers” of modern AI and senior executives at OpenAI and Anthropic have warned governments to prepare for an AI “intelligence explosion”, which they say could be the most consequential technological development in history. Petrol | The price of diesel on UK forecourts has hit an all-time high average of 199.18p a litre, as the conflict in the Middle East continues to drive the cost of fuel to record levels. Ebola | A senior member of the Democratic Republic of the Congo’s ruling party was beaten to death on Sunday after appearing on a radio programme to raise awareness about the Ebola outbreak, a party representative has said. In depth: What we do (and don’t) know about a suspected bomb plot in the Cotswolds In the early hours of Sunday, a farmer from the village of Whelford was travelling home from a party along quiet rural roads. She was about to drop off a friend, while her husband dozed in the passenger seat. Around 1am, however, she encountered three vans “parked in a really weird fan shape” blocking the path to her farm, close to RAF Fairford, an airbase operated by the US air force. Forced to turn around, she then described seeing “a large group of hooded and masked men” at a nearby junction, who quickly dispersed. After a failed attempt to contact the Ministry of Defence, she phoned the police at 1.36am and posted in the local residents’ WhatsApp group. Roughly 10 minutes later, armed officers were on the scene. Five men were arrested 300 metres from the base’s perimeter, first under the Explosives Act, and subsequently also on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act. All five – UK nationals from London aged between 23 and 25 – were released on bail yesterday. In interviews, the farmer, who has remained anonymous, reiterated her belief that her tip off “foiled whatever plans” were unfolding. “I am absolutely staggered that it was left to me, as a member of the public, to see and report this,” she said. That the high-security site was so exposed, and that the vans suspected of carrying explosives in its vicinity went totally unnoticed, has since raised questions. While thanking the farmer for her efforts, defence secretary Wes Streeting was quick to cast doubt on her assertions, hinting that UK security services were aware and that her account only offered “a partial picture”. Donald Trump has claimed the US and UK agencies worked together and had the five men “under view for a long time”, adding the suspects “were looking to do big damage to our fort, and working with the British worked out great”. The farmer acknowledged there had been “activity” by what she “assumed were plain-clothed police officers” in the area in recent days. Another local told the BBC that while walking their dog early on Saturday evening they were stopped by armed police and told to return home. Gloucestershire constabulary said they were first alerted to the suspicious vans at 12.45am on Sunday – almost an hour before the farmer’s 999 call. Counter-terror police have confirmed the three vehicles had been travelling overnight and been subject to extensive examination, with the support of military assets and forensic experts. It is now understood that the material found inside them was not viable explosives, but police have said the investigation is continuing. And then there’s the expeditious nature of the response: the speed with which armed officers and police helicopters arrived at a rural location in the middle of the night appears improbable. *** Questions around the arrests Police are still working to establish motive. Yesterday afternoon, the head of UK National Counter Terrorism Policing, Laurence Taylor, confirmed it may have been the work of proxies, or individuals working on behalf of a foreign state. On Monday night, US secretary of state Marco Rubio told Fox News that a foreign actor was involved in the suspected plot, but provided no evidence for his claims. Iran is the centre of speculation, having explicitly stated it considers RAF Fairford “a legitimate target”. Yesterday, the Iranian embassy said it “categorically rejects” any involvement. Used by the US military for decades, RAF Fairford’s two-mile long runway was specially constructed by the Americans to allow long-range bombers to take off and land. Fairford has played a significant role in Trump’s war on Iran; since former prime minister Keir Starmer allowed the US to use UK bases in its assaults, bomb-laden American B-52 and B-1 planes have regularly been spotted taking off. The airbase is one of only two available to the US in Europe that can facilitate these operations, after Spain, France, Italy and Switzerland rejected similar American requests. “Most observers and analysts would place Iran at the top of the list of potential suspects here,” Jason Burke, the Guardian’s international security correspondent, tells me, “though we have very little in the way of information to work on, so it’s entirely possible an altogether different scenario is at play.” As for the five suspects, their being British nationals is likely of little help when determining who may be behind the plot. “The Iranian modus operandi – borrowing a leaf from the Russian playbook – relies on using local hires,” Jason says. “Instead of deploying their own intelligence operatives, they recruit low-grade agents on the ground, some of whom may not fully realise what they are involved in.” *** Growing security concerns Since the US-Israel war on Iran began, a series of UK security incidents have been linked with Iran. Earlier this month, a man and a woman were arrested after raids on homes in north London on suspicion of assisting Iran’s foreign intelligence service. In March, four Jewish community ambulances were destroyed in an arson attack – counter-terror police explored the possible involvement of Iranian proxies, though aside from a reference to a “terrorist connection”, no mention of Iran was made by prosecutors in court when four men admitted responsibility. Similar suggestions have been made about tens of other antisemitic attacks in the UK and Europe – Iran’s embassy in the UK has denied any involvement. In April, Jason reported that, while direct proof of Iran’s involvement in incidents on UK soil remained elusive, the consensus among security officials was the attacks look to be part of a campaign of hybrid warfare launched by Tehran. Since then, Jason says, more evidence has emerged, in part due to the prosecution of 32-year-old Iraqi national Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi in a US court. “This case laid out in extraordinary detail how he, on behalf of the Iranian Revolutionary Guards Corps, commissioned, organised, and executed a series of attacks in Europe, including in Britain.” *** A significant escalation If Iran is proven to be responsible, an intended attack on this scale would represent a significant escalation. “It would be a major step up from targeting synagogues, Israeli embassies and US-owned banks,” says Jason, “given this is a piece of major military infrastructure in Britain.” With Andy Burnham leading a new government, it’s possible there may be a recalibration of UK foreign policy. He has said he’d be willing to deviate from Trump when necessary. Burnham’s foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, was reportedly central to attempts made during a national security meeting to dissuade then-PM Starmer from granting the US permission to use UK bases. But this would not significantly alter the risk of attacks, Jason says. “Iran’s targets are not necessarily chosen to directly punish a country; most experts believe they are selected to sow division in societies, distract policymakers, and divert resources.” For now, the investigation continues. What else we’ve been enjoying Palliative nurse Jane Turner makes a poignant point in this column: regardless of your belief about assisted dying, every side agrees on the need to radically improve end-of-life care in the UK. Charlie Lindlar, newsletters team I devoured Jess Cartner-Morley’s interview with Celia Birtwell, in which Birtwell talks about her friendship with David Hockney and her marriage to Ossie Clark: “He was spectacular, at the beginning,” says Birtwell – even if he did leave her the day after their wedding, pregnant, to honeymoon in Barbados on his own. Lucinda Everett, newsletters team Some vital tips in this piece by Sarah Phillips on the conversations every couple should have to keep a household running safely and happily – I’ve already pencilled in my first weekly “check-in”. Charlie All of the photographs in this gallery of the Porthcawl Elvis festival are wonderful. But my favourite has to be of Brian, AKA Smurf Elvis, who remixed his costume this year after a decade of attending the largest gathering of Elvis fans in Europe. Lucinda Rob Draper’s look back at how Arsenal’s hiring of Arsène Wenger changed football is brilliantly reported – make sure to share it with your nearest mustachioed graphic designer friend called Sam, Ed or Harry. Charlie Sport Nations League | Israeli football team captain Manor Solomon has hit out at Ireland after his team’s 3-o loss in a politically charged Nations League game, saying “They hate us and we don’t like them.” Rugby | In west Wales, fans want to know why the Scarlets and Ospreys, two teams who have won titles and turned out hundreds of Test players, are on the chopping block under the Welsh Rugby Union’s proposal to cut a club by 2028. Football | The Fifa president, Gianni Infantino, is poised to bow to demands from Uefa and Concacaf to distribute more money from its $6bn cash reserves to member associations. The front pages The Guardian splashes on “PM unveils electricity grid plan in push for public control of utilities”. The Mail leads with “PM to vow public control of energy, water and housing” and the Mirror looks at Burnham’s energy prices pledge with “Taking back power”. The Financial Times also reports “Burnham to outline plans for social care, welfare and ‘control’ of utilities.” The Times goes with “Labour split on prospect of ending triple lock”, the Telegraph has “Burnham signals end of triple lock”, while The i Paper says “End of UK state pension triple lock moves a step closer”. The Sun looks at the RAF terror drama, asking “Plot’s going on, PM?” Today in Focus The Pussy Riot activist turned Kremlin informer In August, Rita Flores, a Russian artist, activist and former member of the Pussy Riot collective, revealed in a video that she had been working as an informant for Russia’s FSB security service, a cooperation she only broke days after fleeing the country. Masha Alekhina, a founding member of Pussy Riot who was jailed for her support of the group and fled the country, tells Helen Pidd about why she does not feel angry at her former comrade in activism. Cartoon of the day | Ben Jennings The Upside A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad Our weekly series The pet I’ll never forget is always a source of joy. And the story of scruffy little terrier Dennis is no exception. Sophia Money-Coutts got Dennis in 2024 with her then-boyfriend, but within three months the couple had split. “I was distracted from my sadness by this small, bouncy, intensely disobedient dog,” says Money-Coutts, explaining that he raced after every squirrel, raided her bins, licked a man she was dating during an amorous moment, and “once farted on Jilly Cooper’s sofa”. Dennis had accompanied Money-Coutts, a journalist, to an interview with the animal-loving novelist, whose response was typically indulgent. “It doesn’t matter a bit, does it darling?” she recalls Cooper crying, clutching Dennis closer to her. “He can do whatever he likes.” Sign up here for a weekly roundup of The Upside, sent to you every Sunday Bored at work? And finally, the Guardian’s puzzles are here to keep you entertained throughout the day. Until tomorrow. Quick crossword Cryptic crossword Wordiply

title: Saving the Siamese crocodile: Cambodia moves to protect one of the world’s last wild populations
summary: Indigenous communities play crucial role, as ‘genetic bank’ area of wetland offers hope for critically endangered reptile
text: In the 1990s, conservationists in Cambodia feared the Siamese crocodile had disappeared for good. Fishing and hunting had devastated the species throughout the 20th century, leaving populations across its native south-east Asia on the brink of extinction. But in villages dotted among the wetlands of the remote Cardamom mountains, Indigenous Chorng communities still reported seeing them. Passing this knowledge to researchers surveying the area in 2000 led to an official recording of the species – and bolstered the mission to revive the population. “[The Chorng] share a spiritual relation between nature, sacred species and the forest,” says Sony Oum, the country director for Conservation International in Cambodia. “They believed that [the crocodiles] were there, and they helped the scientists and researchers to spot the sites.” Now, more than a quarter of a century on from the initial sighting, a 315-hectare (778-acre) wetland in Pursat province at the northern end of the Cardamom mountains has been formally declared a genetic conservation area to protect the habitat of one of the world’s last wild populations of Siamese crocodiles. The area, formally designated by Cambodia’s environment ministry on 22 July, will be home to at least 40 Siamese crocodiles that are thought to live there, making it a crucial site for a species still classed as critically endangered on the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) red list. Habitat destruction, poaching and cross-breeding with crocodiles kept on farms have left few genetically intact wild populations of Siamese crocodiles. With small, isolated groups in the wild vulnerable to inbreeding, conservationists say preserving genetic diversity can improve the animals’ ability to reproduce and withstand disease. Oum describes the site as a “genetic bank” for the species – a population that, if it remains healthy and expands, could one day help support crocodile recovery in Malaysia, Myanmar and Indonesia, where the reptile is thought to have become extinct. The new protection area is the latest stage in a conservation effort that has undertaken an extraordinary task. In 2011, the conservation charity Fauna & Flora International set up a Siamese crocodile breeding facility to boost numbers of genetically pure Siamese crocodiles for release into protected rivers. The charity has released 246 Siamese crocodiles into the wild since then, with 100 of those released since 2024. “Natural recovery of this species takes a long time,” says Vanny Lou, who manages the Siamese crocodile programme in Cambodia for Fauna & Flora. “This is one of our approaches to boost the species’ recovery from the brink of extinction.” “We have 648 individuals [at the breeding centre], including the parents,” he says. “Seventy-one of those are breeding parents – 54 female and 17 male.” Lou says it takes three to four years to get a baby crocodile to the appropriate age and size to release back into the wetlands. Before release, some crocodiles are fitted with acoustic tags, allowing conservationists to track where they move and target protection efforts. Local community wardens then help monitor the animals and their habitats. The wardens help the conservation organisations by identifying potential nesting sites, monitoring rivers, patrolling for illegal fishing and poaching, and reporting threats to government officials. And who better than the people who put the species back on the map – the Chorng. Oum says the fact that Chorng communities have lived alongside the crocodiles for generations and regard them as sacred guardians of the rivers and forests makes them the perfect people to assist the conservation. “The Indigenous people have a strong belief in the connection to nature,” says Oum. “They do some cropping and farming alongside the river, and when the Siamese crocodiles come to destroy the crops, [the Chorng] smile happily and feel blown away. They’ve been coexistent for a long time.” In 2024, five wild Siamese crocodile nests containing 106 eggs were found in the Cardamom mountains. Community wardens monitored them and saw 60 hatchlings emerge – the species’ largest recorded breeding event in the wild this century. “Without active involvement from the community as the frontline, our programme would not be successful,” says Lou. Sim Khmao, a Chorng community warden, says they are happy to do it. “They are not afraid of the crocodiles,” he says. “They understand them – because they have been here since our ancestors’ period.” Find more age of extinction coverage here, and follow biodiversity reporters Rebecca Ratcliffe, Phoebe Weston and Patrick Greenfield on the app for all the latest news and features

title: Why is South Korea so angry with Ukraine over two North Korean prisoners of war?
summary: Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s mention during a UN speech that Kyiv had sent two prisoners of war to South Korea has spiralled into a most unexpected crisis
text: South Korea and Ukraine are locked in an escalating diplomatic dispute over who agreed what regarding the circumstances of two prisoners of war captured fighting for Russia. Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, told the UN general assembly last week that his country had “sent two North Korean prisoners of war to the Republic of Korea”. Seoul had long said it would take the men. But rather than celebrate, on Monday South Korea summoned Ukraine’s most senior diplomat in Seoul and demanded an apology. Here’s a brief guide to what has happened, and why. Who are the PoWs and what has happened to them? Ukrainian forces captured the two men in Russia’s Kursk region in January 2025. They were among thousands of troops Pyongyang sent to fight for Moscow. Both men later said they wanted to go to South Korea, which regards North Koreans as its own citizens. In July, Zelenskyy and South Korea’s president, Lee Jae Myung, agreed to resolve the issue while respecting the soldiers’ “free will”. The captured pair reportedly arrived in South Korea via a third country earlier this month. North Koreans arriving in the South as defectors are usually questioned by the National Intelligence Service before being sent to a state resettlement centre, although sensitive cases can reportedly bypass the centre. Why is Seoul so angry? Seoul says Kyiv requested secrecy about the transfer, fearing domestic criticism for passing up the opportunity to exchange them for “a large number” of Ukrainian prisoners. South Korea says it agreed, citing the safety of the two men and their families as well as diplomatic and security considerations. After Zelenskyy revealed the transfer in his UN speech, Lee said on X that Ukraine had broken a “non-disclosure agreement” and that this was regrettable. Zelenskyy’s adviser Dmytro Lytvyn responded on Facebook that there had been no such agreement, prompting accusations from Lee’s critics that the president, whose approval rating has hit a low of 37.9%, had lied. Lee’s office called Kyiv’s statement “false” and said its conduct “seriously damages trust” between the two governments. On Monday, the foreign ministry summoned Ukraine’s chargé d’affaires, demanding an apology at governmental level. Was there actually an agreement? South Korea’s foreign ministry told Ukraine’s envoy there had been a “clear agreement”. Asked by the Guardian the same day whether anything had been put in writing, the ministry said only that the two sides “had decided to handle it confidentially”. Ukraine’s embassy in Seoul did not respond to a request for comment. Has North Korea said anything? No. South Korea’s unification ministry said it had “not identified any related developments so far” and would continue monitoring. North Korea has glorified soldiers who killed themselves rather than be captured. The transfer of two who survived and chose the South is “a fatal matter” for Pyongyang, says Cho Han-bum of the Korea Institute for National Unification. Having built a “heroic narrative” around its troops, the regime is unlikely to disclose the transfer domestically, he says. How big a diplomatic incident is this? After Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, South Korea condemned Moscow’s actions, joined western sanctions and, in July, pledged a $100m support package. But it has kept the war at arm’s length, refusing to send weapons directly to Kyiv, in line with its practice of not supplying lethal arms to countries at war. Before the war, Russia was one of South Korea’s biggest trading partners. Lee’s government is also keen to improve relations with Pyongyang. The row has turned that cautious support for Kyiv into open criticism, largely from Lee’s own camp. Kim Byung-joo, a Democratic party lawmaker, said there was “no reason or need” to support Ukraine and has urged the government to review its aid “immediately”.

title: Country diary: A tangle of butterflies and battle re-enactments | Paul Evans
summary: The Marches, Shropshire: On a day of micro-dramas past and present, we witness a Welsh victory over the English, just as it was 861 years ago
text: I’m telling the story from a pub in the bailey opposite the ruins of Oswestry Castle. There in 1165, Henry II, the Angevin (Anglo-Norman) king of England, gathered troops from the Marcher Lords to advance on an alliance of Welsh princes for control of the Marches. The previous Sunday, 861 years later, we went the same way as Henry’s army to Chirk Castle, Castell Y Waun a’r Ardd, to see a re-enactment of the Battle of Crogen. The present castle wasn’t built back then and the battle at Crogen was in the Ceiriog Valley below. Henry had sent woodsmen to raze woodland in the valley to remove the Welsh advantage, but he left one oak, Quercus petraea, at which Owain Gwynedd gathered his army. That tree became the Pontfadog oak – a giant, the oldest British oak, and survived as the National Tree of Wales, much loved and storied until it blew down in a storm in 2013 at an estimated 1,600 years old. I have a small fragment of it given to me by the longtime Guardian environment editor John Vidal. The battle re-enactment, with crashing swords and shields in the colours of Marcher lords and Welsh princes, fine horses and boinging arrows, was fun to watch with a running commentary giving a sense of what was happening and who was doing what. Histories vary about whether this was a great battle, isolated harassments or no fighting at all, but the outcome was the same: the Welsh won. The history of the Marches, like the traumatised, ghost-ridden ground itself, has been a contested space for centuries. It was fascinating to talk to people dedicated to making the past come to life for modern audiences. Over the castle garden wall, the past and present were weaving together in micro-dramas of moment. Two clouded yellow butterflies, Colias croceus, which had migrated here from north Africa or southern Europe, were flickering over herbaceous borders and lawns. Given the massive decline in insect populations, that pastoral scene had a spirit of resistance. And as if to demonstrate a mystical kind of heraldry and valour of a far more ancient territorial warrior, a small copper, Lycaena phlaeas, flourished his wings. • Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024, is available now at guardianbookshop.com

title: ‘Intimidatory’ far-right marches should not be allowed, says Angela Rayner
summary: The UK communities secretary decried protests by ‘men in black wearing face masks’ and those ‘whipping up hatred’ towards lifeboat volunteers
text: Far-right marches led by the self-styled “Danny Tommo” should not be treated like normal protests, the communities secretary, Angela Rayner, has said, calling the marches “intimidation” that should not be permitted. Rayner said the behaviour of some masked marchers – who have blocked roads and transport hubs – was not an acceptable form of protest. Daniel Thomas, the instigator of the marches over the past month, was arrested and charged last week after allegedly using a blade to slash an inflatable dinghy in the Channel while a rescue worker was onboard. Rayner said the marches were frightening local people. “When you see hundreds of predominantly men in black wearing black face masks shouting, going down the street, that is intimidating,” she said. “Whether you agree with the message or not, it’s intimidating.” She added: “It is not a protest. I’ve been on many protests myself when I was in my union days. We have music, we have banners, but we don’t wear balaclavas and shout divisive rhetoric down the street. “There’s a line, and I think organising to disrupt and cordon off areas to stop people going through public highways, this is all behaviour that is intimidatory and is not acceptable.” Thomas has recently brought dozens of nationalist protest groups together under the umbrella name of Patriot Platform. Masked and hooded anti-migrant activists from the movement have convened in English coastal towns and ports, in one case blocking traffic in and out of the port of Dover. Rayner said she was deeply concerned by the way social media was amplifying extreme voices – especially those targeting the RNLI. On the day that a 10-year-old child and two women died ⁠attempting to cross the Channel, Rayner said there needed to be more humanity about how migrants were described and treated when they attempted to cross in small boats. “How can we get to the point where we dehumanise like this,” she asked. “Yes, we can have an argument about the criminals putting people on these boats, the legitimacy of someone’s claim. But when you’ve got a human being at risk of death, do we let them drown? “That is ultimately what it comes down to. Yes, we politicians have a discussion about policies, about people we give asylum to, about how we stop boats. But [to] attack volunteers that save people from drowning? “These are volunteers. If there’s a risk to life at sea, an RNLI volunteer without any political persuasion at all or any ideology will go out and will save lives at sea. “To whip up hatred as if they are making a judgment on the value of these lives that they’re saving or not, and to put their faces up, identify them, to whip up online hatred towards volunteers whose sole job is to give up their time to save lives at sea. It’s not acceptable.”

title: ‘It keeps growing’: the tent camp that stands against Spain’s housing crisis
summary: An encampment is sprawling across Puerta del Sol plaza in central Madrid in protest against the ‘rentier economy’
text: Wielding a broom and dustpan, Marta García, 60, darted past the edges of tents, sweeping up bits of litter as she passed a poster that read: “What kind of times are these, when we need to defend the obvious?” On Saturday, as tens of thousands of people took to the streets of Madrid to protest against the country’s deepening housing crisis, the retired schoolteacher was among a small group who had sought to take the protest one step further. “At first we were 10 tents,” she said, gesturing to the sprawling encampment set up in the central Puerta del Sol plaza behind her. “Now, we’re more than 300 tents, and it keeps growing.” Days earlier, many across Spain had watched in shock as news channels showed Maricarmen Abascal, an 87-year-old woman with a disability, being evicted from the home where she had lived for seven decades. The shock soon gave way to anger as the octogenarian was shown being brought out of her home on a stretcher, flanked by protesters on one side and police officers on the other. Housing campaigners seized on the moment. “The whole country has seen that housing speculation has no mercy on anyone,” said Alicia del Río of the Madrid Tenants’ Union. “We’re not sad, we’re angry. And we’re not going to stop until we change things.” Abascal’s lawyers reportedly reached a deal for her to return home on Monday evening. “If this agreement we have reached is signed, it will obviously be a better and happier outcome for everyone,” her lawyer, Beatriz Duro, told reporters, saying it could “help to change the paradigm when it comes to housing in general”. At the encampment earlier on Monday, many described the days of nationwide protests and the encampment as a turning point in a movement that had long simmered as rents rose by 80% within a decade, while the cost of homes climbed by 63%. “We need stability,” said David Iglesias, 25, as he described how the ever-soaring prices had forced people to put their lives on hold to try to keep a roof over their heads. “People who want to have children should be able to do so, even if they are renting. People who dream of becoming musicians or barbers should have the chance to do so and not have to worry that they need to work, work, work to pay for housing,” he said. “It’s an endless loop that is undermining the mental health of young people.” As he spoke, a large banner flapped nearby, reading: “You can speculate on watches, jewels, cryptobros and Ferraris. But not on our fucking homes.” The swelling encampment had prompted a raft of comparisons to 2011, when the Indignados, or 15M movement, began with a month-long occupation of the same Madrid plaza before snowballing into a force that had reshaped Spanish politics. Iglesias, however, brushed off the similarity. “That was about a general demand for change,” he said. “But we have a goal, and if this goal isn’t met by Tuesday, we’ll have to take action somehow.” It was a nod to the informal camp slogan, launched by housing campaigners and oft-repeated by protesters in recent days: “Either the rentier economy falls, or the government does.” As Spain’s government gears up for its weekly Tuesday meeting, campaigners have put forward a list of demands, from measures to halt evictions to the regulation of short-term and room rentals, making it clear that this is being seen as a make-or-break moment. On Sunday, Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, said his government was “working around the clock to introduce a royal decree on housing on Tuesday”. The protests have put the Socialist leader in a complicated spot; while his coalition government includes leftwing forces who have long pushed for change, Spain’s fractured parliament means his chances are slim of attracting support for measures that could bring about real change. Still, the momentum has continued to grow across the country, fuelled by the campaigners who occupied the offices of Madrid’s social housing agency on Monday to those in Barcelona who began the day by blocking off major thoroughfares. “Today cannot be a day like all others,” said Enric Aragonès of the Barcelona Tenants’ union, ahead of a protest planned for Tuesday evening in the city. “There are only 24 hours left until we find out whether the government will approve a decree that is a sham or genuine.” In Madrid, the calls for change had attracted a diverse group, including Oscar-winning film director Pedro Almodóvar, who visited on Sunday to voice his support for the protesters. “The housing problem is paralysing Spanish life,” he told broadcaster RTVE. Sitting cross-legged in a tent and knitting to pass the time, Guillermo Esteve said he was part of a group of vegans who had decided to show their support by joining the encampment. “We’re a group of people who believe we can do things better,” he said, describing his hope that this would be part of a sweeping change that would start with the real estate sector, then address the precarity of the labour market and eventually tackle production systems. “We want laws that give us hope, not what we have now.” The sentiment was echoed by García, the retired schoolteacher. “This camp is an example of how people still believe that things can change,” she said. “I have my life sorted out; I have a house. But I have two daughters who are sharing bedrooms because they have no other choice. So I can’t just sit around doing nothing.” This was how she had ended up in the heart of Madrid on a Monday afternoon, sweeping the city’s central plaza, she added with a laugh. “Look, if I didn’t think this was going to amount to anything, I would just stay home and cry,” she said. “But I have to stay helpful.” With contribution from Stephen Burgen in Barcelona
