title: Vietnamese government accused of abducting human rights activists
summary: Detained anti-human trafficking campaigners include Tran Hiep, a Vietnamese Australian, not heard from since 18 September
text: Vietnamese authorities have detained three activists, including a Norwegian and an Australian, on what have been described as “fabricated” charges. The Vietnamese government said the three confessed to being members of Viet Tan – a pro-democracy organisation – which it describes as a terrorist group. In a statement, Viet Tan said it “strongly condemns the abduction of two of its members in Cambodia and the fabricated charges issued by the Vietnamese communist authorities to cover up an act of transnational repression”. It is not clear if the third person is a Viet Tan member as well. Australia’s Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade said it was “making urgent inquiries with Vietnamese authorities to confirm reports that an Australian citizen has been detained” and was giving the family consular assistance. Tran Hiep, a 50-year-old Vietnamese Australian democracy campaigner, was due to return to Bangkok, Thailand, to reunite with his wife, Chloe Dang, after a short trip to Phnom Penh, Cambodia, to meet with human rights defenders. Earlier, his wife implored the federal government to find him and bring him home after he failed to board his flight. He had not communicated with his wife since 18 September, leaving her worried for his safety. “My family and I are really worried about his safety, and we just only want to know where he is and what happened to him,” Dang said from Bangkok airport before boarding a flight to Melbourne. “My husband deserves protection, and I really hope the Australian government will continue to put pressure on Cambodia to do an investigation to find out where he is right now.” Anthony Albanese said the government was providing consular assistance. “That’s what Australian governments do for our citizens. And we’ll continue to engage directly with the family,” the Australian prime minister said. Hiep, a freelance IT professional who founded the Australian Alliance to Combat Human Trafficking, was travelling with another human rights activist Nguyen Duc Thuan, who is also Vietnamese and holds a Norwegian passport. The pair travelled to Cambodia to meet with dissident Vietnamese activists for training. According to a Vietnamese government statement, they were arrested entering Vietnam from the Cambodian border along with a third person, Thai Cong Truong Son. The statement describes the three Vietnamese-born people as illegal immigrants and says they will be investigated for alleged terrorism and forging identity documents. Viet Tan says it aims to “overcome dictatorship and build the foundation for a sustainable democracy”, and that it was “committed to peaceful, nonviolent struggle”. “We are convinced that nonviolent means are most effective for generating maximum civic participation,” the organisation said on its website. Human Rights Watch has previously described Viet Tan as “an opposition political party … which operates openly and lawfully in many countries including Australia, but which Hanoi arbitrarily labels ‘terrorist’”. Vietnam in recent years has ramped up its crackdown on dissidents, with more than 55 activists arrested under broad criminal laws in 2025. On 18 September, Human Rights Watch said more than 160 political prisoners were currently locked up in Vietnam, and that activists faced “police harassment, intimidation, surveillance, and interrogation on a daily basis”. Viet Tan urged the Norwegian and Australian authorities to ask for access to the Hiep and Thuan, to “ensure their wellbeing and access to needed medication”. It said the pair had “no intention” of entering Vietnam and the claim they had done so illegally was a “blatant fabrication” to cover up their abduction. “Viet Tan is particularly concerned that To Lam’s police state is using its security apparatus to pursue and repress activists and foreign nationals even beyond Vietnam’s borders,” it said. “Meeting with, exchanging ideas with, and supporting human rights defenders, democracy activists, and civil society is a peaceful form of advocacy to advance freedom, democracy, and human rights in Vietnam.” Civil society groups and United Nations human rights experts have repeatedly warned of growing cooperation between Vietnamese authorities and neighbouring governments targeting advocates. Viet Tan, a pro-democracy diaspora political party, had earlier described the pair’s disappearance as concerning given previous cases involving Vietnamese dissidents vanishing in neighbouring countries and subsequently appearing in custody in Vietnam. “Their disappearance is not an ordinary ‘missing person’ incident. Both men are longtime human rights advocates and Viet Tan members,” the organisation said. Asia Human Rights & Labour Advocates director Phil Robertson labelled it an “unacceptable outrage” and that countries like Australia “continuing business as usual” was not acceptable. “[It] demonstrates yet again that Hanoi is arguably the most vicious and pernicious practitioner of transnational repression today in Southeast Asia,” he said. Dang, 36, said fretting over her husband’s whereabouts had taken a psychological toll. “It’s been 11 days and I’m really in the dark,” she said, choking back tears. “I don’t know where he is and how he’s doing – it’s driving me crazy. “Everything is really uncertain.” The families of the missing men have filed an appeal with the UN working group on enforced or involuntary disappearances.

title: ‘Children are dying’: Fiji hopes declaring an HIV emergency will help it tackle crisis
summary: One in 60 adults Fiji lives with HIV but a recent emergency declaration may help address key issues such as syringe sharing
text: On a recent Friday night, Dr Kesaia Tuidraki’s medical team parked its mobile clinic outside McDonald’s in downtown Suva, Fiji, and grabbed any kid they could to be tested for HIV. Of the 97 people screened, mostly teenagers – some on their way to get a burger, others to buy drugs – one in six tested positive. “Children are suffering, children are dying, and if that doesn’t move you I don’t know what will,” Tuidraki, country director of Medical Services Pacific, tells the Guardian. Fijian authorities this month called a national health emergency to deal with surging HIV cases, with an estimated one in 60 adults now living with the virus. It comes as new infections surge, with 2,016 new cases diagnosed in 2025 – rising by 27% in a year, and representing a 12-fold increase since 2010, according to UNAids. In a close-knit island nation of about 930,000 people, an estimated 9,100 are now living with the virus. But only a fraction of those are tested and access treatment, prompting the government to scale up its pandemic announcement – first made in February 2025 – and mobilise urgent measures to prevent its spread. Dr Jason Mitchell, the head of Fiji’s HIV epidemic response, said it could take between five and 10 years to get a handle on the virus, and in the meantime he would expect numbers to rise. Critics say moves to stem the spread of a disease that is being driven by cases in the young, with new diagnoses highest in those aged between 15 and 34, has been too slow. The crisis is complex and inextricably linked to the drug epidemic – more than 42% of new cases in 2025 were due to sharing contaminated needles or equipment. Health advocates and social workers say primary school-age children are among those injecting themselves and friends are using the same contaminated needle, a problem raised by advocates as far back as 2019. “I know these young boys, they ask me for syringes,” injecting drug user Rochelle*, who is living with HIV, tells the Guardian. “Whenever I have them I give them out. Someone has to give them, they’re already accessing the drugs.” Rochelle, 38, says she tries to tell the boys not to share. Sometimes the kids listen – but not always. Under current law, giving out syringes is technically considered aiding and abetting drug use. A concern among some politicians and medical professionals is that providing needles would encourage drug use – despite evidence from UNAids that this is not the case –and advocates are urging the government to let them distribute thousands of needles and syringes sitting untouched in a Suva warehouse. “It’s really sad, honestly. We can’t wait any more, there are boxes and boxes already here,” Tuidraki says. Mitchell says he expects a change to the HIV Act to be passed within the next two weeks, allowing public health workers to distribute needles. He adds that the government has been “cautious” in announcing the emergency, which his unit had been asking for since June. Those leading the response say increased powers arising from the emergency declaration will help to quell the rapid spread of HIV, including to vulnerable populations like mothers and babies, at an estimated extra cost of $23m FJD (US$10.2m) a year. “The immediate crisis right now is the spread of HIV, which is why the needle and syringe programme is critical,” UNAids, the UN agency that fights HIV and Aids, regional director Eamonn Murphy said. ‘People are scared’ The epidemic is complex but heavily linked to methamphetamine use. Fiji is a drug-running hub in the Pacific for methamphetamine bound for Australian and New Zealand markets, but use escalated during Covid when borders were closed and it began circulating domestically. While Fijians want the crisis addressed, there has also been a backlash. Only 39% of those living with HIV in Fiji know their status, according to UNAids, and some of those spoken to by the Guardian continued to live in denial or refuse testing. “There are people blaming the [queer] community, blaming women as irresponsible people, there’s a lot of cyberbullying. Minorities are being attacked online,” Mark Shaheel Lal, an advocate who lives with HIV, says. “Now it’s more like a scandal and people are scared.” UNAids is also concerned about the spread of the virus to the Pacific, with rising cases seen in Solomon Islands and Papua New Guinea. In November, Australia’s minister for foreign affairs, Penny Wong, announced A$48m for Pacific countries to fight HIV/Aids, while New Zealand committed NZ$4.2m to Fiji in July. The introduction of PreP – or pre-exposure prophylaxis – an HIV prevention drug, would be a “gamechanger,” says Mitchell, who adds that one injection could be offered every six months for those at higher risk. It would be especially important for women who are not able to push for safe sex practices with partners. Two in every 100 pregnant women now have HIV. “You can’t hide a bottle of pills, but you can get an injection,” says Michell. For now, women are already being offered three HIV tests during pregnancy and sexual reproductive hubs are operating at the three main hospitals. ________ “There’s no miracles in the HIV response, it does not happen overnight. Unfortunately people are thinking this is like Covid, it’s very much not,” Mitchell says. His team plans to open new clinics, integrate testing and treatment into GP services, work on harm reduction, and hire at least 100 more staff. He says that the increase in cases means more people are getting tested, which is a positive. “Burnout is a major concern – we didn’t just start working yesterday, we’ve been working for 21 months. It’s difficult, and the difficulty is that all of it is preventable. It should not be happening.” But in many areas, including rural localities, access to treatment continues to lag. Drug Free World Fiji founder and campaigner Kalesi Volatabu is still haunted by the 15-year-old girl she met when she started pushing for a safe needle programme six years ago. A drug mule who smuggled methamphetamine to New Zealand and Australia, she had names for the three main veins on the back of her hand; breakfast, lunch, and dinner. “We had no idea of the severity, of the depth of the drug trade in this country, of the HIV crisis. Even I was naive, at the beginning, and everything was unreported for the longest time. We failed to act then – will we now?” *Name has been changed

title: Tennessee to execute a woman for first time in 200 years after governor denies clemency
summary: Lawyers for Christa Pike, 50, convicted of killing classmate in Knoxville in 1995, ask supreme court to grant stay
text: Christa Pike, a woman who was convicted of murder 30 years ago, is set to be put to death on Wednesday after her request for clemency was denied by Tennessee’s governor, Bill Lee, on Monday. If the execution goes through, she will be the first woman executed in the state in 200 years. Pike, who is now 50, was 18 when she and her boyfriend, who was 17 at the time, killed 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, one of their classmates at Knoxville Job Corps in 1995. The case received widespread attention because of the brutality of the killing, the ages of the people involved, and because a satanic symbol was carved into the victim’s body. Pike was convicted of first-degree murder the following year and sentenced to death, making her the youngest woman to be put on death row in modern US history. Since her sentence, her history as a victim of sexual abuse and mental health challenges has come to light. As her execution date approached, civil rights groups like the ACLU and Amnesty International have called on the public to reach out to the governor’s office to ask that he take Pike off death row. But Lee declined to halt her execution. “After deliberate consideration of Christa Gail Pike’s request for clemency and after a thorough review of the case, I am upholding the sentence of the State of Tennessee and do not plan to intervene,” he said in a statement. In response to Lee’s decision, Pike’s attorneys said that they were “deeply saddened and heartbroken” by the governor’s decision and that through this choice the state was dismissing decades of research about the amount of responsibility an 18-year-old – especially one with severe trauma – should bear for their criminal actions. “Throughout her childhood, Christa was failed by people and institutions that should have shown her care and meaningful intervention,” Pike’s attorneys said in a statement. “The 18-year-old girl suffering from severe mental illness and near-debilitating trauma no longer exists. Christa is a 50-year-old remorseful woman who understands her actions, receives proper treatment for her mental illness, and provides for and guides fellow incarcerated women.” Pike’s attorneys have also asked the supreme court to stay the execution. Assistant federal defender Stephen Ferrell said Pike was sexually abused starting from when she was a toddler and that she was raped at 11 and 17. He said Pike’s lawyers at the penalty phase of her trial did not present the jury with what he said was critical information about her past or argue that her age should be a consideration. Pike, who has never denied her role in Slemmer’s killing, was later diagnosed with bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder. “I was a mentally ill 18-year-old kid. It took me numerous years to even realize the gravity of what I’d done. Even more to accept how many lives I affected. I took the life of someone’s child, sister, friend. It sickens me now to think I had the ability to commit such a crime,” Pike said in a statement included in her clemency petition. Ferrell said more was known today about adolescent brain development and that Pike’s death sentence was an outlier. He noted that Pike’s boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, who was 17 at the time, was sentenced to life with the possibility of parole because of his age. He was denied parole last year. A third teen admitted to being an accessory and received probation. May Martinez, Slemmer’s mother, told the Associated press that her daughter volunteered with the Special Olympics, loved roller skating and wanted to pursue a career in computers. “She was easygoing. She was a computer geek to begin with. She and my husband would build and tear apart the computers constantly,” Martinez told the outlet. “She trusted everybody, and that was her downfall.” The last woman executed in Tennessee was in 1820, according to the Death Penalty Information Center. Martin Eve, charged with being an accessory to murder, was executed by hanging. Most recently, Missouri in 2023 executed Amber McLaughlin, a transgender woman, for a 2003 killing, in what is believed to be the first execution of a transgender woman in the US. In 2021, the federal government executed Lisa Montgomery, marking the first time in nearly seven decades that the US government has put a female inmate to death. Georgia executed a woman in 2015.

title: Ukraine war briefing: Putin orders army expansion as Zelenskyy says more North Koreans to be deployed in Russia
summary: Putin’s order comes as both Russian and Ukrainian forces suffer mounting casualties. What we know on day 1,679
text: Russian president Vladimir Putin has ordered ⁠an increase in the size ⁠of the army to 1.55 ⁠million active ‌servicemen, according ‌to a ‌presidential decree on Monday. The order comes as both Russia and Ukraine suffer mounting casualties in the more than four-and-a-half-year Ukraine war. The expansion, which follows a similar increase ordered in August, ‌will put the size of Russia’s armed forces at ⁠2,441,630. Of those are 1,550,000 active servicemen, an increase of 15,500. Ukrainian president ⁠Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on X on ‌Monday ‌there were now more than 8,000 ‌North Korean troops on ⁠Russian territory and preparations were under way to ‌deploy another 10,000 troops. Putin and North Korean leader Kim Jong-un confirmed for the first time last year that North Korea had sent troops to fight for Russia in the war with Ukraine, with both leaders describing the soldiers as “heroes”. Citing “new data” on the deployment of North Korean troops to Russia, ⁠Zelenskyy said they were “being selected for training and subsequent deployment to Russia”. North Korea has sent an estimated 14,000 to 15,000 ⁠troops to support Russia’s war in Ukraine since 2024, according to Ukrainian and South Korean estimates, with most deployed in the Kursk region to help repel a ‌Ukrainian incursion. Explosions ⁠were heard in the Ukrainian capital of ⁠Kyiv early ⁠on Tuesday, a Reuters witness said, as Russia ⁠continues its near-daily attacks. Missile ‌debris fell in the ‌courtyard of a residential building, among other damage, and a non-residential building caught fire in another ‌part of the city, Kyiv mayor Vitali Klitschko said on Telegram. On Monday, Zelenskyy said nine ⁠people had been killed and more than 80 injured in Russian drone strikes throughout ‌the country, including in Kyiv. Pope Leo urged Russia and ⁠Ukraine to sit down and discuss how to end their war, hours after ⁠he had urged ⁠European leaders seeking to end conflicts to make concessions to achieve peace. Addressing a press conference aboard his flight to Rome on Monday after ‌a four-day trip ‌to France, Leo said the 1.4-billion-member Catholic church had an obligation ‌to call for peace and respect of human life. “The Church has a responsibility to promote these values, continually inviting leaders – from Russia and Ukraine, as well as other countries – to come together, sit down, engage ‌in dialogue,” the pope said. Nato’s top military commander said Russia’s sabotage campaign in Europe was failing to put countries off supporting Ukraine. “State-directed sabotage is growing increasingly brazen,” US general Alexus Grynkewich told a committee of EU lawmakers on Monday. Nato’s supreme allied commander for Europe cited recent incidents including the discovery of an explosive-laden drone at a German airport and a Russian naval ship firing flares at a Danish helicopter. “These are clear examples of attempts to instil fear and fracture our unified support to Ukraine. It isn’t working,” he said. Ukraine will postpone some spending commitments, including reconstruction work, because of delays in receiving aid from its foreign backers, Ukraine’s prime minister said. The government would carry out these projects eventually, “but for now, all resources must be directed toward critical areas”, Sergiy Koretsky said on Telegram on Monday. Russia’s offensive has battered Ukraine’s economy, causing billions of dollars in destruction and punching a huge hole in its neighbour’s finances. Putin has ordered the Russian assets of German retailer Metro AG to be placed under temporary administration, amid Russian-German tensions over the Ukraine war. The order, posted on Monday on the government website, did not state a reason. The step follows similar steps against the Russia businesses of global food company Nestlé and French retailer Auchan under a 2023 decree aimed at businesses associated with “unfriendly countries”. Temporary administration has led to local owners taking over the Russia businesses of French dairy concern Danone and Danish brewer Carlsberg at knockdown prices. A Russian jet-powered drone struck a Ukrainian village near the Polish border earlier on Monday, damaging a border checkpoint, a regional Ukrainian official said. The official did not give details about the nature of the checkpoint or extent of damage from the blast. Russia has launched multiple attacks near Ukraine’s border with Poland in recent weeks, drawing condemnation from Warsaw and its European allies.

text: A married couple in their 70s have been arrested for allegedly shooting and killing their son-in-law, a New York Times engineer, in broad daylight at a suburban Bay Area park. A police officer found Jonathan McKinsey, 40, lying on the ground with multiple gunshot wounds in a park in Dublin, California, a small city about 35 miles (56.3km) east of San Francisco. He had been the head of engineering for the New York Times’s games department for nearly four years, according to his LinkedIn page. Witnesses told police that the suspected shooters, identified as Shouyong Zhang and Shili Chen, both 77, were still in the area. Witnesses also told CBS News that the suspects were both wearing masks, and each took a turn shooting the victim. An arraignment is scheduled for Wednesday, the San Francisco Chronicle reported. Police have not indicated a motive for the shooting. Court records cited in local media reports show McKinsey and his wife had been engaged in a legal battle over child custody and allegations of domestic and child abuse. title: Investigation of alleged gang-rape at Cornell University fraternity house reopened
summary: Outrage over treatment of alleged offenders, members of Chi Phi fraternity, has grown since lawsuit was made public
text: Prosecutors in New York said on Monday that they have reopened an investigation into the alleged gang-rape of a student at Cornell University after an outcry over “leniency” shown to seven fraternity members named as the perpetrators. According to lawyers for the student, who filed a civil lawsuit against the university and her alleged attackers earlier in September, only two members of the Chi Phi fraternity were expelled after the October 2024 incident, in which she said she was drugged and repeatedly raped over the course of seven hours. None of the seven were arrested, they said, and the others were made to write essays, attend workshops or serve short suspensions. On Monday, Matthew Van Houten, the Tompkins county district attorney, said his office was looking again at the case, after the woman, who was 20 at the time of the alleged assault, presented allegations in her lawsuit that were “dramatically different” from the statement she gave to police two years ago. Later on Monday, Van Houten released a fuller statement defending his office’s past decision to not seek charges. “While I generally refrain from commenting publicly on criminal investigations, the community outrage stemming from the incomplete news and social media coverage requires that I provide an answer to why the investigation resulted in a lack of criminal charges,” he said. He went on to say: “Jane Doe’s sworn statement in November of 2024 did not allege that she was drugged against her will or gang raped. On the contrary, Jane Doe’s statement described her participation in drug use and sexual conduct as voluntary, conscious, and consensual. My office obviously did not and could not have based our November 2024 decision on the allegations in a civil lawsuit that would not be filed until nearly two years later. “Furthermore, I have never been contacted by Jane Doe’s attorneys. Not to inform me the original statement was inaccurate and not to ask me to reconsider our decision. Rather, I reached out to Jane Doe’s attorneys after the lawsuit was filed to understand the discrepancy between the original statement and the lawsuit’s allegations and the proper path forward in light of the lawsuit’s allegations,” Van Houten continued. The district attorney said that he has asked a senior female prosecutor to prepare a case for a grand jury, adding that he “recogniz[es] that the process of healing from trauma is personal and different for every human”. “Seeking justice sometimes requires us to reconsider or reopen cases when we are provided with additional evidence,” he said. Van Houten also released a summary of a “six-page, single-spaced, typewritten statement” that Doe provided to the Cornell University police department in November 2024. According to the summary, Doe told police that she agreed to engage in sexual activity with two Chi Phi members, “due to how attracted [she] was to [Male Number 1 ] on top of [her] drunken curiousness”. “When she learned that Male Number 2 would be the third participant, Jane Doe ‘remembered being excited because [she] thought that [Male Number 1 and Male Number 2] wanting to have a threesome meant that they were gay’,” the summary said. The summary added that another man entered the room and shook Doe’s hand. “When [Jane Doe] made contact with [Male Number 3’s] hand, [Male Number 3] pulled [Jane Doe] into him and [they] began making out. While [Male Number 3] was kissing [her], [Male Number 2] began groping [her]. Eventually, ‘[Male Number 2, Male Number 3, and Jane Doe] would end up on the bed next to where [Male Number 1] was sleeping and [they] began to have a threesome,’” according to the summary, which said that four men later entered the room. “Jane Doe had difficulty remembering parts of what happened next. She remembered ‘[Male Number 7] said something very rude and mean to [her].’ Male Number 7 apologized and ‘grabbed [her] face and started kissing [her]’. Jane Doe ‘quickly backed away to stop [Male Number 7] from kissing [her]’,” the summary said. It went on to say that some of the Chi Phi members started to compliment Doe’s looks and asked if they could take drugs off her body. “Jane Doe responded, ‘Sure.’ While the men were doing drugs off of her body, ‘[Male Number 3] and [another male] entered the room and said something like, ‘Ok we’re shutting down whatever the f*** this is,’” the summary added. Outrage over the treatment of the alleged offenders has grown since the lawsuit was made public. The woman, who quit the university afterwards, said she went to visit a friend at the Chi Phi frat house in an already intoxicated state. “When plaintiff arrived at Xi chapter’s fraternity house, plaintiff was visibly intoxicated as she had consumed about 10 standard drinks within the past 3 hours,” Doe’s lawsuit said. According to the lawsuit, one of the defendants “pulled [her] off to a quieter area and propositioned her with having a threesome with her and another one of his fraternity brothers. In her drunken state, plaintiff was incapable of consenting to this proposition.” The lawsuit then alleges that two men “pressured plaintiff into snorting the alleged Ketamine with them, a drug she had never done before. During this time, [the two men] also plied plaintiff with marijuana and ‘Jamaican Liquor’ believed to be some type of high-proof rum.” While they sexually assaulted her, she alleges, a message was sent to a frat house Snapchat group called Chi Phi Actives that stated there was “free pussy upstairs”. At least five other frat members showed up and joined in, she said, and her ordeal lasted until about 5.45am “and plaintiff lost consciousness”, the lawsuit said. It also alleges that Doe was “slapped” multiple times and that her “phone was on the other side of the room and she felt as if there was no way for her to escape this room full of predatory, fraternity men”. “When plaintiff awoke later that day, on October 20, 2024, plaintiff returned to her residence within the Alpha Beta chapter sorority house. At this point, plaintiff was in a state of shock. At her residence, plaintiff noticed a large bruise that had formed on her buttocks and took pre-emptive medication for a urinary tract infection,” the lawsuit said. She made a report to campus police about three weeks later. Cornell’s vice-president for university relations, Kyle Kimball, issued a statement on 21 September calling the allegations “deeply disturbing”. Kimball’s statement claimed the Ivy League institution’s offices of civil rights, student conduct and community standards carried out a number of inquiries at the time. Following the district attorney’s decision to reopen the case on Monday, Kimball said: “Cornell University supports the decision of the Tompkins County District Attorney (DA) to provide an opportunity for the victim’s story in the 2024 Chi Phi fraternity sexual assault case to be heard by a criminal grand jury.” Kimball added that the “involved fraternity chapter was closed in 2024 and remains barred from campus”. An attorney for the student told CBS News that none of the alleged perpetrators faced legal consequences for their conduct, and nobody in the frat house that saw the message did anything to stop the rapes from taking place. “Not one of these guys was arrested,” said the lawyer, Thomas Giuffra. “Not one. That I can tell you for a fact. “There were so many people that could have prevented it and they didn’t. I’ve never seen anything like it.” Giuffra also countered the statement of Van Houten, the Tompkins district attorney, which lays out what he said the alleged victim stated in her original police complaint from November 2024. “She never says that she was drugged without her knowledge,” Van Houten said. “She admits to taking drugs and alcohol voluntarily and with knowledge. She does not allege that she was forced to engage in any acts. She does not say that she was physically helpless or unconscious or incapacitated at any point during the time at the fraternity house.” Giuffra told ABC News that neither the district attorney or Cornell police ever followed up with his client. “In my experience, speaking with an abuse survivor requires delicacy, understanding and specialized training,” he said. “An average university police officer would not have these skills. It would be the role of a specially trained detective or district attorney. However, Ms Doe was never contacted by anybody with those skills.” Giuffra also said: “My client went to the Cornell University police because a crime was committed. It was the obligation of the police to investigate the complaints. They were given the group chat inviting the members of the fraternity to rape my client. “This was a critical piece of evidence supporting that a crime had occurred. Despite this there was no follow-up with Ms Doe either by the Cornell police or the Tompkins county district attorney,” he added. Named defendants in the lawsuit are Matthew Ingalls, Johnathan Newell, Winston Lee, Gillio Lopes, Diego Sarabia, Scott Norris and Scott Kretzschmar. Two of those defendants denied the allegations in statements to ABC News. “At bottom, Scott never sexually assaulted or even touched the plaintiff in any way,” Jeremy Saland, an attorney for Kretzschmar, said. “Period.” Norris denied engaging in sexual activity or drug use – but acknowledged he sent a message that was included in the complaint. “I thoughtlessly engaged in Snapchat and briefly stopped in the room where misconduct happened but not when it happened,” he said. On Sunday, the Academy Award-nominated actor Florence Pugh posted a lengthy statement on Instagram about Giuffra’s client, praising the “unbelievably powerful” victim and her “strong will”. “This is really the moment where we need our men to be as horrified and as sickened as us,” Pugh wrote. “You need to be leading conversations about how we change the allowance and complicity of this behaviour as much as we are.” Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organizations. In the US, Rainn offers support on 800-656-4673. In the UK, Rape Crisis offers support on 0808 500 2222. In Australia, support is available at 1800Respect (1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found at ibiblio.org/rcip/internl.html

title: Five UK nationals arrested near RAF Fairford released on bail
summary: Police say alleged offences could have been committed ‘knowingly or unknowingly’ on behalf of a foreign state
text: Five men arrested over a suspected bomb plot at RAF Fairford have been released on bail as police investigate why they were so close to the airbase in three vans with suspicious material in the back. The five suspects were revealed to be British men, all in their 20s and from London. They had been arrested in the Gloucestershire countryside early on Sunday morning on suspicion of explosives offences and preparing an act of terrorism, with an Iranian link a key line of inquiry. Their release on police bail suggests detectives believe it is unlikely they were on the brink of a mass casualty attack by exploding a bomb close to the base, sources said. An Iranian link is still under investigation, as is whether any of the five were paid to gather in the village of Whelford, two miles from RAF Fairford. On Monday, Donald Trump expressed surprise that the suspects had been bailed. The US president said: “I would not have released them.” The prime minister, Andy Burnham, called a meeting of the government’s crisis committee Cobra over the events and Iran’s possible role. An initial examination of the vans led police to suspect they carried explosive materials, with assessments made as to whether they were viable improvised explosive devices. After the suspects’ release it emerged that no explosive material had been found. The head of UK counter-terrorism policing, the assistant commissioner Laurence Taylor, said the release of the men on bail did not mean the investigation was over and that they were subject to “stringent conditions”. He said: “I know there is significant interest in whether the current geopolitical context has a bearing on this incident. At counter-terrorism policing we are working within this context every day, and at this stage we are keeping an open mind in this investigation. “We have, as you would expect, ensured that our protective security advice and posture remain commensurate to the threat. But be assured, we are considering this from every possible angle. Including, that this may be activity committed by proxies, or individuals either knowingly or unknowingly working on behalf of a foreign state.” Iran is suspected of using proxies in the UK, in incidents ranging from alleged arson attacks against Jewish targets to men flying a basic drone near the Israeli embassy. Taylor said: “Often this threat becomes visible to us as criminal activity, often at a small scale and committed by individuals whose primary aim is not terrorism but a quick financial gain. It can be harder to spot, and to that end I would ask the public to remain vigilant and report anything suspicious to police.” Trump claimed on Sunday that the men “were looking to do big damage” at the base, used by the US air force, which was taken as revealing a serious terror plot. Taylor said: “I can confirm that following extensive interviews and inquiries, the five men who were arrested are being released on police bail this afternoon. They absolutely remain under investigation as we explore multiple lines of inquiry.” Police said the five men were all from London, one aged 23, three aged 24, and one aged 25. They were arrested after a farmer driving home from a party spotted them. She said she believed they were wearing balaclavas and they ran away when her headlights illuminated them. She then called the police. Trump also suggested the plot was known to the US authorities. But British sources suggested the specific activities of the men were unknown. The base had been at its highest state of alert, called delta, for several days beforehand because of a general threat, with extra security measures. The farmer said she was surprised it had been left to her to disrupt the activities of the men. In a round of broadcast interviews, the defence secretary, Wes Streeting, said the woman had only a “partial picture” of the events. About 85 households in the Cotswolds village of Whelford were evacuated early on Sunday morning to a leisure centre, with a 400-metre cordon placed around the white vans as bomb-disposal robots examined them. At the Labour party conference, the home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, said the evacuated residents should shortly be able to return home. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps had made threats against RAF Fairford in July. Iran’s embassy in London denied any involvement in the events in Whelford. It said: “The embassy of the Islamic Republic of Iran in London categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations published by some British individuals and media outlets attempting to link Iran to arrest of five suspects in the vicinity of RAF Fairford base. “The circulation of such fabricated speculations, particularly in the aftermath of the criminal acts of aggression committed by the United States and the Israeli regime against the Iranian people, will serve no purpose other than to fuel Iranophobia propaganda in the UK.”

title: Questions remain over Iran’s link to alleged RAF Fairford bomb plot
summary: Tehran has been trying to step up attacks on targets in the west but its track record has been mixed
text: Investigators may be some way from determining exactly what led five men with three vans to a village just outside RAF Fairford in the small hours of Sunday – but the fact they have all been released on bail without immediate charge suggests they are not deemed to pose a serious and violent threat. In a moment where wider geopolitical tensions mean external threats are perceived to be close, the question of whether Iran had a hand in the alleged plot remains open. Nonetheless, the bailing of the men is a mercifully lower-key development in an investigation that appeared of the utmost gravity. Nigel Farage, the leader of Reform, had earlier insisted that the Fairford incident “proves my point on Iran” and argued that anybody arriving on small boats should not be allowed to move around in the UK. The latter point was an irrelevant argument, already weakened when police said at lunchtime that all five were UK nationals from London. Though the five were arrested on suspicion of carrying explosives and involvement in a terror plot, after more than 24 hours of searches, nothing had been discovered that would prompt further police action – perhaps explaining why MI5 had no idea that the men and their vans would turn up a mile from the base with unclear intent. British officials admitted on Sunday the arrests were not led by intelligence, but rather last-minute warnings on the ground. Counter-terror police said they were first aware of three vehicles travelling to the base at 12.45am on Sunday, while a local farmer phoned 999 at 1.36am after the vans blocked the entrance to her drive. The next day Trump made a characteristically inflated claim that the US and UK had been monitoring the men for “a long time” and that they had been trying to do “big damage”. Threat levels at Fairford have been at the highest level for several days, apparently backing this up – but UK sources say this was related to wider concerns about threats to US bases, not specific to the site. RAF Fairford is the European home for US air force bombers, essentially an American base on British soil. It has been used by the US in its bombing campaign against Iran, after the former prime minister Keir Starmer agreed to allow American strikes on Iranian missile launch sites in the war Donald Trump started in the spring. The base has also been a source of explicit interest to Tehran. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) issued a statement on 23 July, as the US carried out a 13th day of consecutive bombing attacks. It said that any bases used by the US to attack Iran, including Fairford, were “legitimate targets”. That would give Fairford an obvious value, though it is not clear why anyone from London would feel bold enough to attack a military base, given it would be expected to be protected by armed personnel. Rational plotters probably would not expect to survive, and would at least expect the most serious penalties available under law. When the suspects’ release was announced, there was no firm information from UK counter-terror police about what explosives were found or whether there was deemed to be viable devices in the vans – the kind of information that would immediately point to the degree of intent in any terror plot. Subsequently, it emerged no explosive material had been found. Tehran has been trying to step up attacks on targets in the west over the past three years, as fighting in the Middle East has sprawled and expanded after October 2023, and particularly after Trump joined Israel to start a full-scale war on Iran in February. But while its propagandists make heavy threats about British military bases online, Iran’s actual threat is mixed. A year ago, Ken McCallum, the head of MI5, said the Security Service had “tracked more than 20 potentially lethal Iran-backed plots in just the one year”. Two Romanian men were found guilty in July of stabbing the Iranian journalist Pouria Zeraati in the leg in Wimbledon two years earlier in a state-directed attack; he worked for the independent Persian channel Iran International. Yvette Cooper, then home secretary, sanctioned an IRGC-backed terror group, Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamia, in July after it claimed responsibility for a series of attacks in the UK, including the burning of four Jewish community ambulances in March. But while four men have pleaded guilty, evidence in the case has yet to be heard in court, with prosecutors only saying so far there was a “terrorist connection”. In April police closed and searched part of Kensington Gardens near the Israeli embassy in London after an online video appeared to suggest the building had been targeted by drones containing hazardous substances. On that occasion, nothing was found.

title: Burnham promises to roll back privatisation with government-backed grid plan
summary: Exclusive: Creation of GB Grid will be major step towards putting Britain’s utility companies into public control
text: Andy Burnham will take his first major step to putting Britain’s utility companies into public control when, at the Labour conference, he announces a new government-backed body to invest in the electricity grid. The prime minister will use his first speech as party leader to announce the creation of GB Grid, which will use money previously allocated to Great British Energy to compete with privately owned companies such as National Grid. In a speech focusing heavily on undoing what the prime minister calls “40 years of neoliberalism”, he will promise greater public control of energy, water and housing. He is also set to lay out more details on how he will pay for his pledge to create a national care service, with senior ministers refusing to rule out scrapping the pensions triple lock after the next election to free funding. Government sources have suggested Burnham would signal his willingness to review the policy, but stop short of a pledge to scrap it altogether. Burnham will tell the conference on Tuesday: “We have a cost crisis. We all know it. The price of energy is crippling for businesses, and British bill payers pay some of the highest energy costs in Europe. “We have an energy system where prices are dictated in markets miles away, while families and businesses here shoulder the costs. Once again, the British public has lost control.” He will add: “Within 10 years, I want our energy costs to be in line with other nations in Europe. That means we must reform a broken energy market so it serves the public interest.” Burnham’s first conference speech as leader and prime minister caps a remarkable turnaround in his political fortunes since this time last year, when he was criticised by many in the party for talking openly about his desire to replace Keir Starmer. Having ousted Starmer from office, Burnham has spent much of his first few weeks promising a radical shift in tone and policy. He will tell the conference on Tuesday: “We can’t carry on as we are. Politics as usual has taken Britain backwards. More of the same isn’t good enough and isn’t going to get us where we need to be.” Though the conference has been upbeat, Burnham will tell Labour delegates he wanted to strike a serious tone with his speech and address some of the most intractable issues in British politics, such as social care, energy costs and youth inactivity. In the speech, the prime minister will say that he will resist “the usual tub-thumping conference speech … the patriot in me tells me something very different is needed”. He will say “everyone wants less drift and more direction” and that he will “answer that call” today. His offer – expected to contain a number of new policies – will be “a more serious prospectus for Britain than people have been offered in a generation”. “I accept people will not agree with every part of it, but I believe it can turn Britain around,” he will say. The creation of GB Grid is his first significant step to challenging the power of private companies to run Britain’s infrastructure. The organisation will be given access to a pot of £4bn that has already been allocated to the government-backed Great British Energy – although it is not expected to use all of that money. With businesses complaining about how long it takes to get a grid connection for new buildings and projects, GB Grid will use the funding to build more connections, as well as to maximise and speed up the rollout of renewables across the UK. It will be the first publicly owned player in electricity networks since privatisation. Officials said the government would also expand the rights of businesses to build their own connections, allowing them to tap GB Grid’s funding to help pay for it – a move which they said helped speed up connections in Ireland by 11 months. Speaking to the Guardian’s Politics Weekly podcast on Monday, the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, said: “One of my frustrations with the last government is that they didn’t recognise the need to invest in the system, and so we’re having to do that at record pace over the course of the next decade.” On social care, the prime minister will promise “an honest conversation” with the public, saying: “Hope comes from honesty and from saying the things politicians usually avoid.” His promise to “rip the plaster off” when it comes to funding for the national care service has sparked speculation he could use the next Labour manifesto to scrap the pension triple lock and use the savings for social care instead. The triple lock – which guarantees the state pension will rise by the highest of inflation, earnings and 2.5% every year – is forecast to cost £15.5bn by 2030, but so far no major party has remained committed to scrapping it. Speaking to ITV’s Robert Peston on Monday, the chancellor, John Healey, repeatedly refused to commit to funding the triple lock beyond the next election. “I’m not telling you what the next manifesto will or won’t contain – I can’t do that,” he said. “I’m not going to tell you what the budget in a month’s time is going to take.” The prime minister is also set to talk about youth unemployment ahead of a planned report by former minister Alan Milburn on why the number of unemployed young people is rising. While the government has already announced additional support for young people to get into work, ministers have said relatively little about whether they will reduce benefits for those who remain out of work in the long term. Answering calls on LBC Radio on Monday, Burnham said he would use his speech to outline “how I think we should go forward in the next decade”. “It will require some significant changes, but I’m doing it with the best of intentions,” he said.

title: Two people sentenced to 60 and 45 years in prison in death of Telemundo reporter
summary: Danette Colbert and Rickey White sentenced in Adan Manzano’s death for racketeering and negligent homicide
text: A Louisiana judge has handed lengthy prison sentences to two people convicted of roles in a criminal enterprise that targeted New Orleans tourists led to the death of a reporter covering the 2025 Super Bowl there. Nancy Miller, a state court judge, on Monday sentenced Danette Colbert, 49, to a total of 60 years in prison: 50 years for racketeering and a consecutive 10 years for negligent homicide in the death of Adan Manzano, a journalist for the Spanish-language news outlet Telemundo Kansas City. Colbert’s accomplice, Rickey White, was sentenced to 45 years’ imprisonment for racketeering. The sentences come just days after a jury in the suburban New Orleans community of Jefferson parish, Louisiana, convicted both Colbert and White, 35, for their roles in the 5 February 2025 death of Manzano, 27. Manzano had traveled to the New Orleans area to cover the Kansas City Chiefs’ Super Bowl clash with the Philadelphia Eagles. He was found dead in his hotel room in Kenner, Louisiana, the suburb where New Orleans’ international airport is, days before the Chiefs lost the big game to the Eagles. The Jefferson parish coroner’s office, whose jurisdiction includes Kenner, said Manzano died from positional asphyxiation. An autopsy found Xanax and alcohol in his system. Prosecutors said Manzano was among the victims of a years-long operation in which Colbert, White and a co-defendant who testified against them – Christian Anderson – targeted unsuspecting tourists in the city’s French Quarter. The group allegedly lured victims with the promise of sex before drugging and robbing them. Prosecutors said the criminal enterprise dated back to 2012. Manzano’s father addressed his son’s death at Monday’s sentencing via a videoconferencing platform. According to a statement from Jefferson parish district attorney Paul Connick’s office, Manzano’s father called the sentencing “a sad day for me and my family”. “May the laws of this country lock up the people that destroyed my life,” he testified. “I respectfully ask that you give them the sentencing they deserve.” According to local news channel WVUE, the father added: “They snatched his dreams, life and family as we were seeing him happy and successful.” Manzano’s mother, meanwhile, said: “I don’t want to say anything to the people that committed this crime, because they are beings of darkness, beings that don’t have God in their lives. “But I don’t think they should go on with life causing harm and killing people – because I still can’t accept that Adan is not here … This loss, I’ll never overcome it. I don’t wish this on anybody, on any family.” A cousin of Manzano, Carlos Castillo, reportedly said: “I want to look you guys in the face and say that you should pay your entire life for this … Every time the cell opens and you cannot see the light, you think of my cousin.” Manzano’s wife, Ashleigh Boyd, was killed in an April 2024 car crash in Topeka, Kansas. A Topeka judge found Todd W Armstrong guilty of vehicular homicide, speeding and driving on the wrong side of the road after a one-day trial on 21 September, four days after the jury verdict in Manzano’s death in Louisiana. Boyd and Manzano’s daughter – Eleanor, now three – is being raised by her maternal grandparents. Months after Manzano’s death, Colbert received a 25-year prison sentence for being found to have violated her probation on a prior theft and fraud conviction and being classified a habitual offender. Miller on Monday told Colbert that her “behavior in this matter [is] quite alarming”, according to WVUE. “You were indifferent to the impact that your actions had,” Miller said. “That is evident by your consistent pattern in your criminal history. Apparently, you’ve been doing this for quite some time. It’s finally caught up to you with the death of one of your victims.” Note: Colbert was re-sentenced on 14 October to life imprisonment under Louisiana’s habitual offender law, according to prosecutors.

title: Corporations claim their fossil fuel emissions are a drop in the ocean. But what if we could count the real cost?
summary: A new tool called Carbon Impacts Tracer can be used to estimate climate impact from emissions across eight metrics, including lost food production
text: The biggest coal project before authorities in New South Wales, the Hunter Valley Operations mine, will emit the equivalent of about 809m tonnes of climate-warming carbon dioxide if it wins approval. That number, for most people, will carry little meaning, as might the calculation that adding that amount of greenhouse gas to the atmosphere will cause an extra 0.00036C of global heating. But what if the public was instead told that that amount of carbon dioxide would expose almost half a million people to unprecedented heat, or kill nearly 15 million coral colonies on the Great Barrier Reef every time it bleaches, or lead to more than 100 additional deaths from heatwaves in Europe to the end of this century. All those statistics come from a new tool that translates the emissions from burning fossil fuels into estimated real-world climate effects taken from peer-reviewed climate studies. “Small numbers in global warming can mean catastrophic impacts,” says Prof Sarah Perkins-Kirkpatrick, a climate scientist at the Australian National University who is part of a team launching the Carbon Impacts Tracer. The NSW Independent Planning Commission is expected to make a decision this week about the future of the HVO mine, with the joint owners Yancoal and Glencore hoping to keep digging at the Hunter Valley site until 2045. Plugging the project’s expected emissions into the tracer suggests, for example, the extra heat trapped in the atmosphere by its emissions will reduce crop production every year by an amount that is the equivalent to the minimum dietary requirements of 276,129 people. The tool can be used to estimate the impact of carbon dioxide emissions from any project, company or state – or for any known amount of emissions – across eight different factors including the loss of labour hours due to excess heat, the loss of glaciers, the death of corals or lost food production. Central to the tool is a metric known as Transient Climate Response to CO₂ Emissions (TCRE) – an established calculation that every 1,000 billion tonnes of CO2 causes about 0.45C of global heating. Once an amount of CO2 is known – such as from a major fossil project – its contribution to global heating can be calculated and, from there, says Perkins-Kirkpatrick, measured against already published studies. “Every tonne of CO2 matters and we’ve known this for decades,” she said. “To pinpoint what this means with a high degree of confidence has taken us a long time. This [tool] is to hold big fossil fuel emitters accountable. It is not meant to be a blame game. It just shows that all emissions have impacts and now we can prove it.” All the results are presented as the best estimate within a likely range of uncertainty, with links back to the original scientific studies used for the calculations. Perkins-Kirkpatrick accepts some may be sceptical of the results, but counters “we are not making these numbers up for shits and giggles”. “This is based on the best analysis published in the peer-reviewed literature,” she said. And this is only the tip of the iceberg when it comes to the impacts [of fossil fuel burning].” The Carbon Impacts Tracer was developed by scientists at the Australian National University, the Australian Research Council Centre of Excellence for the Weather of the 21st Century and the Lethal Humidity Global Council, and was funded by the Minderoo Foundation. Maria Nawaz leads the Australian Climate Accountability Project at the Australian Human Rights Institute at the University of New South Wales – a partner in the tracer project. “One of the major challenges in climate litigation has been establishing a direct link between a government or a corporation’s actions and climate harms and suffering,” she said. “Governments and corporations have argued their emissions are ‘just a drop in the ocean’ and too small to measure. “But we can now refute this defence and show the emissions of any state or corporation can be tied to a global warming figure and then human and ecological harms. It is transformative.” Elaine Johnson, an experienced climate lawyer and director of Johnson Legal but not involved in the work, said there will be governments and corporations that will not welcome the development of the tool. “Fossil fuel companies do not want people to be able to make that connection between their products and, say, deaths from heatwaves. “But now the science is at the point where we can make those connections clearly. That is a story the industry does not want told.” The Guardian approached Glencore, a partner in the HVO mine, for comment, but received no response. • Graham Readearn is Guardian Australia’s environment and climate correspondent • This article was amended on 29 September 2026. The TCRE metric states that every 1,000 billion tonnes of CO2 – not “every billion tonnes of CO2”, as an earlier version said – causes about 0.45C of global heating.

title: Trump announces $15bn Iowa steel plant as he bids to boost flagging midterm hopes
summary: President says plant will be built by Indian-owned company and calls it largest such facility in American history
text: Donald Trump on Monday announced what he called the largest steel plant in American history to be built in Iowa, giving Republicans a jobs message to take to voters in a state that could help decide control of the Senate in November. “Using advanced steelmaking technology, the plant will produce some of the highest quality, most affordable steel anywhere in the world,” Trump said in the Oval Office, flanked by Iowa’s top Republicans. The plant, which “they’ve already started building”, Trump said, will be built in eastern Iowa by the foreign-owned steelmaker Mesabi Metallics and is expected to cost about $15bn, according to a White House official. It aims to begin production in 2030, years after voters go to the polls in November. In his announcement, Trump singled out Iowa’s Ashley Hinson, the Republican congresswoman who was in the Oval Office and who is running for the Senate seat being vacated by Joni Ernst, also in the room. “I saw some good polls just recently,” he told her. “Looks like you’re doing well.” But the polls for that race are less rosy than Trump suggested. A Marist survey published last week found Hinson trailing Democrat Josh Turek by eight points in the conservative state, while an earlier Emerson College poll had Hinson narrowly ahead but found voters worried about tariffs. Democrats see the seat as one of four they need to retake the Senate. Trump said the plant would run on iron ore from the company’s mine in Minnesota, which accounted for roughly 60% of iron ore production in the US in the 20th century. The president took the chance to attack that state’s Democratic governor, Tim Walz. “They have one of the worst governors in history, a real stupid guy, but they do have good iron ore, which is more important, I guess,” Trump said. The two men have clashed over mining in the state, most recently over Walz’s August order halting permitting for mining projects near the Boundary Waters wilderness. The Mesabi Metallics company itself, however, is owned by the India-based Essar Group, and US taxpayers are helping to pay for the expansion: the Export-Import Bank, a federal agency, will provide up to $10bn in financing. When asked whether global outsourcing would be needed to build the plant, the chairman of Mesabi Metallics, Rewant Ruia, said “most of the critical materials” would come from the US but added “there are some materials that might be used that need to be imported for making and refining the highest quality steels”. Still, the president credited his tariffs – the taxes the US charges consumers on imported goods – for the investment. “Everyone’s building their plant here because they don’t want to pay tariffs,” he said. “It’s really not that complicated. A lot of people say they don’t understand it, but they do. They just don’t like to give us credit.” Trump said the project was “expected to create up to 6,000 new construction jobs, nearly 2,000 manufacturing and mining jobs, and add another $95bn to the US economy”.

title: Cost of green transition could be spread among UK taxpayers, energy secretary suggests
summary: Miatta Fahnbulleh says Britain must look at how costs are recovered – and that could mean money off bills
text: Billions of pounds worth of green levies could be taken off bills, the energy secretary has said, as the government investigates funding green infrastructure through taxes instead. Miatta Fahnbulleh is looking at how green projects are funded, including varying levies between customers and funding them all through general taxation. Such a move could save customers an average of £120 a year, but could involve putting up taxes by as much as £3bn. With households facing a predicted rise in electricity bills next year of more than £400 largely because of the Iran war, ministers are looking for ways to bring down costs in the short term. Paying for schemes such as windfarms, solar panels and home insulation through taxation however would either mean cuts elsewhere or raising taxes. Fahnbulleh told the Guardian’s Politics Weekly podcast: “There is a question that needs to be answered … we have to think about the costs and how we recover it in the most fair way. “And so the question that I am generally asking is: given that there will be fixed costs, if we want a system that is resilient, if we want a system that can cope, if we want a system that ultimately can deliver the diversity of energy that we want, what is the fairest way in which we pay for it? “That is both across the exchequer versus our bill payers, and then within our bill payers. So we have to ask that question. Every other country is asking that question, and ultimately we’ve got to come to a fair deal.” Campaigners have long argued that Britain’s model of paying for its energy transition through bills is unfair compared with systems in other countries that spread the cost among taxpayers, with repayment based on how much a person earns. Analysis by the MCS Foundation, a green energy charity, recently found such a move would save about £120 a year on bills but would cost the Treasury a little more than £3bn a year. Fahnbulleh said she would cut bills, but did not recommit to her predecessor Ed Miliband’s pledge to bring them down by £300 a year. “My mark of failure or success is whether I can get bills down or not,” she said. “That’s the only thing I’m in this job to do.” But she also promised to keep pushing action to tackle the climate crisis, even in the face of increasing political attacks by Reform and the Conservatives. “My challenge to Reform and to the Tories is, when we come to the next election, and I can point to the jobs that have been created, I can point to the industries and the factories that we’ve created, I will say to them: ‘If you want to pull the rug on that, you go talk to those communities,’” she said. “And in the end, I think they will bow because they are on the wrong side – not just of economics, but they’re on the wrong side of history on this.”

title: Nvidia unveils security platform to rein in AI agents and $150bn stock buyback
summary: Chipmaker says new system was designed to prevent AI agents from going rogue amid incidents at top companies
text: Nvidia on Monday unveiled a new security platform that the chipmaker said can stop artificial intelligence agents from going rogue. The company announced a $150bn stock buyback the same day, the largest in US corporate history. The chipmaker said that its Open Agent Safety Platform includes open source software that “sets boundaries for agents” and follows a series of revelations from top AI companies about their models escaping and breaking into other organizations. The disclosures have sparked furious debate about the safety of advanced artificial intelligence systems, including self-improving models that some fear could race out of human control. Nvidia executives said in a media briefing that the new system could have prevented a recent incident involving a swarm of OpenAI agents that autonomously hacked into the AI company Hugging Face. “From what we know, this new security platform could have stopped the breach if it was being used in frontier labs for model evaluation early on,” said Justin Boitano, the company’s vice-president of enterprise AI, referring to companies at the forefront of AI. Nvidia also said its board approved expanding its share repurchase program by $150bn, raising the total amount to $235bn. The previous record was held by Apple with its $110bn buyback in 2024. “Our cash generation gives us the capacity to invest in the technologies that advance this transformation and return capital to shareholders,” Nvidia’s CEO, Jensen Huang, said in a statement. Last month, Nvidia forecast about ⁠70% revenue growth for fiscal 2028, reassuring investors who have questioned how long the AI spending surge can last after years of explosive growth. The Hugging Face incident was a high-profile breach that inflamed safety concerns about AI, which were followed by similar rogue actions involving OpenAI’s models including breaching an Australian health department website. Anthropic and Meta have also disclosed that their AI systems hacked into other organizations on their own. Nvidia’s software, called OpenShell, lets developers “formally verify an agent has enough authority to do its job and no more”, Boitano said. Because it is open source, it can be “extended” to run on rival computing platforms including those from Arm and Intel. The platform also includes a separate security layer called Sentry that runs onboard a chip to continuously monitor AI agent activity and can “intervene instantly” if the agent starts trying to move beyond its target, the company said. “It can quarantine a suspicious agent in milliseconds,” Boitano said. “OpenShell governs the agent’s actions, and then Sentry independently monitors and contains suspicious behavior,” Boitano said. Nvidia said more than 100 organizations were using the platform at its launch, including Microsoft, Perplexity, Accenture and JPMorgan Chase. The AI safety debate has divided the industry, with the heads of Anthropic and OpenAI championing a coordinated slowdown of AI development to let safety efforts catch up. Others, including Huang, say it should be up to individual companies to make sure their models are safe for release. Huang, during the annual Salesforce technology conference held earlier this month, characterized AI safety, including the danger of rogue agents, as an engineering problem that software developers can address.

title: Local representatives question official accounts after suspected bomb plot at RAF Fairford
summary: Amid conflicting statements, local MP and councillors demand answers over how suspects were allowed to enter residential areas of nearby village
text: An MP and councillors representing the residents of the village near RAF Fairford who were evacuated due to a suspected terror plot have expressed scepticism and concern over the security response to threats made by Iran. About 85 properties in Whelford, Gloucestershire, were evacuated on Sunday morning after five men were arrested on suspicion of explosives offences in the village. The men, who were later re-arrested on suspicion of terror offences, were released on bail on Monday. It is understood some residents were returning to their properties late on Monday, but a cordon remains around the village. As speculation mounted over the circumstances surrounding the incident, concerns emerged about how events were handled by the authorities. In July, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps noted RAF Fairford’s use by US bombers, warning the UK that “any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces”. However, it remains unclear who or what was behind the alleged activity. Iran has denied any involvement. Tehran’s embassy in London condemned what it described as “unfounded and malicious speculation” linking the country to the incident in the vicinity of the military base in Gloucestershire. Roz Savage, the MP for South Cotswolds, said she had many questions about the circumstances of how the alleged terror plot was averted. The Liberal Democrat MP, whose constituency covers the military base, said she would be writing to the prime minister and the defence secretary with her concerns. “Ever since it was first announced six months ago that RAF Fairford was going to be used as the base for US military airstrikes on Iran, I’ve been asking questions of the government about whether they can assure my residents, my constituents, of their safety,” she said. “They had given that assurance. However, I feel that the events of this weekend do cast that into doubt.” She went on: “Who knew what? When did they know it? Where was the ball dropped? What more could have been done to secure the safety and security of my constituents? “We are already in the process of writing to the secretary of state for defence and to the prime minister to try and ascertain the answers to some of these questions.” There have been conflicting statements about who knew what and when. A farmer from Whelford told reporters she called police in the early hours of Sunday to report suspicious activity – which then triggered a rapid response. But the US president, Donald Trump, also suggested to reporters the men had been under surveillance. Now, the men have been released on police bail. Tristan Wilkinson, a cabinet member for Cotswold district council and councillor for the Lechlade, Kempsford and Fairford South ward, which covers Whelford, said: “The American president indicated last night in front of journalists that there was some intelligence and that these individuals were under surveillance. “If that was to be true, that they would have been allowed to get so close to the base and drive what was, at the time, believed to be bombs into residential areas of a small village, I can’t imagine the security services allowing that to happen. “I would have expected them to have done a hard stop on the van before they got to people’s homes. So that that doesn’t feel right. “It seems insane that this appears to have been a tipoff from a member of the public, and the security services are claiming that there was a level of intelligence involved as well. I don’t see how those two things can both come through at the same time.” He went on: “Back in July, the Iranians issued a statement saying that any countries that were providing military and practical support for the American effort were legitimate targets and at the time they named RAF Fairford specifically. “So at that time, I and other civic leaders were calling for a more visible police presence to reassure residents, and that did happen. “So from July, if you were around the base, you would have seen more police patrols. “So if you’d parked a car up in a layby or somewhere near the base in the last few weeks, then you probably would have had the police contacting someone quickly to find out who you are and what you are doing. “But I do think there’s been an increase in police presence in the last week as well. So I went past the base last Monday and I noticed that the non-manned entrances to the base have been fortified with vehicles. “They put diggers and heavy vehicles in place that I’ve never seen before. So that’s quite an unusual step to block an emergency exit. So that led to speculation that maybe there was an increased level of concern from the base for them to use those measures. “I wouldn’t expect the RAF to give a running commentary,” he added. “However, I think there’s always room for improvement. We have a significant military presence surrounded on three sides by residential housing. You can walk right up to the perimeter fence. There’s lots of military bases around the world that are quite remote for good reasons. So, the reality is this is a big military presence in a rural community. “I will be asking for us to look at ways at how we can improve ongoing relations, and it’s not just relating to security matters. You know, we have other issues that you know with regard to flooding and noise, so there’s always more we can do.”

title: Michael Wynn-Jones, husband of Delia Smith, dies aged 85
summary: Former journalist and honorary life president of Norwich City FC died peacefully at home on Monday
text: Michael Wynn-Jones, the journalist and husband of the TV chef Delia Smith, has died at the age of 85. Wynn-Jones was honorary life president of Norwich City football club, which said everyone at the club was “deeply saddened” by his death. The club said in statement: “Michael died peacefully at home on Monday morning, aged 85. He will be greatly missed. His family are grateful for the wonderful care provided by the community nursing team at St Elizabeth hospice in Ipswich. “Our deepest condolences are with Delia and Tom [Smith, the couple’s nephew], and with all of Michael’s family, friends and loved ones. At the family’s request, we ask that their privacy be respected at this difficult time.” Wynn-Jones lived with Smith near Stowmarket in Suffolk and they had been married for more than 50 years. The couple oversaw several promotions to the Premier League for the Canaries, putting the club on a solid financial footing. Smith had a more prominent, public role at Norwich City but Wynn-Jones was reportedly regarded as a trusted adviser and influential figure in the boardroom. Darren Huckerby, a former player for the club, posted a tribute saying Wynn-Jones “stayed out of the limelight but all at Norwich City FC owe him so much”. Wynn-Jones worked as a journalist for titles including the Daily Mirror and the Spectator and founded his own publishing company. He began attending Norwich City games in April 1955 at the age of 13. He wrote fondly of the club’s unlikely run to the FA Cup semi-final in 1959. Norwich City Fans Social Club said in a statement: “All of us at NCFSC are devastated to hear the news about Michael Wynn-Jones passing. Michael is a true NCFC legend and what he did for the club cannot be underestimated. We are thinking of Delia, Tom and all of Michael’s family at this incredibly sad time. Rest in peace, Michael.” Delia Smith previously told BBC Radio 4’s Desert Island Discs that she and Wynn-Jones bonded over their passion for food and football. She said in 2021 she rarely cooked at home, leaving Wynn-Jones to hover over the stove while she went “to the end of the garden”.
