title: Absence of violence in Drumcree does not make standoff any less significant
summary: Row comes amid rising division and a tendency towards cynical political posturing in Northern Ireland
text: Three decades ago, it took the deaths of three children from a Roman Catholic family – the Quinn brothers, Jason, nine, Mark, 10, and 11-year-old Richard – in a petrol bomb attack to bring an end to the Drumcree dispute. “No road is worth a life, let alone the lives of three little boys,” the Orange Order’s County Armagh chaplain said at the time. It is perhaps extraordinary to think that this could ever have needed saying – but that was then. Northern Ireland is very different place today. Passions are running high, but the attempt by 35 members of the Protestant Orange Order to walk down Garvaghy Road, a main thoroughfare in a predominantly nationalist part of Drumcree in Portadown, County Armagh, did not lead to violence on Sunday or Monday. Faced with thousands of members of the nationalist community standing in their way and a police line ordering them back, Orange Order district master Nigel Dawson concluded: “There’s no point getting wet unnecessarily,” as he instructed members of the order back inside the church hall to shelter from the rain. Every half-hour on Monday, the Orange Order members walked up to police lines only to be turned back by Supt Brendan Green, but the process was peaceful and respectful. The blessed absence of the old ways does not make what is happening at Drumcree any less significant, however. History doesn’t repeat itself, and although hope and history sometimes rhyme, more often we hear echoes of history returning to us. The divisions and tendency towards cynical political posturing in Northern Ireland, papered over by the 1998 Good Friday agreement – when all sides were exhausted by the hate and misery of the three decades of Troubles – have been all too evident of late. This particular dispute can be reasonably argued either way. The independent Parades Commission has ruled that the march down the Garvaghy Road is permissible. The marchers are simply taking advantage of their rights, it may be said. But is it really necessary to take this road after 28 years of the march being banned? Who is served by the provocation? The detail of the argument is perhaps less important than the fact that it is happening, and what that says about Northern Ireland today, and what it may mean for the future. On the nationalist side, there has been growing and bristling self-confidence about the prospects of a border poll on a united Ireland. This was only inflated by Donald Trump’s recent suggestion that a unified Ireland should happen sooner rather than later. “The days of unionist supremacy and domination are gone,” said the first minister, Michelle O’Neill of Sinn Féin, on Monday after appearing herself in Drumcree. “We will not be going backwards.” The numbers gathering from the nationalist community, some of whom were bussed in from Belfast and Derry, appeared to surprise the Police Service of Northern Ireland. It was a moment of unity within an often fractured nationalist community. Those in attendance included Colin Duffy and his brother Paul, who were both acquitted of terror charges in 2015, along with the SDLP party leader Claire Hanna, a vehement critic of those who reach for violence as an answer. Meanwhile, for the unionists, the changed relationship with the rest of the UK brought about by the Brexit deal and changing demographics has arguably engendered a distinct lack of confidence about the future. Gavin Robinson, the leader of the Democratic Unionist party (DUP), the largest unionist party, claimed on Monday that “standards have been shattered” by the presence of the first minister with the protesters in Drumcree. When O’Neill and Mary Lou McDonald, the leader of Sinn Féin in the Republic of Ireland, arrived at the protest, it was to chants of “bring it down” and “fuck Stormont”, in reference to power-sharing arrangements in Northern Ireland, structured to make unionists and nationalists work together. “How we can go forward when there is such a level of disdain for the simple fundamental democratic principles of society?” asked Robinson of the attempt by the first minister to block a lawful march. It is likely that the prospect of elections for the Northern Ireland assembly next year, and the need to rally the faithful to their respective cause, is not helping to calm the rhetoric. In Stormont, the speaker, Edwin Poots, a former leader of the DUP, condemned the first minister for her “gross discourtesy” and “contempt” in not coming to answer an urgent question about the crisis. In this context, there is concern that even if Sinn Féin’s leaders, with the crowds’ chants ringing in their ears, do not walk out of the Northern Ireland executive, that the DUP could well do so. After a prolonged period in which agreement on a budget for Northern Ireland’s collapsing public services has not been found with Westminster, such further fracturing risks a whole new level of instability. The Northern Ireland secretary, Chris Bryant, spoke to Breandán Mac Cionnaith, from the Garvaghy Road Residents’ Coalition, on Monday. The possibility of mediation was discussed, Mac Cionnaith said. Speaking in the Republic, Micheál Martin, the taoiseach, called for cool heads. “No one wants to go back to the past divisions, to past trauma that we experienced at Garvaghy Road, Drumcree, in the past,” he said. “I would say to Sinn Féin and to everybody else: time to dial back now and time to engage in dialogue, and to work this out in a sensible, community-based way.”

title: Dengue fever outbreak prompts Florida counties to declare state of emergency
summary: CDC says 392 cases of Dengue were reported for the year so far in the state, along with different county-level data
text: Several Florida counties recently declared a state of local emergency in response to a spate of dengue fever infections. Hillsborough county, Florida, officials made the declaration on 24 September as health authorities recorded 134 confirmed cases of dengue fever, which is a mosquito-borne sickness typically found in countries outside the US. Officials said that the spread of the illness poses “an immediate and widespread threat to the public health, safety, and welfare of the residents and visitors of Hillsborough county”. Controlling the tropical disease – often referred to as breakbone fever because it can cause extreme pain – requires “immediate, aggressive, and continuous” measures such as pesticide application, public education and emergency resource planning, officials said. Dengue cases have become more common in parts of the US. In 2023, Long Beach and Pasadena reported the first ever known locally acquired cases in California. The spread of dengue mosquitoes outside tropical and subtropical locales has even hit England, with authorities recently announcing that Aedes aegypti had been found in east London homes. Scientists have said that global warming is poised to intensify climate-related diseases. Declaring a local state of emergency enables Hillsborough county – whose seat is the city of Tampa – to request “any available and necessary state, federal, and local emergency funds, grants, financial assistance, and mutual aid” in their ongoing fight against mosquitoes carrying dengue. The initial declaration was put into effect for one week, but officials can extend it. Neighboring Pasco and Pinellas counties have also declared similar states of emergency in relation to dengue reports. The Florida department of health said in its recent report on mosquito-transmitted viruses that there were 26 cases of international travel-linked dengue reported in the state during a six-day period beginning on 13 September. There have been a total of 212 known travel-related cases in Florida reported so far in 2026. Over the same period, there were 38 locally contracted dengue cases reported in Florida. They were among 190 cases of locally acquired dengue across Florida, the state’s health department said. Numbers from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) differ slightly. As of Monday, the CDC noted 392 cases of dengue had been reported overall in Florida for the year so far, along with different county-level data. Dengue is contracted through the bite of some mosquito species, largely Aedes aegypti, as well as Aedes albopictus. Both species are present in Florida. Symptoms show up between three days and two weeks after a bite from an infected mosquito. Among the symptoms are “sudden onset of fever, severe headache, eye pain, muscle and joint pain … and bleeding. Gastrointestinal symptoms like vomiting and diarrhea may also be present in some cases,” Florida’s state health department said. The symptoms typically span four days to one week. A rarer form of the illness called dengue hemorrhagic fever can be fatal without the administration of proper supportive care, the state health department said. Hillsborough county authorities have expressed optimism that dengue infections might slow down in the coming weeks, with zero “mosquito test pools” testing positive recently, according to the local Bay News 9 outlet.

title: Arizona frat suspended after allegedly making new recruits swallow live goldfish
summary: Case of alleged hazing at the University of Arizona is latest in series of controversial incidents involving US fraternities
text: A college fraternity at the University of Arizona has been suspended after new members were allegedly plied with alcohol and forced to swallow live goldfish. College officials informed the university’s Sigma Tau Gamma chapter by letter earlier in September that it was under investigation for multiple alleged violations of the student code of conduct, including “endangering, threatening, or causing physical harm” to members of the campus community. It is the latest in a series of recent campus hazing cases across the US, which have included the discovery of dozens of partly clothed young men locked in the basement of a fraternity house at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, where they were covered in food as part of a pledging ritual. Meanwhile, in New York, prosecutors said on Monday that they had reopened a 2024 investigation into the alleged drugging and gang-rape of a female student by seven members of Cornell University’s Chi Phi fraternity. The alleged hazing of new recruits to the Arizona fraternity took place in the fall semester of 2025, according to the letter to the chapter from Jasmin Hayes, the university’s senior student rights and responsibilities coordinator. “New members of Sigma Tau Gamma fraternity were subjected to hazing,” Hayes wrote. “Specifically, new members were forced to consume large quantities of alcohol and live goldfish. Additionally, new members were subjected to screaming, degradation, and threats from active members.” The chapter is banned from all activities except essential business meetings while the university’s investigation concludes, Hayes wrote. A repeat violation or attempt to contact or interfere with witnesses could result in more severe consequences, she warned. A separate University of Arizona fraternity, Sigma Phi Epsilon, was placed on probation for 12 months and fined $4,000, for breaches of the student code of conduct relating to hazing, Tucson’s KOLD news station reported in May. In all, six University of Arizona fraternity chapters have been investigated for hazing in 2026, the outlet reported. Among the allegations are forced alcohol and drug use – and incidents of violence and intimidation resulting in hospitalizations. The Guardian has contacted Sigma Tau Gamma for comment. On its national website, the fraternity promotes virtues including “integrity”, “excellence” and “citizenship”. In 2020, the Pennsylvania State University and Sigma Tau Gamma’s board of directors announced jointly that they had permanently closed its Alpha Psi chapter for hazing offenses, including providing alcohol to minors. “Hazing has no place in Sigma Tau Gamma,” the fraternity said in a statement at the time.

title: Marine Le Pen hails RN senate surge as ‘milestone’ towards French presidency
summary: National Rally and allies gain record 14 seats and can form senate group for first time after indirect vote by local officials
text: The French far-right leader Marine Le Pen has said her 2027 presidential campaign will be boosted after her anti-immigration party, the National Rally (RN), and its allies improved to a record 14 seats in partial senate elections this weekend. Le Pen called the results a “historic victory” and a “major milestone” after her party cleared the 10-seat threshold to be able to form a senate group for the first time, after an indirect vote by local officials including mayors and councillors. The party’s progress in the senate will allow it higher visibility and more funding in the second house of parliament before next spring’s presidential election. Le Pen is polling high as Emmanuel Macron prepares to step down after 10 years in office. The French investigative website Mediapart reported on Monday that the RN party president, Jordan Bardella, allegedly made antisemitic comments in writing in 2013, when he was a young party member. The alleged comments in a chat, which Mediapart said it had authenticated, included: “The Jew has to dominate other peoples, crush them, and rob them; a Zionist is necessarily a Jew, and fundamentally so.” He was also alleged to have written “all the banks are owned by Jews”. Bardella responded on X that he “formally” rejected the allegations, which he described as “crude forgeries”, saying he would take legal action. The RN MP Sébastien Chenu called the senate gains “a boost for the presidential campaign” and said there was “no more glass ceiling” for the party. Edwige Diaz, who secured a large senate win for the RN in Gironde outside Bordeaux, told Le Parisien: “This will be very useful for us before the presidential election.” The 348-seat senate is France’s second chamber of parliament alongside the national assembly. Final results on Monday morning showed the senate remained dominated by the traditional right and centre right. The upper chamber’s president of more than a decade, Gerard Larcher, 77, from the rightwing party Les Républicains, is expected to be re-elected next week. Although the RN is now the biggest single opposition party in the national assembly and has the largest number of French members of the European parliament, it has until now never had a grouping in the senate, where its presence has been small. Nine RN senators were elected on Sunday, in addition to the three who won seats in 2023. The RN ally, Éric Ciotti’s Union of the Right for the Republic party, won two seats. The RN had entered the senate for the first time with two seats in 2014, when it was known as the Front National. The senate has an indirect voting system, with local elected officials choosing new senators for half the upper chamber every three years, each to serve a six-year term. Sunday’s vote by local mayors and councillors reflected the RN’s growth in support in medium towns at the last local elections in March. It also showed the party has support among independent rural mayors. Bardella called on politicians on the traditional right to join forces with his party. The Socialist senator Laurence Rossignol said a crucial question would be whether the right and centre right in the senate now moved closer to the RN and hardened their own stance on issues such as immigration and welfare benefits. She told Public Sénat TV: “Will there be a republican barrier against RN ideas? That will be key.” The right, the centre and the left’s Socialists remain the three major forces in the upper house. The radical left party La France Insoumise won a senate seat for the first time, with Gabriel Amard elected in the Rhône. Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the party’s leader, who is the highest-polling left candidate for the presidency, said Amard’s win was a “good omen” for his own 2027 presidential campaign.

title: Reality pays a visit to the Labour party conference, but it’s the ‘Hope Again’ that kills you
summary: Most MPs are clinging to this year’s Beckettian slogan, but the chancellor brought his own brand of despair
text: It could be just me, but I’m beginning to find that all this “hope” stuff is getting me down. Everywhere you go at the Labour party conference, you are being urged to “Hope Again”. It’s on the screens in the main hall and on banners in the exhibition area. It’s on T-shirts, balloons and coffee mugs. It’s all just a bit much. Overkill. You now bump into Labour MPs who are visibly collapsing under the strain of having to walk around with an optimistic perma-grin. And the conference is only into its second day. Come Wednesday they will all be on intravenous Valium. What does “Hope Again” even mean? Is it an instruction? Have we all been hoping in a highly unsatisfactory way so far? Are we being sent back to hope school to learn how to be more upbeat? In which case, I rather think these remedial classes in hoping will be wasted on me. I’ve always been a bit miserable. It feels a bit like someone going round and telling you “Smile. It may never happen.” Or to “Keep calm and carry on.” There are also distinct echoes of Samuel Beckett: Fail again. Fail better. Only in Liverpool it’s: Hope again. Hope better. You also can’t help feeling that all this talk of hope is wasted on John Healey. He is a man with a naturally low-energy vibe. Someone in touch with the darker, more depressing side of his own personality. A man after my own heart. As someone with the touch of Harry Potter’s Dementors, ready to suck the joy out of any occasion, he knows that anything that can go wrong almost certainly will go wrong. Anything good is merely a transitory, illusory state. Take Healey to the football and he will show you a bad time. His home team of Rotherham might go 2-0 up in the 88th minute and John will assure you they’ve peaked too soon – they are nailed on to lose 3-2. I speak from experience. I’ve done it myself. John, meet John. Luckily for me, no one is expecting me to be a ray of sunshine. That’s way above my pay grade. Unfortunately for Healey, optimism was precisely what he was required to deliver in his first speech as chancellor to a nearly full Labour conference hall. To be the fiscal embodiment of “Hope Again”. To give us all a reason to live just a little longer. Only he just couldn’t do it. He was never going to be able to do it. When John sees a “Hope Again” banner, what he reads is “Despair Again”. Come the end of his half hour on stage, he had managed to convert most of the audience to his way of thinking. At lunchtime, the queues for the assisted dying helpline tailed back into the city centre. Not that Healey didn’t give it his best shot. He dropped the word hope into almost every sentence – or his minders had dropped it in for him – and every time, the lights seemed to get a bit dimmer. It was a battle of hope against hope. People had come willing him to succeed. To pull off one of the most astonishing personality transplants of the year. Within minutes, though, a pall of depression hung over the hall. We were all just waiting for it to end. Hardly anyone could be bothered to even clap. The only standing ovation came for the reintroduction of the £15m Union Learning Fund. To give this some perspective, £15m is just a bit more than what the London townhouse of the Tory shadow chancellor, Andrew Griffith, is worth. Not that it’s a bad idea. It’s just not going to reboot the economy. And it’s hard to blame Healey. Maybe another more dynamic and charismatic chancellor could have shifted the mood in the hall with feelgood vibes. But as well as being a bit miserable, Healey is also a realist. He knows things are tough and likely to get tougher. No amount of energy price caps and £2 bus fares are going to make a major dent in a cost of living which is only heading in one direction. Nor is it his fault. He is not responsible for austerity, Brexit, the war in Iran and the cost of borrowing. But he is the current fall guy. The chancellor tasked with fixing the unfixable. So what we got instead was a touch of nostalgia. A deep dive into the stories Labour has written about its achievements. Times when hope was very much alive. Just not now, no matter how often Healey prefixed his sentences with the H-word. Inevitably, though, the truth came out. How he wished he was chancellor back in the late 90s when the economy was on track and there was money to spare. Instead, we were where we were. You can tell people that the UK is the fastest-growing economy in the G7, but it counts for little if everyone still feels broke and broken. There was talk of growth. Of reindustrialisation. But mostly of the need for fiscal discipline. Which is code for saying that the budget in four weeks’ time is unlikely to be a bundle of fun for anyone. Look forward to some tax rises and welfare cuts. There was also a commitment to spend £6m on shipyards to build the UK’s nuclear submarines. Money that had already been promised. Always the best money for a government to spend. Old money repurposed as new. Come the end, no one could have been in any doubt about the scale of the challenge ahead. Despite trying to be someone else, Healey had not been able to be anything but himself. And why not? It’s not as if there are any easy answers. Nor do the Tories and Reform have any solutions. They are just chancers peddling pipe dreams. But most of the Liverpool audience hadn’t come for this. They had been told to come for hope and they wanted half an hour off to enjoy themselves. Instead they had been confronted with cold reality.

title: Nandy labels Farage ‘master of conspiracy theory’ over Fairford claims
summary: Culture secretary criticises Reform leader after he tried to link suspected bomb plot to small boat crossings
text: Nigel Farage has been described as a “master of the conspiracy theory” by the culture secretary, Lisa Nandy, after he tried to link events at RAF Fairford to small boat crossings. The Reform UK leader was criticised over his reaction to the arrests of the men on Sunday, when he said he had been warning for months about “Iranian agents” coming into the UK across the Channel in small boats. “We deserve to be told the truth about the Fairford bomb plotters’ identities,” he added in his post on X on Sunday. On Monday he posted a video in which he claimed to have received intelligence that the Iranian regime was using the small boats “to get their operatives into Britain”. Less than an hour later, Counter Terrorism Policing (CTP) said that the five suspects were all British nationals. The men – three residents of Westminster and two others from Camden and Willesden, all London boroughs – have since been released on bail while the police investigate “multiple lines of inquiry”. Nandy told the Guardian at Labour party conference on Monday that Farage was a “master of the conspiracy theory” when asked about his comments. “I think that he’s good at using the very real sentiment that a lot of people feel, of anxiety and distrust,” she added. “Particularly in this era of mis- and disinformation, I think he’s very agile at exploiting that for political gain.” Defending the authorities’ not having immediately released identity details of the suspects, Nandy said the first job of the government was to reassure the public that they were taking the right steps to keep them safe, which sometimes means “withholding information where it is in the public interest”. “More information is usually better than not,” she added, but it was “not always a conspiracy” when it was held back. Police involved in the investigation have also appealed for patience, without the pressure from speculation, while they conduct their inquiries. CTP senior national coordinator, deputy assistant commissioner Vicki Evans, said in an update: “I am very aware of the levels of speculation about the motivation behind this incident, and the geopolitical questions that are being raised. However, I ask that at this time, Counter Terrorism Policing are given the space to work carefully and clearly.” Farage was also accused of “irresponsible nonsense” by Jenny Jones, a Green Party peer, who said: “Once again Farage’s attempts to whip up division by scapegoating some of the world’s most vulnerable people has left him with egg on his face.” Speaking after the police said that the suspects were British nationals, Farage denied any suggestion it had been irresponsible speculate about the incident while the government was carefully calibrating its responses to the security operation in Gloucestershire. “I have been saying it for years. I didn’t say anything different yesterday. What I have been saying for years and saying all summer, our national security is threatened from the outside by weakness on borders like it has never been before,” he told Sky News. Other Reform UK MPs including Robert Jenrick and Richard Tice also rushed to try to link the RAF Fairford incident to small boat crossings. Jenrick said that “we may now be seeing the consequences” of “complacency” by the Home Office after he had previously said terrorist were using small boats to enter the UK. Later on Monday, Tice shared an X post by his partner Isabel Oakeshott, who said UK law recognised six types of British nationality and that asking for the suspects’ “countries of origin” was among “perfectly reasonable questions”. The Reform deputy leader added: “Ethnicity? Dual nationals? Asylum seekers? Previous convictions? Known to Prevent / Authorities? Benefits claimants? Living in social housing?”

title: Merseyside blaze that killed mother and three children caused by lithium-ion battery
summary: Local fire and rescue service says tragic incident early on Tuesday highlights risks the batteries can pose
text: A fire that left a mother and her three children dead was caused by a lithium-ion battery, firefighters in Merseyside have said. An electrical event caused the battery, of a type commonly used in vapes, ebikes and e-scooters, to go into “thermal runaway”, Merseyside fire and rescue service said. Crews arrived at the blaze, which ripped through the house in Bootle, at about 3.45am on Tuesday 22 September. Four people were discovered in an upstairs bedroom showing no signs of life, a fire service spokesperson said. North West ambulance’s hazardous area response team later confirmed that all four had died. They were named by police as Elisha Brabin, 36, Leo Brabin, 16, Ellis Brabin, eight, and seven-year-old Prudence Brabin. At the fire’s height, six crews were on the scene and eight firefighters entered the house. The fire service’s head of prevention, Kevin Johnson, said: “This is a devastating incident and our thoughts are very much with the family and friends of the mother and children who lost their lives and those who were injured. “This tragedy highlights the very real risks posed by lithium-ion batteries, which we confirmed as the source of the fire.” The service did not confirm what the lithium-ion battery at the home was being used for. Johnson said: “We’re urging people to follow the manufacturer’s instructions, only using batteries and chargers which have been supplied with the vehicle or approved by the manufacturer, as anything else can pose a huge fire risk. “It’s also important to know and recognise the signs that your lithium-ion battery may be failing – if it is swelling, making unusual sounds, has a strong smell, is failing to charge or is smoking, please stop using immediately.” In a tribute issued on Wednesday, relatives of the victims said: “Elisha was our beloved daughter, wife, mother, sister, aunty, niece and cousin. She was a devoted and loving mother who lived for her children. They were her whole world, and she meant everything to us. “Our beautiful babies, Leo, Ellis and Prudence, were loved beyond measure and brought so much joy, happiness and love to our family. They filled our lives with laughter and precious memories that we will cherish for ever. “The tragic loss of Elisha and our three precious children has left us heartbroken. They have all been taken from us far too soon. The loss we are experiencing is unimaginable, and the impact on our family will be felt for ever.”

title: Trump appointee overseeing election investigations steps down from FBI role
summary: Andrew Bailey will resign as FBI co-deputy director about a year after assuming the position
text: Andrew Bailey, a deputy director of the FBI who has been overseeing some of Trump’s election-related investigations, will step down from his position approximately one year after assuming his role. “I am announcing that I am stepping down to return to my family in Missouri,” Bailey wrote in an X post on Monday amid an ongoing shake-up at the bureau. “I am confident Director Patel will continue to reform the FBI, combat violent crime, defend the homeland, ensure strong organizational accountability, and restore public trust in this institution of excellence,” he added, thanking the FBI director, Kash Patel, Donald Trump and the attorney general, Todd Blanche. Bailey, a hardline conservative and former attorney general of Missouri, began serving in the unusual co-deputy director position with former deputy Dan Bongino, a podcaster who had no formal FBI experience, in September 2025. Since Bongino left the FBI in January, Bailey has been serving as co-deputy director with Christopher Raia, a former FBI special agent and New York field office official. It is unclear whether Trump plans to pick another deputy director to serve alongside Raia. In his role at the FBI, Bailey had been overseeing some of Trump’s election-related investigations, including one related to 2020 ballots in Georgia. He was present in January when FBI agents executed a search warrant at an election office in Fulton county and seized ballots among other materials from the 2020 presidential election. MS Now was the first to report on Bailey’s resignation. Under Patel’s leadership, the FBI has seen mass departures of career agents, some of whom have been forced out for perceived political bias; some have left voluntarily for fear of retribution or to avoid carrying out orders they do not agree with. Though Bailey said he was leaving to spend more time with family, a New York Times report indicated that Bailey and Raia had somewhat of a contentious relationship with Patel and went long stretches without speaking to each other. When asked for comment, the FBI referred the Guardian to Bailey’s social media post announcing his resignation. On X, Patel thanked Bailey for his dedicated service. “Although Andrew is leaving the FBI in order to return to his family in Missouri, his fantastic contribution instituting critical reforms which resulted in our historic success will live on. Andrew’s leadership at the FBI will be missed but we are grateful he answered the call to serve!” Patel wrote.

title: Labour’s modest reheat of help to buy is worth a try | Nils Pratley
summary: Turning to George Osborne’s playbook may look awkward, but cutting deposits to 2.5% could jolt a housebuilding sector stuck in a funk
text: There may be three reasons why the Labour government has hesitated until now to reheat the Tories’ decade-long help-to-buy scheme. First, the inflationary risks of throwing subsidies at the housing market at a moment when wider inflation, driven by energy prices and the Iran war, is on the march. Second, the political awkwardness of turning to George Osborne’s playbook. Third, the spectre of Jeff Fairburn, the shameless former boss of Persimmon who bagged a £75m bonus in 2018 as help to buy turbo-charged the value of his share-based incentives. The government would look foolish if, in its desperation to meet its housebuilding targets (or just miss them by a smaller margin), it created more Fairburns. So is Your First Home – Labour’s incarnation – justified? On balance, it’s probably worth a punt. Something has to happen to try to shift the housebuilding sector out of its current funk. The way things are going, and the way mortgage rates are heading, Labour won’t merely miss its target of 1.5m new homes in England in this parliament, it will be short by a few hundreds of thousands. Like it or not, the government needs the private firms to boost construction. At the moment, the prevailing narrative is grumbles over labour costs, raw material costs, tax, regulation and more. Share buy-backs are being preferred over new projects. A tweak on the “affordability” dial at least has the virtue of getting results. Or, at least, that was a top-line conclusion in the official independent report published by the housing department earlier this month on help to buy. The scheme represented “very high value for money”, it said, with a net present social value of £25.1bn, in 2025 money, over its 2013-2023 lifetime thanks to the increase in housing supply. As for the inflationary impact, the report put it at two percentage points – far lower than popularly believed. From the government’s point of view, those trade-offs will look attractive when there is little else to excite in the economic outlook for 2027. Being seen to do something for aspiring first-time buyers unable to get on to the housing ladder is rarely a bad political look. Just don’t expect miracles. The 10%-plus jump in housebuilders’ shares prices on Monday, from beaten-down levels, may give a misleading impression. Your First Home will reduce the first-time buyer’s deposit to as little as 2.5% of the price of the property, from 5% under help to buy, but it is being launched in a very different climate. Back in 2013, interest rates were on the floor, and they would remain so for years. Now, the Bank rate stands at 3.75%, and the debate is about how many hikes Threadneedle Street has in store. A 20% equity loan from the government, with an interest-free period, makes a difference but obviously does not remove the impact of borrowing rates on the rest of the mortgage. And in this case the housebuilders will have to pay a fee to access the scheme – quite rightly, but they will presumably look to recoup some of that expense in the selling price. Full details, including the household income cap, the property price caps by region and the interest-free period, will arrive in the budget next month. All matter, so it’s too soon to make firm judgments. But the general principle here is to try to stimulate more supply of new-builds by modestly improving affordability for first-time buyers. In current circumstances, it’s not unreasonable.

title: Jean Clark obituary
summary: Other lives: Labour party activist and longstanding Harlow councillor
text: My friend and former colleague Jean Clark, who has died aged 92, was a successful teacher, lecturer and a key figure in Labour politics in Harlow, Essex. After moving to the town as a newly qualified English teacher in the 1950s, Jean became a great community activist, as a Labour party member, and as a member of Victory for Socialism, a leftwing pressure group within the party, which helped to get Stan Newens elected as Harlow’s Labour MP in 1964. Joining the International Socialists, she played a leading role in the Harlow Tenants’ Action group, which staged a rent strike in 1968 against Harlow Development Corporation’s rent rises and succeeded in getting them reduced. The following decade she returned to the Labour cause, and became secretary of the constituency party. In that role, she helped lead my campaign for election as Harlow’s MEP in 1994. She then became a longstanding Labour councillor in Harlow, serving until her retirement in 2023. Jean, as she was known all her life, was born Valerie Jean, in Exeter, to Ernest and Daisy Tucker, who owned a hardware shop. She was brought up in the West Country, where she was a county-level tennis player in her youth. After qualifying as a teacher in Lyme Regis, Jean moved to the rapidly growing new town of Harlow, where she taught English at Brays Grove school. Jean married a fellow teacher, Brian Clark, in 1957. They divorced while still relatively young and he later became known as the writer of the play Whose Life Is It Anyway? In the 1960s Jean gained a degree in sociology at London School of Economics, then became a lecturer at Balls Park teacher training college in Hertford, which later became part of Hertfordshire University, from where Jean retired as a senior tutor. Jean was warmly regarded by her colleagues and had many friends. A lifelong Guardian reader, she would walk every morning to Harlow Town station to buy her copy of the paper. A special tribute to her was held by Harlow council.

title: High screen time can hurt children’s learning and language skills, study suggests
summary: Effect of elevated screen exposure could be as significant as parental behaviour and premature birth, report says
text: The effect of high screen time on children is as significant as parental behaviour and premature birth, if not greater, a global study has found. Researchers examined data on more than 2.8 million children across 64 countries and concluded that elevated screen exposure could affect children in areas including academic achievement and emotional problems. It is one of the largest ever studies on the subject. The impacts are “similar in magnitude to or larger” than other factors linked to child development and mental health outcomes including family wealth, the behaviour of parents and whether or not children were born prematurely. Higher screen use for gaming, social media and streaming can lead to lower academic achievement and language development issues, the study suggests. Some experts said the report had limitations, arguing that the findings in “no way” support the belief that screens are the main cause of adolescent distress. Researchers found in the review, published in the journal JAMA Pediatrics, that children who spend more time on screens have higher “socioemotional” and mental health problems. Academics conducted a so-called umbrella review, which summarises results from previous large reviews on the topic. Researchers found that longer durations of digital and social media use were linked to “less favourable outcomes across multiple (although not all) measured domains of children’s developmental health”. The analysis covered a variety of devices, from smartphones to televisions, and a range of activities including scrolling social media, gaming and FaceTime calls. “Together, the findings suggest that screen use may represent one potentially modifiable factor associated with children’s wellbeing across multiple domains,” the report said. It found that greater screen exposure was associated with overall lower grades at school. When academics examined specific subjects, screen time did not appear to be linked to maths, reading or science attainment, but the researchers said these were “among the least studied”, so the finding may be due to a lack of evidence. The researchers, led by academics at the University of Calgary in Canada, did find that higher screen time was also linked to poorer language development. When they looked at mental health, they found that higher screen use was linked to emotional and “peer problems”; “internalising behaviour”, which includes symptoms of depression and anxiety; and externalising behaviour, including aggression and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder symptoms. “Our review revealed that higher so-called doses of screen exposure are associated with lower overall academic achievement and poorer language development, as well as higher internalising and externalising behaviour, emotional problems and peer problems,” the authors wrote. “Notably, these effect sizes are similar in magnitude to or larger than those reported for other well-established predictors of children’s outcomes, such as socioeconomic status, parenting behaviour and preterm birth.” Tatiana Íñiguez Berrozpe, a senior lecturer in sociology at the University of Zaragoza in Spain, said the report showed an association between screen time and poor mental health and academic performance, but it was small. “This is not an insignificant finding, but it in no way supports the mantra that screens are the main cause of adolescent emotional distress,” she said. “Screen use alone does not explain why a teenager is emotionally distressed or performs less well academically.” Esther van Sluijs, a professor of behavioural epidemiology at Loughborough University, said the study was “high-quality” but could not differentiate between different types of screen use. “It cannot draw robust conclusions about specific types of screen use, like social media use or gaming, as there was not enough data to study this. We should therefore be cautious in interpreting these results in the context of young people’s current screen use habits,” she said. Additional reporting by Press Association

title: German Town Votes to Stop Adding Memorials Outside Homes of Slain Jews

title: Trump’s deportations to third countries violate human rights, UN experts warn
summary: Sending migrants to countries they do not come from can have deadly consequences and must be halted, says report
text: The deportation of thousands of migrants from the US to third countries has set off a “cascade of human rights violations” that could have “deadly” consequences, two dozen UN human rights experts have warned. Since Donald Trump returned to power in 2025, the US government has been offering millions of dollars to foreign governments to take in migrants, including refugees and asylum seekers, with no ties to their countries. Deals have been struck with 35 nations, nearly a third of them in Africa. About 20,000 people have been taken by bus to Mexico, according to Refugees International and Human Rights First. More than 5,000 others have been put on flights to countries in Africa, Latin America, the Caribbean and central Asia. On Monday, 24 experts who advise the UN Human Rights Council – backed by a special rapporteur for the African Commission – said they had contacted the US and each of the 35 countries to express their concerns and call for an immediate halt to the policy. “The harms caused by this US government scheme are no longer hypothetical,” they said in a joint statement. “The arrangements are triggering a cascade of human rights violations. For migrants in situations of particular vulnerability, the consequences can be deadly.” Those being banished to countries where they had no connections faced an increased risk of torture and ill-treatment, as well as enforced disappearances, they noted. “These migrants are being transferred to countries or territories with which they have no ties, which can be a traumatising and isolating experience that compounds harms already suffered which triggered their fleeing to the US in the first place. Others are sent to places where they risk further violence or discrimination based on gender, sexual orientation, gender identity or human rights advocacy.” The Trump administration says deportations are focused on removing criminals from the US. However, an investigation by the Guardian as part of a consortium of journalists coordinated by the Forbidden Stories network uncovered the ordeals of some who have been deported. They included an Iranian woman who had sought safety in the US after protesting against the regime and a gay man who had fled Ghana after he was outed, then hunted, by members of his own family. On Monday, the UN-linked experts warned that deportations to unfamiliar countries could leave people vulnerable to other violations, from trafficking to slavery. In some cases, the countries that have struck deals with the US are engulfed in conflict, meaning US arrivals were turning up in places where people were already grappling with displacement, starvation and debilitating poverty. These countries, the statement noted, “lack the capacity to protect the rights of migrants sent there by wealthy nations seeking to shirk their international obligations”. Human rights lawyers say the deportations allow the US administration to skirt around its legal obligations because US law does not allow people to be sent back to countries where they are likely to be persecuted. Instead, the Department of Homeland Security has been deporting migrants, including asylum seekers, to third countries. From there, they are often moved on to home countries they had fled. Monday’s statement pointed to the severe impact this could have on people who were already vulnerable: “What is at stake is not merely migration policy, but the lives, safety, dignity and rights of people who may already have endured grave harm and who, in many cases, are fleeing life-threatening persecution and violence in their home countries.” It was the first comprehensive statement of its kind, according to Beatrice Njeri of the Global Strategic Litigation Council, which has represented people expelled from the US to third countries. “It comes at a very important point in time when we are continuing to see extreme human rights violations that are super horrific,” she said, citing two men expelled to Equatorial Guinea who had been bound, fitted with bags over their heads, beaten and pushed down a flight of stairs. Njeri, who works as the organisation’s regional litigator for Africa, said the African states involved in the scheme had paid little attention to any of the pleas, litigation and advocacy aimed at halting these arrangements. “So, it has felt like we’re screaming into a void. And we hope that this statement will contribute to trying to hold these states accountable.” She said some EU countries were ramping up their own calls for the creation of offshore centres for migrants. “This is a good warning to them not to follow suit,” she said. “European states now clearly know how African states are implementing the agreements, violating people’s rights and offering no redress. And so they have no excuse.”

title: ‘Starship is in orbit’: cheers go up as huge SpaceX rocket circles Earth for first time
summary: Mission goes ahead despite some fears an initial engine failure after the Texas launch would scupper the attempt
text: SpaceX has sent its enormous Starship rocket into Earth’s orbit for the first time on a milestone flight intended to pave the way for future missions to the moon and Mars. The rocket, the largest and most powerful ever built, blasted off from SpaceX’s Starbase launch facility in Texas at 7.48am local time (1.48pm BST), marking its 14th test flight and first attempt to circle the planet before falling back to Earth. Despite an engine failure on ascent that threatened to prevent Starship from reaching orbit, mission controllers decided it was safe to press ahead with a burn that pushed the ship on to a planned trajectory to take it around the planet. Cheers and applause broke out at SpaceX after initial suggestions that the orbit attempt might be abandoned were quashed and the decision to go ahead was announced. Moments after the orbit burn, Daniel Hewitt, an engineer who was narrating a live stream of the launch, declared: “Starship is in orbit.” Elon Musk’s company has flown Starship in its full form since 2023 but previous test flights have only sought to put the rocket into suborbital trajectories, which are simpler and carry fewer risks for the public. For suborbital flights, the trajectory is such that if the rocket explodes or malfunctions mid-flight, the remnants come down in the Indian Ocean far from populated areas. The risks are harder to control when rockets are on full orbital paths around the planet. Starship soared to an altitude of about 171 miles (275km), with the original aim of completing six loops of Earth in nearly 10 hours before splashing down in the Pacific Ocean somewhere west of Chile. More than an hour into the mission however, SpaceX said Starship would come back early, aiming for a landing about three hours after launch in the north Pacific. Martin Barstow, a professor of astrophysics and space science at the University of Leicester, said: “This is an important milestone for SpaceX, with Starship successfully reaching orbit, and at the first attempt.” The achievement “marks the beginning of the transition from the testing and development phase to becoming a working vehicle able to deliver the large payloads needed to return to the moon,” he added. “Congratulations to the whole SpaceX team. Having this large launch capability will also be transformational for the whole space industry.” On the launchpad, the rocket stands more than 120 metres tall, with the Starship upper stage sitting on the “Super Heavy” booster stage. To remain in orbit, the rocket is required to travel at about 28,000km/h (17,400mph). A successful mission will be a relief for SpaceX and Nasa, who hope to use Starship to carry astronauts to the moon as part of a new era of lunar expeditions. It will also cheer investors after the company’s high-profile launch on the stock market in June. The company’s stock price rose sharply in the initial public offering before falling back. It has since recovered some of those losses. During the mission, SpaceX staff watched the booster launch, ascend and separate from the Starship upper stage, then return to an offshore landing point in the Gulf of Mexico. The company did not intend to catch the booster in giant mechanical arms, as it did after a previous test flight in 2024. Engineers modified the rocket’s hardware and software to overcome glitches that emerged during the last test flight. After stage separation, the booster should flip over and fire its engines to send it back to Earth, but on the last test flight the manoeuvre was ended early because three engines started to clog up with ice. The booster then attempted a landing burn with only eight of 13 planned engines reigniting, leading to a hard landing in the water. On the latest test flight, Starship deployed 26 next-generation Starlink satellites. Three carried cameras to capture images of Starship’s heat shield that will feed into testing for future missions. On coming back to Earth, Starship used its four aerodynamic flaps to control its speed and orientation and bellyflop horizontally towards its designated landing zone in the north Pacific. As it approached the water, the ship righted itself and slowed down before erupting in a ball of flames. Musk has set himself the ambitious target of developing fully reusable rockets to speed up mission turnaround times and reduce the costs of future space travel. But several Starship test flights have ended in failure. In March last year, the rocket exploded soon after launch and scattered debris over the Bahamas. Two months later, Starship span out of control shortly after separating from its booster. A month after that, the rocket exploded during preparations for a test flight.

title: Dozens arrested at pro-Palestine protest on Sunday outside Labour conference
summary: Merseyside force says 82 people arrested and another 79 reported for summons during demonstration
text: More than 160 people were arrested or reported for summons at a pro-Palestine demonstration outside the Labour party conference on Sunday, police have said. Officers arrested 82 people on suspicion of wearing or carrying an article supporting a proscribed organisation, according to the Merseyside force. They were taken into police custody before being released on bail. A further 79 people were reported for summons. In a protest organised by Defend Our Juries, scores of people sat outside the conference centre in Liverpool, many holding handmade banners saying they supported the banned group Palestine Action. In a statement, Merseyside police said it estimated 180 people attended, and that “not everyone present was committing a criminal offence”. Two activists also confronted the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, during a meal in Pizza Express in the city centre where he was challenged about the arrests. Video of the incident showed one of the protesters urging Miliband to declare a genocide in Gaza and de-proscribe Palestine Action. Miliband said he was happy to discuss the issue but at another time, before the protesters were ushered out. The number of arrests this year is 16 more than were arrested at a similar pro-Palestine demonstration on the first day of Labour’s conference last year in Liverpool. A police statement said: “Merseyside police respects everyone’s rights to protest lawfully, while also aiming to keep the peace and ensure the public are safe. “The force makes detailed and coordinated plans ahead of such events to ensure it can apply this consistently, fairly and proportionately.” Supt Peter Clark of force operations at Merseyside police said: “We have a comprehensive policing plan in place to deal with incidents, and have been working closely with partners including Liverpool Experience Campus, event organisers and security providers to ensure the smooth and safe running of the Labour party conference. “Merseyside police respects the right to protest, but where offences are committed, proportionate action will be taken.” Defend Our Juries claimed more than 200 people took part in the protest. It said: “Inside the Labour party conference today, Ed Miliband will tell campaigners and party members that they were right to build political pressure over Gaza with their protests. “The hypocrisy is breathtaking. If he means what he says, why are those taking a principled stand against genocide still being arrested as terrorists?” The group said one of those arrested was the 94-year-old human rights barrister Margaret Owen.

title: Avanti West Coast to be renationalised in March as ministers float public ownership of new trains
summary: Andy Burnham hails nationalisation of much-criticised service between London, Birmingham and Glasgow
text: Britain’s biggest intercity rail operator, Avanti West Coast, will be renationalised in spring, ministers have announced, while new trains could also be publicly owned under plans to reduce costs paid to private firms. Avanti, which has been one of the worst rail firms in the country for train delays and cancellations, will come under public ownership from 7 March when its contract ends. Andy Burnham said “enough is enough” for passengers who had put up with a rail service “that has failed them time and time again”. The Labour government has been nationalising passenger rail services across the country as their contracts have expired, as the public body Great British Railways prepares to take full oversight in 2027. The transport secretary, Heidi Alexander, formally announced the decision to nationalise Avanti at the “earliest opportunity” in her speech at the Labour conference on Tuesday afternoon, and said the government would also explore bringing trains into public ownership. Train operators currently lease trains from private rolling-stock companies (Roscos) at the cost of several billion pounds a year. Alexander said the practice since privatisation meant train operating companies “saved money upfront, but it also brought significant long-term costs”. “In 2024, franchised train operators spent over £4bn leasing and maintaining trains they didn’t own – £4bn, that is about a third of the total day-to-day running costs of operating railway services. “Every Rosco contract includes financing and transaction costs and investment returns, costs which are ultimately borne by taxpayers and passengers. “So, as we set up Great British Railways, we will explore whether the state can directly own the new trains we order.” She added: “If GBR owning trains would best serve taxpayers and passengers, then we should do it.” Unions welcomed the news. The RMT’s general secretary, Eddie Dempsey, said Roscos were “sucking much-needed money out of the railways and into offshore bank accounts”, adding: “This should be the start of a process of winding up the rolling stock racket once and for all.” Dave Calfe, the general secretary of Aslef, the train drivers’ union, said it was “a big step forward for our railway”, adding: “Billions of pounds haemorrhage from the network in profits and dividends which could – and should – be invested in our railway and help keep fares for passengers down.” However, the government said that owning new trains would happen on a “case-by-case basis”, and a rolling stock firm director who had been briefed indicated there was no question of nationalising existing trains. For now, the confirmed nationalisation date of Avanti brings into public ownership a service which had been notorious with unions and passengers – including the prime minister. The company connects the north and south of England, with its service running from London to Manchester and Liverpool. It also runs services through the north-west of England and on to Wales, Glasgow and Edinburgh. The prime minister has previously complained about high prices on Avanti, with tickets for peak-time returns from Manchester to London costing as much as £300. Burnham wrote on social media that “for years, people have been expected to put up with Avanti’s cancellations, delays, overcrowding, and a service that has failed them time and time again”. “So my Labour government is bringing Avanti West Coast into public ownership at the earliest opportunity in March next year. That means passengers, not shareholders, will come first. “More investment, fewer delays, and a renewed focus on getting the basics right. We’re putting essential services back in public hands and building a railway that actually works for the people who use it.” Avanti has the worst punctuality rating for any large rail company in the UK. Andy Mellors, the managing director at Avanti West Coast, said: “We’re proud of what we’ve achieved over the last six years – from refurbishing our Pendolino fleet and introducing our new Evero trains to running more services than ever before.” He said the improvements had given “customers greater choice, more capacity and better connectivity, while we’ve continued to innovate to shape the future of the west coast and wider rail industry”. Earlier this month, Chiltern Railways became the latest train operator to enter public ownership, becoming the sixth to be nationalised under Labour, with the remaining four to follow by the end of 2027. The next operator to transfer into public ownership is scheduled to be Great Western Railway in December. East Midlands Railway is scheduled to be nationalised between this winter and mid-2027, and the last is CrossCountry, in autumn 2027.

title: Texas Republican called for public execution of Democratic leaders – report
summary: Bo French, who is running to lead a state agency, has in the past posted controversial and racist statements online
text: Bo French, a Texas Republican running to lead a powerful state agency, has a history of making controversial social media posts, including calling for the public execution of Democratic leaders, according to a recent investigation from CNN’s KFile team. French, who is running to lead Texas’s railroad commission, has recently faced criticism from members of his own party after making a racist post on social media. Powerful Republicans, including the Texas senator John Cornyn, said they would not support French in the upcoming election. But the latest spat over French’s social media has led to a deeper look at his online history. In a review of old posts from social media accounts that seemingly belonged to French, CNN’s KFile team found that the Texas Republican repeatedly called for public executions of opponents. In 2020, French used a now-suspended X account to seemingly call for the execution of former president Barack Obama and other Obama administration officials that he believed had disseminated false information about Russia’s involvement in the 2016 presidential election. In February 2025, French used his X account, under a former handle, to call for other public executions, including Senator Adam Schiff. The Guardian has asked French’s campaign for comment. French is no stranger to posting controversial statements online. Over the last year, he has used his platform to assert that the entire religion of Islam should be banned; claim childless women were “selfish” and “responsible for the demise of our culture”; and posted a poll to ask whether “Jews” or “Muslims” posed a bigger threat. According to CNN/KFile’s investigation, in May 2020 French used an account under the name “rwbofrench”, which has since been suspended, to encourage Donald Trump to “hang” Obama-era officials believed to be part of the “Russia hoax”. The posts came after Trump accused Obama administration officials of “treason” to dismiss reports that Russia tried to interfere with the 2016 presidential election to assist Trump. In response to Trump’s “Drain the Swamp” post, French wrote: “I agree. But you can not do that until your DOJ charges and prosecutes the treasonous bastards who spearheaded the Russia hoax. The death penalty for the Obama conspirators will be the only thing that pulls the stopper out of the drain. #HangEmHigh.” Minutes later, French responded to another social media user who accused Obama of running the Russia interference, seemingly promoting the death penalty for the former president. “The penalty for treason used to be death. Even for a former president. #HangEmHigh,” French wrote. It was unclear why the account was suspended. In another instance of calling for public executions, French used his current social media account, under the former handle “Bo_French_TX”, to call for the death of government officials identified by Elon Musk’s Doge team. “I want more than perp walks. I want public executions,” French wrote in a now-deleted post from February 2025. In another post, French called for the public execution of Schiff, who led the House committee that released the report on Russia’s interference in the 2016 election. It was unclear whether the latest social media posts were deleted by French or a member of his team.
