title: Palestine has become electoral issue in UK for first time, says solidarity campaign chief
summary: Anger over Israel’s war in Gaza is mobilising British voters, according to Aimee Shalan
text: Palestine has become a domestic electoral issue in Britain for the first time, according to the incoming head of the country’s largest Palestinian solidarity organisation. Aimee Shalan, who will take over as director of the Palestine Solidarity Campaign (PSC) in November, joins the organisation as demonstrations against Israel’s war in Gaza have snowballed into what organisers describe as one of the most sustained protest movements in modern British history. She said public anger over Israel’s treatment of Palestinians and Britain’s response was increasingly being expressed not just through demonstrations but at elections, in workplaces and trade unions and through consumer campaigns. Speaking before a PSC protest at the Labour party conference, Shalan said: “We’re seeing for the first time in British history Palestine become a domestic issue, electorally, at the national level and at the local level.” The shift was visible at the 2024 general election and 2026 local elections, where pro-Palestinian candidates made major breakthroughs. Shalan pointed to the foreign secretary Ed Miliband’s announcement of sanctions against settlements in the occupied Palestinian territories as a notable success for their movement. Miliband said at the Labour conference on Monday: “I want to say to the millions of people in this country and indeed elsewhere who have been moved and outraged by the plight of the Palestinian people: we hear you, you were right.” He described the sanctions as a definitive change in how Labour would approach the situation in the Middle East. Shalan said: “That shift is a testament to the mass movement. Both internationally, but specifically also here in Britain, with hundreds of thousands of people marching, campaigning, lobbying. “He [Miliband] says he hears the British public, but his announcement falls far short of the clear and immediate actions millions of people have been calling for: full sanctions on the state of Israel, including a two-way arms embargo, an end to material support for Israel’s military operations and an end to British political and diplomatic support for an apartheid state.” Shalan welcomed the shift within the Labour government but said the sanctions announcement would be “very little solace for Palestinians whose lives have been brutally destroyed through Israel’s relentless oppression and genocide”. She pointed to the 70,000 Palestinians killed in Israel’s war in Gaza and the more than 1,300, including at least 300 children, killed since a ceasefire was signed last year. The PSC says its individual membership has more than doubled from 7,800 at the beginning of 2023 to nearly 17,000, with subscribers to its newsletters rising from 70,000 to about 300,000. Along with partner groups, it has organised 36 national demonstrations since October 2023, some drawing hundreds of thousands of people. Organisers say the demonstrations represent one of the largest and most sustained protest movements in British history. Shalan said: “It’s been uplifting to see the level of support and the connections that people are making between their own lives, and other liberation and social justice struggles, and the Palestinian cause.” But the demonstrations have been contested. Some politicians and campaign groups have raised concerns about antisemitism surrounding pro-Palestinian protests, with critics describing them as “hate marches”. Shalan rejected that characterisation as a smear against the movement, saying: “Those marches have been a really wonderful coming together of communities of all sorts of different faiths, of all sorts of different backgrounds, young and old, of all sorts of different ethnicities.” Shalan also rejected calls for the PSC to be designated an extremist organisation, arguing that attempts to criminalise parts of the Palestine solidarity movement were increasingly at odds with public opinion. “You can try and criminalise, but all it will do is anger the public more,” she said. “That’s why we’re seeing people going out on the streets and risking being arrested because they refuse to be hobbled by this effort to criminalise both Palestinians and those that stand in support. “Those who are responsible for trying to criminalise support for Palestinians and their rights, and supporters trying to end a horrific genocide, should hang their heads in shame.” Supporters attending national demonstrations are directed toward a network of more than 100 local branches, which organise campaigns in communities, workplaces and universities and lobby councils and MPs. The PSC says 34 councils in England and Wales have committed to supporting the divestment of their pension funds from companies that campaigners accuse of complicity in Israel’s actions. The PSC’s influence has also grown within the trade union movement. The Trades Union Congress is backing the Palestinian-led boycott, divestment and sanctions (BDS) movement, supporting workplace campaigns and divestment from companies it says are complicit in abuses against Palestinians. Shalan defended BDS after Miliband said he “wholeheartedly” opposed the campaign. “BDS is a set of tactics that provide a peaceful way for people to campaign for human rights, for justice, for accountability,” she said. Shalan, who is British Palestinian, has spent nearly three decades campaigning for Palestinian rights. She is the director of Makan, a Palestinian-led educational organisation, and has served as chief executive of Medical Aid for Palestinians and as director of Friends of Birzeit University, which has changed its name to Friends of Palestinian Universities. She holds a doctorate on the politics of Palestinian literature. The group’s Pledge for Palestine campaign was signed by more than 2,200 candidates before this year’s local elections and it plans to repeat this at the next general election. “There’s a very short time before the next election and we need to have a very robust movement that ensures that we don’t sleepwalk into what appears to be a really deeply authoritarian future,” Shalan said. She compared the Palestine solidarity movement to the international campaign against apartheid South Africa, while stressing that the histories were not identical. “People can’t unsee what they’ve seen,” she said. “People are finding ways to be mobilised in different spheres. And support for Palestinian freedom and justice will only continue to grow”

title: Trump administration to slash clean car rules aimed at cutting climate emissions
summary: Environmentalists decry move that relaxes requirements on automakers to control pollution from gas-powered cars
text: The Trump administration on Monday announced it was slashing clean car rules that had been aimed at reducing planet-heating emissions and boosting electric vehicles. The move, which was criticized by environmentalists, relaxes requirements on automakers to control pollution from gasoline-powered cars and light trucks for model years 2022 through 2031. The new rule, announced by the Department of Transportation, reverses a push by the Biden administration to accelerate the transition to EVs. Transportation is the largest source of climate emissions in the United States, accounting for about 28% of total US greenhouse gas emissions according to the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). Monday’s move follows the Trump administration’s rollback of the government’s ability to impose requirements to track, report and limit climate-heating pollution from cars and trucks. Donald Trump said on Truth Social on Saturday that the less stringent mileage requirements would “take the waste out of building cars in America” and save families “thousands on a new, beautiful and safe car”, while boosting auto production in the US. Trump has repeatedly pledged to end what he falsely calls an EV “mandate”, referring incorrectly to Joe Biden’s target that half of all new vehicle sales be electric by 2030. No federal policy has mandated auto companies to sell EVs. Sean Duffy, the US transportation secretary, hailed the new initiative – called Freedom Means Affordable Cars – which the agency said would reduce the average cost of new vehicles by $1,300, and save consumers $138bn over the next five years. Duffy said: “Thanks to President Trump’s leadership, we have finally ended the illegal mandate that forced automakers to produce more expensive electric vehicles that American families didn’t want.” Green groups condemned the new rules. Dan Becker, director of the Center for Biological Diversity’s safe climate transport campaign, said that the final rule “ignores the feasibility of clean technology and the millions of fuel-efficient cars already on the road”. “Trump is tanking sensible mile per gallon standards at the worst possible time for consumers, who are getting hit with sky-high prices at the pump,” Becker said in a statement. “Consumers will pay the price for these reckless rollbacks while Trump’s Big Oil and Big Auto buddies reap the short-term profits.” Katherine García, director of the Sierra Club’s Clean transportation for all campaign, vowed the environmental group would fight the rule and said that the loosening of fuel standards would “make driving more expensive too”. Fuel economy requirements set out how far new vehicles need to travel on a gallon of gasoline. The Biden administration had increased required fuel efficiency for cars by 8% annually for model years 2024 and 2025, 10% for 2026 and 2% annually from 2027 to 2031. The Trump ‌administration ⁠in December proposed retroactively revising down the 2022 model year fuel economy standard and then raising it between 0.25% and 0.5% annually through 2031. It estimated its proposal would cut average ⁠new vehicle costs by $930 each. But it would increase fuel consumption by about 100bn gallons through 2050, fuel spending by $185bn and carbon dioxide emissions by about 5%, the department said. The American Lung Association’s president and CEO, Harold Wimmer, said the new rule will “create more air pollution, harm health and accelerate climate change”. Wimmer added: “For decades, fuel economy standards have ensured that new cars, SUVs and pickup trucks are more efficient, which saves lives and money. There is no reason to weaken standards that are technologically feasible and have a direct benefit for the quality of the air people breathe. “Children are particularly vulnerable to the effects of traffic pollution, which can impede lung growth, cause new cases of pediatric asthma, make asthma symptoms worse and increase kids’ risk of respiratory infection and diseases.” Wimmer added that making new cars cleaner had widespread public support, citing a poll the group did that found a strong majority of voters supported stricter limits on vehicle emissions.

title: DRC politician beaten to death after radio appearance about Ebola outbreak
summary: Marie-Celestin Karondwa was attacked on Sunday after promoting measures to prevent spread of disease, his party says
text: A senior member of the Democratic Republic of the Congo’s ruling party was beaten to death on Sunday after appearing on a radio programme to raise awareness about the Ebola outbreak, a party representative has said. Marie-Celestin Karondwa, the acting president of the Union for Democracy and Social Progress (UDPS) party’s federal executive committee in Butembo, a new hotspot for the outbreak, was attacked after taking part in a radio show during which he ‌promoted prevention measures for the disease, ‌the UDPS federation in the city said in a statement, Reuters reported. The party ‌said the attackers beat Karondwa, stole his belongings and set his house on fire, and that he later died from his injuries. It was not immediately clear who carried out the attack, how many people were involved or what motivated it, but the party said Karondwa was “an innocent victim for having defended ‌the party’s position on the existence of the Ebola virus disease … and the threat it poses to the population”. Karondwa’s death comes after a series of attacks on healthcare workers and treatment centres that experts say are fuelled by rumours and misinformation about the disease and distrust of health responders. The incidents have included violence, riots and property damage and the disruption of essential services. On Saturday, armed men attacked a hand-washing checkpoint in the nearby Beni territory, killing at least one person and wounding ‌several others, a local civil society group reported. First identified in 1976 in what is now the DRC, Ebola is a highly contagious and often fatal viral disease that affects humans and non-human primates. It spreads through body fluids or contaminated materials and causes organ damage, blood vessel impairment and sometimes severe internal and external bleeding. The current outbreak is caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, which has no approved treatment or vaccine. It was first announced on 15 May and has infected 8,067 people and killed 3,901, according to data from the DRC’s health ministry. Cases of the disease have been confirmed in seven provinces. The outbreak is the largest and deadliest in the DRC’s history and second only globally to the 2014-16 outbreak in west Africa, which infected more than ‌28,600 people and killed more than 11,000. Data from the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention shows the current outbreak has outpaced the west African one. Last month, the World Health Organization warned it was on track to surpass the west Africa outbreak. Experts say the spread of the disease has been intensified by several factors, including conflict, aid cuts and the attacks on healthcare workers and treatment centres. Reuters contributed to this report

title: Gene-edited bananas that don’t go brown could hit UK supermarkets
summary: Scientific breakthrough could reduce food waste and make it easier to add the fruit to prepackaged food
text: It is the bane of every fruit bowl: sliced banana that turns brown before it has reached the table. But such woes could soon be a thing of the past, with gene-edited bananas that keep their freshly peeled colour now one step closer to reaching British shoppers. According to Tropic, the Norwich-based agricultural-biotechnology company that developed the fruit, the bananas have the same taste and texture but stay “fresh, yellow and appetising long after peeling and slicing”. Gilad Gershon, the chief executive of Tropic, said the flesh of the new banana resisted browning for an extra day or two – and longer if chilled. He added that the innovation could make it easier to add bananas to prepackaged products such as fruit salads and breakfast pots, as well as reducing waste. The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) last week approved a marketing notice for the bananas, confirming their precision-bred status – one of two important requirements for them to be placed on the market. According to the Food Standards Agency (FSA), precision-bred status is given only if the genetic changes made could have been achieved through traditional breeding methods. This is different from genetic modification because precision-bred organisms do not contain DNA from unrelated species. Prof Cathie Martin, a project leader at the John Innes Centre in Norwich, who has worked on gene-edited tomatoes, said the next stage for all crops that had received marketing approval – including the new bananas – was a review by the FSA to ensure the safety of the products. “It is not entirely clear how long this will take,” she said. Tropic developed the bananas by using a gene-editing technology called Crispr-Cas9 to alter all three copies of a single gene within the fruit. As a result, they were able to reduce the production of polyphenol oxidase, an enzyme that causes browning. A similar approach has been effective in reducing browning in other produce, including mushrooms. Tropic said the non-browning bananas could reduce food waste and CO2-equivalent emissions along the supply chain by more than 25%. “This could support an annual reduction in CO2 emissions of over 9m tonnes in the banana export market alone,” the company said. A government study found that 1.4m edible bananas were thrown away each day. A third of consumers (30%) said they had discarded a banana owing to a minor bruise or black mark on the skin. Gene editing has been used by researchers to develop sweeter-tasting strawberries, disease-resistant crops and tomatoes that are more compact or high in vitamin D. Regulations for precision-bred plants came into effect in November last year and apply only to England. However, the FSA notes precision-bred foods that are authorised and placed on the market in England can be sold in Wales and Scotland, provided they are not processed further, with similar rules for Northern Ireland. No precision-bred organisms have been granted market authorisation for sale in England. Gershon said Tropic had gained regulatory approval for the non-browning bananas in 10 other countries including Japan, Brazil and the Philippines. The fruit is already being grown in Latin America. A Defra spokesperson said: “Precision breeding offers huge potential to boost food security, cut pesticide use, increase crop yields and enhance disease resistance. “[The non-browning banana] is a great example of how innovation could help to reduce food waste and improve the sustainability of our food system while keeping our world-leading standards in place.”

title: Shabana Mahmood hints she could water down plans on leave to remain
summary: Home secretary under pressure over changes that would make it harder for foreign workers to claim permanent residence
text: Shabana Mahmood has signalled she could water down her plans to make it harder for foreign workers to claim permanent residence in the UK, amid growing demands for a U-turn from cabinet colleagues and unions. In a speech to the Labour party conference, the home secretary said the government would “come to a position that balances fairness for those who came here legally and fairness to British citizens across this country”, after acknowledging that “some have said elements of these reforms are not fair”. Her comments follow demands from Angela Rayner and from Unison’s general secretary, Andrea Egan, to drop changes to indefinite leave to remain that would penalise overseas care workers looking after the UK’s older citizens. Mahmood told the conference in Liverpool: “As we restore control and fairness to our asylum system, we must do the same for legal migration too. Fair to those who seek a new and better life here, like my parents did, and fair to those already here, including British workers, and especially the young. “That same principle underpins my reforms to the right to live here indefinitely, ensuring settled status is earned by those who have shown a consistent commitment to this country. I know that throughout our consultation process some have said elements of these reforms are not fair. To that, let me say this: we will come to a position that balances fairness for those who came here legally, and fairness to British citizens across this country.” Last year the government changed visa laws to end the recruitment of care workers from abroad in an attempt to reduce net migration. It also banned care workers from bringing family dependants with them. Mahmood’s plans would increase the timeline for permanent residence from five to 15 years for social care workers who arrived on health and care visas. The changes would apply retrospectively to people who have arrived since 2021. Rayner, the housing, communities and local government secretary, said over the weekend that Mahmood’s plans would hit foreign care workers who had “moved their lives here to look after our loved ones”. Speaking to the Guardian’s Politics Weekly podcast, the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, who was brought to the UK as a child fleeing the civil war in Liberia, admitted her family would have found Mahmood’s changes tough. “It would have been tough,” she said. “I represent a constituency which is hugely diverse, where we’ve got first-, second-, third-generation immigrants, and how we navigate this landscape has been tough.” A protest outside the conference on Monday by a leading trade union called for migrant workers not to be made scapegoats for the failure to invest in public services. Egan said: “People who came to this country to help look after our loved ones are forced to work on restricted visas under harsh rules which make them second-class citizens. Now the promise of being able to settle in the country after five years is not only being broken but replaced with the threat of 15 years of insecurity and exploitation. Moving the goalposts at this stage in the game is wrong and unfair.” Sources close to Mahmood said no decision had been made on the indefinite leave to remain proposals, adding that the speech set out the principles underpinning those decisions. In a further development, Mahmood said that from next month the government would begin accepting applications from charities and nonprofit organisations to sponsor refugees through new safe and legal routes. “This will start with a community sponsorship route, allowing local communities to host refugees, and a student sponsorship route, allowing universities to do the same. Applications will open in October, with the first arrivals in autumn of next year,” she said. She confirmed that the government would reopen the UK resettlement route in partnership with the United Nations. “We will take vulnerable refugees from across the world and give them the chance of a new and better life here in Britain, with the first arrivals beginning this year. I am proud to say that around a quarter will be Afghan women and girls fleeing persecution under the Taliban, and Palestinians who have fled the horrors of Gaza,” she said. Immigration experts and refugee charities have welcomed the plans but said the numbers who would be eligible for the schemes were too small to deter asylum seekers from crossing the Channel in small boats. In a personal section of the speech, Mahmood said her parents came to Britain from rural Kashmir “because they knew they would get a fair shot at a better life here; a fairer shot than they could ever expect back home, where past was precedent and your birth dictated your future.” She said: “They were largely welcomed to this country, because most Brits thought it was right to welcome people who come here legally, [to] build a life, and contribute to our nation. There were exceptions to that welcome, of course. This was the 1970s. But they were exceptions, not the rule. “Fairness is what unites us in this country. And a fair society unlocks the very best of us. When fairness isn’t present, the opposite is true. When this country feels unfair, people turn inwards. A Britain that is unfair is one that is smaller and colder for those who look like me.” Mahmood’s successful moves to bring down overall migration by restricting visas are expected to give the chancellor, John Healey, an even bigger challenge after immigration significantly undershot projections from the Office for Budget Responsibility. The Institute for Fiscal Studies thinktank estimated last month that the success of Mahmood’s measures, which have led to net migration being cut to the low hundreds of thousands, could cost Healey about £4bn. On Monday, the Times reported sources familiar with the budget process as saying the figure was now closer to £6.5bn.

title: Did you solve it? Isaac Newton’s tower drop puzzle
summary: The solution to the seventeenth century stumper
text: Earlier today I set you a puzzle that Isaac Newton posed in 1679 in a latter to Robert Hooke. I mentioned that the answer is counter-intuitive, and also gave you the hint that it might have something to do with figure skating. Here’s the problem again, with its solution. The tower drop An object is dropped from a high tower. Bearing in mind the rotation of the Earth itself, where will the object land? slightly to the west slightly to the east exactly at the bottom Solution 2. slightly to the east. The Earth rotates from west to east. Our first thought might be that the object falls slightly to the west, on the grounds that as the object is falling the Earth will rotate slightly to the east. But such an argument ignores the fact that the object is originally – like the tower itself – rotating with the Earth. Our second thought might be that it lands exactly at the bottom of the tower. Again wrong! The object lands slightly to the east because as it falls it spins about its axis slightly faster, by essentially the same mechanism that makes a spinning ice-skater spin faster when they pull in their arms. It is in this way, then, that the object lands slightly to the east. The effect is small, but not absurdly so. If the Eiffel tower were on the equator the deflection to the east would be about 11cm. In more technical detail, the result follows from conservation of angular momentum, which is a measure of the momentum of an object rotating about an axis. When an object is falling from a tower, gravity is pushing it towards the centre of mass of the Earth. Yet the object is also spinning in a circle around the centre of the Earth. As the object falls its angular momentum stays the same. Which means that the expression wr2 – where w is the object’s angular velocity and r is its distance to the rotational axis (in this case, the centre of the Earth) – stays the same. Since the value of r decreases during the fall, the value of w must increase, which means that the object spins faster. If it spins faster than the Earth is spinning it will land slightly to the east of the position directly underneath the tower. Thanks to David Acheson for today’s puzzle. He is the author of a new book, Wonders in Motion, The Story of Dynamics, which among other things explains the background to Newton’s puzzle in more detail. I hope you had fun. I’ll be back in two weeks. Wonders of Motion by David Acheson is on sale at the Guardian Bookshop. I’ve been setting a puzzle here on alternate Mondays since 2015. I’m always on the look-out for great puzzles. If you would like to suggest one, email me.

title: Golders Green stabbings no longer being treated as suspected terrorism
summary: Police say attack on two Jewish men in north London in April now being treated as alleged hate crime
text: The stabbings of two Jewish men in Golders Green, north London, in April are being treated as an alleged hate crime and not as a terrorist attack, police have said. Essa Suleiman, 45, was arrested by the Metropolitan police on suspicion of attempted murder shortly after the stabbings on 29 April. At the time, police said they were treating the attacks, in an area with a large Jewish population, as suspected terrorist offences. Suleiman has also been charged with attempted murder over the unconnected stabbing of another man earlier that same day. On Friday, Suleiman appeared in court for a pre-trial hearing where he denied all charges and the prosecution said the case was no longer being treated as a suspected terrorism case. In an email message sent to communities across London on Monday, the Met said: “At the hearing, the Crown Prosecution Service advised the court that it will not be pursuing a terrorist connection as part of the criminal proceedings.” It said it would treat it instead as a suspected hate crime. “We understand this announcement may cause concern, particularly within the Jewish community, given the impact this incident had locally and against the backdrop of recent incidents affecting Jewish communities across London. We would like to reassure residents that the seriousness with which this matter is being treated has not changed.” Cmdr Helen Flanagan, the head of counter-terrorism policing for London, said: “I fully recognise the impact this incident has had on the three victims as well as the public, particularly the Jewish community. “I’m also aware this news comes shortly after the arrests of two men in Manchester for a suspected plot to target the Jewish community during the High Holy Days period. Counter-terrorism policing continues to work closely with the Met police to provide as much visibility and security as we can to Jewish communities across London.” The victims of the Golders Green attacks were Shloime Rand, 34, and Moshe Shine, 76. The victim of the other stabbing earlier the same day in south London was Ishmail Hussein. The case continues and the full trial is scheduled for March 2027.

title: How a $60 loaf of rye bread went viral in New York City: ‘It’s a conversation piece’
summary: Bread experts weigh in on whether the rye sourdough that bakers ‘feed every day’ is worth that much
text: A loaf of bread has become New York City’s latest viral hit and, somehow, status symbol. At Rye, the first US outpost of Austrian bakery Martin Auer, a 3.3lb loaf of 100% rye sourdough sells for $60 in SoHo. Made with just water, flour, salt and time, the bread has attracted the kind of attention once reserved for rainbow bagels, cronuts and skyscraper milkshakes. Which raises the inevitable question – is it actually worth that much? The answer depends, in part, on what someone believes they are really buying. For Rye’s owners, the price reflects much more than a list of ingredients. The loaf is unusually large and is sold whole for $60, by the half for $30 or by the quarter for $15. The large Landbrot costs €12.97 at Martin Auer’s bakery in Graz – and €14.27 at the one in Vienna. The smaller one goes for €4.48 and €4.93, respectively. And in New York of course, there’s the expense of operating in lower Manhattan, importing organic rye flour from Austria and producing the bread on site. There’s also a very technical process. “You need to ferment the rye sourdough,” co-owner Tim Auer told People. “You need to feed it every day. That takes about 24 hours before you can use it again. Then you need to make the dough, ferment the dough of the bread, shave the bread, ferment the dough again, bake it, and then you have to let it rest.” It’s clear Rye is not presenting its bread as a basic grocery staple. It is presenting bread as craft, a tradition and even a legacy, as it was Tim Auer’s great-grandfather who began the business. That distinction matters, especially in New York, where consumers routinely pay premium prices for food not simply because they’re hungry, but because they’re curious. An unusual product is often something to cross off a bucket list. And there’s nothing inherently wrong about that. Gadi Peleg is the founder of Breads Bakery, an award-winning NYC-based bakery credited with offering the city’s best chocolate babka and a favorite of Martha Stewart’s. He is also among the $60 loaf’s defenders. He attended Rye’s opening, met the minds behind it and tasted the bread. His assessment is an enthusiastic one. “It’s amazing,” Peleg said. “Martin is a rye genius, and I love what he’s doing.” Peleg also cautions against focusing on just the $60 figure without accounting for context. The loaf is enormous compared with others on sale, and customers have the option to buy smaller portions. A quarter loaf, Peleg said, could be comparable in size to a standard loaf elsewhere. He also sees a bigger benefit in Rye’s viral success: more attention for a style of bread he has spent years championing. “I’m so thrilled that somebody else is now talking about rye in New York,” Peleg said. “It’s awesome.” Peleg’s reaction points to an often-overlooked side of viral food. Hype can introduce people to unfamiliar ingredients, traditions and techniques. Someone who walks into Rye because TikTok showed them a shocking price tag will leave having tasted a dense, fermented Austrian-style rye they otherwise never would have sought out. That kind of experimentation is part of what makes New York’s food culture so vibrant. But all the hype has another side. Several New York culinary professionals questioned whether the price of Rye’s loaf can be justified by production costs alone. Mille-Feuille Bakery is one of New York’s most famous French bakeries with several locations across the city, including one that’s a 10-minute walk from Rye. Mille-Feuille offers a variety of baked goods such as croissants, macaroons and éclairs, all of which, most cooks will tell you, require significantly more skill and effort to make than rye sourdough bread, especially when you take into account the training these pastry chefs must endure to learn their trade. Dimitri Viaud, executive chef at Mille-Feuille Bakery, said his bakery also uses lengthy fermentation methods for its sourdough, including roughly 24 hours of fermentation, yet sells a roughly 2lb loaf for about $12. “Bread is supposed to be a popular product,” Viaud said, one that is accessible to everyone. For his bakery, that means balancing craftsmanship and quality with a price customers can return to regularly. He does recognize some of Rye’s perspective. High rent, investment, imported ingredients and the broader experience surrounding the product can all raise a bakery’s costs. But he sees the $60 loaf as selling not so much the bread itself as the novelty of purchasing it. “They sell more of the experience behind this bread,” he said. His colleague Nicolas Buchot, executive sous-chef at Mille-Feuille, visited Rye and came away impressed by the space itself. The bakery, he said, was “gorgeous”, with striking displays and the bread he tasted was “great”. “It looks like luxury,” Buchot said, comparing the “golden” presentation to a high-end fashion store. But despite the obvious quality, he’s not sure it represents a sustainable model. The luxury comparison seems particularly apt. Most people, even in NYC, don’t walk around wearing Dior or Balenciaga. But if even a handful of people are willing to pay $2,500 for a pair of pants, then that will be more than enough to justify the existence of luxury brands. Rye seems to be working on a similar philosophy. Rick Camac, executive director of industry relations at the Institute of Culinary Education, longtime restaurateur, consultant and self-described “bread freak” sees the phenomenon through the lens of consumer psychology. To him, viral luxury foods often function more as something to talk about than something to eat. People may want to say they tried the expensive loaf in the same way they want to try caviar-topped comfort food, a wildly priced exotic burger, a $20 strawberry or any other internet-famous creation. “It’s a conversation piece,” Camac said. “To some degree, people think that it’s bragging rights.” Carmac emphasized that he was not one to shy away from paying a tidy sum for a high-quality meal. “I’m out to dinner four nights a week in New York City. A cheap night out is $250. I’m not afraid of spending money on food, but I’m pretty sure even I wouldn’t spend $60 on a loaf of bread.” But Camac has not yet tasted Rye’s bread, and does not claim to know whether its flavor could change his opinion. But he believes novelty and social currency are doing the heavy lifting in driving the fascination. In 2004, writer Patrick J McGinnis coined the term “Fomo” which stands for “fear of missing out”. It has become a popular phrase thrown around social media, but more importantly, the doctrine behind it seems to have embedded itself into the collective psyche of the online gen Z. On social media, participation is visible. Buying the loaf gives a consumer content to share. Not buying it can feel, however irrationally, like missing a moment in history. Still, it would be far too simplistic to portray everyone who buys into viral trends as victims of marketing ploys. Millennials were relentlessly shamed for liking avocado toast, which, like rye bread, is actually healthy on top of being delicious. At a time when young people are facing rising unhappiness and an unforgiving job market, perhaps we should not be so quick to judge people for indulging in one of life’s most consistent joys: good food. Peleg has confidence that Rye’s appeal goes deeper than a social media stunt. Martin Auer, he noted, has been baking for years and has already demonstrated the ability to sustain a business. He’s not any ordinary viral sensation, but an established, renowned chef. But the NYC food scene is a tough market, and getting tougher. Buchot, whose bakery has been operating in the city for 15 years, questioned whether a concept centered so heavily on one signature product can remain sustainable over time without evolving. Viaud made a similar distinction between a neighborhood bakery, where customers can return for everyday purchases, and a shop people may visit once for a novelty. That may be the real test for Rye. Not whether enough people are willing to pay $60 for bread, but if enough of those people are willing to come back. For what it’s worth, reviews of the lavish rye sourdough bread appear overwhelmingly positive. But that’s not surprising all things considered, and it doesn’t necessarily justify the exorbitant cost. Food & Wine put it most succinctly: “This bread is good, but it’s not that good.” But as any follower of the Fomo philosophy will ask you: can you really believe that without trying it yourself?

title: AI godfathers warn of runaway ‘intelligence explosion’
summary: OpenAI chief scientist also among authors of report on prospect of ‘most consequential technological development in history’
text: Two of the “godfathers” of modern AI and senior executives at OpenAI and Anthropic have warned governments to prepare for an AI “intelligence explosion”, which they say could be the most consequential technological development in history. A report co-authored by the Nobel laureate Geoffrey Hinton and the Canadian computer scientist Yoshua Bengio, considered godfathers of modern AI for their work in the field, urges politicians to act now before there is runaway progress in the technology. The authors say they are concerned about an “intelligence explosion”, which they describe as a “dramatic AI-driven acceleration of AI progress, compressing advances that would otherwise take years into months or less”. The paper, titled “What if automating AI R&D triggers an intelligence explosion?”, is authored by more than 20 people including Hinton and Bengio. Other authors of the paper include Jack Clark, a co-founder of Anthropic, and Jakub Pachocki, the chief scientist at OpenAI. Their concerns focus on the possibility of AIs being able to improve themselves without human intervention, a process known as “recursive self-improvement”. In the paper it is broadly referred to as automated AI research and development. Once AI systems reach expert-level capabilities at AI R&D, a single developer could run a workforce equivalent to “millions” of top human researchers, the paper says. The authors say the automating of AI R&D is the most likely source of an intelligence explosion, because AIs are already contributing to improving their own technology and the resulting improved systems can be rapidly deployed once built. “An intelligence explosion could be the most consequential technological development in human history, compressing years of progress into months or less, threatening human control over AI systems, and severely eroding checks on power within and between states, companies, and branches of government,” the paper says. Urging governments to take action quickly, the authors say: “Once an intelligence explosion begins, the window for action may close.” They recommended a trio of policy priorities: requiring transparent progress reports on AI-related R&D, including embedding independent auditors in companies; finding ways to constrain breakneck AI development; and preparing to adapt to an intelligence explosion. Anthropic and OpenAI have both agreed to having independent evaluators assess their models after warning that AI development was reaching a critical pitch in terms of safety. Anthropic says AI now produces 80% of its own code, while OpenAI uses autonomous AI agents in areas such as the training of new models. “Preliminary evidence suggests that a software-driven intelligence explosion is possible,” the paper says, adding this would lead to the “extremely rapid development of highly capable or superhuman AI systems”. While this could produce medical breakthroughs and technological leaps, it would bring a trio of risks: powerful systems could enable biological and cyber threats that develop faster than the measures needed to counter them; as humans become less involved in AI R&D they could lose the opportunity to control systems; states could use an intelligence explosion to convert a modest lead in areas such as cyberspace into a decisive one. The report acknowledges these impacts are “uncertain”. For instance, a technological breakthrough could take time to implement given the need to set up supply chains for any special materials involved or to comply with regulations. AI systems could also accelerate the speed at which risks are mitigated, say the authors. If such a breakthrough happened, the authors say, AI systems could rapidly eclipse human experts in most fields and “radically accelerate” technological progress. Preparing for this “should be an urgent priority, including at the highest levels of government leadership”. They say governments should consider policies that address the potential for an intelligence explosion, including: requiring transparent progress reports on AI-related R&D, including embedding independent auditors in companies; limiting how fast an AI can improve in a certain time period; working with datacentres to enable pausing certain AI R&D projects; making sure automated AI R&D systems are fully isolated and cannot escape human control; creating “emergency response plans” for the various scenarios that could emerge from an intelligence explosion. Despite some glitches shown by systems, such as disobeying instructions, R&D projects that would take humans months to carry out could be fully automated by AI by 2028. “Productivity gains from AI R&D automation have not yet reached the threshold needed to trigger an intelligence explosion, but gains from newer systems are likely approaching that threshold,” they said. The AI doomsday threat: Distinguishing facts from fear On Thursday 15 October, join Dan Milmo and Prof Dame Wendy Hall as they discuss the warnings surrounding artificial intelligence and how we can separate fact from speculation. title: ‘Are these chemicals in my blood?’ How one community learned the truth about Pfas pollution
summary: People living next to a chemicals plant near Blackpool were tested for ‘forever chemicals’. Last week they received the alarming results
text: Last February, I got a call from a woman called Sam Hammond. We had been speaking on and off for a while over her growing concern that her garden could be affected by pollution from a nearby chemical plant. That morning, Sam had been hand-delivered a letter from her council informing her that her pet ducks’ eggs, reared in her garden, were contaminated with Pfas chemicals. “Are these chemicals in my blood?” she asked me at the time. Seven months later, Sam has an answer to that question. Pfas are a group of thousands of synthetic compounds known as “forever chemicals” because of their persistence in the environment. In 2024, Wyre borough council and the Environment Agency launched an investigation into contamination of one type of Pfas – Pfoa, a group 1 carcinogen that was globally banned in 2020 – in the vicinity of the AGC Chemicals Europe factory in Thornton-Cleveleys, a town to the north of Blackpool. Pfoa was emitted in huge quantities from the AGC Chemicals factory up until 2012. The level of Pfas in one of Sam’s duck eggs was so high that if she ate just one a week, she would exceed the European safe level 10 times over. Sam and her children had been eating these eggs every day for decades. The risk was increasingly clear, but residents did not yet know if the Pfas had entered their systems until last week when the law firm Leigh Day, working with Dr Dave Megson, a forensic environmental scientist at Manchester Metropolitan University, and in association with Watershed Investigations, published the blood test results of 49 individuals who live around the factory. In the UK, there is no guidance on what constitutes a safe level of Pfas in blood. However, in the US the guidelines state that if the sum of seven Pfas chemicals is above 20 nanograms per millilitre, there is an increased risk of adverse effects and that clinicians should consider more frequent, targeted health screenings. The results showed that 70% of those tested in Thornton-Cleveleys had a combined Pfas level above 20ng/ml. Sam’s level is 25ng/ml, putting her firmly in this high-risk category. But what is perhaps even more alarming is the level of Pfas in her son’s blood: 111 ng/ml. “I feel quite sick about his results,” she said. “My concern all along is what have we done to the kids. We moved here, chose this property, and I feel guilty because I’ve exposed them to that, even though I know it’s not my fault.” The results specifically revealed that nearly 70% of those tested had increased levels of Pfoa. Pfoa exposure is linked to a range of serious illnesses and has been linked specifically to kidney cancer. In June, a government-commissioned study found no higher-than-expected rates for most cancers but found that two areas – one south-east of the factory and one north of Blackpool – had recorded higher than expected rates of kidney cancer. A detailed review found no evidence of a statistically significant excess of kidney cancer cases and no evidence of a cancer cluster or an environmental association, and argued it could be the result of random variation because of the small sample size, concluding: “No further cluster investigation is warranted at this stage.” These findings were immediately questioned by experts, who advised further investigations. Megson, who was not involved in the study, described this conclusion as being “very contradictory” and said it “seems to downplay the findings rather than assess it objectively … Personally, I fear that this data is giving us strong evidence that … significant harm has already been caused.” One woman, who asked to remain anonymous, has a Pfas level of 436 ng/ml. She recently had a tumour removed from her back and is now left questioning whether her persistent health problems may be linked to this chemical exposure. “I thought I was just unlucky, but when I found out that result I thought it must have something to do with it,” she said. While the test result has given her some answers, it has left her with even more questions. “How can I get this out of my body? Who can help me? Where do I go from here? I just want this out,” she said. In the UK, there is no clear guidance on what to do if you have high levels of Pfas in your blood. However, the council has advised residents within a 1km radius of the factory to wash and peel homegrown produce and not to eat eggs from locally reared birds. Because of the potential risks to human health, the council has also announced plans to shut down two allotments close to the factory. For the past five years, Alan Hodson has had a plot on one of the allotments that borders the AGC Chemicals site. The allotment was his sanctuary. But last year he received a hand-delivered letter informing him that his beetroot contained the highest level of Pfoa of all of the products tested. “I just think of all that time I spent here – I could’ve been doing something else. It’s just wasted time,” he said when I visited him earlier this year. Alan has now found out his blood contains 43ng/ml of Pfas. “You get an allotment and you grow homegrown veg to be more healthy and then all of a sudden you’re told it’s polluted,” he said. “I’m worried, but you’ve just got to crack on. If you dwell on it, it takes over your life.” Following the recent news of AGC Chemicals’ planned closure, Megson is calling on central government to step in to provide more support to residents. “That is what has happened across the globe for the last 50 years when potential chemical pollution disasters like this are uncovered. In other places there has been swift widespread biomonitoring offered to residents. This helps clearly establish how localised the problem is,” he said. A spokesperson for AGC Chemicals Europe Ltd said: “We are aware of the recent blood testing initiative, and we understand the concerns this may have caused amongst local residents. Whilst the parties conducting these tests have chosen not to share their findings and data with us, we would emphasise that the UK government’s position is clear: Pfas blood testing does not predict future health problems and can sometimes create unnecessary concern. For these reasons, Pfas biomonitoring is not currently recommended through the NHS or private blood tests. “The Hillhouse site and surrounding area has been dedicated to industrial chemical manufacturing for well over a century – long before AGC Chemicals Europe Ltd was established – and a wide variety of historical users have operated on the site. Since the wider multi-agency investigation is still ongoing and no formal determination of land contamination has been made under part 2A of the Environmental Protection Act, we cannot speculate on future outcomes or next steps. “AGC Chemicals Europe Ltd has been part of the Thornton-Cleveleys community since 1999. The health, wellbeing and safety of our employees and the local community remain our priority.” The government has been contacted for comment.

title: Boston sues Trump administration over infrastructure grant withdrawal
summary: City challenges transportation department’s decision to cancel funding that included money for EV charging
text: Boston has sued Donald Trump’s administration over the withdrawal of a $20m grant for infrastructure improvements in the latest example of cities across the country mobilising against the federal government. Boston is challenging a decision by the transportation department to cancel funding for a project on the basis that it included a small allocation for electric vehicle charging. The grant was awarded to Boston during Democrat Joe Biden’s presidency under the Rebuilding American Infrastructure with Sustainability and Equity (Raise) programme. The city argues the Roxbury Resilient Corridors project would improve safety, public transport, accessibility and traffic flow. Three streets identified for improvements are in the top 3% of Boston’s streets in terms of concentration of traffic injuries and fatalities. They are in an area classified by the transportation department as one of “persistent poverty” and a “historically disadvantaged community”. Boston says the department gave a single reason for withdrawing the grant in September last year: it included electric vehicle charging infrastructure. However, the city contends this accounted for less than 1% of the project’s costs. The lawsuit argues that the decision was unlawful and overtly political and contradicted the purpose of the Raise programme, which Congress established to support infrastructure projects promoting sustainability, safety and technological innovation, including in underserved communities. Michelle Wu, the mayor of Boston, said: “We’re fighting for every dollar of investment to improve quality of life for Roxbury residents, commuters and businesses. “Boston earned this competitive grant to meet community needs and address long-needed infrastructure upgrades. The City of Boston will continue to fight back against lawless federal attacks, and we urge the court to reverse the Trump administration’s illegal actions and restore these critical funds for Roxbury.” The Democratic congresswoman Ayanna Pressley, whose Massachusetts district includes Roxbury, said: “These funds are an essential investment in Roxbury and the unlawful cancellation of this grant is more evidence of Sean Duffy and Donald Trump’s contempt for the people we serve.” She added: “There was no good reason to rescind these funds – DOT should reverse course so we can move this project forward, improve the daily lives of commuters, and enhance the climate resilience of at-risk communities—just as Congress intended.” The lawsuit argues that federal agencies cannot change the terms of a programme established by Congress to reflect changing political priorities. The case, City of Boston v Duffy, names the transportation secretary, Sean Duffy, and was filed in the US district court for the district of Massachusetts. Boston city says it will have filed nine lawsuits against the administration once the latest case is included, eight of them in partnership with the Public Rights Project. Toby Merrill, litigation director at the Public Rights Project, which is providing pro bono legal counsel to Boston, said: “Boston lost a $20m infrastructure grant over electric vehicle chargers that represented a fraction of 1% of the funding – infrastructure the federal government itself encouraged.” Cities including Chicago, New York and Los Angeles and states across the US have brought a series of lawsuits against the administration over federal funding decisions and other policies since Trump returned to the White House.

title: Andrew Bailey, a Deputy Director at the F.B.I., Leaves His Job

title: Aldi to invest £900m in UK and open 40 more stores next year
summary: Supermarket chain declares ‘increasing confidence’ in its growth plans after posting record annual revenue of £19bn
text: Aldi says it is stepping up investment in the UK with plans to spend £900m and open more than 40 stores. The company, which operates 1,092 budget supermarkets in the UK and Ireland, revealed sales rose 5% to a record £19bn last year. It opened 40 stores but profits slipped by £2.6m to £433m as it cut prices despite cost inflation. Giles Hurley, the boss of Aldi’s UK and Irish arm, said the German-owned business had “increasing confidence around growing our business”, claiming it already was the third largest UK supermarket in terms of items sold and customer numbers. Asda is classed as the UK’s third largest supermarket by value of sales, just ahead of Aldi. Leeds-based Asda is less than one percentage point ahead of its rival, with a market share of 10.6% in mainland UK, according to the latest data from Worldpanel. Aldi will open 42 stores this year, with 30 opening in the next 10 weeks. It plans a similar number next year, stepping up investment by about £100m to £900m. In the longer term it is aiming for 1,500 outlets in the UK and Ireland. “We could probably grow faster but we need to find the right sites in the right locations and have to go through a planning process which can, at times, be challenging,” Hurley said. He said consumers were “feeling the pinch” against a backdrop of persistent inflation, and the “continuity and clarity” of Aldi’s range of cheap groceries had attracted 425,300 more customers. He said the outlook for grocery inflation, which stood at 2.8% in August, according to the British Retail Consortium, was difficult to assess until the impact of drought and extreme heat on UK crop yields was clear. He said the industry was “not seeing systemic food shortages” but the climate crisis was creating “a real challenge” for food producers. He urged the government to treat the UK’s food system as “a national strategic priority” because “relying on imports leaves us exposed”. Hurley claimed Aldi was the only grocery chain reducing prices. He said the loyalty discount schemes offered by many rival chains, including Tesco and Sainsbury’s, were “definitely a roll of the dice for customers and questions remain about how much of the value [they offer] is perceived rather than real”. He said Aldi was winning over customers because it remained the cheapest place to shop in the market and it would continue to invest to maintain that position by cutting prices. However, Aldi does not reveal sales performance in established stores – those open for more than a year – making it difficult to gauge how much growth is just the result of expansion. Aldi’s growth is much slower than than that of its rival Lidl, which is gaining market share with a loyalty scheme while allowing shoppers to order online and pick up in a store. Aldi has signed a deal withDeliveroo under which the courier firm’s workers will pick, pack and deliver Aldi groceries sold through its app. The supermarket chain said it had committed to sourcing at least half its products through long-term supplier agreements by next year, giving its producers and manufacturers greater confidence to invest and make Britain’s food system less reliant on imports. Aldi said it spent £14bn with British suppliers in 2025 and about 80% of its sales came from them.

title: Farmer who alerted police to RAF Fairford suspected bomb plot says there was ‘no follow-up’
summary: Woman who spotted suspicious vans and masked men says authorities did not contact her after five men were arrested
text: A farmer who claims to have alerted the police to a suspected terrorist bomb plot at RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire has said she has had “no follow-up at all” from the authorities. The woman told reporters on Monday that she did not see herself as a hero for having reported vans blocking a road near the base while on her way back from a party. Five men from London were arrested in the village of Whelford, near to RAF Fairford, on Sunday on suspicion of explosives and terrorism offences. The village remained shut off on Monday afternoon, with people evacuated from their homes dispersed to family, friends, hotels and a leisure centre. The farmer, in her 50s, said she had been travelling home with her husband and a “young lad” who works for them when she spotted the vehicles parked in a “really strange formation”. She said: “You couldn’t drive between them on the road, and you also couldn’t drive up the farm drive, and I think this has been one of the funny things that people are saying: ‘How could you notice?’ But when you live in Whelford, you notice everything. We all know what cars each other drive, we know who we are, we know the people that cycle through regularly.” She said one of the vans had some “strange sign writing on it” and she initially believed it belonged to undercover police. She said: “We had a bit of a look at the vans, established there was no one in there, tried to phone the number on the side, just in case we could get it moved so we could drive down to the farmyard, and the number didn’t work.” After dropping off their employee, the farmer and her husband turned around and drove back the way they had come. “We suddenly saw a large group of men,” she said. “They were panicking … I suppose they were panicking because anyone saw them, but our vehicle is quite similar to the patrol vehicles that they use, and we had our lights on main beam. “I think we sort of dazzled them, and they started to run, and some of them ran straight ahead across the road into the field, and some turned and started going down towards Kempsford, which is our next village.” Despite five men having been arrested, the farmer said there were “definitely more than five” and estimated she saw between eight and 10 people with their faces covered and wearing “slim-fitting clothes”. Authorities have previously said the incident was contained. The farmer said she tried to call the MoD police, but the phone “just rang and rang and rang and no one answered”, before she phoned 101 and was put on hold. She then phoned 999 and messaged the village WhatsApp group to alert people to the unusual activity. “Literally within five minutes of that, everything sort of kicked off and armed police arrived – the guys were arrested,” she said. “The helicopter was up searching, probably for a couple of hours, and there was a lot of shouting.” She added: “The strange thing is, there was no kind of follow-up. The police didn’t ring me – they had all my details, they didn’t phone me back, and nobody told anyone in the village what was going on apart from me. “It wasn’t until probably half six in the morning when they suddenly decide to evacuate people. Meanwhile, those vans were right in the middle of the village, next to everyone’s houses and no one did anything.” Responding to her account, the defence secretary, Wes Streeting, said earlier on Monday that she had only “a partial picture” of the situation. The farmer in turn told reporters: “I know it’s been said by some of the higher-ups today that I didn’t have the full picture, but the picture I had was three extremely unusual vehicles parked in the middle of our village and a group of unknown men running around.”

title: Foie gras, live dolphins and toasters: China and US cut reciprocal tariffs on $30bn each of goods
summary: World’s biggest economies release lists of products in latest move away from trade war – but no strategic goods are included
text: The US and China have released reciprocal lists of goods worth about $30bn each on which they plan to cut tariffs, ranging from consumer electronics and agricultural products to artificial flowers and live dolphins. The announcements are the latest tack away from the intense trade war between the world’s two largest economies that dominated much of last year, though major strategic products are not included and no timeline has yet been given for the reductions. The US list includes 77 categories of Chinese products including bed linen, garden umbrellas, toasters, fish hooks and billiard balls. The reciprocal Chinese list features 1,619 types of US product including a broad range of food such as butter, offal, lobster and foie gras. It also includes coal, scientific devices such as MRI systems, rabbit hair and several types of animals for breeding. Han Lin, the China country director at The Asia Group, a strategic advisory firm, said: “The animal list is certainly eye-catching: donkeys, mules, horses, whales, dolphins and dugongs. But I’d read it less as an exotic trade story than as evidence of how granular tariff codes can be.” The news comes days after Xi Jinping and Donald Trump met in Washington for an optics-driven summit aimed at stabilising the two sides’ volatile relationship. Zhu Tian, a vice-president and co-dean at the China Europe International Business School (CEIBS) in Shanghai, said: “It is a positive step, but not a major breakthrough.” He noted that the reductions covered a relatively small share of US-China trade, and that other tariffs on more strategic goods remained in place. “Still, it is significant that the two sides are moving from simply avoiding further escalation to actually reducing some tariffs,” he added. The agreement has been brokered through the US-China Board of Trade, set up during Trump’s visit to Beijing in May. The US trade representative Jamieson Greer said each side had recommended $30bn of non-sensitive trade that “could benefit from more favourable tariff treatment in the future”. The list represented “improved market access for about 30% of US exports to China”, he added. The Chinese commerce ministry said levies on more than 90% of the products would be subject to “most favoured nation” levels, according to state media. Sensitive product categories such as semiconductors, batteries and electric vehicles are not covered in the $30bn tariff cut lists. US whole soya beans imports – which became a Chinese target during 2025’s trade war – are not on Beijing’s tally, Reuters news agency noted, meaning they still face an additional tariff of 10%. Meanwhile, the Xi-Trump meeting last week yielded only a two-month extension to a wider trade truce first established by the two leaders in Busan, South Korea, last year. Lin said: “Both sides are carving out non-sensitive trade where cooperation is still possible. It’s managed stabilisation, not a trade reset.”

title: Heat pump sales soar across Europe after states cut electricity taxes, data shows
summary: EU to push member states to cut tax rate below duty on gas, with 11% surge in sales also put down to fallout from Iran war
text: Sales of residential heat pumps increased 11% across Europe in the first six months of the year as the Iran war sent oil and gas prices rocketing and some countries lowered electricity taxes. Homeowners bought 1.16m heat pumps across 12 European countries, up from 1.05m in the first half of 2025, according to the European Heat Pump Association (EHPA). Iran’s de facto closure of the strait of Hormuz, an important shipping passage, severely disrupted the flow of oil and gas shipments and sent the price of crude oil as high as $126 a barrel in late April. Soon after the US-Israeli attacks on Iran on 28 February that started the war, the European Commission published plans to encourage EU governments to lower electricity taxes and speed up the shift from fossil fuels oil and gas to renewable sources of energy. Soaring energy prices and electricity tax changes have fuelled the growth in heat pump sales so far this year, said the EHPA, which has long argued that the popularity of the heating systems depends heavily on the price of electricity. Rather than generating heat from burning fuel, the pumps transfer heat energy from one place to another and can be used for warming and cooling a home. In its electrification action plan, the commission said tax on electricity should be no higher than that on gas. Brussels hopes to amend the network charges that consumers pay on their utility bills to reward flexible options such as heat pumps. Heat pump sales have risen in European countries where electricity taxes have been cut, the EHPA said. In Germany, a subsidy scheme has led to heat pumps being the No 1 heating tech being installed, it added. The 12 countries covered in the data are Austria, Belgium, Switzerland, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Norway, Portugal and Sweden. Paul Kenny, the EHPA director general, said: “Europe is ending its addiction to a toxic, costly drug from dodgy suppliers: gas. The sooner electricity becomes the most affordable solution, the quicker we’ll get clean. “The fix? Dropping taxes on electricity and shifting them over to fossil fuels. The European Commission has made this clear – but now all EU governments must enact it, following in the footsteps of the Netherlands and Belgium.” The industry body found that taxes on electricity were often higher than on gas, which drives up the cost sharply. In the UK, electricity costs more than four times as much as gas, similar to Belgium. The only country where the ratio is higher is Romania, where electricity prices are five times as high as those for gas. The EHPA said countries that taxed electricity more than gas saw slower adoption of heat pumps and were more dependent on fossil fuels. It pointed to Belgium, where heat pump uptake remains low, although the government announced tax changes for 2026 that will cut electricity costs by 3% and raise gas costs by 3%. Separately, a two-year study by the London-based Centre for Net Zero found that installing solar panels and a battery in a UK home saves £681 a year on average. Families’ annual bills fell by almost two-thirds (62%) after they received free solar panels and a battery, based on smart meter data used to calculate their electricity bills, in news first reported by the Times. Great Britain recorded more new solar power installations in the first half of this year than in any six-month period since 2011, according to government figures published in July.
