title: Healey offers upbeat vision but sheds little light on how it will be paid for
summary: With the budget only a month away, the chancellor gave little indication of where money will come from to reindustrialise Britain
text: John Healey cheered the Labour faithful with his first conference speech as chancellor, offering an upbeat vision of a reindustrialised Britain with fresh opportunities for young people, but he gave little sense of how he intends to pay for Andy Burnham’s radical plans. Healey’s budget next month is widely seen both inside and outside Labour as the moment when the prime minister’s radical rhetoric about ditching 40 years of neoliberal orthodoxy risks crashing into fiscal reality. With the global bond sell-off driving up government borrowing costs, and eye-watering energy prices likely to push up household bills in the new year, he did deliver some home truths to Labour members and cabinet colleagues. He deliberately and repeatedly highlighted his role in the last Labour government, as an aide to Gordon Brown, at one point recalling lending Brown a tie to deliver his conference speech, which Healey wore as he spoke in a neat nod to that era. However, the chancellor cautioned: “The money New Labour had in the 90s is simply not there now.” “The worldwide economic shocks – conflicts, trade tensions – are felt hard at home,” he added. “Britain has it harder now.” Like Rachel Reeves before him, Healey sought to argue that fixing the public finances was a precondition for rebuilding the economy. “The rock of fiscal discipline. It underwrites every promise this government makes … we can’t succeed without it.” Attacking the Conservatives for driving the UK further into the red during their 14 years in power, he claimed that current levels of UK debt were “an assault on our common sense; they’re an affront to our values” – although Reeves deliberately redefined the government’s fiscal rules to allow more borrowing to fund long-term investment, which Healey presumably doesn’t resile from. Much of the speech hailed the benefits of an industrial renaissance, creating good jobs for young people. An apprentice called Steve, who helped build the new Mersey ferry, had been invited along. A clearer picture is beginning to emerge of how Labour intends to go about reindustrialisation. Healey highlighted the government’s intention to use rising defence spending to create work in the UK, including through £6bn worth of contracts with British shipyards. And in a signal of Labour’s intention to devolve more employment support measures, he announced the creation of new local apprenticeship teams, overseen by regional mayors, which will match firms to young people. “These times demand of us a greater resolve, a greater determination and a greater hope,” he said as he promised to pursue what he called the “moral duty” of finding work for the almost 1 million young people not in education, employment or training, echoing language also used by the work and pensions secretary, Pat McFadden. Also like McFadden, he highlighted the fact that too many young people were being written off by the benefits system – a heavy hint that welfare reform will form part of the package of changes recommended in the soon-to-be-published Milburn review. Healey also sought to fill in some of his own personal story to those outside the hall less familiar with a man who, he said, had given his first Labour conference speech a full 40 years ago, in 1986. He spoke of his wife, Jackie, whom he became engaged with a fortnight after their first meeting at a Labour function, and his first job as a pot washer in a pub, which taught him the joys of a hand-pulled pint. Yet he threw little light on how he was approaching a budget now exactly a month away, other than to recommit to Reeves’s determination to balance the books, which will take more than optimism and a good story.

title: Base jumper dies in Utah after wingsuit fails in remote mountainous region
summary: Identity of man, 27, being withheld pending family notification after 700ft plunge
text: A Base jumper died on Sunday in Utah after his wingsuit failed while he plunged from a 700ft height, according to authorities. Local news reports cited the Cache county sheriff’s office, which said that the man fell to his death at age 27 in a mountainous region of Hyrum, which is east from the city of Millville. His death came several months after two other Base-related fatalities in Utah, including that of the extreme athlete Andy Lewis, who rose to prominence for his 2012 Super Bowl performance with Madonna – drawing more attention to the activity’s many dangers. Search-and-rescue teams on Sunday were deployed to an area called Leetham’s Hollow, described by NBC News as having “walls and cliffs not unlike the Grand Canyon’s”. Those crews declared the man dead on the scene. “On today’s jump, something went wrong, and he did not have enough lift with his wingsuit,” Doyle Peck, a Cache county chief sheriff’s deputy, was reported to have said. “He impacted the ground at a high rate of speed resulting in his death.” The search and rescue personnel helped transport him out of the hollow, the Salt Lake Tribune reported. Peck said that the man, whose identity is being withheld pending family notification, had experience in Base jumping and was among a group engaging in the activity, according to NBC News. The local news outlet KSL also reported that the sheriff’s office expressed “deepest sympathies to the family and friends of this individual”. Base is an acronym for building, antenna, span and earth – four objects from which participants can jump. A 2019 National Geographic report referred to wingsuit Base jumping as the world’s “deadliest sport”. Before Sunday, the Base Fatality List had registered 548 deaths worldwide since the registry started in 1981. There had been 15 deaths so far in 2026, according to the list.

title: Schools forced to shut amid burst Thames Water pipe ‘leaking 750 litres a second’
summary: Leak causes outages and low pressure in parts of London and Surrey, affecting 6,000 properties and leaving some without water
text: Schools, businesses and homes across seven boroughs in England were hit by a Thames Water outage on Monday, from a burst water main reportedly leaking 750 litres a second. About 6,000 properties across five south London boroughs and two Surrey boroughs had no water supply or low pressure, Thames Water said. Thames Water apologised for the lack of water. A spokesperson said: “Our specialist team is now on site and working to stop the water flooding from the broken pipe.” Schools and colleges were forced to close across the boroughs. Esher College, a sixth-form college for 2,000 students, was among those forced to send pupils home and shut their doors. The college said: “Due to a major water outage effecting the KT10 area and our campus we are closed on Monday 28 September.” Kingston grammar school also closed, as did Long Ditton infant and nursery school, Thames Ditton infant school and Hollyfield school and sixth-form centre in Surbiton. Monica Harding, the Liberal Democrat MP for Esher and Walton, Surrey, said it was her understanding that water was leaking at 750 litres a second early on Monday morning after a large main burst. The community was left without water from about 5am. “It is completely unacceptable,” she said. “We need an urgent response from Thames Water to get water supplies back on as soon as possible and to protect vulnerable communities.” Some reports said a contractor had struck the water pipe with a digger, causing a 4ft rupture in the pipe in the Walton section. Helen Ryder, who runs a flower shop in Thames Ditton, said: “Our priority is to make sure staff have water, but we need to make sure the flowers do too. Hopefully we have enough water, but people come before flowers.” Parents at Hollyfield school and sixth-form centre received a message from the school which said: “There is a significant issue with water supply in the local area … Whilst we have water at the moment it is not replenishing at the same rate it is being used and so our supply will run out at lunchtime. This means that it is unsafe for students to remain on site.” Thames Water said it would deliver water to registered vulnerable customers and open bottled water stations later, at locations yet to be confirmed. Thames Water said the following postcodes could be affected: CR4, KT1, KT10, KT12, KT2, KT3, KT5, KT6, KT7, KT8, SM4, SW16, SW17, SW18, SW19, SW20, TW10 and TW16. Paul Kohler, the Lib Dem MP for Wimbledon, said he had contacted Thames Water for more information after reports of a water outage across Wimbledon, New Malden, Raynes Park and Morden, in south London. He told followers on X that he would share any updates he received. Harding said: “My worry is that decades of underinvestment in our infrastructure and poor regulation may be causing incidences like this. Right now, however, the priority must be getting water back in our taps.” A spokesperson for Thames Water said: “Our engineers are making progress on repairing the burst in Molesey but it is likely to take some time to complete. “We are rerouting water in the area to reduce the impact on customers while we work to fix the burst. Water deliveries are being made to customers who are on our priority services register. We will be opening bottled water stations this afternoon and will provide their locations once confirmed. “The number of properties affected has now been reduced to less than 6,000. We again would like to say sorry to our customers and reassure those who are still affected that we are working to restore their water supply as quickly as possible. “The latest updates will be posted on our website, thameswater.co.uk.”

title: Healey signals welfare reform push and new apprenticeships scheme
summary: Chancellor sets out measures to support jobs and growth in Labour conference speech but vows fiscal discipline in budget
text: John Healey has signalled Labour will stage a fresh attempt at welfare reform as he pledged to put fiscal discipline at the core of next month’s budget, alongside measures to inject hope into Britain’s economy. In his first speech as chancellor to the Labour conference, Healey warned that next month’s highly anticipated tax-and-spending event would need to take into account a challenging global backdrop. Setting out measures to support jobs and growth, the chancellor announced a new local apprenticeship service, to be led by mayors, targeted at young people to deliver “thousands more apprenticeships” across the country. However, he also gave the clearest indication yet that job support would be accompanied by changes to the welfare system designed to incentivise employment while curbing a soaring benefits bill. Rolling the pitch to avoid a repeat of the welfare rebellion that forced his predecessor, Rachel Reeves, into a costly U-turn, Healey argued Labour had a “moral duty” to overhaul the system to encourage people to find a job. “Our social security system must always be there for those who can never work. But for everyone else, benefits should be a bridge to work, to wider participation, to a better life, not a trap that people can’t escape,” he said. “And, conference, it is simply not progressive to allow a bigger and bigger benefits bill and a system which offers an income but doesn’t offer a future. So, once again, as a Labour government it falls to us to act.” Insisting he would balance the books while fleshing out Andy Burnham’s plans to strengthen “growth in every postcode”, Healey said he and the prime minister were in lockstep in their commitment to balance the books. “That commitment is so important. There is nothing progressive about losing control because it’s always working people who pay for it,” he said. Against a backdrop of jitters in financial markets as the Iran war rattles the global economy, the UK government’s borrowing costs have risen to the highest levels for almost two decades. Economists have warned that the chancellor could be forced to increase taxes or cut spending in response to rising pressures. However, with Burnham having promised to stick to Labour’s manifesto promise not to raise income tax, national insurance or VAT, investors view benefits reform as a totemic issue that could help the prime minister to demonstrate his commitment to balancing the books. Since he replaced Keir Starmer this summer, Burnham has signalled that Labour remains willing to overhaul welfare, amid predictions that the overall cost of pensions and welfare benefits could reach £409bn by 2030. In a speech aiming to strike a balance between promising to fund the new prime minister’s priorities and committing to fiscal discipline, Healey drew a comparison with the 1990s when he was an adviser to Gordon Brown. Wearing a red tie that he had lent to Brown, then chancellor, to wear for a Labour conference speech in Bournemouth more than two decades ago, he said the money New Labour had in the 1990s “is simply not there now”. Teeing up a tough budget on 28 October, in which Burnham has warned “difficult decisions” will need to be taken, Healey said the government needed to hold firm on its main fiscal rule requiring day-to-day spending to be matched by revenues by 2030. Rain Newton-Smith, the chief executive of the business lobby group the CBI, said: “The speech sent many of the right signals. The budget now needs to turn them into action if we are to fundamentally change firms’ willingness to invest, take a chance on a young person, and scale a business here in the UK.” Healey sought to draw a distinction between Labour’s approach and that of the Conservatives, saying Britain was suffering from the “reckless actions” the Tories had taken since 2010. He accused Reform UK of prioritising the interests of “dodgy” billionaire donors, saying Nigel Farage was “Liz Truss with a bitcoin account”. Healey’s local apprenticeships announcement comes as ministers await recommendations from two reviews of the welfare system expected to be published this autumn – on young people by Alan Milburn, and on a key disability benefit by the Timms panel. Milburn, a former Labour cabinet minister, has signalled that changes to welfare would be central to his recommendations, alongside measures to boost access to job support, education and training opportunities. Aiming to strike a balance between a message of fiscal discipline and an upbeat approach, Healey used his conference speech to argue that his budget would inject hope into the economy. The chancellor said actions would be taken to devolve power to regional mayors, alongside measures to support young people to find work and to reinvigorate business confidence. Healey also said he would allocate £6bn from the government’s defence investment plan to contracts for British shipyards, as part of a project to reindustrialise Britain. “Let’s bring back hope to Britain. For the next generation of young people. For a new age of industrialisation. For growth made here, by British firms and British workers,” he said.

title: Decades of fossil fuel influence paved way for Trump’s assault on university research, study says
summary: Fossil fuel firms have spent years trying to regulate climate research by donating to US universities, study authors argue
text: Recent attacks on US universities by the Trump administration have built on decades of efforts by libertarian donor networks, fossil fuel companies and conservative thinktanks to reshape university governance and increase outside influence, according to a new study. The authors of the new perspective study argue that the erosion of university autonomy has left colleges more vulnerable to corporate interests, especially within climate and energy research. In 2025, the Trump administration froze billions of dollars in research funding, launched investigations into 75 institutions and pushed colleges to sign agreements supporting administration policies in exchange for federal funding. The federal government canceled $4m in climate research grants at Princeton University alone and accused scientists of fueling “climate anxiety”. If you’re a young researcher watching that, you might think twice about asking a question that could cost you your funding, said Noel Healy, of Salem State University, the lead author of the study published in the journal Energy Research & Social Science. “Climate policy is only as good as the evidence behind it. When the industry being regulated gets to shape the questions researchers ask, it ends up shaping the policy too,” he said. The Academic Freedom Index, which measures how freely scholars and universities can teach, research and express ideas without interference, found that US institutional autonomy fell from 3.3 in 2019 to 1.7 in 2025, on a scale of 0 to 4. “Since 2025, scientists have been deleting words like ‘climate change’ from their grant applications because those words can get an application rejected,” Healy said. “Some universities have shut down programs before the government even asked them to, hoping to avoid becoming a target. You don’t have to ban speech if people fear that speaking up will cost them their funding. People start deciding it’s safer to stay quiet.” Outside influence on US universities is not new. In the 1920s, electric utilities worked with academics to defend their monopoly positions and oppose regulations. Fossil fuel companies followed suit in the 1950s, funding research to sow doubt about the public health impacts of their products. Internal industry documents have shown that companies viewed academic research as a way to build credibility and influence public debate. Corporate-funded research was only one way powerful interests influenced universities. Libertarian donor networks also influenced program content, faculty hiring and gained appointments to university governing bodies. For example, David Koch, the billionaire industrialist whose wealth came from Koch Industries, gave more than $185m to his alma mater, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), and served as a lifetime member to the elite research university’s highest governing body. Between 2010 and 2020, six fossil fuel companies alone gave more than $700m to US universities, helping to legitimize industry solutions to the climate crisis and undermine regulatory approaches. Some of this funding came with donor agreements that gave outside actors control over decisions traditionally made by faculty, such as in hiring and curricula. At the same time, donor-influence models were written into state law. For example, in 2016, the Arizona state legislature created the first publicly funded libertarian academic center. Other states have followed suit. These centers bypass faculty control, instead answering to legislators. These centers are expected to receive $50m in US taxpayer dollars during the 2025-2026 school year, according to reporting by the Hechinger Report. State legislatures have also tried to limit faculty power through legislation that could abolish tenure, block faculty participation in lawsuits and police educational programming. From 2021 to 2023, more than 150 state bills were introduced targeting tenure, faculty governance, and diversity, equity and inclusion, according to the Energy Research & Social Science perspective. Soaring tuition and student debt, which are also products of the corporate model, have contributed to mistrust in higher education. The authors of the study argue that to regain public trust, administrators must confront how corporate donors have reshaped their priorities, disclose donor contributions and influence, and give faculty committees the ability to reject funding that undermines the university’s public mission and create conflicts of interest. Union contracts can protect faculty and empower them to confront corporate capture. “Transparency lets you see the deal, but it doesn’t let you stop it. Faculty need the power to review major gifts before they’re accepted and to refuse the ones that threaten academic freedom,” Healy said. Universities don’t have to start from scratch. For example, the national UnKoch My Campus campaign published a model gift-acceptance policy that gives faculty a say before gifts with conditions are accepted, makes donor agreements public and sets clear grounds for rejecting gifts that give donors influence over hiring or teaching. Universities can draw on examples like this to write their own rules, Healy said. “In other countries, attacks on university legitimacy paved the way for faculty purges, campus closures and centralized political control,” he said. “Universities came under attack before those governments had full control, not after.” MIT has previously said it would not divest its endowment from fossil-fuel companies, arguing that working with industry could help develop climate solutions. The MIT Energy Initiative has also said that funders have no control over the content or findings of its research reports.

title: Teachers at Euan Blair firm report ‘horrendous stress’ after AI used to rate their work
summary: Exclusive: Instructors at tech training company Multiverse hit out at ‘remorseless’ and ‘unnerving’ monitoring system
text: Teachers at Euan Blair’s £1.6bn tech training company, Multiverse, have blown the whistle about “horrendous stress” and feeling constantly watched after bosses started using AI models to surveil and rate their teaching. Staff delivering apprenticeship training in computer and AI skills to thousands of UK public and private sector workers now have transcripts of online classroom sessions analysed and scored by an AI programmed to alert human managers when they are suspected of doing things wrong. The AI is trained to flag problems in their performance ranging from not fixing a disruption to the online connection quickly enough – within about a minute – to using too many “filler” phrases, such as “sort of” and “kind of”. Teachers called the newly introduced system “remorseless” and “unnerving”, and said some staff were on edge, losing sleep and seeking therapy. Multiverse was co-founded by the eldest son of the former prime minister Tony Blair and employs more than 800 people. It supplies AI and digital skills training to workers in the NHS, local councils, universities and the private sector (including the Guardian), mostly funded through the government’s apprenticeship levy. Alongside his father, Blair is a supporter of wider AI adoption in the UK economy, claiming last week that “every single worker is going to need to be retrained” and that employers want their workforces “as AI-pilled as possible”. Multiverse uses a mix of AI models including Anthropic and OpenAI products. Its new AI teacher monitoring system tags each instructor by their “risk status”, calculates a “percentage confidence score” and produces written comments about teachers’ work for managers to see at a glance. It is only the latest example of employers using AI to track worker behaviour. Earlier this year Burger King started using AI to track restaurant workers’ customer interactions and this summer Meta paused tracking of employees’ computer keystrokes amid data privacy concerns and a staff backlash. With critics warning AI monitoring risks eroding human agency, one study has suggested it can backfire by turning workers rebellious and new research to be published this week reports that workers in the wider UK tech industry are finding AI degrades work satisfaction. The United Tech and Allied Workers branch of the Communication Workers Union concluded AI causes “cognitive surrender” as workers lose skills and confidence and often intensifies rather than eases work. “Since all of this has come in, the stress level has been absolutely horrendous,” said one of several Multiverse teachers who spoke on condition of anonymity. “It has affected sleep, and not just for me. I’ve gone through a lot of things in my life, and I haven’t ever been in a position where I’m waking up in the middle of the night.” Previously instructors were observed monthly by a human manager but are now watched for several hours a day by an AI. It is trained to consider marking instructors down if they give vague or uncertain answers to questions, if learners go quiet when asked to contribute and if the teacher gets pulled into a prolonged one-to-one exchange that sidelines the group. “This is inducing stress because you consistently have to be cautious,” one teacher said. “Your attention is no longer delivering [the lesson] and listening to the learner [but] ‘am I saying the right thing so the AI doesn’t mark me down for something stupid that I’ve mistakenly said’.” Another teacher called it “very uncomfortable”. Multiverse says the AI does not replace human judgment but “directs human time to where it’s needed most” by highlighting problems. A spokesperson said it was “using AI to improve the experience of learners and customers”, and that only human managers wrote teachers’ performance reviews. They did not directly address complaints the system caused stress and anxiety and felt “remorseless”, but said its introduction was communicated in advance and teachers will have access to the data the AI collects. “This agent provides instructors with improved advice on development and feedback – exactly how any learning organisation should be deploying AI,” the spokesperson said. “The most consequential performance management action it can take is to recommend that a human personally reviews a session.” Blair owns a large minority stake in Multiverse, putting his personal net worth at an estimated £350m. The company was recently valued at £1.6bn albeit on a turnover of £118m and losses of £28m last year. In February, Ofsted, the UK education inspectorate, found Multiverse failed to meet expected standards in several areas, but praised the instructors as “skilled, effective teachers”. Its AI monitoring agent, introduced in recent weeks, is trained to spot signs an instructor has not fully internalised the teaching material. It is instructed to count verbal tics that point to that conclusion and to “judge the PATTERN across the whole transcript, not isolated instances”. It says: “1-2 hedges or filler words in an otherwise direct, well-internalised explanation do NOT fail this standard … What fails the standard is a PERVASIVE REPEATED pattern of filler, hedging or re-explanation.” When a trainer is setting a task “if the instructor is visibly confused themselves or had to self-correct while giving the instruction, that confusion itself counts as evidence the instruction was not clear the first time”. The AI is told to apply a negative mark “even if it was eventually straightened out”. The workers said the AI monitoring had led to managers pulling them up for suspected “digressions” when in fact they were answering a student’s question. “It’s impossible for me not to be affected by this mentally,” one teacher said. “I feel like I’m under continuous scrutiny,” another said. “It’s all about what I didn’t do in this session rather than what I did do. Did I do something incorrectly yesterday? What will I mess up on today? It’s remorseless. I don’t know why this is happening.” John Chadfield, the national tech officer at the CWU, said the public would be horrified to hear of bosses “deploying deeply intrusive surveillance on workers” but that “this news won’t surprise tech workers who feel the reality of the tech sector – an industry in serious need of further regulation”. He called for new laws to ensure AI was deployed in a socially responsible way and not to “shut off job opportunities for young people, degrade the craft of skilled workers and make astronomical profit for a few”. Anonymous: ‘An AI judges my lessons. Multiverse calls it quality assurance – it feels like surveillance’ Being constantly monitored by an AI is deeply uncomfortable. Imagine every word you say on the job being checked against a rubric that dictates what you’re expected to say and how. That’s the reality for me and my colleagues: every session we deliver to apprentices is now recorded and transcribed. It feels intrusive. Multiverse calls it quality assurance, but it feels like surveillance. Managers can now look at a dashboard showing how the AI has judged each of our sessions. It assigns a risk level to each of us: the risk of not having said the right things. That’s stressful, for several reasons. First, the AI isn’t always accurate. Managers are now tasked to investigate trainers for not following the script – at least according to the AI – when actually they were adapting the lesson to a learner’s needs. The threat of being questioned in such detail, at any time, is a constant source of anxiety. Second, there is no transparency. During the rollout, all delivery staff were kept in the dark while the system was developed. We have no insight into the AI’s analysis. The company says staff will get dashboard access in time, but for now only managers can see it. The need to always be cautious warps your priorities. Instead of focusing attention on the learner, you become obsessed with whether you’re saying the right thing. Being on camera for most of the day is stressful in itself; being haunted by an AI makes it worse. A more productive way to use AI would be to improve the teaching materials and raise the standard of what we teach. Instead, the AI is checking whether the teacher managed to fill the gaps? As it stands, this is surveillance, not empowerment. And I’m worried about what this data is for. In a climate of AI replacing people, I can’t help but worry it will be used to train AI to replace coaches and instructors altogether. Apprentices don’t want that and neither do I, and I would never consent to my sessions being used this way. • This article was amended on 29 September 2026 to include reference to the Guardian’s current contract with Multiverse; the training company provides an AI apprenticeship for a number of staff.

title: Three people dead, including a child, in attempt to cross Channel to UK
summary: Official says deaths – and dozens of injuries – were probably caused by crushing on boat carrying 105 people
text: A 10-year-old child and two women died ⁠attempting to cross the Channel on Monday, French authorities have said. Their deaths and the injuries of dozens of others in a large dinghy were probably caused by crushing, according to a French official. France’s maritime police ‌said ‌they received a ‌distress call in the early hours from an inflatable dinghy carrying 105 people that had ‌run into trouble in calm seas. The three passengers were treated onboard but were later confirmed dead by an emergency medical team flown out by helicopter. François-Xavier Lauch, the prefect of Pas-de-Calais, told a press conference: “Apparently there was no drowning, it was likely crushing – which is just as dreadful, especially if we think of the 10-year-old child.” The incident happened off the coast of Wissant, a village about 14 miles (23km) from Calais. A spokesperson for the local prefecture confirmed “a provisional total of three deaths and many more injured”, adding that “sea conditions were calm – the weather is good”. The prefecture described the boat as a “water taxi”, saying it had arrived relatively empty from an inland waterway before picking up passengers from the beach at Wissant. At 10.30am local time (9.30am UK time) six rescue boats were still at the scene searching for people in the water. At least 17 people, including women and children, have died in the Channel this year while attempting to reach the UK. Many have drowned, while others have died in incidents involving overcrowded boats. Three bodies were found last week after chaotic “water taxi” departures of this kind in northern France. So far this year, 18,609 people have made the Channel crossing – more than 40% fewer than at the same point last year. The number is also more than 25% lower than at this stage in 2024, when 25,165 people had crossed the Channel. Last week there were two uncontrolled landings in the UK, where dinghies arrived without being intercepted by authorities. It comes as more than 80 people, including a baby, are feared to have died while attempting to reach Spain’s Canary Islands by sea in August. On Monday, a rescue boat arrived at the port of Calais in the mid-morning, where it began disembarking people rescued from the accident. A coach, fire service and police vehicles were deployed at the scene. The northern beaches of France have become a key crossing point for people without visas hoping to cross the Channel. They pay people smugglers to board unstable rubber dinghies to make the journey across one of the world’s busiest shipping routes. At least 29 people lost their lives last year trying to cross the Channel, according to an Agence France-Presse tally based on official French and British sources. Official figures cited by the UN refugee agency, the UNHCR, show irregular migration to the EU – notably via Mediterranean sea routes – has plummeted since its peak during the 2015 refugee crisis. Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, will on Monday announce the reopening of a scheme to resettle refugees in the UK as she says “fairness” is at the heart of her vision for the Home Office. It will come as she focuses on safe and legal refugee routes to the UK in her Labour party conference speech. The UK resettlement scheme will reopen immediately, with about a quarter of those admitted to the UK under it expected to be Palestinians and women and girls from Afghanistan. UK government sources said officials were aware of the fatalities.

title: Tensions rise as Orange Order members vow to continue with march blocked by police
summary: Talks expected on Monday after Sinn Féin leaders join those on streets opposing decision to allow unionist parade for first time since 1998
text: Tensions between unionist and nationalist leaders in Northern Ireland have escalated as a number of Orange Order members remain at Drumcree church, vowing not to leave until they can proceed with their march down a nationalist road in Portadown. Members of the loyalist Orange Lodge made a third attempt to proceed down Garvaghy Road at 4am on Monday morning, but a line of police Land Rovers blocked their path. While protesters at the head of Garvaghy Road were dispersed late last night, there are fears that the tensions between Sinn Féin and the Democratic Unionist party (DUP) have reached a level that could lead to the collapse of power sharing at Stormont. Speaking to the Irish broadcaster RTÉ on Monday morning, Claire Hanna, the leader of the Social Democratic and Labour party, said collapsing Stormont “solves nothing” as it would halt critical decision-making. “Too often, we have reached for these collapse mechanisms only to have to come back six months later,” she said. The leader of the Ulster Unionist party, Jon Burrows, also said he did not “want to see the executive fall”. He told the BBC: “There are people waiting for health appointments, there are people that wait too long in A&E, people that wait too long for an ambulance, there are lots of initiatives that [health] minister [Robbie] Butler and his predecessors need delivered. We can’t risk those.” Power sharing at Stormont has collapsed several times before, whenever one of the two parties has pulled out of the pact between unionists and nationalists. All eyes will now be on the DUP’s commitment to the executive, given it accused the Sinn Féin vice-president and Northern Ireland first minister, Michelle O’Neill, of breaking the law on Sunday by showing up at an illegal protest at Garvaghy Road. The Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) was maintaining a low-key presence near Drumcree church as political efforts to resolve the dispute over the parade intensified. Breandán Mac Cionnaith from the Garvaghy Road Residents’ Coalition told protesters he would meet the Northern Ireland secretary, Chris Bryant, and the PSNI chief constable, Jon Boutcher, on Monday morning for talks. O’Neill told reporters shortly after midnight that the Garvaghy Road community had won a “victory”. Hundreds of protesters spent Sunday blocking the route of the hugely contentious parade after a court gave late-night clearance for the Orange Order to march on the historically significant road for the first time in nearly 30 years. The parade along the mainly nationalist Garvaghy Road was given the go-ahead by the Parades Commission for the first time since 1998, a decision denounced by Sinn Féin as “madness”. It led to a weekend of intense legal wrangling which concluded at 2.15am on Sunday when the court of appeal said it could not interfere with the commission’s decision. In driving rain on a cold Sunday morning, hundreds of nationalist protesters gathered to block the route. Many linked arms and sang songs as announcements were made over loudspeaker that they were liable to arrest and prosecution. The Orangemen spent the day ensconced a mile away in a church, the proposed start of the march, and said they would wait until police told them the road was clear. Among the protesters earlier in the day was the Sinn Féin president, Mary Lou McDonald, who said the decision to allow the parade was “madness” and “primitive treatment of any community in the year 2026. It is intolerable, and it will not be tolerated.” She added: “The mood here has been peaceful. It has been united and orderly. This is a dignified and united community and they are absolutely determined that they and we will not be drawn back into the past.” O’Neill was also there and said reigniting the dispute brought “into question how this whole peace process works”. She told reporters: “We’re meeting families who feel collectively traumatised, who feel individually traumatised. Does anybody think that this is a good idea? “No right-minded person would make this decision. I still do not know the answer to this question – why, after 28 years of a determination to block a march down this road, the Parades Commission thought that this was the right idea today to bring this mess back on to this community.” The local DUP MP, Carla Lockhart, accused O’Neill of “whipping up hysteria” at an “unlawful” protest. “It is unreal that we have a first minister behaving the way she is behaving,” she said. “If I did it, or if any of my colleagues did it, I would be in the back of a Land Rover.” Gavin Robinson, the DUP leader, said: “We now have lawmakers acting as law breakers,” and he accused O’Neill of “giving two fingers to the courts, the police, the rule of law”. Bryant cut short his attendance at the Labour party conference in Liverpool to travel to Belfast, but said he did not have the powers to call the march off unless police formally requested him to do so. He said the nationalist protest was unlawful and called on politicians to “calm things down”. Bryant said: “It is incumbent on everybody in political office to take this moment very, very seriously and to take the temperature down, to think twice before … inflating any argument and to think about what somebody else who doesn’t share your opinion might think about the way you’ve put your case.” Earlier on Sunday the tense standoff drew in the prime minister, Andy Burnham, who appealed for “calm on all sides”. The Irish taoiseach, Mícheál Martin, echoed that but described the Parades Commission decision as “incomprehensible and wrong”. He called for the situation to be mediated sensibly in a way “that protects the gains that have been made and the peace and harmony that has prevailed for so long”. The Drumcree parade on Garvaghy Road – a Catholic enclave in a largely Protestant town – previously sparked some of the most serious and violent disorder in Northern Ireland’s history. On Friday, the Parades Commission granted permission subject to restrictions, including a limit of 35 participants, an 8am start time instead of 1pm, and that it should be held in silence. The decision was challenged and blocked on Saturday by a judge, Justice Patricia Smyth, who said the “long-running dispute has the potential to escalate” across Northern Ireland. That decision was then challenged by the Orange Order, leading to two further hearings on Saturday night and Sunday morning. The final, time-limited sitting, which began at 20 minutes past midnight on Sunday, was heard before Mr Justice Humphreys, who acknowledged the “unusual if not unprecedented circumstances … with a parade scheduled to begin in just over six hours’ time”. Outlining his decision, Humphreys cited case law that as a public body the courts must respect the commission’s judgment and “their decisions will not be lightly interfered with”.

title: Israel does not have right to close UK consulate in Jerusalem, Foreign Office advised
summary: Former attorney general Dominic Grieve says Israel is not entitled to shut mission in occupied Palestinian territory
text: Israel does not have a legal right to act on its plan to close the British consulate in East Jerusalem, the former attorney general Dominic Grieve has advised the UK Foreign Office. Israel has said it intends to shut the consulate on 8 October in response to the sweeping ban on trade with goods from Israeli settlements announced by the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, this month. Israel said on Sunday that it planned to revoke the credentials of Dutch diplomats from the country’s mission to Palestine, in response to the Netherlands’ ban on imports from illegal Israeli settlements. Grieve, who was a Conservative MP between 1997 and 2019 and attorney general from 2010 to 2014, said Israel did not have the right to shut the consulate since it was situated in East Jerusalem, which is recognised by the United Nations and most of its members, including the UK, as being occupied Palestinian territory. When challenged in the Lords by the former UK ambassador Lord Hannay on the legality of Israel’s action, the Foreign Office minister Lord Wood said his fellow peer may have a point, and knew more about the subject than he did, but that he feared Israel de facto could make the consulate inoperable. Grieve said the UK should challenge the decision in the courts, arguing Israel was asserting a right it did not possess as an occupying power to impose sovereign control over East Jerusalem. The UK mission in Jerusalem dates from 1838, predating the creation of the state of Israel by more than 100 years, and is separate from the embassy based in Tel Aviv. The consul general reports direct to the Foreign Office, and has its own staff and a distinct diplomatic role, covering Jerusalem, the rest of the West Bank and Gaza. Grieve argues in an advisory paper sent to the Foreign Office by the British Palestine Project that “retaining a consulate general in East Jerusalem after recognition of the state of Palestine preserves the UK’s position that Jerusalem’s final status remains to be determined. It does not concede Israeli sovereignty.” Grieve said the UK government had a duty to oppose the move. He pointed out the UK government had formally accepted the July 2024 advisory opinion of the international court of justice that governments should recognise Israel’s presence in occupied Palestinian territory as unlawful. Separate from the legal position, Grieve said the closure of the consulate was a measure designed to fall on Palestinians, not on Britain alone, because it would hamper aid, oversight and reporting from the West Bank and Gaza. He said: “Israel’s method in the city has been to create facts on the ground through unlawful settlement building and property seizure, and to press states to recognise those facts diplomatically. The closure should be challenged as a further attempt to exercise powers outwith those permitted to an occupier.” In closing the consulate, the Israeli foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, asserted Israeli sovereignty over the whole city of Jerusalem, which the UN security council has expressly said Israel does not possess. The decision to revoke credentials of Dutch diplomats, announced by Sa’ar on Sunday, also in effect bars them from Israeli-controlled East Jerusalem and is likely to force the closure of their representative office in Ramallah. The Netherlands’ ban on imports from occupied Palestine came into force on 22 September. The guidance applies to companies and individual travellers, and covers items bought before or after the legislation came into force, including gifts, souvenirs and items for personal use, the Dutch customs authority said. Israel’s military occupation of the West Bank, East Jerusalem and Gaza means diplomats need Israeli accreditation to operate in Palestine. Sa’ar claimed that Dutch diplomats from the Ramallah mission could continue representing their nation’s interests “from Palestinian Authority territory, rather than from the territory of the state of Israel”. The Israeli foreign ministry did not immediately respond to questions about how this would work in practical terms. When Israel took the same measures against Norwegian diplomats in 2024, in response to the country’s decision to recognise Palestine, it was forced to close its mission based in the West Bank town of al-Ram. “We consider the Netanyahu government’s decision to be extreme and unreasonable,” the Norwegian foreign minister, Espen Barth Eide, said at the time. Diplomats based in Jordan have supported Norwegian relations with Palestine since then.

title: ‘Counting window’ seen as high-risk time for Trump to cast doubt on midterm results | First Thing
summary: Experts warn Republicans may try and sow distrust and claim ‘foreign interference’ in crucial hours after counting begins
text: Good morning. Election experts have warned that Donald Trump’s administration could use the crucial hours and days after November’s midterm elections to disrupt the results after struggling to enforce the crackdown it wanted on voting. After a succession of court setbacks to plans to restrict voting access, and with less than six weeks remaining until polls close, the post-election “counting window” is being seen as a particularly vulnerable moment by former US federal government officials. How might Republicans cause doubt over results? Caitlin Durkovich, a former deputy homeland security adviser, said: “I think because the administration has lost so many of their attempts to disrupt the normal process in court, that they are going to use the claim of foreign interference at the end of voting days to either seize equipment or to seize ballots, whether they’re legally justified to do so or not.” What are Democratic prospects for the midterms looking like? With control of the US Congress in the balance, Shrai Popat has interviewed Yasmin Radjy, a grassroots organizer, about what Democrats are getting right – and wrong – in the election run-up. UK counter-terror police investigate Iran link over suspected bomb plot at English base used by US forces British counter-terrorism police are investigating whether Iran is behind a suspected bomb plot after armed officers found explosives in three vans parked minutes from an RAF base used by the US military. After five men were arrested on terrorism charges, investigators were examining materials found in the vans near RAF Fairford, with an initial view being that they were consistent with improvised explosive devices. What have authorities said about the plot? Counter-terrorism police said: “At around 12.45am Sunday, police received a call relating to three suspicious vehicles which appeared to be travelling towards the airbase. Armed officers responded and five men were arrested.” How did the arrests unfold? A resident of the village of Whelford was driving home from a party when she saw three white vans parked on a country road. She was immediately suspicious, she said, and became all the more so when she spotted a “large group of hooded and balaclavaed” men. She called emergency services and police arrived on the scene 15 minutes later. You can follow the latest developments in this story in our live blog. What has the US ambassador to the UN, Mike Waltz, said about attempts to end the US-Iran war? “They were asking for everything upfront with a promise that they would then talk,” Waltz told CNN. “The president is just not confident that the Iranians are coming in good faith and that we will truly negotiate the end of their nuclear program.” Republican senator criticizes White House for taxpayer-funded Trump ads The US senator John Kennedy told CBS News on Sunday “there ought to be a rule” against the White House expanding a taxpayer-funded advertising campaign to promote Donald Trump’s political agenda before the November midterm elections – before tacitly admitting such spending is “probably” illegal. Kennedy appeared to also be acknowledging the argument made by Jamie Raskin, a Democratic congressman, that any government employees who worked on the pro-Trump ads may have committed a felony violation of the Hatch Act, a law that bars government workers from partisan campaign activities. US attorney general defends Trump’s White House media ban Donald Trump’s attorney general, Todd Blanche, argued that the administration was permitted to ban three news outlets from the White House because “it is a privilege and not a right to be there”. On Thursday, a judge issued a temporary restraining order requiring the White House to temporarily restore the credentials of affected journalists at CNN, MS Now and Politico, and they were allowed entry to the executive complex. However, on Saturday CNN said its journalists were barred from joining the press pool traveling with the president on Air Force One. Pressed to point to a specific report the administration objected to, Blanche seemed to suggest that any negative reporting about Trump must be inaccurate, saying: “The information coming out of CNN and some of these other networks is wholly and completely, almost 100% negative toward the president.” Without providing any evidence, Blanche repeated the administration’s position that the affected three outlets’ reporting amounted to a “national security problem”. In other news … Madonna and Taylor Swift triumphed at the 2026 MTV Video Music awards, with the former winning three trophies and the latter winning the night’s top honor, extending her run as the most-awarded artist in VMAs history. Bill Gates has called on the US to regulate the development of artificial intelligence, saying that the technology left unchecked could cause “a billion deaths”. Datacenter developers are manipulating the EPA’s air pollution permitting process to avoid emission controls and scrutiny of their projects, environmental advocates allege. France’s far-right National Rally has surged in senate elections, with Marine Le Pen hailing a “historic victory”. Stat of the day: 61m tonnes of rubble – Gaza aid workers face delicate task of clearing ruins concealing up to 10,000 bodies The removal of the war debris, in which lives, memories and unexploded Israeli bombs lie buried, is one of largest clearance operations in modern history. Seham Tantesh reports from Gaza City for the Guardian. Building Power: Climate protesters call out big tech’s disconnect from reality In New York City activists gathered outside the OpenAI offices during climate week as figures showed that from 2024 to 2026 at least $64bn in proposed datacenter buildout was blocked by local organizing. Don’t miss this: US states grapple with uptick in encounters between bears and humans Experts largely attribute the increase in human-bear encounters – up in 15 states – to the impact of unusual weather on the animals’ food sources and a rebound in recent decades in black, brown and grizzly bear populations. … or this: A new museum coaxes Austrians to embrace The Sound of Music It is a beloved classic all over the world – except where it was filmed. Now a new museum aims to lift the profile of The Sound of Music in the beautiful Austrian city of Salzburg, where much of it was made. Climate check: Hurricane Nolo still threatens Hawaii as nor’easter storm batters US east coast Hurricane Nolo was moving away from the Hawaiian islands on Sunday, but the threat of heavy rain, flash flooding and strong winds persisted. Mexico’s National Meteorological Service said Polo was expected to make a Baja landfall on Monday. Meanwhile, a nor’easter storm was battering the US east coast with heavy winds causing power outages.
