title: Concern mounts over slow-moving, planetary-scale ‘Kelvin’ wave heading for California
summary: The ocean phenomenon could raise sea levels by up to a foot as El Niño keeps warm water trapped along the coast
text: Concerns are mounting about an ocean phenomenon known as a Kelvin wave that could raise sea levels along the California coastline by up to a foot, as scientists say El Niño is supercharging the threat of storm surges and flooding in the coming months. As an incredibly strong El Niño continues to develop in the Pacific, the phenomenon brings with it a strange shift in the ocean. The Kelvin wave phenomenon is created when trade winds that usually blow from South America towards Asia die down or reverse in El Niño years, setting off a massive, slow-moving slosh of water. Kelvin waves are not like crashing waves at the beach. They are planetary in scale, spanning thousands of miles. And when a Kelvin wave kicks off, it brings with it an untold amount of warm water that slowly moves from the western Pacific, along the equator, towards South, Central and North America. “You can follow them along … we see the higher sea levels along the equator, and when the wave reaches the coast of South America, it cannot continue to go eastward,” Severine Fournier, a research scientist studying ocean circulation at Nasa’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory, said. “So it goes north and south.” One such wave hit the northern tip of South America in late August and has begun moving up towards the west coast of the US. That wave could reach California shores within days, and when it does, ocean scientists say it may raise sea levels by up to a foot for months as El Niño lingers and keeps that warm water trapped along the coast. Nate Mantua, a research scientist at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s Southwest Fisheries Science Center, explained that in a typical year, there is a thick layer of warm water in the western Pacific. “When the wind stops blowing or weakens, the force that’s holding that pile of water in place goes away, so that water surges or sloshes back towards California,” he said, noting researchers expect the influence of the Kelvin wave to linger through the winter and into early next year. Mantua said Kelvin waves were a natural phenomenon that have been happening for thousands of years and measured by agencies like Noaa since record-keeping began. But sea levels have already risen about 8in over the last century, meaning Kelvin waves will add more water on top of a figure that’s already going up. “We can predict a lot of the impacts,” he added, “but not all.” This year’s El Niño is likely to be the largest in at least 1,000 years. Climate readings have already surged past the highest temperature ever recorded for the phenomenon several months before it is expected to peak. The climate pattern also brings with it the threat of more severe storms, storm surges, flooding and coastal erosion. For California, all of those effects will happen on top of the sea level rise the Kelvin wave brings, making the threat even worse. “It’s a wave unlike the ones you’re used to at the beach. They don’t crash, you can’t really seem them come by,” said Mike Jacox, a research oceanographer at the Southwest Fisheries Science Center. “This winter, we’re supposed to have some really high tides around Thanksgiving and Christmas. If you also have more storms, then you have storm surge. It’s just like you’re raising the floor on all that stuff that happens.” California is already taking steps to prepare for a potentially catastrophic season. This week, the state’s governor, Gavin Newsom, declared a state of emergency, mobilizing resources before any future winter storms, coastal flooding or other impacts. Road-closure and snow-removal equipment is being staged along highways; the state national guard will be prepared for any necessary search-and-rescue efforts; and agencies are finding ways to cut red tape in the event of a natural disaster. The California Coastal Commission, which plans and regulates the use of land and water along the state’s coastline, has urged homeowners and residents to prepare now. That includes inspecting any areas vulnerable to flooding or erosion, adding drainage and addressing any causes of damage before severe weather arrives. “A key observation from past El Niño events is that the most damaging storms are often those that coincide with the highest tides,” Kate Huckelbridge, the head of the commission, wrote in a memo earlier this month. “Storms that peak during high tides are far more likely to cause damage than if the same storm peaked during low tide.” Mantua said past years with exceptionally strong El Niño’s – 1983, 1998, 2016 – had helped researchers better predict what can happen, and where. But with rising sea levels and the “really exceptional intensity of this event”, he said, “it may end up causing even more damage than we’ve seen in major El Niño winters”. “Other things have been happening, right?” he said. “In the El Niño winters in the northern Pacific, we tend to have a lot of storminess, we tend to have more storms and big storm waves in the ocean than we typically do. So you add that on top of this elevated sea level … then you just expose places to more of the ocean’s energy and simple inundation.”

title: Gouged: why Americans are being ripped off – and what to do about it
summary: How can we fix our pricing crisis? Economic sociologist Lindsay Owens urges tough new rules – and a consumer uprising
text: “Repeat after me: it’s not my fault, it’s not my fault, it’s not my fault.” That’s the message to frustrated US shoppers in Gouged: The End of a Fair Price – and What That Means for Your Wallet by Lindsay Owens, economic sociologist and head of the Groundwork Collaborative, a progressive Washington thinktank. Consumer rage is rising and no wonder – we are all living through the “reinvention of the rip-off”, Owens told the Guardian, an experience that is undermining Americans’ trust in the economy. Nothing short of a consumer uprising and a slate of tough new rules is going to fix the problem, she believes. The book concludes with a “shoppers’ bill of rights” that lays out how local and federal governments could write rules to fix the problem: ban companies from using shared software to coordinate prices, it urges, and require AI “shopping assistants” to act in consumers’ best interest, not steer them to higher-price items, among other moves. “A cost of living crisis is the right time to build the constituency for a revived consumer movement in this country,” Owens says. The following interview was compiled from several conversations and edited and condensed for clarity. Why did you write Gouged? Right around the time that America started experiencing rising inflation and cost of living in 2021, I started to realize that there was something else going on besides just high prices. The way companies were talking about pricing was starting to shift. Their costs were going up but they weren’t too worried about it. They were planning to pass all of their rising costs along to us, and they were pretty bullish about gilding the lily and going for more. In an economy with competitive pricing, that shouldn’t happen, right? I started to see a little bit of a breadcrumb trail: “Oh, these companies are bullish because they have a plan for this, right?” They have some new techniques and technologies they’re planning to deploy, they have some new partnerships, they’ve been buying up AI pricing companies … they were ready for this moment. What actually changed inside corporate boardrooms? Cost-cutting hit bone. I cut my teeth in academia and the Senate studying the ruthless form of American capitalism that’s centered around it: bust unions and keep wages down, pass Nafta and outsource labor, bring in the bean counters from the big four accounting firms and ask: “How do we limit our regulatory costs?” Low prices were part of that part of capitalism. But there’s been a shift toward the revenue side of the ledger that includes getting better on price hiking. That’s easier to do when there’s less competition, but it’s also the result of new technologies. Gouged details data-mining companies unknown to the average consumer, like EverSight, Kronos, Plexure. How important have they been to the “gouging” problem US consumers are facing? Hugely important. Their dossiers contain thousands of data points and inferences about consumers, including their age, income, health, religion and even partisan affiliation. Virtually no one evades data brokers’ grasp. One data broker claims to have data profiles on roughly 95% of adults. With these troves of personal data in hand, retailers increasingly rely on outside consultants and AI startups who specialize in the “art and science behind pricing decisions”. They run experiments on consumers – and even personalize prices to each consumer’s pain point. Should these companies exist in an economy that’s also fair to workers and consumers? Profit maximization is not intrinsically problematic. In a competitive marketplace, companies would have to compete on price and quality in order to win over consumers, resulting in better products and better deals. However, as competition disappears and the law struggles to keep pace, new technologies and newer, more brazen methods of corporate profiteering erode the basic social contract between shoppers and retailers. Companies whose sole purpose is to harvest consumer data would probably cease to exist if Congress had passed adequate privacy protections. Companies should not get a gold star for refusing to gouge customers; they should be required not to. There’s a lot of telling history in this book, like the lightbulb that has been burning in California for 120 years, and how manufacturers banded together to make sure they never lasted that long again. Yet we’re still surprised by “planned obsolescence”. Have modern US consumers just been too naive? I think we all have a sense that this is going on and something has shifted, but we don’t fully appreciate how systematic and how purposeful this is. Whether it’s making the jar of Skippy peanut butter concave, degrading product quality, locking you out of something you bought, forcing you to pay top dollar for parts and repair – all of that is really baked into how companies operate these days. I don’t think Americans are naive. But every 10 or 20 years we need to have a conversation about what we’re owed as consumers and shoppers. It’s time to update the rules. How are American shoppers doing right now? I think American shoppers are exhausted. High prices make shopping pretty treacherous. The amount of basics Americans are putting on credit cards, the amount of Americans who are using things like “buy now, pay later” shows how difficult it is. Adding insult to injury is the increasingly opaque manipulative and volatile way that corporate America does pricing. This reinvention of the rip-off that we’re all living through has undermined trust in one of the major ways we participate in the economy. Comparison shopping is almost impossible now. Trying to get a refund is a three-day battle with a chatbot, and even if you think you won, you’d better remember to check with your bank to make sure they actually follow through. Where are we in the current inflation and rising cost cycle? I don’t even think we’re even at the halfway point. This is something I’ve been saying since 2022. Every time I was on the Hill, I was screaming at the Biden administration to focus more on prices and cost of living. This is a once-in-50-year period of high inflation. Something has completely changed in our culture and our economy, in our politics, and you have to be responsive to it. You wrote Gouged before the US and Israel attacks on Iran, which have ramped up inflation. Yes. I do talk in the book about Trump’s trade war, and its impact on prices. The Iran war is similar. Most Americans do understand how gas prices ripple through the whole economy. The fog of war, the fog of crisis, is really powerful. It makes it so that Americans have a hard time discerning which piece of the price increase is indeed because of import costs, and which is companies gilding the lily. Buckle up. You expect companies to take advantage of the war? Absolutely. What about your personal shopping? How are you and your family navigating this situation? The first thing I will say is I am not the “points guy” for e-commerce. I, like you, am being screwed by these companies. Most Americans are balancing trying to get a good deal with figuring out how much time they could possibly spend on not getting ripped off. So I updated how I comparison-shop. I look at brick and mortar, on the app, logged in, logged out. I try not to buy in-app. I run experiments. Call your friends and say: “What price are you seeing?” My husband and I sit in bed with our laptops open, figuring out which of us gets the better deal. Whoever gets the better deal buys the plane tickets. One thing I often hear from readers is “nothing is ever going to change” – a sort of pessimism about reforming the system. I do think the deck is stacked against us and we have our work cut out. It feels like Whac-A-Mole – you get a win in one city, you find out your bill is vetoed in another. [Colorado governor] Jared Polis vetoed surveillance pricing legislation. We’re still waiting for [New York governor] Kathy Hochul to sign a bill that passed there. But when Americans find out that companies are partnering with AI companies to spy on you and figure out how to take your last three pennies for every item in your grocery cart, they get pretty ticked off. I think the optimism I have is the sort of public anger, and, frankly, the groundswell of public conversation around this. The Federal Trade Commission is sorting through about 1,000 comments from Americans about surveillance pricing regulation. Wendy’s had to cry “uncle” and say they wouldn’t do surge pricing on their electronic menu board. Delta cried “uncle”, and so did Instacart two weeks after Groundwork exposed their algorithmic pricing experiments. I think all of that is a really important part about how we stick the genie back in the bottle, combined with legislative activity. If Democrats take the House and Senate, there’s a long list of things they are expected to address related to the Trump administration, national security et cetera. Where should this be on the priority list? The top issue for the American people, and it has been this way since 2022, is prices and the cost of living. Anything that takes on the economy is going to be top of the list. The only that could shift could be rising concern about AI – and a lot of the most sinister nefarious and opaque pricing practices that corporate America is using are powered by AI. We’re seeing interest from Republicans as well. I testified in front of [Missouri senator] Josh Hawley on this a couple weeks ago, at his request, as a majority witness, which has never happened to me before. You ask readers to repeat “It’s not your fault” three times before they try to confront this new landscape. Why? From the bottom of my heart, I don’t believe it should be Americans’ job to duck and dodge and beat the machine. The most dystopian version of this world is one in which there’s a “points guy” for everything. Outsmarting price-gouging on your own is like trying to solve climate change by yourself. Gougers are always reinventing themselves, always figuring out newer, more cunning ways to stay one step ahead. And all that effort eats up one of your most precious resources: time. Companies know this – and they are banking on it. What are you hoping to change, near term? It’s been a really long time since the consumer laws have been updated. I do think e-commerce and agentic commerce begs a new type of policy regime. This year alone, there are 90 pieces of legislation throughout the country, in states and cities to try to curtail algorithmic price fixing. A cost of living crisis is the right time to build the constituency for a revived consumer movement in this country.

title: ‘Contract between humans and river’: Bristol Avon’s rights enshrined in charter
summary: River charters part of wider movement establishing ‘moral’ framework to protect nature and hold institutions to account
text: One Monday morning in spring last year, 12 people gathered in the morning drizzle at Joyce’s Pool, one of the sources of the Bristol River Avon, and took the first steps of the inaugural Avon pilgrimage. Over the course of eight days, a revolving cast of pilgrims walked about 100 miles from the source of the river to the point at which it reaches the sea, in some cases bivvying on the riverside at night. Along the way they planted trees, sowed seeds, restored footpaths and presented councillors and decision-makers with a fledgling Avon charter, developed by the Bristol campaign group Conham Bathing. “The reception was so good across political parties and interest groups,” recalls pilgrim Hamish Evans, who co-founded We Are Avon, which organised the pilgrimage and is building a movement to regenerate the Avon bioregion. “It felt inevitable that we would one day achieve better rights and representation for this river.” On Sunday, World Rivers Day marked a breakthrough for the annual pilgrimage and wider Avon campaigning. Councillors, environmental groups, river guardians, and members of the public gathered at 11am at Parade Gardens in Bath to publicly sign the Avon bioregional charter of river rights (ABCRR). The charter enshrines the Avon’s rights to exist, thrive, and evolve naturally, to flow sustainably, to not be polluted, to preserve its biodiversity, to aim for regeneration and restoration, to build cultural and community connection, and to represent and advocate for the rights of the river. River charters are part of a national and international movement to establish legal rights and stronger agency for nature. Recent UK initiatives include Lewes town council recognising the rights of trees, organisations putting nature on the board, “interspecies councils” exploring interspecies decision-making, and a nature’s rights bill being debated in parliament. About 40 river charters have emerged since the Sussex River Ouse became the first in England to have its rights recognised by a local authority, in February 2025. The ABCRR contains similar language, but it also breaks new ground. An unprecedented nine councils have endorsed it, including Bath and North East Somerset (B&NES), Bristol City, and North Somerset (under its motion for the ocean). More are expected to follow. We Are Avon’s bioregional movement also represents a new model for upholding charter rights. River charters do not replace statutory duties, create legal obligations, or explain how competing rights should be handled. But proponents argue that they can align governance bodies around clear moral rights, empower grassroots stewardship and hold institutions to account. Josh Levene, a founder of the UK River Rights Network, says the best charters are “social contracts between humans and the river”. The more integrated they are with existing institutions such as councils and catchment partnerships, he says, the stronger they become. Through the charter campaign, We Are Avon convenes cross-council workshops exploring bioregional river governance for the first time. This has increased communication between councils, Wessex Water, and the West of England combined authority. Individual councils are yet to publish implementation plans, though B&NES has appointed a river advocate to represent the Avon. The councillor Oli Henman says the charter also “allows us to embed some of those principles into our [climate and nature] strategy”, due in early 2027. The Bristol Avon catchment partnership has not officially endorsed the charter, but is collaborating with We Are Avon. Henman says the charter “is really about re-energising, stepping up ambition, expanding that partnership”. The We Are Avon movement, unique among UK river charters, plans to push existing institutions to uphold the charter – while also modelling alternative approaches. Bioregionalism advocates for environmental governance that maps on to ecological systems – in this case the Avon catchment. Since 2023, We Are Avon has been mobilising farmers, river guardians, and other groups around bioregional ecology, grassroots stewardship, and river rights. Levene says the “Avon is furthest along the way to showcasing the bioregional approach”. The campaigner Meg Avon, who “married” the Avon in 2023 to highlight river pollution, says 18 Avon guardian groups now test water quality, pick litter, and “maintain that relationship with their local tributary or section”. For Paul Powlesland, a co-founder of Lawyers for Nature, this groundswell is critical. “River rights charters are an amazing way to begin changing our attitude towards rivers, but they don’t change the law by themselves,” he says. “Most important is what comes next. The Avon is lucky to have an amazing community of river guardians and supportive councils who can begin to make these rights a practical reality.” We Are Avon is not relying on existing governance structures. “We want to keep the pressure on councils, but don’t want to wait for that,” says Evans. “We’re also making our own table.” This means growing the movement and empowering local actors to step into charter implementation without top-down guidance. As well as guardian groups, We Are Avon is convening farm clusters to share regenerative practices, and preparing a campaign to acquire a community-owned hub to demonstrate regenerative land management. “If the community doesn’t have more autonomy over those things, the issues will perpetuate,” says Evans. Movement building means shifting narratives – something charters can support. “Charters give people hope, which is in short supply,” says Levene. “They give people a sense of what they feel they’ve been missing for a long time – agency.” Meg Avon has witnessed this. “We’re already starting to shift cultural consciousness into acknowledging that rivers are alive and subjects worthy of rights,” she says. “People are willing to go wading in shit because they get so much joy out of walking with us.” If We Are Avon’s model strengthens charter enforcement, more than local pilgrims may soon be walking in its footsteps.

title: As the US midterms approach, Trump’s boasts on the economy fall flat with voters
summary: Trump’s tariffs and his war against Iran caused prices to to rise, but the US president continues to claim it’s ‘the greatest economy in history’
text: Donald Trump has taken to repeating a familiar boast: “We have the greatest economy in history,” Trump said recently at a White House press gaggle. The boast comes even though inflation is higher and economic growth lower than when Joe Biden left office, even though gas prices have jumped about 50% since the war against Iran started, and even though 73% of Americans think the economy is in fair or poor shape (48% say it’s in poor shape). What’s more, the Federal Reserve is so worried about inflation that it just raised interest rates. “It’s bluster, it’s gaslighting for him to say the economy is the greatest ever,” said Darrick Hamilton, chief economist for the AFL-CIO, the nation’s main union federation. “The economy is trending down by many measures. A lot of that has been caused by Trump’s unforced errors.” Hamilton said those errors include Trump’s tariffs and his war against Iran, both of which have pushed up prices – inflation is running at 3.4%, up from 3.0% when Biden left office. One unfortunate result is that prices have been rising faster than wages, worsening Americans’ affordability problems. A New York Times/Siena Poll found that 71% of voters disapprove of how Trump is handling the cost of living. Over the past 12 months, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, fuel oil prices have soared 52%, while ground beef is up 7.2%, fish and seafood up 6.5%, coffee 6.1%, sugar and sweets 6.1% and electricity up 3.8%. The administration boasts that egg prices are down 23%, even as gas has soared to an average of $4.47 per gallon nationwide. With the economy growing at a modest 1.5% rate in the second quarter, Trump stretches the truth when he boasts of a great economy, considering that under John F Kennedy, Lyndon Johnson and Ronald Reagan, there were full years when GDP growth – the broadest measure of the nation’s economy – averaged over 6%. (The economy grew at a 2.7% annual rate during Biden’s last six months in office.) Consumer sentiment has slid sharply in light of today’s stubborn inflation, mixed with slower economic growth, high interest rates and huge economic uncertainty about trade wars and AI. According to a University of Michigan poll, consumer sentiment fell in September to its second lowest level ever in the poll’s 74-year history. Only this past May was lower. Kush Desai, a White House spokesman, said: “President Trump has always been clear about temporary disruptions as a result of the Iran conflict, but the Trump administration has remained laser-focused delivering on the president’s long-term economic agenda on the home front.” As good news, Desai cited “continued private-sector job growth” and “booming investments”. The unemployment rate has been fairly low during Trump’s second term – at 4.1%, it’s about the same rate as in Biden’s last year. But the jobless rate has been lower under several previous presidents; it sank to 2.5 % at one point under Dwight Eisenhower and below 4% at times under Bill Clinton, Richard Nixon and Johnson. But in a not-so-great statistic, job growth has been mediocre since Trump returned to office – just 43,000 a month on average, less than one-third the 145,000 average during Biden’s last two years in office. Although Trump said his tariffs were aimed at revving up manufacturing, the US has lost 35,000 factory jobs since he returned to office. Last month, however, there was good news on job growth – the nation added an impressive 162,000 jobs. Desai said the Biden administration “padded employment growth” by “adding hundreds of thousands of government or government-adjacent jobs that relied on runaway federal spending”. He added, “President Trump is slashing regulations and taxes to create sustainable private-sector jobs – not juking the statistics by drumming up government spending.” Michael Strain, director of economic policy studies at the American Enterprise Institute, a center-right thinktank, had an upbeat view, saying: “The economy is strong.” Strain added, “the unemployment rate is very low,” and “the economy is very resilient in the face of high energy prices, and consumers are resilient in the face of the trade war.” He noted that “investment spending is very strong”. “Where we’re not doing well is inflation,” Strain added. “It’s eroding wages and income. Inflation is a headwind that households are facing.” Responding to the widespread concerns about inflation, Desai said: “The last two inflation reports [show] dramatic month-over-month price reductions in beef, prescription drugs, and auto insurance.” He said this was “proof that the administration’s targeted policy interventions to lower costs are delivering”. Responding to concerns about inflation, Desai said: “President Trump had always been clear about market disruptions as a result of the Iran conflict, but the last two inflation reports showing dramatic month-over-month price reductions in beef, prescription drugs, and auto insurance are proof that the administration’s targeted policy interventions to lower costs for American families are delivering.” Lindsay Owens, president of the Groundwork Collaborative, a progressive thinktank, was far more downbeat about the economy. “I think it’s going pretty poorly,” she said. “The Federal Reserve just raised interest rates, when Americans were already concerned about high interest rates. That’s not going to do anything to help people who want to buy houses when mortgage rates are already high. Americans are feeling that things are pretty grim. “Trump’s approval rating on the economy was his superpower in his first term,” she continued. “But now it’s absolutely in the toilet.” Just 28% of Americans approve of how Trump has handled the economy, according to a new Marquette Law School poll. Just 29% of Republicans say the economy is better than a year ago, down from last January when 72% of Republicans said the economy was better than a year earlier, Owens said AI has been crucial for Trump’s economy, helping fuel GDP growth, business investment and repeated stock market records. “The pieces of the economy that are doing well are completely propped up by AI investment,” Owens said. “That’s the whole story. That’s what Trump has going for him. “But,” she continued, “that’s an increasingly precarious place for him to be right now,” considering the fast-growing worries about AI, including the fierce opposition to datacenters in many communities, the recent calls to slow AI development for safety reasons, and Wall Street’s increasing skittishness about AI stocks. Owens pointed to a second factor that’s sustained the economy: the vast spending power of the richest 10% of Americans. She said they account for nearly 50% of consumer spending, and while the bottom 50% by income are feeling squeezed, it’s the top 10%’s buying power – whether on new cars, airline tickets, or home renovations – that has kept consumer spending and the economy from faltering. “It seems to me the president doesn’t care about how average Americans are doing,” Owens said, pointing to such Trump statements as “I don’t think about Americans’ financial situation,” which Trump said last May when asked about how the Iran war was affecting Americans. And last week, he downplayed consumers’ dismay about the surge in gasoline prices, saying, it was “a little higher” and “it’s a very inexpensive price”. Owens said responsibility for high gas prices and higher inflation rests squarely with Trump. “This is not a situation where the economic conditions are beyond his control,” she said. “He has made a deliberate series of choices that cut against his promises to reduce prices.” According to the Yale Budget Lab, the average American household will spend $1,100 more this year due to Trump’s tariffs, while Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody’s Analytics, says the average household will have to spend $1,000 more this year because of higher fuel, food and other prices caused by the Iran war. “The biggest drivers of inflation are his tariffs and the war against Iran,” Owens said. “These are policy-driven price hikes,” The White House sees it differently. “The hard data of actual consumer spending and retail sales has remained robust throughout President Trump’s term so far. American consumers remain resilient and are voting with their dollars,” said Desai. How consumers really feel will become clear in November, when the real voting takes place.

title: Hormone-disrupting herbicide contaminating 25% of continental US rivers, report finds
summary: Atrazine, banned in 60 countries, polluting rivers at levels that can harm wildlife and may threaten human health
text: The hormone-disrupting herbicide atrazine is contaminating nearly 25%, or about 860,000 miles, of all continental US rivers at levels that can harm wildlife and may threaten human health, a new review of federal records has found. The waterways cover over 20% of surface drinking water intakes across the country, and over 675,000 private and commercial wells. Atrazine can have severe impacts on human and animal hormones, especially for developing children. It was found to “chemically castrate” frogs, and cause some to change sexes. The herbicide is so dangerous that it has been effectively banned in 60 countries, including the European Union, since 2003. Litigation in the US seeks to strike down its approval, but it remains the second most widely used pesticide here, with about 70m pounds sprayed on the nation’s cropland annually. The report, compiled by the Center for Biological Diversity, which advocates for stricter pesticide regulations, marks the first time anyone has analyzed all the EPA’s atrazine records and identified the threat’s extent. “The problem is vast,” Nathan Donley, a report co-author and environmental health science director at the Center for Biological Diversity, told the Guardian. “Everyone recognizes this is a big problem, but the EPA has utterly failed to do anything about it for the last three or four decades.” Atrazine is primarily used on commodity crops like corn, sugarcane and sorghum. The research around its health impacts is robust, and it is classified as a probable carcinogen by the International Agency for Cancer Research. It is an endocrine disruptor that is especially dangerous for developing fetuses and children at even very low levels of exposure, and is linked to impaired fetal growth, pre-term birth, birth defects and low birth weight. Atrazine can be particularly harmful to reproductive systems, and is linked to the “feminization” of the male gonads, irregular menstrual cycles, lower sperm counts, poor semen quality and lower fecundity in men and women. In animals, it also causes liver, kidney and heart damage. Exposure at levels as low as 0.1 parts per billion (ppb) in water has been shown to harm reproductive organ development in frogs, potentially leading to population decline. The current allowable level of atrazine in human drinking water is 30 times higher, at 3 ppb. It was “no surprise that the pollution is so widespread”, said Tyrone Hayes, a University of California, Berkeley pesticides researcher who discovered atrazine’s impact on frogs’ reproduction systems in the early aughts. He was also in the late 1990s hired by Novartis, which produced atrazine until it was bought by Syngenta, to study the chemical. “At the time it was known that atrazine was the most common pesticide contaminant in drinking water, rain, surface water and groundwater. You name it – atrazine was there,” Hayes told the Guardian. He noted it also travels via the atmosphere, and the US government found atrazine sprayed in Kansas can rain down on Minnesota. “The effects are very clear, and in my opinion there is no safe level at which atrazine can be used because it is active in amphibians at 0.1 ppb, and there can be atrazine at 100 times that in rainfall,” Hayes added. The Center for Biological Diversity and other public health groups have sued over the EPA’s approval of atrazine, and in 2020 the agency said it would put together a plan to address the water pollution, Donley said. A 2024 draft he reviewed showed an inadequate plan that “is not worth the paper that it’s printed on”, Donley said, and it is likely that the lawsuit will resume once the final plan is published. The EPA has failed to act, Donley said, because atrazine is chemical giant Syngenta’s flagship product, widely used, and profitable. Analysts estimate $2-3bn in US sales in 2025. “It’s the one of the most powerful pesticide industry lobbies behind glyphosate, because of the amount of money being made, and it’s the result of political malfeasance,” Donley said. The EPA and Syngenta did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Among five hotspots where pollution is most concentrated are the Chesapeake Bay region, the midwest corn belt, Florida’s Lake Okeechobee, the lower Mississippi River and the Texas Gulf coast. The report highlights the unique risks in each area. In the midwest corn belt, including Kansas, Nebraska, Iowa, Missouri, Illinois, Indiana and Ohio, over two-thirds of river miles are contaminated, EPA records show, and that covers about half of the region’s wells and 68% of its drinking-water treatment facilities intakes. States in this region have rapidly rising early-onset cancer diagnoses compared with the rest of the country. This high level of contamination in the Chesapeake Bay watershed largely stems from the high concentration of corn grown in the region, which is home to 18 million people and more than 3,600 species of plants and animals. Meanwhile, atrazine-contaminated watersheds run nearly the entire length of the lower Mississippi River, many at concentrations more than five times the level the EPA has found harmful to aquatic ecosystems. “We need to follow the lead of over 60 countries around the world and ban atrazine once and for all,” Donley said. “Failing to do so will mean disease, death and dirty water in America for decades to come.”

title: Trump asked Xi Jinping if China would like to buy US weapons, American ambassador says
summary: David Perdue’s remarks come after a Taiwanese minister spoke of the ‘severe’ military threat posed by Beijing to the self-ruled island
text: Donald Trump offered to sell weapons to China while hosting its leader, Xi Jinping, last week, the US ambassador to China said on Sunday. David Perdue told Fox News on Sunday: “President Trump continues to say, hey, we sell arms to other people around the world. He actually asked President Xi, would he like to buy some at one point.” On Monday, Chinese state media praised the “extraordinary level of courtesy” that Trump had shown Xi on the Chinese leader’s visit to Washington. The extraordinary claim came during an interview about US policy on Taiwan, which has been waiting for months for Trump to approve a new arms sales ⁠package worth $14bn (£10.5bn), after a record multibillion-dollar deal was announced in December last year. Trump’s level of commitment to protecting Taiwan has previously been questioned. At a meeting with Xi in Beijing in May, ⁠Trump said he was keeping the $14bn Taiwan arms sales package in abeyance, describing it as a “very good negotiating chip” in dealings with China. Washington has long maintained a strategically ambiguous stance on whether it would defend Taiwan in the event of an invasion. But under the decades-old Taiwan Relations Act, it is required to provide Taipei with sufficient military equipment to defend itself. Beijing has repeatedly said it “resolutely opposes” Washington’s arms sales to the island democracy, which it regards as a breakaway province, despite never having ruled it, and has not renounced the use of force to take it. During their Washington meeting last week, Xi urged Trump to oppose “Taiwan independence”, according to a readout from the official Chinese news agency Xinhua. After Perdue’s interview, the White House told the New York Times the US had no plans to sell arms to China, while the state department said: “US law prohibits arms sales to China and there is no offer or plan to sell arms to China.” China is a net exporter of weapons. Of the arms that it does import, most come from Russia, but the volume is rapidly falling thanks to advances in China’s own military manufacturing capacity. China’s arms imports fell by 72% between 2021 and 2025 compared with the previous five years, according to data from the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute. Before the interview, the Taiwanese deputy foreign minister, Chen Ming-chi, spoke of the severe military threat China posed. “Taiwan faces a severe situation in the Taiwan strait. Even though China’s economy is declining, it continues investing more resources into building military capacity. Under ‌this context, the US very much understands our defence needs,” he told reporters in Taipei. On Sunday, a Taiwanese official, Shen Yu-chung, also pushed back on what he said was an attempt by Beijing to “falsely claim that the Chinese Communist party and the US were allies” in the second world war. A fact sheet released by the White House after the Trump-Xi summit had said China and the US “fought side by side to win” in the war. China’s government during the second world war was the Republic of China led by Chiang Kai-shek. Chiang’s government fled to Taiwan in 1949 after losing the Chinese civil war to the communists, who established the People’s Republic of China in 1949. In recent years Taiwan has sought to emphasise its history of fighting alongside western democratic allies as it hopes to bolster international support against aggression from Beijing. Trump has not mentioned the sale ‌since last week’s summit, saying ‌only on Saturday that Xi understands his position on Taiwan. Perdue told CNBC on Friday that there had been no change in Taiwan policy by Trump, including on arms sales. Reuters contributed to this report

title: John Fetterman accidentally calls himself ‘a lifelong Republican’
summary: Social and news media commenters seize on senator’s gaffe, with some characterizing it as a Freudian slip
text: With speculation about whether he may defect from the Democratic party swirling around him, the US senator John Fetterman described himself seemingly unintentionally as a “lifelong Republican” during a fireside chat in Texas over the weekend. Fetterman made the comment when someone listening to him speak with CBS News political correspondent Major Garrett at the Texas Tribune Festival on Saturday asked the Pennsylvania senator why he had not become an independent. “Because I’m a lifelong Republican,” Fetterman replied. Garrett promptly corrected him by saying, “Democrat,” as Fetterman raised a hand and shook his head in disbelief. “That’s a moment right there that’s clippable, ladies and gentlemen,” Garrett said amid laughter from the audience. “Go, go, go – internet, spin wildly! Wildly spin, internet!” Fetterman then remarked, “Yeah – I guarantee you that’s going to break through. That’ll get … clipped – yeah. I’m a lifelong Democrat, though, and that’s … the point.” Social and news media commenters quickly seized on video of Fetterman’s gaffe, with more than one characterizing it as a Freudian slip. Fetterman has drawn questions over his loyalty to the Democratic party after joining Republicans in opposing his party’s efforts to end the US war with Iran as well as to cut off military aid to Israel, which has been accused of committing genocide in Gaza. He also appeared in a video praising the Republican Pennsylvania US senator Dave McCormick at a convention held by the latter’s party in Dallas on 9 September. Fetterman – who was elected to the US Senate in 2022 – has denied that he intends to defect to the Republican party. He has said he would only abandon the Democrats if they became “the anti-Israel party”. “I’m not going to be a Republican,” Fetterman told a reporter at the US Capitol in a video published online by C-Span on 15 September. “Why can’t you guys just wait till the midterms? And if I turn a Republican, then I’ll be a liar.” At the Texas Tribune Festival on Saturday, Fetterman expressed his belief that it was “entirely possible” for the Democratic party to clinch a majority in the Senate during the federal midterm elections in November, with Republicans being predicted to lose seats in Congress. But he declined to indicate with whom he may side if he ends up holding a tie-breaking vote on any given issue in the 100-seat Senate after the midterms. “Let’s revisit after the midterms, and let’s see what happens – you know – if I happen to be 51,” said Fetterman, who was elected to the US Senate in 2022. “I don’t know.”

title: Boss of Beaverbrooks urges government to give businesses ‘a bit of a break’
summary: Jeweller reports flat sales and fall in underlying operating profit as retailers anticipate October budget
text: The boss of the family-owned jeweller Beaverbrooks has called on the government to give business “a bit of a break” by halting cost increases amid flat sales and falling profits. The retailer, founded in 1919, revealed a 9% fall in underlying operating profit to £7.8m last year after an increase in employer national insurance contributions (NICs) and the legal minimum wage introduced by the former chancellor Rachel Reeves. Anna Blackburn, the managing director of Beaverbrooks, said she was positive about the performance against the backdrop of a challenging retail market: “Everything we hear in the jewellery industry [suggests] this is a pretty strong performance,” she said. Total sales slipped 0.1% to £217m at the group, which operates 56 Beaverbrooks and four Loupe stores as well as 22 outlets for specific brands including watchmakers Omega, Breitling, Tudor and TAG Heuer. Blackburn said she wanted to see the government help boost consumer confidence and provide stability by tackling unemployment and inflation and not adding new taxes in next month’s budget as retailers prepare for Christmas. She said: “[The government] can’t increase business costs much more. Give business a bit of a break and stimulate some growth and confidence. A long-term, joined-up strategy is critical.” Blackburn said Beaverbrooks was outperforming its rivals in tough conditions as it continued to invest in its stores and staff, modernising its online operation and developing new products. “Our business has remained strong for 107 years because we believe in the high street and the importance of exceptional products and customer service.” The group has just opened its fourth Loupe watch boutique, in Sheffield, and is investing in revamping its outlets in Manchester’s Trafford Centre and Lakeside in Essex in the year ahead. Blackburn’s comments come after the since-departed boss of the John Lewis department store chain, Peter Ruis, said the chancellor’s budget would come at a “critical period” for retailers and he wanted to see more help on business rates. The boss of fellow retailer JD Sports has also said Reeves’s move to increase employer NICs at the same time as a chunky rise in the legal minimum wage had been “really a wrong movement” and pushed retailers to use more technology and hire fewer young people. The government faces a tricky budget as the high price of oil and government borrowing put the squeeze on its finances – and on household bills. The chancellor, John Healey, is reportedly considering shifting more green subsidies from energy bills into general taxation, examining fuel duty and targeting help at the poorest households.

title: UK security forces were aware of RAF Fairford suspected bomb plot, hints defence secretary
summary: Wes Streeting indicates farmer who alerted police and said security forces had ‘dropped the ball’ only ‘had a partial picture’
text: UK security services were aware in advance about a group of men arrested in connection with a suspected bomb plot against an RAF base used by the US military, Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, has indicated. Five men were arrested on suspicion of terrorism offences after armed officers found explosives in three vans parked minutes from RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire, from which the US air force flies missions against Iran. Police were alerted after a local woman driving near the base in the early hours of Sunday saw the vans and men acting unusually and called 999. Speaking to the BBC on Monday morning, the woman said security services had seemingly “really dropped the ball on this”. Speaking later to BBC Radio 4’s Today programme, Streeting said that while he wanted to thank the woman – who has chosen to remain anonymous – for calling police, she had “a partial picture”. He praised police and security services for their work, referencing comments by Donald Trump who claimed the suspects had been under view for a long time. Trump alleged the men “were looking to do big damage” and said of the response: “It was fantastic. Working with Britain, it was an amazing job.” Streeting, when asked if he was saying Trump had been correct, did not reject this. “Our security services and our police, they don’t ask for praise, but I think it was a proud moment yesterday to see the president of the United States recognise the extraordinary work that our police and our security and intelligence services do every day throughout the year and throughout the world to keep us safe. That’s all I want to say this morning on that,” he said. It is understood that UK officials believe there is no contradiction between Trump’s comments that the men were being watched and the fact that an alert was made to police by a member of the public, indicating that they were likely to have been intercepted anyway. Streeting declined to give any details about any prior information about the suspected plot or the identities of the men arrested. He said: “There’s a live police investigation, and as a matter of course we don’t comment in detail on operational security matters, because often the more that we might say, the more insight we give to those who would wish us harm and do us harm, given the opportunity.” Images showed shirtless men being handcuffed in a dark country lane after police were called to reports of three suspicious vans travelling towards RAF Fairford. During the major incident, the residents of 85 households in the Cotswolds village of Whelford were rapidly evacuated to Cirencester leisure centre and a 400-metre cordon was placed around the white vans as robots from the army’s bomb squad examined them. In comments read out by a member of BBC staff, the local woman who called the police said she had been driving home late from a party but that when she reached her farm she found the driveway and the road blocked by three white vans. Thinking this was related to security operations at RAF Fairford, she turned her car around, but then she saw a group of men wearing hoods and masks, who she said ran away when they saw her. Suspicious, she called Ministry of Defence police and then 999. She said: “I think it was pure luck that I arrived in the village at a similar time to the vans. I am absolutely staggered that it was left to me, as a member of the public, to see and report this. “The airbase were operating a roadblock close to the entrance to the base, but not on any of the other roads. But we assumed someone would be monitoring the roads around the base perimeter and taking regular patrols in the village.” She said: “I’m just really keen to highlight that it appears someone really dropped the ball on this.”

title: Bangkok declared a ‘disaster zone’ after flooding, as rainstorms shift direction
summary: Capital city submerged in waist-high flood water, while elsewhere Hurricane Nolo threatens Hawaii’s Big Island
text: Bangkok was declared a disaster zone by its city officials towards the end of last week, after streets in Thailand’s capital city were submerged in up to waist-high flood water. The flooding stemmed from an active cell of low pressure across central Thailand that brought continuous heavy rainfall and thunderstorms to Bangkok and surrounding regions. The heavy rain began early on Thursday when the weak area of low pressure travelled north-westwards up the gulf of Thailand before then sitting over central Thailand by Friday morning. For most of the following two days this low pressure remained roughly in situ, which allowed unrelenting downpours over Bangkok and nearby areas. One weather station near Prachin Buri, just north-east of the capital, recorded 213.5mm within a 24-hour period between Friday and Saturday evening local time – for comparison, London receives an average 585mm a year). Fortunately, the centre of the low-pressure cell shifted north-westwards on Sunday and brought an end to the torrential rainfall. Out in the central Pacific, meanwhile, citizens of Hawaii’s Big Island were threatened by Hurricane Nolo over the weekend. The system initially approached the archipelago early last week, bringing heavy rainfall from around Tuesday evening. By the early hours of Saturday Nolo was a category 2 hurricane, with sustained windspeeds of 85-90knots (98-104mph), situated at its closest to the archipelago at approximately 145 miles (233km) south of the Big Island. Strong winds were not the only threat to the Big Island, as the vast quantity of rainfall raised concerns over flooding and mudslides. Since the impacts of Nolo started late on Tuesday 22 September, weather stations in the north-east of the island have received over 530mm of rainfall. Fortunately, Nolo has propagated westwards away from Hawaii where it is forecast to peak in its intensity on Monday 28 September, with current predictions of achieving category 4 status. Meanwhile, farther east in the Pacific Ocean, Hurricane Polo is now forecast to make landfall with the Baja California peninsula late in the day on Monday 28 September. The once category 5 hurricane will downgrade to category 2 by landfall with sustained winds of 96-110mph. A hurricane warning has been issued in coastal regions due to the risk of a storm surge where winds are onshore. Polo will also bring intense downpours while traversing the peninsula with 100-200mm expected, potentially reaching up to 250mm locally. The bulk of this rain falling within a 12-hour period and bringing the risk of life-threatening flooding and mudslides. The storm will continue to weaken while propagating north-eastwards across the Sonora region in Mexico.

title: Anthropic will not appear at Senate inquiry into AI and datacentres amid fallout from OpenAI hack
summary: Company behind Claude chatbot expected to attend separate Australian government hearing on AI next week
text: The chief executive of Anthropic will turn down an invitation to appear at a Senate committee hearing on AI this week, in the wake of the revelation that OpenAI agents had breached Australian government websites. However, the company will make an appearance before another committee early next week. The chair of the Senate inquiry into AI and datacentres, Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young, wrote to OpenAI and Anthropic last week asking for their US-based chief executives to appear before the committee on Thursday this week. The invite came after the prime minister’s revelation that OpenAI’s agents had infiltrated systems run by the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, Victoria’s Department of Health, the New South Wales Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research, and the Medicare statistics reporting service portal of Services Australia. Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here Neither company’s executives could be compelled to appear before the Senate committee, given they are based outside Australia, and it is understood that Anthropic – the company behind Claude – will not attend the hearing this week. It is understood the company’s local team is not in Australia, and the invite was considered last-minute. An alternative date for the hearing has been sought. Anthropic is, however, expected to attend a separate joint standing committee hearing on AI next week. Anthropic’s chief executive, Dario Amodei, will not attend, but it is understood representatives of its Australian and US operations will appear. The company has made a submission to that committee in which Anthropic warned that governments had a critical role in reinforcing a responsible approach to AI by industry, while also arguing that frontier AI was not just an economic capability but also a “national security capability”. “It matters which countries build the most capable models, and on whose terms they are deployed,” Anthropic said in the submission. “The most capable AI models are built in the United States. Broadening that development out to trusted allies like Australia is critical and will support efforts to ensure that the capability of democracies outpace those of authoritarian states.” OpenAI was approached for comment. The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, who was in the United States last week when announcing the hack, said he had spoken with OpenAI’s chief executive, Sam Altman, “to express Australia’s extreme concern about this incident”. The finance and government services minister, Katy Gallagher, flagged new mandatory reporting rules could be introduced for AI data breaches. After criticism of the government’s slow response to the incident, Services Australia has put in place new procedures to ensure real-time monitoring of information sent to the public-facing email address used by OpenAI to report the hacking. But Gallagher rejected Coalition claims the government had politicised the Medicare breach, rejecting suggestions Labor had delayed a public announcement or overstated the significance of the rogue agent’s actions. “It is the first time that we’re aware that an agent acting on its own, not with the authority of OpenAI, was able to get into one of our data systems, and I think we did the right thing,” she said. Cabinet was briefed on the ongoing investigation on Monday, as the company continued to cooperate with Services Australia and the intelligence agency, the Australian Signals Directorate. Gallagher said the investigation would take a matter of weeks to be completed but confirmed the statistical website accessed in the incident had been decommissioned and the data transferred to a new portal. The taskforce would also review how OpenAI’s agent had interacted with the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare’s website. An obscure German wiki site that was reportedly hijacked and used as a message board for the agents to communicate with each other included messages showing the agents tried and failed to access the AIHW website data over multiple days in June this year, as first reported by the ABC. Part of $160m in new funding for cybersecurity improvements at Services Australia, announced in the May budget, will be used for the response to the OpenAI incident. “The kind of cyber protections of a public-facing website, versus our systems of government significance are quite different, and they are under constant, constant attention from people who would like to get in,” Gallagher said. “Those systems are the ones that the upgrade will be focused on.” The opposition leader, Angus Taylor, said every cyber-attack was serious, but criticised Albanese for waiting to reveal the incident publicly.

title: Children forced to give up school for work as fighting upends daily life in Yemen
summary: Renewed fighting between Iran-aligned Houthis and Saudi-backed Yemeni forces has shattered four years of relative calm
text: In the mornings, 13-year-old Muneer Farie went to school, and in the afternoons he helped his father feed the livestock. He took his studies seriously, dreaming of becoming the first teacher in his family of farmers. As fighting approached his village in al-Wazeyah district in Taiz, Yemen, two weeks ago, Muneer’s focus started to drift from his lessons. The classroom echoed with the distant sounds of explosions and gunfire. His home was suddenly on the frontline of renewed fighting between the Iran-aligned Houthis and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government. “We heard there was fighting in surrounding areas but we didn’t expect it would reach our village that fast,” Muneer said. “As soon as the sounds of clashes approached our village, we took our livestock and important belongings and fled home early in the morning.” He and his family fled south-west, moving to a camp set up for displaced people in al-Shimayateen, Taiz. They arrived penniless and lacking even the most basic supplies. Muneer and his family are some of the more than 130,000 people displaced by recent fighting in Yemen, which started in September when the Houthis launched a renewed military campaign and rapidly moved south-west, seizing control of towns along the Red Sea coast. The Houthis’ campaign interrupted years of relative calm that had prevailed over Yemen, with frontlines remaining broadly static since a UN-mediated ceasefire came into force in 2022. The Houthis are now battling government forces and a Saudi air campaign to seize strategic highlands and supply lines on the outskirts of Taiz. Civilians have been driven out of their homes by the fighting, fleeing airstrikes and missiles. Muneer and his brother, instead of studying, now sell socks and other cheap products in the markets outside his displacement camp. His classroom has been replaced by a small tent where he and his five siblings and parents crowd together in the humid night air. He joins the more than 3.2 million children whose studies were interrupted by Yemen’s civil war prior to this month’s escalation. “Studying is important, but not in a situation like this where we are struggling to get enough food, water and other necessities,” he said. “For now, I will keep working until the war ends.” His father, Ghaleb Farie, has been forced to ask his sons to work so that the family can scrape together enough to survive life in the displacement camp. Farie hopes the camp will be only a temporary home and that he can soon return to his village, but he is not optimistic as new displaced people arrive every day. “What I was told by neighbours who have been displaced for longer is that the first few months are difficult and I will adapt,” Farie said. Life has also grown harder for those who have remained in their homes. Abdulwasea Abdu, the principal of Musaab Ibn Umayr school in Taiz, tried to keep the doors of his school open for as long as possible to give children a sense of normality. But that normality was shattered two weeks ago when a missile fell nearby, exploding in sight of the students. “On the day the missile struck, we witnessed severe panic among them, with crying and screaming due to the explosions. Some children showed psychological trauma as a result of the intensity of the blasts,” Abdu said. The school was forced to close its doors, depriving the more than 600 pupils of their education. Abdu watches the battlefield developments closely, searching for a let-up that will let him resume classes, but so far the situation has been too chaotic. “The area faces fighting from multiple fronts – south, west and north – which makes it difficult to take any steps toward resuming classes at the moment,” Abdu said. He fears that many of the children out of school and displaced will be forced into child labour. The resumption of fighting has upended life for residents of south-west Yemen. Clashes severed the main road between the now Houthi-controlled port city of Mocha and government-controlled Taiz. The road is a vital artery for goods as it is one of the only in the area wide enough for large trucks and passenger buses. Interrupted commerce has increased the price of basic goods, compounding the crisis, particularly for displaced people. “It is civilians who bear the cost of military escalation, and it seems that we in Taiz are paying a particularly heavy price, as commodities no longer reach us easily,” said Essam Nabil, a 56-year-old carpenter in Taiz city. He added many people had begun giving up meat and resorting to cheaper foods. The fighting has disrupted other, more mundane facets of daily life. Asaad, an expatriate who works in Saudi Arabia and asked to be identified only by his first name, can no longer take a direct trip back from Yemen. “This reminds me of the early years of the war in Taiz, when the main roads were blocked and we had to travel through Aden before heading to Saudi Arabia,” Asaad said. “Now, we are repeating the same expensive and arduous journey.”

title: Counter-terror police investigate Iran link over suspected bomb plot at RAF base used by US
summary: Five men arrested on terrorism charges after explosives found near RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire
text: Counter-terrorism police are investigating whether Iran is behind a suspected bomb plot after armed officers found explosives on three vans parked minutes from an RAF base used by the US military. The Guardian understands that after five men were arrested on terrorism charges, investigators were examining materials found in the vans, with an initial view being they were consistent with improvised explosive devices. Images circulating on Sunday showed shirtless men being handcuffed in a dark country lane in the early hours of Sunday after police were called to reports of three suspicious vans travelling towards RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire, which hosts US air force missions against Iran. The suspected plot appears to have been foiled by chance when a member of the public spotted unusual behaviour late at night in the countryside from a group of men and called 999. During the major incident the residents of 85 households in the Cotswolds village of Whelford were rapidly evacuated to Cirencester leisure centre and a 400m cordon was placed around the white vans as robots from the army’s bomb squad examined them. Tests were ongoing to find out whether the suspected explosive devices were viable, with bomb robots deployed in the Gloucestershire countryside as investigations continued. After their initial arrest over explosives offences, the five men detained early on Sunday were further arrested later in the day on suspicion of the preparation of a terrorist act. The pictures of the men with their shirts off could point to a precautionary measure against the risk of suicide vests or concealed weapons. At least one van carried the logo of a fuel company and a phone number missing a digit. A real fuel company of the same name firmly rejected any connection to the incident and said: “We are extremely concerned that our company’s name has been used without our knowledge or permission.” It said it was cooperating with the authorities. In a statement, counter-terrorism police said: “At around 12.45am today (Sunday 27 September), police received a call relating to three suspicious vehicles which appeared to be travelling towards the airbase. “Armed officers responded and five men were arrested in the Whelford area on suspicion of committing offences under the Explosives Act. They were further arrested on suspicion of preparation of a terrorist act, contrary to section 5 of the Terrorism Act.” The arrests come as the war between the US and Iran limps on. In July Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps noted RAF Fairford’s use by US bombers, warning the UK that “any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces”. Counter-terror police and the security services are searching for the motive. The circumstances of the arrest near the base and prior warnings from Tehran leave an Iranian motive high in the investigators’ and government’s thinking. But sources warn nothing is being ruled out, including a jihadist or other motive, and the UK threat level remains at severe, the second highest, meaning an attack is highly likely. Whether there was any foreign involvement forms part of the investigation, and Iran’s ministry of intelligence and security has orchestrated attacks overseas before. Any proven link with Iran would be a dramatic escalation in hostilities between the UK and Tehran. While several recent incidents in the UK have been linked to the Middle-Eastern country, including the antisemitic arson attack on four Hatzola ambulances in Golders Green, the alleged plot at RAF Fairford appears to be significantly more serious. And it raises urgent questions for the UK security services after it appeared the authorities had been unaware of the alleged plot, with police only moving on the three vans after a 999 call from a resident who spotted them as she drove home. The US president, Donald Trump, claimed to have had the suspects under view for a “long time” and alleged the men “were looking to do big damage” – although the Guardian understands the operation was not intelligence-led, suggesting investigators had not known about any potential plot in advance. “It was fantastic. Working with Britain, it was an amazing job,” Trump said. The UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, was being updated on the matter from Liverpool, where the Labour party conference is taking place. He cancelled plans to take part in a journalists versus politicians football match in order to take calls about the incident. He said it was “deeply concerning” and the government will “always take every step necessary” to protect people. Fairford has a particularly long runway, which extends almost 2 miles (3km). It is reinforced to support heavy bombers such as the B-1 and B-52, which have been deployed in attacks on Iran. The aircraft are capable of carrying large payloads, including “bunker buster” bombs. In March this year, after then prime minister, Sir Keir Starmer, granted permission for “defensive” US action against Iranian missile sites from UK bases, four American bombers landed at RAF Fairford and the US started using British bases for “specific defensive operations”. There have been protests in recent months over the UK government’s decision to allow the US to use RAF Fairford to carry out strikes on Iranian missile sites that are attacking ships in the strait of Hormuz. At the time of Iran’s warning in July, a government spokesperson said: “Our armed forces are ready to keep the United Kingdom safe from any kind of attacks, whether it’s on our soil or from abroad. The UK stands ready 24/7 to defend itself.” Evacuated residents of Whelford spoke of “heightened tensions” in recent weeks around the base with more frequent, visible police patrols. Outside Cirencester leisure centre, Jason, a resident of Whelford who declined to give his surname, said: “There have been heightened tensions recently around the base, we are aware it is used by the USAF … It always feels pretty safe. Some residents have seen increased police patrols.” It was unclear when people would be able to return to their normal lives; those at the leisure centre said they had been asked by authorities if they had anywhere else to stay on Sunday night. The Fairford youth football club, about 1.5 miles (2.4km) north-west of Whelford, was taken over as a temporary base for the emergency service response to the incident. There were several police vehicles, ambulances, fire engines, pop-up tents and a large mobile command-unit vehicle in the grounds. Richard Ocone, the assistant chief constable with Gloucestershire constabulary, said: “We appreciate the disruption this will have caused and would like to reassure them we are working as quickly as we can to get them back in their properties.”

title: Can you solve it? Isaac Newton’s tower drop puzzle
summary: The problem that changed the world
text: Today’s puzzle played a pivotal role in the birth of classical physics. The tower drop An object is dropped from a high tower. Bearing in mind the rotation of the Earth itself, where will the object land? slightly to the west slightly to the east exactly at the bottom The answer is counter-intuitive. Or, in the words of Isaac Newton, who posed the problem in a letter he wrote to Robert Hooke in 1679, the answer is “quite contrary to ye opinion of ye vulgar.” Some hints. Think about how the spin of the Earth might affect the downwards trajectory. Also think about what happens when a spinning figure skater pulls in their arms. I’ll be back at 5pm UK with the solution. PLEASE NO SPOILERS. Instead discuss your favourite seventeenth century scientists. UPDATE: You can read the solution here. Today’s puzzle was suggested by David Acheson, emeritus professor of maths at Oxford and the author of several excellent popular maths books. His latest is Wonders in Motion, The Story of Dynamics, a beautifully accessible introduction to the science of motion. Acheson’s book includes more background about the tower drop puzzle. Hooke’s correspondence with Newton rekindled Newton’s interest in gravity and motion, which ultimately led to his formulation of the mathematical foundations of classical physics in the Principia. Wonders of Motion by David Acheson is on sale at the Guardian Bookshop. I’ve been setting a puzzle here on alternate Mondays since 2015. I’m always on the look-out for great puzzles.
