summary: Researcher says sightings of the endangered moth have increased over the last two years but ‘this year has blown them out of the water’
text: Swarms of bogong moths have surprised New South Wales residents over the last few days – with experts saying sightings of the endangered native insect are cause for excitement rather than alarm. Hundreds of moth sightings in coastal areas were posted over the weekend to the iNaturalist page for Bogong Watch, a citizen science initiative run by Invertebrates Australia. Spring marks the beginning of an annual bogong moth migration: huge numbers of the insects migrate up to 1,000 km to a small number of cool caves in the Australian Alps, where they spend the summer escaping the heat. Bogong Watch project manager Linnea Emneby said their bogong “sentinels” – dozens of volunteers spread in all directions from Mount Kosciuszko, who use non-lethal bug lanterns to monitor the moths – were reporting high numbers of the insects. Three NSW households each reported dozens of moths on Monday, while one sentinel sighted more than 200 bogongs on Sunday night, she said. Emneby said the moths – which are about the size of a 50-cent piece and weigh a third of a gram – were important both “culturally and ecologically”, playing a critical role as pollinators and also a key food source for the critically endangered mountain pygmy possum. “We’re absolutely thrilled with what we’re seeing,” said Dr Marissa Parrott, a reproductive biologist at Zoos Victoria, which runs a separate citizen science program Moth Tracker. “The reports just keep coming in … one of my team members was in tears with excitement this morning.” Sightings of the endangered moth had increased over the last two years, but “this year has blown them out of the water”, Parrott said. “In September alone … we’ve had more bogong moths sightings come in than all of last year. “We’re hoping this means a stronger recovery of this endangered species. “Those big numbers really are in NSW and the ACT – Victoria is still behind,” Parrott said, adding that “wetter, cooler weather” had likely yielded favourable conditions for the moths. “They do come in waves,” Parrott said, with the insects taking days to weeks to complete their migrations to the Alps. “This is what should have happened in the past, seeing these big swarms of moths coming through Canberra, Sydney, Newcastle and Melbourne, across those south-eastern Australian migratory zones.” An estimated 4 billion moths used to arrive in the Alps each year, until the population collapsed catastrophically – by up to 99.5% – between 2017 and 2019. They were once found in huge numbers, periodically swarming into Parliament House in Canberra. During the closing ceremony of the Sydney Olympic Games in 2000, a swarm of bogongs drawn by stadium lights was so huge that weather forecasters mistook it for a rain cloud. The moth has been listed as endangered by the International Union for the Conservation of Nature since 2021, but is not listed as a threatened species under federal conservation laws. “They migrate generally more inland, but they can move around depending on weather and wind,” Parrot said. Moth Tracker sightings from last year showed that “they even get blown across to New Zealand”. The nocturnal moths are the only invertebrate known to navigate using a map of the stars as a compass. “Hopefully the ones blown off course will be able to navigate back safely,” Parrott said. The strongest El Niño on record, and the drier, hotter conditions the climate pattern can bring to Australia, was cause for concern, Parrott said. “While the [bogong] numbers are looking good now, and I think that’s something we can all celebrate, we do worry what’s going to happen over the next couple of years.” For members of the public who encounter bogongs on their migration, experts suggest turning off unnecessary outdoor lights, refraining from insecticide use, and uploading sightings to the Moth Tracker or Bogong Watch platforms. “If any come into the house, gently place them back outside,” Parrott said. “Females can have 2,000 eggs, so every moth is precious. “They don’t do any damage, they don’t eat clothes. They pollinate the plants as they go through, so that’s a big help for people who love their gardens. “The moths are gentle, beautiful little animals that will move on on their own.”

title: Monday briefing: Who ​profits​ from the illegal global gambling empire?
summary: In today’s newsletter: A major data leak from Curaçao’s gambling regulator has exposed the people​ and companies behind thousands of offshore casinos used by British punters
text: Good morning. Every year, British people bet billions on unregulated gambling sites. Given how ubiquitous legitimate betting shops are on UK high streets, and how inescapable ads for online casinos are on social media, sport and primetime TV, the scale of underground operations appears baffling. But the offshore online gambling market is one of the world’s most profitable – and least regulated – industries, estimated to be worth tens of billions. Opaque ownership, offshore licences and international inaction has made these often easily accessible and widely advertised digital casinos an attractive hunting ground for organised crime and corruption. Now, however, we’ve had a rare glimpse into the murky world in which they operate. A German hacker has released tens of thousands of previously confidential documents in what has been labelled the “Casino Secrets leak”, exposing the inner-working of thousands of unregulated gambling sites. In today’s First Edition, Guardian reporter and author of Jackpot: How Gambling Conquered Britain Rob Davies explains what this data could reveal, and why illegal gambling is running rampant in Britain. Before that, a roundup of this weekend’s biggest stories. Weekend roundup Labour | Going into his first party conference as prime minister, Andy Burnham revealed a set of new initiatives, from a new help-to-buy loan scheme for first-time buyers to a vision for universal free social care. UK news | Counter-terrorism police are investigating whether Iran is behind a suspected bomb plot after armed officers found explosives on three vans parked minutes from an RAF base used by the US military. Northern Ireland | Hundreds of protesters spent the day blocking the route of a hugely contentious parade after a court gave late-night clearance for the Orange Order to march on a historically significant road for the first time in nearly 30 years. US politics | Experts warned on Sunday that Donald Trump could use the hours and days after November’s midterm elections to disrupt the results after struggling to enforce a crackdown on voting. UK news | On Saturday, the stepson of Sir Ranulph Fiennes launched a crowdfunder to pay for “specialist legal advice” in an attempt to locate the explorer, who hasn’t been seen in public for more than two years. In depth: ‘The major concern is the exploitation of vulnerable people’ The hidden gambling market is seriously big business. Gaming Compliance International (GCI) estimates the global illicit gambling market saw bets made worth $5.9tn in 2025, having steadily increased in previous years. A 2024 report by the UK Betting and Gaming Council (which represents the interests of the industry) suggested £2.7bn was being staked annually on illegal, unregulated gambling sites in Britain. Without a licence from the Gambling Commission, it’s illegal for online gambling sites to offer their services in England, Scotland and Wales. “Despite its flaws, this regime has been developed over many years and is extremely stringent in certain aspects,” says Rob: imposing anti-money laundering and terrorist financing checks, setting of stake limits, enforcing responsible gambling rules which (in theory) protect vulnerable customers. Britain isn’t short of legal online betting sites and casinos. According to the most recent data, there are 25.7 million total active accounts on licensed gambling sites in the UK. Still, users are increasingly being enticed underground: from gambling addicts who have previously banned themselves from regulated sites looking to bypass their own self-exclusion to high rollers who prefer to operate without oversight. Some UK operators restrict or refuse bets from highly successful sports betters, and you cannot legally bet in the UK using cryptocurrency, prompting these users to seek alternative options. “The gambling industry would argue intrusive overregulation drives users to unlicensed sites,” says Rob. Licensed websites run affordability checks, ranging from background soft credit searches to requests for bank statements and digital payslips. There’s no need to venture on to the dark web to find an unregulated outfit. If a UK customer tries to visit a non-UK licensed casino, the website should display a message stating it’s unavailable. But “some sites simply don’t bother blocking access,” says Rob, “and users can easily bypass these blocks using a simple VPN.” Some users simply aren’t aware of the licensed/unlicensed distinction. For users, most platforms look virtually identical. Advertising further blurs these lines. While unlicensed operators can’t technically publish ads in the UK, sponsorship deals offer a loophole. Premier League football clubs frequently advertise unlicenced in Britain offshore gambling on their kits, while other clubs have their own commercial deals. These practices are currently legal, though there are moves to clamp down. (For more on the football front, this piece on Josimar is well worth reading). And plenty of these sites do have legit-looking credentials, licensed not in the UK, but offshore where there are looser regulations. Many are registered in the Caribbean nation of Curaçao, which has over 8,000 online casinos in its jurisdiction – that’s one for every 20 of its residents. *** ‘Under the bonnet’ of offshore gambling The Curaçao files were accessed by 31-year-old German hacker Lilith Wittmann. It “wasn’t hard to access” the data, she explained to me this weekend from Berlin. “It took me only six hours to find a vulnerability to then monitor The Curaçao Gaming Control Board for nine months in real time.” Specialist reporters like Rob are still combing through the files, but they include information about the owners of some of the world’s largest offshore casinos and details including the source of their wealth. “This data can take us under the bonnet and show us who is applying for the licences, and who may be profiting from illegal gambling.” Rob has previously reported on the Curaçao-based Santeda network, which “operates six or seven of the largest offshore casinos that people use in the UK.” Their data is in the leak – expect more stories to follow. Also exposed is the lacklustre nature of much oversight that does take place. Some casinos have submitted detailed balance sheets, but Rob says that “in one case I looked at, a bloke had just written ‘cryptocurrency investments’ on a piece of paper as his source of company funds.” “What’s already clear is that these are global networks, all gravitating to Curaçao, as a gateway to millions of wallets.” *** Respectability without scrutiny From a punter’s perspective, looking for a licence when you’ve already opted for an unregulated betting site is unlikely to be a priority. But, these licences are often vital for the casinos to function, Rob explains: banks, payment providers, game developers etc can “point to this fig leaf of respectability” to justify working with these sites and making them operational. “Curaçao has very cleverly marketed itself as a kind of international gambling hub,” says Rob. “It became the go-to because it had just enough respectability without any real scrutiny.” Still, in recent years even Curaçao has taken a slightly more rigorous approach, says Rob, with casinos venturing elsewhere, where rules are even lighter, such as US and Canadian First Nation jurisdictions like Kahnawake and Tobique and the Indian Ocean island of Anjouan. *** ‘Nobody will come after you’ There’s certainly a financial incentive for governments to crack down. The Office for Budget Responsibility estimates betting and gaming duties will raise £4bn in 2025/26. Above board operators aren’t just liable for corporation tax – they also pay HMRC a 40% levy called Remote Gaming Duty on stakes they profit from. Unlicensed casinos avoid such obligations. “From my reporting standpoint, the major concern is the exploitation of vulnerable people,” says Rob. He has reported on the gambling industry for years, covering “plenty” of poor behaviour by British licensed operators. “But you’re definitely safer with these companies,” he says. Unlicensed operators offer no safeguards, and in some cases, have simply refused to pay out winnings to players, who then have no legal recourse. Rob has interviewed many people who’ve lost significant amounts on unlicensed sites, who’d received “no intervention whatsoever when they were displaying obvious signs of problem gambling”. If a UK-licensed operator acted similarly, “they could face a multimillion pound fine or even a suspension of their licence.” There are ongoing efforts in the UK to wrest back control, with legislation expected soon to give the Gambling Commission greater powers to intervene. “Really it needs a coordinated international response,” says Rob, “but ultimately it will be very, very difficult to achieve anything substantial.” Casinos can virtually relocate faster than jurisdictions can be targeted. Shut down a website, and a replica can pop up within a few seconds with a slightly different domain name. “And there are always going to be countries where the governments don’t have the will or the capability to act, especially today with Belarus and Russia.” That’s not to say we shouldn’t try. “When it comes to drug or sex trafficking,” says Rob, “there’s an enormous coordinated global effort globally to crack down with very serious consequences for those involved. But with unregulated gambling – essentially a licence to print money, deeply connected to organised crime – nothing is being done. And nobody will try to come after you.” Whether that’s also true for the hacker, Lilith Wittmann, remains to be seen, as she waits to hear if legal proceedings might soon be mounted against her. She seems entirely unfazed at the prospect. “There was a legitimate public interest defence in accessing this data,” she tells me, “so we all know how much tax revenue is being lost and who is profiting.” Whether a German court will agree is another question. Thursday | Nasa and SpaceX’s Crew-13 mission to the International Space Station is expected to launch from the Kennedy Space Center, Florida. title: Starwatch: Tracking down the faint stars of Pisces
summary: Below the southern edge of the Great Square of Pegasus lie the fishes, linked by two strings
text: This week we will track down Pisces, the fishes. Despite being one of the largest zodiacal constellations, it can be surprisingly difficult to identify because it contains no bright stars. The chart shows the view looking east from London at 10pm on Monday. As the week progresses, the bright waning moon will rise later and later in the evening, allowing the faint stars of Pisces to be more easily seen. Start by finding the Great Square of Pegasus. Look below its southern edge for a small, faint ring of stars. This is the Circlet of Pisces. Seven stars make up the pattern, although you will not see them all from a semi-urban location. The circlet represents one of the two fish. From here, a long string of faint stars heads to Alrescha, an Arabic name meaning “the cord”. Another string leads to the second fish, forming a V-shape of stars. Pisces is one of the second-century astronomer Ptolemy’s original 48 constellations. In Greek mythology, the fishes were associated with Aphrodite and her son Eros, who escaped the monster Typhon by taking the form of fish. They tied themselves together so they would not become separated. From the southern hemisphere, Pisces is also well placed in the evening, appearing higher in the sky.

title: Country diary: A young shieldbug has found a safe place to hide – or so it hopes | Nic Wilson
summary: Bedmond, Hertfordshire: Serge Hill Project is a haven for humans and wildlife, and there’s much to find in its collection of drought-tolerant plants
text: Looking across a swathe of golden oat grass to the Apple House, it seems almost inconceivable that the M25 and M1 motorways are just beyond the treeline. I’m exploring the Serge Hill Project for Gardening, Creativity and Health: a therapeutic resource for local schools, community groups and charities, founded three years ago by Tom and Sue Stuart-Smith. All around me, a diverse collection of drought-tolerant plants is thriving in a six-inch layer of sharp sand in the uppermost section of the Plant Library, despite not having been watered once during our sweltering summer. Among the many plants I’ve not met before, Crete scabious is the epitome of autumn glory. Its pale lilac flowers have transformed into globular seed heads that quiver in the breeze. Each sphere is a fanfare of tiny trumpets, their flared funnels marked with brown stripes. On closer inspection, I can see that some of these papery alcoves harbour hairy shieldbug nymphs, Dolycoris baccarum. Elsewhere in the garden, troops of adults and juveniles cluster on sunflower stems and wine-red dahlias, but nowhere is the nymphs’ camouflage as successful as on the scabious seed heads. While the adults invite attention with their black and white striped antennae and connexivum (edge of the abdomen), and reddish-brown forewing bases and pronotum (a hardened plate covering the front of the body), the young bugs’ markings shield them from sight. Golden-brown bands on their abdomens and along the connexivum break up their oval outlines, and the colour match between plant and insect helps them sink into sepia obscurity. Their sanctuary – Crete scabious – is one of many Mediterranean species planted in the garden as part of the project’s research into climate-resilient landscapes, so it’s encouraging to see the shieldbugs making themselves at home. So far, almost 350 invertebrates (including five species of shieldbug) have been recorded across more than 2,500 herbaceous perennials, low shrubs and bulbs in the Plant Library. Like the children and adults who come to this inclusive garden to connect with nature, the Serge Hill Project provides wildlife with a safe space to shelter and develop. And all within a mile of the London orbital, Britain’s busiest motorway. • Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024, is available now at guardianbookshop.com

title: ‘You were right’: Ed Miliband tells critics Labour was wrong on Gaza
summary: Foreign secretary will tell party’s conference ‘we are not here to accept the status quo but to change it’
text: Ed Miliband will tell campaigners and party members who raised the plight of Palestinians they were right that Labour’s approach had not been enough, saying he was heeding the calls of millions of people by imposing sanctions on Israeli settlements. The foreign secretary will tell the Labour party conference that the government will take more explicitly progressive foreign policy positions under Andy Burnham, and that the UK will be a leader among like-minded countries in a new age of diplomacy. He will say there is a “fundamental and wider lesson from Israel and Palestine about how we have changed our approach as a party”, saying Labour will succeed “because of, not in spite of, our progressive values”. He will talk of the start of a new and more muscular foreign policy. “We are not here to accept the status quo but to change it at home and abroad,” he will say. The party’s conference hall was often the scene of fierce opposition to Keir Starmer’s stance on Israel and Palestine in Labour’s final year of opposition and early in government. Since becoming foreign secretary, Miliband has announced sweeping sanctions on trade with Israeli settlements against a backdrop of increasing settler violence in the West Bank, which has resulted in 12 countries – including France and Canada – announcing they would also impose sanctions. The Guardian understands Miliband will say in his speech that the sanctions marked a definitive change in how Labour will approach the situation in the Middle East. “I want to say to the millions of people in this country and indeed elsewhere who have been moved and outraged by the plight of the Palestinian people: we hear you, you were right,” he will say. “And under Andy’s leadership, we have reset our approach. We call out ethnic cleansing by the settler terrorists in the West Bank. We call out the evidence of war crimes in Gaza. We call out Israel’s illegal occupation of Palestine. And we match words with actions. “We will ban the import of goods from illegal settlements. We will disrupt the supply lines of British finance, British construction and British services for illegal settlements. And when it comes to the attempt to destroy the two-state solution, this party, this movement, this government, says ‘we will not let you succeed’.” Miliband will pay tribute to those who have campaigned against the Israeli onslaught in Gaza, though his warm words are likely to raise questions about whether the government will review the proscription of Palestine Action. Police arrested a number of demonstrators outside the conference hall on Sunday. “The bonds of solidarity between the British people and those who yearn for peace in Israel and Palestine are too strong to be broken,” Miliband will say. “Our decision to act mobilised the international community, country after country. This is how to make change happen in today’s world. Doing what is right and galvanising others to act too.” Miliband will say in his first speech to the party conference as foreign secretary that cooperation in imposing sanctions will be the beginning of a new bond with “likeminded countries” such as France and Canada, though it is also likely to be interpreted as being more willing to sideline the US. Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, has made an explicit argument for middle powers to do more to build alliances with each other outside traditional structures, and was direct in his desire to forge closer ties with and among European countries in a speech in Brussels earlier this month. A source close to Miliband said that would be a key theme of his time in office. “Britain’s interests are served by standing up for our values on the world stage. Our ability to build coalitions on big global issues depends on our ability to bring countries with us,” he will say. “This Israel/Palestine reset is a sign of how we want to do business. We are going to be propositional in bringing countries with us on the issues we really care about.”

title: ‘The same struggles as 100 years ago’: exhibition highlights lives of Sami people in Sweden
summary: Show at Kin Museum in Kiruna marks handover of long-awaited report on abuses committed by the state against the Indigenous people
text: From a detailed multi-perspectival drawing of reindeer to written accounts of belief systems and childbirth, Johan Turi’s work offers unparalleled insight into his life as a Sami person living in northern Sweden at the start of the 20th century. In the face of racist discrimination, land disputes and the spectre of encroaching industry, Turi wanted his 1910 book Muitalus sámiid birra (An Account of the Sami) to set the record straight about the lives of Europe’s only recognised Indigenous people. Turi is widely regarded as the first Sami author to write about Sami life in his own language, but until now his pioneering works had not been on display for almost 100 years. To mark the handover to the Swedish government this week of a long-awaited report by the Truth Commission for the Sami People on abuses committed by the state against the Sami, his writings, drawings, paintings and Duodji (traditional Sami handicraft) now form the centre of an exhibition at the Kin Museum of Contemporary Art in Kiruna, the area in which he used to live. The title of the exhibition, On the Ugly and the Beautiful, draws from a quote by Turi, who died in 1936, about his belief that everything, positive and negative, has a place to be shown. His work is on display alongside two contemporary artists, Outi Pieski and Johanna Minde. The museum’s director, Maria Lind, said An Account of the Sami, which was published in Sami and Danish before being translated into Swedish seven years later, is “about Sami life, small and big – external and inner life”. Turi was born in Guovdageainnu (Kautokeino), the Norwegian part of Sápmi, in 1854 but as the imposition of formal national borders began to have a bigger impact on the lives of the Sami, his family, who were reindeer herders, moved to Kiruna. “He had dreamed about writing a book about the Sami with the purpose of making the population in Sweden understand how difficult it was for the Sami because those were difficult years,” Lind said, citing the arrival of settlers, industry, including mining, and the railway. “He wanted the king to read his book because he felt if the king knew then things would change. Most likely the king did not read his book, but it became a success,” she added. The problems facing Sami people today are not dissimilar to those Turi would recognise. Industry – especially the search for rare earth minerals and wind energy – is an ever-increasing threat to reindeer herding and nature. Anti-Sami rhetoric is on the rise, including from political leaders, despite the seeming progress symbolised by the truth commission and its report, which will be presented on Wednesday. Similar commissions have also been held in Norway and Finland. But unlike in Turi’s time, there is now the escalating impact of the climate crisis, particularly visible in the Arctic and northern regions. As the report, which is intended to form the basis for reparation and reconciliation discussions, is handed over at Mid Sweden University in Staare, the Kin Museum will put on a special tour of the works, after which there will be a reading of testimonies at the culture house next door. Pieski, who lives on the Finnish side of Sápmi, said she grew up with Turi’s writings and drawings, in which she sees the paper as the land itself. “And then humans, animals, everything is grounded on that paper,” she said. “It’s not a western way of seeing a landscape as a beautiful view that you look at from a distance. But the actual place where you are, physically placed, and you are an active member of this network of land.” Her research and exploration with Eeva-Kristiina Nylander around the subject of the ládjogahpir, a traditional hat historically worn by Sami women, is also part of the exhibition. Their work has helped to bring it back into use. It has, said Pieski, become a “new symbol for decolonial feminism”. She said that in many ways Turi’s work started the current process of truth and reconciliation by writing about life and Sami culture from his point of view. “It’s very sad that we are kind of in the same spot still now, 100 years later,” she said. “And I know the same struggles are still existing that Johan Turi brought out with the fight for industrial land use and so on. “No nation can exist without their own spoken or written histories. Ignoring it is a very simple colonial tool [that does] not give existence to one nation that we are here.”

title: ‘You can taste the land’: the Somerset farmer bringing wildflowers back to cheddar
summary: Tom Calver has sacrificed milk yields to give his cows a more varied diet of plants and believes the result is better cheese and richer farmland
text: In the rolling hills of Somerset, hundreds of thousands of cows placidly munch lush green grass to produce milk for cheddar. But six fields stand out. Rather than uniform grass, they have technicolour wildflowers sprouting across the meadows. Farmer Tom Calver said that to allow the flowers to grow he has to keep fewer cows and leave some fields ungrazed as they mature. “Other farmers thought we were nuts for doing this,” said Calver, who runs the Westcombe dairy in the eponymous hamlet in Somerset. He is pioneering emerging research that suggests that when cows are fed in an organic way, their microbiome is healthier and more complex than when they are given modern feed. It is thought that feeding cattle a wide range of plants creates a healthier gut microbiome still. “We have actually lost milk production in what we’re doing,” Calver said, but added the cheese tasted better than ever as it is “meadow flavoured”. Cheddar has been made in the county for over 850 years, and cows once grazed more varied pasture, much like Calver’s black-and-white herd do now. Calver believes his Westcombe cheddar, which is raw and unpasteurised, has a much more complex taste than the average supermarket block and this is because of its microbiome. “If you look at the diversity of what cows have been eating before, we were growing lots of maize and Italian rye grasses,” Calver said. “Now, actually, the cows are out into 19 different species of plants in our paddocks. What’s living on those plants is a huge, diverse range of microbiome, and I think you’ve probably heard a lot about how the microbiome is actually helping our guts and minds and everything else like that. It also actually has a massive input in the flavour profile.” Calver, a trained chef, said he didn’t understand why cheese couldn’t have a “terroir” – a taste of the land where it was created, just like wine does. “You talk to viticulturists, winemakers, and they talk about terroir, and I think that’s amazing. It’s what we can actually use to improve diversity in our landscapes and in the flavour of our foods.” The drawback is that his way of farming is “much more expensive”. But Calver believes it’s worth it. He said that growing wildflowers rather than just maize and grass has boosted nature on his farm, and he also prefers the taste of the cheese now: “You can actually like taste the land. You can taste everything around it.” Calver said it had been hard to market the cheddar as it tasted different every time due to the diversity of the plants the cows are fed. “One of the things that we are very bad at, I think, is wanting to have the same thing every single day. When you’re working with nature and you’re actually trying to farm in that particular way, you have to embrace diversity, even of the actual flavour profiles that you’re actually creating as well, which makes it very difficult for a retailer to actually market that. It is quite a challenge.” Growing deep-rooted wildflowers in the meadows helped the farm during this year’s drought, too. “We’ve got lots of chicory that’s actually going down and accessing water from subsoil and actually bringing that up. So we’ve done rather well.” Farmers trying to graze their cattle on parched fields looked at Calver’s comparatively greener land with envy. “I think there’s been a lot of other farmers locally who have been, hopefully, maybe inspired by taking a slightly different approach,” he said.

title: Ukraine war briefing: Zelenskyy says Moscow terrorising Ukrainians as fresh strikes kill eight
summary: Ukraine president says Russia shows no signs of slowing the war, calls for sanctions packages to take effect in October. What we know on day 1,678
text: As Russian drones struck Kyiv and other parts of Ukraine on Sunday, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia was showing no signs of de-escalating the war despite assurances to the US that it would. In a statement on X, Zelenskyy accused Russia of terrorising Ukrainians with its latest attacks, which he said included setting on fire a market outside Kyiv, and striking kindergartens, schools, homes and communications facilities. “Anywhere in the world, this choice of targets would be called by one word – terrorism. Russia has no military objective whatsoever in doing this – it is purely an attempt to break people and inflict as much harm as possible on our society,” Zelenskyy said. “If Russia were truly preparing for any real steps toward de-escalation – as it claims, particularly to American negotiators – this wave of … terror would not be happening,” he said, calling on the US to fully implement the Lindsey Graham Act, which enables sweeping sanctions on Russia aimed at pressing it into ending the war. Zelenskyy’s comments came ahead of the conclusion of the UN general assembly in New York on Monday. On the weekend, the foreign ministers of Russia and Germany met in New York on the sidelines of the ⁠assembly to discuss the war but Russia’s top diplomat dismissed Germany’s calls to ease off its “dangerous path of escalation” towards Europe. Zelenskyy said on X that Ukraine was relying on “effective decisions” being made by other countries and stronger pressure from its partners in the G7 and G20, “so that Russia sees that manipulating diplomatic signals will not allow it to keep winning more and more time for war and terror”. New sanctions packages targeting financial networks, supply chains and companies and individuals helping produce Russian weapons “must take effect as early as October” Zelenskyy said also, to provide a stronger foundation for changing the situation and “pushing Russia toward real diplomacy”. Russian strikes killed eight people across Ukraine on Sunday, according to authorities while Zelenskyy said Russia had fired about 3,900 drones, aerial bombs and other missiles at Ukraine over the past week. Ukrainian prosecutors said a drone attack hit a market in Sofiiska Borshchahivka on the western outskirts of Kyiv, killing two and injuring about 10 people. Others died in strikes in different regions and Kyiv also came under attack, local officials said. In the capital, ⁠Mayor Vitali Klitschko said nine people were injured, including a child. Russia also hit the headquarters of Kyivstar – Ukraine’s largest mobile service provider – on Sunday, the company told local media. On Monday a ⁠guided Russian ⁠aerial bomb injured 22 people, including ⁠children, as it struck ⁠an apartment building in ‌Ukraine’s ‌second-biggest city of Kharkiv, mayor Ihor Terekhov said on Telegram. Moscow has recently waged a sustained bombardment of Ukrainian ⁠datacentres and communications infrastructure. Peter Beaumont and Artem Mazhulin have reported on the dire living conditions inside Oleshky, across the Dnipro River from the southern city of Kherson. Life in the city – once home to 24,000 people but now with only 2,000 remaining – has become “a hell on earth”, according to Ukrainians familiar with conditions there. South ⁠Korea has demanded an official ⁠explanation and apology from Ukraine, accusing Kyiv of disclosing the transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea and then falsely denying that the two sides had agreed to keep the move ⁠confidential, according to a report from Reuters. “The presidential office expresses strong regret over Ukraine’s unilateral disclosure and its subsequent false announcement that there had not been a non-disclosure agreement,” Seong Ghi-hong, senior presidential secretary for public relations, said in a statement on Sunday. According to the statement, President Zelenskyy disclosed the transfer in his address to the UN general assembly. Ukraine’s embassy in Seoul did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment.

title: Republican senator criticizes White House for taxpayer-funded Trump ads
summary: John Kennedy pushes back against such spending as pro-Trump ‘public service announcements’ air before midterms
text: As the White House expands a taxpayer-funded advertising campaign to promote Donald Trump’s political agenda before the November midterm elections, Senator John Kennedy told CBS News on Sunday “there ought to be a rule” against such spending – before tacitly admitting such spending is “probably” illegal. Kennedy, the US president’s fellow Republican, was asked by Margaret Brennan, the CBS Face the Nation host, about the White House spending to air multiple ads featuring Trump – including one that was produced for his 2024 election campaign. Brennan first reminded Kennedy that in March he had rebuked Kristi Noem, then Trump’s homeland security secretary, for spending millions in government funds “to bolster her public image” in a $220m series of ads she starred in. She then asked the Louisiana senator to comment on the new ads featuring Trump, which the White House calls “public service announcements”. “Our viewers are going to see a 30-second commercial on this program,” Brennan said. “It’s on all major networks – it’s on the cable networks as well. It prominently features President Trump, and there’s a voice praising him as ‘the toughest, most resilient person I ever met’. And at the end, it says ‘paid for by the US government’. Is that the best use of taxpayer money?” Kennedy replied: “Well, first, as to Secretary Noem, what she did was masterclass dumb. She spent $220[m] on commercials about her, and I called her out on it.” “This looks like a commercial about President Trump,” Brennan noted, referring to the first ad in the series, a 30-second highlight reel of Trump’s second presidency, punctuated by on-screen text driving his political agenda and suggesting Democrats are communists. “I don’t think any public official, including President Trump or Kristi Noem or John Kennedy, should spend public money … on private ads for themselves,” Kennedy replied. “Now, the White House sees it differently. But … I think there ought to be a rule that you can’t – well, there probably is a rule – you can’t spend public money to promote yourself.” Kennedy, a lawyer with degrees from both the University of Virginia and University of Oxford, appeared to be tacitly acknowledging the argument made by Jamie Raskin, a Democratic congressman and legal scholar, that any government employees who worked on the first pro-Trump ad – “or used government resources to make it” – may have committed a felony violation of the Hatch Act, a law that bars government workers from partisan campaign activities. According to Medium Buying, a company that buys airtime for Republican candidates, the Trump administration used more taxpayer funds to broadcast another partisan ad featuring the president that aired nationwide on Saturday during a college football game between Ohio State and Illinois on Fox. It aired again during Fox News Sunday. That 30-second spot shows a moody, black-and-white shot of Trump staring into the camera as the soundtrack plays the closing riff of a campaign speech he gave dozens of times in 2023 and 2024. “This is the final battle,” Trump says in the ad. “With you at my side, we will demolish the deep state; we will expel the warmongers from our government; we will drive out the globalists; we will cast out the communists, Marxists and fascists,” he continues, with cheers from a crowd. Those cheers indicate that the audio was recorded during a campaign rally and at a time before he used his power as president to start a war with Iran that has left some supporters feeling betrayed. “We will rout the fake news media, and we will liberate our country from these tyrants and villains once and for all,” Trump can be heard promising in language clearly calculated to appeal to Christian supporters by echoing the biblical story of Jesus driving merchants and money changers from the temple in Jerusalem. The newest ad, with on-screen text reading “Paid for by the US Government”, is even more obviously a partisan product than the first one. In fact, the ad was created for Trump’s 2024 election campaign. And it was posted on his Truth Social account in 2023 and 2024 with a plea for funds from supporters. The rhetoric was written in to Trump’s standard campaign speech as early as July 2023, and then repeated by him again and again at dozens of rallies and appeals for donations. The ad was even played on giant screens during the 2024 Republican national convention before Trump’s speech accepting his party’s nomination. When it was broadcast during the convention by C-Span on 18 July 2024, the ad was identified as material “provided by the Republican National Committee”. At the end of his interview with CBS on Sunday, Kennedy volunteered that he also opposed Trump’s drive to put his own name on public buildings. “I also think that we ought to have a rule that no politician can have a building named after him while he’s alive,” Kennedy said, before adding that there was such a statute in his home state. “Well, we’ll watch, Senator, if you introduce that,” Brennan responded.

title: Failure to protect free speech could cost Labour votes at next election, says Liberty
summary: Polling for rights group shows issue is concern for voters and many feel recent policies have had negative effect
text: Free speech will be a big concern for voters at the next general election, with the government’s current approach on the issue perceived by many to be bad for Britain, polling suggests. Three in five people said a political party’s position on free speech would affect how they voted at a general election. The human rights organisation Liberty, which commissioned the polling from More in Common, claimed the results showed that Labour’s failure to protect free speech could cost it votes. A significant proportion of those polled felt certain policies and rhetoric by politicians had been detrimental for free speech. For example, two in five said arrests of people for holding signs in support of the banned group Palestine Action had had a negative effect on freedom of speech. That compared with one in five who said it was positive. Only about one in seven thought Andy Burnham cared more about protecting free speech than his predecessor, Keir Starmer. Akiko Hart, the director of Liberty, said: “The ability to express ourselves freely makes us all who we are, and free speech is of vital importance to the British public. These findings should serve as a stark wake-up call for the government, which has lost the public’s confidence on protecting this fundamental human right. “We’re fortunate to live in a nation shaped by many identities and perspectives, which means differences of opinion and sometimes uncomfortable views that could upset or offend others. This requires the government to adopt a consistent, non-partisan approach to safeguard everyone’s right to speak freely while protecting people from discrimination.” The polling, released ahead of a joint Liberty and More in Common panel event at the Labour party conference on Monday, also found that more than a third of people believe politicians calling for phrases to be banned at protests is bad for free speech, compared with just over a quarter who think it is positive. When asked about police getting greater powers to restrict protests or marches, a similar proportion – a third – believed it was good as thought it was bad. More than half of people polled said calling protests “hate marches” or “thuggery” had been bad. Starmer called for “tougher action” against people who used phrases such as “globalise the intifada” – intifada is an Arabic word that translates as uprising or “shaking off” – at pro-Palestinian demonstrations, and there have been arrests. The Crime and Policing Act, which received royal assent in April under Starmer, gave police increased powers to restrict protests, including requiring them to consider the “cumulative impact” of repeated demonstrations in the same area when imposing conditions. Many civil society groups were critical of the measure. Since Palestine Action became the first direct action protest group to be proscribed, in July last year, more than 3,600 people are believed to have been arrested for showing support for the organisation, most for holding placards saying “I oppose genocide, I support Palestine Action”. Arrests have continued since Burnham entered office. The UK supreme court will hear an appeal against the ban in November, having decided it is arguable that proscription represents a disproportionate interference with articles 10 and 11 of the European convention on human rights, which protect the rights of freedom of speech and protest respectively. Both left and right have complained about so-called “cancel culture” in recent years, with each side portraying the other as the chief culprit. Hart said: “The prime minister must show urgent leadership on an issue that is dividing the country, and change course away from heavier restrictions and towards a principled defence of free speech.” A Home Office spokesperson said: “Freedom of speech and peaceful protest are fundamental rights that this government will always protect. But there is a clear difference between expressing a view and engaging in unlawful behaviour – such as inciting hatred and violence or supporting proscribed organisations. It is right that as a society and a government, we draw that line clearly.” The Labour party was also approached for comment. More in Common polled a nationally representative sample of 2,017 people in Great Britain between 11 and 15 September.

title: Dog dies trying to protect northern California couple from bear attack
summary: Couple was seriously injured after attack on 19 September and are mourning the death of their French bulldog
text: A bear attack last weekend has left a California couple seriously injured and mourning the death of their French bulldog, who tried to protect them from the animal. In the early hours of 19 September, Jeff Wilson, who lives in rural northern California, let his dog Cassie go outside, the San Francisco Chronicle reported. When Jeff went to bring Cassie inside, a cinnamon bear, a subspecies of the black bear, appeared, slamming him into the side of his home and breaking two of his ribs, according to the paper. His wife, Mallory Wilson, was roused by sounds of a struggle and ran outside to a harrowing scene. The bear had Cassie in its mouth and her husband was bleeding on the ground. Mallory jumped into action, striking the bear with a piece of patio furniture. The bear knocked her down and grabbed her by the back of the head, injuring her neck, before fleeing. The family’s dog died two days after the attack from her injuries, according to a GoFundMe organized for the couple. “Jeff suffered two broken ribs and numerous bite and claw wounds, while Mallory sustained serious injuries to her head and face, and other bite and puncture wounds. Both are now facing continued medical treatment and recovery”, their friend wrote in the online fundraising appeal. “Mallory and Jeff have built their lives and livelihood surrounded by nature. They operate a small hospitality business, have years of experience living and working alongside wildlife, and take precautions to peacefully coexist with the animals that share their land,” the appeal continued. “They are passionate animal lovers, which has made this extraordinarily rare encounter and the loss of Cassie heartbreaking on so many levels. Cassie was a deeply loved member of their family, and in the moment Jeff needed her most, this little dog courageously put herself between him and a bear.” The northern California attack comes as there has been a surge of bear-human conflicts across the American west. In some cases, changing climate conditions have squeezed the food supply of bears, who turn to residential properties in search of nutrition before the winter denning season.

title: Late-night drive and a 999 call: farmer’s chance encounter that led to terrorism arrests at RAF base
summary: Local people say members of WhatsApp group noticed suspicious activity around vans in Whelford overnight
text: In the early hours of Sunday morning, a resident of the village of Whelford was driving home from a party when she saw three white vans parked on a country road. She was immediately suspicious, she said, and all the more so when she spotted a “large group of hooded and balaclavaed” men. She called 999 and police arrived on the scene 15 minutes later. The resident, who asked not to be named but reportedly is a local farmer, told the Press Association: “It would appear that by doing so I just derailed whatever they [the men] were planning. A plucky amateur shouldn’t be spotting an unusual bit of activity at 1am when the airbase is on high alert. I think it’s absolutely astonishing.” If there had been no 999 call, it appears the authorities would have been unaware of the vans and the potential threat they posed to nearby RAF Fairford. People living in the area have been used to disturbance from protesters and a heavy police presence ever since the decision to allow the US air force to use Fairford as a base for attacks on Iran. But in recent weeks they have noticed dramatically increased security measures, with the gates of the base newly barricaded. “In the prior few weeks they have put heavy, very heavy vehicles across all gates,” another resident said. She described them as “very big tractors and things like that” parked behind gates into the base, adding: “So obviously they’re taking security seriously.” The resident said “great big concrete walls” had also been placed behind some gates, including on Dunfield Loop and Whelford Road. If local people had questioned the necessity of those steps, they may have been persuaded this weekend. In the early hours of Sunday morning, others in Whelford became aware of suspicious activity as the local WhatsApp group lit up with messages. One resident of Whelford, named Jason, who declined to give his surname, said they were first alerted that something was happening at about 1.30am when people in the chat group started discussing the vans. Julian Tudsbery, who has lived in Whelford for 30 years, said the 999 call had only come after an attempt to contact the airbase itself. “Evidently, they phoned the airbase police, who didn’t answer the phone,” he said. “It just rang out, so she dialled 999.” A photograph published by the Daily Mail showed police arresting five shirtless men at night. Police later confirmed that five men had been taken into custody on suspicion of explosives and terror-related offences. Residents were then woken at 6am by police banging on their doors and telling them to leave immediately. People from 85 households were taken to a nearby leisure centre. Tudsbery said: “[The police] were banging on the door, so I went downstairs in my dressing gown. There were several police, three police cars in the drive, and they said you need to evacuate, there’s been a major incident, said he couldn’t elaborate.” Thirty emergency vehicles were seen in the village, with the army, a bomb squad and counter-terrorism police all investigating at the scene. Explosives experts were seen examining three vans. The RAF base has come to prominence since March and the beginning of the US-Israeli war with Iran. From the perimeter of the RAF base it has been possible to see heavy bombs being loaded on to American aircraft. Fairford has a particularly long runway, which extends almost 2 miles (3km). It is reinforced to support heavy bombers such as the B-1 and B-52, which have been deployed in attacks on Iran. The aircraft are capable of carrying large payloads, including “bunker buster” bombs. Jason, 50, was evacuated to Cirencester leisure centre at 6am on Sunday with his family and 11-week-old puppy, Poppy, and friends who were visiting from London. “We went to bed [the previous night],” he said. “It was early the next morning when the doorbell rang. It was the police asking residents to evacuate as there had been a major incident.” Jason, who works in consulting, said there were about 40 to 50 people in the leisure centre, ranging from toddlers to elderly villagers, as well as a number of dogs. He said they had been given no more details than those that had been released publicly by police. The Fairford youth football club, about 1.5 miles north-west of Whelford, was taken over as a temporary base for the emergency service response to the incident. There were several police vehicles, ambulances, fire engines, pop-up tents and a large mobile command-unit vehicle in the grounds. It was unclear when people would be able to go back to their normal lives. Those at the leisure centre said they had been asked by authorities if they had anywhere else to stay on Sunday night. By Sunday afternoon, the cordon around the village had expanded so no one could get anywhere near it. Access to the village of Whelford remained closed. With RAF Fairford located along one side of the road, a single police vehicle acted as a blockade against further passage into the village. Tudsbery said he hoped he could get home soon. He had left his cat, Misty, behind.

title: Nor’easter storm batters US east coast with heavy winds and power outages
summary: At least one person killed and about 110,500 households still without power from North Carolina to New England
text: A strong, deadly storm known as a nor’easter battered the US’s east coast over the weekend, bringing power outages, flooding, damaging winds and hazardous ocean conditions. Trees and power lines were knocked down across the region, at least one person was killed and hundreds of thousands were left without electricity. There was significant coastal flooding, rough surf, powerful winds, rain and dangerous rip currents from North Carolina through New England. Boston and the New York City tri-state area were among the regions affected. Power was slowly being restored by Sunday afternoon , with about 110,500 households still without electricity, according to the website Poweroutage.US. In New York, more than 21,000 customers remained without electricity, while the power was out for about 11,940 customers in New Jersey. The National Weather Service said the nor’easter was expected to weaken on Sunday night, with heavy rainfall persisting into Monday in several regions of the mid-Atlantic and New England. Coastal flood warnings were canceled several regions of New York, New Jersey and Connecticut. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) advised travelers to check with their airlines for updated flight information. FlightAware reported more than 5,000 US delays and nearly 550 cancellations. In Massachusetts, a temporary ground delay was issued at the Boston Logan international airport amid the weather. As a result of the storm, New York’s governor, Kathy Hochul, declared a state of emergency covering the Bronx, Kings, Nassau, New York, Queens, Richmond, Suffolk and Westchester counties. A fallen tree in the east New York City borough of Brooklyn resulted in a death on Saturday during the nor’easter. A 56-year-old New York City housing authority employee was killed when a tree came down on him in a parking lot. Police said he was pronounced dead at Brookdale University hospital. Authorities had not immediately determined whether wind caused the tree to fall. In Queens, high winds caused widespread disruption after a tree fell at about 5.40pm in the Glendale area, with downed power lines forcing authorities to close the roadway. As a precaution, the New York City fire department evacuated a nearby building. No injuries were reported in that incident. Along the Jersey Shore, residents spent Saturday removing debris and cleaning up between periods of high tide after the nor’easter forced flood water into streets and homes near the New Jersey coast. Eight counties in New Jersey remain under a state of emergency issued before the coastal storm arrived. The storm struck the mid-Atlantic and New England over the weekend and was forecast to continue into the early part of this week. As the week continues, flooding was expected to rise and recede along with the tides. The National Weather Service (NWS) expected coastal flooding to bring significant flooding from the Jersey Shore south to the northern Outer Banks of North Carolina, with more moderate flooding forecast along the Massachusetts coast.

title: Blanche defends Trump’s White House media ban: ‘It is a privilege, not a right’
summary: US attorney general argues that president was ‘sick and tired’ of inaccurate reporting by CNN, MS Now and Politico
text: Donald Trump’s attorney general, Todd Blanche, argued on Sunday that the administration was permitted to ban three news outlets from the White House because “it is a privilege and not a right to be there”. Appearing on the ABC News program This Week during the second week of the White House’s dispute over press credentialing and access, Blanche also said that the administration took the decision to ban CNN, MS Now and Politico beginning on 19 September because the president was “sick and tired” of what he considered to be those media outlets’ inaccurate reporting. Blanche offered no evidence for his claim that the outlets’ reporting was inaccurate, rather than simply unflattering to the president. Pressed by the interviewer, Martha Raddatz, to point to a report the administration objected to, Blanche seemed to suggest that any negative reporting about Trump must be inaccurate. “Wait, give you an example of when CNN doesn’t report accurately? You cannot be asking me that,” Blanche replied. “There’s not even a real dispute that the information coming out of CNN and some of these other networks is wholly and completely, almost 100% negative toward the president.” On Thursday, a judge issued a temporary restraining order requiring the White House to temporarily restore the credentials of affected journalists, and they were allowed entry to the executive complex. But on Saturday, CNN said its journalists were barred from joining the press pool traveling with the president on Air Force One. “The president hasn’t denied access,” Blanche told ABC. “That’s not the right way to describe it.” The continuing dispute between the administration and the White House press corps had appeared to be resolving before CNN was again blocked from providing pool TV coverage of Trump on Saturday. That was after outlets stood in solidarity with CNN, MS Now and Politico by briefly refusing to provide any pool TV feeds of the president. On ABC, Blanche said it was not unusual for a news outlet to not be allowed on to the president’s plane. “The White House routinely decides who can go on Air Force One,” Blanche said. “This wasn’t a one-time denial of CNN. There’s all kinds of times when certain reporters are not flying or are flying. “It’s not unusual, and as a matter of fact, it’s common every time the president travels that he and his team decide which reporters get to travel with the president.” What Blanche did not explain is that, before Trump’s second term, the choice of which correspondents were part of the pool covering presidential travel was left to the White House Correspondents’ Association and the broadcast networks that take turns providing camera crews. After Trump returned to office last year, the White House took control of which outlets would be permitted in the Oval Office, or on Air Force One, leading to increased access for partisan, pro-Trump journalists. Blanche repeated the administration’s position that the affected three outlets’ reporting amounted to a “national security problem”. Raddatz reminded Blanche that Trump himself said he had banned CNN, MS Now and Politico, because, he said, “they purposely write negative news, and they do that because they want to diminish the Republicans and a Republican administration”. In the ruling to temporarily restore the three banned outlets’ White House access for 14 days, US district judge Timothy Kelly said there was nothing in the record suggesting that revocation of the press passes was motivated by national security concerns. “Certainly, that is not what President Trump said when he announced that he was ‘banning’ plaintiffs from the White House – instead, he focused on the alleged lack of truthfulness and negativity of plaintiffs’ reporting,” Kelly wrote in his ruling. Trump was faced with a gloomy political landscape with just over a month before the federal midterm elections in November. A recent Reuters/Ipsos poll found Trump’s overall public approval rating to be at 32%, an all-time low. But confidence in the news media polls lower, with just 28% expressing a “great deal” or “fair amount” of trust in newspapers, television channels and radio outlets to report the news fully, accurately and fairly, according to a 2025 Gallup survey. Bill Clinton recently commented on the battle between what the news media see as a crude effort at censorship and a denial of constitutional rights – and what the White House views as unfairly negative reporting. “There were lots of times when I wanted to ban the White House press corps,” the former president said at the Clinton Global Initiative 2026 summit. “And there’s a reason we have a constitution – because none of us are immune from being pissed off. “But I’m glad I never did, and I’m glad I couldn’t. And these people shouldn’t. The law should be what it is.” Blanche was asked what the US constitution’s first amendment – which guarantees the right to a free press – meant to him. “The law says – what the free press can do is they are free to report whatever they want,” Blanche remarked. “Of course, they can. But when it comes to the White House, it is the people’s house. It is a privilege and not a right to be there.” He added that “it is absolutely the president’s duty to make sure that the American people are hearing accurate news.”
