title: Andy Burnham to fight next election with plan for NHS-style care service
summary: PM says he is willing to expend political capital to bring in universal service for England funded by ‘everybody’
text: Andy Burnham will fight the next election with a pledge to finally fix the broken social care system, acknowledging he is willing to expend political capital by asking taxpayers to cover the cost. As Labour’s party conference began in Liverpool, he pledged to “rip the plaster off” to radically transform care, setting out a vision for a universal service that would be free at the point of use for everyone in England. The prime minister said the new NHS-style service would be funded by “everybody” but did not give further details on how his long-term plan would be paid for, indicating that a tax rise may be on the cards. One option could be to link reform of social care with looking again at the pensions triple lock, with government insiders not ruling it out in the future. He said Labour would put the proposals into its next general election manifesto so voters could give their endorsement, in the hope of reducing the risk that political attacks over “death taxes” would sink the policy. Burnham acknowledged there were risks in a nationwide reform, likely to be costly and complicated to implement, although he rejected suggestions it could cost £18bn a year. “It’s not that high,” he told the BBC. “Somebody needs to grasp the nettle. I will be the one to do that,” he said. “I realise it might require me to spend some political capital, that it might make me unpopular with some, but that isn’t going to stop [me].” But he said he would take his time to work out how it could be fairly funded. “The challenge in the public finances is real. So it has to be done carefully, without putting extra strain on the public purse. But I will bring forward proposals.” Labour’s annual gathering is intended to be an upbeat affair, with the prime minister wanting to restore hope that some of the country’s most intractable political problems can be solved despite severe economic headwinds. With political courage a theme of the conference, he said in an interview with the Guardian at the weekend: “There’s always things you can do, it’s just whether you’re prepared to do them.” Burnham acknowledged the public finances were “challenging” ahead of next month’s budget but he said delivering fiscal stability would be “crucial”, because only then would the government be able to focus on fixing bigger problems. A series of global economic shocks, including the Iran conflict, has put the UK economy under intense inflationary pressure and pushed up borrowing costs, leaving the government with limited room for manoeuvre. On Sunday, Burnham said he did not want to focus on a “narrative of doom” about the UK’s economy but that he would show in his leader’s speech that he was prepared to take tough decisions. He acknowledged there was “real concern” in the financial markets about the state of the British economy, pointing to the “febrile” global backdrop. He said he was willing to cut government spending to balance the books, and he believed money could be saved by taking a more “productive” long-term approach to issues such as rough sleeping and youth unemployment. Amid concerns that the government could be hemmed in at the budget by the parlous state of the public finances, he said the chancellor, John Healey, would be “highly prudent” in running the economy. “I won’t do what the previous Tory government did and take risks with the economy that are actually still hurting us right now,” he said. Burnham suggested to the Guardian that a significant fiscal buffer would be necessary, with speculation that the Treasury could now consider £15bn acceptable. “I do think it is crucial to have stability and to show that there’s a willingness to face up to the reality of some of these difficult things,” he said. “But actually from that stability, the permission can come to make bigger change that, in the end, could put the country in a stronger position in relation to the public finances.” Louise Haigh, the de facto deputy prime minister, and Healey are using the conference to stress the government’s commitment to boosting British manufacturing through procurement. Healey will tell the conference on Monday he plans to commission three new floating docks to service navy submarines, with the tendering process only open to British companies. The chancellor will promise “a new age of industrialisation”. Meanwhile, Haigh is using her speech to announce a £115m marine research vessel for assessing fish stocks, mapping the seabed, monitoring pollution and responding to marine incidents. Sadiq Khan, the mayor of London, said the “heavy lifting” on making the case for rejoining the EU needed to be done by the government now, after Burnham signalled that the move could be in the next manifesto. “The pitch rolling must be done now, explaining to the country the dis-benefits of being outside the European Union and the benefits of being part of this family,” Khan said. However, the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, appeared to criticise Khan – and Burnham – telling Politico that the speculation “frankly cause[s] a lot of uncertainty for business”. Meanwhile, plans for a third runway at Heathrow are once again up in the air after Burnham refused to say whether he backed the “contested” project, which is delayed by up to four years, saying it was “principally” a matter for London.

title: Republican says Trump’s support of Ken Paxton in Texas primary was ‘colossal mistake’
summary: Thom Tillis says Trump’s decision to back Paxton instead of John Cornyn has put the Senate seat at risk for Republicans
text: The US senator Thom Tillis on Sunday criticized Donald Trump, his fellow Republican, for the president’s support of Ken Paxton over incumbent John Cornyn in the Texas Senate Republican primary. “He made a colossal mistake,” Tillis, a frequent Trump critic from North Carolina, said during an interview on CNN’s State of the Union in reference to the president’s support of Paxton who defeated Cornyn in the May primary. “John Cornyn’s a great member of the US Senate. Paxton has his challenges,” the retiring Tillis added. “We would not be spending tens or hundreds of millions of dollars in Texas if Cornyn had won.” Tillis pointed to the president’s involvement in the contest and described Trump’s decision to back Paxton instead of Cornyn as an “unforced error” that has put the Senate seat at risk for the GOP. Trump endorsed Paxton just days before the Texas attorney general defeated Cornyn, a four-term senator, and advanced to face the Democratic candidate, James Talaricc, a in the general election on 3 November. The race had wide implications for Trump’s strength heading into November’s midterm federal elections. Paxton will now face Talarico, a pastor and state legislator whose message of peace and populism has attracted much attention. If he wins, Talarico would become the first Democrat in more than 30 years to win statewide office in Texas. When he chose to support Paxton over Cornyn, Trump highlighted the Texas attorney general’s record as a steadfast supporter of the president’s Make America Great Again (Maga) movement. Cornyn had previously said during the 2024 presidential campaign that Republicans should move on from Trump. In a social media post shortly before the election day, Trump said Cornyn had been “VERY disloyal” to him and implored voters in Texas to “REMEMBER!” Paxton, meanwhile, is struggling to overcome a series of political scandals. He was impeached in 2023 after being accused of corruption and later acquitted in a trial in the Texas senate. He was also indicted on charges of felony securities fraud, but the case was dismissed after a 2024 pre-trial diversion agreement. In July 2025, his wife of 38 years, Angela Paxton, filed for divorce “on biblical grounds”, citing adultery. Tillis is one of a handful of Republicans to repeatedly break with Trump and publicly criticize the president’s decisions. In April, he spoke out in defense of the Nato military alliance after Trump said he was “absolutely” considering withdrawing the US from it. “Any president that contemplates attempting to withdraw from Nato is not only fulfilling [Russian leader] Vladimir Putin and [Chinese premier] Xi Jinping’s greatest dreams but would be undermining America’s own national security interests,” Tillis said at the time. He also called for then secretary of homeland security Kristi Noem’s resignation after immigration agents killed two US citizens in Minneapolis in January, calling her leadership “a disaster” during the last Senate hearing before her firing. Tillis was one of a small number of Republicans on Thursday to vote in favor of a Democrat-led war powers resolution that aimed to end the US war with Iran. Despite gaining some Republican support, the proposal failed to pass in the Senate by a 49-50 vote.

title: ‘Don’t squander it’: Can Labour hang on to the Burnham bounce?
summary: Conference delegates grateful ousting Starmer has paid off, but relief tempered by fiscal headwinds ahead
text: Even Andy Burnham’s closest allies accept that deposing Keir Starmer to install their man as leader was a huge political gamble. But if the mood at the Labour party conference in Liverpool is anything to go by, it is one that – so far – has paid off. The contrast with last year, when Starmer retained his grip on the party and Burnham slunk away from Liverpool early, could not be more stark. Their relief at their turn of fortune is tempered only by the fiscal headwinds ahead. Cabinet ministers recount how at their political meeting two weeks ago, they were shown a series of charts showing the metrics behind the Burnham bounce. One in particular stood out to those in the room. It was a graph showing whether the public felt the government was heading in the right direction. Until the end of June, it had been on a downward trajectory as public frustration mounted over Starmer’s leadership. But once Starmer announced his intention to step down and Burnham took over in July, the line suddenly rebounded and, while still in negative territory, has been moving definitively upwards since. “We’ve got a second hearing with the public,” one cabinet minister said. “We can’t squander it.” This time last year, just 14 months after coming to power, several were privately despairing about Labour’s electoral prospects. But with an energetic new prime minister and after a difficult summer for Nigel Farage, they now believe that a second term is winnable. It is perhaps unsurprising, then, that speculation about a snap election escalated in the run-up to the conference, to the extent that Burnham felt compelled to “knock that dead” and confirm a 2029 date instead. Some of the prime minister’s closest advisers wanted him to rule out an early election from the off, pressing him to be explicit. “The polling isn’t good enough. We could end up being the biggest party but we could lose our majority,” one said. Another said: “Elections have to be about a choice, not a referendum on an alternative plan.” But others inside No 10 felt he should go to the country while the polling was good, Farage was on the back foot, and before Burnham’s big plans for change ran headfirst into fiscal reality. “Right now the public is willing to give us the benefit of the doubt – that won’t last for ever,” one said. For his part, Burnham claims he can deliver on his promise of radical change for the country despite the severe economic headwinds, by delivering tangible – albeit smaller – improvements in the short term while setting out a longer-term vision to transform things such as social care and youth unemployment at the same time. “There’s always things you can do, it’s just whether you’re prepared to do them,” he told the Guardian at the weekend. “I do think it is crucial to have stability and to show that there’s a willingness to face up to the reality of some of these difficult things. But actually from that stability, the permission can come to make bigger change.” The slogan of his first conference as leader has been “hope again” – but with the bleak global economic landscape there is less hope around than there was when he walked into Downing Street two months ago. The first crucial test for Burnham will be next month’s budget, at which he said the government would be “highly prudent” with the public finances, amid concerns that Labour needs to reassure the markets. But if the budget is about intent, next summer’s spending review is about proof, and as such, that could prove to be a make-or-break moment for this prime minister. It’s easy to make the promises, but much harder to deliver on them. With obstacles ahead, the relief felt by Labour MPs and ministers in Liverpool is heavily caveated. One cabinet minister quoted Alastair Campbell’s election mantra as a warning to colleagues who might be getting ahead of themselves: “Lots done, lots to do, lots to lose.”

title: UK to open new refugee resettlement routes for Afghan women and Palestinians
summary: Exclusive: Move by Shabana Mahmood comes after closure of Afghan scheme last year but experts say numbers too small to deter Channel crossings
text: Shabana Mahmood will announce a new legal route for refugees that prioritises Afghan women and girls and Palestinians, unfreezing a scheme that will put the most vulnerable refugees on a faster path to permanent status. The change marks a shift in Mahmood’s approach to asylum seekers after the abrupt closure of the Afghan resettlement scheme last year and changes that will keep refugee status under constant review for two decades. The home secretary is to say the changes will show there is fairness in the immigration system to support the most vulnerable refugees and that a balanced system will “unlock the inherent generosity of this country”. However, immigration experts and refugee charities have said the numbers who will be eligible are too small to deter asylum seekers crossing the Channel in small boats. The reopening of the scheme is likely to attract criticism from the right, especially as women and girls and people with disabilities are the most likely to be dependent on the welfare state. Reform UK and the Conservatives are also likely to raise questions about security checks – which the Home Office says will be carried out – after the Sunday Times revealed that a former Hamas bodyguard had been granted asylum in the UK and was recently arrested on suspicion of being part of a terrorist plot. Mahmood will tell the Labour conference on Monday that she will reopen the UK resettlement scheme, which was in effect suspended for two years, though never formally closed. The home secretary will say that a tougher migration system, combined with a new scheme for the most vulnerable, will be the best way to ensure there is still broad consensus for helping refugees. “Fairness is what unites us in this country. A fair society is what unlocks the very best of us. Because when people think this country is fair, they are more open and generous to others. When this country feels unfair, people turn inwards. They grow less willing to tolerate difference,” she will say. “I know the British people have not given up on their belief that we should be compassionate, live up to our international obligations, and save the lives of those fleeing war and persecution. But I also know this process must be capped and controlled, and communities must be ready and able to welcome those who come here. “This is what we can do and who we can be as we restore control to our borders, bear down on the small boat crossings, and unlock the inherent generosity of this country.” The Home Office expects about one in four arrivals to be Afghan women and girls and Palestinian refugees, though numbers will initially be very small and capped each year. Under the scheme, potential refugees will undergo security and criminality checks. Those who arrive via the scheme will have a far more generous route to permanent settlement – granted indefinite leave to remain, which will give them a five-year path, in contrast to the constant review of status for those who arrive via irregular routes such as small boat crossings. The home secretary will also formally open another scheme announced earlier this year allowing community sponsors from next month to apply to bring refugees to build a new life in the UK. A sponsored work route for refugees is expected to follow in the spring. Home Office sources said the plan would be to begin with numbers in the hundreds and grow to the low thousands as levels of illegal migration fall. A cap would be set each year, sources said. Refugees will be identified by the United Nations refugee agency (UNHCR) and the International Refugee Assistance Project (Irap). The scheme had stopped taking any new referrals in December 2024. By that point, it was being used by only a tiny number. It will be reopened immediately, Mahmood will announce, with priority given to people with disabilities and for women and girls deemed to be vulnerable. Family units will be able to come together under the scheme, though not extended families because of a crackdown on family reunification introduced earlier by the government. Government statistics show that almost 300 “legacy cases” arrived under the existing UK resettlement scheme over the first half of this year. Officials said they were people who had been referred under the scheme before it was suspended and who had taken time to arrive in the UK. Mahmood will also confirm two of three other settlement schemes that have previously been announced. Starting in October, charities and nonprofits will be able to apply to become sponsors, allowing communities and universities to host refugees. The first batch of arrivals on that scheme are expected to arrive by autumn next year. Applications for sponsors for a work sponsorship route, under which companies will host refugees, will open in spring 2027. Sponsors must provide accommodation, integration support and help finding work, with the aim of reducing pressure on local authorities. Numbers across all of the schemes are likely to be tightly limited, meaning the vast majority of refugees in the UK who arrive via irregular routes will still be subject to new and harsh restrictions on their status. Mahmood has previously announced that refugees will have their status reviewed every 30 months for up to 20 years, with the possibility of returning them to their home countries should those be deemed safe. Madeleine Sumption, the director of the Migration Observatory at the University of Oxford, said the reopened route bore similarities to a scheme that was closed by Labour last year, and that its impact would depend on the numbers allowed to enter the UK. “It has been framed primarily as a matter of principle – in other words, the UK should be doing its bit, and not as a strategy to reduce unauthorised arrivals. “That is just as well, because there is no reason to believe that resettlement would have a large impact on unauthorised arrivals,” she said. Allowing in the “most vulnerable” in the resettlement part of the scheme would be a “trade-off” because of rising costs to the state, Sumption said. “On one hand, there is widespread political support for the idea of prioritising more vulnerable refugees who would not have been able to make it over on a small boat. “On the other hand, previous data suggests that these more vulnerable refugees, for understandable reasons, struggle more to support themselves in the UK, and fare considerably worse in the labour market, for example, than people who arrive through the asylum system,” she said. Responding to the announcement, Jon Featonby, the chief policy analyst at the Refugee Council, said: “The government deserves credit for creating new safe and legal routes that will help refugees reach the UK without risking their lives. Safe and legal routes are essential to undermining people-smugglers’ business model, but they only work if they operate at scale. That means thousands of places, not hundreds.”

title: Facing up to the threat that Reform poses to our democracy | Letters
summary: Letters: Readers respond to an article by John Harris in which he urges Labour to offer hope and change
text: John Harris writes: “Reform is apparently in deep trouble, yet also still in with a serious chance. How come?” (Don’t discount Reform because it’s had a bad year. In our angry, fragile democracy, anything can happen, 20 September). Because it is a cult, just as Maga is a cult. It is sustained by faith, not fact. It offers simple solutions to problems of such complexity that most of us are incapable of understanding them. Reform UK would not exist without Nigel Farage. All his other “parties” only existed because of him. Its self-designation as outside “the establishment” is one of the few truths to be relied on – in the sense that it’s beyond the pale. It is an ethics-free zone. Farage is the tool of the US hard right in the UK. All that’s missing is the Christian end-times nihilism, and not many would be surprised if that clawed its way to the surface soon. Harris maintains that the next general election will be driven by emotion – all choices are. Our biochemistry sees to that before our prefrontal cortex even engages. And the choice will be stark. It will be about “me” or “we”. Do we each retreat to our own little “green zone” or do we hang on to that glimmer of hope and work together? I believe Andy Burnham is sincere in his desire to do politics differently, but I am disturbed that he has said nothing yet about the systemic change necessary for a new, people-focused politics. The founding of a commission to inform a citizens’ assembly on voting reform would be a clear indication that he means what he says. I live in hope. Lyn Dade Twickenham, London • The threat that a Reform-led government poses to the UK is summed up in John Harris’s use of the phrase “munificently funded barbarism”. The rise of Reform and its ruthless rhetoric has helped generate the growth of violent racist militia-styled groups on our streets, whose increasing presence not only intimidates whole communities but creates an atmosphere of lawlessness and insecurity. Simultaneously, billionaires suddenly see an opportunity to buy influence in the UK’s democracy – loudly denied – and elsewhere tax exiles such as Jim Ratcliffe seem empowered to rant about Britain’s decline from when it was the greatest empire in the world. Barbarism, it seems, can attract both interest and vast sums of money from some of the wealthiest people in the world. That alliance of munificent funding and barbarism should alert Andy Burnham and his Labour colleagues and all of us who value and want to protect our increasingly fragile democracy. Peter Riddle Wirksworth, Derbyshire • John Harris mentions Aneurin Bevan, one of whose most famous quotes was: “The language of priorities is the religion of socialism.” This is something that many Labour MPs, and perhaps Harris, having read many of his opinion pieces, need to engage with. Their blanket kneejerk opposition, for example, to any justifiable scrutiny of the welfare budget is music to the ears of Reform. Hope and communities at ease with themselves will only follow from credible policy priorities married to fiscal competence. Roger Whitmore Bath • Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Please email us your letter and it will be considered for publication in our letters section.

title: Formerly enslaved people in Guyana embraced collective action | Letter
summary: Letters: We should learn about emancipated people’s extraordinary capacity for mutual endeavour, writes Prof Kathryn A Monk, in response to an article in the Cotton Capital series
text: Your report (British corporation continued trafficking of enslaved Africans to Guyana 40 years after abolition, 23 August) tells one important part of Guyana’s post-slavery history. There is another that deserves to be better known. In 1839, little more than a year after full emancipation in British Guiana, 83 formerly enslaved men and women pooled their savings to buy the 200-hectare (500-acre) Northbrook plantation. They renamed it Victoria. Other purchases by other groups followed, developing into what became known as the communal African village movement. These were not simply individual acts of property ownership. Many had kept their hard-earned savings buried for safekeeping; the first payment for Northbrook was reportedly carried to Georgetown in coins in a wheelbarrow. Formerly enslaved people went on to buy land collectively, establish villages and devise their own arrangements for managing roads, land and other shared resources. Victoria had established its own code of local government by 1845. Having worked in Guyana, I have always found this one of the most remarkable parts of its history. At almost the same moment that plantation interests were trying to perpetuate the old system, people emerging from slavery were demonstrating an extraordinary capacity for collective action, self-government and mutual endeavour. The history of emancipation is not only the history of what was done to formerly enslaved people, but of what they chose to build once they were free. Prof Kathryn A Monk Bristol

title: Silver linings in the garden's snail trails | Brief letters
summary: Brief letters: Country diary | Benjamin Netanyahu | Fried-egg crisps | Manchester City FC | David Pannick
text: What a wonderful piece of writing by Josie George on the snails in her garden, with her perceptive reading of snail trails as art (Country diary, 24 September). John Bunyan wrote that the snail “goes but softly, but she goeth sure” and that “others range and gare, but find no good”. As George says, we are as a species “cruelly dismissive of everything that is not us”. Three cheers for resilience and for the small, disregarded and humble. title: Drumcree standoff shows Northern Ireland’s troubled past still threatens its peace
summary: Governments will be hoping row over the contentious Orange Order march down Garvaghy Road can be defused
text: Like a ghost from its troubled past, Drumcree has unexpectedly reappeared to remind people how far Northern Ireland has changed in 30 years but also how easily history can undermine the present, if imperfect, peace and stability. Three decades ago parts of Northern Ireland came to an almost annual standstill as Protestant Orange Order protesters blocked roads in support of members wanting to march down what they called its traditional route, the Garvaghy Road, on the Sunday before the annual 12 July parade. Because the Garvaghy Road is a main thoroughfare in a predominantly nationalist area, residents opposed the march. The standoff led to violence and murders at a time when Northern Ireland’s fragile peace process was in its infancy. In 1998, the newly formed Parades Commission was established to defuse tension around controversial marches and to regulate parades. The commission, which was opposed by the Orange Order and unionist political parties, banned the Drumcree parade and has done so every year since, until 2026. In August, the high court overturned a Parades Commission ruling preventing the march, saying the commission had erred in not following its own rules and procedures in its decision. That Parades Commission ruling has been described by the Irish taoiseach, Micheál Martin, as “incomprehensible and wrong”. The decision then allowed the order to resubmit an application giving the statutory 28 days’ notice for this year’s controversial march, which was opposed once again by residents. Over the last few days, the issue returned to the courts several times as those opposed to the parade sought to prevent it happening. On Saturday, Justice Patricia Smyth in the high court blocked the commission by means of an injunction, saying the “long-running dispute has the potential to escalate” across Northern Ireland. She urged the parties involved to, “be big enough to step back from the abyss”. The injunction had the effect of pausing the Orange Order’s notification of the parade; that was described by the order’s barrister as “rewriting history”. But that ruling, which was described by Siobhan Keegan, Northern Ireland’s lady chief justice, as “unfortunately” an error in law, was in turn appealed against and led to the high court in the early hours of Sunday morning ruling the initial Parades Commission decision to allow the march to take place had to be respected. But the ruling has not gone down well with residents, their supporters and political leaders who blocked any march by 35 Orangemen, saying that after 28 years there could be no return to the past. Northern Ireland now is, however, very different from three decades ago. There is no longer a unionist majority; indeed the first minister, Michelle O’Neill, is from Sinn Féin. After Brexit, Irish nationalism is more self-confident and is pushing – some would say, if not unrealistically, then certainly prematurely – for preparations for a border poll on unity with the rest of the island. Changing demographics and the Brexit-inspired sea border on trading goods between Britain and Northern Ireland have made many unionists uneasy. That and a barely functioning multi-party executive at Stormont ahead of assembly and local elections next year are the background to the Garvaghy Road standoff. And so we have unionists who opposed the Parades Commission accusing nationalists of refusing to respect the law and those nationalists, who, in the past, called for respect for the commission’s rulings, refusing to comply with its latest. The two governments will be hoping the standoff can be defused so the ghosts of the past can no longer haunt today’s still emerging Northern Ireland.
