title: ‘We’ve done everything by the book’: EU citizens left in limbo after UK government strips post-Brexit residency status
summary: Home Office faces legal action after 1,473 people living in UK before Brexit told settled status was granted in error
text: The Home Office faces legal action over a policy to strip residency rights from EU citizens who were in the UK before Brexit on the grounds that it gave them the status “in error”. It comes as a Home Office minister revealed that the government has contacted 1,473 citizens with post-Brexit residency rights to tell them the original decision to grant them residency was made in error. The campaign group the3million, which is aware of at least 50 cases, has put the Home Office on notice that it is seeking a judicial review of the policy, which it enacted in late 2025 but has only recently come to light. “In many cases, the Home Office is actually wrong to say there was a mistake. So people whose status was properly granted are now fighting not to lose it – this is a clear breach of the withdrawal agreement,” it said in an appeal to supporters to fund their case. Some of those who received notice were told they were not entitled to pre-settled or settled status because they did not submit passports with their original application. This includes a group of Brazilians and others with dual Italian nationality by birth whom the Home Office claimed were not Italian at the time of their pre-Brexit residency applications. Among them is a 33-year-old Italian engineer who has been in London since 2018, when he arrived for a PhD, and now has “settled status” – permanent residency granted after five years. As a consequence of the alleged Home Office error, he stands to lose withdrawal agreement rights to have his wife living with him, causing him great stress when he received the letter. “It was quite devastating for both of us. We have been here for a long time. We have done everything by the book, and we’ve always felt very welcome here and I always thought this is somewhere I could grow my career,” Fabio (not his real name) told the Guardian last month. A woman working in the NHS and researching a PhD, who also received the “error” notification, said her life had been turned upside down. “I can lose my job, I maybe don’t have the right even to rent the property that I’m living in now, because of course I have to prove my right to live here to the landlord to rent a place,” she said. The Home Office said those granted pre-settled status in error were “not withdrawal agreement beneficiaries” but could provide evidence to the contrary if they had it. “A person granted PSS in error can also make a further valid application to the EUSS [EU settlement scheme] which, if refused, will give rise to a right of appeal,” it said. The Home Office recently conceded it was wrong in one case that was taken to an administrative court. It agreed to withdraw its decision that the claimant’s pre-settled status had been “granted in error”, and that the receipt of a physical Italian passport after Brexit was not the date at which her Italian citizenship started. For Fabio, the case gives hope but the judicial review would give a determination for everyone in his situation. “Despite being hopeful, we are still in a limbo as we started an appeal process and haven’t received any communication from the Home Office regarding the fact that they are now conceding their mistake,” he said. He said he was concerned they would have continue with a costly court case to resolve the matter which could leave them with a bill of more than £5,000.

title: What Democrats are getting right – and wrong – in run-up to midterms: ‘We can’t just be anti-Trump’
summary: Grassroots organizer Yasmin Radjy on the Democratic ground game leading into the midterm elections
text: In the run-up to the US midterm elections, Swing Left – a grassroots political group focused on electing Democrats to office – has spent time canvassing in dozens of districts across the country to hear from hundreds of thousands of voters. Now, with fewer than 40 days until the US midterm elections, the group’s executive director, Yasmin Radjy, sets out what she feels Democrats have been getting right and wrong this election cycle, and why these races are vital for the party’s future control of the US Congress in the years to come. We are now five weeks out. What do you feel have been, and will continue to be, the defining issues of these midterm races? Yasmin Radjy: The two things head and shoulders above everything else that we’re hearing about: one is a feeling like the system is broken, and soon after that are various issues around cost of living. The two are often related, but there are very few conversations where one or both of those issues are not coming up. Everyone’s gotten the memo that we need to talk about affordability. I don’t think there’s a Republican or a Democrat who’s not aware of that. The candidates who are really standing out this cycle again across the ideological spectrum, from Abdul El-Sayed [in Michigan] to Mary Peltola [in Alaska]. And on the House map, Paige Cognetti [in Pennsylvania], to Amish Shah [in Arizona]. They are connecting those dots in a way that is specific and that is also mirroring the nature of those districts. What do you think the party needs to focus on to regain trust, and establish a clear sense of identity with voters moving forward – particularly after 2024? We have to follow up with people when they express urgency around the very real and material concerns that they have. When they express disappointment, we can’t pretend like everything is going great. We also need to acknowledge that a lot of the things we’ve been doing aren’t working. That requires having tough, not just conversations, but introspection, and openness to trying new things, testing new things and taking bigger, riskier swings than we’re accustomed to. On one of the must-win races you mentioned – the open Senate seat in Michigan – what do you feel voters are responding to with a candidate like Abdul El-Sayed? What do you think he needs to do in order to win over voters in that state that Trump won? I think something he is modeling is a “talk to everybody and engage with everyone” approach, not just talk to the people who already agree with you. I think he really won his primary because of organizing. In terms of the issues and themes in Michigan, what we’re hearing is very similar to elsewhere with subtle differences: both parties suck, and no politician cares about that voter, their community and people like them. That is ubiquitous. What he is able to speak compellingly on with a lot of authority is his feeling like the system is broken, and he is doing a good job of tying that to affordability and a whole host of other issues. I’m curious what you think might be the biggest obstacle for Democrats in this cycle? What could be getting in the party’s way? One is that we continue to not have a sufficiently clear answer, for a time when the winds are not blowing in our direction, of what Democrats stand for besides being anti-Trump. We need to start answering that now – and it’s OK if that answer has shades of difference in Michigan, Alaska and North Carolina. The second piece is we cannot assume our base will be with us again because of anti-Trump sentiment in a way that can sustain durable power. Something under-discussed that keeps me up at night is if we are not building long-term, durable power, by 2030 we are going to wake up to an election where, if we don’t have power in the states, we will not be able to win congressional majorities because of how bad redistricting will look. Population shifts are clear in California and New York – two big blue states essential for presidential math – and they will be losing electoral college votes starting in 2030. Texas and Florida are the inverse – they are going to gain power. If we don’t treat the midterms as our most important moment to build infrastructure while there’s money pouring in, while there’s energy to have a shot at winning tough Republican seats in a way we can sustain, we are going to lose without question in the future, because we will have squandered an opportunity. I want to discuss the concerns about progressives, from establishment Democrats. What’s your response to those in the coalition who question whether these progressive candidates have a real shot in battlegrounds that the party wants to either retain or flip? We have members who are Democratic Socialists of America members. We have members who think DSA is a huge threat to democracy – we’ve got the full gamut. Our perspective is that the fixation on ideology and the DSA-versus-centrist divide is a completely false binary. We need to win a majority, and there is a level of pragmatism among the grassroots that is underappreciated. The binary will crumble, not because it doesn’t exist in our institutions, but because that’s not how voters are. We talk to voters every day who might be DSA-aligned on healthcare and Blue Dog-aligned on the border, and it’s the same person. If we lead with genuine curiosity and openness to listening to voters, we immediately see that voters are idiosyncratic, strange and full of contradictions because they’re human. Linked to this, I’m thinking about James Talarico [the Democratic nominee for the US Senate seat in Texas] and Rob Sand [the Democratic gubernatorial nominee in Iowa]. They are showing a pivot in their messaging, particularly when it comes to trans rights. Do you feel that is a necessary strategy right now to court those swing voters, independents and moderates in newly competitive battleground states? I think when you go out and really talk to people, specifically on the issue of trans rights, most Americans want trans people to have rights – and the areas of discomfort range from lack of knowledge. Their worldview on trans issues is curated by Fox News, so there is an information gap. Most voters, including many Democrats, have complicated feelings about the trans people in sports issue. The answer is not to start repeating Fox News talking points. The way to talk about these issues – and this is what the data shows – is to break down the pieces: all Americans want every American to have a certain set of freedoms. The trans and sports issue is complicated, and it is not really a decision for governments, it’s a decision for the leagues. I think Sarah McBride is a perfect example of this – leading with grace, recognizing that changing hearts and minds takes time, and that people use clunky language along the way. Looking ahead, do you think Democrats are doing enough to respond to Donald Trump’s efforts to undermine elections in this cycle in particular? I would say there is an asymmetric investment in election protection right now. And that asymmetric investment is on the litigation front, it is on the donor-organizing and on the grassroots-organizing fronts. And I feel really confident and really relieved, candidly, that the amount of investment of time, talent and strategy has been placed on that. The flip side is the progressive ecosystem, overall, has not invested as much in the actual act of winning the election, and there is nothing more important for election protection than winning each competitive race by a big enough margin that Trump doesn’t have the incentive to try any kind of funny business. We are not where we should be in some of the most competitive races in the country in terms of dollars invested and volunteers ready to help that candidate, and to me, that is the most essential ingredient to election protection. This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

title: How the Trump administration is trying to defend its firing of Maurene Comey
summary: Star federal prosecutor is fighting her no-cause firing, as DoJ dances around Trump’s loathing of her father, James Comey
text: Two weeks after Maurene Comey secured a guilty verdict against Sean “Diddy” Combs, the Manhattan federal prosecutor received a three-paragraph letter from top justice department authorities. “Your employment with the Department of Justice is hereby terminated, and you are removed from federal service effective immediately,” the 16 July missive from Francey Hakes, director of the DoJ’s executive office for United States attorneys, said. The shocking firing of Comey – whose extensive list of successes included prosecutions against Jeffrey Epstein, Ghislaine Maxwell and Robert Hadden – has prompted questions about whether it was politically motivated, given that her father is former FBI director James Comey, whom Donald Trump publicly considers an enemy. Now justice department officials’ recent defense of Maurene Comey’s firing – both in an 18 September court proceeding and legal filings – has lifted the veil on the apparent politicization of Trump’s DoJ and as well as his seeming desire to dramatically expand presidential power. Justice department officials have insisted that under article II of the US constitution, which establishes presidential power, Trump and his attorney general can fire line prosecutors: employees who are not political appointees. DoJ attorneys have also invoked Comey’s familial “nexus” in court proceedings and the DOJ has said in court that former Trump Attorney Pam Bondi directed Comey’s firing. But critics and legal observers say that the testimony has instead shown how the justice department has become warped under Trump and bent to his will to pursue his personal vendettas against his perceived foes – and apparently their close family members. “It’s no secret that the Department of Justice is highly politicized,” said Neama Rahmani, founder of West Coast Trial Lawyers and a former federal prosecutor. “A lot of career prosecutors have left voluntarily. Others have been forced out.” “They’ve taken a very broad view of presidential power in many different areas of the law,” he said in reference to the DoJ’s article II argument. Comey sued the DoJ on 15 September 2025 over her firing, with attorneys Ellen Blain, Nicole Gueron and Deepa Vanamali arguing that she was fired “solely or substantially because her father is former FBI director James B Comey, or because of her perceived political affiliation and beliefs, or both”, in violation of her first amendment rights. Comey’s attorneys maintain article II does not give the president or his attorney general power to fire legally protected civil servants without cause. “It is far more plausible that she was fired for reasons that violate the first amendment than anything else. What else could it be? What would they have us believe, that her name was pulled out of a hat? It doesn’t pass the laugh test,” Gueron told Manhattan federal judge Jesse Furman during legal arguments on 18 September. “By admitting there was no cause to fire her, they raise the immediate question … why was she fired, and is there some reason other than a first amendment violation for her firing?” Gueron referenced a line in an August DoJ filing that stated Comey “is thus wrong to assert that no ‘nexus’ exists between her familial relationship and ability to carry about her duties”. “What does that mean? What is the nexus between her family and her job?It is not her ability to do the job. They have conceded she was fired without cause. It is not some kind of performance-based failure. So what is the nexus that they are referring to?” Gueron argued. “It can only be that they believe, because she is a member of a family that is politically disfavored by this administration, she is presumed incapable of doing her work, of serving her country, and presumed to hold disfavored political opinions. “She’s basically deemed a political enemy, a thought criminal.” During the proceeding, Furman asked the DoJ lawyer Tyler Becker: “When you referenced the nexus between Ms Comey’s familial relationship or family, or name, or whatever the case may be, and performance here, what did you mean by that?” “The idea that the government could never consider the speech, or otherwise, of a family member in determining whether there is an appropriate nexus, just doesn’t make any sense in the ability to carry out their duties,” Becker responded. He continued at one stage to say: “Given there may be some trust issues or something like that from the government, in terms of giving you that power due to certain familial relations.” Furman asked: “In your view, is there a nexus between her family relationship, her last name, and her ability to carry out her duties?” “We have not asserted any sort of nexus that exists,” Becker said. “We have just asserted that the attorney general can remove Ms Comey without cause. So we have not asserted that that is the reason for her termination whatsoever.” Blain, who represents Comey, pressed on this moments later, saying that DoJ lawyers “couldn’t find an answer” and “struggled” when asked about this nexus. “The government actually said that there may be trust issues due to familial relations,” Blain said. If that’s the nexus between her firing, then that “clearly violates” the constitution. As for the government’s assertion that assistant US attorneys can be terminated without cause, Becker said criminal prosecution falls under the president’s executive powers – and that the ability to fire without cause was in keeping with good government. “All the executive power is vested in a democratically elected president, and the accountability for serious prosecutorial decisions must not go to people who – or to bureaucrats in the government – who are not accountable to the people,” he said. The claim that accountability necessitated unchecked firing power over workaday prosecutors appears to contrast with longstanding agency hierarchy. Speaking in general and not about Comey’s case, attorney Jackie Kelly, a former Manhattan federal prosecutor who now works at Boies Schiller Flexner, said there is a “chain of command” in US attorneys’ offices. A line prosecutor has “numerous supervisors, both direct and skip level, within the office. They are directly supervised by their unit or section chief.” “Those unit or section chiefs are, in turn, supervised by the chief of their division,” Kelly explained. “Those criminal and civil division heads are underneath the first assistant or the deputy US attorney, who reports to the US attorney.” Assistant US attorneys, generally speaking, do not act “unilaterally”. “There are numerous kinds of inflection points, or decision points, where supervisors are involved during the life of a case,” said Kelly, who worked with Comey at the Manhattan federal prosecutor’s office. Assistant US attorneys can be fired for cause – they’re not insulated in the event of bad performance. But that bad performance has to be spelled out. “Anytime you have power, there’s the risk of the abuse of that power, so I think it’s really important that [assistant attorneys general] and other federal employees can be removed for cause,” Kelly said. “That’s kind of far afield from the idea that the executive can, on a whim, remove someone from their job without any regard for those protections. “It’s impossible to seek justice and to do the job the right way if you’re looking over your shoulder in fear that you might get fired, or if you’re trying to seek favor with the executive.” For Carl Tobias, the Williams chair at the University of Richmond School of Law, Furman’s questions suggest that he is not swayed by the DoJ’s arguments. As for what the case says about the DoJ under Trump, Tobias returned to what many believe is the main issue: Why was Maurene Comey actually fired? “Even the government lawyers seem to admit that she was a model employee, and she had won a number of high-profile cases,” Tobias said. “That then leads to the question of whether it’s because of her father and those kinds of issues.”

title: Grizzly reality: US states grapple with uptick in encounters between bears and humans
summary: Bears are increasingly entering places where humans live in the US, forcing wildlife workers to make tough decisions
text: Dan Thompson, supervisor of the large carnivore section of the Wyoming game and fish department, enjoys the field work of capturing mountain lions, wolves, black bears and grizzly bears to study them. “I have always been personally intrigued with carnivores and their role throughout any ecosystem,” Thompson said. “I actually feel very fortunate to get paid to do what we do.” Still, like most jobs, there are tasks he does not enjoy but must do: grappling with attacks and human injuries, having to sometimes put animals down and then facing the public blowback. This year, he expects the number of bears he and other state workers have to kill to be among the highest on record. That is because Wyoming, like other states, has seen a significant uptick in the number of encounters between humans and bears. There has been an increase this year in at least 15 states across the US, the Washington Post reported, revealing a national picture of more, and more intense, encounters between humans and bears. Experts largely attribute the increase to the impact of unusual weather on the animal’s food sources and a rebound in recent decades in black, brown and grizzly bear populations. The animals entering places where humans live forces people like Thompson to do something he doesn’t like or face tragic consequences. “None of us got into this job to kill the animals we love,” Thompson said. After persecution and habitat loss during the 19th and 20th centuries drastically reduced many bear populations in North America, restricting hunting and preventing the complete clearcutting of forest ecosystems – instead, just doing sustainable logging – has caused bear numbers to grow over the last 50 years, said Nate Bowersock, a biologist with the Missouri department of conservation. Meanwhile, human development has expanded, and visits to US national parks, where bears roam, have increased. In 1994, the parks saw 268 million visitors; in 2024, 331 million people visited, according to the National Park Service. “We definitely are seeing more people moving into areas where bears are common, and so that does lead to more encounters,” said Bowersock, who also chairs BearWise, an organization dedicated to helping bears and humans coexist. This year, the western US experienced a warmer winter and severe drought conditions, which limited vegetation, like berries and acorns, that bears eat to regain fat after hibernating. That prompted some bears to seek food in developed areas. “Their whole lives revolve around recovering from hibernation and preparing for hibernation, and they have really high caloric needs and so when they can’t find their natural food sources, they have to go look for alternatives,” Bowersock said. Connecticut has had a steady increase in bears entering homes over the last decade. From 2014 until 2020, there were less than 25 reports each year, according to the state. In 2022, 2024 and 2026, the state had at least 60 annual reports. In Florida, the fish and wildlife conservation commission received an average of 2,500 complaints concerning bears annually from 2006 to 2010, according to the state; from 2021 to 2025, the state average was more than 6,400. Black bears were once designated an “imperiled species” in the state; in 2025, the population had grown enough to where the state allowed black bear hunting for the first time in a decade. In Colorado, there have been more than 8,600 reports of bear sightings and incidents this year, more than twice as many as last year, according to the state parks and wildlife department. The agency has euthanized 294 bears, three times the 2025 amount. And there have been 10 confirmed bear attacks in Colorado, the highest number on record. This month, a black bear bit a woman on her forearm through her tent, and a black bear entered a condo through a bedroom window in the middle of the night and scratched a woman. In August in New Mexico, which also has had more bear encounters this year, one killed a 67-year-old wildland firefighter inside his home. The depleted natural food sources had “pretty much forced [bears] to take higher risk food opportunities, so stuff like going into communities and getting in the garbage or maybe investigating a campsite or even investigating a person as maybe a potential source of food”, said Wes Larson, a bear biologist who hosts the podcast Tooth & Claw and maintains a popular Instagram account. Still, bear attacks remain rare. Humans can minimize their risks by not leaving pet or human food outside, securing garbage inside a bear-resistant container and not feeding bears. When exploring the outdoors where bears live, people should carry bear spray and store food and toiletries in bear-resistant containers rather than in tents. If a bear approaches, people should hold their ground, wave their arms and yell “hey bear,” until it leaves, according to BearWise. Such measures don’t just save people; they help keep bears alive too. “Once bears have obtained food rewards that they associate” with people, “we call that human-food conditioning. Once they are at that level, we are going to have to put that bear down,” Thompson said. But with proper precautions, seeing a bear in the wild is not necessarily cause for alarm. “If they have done a necessary amount of education to where they know how to respond to a bear, it puts them in a headspace that they can then enjoy that encounter rather than be afraid,” said Larson, who has received more photos and videos of bear encounters this year than ever before. “In a perfect world, I would love that every encounter between human and bear is full of wonder and awe. But unfortunately, there are some that become a lot scarier or even violent.” Despite that increase this year and projections that the climate crisis will produce more severe droughts, Thompson, who has been with the Wyoming department for almost two decades, thinks this year is an anomaly. “I have seen over the years and decades that things ebb and flow,” he said. “The high level of animals that were removed in conflict, that takes those out of the equation, right? And so for all those reasons, I would not expect this to be the norm.”

title: Bad language: profane Trump brings presidential swearing out into open
summary: President has let rip with swearwords in recent months, redefining norms about acceptable language in public office
text: With a lifetime of political memories stretching back to John F Kennedy’s assassination and the Black civil rights struggles of the 1960s, Cheryl Johnson had one complaint above all else about today’s politicians: the swearing. “All this cursing in politics, we never heard that before,” said Johnson, a retired social worker living in the Pittsburgh area. “Words are very powerful, and the past 45 presidents of this country, have not used such vile language. “Is that how teachers, corporate leaders, nurses, doctor, dentist speak in their work environment? It’s not OK. It’s a decline in respect and honor, period.” Over the past decade, Donald Trump has been at the vanguard of redefining public standards of what constitutes acceptable language. Having already been criticized for debasing and coarsening the public discourse during his first presidency – when he was memorably reported to have complained that US was admitting immigrants from “shithole countries” – Trump has let rip during his second. He has repeatedly used, and seemingly normalized, words never previously heard in public from a US president, at least not intentionally. A taboo seemed to be broken in June 2025, when Trump profanely condemned Israel and Iran for continuing firing at each other even after hostilities were thought to have been halted following a 12-day war. “They don’t know what they fuck they’re doing,” he told reporters on the White House lawn. Lest that should be taken as slip of the tongue, Trump indulged his growing taste for public obscenity again in October 2025, when asked about Venezuela’s then president, Nicolas Maduro. “He’s offered everything,” claimed Trump. “You know why? Because he doesn’t want to fuck around with the United States.” (Months later, Maduro was seized by US special forces. He is now in custody in New York, awaiting trial.) Trump has used profanity even more starkly in recent social media posts, deploying it to raise rhetorical pressure on Tehran after it closed the strait of Hormuz following Trump’s decision to launch the US-Israel war on Iran in February. “Open the Fuckin’ Strait, you crazy bastards, or you’ll be living in Hell - JUST WATCH,” he posted on his Truth Social platform in April. “President Trump doesn’t have a very strong sense of decorum,” said Michael Adams, a professor of English language at Indiana University Bloomington, and author of In Praise of Profanity, a study of swearing’s place in society. “The swearing has a whole range of aspects to it. Some of it is this emphatic diplomatic persona, and some of it is believing in the unpredictability of the president, and his general sense that he doesn’t care.” Civility in politics Trump is hardly the first president with a taste for the profane. Lyndon Johnson and Richard Nixon were both renowned for liberal use of earthy vernacular, but in private. Their bad language was only exposed when tape recordings of their conversations were released after their presidencies. In Nixon’s case, his swearing became an issue during Watergate, when the White House released heavily-redacted transcripts of his taped conversations – with repeated use of the telling phrase “expletive deleted”. Trump’s increasingly cavalier approach to obscenity is a far cry from George W Bush’s mortified response when he was a US presidential candidate in September 2000. During the campaign, a live mic picked up his description of a New York Times journalist as a “major-league asshole”. A chastened Bush, running on a pledge to restore civility to politics, voiced “regret” that his remark was heard. These days, by contrast, politicians are only too keen for voters to hear what would once have been indiscretions, according to analysts. While Trump may have opened the floodgates, other officials and candidates – Republican and Democrat alike – have followed through. Joseph Phillips, an American politics professor at Trinity College Dublin, puts this down to a search for authenticity in an era when politicians have fallen in public esteem. “The incentive for politicians to use profanity [comes from] a change in how people view the profession,” Phillips said. “The level of political trust that Americans have has declined a lot, and this has changed how people see politicians. “Politicians have the incentive to buck that particular trend of appearing unscrupulous and unrelatable by doing a very cheap thing that we all can do, which is using language more typical of ordinary people, which would include cursing.” In that vein, US vice-president JD Vance has commonly used the word “shit”, in speeches and on social media, to bait political opponents and critics. Speaking at a military base in Kentucky on Thanksgiving last year, Vance drew criticism after telling soldiers who raised their hands when asked if they liked eating turkey that they were “full of shit”. Pete Hegseth, the defense secretary, has used scatalogical terms to deride previous practices in the armed forces he regards as woke, telling a gathering of generals at a marine base in Quantico, Virginia last September: “We’re done with that shit.” Democrats, too, have embraced verbal vulgarity. Minneapolis mayor Jacob Frey told Immigration Customs and Enforcement (ICE) agents to “get the fuck out” of the city after an agent shot dead a mother-of-three, Renee Nicole Good, in her vehicle in January. Earlier this week Tammy Duckworth, a Democratic senator from Illinois, told a Washington thinktank she was “tired of fixing shit that Republicans break”. Arguing against being polite if the Democrats regain control of the Senate in November’s midterm elections, she said: “Fuck that shit.” A rhetorical maneuver While the long-term impact may be to reduce public respect for politics even further, those competing for office are unlikely to care. “The incentive of an individual politician is probably not to regain the esteem of the profession, but instead to ensure their own election or re-election,” argued Phillips. “It wouldn’t be the first time that politicians have run sacrificing a broader institution for personal gain.” Adams, of Indiana University, said politicians were seeking “covert prestige” in descending into coarse language. “There is a covert prestige to swearing that has to do with the swashbuckling image of the inveterate swearer – a sort of devil-may-care attitude that attracts people,” he said. “People do swear, and if you never swear, then people wonder if you’re really like them enough that you would be a good president for them. “It’s comparable to when George W Bush and Barack Obama were campaigning and people asked: ‘Would you want to have a beer with them?’ It wasn’t a glass of vintage wine, or a very old single malt – it was a plebeian drink with the plebs. Swearing fits into the same rhetorical maneuver.” Benjamin Bergen, a professor of cognitive science at the University of California, San Diego, and author of “WHAT THE F: What Swearing Reveals About Our Language, Our Brains, and Ourselves,” suggested the heated language was being fueled by the fact that “we are in a very strident time of political disagreement”. The polarized atmosphere, he said, could mean it is only a matter of time before previously unthinkable – let alone utterable – profanities crop up in presidential inaugural speeches, or State of the Union addresses. “I don’t see any reason why there’s anything special about a State of the Union address or a speech in front of the UN, or anything like that,” said Bergen. “I think the language norms are just changing.” But the pendulum could eventually swing back from the current profane trends, he suggested. “If politicians of one generation are seen to be swearing all the time, the next generation may just reject that entirely.” In a curious transatlantic distinction, Phillips – who previously worked in the UK – said the US tendency towards swearing has yet to be replicated in British and Irish politics. “We’re dealing with similar loss of political trust in all three countries,” he said. “However, there is one way in which the US differs, and that’s in the incentives for politicians to build personal brands. “Politicians’ fates in the UK and Ireland are much more tied to the fate of the party. So the incentive to change an established mode of behavior just isn’t quite as high.”

title: Houses can be built on floodplains despite failing safety test, says high court
summary: Decision to allow 190 controversial new homes in north Somerset sparks campaign for change in the law
text: Houses can be built on floodplains even if they fail a crucial safety test, according to a high court judgment that will be of “immense interest” to developers across England and Wales. The ruling clears the way for a highly controversial development of 190 new homes on north Somerset’s floodplains, despite the site being in “flood zone 3a”, the highest level of flood risk before land is considered a functional floodplain. Ministers and experts are so disturbed by the decision that it was agreed at a flood resilience conference on Wednesday to campaign for a change in the law that would stop the ruling setting a national precedent. As a result, Tessa Munt, the chair of the flooding and flooded communities all-party parliamentary group (APPG), will now meet Matthew Pennycook, the housing and planning minister, to ask him to change the national planning policy framework (NPPF). “This is a dangerous and nationally significant exploitation of planning loopholes,” Munt said. “Tragically, we’ve lost the battle in north Somerset, but we need to change the framework as a matter of urgency, so this ruling doesn’t result in planners and developers across the country making similar speculative housing applications.” Charles Banner KC, who represented Persimmon Homes at the court case brought by the local council, agreed the decision was of national significance. His chambers, Keating Chambers, said the result was “hugely important”. “This decision will be of immense interest to the planning and development sector,” it added. Persimmon Homes won permission despite failing the “sequential test”, which is designed to be the ultimate barrier for floodplain development UK planning policy, after the inspector found 12 alternative sites at less risk of flooding. They also overcame heavy opposition from politicians, local and regional tiers of authority and locals – many of whom fear houses surrounding the site will be at increased risk of flooding. Munt said the high court judgment “flies in the face of everything insurers, lenders, Flood Re – a joint UK government and insurance industry initiative that makes the flood cover part of household insurance policies affordable – the Environment Agency and Defra are trying to do on a national policy level”. The Environment Agency objected to the development on flood risk grounds. But the high court agreed that even though the sequential test had failed, the inspector was entitled to consider the development’s wider benefits and whether it could be made safe for its lifetime when weighing the application. Annemieke Waite, North Somerset council’s cabinet member for planning and environment, accused Persimmon of exploiting a legal loophole. “We’re not being nimbys, we accept we need to build these homes,” she said. “But we don’t accept the establishment of a highly controversial legal precedent whereby vital local environmental protections can be overridden to build on floodplains across England and Wales.” Local people living around the site are distraught. With just a few hours’ notice, 51 residents converged at the site earlier this week to meet the Guardian’s photographer, many leaving work early to be there – and one coming straight from a hospital bed. “We represent everyone living in areas at risk of flooding in England and Wales,” said Sue Gardiner, whose living room window opens out over the site. “This ruling massively increases the likelihood of developers building up near you, without having to answer for your increased flood risk.” Gazing over the fields, Gardiner broke down. “I’m petrified,” she said. “Persimmon claims we’re not at any significant greater risk of flood, but no one else agrees: we’ve been refused by three major house insurers on the grounds of increased flood risk on the back of these plans. “Without insurance, our home – the home we worked hard throughout our lives to pay for so we could leave it to our children – could become unmortgageable, and then unsellable,” she said. “Thanks to Persimmon, our only asset could become a dangerous flood hazard for us – and a worthless inheritance for our children.” Richard Croucher, whose home also abuts the site, agreed. “The value of our home was supposed to fund our care when we get old,” he said. “Now we’ve got nothing for when we’re old and in need: that’s terrifying.” Persimmon Homes said: “Our proposals to deliver much-needed new homes in Yatton were subject to detailed scrutiny at a public planning inquiry before being approved by an independent planning inspector. “Flood risk was considered in detail through the planning process, including at the public inquiry by the inspector, before planning permission was granted.”

title: Burnham’s plan for a radical reset collides with economic reality | Heather Stewart
summary: Surging energy bills, higher borrowing costs and rising inflation have left the PM and his chancellor in a fiscal bind
text: As Labour heads to Liverpool this week, Andy Burnham has promised to deliver “stability” in the public finances; but the economic backdrop is anything but stable. The longer the US-Israeli war on Iran persists, the more likely it is that UK consumers will have to swallow higher mortgage rates and energy bills – just as the government is wrestling with its own surging borrowing costs. We are only a few weeks into the three-month period tracking energy price moves that the regulator for Great Britain, Ofgem, will use as a basis to set the energy price cap in January – but it’s been a pretty bleak period so far, with the cost of a barrel of crude above $100 for much of that time. Based on the pricing in energy futures markets, the Bank of England reckons Ofgem could increase the energy price cap, which sets the maximum energy rates paid by homes on standard tariffs, by an eye-watering 24% in January. At the same time, the Bank’s policymakers – from the governor, Andrew Bailey, down – have repeatedly signalled that while they are reassured high energy prices have not yet fed through into wider inflation, they can’t hold off from raising rates for much longer. “We’ve made it quite clear … that it’s going to be harder to maintain that stance, the longer we have high energy prices,” Andrew Bailey said on Friday. Or as his deputy, Sarah Breeden, who like Bailey did not vote to raise rates in September, put it: “The more sparks we’re throwing in the tinderbox, the more likely we might have to turn the hose on it.” Donald Trump made clear over the weekend that he has no intention of staunching the flames himself, by bringing the conflict to a close. “I’m rejecting their deal,” he told reporters, after Iran made a fresh proposal. “They want to make a deal where they open the strait immediately because they’re losing so badly … we’re winning tremendously.” With UK inflation already above 3% and likely to rise further, markets are expecting the Bank to raise rates four times, to 4.75%, over the next 12 months. Such a situation almost certainly won’t happen – the economy would probably be clobbered into submission long before they got there, and inflation with it. But Bailey and his colleagues are widely expected to make a start in November, the week after John Healey’s first budget. Policymakers will also have to reckon with the impact on prices of what is expected to be the most powerful El Niño weather system in 1,000 years, which as well as being devastating to human life, is likely to drive up the cost of important foodstuffs. Burnham has made offering the public a “breathing space” from higher costs a hallmark of his early weeks in power, with sensible but modest policies, such as the £2 bus fare cap. A new iteration of the Tories’ help-to-buy scheme for first-time homebuyers will follow at the budget, he announced this weekend. But while these offerings show a government keen to help, they risk being overshadowed by the wider picture. With the threat of a surge in energy bills looming, the government is keen to avoid announcing a large new support package, conscious of the cumulative cost of Labour’s interventions over the last year. “I think people need to remember that measures have already been taken,” Burnham said this weekend. These include the £2.3bn Rachel Reeves spent on lowering energy bills – including by shifting some green levies on to general taxation – and his own VAT cut on domestic electricity, which the Treasury has yet to explain how it will fund. Yet if, as Trump has hinted, the conflict continues until after the midterm elections in early November, global oil and gas prices could remain high for many more weeks – locking in a sharp rise in bills for UK consumers in the new year. Economists are urging Healey to be bold on energy in the budget, rather than wait and hope. Experts at the research and innovation foundation Nesta are calling for a gas price stabiliser, for example, that would cushion the blow of higher prices now, at the Treasury’s expense – but bring in additional revenue as market prices dropped in future. Any policy that cuts utility bills has the added bonus of bearing down on inflation, helping ease the pressure on the Bank to act. Adding to Labour’s woes, though, the government’s cost of borrowing has risen sharply in recent weeks, alongside that of other big economies, as the global bond selloff has gathered pace. It has been yet another harsh reminder of how exposed the government’s fiscal position is to the vagaries of global markets, with a knock-on effect for the budget forecasts. There are growing warnings, too, about the risks of market instability caused by the interaction of febrile bond markets and the AI mega-bubble. Labour was already in a tricky fiscal bind, given demands for higher defence spending – not least from Healey himself, who now has the job of finding the resources. The difficult decisions about how to do so – let alone fund Burnham’s wider priorities – look likely to be delayed until a spending review some time in 2027. It is very hard to see how that won’t necessitate a fresh round of tax rises. The plan had been for a relatively modest budget, focusing on plans for devolution, and filling the gaps in the defence investment plan announced in the summer. This caution looked out of step with Burnham’s promise of a radical political reset and may be untenable if energy bills are going to soar. He and Healey face a tough autumn.

title: ‘Hell on earth’: last residents eat weeds to survive in Russian-occupied Oleshky
summary: Ukrainian forces airdrop supplies to city where bodies are left to be eaten by dogs because of deadly risk from drones
text: The phone message sent out of Russian-occupied Oleshky was grimly matter-of-fact: food had finally run out for the 2,000 or so civilians, including 50 children, remaining in the city and its surrounding villages. “We’re in Oleshky [and] we can’t get out. We’re going hungry … Right now, I’ve got absolutely nothing to eat,” read the message from a woman in the besieged city who was waiting to be evacuated by the occupying forces. Before the war, she had weighed 110kg (17st); now she weighed just 67kg, she wrote. “At first I was glad [to lose some weight], but now I realise I’ll die without proper protein-rich food. It’s very hard. The house where we stayed last winter was also destroyed and burned down. Just like our own home … We’re still alive.” Oleshky, across the Dnipro River from the southern city of Kherson, has become “a hell on earth”, according to Ukrainians familiar with conditions there. This weekend, military authorities in Kherson carried out a large-scale airdrop of emergency food, water and medical supplies into the city and surrounding areas, using large drones, after Russia reportedly again rejected a ceasefire to evacuate civilians. The military governor’s office in Kherson said an operation had dropped about four tonnes of food to 100 locations, but it was unclear how much the Russian military had intercepted. The Ukrainian foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, raised the situation in Oleshky at the UN general assembly in New York this week. A “Save Oleshky” banner was lifted at a Ukraine-Hungary Nations League football match on Friday. In a statement published on Monday, Sybiha warned of a “humanitarian catastrophe” and called for an immediate evacuation, accusing Russia of standing as “the only obstacle”. He said in an address during the general assembly: “Russia is deliberately making life there impossible. They are starving them to death.” The Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, this month acknowledged the “critical situation” in Oleshky but accused Ukrainian forces of blocking humanitarian supplies intended for its residents. Until May, food supplies were still getting through to residents of a city that had once been home to 24,000. But since May, as the occupying Russian forces expanded minefields and drone cover, the trickle of supplies has entirely halted. Compounding the issue for civilians is the fact that Ukraine’s highly successful summer drone campaign against Russian supply lines has caused shortages for the invading forces’ frontline troops, who in turn steal what little food Ukrainian civilians have managed to save. In messages shared with the Guardian, residents said they were down to one meal a day: soup without potato, made with courgette grown in what once were the flower boxes of the city’s apartment houses, sometimes with the addition of foraged purslane, an edible weed. “We’re running out of everything,” said a resident early in the summer. “By August, the situation will be critical for us. And come autumn, we’ll definitely die. I’m already dying. I’m getting weaker by the day.” On 1 September, a food convoy heading to the city was attacked. Moscow blamed the Ukrainian armed forces for the attack, while Kyiv blamed Russian troops. Ukrainian officials say attempts to drop food by drones have done little to help: the supplies are seized by Russian soldiers and in at least one case the intended recipient was arrested. Commenting on the airdrop over the weekend, Kherson’s military governor, Oleksandr Prokudin, described it as the largest operation of its kind so far. “Food was delivered directly to 100 distribution points. And now I would like to address the Russians,” he said. “Civilians have absolutely nothing to do with the Ukrainian armed forces. Because of the conditions you have created in Oleshky, people simply have no choice but to take food. Do not deprive people of the chance to survive and avoid starvation. “Russia, as the occupying power, is obliged to provide people with food, medicines and adequate conditions for healthcare and hygiene. If its own resources are insufficient, the occupying authorities must consent to humanitarian operations by international organisations and other states. Instead, we are seeing the opposite.” He continued: “Russian occupying forces are obstructing the provision of aid to the civilian population. They are destroying vehicles attempting to deliver humanitarian supplies. And they are killing people trying to bring in food and medicines. They are also blocking all initiatives and agreements regarding the evacuation of people from Oleshky.” According to Tetiana Hasanenko, a Ukrainian official serving from the western side of the Dnipro as the head of the Oleshky military administration, problems began in earnest late last year as access to the city from the Russian side for Ukrainian civilians became ever more difficult. “The density of the minefields has become very high,” she told the Guardian. “From December onwards, food deliveries became much less frequent because vehicles were hitting mines and being targeted by drones. By winter, supplying food had already become very difficult. “And it’s already been very hard. There’s no other infrastructure, electricity, therefore no ATMs, no cash. Oleshky isn’t functioning. People used to grow food in their vegetable plots before the war. There was not only enough for themselves but they used to sell it to Crimea and Kherson city. Now they cannot even grow it for themselves.” Hasanenko described a reported incident where a 74-year-old man was digging out a cellar that had been flooded with mud after Russia blew up the Kakhovka dam in 2023, looking for stored food. Refusing to allow the soldiers into the cellar he was excavating, he was murdered by the soldiers. “Some people have been digging out these cellars looking for canned vegetables, pickled vegetables and canned meat that people were storing up for winter,” she said. Despite the horrific conditions in the city, Ukrainian officials believe the occupying forces are dragging their feet with the evacuation of the remaining civilians in order to discourage a Ukrainian counterattack. Hasanenko said: “The Russians are afraid that an offensive [against Oleshky] will start from Kherson city and they are just keeping people, civilians, as human shields.” She added: “It’s an old city. It has existed for almost a thousand years – and in all this time, people never lived in such horrible conditions, in such a hell like they do now. There are dead bodies not only in the basement of the hospital, but all over the city. They’re just lying there because you cannot pick up the dead body. The drones are flying constantly and then the dogs are eating the bodies.” In a text message, another resident said simply: “All supplies are running out.” Another messaged: “A week ago, the orcs [a Ukrainian term of abuse to describe Russian soldiers] came into people’s yards and dug up all the potatoes, onions, and garlic. “They took all the food supplies from the elderly women. When one of the grandmothers started shouting, they replied that people ‘soon to be living in heaven’ like them should subsist on nothing but water.”

title: ‘It’s hard to sell a house when it’s covered in baboon faeces’: Cape Town divided over plan to remove its monkeys
summary: Two troops of chacma baboons are breaking into homes and shops but animal rights activists insist coexistence is the answer
text: Cape Town’s city council has said it will “imminently” round up two baboon troops coming into repeated conflict with residents. The animals will be sterilised and permanently moved to a newly constructed sanctuary. The plan has been fiercely criticised by animal rights activists, who say the monkeys should remain roaming freely, and that less destructive options have not been properly considered. Cape Town’s baboon problem has been brewing since the 2000s, after the city stopped culling troops in the late 1990s after pressure from the public. But in the past two years it has reached boiling point. A 2025 census found that the population had grown by a third since 2000, from 360 baboons to 493, (including a peak of 519 in 2023), now living in 12 managed troops. As a result of the population boom, troops of chacma baboons on the city’s peninsula regularly rip off roof sheeting, sneak into unlocked cars and raid food pantries. Some monkeys forage naturally, but others are now staying up late into the night to break into homes in Simon’s Town and nab snacks from convenience stores. Residents can no longer barbecue or host garden parties for fear of the marauding baboons. “It’s depreciated property values because it’s hard to sell a house when it’s covered in baboon faeces and paw prints, and you know they’re coming every day,” said Justin O’Riain, a behavioural ecologist at the University of Cape Town who has long studied the local baboons. Cape Town’s geography is partially to blame. Much of the problem is confined to the Cape Peninsula, a narrow sliver of land stretching from the city centre to Cape Point. Here, baboons are boxed in between the steep, protected area of Table Mountain national park and the sprawling urban development that stretches to the Atlantic Ocean. “The underlying issue is that baboons will seek low-lying land. That is their natural drive – it’s better access to water and more productive vegetation,” said Joselyn Mormile, who leads the Cape Baboon Partnership (CBP), a nonprofit organisation that works to manage the baboons. “But throughout the peninsula, we’ve developed most of those places. It’s a constant battle between the two.” Initially, the 2025 management plan, drawn up by the CBP which includes the City of Cape Town, South African National Parks and Cape Nature,proposed to move four troops to a sanctuary. That was revised, Mormile said, to give two other troops living in the northern section of the peninsula “the benefit of the doubt to see if they can adjust in that remaining space … We believe that they could settle quite nicely.” The baboons have proved an especially divisive – and expensive – issue. Cape Town’s baboon management programme costs about 20m rand for 18 months (£920,000), with full-time rangers watching over most of the troops to try to head off any trouble. In addition to moving the Waterfall and Seaforth troops to a sanctuary, a baboon-proof northern boundary fence will be erected between urban areas and nearby mountains. Animal rights activists, who have been staging peaceful protests for months, and some scientists say the city should build a fence to exclude the Waterfall and Seaforth troops rather than remove the animals from their environment. However, O’Riain said it was likely that the baboons would simply move along to the next area of low-lying land where the fence ends, as there was not enough food for the baboons behind the proposed southern fenced area. Opponents argue that removing the other baboons will cause long-term psychological distress and social disruption, and that the baboons play an important ecological role by dispersing plant seeds. Chacma baboons are not considered endangered. And the welfare of the animals is already in question: baboons are being poisoned, hit by cars, chased by dogs and shot. “No one should ever shoot a baboon, but if people feel the authorities are not doing anything, they will take action – and that action is never nice,” O’Riain said. “Just a few days ago, a baboon was shot straight through the chest. “How many more millions of rand are we going to throw into these troops only to end up in exactly the same place in another 10 years’ time?” he said. “Which is shocking baboon welfare, shocking baboon health, and a very poor quality of life for the people who are living in these areas.” Find more age of extinction coverage here, and follow the biodiversity reporters Rebecca Ratcliffe, Phoebe Weston and Patrick Greenfield in the Guardian app for more nature coverage.

title: ‘Rip the plaster off’: Andy Burnham sets out vision for universal free social care
summary: PM says he will put proposals for NHS-style service funded by everybody into Labour’s next general election manifesto
text: Andy Burnham has said that he is going to “rip the plaster off” to fix the broken social care system, as he set out a vision for a universal service that would be free at the point of use for everybody in England. The prime minister said the new NHS-style social care service would be funded by “everybody” but did not give further details of how his radical long-term plan would be paid for. Speaking to Laura Kuenssberg on the BBC as the Labour party conference began in Liverpool, Burnham ruled out implementing reforms before the next general election – currently due in 2029. He said Labour would put the proposals into its next general election manifesto so that voters could give their endorsement, in the hope of reducing the risk that political attacks would sink the policy. The prime minister acknowledged that there were risks in a nationwide reform, likely to be costly and complicated to implement. “Somebody needs to grasp the nettle. I will be the one to do that,” he said. “I realise it might require me to spend some political capital, that it might make me unpopular with some, but that isn’t going to stop [me].” The current social care system in England was “as unfair as American healthcare” where the “most vulnerable in society can lose everything, they can be wiped out”, he said. He told Kuenssberg: “I’m going to rip the plaster off, if I can put it that way, because someone has to do it.” Burnham declined to give details about how a new system would be funded, saying a review was continuing and promising more details in his conference speech on Tuesday. The death two weeks ago of his father, Roy, who had Alzheimer’s, had pushed him on, he said, as he praised the “humour, humanity and skill” of those who cared for him. “If I look at the people who cared for my dad, they must just feel invisible to the political class,” he said. “They work day in, day out, with huge humour and humanity and skill in what they do … caring for other people’s parents on poverty pay. How have we let this go on so long?” Burnham claimed that the annual cost of delivering an NHS-style social care service was “not as high” as the £18bn that had been suggested – and said he would take his time to work out how it could be fairly funded. “The challenge in the public finances is real,” he said. “So it has to be done carefully, without putting extra strain on the public purse. But I will bring forward proposals.” Asked if social care was going to be like the NHS, free at the point of use and paid for through general taxation, Burnham replied: “It will be a system of that kind. So everyone contributes, everyone’s covered, but not precisely necessarily in the same way that we currently pay for the NHS. This is for Baroness Casey to advise us on.” Changing social care has long been a political priority for Burnham. As health secretary in 2009, he proposed a national care service modelled on the NHS, but the Conservatives called it a “death tax” because it proposed a system funded by a new tax on estates after people died. Labour went on to lose the general election in 2010 and the plan was abandoned. Asked if he would go back to that system, he said that nothing was off the table. “That doesn’t mean that I’m going straight back to the proposal that I had in 2010,” he said. Trying to head off inevitable blocks from opposition parties, Burnham said that though consensus was necessary, scaremongering would block vital reform. “If we continue to approach this issue with politics as usual, where people are scoring points and they’re taking a proposal and then trying to frighten the public at home about it, we will never fix it,” he said. “And can we honestly justify that? That politics in this country cannot face an issue like this and deal with it because we’re too scared of it?” Burnham acknowledged there was “real concern” in the financial markets about the state of the British economy, pointing to the “febrile” state of global backdrop. The prime minister said he was willing to cut government spending to balance the books – but also that he believed money could be saved by taking a more “productive” long-term approach to issues such as rough sleeping and youth unemployment. Amid concerns that the government could be hemmed in at the budget by the parlous state of the public finances, he said that the chancellor, John Healey, would be “highly prudent” in running the economy. “I won’t do what the previous Tory government did and take risks with the economy that are actually still hurting us right now,” he told the BBC.

title: Trump allies could use midterms ‘counting window’ to disrupt results, experts warn
summary: Fears grow that loyalists in key states could use critical period when votes are counted to amplify false claims
text: Election experts have warned Donald Trump’s administration could use the crucial hours and days after November’s midterm elections to disrupt the results after struggling to enforce a crackdown on voting. With less than six weeks remaining until polls close, and control of US Congress in the balance, the post-election “counting window” is seen as as a particularly vulnerable moment by former US federal government officials. While the US president’s bid to impose sweeping restrictions on mail-in ballots was rejected by the supreme court earlier this month, there is apprehension that Trump and his allies could use the period while votes are counted to amplify unfounded allegations in a bid to challenge results that don’t go their way. “I think because the administration has lost so many of their attempts to disrupt the normal process in court, that they are going to use the claim of foreign interference at the end of voting days to either seize equipment or to seize ballots, whether they’re legally justified to do so or not,” Caitlin Durkovich, a former deputy homeland security adviser for resilience and response on the national security council, told a briefing staged by the Brennan Center for Justice earlier this week. Some states take days – even weeks, in California’s case – to complete a count of votes after an election. Control of the House of Representatives and Senate may hinge on results in states with a delayed result. “That period, that waiting time, is where doubt begins to surface,” Durkovich said on Tuesday. “And when it is then amplified by foreign actors and, frankly, by domestic actors, it starts to cause distrust in the integrity of the process.” State-level elections officials are trying to prepare the public to understand the process now, to head off a manufactured controversy later, said Larry Norden, vice-president of the elections and government program at the Brennan Center. “To me, this is the biggest threat right now,” he said. “I think a lot of people may think just because they’re seeing all these headlines being thrown at them that things have changed – that it’s become more difficult to vote,” added Norden. “In the history of American elections in some ways, there have never been more options for the way that people can vote, and they are still in place going into this election.” Early voting eliminates most of the threats voters apprehend ahead of an election, he suggested. “The earlier they vote, the more secure they can feel that their vote is going to count, and I think that’s a really important message for us to be delivering to people.” The power of doubt about the validity of votes, and the risk of Trump unveiling “emergency” measures on ballots or voting machines around election day, looms large. “Every state in the country now has live ballots out,” said Ben Hovland, former chair of the Election Assistance Commission. “That really means the election is here, and it means that needs to be taken into consideration for any court rulings we’re looking at.” A supreme court decision this month upheld a lower-court injunction on the Trump administration using the US Postal Service and the Department of Homeland Security to vet mail-in ballot deliveries. But groups such as the NAACP, the National Urban League and other rights organizations remain concerned about the Trump administration’s insistent claim – without evidence – that the 2026 midterm elections will be illegitimate unless the federal government intervenes. Normally, the Department of Justice and the FBI enter a “quiet period” just ahead of elections, to avoid influencing the results. That has not been the case this year. The Department of Homeland Security continues to pursue voter-roll lists in states that would not turn them over voluntarily. The federal government has asked states to retain their 2024 election documentation for later inquiries. And DHS is pursuing an independent “unlawful voter initiative” to find non-citizen voters on state rolls, one that an anonymous whistleblower told congress last week that is using “highly questionable data” and may be unlawful. The federal government’s claims of illegally-registered voters – claiming numbers that do not bear up under scrutiny – and Trump’s rhetoric alleging fraud without evidence, “back up a narrative of fraud to undermine confidence in the elections”, Hovland said. Much of the president’s election rhetoric revolves around foreign interference. Experts make a distinction between foreign influence – propaganda, essentially – and foreign interference , or directly manipulating vote counts. “It’s very important for people to understand that we don’t have any examples of a country trying to interfere in the electoral process, in that technical process,” said Beth Sanner, a former deputy director of national intelligence who is now director for geopolitics and strategy at International Capital Strategies. “It just didn’t happen,” she said. “It didn’t happen in 2020.” Election security has improved across the country, partially as a reaction to false claims about Trump’s 2020 defeat. “Every state audits its results,” said Geoff Hales, former chief of joint cyber defense collaborative partnerships at the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, or CISA. “Election officials across the country have really taken cybersecurity seriously.” Despite the president’s insistence that the country faces a foreign threat to elections, Hale said the federal government has sharply cut staff and spending on elections security at CISA, and with it the technical assistance that once flowed to state election’s officers. “The federal support that used to be there has pulled back sharply,” he added. “This means that cybersecurity services have been reduced, funding for information sharing environments have been cut, the threat briefings about nation-state adversaries that used to occur dozens of times a year are occurring rarely or not at all.”
