title: ‘Miracle on the Hudson’ pilot Chesley Sullenberger inducted into US Aviation Hall of Fame
summary: Sullenberger landed a disabled passenger plane safely in the Hudson River in 2009 without any loss of life
text: Capt Chesley “Sully” Sullenberger III – the pilot known for safely landing a US Airways flight in New York City’s Hudson River during a 2009 emergency – has been inducted into the US’s National Aviation Hall of Fame, two months after he went public with an Alzheimer’s disease diagnosis. Sullenberger, 75, received the honor during a ceremony held in Washington DC on Thursday, 17 years after he engineered what has become widely known as the Miracle on the Hudson. His actions that day – which saved more than 150 lives – set the stage for him to be inducted alongside the six-member 2026 hall of fame class, including Nasa astronauts and aviation researchers. Sullenberger participated in the ceremony remotely by video, saying: “I want to congratulate the other [inductees] on lifetimes of accomplishments. And I thank you for the honor of enshrinement in the National Aviation Hall of Fame.” During his remarks, he recognized that the dramatic events of 2009 – which were eventually the basis of a Tom Hanks movie – played a major role in his enshrinement. But he made it a point to say: “My career was much more than one flight. “From a very young age, I knew I wanted to fly airplanes. That was the beginning of a lifetime following that dream. I was so fortunate to spend an entire working lifetime doing something I loved.” A former member of the US air force, Sullenberger was piloting US Airways Flight 1549 on 15 January 2009. The aircraft had departed New York City’s LaGuardia airport en route to Charlotte, North Carolina, carrying 150 passengers and five crew members. Not long after takeoff, the aircraft struck a flock of birds, resulting in a total loss of thrust from both engines. Sullenberger ultimately realized that the plane would not be able to make it back to LaGuardia – so he instead landed the aircraft in the Hudson River. All 155 people aboard survived. Sullenberger in July disclosed that he had been diagnosed with Alzheimer’s disease, which had given him another way to think about public service. “This new phase of my life has challenged what it means to be of service,” he said in a statement shared at the time. “And the answer is to speak up. It is my hope that by sharing this, other families living in the shadows with this disease will feel they too can step forward.” Speaking in an interview on Wednesday with the ABC program Good Morning America, Sullenberger described his reaction to learning of the diagnosis. He said he experienced “all those emotions, the shock, the anger, why me?” “We’re part of this community who are trying to make the best of a bad situation.” Figures from the Alzheimer’s Association indicate that about 7.4 million people who are age 65 or older are living with clinical Alzheimer’s dementia. Roughly three out of four are 75 or older. “This is a disease – not a character flaw,” his wife, Lorrie Sullenberger, said on Good Morning America. “I think we need to talk about it more openly, and maybe other people can do the same.” • The headline of this article was amended on 28 September 2026 to correct the spelling of the first name of Chesley Sullenberger.

title: Seattle prosecutors mull hate crime charge for woman who bit circle in victim’s forehead
summary: Suspect, charged with felony assault, under investigation for making racist and homophobic comments before attack
text: A Seattle woman will need surgery for a gnarly wound, after a stranger, who called her “an inferior race”, took a bite of flesh from her forehead in a surprise attack. The incident occurred in broad daylight on 18 September when Diana Gonzalez, 36, was walking to a local convenience store and the alleged assailant, identified by prosecutors as Kamilia Chadli, threw a food wrapper at her, the victim told Seattle police. After Gonzalez asked the woman why she had done that, Chadli allegedly yelled, “You’re the inferior race,” as well as used a homophobic slur, before spitting on Gonzalez and dragging her to ground. The suspect then sank her teeth into Gonzalez’s forehead and gnawed out a 1in-diameter chunk of flesh. Officers who responded to the scene said they found a piece of the victim’s flesh the suspect spat into a grate. “It looks like a zombie bite in a movie that you would see – like it’s a full circle,” Gonzalez told KOMO-TV, a Seattle ABC affiliate, wearing a bandage on her forehead. “This is my face. I’m going to have a scar permanently.” Gonzalez said she learned from a police report that the woman was unhoused. KOMO-TV reported that court documents indicate Chadli was living in a shelter across the street from the crime scene, and police reports from her prior encounters with officers described her as having a “history of mental health and substance abuse issues”. Gonzalez noted that she and Chadli, who is the same age, share a similar complexion and both have curly hair. “I was like: ‘Do you think I’m white? Do you think I’m Black?’ She’s like: ‘I don’t care,’” Gonzalez said, adding the woman repeated her racist remarks. Chadli allegedly fled the scene, but was chased by a witness, who flagged down a marshal at a nearby courthouse. Chadli has been charged with second-degree assault, which is a felony, and is detained with bail set at $150,000. Her arraignment has been scheduled for Monday. A hate crime investigation is also under way, jail records show. “Though a hate crime is not charged now, that charge may still be added later in the case if the evidence can meet the burden required by state law – which is often higher than what people understandably think the proof burden is,” the King county prosecutor’s office said in a statement to Seattle’s CBS affiliate, KIRO 7 News.

title: Third person arrested in death of Tasia Fortune, as police say hanging was staged
summary: Eric Clark, 45, charged with murder as autopsy concludes Fortune was dead days before body discovered in tree
text: A third person has been arrested in the death of 29-year-old Tasia Fortune in Mississippi’s capital city, while investigators said they had determined the scene where her body was found hanging had been staged. Eric Clark, 45, surrendered to authorities on Friday and was charged with murder, according to the Jackson police department (JPD). Clark was scheduled to make a court appearance on Monday. Police disclosed Friday that an autopsy investigation concluded “the scene and the hanging were staged”. Authorities did not release additional information about the circumstances surrounding Fortune’s killing or why investigators believe the scene was faked. Clark’s arrest comes after two other men, Earnest Lloyd Jr and Jarques Ratliff, were charged with murder in connection with Fortune’s death. The case leading to the arrests of Clark, Lloyd Jr and Ratliff had drawn national attention because of the severity of Fortune’s killing and Mississippi’s history of racist violence and lynchings. Clark, Lloyd Jr, Ratliff are Black, as was Fortune. “The Jackson police department’s robbery-homicide division will continue its investigation until all individuals believed to be involved are held accountable for their actions in connection with Ms Fortune’s death,” a news release shared with multiple news outlets states. Fortune, a mother of four, was discovered on 3 August hanging from a tree behind a vacant home on the 500 block of Road of Remembrance in the western part of Jackson. Investigators have said Fortune was not killed at the location where her body was found. JPD detective Samuel Dukes previously described Fortune’s hanging in court as “staged”, saying investigators believe she was killed somewhere else before her body was placed in a hanging position in the tree on Road of Remembrance. He added investigators determined Fortune had been dead for two to three days before her body was discovered. Police have released few details about the events leading to Fortune’s death. Detectives have interviewed as many as 15 people, according to the police news release. Local TV news station WLBT reported an alleged physical altercation between Lloyd, 25, and Fortune that occurred shortly before her death. Police accused Lloyd of using a black cable cord to hang Fortune, according to WLBT. Ratliff and Lloyd have both reportedly pleaded not guilty. Each has been denied bond. Fortune’s mother, Christy Spivey, has said she was certain her daughter would not have killed herself.

title: Greek authorities seek answers after six killed in Athens apartment block explosion
summary: Emergency teams discovered victims after two-storey building in historic Plaka district collapsed ‘in seconds’
text: Greek authorities say they are trying to discover what caused a two-storey apartment block in the heart of ancient Athens to collapse “in a matter of seconds”, killing six people. Emergency teams found the victims, including four American tourists, on Saturday, more than 24 hours after the early morning explosion in the historic Plaka district. The fire service said the bodies of three women and three men had been found, but stopped short of identifying them. A Briton and his Greek wife, 77 and 78, who lived in a flat on the building’s upper floor, were among those killed, the Guardian was told. “The bodies have been taken to the morgue where postmortems will be conducted,” the city’s vice-mayor, Paris Charlaftis, said in a telephone interview from the blast scene. “Our focus now is on the explosion’s cause. What could have happened to bring the building down in a matter of seconds?” Rescuers had deployed thermal cameras and geophones, used to detect deep subsonic frequencies, in the hope of finding survivors. Earth-moving machines and specially trained search dogs were brought in to move and comb mounds of rubble through the night. Before the bodies were pulled from the ruins on Saturday, police put the missing at six, saying four were Americans staying in a short-term rental on the building’s first floor. Two brothers and their wives, all four were due to fly to the US on Friday, just hours after the explosion. “When they failed to turn up for the flight they had checked into only a day earlier, that gave us a further lead,” a source said. “It became clearer that they must have been there when the blast occurred.” The Briton, a talented artist, who lived with his wife on the second floor, was described by Charlaftis as being partially disabled. “He had kinetic issues, and it was thought likely they, too, were in the building [at the time of the blast].” Nestled around the foot of the fifth-century BC Acropolis, Plaka is especially popular with tourists. The picturesque district draws thousands of visitors daily, with many staying overnight in the hotels and short-term rentals in neoclassical houses and small apartment blocks along its alleyways and narrow streets. The mayor of Athens, Haris Doukas, who rushed to 15 Lysikratous, where the mid-20th-century building had once stood, was quick to describe the incident as an “unprecedented disaster”. At least three people were known to have been injured when the explosion occurred at 7.30am, shattering the windows of nearby buildings and scattering debris far and wide. A motorist driving down Lysikratous described how his car was lifted into the air by the sheer force of a blast that some in the neighbourhood likened to an earthquake, others to a bomb. Emergency workers could be seen hastily removing two women on stretchers from a building next door who had been wounded by flying debris. Speculation is rife that a gas leak triggered the collapse but officials said there were many “cogent theories” at play. Fears of the leak emanating from the first-floor short-term rental was among them. As part of efforts to address a burgeoning housing crisis, Greece’s centre-right government has sought to ban short-term rentals in Plaka – clamping down on permits and tightening regulations. On Saturday, as speculation mounted over the cause of the blast, criticism grew over the ability to “properly control” establishments that were often unregulated. “This awful incident will fuel further debate over who inspects short-term rentals that no one who lives in Plaka wants anyway,” said Giorgos Zafeiriou, an architect who heads the local residents’ committee. “Hotels have chambers that regulate them but who inspects and controls Airbnb and serviced apartments that often may not be up to par?” Civil protection crews and emergency disaster management teams have been ordered to remain on site until the cause of the explosion is found, officials said. “It was a huge explosion, so getting to the bottom of it must now be the priority,” added Zafeiriou. “Six people have lost their lives.”

title: ‘I can deliver’: Burnham pledges radical change on eve of Labour conference
summary: Exclusive: UK prime minister says delivering fiscal stability would be ‘crucial’ to be able to fix bigger problems
text: Andy Burnham has said he can deliver on his promise of radical change for the country despite severe economic headwinds, telling the Guardian: “There’s always things you can do; it’s just whether you’re prepared to do them.” The prime minister acknowledged public finances were “challenging” ahead of next month’s budget but said delivering fiscal stability would be “crucial”, because only then would the government be able to focus on fixing bigger problems. A series of global economic shocks, including the Iran conflict, has put the UK economy under intense inflationary pressure and pushed up borrowing costs, leaving the government limited room for manoeuvre. Ahead of his first Labour conference as prime minister, however, Burnham sought to reassure voters he was willing to make tough decisions to deliver change and show the markets he could ensure fiscal stability while preparing the groundwork for more substantial change ahead. Speaking to the Guardian on the eve of his first conference as Labour leader, he said: “The public would have more respect for us if we go and grab something difficult … and say, ‘Right, we’re going to do something here’, rather than constantly playing the political game before fixing the problems. “It’s challenging, definitely, but there are still things that you can do. Always in politics, there are things that you can do. The question is sometimes: Are you prepared to do them? Yeah, I am prepared to do them.” When asked about the need for a large fiscal buffer against shocks, he said the key thing was stability, indicating that he understood the need to reassure the markets, but that more radical transformation of the state would follow. “I do think it is crucial to have stability and to show that there’s a willingness to face up to the reality of some of these difficult things. But actually from that stability, the permission can come to make bigger change that, in the end, could put the country in a stronger position in relation to the public finances,” he said. “You have to have stability, but you have to do what you can within that. You can’t pursue a major programme of change, which is what I believe the country needs, in a chaotic situation.” After ruling out holding a snap general election before 2029, Burnham said he wanted to set out a clear path for how the country could move to a better place – and that he hadn’t been spending his time “sitting politicking and strategising” but instead was focused on fixing problems. His ambition to give people “a bit more belief that things can improve” across the country, he said, would not come from “endlessly running elections and referendums”. He denied having had discussions with his senior team about whether to call an early election. “The speculation in no way matches the internal discussion because there isn’t one,” he said, rejecting claims he did not have a mandate as the public had voted for the Labour party. However, Burnham acknowledged he was hemmed in on tax and the fiscal rules of Keir Starmer’s manifesto commitments, and suggested he would have done it differently had he been in charge at the time. “I’ve inherited those positions and, as I say, I think the main thing for me is to focus on the here and now for people, not to be self-serving about ‘oh, what would suit me?’ and playing politics. That’s not where my mind is, and possibly would have framed it different, but we are where we are, you know, and that’s the reality.” Burnham played down speculation that Labour may give more support for energy bills, with the price cap set to soar from January. “I think people need to remember that measures have already been taken,” he said, referring to VAT on electricity bills being scrapped from next week. The prime minister also reiterated that while he thought the welfare bill was too high, the will among Labour MPs was “not there for crude cuts” because they would push people into crisis, so a longer-term approach to reform was required. After warning of the risks, as well as the opportunities of artificial intelligence at the UN last week, Burnham admitted to concerns about rogue AI agents attacking state institutions in the UK, after the Australian medicare system was hit. Burnham addressed the presence of far-right protesters on the streets of Britain, accusing Daniel Thomas, who has led black-clad anti-migrant vigilantes on the streets of some English towns, of “creating fear” but did not go as far as Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, who accused him of being an “outright racist”. Speaking of Thomas’s masked gangs, he said: “I mean that’s not Britain. That’s not what we want to see in people’s communities. There’s legitimate concerns about issues, and then there is intimidation – and that is intimidation,” he said. The prime minister also addressed political funding, which has been in the spotlight since Reform UK received two record-breaking £36m donations from cryptocurrency billionaires, saying that – contrary to reports – he would not rule out a domestic donations cap. “You know I think we do need to continue to have a cross-party discussion about how do we uphold trust in politics? How do we not give the impression that politics can be bought and that people are, if you like, unduly influenced?” He was also open to looking at election spending limits, he said, which are now being examined by the Electoral Commission, adding that he has “real concerns” about crypto-fuelled politics. An emotional Burnham revealed that the death of his father, Roy, last week had made him more determined to deliver. “I’m in this job for what I can do for people, not for what it can do for me … to make the changes that my dad, for instance, long pushed me to make,” he said. “It’s been a hard thing, if I’m honest, coming into this position in the last three months when I also knew in my heart that I was starting this journey as my dad was ending his. “Although that’s hard, and I’m not seeking sympathy in saying it, I say it because the coming together of those two things increases my determination to make a difference on the things that I’ve long said I want to fix.” With political courage expected to be a focus of his speech to Labour’s conference in Liverpool, Burnham said he was willing to be honest with the public about what needed to happen, even if it was difficult to hear. “I think the public want to see, number one, honesty about things. So not spin or putting things a certain way that’s self-serving. They want honesty, and then they want, I think, difficult but real decisions,” said Burnham. “Not difficult decisions and making a fetish out of that, but actually grasping nettles and then moving things forward. I don’t think politics has been prepared to do that enough in recent times.” Burnham criticised previous governments for failing to tackle difficult issues such as social care, housing supply and youth unemployment, saying longer-term reform was needed because there were no “easy or quick wins”. He revealed there would be a new help-to-buy scheme aimed at giving first-time buyers who cannot rely on the “bank of mum and dad” the keys to their own home. It will be funded by reallocating existing budgets, although it is unclear which ones, rather than through extra borrowing. Burnham also said he wanted to deliver significant progress on social care reform – a manifesto commitment – before the next election. “Who is going to do something to actually make it real? I’m saying to you that I am going to address this directly.”

title: Andy Burnham announces new homes scheme for first-time buyers
summary: Exclusive: Policy initiative for England will help more young people on to property ladder, prime minister tells Guardian
text: A new help-to-buy scheme aimed at giving first-time buyers who cannot rely on the “bank of mum and dad” is to be introduced in a big policy announcement by Andy Burnham. The programme, called “Your first home”, is intended to help buyers in England who have a regular income but have been unable to save for a large deposit or don’t have financial support from their family. Under the scheme, first-time buyers will get a 20% equity loan to help them buy a new-build home, with an initial interest free period and a requirement of a minimum deposit of just 2.5%. Household income caps and a deposit cap will be introduced to exclude those on the biggest salaries and with big savings pots, with the scheme targeted at those who may struggle to buy a home on their own. Price caps will ensure people can only buy modest houses. In an interview with the Guardian on the eve of Labour’s party conference in Liverpool, the prime minister said: “Too many young people are struggling with housing, with many giving up hope on ever having a home to call their own. “So we are going to help more first-time buyers on to the housing ladder, especially those who can’t call on the bank of mum and dad. “‘Your first home’ will get them the keys to their own front door, and give builders the confidence to deliver the high-quality new homes the country needs.” Burnham also unveiled plans to strengthen the powers of local leaders to take over long-term empty and derelict homes, reversing changes made by the Conservatives. Housing ministers and officials under Keir Starmer’s government argued for a new version of help to buy but were ultimately overridden by then chancellor, Rachel Reeves, who wanted to focus more on boosting housing supply. Some changes have been made to George Osborne’s original scheme, under which 387,000 people were supported, after concerns it was targeted at those who would have got on the housing ladder anyway and contributed to soaring house prices. “We think some adjustments needed to be made to it to make it focus on the people who really need support, and I think our scheme does that,” Burnham said. Officials said the programme, which will be announced by John Healey in the budget and open for registration by the end of 2026, would be funded by reprioritising existing government budgets. It was not immediately clear whether the money would come from funding already earmarked for housebuilding, or would mean cuts elsewhere. Developers will pay a fee related to property values to participate, which will contribute to its running costs. Burnham denied the scheme would just push up house prices even higher by driving up demand, saying that the government would also make sure more homes were built across the board. “No, it’s also about making sure that we are building more homes across the board … We are working actually to increase supply of housing, which also helps in terms of not pushing prices up,” he said. However, Angela Rayner, the housing secretary, acknowledged last weekend that there was only a “slim chance” the government would meet its target of building 1.5m homes in England by the next election. In 2013, George Osborne announced the first help-to-buy scheme, offering taxpayer-backed loans to reduce the deposit buyers would need. Later that year, he launched a second version. Both applied to homes worth up to £600,000, and by 2014-15, they supported about a fifth of first-time buyer purchases. The schemes proved popular, but were criticised for failing to help those who needed them most. In 2020, a further iteration of the scheme allowed buyers to borrow up to 20% of a new-build property’s value, or 40% in London, but was no longer available to movers and was subject to new regional caps on prices. Help to buy represented “very high value for money”, according to a government review, which calculated it provided £25bn of social value to the UK in the last financial year, despite criticisms over cost and impact. The government will also update empty dwelling management orders (Edmos) to allow councils to make more than 300,000 dwellings classed as “long-term empty” available to provide housing for families in need. The period a property must be empty before it becomes eligible for an Edmo will be reduced from two years to six months, to prevent homes from falling into serious disrepair and accelerating their return to use. Local authorities will no longer face the same evidential requirements to provide to the residential property tribunal, simplifying the process and empowering empty homes officers to act more decisively and with greater speed.

title: Ranulph Fiennes’ stepson appeals for funds to ‘locate and safeguard’ the explorer
summary: Alexander Millington-Cotes is concerned for welfare of the 82-year-old, who hasn’t been seen in public for two years
text: The stepson of Sir Ranulph Fiennes has launched a crowdfunder to pay for “specialist legal advice” in an attempt to locate the explorer, who hasn’t been seen in public for more than two years. Alexander Millington-Cotes, 31, has set a target of £55,000 for the fundraiser, to enable him to instruct lawyers to “locate and safeguard” Fiennes. Millington-Cotes’ mother, Louise, from whom he is estranged, has lasting power of attorney in relation to Fiennes’ care, which her son wants to see revoked. Friends and family are growing increasingly concerned for the welfare of the renowned expedition leader, who is 82 and has Parkinson’s disease. It is understood that Louise, Fiennes’ second wife, has installed him in a succession of care homes where he has not been allowed to receive visitors. According to the Telegraph, the former soldier had previously spent time in a care home in Wales under a pseudonym. It reported a watchdog had concluded his living arrangements amounted to a deprivation of his liberty because his wife had failed to ensure adequate legal safeguards were in place. The newspaper also said that Fiennes, widely considered the world’s greatest living explorer, had spent time in another care home in London, where visitors were apparently asked to sign non-disclosure agreements by Louise, 59, before being allowed to see him. Arabella McIntyre-Brown, sister of Fiennes’ late first wife, Ginny, said she was so concerned about his welfare that she checked into the London home for a week in an attempt to speak to him. She told the Telegraph that he expressed a wish to see his friends. Millington-Cotes’ crowdfunder had raised almost £3,000 on Saturday afternoon. He told supporters: “Ran has spent his entire life pushing boundaries for others and representing the best of human endurance. Now, he needs us to fight for him.” He added that donations would cover “specialist legal representation and advice”, court fees and the cost of “determining [Fiennes’] exact location, to be shared with the relevant authorities”. Millington-Cotes said he had a difficult relationship with his mother, who told him he was unwelcome at the family home two years ago. About this time, Fiennes, the first person to cross Antarctica on foot, failed to appear at a gala evening organised in his honour at the Royal Geographical Society in Kensington, west London. Instead, he delivered a brief, prerecorded message from home, saying he was “not well enough” to attend in person. He has not been seen publicly since. Millington-Cotes alleged that he had been forced to visit his stepfather in secret after the breakdown of his relationship with his mother. “Since being asked to leave the family home and not come back, I can only imagine the amplification of Ran’s difficulties and isolation,” he said. “His isolation would consist of being effectively annexed in the other end of the house, with relatively minimal contact. “I remember him gleaming the occasional times I would appear unannounced with some sweet treats, which I’d had to haul with me as I climbed over the seven-foot industrial entrance gate. “The last time I saw Ran was when he whisked me away while I was walking up the drive on one of my infrequent visits, sadly neither him or I realised that it may be the last time we’d see and hug one another. “This is the moment he told me he was proud of me, a sweet moment in my memory.” He said that, over the past two years, he had “tried multiple avenues” in an effort to locate his stepfather, whom his mother married in 2005. Ginny, to whom Fiennes was married for 34 years, had died of cancer the previous year. Louise gave birth to a daughter, Elizabeth, in 2006, Fiennes’ only biological child. While Millington-Cotes described his stepfather as “a man of immense heart, kindness, and selflessness who supported me for years”, he said his strained relationship with Louise had caused him “great pain and distress”. “Upon learning from other friends and family that Ran was considered missing, I put aside my own pain and immediately felt anger,” he said. “Anger that similar experiences I’d had were now being cast on to Ran. A man for as long as I could remember was completely selfless, kind and abided by an excellent moral code.” He added that he had visited various care homes hoping to find Fiennes “to have a simple conversation with him, or to be able to take him for a brief coffee”, but had so far been unsuccessful and had “left with a feeling of dismay and a slightly emptier heart”. Millington-Cotes said that any excess funds would be donated to Marie Curie and the British Heart Foundation, favoured charities of Fiennes.

title: US strikes on Ecuadorian fishing boats raise humanitarian concerns but Trump admin not wavering
summary: Attorney says fishers ‘losing their livelihoods’, but Marco Rubio maintains US still willing to ‘blow up ships if need be’
text: While the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, was being decorated in Quito by Ecuador’s president for “helping to promote peace in the region”, 10 Ecuadorian fishers whose boat had been blown up by US forces were adrift in the eastern Pacific. On 8 September, a day before Rubio arrived, a US patrol vessel intercepted the fishing boat Don Rufo in international waters near Ecuador. “The gringos were all armed as if they were going to war,” said the boat’s captain, Mero Calderón, 50. “I tried to show them our catch to prove that we were there working, but they wouldn’t listen,” he added. “They brought two huge bombs aboard, took us to their ship, handcuffed and blindfolded us, and blew our boat to pieces,” said Calderón, who along with five other fishers, was handed over to local authorities. But another 10 crew members were fishing farther out to sea in a smaller boat that was not equipped to make it back to shore. The Ecuadorian navy only rescued them on 10 September, when Rubio was already in Peru preparing to return to the US. US Southern Command posted an edited 14-second video of the operation and said “intelligence confirmed” that the vessel was being used by a gang as a “floating refuelling station” for speedboats allegedly carrying drugs – which the fishers deny. It was one of eight operations involving Ecuadorian boats in just more than two weeks – the latest on 16 September – to follow the same pattern. Unlike the nearly 70 US airstrikes in the Pacific and Caribbean that have killed 234 people since last year, crews were removed before the vessels were sunk. Also, rather than unilateral US attacks, the new wave of operations has the open support of Ecuador’s far-right president, Daniel Noboa, who is calling them “joint operations”. Donald Trump has compared the drug trafficking operations to the campaign against the Islamic state. “Like ISIS, they should be killed, exiled or detained as enemy combatants without the possibility of release, which is what we’re doing,” Trump said on Tuesday. Some analysts see the shift as an indication that the US’s military strategy against drug trafficking in Latin America has entered a new phase. “Noboa has offered Ecuador as a ‘laboratory’ for the implementation of this new phase,” said Will Freeman, a fellow for Latin America studies at the Council on Foreign Relations. Although Ecuador does not produce cocaine like neighbouring Colombia and Peru, over the past decade it has become a major trafficking hub because of its access to the Pacific, including the area where the attacks on boats have been taking place. Noboa has responded with a controversial “iron-fist” approach to the gangs, issuing repeated states of emergency and expanding the role of the armed forces. This crackdown however has done little to reduce violence, and instead has eroded human rights. The most notable example of human rights abuse came last year in the case of the “Guayaquil Four”, the forced disappearance of four Afro-Ecuadorian boys between the age of 11 and 15. All four boys were found dead, there bodies charred and dismembered. Despite pushback from voters, Noboa signed an agreement with the White House authorising joint operations and granting US military personnel involved in counter-narcotics operations immunity from criminal prosecution. The operations have also extended to land, with US troops taking part in raids last Thursday. “Noboa is interested in the optics of a very lethal crackdown and in making Ecuador a place where the Trump administration can refine those methods and show them off,” said Freeman, who has also reported on the boat attacks in Ecuador for the New Yorker magazine. Trump has pressured Latin American presidents to join an anti-drug cartel coalition he created called Shield of the Americas. With Peru and Colombia recently joining, the group now includes all but the few countries still governed by the left, such as Mexico and Brazil – where a far-right senator is a serious contender in October’s election. So far, the coalition’s primary goal appears to have been increasing joint operations against alleged drug traffickers. Adam Isacson, director for defence oversight at the Washington Office on Latin America, expects joint operations to expand across the region. Isacson stressed that though more people are being turned over to local authorities instead of killed, the US is “still doing the bad old stuff”. On 19 September, four people were killed in the Caribbean. As with the other airstrikes, the US has not disclosed their identities or any of the alleged evidence linking them to criminal activity. During his trip to Ecuador, Rubio said the decision on what approach to take was “a strike-by-strike or operation-by-operation determination” that depended on the threat and location of the boat, but that the US would “still blow up ships if need be”. Human rights organisations have described the airstrikes as extrajudicial killings, and a special rapporteur for the UN human rights council has concluded that there are “reasonable grounds to believe” that they constitute “crimes against humanity”. Despite Trump’s claims, available data show they have had no impact on the volume of cocaine entering the country. Journalists and human rights groups have managed to identify some of the victims, who in many cases were innocent or, when suspected of involvement in criminal activity, poor people at the bottom of trafficking networks. In Ecuador, the local NGO Permanent Committee for the Defence of Human Rights estimates that more than 220 fishers have been subjected to “violent boardings, arbitrary detentions, enforced disappearances, torture and the destruction of vessels” in this year’s US operations. None of the fishers remains in custody and, while some are still facing prosecution, many have already been acquitted for lack of evidence. “Fishers are losing their livelihoods when the US destroys the boats. Besides, if the US says the vessels were being used to refuel drug boats, why destroy the evidence?” said the committee’s lawyer, Fernando Bastías. A US Southern Command spokesperson said it conducts operations “in compliance with US and international law” and that leaving boats “intact could permit their reuse by criminal networks”. Although the US and Ecuador have celebrated the recent operations on social media, three cases from earlier this year remain unclaimed. The first was on 20 January, when the fishing vessel Fiorella disappeared with eight crew members on board; days earlier, some of them had told relatives they were being monitored by drones and by a vessel on which they said they had seen a US flag. Human rights organisations and journalists identified two more cases with similar patterns in late March, although the fishers survived. The Washington Post reported that the three cases were part of a covert CIA programme, and the agency declined to comment. A US Southern Command spokesperson said it had no knowledge of, nor were its forces “involved in the incidents described in reports involving the Fiorella”. Both the husband and brother of María Mero, 43, were aboard the Fiorella: Gabriel Aladino Mero Delgado, 44, and Jefferson Ariel Mero Cueva, 25. “Where did they take them? Do they have them in the US, in a prison somewhere? We don’t want any trouble; we just want them to send them back to us,” she told the Guardian. The families say they have spent months trying to get answers from the Ecuadorian government, so far without success. “They were fishers, not criminals. Let the great president come here to my house and see whether I have luxuries, anything that would show I’m a drug trafficker. No, because all of us here are poor, and we just want our loved ones back,” added Mero.

title: Pope Leo celebrates open-air mass before 700,000 people in Paris
summary: Crowds line Place de la Concorde on second day of pontiff’s first official papal visit to France in 18 years
text: Hundreds of thousands of people lined the Avenue des Champs-Élysées in ⁠Paris on Saturday to attend an open-air mass with Pope Leo, on the second day of his visit to France. The Vatican estimated 700,000 people turned out for the outdoor mass with the 71-year-old American pope – about 100,000 more than the number of people who had registered to attend. It took place at the Place de la Concorde, the site of bloody executions by guillotine during the French Revolution – when Louis XVI’s staunchly Catholic rule was overthrown – and now the centre of the secular republic. The choice of the site, a symbol of the French republic to many, was criticised by supporters of France’s strict legislation separating church and state in public life. But cheers rang out in the crowd as the pope thanked ‌God in his homily for the chance to ‌visit France on a whirlwind four-day, three-city tour to promote Catholicism and its teachings. It is the first official papal visit to France in 18 years. Pope Leo asked those in the crowd not to keep their faith to themselves. “Let it overflow, so that those you meet may be refreshed and their thirst satisfied,” he said. “From this beautiful city of Paris, I pray fervently that the living water of the Holy Spirit may flow throughout France.” He told Catholics that only their faith, and not material things, can provide true happiness. “Only God can fill the emptiness within us,” he said. The security zone for the event – the biggest of the papal tour – stretched about 1.4 miles (2.2km), shutting down road traffic in central Paris from the Place de la Concorde to the Arc de Triomphe and beyond. Chanting “Leo, Leo” and “Long live the pope”, crowds of people waved French and Vatican flags as the pontiff rode slowly down the grand boulevard of the Champs-Élysées aboard a popemobile – a specially designed, partly open vehicle used during public appearances. He stopped frequently along the way as babies were lifted out of the crowd and brought to him to receive a papal caress on their heads. The city centre was sealed off for the service, with helicopters circling overhead and snipers positioned on rooftops. About 14,500 police officers, gendarmes, military personnel and firefighters were deployed to the event, which was attended by 2,400 priests and deacons, and about 100 bishops. Marie-Élisabeth, a 44-year-old nun from Burgundy, told a reporter for France 24: “This event is a way for us to say loud and proud that Christians are here.” Speaking to reporters from Agence France-Presse, Sylvie Leclerc, a 51-year-old teacher, also said she and her fellow Christians want to share their fervour for their faith. “You don’t hear much from us Catholics, but now we’re going to make some noise!” she said. “But to proclaim love, peace, joy.”

title: California man charged in the killing of his ex-wife – two decades after she vanished
summary: Authorities discovered a body hidden in a home’s crawlspace in 2020, 13 years after Jill Maiorca disappeared
text: A man was recently charged in California with the killing of his ex-wife six years after her remains were discovered in a crawlspace beneath a home – and about two decades after when she went missing, according to investigators. Jeff Maiorca, 53, faces a charge of murder in the death of Jill Maiorca, who was 29 when she was killed, authorities said in discussing what could be one of the latest cases in the US to be solved with modern DNA techniques. Jill Maiorca’s disappearance was reported in the southern California city of Big Bear Lake in 2007, a statement from the local San Bernardino county sheriff’s department said. The path to finding Jill Maiorca then began in late October 2020, when San Bernardino sheriff’s deputies received a call to investigate “a suspicious discovery in the crawlspace under [a] residence” in Big Bear Lake. The deputies and members of the Big Bear fire department ultimately located human remains in that crawlspace. Although the remains couldn’t immediately be identified, an autopsy determined the manner of death in the case was homicide, the San Bernardino sheriff’s office statement said. The agency said its cold homicide case team in 2023 then submitted the unidentified remains for additional investigative DNA analysis. Such analysis determined the remains were those of Jill Maiorca, according to the sheriff’s office. The sheriff’s office also said that its investigators had come to consider Jeff Maiorca – who had been Jill’s husband and had filed to divorce her in 2004, court records showed – as a suspect. Citing unspecified evidence, the sheriff’s office’s statement asserted that Jill Maiorca had been murdered in November 2006. Her remains were then concealed – “without the homeowner’s knowledge” – beneath the residence where they were later discovered, the sheriff’s office said. The agency did not elaborate on the hiding of Jill Maiorca’s body. Business records reviewed by the Guardian link Jeff Maiorca to a heating, ventilation and air conditioning company. Other records showed his divorce from Jill Maiorca was classified as one involving children. The San Bernardino sheriff’s office said it arrested Maiorca on Monday. He was formally charged with murder as well as with the use of a deadly weapon, and he had an initial hearing on Wednesday in San Bernardino county superior court, as NBC News first reported. Jeff Maiorca remained in custody on Saturday at the High Desert jail in Adelanto, California, records indicated. Multiple media outlets reported that he was being held there without bail, and he was tentatively scheduled to appear in court again on 12 October.

title: Jill Dando murder: technological advances allow police to review CCTV 27 years later
summary: BBC broadcaster was shot in 1999 in case detectives have previously said may never be solved
text: Technological advances are allowing police to review old CCTV footage in the unsolved murder of the BBC broadcaster Jill Dando, Scotland Yard has revealed. Advances in CCTV enhancement technology have allowed detectives to return to 27-year-old footage of Putney Bridge Underground station, Scotland Yard said. But detectives stressed that the review was part of existing inquiries – not a new investigation. The former Crimewatch presenter was 37 years old when she was shot and killed outside her home in Fulham, west London, on 26 April 1999. An unidentified person, referred to as “Man X”, was captured on camera near Putney Bridge station – about a mile from Dando’s home – shortly after the attack. A driver had seen a man “running for his life” on Fulham Palace Road around the time of the shooting, the Mirror reported. She later picked out Man X in the station CCTV as the person who had been sprinting. A Met spokesperson said: “In the 27 years since Jill Dando’s murder, the investigation has been subject to numerous reviews, aiming to identify whether matters could be progressed with advances in technology and forensics. “Recent advancements in CCTV enhancement technology have provided investigators with the opportunity to re-examine original footage from Putney Bridge train station. “The review of CCTV footage forms part of ongoing inquiries and should not be interpreted as a significant line of inquiry nor as a new investigation being opened on this matter.” Outside her work on Crimewatch, Dando was also seen during the 1980s and 1990s on BBC shows including travel show Holiday and The Antiques Inspectors. She began as a reporter at her local paper The Weston Mercury in Weston-super-Mare, Somerset, before moving to the morning programme Breakfast Time, which later became BBC Breakfast. In 2019, the detective who led the inquiry into Dando’s murder expressed doubt the case would ever be solved. Speaking in a BBC documentary to mark 20 years since the television presenter’s shooting, Hamish Campbell said he did not think any new suspects would ever be brought to court. “Do I think somebody will come back to court? Probably not, no. Sometimes, I felt we were a day away from solving it and other times, I thought: ‘No, we’re a long way away’. Senior officers were asking: ‘What are the likelihoods of this case being resolved?’ “We had over 2,000 people named as potential suspects or responsible. Some actions to trace and eliminate one person might take a day. One action might take two weeks. But there’s thousands of them and that’s the issue of managing stranger homicides.”

title: Pennsylvania measles outbreak spreads, with 55 new cases reported since Wednesday
summary: Less than 1% of infected have been vaccinated, with 173 people hospitalized and four deaths so far
text: The Pennsylvania department of health (DoH) announced on Friday that 55 new measles cases had been reported in the state since Wednesday, with officials continuing efforts to contain an outbreak of the disease that has spread across dozens of counties. In a news release, the DoH said that 890 measles cases had been confirmed across 39 counties in the state so far for the year. The outbreak had resulted in 173 hospitalizations in the state and four measles-associated deaths, the statement added. State health officials said fewer than 1% of reported cases have occurred among individuals vaccinated against measles. And according to the state data, 31% of the cases are among people younger than 18. In addition to announcing that 55 new cases had been reported during a two-day period beginning on Wednesday, the DoH said it was “proactively working with residents, community organizations and healthcare providers to combat the measles outbreak … through access to fact-based information and access to the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine”. The update about the measles outbreak on Friday from Pennsylvania came after the Trump administration’s health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr – a longtime vaccine skeptic – has sought to cast doubt on deaths related to the disease in the state, writing on social media that they “may even have been altogether fabricated” for political reasons. In August, the new director of the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) ordered agency staff not to include two measles-associated deaths reported by Pennsylvania in its national tally, as the agency said it was reviewing “additional information” regarding the deaths. Pennsylvania’s Lancaster county has recorded the highest number of cases in the state for the year so far, with 359 positive cases, according to state data. State health officials said that since “the outbreak began in late April” they had “administered more than 5,300 MMR vaccinations at 165 pop-up vaccination clinics in the affected communities”. Dozens of additional vaccine clinics are also scheduled in the coming weeks and months, based on community interest and need, they said. In total, state health center staff have administered more than 7,900 MMR vaccine doses to residents across Pennsylvania this year, according to the statement. It added that healthcare providers across the state have also seen a “surge of interest from residents seeking MMR vaccinations”. The DoH said on Friday that the “best protection against measles remains getting fully vaccinated” and that the MMR vaccine “boosts a person’s immune system and provides 97% lifetime protection”. Measles is a highly contagious virus that can cause serious health complications. The DoH said that death from measles, though rare, “occurs in one to three patients per 1,000 cases”. It had been declared eliminated from the US in 2000, but the virus has more recently spread in under-vaccinated communities. According to the CDC, measles can spread to others through coughing and sneezing – and it can live for up to two hours in an airspace after an infected person leaves an area. Symptoms usually begin seven to 14 days after infection, the CDC says. They can include high fever, cough, runny nose and red, watery eyes, followed by a rash that spreads down the body. The CDC advises that two doses of the MMR vaccine “provide the best protection against measles”. According to data from the CDC, as of 24 September more than 3,659 confirmed measles cases have been reported in the US so far for the year. For all of 2025, a total of 2,289 confirmed measles cases were reported nationwide.

title: ‘I’m not JD Vance’: the Appalachia memoir author running for Congress
summary: Beth Macy, author of Dopesick, is drawing on her reporting experience to win Virginia voters in a longtime Republican district
text: Virginia’s sixth congressional district has been in Republican hands for over 33 years, but Beth Macy, a longtime reporter with the Roanoke Times and author of Dopesick, a powerful account of the opioid crisis that swept through Appalachia two decades ago, has a plan to change that. The plan, drawing on her experience as a reporter, is to canvass the district in the mountainous west of the state, knocking on doors, going to food pantries, meeting with veterans. It’s what any political hopeful might do, but with a twist: Macy carries her reporter’s notebook and jots down the good stories she’s been told. One came at a recent fundraiser: two couples whose land had been in the family for 300 years approached Macy to tell her that a datacenter had been proposed on land next door. Macy does an intro to camera: “Hey I’m Beth and I’m running for Congress.” Then they tell their stories that then get posted on social media. “It’s been really effective because it show the real issues that people care about and people who are independent or moderate Republican who are maybe changing their mind and starting to cross over …” she says. “If it’s enough, I don’t know.” Macy has challenged Republican congressman Ben Cline, who was elected by nearly 30 points in 2024, to three debates ahead of November’s vote. Cline agreed to participate in three, but then appeared to limit them to something less – candidate forums. Macy told her former paper that amounted to “a chicken-you-know-what response”. Many races in this cycle have been upended or at least complicated by the datacenter debate. Three hours to the north-east of Roanoke lies Loudon county, the data processing heart of the US. But this is farm county, typically Republican, and farmers are being buffeted by high diesel prices and fertilizer costs as well as the loss of immigrant workers. A sign on a country road to Glasgow, 30 miles north of Roanoke, read: “Farmers for Beth Macy: Protect Family Farms, Stop Data Centers.” Democrats hope Macy can pull of an upset win despite Virginia’s state supreme court striking down a voter-approved re-districting plan that would have helped the party. The decision has energized Democrats locally and with the political mood across the US turning against incumbents – but especially Republicans – Macy could pull it off. In Macy’s view, there is a more than a notional parallel between the opioid crisis and the data center issue. In the first, the public were told Oxycontin prescribed for pain relief was not addictive, only to find it was. In the second, data centers may be being foisted on the public without sufficient knowledge of their consequences to water and electricity supplies. “It’s the idea that this thing was done to people without their knowledge,” Macy says, pointing to the construction of a multi-building data center campus on a 312-acre site in Botetourt county, Virginia. “Only relatively recently did the people of Botetourt even find out they were doing it. “It’s just like when Purdue Pharma told doctors and conned congressmen with nice checks that their drug wasn’t addictive. It’s the same thing … they occluded the fact of the matter and how people were going to be hurt.” The opioid crisis, she points out, remained hidden from view for years because of the shame that addicts and their families carry, but the data center issue now blowing up in the faces of politicians from both political parties has changed the narrative. The amount of water that the Botetourt data center, codenamed “Project Raspberry”, would require only came to light after Henri Gendreau, founder of the Virginia-based news publication the Roanoke Rambler filed a public records request under the Virginia Freedom of Information Act (VFOIA). Macy, 62, has published five books: Factory Man, about a furniture factory owner in rural Virginia: Truevine, about two Black brothers who were kidnapped and forced to perform in circus freak shows during the Jim Crow era; Dopesick, which later became a Hulu series; Raising Lazarus about the opioid crisis aftermath; and, last year, Paper Girl, a memoir about her Ohio childhood and the seeds of rising political division. That has brought a natural – though to her unwelcome – comparisons to Donald Trump’s vice-president JD Vance, whose 2016 memoir Hillbilly Elegy traced his upbringing and his mother’s heroin addiction in Ohio and became a launch pad for his political career. “Oh my God,” Macy exclaims, “I hate that comparison. I’m my own person, I’m not JD Vance. I’m 20 years older than he is. It’s not the exact same part of Ohio. He grew up with addiction and poverty. Okay, I’ll take that. Tough grandma, I’ll take that. But he mocked poor people for being poor and said it was a lack of masculinity and a lack of thrift. I would never blame poor people for their poverty.” In Paper Girl, Macy describes how she received a Pell Grant to go to Bowling Green state university, Hollins university and a fellowship in journalism at Harvard, much as Vance received a grant under the GI Bill to attend Ohio State and later a scholarship to attend Yale. “What I’ve tried to do is amplify the voices of people like me who don’t grow up with everything handed to them. He got out of that, went to Yale, became a venture capitalist, a senator and now the vice president, and now wants to yank up the ladder behind him,” Macy contends. Running as a Democrat in rural Virginia is of course very different from running under the same banner in a naturally blue or toss-up purple district. One of the hurdles a Democrat candidate running in a red district must address is the shortcomings of Biden administration policies. Macy acknowledges that Democrats the last time screwed up the border. “It was wide open and they sent Kamala [Harris] down there, or she was supposed to,” she said. Democrats, she says, have to talk about what they got wrong. She mentions the North American Free Trade Agreement (Nafta) under Bill Clinton and the Communications Decency Act of 1996 that immunized websites and social media networks from responsibility for what is posted online. “We’ve got to talk about that stuff,” she says. “and we haven’t renewed immigration since 1996. We’ve got to have a solid H-2A program (for temporary or seasonal agricultural jobs) for folks. I’ve done a lot of solid reporting on tobacco workers who would love to go home once a year.” One aspect of Macy’s platform is to recognize that white-collar jobs filled typically by indebted college graduates are likely to disappear with AI, while the market for blue-collar or trades jobs will increase. “I think the trades are going to become highly coveted and you’re going to see people who might have gone to college or come from wealthier families go after the trade jobs. So I’m calling for free community college, and I think Google or all these data center companies should be paying for that.” Macy has called for a moratorium on data centers until “some kind” of AI czar can be found “to protect our jobs, our land, our electricity, our water, because it’s moving so fast now it’s endangering all of us.” Macy recently received an endorsement from the AFL-CIO, the largest federation of labor unions in the US. She may be slowly opening the door in Virginia that has been closed to a Democrat for decades. At a fundraiser on a horse ranch – a largely favorable crowd – Macy says she believes Virginia voters who might have been resistant are loosening up. “They’re feeling the pain and they’re getting to know me a little bit ... I know what it’s like to worry that the electricity is going to get cut off, or might go hungry and eat government cheese, or my grandmother accepting food stamps.”

title: ‘Traffic is going to get a lot worse’: San Francisco Bay Area faces potential death spiral of transit system
summary: A marvel of engineering and a model of sustainability, Bart has been financially distressed since the Covid pandemic
text: A marvel of engineering and a model of sustainable public transportation, the San Francisco Bay Area’s transit system, financially distressed after years of declined ridership, is now staring down a fiscal cliff – and a potential death spiral that would have massive repercussions for everyone in the globally influential metropolis. As soon as early 2027, Bay Area Rapid Transit could be forced to close as many as 15 stations, reduce frequency of service by 63%, increase the cost of rides and parking fees by 30% and end all service at 9pm. If service becomes less frequent and more expensive, there will be fewer commuters, less fare revenue and a downward cascade of financial austerity with ripple effects for all Bay Area residents, not just those who use public transit regularly. In a doomsday scenario, the whole system could be deemed unsafe and shut down. The transit system, known locally as Bart, has served the Bay Area for more than five decades, connecting 50 stations in five counties. Given the region’s sprawling geography, formed around a large body of water, the area’s freeways and bridges are notoriously gridlocked. With 131 miles (210km) of track linking cities like San Francisco and Oakland with the wider south and east bay regions, Bart allows commuters to bypass congested roads and hefty bridge tolls. Bart is also a feat of engineering. Its underwater tunnel, known as the transbay tube, sits 135ft (41 meters) beneath the chilly waters of the San Francisco Bay. It was designed with flexible joints to absorb the seismic activity of the region’s two active faultlines, and emerged from the 1989 earthquake unscathed. Bart is a model of self-sufficient funding, and was the first US transit system made fully accessible for people with disabilities. At its high point in 2016, the agency boasted 435,000 riders each weekday and brought in nearly half a billion dollars annually. But since the pandemic, it has struggled to regain enough riders to sustain its funding model. Now its future is riding on voters approving a 0.5% sales tax across four Bay Area counties and a 1% sales tax in San Francisco. The regional transit measure would generate approximately $1bn annually to fund the four largest transit operators for 14 years. For voters in San Francisco, it is one of two transit taxes on the November ballot. “Losing Bart destroys the Bay Area economy,” said Jeffrey Tumlin, former head of the San Francisco Municipal Transportation Agency (SFMTA), now on a sabbatical. “All of the large Bay Area technology companies and the business associations that represent them understand that there’s no Bay Area tech economy without Bart.” ‘Traffic is going to get a lot worse’ On a Wednesday morning, the yellow line from Antioch bustles with commuters relaxing as they glide past the gridlock. Out the window, the highway is already choked with cars crawling along into Oakland, Berkeley, San Francisco and other hubs for work and study in a region home to more than 7.5 million people “Sometimes I sit here on Bart and just look out the window and laugh – ha, ha, ha! – at the people in traffic,” said Carissa Spencer, an executive assistant for Airbnb in her 40s who takes Bart almost daily from Antioch to downtown San Francisco. The prospect of losing this rail line and ending up in traffic seems like a cruel joke. “It just is shocking to me that that’s how we operate in the United States of America in 2026, where people have to have a car to be able to survive,” she said. As slow as traffic is today, it could more than double if voters reject the ballot measure. Riding the red and yellow Bart lines during the early morning commute, the Guardian spoke with families and commuters from the outer reaches of the Bay Area who rely on the system to take them to schools, and jobs at banks, universities, hospitals, tech companies and fast-food chains. Unlike transit systems in other world-class cities that receive significant government funding, Bart has generated 60%-70% of its operating revenue through passenger fares, making it uniquely self-sustaining – and uniquely exposed to the low ridership during the pandemic and the Bay Area’s nation-leading shift to remote and hybrid work. To lure back riders, the agency upgraded safety, cleaning, restrooms, fare gates and payment systems, while shortening trains, retiring legacy cars, re-aligning schedules for off-peak demand and syncing operations regionally. Despite multiday delays due to old equipment overheating earlier this month and the rocky rollout of the new Clipper 2.0 card, Bart has a 95% customer on time performance and record high rider satisfaction. David, 42, a surgeon taking Bart’s red line to work at dawn, supports the ballot measure, but would like to see big companies in the region who benefit from Bart to step up: “I think that they should pay some portion of the subsidy for our transportation to work for them,” he said. The economic, climate and equity stakes of both measures failing at the ballot box couldn’t be higher. A new report by the San Francisco Bay Area Planning and Urban Research Association (Spur), which spearheaded the regional transit measure, paints the bleakest picture yet: traffic delays on the Bay Bridge and other chokepoints would more than double during peak hours. “Traffic is going to get a lot worse and I think this is a best-case scenario,” said Laura Tolkoff, the transportation policy director at Spur and author of the report. The transit system is largely what keeps the road systems moving, and people who cannot switch to driving, including low-income workers and people with disabilities, will be hit hardest. Alvina, 70, takes Bart every day from Oakland to her job at McDonald’s in Lafayette. If Bart goes down, she would use Uber, she said in Spanish, which would significantly cut into her hourly wage. On the yellow line between Oakland and Antioch, the Guardian spoke with a half dozen riders who made decisions about buying homes or working certain jobs because of the area’s relative affordability and proximity to the Bart. Now that segment of rail could be gutted. Regina, 34, who studies risk for JP Morgan Chase, said she and her husband bought a house in Antioch three months ago because her job required her to commute into the office every day and she hates driving: “The biggest reason why I moved out here is knowing that there was a Bart line.” Commuters displaced from transit to cars would potentially face multiple bottlenecks and have to drive an additional 10 miles (16km) each way to reach an open station, according to Spur estimates. They would also incur an estimated $3,280 per year in additional transportation expenses – the sales tax, Spur estimated, will cost 3% of that. Campaigning for Bart On a Friday evening in San Francisco’s Sunset district, nearly three miles away from the closest Bart station, a group of young men with signs, clipboards and polling data went door-knocking in search of persuadable voters. Anki, a 33-year-old software engineer, has spent months walking up to strangers at bus stops, farmers’ markets and protests to pitch them on approving the ballot measures. Motivated by fear of how the cuts will affect him personally and the region as a whole, he gathered a record 2,501 signatures to get the measures on this November’s ballot. Though polling looks promising, it is still within the margin of error, and he plans to be out canvassing until November in early El Niño rains if he has to. “We refuse to wake up in January to creeping highways and choking bridges; to abandoned bus routes and boarded up Bart stations,” Anki said in a speech launching the final campaign push to save public transit. “We will not stand clear of the doors.” • This story was amended on 26 September 2026. An earlier version said Bay Area Rapid Transit’s future was riding on a half-cent sales tax across four Bay Area counties and a $0.01 sales tax in San Francisco; this should have said a 0.5% sales tax across the four counties and a 1% sales tax in San Francisco.

title: New research finds 485 chemicals in US pesticide products linked to breast cancer
summary: Paper raises questions about safety of food and other products as early onset breast cancer rates surge worldwide
text: New research has identified at least 485 chemicals used in US pesticide products that are linked to breast cancer, raising questions about the safety of food and other products at a time when early onset breast cancer rates are surging worldwide. The new peer-reviewed paper, published in Environmental Health Perspectives, a top journal from the American Chemical Society, highlights what public health advocates say are a range of deficiencies in how US pesticides are regulated. The review includes active pesticide ingredients, but also hundreds of so-called “inert”, or inactive, ingredients that typically do not undergo a thorough safety review. The Environmental Protection Agency only considers each pesticide ingredient’s individual health risks, and does not consider the entire pesticide formula, or exposure to multiple pesticides. The chemicals are not just found in pesticides used on crops, but also in lice treatments applied to children’s scalps, home lawn fertilizers, and flea and tick treatments. “Adding these exposures up gets pretty consequential and concerning,” said Jenny Kay, a report co-author with the Silent Spring Institute non-profit. “We wanted to bring more attention to the pesticides in different products.” Beside skin cancers, breast cancer is the most commonly diagnosed cancer in the US. Incidence rates for breast cancer have notably increased by 1% per year, according to the American Cancer Society, and that rise has actually been slightly faster in women younger than 50 (1.4%). Pesticide use has also increased in recent years, as federal health data via the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) shows 84 of these specific breast cancer-linked chemicals are present in the general population. But that number, scientists say, is an undercount because it does not track most of the compounds the Silent Spring Institute identified. The pesticide review is part of a broader systematic effort by the institute to identify where in the economy, and across everyday life, people are exposed to breast cancer-linked chemicals. It identified about 500 in common consumer goods, and 462 in drinking water. Only about 145 of the pesticide chemicals identified were registered with the EPA as active ingredients, meaning that the chemical industry is either using the inert status to avoid health scrutiny, or exploiting other loopholes. Inactive, or inert, ingredients are usually added as surfactants or penetrating agents that help disperse the active ingredients or make them more absorbable. About 4,000 inert ingredients are approved for use by the EPA, among them Pfas “forever chemicals”. They are often added to make the pesticide more toxic to a living organism. “They are not biologically inert, they are just called inert because they do not target the pest,” Kay said. In other words, the body does not distinguish between inert and active ingredients, and inactive substances are no less of a danger to human health. “It is a regulatory blind spot,” Kay said. The EPA in 2023 rejected a legal petition to start more stringently reviewing inert ingredients. Kay said another problem lies in hormone-disrupting chemicals causing disease at lower levels of exposure, but not higher. This “non-monotonic dose response” has led the EPA to dismiss some chemicals’ risks, and ignore that they can cause cancer at low levels. The top officials in the EPA’s pesticide and chemical safety offices are former industry lobbyists. The pesticide office in particular has been viewed as being heavily infiltrated by industry, and subjected to its influence. “I’m not in the head of EPA scientists, but I do worry a lot about industry pressure and the revolving door between EPA and industry employees because all of that factors into the way the EPA considers and regulates chemicals,” Kay said. The Silent Spring Institute called for an expansion of California’s Proposition 65, which requires warnings for chemicals known to cause cancer or reproductive harm. The study identified 16 pesticides that are not listed under Prop 65, and the authors say adding these chemicals could discourage companies from using them. People can protect themselves by buying organic produce, or products that have not been treated with pesticides, as much as possible. If that’s not possible, Consumer Reports has an easy-to-use guide on which fruits and vegetables typically have the highest levels of pesticide residues on them. Among those are blueberries, watermelon, kale and green beans. A recent report found about 25% of the nation’s water intake and around 675,000 wells draw water contaminated with dangerous levels of atrazine, a hormone disrupting chemical linked to breast cancer. Water-filtration systems can filter pesticides from water, and though no system is perfect, activated carbon and reverse osmosis generally do the best job.

title: White House blocks CNN from Air Force One in latest escalation with news media
summary: Outlet had been scheduled to fly with Donald Trump to Tennessee for a college football game, network said Friday
text: The White House has blocked CNN from traveling aboard Air Force One on Saturday, impeding its TV press pool duties in the latest escalation of the administration’s battle with the news media. CNN had been scheduled to fly with Donald Trump to Tennessee for a college football game, the network said on Friday. The White House confirmed CNN’s exclusion when it did not list the network on guidance sent to the press corps regarding Trump’s schedule for Saturday. CNN’s exclusion from Air Force One was first reported by the Washington Post. The White House did not immediately return the Guardian’s request for comment. The incident comes a week after Trump, a vocal critic of what he deems the “fake news media”, revoked White House access for CNN, Politico, and MS Now, citing unfavorable reports about his presidency. The Republican president published a post about the topic on his Truth Social platform early on Saturday which read: “Why should perpetrators of FAKE NEWS … be allowed access to a very sacred place, the White House? Despite my big Election Win, almost 100% of ‘TRUMP’ coverage is negative, and has been for years!” The post singled out CNN and MS Now, referring to the latter as MSDNC, which combined the outlet’s name with the Democratic National Committee. He published it days after a recent Reuters/Ipsos poll found Trump’s overall public approval rating to be at 32%, an all-time low. The extraordinary access revocation prompted swift backlash from the White House press pool, who suspended their video coverage of Trump in protest. The press pool is a rotating group of journalists charged with covering presidential travel and disseminating written and multimedia reports to news outlets that may not be present at a given White House event. Since the beginning of Trump’s second administration in 2025, the White House has decided which outlets cover the president via the pool each day, a task previously coordinated by the White House Correspondents’ Association. In a joint statement Monday, the White House television pool said: “The public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government. No administration should restrict a news organization because it objects to its reporting.” In a subsequent lawsuit, CNN, MS Now and Politico argued the White House ban was a violation of the first amendment. Meanwhile, the Department of Justice’s attorneys suggested the ban was in the interest of national security, pointing at media reports involving “sensitive” and “classified” information. The US district judge Timothy Kelly sided with the outlets, ordering the Trump administration to restore their White House access. CNN, MS Now and Politico’s journalists sought to enter the White House on Thursday morning, but were not granted entry until midday. Hours later, CNN’s editorial team along with an MS Now reporter were blocked from covering the state dinner commemorating Chinese president Xi Jinping’s visit.
