title: Ex-American Idol contestant told lover he dreamed of killing wife, murder trial hears
summary: Alleigha Botner tells court Caleb Flynn, charged with murder of wife Ashley Flynn, sent her AI love songs
text: The Ohio former pastor and American Idol contestant accused of fatally shooting his wife fantasized to his then lover about killing his spouse and sent her AI-generated love songs, according to evidence presented at trial this week. Caleb Flynn, 40, is on trial for aggravated murder in connection with the 16 February shooting death of Ashley Flynn. He also is charged with two counts of felonious assault and three counts of tampering with evidence, according to a March indictment. Flynn has pleaded not guilty to the charges. Prosecutors say Flynn – motivated by a desire to be with his girlfriend, Alleigha Botner – shot his sleeping wife twice in the back of the head. He allegedly altered the crime scene to look like a deadly home invasion. Flynn’s defense team has acknowledged the affair, but said at trial it does not make him a murderer. “A man can make selfish decisions without committing a crime,” defense attorney Emily Smith said. Investigators recovered songs from Flynn’s phone, where he reflected on his friendship with Botner evolving into a romantic relationship. “That first time I saw you the room disappeared, love at first sight even though I was scared,” a voice sang in a style reminiscent of Christian rock, according to video broadcast by Court TV. “Life is now empty, since the moment I lost you,” the song ended. A second version with similar lyrics but delivered in a somber tone was also played to the court. Botner was 20 when she met Flynn at their church, Botner testified. Flynn was 36 or 37 at the time. “At first it was: I want her dead. I wish she was gone. And then it was: if I could kill her and not go to jail, I would. And one night, he was up really late – he told me he was thinking about ways to kill her,” Botner, now 24, said. Flynn also repeatedly said he hated his wife in several texts to Botner. During an August 2025 cruise to celebrate the married couple’s 15th wedding anniversary, Ashley Flynn found texts her husband had sent to Botner. She tried to arrange a coffee meet-up with Botner. Botner avoided the conversation, saying she was busy. In January, Botner gave Caleb Flynn an ultimatum: leave your wife or it’s over. At about this time, Flynn sent her the AI-generated songs. On 14 February, two days before Ashley was shot, Botner testified that Flynn said he was getting a divorce and would finally be free of his wife, to which Botner said she did not believe him. “I told him that I don’t trust him and that I’m moving on with my life,” she said on the stand. When Ashley Flynn was found dead, her sister Kayla Keyt did not have knowledge of the affair. She told police when Caleb was arrested that they had the wrong guy. “I trusted Caleb with everything I had in me … He was completely innocent. I really believed that with all of my heart,” Keyt said. The FBI subsequently informed her of the affair. Keyt said news of the affair made the couple’s two daughters “mostly broken-hearted for mommy”. “They said she loved daddy more than anyone else in life. So why did daddy not love her as much?” she testified. Flynn appeared briefly on American Idol’s 12th season in 2013, describing music as his passion and saying his wife nudged him to go on the show. The trial, which is expected to wrap by the end of next week, will resume on Monday.

title: Trump and Chinese president Xi end summit without major agreement on AI
summary: Xi’s state visit to the US emphasized personal rapport with the US president, rather than substantial agreements to pause their respective countries’ AI arms race
text: Donald Trump and Chinese president Xi Jinping wrapped up their Washington summit on Friday, facing criticism that they had squandered an opportunity to pause their countries’ artificial intelligence (AI) arms race. The three-day state visit emphasised pageantry and personal rapport rather than substantial agreements. The US president and Xi discussed the wars in Iran and Ukraine and the status of Taiwan. Their biggest policy announcement was a modest two-month extension of a trade truce. But despite the presence of top tech executives at a White House state dinner on Thursday night, Trump and Xi failed to deliver the AI breakthrough that some experts and foreign governments had hoped for amid warnings that the technology could pose an existential threat to humanity. “It was such a layup,” said Ro Khanna, the top Democrat on the House of Representatives’ select committee on China. “If [Trump] had just said, look, we have established technical working groups and we’ve agreed to a framework that has called for DeepSeek and Moonshot and Alibaba to sit down with Anthropic and OpenAI and Gemini and with technical experts and they’re going to commit to at least a pause on any self-improving AI, he could have looked like he was a statesman taking the lead. “I believe Xi Jinping would have agreed to some of at least the technical working groups. But he [Trump] didn’t want to; he has no interest in doing that.” It was the first visit to the White House by a Chinese president in more than a decade and Xi’s second state visit to the US. Three days of pomp and circumstance culminated on Friday with Trump and Xi drinking tea. Trump said ⁠the summit ⁠had produced great strides and that “our farmers are going to be happy,” but did not provide details. The pair then went to the National Archives, where Trump and Xi looked at the original Declaration of Independence, the constitution and Bill of Rights. Trump told reporters they were comparing China’s documents to America’s founding documents. “Ours goes 250 years, which is great, and we’re proud of. Theirs goes 6,000 years. So there’s a little difference between 6,000 and 250. But we’re very proud of our 250.” On Thursday, Xi acknowledged that the US and China have the “responsibility to develop and manage AI for good” and “ensure that the development of AI is always under human control”. China aims to have next-generation smart terminals and AI agents reach more than 90% penetration by 2030. But Trump – who has repeatedly said the US must forge ahead to maintain its lead over China – appeared more focused on his push to rebrand artificial intelligence as “super intelligence”, later claiming on social media that Xi “seems to like” the term without divulging the substance of their discussions. Later Trump hosted a black-tie state dinner attended by titans of the tech industry. Bernie Sanders, an independent senator of Vermont, used social media to label a photo of Trump and Xi’s table with guests’ net worth: Elon Musk of SpaceX and Tesla ($928bn), Lisa Su of Advanced Micro Devices ($3.5bn), Jensen Huang of Nvidia ($186bn) and Tim Cook of Apple ($3.1bn). Sanders commented: “A government of, by and for the billionaire class.” But their counterparts in the Chinese tech industry were not present and there was little sign of either country making even a symbolic gesture to apply the brakes. Khanna commented: “Trump didn’t have to have some groundbreaking treaty like Reagan and Gorbachev did [on nuclear weapons]. He could have at least said, look, we’re going to have a working group of Chinese and American technologists working together to make recommendations and enforcement and verification of the labs.” Jonathan Czin, a fellow in the China Center at the Brookings Institution thinktank in Washington, agrees that an opportunity was missed. “We are in this potentially transformative moment for both countries and for the world and for technology and, instead of having a meeting that would meet the moment, you got theatre of the absurd in lieu of that,” he said. “Even going into this meeting, you’re dealing with a septuagenarian and octogenarian who may or may not have ever had first-hand contact with actually using AI and what happens with this technology rests on their two shoulders. The only thing they seemed to agree about is that neither of them wants to slow down with this technology, regardless of their actual understanding of it.” The state visit underlined the contrast between Trump’s treatment of democratic allies such as Canada and authoritarian rivals such as China. He broke from tradition to give Xi a red carpet welcome when he landed at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland. He also found time to show Xi around the White House, including a gallery wall of presidents where Joe Biden is mockingly depicted as an autopen, a construction site for his White House ballroom and a new helicopter landing pad. “He’s an expert on stone, aside from many other things, and he loves good granite,” Trump said. But the summit was somewhat overshadowed by Trump’s decision last week to bar CNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House, sparking a legal fight. On Thursday, Chinese state media were welcomed into the White House grounds even as members of America’s free press were frozen out, though later they gained entry. As in May, when Trump visited Beijing, the leaders did not hold a press conference. Czin of the Brookings Institution added: “I had very low expectations going into this meeting for anything of substance and the meeting managed to underwhelm even those low expectations. We went from the mezzanine down into the basement. In terms of the substance, it’s not clear to me what the US got out of this.” Senate Democrats also criticised the summit, arguing that Trump failed to secure meaningful concessions from Beijing on trade, security, human rights or AI. Chuck Schumer, the minority leader in the Senate, said: “As usual, Trump acts based solely on who flatters him at the moment, where the nearest photo op is, and what headline he covets. If you’re a foreign authoritarian, Trump won’t just invite you to visit America, he’ll greet you plane-side.” Trump and Xi are on track to meet twice more this year. In November, Xi will host the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, and in December the Group of 20 summit will be held at the Trump National Doral Miami golf club in Florida.

title: Turning Point USA knew of security concerns yet insisted Charlie Kirk speak outdoors, report says
summary: According to report, school staff recommended event move to a more secure location weeks before Kirk was fatally shot
text: A new report says that Turning Point USA insisted the conservative political group’s leader Charlie Kirk speak outdoors at Utah Valley University – where he was ultimately assassinated – despite security concerns raised with his team by the school’s leaders and its police chief. The independent report with those findings was commissioned by UVU and released on Friday. The report examined security procedures leading up to the 31-year-old’s fatal shooting on 10 September 2025 during a talk at the university’s campus in Orem, Utah. According to the 158-page report, school staff recommended Turning Point USA (TPUSA) move its event to a more secure location weeks before Kirk’s slaying. However, TPUSA “insisted upon” an outdoor location which “created significant protective operations considerations”, the report said. It added that a face-to-face, pre-event briefing and walkthrough with UVU police chief Jeff Long and the TPUSA protection detail – including the organization’s security supervisor Dan Flood – “should also have occurred” on UVU’s campus hours prior to the event. “Chief Long texted Dan Flood to meet on the Hall of Flags outdoor pedestrian walkway at 11[am], however, this face-to-face meeting did not occur,” the report said. Kirk was shot and killed by a sniper that day in the early afternoon. According to the report, the university also asked TPUSA for an estimated attendance figure. But the organization never provided one, despite saying it would control ticketing for the event, Utah’s Salt Lake Tribune newspaper reported. “Based on our review of all available information, that at no time during the events leading up to the assassination of Charlie Kirk, or in its aftermath, did any employee or agent of UVU act in bad faith or in willful and wanton disregard for the safety of others,” the report said. However, it also noted UVU’s having deferred to TPUSA on various event logistics. “Several key event security decisions were deferred to the TPUSA field representative even though UVU staff members raised concerns, including concerns related to holding the event in the outdoor fountain courtyard area and using TPUSA’s ticketing process,” the university’s report said. “Those decisions placed the event in an area that was more difficult to control and limited UVU’s ability to obtain reliable, real-time information regarding anticipated attendance and crowd size.” The report added: “UVU should have retained decision-making authority over key security-related issues, including venue selection, ticketing, access control and other conditions necessary to support campus safety.” In response to the report, Kirk family attorney Brett Parkinson said: “UVU hosted this event, and in doing so, assumed responsibility for the safety of all in attendance, including Charlie. The buck stopped with UVU leadership and law enforcement. “Justice for Charlie and his family requires true accountability for UVU’s fatal shortcomings that day.” Meanwhile, a statement from Jon Anderson, UVU’s president, said the university had a responsibility to “learn from the findings of this review, and follow through on its recommendations”. “This requires humility, an honest examination of our policies and practices, and a commitment to act on what we learn,” Anderson’s statement also said. Anderson, who became the university’s president in August, also said in his statement that UVU had made “meaningful progress in strengthening campus safety over the past year”. Kirk’s family is planning to sue the university. His family alleged in a 16 September legal notice presaging wrongful death litigation that UVU had placed “a politically controversial figure like Charlie Kirk in an outdoor event … surrounded by tall buildings and other elevated observation platforms” – and that the setup was like “walking him into a fishbowl”. UVU said it was aware of the notice and said it “addresses legal matters consistent with our established processes”, according to the Tribune. Utah resident Tyler Robinson has been charged with aggravated murder in connection with Kirk’s killing. He has pleaded not guilty, and no trial date had been set for him as of Friday. The Associated Press contributed reporting

title: Nearly 200 people wrongly identified on Nevada’s voter rolls as non-citizens
summary: State election officials said they reviewed 185 records homeland security sent them and confirmed they were US citizens
text: The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) wrongly identified 185 people on Nevada’s voter rolls as non-citizens, state officials said this week, escalating concerns over the shoddy methodology the government is using to raise fear about non-citizen voting ahead of the midterm elections. In July, Donald Trump gave a speech saying DHS had found a combined 278,000 non-citizens on the rolls in Nevada, California, Pennsylvania and New Jersey. Follow-up letters to each of those states weakened the claim, saying there only could be as many as 278,000 non-citizens on the rolls, including up to 15,903 in Nevada. In August, DHS officials told staffers in the Nevada secretary of state’s office that they had reviewed the numbers and confirmed only 185 were non-citizens. DHS officials said they still needed to review more than 14,000 records. But on Wednesday, Nevada election officials said they had reviewed the 185 records DHS sent them and confirmed they were US citizens. “As for the 185 individuals, our records indicate that they were citizens. You have provided nothing of substance to suggest otherwise,” Greg Ott, a deputy attorney general, wrote to DHS this week in an email obtained by the Guardian through a public records request. The message was first reported by the New York Times and Nevada Independent. In a statement on Friday, a DHS spokesperson did not address whether the department still believed the 185 were non-citizens. The spokesperson said the agency “is providing a service to the citizens of Nevada”. “The list of 185 were simply a subset of individuals that had gone through a rigorous manual review process at that time of the call. The list shared with Nevada last month also included 6,218 individuals with the highest number of matching attributes to an alien in DHS records,” the spokesperson said. In his email, Ott lamented DHS had not been transparent about the methodology DHS had used to flag alleged non-citizens nor had it shared adequate information. When Nevada officials requested DHS provide the first name, last name, address, and any other data point DHS officials matched, the department said they were only going to provide the voter ID number. In Nevada, a voter registration number can belong to multiple people, he wrote. Each of Nevada’s counties used to maintain their own registration system, but Nevada recently transitioned to a single statewide voter registration system and gave voters new state voter identification numbers. “As a result, the same number may appear at different points in time in connection with different voter records,” he wrote. “The number also doesn’t tell us whether an individual was born in the United States, naturalized, derived citizenship through a parent, or holds any particular immigration status. Election records commonly reflect the information supplied during registration,” he added. “For example, if someone registered to vote in 1970, the registration record may be incomplete; the name, address, and date of birth may be incomplete, changed, entered differently, or shared by more than one person. A number that matches a voter record thus establishes only that a number exists in, or once existed in, a voter registration system.” The news outlet Votebeat also reported earlier this month that election officials in Pennsylvania have also pushed DHS for information on its basis for claiming there were as many as 14,576 non-citizens on its rolls. In an August letter obtained by Votebeat, Al Schmidt, Pennsylvania’s top election official, said DHS representatives had indicated they did not have “high confidence” in that number.

title: New Jersey lieutenant governor resigns after sexual harassment accusation
summary: Investigation determined Dale Caldwell violated state ethics rules and engaged in harassing behavior
text: Dale Caldwell, the lieutenant governor of New Jersey, resigned from his position on Friday, after the release of a report accusing him of sexually harassing a female staffer, among other ethics violations. New Jersey’s governor, Mikie Sherrill, announced on Friday afternoon that Caldwell had submitted his resignation to her earlier in the day. The decision by Caldwell, 66, came one day after Sherrill called on him to step down after an investigation determined he violated state ethics rules and engaged in behavior that constituted sexual harassment. The 61-page report said it found credible evidence that Caldwell made romantic advances toward a female staffer’s friend, tried to secure a promotion for his girlfriend and gave tickets to personal guests without reimbursement. The New Jersey Globe was the first to report on Caldwell’s resignation. Thomas Calcagni, a lawyer for Caldwell, said in a statement they would “continue to forcefully challenge the report”. “Dr Caldwell’s resignation, submitted to put an end to the targeted campaign to discredit his character, does not in any way diminish our outrage concerning the investigative process and its specious findings,” Calcagni said. “Counsel is fully exploring all legal remedies to ensure a true, balanced, and unbiased record.” Sherrill, a Democrat, said she would appoint the state’s acting comptroller, Shirley Emehelu, as the acting secretary of state. “We can no longer tolerate the culture of silence, sweeping things under the rug or kicking cans down the road,” Sherrill said Friday at press conference in Trenton, the state capital. “New Jerseyans deserve fairness and they deserve accountability.” The change-up comes just weeks before midterm elections, which the lieutenant governor is responsible for overseeing. The New Jersey governor initiated an investigation into Caldwell in May after receiving an anonymous letter that accused him of “bringing uninvited female guests to events while traveling using taxpayer funds” and “hitting on women at functions”. Ultimately, investigators concluded that aspects of the allegations were credible. In one instance, investigators said Caldwell made a romantic advance toward a female staffer’s friend and then made a “derogatory or demeaning reference” about women after his advances were rebuffed. Caldwell allegedly told the staffer that women like them were ambitious and successful and needed a man in a position to help them, “but you young women are looking for young sperm”. Investigators also found that Caldwell advocated for the promotion of his girlfriend, a state employee, to a “senior leadership position”. Caldwell acknowledged that he did not disclose the nature of his relationship with the state employee until he was confronted. Caldwell had pushed for his girlfriend’s promotion, even after being informed he was under investigation. Ultimately, she did not get the promotion and no longer works in state government. Credible evidence also determined Caldwell brought at least three personal guests, including his girlfriend, to ticketed events, in his capacity as lieutenant governor, without advance authorization or payment. After Sherrill announced the report’s findings and called for Caldwell to resign, it was unclear whether or not he would step down. As lieutenant governor, Caldwell was also serving as New Jersey’s secretary of state, who is the chief elections officer. With just 39 days until the midterm elections, Sherrill said she was tapping Emehelu to ensure “all eligible New Jerseyans can make their voices heard”. “Shirley is a veteran of the US Department of Justice and the New Jersey attorney general’s office. She has the judgment to run these elections and the strength to stand up to Trump’s attacks on voting,” Sherrill added. Sherrill has 45 days to name a permanent replacement for Caldwell. • This story was amended on 26 September 2026. New Jersey governor Mikie Sherrill said she would appoint the state’s acting comptroller, Shirley Emehelu, as the acting secretary of state, not as lieutenant governor as a previous version stated.

title: In latest blow to Obamacare, Trump is threatening the entire US health system
summary: The Trump administration is removing 760,000 people enrolled in the Affordable Care Act marketplace
text: The Trump administration is removing 760,000 people enrolled in the Affordable Care Act (ACA) marketplace on allegations of fraud, officials said on Tuesday – adding to previous efforts to chip away at federally subsidized insurance programs and likely causing some of the lowest-income Americans to forego healthcare, experts said. The US government is also investigating about 420,000 people whom they suspect of fraud, and they are putting a six-month enrollment moratorium on new agents and brokers selling Obamacare policies, officials said at a press conference. The removed enrollees are a mixture of “phantoms” and “ghosts” as well as people who don’t meet the eligibility requirements of Obamacare, said Mehmet Oz, the administrator for the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS). “These are not real people,” he said, claiming that expelling them from the ACA marketplace would save the federal government $2.2bn. JD Vance, who is leading a federal taskforce on fraud, claimed: “We’re actually making sure that the people receiving Obamacare subsidies are actually entitled to receive them.” No details were provided about how many enrollees were fictional, enrolled by fraudulent brokers without their knowledge or expelled because of income restrictions. “There’s no transparency about who these people are and why they’re being disenrolled, but I think it’s a reasonable concern that some number are being disenrolled inappropriately,” said Edwin Park, a research professor at the Center for Children and Families at Georgetown University’s McCourt School of Public Policy. “A common theme here is to make it incredibly burdensome for individuals to enroll and stay enrolled in their health coverage.” Without more information, “there is no way to know how many legitimately enrolled people had their plans canceled”, said Cynthia Cox, senior vice-president and director of the Program on the ACA at KFF, an independent health policy organization. The move follows recent rules and legislation to reduce enrollment in Medicaid, Medicare and the ACA, said Park, who added: “A lot of these actions are intended to sharply undercut the success of and the long-term viability of the ACA’s coverage expansions, which have been an incredible success in terms of reducing the number of people without health insurance.” About 19.2 million Americans are enrolled in the ACA marketplace, but nearly 3 million people lost their coverage between February 2025 and February 2026, according to the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities. The fraud taskforce has also withheld $2.2bn in Medicaid payments from California and Minnesota over alleged fraud – primarily in home health aide programs, which disability advocates say are a lifeline. Officials followed an unusual path to verify ACA enrollment, experts said. The administration sent to insurers a list of more than a million people suspected of being fraudulently enrolled in the ACA marketplace, also known as Obamacare. Officials said on Tuesday that they used AI tools to identify the enrollees. The people were identified by three factors: they’d been enrolled by a broker or agent, had all of their ACA premium paid by the tax credit, and they had not supplied social security numbers or immigration documents. Insurers were asked to try to make contact with those enrollees; they were permitted to filter out people who had a previous claim or had communicated with the insurer. The enrollees had 30 days to respond, or their coverage was canceled. “It is entirely possible that many of these people were enrolled without their knowledge or were so-called phantom enrollees,” Cox said. “It is also entirely possible that many of these people were legitimately enrolled and simply did not respond in time.” People can appeal and be reinstated once they prove their identities – but this will likely function as an additional hurdle making it harder for people to stay enrolled, Park said. “We know that when you add a lot of red tape, increase the amount of complexity and the requirements for paperwork,” Park said, that “leads to eligible people being disenrolled.” Vance spoke of two fraudulent brokers who were convicted of quietly enrolling people to collect commissions from insurance companies, acknowledging that “some of those people were probably legitimate”, but he did not speak of the steps necessary to reinstate them or to prevent future disenrollments. Ending unscrupulous broker practices has been a bipartisan issue, and the Biden administration was the first to act, finalizing a rule to crack down on shady brokers. Officials under Biden decertified about 200 such brokers – but Trump administration officials recertified them last year. About 35% of ACA enrollees have never used their health insurance, Oz said. “That’s just not possible,” he said, adding, “So we know there is fraud.” But it’s not unusual for healthy people to be enrolled in insurance and not need to use it, Park noted: “You can expect in any insurance risk pool that there’s going to be a lot of people who don’t use much healthcare or use healthcare at all.” By removing lower-risk enrollees, insurance premiums could increase or insurers could decide to leave markets entirely, he said. Some enrollees also appear to have been cut because they are low-income. The Affordable Care Act was intended to include a Medicaid expansion for those living under the poverty line, but a supreme court decision made the expansion optional. In states that chose not to expand Medicaid, there is a group of low-income people who make too much money to qualify for Medicaid – earning between $16,000 and $22,000 per year – but don’t make enough to qualify for the ACA. “We’re going to make sure that they actually meet the income threshold requirements in order to receive these Obamacare benefits,” Vance said of this group. Oz called their disenrollment “a little bit painful”. Park said that there have been a series of “at best misleading” allegations arguing that a large share of current marketplace plan enrollees are fraudulently or inappropriately enrolled. Reports from the Paragon Institute and the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) have indicated millions of fraudulent enrollees – but those analyses are “flawed”, Park said. These reports directly compare administrative data and unadjusted census data, but income and household sizes are calculated differently in these two measures. The census counts all individuals living in the household, while Medicaid and the ACA marketplace exclude non-dependent relatives. “That has a big effect on the number of people who appear to be in certain income ranges,” Park said. “That has been used to say a huge percent of people don’t look like they have incomes in the right eligibility range.” These disenrollments are happening in the context of major cuts to the marketplace. Premiums skyrocketed, doubling or tripling for some enrollees, after Republicans opposed extending the enhanced tax credits at the end of last year. Alongside other financial pressures, like higher energy and food costs, “there’s going to be an increasing number of people who can no longer afford their share of the premium”, Park said. The healthcare cuts of the budget reconciliation law HR1 “in many ways were designed to undermine the Affordable Care Act coverage expansions” without explicitly repealing it – a longtime Trump promise, Park said. The Trump administration has also created new regulations to restrict marketplace enrollment, he noted, adding: “You add it all together, and you’re going to have certainly significant reductions in enrollment – with those enrollment losses increasing over time.” When people lose their health insurance, it has ripple effects – including added pressure on health systems that affect all patients. “Providers, particularly safety net providers, operate under thinner operating margins. If they’re facing payment cuts, they’re facing higher uncompensated care costs, as a result of more uninsured [patients],” Park said, which may lead hospitals to cut services or staff, or close their doors entirely. “And that makes it harder for everyone to access the care they need.”

title: US senators propose legislation to limit ICE arrests and indefinite detention
summary: Exclusive: Democrats Dick Durbin of Illinois and Alex Padilla of California seek to prevent unlawful arrests
text: US senators have introduced legislation aimed at cutting down warrantless or specious ICE arrests, and curbing the agency’s ability to indefinitely detain immigrants who do not pose any danger to their communities. The new legislation, shared exclusively with the Guardian, would require immigration officers to obtain an administrative warrant from a supervisor outlining a probable cause for detaining someone. Such a warrant must also be presented to each person who is detained, the bill says, alongside notice of when the detainee must appear in immigration court. The bill would require a bond hearing within 24 hours of any warrantless arrests, and custody review of every noncitizen in immigration detention every 60 days by an immigration judge or US district judge – ideally ensuring that detainees are not held in ICE custody indefinitely without clear cause. The Democratic senators Dick Durbin of Illinois and Alex Padilla of California – – said they are introducing the “Immigration Warrant Reform Act” to prevent unlawful arrests and detentions following reports that US citizens and immigrants with legal status were being apprehended. By clarifying how and when ICE can make arrests and detain individuals, the senators said, they also hope to stop the agency from racial profiling or detaining people for arbitrary reasoning. “This bill would establish stronger accountability and oversight,” Padilla said, referring to Americans and noncitizens alike. “The disturbing reality today is that many American citizens and immigrants with lawful status have been caught in the Trump administration’s indiscriminate and violent immigration enforcement dragnet across the country,” said Durbin. “[The legislation] is commonsense, and I encourage my colleagues on both sides of the aisle to support it.” With Republicans in the majority in both chambers of Congress, there isn’t an easy path for the the bill to become law. But Durbin said he was compelled to do something after seeing civil rights abuses during the Trump administration’s Operation Midway Blitz – the militarized immigration raid in Chicago last fall and winter. Immigration advocates and attorneys who reviewed the legislation were concerned that it still left several groups of immigrants vulnerable to arbitrary arrest and detention by granting ICE officers broad leeway in deciding when to conduct a warrantless arrest. The proposed law states, for example, that a warrant isn’t required when someone poses an “imminent danger to the community” – but doesn’t clarify what that means. “The framework neglects how the current administration routinely weaponizes unsubstantiated national security allegations to advance its anti-immigrant agenda,” said Faisal Al-Juburi, the co-chief executive of Raíces, a Texas-based humanitarian aid and immigration services non-profit. Donald Trump and his administration have specifically claimed that Venezuelan asylum seekers without criminal records pose a national security threat, or arbitrarily proclaimed that families who have lived in the US with temporary legal status for years are dangerous criminals. It is also unclear, advocates said, how the bill would hold ICE accountable for violating these standards. Durbin’s office said the bill codifies constitutional safeguards, by requiring immigration agents to prove they have a probable cause to detain someone – and if not, release them within 24 hours. Requiring that detainees get a hearing every 60 days would also force the government to justify its reasoning for the continued detention. The bill would “help prevent these due process violations while ensuring noncitizens who present a threat to public safety are not released”, Durbin said. Al-Juburi said he was skeptical the bill meets the moment. And a bigger question raised by the bill is whether immigrants should be detained at all for civil violations such as entering the US without authorization, he added.. “My concern here is that this approach fails to reject the inhumane notion that people should face detention, and loss of liberty, for non-criminal matters,” said Al-Juburi. “Detaining people for civil immigration enforcement stands in direct conflict with what are ostensibly core constitutional protections.”

title: ‘He looked at me and said: “So you really are working class”’: Alan Johnson on the need for better paternity leave
summary: Exclusive: Former Labour minister says working-class fathers are being shortchanged and budget should correct it
text: Parliament was in recess when Tony Blair called Alan Johnson up to his flat above No 11. The former prime minister was relaxed, padding around in his socks, while his son Leo played with his toys. Johnson, then the education secretary, spoke about his own son from his second marriage, who was a similar age. “Tony said: ‘Oh you’re a father?’” recalled Johnson. “I said: ‘Tony, I had three kids by the age of 20!’ He looked at me and said: ‘So you really are working-class …’” It may be almost a quarter of a century since Johnson introduced paid paternity leave during his time as the trade and industry secretary, but working-class fathers are still being shortchanged, the former minister has told the Guardian. Johnson has added his name to a growing number of current and former MPs and senior Labour figures calling for six weeks of paternity leave paid at 90% of earnings, capped at £1,200 a week, with the offer extended to self-employed fathers, who are currently the only parents with no entitlement to paid leave. The author married his first wife, Judith, when he was 18, adopting her daughter and going on to have two more children by the time he was 20. His fourth child, with his second wife, was born when he was a minister in the New Labour government in his 50s. Johnson recalls that when his second child was born, he came home from work on a night shift in the postal service to find a note from his wife telling him she had gone to hospital to have a baby. He slept for a few hours and went back to work. “Men were meant to go down the pub, buy everyone a drink, smoke a cigar, and leave all the kind of hard work to their partners,” he said. “By the time my fourth child was born, it was practically compulsory to be at the birth – things move on and the law has to move with it.” Working-class fathers are still far less likely to take up the current paternity leave of £187.18 a week for two weeks, among the least generous offerings in Europe. According to analysis of HMRC data by the campaign group the Dad Shift, 90% of paternity leave in 2024-25 was claimed by fathers in the UK’s top half of earners – those who generally make more than £37,800 a year – and 95% of claims for shared parental leave were made by fathers or partners in the top 50% bracket. Many fathers and partners would still be in the position of having to go back to work the day after the birth of a child, just like he did, added Johnson. “The statistics about who is actually accessing paternity leave is just stunning. It shows that it’s a class issue,” he said. “It’s great that more prosperous dads are taking paternity leave, but we’ve got to do something to increase the take-up among the lower paid.” The Joseph Rowntree Foundation estimates that introducing the new policy of six weeks at 90% of pay in the forthcoming budget would cost the government an additional £1bn, but increased tax receipts from women going back to work could reduce that cost to £220m. Asked if the government should introduce the change in the next budget, despite the strong economic headwinds faced by the chancellor, John Healey, Johnson was in no doubt. “Absolutely. In government terms, the cost is money down the back of the sofa,” he said. “And actually if the finances are preventing couples from having children, ultimately that is bad for society. Society needs children, mankind needs to procreate. So encouraging childbirth is good for society, full stop.” The policy would be popular, and unlikely to be opposed, he added. “If it was, in pure political terms, it’s a good dividing line for Andy Burnham and the Labour party to take,” he said. “It’s an excellent dividing line.”

title: Alarm at UN over sanctions threatened by US on international criminal court
summary: Group calls for proper enforcement of ICC rulings as Trump administration widens attacks on court
text: The US threat to impose sanctions on the international criminal court (ICC) as an institution, not just its leading judges, could fundamentally disrupt its operation and needed to be resisted, a coalition of countries to defend international law heard at the United Nations on Friday. Ronald Lamola, South Africa’s foreign minister, issued the warning at an event during the UN general assembly called to protect the system of international law from a growing array of threats, including open flouting of its tenets and rulings by Israel. The meeting was organised by the Hague Group, of which Lamola is co-chair, and which was set up in 2025 to protect international law and to call for the proper enforcement of the rulings of its two primary bodies: the ICC and the international court of justice (ICJ). Lamola told the gathering that the US had already sanctioned ICC judges and prosecutors, but was now planning sanctions against the ICC itself. “If imposed, such measures could fundamentally disrupt its operations,” he said. “An independent court remains independent only if judges and officials cannot be punished for carrying out their mandates.” The head of the ICC, Judge Tomoko Akane of Japan, was sanctioned by the US in August, along with senior trial lawyer Abdoulaye Seye of Senegal, for engaging in the ICC’s efforts to “prosecute officials whose government has not consented to ICC jurisdiction”. The attack on Akane was condemned this week by the Japanese prime minister, Sanae Takaichi. The US has admitted it seeks to dismantle the Hague-based ICC. In his address to the UN general assembly this week, Donald Trump once again criticised the “out of control” court, which he smeared as an “evil group of people” and urged other nations to reject. The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, has accused the court of being “a corrupt and fatally politicised supranational court that has maliciously abused its authority and exceeded its mandate. We will not tolerate its assault on state sovereignty.” The next step by the US is likely to be to impose secondary sanctions on anyone who cooperates with the court, as opposed to sanctioning its senior judiciary. A designation of the whole institution would reach every European bank, insurer and technology supplier serving the court, which sits in the Netherlands. The Dutch government, as the host of the ICC, is taking the lead in trying to warn the US away from the effective immobilisation of the court. The Dutch prime minister, Rob Jetten, told the UN general assembly: “International law either works for everyone or for no one. This court was established to protect us against impunity and it was built on the foundations of the Nuremberg and Tokyo trials. And now, with the ICC under attack, the writing is truly on the wall. “After all, how can you possibly be opposed to prosecuting the very worst crimes? And I believe there can be only one response: to say, hands off the ICC and all those other institutions that protect the international legal order.” William Schabas, a specialist in international law, noted to the meeting the irony that the resort to international law and courts was increasing dramatically even as the institutions were under attack. He said nations needed to strengthen the ICC, including by ensuring positions are not traded and only the highest calibre judges are elected. Diana Buttu, the prominent Palestinian lawyer, was among many to complain of western powers’ partial resort to international law. “The greatest threat to international law is not the state that openly defies it,” she said. “The greatest threat is our selectivity – the quiet decision that is made in capitals and rooms that the rules don’t bind everybody, they only bind some. It is the belief that we can excuse some because they are our allies, our partners and our friends.”

title: Overcrowding and racism at Manston asylum centre linked to government decisions, inquiry hears
summary: Kent facility became dangerously overburdened after ministers halted transfers to hotels
text: A catalogue of failures including racism, use of force and chronic overcrowding at a Home Office processing site for people who arrive on small boat were linked to decisions made at the highest level of government, an independent inquiry has heard. The government commissioned the Manston independent inquiry to look at problems under the Conservative government between 1 June and 22 November 2022 at the facility in Kent. Almost 200 asylum seekers detained at Manston are participating in the inquiry along with the former home secretaries Suella Braverman and Priti Patel, several government departments including the Home Office, Treasury, Ministry of Justice and Ministry of Defence, and HM Inspectorate of Prisons and the UK Health Security Agency. The problems began when the site became vastly overcrowded. Manston was designed to hold a maximum of 1,600 new arrivals for no more than 24 hours as there are no proper sleeping or other facilities there. But after decisions by ministers to pause transfers of many of the asylum seekers to other accommodation such as hotels the site became dangerously overcrowded. Up to 4,000 people were accommodated there unlawfully for several weeks at the peak of the crisis, most of them sleeping on the floor in profoundly insanitary conditions. There were outbreaks of infectious conditions including scabies and diphtheria, the latter of which can be fatal in approximately 30% of cases in unvaccinated populations. There were also reports of assaults and drug use by guards, racist abuse from guards, and the death of a man after contracting diphtheria. The inquiry, chaired by Sophie Cartwright KC, heard that two former prime ministers, Boris Johnson and Rishi Sunak, who were both in post at different points in 2022, were involved in decision-making about the Manston site. Laura Dubinsky KC, representing some of the participants, told the inquiry that the decision to pause sending many asylum seekers on to hotels was in line with the thinking at No 10. “No 10 clearly did play a decision-making role,” she said. Patel has provided evidence to the inquiry that funding was deemed inadequate to address the small boats issue, including funding for Manston and onward accommodation. The inquiry heard that events in Manston “raise very serious questions for ministers”. Clair Dobbin KC, counsel to the inquiry, said it was taking place in a “crucible of hostility” at a time when the arrival of small boats remains a significant issue. She added that “to put it bluntly” the inquiry would look at whether at certain points “the entire operation at Manston was outside the law”. One senior Home Office official wrote a report saying: “To be frank, I’m struggling for words,” after observing what he said were “the worst conditions I have observed working in this environment”. Hussein Haseeb Ahmed, 31, was taken to Manston after arriving in a small boat. He died in hospital after becoming ill with diphtheria. He was belatedly admitted for care and was kept in handcuffs as he lay dying. The handcuffs were only removed two and a half hours before he died. According to the inquiry, evidence about his death suggests “a succession of missed opportunities”. The inquiry also heard that “very racist language was used towards detainees by some staff”. Sixty families were crammed into 11 rooms in a barracks building with no hot water, showers or clean clothes for nine days with one toilet for 81 people, and no soap or sanitiser available. Some used toothpaste to soothe bites and one used a croissant wrapper to dress wounds. Questions were raised about whether some unvetted staff were working legally at Manston. Shu Shin Luh, one of the lawyers representing participants in the inquiry, said: “Why were people treated as less than human?” Stephanie Harrison KC, also representing some of the participants in the inquiry, accused the Home Office of presiding over “an institutional culture defined by impunity with widespread illegality and non-compliance with the law”. Future dates for inquiry hearings have not yet been confirmed.

title: Partner of woman killed by US hunter who allegedly mistook her for deer says death ‘no accident’
summary: Walter Moorhead, arrested on suspicion of manslaughter, murdered Santos Maria Chilel Soto, partner alleges
text: The partner of a Delaware woman who was shot dead by a hunter allegedly mistaking her for a deer has said the killing was “senseless” and the hunter had “no excuse”. “I have never seen a deer with only two legs,” Minivaldo Velásquez told the Delaware public news outlet WHYY in an interview published on Thursday about the death six days earlier of Santos Maria Chilel Soto. “It doesn’t make sense – no.” Velásquez’s comments came after authorities investigating the case arrested 74-year-old Walter Moorhead on suspicion of manslaughter, which Delaware defines as recklessness causing the death of another person. State police investigators had previously said Moorhead was hunting from a ground blind near the community of Ellendale at about 7.40pm when he thought he spotted a deer and fired his rifle. Yet it was actually Chilel Soto whom Moorhead shot at and struck, according to authorities. Velásquez told WHYY that he, Chilel Soto and two of her children were walking through a harvested cornfield at the time of the shooting after going to dinner as a family. “She had a yellow blouse, and I was wearing a blue T-shirt,” said Velásquez, who also said the shooting happened about an hour earlier – when it was presumably more visible – than the time listed by police. Velásquez reportedly told police he applied pressure to Chilel Soto’s gunshot wound – which was to her torso – and called emergency responders. She was then brought to an area hospital and pronounced dead there, state police said. Investigators said they jailed Moorhead after speaking with him and determining that he shot Chilel Soto, purportedly thinking she was a deer. Hunting deer with a rifle was not in season at the time of the shooting, according to Delaware’s laws. But WHYY, citing information from Delaware’s department of natural resources and environmental control, reported that the property where Chilel Soto was killed had a permit authorizing the harvest of antlerless deer there outside the normal season. Investigators booked Moorhead on counts of manslaughter, possession of a firearm during the commission of a felony, and reckless endangering. In Delaware, the first two of those counts are considered class B felonies, which can carry up to 25 years in prison. Moorhead – a resident of Salisbury, Maryland – posted a $43,000 bond to secure his release from custody pending the outcome of the case, state police said. Velásquez later told WHYY that Chilel Soto’s killer has “no excuse – the excuses are unacceptable and senseless”. “That was a cold-blooded murder,” Velásquez continued. “It was not an accident. It was 100% not an accident.” WHYY reported that Chilel Soto was a mother of five originally from Guatemala. The outlet reported being told by one of Chilel Soto’s sisters, Yolin, that sane people trying to hunt “should make sure it really is an animal before shooting – and what kind of animal”. Yolin Chilel Soto also suggested there may have been a component of “racism” to her sister’s killing, according to WHYY. “This person should receive psychological help before carrying a weapon – and not just at the beginning. They need it continually,” Yolin Chilel Soto reportedly said. Attempts to contact Moorhead for comment have not been successful. He waived a preliminary court hearing on Friday, the Delaware news station WDEL. WDEL also reported that dozens of people in support of Santos Maria Chilel Soto gathered outside and in the courthouse on Friday.

title: Hurricane Nolo predicted to bring ‘life-threatening flooding’ to Hawaii
summary: Forecasters say storm will cause heavy rains and large waves along the coast, near communities still recovering from extreme weather
text: Hurricane Nolo is expected to bring potentially life-threatening and catastrophic flooding to Hawaii on Friday, affecting communities that are still recovering from devastating storms earlier this summer. The state activated more than 230 Hawaii national guard members and closed schools ahead of the storm. Nolo is expected to move west on Saturday and not directly hit the islands, but forecasters say it will still cause heavy rainfall, as much as 25in, as well as large and damaging waves along the coast. It comes as remote communities are still recovering from extreme weather in recent months that destroyed homes, washed away roads and left neighborhoods without power. Nolo is forecasted to bring the heaviest rain to an area hit hard by Hurricane Lala in August, where some people remain displaced. Residents still grappling with the effects of the previous storm told Honolulu Civil Beat they were on edge over this bout of bad weather and hoping their homes would survive. “We’re slowly starting to rebuild, but now it’s almost like if this storm hits, it’ll smash us back down,” said Troy Gacayan, a high school teacher and pastor, to the outlet. As of Friday morning, Nolo was just over 200 miles south of the Big Island and expected to head north-east, bringing tropical storm conditions by the evening before strengthening to a major hurricane on Saturday. “This rainfall could produce catastrophic life-threatening flooding and mudslides, especially in areas of steep terrain,” the US National Hurricane Center said. Meanwhile, residents and tourists alike were preparing for the storm to approach the Big Island. “I guess that’d be my concern – whether we’re getting out of here or not, but, you know, as far as the weather goes, it is what it is,” said Daniel Compton, who was visiting from Seattle. Hawaii’s emergency management agency has advised residents and visitors to review emergency plans and supplies, ensure properties are prepared for flooding, high winds and power outages, and to consider evacuating to safer areas. Earlier this week, Josh Green, Hawaii’s governor, requested an emergency disaster declaration for four Hawaii counties in order to access federal funds and emergency support. The request still awaits approval from Donald Trump. In remarks to Congress earlier this week, Brian Schatz, a Hawaii senator, lamented the destruction on the islands and pointed to the role of the climate crisis. “There is a reason these destructive disasters are piling up one after another, leaving communities exhausted and governments depleted. It is the warming planet,” Schatz said, urging the US to reduce pollution, increase clean energy and help communities prepare for worsening disasters. The Associated Press contributed

title: Earth microbes survive simulated conditions of Saturn moon’s ocean
summary: Experiment suggests organisms could live in harsh environment under Enceladus’s icy crust, strengthening possibility moon could support life
text: From the moment scientists spotted plumes of water erupting from Enceladus, one of Saturn’s moons, it became the most tantalising place in the solar system to search for life beyond Earth. Now the case is even more compelling after researchers found that organisms that live in deep-sea waters off Japan can survive the harsh conditions expected in the briny ocean that lurks beneath Enceladus’s icy crust. The microbes, which thrive near hydrothermal vents on the seafloor by converting hydrogen and carbon dioxide into methane, survived in a brine that mimicked the Saturnian moon’s ocean. The work suggests the distant world may be habitable, if not exactly hospitable, to at least some forms of life. “If we use the cellular definition of life that we understand on Earth today, the experiments tell us that if this organism, or something similar to it, was on Enceladus, there’s a good chance it could survive,” said William Orsi, a professor of geomicrobiology at Ludwig-Maximilian University in Munich. Saturn has more moons than any other planet in the solar system, with nearly 300 known to orbit the gas giant. For more than two centuries, Enceladus, a 300-mile-wide ice ball, did not seem particularly remarkable. But that changed with the arrival of robotic spacecraft. Since the 2000s, observations from Nasa’s Cassini probe and, more recently, the James Webb space telescope have revealed gigantic plumes of water vapour and ice grains spewing from Enceladus and evidence for a huge saltwater ocean under its frozen crust. The seafloor is thought to be dotted with hydrothermal vents that warm the water around them. Last year, scientists found organic substances in samples collected by Cassini as it swooped through one of Enceladus’s spectacular plumes. Orsi and his colleagues wanted to see if they could concoct a miniature version of Enceladus’s ocean to study in the laboratory. By combining water with salts and carbonates and adding powdered rock, they recreated not only the extremely alkaline environment of the ocean but also crucial reactions that take place between the water and the rocky seafloor. The rock-water reactions were active enough to start churning out hydrogen, a process that seems to happen in the ocean on Enceladus. It led the researchers to wonder whether Earthly microbes called methanogens, which survive by converting hydrogen and carbon dioxide into methane, could survive in the solution. “It was a long shot,” said Orsi. To find out, the scientists turned to microbes originally found near deep-sea hydrothermal vents in the Okinawa trough between Japan and Taiwan. Hydrothermal vents are hot springs on the seafloor that release hot, mineral-rich water. Surprisingly, the microbes grew in the simulated ocean despite its pH reaching 11, which is far more alkaline than the organisms’ known limit. The microbes even adapted their metabolism to cope with low concentrations of carbon dioxide in the water. Details are published in Science Advances. David Rothery, a professor of planetary geosciences at the Open University, said that by showing that methanogenesis – the process that sustains the microbes – was possible in the simulated Enceladus ocean, the work “removes another barrier to the viability of microbial life there”. Orsi stressed that if life ever evolved on Enceladus it could be radically different from that on Earth. Even if similar bugs did somehow arise, it is not clear if methane-making microbes would thrive in the moon’s ocean: his experiments lasted only days. “Could they survive for a year? Could they survive for a million years? We don’t know,” Orsi said. In a second paper in the journal, some of the same researchers describe how ice grains in Enceladus’s plumes freeze and fragment in a way that separates the different constituents of the ocean. If ocean droplets contained bits of alien microbes, these might turn up in a small fraction of ice particles but be highly concentrated within them. That would be “great news” for the search for life, said Frank Postberg, a professor of planetary sciences at the Free University of Berlin, who said it would be relatively easy to identify signs of life with today’s technology. The tantalising science around Enceladus has fuelled interest in a return trip. The European Space Agency’s L4 mission aims to combine a Saturn orbiter with an Enceladus lander that would touch down at the moon’s south pole and hunt for biosignatures in the plumes erupting from its ocean. But scientists face a long wait: with a launch proposed for about 2042, it would not reach Saturn until the 2050s. Dr Rachael Hamp, also at the Open University, who has worked on Enceladus’s plumes, said: “It’s fantastic to see new research pushing our understanding further and providing additional evidence for the potential habitability of this little icy world. I think this makes the European Space Agency’s proposed mission to Enceladus even more exciting.”

title: Burnham pledges extra £210m towards regenerating boarded-up high streets
summary: Funds to help local people turn empty shops, pubs and clubs into community hubs, shared workspaces and cafes
text: The UK government has pledged £210m to regenerate high streets by taking boarded-up shops, pubs and clubs and turning them into shared workspaces, cafes and community hubs. Andy Burnham said the funds would “help put power back into the hands of locals who know their area best” as part of his effort to “restore pride and bring hope back”. High streets continue to struggle, despite multiple government attempts at regeneration, after a shift to online shopping and services such as banking and estate agents, as well as higher business costs including taxes, energy and labour. The cost of living crunch has also prompted people to rein in spending on non-essentials and driven a shift to dining and drinking at home instead of spending on eating out. Burnham said it was important to find ways of reviving high streets despite the challenges. “People don’t measure growth by looking at a spreadsheet,” he said. “They measure it by looking at their local high street. Are shops opening or are the shutters down? Does the place feel like it’s moving forward or being left behind? “The truth is that too many high streets have been left to hollow out, leaving town centres a shell of what they once were. That must change, and today’s funding will help put power back into the hands of locals who know their area best. “That’s how we restore pride and bring hope back. Not by telling people things are getting better, but by giving them the power to see and feel the difference where they live.” A new £125m derelict buildings fund will support local councils to revamp vacant shopping centres, disused cinemas and other abandoned buildings into locally needed spaces such as community halls and health centres. A further £65m will help communities in England rescue and revamp buildings and businesses at risk of closure, such as pubs and clubs. Another £20m will be equally split between funding co-operative ownership of businesses important to communities such as pubs and clubs and funding council high street rental auctions to fill properties left vacant for a year or more. The decision directs existing funds already earmarked for high street regeneration towards community-led schemes. It is in addition to the existing £5.8bn pride-in-place programme that is handing 284 deprived communities up to £2m a year for 10 years towards local regeneration projects. The government is to announce later this year a full high streets strategy aimed at improving town centres across England. Research by the University of Southampton found people feel high streets have declined more than any other part of their local area over the past decade as household chains, from BHS to Debenhams, have collapsed while shoplifting has increased. Rose Marley, the chief executive of trade body Co-operatives UK, said the new specialist fund to back the creation of mutuals was “a game changer”. Labour pledged to double the number of co-operatives in the UK but its figures showed the number rose by just 0.4% last year to 8,005. Amid difficult times in the hospitality sector, co-operative pubs are on the rise – up 48% in the last five years – but they remain a tiny fraction of the industry with just 377 pubs and other hospitality businesses in the UK at present. However, Marley said: “This funding shows a government that understands how giving power and agency to communities brings positive change and improves lives, with community, business and local government all working together.”

title: Why a supercharged El Niño is putting Hawaii in the bullseye of more storms
summary: Hurricane Nolo is the latest storm to menace the islands as sees warming ocean temperatures fuel more severe weather
text: With Hurricane Nolo, the islands of Hawaii are grappling with the third major tropical storm in recent months. Hurricanes Lala in August and Lowell in early September flooded homes and roads, downed trees and toppled electricity lines across the islands. Nolo, which strengthened to a hurricane on Thursday night, is expected to batter the islands with rain and high surf. Despite its location, stretching across roughly 1,500 miles in the central north Pacific Ocean, Hawaii typically avoids the worst effects from hurricanes. In fact, the island chain so often dodges direct hits from the violent storms that it’s been quipped they have a force field around them. But the islands have seen an unusual amount of severe storms this year. Already, more than 500 homes have been damaged or destroyed as Nolo threatens to unleash downpours that could measure in feet instead of inches. “An event of this magnitude is somewhat rare,” Michael Brennan, director of the National Hurricane Center, said during a broadcast discussion as Lowell swirled closer last month, adding that Hawaii has not had a direct hurricane landfall since Iniki in 1992. That violent storm unleashed 145 mile-per-hour winds as it tore through Kauai, destroying or damaging roughly 70% of the island’s homes and businesses. It’s not luck (or a force field) that typically protected the islands, but location, according to Dr Nicholas Grondin, assistant professor of environmental science at the University of Tampa. Among the most isolated chains of islands on Earth, Hawaii is simply a small target in the vast open ocean, Grondin explained in an editorial published by the Conversation. Most approaching storms also must pass over cooler water temperatures to the east of the islands, which helps calm them. “Without warm oceans to provide fuel, hurricanes tend to weaken and fizzle out as they approach the islands,” Grondin said. Sea-surface temperatures in the tropical Pacific are, however, exceptionally warm this year due to El Niño. The climate phenomenon typically limits hurricane activity in the Atlantic and enhances the development and strength of storms in the Pacific. El Niño has already developed, but is expected to strengthen through the coming months, and forecasters have warned there is a high probability it will reach a historic intensity. El Niño has caused hurricanes to form further to the south and west this year, according to Matthew Rosencrans, National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s lead forecaster for the seasonal hurricane outlook, which “puts them in a place where they could make that westward run towards the Hawaiian islands”. It also makes for a lagging storm season. Hurricane risks typically extend from July to the end of November but fall off into the later months. September and October are far busier in El Niño years. The climate crisis has also played a part in strengthening the storms. The effects of El Niño are layered on top of the warming trends. “The oceans are absorbing 92% of the excess heat to the climate system from the addition of heat-trapping pollutants to the atmosphere,” Union of Concerned Scientists climate scientist Dr Marc Alessi said in a thread shared on Bluesky. According to Alessi, the energy added to oceans over just the last year is on par with roughly 12 Hiroshima bombs of heat released every second. “For the next year, we can expect to see precipitation and other weather extremes unlike anything we’ve seen before,” he said. For Pacific storms, Rosencrans said, it means they may carry more moisture and produce stronger winds. As efforts begin to clear debris and repair roads and infrastructure damaged during Lowell, emergency management officials must continue keeping close watch on the waters for the next big storm. “They just need to reset and regard any potential upcoming impacts,” Rosencrans said. “The season is not over – there is still a long bit to go.”

title: US supreme court lifts restrictions on controversial voter database
summary: Trump and officials claimed database combats noncitizen voting but critics said it could disenfranchise eligible voters
text: The US supreme court has lifted restrictions on a controversial federal database of voters as Donald Trump seeks to impose tougher restrictions on voting ahead of November’s midterm elections. The ruling issued Friday by the chief justice, John Roberts, in the name of the court temporarily sets aside an injunction issued by US district judge Sparkle L Sooknanan, who ruled on 22 June against the Trump administration’s plan to use the Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements – Save – database to vet voter registration eligibility. A federal appeals court later declined to pause that ruling. The ruling sends the case back to the DC circuit court of appeals to be heard. “Today’s decision is profoundly disappointing, as it puts millions of Americans at risk of being unlawfully targeted by the administration’s unreliable voter purge database weeks before the midterm elections,” the League of Women Voters said in a prepared statement. “However, this case is not over. The D.C. district court ruled that the expanded SAVE program violated multiple laws. We will be doing everything in our power to protect Americans’ voting and privacy rights by ensuring that the district court decision stands.” The case stems from an executive order issued in March 2025 with the stated purpose of improving enforcement of laws barring noncitizens from voting in US elections. Among its provisions, the order directed the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and other agencies to make federal databases of citizenship information available to state elections directors. Other provisions of that executive order, like its demand to states to turn over their voter rolls to the federal goverment, remain bottled up in court. The League of Women Voters, the Electronic Privacy Information Center and other groups sued to block the use of the Save database, arguing that it was riddled with inaccuracies, and that taking social security numbers from the Social Security Administration violation of the Privacy Act, Social Security Act, and the Administrative Procedure Act. State officials had used social security numbers and other information obtained by DHS to conduct sweeping checks of the citizenship status of registered voters against federal records. Federal law prevents state election administrators from systematically striking people from the voter rolls within 90 days of an election, with or without the use of the Save database. However, the Friday ruling notes that “all agree that the order prevents the Federal Government from using the modified SAVE program to conduct individualized inquiries, which are permitted under federal law during this period.” That distinction matters in light of a DHS whistleblower’s allegations that the department has as part of its “Unlawful Voter Initiative” directed federal agents to impersonate voters in violation of state laws, using social security numbers and other information to look up voter history on state websites. US senators Alex Padilla and Adam Schiff, both California Democrats, sent a letter Monday to the state’s attorney general, Rob Bonta, asking for an investigation. “As you know, the U.S. Department of Justice has been unsuccessful in its attempt to compel California to provide its voter information to the Trump Administration, raising serious questions about what this data is, how DHS obtained it, and whether they complied with the law in collecting and using this data,” the letter said. “The fact that the DHS data was compiled with something called ‘supplemental magic’ does not provide reassurance.”

title: No general election before 2029, Andy Burnham says
summary: Prime minister quashes speculation that Labour’s revival in the polls could prompt early contest
text: Andy Burnham has said he will not call a general election before 2029, after days of speculation that Labour’s revival in the polls could tempt him to call an early contest. The prime minister was repeatedly questioned on the prospect during a round of broadcast interviews to regional media on Friday. He initially said he was “not particularly” tempted by the idea of an early election, but later became firmer, saying he would “knock that dead” and he was “not going to do that” because he was focused on getting on with the job. Asked by ITV Calendar whether the next election would be in 2029, Burnham said: “Well, yes, that’s when the next election will be. All of this speculation on an early election – I can knock that dead. “You know, people want me, new in office, to be getting on with the job of delivering on the things that we’ve discussed, rather than putting self-serving politics before that, which was what I would be doing if I call an election. I’m not going to do that.” Talk of an early election had grown during the last week after polls showed Labour pulling into the lead with support in the low 20s, and the Conservatives and Reform neck-and-neck a few points behind them. Westminster sources said Downing Street advisers and MPs had been discussing the merits of an early poll but that even though the right was split, Labour would be at risk of losing its majority and having to form a coalition. The Guardian revealed on Friday that Ravinder Athwal, the economist who wrote Labour’s 2024 manifesto, was taking on a senior role as an adviser to John Healey, the chancellor, to strengthen his team before the budget. This fuelled further speculation that the party’s preparations for a campaign were gathering pace. Athwal, a Cambridge economics graduate, devised Keir Starmer’s five “missions”, which were meant to shape Labour’s approach to government. Healey poached Athwal to be his senior special adviser from the business advisory group Flint Global, previously run by Burnham’s chief of staff, James Purnell, a Blair-era cabinet minister. All the parties had begun increasing their preparations for a potential campaign since Burnham replaced Starmer in the summer, in case he decided to take advantage of the bounce in his popularity. However, the prime minister has repeatedly ruled it out, both before and after taking office. In his regional interviews, he stressed his attention was on the party’s autumn conference, saying a big focus of his speech would be on setting out more details of a new model for the water industry that increases public control. He told BBC South: “As we go into the Labour conference, we will set out more thinking about the change that we need to see in the running of water across the country. But it is clear to me that what we’ve had in the last 30 years is nowhere near good enough and is actually letting the public pay.” During the interviews, Burnham confirmed reports that he would not be giving any exclusive interviews or articles to the Sun. The policy of declining special interviews with the newspaper has arisen from solidarity with victims of the Hillsborough disaster over the media outlet’s coverage of the 1989 tragedy that falsely blamed Liverpool fans for the deaths of supporters – for which it has since apologised. Leading up to the conference in Liverpool, Labour members have been cheered by Burnham’s takeover, which has led to a modest recovery in the party’s popularity. An MRP poll of more than 8,000 voters reported by the Guardian this week showed a significant shift of left-leaning voters towards Burnham’s Labour. This encouraged those in the party who have been thinking of gambling on an early election while Reform’s ratings are ebbing and while leftwing parties such as the Greens appear to be losing momentum. Twice as many voters have returned to Labour from the left as from the right since April. The previously unreleased research, including a seat-by-seat MRP model, was conducted by Survation and the progressive activist site 38 Degrees in Burnham’s first month as prime minister. It also showed progressive voters could push Reform UK into fourth place and put Labour within touching distance of a majority if tactical voting was widespread. Burnham is beginning to attract a significant number of left-leaning voters back to Labour, motivated by a desire to stop Nigel Farage, the results suggest.

title: Spacecraft returns to Earth after rescue mission for ageing Nasa telescope fails
summary: Series of in-flight problems meant Link, a ‘commercial space robot’, could not salvage the Nasa observatory
text: A spacecraft that was launched in July on a mission to rescue a decaying Nasa space observatory plunged back to Earth on Friday, concluding a failed mission that will be followed by the telescope’s own demise in several weeks’ time. Link, billed as “America’s first commercial space robot”, lifted off on 3 July from Kwajalein Atoll in the South Pacific islands with the objective of lifting the orbit and prolonging the life of the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory, a satellite that has studied gamma-ray bursts and other cosmic events for the last 22 years. It got as close as 7 to 9 miles (12km to 15km) to Swift and was able to take a series of images detailing its condition, but a series of earlier in-flight problems that hampered motion control and communications meant Link was unable to capture the observatory as planned and release it at a higher altitude. Katalyst Space Technologies, the company based in Flagstaff, Arizona, which won a $30m Nasa contract for the salvage mission in September 2024, and put together an ambitious rescue plan inside 22 months, announced in a press release Friday morning that its three-armed spacecraft had re-entered Earth’s atmosphere after 85 days in orbit. Without the altitude lift, Swift, a collaboration between Nasa and Penn State University that was launched in November 2004, will follow its own descent in the coming weeks, and is expected to re-enter Earth’s atmosphere in November. “From the beginning, this was a high-risk, high-reward mission,” Shawn Domagal-Goldman, director of Nasa’s astrophysics division, said in a statement. “While we’ll be sad to see Swift’s mission come to a close, we knew this boost effort would be worthwhile either way – advancing US spacecraft servicing technology, challenging us to meet unprecedented mission timelines, and testing how we operate satellites to extend their time in low Earth orbit.” Jared Isaacman, Nasa’s administrator, also praised the mission in a statement. “Nasa should be willing to move quickly and take smart risks when the potential return is worth it, and that is exactly what we did with this mission,” he said. “This is not the outcome we were working toward, but it does not change why this mission was worth attempting. The team moved with extraordinary speed to give Swift a chance to carry out more science while advancing capabilities America will need for satellite servicing in the future.” Ironically, Swift’s expected lifespan was shortened by the very intense flare-ups from the sun, which it was sent up to observe. Nasa suspended its observations earlier this year and repositioned Swift to try to minimize the atmosphere’s downward drag while preparing the rescue mission. Electronics issues on board Link after launch rendered inactive two of its three reaction wheels required for maneuvering, and at one point the spacecraft went into a deep spin. Communication and control were restored, but mission managers abandoned the rescue effort last month when it became clear there was insufficient fuel left.
