title: Healey appoints Labour manifesto writer, adding to election speculation
summary: Economist Ravinder Athwal, who worked in Keir Starmer’s team, is poached from Flint Global
text: Ravinder Athwal, the economist who wrote Labour’s 2024 manifesto, is taking on a senior role as an adviser to John Healey, in a move likely to fuel speculation about an early general election. The chancellor is keen to strengthen his team before the critical budget on 28 October, as the economy is buffeted by high oil prices and rising government borrowing costs. Healey has poached Athwal to be his senior special adviser from the business advisory group Flint Global, previously run by Andy Burnham’s chief of staff, the former Blair-era cabinet minister James Purnell. Athwal, a Cambridge economics graduate, was closely associated with drawing up Labour’s manifesto, and devising Keir Starmer’s five “missions”, which were meant to shape Labour’s approach to government. He worked as a senior economic adviser in Starmer’s Downing Street team but left after a year to join Flint Global. A source close to Healey said: “Having Rav join John’s team as an experienced heavyweight economist at the Treasury ahead of this budget will be invaluable. His political nous will add to the special adviser team, providing John with guidance and counsel to the chancellor.” Burnham flatly denied that he planned to call an early election on Friday. Asked by ITV Calendar whether the next general election would be in 2029, he said, “well, yes, that’s when the next election will be. All of this speculation on an early election, I can knock that dead.” Nevertheless, Athwal’s presence on Healey’s team could be seen as a strength if the prime minister did decide to draw up a fresh manifesto. Athwal’s arrival is also likely to increase concerns among some in Labour that the Treasury’s instinctive caution is fuelling a “continuity Starmer” approach to economics. The pledge at the heart of the manifesto not to increase income tax, national insurance or VAT was seen by Starmer’s team as key to Labour’s landslide victory two years ago. But it is widely agreed that it has restricted the party’s room for manoeuvre once in power. People with knowledge of Athwal’s thinking suggest he has learned from the travails of Labour’s early months in office, however. One left-of-centre economist said: “I’d say he was at the more interesting and curious end of the Starmerite project.” Before joining Labour, Athwal was a Treasury civil servant, rising to be head of growth strategy. One former colleague described him as “nice and clever – a good combination”. After taking over at the Treasury in July, Healey hired Will Straw, who played a leading role in the remain campaign during the Brexit referendum, to be his chief of staff; some of Rachel Reeves’s economic advisers, including Spencer Thompson, stayed on. Reeves’s chief economic adviser, the former Clean Bandit violinist Neil Amin-Smith, who was closely involved in her plans to devolve more tax revenue to local leaders, has moved across to Burnham’s No 10. Athwal is expected to arrive in post next week, a month before Healey’s first budget. With inflation and borrowing costs expected to have wiped out at least half of the headroom Reeves had built up against Labour’s fiscal rules, Healey faces a series of tough decisions. He has promised to maintain a “buffer against uncertainty” but this is widely expected to be significantly smaller than the £24bn in the spring forecast. Depending on the Office for Budget Responsibility’s forecasts, restoring the cushion in full would be likely to require large tax rises or spending cuts. But government sources say Healey wants this to be a “focused” budget, after Reeves used her two budgets as chancellor to increase taxes by £70bn a year. Key decisions about future tax and spending appear likely to be delayed until a Treasury spending review next year, which will come after Burnham has set out his long-term priorities in a 10-year plan, expected after the budget. Healey has made clear he does not intend to set a timetable for when the UK will spend 3% of gross domestic product on defence at the budget, for example – a target he insisted, when he resigned from Starmer’s government in June, must be met by 2030. However, hopes of a low-key budget are under pressure from persistently high global oil and gas prices, which make it likely that the energy price cap, which determines UK consumer bills, will rise sharply in January. Treasury sources have said officials are working “at pace” on options for consumer support, though help is expected to fall far short of the costly universal approach taken by Liz Truss in 2022. Flint Global was approached for comment.

title: Alberta’s self-image as world’s only rat-free region shattered by discovery of rat
summary: Province’s rat patrol called in to investigate as town of Bowden announces discovery of dead vermin
text: For more than seven decades, residents of Alberta have shared something in common with Antarctica and the high Arctic: all locations are officially free of rats. But on Thursday the Canadian province’s reputation as a firewall against rodent infestation took a hit when the town of Bowden announced the discovery of a dead rat and called on the province’s “rat patrol” to investigate. “If you’ve noticed rat droppings or any signs of rats, please contact Rat Patrol Alberta so they can follow up,” the town said in a statement. “Please stay alert and report any sightings.” Officials in Bowden did not say where in the town the rat was found. But as global temperatures increase, rat numbers have surged in major cities. Over the past decade, rats increased by 390% in Washington DC, 300% in San Francisco and 162% in New York, according to researchers, who analysed public sightings and infestation reports. Toronto, Canada’s largest city, is facing a “perfect rat storm”, with numbers up 186% in the last 10 years. Unlike other regions in the world that have been overrun by the wily and adaptable urban mammals, Alberta has actively fought rats from entering at all. “Albertans have enjoyed living without the menace of rats since 1950 when the Rat Control Program was established,” the province says in its rat guide. It cites both the province’s unique geography, with mountain ranges and boreal forest surrounding most of Alberta, and the fact that the Norway rat – “one of the most destructive creatures known to man”, the province claims – cannot survive in vast natural areas and cannot overwinter in cultivated fields. The very lack of the humans and their structures that rats need to survive has given the province a chance to ward off infestation. In the 1950s, suspecting rats might try to enter from the east by way of neighbouring Saskatchewan, Alberta officials created a “rat control zone” – a strip of land measuring 373 miles by 18 miles (600km by 30km) – to monitor incursions that ranges from Cold Lake in the north to the Montana border in the south. In addition, from June 1952 to July 1953, 140,000lb of 73% arsenic trioxide powder was used to treat 8,000 buildings on 2,700 farms to slow the spread of rats. The province also amended the Agricultural Pests Act of Alberta in 1950, obliging “every person and municipality” to destroy rats they found; made posters reminiscent of a national war effort; and hosted a radio show, Call of the Land, to educate residents. Today, there are dedicated telephone lines and an email address to report rats. But while the rat patrol receives hundreds of calls each year, it says the vast majority are not rats but muskrats, voles and field mice. Still, it concedes there are exceptions. “Alberta’s rat-free status means there is no resident population of rats and they are not allowed to establish themselves. It does not mean we never get rats.”

title: The dark art of maths and the AI revolution | Letter
summary: Letter: Bev Littlewood reminds us that mathematics has been the prime driver of the rise in AI, in response to an editorial
text: You report in your leader that some mathematicians feel discomfiture at the AI solution to a Navier-Stokes problem (The Guardian view on AI v mathematicians: humans are still vital to the field, but tech firms refuse to see that, 20 September). I fear that they have been hoist by their own petard: mathematics, after all, has been the prime mover of the AI revolution. As a somewhat lowly mathematician, let me remind others of the famous quote of Augustine: “The good Christian should beware the mathematician and all those who make empty promises. The danger already exists that the mathematicians have made a covenant with the devil to darken the spirit and to confine man in the bonds of hell.” While the accuracy of the quote, and Augustine’s meaning, are in some dispute, its appropriateness here is too good to waste. Bev Littlewood Emeritus professor of software engineering, City St George’s, University of London • Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Please email us your letter and it will be considered for publication in our letters section.

title: Why Ed Miliband has embraced his ‘awkward dad’ image in viral TikTok video
summary: About 1.5 million people have watched footage of foreign secretary that capitalises on social media’s love of a cringe moment
text: It sparked delight among the diehard Milifans and a begrudging smile from those less keen on the foreign secretary, but a viral video of Ed Miliband has – possibly – confirmed his status as the internet’s awkward dad. About 1.5 million people have viewed an interaction between Miliband and the TikTok personality Feroz Khan on the streets of New York, during which the digital content creator asks Miliband a series of questions including his name, job and his top piece of advice. Following the same formula employed by Khan in every video, Miliband is stopped in a seemingly – though of course not at all – impromptu manner by the influencer who says: “You’re very well dressed, what do you do for a living?” When Miliband, in New York for the UN general assembly, explains that he is the foreign secretary (adding that he is the UK equivalent of Marco Rubio when Khan claims not to know what that is), the influencer asks: “What makes your work so special?” Miliband gushes that he is “trying to make the world a better place”. So far, so soft serve. But it is when Miliband is asked about any challenges he has faced and, with the charm of an ingenue, replies – “Oh wow! I ran to be prime minister of Britain. It didn’t go so well … but I kept going!” – that it is clear his media team have fully capitalised on social media’s love of the cringe moment. Miliband has been on a journey since May 2014, when the then Labour leader was photographed ineptly eating a bacon roll during a campaign visit in New Malden. It was an image that launched a thousand memes and, occasionally, if daftly, was pointed to as a reason that Labour lost the 2015 general election. Freed of the shackles of leadership – and embraced by a generation that frames mortifying incidents as unifying moments – Miliband is now free to take pleasure in the delights of a vegan fruity flapjack, safe in the knowledge that the video of him doing so will probably bolster his particular internet aura rather than damage it. While Reform UK’s Lee Anderson wrote thunderously of the video, “Our Foreign Secretary! Putin will be quaking in his boots!”, his team were perhaps notching up the hits and watching Miliband’s expanding online presence. The PR consultant Mark Borkowski said: “Ed Miliband has finally worked out that the awkward dad thing isn’t a reputational defect. It’s his brand. In an age of politicians desperately trying to manufacture authenticity, the slight cringe actually makes him feel human. He’s not trying to be cool, he’s letting the socials enjoy the fact that he isn’t.” While the video nods to content consumers being in on the joke, some observers have pointed out that it is clearly staged rather than spontaneous, because Miliband’s aides do not stop when the foreign secretary starts speaking with a “stranger” and his answers seem rehearsed. A government source agreed that it may well indeed have been a remarkable coincidence if Miliband had just bumped into an internet celebrity who also just happens to bump into famous people including Jennifer Lopez, Sydney Sweeney and Bradley Cooper. “This isn’t Ed trying to hoodwink anyone. This is how these videos work – it’s really exciting working with content creators, but you have to outsource editorial control,” they said. “The vast majority of people who watch a video like this understand that the tone is native to the format.” With the clock of views ticking up, the video had clearly reached a lot of people who may have been unfamiliar with Miliband’s early oeuvre. But Borkowski said there was potential for the knowing nod about Miliband’s maladroit moments to backfire. “The danger comes when the choreography becomes visible,” he said. “Awkwardness works because it feels accidental. Once people think the ‘dad dancing’ has been Blackfriars Road focus-grouped, the joke shrivels.”

title: Ketanji Brown Jackson criticizes supreme court’s handling of emergency docket
summary: The associate justice called out her colleagues in a speech she made at the UDC school of law, hours after Trump filed his latest request
text: US supreme court justice Ketanji Brown Jackson acknowledged serious concerns about her colleagues’ handling of emergency requests, the method Donald Trump often uses to seek approval from the court. Jackson, one of the three liberal members of the supreme court, criticized the justices’ willingness to issue rulings via the “shadow docket”, saying it undermines the public’s faith in the judicial system. “There is a serious concern that the supreme court’s modern stay practices are having a disruptive and potentially corrosive effect,” Jackson told faculty and students at the University of the District of Columbia’s David A Clarke school of law on Thursday. Her comments came just hours after the Trump administration filed its latest emergency request – this time asking justices to allow officials to continue deporting immigrants to countries other than their own. The emergency docket, sometimes also referred to as the “shadow docket”, is where plaintiffs can request immediate relief from the supreme court in consequential cases. Justices can quickly grant or dismiss requests without conducting the same legal review that is typically required in merit cases or providing a lengthy explanation to the public. The Trump administration has used the method to rapidly push forward the US president’s agenda. Since returning to office in January 2025, the administration has filed more than 30 emergency requests. Many have been granted. Via emergency requests, the conservative wing of the supreme court has allowed Trump to temporarily end protections for migrants seeking asylum, eliminate transgender rights, roll back environmental protections, fire the officials in charge of independent federal agencies and more. The justices have faced criticism for their handling of emergency requests from members of Congress and the public. However, in July, justice Elena Kagan, another member of the liberal wing of the court, told Congress that she thought they were improving its handling of requests by providing some justification. Jackson pointed to that on Thursday, telling the audience that while the court “began to explain more”, it was “still not the full kind of explanation” that cases receive on the merits docket. “If we’re not careful, the emergency docket can and will become an end-run around the standard review process,” she added. As Jackson critiqued the court’s current methods, which have become more prominent under the second Trump administration, three of her colleagues dined with Trump and Chinese president Xi Jinping at the White House. Chief justice John Roberts and justices Brett Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett joined other officials for the state dinner to welcome Xi.

title: Pope Leo warns of AI threat to humanity at start of three-day France visit
summary: Pontiff says artificial intelligence must remain at service of people in first official papal visit to country in 18 years
text: Pope Leo has warned against losing humanity in a “paradise of machines” as he addressed global concerns over the dangers of artificial intelligence at the start of a three-day visit to France. “If we are to avoid losing our humanity amid a paradise of machines invading and conditioning our daily lives, there is an urgent need for people to be educated in ethical discernment, capable of seeing what is morally right,” he said in a speech at the Élysée. At a second address on Friday, the 71-year-old head of the Catholic church insisted that new technologies must “remain at the service of the human person rather than becoming yet another instrument of domination and injustice” in remarks to a gathering at the Paris headquarters ⁠of the UN culture and education body, ⁠Unesco. “Every science risks losing its proper meaning when pursued without ethics,” he said. “Certain artificial systems have even been given the name of our human faculty of thought: intelligence. At the same time, however, our ideas and relationships risk being impoverished by a process of dehumanisation.” He added: “While intelligence is attributed to computational systems, we struggle to recognise the inalienable dignity of human persons whose lives are judged according to the criterion of efficiency and when deemed no longer productive, rejected and discarded.” Leo also criticised world leaders who disrespect the ⁠rule of ⁠law, without naming individuals. “Instead of respecting ‌the law, ‌those in power invoke ‌it when it serves their interests and disregard it when it restrains them, treating even justice itself ‌as though it were a commodity to be bought and sold,” he said. Leo, who became pope in 2025, ⁠has been critical of the direction of global leadership in recent months. He said ‌the world was “being ravaged by a handful of tyrants” last April. The first official papal visit to France in 18 years comes as Emmanuel Macron’s decade in office draws to an end ahead of next spring’s French presidential election, for which the far-right, anti-immigration Marine Le Pen is polling high. Pope Francis did not make a full state visit to France during his 12-year pontificate and refused to join the inauguration of the rebuilt Notre Dame Cathedral in 2024. After France passed legislation in June granting some adult patients the right to assisted dying, the pontiff said he was concerned by trends “that risk turning science and technology into profit-driven ventures promoting genetic manipulation, surrogacy, the trade in human organs or the possibility of arranging one’s own death.” A key moment of the three-day visit will be a giant outdoor mass on Saturday, led by the pontiff at Place de la Concorde. The pope, whose paternal grandmother was born in France, on Friday urged Paris to remain a “tireless champion of peace” worldwide. On Monday, he will deliver a speech on European peace in the eastern city of Metz as Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine continues into its fifth year. Leo called on the world not to ⁠become indifferent to the pain caused by “the scourge of war”. He told Macron and other French politicians: “I urge you ‘… never to grow resigned to the prospect of war or to ⁠consider it ‘inevitable’.” Leo will also visit Lourdes, a pilgrimage site for Christians worldwide, where he will privately meet seven victims of clerical sex abuse. After some survivors’ groups suggested a larger number of survivors should have been canvassed, the Catholic church said the pontiff was seeking in-depth dialogue with individuals. France’s Catholic bishops’ conference has agreed to provide compensation after a 2021 report estimated that 330,000 children were sexually abused over 70 years by priests or other church-related figures in France. The report described a “systemic” cover-up by church officials. In recent years, further accusations have emerged, including against workers at the elite Catholic boarding school Notre-Dame de Bétharram, near Lourdes. On his flight to Paris, Pope Leo told reporters they were welcome to cover him, as he responded to the Trump administration’s attempt to bar US media from the White House and affirmed the importance of journalists covering public figures. Asked by a CNN reporter about Donald Trump’s attempt to bar CNN and other reporters, Leo said the media were welcome on his plane. “I am very happy that here, you are all welcome,” he said.

title: Trump faces tough choices as Iran dangles deal to reopen Hormuz before US midterms
summary: Iran’s seven-day timetable would restart nuclear talks, but will the US be willing to deliver on terms that include reining in Israel in Lebanon?
text: Iran’s seven-day timetable to reopen the strait of Hormuz and start talks on its nuclear programme has been pitched as a deal that could rapidly extricate Donald Trump from a political crisis but requires the US president to make difficult concessions. In the five days left before the proposed reopening of the strait, which is expected to relieve pressure on global energy markets, Trump would need to lift Iranian asset freezes, permit Iran to export its oil and, probably most difficult of all, order Benjamin Netanyahu to end Israel’s attacks on Hezbollah in Lebanon, thus achieving the “ceasefire on all fronts”. Iranian diplomats in New York said they thought a three-hour meeting earlier this week with the US envoy Steve Witkoff in which they laid out the seven-day plan was productive, but were doubtful the US would deliver. Iran nevertheless feels it has done the diplomatic spadework, taking the proposal to China for endorsement and ensuring that Oman, located on the south side of the strait, was also on board. The foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, explained that the idea was to take the elements of the Iran-US memorandum of understanding that Trump signed in June and repackage and accelerate the process since, as they understood it, Trump had come to hate the MoU. “The conditions we have asked the US to meet is nothing new, nothing more than what was already in the Islamabad agreement, which was signed by the US president,” Araghchi said. But what is new is the speed. In the first four to five days under this timetable, the US would have to lift the naval blockade on Iran’s oil ports, restore the waiver that lifted sanctions on Iran’s oil exports, end the war on all fronts and permit the release of some of Iran’s frozen assets. On the sixth day, the strait of Hormuz would be reopened by Iran, with ships using a new route designated by Oman and Iran. And on the next day, negotiations would start on the future of Iran’s civil nuclear programme, including a protocol to allow UN nuclear inspectors back in to look at Iran’s damaged sites and the stockpile of highly enriched uranium. This accelerates the point at which nuclear talks would begin, from 60 days in the June agreement to seven. Those talks could, of course, take a long time, but from Trump’s perspective, the strait of Hormuz would be reopened before the midterm elections, a point in the political calendar that the Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, says has never been a factor in Iranian thinking. Trump had claimed Iran was waiting until after the vote to offer a deal. Iran, Araghchi argued at a largely off-the-record briefing with reporters – at which Pezeshkian was also present – had every reason not to negotiate with the US. In particular, he admitted to being sceptical that Witkoff could deliver. He recounted how he had twice held talks with Trump’s special envoy, after which Witkoff had described them as “productive and good”, only for the US to bomb Iran the next day. Other Iranian diplomats say Trump’s willingness to rein in Netanyahu in Lebanon remains key. If he could do that, a deal would be feasible. It is a difficult deal for Trump to swallow since the strait would reopen largely on Iran’s terms, with the new route predominantly going through Iranian waters. Saudi Arabia is also concerned that the route deal is bilateral between Iran and Oman, and not with the Gulf states as joint signatories. Trump says he has a choice to make between the annihilation of Iran and engagement – an engagement that, he says with typical hyperbole, could make Iran one of the great countries of the world. In reality, the judgment he has to make is more prosaic. Is he prepared to go back to war with Iran after the midterms and, if not, does he believe the US can squeeze the Iranian economy so hard that the leadership will succumb. Pezeshkian, who handed all questions about the talks to Araghchi, admitted Iranians wanted the war to end and did not deny the economic pressure, but said the public had withstood sanctions for 45 years. He also insisted Iran’s decision-making machinery was functioning. The reclusive supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, was completely healthy, he claimed, a testimony based on spending seven hours in his presence. He did not explain why, apart from security, Khamenei had not issued a voice recording, photograph or video as proof of life.

title: Republican Florida congressman introduces bill requiring warrants for Flock Safety cameras
summary: Greg Steube’s Flafo Act would require federal agencies to obtain warrants before accessing or sharing data from networked license plate readers
text: A Florida Republican has introduced a bill that would bar US federal agencies from using Flock Safety’s licence plate cameras and similar systems without a warrant, amid a nationwide backlash against the surveillance company. Greg Steube’s Facilitating Liberty and Accountability for Flock Observations (Flafo) Act, introduced on Friday, would require a judicial warrant before federal agencies could buy, operate, access or share data with networked licence plate readers. It would also make US Department of Justice grants to local police conditional on their adopting similar rules. “Americans should not be tracked everywhere they drive without a warrant,” Steube wrote in a statement. “The government has no business tracking law-abiding Americans.” Although the bill covers any company that makes the technology, it is aimed squarely at Flock. The Atlanta-based firm operates about 120,000 readers (with thousands more planned) across every state except Alaska, according to its website, and accounts for more than 80% of the market. Its cameras photograph passing vehicles and log their plate numbers, make, model and location into databases that police in other jurisdictions can search. Steube pointed to investigations in Florida, Indiana, Illinois and Wisconsin that found officers had misused those databases. His proposal is the third of its kind in a month. On 2 September, Thomas Massie, a Kentucky Republican, introduced the Flock-Off Act, which would prohibit federal money from being used to buy, install, maintain, operate or upgrade licence plate readers and biometric surveillance cameras. The bill drew co-sponsors from both parties, including the California Democrat Ro Khanna and the Republicans Chip Roy and Lauren Boebert. Two weeks later, Raja Krishnamoorthi, an Illinois Democrat, and Michael Cloud, a Texas Republican, introduced the No Flock Act in response to reports of officers using the technology to stalk former partners. That bill would give states two fiscal years to limit the cameras to five approved uses or lose 10% of certain federal transportation funding. The Republican critics are at odds with Donald Trump, who told reporters aboard Air Force One this month that he liked the cameras because of their value to law enforcement. “Some people don’t. They think it’s an infringement,” he said. “I like them.” But the cross-party interest in Washington reflects the displeasure nationwide. Anti-surveillance watchdog Secure Justice’s Flock Termination Tracker found that cities in 36 states from Florida to Colorado have cancelled their Flock contracts so far, with Santa Cruz becoming the first California city to drop the company in January, and more than a dozen others in the state have followed. In Indiana, Fort Wayne and several counties have voted in the past month to cancel or not renew their contracts. In Arizona, Chandler ended its contract after an investigation found an officer had misused the system. The Institute for Justice, a libertarian law firm, says it has documented more than 200 cases of abuse stemming from automated license plate readers, including stalking and wrongful stops. Steube’s home state has already moved. At the start of September, Florida’s transportation department revoked all permits for local police to operate license plate readers on state roads, ordering existing cameras removed within 30 days. The week before, Texas governor Greg Abbott halted state funding for the cameras, pre-empting a Texas Tribune investigation that a state agency had spent at least $30m building out the state’s Flock network. Flock did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

title: Couple jailed for at least 21 years for murder of vulnerable man in their care
summary: Kenneth Newton and Melanie James filmed themselves mocking and abusing Rubin Blount, 28, who weighed 40kg when he died
text: A couple convicted of murder after inflicting “deliberate cruelty” on a vulnerable 28-year-old man in their care, who at the time of his death weighed just 40kg (6st 4lb), have been jailed for life. Rubin Blount was made to stand for long periods of time, left to lie in his own urine and forced to eat out of bins by his stepbrother Kenneth Newton and Newton’s partner, Melanie James, at a property in Tamworth, Staffordshire, Stafford crown court heard. Newton, 58, and James, 64, both from Birmingham, who had filmed themselves mocking and abusing the victim, were convicted by a jury in July of his murder. Jailing them each for a minimum of 21 years, Mrs Justice Jefford said they had been in a position of trust which they had abused and had shown an “abject failure to help him when he was in pain and suffering”. Blount was severely dehydrated and malnourished when he was taken to hospital after he became unwell, and he had a cardiac arrest upon arrival. He died three days later on 30 November 2022. Doctors found he had extensive pneumonia, severe infection, fractures to his ribs and spine, and burns, lesions and grazes. He had 50 rib fractures, 47 of which had been inflicted in the weeks leading up to his death. Jennifer Josephs KC, prosecuting, told Friday’s sentencing hearing that Blount had been described as “considerably mentally impaired” and was particularly vulnerable, and that the defendants’ “cruel” behaviour towards him was demonstrated in videos shown to the jury. Josephs said Blount must have been in “extreme pain and suffering” before his death, and the couple had denied him access to medical care until he was “beyond help”. “Mr Blount’s death was the culmination of a prolonged course of conduct perpetrated against a man who was unable to speak for himself,” she said. Blount’s mother, Jeanette Blount, said in a victim impact statement that her son was vulnerable and deserved “compassion, dignity and a chance to live his life”. “We all believed they loved him and would take care of him. We had no reason to believe otherwise,” she said. The judge said a series of videos made by the defendants on 2 November 2022 “show Rubin emaciated, gaunt, stooped and broken, standing in the doorway”. Videos showed the pair mocking him and flinging abuse at him while he was “unable to defend himself or even walk away”. “The first 25 rib fractures were inflicted before or shortly after this recording was made,” she added. James sobbed as the court was told that the abuse and violence inflicted on Blount went on for months. Rebecca Wade KC, defending James, said: “No one could fail to be disgusted by Melanie James’s actions towards this vulnerable man. She is a woman who has had a difficult life of her own. “There is some evidence to show that at one point she did care for Rubin and did love him, and him her.” Something “shifted”, she said, due to James’s “ability to cope with the stresses and strains of life and that was much to Rubin’s detriment”. Mark Heywood KC, defending Newton, said Blount was, through no fault of his own, a “challenging” person to care for. The circumstances leading to his death “can’t be dealt with as simply as saying he was financially advantageous for them, or that he became a burden”, he said. The couple were “ill-equipped”. Speaking outside the court, DCI Ian Fitzgerald, of Staffordshire police, said: “The extent of the injuries Rubin suffered, the state that he was in and the arrogance [of the defendants] in the way they thought they could try and get away with it and blame him for his injuries was shocking and very, very distressing.”

title: OpenAI hack on Australian government reveals anxiety at heart of global artificial intelligence dilemma
summary: As the UN warns traditional safeguards are ‘unravelling’, Donald Trump says he will encourage, not restrain, the AI race
text: When the Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, sat down for an interview in the heart of Silicon Valley at the weekend he had known for two days that his was the first government known to have been attacked by a rogue AI agent. He didn’t reveal the attack then, but he sounded a warning about the march of AI: “the risk is that AI develops in a way in which humans are no longer in control of what AI is producing.” But Albanese noted, too, that two countries – the US and China – would dominate the world’s response to the new technology. “The truth is they’re the big two giants here, and so we want to see cooperation,” Albanese said. “The US is essentially ahead of China when it comes to the race that is on for the development of this new technology. But it is in the world’s interests that there be engagement.” Days later, Albanese used the global attention of the United Nations general assembly meeting in New York to reveal that Australia’s government healthcare system, Medicare, had been attacked by an OpenAI agent in June, but that it was three months before his government was told. Again he warned of “the potential risks of allowing frontier AI to develop too fast without guardrails”. China’s president, Xi Jinping, skipped the general assembly in favour of a bilateral meeting with the US president, where he emphasised the responsibility to manage AI “for good, and ensure that the development of AI is always under human control and serves the wellbeing of the people”. But the president of the United States – the nation which is the global leader in artificial intelligence – used his general assembly address to insist he would only encourage, not restrain, the AI race. Alarms sounding To little fanfare earlier in the week, the UN’s independent international scientific panel on AI warned a threshold had already been crossed. There was, the panel, said: “no assurance that humans can reliably keep AI agents under control today, particularly as they become more capable, harder to monitor and better at finding loopholes or hiding their activity”. The Australian government had known the reality of this for more than a week. OpenAI had known it more than a month. Two days after the panel’s statement, the Australian prime minister belatedly revealed an OpenAI agent had hacked medical data held by Australia’s universal health care provider, Medicare. No patient data had been accessed, but the agent had gained unauthorised access to “non-public files”. OpenAI’s agent hacked the government sites in June of this year. OpenAI discovered its agent had gone rogue in August. It did not tell the Australian government until 10 September, and then only with a solitary email to a generic public email address not checked until the next day. The prime minister was informed on 18 September. It was another week before the Australian people were told. Australia has promised, if it is possible, to lay criminal charges, though this is complicated by the fact that OpenAI claims the hack was committed by an AI agent – apparently acting beyond its instructions (euphemised by OpenAI as “misaligned behaviour”) – not a person. The hack on Australia’s Medicare statistics reporting service portal, as well as three other government sites, follows the Hugging Face incident in July, in which autonomous AI agents developed by OpenAI broke out of their isolated testing environments, coordinated themselves into a “swarm” and launched a cyber-attack on competitor AI platform Hugging Face. The UN panel, investigating that attack, warned “the traditional method of safeguarding is unravelling” as AI agents act autonomously to breach protections. “The default interpretation and immediate lesson is that basic cybersecurity practices were overlooked, and safeguards are not advancing at the pace of capabilities. The more insidious and grave concern is that current training methods can lead agents to adopt goals of their own, knowingly violate safety instructions, and conceal their actions.” Twenty countries (including Australia) and the EU this week signed a statement arguing the rapid development of frontier AI models posed serious risks to safety and security if not properly managed. “AI must remain under human direction, oversight and control. It must be developed and used in line with international law.” Too soon? Even those running AI companies have warned the technology is developing too rapidly for humans to control. Appearing before the UN security council this week, OpenAI’s chief executive, Sam Altman, warned: “some of the things people working to build AI have said are so dystopian that they sound like the plot of bad science fiction movies”. “As AI systems become more capable and more autonomous, they can move faster than our institutions … or make decisions that people no longer understand or control.” But there are at least two – very loud – voices in opposition to any external regulation of the AI industry. Elon Musk, who co-founded OpenAI with Altman before falling out with him, said in a recent interview the “smart move” would be to have the “leading AI companies at least just meet or have some sort of call once every few weeks and just discuss any safety and security issues”. Musk said AI would probably be beyond the control of humans within a decade, and that humanity should “enjoy the ride”. “I still think there’s risk associated with AI and robots. It’s not zero … my sort of philosophical conclusion is to look on the bright side. I can’t see any way to really stop this incredible momentum of AI and robots. “If there was a stop button, we probably shouldn’t press it, because the most likely outcome is incredible abundance for all.” Donald Trump used his speech to the UN general assembly to attempt to rebrand AI, and insist it should never be reined in. “The United States also totally rejects any attempt to construct a globalist scheme to control for the artificial intelligence being spoken of so much now,” the US president said. Trump wants to re-label artificial intelligence “superintelligence”. “I’m not going to stifle growth of something that will be bigger than the Industrial Revolution. “We’re going to encourage it, not rein it in.” Trump said the US was “leading China by a lot” in AI, and would continue to do so “safely and responsibly”. “Whoever wins superintelligence, wins.”

title: ‘Major milestone’: TfL to launch new public bus operator in London
summary: Buses for London aims for ‘greener, safer and better-value’ service but private operators say move will not fix problems
text: A publicly owned company, Buses for London, will start running services in the capital next year, Transport for London has announced. TfL said the launch was a “major milestone” in its plans to improve buses for drivers and passengers. The new public company will take over a handful of London’s bus routes, which number nearly 700 in total, from late 2027, starting with route 6, which runs between Willesden and Victoria station. A further four routes to be run by the public company from 2028 are to be announced. TfL said the creation of a publicly owned bus company would give it greater control over how services were run, allowing it to make buses more reliable and safe, and to reinvest profits into improving the transport network. At present, TfL contracts bus services to eight privately owned operators. The mayor of London, Sadiq Khan, said: “This is an opportunity to reimagine our bus network so that it provides better value for money, supports our climate goals, makes our roads safer, and overall just works better for passengers and drivers alike.” London’s buses have been getting gradually slower and passenger numbers have fallen over the past decade, as they battle with congestion and demands on road space in the capital. Lorna Murphy, TfL’s director of buses, said the public company marked “an exciting new chapter”, with a depot in the Old Oak regeneration area that would be “the first home of a new generation of zero-emission buses … helping us to build on the progress we’ve already made towards a more sustainable transport system”. Unions welcomed the move but private operators said the taxpayer would foot the bill for investment and take on more risk. The Unite general secretary, Sharon Graham, said: “Unite has long been calling for London’s bus services to be returned to public ownership. Outsourcing to private companies hasn’t worked well for workers or passengers. “For too long, bus workers have been subjected to intolerable working conditions and passengers have experienced worsening services, while bus firms and their shareholders rake in huge profits.” The union’s national officer for passenger transport, Wayne King, said it was “only the beginning”. He said Unite expected Buses for London to “lead the way in workers’ pay, terms and conditions and treatment and will hold TfL and the mayor to account on this”. The Confederation of Passenger Transport, representing bus firms, said it would not fix London’s buses. Graham Vidler, the chief executive of CPT, said: “Passengers don’t need a new public bus operator. They need faster, more reliable journeys and investment should be made where passengers will actually feel the difference: tackling congestion, giving buses priority and getting London moving. “Regardless of who operates the service, buses typically travel at just 9 mph in London – slower than the average cyclist.” He said private operators had made significant investment in London’s bus network, including new vehicles and technology, adding: “The uncertainty created by a new publicly owned operator risks making it harder for private operators to make the case for continued investment in London in the future.” Labour’s bus overhauls since 2025, which push wider franchising and public control of services, have also made it possible for local authorities nationwide to establish new publicly owned companies. A few municipal companies, such as Reading, Blackpool and Nottingham, survived deregulation and privatisation in the 1980s.

title: ‘Robust little’ vessel begins treacherous 22,000km journey around Antarctica in the name of climate science
summary: Powered by sun and wind, the uncrewed vehicle will collect data to help Australian scientists better understand how oceans absorb emissions
text: A small uncrewed vessel has embarked on a lap around Antarctica and may not return for months. The seven-metre craft, which looks like a large kayak in hi-vis orange, is expected to travel about 22,000km through inhospitable waters, propelled by powerful westerly winds and energy from the sun. The journey is seven times the distance between Sydney and Perth. Along the way, it is expected to encounter massive waves, freezing temperatures, ferocious winds, and even the odd curious seal or albatross. The mission? To collect data on carbon dioxide in the ocean and atmosphere, to help scientists better understand the role of ocean sinks. Dr Elizabeth Shadwick, a principal research scientist at the CSIRO, said that after leaving Hobart the vessel would travel east towards New Zealand, “eventually scooching through the Drake Passage between the bottom of South America and Antarctica, then coming along past South Africa and back to us here, where we’ll pick it up.” She hoped to see it again in seven to nine months. The autonomous vehicle made by the US maritime company Saildrone was designed to withstand the intrepid voyage, with a heavy keel keeping it upright, a rudder to steer and a fixed solar sail poking above the surface. It would be remotely monitored by the company, who would check in regularly via satellite, and, if necessary, nudge it in the right direction. “It’s already been bashed around pretty heavily,” Shadwick said. “It’s quite a robust little device. We saw some eight metres of waves just the day after we deployed it and a 35-knot wind.” Measurements taken throughout its journey – including wind speed, atmospheric pressure, solar radiation, ocean temperature, salinity and chlorophyll, as well as carbon dioxide levels in the water and air – were expected to assist scientists in better understanding the role that oceans play in global heating. “The ocean is doing all of us a great service by absorbing about a third of anthropogenic or human emissions every year,” Shadwick said, and the Southern Ocean, around Antarctica, played a significant role. “If we want to continue to rely on this ocean service of absorbing our human emissions, we need to understand how it might change in the future.” Crewed research vessels that travelled between Hobart and Antarctica traversed only a limited patch of the ocean, she said. The autonomous craft would gather data over a greater distance and time, including crucial measurements during the polar winter. The vessel is the first in a fleet of four. Others are planned to be launched at three-monthly intervals. They will be spread across the Southern, Pacific, Atlantic and Indian oceans, particularly during winter. The scientists will be able to access information in near real time via a mission portal, and once the vessels return to home base, all data and observations will undergo quality checks before they are made available for further research. Dr Pep Canadell, a chief research scientist at the CSIRO, said for every tonne of carbon dioxide released by burning fossil fuels, about 500kg were removed by ocean and forest sinks. “This is like a 50% discount on climate change,” he said. But the amount absorbed by the oceans could change due to multiple drivers: warming waters, westerly winds, melting ice, ocean acidification and the hole in the ozone layer. Observations would enable scientists to more accurately model these processes and understand how they could change in the future, he said. The University of New South Wales professor Matthew England, who studies the role of ocean circulation in global climate but was not involved in the research project, said measuring how much the oceans absorbed and how that was changing was critical. “We’ve obviously got a surge of emissions going into our atmosphere. Both the terrestrial vegetation on land and the oceans absorb a big chunk of that,” he said. “We need to track that carbon uptake and understand exactly how big the absorption is. If it starts to decline in a significant way, then it tells us that we have an even bigger problem of carbon emission reductions.” The Southern Ocean was “inhospitable” with huge swells, gale force winds, sea ice and storms. “These are very tough measuring conditions for a research vessel.” So gathering data using an autonomous vehicle, without burning fuel, was “an incredible deployment of technology”, he said.

title: I saw pedestrians swear at plovers when they swooped. But I admired the birds
summary: Many people despise these birds for violently defending their babies in nests they create in ridiculously vulnerable areas. My community, however, became devoted to them
text: It was early September when the two spur-winged plover chicks hatched. They hit the ground running, literally. Shortly after emerging from the speckled brown eggs their mother had laid in a shallow divot, they were scurrying around on their disproportionately long, stilt-like legs. They looked like fluffy brown and white cotton balls that could blow away in the wind. The nesting ground was on the headland above a popular tidal pool in Maroubra, in Sydney’s south-east. Adorned with black crowns and bright yellow masks on either side of their bright yellow beak, the chicks’ parents were always close by – and always on guard. They provided protection from the cold, letting their free-roaming chicks tuck themselves under their fluffy white breasts for warmth. And, like all good plover parents, they took turns swooping any intruder – person, dog or drone – who ignored their warning call and came too close – a loud “kekekekekekekek”. A few times I thought I was watching the family from a safe distance only to find myself having to quickly duck to avoid their grey-brown wings clipping my ears. Plovers, otherwise known as masked lapwings, are common throughout northern, central and eastern Australia. These long-legged birds resembling masked superheroes typically inhabit mudflats, marshes, beaches and grasslands – but they’re often seen in urban areas too. They are sometimes referred to as spur-winged plovers due to each wing being armed with a yellow spur, which they use when diving at intruders during breeding season. Both sexes share the building of the nest, which is a very shallow scoop in the ground away from ground cover where they also both take turns sitting on their precious eggs. In urban areas, these shallow homes can be found on playing fields, or median strips, or sometimes the roofs of buildings. Many people despise these birds for their apparent mix of stupidity and stubbornness – insisting on violently defending the nests they’ve created in ridiculously vulnerable areas. Indeed, I saw several pedestrians swear and shout at the plovers on the headland when they swooped. But I admired how fiercely and fearlessly they protected their family. I became devoted to them. They lived a short walk from my apartment, and every morning and evening I wandered down to check on how the chicks were faring. Amid all of the bleak news of mass bird deaths caused by the arrival of H5N1 bird flu in Australia, they were a source of much-needed hope. Focusing on them – even if just for a few minutes each day before and after work – made me feel just a little less despairing. But I was also nervous for them. This was the third consecutive season the parents had nested in this place. With unlimited ocean views and open grassland, it’s a fine spot to raise a family. But it also comes with many risks for vulnerable chicks: dogs, cats, foxes, resident birds of prey, cars, steep cliffs that drop into the ocean. The parents knew about these risks all too well. The last two breeding seasons ended in tragedy. All of the chicks died, some squished on the nearby road by speeding cars only days before they might have taken flight. As happened during the last two unsuccessful breeding seasons, there were several other locals watching over the family this year, reminding people to keep their dogs leashed to give the chicks the best chance of survival. Volunteers from the local branch of Wires, the largest wildlife rescue organisation in Australia, placed signs around the perimeter of the nesting site to reiterate the message and warn of heavy fines for harming native wildlife. Some people listened. Many did not. I feared something bad had happened when I walked down to check on the chicks one morning, about a week after I first spotted them. I could not find them at their usual spot. They weren’t there that evening, nor the following day. I texted one of the local Wires volunteers to ask if she had seen the chicks in the past few days. She hadn’t – nor, she added, had anyone else she knew who was keeping watch over them. “I think we’ve lost them again,” she said. The parents had disappeared from the headland too. Were they grieving the loss as I and other locals were? Nonhuman animals at the very least respond to the death of a companion or offspring. Humpback whales, for example, have recently been observed caring for a deceased newborn calf off Australia’s Gold Coast. Orcas have been seen carrying their dead calves through the ocean for weeks. Elephants visit the bones of dead family members. Crows gather around the corpse of one of their flock, in a funeral-like ritual. The parents are now back at the headland, where the Wires signs still stand like solemn grave markers. Without chicks to protect, they have become shy and timid again, moving away from anyone who walks by rather than swooping and shrieking as they once did. It’s easy to wonder why they don’t learn to go elsewhere, given the repeated tragedies they’ve experienced here. But perhaps it’s better to wonder about how we might learn to live more harmoniously with them, as well as all of the other animals we share our suburbs and cities with. I’ll show up to check on any chicks that might hatch in future, however futile it seems. From my apartment, I can still hear the birds calling in the distance, and I’m grateful for their persistent “kekekekekekekek” ringing out across the neighbourhood.

title: It’s going to take more than an email to a public inbox to protect Australians from potential AI doom | Tom McIlroy
summary: OpenAI’s hack of Medicare suggests safeguarding civilisation is the task facing leaders in this extraordinary new era
text: More than 130 world leaders descended on the United Nations headquarters in New York this week, joining the pageantry and speechmaking of the annual general assembly. Many of the visiting presidents and prime ministers delivered their set-piece addresses to a sparsely populated hall, but contributions from two unlikely visitors in the nearby security council chamber stood out. OpenAI boss Sam Altman and Dario Amodei of Anthropic gave briefings on the safety of artificial intelligence on Wednesday, as a nervous world watched on. Speaking in the room where some of the biggest questions to face humanity have been deliberated on since the end of the second world war, Altman said the world faced a choice. AI could be like a renaissance of creativity and discovery, he said, or more like a new Industrial Revolution bringing upheaval and disarray. “If AI is to be democratic, the most important decisions cannot be made by labs in San Francisco alone. They must be shaped through democratic processes and by governments accountable to the people that they serve,” Altman said. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email The words rang hollow less than 24 hours later, when Altman was the subject of an angry phone call from Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, after revelations a rogue OpenAI agent had hacked into sensitive Medicare systems in Australia. Altman and his colleagues had kept the incident secret for two months. As people become more anxious about the risk posed by AI to civilisation, Albanese grasped the company’s transgression as proof that democratically elected governments need to impose guardrails on the technology. Already, many believe the risk of AI slipping out of human control is a threat akin to the Covid-19 pandemic or a nuclear arms race. Like his government’s moves to ban children under 16 from using social media, and forcing platforms to give users the ability to opt out of powerful algorithms, Albanese wants to use new AI laws as a way to curb the creeping sense of helplessness so many people feel in the face of big tech. But Thursday’s announcement that government websites had been compromised by OpenAI showed that serious vulnerabilities and failures of process exist within both the company and the federal government. The hack happened in June, but it took OpenAI executives until September to alert Services Australia that statistical data on Medicare use had been accessed. Despite the company’s corporate might – and an army of well-paid government relations executives and lobbyists – OpenAI deemed it appropriate to send an email to a public-facing Australian government address to raise the alarm, months after the hack. It’s incredible the email wasn’t mistaken for spam. Wholly inadequate to the point of recklessness, the company’s actions show contempt for the Australian government and its citizens, whose healthcare data had been stolen. Worse, Altman met with Australia’s defence minister, Richard Marles, in early September but did not tell him about the hack. It took time for the public service to react to OpenAI’s email. Because the public inbox is checked routinely only once a day, the email was first read by staff within Services Australia on 11 September. It was not until 15 September that the intelligence agency the Australian Signals Directorate was informed, and two more days before the relevant minister, Katy Gallagher, was alerted. Then on 22 September, public servants asked OpenAI for more information about the scale of the hack. An investigation was quickly launched and the public finally informed. Albanese himself was only told after leaving for New York. The government’s planned AI legislation – expected to be finalised before Christmas and considered by parliament next year – must surely include mandatory reporting requirements for AI companies. Future notifications must come from senior officials within the responsible entity to ensure they are taken seriously. Sending an alert to a public email inbox will not cut it. On Friday, the assistant technology and digital economy minister, Andrew Charlton, said the government would take advice on possible referrals for criminal investigation, and that any legal liability would have to be traced back to the intent of a person or a company that created or directed an AI agent to hack. The terms of reference for a rapid investigation, released by the prime minister’s department on Thursday, cover reporting requirements for AI-driven cyber-incidents and vulnerabilities; governance and information sharing responsibilities for federal officials; obligations on AI firms for timely disclosure of breaches; gaps in existing laws; and mechanisms to boost protection against hacking that targets the federal government. Before leaving the US on Friday, Albanese floated the idea of creating an international authority with governance and investigative powers to help governments protect their people. The general sense of vulnerability to AI comes after a top safety researcher at Anthropic this month warned AI is advancing so quickly there is a greater than 10% chance it “could kill all humans” within the next decade. Not helping is the spectacle of Donald Trump and Xi Jinping dining with Altman and other tech bosses at a White House state dinner. Trump has resisted pressing the breaks on AI for fear China will develop a new strategic advantage over the US. Behind closed doors Xi apparently proposed continuing a dialogue with Trump to prevent AI “misuse and abuse”, while ahead of an expected drubbing in the November midterm elections, Trump said AI “concerns the future of humanity”. The latest revelations from OpenAI will have done little to reassure anyone in Australia. In this extraordinary new era, world leaders must address our creeping sense of helplessness and start protecting civilisation. Tom McIlroy is Guardian Australia’s political editor

title: ‘We will get stuff done’: Burnham seeks to banish ghosts of Starmerism at Labour conference
summary: The PM returns to Liverpool, where he was mocked last year, with a promise that no one will be left wondering what he’s trying to do
text: Andy Burnham was not even in the audience for the prime minister’s speech at the Labour party conference this time last year. As Keir Starmer made the case for continuity to his restive party, Burnham was spotted slipping out over the bridge towards Liverpool’s Albert Dock. The then Greater Manchester mayor had been vying for the spotlight throughout the party’s annual gathering, presenting the argument for change. But even he could not have envisaged the schism that would take place in the ensuing 12 months and would put him on the main stage as prime minister at this year’s conference, beginning in Merseyside on Sunday. At the time, Starmer retained a tentative grip on the party, while Burnham was mocked for leaving Liverpool with his tail between his legs, awkward and abashed, especially over his controversial comments about the government being too “in hock” to the bond markets. But below the surface, disquiet was starting to take shape in the party. Several cabinet ministers confided privately in Liverpool last year that they believed Burnham would ultimately be seen as the party’s Cassandra: comically ham-fisted, but nonetheless telling hard truths about the party’s problems. After he succeeded Starmer in the top job in July, Burnham has made “Hope again” his conference slogan, with No 10 strategists pitching this year’s event as a definitive break with the past. Burnham has been promising to defy the political and economic consensus of the last 40 years since he was elected as MP for Makerfield in a byelection that proved to be the final domino for Starmer’s faltering leadership, and he will use this conference to set out how he aims to do this. It will also attempt to break old habits in the Labour party’s way of doing business, which has often been hindered by pessimism, fear and factionalism. Cynics in the party will wonder if this effort can withstand current economic pressures, given soaring borrowing costs. Hayden Munro, Burnham’s new political director, has told cabinet ministers and special advisers they must defy such cynics, and every message they send must be about how there is renewed faith in Britain. Munro, a former strategist for Jacinda Ardern, who colleagues say is the “in-house hype man”, told them the theme of conference would be how help was coming for ordinary working people. Burnham’s government would put care of people as the first consideration, he told them, restoring “the right values” – a nod to the widespread fears in Labour about the rise of overt racism across the political sphere. Ministers have been tasked with announcing policies that deliver immediate breathing room for families, but also long-term plans and investment to make everyday life easier and more affordable, with a particular focus on public control of essential services. Burnham will emphasise again that he intends to deliver the biggest change to Britain in 40 years. But the other theme of the conference will be courage, that this will finally be a government that will fix problems long been thought to be intractable: rough sleeping, social care, and youth inactivity. “‘It’s too hard’ will no longer be used as a justification for not acting,” Munro wrote in his note to advisers. “We will get stuff done.” Addressing the Labour conference in Liverpool is a kind of homecoming for Burnham, even though he is most closely associated with Manchester. He was born in its suburbs, it is where he had his formative political awakening on the Hillsborough injustice, and the area where he returned just a fortnight ago in tragic circumstances, after his father’s death from Alzheimer’s. Burnham writes all of his own speeches and has spent the last few weeks, in between meetings and travelling by train between London and Manchester, working through his ideas. He told reporters at the UN general assembly in New York this week that his conference speech would be his own political philosophy spelled out in primary colours. “I keep saying: ‘Nobody won’t know what I’m trying to do.’ People will know, you can make your judgment on whether it’s right or wrong. But people are going to know the direction I want to take this country in,” he said. This approach marks a definitive break with Starmerism. One Labour strategist said: “If we achieve one thing at this conference, it will be that no one will ever say about Andy Burnham what they said about Keir Starmer. You can never say ‘we don’t know what he stands for’.” Burnham is the beneficiary of a gentler political landscape than Starmer was a year ago, when Reform and the rapid rise of far-right demonstrations had dominated the summer. Labour had been sinking in the polls even before the scandal-fuelled resignations of Angela Rayner and Peter Mandelson just weeks before the event. Going into conference now, Labour is in the lead with all pollsters for the first time since October 2024, partly thanks to Burnham’s own bounce but also as a result of declining trust in Reform after a series of scandals. There is very little appetite for rebellion among the Labour rank and file who have often made it awkward for Labour leaders with votes on the conference floor. “It is going to be very boring,” one senior party figure said. “Everyone is desperate to make it work.” Activists will be pushing for conference to commit to a commission on electoral reform, which Burnham has said he will put in Labour’s next manifesto but which strategists do not want to make a major topic of his first months in office. At least three dozen local parties have submitted motions on the subject, more than on any single policy issue since conference rules were tightened in 2023, making it likely it will be one of the priority topics for debate. The only other unwelcome surprise would be an emergency motion on Israel and Palestine. Ministers had hoped Ed Miliband’s announcement of sweeping sanctions against West Bank settlements would be an answer to calls for Labour to take a much more robust position on Israel. But party staff believe something more could come when emergency motions are tabled this weekend. “There is always another demand, and conference will always vote for almost anything put in front of it on this,” another senior figure said. “The unions have very left policy mandates.” Most of the exiled former cabinet ministers and Starmer loyalists are swerving conference this year – the exception being Darren Jones, the former chief secretary to the prime minister, who will take part in some keenly watched fringes. But few have his inclination. One ex-minister said he did not feel welcome. “No one wants a spectre at the feast,” he said. “Any appearance is going to attract some unwelcome attention. I do think more of us will start to speak out, whether on oil and gas, on the economy, maybe on Europe, but frankly doing that at conference is too unhelpful – even if it’s the kind of tactic that Andy himself has been doing for years.” Many said they saw it as a chance for a break. One former minister close to Starmer compared himself to Arsenal’s Declan Rice, who played more minutes last season than any other English footballer but who will now sit out England’s matches over the international break. “I haven’t had a rest in about six years. I think it makes sense to miss the first Labour conference in about 15 years,” he said. There will be time for interventions – helpful or otherwise – in the coming months. Conference is the first of four phases that No 10 views as opportunities for Burnham to seize public attention and set direction. After that will be the budget, his 10-year plan expected later in the autumn, and then the spending review next year. But if conference gives Burnham another poll boost, it will add to the chatter in Westminster that he could decide to call a general election sooner rather than later. “Conference could be make-or-break for that decision,” one MP said. “If the left looks united, if the polls continue as they are – and if we then beat [the Greens’ Zack] Polanski in Holborn and St Pancras then there will never be a better time.” Most cabinet ministers are wary. “Why are we here if not to use this majority we have got to improve the country?” one said. “If we are saying we are here to get things done, then let’s do them now.” For now, Burnham seems to agree. Speaking to broadcasters before the conference, he said he was “not particularly” tempted to call an election. “I see all the speculation and it just races ahead,” he told BBC West’s political editor, Paul Barltrop. “The time has come: draw a line, get the country looking forward, pulling together, people feeling a bit of hope in their lives again. That’s what I’m trying to do, and I hope to take it further in the coming period rather than putting people back into an election cycle.”
