title: The daily toll of an ICE arrest on a mother and three young kids: ‘Why did they take my dad?’
summary: Like many other families coping with a family member’s detention, Alma Ramirez and her children have faced financial struggles and mental health tolls
text: A version of this story was originally published in La Opinión. Read the story in Spanish here. Every night, for months, as they settled into bed at their home in Watts, California, seven-year-old José, named after his father, would look over to his mother, Alma Ramirez, and ask her one question: “Why did they take my dad away?” His father, 41-year-old José Padilla, was detained on 27 January, 2026, by Immigration and Customs Enforcement while he was working as a car washer in Los Angeles. The father of four, who has been living in the United States for more than 20 years, was one of more than 1,400 people detained in the LA area that January, according to the Deportation Data Project, and one of at least 373 car wash workers detained from June 2025 through January 2026, according to data compiled by the Clean Carwash Worker Center. Like many other families who have lost the head of their household due to ongoing immigration raids across southern California, Ramirez and her children have faced intense financial struggles coupled with the emotional and mental health toll of family separation. “It impacted the kids more because they had their dad every day. Even if he came home tired from working in the hot sun, he would come and play with them,” said the 31-year-old mother of three while sitting in her living room. “And he took care of us. He would pay our bills, help me around the house doing chores, and bathe [the kids.] He was a real present dad. That’s what I love about him.” “Now that he’s not here, we really feel his absence and how much he helped us–not only with the bills, but also just by being there for the kids, for me, and for my parents,” Ramirez said. “It’s been hard for us to be without him. He was our person. Honestly, he was everyone’s person.” The psychological toll of immigration enforcement has been immense. For children in mixed-status families, these disruptions and absences can cause enduring symptoms of PTSD, anxiety and depression. According to a report from the University of California, Riverside’s school of medicine, the worksite raids and arrests during federal immigration enforcement operations are creating what they describe as a “public health emergency” for millions of kids like José and his brothers. Dr Lisa Fortuna, professor and chair of psychiatry and neuroscience at the UCR school of medicine and the lead psychiatrist behind the report, said these types of separations from a caregiver “fundamentally reshape a child’s development and mental health”. In Ramirez’s case, two of her children, José and Alex, who has autism, both experienced some type of disengagement in school following their father’s detainment. José’s eldest son, Alex, depended on his father, who helped him with everything from bathing and schoolwork to attending school meetings. “The reason José decided to work a carwash job was for the kids, especially Alex, because he requires extra care,” said Ramirez as she waited for Alex to be dropped off by the school bus. “He wanted to make sure he could be available for all of them at any given moment.” That June, Alex and his brothers had been away from their father for five months, and during those months both of the eldest kids began therapy. “They are learning different ways they can manage those big feelings,” she said. “My seven-year-old tries to be a tough little kid, but I can tell he misses his dad.” In a letter to the immigration judge supporting his dad, Alex wrote about how much he missed his father and how badly he wanted to see his dad in “real life”, not through a phone or tablet. Routines interrupted For seven-year-old José Jr, his two-year-old brother Joaquin, and 17-year-old stepbrother Alex, their father José was a constant figure of safety and stability. They played together every evening after finishing their homework; he would read to them and, along with Ramirez, often go on family outings. At night, part of José’s kids’ routine included them cuddling in between their father’s arms as he soothed the little ones to sleep. “We had our routines, each morning and evening, and all that went away,” Ramirez said. According to Ramirez, the family unit deteriorated the moment José was detained. “From one day to the next, everything was on me,” she said, bouncing her two-year-old son in her arms. “And I don’t mind stepping in, but you have to understand, we were such a great team; we really helped each other. When I suffered postpartum depression, he was patient; he took care of everything, and he helped me get back to myself.” Ramirez and her partner, whom she jokingly calls her mari-novio, a word combining husband and boyfriend, have been together since 2014 and are a mixed-status family. She met José when he was a single dad of two and when he worked at her father’s car washing business. Like any parents, their life goal is to give their kids a good, stable life. On the day José was detained, he and Ramirez had gone about their regular morning routine: they helped get the kids ready for school; one helped bathe and dress them, while the other made breakfast. Then, Ramirez would take her son and nephew to school while José stayed home with their youngest and did some light cleaning around the house before getting ready for work. The only difference that morning was the time José left for work. According to Ramirez, José would typically leave the house by 9am, but that day he left extra early to pump gas, something he didn’t normally do, but he had forgotten to fill the car the day before. “He was rushing out the door when I told him, ‘No, you have to eat,’ and I gave him two burritos and a coffee, and he took off,” she said, trying to hold back her tears as she recalled the details of that morning. Ramirez was standing in her mother’s kitchen when she got the call. “The guy on the other end asked me if I knew Morro, which is José’s nickname, and when I said yes, he said, ‘ICE just detained him.’” “I broke down; we were all devastated. We couldn’t believe it.” Ramirez remembers having to hand over the phone to her mother and sister because she couldn’t contain her tears. As a family, they had observed the ongoing ICE raids in their neighborhoods and had only discussed safety measures like sharing each other’s locations, but she said they never discussed what they would do if José was actually detained. “We just felt like, you know, it won’t happen to us if we’re careful. Until it did,” she said. José was eventually transported from downtown Los Angeles to the Adelanto detention facility, before being transferred one final time to the California City detention facility in Kern county. The drive from Watts to the detention center is a hefty three-hour ride, so with a busy schedule, a family to take care of, and a car that isn’t reliable for such a drive, Ramirez and her family mostly communicated with José through video phone calls every other night. ‘I need my dad’ On a Friday afternoon in June, Ramirez laid out family photos on her couch. In her hands was a Valentine’s Day gift she had made just for José, before he was detained. “We didn’t get to celebrate Valentine’s Day how we wanted, but it’s ok, this is waiting for him when he gets out,” she said, feeling optimistic about his return. “Look, that’s him!” she said, pointing to José, who was being embraced by his seven-year-old in a photograph – both sporting huge smiles on their faces. Ramirez said each kid has been impacted differently, and the changes differ from child to child. Her youngest boy, two-year-old Joaquin, is taking it the hardest. “He’s still little, so it’s hard for him to understand why he can’t see his father,” Ramirez explained. “He was the one who was used to sleeping in his dad’s arms, so every night he turns to see the empty space next to me, and he says ‘Me hace falta mi papa,’ ‘I need my dad.’” The Children’s Equity Project at Arizona State University found that the detention and separation of children and parents, even for a short amount of time, can trigger toxic stress. “Psychological science is clear: detention, deportation, family separation, and the constant threat of such actions create chronic stress that increases anxiety, depression, trauma-related symptoms, and long-term health risks”, said APA CEO Dr Arthur Evans Jr, in a report by the American Psychological Association. “These harms are especially severe for children, whose emotional development depends on stable and secure caregiving relationships.” A mother trying to keep afloat For months, the mother of three managed her children, household duties and school as best as she could. At the time of José’s detainment, she was a stay-at-home mom and a student studying for a test to become a certified phlebotomist. Unfortunately, she had to retake the test a few times because, after losing her partner’s support, she had little to no time to study. “It’s been very hard. I just find myself crying all the time, some days are harder than others,” she said. Ramirez and her kids live with her parents and pay rent, but she said that even though she is in a better living situation than most, paying bills and managing it all while trying to keep her partner’s spirits up has been difficult. She explained that she and José have had to find ways to balance the financial and emotional load. “José got a job at the detention center kitchen because he said he didn’t want to drown in depression. He wants to make the time pass by, and he says any money he makes he can use to buy himself soups and snacks because he didn’t want me to worry about putting money in his account,” she said, with a slight smile on her face. It was another reminder of why she loved him and how hard he is still trying to care for them even while detained. According to a 2020 study in Pima county, Arizona, an immigration arrest can cost households an average of more than $24,000. In addition to lost income, this amount includes out-of-pocket legal fees, the value of belongings that were seized during arrest and not recovered, and other expenses related to supporting a family member as they navigate the immigration court system. She said her morning begins before 5am. She usually gives her mother a ride to work early in the morning, allowing her about an hour to herself before she has to get the kids ready for school, which she spends trying to study. “It’s been a struggle managing time and finding a new flow,” she said. “I have to study either really late at night or really early in the morning because it has to be when the kids are asleep, so I hardly get rest.” Ramirez has not been able to pass her test but hopes to retake it soon, once she can adjust to her new routine. As for José, she hasn’t lost hope. “I do have a lot of faith and hope that he will be freed,” Ramírez said in June. “I can’t wait for the day my kids have their father back.” *** On 4 August 2026, six months after his detention, Ramírez and her kids got the news they’ve been waiting for. José was released from immigration detention, and his kids welcomed him at Union Station in Los Angeles. The Immigrant Defenders Law Center, which helped José and his family with his case, captured the emotional reunion. “Who’s that papa?” Ramirez tells her seven-year-old as they turn the corner; no words come out, just smiles and tears of joy and relief. The family’s healing journey is far from over. While José has regained his freedom, he is still fighting his case and hoping he can stay in the country where he has built a life with his family. Ramirez shared that, to help with attorney fees, they have left his GoFundMe open. For now, Ramirez and her kids rejoice as they are all once again in José’s arms, enjoying the warm embrace they longed for for six months This article was produced in collaboration with the Ethnic Media Health Reporting “Healing California” initiative at the USC Annenberg Center for Health Journalism and the California Local News Fellowship program at the University of California, Berkeley.

title: Jeffrey Donaldson could face more than 10 years in jail for child sexual abuse, court told
summary: Age difference between former Democratic Unionist party leader and his victims an aggravating factor, say prosecutors
text: Jeffrey Donaldson, the former leader of the Democratic Unionist party in Northern Ireland, could be sent to prison for more than 10 years over the sexual assault of two women when they were children, a court heard on Friday. The disgraced politician, who headed the DUP between 2021 and 2024, was found guilty of 18 counts of sexual abuse including one count of rape against the women in June. Recounting the case, Rosemary Walsh KC reminded Judge Ramsey how the distress felt by Complainant B while giving evidence was “palpable” in the court room. Referring to a victim statement already with the judge, she told how Complainant B had described the trial as “a terrible experience” and how the abuse she suffered as a child “affected her every day” of her life. Sometimes she struggled so much she “wishes she could die”, Walsh said, adding that as a result of the abuse she “does not know what love and trust really is”. The other victim, Complainant A, wrote in her victim impact statement that she felt her childhood had been “stolen from her” and this had led to feelings of shame and anger. Her sleep and sense of wellbeing were affected to this day and sometimes she felt burnt out from the emotional stress. Walsh spoke of various tariffs for the offences, several of which carried a maximum sentence of two years, but others which carried a maximum sentence of between 10 and 14 years under historical tariffs for crimes, she told the court. She said historical legislation did not differentiate between a child and an adult victim in all the counts, so the disparity in age between Donaldson and his victims should be considered an “aggravating” factor in sentencing. She said Complainant B was “nine or 10” during some of the offending by Donaldson when he was 25 or 26 years old. She had described how she felt “sick” when he abused her and “wanted to scream out” but thought it was her fault. Complainant B suffered other types of sexual assault by Donaldson when she was as young as “seven or eight”. Donaldson, 63, who is planning to appeal, sat stony-faced throughout the 70-minute pre-sentencing hearing in Newry courthouse. Kieran Vaughan KC urged the judge to take into account several “mitigating” factors including Donaldson’s current age and that he was a man of “previous good character”. He also told the court “there was no offending of this type” in the past 18 years and during this time Donaldson had significant achievements which were “obliterated” by the conviction. Donaldson’s wife, Eleanor, has already lodged an appeal against the court’s finding that she had committed acts alleged in relation to five of the charges he had faced. She was found unfit to stand trial on mental health grounds, meaning the jury was asked to find out if she did or did not commit the acts of which she was accused. She cannot be sent to jail but is appealing to have the court conclusions overturned. Donaldson is expected to be sentenced next month.

title: Cyber-attack on Dyfed-Powys police ‘may have accessed staff information’
summary: Welsh force says incident disrupted ‘some non-emergency systems’ and public data was not affected
text: A police force in Wales has said staff information may have been “accessed or compromised” in a cyber-attack. Dyfed-Powys police, which has more than 2,000 officers and civilian staff, said it was hacked on 14 September in an incident that disrupted “some non-emergency systems”. The force said there was no evidence that personal data belonging to members of the public had been affected. The Dyfed-Powys force covers the counties of Carmarthenshire, Ceredigion, Pembrokeshire and Powys in Wales. A spokesperson said: “At this stage, our investigation has found no evidence that members of the public’s personal data has been accessed or compromised as a result of this incident.” However, the force said it was continuing to investigate the possibility that staff information may have been accessed or compromised, with the implication that it could have been taken by hackers. “We are … continuing to investigate whether any information relating to our staff may have been accessed or compromised, and are taking all appropriate steps to protect that information, and will provide appropriate advice to colleagues if required,” said a spokesperson. The force said it was receiving support from cybersecurity specialists and its systems had been subjected to “precautionary measures” while an investigation was under way. Online and email contacts for the force were unavailable after the attack, which was identified on the day it happened, but have since been restored. The Information Commissioner’s Office, the UK’s data watchdog, has been notified of the incident. A spokesperson for the force added: “We understand the potential concern this may cause and want to reassure the public that we have and will continue to take all necessary steps to protect our information and maintain the security of our systems. “We will provide further updates when we are in a position to do so.” The area served by Dyfed-Powys police equates to more than 500,000 people, a number that rises significantly with tourists each year. The investigation is being managed by Tarian, the regional organised crime unit (ROCU) for southern Wales, and force systems are being monitored. A spokesperson for the ICO said: “We can confirm we have received a breach report from Dyfed-Powys police and we are assessing the information provided.” In July it was revealed that hackers had breached the police national legal database (PNLD), which provides legal assistance to UK police forces. The cybercriminals claimed to have taken 135,000 pieces of data. The PNLD said the details taken related to “police officers and those working in criminal justice including their name, the force or organisation they work for and their work email address”. However, the database does not contain confidential victim, witness or offender information.

title: Noah Woods died after leaving playground through gap in fence, inquest told
summary: Three-year-old became separated from a relative in Suffolk and went in direction of pond where he was later found dead
text: A three-year-old boy who was found dead in a pond after going missing from a playground had left the play area “through a gap in the fence”, an inquest heard. Noah Woods became separated from a relative after visiting the playground in Merriam Close, Brantham, on the afternoon of 15 September, Suffolk police said. About 1,300 members of the public joined a search to find Noah, who police said was non-verbal, partially deaf and had been undergoing an assessment for autism. Met police divers recovered his body from what is known locally as Decoy Pond on the afternoon of 16 September. Suffolk police said his death was not being treated as suspicious. After the inquest into his death was opened and adjourned in Ipswich on Friday, Noah’s family said they would like him to be remembered as “the happy little boy that he was”. In a statement, they said: “Noah was a happy, cheeky, playful three-year-old boy who loved to laugh, loved to giggle and who brought joy wherever he went. He was part of a loving and caring family, living with his mummy, daddy and his little baby brother. He was at the centre of our world. “Noah was being assessed for autism, although he had not received a diagnosis. He also had mild hearing loss and was speech delayed. “Despite the challenges he faced, he was learning every day. He was saying new words all the time and had only just started finding and using his little voice. One of the things we miss most is the special sound of his voice. It was unique, wonderful, and something we will carry with us forever.” Noah was “the most affectionate” boy who had an “incredibly special” bond with his brother, the statement said. DCI Matthew Connick told the inquest that on 15 September, Noah, of East Bergholt, Suffolk, was being “looked after by relatives and this was part of a normal routine for Noah”. He said they walked to an under-fives play area and CCTV footage in the park “showed Noah playing with his relative”. The first piece of footage was timed at 2.13pm and he was last seen playing at 2.37pm, said Connick, who added that the CCTV was motion-activated so did not provide continuous footage. He said the relative, who was not named at the hearing, had provided a statement to police. The officer said Noah “left through a gap in the fence leading to the memorial garden where he left through an open gate”. He said Noah went in the direction of Decoy Pond and he was “being closely followed by his relative who was trying to keep up with him”. He said the relative “shouted after him” but after 200 metres Noah could not be seen. “Police were called and a large-scale search operation began,” Connick said. Noah was found by a Met police diver “approximately 5 metres from the bank and within submerged tree roots”. The depth was estimated at 1.8 metres at that point, he added. Noah’s death was confirmed at 4.31pm by paramedics and his identity was formally confirmed by his mother, Charlie Peck, at Ipswich hospital that evening. A postmortem examination at Addenbrooke’s hospital mortuary in Cambridge recorded his medical cause of death as pending further investigation, Connick said. The Suffolk assistant coroner Jyoti Gill said at the outset of the hearing, which was not attended by the boy’s family: “I would like to express my deepest condolences to Noah’s family and friends and all those affected by Noah’s death.” She said at the end of the six-minute hearing: “The inquest is adjourned to a date to be fixed in due course.” Noah’s father, Rhys Woods, had paid tribute to his son in a message shared on a community Facebook group last week. He described Noah as the “sweetest and most innocent little boy, with nothing but love to give”, and added: “We are going to miss him so very much.” Football players paid tribute to Noah during Everton’s home match against Ipswich Town on Saturday by wearing black armbands.

title: Pakistan locks down Islamabad as Imran Khan’s party vows to march on capital
summary: Tens of thousands of police deployed and roads barricaded as PTI demands release of jailed former PM
text: Leaders from Imran Khan’s party have vowed to go ahead with a nationwide demonstration in Pakistan to demand the former prime minister’s release, even as the government deployed tens of thousands of police to Islamabad, barricaded highways and issued arrest warrants to try to stop the march. The state has taken extreme measures to prevent Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party from proceeding with the march. It was announced after mounting concerns of the treatment of Khan, who has been in jail since 2023 on corruption charges. On Friday, PTI leaders said they would postpone the start of the march until 4 October, a week after the original 27 September date, saying they hoped the delay would put further strain on the government. Analysts said the protest could present a major challenge to the military-backed government, which is widely regarded as weak, illegitimate and unpopular, while Khan remains a popular rallying figure. The ruling coalition is led by the prime minister, Shehbaz Sharif, but the army chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir, is widely seen as the country’s de facto leader. This week, dozens of PTI leaders and ministers have been detained or made subject of arrest warrants, while Khan’s three sisters were arrested on Monday and remain in jail, charged with posing a grave threat to security. Among those facing arrest is Sohail Afridi, the chief minister of Khan’s home province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, PTI’s stronghold, from where thousands of supporters are expected to join the march to the capital. Afridi said the PTI would carry out the march unless the government made significant concessions over Khan’s treatment and conditions in jail, including a fair hearing for Khan’s cases. “The government is panicking – that’s why they have put Islamabad under siege, that’s why they are abducting our ministers,” he said. “But Imran Khan is the most popular leader of the country and people will come out for him. I am certain they won’t be able to stop the public power of the masses when they come out on streets and take to Islamabad.” Afridi acknowledged that the scale of the security deployment had led many to fear there could be a violent confrontation to prevent Khan’s supporters from entering the capital, as had been seen in previous demonstrations. The government has already deployed tens of thousands of security officials to Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and shut down the main highway connecting the provincial capital, Peshawar, to Islamabad. “I know they can go to any extent to stop us by brute force, we have no doubt about it,” Afridi said. “But if we have a large number of people, they can’t open fire at us. Our plan is to bring so many people that they surrender.” Faisal Karim Kundi, a central government appointee as governor of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, defended the security measures being taken against PTI as precautionary and accused the party of trying to create “instability and violence”. “The state can’t allow any violent group to march on Islamabad,” Kundi said. Public frustration has mounted in Islamabad as the government’s measures to stop Khan’s party supporters having any way to enter the capital has led to the city resembling a high-security fortress. More than 1,000 shipping containers, many fortified with spikes, have blockaded roads and sandbags were placed on bridges, while a key highway into the capital was closed. Public gatherings have been banned in Islamabad and 22,000 police and other security personnel have been deployed across the capital. The government’s shutdown has fuelled anger and frustration in the capital, with many businesses unable to get supplies. Shahid, 76, a retired businessman, said: “The entire city is suffering. The government has shut down the whole city and we, as citizens, are helpless. I have never seen such a situation. Joblessness, inflation and insecurity has made our lives hell but does the government care? No.” Despite the considerable efforts by the government and the military to crush Khan’s party and remove the former prime minister from the public consciousness – with media organisations instructed to not even refer to him by name – Khan is still viewed by many as the political alternative to the current regime. The PTI alleges Khan is being held in solitary confinement and has been denied adequate medical treatment and any contact with his family or his lawyers for months. Khan denies all the charges against him and alleges he is being imprisoned due to the political threat he poses to the government and the military. All but one of the court rulings against Khan have been overturned. Analysts say the government and its military backers fear the PTI protest could escalate into a movement that could topple their administration, similar to protests seen in nearby Bangladesh, Nepal and Sri Lanka. “They have an eye on what has happened in south Asia over the last five years, where country after country has seen huge protests snowballing suddenly out of nowhere and sweeping away a government,” said Niaz Murtaza, a Pakistani political columnist. “Given the breadth of grievances in Pakistan at the moment, the performance of the government has been so poor on the economy and security, while the repression is so high, that they are very nervous that the whole situation could combust very quickly.”

title: ‘Significant’ nor’easter brings high winds and heavy rain to US east coast
summary: Forecasters say up to 40 million people in multiple US states could be affected by the early season northeasterly storm
text: High winds and heavy rain were beginning to batter New England on Friday as a “significant” nor’easter, the first such storm of the fall, threatened to disrupt weekend plans for millions. In the Pacific Ocean, meanwhile, three separate hurricanes, one threatening “catastrophic flooding”, including life-threatening flash floods, in Hawaii, were churning as a record-setting El Niño continued to amplify severe weather events on a global scale. Forecasters said up to 40 million people across multiple US states could be affected by the early season northeasterly storm that was already lashing coastal areas of Rhode Island, Massachusetts, Connecticut and New York’s Long Island by Friday morning. “Strong winds and rough seas along with a prolonged period of steady rain across the region are expected through this weekend,” the National Weather Service’s Boston office warned in a post on X, adding that rain could last until Monday. “Beach erosion, coastal flooding, and wind damage including downed limbs and power outages are our main concerns.” Areas farther inland were also bracing for the arrival of the storm, which has the potential to deliver hurricane force winds despite uncertainty over exactly where it will go. The online AccuWeather service said winds of 40mph-60mph were expected along the coast from New Jersey to Maine, beginning late Friday, and up to 80mph in and around Montauk, New York. “The nor’easter has strengthened over the Atlantic and is expected to stay closer to the shoreline. This will bring more rain inland, but more importantly stronger winds closer to shore,” Elizabeth Danco, an AccuWeather expert meteorologist, said in a statement. “This region has experienced soaking rains in recent weeks, making it particularly susceptible to falling trees and flooding.” While the worst of the impacts, especially flooding and beach erosion, will occur closer to the coast, travelers were warned to expect significant flight cancellations and delays, and difficult driving conditions. Up to 8 inches of rain were forecast for some areas of south-eastern Massachusetts, and up to 2 inches in Boston on Friday into Saturday, and the same in New York City a day later. High wind warnings were in place in Boston and neighboring areas on Friday morning. “New York City and especially Boston need to stay weather aware this weekend, and prepare the same as you would for a tropical storm,” the Weather Channel said on its website. It also addressed the existence of the nor’easter so early in the season. “You might think it is too early for a nor’easter, but the criteria are met more often than you would think,” the Weather Channel said. “Most people usually think of snow and ice with nor’easters because [they] do tend to occur more in the late fall and winter.” Extreme weather is also occurring in the Pacific, where hurricanes Nolo, Odalys and Polo were bringing varying impacts on Friday. Nolo was menacing the islands of Hawaii, and expected to be a major category 3 storm as it passes about 80 miles south of Big Island early on Saturday. Although not forecast to make landfall, Nolo will bring “five days of torrential rain through Monday, catastrophic flooding and mudslides”, AccuWeather’s hurricane experts said. Polo, which intensified rapidly from a tropical storm to a category 5 monster hurricane earlier this week, remained offshore of Mexico on Friday, about 250 miles south-south-west of the Jalisco coast. Its 160mph winds “are likely to cause life-threatening surf, rip currents, and coastal flooding”, in the region, the National Hurricane Center in Miami said. The storm was forecast to curve around and make landfall somewhere in Baja California on Sunday night or Monday morning as a much-weakened hurricane. Odalys, a category 4 hurricane, was forecast to remain at sea with few to no impacts on land. The El Niño that has contributed to 18 named storms in the Pacific basin this season has had a converse effect in the Atlantic where, for the first time since 1914, no hurricanes formed by 21 September. Both seasons run until 30 November.

title: Daniel Thomas pleads not guilty after alleged dinghy slashing in Channel
summary: Far-right activist who was filmed appearing to slash boat with blade is refused bail as he denies charges
text: The far-right agitator Daniel Thomas has pleaded not guilty to causing criminal damage after he was filmed apparently slashing a boat in the Channel with a blade while an emergency responder was onboard. Thomas, 37, appeared at Basingstoke magistrates court on Friday morning. He also pleaded not guilty to failing to disclose to police the pin number of his phone, under section 53 of the Regulation of Investigatory Powers Act 2000. The prosecutor Kevin Lucie, outlining the basis of the criminal damage charge, alleged Thomas slashed an adrift boat with a knife. He told the court: “On 22 September, around 4.30pm, the defendant on his social platform livestreamed himself from a boat on the English Channel. He broadcast to a significant number of people a boat of migrants being supported by the RNLI in the English Channel. It was a single Rib [rigid inflatable boat] which was adrift. “He armed himself with a knife. He slashed the boat.” Lucie said Thomas was arrested at a BP service station and taken into custody, where his mobile phone was seized but he allegedly refused to provide the pin code. When asked about the boat, Lucie confirmed he was unsure if the damage was worth more or less than £5,000, and said: “Unfortunately, it is the case that it did go back to France. We have asked for the cost of the damage.” Thomas, also known as Danny Tommo, was refused bail. The father of four, described as a professional roofer, was seen dabbing his eyes with a tissue at one point during the hearing. He appeared for the hearing via video link, wearing a black top and grey coat, and spoke only to confirm his name and date of birth. He was supported in court by his teenage son, as well as fellow far-right activist Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, also known as Tommy Robinson. Other supporters were placed in a separate room to watch a live stream from the court, a routine measure when interest in a case outstrips the space available in a courtroom. There was a visible police presence, with an officer in the public gallery of the courtroom, another at the courtroom door and third in the seated waiting area outside the courtroom. On Thursday evening, several hundred people, many wearing black, gathered outside a police investigation centre in Basingstoke, apparently in the belief Thomas was inside. Dozens of police officers could be seen monitoring the group as the protest continued for several hours. Thomas has said he would like a crown court trial. A hearing will take place in Portsmouth crown court on Tuesday 29 September. His lawyer, Simon Pentol KC, said: “This defendant is not charged with an offence of political activism, whether you agree with it or not, that is not the issue. He has elected crown court trial over criminal damage simpliciter and nothing more, and for not acquiescing to a notice requiring him to provide a pin number.” He added: “I invite this court to bear in mind it’s dealing with a 37-year-old man who lives with his long-standing partner and their four children, all aged between 18 and three, his partner is pregnant once again, four months. She is a full-time mother, he is the full-time provider, or breadwinner, as they used to say. “He is a professional roofer by trade. He is, therefore, having to look after his family who, through his political activism, have been under huge threat and due to publication of his mother’s home address, she has had to move home.”

title: Pomp over progress in Xi’s US summit with Trump is a win for China
summary: While US president hailed visit as ‘great’, almost nothing of substance was achieved on resolving thorny issues
text: If the Beijing meeting between Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in May was the “stalemate summit”, the second round of talks between the presidents of the US and China this week seemed to give up entirely on the idea of breakthroughs. Instead, it was described as a celebration of “diplotainment” rather than diplomacy, where pomp prevailed over progress and where one of the main outcomes was the news that two giant pandas would soon be sent from China to Atlanta zoo. Trump rolled out the red carpet for Xi’s arrival on Wednesday and broke with decades of precedent to meet the Chinese leader at Joint Base Andrews. Thus began a three-day state visit that involved a tour of Trump’s new helipad and the Marine One helicopter, and a 90-minute meeting that Trump described as “great” and that revealed, according to Trump, that Xi “has great interest in granite”. “The biggest takeaway is that Trump has been displaying an extraordinary degree of deference to Xi Jinping,” said Julian Gewirtz, who served as a senior China official in the Biden administration. But what of actual substance? Expectations going into the summit were low. But the outcomes somehow still fell short. One of the biggest issues in the US-China relationship is trade. Last year, as Trump unveiled successive rounds of tariffs on Chinese goods, the White House accused China of unfair practices that it said contributed to the loss of 3.7m US jobs and inflated the trade deficit. The tariffs were supposed to suppress the volume of Chinese imports to the US and put pressure on China. To some degree, they worked. The US trade deficit with China in 2025 fell to $200bn, down from nearly $300bn in 2024. But experts have noted that some of this shortfall is made up for by Chinese goods being shipped to the US via third countries, a trend underlined by the fact that China’s trade surplus surpassed a record $1tn last year. With the US and China accounting for 43% of global GDP, their trade war has far-reaching implications for the world economy. So it was a relief not just to Beijing and to US consumers when the two countries agreed a temporary truce in Busan last year. That truce is due to expire in November. China, where the economy is heavily reliant on exports, was reported to be pushing for the truce to be extended until the end of Trump’s term, in January 2029. On Thursday, it was revealed that Xi’s first state visit to the US in more than a decade had resulted in a mere two-month extension. That reflects “the lack of preparation for this summit beyond the pomp and circumstance”, said Neil Thomas, a senior fellow at the Asia Society. William Yang, a senior analyst at the International Crisis Group, said: “This summit largely achieved symbolism and ritualism over substance. That is very clear.” The short extension “reflects the level of fundamental differences that still exist between the two countries over a variety of issues”. China’s most powerful response to Trump’s tariffs was the decision to block the export of rare earths, critical minerals vital to US manufacturing and military supply chains. That seemed to skewer Trump’s leverage over China. Gewirtz said: “Beijing’s retaliation … seems to have had a profound effect on [Trump] and his administration’s willingness to take risks vis-a-vis China.” Apart from the trade war agreement, the summit failed to achieve any meaningful progress on thorny issues in the US-China relationship such as artificial intelligence, Taiwan, the wars in Iran and Ukraine, and human rights. On Taiwan, which Beijing considers to be the most important issue in the relationship, Xi put pressure on Trump to weaken the US’s support for the self-governing island that China claims as its own. According to the Chinese readout of the Xi-Trump meeting, Xi told Trump he hoped “the US side will adhere to the correct position of opposing Taiwan independence”. For the US to state that it “opposes” Taiwanese independence would be a rhetorical shift from the current position of “does not support” such a claim, and would be a move welcomed by Beijing. Trump has not yet commented on whether he agreed to such a statement. But it does seem he is no closer to approving a $14bn arms sale package for Taiwan, a sale that Beijing would like to see disappear completely. On Thursday, US Senate Democrats lambasted Trump for opting for “pageantry over purpose” and for failing to deliver agreements on “the economic and security issues that will shape America’s future”. Trump ignored recent warnings about the dangers posed by AI, writing on social media on Thursday: “I want to leave it exactly where it is,” adding: “That is China’s position also.” For China, the lack of big news from the visit is a win in itself. “The summit went excellently from the Chinese perspective,” Thomas said. Xi “got a huge amount of respect from the American president, the full state visit treatment [and] really great images beaming back to China of the Chinese and the American presidents interacting as peers on the global stage, without having to make any meaningful concessions or compromises.”

title: Joe Harkness obituary
summary: Writer, teacher and naturalist who explored the effects of the natural world on neurodivergency
text: The writer, teacher and naturalist Joe Harkness, who has died aged 39, was an inspiring advocate for the role that wild nature can play in alleviating depression and helping all minds, but especially neurodivergent ones, find joy and peace. His first book, Bird Therapy (2018), was a notable success from a new generation of authors who found readers online and crowdfunded their publication via the now defunct Unbound. In Bird Therapy, Harkness told the story of his own breakdown, near-suicide and subsequent recovery through watching birds near his home in rural Norfolk. Readers responded to his honesty and heartfelt practical advice, as well as the obvious pleasure he found in nature. “In that moment, watching the flock of finches, I was allowing myself to become lost and absorbed in the sights in front of me,” he wrote. “I started to notice that when I was out, on my own, experiencing nature and birds in a personal and intimate way, I was more relaxed than I’d ever been before. My breathing rate slowed and I closed my mind to repetitive thoughts and worries. My only focus was observing birds and learning about them. I was losing myself in birds, in a positive way.” Following the success of the book, Harkness continued his day job as a teacher of pupils with significant learning disabilities. In 2025, he published Neurodivergent, By Nature, an original and deeply researched exploration of neurodivergency and the natural world sparked by a belated diagnosis of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). It was also inspired by a joyful new obsession – moths. Here, as with his interest in birds, he rapidly surpassed the skills of his naturalist friends in identifying obscure micro-moths. The book featured fascinating interviews with neurodivergent conservationists, and was a plea for embracing neurodivergency to better restore biodiversity. It was shortlisted for the East Anglian Book Awards as well as the 2026 Wainwright prize for conservation writing. Harkness, a devoted father who continued to experience depression, took his own life two weeks before the prize ceremony. Born in King’s Lynn, Norfolk, from the age of four Harkness was raised by his single working mum, who worked as an administrator. Harkness credited his maternal grandad’s quiet passion for the natural world with his later rediscovery of it. He enjoyed a close relationship with his mother who, in an interview after the success of Bird Therapy, described Harkness as a young boy as “very talkative, very bright, very intelligent, very inquisitive, had boundless energy, a keen eye for detail, loved nature, and was very good at reading, especially the Argos catalogue”. Harkness later called himself “a proper nightmare” at school but also reflected upon the obviousness of his ADHD behaviours and the failure of school and health professionals in the early 2000s to offer him a diagnosis. “I just flew under the radar, like so many other children in my generation,” he wrote in Neurodivergent, by Nature. “Instead, in the eyes of society, and my teachers, I was the archetypal product of a single mother in social housing, and of course I was going to act up to that.” During his teenage years, he self-medicated with various drugs, which he later said contributed to his chronic anxiety. He dropped out of sixth form and did not pursue further education. In his 20s, Harkness drank heavily and took drugs, but also managed to build a career, working as a development worker for the Prince’s Trust and a support worker at the charity Mencap. In 2013, he was stopped from a suicide attempt, had a breakdown and took three weeks off work. During a country walk with Emma, his future wife, he saw a pair of common buzzards displaying over a tree-line. The buzzards were a gateway into a new passion: birdwatching. Permanently quitting all drink and illegal drugs, Harkness found new naturalist friends, who were astonished by how quickly he became a proficient birder, rapidly able to identify birds by flight, call and song. He began teaching teenagers excluded from mainstream education and also attracted a growing following on his Bird Therapy blog and on Twitter, where he shared his thoughts on his recovery through nature. When a follower suggested he could publish the blog as a book via Unbound, he approached the publisher, who wanted him to raise £18,500 to bring it out. “It really scared me,” he later said. The sum was raised in just five weeks. Bill Bailey donated £1,000 and Chris Packham wrote a glowing foreword, predicting that the book would save lives, and it was endorsed by Stephen Fry and the novelist Melissa Harrison, who called Harkness’s writing “inclusive, unpretentious and evangelical in the best way”. Bird Therapy’s success in the UK led it to be translated into five languages. Harkness was told by readers that they owed their life to him. However, his entry into what he called the “guild” of nature writers was disillusioning. He found his fellow writers competitive and self-obsessed. Social media contributed to growing anxiety. “The more open I was on social media, the less people engaged with me. If you’re already struggling with self-esteem, it is hell to be on it,” he said in 2020. He closed his accounts. He was more comfortable devoting time to his family, alongside his responsibilities as a special needs teacher at Cromer academy, a Norfolk state school, and latterly as a senior teacher at Parkside, Norwich, where he worked with pupils with autism, ADHD, Down’s syndrome and learning disabilities. In 2023 he wrote Inside/Outside, a teachers’ nature-themed resource book for promoting emotional literacy. His pupils, like his readers, found Harkness to be warm, inclusive, enthusiastic, empathic and a lover of bad jokes. He said he made a point of talking about mental health with his students every day. One day at work, a mental health nurse asked Harkness if he had ever considered that he may have ADHD. It took more than three years to obtain a formal diagnosis, in 2022, and when it came it was a relief. “The whole idea completes me,” he wrote. It also enabled him to access helpful drug treatment, and set him on a path to write Neurodivergent, by Nature. Before his death, Harkness had just finished an extensively revised edition of Bird Therapy, which is due to be published by Bloomsbury next year. He is survived by Emma and their two daughters. • Joe Harkness, writer and teacher, born 23 December 1986; died 4 September 2026

title: The comedians turning AI anxiety into punchlines: ‘It’s so good, it’ll completely alter our grasp on reality’
summary: Across videos, standup and cartoons, humorists are skewering big tech’s attempt to make AI ubiquitous and inevitable
text: “Best case scenario, we never have to do any admin again,” says an AI CEO. “Worst case, we all die.” A young man struggles to the top of a beautiful mountain, words echoing in his ears: “AI will most likely lead to the end of the world, but in the meantime, there will be great companies created.” At the top of the mountain, he triumphantly holds up a sign: “Build a datacenter here.” On the New York subway, posters herald what appear to be AI startups. “What if forks were spoons?” asks an ad for Cutlery.ai. Another advises viewers that Ziplink is now known as Froggle. The posters are real, but the companies aren’t; the CEO and datacenter scenarios are social media sketches (though the “great companies” quote is a genuine piece of wisdom from Sam Altman). It’s all part of a recent wave of comedy inspired – but absolutely not generated – by AI. The comedy extends across all forms of media: social videos, standup, songs, humor columns, comic strips and art installations. It takes aim at companies’ attempts to make AI ubiquitous, the dangers of believing its every word, its threats to society and the environment. It effectively punctures tech CEOs’ relentless narrative: that artificial intelligence represents humanity peaking; that it is inevitable and all-powerful; that we have no idea where it’s going and it could kill us all, but for some reason it is absolutely essential to pursue. It’s no surprise that a topic as pervasive as AI in 2026 would end up in comedians’ crosshairs. A March Gallup poll found 79% of Americans believe AI will reduce jobs. In a CNN poll this week, 81% of respondents said they were more concerned than excited about how the technology could “fundamentally change our way of life”. Only 11% of Americans would support the building of a datacenter locally, according to UMass Amherst. Meanwhile, a handful of impossibly wealthy weirdos wander between podcasts and conference stages boasting about their plans to fundamentally alter what it means to be human. One way to expose the absurdity of the AI companies’ story is by exposing the flaws in their products. Ty Eveland, for instance, trolls AI doctors and HR professionals – the video bots you might awkwardly encounter at a virtual doctor’s appointment or job interview. Asked about marketing, he tells one bot interviewer he takes “everything with a grain of salt and maybe a little bit of pepper”. The bot, portrayed as a generically handsome blond man, responds earnestly: “When you say you take things with a grain of salt and pepper, what does that actually mean for a brand’s social media strategy?” If bots are approaching superintelligence, this one has clearly been left behind. Other comedians parody the user experience: the comedian Aya Huseen, repeatedly popping out from behind a door, personifies tech companies’ desperate attempts to get users hooked on new AI features: “You sure you don’t want to try it with AI?” “This would be so much funner with AI.” “Just try generating it with AI.” The comedian Tom Nestor imagines “how people who love AI think we see them,” telling a friend on the phone: “Do you know what I also really like? It’s not so good now but in years to come it’ll get so good that it’ll just completely alter people’s grasp of reality.” In the Atlantic, the humorist Alexandra Petri recounts a dream in which everything in her life has pivoted to AI, from children’s books – Goldilocks and the 4.5 Bears – to her cereal, which features “subtle changes in the recipe, such as the nuts now being the hard, metal kind”. Pro-human comedians have also taken aim at AI’s artistic pretensions. “If you are somebody who uses ChatGPT to generate videos, images, art, text, in an artistic capacity, to write for you, you are not somebody who deserves to be taken seriously,” said the comedian Caleb Hearon in a serious moment on his podcast. A comic strip titled “AI Design Logic” puts it more succinctly: “Get me a cheese pizza,” a diner tells a waiter. When the pizza arrives, the customer takes credit, exclaiming: “Wow, look what I made!” It’s simple, scathingly effective, and highly meme-able. Even more succinct is a T-shirt worn by the actor Ayo Edebiri: “Do not talk to me about AI. I will kill myself.” The Altmans and Musks of the world may be louder than these comedians, but the collective weight of their jokes provides a counterbalance to the pro-AI declarations. “I would like to think that some of these [companies] are looking at the ridiculousness of where we’re at” and might be swayed by the success and relatability of comedy mocking their products, says Marwan Shaffey, whose videos include a takedown of a water-guzzling Google in 2026, with its Gemini-generated search results that are more about vibes than accuracy. “It does seem like the sentiment is changing, but I think it will take time.” Comedy, of course, can cut through the noise in a way that serious lectures may not. That has been the experience of Alberta Devor, who spent six and a half years as a software engineer at Google. In one recent video, she offers a cool hack for when someone asks you a tricky question: instead of pulling out your phone and asking AI, it’s actually possible to use the LLM in your brain to produce a response. When a colleague wonders what “EOD” means, she immediately tells him. “How’d you ask Claude that so fast?” he asks. “I trained a model in my head,” she replies. “I just consumed a lot of media, a lot of books.” Devor herself is a regular AI user. Still, she’s concerned about overreliance on the products, whether they’re being used to seek information or to code. “The message that I want people to take home is to actually understand what they’re asking AI, to actually understand what the limitations of it are,” she says in an interview. Her serious videos on these topics often meet with some backlash. Comedy, she says, tends to find a more open audience. “It makes people want to engage more, and then you can start to get through to these more complex ideas,” she says. “Like maybe we should be using our brain.” Not all the AI takedowns are themselves digital. The New York subway signs are the brainchildren of two comedians, Harris Alterman and Dave Ross, who designed a campaign mocking the inscrutable – and insufferable – language of bus-stop tech ads and San Francisco billboards. “It was the quickest writing and creative process I’ve ever had,” Ross said. The tech advertising tropes were so clear, and so different from how any human has ever talked, that it was easy to satirize. “We made a big Google Doc of every keyword from all these things – ‘agents’, ‘democratize’ – and then we made 50 frameworks of these ads”: “finally, X that you can Y, or from X to Y in just one Z”. They rearranged and filled in the frameworks, Mad Libs-style, and had them printed. Initially, the concept just seemed funny. “The more I talk about this, and it’s been months now, the more I realize just how disgusted I am with it,” Ross says of the ads’ language, which is “borderline offensive to the human brain”. Other comics are equally clear-eyed in their message, and more direct in their advocacy. The British comedian Cody Dahler, condemning “techy tits” such as Palantir CEO Alex Karp, AKA “evil Art Garfunkel”, for creating systems “designed to set fire to everything we value as human beings”, has directly urged followers to speak out. Charlie Berens of Wisconsin has led a fight against datacenters in that state. His parody news broadcasts – warning it could soon be “goodbye, America’s dairyland and hello, America’s motherboard” – led to him headlining gatherings of hundreds. Sure, it may be “a little lofty to expect that your comedy could topple a billion-dollar corporation”, as Ross says. But we shouldn’t underestimate the power of comedy wielded en masse. Altman, the human face of ChatGPT, was recently presented with a clip of Husk, a former landscaper who recently reached a million followers, asking the bot to time a supposed long-distance run, which it got wildly wrong. Altman appeared sheepish: “It’s a known issue.” Ross doesn’t believe comedians should be seen as philosophers, but it would be “wonderful”, he says, if humor “woke up an understanding in people’s minds that they’re also upset, and drove them toward questioning” our AI future. It’s easy to feel helpless against a tide of supposed robotic inevitability. But each small act of comedy offers permission to question our self-appointed AI overlords – a little win for the humans.

title: Trump’s executive order on recreational fishing is a ‘giveaway of fish and ocean ecosystem’, advocates warn
summary: Federal agencies told to prioritize recreational fishing and to reconsider scientific standards as well as regulations
text: Donald Trump’s latest fishing order is raising new concerns about US marine protections, as it directs federal agencies to prioritize recreational fishing while reconsidering the scientific standards and environmental regulations that govern American fisheries. The National Marine Fisheries Service hailed last Thursday’s order, Restoring American Saltwater Angling and Recreation, telling the Guardian: “By addressing long-standing flaws in federal data collection, streamlining permitting, and expanding marine habitats, this action delivers long-overdue stability to America’s $1.2tn outdoor recreation economy.” However, conservation advocates say the order marks another step by the Trump administration away from science-based marine management and conservation. “That progress is now being dismantled, bit by bit,” said Lance Morgan, president of the Marine Conservation Institute, adding: “The current administration has moved to gut most ocean protections, threatening to take the US from a global leader in marine conservation to nearly a bystander.” The order directs the commerce department to review fisheries guidelines under the Magnuson-Stevens Act, the primary 1976 law that governs marine fisheries management in US federal waters. The review of the guidelines should “ensure they appropriately account for the … recreational fishery”, the order says. Gib Brogan, senior campaign director at Oceana, said the review is not inherently unusual. However, according to Brogan, the concern is how the Trump administration could reinterpret the standards. “The concern comes in the way that this administration has been implementing the bedrock environmental and conservation laws,” Brogan said. “We’re very concerned about how this administration will attempt to reinterpret things like overfishing and rebuilding, or what constitutes ‘best available science’,” he added, pointing to language used by Trump administration officials. The order also directs the interior department to establish a program facilitating the conversion of decommissioned offshore oil and gas structures into permanent artificial reefs. Kristen Monsell, oceans legal director and senior attorney at the Center for Biological Diversity, called the provision “a handout to the oil industry”, saying that it is “another blatant demonstration of Trump’s desire to let the oil industry avoid any responsibility for the mess it continues to leave in our oceans”. “Offshore platforms were never designed to function as healthy reefs and are known to serve as hubs for invasive species, including non-native corals and fish. They can also leach harmful chemicals into the ocean,” Monsell said. Meanwhile, Arlo Hemphill, Greenpeace USA’s ocean sanctuaries project lead, said some rigs could provide useful habitat but questioned whether converting them into reefs is appropriate in every location. “You don’t just put [artificial reefs] anywhere just because there happened to be an oil rig there,” he said, pointing to obstacles including rigs located in navigational lanes, areas with strong currents that may be unsuitable for artificial reefs, or places that already have abundant habitat. Hemphill also cautioned that attracting fish to a structure does not necessarily mean creating new fish populations. “They do have the potential to build the population by creating new habitats. But the first fish you’re going to see are not fish that were created by that habitat being there. It’s fish that were in all the surrounding area and then were drawn in by … a new habitat … It’s just making them easier to catch,” he said. The order also calls for the establishment of an “Interagency Shark and Pinniped Depredation Task Force” to address cases where sharks and marine mammals take fish from anglers’ lines. The taskforce is directed to examine barriers to shark fisheries, including international agreements and listings under the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES). Andrea Treece, deputy managing attorney for oceans at Earthjustice, said the provision appears aimed at easing restrictions on the shark trade, which has been largely prohibited under US federal law. “It seems to be aimed at killing more sharks and that is really short-sighted,” Treece said, pointing to the critical role sharks play in ocean ecosystems, including regulating food webs and supporting the health of coral reefs. “Most shark populations in the US are a fraction of what they were before the rise of industrial-scale fishing in the mid 1900s,” Treece said, adding: “To the extent that recreational fishers in some places are experiencing more sharks biting fish off lines, it’s worth asking why that is … We should be looking at, for example, is it that fish and increased recreational fishing numbers are competing for fewer fish?” “We should be looking at … ways we can actually conserve and foster more abundant fish populations for everybody instead of just killing off the competing predators in the ocean, which is just going to destabilize the system in the end,” she continued. Grace Casselberry, a postdoctoral shark depredation researcher at the University of Massachusetts Amherst, also urged caution. “While some shark populations have seen various levels of recovery, we also have more people fishing recreationally than ever before, which creates a perfect storm for these encounters … It has taken decades to get to the point where sharks are beginning to recover, and that progress could be quickly undone,” Casselberry said. “We must ensure that changes to the current strict harvest limits are based on the best available science and any adjustments continue to promote population growth and sustainability.” The executive order also directs agencies to “suspend, revise or rescind regulations that overly burden boaters, anglers and outdoor businesses”. Monsell warned that the order’s deregulatory push could threaten protections such as the vessel-speed rule aimed at reducing deadly collisions between ships and endangered North Atlantic right whales. The measure requires ships to slow to 10 knots or less in certain areas and at certain times, reducing the risk of fatal strikes. “The speed rule is an effective, life-saving measure that reduces the risk of deadly strikes,” Monsell said, adding: “Right whales are facing threats from all directions, and the speed rule is one of their few protections.” The executive order is the latest move by the Trump administration to roll back environmental protections and reshape federal marine conservation policy. Since returning to office last year, the administration has expanded deep-sea mining, weakened protections for marine national monuments and dismantled key protections for endangered species across the US. “If every administration rollback proposed survives legal challenge, US waters could end up with just 4% under any form of protection – down from 26% – a number that is far too small to sustain marine biodiversity,” Morgan said. “Calling this a science initiative isn’t an improvement, it’s a giveaway of our fish and our ocean ecosystems, dressed up in credible-sounding language,” he added.

title: DNA database of UK dogs could help police collar criminals
summary: Experts working on database that could identify particular breeds involved in crimes, or rule out canine suspects
text: From tracking criminals to sniffing out drugs, dogs have long helped police crack cases. Now experts are hoping a database of canine DNA could offer vital leads. While hair, saliva and other canine material may be found at crime scenes, or on individuals connected to incidents, scientists say they are often not fully investigated. Yet such traces could provide valuable clues, from the identity of a canine perpetrator to evidence a dog’s owner was present at a crime scene. “You might have a human case, kidnapping, for example,” said Prof Denise Syndercombe Court, a forensics expert at King’s College London who is leading the work. “Lots of us have dogs. We live with dogs all the time. And so if you can identify canine material associated with a crime like that, then that can be very powerful in being able to provide intelligence to help solve a human case where there’s no other evidence.” As a result, researchers at King’s College London and the Royal Veterinary College have teamed up to harness the potential of canine DNA. It is not without its challenges. “Forensically, we don’t have loads of DNA,” said Syndercombe Court. “You have a few cells that are left at a crime scene … So you’ve got to make something useful out of that.” One approach is similar to that employed in the forensic analysis of human DNA, which is to focus on very small segments called short tandem repeats (STRs). This technique involves looking at the number of times these small segments are repeated in the DNA, resulting in two numbers for each STR – one inherited from each parent. Syndercombe Court noted the set of numbers provided a virtually unique profile – be it for a human or a dog. What is more, in dogs some sets of numbers are more common in some breeds than others. By focusing on STRs the team has built a database covering 80 different breeds – the first of its kind in the UK. For the 10 most common breeds, including labradors, cocker spaniels and miniature schnauzers, samples were taken from at least 50 dogs of each breed. The upshot is that canine DNA from a crime scene can be analysed and the results either compared with those from a particular dog – allowing that animal to be confirmed or ruled out as being linked to a crime – or screened against the database, potentially allowing experts to identify the breed of dog from which it came. The latter could be particularly useful where the dog thought to be linked to a crime is unknown, or where samples cannot be taken from a canine suspect, or where the sample does not match the DNA of a dog under suspicion. Syndercombe Court said her team now hoped to expand their database to include breeds such as pitbull terriers, American XL bullies and Japanese tosas that are banned in the UK. While the STR analysis focuses on DNA from the nucleus of a cell, the team have also created a database using another approach: sequencing DNA from within mitochondria – the tiny structures that power cells. With many mitochondria per cell, this approach can be useful where there is very little material to work with – although it is more limited as this DNA is only passed from mother to offspring. The focus on doggy DNA has already offered insights for police investigations. In one case, the approach shed light on whether serious injuries sustained by a man were down to another person – as he claimed – or occurred when he tripped over his own dogs as they attacked the accused. Forensic analysis supported the latter. “We looked at the T-shirt [of the accused] and there were holes in the T-shirt,” Syndercombe Court said, adding the team also found DNA from two different dogs on the garment. In another case, the DNA analysis shed light on a sheep attack. “We got some decent DNA from the crime scene, and the police thought it was a particular person’s dogs,” said Syndercombe Court. However the DNA from those dogs did not match the DNA recovered from the crime scene. “So we were not only able to exclude his dogs, which were of a particular breed, but also say the breed of dog that [did] this attack was very likely to be [another breed],” said Syndercombe Court. Dr Nicholas Dawnay, an expert in forensics at Liverpool John Moores University – who was not involved in the work – said research assessing how best to use canine DNA collected from crime scenes was hugely important. “Whether it is a dog attacking a human or livestock or wildlife species, the ability to match the individual dog back to the attack is the primary goal. Obtaining breed information at the early stages of an investigation may help narrow down the pool of possible dogs, which is exciting,” he said. But Dawnay said a big challenge remained regarding the funding of canine forensic casework: “Police budgets are stretched and without effective funding, the benefits of this research may struggle to be realised.”
