title: Meloni accused of ‘running scared’ with cap on foreign children in classrooms
summary: Critics say decree also banning burqa in schools shows Italian PM worried about losing far-right voters in next year’s elections
text: The Italian government has been accused of ramping up divisive rhetoric to try to court far-right voters ahead of next year’s general election after it passed a decree aimed at capping the number of newly arrived migrants in classrooms and banning the burqa and niqab in schools. The prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, who leads the far-right Brothers of Italy party, said her government had approved what she called “commonsense measures that do not divide but genuinely help to integrate”. Writing on social media, she said the measures included: “A limit of 30% in classrooms for students who do not adequately know Italian, plus tools to learn our language and a halt to burqas and niqabs in school.” The announcement was a toned-down version of comments she had made earlier in the week at an event organised by Brothers of Italy’s youth division. “It cannot be that in the classroom it is Italian children who feel left out because they’ve become the minority,” Meloni said as she vowed to “legally set the number of foreign students per class”. Thursday’s decree also sets out that in cases where students show persistent problems with integrating or struggling to learn the language, their parents will be referred to social services and will have to take free literacy and Italian language classes. Parents’ failure to comply could result in fines of up to €1,000. The education minister, Giuseppe Valditara, said the measures, set to take effect in the 2027-28 school year, would affect about 1,000 classrooms, or about 0.3% of the total nationwide. Rights campaigners were swift to link the measures to next year’s election, in which Meloni’s premiership is facing an unexpected challenger on the right. “She’s creating an emergency that is not a real emergency at all,” said Daniela Ionita, of the campaign group Italians Without Citizenship, pointing out that an estimated 60% of the pupils who could be described as foreign were born in Italy but faced a myriad of hurdles when it came to accessing citizenship. “Because there are now new parties pushing from the right, I think Meloni is scared,” she said. The government said students born and raised in Italy or who had attended at least two years of nursery school or completed three years of schooling in Italy would be exempt from the measures. Ionita said the ramped-up rhetoric was an attempt by the government to mask how little it had accomplished during its time in power. “If you remove every decree linked to security or to migrants, the government’s political and economic programme will fall apart, and very little concrete remains of one of the longest-serving governments of the last years in Italy,” she said. Marco Tarchi, a political scientist who focuses on the extreme right and teaches at the University of Florence, said the measures were “undoubtedly” driven by fears of a new political challenge on the right. Since February, a new party, Futuro Nazionale (FN), has galvanised the extreme right, with polls suggesting it could capture about 8% of the vote in an election expected as early as spring 2027. Led by Roberto Vannacci, a former army general best known for self-publishing a book rife with racism, homophobia, Islamophobia and antisemitism, the party’s popularity in polls has eclipsed that of Brothers of Italy’s two coalition partners, the League and the conservative Forza Italia. Those who have shifted allegiances include some who had enthusiastically lined up behind Meloni years ago as she spoke of “ethnic substitution” and vowed to install an all-out naval blockade to prevent migrant arrivals from north Africa. Tarchi said: “Many of the FN’s potential voters are former supporters of Giorgia Meloni’s party who are disappointed that, once in power, the leader softened many of her previous stances regarding the European Union, which she had harshly criticised; immigration, on which she had made radical proposals that were later abandoned; and other issues.” He said Vannacci had capitalised on this, capturing voters with an extreme manifesto that promised “remigration” and limits on the number of foreigners in the country, as well as curtailing LGBTQ+ rights and negating the right to abortion. He said that in order to win back this support, Meloni may have to adopt positions closer to those she held in opposition. A glimpse of what this could look like came this summer when Meloni seized on the sudden entry of tens of thousands of people into the tiny Spanish territory of Ceuta in north Africa, said Elisa De Pieri, a researcher at Amnesty International. “Meloni immediately exploited the situation in Ceuta, which had absolutely nothing to do with Italy and nothing to do with the Schengen space, but she made it into a supposed crisis for Italy,” she said. “And so that’s the mode that I think we’re going to see in the next months.” De Pieri predicted that Meloni “won’t be talking too much” about Italy’s offshore detention agreement with Albania on the grounds that it had not been as successful as she would have hoped. “It’s been very costly, and it’s been struck down repeatedly by national and international courts,” she said. Instead, she expects Meloni will adopt a more aggressive tone on migration more generally, leading to a polarising electoral campaign that would have a disproportionate impact on migrant communities. The view was echoed by critics of the new measures who pointed out the rarity of burqas or niqabs in Italian classrooms and said the government was simply repackaging previous, unenforced policies, given that the 30% threshold was previously floated by the education ministry in 2010. Save the Children said the overall impact would be to “create ‘first-class’ and ‘second-class’ students”. The leader of the Democratic party, Elly Schlein, described the decree as “shameful” and accused the government of “living on a different planet”. She said Italian parents were grappling with a very different set of issues, citing crumbling school buildings, the high costs of textbooks and low teacher salaries. “Faced with all this, the government’s response is to kick foreign children out of the classroom,” Schlein said. “Who do they think they’re kidding? After four years of cuts and no serious investment in school buildings, they’re inventing a witch-hunt that targets the youngest children.”

title: When Trump’s narrative meets voters’ realities
summary: By Donald Trump’s telling, we’re in a US ‘golden age’. Americans may feel differently. Plus: Anger at the elite and a gunfluencer runs in Texas
text: One of Donald Trump’s greatest talents – deployed during his time as a real estate tycoon, source and subject of tabloid gossip, reality TV protagonist, and president of the United States – is his ability to tell stories. With six weeks until the US midterm elections, he is likely to lean on this instinct more than ever. Rarely does the US president appear more comfortable than when behind a microphone, speaking without interruption, sometimes for multiple hours. Long before entering the White House, he wholeheartedly embraced social media as a means of crafting his narrative, going so far as to launch his own social network when booted off others. Earlier this week, his administration launched a YouTube channel, which critics quickly dismissed as a “state-run” TV network. Such platforms give Trump the ability to deliver his unfiltered narrative – unencumbered by open discussion, or its often tenuous relationship with the truth. Only when his stories leave the spaces where he has complete control, and enter the real world, do challenges arise. The president has long both courted and criticized the media, seeing the very publications and outlets he claims to loathe as opportunities to amplify his message. He bristles when they fail to do so. Last Friday, Trump abruptly announced a ban on CNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House over their coverage. The outlets swiftly sued over the move, setting up an acrimonious legal battle over press access. In the early hours of this morning, a federal judge ordered Trump to restore their ⁠access. “You said you weren’t going to cover me,” Trump told CNN, which had said no such thing, upon his arrival at the United Nations this week. “You shouldn’t be covering me.” *** Americans don’t need to tune in to Trump TV or log in to Truth Social to find out how much it costs to buy a home, feed their families or fill up their cars – factors that, time and again, have influenced which way they vote in elections. By the president’s telling, his controversial war on Iran has been about to end since not long after he launched it in February. Tariffs are meanwhile enriching the US economy. A new “golden age” is under way. When news outlets report otherwise, the president – a voracious media consumer – has a choice. He can engage with the message. The Iran war, more than 200 days since it started, is not over. The US economy is under pressure, despite a boost from vast investment into AI. And while the president and his allies seem to be doing OK, millions of Americans have yet to see tangible evidence that a “golden age” is under way. Or he can blame the messenger. Railing at all hours against the “Fake News Media”, Trump has filed lawsuits against the Wall Street Journal, the BBC and CBS, among others, over their coverage. “I believe in the free press more than anyone in this room does,” Trump claimed at July’s White House correspondents’ dinner. “Hmm,” he added. “Maybe not quite.” *** None of this marks a dramatic departure from the past 11 years, of course. But with Trump’s party facing a crucial electoral test in November, and Republicans increasingly nervous of an impending “bloodbath”, his hunger to control the narrative is set to grow. In this final stretch of the campaign, we can expect to see the president intensify efforts to hammer his narrative – from a purported “communist” infiltration of the Democratic party to a supposed economic boom across the nation – and attack those who dare to question it. This remarkably volatile president has shown a striking ability to stick to a message like glue in the final stages of an election. In 2024, this included relentlessly blaming Joe Biden for a surge in consumer prices, and promising Americans that he would fix it. We have a good sense of what it will include in 2026. After summoning Republicans for the party’s first ever midterm convention in Dallas this month – another chance to get behind a microphone, uninterrupted by reporters, or reality – Trump asked supporters to do him “the biggest favor” and “pretend” they were voting for him. In truth, his name will not appear on a single ballot paper. As polling day edges closer, the president is escalating his fights with the media. My colleague Chris Stein noted earlier this week that polls continue to show Democrats with an edge on the generic ballot, a key indicator of voter sentiment in congressional races, as well as in some key Senate contests. Once all votes are cast and counted, there is a world in which the president and his party retain control of Congress – defying frustration over the Iran war, concern over their handling of the economy and broader anger over the status quo – in an extraordinary display of political resilience. There is also a world in which they endure a painful rejection by voters and lose control of both congressional chambers, leaving Trump to serve out his second term as a lame duck in the White House. The president’s version of events is only likely to accept one of these outcomes. Quoted “Most people around the country, many of whom don’t even identify as Democrat or Republican or whatever, are 10 out of 10 pissed off, angry and willing to take that anger into action against the status quo.” – Maurice Mitchell, the national director of the Working Families party, a progressive third political party that has seen its endorsees winning bigger than ever this year Read more: ‘People are pissed off’: anger at the elite and the establishment is fueling this year’s midterms Meet the candidate: Brandon Herrera Brandon Herrera, a 30-year-old YouTuber with more than 4 million subscribers, has made a name for himself making outrageous pro-gun statements. He’s also the frontrunner in a race to represent Texas’s 23rd congressional district, where 23 people were killed in a mass shooting at a Walmart in 2019 and an 18-year-old former student killed 19 children and two teachers in the Uvalde school shooting. Democrats are hoping that such an extreme candidate, even by Texas’s standards, could be vulnerable at the ballot box. They aim to flip the seat that has been in Republican hands since 2015. Should he win the midterm election, Herrera will take what he calls his “second amendment absolutism” to Washington, with possible ramifications for nationwide gun laws and debate. title: Tall, dark and hated: plan to renovate ‘Paris’s ugliest building’ put on hold
summary: Tour Montparnasse modernisation project at a standstill after clashes over pricing and other issues
text: It has been called a carbuncle on the Paris skyline, a sombre skyscraper where visitors to its viewing platform often joke that the city looks better when you can’t see the building itself. The much-maligned Tour Montparnasse, a lone, dark monolith with tinted windows rising above a historic neighbourhood in the south of the city, is once again at the centre of controversy after its long-awaited renovation was halted this week because of disagreements between its many private co-owners. The tower, which opened in 1973, is the tallest skyscraper in inner-city Paris and is also considered its ugliest building. For more than a decade, plans have been thrashed out to overhaul the building and brighten its looming presence and modernise the area around it. Architects had planned to entirely refit the 210-metre structure with a new glass exterior, adding vegetation throughout, with a garden terrace on the 16th floor and an agricultural greenhouse at the top. The plans included a hotel on three floors of the 59-storey building, as well as new office and leisure spaces. But alongside a significant operation to remove asbestos, the estimated price of the project more than doubled to €800m (£688m). The building’s private co-owners, which include French investment funds and insurers, met this week for a final vote on the start of a first phase of renovation, with asbestos removal, interior stripping and a partial facade removal. After clashes over plans and pricing, more than three-quarters of the co-owners voted against the project. It was the last opportunity to launch the project before the building permit granted for the tower’s renovation expires at the end of November. There are now concerns that the building, which has been emptied and closed for renovation, will loom deserted. This summer, fire officers intervened after bits of glass fell off the building and landed on the street below, although no one was hurt. “Everyone needs to come to their senses,” said Philippe Goujon, the rightwing mayor of Paris’s 15th district where the tower is located. He told Agence France-Presse: “I cannot accept seeing a project that took 10 years to develop thrown away, or allowing this world-renowned landmark to fall into neglect.” Four of the co-owners who still want a renovation, including the tycoon Xavier Niel, said in a joint statement: “We would like all the co-owners, financial partners and public authorities to meet soon to examine all the solutions to transform the Montparnasse Tower.” Some co-owners hope that a new, scaled-down project could be agreed upon. Separately, the architect Renzo Piano has been tasked with overhauling the shopping centre beneath the tower and other buildings nearby, opening up new pedestrian spaces and moving from grey concrete to a greener, planted space. Local officials want to avoid delays to that project if the tower’s renovation stalls. The office of the Socialist mayor of Paris, Emmanuel Grégoire, said it wanted “an alternative solution to be proposed” so the site does not stay at a standstill. Opposition councillors on the left have suggested the “obsolete” tower should instead come down and be replaced by a park that would have a cooling effect during summer heatwaves.

title: ‘Your body fights to stay cool’: workers toil in record heat as federal rule frozen
summary: Trump officials and Republicans are rolling back protections against heat-related illnesses and deaths
text: When it’s 90F on a hot summer day, Esther Minton wears a long-sleeved shirt to work. “Working outside, you don’t have cover. There’s nowhere for you to really go if you’re on a roof or if you’re on the side of a building,” said Minton, a member of the Sheet Metal Workers Local Union 28 in New York City. “Having the sun beaming on your skin all day long, you’ll never make it through, so what you wear makes a difference.” Working outside during the brutal summer months means learning how to stay properly hydrated, dealing with port-a-potties that get much hotter than outside temperatures and handling heated copper metals exposed to direct sunlight. “Before the day is over, by the time you’re at break at lunchtime – say 12pm, when the sun is really out and doing its thing – you are drained,” Minton said. “Your body fights hardcore to stay cool, your body fights hard to not be dehydrated.” This summer was the hottest on record in the US, and workers are caught on the frontlines of a heat crisis that is expected to drive up heat-related illnesses and deaths. The rising temperatures come as the Trump administration and Republicans in Congress are rolling back federal rules meant to protect workers from heat injury and illnesses. In January 2025, the White House indefinitely froze Biden-era heat safety regulations that would have mandated water, shade, breaks, training and prevent plans for workers. House Republicans have also been pushing legislation that would prohibit the Department of Labor from enacting any workplace protections for heat exposure. Republicans in Florida and Texas have passed similar legislation prohibiting local city and county governments from passing heat protections. Big business groups and lobbyists, including from the agricultural and construction industries, have strongly opposed heat protection standards for workers, claiming employers already do what would be mandated and claim the rule would be a burden on employers. Workers at a recent Climate Week roundtable in New York City strongly disagreed employers are doing enough to protect workers from heat. Donald Nesbit, executive vice-president of Local 372 and former school cafeteria worker, recalled working in an old school building every summer in a kitchen basement as he prepared meals for students. “It was torture. We clocked temperatures at 130F to 140F in school kitchens during these summer conditions,” said Nesbit during the roundtable. “If we were to lock our animals in a car with those same conditions, we would be arrested, right? And yet, workers are working in those conditions, right, so there [have] to be protections. We have to push as a society to make protections better.” Currently, only seven states have enforceable heat prevention standards in place for workers. A December 2025 a study published in the journal Health Affairs found California’s outdoor heat protections had resulted in at least a 33% reduction in heat-related workplace fatalities since 2010. “We need a federal heat standard in this country,” said Julie Su, deputy mayor of New York City for economic justice and former secretary of labor under Biden. In June, Su and Zohran Mamdani, New York City mayor, issued heat protections for New York City workers, citing the White House’s pullback. “We had one proposed and the administration is not moving on it. There are also lots of states that have a standard, and New York does not have one,” Su said. “In the city, we are doing everything we can with the powers that we have.” The Occupational Safety and Health Administration (Osha) estimates over 550 US workers die and nearly 28,000 are injured annually from heat exposure. Heat has caused more than 2,300 deaths in the US in 2023 and 2024 combined, the highest numbers in 45 years of records, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. A spokesperson for the Department of Labor said in an email: “OSHA is currently reviewing comments from the public hearings on the proposed rule ‘Heat Injury and Illness Prevention in Outdoor and Indoor Work Settings.’ OSHA provides compliance assistance to employers regarding potential workplace hazards, including guidance on how to keep employees safe in the heat.”

title: ‘We don’t have time for more promises’: the Croatian town that took on an illegal waste dump
summary: After years of illegal mass flytipping in Gospić, fed-up residents decided to take matters into their own hands
text: “Gospić is our home,” Željka Šikić shouted to a crowd of 40,000 people outside the Croatian parliament earlier this month. The slogan is the name of a campaign she helped to set up to protest against the illegal dumping of waste in Gospić, a town in the mountainous Lika region of central Croatia. Between 2022 and 2024, waste was illegally abandoned at several sites in the town. At one of the biggest, just 50 metres from Šikić’s home, an estimated 35,000 tonnes of waste, some of it hazardous, was dumped and buried. In the dead of night, lorries heaving with waste would pass her front door and enter a nearby industrial site. This activity went largely unnoticed by the local authorities and police. But residents in Gospić were well aware and started taking it in turns to stay up to photograph the vehicles coming in and out of the site. “I don’t think it should be our job to stay awake all night to see what’s going on,” Šikić says. The waste became a blight on the community and a recent report from the Croatian Institute of Public Health revealed Pfas “forever chemicals” had been detected in groundwater samples nearby. Elevated concentrations of copper and lead were also detected in the soil. Pfas are a group of thousands of synthetic chemicals that have been linked to serious health conditions, including several types of cancer. They are known as “forever chemicals” because of how long they persist in the environment. Despite assurances that their drinking water is safe, a lack of trust means many residents have resorted to buying bottled water. “I’m really scared,” Šikić says. “I would like to move house but I don’t know who would pay for the house on the first road next to the waste. I feel betrayed.” In February 2025, years after the activity began, police and law enforcement officers arrested 13 people on suspicion of being part of the environmental criminal network involved in dumping the waste. The main suspects, two Croatian nationals, were considered high-value targets by Europol and were believed to have orchestrated the illegal import of hazardous waste from Italy, Slovenia and Germany. It is thought the criminals generated upwards of €4m (£3.4m) in profit from this activity. Waste crime is big business. Criminal networks often take advantage of the high costs associated with treating and disposing of waste properly. By falsifying documents to declare the waste as destined for recycling, they can save on the costs and pocket the difference. Residents in Gospić had hoped the arrests would finally mean the site was shut down and cleaned up. But 18 months later, it is still there. Frustrated by the lack of action, Šikić and 16 other residents joined together to form the “Gospić is our home” movement. Ivana Rukavina Sarić, another member of the campaign group, says: “We called people from different professional backgrounds because we knew from the beginning that this would be highly complicated and would need a multi-disciplinary approach.” Having shared information about their struggles online and with Croatian media, Sarić says the campaign turned national, with the group now getting calls daily from other affected communities. “There are so many waste hotspots in the whole of Croatia and so many people facing similar problems. The problem we have in Gospić is the drop of liquid that overflows the glass,” she says. “It’s become a national, even global problem.” Similar dumping has been reported in several other Croatian towns, but the issue extends far beyond national borders. The United Nations estimates that 15% to 30% of EU waste shipments are illegal, and a recent investigation by the Guardian uncovered irrigation canals contaminated with microplastics in Turkey, a major destination for UK waste exports. Anger at the scale of the problem prompted tens of thousands of people from across Croatia to descend on the capital on 5 September. It is thought there were upwards of 40,000 people marching through Zagreb. “The capital was full,” Sarić says. The group is demanding a comprehensive remediation of the site and the urgent removal of the buried waste. It also wants all known waste hotspots in Croatia to be included in a national waste strategy. The government has opened two public procurement procedures for the removal, disposal or recovery of the waste. But with the waste still there four years since the illegal activity began, and concerns mounting over potential health and environmental impacts, the group plans to head to Brussels where it will protest at the European parliament. “We’ve lost so much time, we don’t have time for more promises,” Sarić says. “We want clear information, clear deadlines and clear action.” The Croatian government did not respond to a request for comment.

title: Netanyahu lambasts Israel’s critics at UN as New York protesters detained | First Thing
summary: More than 100 people arrested while Israeli PM claims war on Gaza is ‘the opposite of genocide’
text: Good morning. Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, delivered an inflammatory address to the UN in New York, decrying what he said was a global anti-Jewish conspiracy and taking aim at critics of the humanitarian crisis in Gaza. He branded Turkey’s president, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, a “tyrant”, described Zohran Mamdani as the “antisemitic mayor of New York”, and declared that Israel’s war in Gaza was not a genocide, “it’s the opposite of genocide”. Netanyahu delivered his address just hours after the Palestinian leader, Mahmoud Abbas, said his delegation was “unlawfully” denied visas by the Trump administration to attend the meeting. Dozens of delegates, inspired by a Palestinian call, walked out of the General Assembly Hall of the UN headquarters as Netanyahu took the stage. What was the reaction on the streets of New York? More than 100 people were arrested outside the UN headquarters as hundreds of Jewish, Palestinian, Iranian and Lebanese New Yorkers, among others, protested during Netanyahu’s address. Susan Sarandon and Hannah Einbinder were among those detained. What has rapper Macklemore announced? The US rapper, removed from Ed Sheeran’s US tour after voicing his support of Palestine, has convened a Free Palestine tour to benefit humanitarian aid organisations. The charity show will visit Dublin, Paris and London, with a North American run to be announced. Iran awaiting response from Trump on proposal to open strait of Hormuz in six days Iran has said it has told Donald Trump it is willing to open the strait of Hormuz in six days, and to start talks on its nuclear program the day after, so long as the US lifts sanctions on Iran’s oil exports in return, ends the war on all fronts – including in Lebanon – and releases some of Iran’s frozen assets. Privately, Iranian officials believe they could reach a deal with the Americans, but fear Israel will use its influence to pull the US president away from the proposal due to the inclusion of demands over Lebanon. What happened in the Senate about the war? Senate Republicans have blocked a Democratic effort to end the US war against Iran, voting down a House-passed war powers resolution. The measure, which passed the House last week with bipartisan support, failed in the Senate by a 49-50 vote, attracting some Republican support, but not enough to pass. What other developments have there been in the Middle East? Saudi Arabia says it intercepted six ballistic missiles fired by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis, with the latest attacks pushing oil prices ⁠to a one-week high over fears of spiralling supply disruptions. Texas woman triumphs as court upholds acquittal in voting error case The nearly decade-long case of a Black Texas woman who was sentenced to five years in prison in a controversial illegal voting case will end with an acquittal, the state’s highest criminal court has ruled in a 5-4 decision. Crystal Mason has been appealing ever since her 2018 conviction for casting a provisional ballot that ultimately was not counted. What is the latest voting controversy in Nevada? The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) wrongly identified 185 people on Nevada’s voter rolls as non-citizens, state officials said this week, escalating concerns over the shoddy methodology the government is using to raise fear about non-citizen voting ahead of the midterm elections. Why is there backlash against a sheriff in California over voting? The Republican sheriff Chad Bianco must return more than 650,000 ballots his department confiscated earlier this year in an unprecedented move that violated election law, a state supreme court has ruled. Xi Jinping lays out terms to avoid US-China military conflict Xi Jinping has called for extensive cooperation with Washington to avoid a trap that could put the US and China on a military collision course amid rising tensions over artificial intelligence, trade and Taiwan. Rather than confrontation, conditions for “achieving the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and making America great again go hand in hand” and should be the goal, Xi said. Mark Saunokonoko has this list of key takeaways from the summit. In other news … Mary Peltola’s campaign says reports of her using slurs and shoving a staffer are exaggerated, but acknowledges the Democratic nominee in Alaska’s pivotal Senate race struggled after the deaths of her husband and mother. Trump’s Food and Drug Administration commissioner nominee, Dr Heidi Overton, has said the MMR vaccine shot is “safe and effective”, weeks after standing behind Trump as he suggested the shot could be “quite lethal”. US mortgage rates passed 7% for the first time since January 2025, according to federal lender Freddie Mac. Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s presidential campaign has accused Donald Trump of wanting to “colonise” Brazil in order to capture its natural resources by meddling in next month’s election there. Stat of the day: ICE has wasted tens of millions to carry out Trump’s mass detention agenda US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and other federal agencies have wasted tens of millions of dollars pursuing controversial plans to rapidly increase detention capacity – and the total will likely rise due to continuing mismanagement, congressional investigators have warned. Culture Pick: My dad was a monster! Sara Karloff on reviving Frankenstein, 95 years on Boris Karloff’s daughter and the composer Michael Shapiro, who has written a 21st-century musical score for the 1931 classic, talk to Pamela Hutchinson about how it became so loved – and the strange experience of watching your father be Dr Frankenstein’s creation as a teenager. title: Digested week: I had Nigella down as tradwife burlesque but her Bake Off debut won me over | Emma Brockes
summary: Plus, Prince Harry spreads his love of Marmite to his kids, and Dolly Parton’s nephew turns out to be fairly unusual
text: Monday It was a big week at the UN, Buckingham Palace and the White House, but for all sentient people of Britain, the top story this week was that Bake Off is back and we need to talk about Nigella. (“Isn’t that the thing you use on cold sores?” said my gen Alpha child, as yet uninitiated into the lifestyle icons of our age. “That’s Bonjela,” I said.) I went into the opener of the show’s 17th season crankily resenting the departure of Prue Leith, who I love, and who offers, apart from anything else, a corrective to all the women on TV at the moment lecturing us about how to age from behind Maga-style glow-ups. (Youth on HBO anyone? No thanks!) And in the first half of the show, Nigella did indeed seem to struggle. She was quiet, watchful and seemingly unsure of herself in the face of the wide array of personality types on the show, who were also struggling to adapt to new surroundings. This isn’t working at all, I thought, and then halfway through the show she clicked, or possibly I did. I should say that going back I was never a big Nigella person. I bought her first cookery book a million years ago and loved the excess of all that butter and cheese. But over the years, as her brand grew and refined, I just assumed she was part of the large cohort of women who aren’t really for me – broadly speaking, who commit themselves to a kind of tradwife burlesque that, even at ironic remove, seethes with the conventionality of the thing it’s critiquing. Anyway so much for that. As Bake Off unfolded, I crumbled like a flapjack in biscuit week (don’t email; per UK tax law, a flapjack is, indeed, a biscuit). It is so rare to watch someone of Nigella’s star power comport themselves on telly in such pensive style, so that even when she’s trying to be saucy, it seems to me, her natural state is one of anxious enthusiasm and a depth of feeling that comes out in odd places. “May I just say, I love salt,” she said, with the mad emphasis of someone correcting a widely held but incorrect assumption about themselves and instantly, of course, I loved her. Tuesday While the rest of the House of Windsor wrestled with the fallout from Tuesday’s publication of Charles Spencer’s book, Prince Harry – surely closer to his uncle in thought and style than anyone else in the family – gave us some benign royal news in the form of an update on his children’s eating habits. Since moving from the US to the UK last month, the prince said his two children were enjoying Marmite for the first time – and I’m going to have to run the quotes in full here, for their jolliness and mild strangeness. “Is that a British thing?” said Harry to Hello! magazine at the WellChild awards this week, referring to Marmite. “Because it’s always been in my life, and now the kids are eating Marmite on crumpets, which is big for me.” I mean, what’s that about? Of course he knows it’s British; perhaps he feels in brand competition with the iconic British spread. Anyway, on he went: “They used to diss me for having Marmite in the house, and now they’re in the UK it’s like that’s kind of like water under the bridge, so it’s good.” That’s nice; I mean it. I was happy when one of my two accepted that Marmite was the only way, although I’ve never had much success with any of the other British staples and nor has Harry, who said his attempt to put his kids on to beans on toast “hadn’t gone down very well”. I’d watch a full series on this, in which Harry puts toad in the hole, yorkshire pudding and the full English (“is that a British thing?”) in front of his kids – but no one tell Brooklyn Beckham or he’ll be round with his cookbook. Wednesday Disappointing news from the Dolly Parton estate, where that very nice-seeming nephew of hers who broke the news of her death in a video statement last month has turned out, judging by court papers filed by the Parton estate in Tennessee this week, to be – how to put this? – fairly unusual. Bryan Seaver, who Parton employed for more than two decades as her head of security, is alleged to have sent Danny Nozell, Parton’s manager who runs the late singer’s estate, a series of communications, including the lines, “I’m a killer” and, “I’m literally an international arms dealer and mercenary. All I do is warfare. Everyone needs to be worried about what I might do.” Meanwhile, in trying to explain himself to TMZ this week, Seaver apparently made things worse with the explanation: “I am a career soldier and military contractor and do conduct arms deals for foreign governments. I am a security professional and I am a killer. However, nothing in this lawsuit were threats and most of the comments I stand by.” So that’s OK. To be fair to Seaver, “all I do is warfare” is a great line I will be trying to work into my own conversations from now on. One wonders what this scene was like while Parton was alive. Famously, the singer employed large numbers of her family at Dollywood and elsewhere, and one has to assume kept any awkward characters in check. Now the queen is dead, can the centre hold? Thursday News of the one-in-a-thousand-year El Niño coming down the pike is so grim, let’s cling to the odd bit of cheer from the climate frontline. This week in West Bengal, news of a baby elephant calf, separated from its mother and drowning in flood water, was rescued by two heroic fishers who spotted its trunk, waving out of the water like a periscope, and after following it for 3 miles into shallow water, managed to fish it out of the murk. The calf, which was a few days old, had lost its mum and the rest of the herd at the Teesta River and, improbably, after wrestling it on to the boat, the fishers managed to find the herd and reunite it with its mum, who got in such a frenzy at the sight of her missing baby that onlookers fleetingly worried she’d kill it. Instead, she wrapped her trunk around its body, splashed its head with water and flapped her ears with abandon, making witnesses on the bank hold themselves in at the beauty of it all. Friday Week two of trying to change mobile phone providers comes to a close without success and what have I learned? That the phrase “I know it’s not your fault” followed by a giant rage spiral doesn’t achieve the desired outcome. That the phrases “why are you like this?” and “what is wrong with your company?” equally have little to no effect. And that inserting “literally” into the sentence “we’re talking about a £10-a-month contract, literally what’s wrong with you?” doesn’t provide the needle-moving emphasis I’d hoped. Time for a lie down and a rethink. The week in pictures

title: Hurricane Polo barrels towards Baja California region of Mexico
summary: Area’s second-most intense hurricane on record being fuelled by exceptionally warm Pacific waters
text: Hurricane Polo is barreling towards the Baja California region of Mexico, the latest system in a Pacific hurricane season that has been notably active in recent months. On 22 September, a measurement of 892 millibars was registered for Hurricane Polo, making it the second-most intense hurricane on record in the east Pacific. It is fuelled by exceptionally warm waters across the Pacific Ocean, providing favourable conditions for the system to maintain its considerable strength. Polo is expected to turn towards the west-north-west, before taking a more north-westerly trajectory on Saturday. It has maximum sustained winds of around 150mph, with even stronger gusts occurring within the most intense parts of the hurricane. Hurricane-force winds extend outward for approximately 40 miles from the centre, while tropical storm-force winds reach as far as 125 miles. These powerful winds, combined with torrential rainfall and dangerous seas, could have significant impacts. Although some fluctuations in intensity are possible over the coming days, Polo is expected to remain powerful as it tracks north-westwards. In India, a deep 988-millibar low-pressure system – a tropical storm in this case – is centred along the east coast, bringing widespread and potentially disruptive weather conditions to Odisha and surrounding areas. The system is producing heavy rainfall across the region, with the latest forecast models suggesting totals could exceed 200mm in some locations over a 24-hour period. Rainfall rates are expected to be particularly intense at times, with hourly totals potentially exceeding 30mm in the heaviest downpours. Such intense rainfall could cause significant surface water and localised flooding, particularly in low-lying areas and places with poor drainage. Strong and gusty winds are also affecting coastal parts of Odisha. Winds are forecast to reach around 50-60mph, creating hazardous conditions in exposed areas and potentially causing disruption to travel, infrastructure and power supplies. Authorities have closed numerous schools across the affected districts for safety reasons. Meanwhile, in Iberia, the relentless heat of summer is extending into meteorological autumn, with temperatures rising into the high 30s celsius on 23 September. Alvega, in Portugal, recorded a maximum temperature of 41.7C on that day. Such temperatures would have been record breaking 30-40 years ago in July and August, highlighting the severity of the heat in today’s climate.

title: TalkTalk races to sell consumer and broadband arms as administration looms
summary: Customers and jobs ‘top priority’ as company closes in on deals with Opus Broadband and investment group Octopus
text: TalkTalk is scrambling to secure its future amid the threat of administration, closing in on deals to sell its consumer and broadband arms as it seeks to save 900 jobs. The telecoms company said on Friday it was in the final stages of sealing deals to sell its consumer business as well as its wholesale operation, PXC. “The company expects to conclude both transactions imminently,” TalkTalk said. The UK’s fourth-largest broadband company was founded in 2003 by Charles Dunstone as a subsidiary of Carphone Warehouse. It has struggled in the highly competitive telecoms market, with its customer numbers shrinking from 4 million in 2019 to about 1.5 million. The debt-laden business is close to sealing a £100m deal to sell its consumer operation to Opus Broadband, and to sell its wholesale operation PXC to Octopus Investments for an undisclosed sum. A spokesperson for Opus said: “[Our] top priority is to ensure that every customer stays connected and that all TalkTalk employees’ roles are protected.” Octopus Investments declined to comment. “I’d be surprised if there is real disruption for TalkTalk customers if the deal with Opus goes ahead,” said Karen Egan, a telecoms analyst at the research and consultancy firm Enders Analysis, told the BBC. “They would take over the running of the operations I would expect. “They may look to move the customers to their own platform but I’m sure [the industry regulator] Ofcom would be focused on that being a very smooth transition, especially given that around 250,000 of TalkTalk’s customers are deemed to be vulnerable.” If the cut-price deals go through TalkTalk’s owners, which include Dunstone, will have to write off about £1bn in debt. PXC works with the Ministry of Defence although the sale process is unlikely to interrupt the services it provides. It is understood that work with the MoD is through a third-party reseller, not PXC directly, and that regulations mean there is always at least one other telecoms company to prevent disruption. It has been reported that Dunstone and TalkTalk’s biggest shareholders, including the private credit company Ares Management, could inject more money to take control of the consumer business if a deal cannot be reached. Shareholders have provided £350m in emergency funding over the past two years. Dunstone established TalkTalk in 2003 as a subsidiary of Carphone Warehouse in an attempt to shake up the UK broadband market. The business was later demerged, and floated on the London Stock Exchange in 2010. Initially a success story, at its peak in 2015 TalkTalk’s market value hit almost £4.8bn. But the company struggled at the budget end of the market, unable to invest at scale to compete with rivals such as Sky and BT. As customer numbers dwindled, Dunstone engineered a £1.1bn deal with Toscafund Asset Management in 2021 to take the company private, which saddled the business with debt. He has been seeking a buyer for TalkTalk for a number of years, with Virgin Media O2 and BT reportedly considering deals, but rivals and investors have been wary of the company’s embattled position at the budget end of the broadband market. Dunstone remains chair of TalkTalk but the business is effectively under control of its lenders, led by Ares.

title: Pow! Man in Batman costume chases down suspected Norwich handbag thief
summary: Superhero, who was joined by others dressed as comic book characters, retrieved stolen bag after scaling wall
text: A scene from the fictional comic metropolis of Gotham City played out for real in Norwich last weekend when a man dressed as Batman chased a suspected thief and recovered a woman’s stolen handbag. Sonni Mason, 25, was attending a friend’s fancy dress party on Saturday night in a Batman costume when he witnessed a handbag being snatched after a row in a queue for a nightclub in the city. Mason was joined in the chase by others dressed as comic book characters including Mister Fantastic from the Fantastic Four, and Poison Ivy, another character from the Batman franchise. They flagged down a group of police officers on their way before catching up with the suspected thief. But the suspect no longer had the bag. After a tip-off the bag was eventually discovered about 300 metres from where it was snatched, on top of a high flint wall on the perimeter of Norwich Cathedral. Failed attempts were made to get the bag down with a roll of toilet paper, before Mason, still in his Batman costume, scaled the wall and retrieved the bag. He returned the handbag to its grateful owner with all the contents still inside. Much of the incident was captured on a TikTok video uploaded to Mason’s account. In a post about the incident he wrote: “On a night out for a friends birthday, someone swiped someone bag over a pack of cigarettes out of spite …. myself as Batman, Poison Ivy, Mr Fantastic and various other heroes chased him down.” Speaking to SWNS news agency, Mason, who is from London and works in a cafe, said: “I hope I can inspire people to be a little bit more like Batman. Not so much the running around in the dark in a costume but helping others out. I didn’t expect to be scaling up a wall.” He added: “Everyone needs a little bit of Batman. You have to be brave, bold and kind. I would hope everyone else would do the same, whether or not they are wearing a cape or a cowl.” Rather than jump off rooftops or beat people up, he just wanted to make sure everybody was all right, Mason said. “That’s what [Batman] is about. He’s a protector. “I just hope more people will be inspired to do the same if they see someone being mugged or feeling uncomfortable on a night out. It shouldn’t take a superhero costume to make you want to do that.” A Norfolk police spokesperson said: “Officers on routine night-time economy patrols in Norwich were approached by a member of the public, on Saturday September 19, who requested help to find a missing bag. “Following inquiries at the scene, the bag was located with all of its contents intact and subsequently returned to its owner.”

title: Sagal Abdi-Wali: Labour’s candidate in Starmer’s former seat zeroes in on local issues amid Green challenge
summary: Camden council leader’s message is clear: she’s ‘visible, committed and local’, and has been for a long time
text: Sagal Abdi-Wali does not want to be the prime minister. She doesn’t even want to lead her party. Labour’s candidate for Holborn and St Pancras laughs and shakes her head with unusual vigour when asked if she would like to follow in the footsteps of the last member of parliament for the constituency, Keir Starmer. “No, no, no, no, that’s not at all, in any way, what I’m trying to do,” she says during a break in campaigning in the Primrose Hill cafe in Regent’s Park. “I’m literally trying to get through the next few weeks and trying to be the member of parliament for this constituency, and that’s all I care about.” It’s a message the 42-year-old leader of Camden council returns to with ruthless discipline ahead of a byelection on 8 October. It is plastered all over her campaigning material and brought up by every door-knocking Labour activist – every mention an implicit comparison between herself and her high-profile opponent Zack Polanski. “All I’ve done, all my life, is be a committed champion for people here,” says Abdi-Wali. “Whether it’s volunteering as a teenager or being a councillor, and all the work I did in between, that’s all I’ve ever done. All I want to be is someone who will be visible and local and committed every single day.” Labour HQ is in no doubt of the stakes in this high-profile byelection, triggered after the former prime minister was unceremoniously dumped by his own MPs and quit the seat to concentrate on international affairs. If the party wins here, Andy Burnham can argue that he saw off Reform in Makerfield and can kibosh the Greens in the capital. Spinners will say his appeal is national and point to victory in this part of north London as proof that his homespun northern charm works south of the Watford Gap. If he loses, his relatively lengthy honeymoon period in Westminster is over. The constituency is young, popular with students, and diverse. About 45% of constituents were born overseas and 48% are aged between 18 and 34, compared with the UK average of 28%. The borough was once among the most ironclad of Labour strongholds but the party has lost support here since Starmer first won in 2015, its majority cut in half from 2019 to the 2024 general election. “All things being equal, Labour win,” says More in Common’s Luke Tryl. “But if Polanski can excite his base enough, and tap into some on the soft left who see it as a way to keep Burnham true, then the Greens could nick it.” Despite failing to persuade the Green party to put off its annual conference, Polanski is flooding the area with members, focusing heavily on Gaza, delivering leaflets saying no Labour councillor has taken up an invitation to sign a statement of solidarity with Palestine. The fact Abdi-Wali did not attend a Camden Muslim Network hustings on Tuesday has been leapt on by Green activists. Abdi-Wali insists she is not focused on what any other candidate is saying, and she won’t be drawn on the Greens ground game or digital air war. Her nonattendance at the hustings was due to a last-minute invitation and a prior obligation, she says [see footnote]. She won’t say if she thinks the Labour government needs to go further on Gaza, only that the foreign secretary’s decision to call Israel’s occupation of the West Bank unlawful and announce sweeping sanctions on trade with Israeli settlements was welcome. “People have seen what’s been happening over the last three years – the 70,000 Palestinians killed by the Israeli government and the atrocities of Hamas on October 7th,” she says. “In our communities we’ve seen a rise in hate and we’ve been doing a lot of work in making sure those communities feel supported.” Abdi-Wali arrived in London in the early 90s, speaking no English, after fleeing war in Somalia with her four brothers and her mother, who trained as a lawyer in Somalia. “The way we made friends was through sport, was through football, and we just all spoke this universal language,” she says. She moved to Gospel Oak when she was seven, and her father later joined the family. He stood as a candidate for the Liberal Democrats in the 2010 local elections, but it is her mother, a community activist, who provided her inspiration, says Abdi-Wali. So why did she not remain a community organiser, or lead on local issues as the leader of Camden council, a position she took up only in May? “I’ve seen as a councillor, and as a council leader, a lot of the issues that particularly impact this community like housing and the climate emergency need national-level policy and national advocacy,” she says. It was seeing a rise in homelessness around King’s Cross that pushed her to join the Labour party in 2015. “In the 2000s it was almost eradicated, but when I came back to Camden from university, homelessness was really rampant,” she says. “It was a political choice … I realised it needed political solutions.” Housing is a big concern in the constituency where, despite the proliferation of millionaire’s mansions, 76% of residents rent, compared with the UK average of 36%. But Abdi-Wali is wary of rent controls, saying they can help those already in housing but reduce the availability of stock for others. “It’s not a solution for the vast majority of people,” she says. “But I think everything should be looked at as an option to see how we can really tackle the housing crisis.” Abdi-Wali admits she was unsure about putting her name forward as Labour’s candidate, but as well as receiving lots of positive encouragement, it was a nudge from a very different source that made her apply. When her name began being mentioned, the Reform UK home affairs spokesperson, Zia Yusuf, wrote on social media that Abdi-Wali was being “foisted” on the people of Holborn, despite being “born in Somalia” (adding, if the subtext were not clear enough, “do you understand what’s happening?”). Did Yusuf’s comments tip the balance? “It was more that I think people like me should be in this arena,” she says. “And wanting to make sure that young people that look like me – or don’t look like me – can understand that it’s not just divisive, hateful rhetoric that gets you here. Actually just being a local person committed to your community and wanting to do better for it can also do that.” • The subheading and main text of this article were amended on 25 September 2026. Sagal Abdi-Wali is the current, not former, leader of Camden council. • Footnote added 5 October 2026: Camden Muslim Network contacted the Guardian after publication to state that their invitation to Sagal Abdi-Wali was sent out at the same time as other candidates; however, it was not received by the Labour party until closer to the date.

title: Would you bet on the future of our planet?
summary: Prediction markets are focusing on extreme weather and the climate crisis. But as scientists warn of an increasingly unpredictable planet it’s led to questions about what exactly people are betting on
text: How hot will it get in your nearest city tomorrow? How quickly will the planet’s ice melt and its corals die off? How many huge, costly climate disasters will hit this year? If you’re inclined to do so, you can now place online bets on how the weather and the broader, longer-term climate crisis will play out. In the US, big online prediction markets like Kalshi and Polymarket are considering a new area of growth beyond mere sport and crypto: the climate itself. Kalshi recently reported 500% growth in weather and climate wagers over the past year, taking the market to a $1.1bn, and is now partnering with the Weather Company, which owns the Weather Channel, to boost its credibility in this new arena. What does this mean for our ability to predict the future of our climate? More, after this week’s most important reads. Essential reads Huge El Niño projected to cause more than 450,000 deaths by February ‘Planetary boundaries’ necessary for flourishing of life have been massively breached, scientists warn British people understand the climate crisis threat. Today I’m empowering them to tackle it | Andy Burnham In focus Betting on the weather isn’t new, but some climate scientists have been left feeling queasy about people placing bets on the well-documented breakdown of a stable climate, caused by the burning of fossil fuels. Such bets, they argue, trivialise and gamify raw human suffering, distancing people rather than rallying them to act on the climate crisis. Particular alarm has been raised about the consequences of betting on wildfires, after large wagers were placed on the Los Angeles fires last year (Kalshi and Polymarket stress they have banned such betting, due to unintended incentives for would-be arsonists). “I find it depressing because it’s distracting us from what we should be focusing on,” said Kaitlyn Trudeau, a scientist at the non-profit Climate Central. Trudeau’s own grandfather lost his home in the LA fires, and she was aghast to find that people had been betting on the disaster. “I’m not against prediction markets in general but we need to be clear about the downsides,” she said. “They aren’t going to reduce the risks of climate change or solve climate change.” When I covered the story this month, though, it was striking to me how these prediction markets, which are essentially a gauge of public opinion, see their role as forecasting events in the natural world. A Kalshi spokesperson told me the company sees itself as part of “well-calibrated forecasting data” – essentially using the wisdom of the market to help predict how hot it will get, how bad floods will become and other such environmental outcomes. A growing array of data, and the use of artificial intelligence in harnessing it, is indeed helping scientists work out thorny questions over how the climate crisis is set to unfold. Perhaps prediction markets will be able to add to this in some way. But recent evidence suggests that anyone predicting exactly what will happen to our planet – other than it generally getting hotter, more chaotic and more dangerous – over this century will have a tough task. The United Nations recently conceded that a foundational international target to restrain the global temperature rise to 1.5C beyond pre-industrial times – a promise made just a decade ago – is now already effectively trashed. Global heating is too rapid, and too unrestrained, to meet the 1.5C goal, which will cast billions of people into the throes of extreme weather, food insecurity and heightened risk of the sort of cataclysm we recently saw in Nepal. Conversely, the advance of clean energy means that the very worst previous scenario, a pathway known as RCP8.5 and lined with rampant coal burning, is now unlikely. The absolute worst, but also the most optimistic, scenarios have been swept from the table, all in just a handful of years. The world itself will have further surprises in store for us as we blunderingly fiddle with its chemistry. “Feedback loops” from natural systems such as thawing permafrost, supersized wildfires and overheating wetlands mean that planet-heating emissions coming from such sources could accelerate overall global heating by as much as 30%, a recent study found. This will add as much as 0.4C to the overall global temperature – a large chunk on top of what is already set to be a disastrous rise in heat. But even in this stark new study, researchers caution that there are uncertainties. While for now we still retain some control over our own destiny, the situation could still gallop away from humanity – the planet, once provoked, could unleash far hotter temperatures than this. Perhaps – hopefully – it will be less sensitive. But do you really want to bet on that? title: Friday briefing: How a ​grassroots ​film ​is ​turning ​climate anxiety ​into ​action
summary: In today’s newsletter: The People’s Emergency Briefing delivers a stark warning about ​o​ur future in a warming world. ​B​ut sharing difficult truths collectively​ shows us that there is still hope to be found
text: Good morning. Here we are, stumbling into an oddly warm autumn and with the aftermath of a ceaselessly dry summer all around us in our parched parks and fire-ravaged forests. With the change in season, the headlines are no less gruelling. At the start of the week, more than 450,000 people are predicted to die from an unprecedented El Niño over the next six months. At the end of the week, a report by UK intelligence chiefs reveals the extent to which the collapse of natural systems threatens security and defence around the world – a report which, as the Guardian revealed, was suppressed under former prime minister Keir Starmer’s leadership. Meanwhile, as Hettie has written about in a previous newsletter, right-leaning climate sceptics continue to seed doubt about the glaring reality wherever they may. Overload, silencing and misinformation can generate fear, suspicion, grief, helplessness, a compulsion to look away or to focus on paying the next bill. But this summer, I’ve been hearing about another climate briefing – in film form – that aims to engage all of those emotions. It’s as much about giving people the information they deserve as it is about helping them deal with it once they have it. You won’t see it on Netflix, but your neighbour might be screening it at the local scout hall this weekend: for today’s newsletter, I spoke to Nick Oldridge, co-founder of the People’s Emergency Briefing, about how a film about the end of the world became a grassroots movement. First, the headlines. Five big stories UN general assembly | Benjamin Netanyahu delivered an inflammatory address to the United Nations, decrying what he said was a global anti-Jewish conspiracy and swatting aside criticism of Israel’s war in Gaza. UK news | Far-right agitator and anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas has been arrested after he filmed himself appearing to slash the side of a dinghy while a rescuer was onboard. Iran | Iran says it has told Trump it is willing to open the strait of Hormuz in six days, and to start talks on its nuclear program the day after, so long as the US lifts sanctions on Iran’s oil exports, ends the war on all fronts – including in Lebanon – and releases some frozen assets. Ukraine | Ukrainian refugees fear they could be left homeless after the government quietly axed 70% of funding for hosts of the Homes for Ukraine scheme, reducing monthly “thank you” payments. World news | Xi Jinping has called for extensive cooperation with Washington to avoid the “Thucydides trap” that could put the US and China on a military collision course amid rising tensions over AI, trade and Taiwan. In depth: ‘It’s clear evidence that this model works for engaging politicians’ Have you seen that climate film yet? You know, the one you read about on the Guardian website and then a friend of a friend emailed you about it, but other things got in the way until your best pal watched it and said you absolutely had to see it and then you looked it up and realised there were screenings happening all around you. That was my experience, at least. The People’s Emergency Briefing began life, in real life. Last November, nine climate experts delivered a “first-of-its-kind national emergency briefing” to an audience of MPs, civic and business leaders in Westminster. It was, by all reports, a galvanising event. The organising team – including pioneer in carbon footprinting Prof Mike Berners-Lee and TV environmentalist Chris Packham – then crowdfunded to turn the in-person briefing into a film, which anyone can register to screen in their local village hall, faith centre, workplace or wherever else they can get bums on seats. I watched the briefing myself at an arts centre in Paisley on a sunny Friday evening last month. The 50-minute film felt like 15, as the roster of experts set out in plain language how global heating is affecting all aspects of life in the UK: the economy, food, healthcare, nature, national security. It’s a hard watch. The alarming – but never alarmist – message is that the climate is changing much faster than expected, and that we are woefully unprepared for it. The grinding frustration of these experts – who have been repeating these stark facts to a sclerotic government and a sceptical public for years – is evident, but there is also hope. The aim is to demand that the prime minister convenes a Covid-style primetime emergency briefing on the climate and nature crisis, led by independent experts. As Packham says as he introduces the film: “I understand it’s human nature to prefer not to know, to try to bury our heads in the sand. But if we all take a breath and watch this together, well first of all that’s a huge relief and second we can figure out what to do about it.” *** Do it like Gogglebox What’s unique about the film is both how it’s framed and how it’s watched. “We knew you can’t just film people talking at podiums,” Oldridge explains, “so we decided: ‘We’ll do it like Gogglebox’.” Spliced between the expert commentary, members of the public sit on a sofa across from Packham and talk about what they’ve just watched. “This is the nub of it,” says Oldridge. “This film has got to be watched in groups, people who experience it together and then talk about it, instead of the isolated way we usually consume media.” Since the first community screening on 7 April, the film has become a word-of-mouth phenomenon – so far 2,789 screenings have taken place, with a further 1,395 planned. Readers across the country, from the south of England to north-east Scotland, have contacted the Guardian’s Environment desk to tell us about their involvement. Anna Taylor, trustee of Wendover Climate Action, who organised a packed screening in the Buckinghamshire village after reading about the original Westminster event in the Guardian, told me: “It’s spurred me on so that, if nothing else, my kids will know I tried to make things better for them”. Any group can register to host a screening, and will receive a carefully scripted guide for steering the discussion afterwards as viewers process some difficult material. Organisers have told me how essential it felt for people to sit together and share their immediate reflections on what was a shocking film for many, even those who considered themselves familiar with climate science. That was my experience: the lump in my throat got smaller as I listened to other people talking about their visceral shock, anxiety and plans to take action. Groups are also encouraged to invite local politicians – not to put them on stage to shout at but so they can sit among the audience as another community member. (Eleven were invited to the Paisley screening, none came – you know who you are!). *** Will it burst through the eco-bubble? One of the threads we unravelled in the discussion after my screening was how to normalise climate conversations: “How do we reach people who don’t even believe climate change is happening?” asked one woman. (It’s worth interjecting here that tracker polling suggests this summer’s extreme weather has prompted a big jump in voters’ ranking of the environment as an issue.) But it’s a question that the People’s Emergency Briefing team have wrangled with extensively. Inevitably there’s an element of self-selection with community screenings, but there’s ongoing work to bring the film to wider audiences at Quaker meeting houses, churches and cathedrals, the Women’s Institute, hospitals, school staff rooms, the national lottery, the V&A, Channel 4, and even here at the Guardian. All the organisers I heard from had plans to run more screenings and diversify audiences, while viewers reported feeling more hopeful, better informed and more motivated to act. “We first realised something was happening when we watched the booming community screenings,” says Oldridge. “But now all these big brands are doing it too. You’re always trying to break beyond the eco-bubble and I think we’ve got a very good chance of doing that now”. *** What difference can it make? In recent years, the orthodoxy around climate communications has tended towards telling only hopeful stories, with a recognition that the public were beyond capacity for bad news. “But we felt quite strongly that we need to reset the baseline of understanding,” says Oldridge. “Most surveys show people are worried, but they see it as a far away problem. And they don’t have all the facts that relate to the UK and their own lives.” This is especially salient when the right weaponise net zero as a threat to the economy. Mindful of this context, the film is trenchant in its optimism. It avoids finger-wagging; there’s no scolding of those of us who still fly or eat cheese. There’s a recognition that – however helpful individual effort can be – climate change isn’t a problem that isolated action can solve. Rather, it calls for an emergency response equal to that rolled out during the pandemic, or a war. “Our effort is focused purely on change driven by government, helping the public understand that they are one of the pieces of the jigsaw that enable the government to be bold enough to make those changes,” says Oldridge. A major academic study of the film’s impact will be published next month and early findings suggest that every screening in a constituency makes its MP more likely to back a televised emergency briefing. “It’s clear evidence that this model works for engaging politicians.” There is engagement too at the top of government, according to our environment editor Fiona Harvey. She reported this week how Ed Miliband brought the national security warnings to global attention at the UN general assembly in New York, with the backing of Andy Burnham. It marks a growing openness from the prime minister towards climate action, she believes, encouraged by Miliband and that goes beyond campaigning pragmatism ahead of the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, where Labour is taking on Green leader Zack Polanski. Perhaps there is room for guarded optimism, as there is in this devastating film about the systemic collapse of society that is paradoxically hopeful. As one member of the public says on screen: “It’s not as if we need to go off and invent all the solutions. They’re right there. We just need to use them”.
