title: Nepal’s PM says flash flood was ‘warning to world’ as he scolds leaders at UN over climate change
summary: Shah ⁠said ​Nepal’s recovery and reconstruction needs were estimated at about 10% of GDP, as he appealed for more international support
text: Nepal’s prime minister scolded world leaders at the UN on Thursday, saying last month’s catastrophic deadly flood was a reminder that climate change keeps hurting people who didn’t cause the crisis. The disaster “was a warning to the world,” Balendra Shah told the general assembly. “And I ask you today: Have you really heard that warning?” International scientists have connected melting permafrost caused by changes in the climate – linked to burning coal, oil and gas – to the instability of the glacier, which partly collapsed and triggered a massive flood that killed at least 1,400 people. Shah said that Nepal contributed less than one-tenth of 1% of the heat-trapping gases behind climate change. “We did not create this crisis, yet we are paying a colossal price for it,” said Shah, 36, a former rapper and engineer, who wore a traditional Nepali hat and dark sunglasses, which he uses for medical reasons. Shah ⁠said that Nepal’s recovery and reconstruction needs were estimated at about 10% of gross domestic ⁠product following the flood that struck four weeks ago, and argued that vulnerable countries should not be ⁠forced to take on additional debt to rebuild from catastrophic climate events. “When a climate-driven disaster destroys ‌infrastructure of a poor ‌country, the answer cannot simply be another mega loan or ‌a patchwork of small grants,” he said. “We need adequate grant-based support from the world.” He urged closer cooperation between Nepal, India and China on climate resilience, calling for an urgent Himalayan mechanism to share satellite data, monitor glacial lakes, strengthen early-warning systems and coordinate disaster ‌responses across borders. Shah didn’t ask for a specific amount in international aid, but he called the financial aid system inadequate and too bureaucratic. The Nepalese leader said the flood had swept away roads, bridges, schools, homes and livelihoods, interrupting Nepal’s development progress. Weeks later, search and recovery operations were still under way, with more than 6,000 people remaining missing in the area. Shah ‌said many of them may never be found. The World Bank earlier this week made available up to $170m in emergency financing to help Nepal respond to the disaster and begin recovery efforts. Over the past 75 years, the US has emitted about 1,500 times more carbon into the air than Nepal, according to the Global Carbon Project, a group of scientists that track greenhouse gas emissions. The US this week announced $31m in aid to Nepal for flood recovery, which brings America’s total financial help up to $36m. Shisir Khanal, Nepal’s foreign minister, said Wednesday at the UN climate summit: “What happened in Nepal is not an isolated disaster but a preview of what awaits many vulnerable nations.” Speaking to the Guardian earlier this month, Khanal said Nepal had written a joint letter to the UN’s fund for responding to loss and damage – set up in 2022 in line with the Paris climate agreement – to request $20m in climate-related damages.

title: ‘We wanted to prove we didn’t need air conditioning’: the airport cooled by natural ventilation
summary: At Roland Garros airport on Réunion island, the ceiling design funnels a light tropical breeze into the terminal
text: At the arrivals terminal at Roland Garros airport on Réunion island, visitors are greeted by floor-to-ceiling windows framing the lush green mountains of the French Indian Ocean territory. What they may have also expected was the icy chill of air conditioning; this island just off Madagascar sits in the tropical zone to the south of the equator. But instead, the terminal is cooled by a light tropical breeze, the result of natural ventilation built into its unique design. The genesis of the project was in 2016, as part of a wider effort by airport management to reduce its carbon dioxide emissions. Marc Delanoë, who was then leading the airport’s environmental and energy team, was determined from the beginning that the new arrivals terminal, which was being built completely from scratch, would not use air conditioning. “I took on the responsibility to prove to my management that not using air conditioning was feasible,” said Delanoë, now the airport’s sustainable development director. “So, from the start, we never thought of this building having air conditioning being an option. It was a risky bet, but the further we went with our studies, the more we realised that we were right.” The roof of the terminal, which opened in 2024, curves upwards from each of the rectangular building’s long sides in gentle waves. But, instead of meeting in the middle, the roofs end abruptly to form a “canyon”. The creation of an area of low pressure funnels wind into the building through vents on each side that are adjusted depending on the weather conditions. Ceiling fans with a 7.5-metre (24.6ft) diameter help to circulate the air. In the 30C (86F) humid heat of Réunion’s wet summers, which last from around November to April, the resulting breeze reduces the perceived temperature by four to five degrees, to almost the same level usually set for air conditioning. Less air is allowed to flow in during the island’s dry winters, when the coastal daytime temperature falls to 25C and below. During a cyclone, the entire building is closed up. The building’s lead architect, AIA Life Designers, said it wanted to challenge the assumption that adjusting temperature was the only way for humans to cope with heat. “It is precisely this pitfall – understanding summer comfort solely through the lens of indoor temperature – that we want to dismantle, a pitfall that traps us in the logic of air conditioning as the only answer to comfort requirements,” said Éric Bussolino, the firm’s engineering and environment director. “Our objective is to maintain an indoor air temperature identical to the outdoor temperature while generating an airflow of 1 metre per second to reduce the perceived temperature for passengers.” AIA, chosen for its expertise in designing airport buildings, partnered with a local architect, Olivier Brabant, who had the necessary expertise of designing buildings for the island’s tropical maritime climate, Delanoë said. Local architects were already using natural ventilation on the island, in everything from offices and libraries to a university amphitheatre designed by Brabant. “We simply had to change the scale,” Delanoë said. “You have to channel the air, play with the elements … That’s exactly what our ancestors did on La Réunion,” he said. “They built houses according to the direction of the wind, with a central corridor, and they opened the windows or closed the doors depending on the amount of air that they wanted to let in. If they were cold, they closed them; if they were hot, they opened them.” Building the arrivals terminal cost €75m , of which €15m went on a new baggage sorting system and €60m on the building, said Delanoë. Since opening two years ago, the airport has saved €150,000 a year in energy bills, he said. AIA said this amounted to savings of about 60% compared with an air-conditioned building, while carbon emissions were lower by a factor of eight. Delphine Robert, who leads the local tourism board’s welcome team, works in the terminal once a week and said she preferred it to other offices. “It’s very airy. It’s comfortable – a lot of light, the ventilation is optimal,” she said. “I find it better working in this building, because I am often sick. And that’s the result of air conditioning, which is very strong in offices. So that’s why it’s more pleasant to work in a building where the air circulates, but it is natural.” The lessons from the terminal’s natural ventilation will be harder to apply in large, polluted cities in mainland Europe, said Delanoë. “You will concentrate the pollutants inside – it doesn’t work,” he said. “We are lucky, we are on an island, there is no pollution around.” Continental Europe, which is struggling to adapt to heatwaves being made ever more severe by the climate crisis, would also have to eschew air conditioning to make use of natural ventilation, Delanoë said. “The problem is that if you have air conditioning at home and you have air conditioning in your car, when you get to the office, if you don’t have air conditioning, you’re going to be hot, he said. “That is to say that if you reduce air conditioning throughout your life … when you get to 30 degrees in the office, you won’t be hot. In La Réunion, people are used to 30 degrees.”

title: ‘We can’t ride this storm’: the English farmers facing uncertainty after sustainability funding runs dry
summary: After the available money ran out after just six hours, some fear they will have to reverse efforts to boost nature
text: On Tuesday morning, farmer Peter Hatley logged on to his computer at 10am. England’s 2026 sustainable farming incentive (SFI) was opening for applicants and, after three bad harvests, the money would be a lifeline. But Hatley, who runs a 240-hectare family farm in Cambridgeshire, was faced with repeated error messages. He called the government’s helpline, which he says acknowledged there were problems with the scheme, but says by the time the problem was fixed, the money had gone. “We tried our utmost. We were fully prepared; everything was checked and triple-checked and through no fault of our own we were denied this opportunity. I’m shell-shocked,” he says. By 4pm on Tuesday, just six hours after it launched, the SFI had run out of money after a rush some compared with “the scramble for Oasis tickets”. SFI is part of a package of payments that replaced the EU’s common agricultural policy, paying farmers to look after nature, soil and other public goods, rather than simply for farming and owning land. Figures suggest that up to 10,000 farmers with funding agreements that will expire in March 2027 either chose not to apply or could not apply. Historically, Hatley says his farm could weather a level of uncertainty with confidence that, if he had one bad harvest, the next would probably be good. But in the face of the rapidly changing climate, this is no longer a given. “In 2024 we had extreme rain, in 2025 a lack of rain caused depressed yields and then this year, I mean, it’s 25C at the end of September. We’re at breaking point. We can’t ride this storm,” he says. Farmers across the country are reporting a devastating outlook, with crop-destroying heat and drought, and soaring fertiliser costs tied to the war in Iran piling pressure on what has already been a challenging few years. Hatley has spent years slowly diversifying his farm and creating space for nature but says without the SFI funding he has no choice but to reverse this. “I will undo all the hard work over the last 20 years and move to a mono crop with maize. It’s not a threat, it’s what I will do for my family. It will break our hearts but my children come first. I’m just thankful my father is not here to see it,” he says. “The skylarks, the lapwings, they’ll go. I’ll have to put more cows on my grass so the bugs and the dragonflies will suffer. If I said this to anybody else, it would sound like blackmail, but it’s not; it’s a business fact. How do I explain to the bank manager that I can’t afford to pay my mortgage this month because I put wood pigeons and birds of prey first?” Martin Lines, chief executive of the Nature Friendly Farming Network, said the speed at which the funding ran out showed the “desperation” many farmers were experiencing. Mat Cole, an uplands farmer in the south of England, could not log in to the scheme as it launched because he was busy at market day. But as soon as he could, he rushed home and by noon was ready to apply. After spending a few hours preparing his application, he submitted it at 3.50pm, only to be greeted by an error message. “I then understood they had run out of money,” he said. “I thought I probably had a week or so to apply.” Like Peter, he has been left in an uncertain situation, not knowing if he can continue with the environmental improvements he has been making on his farm. “We’ve engaged with these schemes to try and improve our environment. We’ve used the money to improve hedgerows, grasslands and water quality. To have the drawbridges pulled up like that, it’s just shambolic,” he says. The last few years have presented farmers with a number of financial challenges, on top of dealing with a changing climate. Brexit meant losing access to the basic payment scheme (BPS) through the common agricultural policy; the BPS is being phased out, however, and replaced by a complex system of funds for environmental management, which seem much more likely to run out or be unexpectedly wound up for the year. This comes as basic costs for fuel and inputs are also soaring, thanks to global conflict. The National Farmers’ Union is calling on the government to commit now to the 2027 SFI scheme. “For food-producing businesses already questioning whether they can survive the year ahead, this clarity is critical,” said Robyn Munt, the union’s vice-president. Farming Minister Stephen Morgan said: “Farmers will receive almost a third of a billion pounds each year for three years under new SFI26 agreements. That’s nearly a billion pounds invested in resilient farming. “Previously a quarter of funding headed to just 4% of farms making claims. That’s why this government developed a fairer system to reach more farmers by capping applications at £100,000 and ensured small farms and those new to environmental land management schemes were prioritised. “I know some farmers who wanted to join SFI26 will be deeply disappointed not to have secured an agreement during Window 2, particularly given the challenges the sector has faced this year. I have heard those concerns and am determined to work closely with farmers as we learn lessons from this year and shape SFI27, including exploring alternatives to a first-come, first-served application process.”

title: Skylarks and sandwich terns among new birdies on reserve created from ‘boring old golf course’
summary: National Trust has transformed Sandilands in Lincolnshire into a nature reserve with wetlands and wading pools
text: There is no chance of a birdie or an eagle any more. But there are skylarks, short-eared owls, avocets and curlew. Sandilands, a former golf course on the Lincolnshire coast, has been transformed by the National Trust into a 2km-long nature reserve with wetlands, wading pools, rough grassland and coastal scrub. The new reserve opens to the public on Saturday but the birds have already flocked in: little ringed plovers and avocets nested this summer as soon as fairways and bunkers were turned into shallow pools and islands for shore and marsh birds. Marsh harriers have been hunting over the reserve, with water rail, sandwich terns and spotted redshank also flying in. “It’s been super-exciting to see the transformation from a boring old golf course – sorry golfers,” said Katie Scott, an area ranger for the National Trust at Sandilands. “It was quite flat and the grass was cut when it was a golf course but now with all the mounds and undulations – and just by not mullering the grass – so many new plant species have come up. It just goes to show that nature is always there waiting to push through.” Scott said there were a few local people who mourned the loss of the course, which was founded in 1894, but the private club went into liquidation in 2018 before the trust stepped in, ensuring the coastal site was not developed or turned into a caravan park. What was once a site only accessible to a few hundred golf club members is now open to everyone. Sandilands is on the edge of Mablethorpe, a deprived seaside town, and the trust has been deluged with offers of support and help from local people, with 50 already volunteering on the new reserve. “As soon as the office cabin was put on site, people came knocking saying they wanted to get involved,” said Anstee Stratigou, the community, participation and volunteering manager for the trust. “We’ve worked so hard with the local community talking about the work we’re doing and encouraging them.” One volunteer, Sue Cushen, said: “What’s happened over the last few years here is remarkable and it is going to get better. I grew up around here and it was a pretty ordinary golf course to be fair. Now we’ve got really nice nature on this part of the coast and the birds are coming back. It’s great. It’s also hard work.” As with many nature restoration projects, annual “weeds” such as thistle and ragwort are the first to colonise the disturbed ground and Cushen and fellow volunteers have spent much of the summer hand-pulling ragwort, “our nemesis” as she called it, to keep it under control. Some local people complained about the number of thistles on the new nature reserve but Scott explained that they would boom for a year or two before being replaced by a natural cycle of perennial grasses and flowers. Green hay from a nearby Lincolnshire Wildlife Trust reserve has been spread to establish local native species including wild carrot, yarrow, yellow rattle and red clover. “We left the thistles this year and we had a massive explosion of painted lady butterflies,” said Scott. The coastal reserve, which includes a timber-framed community centre and cafe and an accessible pathway weaving through the long site, was originally coastal wetlands before the golf course was established, and as soon as shallow ponds were dug, reed and reed-mace sprouted up naturally. The pools and marshes of Sandilands will become a mecca for birdwatchers with the reserve sitting within the internationally important “East Atlantic flyway”, one of Europe’s major migration routes. Every year, thousands of birds travel along Britain’s east coast between Arctic and northern European breeding grounds and warmer wintering areas farther south. Rare migrants blown into Sandilands will find shelter in some of the 36,000 native shrubs, including sea-buckthorn, blackthorn and gorse, planted by the volunteers. The transformation was funded thanks to £2m from Mablethorpe Towns Fund, along with £1.5m from National Highways and £200,000 from the government’s shared prosperity fund, as delivered by East Lindsey district council. Highland ponies will be introduced to the site to provide conservation grazing and the trust hopes to reintroduce the rare natterjack toad once the pond habitat is ready. While the Guardian visited, a skein of pink-footed geese flew over, and birders reported seeing black-tailed godwits on the site, with gannets, red-throated divers and shearwaters passing just out to sea. Martin, a day tripper visiting the new reserve from Melton Mowbray with his dog, Alma, said: “Walking between the pools and seeing all the wildlife is lovely, it really is. It’s so peaceful.”

title: Country diary: Before Hastings was the Battle of Stamford Bridge. And it happened right here, 960 years ago today | Amy-Jane Beer
summary: Low Catton, East Yorkshire: It was King Harold’s last taste of victory. How chilling it is to visit this unassuming spot and imagine the bloody scene back in 1066
text: The field with freshly sprouted winter wheat sloping down to the River Derwent looks ordinary; however, today feels anything but. Just standing here, strange chills are swarming through my body and converging in my chest. It happened here. I’m standing on what has recently been identified as the battleground of Stamford Bridge, where on 25 September 1066 an English army led by Harold Godwinson surprised and devastated the Viking and rebel forces of Harald Hardrada and Godwinson’s brother, Tostig. A famous victory, but short-lived: Harold’s luck ran out catastrophically just three weeks later at Hastings. Despite many aspects of the battle being colourfully documented, the land around the modern village of Stamford Bridge has never offered any physical trace . But in 2022, the metal detectorists Simon Richardson and John Benfield turned their attention a mile downstream, where traces of Roman settlement hinted at a second ancient crossing point. Their systematic search has since yielded an astonishing array of 11th-century Saxon and Viking weaponry: spear points, arrow tips, an axe head, sword and scabbard fragments, scraps of chainmail. There can be no doubt that this is the place. I walk upstream to cross the river and loop back to the spot where the Roman bridge must have stood. New signs forbid digging and unauthorised metal detecting, but there’s no prohibition on imagination, and mine is in overdrive, conjuring roars, screams and gasps, the thwack of metal on metal, metal on bone; the reek of sweat and mutilated flesh. Are these insouciant crows descendants of those who feasted then? Were there slim-bodied fish (bleak, a friendly angler tells me) in the water then as now, to taste the blood? There hasn’t been a bridge here for centuries, so to return to my starting point I undress, stuff my clothes in a drybag and slip into the river. Cool green water carries me under the sun-dappled boughs of goat willow and oak where dragonflies and bumblebees cruise, but my mind is winding along the silty bed below, peering at bent and corroded weapons untouched since they were dropped. What was really won that day 960 years ago, I wonder? Because right now, I am more aware than ever that England is a dream, and the battle for her is still going on. • Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024, is available now at guardianbookshop.com

title: Lula says Trump wants to ‘colonise’ and capture Brazil’s resources by meddling in election
summary: A TV spot claims the US president is trying to sway October’s presidential vote in favour of Lula’s far-right opponents
text: Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s presidential campaign has accused Donald Trump of wanting to “colonise” Brazil in order to capture its natural resources by meddling in next month’s presidential election. The accusation came in a campaign advert that was published on social media on Thursday night by Lula’s team and will air on television on Friday amid growing fears over the impact alleged US interference could have on the vote. The TV spot claims the US president is trying to sway the election in favour of Lula’s far-right adversary in the election, Flávio Bolsonaro, in order to advance Trump’s interests in the South American nation. “Flávio Bolsonaro is Trump’s candidate and what Trump wants is to colonise Brazil, take our riches, steal our future and leave us in the dust,” the female narrator tells viewers in the minute-long video. The state department has denied claims the US is meddling in Brazil’s election. “Any insinuation of a ‘ploy’ to undermine a democratic nation’s election is a baseless lie,” it said last month in a statement. Writing on X, Lula accused Bolsonaro of wanting to “hand our natural resources over to the United States”. “If it’s up to him, Brazil will become a colony again,” the incumbent leftwing president added. With just over a week to go until the 4 October first round vote, Lula and Bolsonaro are neck and neck in the polls. A second round run-off will be held on 25 October if no candidate secures more than half of the votes. In recent weeks, there has been growing alarm – both in Brazil and overseas – about Washington’s apparent attempts to influence the result, with a campaign of diplomatic and economic pressure, including 25% tariffs on Brazilian imports. Speaking at the UN general assembly in New York this week, Lula indirectly criticised the US’ perceived meddling, telling delegates: “We will not allow the enemies of democracy – internal or external – to attack the will of the people. Brazilian democracy belongs to the Brazilians.” Earlier this week, dozens of Democratic party congresspeople wrote to secretary of state, Marco Rubio, to denounce the Trump administration’s “apparent effort to interfere with, and potentially undermine” Brazil’s elections through what they called a “sustained, multifaceted campaign of interference and destabilisation in Brazil”. The narrator of Lula’s campaign ad cited a series of recent media stories relating to alleged acts of US meddling. They include reports about the alleged interference of Big Tech companies as well as a confidential document sent to electoral authorities by Brazil’s intelligence agency warning of a “critical level” of risk of US interference. The campaign video also highlighted recent claims about links between Bolsonaro’s campaign and the conservative donor network Rockbridge, which was co-founded by Trump’s vice-president JD Vance. Éden Valadares, the communications secretary for Lula’s Worker’s party (PT), said the campaign ad was part of efforts to “alert the Brazilian people” to the ideologically-driven US campaign. “We don’t believe it will work but nor will we sit back and do nothing,” Valadares said. “President Lula has instructed us … to mobilise Brazilian society … [and] to react in the streets,” added Valadares, who said a nationwide series of events were being planned for this Sunday. Fears over US meddling are not confined to the Brazilian left. This week, another of the right-wing candidates in Brazil’s election, Renan Santos, also denounced Trump’s behaviour and said he did not want Brazil to become a US vassal state. “They want to interfere in Brazil’s elections to secure satisfactory contracts involving rare earths,” Santos claimed in a social media video. Recalling the US invasion of Venezuela in January, Santos added: “I don’t want to see Latin America become an American protectorate.” In the letter sent to Rubio on Friday, the Democratic lawmakers wrote that “rather than helping defend Brazilian democracy”, the US was “acting as an agent of interference and destabilisation – using diplomatic, economic and political pressure in ways that risk weakening the country’s democratic institutions, undermining confidence in Brazil’s electoral process, and inflicting further damage on our relationship with a strategic US ally and trading partner”. They asked Rubio if Trump’s administration would commit to respecting Brazil’s electoral process and requested a response by 1 October. The state department has not yet responded to a request for comment.

title: Diplomacy or ‘diplotainment’? Key takeaways from the Trump-Xi summit in Washington
summary: Xi Jinping’s visit heavy on symbolism but no sign closed-door meeting yielded breakthroughs on thorny issues such as AI, trade, Taiwan and Iran
text: Donald Trump welcomed Xi Jinping to the White House on Thursday, with talks on AI, trade and a growing US-China strategic rivalry expected to feature on an elaborate state visit that critics say went big on style but lacked substance. Here are the key takeaways from Xi’s first visit to Washington in more than a decade. Diplomacy or ‘diplotainment’? Senate Democrats criticised Trump’s summit with Xi, saying it prioritised pageantry over substance on the major issues. There was no sign a brief closed-door meeting yielded breakthroughs on the thorny issues of AI, trade, Taiwan and the war with Iran. Both countries agreed to extend until 10 January an agreement pausing their trade war, but experts said there were few other obvious tangible outcomes. Xi once again invoked the “Thucydides Trap”, an academic theory that competition between a rising power and an established one often results in war. Xi said the risk “can be overcome” and urged cooperation. After their meeting, Trump gave Xi a tour of the new helipad he had recently constructed on the White House’s South Lawn. “He loves good granite,” Trump told reporters, adding the two men had a “great meeting” without elaborating. Danny Russel, a former US diplomat serving in the Obama administration, expressed concern that the two leaders spent more time on social and ceremonial events than the actual meeting, which was about 90 minutes. “Pageantry and protocol don’t add up to progress. Pandas are cute, but what America needs are rare earths,” said Russel. “What we’re seeing isn’t diplomacy so much as ‘diplotainment,’ which won’t do much to solve the serious problems in the US-China relationship.” AI unchecked AI analysts were forced to read between the lines to gauge the outcome of AI discussions between the pair. Trump had written in a Truth Social post on Thursday morning that he and Xi would discuss “super intelligence” (Trump’s newly coined term for AI) but suggested he had little interest in new regulations, despite concerns from industry leaders that AI could eventually pose a threat to humans. “Super Intelligence (SI) will be a big topic of ⁠discussion, but I want to leave it exactly where it is,” Trump wrote. “That is China’s position also.” During his comments on Thursday, Xi said both countries must “ensure that the development of AI is always under human control”. Analysts say intense competition between the two powers in AI is likely to limit the scope for anything beyond symbolic agreements. Taiwan and stalled $14bn arms deal During the afternoon discussion, Xi urged Trump to oppose “Taiwan independence,” according to a readout from the official Chinese news agency Xinhua. The White House did not immediately provide its own summary. Xi was expected to press Trump to halt arms sales to Taiwan. After his visit to China in May, Trump said he was holding in ⁠abeyance an arms package to Taiwan worth about $14bn and called it a “very good negotiating chip” – rattling some US allies in Asia. In a statement signed by at least 19 ⁠of 47 members of the Senate Democrats caucus, seen by Reuters, Democrats on Thursday called on Trump to ‌immediately deliver the security assistance package Congress has approved – $1.3bn in funds and the $14bn arms sale. China claims democratically governed Taiwan as its own territory and has not ruled out using force to gain control over the island. Unusual airport greeting Trump greeted Xi on arrival with a red carpet on the tarmac at Joint Base Andrews, the ‌first time a US president has welcomed a foreign leader there since Barack Obama met Pope Francis in 2015. Normally, presidents wait for state visit guests to arrive at the White House before offering a formal welcome. For months, Trump has derided Democrats as “communists”, but the president’s welcome for Xi included Chinese flags adorning the roof above the Oval Office alongside US flags. Despite the fanfare, Trump and Xi’s remarks during the trip were not carried live by any US television networks, which refused to provide footage in protest of the White House’s ban of CNN, MS Now and Politico. Tech billionaires dine out at state dinner Thursday’s state dinner for Xi featured Washington powerbrokers and a cavalcade of billionaires, including: Apple’s Tim Cook, Amazon’s Jeff Bezos, Alphabet’s Sundar Pichai, OpenAI’s Sam Altman, Tesla’s Elon Musk and Nvidia’s Jensen Huang. First lady Melania Trump’s menu featured yellow squash velouté, sesame-crusted sea bass and a vanilla crémeux with sour cherry confit. In a continuation of Trump’s beef with certain media outlets, CNN and MS Now reporters were barred from attending. While outside the gate, a group of loud protesters shouted slogans like “China out ⁠of Hong Kong” that were clearly audible to the leaders ⁠as they posed for pictures on the red-carpeted White House steps. Reuters and Associated Press contributed to this report

title: Saudi Arabia intercepts wave of Houthi missiles as oil climbs to one-week high
summary: The ⁠Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said the missiles were ⁠aimed at Taif and the Yanbu area on the Red Sea, the main alternative route for Saudi oil
text: Saudi Arabia says it intercepted six ballistic missiles fired by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis, with the latest attacks pushing oil prices ⁠to a one-week high over fears of spiralling supply disruptions. The ⁠Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said the missiles were ⁠aimed at Taif in western Saudi Arabia and the Yanbu area on the Red Sea, with the Houthis claiming their attacks were aimed at “a sensitive target” in the capital Riyadh and on Saudi Aramco facilities in Yanbu. Oil prices climbed about 3%, but trade was volatile and prices came off session highs after reports the US and Iran discussed reopening the strait of Hormuz. The escalating attacks threaten Saudi Arabia’s ⁠ability to export oil through the Red Sea at a time when the strait of Hormuz is disrupted and the kingdom’s east-west pipeline is only now resuming operations after drone strikes earlier this month. The Houthis declared a naval blockade on the kingdom in July, opening a ‌second theatre in the US-Iran war. It was ‌not clear whether there was any damage or casualties in either Taif or Yanbu, the main alternative route for Saudi oil. The Houthis seized the whole Yemeni western coast in a lightning offensive nearly two weeks ago that brought them to the shores of the Red Sea’s strategic Bab el-Mandeb waterway. Yemen’s internationally recognised government pressed world leaders on Thursday for help defeating the militants, saying that their new perch along one of the world’s busiest waterways presents an international economic risk. While claiming that their blockade only applies to Saudi shipping and there remains no threat to commercial shipping on the Red Sea, the Houths have also warned other nations not to get involved. But the vice-president of the internationally recognised government council urged world leaders at the UN general assembly not to trust the Houthis’ assurances – and to see a bigger picture in the crisis around the strait. “The Houthi militias’ use of the safety of navigation as a tool for blackmail threatens not only Yemen. It is taking hostage the entire global economy,” said vice-president, Abdullah Abdulkader al Alimi-Bawzer. Arguing that protecting the strait “is the responsibility of every economy that depends on secure supply chains, energy security and freedom of navigation,” he urged the international community to keep weapons and technology from getting into the rebels’ hands. The Saudi-backed government’s forces had earlier repelled overnight attacks by the Houthis on a key supply route to Yemen’s third-biggest city Taiz from the southern port city of Aden where the internationally recognised administration is based, government sources said. The Houthis ⁠have kept up pressure along a steep, winding mountain pass known as Hejat al-Abd, a lifeline for government forces and the only route for goods and residents to reach Taiz and travel abroad. Seizing parts of the road could allow the Houthis to tighten their grip around the city and deal another blow to the government, which has struggled to regain the initiative since losing the western coast. Riyadh’s foreign ministry said on Friday that Saudi ⁠Arabia, Turkey and ⁠Pakistan would ⁠hold an urgent ⁠meeting of their chiefs ⁠of staff ‌to ‌discuss ways to ‌support repel the Houthi attacks under their joint ‌defence agreement. Under the defence pact, all three countries agreed that an armed attack on any one of them would be treated as an attack on all three. Officials in Pakistan are said to be deeply worried about being dragged into the never-ending war unfolding across the Middle East. With Reuters and the Associated Press

title: CNN and MS Now journalists denied access to White House state dinner despite court ruling
summary: Officials deny entry even after federal judge rules Trump administration must grant banned journalists access
text: Journalists for CNN and MS Now were denied access to the White House state dinner in honor of Xi Jinping, China’s president, on Thursday evening, hours after a federal judge ruled the Trump administration must allow them in after imposing a ban last week. “About an hour before Xi’s arrival was scheduled, the White House said CNN could cover the event, but only with a photojournalist and audio technician, notably excluding the network’s editorial team consisting of a reporter and producer,” CNN reported. MS Now, another outlet banned from the White House by Trump last week for what he calls overly negative coverage of his presidency, also said its White House reporter, Laura Barrón-López, was prevented from covering Xi’s arrival for the state dinner despite applying for credentials to cover the event. When Barrón-López asked a White House staffer why she was denied access, the staffer said she should “talk to Steven”, apparently meaning White House communications director Steven Cheung, MS Now reported. Xi’s arrival for the dinner, with his wife, Peng Liyuan, was streamed live on YouTube by the White House, but none of the major US networks provided live broadcast video of the event in solidarity with CNN, a member of the broadcast pool. Earlier on Thursday, journalists for CNN, MS Now and Politico, which was also part of the ban issued last week, were finally granted access to the White House after days of being barred from the building. Earlier attempts by the journalists to enter the building had been unsuccessful, and lawyers representing the three organizations had told a judge that the White House has already “repeatedly violated” his overnight order requiring the Trump administration to return the press badges of journalists from the three news organizations. Timothy Kelly, the US district judge who appeared skeptical of arguments from lawyers representing the White House during a hearing on Wednesday, issued an early morning order forcing the administration to return access for a 14-day period. But journalists from the three affected networks reported being barred from the building, with some having their badges taken for the first time. “This morning journalists from each of CNN, MS Now, and Politico attempted to enter the White House and were turned away, and Secret Service agents confiscated the hard pass of journalists whose hard passes had not previously been confiscated,” lawyers for the three news organizations wrote in a brief requesting a video or telephone conference “as soon as possible this morning”. In a legal filing on Thursday afternoon, Micah Stopperich, the White House director of press operations, said in a sworn statement that the operations team was notified at 7.10am to restore access, and that it began reinstating badges at 7.25am. She said that US Secret Service indicated that badges were re-activated as of 9.07am, and that confiscated badges were dropped off at the entry to the building just before 10am. “United States Secret Service has represented that press passes that were turned on were available for pick up at the press gate as soon as they were delivered,” she said. The badges were revoked on Saturday, after the president abruptly ordered the three outlets to be banned over “their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS”. The outlets swiftly sued over the move, which sparked widespread criticism from other news organizations and press freedom advocates. In a legal filing earlier this week, Department of Justice lawyers argued that the ban was necessary for national security reasons, and listed examples of articles that relied on non-public information. But Kelly was unswayed, and argued in his ruling that the way in the which the White House banned the organizations had likely violated due process protections for journalists – and well-established legal precedent set in two press access cases by the United States court of appeals for the District of Columbia. “Plaintiffs are also likely to succeed in showing that their hard passes were revoked without constitutionally adequate due process,” he wrote. “The ‘general rule’ is that ‘individuals must receive notice and an opportunity to be heard before the government deprives them’ of a constitutionally protected interest.” The judge said that, based on case law, before a press pass can be revoked, the White House “must promulgate rules or standards governing the conduct that would lead to such revocation. And the reporter must ‘receive fair notice not only of the conduct that would subject him to punishment, but also of the magnitude of the sanction that the White House might impose’.” The three news organizations were not given advance notice that they were in violation of any set of standards and only received formal notice – in letters sent to each news organization on Tuesday – that they “exhibited behavior in violation of the standards of professionalism and decorum expected of those given access to the White House Complex, including by trafficking in verifiable falsehoods about national security and other issues, and publishing sensitive or classified information”. Michael Kenneth Velchik, a justice department attorney representing the Trump White House, argued that such a process had been laid out in the letters, which informed each news organization that they had until 5pm on Friday to contest the ban. (The letters said that if the organizations did not submit such a challenge, it would become final.) But the judge said the standard mentioned in the letters was “so vague it hardly does the trick”, and concluded that even the defendants “do not dispute that plaintiffs did not receive notice and an opportunity to be heard before their hard passes were revoked”. The judge also wrote that he was “skeptical … that defendants’ interest in safeguarding national security is the actual motivation for, or is even advanced by, the revocation of Plaintiffs’ hard passes”. He cited comments from Trump about how the ban was for content-based reasons. A hearing for a preliminary injunction will be expedited to be held during the 14-day period in which the passes are returned, the judge said. title: Ukraine war briefing: Finland urges Elon Musk to expand Kyiv’s Starlink coverage over Russia
summary: Ukraine believes that turning on Starlink over Russian territory would help it target missile launchers. What we know on day 1,675
text: Finnish President Alexander Stubb has said he pleaded with SpaceX owner Elon Musk to expand Starlink satellite internet coverage for Ukraine so it can strike Russian ballistic missile launchers located inside ⁠Russian territory. Ukraine ⁠has an acute shortage of air defences to repel Russian ballistic missiles and Kyiv believes that turning on Starlink over Russian territory would help it target the launchers that fire the missiles. Musk switched on the Starlink satellite internet service over ‌Ukraine shortly after Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022. It has become the lifeblood of Ukraine’s battlefield communications and a tool for piloting drones, but it does not work over Russian territory. Volodymyr Zelenskyy has met with senior Wall Street executives on the sidelines of the UN general assembly in New York, ⁠as Kyiv seeks to attract investments to help finance the country’s rebuilding efforts. The meeting focused mainly ⁠on areas such as helping Ukraine get through the winter and supporting its economy, the Ukrainian ⁠government said. Ukraine faces a brutal winter as stepped-up Russian strikes on its infrastructure and key ‌export industries deepen ‌the country’s budget crisis. The daily cost of the war ‌grew to about $190m this year. The meeting, attended by more than two dozen US companies, was facilitated by US banking giant Citigroup and the US chamber of commerce. Russia could launch a limited military attack against a Nato country in the coming months, Danish intelligence said, in one of the starkest warnings yet by western security services. In a report published on Thursday, the Danish defence intelligence service warned of a “low but growing risk” that Russia could launch long-range strikes on Nato infrastructure supporting Ukraine, or carry out a limited incursion into a neighbouring country with a small number of troops, potentially operating without insignia. The report came hours after a fire at a Starlink satellite station in central Poland that local authorities described as an “act of sabotage”. Nato is capable of handling sabotage and drone incidents in Europe and has good action plans in place to deal with them, the alliance’s secretary general said after the warning from Danish intelligence. Secretary-general Mark Rutte said he believes the rising number of hybrid incidents in Nato countries shows that Russian President Vladimir Putin is losing the war in Ukraine. He said that citizens of the 32 Nato countries can remain calm. “Putin is in a bad place,” Rutte said. “He is not winning the war in Ukraine.” Russian drone and missile strikes on Kyiv and Ukraine’s north-east killed eight people on ⁠Thursday in attacks that included ⁠a maternity hospital and a farm, officials said. Two people died ⁠in the assault on Kyiv, Zelenskyy said. “As people were sleeping, flashes from explosions lit up the sky,” the president said on Telegram. Police said nine homes, a post office, warehouses and dozens of cars were also damaged in Kyiv. A separate ‌Russian attack on a vegetable storage ‌facility at a farm in a village of the north-eastern Kharkiv region killed six people and injured a further 12, prosecutors said. ⁠Turkish president Tayyip Erdogan said Turkey ⁠had ⁠stepped up efforts to re-establish the Black ⁠Sea grain corridor. “We have now increased ⁠our efforts to re-establish ‌the grain corridor. ‌We are also ‌accelerating our diplomatic steps for this,” Erdogan told a group of Turkish journalists ‌in New York. Erdogan said ⁠he had discussed the issue again with Zelenskyy ‌and received a positive response.

title: At Trump meeting, Xi Jinping lays out terms to avoid US-China military conflict
summary: Chinese president’s proposals for lessening tensions come amid period of intense competition between the two countries over AI and trade
text: Xi Jinping has called for extensive cooperation with Washington to avoid the “Thucydides trap” that could put the US and China on a military collision course amid rising tensions over artificial intelligence, trade and Taiwan. At the start of his summit meeting with Donald Trump in the White House, the Chinese president laid out terms for a mutual understanding that he said could steer the two competing superpowers away from future military conflict and on to a road of mutual gain. Rather than confrontation, conditions for “achieving the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and making America great again go hand in hand” and should be the goal, Xi said, citing Trump’s political catchphrase. “We should strengthen communication. China and the United States are different in national conditions, but through candid, in-depth and continued dialogue, our two countries can understand each other better, seek common ground while shelving differences, and build up mutual trust,” said Xi, with Trump looking on. “We should coexist in peace. China and the United States, as two major countries, stand to gain from cooperation and will both lose in confrontation. Our two militaries should maintain regular dialog and improve mechanisms for crisis communication and prevention.” With such conditions in place, Xi said, “the Thucydides trap can be overcome”, referring to the phenomenon, defined by the Greek historian, of tensions that arise when an emerging power challenges the dominance of an established power. Xi invoked the phrase in his meeting with Trump in Beijing in May, asking the US president how he planned to avoid it. His proposals for lessening tensions – which also included the invitation of 100,000 young Americans to visit China on student exchanges – come amid a period of intense competition between the two powers over artificial intelligence and trade, with each side imposing tariffs on the other. Trump had earlier welcomed Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, to the White House, noting that he was the first Chinese leader to make a second state visit to the US. The previous visit occurred in 2015, when Barack Obama was president. “President Xi and Madame Peng arrive at an important moment for America, the 250th anniversary of our founding,” he said. Trump said he had forged “a truly great friendship” with Xi. “President Xi and I have made tremendous strides on the issues facing our two countries,” he said. “Our teams have been working to encourage a more balanced trading relationship, including the new market access for American farmers and ranchers.” He said the current visit would include discussion over security, technology and AI – which he called “super intelligence”, a term he introduced in his speech to the United Nations general assembly on Tuesday. Xi also extolled his personal relationship with his American counterpart, saying: “President Trump and I have respect for each other. We have built personal rapport and stayed in touch.” Addressing Trump directly, he said: “During your visit to China this year, we agreed to build a constructive China-US relationship of strategic stability. I am ready to work with you to steer the giant ship of the China-US relationship on a steady course towards the future.” The White House welcome ceremony came after Trump had taken the unusual step of going to Andrews air force base in Maryland the evening before to greet the Chinese leader and his wife on the tarmac. Much of the same pageantry was repeated in Thursday’s ceremony, with both countries’ national anthems being played. Trump was flanked by his wife, Melania, while members of his cabinet and senior aides – including Natalie Harp, Trump’s dedicated assistant nicknamed “the human printer” by fellow staffers – looked on. Trump and Xi held bilateral talks after the ceremony and the welcoming speeches. Later on Thursday, Trump hosted Xi at the White House for a state dinner. Notable invited guests from the tech world included Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, Apple chair Tim Cook, SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk, and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman. Trump gestured to the titans of the industry in his remarks to the dinner, recounting when Chinese diplomats first arrived in the US 158 years ago, meeting American intellectuals like Henry David Thoreau and prominent political figures. “Tonight, we revive the spirit of that first encounter here on American soil as we are joined by some of the top leaders in business, culture and government from our own time,” he said. “On one side, China draws on thousands of years of history and tradition from Sun Tzu to Sun Yat-sen. For Americans, we inherit a legacy of faith from Jerusalem to Rome, democracy of ancient Athens, the triumphs of Sparta and the freedom proclaimed in Philadelphia 250 years ago.” Trump also touted his relationship with the Chinese leader. “President Xi and I both understand we represent different systems, but the ties between our people endure, and we’ve never gotten along better,” he said. Xi also addressed the dinner, saying talks with Trump during the visit had yielded “common understanding on many issues”, and suggesting the US and China find a new approach to working together. “China ⁠and the United States must act as responsible major countries,” he said. Despite the harmonious tone adopted by both leaders, analysts have voiced scepticism about the possibility of longstanding stable arrangements being arrived at over a host of issues. In the race for AI, the US has placed strict export controls on microchips, semiconductors, software and chip-making equipment in a bid to slow China’s development. A truce agreed between Trump and Xi in South Korea last year aimed at keeping tariffs lower had been due to expire in November but has now been extended until February, the US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent said. Analysts believe the extension suggests Trump continues to be dissatisfied with Xi’s concession offers on trade and wants to keep the pressure on in the hope of getting a better deal if the two meet again at the G20 summit scheduled to be held in Miami in December. Despite the trade war between the two countries, Chinese imports have continued to surge into the US. China is on course to run a $1tn trade surplus for the second year running. Uwa Ede-Osifo contributed reporting • This article was amended on 24 and 25 September 2026. Misspellings of Xi Jinping in the headline and text were corrected. And China is on course to run a $1tn trade surplus, not deficit.

title: Netanyahu’s speech at UN spurs protests in New York City: ‘Let Gaza live’
summary: Actor Susan Sarandon, whistleblower Chelsea Manning and comedian Caleb Hearon are detained by NYPD
text: More than 100 people were arrested outside the United Nations’ headquarters in New York City on Thursday as Benjamin Netanyahu addressed the general assembly, a speech that also prompted dozens of UN delegates to walk out in protest. The protest outside the UN, one of several this week against the embattled Israeli prime minister, drew hundreds of Jewish, Palestinian, Iranian and Lebanese New Yorkers, among others, as well as several elected officials and candidates in the November election, and a number of celebrities. Many wore shirts reading “Fund people not bombs” and chanted slogans like “Let Gaza live” and “the whole world is watching.” Official vehicles heading to the UN were diverted as protesters sat down in the middle of the street for more than an hour, unfurling banners that called to “end the genocide” and flying a kite reading “Free Palestine” – a reference to Israel’s threat earlier this year that it would target Palestinian children flying kites, organizers said. A few hours later, an estimated few thousand people marched from nearby Bryant Park to the UN in protest of Netanyahu’s visit to the city. Swathed in keffiyehs and carrying Palestinian flags, accompanied by a brass band and drummers, protesters held banners calling on UN member states to sanction Israel, others with illustrations of Netanyahu’s face. “The US and Trump and Benjamin Netanyahu are using the UN as a bully pulpit to basically project their vision of the world, which is one based on brute force and international crimes of aggression and illegal forever wars,” said Nas Issa of the Palestinian Youth Movement, which planned the afternoon protest. “It’s incumbent on member states of the UN to challenge the immunity that America and Israel have enjoyed for decades, but particularly in the past three years since the start of the Gaza genocide.” On Wednesday, members of the Democratic Socialists of America’s New York City chapter rallied at the city’s John F Kennedy international airport in protest of weapons and explosive materials destined for the Israeli military being flown out of the airport on commercial aircraft. “What we made clear today is that New Yorkers, including Jewish New Yorkers, do not want war criminals and the architects of genocide coming to our city,” said Beth Miller, political director of Jewish Voice for Peace Action, which coordinated the first protest outside the UN. “This is something that we have been saying for years, especially over the last three years during which Israel has killed over 75,000 Palestinians in this genocide – and to be clear that is a severe undercount.” Protests have long been a staple of Netanyahu’s appearances at the UN, but as Israel’s political isolation has deepened against the backdrop of its destruction of Gaza, the tone of this year’s demonstrations reflect many Americans’ growing anger at their own government’s continued support to the Israeli military. “We will not be silent as our government fully funds a genocide in Palestine,” said actor Hannah Einbinder, who has frequently spoken out for Palestinians’ rights and who was arrested on Thursday, ahead of the protest. “This moment calls on each and every one of us to speak out and demand the US stop funding genocide.” She said she felt a moral obligation to join the protests “as a Jew, as an American, and as a human being”. Fellow actors Susan Sarandon and Debra Winger, whistleblower Chelsea Manning and comedian Caleb Hearon were also among those detained by the NYPD, along with model and actor Indya Moore, author Glennon Doyle, activist Linda Sarsour, rabbi Abby Stein and writer David Velasco. Many demonstrators remained on the scene after police ordered them to disperse, but they did not appear to resist arrest. Opposition to Israel’s war in Gaza has prompted a seismic shift in US public opinion of Israel, a change that has begun to trickle into US elections, with scores of leftist candidates winning primaries earlier this year while openly calling to end US aid to Israel. While reflexive support for Israel was once a prerequisite for anyone running for office, in some districts it has increasingly become a liability. Many of the openly pro-Palestinian candidates who seized primary wins earlier this year were also at Thursday’s protest, including New York’s Darializa Avila Chevalier and Brad Lander, Pennsylvania’s Chris Rabb, New Jersey’s Adam Hamawy, and Colorado’s Melat Kiros. Several New York City and state officials and candidates were also in attendance and at least 10 were arrested, including city council members Chi Ossé and Tiffany Cabán. “I think it is really important to send a message that New Yorkers do not stand for this,” Chevalier, a pro-Palestinian activist whose primary win in June stunned the political establishment, told reporters at the protest shortly before being arrested. “It is really important that we show that we are willing to fight back against our tax dollars being used to commit war crimes.” Hamawy, an army doctor who participated in a medical mission in Gaza in 2024, told the Guardian as police moved in to make arrests “we’re ready to do what we have to do. We shouldn’t have to do that to stop a genocide. It’s ridiculous that we have to come out on the streets and protest when we have the body that’s supposed to be upholding international law right there in front of us, inviting Netanyahu as a guest rather than trying him as a war criminal in The Hague.” The NYPD did not immediately confirm the number of arrests but organizers estimate it was more than 100. The office of New York mayor Zohran Mamdani did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The protests presented a challenge to the mayorMamdani, who at one point pledged to arrest Netanyahu should he come to town, and who has long said his administration supports New Yorkers’ right to protest. Mamdani has repeatedly called Netanyahu a “war criminal” who is “not welcome in New York City” but admitted earlier this year that he does not have the legal authority to order his arrest, calling instead on the federal government to do so. At a press conference earlier this week, Mamdani said that he had no plans to attend any protests outside the UN but made clear that New Yorkers were free to do so. “To New Yorkers, I have never encouraged them to protest, what I have always told them is that they have the right to do so in this city,” he said. “We respect that right and this is a city that is proud of the constitution and proud of the first amendment.” Mamdani’s own election, after a historic campaign in which his criticism of Israel played an outsized role, was a sign of just how much how many New Yorkers had turned on Israel. “Mayor Mamdani campaigned and won his election speaking about a promise to arrest Benjamin Netanyahu and that was something that thousands and hundreds of thousands of New Yorkers voted for,” said Aber Kawas, who in November is slated to become the first Palestinian-American elected official in the New York legislature and who was also detained at Thursday’s protest. “Him winning is sending a message that this is what constituents want to see,” she added. “They do not want Benjamin Netanyahu to be allowed to enter into New York City and they want Benjamin Netanyahu to be arrested.”

title: Susan Sarandon and Hannah Einbinder arrested at anti-Netanyahu protest in New York
summary: Actors detained at Jewish Voice for Peace demonstration against Israeli prime minister’s address to the UN general assembly
text: Oscar-winning actor Susan Sarandon and Hacks star Hannah Einbinder were among people detained by police in New York on Thursday as they moved in to break up a protest against Benjamin Netanyahu. Agence France-Presse footage shows NYPD officers cuffing Thelma & Louise star Sarandon at the demo in the city as the Israeli prime minister was readying to address the United Nations general assembly. The New York Post reported Einbinder had also been marched away from the demonstration organised by Jewish Voice for Peace, where protesters held banners that read “Stop Arming Israel” and “End the Genocide.” A spokesperson for the NYPD said officers had responded to reports of an “unscheduled demonstration” where people were blocking an intersection. “Members of the NYPD Community Affairs Bureau issued … warnings, advising participants that they should leave,” the spokesperson said. “They continued to block the intersection. Multiple individuals who didn’t comply were taken into custody,” she said, without providing the number of people arrested. Democratic congressional candidate Darializa Avila Chevalier and New York ⁠City council member Chi Ossé were also among those arrested. Inside the general assembly, dozens of envoys from across the world walked out as Netanyahu began his speech, where he assailed both enemies and allies that have crossed him in recent months, including Britain and France, which have recently moved to recognise the state of Palestine. “They accuse Israel, tiny Israel, of colonialism – some colonialism. And who’s accusing us? Among them are people in Britain and in France. For God’s sakes, they invented the term,” he told the assembly. Sarandon, whose movie hits also include The Rocky Horror Picture Show, Dead Man Walking and The Witches of Eastwick, is no stranger to protests over Israel’s war in Gaza. The US actor told journalists at the Venice film festival this month she was losing work because of her outspoken views. “I’ve still had movies taken away recently because there are agencies that are telling people not to hire me still. But that’s the power structure,” she said. “I think there has been a change in terms of the understanding of the situation and the general public, but there are still very strongly held positions within my industry that are held by Zionists and who have not relaxed their feelings towards me. “But I found my family, I found my people, and I’m OK,” she added. Einbinder has previously said the cost of not speaking up about Palestine is greater than losing her Hollywood career, citing industry backlash to actors such as Sarandon and Melissa Barrera. “I think what they know is what I know, which is that the cost of not speaking is higher,” she told Cannes film festival earlier this year. “There is a greater toll in not speaking and you’ve just got to have your priorities straight. I am under no impression that my small career could ever measure up in comparison to even one human life. It’s an obligation and I will always do it.” Agence France-Presse contributed to this report

title: Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes reportedly to be transferred to halfway home next year
summary: Holmes was sentenced to 11 years in prison in 2022 but has seen her sentenced reduced several times
text: Elizabeth Holmes, the disgraced founder of blood testing startup Theranos, will reportedly be transferred from a minimum security prison to a halfway home next August. In 2022, Holmes, 42, was sentenced to more than 11 years in prison for defrauding Theranos investors out of hundreds of millions of dollars and ordered to pay restitution. The company falsely promoted its technology as being capable of detecting diseases, including types of cancer, from drops of finger-pricked blood. The Federal Bureau of Prisons (BOP) informed Holmes’s victims of the upcoming move to the Austin transitional center in Del Valle, Texas, according to ABC News. The New York Times and NBC News confirmed ABC’s reporting. While Holmes has been incarcerated at the federal prison center in Bryan, Texas, her prison term has been reduced several times. The US district judge Edward Davila wrote in court filings that her shortened sentence did not diminish the weight of her fraudulent behavior. “Holmes’s revised sentence continues to reflect a just punishment for her serious offense and serves as a reminder that the scales of justice will balance,” Davila said, according to ABC News. She is set to leave prison in February 2030, BOP records show. ABC News reported that Holmes plans to reside in Austin after her release. Holmes has faced renewed interest as the subject of comedian Nathan Fielder’s upcoming documentary You Can See Everything. The enigmatic project follows Holmes and her partner Billy Evans before her prison term and through the start of her incarceration. In May, NPR reported that Evans had raised millions for a new medical testing startup, a revelation that fueled speculation over Holmes’s post-prison plans.

title: UK food and drink trade deficit largest since 2000 at £21bn
summary: Industry leaders call on government to protect homegrown produce in the interest of national security
text: The gap between Britain’s food and drink exports and imports has neared its highest this century, as a combination of Brexit, war in the Middle East and US tariffs dented deliveries overseas while imports soared. The UK’s food and drink trade deficit has risen to more than £21bn – the largest since 2000 – in what industry leaders said was a “wake-up call” for the government to protect homegrown produce in the interest of national security. UK food and drink export volumes fell by more than a tenth (11.7%) in the first half of 2026 to 4bn kg, only marginally above levels at the height of the Covid pandemic and in the aftermath of the 2001 foot-and-mouth disease outbreak, according to analysis by the Food & Drink Federation (FDF). Exports to the EU continued to fall – down 0.9% in value – amid the additional costs and complexity of trading since Brexit. The FDF recorded an even larger fall in exports beyond the EU – down 6.9% in value terms. That was partly driven by disruption in sales to the Middle East, with exports to the UAE down by almost a quarter as a result of the US-Israel war on Iran. The US’s introduction of a 10% import tariff hit cross-Atlantic sales by 16.5%. Food and drink imports were 19.1bn kg in the first half of this year, the second highest ever, only beaten by the same period last year. Imports from outside the EU are up more than a fifth since 2023 as restrictions have been eased through trade deals, particularly with Australia which now sends 25% more in value terms to the UK than a year ago including meat, oils, vegetables and even whisky. The suspension of tariffs on a range of manufactured foods, including chocolate and biscuits, this year as part of the former chancellor Rachel Reeves’s package to ease the cost of living has also raised import levels. In addition, EU food producers increased deliveries to the UK in value terms – up 0.8% year-on-year – having recovered in volume terms since Brexit. Tom Bradshaw, the president of the National Farmers’ Union of England and Wales, said: “These figures should be a wake-up call. At a time of growing geopolitical uncertainty, we cannot afford to take our food production capacity for granted.” He said the widening trade deficit underlined the need for a long-term plan to support British production and recognise “a simple truth that food security is national security”. “The pressures facing farm businesses are immense, from rising costs and regulatory burdens to extreme weather and global market volatility,” said Bradshaw. “If government is serious about food security, economic growth and national resilience, it must create the conditions that give businesses the confidence to invest, innovate and grow.” The FDF, which represents hundreds of food and beverage producers, said pressures on manufacturers were “significant and growing” as the cost of energy, ingredients, transport, packaging and labour continued to rise. It said changing regulation also added to pressures on the industry. Karen Betts, the chief executive of the trade body, said: “Our food and drink trade deficit is growing and is now the largest it’s been in over 25 years. In a world beset by conflict and the ever-increasing impacts of climate change, this poses some stark questions about our food security. “When the government then chooses to remove tariffs on, for example, biscuits imported from China, it’s not surprising that they’ll be sold more cheaply here than biscuits made in the UK.”
