title: US mortgage rates top 7% for first time in 20 months
summary: Increase comes after Fed decision to raise interest rates, as Americans struggle with high prices and stagnant wages
text: US mortgage rates surpassed 7% for the first time since January 2025, according to federal lender Freddie Mac, aggravating a housing market that has endured years of high interest rates and low supply. The increase comes after the US Federal Reserve hiked interest rates, which directly affect mortgage rates, for the first time since 2023, citing high inflation. Rates on 16 September went up by a quarter of a point, to a range of 3.75% to 4%. In new projections, a majority of the Fed’s rate-setting committee predicted at least one additional rate hike before the end of this year. Last year, the Freddie Mac 30-year-mortgage rate, commonly used on home loans across the country, had been trending down from 7.79% – a generational high reached in late 2023. But rates have been creeping back up since late February, when the US and Israel launched its war with Iran. The conflict drove inflation to its highest levels in three years and sharply increased energy prices. Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil, topped $105 earlier on Thursday. On Thursday, the 10-year US treasury yield – which underpins the 30-year mortgage rate and other borrowing costs – also reached its highest level since July 2007 and the 30-year Treasury yield hitting its peak since 2004 as investors raised expectations for another Fed rate hike next month. Earlier in September, US treasury secretary Scott Bessent announced the Treasury would triple its buyback of government debt, but yields have continued to rise. The housing market has long been in a slowdown, said Anthony Smith, a senior economist at Realtor.com, with existing home sales hitting their 2026 low so far in August and pending sales that have turned negative year over year. “A 7% handle is as much psychological as mathematical, and it arrives at the point in the season when leverage usually shifts toward buyers,” said Smith. High mortgage rates are just one of the many reasons why Americans are struggling to attain home ownership. Wages have not kept pace with higher inflation, and everyday costs are higher. The frustration is expected to show up in November’s midterm elections as Republicans struggle to maintain control of Congress. Nearly three-quarters of Americans disapprove of Donald Trump’s handling of the economy, according to a recent CNN poll conducted by SSRS, and two-thirds of registered voters rate the economy as “extremely important” to their vote.

title: Trump’s FDA nominee says MMR shot is ‘safe and effective’ at Senate hearing
summary: Dr Heidi Overton faces confirmation hearing weeks after standing behind Trump as he suggested shot could be ‘quite lethal’
text: Dr Heidi Overton, Donald Trump’s nominee to lead the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA), has told senators the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine is “safe and effective”, weeks after standing behind the president as he suggested the shot could be “quite lethal”. At a confirmation hearing on Thursday, Overton described the MMR vaccine as “safe and effective”, adding: “It is our best tool right now in the public health response to the measles outbreak.” Asked whether any vaccine on the US market was unsafe, she said: “Every vaccine on the US market right now is safe and effective, according to the FDA.” Overton faced questions from Bill Cassidy, the Louisiana Republican and physician who chairs the Senate health committee, whose vote is seen as pivotal. He had called her role in Trump’s August vaccine executive order “almost disqualifying”. The hearing comes as the US records its highest number of measles cases since 1991. When Cassidy asked what Overton would do if the president asked her to break those assurances on vaccine safety, she replied: “I would give him my best advice, and I would follow the statutory requirements for the role of FDA commissioner regarding individual product determinations for safety and efficacy.” When Bernie Sanders, the independent Vermont senator, asked whether she would have “the courage to stand up to” a president who he said “lies all of the time”, Overton did not answer directly. “I have worked for the president for a long time now, and earned his trust because I have been part of robust discussions to bring him the best advice,” she said. In her opening statement, Overton framed her agenda around speeding up drug development to protect US leadership in biotechnology. “We can protect America’s global leadership in biotechnology, but we have to act fast,” she said, pledging to make the FDA “the agency of the possible, rather than the impossible”. Overton, whose father leads a church in her home town of Gallup, New Mexico, has described Colossians 3:23 (“Whatever you do, work at it with all your heart, as working for the Lord, not for human masters”) as one of her life verses since childhood. Susan Collins, the Maine Republican senator, challenged her over the FDA’s August authorization of flavored vapes and nicotine pouches, including blueberry, mango and cappuccino. Collins said nearly 90% of young e-cigarette users choose flavored products. Overton said there was “100% agreement from this administration that we must protect kids”, but defended the decision as recommended by career staff because “so many adults are using flavors preferentially”. She added: “If that standard is not appropriate, we should work on statutes to fix that.” If confirmed, Overton, 37, would be the youngest ever FDA commissioner. A surgeon by training, she is now deputy assistant to the president for domestic policy, and served as a White House fellow during Trump’s first term. In a February 2023 issue brief for the conservative America First Policy Institute, where she was chief policy officer, she criticized federal policies that allowed abortion pills to be sent through the mail, writing that abortion “is corrosive to children, women, and society broadly”. She would replace Marty Makary, who resigned in May, and take over an agency still recovering from 2025 layoffs that cut its workforce by nearly 20%.

title: Vistry is the laggard in a housebuilding sector full of cracks | Nils Pratley
summary: Group shrinks ambitions from 20,000 to just 12,000 homes a year in an attempt to balance the books
text: The entire housebuilding sector is in a funk, grumbling about energy prices, the cost of labour, regulation, planning delays, taxes and more, but few have messed up a bad hand quite like Vistry. Three years ago this mashup of the Bovis, Linden and Countryside brands aspired to build 20,000 houses a year, and made itself the darling of the incoming Labour government by betting big on “affordable mixed-tenure housing” in partnership with councils, housing associations and institutional landlords. The City, too, fell for former executive chair Greg Fitzgerald’s promise that a “capital light” approach of pre-selling homes via a partnership model would yield oodles of cash. The share price doubled to almost £14 between October 2023 and August 2024. Fitzgerald departed in May after too many profit warnings and now, with the shares down to the bare foundations of 262p, it’s time for new chief executive Adam Daniels’ review of what happened. Short version: the logic of the partnership stuff wasn’t so silly, but the execution was horrible, especially in the south of England. “The pace of change meant that the operating model, controls and culture did not scale consistently with the group’s volumes [of construction],” he said, a polite summary of a growth strategy gone awry. For good measure, a proportion of the land bank would not be acquired “under the investment approval criteria that will be applied in the future”, which read as a confession that Vistry simply overpaid for plots. The good news, of a sort, for shareholders is that the damage to the balance is not deemed so severe that fresh equity is required. Daniels’ prescription for recovery, however, is a long exercise in getting smaller and living with shrunken ambitions. The aim is to build 12,000 houses a year, rather than the 20,000-plus imagined by Fitzgerald. A greater proportion of those homes will be in the north of England. As for return on capital employed – a critical metric for housebuilders – the old idea was 40%. That’s been cut to 30%, and only by 2031. It all sounds perfectly reasonable: keep things simple, fix the balance sheet by eating into the land bank, and concentrate on the parts of the country where market prices (which still matter for a mixed-tenure model) are holding up better. In Vistry’s favour is the fact that, for all its financial troubles, it’s still in the government’s good books. Last month, the company received a £350m direct grant to construct 3,000 affordable homes under the £39bn social and affordable homes programme. If you take the long view, there is a possibility of a turnaround if Daniels can live up to the promise of better execution. At the age of 35, he has time on his side – and may need it. The wider message for the government’s target to build 1.5m homes in England during this parliament, however, is as discouraging as ever. Vistry is an extreme example but virtually everybody is reining in ambitions in the name of financial discipline and cash generation. Even Barratt Redrow, the biggest of the lot, said in April it would be scaling back its land purchases. Angela Rayner, the housing secretary, has taken to calling the 1.5m figure a “stretch target”. Indeed, the only real question is by how much it will be missed. By an embarrassing margin, on current form.

title: Russia could attack a Nato country within months, Danish intelligence says
summary: Warning comes hours after Poland says fire at Starlink satellite station was ‘act of sabotage’
text: Russia could launch a limited military attack against a Nato country in the coming months, Danish intelligence said, in one of the starkest warnings yet by western security services. In a report published on Thursday, the Danish defence intelligence service warned of a “low but growing risk” that Russia could launch long-range strikes on Nato infrastructure supporting Ukraine, or carry out a limited incursion into a neighbouring country with a small number of troops, potentially operating without insignia. The report came hours after a fire at a Starlink satellite station in central Poland that local authorities described as an “act of sabotage”. Krzysztof Gawkowski, the deputy prime minister of Poland, said the blaze, which broke out overnight in the Masovian voivodeship, had been “deliberately designed to disable the station”, disrupting internet access for a number of institutions, including the Ukrainian military. Gawkowski said it had not been established who was responsible for the fire, but that “many signs suggest this aligns with Russia’s new ‌doctrine ⁠of attack. “While everything is operational today, we must recognise, as prime minister [Donald] Tusk recently noted, that this is an element of hybrid warfare,” he said. Starlink has become a key part of Ukraine’s military communications, and the incident comes amid a spate of suspected Russian sabotage operations across European infrastructure supporting Ukraine. Earlier this month, Germany publicly blamed Russia for an attempted drone attack on Leipzig/Halle airport, while a series of other incidents – including fires at drone factories and sabotage targeting rail infrastructure – have also been investigated for possible links to Moscow. Russia has denied involvement in such attacks. In recent weeks, several European intelligence chiefs have warned that Russia may be preparing more assertive actions to test Nato countries’ commitment to supporting Ukraine, though officials differ over how imminent such a move may be. Russia is expected to intensify its hybrid attacks against European countries with “greater consequences” for those targeted in the coming months, the Danes warned, including “destructive cyber-attacks that cripple societal functions as well as sabotage attacks that carry a high risk of casualties”. A source familiar with Moscow’s thinking agreed that Russia was likely to step up its hybrid attacks. “Russian military top command is convinced some Nato countries are directly involved in the war against Russia – not just by supplying Ukraine with weapons and intelligence, but by helping to guide missiles and drones,” the source said, speaking on condition of anonymity. “They therefore believe Nato is already waging a hybrid war against Russia, and that Russia has the right to respond in kind,” the source added. “Hybrid attacks” are broad terms generally used to describe non-military tactics aimed at pressuring or destabilising an adversary, including cyber-attacks, sabotage and disinformation. The aim of Russia’s actions would be to divert European resources away from supporting Ukraine, and deepen divisions within Nato if the alliance failed to agree on a collective response, the report added. The service believes it remained “highly unlikely” that Russia would launch an outright invasion of a Nato country, but notably said it “cannot be ruled out”. The Danish services said Russia could seek to test Nato’s article 5, which commits members to collective defence. They warned there was “a risk that Russia assesses that the Nato countries will not respond collectively”, particularly if Moscow believes the US is unable or unwilling to support its European allies in a potential war with Russia. There have been ongoing jitters among Nato members over whether the alliance’s most powerful member, the US, would come to Europe’s defence under Donald Trump in the event of a Russian attack. Questions over unity within Europe are also growing. Last week, Slovakia’s prime minister, Robert Fico, who has maintained close ties with the Kremlin, cast doubt on his country’s commitment to Nato’s collective defence principle, saying he did not want Slovakia drawn into a military conflict “because of some article 5”. Speaking at the UN general assembly on Wednesday, Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned that Russia continued to threaten countries beyond Ukraine, including Moldova, Poland and the Baltic states, while showing “no respect” for the sovereignty of countries in the south Caucasus and central Asia. “The more freedom Putin has to act, the more dangerous the world becomes for everyone else,” he said.

title: Reported assaults on Great Britain’s railways rise by fifth in a year
summary: Unions say record high of nearly 25,000, including assaults on rail workers and public, shows need for more staff and policing
text: The number of reported assaults on Great Britain’s railways has risen by a fifth to a record high of almost 25,000 incidents in a year. Unions said the “horrendous” figures showed the need for more staff and policing, as the Office of Rail and Road (ORR) revealed a sharp increase in assaults on the travelling public and on railway staff last year. There were 13,464 reported assaults against passengers and members of the public on the mainline railway in 2025-26, up 36% on the previous year and the highest number recorded by the ORR since it started tracking the figures in 2004. Assaults on rail staff were up 12% in a year to 11,289 reported incidents, mainly verbal abuse but including nearly 2,500 physical assaults – an average of about seven every day. The assaults on members of the public included startling rises in cases of harassment, up 52% year on year, and common assault, up by 30%. The figures partly reflect increased reporting and zero-tolerance campaigns on public transport, but also underline concerns flagged by unions about the threats to frontline workers as well as passengers, and the availability of transport police. The RMT general secretary, Eddie Dempsey, said the numbers were horrendous but chimed with the union’s own surveys showing two-thirds of its members had experienced some form of violence at work in the past year. He said: “We are calling for a significant increase in staffing across public transport, including an end to lone working. We also clearly need stronger legal protections for public transport workers against assaults at work. “British Transport Police funding cuts have also been disastrous which has undermined a proper policing presence on all public transport.” The TSSA union’s general secretary, Maryam Eslamdoust, said: “These new figures are shocking but not surprising because we have been warning for many months that violence on the railways is spiralling out of control.” The government said it was increasing police funding and taking the issue “extremely seriously”. A Department for Transport spokesperson said: “The rise in assaults on the railway is deeply concerning and completely unacceptable. No passenger or rail worker should face violence, threats or abuse, and we encourage anyone affected to report incidents to the police. “The government and rail industry are taking this extremely seriously, with a £63m increase in British Transport Police funding by 2028-29, which will see over 200 additional officers recruited.” New measures called railway behaviour notices were introduced in June 2026, strengthening the railway’s ability to exclude repeat offenders from stations. BTP said they had been encouraging greater reporting of all types of assault by staff and passengers, including record use of the 61016 discreet text-to-report number, which partly explained the growing numbers. Nonetheless, the BTP assistant chief constable said: “These figures are a stark reminder of the violence and abuse rail workers face simply for doing their jobs. We will never tolerate violence or abuse directed at passengers or staff on the railway, and anyone committing these crimes can expect a robust response from us. “We remain committed to driving down these offences and ensuring the network is safe for everyone.” The chief inspector of railways, the ORR’s Richard Hines, said the increase in reported assaults was concerning, adding: “No one on the railway should be subjected to violence, threats or abuse.” He said the ORR had set out guidance for employers on the risks, effective controls and encouraging staff to report incidents. A spokesperson for Network Rail and train operators said: “Violence, abuse and intimidation directed at passengers or staff are completely unacceptable. The rail industry works closely with British Transport Police to investigate incidents, support victims and bring offenders to justice.” They said the numbers also reflected greater intelligence sharing, improved reporting processes, and more CCTV and body-worn cameras for frontline staff. The ORR report noted that the headline numbers of reported assaults can include multiple counts in a single incident, for example for both harassment and common assault, while workforce assaults are now recorded even if no physical injury occurs. On the London Underground, where there is single counting, the number of assaults on the workforce fell slightly last year. The chief executive of the Rail Safety and Standards Board, Mark Phillips, said the rail industry was taking action to better protect staff, but the figures “underline the need for a change in public behaviour and greater respect for the people who keep the railway running safely every day”. Reports in recent years have highlighted that women and girls were at particular risk, while the growing number of assaults year on year since the pandemic has coincided with pressure on British Transport Police numbers. The abuse and intimidation faced by frontline staff on the railways has also been seen in sectors including retail and in the NHS. The British Retail Consortium warned over “endemic” violence towards shop workers earlier this year, while the number of reports of violence against NHS staff by patients surpassed 100,000 in 2025.

title: Rick Wakeman performs piano concert to 150 rescued moon bears in Vietnam
summary: Former Yes musician plays at sanctuary to raise awareness of animals that remain stuck in cages at ‘bile farms’
text: Rick Wakeman has played to all kinds of people around the globe, but he has now performed to an audience he had never encountered before – an enclosure of 150 bears. The former Yes musician, who has gone on to have a prolific solo career, played the piano at a Vietnamese bear sanctuary. “Before you ask, I won’t be playing the teddy bear’s picnic,” he joked ahead of the performance. Wakeman, who is a supporter of animal welfare causes and has rescue dogs and cats of his own, is conducting the concert to raise awareness of moon bears kept in cruel conditions for the extraction of their bile. He said he was a bit worried about how hot it is going to be. “You know the heatwave we had in England? It’s double that,” he said. “They offered to rig up a fan for me, but I figured that will just blow more hot air around.” His concert was performed live on a Yamaha grand piano positioned in Animals Asia’s bear sanctuary in the Tam Dao national park, and Wakeman had written some new compositions especially for rescued bears. Asked whether the bears would enjoy the music, he said: “They’ve not got much choice, really. It’s a well-known fact that all animals react to music, especially gentle melodic music. So what I am going to do is piano music that is melodic, and I can only hope that they will come up to the perimeter of the sanctuary and have a listen.” Wakeman has been sponsoring rescue bears since 2016 and recently adopted a new one: “He’s only 20 months old, a big fella, I went to see him today. He came out right to the edge and stood on his back legs and just stared at me, it was brilliant.” Bile is extracted from bears for traditional Chinese medicine by putting a needle into their gall bladder and drawing it out. The bears are kept in poor conditions in countries including China and in Vietnam, where it has just been banned, but where some bears are still in captivity in cramped enclosures. It is the fourth-biggest market in the illegal wildlife trade in east Asia, resulting in a dramatic decline in the Asiatic black bear populations in Vietnam, with nearly a third of their numbers lost around the world in just 30 years. Of the sanctuary, which he has been visiting this week, Wakeman said: “To see the bears be rehabilitated, having a life they never had before, some have never put their feet on grass before. They are so wonderful, that we can do such horrendous things to animals is beyond belief. Before this, they were chained in cages sometimes for 10 or 20 years in conditions where they couldn’t even turn around.” He is playing to raise awareness for the bears still stuck in cages in Vietnam and to urge the government to get them released: “We have 150 bears at the sanctuary, but there are 125 bears left in cages in the old bear bile farms, and there are four dying a month. We have to get them out quick and into the sanctuary.” He treats his rescue dogs and cats to music back at home in Suffolk. “I had one cat who used to jump on the grand piano, and if I stopped playing he would put his paw in the strings and rattle them until I played again. I know if my dogs don’t like it, they will get up and walk out, and my cats don’t like metal, grunge or rap. They want a melody.” Wakeman spends hours watching the bears. “If you see these bears it is hard to put into words, they are almost human the way they look at you,” he said. “If you see them, you can’t help but be moved. They aren’t tame but they are very safe, very happy, they play, they romp. I witnessed two today jumping in a bubble bath and playing. They’ve got a life back.” Dr Jill Robinson, the founder and CEO of Animals Asia, said: “We are beyond blessed to have Rick’s support for Animals Asia and the bears. His love for them is immeasurable and can be heard in the beautifully haunting music he has written for them. We’re all so excited to hear his performance in the open air at our sanctuary in the stunning setting of Tam Dao national park. I can’t wait to see how the bears respond.” Wakeman added: “I hope they lay down and have a listen, that would make my day. I would have a big grin on my face.”

title: Rebel offensive against Ethiopian army stokes fears of return to civil war
summary: Fighting escalates after Tigrayan rebels form new coalition aimed at overthrowing Abiy Ahmed government
text: There are growing fears of a return to civil war in Ethiopia after an offensive by fighters from Tigray into the neighbouring states of Afar and Amhara and the formation of a new rebel alliance aimed at overthrowing the government of the prime minister, Abiy Ahmed. About 600,000 people died between 2020 and 2022 during a devastating war between the Ethiopian army and the political party and paramilitary group the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF). Both sides are now accusing the other of triggering a return to open conflict. On Sunday, seven armed groups from around the country, including the TPLF, announced the formation of the Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Alliance for Survival, aimed at deposing the government in Addis Ababa. Then, on Wednesday, the TPLF seized control of three airports from federal police. The state-owned carrier, Ethiopian Airlines, said it had suspended flights to the region “due to the current situation”. The TPLF also launched attacks into Afar and Amhara. A humanitarian source in Afar told Agence France-Presse there were heavy artillery attacks by the group on Thursday as they attempted to take control of the town of Yallo, near the Tigrayan border. Flights to the historic Ethiopian town of Lalibela were also suspended on Thursday because of nearby fighting, while people in Tigray stocked up ⁠on food and cash, with one resident telling Reuters that people there feared they could face siege conditions similar to those during the previous war. A resident of Adigrat, a city close to the Eritrean border, ‌described panic-buying and shops emptying. “Food shortages are worsening as market shelves sit empty … Essential medicines remain scarce and astronomically expensive,” he told Reuters. “Daily survival has become a constant calculation.” The TPLF’s vice-president, Amanuel Assefa, told AFP: “We are in the situation of full-blown war now.” He confirmed Tigrayan forces were fighting alongside local armed groups in Afar and Amhara. The group took control of Abala, also on the Tigray-Afar border, on Wednesday, a foreign security source based in Ethiopia told AFP, while a TPLF source said they had seized several other towns in Afar. The foreign security source also said there was fighting around the Amhara town of Weldiya – one of the few routes to the capital. In its first public comments on the fighting, Ethiopia’s army said on ⁠Thursday it had foiled the attacks and killed, wounded or captured more than 500 enemy fighters. Analysts say the TPLF has support from Ethiopia’s neighbour and historic adversary Eritrea, which fears landlocked Ethiopia is planning to invade its territory to gain access to the Red Sea. The TPLF’s Assefa told AFP “we have no information about Eritrea’s plan”. Asked if they would request Eritrean intervention, he said: “Not yet.” The current fighting reflects shifting dynamics from the civil war, when Eritrea and Fano, an insurgent group that is now part of the new alliance, both fought with the government against the Tigrayans. Speaking at the UN general assembly on Wednesday, the Ethiopian president, Taye Atske-Selassie Amde, decried “the forces of destruction and mayhem” and “interference in our internal affairs by adversarial elements”. He said Ethiopia had exercised “immense restraint” and made progress with its neighbours. Abiy’s spokesperson, Billene Seyoum, said members of the alliance had been collaborating for a while with the financial backing of Eritrea. Eritrea has repeatedly denied similar accusations. The TPLF ruled Ethiopia from 1991 to 2018 before being sidelined by the rise of Abiy, eventually triggering the civil war. The renewed fighting marks the most serious challenge yet to the 2022 Pretoria agreement, which ended the civil war and maintained an uneasy calm until late last year, when clashes resumed. It raises fears of a broader regional conflict that could draw in armed groups from across and further destabilise a region already strained by war in neighbouring Sudan and tensions along the Red Sea. On Wednesday, the African Union chair, Mahmoud Ali Youssouf, urged “utmost restraint” from the warring parties and resumption of direct talks. An EU spokesperson called for “immediate de-escalation” and a recommitment to the Pretoria agreement. In the 2020-22 war, Tigray was largely cut off from the outside world as communications were severed, and access to food, cash and medicines was severely restricted, pushing hundreds of thousands of people into famine-like conditions. AFP and Reuters contributed reporting

title: Firms fined £1.3m after man killed by window that fell from luxury property in London
summary: Mick Ferris was crushed to death when the 130kg pane fell 26 storeys from the Corniche housing development
text: Two companies have been fined a total of £1.3m over health and safety breaches after a coach driver was killed by a falling window pane. Mick Ferris, 53, was crushed when a window fell 26 storeys from the Corniche, a luxury development in Vauxhall, London, on 2 October 2018. The property developer St James Group Ltd was fined £1m and the specialist facade contractor Lindner Prater was fined £300,000 at a sentencing hearing at Inner London crown court on Thursday. The firms were also ordered to pay costs of £125,000 each. In August, the firms were found guilty of ignoring “foreseeable risks” and convicted of “failing to discharge a duty” under the Health and Safety at Work Act 1974. Ferris, who was a driver for Clarkes of London, had been returning to his coach when the window pane, which weighed 130kg and was roughly 85cm wide and 190cm tall, fell from a height of about 90 metres (300ft). During the trial, the court heard that a window panel had previously fallen from the same development in August 2017, but that the design had not subsequently significantly changed. The Corniche, located on Albert Embankment alongside the Thames, has panoramic views over the Houses of Parliament. Luxury flats in the building – containing a gym, pool and spa – have been listed for sale at £3m. Ferris’s widow, Rachel, said his death “could have happened to anybody” and could have been prevented. In a statement read out in court, she said: “If somebody had done something differently – anything – it would have changed our lives. One person could have asked: ‘Can’t we do this better?’ What those companies did killed my husband. “Mick was just minding his own business. One minute there, one minute gone. The thought this could have happened to anybody is always with me. It could have been a child.” The trial heard that the design of the window in the Corniche was not safe because it opened outwards and was held in place by a single metal restrictor, meaning it could be prised off by the wind. Mr Justice Boyle said he was not sentencing the firms on the basis of the design itself being unsafe as the windows were “common within the industry” and there was no Health and Safety Executive (HSE) guidance prohibiting their use. The judge said St James should have been more robust in “ensuring the critical safety component was present and engaged”. Speaking outside court, HSE’s principal inspector, James Goldfinch, said Ferris “lost his life due to the failings of two leading companies in their field. The fact lessons had not been learned from a near miss the year before makes what happened on that day all the more galling. For a window to fall once was quite extraordinary; for it to fall again was simply criminal.” A spokesperson for St James said: “The death of Mick Ferris in 2018 was tragic. Our thoughts remain with his family and friends. We acknowledge the court’s sentencing decision and the fine imposed.”

title: TikTok drops appeal against £12.7m fine for not keeping under-13s off platform
summary: UK watchdog fined video app in 2023 for failing to enforce minimum age limit and remove underage users
text: TikTok will pay a £12.7m fine to the UK’s data watchdog after dropping an appeal against a ruling that it did not do enough to keep children below the age of 13 off the platform. The video app was punished by the Information Commissioner’s Office in 2023 for inadequate checks of who was using the platform, and failing to remove underage users. When issuing the fine the ICO said TikTok had done “very little, if anything” to address underage use of its service. TikTok has a minimum user age of 13 but failure to enforce that limit resulted in up to 1.75 million UK children under 13 using the service in 2020, the ICO said. TikTok also failed to provide users with information about how their data was being collected and used, and neglected to obtain parental consent. Emily Keaney, the ICO’s deputy commissioner, said: “Our successful action against TikTok shows how important it is for companies to have the right protections in place, including to prevent access by children who are not old enough to be using their services.” Chinese-owned TikTok said it disagreed with the ruling but had decided to pay the fine because it related to a period between 2018 and 2020, after which it had implemented “many youth safety measures and policies”. TikTok, which has more than 30m users in the UK, has also withdrawn an appeal against an ICO request for information about how its algorithm processes teenagers’ personal data – and how it serves potentially harmful content. The ICO said it would now resume the investigation. At the time the fine was issued, the then information commissioner, John Edwards, told the Guardian that TikTok was “not doing enough” on multiple fronts. “Our findings were that TikTok were not doing enough to prevent under-13s accessing their platform, they were not doing enough when they became aware of under-13s to get rid of them, and they were not doing enough to detect under-13s on there,” he said. Age-checking measures at tech platforms will be at the vanguard of the government’s new under-16 age limit for accessing social media platforms, which comes into force next year. The UK’s communications watchdog, Ofcom, has said “more action from the tech industry is needed” on enforcing age limits as the ban approaches. In Australia, which introduced a social media ban for under-16s last December, the eSafety commissioner has said a “substantial proportion” of under-16s in the country have kept their accounts, managed to create new ones or bypassed age-gating systems.

title: Australia’s newest chicken factory looks like a modern art gallery – but will it improve animal welfare?
summary: Three million chickens a week will be processed at the state-of-the-art facility in Tamworth – a fifth of all those eaten nationwide
text: Is it for birds? Is it for planes? The sleek, rust-coloured saucer settles into the earth, mirroring the surrounding hills. It looks like an art gallery or a high-end conference centre – an architectural masterpiece designed to sit lightly on the land. Until you see the shed behind it. The sweeping lines are the gateway to a $600m poultry processing plant that will, at full capacity, process 3 million chickens a week. Located in Tamworth, 300km north of Sydney, the new facility is owned by Baiada, one of Australia’s two largest chicken producers and the owner of household brand names Steggles and Lilydale Free Range. At its height, two lines will process 15,000 birds an hour as chickens fly through state-of-the-art chilling systems and automated packing machines en route to supermarkets across the state. The new plant will support more than 1,000 jobs, with workers able to spend their lunch breaks at an on-site cafeteria, at a gym or in landscaped gardens. Jeff Budd, the deputy mayor of Tamworth regional council, has toured the facility, which opened last week. He says the unusual design creates a gem for the city and will attract the skilled workers and technicians needed to run kilometres’ worth of conveyor belts and systems. “I think it’s massive for the entire region,” he says. “The Baiada company … certainly made it look that way. Once you’re inside that main building at the front, it’s like a five-star hotel.” Australians are voracious chicken eaters, consuming an average of 55kg of chicken meat per person per year. Almost half of all meat eaten in Australia is chicken, and consumption has doubled in the past 30 years. More than 800 million chickens will be slaughtered this financial year to meet the demand. Once fully operational, the Oakburn facility will account for almost 20% of that. “We’re happy to see a commitment from a Sydney-based company to one of their regional hubs, to put in such a sophisticated [facility],” says Prof Stephen Walkden-Brown, the interim director of Poultry Hub Australia at the University of New England. “It’s a pretty big development, one of the most modern plants in the world.” Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email In a media release, Baiada said the company had “grown alongside” the Tamworth community for six decades, and the facility reflected the company’s commitment to the city. “This is a long-term investment in Tamworth and the people who have supported Baiada for generations,” the managing director, Simon Camilleri, says. “Our history in this region stretches back to the 1960s, when Charlie Baiada first established operations here, and this facility reflects our confidence in the future of Tamworth.” But it did not answer questions about whether the new facility would also deliver improved animal welfare outcomes. Jed Goodfellow, the director of policy and government relations at the Australian Alliance for Animals, says while the Baiada building may be state of the art, he believes “the welfare model behind it is anything but”. Slowing the growth A leading welfare issue, Goodfellow says, is the speed at which meat chickens grow. “Chickens are still being selectively bred to grow at extraordinary speeds, with their bodies paying the price for ever greater efficiency,” he says. “Healthier, slower-growing breeds are now being used in many parts of the world, particularly Europe, with Norway, the Netherlands and France producing higher welfare breeds at scale. “It may cost slightly more but, as their experience shows, the increase is not prohibitive, as European consumers increasingly opt for the healthier option.” Melina Tensen, the senior scientific officer for farm animals at the RSPCA, says about 97% of chicken meat sold in Australia abides by the organisation’s welfare standards. “It’s a pretty big deal to have most of industry achieving standards to go well above the legal minimum,” Tensen says. “Wherever animals are farmed for food – and they’re going to be farmed for food for a long time to come – we want to be in there making sure that animals are raised and handled and transported and slaughtered in ways we find acceptable.” Welfare standards were updated this month to promote lower stocking density, variable light intensity in sheds – to allow chickens to choose between brighter and darker areas – and the phasing out of a slaughtering method called electrical water bath stunning. Those changes must be enacted by 1 January 2031 for businesses to keep their RSPCA certification. At the same time, the RSPCA has released a new category of “enhanced” welfare standards, which are primarily focused on encouraging producers to rear slower-growing breeds. Most of Australia’s commercial chickens are two fast-growing breeds, the Ross 308 and the Cobb 500, which reach slaughter weight at between four and six weeks of age. Tensen says the RSPCA would ultimately like to see chicken meat producers replace fast-growing breeds with slower-growing breeds but consumers would have to help achieve that transition. “The longer it takes to grow, the greater cost,” she says. “We definitely encourage consumers to be vocal about supporting this transition … because every dollar you spend is a message to the retailer.”

title: Germany investigates 105-year-old suspected former Nazi prison camp guard
summary: Man accused of being accessory to murders at Stalag 326 VI K amid race to prosecute suspects before they die
text: A 105-year-old man is under investigation on suspicion of being an accessory to multiple murders at a Nazi prisoner of war camp, German prosecutors have said. The case, which is being handled by the public prosecutor’s office in Dortmund, centres on the Stalag 326 VI K camp in western Germany, in what is now the state of North Rhine-Westphalia. “The 105-year-old suspect is thought to have been a guard at the prisoner of war camp Stalag 326 VI K in the Senne region of western Germany,” prosecutors said in a statement. The man is “accused of being an accessory to multiple murders owing to his activities there”, they said. The Senne camp housed between 180,000 and 200,000 Soviet prisoners of war between 1941 and April 1945, when it was liberated by American troops. The investigation is the result of an urgent last-minute scramble by the judiciary to prosecute alleged participants in the Nazi killing machine before they die. The judicial efforts stem in part from a recognition that many of the suspects who have escaped prosecution in the eight decades since the end of the second world war on the grounds that they were considered to have played an insignificant role were in fact integral to the implementation of the Hitler regime’s murderous aims. A judicial precedent was set by the court case of John Demjanjuk, a former guard at the Nazi Sobibór death camp in occupied Poland, who was convicted in 2011 of being an accomplice to the murders of more than 28,000 Jews that took place in the time he worked there. Prosecutors had sought Ukraine-born Demjanjuk’s extradition from his Ohio home to Germany for years, arguing that he was complicit in the crimes committed at Sobibór despite a lack of evidence that he had directly killed anyone. Demjanjuk died aged 91 in March 2012 awaiting an appeal due to his age and frailty, which meant he did not go to prison. The Demjanjuk case lowered the bar for proof of complicity, paving the way for other nonagenarians and more recently centenarians to stand trial. The most prominent trial of recent years, and representative of what Hannah Arendt, a political theorist, described as a Schreibtischtäter (desk perpetrator, or bureaucratic mediator), was that of Irmgard Furchner, who worked at the Stutthof concentration camp between 1943 and 1945 as a secretary to the camp commandant. She was given a two-year suspended sentence for her role as an accessory to murder. Her trial was, contrary to normal rules, filmed for historical purposes. Furchner made headlines after running away from her retirement home on the scheduled opening day of her trial. Josef Schütz, a former guard at the Sachsenhausen concentration camp north of Berlin, was sentenced for being an accomplice to murder to five years in prison in June 2022. He died the following year, aged 102. In April last year an alleged former guard at Sachsenhausen died before he was able to face trial over charges of complicity in the murder of more than 3,300 people. A separate investigation was opened last year by Dortmund prosecutors into a 100-year-old former guard at a PoW camp in Hemer, North Rhine-Westphalia, which also held mainly Soviet prisoners. He is suspected of participating in executions of prisoners between December 1943 and September 1944. The new investigation was initiated by the Central Office for the Investigation of National Socialist Crimes in Ludwigsburg, in the southern state of Baden-Württemberg, which passed its preliminary investigation into the man to public prosecutors along with that of another former guard. The other suspect has since died, according to German media. If the trial goes ahead, like other recent cases it is expected to throw light on the Stalag system in general and on Senne in particular, drawing survivors and historians to give evidence. Up to 5.7 million Soviet prisoners were held captivity in Germany. More than half did not survive.

title: EU says Trump’s plan to ban US diesel exports would ‘negatively impact both sides’
summary: US president’s suggested 90-day export ban before midterm elections could bring even higher fuel prices across Europe
text: The EU has warned Donald Trump against plans to ban US diesel exports to the global market, saying the move would negatively affect Europe and the US. The European Commission has reacted with “concern” to reports this week that the US president could prevent diesel from reaching the global market. Trump is reportedly considering a 90-day export ban to provide a temporary respite from high pump prices for US households before the midterm elections, after US diesel reached a record average of $6.52 (£4.93) a gallon. “I’ve said let’s not send ‌out the diesel. ‌We make a lot of diesel … I’ve called for it. ‌I’ve called for it within my people,” he said. Olof Gill, a spokesperson for the EU’s executive arm, said on Thursday “any disruption would risk negatively impacting both sides” and the EU expected “close partners to consult each other before taking measures that affect shared markets”. The EU made the diplomatic intervention as experts said that the potential export ban could be “devastating” for Europe, and traders scrambled to assess the continent’s reliance on imports from the US. The US energy secretary, Chris Wright, has warned at an Economist event in New York that banning exports was a “blunt tool” that could harm US fuel supplies in the long term. For Europe, the ban could be far more damaging. US diesel exports have made up a third of the continent’s imports this year, as supplies from war-damaged refineries in the Middle East and Russia have plummeted. By August, the US supplied about half of Europe’s diesel imports. Pump prices have already climbed to record highs across Germany and the Netherlands, leading to calls for political leaders to protect households from rising costs. In the UK, motorists may be only days away from fresh all-time highs, raising concerns over the economic impact of further price hikes for hard-pressed households. The RAC said the average cost of diesel was 197.75p a litre on Thursday, up from 142.38p before the start of the Iran war. “A US export ban would be devastating for diesel supply in Europe, which would struggle to replace supply,” said Josh Michalowski, the head of European diesel pricing at Argus Media, a commodities data provider. Fuel stations across Europe are unlikely to run dry, because Europe produces about 70% of the diesel it consumes from domestic refineries. It also stores fuels in reserve. But experts fear that competing for cargoes on the global market would lead to higher market prices. So far the market for diesel cargoes has remained relatively quiet since reports of a potential US diesel ban emerged this week, according to Benedict George, the head of European products at Argus. He said traders were still weighing up the degree to which the White House might limit US exports. “If this prospect became even relatively serious [in the White House], it would be very serious for European markets. There would be some degree of panic given how reliant buyers have become on US cargoes,” George said. “There’s enough European diesel production to ensure that we wouldn’t run out, but losing US cargoes would mean buyers would have to compete with buyers in Asia for the few available cargoes from the Middle East and India, in what is already a very competitive global market.” The price of diesel has outpaced the rising price of global oil markets due to severe disruption to refineries in the Gulf and in Russia. The price difference – known as the “crack spread” – reached a record high earlier this month and could climb further still. “A US ban on diesel exports would pose a significant challenge for the UK, given the country’s growing reliance on American refined fuel,” said Thomas Pugh, the chief economist at the audit, tax and consulting firm RSM UK. The UK has only four operating oil refineries after the closures of Grangemouth and Lindsey last year. Both produced diesel for the UK market. Pugh warned that losing almost 90,000 barrels a day of US distillate, or 18% of the country’s total consumption, would leave the UK even more exposed to global diesel prices. He added that, while shortages of fuel were unlikely immediately, a longer-term ban would make them a “real possibility”. Although the number of motorists driving diesel passenger vehicles has fallen, it remains the lifeblood of the UK’s agricultural and logistics sectors by fuelling heavy machinery, lorries and vans. The European Commission spokesperson said: “High-level contacts between the European Union and the US administration are ongoing.” A UK government spokesperson said: “Forecourts in the UK are being supplied with petrol and diesel as normal and we have a diverse and resilient supply. We continue to engage with our international partners and the UK fuel industry.”

title: The eyes have it: Rory Stewart’s ‘magnificently strange’ Newsnight moment goes viral
summary: Clip of the former Tory MP staring intently at fellow panellist is shared widely online
text: Rory Stewart has been an Afghan NGO leader, a Conservative leadership candidate, a Harvard professor, a popular podcaster, and the deputy governor of an Iraqi province. This week, he created a moment that drew wider attention than any of them: he fixed a beady gaze on a fellow Newsnight panellist for the longest four seconds in television history. Stewart, who now co-presents The Rest Is Politics podcast with Alastair Campbell, appeared on the BBC programme on 18 September – but in the last few days, a clip of the moment in question has taken on a life of its own on social media. Stewart appeared alongside the former Labour leader Neil Kinnock and the New Statesman’s political editor, Ailbhe Rea, to discuss the day’s main news stories, including the race between China and the US to develop artificial intelligence (AI). After Stewart made his comments, the presenter Matt Chorley asked Rea what Westminster could do about the development of AI. Stewart then swivelled around in his chair and stared directly at the journalist with an expression – and posture – of absolute focus. Chorley told the Guardian the behaviour had not appeared overly strange in person: “I didn’t notice Rory looking particularly intently at anyone during the course of the programme,” he said. He only became aware of what had happened when several friends texted him. “You know a moment from Newsnight has cut through when friends and family who don’t normally watch it are suddenly sending me clips,” he said. “But it is just quite a funny moment.” He added that as it was the first Newsnight episode to move to the programme’s new earlier slot at 7pm, it had been “quite manic” in the runup. He had even joked to the panellists: “Anything that can be used to go viral, maybe a punchup or whatever, a tiff at the table, if you want to do that, that’d be great.” Chorley observed that Stewart was “used to this”, after another clip of him taking his tie off during a Tory leadership debate had gone viral in 2019. “It’s not the first time that something he’s done has gone wild online. I think he was genuinely probably just intently listening to what Ailbhe had to say. But there was something about the camera angle and his very direct look,” he said. Many behaviours that appear normal in person can look strange on screen, Chorley added. He said he had learned to “remember you’re always on” and to control his naturally emphatic hand movements, which can “look crazy” on screen. He also recalled an early Newsnight episode which had surprised viewers when Tim Stanley, a columnist at the Telegraph, winked at the camera. “This is just the beauty of live telly,” he said. “It’s a reminder that even when the camera is on the person who’s talking, you might be in shot.” Rea, who was on the receiving end of the stare, posted the clip on X to joke that she would “please like attention levels like this on my latest interview” after sharing a link to her most recent reporting. The clip has turned into a meme online, with commenters imagining situations in which the stare could have taken place. The Larry the Cat social media account posted: “When HR tells you that you need to listen better to female colleagues.” Total Politics Group’s chief executive, Mark Wallace, compared Stewart’s behaviour to the comedian Kevin Eldon’s surreal style, writing: “There’s a high degree of Kevin Eldon energy to this. Magnificently strange.”

title: Leaders join push to create UN body to tackle ‘awful reality’ of inequality
summary: Body would be modelled on climate panel and recognise inequality as a global challenge threatening world security
text: Plans to set up a global UN body on inequality modelled on the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) are likely to be proposed to a meeting of the UN general assembly in the coming months. Speaking at an event on the sidelines of the general assembly in New York, left-leaning leaders from Brazil, Norway and Spain claimed momentum was building behind calls for a standing international panel on inequality that would recognise the issue as a global challenge threatening world security. Two G7 countries – Germany and Japan – have given public backing. Joseph Stiglitz, the Nobel prize-winning economist, recommended the establishment of the new body in a report commissioned by South Africa for its G20 chairing last November. The dislocation caused by inequality was also the focus of the 2024 G20 meeting, chaired by Brazil. But the proposal is likely to make little political headway during this year’s G20, to be led by Donald Trump, and some countries are wary of talk about new globally imposed taxes, or assertions that economic analysis can be compared to climate science. The UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, has said he wants inequality to be part of the agenda of the UK-chaired 2027 G20, but no British diplomat spoke at this week’s high-level event on the issue. Cyril Ramaphosa, the South African president, told this week’s meeting that inequality was “the new multilateral frontier”. “Inequality is not inevitable but a problem that can be solved with evidence, analysis and political action,” he said. The panel would not just track trends but propose solutions, though many would be likely to face opposition from multinationals and billionaires. The Spanish prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, argued: “Inequality is not an abstract concept but an awful reality. It is about disaffection and whether the people feel the system is working against them.” He added: “Think what the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change has done for climate change – bringing together the best available knowledge, independently assessing the evidence and giving governments around the world a scientific basis on which to act. We need something similar for inequality, and we need to do it now. Not ideology but knowledge. Not another layer of bureaucracy but instead a tool for better policymaking.” Spain’s foreign affairs minister, José Manuel Albares, said progressive tax systems and better tax cooperation were necessary to prevent tax evasion. The UN deputy secretary general, Amina Mohammed, told the meeting: “We see breathtaking levels of income and wealth inequality; the richest 10% earning 75% of all wealth. This emergency could get worse – and fast. The breakneck emergence of frontier technology, and the concentration of this technology in a tiny number of hands, could unleash global inequality on a scale far beyond what we have ever seen. A world in which only a few powerful countries are wealthy is a ticking timebomb.” Stiglitz, an advocate of a billionaire’s wealth tax in California, said: “Inequality within and between nations is a collective threat to the functioning of our economies, and our ability to support human dignity. This kind of global stress akin to the crisis of climate change needs to be very much better understood and studied in the same way.” Mia Mottley, the prime minister of Barbados, said the need for a groundbreaking general assembly resolution to establish the panel was urgent. She asked: “Who is really participating in growth, who owns the assets and who shapes the rules?” Referring to a UN resolution in March condemning the transatlantic chattel slave trade as the “gravest crime against humanity” and calling for reparative justice, she added: “If we condemn slavery, we condemn the notion of people exploiting other human beings in order to make profit, but slavery is just the extreme condition, and as I have come to reflect more and more, the mens rea [criminal intent] that informs slavery, regrettably, is still existent in the modern world.” Drawing on the Stiglitz report to last year’s G20, she said that between 2000 and 2024 the richest 1% captured 41% of all new global wealth, while 50% of the world’s population received just 1%. “Equal effort therefore does not guarantee equal opportunity,” she said. Sarah Colenbrander, the director of the climate and sustainability programme at the London-based thinktank ODI Global, said: “The IPCC has consistently demonstrated the overwhelming scientific consensus on the importance of cutting emissions and the consequences of failing to do so. A panel on inequality could likewise cut through the noise and make the case for poverty reduction and wealth redistribution. But she warned: “We have seen that the IPCC’s summaries for policymakers have consistently been watered down by countries with fossil fuel interests. In the same vein, it is hard to imagine that billionaires – and the world leaders among them or in their pockets – would engage constructively.”

title: After so long in Trump’s sights, hopeful Greenlanders breathe a collective sigh of relief
summary: Locals hope agreement signed this week is step towards independence and end to US threats to annex island
text: Greenland’s prime minister, Jens-Frederik Nielsen, and Múte B Egede, the foreign minister, received a hero’s welcome when they landed back in Nuuk from New York on Wednesday night – and a nation took a collective sigh of relief. Colleagues, friends and members of the public turned out to greet them at an airport where, just 20 months ago, the landing of a Trump-branded plane containing Donald Trump Jr had kickstarted a geopolitical crisis that the people of Greenland now hope is over. To cheers and applause, and waving red and white Erfalasorput flags, the politicians were credited with saving the nation thanks to a new defence agreement between Greenland, Denmark and the US signed this week at the UN in New York. It comes after an unprecedented period of turbulence in which Donald Trump repeatedly threatened to invade the Arctic island and almost tore apart Nato in the process. “Welcome home,” the speaker of Inatsisartut, the Greenlandic parliament, Kim Kielsen, said. “Welcome to a country that we were about to lose. You have ensured that we have a future here.” Like many Greenlanders, for the last year-and-a-half he said he had been holding his breath. Nielsen, who became prime minister last year in the middle of the crisis, told the crowd: “We can be calm. Our land will not be taken. Our land will not be bought. The road has been long, and it has been very difficult and dangerous.” Hundreds then attended a celebratory coffee party at Katuaq, the Greenlandic capital’s cultural centre. Aqqalukkuluk Fontain, 38, who was there with his girlfriend, Stella, and their youngest daughter, Aura, who is three, said the collective release of tension was palpable. “It was a joyous moment. It’s going to linger for a while,” said the IT manager, who earlier this year organised a protest outside the new US embassy in Nuuk. He cautioned he could not entirely relax – concerned that, after the midterms, Trump could change his mind and relations could “take a turn for the worse” – but hailed the deal with the US as a moment of pride for Greenland and a stroke of “strategy genius” from Greenlandic and Danish negotiators. “Trump is trying to angle it that he made a great deal. But he wanted total control, ownership of Greenland. He didn’t get that,” he said. Its full text contains some key differences from the 1951 defence agreement it is intended to update – for example, the US gets underwater access to Greenland and specific permission to construct a missile defence system – but is a far cry from Donald Trump’s original threat to annex the Arctic island. And in terms of tangible outcomes, the biggest winner is arguably Greenland, where it is seen as a potential stepping stone to future independence. When the 1951 agreement was signed, Greenland was still a colony of Denmark. Now, it is a largely autonomous territory that has signed an agreement alongside Denmark with the US that it played a central role in negotiating. A big question hanging over Greenland independence was what would happen to its status within Nato and relationship with the US. The new agreement answers that question. It stipulates that if it did become independent, the governments of Greenland and Denmark would “together ensure that the independent Greenlandic state will agree to remain in Nato, including by applying to become a member if necessary”. The centrality of Nato to the agreement is also seen as a boost for an alliance that was creaking under US claims against one of its fellow members’ territory. Greenlandic politician Qarsoq Høegh-Dam, who earlier this year became the first member of the pro-independence party Naleraq to be elected to the Danish parliament, said there was still considerable work to do in terms of gaining independence but that “a lot of what ifs” have now gone. “It’s a point of relief for Greenlanders,” he said. “They can lower their shoulders a bit, so we can talk about domestic issues, the road to independence more freely, instead of the search of what if?” Much of the agreement already existed in practice, he said, but now “it is written in ink” with Greenland’s explicit involvement. “It’s a continuation of an agreement since the 1950s. The difference is now that Greenland has some say in it. They want to agree for themselves instead of a country overseas agreeing on behalf of them,” he said. “That’s the difference first and foremost and it is significant.” He said, however, there were still questions about what the words will equate to in practice, for example on investment. “It’s a good foundation, but the details are missing,” he said. Given that just a few months ago Trump was threatening to invade Greenland, and a few weeks since he posted a map of Greenland covered with the US flag to social media, in many ways the very fact that a diplomatic agreement has been reached is a victory in itself. Ulrik Pram Gad, a senior researcher at the Danish Institute for International Studies (DIIS), said: “For Danes and Greenlanders, it’s a win to be able to force Trump into doing something diplomatically. And if this actually puts the Greenland crisis to rest, it will be felt as a win for Greenland, Denmark and Europe because then we can concentrate on real problems and trying to find ways to work with the US on that.” Aviaja Fontain, 41, a student from Nuuk, said the agreement puts to rest months of anxiety. At one point, amid government warnings about preparedness, she thought Nuuk was being attacked by the US during what turned out to be a power cut caused by a storm. “Many of us have been afraid that Trump will use force, but now I can feel relief,” she said. Now she feels she can finally relax. “We don’t have to think about getting attacked and just live our peaceful life again.”

title: ‘Eat the rich, save the planet’: climate protesters call out big tech’s disconnect from reality
summary: Activists gathered outside the OpenAI offices on Monday during climate week in New York City
text: On Monday evening, protesters gathered outside the unmarked Manhattan offices of OpenAI, maker of ChatGPT, holding signs calling to “Eat the rich, save the planet”. Over the next two days, groups also picketed outside the offices of fellow tech giants Google and Amazon; other protesters, including clergy, were arrested while disrupting a closed-door AI health summit in the city. Tonight, protesters will target a Brooklyn gas power plant that was set to close – until it was purchased to power AI datacenters. The protests come on the heels of an Anthropic employee quitting his job with a warning that intensified an already-growing AI panic: “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.” Though it was far from the first time an AI expert had issued a doomsday message about the threat the tech poses, this time it dominated public attention, arriving as trust in big tech has hit an all-time low and communities across the country are trying to stop the building of datacenters. From 2024 to 2026, at least $64bn in proposed datacenter buildout was blocked by local organizing. Today, bans have been passed in at least 18 states at the local or county level, and New York passed a statewide moratorium this summer. “They are claiming that they have the power to end humanity, but at the same time can’t get AI to do a lot of major things that they’re pushing for,” said Jonathan Westin of Climate Defenders and the Stop Funding Billionaires campaign, which organized the “unplug AI” week of action. Like Westin, many of the protesters at the anti-AI protests this week were part of climate organizations, in town for New York’s climate week, a global gathering of elected officials, policy experts and advocates timed to the meeting of the United Nations general assembly. Datacenters require significant amounts of water to function and an immense amount of energy to power, often using fossil fuels, bringing pollution into communities. Organizers are calling for more datacenter moratoriums and stronger commitments to protect water access and to block fossil fuels. They say tech companies’ greed is the real threat to the environment. Even Wall Street has warned the AI boom could cause another economic bubble to burst – one that, protesters say, will be carried on the backs of working Americans. “Regular people shouldn’t be left holding the bag for a bunch of billionaires and trillionaires to play Monopoly with our economy,” Westin said. Other groups at this week’s protests, like the anti-war organization Code Pink, called attention to how many big tech corporations work with the US military: the US has used tech made by Palantir, xAI and Anthropic to establish targets and rain down bombs in the war in Iran – all with far-from-perfect accuracy. Alex Hanna, director of research at the Dair Institute, an AI research organization centering communities facing environmental damage and extraction from AI, said the doomsday prophesying from tech companies and former employees are a distraction amid “the climate and ecological crisis, the rising fascism that is borne out of climate politics, the making of climate refugees, and the growing inability of people just to get by from day to day. It’s such a disconnect from what seems to be actually happening.” Some protesters outside the OpenAI offices Monday had traveled from New Mexico, where a planned datacenter threatens the already-sapped Rio Grande and a community facing a 20-year drought. Oracle’s Project Jupiter, which is contracted to OpenAI, was pitched as a job creator for the community, but organizers say the companies aren’t talking about how it would drain the area’s limited water resources. “There’s just so much misinformation that’s being sold, not only to the elected [officials], but to the community, and I think it’s really a disservice to the people of New Mexico for these companies to come in and just basically lie about what they’re going to do and how these projects are going to benefit communities,” said Daisy Maldonado, a resident of Doña Ana county, the planned site of the datacenter. At an AI sustainability conference elsewhere in the city on Tuesday, five protesters were arrested for disrupting a keynote on using AI to solve the energy grid crisis. Activists called out the conference framing as “greenwashing”, or using misleading descriptions to brand something as eco-friendly or less harmful. “We do not want to greenwash these datacenters that are being built,” said Adrosto de Silva, who also traveled from New Mexico to the OpenAI protest. “There is no way that you can do harm reduction in any sort of datacenter whatsoever.” At Monday’s protest, attendees – including the Tennessee state representative Justin Jones, who dropped in while in town for climate week – emphasized that many of these fights are happening in communities of color and poor communities, where the companies thought they wouldn’t face local backlash. “This building behind me is a danger to humankind,” said Jones, gesturing at the OpenAI offices. “The confluence of this techno oligarchy is a threat to us all. I’m here because if they come for one of us, they’re coming for all of us.”

title: Injunction blocking publication of ex-SAS soldier’s book on counter-terror op extended
summary: MoD claims book by soldier known as Christian Craighead contains alleged breach of confidentiality contract
text: An injunction preventing a former member of the SAS from publishing a book about his role in a counter-terrorism operation has been extended after an application by the Ministry of Defence. The block on publication of the book in the UK will continue until the conclusion of a government legal action against the soldier, who is known only by the pseudonym Christian Craighead. Craighead received the Conspicuous Gallantry Cross – a medal one level down from the Victoria Cross – for his involvement in an incident after an al-Shabaab attack in the Kenyan capital of Nairobi in 2019 in which 21 people died. Craighead claims to have saved more than 700 people from a hotel complex in Nairobi after a group of armed militants launched an assault. The MoD claims that Craighead’s book contains an alleged breach of a confidentiality contract that he had freely signed on joining the UK’s special forces. An interim injunction was issued this month, with government barristers returning to the high court on Thursday to ask for it to be extended until the legal claim is resolved. Oliver Sanders KC, for the MoD, told the court in London the claim that Craighead had breached the contract was “straightforward and really unarguable”. The book has been published in the US but Sanders said that this was not relevant because “the only reason it is available overseas is through the defendant’s own wrongdoing”. Craighead did not appear in court and was not represented. In a ruling extending the injunction, Mr Justice Saini said Craighead “willingly entered into” the contractual agreement and was “clearly and consistently told by his superiors” that he would not be permitted to publish the book. The judge said he believed the MoD had an “overwhelming case for an injunction” and that Craighead appeared to have committed a “flagrant breach” of the contract, which he did “having his eyes open to the potential consequences”. Craighead lost a legal challenge against the MoD in 2023 after it refused to allow the book’s publication, citing national security concerns. Craighead joined the armed forces in 1992 and served in the special forces from 2006 to 2020. The court was previously told that when joining the special forces Craighead signed an agreement preventing him from disclosing information about his time in the SAS. The confidentiality contract stated that Craighead would give a “solemn undertaking binding me for the rest of my life” not to disclose information relating to his special forces service without “express prior authority in writing” from the MoD, which has not been given in relation to the book. Sanders said: “If he had not signed the contract, he would not have served in the UK special forces. He would not have been in Nairobi; he would not have had the training, the equipment, the weapons, the support. While he does not like it, this is what he agreed, and as a matter of contract law it is very, very straightforward.”
