title: UK ‘losing up to £6.5bn a year in EU trade’ without post-Brexit product deal
summary: IPPR finds failure to align testing standards costing 0.18% of national income and has seen companies abandon exporting to EU
text: The UK is losing out on annual exports to the EU that could be worth as much as £6.5bn without a deal with Brussels that allows manufacturers to jettison duplicate product testing. In the latest attempt to calculate the loss of trade with the EU after Brexit, the IPPR thinktank said many companies have given up selling goods to the EU or set up subsidiaries inside the trade bloc after successive governments failed to secure a mutual recognition agreement that would avoid the extra administration costs. The thinktank estimated that the absence of such a deal may have cost UK exporters between £3.7bn and £6.5bn each year in lost revenue since the UK’s post-Brexit trading arrangements came into force in 2021. It urged the government to reopen talks with the EU, saying that the loss of trade amounted to about 0.18% of annual national income, or about three times what the UK government expects to gain from its trade deal with Japan, Canada, Australia and Singapore, known as the CPTPP deal. At this week’s Liberal Democrat conference, the party’s leader, Ed Davey, said that should the party take control at Westminster, he would begin talks to rejoin the EU single market and customs union. He said the move would bring the UK into alignment with its largest trading partner, boost exports and kickstart growth. Earlier this year, the Starmer administration pitched the creation of a single market for goods between the UK and EU to Brussels, but the proposal was rejected by EU officials. EU officials said they wanted deeper cooperation with the UK, but this had to be in line with fundamental principles, including no cherrypicking of EU policies. The IPPR said a mutual recognition agreement (MRA) based on “dynamic alignment” – where the UK keeps relevant product rules in step with the EU – would allow UK and EU authorities to recognise each others’ product assessments, reducing costs and uncertainty for exporters. The estimated losses are concentrated in three industries: Motor vehicle and part exports would have been between £2.48bn and £3.42bn higher each year. Electronic exports could have been between £1.17bn and £1.67bn higher. Pharmaceutical exports would have had an estimated annual uplift of between £740m and £820m. “The findings highlight the scale of trade missed out on as a result of post-Brexit regulatory barriers, providing one of the clearest opportunities to reduce friction in UK-EU relations,” the report said. Joseph Sassoon, an economist at the IPPR and co-author of the report, said the report was the first attempt to find the cause of the loss of trade caused by the lack of an MRA after Brexit by isolating its impact from other factors that could also have caused exports to decline. He said researchers tested whether Covid-related disruption, changes in global supply chains, sanctions on Russia, energy market shocks or shifts in re-export patterns could be to blame for the decline. “The estimated impact of not having an MRA remained large and statistically significant throughout,” he said.

title: Alarm bells sound in Brussels as EU sales of Chinese hybrid cars rocket
summary: Explosive growth in imported vehicles omitted from EV tariffs fuels concern for future of European carmakers
text: Sales of Chinese hybrid cars have rocketed in the EU in the past four and a half years, data shows, underlining growing concerns in Brussels over the future of the European car industry. In 2022, just 659 Chinese-made fully hybrid cars (vehicles in which the petrol or diesel engine charge the motor and battery) were sold in the EU. However, after Brussels imposed anti-subsidy tariffs on fully electric cars from China in 2024, sales of hybrids have shot up to 160,662 in the first seven months of this year. Eurostat figures show that sales of Chinese-made plug-in hybrid vehicles – models popular for longer driving distances that can recharge via both the fuel engine and an external power source – have also soared, rising from 56,706 sold in 2022 to 217,764 from January to July this year. The volume of Chinese hybrids on the roads is now spooking the car industry and Brussels, which has asked China to voluntarily reduce its hybrid exports to the EU or face safeguards, likely to be quotas. On Thursday the German car industry for the first time indicated it would be willing to consider tariffs on Chinese hybrids specifically. The German Association of the Automotive Industry, VDA, called on the European Commission to carry out a comprehensive assessment of the impact of any trade safeguards, which can range from quotas to price floors and tariffs. It said: “The EU must also have an effective and up-to-date set of trade defence instruments at its disposal. Where unfair conduct is proven, the use of WTO-compliant trade defence instruments must be considered; these are legitimate and tried-and-tested means of achieving a level playing field and safeguarding fair conditions of competition.” According to new figures released by the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association (ACEA), hybrid cars now account for almost 37% of the overall market, with electric cars making up just over 21% of the market. The ACEA figures show three Chinese manufacturers – BYD, Chery and Leapmotor – making significant inroads with triple-digit growth in the EU. A fourth firm, Geely, has had a steady 8% increase in the first eight months of the year and remains the most popular Chinese brand in the EU, with 205,000 cars sold in the first eight months of the year. Its brands include Sweden’s Volvo and Polestar, the EU’s only all-electric car manufacturer. BYD is catching up with Geely, with sales rocketing by 163% year on year with 177,000 units sold. Both firms, along with a fifth Chinese manufacturer, SAIC, are now firmly ahead of Elon Musk’s Tesla, which sold 142,000 cars across the bloc in the first seven months of the year. European car manufacturers still dominate, with the Volkswagen group selling 2m cars in the first eight months of the year. Sales of electric cars are also growing fast in parts of Europe including Germany, up 75% to 69,000 units in August, and in France, where sales are up by 112%. In Slovenia, sales have increased by 266%. This compares with the UK, up 27% in August to 28,000 EVs sold, and Ireland, up just 7% to 2,200 units. Earlier this month, the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, described the now €1.18bn-a-day trade deficit between the bloc and China as having reached an unsustainable “tipping point”. The EU’s trade commissioner Maroš Šefčovič and his Chinese counterpart Wang Wentao will meet on 8 and 9 October to try to build a truce. Also hoping for a trade truce are Donald Trump and Xi Jinping, who meet in their third summit in 12 months in Washington on Thursday. Trump agreed in South Korea last October to drop tariffs on certain Chinese imports in exchange for a suspension of China’s export restriction on rare earths, critical to the car industry across the US, EU and the UK. Some believe a deal may not have been reached yet and the suspension may not be announced until the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation conference next month.

title: Beleaguered at Home, a Bellicose Netanyahu Heads to the U.N.
summary: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel will take to the world stage while fighting for his political future in a critical national election.

title: Benjamin Netanyahu to deliver defiant UN speech while facing protests and political isolation
summary: Prime minister will ‘highlight Israel’s achievements’ as he heads towards his toughest re-election challenge
text: When he takes the stage at the UN on Thursday, Benjamin Netanyahu will deliver a familiar message of defiance even as protests and international condemnation leave the Israeli leader in growing isolation. Netanyahu is facing his toughest re-election challenge in a political career spanning decades with three ongoing conflicts in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran, and a growing campaign of violence by Israeli settlers in the West Bank. Internationally, Israel is facing growing condemnation. The UK, France and Canada are planning to sanction Israeli settlements in the West Bank, and the British foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, has accused Israeli settlers of committing ethnic cleansing of Palestinian communities. And the US is in the midst of a historic shift in public opinion against Israel, with 62% of respondents telling Pew in July they had a negative opinion of Netanyahu’s government, and 60% of American Jews in a poll released this week hoping he is voted out in October. Protests are expected both in the UN’s general assembly hall and on the streets of New York City, where mayor Zohran Mamdani has tempered his earlier promises to arrest Netanyahu as a war criminal to assure demonstrators this week that he would protect their “right to [protest] in this city”. Danny Danon, Israel’s ambassador to the UN, defended Netanyahu’s government in a telephone interview before this week’s speech seeking to cast criticism of Israel’s actions as the product of misinformation and bias. “We are aware of the fact that we had a very challenging three years since October 7,” said Danon. “We accomplished a lot, but we were criticised. We were under the spotlight, and for us, I think, we are proud of our achievements.” “At the same time, we will work harder to improve the image of Israel, and we know there’s a campaign against us,” he added. Anger at Netanyahu will be on full display in New York City on Thursday, where several protests have been scheduled, including one from Bryant Park in midtown Manhattan to the UN headquarters in Turtle Bay to “reject war criminal Benjamin Netanyahu and the genocidal Zionist project”. “Netanyahu is coming to New York amid a political environment that has made it crystal clear that he is not welcome here,” said Beth Miller, the political director of Jewish Voice for Peace Action. She described a “mainstreaming” of public opinion that “Americans do not want to be supporting Israel’s genocide. We do not want to be supporting Israel’s apartheid. We do not want to be arming Israel or supporting Israel.” And Palestinian representatives are calling for diplomatic missions to bring staff for a planned walkout of Netanyahu’s speech to “send a clear message to Netanyahu and his government that no one is willing to aid, abet, or be complicit in its genocide and war crimes and illegal occupation, which all peace-loving states and peoples demand must come to an end”. But in Danon’s telling, Israel’s problem was largely one of public relations rather than of policy, and he cited a “wave of misinformation” as the reason for the precipitous shift in polling. Netanyahu would use his speech to “highlight Israel’s achievements”, he said, and to lay out “what still should be done, and how should we verify that we actually achieve the goals of the war?” He did not elaborate on those specific measures before the speech, but the White House and US policymakers will be listening as they calibrate their message to voters – as well as the backlash of public anger – ahead of the upcoming midterm elections. Netanyahu is expected to deliver a hardline message aimed not just at world leaders, but also to his own electorate in Israel ahead of the October elections. “I think that he is trying to demonstrate to the Israeli populace that he still maintains some level of control over the situation,” said Miller. “And I think that he is trying to speak to a rightwing audience and a Trump-Maga audience in this country to try to rile up the hatred and Islamophobia.” Donald Trump and top US officials are not expected to meet with Netanyahu, however, during a visit expected to last less than 24 hours. Trump will be in Washington DC to host the Chinese leader, Xi Jinping, and Netanyahu has cited Israel’s electoral campaign and the holiday of Sukkot as his reason to head home quickly after the speech. A Trump administration official said Netanyahu’s delegation had sought a high-level meeting during the visit but none was organised. There are also no plans to meet congressional leaders, Danon said. With criticism from top Republicans, including the vice-president, JD Vance, and leading democratic presidential contenders, Israel could face a 2028 campaign with two candidates who no longer support arms sales to Israel or the broad diplomatic support that it has enjoyed in the past. Even within the Maga base there are fractures, Miller noted, with “more and more people who don’t really want to be sending our tax dollars to support the Israeli government”. Danon said of a potential shift in the US-Israeli security relationship: “I think that we are still sharing the same values, and that’s why I’m sure that we will continue to have the support from the US.” But there are multiple flashpoints now for anger from both US political parties, as well as the international community, including dire humanitarian concerns and the lack of reconstruction in Gaza, the expansion of settlements in the West Bank, and continued conflicts in Lebanon and Iran, where the US has found itself mired in a conflict that has driven up global energy prices. Asked if a controversial $2.8bn (£2.1bn) arms sale indicated that Israel is preparing to resume its offensive in Gaza, Danon said Israel “hopes that we will see [Hamas’s] disarmament without our involvement”, nodding to efforts by the Trump-backed Board of Peace. But he said Israel “will do it ourselves” if that does not change, adding: “We can not leave it forever like that.” He was equally resolute on the West Bank, saying that Israel would not be swayed by recent criticism led by the UK over plans to expand settlements including E1, the planned construction which would sever East Jerusalem from the rest of the West Bank. Senate Democrats are also introducing a bill on Wednesday to sanction facilitators of the new settlement, and Senator Chris Coons, a co-sponsor, said in a statement that “as Palestinian civilians face a campaign of devastation and fear from violent extremist settlers, the United States must send a strong message that this behaviour is unacceptable”. The protests began even before Netanyahu arrived in New York. Already on Wednesday, several members of the Democratic Socialists of America’s New York City chapter rallied at the city’s John F Kennedy international airport in protest at weapons and explosive materials destined for the Israeli military being flown out of the airport on commercial aircraft. Aber Kawas, who in November is slated to become the first Palestinian-American elected official in New York state, spoke at the event and later told the Guardian she plans to join many other New Yorkers protesting Nethanyahu’s UN speech on Thursday. “Thousands of people are against his presence in our city,” she said. Even though some had hailed Netanyahu’s decision to cut his visit short as a victory, she added, “the fact that he is coming shows he continues to have a sense of entitlement to be centred on the world stage while being the head architect of a genocide”.

title: Big-eyed bugs and praying mantises: climate crisis drives new visitors to UK shores
summary: Britain has seen an explosion of migrating insects – in some cases from as far as northern Africa
text: It was a stifling evening in July and Matt Phelps was out for a stroll, when a piercing, whirring noise stopped him in his tracks. As an ecologist, Phelps knows his fauna – and he could think of no UK creature that could emit such a sound. “It was like the classic sound effect of a cricket in a film, a beeping sort of little trilling sound,” said Phelps, who works at Knepp Estate in West Sussex. He returned with entomologist Graeme Lyons to track it down. But the sound, though incredibly loud, “seemed to be all around us … it was very ventriloquial”. The duo hunted for three hours. Night fell before they realised their quarry was, said Phelps, “literally below the ground where we stood”. Sure enough, in a crack in the parched clay they made the first identification of a Verge (or Bordeaux) cricket (Eumodicogryllus bordigalensis) in the British Isles. Once they announced it, other reports poured in. “It turns out there’s been this wave of them right at the moment when there was an enormous wildfire in Bordeaux,” said Phelps. “And it made you think: have some of these things fled the flames of southern Europe?” Verge crickets are just one of many “first sightings” of insects on the UK mainland this summer. It’s been an “extraordinary flood”, he said. And it’s not just the professionals who are finding them. Jackie Harmer, a retired secretary from North Cheshire, was one week into her new hobby of moth-trapping when she found an odd-looking creature native to the Iberian peninsula, Odice pergrata – a first for the UK. And David Cousins, a city trader who collects moths by night at his home in north Essex, opened his box one June dawn to find a white moth with bluish markings. “I just knew it was something really unusual,” he said. It turned out to be not just a new moth but “a completely undiscovered genus in Britain”. In north Africa and southern Europe it’s known as a spotted seal moth (Enolmis acanthella). Then there’s Olly McKeown, 18, in Truro, who didn’t even leave his room to discover what were pronounced in August to be the UK mainland’s first breeding praying mantises. “I sat at my table doing some work and then one was crawling across my keyboard – and then I saw one on top of the chair and then I just started spotting loads all around the tables, chairs and then some on the walls as well,” he said. McKeown’s sighting has subsequently been trumped by reports of others that predate his, in places such as the New Forest. The Cornwall Wildlife Trust said: “There are a few sites now where experts agree that the species has likely bred.” Liam Crowley, a fellow of the Royal Entomological Society and entomologist at Oxford University, said that the simplest explanation of these shifts is that the world is warming up and insects are moving northwards.. But, he added, “there’s a lot of different dynamics going on and it’s hard to know the true cause”. For example, insects that inhabited the UK a century ago may have gone locally extinct because of habitat destruction – only to return now if nature is restored, or if the climate crisis makes it the least-worst option. Some arrivals may even be part of events unfolding since the ice age ended 11,700 years ago, said Crowley. “As humans, we tend to obsess and focus on our own timescales.” He said there was also an explosion of migrating insects this summer. “Every year there are trillions of insects arriving in the UK, migrating up from the continent and in some cases even northern Africa. They fly up high into the air streams and they use that as a bit of a lift. “With the record-breaking heat, it’s been an absolutely bumper year [for migrating insects], particularly for very noticeable species.” Crowley highlighted hummingbird hawk moths and hoverflies, while others point to vast numbers of cicadas, striped hawkmoths, painted lady butterflies and clouded yellow butterflies. “Some of these species are starting to breed and establish and potentially survive through the winter in the south,” he said. Harry Witts, who discovered two new species in July, said he had mixed feelings about them. The excitement of discovery is balanced by the knowledge that “it’s only occurring because of climate change – a symptom of a very damaging force in our world”. Witts, who works at the Essex Wildlife Trust, described the moment at Colne Point, Essex, when “this grasshopper with blue wings jumped out in front of me”. It was bigger than most UK grasshoppers, with much broader wings, which helped him identify it as a blue, slender-winged grasshopper (Sphingonotus caerulans). He thinks he was the first witness of its “natural arrival” on the mainland: other specimens found in Kent this summer were probably Channel tunnel stowaways, he said. A few days later he and colleague Joss Carr found a new species of big-eyed bug (Geocoris megacephalus) in the same place, lurking on a piece of driftwood. Crowley said that most of these arrivals, if they survive the winter and settle, will find their niche and get on with life and may even enhance the ecosystems. “Occasionally,” added Phelps, “you’ll get something that becomes more problematic because it’s out-competing other species. But generally a lot of the ones that turn up by themselves don’t tend to do that.”

title: Mass sardine die-off pits survival of South Africa’s penguins against fishers’ livelihoods
summary: Known as the ‘energy bars of the sea’ the fish are a key food source for many species, but closing fisheries to allow numbers to recover would cost millions
text: It began on 28 July, when fishers near Saldanha Bay on the west coast of South Africa reported seeing dead sardines (also known as pilchards) floating at sea. Then, in early August, more dead sardines began washing up on beaches near Cape Town. In the weeks that followed, similar reports came in from places across a vast area spanning 2,600km (1,600 miles) of coastline, such as Henties Bay in Namibia and Mbotyi in the Eastern Cape province of South Africa. Sardines, sometimes described as “the energy bars of the sea”, are a key food source for seabirds – including the critically endangered African penguin, which only feeds on sardines and anchovies – seals, common dolphins and other fish. Meanwhile, the commercial sardine fishery contributes billions of rands and thousands of jobs to South Africa’s economy. “We’ve never had an event of this scale,” says Dr Janet Coetzee, of the Department of Forestry, Fisheries and the Environment, a scientist who specialises in small pelagic fish. “We are taking it very seriously. The minister got involved from the start, establishing a high-level task team comprising local management authorities, scientists, the fishing industry and municipalities to oversee a coordinated response.” Dead fish were sent for testing, and pilchard herpesvirus (PHV) was quickly identified as the primary culprit. The virus is specific to sardines and is not a threat to humans or animals who eat infected fish. While the source is still to be confirmed, it is likely that it was brought to South Africa via imported frozen pilchards used by the canning industry or as bait by commercial fishers. While herpesvirus is endemic in some sardine populations, naive populations are especially vulnerable to the virus. A paper published in 2016 did not detect PHV in South African sardines and cautioned against importing frozen sardines to South Africa for precisely this reason. There is a precedent. A PHV epidemic in Oceania, probably caused by importing sardines as feed for offshore bluefin tuna farms, in 1995 (and another in 1998-99) killed up to 60% of affected populations. Eventually the Australian population developed herd immunity, but it took years for the numbers to recover. Against this backdrop, the South African task team met in early September to chart a way forward. A group of 12 scientists (who do not sit on the task team) representing several universities and conservation NGOs prepared a document calling for an immediate halt to commercial sardine fishing while the extent of the die-off was being assessed. The Southern African Pelagic Fishing Industry Association, meanwhile, stressed the socioeconomic consequences of a moratorium: “A fishery closure would dent the South African economy by over 1.2bn rand [£55m],” says the association’s Mike Copeland, who is on the task team. “The impact on fishers, workers and the communities where they live would be devastating.” After careful consideration, says Coetzee, the task team concluded “that the available evidence didn’t suggest a very large reduction in the population … We looked at what the trajectory would look like if we closed versus if we didn’t close, and we didn’t see much difference.” Dr Alistair McInnes of BirdLife South Africa questions the evidence used to reach this decision. “The only thing we know is that the range of the die-off is extensive. We don’t know how many sardines have died because most of the dead fish end up at the bottom of the ocean. But we do know that a similar event in Australia was devastating.” McInnes and many other conservationists believe that the only responsible action is to pause fishing until the results of an annual hydroacoustic biomass survey are received. This survey, which takes place every October and November, is used to establish quotas for the next year’s fishing season, which opens on 15 January. McInnes is especially concerned about what happens when African penguins start to moult in October, a process that continues until February. “There is a strong link between penguin survival and sardine biomass,” he says. “Of course I can appreciate the socioeconomic impacts of a closure, but the impacts of a fishery collapse – as has happened in California and Namibia – would be even worse. It doesn’t seem worth the risk for a few months of fishing.” While Coetzee acknowledges that the only way to gauge the extent of the problem is to wait for the results of the biomass survey, she is adamant that the government’s approach has been cautious. “The temporary restriction was all about buying time. It stops rights holders from rushing out and catching as much as they can. We’ve also made it clear that come 2 October there is no guarantee that fishing will continue.” Tensions between conservationists and the fishing industry are nothing new. In March 2025, the two parties reached an out-of-court settlement pertaining to no-catch zones near penguin breeding colonies. Despite the current disagreement, both sides have been brought together by a common hope that PHV mortality rates seen in Australia are not replicated in South Africa. The bioacoustics survey results are released in early December, when all will be revealed.

title: Thursday briefing: Andy Burnham wants to remake Britain from the regions up. Can it work?
summary: In today’s newsletter: The newish prime minister wants to shift power out of Westminster, but fragile councils, patchy financial scrutiny and dwindling local journalism could put his plans at risk
text: Good morning. Over the summer, I interviewed more than 40 people who are trying to influence the new Labour government for the Guardian Long Read, among them thinktank researchers and politicians. The piece, published this morning, tries to work out how radical Andy Burnham intends to be. So far, his big idea is to give more power and money to England’s regions than ever before – and while “devolution” isn’t a word that sets pulses racing, this plan could be genuinely transformative. Yet, since writing the piece, one thing that has nagged at me is the wider picture. Local media has been gutted. Mechanisms for scrutinising local authority finances have disappeared. Local services and the public realm have been vaporised. Cash-strapped councils have made risky investments and gone bankrupt. All of this amounts to something bigger than a single crisis of accountability; the state’s legitimacy has been eroded, leaving people disenchanted with and distrustful of politics. Burnham is hoping that devolution will renew people’s faith in democracy. But the wider context poses huge risks to this project before it has barely even begun. Today’s newsletter discusses these risks and opportunities with Josh Halliday, the Guardian’s north of England editor, who wrote yesterday about the need for greater scrutiny of mayors. First, the headlines. Five big stories Climate crisis | The UK has warned that the climate crisis and coming El Niño threaten national security and defence around the world, presenting foreign ministries with the findings of an explosive report suppressed under Keir Starmer. US news | A federal judge has ordered the Trump administration to restore ⁠White House ⁠access to journalists from CNN, MS Now and Politico, ⁠saying his ban on the three media outlets was ⁠likely unconstitutional. Education | Teenagers are to be offered a range of new vocational GCSEs under a radical shake-up of the school system in England designed to tackle a crisis that has left nearly a million young people out of work or training. Conservatives | People claiming universal credit would have their payments cut by a third if they have not paid enough national insurance, under a Conservative plan condemned by one charity as “a fast track to increased poverty”. Football | Andy Burnham has signalled he may lift the ban on drinking alcohol in the stands at football matches, suggesting it is “unfair” for fans to be singled out when it is permitted for other sports. In depth: ‘A seminal moment … but the risks are huge’ Burnham, with his behind-the-scenes TikTok video of No 10 North, has made devolving power away from Westminster his central big idea. “If anything had brought me into parliament, it was a mission to close the North-South divide,” he wrote in his 2024 book, Head North. “Seeing how things worked from the inside, I finally understood why England has always felt like two countries.” The clearest statement of this intention since he became prime minister is a paper his cabinet published in July, which outlined plans to let mayors keep a share of income tax generated in their areas and give them greater control over skills, transport and public services. “These plans are a seminal moment in terms of how Britain is run,” Josh Halliday tells me. “But the risks are huge. It just takes one or two bad scandals – such as the bankruptcy of Birmingham council – to really damage the legitimacy of the whole project.” Here’s how those risks break down. *** The media | A shrinking local press Burnham was the mayor of a city comparatively well-served by the media. The Guardian was founded in Manchester and continues to have a newsroom of reporters there (including Josh). Despite the ongoing decline of regional journalism, flourishing media start-ups and subscription newsletters in cities like Manchester, Glasgow, and Birmingham have proven there is still demand for quality local journalism. There have also been wider initiatives to address England’s “news deserts”, such as the BBC Local Democracy Reporting Service. But the bigger picture is one of endless closures and cuts. Reach, the owner of regional titles in England, announced a further round of 220 redundancies (though plans to create 60 new roles) two weeks ago. Even Burnham, who started his career writing for publications such as Tank World, moved to London to find work in journalism. Josh, who graduated from Sunderland university in 2010, used to dream of working for a local newspaper, but found it difficult to even get a work experience placement. “There are fewer and fewer local journalists, which means fewer people keeping an eye on council meetings or scrutinising budget reports,” he tells me. “And that’s really worrying.” *** Local democracy | Participation has been ‘squeezed’ Journalism isn’t the only institution that holds politicians’ feet to the fire. Civil society plays a crucial role, but the cost of living crisis and the gradual erosion of the institutions that bind people together have diminished people’s involvement in politics. “We often talk about the cost of living crisis as a financial squeeze,” Sarah Longlands, the chief executive of the Centre for Local Economic Strategies in Manchester, tells me. “But it’s also squeezed people’s ability to turn up at local campaign groups, to attend town council meetings, to run as councillors themselves, because they’re just focused on the day-to-day of getting by.” For most people, politics isn’t about nuclear deterrents or Westminster white papers, but about how often the bins get emptied or whether the library stays open. In recent years, local authorities have sold off local assets and outsourced public services to faceless providers. This, Sarah says, has robbed people of institutions that give them a stake in their communities. “Take away publicly funded local services, and you take away the frontline engagement and relationship between councils and communities that form part of democracy,” she says. She is particularly concerned that Burnham may decide to go ahead with a plan to reorganise local government that he inherited from his predecessor. Those plans are now on pause, but two professors recently described in the Guardian’s letter pages how the scheme could result in the disappearance of as many as 75% of England’s existing councils, eliminating institutions that have close ties to communities, and making services even more anonymous and detached. *** Scrutiny | Who will keep an eye on the money Over the last decade there’s been a vacuum of information about the financial decisions taken by councils. In 2015, David Cameron abolished the Audit Commission, a body that scoured local governments’ accounts every year. Since then, some struggling councils have gone on reckless spending sprees, buying office blocks and shopping centres while cutting back on local services. Some have since declared bankruptcy. “The National Audit Office will get called in to investigate, but only once there’s already been an emergency,” Josh tells me. “They’re not a safeguard against financial crises.” The Starmer government introduced plans for a new Local Audit Office, which should help address some of these problems, and Burnham’s government is expected to publish further details of its plans for accountability in a few weeks’ time alongside its first budget. Amid all this is a wider question about how to make the devolution of power genuinely democratic. Sarah suggests that any new authority or mayoralty should commit to an ongoing citizens’ assembly, where residents can collectively decide how new resources are allocated, and scrutinise government spending. “The government mainly talks about devolution as a way to drive growth,” she says. “But this could be a cutting edge way to redesign British democracy, so it really works for people.” What else we’ve been enjoying Nesrine Malik examines why enslavement remains absent from mainstream British history in our sister newsletter, The Long Wave, after the Guardian revealed new detail of domestic slave traders and the institutions they funded. Libby Ammar Kalia’s ranking of 100 unusual crisp flavours is both useful and an absolute hoot. It also seems to have been a brave undertaking, considering some of Ammar’s verdicts: “they leave a luminescent blue powder on your fingers and smell of urinal cakes”. Lucinda Everett, newsletters team Not only are adults failing to act effectively on the climate crisis, we’re also rubbish at explaining its realities to kids. So I was pleased to read that New York Climate Week is getting some help from Sesame Street. Libby I enjoyed Matthew Pearce’s interview with author Russell Warfield, who argues that Zack Polanski’s “eco-populist” package is “not a departure from Green tradition, but the culmination of a 50-year evolution which has turned the party into the main electoral force on the British left.” Lucinda Dani Garavelli’s diary of her visit to Mussolini’s birthplace in this week’s London Review of Books is a timely reminder of the echoes of Il Duce in Italy’s current politics. Libby Sport Football | Manchester United have reported an annual loss for the seventh successive year, taking the club’s combined losses to £444m since 2019. Rugby | Steve Borthwick has secured a boost for his preparations for next year’s World Cup thanks to an overhaul in the refereeing of Prem matches for the coming season designed to help England’s hopes in Australia. Football | Cristiano Ronaldo said he considered quitting international football after the World Cup, but confirmed he plans to play on for Portugal and hopes to reach 1,000 goals for club and country. The front pages The Guardian leads with “PM unveils new vocational GCSEs in biggest exam shake-up in decade”. The Telegraph has “Tories to ban spending benefits on alcohol”, while the Times follows the same story with “Tories to cut benefits for long-term unemployed”. The Mail characterises the announcement as “Kemi’s ruthless crackdown on benefits street”. The i has “EU Brexit chief: UK can get a Canada-style membership deal with us”. The Financial Times reports “Healey weighs smaller fiscal headroom to reduce tax rises”. The Mirror covers the crash of an RAF jet under the headline “Miracle no on was killed”. And the Sun looks at the reported axing of alcohol bans in football stadiums with “Going down going down going down.. rather nicely!” Today in Focus: The Latest Has Burnham proved he can handle Trump? Andy Burnham has navigated his way through a first high-stakes meeting with Donald Trump at the UN general assembly in New York. The prime minister’s aides were delighted with how the meeting went, as Trump praised the US-UK relationship and described Burnham as a ‘natural businessman’. The anticipated sticking points – the Chagos Islands, West Bank settlement sanctions and Ireland – appear not to have derailed the talks nor cast a shadow over the future relationship. Lucy Hough speaks to policy editor Kiran Stacey. Cartoon of the day | Ben Jennings The Upside A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad The landmark documentary 7 Up, which launched 63 years ago, followed the lives of 10 boys and four girls in England, beginning when they were seven years old, and returning every seven years. As its final season, 70 Up, concludes, seven people have shared the profound effects the show has had on them over the decades. “The series changed my life,” says Martin Forsey, 65. “I retrained and became a sociologist and anthropologist because of it.” Lyle Jackson, 72, was inspired to become a documentary photographer and producer, and went on to win 18 regional Emmys. And others found important life lessons within the show. “It seemed that the real measure of success was not academic or material achievements after all,” says Sheila Lambe, 63, “but familial love and finding peace.” Sign up here for a weekly roundup of The Upside, sent to you every Sunday Bored at work? And finally, the Guardian’s puzzles are here to keep you entertained throughout the day. Until tomorrow. Quick crossword Cryptic crossword Wordiply

title: Australians ‘scrambling’ for second jobs to deal with rising mortgage repayments and cost of living
summary: Latest data also shows unemployment at highest level since the pandemic, which analysts doubt will stop RBA hiking interest rates
text: Australians are “scrambling” to find more work to cover soaring living expenses and prepare for higher mortgage costs, economists say, after new data showed unemployment ticked up to its highest rate since the pandemic. The key jobless figure lifted to 4.6% in August, from 4.5% the month before, according to the Australian Bureau of Statistics. Analysts had predicted unemployment to remain steady, but said the unexpected increase would not be enough to stop the Reserve Bank from hitting mortgage holders with a fourth interest rate hike next Tuesday. If raised – as is widely expected – the RBA’s cash rate will go from 4.35% to 4.6% – its highest in nearly 15 years. Central bank officials over recent days and weeks have repeatedly warned that inflation, at 3.5%, remains too high and does not appear to be tracking lower, as hoped. As higher fuel costs threaten to add to price pressures amid the ongoing US-Israel war on Iran, experts and the financial markets are predicting a good chance the central bank could hike again on Melbourne Cup day. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Details in the labour force data showed the number of employed people jumped by 39,000 last month, but that this reflected a surge in part-time employment, offset by a 6,000-person drop in full-time work. The lift in the unemployment rate, despite the rise in employment, reflected an influx of new people looking for work, analysts said. KPMG’s chief economist, Brendan Rynne, said the numbers reaffirmed that the economy is weak and growing weaker. “Households are still feeling the pinch of higher inflation and anticipatory higher mortgage rates which can be seen through a rise in the participation rate to just below all-time peak level of 67.2%,” Rynne said. “This suggests households are scrambling to find more income to help cover their rising day-to-day expenses and future increases in mortgage payments.” Earlier this month, ABS figures showed the number of Australians working more than one job had passed 1 million for the first time. The share of employed people working more than one job pushed to an all-time high of 6.9%, or about 1 percentage point higher than before the start of the new inflationary era from 2022. Ryan Wells, a Westpac economist, said “while a softer economy and sub-par employment growth would typically discourage some individuals in their search for work, cost-of-living pressures and interest rate rises are acting as a counterweight, encouraging more people into the labour market”.

title: ‘Cash to trash’ levy on house developers too low to offset damage to Norfolk Broads, say critics
summary: Exclusive: Levy that allows almost 16,000 houses to be built on Norfolk Broads will not cover cost of mitigating environmental damage, critics say
text: A new levy on developers to allow almost 16,000 homes to be built in the environmentally protected Norfolk Broads has been cut by tens of thousands of pounds per house, the Guardian can reveal. Ministers say the government’s environmental delivery plans (EDPs) were created to unblock housing growth across the country and are a “win-win” for development and nature. They allow environmental damage to protected habitats and species to be overlooked as long as developers pay into a nature restoration fund, which is used for conservation actions at a later date designed to address the impacts. Once the first instalment of the fee is paid, work can start immediately. Labelled by critics as “cash to trash”, the first EDP was published last week by the government’s nature adviser, Natural England. It allows 15,780 houses to be built within the Norfolk Broads, a heavily protected wetland network of 60 shallow lakes and winding rivers that is home to some of England’s rarest species. The published plan, which is open for consultation for 28 days, states that the developer will pay £2,675 per house – £42m in total – into the nature restoration fund to cover compensatory actions including fenland creation and restoration, a change in use of agricultural land to semi-natural habitat, catch-dyke restoration and deer management. But a previous draft of the EDP, seen by the Guardian, set the levy much higher. Ecologists said this was to properly reflect the realistic costs of mitigating the increased nutrient pollution from increased sewage pollution and urban run-off into protected chalk stream rivers – the Wensum, Bure and Yare – caused by the development. The fee was to be between £5,400 and £60,500 per house, depending on the scale of total nutrient pollution that the development would cause. The fenlands, marshes, bogs and mires of the Broads are a biodiversity hotspot, home to more than a quarter of the rarest wildlife in the UK such as the otter, cuckoo and fen orchid. Natural England acknowledges that the new homes will cause environmental harm in the form of physical, chemical, hydrological and biological damage to the habitats and rare species in the Broads from increased nitrogen and phosphorus pollution. But the EDP states that the payment of the levy and the conservation actions it funds “will materially outweigh the negative effect of the maximum amount of development on the conservation status of each identified environmental feature”. Critics point out that Natural England is being funded by the developer’s £42m levy to carry out the works, raising concerns of a conflict of interest. Environmental lawyers, ecologists and environmental professionals say the levy is too low. They say none of the conservation actions created by Natural England address reducing the nutrient pollution coming from the development. Analysis of the figures in the EDP reveal that an extra 7,695kg a year of nitrogen will enter the protected waterways, amounting to 83% of the development’s pollution load, and up to 435kg a year of extra phosphorus, according Alexa Culver, legal counsel at RSK Wilding. “Developers will be paying a levy that green-lights more pollution rather than solves the problem – quite literally the definition of ‘pay to pollute’ or ‘cash to trash’,” Culver said. The Norfolk Broads EDP is the first since the Planning and Infrastructure Act came into force. Others will be rolled out to allow development alongside and within some of the UK’s most protected sites. Sally Hayns, the chief executive of the Chartered Institute of Ecology and Environmental Management (CIEEM), said: “It is important to get this right because this first EDP is effectively the blueprint for all the other EDPs targeting nutrient pollution that are going to follow: these are already in preparation and will be coming thick and fast. “This EDP is an articulation of the government’s ambition to deliver a win-win for development and nature through the Planning and Infrastructure Act. We finally get to see what that looks like in practice – and there is real concern.” Hayns said the levy seemed low. “I think there has been a very conservative estimate of how much things are going to cost, with minimal contingency built in.” Not one avoidance measure has been included in the EDP. Hayns said she was at a loss to understand why recognised solutions to strip out nutrient pollution before it enters waterways, including sustainable drainage systems, and integrated constructed wetlands – pools and marshes to filter out nutrient pollution – had not been included. The Broads are already so polluted by nitrogen and phosphorus from sewage, agriculture and run off that they are on the red list of concern and severely depleted. “If nutrient pollution gets worse we will end up with choked, poisoned waterways and we will lose some of our most vulnerable and rarest species,” Hayns said. Dr Justin Neal, the head of legal at WildFish, said the delivery plan was full of holes and set up a worrying “pay to pollute” system that was being used to sacrifice countryside for concrete. “Norfolk’s chalk streams and wetlands are protected for a good reason,” he said. “The Yare and Wensum, for instance, hold white clawed crayfish and lamprey. They shouldn’t be sacrificed on the altar of growth.” Bradley Tooze, the nature restoration fund director at Natural England, said: “The environment delivery plan aims to deliver better outcomes to protect the precious habitats of the Norfolk Broads while enabling sustainable development, including through river restoration measures and wetland habitat creation. “The consultation on this first plan is now open. We welcome all views on our proposals and encourage stakeholders to share their expertise to help shape this new approach to nature restoration.”

title: An OpenAI agent infiltrated Medicare – and Australia only found out months later. Here’s what we know so far
summary: Experts say ‘fairly minor’ breach is a portent of things to come and proprietary closed systems like OpenAI are ‘the least of the worries’
text: Anthony Albanese says an artificial intelligence agent developed by OpenAI hacked Medicare and three other systems in June – and the company only notified Australia earlier this month. The prime minister has expressed his “extreme concern” over the incident, although he noted no personal information is believed to have been accessed in the breach. Here’s what we know. What happened? An artificial intelligence agent built by the American firm OpenAI hacked into Medicare, Australia’s universal healthcare system. The agent gained unauthorised access to both public and non-public files in the Medicare statistics reporting service portal. The actions of the agent have been described as “misaligned behaviour” after it was assigned a benign research task compiling health and medical statistics. The agent also accessed the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, the Victorian Department of Health, and the New South Wales Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research. At this stage it is believed that no personal medical information has been compromised, but investigations are continuing. The prime minister has said: “this situation is obviously unacceptable”. What is an AI agent? An artificial intelligence agent is a system that autonomously solves problems, makes decisions, plans and performs complex tasks on behalf of another user or system, using all available tools. OpenAI was co-founded by Elon Musk and Sam Altman (who remains CEO) in 2015. It is valued at more than US$1tn. Both have recently raised concerns about the pace of, and lack of controls around, the development of AI. “There are many things that AI cannot and should not automate,” Altman told the UN security council this week. “As AI systems become more capable and more autonomous, they can move faster than our institutions … or make decisions that people no longer understand or control.” How did Australia find out? OpenAI, one of the best-resourced AI companies on Earth, sent an email to a public-facing Australian government address, three months after the hack. OpenAI said it found out about the agent’s access in August. On 10 September, it sent an email to a general Australian government email address which is monitored once a day, advising its AI agent had hacked the country’s universal healthcare system. The email was read on 11 September. On 15 September, Services Australia notified the Australian Signals Directorate. The minister for government services, Katy Gallagher, was notified on 17 September. Services Australia’s first interaction with OpenAI – asking for more specific details of the hack – was on Tuesday this week, 22 September. “It took the company way too long to inform the government what had occurred,” Albanese said, “and the nature of the way that that notification occurred as well was unacceptable.” The acting prime minister, Richard Marles, met with Altman earlier in September, but Marles said Altman did not mention his company’s hack of Australia’s health system to Marles at that meeting. How did Australia respond? Albanese, currently in the US, said he spoke with Altman “to express Australia’s extreme concern about this incident”. The prime minister announced he would establish a taskforce – involving the national cybersecurity coordinator, the office of AI, the Australian Signals Directorate, the Australian AI Safety Institute and Services Australia – to conduct an “urgent and immediate” review into the incident. Terms of reference for the investigation, released by the prime minister’s department on Thursday, cover reporting requirements for AI-driven cyber-incidents and vulnerabilities; governance and information sharing responsibilities for federal officials; obligations on AI firms for notification of future incidents; the adequacy of existing laws; and mechanisms to boost protections against hackings within the federal government. The incident has also been referred to parliament’s joint select committee on artificial intelligence. To date, OpenAI has not faced any sanction. How serious was this attack? At a press conference in Sydney, Marles said the incident itself was “relatively minor” and that it appeared no personal health information had been accessed. But he said the government regarded the hack as a “salutary warning … about the technology being developed without safeguards and without guardrails in place”. Dr Joel Pearson, a professor of neuroscience and neurofuturism, and the deputy director of UNSW’s AI Institute, said the breach appeared to be a “fairly minor security incident”, but was a portent of more serious attacks to come. “What I would worry about is the latest open-weights and open-access models from China that are going to be used at scale by nefarious organisations and nations, perhaps particularly Russia: these things are going to be used at scale to do things much more damaging and much more costly to Australians than a small breach to some non-personal Medicare data.” Cory Alpert, a PhD student studying the impact of AI on democracy at the University of Melbourne, said OpenAI’s attack appeared to be the first instance of a frontier AI model hacking into another country’s government systems of its own volition. “This raises very important questions about the foreign attack vectors. Had this been a Chinese or a Russian model, the reaction would have been markedly different than a stern call to Sam Altman, and yet it is still a massive vulnerability.” Is Australia doing enough to address the risks posed by AI? Pearson said it was “pretty clear that we are way behind, the government is behind in all things cybersecurity, in most things AI”. “I would say that the least of the worries should be these proprietary closed systems like Anthropic and OpenAI. It will be the open-source Chinese models in the hands of spammers, scammers, and nefarious individuals and foreign nationals, and the spy agencies coming at us from all different angles. That will be the big threat and that’s where the government really has to step up.” Pearson said none of the frameworks established in Australia – government or private – were equipped to deal with the rising threat. “From the government all the way down to companies and boards and CEOs, everyone is scrambling, trying to understand and update frameworks, including the legal process. It’s just all moving too slow compared to the exponential speed of AI.” What does this incident say about big tech and transparency? A spokesperson for OpenAI said the company was conducting an extensive review of “misaligned model activity” during training and evaluation, and notified third parties whenever the review identified potential impacts to their systems. The spokesperson said “our models took actions we did not attend”, but there was “no evidence of patient records being accessed”. “Our overall review is ongoing, and we remain committed to transparency about these issues and to sharing what we learn as that work continues.” Prof Toby Walsh, the chief scientist at UNSW’s AI Institute, said he believed Australia should be prosecuting OpenAI, a company known to have “terrible agent governance”. “For a trillion-dollar company, their cybersecurity was woeful. The officers of this company need to be held accountable. These hacks could have easily been stopped, indeed never need to have taken place. We would prosecute humans who did such hacking.” Walsh said it displayed operational incompetence on the part of OpenAI. Dr Rob Nicholls, senior research associate at the University of Sydney, said the three-month delay in informing Australia of the breach exposed the ineffectiveness of Australia’s laws. “An AI agent broke into a government Medicare system and helped itself to non-public files, and OpenAI sat on that for three months before telling us. If a person had done this, we’d call it hacking. The fact it was an AI agent doesn’t make it less serious, it makes our disclosure laws more out of date. “This is the clearest case yet of an AI agent operating autonomously and breaching Australian government systems without a human directing it to. It is a live test of whether Australia’s AI and privacy settings can keep pace with agentic AI, not just chatbots.”

title: Israel facing water shortages caused by destruction of Gaza’s treatment plants
summary: Five desalination plants shut down for days, while Gaza remains in grip of severe water and sanitation crisis
text: Israel is facing weeks of water shortages after an exceptional algae bloom crippled much of its desalination capacity, in a crisis scientists say was triggered when Israeli attacks destroyed much of Gaza’s wastewater infrastructure, causing a massive discharge of untreated sewage. “Pollution does not recognise political borders,” said the Zalul Environmental Association, an Israeli NGO dedicated to protecting the country’s seas and shores. “The discharge of untreated sewage from the Gaza Strip into the sea is contributing to the worsening crisis affecting the Israeli desalination facilities. The wastewater contains nutrients such as nitrogen and phosphorus, which feed microalgae and cyanobacteria and may intensify their blooms.” Despite last year’s US-brokered ceasefire, Gaza remains gripped by a severe water and sanitation crisis. The Palestinian territory is plagued by rodents, and sewage floods its coastline after Israel destroyed its wastewater treatment plants. Just across the border, a vast bloom of microalgae stretching up to 60 miles (100km) long has clogged filters at five of Israel’s six main desalination plants, which were shut down for days and have since been operating at a reduced level. Experts say that after nearly three years of war, the environmental consequences of the destruction in Gaza are now spilling back into Israel. “The discharge of untreated sewage from Gaza into the sea increases risks to Israel’s water production infrastructure along the southern Mediterranean coast,” said Jack Gilron, a professor emeritus and desalination expert at Ben-Gurion University’s Zuckerberg Institute for Water Research. “The current incident reinforces the need to prepare against threats to one of Israel’s main sources of drinking water.” Since 7 October 2023, Israeli bombardment has destroyed 90% of Gaza’s water and sanitation infrastructure, according to a report by Médecins Sans Frontières. Direct strikes have been carried out on wells, carrier lines, reservoirs and desalination units. Gaza’s water crisis remains severe. Before the war, 80% the territory’s supply came from an aquifer under the coastal strip, but that supply is now contaminated by seawater and wastewater and unfit for human consumption. Most of Gaza’s drinking water came from desalination plants and three pipelines controlled by the Israeli water authority, but those pipelines were cut at the start of the war and have only partially reopened. Meanwhile, damaged or destroyed distribution networks have left much of the population reliant on water trucks. For many, this means a stark choice between drinking an extra cup of water or saving it to wash their hands and prevent disease, with acute diarrhoea among the leading causes of illness. “We carry water in jerry cans,” said Nas al-Barawi, 34, a mother of five from Beit Lahia. “We walk with heavy containers or wait for hours in queues. Much of the water is unsafe, and children suffer recurring stomach infections, diarrhoea and skin rashes. Damaged sewage networks and failed pumps have also left wastewater flowing between tents and through residential areas.” Omar Shatat, the deputy executive director of the Coastal Municipalities Water Utility in Gaza, said all five of the territory’s wastewater treatment plants were out of service, leaving an estimated 45,000 cubic metres of untreated sewage to flow into the Mediterranean every day. In addition, about 15,000 cubic metres of untreated waste a day seeps into the groundwater from soakaway pits, particularly in the informal camps in al-Mawasi. “This is a catastrophic situation environmentally and from a public-health perspective,” Shatat said. “The sea is heavily polluted, and the first people affected are Gaza’s residents and displaced people because they are in direct contact with the highest concentrations of sewage.” Pat Griffiths, the International Committee of the Red Cross’s spokesperson in Gaza City, said the situation was only likely to get worse with the onset of winter. “Palestinians live surrounded by wastewater. It’s all around them. It’s where they eat, where they get water, where they walk,” he said. Shaimaa al-Katari, 37, who has been displaced to al-Mawasi, said: “We have nowhere to dispose of the water from washing dishes and clothes. We have to let it run into the street, which causes pools of stagnant water to form. Algae and mosquitoes then spread around them and the streets become dirty. We suffer from foul smells, mosquitoes at night and flies during the day, as well as rodents.” Rats have infested parts of Gaza for months, thriving amid raw sewage and piles of rubbish accumulating around overcrowded camps for displaced people. Israeli communities near the Gaza border have also been grappling with an unprecedented rat infestation, with rodents swarming homes and gardens. “The consequences [of the war] do not stop at the border,” said Nada Majdalani, the Palestine director of EcoPeace Middle East, an environmental peacebuilding organisation. “We are already seeing an increase in hepatitis A in Gaza. I believe we are on the verge of a catastrophe. And a serious outbreak in Gaza would not necessarily remain within Gaza’s borders.” In Israel, authorities are urging people to use water “judiciously” until the system is fully restored. Water supplies have been reduced in the south of the country, and farmers have been instructed to halt irrigation, which economists say will cause food prices to rise. Zalul and EcoPeace urged Cogat, the Israeli agency charged with administration of Gaza, to help restore the territory’s sewage system and allow wastewater to be treated in Israeli-controlled areas. Cogat did not respond to a request for comment. Zalul said: “If the pollution continues, its impact could eventually be felt throughout the country. When the marine environment is contaminated, both people and nature suffer. Regardless of which side of the border they are on.”

title: Country diary: The snails are back to reclaim my garden – and leave behind a little artwork | Josie George
summary: Stoke-on-Trent, Staffordshire: So much to admire in these creatures, from their resilience over summer, to the detailed pattern of their trails
text: Here’s a lovely word: aestivate. It’s what my garden snails did through the parched weeks of our summer drought, pulling their bodies high up into their shells and closing the door. Here’s another: epiphragm – the pearl-like door they make to keep moisture in as they slow their hearts and their breathing, until just a thread of life remains. Pretty words, but such power in them. Over the summer I’d find these snails, dry and still, and hold them in my hands before tucking them back behind my garden pots. This is it, I’d think, the irony of our times: there’s us humans, all-powerful and cruelly dismissive of everything that is not us, hurtling towards changes in our climate that our bodies are entirely unequipped to deal with. And then here are snails, not invulnerable either, but with more forbearance than we could ever dream of. Even so, both my small friends and I have been celebrating since the rain returned. I keep stepping into my garden, tipping my face to the sky, and seeing them move slowly and determinedly across the slick walls and paths to eat everything that remains from the summer – the clematis, the hostas, the snapdragons. Yes, autumn is here and the snails are back to rule their world again. What deep comfort there is in that. And what do they leave in their wake? Art. My dirty garden furniture has become a canvas. Lacy, spiralling lines cut through the algae. Look closely and you’ll see the triangular pattern of their radula – a kind of conveyor-belt tongue covered in microscopic teeth – as they scrape, move, scrape. Keep your eyes open and you’ll see their mark everywhere; the bridge over to our local Sainsbury’s has become a veritable gallery for snail expression. Like all great art, it isn’t surface decoration but an act of reclamation and defiance. Here’s to resilience, then, and the ability to turn the necessary business of living into something slow, delicate, meaningful – something that leaves beauty in its wake. • Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024, is available now at guardianbookshop.com
