title: ‘The eels were climbing out of the water to die’: why did every fish in this idyllic lake perish overnight?
summary: Furnace Brook in East Sussex was home to carp, tench, bream, roach and trout – and 15 trailer-loads had to be buried. The mystery led to a neighbouring farm, and a story of waste, pollution and dirty rivers that reveals a lot about Britain today
text: When Alistair and Diane Gould bought Furnace Brook in 2013, they had big plans. It was an idyllic spot: a stream-fed fishing lake nestled in a secluded valley in the High Weald, East Sussex, surrounded by woodland and fields. “People loved to come fishing here because it’s so beautiful,” says Diane. “Some of them had been coming for so many years that they got to know the individual fish.” Diane moved here from Kent in 2000, when Furnace Brook was owned by a distant relative. Her two younger sons, then 10 and 14, flourished. They would chat to the anglers about the fish they were catching and throwing back in, and sell them bacon sandwiches. Her elder son, Simon, moved from London to join them in 2006 and became a keen angler himself, and then the fishing manager, or bailiff, looking after the fish and the landscape around the lake. Diane, who is 68, and Alistair, 69, met in 2008. After Diane’s relative died, they decided to buy the property. Alistair, an ecological consultant with a background in low-carbon design, had drawn up a plan to restore the entire ecosystem of the eight-hectare (20-acre) site. But two years ago, their plans were blown out of the water. On the morning of 20 June 2024, Alistair and Simon walked down to the lake and noticed dead fish floating on the surface. “We looked at it and thought: ‘This is a bit odd,’” says Alistair. On further inspection, almost everything in the 2.4-hectare lake was dead. “It brings tears to my eyes,” says Diane. There were at least 15 species of fish in the lake, she adds: carp, tench, bream, roach, trout and some large eels. “You get a sort of relationship with them, as living beings.” The larger fish even had names. “It was very traumatic for us all,” Alistair continues. “Obviously for nature directly, but also seeing all these fish on the surface and the fact that Simon has been a fishery bailiff here for 15-plus years and these are his babies, and he’s just seeing them all curl up and die.” Diane continues: “More than 2,000 fish were dead. Plus, the ones we don’t know about that sank to the bottom. The eels were climbing out of the lake to die.” Eels are pretty hardy, says Alistair; they can even travel over land if they need to. To see them gasping and dying on the banks was heartbreaking. “It was apocalyptic.” At first, the Goulds thought it must be their fault, that they had mismanaged the fish stocks somehow. But when Alistair walked to the top of the lake, he saw that Clippenham stream, which feeds the lake, was also full of dead fish. “That’s when I twigged: ‘This isn’t us. There’s something else going on.’” It seemed clear to him that pollution was coming from somewhere upstream. “All down the stream, our friends were finding dead fish: lamprey, brown trout, freshwater mussels,” says Diane. The stream runs to the Pevensey Levels on the south coast, where water is extracted for drinking and agriculture. They immediately called the Environment Agency (EA), the body responsible for the “protection and enhancement” of the environment in England, which visited two days later and declared it a Category 1 incident, the most severe kind, meaning it had “a serious, extensive or persistent impact on the environment, people or property”. The Goulds and their team removed 15 trailer loads of dead fish from the lake, which the EA advised them to bury. Their angling business was gone overnight. They estimate they have lost £500,000 in income so far. A biologist later estimated that the lake would take 10 to 15 years to recover. “It’s not just the loss of money,” says Alistair. “It’s the loss of the ecological function.” The story of Furnace Brook could be Britain in microcosm. We take pride in our rural heritage, in the natural beauty of our countryside, but the illusion that it is an unspoilt, unchanging idyll is becoming ever harder to maintain. River pollution has become a national scandal. The release of sewage by privatised water companies – illegal but persistent and apparently unpoliced – has devastated landscapes throughout England. Often, we register this in terms of how picturesque our rivers are or how safe they are to swim in – how the pollution affects us directly – but beneath the surface, decades of pollution have decimated how much life they can support. According to government statistics from 2025, just 14% of England’s rivers and lakes have a “good ecological status” and every one of them is polluted with chemicals. Illegal dumping has become a separate scandal, the scale and effects of which also seem beyond authorities’ control. In the past 12 months, there have been high-profile cases such as the 150-metre-long mountain of rubbish “discovered” in Kidlington, Oxfordshire, or the 35,000 tonnes of rubbish dumped in Hoad’s Wood, Kent, the latter of which cost an estimated £15m to clean up. In August, Andy Burnham visited another huge, foul-smelling illegal dump, in Midland Road, Bradford, where he vowed to take action, declaring: “The days of making easy money out of waste are over.” He has a (waste) mountain to climb. Over the past two decades, successive governments have loosened environmental regulations and removed protections – not least by neutering the EA. The fact that this is happening in the countryside, sometimes in isolated areas, makes it hard to monitor or police. Furnace Brook is a symptom of all these problems, although it could also become a model for how to overcome them. The Goulds are working on a plan not only to restore the landscape, but also to show how we could reset our relationship to it in a more sustainable, nature-friendly, community-oriented way. In the case of Furnace Brook, the water companies were not to blame. So the Goulds set out to discover what was. “I thought: ‘I bet I know exactly where that’s come from,’” says Jack (not his real name), Furnace Brook’s former ecological consultant, who has worked in the area for decades and knows the landscape intimately. He remembers walking up Clippenham stream two days after the pollution event. “It was hot weather and the whole of the valley stank. It smelled of dead fish and aquatic life. I thought: ‘It’s probably something that’s come off another property. And if any of the properties around here are likely to be doing something unpleasant like that, I’ll put money on it that I know which one it was.” He headed about half a mile up the valley to a tributary joining the stream from a neighbouring property named Morgans Farm. “You could clearly see the water upstream [of the tributary] was totally normal, a sandy colour with clay silt in it, and what was below it had gone a blue-black colour. You could see dead brook trout, wild eels, and there was a dead crow or raven, which may well have eaten something poisonous from the river.” In some places, he says, there was a thick layer of blue-grey scum on the water, which he later learned is sometimes called “bacterial cheese”. “There’s so much nutrient [sic] in the water that it allows for a bacterial colonisation explosion.” The bacteria take up all the oxygen, which causes most of the fish, especially the older, larger ones, to die. Jack followed the polluted tributary up through Ann Wood, a small pocket of ancient woodland on Morgans Farm. The source of the tributary seemed to be a large hole or pit at the north-west corner of the wood, in a cleared area, accessible by heavy vehicle. In one council document, it is referred to as a “slurry lagoon”. Shortly after the pollution incident, this hole was filled in and covered with waste soil. When I visited in September 2025, the area where the hole had been was obscured beneath a stack of hundreds of plastic-wrapped hay bales. When EA officers visited in the days after the pollution event, they were shown the devastation and the suspected source of the pollution. They took water samples from various locations. One officer also visited Morgans Farm. The EA has the power to investigate and prosecute those in breach of environmental protection laws, which can result in fines or even imprisonment for offenders, but the process is notoriously slow. Investigations can take years and rarely result in meaningful penalties. More than two years later, the EA has yet to take action over the incident at Furnace Brook. In the interim, Alistair and his team took matters into their own hands. They bought equipment to test the water for factors such as dissolved oxygen, dissolved solids and conductivity. They also tested for heavy metals, such as lead, cadmium, arsenic and mercury, which are usually a byproduct of industrial, rather than agricultural, processes. You can do crude tests for them with a paper strip that changes colour from orange through to dark purple. When they tested the water coming from Morgans Farm, it was “off the chart”, says Jack. “This went about as deep into the purple as you possibly could go.” A year later, in July 2025, Furnace Brook sent samples of water collected from the lake to an independent testing lab. The results still found unusually high levels of heavy metals, ammonia levels that were “well outside acceptable limits for any freshwater life” and nitrogen levels that were “toxic to all aquatic life”. *** What was going on at Morgans Farm? Quite a lot, according to its neighbours. Going by planning statements submitted by Morgans Farm, the owners farmed “a mix of cattle and sheep spread out over 243 hectares throughout Sussex”. Several large agricultural barns and other buildings have been constructed on the property, with planning permission. In 2022, the owners also applied for planning permission to extend an existing forestry track down one edge of Ann Wood, parallel to the suspected tributary. Permission was withheld – the woods are classified as “ancient and semi-natural woodland” and an “irreplaceable habitat” – but a 300-metre surfaced track was built anyway. Over the years, Furnace Brook and other neighbours have seen a steady succession of tipper trucks arriving at Morgans Farm and depositing material on the land, some travelling down the new surfaced track and on to the lower part of the farm, closest to Clippenham stream. This activity preceded the pollution incident, but increased afterwards and has continued since. Some days, trucks arrived every 10 minutes, says Jack. They would queue up, he says, pointing across the valley to the main road that passes Morgans Farm, before “travelling down and going into various different meadows and just tipping these heaps”. They have also observed material from the trucks being tipped into dug trenches in the fields, before soil is spread over the top. There is a mechanical excavator and a bulldozer on the site, says Jack: “They were using both of those flat-out, day after day, week after week, month after month, piling individual piles up into huge single piles. “Then we noticed other activity: the excavator was making enormous, deep holes in the ground and they were bringing lorries in and emptying stuff into the holes, then using other soil from the site to cover the holes over. We were like: ‘What are they putting in? What are they digging and burying and then covering over?’ Because that’s, I believe, how the original spill took place.” On my first visit to Furnace Book, in April 2025, large heaps of what looked like soil and manure were clearly visible on the lower fields of Morgans Farm. Jack has seen them up close. “The heaps were a very, very low grade of kind of compressed clay topsoil, sort of slag mixed with chunks of ceramic, red brick, tarmac scalpings – which are toxic to aquatic life and have to be controlled and licensed in their storage and their implementation on farmland, according to the government’s own laws. There was a lot of plastic refuse in there, plasterboard, all sorts of foreign objects, which I would not consider to be a clean, acceptable level to be putting all over permanent pasture in a protected landscape.” When I returned in September 2025, there were even more signs of activity: previously green pastures now appeared to be barren brown fields, with soil or construction waste spread across them. “When it rains, that leaches huge amounts of very negative ammonia and nitrates into the watercourses,” Jack says. He and the Furnace Brook team have been testing the water continually since the pollution event. They have continued to find high levels of heavy metals, ammonia and long-chain hydrocarbons – compounds associated with industrial processes. Other neighbours also say they have witnessed the trucks, sometimes as many as 30 to 40 a day, and into the night, arriving full at Morgans Farm and leaving empty. Material is now being deposited on the upper part of Morgans Farm as well. Where once there were pastures and ponds, now it is mostly bare soil and rubble. “England’s green and pleasant land,” the neighbour says sarcastically. One of the neighbours shows me drone footage they took in March 2022 that appears to confirm Jack’s observations. It clearly shows a deep hole on Morgans Farm – about four metres in diameter and 10 metres deep – in a different location from the suspected source of the pollution incident. A large mechanical digger is scooping material out of the hole, as a truck full of an unknown substance reverses towards it. Almost all the trucks seen bringing materials to Morgans Farm have come from one company: Robins of Herstmonceux, a family-run waste transfer company and supplier of topsoils and building materials, which has operated in the area for more than 60 years. Its vehicles are a familiar sight in the area. The company’s website claims it is “able to recycle 100% of inert waste received” and to produce and deliver “recycled materials such as crushed concrete … and screened soils”. There are complex rules concerning what materials can and can’t be put on farmland, in what quantities and for what uses. In March 2024, three months before the pollution incident, Robins of Herstmonceux and Morgans Farm obtained what is known as a U1 exemption from the EA. This means they were permitted to use a limited amount of “suitable waste for construction projects and maintenance work” on the site: up to 5,000 tonnes of non-hazardous waste from construction over three years, for example. By Furnace Brook’s estimate, in 2025 alone, counting the number of trucks that have come into the farm, more than 15,000 tonnes of material was deposited at Morgans Farm. Even so, this activity may not have been illegal. As well as the U1 exemption, there is another route landowners can take to import materials on to their land, known as CL:AIRE, which stands for Contaminated Land: Applications in Real Environments. The CL:AIRE scheme, a registered charity, enables the reuse of excavated material “without the need for traditional waste regulatory controls such as permits and exemptions”, according to its introductory video. Essentially, it connects people generating large amounts of such material (construction sites, say) with people who might have a use for that soil “in a pre-identified place for a pre-identified purpose”. This makes sense from a sustainability perspective – the waste soil would otherwise go into a landfill. According to CL:AIRE, the process has plenty of checks and balances: each project requires a detailed “materials management plan” and a “qualified person” (such as the landowner) who must submit a declaration to the EA, as well as a verification report after the work is completed to confirm that it was done properly. However, the CL:AIRE code of practice is apparently self-regulated and details of its extent or participants are opaque. Morgans Farm was mentioned as being part of the CL:AIRE scheme in a letter from the EA, but in response to requests for more details, CL:AIRE replied that “we cannot share any scheme-specific or participant-level information with you” and that “managed schemes are treated as strictly confidential”. That leaves a great many questions unanswered. How much material was Morgans Farm permitted to import under this scheme? How well was it being monitored? Where was all this material coming from? How many other properties are operating under similar conditions? Morgans Farm and Robins of Herstmonceux were approached for comment regarding these issues, but neither responded. Environmental groups, politicians and employees from government agencies all told me of their frustration at how powerless they are to act over what is happening at Furnace Brook and in many other cases like it, locally and nationally. “It brought me down to earth with a bump to discover how little power a district council appears to have over such things,” says Greg Collins, a Green party councillor for Wealden district council, in which Furnace Brook is situated. Wealden is one of five district and borough councils within the county of East Sussex and at present it is under joint Green and Liberal Democrat control. (Diane Gould has been a Green party councillor for Wealden since July 2025.) Collins continues: “My understanding is – and I am satisfied that I’ve kicked the tyres hard on this – that the district council has no effective powers in respect of the event that damaged the ecology of Furnace Brook. That is an EA matter. They own the regulatory regime that would deal with that and my understanding is that they’ve effectively gone: ‘Nothing to see here. Move along. Hey-ho, life’s a bit shit sometimes.’” The EA investigation is showing little apparent progress, nearly two years later. In a letter last July, the EA wrote that it had visited Morgans Farm in late 2024 and early 2025, alongside other district and county council officials. “Having regard to all the circumstances, and in consultation with other agencies, we, the Environment Agency, have not found any evidence of the illegal importation of waste to Morgans Farm,” it wrote. The EA was approached for comment and responded: “We take the incident at Furnace Brook Fishery very seriously and are progressing with our investigation. As this is an ongoing case, further details cannot be provided at this time.” In the recent Channel 4 series Dirty Business, a docudrama that exposed water companies’ role in river pollution, the EA is portrayed as under-resourced, reluctant to take action and unhealthily close to the corporations it is supposed to police. There is evidence to support this. In January 2022, three EA officers told the Guardian the agency was increasingly unable to hold polluters to account or to improve the environment as a result of the body’s policies. Government grants to the EA have grown from £800m in 2016-17 to £1.8bn in 2024-25, but its powers apparently continue to diminish. “Should a polluter be caught, any tools that were at [the EA’s] disposal to take action have been systematically removed,” a whistleblower said in 2022. “Officers are actively encouraged not to take enforcement action.” Another whistleblower last year revealed that the EA did not send investigators to nearly a third of reported water industry incidents in 2024. In July 2025, the EA admitted that, due to staff shortages, thousands of water samples from pollution incidents had not yet been tested, or never would be. While water and river pollution are ostensibly the EA’s domain, matters of waste, dumping and contaminated land ought to be policed by local government. But, again, a lack of funding and resources has hampered this, says Rachel Millward, the leader of Wealden district council and the deputy leader of the Green Party in England and Wales. She says: “The basic issue is that the policy is there, but it has no teeth, because it doesn’t have funding so that the authorities who are meant to do it can do it, and then there’s no real threat of prosecution.” Millward and other councillors point to the contaminated land regime, laid out in part 2A of the Environmental Protection Act, which requires local authorities to identify and monitor contaminated sites in their district. According to Wealden district council’s website, “there are no formally determined contaminated land sites in the Wealden District” and, owing to lack of funding, “the council is not currently pursuing strategic site inspections”. In other words, says Millward: “Councils have stopped making contaminated land registers and stopped updating them because they can’t afford to do it.” Contaminated land is often identified only when a developer comes along and wants to build on it. Then the developer must pay for removing those contaminants; it becomes a planning matter, rather than an environmental one. But the planning system is also underfunded and incapable of monitoring such issues, according to insiders. “The planning system is designed to encourage development; it’s not designed to prevent it,” says Collins. “The rules are there to create the impression in the minds of the public that there is some sort of jeopardy if you break the rules. They are not there so that you actually experience that jeopardy.” The pressure to build new homes only puts more strain on rural areas. To meet government targets, Wealden district council is expected to add more than 1,400 new homes a year to its housing stock. According to one planning expert, the town of Hailsham, five miles from Furnace Brook, has more than doubled in size in the past decade. Several sources wondered if there were connections between this scale of construction and the materials arriving at Morgans Farm. A spokesperson for Wealden district council responded: “The council does not accept the assertion that planning enforcement is weak. Our planning enforcement team investigates reported breaches and takes proportionate action in line with national policy, legislation and the council’s adopted enforcement approach. Planning enforcement is intended to remedy unacceptable harm caused by breaches of planning control; it is not a mechanism for preventing development that has planning permission.” In terms of illegal dumping, the local picture is also bleak, says Collins. “Anybody who drives around the district sees so much casual fly-tipping. If they stopped to think about it, it would be hard for them not to come to the conclusion that there is a large-scale problem.” Other sources close to local government in East Sussex, who did not wish to be identified, are in despair at the situation. “There is so much to do with illegal waste disposal, organised criminality and the failure of agencies to apprehend these issues that it’s just depressing and extraordinary,” one insider says. “It’s so expensive to dispose of waste legally that many people attempt to do it illegally. And there are plenty of dubious arrangements to be arrived at between operators and landowners which are financially beneficial to both. It’s very difficult with our resources to keep up with those.” Wealden district council responded that it has “one of the lowest reported levels of fly-tipping in East Sussex” and that “the number of recorded incidents in the district has fallen over the past five years”. A report shared with the Guardian in November 2025 found that there were at least 8,000 illegal dumping sites in the UK, containing approximately 13m tonnes of rubbish. When Air & Space Evidence, the satellite company that helped compile the report, presented its findings to the EA, it said there was little interest at the management level. “From the outside, this looks like a fear of finding out. If the Environment Agency finds more illegal waste sites, then they feel they will have to do something about them. So, they would rather not know.” The EA has said it stopped activity at 743 illegal waste sites in 2024-25. It received 10,238 reports of suspected waste crime in 2025. This March, the House of Commons’ public accounts select committee issued a report on environmental regulation in England. It concluded that the system needs to be overhauled. It stated: “We are concerned about the recent rise of illegal waste dumping. Gaps in the Environment Agency’s powers and intelligence have led to delays in responding to a problem that is out of control.” *** If Furnace Brook is Britain’s polluted countryside in microcosm, it could also become a model for how to fix it. The pollution event was “a huge lag at one level, but a huge opportunity at another”, says Alistair Gould. Before the events of June 2024, his plan was to establish Furnace Brook as a “living laboratory”, a showcase for how to transform a landscape degraded by industrial farming into something richer and more resilient on every level: soil and water quality, biodiversity, food security, sustainable energy, community participation. That is still the plan, he says. They are starting several steps further back, but with a broader canvas: the Goulds recently acquired a neighbouring farm, quadrupling the size of the Furnace Brook site. Much of Gould’s career as an environmental consultant was spent thinking about and researching these problems: clean technologies, decarbonising the environment, permaculture principles. He is plugged into what has become a global network of people pursuing similar goals and he has gathered a team of colleagues, volunteers and like-minded experts to help at Furnace Brook. The immediate challenge is restoring the fishing lake. The emphasis is on “bioremediation”: removing pollutants and toxins using natural materials and processes – everything from plants to fungi, bacteria to rocks, explains Cassandra Shaffer, an ecological consultant from Oregon who is leading Furnace Brook’s restoration. For example, the team has been testing floating islands of straw and reeds in the lake, which use biochar – a form of charcoal – and fungi-based “mycorrhizal filtration systems” to trap sediment and encourage the proliferation of micro-organisms that digest the pollution and clean the water. The area upstream from the lake will be a “constructed wetland” – a managed landscape of reeds, wildflowers and other plants. Particular plants have been found to be good at absorbing particular pollutants, says Shaffer. For example, species of Juncus have proved to be particularly effective at removing cadmium. “You plant specifically to the qualities of chemicals or pollutants that you find in your system.” It sounds highly experimental, but these low-tech methods are tried and tested, says Bryan Spooner, a former colleague of Gould’s and an adviser on the project. “This is exactly how mother nature keeps our water clean. If you look at what beavers do, if you look at how an estuary works, if you look at how waterfalls operate, nature is full of examples.” If all goes to plan, these techniques should accelerate the healing of Furnace Brook’s damaged ecosystem. “You should see a very near complete remediation within 18 months,” says Shaffer. The project is also envisioned as a teaching resource for students and organisations. That is the ethos of the “living lab” – to show other people what can be done and to give them a role in it. “We hope that the community members around us would be able to come and help us on volunteer days, and that way they get some hands-on experience,” says Shaffer. She has worked on similar projects in the US and elsewhere in Europe and has seen how approaches benefit people as well as the landscape. “They’re faced with looking at the news and seeing everything that’s happening with these heatwaves, climate catastrophe, huge pollution spills, and it seems so out of our control and so much bigger than us.” When people are able to participate and see results such as water quality improving within a few weeks, she says: “It makes a huge difference in their mental aspect, in the way they communicate, in the way they make friends.” Beyond the restoration, Alistair Gould sees Furnace Brook as a model for a new kind of rural community, where people jointly own and manage their landscape, to cater to local needs. “At the heart of the model is the idea that land should function as a shared foundation for regenerative activity, rather than as a commodity,” he says. “The land is bought so that aligned farmers, entrepreneurs, educators and families can steward it together, generate real value from it and use that value over time to repay the original purchase, enabling ownership to move into more permanent, community‑anchored forms and allowing the original capital to support similar projects elsewhere.” He lays out aspects of the bigger plan: care for elderly people; cohousing projects; reconditioning dilapidated farm buildings; supporting local businesses. Food is a big part of it, including community farming, food storage and food resilience – as in preserving produce locally to feed the community in the event of an emergency, rather than growing it to sell to large, centralised suppliers. This is effectively a reversal of the corporatised industrial model that has done so much to degrade our rural landscape, whether that be industrial farming, privatised water companies mismanaging rivers or operators dumping waste in the countryside. “It extracts from the rural areas and it doesn’t really reinvest in them,” says Spooner. “If you turn that around and start looking at the opportunities to build local community resilience, food resilience, and then looking at what that means in terms of new skills, new employment, new supply chain lines, and localising things again, the economic opportunities are massive.” The community engagement aspect of the plan is already under way, with some help from Maarten Klop, a Dutch organiser who has developed similar initiatives in the Netherlands, organising events, bringing people together, “thinking about how to make these eco-social topics something fun and include everyone”. On a small scale, they are developing locally produced wares such as a “Clean the Lake” lager (Diane already runs a craft brewery at Furnace Brook) and a “cookie of resilience”, the profits from which will go towards the restoration, to draw people deeper into the story of the project. There are plans for beekeeping, forest schooling, market gardening for local restaurants and community fridges and pantries. The soil consultant Michael Kennard has set up a “community compost club”, which collects food waste and turns it into nutrient-rich compost. “You don’t have much room for trying new things if you’re running a commercial farm. We have the space here to experiment and exemplify,” says Klop. Amid a global crisis, all this may sound like a drop in the ocean, but “locally is the only place where we can fix ecological or social challenges”, says Klop. “We can plant a tree, harvest a vegetable, experience community, but if we want to change to a new system, then it needs to happen everywhere all at once. And, luckily, it’s been happening all over the world for decades already.” In the meantime, the prospect of the Goulds receiving any compensation for the damage done to their land remains as remote as ever – they continue to await action by the EA while the truck deliveries continue to roll into Morgans Farm. But the Goulds are focusing on the future, rather than anger or despair. As much as they want to restore the land and model a sustainable rural future, they also want to see the return of the community that made Furnace Brook what it was, says Diane. “The ones who really valued this place, the ones who were really touched by it,” she says. “I really would like to see it open for them. It would be again a place of peace, tranquillity and healing.” • Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Elif Eralp: ‘Germany’s Zohran Mamdani’ who vows to be a mayor for all Berliners
summary: Die Linke candidate, a lawyer affected by her experiences as the child of political migrants from Turkey, poised to head Berlin coalition government
text: Elif Eralp launched her election bid last autumn with the blunt statement: “People like me are actually not supposed to become mayor in this country.” So the fact that the 45-year-old lawyer and daughter of political migrants from Turkey is on the verge of becoming Berlin’s next mayor and the capital’s first leader of Turkish origin is quite the moment in German politics. After last weekend’s city state election, in which her far-left party, Die Linke, came first with more than a quarter of the votes, Eralp has become a household name. The mood at Die Linke’s election celebrations on Sunday night was electric. Eralp, whose candidacy has helped propel the party from the doldrums to the brink of heading a coalition government in Berlin for the first time, was feted as a star. Some commentators suggested Germany was “having a [Zohran] Mamdani moment”, in reference to the democratic socialist mayor of New York. (One of his advisers was summoned to Berlin to help Eralp weeks before the poll. Her campaign was modelled on that of the veteran US senator Bernie Sanders.) “In our city, love and justice won over hate … this signal goes out into the world,” Eralp said at her victory party, the “hate” a pointed reference to the far-right Alternative für Deutschland, which was celebrating coming first in another regional election. Even in liberal Berlin, the populist party made considerable gains. It was Die Linke, however, that came out on top. With about 26% of the vote, the party not only outperformed the centre-left Social Democrats, whose presence has dominated Berlin politics for decades, and the Greens. It was also well ahead of the Christian Democratic Union (CDU), the conservative party of the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, which had previously held the mayoral position. A lot is now at stake for Eralp, who has promised to be “a mayor for all Berliners”. Eralp, who was chosen in particular by the young (47% of whom voted for her) and who mobilised thousands of otherwise non-voters thanks in part to intensive door-to-door campaigning and social media, generated most interest with her ambitious promise to take on corporate giants over unaffordable housing in the German capital. Once described as “poor but sexy” by a former mayor for its low cost of living, Berlin’s rents have soared in recent years. In her nomination speech, the lawyer said: “I’m running so that our city becomes affordable again, so that real estate speculators don’t decide what happens to our city, but rather we do together.” She called sky-high rents a defining social issue, saying: “This city belongs to all of us, not to the speculators.” Merz has led the charge against Eralp’s plans to expropriate more than 200,000 Berlin flats from their corporate landlords, saying her policy – decried by some as “socialism on speed” – would have “calamitous effects” on the economy. The chancellor has said he will push for laws to prevent her plans. Eralp has pledged to plough on. It is not a given that Die Linke will take control of Berlin’s towering Rotes Rathaus, or red city hall, named after its red brick and not its association with leftwing politics. Eralp’s victory has been overshadowed by accusations that Die Linke has failed to tackle antisemitism within its own ranks as well as charges that the party has tolerated – and at worst courted – the support of criminal gangs. The Social Democrats and the Greens, potential coalition partners, have said they need urgent clarification on these alleged affiliations before they agree to be associated with Die Linke. Die Linke’s leadership has repeatedly denied the accusations while vowing to clampdown on any antisemitism in its ranks. On Tuesday it announced that one of its Berlin MPs, who is alleged to have connections both to criminal gangs and a terrorist-related, pro-Hamas organisation, would “suspend his parliamentary duties until further notice”. On Monday, Eralp sought to reassure critics. “Any form of glorification or trivialisation of violence or terror is completely out of the question,” she said. “I stand by that, and for me the promise of protection applies unequivocally to Jewish people just as it does to Muslims, Christians and all people in our city.” Eralp has been keen to stress the ordinariness of her life. She lives with her husband and two children in a rental flat in her own constituency of Kreuzberg, in south-central Berlin, one of the city’s most diverse quarters and home to one of Germany’s liveliest Turkish communities. Her children attend a state school in her kiez, or neighbourhood, and she has kept her family away from the cameras “for their own safety”, she says. Much of her campaigning in the district was carried out in Turkish. Unlike most Turkish migrants, Eralp’s parents did not come to Germany as Gastarbeiter, or guest workers, from Eastern Anatolia but were trade unionists and socialists from Istanbul who were imprisoned after a military coup for their political beliefs. Her mother, Hülya, a well-known feminist in Turkey, was only allowed out of jail because she was heavily pregnant with Eralp. She and Eralp’s father, Selçuk, a doctor, fled to Germany, where their daughter was born in Munich in 1981. The family experienced a complicated asylum process, which Eralp has said helped shape her view of the world. “I’ve experienced a lot about what it means when authorities make decisions you don’t understand. I’ve also felt racism and discrimination first-hand, so my life story has a lot to do with where I’ve ended up now,” she has said. She recalls how her parents often put up asylum seekers in their home over many years, and the 15 years of struggle that her mother, a trainer for nurses, faced before her qualifications were recognised in Germany. At the age of 10, Eralp founded a conservation club with friends in her parents’ garage, and later she went into the anti-nuclear movement. After studying law at the University of Hamburg, she moved to Berlin for two years of obligatory practical legal training, ending up working in the parliamentary group of Die Linke and later switching to the Berlin state parliament. She said she was inspired to join Die Linke in 2017 in direct response to the entry of AfD, an anti-immigration party, into the Bundestag for the first time. In 2019, with fellow members and supporters of Die Linke who had refugee and migrant backgrounds, she co-founded Links*kanax, an alliance that aimed to increase the visibility of the migrant-progressive voice within the party and beyond. When she was 12, Eralp says, she wanted to become a human rights lawyer “to fight against all these injustices I’d seen”. Now, she says, “I’m doing what I set out to do, not in a courtroom, but in the political sphere”.

title: The long-range drone war: Ukraine and Russia scramble for supremacy in the skies
summary: A conflict that began with tanks and then artillery is now pivoting around a new generation of drones focused on military, industrial, economic and civilian targets
text: Finally, in the dead of night, the threat above has passed. The rain has eased and the Ukrainian drones are ready, prepared by a ground crew shrouded in hard-to-detect green and red lights. A small succession of Ukrainian Fire Point FP-2 craft, miniature monoplanes with a 6-metre wingspan and more than 100kg of explosive, line up for an attack mission into occupied Luhansk, over 200 miles away. The drone’s main piston engine is a familiar scooter’s buzz, but its launch booster is something else. The jet sound reverberates, almost painfully. A burst of fire lurches into the distance, the last of which signifies it is time for Ukraine’s 413 Raid drone regiment to pack and go. The launch of an FP-2 drone during the mission into occupied Luhansk It is a scene that is now played out nightly by dozens of Ukrainian crews, reflecting a fast-changing conflict that began with tanks, then artillery, but is now pivoting beyond a first generation of drones. Death and destruction are delivered by new weapons in growing volumes, hundreds of miles beyond the frontline, and at targets that are military, industrial and economic but that affect civilians too. But just as Ukraine has developed its drone and missile capability to almost match Russia’s – after its cities were subject at times to hundreds of drone strikes a day – Moscow has transformed its drone arsenal with a jet-powered revolution. The balance of power remains uncertain. Pilots of the 413 Raid drone regiment preparing an FP-2 for launch Raid is a specialist drone unit, created two years ago, and has been operating Ukrainian-designed and -built FP-2 attack drones since last autumn, according to Skipper, a former corporate IT worker with a master’s in computer science who is now one of its commanders. If, he says, there was only one crew that could run two missions a week when they started, today he says “we can do 10 times more, or even more”. Speaking in a car as the rain pelts down, Skipper cautions there is “a flipside” when asked if long-distance wars are easier to fight because nobody has to be killed visibly. “They can do it as well,” he says – Raid’s crew are targets too. “Maybe you don’t see the enemy with your own eyes, but still it’s a very dangerous game,” he adds. The FP-2 was only first publicly acknowledged by Ukraine last September. It is designed to attack hardened targets at a mid-range, to disrupt Russian logistics to the frontline. The success of Raid and others engaged in mid-strike bombing has helped grind the pace of the invaders’ advance to a near halt. Russia gained a modest 90 square kilometres of Ukraine in August, compared with 505 sq km a year earlier, and western officials estimate it is losing 6,000 more soldiers a month than it can recruit. In Ukraine’s sprawling military, the specialist drone units of the Unmanned System Forces, including Raid regiment, work and overlap with army units working closer to the frontline and special forces. A major attack, such as the attack that disabled the Moscow refinery about 300 miles from the border on 20 September, involves several working at once. A long-range attack could involve launching up to 300 drones, though the target is to be able to launch 1,000 a night, in what soldiers describe as an “orchestra”, where cheap drones identify an air corridor towards the final target. An employee walks past a plume of smoke rising from a fire at the Russian e-commerce firm Wildberries’ logistics complex near the town of Podolsk, outside Moscow, on 16 August. Photograph: Tatyana Makeyeva/AFP/Getty Images The long-range, $75,000 FP-1, sister to the FP-2, has been used to repeatedly attack warehouses, refineries and other military-economic sites at a depth of 1,800 miles inside Russia, causing the country’s crude oil production to fall by 7.7% in a year, according to figures from the International Energy Agency, and interest rates to remain at 14%. “Both sides are getting better at translating deep strikes into economic effects,” says Sidharth Kaushal, of the Royal United Services Institute. A refinery burning in Moscow after Ukrainian drones strikes, 21 September. Photograph: EyePress News/Shutterstock Mission planning is rarely shown, but a short-range drone unit operating in the eastern Donetsk front – Unit 17, Special Operations Centre – is happy to show their war work from their dacha. Znakhar, 33, a software coder before the full Russian invasion, is one of a squad of English-speaking men in their early 30s. During the day, he clicks on fresh, static targets – artillery, electronic jamming systems – that have been added to a common system from western satellites or Ukrainian reconnaissance drones, studying their pictures for extra information. Pilots of Unit 17, Special Operations Centre, posing for a portrait next to a Sych mid-strike drone The temporary base of pilots of Unit 17, Special Operations Centre. Right: the ‘drop bombs’ Unit 17 used for middle strikes At night, the crew use a $25,000 Sych drone, which looks like a large model aeroplane. If the rain holds off, they can fly two to six bombing runs, dozens of miles behind enemy lines. Znakhar, whose call sign means healer or herbalist, draws up an initial flight path in seconds with a few clicks on a map, then adjusts the route to avoid population centres, high ground and known interceptor drone launch sites. What’s changed recently? “More drones,” he says. “Russian drones.” Colleagues such as Ananas, 30, head out at night, taking more precautions than they did when the unit started drone work two years ago, preparing launches underground where once they could work in a field. He studied architecture, then worked as a 3D artist in a video game studio. “I play a lot of video games,” he says, “so I’m good with a gamepad. It’s a big plus because now I’m a pilot.” It’s a narrowing of the gap between fiction and reality. *** On the other side, Moscow always has ballistic and cruise missiles available, allowing it to bomb anywhere inside Ukraine since February 2022. It imported delta-winged Shahed drones from Iran in the war’s first year to boost its long-range attack numbers, and developed a family of cheap battlefield drones plus its own version of the Shahed. But since May there has been a notable set of upgrades, allowing Russian forces to strike Ukraine more effectively with fast, jet-engined drones, allied with a new ruthlessness of targeting. Firefighters working at the site of a Russian drone strike on Kyiv business centre on 23 September “Russia never stops,” Serhii Beskrestnov, Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s defence technology adviser, said during an interview in Kyiv punctuated by an air raid and explosions in the distance. The original Iranian delta wing Shahed (known by Russia as the Geran-2) has been redesigned and a jet engine added. The new Geran-4, with more aerodynamic wings, flies at anywhere from 300km/h (186mph) to 550km/h, while the cigar-shaped Geran-5 is even faster, at closer to 600km/h. It is similar in speed to a new light cruise missile, the Banderol. The prediction is that Russia will make 36,000 jet Shaheds in 2027, a further 10,000 Banderols, plus a similar number of cheap cruise missiles, the Dan-T. All could be used to bomb Ukraine’s strained electricity, heating and water systems this winter. The new weapons, whose Telefly engines are made in China, are faster than the Ukrainian interceptors, designed to stop the old piston-engined Shahed Geran-2s. Shahed interception rates, once over 90%, are down to 60% against Russia’s newer models, with predictable results. The aftermath of a Russian attack on ammunition storage in Myla village, Kyiv region, in August A mix of jet- and traditional-engined drones made a rare morning attack into the centre of Kyiv on Wednesday, bombing a market near the central railway station and business centre, killing two people and injuring 41. At the end of August, a Geran-4 hit an ammunition dump at Myla, outside Kyiv, killing 38 and destroying homes nearby. Another struck Ukraine’s SBU domestic intelligence agency in the centre of Kyiv, though it may have been controlled in its final phase by a Russian agent on the ground. Food supplies in Kyiv supermarkets are uneven after sustained attacks on warehouses in August; petrol stations in the capital were targeted in early September. The aftermath of a Russian Geran-5-type jet-powered drone strike on an Ukrnafta petrol station in the Holosiivskyi district of Kyiv, 15 September. Photograph: Libkos/Getty Images *** Ukrainian military propaganda is excellent at highlighting successful missions on social media, but the wider picture of the impact of its drone strikes on Russia is harder to discern. “This spring we had a really nice time and almost every night we could see one, two, three, four systems destroyed,” Skipper says. “Since June, July, they are just hiding.” Other Ukrainian military sources emphasise that Russia has improved its jamming capabilities, and cheap strike drones are simply not as accurate now. In this long-distance war, civilian casualties are climbing. New UN figures show 2,222 killed in Ukraine during the first eight months of 2026, more than in all of 2025. In August, 368 were killed in Ukraine and a further 113 reported dead in Russia. Warehouses owned by Ukrainian supermarkets, its Nova Poshta postal service and e-commerce groups were hit at least 32 times. Wildberries and Ozon warehouses in Russia were bombed 17 times by Ukraine. Firefighters at a warehouse in the Kyiv region after a Russian attack The impact could be harder for Ukraine. “Russia has advantages that Ukraine does not,” says Kaushal. “A more diversified range of long-range weapons, more of an air defence network and more slack as a society, because its people have not faced so much pressure for so long.” Ukraine, meanwhile, faces economic pressure at a time when its war budget is overspent and needs to find £40bn more next year. Yet, though war is escalating as the technology changes, neither side is close to defeat or a crisis. Tests will come if Russia tries to mobilise up to 300,000 men after parliamentary elections – and as Ukraine tries again to refinance and, most urgently, get through the winter. Back in their soldiers’ dacha, Ananas and Znakhar wonder if the war will ever end. “Sometimes I catch this feeling,” Ananas admits, then Znakhar comes in: “We just need to hang on one more day than them.”

title: Defiance, threats and a ‘rebirth’: five key points from day two of the UN’s big gathering
summary: Iran took a combative tone, a new Venezuela is announced, and Ukraine’s president aims at the Kremlin’s coffers
text: The rubber hit the road this week at the UN general assembly at a time of global urgency, with the Middle East crisis reverberating through markets around the world, AI sparking existential concerns, and few signs of cooperation between the US and China in their great power rivalry. World leaders have gathered in New York to make their feelings known, both at the podium and at crucial meetings on the sidelines. Amid the chaos of the politicking and background briefings, here is a selection of key points we saw on day two. No bending the knee for Iran Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, balanced defiance against the US with an openness to dialogue, in an address that had been in doubt as it was unclear he would be issued a visa to enter the country. “We have only defended ourselves. We are not terrorists,” he said. “Our innocent people have been the targets of cowardly attacks and aggressions imposed upon our country.” Referring to the United States, Pezeshkian added: “Yes, they did hit us, but we did not bend the knee.” The US delegation walked out of the room. At the podium, Pezeshkian held up images of children killed in the strike on a school in Minab, which a UN fact-finding mission had found “reasonable grounds” to say was carried out by the US. Despite Donald Trump’s earlier public musings on whether to “annihilate the Islamic Republic”, the US president said there had been a “very good” meeting on the fate of the strait of Hormuz between Tehran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, and US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. Xi Jinping gives it a miss The biggest thing not happening at the UN general assembly could well be any involvement by Xi Jinping. Amid crises in Ukraine and the Middle East that have seen Beijing accused of being at best unhelpful, Donald Trump rolled out a 100ft red carpet to personally meet his counterpart at Joint Base Andrews instead of the White House, a move not seen for decades. The two will talk about AI, trade and Taiwan during a state dinner and tea, but China will be represented at the UNGA by vice-president Han Zheng. On his arrival, Xi said “our two countries should be partners rather than rivals”, according to state news agency Xinhua, and a modest extension of their trade truce was announced, but expectations of a big breakthrough are low. ‘Today, Venezuela is being reborn’ Venezuela’s interim president described the “rebirth” of her country, as she addressed for the UN for the first time since the abduction of her old boss on the orders of Trump. Delcy Rodríguez, speaking as Nicolás Maduro languished in a prison nearly in Brooklyn, promised elections at an undisclosed point in the future and said her government had started a “political dialogue with opposition sectors”. Earlier, she had watched as Trump defended the US intervention in her country, saying: “It was a war … [and] to the victor belong the spoils”, an allusion to the controversial 65bn-barrel oil deal she agreed, which the president called “the largest oil deal in history”. ‘Russia’s revenues must remain a target’ As the war grinds towards its fifth winter, Ukraine’s president was clear-eyed about how to hurt Russia: hit the Kremlin’s coffers. “Russia’s revenues must remain a target,” Volodymyr Zelenskyy told the assembly. “When someone gives Russia more money through trade, they give this war more time. And that is exactly why we insist on limiting trade with the aggressor, and why we are burning Russia’s revenues ourselves,” he said. The president flagged that the upcoming winter could be “very harsh for us”, given the annual onslaught against its energy infrastructure, but warned that Kyiv could “make it painful for Russia too”. Ukraine has used long-range drones to strike Russian warehouses, ‌port infrastructure and oil refineries, but Trump has pressed Zelenskyy to “stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia” because it was causing a global shortage. Although Russian president Vladimir Putin is not at the UN, Trump has invited him to December’s G20 in Miami, which would mark a significant step in welcoming Putin back on to the world stage. Coming up ... Netanyahu New York is bracing for protests, both in the assembly hall and on the streets, when Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu speaks on Thursday against a background of growing international condemnation, most recently over violence by Israeli settlers in the West Bank. New York mayor Zohran Mamdani told demonstrators this week he would protect their “right to [protest] in this city” but tempered his earlier promises to arrest Netanyahu as a war criminal. Palestinian representatives are calling for diplomatic missions to bring staff for a planned walkout of Netanyahu’s speech. Netanyahu is expected to deliver a hardline message aimed not just at world leaders, but also to his own electorate in Israel ahead of elections next month. Trump and top US officials are not expected to meet Netanyahu, but will be listening carefully to his words – 60% of American Jews in a poll released this week hope Netanyahu is voted out in October.

title: ‘Hanging on by a thread’: 11th hour decision to protect endangered birds from SA space project plans welcomed
summary: The Eyre peninsula site is ‘precious and important’ habitats for southern emu-wren and home to 80% of the mallee whipbird population
text: Conservation groups have welcomed an 11th-hour decision to protect “precious and important habitat” on South Australia’s Eyre peninsula from plans for a rocket launching facility. The Whalers Way “orbital launch complex”, which could see as many as 42 rockets a year take off from conservation land, had already been approved under federal and state planning and environment laws. But a recent decision by the state’s independent Native Vegetation Council could scuttle the space project, located about about 32km from Port Lincoln. The 23-hectare site is protected under a long-standing heritage agreement, a type of covenant on private land designed to protect native wildlife and habitat in perpetuity. The developer, commercial aerospace company Southern Launch, had sought to amend the agreement – to enable its project to proceed – but this was rejected by the council earlier this month. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email The chief executive of BirdLife Australia, Kate Millar, welcomed the council’s decision to protect “one of the most precious and important habitats in the state”, which was a stronghold for one of Australia’s tiniest birds, the endangered Eyre Peninsula southern emu-wren, and home to 80% of the endangered mallee whipbird population. Since the development was proposed about eight years ago, conservation and community groups have fervently opposed the location, which Millar described as the “worst possible place” for a rocket launching facility. “These birds are hanging on by a thread,” she said. “What we should be doing as government and community and business, is seeking to improve and restore [their habitat], and give them every chance of avoiding extinction.” She said the decision under the state’s Native Vegetation Act would have been a “tough call” for the council. “I think they understand what’s at stake here.” South Australia’s natural environment had been under sustained pressure, with the harmful algal bloom, the arrival of H5 bird flu and now the threat of a “horrendous bushfire season”, Millar said. The “wrong development, in the wrong site” would have been “one more nail in the coffin for these species that are found nowhere else on the planet.” The chief executive of the Conservation Council of SA, Kirsty Bevan, called on the state government and the developer to back the council’s decision and seek alternative sites. “We commend the Native Vegetation Council for the expertise and diligence they brought to this assessment, and for upholding the integrity of the Heritage Agreement process and framework that protects places like Whalers Way,” she said. A state government spokesperson said Southern Launch had been told that its application to vary the heritage agreement had been rejected. It could alter the application and send the matter back to the Native Vegetation Council for reconsideration, however. According to the company’s website, the site was selected based on its “favourable launch conditions”, including its coastal location, stable weather and low ship and air traffic. A spokesperson for the Australian Space Agency said there were several launch facilities in operation around the country, including the Bowen Orbital Spaceport in Queensland and the Koonibba Test Range in South Australia, and several others in development. “Australia’s unique geographic advantages make it an attractive destination for space launch and return activities, with vast open areas, access to a broad range of targeted orbits, and a stable political and regulatory environment”, the spokesperson said. Guardian Australia contacted the developer Southern Launch for comment but did not receive a response.

title: Eight USS Lincoln personnel have attempted suicide, US navy confirms
summary: Hung Cao, acting US navy secretary, answered questions from US senator Kirsten Gillibrand in a letter
text: Eight US navy personnel assigned to the USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group have attempted suicide since the start of their lengthy deployment as part of the US war on Iran, Hung Cao, the acting US navy secretary, revealed in a letter to the US senator Kirsten Gillibrand on Tuesday. “Since the beginning of Lincoln’s deployment, there have been a total of eight suicide attempts across the strike group,” Cao wrote, responding on behalf of US defense secretary Pete Hegseth to Gillibrand’s inquiry about the quality of life aboard the fleet. “This number includes the Lincoln crew and sailors from the carrier airwing, strike group and destroyer squadron staff, escorting destroyers and all embarked aviation squadrons.” CNN first reported on Cao’s response to Gillibrand. The crew of the Lincoln, which was at sea for 286 days, disembarked on 1 September in a Thai resort city. The crew had been scheduled to wrap their deployment in May, but it was extended amid the unresolved war. In August, two military newspapers reported on sailors’ deteriorating mental health, including multiple attempts to jump overboard. The reports prompted outcry from Democrats, who called for an investigation of the conditions onboard. In March, one sailor’s attempt to go overboard was thwarted by shipmates, according to Cao. In August, one sailor did go overboard. The individual was rescued and received medical treatment, before being “transferred off-ship for follow-up care”, Cao wrote. MS Now also reported in August on alarming allegations of mold in the ship’s showers and dwindling supplies of food and soap, among other basic necessities. The number of entrée options was temporarily reduced from two to one, Cao wrote in his letter, a measure “implemented to optimize endurance and ensure sustained time on station”. He said four nutritionally balanced meals were served daily. He acknowledged certain delays in replenishing crew supplies. As details of low morale trickled out of the Lincoln, Hegseth downplayed the media coverage, saying news outlets “completely misrepresented” the situation. “We make sure every ship, every crew, every captain has everything we can provide them at every single moment,” he told reporters in August. “What Trump and Secretary Hegseth dismissed as ‘fake news’ turned out to be serious and deteriorating conditions for our service members,” Gillibrand said in a Wednesday statement to the Guardian. “Our troops and their families make immense sacrifices every single day, yet the president dismissed them with open disrespect. That this administration can find endless taxpayer dollars for bombs, ballrooms, and billionaires, but cannot take care of our service members, is completely unacceptable.” “The Navy and the Navy secretary are very committed to sailor health, wellbeing and morale,” a US navy official told the Guardian on Wednesday. Here is the complete text of Cao’s response to Gillibrand’s questions: • In the US, you can call or text the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org. In the UK and Ireland, Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123. In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found at befrienders.org

title: Ukraine war briefing: Moscow hammers Kyiv as Zelenskyy urges leaders at UN to keep choking Russia’s revenues
summary: Two killed and 41 wounded in Kyiv as Russian drone attacks that began on Wednesday stretched into Thursday
text: Russia hammered Kyiv with drones in daylight attacks on Wednesday hours before Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy met with world leaders at the UN general assembly. Two people were killed and 41 wounded in Ukraine’s capital. Palls of black smoke floated above the city following the latest in what have been daily Russian attacks that torment Ukrainian civilians. The drones set off fires and damaged buildings in Kyiv and elsewhere in Ukraine overnight, authorities said. The attacks continued early into Thursday with emergency crews dispatched to three ⁠districts, said Kyiv mayor Vitali Klitschko. “Explosions in ‌Kyiv, The ‌capital is under attack ‌from ballistic missiles. Remain in shelters!” Klitschko wrote on Telegram. Unofficial Telegram channels showed what was described as a fire lighting up the horizon. A Russian ⁠aerial bomb attack ⁠also killed five people ⁠and injured six on Wednesday ⁠in the village of Oleksandrivka ⁠in Ukraine’s eastern ‌Donetsk ‌region, the regional governor ‌said. Vadym Filashkin, writing on Telegram, said Russian forces had dropped ‌four bombs on the village, near the city of Kramatorsk. Zelenskyy urged world’s leaders Wednesday to keep choking Russia’s revenues and impede its war efforts, telling the UN general assembly that “Russia’s revenues must remain a target.” “When someone gives Russia more money through trade, they give this war more time. And that is exactly why we insist on limiting trade with the aggressor, and why we are burning Russia’s revenues ourselves,” he said. Zelenskyy also reiterated his warnings to Moscow that Ukraine would strike back and make the coming winter deeply painful for Russia, if the two sides ⁠cannot agree a truce on energy ⁠attacks before the cold sets in. Ukraine and its allies are racing to secure limited agreements on energy infrastructure and Black Sea shipping before winter, fearing renewed Russian strikes on power and heating facilities, while Moscow continues to show little interest in wider negotiations ⁠to end the war. “Ukrainians understand that this winter could be very harsh for us. But in response, we will have no choice but to make it painful for Russia too,” Zelenskyy told the UN meeting. ⁠The US has invited Russian president Vladimir Putin to a December G20 meeting in ⁠Miami, Florida, where ⁠he could hold a summit with Donald Trump, US secretary of state Marco Rubio ⁠said on Wednesday. The Kremlin said Russia would consider the invitation. Rubio, speaking after meeting Russian foreign minister Sergei ⁠Lavrov on the sidelines of the UN general assembly, said the US remained ‌open to engaging ‌with Russia on the war in Ukraine, despite stalled efforts ‌to bring an end to the conflict. “We’ve invited President Putin to the G20. We think it’s an opportunity for him to engage not just with the president but with other world leaders. We hope that’s an invitation ‌he’ll accept,” Rubio said. Zelenskyy said on Wednesday he had signed a “drone deal” with Finland’s president, ⁠another in a series of agreements offering to combine Kyiv’s technical expertise with other countries’ industrial capacity. Zelenskyy met Finnish ⁠president Alexander Stubb, ⁠along with Norwegian prime minister Jonas Gahr Stoere in New York. “And today we just signed a Drone Deal with Alex (Stubb) – an important step for jointly protecting our ⁠people and an even stronger partnership between our countries,” Zelenskyy wrote on Telegram. Ukraine has transferred two North Korean prisoners of war to ⁠South Korea, Zelenskyy said on Thursday in his address to the UN. “Recently, we sent two ⁠North Korean prisoners ⁠of war to the Republic of Korea,” Zelenskyy said in his speech. “These guys are not easy to capture alive. One of them, ⁠when he realised he was going to be taken prisoner, tried to kill himself. And he was shocked that fate did not let him ⁠die.” Zelenskyy did not provide more details about the return. According to some estimates, North Korea has sent up to 15,000 soldiers since 2024 to support Russia’s war against Ukraine. Australian prime minister Anthony Albanese has announced that Australia will provide $60m more in support for Ukraine’s fight against Russia’s invasion during an emotional meeting with ⁠Zelenskyy in New York. Albanese became emotional as he paid tribute to his “friend” Zelenskyy in his fight against Russian aggression. “[His] leadership has been, I think, quite extraordinary, leading people in circumstances which are extraordinarily difficult,” he said.

title: In historic first, tropical turtles spotted nesting on California beaches
summary: What caused the turtles to begin nesting farther north than usual is the ‘million dollar question’
text: A sea turtle crawled out of the surf in southern California last weekend around sunset and started laying eggs in the sand. People on Huntington Beach who saw the female olive ridley sea turtle were shocked and excited. And they weren’t the only ones freaking out, said Justin Viezbicke, the California stranding coordinator for the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Association (Noaa). “This is the first documented case of a turtle nesting on the west coast,” Viezbicke said. What made the sighting even more noteworthy is that two different olive ridley sea turtles were identified laying eggs on Orange county beaches in the last week, the first on Seal Beach and the second on Huntington Beach. It’s a pattern that has scientists questioning whether the nestings are a freak occurrence, or the beginnings of a more lasting trend. While early news reports suggested that a single female turtle laid eggs on both California beaches, scientists further analyzed photographs of the turtles’ shell shape and barnacle patterns and determined that two separate olive ridley turtles had begun nesting on the US coast, Viezbicke said. Olive ridley turtles typically lay their eggs on beaches much further to the south, in Mexico and Central America, Viezbicke said. What caused the turtles to begin nesting further north than usual is the “million dollar question”, he said. Scientists are examining several different theories, including the environmental factor of warmer coastal waters, to other effects of El Niño, or whether the turtles “could have been blown off course by the recent hurricane”. “There’s been a lot of activity in the Pacific Ocean,” Viezbicke said. While it’s too soon to tell, it’s also possible that these first recorded US coastal nests could herald a broader northward shift in the olive ridley turtle’s nesting patterns, one driven by climate crisis and the warming ocean waters in the turtles’ native nesting areas, said Lance Adams, an aquarium veterinarian at the Aquarium of the Pacific in Long Beach. The sex of the olive ridley turtle is determined by temperatures where the eggs hatch, and warmer temperatures produce more female turtles. “After about 87.8F, they’re almost all female,” Adams said. To achieve a balanced population, the sea turtles might need access to cooler nesting areas. On the other hand, it’s hard to generalize from just two sightings, Adams said: “The turtles could be here by mistake.” Because the nesting season is not over and individual olive ridley turtles typically lay multiple nests of eggs, “We might see additional sea turtles making beach crawls to nest in the next 30 to 90 days,” Adams said. For protection, the new turtle nests have been surrounded by fencing. But there’s only so much local officials can do to protect the eggs, which typically take 45 to 60 days to hatch, Viezbicke said. It’s not just the dangers from local predators, such as coyotes, or from interfering humans. New hurricane swells and high tides are expected as soon as Monday of next week, Viezbicke said – and there’s a risk of the extreme weather “washing away that part of the beach”. Californians who spot sea turtles on a local beach should not interfere with them, and should keep at least 50 ft away, Adams, the aquarium veterinarian, advised. To advise authorities of a new turtle sighting, tell a lifeguard, or call Noaa’s marine animal stranding hotline, he recommended. Getting close to the turtles’ fenced-off nesting spots is not a good idea, he said: “People won’t see anything.” If locals want to observe live sea turtles in action, they can visit rescued turtles on display in rehabilitation tanks at an aquarium. Olive ridley sea turtles are one of the most abundant turtle species worldwide, but are protected under the US endangered species act. Warmer ocean temperatures have led to sightings of all kinds of sea creatures that aren’t typically spotted on the California coast, he noted, including different shark species, rays, sea horses and the venomous yellow-bellied sea snake. People should aim to adapt to shift in wildlife patterns, and, in general, keep their distance, Adams said, though new unexpected species present different potential risks. “Turtles aren’t particularly dangerous to humans. They can bite. They can slap with their flippers. Someone could potentially get hurt, but probably not seriously,” he said.

title: The Coalition says it wants cheaper power, not ideology. But its evidence-free plan is all ideology | Adam Morton
summary: The reheated plans to scrap renewable schemes, boost fossil fuels and revive nuclear are transparently Trumpian
text: Give the Coalition points for chutzpah, if nothing else. In a press release on Wednesday, first given to the Australian for a not exactly hard-won “exclusive”, it declared “Australians need cheaper power, not more ideology”. You don’t have to get far beyond that headline to find its position comes from a worldview that is ideology on steroids. That worldview says climate breakdown is not real, or at least not a real concern, and Australia should abolish nearly all plans to respond to or prepare the economy – and people’s lives – for the changes under way. As one campaigner put it, it is a plan to let climate change rip. Greenhouse gas emissions would be much higher than on the current trajectory. From a here-and-now consumer point of view, it is a plan that is based on the fallacy that the big jump in power bills in recent years is due to renewable energy and a legislated net zero emissions target. Evidence and most experts clearly say otherwise. But both are disregarded. Most of what the Coalition announced wasn’t actually new. The fresh bit is that it has promised to package up eight commitments in a new bill that would be introduced within 30 days if it was elected. Remarkably, at least half of those commitments are to abolish policies that were introduced under Coalition governments led by Scott Morrison, Tony Abbott and John Howard. Sign up to get climate and environment editor Adam Morton’s Clear Air column as a free newsletter Angus Taylor and Matt Canavan say they would tear up the safeguard mechanism, introduced under Abbott, ostensibly to put a limit on pollution from major industrial sites. They would abolish the mid-century net zero emissions goal brought in by Morrison and Barnaby Joyce and legislated under Labor. They would repeal the Howard-era ban on nuclear energy. They say they would scrap Labor’s capacity investment scheme, which is meant to underwrite solar, wind and energy storage developments, and replace it with a scheme that could also use public money to encourage fossil fuels and nuclear generation. And they would abolish the vehicle efficiency standard that requires auto companies to lower the average emissions of their new car fleets – a policy that has belatedly seen a substantial increase in electric vehicle models available, including at the more affordable end, ending the farce in which Australians had far less opportunity to buy clean cars than any similar country. Bizarrely, the Coalition claims the latter policy has somehow reduced vehicle choice. Tell that to the 25% of new car buyers who chose an EV last month – a higher percentage than bought a petrol or diesel car – and who are now enjoying much lower running costs. Many of these policies are transparently Trumpian. They otherwise mostly fly in the face of global trends. For the first time, renewable energy – solar, wind and hydro – last year overtook coal-fired power as the leading source of electricity. Solar energy capacity expanded by 30% in one year. According to the International Renewable Energy Agency, 85% of new power capacity built last year was renewable, and 90% of the renewables built were cheaper than the lowest fossil fuel alternative. Global EV sales are up more than 10% this year and expected to account for nearly 30% of the global total, with China leading the way. Clean solutions are rising due to governments taking some action to reduce emissions and limit an accelerating climate crisis that is killing thousands of people. But cost is at least as big a factor, particularly in electricity generation. In Australia, that argument has been muddied by events. As we have pointed out before, power bills increased dramatically after Russia’s attack on Ukraine sent global gas prices skyrocketing four years ago. About the same time, coal power prices were pushed up by flooding at east coast mines and outages at ageing generators. Combined, these issues pushed up the wholesale cost of electricity by about 20% not long after Labor had overconfidently suggested that bills would come down by $275. Despite claims to the contrary, renewable energy was not a major issue. Correlation is not causation. In fact, wholesale prices have fallen in some cases due to the influx of batteries that have allowed cheap excess solar power to be stored and used at night. That’s the good news. The more complicated news is that replacing an old coal-fired system is expensive, however you do it. A renewables-dominated power system may not bring prices down much, if at all. But there is clear evidence that it will be cheaper than other options. It will also cut heat-trapping pollution that is doing escalating damage and could allow an industrial shift that sets up Australians for a potential economic future as demand for fossil fuels falls. This is not to say the Albanese government is doing enough. The renewables transition is at risk of slowing and new coal and gas export developments are still being approved. The prime minister gave a keynote speech at climate week in New York in which he avoided saying fossil fuels are the problem. But Taylor goes further. On Wednesday, he implicitly dismissed climate change as a threat. He suggested all types of energy, dirty and clean, should be equally available. He claimed this would lower bills. Evidence? That’s not how this ideology works. • Adam Morton is Guardian Australia’s climate and environment editor
