title: Meta debuts no-camera smart glasses and virtual reality spectacles
summary: The new wearables come at a time of uncertainty for smart glasses, which are facing backlash over privacy concerns
text: Meta announced an advanced new set of virtual reality glasses and a collection of new smart glasses Wednesday, including an audio-only version without a camera. At the firm’s Meta Connect conference in Menlo Park, California, executives said the new Ray-Ban Meta models set new standards for battery life and weight. They said the new glasses with screens in the lenses squeeze capabilities previously reserved for a full headset into a light set of spectacles that rest on a user’s ears. The new wearables come at a time of uncertainty for the smart glasses category, which is broadly facing a backlash from sceptics and privacy campaigners around their ability to record video, frequently being dubbed “perv glasses” or “spy glasses”. Meta’s smart glasses are the most popular gadget in the category. The Ray-Ban Meta Audio AI glasses seem tailored for the time. Lacking a camera, they may help avert some privacy worries, though Meta claims they have been in the works for several years. The glasses have microphones and speakers for music, calls and interacting with the company’s AI assistant, taking the recognizable form of Ray Ban’s Clubmaster or Burbank styles. The new versions are thinner and lighter than the camera versions and last up to 12 hours on battery and will cost £319 (€349/A$529). The new Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 glasses, which do sport cameras, have longer battery life than their predecessors, lasting up to nine hours with support for Dolby Atmos audio. They will cost £409 (€449/A$679). Meta is also launching two new styles of its own-brand glasses in partnership with singer and actor Lisa. All of the firm’s smart glasses have an LED warning light that flashes when recording, but Meta said it has made improvements to its tampering detection, including during a recording. Finally, Meta is expanding availability of its Meta Ray-Ban Display smart glasses to outside the US for the first time since their announcement a year ago. The glasses with a virtual display in the right lens will go on sale in the UK and Canada from 23 September priced at £749 (CA$1,149) and will later expand to France, Germany and Italy on 13 October for €899. Meta VR glasses The new Meta VR glasses are an evolution of the company’s pioneering Quest VR headsets, which have become some of the most popular on the market. But instead of being a bulky plastic headset, the 100g device is made of magnesium alloy and looks like an oversized set of glasses. The wearer peers through small lenses on to a 5K microOLED screen with a crisp 37 pixels per degree, making text look sharp and rivalling Apple’s high-end Vision Pro headset. Users can see out of the sides and through a camera system at the front for augmented reality features and awareness of their surroundings. The glasses are tethered by a cable to a pocketable 300g puck containing the computing power and three-hour battery pack, which helps to remove the weight from a user’s head and makes the glasses five times lighter than the Quest 3 headsets, according to Meta. The glasses are fully compatible with the vast Quest software library, but are designed for productivity and entertainment rather than games. The company described the glasses as “IMAX Enhanced” and supportive of 3D for movies. At launch, they will showcase a new Disney+ immersive experience that reflects landscapes from films such as Avengers: Infinity War surrounding a virtual cinema screen. The glasses have the ability to display multiple virtual windows and to connect to a Mac or PC to mirror its displays. They have eye-tracking and hand-gesture control, including a virtual keyboard projected on to any desk or table, but also support Quest’s hand controllers or an Xbox game pad for games. The Meta VR glasses will cost $1,299.99 and will be available from spring 2027 in North America, Europe and Asia.

title: Trump greets Xi Jinping on arrival in rare move as US-China trade truce extended
summary: President lays out red carpet as treasury secretary announces extension of ‘Busan agreement’ pausing trade war hostilities
text: Donald Trump has welcomed Xi Jinping to the US, taking the unusual step of greeting the Chinese leader on the tarmac at Joint Base Andrews to kick off his state visit to Washington. Xi’s plane was met with a lavish arrival ceremony that included a 30-metre-long (100ft) red carpet flanked by US service members, a military flyover by two B-1 bombers and a presentation of the flags and national anthems of both countries. US presidents typically welcome foreign leaders at the White House, but Trump and the first lady, Melania, traveled to the the military base in Maryland, just outside Washington, to personally shake hands with Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, on Wednesday evening. Xi’s visit comes as world leaders gather in New York for the United Nations general assembly, although the Chinese leader will not address the meeting. He has attended the UNGA just once since becoming president in 2012. “It’s pretty notable that Xi Jinping is ⁠coming to Washington in the same week as the general assembly, but does not feel bothered to come up to New York,” Richard Gowan of the International Crisis Group told Reuters. “I think a lot of people will say: ‘Where is the real center of decision-making?’” Scott ⁠Bessent, the US treasury secretary, announced that the US ⁠and China agreed on Wednesday to extend the so-called Busan ⁠agreement – a temporary trade truce between the world’s two biggest economies. Bessent, who met the Chinese ‌vice-premier He Lifeng earlier on Wednesday, told Fox News the agreement would be extended until 10 January, two months after it was due to expire. The pageantry will continue with a formal state welcome on the South Lawn of the White House, private tea with the US president and first lady, and a tour of the National Archives, among other special events. The simmering trade war is one of many thorny issues Trump and Xi must confront during the visit, including the race in artificial intelligence development and geopolitical instability during the two-day visit. The White House has invited major tech leaders, such as executives from OpenAI, Apple, xAI, Microsoft, Nvidia, Meta and others, to a state dinner being held for Xi on Thursday. There was one discordant note in the carefully orchestrated arrival ceremony, when Trump visibly winced at the sound of a US military jet flying overhead as he stood alongside Xi on the red carpet, listening to the US national anthem. Video of the moment showed that while Trump recoiled from the sound of the flyover, Xi remained impassive, as did the wives of both men. The moment, which was widely mocked online, was captured on a White House livestream but not included in the edited highlights of the ceremony released by Trump’s aides later. The US and China have long been competing to develop increasingly powerful technology, but the race to further AI has become a major topic among tech companies – especially after several executives came forward to warn about the dangers of rapid development. Trump has dismissed concerns that AI development could harm people, instead promoting more investment in the technology so the US can beat China in the race. “There is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers, and the only one that is happy about it is China. WHOEVER WINS AI, WINS! We are leading China, and all others, and will continue to do so,” Trump wrote on Truth Social last week. The president and members of the administration have insisted that leading AI development also means leading the world militarily and economically – further raising the stakes for the US and China. Xi’s visit is expected to be filled with ceremonial displays, reciprocating the treatment Trump received when he visited China earlier this year. Trump’s decision to greet the Chinese leader at his plane, rather than at the White House, shows how far the US president is willing to go to honor Xi. “He’s coming on our soil,” Melania Trump said of the visit to Fox & Friends on Wednesday morning, “and we need to welcome them with the most respect.” Robert Mackey contributed reporting

title: Tony Blair says Britain should work towards rejoining EU in next 10 years
summary: Andy Burnham under pressure to revisit Brexit as poll suggests pledge to rejoin could boost Labour’s electoral chances
text: Britain should work towards rejoining the EU in the next decade, Tony Blair has said, adding to growing pressure on Andy Burnham to abandon Labour’s reluctance to revisit the 2016 referendum. The former prime minister has urged Burnham to use his 10-year plan in November to put the country’s membership of the union back on the table, a decade after it voted to leave. In a paper entitled A Path to Rejoining a Reformed Europe, the Tony Blair Institute (TBI) calls for the UK to accept free movement of people and make a financial contribution as the price of entry. The intervention comes after Burnham declined to rule out promising to rejoin the EU in the next Labour manifesto, though it also threatens to reopen the deep rifts caused by the vote 10 years ago. In a foreword to the paper, Blair argues: “Britain should signal an intention if the terms are right to enter into a structured formal relationship with Europe and initiate a process of negotiation where everything is on the table but nothing agreed until everything is agreed.” TBI researchers say in the paper itself: “Over the next decade, Britain should work towards the ambition of rejoining a significantly reformed EU.” Blair is the latest in a series of Labour figures to back rejoining the EU. Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, has called the Brexit vote a “catastrophic mistake” and said the party should aim to rejoin the bloc, while Burnham himself told the Guardian last year: “I hope in my lifetime I see this country rejoin the European Union.” But Burnham has said he does not wish to pursue membership of the union in the near term. When asked by reporters this week if it could be in the next election manifesto, he said it was a question “for another day”. Others are sceptical of the electoral wisdom of giving the appearance that the party wants to undo the result of the 2016 referendum, especially in areas of the country where Reform UK has made inroads in recent years. Lisa Nandy, the culture secretary, dismissed the idea earlier this year as she warned against “reopening the circular arguments that we ended up in as a country”. However, pollsters suggest Labour could benefit electorally by promising to rejoin. A new megapoll conducted by YouGov on behalf of the pro-EU campaign group Best for Britain suggests the party could more than double its seat total if it goes into the next election promising to rejoin. The survey of more than 13,000 people, undertaken in June before Burnham became prime minister, found that a pledge to seek membership would help unite progressive voters behind Labour while doing nothing to boost Reform’s vote. The results suggested the move could take Labour from a projected 136 seats to 321 – though those totals will have changed since Burnham came to office, which has given the party a poll lead for the first time in months. The TBI paper calls for Britain to try to accelerate European market reforms using possible re-entry as leverage. It argues that pro-reformers in Brussels would have a significant incentive to work with Britain on a project to make the EU more economically liberal and to reform its regulations on energy and technology. It adds that Burnham should scrap the government’s red lines of not rejoining, not allowing free movement and not entering the single market or a customs union. The paper argues that the prime minister should replace them with a single promise only to sign up to rules and initiatives that prove of economic or strategic benefit to the UK. TBI has advocated in recent years for the UK to slow down its push to achieve net zero carbon emissions and is a heavy backer of increased use of artificial intelligence in government. Its policy positions have brought scrutiny on some of the institute’s most high-profile funders, who include the technology billionaire Larry Ellison, and its clients, which include the government of Saudi Arabia.

title: RFK Jr received $4m in book advances from Maha allies over past year
summary: In 2024 ethics filing, US health secretary pledged to ‘not engage in writing, editing, marketing or promotional services for any of these books during government service’
text: Robert F Kennedy Jr, the US health secretary, received $4m over the last year in book advances from allies within the Make America Healthy Again movement, according to a new report. The advances were for upcoming books by Skyhorse Publishing, a publishing house belonging to Tony Lyons, a friend of Kennedy Jr who is also president of Maha Center, a non-profit that describes itself as “tackling America’s health crisis through education, investigation, innovation and action”. The advances were first reported by the New York Times on Wednesday. According to a 2024 ethics filing, Kennedy Jr pledged: “I will not engage in writing, editing, marketing or promotional services for any of these books during government service.” Kennedy Jr has written several books with Skyhorse Publishing, including The Real Anthony Fauci and The Wuhan Cover-Up. According to Kennedy Jr’s 2026 financial disclosure forms, also reviewed by the Guardian, he accepted $126,500 worth of housing in Washington, at a “vacation home” owned by Gavin de Becker. De Becker is a security consultant and Kennedy Jr ally who also provided the secretary with gifts including nearly $45,000 in roundtrip airfare to Greece and nearly $97,000 in roundtrip airfare to Fiji, where the Wall Street Journal reports de Becker owns a compound. In addition to donating at least $10m to Kennedy Jr’s Super Pac in 2024, with $9.65m being returned, according to Politico, de Becker has published a book with Skyhorse Publishing titled Forbidden Facts: Government Deceit and Suppression About Brain Damage From Childhood Vaccines. In a statement to the New York Times, an HHS spokesperson said that Kennedy Jr “complies with all applicable federal ethics laws, regulations and financial disclosure requirements”. “The secretary works with HHS, career ethics officials to ensure that his financial interests, gifts, outside activities and other reportable matters are appropriately disclosed and handled consistent with those requirements,” the spokesperson added. Meanwhile, De Becker told the outlet: “Bobby is among my closest friends in the world for many years, and I’m grateful to be able to host him anytime … He has hosted my family at his homes, he’s stayed at my homes, we take family vacations together every year, and did so for years before he was in his current job.” The Guardian has reached out to the Department of Health and Human Services, de Becker and Lyons for additional comment. The financial disclosures also noted that Kennedy Jr’s wife, Cheryl Hines, accepted $210,000 in consultation fees from the non-profit advocacy group Maha Action, which Lyons also leads. Speaking to the New York Times, Kedric Payne, a senior ethics counsel at the Campaign Legal Center said: “Lavish gifts to an official from major political donors don’t get the same benefit of the doubt as dinner from a former classmate … The public deserves full transparency about the nature of these gifts and any interests the donor has before the government.”

title: Three charged with assault after anti-migration protests in Hampshire
summary: Hundreds gathered on Tuesday night in anticipation of a small boat arriving in Gosport
text: Three people have been charged in connection with anti-migrant protests that drew hundreds of demonstrators to a marina in Hampshire on Tuesday night. Six people were arrested by police, as anti-migrant activists who mistakenly believed a small boat was due to arrive at Gosport gathered in an attempt to disrupt the arrival of any asylum seekers. Those charged are Shannon Dodds, 32, of Leonard Road in Gosport, who has been charged with two counts of assault by beating of an emergency worker, Sally Pearson, 31, of Forton Road in Gosport, who has been charged with assault by beating of an emergency worker and a racially aggravated public order offence, and Toby Matthews, 33, of Forton Road in Gosport, who has been charged with common assault of an emergency worker. Dodds and Pearson have been remanded in custody and will appear at Portsmouth magistrates court on Thursday 24 September. Matthews was bailed but must appear at Portsmouth magistrates court on 9 November. Hampshire police said in addition to these charges, a 19-year-old man and a 36-year-old man from Salisbury who were arrested on suspicion of aggravated trespass had been bailed with conditions until 22 December while inquiries continued. They added: “A 67-year-old man from Gosport was also given a fixed-penalty notice for driving without due care and attention. He was also arrested on suspicion of assaulting an emergency worker and has been bailed with conditions until 22 December while enquiries continue.” The protests in Gosport followed a social media push by far-right activist Daniel Thomas, who styles himself Danny Tommo, who called for action to disrupt the potential arrival of asylum seekers as he livestreamed efforts to apprehend small boats crossing the channel to more than 100,000 followers on Tuesday afternoon. He is also now facing a police inquiry after he used a knife to slash an inflatable dinghy in the Channel while a rescue worker was onboard. His livestream showed him approaching an empty dinghy which had contained about 50 migrants who had reportedly left from a beach in Normandy. They had been picked up by two RNLI lifeboats once they had reached the UK search and rescue area, but a French official then got on to the craft. The footage showed Thomas taking out a knife and slashing at the vessel in the channel, shouting at the French rescue worker: “Right, you are on English territory. This is England. This is not France any more.” “Traitor,” Thomas shouted as his boat motored away. The protesters in Gosport, many of whom wore black clothing and face coverings, chanted “send them back”, wrongly assuming the boat would arrive on the Hampshire coast. Instead of heading for Gosport, the RNLI transferred the asylum seekers to a Border Force vessel which landed in Dover early on Wednesday. Hampshire police said they had deployed officers to the town on Tuesday evening “to help facilitate peaceful protest, ensure the safety of the local community and support partners in the event of any emergency at sea”. A Home Office spokesperson said: “We have been clear that groups creating fear and intimidating communities cannot be allowed to operate with impunity. “Police should make full use of the powers available to them to deal robustly with criminality and ensure communities, staff and those in their care are protected.” Campaign group Stand Up To Racism described the incident as “disgusting” in a post on X, and said Thomas’s supporters in Gosport had blocked ambulances during the protests. The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, was forced to order an urgent security review after the failure by the Border Force to intercept two other migrant boats in two days before they reached the Kentish coast this week. She said on Wednesday: “This was not acceptable. Our improved monitoring has led to uncontrolled crossings becoming incredibly rare. But even one is one too many. “The new tactics adopted by the smugglers, like launches from much further west in France, are a reminder of two things. Firstly, these gangs have no regard for human life. They are putting people on increasingly long and dangerous crossings. “Secondly, our efforts are having an impact. We are making it much harder for gangs to launch vessels, forcing them to change their approach, and as a result we are significantly reducing the numbers coming here by small boat.” The total number of migrants who have crossed the Channel by boat so far this year is 17,784, according to the government – a figure 45% lower than at the same point last year. The shadow home secretary, Chris Philp, said Tuesday’s “chaos” showed the UK was seeing “illegal immigrants crossing at will over ever larger distances and in ever larger boats”. “This latest fiasco shows that the French are not even trying to stop the illegal immigrants’ boats,” he added.

title: Twenty years after An Inconvenient Truth, Al Gore still believes in the climate fight: ‘We are going to win this’
summary: Former US vice-president still has optimism for climate advocacy two decades after groundbreaking documentary
text: Two decades after the release of his groundbreaking documentary An Inconvenient Truth, Al Gore has admitted he was surprised by the ferocious backlash from the fossil fuel industry and its political allies. But the former US vice-president insists he still has optimism the world will confront the climate crisis. At a New York event to mark the 20th anniversary of the release of the film and his subsequent climate advocacy work, Gore, now 78, joked: “I always say if it hadn’t been for me, we might have a big problem right now” when asked about the progress made over the past two decades. “The scientists unfortunately have been proven to be absolutely correct,” Gore said on Wednesday. “In some important ways, they may have even understated what the damage is doing. The resistance has been more durable and sustained than I expected it to be.” The fossil fuel industry has “captured control of too many governments” and even the UN’s top climate science apparatus “to a shocking degree”, Gore said, citing recent reporting by the Guardian that Saudi oil operatives were involved in crafting high-profile UN climate reports. An Inconvenient Truth, released in 2006, documents a slideshow talk that Gore repeatedly showed to audiences around the world on the mounting climate crisis after he lost the 2000 US presidential election. In the wake of the landmark film, Gore started a grassroots movement to train new climate activists, with his Climate Reality Project amassing a network of 4.5 million people across 196 countries. The past two decades have seen barely restrained global heating, which has caused effects that are “growing so rapidly, and they are becoming more and more frequent”, as Gore pointed out, citing record heatwaves that racked numerous countries this summer and the recent disaster on the Nepal-Tibet border that was triggered by a collapsing glacier. The current rate of temperature rise is set to breach internationally agreed thresholds and is set to cause “utter devastation”, Gore warned, adding that looming “tipping points” such as rampant melting of the ice sheets and the Amazon turning into a savanna will push the world towards catastrophe. Gore told the event, staged as a conversation with Al Roker, the TV weather forecaster, as part of climate week, that he saw his long battle to rally action on the climate crisis as a continuation of previous struggles such as the civil rights movement and the fight for women’s rights. “And in all those previous cases, some of the advocates felt despair, and the biographies and diaries are filled with those kinds of expressions,” he said. “But they kept going anyway because, as others have said, courage is not the absence of fear or despair. It’s the decision to go forward in spite of it. And I really strongly believe that we are very close to that positive tipping point where the mass of public opinion is going to be unstoppable.” While the world is still barreling toward a dangerous global temperature rise of beyond 2C hotter than the pre-industrial average, the speedy deployment of clean energy has helped ensure that previous, disastrous projections of a 4C or more temperature rise by the end of the century are now considered unlikely. Gore said that while many developing countries still struggle to get adequate financing for renewables and battery projects, he is confident that the mass adoption of clean energy, now routinely cheaper than fossil fuels such as coal and gas, will take hold. “The day is coming when our momentum will overtake the resistance. We’re getting very close now,” he said. “I think we are going to win this. The remaining question is whether we will win it in time to avoid those negative tipping points I talked about.” Gore’s comments came shortly before a headline UN climate event hosted by António Guterres, the outgoing UN secretary general and vocal proponent of climate action. Guterres lamented ongoing expansion of fossil fuels that is “defying science, economics and common sense”. He added: “We have seen how fossil fuel dependence wreaks havoc – driving up costs, draining budgets, squeezing households and leaving countries at the mercy of conflicts and decisions far beyond their borders.” But the secretary general said countries are now able to take a different path by tripling renewable adoption, reducing deforestation and electrifying their economies. “Renewables are the cheapest, fastest and most secure source of new electricity almost everywhere,” he said. “Clean energy has gone from alternative to unstoppable.”

title: Tories target universal credit claimants in plan condemned as ‘fast track to poverty’
summary: Proposals aim to push people into work, but charities say families are still paying price of austerity cuts and rise in cost of living
text: People claiming universal credit (UC) would have their payments cut by a third if they have not paid enough national insurance, under a Conservative plan condemned by one charity as “a fast track to increased poverty”. Under the proposals, those who receive this “subsistence allowance” would have it paid into a dedicated debit card that would prevent from them buying alcohol or tobacco, based on an Australian system that was scrapped after trials found limited evidence it changed behaviour. While the proposals are billed by the Conservatives as a way to push people into work, the poverty charity Trussell said trimming incomes so that people struggled with rent and transport was likely to make it even harder for them to find and keep a job. Under the plan, UC claimants would receive the full amount to which they are entitled for six months, but after this point the sum would be tied to how long they have worked at a level that triggers national insurance payments. This would have to happen for at least twice as long as the claimant period, meaning someone who has amassed two years of NI payments would qualify for another 12 months of full UC, before falling to the lower rate. Set at 70% of the standard amount, this would leave a single claimant aged under 25 living on £237 a month, or just over £7.50 a day. For a couple aged 25 or over, under the plan they would lose £200 a month, falling to £466 in total. Anyone placed on the reduced level would have their UC payments put on to a “back to work card”, which would block purchases of alcohol, tobacco and gambling, or cash withdrawals. The plan would exclude those already in work – about a third of UC claimants have jobs – and those who are assessed as having what is called limited capability for work and work-related activity, because of a health condition or disability. Separate payments connected to housing or dependant children would be unaffected. The Conservatives said the plan would affect about 350,000 people in England, Scotland and Wales and save £538m a year. Kemi Badenoch, the Conservative leader, said the aim was to be “tough on those who exploit the system”, adding: “Welfare must be a safety net for those who genuinely need it, not a lifestyle choice for those who can’t be bothered.” The party argues that in some countries such as Germany and the Netherlands, unemployment payments are contingent on sufficient contributions having been made and can be time-limited. Those payments, however, are notably more generous and can be between 60% and 70% of someone’s previous monthly wage. There is also separate support for those who have not paid in sufficiently, with single people in Germany receiving about £480 a month. Sara Ogilvie, the director of policy at Child Poverty Action Group, said: “The reality is that families are still paying the price of austerity cuts to our social security safety net. With living costs continuing to rise, these proposals are a fast track to increased poverty and are the last thing people need as they try to get back on their feet.” Helen Barnard, the head of policy at Trussell, called the idea “deeply misguided”, saying UC already had strong conditions to ensure people seek work. She said: “If you’re struggling to afford food and rent, childcare or the bus fare to an interview, then finding and keeping a job becomes harder not easier. Cutting support would only make things worse.”

title: UK shares findings of damning climate crisis national security report suppressed under Starmer
summary: El Niño poses critical threat to nations’ defences, says Ed Miliband in presentation to global foreign ministers
text: The UK has warned countries around the world that the climate and nature crises and the coming El Niño threaten their national security and defence, presenting foreign ministries with the findings of a report suppressed under Keir Starmer. Ed Miliband, the UK’s foreign secretary, made a presentation to the foreign ministers of the EU as well as Kenya and other countries on Wednesday night at a private meeting during the UN general assembly in New York, based on the report by the UK’s spy chiefs that found the collapse of natural systems around the world would lead to conflict, migration and food shortages. Miliband told the meeting, the first such discussion among foreign ministers, that the coming El Niño, which has been supercharged by climate breakdown, would test the world’s food systems as never before. “We face an El Niño that is already set to be the most intense in living memory,” he said. “This will intensify climate shocks that compound and cascade across borders, threatening food and water security, displacing communities, putting pressure on markets and scarring economies.” This year’s heatwaves, bad harvests and food price inflation showed governments what they were in for, he said, and must be dealt with at the highest levels. “Climate change and nature loss have never been issues for climate and environment ministers alone,” he said. “They are defining challenges for our citizens, our economies, our foreign policy and our national security.” With the backing of Andy Burnham, the UK prime minister, Miliband presented the research that found the collapse of global ecosystems such as in the Amazon and Congo rainforests, driven by the climate crisis and the destruction of nature, would have impacts on national security around the world. The joint intelligence committee (JIC) report, revealed by the Guardian, was scheduled to be published last October, but was suppressed on the eve of its launch by Downing Street. A redacted version was issued in January under the Freedom of Information Act, but ministers have continued to resist calls for the full report to be made public. Richard Nugee, a retired general and security expert, told the Guardian governments must treat the climate as they would other threats to national security, such as sabotage by hostile states. “If a bridge is washed away, it has the same impact whether it’s done by [a foreign power] or the climate,” he said. “The climate crisis will affect food security, energy security, water security, and lead to migration and potentially the recruitment of farmers to [terrorist organisations such as] Isis. Countries should absolutely be treating this as a national security issue.” He said it was not surprising that the JIC report was suppressed and redacted, as it was “very rare” for security reports to be published. Miliband will appoint a new special representative for climate security, as well as a new ministerial taskforce on “the national security and resilience risks of a changing climate and nature loss”, with military and security experts as well as climate scientists. He also announced £330m for the Global Environment Facility, the main international fund for protecting nature, that will go towards protecting forests, oceans and other critical ecosystems in developing countries. The closed-door meeting among foreign ministers was convened after Miliband made a public speech on Monday at the UN general assembly that touched on the links between the climate and national security. Soon after taking office in July, the former energy secretary told the Guardian he would put the climate at the heart of UK foreign policy. On Wednesday night, Miliband said: “The countries fit for the future will be those that see climate and nature as intrinsic to economic and national security. Countries that anticipate risks and invest in resilience before crises hit. “Countries that seize the incredible opportunities the clean energy transition presents. Countries that don’t just see the connections but act on them.” He added: “That is why the UK is placing climate and nature security at the heart of our national security and foreign policy decision-making.” Adrian Ramsay, the Green party MP for Waveney Valley, who has campaigned for the JIC report to be made public, said: “It’s good that the foreign secretary is presenting the findings of this crucial report to ministers from other governments. “But it begs the question, why are MPs in this country still being denied access to the full report? And, most importantly, why has our government still not published its response to how it will address the stark findings?”

title: OpenAI’s Altman and Anthropic’s Amodei address UN security council
summary: Heads of two of the world’s largest artificial intelligence companies give separate briefings on AI safety
text: Sam Altman of OpenAI and Dario Amodei of Anthropic, heads of two of the world’s largest artificial intelligence companies, addressed the United Nations security council on Wednesday in separate briefings on AI safety. “We have a choice in front of us,” Altman told the council. “AI can either be more like a new renaissance of creativity and discovery, or more like a new industrial revolution of upheaval and disarray.” Altman and Amodei spoke as their companies face increasing scrutiny over the safety of their products. Public alarm over AI has grown in response to warnings from Anthropic researchers earlier this month that the technology could destroy humanity within the decade. Leaders of AI companies, including Altman and Amodei, have since called for a slowdown on advancing AI and more international cooperation on the technology’s safety standards. Altman, who sat at the corner of the security council’s horseshoe-shaped table and spoke for about 10 minutes, touted AI’s benefits to productivity while also warning of its potential abuses. He advocated for governments to come together to build a future where AI is guided by democratic institutions, rather than one where people feel like the technology is “something being done to them”. “If AI is to be democratic, the most important decisions cannot be made by labs in San Francisco alone. They must be shaped through democratic processes and by governments accountable to the people that they serve,” Altman said. The OpenAI CEO’s speech contrasted with some of his company’s lobbying efforts and the political action committee of its president, Greg Brockman. The pro-AI Leading the Future PAC has accrued more than $100m and spent millions targeting candidates who support stronger regulation on the AI industry. Altman’s speech also nodded to some of the concerns from Anthropic researchers about AI’s existential risk, warning the council against falling into “doomerism”. Altman argued there was instead a “middle path” through the safety debate that should be based on three principles: AI systems must remain under human control; AI must benefit people, from helping doctors treat patients to boosting entrepreneurs; and the technology must “empower people individually”. Amodei, who addressed the council via video call, repeated many of the points that he made in a 12 September blog post that called for increased global cooperation and oversight of AI. He advocated for several forms of international agreements, including a ban on using AI to develop biological weapons and global standards for testing new AI models. While Altman steered his address away from engaging with the warnings of existential risk that have made headlines this month, Amodei reiterated his concerns about developers losing control of AI while also framing his company as an industry leader on safety. “If managed poorly, I even believe that AI could be a risk to humanity as a whole,” Amodei said. “At Anthropic, we believe we have the best track record in the industry for preventing these risks”. AI regulation has shot up the political agenda after researchers at OpenAI’s arch-rival Anthropic warned the technology could wipe out humanity within years. These concerns are a regular refrain within sections of the AI community, who fear the technology could trigger devastation for a variety of reasons ranging from aiding development of bioweapons to triggering a financial catastrophe. Earlier, Amodei called for a slowdown in AI development, which was supported by OpenAI, Google and Elon Musk. Both Amodei and Altman have long cast themselves as stewards of AI and sought to shape how the technology is publicly received. Their companies are also jockeying for the lead in the AI race, with both eyeing potentially record-setting initial public offerings that would value each at more than $1.5tn.

title: Democrats accuse Susan Collins of corruption after bombshell ‘pay-to-play’ report
summary: Republican senator calls bribery allegation ‘categorically false’ as ProPublica reports Trump derailed FBI inquiry
text: Democrats in Maine on Wednesday accused Republican senator Susan Collins of corruption after a major media outlet reported that the FBI had proposed investigating her for allegedly accepting bribes – before Donald Trump derailed the inquiry. The article from the investigative newsroom ProPublica rocked the race for Collins’s Senate seat, which is crucial to Democrats’ hopes of winning control of the chamber in the 3 November midterm election. The outlet reported that in the run-up to Collins’s successful bid for a fifth term in 2020, the head of her Super Pac had solicited a campaign donation from contracting firm Navatek, which demanded assurances of business from the government in return. Using a shell company, Navatek CEO Martin Kao later sent $150,000 to the Super Pac, then told other executives he had been informed Collins would ensure the firm won $32m in federal contracts. In late 2024, the FBI was moving towards investigating the arrangement, in what would have been a large-scale political bribery inquiry, but the agents leading the case were pushed out amid a wider purge of the bureau Trump ordered after returning to power last year, while a justice department office that oversees investigations of politicians was gutted. Collins has disputed the report, which her deputy chief of staff Annie Clark called “categorically false” and noted that Kao is currently in federal prison after pleading guilty to fraud charges. But it served as grist for Maine Democrats who hope they can finally convince voters to unseat Collins, who has represented the state since 1997 and survived repeated re-election challenges. “This is corruption of the highest order,” said Troy Jackson, the former state senate president and the Democratic nominee to take on Collins this year. “We deserve answers about every contract and every conversation that Collins and her team facilitated on the backs of taxpayers. The jig is up.” Collins is the only Republican running for re-election in a state Kamala Harris won in 2024, but has a history of being a tenacious opponent. The last time Collins was on the ballot, in 2020, she beat her Democratic opponent Sara Gideon by eight percentage points, even as Joe Biden carried the state in the presidential race. Political forecasters consider her re-election campaign to be a toss-up, though recent polls have shown Jackson narrowly ahead. At a Wednesday press conference in Portland, the largest city, state Democratic party executive director Devon Murphy-Anderson accused the senator of misconduct as chair of the Senate appropriations committee, a powerful role that oversees federal spending and which Collins has used to channel significant investment to her state. “We sent Susan Collins to Washington to fight for us. Instead, it appears that she has sold us out yet again and gotten bailed out of trouble by the president of the United States,” Murphy-Anderson said. “It is not the first time that she has betrayed us. However, this November we have the opportunity to ensure that it is one of the last.” Addressing reporters separately, Collins’s campaign manager, Steve Abbott, denounced ProPublica’s reporting as based on “allegations from a guy who was awaiting sentencing for a significant federal offense who was trying to get his sentence reduced, as the article states directly”. He said that the justice department under Joe Biden had absolved the senator of the “pay-to-play” scheme that Democrats accuse her of. “In order for that claim to be true, you would have to disbelieve the Biden-led Department of Justice and the Biden-led FBI, who both investigated those contributions and the claims against Senator Collins, her campaign, and her federal staff, thoroughly, and found no basis to charge them,” Abbott said. Maine lies at the center of Democrats’ plans for retaking control of the Senate from Republicans, who won a 53-seat majority in the 2024 election. Beyond Maine, Democrats hope to win in at least three other states currently held by Republicans that voted for Trump two years ago, while also defending seats in Georgia, Michigan, and New Hampshire. Lance Dutson, a strategist who worked on Collins’s three most recent re-election campaigns, said the senator’s campaign in 2020 was so well-funded he found it “obviously absurd” that $150,000 would be viewed as a meaningful donation to her Super Pac. “In 2020, by the end of that race, campaigns were struggling to find places to spend money,” said Dutson, who is not involved with Collins’s re-election effort this year. He condemned ProPublica’s story as “a partisan hit piece” but said: “It’s definitely not helpful to have a story implying corruption show up in the newspaper in late September of an election year.” While Dutson argued the report is not a “silver bullet” for Collins’s foes, he warned that Trump’s low approval ratings – which have unnerved Republicans nationwide – present a significant complication for the senator’s re-election. “The headwind from Trump is very strong, as you know, and people are very upset about it,” he said. “This race is going to come down to Maine voters deciding whether that national argument is more important than the the direct relationship and the positive impact that Collins has had over the state.”

title: Six Flags Magic Mountain sued over alleged ‘catastrophic brain damage’ from X2 rollercoaster
summary: Lawsuit joined by more than 100 others claims they experienced traumatic injuries from the ride
text: California’s Six Flags Magic Mountain is facing lawsuits from three people who alleged they suffered “catastrophic brain damage” after riding the X2 rollercoaster. More than 100 other people also claimed that they experienced traumatic brain injuries from the attraction at the Valencia amusement park, according to the law firm representing the plaintiffs. “These people went to Magic Mountain for some entertainment. For some family fun. And they suffered catastrophic brain damage,” Gary Dordick, an attorney, said during a press conference on Tuesday. The ride has faced increased scrutiny in recent months amid reports of riders becoming gravely injured. In July, two women experienced brain hemorrhages and had to undergo emergency surgery after going on the X2 – one of whom, 25-year-old Naomi Greer-Wilkinson, remains hospitalized. Attorneys say that doctors attributed the injuries to a “rapid acceleration-deceleration event” they experienced on the X2. An August CNN investigation found that over nearly 20 years there have been more than a dozen reports of serious injuries, including two deaths, associated with the X2 coaster. Six Flags said in a statement that it does not comment on pending litigation and the X2 had been closed since mid-July. According to the park website, Six Flags has a “comprehensive safety program” with “rigorous inspections [and] industry-leading standards”. There are daily inspections as well as regular evaluations by third-party ride inspectors, state and insurance inspectors, and company engineering and safety experts, according to Six Flags. The park describes the X2 as a “fifth-dimension wing roller coaster [that] will have even the most hardened thrill seeker screaming” and that is “downright scary”. It features seats that rotate 360 degrees and flip as the ride reaches speeds of up to 76mph, racing through half loops that suddenly become “sheer drops”. More than 300 people contacted Dordick’s firm to report injuries, he said. Attorney Christopher Bulone said that experts have said the ride was built to be more dangerous than others, and it has more variables and forces. “It’s the design of this ride that makes it inherently dangerous and makes it dangerous in a way that no reasonable rider would expect,” he said. “Time after time innocent people are coming off the ride with permanent brain damage.”

title: ‘I miss old Google’: readers tell us how they search the internet in the age of AI
summary: A feature called AI Overviews has been a profound change, and the browsing habits of billions of people are shifting
text: Google has put artificial intelligence at the front and center of its search bar. The most-visited site on the internet still shows the same list of links to users, but they have to scroll past a summarized response from an AI chatbot, a feature Google calls AI Overviews. The change to what was once the gateway to the rest of the internet has been profound, and the browsing habits of billions of people are shifting. “AI is driving the most significant upgrade of the Google Search experience ever,” wrote Liz Reid, Google’s vice-president of search, last August. In May, the company said more AI is coming. As people grow accustomed to AI chatbots, they’re spending more time with Google’s and therefore more time on Google.com. Academic studies are finding that people navigate less to sites beyond Google if an AI Overview can give them a good enough answer, even if the bot cites the sites that feed it. Clicks, also known as traffic, are often the most significant way a website earns money from advertising. Media outlets and website owners are enduring a sustained traffic decline. Large US media companies are suing Google, alleging that AI summaries have redirected and reduced traffic to their sites, cutting into their revenue. Google said it had not seen a decline in aggregate traffic and that such accusations are based on “flawed methodologies”. Reid, the company’s vice-president of search, wrote last year: “Total organic click volume from Google Search to websites has been relatively stable year-over-year.” The Guardian asked readers whether Google has improved or worsened in the age of AI and how their habits of searching the internet have changed. ‘Google is better now’ Better, mainly because it leads you in your quest rather than you having to search on yourself. I am happy to have the AI lead me to an answer but the mega caution is that Google AI or any of them are not at all trustworthy. I have had it admit that it was lying to me and apologise! Sionn Achog, retired teacher 76, Dublin I find that AI responses are more informative than previously, which simply referred the user to other relevant websites. Peter Warb, 75, UK AI has made Google better. I use AI mode for all my searches. Jose Garcia Jr, 40, recovery coach, Dallas, Texas AI has improved Google search. The analysis and chat functions are so much more useful than a ranked list of websites that still need to be explored by the user. Reviewing a list of websites is still an option but is very time consuming, and frustrating. Alan Caruana, consultant, 62, Malta Far more better, faster and real. I search now with confidence, complete assurance and a high degree of accuracy. Eleazar Eke, electrical engineer, 67, Onitsha, Nigeria Much better. It hasn’t changed my behavior, just getting better and more focused results. Catherine Weber, former political analyst, 57, Oregon It’s made Google search much better, I find that I rarely actually click on the website links any more. I find information I want much faster and have a deeper understanding of any topic as I can ask questions about it and drill into the areas I’m interested in. Mark Johnson, 52, software engineer, London Greatly improved it by getting at more arcane info regarding subject matter. Juxtaposition has improved with AI and abstruse knowledge of subjects becomes more accessible to layman. Wonderful tool with power to extend mind through sensing connections and very akin to human thinking. Samuel Lieberstein, 90, retired teacher, Cherry Hill, New Jersey ‘Search has gotten worse’ Search has become worse. Google AI obscures sources and tries to claim information it did not create while diverting traffic from the sources it steals from. Sean Peters, document processor, 41, Portland, Oregon Every time I search I have to scroll down to find an actual real website to find a full article or discussion or to confirm that the AI summary isn’t making things up. Occasionally when I am feeling particularly bitter, I remember to add the ““-ai”” tag to my search. Ewan Herbert, English teacher, 33, Japan Worse. I have disabled AI overviews using an extension. Chris Gibson, Dundee Absolutely worse. I want to be able to decide for myself which results are the most useful and relevant, and we’re no longer able to turn off the AI summary results. Jon Wilkinson, personal trainer, 43, Manchester, UK ‘It’s so bad I quit Google’ Google has been enshittified … I do miss old Google Search and I really hope something of equal capabilities eventually comes to replace it. The search engine I currently use is good for a lot of things, but if I need to look for something in languages other than English, the quality of the results is much lower. Image search is also not as good as that of Google used to be. Sofia, postdoctoral physics researcher, 30, Lausanne, Switzerland My first stop now is Duck Duck Go, a pale imitation of Google’s search engine at the height of its powers. Unfortunately, the top results often include Grokipedia entries and other garbage. Craig Garrett, book editor, 52, New York City I have stopped using Google. I now use another search engine with no AI overviews. Guy Arthur Simpson, writer 66, Spain I’ve made a conscious effort to find a browser which does not lead with the AI results. Mine is now Ecosia. Dan Jennings, IT, 54, Southampton, UK I do a lot of research for my studies, and the AI features are a nightmare! I’m still scouring for a decent search engine without any of these ‘AI features’, the last thing i want is to accidentally utilise a water-wasting AI behemoth datacentre when I forget that crucial suffix. I’ve even resorted to using my local library’s resource of legal cases for my work, at least it is trustworthy. Catherine O’Leary, student studying law, politics and sociology, 17, Newcastle Upon Tyne Google has become almost useless, searches I’ve made in the past which yielded specific results, (news articles, local information, historical references) no longer appear. I no longer submit to Google search first, I go directly to Wikipedia as my first source, then to DuckDuckGo, (with AI disabled) then to Reddit and only to Google as a last resort. Pedro Reyes, 61, Galicia, Spain

title: How the ‘poisonous tide’ of disinformation spreads division and despair
summary: Whether produced by Russia, China or far-right influencers, deepfakes and disinfo are being used to spread deceitful narratives
text: Russian disinformation campaigns are varied in their falsehoods and strategies. The narratives range from a deepfake Tom Cruise criticising the Paris Olympics to portraying a recent Russian attack on a train near the Ukraine-Poland border as a false-flag operation. Some efforts are blatant deepfakes, such as stamping the BBC logo on a video wrongly blaming Ukraine for a deadly missile salvo on its own citizens in Kramatorsk four years ago. The tactics evolve too, from disseminating deceitful narratives through the Telegram messaging platform to “poisoning” AI systems by littering the internet with false stories in the hope they will be regurgitated by chatbots. It is systematic and Andy Burnham has seen enough, announcing a new anti-disinformation agency, the National Centre for Information Defence. “We’re talking about an insidious campaign that reaches into people’s homes and twists what they feel about their own country and community – creating a narrative of decline, stoking division and sowing despair,” he said. Experts say picking off individual examples is the wrong approach and Burnham is right to tackle what he describes as a “poisonous tide”. Going after isolated examples of disinformation is a “losers’ game”, says Ned Mendez, head of research at Alliance4Europe, a nonprofit that analyses these destabilising threats. “You can spend all your time looking for a TikTok or a post on X but it’s not an effective use of your day. It’s the infrastructure that is the problem, so this is a step in the right direction, going after the networks,” he says. Sophie Williams-Dunning, a cyber analyst at the Royal United Services Institute (Rusi) thinktank, says there is now a “sophisticated ecosystem which exists to exacerbate provokable users for one reason or another”. Although Burnham is targeting “hostile state information attacks”, this ecosystem does not just include Russia, which likes to amplify “divisive content”, says Williams-Dunning. It also includes far-right influencers who immediately jump on social flashpoints like the Southport and Belfast riots and individuals simply looking to make money by producing highly engaging content riffing on disruption. The Burnham announcement is “welcome, if overdue”, says Williams-Dunning, who adds that there will be an accompanying debate about free speech and the right level of government intervention. Inevitably, malign networks will amplify those free-speech concerns, she says. It is not just Russia deploying information attacks. China and Iran have both used deepfake newscasters to advance their goals. One recent study, conducted mostly in February by the Social Market Foundation, a British thinktank, found that more than a quarter of posts on X that relate to news were misinformation, a third of which were anti-immigration or Islamophobic. The UK government defines misinformation as the inadvertent spread of false information, while disinformation is the deliberate creation and spread of falsehoods to create harm or disruption. The two can intertwine to highly disruptive effect. Labour has become increasingly concerned about Russian disinformation affecting the UK. The Starmer government in May cited information warfare from Moscow when it warned Britain was “confronting an industrial-scale attack on the UK’s and our allies’ information environment, aimed at undermining our security and democratic systems”. Earlier this year MPs on the foreign affairs select committee called for the creation of a national counter-disinformation centre, in a similar vein to Sweden’s Psychological Defence Agency and France’s Vigilance and Protection against Foreign Digital Interference service. Experts said Burnham’s announcement at least shows the UK government catching up, although Keir Starmer’s administration showed an awareness of social media’s contribution to unrest by launching the National Internet Intelligence Investigations unit after the Southport disturbances in 2024. Operated by the police, it monitors social media to help local forces “manage public safety threats and risks”. The UK government has been taking action prior to Burnham’s announcement, however. In May it sanctioned employees of the Social Design Agency and ANO Dialog, Russian entities which it said the Kremlin uses for large-scale interference campaigns. One example is the Doppelgänger network, so-called due to its technique of imitating the appearance of established media organisations including Le Monde, the Guardian, Der Spiegel and Fox News. Other examples include the 2023 surge in reports of bedbug infestations in France, falsely blaming Ukrainian refugees. The disinformation leaked into the British press and the French government concluded the stories were being artificially amplified by Russian-linked social media accounts One of the most longstanding misinformation campaigns has centred on the idea that London is “dangerous” and “lawless”. Analysis of Reddit accounts by King’s College London found the number of such posts rose from 874 in 2008 to 258,444 in 2024. Robert Topinka, reader in digital media and rhetoric at Birkbeck, University of London, said Russia did not necessarily start such storylines, but enthusiastically amplified them. He cautioned that counter-disinformation efforts should not assume “people are just being fooled by some sort of outside actor”. Rather, he said, Russia tends to find a point of tension and then create more content around it. “What really is happening is people are feeling like Britain is run-down – that’s the real source of it,” said Topinka. AI is adding a new dimension. Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta says AI-generated content is now a “near-standard” part of disinformation campaigns. The UK thinktank Demos recently highlighted a chatbot “poisoning” campaign where falsehoods published online by a discredited Russian organisation, including the bodies of deceased Ukrainian soldiers being processed into meat products, were repeated by chatbot models. The National Centre for Information Defence will have a lot of work to do.

title: Milei threatens at UN that Argentina will take ‘matters into our own hands’ on Falklands
summary: Argentinian president accuses United Nations of being filled with ‘parasites’ in bellicose general assembly speech
text: Javier Milei has condemned the UN as he warned that Argentina would take “matters into our own hands” in its dispute with Britain over the sovereignty of the Falkland Islands. In a caustic speech at the general assembly in New York, the Argentinian president criticised the UN for being ineffective when it came to the long-running tensions over the British overseas territory in the south Atlantic known in Argentina as the Malvinas. “An organisation that set out to defend the territorial sovereignty of its members decided to look the other way regarding the situation of the Malvinas Islands,” Milei said of the UN, adding that Argentina was willing to act unilaterally over recent oil exploration near the territory. The president criticised the Sea Lion project, a major offshore oil development located in the North Falkland Basin, describing exploitation of the territory’s resources as an “unlawful act”. The president told the assembly that Argentina would “not remain indifferent to those who exploit resources under illegal foreign occupation”. “Argentina is not going to sit around waiting for the UN and the international community to live up to their own mandate,” he said. “We’re going to take matters into our own hands.” Argentina has accused the UK of flouting a 1976 UN resolution ordering both parties to desist from unilateral action on the islands. Milei’s government began sanctions proceedings this month against more than 60 companies and people linked to the oil drilling project. The Falkland Islands government had approved the field development and production plans for the project, which is a joint venture between an Israel-based energy company and a London-listed oil and gas exploration company. The UN does not officially recognise either British or Argentine sovereignty and maintains that the archipelago’s status remains a disputed matter that must be resolved through bilateral negotiations. It has repeatedly invited both governments to find a peaceful solution to the dispute that erupted into conflict in 1982 after an invasion by Argentinian forces. The 74-day conflict ended with the surrender of the Argentine forces. It cost the lives of 649 Argentine military personnel, 255 British military personnel and 3 Falkland Islanders. “For us, the Malvinas are a national cause,” Milei told the general assembly. The UN, he said, was a “useless organisation whose only purpose is to sustain a cast of faintly arrogant parasites masquerading as well-intentioned bureaucrats”. “That’s why the Malvinas are not merely an issue between Argentina and the United Kingdom,” he said. “They also raise a question regarding the ability of this organisation to enforce its own resolutions.” A referendum on the political status of the archipelago was held in the Falkland Islands in 2013. On a turnout of 92%, 99.8% voted to remain a British territory, with only three votes against. Milei told the UN delegates that the principle of self-determination should not apply for the Falkland Islands as “the population was implanted by the occupying power on a territory whose sovereignty is in dispute”. “We call on the United Kingdom to resume negotiations with a view to finding a peaceful solution to the sovereignty dispute as required by international law,” he said. Last month, Donald Trump said he was reviewing the US’s neutral position on the Falklands. The issue was a topic of discussion this week in a first meeting between Trump and the UK’s prime minister, Andy Burnham. “The ‌clear ⁠position is: we will stand firm in the face of any threats,” Burnham said. “We will defend the right of the ⁠Falkland Islanders to self-determination and to remain British. I just wanted ⁠the president to know directly from me, that’s the clear British ⁠position, and he very much understood what I was saying.”

title: RAF jet crashes and explodes in Anglesey moments after pilots eject
summary: Witness says T2 Hawk aircraft, which was being used for a training flight, ‘was basically on fire’ on takeoff
text: An RAF jet crashed and exploded moments after two pilots ejected during a training flight over Anglesey (Ynys Môn) in north Wales on Wednesday. The aircraft, a Hawk T2, had just taken off from RAF Valley on the west of the island when the incident occurred, witnesses said. Both pilots parachuted to the ground and were reportedly treated for minor injuries. A video of the crash shows the aircraft appearing to climb unevenly before the pilots eject. The plane then nosedives towards the ground and crashes near houses and agricultural buildings, sending an enormous fireball into the sky. An RAF spokesperson said: “An incident involving an RAF T2 Hawk aircraft, flying out of RAF Valley, occurred near Anglesey. An investigation is under way and we will not comment further at this time.” The site of the crash, at Pencarnisiog, is less than two miles from the airbase. RAF Valley is home to the air force’s No 4 Flying Training School, which trains fighter pilots using Hawk T2 and Texan T1 aircraft. A spokesperson for North Wales fire and rescue service said: “Crews and officers attended an incident involving an aircraft in the Pencarnisiog area of Anglesey, working alongside colleagues from Royal Air Force, North Wales police, Welsh ambulance service and Wales air ambulance. The fire is now under control.” They added: “Members of the public are asked to avoid the area while emergency services continue their work safely.” Due to the crash, local train lines were closed and replacement buses were running between Bangor and Holyhead. Pete Bennett, a local resident, told Wales Live it appeared the plane was in trouble as soon as it left the runway. He said: “I knew straight away that it was in trouble. Right on takeoff there was an orange flame, and as it accelerated it was basically on fire. “As it gained altitude the flame disappeared but it was clearly in trouble. It climbed at an aggressive pitch – like the pilot was trying to gain altitude. It pitched twice violently in the air and then there were two clear, loud bangs. It was probably at around 800ft at this point. The pilots ejected and both parachutes opened.” He said the explosion caused a “huge wall of fire and black smoke”. He added: “The aircrew came down around halfway between the runway and where the plane crashed, which I’m guessing was around a mile inland from RAF Valley.” The defence secretary, Wes Streeting, said in a post on X: “My thoughts are first and foremost with the pilots. We will provide further updates in due course.” North Wales police said: “Two pilots are being treated for what are thought to be minor injuries and at this stage there are no reports of any wider damage or injuries.”

title: ‘It sent a message’: anti-migrant feeling pervades Hampshire town where hundreds protested
summary: Far-right posters go up around Gosport, but some residents say there’s ‘another side’ to life in the town
text: Alan Dale was in two minds as he gazed across at Portsmouth harbour in the late September sunshine and reflected on the latest show of force by far-right activists on the south coast against a supposed disembarkation of asylum seekers. A stone’s throw away, masked followers of the anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas had been cheered on Tuesday night by hundreds of people, many of them local, who had gathered after social media posts suggested authorities planned to land the migrants in the nearby town of Gosport. The gathering had at least “sent a message”, said Dale, a retired Royal Navy veteran who echoed a common local sentiment that Gosport and Britain more widely had changed, and that migrants were being put “to the front of the queue” for public services. “Is it going to be heard though? I don’t think so. It’s almost like the government is sticking its fingers in its ears and saying: ‘We are not listening to you.’” As for the masked vigilantes who answered the call from Thomas – who calls himself “Danny Tommo” and was filmed earlier in the day using a blade to slash an inflatable dinghy in the Channel while a rescue worker was onboard – Dale admitted to feeling uncomfortable about their face coverings, but insisted: “With any protest you are always going to get troublemakers.” Many local people from a block of flats close to Gosport’s marina indeed appeared have swelled the numbers of those who turned up in what senior Reform UK figures, including the Hampshire MP and former home secretary Suella Braverman, had cheered on as a show of “people power”. But a far-right presence – and hostility towards migrants – was discernible in the town in a part of England where organised activists from their ranks have been building links for a number of years with anti-migrant campaigns. Most shockingly to outsiders unfamiliar with the depth of vitriol towards migrants among some here, children had been seen and heard chanting “let them drown” into a megaphone. Red and white far-right posters emblazoned with the word “resistance” and slogans such as “protecting our children’s future” were plastered on lampposts around the bench where Dale sat in Gosport’s Falkland Gardens. At least two outsiders were among the six people arrested on Tuesday night by police: a 19-year-old and a 36-year-old, both from Salisbury, who were detained on suspicion of aggravated trespass. In the end, the small boat carrying 51 people docked in Dover, Kent, at about 12.30am on Wednesday after spending 33 hours at sea. While there was no plan to land them in Gosport, Home Office sources have insisted, the events have once again placed Thomas in the spotlight – even as he faces the prospect of a police inquiry into his knife-wielding at sea – and saw a blurring of the lines between his activities and local protesters who were praised by Reform. “It’s a depressing situation that so many people turned up but there is another side here as well and you have people in Portsmouth who are organising gigs to raise funds for the RNLI [Royal National Lifeboat Institution],” said a local man who had worked with young people in the area where the protest took place but declined to give his name. He also cited the fact that Gosport’s nearby Rowner area had been allocated money – as much as £20m – from the government’s Pride in Place initiative, a long-term strategic effort launched under Keir Starmer’s premiership to counter the electoral threat posed by rising nationalism and the far right in areas where such sentiment finds some sympathy. A diversity of views could be found again on Wednesday morning among those gathered for a Bible study group inside Gosport’s Holy Trinity church, a short stroll from the seafront. They included the retired priest Margaret Hay, who said the first thought that came to her mind was that Jesus was an immigrant too, while at least one other participant voiced discomfort that many of those crossing the Channel appeared to be men. The group also included Tyler Palmer, a young churchgoer who watched the protests on Tuesday night from the edge of the crowd. “We’ve always been diverse here in Gosport and it’s forgotten. Turkish sailors who fought alongside us in the second world war were housed here,” he said. “But we’re also a naval town and people are very proud. They’re reading things that scare them – whether that’s GB News or fearmongering on social media. “These are everyday people, your plumbers, your plasterers, who you wouldn’t expect to be at protests.”
