title: Bentley launches first fully electric car – with fake engine sounds to replace classic growl
summary: Torcal SUV can travel up to 375 miles on a single charge and is part of a £350m investment in the VW-owned carmaker’s UK business
text: Bentley is launching its first fully electric car – complete with a drum soundtrack to replace the growl of a combustion engine – as part of a £350m investment in its UK business. The vehicle, an SUV called the Torcal, is Bentley’s cheapest, starting at £173,000, and will be built at its factory in Crewe, securing the jobs of the 4,000 workers there. Bentley hopes to win over both EV refuseniks and younger customers with a new synthetic engine noise built from drum recordings based on its old eight-cylinder engines. The feature is designed to give “emotion to the car” and “bridge the gap” to new buyers, said Bentley’s chief executive, Frank-Steffen Walliser. “We expect a younger clientele,” he added, pointing to a more muscular vehicle body shape than previous models and the comparatively low price, which gives “easier access” to the brand, whose cars can cost up to £1.7m for one-off vehicles built to be showstoppers for billionaires. The Torcal launches into a thin market for fully electric luxury SUVs. Arch-rival Rolls-Royce’s only EV is a two-door coupe called the Spectre, which starts at about £330,000. The recently announced Range Rover Electric – considered part of the premium segment rather than luxury – begins retailing at £154,070. It also marks a more tentative entry into the EV market than Bentley once predicted. In 2024, it was forced to abandon plans to launch new electric cars each year from 2025 to 2030, citing poor demand. Walliser said that while early indications showed demand would be strong in the UK, Europe and the Middle East, he admitted: “We managers always say we know but to be honest we don’t know [how much demand there will be].” There are “no plans at the moment” for a second EV launch, he added. “I revised so many long-term plans in the last 10 years that one has to be careful of it.” It is the third big funding announcement in just over a week for Britain’s automotive sector. Nissan has said it will invest £170m to build a new model at its factory in Sunderland, while McLaren will spend £500m on a new factory, creating 1,000 jobs and its first SUV. However, carmakers remain under significant pressure from US tariffs, competition from Chinese rivals and high industrial energy costs. Jaguar Land Rover recently said it would cut 4,000 jobs, citing “intense competition and ongoing geopolitical uncertainty”, while Bentley’s owner, Volkswagen, is cutting 100,000 jobs by 2030. Asked if Bentley was immune from the cuts at VW, Walliser said: “Immune would be the wrong wording. But there’s a very simple rule in Volkswagen. If you’re successful you can run your business. And we consider we are a successful business … it doesn’t bother me too much at the moment.” Bentley itself cut 245 jobs in Crewe earlier this year to reduce costs, and sales have fallen by a third since a 2022 peak of 15,200 cars. Walliser said a period of strong margins after the pandemic was a “post-Covid boom … now we are back to normal”. Walliser said headcount in Crewe will not grow with the investment “for profitability reasons”, but he insisted that “the statement cannot be clearer” about investing in the UK and that the money will partly go towards a new assembly line. Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, said it was the “third win in just seven days for our world-class automotive industry, which truly shows the confidence that businesses have in Britain”. But Walliser said the landscape remained “difficult” for Bentley suppliers. “We see a lot of impact on especially the smaller businesses,” he said, citing new EU rules of origin and high industrial energy prices both in the UK and Europe. “There’s a lot of pressure,” he said. The Torcal can travel up to 375 miles on a single charge, and can power up from 10% full to 80% full in 20 minutes using an ultra-fast charger. The car marks the fourth model in Bentley’s lineup, alongside the Continental, Flying Spur and Bentayga.

title: ‘We hope he’ll accept’: US invites Putin to G20 summit at Trump golf club
summary: Invitation announced by Marco Rubio is likely to raise concerns from Ukraine and EU countries
text: The United States has invited Vladimir Putin to take part in the meeting of the G20 scheduled in Miami in December in what would be the first major summit with the Russian leader present since he launched his invasion of Ukraine in 2022. The invitation, which marks a significant reversal by the Trump administration of Russia’s international isolation, was announced by Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, during a press conference on the sidelines of the United Nations conference in New York. “We’ve invited President Putin to the G20,” Rubio said in a televised press conference following a meeting with Russian foreign minister Sergei Lavrov. “We think it’s an opportunity for him to engage not just with [Trump] but with other world leaders. We hope that’s an invitation he’ll accept.” The Kremlin has not yet responded publicly to the invitation, which is likely to raise concerns from Ukraine and other European leaders who have recently accused Russia of launching hybrid attacks to disrupt logistics and spread political uncertainty among Kyiv’s allies. Russia remains a member of the G20 but Putin has not attended a summit of the body since 2019. He did attend one session virtually in 2023. The December summit is set to take place at the Trump National Doral golf club. Rubio framed the invitation by saying that Trump was willing to meet with “virtually anyone” and that “in order to solve problems, you have to meet with people you disagree with”. He said Trump remained open to meeting with Putin one-on-one in other forums, if “there’s a purpose behind the meeting”. The G20 is a forum of the world’s largest economies and includes the European Union, China, India, the United States, the United Kingdom, and other major countries. European officials were upset by a decision to invite Russian finance minister Anton Siluanov to a meeting of the group’s top economic officials in August and refused to pose in a “family photo” with him at the summit. Zelenskyy had said earlier this month that he would be ready to travel to the summit and would meet with Putin if he attended. “We have to come. We have to meet, to speak and make decisions,” he told German broadcaster Deutsche Welle in an interview. “It’s not about words. What I will tell him or what he wants to tell me, it doesn’t matter. It doesn’t matter. [...] Results matter. That’s it.” On Wednesday, Zelenskyy addressed the United Nations, urging world leaders to keep choking Russia’s revenues and impede its war effort. “Ukrainians understand that this winter could be very harsh for us,” said Zelenskyy. “In response, we will have no choice but to make it painful for Russia too.” Zelenskyy also warned that the war could spread beyond Ukraine if Putin was not stopped. Rubio on Wednesday also indicated that he had spoken with Lavrov about the accusations of “hybrid attacks” in Europe, saying that one concern about the war was that “it could metastasize and spread into other places”. Trump is currently seeking to negotiate a partial ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine that would include attacks on Russian oil refineries in order to take pressure off global energy prices. In particular, Trump has called on Zelenskyy to halt attacks against Russian oil in order to reduce prices on diesel fuel, which have spiked to almost double their price last year in the United States before midterm elections for Congress. Trump and Zelenskyy met on the sidelines of the United Nations on Tuesday for a rare face-to-face discussion of measures to end the war. Zelenskyy called for a trilateral meeting with Trump and Putin to end the war, but the Kremlin has declined past attempts for direct meetings with Zelenskyy. “President Trump, our teams, and I spoke about how to end the war. This is the priority. We are ready. I’m not sure Russia is ready as of today, but anyhow, we spoke about an energy ceasefire,” Zelenskyy said on Tuesday. Despite efforts to broker a ceasefire, however, Russia has continued to pummel Kyiv and other major Ukrainian cities with drone and missile attacks. Kyiv hit a major Russian oil refinery over the weekend in its largest attack on Russia’s capital yet. For the past two days, Kyiv has come under particularly severe attack from jet-powered Shahed drones – swifter and harder to intercept than their predecessors. As has been the case since mid-August, the drone attacks have come in the daytime as well as at night, disrupting ordinary life, schools and kindergartens. On Wednesday morning an acrid stench of burning filled the city centre after multiple explosions, and the clear autumnal sky was clouded with plumes of black smoke. A petrol station, warehouses, a business centre and a transport infrastructure building were hit, according to Kyiv’s mayor, Vitali Klitschko. As of mid-morning, one person had died and eight had been injured. Explosions were seen near the capital’s main railway station. Congress last week passed a sweeping sanctions bill against Russia that would also give Trump the authority to levy 100% tariffs against top purchasers of Russian energy exports, including China and India. Democrats, who mostly opposed the bill, said that it gave Trump too much power to levy tariffs and that they could be used against US allies as well. In response to what has happened, the Democratic members of the House foreign affairs committee posted on X: “Trump signed the Russia sanctions bill 5 days ago. Today Rubio makes clear the administration has no intention of isolating Russia for its war of aggression in Ukraine.” Charlotte Higgins contributed reporting from Kyiv • This article was amended on 27 September 2026 to clarify that the Democrats on the House foreign affairs committee posted the X comment on the Russia sanctions bill.

title: McDonald’s to take on KFC and rivals as Gen Z flock to fried chicken
summary: Fast food giant aiming to increase share of global chicken market as rising cost of beef hits profits
text: McDonald’s is betting on fried chicken as health concerns and the rising price of beef shift dining habits. The company said that it aimed to take an extra 1.5 percentage point-share of the global chicken market by 2030, with an aim to increase its share of drinks by the same proportion. McDonald’s said the growth in chicken, a lower-priced protein, would not come at the expense of beef burger sales, saying it aimed maintain its “leadership position in beef”. Chris Kempczinski, McDonald’s chair and chief executive, told investors in May that the chain’s share of the chicken market was in the “high teens”, compared with about 45% in beef, but the chicken market was bigger and growing at twice the pace of its red meat counterpart. McDonald’s has warned that the rising cost of beef, as well as energy, was hitting profits for its franchisees. The chain also faces heavy competition from the rapid rise of chicken shop chains including Popeyes and Wingstop as well as expansion by the more established player KFC, driven particularly by the popularity of fried chicken among younger Gen Z consumers. “McDonald’s has the unmatched scale, customer insights, brand loyalty and operational capabilities to not only adapt to the next wave of change in our industry, but to turn it into an advantage,” said Kempczinski. The chain also said it would spend about $8.5bn (£6.4bn) to help franchisees with rent and improve their restaurants. The change comes amid the rapid rise in chicken shops and sales of chicken and the surging price of beef, which has risen by more than 20% in the past two years in the US and the UK, according to figures from the UK’s Agriculture and Horticulture Development Board. Peter Backman, an independent food service industry analyst, said “chicken is cheaper and perceived as healthier”. He said the rising price of beef was likely to be a “drag on the market” for burgers and offering more chicken would enable McDonald’s to sell more to its fans and “steal a bit of market share from other quick service operators”. He said higher drinks sales were probably attractive as beverages tended to be more profitable. In the UK, 39% of consumers used chicken shops in 2025 compared with 37% in 2023, according to market research firm Mintel, with Gen Z usage hitting 52%, almost matching pizza outlets at 56%. A plethora of other options, including Asian-inspired chains such as Wagamama, are also eating into the market share of burgers and pizza. Late last year Domino’s Pizza Group announced that its chief executive of two years had stepped down with immediate effect, less than two weeks after he appeared to suggest the UK may be approaching “peak pizza” and that the chain should try to broaden its menu to sell more chicken.

title: No signs Chagos deal can be adapted to suit Trump, say UK officials
summary: Agreement with Mauritius over Diego Garcia unlikely to be revived unless president changes his mind, insiders believe
text: The Chagos Islands deal is on hold for as long as Donald Trump objects to it, UK officials believe, with no immediate signs it can be adapted to suit the US president. After Trump savaged the three-way plan as “a terrible deal” during a meeting with Andy Burnham at the UN general assembly, the prime minister said he was “confident” the UK would be able to find a solution to revive the idea. But while efforts are still taking place to do this, there is an acceptance in the government that it is extremely unlikely unless Trump has another change of heart. “Until the president changes his mind there will not be any progress,” one official said. “We are where we are. We were waiting for the president to present a view, which he has.” The UK signed a treaty last year to transfer sovereignty over the Chagos Islands to Mauritius, while retaining control of the joint UK-US military base on Diego Garcia, part of the Indian Ocean archipelago, under a 99-year lease. Mauritius was set to receive £165m for three years and £120m a year from the fourth year. Wes Streeting, the UK defence secretary, said on Wednesday morning that payments worth at least £120m to Mauritius were on hold given the deal could not go ahead without US support. “This deal as it is currently constituted can’t go ahead without American support,” Streeting told BBC Radio 4’s Today’s programme. “So we have to get a deal to a place where it commands American support as well as the agreement of the government of Mauritius and our government.” The US had supported the plan, but Trump changed his mind amid a wider deterioration of relations with Keir Starmer over the lack of UK support for the US attacks on Iran. Speaking after their first in-person meeting at the UN in New York on Tuesday, Trump praised Burnham but gave no ground on his scepticism about the Chagos deal. “I don’t support it. I think it’s terrible,” Trump told reporters. “It was a terrible deal. [Mauritius] all of a sudden say they have ownership. Somebody has ownership that never showed up before, after decades and centuries. I think it’s ridiculous.” Burnham later said he had “inherited the situation” and had told Trump “that we will work to find that resolution between the different sides”. He added: “It was clear that we need to come to that agreement, but I’m confident we can find it working with our US partners.” Given Trump’s objections appear based on the core element of the deal – the transfer of sovereignty to Mauritius – there appears to be no immediate way forward. The UK government has previously made clear that Washington’s approval is a prerequisite for the plan. UK officials stress, however, that while Burnham inherited the impasse from Starmer, there is no intention to deprioritise a plan, begun under Rishi Sunak, that the government says is vital to ensure the future of the strategically vital Diego Garcia base, given Mauritian claims to sovereignty of the archipelago. “It’s not back to the drawing board, as we do need to find a diplomatic solution to this,” another UK official said. “Everyone agrees something has to be done, which is why several prime ministers and even more foreign secretaries have tried to get it over the line.” Streeting stressed the same point to the BBC, saying: “The ostrich strategy of sticking our heads in the sand … I would caution is not a wise strategy when it concerns one of the most sensitive national security assets we have anywhere in the world.”

title: UK to launch military squadron to protect satellites in space
summary: New RAF unit will warn of incoming missile attacks, and support offensive and defensive operations
text: A new military unit dedicated to defending satellites, protecting services people need on Earth and potentially supporting offensive operations is being launched by the UK. The No III Space Effects Squadron will be announced on Wednesday, with the defence secretary, Wes Streeting, warning that Britain needs to “keep pace in the new space race”. “Control of the waves was the essential ingredient in 19th-century deterrence,” he will tell the Space Power conference. “That is why Britain built the finest naval power in history. In the 20th century it was control of the skies, and so we built a world class air force to protect us. This century will depend on control of space.” The new Royal Air Force (RAF) squadron will protect satellites used to warn of incoming missile attacks, provide communications and help guide ships, the Ministry of Defence (MoD) said. It will bring together specialist personnel from across the armed forces to counter hostile activity in orbit and defend satellites the nation depends on every day. Two existing units – No I Space Operations Squadron and No II Space Warning Squadron – already allow the RAF to watch and warn of threats in space. The MoD said the new squadron would act against those threats, using advanced technology, including electronic warfare, “to disrupt, degrade and deny hostile actions”. It is intended to support offensive and defensive space operations and will expand over time as new capabilities enter service. The chief of the air staff, Air Chief Marshal Sir Harv Smyth, will say on Wednesday: “Space no longer supports operations from the sidelines. It’s a domain of direct competition, where our military advantage can be won or lost.” The UK has formally ruled out destructive anti-satellite missile testing and the government said on Wednesday that it continues to work through the UN committee on the peaceful uses of outer space to promote norms, rules and principles of responsible space behaviours. Smyth and Streeting are speaking at the conference in London which being promoted by the Space Command wing of the RAF. The moves come after warnings that other nations have been building up military capabilities in space. The UK Space Command said last year that Russia was attempting to jam UK military satellites on a regular basis. The US, which established the United States Space Force in 2019 as the sixth branch of the its armed forces, said earlier this month that it had deployed weapons in space for the first time. Responding to the US announcement, China’s foreign ministry said Washington was “preparing for war in outer space”, and warned against turning space “into a battlefield, as well as an arms race there”. The UK announcement on Wednesday comes weeks after the release of a government strategy designed to strengthen defences against threats from space.

title: Philadelphia teacher admits to lying about being Palestinian and Black: ‘I hid the truth’
summary: Local advocacy groups say they have cut ties with Hannah Gann, who ‘fully lied about her identity and background’
text: A Philadelphia teacher is facing criticism from her fellow colleagues and activists after it was revealed that she fabricated being both Palestinian and Black. The Racial Justice Organizing Committee (RJOC) and Philly Educators for Palestine (PEFP) announced over the weekend that it was cutting ties with “one of their long-time members”, Hannah Gann, who “completely lied about her identity and background, claiming at various times to be Palestinian, Tunisian and Black”. Members of both organizations met with Gann and questioned her about her background. After over an hour of discussion, Gann “finally admitted she lied”, the joint statement said, adding: “We asked her to publicly acknowledge that she is a white woman of Jewish heritage and an Israeli settler family. “We will no longer work with Hannah, and she will no longer be welcome in any of our organizing spaces … We recognize the profound harm this has caused; Palestinians whose identity and struggle were appropriated, the Black community, young people, organizers, and organizations whose trust and resources were exploited,” PEFP and RJOC continued. Gann released a separate statement on Instagram a few days later, saying in a video: “One of the most sickening aspects of facing what I’ve done is seeing the way that the blowback is falling on people, groups, communities and causes I genuinely care about. I recognize it’s far too late for me to mitigate all the damage I’ve done, but I’m determined to try to do what I can. “I hid the truth or outright lied about my background to everyone in my life. There is not a single person on this planet … who knew what I was doing … The fact that I lied about who I was does not mean anyone else who speaks up for Palestine is lying and does not erase the urgency of listening to voices on the ground, voices who are courageously telling us about an ongoing genocide, even as the state of Israel deliberately targets journalists and others who are speaking the truth for extermination,” she continued. The Guardian has reached out to Gann for additional comment. Videos and local news articles online showed Gann’s involvement over the years in local pro-Palestinian activism, with one Facebook video posted by RJOC in November 2025 featuring Gann addressing attendees at a teach-in. “Philly Educators for Palestine is bigger and stronger than ever before. Curious about who we are and what our purpose is? Listen to these powerful words from one of our founders, Hannah Gann, as she welcomed attendees to our most recent teach-in,” the video caption said. Gann, who teaches at Philadelphia’s Workshop School, according to the Philadelphia Inquirer, was also the subject of a moving billboard outside her school in 2024. The mobile display featured a photo of her wearing a keffiyeh alongside the words: “Hannah Gann: 10th Grade Teacher & Philadelphia’s Leading Antisemite,” the grassroots outlet Rethinking Schools reported. The Philadelphia Inquirer, which reviewed a document compiled by the Philly Palestine Coalition, noted that Gann often made references to alleged Palestinian relatives “including a Palestinian-born grandfather whom the PPC found was actually born in Baltimore, citing historical draft records and her great-grandfather’s US naturalization papers”. Meanwhile, a former University of Pennsylvania classmate told the Philadelphia Inquirer that Gann was known in college “as a self-proclaimed white Jewish woman with family in the occupied West Bank. I watched her sudden transformation after she returned to Philly from the Peace Corps [in Rwanda]. She was clearly making herself look darker using makeup and fake tan, and speaking using [African American Vernacular English.]” In a statement to the Guardian, a spokesperson for the Philadelphia school district said: “The school district of Philadelphia is aware of social media posts concerning a district employee and her involvement with an outside advocacy organization. The posts reference the employee’s involvement in an external group. The district is making support available to The Workshop School staff and students, as needed.”

title: Iran’s president hits out at ‘bully’ Trump in UN speech but signals willingness to talk
summary: Masoud Pezeshkian says Tehran is ready for dialogue and diplomacy ‘but without the language of force’
text: Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, turned the tables on Donald Trump, describing the US as the true bully and terrorist in the Middle East while insisting that Iran had always shown a commitment to the negotiating table. In a defiant speech to the UN general assembly in New York, his first since the US and Israel launched an all-out war on Iran, Pezeshkian repeatedly vowed that Tehran would never bend the knee to the US. But he balanced defiance with a willingness to talk, saying: “It must be understood by President Trump and those who seek to bully us that we are ready for dialogue and diplomacy and negotiations but without the language of force.” On Tuesday, the US president had told the UN he was weighing whether to “annihilate” Iran, but went on to hail renewed talks between Tehran and Washington’s negotiators. A surprise three-hour meeting between Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, and the US special envoy Steve Witkoff on the sidelines of the assembly the same day was regarded as constructive by both sides. It was the first such meeting since June, but did not stop the US delegation from walking out at the start of Pezeshkian’s speech. The Iranian president did not go into any details about the talks, but conveyed the impression that he was focused on winning the support of Iran’s Arab neighbours for the proposals Tehran has drawn up for the future of the strait of Hormuz, the vital waterway that has been intermittently blockaded since the start of the war, causing global energy prices to soar. He made it clear Iran could not tolerate the strait being used to transport arms that could then be used against it, a statement that suggests the Islamic republic will demand the right to inspect ships travelling through the strait in the future. Iran’s goal, he said, was to live independently. Pezeshkian accused Washington of “terrorism” for assassinating the supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei at the start of the war. He held up photographs of the dead leader and more than 150 schoolchildren killed in the opening days of the conflict, before insisting Tehran had never started a war. “We have only defended ourselves. We are not terrorists,” he said. “Our innocent people have been the targets of cowardly attacks and aggressions imposed upon our country.” He said Iran had the right to pursue a peaceful civil nuclear programme and it did not want to build nuclear weapons. He repeatedly argued that the answer to regional security lay in agreement within the region and not with outsiders such as the US. Iran did not see its neighbours as security rivals, he said, but as partners in security. “In today’s world, those that are unable to defend themselves will be trampled upon,” he added. Iran has repeatedly targeted US allies in the region since the start of the war. Insisting Iran was the true victim of terrorism, Pezeshkian questioned why “Israel kills, yet Iran is subject to sanction”. He added: “They kill, we are sanctioned. Iran did not seek special treatment but wanted equal rights.” Pezeshkian’s speech received domestic praise, but the hardline secretary of the supreme national security council, Mohsen Rezaei, refused to describe the talks with the Americans as negotiations. He said: “Mr Araghchi [Iran’s foreign minister] has announced Iran’s conditions, and until Iran’s conditions are implemented, the strait of Hormuz will not be opened nor will there be any negotiation.” He warned Iran’s neighbours implementing a US-induced ban on Iranian travel: “If you stand alongside the United States, we will not stand by and watch.” He cautioned that should Iranian flights face bans through regional cooperation with Washington, “their airports will have no flights either”. Pezeshkian’s attendance at the UN’s signature diplomatic event, in the heart of Manhattan, had been in doubt as it was unclear whether the US would issue a visa. Ultimately, Washington granted the permit but denied visas to several members of Pezeshkian’s entourage. In Tehran, the foreign ministry spokesperson, Esmail Baghaei, confirmed talks had taken place between the two sides but appeared not to confirm any shift in the Iranian negotiating position. He said: “The interaction that took place with the American side was through Qatari mediation. This interaction was aimed at conveying Iran’s conditions, including the end of the war in all its dimensions, the cessation of American aggressive actions, the naval siege, and the economic war, the release of Iranian assets and so on.” Aware of the potential domestic backlash, he added that Iran’s conditions had been conveyed. Iran set seven preconditions before returning to talks, and in a new development over the past 48 hours it said the strait of Hormuz could be reopened within seven days if those conditions were met. It is likely that the US and the Gulf states would have to accept a navigational route for shipping in the strait of Hormuz that requires commercial shipping to enter through a sea lane mainly in Iranian waters and under Iranian rather than Omani control. The fact that the talks lasted three hours suggests some progress was made. The US side is under pressure to leverage down oil prices and increase the availability of refined oil before the midterm elections in November. The latest published figures suggest the number of identifiable tankers making it through the strait is fewer than five a day. The blockage in the strait is made worse by uncertainty surrounding the control by the Houthis – the Iran-backed Yemeni paramilitaries – of a second energy transport choke point, the Bab al-Mandab strait that leads from the Red Sea into the Indian Ocean. There is little sign that Trump wants to relaunch a full-scale war with Iran, or indeed with the Houthis, as Republicans battle to turn the domestic political agenda away from a hugely unpopular conflict that Americans think they are losing. Iran is under ever more intense pressure from sanctions, and a US naval blockade is making it nearly impossible for it to export oil, depriving the country of badly needed foreign currency. Iran’s civilian aircraft on Wednesday faced a potential worldwide grounding owing to the threat of US secondary sanctions on any entity that engaged with Iran’s civilian fleet. Iranian officials negotiated frantically with neighbouring countries to try to maintain an air bridge, but it appears that Oman and Iraq have been forced to close their airspace to Iranian civilian planes.

title: Farewell, nimbys of Piddington… | Letters
summary: Letters: Readers respond to the news that an Oxfordshire village has voted to leave the UK over plans to house asylum seekers nearby
text: So the people of Piddington have spoken – an overwhelming majority want to leave the UK (English village votes to leave UK in protest over migrant housing plan, 16 September). They didn’t really consider the consequences, did they? We can say goodbye, but to protect our borders we would need to erect a solid barrier around the village. Obviously anyone who works in the UK outside Piddington’s borders would need a work visa now, and travel visas will be needed by people wanting to visit supermarkets – or relatives. I note that there’s a small river running through Piddington. Any attempt to leave on small boats should be dealt with like any other attempted illegal entry. I’m not sure they really thought through the reality of leaving, preferring instead a mix of populist soundbites and protest votes. It’s going to go badly. Where have I heard this before? Neil Knowles London • Lisa Nandy rightly pointed out that all communities should shoulder the burden of asylum seekers, not just those areas with cheap accommodation as was the policy under the Conservative government. We are all susceptible to a bit of nimbyism, but this “vote” was based on ignorance of the facts and on prejudice whipped up by the rightwing media. Linda Karlsen Whitstable, Kent • I note with interest that Piddington has voted to leave the UK. But if they can have a vote, why can’t the rest of us get a say in this? If given the chance, I’d vote for the nimbys of Piddington to be expelled from the UK. It would be interesting to see how long they’d last without us. Chris Jones York • Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Please email us your letter and it will be considered for publication in our letters section.

title: Germany pledges to phase out fossil fuels for first time with target of 2045
summary: Campaigners say plan marks notable shift away from oil and gas as previously pledges were only for carbon neutrality
text: Europe’s biggest economy, Germany, has committed to phasing out fossil fuels by 2045, despite fierce debate about its green policies. In a roadmap published on Wednesday, the German government set out for the first time an explicit promise of “transitioning away” from fossil fuels. Previous pledges were only for “carbon neutrality”. The plans include ramping up renewable energy from 55% to 80% of electricity generation by 2030, with an additional 12GW of onshore wind, and a target of 215GW of solar energy by 2030. The previously stated target of winding down coal use in the next decade, with a view to an exit from coal in 2038, was also reaffirmed, with the potential for an earlier target of 2035. Emissions of methane, a greenhouse gas 80 times more powerful than carbon dioxide, will be cut by 30% by 2030, in accordance with a global methane pledge signed in 2021. Andreas Sieber, head of global political strategy at 350.org, said the plan marked a “notable shift” in making the phaseout of fossil fuels an explicit policy goal. But he warned that Germany’s ministry for economic affairs and energy was also pushing intensely for greater use of gas. “The economic ministry keeps sabotaging the transition away from fossil fuels,” he said. “This year has shown in the starkest terms that fossil-fuel dependence is a risk for everyone as it exposes households and businesses in Germany and around the world to price shocks, volatility and geopolitical insecurity.” Germany’s former climate envoy Jennifer Morgan said the government must put more effort into electrifying transport and heating. “Accelerating the shift from coal, oil and gas to clean renewables will bolster energy independence and insulate consumers from price shocks at a critical moment,” she said. “However, a roadmap is only the starting line.” She said the strategy must be paired with a faster, more deliberate rollout of green electrification. The push for heat pumps to replace gas boilers came under attack from the far-right wing of German politics after a heating law was passed in 2023 that would have banned the installation of most oil and gas heating. Alternative für Deutschland made the issue a key campaigning point and forced a watering down of the rules earlier this year, while the party’s co-leader Alice Weidel has described wind turbines as “windmills of shame”. Heat pumps now make up about half of all new domestic heating systems. Germany is the third major developed economy to publish such a roadmap, after France and the Netherlands, after a major international conference in Colombia in April at which all participants promised to set out plans for a full phaseout of fossil fuels. It comes after nations debated how to expand their currently inadequate efforts to tackle the climate crisis at the UN general assembly in New York. António Guterres, the UN secretary-general, has been a strong advocate of climate action for his 10 years in office, but the end of his term this December has raised fears that his successor may be less firm. The UK has still not published its pledge to phase out fossil fuels, and will take up the presidency of the G20 group of developed and developing economies in December, for which the climate and the soaring costs of oil and gas are expected to be key issues.

title: Does Airtel Money mark the end of London’s listing drought? Not yet | Nils Pratley
summary: The biggest flotation in five years was a bit of a shoo-in. Let’s see what happens when overseas competition is tougher
text: A win is a win, but we should probably contain our excitement about the biggest flotation in London for five years. Airtel Money, a payments processor that operates in 13 African countries and should be worth between £6bn and £7bn, is a welcome addition to the stock market but it would be a stretch to say the event marks a definitive change in the weather to end the listings drought. Why? Because, in a sense, Airtel Money is already here. It is a 78%-owned subsidiary of Airtel Africa, an established FTSE 100 firm with a market value of £11.3bn ultimately controlled by Bharti Enterprises under the Indian billionaire Sunil Bharti Mittal, also known for his 25% stake in BT. That means this was a home fixture for London in the competition with other venues. The Airtel/Bharti collective still had a look at the Middle East, the US and the rest of Europe, we’re told, but London will have started as a heavy favourite. It is simply easier to spin off a subsidiary on a market where the parent is already known – and, indeed, a market where Airtel Africa was a top-performing Footsie stock last year. Ian Ferrao, the chief executive of Airtel Money, still made all the right noises to please exchange officials. London got the nod on account of its deep capital pools plus investors’ enthusiasm for fintech firms and their general understanding of African companies, he said. All true, but it’s also the case that it would have been simply odd to list Airtel Money on a different market to Airtel Africa. The latter is likely to remain the largest shareholder for years yet, and the two businesses are closely linked operationally. Airtel Money has grown out of Airtel Africa’s telecoms business, and one of its key growth opportunities is to persuade even more of the telephony customers to join the payments service. There are 75 million potential recruits to go at, on top of the established 53 million monthly active users, so there is a decent story to tell. It is one reason why the listing should go well, assuming the wider stock market environment remains calm. Airtel Money is capital-lite, converts a chunky proportion of its earnings into cash, carries the buzzy fintech vibe and is growing at about 20% a year. The cash-generative qualities mean no new equity is being raised, so it is really an opportunity for existing shareholders – including minority owners including TPG, Mastercard, the Qatar Investment Authority and Chimetech Holding – to cash in a few chips. As long as they don’t get greedy on price, it looks a relatively easy pitch for the promoters. For London, the listings game is really about winning a few high-profile names where the competition from overseas markets is tougher. The biggie remains Norway’s Visma, one of Europe’s biggest software companies. A listing was delayed earlier this year because of the so-called “Claude crash” – the sell-off in data-related sectors deemed to be under threat from AI tools – but private equity-backed Visma remains a top target given its valuation a year ago was put at almost €20bn (£17.2bn). The listing venue for Visma looks to be a shootout between London, Stockholm and Amsterdam. Win that one and it may be time to turn more cheerful about the UK’s pulling power. We’re not there yet.

title: Janet Davies obituary
summary: Other lives: Dedicated worker for Christian Aid in Merseyside and the north-west
text: My sister, Janet Davies, who has died aged 89, dedicated most of her adult life to international development, ecumenical partnership and social justice. From 1968 to 1986 she worked for Christian Aid in Merseyside and the north-west, and later became regional organiser. Based in Liverpool, and supported by Edward Patey, then dean of the city, Janet used her formidable communicating, networking and nurturing skills to forge grassroots alliances across denominations to deliver and celebrate the practical demonstration of ecumenism that was Christian Aid Week. Her work in the establishment of the Merseyside Churches Ecumenical Council also helped to lay the foundation for the “Better Together” partnership of Bishop David Sheppard and Archbishop Derek Worlock. Born and raised in Formby, Lancashire, to Margot (nee Rose) and Philip Crisall, a civil engineer, Janet went to Streatham House school, Crosby, and later trained and worked as a secretary. Janet was a gifted pianist and choral singer. At the Southport Gramophone Society in 1968, she met and later married Alan Davies, an occupational therapist at Moss Side high security hospital in Maghull, Merseyside. He was a great supporter of her Christian Aid work. His death from cancer 11 years later was a great loss. In her overseas work on behalf of Christian Aid, Janet became transformed by encountering and standing with those in dire poverty. She told of being up to her knees in filth and excrement in the shantytowns of Calcutta (now Kolkata) in 1975, of the horrors of racial segregation in apartheid South Africa in the late 1970s and early 80s, and how deeply this had affected her spiritually. A great motivational speaker, never using notes, Janet was undaunted by addressing an audience of 1,500 at the Royal Liverpool Philharmonic Hall where, in 1985, she publicly received a cheque for Christian Aid’s appeal for the Ethiopian famine, the proceeds of a concert featuring Paul Tortelier playing the Elgar cello concerto. A classic late developer, Janet studied for and gained a certificate in theology from Birmingham University in 1994. Returning from the first of many visits to Lebanon and the occupied Palestinian Territories in 1982, she wrote movingly about her “alternative pilgrimage” in They Came and They Saw: Western Christian Experiences of the Holy Land (2000), edited by Michael Prior, in which she catalogued the need for peace and justice in those tormented lands. Becoming a driving force in Middle East peace advocacy, she led related programmes for USPG (United Society Partners in the Gospel) from the mid-80s to the early 90s and the United Reformed Church (1992-95), and in retirement established Sabeel-Kairos UK (formerly Friends of Sabeel-UK), a charity committed to solidarity with the Palestinian Christian community. She is survived by me, and nine nieces and nephews. Our older brother, Chris, predeceased her.

title: Harvey Weinstein sentenced to 15 years after sexual assault conviction
summary: Sentencing comes after years of appeals and retrials in case involving former TV production assistant Miriam Haley
text: Harvey Weinstein was sentenced to 15 years on Wednesday after being convicted of sexually assaulting former TV production assistant Miriam Haley in 2006 at his Manhattan apartment. Haley appeared in court on Wednesday morning and delivered a victim impact statement. In her statement, Haley spoke about the harassment and humiliation she has endured over the past seven years, saying she was publicly smeared by Weinstein, his defense team, and podcasters she suspects were paid to damage her image. Haley added that her experience following the assault has “already been a life sentence” for her, and asked the judge to take all of this into consideration. New York assistant district attorney Nicole Blumberg addressed the court on behalf of the prosecution. She asked the court to sentence Weinstein, 74, to 20 years with five years of post-release supervision, stating he never showed any type of remorse for his crimes. Weinstein said in his statement he has remorse for Haley. “I live with many regrets and sincerely apologize for my actions,” he said. Weinstein’s defense had also argued that their client is too sick to serve a long sentence following a diagnosis of several health conditions including blood cancer and heart disease. The defense asked for a nine-year sentence. Before sentencing, Judge Curtis Farber acknowledged that Weinstein would be remembered not just for producing films, but for being the face of the #MeToo movement. Farber said Weinstein took advantage of Haley’s dreams of working in the film industry. “You had it all,” Farber said. “Your legacy could have been cemented with greatness. But you threw it all away by assaulting Miriam Haley.” The latest sentencing comes after years of appeals and retrials in the closely watched case. Weinstein was sentenced to 23 years in prison in 2020 after a jury convicted him of sexually assaulting Haley and raping aspiring actor Jessica Mann. But in 2024, New York’s highest court overturned the convictions, saying Weinstein’s trial had been prejudiced by the judge allowing woman who alleged they were sexual assault victims of Weinstein to testify, despite not being plaintiffs in the case. Weinstein went on trial again in 2025 and was once more convicted of a criminal sexual act involving Haley. Jurors acquitted Weinstein of a separate sexual assault charge involving former model Kaja Sokola but could not reach a verdict on the rape charge involving Mann. Prosecutors retried the Mann charge earlier this year, but the jury deadlocked in May. The charge was later dropped after Mann said she could not endure another trial. Weinstein is also awaiting resentencing in a separate California rape case. In June, a California appeals court upheld Weinstein’s 2022 rape and sexual assault conviction. He was found guilty of assaulting an Italian model in her hotel room during a film festival. He could serve the California sentence before beginning the sentence imposed in New York. Farber said at Wednesday’s sentencing that California will have the final say on whether Weinstein’s sentences run consecutively or concurrently. The accusations and subsequent charges against Weinstein were one of the biggest factors in launching the #MeToo movement. More than 80 women have come forward with allegations of sexual assault or misconduct against him.

title: Criminals recruiting students on social media to be ‘parcel mules’, say police
summary: Organised crime groups offer cash to move packages containing drugs or weapons, says West Yorkshire force
text: Students are being recruited by criminals to transfer illegal packages containing illegal drugs, prohibited weapons, stolen goods and dirty cash, say police in West Yorkshire. Organised criminals are using social media platforms including Snapchat, Instagram, TikTok and Facebook to recruit people to help them move illicit goods, particularly targeting students and vulnerable adults. They offer cash to “parcel mules” to accept criminal packages in what West Yorkshire police has described as a new trend, which could see those not otherwise involved in crime landed with a criminal record. Parents are being warned to speak to their university age children and advise them against becoming involved with the gangs moving criminal property around West Yorkshire. The social media adverts typically contain phrases such as “Work from home”, “Easy money”, “No experience needed” and “Earn £100-£500 per week”. Police are warning that the suspect packages could contain anything from illegal drugs to offensive weapons, as well as stolen goods, counterfeit items or fraudulently purchased products. Some may also contain criminal cash obtained through illegal activities. Officers have warned that not knowing what is in a parcel may not always protect those handling it from criminal investigation, and ultimately receiving a criminal record. Depending on what the parcel contains, they may face charges for anything from possession of controlled drugs or prohibited weapons to handling stolen goods or money laundering. Anyone receiving the parcels may also find themselves charged with conspiracy offences. Officers have said that warning signs to look out for include being offered money simply for accepting deliveries, being asked to use your address without being told why, someone using multiple names or addresses, or being asked to accept a parcel but not being told what is inside it. Police have also said to be wary of anyone saying “don’t worry it’s legal” without further explanation, anyone pressuring the recipient into making a decision, or saying they want to collect the parcels quickly after delivery. Officers have said that criminals may talk their victims into accepting packages by saying things such as “it’s just because I’m not home during the day,” or “you’re not doing anything wrong,” or “nobody will ever know.”. West Yorkshire police Ch Insp Michelle Swift said: “What may seem like an easy favour or a way to get quick cash could leave you facing a police investigation and a criminal record. “Criminals will often use social media like SnapChat, Instagram, TikTok and Facebook to recruit people to help them. “If something doesn’t feel right, trust your instincts and report it to us. “We hope by raising awareness of this type of crime, people will be alert to the risks and tactics used by organised criminals. “We would particularly encourage parents to have this conversation with their university age children to make them understand this type of trend and the dangers that are associated with it.” Earlier this year, Lincolnshire police issued a similar warning, advising people to beware of “anyone offering money or favours for accepting deliveries,” as well as parcels arriving addressed to unfamiliar names, and packages arriving from overseas with no clear sender. The force warned that in some cases, individuals and addresses were being used without their consent, as part of organised fraud or delivery scams. Anyone who suspects they may have been recruited as a parcel mule is advised to stop involvement immediately, keep messages, emails or screenshots and report their concerns to the police. Anyone who has received a parcel not addressed to them is advised not to open it, and to contact the delivery company to arrange return or collection.

summary: Phil Knight and wife, Penny, make largest known donation to a public university to fund a new engineering school
text: Nike co-founder Phil Knight, and his wife, Penny, have donated $1bn to the University of Oregon in what the institution described as the “largest gift ever made to a comprehensive public university”. The donation is intended to be used to establish a new engineering school in Eugene. In a news release seen by the Guardian, the university said the new school would “educate engineers and applied scientists in bioengineering and other high-demand disciplines, attract faculty and researchers to a growing campus, and accelerate the university’s ability to move discoveries out of the laboratory and into products, therapies, technologies and companies”. The University of Oregon president, Karl Scholz, said in a statement that the Knights have “a long history of believing in things before they exist” and that “they did it in 2016, and they are doing it again now, at a scale that is genuinely hard to take in. I am grateful to them, and I am grateful to be here for it.” Knight, 88, is a graduate of the university. The latest donation brings the Knight family’s known total giving to the University of Oregon to more than $2bn, according to the New York Times. The school said in the news release on Wednesday that the gift is the third commitment the Knights have made at this scale in 10 years, following $500m in 2016 and $500m in 2021 that created and expanded the Knight Campus. The school also said the new engineering school will be located at the Phil and Penny Knight Campus for Accelerating Scientific Impact. In the announcement, Knight also shared a statement noting that “to make an audacious dream a reality requires more than a vivid imagination”. “It also requires the sort of opportunity that our great American universities, both public and private, have historically provided,” he said. “This is no time to abandon them.” He added: “Penny and I are grateful for the chance to invest in our most promising young people’s future in this important way.” Bob Guldberg, vice-president and Robert and Leona DeArmond executive director of the Knight Campus, said in a statement that the creation of a college of engineering “builds on the original vision put forward by UO faculty who inspired Phil and Penny to invest in the idea that we can do better translating the great work we do out into the real world”. “The Knight Campus stands on the foundation of a remarkable Oregon legacy: the belief that bold innovation can unlock human potential,” Guldberg said. “Today, we carry that same belief forward, applying it to science, technology, and human health.” Scholz, the university president, said in an interview with the New York Times about the donation that “one of the most successful businesspeople in the history of humanity, and one of the most generous philanthropists in the history of humanity, has said higher education is worth an investment of this magnitude. “At a time when we’re all feeling a little bit under siege, this is tremendous news,” he said, adding that the gift amounted to “a screaming endorsement of the importance of what we’re doing”. Senator Ron Wyden, an Oregon Democrat, said in a statement: “This groundbreaking gift from Phil and Penny Knight stands out for its extraordinary generosity and monumental impact at a public university. “As a proud University of Oregon alumnus, I know my alma mater will put this massive investment to great use by educating students who will meet the ongoing need for engineers so essential to the economy in our state and nationwide.” The news on Wednesday comes as earlier this month it was announced that the Knights were committing $1.1bn to Providence St Vincent Medical Center and to Providence Heart Institute to create Oregon’s first hospital dedicated exclusively to women’s health. “Penny and I have always believed that real breakthroughs come from people willing to take on the toughest challenges,” Knight said in a statement earlier this month. “Providence has shown that kind of ambition in cardiovascular care, and we see the same opportunity to do something truly distinctive for women’s health. We’re proud to invest in teams that will change what’s possible for communities across Oregon and beyond.” Last year, Oregon Health & Science University announced that it had received a $2bn commitment from the Knights to its cancer institute, which the university said would “transform the future of cancer care and set a new standard globally”.

title: Single, couple or family: not all Australian middle-income earners are equal | Greg Jericho
summary: The latest Hilda report tells us wages have become more equal, but comparing living standards gives a better understanding of households’ wealth
text: The latest Household, Income and Labour Dynamics in Australia (Hilda) survey released on Thursday provides vital details on the lives of Australians. It also helps answer the question of how much you need to earn to be a middle-income Australian. The Hilda survey by the Melbourne Institute is a longitudinal study that follows the same group of about 17,000 people to get a sense of how Australia is changing across a range of economic and social measures. For example, the latest survey, which covers 2024, found there has been a slight decrease in the share of Australian households made up of couples with either dependent or adult children, but an increase (from 20.4% to 22.1%) of couples without children: If the graph does not display click here The survey also found households now spend more on childcare than they did in 2002 – but the costs have stabilised over the past decade. If the graph does not display click here The report also reveals that wages have become more equal, which has helped counter the increased inequality of non-wage income (such as investments): If the graph does not display click here This poses the question of how we measure income and what is the “middle”, as opposed to the “average”, income of Australian households. This is a tricky, but important subject. For example, I regularly use per capita (or average) household disposable income to compare house prices to income. I calculate this from the national accounts, which come out every three months. The Hilda survey uses both median and average household income, and pleasingly, my measure is relatively similar to the median household disposable income in the Hilda survey: If the graph does not display click here The problem however is there are a multitude of ways to measure income, and also to split up the population. Firstly “median” and “average” (more strictly, “mean”) are quite different. Median is the midpoint (ie half earn more and half earn less), whereas average is just the total amount of income divided by all the people. As a result, average income is always a lot higher than the median. The Hilda survey found that in 2024 the median income across every household in Australia was $103,166. But that actually isn’t very useful. Yes, if the total disposable income in your household is more than $103,166 you can say you have more income than half of Australian households, but that says nothing about your living standards. Obviously if you are a single person with a disposable income of $103,166 you are much better off than if that is the income for a family of four. This is why the Hilda calculates a measure called the median “equivalised” disposable income. Essentially this is the income of a single person with median living standards. In 2024 this was $66,311. By contrast someone in the 90th percentile (ie with living standards better than 90% of Australians) had an income of $122,675, and someone in the bottom 10% earned just $30,842 after taxes: If the graph does not display click here Because most people think about gross income (ie before tax), this means that for a single person to have median living standards they need to earn $83,969 before taxes (assuming 2% Medicare levy). But the ABS records that median total earnings in 2024 was just $78,567. The reason why it is less is that it only counts wages and salaries, not income from investments and other sources. The Hilda survey also suggests that a pre-tax income of $170,513 puts you in the top 10%: If the graph does not display click here But again, this is only slightly more helpful because it is just for a single person. What about for a couple, or for a couple with two children? This is where we shift from talking about median incomes to living standards and try to work out what you would need to earn to have the same living standards as a single person on median income. The standard formula is to count every extra adult in a household as requiring 50% more income, and each child 30%. This is because a couple living together does not for example double the cost of electricity or even rent. So, for a couple to have the same living standards as a single person they need to earn 1.5 times more. Similarly, for a couple with two children they would need 2.1 times the income as a single person. This means for a couple to have the same living standards as a single person on median income, they need a combined household disposable income of $99,467, while a couple with two children needs $139,253: If the graph does not display click here If we assume each couple earns a 60/40 split of the household income, we can also estimate the pre-tax household income required for each family size to have median, average or top 10% living standards: If the graph does not display click here On this score, a household income of $176,219 is needed to deliver median living standards for a family of two adults and two children – about $25,000 less than what you need to have “average” living standards. So when you hear a politician talk about average income, always remember to ask if they are talking about a single person or a family, and whether they are really trying to pretend they are talking about middle income. • Greg Jericho is a Guardian columnist and chief economist at the Australia Institute

title: Bats originated in Europe, rewriting mammals’ family tree, study reveals
summary: Biggest study of its kind provides insights into bats’ evolution – a potential gamechanger for research into human virus and cancer treatment
text: In the northern forests of the Congo-Brazzaville, as the sun slips away, a distinctive honking fills the dusky sky. Every evening, thousands of hammer-headed fruit bats depart their daytime roosts in search of mates, calling out through large, box-shaped snouts that give the flying mammals the appearance of a winged moose. Here, along the Congo River, scientists have been collecting DNA swabs and tissue samples from the bats for years, working deep into the night in spacesuit-like protective gear. Those hard-won samples are now among the thousands of specimens gathered from bats across the world that have helped to reshape what we know about the bat family tree. In a landmark study published today in the journal Nature, a team of more than 130 international researchers combed through ancient bat fossils and genomic data from living species to establish that bats likely originated in Europe about 65m years ago – not in Africa, Asia or North America, as had previously been thought. Rather, it seems that the earliest ancestors of modern bats dispersed from Europe into Africa, then expanded onwards to Asia, the Americas and Australia. The findings also reveal that echolocation, like flight, also evolved near the dawn of bat evolution. “Bats, on a scale of amazing to amazing, they’re super amazing,” said Sarah Olson, one of the study’s authors and director of health research at the nonprofit Wildlife Conservation Society. “It’s fun to have part of that puzzle piece in the block, and then we can keep finding and adding other puzzle pieces to it now.” The work is part of a larger global effort known as Bat1K, launched in 2017, which seeks to sequence the genomes of all the living 1,500 bat species – the second most diverse mammal species in the world, and accounting for one-fifth of all mammals. Genomes are an organism’s complete set of genetic constructions, containing all the DNA needed to build, grow and live. The Nature study ultimately drew on 103 bat genomes from 21 bat families, alongside 44 fossil bats – mostly their teeth – unearthed across the globe. Olson said their findings lay the groundwork for better understanding bat physiology and, critically, how the mammals have evolved to be so resistant to disease. Bats are often identified as reservoirs of fatal zoonotic viruses, including Ebola, Nipah and Marburg – but the bats don’t get sick themselves. “How are they living with these viruses that, when they get into us, they cause so much damage?” Olson said. “What we have now is a kind-of code book of life.” A 2025 study based on the Bat1K genomic work found that early bat ancestors seemed to have excessive immune gene adaptations. “We showed for the first time that these adaptations associated with viral tolerance and disease resistance probably evolved at the same time that all bats evolved,” said the evolutionary biologist Ariadna Morales, who worked on both studies. Bats are also unique among mammals in that they live exceptionally long for their size, showing few signs of ageing or cancers. Now, scientists say they will be able to investigate the genes driving those traits. What they learn could be a gamechanger for research into human ageing, immunity and disease resistance. “With the genetic information that we can find in bats, it could be used to develop therapeutics associated with zoonotic disease. And they could also be models to develop treatments for cancer,” Morales said. Olson added that the research can also strengthen our understanding of “what makes a healthy bat a healthy bat, and what are bats going to be susceptible to?” About half of the known bat species have unknown or decreasing populations, with 18% of species considered threatened by the International Union for the Conservation of Nature. Bats are at risk from the climate crisis, habitat loss, and bat persecution and harvesting, said study co-author Liliana Dávalos, a conservation biologist at Stony Brook University in New York. At the same time, bats play an important role in ecosystems, helping to pollinate plants, spread seeds, and keeping insect numbers – particularly mosquitoes, another spreader of disease – in check. “Unlike most small mammals, all but one bat species have very small litters of one or two pups, so when individuals drop dead from scorching temperatures, or get killed through persecution or harvesting, populations cannot quickly recover their numbers,” Dávalos said. And while bats have shown resilience to Ebola and Marburg, in Canada and the United States bats have perished by the millions from a fungal pathogen called white nose syndrome, which grows on the skin of hibernating bats. “This research can help us go back and look at what makes the myotis bat species more susceptible to these fungal diseases,” Olson said. “There may be some interesting findings that other researchers can take from this study … to go back and piece together what’s happening with white nose syndrome.” • Find more age of extinction coverage here, and follow the biodiversity reporters Rebecca Ratcliffe, Phoebe Weston and Patrick Greenfield in the Guardian app for more nature coverage.

title: Six arrested after anti-migrant protest at Gosport marina
summary: Heeding calls from far-right activist Daniel Thomas, hundreds of protesters turned out in Hampshire
text: Six people have been arrested after anti-migrant protesters gathered at a marina in Hampshire in the mistaken belief that a small boat was due to arrive. Heeding calls from the far-right campaigner Daniel Thomas, hundreds of protesters gathered early on Tuesday evening at Gosport in Hampshire, aiming to disrupt any disembarkation of asylum seekers. The Border Force vessels carrying them landed instead in Dover early on Wednesday. Thomas, who styles himself as Danny Tommo, spent Tuesday afternoon in a speedboat in the Channel broadcasting his pursuit of the asylum seekers to more than 100,000 people. He is facing a police inquiry after using a blade to slash an inflatable dinghy in the Channel while a rescue worker was onboard. Hampshire police said two men from Salisbury, aged 19 and 36, had been arrested on suspicion of aggravated trespass; and four people from Gosport – two men aged 33 and 67, and two women aged 31 and 32 – were held on suspicion of assaulting an emergency worker. The 67-year-old was also held on suspicion of careless driving. Police are “conducting inquiries” into footage of Thomas slashing the side of an inflatable boat while a member of a rescue team was still on it, then sailing away shouting: “Traitors.” The arrests were made after unions representing Border Force staff discussed security concerns with the Home Office following increasingly aggressive tactics by anti-migrant activists. The discussions followed attacks on Border Force vehicles and attempts to record and identify staff members by some anti-migrant activists. The Home Office plans to use public order powers to stop the harassment and possible doxing of government staff who pick up small-boat arrivals at sea. Lucy Moreton, of the Immigration Services Union, said: “Following several conversations with the ISU regarding staff safety, the Home Office is working with local police and MoD [Ministry of Defence] to ensure that staff, and migrants, are properly protected using existing police powers and civil service support networks.” Fran Heathcote, the general secretary of the PCS union, which represents Border Force guards, said: “PCS unreservedly condemns this life-threatening and criminal behaviour. Our members do an important and dangerous job and this inference is reckless in the extreme.” A Home Office spokesperson said: “We have been clear that groups creating fear and intimidating communities cannot be allowed to operate with impunity. “Police should make full use of the powers available to them to deal robustly with criminality and ensure communities, staff and those in their care are protected. “Recent events demonstrate the need to learn lessons and adapt our response to new tactics, ensuring police have the tools, intelligence and operational plans needed to act quickly and effectively.” Some of the protesters in Gosport wore black clothing and face coverings, and chanted “send them back”, wrongly assuming the boat would be guided to the Hampshire coast. In fact, it docked in Dover, Kent, at about 12.30am on Wednesday after 51 people onboard reportedly refused help from a French ship and spent 33 hours at sea. It emerged on Tuesday that a second small boat had arrived on UK shores within the last 24 hours without being detected and intercepted. The boat reached Samphire Hoe, near Dover, on Tuesday afternoon. Border Security Command has detained 21 migrants so far. On Monday, five people were detained and passed to Border Security Command after a dinghy made it to shore at Folkestone, also in Kent. The defence minister Luke Pollard dismissed suggestions the government had lost control of the border. “Our borders are secure, but we want to make them stronger,” he told LBC Radio, adding that a Home Office investigation was under way into what had happened. A man was found dead on a beach in northern France on Wednesday, French authorities have said. In a translated statement, a spokesperson for the Pas-de-Calais prefecture said: “The lifeless body of a man, who appeared to be of African origin, was discovered this morning on the Neufchâtel-Hardelot beach. “An investigation has been launched.” A total of 17,480 migrants have arrived in the UK after crossing the Channel by boat so far this year, including 5,011 since Andy Burnham became prime minister. The total so far for 2026 is down 46% on the same point last year. Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, has ordered a review after the Border Force failed to intercept a second dinghy in two days. A government spokesperson said on Wednesday: “Border Security Command officers alongside Kent police have been responding to an incident in Dover. “Twenty-one individuals have already been detained under a swift enforcement response. There is a thorough investigation and it would be inappropriate to comment further.”

title: The EU’s Canada offer is more mood than reality but it could hint at a future geometry for the bloc
summary: While Brussels and Ottawa desire a deeper partnership born of Trump-era volatility, ​the EU has no legal framework to accommodate it
text: The EU and Canada, Ursula von der Leyen said last week, “see the world with the same eyes”, with shared stances on everything from AI to the climate crisis, the Ukraine war and the unholy chaos unleashed by the current occupant of the White House (OK, she didn’t actually say that last bit. But I like to think she almost certainly thought it.) So, the European Commission president went on, Canada should become “the first associate member of the EU”. In the audience, Mark Carney beamed with delight. The next day, Canada’s prime minister enthusiastically embraced the idea of an “alliance for the future”, to build “collective resilience” through “deep cooperation”. Cue standing ovations, warm handshakes – and a great deal of head-scratching in Brussels and assorted EU capitals. Because “associate membership” of the EU is not, in fact, a thing. Nor, as a Guardian editorial pointed out, is there “any blueprint for what such a thing might involve”. The term was, the editorial argued, “a political hypothesis”, describing “a relationship of intimate strategic alignment with the EU, stopping short of actual membership, in ways that are significant but undefined”. So what exactly are the commission and Canada playing at here, and where might it lead? You can see where they’re coming from. On paper, in a world of unpredictable and increasingly aggressive great powers, it makes perfect sense. For Canada – which already has the Ceta free trade agreement with the EU – the catalyst for even closer cooperation is clearly Donald Trump: incessant tariff threats, an escalating trade war, bullying talk of Canada as the “51st state”, the renaming of Lake Ontario – all have left Ottawa eager to diversify its relations. Aligning with European industrial strategy, working together on defence and AI, and joining EU scientific research and student exchange programmes would offer Canada a reliable counterweight to its all-too-unreliable southern neighbour. (Unsurprisingly, Trump called the tie-up “laughable”, and threatened more tariffs.) For the EU, meanwhile, Canada is a dream partner: a stable, like-minded “middle power” rich in critical minerals, rare earths and – as Carney couldn’t resist noting – good manners. Plus, Canada’s unbridled EU-enthusiasm is a pleasing boost to the bloc’s bruised ego after Iceland’s recent rejection of more EU accession negotiations. There’s only one problem: “associate membership” is not a status in the EU treaties, and creating such a status would mean treaty reform, which member states won’t contemplate. There are things called “association agreements”, such as with Ukraine, Moldova or Georgia, but those are essentially stepping stones to full membership – which Canada can’t aspire to, for the very good reason that it isn’t in Europe. But if “associate member” sounds vaguely familiar, that’s because the EU has been talking about a “second circle” since the days of Jacques Delors: an outer ring of countries bound by shared values, free trade and security cooperation to an inner core of members, but without full voting rights or complete regulatory integration. Emmanuel Macron’s European Political Community is a variation on this theme, and Germany’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz, recently floated “associate member” status for Ukraine. Indeed, non-EU nations in the European Economic Area (EEA) and European Free Trade Association, such as Norway, Iceland or Switzerland, already function as quasi-associate members, enjoying single-market access while being largely “rule-takers”: adopting EU rules without having a vote in Brussels. Writing in the Guardian, Fabian Zuleeg suggested that Canada and Europe actually need more of an “integrated partnership” – a model that leaves single market access to one side, focusing instead on concrete collaboration in areas such as defence, supply chains and EU programmes like Horizon and Erasmus+. Alberto Alemanno, a professor of EU law, noted that a realistic EU-Canada landing zone would have to go further than Ceta and might more resemble the kind of tailored framework of the EU-Swiss relationship. But the real significance of any formal new status, he said, was that it could make the EU “an institutional hub around which other democracies organise strategic autonomy – but without joining the union”. What that might actually look like is anyone’s guess: visa-free work access, shared military procurement, Canadian seats on EU regulatory committees? For the moment, Canada’s hypothetical “associate membership” is more of a mood than a reality: the expressed intent of a democratic bloc and a middle power to deepen ties in the face of mounting global uncertainty. Does it, all the same, hold any hope for Brexit-regretting Britain? As Jill Rutter of the Institute for Government highlighted, the EU’s sudden willingness to display “institutional imagination” at least shows that the bloc is willing to think about adapting when geopolitical pressures demand. But a new deal for Canada won’t automatically fix the UK’s issues. As Joël Reland of UK in a Changing Europe pointed out, the vagueness of the EU offer to Canada might look promising for the UK. But Canada wants “deep cooperation” without touching single-market rules, and the UK’s main problem is that it is now shut out of that same market. Whatever Canada eventually gets, it’s unlikely to work for the UK. *** A miserable time for Merz Friedrich Merz is in trouble. A fortnight after the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) swept to a crushing victory in one state election in Saxony-Anhalt, the German chancellor’s centre-right CDU failed to clear the 5% threshold needed to enter the state parliament in another, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. It fared a little better in Berlin, where it was the incumbent, but was still beaten – by a clear five-point margin – by the far-left Die Linke. And the AfD made headway in the capital, too, surging to a double-digit result. The embattled chancellor has vowed to fight on, but faces an uncomfortable choice: revise the unpopular economic reforms he insists are essential, or risk oblivion defending them. Meanwhile, as long as he refuses to step aside and no one is actively seeking to replace him, a volatile and damaging deadlock will reign in Europe’s biggest economy. After 16 months in office, it is becoming increasingly clear – as a Guardian editorial noted – that Merz is “ill-suited for the job” of defending Germany’s democratic future against the far right.
