title: UK to join EU ocean science scheme to better predict extreme weather events
summary: Cooperation on OceanEye, which aims to better anticipate climate events, comes amid efforts to boost ties with bloc
text: Britain is to join a major new ocean science programme, led by the EU, to better forecast extreme weather and climate events, the environment secretary is to announce in New York. The announcement on Wednesday will come as Andy Burnham’s government aims to rebuild the UK’s relationship with Europe, and follows warnings this year’s “supersized” El Niño, tracked in the Pacific Ocean, will fuel more extreme weather globally. Scientists have warned that the global marine monitoring system, which is vital to predict extreme weather events and ultimately to save lives, is under strain after threats by the US administration this year to dismantle its substantial share of global ocean observations. In June, the EU launched a €92m (£78m) initiative called OceanEye, to boost its role in ocean observation and to provide data-backed marine intelligence to deepen understanding and management of the ocean. It plans to create a digital “real time” replica model of the ocean, collected by satellites, sensors and other models by 2030, to help decisions on ocean protection and security. The EU introduced an international alliance with Canada as part of OceanEye, to address critical gaps in under-monitored regions and strengthen cooperation between nations. In addition to weather and climate predictions, ocean observations also underpin national security, global trade and marine protections. Angela Eagle will announce the UK is to join the scheme at a meeting attended by the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, and Mark Carney, Canada’s prime minister, at the UN headquarters in New York. Britain will share more data from the Met Office and other agencies with the EU and Canada than before. The environment secretary will tell the event: “As an island nation and a global leader in climate science, we know that data from ocean monitoring is essential to our ability to protect and restore our oceans, and anticipate and respond to the huge threats they face, because we cannot save our oceans if we do not understand them.” “Changing weather patterns and currents are fuelling the extreme weather which is already impacting all of our nations – through floods, droughts, storms and extreme heat. That’s why the UK is so committed to maintaining our vital global network of observation systems, which span coastal waters, shelf seas and the open ocean, including some of the longest-running observations in the world.” Joining the alliance to support and provide data to the Global Ocean Observing System (GOOS) would help better protect Britain from the impacts of climate change, said the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs. Currently, the global ocean observing capacity has significant gaps, at the poles, the deep ocean and of biological measurements. The US, which provides over half the ocean observing platforms and much of the technology, has reversed a proposal to scrap its $368m (£275m) funding for its Ocean Observatories Initiative after a backlash from scientists. However, moves to cut funding for US ocean agencies have left GOOS vulnerable to changing priorities of the US administration.

title: Burnham stands by claim UK is ‘in hock’ to bond markets
summary: PM says his comments last year were deliberately misinterpreted by Keir Starmer and his advisers
text: Andy Burnham has said he still believes the UK is far too exposed to global shocks, defending comments last year when he said the UK should be less “in hock” to the bond markets. He said the comments had been deliberately misinterpreted by the former prime minister Keir Starmer and his advisers and said his aim was not more borrowing and spending but a far more resilient economy. Burnham’s comments in an interview with the New Statesmen last year made waves before the Labour conference because of the then Greater Manchester’s clear ambitions to replace Starmer as prime minister. In a fresh interview with the magazine on Wednesday, he said he had intended to highlight how vulnerable the UK was to global price fluctuations. Government borrowing has climbed again over the past months as energy prices have risen in response to continued deadlock on the Iran war. The UK government borrowed a higher than expected £18.3bn last month, putting further pressure on the chancellor, John Healey, as he prepares for next month’s budget. Burnham said he wanted to build an economy that was far less vulnerable. “I mean, the point about the bond markets, it holds – in that what I was saying was the country has left itself over-exposed,” he said, telling the magazine he was arguing for a “much more streamlined, productive state”. He said criticism from Starmer and the then chancellor, Rachel Reeves, was unjustified. “They couldn’t understand why I was saying some of the things that I was saying … [They] didn’t know what to do with it, but they did what they always do, which is they pulled one line out of it and then framed that one line within their world, rather than the one that I was talking about.” Burnham also addressed criticism from the Conservatives after he said during an exchange at prime minister’s questions that national security “should not come at the expense of social security” – which opponents said showed he was not willing to cut the welfare budget to fund increased defence spending. “It oversimplifies the political discourse that we need to have, doesn’t it?” he said. Burnham, who will address his first Labour conference as prime minister in Liverpool next Tuesday, said he would set out his political vision, which would be a break from the economic and political mainstream of the past 40 years. “It’s about control,” he said. “If you strip it back, and all the fluff and, you know, the verbiage, you can actually strip it back to one word, which is control.” He said that would be a business-friendly approach, rather than purely statist. “People aren’t going to come in and invest in a significant way where the place isn’t functional and it’s in major decline,” he said, saying it was the state’s job to “create the optimum conditions for private-sector investment”. “We’ve just got to get that belief back into Britain that, yeah, we know what we’re about, we know what we stand for, that is what we’ve always been, so we can do it again.” In attempts to calm jittery bond markets, Burnham has previously said his budget would “stick to the fiscal rules” on debt and borrowing set out under Reeves, “but at the same time we will help reduce cost of living pressure on our constituents”.

title: New York and Boston face weekend nor’easter with high winds
summary: First such storm of fall could have wind gusts of 70mph in places, flooding and power outages, forecasters warn
text: New York, Boston, and much of New England could face a weekend nor’easter storm with wind gusts of 70mph in places, and “significant” impacts including beach erosion, flooding, and power outages, forecasters warn. Effects from the season’s first such storm since Tuesday’s official start of fall could last through the weekend, especially if the system sits swirling off the coast, a scenario experts say is looking increasingly likely. “If the storm nearly stalls, several days of persistent onshore winds and pounding surf could take a significant toll on beaches and vulnerable coastal communities, especially with astronomical high tides coinciding,” said Alyssa Glenney, an AccuWeather meteorologist. The online weather service predicted “a long-duration storm for many areas along the mid-Atlantic and New England coasts”, with impacts beginning late Wednesday, spreading to New England late Friday or Saturday, and lasting through Sunday in some places. The Weather Channel said coastal flood alerts were in place across the mid-Atlantic, and winds were likely to bring sea rise up to 3ft above normal levels. But it said uncertainty remained about exactly where the system would be at the end of the week. “Forecast models are picking up on the low, but two models show that the timing and duration of the storm could differ,” the Weather Channel said on its website, weather.com. “The European model brings the low close to the coast as a strong storm, but it moves slower. It could even meander around the east coast until it fizzles. Under this scenario, there would be more time for strong winds to cause significant power outages, heavy rain-induced flooding, and coastal erosion.” The GFS model, meanwhile, brings the storm in faster, and approaching New England by Saturday afternoon. “A faster storm could mean winds, rain and coastal erosion would be less severe and lessen disruptions to travel and weekend plans,” the Weather Channel said. “However, this model calls for a stronger storm by the end of the weekend as it moves away from the north east, meaning some coastal areas could experience longer-lasting impacts.” Nor’easters are more prevalent from September to April, the National Weather Service said. They usually develop within about 100 miles of the cost between Georgia and New Jersey, and progress steadily north eastward, typically attaining maximum intensity near New England and the maritime provinces of Canada. AccuWeather’s forecasters agreed with the Weather Channel that the exact track of this weekend’s storm remained important for communities farther inland. “A track closer to the coast could bring heavier rain, stronger wind gusts and travel disruptions from Washington DC and Philadelphia, to New York City and Boston, while a track farther offshore would limit inland rain and wind impacts,” the service said.

title: DoJ defends Trump media ban: ‘Access to the White House is a privilege’
summary: Justice department cites national security to support ban on CNN, Politico and MS Now as trio file lawsuit in response
text: The US Department of Justice has defended Donald Trump’s decision to ban three new organizations from the White House, arguing in a court filing that access to the grounds was a “privilege” and citing national security concerns. Lawyers for the US president doubled down on Trump’s claims about CNN, Politico and MS Now reporting “Fake News”, and insisted the ban did not violate the first amendment because “access to the White House is a privilege, not a right”. In the filing, justice department lawyers argued that Trump had concluded that the news outlets “fail to satisfy the minimum requirements of professionalism” by relying on anonymous sources, and not giving the White House enough time to comment. Trump’s lawyers also claimed the three organizations had violated “decorum” by publishing classified or sensitive national security information. The justice department asked Timothy Kelly, the federal judge overseeing the case, to allow Trump to enforce his White House ban on reporters from CNN, Politico and MS Now. The judge is expected to hold a hearing on the new organizations’ request for a temporary restraining order on Wednesday at 3.30pm ET. CNN, Politico and MS Now sued Trump on Monday, days after the president announced he would institute a White House ban. His accusation of “fake news” is one the US president has repeatedly made against media outlets, often without citing evidence. The three news organizations are asking Kelly to stop Trump from enforcing his ban and to restore their hard passes to the White House, claiming the ban violates the first amendment. But Trump and his justice department insist the ban does not infringe on the right to the free press, saying instead it addresses “national security” threats. In Tuesday’s filing, lawyers for the justice department said it sent letters to CNN, Politico and MS Now outlining examples of reports that violated “the standards of professionalism and decorum expected of those given access to the White House complex”. The letters cited various “reporting incidents”, including some that “threatened national security and spread falsehoods”. That includes CNN’s reporting on construction of the East Wing bunker under the White House ballroom; MS Now’s reporting on an alleged leak investigation; and Politico’s reporting on how the US Secret Service would invest money into security improvements for Trump’s ballroom.

title: ‘Watermelons’: Zack Polanski and the rise of the ‘green outside, red inside’ eco-populists
summary: Author Russell Warfield argues the Green leader’s brand of politics is not new but has evolved in the party over time
text: Watermelons: the term used to describe the members of the Green party of England and Wales who are green on the outside and red on the inside. People in this faction are environmentalists but bleed socialist ideologies. Of the roughly 160,000 people who have flocked to the party since Zack Polanski became leader last year, most are thought to be in this camp, drawn to a political space on the left that they see as vacated by the Labour party. But the author of a new book – The Green Socialist: Zack Polanski and the Battle for Britain’s Future – says this flavour of Green is nothing new. “What you’ve got to understand is that the party has been watermelon for at least 10 years,” says Russell Warfield, a former party staffer who has worked on election campaigns, including Polanski’s. “There’s often this dichotomy presented that there’s this ‘real core’ Green party who are these ecologists who really just care about conservation of the environment, then there’s this new cohort of hard leftists,” Warfield says. “Actually, this has been both an organic process but also one which reaches much more deeply into the past of the party, where a lot of the fundamental positions of the party can be traced back to the early 1970s.” His book unpacks the history of the party to explain how Polanski fits into it, arguing that the leader and his “eco-populist” package is not a departure from Green tradition but the culmination of a 50-year evolution that has turned the party into the main electoral force on the British left. Not everyone agrees. During the leadership contest between Polanski and co-runners Adrian Ramsay and Ellie Chowns in 2025, a senior Green source described Polanski’s rise as a “hostile takeover”. Even Caroline Lucas, the Greens’ first MP and a former party leader, has said, when pressed, that she would love him to talk about the environment more. “It’s just obvious nonsense,” Warfield says of the hostile takeover comment. “Look at the mandate, it was 85%,” Polanski’s landslide leadership win. “He won across every wing of the party.” But how green are the Greens? Since Polanski took over, he has been splashed across newspapers and TV screens discussing subjects ranging from Gaza to wealth taxes – progressive politics, but not necessarily or overtly green. Warfield responds with a statistic: 34% of voters trust the Greens more than any other party on the environment, according to YouGov polling – the highest level of trust recorded for any party on any issue. “There is not a voter in this country, leftwing, rightwing, old, young, rural, urban, whatever, that does not strongly associate the Green party with taking action on the environment.” Because of that starting point, he argues, the sensible move forward was to evolve into a broader message – one previous leaders paved the way for. “The reason the party exists is in recognition of the fact that just having a bunch of environmental conservation movements isn’t addressing the root political and economic causes of environmental degradation. “We tried 50 years of that. And it got us so far, but the manifest moments of material advancement have been tied to moments where we’ve been able to be more responsive to the actual political context of the day.” Warfield points out that many of Polanski’s positions are not his alone. Green party members vote on policy and the leaders are constitutionally duty bound to advocate for it. “Take the wealth tax,” Warfield writes. “He did not arrive at this policy personally. A ‘wealth tax’ is called for as ‘a means of limiting large accumulations of wealth’ in a Green party manifesto published long before Polanski’s leadership.” The book finds links between the party’s past and present, even in unlikely places. It’s unavoidable, Warfield writes, that there were “some distinctly rightwing people present at the formation of the Green party”. The first key figure was Teddy Goldsmith, an environmentalist part of a famous Tory family. His writings formed key texts for People, the political party from which the modern Greens descend. But even Goldsmith – whose “deep ecology” philosophy leaned into Malthusian concerns about human population and misanthropic views that blamed humanity as a monolith for ecological degradation – shares threads with Polanski’s Greens, Warfield says. Both share the golden Green rule that infinite economic growth and endless extraction are impossible on a planet with finite resources. Both reject the idea that capitalism can simply carry on with business as usual, green or otherwise. As the party has shifted towards social ecology over the years, Warfield says Polanski’s eco-socialism simply represents a modern evolution: arguing that capitalism and the 1% – not all of humanity – are the root cause of environmental destruction. But Polanski’s tenure has also brought controversies. There was his criticism of the police response to the Golders Green attack, which the Met commissioner, Mark Rowley, called “inaccurate and misinformed”. There was the false claim he was a British Red Cross spokesperson and the sharing of a photo of a man with a T-shirt showing a guillotine and the phrase “we’re only making plans for Nigel”, a reference to Nigel Farage. YouGov polling shows Polanski’s approval rating has slumped since he became leader, while Green voting intention has dropped from 21% of the electorate in March to 11% this month. Should the party take Polanski’s social media away? “Golders Green was a misstep,” says Warfield. “But what you don’t want to do is to get to a situation where every post needs double-tick signoff from different members of staff and you can’t just let Zack engage with social media in the way that allows him to reap the political points of authenticity.” Polanski was criticised for his refusal to apologise for sharing the Farage guillotine picture. “Reform were trying to goad him into apologising for incitement to murder,” Warfield says. “If you do that, you legitimise the claim that they’re making. I think there’s a lot of strength in not succumbing to the pressure of playing that game.” On 8 October, Polanski will contest the Holborn and St Pancras byelection after Keir Starmer announced his decision to vacate the seat. Warfield thinks Polanski can win. “You could vote Labour again and you get another backbencher who is one among literally hundreds of Labour MPs and that doesn’t make much difference to anything,” he says. “Or you can put a really prominent, independently minded Green in there and continue to put pressure on the Burnham project from its left.”

title: New powerful synthetic opioids behind sharp rise in Scottish drug deaths
summary: Eleven per cent increase in fatalities last year partly down to presence of nitazenes in Scotland’s illicit drug market
text: New forms of a powerful synthetic opioid have contributed to a sharp rise in Scottish drug deaths, with the latest data showing an 11% increase in fatalities last year Annual figures released by National Records of Scotland (NRS) on Wednesday recorded 1,133 drug-related deaths in 2025, 116 more than the previous year. The 2025 figures are the sixth highest on record. Opiates and opioids, which include drugs such as heroin, remain the most deadly drug types, implicated in 78% of all deaths. But the presence of nitazenes – a highly potent type of synthetic opioid – rose by more than 200%, from 76 deaths in 2024 to 247 in 2025. Maree Todd, the minister for mental wellbeing, public health, sport, alcohol and drugs, said an “increasingly toxic and unpredictable drugs supply” required “more coordinated action across the country”. Last year’s data showed Scotland’s lowest drug deaths since 2017, but the charity Scottish Drugs Forum (SDF) warned at the time that this was most likely a blip, masking a recent surge in synthetic opioids in Scotland’s illicit drug market. Unlike plant-derived drugs such as heroin, nitazenes are created in illegal laboratories and can be hundreds of times stronger than traditional opiates and opioids. They are also often mixed with other drugs, increasing the risks to users who do not always know what is present in the supply. SDF’s chief executive, Kirsten Horsburgh, said the increase in drug deaths reflected a range of factors “including an increasingly unpredictable drugs supply”. The increased presence of nitazenes was “a stark indication of [the] changing risks”, she added Horsburgh said: “It is too simplistic to say that 1,133 people died because of the contaminated drug supply, or indeed because of drug use itself. The truth is that these deaths are shaped by a much wider set of factors, including poverty, trauma, deprivation, housing insecurity and mental health inequality.” The figures showed drug-related deaths were 15 times higher in Scotland’s most deprived areas than in the least deprived. There was a 19% rise in deaths among men, withthe average age of death 46. Todd said the government had funded more than 1,100 residential rehabilitation placements last year and widened access to treatment. But, she added, “despite these policy interventions, and the actions of our valued frontline workers, it is clear we need to do much more to reduce this tragic loss of life”. The new figures mean Scotland remains Europe’s “drug deaths capital”, with the worst fatality rate in the continent. Before the figures were published, the Scottish government announced that a new drug-checking service, which will allow users to submit drugs for rapid testing and provide harm reduction advice, would open early next month in Glasgow’s safer drug consumption facility. Similar drug-checking services have been approved in Aberdeen and Dundee, with a fourth expected in Edinburgh.

title: Delays in Covid shots for kids is latest bid by Trump officials to restrict vaccines
summary: Administration is holding back Covid vaccines for all children in at least 11 states and one US territory
text: The Trump administration is holding back Covid vaccines for all children in at least 11 states and one US territory, and officials have not indicated when or whether the shots will become available. It’s the latest step by top officials to restrict vaccines in the US – and it sets a precedent for holding back other immunizations, experts said. “They’re using every means possible to try and make it harder to get vaccinated,” said Daniel Jernigan, the former director of the National Center for Emerging and Zoonotic Infectious Diseases at the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). These actions could be a way of “testing the waters” on halting other vaccines in the federal Vaccines for Children (VFC) program, Jernigan said. “There’s nothing preventing them from doing that for the other vaccines as well,” he added. More than half of children in the US receive vaccines through VFC, and some states and American Samoa are also known as “universal” vaccine purchasers, which means they buy vaccines through this system for all children in the state or territory, regardless of their insurance status or ability to pay. But as updated pediatric Covid shots roll out throughout the country amid a Covid wave, HHS is not providing Covid vaccines through the VFC program, with no timeline on when the vaccines will be sent. That means the 52% of children who are eligible for VFC – because they are Alaska Native or American Indian, under- or uninsured, or enrolled in or eligible for Medicaid – as well as all children in universal VFC states don’t have access to Covid vaccines. “The delay in VFC means delays in these states’ ability to get vaccine for all children,” said Demetre Daskalakis, former director of the CDC’s National Center for Immunization and Respiratory Diseases and chief medical officer at Callen-Lorde Community health center. The states with universal purchase programs include Alaska, Connecticut, Hawaii, Maine, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, New Mexico, Rhode Island, Vermont, Washington, and Wyoming. Some states, like Idaho, also purchase some of the recommended vaccines in this way. Emily Hilliard, a spokesperson for the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), confirmed that Covid vaccines are not available through VFC. Because Covid can circulate at other times as well, including in the summer, “an arbitrary September date should not be treated as a public-health deadline for Covid-19 vaccine procurement”. The CDC is “finalizing decisions” about Covid vaccine procurement through the Vaccines for Children and Section 317 programs, and “additional information will be available soon”, Hilliard said. She did not respond to the Guardian’s questions about the effects on universal VFC states. The updated Covid shot provides the best protection against variants that are circulating now, Jernigan said. “Getting the updated vaccine out there is going to provide the most protection to kids,” he said, adding that HHS is “not allowing the best vaccine to be out there to prevent the most disease”. Previous vaccines expired earlier this year. Vaccinating children is especially important early in life; infants have one of the highest hospitalization rates from Covid after the 65-plus age group. “Those are kids that have never been exposed to Covid,” Jernigan said, adding that vaccination can help prevent these severe outcomes. “It’s, in a sense, almost derelict that you would not make it available to those most vulnerable to severe disease,” he said. Jernigan is concerned about the vaccines that were recently designated “shared clinical-decision making”, including hepatitis B, meningococcal vaccines, and the flu shot; a judge’s order has stayed such changes for now. Robert F Kennedy Jr, HHS secretary and longtime vaccine opponent, has claimed that these changes have not affected vaccination, even as public confidence in vaccines sags after years of misinformation. “We have not taken vaccines away from anyone. We have preserved access,” he said at an anti-vaccine conference last week. Hilliard, the HHS spokesperson, did not respond to a question about how Kennedy’s statement squared with the decision not to make Covid vaccines available. “Not allowing universal ordering states to order vaccine is limiting access,” Daskalakis said. The restrictions on vaccines are part of a pattern at HHS, Jernigan said, “trying to find each lever to keep the vaccine from being accessible”. The administration has taken multiple steps to decrease the availability of vaccines, “just making it harder and harder” to get them, he said, calling it “death by a thousand cuts”.

title: Beluga whale rescued from closed Canadian marine park dies in US
summary: Osiris, one of 30 belugas removed from Ontario’s shuttered Marineland, struggled to acclimate to her Illinois home
text: An Illinois aquarium has said that a third beluga whale it rescued from a closed marine park in Canada this summer has died after it struggled to acclimate to its new environment. Osiris, a 26-year-old female, was one of 30 belugas removed from Ontario’s shuttered Marineland amusement park, and among 10 rehomed at the Shedd aquarium in Chicago, which said the whale died there on Monday. Over the last month two other rescued belugas, named Peekachu and Rain, have died at the Shedd; and a 19-year-old male, Jelly Bean, one of two relocated to Oceanogràfic de València in Spain, died “suddenly and unexpectedly” last week. “When Shedd was asked to help with this rescue, we understood that these animals arrived with significant vulnerabilities and that the outcome for every individual could not be guaranteed,” the aquarium said in a statement. Beluga whales are particularly vulnerable to changes in their environment, such as climate change, pollution and other sources of stress, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (Noaa). Native to Alaska’s Cook Inlet, belugas are classified as an endangered species, and their numbers have declined by almost 80% from 1979 to 2018. The 30 whales, and a number of bottlenose dolphins, became the subject of what marine activists said was akin to a hostage situation following the 2024 closure to the public of Marineland, a troubled theme park on the southern shores of the Niagara river. More than 20 whales and dolphins had died there since 2019, and a calamitous drop in visitor numbers and income forced the owners to abandon the venture. The Canadian government blocked the sale of the surviving animals to China, leaving them facing the threat of euthanasia. A complex international operation moved 30 whales to aquariums in the US and Spain over the summer, but many did not take well to their new surroundings. The deaths were sudden and unexpected as their health wavered amid the challenges of adjusting to a new home, according to statements from the aquariums. The rescued belugas were moved in custom-made slings and temperature-controlled containers, Shedd staff told the Associated Press. Aquarium personnel traveled to Marineland to examine their health records in preparation for the move. They have monitored their health minute by minute since they arrived, staff said. Peekachu and Rain died at the Shedd in late August and early September after arriving from Canada. Another beluga, at the aquarium for decades, died around the same time. Osiris was a “whale of clinical concern” since she arrived, according to the aquarium. The whale did not eat as consistently as her fellow animals, which complicated the efforts to keep her well-fed and hydrated, according to the statement. “Osiris experienced periods of meaningful progress, both nutritionally and socially, but her overall condition remained closely monitored,” the aquarium stated. Osiris’ caretakers noticed sudden changes in her behavior and breathing patterns the morning of her death, according to the aquarium. She was moved to the medical habitat, but “her condition declined rapidly,” and she “passed away despite lifesaving efforts”. José Rafael Serra Díez, spokesperson for Oceanogràfic de València, said Jelly Bean’s death was also unexpected. The whale “experienced feeding difficulties, prompting the veterinary team to intensify her monitoring”, despite periods of improvement, the spokesperson said in an email to the AP. The Georgia aquarium and SeaWorld locations in San Diego and San Antonio have also accepted whales from the Canadian park. The two rescued whales at the Georgia aquarium showed decreased appetites and were examined, but no issues were found, the aquarium said in a social media post on Friday. The whales at SeaWorld are in “stable health”, according to AnneMarie Iturrizaga, a spokesperson for the company that owns the parks. The Shedd aquarium notified Noaa of Osiris’s death Monday, according to John Chu, a spokesperson for Noaa Fisheries. Within 30 days of the whales’ deaths, the aquarium must formally submit their names and causes of death, and on request, provide copies of necropsy reports, Chu said. The Shedd aquarium said it will conduct necropsies and share the confirmed results. The Associated Press contributed to this report

title: Delcy Rodríguez poses with Trump in New York as Maduro languishes in jail nearby
summary: Venezuela’s interim president hails ‘historic meeting’ and does not say whether she will visit snatched predecessor
text: Venezuela’s interim president, Delcy Rodríguez, has celebrated a “historic” meeting with Donald Trump in New York, posing for a smiley photo with the US president, less than nine months after he ordered the abduction of her boss, Nicolás Maduro. The former foes met at a five-star hotel a few blocks from Trump Tower in Manhattan late on Tuesday on the sidelines of the UN general assembly. The hotel is about 7 miles from the Brooklyn prison where Maduro has been held since he was snatched during a special forces raid on Caracas in January. On the eve of Tuesday’s encounter, an American reporter asked Rodríguez if she would be visiting Maduro, under whom she served as vice-president, during her stay in New York. She did not reply. But she did find time to meet Trump at the luxury Lotte New York Palace hotel, with the get-together seen as a key part of Rodríguez’s push for international legitimacy after years of Venezuela’s diplomatic isolation under Maduro’s dictatorship. On Wednesday she is expected to address the annual UN assembly. “We held a historic meeting with … Donald Trump, with whom we discussed strengthening the bilateral relationship between our countries and advancing a cooperation agenda in strategic areas such as energy, mining, security and other matters of common interest,” Rodríguez wrote on Instagram, in a 133-word statement that made no mention of her incarcerated ally. Oliver Blanco, one of Rodríguez’s top diplomats, claimed the meeting marked “a new stage of dialogue and understanding between both countries” and was “an important step toward new opportunities for our country and our people”. Blanco also posted a cheery photo in which he and Trump smiled and gave the thumbs up to the camera. A White House aide said the meeting was also attended by top US officials including the secretary of state, Marco Rubio, and the deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller. “It was a short meeting but it was an important meeting,” Rubio said on Wednesday, telling reporters it had focused on Venezuela’s economic recovery and political transition. Hours earlier, Rodríguez had sat in the general assembly hall watching Trump celebrate the “massive military operation” during which Maduro – whom he called an “outlaw dictator” and “a real criminal” – was captured. “It was a war … [and] to the victor belong the spoils,” Trump bragged of the recent oil deal between the US and Venezuela, as Rodríguez appeared to wince. Some observers also detected signs of discomfort in the body language captured in the photo of Trump and Rodríguez, who appeared to be clenching her left fist. Some of Rodríguez’s critics in Venezuela called her treatment by Trump an unmitigated humiliation for a socialist party politician who has spent years railing against American imperialism. After Maduro’s capture, Trump warned that Rodríguez would “pay a very big price, probably bigger than Maduro,” if she did not toe the US line. Since then, Rodríguez has made a series of concessions, including ceding control of Venezuela’s oil revenues to Washington and agreeing to a controversial 65bn-barrel oil deal that Trump on Tuesday called “the largest oil deal in history”. One opposition figure denounced the Rodríguez-Trump meeting as an encounter between a “shameless puppet and her unscrupulous puppeteer”. But Rodríguez has succeeded in consolidating power, with Trump seemingly more focused on gaining access to Venezuela’s natural resources than pushing for a fresh presidential election that would move the South American country back towards democracy. Trump has repeatedly praised Rodríguez’s “fantastic” and “terrific” leadership while sidelining her main rival, the opposition leader María Corina Machado. Machado, who left Venezuela late last year to receive her Nobel peace prize in Oslo, has been unable to return and is exiled in Panama. She reportedly made three attempts to return to Venezuela this week but failed. Orlando Pérez, a Latin America expert from the University of North Texas at Dallas, rejected the idea that Rodríguez had been humiliated by her meeting with Trump. “It’s a huge triumph [for her]. She got the photo op she wanted. I frankly don’t think you can overestimate how important the photo op was for her,” said Pérez, who believed the image legitimised Rodríguez’s position as president and signalled that Washington was happy to keep working with her and for other leaders to engage with her. For Trump, meeting Rodríguez was a way to show Maga voters he had “won Venezuela” by commandeering its massive oil reserves with January’s invasion. “So that picture was a win-win for Delcy and for Trump,” Pérez added. Before Tuesday’s tête-à-tête, the presidents of the US and Venezuela had last met in 2015, when Barack Obama and Maduro spoke briefly during a regional summit in Panama. In the decade that followed, Maduro became an international pariah as he led his country into economic chaos and increasingly authoritarian rule, and Venezuela was hit by punishing international sanctions. At the 2015 summit, Obama conceded that the days in which “the US could meddle with impunity” in Latin America were over. But Trump has dramatically different ideas and has been forging ahead with attempts to reassert US dominance in a region it has long considered its back yard. As well as capturing Venezuela’s government and trying to topple Cuba’s communist government by strangling its economy, Trump’s push for hegemony has also seen the US accused of trying to swing Brazil’s presidential election in favour of the far-right candidate Flávio Bolsonaro through diplomatic and economic pressure. Addressing the UN assembly on Tuesday, the Brazilian president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, hit back at such efforts, without directly citing the US. “We will not allow the enemies of democracy – internal or external – to attack the will of the people. Brazilian democracy belongs to the Brazilians,” said Lula who is facing a tough battle to win re-election in October’s vote. “Brazil doesn’t fit into anyone’s back yard,” added Lula, who also called for elections in Venezuela. He did not meet Rodríguez during her visit to New York but said the “people of Venezuela deserve to decide their own future”.

title: Trump addresses UN with mixture of boasts, threats and jibes | First Thing
summary: US-Iran meeting takes place on sidelines despite president’s threat to ‘annihilate’ Tehran regime. Plus, one man’s month-long pilates odyssey
text: Good morning. Donald Trump has used the platform of the UN general assembly in New York to threaten to “annihilate the Islamic republic” of Iran, “and do it quickly”. He called on countries to unite to isolate Tehran and bring down global energy prices. Despite his bombastic rhetoric, Trump also said Iranian officials held three hours of talks with the US special envoy Steve Witkoff on the sidelines of the meeting. Witkoff said he felt very good about the meeting, the first such contact since the US vice-president, JD Vance, met an Iranian delegation in Switzerland in June. A senior Iranian official also indicated that Iran was prepared to reopen the strait of Hormuz within a week. What else did Trump say at the UN? The president doubled down on his defence of AI development, saying warnings about runaway agents were a “hoax”; announced the US would build new military bases in Greenland; attacked the international criminal court as a “rogue organisation”; and prompted the Cuba’s delegation to stage a walkout when he described the country as a “failed state”. Did he continue his attacks on US media networks? Trump scolded a CNN anchor for covering him at the UN, saying “I’m surprised that CNN is here covering me. You should not be here covering me. You said you weren’t going to cover me.” Last week, the president announced he was banning CNN, Politico and MS Now from the White House. Follow UN proceedings live today here. Republican calls for Senate investigation of Trump Jr wedding paid for by Russian oligarch A Republican senator has accused Donald Trump Jr of corruption and demanded a Senate investigation into revelations that a Russian oligarch bankrolled part of his recent wedding in the Bahamas. John Curtis, of Utah, wrote to the leaders of the US Senate judiciary committee on Tuesday, urging them to subpoena Trump Jr over his business dealings, his relationships with foreign individuals, gifts he has received – and any occasions where his connection to his father, Donald Trump, “was invoked or understood to provide value”. Where else is the president seeing dissent from Republicans? Another prominent Florida Republican has publicly distanced himself from Trump, days after María Elvira Salazar called out the president’s immigration-enforcement policy targeting law-abiding undocumented immigrants. Byron Donalds, the Republican nominee for governor in November’s midterm elections, launched an updated campaign website on Tuesday that was stripped of almost every mention of Trump. Mississippi grand jury decides not to charge anyone in death of Nolan Wells A grand jury made a unanimous decision to not bring criminal charges against anyone in the mysterious death of Nolan Wells, a Mississippi teenager who died after a boat outing with friends on 4 July. Wells’s case drew national attention, with many speculating about what happened and suspecting that the 18-year-old’s disappearance and death may have been racially motivated. Wells, who was Black while the friends with whom he was last seen were white, was also the only friend in the group who did not return from the trip that day. Hayden Panettiere’s cause of death confirmed as fentanyl overdose Hayden Panettiere died from a fentanyl overdose, according to the Greenville county coroner’s office. Medical examiners said there were “no signs of trauma” and “the manner of death has been ruled accident”. Panettiere was in her South Carolina apartment with her boyfriend, Brian Hickerson, and his brother Zach when she died on August 16. Panettiere, known for her roles in television series including Heroes and Nashville, began acting at just 11 months old. After her death, her father released a statement, saying: “She was an incredible light and a force of nature who brought immeasurable love and joy to all who knew her – and to the millions who watched her onscreen.” In other news … Ella Langley’s hit song Choosin’ Texas has set a new record, spending 23 weeks at the top of the Billboard Hot 100, unseating Mariah Carey’s All I Want for Christmas Is You, which topped the charts for 22 weeks. An US F-16 fighter jet ⁠in western Germany crashed on Tuesday, the US military said, ⁠adding that one pilot had ejected safely. DoorDash said it would pay $131.5m ⁠to settle a New York City government investigation that found the food delivery company underpaid or waited too long to pay workers. ‘Looksmaxxing’ influencer Clavicular has been charged with rape and drug offenses in Massachusetts. The 20-year-old, whose real name is Braden Eric Peters, has been scheduled for a 14 October arraignment. Qantas says travellers will be able to fly between Sydney and New York in just 18 hours from mid-2028 when the airline launches its second ultra long-haul route. Well Actually: Get tested and talk to your partner – how to have safer sex after age 50 We are long past the era when sex was for young married couples trying for children and nobody else. Amanda Zuckerman Klarsfeld has compiled this thoughtful selection of advice for older lovers. Don’t miss this: Why public transport in global cities is slowing to a crawl – visualised The UK capital’s iconic red buses have a problem: they are getting slower. And it isn’t just an issue in London, but a growing worldwide problem for transit networks, with worrying implications for the poorest in society. Our visuals team have put together this rich explainer to explore why. … or this: Will anyone topple soccer boss Infantino? Since Fifa abandoned its controversial World Cup sell-off plan last month, causing deep divisions among the global administrators of soccer, the governing body’s president, Gianni Infantino, has continued to lobby for re-election. title: Not set in stone: teachers are defying mandates to display the Ten Commandments in classrooms
summary: Some educators are pushing back in class and in court against the display of the religious code in public schools
text: When history teacher Chris Dier sued Louisiana two years ago for mandating that the Ten Commandments be displayed in classrooms, he said it was not about taking a stand against Christianity. “It’s a defense of many different types of values, including civil liberties and religious freedoms,” Dier said, who teaches at a New Orleans high school. “I spent over 16 years teaching students that the constitution protects everyone of every faith – students of no faith too.” While Dier’s lawsuit has stalled, posters of the sacred text have appeared in schools across the state. Dier said he would not hang up a copy even if one is dropped off at his door, and he is willing to accept the consequences. “I want people to know there are teachers out there who want to demonstrate that we can take a stand,” he said. “We don’t have to let schools become battlegrounds.” Louisiana is among four states (including Texas, Arkansas and Alabama) that have recently enacted laws requiring the Ten Commandments to be posted in all public school classrooms, from kindergarten to college. A host of other southern states, including West Virginia, Mississippi and South Carolina, are debating similar legislation. The laws, which raise thorny questions about the separation of church and state, are gaining renewed attention as the supreme court is expected to consider a number of challenges to them, including Dier’s, in the fall. Public school teachers caught in the crosshairs of the escalating culture war are fighting back, some taking the legal route and others quietly defying the law in their own classes. At least two teachers in Texas, theater teacher Gigi Cervantes and band director Johnnie Cotton, have quit in protest. “I believe very strongly that politics and religion have no place in the public schools,” Cotton said in a Facebook post announcing his resignation. “I spent my 42 years as a teacher and administrator making sure that my classroom/campus stayed neutral on both counts.” ‘It is Christian nationalist bullying’ Taria Usher, a kindergarten teacher in a district near Houston, said she was furious when copies of the Ten Commandments were delivered to her school in late May. By law, she is obliged to display one in her class. “I’m personally Christian, but professionally, a secular teacher,” Usher said. “Publicly funded classrooms are not the place for religious tenets to be put up.” Rather than simply complying with the mandate, Usher ordered posters with different religious teachings – the Five Pillars of Islam, the Five Precepts of Buddhism and the Yamas and Niyamas of yoga – and hung them around the Ten Commandments. Then she launched a petition demanding that the school board join in the ACLU’s lawsuit against the state or allow teachers to take down the posters without any backlash. Usher read out the demands at a school board meeting this month. “For me, it is Christian nationalist bullying,” she said about the state mandate. “I am going to fight against it.” Other groups and opponents of the law have organized resources for teachers, including the website IllegalPoster.com, which offers free LGBTQ-themed posters of the Ten Commandments, as well as companion posters explaining why the mandate is unconstitutional. The Texas law requires that the commandments be displayed in a “conspicuous place” on posters of at least 16 by 20 inches in size, and the text has to be easily read by anyone with “average vision”. One stipulation: schools are not required to buy the posters with district funds, but they must accept donated copies. That hasn’t stopped some districts in Texas from spending thousands of dollars to print their own posters. Well-funded Christian groups have also been raising money to buy and send copies of the Ten Commandments to schools. Texas’s attorney general, Ken Paxton, and other proponents of the law have argued that the Ten Commandments are “irrevocably intertwined with America’s legal, moral and historical heritage”. It’s a perspective that Usher said she “unequivocally” rejects. “As an African American woman, American heritage has been oppression and slavery,” she said. “I see a push in certain ways that some people in this country want to go back to those things. The last thing I see is people obeying the Ten Commandments.” Fight could head to the supreme court Daniel Mach, the director of the ACLU Program on Freedom of Religion and Belief, said the Ten Commandments policies are part of a broader movement by the Christian right to inject religion in public schools, including efforts to install chaplains on campus and create religious charter schools. “There are plenty of people who want to take a wrecking ball to the wall separating religion and government,” he said. But there’s a nearly half-century-old supreme court precedent protecting this wall, Mach said. In a 1980 ruling, the court ruled that a similar Kentucky law violated first amendment rights, which bars the government from establishing or favoring a religion. “The court then said what we’re arguing now, which is that these laws violate the important constitutional protection that we have against government religious favoritism,” he said. Many parents are also fighting back, joining forces with the ACLU and other legal groups to file a flurry of lawsuits against the mandates. After seven Arkansas families with children in public school sued the state last year over its Ten Commandments mandate, a federal judge struck down the law in March, arguing that “nothing could possibly justify hanging the Ten Commandments – with or without historical context – in a calculus, chemistry, French or woodworking class, to name a few”. (The state has said it intends to appeal the ruling.) In Texas, two dozen families from multi-faith backgrounds asked the supreme court last month to take up their challenge against the state law – after the US fifth circuit court of appeals ruled against them. The supreme court is expected to consider two challenges to the Texas law this fall. The Rev Mara Richards Bim, a Dallas-based Baptist pastor and parent who is part of the Texas litigation, said the law violates the “separation of church and state” principle that is integral to her faith. “As a Baptist, I am opposed to the state imposing their version of faith in classrooms,” Bim said. “Scripture and faith traditions are best taught at homes and in church.” Two other plaintiffs, Ted and Rebekah Lowe, are raising their children in a Christian and Jewish family. They said they don’t oppose the teachings themselves but felt that the government has no right to privilege one religion over any other. “When it comes to religious instruction like the Ten Commandments, it’s my job as a parent to teach it,” Ted Lowe said. “I don’t want government officials inserting themselves into our children’s religious education.”

title: Police use teargas on protesters as disabled woman, 87, evicted from Madrid home
summary: Housing rights campaigners decry landlord’s ‘barbaric behaviour’ after apartment Maricarmen had lived in for 71 years was bought by a developer
text: There were violent scenes in Madrid on Wednesday as riot police fought with protesters trying to prevent the eviction of an 87-year-old disabled woman from her apartment in the Retiro district. Hundreds of protesters had gathered, many of them overnight, in an effort to block the fourth attempt to carry out the eviction. Activists from the Madrid and Barcelona tenants’ union, and celebrities including the actor Carlos Bardem and the singer and actor Ana Belén, joined the protest. Police fired rounds of teargas and made repeated baton charges as they tried to open a path for a judicial committee to carry out the eviction order, which was eventually executed on Wednesday morning. The tenant, known simply by her first name, Maricarmen, is about to turn 88. Demonstrators chanted “Ayuso’s attic for Maricarmen”, a reference to the scandal surrounding the Madrid regional president Isabel Díaz Ayuso’s alleged purchase with public money of a €6.3m residential apartment for her use as a temporary office. Behind the building’s locked door, more protesters occupied the staircase leading to Maricarmen’s flat while neighbours handed out snacks and offered the demonstrators the use of their bathrooms. When a developer bought the building Maricarmen had lived in for 71 years, she was offered the chance to buy her apartment for €247,000 (£212,000), an impossible sum for a pensioner. They then raised her rent from €500 to €1,650 a month, while she receives a state pension of €1,350. An unnamed “prominent” writer offered to pay the €1,150 difference indefinitely but their offer was ignored. In a video recorded by the local tenants’ union before the eviction, a tearful Maricarmen said: “Good morning, everyone, I thank you for the action you are taking, spending the whole night sleeping in the street. Please, keep going, but don’t hurt one another. This has to be peaceful. “I can still hear all your noise. A hug to everyone and to all the people who are supporting me in this cruel struggle against a person who wants to make money but who should not forget that they have parents and that one day they could find themselves in the situation that unfortunately I am in.” The original 1956 contract for the flat was in Maricarmen’s father’s name. When he died, the apartment passed to his wife, and on her death in 2008 it was then sublet to Maricarmen. The landlords, Urbagestión SL, successfully argued in the supreme court that this subletting was invalid and that the contract was no longer valid. Urbagestión SL has been approached for comment. Speaking at the scene, Aldo Reverte, a spokesperson for the Confederation of Tenants’ Unions, said: “Maricarmen’s case is just one more example of what happens when housing is put in the hands of landlords. The difference is that a lot of people have become aware of her situation and the tenants’ union has shown that we can fight this type of barbaric behaviour.” However, for all their efforts, the protesters were unable to stop the eviction. Beatriz Duro, the lawyer representing Maricarmen, said: “The owner isn’t prepared to negotiate or accept any sort of offer. We have asked for a place where we can take Maricarmen’s personal belongings.” So far this year, 4,000 evictions have been carried out in Spain.

title: Legal & General to cut 1,000 jobs by mid-2027
summary: Programme will initially involve voluntary redundancies in the UK but the insurance and pensions firm will consider mandatory job cuts depending on the take-up
text: Legal & General plans to cut 1,000 jobs by the middle of next year, about a tenth of the British insurance and pensions firm’s workforce. António Simões, the chief executive, is wielding the axe as part of his attempts to create a “leaner organisation” since taking over from longtime CEO Nigel Wilson in January 2024. L&G described the move as “the next stage of that transformation”. The London-headquartered firm told staff on Wednesday that it had begun moves to eliminate about 1,000 roles by mid-2027, which had first been reported by Bloomberg News. Most of L&G’s 10,000 employees are based in the UK. The programme will initially involve voluntary redundancies in the UK but L&G will consider mandatory job cuts depending on the take-up. The fund management division, which oversees £1.2tn in assets, is excluded as it has its own restructuring plan. Simões, who previously worked for Santander and HSBC, announced a sharper focus on L&G’s booming pensions arm in June 2024 and reduced the group’s four businesses to three, by merging its asset management divisions. It sold several “non-strategic” assets, the biggest of which was the housebuilder Cala Homes, along with legacy land and real estate. He also brought in a new executive team and pledged to return more than £5bn to shareholders between 2025 and 2027 through dividends and share buybacks. Simões told employees in an email: “Over the past two-and-a-half years, we have made significant progress executing our strategy, simplifying L&G, establishing three core businesses, and creating a more focused business. “However, over the last decade, different structures, processes and ways of working have developed across L&G, making us more complex than we need to be… we need to change how we work today and, through this, become a leaner organisation.” An L&G spokesperson said the changes “will help us focus our resources and investment on the areas where we see the strongest opportunities for long-term growth”. The spokesperson added: “We recognise and take seriously the impact on colleagues and are committed to supporting our people throughout the process and consulting with our unions.” The company expects £500bn of transactions in the UK pensions market over the next decade, as employers transfer their old defined benefit pension plans to insurers and pension companies. L&G said it was also benefiting from strong auto-enrolment of staff in their companies’ pension schemes, with about £1bn of new inflows each month.
