title: Indian billionaire’s payments firm plots biggest London flotation in years
summary: Sunil Bharti Mittal’s Airtel Money targets $9bn IPO in boost for ailing UK stock market
text: A payments business that operates across Africa and is ultimately controlled by an Indian billionaire has announced its intention to float on the struggling London Stock Exchange. Airtel Money, the mobile money arm of Airtel Africa, is planning one of the biggest UK listings in years, in a boost for the shrinking London market that has faced a string of recent departures. The company is understood to be hoping to raise about $800m (£601m) from the initial public offering (IPO) and is targeting a valuation of $8bn to $9bn, which would make it one of London’s largest listings in recent years. Airtel Money has 53 million monthly active users across 13 countries in sub-Saharan Africa, including Uganda, Zambia and the Democratic Republic of Congo. It operates through a network of branches and kiosks, which enable customers to load money on to their phones, withdraw cash and access other money services, and the company generated revenues of just under $1.4bn in the last financial year. Airtel Money’s parent company is Airtel Africa, a telecoms provider that is part of the Indian conglomerate Bharti Enterprises, which is ultimately controlled by the billionaire Sunil Bharti Mittal. Airtel Africa is already listed on the FTSE 100 but said it wanted Airtel Money to be listed separately. “From a company perspective, [the listing] gives us flexibility for the future,” said Airtel Money’s chief executive, Ian Ferrao. “We evaluated multiple [stock] exchanges, including the Middle East because we’ve got a headquarters in Dubai, along with European and North American exchanges. Ultimately, shareholders felt that London was the right choice. We still believe there is deep capital available … all the global institutional investors are here.” Ferrao added: “Most importantly there’s a deep understanding of emerging markets in the London market and Africa specifically.” Airtel Money said it would announce more details about the float in early October, including the indicative price range and number of shares to be offered, with final pricing to follow later in the month. Airtel Africa had originally targeted a listing in the first six months of 2026 but delayed it to the second half of the year, blaming unfavourable market conditions as a result of the US-Israeli war on Iran. Several other companies also pushed back planned IPOs amid the market volatility caused by the conflict. Airtel Africa owns just under 78% of Airtel Money and will remain a long-term investor after the IPO. Minority stakes are held by TPG, Mastercard, the Qatar Investment Authority and Chimetech Holding. Revenue in Airtel Money’s most recent quarter to 30 June climbed 38% to £399m, according to Airtel Africa. The decision to float Airtel Money in the UK could mark a turning point for the City, which has struggled to attract listings in recent times and has also been hit by departures, partly as a result of overseas takeovers of UK companies. Airtel Money’s planned listing could be one of the biggest debuts since the international payments company Wise floated in 2021 with a valuation of £8.75bn. Wise has since moved its main listing from London to New York.

title: Stung by Trump, machinists union campaigns for affordability in midterms
summary: One of the largest labor unions in the US targets eight battleground states in ‘workers v billionaires’ campaign
text: The International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers (IAM), one of the largest labor unions in the US, has launched a “workers v billionaires” political campaign tour targeting members in eight battleground states and encouraging them to support pro-worker candidates in the midterms. IAM has nearly 700,000 active and retired members in North America, covering workers at corporations that include Boeing, Lockheed Martin, United Airlines and Harley-Davidson. The union is targeting members and voters in Maine, Pennsylvania, Michigan, Texas, Ohio, Georgia, Arizona, Nevada and Illinois. “We made a strategic commitment that we’re going to be the most engaged that we have ever been in the history of our union in working,” said Brian Bryant, international president of IAM. “We’re living in an economy that only favors billionaires and does not favor working people, and it’s time that Congress and this administration realize who they should be looking out for.” Bryant emphasized that several union members, including those with IAM, voted for Trump in 2024 because of promises that he would fix the economy and make things more affordable. Throughout his 2024 presidential campaign, Trump repeatedly claimed: “When I win, I will immediately bring prices down, starting on day one.” Yet since Trump took office, inflation has increased from 3.0% in January 2025 to 3.4% in August 2026, health insurance costs are soaring due to the expiration of Affordable Care Act subsidies and gas prices are on average $1 a gallon higher due to Trump’s war with Iran. The union will “send a message to this administration that what the status quo is right now is not acceptable, and they’re going to have to stand up and pay attention to working people”, Bryant said. Jason Gayler, president of IAM local 776A in Fort Worth, Texas, said his state “is more purple than what people put out to be”. As Democrats are seeking to flip several seats, polls are showing that races are the most competitive they’ve been in decades. “The price of just the cost of living in north Texas now has absolutely skyrocketed, and it’s starting to really affect a lot of our members, which is motivating them to back candidates that focus primarily on the working class,” Gayler said. He also noted that the machinists recently elected their first rank-and-file member to the Texas senate; Taylor Rehmet, president of the IAM’s Texas state council, won a special election in January, flipping a state senate district that Trump won in 2024 by 17%. Shay Blodgett, an Alaska Airlines worker in Phoenix who is helping to lead IAM’s political program in Arizona, said the union has worked to oppose Republican-led state legislation that would have restricted public sector workers’ ability to organize and supported the Arizona AFL-CIO “labor 2026 blitz” campaign. “We’ve been conducting member-to-member engagement this summer, reaching out, asking members what matters to them,” Blodgett said. “We heard them loud and clear. The No 1 thing was the economy, cost of living, fuel prices, healthcare and food costs.” Co-workers have expressed regret over voting for Republicans in the last election, especially since transportation workers are exempt from the temporary no-tax-on-overtime deduction that was passed as part of Republicans’ One Big Beautiful Bill Act that was passed last summer. “The majority of our airline workers in the state will be entering contract negotiations in early 2027, and we need elected officials that will fix the economy and allow airline workers to fulfill the American dream of home ownership and raising families in Arizona,” Blodgett said. Rich Howell, former president of IAM local 1776, a longtime member of the union and worker at Philadelphia international airport, said the union is supporting Democrats in Pennsylvania who are trying to flip four congressional districts and the state senate while maintaining control of the governorship and statehouse. Trump “said he was going to bring down the prices a year and a half ago. That was his campaign message. If you go back and see all the promises, there wasn’t one that he held,” Howell said. He noted this is a difficult election year due to the amount of money billionaires are pouring into politics – more than $1.6bn in the 2026 midterm elections so far – but noted that “money doesn’t buy a race”. “Trump put the tariffs on, cutting more jobs, hurting more people in our industry,” Howell added. “It’s billionaires versus the workers, and that’s the stance we’re making. They are getting rich and we’re paying for it. We’re paying for it out of our pockets.” • This article was amended on 23 September 2026. It is $1.6bn that has been poured into the 2026 midterm elections so far. An earlier version incorrectly stated it was $1.6tn.

title: Nazi jokes and ‘cum trophies’: meet the Texas gunfluencer who could soon represent Uvalde
summary: Brandon Herrera, a YouTuber known for making outrageous pro-gun statements, is the frontrunner to represent a district devastated by mass shootings
text: The video begins with Brandon Herrera staring intently into the camera. He is filming himself in a hotel room seated between twin beds, his black hair slicked back and beard neatly trimmed. He is wearing a T-shirt branded with his trademark nickname, “The AK Guy”, above the image of a semi-automatic rifle primed for action. Three days earlier, on 3 August 2019, a white nationalist armed with a semi-automatic firearm not dissimilar to the one stamped across Herrera’s chest entered a busy Walmart store in the Texas border city of El Paso and opened fire. Within minutes the shooter had unloaded about 90 rounds, killing 23 people and injuring 22 more. With the massacre still dominating headlines, most public figures were limiting themselves to vanilla expressions of “thoughts and prayers”. Not so Herrera. He opened his video with a warning: what viewers were about to hear might sound “a little harsh”. But, he assured them, it was “data driven” and came from “a place of empathy”. Then he said: “With these terrible mass shootings, you should be really glad that some of these people are using guns to do this … I think we are fortunate that these people are using guns.” Had the perpetrator of the El Paso massacre used a truck, or a fertiliser bomb, the death toll might have been much higher, Herrera opined. He then attempted to back up the argument with statistics: the average victim count in mass shootings is 15; the Oklahoma City bombing killed 168. Such sophistry could not disguise his core argument, however. With the blood barely dry on the Walmart floor, Herrera was urging his viewers to celebrate the choice of weapon used in the carnage – a military-style AR-15 semi-automatic rifle. Herrera, 30, has made a name for himself producing such extreme out-of-the-box pro-gun statements. It is what launched him as a prominent “gunfluencer” with 4.27m subscribers to his YouTube channel, where his videos have been viewed almost 860m times. And now, he is the frontrunner in the race to represent the border district of south-west Texas in November’s midterm elections. Texas’s congressional district 23 is being closely watched as potentially decisive in the battle to control the House of Representatives through Donald Trump’s final two years in the White House. Democrats are hoping that such an extreme candidate, even by Texas’s standards, could be vulnerable at the ballot box. They aim to flip the seat that has been in Republican hands since 2015. Should he win the midterm election in Texas’s congressional district 23, Herrera will take what he calls his “second amendment absolutism” to Washington, with possible ramifications for nationwide gun laws and debate. Locally, the implications are even more poignant. It would mean that a Republican committed to loosening America’s already lax gun laws would become the voice in Congress for those who live in the outskirts of El Paso, the city left devastated by that 2019 Walmart mass shooting. More chillingly still, Herrera would also represent the town of Uvalde where, in May 2022, an 18-year-old former student killed 19 children and two teachers. Shannon Watts, the founder of the gun safety group Moms Demand Action, has been a target of Herrera’s aggressive use of social media. Should he win, she says, there could be long-lasting consequences. “His idea that somehow we should be grateful that firearms are being used in mass killings is a very cynical ploy to numb people to gun violence, to make them expect it and even accept it. The more Brandon Herreras we elect to Congress, the more likely that will be our destiny.” *** Herrera has been presenting himself on the campaign trail as a Trump-endorsed “America First” Republican. He has promised the more than half a million voters scattered across the sprawling, majority-Latino district that he will impose no new taxes, double down on the border crackdown and oppose government funding for abortion. But it was guns – and specifically the Uvalde school shooting – that brought him into politics. Herrera grew up in a military family in Fayetteville, North Carolina, and dropped out of college to build his own firearms manufacturing business, focusing on the growing market for semi-automatic rifles. He spent years developing his own spin on the Soviet Kalashnikov rifle, the AK-47. He scaled up the weapon so that it was capable of taking huge 0.50-caliber cartridges, ammunition developed for Browning heavy machine guns more than a century ago. He called his invention the AK-50, and began marketing it through his company, The AK Guy Inc. Citing frustrations with state-wide Covid restrictions, Herrera relocated the company to San Antonio, Texas, in 2020. Two years later, Uvalde became the site of one of the worst school shootings in American history. The massacre lasted 77 minutes, the shooter killing his victims at close range as police held back for more than an hour before they finally broke into the classroom and killed him. Riding the ensuing wave of revulsion, Joe Biden signed into law the Bipartisan Safer Communities Act, which strengthened background checks for buyers under 21 and tightened restrictions on firearm possession for some domestic-abuse offenders. Eric Ruben, an expert on gun policy at the SMU Dedman school of law in Dallas, Texas, says that Uvalde “jolted Congress into passing its first major piece of gun safety legislation in a quarter of a century”. Herrera had a starkly different response. Furious that Tony Gonzales, the Republican congressman representing Uvalde, had backed Biden’s Bipartisan Safer Communities Act, Herrera decided to challenge him for his seat. “If you vote against our interests, if you vote against gun rights,” he warned Gonzales in 2024, “we will primary you, and we will take your fucking job.” He did challenge Gonzales that year, losing to the incumbent narrowly, and was repeating the effort this April when Gonzales abruptly resigned from Congress in a sex scandal. His departure has cleared the way for Herrera to claim the Republican nomination. He is now free to blast his extreme view of gun rights across Uvalde, across the district, through the state of Texas and, should he be successful, nationwide. Energised by his vast YouTube following and the large sums it passes his way, Herrera is in a position to weaponise his gun rights absolutism. He has vowed to resolutely oppose any new gun safety laws, including raising the age of ownership of an AR-15-style weapon from 18 to 21 or introducing so-called “red flag” laws that allow courts to temporarily remove firearms from people who pose a threat to themselves or others. Both measures have been championed by families of Uvalde victims, some of whom have devoted themselves to pushing for stricter gun laws in the hope of preventing other mass shootings. Veronica Mata, a founder of the gun safety group Lives Robbed who lost her 10-year-old daughter, Tess, in Uvalde, has put it this way: “Just like we can never turn around and see our daughters again, we’re not going to turn around and walk away.” *** To people outside Texas, and beyond America, one of the state’s enduring mysteries is its fierce loyalty to the most extreme form of gun rights, especially in the wake of such human suffering. There are more than 1m gun licenses in Texas – twice as much as the next state, Florida – with about half of all households in possession of at least one weapon. But as Ruben, the law professor, points out, until the 1990s Texas was relatively restrictive in its gun laws. In 1995, George W Bush, then governor, signed a law allowing licensed Texans to carry concealed handguns in public. He said it would make Texas a “safer place”, an argument that meshed well with the state’s culture of rugged individualism. Herrera’s position echoes that logic: he has argued that the way to protect children is to hire more armed security officers and turn schools into “hard targets”. Since then, Texas’s policies have taken a pro-gun turn in lock step with the tightening grip of an increasingly hard-right Republican party. “Texas has largely tracked the broader effort of the gun rights movement to relax policies on firearms,” Ruben said. And yet, Texans are not universally wedded to the idea of firearms supremacy. A 2025 opinion survey by the Hobby school of public affairs at the University of Houston found that 85% of Texans support raising the age of buying an AR-15-style rifle from 18 to 21. The reform is especially relevant to Uvalde, given that the shooter legally bought two AR-style rifles with 30-round magazines just days after his 18th birthday. The same survey showed a clear majority of Texans wanting firmer background checks on gun buyers, a ban on all AR-15 style rifles, and supporting red flag laws. After the El Paso mass shooting, Republican lawmakers introduced permitless carry, allowing anyone to pack a concealed, loaded handgun in public without a licence or training. It was the polar opposite of the gun safety measures they had promised immediately after the massacre. The law was the end result of an intense lobbying campaign from hard-right gun activists. When he signed permitless carry into law in June 2021, the Republican governor Greg Abbott did not refer to the El Paso shooting. Rather, he presented it as a defiant act to stop the federal government taking Texans’ guns, arguing that arming yourself was a form of self-defense “against attacks by others”. Herrera wants a similar law to be imposed across the country. He wants what he calls “concealed carry reciprocity”. It would override regulations in states that take a more stringent approach to gun safety. Watts, the Moms Demand Action founder, described the end result Herrera is seeking: “His goal is that if you can carry a gun in Texas, no questions asked, then you should be able to carry that firearm down into the New York City subway.” *** Shannon Watts had already experienced Herrera’s particular style of political combat first-hand. He unloaded a stream of obscene invective at her on X in January 2023. Speaking directly to her in a video posted on the platform, he ridiculed the group she had founded. Rather than debate her on gun policy, he opted for vulgar phrases drawn from the pornography industry. “Just because you let somebody creampie you doesn’t mean I have to give a shit about your political opinions,” he said. Referring to her role as a mother and an activist, he continued: “The fact that you kept your cum trophy doesn’t make you any less wrong about the dumb shit that you say.” Watts told the Guardian that she was unsurprised by his virulent attack, as she has been frequently assailed over the years by male gun rights activists. “It has always been about misogyny. How dare a woman and a mother use her voice. That strikes at the heart of every gun extremist, that women could take away their manhood.” Herrera’s ascent and its impact on the gun discourse bears comparison to what Trump has done to the Republican establishment. Herrera and other “guntubers” have filled the void left by the self-implosion of the once almost monopolistic National Rifle Association (NRA), the gun rights group that held an iron grip on Republican politicians and used that power to resist public safety measures. Over the past few years, the NRA has been badly weakened by financial scandals and internal disputes. Into that vacuum has stepped a plethora of even harder-line gun-rights groups and social media influencers: louder, more brazen and pushing at the boundaries of a second-amendment free-for-all. The Guardian repeatedly asked the Herrera campaign whether the candidate would explain his policy stance in an interview, but received no reply. We followed up with a list of detailed questions about his past comments and current positions, including his reductivist view of a child as a “cum trophy”, but that also went unanswered. He did agree to talk to the New York Times recently, swatting away criticism of the base language he uses on the videos and in social media posts by presenting it as a “comedy performance”. Then there’s the company that Herrera keeps. He has been endorsed by Kyle Rittenhouse, the gun rights activist who, then 17, shot dead two men and injured another amid 2020 street protests in Kenosha, Wisconsin. (He was later acquitted of homicide.) Days after the Kenosha incident, Herrera had made another of his “jokes” on video – this time about the death of Rittenhouse’s victims. “Good luck, kid. You minted some good commies,” he said, adding that he was not encouraging anybody to go “get themselves into some shit … it’s not worth it.” The duo have now campaigned together and fired a machine gun in unison out of a helicopter. But sometimes, even some of his followers recoil from the “edgy” humour. One of the remarks that has drawn the strongest condemnation came on the Unsubscribe podcast, when he said he often thought about “putting a gun in my mouth, so I’m basically an honorary veteran”. In 2023, the latest year for which records are available, 4,690 US military veterans died by suicide using a gun. In 2025, more than 28,000 people in the wider US population died by firearm suicide. Another disturbing “joke” he has made relate to the Nazis and the Holocaust. In a 2022 video viewed 2.3m times, he calls the MP 40, the submachine gun used by the Germans in the second world war, “the original ghetto blaster”. Later in the video, he and an associate goosestep to the sound of Ericka, the military marching song adopted by the Waffen SS. The Nazi references were not the only evidence of Herrera’s flirtation with far-right historical imagery. The news outlet Jewish Insider uncovered private videos produced by a younger Herrera in North Carolina on behalf of the Fayetteville chapter of the Sons of Confederate Veterans. The group has promoted the “Lost Cause” narrative which reframes the civil war as a struggle over states’ rights rather than slavery. Herrera described SCV as an “historical honor society dedicated to preserving confederate heritage”, without mentioning its longstanding links with white supremacist groups. His involvement with neo-Confederacy activity continued until at least 2019, the newspaper reported. Such an unsettling back catalogue has provoked objections to his candidacy even from within Texas conservative circles. Brendan Steinhauser, a Republican strategist based in Austin, challenged Herrera by saying there should be zero tolerance for making light about Nazi Germany. “I don’t think the Holocaust is something we should be joking about,” he said. “I don’t think we should be singing the song of the stormtroopers.” Steinhauser told the Guardian that anything perceived as antisemitic was likely to play negatively with Texas Republicans and independent voters, both of whom tend to be strongly pro-Israel. True to form, Herrera lashed back at Steinhauser, posting on social media: “When did conservatives become pearl clutching virtue signalers?” *** Could this toxic screed prove to be Herrera’s political undoing?Nationally, the Democratic party has begun to wake up to the possibilities. In August, the Democratic congressional campaign committee added Texas 23 to its target list, denoting a shift in strategy from previous assumptions that the district was irredeemably Republican. Opinion polls have been few and far between, and those that have been conducted came from partisan sources. A survey back in March was carried out by the House Majority Pac sponsored by the Democratic party. It put Herrera’s Democratic rival, Katy Padilla Stout, two points up. A poll conducted from the other side of the aisle last month put Herrera ahead by six points. That came from the Remington research group, on behalf of the rightwing website Breitbart. On the ground, his opponent Padilla Stout sees his most egregious outbursts as a turn-off for many voters, especially his depiction of children in the wake of the Uvalde massacre at Robb elementary school. “So many children in Uvalde were affected by the shooting. When people hear the way he describes children, their jaws are on the floor,” she said. And yet, Padilla Stout has a palatability problem. How do you talk about “creampies” and “cum trophies” without offending voters anew? “As a mother myself, that’s a hard thing for me to put on thousands of doors.” Texas 23 is a deeply rural and relatively sparsely populated district that has hunting and shooting in its DNA. Padilla Stout herself grew up within that culture. “My dad bought a ranch shortly before I was born, it was part of his American dream,” she said. “And that aspect of gun culture, the hunting and ranching part, I’ve been part of it all my life. I have cousins who would get their first shotgun on their 12th birthday, that’s our family tradition.” Given the prevalence of guns in the local way of life, she hasn’t made Herrera’s gun rights policy front and centre of her campaign. Voters, she said, rarely raise it. Her first campaign ad focused on the cost of childcare and groceries, and the prolonged drag of the Iran war. But she told the Guardian that she would continue to sound the alarm whenever she is able. “Herrera is a gun manufacturer who makes money off his gun absolutism. That’s his end goal. He wants to remove all boundaries on the second amendment, and dismantle public safety piece by piece.”

title: Iran denies dropping preconditions amid ‘very productive’ three-hour UN talks in New York
summary: Trump says further talks possible as barrel of Brent crude falls to below $100 for first time in two weeks
text: Iran has pushed back on claims that it dropped former preconditions for reopening the strait of Hormuz in surprise talks held in New York under the mediation of Qatar between Tehran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, and Donald Trump’s envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. Trump said the three-hour talks held in a room at the UN headquarters had gone very well and been very productive. He suggested further talks were possible imminently, which led to the price of a barrel of Brent crude to fall to below $100 (£75) for the first time in two weeks. Witkoff said the talks had been “encouraging, constructive and successful”. In his speech to the UN general assembly, Trump said he had a decision to make very soon on whether to “annihilate the Islamic Republic” or help turn it into one of the great countries of the Middle East, the kind of bombastic threat Trump often deploys during talks with Iran. In Tehran, the foreign ministry spokesperson, Esmail Baghaei, confirmed the talks had occurred, but appeared not to confirm any shift in the Iranian negotiating position. He said: “The interaction that took place with the American side was through Qatari mediation. This interaction was aimed at conveying Iran’s conditions, including the end of the war in all its dimensions, the cessation of American aggressive actions, the naval siege, and the economic war, the release of Iranian assets and so on.” Aware of the potential domestic backlash, he added that Iran’s conditions had been conveyed. Iran set seven preconditions before returning to talks, and in a new development over the past 48 hours said the crucial strait of Hormuz could be reopened within seven days if those conditions were met. It is likely that the US and the Gulf states would have to accept a navigational route for shipping in the strait of Hormuz – a key waterway for transporting oil – that requires commercial shipping to enter through a sea lane mainly in Iranian waters and under Iranian rather than Omani control. The fact that the talks lasted three hours suggests some progress was made. The US side is under pressure to leverage down oil prices and increase the availability of refined oil before the midterm elections in November. Latest published figures suggest the number of identifiable tankers making it through the strait is fewer than five a day, but estimates of the US navy are much higher. The blockage in the strait is made worse by the uncertainty surrounding the control by the Houthis’ (the Iranian-backed Yemeni paramilitaries) of a second energy transport chokepoint, the Bab al-Mandab strait that leads from the Red Sea into the Indian Ocean. There is little sign that Trump wants to relaunch a full-scale war with Iran or indeed with the Houthis as Republicans battle to turn the domestic political agenda away from a hugely unpopular war that the Americans think they are losing. Iran is under ever more intense pressure from sanctions, and a US naval blockade is making it nearly impossible for Iran to export oil, depriving the country of badly needed foreign currency. Iran’s civilian aircraft on Wednesday faced a potential worldwide grounding owing to the threat of US secondary sanctions on any entity that engaged with Iran’s civilian fleet. Iranian officials negotiated frantically with neighbouring countries to try to maintain an air bridge, but it appears Oman and Iraq have been forced to close their airspace to Iranian civilian planes. The president of Iran, Masoud Pezeshkian, is due to address the UN general assembly on Wednesday after arriving in New York on a flight from Tehran as talks were under way. Pezeshkian is an advocate of negotiations with the US but has not played a direct role in the talks. He has said the memorandum of understanding (MoU), agreed with the US on 17 June, remained the starting point. Implementation of the MoU fell apart after the two sides accused one another of breaching its terms by trying to take control of the strait. Iran said the MoU clearly left Iran in control of the strait for an interim period before a long-term agreement on its management was reached, including the possibility of Oman and Iran charging fees for navigational services. Pezeshkian is expected to condemn western double standards over what he regards as an illegal US assault on Iran that has left schoolchildren dead and infrastructure ravaged. Europe’s preparedness to call out Russia for its invasion of Ukraine, and its reticence in criticising the attack on Iran, or Israel’s treatment of Palestinians in Gaza, has been a constant theme of Pezeshkian’s remarks. Many of the most powerful speeches on Tuesday at the UN general assembly came from European and Arab politicians who decried the inability of the west to enforce peace. In his farewell speech to the UN, the French president, Emmanuel Macron, criticised the attempt to overthrow the Iranian government by the US and Israel, arguing: “Every time a few states, sometimes even in the name of international order, have tried to replace the people in order to change a regime or a system, they have plunged those states into even greater chaos.” He also said that the west had not imposed a peace in Gaza. “Some boast of a supposed peace. But this peace hasn’t reopened humanitarian routes for a single second. Must we stand by and watch this spectacle that shames us all? Never!” Macron landed himself in hot water with Israel when he suggested Hamas was not present in the West Bank, as opposed to Gaza. Netanyahu’s office responded, using the biblical name for the West Bank: “Hamas terrorists carry out attacks against Jews almost every day. They have murdered countless Israeli civilians in Judea and Samaria.” Jordan’s King Abdullah II attacked the Israeli government for “moving the goalposts”, for continuing attacks and the destruction of civilian infrastructure in Gaza, and for refusing to withdraw from the war-torn Palestinian territory. This has forced the Palestinian population in Gaza into barely one-third of the territory, he said. Observers must no longer treat Israeli policies as “temporary military measures” or a “consequence of war”, he said. “Accountability begins when we call things what they are: an attempt to erase Palestinian life and impose a new territorial reality in Gaza,” he added.

title: Chagos Islands deal ‘can’t go ahead’ without US support, Streeting says
summary: Defence secretary places annual payments to Mauritius on hold as UK government reviews deal over Diego Garcia base
text: Wes Streeting has said annual payments worth at least £120m to Mauritius are on hold as the government reconsiders its deal over the Chagos Islands, after Donald Trump refused to back the agreement. The defence secretary said the payments would not be made “at this stage” and confirmed the deal “can’t go ahead without US support”. Last year, the UK signed a treaty to transfer sovereignty over the Chagos Islands to Mauritius, while retaining control of the joint UK-US military base on Diego Garcia under a 99-year lease. Mauritius was also set to receive £165m for three years and £120m a year from the fourth year. Asked on BBC Radio 4 Today’s programme if the payments would still go ahead, Streeting said: “Not at this stage. We’ve got to get to a point where we can agree a deal … This deal as it is currently constituted can’t go ahead without American support. So we have to get a deal to a place where it commands American support as well as the agreement of the government of Mauritius and our government. “And the reason why that is important is because we are trying to safeguard, not just now but for the longer term, the base at Diego Garcia, and the capability it provides the United Kingdom and the United States for our national and collective security.” Streeting said the payments would be a “price worth paying” if they secured Britain’s long-term ability to operate from Diego Garcia. Trump doubled down on his criticism of the agreement when he met Andy Burnham at the UN general assembly in New York on Tuesday, describing the deal to transfer sovereignty over the Chagos Islands to Mauritius as “terrible”. “I don’t support it,” Trump told reporters after a bilateral meeting with Burnham on the fringes of the general assembly adding: “I think it’s a terrible deal.” After meeting Trump, the prime minister said the government would “work hard” to find a resolution that was acceptable to the different sides. Streeting said Trump’s criticism had not come as a surprise to ministers. “This isn’t news to us,” he said, “President Trump has been clear that he has concerns about the deal as it’s currently constituted. We will work through the detail of the US concerns and seek to reach a point that all of us can sign up to.” The agreement can’t proceed as it is without US support because of the importance of the joint UK-US military base on Diego Garcia, Streeting said. The defence secretary also warned that Britain could not adopt an “ostrich strategy” of sticking its head in the sand and hoping the row over the Chagos Islands would go away, as he warned settling the dispute would involve “painstaking work”. “The strategy is not to wait out President Trump. I think the approach will be to work with President Trump and his administration,” Streeting told Times Radio. “I’m not pretending that’s an easy position and that resolving this is not going to be difficult. It is difficult and necessarily painstaking work, but it is necessary. “And the ostrich strategy of sticking our heads in the sand … , I would caution is not a wise strategy when it concerns one of the most sensitive national security assets we have anywhere in the world,” Streeting added. He also warned ignoring that Mauritius’s claim to sovereignty posed its own risk to the military base’s future. He said the ruling from the international court of justice in 2019 is “advisory now, [but] there is a potential further course of legal action avenue open to the government of Mauritius”.

title: At Climate Week, Elmo recalls a storm on Sesame Street: ‘Courage is when you still help others’
summary: New York event hears about the red Muppet’s fears during a recent storm as climate crisis increasingly affects children
text: A generation of political leaders has failed to galvanize sufficient action on the climate crisis for so long now that it was perhaps little surprise that an audience in New York City turned to a three-and-a-half-year-old red furry monster for inspiration on Tuesday. Elmo, the Sesame Street denizen, made a starry appearance at a Climate Week event that highlighted how the impacts of global heating affect children. The red creature, who frequently refers to himself in the third person, recounted to the audience his fear when a storm hit Sesame Street, an event depicted in a recent episode that featured the singer Post Malone. “We all feel scared sometimes, but courage is when you feel scared but you still help others,” Elmo said at the event, which was named “Big Storms, Big Feelings”. “I tried to help others by giving lots of hugs and playing music on Elmo’s xylophone. When the storm passed Sesame Street didn’t look like Sesame Street, there was trash and branches all over the place.” Elmo revealed that, much like a prepper, he had a “go bag” ready for the disaster and that the residents of Sesame Street banded together to help their neighborhood clean up after the storm. “Home is the people who make the place special,” he added. “So long as you’re with the people you love, you’ll be home. And that’s true in any weather.” These sentiments were warmly received by the New York audience, who had clearly moved on from Elmo’s ambiguous support of the New York Knicks in last season’s NBA basketball playoff finals. While media and political focus on the climate crisis has waned, despite a cavalcade of recent disasters, a Sesame Street executive at the event said the show is looking to find avenues for children to talk about the issue. Kim Foulds, the vice-president of research and insight at Sesame Workshop, said a study was taken to “understand how children make sense of extreme weather and how their parents navigate those events across a global, diverse context”. What the show heard back from parents was alarm over extreme weather events and accounts from children of severe heat, flooding and other disasters. This is affecting children around the world physically, she said, as well as upending their day-to-day lives. “The biggest disruption that they’re causing to young children is how they disrupt their routines,” Foulds said. “So inability to go to school, lost time outside, and play with their friends, with their parents. And while there were some differences in the extreme weather events, we did hear across all geographies, they all experienced extreme heat in different ways.” Experts at the event, including a climate scientist, a Unicef official and a young climate campaigner, all agreed that while parents often find it difficult to raise the climate crisis with their offspring, children are able to grasp the concept in surprising ways and can get involved in small-scale but direct actions such as planting trees. “The most important thing to share, science actually shows, is that others care and there are solutions that work,” said Katharine Hayhoe, a climate scientist, on what to tell children. “Those are the two most important things to share with anybody between the age of five and 95. Others care and there are solutions and kids get that faster than adults.”

title: Republican jitters grow as unpopular Trump fuels midterm ‘bloodbath’ fears
summary: Iran war, rising prices and president’s low ratings give Democrats advantage, but Republicans have poured cash into key races – could it be decisive?
text: Donald Trump pulled out all the stops at the Republican party’s midterm convention two weeks ago. In speeches aimed at the voters who will soon decide whether to keep Republicans in control of Congress for the final phase of his presidency, the president dangled $5,000 checks, and warned the United States would turn into a “communist country” if Democrats are elected. The unprecedented political gathering amounted to a Hail Mary pass at retaining control of Congress, which history indicated Trump’s Republican allies had always been likely to lose in the 3 November vote. Two weeks later, with election administrators in several states already sending out mail ballots, there is no indication the gambit has worked. Polls have continued to show Democrats with an edge on the generic ballot, a key indicator of voter sentiment in congressional races, as well as in some key Senate contests such as North Carolina and Georgia, both states where Trump won two years ago. Forecasters have moved their ratings of other battleground races almost uniformly in Democrats’ favor, despite Republican-led states’ concerted effort to redraw House districts in the party’s favor. Trump’s approval ratings remain low, with some surveys finding him plumbing new depths. Prices for gasoline and diesel have started climbing again amid the ongoing war with Iran, prompting the Republican Senate stalwart Chuck Grassley of Iowa to publicly encourage the president to do more for farmers, whose businesses have been particularly hard hit by the conflict’s economic shocks. Top Republicans suddenly appear worried about the fortunes of incumbents standing for re-election in some of the reddest states in the country. Last week, vice-president JD Vance campaigned in Kansas, which has not elected a Democrat to the Senate in nearly a century, but where Adam Hamilton is seen as a strong challenger to the Republican incumbent Roger Marshall. Back in Washington, the extent of the House GOP’s jitters became clear when Democrats forced a vote on a war powers resolution to end the fighting with Iran, and three Republicans who had not backed the previous five efforts supported this one, ensuring its passage. “This midterm is going to be a fucking bloodbath,” said Nancy Mace, the outgoing congresswoman who was among the trio of new converts, and predicted that her party would not keep control of the Senate and House of Representatives when ballots are tallied in a month and a half. In the days that followed, more Republicans in competitive races came out against the Iran war. “The war with Iran needs to end, and end quickly,” Mike Rogers, the Republican nominee for Michigan’s open Senate seat, said in a campaign ad released on Monday. Ashley Hinson, the congresswoman who is running to represent Iowa in the Senate, wrote on social media “the war needs to be brought to a successful and immediate end”. She had voted against the Democratic war powers resolution, as had John James, the congressman who is the Republican nominee for governor of Michigan, but on Tuesday, the Detroit News reported he told reporters: “We need to end this war quickly. Because war is terrible, and no one likes war.” Democratic operatives have long maintained that Trump was leading the GOP’s congressional majorities into oblivion, and are now being joined in that prediction by veteran politics watchers, who see the toxic combination of rising prices, poor approval ratings and dampening enthusiasm among voters as likely fatal for Republicans’ hopes of keeping control of the House, if not the Senate. “We are seeing a dramatic souring and just overall level of anger at the broken promises of Trump and House Republicans, like, issue after issue after issue. Like, people are just unhappy right now,” said a Democratic strategist who did not want their name to be used. Talk has even re-emerged of a “blue wave” in November that will see Republicans lose in deep-red corners of the country. “Republicans should brace themselves: the three most plausible outcomes are that it will be bad, really bad, or truly horrible,” wrote the veteran analyst Charlie Cook. Yet not everything is necessarily going Democrats’ way. In the battle for the Senate, Republicans have grown increasingly optimistic about their Senate candidate winning in New Hampshire, which some major forecasters now view as a toss-up. The party may also have come out ahead in the mid-decade redistricting push, and definitely has more financial resources this year than the Democrats – a reversal from most midterms prior. “House Republicans are running with a more favorable map, historic fundraising, stronger candidates, and a commonsense agenda, while Democrats are burdened by unelectable far-left nominees and deeply unpopular policies that make their path to the majority far more challenging than the pundits suggest,” said Mike Marinella, a spokesperson for the National Republican Congressional Committee. After much speculation about when he would act, Trump’s Maga Inc Super Pac has started spending its $400m war chest, buying $15m in advertisements to support the Republican Ken Paxton in the Texas senate race. Fairshake, a Super Pac connected to the cryptocurrency industry, will reportedly spend $30m against Sherrod Brown, the Democratic former senator from Ohio and cryptocurrency adversary seeking to return to the chamber, after the industry spent $40m to see him defeated in 2024. Republicans and their allies have thus far put $384.5m into Senate races, to Democrats’ and their supporters’ $112.7m, according to data compiled by political analyst Rob Pyers. In the House, Republican supporters have spent nearly $65.7m to the Democrats’ $51.1m, but Politico has reported that much of that money has gone to districts where Trump won two years ago, a sign that the GOP is playing defense. Winning the Senate will require Democrats to oust at least four Republicans in states that Trump won in 2024. The House seems an easier target for the party, since the GOP controls it by a low single-digit majority. House Republican leaders including the speaker Mike Johnson nonetheless insist that voters will expand rather than disband their majority in November. They note that 23 Democrats represent districts that voted for Trump in 2024, a number that has increased due to GOP-led states’ redistricting, while only eight Republicans represent districts that backed Kamala Harris. The party also believes that voters are still too disenchanted with Democrats overall to put them back in charge in the Capitol. “Voters might not like Trump. They might not even like Republicans. But the polling shows that they hate Democrats even more,” a Republican strategist said on condition of anonymity. In a statement, Julie Merz, the executive director of the House Democrats’ campaign arm, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, acknowledged the party’s fundraising struggles but said they were still on track for a return to power. “We are confident we’re poised to win the majority, and that’s why Republicans in deep red territory are running scared,” Merz said. “If Democrats want to break the Republican gerrymanders in the south and get the largest majority possible, more resources ensure we can flip those seats too. We need more cash.” Money isn’t everything, as Democrats know – Harris and her supporters outspent Trump and his allies in 2024, a year of resounding Democratic losses. And many of the factors that will decide the election outcome may already be baked into the result, said John T Woolley, co-director of the American Presidency Project at the University of California, Santa Barbara. “Inflation, employment rates – they’re just not going to change a whole lot. So the kind of thing that’s left, the seats, those are fixed, [you] can’t change that stuff. So the only thing that’s left is the president’s approval,” Woolley said. “What that means is the president has to shift swing voters, independent voters, voters who don’t identify as either Republican or Democrats.” But that group, too, appears to have soured on the GOP: a New York Times and Siena University poll released last week found 57% of independent voters were planning to vote Democratic in the midterms, and just 34% for Republican candidates.

title: Former Fox News host Gretchen Carlson urges reporters to ‘speak up’ against Trump insults
summary: Co-founder of Lift Our Voices condemns president’s ‘highly offensive’ misogynic outbursts – ‘It’s my hope other journalists will start speaking up when that happens’
text: Donald Trump has achieved something rarely seen in Washington: uniting rival television networks against him. When he banned CNN and MS Now – along with Politico – from the White House, their competitors suspended shared coverage of the US president’s events. Gretchen Carlson, a journalist, author and former Fox News host, hopes this will not be the only example of solidarity from a White House press corps facing what she describes as an “outright onslaught” from the administration. In a phone interview with the Guardian before the media ban news, Carlson, 60, called on reporters to push back against Trump’s brazen misogyny, which has included calling female reporters “stupid”, “piggy”, “incompetent” and “a horrible person”. “That’s highly offensive to any human being, much less journalists whose job it is to cover the president with respect and dignity,” said the co-founder of Lift Our Voices, a non-profit that aims to end the silencing of voices in the workplace. “To be called those kinds of names and still have to maintain your composure and do your job is something that no journalist should have to endure.” She called for solidarity across the White House press corps in response to the president’s sexist insults. “It’s my hope that other journalists will start speaking up when that happens and repeat the question that was asked, because it likely wasn’t a stupid question,” she says. “It was likely an appropriate question that many Americans want the answer to like, when will the Iran war end? My hope is that the questions will be asked until they are answered and that it’s not just from the one who’s attacked.” Carlson also urges the media to take a more robust approach with Trump despite the risks of being barred in the future. “It’s also my hope that journalists will say: you can’t speak to people that way. Now, I’m not naive, I understand there’s a conundrum here for journalists, because this is all about access to the president of the United States and access to this administration. If you speak up and cross this president, he’ll come after you. “But we have to find a happy medium here because the end result is allowing this to continue is the promulgation of misogyny in our society.” One potential barrier to collective action is an influx of “Maga” media outlets, ever ready to ask the president favourable questions and unlikely to speak up on behalf of “mainstream media” colleagues. The president can call them at any moment to blunt the momentum of the questions coming his way. Carlson acknowledges the point but responds: “There’s still plenty of other journalists who might. There is the White House Correspondents’ Association. They were able to plan a second dinner after the assassination attempt so they could certainly come together and decide that they’re going to have a certain reaction to those kinds of attacks. “When you get attacked like that and another reporter just goes on to the next question, it makes it look like there’s nothing wrong and so if you’re watching this press conference, you normalise that then, and you’re like, oh, I guess that’s how we should treat everyone. “It’s damaging to young men about how they can treat women and young women about how they feel they should be treated. We’ve been trying to raise up our young women for generations and we’re doing a great job of it and now, all of a sudden, you can just treat women like this and nobody says anything?” As if channeling the 1960s-set TV drama Mad Men, Trump has repeatedly singled out Kaitlan Collins, the chief White House correspondent of CNN, complaining: “I don’t think I’ve ever seen a smile on your face.” Carlson notes it is not the kind of comment he would ever make to a man. “Ask any woman on the street how many times have you been told in your life you need to smile more. Barf. I mean, really? We’ve all heard that before: put a smile on your face and just go out there and deal with it. No. That’s like, you go in to negotiate for higher pay, the man just asks for it, the woman has to put a smile on her face in order to get it. It is such an old school way of looking at the different gender types and the way in which we respond to a request if it’s by a man or a woman.” Carlson rejects the implication that women in media should maintain a happy demeanour when asking tough questions about conflict, economic strife or foreign policy. “She’s not supposed to be smiling when she’s asking tough questions of the president of the United States. “You’re not supposed to be smiling when you’re out as a journalist covering a triple murder or raging wildfire. There’s plenty going on in America right now where we don’t need to smile about it – high gas prices, high grocery prices, the Iran war, tariffs. It is almost 10 years since Trump was first elected. It is also 10 years since Carlson sued Roger Ailes, then the chief executive and chairman of Fox News, for sexual harassment. In the following weeks more than 20 other women came forward with allegations that Ailes had abused them. The #MeToo movement, raising awareness of sexual misconduct by men, was in the ascendancy. Despite the regression personified by Trump, Carlson sees evidence of progress in unexpected places – notably in the Capitol Hill campaign surrounding the disclosure of files relating to Jeffrey Epstein, who exploited and trafficked underage girls. The effort produced an unusual alignment between Democrats and Republicans, demonstrating that survivor advocacy can break through. “It was an amazing bipartisan movement,” Carlson notes, citing Democrat Ro Khanna and Republicans Thomas Massie, Marjorie Taylor Greene, Lauren Boebert, and Nancy Mace. For Carlson, the driver of this breakthrough is a fundamental shift in public opinion. A decade ago, she contends, victims of high-profile abuse were routinely dismissed or discredited. Today the baseline has changed. “The most credit goes to the survivors because they keep pushing forward,” she says. “A lot of times people say to me that the #MeToo movement is in a downward spiral because we’re still not getting all the files released and people aren’t being held accountable. But I look at this as a leader in this movement and say we have to look at the progress. “People actually believe the Epstein survivors now. Ten years ago, they would not have believed them. Every time they come to the Hill and hold a press conference, they take the power right back.” Despite the rise of the “manosphere”, “trad wives” and a tsunami of online misogyny, Carlson rejects the narrative that the movement against workplace abuse has stalled or been defeated by reactionary cultural backlash. “It’s very easy to say the #MeToo movement is dead when you look at all the negative stuff,” she admits. “I’m not naive enough to say that everything is perfect right now–it’s not. But movements ebb and flow. If you look at any major cultural movement, whether it was the civil rights movement or women getting the right to vote, these things did not happen overnight. There were many ups and downs.” Carlson points to legislative milestones that have altered employment law across the US. Through Lift Our Voices, she spearheaded the passage of two pieces of federal legislation in 2022 that curtailed forced arbitration clauses, preventing corporations from hiding systemic abuse behind secret, binding proceedings. “People ask me every single day: how did you do that?” Carlson reflects. “These are the kinds of things we have to focus on. Yes, there are blips along the way and hurdles to overcome, but we have to keep pushing forward. There have been laws passed, and state laws passed banning non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) completely for these types of things.” Her focus remains the total elimination of contractual silencing mechanisms – such as non-disclosure agreements and non-disparagement clauses – that allow toxic workplace cultures to persist in secret. Carlson insists that workplace safety and anti-silencing reform must remain strictly non-partisan. When high-profile misconduct allegations surfaced surrounding Democratic candidate Graham Platner in Maine, Carlson condemned attempts by some Democrats to shield their own candidates from accountability. “There is no room for hypocrisy with regard to this kind of behaviour, and the American public is onto this,” she asserts. “The idea that you want to not call out this behaviour because it’s a Democratic candidate and you’re a Democrat is wrong – and the same thing on the flip side.” At Lift Our Voices, the rule is evaluate the conduct, ignore the party label, she says. “We believe women and we take politics out of it. By the way, it’s been proven all across the board that politics has nothing to do with sexual harassment or sexual assault. “Before somebody decides to do either of those to you, they don’t ask you what party you’re in. They don’t care. This is about power.”

title: Top South African police officer charged with raping woman, 18, and grooming 16-year-old girl
summary: Arrest of Shadrack Sibiya comes as country reels from cases of femicide and alleged police corruption and criminality
text: One of South Africa’s most senior police officers has been charged with raping an 18-year-old woman and grooming a 16-year-old girl, as the country’s police face allegations of corruption and failing to tackle violence against women and girls. Shadrack Sibiya, who was already suspended from his role as deputy national police commissioner over allegations he interfered with political killings investigations, was arrested on Monday. He is facing charges of rape, people trafficking, promoting the sexual grooming of a child and two counts of grooming a child. Sibiya appeared briefly in a Johannesburg court on Tuesday. He was then taken to prison in the capital, Pretoria, before a bail hearing on 29 September, as prosecutors had argued he was an escape risk. South Africa is reeling after the discovery of nine women’s bodies across Ekurhuleni, the municipality east of Johannesburg, in September. Meanwhile, the Madlanga Commission judicial inquiry has been examining allegations of corruption and criminality within the police for the last year. Puleng Dimpane, the acting national police commissioner, said: “Police officers are entrusted with protecting women and children. They cannot themselves be implicated in conduct that undermines this responsibility. As the country continues to confront the scourge of gender-based violence and femicide, there can be no room for anyone within the police service who is alleged to abuse their position or violate the rights of women and children.” Sibiya is accused of raping an 18-year-old woman at a hotel in May in the Sandton business district of Johannesburg. The alleged rape took place “whilst she was passed out due to intoxication administered by the accused”, according to a copy of the charge sheet. The alleged grooming of the 16-year-old girl took place over WhatsApp between 20 July and 3 August, according to the charge sheet. This allegedly included Sibiya sending the girl naked photos of herself, which she had not sent to him. Sibiya did not enter a plea at the hearing on Tuesday. His lawyer told the court that they needed more time to consult with and get instructions from him, according to News24. Firoz Cachalia, the acting police minister, said: “We strongly condemn the alleged conduct. “Where allegations of sexual offences are made against a member of the service, they must be investigated without fear or favour.” When Sibiya appeared before the Madlanga Commission in February he denied allegations that he had moved 121 political killings investigations from KwaZulu-Natal province to the national head office without explanation. Sibiya also denied that he had received a gift of 20 impalas from Vusimuzi ‘Cat’ Matlala, a businessman who received an allegedly fraudulent 360m rand (£16.7m) police health services contract soon after the alleged gift. Matlala, who has been charged with attempted murder, alongside several other charges including fraud and money laundering, declined to comment on the impalas when he appeared at the Madlanga Commission in August. He said he did not want to incriminate himself as the matter was under investigation.

title: Three international bodies warn of risks of rising debt and soaring borrowing in major economies
summary: IIF highlights challenges facing US, France, UK and Japan, while OECD and IMF also voice global concerns
text: Three heavyweight international bodies have issued stark warnings about the risks of rising debt levels and soaring borrowing costs across large economies. The Paris-based Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the International Institute of Finance (IIF), the voice of global banking, on Wednesday highlighted the dangers of soaring interest rates on $365tn (£275tn) in global borrowing. In its quarterly debt monitor, the IIF predicted a “structurally debt-intensive future” as governments and companies scramble to invest in new technologies and bear the costs of ageing societies. “The buildup in global debt is set to accelerate as governments and corporates compete to boost growth and secure their positions in an economy reshaped by structural changes,” it said. It compared the current status of some of the world’s largest economies, including the UK, with crisis-hit emerging countries. “The US, France, the UK, and Japan face persistently large deficits and rising interest expenses – challenges long associated with debt-distressed emerging market sovereigns.” With many politicians facing elections in the coming months, and belt-tightening unlikely to be popular with voters, it said: “The risk is that already-unsustainable debt trajectories continue to deteriorate.” While in New York this week for the UN general assembly, the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, denied reports that he had been shocked by the parlous state of the public finances since he came to power in July. “It’s not the case that we were surprised when we came in, not least because I was in access talks and understood very clearly the position,” he told reporters. “The truth of the matter is that because of the situation in the Middle East, the position changed, and has changed over the time I’ve been in. That’s just the reality of the situation that we’re in.” The IIF’s warning came as the OECD highlighted the rising cost of servicing government debts as one key risk to the global economy in the coming months. In its interim economic outlook the OECD said global growth had been more resilient than expected given the strains of the US-Israel war on Iran. However, presenting the report, its secretary general, Mathias Cormann, warned: “Fiscal and financial risks have grown. Thirty-year government bond yields are at their highest in 15 years or more in six of the G7 economies. That means higher debt-servicing costs for governments whose budgets are already under strain, and it means higher borrowing costs for businesses and households.” His words echoed a warning by the managing director of the International Monetary Fund, Kristalina Georgieva, who told the BBC the world’s advanced economies must take action to reduce their borrowing and bring down debt levels. Georgieva said a succession of global economic shocks had been “pushing debt levels up like a staircase not to heaven”, with governments taking “no action to contain that service cost. [It’s] time to take that action,” Georgieva said, adding that courage was needed by politicians to take the necessary steps. In its quarterly forecast update, the OECD highlighted the better-than-expected growth performance of the global economy this year but warned that the recent resurgence in oil and gas prices posed risks for the coming months. “Global economic prospects remain heavily dependent on whether a durable resolution to the Middle East conflict is achieved,” it said. It projected global economic growth of 2.9% this year – a modest 0.1 percentage point upgrade from the 2.8% it forecast in June. At the same time, it trimmed the outlook for next year slightly, from 3.1% to 3%. It also identified the record-breaking El Niño weather system – expected to be the strongest in 1,000 years – as a “significant downside risk” to the global economy, warning that it could hit agricultural production and push up food prices.Looking at the UK, the OECD significantly cut its inflation forecast for this year, from 3.7% to 3.1%, after prices rose less dramatically than expected. Economic growth for the UK is forecast at 1.1% for 2026, up from the 0.9% it had forecast in June and 0.7% in March, “with consumption expected to be supported by newly announced government support measures”.

title: North Carolina father and son receive hero awards for saving man from burning car
summary: Larry Pickett Sr and his son, a US army cadet, pulled David Denton from vehicle fire in upstate New York in 2025
text: A North Carolina man who helped his son – a player for the US army academy college football team – pull a wrecked car’s driver out of the vehicle moments before it burst into flames has earned the highest honor for civilian heroism in the United States and Canada. Larry Pickett Sr earned the Carnegie medal for heroism for a daring rescue alongside his son, Larry Pickett Jr, on 31 August 2025 outside Fort Montgomery, New York, that was captured in headline-grabbing cellphone video, according to a recent announcement from the non-profit organization that administers the award. A statement from the Carnegie Hero Fund Commission said the motorist whom the Picketts rescued – 65-year-old David N Denton – was semiconscious inside his sport utility vehicle after it left a roadway and struck a power pole. The crash caused the pole and power lines – carrying a total of at least 14,000 volts – to fall on to the road and Denton’s SUV as Pickett Sr, 46, drove by the wreckage with his family. Pickett Sr immediately parked before he and Pickett Jr, 20, realized Denton was semiconscious inside his SUV, which had flames burning on the exterior of its passenger side, according to the Carnegie commission. The father and son then advanced toward Denton, opened his driver’s door and each took turns reaching in for him, stepping over a perilous downed power line. There was evidence of electrical arcing beneath the crashed SUV, the commission’s statement said. Pickett Sr successfully removed Denton’s seatbelt after four tries. He and his son together then freed Denton from the car, the commission recounted. The elder Pickett then tripped and fell next to the car – within inches of one of the downed power lines. But he quickly got back on his feet, and Pickett Jr carried Denton across the four-lane road and laid him down on grass, the commission said. The commission noted that an eruption of flames enveloped Denton’s car seconds later. Firefighters subsequently arrived to extinguish the blaze from a distance out of caution for the live power lines nearby. The power was not shut off until after that – and even then, it was done remotely, according to the commission. “A fire chief at the scene and an electrical engineer later consulted about the incident both agreed that the car’s exterior and surrounding area should have been electrified under the circumstances and could not explain how Pickett, his son and Denton avoided electrocution,” the Carnegie commission’s statement said. Denton emerged from the dramatic episode with only abrasions. He was taken by ambulance to a hospital for treatment, was discharged and ultimately recovered. Neither of the Picketts was injured. On the night that he and his father crossed paths with Denton, Pickett Jr had just played a game for the army college football squad at its home stadium in West Point, New York. He and his family encountered Denton’s crash on their return trip from having dinner at Times Square in New York City. Pickett Jr’s sister, Lauren, recorded video of his and Pickett Sr’s efforts to save Denton. The footage – widely circulated on social media – captured a woman screaming, “Larry, come on! Come on, get him out – that’s it!” Viewers can see the car engulfed in fire and surrounded by sparking wires. In another part of the video, a confused man can be heard saying over popping sounds in the background, “What car is this?” Another man can be heard saying, “That’s your car. You hear it? That’s the tires popping.” Pickett Sr later spoke with WTVD of his home town Raleigh, North Carolina, and explained how there was “no discussion” between him and his son about whether to aid Denton. “My son just jumped right into action,” Pickett Sr, a business owner, told the news station. “He mentioned his military training kicked in, and we pulled him out.” Of his namesake, Pickett Sr also said to the channel: “It’s just amazing to see him in action. And it’s just not surprising because we’ve watched him his whole life do amazing things.” Pickett Jr received the US army’s soldier’s medal in March, which is the military branch’s highest honor for noncombat actions. Pickett Sr was among 16 Carnegie medal recipients named on Monday. The medal recognizes those in the US and Canada “who enter extreme danger while saving or attempting to save the lives of others”, the Carnegie Hero Fund Commission said. Philanthropist Andrew Carnegie created that commission after two men sacrificed their lives attempting to rescue others after a deadly 1904 coal-mining accident. The Carnegie medal has been awarded to nearly 10,600 individuals since its inception, with more than $47m being given in one-time grants, scholarship aid, death benefits and continuing assistance, according to the hero fund commission.

title: New UK agency to fight ‘information warfare’ from likes of Russia, Burnham tells UN
summary: PM aims to ‘stem poisonous tide’ of disinformation and deepfakes with National Centre for Information Defence
text: Security chiefs will set up a new national centre to tackle disinformation and deepfakes from hostile states such as Russia, Andy Burnham has announced, saying the government had a duty to “stem the poisonous tide” from damaging British interests. The National Centre for Information Defence will “detect, attribute and disrupt” information attacks by foreign powers, many of which are enabled by AI, bringing together the intelligence agencies, law enforcement and social media companies. It will be tasked with making sure the UK has the defensive capability necessary to combat information warfare and build national resilience by helping communities to identify and combat disinformation, preventing a “distorted and untrue” narrative about the UK. Burnham said the country would have to go into the next decade “eyes wide open” about “insidious” campaigns, many of which had been orchestrated by Russia, which “twisted” what people at home felt about their own country and community. In eye-catching remarks, the prime minister suggested that Britons who were struggling with the cost of living and young people not in education, training or employment may be particularly susceptible to foreign influence online, underlining how inequality further undermined society. In his speech to the UN in New York on Tuesday night, Burnham said: “We’re talking about an insidious campaign that reaches into people’s homes and twists what they feel about their own country and community – creating a narrative of decline, stoking division and sowing despair. “On top of that, we have seen cyber-attacks on our companies and institutions. We know that AI will multiply the threat. We have tiptoed around this for too long. Over the last decade we have given too much ground to those who want to run a negative, corrosive narrative about life in Britain, which bears no resemblance to reality. Well, no more. “We are going to face the new decade in a different way – with our eyes wide open. We are going to be much prouder in standing up for our values and the rule of law. And we are going to help our people to strengthen their resilience – because, faced with this information warfare, security starts in every home.” Burnham’s speech came after Donald Trump – during a press conference at the UN with Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelenskyy – said that Keir Starmer’s rhetoric had been “too tough” towards Moscow and that London “needs to be a little bit careful”. Downing Street pushed back on the US president’s remarks, saying that every UK prime minister – up to and including Burnham – had been consistent in the view that Russia’s threats, whether hybrid attacks or rhetoric, were “egregious and unacceptable”. “The UK is united with our allies on the importance of defending ourselves, and Russia’s aggression will not deter us from supporting Ukraine,” the prime minister’s official spokesperson added. In his speech, Burnham singled out Russia, saying the Kremlin spent around £1.3bn each year on manipulating information. “Russian agencies have used every means at their disposal to spread lies and disinformation and prey on people’s fears. They’ve used bots and fake websites. Falsified newspaper articles,” he said. “Forged the branding of 28 British organisations – including universities and the BBC. They’ve amplified far-right narratives. And we have evidence that they tried to interfere with the 2019 general election. “We also know that they have tried to stoke tensions and unrest in the wake of horrific events. The idea that anyone would try to use such things to their advantage is just repulsive – but it is what they do.” The prime minister suggested that certain groups of people who felt their own lives were not improving may be more vulnerable to disinformation and deepfakes. “If you’re struggling with the cost of living and your life is not improving – or if you’re a young person not in employment, education or training – then you are going to be much more vulnerable to this kind of influence,” he said. “So part of the challenge is to lift our people up and create the opportunities they need. When inequalities grow too wide, our societies are at greater risk. So we will work to make life more affordable. And we will put in place the architecture we need to stem this poisonous tide.” The UK plans to share its experience of being on the receiving end of information attack with other countries, and has already supported Moldova, for example, to protect its elections from Russian interference. “As more elections approach across Europe, more nations are grappling with these issues – some for the first time. So we’re ready to share our understanding of how these actors work, and how we can respond – because this is vital for our collective security and resilience,” Burnham added. Emily Thornberry, the chair of the foreign affairs select committee, said: “I’m absolutely delighted the prime minister has announced a new centre to tackle the threat of disinformation, which was the major recommendation of the foreign affairs committee’s March 2026 disinformation diplomacy report. “For too long, the approach of successive governments to disinformation has been disjointed and without organisation, allowing states like Russia to amplify lies about this country, to sow division and stoke tensions. This new National Centre for Information Defence is an opportunity to finally take on this very serious threat.”
