title: Glimpses into lives of Roman suburbanites in Bath revealed in rare finds
summary: Exclusive: Restoration work at Bath Assembly Rooms unearths Roman ditches containing pottery, coins and fragments of a military helmet
text: The restoration of a Georgian building in Bath once frequented by Jane Austen has unexpectedly provided a tantalising glimpse into the life of the city’s Roman suburbanites. A network of Roman ditches containing pottery, coins, glassware and a fragment of a military helmet has been found beneath Bath Assembly Rooms in the north of the city. Experts say the finds expand the known extent of Roman occupation in Bath and suggest further remains are likely to lie under neighbouring Georgian buildings and streets. The Roman baths that give the city its modern name are one of the best-preserved ancient sites in northern Europe, attracting more than 1 million visitors a year. Previous archaeological finds have revealed that in Roman times there were suburbs around the baths complex and, further away, comfortable country villas. But relatively little had been found in an area north of the city, partly because the city’s Georgian buildings and streets are so solid – and well protected by conservation laws – that the sort of construction project that might unearth remains rarely takes place. Marek Lewcun, of Wessex Archaeology, said this made it all the more exciting when Roman artefacts were discovered beneath Bath Assembly Rooms. “There was a gap in our knowledge and this helps fill in a missing link,” he said. Lewcun said the finds suggested the residents of this part of Bath were the sort that might live in the outskirts of a modern city: “So we’re probably looking at the ordinary folk that you might find in a modern suburb today, people who had small shops supplying pottery, bread, things like that. “We are looking at people who had gradually integrated with those who had come from all over the Roman empire. Before they arrived we were living in mud huts, more or less. We’ve gone from that to living in buildings that have got roofs, heating, water.” Lewcun said people with more money or status, such as retired military leaders, were probably living further up the hill in villas. “That may have been the equivalent of retiring to somewhere in the sun today.” The archaeologists found almost 60 fragments of Roman pottery, glass vessels, animal bones, roof tiles, Roman coins and a limestone tessera which may once have formed part of a mosaic floor. Among the most intriguing discoveries was a fragment of a Roman military helmet. This is seen as further evidence that military personnel were involved in the construction of the settlement. A slot for a beam was also found, showing that a Roman building had once stood here. Lewcun and the team were helped by the fact that the builders of Bath Assembly Rooms in the late 18th century did not create deep foundations, knowing the thick clay was strong enough to support the structure. It meant the Roman ditches were left untouched for the 21st-century archaeologists to probe. The bath complex was built by the Romans around mineral-rich hot springs after the defeat of the British queen Boudica in AD60 and 61. Known as Aquae Sulis (the waters of the goddess Sulis), it became a place of pilgrimage for people seeking healing in the apparently curative water. Jane Austen lived in Bath in the early 19th century and visited Bath Assembly Rooms, where dancing, coffee-drinking, billiard-playing and gambling took place. Unsurprisingly, beauty products, wig curlers, wine bottles and tobacco pipes from the rooms’ heyday have been found during the restoration project but the Roman remains are regarded as a joyful bonus. Tatjana LeBoff, the National Trust project curator at Bath Assembly Rooms, described the Roman discoveries as significant. “It’s so wonderful to find Roman remains under our Georgian building,” she said. The £20m restoration project includes refurbishing the upper rooms heavily damaged by bombing in the second world war and conserving 10 original Georgian chandeliers. The building is due to reopen next year with a new Georgian visitor experience and a place for 21st-century assembly.

title: Fears mount that next UN chief will downgrade climate action
summary: Experts say some of António Guterres’s possible successors could be ‘disastrous’ for efforts to tackle crisis
text: Fears are mounting that the next UN secretary general will downgrade the priority of the climate crisis, according to climate and civil society experts. The current secretary general, António Guterres, has been the most forthright on the subject, calling fossil fuel companies “the godfathers of climate chaos” and warning governments they are rushing down a “highway to hell” by failing to cut greenhouse gas emissions. His repeated championing of the urgency of the crisis and willingness to take on vested interests are credited with significant global impacts, forcing governments to confront their policy failures and keeping alive the aims of the 2015 Paris climate agreement, despite the rising tide of populism and disinformation. Guterres must step down at the end of his second five-year term on 31 December and the choice of his successor will be one of the top concerns among the scores of heads of government meeting in New York this week for the UN general assembly. Many of Guterres’s most likely successors have shown less enthusiasm for tackling the climate crisis, despite rising alarm at its impacts, and experts have told the Guardian that some of the candidates could be “disastrous” yet could enjoy the support of influential countries including the US and its allies. Three candidates in particular have raised concerns: the Argentinian diplomat Rafael Grossi, who heads the International Atomic Energy Agency; Macky Sall, the former president of Senegal; and Olara Otunnu, a Ugandan former presidential candidate who has served as UN undersecretary general for children and armed conflict. Numerous insiders and experts told the Guardian that Grossi was “trying to be a friend of Donald Trump” and maintained close links with Argentina’s populist president, Javier Milei, a climate denier. “Grossi is not a climate denier himself, but those links could lead him to downplay climate,” said one close observer, who could not be named. Sall is seen as a potential champion of gas in Africa as a “transitional fuel”, which many African leaders want to exploit. “I wonder how far he would be willing to push [climate action] when it conflicts with African [fossil fuel] energy interests,” said the observer. Otunnu may feel national pressure on the politics of African gas and oil exploration, as Uganda has discovered large oil and gas deposits that it plans to exploit. “He’s a big question mark,” said another expert. “Given the fossil fuel politics of Uganda, would he make climate constraints politically binding when they conflict with development priorities?” Andreas Sieber, the head of political strategy at the campaign group 350.org, said: “The gender gap is impossible to miss: all five women candidates range from credible to genuinely compelling, while the men could be auditioning for a job description from the past century.” Some candidates have a stronger climate record. Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett of Guyana has pushed strongly for Indigenous rights and social development, particularly on fairer finance. Rebeca Grynspan, an economist from Costa Rica, has linked the climate crisis to debt in the developing world, arguing both crises need to be tackled together. Michelle Bachelet, the former president of Chile, has said governments can no longer treat climate action as a choice but a necessity, but she was reported this week to have dropped out of the race. María Fernanda Espinosa, a former foreign minister of Ecuador, led the country’s negotiating team at several UN climate Cop summits. Ivonne Baki, also known as Ivonne A-Baki, another Ecuadorian former minister, has pioneered several conservation schemes but expressed doubt over the efficacy of emissions reductions, to the consternation of climate campaigners. A spokesperson for Baki told the Guardian: “Ambassador A-Baki’s commitment to climate action is longstanding and unequivocal. What she has questioned is not the need to reduce emissions, but whether climate policy will succeed if it becomes detached from economic realities, development needs and the livelihoods of the people it is intended to protect. Her position is that the world must pursue emissions reductions while dramatically strengthening adaptation, climate finance and protection of the natural systems on which human security depends.” Carlos Lopes, a professor at the Nelson Mandela School of Public Governance at the University of Cape Town, said: “There is a real risk that the next secretary general may be less forceful on climate than Guterres has been, not necessarily because of the individual ultimately selected, but because the political environment has changed considerably: climate diplomacy is facing stronger geopolitical headwinds, the multilateral system is under greater strain, and we are seeing forms of ‘climate hushing’, including among countries that only a few years ago wanted to be seen as leaders.” He added: “A new secretary general may understandably want to establish a distinctive agenda, but climate cannot now be treated as one issue among many competing for attention.” Continuing Guterres’s strong sense of mission on the climate must be the minimum for his successor, experts told the Guardian. “It’s absolutely critical that the climate remains at the heart of what the UN does,” said Cosima Cassel, the climate diplomacy programme lead at the E3G thinktank. The new incumbent must take on fossil fuel interests emboldened by the Trump administration and with profits bolstered by soaring fuel prices. Against a rising tide of climate denialism and misinformation, the UN is also asking governments to regulate AI, a task begun under Guterres but which will fall mainly to the next head, and could be crucial in determining whether AI becomes a vast new source of emissions. Focusing on methane – a greenhouse gas 80 times more powerful than carbon dioxide, which comes from leaky oil and gas operations, waste landfills and agriculture – should be a top priority, said Durwood Zaelke, the president of the Institute for Governance and Sustainable Development. “Cutting methane is the single most important strategy to slow near-term warming,” he said. “If we want to stop the punishing heatwaves, we need to turn off the methane blowtorch.” Countries have few constraints on the gas at present: even basic efforts such as plugging abandoned coalmines are still lacking. Electrification, which will be under the spotlight at the Cop31 summit this November, should also be a key push, aided by concerns over oil dependence raised by the Iran war. And climate finance is still not flowing to poor countries: as the tragedy in Nepal demonstrated, countries stricken by climate disaster are not receiving “loss and damage” money promised for their rescue and rehabilitation. The new UN chief must threaten and cajole rich countries into paying their share, even while the UN faces budget cuts of its own amid the withdrawal of US cash. Claudio Angelo, of the Observatório do Clima network in Brazil, said: “A secretary general can only be as good as the institution they head, and the UN is being hollowed out by the US.” Many prominent figures in climate diplomacy see the UN as an essential linchpin in climate action. Mary Robinson, the former president of Ireland, said: “We are watching the planet’s life support systems collapse around us. This could not be more urgent. The next secretary general doesn’t just need to match the ambitions of previous SGs, they have to make this one of their top priorities and be a beacon for leaders all over the world to phase out fossil fuels.”

title: Wednesday briefing: ​Can Burnham ​seek a ​different ​path​ to Trump’s world order?
summary: In today’s newsletter: The PM’s first face‑to‑face with​ the US president marks a fragile reset
text: Good morning. In the early hours of Tuesday a plane carrying Andy Burnham, a handful of UK ministers, an excited group of British political journalists, and Burnham’s wife, Marie France, landed at a New York airport for one of Burnham’s first major outings as prime minister: a face-to-face meeting with Donald Trump. Considering the president once described Burnham as the mayor of “a town,” and the prime minister once said Trump wouldn’t be welcome in said town (Manchester), the meeting yesterday afternoon went remarkably well. That was the feeling among observers at the UN general assembly, an annual festival of hobnobbing and dealmaking for global leaders. Save for a few minor hiccups (Trump described Burnham as a “natural businessperson,” which will be news to Burnham), their meeting was relaxed. Marie France was entertained at a “spouses lunch” with Melania, and Burnham will no doubt have ended the day with a sense of relief. But for all the warm words in Manhattan, Burnham and his foreign secretary Ed Miliband still have tricky questions to answer about how they deal with Trump. Faced with a resurgent far right that has been emboldened by his administration, how should Burnham approach the country that was – until recently – the first ally Britain would call in a diplomatic crisis? Today’s newsletter tries to answer that question with the help of our political editor, Pippa Crerar, who was on the plane. First, though, here are the headlines. Five big stories UN general assembly | Donald Trump has called on nations to unite to isolate Tehran and bring down global energy prices, as he gave a bellicose defence of his administration’s foreign policy and decision to strike Iran. The far right | Charities have condemned footage of a far-right activist using a blade to slash an inflatable dinghy in the Channel while a rescue worker was onboard, in a further escalation of organised anti-immigration protest. UK news | Children as young as 13 in the UK have been referred to a specialist clinic for a “devastating” bladder condition linked to sustained use of ketamine. West Bank | British banks and financial institutions are receiving warnings from MPs that they should not invest in Israel’s E1 settlement project. UK politics | Andy Burnham has opened the door to fighting the next election on the UK rejoining the EU, but said his immediate priority was continuing to rebuild bridges with European allies. In depth: ‘There are some really thorny issues coming up’ A non-exhaustive list of Trump’s recent foreign policy achievements is a good reminder of just how swiftly he has destroyed what is rosily described as the “rules-based international order”. Since taking office in 2025, he has installed loyalists in key positions, flirted with the idea of withdrawing from Nato, abolished USAID, gutted the US state department, threatened to acquire Greenland “by any means necessary”, captured the president of Venezuela and recast foreign policy as a brutal means of putting “America first”. His administration’s national security strategy, published in December 2025, was described by one former Pentagon official as a “manifesto for the global far right”. It declared that Europe faces the “stark prospect of civilizational erasure” (echoing the far-right conspiracy of a “Great Replacement”) and said that America would encourage the promotion of “patriotic European parties”. Despite this, western leaders have taken a while to adjust to the second Trump presidency. “Starmer got quite a lot of criticism for being obsequious to Trump,” Pippa tells me. His reverence was on full display when he placated Trump with a royal visit that included a dinner-party seat next to the Princess of Wales, and when he struck a controversial trade deal that will force the NHS to spend more on US-branded drugs (the deal, for which the US agreed not to put tariffs on British pharmaceutical exports, could cost the NHS as much as £44.7bn by 2030, my colleague Aditya Chakrabortty reported in June). Starmer’s stance gradually toughened as he realised that placating Trump was no guarantee of protection. Later in his premiership, he refused to let Trump use UK military bases in America’s initial strikes on Iran. “But he was seen by some inside the government as being too flattering and fawning,” says Pippa. *** What’s changed? On the surface, not much. Within hours of arriving at the UN, Trump managed to alienate just about everyone, telling a journalist from CNN, one of the three networks he’s banned from the White House, “you should not be here covering me,” openly contemplating the annihilation of Iran, a UN member state, taking a shot at Cuba and attacking the UN for “imposing a radical left-wing agenda”. Burnham, meanwhile, wasn’t that different in tone from Starmer. He shook Trump’s hand, forgave him for once describing him as the mayor of a town, made the obligatory noises about loving the US, and appeared to nod along while Trump excoriated the Chagos Island deal (Starmer’s proposal to give Mauritius sovereignty over the island on the condition that the UK can continue to operate the Diego Garcia military base there). “Our understanding is that Downing Street is sticking to the Chagos deal,” Pippa tells me. Even so, Burnham has said he wants to take a different approach to US relations, suggesting in June that he wouldn’t just “go along with anything they say”. The clearest sign of this intention was the sweeping sanctions that Ed Miliband imposed on trade with Israeli settlements earlier this month. At yesterday’s meeting, a journalist asked Trump what he thought about the decision. Trump didn’t take the bait, and instead deferred to Burnham. “It was an unusual show of reticence,” Pippa says. It seemed like a vindication of the careful diplomatic work that took place over the summer, when Miliband and diplomats at the Foreign Office formed a 12-nation coalition to back the policy. Perhaps it will give them confidence that it’s possible to make a principled stand without suffering severe repercussions. *** What were the flashpoints? “It’s impossible to get away from the fact that despite the cordial relations, there are some really thorny issues coming up,” Pippa says. One of those is Iran. Burnham told journalists on the plane to New York that he would be pushing Trump to de-escalate the conflict (Trump said yesterday that he’d strike a deal with Iran after the midterm elections, which seems highly unlikely). Britain has longstanding diplomatic ties with Saudi Arabia, and Burnham recently agreed that Britain would help refuel Saudi jets that are defending energy infrastructure against Houthi rebels. With this decision, he’s treading a fine line between assisting a regional ally, and getting drawn into a wider conflict. In his speech at the general assembly, Burnham announced he would be launching a new international centre to establish global standards on AI. It’s unclear whether he’ll go as far as nations such as Norway and Finland in backing legislation to prevent the launch of new AI models that haven’t undergone rigorous safety testing, something that ministers in Starmer’s government were previously exploring. In any case, his speech on AI put him firmly at odds with Trump, who described attempts to regulate AI as a “globalist scheme”, and declared that from now on, his administration will now be referring to AI as SI: Super Intelligence. *** What should Burnham do next? As the Trump administration has helped to erode old alliances like Nato and the G7, new and temporary alliances have emerged, including the nations that Miliband convinced to back his West Bank sanctions. In a speech at Davos earlier this year, Canada’s Mark Carney spoke of a “rupture in the world order” and called for the world’s democratic “middle powers” to come together to build alliances based on shared values. “Burnham doesn’t want to take the Carney approach of all-out diplomatic war with the US, because the US is still our biggest security and economic ally,” Pippa tells me. “But we live in a world of spheres of influence – the US, China, and the EU – and that means having to make decisions about which sphere we want to belong to, whether geographically, or ethically.” As the Guardian contributor Steve Bloomfield recently wrote in this interesting piece, the idea of foreign policy with an “ethical dimension” of the sort once espoused by the Labour foreign secretary Robin Cook has often been regarded as something of a joke. But in a battle between liberal democracies and an authoritarian far right, demonstrating an alternative to the cruelty and belligerence of the Trump administration is arguably more important than ever. Miliband’s sanctions announcement is a promising start, but nobody knows yet how far Burnham will be willing to go. What else we’ve been enjoying The diary of a 12-year-old boy living in Gaza, part of our powerful Gaza: a week in the life series about the daily routines of ordinary Palestinians, is not an easy read and all the more essential to take in because of that. The 21-year-old has agreed a “multi-year” deal, the Prem champions announced on Tuesday morning. The front pages The Guardian leads on the prime minister’s meeting with the US president, under the headline “Trump praises Burnham but says Chagos Islands deal is ‘terrible’”. title: Burnham navigates diplomatic rapids in first Trump meeting, but turbulent waters lie ahead
summary: British aides express relief, as the prime minister’s team say the meeting was at the ‘top end of their expectations’
text: On the flight out to New York this week, one of Andy Burnham’s senior aides warned him that meeting Donald Trump would be the political equivalent of white water rafting. While there is a well-known playbook the US president deploys when he first meets other world leaders, he remains a deeply unpredictable figure and any dealings with him can leave you crashing into the rocks. Trump’s strategy involves personal flattery, transactional diplomacy and a public evaluation of his guest’s skills. When Keir Starmer first met the president at the White House early last year, it was there in spades. Trump praised his “beautiful” accent, said that Britain was a “wonderful” place and claimed that he had driven a “hard bargain” on tariffs. On the flight home, the clearly relieved former prime minister gave journalists a Trump-style thumbs up, telling them he was “happy” before returning to the front of the plane. But in time, their relationship fell apart. Just over 18 months later, it was an apprehensive Burnham’s turn to head down the diplomatic rapids at the UN general assembly. As the new prime minister faced the press after their talks, the president again deployed the playbook – describing Burnham as a “natural businessperson” who had “lots of assets on his side”, while predicting he would be a “great” leader. The British side, including foreign secretary Ed Miliband and national security adviser Jonathan Powell, could not hide their relief when Trump kept his policy differences with the UK muted – beyond inevitable criticism of what he described as the “terrible” Chagos deal. Even on the issue that fully ruptured Starmer’s relationship with Trump – his refusal to allow the US to use British airbases for attacks against Iran at the start of the war – the president held his punches. “Some countries could have stepped forward. But there aren’t too many countries, frankly, that could have handled that,” he said. Afterwards, British officials – even those who have witnessed the Trump strategy in action before and knew it would not necessarily last – were delighted with how the talks had gone. “It was the top end of our expectations,” said one. “All the issues you guys had written about – the Falklands, a united Ireland, Chagos – all fine.” They admitted the West Bank settlement trade ban was the one area they had worried about most. But a summer of diplomacy got Trump on board, and to their relief, he deferred to Burnham on the question. “It was a bit of a curveball, but it was better than him criticising it,” another aide said. Burnham even managed to use the moment to steer the raft – briefly – into calmer waters, explaining his hopes of drawing an end to the political turbulence that has gripped Britain for more than a decade, and creating a more “positive story” for the country instead. “More than anything, we just needed them to connect, and start building a relationship that we can leverage when we need to,” a third government official said. But just as Starmer found that with time, policy differences between the UK and US made the relationship more difficult to navigate, so his successor is likely to find the same. Burnham’s team is right to be cautious about the unsteadiness that Trump can inflict – his international actions causing ripples in the UK too. The prime minister may have survived the first set of diplomatic rapids, but there are more to navigate ahead.

title: Qantas announces 18-hour direct flights from Sydney to New York with onboard ‘wellbeing zones’
summary: Due to take off in 2028, it is set to be the national carrier’s second ultra long-haul route after Sydney to London
text: Qantas says travellers will be able to fly between Sydney and New York in just 18 hours from mid-2028 when the airline launches its second ultra long-haul route, cutting at least three hours from the travel time. The route will be the second in Qantas’ Project Sunrise expansion plans, with new Sydney to London direct flights planned for October 2027, after some delays. It would be the first commercial direct flight from Kingsford-Smith airport to New York’s JFK airport. Qantas currently offers flights from Sydney to New York with a stopover in Los Angeles, which take 21 hours and typically cost more than $1,400 one way or more than $1,900 return. Qantas has not disclosed prices for the Project Sunrise routes. It has previously suggested direct fares could cost 20% more than stopover fares and said ticket prices are facing upward pressure. Tickets for the Sydney to New York route are set to go on sale in August 2027, Qantas said. It has not specified which month flights will begin. When it announced the London route launch date, the company said it would reveal launch timings in 2027. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Qantas is planning to unveil more 20-hour direct flights from Perth in future but has abandoned references to previous hopes to run routes from Brisbane or Melbourne. The Project Sunrise flights’ initial launch date of 2022 was delayed by the Covid-19 pandemic. Subsequent plans to start in 2025, then early 2027, were waylaid by manufacturing delays at Airbus, Qantas has said. The company has ordered 12 Airbus A350–1000ULRs, fitted with extra fuel tanks, which can fly over 16,000km and up to 22 hours nonstop. The first is expected to arrive in Australia in April 2027. The planes were specifically designed to fly up to 22 hours nonstop for Qantas, to complete some of the longest commercial flights in the world. A test model in July completed a 24-hour, 24-minute flight from Melbourne to Airbus’s manufacturing facility in Toulouse, France, believed to be the longest-ever commercial flight. Each plane will contain a dedicated “wellbeing zone” between the economy and premium economy cabins, where passengers will be able to stretch, watch guided exercise videos and help themselves to snacks and drinks. Only 140 of the A350–1000ULR’s 238 seats are standard economy. It contains six first-class suites, 52 business suites and 40 premium economy seats. The company expects the Project Sunrise flights and sustained premium flight demand to increase its earnings by $400m over the next five years, with profit margins to rise from today’s rate of 4% to 10%. Qantas said demand for its flights in and out of New York have doubled since 2023. Short-term US arrivals to Australia picked up 4% in the year to July 2026 compared with the year prior, according to the Australian Bureau of Statistics. However, Australians travelling and returning from the US dropped 9% in the same period. Qantas’s chief executive, Vanessa Hudson, unveiled the start date at a launch party in a New York cocktail bar, as world leaders gathered in the city for the United Nations general assembly. Hudson said the flights could change the way Australians travel. “Reaching New York nonstop completes a vision we set out many years ago, and it’s a moment of enormous pride for the thousands of our people who have been working hard to make Project Sunrise a reality,” she said. The company is training pilots on its A350 simulator and is teaching engineers about the new aircraft. It said more than 360 pilots and 1,200 cabin crew will be trained to operate the aircraft by the time the entire fleet has arrived.

title: Critics of UK government’s economic forecaster are ‘shooting the messenger’, say MPs
summary: Treasury committee rejects calls for fundamental reform of independent watchdog the Office for Budget Responsibility
text: Attacks on the government’s independent economic forecaster from left and right of the political spectrum are akin to “shooting the messenger”, according to an influential group of MPs. The Treasury committee rejected “siren calls to fundamentally reform” the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) and said it should not be blamed when policymakers had to make tough decisions because of tight public finances. However, the MPs said they were persuaded that ministers should consider instructing the OBR to adopt a 10-year economic forecast to complement the five- and 50-year forecasts that it already publishes. Parliament should also set aside time to debate the OBR’s annual fiscal risks and sustainability report, which sets out threats to the stability of public finances over the next 50 years. Dame Meg Hillier, chair of the committee, said critics of the OBR had sought to characterise it as “a wielder of dark powers with a stranglehold on Treasury ministers and officials”. But she said a review by the committee had found “it’s simply not true”. Hillier said: “The fiscal rules, and therefore the OBR’s forecasts, become more important when government spending operates on razor-thin margins. That is a feature of decision-making by chancellors, not overreach by the OBR.” The OBR was set up in 2010 by the then chancellor George Osborne to provide independent forecasts of economic growth and assess the impact of the government’s tax and spending policies. Since then, it has come under fire for allegedly underestimating the impact of successive austerity budgets under Osborne’s chancellorship and, more recently, overestimating the growth potential of the economy. Prof Jo Michell, an economist at the University of the West of England, and Dr Robert Calvert Jump, an economist at the University of Greenwich, told the committee that the OBR’s forecasts about the level of spare financial capacity, often referred to as headroom, at the end of a five-year forecast had come to dictate government spending policies. “The OBR has evolved into a body that determines the bounds of permissible fiscal policy, despite lacking the democratic mandate to fulfil such a role […] It does not merely produce forecasts; it determines whether the government passes or fails its fiscal rules. As a result, its ‘headroom’ figures have become the binding constraint on policy,” they said. The latest review by the Treasury committee followed the resignation in December 2025 of chair Richard Hughes after the OBR’s assessment of the previous budget was leaked. Hillier said: “Now is the time to preserve the independent voice within our economic debate, not attempt to undermine it. I would like to hear our new chancellor and the wider administration make that point clearly and regularly. “I do, however, think there is merit in looking at both the potential longer-term effects of government policies and the possible path of the economy further out. While these will be highly uncertain, it can help to start a debate on how to break the cycle of short-term thinking, which so often holds this country back.”

title: How opencast mining risks reawakening dormant geological faults
summary: New study finds subsidence caused by groundwater extraction can take place as far as 20km from site of mine
text: The impact of opencast mining goes far beyond the edge of the pit. Studies of an opencast coalmine in western Germany show that opencast mining triggered extensive subsidence in the surrounding area and re-activated dormant geological faults. Underground mines are often associated with ground subsidence, but less is known about the risks associated with opencast mines. Researchers from the GFZ Helmholtz Centre for Geosciences in Potsdam, Germany, studied satellite data and geological field measurements from the area around the opencast Rhenish coalfields, between Aachen and Cologne. Their findings, which are published in Engineering Geology, show that the large volumes of groundwater extraction required for safe mine operations lowered the water table, resulting in widespread subsidence up to 20km (12 miles) from the edge of the mine. And the locations that were most affected were not random; they clustered and intensified along existing geological faults, which were re-awakened by the mining-induced subsidence. Cracks in buildings and roads in the local area demonstrate the impact, including a school that has shifted by half a metre. Mining is still taking place in the area and subsidence will probably continue for decades to come. But the researchers show how satellite monitoring combined with geological data can be used to produce regional subsidence hazard maps, helping communities plan ahead and develop more resilient infrastructure.

title: Japan PM pledges support for international criminal court after Trump calls it ‘out of control’
summary: Sanae Takaichi has been under domestic pressure to publicly support the ICC, after the US sanctioned the court and its Japanese president
text: Japan’s prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, has voiced her country’s “consistent support” for the international criminal court (ICC), after Donald Trump urged member states to abandon the body, calling it “out of control”. In her speech to the UN general assembly in New York on Tuesday, Takaichi said postwar Japan had “emphasised the rule of law in the resolution of all conflicts” – a commitment she said was reflected in its support for multilateral organisations such as the ICC. Japan’s leader had faced pressure at home to publicly support the ICC, whose president, Tomoko Akane, is Japanese, after failing to come to its defence in response to Trump’s announcement in August that the US would impose sanctions targeting the entire organisation. On Tuesday, Trump intensified his criticism of the ICC in his speech to the general assembly. “The United States is equally opposed to the out-of-control institution known as the international criminal court,” he said. “I call on all nations that are members of the ICC to officially resign from this rogue institution immediately.” The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, has called for the ICC to be dismantled “brick by brick”, describing it as an “intolerable threat to US sovereignty”. Takaichi avoided direct criticism of the US administration in her UN speech as she seeks to keep Washington on side amid rising tensions in the Asia-Pacific, including a commitment to support democratic Taiwan and address Chinese military activity in the South and East China Seas. Officials in Tokyo are reportedly concerned that Trump could use Taiwan as leverage when he discusses trade with the Chinese leader, Xi Jinping, in Washington on Thursday. Washington is legally obliged to provide Taiwan with the means to defend itself. Beijing regards the self-governing island as a province and has vowed to “annex” it, including by force if it can’t convince or coerce Taiwan into accepting what it calls “reunification”. Takaichi’s most recent comments on the ICC come after a cross-party group of MPs in Japan urged her to demand that Trump withdraw the sanctions, announced in response to its decision to issue a warrant for the arrest of the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, and an ongoing investigation into alleged war crimes by American troops in Afghanistan. One of the Japanese lawmakers, former defence minister Gen Nakatani, said the UN general assembly was “a place where a country should make its case to the world”, adding: “We want Japan to protect the ICC through the [prime minister’s] address and contacts with other countries.” Takaichi said on Tuesday that she and Trump had a “candid exchange” about the ICC during discussions on the sidelines of the general assembly. In the past, Takaichi had drawn criticism for her lukewarm defence of the ICC, having initially described US sanctions as “very unfortunate”. She later said the measures were “incompatible” with Japan’s stance on the work of the court. Akane, who has led the ICC since 2024, said she would not be intimidated by the threat of sanctions. Speaking soon after the measures were announced in August, she told reporters: “The ICC will never be defeated. Justice will and should prevail, and we will stay true to that belief.”

title: Country diary: An autumn bounty of fruits is well on its way | John Gilbey
summary: Cardigan: Taking a walk beside the River Teifi, I encounter trees beginning to fade into new season colour, and the low blur of a weasel
text: It is rare for me to visit the same place twice within a couple of weeks, but my walk in the Teifi Marshes recently was curtailed by heavy rain, and I feel that I have unfinished business. Last time I started from the Cilgerran end of the marsh, so today begin at the seaward side – crossing the bridge over the Teifi and heading upstream past the site of the old, sadly long-departed Cardigan railway station. My route follows the former course of the railway line, but I briefly divert along a boardwalk into the broad reedbeds at the heart of the marsh. Here, I am surrounded by the ambient sound of the wind in the reeds, which ebbs and flows with an almost animate organic static – pushing back the distant sounds of traffic on the main road. Scrub and small trees interact with the reeds at the margins, their autumn bounty of fruits already well advanced. The blackberries are almost over, but the sloes are plump and mature with the promise of a warming winter spirit to come. Back on the main trail, a weasel, a low blur of fur and legs, dashes across the path in front of me just as the sun emerges from banks of grey cloud. The new shadows make me look up. Beyond the mile or so of reedbed, the valley side is wooded with deciduous trees just beginning to fade into autumn colours. Among them, a few bare crowns of what I take to be dead ash trees stand skeletal, awaiting the winter storm. The Afon Teifi is tidal here, and it is about an hour after high water. The level in the creek off the main channel is starting to fall, exposing freshly wetted mud. Along the edge of the water, a pair of dunlin explore what the receding tide has left on offer, hunting with their short bills and jerky movements, while nearby ducks take a more leisurely approach. On my last visit, I caught a glimpse of a kingfisher from this spot, but today it is absent – as is the heron I had hoped to get a better picture of. Next time, perhaps. Next time. • Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024, is available now at guardianbookshop.com

title: Thinktank linked to Reform UK calls for abolition of state pension
summary: ‘Radical’ report likely to influence party’s platform also proposes abolishing inheritance and capital gains taxes
text: A thinktank linked to Reform UK has called for the abolition of the state pension and £75bn worth of sweeping tax cuts in a “radical” report likely to influence the party’s platform for the next election. The Centre for a Better Britain’s (CFABB) report – which also calls for weaker rules for UK banks and Trump-style investment accounts offering £1,000 to newborns – will be formally launched at a private event with City executives on Wednesday. The 183-page report, entitled “Boosting Britain”, proposes abolishing taxes typically levied on wealthy Britons, including capital gains tax and inheritance tax, which it says disrupts family businesses and encourages people to move their wealth out of the UK. The CFABB – founded and led by the former Reform chief operations officer Jonathan Brown – also calls for the elimination of stamp duty on property and shares, digital service tax and air passenger duty, and a drastic reduction in “internationally uncompetitive” corporation tax from 25% to 15% over eight years. That would effectively “remove up to 50% of the existing tax code” at a £75bn cost to the public finances. The report said it amounted to a “a programme of radical reform to Britain’s financial system and tax code, designed ultimately to raise productivity and living standards through better-paid jobs, higher retirement incomes, higher business investment, more businesses starting and scaling, and less time and money spent on unproductive activity”. The report stresses that any tax changes would have to be matched by cuts to public spending – to avoid a Liz Truss-style market meltdown – but stopped short of outlining how exactly to match all of those cuts with cost savings. However, the CFABB says some ways to cut spending could involve closing the coveted public pension plan to new teachers and civil servants, and eradicating the state pension. The Department for Work and Pensions forecasts the state pension will cost the public purse £146.1bn in 2025 to 2026. “The issue with the state pension is that it’s essentially a Ponzi scheme,” Brown told reporters at a briefing on Tuesday, suggesting workers were unfairly funding current retirees. Instead, a “lifetime investment account” would take its place. The Trump-style investment accounts would come as a £1,000 starter pack to children at birth, with account holders later contributing up to 15% of earnings into their personal retirement pot. The state pension would only remain as a “means-tested safety net” for the worst-off. The report has been released weeks before the prime minister Andy Burnham’s government is due to reveal its first budget. The CFABB launched formally last year, after raising fresh funds under its previous guise, Resolute 1850 – a reference to the ship whose timbers were used in the White House’s Oval Office. Its report is likely to prompt debate, having also called for a sliding scale for bank taxes, breaking up the Treasury – moving some responsibilities to a new “department for economic growth” – and making sure senior bosses at the Bank of England have their pay linked to hitting inflation targets. That would include positions such as the governor of the Bank, currently Andrew Bailey, the thinktank authors confirmed. The CFABB’s funding is unclear. It has notable ties with Reform UK, with its operations based in Millbank Tower near Reform’s headquarters, but authors insisted that their work had yet to be reviewed by the party. The CFABB has five staff, and previously counted James Orr – Reform UK’s former head of policy – as the chair of its advisory board. Orr was suspended from Reform UK earlier this month after being filmed in an undercover investigation appearing to help orchestrate a plot to get around electoral laws on foreign donations. Orr denies wrongdoing. A spokesperson for the CFABB said Orr stepped down from the thinktank role when he took a job at Reform in February, and was not replaced.

title: Huge El Niño projected to cause more than 450,000 deaths by February
summary: New report predicts a heavy toll from Nigeria to the US – and comes on top of existing impacts of the climate crisis
text: More than 450,000 people are projected to die from the additional heat brought by the super El Niño by February, according to estimates by climate scientists. The toll is on top of the early deaths resulting from temperatures already driven up by the climate crisis. It will strike across the globe, from Indonesia to India, and Nigeria to the US. Many further deaths are expected from the droughts, wildfires and flooding that El Niños bring. The heat deaths have been estimated at regional level, and the researchers said the projections therefore identified where measures to protect people could be put in place and save lives. Such actions could include better heat forecasts, cooling centres where people can shelter, increased staffing for medical facilities at the hottest times and protections for outdoor workers. The El Niño currently heating up the planet burst through the highest temperature ever recorded for the phenomenon on Monday, several months before its expected peak. The heat is so much greater than previous events that scientists have called it “mind-blowing” and “Godzilla-level”. El Niños are natural climate events but may be made worse by global heating. “The estimate of 451,000 people is such a large number that it can be numbing, but it is made up of parents and children, grandparents and neighbours, people going to work, caring for families, and living their lives,” said Prof Michael Greenstone, co-founder of the Climate Impact Lab and at the University of Chicago, who co-authored the report. The estimate of deaths is for the period June 2026, as some heat deaths will have already occurred, to February 2027, which is when current temperature forecasts end. But elevated levels of heat deaths are expected to continue until June or July 2027. The most affected countries in the next six months are the tropical nations of Nigeria, Indonesia, Sudan, India and Brazil. The US is in the top 20 most affected nations, with 3,500 projected additional heat deaths. More broadly, the Sahel region in Africa and south-east Asia are heavily affected. The El Niño is also a “postcard from our future”, the researchers said, pushing up temperatures to the level the climate crisis is projected to deliver in 20 years’ time. “Increasing emergency response and better targeting our efforts can save many lives this year,” said report co-author Dr Tamma Carleton at the University of California, Berkeley. “But 20 years from now, once today’s extreme temperatures become the new normal, we don’t want to be in a constant state of emergency.. We need to mobilise now to design, deploy and evaluate the tools that will save lives in the years ahead.” The projections were made using peer-reviewed methods that track the month-by-month relationship between temperature and additional heat deaths in 24,378 regions across the world. This was combined with the forecasts for higher temperatures due to El Niño in the months ahead. The baseline was the number of heat deaths in the average month from 1996 to 2025. “People have been able to forecast when there’s going to be shocks to crops, and give advance warning of that,” said Greenstone. “This new report is opening the door to being able to do it for an even more important outcome – I would say the most important outcome – which is death.” The report will be submitted to a peer-reviewed journal, but Greenstone said that, given the urgency of the situation, “it would have been irresponsible to sit on it”. Food supplies will also be hit by El Niño, with the World Food Programme warning in August that its impacts were likely to push about 50 million people into acute hunger and drive prices up. A major El Niño in 1877-1878 led to more than 50m deaths due to drought and famine, with India, Brazil and China severely affected. Prof Friederike Otto, at Imperial College London, told the Guardian on Monday: “The [current El Niño] event is a huge redistribution of energy in the climate system and is dangerous, because it is unfolding on top of a much warmer, human-influenced climate system. “So, in many places around the world we will see never-before-experienced heat extremes, with all their consequences on health, food security and water stress. El Niño comes and goes, but as long as we continue to burn fossil fuels, it occurs on an increasingly hotter baseline, making it much more difficult for communities to deal with the consequences.” The Guardian’s climate forum 2026: On Tuesday 20 October, join Damian Carrington, and our panel of experts—including Professor Andy Haines, Katie White MP, Asad Rehman, Shruti Suresh Gareth Thomas and Amy Fairman for a hopeful and solutions-focused evening. Book tickets here or at guardian.live • This article was amended on 23 September 2026. Owing to information provided, an earlier version said that the figure for 450,000 projected extra deaths due to El Niño covers the period from September 2026 to February 2027. In fact it covers the period June 2026 to February 2027.

title: As Japan swelters, farmers turn to new heat-resistant rice varieties to boost staple crop
summary: New rice varieties give hope that farmers can overcome the climate emergency and a warmer future that threatens harvests
text: When schoolchildren in Shiroishi were enlisted to plant rice seedlings in June, Shinto priests blessed the land and asked the deities for a bountiful crop. Judging by the fields behind farmer Haruki Kawasaki, their prayers have been answered. The 63-year-old is preparing to harvest this year’s crop of hinatamaru, a variety of rice whose plump grains have thrived despite exposure to another hot and dry summer, conditions that typically punish rice yields. Hinatamaru is one of growing number of heat-resistant rice varieties that are giving fresh hope to farmers across Japan that they can overcome a climate emergency that is threatening the country’s staple crop. Kawasaki and his team once spent the entire day in the fields, but the heat has made that impossible. “Now we start early in the morning and work until around noon,” he says. “It’s way too hot in the afternoon … although the mornings are not what you would call cool.” Kawasaki and other farmers in Saga are at the centre of the boom as Japan finds ways to cope with a warmer future. The long process of developing heat-tolerant strains involves cross-breeding existing varieties, cultivation in controlled environments and, finally, real-world trials. Japan’s ageing farmers have toiled through record-breaking heat and below-average rainfall over the last three summers. After heat records were broken again this year, the meteorological agency added a new category – “cruelly hot days” – when the mercury exceeds 40C. El Niño is expected to bring even more extreme weather. Those conditions create havoc with crops of Japan’s staple cereal, producing chalky, anaemic grains that are susceptible to cracking when polished for commercial sale. When the temperature stays abnormally high for prolonged periods after rice plants have flowered, what should be translucent, starchy seeds end up as immature grains that can’t be sold as grade 1 polished rice on the open market. In a report published this month, Greenpeace Japan warned that four of the country’s “iconic” autumn crops, including rice and sweet potatoes, were at risk because of exposure to long periods of high temperatures. “Over 50 years of accelerating heatwaves have pushed Japan’s most iconic agricultural hubs past their thermal limits, placing both crop viability and supermarket prices on the line,” Ikumi Toyota, from Greenpeace Japan, said in a statement. “While farmers are showing incredible ingenuity to adapt, single operations cannot outrun systemic climate disruption. When the people who feed us run out of options, national food security becomes everyone’s crisis.” Embracing heat-loving crops The climate crisis has made growing traditional rice varieties a calculated risk that fewer farmers are willing to take. In Saga prefecture, located on the coast of the Ariake Sea in Kyushu – a large island in Japan’s south-west – growing numbers are instead taking a chance on something new. According to the agriculture ministry, Saga now leads the county in the adoption of new strains that can withstand the stifling, bone dry summers that have become the norm. Heat-tolerant varieties account for almost 67% of Saga’s rice acreage. Neighbouring Nagasaki follows with just under 50% and Shimane, on the Japan Sea coast, with 47%. However, uptake in regions in the north-east, where farmers are traditionally more accustomed to battling cold weather, is still very low. Heat records have tumbled in Japan in recent years. Record-breaking heat in 2023 was partly to blame for the “Reiwa rice crisis” the following year, when the government was forced to take the unprecedented step of releasing emergency stockpiles to ease severe shortages and price hikes. Farmers in Saga raised the alarm a decade ago, when low yields of poor quality rice sent prices plummeting. “They were determined to grow delicious rice that could withstand the heat,” says Kazuhiro Matsumoto, a senior official in the crop department of the Saga Prefecture Agricultural Testing and Research Centre. The solution came in the form of hinatamaru – the product of 12 years of research that is now spreading quickly after successful trials in 2024 – propelling Saga prefecture to the forefront of agriculture’s rearguard action against climate change. Kawasaki’s crop of hinatamaru is this year is expected to total a modest 600kg but the outlook is promising. And other regions in Japan are following suit. The use of heat-tolerant rice has expanded to all but three of Japan’s 47 prefectures as agriculture officials rush to combat declines in quality and yield. They covered 248,000 hectares last year – a record 18% of the overall rice crop – according to the agriculture ministry, a dramatic increase from the 42,000 hectares the previous year. The climate emergency is also changing the way Japan’s farmers work. Fruit and vegetable farmers in some regions have taken to inspecting their crops at night, to avoid higher temperatures, while others are switching to heat-loving crops such as avocado, bitter melon and okra. Kawasaki, who has been growing rice for more than three decades, says the day could come when farmers across Japan are all growing new heat-resistant varieties. “The priority is that it has to taste good.” As he prepares to harvest this season’s crop – some of which will be included in an annual ritual at the imperial palace in Tokyo – Kawasaki also notes the spread of heat-tolerant grains as a race against time. Almost 70% of Japan’s agricultural workers are 65 or older. “Lots of farmers around here are in their 70s, and I’m in my 60s,” he says. “So as a farmer, I’m just grateful that we have found something that works. And it tastes great.”

title: AI looms large over Trump-Xi meeting amid deep distrust between US and China
summary: Fears persist about Trump ‘sucking up’ to Xi on Taiwan, but few concrete outcomes anticipated from US meeting
text: When Xi Jinping, China’s leader, touches down in Maryland on Wednesday, he will step out into the arms – perhaps a hug, if Donald Trump’s wishes come true – of a US president who has shown China more bonhomie than any of his recent predecessors. The meeting between Xi and Trump this week will be the second time that the leaders of the world’s two biggest economies have talked face to face this year. At the previous summit, held in Beijing in May, there was much talk of building a “strategic stability” between the two powers. But there was little by way of concrete outcomes: the countries remain at loggerheads over trade, export controls and geopolitics. Despite the goodwill built in May, few anticipate any major breakthroughs this week when Xi makes his first state visit to the US since 2015. “Expectations are very low,” said Bonnie Glaser, a managing director at the US thinkthank the German Marshall Fund. “Nobody is using the term ‘deliverables’.” One area in which Trump and Xi may reach some consensus is on artificial intelligence safety. Tech executives including Jeff Bezos of Amazon, Sundar Pichai of Alphabet, Sam Altman of ⁠OpenAI, Tim Cook of Apple, Elon Musk of Tesla, Mark Zuckerberg of Meta and Jensen Huang of Nvidia will reportedly attend a ⁠state dinner at the White House on Thursday evening. ‘Whoever wins AI, wins’ In the past few weeks, the US has been beset by worries that AI is progressing too fast, but that the US must strive to defend its lead over China in the frontier technology – and Trump has pushed back hard against calls to slow its development. “We’re leading China in AI,” Trump said recently. “And frankly, I want to ⁠keep it that way, because whoever wins AI, wins.” On Sunday, Scott Bessent, the US treasury secretary, concluded talks with the Chinese vice-premier He Lifeng by proposing an AI safety mechanism to be established between Washington and Beijing. The mechanism appears to stop short of a major safety agreement. Tuesday’s front page of the People’s Daily, the official newspaper of the Chinese Communist party (CCP), ran an article saying that the US and China should “make AI a new frontier for China-US cooperation” and “make good use of the intergovernmental dialogue mechanism on AI”. António Guterres, the UN secretary general, called on the two countries to establish a dialogue on AI similar to the communication between the US and the Soviet Union during the cold war. “Governments with the greatest AI capabilities have the greatest responsibilities to humanity, to establish channels for dialogue, transparency, trust and cooperation,” Guterres said. Still, China does not agree with US assessments about the grave threat posed by its AI developments. China’s foreign ministry responded to an essay by Dario Amodei, the Anthropic chief executive, which called for Washington to impede Beijing’s progress by saying “fearmongering, confrontation and vicious competition will only disrupt the process of global AI governance”. China has already taken steps to mandate the labelling of AI-generated content, to restrict the ability of children to use AI companions and, in keeping with the CCP’s desire to keep tight control on all information, to restrict what can be said by chatbots. China may be more concerned with what it sees as US attempts to limit is growth. Washington has for years restricted China’s ability to buy the most advanced semiconductors needed for AI development, and this year the US banned the sale of Chinese humanoid robots. Amanda Hsiao, China director at the Eurasia Group, a political risk consultancy, said: “China doesn’t necessarily see the threat in the same way that the US does. There is a lot of distrust that’s in the way of cooperation. The Chinese are inclined to think of every US call for safety standards or calls from companies for pacing the frontier as means of suppressing Chinese development.” Trade tensions persist Next on the agenda will be trade. Washington and Beijing struck a temporary truce in the trade war last year at a summit in South Korea. That truce – which included a pause on tariffs, as well as an agreement for Beijing to loosen restrictions on the export of rare earths – will expire in November. Beijing is hoping for a longer-term commitment to banish tariffs, which pose a threat to China’s export-driven economy. But reports suggest that the US is unwilling to agree to anything that would weaken its future bargaining power. Glaser, of the German Marshall Fund, said: “The US side views this as leverage over China and ensuring that they can get deliveries of the rare earths and magnets that American companies need.” China may not feel the need to negotiate, either. Despite the trade war, China’s exports have surged, and it is on track to reach a $1tn trade surplus for the second year running. ‘This is not a G2’ One aspect of the relationship that has shifted since May is the issue of Taiwan. After the Beijing summit, Xi secured a major concession from Trump, when he agreed to pause a $14bn package of US arms sales to Taiwan. US presidents have traditionally excluded the issue of arms sales to Taiwan, a self-governing island that China claims as part of its territory, from the US-China relationship. But Trump has described future weapons sales as a “very good negotiating chip”. The US is now reportedly considering delaying further sales until after the Apec and G20 summits later this year, where Trump and Xi are expected to meet again. Tuesday’s People’s Daily article said that a stable China-US relationship would “bring more peace, prosperity, and progress to the world”. But for all the talk in Beijing of “strategic stability”, Scott Kennedy, a senior adviser at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, notes that “this is not a G2” alliance of the world’s two dominant powers. “They are finding a way to manage the bilateral relationship, but they are not whatsoever working together as co-stewards of the international order,” Kennedy wrote in a recent commentary. China is Iran’s biggest oil buyer and trading partner. After Trump launched strikes against Iran in February, China reportedly put pressure on Tehran behind the scenes to come to the negotiating table. It also slashed oil imports by nearly one-quarter in the first six months of the war, limiting global inflation. Da Wei, a professor of international relations at Tsinghua University, wrote in a recent essay that this reflected “a more confident China” that “did not exploit the difficulties that the United States faced in the war with Iran”. But Beijing has otherwise done little to resolve the crisis in the Middle East, which it sees as being a mess of Trump’s making. Last month, Bessent announced an “economic D-day” against Iran and its enablers. The US treasury secretary subsequently claimed to have had “very good private discussions” with Chinese officials over ending the country’s economic ties with Iran. When it comes to Ukraine, Beijing has shown unwavering support for Moscow since Russia’s president, Vladimir Putin, launched his full-scale invasion in 2022. Ali Wyne, senior research and advocacy adviser on the US and China at the International Crisis Group, said: “The contrast between the world’s incumbent power and its principal challenger will be even sharper in Washington than it was in Beijing in May: while the former is mired once more in the Middle East and straining longstanding alliances, the latter is casting itself as a stabilizing counterweight and the leading champion of a more multipolar order.” High vibes, low ambition The lack of momentum on thorny geopolitical issues, combined with China’s emphasis on maintaining “strategic stability” above all else, means that few expect there to be major breakthroughs at this week’s summit. Hsiao added: “It is going to be yet another summit that is high on positive vibes and relatively low ambition in terms of substance.” Democrats in Washington have urged Trump to raise concerns over China’s treatment of political prisoners, but are already sounding the alarm that he could make too many concessions to Xi. Senator Tammy Duckworth told an audience at the Center for American Progress thinktank on Tuesday: “He’s not very good at making deals with the PRC [People’s Republic of China] that they actually follow through on. If you look at the result of the last summit they had, they promised the purchase of 200 Boeing aircraft and $17bn in agricultural products. Neither one of those has come to pass.” “At the same time, he violated our longstanding position on Taiwan by engaging in discussions on arms sales to Taiwan with President Xi,” Duckworth added. “I worry that it’s going to be a repeat of that and President Trump basically spends too much time sucking up to President Xi. He’s very distracted. When he focuses on the Indo-Pacific, it’s about him cozying up to an authoritarian regime at the expense of our friends and allies in the region.” Additional research by Yu-chen Li

title: Jamaica hails King’s decision to refer slavery reparations petition to privy council as ‘really big deal’
summary: The move comes after Jamaica’s culture minister Olivia Grange travelled to the UK earlier this month to lodge the historic petition
text: King Charles has referred a landmark slavery reparations petition from Jamaica to a high-level UK appeals court for legal advice, Jamaica’s culture minister announced in parliament on Tuesday. Referring to the move as a “really big deal”, Olivia Grange told Jamaica’s MPs the monarch had confirmed that their legal questions have been passed on to the London-based privy council – the final court of appeal for UK overseas territories and some Commonwealth countries. The petition seeks guidance on three questions: whether the forced transport of Africans to Jamaica was lawful; whether it constituted a crime against humanity; and whether Britain is under an obligation to provide restitution for slavery and its enduring consequences. “Indeed we went fearless and boldly into this chapter when we petitioned the king on Monday, September 7, 2026 – one day after the 245th anniversary of the commemoration of the Zong massacre, an event that captures the barbarity of chattel enslavement,” Grange said in parliament. “The king could have ignored us. The king could have delayed responding to us. The king could have made a decision not to refer the questions to the privy council, or he could make a decision to refer the questions,” she said, before adding “King Charles has referred the petition filed on the 7th of September, 2026, on behalf of the people of Jamaica to the Judicial Committee of the privy council.” Jamaica had activated a rarely used mechanism in the Judicial Committee Act 1833, which allows the king to refer questions of “legal or constitutional nature” to the privy council when they cannot be resolved through ordinary courts, according to the country’s legal counsels. The minister said that taking the matter to the International Court of Justice, was not an option for Jamaica. “The United Kingdom has placed specific reservations on the compulsory jurisdiction of the ICJ which prevent the Court from adjudicating on disputes between the United Kingdom and the government of any other country which is or has been a Member of the Commonwealth”. A privy council opinion would not compel the UK government to pay reparations, but Jamaican officials believe it could shape negotiations and legal options and set a precedent for other Commonwealth nations seeking reparations. Earlier this month, Grange led a Jamaican delegation to London to officially lodge the petition. While in the UK, the group, lawyers and members of the country’s national council on reparation met diaspora communities, MPs, church leaders and cultural institutions – among them the British Museum, from which Jamaica is seeking the return of artefacts taken during colonial rule. Tuesday’s announcement follows the Caricom Regional Conference on Reparations, which took place in Barbados last week. Officials at the conference said that Caribbean nations are drawing up a multi-pronged “action plan” with legal options to push the UK into negotiating a decades-long slavery reparations deal. Leaders in the region are hoping the UK would agree to targeted and constructive negotiation talks at upcoming Commonwealth and UN summits, but they are ready to take the matter to international courts if Britain continues to resist diplomatic options. Speaking at the conference, Prof Sir Hilary Beckles, the chair of the Caricom Reparations Commission, said reparations was a matter of justice, adding that countries in the region were forced to create viable democracies “out of the mess” of colonialism, which was still having an impact today. He said: “When Jamaica took its petition to the UK, we had to surround that petition with the fact that when Jamaica became independent in 1962, 80% of the black people in Jamaica could not read or write. After 300 years of British colonisation, they moved into independence with 80% illiteracy. How do you build a modern nation, not even a competitive economy, with 80% illiteracy?” Earlier this month, a spokesperson for Andy Burnham reiterated the British government’s long‑held position that “the UK does not and will not pay reparations”. Grange told parliament that the country is “awaiting directions from the Judicial Committee of the privy council as to the next steps to be taken in the case. And the attorney general is preparing to deal with the case”.

title: Ukraine war briefing: Zelenskyy ready for ‘energy ceasefire’, as Nato warns Putin becoming ‘increasingly cavalier’
summary: Meeting on sidelines of UN general assembly, Ukrainian leader says Kyiv open to deal not to attack energy targets if Russia agrees. What we know on day 1,673
text: Volodymyr Zelenskyy discussed with Donald Trump on Tuesday efforts to end the 4-year-old war with Russia, ⁠including a potential bilateral ceasefire on energy-related targets. “We are ready for any kind of format of energy ceasefire” if Russia agrees to “not attack our energy system,” Zelenskyy told journalists after meeting with Trump at the UN headquarters in New York. The Ukrainian leader expressed hope the “American side will find a way … to bring them to any kind of negotiations.” Zelenskyy said that he also was ready to meet the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, at a trilateral meeting with Trump. Trump insisted he was working with both sides to end the war, despite little evidence of Putin being open to any settlement. “It’s going to happen, I think, more quickly than people understand,” Trump said in his UN speech. Efforts led by Washington to broker a deal to end the hostilities, which have raged since Russia launched its all-out invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, have stalled in recent months as the US has shifted focus to its war against Iran. Zelenskyy claimed the war with Russia would end if Trump applied more pressure on Putin, and if China and India stop buying oil from Russia. “It’s enough to stop them, they will not have enough money,” Zelenskyy told The Wall Street Journal on Tuesday. Zelenskyy said Russia’s energy sales to China, India and Turkey were propping up Russia’s economy. During the same interview, Zelenskyy said that Trump on Tuesday did not ask him to stop bombing Russian oil refineries. However, he acknowledged the issue has been raised before by American partners over concerns of rising energy prices. Zelenskyy also met with the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, in New York, who said he lobbied Trump to press for a Ukraine-Russia energy ceasefire in his meeting with his Ukrainian counterpart. Burnham promised further financial support to Kyiv for infrastructure. Putin is becoming “increasingly cavalier, dangerous and risk accepting,” as his war in Ukraine drags on and as he seeks to divide western allies, Nato’s deputy commander in Europe said Tuesday. Air Chief Marshal Sir John Stringer spoke to The Associated Press at a security conference in Estonia amid warnings from some European leaders that Moscow is planning to test Nato’s collective defence pact with bolder attacks that have already included sabotage and espionage. Stringer warned that Nato members need to be aware of the “febrile environment” and be careful in their response because Putin would like to provoke the alliance into an “overreaction”. Officials in Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, which border Russia, have been more cautious about the prospect of a serious escalation. “Ukraine is fighting. Russia is absorbed in Ukraine. We do not observe any buildup near our borders. And from that part, I think that most would agree that the perspective of direct military attack is not correct,” Latvian president Edgars Rinkevics told reporters on the sidelines of the UN meeting. European countries have already faced multiple incursions of Russian drones – and several missiles – as well as a campaign of covert Russian disruption which began after the war. Ukraine has continued to press the US for more Patriot interceptors to defend against Russia’s ballistic missiles, but is yet to get any confirmation, Zelenskyy told reporters. “They are positive to help us, but I didn’t get the very concrete answer,” he said. Defence experts say the US has been experiencing a global shortage of Patriot interceptors because many have been expended to defend against Iranian attacks on US and allied bases in Middle East. Zelenskyy spoke of the urgency of needing the weapons, which can shoot down Russia’s more advanced ballistic missiles. The shortage in Ukraine has left Kyiv and other cities increasingly exposed to devastating attacks.

title: Sri Lanka Easter bombings: 15 sentenced to hundreds of years in prison each over deadly terror attacks
summary: Islamic State-inspired bombings of churches and hotels in 2019 was one of the country’s worst ever attacks
text: A court in Sri Lanka has convicted 15 men on terrorist charges for their involvement in the deadly 2019 Easter bombings and sentenced them each to at least 220 years in prison. The terror attacks, which targeted luxury hotels and churches as they held Easter services, left 267 people dead and wounded almost 600. The bombings, which were inspired by Islamic State (IS), were among the deadliest terror attacks in Sri Lanka’s history and sent shockwaves through the country. Two Sri Lanka-based Islamist militant groups were believed to have orchestrated the attacks. A video, recorded by the suicide bombers the day before the bombings, showed the attackers with their faces covered, armed with rifles and swords and pledging allegiance to the then-IS leader Abu Bakhr al-Baghdadi to make Sri Lanka an Islamic nation and wage war. The attacks were carried out by nine suicide bombers who died in the blasts. None of those who directly participated survived. Those on trial were accused of conspiring and aiding the bombings, which had deliberately targeted the minority Christian community and foreign tourists. The proceedings had spanned nearly five years, with the slow pace of justice frustrating victims and their families. In 2021, authorities filed 23,270 charges against 25 suspects whom they accused of planning or inspiring the attacks: three at churches, three at tourist hotels, one at a motel where an attacker killed himself, and two others after aborting a plan to attack a fourth hotel. The charges included murder, conspiracy to commit terrorism, and firearms and explosives offences under the Prevention of Terrorism Act. The verdict was finally delivered on Tuesday by a three-judge high court amid tight security, with hundreds of police deployed around the courthouse. In total, 15 defendants, who were all from Sri Lanka’s minority Muslim community, were sentenced to more than 200 years each. The judges also ordered the property of the defendants to be confiscated. Nine defendants were freed after the court found that the charges against them were not proven. One other died before their case reached trial. “Finally, we have justice,” said Catholic priest Jude Fernando. “It has taken a long time to get to this point.” However, the completion of the trial is unlikely to offer full closure for some. Sri Lanka’s Catholic church has long alleged that perpetrators put on trial were not the masterminds behind the bombings. Since Sri Lanka’s new government was elected in late 2024, there have been renewed investigations into allegations that elements within the Sri Lankan state – tied to former president Gotabaya Rajapaksa and his powerful family dynasty – may have had links to those responsible for the attacks. Investigators have alleged the Easter bombings were part of a conspiracy to manufacture a security threat, that would create chaos and help bring Rajapaksa, a former defence chief, to power. Rajapaksa was elected as president just a few months after the attack, on the back of a campaign that portrayed him as a strongman leader who was tough on terror. A parliamentary committee found that police and intelligence officials failed to act on repeated intelligence warnings of the attacks. In July, a former police chief and a former senior defence ministry official were sentenced to death for failing to act promptly on foreign intelligence warnings of possible attacks. Earlier this year, police also arrested Suresh Salley, a former intelligence chief and retired army major general, alleging he had prior knowledge of the attacks and worked with Islamist extremists before the bombings were carried out. He remains in custody but denies the charges. The country’s defence ministry and the Rajapaksa family have denied any involvement in the attacks.
