title: Far-right activist Daniel Thomas slashes dinghy in Channel with blade while rescue worker onboard
summary: Thomas called followers to protest against arrival of asylum seekers in Gosport, but Border Force instead transported them to Dover
text: Charities have condemned footage of far-right activist Daniel Thomas using a blade to slash an inflatable dinghy in the Channel while a rescue worker was onboard, in a further escalation of organised anti-immigration protest. Hundreds of protesters gathered early on Tuesday evening at Gosport in Hampshire, aiming to disrupt the planned disembarkation of asylum seekers, but the Border Force vessels carrying them landed instead in Dover early on Wednesday. Thomas, who styles himself as Danny Tommo, spent Tuesday afternoon in a small boat on the Channel, filming himself as he tracked two dinghies carrying asylum seekers from France to the UK. As rescue workers assisted them on to rescue boats, Thomas approached one of the dinghies, shouting: “Let’s get rid of that boat.” The black inflatable dinghy was full of dozens of lifejackets, recently left by the passengers. As Thomas drew close to the vessel, a rescue worker wearing an orange hi-vis outfit and yellow helmet stepped into the boat from the larger rescue boat. In footage livestreamed to 100,000 viewers, Thomas filmed himself stabbing a knife into the inflatable dinghy several times and slashing its side. The noise of escaping air was audible, and Thomas shouted: “This is England. This is not France any more.” Spotting that there was a rescue worker onboard, Thomas shouted: “Get off the boat. You’ve got time to get off the boat.” Thomas shouted to his colleagues: “Let’s go lads. Let’s go” and his boat motored away before the rescue worker climbed back on to the larger boat. The stream did not show what happened to the rescue worker. His action was condemned as violent and dangerous by the refugee charity, the Joint Council for Welfare of Immigrants. Stand Up to Racism posted on X: “Danny Tommo already has a conviction for knife crime. The footage of him going wild with a knife and slashing a boat with [an emergency worker] on it in the Channel today is disgusting.” Hampshire and Isle of Wight Constabulary said it was conducting inquiries into the boat-slashing incident. It said officers had made six arrests for offences including assaulting an emergency worker and aggravated trespass. All six people were in custody on Tuesday night. According to RNLI, the rescued asylum seekers had been in the water for 36 hours, which is thought to be the longest time small boats passengers have spent crossing the Channel. RNLI said that there were concerns for their deteriorating health and fears of a “catastrophic failure” of their dinghy. The French coastguard said about 60 migrants on a small boat spent more than 33 hours at sea “in precarious conditions”, refusing help as they were “determined to take all risks to reach the United Kingdom”. The RNLI later facilitated their transfer to a Border Force vessel. Thomas, who spent two years in prison for attempted kidnapping, has this summer gathered dozens of nationalist protest groups under the umbrella movement Patriot Platform. He used social media to call on followers to head to Gosport for 7pm to stage a protest at the expected arrival site. Hundreds of people turned out in Gosport, and others also gathered near the Haslar immigration removal centre, an unopened detention site. Scores of police vans and dozens of police officers blocked off roads. It was later confirmed the asylum seekers had been taken away from Hampshire by a Border Force boat to Dover, a 100-mile sea voyage away. Gosport local Dave Palmer, 43, was among the protesters. “We don’t want them in the country at all. They get given everything. I work 70 to 80-hour weeks as an air-conditioning engineer. What does the government give me? Nothing,” he said. A number of men wearing black, several with face coverings, arrived at the front of the protest with chants of “Send them back” from the crowd. The protesters in black remained quiet as they lined up face-to-face with the police officers. Donna Jones, the police and crime commissioner for Hampshire and the Isle of Wight, said she had urged Border Force to transfer the migrants to Dover. “Hampshire is not prepared or set up to process people travelling into Britain this way, and the burden on the police to deal with the arrival and potential protest activity is unsustainable,” she said. Following targeting by far-right agitators, RNLI emphasised that its role was not a political one: “When tasked by HM Coastguard we will rescue anyone in trouble at sea, as we have been doing for more than 200 years, without judgment or preference.” A government spokesperson said: “The Border Security Command works around the clock to protect our border and will continue to detain, check and process every small boat arrival.” Additional reporting by Solent News

title: Pay rent, eat or keep warm? Growing numbers face hard choices as housing benefit gap grows
summary: Wirral mother among renters turning to food banks as gap between a two-bed and housing benefit hits £158 a month – rising to as much as £324 in London
text: Do you prioritise paying the rent, putting food on the table or keeping the house warm in winter? In practice, says Laura Braddock, a single mum from Wirral, Merseyside, you always pay the rent first and improvise the rest. “If I’ve got a roof over our head, then everything else I can muddle through.” The pressing problem for Braddock, 39, is that muddling through is getting harder. The monthly rent for her two-bedroom flat far outstrips the local housing allowance (LHA) she receives – and the gap may widen. She pays her landlord £550 a month, but receives £425 in housing allowance, leaving her to make up a £125 “rent gap” out of her grocery and heating budgets. The former shop worker has a range of tried and tested strategies to cope, and to shield her son as far as possible from cost of living pressures. She may pay half the gas bill. She’ll eat cheap pasta and beans – or skip her own meals altogether. In January, however, these strategies, and the constant juggling with ever tighter budgets, failed. She was forced to go to a food bank for the first time in years to make end meet. It’s hard, she reflects, and the stress can affect her mental health. “When I’m tired or hungry or whatever, that then has an impact on me, the way I parent. I’ve got no energy sometimes … It’s difficult.” Hundreds of thousands of low-income households are feeling the same pressures, said Trussell, the food bank network. Unless the government links LHA more closely to actual rents, it added, many more will be forced to turn to charity food. The growing gap between LHA rates and local rents means more than half (62%) of private renters receiving housing support have gone without food and heating in the past six months because they could not afford them, Trussell estimated. The gap is expected to reach record levels this autumn. According to the Resolution Foundation thinktank, the average difference between rent and LHA faced by a low-income household renting a two-bedroom home in the private sector is £158 a month – rising to as much as £324 a month in parts of London. Trussell wants the government to relink LHA to the cheapest 30% of local rents. It estimates this would lift 105,000 people out of severe hardship by 2028-29, including 40,000 children. The Resolution Foundation estimates this would cost £2bn a year. Campaigners will focus on the LHA gap – the consequence of years of austerity and rising private rents – in the run-up to next month’s budget, arguing it is an effective way to give low-income families “breathing space” from cost of living pressures. Beatrice Orchard, the head of policy at Trussell, said: “Nobody should be forced to choose between paying the rent and putting food on the table. But for increasing numbers of UK renters, this is already a bleak reality. Keeping LHA frozen while rents rise is driving people to food banks.” Governments have often been reluctant to match rents and housing support, fearing landlords will simply put up rents, or that tenants will move to plusher rented homes. Braddock, who fears that her landlord is preparing to put up her rent, tightening her budget even further, disagrees: “If the local housing allowance matched the going rate for a two-bedroom or a one-bedroom [place] then people don’t need to move. It’ll just mean they don’t struggle to get through the month, because the rent’s being paid. “I don’t think the government understands … From a parent’s point of view, you’ve got to think about keeping your kids safe and your kids warm. And they wonder why there’s an epidemic of mental health [concerns]”. A spokesperson for the Department for Work and Pensions said: “We’re tackling the impact of rising rents and the housing shortage with our commitment to build 1.5m homes – including the biggest boost to social and affordable housing in a generation. “Local housing allowance rates are reviewed annually, and future decisions will be taken in the context of the government’s welfare priorities, and the fiscal context.”

title: England’s mayors should face greater scrutiny as powers expand, thinktank says
summary: IPPR North says one bad decision could derail devolution agenda as regions gain control of billions in funding
text: England’s mayors should face much greater official scrutiny to avoid Andy Burnham’s devolution agenda being “derailed by one bad decision”, a thinktank has said. Ministers will set out plans next month to give regional leaders control over potentially billions of pounds of additional funding under a “transformational” shift of power outside Whitehall. From 2028, mayors will be able to keep a share of income tax generated in their areas – giving them greater scope to borrow for major infrastructure projects – as well as retain business rates from 2027 and raise further funds through a “tourist tax”. IPPR North, whose researchers have worked closely with Burnham’s government, welcomed the “bold and ambitious” plans as a step towards “reversing decades of damaging over-centralisation that has held the country back”. It called for mayors to be allowed to keep a 5% share of income tax, which would move an extra £3.8bn a year out of Whitehall and roughly double the funding under their control. However, the thinktank said increasingly powerful mayors should be subject to much tougher oversight. In its 30-page report, IPPR North warned: “A bad decision or mismanaged funding from any one authority risks turning public opinion against devolution and undoing progress.” Its proposals include establishing new regional audit offices to scrutinise how money is spent and what it delivers. It is also proposed that each region should be overseen by a senior accounting officer, similar to the model of permanent secretaries running government departments. Larger mayoral authorities, such as London, Greater Manchester and the West Midlands, should be overseen by beefed-up accountability committees to guard against any “misuse of funds, corruption and elite capture by lobbying interests”, the thinktank said. Burnham, a former Greater Manchester mayor, has placed the transfer of power outside Whitehall at the heart of his government, establishing No 10 North in Manchester to act as the engine room of rapid devolution. Proposals outlined in a Cabinet Office paper in July, weeks after Burnham became prime minister, would represent the most dramatic shift of authority to the English regions in modern times. There are concerns, however, about the capacity of newer and smaller combined authorities to take on these expanded powers, which include employment support, local transport, housing, innovation, local energy and cultural investment. While some mayoral authorities are well established, others, such as the Reform UK-led bodies in Hull and East Yorkshire and Greater Lincolnshire, were only founded last year. Several other planned mayoral authorities, spanning millions of people along the south coast and in north-west England, have not yet been established. Ministers are due to set out a timeline for fiscal devolution to the English regions in a white paper to be published alongside the autumn budget on 28 October. Aditi Sriram, the lead author of the IPPR North report, said Britain was at a “defining moment” in how it is governed and that accountability was essential to the success of devolution. “For too long, mayors have been expected to drive growth with one hand tied behind their backs, reliant on Whitehall for the money and permission to get things done,” she said. “Critics are loud, political trust is faltering, and the public wants to see action, so the devolution agenda cannot afford to fail.” Jim O’Neill, the former Treasury minister who advised Burnham before he became prime minister, said in a foreword to the report that critics would dismiss devolution as an “irrelevance and a probable source of wasted taxpayers’ money”. But he said the best answer to those “cynics” would be to hand mayors of the most populated areas the greatest powers. “This is assuming they have the capacity to cope, the desire to be accountable and, of course, just like Greater Manchester has had, the aspiration to be bold,” he said.

title: US supreme court declines to intervene in custody fight over baby born via surrogate
summary: Surrogate who rejected abortion request had asked justices to halt court order recognizing LA couple as legal parents
text: The supreme court has refused to get involved with a custody dispute between an Alaska surrogate and a California couple whose child was born with a rare and serious heart defect. On Tuesday, Justice Elena Kagan denied an emergency request from McKenna West, an Alaska nurse and surrogate who had asked the US’s highest court to halt a California court order recognizing the couple, Omar Ahmed and Nausheen Gilkar, as the boy’s legal parents. In recent weeks, the case has garnered nationwide attention, sparking broader discussions about surrogacy and abortion. In a 9 September filing, West’s attorneys urged the supreme court to intervene in what they described as “extraordinary circumstances”, arguing that “a life hangs in the balance”. After a scan that discovered the baby having hypoplastic left heart syndrome, a condition that impedes blood flow and requires extensive surgery, Ahmed and Gilkar asked West to abort the pregnancy. According to NBC, the couple signed a contract last August with West that included a clause stating that the pregnancy could be terminated in the case of a “fetal abnormality”. However, West refused to terminate the pregnancy and instead traveled to Texas, where abortion is illegal, to give birth. Republican attorney general Ken Paxton intervened, shining a national spotlight on the case. A Dallas judge subsequently issued an order requiring the baby to receive medical care. Kagan’s refusal to intervene comes just days after the Texas supreme court ruled that the month-old child can leave Texas and relocate to a Los Angeles hospital for treatment. “Sustaining the life of the medically fragile child is the paramount concern in this time-sensitive matter,” the court said. West has since argued for custody of the child, claiming that his legal parents will not provide the necessary medical care because they had previously sought an abortion. West’s attorneys say that because their client “is now completely excluded from the life of the medically fragile infant she brought into the world, much less from the ability to make critical health decisions that protect him, time is of the essence”. In West’s filing to the supreme court, her lawyers argued that “without relief, she will receive no further information about the child she carried for 37 weeks and fought to save”. During a court hearing in Dallas last month, the child’s parents said West was “unstable”. Gilkar added: “He’s our child … He’s the most beautiful person I’ve never seen … He’s the love of our lives. He’s suffering a lot.”

title: Kamala Harris returns to Michigan to campaign for Abdul El-Sayed for Senate
summary: Former VP, who lost state to Trump in 2024 elections, is lending her popularity to unite fractured party
text: Kamala Harris returned to Michigan on Tuesday to campaign for Abdul El-Sayed, lending her popularity among Black voters to a progressive Senate nominee still working to unite a party fractured by a bruising primary – and the former vice-president’s loss to Donald Trump in the state. Appearing with El-Sayed at a Detroit birth center, Harris used a roundtable on Black maternal health to frame that November’s contest against the Republican Mike Rogers as a fight over women’s access to care. “Medicaid is the largest funder for maternity care in America. Donald Trump cut Medicaid funding by a trillion dollars,” she said, hammering Rogers for his support of the president’s agenda. Harris also criticized the Trump administration for halting federal research funding it classified as diversity-related, including studies of fibroids, and said the Senate should act as a check on the White House. “The United States Senate should be a stopgap on the abuses of this administration and I would suggest to you that the fellow sitting to my right would be one of them when elected,” Harris said, nodding to El-Sayed. The crowd murmured in agreement. El-Sayed, a physician, thanked Harris for “uplifting the issues that we are here to talk about today”, noting his gratitude for her work on them. The Senate seat is open following the retirement of the Democratic senator Gary Peters, and holding it is a must for the party’s path to a Senate majority. But even with a win in Michigan, Democrats would need to flip at least four Republican-held seats to control the chamber for Trump’s final two years in office. El-Sayed, who backs universal healthcare and sits to the left of his party’s leadership, narrowly defeated the congresswoman Haley Stevens in August, following a bitter primary that divided key constituencies. Black voters in Detroit, the backbone of the Democratic coalition in the state, tended to favor Stevens, and Rogers has also been courting them in the city. The joint appearance also papers over a rift between the Democrats. El-Sayed has called Israel’s military campaign in Gaza a genocide, a sharp break from the Biden-Harris administration’s military support for Israel, but a position that puts him in step with a growing share of the electorate. A Quinnipiac University poll released this month found 38% of voters more sympathetic to Palestinians and 35% to Israelis, the highest share siding with the Palestinians since the university began asking the question in December 2001. In Michigan, home to a large Arab American community, that shift has already shown up at the ballot box, and El-Sayed was part of it. In 2024, he backed the “uncommitted” movement, which urged Democrats to withhold their primary votes from Joe Biden in protest at US military aid to Israel. He endorsed Harris when she replaced Biden as the nominee later that year. Many of the movement’s supporters did not follow him and the state narrowly went to Trump. The trip also comes amid speculation about Harris’s own political ambitions, as she mulls whether to run again for the White House. Michigan is set to hold the fifth contest on the Democrats’ revised 2028 primary calendar and Harris has further campaign stops planned in Nevada and Georgia. Closing her remarks, Harris urged the room to remind voters “that they have power and voice in the outcome of this election, which will directly impact their lives in many ways”.

title: Spain allows US extradition case against pro-Palestine aid donor to proceed
summary: Lawyers for James ‘Fergie’ Chambers, wanted over alleged support for Hamas, say client is being persecuted
text: The Spanish government has decided to allow the Trump administration’s controversial extradition request to extradite wealthy activist James “Fergie” Chambers to continue in the country’s courts. Chambers, a US citizen and wealthy donor to leftwing and humanitarian projects, is now imprisoned in Madrid. It is the first known case of the US seeking to extradite a citizen over alleged support for Hamas, an accusation tied to money Chambers has donated to support Palestinians, including the Sameer Project, in Gaza. His legal defense team, an array of Spanish parliamentarians, and some celebrity supporters have publicly opposed the request, calling it political persecution, which would render it illegitimate under Spanish law. The 22-member council of ministers could have rejected the US petition outright on Tuesday but instead opted to remand the request to the Spanish justice system, beginning a legal process that could now take months. Meanwhile, Chambers has begun the process from prison of applying for asylum in Spain – which by law makes it impossible for the country to extradite him until the process is concluded, according to attorney Aitor Martínez, part of Chambers’s legal team. The attorney also told the Guardian that a third request to allow his client to be released on bond while his situation is resolved awaits a judge’s decision, after previous requests have been denied since Spanish police detained him in Ibiza on 10 July. Elma Saiz, minister of inclusion, social security and migration, devoted less than a minute to announcing Tuesday’s council decision to the Spanish press, calling it “purely procedural”. Details from the weekly meetings are not public, but sources close to the council told the Guardian: “There was debate, and five ministers from Sumar – including the vice-president – pushed back in the meeting.” Sumar, a leftwing coalition, governs jointly with Spanish prime minister Pedro Sánchez’s Socialist party. Sánchez’s government has repeatedly expressed support for the Palestinian people, putting him at odds with the Trump administration. Baltasar Garzón, the international human rights lawyer leading Chambers’ legal team, said that Tuesday’s decision “sets a dangerous precedent regarding the defense of the Palestinian cause”. “Spain cannot defend international law, the rights of the Palestinian people and the protection of those who provide humanitarian aid while at the same time allowing a request to proceed with an extradition that shows clear signs of political persecution by the US government, as it is directed against an individual because of his political activity and solidarity with Palestine.” Ione Belarra, secretary-general of Podemos – a progressive party also vital to Sánchez’s interests – said the government “has chosen to keep [Chambers] imprisoned by giving the green light for Trump’s political persecution to proceed to the courts”. Belarra appeared in parliament on Tuesday afternoon wearing a T-shirt that said “Free Fergie”. She also noted that Spain must hold a general election by August, and said many of her colleagues in Spain’s Congress “are deeply concerned that by the time Fergie Chambers’ case has gone through the judicial process … Spain could have a more conservative, pro-Israel government”. The possibility of Chambers being extradited “risks opening the floodgates to Trump’s repression reaching into Spain and the rest of Europe and targeting other progressives”, Belarra said. The US government’s case centers on Chambers allegedly laundering $7.5m he wired several years ago from a US bank account to Tunisia, where he lived at the time, and allegedly using the money to support Hamas. His partner, activist and actor Stella Schnabel, told the Guardian last month that the $7.5m went to support Club Africain, a Tunisian football club, paying off debt and past-due salaries as well as rebuilding a training center and building youth football fields. The self-described anti–imperialist’s defense is also asserting that the Trump administration’s charges of “international money laundering” do not hold up because, as heir to one of the richest families in the US, he obtained his personal wealth through legal means. His money comes from a mid-2023 settlement with his family, owners of Atlanta-based Cox Communications, in which he sold them stock worth about $250m. Members of his family severed contact with him at the time and his donations have gone to about 100 projects in 20 countries. Chambers’s views and donations have been extensively profiled in US media. He was interviewed on a TV news station in New Hampshire in late 2023 about a direct action against Elbit Systems, an Israeli defense contractor, staged by a group whose legal fees he paid, then called Palestine Action – a group now proscribed in the UK as a “terrorist organization”. Sealed charges against Chambers were originally filed in New Hampshire. Chambers’s public comments on Israel and Gaza have previously brought controversy. A week after the 7 October 2023 Hamas attacks on Israel, he posted on X about Israel’s response: “Stop calling it ‘collective punishment’ / There’s nothing to be ‘punished’ for / No faction of the Palestinian resistance, Hamas or other, has done *anything* wrong / It’s simply genocide / Like it has been.” He has also been a staunch critic of the US, telling a reporter in 2024: “I think the most important thing for the prosperity of humanity is the destruction of the US.” “I am heartbroken,” Schnabel told the Guardian. The two have a young son and Schnabel is just over three months pregnant. “Fergie could spend the first year of our baby’s life unable to hold them, seeing them only through a pane of glass – even though he has not been convicted of any crime,” she said.

title: US coast guard suspends search for man who reportedly jumped off cruise ship
summary: Agency says it scoured 1,707 sq miles between California and Mexico with no sighting of Tom Gigler
text: The US coast guard has suspended its search for the 56-year-old man who reportedly jumped off a Carnival cruise ship on Saturday. “Decisions to suspend search operations are never easy and are made with careful consideration of all available information. Our hearts are with those impacted by his loss,” said Jessica Davila, chief of incident management for the coast guard south-west district. The agency said it had scoured more than 1,707 sq miles for roughly 41 hours with no sighting of Tom Gigler. The circumstances leading up to the jump remain unclear. Gigler was last seen on Friday evening. By 1.30pm on Saturday, he had been reported missing, according to the agency. Camera footage capturing Gigler going overboard was later reviewed. The Panorama sailed from Long Beach, California, to Puerto Vallarta, Mexico, on 13 September. The vessel was returning from the coastal Mexican resort town when the incident occurred on Saturday. Misty Hernandez, who was aboard the cruise ship, noticed it had reversed direction and was heading back toward Puerto Vallarta. The peculiar about-face came as the intercom system was used to repeat Gigler’s name a few times throughout the morning. “You heard it one time and you’re thinking: ‘Oh, it’s almost the last day. Maybe he has an outstanding bill.’ But when you hear it more than three times, you knew that something was going on,” Hernandez said. The cruise’s passengers were later instructed to return to their rooms for a headcount and were informed of a missing-person search, according to a video shared with the Guardian. The order was lifted hours later when the captain delivered the news of a person having gone overboard. As passengers trickled out of their cabins, Hernandez said, the previously bustling and loud atmosphere turned quiet. She prayed with some women she encountered in a hallway. By evening, fellow passengers had written messages about the missing traveler on a piece of posterboard. Hernandez said she briefly met the man believed to have gone overboard in an elevator with his wife and children. “They had mentioned that it was their anniversary trip,” she said. “My heart just hurts for their family.” In a statement early this week, a Carnival spokesperson said they were providing support to Gigler’s family. “Our thoughts and prayers are with them and their loved ones.”

title: Patrick Clancy interview on 60 Minutes fails to provide big ratings boost for CBS
summary: Amid major overhaul by Bari Weiss, Sunday’s episode draws third-smallest audience for second episode in past 25 years
text: 60 Minutes’ blockbuster interview with Patrick Clancy, the ex-husband of Lindsay Clancy, failed to provide a major ratings boost for the Sunday show, according to audience figures released on Tuesday. Sunday night’s episode of the newsmagazine show drew an average of 6.77 million total viewers, the third-smallest audience in the past 25 years for the second episode of a season, adding to a disappointing debut for Bari Weiss, who, as CBS editor-in-chief, rewired the show, firing several high-profile correspondents in the run-up to the new season. The 59th season debuted on 13 September with an audience down sharply from the 58th season debut, drawing 7.94 million viewers compared with 10 million for last season’s first episode. That episode was the show’s lowest-rated season debut in the 21st century, though CBS News touted it as the most-watched non-sports program of the week and released a statement expressing satisfaction with the content of the program. “We are so proud of the exceptional journalism on display in our season premiere and we can’t wait to bring our audience another amazing show this coming Sunday,” the network said last week. The 20 September episode of the show barely edged last season’s second episode (6.45 million viewers), and it was likely hurt by not having NFL football as a lead-in program in all markets. But it featured what should have been an audience-boosting interview, with new correspondent Ross Douthat sitting down with Patrick Clancy, who described the killings of his children and the aftermath. Clancy’s new wife, fertility doctor Rachel Danis, also gave a brief interview. In a nod to the interview’s cultural significance and importance for the show, Weiss was in attendance for the conversation, sources said. The show also featured a timely segment on pushback against datacenters reported by correspondent Norah O’Donnell, along with a whodunnit piece from longtime sports-focused correspondent Jon Wertheim about Shergar, an Irish racehorse kidnapped in the 1980s. While Douthat’s interview with Clancy received generally favorable reviews, it evidently was not the ratings draw that CBS News executives had hoped. The show’s debut episode had also featured a blockbuster interview, with one of the American fighter pilots shot down over Iran in April. The Guardian has reached out to CBS News about Sunday’s ratings. On a positive note for the network, the episode attracted 179.2m social views, surpassing last week’s record of 116.7m views.

title: Iran and US have held talks on sidelines of UN summit, says Donald Trump
summary: Senior Iranian official indicates willingness to reopen strait of Hormuz if US takes steps to ease pressure on Tehran
text: Iranian officials held three hours of talks with US special envoy Steve Witkoff on the sidelines of the UN general assembly, Donald Trump disclosed on Tuesday. He said there would a further meeting in the very near future. Witkoff said he felt very good about the meeting, the first such contact since the US vice-president, JD Vance, met an Iranian delegation to agree a memorandum of understanding in Switzerland in June. Iranian officials confirmed the meeting with Witkoff involved its foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, and was mediated by diplomats from Qatar. A senior Iranian official also indicated that the country was prepared to reopen the strait of Hormuz within a week, as long as the US took reciprocal steps to ease the military and economic pressure it is applying on Iran. Previously, Iran had set seven onerous preconditions for lifting its blockade on the strait, one of the world’s key oil shipping routes, including an end to the US war “on all fronts” and a commitment by the US to end all aggressive actions against Iran, including sanctions. The new position, revealed amid frantic backstage negotiations at the UN general assembly in New York and set out by an Iranian official in Tehran to the Japanese news agency Kyodo and then to Reuters, would involve relaxing some of those preconditions. The official claimed the position had been approved by Iran’s supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, and the country’s supreme national security council, although some Iranian media close to the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) denied any new position had been adopted, reflecting disputes in Tehran. Diplomats had been testing the ground for possible talks between the US and Iran, with Qatar’s diplomats in talks with Araghchi. A meeting between Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, and Trump had largely been ruled out as too combustible, however. Pezeshkian is due on Wednesday to address the UN general assembly, where most of the Iranian delegation left the hall during Trump’s speech on Tuesday after he described Iran as the bully of the Middle East and the number one terror organisation on Earth. But earlier, the IRGC issued a statement that said there was no contradiction between staging negotiations and waging war at the same time, a position echoed by Iran’s chief negotiator, Mohammad Ghalibaf, in recent remarks delivered online to the Iranian parliament. The official said Iran was seeking signs from Washington that it was prepared to return to negotiations and take steps toward ending its military blockade of Iranian ports and halting military operations related to the strait of Hormuz. In that case, Iran was prepared to reopen the strategic waterway within seven days and return to the negotiating table, according to the official. Such preconditions are less stringent than those issued by other senior Iranian figures in the previous 48 hours. Experience has shown that initially appealing Iranian offers can emerge to be more complex once the small print is revealed, and there is a barely disguised tussle being played out in Tehran between hardliners and figures like Pezeshkian over the value of any talks. Resolving these disputes is not made easier by the low profile kept by the supreme leader, normally the arbiter in such internal ructions. Trump, in his remarks to the general assembly, said he had a big decision to make: whether to annihilate Iran, or to help it become a great country. “Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations?” he asked, adding he expected Iran to make a deal immediately after the US midterm elections. “There are two options; one could be a very bad thing, and the other could lead to greatness and progress for this country. Therefore, I think they want to do this.” Overall, his demeanour, and the mixed signals out of Tehran, suggest the two sides are still too far apart to reach a deal, which would have to start with agreement between Iran and Oman on a new route for commercial shipping in the strait of Hormuz that largely goes through Iranian waters. The Gulf states have not endorsed such a deal. Saudi Arabia also wanted to be a signatory and authoriser of the route, but Iran insisted it had to be endorsed only by the two countries in which the strait’s waterways pass – Iran and Oman. Tehran is also under growing pressure as the US blockade of its oil exports plays havoc with its currency reserves and domestic inflation. In his speech, Trump called on other countries to isolate Iran economically, including by demanding that all nations prevent any Iranian civilian planes from landing at their airports. US diplomats have warned Turkey and Iraq to comply or face sanctions. Many of the Gulf states were also planning to urge Trump to do more to press Israel to meet its commitments under the six-month-old peace plan to withdraw from Gaza. The Turkish president, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, prompted a walkout by the Israeli delegation when he described Gaza as “the world’s largest graveyard and the most inhumane and shameful concentration camp of our time”. He added: “Israel refuses to stop the occupation. We are faced with a genocidal mindset that can never get enough of killing. No one with a sense of humanity, mercy or compassion, no one guided by justice and conscience, can possibly remain indifferent to this picture.” Jordan’s King Abdullah, in his address, claimed: “With Israel, resolutions end where they began on paper. This result is a state without restraint. This government’s sense of impunity has reached terrifying levels. It no longer feels compelled to ask: ‘Can we get away with this?’ It already knows the answer.” He added that what was unfolding across the occupied West Bank was not a series of isolated acts but rather “elements of a single policy to compel an entire population to leave their land. And there is a name for that: forced displacement. And that is a war crime.” A statement from eight Gulf foreign ministers also called on Israel to immediately fulfil its outstanding commitments under the first phase of the Gaza ceasefire agreement, including by ensuring the immediate, safe and unhindered delivery of humanitarian assistance and early recovery supplies, and facilitating the rehabilitation of critical infrastructure. The ministers reiterated their categorical rejection of any measures aimed at the expulsion or the forced displacement of the Palestinian people from their homeland or attempts to alter the territorial or demographic character of the occupied Palestinian territory.

title: Outgoing UN chief says polluters have treated atmosphere like an ‘open sewer’
summary: António Guterres laments world leaders’ inaction and says oil and gas firms ‘must pay’ for climate devastation
text: For one last time, António Guterres tried to fix the world’s gaze upon the dangerously escalating climate crisis. But the departing UN secretary general found world leaders still largely focused on other issues, even after a painful summer of stunning climate-driven disasters. Speaking to assembled dignitaries at the UN on Tuesday, Guterres railed against big oil for treating “the atmosphere as an open sewer” and warned again of the catastrophic effects of the climate crisis. Guterres said: “Three years ago, in the mountains of Nepal, I sounded the alarm on accelerating glacier melt, warning that the rooftops of the world are caving in. Some dismissed it all as overstating dangers. “But as tragic events have shown, impacts are arriving sooner, hitting harder and spreading further than many anticipated.” The UN chief said: “Those who polluted the most – and profited the most – must do far more to repair the damage they caused. Polluters must pay. And to the leaders, cities, civil society and citizens working to hold them accountable – you are on the right side of history. Keep going.” Guterres has been an unflinching advocate for climate action in his nine years as UN secretary-general, and his departure from the role is set to leave a void in a geopolitical landscape consumed by wars, inflation fears and other economic concerns rather than our rapidly heating planet. “António Guterres has been the most climate-forward secretary-general in UN history; and this speech shows why,” said Alden Meyer, a veteran climate policy expert at E3G. “He clearly laid out the stakes on the climate emergency – the horrific consequences of inaction and the tremendous opportunities in deploying the available solutions.” This summer has been roiled by record heatwaves and wildfires across the US and Europe, as well as a catastrophic glacier collapse and landslide on the Nepal-Tibet border. A mounting El Nino event, perhaps the largest in modern human history, is meanwhile set to push global temperatures to new record highs and spur a spike in food insecurity. Yet the climate crisis has slipped from the agenda to the extent it has been little surprise that this week’s UN general assembly is not expected to bear any major new commitments to slash planet-heating emissions or to accelerate the rollout of a clean energy sector that is, while growing, still not on pace to avert further dangerous temperature rises. Even Climate Week, an array of events across New York that overlaps with the UN gathering, is not expected to deliver any major announcements. While a record number of people – more than 100,000 – are set to attend Climate Week events, organizers have lamented an outbreak of “climate hushing” among political and business leaders who have determined the public has tuned out of the planetary emergency. Donald Trump, who has dismantled environmental policies in the US and repeatedly called climate science a “hoax”, has been a major factor in this, even though his UN speech this year dwelled less on the topic than last year’s incendiary version. But those who advocate for action said there was broader blame to be cast upon the complacency of other leaders who have failed to ensure the world does not blow past previously agreed temperature thresholds. There is still widespread public alarm about the climate crisis, polling shows, despite the disconnect by political leaders. “We are in a terrible spot. That is the truth, because hypocrisy has won over concrete action,” said Juan Carlos Navarro, environment minister of Panama, who is pushing for a universal declaration of the rights of nature at the UN this week. “As to the international arena, it’s a terrible situation. Look at the signs. A war in Iran … the other sign that we have is this forthcoming El Nino. So do we need more signs? No, it’s terrible. But what are people doing? Nothing.” While Panama has acted strongly to cut its own emissions, other countries are failing, Navarro argued. “The war in Iran, the El Nino – has it had any impact in terms of countries or political leaders stepping up with bold commitments for real change? Zero,” he said. “All I see around me is hypocrisy, BS, beautiful speeches, zero action. Let’s start telling the truth and start telling the truth to our own citizens. We’re facing climate change and it will have an impact and we’re not doing enough to alter it.” The rays of optimism at Climate Week so far have centered on relief over the fact Trump is set to become a lame-duck president and also the continuing growth of renewables such as solar and wind. “Climate” may have become a taboo term for some, but investment in clean energy, particularly in China, is booming. “The economy is built on batteries and the sun in California, which we know is cheaper,” said Gavin Newsom, the governor of California and potential Democratic candidate for the next presidential election. “You can bottle the sun, you can catch the wind, you don’t have to worry about the sun getting blockaded in the strait of Hormuz. It gets cheaper and cheaper, in the abundance.” Much of this progress is still being overshadowed, Newsom conceded, by Trump. “He’s trying to take us back to the 19th century,” Newsom said of the president. “He’s doubling down on stupid.”

title: Another Florida Republican distances himself from Donald Trump before midterms
summary: GOP nominee for governor Byron Donalds removes multiple mentions of president from his campaign website
text: Another prominent Florida Republican has publicly distanced himself from Donald Trump, days after María Elvira Salazar called out the US president’s immigration-enforcement policy targeting law-abiding undocumented immigrants. Byron Donalds, the Republican nominee for governor in November’s US midterm elections, launched an updated campaign website on Tuesday that was stripped of almost every mention of Trump and removed a photograph of the congressman and his wife, Erika, posing with the president, the Miami Herald reported. Until now, Donalds has proudly touted his close ties with the president, running a Republican primary campaign themed largely on Trump’s endorsement, and displaying a large banner on his website advertising his support. The move comes as Trump’s overall approval rating fell below 30% for the first time, dragged down by dissatisfaction over his handling of the US economy and the Iran war, and Republicans brace for heavy losses in November, including the possible loss of the party’s majorities in the US House of Representatives and Senate. On Tuesday, Sabato’s Crystal Ball, a top election prognosticator, moved the open Florida governor’s race from “likely Republican” to “leans Republican”. “The GOP is still favored in both, but close polling, a bad political environment, and possible exhaustion with long periods of Republican leadership may make both of these races fairly close,” the report’s author, Kyle Kondik, wrote. The Herald’s reporting was based on research by the website tracking service Visualping, which recorded multiple changes to the Donalds site, including the removal of at least eight mentions of Trump from its homepage. Prior to the alterations, Donalds described himself as a “Trump-endorsed proven conservative fighter”, while other since-removed banners featured a “chip in to support Trump-endorsed Byron Donalds” fundraiser and one of Trump’s “run, Byron, run” endorsement announcements from last year. A previous capture by Wayback Machine of the Donalds website’s list of issues features “Enact the Trump agenda” as his number one priority; that has now disappeared, replaced by “affordability”. The only reference to Trump that still appears is his name among a rolling list of endorsements for Donalds by other conservative and rightwing figures, including Elon Musk, Rick Scott, Mike Johnson and the late Charlie Kirk. In a statement, the Donalds campaign said: “Our campaign website reflects Byron’s focus on the issues that matter most to Floridians – affordability, insurance costs and government transparency. He’s running to be the next Governor of Florida, is proud to have President Trump’s endorsement, and has real policy proposals to tackle those issues.” Trump is “still all over the website”, a Donalds campaign official claimed. Donalds clinched the Republican nomination for the election to succeed Florida’s incumbent governor, Ron DeSantis, in August. He has represented south-west Florida in Congress since 2021. Politico reported on Monday that multiple Republican candidates in numerous November races are breaking with Trump, with mail-in ballots already sent out in some states and barely 40 days until 3 November. “These candidates know how to read a poll,” a GOP strategist told the outlet. “They know he is kryptonite.” In a statement, the Florida Democratic party called the purge “trouble in paradise” for Republicans. “Florida voted for Donald Trump by 13 points two years ago. Now, Byron Donalds is pretending he’s never met the guy because he knows it’s his only shot at winning,” spokesperson Evan Ecklund said. “Byron is desperately trying to go no-contact. “But Floridians know the truth: Byron Donalds has been Trump’s right-hand man throughout his disastrous presidency, and a phony last-minute breakup won’t change that.”

title: Hats, pencils and baby pacifiers: Yellowstone staffers retrieve record amount of trash from hot springs
summary: The park is the most highly visited and high winds make trash problem worse, with gusts blowing away items
text: Hold on to your hats – Yellowstone national park staffers have removed a record-setting 20,100 pieces of trash from hydrothermal areas around the geyser-filled park so far this year. The most commonly found items include 280 hats, 54 camera lens caps, 47 hair ties, 42 pencils, 36 pairs of sunglasses, 20 hotel key cards and 17 baby pacifiers. “The issue is made worse by the park’s high winds: unexpected gusts easily blow away tissues, maps, food wrappers, and even heavier items like sunglasses and hats!” Margery Price, a physical science technician with the Yellowstone national park geology program, said in a blog post for the US Geological Survey. That, and park visitors treating the hot springs like wishing wells. The Yellowstone geology team collected more than $18 in coins during summer 2026, in currencies ranging from the dollar and pesos to yen and euros. With more than 4.5 million visitors annually, Yellowstone is one of the most highly visited national parks in the United States. “No matter the type of debris, it needs to be removed. Foreign material of any kind can damage or permanently alter a hydrothermal feature, whether from clogging its water supply, blocking or diverting its runoff channel, or polluting it with chemicals and sediment,” Price said. In the 1900s, the park’s Morning Glory Pool changed color from all of the trash visitors were leaving in the pool, which was nicknamed “trash can” by the 1950s. This year, the park’s geological staff retrieved six Invisalign retainers, eight mini race cars, three golf tees and 15 fake nails. While the park’s staff understands that much of that trash gets swept away by accident, they encourage visitors to “stash your trash” when visiting Yellowstone. That is, packing wrappers, tissues and even hats carefully away in windy areas. At the end of the season though, they’ll be sure to wash and donate all of the hats left behind.

title: Trump made over 1,000 July stock trades worth up to $270m, filings reveal
summary: President made more than 440 purchases and 700 sales despite voter anger over elected officials trading stocks
text: Donald Trump made more than a thousand stock sales and purchases worth between $79m and $270m in July, according to a Guardian analysis of his latest financial disclosure released Tuesday. His two largest sales were of Amazon and Microsoft stock, selling between $5m and $25m each on 20 July. That same day, he also sold up to $5m worth of Oracle and Costco stock, sold from $500,000 to $1m in Nvidia, and bought up to $5m worth of shares in Intuit and Salesforce, among dozens of other transactions. Overall, he made more than 700 sales that totaled between $35m and $137m, and made more than 440 purchases that totaled between $43.5m and $134m. Financial disclosures, which presidents and vice-presidents are required to file by law, only include a date and a range of the transaction amount. The White House said Trump’s stock and bond portfolio was “independently managed by third-party financial institutions” and that there were no conflicts of interests in the latest disclosure. “All holdings are maintained in discretionary accounts and invested through computer-based model portfolios that automatically replicate recognized indexes, such as the Schwab 1000,” said Davis Ingle, a White House spokesperson. “Neither President Trump nor any member of his family has any ability to direct, influence, or provide input regarding how the portfolio is invested or when investments are bought or sold. All investment decisions are made entirely by independent managers.” The July disclosure comes as Trump and the Republican party continue to champion a ban on stock trading among members of Congress, which would exclude him from any restrictions. The president made more trades than all of Congress combined between the start of his second term and June, a Bloomberg analysis found. Trump’s last annual financial disclosures revealed that he made more than $2.2bn last year from his network of businesses and investments, including $1bn in crypto revenue. Disclosures from his staff have also revealed large $45,000 cash gifts to three White House officials, including his close personal aide, Natalie Harp, which sparked calls from watchdog groups for further investigation. Trump also made up to $15.5m from his investments into oil and gas companies, the Senate’s joint economic committee found, because of gas prices driven up by the US war with Iran. The president, vice-president and members of Congress are legally allowed to trade stocks and are required to disclose their trades within 45 days of a transaction. But the practice is widely unpopular with voters. A recent survey from the Economist and YouGov found that about 75% of respondents, which included majorities of Democrats and Republicans, believed that elected officials should not be allowed to buy and sell individual stocks in public office. The Trump-endorsed Stop Insider Trading Act, passed by the House of Representatives in July, would prohibit lawmakers and their families from purchasing publicly traded stocks. The ban, however, would not affect Trump or JD Vance.

title: Trump praises Burnham despite tensions over AI, Chagos Islands and Iran
summary: US president calls UK prime minister ‘a natural businessperson’ as leaders meet at UN assembly in New York
text: Donald Trump has asserted his relationship with the UK is “more up” with Andy Burnham than under Keir Starmer despite tensions between the two countries on a range of thorny issues including regulation of artificial intelligence, the Chagos Islands and the war in Iran. At their first face-to-face meeting, the US president praised Burnham, who sat nervously alongside him, as a “natural businessperson”, saying he thought he had “lots of assets on his side” and would be a “great” prime minister. Burnham, who was joined in the talks by Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary, and Jonathan Powell, his national security adviser, said he and Trump had built on the “good connection” they established early on, in an effort to shore up relations which had splintered over Iran. UK officials reacted with relief that the talks appeared to have gone according to plan. But despite the warm words at the UN general assembly in New York, there were still signs of difficulties ahead. On his way to the US, Burnham had revealed he would urge the US president to de-escalate the Iran conflict, with turmoil in the Middle East pushing up global energy prices, putting the UK economy under intense pressure. Much of the summit has been dominated by geopolitical turbulence, with Trump using his speech to double down on his strategy. The president repeated his threat to “annihilate” Iran, adding he would “drive them into hell” if they did not back down and sign a peace deal with the US. Asked later whether he had any sympathy with allies which were feeling pain over the cost of living as a result of his actions, Trump claimed that “as soon as the war is over the prices are going to come way down”. Trump, who has suggested Iran could agree to a deal after the US midterms in November, said “people understand” the need to prevent Tehran obtaining a nuclear weapon, even if that meant price hikes at the petrol pumps and in shops. In his own UN speech, Burnham was expected to push for greater international control over AI. He revealed to business leaders that he wants a “single set of global principles and standards” to guard against rogue AI, saying the issue would be a main focus of the UK’s G20 presidency next year. But Burnham’s ambition for the UK to be an “honest broker” between countries in that could set him on a collision course with Trump, who has called warnings about AI’s existential threat to humanity a “hoax” and gave a defiant speech in which he intensified his criticism of attempts to regulate the emerging technology. “The United States also totally rejects any attempt to construct a globalist scheme to control for the artificial intelligence being spoken of so much now. We’re going to encourage it, not rein it in,” he said. “Americans have never been a nation that retreats from a frontier or shrinks from a challenge, no matter how great or how daunting that challenge may be … I’m ⁠not going to stifle growth of something that will be bigger than ‌the Industrial Revolution.” Burnham is also under pressure to sign up to an initiative being led by Finland and Norway – and backed by more than 20 countries – to bar AI companies from launching their models commercially without submitting them for safety testing first, amid growing concerns over the risks. In another schism between the two countries, Trump was scathing about the UK’s deal to give away sovereignty of the Chagos Islands to Mauritius, while paying for a lease of the military base of Diego Garcia. “I don’t support it. I think it’s terrible. It was a terrible deal. [Mauritius] all of a sudden say they have ownership. Somebody has ownership that never showed up before after decades and centuries. I think it’s ridiculous,” he said. But he suggested that Burnham may reconsider the deal. “It’s amazing how strategic it is, and I think the prime minister is going to be looking at it,” he said, to which the UK leader nodded and said “yeah”. However, Trump avoided commenting on the UK’s decision to ban trade with West Bank settlements, leaving it to the prime minister to answer the question. He is also understood to have agreed to a request from Burnham to bring up the case of imprisoned Hong Kong dissident Jimmy Lai in talks with China’s Xi Jinping on Thursday. British officials in the meeting suggested Lai could live in the UK. UK officials had been somewhat nervous about the meeting, as Trump had previously dismissed Burnham as “extremely liberal” and described the former mayor of Greater Manchester as the “mayor of a town”. However, his demeanour towards Burnham was mostly cordial. But it appeared to have gone to plan for both sides, with Trump praising US-UK relations, saying: “I think you’re up. Well, they’re more now than they were with your last prime minister, let me put it that way. “I think right now, based on my relationship with your prime minister, Andy, I think we’re doing very well.” Later in the press conference, Trump hit back at reporters questioning why he has banned some journalists from the White House, leading to a wider boycott by media organisations. The president claimed he had a “right to clean out fake news”. In his UN speech, Trump promised there would be peace between Ukraine and Russia “more quickly than people understand”. After talks with Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, he warned that Starmer’s rhetoric had been “too tough” towards Moscow and that London “needs to be a little bit careful”. Many of Trump’s talking points were contradicted, however, by the UN secretary-general António Guterres, who used his speech to warn about the consequences of international conflict, climate change and AI over the past decade. “Geopolitical divides have deepened. Inequalities have intensified. Trust has frayed. The climate crisis went from distant warning to daily reality. And artificial intelligence moved at a speed that has blindsided even those who created it,” he said. Without naming Israel, he added that what followed the Hamas attack of October 2023 “was an onslaught on Palestinians in Gaza, with a scale of killing and destruction unlike anything I have witnessed in all my years as secretary-general”.

title: Call it a win: boredom but no temper tantrums in Burnham’s first face-to-face with America’s King Baby
summary: Meeting at the UN in New York, the UK prime minister showed signs he can handle trash-talking President Trump
text: How do you deal with a problem like The Donald? The simple answer is that you don’t. You can’t. The normal rules of political engagement don’t apply. The US president is like a five-year-old child with the world as his set of toys: a King Baby. Nothing is ever constant or predictable. What’s agreed one day can be forgotten the next. Any deal can be interrupted with a temper tantrum at any time. Trying to second-guess Donald Trump is a fool’s errand. So the primary aim of Andy Burnham’s first face-to-face meeting with Trump was to get out alive with his – and the UK’s – self-respect intact. To take no incoming damage. And whatever he did, not to offer the president a third state visit. Keir Starmer never really lived that one down. Putting out on the first date only encourages the other person to think you’re a pushover. The hoped-for result was a pleasant and almost forgettable bilateral meeting at the United Nations general assembly in New York. It was only scheduled to last 30 minutes, so more like speed dating – one step up from two world leaders shooting the breeze while getting to know each other. Where differences could be acknowledged without causing a major diplomatic incident. All of which falls pretty comfortably within Burnham’s skill set. Andy’s stock in trade is an easy-going self-confidence. He’s comfortable in his skin in a way that Keir never was. Or maybe the artifice is just better concealed. He understands that trash-talking is all in a day’s work for most politicians. In the past, he may have called Trump all sorts of things. Poisoned politics. Someone who would be unwelcome in Manchester. Well, that was then, this is now. Things change. Just like Trump. Now he would be welcoming the US president to the G20 in Manchester next year. Who would have guessed? And it all looked to have gone pretty much to plan. Maybe Trump also wanted this meeting to go well. His poll ratings in the US are dire, the midterm elections look like trouble and The Donald needs all the friends he can get – even if he had just tried to lose a few more of them in his speech to the UN earlier. A speech that had been even wilder and madder than many of his previous ones. Still, at least he hadn’t threatened to invade a Nato country this time. And it’s always good to learn of countries you never knew existed. Anyone for “Kazakhistan”? Taking questions with Trump afterwards, Andy didn’t look quite as self-assured as usual – he seemed very much on edge – but who could blame him for that? This was his first time as prime minister at the UN and The Donald always has it in him to blow any meeting out of the water. It was Andy who went first, trying to remember what they had just talked about. It had all been a bit of a blur. That was it – they had talked about Iran. In his earlier speech, The Donald had suggested it was a toss-up whether he came to a deal with Iran or whether he annihilated it. On the whole, Andy was in favour of a deal. Quickly if possible. The war was causing a massive hit to the cost of living. He chose not to highlight the irony of Trump calling on Volodymyr Zelenskyy to stop bombing Russian refineries as it was playing havoc with the cost of oil. Pots and kettles and all that. Burnham then bigged up the deal with Saudi Arabia. The one where we send one plane to refuel Saudi fighters that don’t need refuelling because their targets are only a few hundred miles away. Finally, he mentioned the Falklands. By now The Donald was looking a wee bit bored. Unsure where the Falklands are or why they had been talking about them. Perhaps he was wondering why he was looking even more orange than usual. Then came the actual questions. Was Andy a man with whom Trump could do business? Sure he was, said The Donald. Andy was a “great businessperson”. Really? And by the way he was a lot nicer and a lot more talented than his predecessor. Poor Keir. Not only is he no longer prime minister, but he’s still getting rubbished at meetings he would have been attending. He really can’t buy a break. But that’s Trump for you. Andy shouldn’t relax too much. That will be him getting trashed one day. On we went. Immigration. Burnham deftly trying to give credit to the immigrants working in the NHS while going on to condemn illegal immigration. Trump was just dreaming of walls and border guards. What about patriotism? Which did the prime minister prefer: Manchester or Manhattan? By now Andy was feeling a bit more self-assured that the whole thing wasn’t about to go tits up, so he joked about the president calling Manchester “some town”. Trump just shrugged. It still is just some town to him, but he wasn’t going to labour the point. He was trying to be on his best behaviour. For a five-year-old. Then a question on the sanctions imposed on illegal settlements in the West Bank. Trump looked bewildered. Had never heard of them. Andy insisted he had personally called the White House to inform the president of the UK’s intentions. It had been done to maintain the possibility of a two-state solution and to restore trust in politics. This was more like the authentic Burnham. Standing up for what he believed. Trump said nothing. Maybe he actually did recognise the prime minister as an equal. There was just time for a mention of the proposed handover of the Chagos Islands – It’s a terrible idea,” said Trump unhelpfully, to which Andy gulped “We’re looking at it” – before we closed with Trump insisting relations with the UK had never been better and that Britain was a country on the up. Some of us could distinctly remember The Donald saying the UK was on the slide only last week. But who’s counting? Then a minder called the impromptu presser to a close and kicked everyone out of the room. Trump looked blank. He often does. Burnham looked relieved. He had got out of his first encounter with the president alive. Both he and the UK were still intact. Chalk this one up as a win.

title: Hurricane Polo, rapidly intensifying from strong El Niño patterns, rages off coast of Mexico
summary: Polo, with sustained winds of 165mph, is churning 215 miles south of Zihuatanejo but is unlikely to directly hit Mexico
text: A tropical storm off the south-west coast of Mexico has intensified into a category 5 monster in fewer than 24 hours, fueled by stronger than usual El Niño weather patterns in the Pacific Ocean. Hurricane Polo was sending out maximum sustained winds of 165mph (266km/h) on Tuesday as its center churned about 215 miles (346km) south of the coastal city of Zihuatanejo, in Guerrero state. On Monday, Polo was only a tropical storm with winds below 74mph (120km/h). Its rapid and sudden growth is testament to the dominance of this year’s so-called super El Niño, which set a record on Monday as the most extreme on record, and has amplified a number of extreme weather events globally. Forecasters at the National Hurricane Center in Miami said Mexico was likely to avoid a direct hit, but warned that further intensification was likely, and that life-threatening flooding and mudslides were possible inland, along with dangerous surf and rip current conditions. El Niño occurs when extended ocean temperatures in the eastern and central Pacific, and near the equator, rise above their historical average. Meteorologists say the phenomenon increases disruptive winds and curtails other conditions favorable to storm development in the Atlantic basin, which remains quiet with less than three months to go in this year’s hurricane season. Conversely, it promotes increased activity in the Pacific, where the 2026 El Niño remains one of the strongest on record. “The water temperatures in two separate areas, the north-central Pacific and off the Mexican coast, are running well above average,” Paul Pastelok, AccuWeather’s lead long-range meteorologist, said in the online weather service’s fall hurricane outlook last month. “We are seeing a strong impact in both the Atlantic and Pacific basins, with extreme wind shear limiting Atlantic storm development, while the Pacific remains quite active, as we expected back in the spring.” Hurricane Polo’s single-day intensification also fits into the assessment of University of Miami senior research associate Brian McNoldy on his tropical Atlantic blog that El Niño, which he said was only “moderate” towards the beginning of September, was “forecast to become very strong, likely the strongest on record, by later this fall and into winter”. Polo is the 18th named storm, and seventh hurricane, of the 2026 Pacific season, which runs from 15 May until 30 November. By contrast, the Atlantic basin, which has a six-month season from June until November, has seen only six named tropical storms and no hurricanes so far. It is the first time in 112 years that no Atlantic hurricanes have formed by 21 September, and 2026 could join 1907 and 1914 as the only years without one being recorded.
