title: Trump’s threat to annihilate Iran to UN general assembly is stunning, even for him
summary: US president may have upstaged the ghost of Soviet leader Khrushchev by musing destruction of fellow member state
text: Donald Trump has a habit of discomfiting delegates to the United Nations general assembly. But this year, he may have upstaged the ghost of Nikita Khrushchev by openly contemplating the annihilation of a fellow UN member state. Eleven minutes into a 40-minute address, the US president announced he had “a big decision to make” over Iran, which has staged a much more determined resistance than Trump anticipated when he decided to go to war against the country in February. “Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild, and create a far greater country than it ever was before?” he asked. “Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again? Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations?” Possibly not since Khrushchev, the late Soviet leader, brandished his shoe and allegedly banged it on a desk in 1960 in protest at a fellow delegate’s speech has the annual gathering witnessed such a display of bellicosity from a superpower leader. But this seemed more shocking. The world may have become inured to Trump’s dire threats to send Iran “to the stone age” or end its civilization – so often have they been issued, only to sometimes be followed by a ceasefire or negotiations. But hearing them voiced in a forum created in the aftermath of the second world war, with the explicit aim of preventing future conflicts, was disconcerting. Iran was the focal point of much of Trump’s speech, which began with a catalogue of familiar boasts of his supposed achievements that seemed better fitted to a domestic audience. Whether or not the latest threat should be taken literally, little of what he said about Iran seemed reassuring. He appeared to play fast and loose with the facts, consciously or otherwise. The US president twice incorrectly asserted that the theocratic regime had held power for 51 years. In fact, the Islamic revolution that toppled the pro-western former Shah, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, and installed the current regime happened 47 years ago, in 1979. Trump also cited apparently inflated figures for the number of Iranians killed in anti-government protests last January, weeks before the war. “The same regime slaughtered over 72,000 of its citizens this year,” he said, in support of his oft-stated declaration that Iran should never be permitted to acquire nuclear weapons. No definitive death toll has been established. But previous estimates of people killed in the brutal crushing of January’s demonstrations – even including those previously stated by Trump himself – have been much lower. The ominous rhetoric was not limited to Iran. Members of the Cuban delegation were seen leaving the hall as he predicted the imminent collapse of the country’s communist regime, which has been struggling to cope with a food security and humanitarian crisis amid tightening US embargoes. “It’s an absolutely failed state, it’s failing like never before, and it will fall,” Trump said. “Marco Rubio [the US secretary of state] is handling a negotiation. He’s deep into negotiations with Cuba. Let’s see what happens.” US actions in Venezuela, where special forces last January seized the strongman president, Nicolás Maduro, and spirited him to New York to face drug-trafficking charges, was also cited as an ominous warning to other adversaries – as well as a vocal statement of how the administration would behave in Latin America, Washington’s supposed “back yard”, if it felt its interests threatened. “Our actions in Venezuela are proof that the United States will no longer permit threats to America to gain a foothold anywhere in the western hemisphere, and, if necessary, we will use our unmatched military might to secure the vital national interests of the United States,” Trump declared. He was brazenly unabashed in hailing a recent US oil deal with the interim Venezuelan president, Delcy Rodríguez, that he claimed put the US and Venezuela jointly in control of more than 60% of the world’s oil. “It was perhaps the biggest deal ever made. To the victor belong the spoils – you’ve all heard that,” Trump said. There was outright antipathy for the international criminal court, which Trump called an “out-of-control institution” and “an evil group of people”. “We will never allow US service members or anyone else to be investigated or given show trials by an anti-American tribunal with no jurisdiction over us,” he said. Given his pugnacious stance towards US adversaries, it probably came as a relief to Washington’s traditional friends that Trump had relatively kind words for them. It was a far cry from his general assembly speech a year ago, when he warned European allies “your countries are all going to hell” because of immigration. This time, in a pointed message, Trump praised Nato’s secretary general, Mark Rutte, as a “great leader” – a marked departure from his previous denunciations of the military alliance as “obsolete” and a “paper tiger”. He lauded Denmark as “an incredible, beautiful country”, just days after announcing an agreement with it over Greenland, following prolonged tensions over the territory, which Trump had previously threatened to annex. With that issue seemingly settled – at least for now – the president declared his intention to flex his muscles on a new battleground: artificial intelligence, or AI. Echoing recent social media posts, Trump likened recent calls to slow its development, on the grounds that its rapid development poses an existential threat to humankind, as a “globalist scheme” hatched by the same forces he blamed for warnings of climate change, a premise he has long erroneously labelled a “hoax”. Part of the answer, he said, was to change its name. Henceforth it would cease to be called “artificial” (“it makes it sound fake – and it’s not fake”) and would be called “super intelligence” in all US government documents. “Welcome to the new world of super intelligence,” he said. “Let’s see if that goes. It’s much more accurate. Let’s see if I have any power. Maybe I do, maybe I don’t.”

title: Donald Trump praises ‘natural businessperson’ Andy Burnham after first meeting
summary: US president says British PM has a ‘lot of assets on his side’ as pair meet at UN in New York
text: Donald Trump has praised Andy Burnham as a “natural businessperson” and said the UK was “more up” than under Keir Starmer. But he berated the UK for its decision to give up the Chagos Islands. In their first face-to-face meeting, Trump gave a warm assessment of the relationship, saying he thought Burnham had a “lot of assets on his side” and would be a “great prime minister”, adding: “We talked about everything from Rolls-Royce to energy to immigration – we covered a lot.” At a joint press conference after their talks at the UN general assembly in New York, Burnham said he and the president had “established a good connection in our early discussions and we’ve taken that further today”. UK officials had been somewhat nervous about the meeting, as Trump had previously described Burnham as “extremely liberal” and called the former mayor of Greater Manchester as the “mayor of a town”. But the meeting appeared to have gone to plan for both sides, with Trump praising the UK, saying: “I think you’re up. Well, they’re more now than they were with your last prime minister, let me put it that way.” He added: “I think right now, based on my relationship with your prime minister, Andy, I think we’re doing very well.” However, Trump was scathing about the UK’s deal to give away sovereignty of the Chagos Islands to Mauritius, while paying for a lease of the military base of Diego Garcia. Asked about the deal, he said: “I don’t support it. I think it’s terrible. It was a terrible deal. They [Mauritius] all of a sudden say they have ownership. Somebody has ownership that never showed up before after decades and centuries. I think it’s ridiculous. “No, we were talking about that, and [the islands are] strategically very important. Very important. You know, we had to send our B-2 bombers … back home to Missouri, as opposed to flying for a short period of time. “It’s amazing how strategic it is, and I think the prime minister is going to be looking at it.” Trump was also questioned over the Iran war and the cost of living, with the president claiming that “as soon as the war is over the prices are going to come way down”. He later hit back at reporters questioning why he has banned some journalists from the White House, leading to a wider boycott by media organisations. Trump claimed he had a “right to clean out fake news”.

title: EU removes two oligarchs from Russia sanctions list as deadline looms
summary: Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman delisted in what Ireland’s EU presidency calls ‘a difficult compromise’ for the bloc
text: The EU has agreed to remove two Russian billionaires, Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman, from its sanctions list, while extending restrictions on nearly 3,000 individuals and companies accused of supporting the war on Ukraine for the next three years. With an end-of-Tuesday deadline looming to preserve the Russia blacklist, the EU’s 27 member states found a compromise that meant delisting the two oligarchs in spite of very few countries wanting this outcome. EU sanctions have to be approved unanimously. France stunned and infuriated EU governments this month when it called for Usmanov, a Russian-Uzbek national, to be removed from the list on “national security” grounds, reported to refer to a prisoner exchange deal involving French nationals and Azerbaijan. Luxembourg then asked for the same treatment for Fridman, the Russian-Israeli magnate, who is suing the Grand Duchy for $16bn (£12bn) for freezing his assets. The exemptions angered many EU countries which believe it sets a bad precedent by allowing member states to weaken sanctions in defence of national interests. Ukraine criticised the removal of the men from the sanctions list as unacceptable. Shortly after the decision emerged, Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, wrote on social media: “No name on the sanctions list is there by accident: each one represents a reason why this war started and continues to this day.” The Ukrainian foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, called the decision “shameful and unjustifiable” on X. “Moscow is celebrating because it got what it wanted: a sense ‌of impunity, the humiliation of the EU, and division among Europeans,” he added. In order to enable the delistings that many EU member states found unpalatable, it was proposed that the sanctions be rolled over for 36 months, rather than the usual six. A spokesperson for Ireland’s EU presidency, which brokered the talks, said the bloc had reached “a difficult compromise”. They said: “Until now, these listings have been reviewed and assessed on a six-monthly basis; today’s decision to renew on a 36-month basis enhances the durability and predictability of the EU sanctions framework.” A decision had been expected earlier this week, but Latvia’s government, facing parliamentary elections on 3 October, announced a last-minute objection to the delistings on Monday. Latvia’s prime minister, Andris Kulbergs, said late on Monday night that he could not accept the proposed compromise and instructed his foreign minister to enter talks with Paris and Brussels to find a solution. Diplomats said Latvia had finally agreed to abstain on the two delistings. The blacklist includes Russia’s president, Vladimir Putin, and foreign minister, Sergey Lavrov, as well as Duma deputies, the country’s major banks, energy companies and military industrial complex. Senior EU officials have promised to present about 1,600 new designations – individuals and entities involved in the Russian military industrial complex – to foreign ministers next month. But the latest standoff, which followed the tortuous agreement on the EU’s 21st round of sanctions in July, suggests the process could be difficult.

title: Woman and three children killed after ‘intense’ fire ravages Merseyside house
summary: One other person being treated in hospital after fire crews respond to early-hours incident at home in Bootle
text: A woman and three children have died after an overnight fire ripped through a semi-detached house on Merseyside. The Merseyside fire and rescue service (MFRS) said crews arrived at the blaze in Bootle at about 3.45am on Tuesday. Speaking at the scene, the chief fire officer, Nick Searle, said four people inside the house had died and another person, outside the property, had been taken to hospital. He said the fire was “intense” and “spread very rapidly”. Four people were discovered in an upstairs bedroom showing no signs of life, a fire service spokesperson said. At the fire’s height, six crews were on the scene and eight firefighters entered the house, which was alight when they arrived, they added. One local person, who did not want to be named, said: “We all came out on the front and we could see smoke coming over from the houses. The sirens woke me up and there were fire engines in the street.” Another person said: “I heard shouting in the early hours but I just thought someone was having an argument, then I came downstairs and saw all the fire engines.” At the scene, Searle said: “Firstly, our thoughts are with everyone who’s been affected by the tragic incident this morning.” He said the MFRS control room received a 999 call at 3.38am and crews from surrounding stations were mobilised, with the first fire engine arriving at 3.45am to find the house “well alight”. “Crews who were wearing breathing apparatus entered the building to search the property for occupants and fighting intense fire, which had spread very rapidly.” Other crews found a casualty outside the property, and he was taken into the care of North West ambulance service and transferred to hospital,” Searle said. “During the course of the search of the property, firefighters discovered four casualties, showing no signs of life, and it’s now been confirmed that all four have tragically lost their lives.” He said MFRS and Merseyside police would carry out a full joint investigation into the cause of the fire. “Our thoughts remain with the loved ones of those lost, and fire crews will maintain a visible and reassuring presence in the community over the coming days.” The MFRS area manager, Kevin Longshaw, said: “This is a devastating incident, and our thoughts are very much with the family and friends of those who have lost their lives and been injured. “We will work closely with relevant colleagues to ascertain the cause of the fire, but in the immediate term, we again extend our sincere condolences to those affected by this tragic incident.”

title: Police believe they have foiled ‘imminent’ attack on Manchester’s Jewish community
summary: Counter-terrorism police say ‘long-running investigation’ disrupted alleged plot days after two men arrested on eve of the holy day Yom Kippur
text: Police believe they have stopped an imminent plot to attack Jewish communities in the Manchester area. The announcement on Tuesday follows the arrest of two men on Sunday at 2.45pm in Manchester and comes during the period of festivals at the beginning of the Jewish new year. Counter-terrorism investigators were unusually explicit about the alleged attack plot, which was halted after an operation lasting several months. Police believe they have detained the main suspects and any materials they may have been planning to use. Deputy assistant commissioner Vicki Evans, senior national coordinator for Counter Terrorism Policing, said: “This has been a long-running proactive investigation which has led to the disruption of what we believe to be a plot to target the Jewish community in the Manchester area.” The arrests and official confirmation of a suspected attack plot comes almost a year after an Islamist-incited attack on a Manchester synagogue on Yom Kippur left two people dead, with the attacker shot dead by police. Arrests were made hours before this year’s Yom Kippur started, with police fearing any plot might be “imminent”. The Jewish festival of Sukkot falls on Friday, with other holy days to follow. Evans added: “We are acutely aware this news will cause further concern to the Jewish community, as well as the wider public, especially given the significant High Holy Day period. “I want to reassure them we are working incredibly closely with colleagues in Greater Manchester police and partners to ensure we’re doing everything we can to keep them and the wider public safe.” The two men in their 30s were arrested under section 41 of the Terrorism Act, meaning police suspected they were terrorists. Police will not officially say what the motive was, nor the nationality or ethnicity of those detained. The Guardian understands that a far-right motive is thought to be unlikely. Sources stress the investigation is at an early stage. Islamist extremism is among possible motives under consideration, and given a spate of recent attacks against Jewish targets, investigators are searching for any sign of a state link. Investigators are increasingly finding it difficult to determine motive until much later in an investigation, if at all. The UK’s terrorism threat level is now at its second highest level of severe. The investigation was led by CTP in London and the two men arrested have been taken to a police station in the capital for questioning. Warrants for their further detention have been granted, meaning they can be held until Sunday. The arrests led to searches in Epworth Street, Liverpool, and Lancaster Road, Salford, which police say have now been completed. Examination of electronic devices such as mobile phones is under way. Evans added: “Counter Terrorism Policing continue to focus our efforts on identifying and disrupting those who wish to cause harm in our communities. “As we have shown with these arrests, where we suspect there could be a threat to the public, then we will not hesitate to investigate and take action. “We are pursuing a number of lines of inquiry and we anticipate these will continue over the coming days as this investigation continues. “Importantly, we do not believe there to be any ongoing threat to the public in relation to this matter, but as ever, we would ask that people remain vigilant and contact police with any concerns.” The Community Security Trust (CST), which works to keep Jewish communities in the UK safe from attack, said: “This is utterly chilling, coming so close to the anniversary of the terrorist attack at Heaton Park Synagogue last year, and is another reminder of the serious terrorist threat facing Jewish communities in this current time. “We urge the Jewish community to remain calm and alert, and to report any suspicious activity to police on 999 and then to CST.” • This article was amended on 23 September 2026. There is no specific Jewish “holy month”, as was mentioned in an earlier version, but rather a period of festivals – including Yom Kippur and Sukkot – following Jewish new year.

title: ‘Worse than the scramble for Oasis tickets’: England’s sustainable farming funds run out in just six hours
summary: Entire £253m budget for 2026 allocated in less than a day, leaving thousands of farmers disappointed
text: Thousands of farmers have been left empty-handed with the government’s 2026 nature funding spent in just six hours. The £253m sustainable farming incentive (SFI) scheme opened for applications from farmers at 10am on Tuesday. SFI is part of a package of payments that replaced the EU’s common agricultural policy, paying farmers to look after nature, soil and other public goods, rather than simply for farming and owning land. But by 4pm on Tuesday – just six hours after it opened – the government confirmed that the 2026 SFI scheme was closed for applications, with all of the budget allocated. For many farmers this was their first opportunity to apply to SFI since the scheme’s sudden closure in March 2025. The next opportunity to apply for funding will be in 2027. “Vicki Hird, the strategic lead on agriculture at The Wildlife Trusts, compared the scramble for SFI funding to “the scramble to get Oasis tickets” and said it was shocking to watch the funding disappear so quickly. “The government really needs to get the budget in order to ensure farmers have the funding they need for nature, food security and national security,” she said. Alice Groom, the head of sustainable land policy at the RSPB, said it was “unprecedented” for the budget to be used up so quickly. “We thought the money would go quickly but not necessarily in one day,” she said. “Defra doesn’t have a way of managing the budget. SFI is supposed to be spent on meeting environmental goals and transitioning to environmental farming, but it’s now first come first served. “There will likely be thousands of farmers who haven’t been able to apply for any funding, which will have implications for their ability to deliver for the environment on their farm,” she said. Throughout the day, farmers who had been experiencing problems with their SFI applications had to wait up to five hours to speak to someone to get help. Martin Lines, the CEO of the Nature Friendly Farming Network, said this will have meant they won’t have spoken to someone until after the scheme had closed. This year has been extremely challenging for farmers because of crop-destroying heat and drought alongside soaring fertiliser costs tied to the war in Iran. The SFI funding will have been seen as a way for many farmers to invest in the future of their businesses, he said. Lines said the fact that thousands of farmers would inevitably miss out on funding was “terribly sad” and showed the “desperation” many farmers were experiencing. “If they can’t get access to the funding, how will they remain resilient?” he asked. Groom added that this would “absolutely” affect the government’s ability to meet its legally binding nature targets, including its statutory target to restore 30% of nature by 2030. “Lots of targets will be missed, we’re really worried,” she said. With farmers having suffered through what the NFU has described as the “toughest summer in a generation”, the employers’ association said the government must urgently set out a plan for the 2027 SFI scheme, with increased budget transparency. Andy Burnham, the prime minister, announced in August that there would be an extra £50m in funding for the 2026 SFI; that money was included in this funding round. The NFU said it welcomed this but “remains concerned that the limited SFI budget endangers longstanding environmental delivery and fails to recognise farmers’ desire to deliver greater environmental outcomes”. A Defra spokesperson said: “This year we ensured small farms and those new to SFI were prioritised – with an exclusive first window in the summer. “In anticipation of high demand in the second window, Ministers decided to allocate an additional £20m to the fund, on top of the £50m announced by the Prime Minister in August, so that we could fund as many agreements as possible. We have therefore allocated a total of £310m to new agreements under both windows.” This article was corrected on 23 Sept 2026: an earlier version said the budget was £233m, but in fact it was for £253m, after Defra allocated an additional £20m.

title: Donald Trump scolds CNN anchor for covering him at the UN
summary: President chided Kaitlan Collins for asking him question at UN after White House ban on CNN, MS Now and Politico
text: Donald Trump has scolded a CNN anchor for covering him at the UN in New York after banning the network and two other media outlets from the White House. Kaitlan Collins asked the US president on Tuesday when the Iran war would end, citing a poll that claims two-thirds of Americans don’t think the US is winning. “It’s an honor to be here. I’m surprised that CNN is here covering me,” Trump began before telling Collins: “You should not be here covering me. “You said you weren’t going to cover me. You shouldn’t be covering me.” Collins told the president on Tuesday that the UN allowed her organization into the general assembly. The Guardian has asked CNN for comment. Last week, Trump announced he was banning CNN, Politico and MS Now from the White House, accusing the outlets – without citing evidence – of “constantly” writing and reporting “FICTION and LIES”. On Saturday, reporters and other staff from the news organizations were denied access to the White House. On Saturday, CNN said: “We will not be deflected from our duty to hold the government and other public bodies to account, and we will continue to report on the actions and processes of this administration without fear or favor.” CNN, Politico and MS Now have since sued the administration, seeking to end his enforcement of the ban and restore reporters’ hard passes that grant them access to the White House grounds. A federal judge is expected to hold a hearing on the matter on Wednesday. Trump’s attempt to restrict press access sparked criticism from other media organizations and first amendment advocacy groups, which have accused the US president of infringing on the right of the free press. Trump has defended his decision, claiming his ban was not “an assault on the Free Press”, but instead designed to address “national security” threats – a claim the US president has recently used to justify building a triumphal arch and a White House ballroom.

title: Trump calls on allies to enforce ‘complete economic isolation of Iran’ in UN speech
summary: US president threatens to ‘annihilate’ Tehran and dismisses threat from AI as a ‘hoax’ in bellicose address
text: Donald Trump has called on nations to unite to isolate Tehran and bring down global energy prices, as he gave a bellicose defence of his administration’s foreign policy and decision to strike Iran. “I call on all nations to help to enforce the complete economic isolation of Iran,” Trump said in a speech to the UN general assembly on Tuesday. “If we stand united, we will soon see a world free of the last 51-year menace of Iranian terror … and oil prices will come plummeting down even lower than they were at the start of the conflict.” Trump’s call for international unity on Iran – he also said he may “annihilate” the country – comes as numerous US allies have complained about soaring energy prices and growing international instability during his US administration. On the first day of the high-level week of the UN general assembly in New York, Trump also reiterated that the US would not seek to rein in the development of artificial intelligence, seeking to rebrand it as “superintelligence” and saying warnings about the threats from out-of-control AI development were a “hoax”. “I’m ⁠not going to stifle growth of something that will be bigger than ‌the Industrial Revolution,” he said. In an address that mostly rehashed his stump speech talking points, Trump announced that the US would build two new military bases in Greenland as part of an agreement with the government of Denmark, after a year of geopolitical haggling that has unsettled the Nato alliance. “We will have the complete ability to do what is necessary to defend the American continent, and also Europe and other places,” Trump said in announcing the two “major” military bases. “No US adversary will ever be permitted to establish a military presence in Greenland any more, or make sensitive investments there without our express written approval.” He denied that the US was running short of critical munitions (“we have more munitions than we could ever possibly even think of using”), attacked the international criminal court as a “rogue organisation” and claimed once again that he was close to settling the war in Ukraine. But this was a less bellicose speech than the one he gave last year, when he excoriated the UN and told European allies that their countries were “going to hell” because of their migration policies. At one point on Tuesday, he stopped and turned around to thank the UN security council for condemning Iranian attacks on shipping in the strait of Hormuz. During the speech, he repeated a threat to destroy Iran, which he has made dozens of times since the US and Israel launched joint strikes in February. “I have a big decision to make: will a deal be made with Iran that let them rebuild and create a far greater country than ever was before,” he said. “Or do I annihilate the Islamic republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill or destroy people and continents?” Trump denied that he was under political pressure to end the war and said the midterm elections would have absolutely no influence on his decision-making around the conflict. “They’re waiting to see how I do in the midterm election. What they don’t realise is that I’m not running,” he said. “It doesn’t even enter my mind. The only thing that does is that Iran will never have a nuclear weapon.” Iran has maintained a stranglehold over energy shipping through the strait of Hormuz since early in the war, and global oil prices have also been driven up by the conflict between Russia and Ukraine, where Kyiv has successfully targeted Moscow’s refining capacity. Trump used the speech to take a pot shot at Cuba, calling the country “an absolutely failed state” – prompting the Cuban delegation to walk out of the hall as the president continued to criticise the US’s neighbour. Trump went on to say his administration was seeking “a fundamental change in the situation in Cuba”. Cuba’s delegation head, Bruno Rodríguez, later rejected Trump’s remarks as “falsehoods” and “slander”. Trump defended the US move to arrest the former Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro in a midnight raid, and the subsequent oil deal he struck with Delcy Rodríguez, Maduro’s successor, who has proved much more amenable to US demands and agreed to a deal sharing the country’s vast oil wealth with the US. “To the victor belong the spoils,” Trump said. Trump’s New York itinerary is a crib sheet of the ways that his presidency has upended global politics in the last two years. After his speech, Trump signed an agreement with Denmark over the future of Greenland, which Trump has claimed could be dominated by Russia and China despite few signs that was the case. Later, he is expected to meet the Ukrainian leader, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, whom he is expected to press along with Russia to conclude an energy truce to help assuage soaring prices on diesel mainly prompted by Tehran’s closure of the strait of Hormuz. Trump will also meet Gulf leaders, who have been affected by Iran’s retaliation to the joint US-Israeli attack, and then will have a pull-aside with the US-backed Rodríguez of Venezuela, another major oil exporter.

title: Russians have a pragmatic approach to politics | Letter
summary: Letter: There has never been a real rebellion for the Kremlin to squelch, writes Mergen Mongush
text: To an old Russian like me, Rafael Behr is as wrong as sin, because he is watching (and describing) the smoke without seeing the fire (To understand the threat to our real democracy, watch Putin’s fake one, 16 September). In their unqualified admiration for your democracy, our leaders have done a lot to emulate it: in 1861, Alexander II abolished serfdom; in 1905, Nicholas II allowed the creation of our elected parliament; in 1917, Kerensky allowed women to vote; in 1990, Gorbachev reintroduced a multiparty system; he, Yeltsin and Medvedev resigned in 1991, 1999 and 2020 respectively (like your Wilson, Thatcher, Blair, Cameron, May, Johnson, Truss and Starmer in 1976, 1990, 2007, 2016, 2019, 2022, again 2022, and 2026 respectively). But ordinary Russians are up to their ears in their age-long que será, será approach to politics. So there has never been a real rebellion for the Kremlin to squelch. Had Mr Behr lived in our provincial towns instead of Moscow in the 1990s, he would have produced a very different article. Mergen Mongush Moscow, Russia • Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Please email us your letter and it will be considered for publication in our letters section.

title: Reform UK-led council ends support for Show Racism the Red Card
summary: Charity’s head coach ‘shocked’ after Sunderland council leader says it will not support ‘politically charged’ groups
text: Anti-racism education in some schools will be scrapped after a city council now led by Reform UK ended its 30-year support for the charity Show Racism the Red Card. Announcing the decision last week, the Reform leader of Sunderland city council, Christopher Eynon, said it would no longer support “politically charged organisations with an agenda”. Gary Bennett, the former Sunderland AFC captain and the charity’s head coach, said he was “shocked and disappointed” that Nigel Farage’s party had withdrawn vital funding. The move prompted a furious backlash from opposition politicians including Labour’s Bridget Phillipson, who described it on Tuesday as “misguided, cruel and in no way backed by the people of Sunderland”. Bennett, who became only the second black player in Sunderland’s history when he joined the club in 1984, was a founding member of Show Racism the Red Card when it was established in 1996. The former centre-back, who remains a cult hero on Wearside, said he was “surprised, shocked and disappointed” that Sunderland council – the first local authority to have supported it – was cutting its ties after 30 years. Bennett said it would immediately disrupt the charity’s ability to teach local children in schools and provide workshops in prisons and workplaces. He said: “We’re not a political charity – they’re trying to say we are but we’re not. Sunderland were the first council to come onboard to help fund us, that’s the annoying thing. For something like this to happen now, we just want to know the reasons why.” Bennett said the racist riots across many English cities including Sunderland in 2024 showed there was “still lots of work to be done”. While Britain had come a long way since the 1980s, he said, there remained issues to confront around attitudes towards asylum seekers and migrants. “You’ve got all different issues going on now. It keeps moving, it’s always something else which causes some form of racism,” he said. “It’s something that is challenging every single day and we’ve got to keep the fight. There’s still lots of work to be done and we can’t just ignore it and think it’s going to go away because it’s not.” Eynon, whose party gained control of the council in May, said the authority was not “stepping back from its opposition to racism or discrimination” and that “racism has no place in Sunderland”. He took issue with Ged Grebby, the chief executive of Show Racism the Red Card, describing Reform as a “very dangerous organisation”. Grebby defended his right to express personal views and said the charity had support across the political spectrum. Separately, Reform UK has been accused of “vice signalling” after its councillors in Bradford proposed to pull out of the Local Authority of Sanctuary scheme, which is intended to show a city is a safe place for migrant communities. The Reform group that runs the council said it would be putting forward a motion at the next meeting in October to end the status, which it said has meant the council had “led Refugee Week engagement and utilised local libraries to celebrate all new arrivals into Bradford”, adding that “public services should instead be prioritised for Bradford residents”. The Reform councillor Jayne Morgan said the move “may upset oversensitive political opponents” but was firmly in the public interest. In response, Imran Khan, the leader of Bradford’s Labour group, said: “Reform failed to deliver on various promises they made to Bradford residents this summer, so instead they fall back on their usual toxic recipe of hate, victimhood and division.” He said pulling out of the scheme would “do nothing to help a single person” in Bradford. “This is vice signalling from Reform and all it does is damage integration and promote division and resentment, which helps no one,” he said.

title: Former Radio 1 DJ Tim Westwood charged with two more offences
summary: Westwood, 68, charged with indecently assaulting teenage girl in 1991 and sexually assaulting 18-year-old woman in 2004
text: The former BBC DJ Tim Westwood has been charged with two additional offences dating back to 1991 and 2004. The 68-year-old will appear at Westminster magistrates court on a date to be fixed accused of indecently assaulting a girl aged 16 or 17 in the borough of Hammersmith and Fulham in 1991, the Metropolitan police said. He is also accused of sexually assaulting an 18-year-old woman in Wandsworth in May 2004. Catherine P Baccas, the deputy chief crown prosecutor in CPS London, said: “Today the Crown Prosecution Service has authorised two further charges of sexual assault and indecent assault against Tim Westwood. “Mr Westwood is already charged with nine counts of indecent assault, two counts of sexual assault and four counts of rape in relation to reported non-recent offences between 1983 and 2016 involving seven women. “These new charges, following an investigation by the Metropolitan police, relate to separate reports of non-recent offences in 1991 and 2004 involving two additional women. “Our prosecutors have worked to establish that there is sufficient evidence to bring these additional charges to court and that it is in the public interest to pursue further criminal proceedings. “The Crown Prosecution Service reminds everyone that criminal proceedings are active, and the defendant has the right to a fair trial.” Last December, Westwood pleaded not guilty to 15 charges. Three of the indecent assault offences he is charged with allegedly occurred at the BBC Studios in 1996. Westwood hosted shows on Radio 1 between 1994 and 2013. Also among the 15 charges were the rape of a female aged between 17 and 18 in London between 1995 and 1996, as well as sexual assault of the same person in central London in a similar period, and the rape of a woman in her 20s in London in 2010. He was also alleged to have indecently assaulted a 17-year-old girl in Fulham, London, in 1983, indecently assaulted a woman in her 20s in Vauxhall, London, in 1986, and sexually assaulted a woman in her 20s in Stroud, Gloucestershire, in 2010. The most recent alleged offence was sexual assault of a woman in her 20s in Finchley, north London, in 2016. He had previously said that he “strongly denies all allegations of inappropriate behaviour”. Westwood began his career on pirate radio in London before joining Capital Radio. He became one of the UK’s best-known names in hip-hop after hosting BBC Radio 1’s first rap show in 1994, remaining at the corporation until 2013. He later hosted a regular show on Capital Xtra, which he left in April 2022.

title: Jim Ratcliffe halts production at Hull chemical plants over ‘ridiculous’ gas prices
summary: Billionaire owner of Ineos says company ‘cannot compete’ with global market despite efficiency of Humberside sites
text: Billionaire industrialist Sir Jim Ratcliffe is pausing production at three chemical plants in Hull, blaming the UK’s “ridiculously high” gas prices. Ratcliffe’s chemicals conglomerate, Ineos, said on Tuesday it would “mothball” three chemical plants because the cost made it difficult to compete in the global market. Production has already been paused at two of the Humberside plants and the third is due to come offline in a few days, according to Ineos. About 240 people are directly employed by the company across the three sites. Ineos said the number of jobs on Humberside that would be affected by a permanent closure would rise to 4,000 including those employed in the sites’ supply chains. “I’m sure people will find it hard to believe that we are being forced to mothball some of the most efficient plants in Europe,” Ratcliffe said in a statement. “[W]e just cannot compete.” The Monaco-based billionaire claimed that gas prices in the UK were 12 times higher than in the US and eight times more expensive than the coal increasingly used by chemical plants in China. The rising cost of gas in recent years has taken a heavy toll on Europe’s chemicals industry, including the Ineos empire, because it is a vital feedstock used to make the chemical building blocks required to manufacture products ranging from textiles and pharmaceuticals to detergents. Gas prices tend to be higher in the UK than in other parts of Europe due to the country’s reliance on gas for heating and electricity generation. Historically this reliance was met by the UK’s domestic North Sea reserves, but as production declines the UK has become increasingly reliant on imports. The co-owner of Manchester United also said that the UK government’s energy policy was “leading to economic vandalism on an industrial scale” by losing jobs to China and the US “and driving up global CO2 emissions at a stroke”. “Not only is the ridiculously high gas price in the UK destroying our manufacturing base and the jobs of hard-working people on Humberside, it is also massively increasing the environmental burden, with replacement products supplied from the USA at double the carbon emissions and from China at eight times the emission level,” Ratcliffe said. A government spokesperson said ministers had taken “bold action” to support the UK’s chemicals industry, including the launch of a £350m co-investment scheme and trade measures on foreign chemicals imports. The spokesperson said the government was preparing to tackle high electricity costs via a pair of discount schemes for manufacturers. The first aims to reduce electricity bills by up to 25% for more than 10,000 manufacturing businesses, while a “supercharger” scheme will cut electricity costs for hundreds of the UK’s most electricity-intensive businesses by more than £400m a year. “While this is a commercial decision from Ineos, we know this will be a concerning time for workers in Saltend and their families,” the spokesperson added.

title: Earl Spencer apologises to Piers Morgan over ‘incorrect assumption’
summary: Brother of Diana, Princess of Wales, says ‘accuracy is important’ as he responds to broadcaster’s threat to sue over claims made in memoir
text: Earl Spencer has apologised to Piers Morgan for incorrectly claiming in his new book about Diana, Princess of Wales, that the former tabloid editor was behind the publication of intrusive photos of the late royal in the mid-1990s. Morgan had earlier threatened to sue Spencer over “fabricated inaccuracies” and “examples of brazen falsity” in the book, which was published on Tuesday. In the memoir, the earl claims Morgan was in part responsible for the publication of photographs taken by an allegedly hidden camera in a gym, of Diana working out in a leotard. But the broadcaster told his audience on YouTube on Monday that the pictures were published in the Sunday Mirror nearly two years before he became editor at the Daily Mirror and when he was working at the Sun. Morgan called on Diana’s brother to pulp the remaining copies of his book and said he had instructed his lawyers to demand the work be pulled from sale immediately. Later on Tuesday, Spencer issued a statement apologising to Morgan and admitting he had incorrectly assumed Morgan had been editor of the Mirror at the time. “Earl Spencer’s account of his conversation with Piers Morgan is accurate. “Morgan was surly and annoyed when Earl Spencer called personally to tell him that he was not welcome at his sister’s funeral,” the statement said. “The book then records Earl Spencer’s assumption that Mr Morgan’s response was because he was editor of the Daily Mirror when the Mirror Group had published highly intrusive photographs of Princess Diana at the gym. “The photographs were published by the Sunday Mirror on 7 November 1993. Mr Morgan has pointed out that he did not join the Daily Mirror until October 1995. As an historian, accuracy is important to Earl Spencer. He therefore wishes to clarify that his assumption was incorrect. Earl Spencer apologises to Mr Morgan for this error.” In his response to Spencer’s apology, Morgan also wrote he was “neither surly nor annoyed” but had been “very respectful” to the earl during their telephone conversation. He wrote: “Earl Spencer’s account of our phone call is also deeply misleading. “I was neither surly nor annoyed, but instead, very respectful to him and his family, as I wrote in my diaries, The Insider. It would seem that Spencer’s recollection of phone calls is very suspect.” Morgan also doubled down on his threat of legal action, writing on social media: “Earl Spencer has apologised to me for his defamatory lies published in his new book, Swan Song, published today. “But I am pursuing legal action against him and his publisher Penguin to have the lies removed, and damages paid to the King’s Trust.” The earl has made a series of claims in Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, including that King Charles said “we’ll forget her soon enough” after she died, which has prompted a war of words between him and Buckingham Palace. The book also contains allegations about Morgan, who has rejected the claims. Speaking earlier on his YouTube show, Piers Morgan Uncensored, Morgan said: “Many allies of his majesty have called into question these facts, ever since the most salacious accusations were serialised by the Daily Mail. “Many royal commentators and experts have lined up to say that they simply don’t ring true. The king himself issued a furious rebuke that is almost without precedent. But, in essence, this has all been about opinions. Recollections may vary, after all. Well, until now. “Because I can exclusively reveal on Uncensored that Earl Spencer’s book contains fabricated inaccuracies which will strike to the heart of his credibility. Spencer recounts how he personally called round the tabloid newspaper editors to uninvite them from Princess Diana’s funeral, after they had all been invited. I remember this well, because I was one of them.” Morgan read an extract from Spencer’s book, which claims the editor “snarled with annoyance before he hung up”, as well as the passage concerning the intrusive photographs. He told his audience on YouTube that the pictures were published in the Sunday Mirror nearly two years before he became editor at the Daily Mirror. He said: “Well, this is all pretty extraordinary stuff, isn’t it? And very damning, particularly about me. I come across in the most despicable manner imaginable. There’s just one problem. It’s all bullshit and very, very easy bullshit for me to prove it. “The photographs which he says that I published were printed by the Sunday Mirror on 7 November 1993. I joined the Daily Mirror in October in 1995. In fact, at the time of the gym pictures, I was doing a showbiz column on the Mirror’s arch-rival, the Sun. About as far removed from responsibility for the Mirror scoop as I could possibly have been.” Morgan, who was the editor of the Mirror from 1995 to 2004, continued: “Earl Spencer was estranged from Diana and living in South Africa at the time of her death. As editor of the Daily Mirror, I had lunch with her at Kensington Palace with Prince William. After that, it wasn’t uncommon for her to call my office or for me to run stories by her … Ironically, by that time in her life I think I was probably talking to her more often than he was. “My question, though, is this: if Earl Spencer can be so incredibly, defamatorily wrong about such basic facts involving me, well, why should we believe anything else he puts in this book?” He later added: “In the meantime, Earl Spencer, you’ll be hearing – and your publishers – from my lawyers.” Bookshops across London were reported to have appeared quiet on the release day of Spencer’s memoir – with the £28 book marked at half its cover price in some stores. Dozens of copies with red “half price” stickers were stacked in Waterstones flagship Piccadilly store – the largest in Europe. It is also marked as half price on the Waterstones website.

title: Briton pleads guilty to ‘recklessly’ causing death of his son in Cyprus
summary: Man’s lawyer says he accepted charge over toddler’s fall from window to avoid harrowing trial for himself and his family
text: A British man has pleaded guilty to “recklessly” causing the death of his son, 10 weeks after the toddler fell from a fourth-floor hotel window in Cyprus. Josh Foster, 37, who appeared before the district court of Paphos on Tuesday, accepted the charge of causing the accident through a “rash, reckless and dangerous act” on the first day of a family holiday near Paphos on 12 July. The case was adjourned until 5 October, when the judge ordered the man to return for sentencing. Under the maximum penalty he could face up to four years in prison. Explaining his client’s decision to enter the plea, the defence lawyer, Alexandros Alexandrou, said the alternative was the prospect of prolonged criminal proceedings. If he had contested the charge, a series of hearings would have ensued, forcing the father to repeatedly confront the circumstances of the two-year-old’s death. His client had broken down inconsolably when he appeared in the same courtroom to be formally charged in July. “[A trial] would be disturbing for him, for his family,” said Alexandrou, emphasising that the Briton, his wife and other relatives were still processing the grief of their “unimaginable loss”. “In order to end this story he accepted [the accusation],” he said, adding the defence would present mitigating factors in an attempt to secure a lenient verdict. “If the maximum sentence were imposed, the defence would appeal. This kind of penalty is not acceptable from our side.” After posting €30,000 (about £26,000) in bail to return to the UK to attend the toddler’s funeral in August, Foster was forced under threat of extradition to return to Cyprus and surrender his passport by 14 September. Until last week Foster had hoped the charge would be suspended. In what amounted to a desperate plea for reprieve, the Briton, a senior employee at one of the big four accounting firms, had appealed to George Savvides, the attorney general of Cyprus, to intervene. As the island’s top legal authority, Savvides has the power to confer clemency by discontinuing criminal procedures on humanitarian grounds. Alexandrou had lodged the appeal saying: “In these exceptional circumstances, we do not believe a continued criminal process serves the public interest. The focus now should be on [the family’s] welfare and recovery.” The request was denied. Addressing Paphos’s district court last week, state prosecutors said that while Savvides recognised the father’s grief, there had been loss of life and it was a matter of “public interest” that the criminal proceedings went ahead. Until the eve of the plea hearing it had remained unknown how the defendant would contest the charge of causing his son’s death. The boy, who would have turned three last week, fell from a fourth-floor window at the King Evelthon hotel and resort on the Chlorakas coastline outside Paphos. The father claims he placed him on the windowsill – along a corridor leading to a lift that his relatives were about to use – not realising the window was ajar. The toddler then fell backwards, suffering fatal cranial injuries when he hit a veranda 10 metres (33ft) below. In a country so dependent on tourism, criticism has mounted as human rights defenders, media pundits and diplomats have questioned the perceived lack of compassion with which officials have approached the case. While the letter of the law had been adhered to so assiduously by police and court officials, “no one had asked why the window did not have bars”, said a diplomat based in Nicosia, the eastern Mediterranean island’s capital. “It’s perplexing that there’s all this emphasis on the father being a criminal and so little focus on the circumstances in which the boy died,” he added. “Why was there even a window there and why was it open? In a country where permits to build hotels are often lax, these are questions that should not be ignored.” In an editorial last week, the Cyprus Mail echoed that sentiment. “Why are authorities so eager to treat tragic accidents as criminal acts?” it asked, after a similar incident in which the three-year-old son of African immigrants fell to his death from the balcony of his family’s sixth-floor apartment in Nicosia. Like the Briton, his parents were held in custody for several days although they were eventually released without charge. The attorney general’s decision to go ahead with the prosecution – described as both disappointing and surprising by Alexandrou – had stirred further debate. The role of Cyprus’s attorney general has long been regarded as one of the most controversial legacies of the island’s former status as a British colony. The island’s leading human rights lawyer, Achilleas Demetriades, said the Briton had fallen foul of “an archaic system” that was long overdue an overhaul. Under Cyprus’s postcolonial justice system, such decisions remained entirely at the discretion of the attorney general and could not be challenged, he said. For years there had been talk of amending the constitution to resolve the anomaly, he added. “It’s in the process of being amended because the office of the attorney general, when it takes this type of decision, should have judicial overview which it currently does not. “Sadly, this man has fallen victim to an archaic system in which one man, the attorney general, has unfettered power. This certainly raises human rights issues.”

title: AOC refuses to rule out run against Senate leader Chuck Schumer
summary: ‘I’ll cross that bridge when I get to it,’ the progressive US representative says
text: Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, the progressive Democratic congresswoman, has refused to rule out a potential run against the party’s Senate leader Chuck Schumer amid mounting speculation around her political ambitions. When asked by the New York Times whether she would challenge Schumer in 2028, when his current term is up, Ocasio-Cortez declined to exclude the possibility – even if Democrats win back the Senate majority. “We’re working hard to have that problem,”, Ocasio-Cortez, 36, told the newspaper of a Democratic majority in the Senate, which she called called “the best possible problem we could have as a country”, adding: “And I’ll cross that bridge when I get to it.” The New York congresswoman emphasized that any decision she makes would be personal, saying: “I don’t think that my decisions would come down to deference.” Ocasio-Cortez has been repeatedly cited as a potential challenger to Schumer, 75, and possibly a Democratic presidential candidate in 2028. She has built a significant profile since defeating a top incumbent Democrat to win her seat in the House of Representatives, representing an area of New York City, in 2018. Her progressive policies have resonated with younger Democrats, women and Hispanic voters, according to recent polling from the New York Times/Siena University. She has become a leading figure in rallying anti-Trump voters. She has also raised more money than many of her House colleagues, securing more than $32m since 2025. As of June, Ocasio-Cortez had more than $15m in cash, according to Federal Election Commission data. But Ocasio-Cortez is also polarizing, with roughly 41% of likely voters and 75% of Republicans finding her unfavorable. That combination has made her an easy target for Republican attacks, particularly from the US president. Though her name is floated as a potential 2028 presidential contender, Ocasio-Cortez has been elusive about her plans, often leaving the door open to a run while acknowledging the hurdles she faces. “I’m not naive to the fact that we are living under a very regressive administration, and I happen to be a woman, and I, you know, happen to be Latina,” Ocasio-Cortez told the New York Times. “And I think that there’s a lot of conversation about electability, and I don’t kind of shy away from those realities.” Taking on Schumer could be Ocasio-Cortez’s first step to fulfilling greater political ambitions. Earlier this year, a survey from the liberal firm Data for Progress found that 55% of likely Democratic voters said they would support or lean toward supporting Ocasio-Cortez, while only 36% would back Schumer.

title: Activists and leaders reflect on Standing Rock a decade on: ‘I would do it again’
summary: Tribal leaders and organizers return to reservation 10 years after demonstrations against Dakota Access pipeline
text: Ten years after major demonstrations against the Dakota Access pipeline, tribal leaders and Native American organizers returned to the Standing Rock Sioux reservation this week to honor the movement and its lasting impacts. In the rural reservation area of Fort Yates, a four-day encampment that centered on the phrase “mní wičóni” – “water is life” – brought together about 150 tribal members and allies for meals, drum circles, sacred ceremonies and memorials. It opened with the lighting of a sacred fire – “peta waken” – using coals preserved from a fire that burned at the 2016 camp. The tradition is a significant spiritual unification between the seven councils of the Oceti Sakowin, or Sioux Nation, tribes, typically done in times of historic and political efforts as a symbol of hope. In November 2016, after nearly two centuries had passed without the ceremony, Sioux tribal elders called for the fire to be relit after protesters – concerned that the Dakota Access pipeline (DAPL), which would run within a mile of tribal lands, might pollute the Standing Rock reservation’s water supply and encroach on Native lands and burial grounds – were maced, attacked by dogs and arrested en masse. Later that winter, thousands more protesters or “water protectors” convened on the Great Plains, and outrage over the pipeline’s construction became a louder, global movement for Native rights and climate justice. But it did not stop Dallas-based Energy Transfer Partners from building the project, and national guard and police cleared the last holdout of protesters in an early 2017 military-style takeover. The pipeline now transports up to 750,000 barrels of oil a day from North Dakota to an Illinois refinery. In a powerful moment Thursday evening, Manape LaMere – an original headsman from the 2016 council and a member of the Sioux nation – retrieved the original coals and lit the fire as he had 10 years ago. One of LaMere’s other responsibilities at the Mni Wiconi gathering was to help perform a spiritual healing ceremony to help those who were at the camps find closure from the trauma of what they experienced. “When we sacrifice in camp the way we did, all that hardship and all that beauty, I always encourage people to call their spirit back,” LaMere said. “But because we got evicted the way we did, a lot of us may not have received that message, and I’ve seen people struggle.” Reunion attendees, at open mic sessions or around fire pits, reflected on how the often-violent standoffs between protesters and law enforcement in 2016 left many with lingering trauma, like for Candi Brings Plenty, a member of the Oglala Lakota Sioux nation. But, Brings Plenty said, while the event left scars, the community formed among camps has created lifelong strength. “I got the best knowledge and woksape, which is a Lakota word for wisdom, being at Standing Rock. I got so much empowerment and even though I got the worst-of-the-worst PTSD and everything that came along with it, you know, I would do it again,” Brings Plenty said. At the Prairie Knights Casino, the inaugural People of the Sun event brought together renewable energy groups, activists and performers for a three-day summit focusing on clean energy solutions. Speakers and panelists said that the protests 10 years ago underscored the need for Native reservations to build more sustainable energy systems that align with tribal values. One group making those systems a reality is the Sage Development Authority, a federally chartered corporation formed by the Standing Rock Sioux nation. The group uses grant funding to build wind farms for tribal district buildings, which allows local leaders to then reinvest that money back into their communities. Joseph McNeil, the CEO of SAGE and an enrolled member of the Standing Rock Sioux nation, said building infrastructure that allows his community to gain energy independence has intergenerational impacts. “The intergenerational poverty has been so dire, and being forced and your economy purposely depressed has been so intentional, that we can be voices for that and try to think of ways to help folks who aren’t there,” McNeil said. “We’re putting the stuff onto the district buildings, but it’s up to the district. We’re not going to dictate you, have your own choices, make your own decisions, and then live with those.” In support of the People of the Sun event was the actor Shailene Woodley, whose arrest at the protest 10 years ago spurred additional public discourse around the pipeline. “Do your research. Learn about the history, the real history of what happened to this country when our ancestors chose to colonize this land. And not from a place of guilt, not from a place of shame, but from a place of empowerment,” Woodley said in an interview. “If we don’t pay attention and if we don’t educate ourselves on what happened, then we’re going to continue to even unknowingly repeat those patterns and feed into the same cycles.”

title: Republican calls for Senate investigation of Trump Jr wedding paid for by Russian oligarch
summary: Putin ally helped cover cost of renting private island in the Bahamas for wedding of Trump Jr and Bettina Anderson
text: A Republican senator has accused Donald Trump Jr of corruption and demanded a Senate investigation into revelations that a Russian oligarch bankrolled part of his recent wedding in the Bahamas. John Curtis, of Utah, wrote to the leaders of the US Senate judiciary committee on Tuesday, urging them to subpoena Trump Jr over his business dealings, his relationships with foreign individuals, gifts he has received – and any occasions where his connection to his father, Donald Trump, “was invoked or understood to provide value”. Trump Jr’s wedding warrants the kind of scrutiny Republicans once trained on Hunter Biden, the son of Joe Biden, Curtis said. “A toaster is a wedding gift. A private-island party paid for by a Putin-connected oligarch is something else,” he wrote in a social media post accompanying the letter to the committee. “Republicans nearly wore out the subpoena machine investigating Hunter Biden’s foreign relationships. We should not unplug it now.” The push follows reporting by ProPublica that Umar Kremlev, the Russian boxing official with close ties to Vladimir Putin, helped cover the cost of renting a private island and staging a fireworks display for the wedding of Trump Jr and Bettina Anderson in the Bahamas in May. Bettina Trump later described Kremlev on Instagram as a “dear friend” who had generously hosted two nights of post-wedding celebrations. Donald Trump, who did not attend the ceremony, defended Kremlev’s involvement but said he was told by Trump Jr that the money would eventually be reimbursed, though explained that giving a wedding party as a gift is “totally allowed” and is also “very common”. It is not the first time Trump Jr’s conduct has drawn scrutiny over ties to Russia. He was a central figure in the Robert Mueller investigation that followed the 2016 election, after it emerged he had attended a Trump Tower meeting with a Russian lawyer who had promised damaging material on Hillary Clinton. The call for a formal committee inquiry marks one of the sharper breaks with the president by a sitting Republican senator. Curtis first flagged the wedding payment as problematic on Friday, calling it “corruption” in a video posted online and promising further comment. He was elected to the Senate in 2024, pledging not to shy away from disagreements with Trump. His letter, addressed to the committee chair, Chuck Grassley of Iowa, and its top Democrat, Dick Durbin of Illinois, lands amid signs of broader unease among Republicans over Trump’s standing heading into November’s US midterm elections, with the party facing pressure over the war in Iran, high gas prices and slipping poll numbers. Republicans in the House of Representatives spent much of 2023 and 2024 investigating whether Hunter Biden traded on his father’s name in his overseas business dealings, an effort that produced a report alleging a conspiracy to enrich the Biden family, but never resulted in impeachment articles reaching a House vote. The Bidens denied wrongdoing throughout. “‘Trust us’ was not enough then,” wrote Curtis, “and it is not enough now.”

title: European drugmakers say they are ‘losing ground’ to US and Chinese rivals
summary: Some of continent’s biggest pharma firms write to national leaders calling for action to safeguard the sector
text: Some of Europe’s biggest pharmaceutical companies have said the continent is “losing ground” to rivals including the US and China in developing new drugs and attracting investment. The chairs of nine companies, including Britain’s AstraZeneca, GSK and Denmark’s Novo Nordisk, wrote to Andy Burnham and the national leaders of other European countries on Tuesday to call for action to “safeguard our companies’ future”. The letter, entitled Europe is Losing the Pharma Investment Race – But the Comeback is Within Reach, called on governments to treat medicines as strategic infrastructure, secure health sovereignty and act now to restore Europe’s competitiveness. It argued that the pharmaceutical sector is one of Europe’s great postwar achievements that is supporting millions of highly skilled jobs and generating an EU trade surplus of more than €220bn (£188bn). “But this hard-won inheritance is at risk,” the letter said. “In our boardrooms, we see Europe losing ground to global competition. Over $600bn in pharmaceutical investment has been announced in the US and China in the last two years alone. “European governments must create conditions that attract investment in next-generation medicines before it’s too late,” said the letter, which was also signed by the chairs of Germany’s Boehringer Ingelheim, Italy’s Chiesi group, France’s Sanofi and Ipsen, and Novartis and Roche of Switzerland. Europe’s share of global pharmaceutical research and development has fallen from 43% in 1990 to 31%, according to the European Federation of Pharmaceutical Industries and Associations (EFPIA). The continent’s share of commercial clinical trials – where new medicines are tested for safety and efficacy before they are submitted for regulatory approval – has halved to 9% from 18% a decade ago. Only 4% of clinical trials are focused on cell and gene therapies. China has overtaken Europe in clinical trials, pharmaceutical patents, and the development of new medicines. The country’s share of global clinical trials rose from less than 10% to almost 30% over the same period. Almost half (49%) of newly approved therapies did not reach European patients last year, up from 46% in 2019; those drugs that do take nearly 600 days on average. This varies hugely from country to country: from a median 56 days in Germany to 1,201 days in Romania, according to data from the EFPIA. The industry body has said the root causes of unavailability and delay to accessing new medicines range from the speed of regulatory processes to insufficient budgets in some European countries. Closing the clinical trials gap alone could generate €53bn and create 82,000 jobs in Europe, the nine pharma companies argued in the letter. “We ask national leaders to work with us to reverse Europe’s declining competitiveness, unleash a new era of medical discovery, and secure health sovereignty. We recognise the fiscal pressures many face. But just like defence or energy, modern medicines should be treated as vital infrastructure and not be left to others to provide,” the letter said. It was signed by industry leaders including Michel Demaré, the chair of Britain’s biggest pharmaceutical company, AstraZeneca; Jonathan Symonds, his counterpart at GSK, the country’s second-biggest drugmaker; Lars Rebien Sørensen, the chair of the Wegovy and Ozempic maker, Novo Nordisk; Severin Schwan at the Swiss company Roche; Giovanni Caforio at fellow Swiss firm Novartis, and Frédéric Oudéa at France’s Sanofi. It comes after a public row last year between the industry and the UK government over drug pricing and availability of new treatments to patients. Ministers agreed in December to spend billions of pounds a year extra on medicines supplied to the NHS after pressure from Donald Trump, who argued that high drug prices in the US were subsidising lower prices elsewhere.
