title: Nick Clegg could make £30m windfall from datacentre startup Nscale flotation
summary: The former UK deputy prime minister is a board member of the UK-based company and owns 917,000 shares
text: Nick Clegg could make approximately $40m (£30m) from the planned float of Nscale as the UK-based datacentre company prepares for a US stock market listing. The former UK deputy prime minister owns more than 917,000 shares in the startup, which is reportedly seeking a valuation of up to $35bn in a flotation. Based on Clegg’s stake of 0.12%, that could yield a valuation of about $42m for the ex-Liberal Democrat party leader. Clegg is a board member at Nscale along with the former Meta executive, Sheryl Sandberg, whose 0.25% stake could be worth $88m if Nscale floats at the $35bn valuation, a figure reported by the Financial Times this month. However, Nscale was last valued in a funding round at $14.6bn, implying lower valuations of Clegg and Sandberg’s stakes of about $18m and $37m, respectively. Forbes has estimated Sandberg’s wealth at $2.4bn, while Clegg has made about £24m from sales of shares in Meta, where he was formerly the president of global affairs. Both are paid an annual retainer of $60,000. The Telegraph first reported Clegg’s potential wealth gain from the Nscale float. UK-based Nscale filed papers for its flotation in the US on 18 September and could make its stock market debut before the year end. The company is preparing to list in New York, reflecting its global ambitions and the depth of funding available in the US for expensive AI infrastructure projects. Nscale reported a loss of $1bn in the six months to 30 June, on revenues of $140m. In the flotation document, Nscale said its losses reflected the “substantial investments” it has made in a “highly capital intensive” business. Josh Payne, the chief executive of Nscale, has said the company sees a “significant” opportunity in sovereign AI, where countries develop their own models and infrastructure, in order to reduce reliance on US or Chinese technology. Christine Lagarde, president of the European Central Bank, and Margrethe Vestager, the former EU competition head, have both called for Europe to do more to develop its own AI infrastructure. “Nscale is well positioned to serve this demand as a trusted, sovereign-capable platform,” said Payne. “This is particularly true in Europe, where the need for sovereign AI infrastructure is especially acute, and where our British domicile positions us as a natural, trusted partner.” Nscale operates five datacentres in Europe and has a further 12 under different phases of construction including in the US. The Guardian revealed this year that one Nscale project in Loughton, Essex, is an undeveloped scrapyard. Nscale has been approached for comment.

title: Mississippi grand jury decides not to charge anyone in death of Nolan Wells
summary: Jury report says ‘no credible evidence’ points to criminal conduct related to death of Mississippi teen after boat outing with friends on 4 July
text: A grand jury made a unanimous decision on late Monday night to not bring criminal charges against anyone in the mysterious death of Nolan Wells, a Mississippi teen who died after a boat outing with friends on 4 July. The Jackson county, Mississippi grand jury, which met from 14 September to 18 September, issued 132 subpoenas during its investigation, considered evidence from 43 witnesses and investigators, and reviewed an independent investigation by Wells’s family. They also considered physical and digital evidence, including mobile phone data and forensic reports, photographs, videos and GPS data. A copy of the grand jury report was posted online by the Jackson county district attorney’s office, which said that there was “no credible evidence to support the public allegations that any persons who rode to or from Horn Island on July 4, 2026 … engaged in any criminal conduct related to the death of Mr Wells”. “The allegations against the occupants of the Triton, the Palm Beach, and the Tideline [boats that traveled to the island] are not based in truth, and are solely the result of public clamor and private malice,” the report says. Wells’s case drew national attention, with many speculating about what happened and suspecting that the teen’s disappearance and death may have been racially motivated. Wells, who was Black while the friends with whom he was last seen were white, was also the only friend in the group who didn’t return from the trip to the barrier island that day. Per the grand jury report, Wells chose to stay behind on the island and come back later with another group as it was “not unusual or suspicious for individuals to return from the island on boats they did not travel … on”. Wells’s family, however, has consistently pushed back on this claim, suggesting that it is not something that the teen would have done. “We always taught him that if you go with a group, you stay with a group,” said Elmore Wonsley, his father, during the Good Morning America appearance in July. “If you go with five, you come back with five. Do not separate from the group. Because I always said: ‘Safety is in numbers.’ So he knew to stay with this group, so why would he split from the group? I don’t know.” Wells’s family, through their attorney Ben Crump, announced the results of an autopsy performed by Dr Roger A Mitchell Jr, a forensic pathologist the team hired, in late July. Mitchell found that Wells had “sustained recent unexplained blunt force injuries to the back of the head and additional areas of his back”. Both the independent autopsy and the state’s chief medical examiner said that the cause and manner of Wells’s death were undetermined. “Drowning is a diagnosis of exclusion,” the grand jury report said. They also found that “the position of, the condition of, time of discovery, and location of Mr Wells’ body is consistent with drowning”. The grand jury found that Wells was not the only Black person on Horn Island on 4 July, and that “false assertions have led to misidentification, speculation, and rumors concerning the death of Mr Wells”, according to the report. “The family, the Crump team, and anyone close to Nolan knew that his disappearance and death were not the result of racial hate or violence,” said Angel Myers McIlrath, Jackson county’s district attorney, in a video posted on social media alongside the grand jury report on Monday. The 23 grand jurors included 13 men and 10 women. Twelve of the jurors were white, five were Black, two were Hispanic, two were Native American, one was Asian and one was identified as “other”, according to information released by the district attorney’s office. “There is absolutely no evidence to support the allegations that Nolan’s disappearance and death were racially motivated,” Myers McIlrath said in the video. Crump, the civil rights attorney who is representing the Wells family, said the grand jury’s decision is an attempt “to close the chapter on Nolan Wells’ death without getting to the truth”. Wells’s legal team is releasing Mitchell’s full report and requesting that the Jackson county district attorney do the same with the state’s medical examiner’s report. Additionally, they are calling on the district attorney’s office to keep the investigation open and active. Crump said that the report “leaves us with more questions than answers”. “Mississippi’s own pathologist found two bruises on the back of this young man’s head and informed investigators of them early in this investigation,” Crump said in a statement. “An independent autopsy documented traces of blood and recent blunt force injuries to the back of Nolan’s head and his back. To this day, not one person has explained how they got there. “Dr Mitchell also wrote that the record does not establish whether Nolan entered the water on his own or was forced, or whether he was conscious when he went in. We don’t know how Nolan died, and neither does the state of Mississippi. Mississippi must keep investigating, and if it will not pursue this to the end, the Department of Justice should.” There is no statute of limitations for homicide cases in Mississippi, something the grand jury report noted. If any evidence were to emerge that suggests that Wells’s death was not accidental, it should be referred to the grand jury for consideration.

title: Hayden Panettiere’s cause of death confirmed as fentanyl overdose
summary: South Carolina medical examiner says ‘no signs of trauma’ and ‘the manner of death has been ruled accident’
text: Hayden Panettiere died from a fentanyl overdose, according to the Greenville county coroner’s office. Medical examiners in South Carolina confirmed the 36-year old actor’s cause of death on Tuesday, saying: “The cause of death has been ruled as toxic effects of fentanyl, 4-ANPP, Alprazolam, Methocarbamol and Quetiapine.” They said there were “no signs of trauma” and “the manner of death has been ruled accident”. The Greenville police department separately said no foul play was suspected, telling Variety: “The preliminary investigation has not indicated any signs of foul play or suspicious circumstances.” “An acquaintance of Ms Panettiere placed the 911 call,” the police department said. Panettiere was in her South Carolina apartment with her boyfriend Brian Hickerson and his brother Zach Hickerson when she died on 16 August. A police report at the time stated that a Greenville police officer observed paramedics performing CPR on an unresponsive woman. It said: “The patient did not seem to have any obvious physical reasons to be unresponsive. “I observed Zach to be very emotional while EMS were working on Hayden. Brian did not become emotional until EMS declared her officially deceased.” Following Panettiere’s death, her father, Skip Panettiere, released a statement, saying: “It is with profound sadness that we share the tragic passing of our beloved Hayden. She was an incredible light and a force of nature who brought immeasurable love and joy to all who knew her – and to the millions who watched her onscreen.” Panettiere, known for her roles in television series including Heroes and Nashville, began acting at just 11 months old. She earned two Golden Globe nominations for her portrayal of country singer Juliette Barnes on the ABC series Nashville. Her other projects included Scream 4 in 2011 and Scream VI in 2023. In 2014, Panettiere had a daughter, Kaya, with her former fiance, Ukrainian boxer Wladimir Klitschko. In 2018, she gave Klitschko full custody while focusing on her recovery from depression, anxiety and substance abuse. Speaking to People magazine in 2022, Panettiere said: “This hasn’t been easy and there were a lot of ups and downs … But I don’t regret even the ugliest things that have happened to me. I feel incredibly accomplished. And I feel like I have a second chance.” In an interview with podcast host Jay Shetty in May, Panettiere spoke about her relationship with her daughter, saying: “I will always want her here. I always miss her … I always want to have my arms wrapped around her, but that’s just not the way life is right at this moment … I have faith that she is going to come to me and that we’re going to have an incredible relationship and bond and friendship that a lot of parents don’t get to have with their kids.” That same month, Panettiere released a memoir titled This Is Me: A Reckoning, in which she detailed her struggled with fame, postpartum depression, addiction and recovery.

title: UK tech workers: do you want to join a trade union?

title: ‘Literally state-run TV’: Trump launches YouTube channel amid boycott by US networks
summary: White House press coverage row continues while anchor-less channel of the administration’s ‘latest and greatest’ streams propaganda for the Maga faithful
text: Donald Trump’s previous television career centred on his role on The Apprentice, but the US president’s latest media venture is a rather lower-budget affair: the launch of Trump TV in the wake of his ban on several outlets from covering the White House. With major US networks agreeing to not cover the president while the dispute continues, on Monday the White House announced the new 24/7 YouTube live stream, which it promised would feature “top past moments, announcements, and the latest and greatest from the administration all in one place”. The anchor-less channel dispenses with traditional broadcast norms. With no schedule, no on-screen description of what is being shown, and zero context for where or when a clip was recorded, the effect of having the channel on in the background is less like watching a news network and more like installing Trump wallpaper – a 24-hour fever dream of self-soothing propaganda for the Maga faithful. On Tuesday, the stream swung wildly between cinematic replays of Trump attending a UK state banquet, emotional footage of Laken Riley’s mother praising Trump as “a man of his word”, an 18-month-old clip of Melania Trump at an awards ceremony, and Trump delivering a long, rambling press conference in February 2025 in which he casually advocated for the US taking over Gaza and absorbing Canada as the 51st state. Despite the channel boasting more than 3 million subscribers, the initial appetite for this unedited stream of consciousness appeared modest at best: live viewer counts hovered at around 1,500. A minute-long trailer for the new service features an uptempo electronic version of The Buggles’ hit Video Killed the Radio Star by Andrew Spencer, while clips from Seinfeld, Modern Family, Breaking Bad, Friends, Parks and Recreation, The Office and many more show a host of familiar faces scrambling to apparently watch the channel on their televisions. The clips originate from a wide range of US networks, including Warner Bros, Fox, Nickelodeon, Sony Pictures Television, Disney and NBCUniversal. While the animation staples Family Guy, The Simpsons and SpongeBob SquarePants feature in the trailer, notably absent is any appearance of characters from South Park, the satirical show that has taken to portraying the US president as being in a relationship with Satan, and frequently mocks the size and appearance of Trump’s genitals. The California governor, Gavin Newsom, a potential Democratic presidential candidate for the 2028 election, decried the launch of Trump TV as “quite literally state-run TV” and “truly autocratic behaviour”, which he said Trump was using to “drown out the fact that he and his corrupt administration are failing”. As part of his escalating row with the media, Trump described established US outlets as a threat to national security, posting on Truth Social: “The White House is not instituting an assault on the Free Press, something which I cherish. It is instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS, something that has grown like Cancer.” With the network pool refusing to cover the president on Monday, a White House-produced live stream covered Trump opening a new helipad at the White House, with his remarks totally inaudible due to the helicopter behind him.

title: Could you be an ‘autumn spotter’? Public asked to track changing colours of trees in England
summary: Forestry England invites people to help it create a record of when and how the season arrives across the country
text: The reds and golds of autumn leaves may be beginning to appear, but exactly when the season arrives is not always as predictable as the calendar might suggest. Now, Forestry England is asking people to help track the changing colours of forests to create a record of when and how autumn arrives across the country. The Autumn Leaf Watch citizen science project invites people to become “autumn spotters” using Forestry England’s new autumn colour tracker. Those taking part can record the most common leaf colour they spot on visits to forests, or search for hues of leaves on specific tree species, including beech, horse chestnut, oak, rowan and silver birch. By collecting observations over the coming weeks and in future years, Forestry England, which is in charge of the country’s woodlands, hopes to build a picture of how the timing and development of autumn colour varies between regions, habitats and tree species. Early observations suggest autumn remains in its infancy, Forestry England said, with most reports showing green woodland canopies. But yellow and orange leaves have already been recorded at Wyre Forest in Worcestershire, Haughmond Hill in Shropshire and Delamere Forest in Cheshire. Silver birch and beech are among the first species showing colour change, while oak has so far remained predominantly green across much of the country. The timing of autumn is influenced by factors including daylight, temperature, rainfall, soil moisture and the health of individual trees. Forestry England said this year’s extremely hot and dry summer had caused some trees to shed their leaves earlier than usual. It is too early to say what effect those climate crisis-driven conditions will have on this autumn as a whole, with weather over the coming weeks helping to determine how the season develops. Chris Sorenson, a forest management adviser at Forestry England, said the UK’s summer of extreme heat made this year particularly interesting to observe. “Some trees have already shed leaves early, but there’s still plenty of autumn to come,” he said. “We want people to get outside, look closely at the trees around them and help us track it.” The changing of the colours is part of the process by which deciduous trees prepare for winter. With days shortening and temperatures falling, trees stop producing chlorophyll, the green pigment in their leaves, causing yellow and orange pigments already present in the leaves to become visible. Some species also produce red pigments. The timing and intensity of the change can vary considerably between species and locations, making observations from across the country useful for understanding how autumn develops from year to year.

title: ‘Looksmaxxing’ influencer Clavicular charged with rape and drug offenses
summary: The Massachusetts case is the latest in a series of legal woes for the influencer whose real name is Braden Eric Peters
text: The online influencer known as Clavicular – who has helped to fuel the rise of the extreme male appearance-improvement trend of “looksmaxxing” – has been charged with rape and drug offenses in Massachusetts. The 20-year-old, whose real name is Braden Eric Peters, has been scheduled for a 14 October arraignment on Cape Cod, according to legal documents seen by the Guardian. He faces up to life in prison on felony counts of rape, drugging a person for sexual intercourse, and a misdemeanor charge of providing liquor to a minor. The offenses are alleged to have taken place in Massachusetts in May 2025. It was not immediately clear if they related to a separate lawsuit filed in April by a teenager in Florida who said that Peters gave her alcohol during a 2025 party at his parents’ home on Cape Cod, then had sex with her while she was passed out. The girl was 16 at the time of that alleged incident. Peters rose to prominence as a promoter of “looksmaxxing”, which analysts have described as a toxic pursuit by young men of altering or improving their facial looks and physiques, using extreme measures such as bone smashing to achieve more chiseled jawlines, oral and plastic surgeries, and lip enhancement. The trend, which moved into the mainstream from its roots in the misogynistic “incel” (involuntary celibate) community, has an online following of millions. It has also been blamed by mental health experts for worsening issues of self-esteem, depression and social anxiety in teenage boys for its messaging that romantic success is tied to physical perfection. The charges against Peters in Massachusetts were filed in Orleans district court on 8 September, the records show, and a summons was issued the same day. A representative of Peters told multiple media outlets that Bulwark, the online news site that first reported the charges, was “exaggerating” the status of the case “to boost traffic” because, he said, the influencer had not been physically served. Peters, who has an online following of more than a million, did not respond to the charges directly. But he posted a cryptic message on X on Monday night accusing the teenager who filed the Florida lawsuit of “trying to get my attention in anyway possible” and calling her “petty”. It was accompanied by a photograph of a letter allegedly written by the teen – who has publicly identified herself – pledging “you have my loyalty 100%”. The lawsuit makes allegations against Peters of battery, intentional infliction of emotional distress, fraud, and unauthorized publication of her name and likeness, according to NBC6 South Florida that reported the developments in April. It stops short of accusing Peters of rape despite the allegations in the lawsuit. According to the lawsuit, Peters initially paid her $1,000 and told her he wanted to make her “the female face of looksmaxxing” – but their relationship soured and went through several highs and lows. When the teen was in Massachusetts in 2025, it said, Peters paid for an Uber to take her to the party at his parents’ home. The age of consent in Massachusetts is 16 – but she alleges that Peters served her vodka despite being under the legal drinking age and “to the point where she was unable to give consent”, then had sex with her anyway. After ignoring her for six months afterwards, the lawsuit said, they rekindled their relationship to a point where Peters was paying her $15,000 a month as a social media promoter. But they fell out again and Peters began an online campaign to discredit her. The teen said Peters also injected her twice against her will with methamphetamine-laced Aqualyx, a substance not approved by the US Food and Drug administration (FDA), to melt fat around her cheeks and jawline. Steven Kramer, Peters’ attorney in that case, said in a statement at the time that his client “denies the claims and disputes the characterization of events”. He said Peters would “vigorously defend himself” through the appropriate legal channels and would not be making any further comment. The Massachusetts rape case is the latest in a series of recent legal woes for Peters, who in February was reported by the New York Times to be earning in excess of $100,000 monthly for his livestreams. In March, he was charged in Florida with firearms offenses for allegedly shooting a dead alligator during a livestream. He pleaded no contest in exchange for six months’ probation and 20 hours of unpaid community service. The same month, he and a girlfriend – Violet Marie Lentz, 24 – were arrested and charged with battery stemming from an alleged assault on a 19-year-old woman at a rented house in Kissimmee, Florida. • Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organizations. In the US, Rainn offers support on 800-656-4673. In the UK, Rape Crisis offers support on 0808 500 2222. In Australia, support is available at 1800Respect (1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found at ibiblio.org/rcip/internl.html

title: UK borrows £18bn in August, putting pressure on Healey before budget
summary: Some economists say it is now ‘inevitable’ that chancellor will need to raise taxes in the budget next month
text: The UK government borrowed a higher-than-expected £18.3bn last month, increasing the pressure on John Healey as he attempts to calm jittery bond markets before next month’s budget. Some economists said it was “inevitable” that the chancellor would need to raise taxes on 28 October if he is to meet demands for extra spending on defence without further borrowing from investors on international money markets. Official figures released by the Office for National Statistics on Tuesday said public sector net borrowing – the difference between government spending and income – was £2.9bn higher last month than in August 2025. It meant that borrowing jumped by £3.5bn above the level expected by the government’s independent forecaster, the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR), taking the deficit over the financial year so far to £77.3bn – £8.1bn above forecast. The £18.3bn borrowed in August was also more than the £15.6bn City analysts had forecast. Healey, the chancellor, has promised to stick within the government’s spending limits, which restrict the amount the Treasury can borrow as a proportion of national income. The August figures come after the government ran a larger-than-expected £1.8bn deficit in July, when analysts had expected the figure to be zero. Thomas Pugh, the chief economist at the consultancy RSM UK, said: “The jump in borrowing in August compared to last year sets the stage for what is likely to be a much trickier budget than Burnham or Healey anticipated when they came to power just a few months ago. Another round of tax rises in October now looks inevitable.” The UK has been among the countries hardest hit by the rise in the interest rate on government bonds amid turmoil in financial markets. While the cost of financing UK bonds has eased in the last week, the Treasury remains under pressure to show it can reduce its reliance on heavy borrowing to maintain welfare spending. On Tuesday, the yield – or interest rate – on 10-year UK bonds rose three basis points (bps) to 5.232%, while 30-year bond yields were also 3bps higher at 5.729% in early trading. Chris Beauchamp, the chief market analyst at IG, said: “The PM and chancellor will be feeling quite claustrophobic today as the walls close in around them. Borrowing costs keep climbing, while borrowing itself is outpacing the teeny rise in tax receipts.” The Institute for Fiscal Studies, a thinktank, said that since April, the government had spent £50bn on debt interest, £2bn more than forecast by the OBR in March. “On those forecasts – made before the most recent hikes in government interest rates – debt interest was set to be more than £100bn every year over the next five years,” said Nick Ridpath, an IFS research economist. Central government spending on social security benefits and pensions climbed by almost £10bn more than in the same period last year – from £135.3bn to £145bn – mostly in response to rising inflation. The consumer prices indexrose last month to 3.1% and, while the Bank of England held interest rates at its latest meeting last week, the central bank warned that the cost of borrowing may need to rise in the coming months if inflationary pressures persist. Martin Beck, the chief economist at the consultancy WPI Strategy, said: “Today’s public finance figures are another unwelcome setback for the government ahead of next month’s budget.” The International Monetary Fund has urged western governments to gain greater control over their public finances to reassure financial markets that they remain safe havens for lenders. Emma Reynolds, the chief secretary to the Treasury, said the government was committed to improving the UK’s economic growth, “but we can only deliver that growth with fiscal discipline”. She added: “At a time when debt interest costs billions of pounds that could otherwise be spent on improving lives, we must always know where the money is coming from to pay for public services.” The Conservative party Treasury spokesperson, Andrew Griffith, accused Labour of losing control of the public finances. “They are borrowing so much they’ve overshot the OBR forecast by an extra £8bn of debt,” he said. “It takes a rare fiscal incontinence to both have the highest tax take in history and see borrowing still shoot up.” However, the OBR has said estimates of government borrowing published early in the financial year should be considered provisional and they are likely to be revised.

title: Ed Davey promises £17bn income tax cut if Lib Dems are elected
summary: Growth created by rejoining EU single market and customs union would fund change, Davey tells the party’s conference
text: Ed Davey has unveiled a plan for a £17bn income tax cut in a speech aimed at shoring up the party’s support among former Conservative voters, but which risked disappointing some Liberal Democrat MPs who want a bolder vision for the party. Addressing the party’s annual conference in Brighton, the Lib Dem leader said the proposal, which would eventually increase the threshold for paying income tax to £15,000 and raise the level at which people pay the 40p higher rate by about £6,000, would be paid for entirely by increased growth. This growth, the Lib Dems argue, would be created through rejoining the EU’s single market and customs union. As making a deal with the EU would take time, the actual tax cuts would only happen in the final year of a parliament, potentially as late as 2034, costing £17bn. In the interim years, thresholds would be raised by inflation, thus keeping levels effectively stable. There would also be a smaller increase to the 45p additional rate of tax, currently payable above £125,000. Setting out what he described as “trusting people to spend their own money, not telling them the state knows best”, Davey took aim at what he called “the post-Brexit stealth taxes” of frozen thresholds, notably on the higher 40p rate. “Thirty years ago, just 2 million people paid it. Now it’s 9 million,” he said. “A tax band designed for stockbrokers is now holding back teachers and nurses. That’s not fair. It’s not right.” The plans mark a distinct shift in the party’s fiscal approach. While it is eyecatching and could appeal to the many former Conservative voters who backed the Lib Dems in 2024, helping them take 60-plus Tory seats, it is likely to cause unease among some of the party’s MPs. A number of them have called privately for a more ambitious and comprehensive vision of what the party stands for, amid polling that shows most voters do not have much of a sense of this. Davey’s advisers, however, argue that the cost of living is the subject that most affects many voters, and that tax cuts – even up to eight years in the future – directly address this. Other elements of the speech included previously-trailed new policies, including a proposal for a global nuclear-style non-proliferation treaty to halt the development of super-intelligent AI. The tax-cutting plan is predicated entirely on the EU allowing a swift deal on single market access, which could become even more difficult if rightwing populists take power in more EU states, and on this then increasing growth. The Lib Dems insist the numbers stand up, saying they are based on a report from an independent economics consultancy, which calculated that a deal with the EU could generate 0.5% growth in the first fiscal year alone. Reform UK has already pledged to increase the personal tax allowance to £15,000, paid for in part by significant cuts to social security. Davey noted this in the speech, saying: “Think about that. Reform say you can have a tax cut, but only if they get to punish disabled people at the same time. We say no. We can cut taxes and support the most vulnerable people in our country.” Opening his speech with a warning that black-shirted, and balaclava-wearing far-right protesters who gathered in Dover and Portsmouth “would tear our country apart”, Davey compared groups such as Patriot Platform to Oswald Mosley’s fascists in the 1930s, the National Front in the 70s and to Nick Griffin and the BNP. “Each time, they tried to turn neighbour against neighbour, tried to pit community against community, tried to turn our streets into battlegrounds,” he said. “But we didn’t let them. The British people said no.” He said this time, far-right vigilantes were not acting in isolation, but were the most visible part of a far-right threat that was “extremely well funded” and promoted by figures such as Elon Musk and given credibility by “cynical politicians like Nigel Farage”. Davey slammed Farage as a cynical politician who was “not just willing, but eager to fan the flames of hatred and intolerance to make himself richer”. He said: “It is the worst of Trump’s America. We must not let it become Farage’s Britain.” Pointing to the £72m donations Reform had received from two crypto billionaires, Davey added: “If there was any doubt before, there can’t be now. We are in the fight of our lives. And it is a fight we must win.”

title: Up to 169 killed in Yemen as Houthis battle for Red Sea coastal heights
summary: Thousands flee renewed fighting as Iran-aligned group seeks to consolidate territorial gains against Saudi-backed government forces
text: As many as 169 people have been reportedly killed in Yemen in the last three days as Iran-aligned Houthis battle Saudi-backed government forces for control of strategic heights on the Red Sea coast, while thousands flee the violence. Houthi military officials said at least 118 people had been killed in clashes as well as Saudi air and artillery strikes on Taiz, al-Jawf, Marib and Saada provinces since Sunday, Agence France-Presse reported. Yemeni government sources have said at least 36 people have been killed on their side of the conflict. The Houthis accused Saudi Arabia of striking the port city of Mocha on Tuesday, killing six civilians, including two children. The group also said a Saudi strike on a prison in al-Jawf province, north-western Yemen, killed nine detainees. The Saudi government, which backs Yemen’s UN-recognised government against Houthi forces, on Tuesday issued an alert in the south of the country before potential strikes, after the Houthis launched strikes at the Saudi capital, Riyadh, at the weekend for the first time in years. The renewed fighting came after a dramatic offensive launched by the Houthis three weeks earlier in which the group seized control of much of Yemen’s Red Sea coast from government-aligned forces. They were the most significant territorial gains in the last four years of the civil war in the country. The offensive has upended global energy markets, which are already reeling from the Iranian closure of the strait of Hormuz, and further expanded the regional scope of the US-Iran war, now in its seventh month. Last week the Houthis took control of Mocha and other strategic cities, which gave them control over the Bab al-Mandab strait, a key shipping lane home to 10% of all global maritime traffic that has gained renewed importance after the closure of the strait of Hormuz. The clashes have compounded an already dire humanitarian crisis, where about 22 million people need humanitarian assistance and 5.2 million people are already internally displaced. Yemen’s civil war started in 2014 when the Houthis seized control of the country’s capital and toppled the government. A Saudi-led coalition then intervened in an aerial campaign on behalf of the internationally recognised Yemeni government and allied militias. A UN-brokered ceasefire was established in 2022, which had largely held until the Houthis launched the current offensive. In recent days, clashes have focused on the strategic Kahboub mountains near the Red Sea coast as the Houthis seek to consolidate recent territorial gains. Government forces have been trying to hold the line against the Houthi advance on multiple fronts to prevent them from seizing the mountain range. Control of the mountains would give the Houthis a strategic vantage point over Red Sea coastal areas and would further cut off Aden, the seat of Yemeni government forces, from the western coast. Seizing the mountains would also complicate future government counterattacks. The Houthis have advanced on multiple fronts, particularly the outskirts of Taiz province and the coastal area of Ras al-Ara, with the greater goal of controlling the Kahboub mountains. Media affiliated with the Houthis have reported gains in the area, while government media said its fighters had successfully repelled Houthi incursions. Since the Houthi campaign was launched, the group has routed government-aligned forces from western Yemen. The prospect of an Iranian-aligned force controlling Bab al-Mandeb has worried Saudi Arabia as it would place two shipping lanes vital to its energy exports in the hands of Iran and its allies. Saudi Arabia has launched hundreds of strikes on Yemen in recent days to try to stop the Houthis, with little success. Donald Trump reportedly considered striking the Houthis over the weekend but called them off at the last minute, while the UK said it would assist aerial refuelling of Saudi aircraft engaged in defensive missions, leaving open the prospect of further international intervention. Members of the G7 have called on Iran to stop arming the Houthis. In a joint statement released ahead of the UN general assembly, member states urged the Houthis to stop their strikes on Saudi Arabia, which have damaged key oil infrastructure and wounded dozens. “We call on the Houthis to immediately cease all military actions, all threats and attacks against civilian shipping, and to return to the political process in good faith,” the statement read. The clashes have killed about 700 people and displaced more than 100,000 people, pushing some Yemenis to flee the fighting via sea. Civilians have fled westwards across the Red Sea to Djibouti, while aid groups warn conditions for those remaining in Yemen are deteriorating. Babar Baloch, a UN refugee agency spokesperson, said on Tuesday that displacement inside Yemen could rise to 230,000 people and more than 10,000 could flee to Djibouti if fighting continued. Saudi Arabia has tried to marshal international support to roll back the Houthi offensive, with the Saudi crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman, asking Trump to strike the Houthis – a request Trump has thus far refused. Trump held a call with the head of Yemen’s governing body, Rashad al-Alimi, on Monday, with al-Alimi asking the US for military assistance. Trump expressed solidarity but did not promise military support, a source told Agence France-Presse.

title: British banks warned not to invest in planned Israeli settlement before UK trade ban begins
summary: MPs send out letter as Israeli government seeks bids for construction of large E1 settlement in West Bank
text: British banks and financial institutions are receiving written warnings from MPs that they should not invest in Israel’s E1 settlement project even though new UK laws banning trade with illegal settlements are unlikely to be in place for months. A letter was sent to banks on Tuesday by the all-party Britain-Palestine group of MPs saying the onus was now on banks to review their obligations not to cooperate with new settlements. The foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, announced two weeks ago plans for a complete ban on trade with illegal settlements and new sanctions on those co-operating with building the settlements. But complex secondary legislation needed for the powers to come into force may take six to nine months to pass through parliament. The issue is urgent since the Israeli government is seeking bids for two tenders for the construction of as many as 3,400 houses, including more than 1,300 for which the tender closes on 25 October, two days before the elections. Israel’s finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, said in 2025 that the E1 settlement “practically erases the two-state delusion” by splitting up territory that would be set aside for a Palestinian state. The settlement plan has long been delayed due to its uncontested political impact on the prospect of a two-state solution, still the main peace plan backed by the west and Gulf states. Finance, insurance and guarantees are required before construction starts. One of Miliband’s motives in acting earlier this month, before the Israeli elections, was not just to express his deep concern at the scale of settler violence in the West Bank but to deter UK finance from helping with the tenders or the construction. It has been alleged that he overrode some diplomatic advice in acting before the elections. The all-party group said: “The immediate question is what commitments institutions were willing to make while the detailed rules are being developed, and how they would respond when restrictions take effect”. The letter, signed by two Labour MPs, Debbie Abrahams and Andy McDonald, states: “Commitments made now may be difficult to unwind when restrictions commence; the allocation of costs will depend on the contracts and applicable law. We ask boards to consider this interim risk before agreeing new or increased commitments.” The letter adds: “We ask you to place potential E1 and settlement-related exposure on the board’s agenda and on the risk register, and to reach a reasoned decision on whether the associated sanctions, legal and reputational risk sits within the institution’s stated risk appetite.” It is argued that postcodes provide the locality of a product’s origin, and nothing is being attempted that would stop trade in general with Israel. Abrahams said: “We are not asking to pre-empt the law. We are asking boards a question they should be able to answer today: what exposure are you prepared to carry while the sanctions regime is written and on what evidence?” The all-party group said it intended to publish replies to its letter by 10 October.

title: High-mileage electric cars are more reliable than petrol ones, study finds
summary: EVs with 90,000 to 120,000 miles on the clock are more likely to pass MOTs than petrol models of the same age
text: Motorists buying a secondhand car with a lot of miles on the clock are likely to find an electric vehicle (EV) ultimately more reliable than a petrol vehicle, according to a study. An analysis of 47.4m MOT tests found that after cars were driven 90,000 to 120,000 miles, EVs were about 25% less likely to fail than petrol models of the same age (based on a failure rate of 16.5% versus 22.1%). Beyond 120,000 miles, 16% of EVs failed, compared with 23.5% of petrol cars. The study found relatively little difference between the two fuel types at lower mileages. The study by the consultancy New AutoMotive on behalf of the industry group the British Vehicle Rental and Leasing Association (BVRLA) comes as a growing number of EVs change hands. Many used to belong to company and leasing fleets so have potentially racked up a lot of miles. Toby Poston, the BVRLA chief executive, said that mileage is “one of the first things people look at when buying a used car, and passing 60,000 or 70,000 miles can have a big impact on how a vehicle is perceived”. He added: “What this data shows is that mileage alone should not put consumers off. A well-maintained, higher-mileage electric car can be an extremely durable used vehicle. “That matters because the used market is where the transition to electric becomes accessible to millions more motorists. Giving buyers confidence in these cars will be critical to creating a healthy and affordable secondhand EV market.” Ben Nelmes, the chief executive of New AutoMotive, which carried out the research, said that high mileage “isn’t a proxy for poor condition in the way buyers have traditionally assumed. The data suggests the mechanical simplicity of an electric drivetrain starts to become increasingly valuable as cars accumulate miles.” The study also identified areas where electric cars performed worse, particularly tyres. EVs recorded nearly twice as many tyre defects as petrol cars and older, low-mileage electric cars showed increased friction-brake defects. Researchers attributed the latter to corrosion associated with the brakes being used less frequently. MOT tests examine statutory roadworthiness, including brakes, tyres, suspension, steering and lights, but do not measure battery health, degradation or charging performance. This information would therefore need to be considered alongside mechanical roadworthiness when assessing any used EV, the researchers said. “This isn’t an argument for buying a used EV without doing your homework,” Poston said. “Buyers should look at its history, condition, tyres and battery health just as they would scrutinise the engine, gearbox and service history of a petrol or diesel car. “What we can now challenge is the idea that an electric car with 80,000 or 100,000 miles on the clock should automatically be regarded as worn out.”

title: Superpowers cannot solve world’s problems, UN chief says in final general assembly address
summary: António Guterres says humanity faces unprecedented convergence of threats but mechanisms for collective action are under growing strain
text: The world’s fault lines have turned from cracks into canyons as superpowers show that they alone do not have the military, economic and technological power to guarantee security or solve the world’s problems, the outgoing secretary general of the United Nations has said in his final address to the general assembly. In a speech laced with despair but also glimpses of defiant hope, António Guterres said that over the last decade, largely spanning his 10-year period in office, “wars erupted with devastating consequences and dragged on with despicable cruelty. Civilians were targeted. Human rights trampled. Hunger weaponised. Humanitarians killed. International law cast aside.” He continued: “Geopolitical divides have deepened. Inequalities have intensified. Trust has frayed. The climate crisis went from distant warning to daily reality. And artificial intelligence moved at a speed that has blindsided even those who created it.” Without naming Israel, he said what followed the Hamas attack of October 2023 “was an onslaught on Palestinians in Gaza, with a scale of killing and destruction unlike anything I have witnessed in all my years as secretary general”. He rounded on profiteering energy companies for “treating the world as an open sewer”, described Africa’s omission from a permanent place on the UN security council as stunning, and called for a new compact to regulate AI. Throughout, the 77-year-old Portuguese politician and diplomat argued that a multilateral system centred on a newly representative UN was the only way to address this new convergence of problems. However, he warned: “At the very moment when humanity faces an unprecedented convergence of threats, our mechanisms for collective action are under growing strain.” Without mentioning Donald Trump once, he said what was required was “a recognition, especially by superpowers, that their power isn’t so super. Their power has limits. The events of recent years have made that unmistakably clear. Military power alone cannot secure peace. Economic power alone cannot command stability. And technological power alone cannot guarantee security.” It was critical to avoid hegemonic tendencies and what Guterres described as the “great fracture” – the division of the world into two rival blocs with separate economic, technological and security systems. The defining challenge of the age, he said, was that world governance, reflecting the power realities of a bygone age, was not adapting to the way power was being redistributed between and within states. At the same time there was “an extraordinary transfer of power away from governments to a handful of private corporations and individuals. Their reach now extends across politics, economies, information flows, technological development, and the civic space on which societies depend,” he said. “Humans are increasingly handing over power to machines – with artificial intelligence agents going rogue, and lethal autonomous weapons going from science fiction to military reality.” The choice was now whether the world was going to continue to fragment with rising tension, transactionalism and shrinking cooperation or change course towards a multilateral system centred on a UN that was balanced and representative. “The test before us is whether power will be exercised with the law – or beyond it,” Guterres said. “We must pass that test. We must defend the charter without double standards. Protect civilians without exception.” He urged world leaders to stop letting civilians pay the price for the cascading conflicts across the Middle East. Demanding that the fighting must stop and humanitarian aid must flow, he pointed out that the international court of justice had ordered last year that the UN be allowed to fulfil its mandates in Gaza. “Meanwhile violence, displacement and settlement expansion in the occupied West Bank are bulldozing the path to peace and raising the spectre of ethnic cleansing. We cannot allow the two-state solution to disappear before our eyes,” he said. In Ukraine, Guterres said, “Russia’s full-scale invasion has subjected a sovereign country to a brutal war in blatant violation of the charter”. But now, he also warned, “in parts of Russia homes, energy and water systems and transport have come under repeated attack, threatening food and energy supply chains globally”. For decades, he said, “big oil has treated the atmosphere as an open sewer – and cashed in on the consequences. Since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, five major western oil companies have pocketed nearly half a trillion dollars in profits. Compare that with just $34bn in international public adaptation finance for developing countries in the latest year reported.” He added: “With a supersized El Niño coming towards humanity, everyday people are paying more for energy, food and insurance.” Although he admitted a 21st-century security council without permanent African representation was unjust and indefensible, he defended the cash-strapped and much maligned organisation, saying the UN was where the powerful were held to account. He announced that the United Nations had “achieved gender parity for the first time in history across all senior leadership … all headquarters … and all professional staff”. “Equality is not a dream. It is a decision,” he said. “If the UN can change, so can businesses, parliaments, governments, peace processes.”

title: Lib Dems quietly commission review into religious inclusion amid case brought by dropped candidate
summary: Richard Newby to chair inquiry commissioned in response to discrimination case brought by David Campanale, who is claiming £790,000 in damages
text: The Liberal Democrats have quietly commissioned a review into the treatment of figures within their ranks who hold religious views, weeks after the Guardian revealed a religious discrimination claim against the party by the former candidate David Campanale. Campanale, a former BBC journalist, was selected in 2021 as the party’s candidate for Sutton and Cheam but was removed in August 2023. He has argued in a civil case against the party that discrimination against his Christianity cost him his political career. Richard Newby, the former Lib Dem leader in the House of Lords, has been appointed to chair the party’s inclusion and faith review, which will examine how the party treats candidates and members of different faith and those without. The inquiry, which has not been publicly announced, was set up in direct response to Campanale’s case, the Guardian understands, with figures at the top of the party understood to be keen to show they take the issue seriously. The Guardian revealed last month that Campanale was seeking almost £790,000 in damages after the party admitted direct and indirect discrimination on the grounds of religion or belief, and failures in dealing with complaints about his treatment. The case prompted the former Lib Dem leader Tim Farron and former deputy leader Simon Hughes to call for an independent inquiry into Campanale’s treatment by the party, as well as an apology. The party cannot comment on court proceedings and will instead use Lord Newby’s review to seek to answer the general question of whether people of faith are being discriminated against, and to what extent any evidence shows this. Hughes told the Guardian he would pursue a separate investigation once Campanale’s case was resolved. “The Newby review is explicitly not about any past or present legal case and cannot be about David’s case, which is still before the courts and with one remaining possible internal party appeal,” he said. “The review however is greatly to be welcomed and I believe it will allow the party to meet one of the two big objectives which David, [the] Lib Dem Christian Forum, I and others were seeking.” The Newby review was announced last week to party members via an email from the Lib Dem leader, Ed Davey, and president, Josh Babarinde, days before the start of the party’s conference in Brighton. It will examine whether candidate approval, selection and deselection processes are inclusive of different faiths, whether candidates receive adequate support, the operation of complaints and disciplinary processes, and training for local party officers. A Lib Dem source said: “This review offers no remorse, no apologies to members misled so badly nor contrition towards the victims of breaches including Campanale and other Christians who once formed a bedrock of activists among our party’s nonconformist tradition. All should have had an apology by now. “As it stands, the review looks like a ploy to impress a court judge as the review of Campanale’s case is meant to be published right before damages are considered.” Another source said: “The review doesn’t recognise the pain [Campanale’s case] brought on members, and it has to be asked why key individuals refused to act when they received complaints or requests to investigate complaints around Campanale’s deselection.” Campanale submitted a schedule of loss that puts his claim at £788,740.75, including interest. It seeks compensation for injury to feelings, aggravated damages, past and future earnings, the loss of an MP’s pension, counselling costs and the “loss of a chance” or “loss of political capital”. In his claim, Campanale said that at a meeting in January 2022 he was questioned about his Christianity by about 30 people and asked whether he was enjoying his “martyrdom just like Jesus did”. Questions have emerged within the party about the remit of the review. A number of Lib Dem figures and activists have also privately criticised its lack of formal announcement. One figure questioned whether Newby would have access to complaints and candidate selection material, and whether the review would extend beyond religious faith to other protected beliefs. There is a particular concern among some members about whether the review will examine the party’s treatment of people with gender-critical beliefs. In a motion passed at party conference on Monday, members rejected official guidance by the equalities watchdog on how organisations should implement the supreme court ruling on transgender people, calling it “discriminatory and unworkable”. The party’s conference fringe programme over the weekend included discussions about Christian nationalism and political use of religion. The Lib Dems previously said the party was “home to people of all faiths and none, including many Christians”, but have declined to comment.

title: The world freaked out about AI doomsday. Now what?
summary: Donald Trump and Xi Jinping will meet each other next week, but it’s unlikely they’ll agree to AI regulation
text: Hello, and welcome to TechScape. I’m your host, Blake Montgomery, US tech editor at the Guardian, writing to you while reading and disagreeing with Jenny Odell’s 2019 book How to Do Nothing. I’m pro-screen time. Today in tech, we’re discussing the upcoming meeting between Donald Trump and Xi Jinping, in which AI will likely feature prominently. Trump, Xi, AI Last week, the world freaked out about an AI apocalypse. Now the two most powerful men, running the countries with the two most advanced AI industries, are going to discuss that possible doomsday. Donald Trump and Xi Jinping are set to greet one another on Wednesday and meet for talks in Washington DC, and artificial intelligence will be high on the agenda. Though their meeting reflects concern for AI at the highest levels of government, which is a generally positive sign, early indicators are not signalling that either nation is willing to put regulatory checks on the technology. The US and Chinese leaders have stressed in recent days that a slowdown of AI development is unnecessary. “We’re leading China in AI,” Trump said. “We’re the most sophisticated country in the world, and frankly, I want to ⁠keep it that way, because whoever wins AI, wins.” “Fearmongering, confrontation and vicious competition will only disrupt the process of global AI governance,” China’s foreign ministry said last week, in a statement that seemingly rejected the possibility of any US-led slowdown. Any AI slowdown would need buy-in from the US and China, but the rival nations see each other as the strongest argument against such a pause. Trump wants AI to go full steam ahead, fortified in that conviction by Silicon Valley leaders who’ve long been wary of Chinese ambitions. Even Dario Amodei, while calling for a global coordinated pause, repeatedly called China a threat. China, meanwhile, sees appeals for a slowdown as a way for the US to solidify American companies’ lead. Would you accept a hobbling proposal from your first-place opponent? That doesn’t mean Beijing shares none of Anthropic’s concerns. Last week, China released the third iteration of its AI safety governance framework. Included in the updates are risks posed by agents, cybersecurity threats from frontier models and the issue of self-improving AI. Amodei has, likewise, highlighted risks on all three fronts. The combative stance between the trans-Pacific rivals doesn’t mean nothing will happen, Trump’s administration is putting on a positive face in the lead-up to the meeting. The US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, has already met with his Chinese counterpart, He Lifeng, to discuss the threat of powerful AI. He called the talks “very successful”. Bessent and He mulled over an international alert system for AI incidents in the same fashion as nuclear alert systems. The two delegations are set to meet again in two months. “The US has proposed that we have a notification mechanism between the two countries, and we want a shared vision of common goals and common threats,” Bessent said. Read more: China bogeyman looms large over American firms’ AI doomsday scenario The present recalls past inaction If the US and China can’t agree on AI regulation, it’s unlikely any AI regulation at all will come. A decade of dire warnings have failed to slow the pace of the AI industry. As today’s freak-out cools, the political response seems to be moving the same way. Trump is calling AI doomsday warnings “a HOAX”. Should a safety bill arrive on his desk, it seems unlikely he would sign it. Read more: ‘Godfather of AI’ says tech regulation is nearing Covid-style pivot moment Though the Vermont senator Bernie Sanders has promised to propose a prohibition on extremely capable AI, no bill will pass both chambers of the US Congress in the near future. Last week, the House speaker, Mike Johnson, dismissed the chamber early for its seven-week midterm campaigning recess, likely preventing meaningful progress on AI safety legislation while the nation is focused on the issue. “It is just beyond the pale that Mike Johnson has called off Congress,” said the representative Yassamin Ansari, a Democrat from Arizona, on CNN. “We’re going home for seven weeks. And during that time, we’re going to see this frontier AI technology continue to evolve, continue to cause damage. And it’s going to get to a point where it will be impossible to go backward if we don’t move quickly now.” Read more: Why a decade of doomsday warnings failed to slow the AI race The AI industry is not united in its calls for regulation, dampening the possibility further. Though Amodei and OpenAI’s Sam Altman have invited new restrictions, and they nearly came to a joint legally binding safety testing agreement, they are but one powerful faction within their business. Nvidia’s Jensen Huang has Trump’s ear, as does the influential adviser David Sacks; both are in favor of accelerating AI development. Huang said on Sunday that “2030 is not going to be the end of the world. There is 0% chance that’s going to be the end of the world. Scaring people is unnecessary. It is irresponsible.” Read more: ‘An out-of-touch Silicon Valley radical’: meet Trump’s AI whisperer pushing for limited regulation Europe, which has played the role of global tech regulator, has little leverage in the debate despite its high concern for safety. Ursula Von der Leyen invited frontier labs to discussions in Europe about pacing the frontier of development, which garnered little response. Read more: Why Europe has been absent from the great AI safety debate In 2023, Geoffrey Hinton, a so-called “godfather of AI” and a Nobel laureate, left Google over his own fears of the risks that AI could be used by bad actors and one day harm humanity. Unlike many whistleblowers, Hinton’s resignation inspired a significant response from lawmakers: an executive order in the US, a congressional hearing and the passage of the EU’s AI Act. Yoshua Bengio, another godfather of AI, told the Guardian much the same last week. Bengio said governments are nearing a Covid-esque moment of rapid action. He’s “more optimistic than many observers because I see the public moving”, he said. Bengio preached his optimism after the Canadian and German governments announced funding of up to £160m for his non-profit organisation, which is dedicated to creating an “honest AI” that will act as a guardrail against rogue agents. I would be optimistic if I were handed £160m. Without such a payout, I am not. The wider TechScape Your AI doomsday questions answered: ‘What, if anything, can people like me do about it?’ ‘Just cut the wires’: why UK conspiracy theorists are destroying traffic scanners Trump to create ‘AI Force’ to monitor technology as fears over out-of-control agents grow Google says its Gemini AI model hacked three other companies Meta ordered to remove UK deepfakes as oversight board criticises ‘inadequate’ safeguards Feeling overwhelmed by the AI doom loop? Here’s the essential reading list to make sense of it all ‘RAMageddon’: tech crunch hikes the price of your next iPhone by £100

title: These journalists share vital reporting with thousands of US immigrants – all by text and WhatsApp
summary: Independent outlets are leaning on social media, chat and other nontraditional methods to fight disinformation
text: When Allan Marrero, an asylum seeker from the Cayman Islands, was released after five months in immigration detention, his family made sure to invite one journalist to his celebration: Eileen Grench, a reporter with the independent, non-profit news outlet Documented. Grench had previously reported on Marrero, who was detained after interviewing with federal officials for a marriage-based green card. But beyond covering his detention struggles, she humanized him, emphasizing his and his husband’s love story. “Most folks in these situations aren’t just victims; they’re fighting and being resilient and maintain the beautiful things about their life, too,” said Grench. The Marreros’ trust in Grench and Documented resulted in full access and rich reporting that received much attention; even NYC’s mayor, Zohran Mamdani, tweeted Grench’s story upon Allan’s release. “To see their story kind of lifted up on to that city stage was really gratifying,” Grench said. Documented is one of many immigrant-serving news outlets across the US meeting the moment when many legacy and mainstream publications are not, whether due to layoffs, lack of resources or being out of touch with immigrant communities. These independent local news organizations are using social media, chat apps and other nontraditional methods to connect directly with immigrants and non-English speakers – especially during recent Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) surges – and they are leaving an impression. “The impacts are phenomenal for relatively new media outlets, and part of it is because they’re operating on such a hyper-local level,” said Angie Chuang, a journalism professor at the University of Colorado Boulder. “Immigrant communities know what they need. They might not be able to access it or make it happen, but they can articulate their own needs. What these outlets are doing is just understanding how amplifying the community’s voices can help them.” Reaching immigrants on WhatsApp Last year, Documented and the Spanish-language news service Conecta Arizona launched the Immigrant News Coalition (INC) with the Listening Post Collective, the Bay Area’s El Tímpano, and the Minneapolis-based Sahan Journal to share strategies and resources for serving immigrant communities – and to ensure their outlets’ survival. Their work has since been bolstered by a $1.5m award from the Press Forward Foundation to “test and spread effective revenue models for immigrant-serving newsrooms” and additional funding from Democracy Fund. Through listening tours and research, the outlets have found that members of immigrant communities in the US don’t always read the news by visiting websites and reading push notifications, especially when English is not their first language. Instead, they rely on other platforms that may have inaccurate information, such as WhatsApp, which over half of Latinos in the US use. To meet specific immigrant communities where they are, Documented runs a WhatsApp group in Spanish, a WeChat group for Chinese immigrants, and a TikTok account in Haitian Creole to combat misinformation about ICE raids and fear-based scams. “Misinformation thrives when there is a vacuum of good information, and immigrant communities are so vulnerable because of the lack of alternatives,” said Madeleine Bair, the founder of El Tímpano. “We’re not translating news into other languages. We’re creating news first and foremost for immigrant communities, and that looks very different than news created for non-immigrant communities.” Adapting to the moment Emmy-winning journalist Maritza Félix started Conecta Arizona’s WhatsApp group, La Hora del Cafecito (Coffee Time), during the pandemic to provide timely, accurate news for immigrant communities in Spanish. The online gathering space, which has thousands of members across platforms, has a weekly Q&A with expert guests, including immigration attorneys, education policy experts and labor rights specialists. But as ICE raids continue, members are engaging less in the public group chat and more in one-on-one direct messages with the staff. “They’re afraid of being a screenshot, or having their message forwarded to someone,” Félix said. “Listening to our community taught us that what works today might not work next week. We are listening to what they say and their silences at the same time.” Having a dialogue with the local Bay Area immigrant community has been crucial for El Tímpano, which is Spanish for “eardrum”. In addition to SMS messaging that reaches more than 7,000 Spanish-speaking immigrants, the outlet’s disinformation defense initiative, Comunidades Informadas, has trained more than 400 Latino immigrants in the Bay Area to recognize and address disinformation and misinformation. “By equipping immigrants with an understanding of how disinformation works, it can empower them, so that when they see a rumor of an ICE raid, their immediate response isn’t to panic,” Bair said. “Instead, they can check with a source they trust or call their local rapid response hotline. We’ve received really positive responses to these workshops and to the information that we provide to combat that fear.” In May, the Alameda county library partnered with El Tímpano for a disinformation defense initiative workshop in Spanish via Zoom for its staff members. Attenders found the content easy to understand, and it helped them articulate how to identify disinformation not just to community members, but also to their own family members. “After going through the workshop, I was like, ‘I can talk to this with my tia and my tios, and explain it to them in the way that I didn’t really have the language before,’” said Jaqueline Martinez, the Alameda county library’s equity services coordinator. Building trust within immigrant communities For many of these outlets, the work and impact started before the recent ICE surge. In 2019, Documented co-founders Mazin Sidahmed and Max Siegelbaum spoke with community organizations across New York that were concerned about workers’ wages being stolen. Joined later by reporter Lam Thuy Vo, they launched an investigation, seeking out New York state and federal wage data for four years. The result was Documented’s Wage Theft Monitor, which inspired NY state legislators to introduce three bills to prevent and punish wage theft. “The dual impact of protecting immigrant workers, but also helping the general public understand how pervasive this issue is, has been one of the most rewarding parts of seeing this project come to light,” Sidahmed said. Similarly, LA Taco, which isn’t part of the INC, originally built trust among Los Angeles immigrant communities through its coverage of food, culture and cannabis. Then last June, as ICE raids swept through Los Angeles, LA Taco journalist Memo Torres began posting daily recaps of ICE activity on the publication’s Instagram account. By reporting verified information about raids during a time when misinformation ran rampant, Torres became one of LA’s most trusted journalists for immigrant communities, increasing LA Taco’s membership from 1,500 to 7,7,00 and earning attention from state and federal government officials. “I was getting information from people, I started reaching out to rapid responders and building trust with them, and then got included in the network with them,” he said, recalling how he started the Daily Memo. Over the summer, the Daily Memo wound down, while LA Taco’s political cartoons by Pulitzer prize finalist Ivan Ehlers, called Sunday Taquitos, took off. In July, his humorous yet poignant illustration about Flock camera surveillance received more than 7m Instagram views and inspired fan-created versions in five different languages. The Ecuadorian American artist said the political cartoons are his short-form way of fighting misinformation and disinformation. “If I can get someone’s attention for five seconds, I can get people to look at important issues and say, ‘Hey, I didn’t know that was happening. Oh man, this is terrible,’” he said. “People will go in and do more research, read more about it, talk to their friends or share it, and that’ll start conversations.” Ehlers has also served as creative director for one of LA Taco’s zines, showcasing the outlet’s reporting on local protests and immigrant communities. Its release in early September was just one of many in-person events LA Taco has held this year to engage with its readers. “The bigger issue is building a community and building support systems and showing people that they’re not alone,” Ehlers said. “We have a lot of people who are willing to fight together, work together and build something together.” This article was amended on 1 October 2026. A previous version said LA Taco’s membership increased from 1,500 to 77,000. The number is actually 7,700.

title: ‘It’s my duty to tell the truth’: UN chief on the climate crisis, capitalism and reasons to be hopeful
summary: Before his final general assembly, António Guterres speaks about why he put climate at the centre of his UN tenure
text: António Guterres, who will finish his second term as UN secretary general on 31 December, has spoken out more strongly on the climate crisis than any of his predecessors. He has criticised “immoral” fossil fuel companies for their “grotesque greed”, warned that we have “opened the gates of hell” and hailed the new “clean energy age”. Before his last UN general assembly, we asked him about making the climate crisis one of the top priorities of his tenure. Why are you so forthright on the climate crisis? Climate is an existential threat. We see political leadership around the world diverted by lots of short-term objectives. Political life lives by the hour, and climate is something whose dramatic consequences will only be seen in the long term. That is why I believe the UN has the obligation to, at every moment, put the climate in the centre of the concerns of the international community, because climate is the most relevant global existential threat. Why have we failed to tackle global heating up to now? There are vested interests that are interested in maintaining the present development model based on fossil fuels. You have a systematic campaign that is strongly financed by the huge profits of the sector that tries to divert attention [from] the impacts of fossil fuels. But also, most people have not yet interiorised the level of risk that we are all facing. I hope public opinion will be more and more impressed by the devastating impacts of climate change, and disasters becoming more and more dramatic. Heatwaves have terrible impacts on health, so there will be a growing consciousness of the devastating impacts of climate change as things get inevitably worse. Is climate breakdown a threat to national security? As the crisis in the Gulf has demonstrated, to base an economy on fossil fuel imports is a severe risk for any country, and security is something that tends to have an enormous importance in decision-making. Scientists tell us we’re coming very close to tipping points that can dramatically accelerate the impacts of climate change. The Gulf Stream [or Amoc, Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation] is slowing, as we know. And we could face a huge acceleration of rising sea levels. It will become a world problem, and it’s a clear security problem – an extremely dramatic problem for the security of all countries in the world. Still in many security establishments, energy security is still seen in terms of fossil fuels. But there is a new generation of institutions and thinktanks alert to the risks of climate change and [the crisis in] biodiversity. What difference can the UN secretary general make? The secretary general of the UN has not much power, and there is no money. But there is one thing that I have: a voice. It’s my duty to use that voice without any compromise, to tell the truth and to alert the international community to the dangers it faces. I have not the power to all of a sudden make everybody invest in renewables, but I have the duty to tell people that unless we accelerate the transition from fossil fuels to renewables, unless we drastically reduce emissions in the next decade, we will be facing dramatic problems that will impact on the whole of humankind. Have you any regrets about your 10 years in office? We should have done more in building powerful alliances outside the traditional political spectrum. We should be able to do more building those alliances [with grassroots organisations and subnational and local governments]. We have given too much importance to our dialogue with the top political decision-makers and not done enough in the mobilisation of society and establishing a stronger alliance with local authorities. Our democratic systems need to be modernised, and communication with the people, especially with young generations, needs to adapt to the new forms of communication [on the internet and social media]. Some people argue that capitalism is the underlying problem and we cannot solve the climate crisis without fixing that. Do you agree? A market economy can be a very good form of allocation and resources. If you call capitalism the market economy, the problem is not capitalism. But a market economy requires effective governance. And that governance must be made through regulations, and that governance must be within the monopoly of political power, democratically elected. So we can have a market economy – and I still believe it’s the best way to allocate resources, as planned economies didn’t prove to be effective – but we need to have regulatory frameworks established by politically democratic institutions. Unfortunately, in many circumstances we have seen regulatory bodies being controlled by private interests. We need to make sure that doesn’t happen. But many of the biggest emitting countries, and countries with the biggest fossil fuel reserves, are autocracies. What can be done with them? I’m in favour of democracies everywhere, but even in non-democratic regimes [tackling the climate crisis] is important – and it’s important that [modern communications] technologies are not used to increase the authoritarian nature of those regimes. Are there any reasons to be hopeful? Clearly we are not doing enough. But they are developing renewable energy at enormous speeds. The crisis of the Gulf will accelerate that trend, because many of the emerging economies that are the biggest emitters are net importers of fossil fuels and they have a vested interest in developing renewables.

title: Death of 27-year-old Presley Gerber being investigated as suspected overdose
summary: Son of supermodel Cindy Crawford and entrepreneur Rande Gerber died at a rehabilitation facility
text: The death on Sunday of Presley Gerber, the 27-year-old son of supermodel Cindy Crawford and entrepreneur Rande Gerber, is being investigated as a suspected overdose, according to police. Gerber died at a rehabilitation facility, Los Angeles county medical examiner records show. An autopsy was performed, but more testing was required before investigators could give a cause of death for Gerber, which the medical examiner did not immediately do. A news release issued later by the Santa Monica police department then said the agency was investigating his death as a suspected overdose. Presley, who was his parents’ eldest child and brother of model Kaia Gerber, had spoken often of his mental health and long-term addiction struggles. On the podcast Studio 22 in 2023, he said he hoped sharing details about his struggles would help others coping with mental health difficulties. “That’s really what I want to do: help people, whether you’re depressed, you’re struggling with something that is having a negative effect on your body,” Presley said. “I mean it could be anything, and there’s no judgment.” His death was first confirmed by Allie Jenkins, a representative for Crawford and Rande Gerber. “The family is asking for privacy during this very difficult and painful time,” Jenkins said in an email. Born in California in 1999, Presley was signed by IMG Models at age 15, making his runway debut in 2016 for Moschino’s Resort show in Los Angeles. He worked with brands including Celine, Calvin Klein, Dolce & Gabbana and Pepsi. The Associated Press contributed reporting
