title: Wasp spider seen in north of England latest ‘climate refugee’ amid global heating
summary: The Argiope bruennichi, spotted in Cheshire for first time, part of worrying trend that could threaten native species
text: She is an unlikely harbinger of the climate emergency: a venomous black and yellow spider who spins mysterious patterns in her webs and eats her mates for breakfast. Native to mainland Europe, north Africa and Asia, the Argiope bruennichi – commonly known as a wasp spider – is rarely seen in the north and west of Britain. But a fully grown female has been spotted in Cheshire for the first time by conservationists from Chester zoo, who stumbled across the large, brightly striped arachnid in a rewilded field. The species, which mimics a wasp to deter predators, is thought to be the latest “climate refugee” extending its range northwards as the planet heats. Females can grow to about 2cm in body length, making it one of the largest spiders found in the UK. “You know your big, chunky house spiders – the ones you think are massive and frighten the life out of you in your living room? A female wasp spider is probably a bit bigger than those,” said Scott Wilson, head of field programmes at the zoo. Although they are not dangerous to humans, they often attack and cannibalise their mates during or after copulation. Males usually reach only about a quarter of the length of the females and studies have found that up to 80% die after their first mating attempt while the rest die after their second. Their body then provides the female with valuable protein as she produces her eggs. It is not yet known how the spread of the wasp spider, which was also revealed to be moving west into counties such as Worcestershire, Herefordshire and Warwickshire last week, will affect local ecosystems in the north. “That’s quite often the risk with these ecological shifts – we don’t know what the implications will be,” said Wilson. The spider recorded in Cheshire was discovered on the Chester zoo estate during a routine “bioblitz” to monitor biodiversity on 80 hectares of land being set aside for nature. An expert from the British Arachnological Society later confirmed it was the first recorded sighting of the species in the county. “It was quite easy to spot,” said Wilson. “It’s a really big, colourful spider and the webs are huge and distinctive … They have this thick zigzag, which some people think is there to reflect UV light and attract insects, but nobody really knows.” The wider zoo estate, which includes wet meadows,grasslands, woodlands and orchards, already supports a diverse range of important UK species, such as great crested newts, badgers and harvest mice. It also hosts nesting barn owls and dozens of dragonfly, moth and butterfly species. Wasp spiders are typically found in sunny, open grasslands across Europe. The species was first recorded in the UK in the 1920s but Wilson said there had only been “a handful” of sightings north of the Midlands to date. Spiderlings are known to travel long distances by ballooning on silken strands in the wind and he fears the spider spotted in Cheshire – which the zoo has nicknamed ‘Wendy’ – is the latest indication of how the warming climate is affecting UK wildlife, creating “climate refugees”. “Her arrival is part of a broader, more worrying trend,” he said. “You get quite excited about spotting a new species, but the bigger picture for climate change impacts on species is generally negative … We’re seeing lots of species change their range.” Ruby Merriman, Chester zoo’s estate biodiversity manager, said wasp spiders were slowly moving north as their southern ranges in Europe warm too quickly for them to adapt. “Some conservation organisations refer to animals driven to migrate by climate change as ‘climate refugees’ – which is a good term. They are moving because of human activity, and we need to make space for them.” Wilson is concerned the trend means invasive non-native species, such as Asian hornets, will spread northwards in the UK in the future, and that native species will go extinct because they are unable to either migrate or survive in the changing climate. As in other countries, the climate emergency poses a major threat to UK wildlife. “We don’t have the big high-profile animals like polar bears – but it’s as relevant to us as it is to any other country … In the UK, we’ve got a very fragmented landscape. So a species that is only found in heathland in a particular county will be under real threat if suddenly that heathland becomes too warm or too cold.” Although the wasp spider can bite, it is unlikely to hurt a human unless harassed. Its venom is “probably about as harmful as a nettle sting”, Wilson said. “To us, anyway,” he clarified. “If you’re a small insect in its web, then it’s a different story.”

title: Kansas judge convicts driver in death of teacher whose husband was killed months later
summary: Ashleigh Boyd died in a car crash in 2024. Her husband, Adan Manzano, a TV reporter, was killed in Louisiana while preparing to cover the Super Bowl in 2025
text: A Kansas school teacher’s fatal car wreck in 2024 led to a vehicular homicide conviction on Monday for the motorist who crashed into her – a verdict delivered just four days after a Louisiana jury found a woman guilty of the drugging death of the educator’s widower while he prepared to cover the 2025 Super Bowl for Telemundo. Todd W Armstrong’s one-day bench trial in an 11 April 2024 traffic collision that killed Ashleigh Boyd in Topeka, Kansas, resulted in the judge, Andrew Holmes, finding him guilty of vehicular homicide, driving on the wrong side of the road and speeding, according to the victim’s father, Brian Hinck. Armstrong, who had pleaded not guilty, was scheduled for sentencing in November, Hinck said. Hinck did not immediately describe a reaction to Armstrong’s guilty verdict. Neither the office of the Topeka district attorney, Mike Kagay, nor Armstrong’s lawyer could immediately be reached for comment late on Monday. Beforehand, Hinck had publicly discussed how much he loathed the idea of Armstrong’s trial happening so soon after the conclusion of a separate one centering on the unrelated 5 February 2025 death in suburban New Orleans of his son-in-law, Adan Manzano. Hinck said he and his wife, Nicole, are raising Boyd and Manzano’s daughter, three-year-old Eleanor, after her parents’ deaths 10 months apart. And he had said it was also bitterly disheartening for him to learn that Armstrong, 55, faced no more than one year in prison even if found guilty of vehicular homicide because Kansas law considers the offense a misdemeanor. Hinck furthermore said he was incredulous that the woman at whose hands Manzano died, according to the Louisiana jury, was on probation at the time of the crime – and that the cases strained his faith in parts of the US criminal justice system. “The disappointment in the justice system is at a peak level in our house,” Hinck had said. Boyd, 24, was in her sedan when Armstrong – in a pickup truck on the wrong side of the road – hit her head-on. The teacher at Topeka’s Lowman Hill elementary school was pronounced dead at the scene, and Eleanor – then an infant passenger – was injured, according to investigators. Court records cited by the Topeka news station KSNT alleged that investigators recovered evidence showing Armstrong’s truck had been parked for five hours at a casino in Kansas City, about an hour’s drive away, on the morning of the crash. Armstrong allegedly told authorities that either a blown tire or mechanical failure caused him to crash into Boyd, though investigators detected no obvious signs of such defects in his truck, said the court records reported by KSNT. There also evidently was a urine drug screen result indicating the presence of cocaine metabolites in Armstrong’s system, as the Topeka Capital-Journal reported. However, according to court records, Armstrong’s attorney successfully argued that the drug screen result should be omitted from being considered as evidence during the defendant’s trial. The Topeka Capital-Journal reported that Armstrong’s lawyer, Kevin Shepherd, had argued for an acquittal during the trial on Monday by pointing to a 2002 Kansas supreme court ruling which said vehicular homicide required more than “ordinary negligence”. Meanwhile, Boyd’s husband, Manzano, was working for the Spanish-language Telemundo affiliate in Kansas City when he traveled to cover Super Bowl LIX in New Orleans. Manzano was found dead in his hotel room in the New Orleans suburb of Kenner, Louisiana, days before one of the teams he covered – the Kansas City Chiefs – played in the big game. Investigators ultimately determined Manzano had been preyed on by a group that descended on victims in New Orleans’ French Quarter, knocked them unconscious by furtively drugging them, and stole their phones and bank cards to drain their financial accounts. Manzano’s autopsy revealed the native of Toluca, Mexico, had died lying facedown on a pillow, having asphyxiated after ingesting a combination of alcohol and the pharmaceutical depressant Xanax. On Thursday, after a four-day trial, a jury at a suburban New Orleans state courthouse convicted Danette Colbert, 49, of negligent homicide in Manzano’s death. That jury also convicted both Colbert and her accomplice, Rickey White, 35, of racketeering. A third defendant in Manzano’s death, 35-year-old Christian Anderson, ultimately testified against Colbert and White, whose sentencing was tentatively scheduled for 28 September. Anderson pleaded guilty to lesser charges of simple robbery and fraud in exchange for a six-year prison sentence. Negligent homicide can carry up to 10 years in prison. Racketeering can carry up to 50 years’ imprisonment. Separately, after Manzano’s death but before her trial, Colbert received a 25-year prison sentence for violating her probation on a prior theft and fraud conviction and being classified a habitual offender. Hinck spoke in between the Colbert–White and Armstrong trials about battling to shield Eleanor from the particulars of the legal fallout surrounding her parents’ death. “We don’t talk about it with her,” Hinck said in reference to his granddaughter. “The only thing she knows is her mom and dad are in heaven, and she will see them one day.” • This article was amended on 22 September 2026 to correct the chronology of the Kansas car crash and the New Orleans killing.

title: EU spends three times more on imports from China than bloc exports there
summary: Days before Xi Jinping’s summit with Donald Trump, new study shows trade deficit ran at more than €1bn daily in July
text: Consumers and businesses in the EU are spending three times more on Chinese imports than their counterparts in China are buying from the bloc, a study has shown. Customs data showed the gap between the EU’s imports from China and exports to China, the trade deficit, ran at more than €1bn (£860m) a day in July. The new data comes just days after the European commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, said the trade imbalance must be arrested, and before Xi Jinping’s summit with Donald Trump on Thursday in Washington. The Mercator Institute for China Studies (Meric) said: “The problem is no longer simply that the EU is buying more Chinese goods. China is selling more to Europe while buying less from it.” China and the EU are locked in talks about averting a trade war, and the EU’s trade commissioner, Maroš Šefčovič, will travel to Beijing to meet his Chinese counterpart on 8 October. “With the bilateral deficit now exceeding €1bn a day, the widening imbalance will almost certainly be high on the agenda at the planned EU-China meeting in October,” Meric said. Analysis of Chinese customs data by Meric showed the EU’s trade deficit hit €36.5bn in July alone, up from €32.2bn in July 2025. From January to July, the total deficit now stands at €234bn, about €21bn more than the first seven months of 2025. “The imbalance has now moved beyond three to one. For every €1 of goods the EU exported to China in July, it imported €3.10. The deficit was equivalent to €1.18bn a day,” Meric said. Sources in Brussels said one of the measures being considered is introducing quotas on hybrid vehicles and certain types of chemicals imported from China. Sales of hybrid vehicles rocketed after the imposition of extra tariffs on Chinese EVs in 2024 omitted to include hybrid electric cars, causing concern in the EU car industry. The latest figures show imports of hybrid cars that do not have to be plugged in have grown tenfold, from just under 4,000 vehicles sold in October 2024, to 50,000 in July 2026. The Financial Times reported last week that the EU has asked China to voluntarily reduce exports of hybrids. China has repeatedly warned it is ready for a trade war but its commerce ministry last week maintained a diplomatic stance before the October summit. “Any solution between China and the EU must ensure a balance of interests, comply ‌with World Trade Organization rules and the respective domestic laws of every side, and fully take into account the interests of industries on both sides,” it said. Chinese exports will be high on the agenda at Thursday’s summit in Washington, with expectations that a 12-month suspension of Beijing’s rare earth export restrictions will be extended. Kurt Tong, the former US consul general to Hong Kong and managing director of the Asia Group strategic advisory firm, said if a reprieve was not announced this week it could be announced at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit next month. China introduced the rare earth export restrictions in April 2025, almost bringing the car industry in the EU, Mexico, US and the UK to a halt amid shortages of permanent magnets. It suspended the ban last October when Trump met Xi in South Korea but did not offer any further concessions when the two presidents last met in May in Beijing.

title: OpenAI’s George Osborne says datacentre nimbys holding back Britain
summary: Former chancellor, now senior figure at OpenAI, says UK needs datacentres to maintain ‘sovereignty’ over AI tech
text: Datacentre nimbys are holding Britain back, George Osborne has said in reaction to nationwide protests about the giant water- and energy-guzzling structures. The former Tory chancellor is now the head of AI for countries at OpenAI, the developer of ChatGPT. His job is to represent the company to governments around the world and he also has a role in enabling the building of datacentres and other infrastructure. Speaking at the Big Brue festival in Somerset on Sunday, Osborne said: “You try and build a datacentre in Britain … I spent my life when I was politician trying to get people to agree to have new roads and railway lines and airport runways, and communities go up in arms – it’s really hard to build a datacentre.” He said the UK would lose its “sovereignty” over tech to the US if it failed to allow datacentres to be built. He explained: “You can either choose to have these datacentres in Ohio and Georgia and Michigan, which is where they’re all being built … we don’t allow these things to be built. They’re going to be built elsewhere, and you know that’s a loss of some sovereign control over the physical location where these things are.” There have been protests about datacentres across the UK, including in central London, Devon and outside Holyrood in Edinburgh. People have said they are a blight on the landscape, questioned whether they will bring jobs to the local area, and argued they will take investment and space that could be used for affordable housing. There are also concerns about the vast water and energy use. The government has classified AI datacentres as critical national infrastructure to get them built more quickly. But the Green party in England has called for a moratorium on building them. Osborne dismissed the concerns over datacentres as nimbyism. He said: “I think a lot of the to opposition datacentres is very much like ‘not in my back yard’. There’s an enormous building boom going on in the United States of datacentres, even as the political opposition undoubtedly is growing.” Verity Harding, the head of the AI and geopolitics project at Cambridge University’s Bennett School for Public Policy, said people had wider concerns over these centres. She said: “The reason everyone hates datacentres has nothing to do with datacentres. It’s the only tangible thing to protest against … [people] just don’t like what’s happening and they don’t feel that anybody’s in control or thinking about the impact of it. “It’s exactly because the tech industry execs are talking in this ridiculous way … You know, you cannot go out on the one hand and say this [AI] might kill everybody one week and then the next week go and appear at a big sales conference saying that you should integrate it into your business.” Bosses of OpenAI and Anthropic, two of the largest AI companies, will be meeting world leaders at the UN general assembly in New York City this week amid debate over the prospect of dangerous, superintelligent AI and whether and how it should be regulated. Osborne said: “The fact that corporate leaders are sitting down with the presidents and prime ministers of the world in the UN security council I would say actually shouldn’t be alarming. It’s actually reassuring that people are beginning to try and use the kind of institutions of the world to think about how we regulate this new technology.”

title: First Thing: News outlets suspend coverage of Trump in escalating media access row
summary: President’s decision to ban three news organisations from White House prompts backlash
text: Good morning. The row over media access to the presidency has deepened, with major US television news outlets agreeing to suspend their video coverage of Donald Trump after the administration banned journalists from several outlets from entering the White House grounds. The president had abruptly announced his ban against CNN, MS Now and Politico, saying he had had enough of “purposely negative stories” about him. On Monday the ban against CNN meant no broadcaster was covering Trump’s midday ribbon-cutting for a new White House helipad. The White House provided its own livestream but the president’s remarks were inaudible over the sound of a helicopter’s engine. How have CNN, MS Now and Politico responded to the ban? A lawsuit seeks a temporary restraining order that would immediately lift the ban. In a statement, the organizations said: “We are filing a lawsuit today to protect our first amendment rights and defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes.” What other significant media developments have there been? Paramount has reached a settlement with California and several other states that sued over its proposed $81bn merger with Warner Bros Discovery (WBD), the California attorney general announced, clearing the way to consolidate some of Hollywood’s most recognizable TV networks and studios under one owner. Trump had earlier blamed Kyiv for the escalating energy war, even as Russia has decimated Ukraine’s economy and launched night barrages of drones and ballistic missiles against Ukrainian cities. What else is Trump expected to say at the UN? The US ambassador to the UN said Trump would speak about how he had “confronted complex problems head-on around the world”. Our writer Robert Tait notes in this analysis, however, that thanks to Trump’s recent social media blitz and self-proclaimed “25 top achievements”, the chances of an uplifting speech appear slim. ICE hides locations of thousands of detainees with final removal orders US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has stopped publicly revealing where it is holding thousands of detainees who are subject to final deportation orders. The unannounced move has made it far more difficult for lawyers and relatives to find them, according to current and former officials familiar with the practice. In a separate development, the US representative Veronica Escobar has said in an interview with the Guardian that federal immigration officials in Texas prevented her from fully conducting her congressional oversight duties. When she arrived to scrutinize conditions at Camp East Montana, she said, she was not allowed to speak with any of the detained immigrants. What has happened to Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez, who was shot by ICE? The Venezuelan man spoke out from detention on Monday afternoon. He was taken from a hospital in Austin into ICE detention, even though he apparently still has a bullet lodged near his spine. “I haven’t received any medical attention. I’m in a lot of pain,” Garcés Pérez said in a phone call to his attorney, adding that he had spent the night sleeping on the floor of a cold room. Houthis move to seize strategic terrain after Trump calls off airstrikes at last minute Houthi fighters are moving to seize strategic heights in Yemen that would cut the Red Sea coast off from areas held by Saudi-backed forces, after Donald Trump called off US strikes on the group at the last minute, reportedly as bombs were being loaded on to aircraft. In a call, Saudi Arabia’s crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman, implored Trump to step in to help halt the Houthi advance. Trump, who had been resisting joining the Saudi war in Yemen, then told the Pentagon to prepare for airstrikes, before reversing course. The UK has agreed to provide defensive air support to Saudi Arabia to help counter Houthi fighters. In other news … Lauren Boebert, the subject of a House ethics complaint about sexual relationships with staffers, has said the allegations are untrue and part of a “politically motivated” campaign against her. Two helicopter pilots died while fighting a fire in Yosemite national park over the weekend. Five Stanford University students who faced prison sentences in connection to a campus protest against Israel’s war on Gaza have had all charges dropped. Meanwhile, a jury has convicted a Vermont man of attempted murder in the shootings of three Palestinian college students who were walking near his home. A Black Tesla employee has accused the company of fostering racial discrimination in a major trial. In another legal development involving Elon Musk’s ventures, a US judge has declined to block the transfer of wildlife refuge land to SpaceX. Clancy’s lawyers have now asked the court to question the juror about his alleged use of a cellphone and his truthfulness. Culture Pick: Nimesh Patel on standup, Palestine and politics The comedian went from being discovered by Chris Rock to making Saturday Night Live history. Now his new Netflix special, Buy the Dip, tackles timely topics with optimism. Radheyan Simonpillai interviews him. Don’t miss this: Nearly 4m records of enslaved people in 20 former British colonies now searchable online The collection, known as the Former British Colonies Enslavement Registers, contains about 300,000 pages, potentially helping millions of descendants across the African-Caribbean and wider African diasporas uncover their family histories. … or this: As he hits 90, master minimalist Steve Reich looks back As Steve Reich approaches his 10th decade, Flora Willson speaks to the composer, who reflects on a life that changed the soundtrack of modern living. title: Poorer nations will be among the last to benefit if global emissions cut to net zero
summary: Scientists found unequal impact of the climate crisis would not be reversed even if implicit goal of the 2015 Paris agreement is achieved
text: The unequal impact of the climate crisis on the world’s poorest people, including those in tropical areas, has been highlighted by new research that finds they will be among the last to feel the benefits if global greenhouse gas emissions are cut to net zero. Temperatures have risen more significantly in tropical areas relative to their historic range than at higher latitudes, including in wealthier countries in Europe and North America. A team of Australian climate scientists found this inequality would not be reversed if global emissions reached net zero – the implicit goal of the landmark 2015 Paris agreement – and could take “many decades to begin to reverse” if carbon dioxide was drawn from the atmosphere under a “net-negative emissions” plan. The research coincided with the UN’s refugee agency releasing a report showing how the climate crisis was increasing the risk of people becoming stateless. The climate inequality study, published in the journal Environmental Research Letters, was led by Dr Andrew King and colleagues at the University of Melbourne. They looked at three sets of computer modelling experiments of the likely temperature changes if global emissions reached net zero and overlaid the results with countries’ gross domestic product. “If we follow a path that is close to net zero, then the inequality we see in present day warming persists indefinitely,” King said. “The wealthier countries that have caused more of the problem are not those that are the most exposed, even beyond net zero. The regions that have not caused the warming are those that experience the most warming.” King said the fate of the planet’s poorest regions, which tend to be concentrated closer to the equator, would depend on how much greenhouse gas was emitted before the world reached net zero. “Even when we get to net zero, we have still emitted an enormous amount of carbon into the atmosphere and its effects will continue for centuries. We can’t easily undo all that damage,” he said. “Getting to net zero sooner means we are less likely to have that long-term warming after net zero. We need to get to net zero sooner to limit that inequality.” King said tropical ecosystems, such as some coral reefs, had mostly evolved to exist in a narrower temperature range than ecosystems at higher latitudes and would continue to be heavily affected for longer as the world cut emissions. A separate report on the impact of climate change on the stateless, commissioned by the UN refugee agency and released with the Peter McMullin Centre on Statelessness, called on nations to support “the continuity of statehood” for countries facing extreme climate damage. It said those at risk included Pacific islands that were losing land to rising seas. The agency estimated about 4.5 million people were stateless but said it accepted the number was probably much larger as stateless people were “invisible to official statistics”. The report said the climate crisis risked creating more stateless people through displacement after climate-driven disasters such as fire, flood and sea level rise. University of Melbourne Associate Prof Radha Govil, a report co-author, said there was a correlation between the regions most affected by climate change and statelessness. The report recommended countries should be helped to digitise citizenship records, and steps should be taken to ensure children were afforded citizenship if they were left without parents after a disaster. It said the risks to children were increased if mothers were not given the same rights as fathers to confer their own nationality to their children. “The recommendations we have set out are absolutely doable,” said Govil. “They can stave of this risk of statelessness and get ahead of this problem.”

title: Why the CDC is excluding measles deaths in Pennsylvania even as outbreak appears to be ‘accelerating’
summary: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention refuses to count four measles deaths in the state though doctors are ‘seeing new forms’ of disease
text: The US Centers of Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) updated its measles dashboard on Friday – but it’s still not counting four measles deaths in Pennsylvania, where the outbreak appears to be accelerating and cases are appearing in ways providers have never seen before. Members of Congress on Monday requested an “immediate briefing” on the decision to change how measles deaths are reported as cases continue to rise throughout the United States, reaching levels not seen in decades. A possible measles exposure was reported in the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia last week. The delay in death reporting is “curious” even after the CDC switched how it counts deaths, said Debra Houry, former CDC chief medical officer. It takes one to two days for the CDC to receive updated data to the National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) after states finish death investigations. “Pennsylvania concluded the investigation on the first two deaths, so CDC would have these records by now,” Houry said. Meanwhile, the outbreak “seems to be accelerating”, said Dr John Goldman, an infectious disease specialist at the University of Pittsburgh Medical Center. “And we’re seeing, actually, types of measles we’ve never seen before,” he added. Doctors are now treating congenital measles – newborns who contracted the virus in utero or at birth – which was once exceedingly rare because most pregnant people were protected by vaccines or, before immunization, surviving measles in childhood. “Because of this, we’re literally seeing new forms of measles,” Goldman said. “We don’t have a lot of information about what happens with it.” Pennsylvania has reported 731 cases, but that number is likely an undercount, he said. Frequently when patients come to the hospital with measles, they mention that others at home are sick as well – but they haven’t been tested, Goldman said. On average, one to three people for every 1,000 cases will die of measles, and one in five will be hospitalized. The current deaths and hospital admissions in Pennsylvania are “definitely not proportional to what would be expected”, Houry said, and she believes the official numbers are “very much an undercount”. Under-testing can make it challenging to do contact tracing and sick people may not realize they need to isolate – both of which can make the spread of measles more likely. Providers are preparing for more cases and more deaths. “It’s not rocket science. If we see more measles, we’ll see more deaths,” Goldman said. “I suspect that we’re not going to see a break until most people in most communities are immune either by vaccine or infection.” Typically, the CDC collects data from states, including causes of death. Death certificates are issued at the state or local level; there are no federal death certificates. But now, the agency is working with the Council of State and Territorial Epidemiologists to define deaths from measles. While the CDC has its own measles case definition, it has relied upon the World Health Organization’s definition of measles deaths. Until a measles death definition is created, the CDC is relying on NCHS data, which “identifies measles as the underlying cause based on death record information submitted by the states”, said Emily Hilliard, a spokesperson for the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS). She did not respond to the Guardian’s questions about why the death count was still delayed, or whether all deaths would receive a CDC definition. Before this outbreak, measles deaths were rare in America; there were none for a decade. “When there aren’t deaths, you don’t need a precise definition,” Houry said. Pennsylvania developed a definition, and the CDC could consider adopting it, she said. Erica Schwartz, the CDC director, denied in an interview that deaths were being miscounted for political reasons, pointing instead to the process of creating a definition. “If someone got hit by a bus, and they happened to have Covid, often that was called a Covid-related death,” Schwartz said, referencing misinformation about how Covid deaths were counted. In reality, Covid deaths were likely under-counted. Pennsylvania’s definition of “measles death” clearly excludes unrelated deaths, so the bus scenario would not apply, Houry said. “Dr Schwartz’s comments are not only not helpful, but contribute to misinformation.” But this isn’t the most important issue right now, she added. “I would focus less on the definition itself and responding to the measles outbreak, and that’s what the focus of the CDC director should be.” Robert F Kennedy Jr, HHS secretary, has cast doubt on the Pennsylvania deaths and reportedly instructed Schwartz not to include them in the CDC tally. Kennedy only mentioned the measles outbreak once in a speech spanning nearly an hour and a half at an anti-vaccine conference on Thursday. He noted only that deaths from measles are headline news and he asked that severe side effects and deaths from vaccines get the same attention. About one to two people in a million experience severe side effects from vaccines, while with measles one in five people are hospitalized and one to three in 1,000 die. Pennsylvania has responded aggressively to the outbreak, standing up more than 100 pop-up clinics and requesting additional vaccination support from the CDC. The state department of health has “done a spectacular job of dealing with this”, Goldman said. Tests have a 24-hour turnaround time. “I have called them up on a Thursday before the holiday weekend and arranged for them to do testing before it closed at noon the following day,” Goldman said. “They have provided us with information, and they have provided us with really really good support.” While there is a likely undercount of cases, “it’s not because they couldn’t get a test”, he said. “It’s because they were sick at home and did not seek medical care.” The response hasn’t been limited to the health department, Houry noted. “Health systems and clinicians are really stepping up across the state to get vaccines to their communities.” Before this outbreak, Goldman was the rare American doctor who had seen measles, once in 1988 and once in 1992. Between 1992 and 2026, he didn’t see a single case. Now, “we’re seeing at least one every day”, he said. He’s preparing for three to six more months of this. “Never in my life did I think I was ever going to see measles again,” he said. He fears for other vaccine-preventable diseases: whooping cough, diphtheria, polio. “In a way, I think this is a warning,” he said. “What worries me is measles is conceivably the canary in the coal mine.”

title: In Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed’s candidacy has split the Jewish community
summary: The Democratic Senate nominee’s views on Israel and comments after a synagogue attack prompted a public debate among Jewish voters
text: When Jess Newman heard that Temple Israel in Detroit was attacked last March, her first thoughts went to her extended family. “I grew up going to services there,” she said. “The attack was awful. My Jewish identity is very important to me.” On 12 March, Ayman Ghazali, a naturalized US citizen from Lebanon, drove his truck into the Temple Israel, causing a fire and injuring a security guard. But even amid her anxiety for her family, Newman was startled by the response from some community members. “The reaction to it from people close to it that I know in my family is: ‘We need AK-47s under our beds,’” she recalled. Today Newman, a political organizer who sits on the Ferndale school board, spends about 10 hours a week volunteering for the campaign of Abdul El-Sayed, a vocal critic of Israel who is the Democratic party’s candidate to become US senator for Michigan in November’s midterm elections. “There is a problem with antisemitism,” she says. “I think it is made all that much harder to deal with when you can’t have a sensible conversation about why violence is happening … you cannot divorce violence invited upon people from violence being done around the world.” Newman’s experiences reflect the broader disagreements facing Michigan’s diverse Jewish communities this year. An estimated 130,000 Jewish Americans live in Michigan, where a 2021 study reported that 61% identified with or leaned Democrat and that Jewish adults are less likely to identify or lean Republican (31%) than all Michigan adults (42%). El-Sayed won the Democratic party’s Senate primary last month by just 15,000 votes. In a battleground state, El-Sayed’s unapologetically progressive campaign focuses on affordability rather than conflict in the Middle East, which has drawn ire from Republicans. But his positions on Israel-Palestine, including calling for an end to offensive and defensive military aid from the US, have become the focus of an active campaign to urge Jewish Michiganders to vote for his Republican opponent, Mike Rogers – as well as a counter-effort on El-Sayed’s behalf. *** Just six miles north-west of Newman’s progressive Ferndale neighborhood, Oak Park is the heartbeat of Michigan’s Orthodox Jewish community, home to Jewish retirement homes, synagogues and kosher bakeries. On the eve of the recent Rosh Hashanah holiday, there was a steady stream of customers buying bread and sweet treats from kosher stores as children furiously cycled from the stores to a nearby synagogue. It was here, last April, that antisemitic graffiti was sprayed on the outside a synagogue. “In the Jewish community, I think we have an awareness that it’s not if something is going to happen, it’s when something is going to happen. This isn’t the first incident we’ve had here,” Rabbi Robert Gamer of the Congregation Beth Shalom told CBS Detroit in April. El-Sayid was criticized for comments he made in March about the Temple Israel attack, saying, in part, that “hurt people hurt people”, referring to the Temple Israel attacker. An FBI investigation concluded that the attacker was inspired by Hezbollah. Ghazali’s two brothers, a niece and a nephew, had been killed in an Israeli airstrike in southern Lebanon days before. The Democratic candidate has also drawn criticism for links to Hasan Piker, the leftwing streamer who has become a target for attacks from Republicans and centrist Democrats. In the Democratic primary, El-Sayed lost Oak Park’s Oakland county to Haley Stevens by nearly 20,000 votes – a number larger than his final winning margin. El-Sayed later apologized for those comments, saying that he had jumped too quickly to provide “context” for the attack, “but it wasn’t the time for context”. Still, El-Sayed’s message has particularly resonated with young Jewish Michiganders angered by the variety of challenges facing working people, and aligned with his positions on Israel. Since his primary win, he has made a concerted effort to meet with Jewish leaders, including the Michigan Democratic Jewish caucus, which has not yet endorsed him. Several campaign initiatives reflect divisions among Jewish communities. An open letter supporting El Sayed, signed by Michigan Jews for Democracy, has about 1,000 signatures. Other rabbis and Jewish leaders have formed the Nonnegotiable Michigan campaign, a petition that demands, among other things, that candidates for office support “Jewish sovereignty in Israel”. (El-Sayed has said he supports “equal rights to peace, dignity, and self-determination” for both Israeli and Palestinians, through whatever political system both peoples choose.) A third initiative is openly calling for Jewish Democrats and independents to back Rogers, claiming: “All of us have felt threatened and alienated by the politics and allies embraced by Abdul El-Sayed.” In June, Jewish Voice for Peace (JVP), a pro-Palestine organization that represents about 750,000 members and supporters nationwide, endorsed El-Sayed in a first for the organization, helping him defeat Stevens, who received tens of millions of dollars from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac), the pro-Israel Super Pac. Others joined after the primary results were settled. “After the primary, some of the members of our [T’chiyah] congregation who voted for Stevens started showing up to the Jews for Abdul meetings because they were just like: ‘We don’t totally align with him on [Israel], but we are very clear that the alternative is really bad,’” says Jackson Koeppel, a 33-year-old Detroit-based volunteer with Jews for Abdul, a group critical of Israel, citing El-Sayed’s platform on universal healthcare and getting money out of politics. Last month, Rogers, El-Sayed’s Republican opponent, asked Aipac not to publicly spend advertising money on his own behalf, acknowledging a growing concern Michigan voters have with the powerful pro-Israel lobbying organization. Polls have put El-Sayed and Rogers in a dead heat. For Josh Whinston, a rabbi at Temple Beth Emeth in Ann Arbor, a reform congregation, it was comments El-Sayed made the morning after his primary win last month that prompted significant concern. “When I hear Dr El-Sayed, the morning after the primary, talk about Israel as bloodthirsty and then in the evening tell me that he cared about my security, that really created such a dissonance in my head,” said Whinston, who has joined the “Nonnegotiable” initiative. He said he viewed the term “bloodthirsty” as playing into an antisemitic trope. At the same time, Whinston, who has met El-Sayed in a one-on-one meeting, says his door is not closed to the idea of voting for the Democrat. “He is an inspiring leader I think he has the potential to do amazing things in our country,” he says. “He is moving in the right direction; he has not moved far enough.” Meanwhile, Republicans and rightwing media have seized on his platform. Last month, vice-president JD Vance spoke personally with a rabbi and a security guard from Temple Israel, who also attended a rally Vance held in nearby Sterling Heights in which the vice-president claimed El-Sayed is “very, very evil”. (Temple Israel declined an interview request from the Guardian.) El-Sayed’s campaign also faces a formidable challenge in the shape of big sums of out-of-state campaign spending. “In Detroit, we have a lot of work to do in terms of getting people excited,” says Newman. Elon Musk has already spent $1m in Michigan on online ads targeting El-Sayed. For his part, Newman, who went on a birthright trip to Israel when she was 18, says the contrast between El-Sayed, an epidemiologist, and Rogers, who with his wife has a net worth of between $7m and $14m, is clear. “He’s principled; he believes in and has actually done work to build better conditions for people in the [Michigan] health departments,” she says. “He’s running a campaign that I can respect; he’s not taking any corporate money, which is a huge piece of this.” • This article was amended on 23 September 2026 to clarify that Abdul El-Sayed is the Democratic party’s candidate to represent Michigan in the US Senate in the midterm elections, rather than a candidate for the Michigan senate.

title: Democrat says ICE restricted her oversight visit to country’s largest detention camp
summary: Veronica Escobar tells Guardian she was prevented from speaking to detainees at much-criticized Texas facility
text: Federal immigration officials in Texas prevented US representative Veronica Escobar from fully conducting her congressional oversight duties at a controversial Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention center, the lawmaker said in an interview with the Guardian. Escobar, a Democrat who represents El Paso and surrounding areas on the US-Mexico border in west Texas, conducted an oversight visit last month at the Camp East Montana ICE tent facility housed in the Fort Bliss military base, after two separate “disturbances” had been reported there in recent weeks. But when she arrived to scrutinize conditions at the camp, the largest ICE detention center in the country, she said she was not allowed to speak with any of the detained immigrants. She also requested surveillance footage of the reported incidents but said she has not received it. “The administration obviously has attempted to block congressional oversight,” Escobar said in a telephone interview with the Guardian. “It’s been very challenging at times. And that has depended on, to a large extent, what the directive has been from the administration.” The constraints placed on Escobar is one of the latest instances in which the Trump administration has limited members of Congress’s ability to conduct oversight visits into federal immigration detention centers. Escobar and other federal lawmakers sued the Trump administration last year for blocking such access. Despite a federal judge ruling in favor of the lawmakers last December, there have been subsequent reports of ICE officials placing limits on or turning away members of congress when attempting to conduct oversight visits. “Oversight, during the second Trump administration, has certainly been significantly more challenging than during the first Trump administration,” Escobar added. Camp East Montana was hastily constructed last summer at the huge army base in El Paso. Unlike other ICE detention centers housed in buildings, this facility is a sprawling “soft-sided” tent camp. It has the capacity to hold up to 5,000 people and has drawn complaints and demands for its closure from the time it opened. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees ICE, reported two separate “disturbances” within one week there in early September. On 1 September, it alleged that detained immigrants assaulted security staff by striking, kicking and throwing tablets at them. On 7 September, a larger group of around 130 detained immigrants allegedly threw items, flipped furniture and disabled security cameras. The detainees also knocked down partitions between the tented living quarters, known as pods, at the detention camp, Escobar said. An ICE official at the facility called 911 during the incident, according to reporting by the El Paso Times. The newspaper’s revelation contradicted what ICE officials apparently told Escobar during her visit. “While there absolutely have been serious issues and mismanagement, fraud, deaths, and a homicide, there had never been a riot,” Escobar said. “There had never been, especially in two weeks in a row, situations where the contractor lost control of the population in their custody.” Escobar said that when she spoke with an ICE official about incidents, the official pointed to the detained immigrants’ nationality as the cause. “The deputy was very quick to blame the nationality of the detainees, saying that the Venezuelans are a difficult population,” Escobar said. It is still unclear what exactly happened during the two incidents. Members of Congress have the legal power to conduct oversight visits into ICE detention facilities nationwide, by visiting the sites without prior notice and speaking with detained immigrants. Lawmakers have claimed that the Trump administration has limited those oversight visits by requiring lawmakers to submit the names and personal information of detainees they want to speak with beforehand. The homeland security department disputed Escobar’s claims in an email to the Guardian, while adding that it considers many oversight visits “a media act”, and also denied that there has been an official request for data and footage. “Any member of Congress can still request to speak with any illegal alien in ICE custody,” a DHS spokesperson said in a statement. “If an illegal alien and a member of Congress agree to meet with one another, ICE will facilitate the meeting. We are not stopping members of Congress from meeting with illegal aliens, including many with criminal histories in ICE custody, or touring ICE facilities.” Since Camp East Montana opened last summer, it has been plagued with accusations of abuse, mismanagement and dire conditions. Immigrants and human rights groups have repeatedly alleged human rights and constitutional violations at the site, including physical abuse, sexual harassment, inedible food and medical neglect. ICE was sued over alleged “dire” conditions earlier this year. At least three people detained at the site have died in ICE custody, including a 55-year-old man whose January death was ruled a homicide after security guards beat him. This year, an internal ICE inspection found a number of deficiencies at the site, including with guards’ use of force. A US government accountability office report also found a series of problems with the facility’s contract, its construction and the conditions. The office made four recommendations to DHS, ICE and the US army. Those recommendations remain “open”, meaning they have not been resolved. “That facility, from my perspective, should not be operational,” Escobar said. “It should have been shut down a long time ago.” During her recent Camp East Montana oversight visit, Escobar pressed for the private contractor running the facility to be held accountable for the recent incidents, not just the detained immigrants deemed responsible. Earlier this year, ICE gave the multi-million-dollar contract for running the facility on its behalf to a new private security company. “The contractor needs to eat those costs [of the damage]. If they were not prepared, if they were unable to control the situation, the American taxpayer should not pay for their incompetence,” Escobar said. “These private contractors are making enormous sums of money. And frankly, there needed to be accountability with this contractor.” The DHS spokesman said that far from closing, Camp East Montana “is upgrading” and claimed that the contractor now running the site was providing more services and “precise quality assurance”. “ICE is always looking at ways to improve our detention facilities to ensure we are providing the best care to illegal aliens in our custody,” the spokesperson said. Amentum Services, a Maryland-based contractor now running the Camp East Montana facility, did not respond to a request for comment. Acquisition Logistics, a small and relatively-unknown company based in Virginia first secured a nearly $1.3bn contract to run the site. Amentum took over this April after previously working as a subcontractor at the site. Meanwhile, there have been further accusations of alleged rights violations at other detention facilities. The Guardian has reported exclusively on a series of force feedings in ICE facilities, including inside two detention centers in Texas. During the first Trump administration, Escobar criticized and investigated ICE’s use of force feeding on hunger strikers in 2019. “It’s a very barbaric practice,” Escobar said. “The rapid expansion of immigration detention, under the [second] Trump administration– and fueled by Republicans’ One Big Beautiful Bill – it is allowing more and more of this absolutely unacceptable behavior by the federal government to continue.”

title: Australia investigating how F-35 fighter jet parts bound for US went missing in Hong Kong
summary: Disappearance of jet components sparks concern some of the program’s technology secrets could have been exposed
text: The Department of Defence is examining how F-35 fighter jet parts bound for the US from Australia were unexpectedly diverted to Hong Kong, the acting prime minister, Richard Marles, has said. Marles said “very much everything that has occurred at the Australian end” would be reviewed, but claimed the technology parts were not “sensitive”, as first reported by Politico over the weekend. The parts, which were being transported by another unknown third party on behalf of manufacturer, Lockheed Martin, still remain unaccounted for months later following their unplanned diversion to Hong Kong. The last known location of the fighter jet components – in Hong Kong, a special administrative region of China – has sparked concern that some of the program’s technology secrets could have been exposed. “We are examining [Australia’s involvement], but the point I would make here is that we are confident about the way in which we’ve engaged with the program, and through the US’s prime contractor, Lockheed,” Marles said on Tuesday. “My understanding is that there is a sense of comfort, and we’re not talking about sensitive equipment here, or sensitive parts. “Ultimately, though, this is an issue which is going to be managed by the United States and by Lockheed in terms of what has occurred.” Politico reported sources said the “sensitive” shipment contained one of the jet’s canopies, which reportedly contains stealth technology. The US Department of War and F-35 Joint Program Office confirmed they were aware of the “shipment issue”. “We are actively working with US authorities and industry partners to retrieve these components, investigate the incident, and place safeguards to avoid a future occurrence,” the spokesperson said. While many details have not yet been revealed, Michael Shoebridge, a director for Strategic Analysis Australia who has worked in intelligence agencies, said there were two reasons why China, or another adversary, would want F-35 parts – to reverse engineer them, or to learn how to better exploit and attack them. Shoebridge added the shipment’s pitstop in Hong Kong was “such an unexpectedly stupid thing” for the manufacturer or Australia to do. “This is an act of incredible ineptitude and stupidity, and so it’s more the Chinese taking advantage of an incredible stroke of luck brought to them by the stupidity of the people involved,” he said. Last week, the US State Department announced that the Trump administration would continue with the sale of 48 F-35s to Saudi Arabia, despite reported concerns from the US intelligence organisations that China could obtain some of the stealth technology. Australia was one of the early development partners in the F-35. The program spreads the development, supply, management and sustainment of the fighter jets across different countries. More than 70 Australian companies have production and sustainment contracts with the F-35 program. In excess of 700 of the fighter jet’s “critical pieces” are manufactured in Victoria alone, according to the state government. Australia also hosts a regional distribution hub for F-35 parts in New South Wales. Australian companies involved in the program’s supply chain have been awarded contracts valued at over $5.2bn, as of September 2025. Shoebridge said the missing shipment of parts could mean the whole multibillion-dollar fleet is vulnerable to adversaries. “They’re all now carrying the risk of whatever vulnerabilities this has brought to the aircraft,” he said. “So it’s not just a US-Australia issue. It’s every operator of the F-35 program [that] has an interest in understanding what happened and what was potentially exposed.”

text: Jacinda Ardern and her husband, Clarke Gayford, have bought a $5.3m home in Sydney’s northern beaches, according to a source with knowledge of the sale. The former New Zealand prime minister settled on a home in Dee Why after looking at properties in the area including in nearby Curl Curl. The sale – handled by Raine & Horne Northern Beaches and first reported by the Sydney Morning Herald – is the biggest the suburb has recorded this year, according to the source familiar with the transaction. The Guardian has contacted Gayford and a representative for Ardern for comment. In February, Ardern’s office confirmed she was living in Australia, following media reports that she, her husband and their daughter, Neve, had attended open home viewings in Sydney’s northern beaches. “The family has been travelling for a few years now,” a spokesperson from her office told the Guardian at the time. “For the moment they’re basing themselves out of Australia – they have work there, and it brings the added bonus of more time back home in New Zealand.” Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email The spokesperson did not elaborate on when the family arrived in Australia nor what kind of work they were doing, but noted it was not unusual for former leaders to spend time overseas after leaving office. Ardern announced her retirement from politics in January 2023, after five years as New Zealand’s prime minister and the leader of the country’s Labour party. When she was elected to the top job in October 2017, Ardern became the world’s youngest-serving female leader, aged 37, and later became the second woman to give birth while holding elected office. Since leaving office, Ardern has taken up dual fellowship roles at Harvard University, continued her work on the Christchurch Call – a project she established to combat online extremism after the 2019 Christchurch mosque shootings – and joined the board of trustees of Prince William’s Earthshot prize. title: Lib Dems torn over whether to be voters’ first choice or the route to block Reform
summary: Party strategists say careful targeting of seats has paid off and should continue, but some say a wider vision is needed
text: One of the more dramatic moments in a Liberal Democrat conference otherwise short of them came late on Sunday, when the party frontbencher Lisa Smart told the polling veteran John Curtice that, in effect, he no longer understood modern politics. Curtice had warned the Lib Dems they risked being left behind, with the lack of a coherent national message seeing them all but ignored outside a few electoral strongholds. Smart’s response? In the new era of five- or six-party politics, and mass tactical voting, this does not matter. It was a distillation of the largely underground debate which has dominated the gathering in Brighton and is likely to define the party’s future. It is a battle between, depending on the stance, strategy versus recklessness, or caution versus ambition – or, more bluntly, whether the Lib Dems want to be the first choice of voters, or their route to block a Reform UK government. The current choice, as decided by Ed Davey and his leadership team and argued forcefully by Smart, is a continuation of the 2024 electoral approach in which the party set aside a fully national campaign to focus relentlessly on a series of target seats, many of them held by the Conservatives. It worked. As Smart argued – after Curtice pointed out that the Lib Dems had won 23% of the vote in the 2010 election – in 2024 such careful targeting helped them take 72 MPs on little more than 12% vote share, adding: “I know which one I prefer.” Party strategists are adamant that with voting patterns atomised, many seats at the next election are likely to be won on tiny margins, with the key factors being tactical voting and a ruthlessly efficient ground game, both Lib Dem specialities. Davey and his team say even in public that they can improve on the 2024 result, the best in a century for the party. In private, there is talk of perhaps 140 MPs, and being the balance of power in a hung parliament. None of this is impossible, but – as Curtice said – it relies on a series of external factors to remain constant, including no noticeable dip in Reform’s fortunes or a boost for the Tories, given the way the strategy hinges on a split vote across the right. But what is more pressing for a number of Lib Dems is the way the tactic can feel like a slightly desperate attempt to appeal to, or at least not alienate, the voters on the right and left that the party needs to enlist. As such, the policy offering on show in Brighton – and there has been no lack of policy – has felt at times a bit disjointed, with economic offerings based on tax cuts and lower regulation balanced by calls to protect human rights. What is lacking, some fear, is a wider vision, or any boldness. “Things need to change,” Carl Cashman, the Lib Dem opposition leader on Liverpool city council, told delegates from the conference stage. “I’m a radical because I’m a liberal, and the fact that liberalism has become synonymous with the status quo – it irks me so much.” Julian Brazil, the Lib Dem leader of Devon county council, was more abrupt still, saying his party was “sleepwalking into irrelevance” under Davey’s leadership. There is, however, no sign at all of a challenge to Davey. Even the more malcontented MPs accept he will take the party into the next election, and in many cases they also accept that his careful approach has merits. Those around the Lib Dem leader say he is aware of the concerns, but feels a huge responsibility to ensure the party wins enough MPs to prevent a Reform government, something Davey sees as the defining mission of his political life. Some argue that the apparent conflict is largely artificial, and it is possible to embrace Davey’s approach to the next election while also trying to redefine liberalism for the longer term. There are, inevitably, still frustrations. “It’s like being stuck on a bumper car, just being buffeted by what the other parties do, with no real control,” one MP said. “Some vision would be nice.” Another took a more hopeful view: “You could argue that we’re not being left behind, we’re just standing still, knowing what we think, while everyone else dashes around in chaos, looking stupid. And maybe we should just let them do that.”

title: Andy Burnham does not rule out Brexit reversal being in next Labour manifesto
summary: PM says immediate focus is on rebuilding bridges with EU as he prepares for first meeting with Ursula von der Leyen
text: Andy Burnham has opened the door to fighting the next election on the UK rejoining the EU, but said his immediate priority was continuing to rebuild bridges with European allies. The prime minister, who will hold his first meeting with the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, on Tuesday, did not rule out including reversing Brexit in Labour’s next manifesto – but suggested the country should focus on securing closer trading ties first. Ministers have expressed fears privately that the EU reset has lost significant momentum since Burnham became prime minister, and a summit on the issue is likely to be delayed again unless the bloc agrees to discuss legislation that could lock British business out of parts of EU industry. Burnham has said he will stick to Keir Starmer’s red lines this side of an election, but he is under pressure from Labour MPs who opposed Brexit to change tack, in part because of the potential boost to growth, even though his own seat of Makerfield voted to leave. Asked by reporters on his flight to New York on Monday for the UN general assembly whether he could rule out a reversal of Brexit being in the next Labour manifesto, he said: “Our focus at the moment is on a UK/EU summit which we hope will take place later this year. “My immediate priority is to build on the good work that Keir did in rebuilding bridges. Because those bridges were broken in the early part of this decade. And Keir did a good job in re-establishing that relationship. “What we have got to do now is go to the next level in terms of reaching practical agreement that will further boost the British economy. And those issues are the substance of the summit alongside EU requests around youth mobility.” The prime minister admitted he had concerns about the bloc’s “made in Europe” legislation, which is designed to curb China’s increasing presence but could also affect British industry and supply chains. He said he would share those concerns “in a constructive spirit” with von der Leyen. “The other issues you discuss, they are for another day,” he said of rejoining the bloc. Burnham said the UK had considerable support among EU member states for its position on the “made in Europe” legislation, which threatens to scupper ongoing negotiations about the reset. “Europe’s argument is not with us. We both suffer the same effects as other countries, particularly steel,” he said. “We are making the argument we are not your enemies here ... we are not the problem. ‘Made in Europe’ is dealing with a different problem.” He also said delicate UK/Ireland supply chains could end up being “collateral damage” of any disagreement with the EU. “Let’s work towards a trusted partner approach that doesn’t cause a problem where there wasn’t a problem and where we have common cause,” he said. In his speech to the UN on Tuesday night, Burnham will reflect on the 10 years since Brexit and say the UK needs to be more clear-eyed about the risks to its democratic system. “I’m reflecting on that last decade,” he told reporters on his plane. “What we’ve experienced is when that turbulence comes, when outside actors seek to manipulate, to distort facts, influence the British democratic process. “Going into the next decade we need to be clear-eyed about that and become stronger and more on the front foot about challenging that. “Perhaps Britain can say we have experienced some of the turbulence before others in terms of the politics of recent times. We need to be clearer where outside forces, our enemies, are trying to manipulate that opinion and feeling to serve their interests, not ours.”

title: Labor MP covers up Woodside logo on Fremantle jumper ahead of AFL grand final
summary: Josh Wilson, federal assistant minister for climate change and energy, joins peaceful campaign against fossil fuel company
text: Labor frontbencher Josh Wilson has become the latest public figure to cover up gas company Woodside Energy’s logo on their Fremantle Dockers jumper, as the team chases its first AFL premiership this weekend. A photograph of Wilson – the Albanese government’s assistant minister for climate change and energy – wearing a Fremantle guernsey with red tape covering the logo of Australia’s biggest oil and gas company was published by The Australian on Tuesday. Opponents of Woodside’s sponsorship of the Dockers have launched the Get Off My Chest campaign, supported by Tame Impala frontman Kevin Parker, who covered up the logo on a Fremantle t-shirt ahead of a performance in Colorado last week. Wilson told Guardian Australia the picture was taken from a family member’s social media account. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email “I’ll be in Fremantle for the [grand final] and I’m looking forward to sharing the nerves and cheers in a sea of purple for what we all hope is a triumphant Wharfie Time. “The photo in question is a family picture, and when I wear my Dockers gear I just want to show my support for Freo. “This week is all about the opportunity to see the Dockers compete on the last Saturday in September, but it’s great that Australia is a place where people have the freedom to express their view and values through a range of creative and peaceful campaigns.” Get Off My Chest campaigner Clare Lagan used spray paint to hide the Woodside logo on a mural of former Dockers players Michael Walters and Nat Fyfe outside the Fremantle markets earlier this month. Lagan said the campaign had provided supporters with hundreds of patches since launching in May. Other supporters include Australian novelist Tim Winton and the independent senator David Pocock. “Woodside has long been one of Australia’s most controversial companies and one of sport’s most controversial sponsors,” she said. “We commend Kevin Parker and call on the Fremantle football club to end their partnership with Australia’s largest fossil fuel company.” “The overwhelming public support for a gas export tax reflects the broad consensus that companies like Woodside are not paying their fair share for resources owned by the Australian people. “Kevin Parker’s statement is clear: this is not something Freo fans can support.” Conservation Council of WA spokesperson, Gerard Mazza, welcomed Parker’s move, linking it to the Browse to North West Shelf gas export project off the Western Australian coast. Woodside calls Browse “Australia’s biggest undeveloped offshore gas resource”. “WA is one of the world’s biggest producers of gas,” Mazza said. “We have more than enough gas to get us through the energy transition and no need for destructive new projects like Browse.” A Woodside spokesperson said on Tuesday the company was proud of its sponsorship agreement with Fremantle, set to run until at least the end of 2027. “We love our partnership of more than 15 years with the Fremantle football club and it’s great to see the success the club is having this year. “We’re looking forward to continuing our work together.” Fremantle will face the Brisbane Lions in Saturday’s AFL grand final. The Dockers are on the hunt for the club’s first premiership since their inaugural season in 1995, in just their second grand final.
