title: Meet Barbie Pig: new documentary reveals the wonders of life on the Pacific seabed
summary: A magical new film captures the secret life of the deep sea in a stretch of the ocean at risk from industrial mining
text: A magical film that explores the wonders of the deep sea through the eyes of a team of scientists and an underwater robot called Isis will be shown in selected cinemas across the UK next month. The documentary, How Deep Is Your Love, offers a playful, irreverent and bittersweet look at our anthropocentric view of Earth, as it switches perspective from humans to deep sea animals and back again. It follows a research team from the Natural History Museum (NHM) in London, who sail for 12 days to reach a remote region called the Clarion Clipperton Zone, a biodiversity-rich area of the Pacific between Hawaii and Mexico. It takes Isis five hours to make the 3-mile (5km) descent to the bottom of this harsh world, where sunlight cannot penetrate, and where nodules rich in minerals mark it out as a hotspot for industrial mining. It is a race against time for the scientists to identify new species before deep sea mining threatens to wipe out fragile ecosystems for ever. Scientists estimate that only 0.001% of the deep sea floor – categorised by some as more than 500 metres below the sea’s surface, where sunlight fades to total darkness – has been observed by humans. The film is an ode, says director Eleanor Mortimer, to the taxonomists and biologists who spend “hours and hours counting the legs of a minuscule animal you can’t even see with the naked eye” and to the strange creatures of the abyssal plain, of which we know so little. Even when painstakingly identified, and DNA collected, it can take up to 14 years to name a species, Mortimer says. “It’s the challenge of the deep sea,” says Mortimer, who shares the scientists’ desire to demystify life in the deep. “Most people never go there, and yet it’s a huge part of our planet we need to connect with. That was the motive behind the film. I want people to fall in love with the deep sea, I want people to connect with it.” She became “obsessed” with the region, but could not work out how to make a film until, by chance, she met Muriel Rabone, the film’s science adviser and co-producer, who told Mortimer about the NHM team. “Their love and curiosity and excitement have become infectious,” says Mortimer. Most of the film takes place at sea, or at the International Seabed Authority (ISA) in Jamaica, which regulates activities in the seabed beyond national jurisdiction. While How Deep Is Your Love does not shy away from complex questions of humanity’s ever-swelling appetite for nature’s resources, it is neither an activist anti-exploitation film like Seaspiracy or a nature-based, David Attenborough Blue Planet-style documentary. Instead, Mortimer’s dreamlike narration poses philosophical questions of the nature of our planet, while sharing the scientists’ sense of wonder, as they watch a series of screens linked to a camera 5,000 metres below. “Oh, I love this sea cucumber,” says one, as a neon pink sea creature, dubbed “Barbie Pig”, comes into view. Other brightly coloured amorphous creatures are given names like Headless Chicken Monster and Psychedelic Elvis Worm. There is a poignant moment, soundtracked by the melancholy strains of Portishead’s Glory Box, which records a dilemma the scientists face: to be studied, a species has to be brought to the surface, a journey the life form cannot survive. “I feel a bit like the Nicole Kidman character in Paddington,” says one researcher: “I want that bear in a jar on my desk!” Another admits to dreaming of tucking sea cucumbers into bed. In a final twist of fantasy, Mortimer brings deep sea animals and humans into the same world. The ghostly stars of the expedition are superimposed on the corridor walls of the ISA – which earlier this year once again concluded negotiations without a regulatory framework and with significant gaps in the data needed to establish environmental thresholds for mining – and in the streets of London at night. “Perhaps the connections made through the film can trigger something like empathy,” says Mortimer. How Deep Is Your Love, a Sandbox presentation produced by Luna Films and Ngauruhoe Films, is opening in cinemas in the UK on 2 October.

title: Trump’s bizarre social media blitz leaves world guessing ahead of UN address
summary: President has been posting on Washington arch, AI and his ‘25 top achievements’ – the chances of an uplifting speech appear slim
text: The annual gathering of the United Nations general assembly has historically been a platform for US presidents to display their most serious face and a positive vision to the world. From Harry Truman and Dwight Eisenhower to John F Kennedy and Barack Obama, over eight decades US leaders have used the setting to expound on grand themes before a global audience at pivotal moments in international affairs. As world leaders and officials gather in New York for the yearly event, and Donald Trump prepares to address them on Tuesday, how he will contribute to this historic catalog of remarks is a matter of speculation. The US president has spent recent days blitzing social media on a variety of topics, from his planned triumphal arch in Washington to a bid to rebrand artificial intelligence, as he contends with an unpopular war and low approval ratings that threaten to drag down his party in November’s US midterm elections. His previous addresses to the assembly suggest that the chances of a non-divisive and uplifting message are low. Last year, Trump shocked the august gathering in his first appearance since returning to the White House the previous January by declaring to those present that their countries were “going to hell” while launching a full-frontal assault on the UN and the concept of open borders. In 2018, during his first presidency, Trump drew laughter from fellow leaders when he opened his address by claiming: “In less than two years, my administration has accomplished almost more than any other administration in the history of our country.” The previous year, he had attacked longstanding allies, singling out Germany for its energy policy, and declaring that the US “can no longer be taken advantage of, or enter into a one-sided deal where the United States gets nothing in return”. This time around, Trump’s recent social media activities hinted at an even more volatile than usual state of mind from a leader who can be erratic at the best of times. Arguably the most eye-catching was his declaration in an early Sunday morning post that he intended to turn his highly controversial planned arch in Washington DC into a military storage facility, claiming – without providing evidence – that the move was requested by the US military. There was a surfeit of others. A post headlined “His Hemisphere” and depicting Trump gazing at a map of the globe ominously hinted at an imperious tone he could strike, less than nine months after US forces seized the former Venezuelan leader, Nicolás Maduro, in his compound in Caracas and spirited him and his wife to New York. The Trump administration has since trumpeted a deal giving it control over a significant segment of Venezuelan oil reserves. In another post, Trump postures as the defender of AI – denouncing recent fears that its rapid development could presage the destruction of the human race. Instead, he painted it as the latest target of “many hoaxes, all generated by the radical left dumocrats, for purposes of destroying our country” and announced his plans for an “AI force”– headed by an “AI Czar” – in the image of the space force, established during his first presidency. “AI is the next Industrial Revolution, or Internet, but will be even larger and more impactful, possibly as much as 25% of our country’s GDP,” he wrote. “We are leading China, and the rest of the world, and I intend to keep it that way.” There is every chance Trump returns to previous themes at the UN on Tuesday. In an echo of his 2018 speech, on Friday he posted a list of his “Top 25 Trump Achievements” since returning to office. Trump’s appearance before the general assembly will be his first since his fateful decision to launch, in tandem with Israel, a war against Iran in February. The conflict – despite his predictions that it would last a few days, and result in the collapse of Tehran’s Islamic regime – shows no signs of ending. The regime still stands. Iran’s closure of the strait of Hormuz, a strategic waterway that was a conduit to one-fifth of the world’s oil exports before hostilities began, has sent global energy prices soaring and stoked inflation in the US, challenging the prospects of Trump’s Republican party in November’s midterms. Polls show a majority of Americans oppose the war, which has further deflated his approval ratings. Further piquancy to Trump’s political dilemma is likely to be added by the presence of Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, at the UN. While Trump has signaled a willingness to meet his Iranian counterpart, Pezeshkian – a relative pragmatist, under pressure from regime hardliners to stand firm and avoid compromise with an enemy still branded by Tehran as “the great Satan” – is thought unlikely to agree to such an encounter. The sting of being snubbed by an Iranian leadership he likes to depict as “dying to make a deal” could add further fuel to a fiery speech before the general assembly and witnessed by a global audience. Traditionally, US presidential speeches to the UN go through a long drafting process and are subject to reviews by the state department, the Pentagon and the intelligence community, as well as fevered last-minute rehearsals. That all may still hold true for this address. Yet equally likely is a no-holds-barred, scattergun diatribe, rehashing the themes of Trump’s recent social media output.

title: Tuesday briefing: Europe thinks Russia is preparing to test Nato’s limits
summary: In today’s newsletter: Intelligence chiefs warn that Russia’s appetite for risk is growing, as sabotage and other covert attacks target countries supporting Ukraine
text: Good morning. As the UN general assembly kicks off in New York later today, we anticipate a heavy focus on the ongoing conflicts in Iran, Ukraine and the Gulf – as well as the inevitable body language analysis of Andy Burnham’s first in-person meeting with Donald Trump. But another related conflict is likely to dominate informal discussions: the intensifying acts of sabotage on European states that are believed to trace back to Russia but deliberately fall below the threshold for military response – a so-called hybrid or “shadow war” with the singular purpose of disrupting support for Ukraine. As Vladimir Putin consolidates his grip on power in tightly controlled Russian elections and the Kremlin welcomed further success for the far-right AfD in German state polls yesterday, European intelligence officers have shared with the Guardian their starkest warnings yet about potential Russian attempts to test Nato resolve with an attack on European soil. For today’s newsletter, I spoke to Shaun Walker, our special correspondent for eastern Europe, Ukraine and intelligence matters, about whether Europe is already at war. First, this morning’s headlines. Five big stories Yemen | The UK has agreed to provide defensive air support to Saudi Arabia to help counter Houthi fighters and restore stability in the Middle East while driving down the cost of living at home, Andy Burnham has said, ahead of his first meeting with Donald Trump. Environment | The “jaw-dropping” El Niño currently heating up the planet has burst through the highest temperature ever recorded for the phenomenon, several months before its expected peak. Gaza | Israeli and UK military commanders could be requested to give evidence to an inquest concerning three British aid workers killed in Gaza when aid vehicles they were travelling in were hit by an airstrike. US | After President Trump’s snap decision to ban CNN from the White House, the four other networks that comprise the White House’s TV pool decided they would cease their pooled coverage of the president. Slavery | Bones of the enslaver Edward Colston are likely to remain interred in a church in Bristol if and when the currently unused building is given a new lease of life as a community resource, it has emerged. In depth: The line between peace and war In a series of interviews with Shaun Walker in Prague and Riga, European intelligence bosses from the Czech Republic, Latvia and Sweden raised the possibility of an imminent Russian test of Nato, with one suggesting a potential attack could come in a matter of “months, not years”. These sources were speaking days after Polish prime minister Donald Tusk told his parliament that intelligence assessments suggested Russia might launch an attack with drones or missiles on Nato territory in the coming months. French president Emmanuel Macron has also summoned party leaders for an emergency meeting to discuss similar warnings. When I catch up with Shaun in a taxi on the way to Warsaw airport, he’s still assessing the gravity of these warnings. “One thing you always have to bear in mind when reporting on intelligence is that – because the way spy agencies gain information usually remains secret – you often don’t know if a source is talking about a very specific intercept of a plan that’s almost certainly going to happen, or if it’s less concrete chatter that analysts have put together.” His view is that these concerns are not at the level of early 2022, when American intelligence repeatedly warned Russia was preparing to invade Ukraine and had hard evidence of the Kremlin’s plans (as Shaun revealed here). What did surprise him was his sources’ willingness to be quoted: “Normally I go into these interviews assuming that we’re going to talk off the record. All of these people were happy to be on the record, which does suggest they want to get a message out.” (Quick note, readers: “off the record” is a phrase that reporters in books, films and even real life throw about with abandon, but what does it mean? Say your source tells you about seeing a piece of fruit in a bowl. On the record means you can report that Jill Bloggs told the Guardian exclusively: “There’s a banana in the fruit bowl.” Off the record allows you to use that information to aid your investigation, but you mustn’t reveal where it came from. You can approach other fruit bowl-watchers, to check if they agree with Jill’s sighting. Then you might write: “Several sources with knowledge of the fruit bowl confirmed that a banana was present.” It’s a journalistic convention with no legal consequences, of course.) *** What is this hybrid war and how can Europe fight it? This systematic campaign has developed since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine four and a half years ago, with common features: designed to seed chaos and anxiety among Ukraine’s allies, while it is often difficult to prove conclusively Russian involvement as Kremlin security services pivot to recruiting local foot soldiers online. Since the beginning of this year, there has been a catalogue of unexplained fires at defence facilities supplying Ukraine in Italy, Bulgaria, Estonia and Slovakia. An explosives-laden drone was discovered next to a Ukrainian cargo plane at Germany’s Leipzig airport. Authorities in Denmark warned Russia is recruiting Danish citizens to sabotage defence firms with ties to Ukraine; in Lithuania, an Ikea was set on fire; and in France, five coffins inscribed with the words “French soldiers in Ukraine” were left under the Eiffel Tower. In the UK, the Rycroft review found online disinformation from hostile foreign states including Russia was warping political discourse when it published in March, while two Russian-linked arsonists who targeted property connected to former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer were jailed in June. Given the recent escalation, it’s not surprising that Shaun observes some EU politicians “getting irritated” with the term ‘hybrid war’, and arguing that such direct attacks amount to more than “grey zone” activity. Although European governments have become much quicker publicly to call out Russian involvement, the challenge for these politicians is deciding what effective measures they can take. After the Leipzig incident, Germany expelled more than 150 Russian diplomats and promised tighter border controls for Russians entering Germany. But the Schengen free movement zone makes this tricky: one of the suspects in the Leipzig incident reportedly entered Europe using an Italian tourist visa. EU sanctions blacklist Russian banks and energy companies, as well as entities in the United Arab Emirates, Thailand and China for helping Moscow evade western restrictions. And there’s a growing willingness among EU nations to clamp down on Russia’s shadow fleet – ships illegally carrying Russian oil and other supplies in the Baltic and North seas. While there are vocal critics who argue these diplomatic and economic measures don’t go far enough, others worry that even more decisive responses would riskdragging the bloc into military escalation. “What Russia is working to is that they know even the most hawkish people in Nato countries would really like to avoid having a direct conflict.” *** What is the mood in Europe? For decades, politicians and analysts in those Baltic states most at risk of Russian aggression have warned western Europe to take that threat more seriously. But that mood has flipped of late, with the secretary general of Estonia’s foreign ministry, Jonatan Vseviov, for example, cautioning against “panic” on social media. These states remain the strongest voices in terms of tangible responses to Russian aggression, but are well aware that the vast majority of Russia’s military capability is tied up in Ukraine. They are also concerned about the impact that a narrative of tanks rolling into Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania has on their societies and economies – which is of course partly the point of concerted Russian psyops. “Somebody put it to me recently – which I thought was the perfect description – that Baltic states prefer western Europe to see it as a chronic rather than an acute problem”. With that in mind, European leaders at the UN in New York this week will be keen to create a united front and wary of interventions from Donald Trump, who has previously dismissed concerns that Russia will strike a Baltic country or other member state to test Nato resolve and repeatedly criticised the alliance. *** Is Europe already at war (and what does that mean)? When Shaun was researching his latest book, The Illegals, about Russia’s deep-cover spies, he waded through archives of KGB documents from the 70s and 80s. They often referred to “the special period”, a Soviet term that described a stage between friendly coexistence and war between communist and capitalist worlds, and was characterised by plans for relentless sabotage. “It sounded a lot like where we are now”, he says. Like Europe, Russia doesn’t want a direct confrontation with the West but it’s clear, adds Shaun, “that their risk appetite is increasing.” The scale of sabotage has led to prominent military voices in the UK and across Europe suggesting that the bloc is already at war – although the very definition of ‘at war’ is now liminal – and that governments ought to be more transparent with their public. Does he agree? Shaun’s one word answer is “no”. The nuance is as follows: “There is a clear campaign from Russia, using methods that are not military, but are pretty aggressive. Some people may consider them as being something close to a war. It’s clearly absolutely nothing like the war in Ukraine.” He suggests that European governments find themselves in a bind domestically. “If they choose to spend on defence rather than social issues, those social issues get worse and voters move to the populist right, the AfD in Germany or Le Pen in France, then you end up with leaders who are very sympathetic to Russia in power.” “There’s a careful path between dismissing this as a fake threat and the kind of alarmist rhetoric that we’re on the path to war and every other issue is secondary.” What else we’ve been enjoying This week, the Guardian is following five Palestinians as they go about their lives, each telling us the story of their day. The latest moving account is from Alaa Hessi, who shares what it’s like to be pregnant in Gaza. Lucinda Everett, newsletters team I learned so many movies by heart in those turbulent adolescent (and younger) years when identities form. So I loved Hannah Marriott’s take on learning Dirty Dancing by heart as a littl’un, and why it’s her feelgood movie as a result. Poppy Noor, newsletters team As someone who has never had the patience (or bladder control) to queue for hours for a front-row concert spot, I was fascinated by Rosalind Adams’ piece about the lengths superfans will go to, to get close to their favourite artists. Lucinda The process of “cuckooing” – where drug gangs take over vulnerable people’s homes – is as terrifying as it sounds, but journalist Max Daly brings another layer to it in his reporting here, that shows the very complex, very human side. Jacqui Housden, newsletters team I loved Rafael Yaghobzadeh’s picture essay about the cold war bunkers in Finland, Sweden and Norway that have been given unlikely second acts as go-kart tracks, swimming pools, children’s soft play centres and more. Lucinda Sport Football | Thomas Tuchel has been rocked by five withdrawals from his England squad because of injuries ahead of the Nations League programme. Football | The Fifa president, Gianni Infantino, has agreed to commission an independent governance review after coming under mounting pressure to do so in the wake of the World Cup sale debacle. Cricket | Harry Brook is hopeful that Brydon Carse will break back into his England white-ball teams once the fast bowler is clear of his ongoing disciplinary, describing him as a “very good mate” who is “working on a few things behind the scenes”. The front pages “UK to give support to Saudi jets in bid to counter Houthi fighters”, is the Guardian’s front page today, while the Telegraph says “Burnham sends RAF to help Saudis”, and the Times writes “PM agrees military aid for Saudis over Yemen”. The i Paper has “UK fires torpedo from undersea drone in new warning to Putin” and the FT leads with “Kremlin-aided forgers moved $7bn through global banks”. The Mail leads on “New small boat farce”, the Express splashes “‘More freedom handed to new arrivals than British citizens’”. The Mirror writes “NHS need 55,00 more nurses”. The Sun has “Letby doc: we need a retrial”, and lastly Metro says “Air traffic out of control”. Today in Focus: The Latest Rise of the far right in Germany: how worried should we be? The German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, has vowed to stay in office despite heavy losses in two state elections that he described as a ‘disaster’. The anti-immigration, Kremlin-friendly Alternative für Deutschland won with 38% of the vote in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, while the leftwing Die Linke was victorious in Berlin. Merz has promised political change, but speculation is growing that his party could soon oust him. Lucy Hough speaks to the Guardian’s Berlin correspondent, Deborah Cole. Cartoon of the day | Ben Jennings The Upside A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad Despite 18 million people in the UK having hearing issues, there is still no dedicated centre for the Deaf community. Now, Amanprit Arnold, an urban planner and activist, is campaigning to create one. The DeafCity Hub would be a national centre for Arnold’s community, as well as a co-working and cultural space, and a home for Deaf-sector charities. It would be designed using deaf-friendly architectural guidelines called DeafSpace principles, which include wide corridors and staircases so people can walk next to each other while talking in BSL. This month, the project has landed a year-long “meanwhile” space (a building awaiting redevelopment), which Arnold hopes “will act as an incubator to develop this idea further.” Sign up here for a weekly roundup of The Upside, sent to you every Sunday Bored at work? title: Country diary: A little love at Larkrise has worked wonders for wildlife | Virginia Spiers
summary: St Dominic, Tamar valley: After just a few years, this rewilded plot of soggy land is home to voles and shrews and vigorously growing indigenous plants
text: At last, proper rain has greened the scorched pastures and washed shrivelled leaves and nut husks along the narrow lanes. Springs dribble and streams remain low; inspection of our well, dug more than a century ago by the legendary “Diver/Diviner” Cullas of Metherell, reveals a water level better than feared, but we remain cautious in our use. On the exposed northern edge of the parish, overlooked by Kit Hill and the distant blue haze of Dartmoor, Larkrise’s rewilded 10 acres of poorly drained land shows ever more growth. The thorny boundary hedge, with purple sloes, blackberries, scarlet hips and masses of haws, encroaches on planted trees – extra protection from predatory deer. The mix of guarded trees are tall and vigorous, interspersed with open patches of seeding knapweed, grasses, plantains and rattle. The guelder rose, spindle, holly and buckthorn already produce berries, less than seven years after this project began. Particularly sturdy are the seedling oaks, growing in-situ near their parent, a 200-year-old spreading oak tree. Formerly grazed off by livestock, rabbits and deer, these strongly rooted saplings have been meticulously marked, staked and guarded and their leaves host spangle and silk-button galls. Despite the drought, none of the recently excavated ponds have dried up completely. Clayey sides and bottoms, and heaps of stony spoil are colonised with vegetation, helped by the owners James and Mary who transplant and spread indigenous plants, seeds and cuttings. Towards the lowest boggy ground, the widest and newest expanse of water is a regular feeding station for skimming swallows. Today, blue sky reflects among water weeds in one of the deeper ponds; two young buzzards cruise overhead, sounding distinctively melancholic; goldfinches swoop among thistledown, and this year’s ubiquitous clouded yellows flit about purple loosestrife and buddleia. Trip cameras record the regular presence of fox, roe deer and barn owl. Moorhens live here and the local small mammal society documents assorted vole and shrew species plus weasels. Homewards, via Down Lane, where hedgerows are thick with incipient hazel catkins, we pass the adjoining farmed enclosure. Inside a gateway of hard trampled earth, bullocks range across the sparse pasture, where grazing is supplemented with winter’s fodder. • Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024, is available now at guardianbookshop.com

title: British Columbia sues OpenAI and Sam Altman over Tumbler Ridge mass school shooting
summary: Canadian province alleges deadly attack could have been prevented if company had warned police of shooter’s ChatGPT use
text: British Columbia has sued OpenAI, saying a mass shooting at a school in the Canadian province could have been prevented if the company had warned local ⁠law enforcement that the shooter ⁠had used ChatGPT to plan the attack. The lawsuit, filed in San Francisco federal court on Monday, names OpenAI and its CEO, Sam Altman, as defendants. It is seeking damages to fund recovery efforts in the province after the February attack, as well as an order directing changes to the way the company handles ChatGPT conversations that could lead to violence. Nine people, primarily children, were killed in the school shooting in Tumbler Ridge, British Columbia. The shooter, Jesse Van ⁠Rootselaar, had been flagged by the company’s safety team after her conversations about gun violence, but the company did not alert police. “The people of Tumbler Ridge have endured an unimaginable loss, and they deserve answers and accountability,” said Niki Sharma, British Columbia’s attorney general, in a statement this week on the suit. AI companies are facing increasing scrutiny over how their products may lead to a range of harms from cyberattacks and disinformation to facilitating violence and worsening mental health. OpenAI is also facing lawsuits from family members of victims in the British Columbia mass shooting, as well as the family of a victim in a Florida State University shooting from earlier this year. Altman published a letter in April to the community in Tumbler Ridge saying he was “deeply sorry” OpenAI had not contacted ‌law enforcement. He promised reforms, but never ‌followed through, despite efforts from British Columbia’s attorney general to engage, the lawsuit says. The school where the shooting took place is in the process of being ‌demolished, and the province has been forced to absorb the costs of a replacement school, mental health care and other effects of the shooting, according to the lawsuit. One survivor, Maya Gebala, recovered from being shot three times, including in the skull. She suffered catastrophic brain injuries and permanent disabilities from the attack, according to court documents. Gebala’s family has documented her life since the shooting in online posts, including sharing images of her celebrating her 13th birthday this week. A spokesperson for OpenAI, Drew Pusateri, called the Tumbler Ridge shooting an unspeakable tragedy. “OpenAI remains committed to working collaboratively with government and law enforcement officials, and continuing to advance our ongoing safety work.” British Columbia alleges that OpenAI has failed to take proper accountability and action for the killing, however, with Sharma stating that the company must strengthen its safeguards and increase transparency on its products. “To date, OpenAI has not taken meaningful steps to address the concerns raised by survivors, families and the Tumbler Ridge community,” the attorney general said. The province’s lawsuit comes after more than 30 family members of victims and others affected by the attack filed lawsuits in California, accusing the company of opting out of a chance to prevent ‌the shooting. Van Rootselaar shot her mother and stepbrother at home before killing an educational assistant and five students aged 12 and 13 at her former school on 10 February, according to police. Van Rootselaar, who was 18, then died by suicide. The incident, one of the worst mass shootings in Canada’s history, devastated the small northern mining town and shocked the country. It also prompted Canadian officials to call in OpenAI executives for questioning, as well as resulted in a call between Canada’s AI minister, Evan Solomon, and Altman. Van Rootselaar’s interactions with ChatGPT were first flagged by the company in June 2025. Safety team members recommended contacting police, but Altman and other OpenAI leadership overruled them, the lawsuit says, citing OpenAI whistleblowers who spoke to the Wall Street Journal in the wake of the shooting. The shooter’s account was deactivated, but she was able to get a new account and continue using the platform to plan her attack. After publication of the Wall Street Journal article, the company said the ⁠account was flagged by systems that identify “misuses of our models in furtherance of violent activities”, but the issues did not meet its internal criteria for reporting to law enforcement. The lawsuit comes after a series of cases against OpenAI have been filed in US state and federal courts in recent months over claims ChatGPT facilitated violence, including lawsuits related to a mass ‌shooting at Florida State University last year. In June, Florida became the first state to sue OpenAI over safety risks, accusing the company of misrepresenting the safety of its ChatGPT platform, which the lawsuit said had harmed children by providing information to school shooters, offering guidance on self-harm and addicting young users. OpenAI, which has denied the claims, has said it trains its models to refuse requests that could “meaningfully enable violence”, and notifies law enforcement when conversations suggest “an imminent and credible risk of harm to others”.

title: Grief, trauma and solidarity as South African running club mourns member killed in wave of femicides
summary: A week after Elizabeth ‘Tsontso’ Moselakgomo’s body was found, runners took part in a morning run to honour her name and demand more protection
text: The runners smiled and laughed, congratulating each other on finishing their 5km or 10km Saturday run, their foreheads glistening with sweat in the early morning sun. They helped themselves to water, instant coffee and sugary snacks, provided by waiting volunteers on the lawn outside a gated community of modern apartment blocks, and then stretched out together. But there were sombre moments too, as they mourned one of their own, who had lit up their Saturday runs around Sandton, an upmarket area of Johannesburg. Elizabeth “Tsontso” Moselakgomo’s body had been found a week earlier, on Saturday 12 September. The 38-year-old went missing three days earlier, after going out for a run alone after work. South Africa has been overwhelmed with shock, anger and grief at the discovery of nine women’s bodies dumped across Ekurhuleni, the municipality adjoining Johannesburg to the east, since 15 July. Six of the women were found in the last two weeks and two still have not been formally identified. Suspects have been arrested in two of the cases. South Africa has one of the world’s highest rates of femicide. Women were killed at a rate of 12.2 per 100,000 people in 2022, nearly six times the global rate, according to the UN Office on Drugs and Crime. Across the country, protesters have marched and running clubs have gathered to demand that police and the national government, which declared gender-based violence a national crisis in November 2025, do more to protect women. “This has really affected all of us,” Moselakgomo’s friend Sakane Mokoena said to her fellow runners, as they stood in a circle with their arms around each other’s shoulders. “I really want to thank each and every one of you for honouring Tsontso’s name. She really came and ran with us. She was an amazing lady.” Mokoena then thanked the men who ran with the majority female club, acknowledging that some slowed their pace every week to make sure that no woman was left behind. The group then bowed their heads for a moment’s silence. “It’s traumatic, scary, confusing,” said Sange, a female runner, who only wanted to share her first name. “Before I joined this group, I was running alone for years in this area … in the mornings, early winter mornings, late winter nights, and with music, earphones in my ears. You know, anything could have happened to me.” “There’s no scenario where women are prioritised,” she said. “The government doesn’t take us seriously. The men of South Africa don’t take themselves seriously. They don’t take us seriously. It’s just dangerous to be a woman in South Africa and it’s very sad to be a woman in South Africa.” The club first came back together to run on 15 September, after Moselakgomo’s body was identified by her family. “I think we all needed that Tuesday run, because we were all sad,” said Nokwanda, who has been running with the group since February last year. “And then we met as a community. And after that, I think we are getting there.” She called on all men to take responsibility for violence against women: “We as women have been fighting for our safety. I think it would be nice to see men fighting and not men saying ‘some men’, but standing up for women.” Thabiso, who had volunteered to provide the post-run refreshments instead of running, agreed. “If there’s a message that I can send out to other men is to be better,” he said. “I think as brothers and men, we need to really leave the animalistic ways behind us. There’s much better ways that we can build a society and we need to not be making these women feel like the country’s so bad.” Meanwhile, the families of the murdered women found across Ekurhuleni are still struggling to come to terms with their loss. Ayanda Nano was admitted to hospital in shock at how her cousin, 38-year-old Dineo Motapane, who she had grown up with, was discovered. “The state she was in is what put me in this hospital bed,” Nano, who is now raising Motapane’s two-year-old daughter, told the local Sunday World newspaper. “She was decomposed, like she had been dead for days. It pains me that she left us this way.” At Moselakgomo’s funeral which was broadcast by South Africa’s national TV news channels, her eight-year-old daughter, dressed in a pale pink padded jacket, took the microphone. “Dearest mother, how heartbreaking that you left me,” she said. “The day feels quiet without your voice. But your love is still here, surrounding me with love … Your beautiful daughter loves you so much. She misses you every day. But I know that I have gained a beautiful angel in you. Love your beautiful princess, Khumo.”

title: Solar and wind generation meet record 80% of power demand on Australia’s national grid
summary: Rooftop solar alone generates more than half of all power used, as clear sunny days and low demand drive record-breaking surge
text: Sunshine and wind met 80.4% of demand on Australia’s main power grid on Saturday, setting a new high bar for renewable electricity. Solar panels on rooftops provided more than half of the power used in the national electricity market, the grid that supplies the eastern states, South Australia and the Australian Capital Territory, for 30 minutes around lunchtime. This was complemented by solar and windfarms, and a small amount of hydro (1%). Fossil fuels, coal and gas, contributed 20%. The energy minister, Chris Bowen, said the milestone meant there was “more clean, cheap, sovereign energy powering our homes and businesses than ever before”. “There’s a long way to go, but expect more and more of these milestones in the future as Labor gets on with the job of the energy transition, and delivering real cost of living relief,” he posted on social media. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Dr Dylan McConnell, an energy systems researcher at the University of New South Wales, described it as “record season” for renewables. Clear sunny days created good conditions for generating power, coinciding with low demand from heating and cooling. It was often the time when a year’s worth of new generation coming on stream was reflected in higher shares of renewable energy. “These records are probably not going to last very long, they’re probably going to be broken in the next couple of weeks.” There was more renewable energy than needed. Some of the excess was being stored by pumped hydro and batteries, and quite a lot of the surplus was curtailed, due to system security rules, network constraints and low prices. Coal generation in Queensland also hit a record low over the weekend, McConnell said. While the renewables record was a sign of progress and illustrated that Australia was “marching towards a higher penetration renewable energy system”, it was not the main game in terms of emissions, he said. “From an emissions perspective, what matters is the annual contributions and how much coal we are burning.” The average renewable share in the year to June was 44%, according to the Australian energy market operator. More than 4.3 million Australian households now have rooftop solar. The weekend record followed new analysis, which highlighted the insufficient investment in new capacity needed to meet Australia’s 82% renewable energy target by 2030.

title: Ukraine war briefing: Sanctions must continue, EU’s top diplomat stresses, as Russian attacks kill five
summary: Kaja Kallas says sanctions vital as bloc scrambles to reach deal on extension; UN sounds warning for civilians on both sides of war as winter approaches. What we know on day 1,672
text: The EU’s top diplomat has urged member countries to maintain sanctions targeting Russia, as Moscow’s forces continued their attacks on Ukraine, killing at least five people. “Sanctions are a core pillar of our response to Russia’s war”, Kaja Kallas told reporters in New York after a meeting of EU foreign affairs ministers. Officials aimed to close talks on a rollover of Russia sanctions soon and have the extension take place swiftly, she said. “We need to have this stability,” with sanctions remaining in place for a longer time, Kallas added on the sidelines of the UN general assembly. She stressed the EU’s position has not changed: “That’s why we are also working on a new package of sanctions.” Discussions on the sanctions are ongoing as some EU member states sought to remove certain individuals from the bloc’s blacklist. EU countries failed on Monday to finalise a deal that involved lifting sanctions on Russian oligarchs Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman. Ukrainian foreign minister Andriy Sybiga denounced the move to remove them as “unacceptable” and said it would send Moscow the “wrong signal”. Negotiations are set to continue in Brussels in efforts to extend sanctions on almost 3,000 other individuals and entities over the war as the bloc scrambles to reach a deal ahead of late Tuesday’s deadline. Russian forces continued their attacks on different ⁠Ukrainian regions along the 1,200km frontline on ⁠Monday, killing at least five people, regional officials said. Prosecutors in ⁠north-eastern Kharkiv region said a drone strike on the town of ⁠Lozova killed one person and injured three. Farther south ‌in Dnipropetrovsk region, ‌a drone killed a car driver ‌in Nikopol. In the Donetsk ‌region, a Russian strike badly damaged an apartment building in the strategic Kramatorsk, killing one person, while another person was killed in ⁠a nearby village. A sustained attack on a village in Mykolaiv region killed a three-year-old child. The attacks could not be independently verified. Russian also bombarded Zaporizhzhia overnight to Monday, hitting apartment blocks, a university and a shopping mall, among other sites, and wounding five people, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said. Donald Trump is expected to press the Ukrainian president on an energy ceasefire during a face-to-face meeting this week, on the sidelines of the UN general assembly, Andrew Roth reports. It comes as world diesel prices have soared due to the war in Iran as well as Russia’s war in Ukraine. Ukraine stepped up its attacks on Russia’s energy sector over the weekend, and the US president said the whole world was suffering due to an energy shortage he said was being exacerbated by the Ukraine war. Russia’s new parliament will include 49 deputies who have taken part in the war against Ukraine, officials said after a landslide victory by the ruling United Russia party in widely criticised elections. Luke Harding reports that the pro-Kremlin party won a record 355 seats in the country’s 450-seat Duma lower house of parliament, according to preliminary figures, further consolidating Vladimir Putin’s grip on power. Escalating infrastructure attacks by both Russia and Ukraine are leaving civilians increasingly vulnerable as winter approaches, UN investigators have warned, expressing fear of a repeat of last winter’s suffering. In a fresh update, the UN’s Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine warned the attacks raised concerns that already difficult living conditions could worsen dramatically with the arrival of winter, as was the case last year. Last winter, Russian forces “continued to launch systematic waves of attacks against Ukraine’s critical energy infrastructure as temperatures plunged to minus 20C”, it said in a statement. “Millions of civilians endured prolonged power outages, shortages or lengthy absence of heating.”

title: US TV networks suspend White House pool coverage over Trump media ban
summary: White House promoted its own ‘Trump TV’ feed online after ABC, CBS, Fox News and NBC decline to participate
text: The major US television news outlets agreed to suspend their video coverage of Donald Trump after the administration banned journalists from several outlets from entering the White House grounds. The collective decision came after the barred outlets – CNN, MS Now and Politico – sued the administration on Monday, saying the president’s actions were a violation of their first amendment rights. The ban was an extraordinary escalation of Trump’s battle against news outlets. After a coalition of networks including ABC, CBS, Fox News and NBC – which along with CNN form a press “pool” that share the responsibilities of capturing and distributing footage of the president carried by news outlets worldwide – announced they would cease coverage in solidarity with the barred outlets, the White House promoted its own feed online, branding it “Trump TV”. The channel purported to show “top past moments, announcements, and the latest and greatest from the administration all in one place”. “Get real-time updates and live events streamed DIRECTLY to your phone,” the White House posted on social media. “No noise. Just the news that matters most – straight from the Trump Administration.” It is extremely rare for a president to travel or make public appearances without the accompaniment of a representative from the White House television pool. Network cameras have provided coverage of the president since 1950. On Monday, the ban against CNN meant that no broadcaster was covering Trump’s midday ribbon-cutting to unveil a new White House helipad. Although the White House provided a livestream, without professional boom mics and audio setup, the president’s remarks were inaudible over the sounds of a helicopter’s engine running in the background. The president abruptly announced his ban against outlets this weekend in a Truth Social post, saying he had enough of “purposely negative stories” about him. Journalists had their press badges confiscated by Secret Service on Saturday. “Effective today, the TV pool will not be covering events designated as pool coverage of the President,” Bryan Boughton, Fox News’s Washington bureau chief who is also currently serving on as TV pool chair, wrote in an email to pool members Monday. The role is rotated each quarter. “This follows the White House’s position preventing CNN from fulfilling its assigned pool duties,” said Boughton. In a show of support with the banned outlets, several outlets, including the Washington Post, the New York Times and the Associated Press, said they would not publish or distribute images taken as part of the White House photography pool including Trump’s departure on Marine One and his events at the United Nations in New York, until midnight ET. In a statement, the Washington Post described the action as part of a “collective effort”. The five news networks, including CNN, wrote in a joint statement: “The public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government. No administration should restrict a news organization because it objects to its reporting.” Although the broadcast networks said they would withhold televised coverage, the print, radio and wire service press pool continues to provide reports detailing Trump’s movements throughout the day. Hours after the broadcast networks’ announcement, the Washington Post said it would also withhold its photographs of presidential events from being published until after midnight ET to support banned outlets. On Friday, Trump abruptly announced he was banning CNN, Politico and MS Now from the White House because, he believes, they “constantly write or report FICTION and LIES”. On Saturday, reporters and other staff from the news organizations were denied access to the White House. Other media outlets and first amendment advocacy groups responded by condemning Trump’s ban, calling it an infringement on the right to a free press. On Monday, CNN, Politico and MS Now filed a lawsuit against the Trump administration, asking a federal judge to temporarily block the enforcement of the ban and restore the reporters’ passes to the White House. On Truth Social, Trump defended his decisions, insisting that his ban was not “instituting an assault on the Free Press”, but instead addressing “national security” threats – a claim the US president has recently used to justify building a triumphal arch and the White House ballroom.

title: Trump and Mamdani appear friendly after ‘wide-ranging’ meeting at Gracie Mansion
summary: Republican president said he hoped the democratic socialist would be a ‘great mayor’ for New York City
text: Donald Trump said on Monday that he hoped Zohran Mamdani would be a “great mayor” for New York, an unusually warm assessment of the democratic socialist leader whom the president and his Republican allies have spent months holding up as a symbol of the Democratic party’s alleged embrace of “communism” ahead of the November midterms. At a news conference following their closed-door meeting at Gracie Mansion, Trump and Mamdani appeared friendly as they have in previous meetings. Mamdani said he and Trump held a “wide-ranging” discussion, which touched on affordable housing and immigration, but did not offer extensive details regarding any disagreements between them. Asked whether he challenged Trump over his decision to ban CNN, MS Now, and Politico from White House grounds, Mamdani said: “I told the president that we’re going to have all of the members of the press here on the lawn, and that is something that I believe in.” “It’s interesting because they said they were going to boycott me, but they never boycott me, so I wasn’t very worried about that,” Trump chimed in, pointing to the large assembly of press on the lawn. The visit to Gracie Mansion, ahead of the president’s speech to the United Nations general assembly on Tuesday, was a measure of Trump’s apparent respect for the 34-year-old mayor of his native New York. It was the first presidential visit to the historic riverside residence in 45 years, following Ronald Reagan, who met there with Ed Koch in 1981. Pressed on why he had invited Trump, Mamdani said he was willing to work with anybody who could “deliver” for New Yorkers, and highlighted their shared interest in building thousands of new housing units at Sunnyside Yard in Queens. For his part, Trump said he believed Mamdani had “great potential”. It was the latest unlikely meeting between Trump, a rightwing populist who has targeted immigrants and Muslims, and Mamdani, a democratic socialist who was born in Uganda and is New York’s first Muslim mayor. Trump has focused his midterm election campaign on denouncing Democrats as “godless communists” who seek to abolish borders and prisons and pose the greatest threat that the US has ever faced. Yet on Monday he said of Mamdani, a member of the Democratic Socialists of America: “I certainly hope he will be a great mayor. You have to understand – I want what’s good for New York. I want what’s good for the country ... I want him to be a great mayor.” The body language again seemed amicable. Trump deferentially stood aside as Mamdani spoke from the lectern and, when the press conference finished, gave him an affectionate double tap on the arm. Trump, Mamdani, Trump’s chief of staff Susie Wiles and Mamdani’s chief of staff Elle Bisgaard-Church were all in attendance during Monday’s meeting. Mamdani said that they discussed the Trump administration’s stripping of protections for Haitian immigrants. “I shared my very strong opinions about how we can keep New Yorkers safe, how we can keep immigrant New Yorker safe, and how important immigrant New Yorkers, especially Haitian New Yorkers, are – not only to the fabric of our city, but also to our city’s economy,” Mamdani said. “The president and I have been very frank about the many disagreements we have,” he added. The meeting came one day after Mamdani, and Clara Brugada, the mayor of Mexico City, met with migrant delivery workers in New York City, who expressed precarity and fear surrounding the increase in Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) arrests. Earlier this month, Mamdani helped initiate a lawsuit against the Trump administration for its “public charge” rule change targeting immigrant communities. The lawsuit was filed by the State of New York and 21 other states against the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and various of its agencies. It is unclear if they discussed the lawsuit during the meeting.

title: Flights resume across US north-east after FAA communications failure
summary: Thousands of flights were delayed or canceled after a primary line failed and a backup fiber-optic cable was severed
text: Airport operations across the US north-east resumed Monday evening after a communications line failure snarled flights at some of the country’s busiest airports, leading to thousands of flight cancellations and delays. Flights were halted at several airports after a primary communications line failed at a key Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) facility in Philadelphia. The backup fiber optic line, which delivers internet service, was inadvertently severed by a railroad construction crew, resulting in a telecommunications crash and hundreds of canceled flights at Newark, LaGuardia, JFK, Philadelphia and Boston airports. Transportation secretary Sean Duffy said in a Monday evening social media post that the backup lines had been fixed and all affected airports were again operating. “It will take some time to clear all existing delays, so please check with your airline for the latest information,” Duffy wrote. The technical problems stem from the same FAA facility in Philadelphia that caused numerous disruptions at Newark Liberty international airport in the spring of 2025. Regional control centers like these have two lines that carry radar and communications data in and out: the primary and the backup. The FAA said a circuit on the primary failed Monday morning, and when the system tried to switch to the backup, workers discovered that the fiber optic line had been cut. Earlier in the day, Duffy said an Amtrak construction crew was to blame. Amtrak, however, pointed to a New Jersey Transit construction crew that was working in the area between Newark and New Brunswick, New Jersey. The disruption coincided with the publication of a government accountability office (GAO) report, which found that the FAA has yet to finish risk assessments or update security documentation covering threats from spoofing, jamming and other attacks on the radio spectrum – prompting a prominent senator to warn of a “major threat” to national security. The FAA also lacks a real-time system to detect all such threats, the report said, meaning it can generally only investigate incidents after they are reported. Investigators warned that a hacker could send fraudulent messages, such as false cancellations of flight clearances, to aircraft, with the potential to cause delays, disrupt airspace or create safety risks. Two systems used to send text messages to aircraft predate modern cybersecurity standards and lack common protections such as encryption, according to the report. The watchdog’s findings prompted calls for swift action. “The FAA’s failure to require the aviation industry to use secure communications is a major threat to US national security, to our economy and the safety of the flying public,” said Ron Wyden, the US senator for Oregon, who has long campaigned on privacy, surveillance and cybersecurity issues. “The FAA needs to issue new standards, as soon as possible, to protect the security of airline communications.” The GAO made nine recommendations, including a formal risk assessment of seven of eight reviewed systems, continuous monitoring for interference, spoofing and jamming, and formal guidance on information sharing. The Department of Transportation, replying for the FAA, agreed with all nine. Monday’s disruption is the latest in a run of problems around Newark. In April 2025, an outage blanked controllers’ screens for roughly 60 to 90 seconds and cut their contact with aircraft, prompting the FAA to halt departures. The FAA later moved the Philadelphia Tracon to a new fiber-optic link with New York on two separate paths, as part of measures to improve reliability. The FAA handles more than 44,000 flights a day and about 3 million passengers, the GAO noted. Wyden, who sits on the Senate intelligence committee, added: “This sobering report from [the] GAO reveals that the technology used by air traffic controllers to communicate with aircraft is incredibly insecure, can be intercepted, impersonated, and jammed, and that hackers and foreign governments can exploit these vulnerabilities to disrupt air travel and even put passengers at risk.” The GAO also pointed to jamming and spoofing abroad. Estonia and Finland have accused Russia of interfering with satellite navigation in their airspace, which Moscow denies. One incident last September involved a Spanish military jet carrying the country’s defense minister. The Associated Press contributed

title: Black Tesla employees accuse company of fostering racial discrimination in major trial
summary: Lawyers say Black employees at Tesla experienced ‘rampant racism’ that was left unchecked for years at their flagship factory in California
text: Dozens of Black employees at Tesla’s flagship plant in California said they were subject to racist slurs, unequal pay and promotions, and bullying by supervisors on a daily basis, a situation management did little to nothing to fix. Their complaints form the basis of a lawsuit brought against the Elon Musk-owned electric car company by the state of California, which began trial with opening statements on Monday. Brett Watson, a lawyer for the California Civil Rights Department, started by showing the court a series of photographs taken throughout Tesla’s Fremont factory. There was the N-word scratched on to a grey-blue metal surface and written in black marker on a wall. “KKK”, swastikas, the Confederate flag, a white supremacist logo and “go back to Africa” had also been found scrawled in bathrooms, lockers, workplace benches and lunch tables, according to court documents. Watson listed a long string of racial epithets workers said were directed personally at them, including one incident where a Black worker said he was asked: “You want to hang from a tree?” “Despite what Tesla might argue, you will hear Black workers were deeply offended,” Watson said. “These experiences cannot be dismissed as a few bad apples … hundreds of complaints to Tesla and [the Civil Rights Department] will show these experiences were not isolated.” Watson said Black employees at Tesla experienced “rampant racism” that was left unchecked for years, and that workers referred to the factory as a “slaveship”, “the plantation” and “The Elon Slave Labor Association” – spelling out TESLA. One Black worker told state lawyers that he heard racial slurs as often as 50-100 times a day. The lawsuit was filed against Tesla in February 2022 and alleges that the company did not comply with the law, violating California’s Fair Employment and Housing Act. It alleges that the factory was racially segregated and Black workers were paid less, promoted less and terminated more frequently than their white counterparts. The state is seeking financial damages and injunctive relief, which could force Tesla to change its labor practices and internal policies. Judge Peter Borkon will make the final ruling in the bench trial, which proceeds without a jury. It’s the first such lawsuit brought against Tesla by a government agency on behalf of dozens of workers to go to trial. Legal experts say the outcome of the trial could have sweeping consequences for the company since the state is not bound by the same arbitration agreements as employees. The trial is expected to continue through the end of October. The car manufacturer has denied any wrongdoing and called the lawsuit “misguided”, saying it has “always disciplined and terminated employees who engage in misconduct, including those who use racial slurs or harass others in different ways”. Tesla said its Fremont factory has a majority-minority workforce and provides “the best paying jobs in the automotive industry” to tens of thousands of Californians. Tyree Jones, the lead lawyer for Tesla, began his opening statements repeatedly saying the N-word in a familiar tone. “What’s up my [N-word], my [N-word] …,” Jones said, adding that “none of which is used as a racial slur.” “By this action, the state of California attacks the way many Black people greet each other,” Jones said. “It’s offensive.” Jones touted Tesla’s accomplishments as an innovative electric car manufacturer and reiterated that the company provides thousands of jobs in the state. “The most prolific employer of California is on trial and under attack by the state,” Jones said. Referring to the racist graffiti around the factory, Jones said: “The state is blaming the employer, when it’s the victim.” After both sides presented opening arguments, the state called three witnesses. All were former Black employees at Tesla who said they either witnessed or were subject to racism at the company. The first witness worked at Tesla from 2021 to 2024 and said he was repeatedly bullied for being Black. In one incident, he alleged he was called the N-word by another employee, and the company gave him a write-up on the situation instead of the instigator. The second witness was a senior security manager who worked at Tesla for six years. He said he habitually worked with human resources when complaints of discrimination came in, and that he witnessed Black employees treated differently than workers of other races. In one incident, he alleged Musk got involved when white employees were caught drinking alcohol on site and the CEO directed management to override company policy and not terminate the workers. Nadia Clark, who previously worked as a police officer and an army officer for decades, was employed as a security manager at Tesla’s Fremont facility from 2020 to 2022. She testified about an incident where a white employee called her the N-word more than ten times in a row in front of other workers. “I likened Tesla to some experiences I had on the street and in the military. It was like a pressure cooker,” Clark said. “These words have a violent landing.” She said the incident shook her and she immediately reported it to human resources, but never got a response. Clark decided to leave Tesla that day. “There were these continuous patterns that were never addressed,” Clark said. “The work environment was unsafe, hostile, and I never returned.” This lawsuit is one of dozens of discrimination suits brought against Tesla, including a case brought by the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, a federal agency. The suits allege the company has routinely ignored complaints of repeated racial harassment. In 2022, a federal jury awarded Owen Diaz, a former Tesla employee, $137m for these claims – one of the largest awards given in a discrimination lawsuit brought by a single worker, although a judge later reduced that sum. Similar suits have been filed by female employees, who allege they experienced physical assaults, harassment and catcalling at Tesla facilities across the country. Tesla has denied wrongdoing in all cases, and has said it implemented various policies in recent years to prevent racist and sexist conduct and punish it when it does occur. Musk, who joined Tesla in 2004 and became the CEO in 2008, has also been accused of racist behavior, including promoting white supremacist conspiracy theories like “white genocide”. The CEO also tends to broadcast his thoughts on X, a social media platform he owns, fixating on anti-immigrant content and theories that the white race is under threat. Musk is not expected to be called as a witness in the trial. He hasn’t publicly addressed the legal proceedings under way and did not return a request for comment.

title: Venezuelan shot by ICE seeks medical care as lawyer says bullet lodged in back
summary: Sshooting of Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez comes months after increased federal immigration enforcement in Austin
text: The Venezuelan man who was shot by a federal immigration officer in Texas on Sunday spoke out from detention on Monday afternoon when he was able to call his lawyer, in the middle of a press conference, and plead for better medical care. Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez, 28, was taken from a hospital in Austin into Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention, even though he apparently still has a bullet lodged near his spine and is in much discomfort. “I haven’t received any medical attention. I’m in a lot of pain,” Garcés Pérez said, in a phone call to his attorney, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch. “I have expressed my pain [to the guards].” He recounted that he had spent the night sleeping on the floor of a cold room in a detention center about 140 miles from Austin, where he was taken hours after being shot by an ICE officer after a traffic stop on Sunday afternoon. Lincoln-Goldfinch had told the Guardian earlier on Monday that the federal officer’s bullet was still inside her client. Garcés Pérez said he had been told it is too close to his spine to operate on to remove at this time. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees ICE, has not responded to requests for more information and comment. In an initial statement issued shortly before midnight on Sunday night, DHS said Garcés Pérez was in stable condition and that he was “in federal custody pending removal” out of the US. The shooting did not come out of the blue, amid an immigration enforcement surge in Austin. ICE had already been active in the Texas capital of late, but then matters escalated dramatically on Sunday as shots rang out. Garcés Pérez was in the process of delivering a DoorDash food order on the city’s north side when ICE encountered him shortly before 1pm on Sunday. Video posted online appears to show an ICE officer getting out of his car and shooting at Garcés Pérez’s car three times. His car, as later visible at the scene, had a large dent on the front passenger side. Garcés Pérez, who was hit once in the back between his shoulder blades, is a Venezuelan national who has lived in the United States for two years, according to his lawyer, but had been ordered removed from the US. Garcés Pérez told onlookers who rushed to the scene that he had been shot because he hadn’t stopped. Garcés Pérez was taken to a downtown hospital for treatment but, according to lawyer Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, was whisked away from there by ICE late Sunday afternoon. For a few hours, his partner and the lawyer could not locate him, then on Monday morning Lincoln-Goldfinch told the Guardian he’d been located at the South Texas ICE Processing Center, in Pearsall. “Bullet still lodged in his back. No pain meds,” Lincoln-Goldfinch said by text on Monday. Garcés Pérez said when he called the attorney on Monday that what appeared to be a normal car had pulled up next to him before veering in his direction. When he eventually stopped and spoke to what turned out to be an ICE officer, he said he asked to move his vehicle to a nearby parking lot because he wanted his car to be there if he was arrested. He was told he could not and when he drove further the ICE vehicle crashed into him and then he was shot, he said. Austin, the politically liberal capital city of conservative Texas, has repeatedly found itself at the crossfire of the immigration debate. The state’s Republican leadership has often sought to make an example out of the city, forcing local leaders to weaken Austin’s policy of not collaborating with ICE. Local leaders said this summer has marked a low-profile but aggressive surge in immigration enforcement in the region, spurred by a jump in ICE acting alone, relying less on state troopers to stop people and hand them over. “As mayor of the city of Austin, I’m very angry about this,” Kirk Watson, a Democrat, said on Sunday. “A person being shot on the streets of Austin by someone purporting to be law enforcement, particularly when it’s ICE, is something that causes me to be unhappy and angry..” TDHS said that it was leading the investigation into the shooting, alongside the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI). However Austin leaders have called for local and state involvement, citing public distrust of ICE. The exact details leading up to the shooting remained unclear on Monday. Video posted on social media shows a man running out of the black SUV and shooting at Garcés Pérez’s almost stationary blue sedan from behind it. Three gunshots ring out. A witness, Nedavia Bolaños, got closest to the scene and shared video with the Guardian of ICE officers standing next to the car as the man clutched his chest, before Austin police officers arrived and were the ones to render first aid. Within an hour, more than a hundred protesters had gathered at the site, chanting expletives against ICE and waving Mexican, American and Guatemalan flags. Several protesters could be seen washing their eyes and mouths in pain, after they were sprayed with what they said was teargas or chemical spray. The shooting came after several months of increased immigration enforcement, particularly in immigrant-heavy neighborhoods, suburbs and exurbs. Austin city council member José “Chito” Vela, who represents the neighborhood where Garcés Pérez was shot, said that he has heard constituents describe an enforcement bump driven by a rise in unilateral action by ICE. While ICE was largely seen making immigration arrests after Texas Department of Public Safety traffic stops for the first year or so of the second Trump administration, they have begun to act increasingly on their own, Vela said. City leaders had previously raised concerns over the increased action. Congressman Greg Casar, an Austin Democrat who leads the Congressional Progressive Caucus, has sent a letter to DHS demanding cooperation in an “immediate, independent investigation” into the shooting, the full release of any footage the federal authorities have of the shooting, and “accountability for any wrongdoing by the agent responsible”. Later on Monday, lawyers representing Garcés Pérez filed both a writ of habeas corpus and an injunction motion in court, hoping to stave off any attempt to deport him before an investigation is complete. In the application for the habeas petition requesting his release, Garcés Pérez’s lawyers argued that he qualified for a type of visa given to victims of crimes.

title: Cut NHS red tape and boost productivity to prevent 20,000 early deaths a year in England, report urges
summary: Boosting productivity could result in four extra years of good health for people on average, report says
text: The NHS in England could prevent 20,000 deaths and save £33bn a year by cutting red tape and boosting productivity, a report says. Research by the Health Foundation found the health service has been held back for decades by excessive regulation, short-term planning and insufficient capability to deliver major change. But rewiring the NHS, the world’s largest single healthcare system, by harnessing new technology, empowering staff and increasing capital investment could save both lives and money, it found. There is “substantial scope to improve outcomes within the funding already available to the NHS”, which could result in up to four extra years of good health for people on average, the report said. In terms of where deaths could be prevented, focusing on diagnosing cancer earlier and finding people with high blood pressure or conditions such as diabetes quicker would be key, it added. The report called for a series of changes, such as releasing the NHS from unnecessary regulation, reporting and compliance tasks, as well as launching a “test-and-learn” approach to scaling up things that could improve productivity, such as use of artificial intelligence. “Our analysis suggests that if the NHS in England achieved outcomes closer to the best-performing comparable health systems, without spending more each year, it could potentially result in 18,500–20,600 fewer deaths each year from treatable causes and 2.5 to 4.5 additional years that people spend in good health on average,” the report said. Increasing NHS productivity is “sometimes … seen as exhorting hard-working staff to work even harder, in a system already under considerable strain” but this view must be challenged, it added. “At its heart, productivity means achieving better health outcomes from the resources available.” The biggest issues affecting productivity included the “constant churn”, too many targets, and not enough focus on health outcomes. Researchers also heard from staff how poor IT wasted clinical time, how limited estate and equipment constrained healthcare and how gaps in administrative support shifted additional work to clinicians. While AI offered opportunities, the “NHS has repeatedly struggled to take advantage of the potential”, the report said. Anita Charlesworth, report author and senior economic adviser at the Health Foundation, said: “This is mission critical for the NHS, which cannot simply keep doing more of the same. “The problem is not a lack of committed and talented people or an absence of ideas; it is that the NHS is not set up to deliver sustained productivity growth. “Our research points to a fundamental redesign of the operating conditions – not another disruptive reorganisation, but a reset to make improving productivity a defining focus for the NHS over the next decade and beyond.” Sir Ciarán Devane, chief executive of the NHS Alliance, which represents and supports the health and care system in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, said he agreed more could be done to deliver further productivity gains but there were “big barriers” that would need to be addressed. “Lack of capital investment has been a long-running drag on NHS productivity. More must be done to turn the tide on years of neglect … We also agree that a more streamlined, supportive regulatory system which encourages local autonomy and innovation will be vital for future progress.”

title: Healthcare in Africa ‘under growing strain’ after US withdrawal from aid programs, report warns
summary: Accra Reset’s report states countries in the region and global south should take greater control of their health development after USAID debacle
text: The United States’ withdrawal from key aid programs has put healthcare in Africa and the global south “under growing strain” a new report warns. The report says the Trump administration’s cuts to programs such as US Agency for International Development (USAID), as well as the Covid-19 pandemic and rising costs of living globally have brought “new urgency” for the need to reform healthcare in the region. The report, titled A Sovereign Future For Health, was created by the Accra Reset, a global health initiative led by John Dramani Mahama, Ghana’s president, that believes countries in Africa and the wider global south should have greater control over their health development rather than being dependent on aid from western countries and international institutions. A key statistic cited by Mahama and Accra Reset is that Africa produces less than 1% of its vaccines while carrying about 25% of the global disease burden. The report cites how abrupt changes to global health financing, such as the US withdrawal from several global health initiatives, forced countries within the global south to urgently restructure their finances. The report points to the Trump administration’s decision to dissolve USAID, which pushed Nigeria to absorb the 28,000 health workers who were previously employed by the agency at a cost of $200m. External financing for health in Africa contracted by close to 70% between 2021 and 2025, the report notes, meaning that African countries historically dependent on aid were forced to adapt quickly. The withdrawal of the US Emergency Plan for Aids Relief (Pepfar) funding for South Africa, which provided over $400m a year annually and is credited with saving 26m lives globally since 2003, led to HIV clinics closing across the country. That left 1.4 million people living with HIV to face uncertainty about their treatment. Such funding cuts caused “severe and devastating” disruption globally, according to research presented at the 26th International Aids Conference in Brazil earlier this year. At the World Health Assembly in May, Mahama said Ghana lost $78m after the closure of USAID programs which affected maternal healthcare, the treatment of malaria, nutrition and HIV/Aids interventions. The initiative’s latest report, published on Monday, comes amid these major cuts to international aid and growing pressure on countries to take greater ownership of their health systems. Mahama refers to these aid cuts as a clear example that donor dependency is not sustainable. “The Accra Reset is not an argument for traditional donors to do less on global health. It is an argument for doing it differently and doing it better. As countries take greater ownership of their health futures, donor countries should step up to support that transition – following the lead of countries that set their own priorities, and work alongside them to determine where outside support is most valuable,” said Naveen Rao, senior vice-president of the health initiative at the Rockefeller Foundation. “The Accra Reset shows how we can evolve to back country-led solutions while advancing our shared health and economic interests.” Mahama notes in the report that the “past few years have shaken global health cooperation to its foundations”. “The Covid-19 pandemic exposed the risks created by concentrated production and unequal access to essential health products; rising debt and fiscal pressures have constrained national health budgets; and declining development assistance is placing programs and services under growing strain,” he continued, adding: “These shocks have brought new urgency to reform debates that have continued for years with limited progress. It was in this context that we launched the Accra Reset and its Sovereign Health Agenda – to give renewed political force to the reform agenda and place the agency of countries of the Global South at its centre.” The report comes alongside a recent survey revealing the progressive attitudes many US citizens have towards foreign aid. About 75% of Americans – including more than one in two (52%) who primarily support Donald Trump – agree that the US should restore disease prevention aid to contain the Ebola virus, according to polling of more than 2,000 US adults commissioned by the Rockefeller Foundation. The polling also revealed that 65% of US adults support international cooperation even if it means compromising some national interests; 64% also believe Americans have a shared responsibility to others, including people in other countries whom they do not know. The Guardian has contacted the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) for comment.
