title: UK to give support to Saudi jets in attempt to counter Houthi fighters
summary: Andy Burnham seeks stability in Middle East to bring down prices at home as first meeting with Trump looms
text: The UK has agreed to provide defensive air support to Saudi Arabia to help counter Houthi fighters and restore stability in the Middle East while driving down the cost of living at home, Andy Burnham has said, ahead of his first meeting with Donald Trump. The prime minister said he had agreed to a request for air-to-air refuelling of Saudi jets to defend energy infrastructure against the Iran-backed rebels and help keep oil flowing from the Gulf to ease global economic turmoil. Burnham also revealed he will use his first meeting with Trump on Tuesday to urge the US president to de-escalate the conflict in Iran, warning that “dark clouds of global instability” are directly affecting people’s lives all over the world. The turmoil in the Middle East has pushed up global energy prices, putting the UK economy under intense inflationary pressure and increasing government borrowing costs to multi-year highs just weeks before a crucial first budget for the new government. On the flight to the United Nations in New York, Burnham told reporters that an RAF Voyager would help refuel Saudi jets for several weeks, in his first military deployment since taking power, after the Houthis advanced to areas adjacent to the crucial Bab al-Mandab strait. The key Gulf ally has used the waterway as an alternative route for oil exports bypassing disruption in the ⁠strait of Hormuz. The RAF operational support is in addition to the UK Sky Sabre air defence system already operating. “We have received a request from Saudi Arabia for military support and … I agreed to that request for defensive air-to-air refuelling. On cost of living pressures and acting to secure the interests of Britain, the wider region … we need to keep those pathways open,” Burnham said. The prime minister also plans to press Trump to wind down US action in Iran, which has destabilised the region, blocked key supply chains and unleashed global economic volatility, including in the UK, where the government will struggle to drive down the cost of living as a result. “Of course the message is that we want to see an end to the conflict as quickly as possible and we stand ready to play our part,” Burnham said when asked if he would raise the issue in talks with Trump. As well as the focus on the Middle East, other major international challenges, including the war in Ukraine and artificial intelligence, are expected to dominate Burnham’s meetings at the UN general assembly. The global security backdrop to the summit is bleak: European leaders have warned that Russia could launch a drone or missile attack on Nato territory within months to test the strength of the alliance. Burnham’s speech to the UN is expected to focus on harnessing the power of AI, amid concerns at home over the safety of the rapidly advancing technology. He will be accompanied on the trip by his AI minister, Kanishka Narayan. The prime minister’s first face-to-face meeting with Trump is a significant moment, with the US president still said to be angry over the UK’s refusal to support his military action in Iran, and ongoing tensions over levels of defence spending. Burnham will attempt to highlight the importance of the security partnership after the UK and US launched a heavyweight torpedo, designed to sink ships and deep-diving submarines, in British waters last week from a Plymouth-made drone named Excalibur. Government insiders, however, are taking some solace from Trump’s low-key response to UK sanctions on trade with Israeli settlements in the West Bank, after weeks of diplomacy with the White House over the summer. They are also hoping to avoid a clash over energy policy. The prime minister is expected to signal to Trump that he is in favour of more drilling in the North Sea, including the Jackdaw gasfield that is likely to get the green light within weeks. Analysts believe the balance of risk for the bilateral relationship has shifted since Keir Starmer was in office, given the Republicans face a difficult set of midterm elections and the US president’s personal ratings are plummeting. Trump is also likely to be more focused on his meeting with the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, and his address to the UN, which comes shortly before the talks on Tuesday. Government sources told the Guardian that Burnham would try to pursue a “third way” in his relationship with the US president, neither as adversarial as the Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, nor as publicly fawning as Starmer’s early approach, and relying on the strength of his personality. Asked whether he felt he could trust Trump, Burnham said: “Yes, of course, we trust our allies. Of course, we do.” Pressed whether this applied to the US president personally, he repeated: “Yes.” Downing Street said the prime minister wanted to use his UN meetings – which will also include the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen – to “drive opportunity and deliver hope”, making progress on areas with the potential to deliver for people at home. Burnham has focused on domestic issues since his arrival in No 10, despite Starmer warning that it would be impossible to separate them from global affairs, given how the Ukraine war is weighing heavily on UK security and the Iran conflict on the economy. On the flight Burnham acknowledged they were inseparable. “[Starmer] was right to say it’s about how we deliver back at home and the situation in the Middle East is a very clear example of that. It is a very big driver of the cost of living pressures that we’re currently facing,” he said. Before the trip, Burnham’s official spokesperson said: “The British people at home are at the forefront of the prime minister’s mission in New York this week. Because to deliver at home, we must ensure we are leading international efforts to brighten a darkening global picture … “To give people the breathing space they need, he is clear we must work with our international partners to face up to the biggest challenges of our generation. So this week at [the UN general assembly] he will be leading the charge on the global issues that impact people’s lives at home.” Burnham will tell world leaders the UK will focus on AI and climate change when it hosts the G20 in Manchester next year, potentially causing ripples with Trump, who has previously criticised the UK’s stance on global warming. The meeting gives Burnham an opportunity, however, to host international allies on his home turf, although the location of the summit was chosen under the Starmer administration. Burnham has been accompanied on the trip by his wife, Marie-France van Heel, who No 10 said would be meeting her international counterparts and supporting the prime minister, whose father, Roy, died last week.

title: Halt super-intelligent AI with non-proliferation treaty, Ed Davey to say
summary: At Lib Dems’ conference in Brighton, leader will accuse Andy Burnham of relying on Donald Trump and ‘tech bros’ to solve problem
text: Ed Davey is to call for a global nuclear-style non-proliferation treaty to halt the development of super-intelligent AI when he makes his keynote speech at the Liberal Democrat conference, accusing Andy Burnham of relying on Donald Trump and “tech bros” to solve the problem. When he addresses the faithful on the final day of the gathering in Brighton, the party leader will call for a global pause on super-intelligent AI, comparing it to a nuclear arms race that could result in technology that could “destroy us all”. Davey is expected to lay out plans in his speech on Tuesday for a new international AI safety agency – modelled on the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) and headquartered in the UK, after numerous warnings from AI researchers that artificial intelligence could wipe out humanity within the decade. “We didn’t leave the atom bomb to a few billionaires to police themselves,” he will say. Davey is expected to call for a new global movement to work together to protect humanity from the risks of super-intelligent AI, saying that the IAEA was built by nations “working together to control a technology that could destroy us all”, but warning that the future of AI is being decided by “a tiny number of the richest and most powerful in California and in Beijing” with no guardrails to slow down development. “As liberals – we know that something as existential as nuclear weapons or climate change cannot be left in the hands of a powerful few. And so it must be with AI. We can’t leave it to Mark Zuckerberg, to Sam Altman, or to Elon Musk to save us,” Davey will say. On Monday, the prime minister announced a new AI partnership with the US ahead of Trump’s address to the UN general assembly on Tuesday. But Davey will say the plan “doesn’t come close to meeting the scale of this threat” and “only risks making us more dependent on a Trump administration in the pocket of the tech bros”. It comes after the Lib Dems’ home affairs spokesperson, Max Wilkinson, on Monday announced that the party proposed a big tech levy and promised to create a new online crime agency focused on offences including child sexual abuse material, trafficking in drugs and weapons, and deepfake AI-generated pornographic images. Wilkinson said the Lib Dems would properly regulate use of Meta’s smart glasses, which he called “perv goggles”, telling the conference that the glasses “are more than a benign piece of tech that provides a bit of fun” and that people – especially women – were being recorded without consent or warning. “This is becoming the new norm, because this government won’t stand up to big tech to protect our civil liberties,” he said. On Sunday Davey set out a proposal to cut fuel duty by 10p a litre for a fixed three-month period, as well as reducing the bus fare cap from £3 to £1 and other transport-related cost of living policies. Davey defended himself in a series of interviews on Monday about complaints his party lacks vision, saying it was pointless to try to compete with the attention-grabbing ideas of the likes of Reform UK and the Greens. “It’s a very noisy environment at the moment,” he told the BBC. “But let me tell you, some of the noise generated by the populists are things that divide our country, that are nasty, or that are just completely crazy. I don’t want to do that. I want to tell people that we have really well thought through policies that will cut their taxes.” Asked if he would propose further tax cuts in the wake of the pledge to slash 10p from fuel duty for three months, Davey replied: “Absolutely.” These would, he said, be financed by higher economic growth due to the Lib Dem proposal to seek entry to the EU’s single market. The Lib Dem leader did praise Burnham for wanting to reform adult social care, but told Sky News the “jury is out” on whether Burnham will deliver as prime minister. But Davey was positive about some of what Burnham has done. “I think it’s good when other parties start talking about Liberal Democrat priorities,” he said. “We have led the debate on social care and carers because it’s so important for our health service. We’ve led the debate on political change because we need to change our political system, and Mr Burnham seems to be up for that.”

title: World leaders address climate crisis before UN meet amid record-breaking El Niño
summary: Prime ministers of Australia and Iceland discuss effects on their countries even as some shy away in face of war and inflation
text: World political leaders are descending on New York for the UN general assembly and some of them are putting the climate crisis on the agenda as they spoke on Monday at the start of the city’s annual Climate Week. This year’s Climate Week – which runs alongside UNGA – comes after months of extreme heat in large parts of the world including Europe and the US, wildfires in Africa, flash flooding in Asia and a record-breaking El Niño. The prime minister of Australia, Anthony Albanese, gave the opening keynote address Monday while Iceland’s prime minister, Kristrún Frostadóttir, gave the closing remarks. Both spoke about the effects of the climate crisis on their countries, the measures they are taking to transition away from fossil fuels, and their support for other countries to do the same. “Global weather has always been treacherous. But the science told us unmistakably that as the world warms these events will become more frequent and intense. And those scientific forecasts have come to be,” Albanese said, highlighting the country’s efforts to support other Pacific nations in fighting the climate crisis. Frostadóttir said the Nordic country’s move to geothermal energy was catalysed by the global oil crisis. In the early-1970s, most Icelandic homes were burning imported oil for heat. “Household budgets were hit and a small island nation, far from every market, every supplier, learned the hard way to depend on something you cannot control,” she said. “So we made a choice. Instead of riding out the volatility, we turned to what was right under our feet.” In a matter of years, Reykjavík built a large-scale geothermal district heating system. Other towns in Iceland followed, many switching within a decade. “This took unwavering political support. Financial support mechanisms that helped ordinary households make the switch without ruinous upfront costs,” Frostadóttir said. “And, perhaps rarest of all in today’s world, across party consensus that outlasted several governments.” Now, nearly every home in Iceland is heated with renewable energy, and more than 90% of it is geothermal. Yet little was said on the opening day of Climate Week about the US government’s recent efforts to block climate action, such as the Trump administration’s move to pay nearly $4bn in taxpayer dollars to stop offshore wind projects and measures to weaken emissions standards for vehicles and coal-fired power plants. Instead of talking about political stalling and backsliding on climate action, speakers focused on the security and economic reasons that are making the need to transition impossible to ignore. Selwin Hart, assistant secretary general for climate action at the UN, said the Iran war had further proven this point. “This crisis, as horrible as it is, is really serving as a wake-up call for countries, businesses and people really to break the fossil fuel addiction and accelerate the transition as fast and as quickly as possible,” he told the Guardian. Lt Gen Richard Nugee, a retired senior British army officer, said that militaries need to be able to operate in the environment in which they find themselves, and those environments are changing. “A really good example of that is the sea in the gulf is getting so hot and is predicted to get so hot that the water won’t cool the engines of our ships,” he said. Nugee said that militaries should be paying attention to climate adaption technologies, not only for their lower emissions but their potential for strategic advantages. “I don’t believe there is renewable energy that will drive a 70-ton tank. It’s not that,” he said. “But our small armed vehicles, why not make them hybrid? Which is better for our stealth, better for the crews because there’s less noise and less vibration.” The UK’s foreign minister Ed Miliband also spoke about the risks of continued reliance on fossil fuels given the Russian invasion of Ukraine and the US’s war in Iran, describing the inherent instability as the “fossil fuel roller coaster”. “Climate and nature must be embedded in national security systems, in threat assessments, and contingency planning,” Miliband said. “Countries need to pool information because a shock beginning in one country can rapidly travel through supply chains, financial markets and migration patterns to other countries.” Meanwhile, the private sector is using the transition to renewable energy to protect its bottom line. Karen Pflug, the chief sustainability officer at Ingka Group, the largest Ikea retailer, said that energy efficiency in their stores has allowed the company to save millions of dollars every year. Pflug said the company just announced a new solar park in South Carolina, which will have 178,000 solar panels. “So regardless of what’s happening from a political point of view I think it’s in fact making good business sense,” she said. “The economic imperative is there.” Leaders also stressed the need to transition sooner than later. Iceland’s Frostadóttir said: “The only real question left for leaders, for all of us in this room, is what it takes to keep moving forward faster than the disruptions that have yet to hit us. Our answer, from a small island in the North Atlantic is this: start before you must. Build the resilience before the crisis tests it.” Climate Week has been held annually in New York since 2009 and organizers said this year’s iteration will be the largest yet, with more than 100,000 attendees drawn from politics, business and activism. But they also admitted an uptick in “climate hushing” whereby business leaders and politicians have shied away from talking about the climate crisis amid a relentless focus on wars, inflation and economic strife that has swept the world. “There has been this disconnect this summer where we have felt climate change like no other year with some massive disasters and the degree to which leaders want to speak about this issue,” said Helen Clarkson, chief executive of the Climate Group, organizer of Climate Week. “Undoubtedly people care about the cost of living but we see in the polling people care about the climate too, they aren’t oblivious to what is going on. A word we heard a lot today in speeches is that we need courage to make that connection to people and join the dots.”

title: Two helicopter pilots killed while battling Yosemite fires
summary: A helicopter assisting in fighting the Dome fire in Yosemite national park crashed on Sunday afternoon
text: Two helicopter pilots died while fighting a fire in Yosemite national park on Sunday afternoon. The pilots were conducting water drops over the Dome fire, which had burned more than 3,000 acres since it ignited last week, when their helicopter crashed around 3pm, according to the Federal Aviation Administration. The pilots were employed by the aerospace company Precision and were working with a wildland firefighting crew that specializes in using ropes to descend from helicopters to reach otherwise inaccessible terrain, known as helitack rappelling. The helicopter went down south-east of Ostrander Lake, said Benjamin Cossel, a spokesperson with the Federal Complex Incident Management Team overseeing the firefighting response. Details about the circumstances surrounding the crash were not immediately released. The crash will be investigated by the Federal Aviation Administration and the National Transportation Safety Board. “It is with unimaginable sadness and broken hearts that we share the loss of two beloved members of our team,” Precision wrote in a social media post. “We are devastated by this loss and are struggling to find the words. We ask for privacy and compassion for their families and our team as we grieve this tremendous loss.” The names of the pilots were not immediately released. Roughly 580 people are fighting the Dome Fire, which started on 15 September near Wawona, California, according to the National Interagency Fire Center. It’s burning on about 4.7 sq miles (12.3 sq km) and is about 15% contained. The lake near the crash site was roughly 9 miles (14.5km) south of Yosemite’s famous El Capitan, and about 7 miles (11.3km) northeast of Wawona. Water-dropping helicopters have been key to fighting the blaze, which has spread across rugged terrain. At least 14 people have died while helping with wildfires in the US this year, the most since 2022 when 25 deaths were recorded, according to government reports. Three firefighters died battling Colorado’s Knowles fire, and an additional member of that crew succumbed to injuries weeks afterwards. The incident was the most deadly entrapment in 13 years. The job has always carried inherent risks,but this year has been especially dangerous. The Trump administration has increased pressure on firefighting forces, amid a critical shortage of federal firefighters. Gabrielle Canon contributed reporting

title: Airlines urge action after UK flights delayed and cancelled again
summary: Nats says fault at Prestwick has been ‘fixed’ after airports in Scotland, northern England and Northern Ireland are hit
text: Airlines have called for “action and accountability” over the UK’s air traffic control services after a technical issue led to flights being disrupted for the second time in a fortnight. Dozens were cancelled and others severely delayed after a fault on Monday morning at National Air Traffic Services (Nats), this time at its second control centre at Prestwick in South Ayrshire. The fault, predominantly affecting Scotland, Northern Ireland and northern England, was fixed by about 10.30am, but only after airlines including British Airways and easyJet were forced to make cancellations. A Nats spokesperson said it had been “working with airports and airlines to safely lift air traffic regulations as quickly as we can to minimise any further disruption”, and apologised for the disruption. They said the problem was “unrelated to the issue two weeks ago”. Despite the relatively quick fix, at least 200 flights in and out of UK airports were expected to be cancelled by the end of Monday, according to the analysts Cirium. The transport secretary, Heidi Alexander, posted on X just after 10.30am, notifying that the latest technical issue had been resolved. She wrote: “I know this will be deeply frustrating for passengers after the previous issue. There may be some delays as things reset.” The incident came less than two weeks after a serious problem at the Nats control centre in England disrupted travel for hundreds of thousands of passengers, and only three days after the company released an initial report that promised to “continually improve the critical service we provide”. Nats said Monday’s incident had been caused by a connectivity issue at its Prestwick centre. Among the stranded passengers at Glasgow were a bride and groom who had expected to fly to their Las Vegas wedding with family and friends. Their BA flight to Heathrow was cancelled, meaning they would miss their connection to the US on Monday, and they rebooked for Tuesday. The bride-to-be, Barbara Ann Stoddart, said: “I’m completely stressed out. I have still to go to the county court in Vegas to go and get the marriage licence, and I’ve got to be there three days in advance … If there’s any hiccups I might not be getting married on Saturday now.” The Civil Aviation Authority said it had reminded airlines of their responsibilities to look after passengers whose flights were delayed or cancelled, but that passengers were unlikely to receive compensation for delayed or cancelled flights. “We consider that disruption caused by the technical issue at Nats Prestwick centre in Scotland on 21 September is likely to be considered the result of ‘extraordinary circumstances’ under passenger rights rules. “This means that although passengers should be looked after by airlines, they are unlikely to be entitled to compensation for delays or cancellations that were directly caused by the incident,” a CAA spokesperson said. Airlines called for action to address repeated failures, with Ryanair reiterating its calls for the Nats chief executive, Martin Rolfe, to resign. EasyJet, one of the most-affected airlines on Monday, said the latest flight disruption “once again calls into question the resilience of Nats’s systems and demonstrates the need for firm actions to prevent these repeated failures”. BA described it as “yet another technical fault with Nats” and said it was disappointing. Jet2’s chief executive, Steve Heapy, said it was “simply not good enough for this critical national infrastructure to keep letting customers down”. “What customers and airlines need now is action, accountability and proper resilience, and we need it urgently,” he said. Ryanair’s chief operations officer, Neal McMahon, said: “Just three days after Nats assured airlines and passengers that it had introduced robust ‘mitigation plans’, its flight data processing system has failed again. “More than 25,000 Ryanair passengers have already suffered disruption, with more than 140 Ryanair flights delayed. “Enough is enough. Martin Rolfe should resign today.” Rolfe, who was paid £1.4m last year including bonuses, has come under increasing pressure since the major outage on 8 September, the third high-profile incident in just over three years. Rolfe apologised and said he took full responsibility, but Nats has denied that the incidents are related. A “radar-related issue” in July 2025 a caused an air traffic control failure that disrupted the journeys of thousands of passengers and forced the cancellation of more than 160 flights. The biggest incident, in August 2023, affected more than 700,000 passengers when flights were grounded across the UK after a “rogue flight plan” sparked a system failure. Alexander has commissioned the CAA to conduct an independent review of Nats and check the findings of its initial report into the 8 September breakdown. She said the government still needed “to urgently understand why this issue was not discovered and fixed before it caused chaos”. Andy Burnham, asked whether the head of Nats should be sacked, said Alexander would have to “get to the bottom” of the problems. “These are clearly serious issues and they need to be fully investigated, and I know the transport secretary is taking these issues extremely seriously,” said the prime minister. “Further issues today do cause even greater concern, but initially this is a matter for the transport secretary to get to the bottom of what is behind this and why there has been a recurrence.”

title: Vermont man convicted of attempted murder of three Palestinian students
summary: James Eaton, 51, faces life in prison after jury rejects insanity defense rooted in claims he was acting on orders from US and Israeli intelligence
text: A jury has convicted a Vermont man of attempted murder in the shootings of three Palestinian college students who were walking near his home, rejecting an insanity defense rooted in his claims that he was acting on orders from the CIA and Mossad. Jason Eaton, 51, faces up to life in prison over the November 2023 attack near the University of Vermont campus in Burlington, which left Hisham Awartani paralyzed from the waist down and wounded his friends, Tahseen Aliahmad and Kinnan Abdalhamid. The jury deliberated for several hours before reaching its verdict after a week-long trial that saw testimony from the three men and psychiatric experts called by the defense and prosecution. Eaton was ordered to be held in jail pending sentencing, which has yet to be scheduled. He stared ahead blankly as the verdict was read. Awartani and Aliahmad, sitting in the front row of the courtroom gallery, smiled and hugged people around them. “Justice has been rendered for Hisham, Kinnan and Tahseen. After three years of sorrow, loss, and struggle, our families finally feel relief,” the families of the three men said in a joint statement. “The verdict cannot undo what happened or erase the trauma our families still carry. But it affirms something fundamental: Jason Eaton is responsible for what he did.” Eaton had pleaded not guilty but did not dispute that he was the shooter. His lawyers argued that he should be found not guilty by reason of insanity, pointing to his claims that the United States and Israeli intelligence agencies transmitted orders to shoot the men to him via FM radio and that God was commanding him to protect his Jewish neighbors. Had he been found not guilty by reason of insanity, he could have been ordered to undergo mental health treatment. In their statement, the families said Eaton had repeatedly used “hateful” words to describe their sons during the trial. “They were not the words of a man confused about who he shot, or why. They are the words of a man who saw three young men celebrating their friendship and wearing what made them feel closer to their far away families and home – and decided to kill them because of his own prejudices. We do not need a jury to tell us why our sons were targeted. We heard it, in his own words. This was a hate crime. We have said so from the beginning.” Thanking their communities in Burlington and Vermont for their support and solidarity, the families added: “That solidarity has mattered even more with each passing year, because our sons’ recovery unfolded alongside the genocide and destruction of Gaza and the escalating ethnic cleansing of the West Bank. While our children fought to heal from being shot in Burlington, they watched Palestinian children lose their lives, their homes, their land, their families. We are grateful our sons’ suffering commanded attention and support. We grieve that so much Palestinian suffering never does. “Hisham, Kinnan and Tahseen have spent three years rebuilding their bodies and their lives after a hateful act almost killed them. We are profoundly relieved. And we continue to work toward a world where hateful violence against Palestinians is called out for what it is – and stopped.” The shooting, a few days after Thanksgiving, shook Burlington and reverberated in the occupied West Bank, where the three men grew up and became friends as schoolmates in Ramallah before moving to the US for college. The shooting, which occurred weeks after the onset of Israel’s military assault on Gaza – widely condemned as a genocide – triggered calls for a hate crime investigation. But no hate crime charges were filed as questions persisted about whether anti-Palestinian animus, an altered mental state or something else had compelled Eaton to open fire on Awartani, Aliahmad and Abdalhamid, who were all 20 at the time. Eaton’s lawyers argued he was suffering from a delusional, psychotic disorder after losing his job at a credit union two weeks before the shooting. Awartani, Aliahmad and Abdalhamid, all of whom are now 23, told jurors of their holiday weekend visit to Awartani’s grandmother’s house, a trip to a bowling alley to celebrate his twin cousins’ birthday, and the walk they took near the University of Vermont campus after dusk that ended in the shooting. Awartani, who was studying at Brown University in Providence at the time, said they were smoking cigarettes and speaking a mix of English and Arabic. Two of them said they were wearing traditional Palestinian scarves known as keffiyehs. Awartani said he noticed Eaton standing on a porch as they approached the apartment house where he lived. Within seconds, Awartani said, Eaton was off the porch and walking towards them. His face was expressionless and he did not say anything. As Eaton got to about five to 10 feet away, “he pulled out a handgun and started shooting at us,” said Awartani, who was paralyzed from the waist down in the attack and now uses a wheelchair. The Associated Press contributed reporting.

title: California braces for record El Niño storms as governor declares emergency
summary: Super El-Niño has already broken temperature records and is predicted to bring an extremely wet winter to the state
text: California is bracing for a record breaking El Niño that is expected to bring severe winter storms and flooding across the state, with the state’s governor declaring a state of emergency in anticipation of extreme weather in the months ahead. The global climate phenomenon known as a “super El Niño” is already breaking temperature records and drawing predictions of an extremely wet winter in places such as California, where El Niño typically brings more severe winter storms and flooding risks. Several coastal California cities have recently faced high surf, flooding and coastal erosion linked to Hurricane Marie as well as El Niño. Experts have said the effects offered a glimpse at what the coming winter could look like. Gavin Newsom declared a state of emergency on Monday to bring supplies to California communities ahead of extreme weather, and ready the national guard to assist with flood response and search and rescue efforts. It also directs state agencies to prepare roads and critical infrastructure. The governor said in a statement that the proclamation was an effort to “[give] communities the support they need, [give] first responders the tools to do their jobs, and [give] families the confidence that their state is ready.” “We are preparing for this El Niño early because every Californian deserves to be safe in their home, connected to their community] and protected when severe weather comes,” Newsom said in a statement. The global climate phenomenon occurs when parts of the eastern tropical Pacific Ocean naturally warm, which affects weather patterns across the world, leading to drought in some areas and fueling severe storms in others, and causes global temperatures to surge. It amplifies the effects of the climate crisis, and recent research found that global heating is supercharging the El Niño climatic patterns. El Niño broke the highest temperature ever recorded for the phenomenon this week, months ahead of the anticipated peak, according to the latest data. This year there is a more than 90% change of a very strong El Niño event and a 75% chance of an event of historic strength, according to a statement from the governor’s office. That could bring severe rain, flooding, landslides and coastal flooding that cuts off neighborhoods, damages communities and causes widespread power outages. “California is already taking steps now to protect communities from a potentially historic El Niño because we know how serious these weather extremes driven by climate change can be,” said Wade Crowfoot, California’s natural resources secretary, in a statement. The governor also approved emergency declarations for several counties across the state that recently experienced significantly damaging severe weather events.

title: Lib Dems reject ‘discriminatory and unworkable’ EHRC guidance on transgender people
summary: Motion passed at party conference calls for new approach to implementing ruling that legal definition of a woman is based on biological sex only
text: The Liberal Democrats have rejected official guidance by the equalities watchdog on how organisations should implement the supreme court ruling on transgender people, calling it “discriminatory and unworkable”. The motion, passed overwhelmingly at the party’s annual conference in Brighton, makes the Lib Dems the first of the big three parties in parliament to call for a new approach to implementing last year’s ruling that the legal definition of a woman is based on biological sex only. The Greens have previously done so. Formal guidance from the Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC), put out in May, is intended to tell service providers and others how they must balance the rights of trans people with the requirement for some spaces to be single sex. It has attracted criticism for being a de facto bar on trans people being in many public spaces by setting out that single-sex toilets and changing rooms must exclude transgender men and women when gender-neutral facilities are not always available. The motion to the conference called the EHRC’s code “discriminatory and unworkable”, saying it “places an undue burden on service providers”. It calls for a revised code, plus a dedicated cross-party parliamentary committee “to review how the law should better protect trans people’s rights”. Proposing the motion, the party member Lucas North condemned the EHRC guidance and noted a rise in anti-trans hate crimes. They added: “The rights of women and the rights of trans people do not have to be placed on opposite sides of a manufactured culture war.” Another speaker for the motion, Rebecca Jones, said that as a trans woman she was “tired of being a culture war prop”. She said: “You now fear using public spaces. You fear anyone that looks at you too much in case they hate trans people enough that they put you at risk. All whilst your government repeats the words ‘dignity’ and ‘respect’, whilst doing everything in their power to ensure trans people do not have them.” But the councillor Mark Johnston, from Reigate in Surrey, said the motion would distract the party from the “realism” needed to ensure Nigel Farage did not become PM: “That realism means accepting the supreme court determination last year is unassailable. “Are we going back to our constituencies to prepare for government, or are we going back to our bedrooms to prepare for irrelevance?” Zoe Hollowood, a party activist, said the party should accept the supreme court ruling: “If we pass this motion, we are telling women we think they are second-class citizens … This policy is totally out of touch with both public sentiment and public priorities.” The mood in the conference hall was strongly in favour of the motion, which was passed easily on a show of hands. Earlier in the day the party leader, Ed Davey, told the BBC he broadly supported the motion, calling the EHRC guidance not “fit for purpose”.

title: Inquest into British aid workers killed in Gaza may call on Israeli and UK military chiefs
summary: Lawyer tells review hearing that families wish to know whether weaponry involved in the deaths was made in UK
text: Israeli and UK military commanders could be requested to give evidence to an inquest concerning three British workers killed in Gaza when aid vehicles they were travelling in were hit by an airstrike. It is also possible that the inquest into the deaths of John Chapman, 57, Jim Henderson, 33, and James Kirby, 47, may examine whether the weaponry that killed the men was made in the UK. Until now, the focus of the inquest has been on the role played by the aid organisation in charge of the convoy and the security firm that was protecting it. But at a pre-inquest review, Maria Voisin, the senior coroner for Avon, indicated that the scope of the final hearing would probably be widened to include the role of Israeli authorities in the deaths. The coroner said she was “minded” to designate the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) and the colonel who ordered the strikes, Nochi Mendel, as “interested parties” for the inquest. Interested parties are often relatives of the person who died or an organisation or individual believed to be closely involved in what happened. Israeli military authorities last month said they would not open criminal investigations into the strike which, along with the three Britons, also killed the Australian aid worker Zomi Frankcom, and one each from Poland, Palestine and the US. The UK, Australian and Canadian governments called the Israeli decision “shameful”. In a written submission to the court, Pete Weatherby KC, for Henderson, compared the case to that of the novichok attack by the Russian state in Salisbury, in which the British woman Dawn Sturgess was killed. In that case, the high court in London ruled the lack of any criminal investigation by the Russian authorities and the strong public concern surrounding the circumstances of Sturgess’s death necessitated the expansion of the scope of the investigation. Lawyers for the three men accepted that it was possible Israel would not cooperate with the inquest but called for UK ministers to try to apply pressure if needed. Another element the families are keen to have investigated is the role the British military may have played in the incident in April 2024. Weatherby’s submission says that a Royal Air Force surveillance plane spent about five hours above Gaza on the day of the attack, seemingly returning to base minutes before the airstrikes were launched. The families want to know what, if any, surveillance the plane gathered about the convoy – and what was shared with the Israeli authorities. The barrister also told the review hearing in Flax Bourton, near Bristol, it was a “matter of public concern” and “great importance to the family” to find out if the weaponry that killed the men was made in the UK. Voisin said she was open minded about which issues the inquest would consider and would keep some under review. “It’s very much a case of throwing the net wide at the moment,” she said. Henderson’s father, Neil Henderson, said in a statement: “We hope the coroner will carry out a thorough investigation into the attack that killed Jim and the others [including] an exploration of all the issues relevant to his death, encompassing the decisions and policies leading to the attack, and what role, if any, UK authorities or military equipment originating from the UK may have played.” Tayab Ali, who is representing the Kirby family, said: “On behalf of the Kirby family they are very pleased that the coroner took onboard their concerns and extended the scope of the inquiry to include those actors that actually caused James’s death.” The scope of the inquiry has also been widened to include inquiries of the IDF and the Israeli defence ministry. It is understood that inquiries will be made of the UK Foreign Office, Ministry of Defence (MoD) and the Israeli arms manufacturer Elbit Systems as well. Ali said after Monday’s hearing: “In order for the inquiry to establish the real circumstances of James’s death it’s crucial that information is provided by the Israeli authorities including the IDF and MoD there, that’s the only way we’ll get to the bottom of how and why he was killed.” A further pre-inquest review will take place in March. No date for the final hearing has been set.

title: Charges dropped against Stanford students over pro-Palestine protest
summary: Students faced prison terms and thousands of dollars in restitution over campus protest against Israel’s war on Gaza
text: Five Stanford University students who faced prison sentences and thousands of dollars in restitution in connection to a campus protest against Israel’s war on Gaza had all charges dropped on Monday. The students also had their restitution severely reduced, ending a two-year legal saga that also saw the lead prosecutor in the case removed by the court. Part of a group of 12, the students had been charged with felony conspiracy to trespass and felony vandalism in connection to an hour-long, June 2024 occupation during which the group barricaded themselves inside the university president’s office to demand Stanford consider a student resolution to divest from Israel, among other requests. Some accepted plea deals or other diversion offers but five of the students went to trial earlier this year. The month-long trial ended with a hung jury but Jeff Rosen, the Santa Clara county district attorney, immediately announced his intention to retry the case before a judge ordered his recusal in May over a conflict of interest that, the judge said during court proceedings, would “render it unlikely that the defendants will receive fair treatment”. The case has since been taken over by the California attorney general’s office, which reached a resolution with the students. That resolution meant dropping all charges in exchange for 100 hours of community service at a nonprofit of their choosing and a total restitution of about $50,000, far less than the $1m prosecutors initially threatened them with and the $ 329,000 they each risked being found liable for at trial. The charges were the most severe handed out against students in connection to pro-Palestine protests on campus. A spokesperson for Rosen referred questions about the case to the California attorney general’s office. A spokesperson for the attorney general said that the office handled the case “with the same level of attention to detail, impartiality, and thoroughness that we bring to every criminal case entrusted to us”. “We believe this outcome serves the best interests of the community and all parties involved,” the spokesperson added. Stanford University did not immediately respond to the Guardian’s request for comment. Three of the students who had previously accepted misdemeanor pleas will also have their convictions withdrawn as part of Monday’s agreement once they complete the required community service. Two of the defendants who went to trial earlier this year, German Gonzalez and Amy Zhai, spoke of their relief in exclusive interviews with the Guardian. The ordeal severely upended their lives and they shared their deep frustration at what they saw as Stanford and Rosen’s effort to criminalize and silence speech in support of Palestinians. They said that they hoped their win would encourage other students to continue to speak out. “The most significant part of this is that I can continue to be involved in the Palestine movement in ways that were kind of curtailed by also being actively a defendant in a criminal case,” said Zhai, who graduated from Stanford as the trial got under way and is now in law school at a different university. “[The prosecution] was intended to silence speech about Palestine, and for everything that they threw at this case, they have failed.” Zhai added: “People still very much care about Palestine but I think they are afraid, and reasonably so, because of everything that’s happened with the escalation of repression over the past two years. It takes victories like this one to encourage people to turn their beliefs into action.” Thousands of students were arrested over their involvement in pro-Palestinian campus protests in the spring of 2024. Dozens were suspended or expelled from their universities, but most of those who also faced criminal charges have seen those charges dropped. Abbee Cox, a member of the Stanford students’ legal team, told the Guardian that Monday’s resolution was in line with those reached in other cases relating to campus protests, which have mostly ended in diversion deals rather than severe sentences. “The attorney general’s office has addressed this in a manner consistent with the way other peaceful student protesters at Stanford have been treated over the years – protesters against apartheid, against the Vietnam War,” she said. “But it took almost two and a half years of this painful and protracted and incredibly stressful battle to get there. And it took a fair prosecutor to get us there in the end.” As protests flared up on campuses across the country in the first year of the Gaza war, the Stanford students briefly occupied the president’s office, renaming the building after Adnan al-Bursh, a Palestinian surgeon who was reportedly tortured to death while in Israeli detention. They were immediately arrested, suspended, and banned from campus for two terms, but it was not until a year later, in April 2025, that Rosen announced criminal charges against the group, declaring at a press conference that “dissent is American, vandalism is criminal”. Rosen was ultimately removed from the case in May, after the students’ legal team submitted evidence to the court that he had used the pending case to fundraise for his re-election, citing it in a webpage dedicated to showcasing his work to fight against “antisemitism”. The page was also emailed to a listserv of more than 600 people, soliciting donations. Rosen responded to the recusal effort by accusing the student’s defense attorney of engaging in a “f—— antisemitic trope” in an interview with a local publication. In pre-trial motions, Rosen had sought to ban the students from discussing “genocide”, as well as the political motivations behind the protest and free speech issues – a request the court denied. But he had successfully blocked the defendants’ efforts to have an international human rights expert testify, and from invoking the first amendment as a defense, on the grounds that the alleged conduct does not constitute protected speech. Gonzalez, a sophomore student at the time of the protest, is set to graduate this year but said he feels under scrutiny by university administrators. “It’s difficult to go to classes and try to walk from your library to your classroom and get followed by campus security,” he said. “It feels demeaning, being surveilled to that degree … All I have done is stand up for what I believe in.”

title: Another day, another Reform Wales leader. Grumpy Nige seems to miss the old one | John Crace
summary: At a low-key event, Helen Jenner replaces Dan Thomas, who was arrested on suspicion of assault and gets warm words from Farage
text: Twenty-five or so Reform members of the Senedd were lined up against a wall. Almost as if they were in a police identification parade. Reform’s need to find a new leader in Wales is becoming habit-forming. First, Nathan Gill was banged up for 10 and a half years on eight counts of taking £40K in bribes to make statements in support of Russia. Easily done. Who among us hasn’t been tempted by the Kremlin? And then last week, Dan Thomas chose to stand down after being arrested on suspicion of assault and coercive behaviour, leaving the Welsh leadership spot open once more. He denies the allegations. It’s almost as if there’s a pattern emerging. That the job of Reform leader in Wales is somehow cursed. Otherwise law-abiding men and women suddenly find themselves accused of all sorts of things. So much so that it’s now the job that no one really wants. Yet politics abhors a vacuum, and someone has to do the job. So it was a decidedly grumpy-looking Nigel Farage who turned up in Cardiff on Monday morning to pretend to be interested in announcing the next Reform Senedd leader. Perhaps he reckoned he had better things to do. The event – if you can call a five-minute announcement that – was supposed to kick off at 11.45. Nige was booked on the 12.18 back to Paddington and had hoped to be in London for a late lunch. No champagne and oysters. There were no undercover reporters posing as Americans trying to make a potentially illegal donation this time. Instead, there was a 20-minute delay. Nige really was going through the motions. He was thrilled by the results in Wales at the May elections, he began. He didn’t sound thrilled. Though that could be because Reform has been shedding support in Wales – as elsewhere – ever since. They have lost seven points in the opinion polls over the course of the summer and are looking less and less likely to challenge Plaid Cymru. “Dan Thomas has been doing a brilliant job,” Nige continued. “I am sorry for his personal difficulties.” This was just weird. Almost as if he hadn’t even considered what Thomas had been alleged to have done. Yeah, Dan. Great bloke. Brilliant Reform leader. Always buys his round in the pub. It’s just unfortunate that he’s been arrested on suspicion of assault and coercive control. But it’s no big deal. He’ll soon be sorted. Nige doubled down, calling the arrest a “bump in the road”. Not a word of sympathy or support for the person he is accused of having assaulted or subjected to coercive control. Besides, he was clear that Dan would come back soon. There would always be a welcome in the Reform valleys for Dan. We all need someone like Dan. After the Song for Dan, Nige made the briefest of introductions to the new leader. Best to skip over the bit where almost half the Reform members of the Senedd had preferred a different candidate. The party in Wales is a hotbed of backstabbing. Not literally, mind. The job was going to Helen Jenner, the former deputy leader and Nige’s old-time Ukip mucker. “I’ve known her for years and I trust her,” he said. Helen mumbled her thanks and said she would build on the good work done by others. It wasn’t clear if Dan would take over from her if he is cleared of the allegations, which he denies. It sounded like a possibility. In which case, I guess Dan might then only be keeping the seat warm for Nathan when he gets early release in 2031. You have to admire Reform’s loyalty. And their amnesia. Because you also can’t help wondering if Nige is beginning to lose the plot somewhat. How else do you explain his recent Substack post in which he claimed that “British politics is awash with dirty money”? I mean, he’s obviously not entirely wrong. But why would he want to draw attention to it when questions remain over money received by Reform and figures associated with the party? There’s the £40K that went to Gill from the Russians. There was the apparent eagerness on the part of Dan Jukes and James Orr to accept overseas donations. A meeting at which Nige was present. Though not listening, apparently. There’s the dosh from Ben Delo, a man convicted of failing to comply with anti-money-laundering legislation in the US. There’s the cash from Posh George and his mum that is somewhat opaque to say the least. There are the police and parliamentary investigations. The £5m gift that went undeclared. With the best will in the world, none of this seems the model of transparency. But what do I know? And it’s good to know that Reform operates in a world where any transgressions are so readily forgiven.

title: Lauren Boebert says claims of sexual relationships with staffers ‘utterly false’
summary: Republican congresswoman rejects ethics complaint and says allegations part of ‘politically motivated’ hit campaign
text: Lauren Boebert, the firebrand Republican subject of a House ethics complaint that she had sex with three staff members, and paid one to keep quiet, has said the allegations are untrue – and part of a “politically motivated” campaign against her. Boebert’s denials came through a formal statement from her office, which said “the congresswoman rejects the claims as utterly false”. She also published a verbose video rant on social media in which she accused the person who filed the document as a “sloppy, desperate, obsessive hack” – and journalists who reported the story as falling victim to a “scam”. According to the complaint, filed on 17 September by David Wheeler, an independent journalist, activist, and founder of the American Muckrakers political action committee, Boebert, who represents Colorado’s fourth congressional district, committed at least seven violations of House ethics rules. The Guardian has reviewed the complaint but not independently substantiated the allegations. Wheeler said his group had direct knowledge of the relationships “through text messages, bank records, court documents, and recorded conversations”. Among the most prominent allegations are that Boebert conducted a four-year “romantic and sexual relationship” with a senior female staffer, named as Clarice Navarro Ratzlaff, then paid her $200,000 when Ratzlaff broke off the affair and threatened to file an ethics complaint of her own. Additionally, Wheeler alleges, Boebert had a sexual relationships around the same time with Raven Finegan, a congressional employee and the congresswoman’s district chief of staff, and Jeffrey Small, who was her chief of staff from 2021 to 2025. The complaint includes detailed financial records of Boebert’s congressional spending, and payments to staff that included more than $450,000 to Finegan to June 2026, and almost $780,000 to Small. Ratzlaff received more than $461,000. The code of official conduct prohibits House members from engaging in sexual relationships with employees under their supervision, or the committees on which they serve, unless a couple is married. Consent, the rules state, is not a defense. The allegations came after Boebert has frequently promoted her own Christian values and has previously been publicly critical of same-sex relationships. In June, she posted on X – without evidence – that Major League Baseball was unduly “forcing” players to promote a LBGTQ+ agenda. Attached to the complaint are numerous photographs of Boebert and Finegan together, and accounts of a number of social trips the congresswoman made to Donald Trump’s Mar-a-Lago resort in Florida with family and friends. Ratzlaff, a Republican former state representative who resigned in 2017 to take a minor role in Trump’s first administration, divorced her husband, Jace, amid the fallout from her relationship with Boebert, the complaint alleges. It adds that Boebert fired Ratzlaff in September 2024 but allowed her to stay on her payroll until January 2025 as a “ghost employee” who performed no work. “These allegations regarding me are entirely false, defamatory, and beyond ridiculous,” Ratzlaff told the Colorado Reporter in a text message. “There is absolutely no truth to any part of this claim.” According to American Muckrakers, Jace Ratzlaff told Wheeler: “I assumed this would eventually surface. I’ll have no further comment on this topic.” A spokesperson for Boebert, in a statement from her office on Sunday, questioned the legitimacy of the complaint, noting that a member of the House needed to certify it had been filed in good faith, and so far nobody had. “Swearing to it does not make it a complaint,” the spokesperson said. “This was a political smear packaged as an ethics filing and published before anyone checked whether it even qualifies under the [ethics] committee’s rules.” Boebert also told news outlet Sources Say News: “I’m not a lesbian or bisexual, and I have never, ever been in any inappropriate relationship, nor have I ever been sexually involved with any staff.” The ethics complaint against Boebert, who filed for divorce from her husband, Jayson Boebert, in May 2023 citing irreconcilable differences, follows similar previous claims. In September 2023, she apologized and said she “fell short of my values” after closed circuit video footage from a Denver theater showed Boebert and a male companion groping each other. Boebert, who was escorted from the building by security, initially denied that she was also vaping against theater rules – but later conceded she had been when further video footage emerged. Boebert said she “genuinely did not recall vaping that evening” and blamed her conduct on a “public and difficult divorce”. In another episode in January 2024, Boebert denied attacking her ex-husband after police were called to a disturbance involving the pair at a restaurant in Silt, Colorado. Boebert in June ended an interview with a Fox News Digital reporter who brought up allegations that she had a relationship with fellow Republican US House member Thomas Massie. In the interview, Boebert had been discussing Republican representatives who had lost their primaries when she mentioned Massie, to which the reporter said: “One of his exes was making headlines saying that you guys – ” Boebert interjected: “Fuck you, first of all. If you’re gonna bring me into this, like, this sexist stuff is out of control. There’s your clickbait that you were looking for. I don’t wanna talk about anybody’s exes and their crazy shit that they do.” She then ended the interview by walking away. In August, Lauren and Jayson Boebert’s 21-year-old son, Tyler appeared in court in Glenwood Springs, Colorado, charged with three counts of sexual exploitation of a child and two counts of contributing to the delinquency of a minor over sexually explicit pictures he allegedly posted on social media in 2024.

title: Race to be next UN secretary general could rest on US and China trade-offs
summary: Numerous possible last-minute entrants being discussed as current field of seven candidates struggle to garner support
text: Numerous last-minute entrants in the race to become the new UN secretary general are being discussed amid concerns that the world powers may not be able to agree a successor to António Guterres from the current field of seven candidates. Three rounds of secret ballots have so far not produced an obvious frontrunner, with probably only three candidates regarded as still having a realistic chance of gathering the required support. The new leader, due to take office in January, will face an organisation at the start of a cost-cutting overhaul programme and seen as marginal to the major global conflicts. But surveys still show strong international support for the institution among a public that blames world leaders as much as the UN itself for its recent failing. A survey by GeoPoll for the UN Foundation published last week found six out of 10 people trust the UN to deliver on the issues that matter to them, but 85% said they had heard nothing or little about the process to choose a new secretary general. The successful candidate must win the support of nine current members of the 15-strong security council with no veto by any of the five permanent members of the council – France, the UK, China, Russia and the US. Achieving consensus among the permanent five is fraught given the breadth of political divisions. Guterres’s term ends on 31 December. Names being mentioned as potential late drafts include Lana Nusseibeh, the minister of state at the United Arab Emirates and a former UAE ambassador to the UN, and Sigrid Kaag, a former UN under secretary general and Dutch centrist politician. She was briefly the senior humanitarian and reconstruction coordinator for Gaza before joining the advisory committee to Donald Trump’s Board of Peace. Other candidates mentioned include Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, the polyglot president of Kazakhstan, and, in deference to the US, Viktor Orbán, the former prime minister of Hungary, who is still much admired by Trump but reviled as a disruptive populist by many European leaders. Vuk Jeremić, a Serbian former president of the UN general assembly who came second behind Guterres in the 2016 race, has also been mentioned. None of the speculated candidates have given any public indication they wish to be drafted. A communique at the end of this month’s Brics summit attended by 21 countries, of which 10 are full members, said: “We note that no woman has ever been elected for the role of secretary general, and only one national from Latin America and Caribbean, and only two nationals from Africa and Asia each have ever occupied this position.” Some would also resent a late candidate, regardless of their origin, entering the field since strenuous efforts have been made to democratise the selection process by holding regional and global hustings. The last general assembly president, Annalena Baerbock, has helped spearhead the attempt to open the selection process. But the need to avoid alienating any of the five, internally divided, veto-wielding security council members inevitably incentivises the candidates to issue slightly bland consensus-seeking statements at a time when the organisation needs firm leadership. All the candidates have said they would like to see the UN return to an active role as a peacemaker – a task often demanded by amateur US diplomats close to Trump. In the third and last straw poll of the 15 security council members on Friday, Rebeca Grynspan of Costa Rica regained the lead after receiving nine “encourage” votes from the security council. She got five “discourage” votes and one “no opinion”. Her fear is that the discourage votes came from Russia and China, an opposition she would need to overcome. In the second straw poll on 21 August she had dropped behind Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett, a Guyanese politician who then came first – receiving eight encourage votes, three discourage and four no opinions. Last Friday, Rodrigues-Birkett maintained the eight encourage votes, but her discourage votes had risen from three to six. A third candidate, the Ecuadorian former finance minister María Fernanda Espinosa, is just about still a viable contender despite the numbers discouraging her reaching six last week, up from three in August. She has been calling for an early warning system inside the UN to help prevent wars, and for a secretary general more willing to take risks in mediation. It will not be until later in the process – when colour-coded balloting reveals if a vote is from a permanent member of the security council or not – that it will be clear whether a candidate faces an insurmountable barrier. In reality the decision may turn on the horse-trading between the US president and the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, and whether Trump accepts that China cares more about the UN’s future than him, and that may mean accepting a candidate that China wants and the US can tolerate. The Trump administration appears to have softened some of its scepticism towards the UN under the US ambassador to the UN, Mike Waltz. The US not only provided $1.8bn (£1.35bn) in additional humanitarian funding in March but also recently sent $827m in dues, admittedly less than a quarter of what it owes the cash-strapped organisation. Michelle Bachelet, a former president of Chile and a human rights campaigner, became the first candidate to drop out of the race at the weekend after she received only one encouragement in last week’s poll.

title: Helen Jenner unveiled as Reform UK’s new leader in Wales after arrest of Dan Thomas
summary: Nigel Farage dismisses loss of previous leader as ‘bump in the road’ and says party will ‘carry on as if nothing has happened’
text: Nigel Farage dismissed the loss of Reform UK’s leader in Wales last week as a “bump in the road” as the party unveiled a replacement. Helen Jenner replaces Dan Thomas, who stood down last Tuesday after he was arrested on suspicion of assault and controlling or coercive behaviours. Jenner, who was previously the party’s deputy leader in Wales, narrowly beat her rival, Jason O’Connell, in a poll of its 33 Senedd members. She joined Farage on the steps of the Senedd, where he said Reform would “carry on as if nothing has happened”. Thomas announced last week that he was standing down after his arrest. He has been bailed and insists he has done nothing wrong. The former Tory councillor, who remains a member of the Welsh parliament, was only announced as Reform’s Welsh leader in February. Jenner is from Neath, near Port Talbot in south Wales, and represents Bangor Conwy Môn in the Senedd. Farage said of Thomas: “I am sorry for his personal difficulties that he is going through. No one’s life is ever seamless and I am quite sure he will come out of these before too long. “But it was pretty much untenable for him to continue as leader while he had these domestic disputes, so we very quickly and rapidly have moved to electing a new leader.” Farage confirmed that a new deputy leader in Wales would be elected, and said: “We will carry on as if nothing has happened, waiting for Dan who is going to stay a member of this place, to come back more actively with us. “We could have done without this bump in the road. But it has happened, we are making the best of it.” Thomas issued a statement last Tuesday after intense speculation about his future, saying that he had been reported to the police the previous weekend and was released without charge. “I stress that I have done nothing wrong, but I do not want the coming headlines to be a distraction from the fantastic work our Senedd team is doing in holding this government to account,” he said. Gwent police said a 45-year-old man from the Aberbargoed area had been arrested on 13 September “on suspicion of assault and engaging in controlling/coercive behaviour. He has been bailed pending further inquiries”. Thomas was perceived by some as having been parachuted in from Reform headquarters in London, which caused tensions, but Jenner is a Welsh speaker who has a track record of involvement with Farage’s parties and was elected to her new role by colleagues. She was a general election candidate for the Brexit party in 2019, and before that was a member of Ukip under Farage’s leadership. She takes charge at a time when Reform is hoping to consolidate and build on its gains in Senedd elections earlier this year. It emerged as the second largest party, largely at the expense of the Conservatives and Labour. She also takes charge after the party was rocked not only by the loss of Thomas but also the defection of another of its Senedd members, Sarah Cooper-Lesadd, to Plaid Cymru, which holds power. Her departure sparked fury in Reform, with the party’s deputy leader, Richard Tice, accusing her of lying to them about her political beliefs. Plaid Cymru said Cooper-Lesadd had been “honest about her political beliefs” and that her views had changed. Cooper-Lesadd, who was elected to the Pen-y-bont Bro Morgannwg constituency, claimed that Reform UK was “far more interested in division, opposition and headlines than in finding solutions”. Before Thomas took up the post, Nathan Gill, who briefly led Reform UK in Wales in 2021, was jailed for 10 and a half years in 2025 for taking bribes to make statements in favour of Russia when he was an MEP.

title: Trump set to press Zelenskyy at UN to agree to energy ceasefire with Russia
summary: US president to meet Ukrainian counterpart in New York as Ukraine steps up attacks on Russian energy sector
text: Donald Trump is expected to press Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelenskyy on an energy ceasefire during a face-to-face meeting this week during United Nations high-level week, as world diesel prices have soared due to the war in Iran, as well as Russia’s war in Ukraine. Ukraine stepped up its attacks on Russia’s energy sector over the weekend, launching its largest reported strike yet on the Moscow region in a barrage that struck a major Moscow oil refinery and killed three people. On Monday, Trump said the whole world was suffering due to an energy shortage that he said was being exacerbated by the war in Ukraine. “Russia has unfortunately lost control of its Diesel Oil Industry due to its War with Ukraine,” Trump said in a Truths Social post on Monday morning. “A large number of their Diesel refineries have been blown up and are, at least temporarily, out of commission.” “This ridiculous and never ending War with Ukraine must be ended,” Trump said. “The whole World suffers as 25,000 people, mostly soldiers, are being killed each month. What a shame!” Trump had earlier blamed Kyiv for the escalating energy war even as Russia has decimated Ukraine’s economy and launched night barrages of drones and ballistic missiles against Ukrainian cities. Zelenskyy on Monday said negotiations were continuing and that there are “ideas on the table for bringing peace closer, starting with strong de-escalation steps”. “Ukraine’s energy sector, critical infrastructure, and our food exports must stop being targets for Russia, and this will lead to matching de-escalation steps on our part,” he said in a statement. “Solutions are possible.” The two leaders are expected to meet on Tuesday during a rare sitdown on the sidelines of the high-level week of the United Nations general assembly. The Russian foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov, will also be in Washington this week, and is expected to meet with the secretary of state, Marco Rubio. During a trip to Ireland last week, Trump directly addressed Zelenskyy, saying he has to do “one thing: he has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia”. “Let him go after targets but not diesel fuel, because he’s causing a shortage,” he said. Trump spoke with Zelenskyy on Sunday in a phone call that one senior Ukrainian official told the Financial Times was about “diesel, diesel, diesel”. Average diesel prices in the United States hit a record $6.50 per gallon on Monday, up from $3.19 per gallon this time last year before the US and Israel launched joint strikes on Iran and Tehran responded by closing the strait of Hormuz to most international trade. The rise in prices is seen as a liability for Trump’s Republican party in the US midterm elections, which will take place in November. Trump is expected to deliver a speech to the UN general assembly on Tuesday morning, and is expected to meet with major energy producers including the Gulf Cooperation Council and Venezuela’s recently installed leader Delcy Rodriguez. In a preview, Mike Waltz, the US ambassador to the UN, said Trump would speak about how he has “confronted complex problems head-on around the world. Many of the peace deals that he has driven to conclusion, or is in the process of driving to conclusion.” Trump last week prematurely announced an energy ceasefire under which Ukraine had agreed not to hit Russian energy targets and that “Russia has agreed to do likewise!” The deal had not been agreed upon, however, and Russian strikes against Ukrainian energy and other critical infrastructure have continued.
