title: Paramount settles lawsuits with 12 US states, clearing way for Warner merger
summary: States including California and New York sued over concerns of ‘extinguishing competition’ with $81bn merger
text: Paramount has reached a settlement with California and several other states that sued over a proposed $81bn merger with Warner Bros Discovery (WBD), the California attorney general announced Monday, clearing the way to consolidate some of Hollywood’s most recognizable TV networks and studios under one owner. Though the merger was approved by the justice department in June, a coalition of 12 states, led by California, had sued over concerns that combining two of the five last legacy studios in Hollywood would “extinguish competition” and lead to fewer movies in theaters and on streaming platforms. Rob Bonta, the California attorney general who spearheaded the antitrust litigation, said in a news conference on Monday that Paramount had made an “enforceable commitment to significantly increase” production in the US and specifically in Los Angeles, which he said would mean “more jobs, more economic activity”. “This settlement is not a vote of support for this merger; it’s not a blessing of the broader merger,” he said. “Broadly speaking, we believe further consolidation in markets that are essential to American economic life doesn’t serve the American economy, consumers or competition well.” Four holdout states – Massachusetts, New York, Connecticut and Minnesota – held out on a deal until this weekend, according to Bloomberg. Paramount, as part of the settlement, agreed that CBS and CNN would maintain independent editorial boards under the merger. Paramount also agreed to spend at least $300m in domestic production, and would be forced to pay a financial penalty ifthe newly merged company fails to distribute 30 films for the first two years of the deal and 32 movies in the three years after. In return, Paramount will not have to sell its cable channels, which include CBS, MTV, Nickelodeon and Showtime, as was discussed in negotiations, the Wall Street Journal reported. Bonta also added that together, the parties would select a trustee to monitor Paramount’s compliance with the terms of the settlement, and would be prepared to go to court if the company ever fails to comply. David Ellison, the CEO and owner of Paramount and son of billionaire tech mogul Larry Ellison, said on Monday that he was grateful to Bonta, other state attorney generals and California governor Gavin Newsom for “engaging in good faith to find a path forward to a resolution”, and reiterated his message that the merger would be “pro-competitive, pro-consumer and pro-worker”. “Our goal has always been to build a stronger Hollywood — one with more stories told, greater choice for consumers and stronger competition,” he said in a statement. “Bringing Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery together will build that stronger Hollywood, creating expanded opportunity for our people and even more great entertainment for audiences around the world.” The legal battle has been a headache for Paramount executives, considering that a closing date past 30 September would have reportedly add millions of dollars to the purchase price. Reports emerged last week that, after months of speculation, WBD and Paramount were in the process of selling their studio lots in California and leaving the state amid the antitrust lawsuit, which would have been an enormous hit to Los Angeles’s already struggling film and entertainment industry. Whispers of Paramount Skydance plotting a California exit had circulated for months, though there was speculation the reports amounted to strategically leaked leverage as the media company sought a bargaining chip in the lawsuit. In an August news release, Ellison called the lawsuit the “final obstacle” to the merger, describing the deal as “pro-competitive, pro-consumer and pro-worker”. Twelve states warned that a merger between Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros Discovery would result in fewer entertainment options and higher prices for consumers. Bonta also has voiced concern about how a merger could affect CNN’s journalism. (CNN is owned by WBD.) Last summer, Skydance Media bought Paramount in an $8.4bn merger, a deal led by Ellison. After US regulators approved the deal, Paramount reached a $16m settlement with Donald Trump over a 60 Minutes interview with Kamala Harris. It also announced the cancellation of the Late Night with Stephen Colbert show, which aired its last episode in May. After the merger, Ellison appointed Bari Weiss as editor-in-chief of CBS News. The network has since been roiled by allegations of bias favoring the Trump administration. In a guest essay published in the New York Times last month, Ellison wrote that the anti-trust lawsuit stemmed from concerns over “whether I can be trusted as a steward of Warner’s CNN”. “I do not aspire to lead these companies to bend their newsrooms to my views. I believe that news should be based on facts and truth,” Ellison wrote. “Great news organizations like CNN and CBS News are here to tell it straight down the middle. That requires newsrooms that reflect the whole world, not one side of it. And it requires independence. Our journalists will continue to answer to the facts and to all the people they serve – not to any party or cause.”

title: Wildlife will be affected by current drought for years to come, UK government says
summary: The number of potentially damaging environmental incidents triggered by this year’s hot and dry weather has surpassed that of 2025
text: Wildlife in England and Wales will be affected by the current drought for years to come, the government has said. This summer saw large parts of England and all of Wales plunged into a serious drought, with both recording their driest Julys since records began in 1836. The lack of rainfall combined with successive heatwaves and new temperature records have placed a significant strain on water supplies, with demand for water increasing by as much as 30% on the hottest days. Scientists said this extreme weather was only possible due to the climate crisis caused by the burning of fossil fuels. Despite recent rainfall, the National Drought Group said groundwater storage and reservoir levels were continuing to decline, with England’s reservoir storage now 19.7% below average for the time of year and most reservoirs classed as notably or exceptionally low. Tony Grayling, the chair of the drought group and the strategic lead for drought at the Environment Agency, said the environmental impacts of the drought would continue to increase. “The short-term impacts of drought have been visible over the summer, but we know the effects on wildlife populations and ecosystems will last for years to come,” he added. “The speed of drought recovery depends both on rainfall and demand for water.” So far this year, 349 environmental incidents have been recorded, exceeding the 321 in 2025. These incidents include algal blooms (which can be triggered by hot and dry weather and reduce oxygen levels in water), fish deaths, water quality incidents and low flows. Natural England said breeding waders and specialist wetland invertebrates had struggled significantly, while some species-rich environments had dried out completely. Natural England is developing a research and monitoring programme specifically focused on the effects of drought and wildfire, as many of the most serious consequences may not become fully apparent until future growing seasons. Oliver Harmar, the chief strategy officer at Natural England, said the country must use nature-based solutions to adapt landscapes to cope with the growing threat from drought. “Restoring the natural hydrology of our landscapes, particularly our wetlands and peatlands, helps them hold on to water for longer, recover more quickly from drought, and reduce the risk of fire taking hold in dried-out ground,” he said. “It also has real benefits for the water that ends up in our taps and rivers, and for the wildlife that depends on these habitats to survive.” The drought group has said it will take months of significant and sustained rainfall for the drought to end. The Environment Agency recently said 120% of average rainfall was needed over the coming seven months for the entire country to be out of drought by next spring. Grayling said: “It is vital we all still use water wisely in the coming months to help our environment recover from the impacts of an exceptionally dry spring and summer.”

title: Stop relying on AI chatbots for customer care, UK banks and energy firms told
summary: Citizens Advice says providers of essential services such as energy, banking, phone and internet should guarantee the ‘right to talk to a human’
text: Stop relying on AI chatbots for customer care and guarantee the “right to talk to a human”, Citizens Advice has urged essential service providers, as research found they wasted time, caused stress and delayed problem solving for more than half of users. The spread of the AI-powered systems to provide help about the provision of vital services such as energy, banking, phones and internet, is making it harder for millions of already digitally excluded people to handle snags, according to the frontline charity that last year provided more than 2.7 million people with one-on-one help in England and Wales. The charity concluded that chatbots caused harm, saying too often they trapped humans in an “endless loop” in which nothing got resolved, and almost half of people who had to use a chatbot found them unhelpful, with some concluding the chatbot seemed rigged to “make me give up”. It called for service providers to respect a new right for customers to speak to a human after it investigated the wider impact of digital exclusion, estimated to affect at least 14 million UK citizens. It uncovered slower and less reliable support for people who struggle with or have limited access to online systems and found the erosion of phone, face-to-face and paper communication had created a two-tier support system. “Going round in circles with a chatbot isn’t just annoying, it can be a blockade to essential services,” said Tom MacInnes, policy director at Citizens Advice. “We’ve seen organisations’ overreliance on chatbots and online forms leaving people unable to fix billing problems, sort out their debt or even access homelessness prevention services. There’s a role for chatbots, but the quiet erosion of face-to-face and telephone services is letting too many people fall through the cracks.” That erosion of traditional ways of communicating means that people without good digital access can face serious difficulties getting simple problems fixed. For example, the charity found that submitting energy meter readings to correct a wrong bill can take less than an hour online if systems are working properly. Without good digital access it takes as long as six weeks offline, putting people “at risk of further harm”. In some locations applying for low-cost social tariff broadband – itself intended to reduce digital exclusion – is being made harder by being digital only, Citizens Advice found after it took evidence from its frontline advisers and hundreds of case summaries. One adviser reported that when people struggled with digital-only applications for homelessness support they ended up “homeless for longer … they’re in danger … they’re losing money … they get into debt” and said: “It can ruin a lot of people’s lives.” The warnings come amid growing frustration with the proliferation of AI customer services. Online message boards with titles like: “I’m so sick of AI Customer ‘Support” Chat Bots” and “Has anyone ever actually had their problem solved by a company’s chatbot?” are filled with tales of woe. Several chronicle frustrated customers’ attempts to circumvent phone-based chatbots by repeatedly yelling “human!”. Only 20% of UK adults polled on behalf of Citizens Advice in July said chatbots were their preferred way to communicate, with phone calls, email and instant messaging all preferred. Gripes about other forms of digital exclusion include multifactor authentication, which requires rapid and dextrous manipulation of more than one device just to log in and time-limits to complete transactions. Of the people who found it difficult or not possible to talk to a human to resolve an issue with their essential services, 49% felt stress or frustration, 27% felt powerless, 44% experienced delays to resolution and 14% gave up trying to resolve the issue altogether. The UK government has previously said it is investing £11.9m in a digital inclusion innovation fund, supporting local projects to help people get online. About 1.7m households in the UK do not have a laptop, tablet or desktop computer. A government spokesperson said: “Businesses have a legal obligation to provide contact information in a manner which is clear and easily accessible.”

title: Catherine Webb obituary
summary: Other lives: Treasury civil servant who went on to become bursar of a Cambridge college
text: My daughter Catherine Webb, who has died aged 47 from metastatic ovarian cancer, was a senior Treasury official during a turbulent period in British politics and latterly bursar of Emmanuel College, Cambridge, where she had taken her undergraduate degree. Having begun at the Treasury in 2000, Katie played a key role in helping ministers to deal with the 2008 financial crisis and Brexit before going on to become the Treasury’s director of operations, managing all the non-policy aspects of the department. Katie was our first daughter, born to Jane (nee Holly) and me, in Bebington, Wirral, and brought up in the mid-Cheshire village of Hartford; my wife was a probation officer and I was a social worker. Katie was educated at Hartford county primary school, Hartford high school and then Sir John Deane’s sixth form college in nearby Northwich, where she was noted for her sophisticated grasp of economics and politics. By then she was already a Labour party activist, and when she moved on to study economics at Emmanuel she continued her political activism in tandem with a vibrant social life. On graduating in 2000 Katie eschewed politics to join HM Treasury. Initially working on labour markets, welfare policy and poverty analysis, she went on to play a central part in tackling the 2008 financial crisis, including on secondment to the Bank of England to work on the team trying to save the failing Northern Rock bank. From 2011 she was key to developing the UK’s economic relationship with China as economic and trade counsellor at the British embassy in Beijing. Katie came back to the UK in 2015, promoted to director level, and held a series of roles at the heart of the UK’s relationship with the EU. She was the only woman among the senior Brexit negotiators, and led teams at the Department for Exiting the European Union and in the Europe Unit at the Cabinet Office. She returned to the Treasury in 2019 as director of operations and member of the management board, leading the department’s response to the challenges of operating under Covid-19 rules and establishing the Darlington economic campus, the northern branch of the Treasury. She was made a Companion of the Order of the Bath in 2020. In 2023 she left the civil service to become bursar at Emmanuel, with the remit to review and restructure the non-academic functions of the college, a task she performed while earning the respect and affection of its fellows and staff. As a civil servant, Katie was valued for her qualities of kindness and empathy as well as her intellect and technical expertise. Wherever she went, she had a gift for making friends and holding them fast. She had a great rapport with children, and was a generous and thoughtful aunt, godmother and significant adult to the children of many friends. Adept at many crafts, including cooking, breadmaking, quilting and sashiko, she was also a keen traveller. She loved to walk and cycle, and was a particularly enthusiastic swimmer, gaining great enjoyment from her membership of the London branch of Out to Swim, an LBTGQ+ aquatic club, and of the South London Swimming Club based at Tooting Bec Lido. She accepted her diagnosis, without rancour or complaint, and when curative treatment failed, decided to prioritise quality over quantity of life. Katie is survived by Jane and me, her sister Elizabeth and nieces Alice and Emily.

title: Key ally urges Trump to back US farmers amid anger over rising prices
summary: Iowa senator Chuck Grassley calls for embargo on diesel exports as tariffs and Iran war drive up costs for sector
text: Donald Trump is facing growing calls, including from within his own party, to boost support for US farmers as his administration faces mounting anger over its treatment of the agricultural sector. Republican senator Chuck Grassley of Iowa called on the US president to place an embargo on diesel exports this weekend and help farmers grapple with high prices. Grassley, who is largely aligned with Trump, suggested the embargo in multiple social media posts, calling on the president to issue a 1970s-style embargo on diesel and agricultural products to help farmers. “If our [government] can embargo chips to China it can embargo diesel to help American farmers & truckers,” Grassley wrote on Sunday. “We need our family farmers who feed&fuel the world [to be] on the strongest footing possible no matter what’s happening across the globe.” For months, farmers – traditionally a reliable Republican voting base – have been angry with the Trump administration because they believe some of its policies adversely affect them. That includes tariffs, which have driven up the cost of fertilizer, machine parts, seed and more; increasing beef imports to lower prices for Americans, which undermines domestic producers; and the Iran war, which has made it more expensive for farmers to operate machinery and transport products. The national average cost of diesel was $6.51 as of Sunday, according to AAA. In Iowa, it was slightly lower at $6.31 – still nearly $3 more than the cost one year ago. Gas prices are not the only rising cost Americans are facing as a result of the Iran war. Groceries have also become more expensive, and the Trump administration has sought to lower some of those prices, particularly beef, by allowing 300,000 metric tons of overseas beef trimmings to enter the US at a reduced tariff rate. But domestic farmers in the US, who are already struggling with smaller herds, say the decision will increase competition and make it more difficult to sell their own. “It takes something big to change long-established voting patterns, but I think there’s a possibility that the Trump administration has done things that are big enough and bad enough from the standpoint of rural America to make some of the voters who shifted a decade ago reconsider their choice,” William Galston, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, told the Washington Sun. Ryan Marquardt, the vice-president of the Iowa Farmers Union, told the Washington Sun he had “never seen farmers more pissed” than when Trump raised the imports of foreign beef. Farmers’ outrage toward the Trump administration has worried Republican politicians, such as Grassley, whose base includes farmers and rural voters. As November’s midterms approach, some politicians closely aligned with farmers have publicly broken with Trump, while others have sought ways to adjust the president’s policies. Iowa congresswoman Ashley Hinson, historically a Trump ally, recently adjusted her campaign strategy to highlight her work across the aisle and has repeatedly voiced opposition to the president’s tariff policies that have affected farmers. When asked by the Gazette, an Iowa newspaper, whether a vote for her would be a vote for Trump last week, Hinson replied: “I vote for me is a vote for commonsense policies, and no matter who is in the White House. That’s what I’m going to focus on.” Grassley, meanwhile, suggested an embargo on diesel, akin to the Trump administration’s embargo on semiconductor chips – though that specific embargo was considered national-security related. When asked for comment, the White House pointed to statements from interior secretary Doug Burgum and executive director of the national energy dominance council, Jarrod Agen, at a G20 meeting in Houston earlier this month. Agen and Burgum dismissed the possibility of implementing a ban on diesel, gasoline or crude oil. “We would consider an export ban if we thought that actually might lower prices, but that’s not the case,” Burgum told reporters. Brooke Rollins, the US agriculture secretary, told reporters on Monday that Trump had called her earlier in the day to discuss the issue of diesel for farmers and that Americans could “expect an announcement very soon on some potential actions”. “It is the direct result, clearly, of the Iran war,” Rollins acknowledged, arguing that the short term “implications” were “not easy”, but necessary, to ensure that Iran never obtains a nuclear weapon. • This article was amended on 25 September 2026. An earlier version said Doug Burgum was the energy secretary; in fact, he is the interior secretary.

title: Gerry Hunt obituary
summary: Other lives: Headteacher who was a community champion in the village of Pill, in Somerset
text: My father, Gerry Hunt, who has died aged 82, was a well-known member of his local community in the village of Pill, Somerset. He moved there in 1966, the same year that he started working as a teacher at Pill primary school. Gerry subsequently worked at Yeo Moor school in Clevedon and Air Balloon Hill in Bristol, where he was headteacher before moving on to become head of Colston’s primary school in the city (now Cotham Gardens school) in 1987. When he retired from teaching in 2001 he turned his attention to a range of community projects in Pill and the surrounding area. He chaired Pill parish council for many years, helped to open its community centre, edited and distributed the Pill Paper, joined the St George’s Players (who produced the Pill pantomime) and in later years set up the Resource Centre, a community hub, where he worked until he was no longer able. He also volunteered at the Victorian gothic revival estate of Tyntesfield for more than 20 years, working there in the inventory team for the National Trust, which bought the estate in 2002; Gerry was instrumental in setting up its bookshop. Born in Barnet, north London, Gerry was one of the four sons of Nancy (nee Butlin), a secretary, and Cedric Hunt, who managed a printing business. He went to Queen Elizabeth’s school in Chipping Barnet, then in 1960 began to study classics at University College London; he later did his teacher training at Redland College, Bristol (now part of the University of the West of England). Gerry met Margaret Higginson when he started teaching at Pill primary; they married in 1968. They were fond of Cornwall, where they went every summer, and my sister, Briony, and I have fond memories of spending long days on Chapel Porth beach, where Gerry loved to surf. He was proudly the Chapel Porth World Belly Boarding Champion, 2003. It is fair to say that Gerry had opinions, which were largely shaped by his daily reading of the Guardian. He is survived by Margaret, his children, Briony and me, his grandchildren, Rory, Joe, Ivy and Sam, and his brother, Peter.

title: Houthis move to seize strategic terrain after Trump calls off airstrikes at last minute
summary: US president reportedly changed his mind over Saudi Arabia’s pleas for assistance as bombs were being loaded
text: Houthi fighters are moving to seize strategic heights in Yemen that would cut the Red Sea coast off from areas held by Saudi-backed forces after Donald Trump called off US strikes on the group at the last minute, reportedly as bombs were being loaded on to aircraft. Amid increasingly heavy fighting in Yemen, which has displaced tens of thousands of people in recent weeks, the New York Times reported on Monday that the US president had flip-flopped wildly in recent days after a call from Saudi Arabia for US strikes on the Houthis. It comes amid the Houthis’ rapid advance on the ground with the group gaining control over much of Yemen’s Red Sea coast from Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces and advancing to areas adjacent to the crucial Bab al-Mandab strait, which Saudi Arabia has used as an alternative route for oil exports bypassing disruption in the ⁠strait of Hormuz. In the call reported by the New York Times, Saudi Arabia’s crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman, implored Trump to step in to help halt the Houthi advance after weeks of such appeals. Trump, who had been resisting joining the Saudi war in Yemen, after the call then told the Pentagon to prepare for airstrikes against the Houthis before reversing course once again, the report said. Trump has frequently given mixed signals to Riyadh, telling reporters during a visit to Ireland earlier this month that the Houthis “called us, and they don’t want to fight us”, adding that the group was “allowing ships to pass” the Bab al-Mandab strait and that the situation would “work out very well”. He added that the Houthi problem was limited to “one country” an apparent reference to Saudi Arabia promising to “take care of fixing that”. The UN says hostilities in Yemen have displaced at least 125,000 people since the start of September. Taiz city has received the largest number of displaced persons, taking in up to 86,000 Yemenis since the recent escalation began. The rapid advance by the Iran-aligned group this ‌month has extended the wider Middle East conflict to a new theatre and further threatened global energy supplies. Washington has so far rebuffed repeated pleas from Prince Mohammed to join the fight in Yemen with the Houthis claiming on Saturday they had fired on Riyadh, where columns of smoke were visible near the main airport. The Yemeni president, ⁠Rashad al-Alimi, ⁠spoke to Trump on Sunday, requesting ‌support for his ‌UN-recognised government in its fight against the Houthis. Trump ⁠made no direct pledge of military support during the call, sources said. Saudi Arabia has launched hundreds of strikes in recent days on Houthi positions in the strategic Kahboub mountains, according to the group, but making little impact on the advance of its fighters. Fighting has centred on the outskirts of the remote Al-Wazi’iyah district in Taiz province and Ras al-Ara along the Indian Ocean coast, which separate the Red Sea coast from the city of Aden, where the government is based. The Houthis aim to secure the rear of their forces around the Bab al-Mandab strait by taking control of the mountains, which would also allow them to open new ‌fronts, according to ⁠sources who spoke to Reuters. The surge in fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis has created a new dilemma for Trump, under pressure to help defend Washington’s close Saudi allies but anxious not to further expand the deeply unpopular war he launched in February against Iran. The US bombed the Houthis for two months in early 2025, but Trump called off those strikes after reaching a ceasefire with the group and has kept out of the conflict since. Amid the broad failure of the US-Israeli war against Iran, and with the US midterm elections looming, the Trump administration’s priorities appear to be to secure at least some oil supplies through the strait of Hormuz, while avoiding a wider entanglement in Yemen. That, however, invites longer-term risks, not least the growing alienation of key US allies in the Gulf, including Saudi Arabia, where Washington is increasingly seen as an unreliable ally, that could also undermine the so-called “security for oil” understanding where the US provides a defence umbrella for Gulf states in exchange for energy supplies. Reuters contributed to this report

title: Chad Gilbert, New Found Glory’s founding guitarist, dies aged 45
summary: Gilbert’s family says he died ‘peacefully in his sleep’ months after My Friends Over You musician shared stage four cancer diagnosis
text: Guitarist Chad Gilbert – a founding member of the US rock band New Found Glory that doled out the early 2000s anthem My Friends Over You – has died aged 45. Gilbert’s family announced his death on Sunday, saying that he “passed away peacefully in his sleep” and “left this world surrounded by friends and family and took his final breaths with his wife and mother by his side, just as he wished”. “We are devastated and shocked by how quickly he left us, yet so grateful for how peacefully and smoothly he went,” Gilbert’s family added, without disclosing his cause of death. In an interview with People magazine from April, Gilbert said that he had been diagnosed with stage four adrenocortical carcinoma (ACC) after doctors discovered three brain tumors, including one “the size of a walnut”. That discovery came as he underwent treatment for metastatic pheochromocytoma – a type of adrenal cancer – since 2021. “On [27 February] I had successful brain surgery and have been recovering in the hospital since,” Gilbert wrote on Instagram in March. “I regained function of my left hand immediately. My radiation oncologist described it like this: ‘This is not a fatal blow and not the end of your story, just the beginning of a new chapter.’” Explaining his ACC diagnosis, his wife, Lisa Cimorelli, told People magazine: “All his treatments were working on his whole body, but they don’t cross the blood-brain barrier. So that’s why this was kind of like the last frontier of a place for things to grow wild, which is unfortunate.” Gilbert revealed in August on Instagram that he “was crushing it and gaining weight” when “suddenly I couldn’t sleep and felt like I couldn’t breathe”. “So I went to the ER and discovered I had 4.5 liters of fluid in my lungs,” Gilbert continued. “So lucky I went in. I stayed for [five] days and they put a needle in between my ribs to drain all the fluid. Not a good time. Now I’m back to the beginning building my strength. But thankful for the nurses and doctors that found it. Definitely kicked my butt. Hoping to feel like myself again soon.” After Gilbert’s death, his family wrote: “The amount of visitors that crowded the hospital lobby at a moment’s notice is a testament to how beloved and cherished Chad was, and always will be. He was a legendary musician, but his favorite accomplishment was being a husband and father. His biggest dreams came true.” Gilbert’s family wrote that his survivors include his wife; his daughter, Lily; his mother, Jackie; and his brother, Brian. Similarly, Gilbert’s bandmates Jordan Pundik, Ian Grushka and Cyrus Bolooki wrote: “Chad’s guitar playing, songwriting, humor, and relentless drive helped shape New Found Glory for nearly three decades. “Through more than a dozen albums, endless tours around the world, and more accolades than we ever could have imagined, Chad challenged all of us to grow as musicians, performers, and human beings. While we are devastated to lose him, we are so grateful for the incredible life he lived, the memories we shared, and the brotherhood we had. “His influence will always be part of New Found Glory and his spirit will be felt on every stage we stand on, with every note we play.” Founded in Coral Springs, Florida, in 1997, the band has been largely celebrated as a one of the most influential pop-punk bands of the early 2000s. The band has been touring throughout the summer, with several more shows scheduled across cities including Orlando, Florida, and Sacramento, California. New Found Glory’s My Friends Over You and its lyrics about prioritizing one’s friendships above blossoming romance with someone else resonated with many teens at the beginning of the 21st century. Some of the band’s other signature songs included Hit or Miss and All Downhill From Here. The band has 14 studio albums to its name, including Listen Up!, the most recent one.

title: US strikes on alleged drug boats may constitute ‘crimes against humanity’, UN expert says
summary: Dozens of US attacks on boats in the Pacific and Caribbean have killed more than 230 people since September 2025
text: A special rapporteur for the UN human rights council has concluded that there are “reasonable grounds to believe” that the United States attacks on boats allegedly carrying drugs in the Pacific and Caribbean “constituted crimes against humanity”. The boat strikes, carried out since September 2025 on the stated grounds of stopping drugs being trafficked by sea to the US, have killed more than 230 people. The latest, on Saturday, killed four people in the Caribbean. The UN itself, along with several human rights organisations, lawyers and international law experts, had already described the bombings as “extrajudicial killings”, but special rapporteur Ben Saul went further. In a briefing note posted by Saul on social media on Sunday night and first reported by the BBC, Saul wrote that, in addition to “serial extrajudicial killings”, the attacks were “in violation of the right to life, being unjustified in national or personal self-defence or under international humanitarian law, the international law of the sea, narcotics suppression conventions, or international counter-terrorism law”. He added: “There are reasonable grounds to believe that the reported 68 attacks that killed 223 people constituted crimes against humanity of murder under customary international law.” The report cites 68 US attacks that killed 223 people. It is unclear how recently the figures were updated – tallies by organisations such as the Washington Office on Latin America put the death toll at 234 people in 66 attacks. US Southern Command, which has coordinated the attacks, posted on Saturday, alongside a grainy video, that it had “executed a lethal, kinetic strike on a go-fast vessel operating along established narco-trafficking routes in the Caribbean. Confirmed intelligence revealed the vessel’s active involvement in narco-trafficking. The operation killed four narco-terrorists”. As has become standard in announcements of such attacks, the US did not identify the victims or provide any details about the alleged intelligence that supposedly confirmed their involvement in drug trafficking. Saul’s report rejects the claim made by Donald Trump before Congress that the strikes amounted to “self-defence” against “designated terrorist organizations”. The special rapporteur wrote that the crews were not “militarily armed and possessed the intent and capacity to launch military attacks” against the US. “Even assuming that the vessels and crew attacked were members of the criminal groups listed as terrorist, such organizations have not mounted any ‘armed attack’ on the United States so as to trigger a right of self-defence,” he added. The US Department of State has not yet responded to a request for comment. Although Trump recently claimed the bombings had stopped 97% of all illegal drugs entering the US by sea, according to available data, the attacks have had no impact on the volume of cocaine entering the US. Journalists and human rights groups have managed to identify some of the victims, who in many cases were innocent or, when suspected of involvement in criminal activity, were at best low-ranked participants in trafficking networks.

title: Chancellor vows to stay on for Germany’s ‘democratic future’ after latest loss to far-right AfD
summary: Merz seeks to shore up support after CDU loses two state elections and is ejected from Mecklenburg parliament
text: Germany’s beleaguered leader, Friedrich Merz, has vowed to keep his fractious coalition government together for the good of the country’s “democratic future” after his conservative party suffered a drubbing at the polls in two state elections. Merz, who has vowed to plough ahead with an unpopular reform agenda, dismissed speculation over his position, saying it was vital that he and his coalition government remained in place. “We are determined to live up to the historic responsibilities our country is facing,” Merz said on Monday. “It is about nothing less, and nothing more, than the democratic future of our country.” Germany faces political uncertainty in the aftermath of three hefty defeats for Merz’s Christian Democratic Union (CDU) this month, which saw it ousted from a state parliament for the first time, and the far right and far left making strong gains at its expense. On Sunday the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) emerged victorious in the coastal northern state ofMecklenburg-Western Pomerania for the third time in a German state, securing 38%. The anti-immigration, pro-Russia AfD party’s leaders predicted Merz would be out of office in months, as they set their sights on securing victory at the next federal election in 2029. “The chancellor certainly won’t make it to the end of the year,” Leif-Erik Holm, the AfD’s top candidate in Mecklenburg, said. “I think the twilight of the chancellor’s era has begun.” Merz described the results as a “disaster”, in particular the CDU’s ejection from Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania’s state parliament, where it failed to reach the 5% barrier needed after losing more than half of its voters to the far-right AfD and centre-left Social Democrats. The result was all the more shocking as Mecklenburg was once a CDU stronghold. In Berlin on Sunday, the CDU fell to second place behind the far-left Linke party, which is on track to lead the next government in the city-state and could give Berlin its first Turkish-born mayor in its lead candidate, Elif Eralp. In Mecklenburg, the SPD under its existing state leader, Manuela Schwesig, is expected to lead a three-party coalition government. Her campaign had focused almost wholly on presenting herself as a buttress against the AfD, as well as distancing herself from the federal government’s reform agenda. The SPD is Merz’s coalition partner in the federal government. Although the CDU’s poor performance had been predicted, Sunday’s outcomes only added to the extreme pressure on Merz already after the CDU’s crushing defeat to the AfD in the state of Saxony-Anhalt two weeks ago, which triggered the first serious speculation over his future as leader. Last week, the CDU’s powerful regional leaders governing in eight states gave their backing to Merz, but questions remain as to how sustained their support will be. At the same time there appear to be few candidates willing to step up to the post, which is increasingly being viewed as a poisoned chalice. On Monday, Merz dismissed the idea that the outcome was a personal rebuke. “The reasons for these election results go far beyond my own person,” he said. “We are witnessing a profound transformation of the political party system in Germany as well as in many other countries around the world.” Karin Prien, the education minister and deputy CDU leader, accepted accusations that the government was failing to take voters’ fears seriously enough. But she said the government had no choice other than to continue trying to reform Germany from within, at a time of chronic economic weakness and global instability. “Without support and steadfastness we will not be able to achieve the necessary reforms, which are by no means a given. Nevertheless, not everything can remain as it is,” she told the broadcaster Deutschlandfunk. “The chancellor knows he will have to change, at least in how he addresses the people … We are a strong country, we have every chance of mastering this challenge together, but I believe that cooperating with each other will be crucial for this, and for the party it means we must broaden our appeal.” Doubts over the efficacy and fairness of the government’s agenda – which includes an overhaul of the pension system, a reduction in overbearing bureaucracy and cuts to income tax for the less well-off – played heavily into both election campaigns. On Monday, SPD leaders said they remained confident in their coalition with the CDU, but said that changes to the agenda were necessary. Lars Klingbeil, the deputy chancellor and finance minister, said: “Saying we will ignore what the voters said to us in three state polls won’t work.” While the country needed reforms, he said, they “must be fair and they need support in the population”. The labour minister, Bärbel Bas, also of the SPD, said the plans needed a “reality check”, but said “nothing would be more lethal than letting this coalition break apart over some technicality”. Rubbing salt into Merz’s wounds, the Kremlin on Monday waded into the election analysis, calling the AfD’s win in Mecklenburg a response to Berlin’s refusal to buy cheap Russian gas, which has jolted the economy and caused prices to soar, contributing to voter dissatisfaction. The Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said: “Naturally, Germans, or at least some of them, are looking for an alternative to the current authorities in order to improve their situation. That is a natural process.”

title: Lucy Letby, the NHS and the rise of managerialism | Letters
summary: Letters: Pete Dorey believes most public services are thoroughly over-managed, Michael Barrett says whistleblowing policies are essential. Plus letters from Frances Kirkham and Jenny Webb
text: Tom Dolphin’s excellent article on the failings of NHS management made sombre reading (The Letby inquiry report makes one thing crystal clear: too much NHS management is scandalously poor, 16 September). Yet I believe that most of our public services are thoroughly over-managed, with frontline professionals neither listened to nor respected by their institutional superiors, and at risk of damaging their careers if they speak out about poor decisions, excessive workloads and impossible targets or “performance indicators”. Like so many of our current woes, the rise of managerialism can be traced back to the public service reforms of the Thatcher governments in the 1980s, and the mantra of “management’s right to manage”. As professionals were supposedly self-serving vested interests, the transfer of power to managers was supposed to increase efficiency and responsiveness to service users. Yet, in many cases, the long-term result has been the rise of excessive, remote and unlistening senior management, and the parallel marginalisation or exclusion of professionals from decision-making in their spheres of expertise, coupled with plummeting morale. Pete Dorey Bath • Dr Tom Dolphin’s article on the failings of NHS management raises some important points about whistleblowing and the regulation of non-medical managers. Hospital board members do have responsibility for their overall management, but how well they exercise their responsibilities depends very much on leadership and the creation of a culture committed to patient care, as well as excellence throughout all the systems delivering that care. One of the essential assurance measures along with risk management and clinical governance is the promotion of a whistleblowing policy that encourages reporting of concerns to board level without fear of repercussions and with certainty that action will be taken if necessary. If there are still any hospital management teams out there without a clear protocol for raising and pursuing problems, confidentially if appropriate, that should be a matter for urgent action. Michael Barrett London • Yvette Cooper states: “This must be a turning point for the NHS”. The cry always goes up: “Lessons must be learned”. But the carefully considered, evidence‑based recommendations made by those who have conducted public inquiries or by coroners are invariably ignored. There is a shelf in government that’s high up – in other words, fairly inaccessible – on which every such report is placed to gather dust. So the lessons are not learned. Frances Kirkham Birmingham • In the wake of the Lucy Letby inquiry, the NHS will no doubt face a barrage of criticism. But we must also remember what a wonderful institution it still is. Earlier this month, after two agonising days and nights, my daughter died in the intensive treatment unit at Leeds general infirmary. Throughout, the service we received was wonderful – not just the medical expertise, but the kindness and loving consideration of all staff, from the consultant to the ward clerk. We were always kept fully informed about what was happening, and in the end we were consulted on the final decision to turn off the life support. By all means, criticise the NHS for its shortcomings. But let us also treasure its strengths, and its potential to help us through some of the most difficult times of our lives. Jenny Webb Chichester, West Sussex • Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Please email us your letter and it will be considered for publication in our letters section.

title: The AfD thrives in the absence of mainstream parties that speak to people’s daily lives | Letters
summary: Letters: Readers respond to Carolin Würfel’s article on the reasons behind Alternative für Deutschland’s recent electoral success in Germany
text: Carolin Würfel is right to see the success of AfD in the eastern states of Germany as a way to protest against west German dominance (I know why many east Germans vote AfD. And no, it’s not an inherited longing for dictatorship, 15 September). But she overlooks the fact that the “takeover” of 1990 could not have been done much differently. Any path more resembling those of other east European nations would have led to mass migration to West Germany. In that sense the current situation is not the fault of western politicians and industrialists. One thing could and should have been done differently, though. An attempt to build a conservative-centrist party representing the east would have been important, instead of just transferring the western parties. Die Linke fulfilled such a role for some time, but from the left, not the centre. Now AfD fulfils this role from the right. In Bavaria, the Christian Social Union has exactly such a role and has helped to keep that state a stable member of the federal republic. A similar “Ost-Union” would have been important, but for that the 5% threshold in the federal voting laws would have had to be replaced by a state-based threshold. A new local party in one state, “Thüringen.Gerecht”, formed by former members of BSW, a split from Linke, could develop into such a role, but without federal representation it will be a very long road. Jürgen Schwarz Berlin • Carolin Würfel’s article highlights a dynamic that is not confined to Germany. The same forces are reshaping politics across Europe and the US, and they all begin with a widening gap between political leaders and the people they are meant to represent. In much of Europe, that gap produces cynicism. Many citizens feel that leaders are driven by party interests, media pressures and broad national narratives rather than the realities of daily life. When people sense that distance, they become receptive to parties like the AfD, which present themselves as the only ones willing to listen. In the US, the emotional response is different. What I see is not just cynicism but a deeper hopelessness – a belief that no leader or institution can address the problems people face. This is the environment in which Donald Trump rose to power. Like the AfD, his appeal comes from exploiting the disconnect between political rhetoric and lived experience. Across democracies, people are responding to the same underlying pressures: deindustrialisation, rapid technological change, climate‑driven disruption and large migration flows from countries experiencing severe poverty, state fragility and deep social fragmentation. These are human problems, not ideological talking points. When leaders fail to engage directly with individuals, frustration and hopelessness become political fuel for movements whose primary interest is power, not solutions. Mickey Wright Utah, US

title: Pakistan jails sisters of Imran Khan before protest seeking his release
summary: Police crack down on family and political supporters of former PM who say authorities are ‘slowly killing’ him in prison
text: Three sisters of Pakistan’s incarcerated former prime minister Imran Khan have been arrested amid a heavy-handed government crackdown on plans for a nationwide protest to demand Khan’s release. The lawyer for the three sisters, Aleema Khan, Uzma Khan and Noreen Niazi, said on Monday that they had all been detained and jailed for 30 days under a warrant that accused them of being a threat to public order. Leaders from Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) condemned the “illegal harassment” of his sisters. Since Khan was arrested and held in prison on corruption charges in 2023, his sisters have been vocal advocates for his release. His family and party allege that Khan is being kept in solitary confinement and has been denied visits and calls from his family for six months, as well as being allegedly prevented from accessing vital medical treatment for an eye condition. The arrest of Khan’s sisters marked a dramatic escalation of a crackdown on PTI members and supporters in the run up to a nationwide demonstration due to be held on Sunday – described as a “long march” – to demand the release of Khan and to protest an alleged erosion of democracy and the constitution under the ruling coalition government. None of Khan’s sisters hold a political position in PTI. Since protesting against their brother’s detention – including by camping outside the prison where he is held, demanding to see him – they have been named in various court cases. This is the first time they have all been held in prison. Aleema was arrested in Lahore on Sunday as she was travelling to a private club; her driver was also picked up by police. Uzma and Noreen were then arrested at around 3am on Monday morning, after they held a press conference to condemn Aleema’s detention at her house in Lahore. According to their lawyer, Rana Mudassir Umar, hundreds of police officers later surrounded the family home as more than 100 entered to arrest Uzma and Noreen, as well as their children, grandchildren – who are four and six years old – and the household staff. The house was raided and all their phones were taken. By 7am on Monday morning, the children and grandchildren had been released but the three sisters were held and charged under the country’s Maintenance of Public Order law, according to Umar. He said: “They have not been allowed any family access, no legal counsellor access and they were not even allowed to bring clothes or basic things. “We have challenged their arrests in the high court in Lahore and [are] hoping we will get a hearing soon.” While Pakistan is ostensibly ruled by a civilian coalition government, the army is widely regarded as the country’s most powerful establishment, led by Pakistan’s army chief, Field Marshall Asim Munir, who fell out with Khan while Khan was prime minister. The current government was brought to power in an election in 2024 which was widely documented as rigged, allegedly by military intervention, to prevent Khan’s party returning to power. Speaking to the Guardian last week, Khan’s two sons, who are based in London and fighting for his release, accused Munir of a “personal vendetta” against their father and alleged the Pakistani authorities were “slowly killing” Khan in prison. Interior minister Mohsin Naqvi said on Monday that the government would “find a permanent solution” to prevent to march going ahead and shutting down swathes of the country “once and for all”. Despite Khan’s lengthy incarceration, he is still regarded as Pakistan’s most popular politician and there are fears among officials that large numbers could turn out to support PTI’s march on Sunday. It is being held as discontentment is rife on the streets amid an economic crisis and crippling petrol shortages due to the turmoil in the Middle East and the Gulf. Disgust at the alleged mistreatment of Khan is also widespread. Khan’s party has faced constant harassment over the past three years, with most senior PTI figures either in jail or pressed to leave politics. Sheikh Waqas Akram, a senior PTI leader, said the government feared that hundreds of thousands of people may turn out to the long march and “topple the government”, as protest movements have done recently in neighbouring countries such as Bangladesh, Nepal and Sri Lanka. Over the weekend, the capital of Pakistan, Islamabad, was transformed into a fortress of heavy security, with barriers and heavy armed security lining the roads and shipping containers placed to block the entrances into the city. “Punjab police are raiding houses, harassing families, bulldozing houses and arresting workers and families,” Akram said. “They are going to insane levels to crush the long march and stop it with violence and arrests. This illegitimate government know they can’t survive if people are allowed to protest and march on Islamabad in huge numbers.”

title: Edward Colston’s remains likely to stay at Bristol church that could become community space
summary: Exclusive: Slave trader is interred at All Saints, which may be given a change of use after being closed for years
text: Bones of the enslaver Edward Colston are likely to remain interred in a church in Bristol if and when the currently unused building is given a new lease of life as a community resource, it has emerged. The dean of Bristol, the Very Rev Mandy Ford, said Colston’s remains would probably stay where they were in All Saints church on one of Bristol’s busiest streets. Colston, who died in 1721, made headlines around the world in 2020 when his statue in the city centre was toppled during a Black Lives Matter protest and thrown into the harbour. The diocese of Bristol has been consulting with Bristolians over what to do with All Saints on Corn Street, which has been closed since 1984. While no final decision has yet been made, it seems likely it will be used as a space to reflect on the port’s connections with the slave trade – and Colston’s remains will stay where they are. Ford said: “There is very, very clear guidance which assumes that you don’t disturb remains that have been given Christian burial, except in exceptional circumstances and so the presumption is that they will stay where they are.” The dean said that if there was to be a radical rebuilding of the space there could be an argument to inter the remains elsewhere. “Otherwise the assumption is that Christian burial is permanent and that’s where they stay.” Ford brings deep expertise to the job of helping decide what happens to Colston’s bones, as when she worked in Leicester she was closely involved in the reinterment of Richard III’s remains after they were found in a car park there. She acknowledged people had different understandings of the theological or spiritual significance of human remains. “But it’s a Christian place of burial and we are a Christian church trying to do the right thing. This is the burial place of a human being who was involved in a practice which we recognise to be utterly sinful and wrong.” The question of what to do about sites connected to Colston in Bristol is a thorny one. After the Colston statue was thrown into the harbour, windows celebrating him were removed from two Bristol churches as the diocese declared the fall of the statue was a “signal” for it to take action. In the same year, Bristol’s concert hall was renamed Bristol Beacon, having previously been called Colston Hall. It is likely to be many months before a final decision is made over the fate of All Saints. But the dean said: “I think people do see that it has potential as a place of learning and also a place of reconciliation. From the work that we’ve been doing in the cathedral and the relationships and the conversations that we have, I think there’s a strong sense that there’s huge potential in Bristol to have difficult conversations and to build a better future on the basis of truth-telling about the past.” She added that work carried out at a new All Saints had the potential to sit alongside projects on Bristol’s history being done by institutions including the University of Bristol and Bristol Old Vic. Ford said: “I think one can see it as part of a much bigger picture, which I think is really important if Bristol’s going to have a peaceful and flourishing future as a civic space and as a city.” The Rev Anjali Kanagaratnam, who is leading the All Saints consultation, has been taking groups into the church. She said there had been a huge range of views. “Each extreme was covered from: ‘I never want to come back into this building’ to ‘Why haven’t I been told that this building is here? I need to bring my children.’ Some people find it a hard space to be in. Some were annoyed by the fact that they didn’t know it was there.” Kanagaratnam said it had been vital to hear the voices of people in Bristol that had been affected by transatlantic slavery but the church had also made sure it heard what people from other communities, such as white working-class areas in south Bristol. Kanagaratnam said there was great potential for All Saints to be a place of “truth-telling”. She added: “I think people do see that it has potential as a place of learning and also a place of reconciliation.”

title: CNN, MS Now and Politico sue Trump after being blocked from White House
summary: Three news outlets filed lawsuit in attempt to regain access to the White House after having badges disabled
text: In what will be one of the largest battles yet between the press and Donald Trump’s administration, three news organizations – CNN, MS Now (formerly MSNBC) and Politico – that have been denied access to the White House have sued to regain their ability to enter the building, accusing the president of violating the US constitution. The suit was filed on Monday morning in the US district court for Washington DC. Journalists for the three news organizations were denied access to the White House and had their badges disabled on Saturday after the president decreed a day earlier that they would lose their ability to enter the building because of his concerns about their coverage. The parties are seeking a temporary restraining order that would immediately lift the ban – and return access for the journalists – while the case plays out. “This morning, we notified the government that we are filing a lawsuit today to protect our First Amendment rights and defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes,” the news organizations said in a statement, referring to the US constitutional amendment guaranteeing a free press. “Without notice or process, the White House revoked our journalists’ credentials because it objected to our reporting. Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public’s right to independent journalism free from government interference.” In their lawsuit and request for a temporary restraining order, the parties argue that because the White House has granted access to journalists, those privileges cannot be rescinded based purely on viewpoint considerations. Case law heavily favors the plaintiffs, including past legal challenges that successfully returned the press badges of journalists Jim Acosta – then of CNN – and Brian Karem, then of Playboy magazine, during Trump’s first presidency. “Defendants took these actions in express retaliation for Plaintiffs’ First Amendment-protected newsgathering and speech because they dislike that speech’s content and viewpoint, and for the express purpose of excluding journalists and news organizations with editorial viewpoints disfavored by the Trump administration from the White House grounds,” lawyers for the news organization wrote in a motion, further alleging that the news organizations were unfairly deprived an opportunity to contest the ban as required by the fifth amendment of the US constitution. Laying out the stakes of the ban, the plaintiffs wrote that “they have been suffering serious irreparable harm”, adding: “They have already lost opportunities to perform their constitutionally protected newsgathering and reporting functions at the White House, impairing their ability to speak and publish as members of the press – and they lose more such opportunities every day that the ban remains in effect.” Trump announced the ban late last week in a post on Truth Social, writing that it was “a result of their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS.” He added: “Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America.” Citing Trump’s own words, the news organizations wrote in their lawsuit that “this ban could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment nor a more blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles.” While there was some uncertainty about whether Trump would follow through, it became clear that the ban was put into effect when journalists from MS Now and CNN attempted to access the building on Saturday morning but were told that their badges had been disabled and were taken. CNN was scheduled to serve as the television pooler on Monday. But the White House removed the organization from the five-member group that provides video of the president’s activities to the rest of the news media. CNN was scheduled to accompany Trump as he traveled to New York City for the United Nations general assembly. On Monday morning, subscribers of the White House television pool received a memo stating that there would be no pool coverage of the president. “This is to advise that, effective today, the TV pool will not be covering events designated as pool coverage of the President,” the memo reads. “This follows the White House’s position preventing CNN from fulfilling its assigned pool duties.” In a statement, the five television networks that make up the primary video pool covering the White House – Fox News, ABC News, CBS News, CNN and NBC News – said: “The public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government. No administration should restrict a news organization because it objects to its reporting.” The suspension of the television pool is an extraordinary escalation and a sign that Trump’s ban of CNN, MS Now and Politico crossed a line for the news organizations that cover the White House. (The Guardian has contacted the White House for comment on the planned lawsuit.) Trump responded to news of the pending lawsuit in a post on Truth Social, writing: “The White House is not instituting an assault on the Free Press, something which I cherish. It is instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS, something that has grown like Cancer in our beloved United States of America. It is corrupt, purposeful, pervasive, fully coordinated, and totally out of control. It is a threat to our National Security, and must be stopped, NOW!” The Knight First Amendment Institute at Columbia University said on Monday that it would support the news organizations in their lawsuit. “We’re glad to see that these news organizations are suing,” Jameel Jaffer, the organization’s executive director, said in a statement. “The president’s decision to bar them from the White House for the content of their reporting is a flagrant violation of the first amendment. It’s an attack both on press freedom and the public’s right to independent information about the government. We will support these news organizations in court.”
