title: ‘So surreal’: woman gives birth while stuck in heavy San Francisco traffic
summary: Doula stopped to assist couple with birth while first responders were also stuck in traffic and arrived on foot
text: A woman stuck in heavy traffic in San Francisco went into labor and gave birth to a healthy baby girl, local authorities have said. The San Francisco fire department said in a statement that a couple had been snarled in heavy congestion near the city’s Golden Gate Park when they were forced to pull over due to the imminent birth. The couple – whom authorities have only named as Karollyn and Nate – had called emergency services. But those first responders also became stuck in traffic and had to eventually proceed to the couple by foot. However, by then, a passing doula, Katie Higgins, had stopped to assist Karollyn and Nate with the birth. Though unconventional, and far from ideal, the delivery of a baby girl went successfully. “Both mother and child were transported to a local hospital in good condition,” the San Francisco fire department’s statement said. “We want to congratulate the family and welcome this new child to the world.” The San Francisco Standard news outlet quoted Higgins as describing the experience as “so surreal”. “We were so fortunate to have the support that we did, especially some medical professionals that were sitting in the same traffic,” the family said in a statement shared through the ambulance company American Medical Response and quoted by the Standard. “Most notably, a doula that helped coach Karollyn through the process until the paramedics arrived.”

title: Meta bans ads for Virginia Woolf play in Spain because they relate to feminism
summary: Theatre told that Facebook and Instagram filter out ads mentioning ‘social topics’ such as civil rights or feminism
text: A theatre in Barcelona has been banned from promoting a stage adaptation of Virginia Woolf’s A Room of One’s Own on Instagram and Facebook because the work includes “social topics”. When the newly reopened Teatre Raval, which seats 193 spectators, asked Meta, the parent company of the two social media sites, why its publicity had been blocked, it was told “any mention of civil rights, feminism or social reform [topics that are central to Woolf’s work] are usually classified as ‘social topics’ by our automatic system” and are filtered out. To resolve the situation, Meta recommended removing “key words” so that the text doesn’t appear to encourage activism. The theatre published a statement saying: “We feel obliged to speak up about the injustice and violation of our rights by not being allowed to promote a feminist work, specifically a work by Virginia Woolf who was born in 1882. “What can we do? As a theatre we have to publicise our activities … and we have to make use of social media so that people are aware of cultural activities.” The stage production, a one-woman show starring Clara Sanchis, is an adaptation of a series of talks Woolf gave in 1928 at Newnham and Girton, which were then the only two colleges at Cambridge University that admitted women. The talks were published as an essay the following year on the situation of women in society and their access to education. Women had been admitted to study at Cambridge since 1869 but weren’t allowed to graduate with a degree until 1948. Woolf said that in order to produce high-quality fiction, “a woman must have money and a room of her own”. She wrote in her diary that she expected to be attacked as a feminist for what she had written. “We don’t know if the publicity has been rejected because of the name of Virginia Woolf or because of the word feminism, or both,” Sanchis told La Vanguardia newspaper. “In any case, it’s a way of erasing from the map advances that have taken centuries to achieve. We have given social media unlimited power and every day we can see how dangerous this is. It’s bias and manipulation.” A Meta spokesperson said: “This ad was removed in error and quickly restored. The ad is live and running as normal.” • This article was amended on 22 September 2026 to add a statement from Meta that was provided after publication.

title: ‘Planetary boundaries’ necessary for flourishing of life have been massively breached, scientists warn
summary: New report shows key indicators of Earth’s health are ‘outside the safe operating space’ as climate disaster looms
text: The planetary life support systems relied upon by humans have deteriorated to their worst levels ever recorded amid ongoing pollution and habitat destruction, according to a key yet grim annual update by scientists. Of the nine “planetary boundaries” that help determine whether life can flourish on Earth, seven are being breached at their highest ever levels of transgression, according to the latest planetary health check, a process that was established in 2009. The seven key indicators in the danger zone include climate change, change in biosphere integrity, land system change, freshwater change, modification of biogeochemical flows, introduction of novel entities and, for the first time last year, ocean acidification. Only two of the assessed areas, stratospheric ozone depletion and atmospheric aerosol loading, have shown improvement over the last decade, although researchers warn that atmospheric aerosols, which can form air pollution, are still a problem in several regions of the world. The coalition of 60 scientists who conducted the analysis of the key guardrails for human life under the auspices of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research warned that the consequences of breaching these planetary boundaries is “becoming increasingly clear all around us”. “The diagnosis is unambiguous – pressure is rising across every planetary boundary already outside the safe operating space,” said Boris Sakschewski, lead author of the report. “It means that the risk of large-scale, persistent and potentially irreversible change is increasing, while our margin for error in tackling these problems is shrinking.” While there is little time to reverse this parlous situation, humanity does still possess the knowledge and capacity to do so, according to Johan Rockström, a climate scientist and report co-author. “Accelerating action to return to the safe operating space across all planetary boundaries is essential to protect lives and livelihoods, and to deliver on the promise of shared future prosperity,” he said. The assessment, which pored over the latest scientific data, seeks to establish the state of the defined areas that provide a “safe operating space for humanity”. Human civilization has developed in the past 10,000 years due to a relatively stable climate and natural resources that sustainably provide us with food, shelter and a safe living environment. These conditions are being badly warped, however, by the ongoing release of huge amounts of planet-heating pollution, from the burning of fossil fuels, and the mass disposal of other pollution, such as plastic into our environment. Habitats such as forests and wetlands are being torn apart, fragmented and flattened to make way for agriculture and urban areas, imperiling animal species and natural systems upon which we depend. The ability of landscapes and bodies of water to cope with this and act as a buffer to the worsening climate crisis is “weakening and may be significantly overestimated”, the new report warns. While forests and oceans have sucked up a vast amount of the carbon dioxide we have emitted, there are signs that these natural systems are faltering. For example, there is a chance that the Amazon rainforest, a huge carbon store, could reach a tipping point where it becomes a savannah, which would have “serious implications for climate stability, food and water security, and human health around the world”, the report states. The report comes on the heels of a series of extreme events around the world in the past year that scientists say have been made far more likely by the upending of our environment. Huge floods hit Pakistan last year, while this year has seen record heat and wildfires across Europe, the hottest ever summer in the US, and a disastrous flood on the Tibet-Nepal border. The oceans, which are absorbing much of this extra generated heat, have hit new temperature records. “These are not separate emergencies; the planet is telling us, in every region at once, that it is out of balance,” said Hindou Oumarou Ibrahim, chair of Planetary Guardians, a coalition of scientists, business leaders and activists. “I hear this same story wherever I go, whether from a pastoralist watching the rains fail season after season or a coastal community watching the sea rise. The 2026 planetary health check puts data behind what communities on the frontlines already know from living it. We do not have the luxury of treating these as separate crises any longer.” The report was released on Monday shortly after the start of Climate Week, a major gathering of politicians, business leaders and activists in New York City that leads up to the UN general assembly. Members of the Planetary Guardians – including Mary Robinson, the former Irish president; Juan Manuel Santos, the Nobel laureate and ex-president of Colombia; and oceanographer Sylvia Earle – attended the launch of the report. They are part of more than 100,000 attenders expected at Climate Week, which organizers said was set to be the largest ever. Despite the record numbers attending talks, announcements and other events aimed at tackling the climate crisis, however, the head of the week’s non-profit organizer acknowledged a general reticence to talk about global heating. Helen Clarkson, chief executive of the Climate Group, said that even though the world had been visibly racked by recent climate-fueled disasters, “I’ve not seen this level of ‘green-hushing’ before. Many companies tell us they will be here, but not very visibly. “But after a summer like this when we saw so much tragedy driven by climate change, this is the time to be loud,” she added. “The world is standing on the edge of the abyss, and people are seeking change.”

title: Putin consolidates grip on Russia as 49 Ukraine war veterans elected to parliament
summary: United Russia party’s record victory in tightly controlled vote likely to be used as evidence of support for war against Ukraine
text: Russia’s new parliament will include 49 deputies who have taken part in the war against Ukraine, officials have said after a landslide victory by the ruling United Russia party in widely criticised elections. The pro-Kremlin party won a record 355 seats in the country’s 450-seat Duma lower house of parliament, according to preliminary figures. The result further consolidates Vladimir Putin’s grip on power and gives United Russia a super-majority bigger than its previous 2016 record of 343 seats. The polls are the first to be held since Putin’s 2022 full-scale invasion. United Russia’s general secretary, Vladimir Yakushev, said 86 veterans from Moscow’s “special military operation” were likely to have been elected. “This is quite a substantial contribution,” he said. He later revised the number to 49. Putin’s press spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, said the vote showed that Russians supported their longtime leader, who has ruled as prime minister or president since 2000. “These indicators, of course, point to the highest level of consolidation within Russian society around the head of state,” Peskov said. Western governments denounced the polls held in Russian-occupied areas of Ukraine as a “sham”. Russia’s supreme court last month banned the only party that opposes the war, Yabloko, from participating, leaving liberal voters with no option to express discontent. Kaja Kallas, the EU’s top diplomat, called the election “another major setback for Russian democracy”. “The Kremlin silenced dissent and shut out international election monitors,” Kallas wrote on X, adding: “The veneer of democracy is all that remains.” The elections come amid speculation that Putin may announce a large mobilisation campaign this autumn, in an attempt to inject fresh momentum to Russia’s bogged down military campaign. Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, has suggested the Kremlin wants to recruit another 300,000 troops. In recent months, Russia has escalated its bombardment, pummelling Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities with jet-powered attack drones. Ukraine has launched its own deep strikes, hitting Moscow’s oil refinery on Sunday, as part of what Zelenskyy has dubbed “long-range sanctions”. Russia’s has also intensified its campaign to seize a string of cities in Ukraine’s eastern Donbas region, including Kramatorsk and Sloviansk. So far, it has been unable to break through, with Ukrainian commanders reporting their own counteroffensive near the city of Lyman. Inside Russia, criticism of the conflict is banned. Anti-war bloggers have been arrested and jailed. A local politician, Boris Nadezhdin, who previously tried to stand in presidential elections on a peace ticket, was barred from September’s elections and accused of being a “foreign agent”. The other parties that won seats in this month’s poll all support the “special military operation”. They include the communists, who came second with 40 seats, the ultra-nationalist LDPR party, with 25, and the New People party, with 20. Chechnya’s leader, Ramzan Kadyrov, a Putin ally, was re-elected and said to have won more than 99% of the votes. Russia’s elections chief, Ella Pamfilova, said United Russia had won a resounding victory with 57.83%, with 95% of ballots counted, up from the 49.8% it won in the last parliamentary election, in 2021. She praised voters for resisting “psychological pressure”. Overnight, Russia carried out what Zelenskyy called a “brutal, targeted attack” on the southern city of Zaporizhzhia. He said a nine-storey residential building, a university building, a shopping centre, and a boiler house were all damaged, with five people injured. A woman in Kharkiv region was killed in a drone strike. Zelenskyy said: “Russia is not scaling back its escalatory actions and is signalling a readiness to expand the war. All this is happening against the backdrop of global stability already having been shattered by this war. We must continue to pressure the aggressor to bring this war to an end.”

title: US hunter charged after fatally shooting woman he mistook for a deer, police say
summary: Walter Moorhead, 74, jailed on suspicion of manslaughter after allegedly shooting a woman while hunting in Delaware
text: A Maryland hunter was recently jailed on suspicion of manslaughter after he allegedly fatally shot a woman whom he mistook for a deer, according to authorities in Delaware. Walter Moorhead, 74, was hunting from a ground blind in a field near Ellendale, Delaware, at about 7.40pm on Friday when he believed he saw a deer and fired his rifle, state police said in a statement. Yet it was actually a woman whom Moorhead fired at and struck as she walked across the field with two children, the statement added. State police troopers who responded to a report of the woman being shot provided first aid to her. The woman – identified as 39-year-old Georgetown, Delaware, resident Santos Maria Chilel Soto – was then brought to an area hospital for emergency treatment but was pronounced dead there, according to state police. Troopers investigating the case spoke with Moorhead, determined he had fired the shot that struck Soto and took him into custody, state police added. The agency said troopers booked the Salisbury, Maryland, resident with manslaughter, possession of a firearm during the commission of a felony and reckless endangering. Delaware law defines manslaughter as recklessness causing the death of another person. The state considers manslaughter and possession of a firearm to be class B felonies which can carry up to 25 years in prison. Moorhead posted a $43,000 bond to secure a release from custody pending the outcome of the case, Delaware state police said. Attempts to contact Moorhead for comment at telephone numbers associated with him weren’t immediately successful. Hunting deer with a rifle was not in season in Delaware at the time of Soto’s killing, according to the state’s laws. Fatal accidental shootings in the context of hunting are relatively rare, according to a database curated by the International Hunter Education Association (IHEA). The IHEA hunting incident database lists 252 fatal firearm-discharge incidents between 2010 and 2025 (an average of 16.8 annually). Failure to properly identify a target was among the most common cited factors for those types of incidents, according to the IHEA database.

title: Eyeing a 2028 Bid, He Used a Weight-Loss Drug to Drop 80 Pounds
summary: Gov. JB Pritzker of Illinois, widely seen as a potential presidential candidate, revealed in an interview on “CBS Mornings” that he had been on a GLP-1 regimen since 2024.

title: Illinois authorities investigate possible ICE wounding of US citizen
summary: Police responded to altercation and found injured man and another person who identified himself as a federal agent
text: Authorities in Illinois are investigating a case on Sunday in which a US citizen was detained by federal immigration agents before ending up at a hospital with injuries. It came the same day that Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) shot and seriously wounded a man in Austin, Texas. Police in the Chicago suburb of Evanston said in a statement that officers were called to an argument between two men just before 10am on Sunday and arrived to find a man on the ground with injuries to his head, neck, and teeth, surrounded by several people who were assisting him. Officers questioned a man in one of two SUVs who was wearing plainclothes and a vest with the word “police” on it. That person “identified himself as a federal agent conducting a fugitive investigation”, the statement said. “The agent told the officer that agents had attempted to identify an individual who resembled a person they were seeking,” the statement added. “He said the individual refused to provide identification, was detained for fingerprinting, and resisted detention. “Agents later determined he was not the person they were seeking and learned that he was a US citizen. He was released.” An officer saw blood on the agent’s hands, the statement also noted, and he said he was injured “while attempting to handcuff the individual”. The statement did not specify which agency the person said he was from. But witnesses told police they believed the persons attempting to arrest the individual were ICE agents. The agent who spoke to the officer said five federal agents had been operating in the area in separate unmarked vehicles and said they had a warrant for the arrest of a person with a Chicago address. “The agent also said the federal agents left the area after protesters began to gather because they feared they would be attacked,” the statement said. Officers later contacted the wrongly detained person, an adult Evanston resident, at a hospital and “photographed and documented his injuries”. The US Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees ICE, did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The episode came as ICE is facing increasing scrutiny over its violent tactics in support of the immigration crackdown that Donald Trump has pursued throughout his second presidency. A 28-year-old Venezuelan man remained hospitalized in Texas in a serious but stable condition on Sunday night after he was shot earlier in the afternoon during an encounter with federal agents in Austin. The shooting followed a traffic stop in the city’s north side. A lawyer for the victim said he was making a DoorDash delivery when he was shot. Austin’s Democratic mayor, Kirk Watson, said he wanted the city’s police department involved in the investigation to provide “clear, third-party eyes”. The incidents follow a ramping up of Trump’s federal immigration crackdown, which saw a record 50,000 people arrested in July. More than half had no criminal record, despite the Trump administration’s pledge to focus the crackdown on dangerous criminals, according to the Deportation Data Project. Also in July, an ICE officer fatally shot 52-year-old Lorenzo Salgado Araujo of Houston, after federal agents driving unmarked vehicles pursued him while he was taking his construction crew to a job site. Among others to be fatally shot by federal agents under the command of the Trump administration were US citizens Renee Good and Alex Pretti days apart in January in Minneapolis.

title: ‘Jaw-dropping’ El Niño bursts through temperature record months before peak
summary: ‘Godzilla-level’ phenomenon is supercharging the climate crisis and will have a huge impact on communities across the world
text: The “jaw-dropping” El Niño currently heating up the planet has burst through the highest temperature ever recorded for the phenomenon, several months before its expected peak. The latest data shows the temperature rise at the heart of El Niño in the Pacific Ocean has now reached 3.05C. That is higher than the 3.02C set in late November 2015, the previous high set in the 150 years of modern records. This temperature is measured against the average of 1991-2020. The preferred measure of most meteorologists uses a 30-year rolling average as a reference and so takes account of human-caused global heating. This metric, called ONI (Nino3.4), is on the brink of breaking the record, just one-hundredth of a degree below the 2015 record. Both metrics are underpinned by data from the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA). The most recent forecasts predict a peak of 4.0C in November and December, according to the average of 14 different models assessed by climate scientist Zeke Hausfather. That is a level so far above previous events that Hausfather called it “mind-blowing”, while others have described it as “Godzilla-level”. Any temperature rise above 0.5C is deemed an El Niño; above 2C is officially called a “very strong” El Niño – often referred to as a “super” El Niño. The current El Niño is likely to be the largest in at least 1,000 years and will pile extra heat into an atmosphere in which temperatures are already rising rapidly due to human-caused global heating. This double whammy means 2027 is expected to “blow apart” previous records and become the hottest year ever recorded. The climate crisis, caused by pollution from fossil fuels, is already supercharging extreme weather and killing people. The El Niño will ratchet up the impacts even further, and has already begun to affect regions across the planet as weather patterns are altered. “Very strong El Niño events like those in 1997/1998 and 2015/2016 were associated with hundreds of billions of dollars in damages globally – this event is leaving those past ones in the dust,” said Hausfather, whose analysis is published by Carbon Brief. Prof Friederike Otto, at Imperial College London, said: “This event is a huge redistribution of energy in the climate system and is dangerous because it is unfolding on top of a much warmer, human-influenced climate system. “So, in many places around the world we will see never-before-experienced heat extremes, with all their consequences on health, food security and water stress,” she said. “El Niño comes and goes, but as long as we continue to burn fossil fuels it occurs on an increasingly hotter baseline, making it much more difficult for communities to deal with the consequences.” Hot and dry conditions in Indonesia have already spurred record wildfires and fatal levels of air pollution, while India has seen vital monsoon rains curtailed. Drought conditions in Central America and the Caribbean are causing crop losses and a slowdown of trade due to low water levels in the Panama canal. The World Food Programme said in August the impacts of El Niño were likely to push about 50 million people into acute hunger and drive prices up. El Niño years also see more intense rains and flooding in some regions, with Peru and Chile already suffering, and access to Machu Picchu is disrupted. The Horn of Africa is also very vulnerable to increased downpours, while the southern US is expected to experience fierce rains in the winter. The southern hemisphere summer is predicted to be hotter and drier as a result of the huge El Niño, meaning greater wildfire risk and droughts in Australia and southern Africa. Typhoons in the Pacific are expected to be more intense, but Atlantic hurricanes are suppressed by El Niño and, unusually, none has yet occurred this year. While the usual impacts of El Niño are well known, scientists are concerned that the multiplying effect of the climate crisis could shift these patterns. This would make it harder for countries and communities to prepare. The UN World Meteorological Organization said it has launched the biggest mobilisation in its 50-year history to support national weather services to deliver “life-saving” forecasts. The UN secretary-general António Guterres said earlier in September: “El Niño is being supersized before our eyes. The science leaves no room for doubt: the planet is in uncharted waters and the world is in the danger zone of extreme weather. The race now is between rising risks and our commitment to take climate action and protect people.” In the Guardian on Tuesday meanwhile, Prof Bill McGuire said: “What is happening in the equatorial Pacific is jaw-dropping and could well mark one of the biggest global weather upheavals in a millennium. “It will spawn a string of weather catastrophes around our world.” He said strong El Niños can have a devastating effect on the global economy: “While the great recession of 2008 resulted in global GDP reducing by around $2tn, the 1997–98 super El Niño resulted in losses of $5.7tn.” That El Niño has already been surpassed by the current one. Recent research shows global heating is now intensifying El Niño cycles, which then in turn intensify the impacts of the climate crisis. Data from analysis of corals, tree rings and historical documents suggest no El Niño has reached this level in the last millennium, added Hausfather. “All effects from El Niño are magnified by global climate change,” said Prof Kevin Trenberth, at the National Center of Atmospheric Research in the US. “The northern summer of excess heat and wildfires in Europe, North America and Asia are but a sample of what is to come.”

title: Epstein survivors struggle financially as they continue to heal their wounds: ‘It doesn’t just go away’
summary: Legislation proposed by House Democrats aims to address survivors’ financial and medical burdens
text: Danielle Bensky wants a typical life. “I would just love to own a house one day and have a dog,” said Bensky, who is among the Jeffrey Epstein survivors advocating for accountability. “I think that’s the dream – literally just to have a normal existence where we’re not trying to fight the government and constantly be facing our own abuse.” For Bensky and many other survivors of the convicted sex trafficker, the simple dreams enjoyed by so many Americans remain out of reach. In addition to the psychological and physical toll of sexual trauma, some Epstein victims face extreme financial pressures related to their pursuit of justice for the well-connected predator. “Right now, I am uninsured,” Bensky said. Bensky has received coverage for mental health treatment because of a settlement between an investment bank and US Virgin Island authorities that led to the creation of a mental health fund. But there are many other costs associated with healing, she said. Physical therapy for a post-traumatic injury costs approximately $200 per visit, she said. Bensky knows she should go more than twice per month, “but I can’t afford it,” she said. The yoga that helps keep Bensky centered comes to about $250 monthly. “I’ve been doing all this advocacy for the year, and I’ve had to take time off from work,” Bensky said, explaining she has now hit roadblocks in securing work due to her advocacy. “There are certain places that won’t even hire some of us now because they’re saying that we’re ‘too political’.” “I’m paying for everything out of pocket,” Bensky said about healthcare. Congressional Democrats Ayanna Pressley, Teresa Leger Fernández and Deborah Ross this week introduced legislation to address survivors’ financial burdens. This proposed legislation seeks to launch a restitution fund in the judicial branch “for survivors of sexual violence whose rights were violated by the federal government, including all survivors of abuse by Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell”. “Though it often goes overlooked or ignored, the deep financial burden that survivors of sexual violence carry – coupled with mental and physical trauma – can be debilitating. Navigating such harm can lead to time away from work or the need to leave a job entirely, resulting in a loss in income while rent is due, daily needs have to be met, and medical expenses to address physical injury and mental health support pile up,” Pressley said in a statement. “The Survivors’ Rights Restitution Act shines a light on this critical gap in support for survivors and would force our government to bring the meaningful accountability and compensation that survivors are owed.” Many survivors support this initiative, but the likelihood of it passing both chambers of Congress and securing Donald Trump’s signature seems unlikely in the near future given heightened partisanship and geopolitical distractions. As a result, an initiative for steadier financial footing is poised more to be a long-term prospect rather than immediate relief. Jess Michaels said that her financial future was derailed after Epstein assaulted her. She had flourished as a professional dancer but the attack left her unable to pursue work. “I would go into auditions and I would lose my nerve,” Michaels said. “I would be unable to finish an audition. I would be unable to go to auditions because I would be stuck in bed, frozen or crying, and that lasted throughout my 20s.” “The career that I had worked for collapsed … What does that end up costing someone?” Michaels said. She noted that for much of the time, “it meant I didn’t even have insurance”. “Sexual harm is an injury that demands first aid care, just like any other injury, before it is a crime demanding an interrogation,” Michaels said. She said she has for years been dealing with physical ailments related to nervous system harm. “That’s why I am someone that deals with gastrointestinal issues, cardiovascular issues, immune system issues, endocrine issues, endocrine system issues,” she said. “There’s something that happens when you have PTSD for a long period of time. It doesn’t just go away.” If the bill passes, Michaels wants to spend money on her health which, she said, had deteriorated over the past year amid the stresses of advocacy. Even though Michaels has health insurance, “a functional medicine doctor that actually understands what I’m going through is expensive, and it’s often not covered by insurance”. “Right now I can’t afford to get the exact type of doctor that I really need,” she said. “I have to wing it with AI, my [primary care provider], my insurance company, and I’m navigating all of those things, which is exhausting all on its own.” Annie Farmer, an outspoken Epstein survivor who testified against his accomplice Ghislaine Maxwell at the British socialite’s 2021 trial, is now able to receive money for therapy from the Virgin Islands mental health fund. But from 2019 until the near-present, Farmer spent “many thousands” of dollars on therapy. Farmer said that her she has not been working this year because her advocacy “has taken over my life”. “That’s obviously a choice I made. I could have kept working and not really been so involved in all the advocacy, but I think it would have been hard to do both in the way at the level I’ve been involved,” Farmer said. “I couldn’t work full-time, certainly, so there’s a cost to that.” Farmer felt as if she had the flexibility to make that choice because she received funds from the Epstein compensation and mental health funds, but said some others are not in that position. “I’ve been able to do this and still be OK and be comfortable, but I think for people that either haven’t received those funds or received significantly less, it is that much more stressful.” Survivors praised World Without Exploitation, an organization dedicated to ending commercial sexual exploitation, for financial assistance with advocacy. But, they said, the cost of participating in advocacy remains steep even with assistance. “I’ve paid a lot of money to be able to be an advocate this year,” Bensky said. “I paid to get myself to the State of the Union [address]. I paid yesterday to go and speak at Ayana Pressley’s press conference.” “The advocacy component of this is so important, and it feels very crucial to many of us,” Bensky said. “So we will always pay to get ourselves there in the name of trying to make it safer and make change.” Michaels said there are costs associated with advocacy even when her travel expenses are covered in full; outside costs, such as dog sitting, could add up to $175 to $200 per day. “People go, ‘Oh, you chose to do it,’ but who’s going to do it for us?” Michaels said. “Nobody’s going to do it for us, and nobody can really do it for us.” “Some victims received very little, while others received a lot. The amount of money received depended on the severity of the abuse and how the abuse affected the survivor,” Spencer Kuvin, chief legal officer of Goldlaw, who has represented multiple Epstein survivors. “Some survivors received tens of thousands while others received millions.” Michaels disabused any potential skeptics who might think that participation in the fund automatically meant a lifelong windfall. Similar sexual assault cases that didn’t relate to Epstein, Michaels’ attorney said, might result in settlements up to $2.5m. “I got a fraction of a fraction of a fraction of that.” Julie Roginsky, who pursued a sexual harassment claim against the former Fox News CEO Roger Ailes and co-launched the non-profit Lift Our Voices, said that many do not understand the long-term ramifications for survivors – even those who have been lauded for their bravery. “After that applause dies down, you’re lying in bed at night at 2 o’clock in the morning, looking at the ceiling and wondering: what the hell just happened to my life? It’s been completely turned upside down,” Roginsky said. In a high-profile case such as with Epstein, barriers to work are not atypical. “That is incredibly debilitating to know that you did the right thing, you spoke up for yourself and for other women, and it’s following you for the rest of your life – not just because of what happened to you, but also because people now refuse to give you a chance professionally,” she added. When survivors come to Roginsky or her colleagues with questions about coming forward, she always tells them that it’s a personal decision because there are ramifications that can be “brutal”. “I absolutely encourage people to come forward for themselves and to hold their perpetrators accountable and to help others, but at the same time, there is a huge cost to that,” Roginsky said.

title: ‘He was well loved’: families mourn victims of Amazon cargo plane crash in Miami
summary: Questions remain over tragedy that killed five as families file wrongful death lawsuits against Amazon and cargo firm
text: Among Junior and Jachel Pineda’s most treasured photographs of their father, Julio, one of five men killed in the Amazon cargo plane crash in Miami earlier this month, is one of him wearing his favorite red apron. Embroidered on the front are the words Chef Mago – the “wizard chef” in English – and Julio is clutching a ladle and tending to a pot on the stovetop. The kitchen was one of the 75-year-old Cuban immigrant’s happy places, where he would cook for his family, his friends and his neighbors in the Hialeah community where he lived. He would feed and entertain them even after an exhausting shift for the aircraft cleaning company he was employed by. “It’s just who he was, an outstanding man who was well loved in his community, who would help people out with anything they needed, and someone taken from his family suddenly in terrible circumstances,” said Mark Lopez-Trigo, an attorney representing the Pineda family. Lopez-Trigo’s firm has filed a wrongful death lawsuit against Amazon, its contracted operator 21 Air and other entities including the pilots over the deadly crash. “It wasn’t just the food, or the magic tricks he’d perform for the neighborhood kids, or the candies he gave them,” Lopez-Trigo added. “The person he was will be missed. He loved his sons, he loved his grandchildren. There’s a lot of pain for the family right now, they’re still in the grieving process.” Pineda’s funeral was on Sunday of last week, seven days after the Boeing 767 cargo aircraft landed too fast on the runway at Miami international airport on a flight from Puerto Rico, and crashed through a perimeter fence and into the van where Pineda was sitting. Four of his friends and colleagues of the Professional Ocean Services Corp cleaning company died with him, and two remain in hospital in critical condition. Three others, including the two pilots and a man in another vehicle, received minor injuries. While many questions remain over the tragedy, and investigators from National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) say it could be months before their final report is ready, information that has emerged so far has leant weight to the lawsuit, Lopez-Trigo said. Officials have said evidence collected from the scene of the crash, including the aircraft’s black box flight recorder, suggest the pilots tried to abort the landing attempt and initiate a fly-around by increasing throttle speed, but the plane never became airborne again. Filing the lawsuit compels the parties to preserve evidence, Lopez-Trigo said, with the aim of determining how the incident happened, and where any blame lies for the deaths. “Justice really comes in three forms, in our opinion,” he said. “The first is being able to recover the body, recover some of the personal items, to be able to lay to rest somebody dear to their heart. “The second form of justice is getting the answers to all of the questions that they have. Who exactly is responsible? Why did the pilots make the decisions they did and make the mistakes they did? “And the third is to make sure this never happens again to anybody else,” Lopez-Trigo said. All five victims were Cuban immigrants who came to the US to make a better life for themselves and their families. Pineda had been in the country since 2001 and, Lopez-Trigo said, and was still working at 75 because he loved the people and staying active. “He’s not really the person who likes to sit and be inside all day. He’s a working man, it’s a hard, laborious job that requires manual labor and long hours, so yeah, he was definitely a hard worker,” he said. “You know, he was just trying to make a living and keep himself busy, just like the rest of us.” The others killed were Rolando Aleman Leon, 55; Yoel Rodriguez Naranjo, 53; Carlos Acosta Fajardo, 53; and Javierkys Reyes Quevedo, 47. Lawyers for Yaraisi Santiso Morejon, Naranjo’s widow, filed an almost identical wrongful death lawsuit two days before the Pineda family, also arguing that the event was foreseeable, preventable and that multiple failures by Amazon, 21 Air and the pilots led to the disaster. Amazon, meanwhile, has severed its partnership with the cargo company. In a statement, spokesperson Kelly Nantel said: “After the tragic incident last weekend, we’ve spent time supporting the investigation and reviewing some of the surrounding circumstances, and we’ve decided to pause our operations with 21 Air, the operator of Flight 7598. “We’ll continue working to support the investigation and everyone affected.” A statement from 21 Air said, in part: “We are confident in our safety policies, procedures and training.” Lopez-Trigo said neither company has reached out to the family directly, but was not surprised given legal action was under way. He said he has spoken with lawyers for the other families and expects to work with them. “A rising tide lifts all ships, and what that means is there’s a concerted effort from everybody to make sure that the appropriate, correct justice is handed down for all these people that are affected,” he said. Robert Clifford, a veteran airline industry lawyer who is not involved in the Miami cases, said he expected the lawsuits to become consolidated at some future point, and that they would likely benefit from the NTSB’s willingness to immediately share what it knows. “It’s very encouraging that the board is issuing this information earlier, and I can tell you that for years they did not,” he said. “Over the years there was so much criticism of the NTSB’s lack of transparency, and now this board, the chair Jennifer Homendy, is trying to change all that to where she’s giving the families a kind of silent voice and assurance that their interests are being properly protected. “You know if the government ends up doing all the investigation for you, then that’s OK. It sure as hell doesn’t hurt them.”

title: Fears over interest rate rise and jobs send UK consumer confidence to three-year low
summary: Blow to John Healey before budget as UK households face ‘notable strain’ on their finances
text: Fears of a steep rise in mortgage payments and increasing job insecurity have sent UK consumer confidence tumbling to a three-month low, according to a leading survey. In a blow to John Healey before next month’s budget, the S&P Global consumer sentiment index dropped to 42.7 in September from 42.9 in August, indicating “a notable strain on financial confidence across UK households”. The chancellor could announce tax rises in his first budget to offset the rising cost of government borrowing, which has soared in response to the conflict in the Middle East. S&P Global said consumers were concerned about the likelihood of an increase in interest rates by the Bank of England. More than 50% of 1,500 respondents said they expected a rise in the cost of borrowing over the next year. Fixed-rate mortgage costs have already jumped to multi-year highs in the UK, while the threat of artificial intelligence and caution among employers about hiring new staff sent consumer confidence in the jobs market plunging to its lowest level in three-and-a-half years. The average two-year fixed residential mortgage rate rose to 5.88% on Monday, its highest since 16 April and up from 5.84% last Friday, while the average five-year is at its highest since October 2023, at 5.92%, up from 5.88%, data from Moneyfacts showed. The rise in mortgage costs is expected to add about £150 to monthly mortgage payments, based on a typical loan of £250,000 over 25 years, since the start of March 2026. Official figures have shown that the average direct debit to cover monthly mortgage costs has risen over the past four years from about £600 to £900. Maryam Baluch, an economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence, said a downbeat mood was spreading across UK households “as improved sentiment surrounding the new government is eroded by renewed worries over energy prices, the cost of living and job prospects”. She said: “Against a backdrop of rising volatility in energy markets linked to tensions in the Middle East, households increasingly reported difficulties accessing credit, suggesting that expectations of tighter monetary conditions are beginning to feed through to borrowing conditions. Together, these factors point to cautiousness about both financial prospects and pose some downside risks to the broader economic outlook.” Analysts believe the jobs market has proved resilient since the US attack on Iran and a steep rise in the cost of fuel and energy, but a steady decline in the number of payrolled employees over the past six months and a drop in vacancies to a five-year low have shown employers are worried about their profitability over the next year. The British Chamber of Commerce has called for the government to give businesses extra support after a series of tax rises over the past two years, including an increase in employers national insurance payments. A survey by the business organisation of 5,000 companies in the second quarter of 2026 found that only 17% were planning to increase investment in the coming months, a post-pandemic low. Last week, Andy Burnham said he will need to take “difficult decisions” on the economy to ensure that it “remains on track”. In response to the growing clamour for tax cuts to support businesses and households hit by the cost of living crisis, the Liberal Democrat leader, Ed Davey, said at his party conference that the UK should cut fuel duty to offset some of the rise in petrol and diesel prices at the pumps. The German government on Monday announced plans for a cut in tax on fuel of about 15p to take effect on 1 October. Healey could limit his tax rises to wealthier groups, including a rise in capital gains tax. However, analysts say he is unlikely to raise sufficient funds from discreet tax rises to pay for higher defence spending and the rise in debt costs while preserving a reserve buffer, often referred to as headroom, of at least £20bn.

title: ‘I have to keep reliving it’: infected blood claimants being asked to prove eligibility
summary: Claimants having to find decades-old medical records to prove they qualify for compensation despite inquiry’s recommendations
text: Suzanne Morgan will never forget the day her mother died. It was nine months after she had gone into hospital with gallstones, where she received a routine blood transfusion. “She went downhill rapidly,” Morgan recalled. Her mother haemorrhaged in her liver, and the next day she was dead. The family were astonished to be told that she had hepatitis C, and doubly shocked to learn that they couldn’t see her because her body was sealed due to contagion risk, leading them to suspect she was HIV positive. Morgan, who was pregnant at the time, said: “I went into full-blown miscarriage. I was in total shock. I was hysterical.” That was 35 years ago, and the family now know Morgan’s mother died because she was given infected blood. Yet Morgan has found herself forced to “keep reliving” the horror through the infected blood compensation scheme. Like many other victims of the scandal and their families, she has been asked to dig out decades-old medical records to prove she qualifies, despite the public inquiry’s recommendations that eligibility be determined “on the balance of probability”. “I have been everywhere to try and get medical notes of any sort. I cannot get them,” said Morgan. Infected blood campaigners who spoke to the Guardian shared their fury that thousands like Morgan face being locked out of the Infected Blood Compensation Authority (IBCA) payment scheme due to its stringent approach. Rachel Halford, the chief executive of the Hepatitis C Trust, said this was “placing an intolerable burden on people who have already endured decades of injustice”. Victims and bereaved families had been asked to prove “even the most basic of things”, such as whether they lived with their deceased spouses or siblings, she added. Some have had to show old school records, tenancy agreements, utility bills or family photos. “People feel they are being treated as potential fraudsters rather than victims of one of the greatest scandals in our history,” said Halford, adding that there have been complaints of unfairness after different compensation awards for people with similar experiences. Halford said the community hoped that Andy Burnham, who has long campaigned for victims of the infected blood scandal to receive justice, would offer his support. “As prime minister, we need him to live up to that reputation and the promises he has made,” she Halford. Yet Rosie McKearney, a policy specialist at the Hepatitis C Trust, said the community was “shocked” that Burnham had moved responsibility for the scandal from a cabinet-level secretary of state to a junior minister. Research from the Haemophilia Society suggests that two years since the IBCA’s inception just 15% of projected compensation claims have been dealt with. In a letter sent to the IBCA’s chief executive, David Foley, the campaigners said they were “concerned and angry at the lack of progress”, especially its “unreasonable and sometimes impossible bureaucratic demands”. The Haemophilia Society is calling for regulatory change to shift the burden of evidence from applicants to the state, meaning that all applicants with a bleeding disorder would be entitled to compensation unless proved otherwise. Kate Burt, its chief executive, said that the current system was “putting haemophilia treatment centres under intolerable pressure”, with staff “asked to sift through patients’ medical notes to find evidence”, knowing that errors could cost the applicant thousands of pounds. “This is highly technical work, relying on expert knowledge to find fragments of crucial information, yet centres are expected to fund this themselves,” she said, adding that one consultant told her they work unpaid on Saturdays to answer the IBCA’s inquiries. Charlotte Evans, a lawyer at Leigh Day who is representing several victims and their families in their IBCA applications, said “the balance of probabilities” was the standard of proof for medical negligence claims. She said it represented a comparatively lower threshold, which considers a risky procedure that took place at the same time as infected blood was used as indicative that a blood product had been administered. Instead of assessing all the available evidence to build up a picture of what most likely happened, applicants are being asked to prove beyond reasonable doubt that they received a specific blood product. “The scheme is supposed to provide a simpler process,” she said, adding that although the government and the IBCA had an obligation to ensure taxpayers’ money was properly spent, “the question is whether those obligations, and IBCA’s understanding of the same, go beyond what the regulations actually require”. The reasons for this disconnect remained unclear, she said. “It may be that certain individuals [assessing claims] haven’t been given the appropriate guidance or training.” Lynne Kelly, the chair of Haemophilia Wales, observed a “tick box” approach from the claims managers she had met. “The Cabinet Office is completely controlling the Infected Blood Compensation Authority scheme. It’s meant to be an independent, arm’s length body,” she said, adding that she believed the eligibility criteria was intended to “minimise the amount of compensation paid out”. For Zena Whittaker, that extra compensation would both give closure and a comfortable retirement, enabling her to stop worrying about putting the heating on. She is still haunted by the memory of asking a doctor how much longer her son Andrew had to live. He replied: “We don’t know, because it depends whether the hep C takes him first, or the Aids.” As a haemophiliac, Andrew received multiple blood transfusions, making it more likely than not that he also had hepatitis C. Yet medical records were destroyed when his hospital merged with another. “It’s just coming up to the anniversary [of his death], which makes everything raw,” Whittaker said. “It’s 31 years since he died and it brought it all back again.” Luke O’Shea Phillips is also struggling with a bureaucratic nightmare. He was given an infected clotting product as a three-year-old, but because he was not given a liver biopsy due to the risk of bleeding for haemophiliacs, he is unable to prove how bad his liver damage was, resulting in a shortfall in compensation he estimates at up to £1m. “I wasn’t told I had hepatitis C until I was 15. So just as life was beginning to open up, I was suddenly told what had already been done to it,” he said. “My infection is my life, and it’s unrecognised in every way.” A spokesperson for the IBCA said: “Missing or destroyed records will not prevent someone from making a claim. We will determine what is most likely from all available evidence. “Our claim managers work with the person claiming to help them gather information from a range of sources to support their claim. We consider all evidence: medical records, witness testimony, and other family records can all be used to support a claim. “Every compensation claim is unique, with individual circumstances, so they cannot be compared.” A government spokesperson said: “The government has listened and learned through constant engagement with the community to make changes to the compensation scheme to ensure the community receive the compensation they deserve. “The government will continue to be held accountable for its work in the usual ways across both Houses of Parliament.”

title: ‘Incredibly encouraging’: healing the scars of traditional anchors in Dorset’s seagrass meadows
summary: Eco-moorings restore seagrass in just five years, boosting sealife such as seahorses, eels and crabs
text: One of the UK’s most precious underwater habitats – Dorset’s seagrass meadows – is recovering thanks to “eco moorings” designed to prevent the seabed being ripped up, a study has revealed. Scars caused by traditional anchors in some areas of seagrass in Studland Bay have almost entirely vanished, which is boosting the number of seahorses that thrive in the submerged meadows. The Studland Bay Marine Partnership, which includes a wide range of organisations including conservationists and boating enthusiasts, hopes the findings could help protect and restore seagrass in other busy marine environments around the UK. Seagrass meadows are considered one of the world’s most valuable ecosystems because, as well as supporting creatures such as seahorses, they store carbon and help protect coastlines from erosion. They are declining globally due to pressures including pollution, coastal development and the climate emergency. The meadows at Studland Bay are particularly at risk because the spot is so popular with leisure boaters. Research conducted by Kira Dunn, as part of her masters degree at the University of Southampton, analysed data collected since eco-moorings were installed by the partnership in 2021. In the area where 10 trial eco-moorings were installed five years ago, bare patches in the seagrass shrank by an average of 94% between 2021 and 2025. In a second study area, where traditional chain moorings remained until 2023, the scars reduced by 65%. Dunn said: “The results clearly show that seagrass is recovering in areas where physical disturbance has been removed. It’s incredibly encouraging to see how quickly this important habitat can regenerate when given the opportunity.” David Brown, the chair of the Studland Bay Marine Partnership steering group and lead ecologist for the National Trust, said: “The impact has been beyond our expectations, and thanks to robust monitoring and research, we have the science to prove how the eco-moorings benefit seagrass and all the species that rely on it.” Studland Bay was designated a marine conservation zone in 2019 and is home to one of the UK’s largest seagrass meadows, supporting numerous marine species including the protected spiny seahorse and the occasionally recorded short-snouted seahorse. Since eco-moorings were introduced volunteer divers who monitor seahorses have reported increases in numbers. Other creatures spotted in the seagrass include conger eels, spider crabs and corkwing wrasse. Eco-moorings consist of a 2-metre helical screw, which is drilled securely into the seabed. Attached to this is a 2-metre elasticated riser that connects to a surface buoy. As the tide rises and falls, the riser stretches and retracts, preventing any scouring of the seabed and seagrass. Ken Collins, emeritus research fellow and diving officer at the University of Southampton and supervisor of the study, said: “This research provides robust scientific evidence that eco-moorings are an effective tool for seagrass conservation and restoration. “The findings support the continued use and expansion of eco-mooring schemes, not only in Studland but in other sensitive marine environments where seagrass habitats are under pressure.”

title: Starbucks baristas reel from surges in health insurance costs: ‘I’m considering a second job’
summary: Several workers say they’re opting to go without health coverage due to premium costs soaring this year
text: Starbucks workers say their health insurance premiums have soared this year, in some cases more than doubling, according to a recent survey conducted by Starbucks Workers United. The survey of more than 130 Starbucks workers in both unionized and non-unionized stores, shared exclusively with the Guardian, found baristas are experiencing significant hikes in costs for their health insurance coverage starting 1 October. Some workers reported their premium costs per paycheck nearly doubling, even as they struggle to afford other basic necessities andare scheduled to work enough hours to be eligible for the benefits. The changes come as Starbucks Workers United launched a boycott last month against the company demanding a union contract, what would be the first since stores started to unionize in December 2021. Since then, more than 700 Starbucks stores have won union elections, with the union representing over 12,000 workers at the company. Several workers said they are opting to go without health insurance coverage due to the costs and the price hikes are forcing them to worry about whether they need to find an additional job. Kaye-Lani Story, who has been a barista in Edina, Minnesota, for nine years, said she took herself and her son to the doctor this month as their health insurance is set to lapse on 1 October. Her health insurance premiums were set to go from $130 a week to $170 a week, a 30% increase. “That is another $40 each week that I am not going to have in my income, if I choose to go with it, and that’s just not something that financially I can afford,” she said. “I have to drop my insurance because the company will not cover those costs when it’s clear that they’re definitely making enough.” In the past, Kaye-Lani was qualified to receive Minnesota’s state health insurance, but switched to the company’s health insurance plan when she made too much income to qualify. “I make too much to qualify for coverage through the state. I don’t make enough to keep my medical coverage through work, and so at this point, I just have to drop it completely,” she added. “During the winter, the heating bill goes up. During the summer, the electric bill goes up from the AC. There are just all these wavering things throughout the year that I have to pull from to be able to apply to expenses just to be able to keep a roof over my head and food on the table and whatnot, and then this happens, and it’s too much.” Cory Wagner has relied on Starbucks’s health insurance for five of the seven years he’s worked as a barista at Starbucks in Woods Cross, Utah, outside Salt Lake City. “This is the first year that [premiums] nearly doubled,” Wagner said. “My insurance rates are going up to a point where I am now having to consider getting a second job, potentially leaving the company.” Wagner relies on a heart medication to be able to work and noted the health insurance premium cost increases have made the out of pocket cost of his medication unaffordable. His health insurance premium cost went from $70 per biweekly paycheck to $122 per paycheck this year. “Now I’m kind of left at a point where I am choosing between paying for this medication and paying for my utility bills, paying for my groceries, paying for the gas that I need to get to work,” he said. “The company has the money to keep our insurance premiums the same. They have the money to help the partners that are actively making them money.” Starbucks Workers United has filed an unfair labor practice charge after the company did not respond to a request for information on health insurance coverage changes regarding what prompted the fee hikes and how Starbucks’s contribution to the healthcare costs were affected. A Starbucks spokesperson did not comment on the unfair labor practice charge but said in an email “like employers across the country, we continue to face rising healthcare costs while remaining committed to providing quality, affordable healthcare coverage for full and part-time partners at Starbucks, beginning at just 20 hours per week.”

title: Millions of dollars in funding but still no plan: can Quebec save its caribou from extinction?
summary: The Canadian government has committed C$25m to try to rescue the caribou in the province – but there is no agreement on how best to save the keystone species
text: The caribou of Quebec are at breaking point. The province, home to 15% of Canada’s population of woodland caribou, has seen numbers crash to about half of what they were a decade ago. For years, local First Nations people, researchers and environmental groups have criticised the provincial government’s lack of action on protecting caribou, an animal considered a keystone species by Indigenous peoples. A recently announced agreement between the federal and Quebec governments has raised hopes that the province will finally be compelled to release a protection strategy. The federal government has committed C$25m (£13m) to the province for caribou over five years, with an additional C$15m for the First Nations communities on whose land the herds live. But one detail of the announcement has caused concern: the continued reliance on maternity pens. Pregnant caribou have been rounded up and enclosed in pens in the hopes that the secure environment will give them and their calves a better chance of survival. But experts say this cannot be a longterm solution. Quebec has herds throughout the province, the majority of which are woodland caribou. There are 13 woodland herds, with 6,800 to 8,900 animals in total. A caribou’s average lifespan is 10 to 15 years; females have a single calf a year, with fewer than half usually surviving their first year. The woodland herds were listed in Canada’s 2003 Species at Risk Act, but 12 of the herds are at risk of extinction in the next 20 years, says Prof Martin-Hugues St-Laurent, an animal ecologist at the University of Quebec at Rimouski. The new funding agreement focuses on only the three most critically endangered herds: in Val d’Or, Charlevoix and Gaspésie. The six remaining animals of the Val d’Or herd were placed in a protective pen in 2020, and hopes were high that the animals would breed and thrive in safety, ready for rerelease. But by summer 2026, the herd had grown by just one animal. The Charlevoix herd was penned in 2022 and numbers 48 animals; the Gaspésie herd was penned in 2023 and has 20 animals. Currently, the Val d’Or and Charlevoix herds are penned throughout the year, while it is intended that some of the Gaspésie caribou will be released every few years. Seven were released this year to join the small number of wild caribou, the first reintroduction since the animals were penned. “When you do not have any confidence that those animals will be able to survive in the wild because you have not solved the problem in the wild then sometimes you convert this maternity penning experiment into a complete permanent penning experiment,” says St-Laurent. Alain Branchaud, director of the Quebec branch of the Canadian Parks and Wilderness Society (SNAP Québec) says the penning experiment has delivered mixed results so far. “The Charlevoix population is doing OK, but nothing happened for the Val d’Or population and two females died from the Gaspésie initiative, so it’s not working well,” he says. Justina Ray, president and senior scientist of the Wildlife Conservation Society Canada (WCS), says that while there is some evidence that maternity pens do help sustain the population, they do not address the underlying problem of habitat loss. “The introduction back into the wild is less of a success story if you haven’t repaired the things that are driving population decline to begin with,” says Ray, pointing to a lack of specifics and accountability in the recent funding agreement. Quebec’s caribou herds are well studied, but that information has not translated into conservation measures such as habitat restoration, despite a decade of federal and provincial money put towards caribou monitoring and recovery, says St-Laurent. “Some, maybe more cynical people, could say that we are the best at monitoring the decline.” Two of Quebec’s major industries, logging and mining, operate within the caribou’s home ranges. To thrive, woodland caribou need about 65% undisturbed forest, but most of Quebec’s caribou populations live in areas that have less than 40% undisturbed, says Daniel Fortin, a biologist at Quebec City’s Laval University. If caribou are released from pens into an environment that has substantially changed, that habitat is no longer familiar to them and they cannot rely on the historical knowledge that aids survival, says Fortin. Although they will slightly shift their habitat in response, they are still more likely to die. But not moving out of degraded habitat also means they are more likely to die, he says. “Putting individuals in pens is a last resort – something that you can do just before extinction,” says Fortin. “Anything else than habitat restoration is a Band-Aid.” There are more than 300,000 miles (500,000km) of dirt roads crisscrossing Quebec’s forests, mostly to access logging areas, on public land. That distance is the length of a trip to the moon and halfway back to Earth, points out St-Laurent. These roads make it easier for wolves to access caribou herds and also change the forest cover. That in turn attracts more moose, which attract more wolves who hunt them. When these roads appear, cabins, shacks and fishing and hunting camps soon follow, says St-Laurent, making closing these roads an unpopular choice. The Quebec government is investing into “interim” measures such as wolf culls and penning, he says. “But because of the public opposition to those road closures and habitat restoration efforts, they’re not investing as much money as needed there.” The Quebec government still does not have a caribou strategy, says Branchaud, even though the creation of one was announced a decade ago. He says the province’s ministry of the environment, climate change, wildlife and parks did have a proposal for one in 2024 but it was rejected by Quebec’s natural resources and forests ministry. The release of a partial strategy was announced in 2024 but has yet to materialise, he says. The ministry of the environment, climate change, wildlife and parks declined to be interviewed for this article. Pascale Déry, Quebec’s environment minister, has been criticised for previous remarks suggesting she did not believe caribou were endangered. A previous minister intended to send the Val d’Or herd to a zoo. That plan was cancelled after an outcry. The Wendat Indigenous First Nation, on whose territory the Charlevoix herd lives, said in a statement: “The Wendat nation has been committed for many years to the conservation and recovery of the Charlevoix yenchehk [caribou] … The nation’s position remains consistent: the protection of the Charlevoix yenchehk is a critical issue, as is the preservation of other species.” The other Indigenous communities where the herds are found – the MicMac, or Mi’gmaq, of Gespeg ; the Anishnabe of Lake Simon; and the Pekuakamiulnuatsh of Mashteuiatsh – declined or did not respond to requests for comment. WCS’s Ray says Quebec’s approach is partially modelled on a successful initiative in British Columbia province, which also included pens. But that plan, she adds, was more holistic and also involved local First Nations, controlling predators and conserving habitats from the outset. One thing that does help forest preservation in Quebec is the economy, says Fortin. As the US is a major buyer of the province’s forest products, when the economy there slows, so does the logging. “It’s a bit sad,” he says. “In other words, it’s not the laws, it’s really the economy that’s been driving it.” But Quebec is running out of forests to log, says St-Laurent, and the increasing number and severity of wildfires in the province caused by climate breakdown is expediting the decrease of loggable trees. “The [loggers] have to access the last remnant of forest that was in protected areas for caribou. So this is a debate that is far bigger than just caribou,” he says. Find more age of extinction coverage here, and follow the biodiversity reporters Rebecca Ratcliffe, Phoebe Weston and Patrick Greenfield in the Guardian app for more nature coverage.

title: Google fined more than €400m by Irish regulator over its use of location data
summary: Watchdog says users may have been unaware their information was used to target adverts or infer their interests
text: Google has been fined more than €400m (£345m) over the way it processed users’ location data, following claims that the tech giant had manipulated users into agreeing to be constantly tracked on their mobile phones. The fine, imposed by Ireland’s Data Protection Commission (DPC), comes after complaints from multiple European consumer organisations that Google was following every step users took. Location-related adverts are familiar to holidaymakers, but seven European consumer organisations had complained that undue use of location data can also lead to a breach of privacy. The DPC inquiry was prompted by research by the Norwegian consumer agency in 2018 which suggested location data could reveal details such as religious beliefs (by tracking places of worship), political leanings (for example knowing a user has gone to demonstrations), health conditions (if a user has gone to hospital) and sexual orientation (if they have gone to certain bars). The DPC launched its inquiry six years ago and set out to find out whether Google had a valid legal basis for its use of location data. It found that Google users could have been unaware that their location was being used to influence them with adverts or to gather details about their health and interests. “Location data is a type of personal data which is processed by way of location tracking, and includes data collected or processed by Google, which by itself or in conjunction with other information an individual’s location can be inferred,” said Graham Doyle, a deputy commissioner at the DPC. “Location data can bring both benefits and harms to individuals. “It can greatly enhance the utility of online services, but it can also reveal a significant amount of information about an individual, including information that is inherently private,” Doyle added. Responding to the DPC’s ruling, a Google spokeperson said: “This case centres around historical policies that have since been updated. From 2019 onwards, we’ve significantly evolved our practices and launched robust tools that make managing location data simple.” The European Consumer Organisation (BEUC) based its complaint on research by the Forbrukerrådet, the Norwegian consumer agency, which claimed Google used “various tricks” to ensure location history and web and app activity were enabled. “Today marks an important milestone in the effort to protect our rights online. People must be able to understand what they are agreeing to without being deceived or manipulated into making choices they otherwise would never have made,” says Finn Myrstad, director of digital policy at the Norwegian Consumer Council. BEUC said that geolocation data was “one of the most invasive forms of consumer surveillance”. Agustín Reyna, director general of BEUC, welcomed the ruling but said “the time needed to come to this conclusion is disproportionate with the seriousness of the infringement” arguing “late enforcement can be as harmful as no enforcement at all”. The DPC inquiry looked at “web and app activity”, “location history” and “location accuracy” between 25 May 2018 and 4 February 2020. Imposing a fine of €403m, the DPC ordered Google to bring its processing into compliance with the EU’s general data protection regulation (GDPR) within six months. It is the fourth-largest fine imposed by the Irish regulator, which has EU-wide responsibility for all the US tech giants with EU headquarters in Ireland. It has previously fined Meta €1.2bn, TikTok €530m and Instagram (also Meta owned) €405m. Doyle said: “The GDPR provides a high level of protection of personal data throughout the EEA, and requires that the processing of personal data must be carried out in a lawful, fair and transparent manner. “As a result of Google’s failures in this regard, individuals could have been unaware that their location was being used to, for example, influence them with ads or to infer their interests, and could lose control over their personal data. “The retention of users’ location data for longer than necessary aggravated this loss of control,” added Doyle. There are three other ongoing statutory large-scale inquiries open that concern Google, all of which are at an advanced stage.

title: Nvidia boss says there is ‘0% chance’ AI destroys the world by 2030
summary: Jensen Huang dismisses warnings from former Anthropic researcher and others as ‘doomsday narratives’
text: The boss of the chipmaker Nvidia has said AI will not develop to a point that will lead to the extinction of the human race within a few years, rejecting such assertions as overblown “doomsday narratives”. Jensen Huang, the co-founder and chief executive of the $5tn AI chipmaker, said the claims made on social media by the former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon that AI could become “superhuman” and kill off humanity within the decade were “irresponsible”. “2030 is not going to be the end of the world. There is 0% chance that’s going to be the end of the world,” Huang said in an interview with CBS News. “Scaring people is unnecessary. It is irresponsible.” Coxon’s remarks, which were backed by two other researchers at the maker of the AI system Claude, prompted an international debate about the dangers and lack of oversight of AI as companies race to develop ever more powerful models. US lawmakers have criticised AI companies over the risks and Anthropic published a threat intelligence report detailing how criminals, state-sponsored groups, spyware vendors, scientists and propagandists have tried to use its powerful AI models to design missiles and bombs, create deadly pathogens and spy on dissidents. Dario Amodei, the chief executive of Anthropic, Sam Altman, the boss of the ChatGPT maker OpenAI, and Elon Musk have called for development of the technology to be slowed down. However, Donald Trump has dismissed anxiety over the AI development as a “hoax” and a “conspiracy”, adding that a slowdown could give China the edge. On Sunday, Scott Bessent, the US Treasury secretary, said the US and China had agreed to set up an AI dialogue mechanism to alert each other to help contain the technology’s potential dangers. Huang said predictions of an extinction-level event caused by AI were “not grounded in science”. Huang also claimed AI companies’ recent calls for national and international safety regulation aim to duck existing laws that would hold them to account. Citing recent cases where AI companies including Anthropic and OpenAI triggered cybersecurity incidents during testing, he said there were plenty of laws to tackle the problems. “You have cybersecurity unauthorised entry laws, you have damage liabilities … if your product does harm, if your product doesn’t perform as you promised, and if you entered into contracts with companies for service level agreements, there are plenty of laws associated with that. My point is, apply those first. And don’t let this doomsday narrative cause somebody to relieve them of the laws that currently exist.” He continued: “Now, go and read between the lines. They’re actually not asking for more laws. They’re asking to be relieved of the laws we do have. And I think that’s a problem.” On Monday the the Tony Blair Institute (TBI) thinktank published a paper arguing that countries risk “profound and compounding disadvantage” if they fail to embrace AI and fall behind other nations. However, it also warned that the institutions meant to support the choices leaders would have to make were not equipped to do so. “The previous [industrial] revolution transformed our world over generations, AI will do so within a decade,” said Tony Blair in a foreword to the paper. “New capabilities are emerging at an extraordinary pace, with profound implications for economies, education, science, labour markets, public services and national security. But the risks are equally profound and growing, and so too is public concern. “Today’s political leaders… must make hard choices that will signficantly alter their countries’ trajectories. However, the institutions of the modern state meant to support political leaders in making these choices are simply not equipped for what is coming.”
