title: Latest German election humiliation puts Merz on borrowed time as CDU unrest grows
summary: Chancellor acknowledges disastrous state election results but vow to push on is likely to further alienate voters, and his own party
text: Friedrich Merz called it a “disaster”, and that was even before the full scale of the catastrophe for himself and his conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) came into view after Sunday’s state elections. In what one outlet called a “power move”, the German chancellor made a highly unusual televised speech just minutes after polls closed in the states of Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, attempting to get ahead of the narrative with a pledge to stay on and fight for his economic recovery programme. But as the results trickled in, it became apparent that the CDU had not only scored its worst-ever result in a state election, in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, it had crashed out of a regional parliament altogether for the first time in postwar history with just 4.9% of the vote in the region on the Baltic coast. The far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) came out on top for the third time in a German state, drawing 38% against 35.5% for the centre-left Social Democrats, Merz’s federal coalition partner. Although the AfD has little chance of taking power because of a “firewall” of non-cooperation agreed by the other main parties, the anti-immigration, Kremlin-friendly party could celebrate a further success in destabilising the German political establishment. In Berlin, the CDU will almost certainly have to vacate city hall once the coalition negotiations wrap up after a stinging defeat to the leftwing Linke party, which is calling for the expropriation of corporate landlords to address a housing crisis. Polls had been predicting the humiliating result for Merz’s conservatives, which came after a historic rout two weeks ago in the former communist state of Saxony-Anhalt, where the CDU scored just 17% to the AfD’s nearly 44%. But the cumulative effect of these losses, coupled with Merz’s dire approval ratings and a far right with clear momentum, can hardly be exaggerated. Despite his vow to stay the course, many regard the German leader to be on borrowed time. “Friedrich Merz is fighting for his political survival,” said the Berenberg bank’s chief economist, Holger Schmieding. “Although Merz has vowed to stay on as chancellor to spearhead the much needed pro-growth reforms, it will not be easy for him to contain the unrest within his party.” Speculation was already rife after the Saxony-Anhalt race about a Kanzlertausch, or chancellor swap. But as long as none of the potential successors appears ready to wield the dagger, and Merz remains unwilling to step aside, a volatile deadlock will reign. Merz, 70, gathered the CDU leadership at the party headquarters in Berlin to watch the exit polls together late on Sunday. Local media reported that some of those assembled loudly objected to the defiant, full-steam-ahead speech he planned to deliver regarding his programme, saying that it amounted to ignoring what voters were shouting from the rooftops with their choices. Merz cancelled a planned trip to New York this week to speak before the UN general assembly, already anticipating he would need to be in Berlin to grapple with the state elections’ aftermath. Now, more than ever, he will have his work cut out for him after just 16 months in office.

title: Tree vaccines and gene-edited butterflies among biotechnology projects funded by UK ‘invention agency’
summary: Exclusive: The tax-funded brainchild of Dominic Cummings hopes to find ways to speed up wild species’ evolution
text: Vaccines for ash trees, skin treatments for newts and gene-edited swallowtail butterflies are among 14 tax-funded projects from the UK’s “invention agency” aiming to accelerate nature’s ability to adapt to the climate crisis. The £54m accelerated adaptation programme from the UK’s Advanced Research and Invention Agency (Aria) – a public body that funds high-risk, high-reward tech projects – aims to investigate applications of biotechnology that can speed up wild species’ evolution and help them to adapt to new threats such as global warming and disease. The 14 teams announced on Monday will receive a share of an initial £30m in grants over the next two years. They will develop tools to protect native British wildlife species, including the English oak tree and critical pollinators such as the buff-tailed bumblebee, said Yannick Wurm, the director of the accelerated adaptation programme at Aria. The world’s natural environments are changing so rapidly owing to the climate crisis and human pressures that many species can no longer adapt quickly enough, said Wurm, a professor of evolutionary genomics at Queen Mary University, London. “This cohort is a first exploration of how we can harness some of the powers of biotechnology to responsibly help wild animals and plants to overcome challenges they face,” he added. The projects aim to work alongside conventional nature conservation measures, such as protected reserves, to give environmentalists a new set of “precision tools” that Wurm compares to mRNA vaccines for humans. Aria is the brainchild of Dominic Cummings, the former chief adviser to Boris Johnson, who said it would fund “crazy” ideas that could “restore Britain’s place as a scientific superpower”. The publicly funded body has attracted criticism for its research into controversial geoengineering techniques and grants that have given millions in UK taxpayer money to US tech companies and venture capital firms. Matt Clifford, Aria’s chair, was forced to stand down this month over what one senior MP called a “clear conflict of interest” after taking a job with Anthropic, the developer of the AI chatbot Claude. One team announced on Monday, led by researchers at the University of Exeter, will use Crispr-Cas9 gene-editing on the swallowtail, a butterfly on Britain’s red list of endangered species, to increase its resistance to insecticides used widely on farms. Another project developed by Rothamsted Research, the 180-year-old agricultural research facility in Hertfordshire, will edit the genes of long-lived tree species such as oaks to reproduce in months rather than decades, meaning they can rapidly develop adaptive responses to drought and invasive pathogens. Environmentalists across the planet have debated using increasingly powerful biotechnology and gene-editing techniques to aid conservation. At the International Union for Conservation of Nature’s (IUCN) world conservation congress last October, more than 90 NGOs raised concerns that these technologies will irreversibly alter natural systems with unpredictable effects. The ban was narrowly rejected after 250 scientists signed an open letter to highlight the potential benefits of synthetic biology, which could allow small islands to eliminate invasive mice that threaten more than 100 birds and reptiles. Instead, the IUCN adopted its first global policy on synthetic biology, including a set of stringent criteria for proposed solutions. This IUCN policy has been one foundation of Aria’s ethical policy, said Marie-Claire Cordonier Segger, the chair of the programme’s ethical and social responsibility advisory committee. Although the projects are intended for the wild, none of the experimental solutions will be released during the programme, which will last until 2030, said Cordonier Segger, a professor of international law at the University of Cambridge. “The decision was made early to have the strongest possible code,” she said, adding that all grantees will work in secure labs. Chris Thomas, founding director of the Leverhulme Centre for Anthropocene Biodiversity at the University of York, said the projects that Aria is funding offer potentially valuable tools at a time when many species and ecosystems face drought, pathogens and other threats. Skin-eating chytrid fungal infections, which have caused population declines in more than 500 amphibian species, seems a “particularly worthy target” for these new approaches, said Thomas, who is not involved in the Aria programme. Biologists have so far had few options to prevent the spread in the wild, leading the Boston-based research lab Cultivarium to propose their project in partnership with Imperial College and Queen Mary University, London. It would genetically engineer a bacteria that lives on amphibians’ skin to produce proteins that “bind and stop” the infection, said Henry Lee, Cultivarium’s co-founder. “We’re not genetically engineering the amphibian; rather what we’re trying to do is we’re trying to give them a shield,” he said. Another project aims to prevent ash dieback – a fungal disease that is expected to kill half of Britain’s ash trees – by injecting the tree with RNA molecules that interfere with the fungus’s ability to infect. “So it is like giving the tree a vaccination,” said project lead Sarah Christofides, a mycologist at Cardiff University. But Thomas cautions that the impact of these solutions will probably be “modest” and difficult to assess. While 90 amphibian species have gone extinct owing to chytrid infection, others show signs of adaptive resistance, he said. Making certain species within a pond more resistant will inevitably affect the species not targeted, he added. To think that these interventions have an important role to play in preventing biodiversity loss “is probably pretty naive”, he said. To be deployed in the field, solutions will not only have to prove they are effective in the lab but win approval from the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs, which has tightly controlled the releases of genetically modified organisms. A further £24m will be allotted to projects that have shown success over the initial two years. Wurm said he hoped that a handful of successes would be “world-changing”. Ultimately, our “most urgent challenge” is to halt and reverse human-controlled drivers of environmental change, he said, but these projects aim to offer solutions in the places where we cannot.

title: Japanese islands brace for Dujuan to become a typhoon again
summary: Storm system expected to hit Izu Islands as it strengthens. Meanwhile, Atlantic hurricane season is unusually quiet
text: Tropical Storm Dujuan is skirting the coast of Japan and despite avoiding a direct landfall, is still expected to leave its mark. Dujuan briefly reached typhoon status on Friday before weakening to a tropical storm again on Sunday morning. But it is expected to restrengthen back to a typhoon by Tuesday morning. Sustained winds could reach 80mph (129km/h), with gusts approaching 100mph. Although mainland Japan has avoided a direct hit, Dujuan’s track takes it across the Izu Islands, where evacuation warnings are in place. Heavy rain, flooding and landslide alerts are widespread, with high waves adding another threat to exposed coastal areas and islands. Some exceptional rainfall totals are expected, with about 200mm (7.9in) possible along the southern coasts of the Chubu and Kanto regions in just 24 hours – roughly equivalent to the average rainfall for the entire month of September. The Tokyo metropolitan area is among the areas facing the heaviest rain, with some models suggesting nearly 90mm could fall within six hours on Monday evening. Further south, the Izu peninsula could receive more than 80mm in just three hours – 38% of the month’s usual rainfall in a single evening. Dujuan is expected to continue north-eastwards before dissipating in the north-west Pacific later this week. The Atlantic hurricane season remains unusually quiet, despite Tropical Storm Fay developing south-west of the Azores over the weekend. Fay is not expected to strengthen further, extending the record for the latest first hurricane to form in a hurricane season during the satellite era. The previous date record was 11 September, set in 2002 with Hurricane Gustav and equalled in 2013 with Hurricane Humberto. South-west Europe may get one last taste of summer with a blast of heat this week. Temperatures across Spain and Portugal will rise significantly above the monthly norm, to the low to mid 30s celsius. Even in north-west Spain, in Santiago de Compostela highs could reach about 35C (95F) on Tuesday, about 12C above the typical daytime high. Heading into the weekend, warmth will spread into central Europe, but most likely with less intensity than earlier in the week across the Iberian peninsula.

title: Baby girls’ greater interest in faces offers clue to nature v nurture debate
summary: Study finds overall differences between groups of newborns by sex that are likely to be determined by biology
text: The question dates back to the first man and woman: how does the world shape the behaviour of the sexes, and what differences, if any, are present at birth? Untangling the contributions of nature versus nurture has proved challenging for scientists, and controversial at times, but a new study of babies sheds light on at least one aspect of the puzzle. When newborns were played side-by-side videos of a face and a toy, girls spent proportionally more time, on average, watching the face than boys did, suggesting that differences in attention may exist when we are born. Because the babies were only a day or so old it is unlikely the effect was driven by culture or social experience. That leaves biological factors such as genetics and exposure to different levels of testosterone in the womb as the leading suspects. “This is a very active and heated debate in the field of sex differences: what are the causes behind sex differences and how early in life are they present?” said Yumnah Khan, a PhD student at the Autism Research Centre at the University of Cambridge. “What our research shows is that at least some differences are present at a small scale very early on in life.” For the study, babies aged from eight hours to three days old watched a laptop while settled on their parent or carer’s lap. The screen showed side-by-side videos with a young woman’s face on one side and a Newton’s cradle toy on the other. An eye tracker monitored where the babies looked as the video played. Both sexes showed more interest in the video of the woman’s face than the clip of the Newton’s cradle swinging back and forth. But the girls favoured the face over the toy more than the boys did. Details are published in the journal Biology of Sex Differences. The findings, based on tests with 130 babies at the Rosie hospital in Cambridge, reveal average differences between groups of boys and girls; they don’t apply to all girls and all boys. There was still plenty of variation and overlap between each sex, the researchers said. Small differences at birth are unlikely to define how children learn and develop, but they may play a role in some long-observed trends. On average, girls learn to talk earlier than boys, for example, and develop certain social skills at a younger age, too. “If they’re showing heightened social interest from birth onwards, that might facilitate the development of these skills,” said Khan, though this is only a hypothesis. Support for the idea could come from further studies that follow the babies until they are toddlers. Another question the Cambridge team is exploring is whether subtle differences between the sexes at birth have any bearing on people’s vulnerability to neurodevelopmental and psychiatric conditions. For example, autism and ADHD are more commonly diagnosed in males, while anxiety and depression are more common in females. “That’s the root issue that we’re really trying to understand here when we’re asking are there any differences present in males and females early in life and what causes these differences,” Khan said. Previous work has found similar on-average sex differences in brain structure at birth. These are thought to be driven by hormones in the womb, with male foetuses exposed to more than twice the level of testosterone as females in the first and second trimesters.

title: Babies ‘will face almost twice as much’ extreme fire weather in Europe than great-grandparents
summary: Children born after 2025 will experience three more years of brutally fire-conducive weather as global heating intensifies
text: European babies will face almost twice as much extreme fire weather as their great-grandparents if climate action does not ramp up quickly, a study has found. Global heating under current policies will expose a child born in Europe in 2025 to three more years of brutally fire-conducive weather over their lifetime than someone born in 1950, the researchers found. The number of days with the most severe conditions for fires to burn hotter and spread further will rise fastest in the Mediterranean, where generation Beta, the demographic cohort born from 2025, is to face five more years of lifetime exposure to extreme fire weather than boomers, born in the two decades after the second world war. The hot, dry and windy conditions that let small fires explode into raging infernos have been exacerbated by one-and-a-half centuries of fossil fuel pollution and the widespread destruction of nature, which has heated the planet by 1.4C. In Europe, which has warmed twice as fast as the global average, the worsening weather has increasingly fuelled monster infernos that overwhelm authorities. Rosa Pietroiusti, a climate researcher at Vrije Universiteit Brussel and lead author of the study, said severe fire weather was a “necessary but not sufficient condition” for the kind of extreme fires that ravaged parts of Europe this summer. “The meteorological conditions are an important element of fire risk – the possibility of that fire happening, being super-destructive and difficult to control, and spreading very fast.” The researchers combined demographic data with outputs from global climate models and tallied the number of days when fire weather was more severe than the worst 5% of days for that region in the reference period from 1985 to 2014. They considered 21 scenarios that resulted in 1.5C to 3.5C of global heating by the end of the century, a spectrum that roughly covers the best- and worst-case scenarios humanity is likely to face. They found that under current policies, which will result in 2.6C of warming, children born today can expect to experience 84% more exposure to extreme fire weather than those born in 1950. They attributed 86% of the increase to climate change and 14% to people living longer. If end-of-century warming is limited to 1.5C – a target likely to be crossed in just a few years – children born in 2025 would face 1.3 fewer years of extreme fire weather than under current policies, the study found. Raúl Cordero, a climate scientist at the University of Groningen, who was not involved in the research, said it highlighted the “inherently intergenerational injustice” of climate breakdown. “Just one month ago, inhabitants of central Europe experienced fire-weather conditions that their parents or grandparents had never encountered. Unfortunately, these conditions materialised in record-breaking fires in Belgium and western Germany,” said Cordero, whose relatives were among the thousands who fled their homes in Germany in August. “An unstoppable fire engulfing a town? This kind of emergency would have been unthinkable for Germans of older generations.” In southern Europe, the number of fires and the area burned have declined over decades as authorities have grown better at suppressing them, according to a study Cordero co-authored in July, but in recent years the trend has reversed. As well as hotter and drier weather, aggressive fire suppression – preventing even low-intensity fires – has led to buildups of flammable vegetation that has fuelled ferocious blazes in years when climatological conditions are ripe. Relentless heatwaves and widespread drought plagued Europe this summer and led to explosive wildfires across France, Spain, Italy and several other countries. Across the EU, the severity of fire weather this year broke records, while the area burned is shaping up to be the third-worst on record. The EU’s civil protection mechanism was activated nine times as countries scrambled firefighting planes and crews to assist overwhelmed neighbours. In her annual state of the union speech on Wednesday, Ursula von der Leyen, president of the European Commission, paid tribute to a Danish firefighter pilot who died with a colleague in Greece last month, and announced plans for the creation of a European firefighting fleet. “I am so proud of Europe’s response, of our European assets flying across the continent,” said von der Leyen. “But clearly, we need to think bigger and learn faster.”

title: Pixel 11 Pro XL: Google’s big-screen superphone with top-class camera
summary: Fantastic display and two-day battery life plus everything that’s great about Google’s more pocketable Pixel Pros
text: Google’s latest super-sized Pixel takes everything that’s great about the relatively pocket-friendly 11 Pro and adds a huge, high-quality screen and a big battery. That makes the Pixel 11 Pro XL one of the largest smartphones available in Europe and the US, competing directly with Samsung’s giant Galaxy S26 Ultra and Apple’s iPhone 18 Pro Max, with an equally sizeable £1,279 (€1,399/$1,299/A$2,099) price tag – £80 (€100/$100/A$100) more than last year with less memory because of the cost of RAMageddon. The XL sticks with the tried-and-tested formula from the previous few years of super-sized Pixels: a fantastic 6.8in OLED on the front, polished aluminium sides and a glass back with a large camera bar poking through it. The new model is 6g lighter and 0.1mm smaller in every dimension than last year’s Pixel 10 Pro XL, but you would be hard-pressed to notice. The phone has the same Tensor G6 chip, 12 or 16GB of RAM (depending on variant) and at least 256GB of storage as the rest of the Pixel line for 2026. The XL feels super snappy in day-to-day use and the chip can handle mid-level gaming but comes up short in raw performance compared with top chips in rivals. Those looking for the best frame-rate or graphics in games best look elsewhere. The battery life is the longest of the current Pixels, lasting just about two days between charges, including more than six hours actively using the screen across a mix of 5G and wifi for browsing, messaging, apps and photos. That’s a few hours longer than the regular 11 Pro but slightly short of last year’s XL model. Most will only need to charge it every other night and it should outlast even the heaviest of use days. The 11 Pro XL runs the same Android 17 as its smaller sibling, with support until August 2033 and an overall very polished experience. It also comes with a six-month subscription to Google AI Pro subscription with access to the video generator Gemini Omni, higher AI usage limits, 5TB of cloud storage and Google Health Premium. Many of the new cutting-edge local AI tools are best-in-class, including the proactive Gemini information suggestions and the turbocharged Rambler voice dictation tool built into the keyboard. Specifications Screen: 6.8in 120Hz QHD+ OLED (486ppi) Processor: Google Tensor G6 RAM: 12 or 16GB Storage: 256, 512GB or 1TB Operating system: Android 17 Camera: 50MP + 48MP UW + 48MP 5x tele; 42MP selfie Connectivity: 5G, eSIM, wifi 7, UWB, NFC, Bluetooth 6, Thread and GNSS Water resistance: IP68 (1.5m for 30 minutes) Dimensions: 162.7 x 76.5 x 8.5 mm Weight: 226g Camera The XL has the same excellent cameras as the regular 11 Pro, including a very good 42-megapixel selfie camera on the front. The triple rear camera is one of the very best on a smartphone, including a 50MP wide, 48MP ultra wide and 48MP 5x telephoto. New for this year is a significantly faster Night Sight low-light mode, which captures photos about three to four times faster with better detail and sharpness. The new Magic Capture mode shoots video and photos automatically with one press, which works great at parties. The Creator Suite has extensive tools to help produce social videos, too. The telephoto camera can perform an excellent 10x magnification crop zoom, with very good digital zoom stretching up to 30x before being processed by generative AI for up to 120x magnification. The new Camera Looks feature allows you to modify how the Pixel captures and processes your photos for the first time, even if that means making your pictures look technically worse, opening up lots of creative potential. Sustainability The battery is rated to last in excess of 1,000 full charge cycles with at least 80% of its original capacity. The phone is repairable by Google, third-party shops or self-repair, with manuals and parts available. The Pixel 11 Pro XL contains 33% recycled materials by weight. The company breaks down the phone’s environmental impact in its report and will recycle old devices for free. Price The Google Pixel 11 Pro XL costs from £1,279 (€1,399/$1,299/A$2,099) in a choice of four colours. For comparison, the Pixel 11 costs £879, Pixel 11 Pro costs £1,079, Pixel 11 Pro Fold costs from £1,799, the Pixel 10a costs £499, the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra costs £1,279 and the iPhone 18 Pro Max costs £1,299. Verdict Google’s super-phone takes everything that’s good about its pocket-friendly Pixel 11 Pro and adds a huge, fantastic screen and a bigger battery. It is wide and quite heavy, making it a two-hand phone most of the time, but its large display offers a similar screen area when watching widescreen video as Google’s Pixel 11 Pro Fold. The camera system is one of the very best, and can be customised extensively for great creative licence. The phone feels responsive, lasts up to two days between charges and is packed with cutting-edge AI, much of which is actually useful. The Pixel 11 Pro XL is a great, massive phone. But it isn’t a dramatic upgrade on those that came before it and falls short in performance and power-user features compared with Samsung’s Galaxy S26 Ultra. Pros: excellent and huge screen, two-day battery life, great camera with 5x and 10x optical magnification and extensive customisation, seven years of software updates, impressive local and proactive AI, Qi2.2 wireless charging and magnetic accessory support, fast fingerprint and face recognition, six months of Google AI Pro included. Cons: very expensive, less memory than before, huge and heavy, face unlock option not as secure as Face ID, raw performance and battery life short of best-in-class, no physical sim card slot in the US, not a massive upgrade.

title: Monday briefing: Inside Trump’s deportation machine – ‘Your fate is out of your control’
summary: In today’s newsletter: The US administration has built a system of removing migrants to countries they have no connection with, often with little warning
text: Good morning. If you want to grasp the true cost of what it means to “secure our borders,” skip the panicked headlines about “mega-dinghies” arriving on British shores and the pictures of Patriot Platform’s black-clad enthusiasts, and look across the Atlantic. Since 2025, the Trump administration has deported about 5,000 people on flights to “third countries” where they have no family ties or history, sometimes as far as Ghana and Sierra Leone. A Guardian investigation published today exposes the staggering cruelty of this sinister policy. It seems deliberately designed to stoke fear, and shows how far-right ideas that once belonged on the fringes of politics have become so mainstream that they’re now barely opposed. These deportations often happen very quickly, with people given little notice of what is going to happen to them. That creates huge challenges for lawyers trying to defend people who are shackled on flights, and for journalists trying to tell their stories. For this morning’s newsletter, I spoke to the Guardian’s investigations correspondent Louisa Loveluck about the lives of the people caught up in this policy, and how the Trump administration has created a deportation machine. That’s after the headlines. Weekend roundup Russia | European intelligence officials have raised the possibility of an imminent Russian test of Nato, with one saying a potential attack could come in a matter of “months, not years”. Domestic violence | About 20,000 disclosures of domestic abuse are estimated to be made to maternity services in England every year, analysis has found. Ed Sheeran | Ed Sheeran has opened a solo concert in Philadelphia with comments about Gaza, saying what is happening is “catastrophic and unjustifiable”, in his first show since his tour was plunged into turmoil. Spycops scandal | Victims of intrusive police surveillance have accused the government of seeking to cut short the spycops public inquiry that has been examining widespread misconduct committed by undercover officers. Royal family | Earl Spencer has said the relationship between the press and the Duke and Duchess of Sussex “echoes” the way the media treated his sister Diana, Princess of Wales. In an interview with the BBC aired on Sunday evening, Spencer described media coverage of Harry and Meghan as having a “cancerous influence”. In depth: The people caught in Trump’s deportation machine The second Trump administration has struck 35 deals with nations such as Eswatini and Central African Republic, allowing it to deport migrants and asylum seekers to nations where they have no connections. Federal officers can deport immigrants with as little as six hours notice, even if they have no assurances that people will be safe from persecution or torture (a US court judgment recently challenged the short timeframe, and the government is expected to appeal it). In many cases, these countries then deport people onwards to the places they fled – something that is technically illegal under US law. Since 2025, more than 5,000 people have been put on planes to countries other than their own, including those in Latin America, Africa, central Asia and the Caribbean. Louisa has been investigating these deportations with journalists from 22 other newsrooms in conjunction with Forbidden Stories, a Paris-based network of investigative journalists. One of the people they interviewed was Rabbiatu Kuyateh, a 58-year-old nurse who had been living in the US for 30 years. During the pandemic, Kuyateh said she had spent much of the pandemic working in a US hospital caring for patients in a Covid isolation ward. Since then, she has worked as a carer for the disabled son of an American family. She was detained during a routine check-in with ICE in July 2025, spent four months in ICE custody, and was then flown to Ghana. Days later, a group of officials dragged her by her hair into a van, which transported her to Sierra Leone, the country she had originally fled with her parents. “The disabled man who Kuyateh was paid to care for was waiting for her on the day she was picked up by ICE,” Louisa says. “And when she could finally speak to her family after she was detained, one of the things she said was: please tell them I’m not coming to work tomorrow.” *** Who is behind this? The policy has been driven by Stephen Miller, the White House deputy chief of staff, who is often described as Trump’s “shadow president”. During Trump’s first term, Miller was behind the administration’s most extreme positions, such as the Muslim travel ban. In November 2024, before returning to the White House, he said on a conservative radio show that the coming crackdown on immigrants would be so prolific, “you’ll set your alarm clock two hours earlier every morning just to get two more hours of daylight to watch the deportation flights happen.” Since then, he’s been in overdrive. Miller has demanded that ICE agents arrest 3,000 people per day on America’s streets, and has strategised with officials from the Department of Homeland Security about how the government can reach its goal of deporting one million people in a year. He hosts daily calls with a small circle of conservative diplomats to press them on third country deportation agreements, and has been trying to accelerate the removal of undocumented immigrant children from the US. His influence is part of a broader strategy to subordinate the federal government’s other priorities to the singular aim of deporting migrants. The Trump administration has disbanded USAID, and repurposed funding previously dedicated to humanitarian assistance towards deportations. It has purged immigration judges deemed insufficiently loyal to this agenda, and has gutted the oversight system that investigates civil rights abuses in immigration detention. “All of these institutions that on some level could have protected refugees, asylum seekers and migrants are being turned inside out to do the opposite,” Louisa says. *** Why the Trump administration doesn’t want you to know the details Trump has made no secret of his gigantic deportation programme (it will be a “bloody story,” he said in 2024). His government has transformed immigration raids into reality entertainment, staged photo ops at migrant detention jails with names such as Deportation Depot and Alligator Alcatraz, and in 2025 arrested two firefighters while they were putting out an active wildfire in Washington State, later deporting one of them to Mexico. But it has been comparatively guarded about its third-party deportation deals. Details of the deals remain opaque, and the government doesn’t publicise most of the deportation flights. Secrecy makes it harder for lawyers to oppose deportations, since they often don’t know when flights are scheduled – or who is on them. It also contributes to a climate of fear and uncertainty for immigrants. “The message is: you are out of control of your own fate,” Louisa tells me. The countries that have struck these deals with the US may not want them to be public knowledge, and by keeping them out of the public eye, the Trump administration can also limit scrutiny of how much they cost. So far, it has pledged at least $410m (£307m) to secure these agreements. The cost of deporting a single person can run as high as $1m. “The administration seems willing to pay whatever it takes to get this done,” Louisa says. (When approached for comment, a state department spokesperson said the administration would use “all legal means” to remove those “with no right to remain in our country”.) *** From far-right conspiracy to government policy The policy is being run from the newly created Office of Remigration, which has borrowed a term used by the far-right to describe the forcible expulsion of immigrants, turning an idea once associated with the political fringes into official government policy. The idea that people who have been living in a country legally for years could be deported in the space of a few hours might sound like dystopian fiction. But as my colleague Jonathan Liew wrote in an opinion piece last year, the remigration discourse has already gone mainstream. In 2022, the UK’s then Conservative government attempted its own version of the third country deportation policy by pushing through plans to send migrants to Rwanda (the first flight was cancelled after a flurry of legal challenges). Reform has now proposed that, if it were to form a government, people who have already secured indefinite leave to remain could be suddenly deported if they don’t meet a new set of rules. And, as we reported yesterday, Nigel Farage has said he would like to “hijack” Trump’s key ICE adviser to secure the UK’s borders. “This is not just an American policy,” Louisa tells me. “This is the language of our political debate right now. And if America is doing this so flagrantly, it makes it easier for others to do the same.” We want to hear from you What do you want to know about the US midterms, and how the Guardian plans to report them? Libby will be putting your questions to our Washington bureau in the coming weeks, so send them in by hitting reply or emailing first.edition@theguardian.com. The week to come Monday | G7’s foreign ministers are set to meet in New York. Wednesday | The disgraced film tycoon Harvey Weinstein is set to face his fourth and possibly final sentencing in New York for sexually assaulting a former assistant. Thursday | US president Donald Trump is set to host Xi Jinping, China’s president, at the White House. What else we’ve been enjoying I loved this interview with Ms Rachel, the toddler whisperer extraordinaire, about being a campaigner on humanitarian issues, politics, and her new album “I’m So Happy”. Sundus Abdi, newsletters team I appreciated this analysis by David Smith on Trump’s battle to rename the Kennedy Centre after himself. On the US president’s motivations, lawyer Norm Eisen said: “You would need an authority in abnormal psychology to get the answer to that question.” Micha Frazer-Carroll, newsletters team What comforted Nazanin Zaghari-Ratcliffe while she was imprisoned in an Iranian jail? Pizza dough, Zumba and sewing, she tells reporter Helena Horton. Sundus Sport Football | Matheus Cunha’s late equaliser gave Manchester United a 1-1 draw at Fulham, who had led through Lisandro Martínez’s farcical own goal. Cycling | Belgium’s Remco Evenepoel won the men’s time trial title for the fourth time in a row, while the Swiss rider Marlen Reusser defended her women’s crown. Darts | Luke Littler has threatened to boycott tournaments in the Netherlands after being booed and whistled at during the World Series of Darts Finals in Amsterdam. The front pages “European spy chiefs brace for Russia to test Nato pact”, is the Guardian’s front page today. The Telegraph has “Labour eyes £14bn tax raid to help the poorest”, the Times says “Half Labour MPs at risk of Pip cuts backlash”, and the Express writes “Stop your tax raid on nation’s high streets”. The Mail runs with “Kemi: I’ll ditch tourist tax to boost Britain” and the i Paper has “We women are all at risk from men, warns minister amid Piddington asylum camp row”. The FT says “BigTech banks of guarantees to keep $300bn AI exposure off balance sheet”. The Mirror’s splash is “Ed: I feel so alone” and Metro writes “I back Team Harry AND Wills” Today in Focus Being trans in Britain in 2026 Transgender people in Britain are navigating a new reality. In August, new guidance – in the form of a document nearly 350 pages long – was published to help institutions interpret last year’s supreme court ruling on trans rights. It means, as Amelia outlines to Helen Pidd, that every time she goes to a pub or restaurant, she is terrified about going to the bathroom. Helen heads to parliament to hear from those protesting over the new guidance, and from senior political correspondent Peter Walker on whether there is any appetite in government to change the law. Cartoon of the day | Tom Gauld The Upside A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad For decades, hopeful entrants to the Royal Horticultural Society’s Britain in Bloom competition have nurtured vibrant flowerbeds and beautiful hanging baskets across the UK’s towns. This year, the charity has launched a new award that has zhooshed up many of our train platforms. Five of the best were shortlisted for the RHS Railway Stations in Bloom competition – featuring boat-planters, pollination-friendly wildflowers and gravel gardens. The winner, the Cardross Community Organic Garden in Scotland, involved a wide range of local communities in gardening activities, from Brownies to volunteering groups. Jane Connolly, who heads the station’s gardening group, said: “Every time we are down there, somebody will come along and peruse it and say how grateful they are with what we have done … People come to our station just to see our gardens.” Sign up here for a weekly roundup of The Upside, sent to you every Sunday Bored at work? And finally, the Guardian’s puzzles are here to keep you entertained throughout the day. Until tomorrow. Quick crossword Cryptic crossword Wordiply

title: Freedom oppressed: the journalists caught up in Trump’s ICE crackdown
summary: Media workers are grappling with increasingly volatile press climate in US, with some detained and even deported
text: As hundreds of masked and armed US federal agents besieged the streets of Minneapolis, turning the midwestern city into the frontline of the Trump administration’s unprecedented crackdown on immigration, the independent photographer John Abernathy was documenting one of the protests that had become a daily occurrence when Immigration and Customs Enforcement tackled him. A photograph of him on the ground, pepper spray running down his face, captured the violence with which ICE agents had for weeks treated immigrants and the thousands of US citizens who had come to their defence. It was also a stark reminder that journalists were not immune to the agency’s aggressive tactics. The US Press Freedom Tracker documented an increasingly volatile climate for journalists across the country in 2025, reporting 32 arrests and 170 assaults, most of them during protests. And things are no better this year. Journalists who are themselves immigrants have at times also become targets of the hardline policy. Estefany Rodríguez, a Colombian reporter covering immigration for a Spanish-language outlet in Nashville, Tennessee, was arrested in March and held in ICE detention centres in Louisiana and Alabama for two weeks, before a judge ordered her release. Rodríguez had reported on immigration arrests at a local courthouse a day before agents surrounded her car, which was marked with her outlet’s logo, and arrested her. It was journalists such as Abernathy and Rodríguez who inspired a multi-outlet investigation, involving staff from two dozen newsrooms in 16 countries and coordinated by Forbidden Stories. The project details the secretive deals the Trump administration has struck with third countries, mostly in Africa and Latin America, to take in deportees the US is unable to send to their countries of origin. In Georgia, ICE agents arrested Mario Guevara, an Emmy award-winning journalist from El Salvador. He had lived in Atlanta for nearly two decades, running an independent Spanish-language outlet and documenting immigration enforcement operations on TikTok. Guevara was covering a “No Kings” protest in June 2025 at the time of his arrest. He spent more than 100 days in detention, mostly in isolation. “They didn’t want me to hear the stories of other fellow prisoners and that’s why they locked me up alone,” he told Forbidden Stories. Guevara was deported to El Salvador last October, while his wife and children remain in the US. He has continued to report on US immigration enforcement from there and remains convinced he was targeted because of his journalism. “ICE had a personal campaign against me,” he said, noting that agents repeatedly asked him why he insisted on documenting their activities when he was not a US citizen. “ICE arrested and deported me because of my journalistic work, I’m sure.” A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security rejected Guevara’s claims, saying allegations he was “arrested by ICE or isolated while in detention because he is a journalist are completely FALSE”. The spokesperson said Guevara was arrested by local authorities for obstruction of law enforcement and deported because an immigration judge had issued a final order of removal more than a decade earlier. “If you come to our country and break our laws, we will arrest you and you will NEVER return,” the spokesperson said. Journalists reporting on the impact of the Trump administration’s third-country removal policy have also faced the hostility of some of those countries’ authorities, particularly in countries where press freedom is already severely restricted. In Cameroon’s capital, Yaoundé, last February, four journalists, including three who were on assignment for the Associated Press, were briefly detained while reporting at a state-run compound where African migrants recently deported from the US were being held. The journalists were accused of criminal trespassing and had their equipment and phones confiscated for a week. During questioning, authorities warned them they would be “crushed” and “disappear[ed] without a trace”, one of the group told the Committee to Protect Journalists. Nalova Akua, one of the journalists detained in Cameroon, told Forbidden Stories he believed they had been targeted because they were exposing the impact of a collaboration with the US government that Cameroonian officials would prefer to keep out of public view. Abernathy tossed his camera to another photographer as agents tackled him to the ground in the hope of saving the photographs he had taken, he previously told the Guardian. “It deserves to be seen, what’s going on around here,” he said.

title: What is Trump’s third-country deportation policy and whom does it target?
summary: Key questions answered about scheme that has sent more than 25,000 people to countries that are not their own
text: Since returning to office in 2025, Donald Trump’s administration has deported more than 25,000 migrants, refugees and asylum seekers to countries that are not their own. Human rights lawyers describe these so-called third-country national arrangements as a “show of force”, intended to make people fear the consequences of entering the US without permission. To compile the most comprehensive account of a policy that has mostly operated behind closed doors, the Guardian joined 23 other media organisations in the Deportation Project, a joint investigation coordinated by Paris-based Forbidden Stories. The consortium interviewed more than 100 people affected by, or involved in, the US drive to extinguish unauthorised immigration, and reviewed documents outlining details of the agreements made by US officials with governments around the world. What are third-country deportations? The Trump administration has struck 35 deals allowing it to deport migrants and asylum seekers to countries that are not their own and where they often have no connections. Human rights lawyers say the administration is using a loophole: under US law it is illegal to send people back to countries where they are likely to be persecuted, and so the Department of Homeland Security is deporting migrants and asylum seekers to third countries instead. In many cases, however, the receiving countries then deport them onwards to the very place they fled. Is this a new policy introduced by the Trump administration? While the Trump administration trialled the policy during its first term, most of the deals with foreign countries have been struck since 2025. The US has pledged at least $410m (£307m) to secure such agreements with 35 countries, almost a third of them in Africa, according to internal records reviewed by the Washington Post as part of the Deportation Project. The drive is being led by the White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller, a fervent opponent of most migration to the US. It is being run out of the newly created Office of Remigration, a new section within the Department of State’s Bureau of Population, Refugees and Migration. The name of the office incorporates a term adopted by the far right to describe the forcible expulsion of minority ethnic immigrants. Who is being deported? About 20,000 people have been bussed to Mexico, while at least 5,000 more have been put on planes to countries in Latin America, Africa, central Asia and the Caribbean. The Trump administration says its deportation drive is focusing on removing criminals from the US. People interviewed by the Guardian for this project include a nurse, originally from Sierra Leone, who was her parents’ main carer in the US; an anti-government protester who fled the Iranian regime; and a gay man who fled Ghana after he was outed, and then hunted, by members of his family. The state department claims that its priority is to deport people with criminal histories, but people interviewed by the Guardian said they had none. Immigration judges had also ruled the people should be allowed to stay in the US because of credible fears they may face harm if sent home. And state department documents indicate that a majority of the 35 countries to have signed deals with the US have specified that they will not accept migrants with violent criminal records. Why would third countries agree to participate? While the fine print of most deals remains opaque, the Trump administration is paying millions of dollars to the 35 countries that have agreed to accept foreign migrants, either temporarily or long term. The state department is also using its foreign aid budget to sweeten the deals, allocating funds to UN agencies that support migrants in some of the third countries. The internal state department records, reviewed by the Washington Post, indicate $30m was earmarked for Cameroon, in order to support UN operations in the country, in return for accepting 1,000 migrants. The US has so far sent only 44. The Democratic Republic of the Congo was promised $50m towards UN operations there in return for accepting 2,000 migrants. It has only received 15, and flights to Kinshasa are on hold because of the country’s Ebola outbreak. A spokesperson for the UN agency that receives these funds, the UNHCR, said it supported “states in fulfilling their primary responsibility to protect refugees and asylum seekers on their territory by helping ensure that, irrespective of the circumstances of their arrival, they have access to asylum procedures and are not returned to places where they face a risk of harm”. Are third-country deportations legal? A US federal appeals court ruled on Friday that the Trump administration’s third-country removals policy was unlawful. A three-judge panel unanimously agreed that the policy violated due process by failing to give people enough notice of the decision to deport them, or the chance to legally contest it. Human rights lawyers said that meant third-country deportation flights should be grounded immediately. But the government has 90 days to appeal against the court’s decision, and is expected to do so. “The third country deportation policy continues,” James Percival, the Department of Homeland Security’s general counsel, said in a statement. The ruling relates to a March 2025 lawsuit arguing that the US was sending people to places where they could be hurt or killed. While a US district judge issued a preliminary injunction in April 2025, resulting in a pause on deportation flights, the supreme court decided two months later that the policy could resume while the legal case played out, and the administration then ramped up the flights.

title: How Saudi oil scientists ended up working on the world’s most important climate reports
summary: Guardian investigation reveals fossil fuel links of IPCC authors, with experts declaring the body’s conflict of interest policy ‘not fit for purpose’
text: On her first day as an expert author on the world’s most important climate reports, Prof Julia Steinberger knew nobody else, so she sat down at a stranger’s table for breakfast. “Hi, I’m Julia. I’m from the University of Lausanne,” she said. The man across the table replied: “I’m Mustafa Babiker. I work with Saudi Aramco.” Aramco, Saudi Arabia’s state oil company, is responsible for more of the carbon emissions driving the escalating climate crisis than any other company in history, and the kingdom has long been a major blocker of climate action. Wasn’t that a conflict of interest, Steinberger asked. The UN’s Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), on which they both now sat, produces the reports that underpin UN climate negotiations and inform national climate policy around the world. No, Steinberger recalls Babiker saying: he had declared the relationship on the IPCC’s conflict of interest form. “That didn’t seem to me a very good answer, but he was friendly and we had a very nice breakfast.” Dr Babiker has worked for Aramco for 20 years. His appointment as a coordinating lead author for the IPCC’s coming Seventh Assessment Report sparked controversy in the climate science community last year. But a Guardian investigation, carried out in partnership with a team of international journalists, has now revealed that Babiker is far from an isolated case. At least a dozen IPCC lead authors are employed by or linked to Saudi Aramco, Saudi institutions and other oil and gas interests, the investigation found. One IPCC vice-chair, part of the body’s leadership group, also represents the kingdom at global climate negotiations as a government employee. The IPCC is the world’s most authoritative organisation on climate science, with its reports approved by 195 countries. They are produced by hundreds of lead authors from around the world with expertise ranging from atmospheric physics to the impacts of extreme weather. The Guardian examined the 223 lead authors in working group III, the part of the IPCC that assesses how emissions can be reduced or removed from the atmosphere. Its work evaluates emissions-cutting policies and technologies and so is directly relevant to the economic interests of countries and companies. Working groups I and II cover the science of climate change and its impacts. The investigation identified 20 cases with strong conflict of interest concerns. More than half involved authors linked to Saudi institutions, a concentration that raises broader questions about the kingdom’s influence on how the reports are produced. The IPCC’s conflict of interest policy has been described as “not fit for purpose” by experts who have reviewed the Guardian’s investigation. ‘It’s the first time we have so many Saudi-linked authors’ Another Aramco employee selected as an IPCC lead author is Dr Diego Armando Moya Pinta, who has worked as an energy and sustainability scientist at the company since 2022. The IPCC lists his affiliation only as Imperial College London, where he is an honorary senior research fellow. As one of 14 lead authors for the chapter on energy systems, Moya Pinta will assess options for reducing emissions across the energy sector, an area with direct implications for Aramco’s business. “I don’t think there would be any question that a case like this would fit under the IPCC’s conflict of interest policy,” said Prof Kevin Elliott, an academic at Michigan State University specialising in research ethics. Yet in March 2026, the IPCC’s conflict of interest committee reported finding no conflicts of interest among any of the authors selected for the Seventh Assessment Report, the next edition of its biggest and most influential publication. The disconnect between the committee’s conclusion and the presence of authors from the world’s largest petroleum company “raises questions about whether the IPCC conflict of interest policy is fit for purpose or being properly applied”, said Rachel Kennerley, a senior campaigner at the Center for International Environmental Law. Alongside the two Aramco employees, working group III includes five authors from the King Abdullah Petroleum Studies and Research Center (KAPSARC), a Saudi government-funded thinktank chaired by the country’s energy minister and whose stated mission is to “advance Saudi Arabia’s energy sector”. Little-known outside energy policy circles, KAPSARC has the same number of authors in working group III as Imperial College London and Vienna’s International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis, making the three institutions the most represented in the group. Another energy systems lead author, Prof Zain Yamani, at King Fahd University of Petroleum and Minerals, was conducting joint research with Aramco’s New Energies Research Division during the past year while also serving in his IPCC role. The resulting paper, co-authored with two Aramco scientists, was published in July. A further IPCC lead author, Dr Syed Masiur Rahman, works at the same university, which advertises its proximity to Saudi Aramco as offering “countless opportunities for collaboration and innovation” between the organisations. A lead author on the chapter on carbon dioxide removal technologies, Prof Hussein Hoteit at the King Abdullah University of Science and Technology, was finalising research based on a demonstration project for underground carbon storage at the time of his appointment to the IPCC. Saudi Aramco conceived the project and provided substantial financial support. “It’s the first time we have so many Saudi-linked authors in the IPCC, above all in working group III,” says Dr Kari De Pryck, a political scientist at the University of Geneva, who is an expert in the organisation’s governance. De Pryck sees the growing presence of Saudi-linked authors in the context of a broader shift in the kingdom’s climate diplomacy. Its longstanding opposition to cutting fossil fuel burning in UN climate negotiations is increasingly complemented by the promotion of technological climate solutions. “When it comes to the IPCC, the Saudi strategy now focuses on advocating technologies like carbon capture that would limit the impact on its fossil fuel economy,” says De Pryck. There is also an overlap between the kingdom’s government and the IPCC’s scientific leadership. Dr Malak Al-Nory, one of working group III’s seven vice-chairs, is a senior adviser to the Saudi energy ministry. Vice-chairs help oversee the assessment process and guide its scientific and technical work. They also evaluate authors’ conflict of interest disclosures and can refer cases to the IPCC’s conflict of interest committee. The IPCC does not preclude government-employed scientists working on its reports. Unusually however, Al-Nory has continued to represent Saudi Arabia in UN climate negotiations while serving as a vice-chair. She was part of the kingdom’s delegation to the Bonn Climate Change Conference in June 2026, underscoring concerns about the compatibility of her dual roles. “Conflict of interest rules aren’t an accusation that someone has done something wrong,” said Tzeporah Berman, founder and chair of the Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative. “They exist to protect an institution’s integrity by ensuring professional, financial or governmental interests that could reasonably be perceived to influence its work are disclosed and appropriately managed.” “If the IPCC’s conflict of interest system can look at an IPCC vice-chair working for the Saudi energy ministry, Aramco employees serving as lead authors, and this concentration of authors from Saudi state-linked institutions and find nothing that needs to be managed, then the policy is clearly not fit for purpose,” she said. A ‘gap’ between policy and reality Until 2011, the IPCC had no institution-wide conflict of interest policy. That changed after a bruising credibility crisis in 2010, when mistakes in its major reports and allegations of financial conflicts involving its then-chair prompted an independent review of the organisation’s procedures. The resulting policy states that its purpose is “to protect the legitimacy, integrity, trust, and credibility of the IPCC”. It adds: “It is essential that the work of the IPCC is not compromised by any conflict of interest for those who execute it.” Kennerley said there was a gap between the IPCC’s written criteria and how it operated in practice. She said national representatives had raised questions over a lack of guidelines on how the policy was enforced, adding that another major problem was transparency. Authors’ conflict of interest declarations are not made public, and the conflict of interest committee provides no detail about its deliberations. A spokesperson for the IPCC said no authors had been referred to its conflict of interest committee as all potential conflicts of interest reported could be resolved by the working group vice-chairs. “The strength of the IPCC lies in its commitment to diverse leadership and author teams, multiple expert and government review processes, and the inclusive nature of its assessments,” the spokesperson said. “These safeguards collectively support the objectivity, integrity, authority and credibility of IPCC reports.” They said details of the review of conflict of interest declarations were confidential due to data protection legislation. “The public can judge whether relevant interests have been adequately assessed and managed [by the] assessment reports themselves, which go through robust, multistage reviews which are [publicly] documented.” Regarding the high number of experts linked to Saudi Arabia, the spokesperson said: “No individual author, institution, sector or country determines the conclusions of an IPCC report. Conclusions are developed collectively by large, internationally and scientifically diverse author teams.” They said IPCC authors were leading experts in their fields and deliberately drawn from a wide range of backgrounds, including government and the private sector. Hoteit, at King Abdullah University of Science and Technology, said: “There is no conflict of interest. My research and contributions related to the IPCC work were fully funded and supported by my employer, which is acknowledged in the referenced paper.” The multi-author paper also states: “We thank Saudi Aramco for conceiving and conducting this pilot project and for providing substantial financial support.” Aramco declined to comment, and none of the other individuals or institutions responded to requests for comment. Eleven of the 20 cases of strong potential conflicts of interest identified by the Guardian investigation were Saudi-linked, with the rest spread across other nations and linked to issues including industry collaboration, fossil-fuel sponsorship of academic institutions’ research, environmental campaigning and sustainable finance. Dr Jeroen Oomen, a climate governance researcher at Utrecht University, said: “The IPCC’s mandate as the arbiter of climate science has always been based on its independence and neutrality. The conflicts [reported in this investigation] risk damaging such a reputation.” Dr Adam Standring, a researcher at the Lisbon School of Economics and Management, said the IPCC was created to bridge science and politics, and it “straddles those two worlds”. That hybrid role was fundamental to its success, he said, but also a source of problems. Berman said: “At a time when fossil fuel interests and some governments are fighting to delay the transition away from fossil fuels, the IPCC should be fiercely protecting its independence. That means strong disclosure requirements, meaningful conflict of interest rules and safeguards capable of addressing both actual conflicts and reasonable perceptions of conflict.” The IPCC said there was no process currently under way to amend its conflict of interest policy. This investigation was developed with the support of Journalismfund Europe and is also being published in L’Humanité in France, Lucy sui mondi in Italy, Visão in Portugal and Nano (3Sat) in Germany, Austria and Switzerland. • This article was amended on 22 September 2026. An earlier version described Tzeporah Berman as “the chair of the Fossil Fuel Non-Proliferation Treaty”. Berman is also the founder of the organisation, which changed its name last year to the Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative.

title: Starwatch: Autumnal equinox in northern hemisphere, spring in the south
summary: Precise moment of equinox in UK is 1.05am on Wednesday – but day and night will not be equal until Friday
text: The September or autumnal equinox takes place this week. It marks the astronomical beginning of autumn in the northern hemisphere and spring in the southern hemisphere. This year, the precise moment of the equinox falls at 01.05 BST on 23 September. It is commonly said the equinox is when day and night are equal, because the name derives from the Latin for “equal night”, but in practice that is not quite true. An equinox occurs when the sun crosses the celestial equator, the imaginary projection of Earth’s equator into the sky. As Earth moves around its orbit, the sun’s apparent position shifts north and south of the celestial equator. At the equinox it crosses from one side to the other. But even then, day and night are not precisely equal. This is because the sun appears as a disc rather than a point of light, and the bending of its rays by our atmosphere means we can still see it even when it is just below the horizon. Together, these effects make the measured daytime several minutes longer than 12 hours at the equinox. In the UK, the date on which day and night come closest to being equal will be a couple of days later, around 25 September. This is called the equilux, for “equal light”.

title: Nearly 3m more lives could be saved in next pandemic if vaccines are shared more fairly, says report
summary: Move would mean deaths would rise in wealthier nations, according to NUS-Lancet Prime commission – which modelled a response to a flu pandemic based on population size, not purchasing power
text: An extra 2.7 million lives could be saved in the next pandemic if countries share vaccines in a less selfish way, a new study has found – although the death toll in richer countries would rise. Researchers modelling a hypothetical global outbreak of flu found that fast-tracking vaccine development could cut deaths from 58.5m to 23.9m. If the vaccines were then distributed equitably, according to population size rather than purchasing power, a further 2.7m lives could be saved overall. However, in high-income countries, that solidarity-based approach would see deaths rise from 2.4m to 3.9m. The modelling, looking at a possible future flu pandemic, forms part of a new report from the NUS-Lancet Prime commission, which found that countries needed to adopt a more comprehensive, society-wide approach in order to be prepared for future disease outbreaks. “Cooperation and solidarity saves the lives of essential first responders, including the health workers who can help stop a pandemic,” said Helen Clark, former prime minister of New Zealand and co-chair of the commission. “[Taking a] more equitable approach means fewer deaths globally and a fairer chance to protect those who need it most. Stronger regional research and manufacturing capacity will also be essential so that, in the next pandemic, vaccines and treatments reach those who need them first.” Boosting confidence in vaccines would reduce the death toll by a further 1.9m, the modelling also revealed. The commission undertook research in 20 countries with communities who had been hit hard by Covid-19 or other crises. They included homeless people in Indonesia, internally displaced people in Ethiopia, and Covid-bereaved families in the UK. The research revealed how systemic weaknesses put communities at greater risk of illness, death and loss of livelihoods and wellbeing, said co-chair Professor Helena Legido-Quigley of Imperial College London. “A person living in a crowded apartment cannot socially isolate, a person with no identity papers cannot access a government payment, and a person who doesn’t speak the dominant language cannot understand health advice,” she said. The commission was set up in 2023 by the National University of Singapore and The Lancet, and includes 41 experts from sectors including health, finance, planning and community. Traditional approaches to pandemic preparedness have been too reliant on checklists covering things like technical capacity, and failed to evaluate whether resources will reach everyone who needs protection, the researchers said. A blueprint for action, based on the findings, includes calls on governments to institutionalise community participation in planning, and commit to protection and be accountable for it. It is being published ahead of a United Nations High Level Meeting on pandemic preparedness in New York on Friday. Dr Githinji Gitahi, global CEO of Amref Health Africa, said countries on the continent had been at the back of the queue for Covid vaccines, and described the modelling results as “both compelling and deeply sobering”. “Plans written in conference rooms in capital cities often fail to reflect the realities that determine whether people can isolate, obtain reliable information, access care or receive a vaccine,” he said. “Trust cannot be improvised once an outbreak has begun. It must be earned now, before the next crisis, through health systems that listen to communities.”

title: Country diary: The biggest burst of partridges I’ve seen on the farm. We must be doing something right | Colin Chappell
summary: Brigg, Lincolnshire: As my attention turns to drilling next year’s cash crops, I create a disturbance out in the fields
text: Sometimes a moment of surprise has years of experience behind it. Last week as I was out in the oilseed rape fields applying a cocktail of microbe food (molasses, humates and fish paste), I had quite a shock when up went a large flock of grey partridges, a covey of 26. Twelve would be considered large, with red-legged partridges only ever appearing in pairs, but I’ve not seen 26 grey here in my lifetime. This is testament to our nature‑friendly approach to farming, including this year planting specific margins to encourage sawfly larvae, crickets, weevils and ground beetles. These insects form the entire diet of grey partridges (and yellowhammers) during their first two weeks of life. In addition, rather than just planting overwinter cover crops and “catch” crops to mop up loose nutrients and protect the soil from the elements, I now add millet, the seed of which is a boost for older birds. The idea is to create a mosaic of habitats that connect through the landscape. Now we have had a decent drop of rain, (almost 100mm in the space of three weeks), we have started to drill the cash crops, starting with the oilseed rape (OSR) and three companion crops that will provide natural defence to it. We plant berseem clover that provides nitrogen for the OSR, buckwheat that scavenges phosphate from the soil and makes it bio-available to the cash crop (through something called root exudates), and fenugreek which with its curry-type odour masks OSR from a pest called cabbage stem flea beetle. Through the winter, the combination of these plants will provide almost complete ground cover to protect the growing crop from the pigeons that can laser focus in on any gaps. Next up will be the barley crops, most of which are tolerant to barley yellow dwarf virus. This virus is spread by aphids and is exacerbated by our mild winters. Thanks to the tolerance, instead of applying an insecticide I can let natural predators feast on the pests, safe in the knowledge that even if they cannot keep up with the numbers, the risk to my crop is minimal. • Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024, is available now at guardianbookshop.com
