title: UK urged to strengthen financial muscle of national wealth fund to aid economy
summary: Unions, thinktanks and others say overhaul could provide investment Britain needs
text: Unions, thinktanks, environmental groups and charities have come together to call on ministers to boost the financial firepower of the national wealth fund to empower it to invest more in Britain and rebalance the country’s economy. Lower energy bills, the revitalisation of the UK’s industrial heartlands and the provision of more high-quality jobs could all be unlocked by scaling up the NWF, according to a statement from organisations including the TUC, Greenpeace, WWF and the New Economics Foundation. The statement calls on the government to overhaul the NWF by turning it into a “world-leading national development bank capable of delivering the investment Britain needs”, while insisting this would be consistent with the government’s existing fiscal rules. The NWF was launched in July 2024 by the then chancellor, Rachel Reeves, with the aim of attracting billions of pounds of private sector money for large infrastructure projects. It was a manifesto promise and aimed to attract a mix of investment – roughly £3 of private funds sought for every £1 of taxpayer cash in schemes such as ports, gigafactories and hydrogen and steel projects. The NWF is not a sovereign wealth fund, such as those owned by Norway and Saudi Arabia, which manage cash generated by the government through state-owned natural sources such as oil, and surpluses from international trade, bank reserves or privatisation projects. Instead, it is designed to boost investment in key industries while giving investors the confidence to park money in the UK by showing the government is willing to share the financial risk of large infrastructure projects. The call to expand its scope comes just before the Labour party gathers for its first conference since Andy Burnham became prime minister and as John Healey draws up his first budget as chancellor, scheduled for 28 October. The group’s statement praises the “important role” played by the NWF in “steering private investment to support clean energy, modern infrastructure and regional growth – for example, through its £500m partnership with the Manchester Good Growth Fund”. However, it calls on such public banks to do more, comparing the £5.5bn available for the NWF to invest each year for the next five years with the €62bn (£53.5bn) lent by Germany’s public investment bank KfW to households, businesses and municipalities in 2025 alone, almost 10 times higher. The statement lays out several ways a scaled-up NWF could benefit Britain, including: Turbocharging the retrofitting of homes and buildings. Giving the public a bigger stake in critical infrastructure through taking part-ownership stakes in key projects. Launching a targeted investment programme to bring new green industries to communities hit hardest by deindustrialisation. Supporting a network of regional banks to funnel money into the small businesses that hold up local economies. This would require the government giving the NWF independence to raise its own finances and invest over the long term, the group said, a practice followed by other public banks around the world. The group said this move would be consistent with the government’s fiscal rules – where ministers match day-to-day spending with their income and only borrow to invest – and would combine “fiscal credibility with economic ambition, delivering visible investment”. Burnham has said since entering Downing Street that he would look at “any flexibility” within the government’s existing fiscal rules to help borrow billions more to invest in infrastructure. A Treasury spokesperson said the NWF had delivered £3.9bn of investments in its first year in projects such as Sizewell C and a second gigafactory in Sunderland, as well as boosting flood defences in Wales. They added that an additional £5.25bn had been generated in private finance, while 11,500 jobs had been secured and created. The spokesperson said: “The government remains committed to the NWF’s long-term mission to crowd in private capital and drive economic growth into every postcode in the country.”

title: ‘It’s unrecognisable’: How being a tax haven has changed Jersey
summary: While global billionaires and multinational companies have been lured to its shores, many islanders feel left behind and priced out, with food bank use increasing
text: On a late Friday afternoon on the Channel Island of Jersey, tourists and locals are flocking to St Helier’s waterfront where the town’s sprawling beach has emerged at low tide. In one direction, they face the calm waters of St Aubin’s Bay, ringed by a seaside promenade and punctuated with a tidal island hosting the 16th century Elizabeth Castle. Back on shore, however, it is all business. Gleaming glass buildings hosting global accountancy firms and and international banks hint at the £4bn offshore finance industry dominating this nine-by-five-mile island’s economy. For decades, low taxes and corporate secrecy have lured the wealth of global billionaires and multinational companies to Jersey’s shores, requiring a high-paid cadre of bankers, accountants and lawyers who now make up more than half of the island’s economic output, and two in every five jobs. It has also made Jersey one of the world’s richest economies, giving its 104,500 population a GDP per head that is nearly 60% higher than the UK. But those tactics have come at a cost, not least to Jersey’s international reputation, with the island consistently securing a top-10 slot in the Tax Justice Network’s international tax haven rankings. It also came under fire after the Panama and Paradise papers data leaks, which shone a light on how elites were hiding wealth in offshore hubs such as Jersey. But Jersey isn’t the only place chasing global wealth, and foreign governments that have built on and replicated the island’s model are now threatening to eat its lunch. “Without urgent intervention, Jersey’s future success as a financial centre is at risk, with inevitable repercussions for the Jersey way of life,” a government-backed review, led by NatWest Group’s former chair Howard Davies, warned in March. In response, Jersey’s government is charging ahead with a £31m four-year plan aimed at slashing red tape, boosting the British crown dependency’s global profile and diversifying into popular crypto assets, all to keep it relevant in a rapidly changing world. “The risk of complacency is real,” the report warns. “Standing still means falling behind.” This is not the first time Jersey has faced an economic crossroads. Its boom and bust history stretches back to the 1700s, when it was home to a lucrative fine knitting industry. Once knitting was killed off by machines, oyster catching and shipbuilding took over, until overfishing and steam power closed shipyards. Entrepreneurial farmers then discovered and bred new exports: the docile and milk-rich Jersey cow, followed by a blight-resistant potato that still bears the island’s name, requiring a swathe of migrant workers to support farmers. “The cycle of Jersey’s industries has tended to see everyone getting involved where there’s a lot of money to be made,” says Lucy Layton, outreach curator at Jersey Heritage. A century later, as postwar Jersey tried to recover from Nazi occupation, tourism boomed, aided by the popularity of the Bergerac detective series. That industry was eventually ruined by discount airlines offering cheap holidays to sunnier European destinations, ushering in a new economic era focused on billionaires and corporations looking for a low-tax home for their wealth. Jersey has crafted an alluring package to draw in global wealth, involving zero inheritance or capital gains tax, and no corporation tax – outside of financial services firms, which are charged just 10% on their earnings. Meanwhile, an army of high-earning bankers, lawyers and accountants face a maximum of 20% income tax on the island, compared with 45% in London. But wealthy Britons have been choosing the glass towers of Dubai over Jersey’s low-rise seaside towns, while rich families overseas are hedging their bets and spreading cash across a number of offshore hubs. The Panama and Paradise papers data leaks have also influenced money flows. “People now are much more selective about the jurisdictions that they deal with,” says Joe Moynihan, chief executive of the sector’s promotional body, Jersey Finance. “They don’t want their organisation, or indeed their family, to be associated with a jurisdiction that could potentially damage their reputation.” However, Moynihan says Jersey’s reputation is strong: “We’re well regulated, with plenty of expertise, good legislation and an independent judiciary, which is becoming increasingly important in the crazy world that we live in.” But Jersey is still losing ground. Authorities say they need to regain a competitive edge, including by diversifying into crypto assets – such as stablecoins and tokens – to draw a younger wealthy client. Ian Gorst, the island’s finance minister, says it is also looking to cut back on “regulatory friction”. To some, that may sound like an opportunity to cut corners, but Gorst insists this is not about watering down rules meant to stop financial crime, corruption or sanctions evasion. Jersey’s ongoing battle with the Russian oligarch Roman Abramovich over his frozen assets is a case in point, he says. “What I think it shows is that Jersey can stand alongside the UK in fighting these issues.” Cooperation with the UK, though, only goes so far. Gorst has so far resisted pressure from Westminster’s anti-corruption champion Margaret Hodge to publicly release its beneficial ownership register, showing who ultimately owns Jersey-based companies. “I don’t intend to make our register public, and I’ve been clear to the UK about that,” he says. But not everyone is on board with the government’s finance-first agenda. Laura Craig, the owner of the Little Wren gift shop in St Helier, has lived in Jersey for 45 years. “For me personally, I would like to see Jersey have more of a balance in industry,” she says, including a return to more tourism. St Helier itself has changed over Craig’s lifetime, with the old granite-frontage that once dominated the town’s waterfront having been reclaimed and built up for the finance industry. “It’s unrecognisable to when I was a little girl,” Craig adds. “All the big buildings on there now are banks and finance houses.” Many say the influx of wealthy bankers has pushed up house prices across the tiny island, just 14 miles off the coast of France. “They just increase the cost of living for everybody,” says Antonio De’Lemos, co-owner of the La Topaze D’or antiques shop in St Helier market. He fears Jersey’s reputation has also taken a blow. “I don’t like to be in Jersey, knowing this is a tax paradise. And let’s be honest, it is,” he says. However, he acknowledges that it has become taboo to criticise the sector. “The establishment don’t like when you speak up.” While Jersey’s authorities are panicked about losing billionaires to Singapore and Dubai, many islanders are struggling to make ends meet. The number of food bank users tripled in the three years to 2024, and demand has continued. Just streets away from St Helier’s financial district, Vini Jones, the general manager of the Grace Trust charity, is helping prepare a free weekly meal at St Paul’s Church for dozens of locals. “You can move here, you can get a job, you could send your kids to school, you can go to your office at the weekends, you go to the beach, and you can have absolutely no idea or concept of what it’s actually like for a lot of people who live in Jersey,” he says. Jones, who moved to Jersey from London in 2000, doesn’t blame the finance industry, which he says helps fund the charity’s work. If the finance sector took a blow “it would be a bit of an earthquake but I think that people can get pretty resourceful”, he says. “We may see a little bit less coming our way in donations if that was the case, but I think there’s still a good community spirit in Jersey that people will rise to.” That community spirit is palpable across the island, including in Gorey, a 15-minute drive up the coast from St Helier. There, 76-year-old Liz Viney is manning a ticket table at the Saturday car boot sale. She says that while some islanders would like to see the bankers go, it would be more painful than they expect. “There’s a large part of the community here who would be quite pleased to revert back to being agricultural and fisheries and everything. But I don’t think we can go back there … who would support [the economy]? Who would pay the taxes? I think we have to live the life that, well, God gives us. And at the moment we are paid by the finance community. That’s what keeps us going.”

title: Whiplashed middle powers seek new alliances as Trump rages on world stage
summary: While world leaders prepare for annual UN gathering, shifts in the global order continue in the face of a disruptive American president
text: In the event of a midterms election battering, it is possible that a deflated Donald Trump, constrained by a Democrat-controlled Congress, will gradually have to face up to the indignity of irrelevance. While continuing to sign off Truth Social posts with his usual, “Thank you for your attention to this matter”, no one will actually be paying much attention. His meandering press conferences will no longer be carried live by TV networks. The Republican party will move on to the question of his successor. Trump could announce he had changed the name of the Champs-Élysées to Sunset Boulevard and even Google Maps will stifle a yawn. He would become that most pitied of political animals, the lame duck. Yet somehow this scenario does not seem to fit the Trump personality, the US media landscape or indeed the recent history of other presidential endings. Just before completing their own terms in office, George W Bush launched the Iraq war “surge”, Bill Clinton got China into the World Trade Organization and Ronald Reagan helped end the cold war. Trump will also surely rage against the dying of the light. Many observers, including the former US secretary of state Hillary Clinton and the former UK foreign secretary David Lammy, predict Trump will concentrate even more on his disruptive foreign policy after November’s midterms, seeking to go even further and faster. Potential legislative gridlock in Congress would block him off from domestic initiatives, so the thinking goes, but much less so foreign policy. The likes of António Guterres, attending his final UN general assembly as secretary general this week, who have tried to impress on Trump that the US could achieve more in alliance with others than alone, are likely to receive short shrift. Those hoping for a return from the orderless world to one of order, loosely built around a set of recognisable values, are likely to be disappointed. In short, there is more to come. *** That assessment is accelerating a trend across the world of countries forming a complex web of diplomatic, military and trading alliances designed to act as protective shields from an unpredictable and predatory US president. These hedging alliances, born out of fear of entrapment or of abandonment, are springing up across the globe, changing the matrix of diplomacy, often but not always in favour of the other superpower of the age, China. John Bew, a foreign policy adviser to four former British prime ministers, describes the process as the creation of “a sub-threshold international order”. As Mark Carney, the Canadian prime minister, urged in a speech at Davos in January, the middle powers are reorganising. The trend is most obvious among former US allies. Mark Leonard, the director of the European Council of Foreign Relations, said: “The world is moving from a situation where countries saw themselves within the context of an alliance system – ‘How do we plug and play and make it all about interoperability with American grand strategy?’ – towards one where the primary goal is: ’How do we hedge and how do we make sure that we can defend ourselves if America isn’t there?’” Wherever one looks it is the alliances in which the US does not feature – from Brics to the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) – that are thriving and deepening. The recent Brics summit in Delhi ended with a declaration 140 dense paragraphs long that centred on how sovereign states can insulate their economies, supply lines, and payment infrastructures from weaponised western financial networks. The aim was to show that the “global south” can shape rules without turning into an anti-American alliance. “The operational strategy does not aim to eradicate the dollar overnight,” the Indian commentator Navroop Singh explained, “but to construct a parallel, non-dollar pipeline through which bilateral commerce, especially in strategic commodities like oil, gas, agriculture, and critical minerals can flow unhindered by extraterritorial oversight of the United States.” At this month’s SCO meeting at Bishkek in Kyrgyzstan, China’s president, Xi Jinping, said: “The overwhelming majority of countries do not subscribe to power politics, do not want conflict and confrontation, and do not wish to remain closed off and left behind. Instead, they aspire to secure an equal place on the world stage through their own development and international cooperation.” Formed to manage border disputes among former Soviet states, the SCO’s activities long ago expanded to include an economic dimension fostering connectivity, trade and investment. By contrast, in the groupings that the US dominates, such as the G7 and Nato, the recent key ambition has been to shape an agenda that avoids a Trump walkout. Success is measured according to whether the west avoids public disintegration. Sometimes these new ad hoc alliances are relatively mundane. Some operate inside existing institutions, others involve the creation of specific new cooperation trading mechanisms such as memorandums of understanding on trade in critical minerals or the development of new overlapping institutions. In the case of the UK, the Chatham House thinktank suggests as many as six different mini-alliances could be formed to build submarines and air engines, share critical minerals, or promote free trade. *** The biggest and most striking recent manifestation of this new order came in the Middle East on 7 August, when Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia signed the Mecca pact – a defensive military alliance that for some is about ending the dependency on the US military umbrella, and for others combatting Iran. Either way, it is likely to rewrite the Middle East’s security architecture. Trita Parsi, from the US foreign policy thinktank the Quincy Institute For Responsible Statecraft, said: “If you sit in the Gulf Cooperation Council countries right now, you must feel tremendously vulnerable because you have put all your eggs in the American security basket and it turned out not only not to work, but it was supposed to be a guarantee that others would be deterred from attacking you. Instead, the US started a war against the wishes of most Gulf countries and within that war, the entire infrastructure of the US bases turned out not to be a deterrent, but a magnet.” Not only were exposed bases pummelled by Iranian missiles and drones to the point, in the words of Gen David Petraeus, that they became “no longer viable”, the Gulf states also discovered the US was prepared to allow Israel to bomb Qatar’s capital, Doha, in the hope of assassinating the Hamas leadership. It was the first such attack on a GCC state, and changed the GCC’s security calculations as to whether Iran or Israel ultimately was the primary threat in the region. The US insists in public it will reinvest in better-protected bases and will shortly lay out a postwar vision in which the US remains indispensable to the Gulf’s security. But Majed al-Ansari, Qatar’s foreign ministry spokesperson, said: “Gulf nations cannot rely solely on the US and other international alliances for their security. Self-sufficiency when it comes to security is the only way forward.” Parsi admitted it was not clear what kind of tree would grow out of the seed sown in Mecca. “Is it another bloc formation that at its core divides the region, leading to rivalry and confrontation, or is it, as the Turks insist, an open constellation that is not targeting anyone but based on collective security?” Saudi Arabia’s Vision 2030, meanwhile, requires foreign investment, tourism and reliable energy routes. Endless wars promoted by Israel and not constrained by the US for purposes not in Saudi Arabia’s long-term interest are a ball and chain on the Saudi economy. In all this, there are deep implications for India, a country dependent on the Middle East for nearly 60% of its crude oil and about 70% of its liquefied natural gas requirements. It may need to form its own hard power security partnerships in the region. Writing in Foreign Affairs magazine, Marc Lynch, a professor of political science and international affairs at George Washington University, asked recently: “If Washington could not even be counted on to consult its allies, defeat its adversaries, or protect its partners from the fallout of its regional misadventures, then what good were its promises? The fundamental bargain the United States offered has crumbled, and it will not be easily rebuilt”. The same set of questions has been posed in Europe, leading to calls for a more Europeanised Nato, most often perceived as an alliance of its five main military powers, a constellation that conveniently bypasses Brexit and would allow Germany, France, Italy, Poland and the UK to work together to face the Russian threat, assuming these democracies next year remain led by forces opposed to Putin’s authoritarianism. Debate about this alliance, promoted at the Munich Security Conference, is driven by the twin fears of the hybrid war conducted by Moscow and the US plan to leave the conventional defence of Europe to the Europeans. Trumpites treat Europeans primarily as trade competitors and sometimes a civilisational threat, not allies. No one can assume that the US would come to Europe’s defence in the event of a Russian attack. Not surprisingly, Poland, the Baltics and Scandinavia have since 2022 increased their defence spending by 71%, 134% and 126% respectively. The call to buy European arms is growing. Such is the concern about where Trump could go next after his threats to Greenland, that some European diplomats privately express relief that the US was unable to repeat the success of Venezuela in Iran. There is no love for the Iranian government, save for its ability to remind Europe of the risks inherent in relying on US military and technological supremacy. *** The country that most acutely faces the American dilemma is of course Canada. Now entering an asymmetric trade war with the largest and most powerful country in the world, it has little doubt about the rupture it is confronting. Bob Rae, a former Canadian ambassador to the UN, recently wrote: “Canada’s nextdoor neighbour is a predatory hegemon [that] tears up treaties, makes a mockery of international law and clearly has a different concept of the relationships between might and right, and between law, morality and self-interest.” But there was an ambiguity deep in Carney’s Davos message. Was he seeking simply to locate new markets blocked by US tariffs, or was he trying to build a network of countries – a third bloc – with like-minded liberal values? Rae argued that for the middle nations alliance to thrive, Carney needed to be clearer about what values Canada stands for, including upholding international law. He wrote: “We can succeed in defeating such aggression only if we are willing to extend economic, political and military support to other countries and jurisdictions facing similar attacks and threats.” In his speech to the European parliament this week while trying to provide the cure to the harsh realities his Davos speech diagnosed, Carney argued that associate membership of the EU would not just be about economics, but an affinity of deep-rooted shared values that implicitly Canada no longer shared with the US. But the rules-based EU does not give access to its markets readily, and the big vision could soon become entangled in the small print Brussels adores. Sometimes this crisis of the west is seen as an exclusively European phenomenon. But South Korea finds itself in a similar place to Canada. Ulchi Freedom Shield, the annual joint military exercise that the US and South Korea held to counter the North Korean threat, was abruptly scaled back by Washington just before it was due to begin in August. Trump ordered the drills cut from 11 days to five, citing costs, his desire to improve relations with the North Korean leader, Kim Jong-un, and South Korea’s reluctance to support his war on Iran. The decline in US military stocks due to the Iran war has hardly helped. It has intensified a debate in South Korea, and in Japan, about pursuing independent nuclear weapons, especially given the apparent indifference of the US and the international community to North Korea’s programme. The friction has given Xi a golden opportunity to promote China to South Korea and Asia as the more reliable ally. Optimists such as Kurt Campbell, who under Joe Biden’s presidency latterly as deputy secretary of state did more than anyone to reconstruct American alliances across Asia after the Trump first term, insists his task can be repeated. There is no need to panic, he said, arguing that “by the winter there will be a dramatic resurgence in discussion, debate, hope and, frankly, optimism about what comes next”. The old centrifugal forces including European aversion to Chinese protectionism and US dominance in artificial intelligence, will resurface. The counterview is that something fundamental has changed. Once bitten, twice shy, the old transatlantic order will not be restored, and something new, less predictable, more fragmented is already taking shape.

title: ‘The physical toll is visceral’: How Indonesia’s fire haze affects millions - visual guide
summary: Intensified by this year’s super El Niño, fires in Borneo and Sumatra are emitting toxic air for swathes of the population in Indonesia and its neighbours
text: For months, parts of Indonesia’s Borneo and Sumatra islands have been ablaze. The fires are sometimes lit illegally as a cheap way to clear land for plantations of oil palm, of which Indonesia is the world’s largest producer. So prevalent is the technique that it even has a special term: slash and burn. Many of the fires begin as small-scale blazes. But in hot, dry conditions, can easily spiral out of control, sending toxic smoke across borders and affecting the air quality of millions in Indonesia and beyond. This year a “super” El Niño could inflame the problem. David Gaveau, a landscape ecologist who runs Nusantara Atlas, which tracks fires and deforestation in Asia, says the worst fires occur on drained and dried out peatland. This type of fire is extremely difficult to extinguish, and can burn for weeks underground. “They go underground, they resurface somewhere else. And then the more water you give it, the more smoke there is,” he says, “These fires are really the legacy of 50 years of forest degradation, deforestation, and particularly on peatland.” If there was an “apex predator” among fires, tropical peatland fires would be a top contender, says Nasa. Fires occur annually in Indonesia, but data from this year indicates it is already looking like a bad year, with the worst hit areas in Sumatra, Kalimantan, the Indonesian part of Borneo, and Papua. Since January at least 895,657 hectares have been burned Indonesia-wide, 34% worse than 2019, according to data from Nusantara Atlas. “It’s trending far higher than 2019 or even 2023,” says Gaveau, “What that means is that this is a terrible year.” In recent weeks, photos from Kalimantan have shown a thick, sepia-toned haze shrouding streets and obscuring cities, schoolchildren wearing masks at their desks, and even rescuers giving oxygen to smoke-affected orangutans. “Ever since the haze hit, we haven’t opened our doors or windows in a long time. The wind carries smoke from the fires all the way to our porch. Ash and smoke seep directly into the house, and the conditions worsen at night,” Ely Marlina, a 46-year-old schoolteacher and volunteer firefighter told the Guardian. “While we sleep, the whole family is just breathing in the smoke,” she says. “The physical toll is visceral; eyes are left stinging and weeping daily … It feels like if we keep breathing in this smog, the dizziness will take over and our bodies will just give out.” As the fires rage, schools have closed, and emergency rooms have been inundated with patients. The numbers of people suffering wildfire-related respiratory illnesses in those provinces had more than doubled to 113,336 by 9 September, from 50,891 on 1 September. Fire emissions from Indonesia in the first week of September reached 19.7m metric tons, accounting for more than a third of the global total, according to Fire Emissions Watch, a portal developed by the European Union’s Copernicus climate monitoring service. The air quality index in Indonesia and its neighbours shows just how much the fires have become a public health issue. According to air quality index ratings, a healthy level of air, signified by green, is ranked between 0 and 50. Anything above 300 is considered hazardous. Every day this September, the air quality in Sampit, central Kalimantan, has been classified as hazardous, going beyond the red and into the worst rating of maroon, according to the Swiss air monitor IQAir. On 10 September, the rating hit 1142. In Kuching, the biggest city on Malaysian Borneo, this month, AQI levels have fluctuated between unhealthy and hazardous. One resident in Kalimantan recently told the Guardian that taking a breath feels like “smoking a cigarette”. When the smoke from these fires crosses borders, it’s called “transboundary haze”. This year, the haze has again plagued Indonesia’s neighbours, blanketing parts of Malaysia, Singapore, Brunei, and even the Philippines. o Carried by monsoonal winds the smoke travelled as far as Manila, with residents urged to stay indoors as much as possible, and to wear mask outdoors. Among the countries hardest-hit, Malaysia has urged the Association of Southeast Asian Nations to review an agreement on transboundary haze from 2003. Indonesia’s environment ministry is investigating 19 companies allegedly linked to the fires, while police have arrested 113 people on suspicion of lighting them. But enforcement has proven a challenge for the country. The government has vowed to crackdown on bad actors; it has also deployed planes, helicopters, drones and the military to fight the fires; and it has bolstered mitigation efforts. Malaysia has offered three helicopters, ⁠an aircraft and 52 personnel to assist, while Japan has also sent in helicopters and a fire-fighting force. Residents are also doing their bit. A team of female firefighters called the Power of Mama conduct daily surveillance activities, fire monitoring and community outreach, including encouraging people not to burn and warning them of the risks. In West Kalimantan, volunteers are going door-to-door to hand out cylinders of oxygen to residents and firefighters ‌struggling to breathe, in a campaign called “Rumah Oksigen”, or Oxygen House. But the next few weeks will be crucial. With this year’s super El Niño, experts say the fires could peak this September, and continue until November, when the rainy season is expected to start, but the phenomenon is not the only factor. “El Niño is an enabler. Of course the more powerful it is, the longer and the more intense the drought, and that’s not good news,” says Gaveau, “But you need a match. And we know what that is; it’s people.” Indonesia’s forestry minister Raja Juli Antoni has also warned that the country is entering a critical phase. “We have not yet escaped the threat of El Niño,” he said. “We are not safe from forest and land fires during this El Niño period. September is our month of struggle, our field of struggle.” Additional reporting by Garry Lotulung

title: ‘People had naive expectations’: How MeToo has changed in China
summary: On Friday, MeToo journalist Sophia Huang Xueqin was released from prison. She returns to a landscape changed by censorship, and a new generation of feminists
text: When Jasmine, a once active member of China’s MeToo movement, organises feminist activities in Beijing, she often does so under the guise of an art or cultural event. She avoids publicising them on social media, instead sharing details privately in her personal circle. It’s very difficult to imagine what happened during the MeToo period, she says, “when one survivor could speak publicly about her experience and trigger a broader discussion about sexual harassment.” On Friday Sophia Huang Xueqin the imprisoned journalist who helped to ignite China’s MeToo movement, was released from prison, five years after her arrest. She will return to see a feminist movement that has dramatically changed in the years she has been detained. In China feminism has become an increasingly private affair. Activists speak of a generational rupture. A movement once inspired by the global hashtag campaign against sexual abuse and harassment has retreated to a less public space. Across Chinese social media survivors post about sexual harassment and successful court cases online. But activists say hashtag campaigns like MeToo and its Chinese language equivalents have largely been scrubbed from the Chinese internet. “A lot of younger, digital-native feminists today don’t know much about those earlier feminist struggles not too long ago, thanks to the state’s intentional annihilation of them,” says Eva Liu, a researcher on Chinese feminism and digital media at Ohio University. Today, Chinese feminists employ creative ways to avoid censorship. They use new expressions to avoid posts being blocked. “It’s really a cat-and-mouse game,” says Liu. She describes an “encyclopaedia” of feminist words banned by Chinese censors. “There are staff specifically tasked with tracking new terms coined by feminists online and adding them to the keyword lists used for automated censorship,” she says. “Even some terms that are not yet popular among feminist users are already part of this automatic censorship list.” Li Sipan, a Chinese investigative journalist and feminist scholar, says: “The Chinese Communist party regards all mobilisation of the public and movements demanding changes from the government as threats. The feminist movement clearly has these characteristics.” Jasmine in Beijing says: “If you want to organise a public event, anything explicitly related to feminism or LGBT issues is basically not possible, at least in Beijing. If you advertise it that way, there’s a risk the event will be shut down. “So usually we frame the event in a more neutral way, without directly presenting it as being about gender or social issues. But once the event is taking place, we may still discuss those topics.” ‘The online environment now is very different’ Huang’s reporting of survivors’ stories helped to propel the MeToo movement into public consciousness in China. She was arrested in 2021 in the city of Guangzhou a day before she was set to leave China to study a masters degree at Sussex University on a UK government-funded scholarship. In 2024 she was convicted alongside labour activist Wang Jianbing of “inciting subversion of state power”. Huang’s friends say they received little information about her from the authorities while she was in detention, amid reports of dramatic weight loss and intense interrogation, resulting in little sleep. Information travelled slowly out of the prison. They sometimes waited months for updates, relying on messages from other inmates who had been released. At the time of her conviction, Huang was also sentenced to four years “deprivation of political rights”. Human right groups say it could prevent her from continuing to work as a journalist or travelling abroad. In a statement released on Saturday, activists pushing for Huang’s release said “though she is released from prison, none of us [her friends] were able to reach her or receive any information from her. “Her whereabouts is also unknown. We are nervous and worried about her current conditions due to the potential severe surveillance she faces.” The Chinese government says the country has made “historic” progress in women’s rights. In a speech last year, president Xi Jinping listed improvements in health, employment and economic participation. China says it will further strengthen gender equality and protect against sexual harassment and sexual violence. Despite the shrinking space for debate, activists say the movement has had a lasting impact on Chinese society. Metoo made sexual harassment a mainstream topic. It led to policy change in universities, although activists say progress stopped at the courts. “I believe the achievements of China’s MeToo are things that many other authoritarian or even democratic countries failed to achieve,” says Lu Pin, a Chinese feminist activist, based in New York. “Under very harsh conditions, MeToo greatly raised women’s awareness of their rights, especially among young women.” In Beijing, Jasmine hopes to meet Huang one day but is unsure if it will be possible. She says she is still in contact with survivors of sexual harassment and believes it’s possible to support them with publicity and legal support. She believes there are other individuals and groups offering similar help, but they must choose carefully how to effect change. “The online environment now is very different from when MeToo first emerged,” she says. Lu Pin agrees. “People used to have naive imaginations and expectations about the internet, but later realised it wasn’t like that, especially for women and feminism.”

title: More Australians will be dying than being born in 40 years as major report predicts future of lower growth
summary: Seventh intergenerational report also outlines how Australia is on the brink of an uncertain age of artificial intelligence
text: There will be more Australians dying than being born in 40 years’ time, according to the government’s latest intergenerational report, which lays bare the fundamental challenges of managing an ageing population at a time of rapid change and lower economic growth. The country’s seventh IGR also outlines how Australia is on the brink of a new and uncertain age of artificial intelligence that will shape the economy and society over the coming four decades. Jim Chalmers, in a speech at the Australian National University to coincide with the release of the analysis, said “this intergenerational report illuminates the road ahead”. “No previous IGR has contended with global challenges this great, with politics this fraught, or a future less certain. The global and generational risks are serious, but Australia’s opportunities are endless,” the treasurer said. The latest 40-year projections show the population will keep getting older as people have fewer children, to the point where falling fertility rates mean deaths are for the first time projected to outnumber births by the 2060s. “This is a milestone that many advanced economies have already surpassed, including Japan, Germany, Italy and the Republic of Korea, with most of the rest expected to do so over coming decades,” the report says. With the population set to grow by 0.9% for the foreseeable future, versus 1.4% historically, alongside a shrinking share of working Australians to support activity and the budget, the IGR predicts the economy has entered into a new normal of lower growth. Living standards will still improve, but not as quickly as in the past, the IGR shows. Real GDP on a per person basis will expand by about 1.2% over the next 40 years, down from 1.5% in the previous four decades, the IGR shows. Even that relatively dour outlook depends on productivity picking back up from virtually zero in recent years to the historical average of 1.2% – an assumption that leans heavily on AI, or what Chalmers described as “the biggest economic transformation of our lifetime”. “The rise and adoption of AI is likely to support the achievement of Treasury’s long-term labour productivity growth assumption over time,” the report says, while the treasurer described its role as “pivotal”. “As a medium-sized economy, Australia’s productivity performance will depend on adopting innovation, supporting investment, developing skills and delivering regulatory reforms that improve the efficient operation of the economy,” the report says. The forecasts underline the tightrope the government must walk between protecting Australians from the worst aspects of the new technology, and not stifling a technology that could almost single-handedly drive future prosperity. The IGR is a five-yearly exercise, although it was most recently published in 2023 after Covid interrupted its scheduling. Peter Costello, a former Liberal treasurer, first conceived of the IGR and formally enshrined it in the Charter of Budget Honesty Act of 1998 as a way to explain how demographic shifts affect the budget over the very long term. First released in 2002, each report has highlighted similar challenges associated with an ageing population: pressures on delivering services to older Australians and how to pay for them – not least dealing with the growing tax burden on a shrinking share of workers. The IGR projects an ongoing, structural budget deficit over coming decades, as it shrinks over the next 10 years before expanding again over the following 40. Government payments as a share of GDP are anticipated to rise by 1.1 percentage points to 27.4% by the mid-2060s. “As the scale and interaction of these structural trends intensify, maintaining a sustainable budget position will require policies and ongoing reforms that manage growing spending and revenue challenges,” the report says. This year’s report also included a section of six “major transitions” for the next 40 years, topped by the AI “revolution” and geopolitical fragmentation. The next four challenges were the energy transition, ageing and the care economy, the country’s “industrial transformation”, and intergenerational equity. “The world is becoming more dangerous, more unpredictable, more unequal, and more divided. These are not just individual threads but part of a bigger fraying of that intergenerational promise, of better times,” Chalmers said. The treasurer said responding successfully to these major challenges would be the key to defeating populist insurgencies that sought to weaponise public discontent for political ends. The IGRs provide a robust argument in favour of the compulsory superannuation regime, which has largely offset the huge budgetary impact experienced in other countries associated with funding retirement incomes.

title: Patrick Clancy, ex-husband of Lindsay Clancy, opens up on children’s killings in first televised interview
summary: In a 60 Minutes interview, ex-husband describes moments leading to the 2023 killings
text: In his first televised interview, Patrick Clancy, the ex-husband of Lindsay Clancy, described the moments leading up to the 2023 killings of their children and how he coped in the aftermath. Patrick Clancy responded to online criticism and conspiracy theories from people who supported Lindsay Clancy and believed he did not provide enough care to his wife at the time. “It’s deeply harmful to the legacy of my children,” Patrick Clancy said. “It is a huge distraction from what really matters here, which is perinatal mental health. And it’s done real harm to real people, myself included but also others.” He called the online response “painful to see”. “And it makes it difficult to be in public and it’s possible that some of those people, after seeing lie after lie after lie, they start to believe it and that’s what we’re left with,” he added. The interview, which aired on Sunday, comes as Massachusetts prosecutors prepare to decide later this month whether to retry Lindsay Clancy for the strangling of her children – Cora, five; Dawson, three; and Callan, eight months old – in the family’s home before trying to end her own life. A judge declared a mistrial on 4 September after a jury deadlocked. Eleven jurors favored clearing Lindsay Clancy of criminal responsibility, finding she was suffering from postpartum psychosis. A single holdout agreed with prosecutors, who maintained that she knew what she was doing. Patrick Clancy said he first noticed his ex-wife struggling with sleep deprivation and anxiety in the fall of 2022, months after their youngest son, Callan, was born. He admitted he “didn’t know how to manage a postpartum illness” before this experience. “I think mental illness has this ability to be tragically deceptive. So I’m sure there are things that I didn’t see,” he added. Lindsay Clancy’s conditions worsened in December, leading to her stay at McLean psychiatric hospital on New Year’s Eve. The children were allegedly strangled 17 days after Lindsay Clancy was released from the hospital. Patrick Clancy said he hoped that Callan might survive after regaining a heartbeat. “I remember just thinking, ‘Just gimme one. Just gimme one kid, and I would raise him as best I could, and I would give him the best life I possibly could. I’d tell him about his brother and sister’,” he said. Callan later died in the hospital. Patrick Clancy attributed the killings of his children to his ex-wife’s mental illness and has forgiven her, rejecting media depictions of her as a “killer mom” or “baby murderer”. “I think I did the best I could with what I had at the time,” he said. “And I live with the outcome. I live with it every day.” Lindsay and Patrick Clancy have each filed medical malpractice lawsuits against doctors and hospitals involved in her care. Lindsay Clancy alleges negligence and medical malpractice, while Patrick Clancy alleges wrongful death. Patrick Clancy said his life came to a “screeching halt” and he admitted he suffered from suicidal thoughts. He eventually moved to New York City seeking anonymity. There, he managed to grieve openly, kept items that belonged to his children and eventually met his second wife at a running club. Speaking to experts at Postpartum Support International had also helped him process what occurred, he said in the interview. “I know I can’t fix – I can’t bring his kids back,” said his wife, Rachel Danis, who joined Patrick during the interview. “But if I can honor them and allow Pat to grieve but also just continue to honor them in the present, it – I guess that’s all I can do.” The Plymouth county district attorney has yet to say whether he’ll seek to put Lindsay Clancy on trial again. She is being held in Tewksbury hospital in Massachusetts. • In the US, you can call or text the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org. In the UK and Ireland, Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123. In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found at befrienders.org

title: Patrick Clancy Describes Grief in First Interview Since Mistrial
summary: Mr. Clancy said in a “60 Minutes” interview that he dreams “all the time” about his three children, who were strangled to death in 2023 by his former wife, Lindsay Clancy.

title: Ukraine war briefing: Russia to ‘intensify’ attacks on Kyiv after Moscow hit with mass drone strikes
summary: At least two killed in Moscow and oil refinery set alight on last day of Russia’s parliamentary elections. What we know on day 1,671
text: Russia has vowed to “intensify” its strikes on Kyiv while accusing Ukraine of attempting to “disrupt” Russian elections after Ukraine fired waves of drones at the Moscow region on the final day of voting, killing at least two people. “In response to the Kyiv regime’s attacks on civilian targets within Russia, the Russian army will continue and intensify its high-accuracy strikes against military targets in Kyiv,” the Russian defence ministry said. The attack was the largest on Moscow since the Kremlin launched its Ukraine offensive in 2022 and involved about 1,600 drones, 450 of which were aimed directly at the capital, Moscow mayor Sergei Sobyanin said. Images showed a gaping hole in a multi-storey apartment building on the outskirts of Moscow. Another showed black smoke pouring from what appeared to be an oil refinery. Volodymyr Zelenskyy praised Ukraine’s attacks, saying: “Our long-range responses had a very significant impact in the Moscow region last night.” The Ukrainian presidient said that among the weapons used in the attack was the Pelican, initially thought to be a short-range ballistic missile, but which sources said later was a winged drone. Zelenskyy said also Ukraine had used its domestically produced Flamingo cruise missiles to strike Moscow. The long-range weapon has previously been used against targets deep inside Russia. Preliminary results from Russia’s election, released by the country’s election commission early Monday, showed the main Kremlin party dominating the vote. The tightly controlled balloting was virtually devoid of opposition to President Vladimir Putin’s policies and all but certain to cement the Kremlin’s dominance. With about 58% of the precincts counted, United Russia had nearly 58% of the vote for the 225 deputies apportioned by party lists, according to the Central Election Commission. The balloting included residents of four Ukrainian regions that Moscow illegally annexed after the war began, but still doesn’t fully control, as well as those in Crimea, the Black Sea peninsula that was illegally annexed by Russia in 2014, in what Kyiv denounced as illegal and the European Union described as a “blatant violation of international law”. Zelenskyy ⁠said on Sunday he had spoken with US President Donald Trump and ⁠the two ⁠agreed to meet in New York for talks that “could change a lot” ⁠in terms of finding a resolution to the war with Russia. The two ⁠leaders will be in New York this week ‌for the UN ‌General Assembly. “There are ideas for de-escalation steps and for addressing fundamental security issues – energy security, food security, and the protection of human ⁠life,” Zelenskyy posted on X. European intelligence officials have raised the possibility of an imminent Russian test of Nato, Sean Walker writes, with one saying a potential attack could come in a matter of “months, not years”. The warnings come after Poland’s prime minister, Donald Tusk, told parliament that intelligence assessments suggested Russia might launch an attack with drones or missiles on Nato territory in the coming months, as part of efforts to prove that “article 5 is more theoretical than practical”. Egypt, one of the world’s largest importers of wheat, is diversifying its source of wheat imports towards France ⁠and other European suppliers, moving away from Ukraine and Russia where supplies have been ⁠disrupted, supply minister ⁠Sherif Farouk was quoted as saying on Sunday. The minister’s remarks were quoted by television ⁠host Ahmed Moussa and later confirmed by a ministry spokesperson. An overnight Russian attack on the Kyiv region ⁠killed four people, including three children, Kyiv regional authorities said on Sunday. Drone attacks persisted in Kyiv and the surrounding ⁠region throughout the day. Drone fragments fell in various districts in the capital. Outside the capital, a mother and ⁠her two 3-year-old children were killed in Kyiv region when a Russian drone strike hit a private home, the emergency service ⁠said. Kyiv region governor Tymur Tkachenko said a girl died in hospital after a separate drone strike in another district. Tkachenko ‌said the region endured ‌more than a day of hostile attacks over several areas.

title: The black robin, once down to just a single breeding pair, wins NZ bird of the year
summary: Fondly known as the ‘goth’ of New Zealand’s bird world, the black robin now has a population of 350 adults thanks to a pioneering breeding programme
text: The black robin, once the world’s rarest bird before an extraordinary conservation project brought it back from brink of extinction, has been crowned New Zealand’s bird of the year, after record voter turnout. The tiny bird is found only in the Chatham Islands, 800km east of mainland New Zealand. Called kakaruia in Māori and karure in Morirori – the language indigenous to the Chathams – the birds are also fondly known as the “goth” of New Zealand’s bird world, for its striking black plumage, black eyes and a little pointy black beak. Habitat loss and introduced pests devastated its population, and by the 1970s there were five birds left. Just one breeding pair remained: Old Blue, the matriarch, and Old Yellow. A breeding programme that pioneered using other species to foster parent the robins’ eggs proved a success, and its numbers have steadily climbed to 350 adult birds, although it is still classed as “threatened”. “They are really cute,” said Jess Mackenzie, spokesperson for the Chatham Islands Landscape Restoration Trust, adding that the black robin has been in the top five birds for the past few years but never clinched a win. “It’s a bird that New Zealanders definitely love and know,” she said. Despite the name, the black robin is not in the same family as overseas robins and is a distinct species. In the Chathams, they live in lowland coastal forest on two restricted, pest-free nature reserves. While a conservation success story, the black robin is not “saved yet”, Mackenzie said. Habitat on their islands is nearly at capacity, and a third pest-free island is needed. The bird of the year competition – run by conservation group Forest and Bird – was launched 20 years ago to raise awareness about the plight of New Zealand’s native birds, many of which are threatened, on the brink of extinction or already extinct due to the introduction of pests, human activity and declining habitats. The 2026 competition attracted a record 105,000 votes. About 88% of the votes were cast from New Zealand. The world’s heaviest parrot, the kākāpō, came second and the 2025 winner, the country’s only falcon, the kārearea, finished third. Over the years, the contest has been subject to scandal, from crowning a bat the winner in 2021, to accusations of Russian interference in 2019, and claims Australians attempted to rig the contest in favour of the shag in 2018. In 2023, British-American comedian and talkshow host John Oliver ran a global campaign for the threatened pūteketeke, which was then crowned the winner that year.

title: Trump reportedly to form health funding board that could veto ‘woke’ initiatives
summary: President’s latest order expected to bring NIH funding under control of Trump administration to align with agenda
text: Donald Trump’s latest executive order is expected to establish a board responsible for approving National Institutes of Health (NIH) grant funding, marking another attempt by the Trump administration to censor topics that do not align with the president’s agenda. The executive order, reported by outlets including the Washington Post and Politico, was discussed in a meeting on Friday in which senior administration officials accused the NIH of funding “woke” initiatives that went against Trump’s political priorities. Russell Vought, the director of the White House’s office of management and budget (OMB), and other administration officials proposed an executive order that would create an external committee that could veto awards in biomedical research that do not align with Trump’s goals, according to several people who spoke to the Washington Post. The board would include Vought and the NIH director, Jay Bhattacharya, according to Politico, and it would be required to reach unanimous decisions on grant awards. The OMB is the White House agency in charge of implementing the president’s policies in the executive branch. Establishing an external commission to award grants based on the president’s ideological agenda breaks with the agency’s traditional process of evaluating proposals on scientific merit. Bhattacharya has resisted cuts to federal research spending and defended the NIH’s grant-making process on Friday, while Vought expressed a desire to reshape federal spending. The reported ⁠move comes as the NIH, the world’s largest public funder of biomedical research, faces a class-action lawsuit by researchers arguing that the Trump administration is hindering and terminating scientific grants to censor opposing views to the president’s ideological agenda. Researchers are accusing the administration of violating the first amendment. “What the first amendment does not allow is the government’s use of its funding power to target or silence the expression of disfavored viewpoints within the biomedical research community,” reads the lawsuit. Since Trump took office for his second term, billions of dollars in federal grants related to health, nutrition, the environment, and disaster relief have been cut or frozen. Research with keywords including “equity”, “racist”, “gender”, “climate change” and others has been flagged by the administration to hinder funding for scientific research. The Department of Health and Human Services, which oversees the NIH, and the White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

title: Lib Dems propose big tech levy to fund £250m online crime agency
summary: Proposal one of many at conference responding to concern voters unaware of party’s policies or what it stands for
text: The Liberal Democrats say they will tax big tech to finance a new online crime agency, as they try to address concerns that not enough voters know what the party stands for. The plan, to be announced at the party conference on Monday by the Lib Dems’ home affairs spokesperson, Max Wilkinson, would create a new Online Crime Agency focused on offences including child sexual abuse material, trafficking in drugs and weapons, and deepfake AI-generated pornographic images. The planned budget of £250m a year would be paid for by an “online crime levy” on large AI and technology companies. Wilkinson is to tell the conference it is “time they picked up the bill” for offences they had enabled. Ed Davey, the party leader, on Sunday set out a proposal to cut fuel duty by 10p a litre for a fixed three-month period, as well as reducing the bus fare cap from £3 to £1 and other transport-related cost of living policies. The party is increasingly concerned that, although it won its best election result in a century in 2024, it does not have a distinctive enough message to reach voters in an increasingly fragmented and noisy political landscape. Polling conducted to coincide with the conference in Brighton, released on Sunday, showed Lib Dem policies are less well known than those of Restore Britain, which launched as a political party only in February and has one MP – Rupert Lowe – compared with the Lib Dems’ 71. The research by More in Common, which was presented at the conference, showed widespread uncertainty among voters about what the Lib Dems stood for. Just 39% said they had an idea, lower than for every other major party, including Restore Britain, which was formed by Lowe after he split from Reform UK. Other parts of the research showed just 16% of voters said they had heard from the Lib Dems in recent months, against 66% for Reform, while 3% said they had seen Davey on social media, compared with 20% for the Reform leader, Nigel Farage. In a round of media interviews on Sunday morning, Davey pushed back against the idea that the Lib Dems, who are static in national polling at about 12%, risked being forgotten in the political conversation amid the rise in prominence of Reform and the Greens. His party, Davey insisted, was making a genuine difference, and not just generating coverage without substance. “I’m talking about real change, not just talking about the bubbles,” he told the BBC’s Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg show. “We have been winning council elections for eight years in a row. That has never happened before – it’s the most successful period that we’ve had.” While there is no talk among Lib Dem MPs about a challenge to Davey, some say they are frustrated the party’s message is too vague and its support too reliant on tactical voting in a limited number of places, mainly in the south of England. One Lib Dem MP told a conference fringe event, at which More in Common’s findings were presented, that the party needed to expand the geographical and social range of its influence. “If we want to be a party of government, then we need to have a message for the whole country, not just parts of it,” said Tom Gordon, the MP for Harrogate and Knaresborough, one of just four Lib Dem-held seats in the north of England, against 58 in the south. Party figures see the conference as a chance to set out a more coherent and striking policy platform, including on the economy and immigration. But there is worry among some MPs that the problem is wider. “We already have quite a lot of policies, if people look at them,” one said. “It’s less about what you get if you vote Lib Dem than why you should – about what we represent. And people don’t really know that.” One longtime party activist said: “The voters only seem to properly notice us once every four years, when there’s an election. It’s a bit like being curling at the Winter Olympics – the rest of the time we’re forgotten. It would be good if we had a more distinctive message, and that needs boldness.”
