title: UK minister warns of impact of Trump’s Iran war on next month’s budget
summary: Bridget Phillipson says Burnham’s past criticisms of US president not an issue as PM prepares to meet Trump at UN
text: Next month’s budget will be made more difficult by Donald Trump’s war with Iran, one of Andy Burnham’s cabinet ministers has said, while adding she did not expect the prime minister’s previous disparaging comments about the US president to be an issue. Burnham is expected to meet Trump early next week at the UN general assembly summit in New York, the pair having previously spoken twice by phone since Burnham entered No 10. As Greater Manchester mayor, Burnham said Trump would not be welcome in the city, saying also that UK politicians who indulged him “should be ashamed”. Asked about the comments, Bridget Phillipson, the Labour chair and minister for women and equalities, told Sky News: “Look, I think what you’ve just described there is politics. The president knows that. This is far from unique. “People will express views at different points on different topics. And that’s no bar to having a strong relationship.” She nonetheless repeated UK condemnation of Trump’s on-and-off military campaign against Iran, which has disrupted global oil supplies, causing significant inflationary pressures, saying this would make life more difficult for John Healey, the chancellor, as he plans the budget. The economy was, Phillipson said, “in a strong position”, especially with growth figures. She said: “But that’s not to take away from the very real challenges that you identify, particularly where it’s come to the conflict we’ve seen in the Middle East and the impact that that’s been having on businesses and on families close to home. “We took the decision not to involve ourselves in that conflict. That was the right call. The US will take their own foreign policy decisions, but I believe, and still believe now, it was the right decision for us as a country not to get involved in that conflict. Of course, something that, had Kemi Badenoch and Nigel Farage been running the country, we would have jumped headlong into a conflict with it without end. “And yet, and we do see the consequences here at home and as we go into the budget, making sure that we are doing everything we can to give people that breathing space to tackle those challenges around the cost of living has been at the forefront of everything that Andy Burnham has done since becoming prime minister. “I know it’s at the forefront of the chancellor’s mind as he’s planning for that budget later on next month.” In a later interview with the BBC, Phillipson was dismissive of comments by Jim Ratcliffe, the petrochemicals billionaire, who said this week he had lost confidence in the UK due to levels of immigration and taxation. She said: “You’ll forgive me if I do take with a pinch of salt what someone who is a tax exile has to say about our country.” Ratcliffe is resident for tax in Monaco. Burnham has previously defended his comments about Trump in a similar way, saying of the US president: “Well, he’s said things as well, and everyone says things as politicians. In the moment, you meet people where they’re at, and you find a connection with people, and that’s always been my style.” With the wider UK-US relationship, there were “differences of opinion”, Phillipson said, while arguing that Burnham could see beyond those differences with Trump in maintaining invaluable ties. She said: “We don’t have the same political outlook, but the relationship between the UK and the US goes beyond any one president, any one prime minister. “It’s something that has stood the test of time over many centuries, despite political differences. They come and go. What matters most is the British national interest. And that’s what Andy Burnham will deliver for our country.”

title: Deaths of three women in sea at Brighton had no criminal involvement, police say
summary: Jane Adetoro, Christina Walters and Rebecca Walters from Uxbridge were found on 13 May
text: The deaths of three sisters found in the sea off Brighton beach did not involve any criminality or third-party involvement, police have concluded. The bodies of Jane Adetoro, 36, Christina Walters, 32, and Rebecca Walters, 31, from Uxbridge, west London, were found on 13 May. A postmortem conducted that month confirmed all three women died by drowning. Specialist detectives worked to trace the sisters’ final movements and understand how they came to be in the water that morning, Sussex police said. The investigation found all three women were dropped off by taxi at Madeira Drive, the road running along Brighton Beach, at 10.20pm on 12 May, wearing everyday clothing. No evidence was found to suggest they visited any nightclubs or local businesses in the area at the time and the investigation concluded all three women entered the water near to where their bodies were found, the police spokesperson added. A spokesperson for the force said: “The purpose of the police investigation was to identify any evidence of criminal offending linked to how the sisters came to be in the water or their subsequent deaths. “We can confirm the thorough police investigation has not found any evidence of a crime being committed or involvement by a third party.” Additional details such as the sisters’ specific movements before their deaths and their potential reasons for entering the water will be considered during the East Sussex coroner’s inquest. Ch Supt Adam Hays said his force had been “acutely aware of the speculation surrounding this incident” and “concerns raised by black communities surrounding the deaths of black people in or near bodies of water”. He said: “Jane, Rebecca and Christina’s tragic deaths sparked a national outpouring of grief, and I would like to thank everyone who supported our investigation by coming forward with information. We will now support the coronial process and ask that the sisters’ family continue to be given privacy to come to terms with their loss.” After the sisters’ deaths, their father, Joseph Jacobson, said there were days when the grief felt unbearable but that he held on to the memories they had shared and “the bond that death can never take away”. In a statement released through Sussex police, Jacobson said: “Jane, Christina and Becky were more than daughters to me: they were my joy, my strength and the beautiful light that filled our family with happiness and love. “Each of you was unique and precious in your own special way. Your smiles brightened dark days, your laughter brought comfort and your presence made life more meaningful. Though your time on Earth was short, the impact you made will remain in our hearts for ever.” A GoFundMe online fundraiser for the women’s funerals has received more than 2,200 donations from members of the public, totalling nearly £46,000.

title: Middle East braces for more violence as Iran claims US is planning to renew bombing campaign
summary: Tensions grow as Trump tells Fox News he is considering ‘wiping Iran out’ after attacks on Riyadh by Houthi rebels
text: Governments across the Middle East are bracing for an escalation of violence after Iran claimed it had received intelligence that the US was preparing for a renewed bombing campaign against the Islamic Republic. In a potential sign of growing tensions before the UN general assembly in New York this week, Donald Trump cut short a weekend visit to the Camp David presidential retreat on Sunday with no official explanation, and a new security alert was issued by the state department to all US citizens in the Middle East. Keeping his options open, Trump reportedly told a Fox News reporter “very big things are going to be happening in the not-so-distant future” and that the options he was considering were “wiping Iran out, letting them rot economically or making a deal”. The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps warned that if an attack does take place, “all US bases and interests in the region will become targets of continuous, effective and painful attacks without any limitations or considerations”. Iran’s leaders also pledged some of the reprisals could extend as far as US naval forces in the Indian Ocean, and accused some Gulf leaders of “double-dealing” by allegedly giving a green light to the US attacks. The outburst of sabre-rattling appears to have been prompted by attacks on the Saudi capital, Riyadh, by Yemen’s Iranian-backed Houthi rebels. The barrage on Saturday marked the first time the capital’s Aramco oil facilities had been subject to such a sustained attack since the Saudi-Houthi ceasefire broke down in June. Riyadh insisted it had intercepted the missiles, but local photographs show smoke pouring from the Aramco facility. The port of Yanbu, vital for Saudi oil exports, was also targeted. The US largely regards the Houthis as a proxy Iranian force and argues that the group’s attacks on Riyadh would not happen without Tehran’s approval, a claim Iran denies. Trump last week provoked profound questions about the level of US commitment to its Middle East allies when he spurned a call by the Saudi crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman, asking the US to come to Saudi’s direct military help. The Saudis wanted US aid after the Houthis suddenly captured strategic ports along Yemen’s west coast overlooking the Red Sea, giving the Houthis control of the Bab al-Mandab strait, the narrow waterway that takes commercial shipping through the Red Sea towards Asia. On the other side of the Arabian peninsular, the strait of Hormuz between Iran and Oman is already effectively closed to western traffic and the pressure on European energy supplies is growing by the day, leading states such as France to take emergency measures to prevent fuel shortages. In an attempt to keep the US out of its war with Saudi Arabia, the Houthis had given commitments to US officials that they would only target Saudi-related shipping in the Red Sea, a commitment that Trump appeared to regard as sufficient to ensure essential US interests would be protected and that the US need not become involved militarily. Pressure on the Pentagon budget and dwindling munitions supplies due to the Iran conflict have also made the US reluctant to broaden the theatre of war. Successive bombing campaigns have not dislodged the Houthis, whose lighting advance to the Red Sea coast took the Saudi-backed Yemeni forces by surprise. Trump appeared to disregard the wider security threat by telling Fox News: “The US is in constant contact with the Houthis and they have agreed not to go to war with the US.” The Houthi government said 318 ships passed through the strait from 10-18 September. France will summon Iran’s ambassador ⁠after Iranian ⁠authorities closed a French-language centre affiliated with its ‌embassy ‌in Tehran, the ‌foreign ministry said on Sunday. The Iranian judiciary accused the centre of conducting “illegal acts that violated diplomatic conventions”. The French foreign ministry said: “This new attack on the French cultural presence in Iran … is unjustifiable and unacceptable.” Trump is due to meet the six member states of the Gulf Cooperation Council when he attends the UN general assembly in New York, in a meeting that is likely to cover Iran, Yemen, Gaza and the future of the US security guarantee. Trump said he was also open to a meeting with Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, in New York, an encounter that would probably be rejected by the Iranians, who refuse to negotiate directly with the US, operating instead largely through mediators. Pezeshkian is one of many world leaders due to address a general assembly that is likely to be dominated, on the sidelines at least, by Trump’s Middle East crisis. In the first sign of a potential change of White House thinking about renewing US military action, the state department issued a security alert on Saturday to US citizens across the region warning that “the security environment remains complex with potential for unforeseen escalation. American citizens in the Middle East should exercise heightened vigilance.” Hizam al-Assad, a member of the Houthi political bureau, said the attacks on Riyadh are a response to “hundreds of airstrikes that Riyadh had carried out against the people of Yemen”. In a lengthy statement to parliament on Sunday, Mohammad Ghalibaf, Iran’s chief negotiator, insisted that Iran was not interested in waging a forever war with the US. But the new secretary of the supreme national security council, Mohsen Rezaei, a hardliner, told Al Jazeera that Iran’s seven preconditions for peace – which include the US lifting its blockade of Iran oil ports, the restoration of its frozen assets and the lifting of sanctions on Iranian oil exports – remained. Rezaei also expressed his anger with the Gulf states, saying they had been invited to a meeting in Salahah in Oman last week to approve the agreed Oman-Iran plan for a new authorised shipping route through the strait of Hormuz, but Saudi Arabia rejected attendance. He said: “We invited them to the Salahah meeting and they reciprocated with a secret meeting in Germany with US Central Command and Israel.” Despite the Houthi victories last week, forces allied to the UN-recognised government of Yemen claimed to be pushing back against the Houthis across the country with 75 Houthi soldiers killed on Saturday alone.

title: Andy Burnham faces a weakened Trump – but the president remains unpredictable
summary: PM hopes to be firmer with US leader than his predecessor without provoking diplomatic warfare, as the Iran war weighs on the UK economy
text: No international relationship has more power to determine the success of Andy Burnham’s premiership. So you might imagine the stakes for the prime minister’s first face-to-face meeting with Donald Trump on Tuesday would be high. Yet Burnham may prove to be a lucky general. The balance of risk has shifted. Trump is unpopular at home, where inflation remains high, and is mired in an intractable conflict in Iran that has the potential to sink his midterm dreams. When Keir Starmer first visited Trump in February 2025, the situation could not have been more different. The notoriously unpredictable president had just won the US election and was at the height of his powers – and was showing muscle on Nato and Ukraine, and with threats of tariffs. Starmer’s “keep calm and carry on” strategy helped keep Trump on board the defence alliance and also protected the UK from the worst of his aggression over trade. But it came with a cost: he was often left looking obsequious and at odds with the national mood. Burnham defended his predecessor’s approach but in June signalled he would take a different direction. “Obviously the relationship is important to the UK, but not to the point where we just go along with anything they say,” he said. “We’ve got in trouble in the past when that happens.” Downing Street insiders expect Burnham to be a bit more forceful when he feels there’s a need to stand up for British interests. But there is no suggestion he will follow the more combative approach of Mark Carney, the Canadian prime minister. Instead, one source said he would probably take a “third way” between Starmer and Carney, pushing back more than his predecessor publicly and privately, but avoiding open diplomatic warfare. A second source said the prime minister had three ambitions for Tuesday’s talks: bond with Trump, make the case for Ukraine, and avoid any drama. Early clues about how the talks might go from the White House perspective have been mixed. In June, Trump suggested Burnham was “extremely liberal” (not as a compliment) and dismissively described him as the “mayor of a town”. The US president remains angry the UK did not join his strikes on Iran, and has attacked the country as a “dying” nation “on the edge of disaster”. More recent comments that he might not help if Argentina again tried to seize the Falklands, and that he would love to see a united Ireland, suggest his displeasure has not abated. But that will not necessarily translate into a strained personal relationship with Burnham. The pair have spoken on the phone twice and are said to have got on. The prime minister’s laid-back, confident style is likely to go down well with Trump, who has already shown with the New York mayor, Zohran Mamdani, that he can warm to leftwingers. On policy too, government insiders point to small reasons for hope: Trump responded warmly to reports the UK government was going to “open up” the North Sea (although the decision to drill at two fields has been delayed) and has – so far – been relatively restrained when asked about the UK’s planned West Bank settlement trade ban. Their meeting will be fraught with tension over both matters, and other areas – such as defence spending and the Iran war – have potential for further clashes. It will help Burnham that Tuesday’s talks will be held on the comparatively neutral ground of the UN, rather than at the White House. As such, he will avoid the jeopardy of an Oval Office press conference that Trump could easily derail. Trump may also decide he has had enough fights for one day. His meeting with Burnham will follow his address to the UN. Last year Trump told world leaders their countries were “going to hell” over their immigration policies. The UK meeting may end up as just a sideshow. Burnham’s views on Trump have also shifted since he took office. As mayor of Greater Manchester, he said the US president would not be welcome in the city, blaming his “poisonous” politics. After winning his seat as an MP in Makerfield, he warned against the “divided, dark politics” of the US. But over the summer, Burnham appeared to shrug off potential divisions, telling reporters that “everyone says things as politicians”. The new prime minister said he would “say what I feel” to Trump but – crucially – would also try to “find a connection” with the mercurial president. With Trump now weaker domestically, political power in the US is starting to shift to who comes next. Burnham is walking into the room with a president who is running out of time. Yet Trump is in power for two more years, and he is nothing if not unpredictable. Burnham’s priority may be on domestic affairs, but his closest aides acknowledge that the biggest weight on the UK right now is Trump’s war in Iran. While the war continues to wreak damage on the British economy, Burnham will struggle to deliver his promises of change. So for the time being, the power still rests with Trump, and Burnham may yet find he has to navigate a perilous path as Starmer did before him.

title: Friedrich Merz vows to stay in office after CDU ‘disaster’ in German state elections
summary: Far-right AfD wins in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and leftwing Die Linke on course for victory in Berlin
text: Germany’s embattled chancellor, Friedrich Merz, has vowed to stay in office and fight for future-proofing economic changes despite heavy losses for his conservatives in two state elections, one to the far right and the other to a leftwing party. Preliminary results indicated Merz’s Christian Democratic Union (CDU) tallied just 4.9% in the coastal region of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, below ⁠the 5% threshold needed to enter the state parliament and indicating they may be excluded altogether. It would be the CDU’s worst-ever state score, which Merz called a “disaster”. The anti-immigration, Kremlin-friendly Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) party extended a streak of strong showings by coming in first in the former communist region with 38.3%, more than doubling its previous score, according to projections on ARD public television. In the capital, Berlin, one of Germany’s 16 federal states, the far-left Die Linke looked on course to win with about 25% of the vote, ahead of the incumbent CDU by a five-point margin. The AfD made headway there too, with a clear double-digit result. The deeply unpopular Merz has been fighting for his political survival after a humiliating series of setbacks with voters this year. Speculation about his ability to hold on as chancellor reached fever pitch after Saxony-Anhalt state’s AfD chapter routed the CDU with a record 44% for the party in an election two weeks ago. The Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania result marked the third time the AfD has emerged as the strongest party in a region, although the party seemed likely to remain shut out of power in the state because of a “firewall” of non-cooperation agreed by the other main parties. In a rare speech on a state election night, Merz admitted the CDU had been bitterly deprived of “tailwinds from Berlin” in both of Sunday’s races. But he said he would remain chancellor and party chair and continue a reform drive on fronts including taxes, healthcare, pensions and reducing bureaucracy. Merz said the German economy was facing “profound upheaval”, while public discourse had become “harsher and more irreconcilable”. “Trust in our country’s institutions is waning and is being actively undermined by radical parties on both the left and the right,” he said. But he added: “Germany is capable of reform. I would even go so far as to say that these reforms are the antidote to the poison of authoritarianism, which is penetrating ever deeper into our society as the fascination with authoritarianism grows.” A jubilant AfD co-leader, Tino Chrupalla, mocked Merz before his speech, saying voters had given his own party a “very clear result” and called on the chancellor to resign. About 2.5 million people were eligible to vote in Berlin and nearly 1.3 million in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. The stinging blows from the latest elections had been expected to put pressure on Merz at a minimum to cede the CDU leadership, which would have in effect ruled out a run for re-election at the next national poll, due in 2029. Merz’s eroding support has created a sense of instability in Europe’s top economy, which is struggling with deindustrialisation, sluggish growth and soaring energy costs. If the AfD’s surge led Merz to abandon the chancellery prematurely, it would give the far right further momentum as France, Italy, Spain and Poland head into elections next year with nativist parties on the march. Germany has high constitutional hurdles to replacing a chancellor against their will and any appointed successor would need to demonstrate a ruling majority. A failure to do so could trigger a new election. The AfD is the biggest opposition force in parliament and is leading national opinion polls with about 30%. It has called for Germany to quit the euro, end support for Ukraine and carry out mass deportations of “irregular” migrants, while citing the “destruction” of the CDU as one of its central goals. The CDU’s debacle in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania – a small, relatively poor state – is particularly bitter for Merz as it was home to the constituency of his arch-rival, Angela Merkel. While she governed Germany for 16 years, Merz appears to be on the ropes after no more than 16 months. Merz took office in May 2025 at the helm of a coalition with the centre-left Social Democrats (SPD) promising to restore the German economy to strength and slash the AfD’s support. A failure to make decisive headway on either front has produced profound disappointment in his leadership, with only one in 10 Germans saying they are satisfied with his performance. An inability to connect with voters appears particularly marked in the former communist east, where the AfD is strongest. In Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, the Social Democratic party state premier, Manuela Schwesig, distanced herself during the campaign from a key pension change backed by her party in Merz’s coalition government. She was expected to hold on to power in a left-leaning coalition even if the AfD came out on top when all the votes were counted. Despite leading the polls for months, the far right failed to garner enough support to govern alone and the remaining parties have ruled out working with it. A confirmed win by Die Linke in Berlin, where the far-left party has called for expropriation of corporate landlords to fight rising housing costs, could see its candidate, Elif Eralp, become the capital’s first leader of Turkish origin.

title: Feeling ‘forced out’ by Badenoch? Lib Dems conference welcomes young Tory defectors
summary: Self-described moderates say Ed Davey’s party offers them a home as Conservatives shift further right
text: Climbing the party-branded stairs of the Brighton Centre with a Liberal Britain tote bag over his shoulder, Cody Butler looks quite at home at the Liberal Democrats’ annual jamboree. But asked how he is finding it, the 21-year-old replied: “Odd.” The former Tory activist resigned as chair of the One Nation Conservative Network and left his old party in July, arguing that centrists, remainers and members worried about the climate crisis and conservation were no longer welcome in the party. A week ago, he joined the Lib Dems. “There is no easy way to describe joining a new political party, because it’s like finding a new family,” he said. “I was brought up in a Conservative association. I was the local Tory boy. So it’s great, but odd.” Butler is one of several youthful former Tories who have publicly defected to Britain’s third party and are in the process of setting up a new group: the One Nation Liberals. It’s a growing group, with other potential defectors believed to be waiting to see if they can survive in Kemi Badenoch’s increasingly rightwing party. Butler has been joined by Josh Bancroft, a former Tory councillor on Cannock Chase council, who left the party to join the Lib Dems earlier this month. “Moderates like me have been forced out of the big tent over the past few years,” he said. “My politics haven’t changed, but the party has.” The 26-year-old said moderates looking for the exit have grown in number since Badenoch embarked on a purge of the Conservative parliamentary party. In July, the Tory leader warned that anyone who supported net zero targets or Britain’s membership of the European convention on human rights would be blocked from standing as a candidate in the next election. The former minister Gavin Barwell lost the whip, and another former cabinet member, Grant Shapps, was blocked from standing again for the party. “The Conservatives have taken leaps to the right and left me and millions of voters behind,” Bancroft added. “The Liberal Democrats can be and should be their new political home.” Bancroft and Butler have been welcomed with open arms into the Liberal ranks, with one MP joking that Badenoch had become the Lib Dems’ most effective recruiter. During a Q&A on the first full day of the conference, party leader Ed Davey repeatedly mentioned Badenoch, referencing her decision to freeze out members and MPs who support net zero policies. “Unlike Kemi Badenoch, who thinks there wasn’t a problem with this summer’s heatwaves, we actually realise you have to take action on climate change and we’re leading that debate,” he said. Despite being stuck at about 11% in national polling, many Liberal Democrat activists and MPs in Brighton are talking with atypical swagger about cementing the foundations of the so-called orange wall. They point to the 72 seats they won in the last election, making them the largest third party in British politics for over a century. And of the 27 seats where the Lib Dems came second in 2024, 20 were taken by the Conservatives. When asked if reaching 100 seats by taking those targets was the aim, Davey insisted there was “no ceiling” to the Liberal Democrats’ ambitions. “If we have great local councillors, great local candidates and great local campaigners, we can beat Reform, the Tories, Labour, Green, the SNP, anyone. We can win anywhere where there’s a multiparty fight.” On Sunday, Davey explicitly ruled out any future pact with the Tories. But when asked about an arrangement with Labour, he said maximising the number of Lib Dem MPs would give his party a stronger hand in any future negotiations. “That means you have to box really smartly,” he said. While that prospect may have some pure-blood Tories running for the hills, it could lure others into the Liberal Democrat ranks, argued Butler. “It used to be that if you wanted power you could only join the Conservatives or Labour, but that reality doesn’t exist any more in a five-party system,” he said. “My message to other One Nation Conservatives is: you can be true to what you believe, and if you back the Liberal Democrats, you’re actually backing the future kingmakers of government. They will write the budget. The Conservatives won’t.”

title: Man, 82, dies after brawl with 76-year-old over sunlounger on Greek beach
summary: Row at Athenian riviera resort turned violent after two elderly bathers reportedly argued over shortage of loungers
text: Greek police are investigating the death of an 82-year-old man after a brawl over a sunlounger at a beach on the Athenian riviera. The man had arrived at the popular bathing spot of Vouliagmeni before 10am on Sunday hoping to secure a sunbed, but he soon began arguing with a fellow bather – described by authorities as a “76-year-old man unknown to him” – when it became clear loungers were in short supply. The row quickly degenerated into a scuffle as others reportedly joined in. The victim, who was with his wife, is believed to have suffered a cardiac arrest during the fight. “It seems that people who were with [the assailant] also participated,” ERT, the country’s state broadcaster, reported. “The 82-year-old was seriously injured, and needed to be transferred by ambulance to Asklepieion hospital in Voula. “Despite the efforts of doctors, at about 11am the elderly man succumbed to his wounds.” A postmortem was immediately ordered. Police arrested the 76-year-old and, initially, a 21-year-old woman who was with him. The beach resort’s manager was also detained for questioning. “The incident is under investigation,” said a source, describing the fight as unprecedented. “In Greece disagreement is expressed vocally, with a lot of screaming and shouting, not in fistfights like this – especially between two elderly men. I think that’s why it is so shocking.” Like other parts of Europe, Greece is undergoing a severe cost of living crisis that has heightened tensions and put strain on social relations. An increase in domestic violence and other disputes has been partly blamed on the pressures of everyday life. In recent years, there has been growing anger over private rental outfits hogging prime coastal areas with exorbitantly priced sunloungers in Greece, where the sea has an important place in national identity. Authorities said “all those” involved in the incident would appear before a magistrate.

title: House Republican doubles down on jab at Trump’s immigration enforcement
summary: Florida’s María Elvira Salazar warns Trump that advisers are ‘compromising his legacy’ and not showing ‘whole picture’
text: María Elvira Salazar, the Republican congresswoman who has accused the president of going too far on immigration enforcement, doubled down on her criticism of the administration on Sunday, warning Donald Trump that some of his advisers were “compromising his legacy”. In an interview with CBS News’s Face the Nation, the Florida representative who is locked in a tight race for re-election pleaded with the US president not to “squander” his relationship with Hispanic voters. Though she couched her remarks as criticism of top administration advisers, it was clear that her focus was on Trump’s much-vaunted ambition to carry out the largest mass deportation of undocumented immigrants in US history. “I’m forewarning him and advising him as a member of Congress from the south Florida area that some of his advisers are just not presenting the whole picture,” she said. Asked by Face the Nation whether she were referring to Tom Homan, Trump’s “border czar”, or Stephen Miller, the White House deputy chief of staff who has spearheaded the removal of undocumented children, Salazar placed the onus on Trump. “He is the only elected official in the White House. He is the one who has to determine who he listens and who he does not listen to. He is the president.” Last week Salazar became a rare voice of internal criticism within the Republican party towards Trump when she released a 30-second advert pointing out that even law-abiding undocumented immigrants were getting caught up in the aggressive federal sweep. The ad said: “In July, 50% of the 50,000 people that were detained had no criminal record. Be careful what your advisers are telling you about immigration policy … The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today.” Salazar’s warning has been backed up by a slew of recent opinion polls that show many Hispanic voters who helped re-elect Trump in 2024 are now turning away from him. They are being repulsed by the rising cost of living and concern about his handling of the economy, as well as by the hardline immigration drive that has led to many hardworking, taxpaying undocumented immigrants being rounded up, detained and deported. In her CBS News interview, Salazar described herself as “a proud Republican”. “I’m first-generation American, and I want to preserve the American values that are entrenched in the [Republican party] and that the Hispanics share”. She is currently facing a tough re-election battle in her Miami-area district against her Democratic challenger, Eliott Rodriguez, despite having won in 2024 by 20 points. Trump also won the district by 15 points that year. Salazar told CBS News that 70% of Americans wanted to see some type of immigration reform. She also pushed back on the administration’s deportation of all undocumented immigrants irrespective of their criminal status. “The average America understands the difference between the narco and the nanny, and the gangster and the gardener.” On Saturday, Trump responded to Salazar’s criticisms, saying: “She obviously doesn’t have a very strong feeling about the border. I do.” He added: “Without me, she wouldn’t have gotten elected.” By breaking her silence on immigration, Salazar has put a spotlight on rising fears within Republican circles that the displeasure of Hispanic voters towards the administration’s policies could cost the party dear in November’s midterm elections. Several House seats in Colorado, Florida, Texas, Nevada and other states could be tipped in the Democrats’ favor as a result. Steve Scalise, the second-most powerful Republican in the US House, acknowledged on ABC News’s This Week that immigration was creating divisions within his party. Asked what he thought of Salazar’s comment that many Hispanic voters feel betrayed, he said: “I don’t necessarily agree with that statement.” He added: “When you look at what María said, obviously we have a lot of disagreements in Congress … Even among Republicans we have disagreements on how to actually get to the secure border that we have.”

title: European spy chiefs warn Moscow is planning more decisive action against Nato
summary: Exclusive: Intelligence officers say Russian campaign could intensify ‘in months, not years’ – but that panic risks playing into Kremlin psy-ops
text: European intelligence officials have raised the possibility of an imminent Russian test of Nato, with one saying a potential attack could come in a matter of “months, not years”. The warnings come after Poland’s prime minister, Donald Tusk, told parliament that intelligence assessments suggested Russia might launch an attack with drones or missiles on Nato territory in the coming months, as part of efforts to prove that “article 5 is more theoretical than practical”. The French president, Emmanuel Macron, called Tusk’s warnings “sound and well-documented”, and on Friday summoned party leaders and 2027 presidential candidates for an emergency meeting in Paris, where they discussed – among other topics – intelligence of a growing threat from Russia. The escalation fears come as the UN general assembly convenes in New York later this week, and amid intensifying airstrikes on both sides of Russia’s war on Ukraine. Kyiv hit Moscow and other Russian regions with hundreds of drones and missiles in the early hours of Sunday, in one of its biggest air attacks of the war. In separate interviews with the Guardian over the past week, in different locations, three European intelligence leaders discussed their views of the potential threat from Moscow. Michal Koudelka, the head of the Czech Republic’s BIS security service, said that as well as increased drone activity, a small-scale invasion of Nato territory that bordered Russia could be part of the Kremlin’s plans. “It’s possible. It could involve a limited incursion, false-flag provocations, a massive influence campaign,” he said, in a rare interview at the agency’s headquarters in Prague. He said this scenario could play out in a matter of “months, not years” but added that “a lot of people are doing everything they can to make sure this doesn’t happen”. Officials in the three Baltic countries, which border Russian territory, have been more cautious about the prospect of an invasion or other serious escalation, citing Moscow’s stretched resources in Ukraine and warning that playing up the prospect of an attack might play into the Kremlin’s hands. “We don’t see indications of an imminent attack,” said Normunds Mežviets, the director general of the VDD, Latvia’s state security service, in an interview at the agency’s headquarters in Riga. He conceded there were signs that Moscow was making preparations for more decisive action in Europe, but said it was not clear whether the plans were simply part of a destabilisation strategy. “It’s still an open question if they have direct and concrete plans or if it’s just within the context of their overall attempts to spread fear and uncertainty in western society,” he said. Baltic politicians, who for many years criticised western Europe for being soft on Russia, now find themselves in the strange position of telling some western leaders to calm down in their public messaging, fearing that talk of an imminent invasion could prove damaging to their societies and economies. On Saturday, the secretary general of Estonia’s foreign ministry, Jonatan Vseviov, decried “panic on social media” in recent days about a possible attack. “If there is reason to fear an attack, rest assured: we will make that clear. Until then, keep calm, carry on and support Ukraine,” he wrote on X. Mežviets said that, overall, it was good that western Europe had woken up to the threat from Russia. “Before 2022, we constantly warned our western European partners about the threat from Russia, but most of the time our voices were not listened to. In 2022, the approach of our partners changed. They said it turns out the Balts and the Poles had been right,” he said. Neither Mežviets nor Koudelka would discuss what specific intelligence might have been obtained about Russia’s supposed planning for the coming months, nor would they comment on whether a surprise trip by the CIA director, John Ratcliffe, to Moscow last month – during which he stopped off in Riga – was partly to warn the Kremlin about the dangers of launching an attack on Nato. After that visit, the Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, dismissed rumours of a Russian attack on Nato. “It has nothing to do with reality and nothing to do with the intentions of the Russian Federation,” he said. However, many in Europe will have the build up to the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 in the back of their minds, when US officials repeatedly warned Russia was preparing to invade and the Kremlin repeatedly denied it. As the full-scale war that ensued approaches its fifth winter, US-led efforts to bring about peace in Ukraine show no signs of success, with Russia and Ukraine intensifying their drone and missile strikes on each other. Ukraine has destroyed much of Russia’s oil infrastructure, targeting refineries and other facilities over recent months. Moscow has frequently said the provision to Ukraine of weaponry, intelligence and military advisers makes western countries participants in the war and legitimate targets, but has so far avoided action that might provoke a coordinated response from Nato. Instead, it has launched what western agencies describe as a campaign of sabotage against targets in countries that are the loudest backers of Ukraine, and one-off incidents apparently meant to test boundaries, such as when more than a dozen drones, flying without ammunition, veered into Polish airspace a year ago. Koudelka said the current Russian tactic was “escalate to de-escalate”, with the Kremlin keen to push at weak points in western societies to tamp down their support for Ukraine’s war effort. “They believe if they escalate enough, then European countries will decide not to support Ukraine,” he said. In recent weeks the Trump administration has made another attempt to kickstart peace negotiations in Ukraine. As well as the Ratcliffe visit to Moscow, the US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner made another trip to Moscow, as well as a first-time trip to Kyiv. While Donald Trump has frequently claimed the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, is interested in a deal, there is scepticism in Europe that the Kremlin has any interest in good-faith negotiations. “I haven’t seen any signs that there is a serious consideration in Moscow about real negotiations,” said Thomas Nilsson, the head of Sweden’s military intelligence and security service, in an interview on the sidelines of a conference in Riga. “My assessment is that they are still thinking that they could achieve their strategic objectives, so they are just playing negotiation theatre,” he added. All three intelligence bosses said that whatever else happened, Russia’s campaign of sabotage in Europe is likely to intensify in the coming months. Nilsson described as a “gamechanger” the recent armed drone incident at Leipzig airport, which German authorities have attributed to Russian intelligence. “To have an armed UAV drone sent in to a busy airport in the middle of Europe … If you have attacks that could result in losses of life or losses of very critical infrastructure that have a huge implication for society, I think that is a gamechanger,” he said. Mežviets said Russia was moving from randomised targeting of sabotage and arson attacks intended to sow panic to specific targets linked to western backing for Ukraine. “We see them looking to attack railway infrastructure, Ukraine support infrastructure. Right now we see a move towards defence industry targets,” he said. “If you do this then the psy-op effect is reached anyway, so you get both things in one,” he added. Nilsson said there were several goals behind the recent intensification of Russian sabotage activity: to reduce support for Ukraine, to introduce splits in Nato and to alarm European populations. “I think Moscow would love Nato to have endless discussion about article 4 consultations, but coming up with no actions,” he said. Koudelka said another effect of the sabotage campaign is the stretch on resources of intelligence services, as doubts often linger even when incidents are caused by other factors. “Now every fire or every malfunction needs to be investigated by intelligence services as a potential terror attack, and that is a good result for them,” he said.

title: ‘An out-of-touch Silicon Valley radical’: meet Trump’s AI whisperer pushing for limited regulation
summary: David Sacks convinced Trump against any restrictions on AI – putting the White House out of step with its own party
text: As lawmakers from both sides of the aisle in the US have joined together calling for the regulation of powerful artificial intelligence models, one of the few vocal naysayers has been Donald Trump. He’s called the perceived dangers of the technology a “hoax” and a “scam”, arguing that the government already has “tremendous CRIMINAL and REGULATORY power over these companies”. It’s a starkly different stance from those of his former adviser Steve Bannon, the Republican Texas senator Ted Cruz and even the heads of the world’s leading AI companies. But it’s directly in line with the opinion of David Sacks – a prominent billionaire venture capitalist and Trump’s onetime AI and crypto czar, who has pushed back publicly and forcefully against recent claims of an impending AI apocalypse. Sacks, who believes regulation will erase the US lead in the global AI race, is seen as Trump’s AI whisperer – the adviser with the greatest influence in the White House on the topic. Time and again, he’s counseled the president to give a soft touch to AI regulation, helping push executive orders and other measures aimed at loosening restrictions on the technology. He also maintains direct financial stakes in multiple AI companies. On Friday, more than 100 AI researchers, professors and technologists signed a public letter urging third-party evaluations of AI models and outlining how that should be done. The signatories included some of the most notable experts in the field, such as Geoffrey Hinton, the “godfather of AI”, and Stuart Russell, a renowned AI computer scientist. Sacks, in characteristic form, dismissed the letter on social media, calling third-party evaluations “pseudoscience” and “censorship and control”. “The last time we had media-generated panics like this (with Russiagate and Covid), social media companies created ‘trust & safety’ teams to censor conservative and dissident voices,” Sacks wrote. “These groups haven’t earned our trust, and their agenda is not our safety.” The next day, Trump proclaimed he would soon create an “AI Force” headed by an AI czar, Sacks’ previous title. It’s not clear if the venture capitalist will assume the mantle again, but he was quick to respond on X, praising Trump’s efforts and deriding a potential pause on AI once again. Derailing AI safety efforts Last December, Trump signed an executive order to halt state laws that limited AI. It was one of the first of several actions by the president that put his alignment with Sacks on full display. The proclamation assigned a federal taskforce to have the “sole responsibility” of challenging states that attempt to pass laws restricting the technology. The order spelled out an influential role for Sacks to direct the taskforce’s litigation against states. Then, just four months later, in March, the White House unveiled an AI policy for Congress that encouraged lawmakers to pre-empt state rules. Again, Sacks was seen as working behind the scenes to make this happen. This pattern has continued throughout the year. In July, Trump and Sacks hosted a fanfare-filled AI summit in Washington. And just this week, Trump called Nvidia’s CEO, Jensen Huang, to discuss AI regulation. In a live demonstration of Sacks’ proximity to the most powerful people in the US, the call came in while Sacks was interviewing Huang at an event on stage. Next week, Trump is hosting China’s leader, Xi Jinping, at the White House and is expected to invite several AI CEOs to be present. Sacks is also slated to be one of the guests in attendance, according to NBC News. Isabel Sunderland, the policy lead for technology reform at the non-profit Issue One, said that Sacks’ relationship with the president shows what happens when money can buy a direct line to power. “David Sacks advising President Trump on AI shows exactly how our political system serves the wealthy and well-connected instead of everyday Americans,” Sunderland said. “This is about more than just AI regulation – it’s about who’s allowed to write the rules.” Trump’s most recent full-throated opposition to AI regulation comes after an Anthropic employee, Jacob Coxon, announced on social media last week that he was resigning from the company, saying AI would soon become “superhuman systems” that could cause human extinction by 2030. After Coxon’s post, other Anthropic employees backed these predictions, with one saying: “We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” The end-of-the-world prognostications whipped up a frenzy of media and lawmakers’ attention over the past two weeks, with US politicians, heads of state and international bodies calling for the tech to be reined in. Dario Amodei, the CEO of Anthropic, issued a proposal to slow down the technology’s advancement and ensure public safety by regulating the industry. In a rare public display of unity, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Google DeepMind chief Demis Hassabis and xAI owner Elon Musk agreed. Sacks, however, pushed back on any regulatory action, instead indicating the proposal was an “election-season psyop” and a bid for “regulatory capture”. In a lengthy social media post responding to Amodei’s proposal, Sacks said: “If the unreleased models are scary enough that you think you should slow down, I support your decision to be responsible. But stop pretending you need anyone else’s permission.” Sacks’ political evolution Sacks, like his tech contemporaries Elon Musk and Peter Thiel, hails from South Africa. He was born in Cape Town in 1972 and then emigrated with his family to the US in the late 1970s. Sacks spent his college career majoring in economics at Stanford, where he met Thiel and worked with him at the conservative student-run newspaper the Stanford Review. The two men also collaborated after graduating, co-authoring in 1995 the book The Diversity Myth: Multiculturalism and the Politics of Intolerance at Stanford, an early glimpse into Sacks’ political ideology. The book rails against “multiculturalism”, “diversity” and the “politically correct” decline of higher education. By the late 90s and early 2000s, Sacks, Thiel, Musk and others worked together at PayPal, becoming members of what’s now known as the PayPal Mafia – an elite group of influential and wealthy tech investors and founders. After founding and working at various startups over the years, Sacks co-founded Craft Ventures in 2017. The fund has raised hundreds of millions for tech companies and has investments in an array of businesses, including SpaceX, Anduril, Palantir, Meta, Airbnb, Lyft and dozens of AI startups. As of 2023, Sacks said the firm’s assets under management totaled $3.3bn. Around the same time as founding Craft Ventures, Sacks started to get more into politics. While he donated to Hillary Clinton’s 2016 bid for president, he quickly pivoted to backing mostly Republican candidates and causes. In March 2020, Sacks launched the popular and influential All-In tech podcast with three other Silicon Valley investors who lean conservative and trumpet capitalist values. Vanity Fair profiled their annual All-In summit in 2025, calling the gathering a “fever-dream capitalist bacchanal where the faithful can stop being ‘guilt-tripped by this woke mind virus’ and get into ‘founder mode’”. Since then, Sacks’ rightward stances and political giving have deepened, according to a profile in the Atlantic. He donated to JD Vance, Blake Masters, Ron DeSantis and Robert F Kennedy Jr, campaign finance filings show. In June 2024, Sacks threw a fundraiser for Trump at his $45m French-limestone mansion in San Francisco’s Pacific Heights. Tickets went for $500,000 per couple. “President Trump is relaxed, happy, and cracking jokes about AI,” Harmeet Dhillon, assistant attorney general at Trump’s Department of Justice, posted on social media from the event. The AI czar’s time in the White House After Trump won the presidency, he named Sacks his AI and crypto czar, a newly created role. The position, as a “special government employee”, only allowed Sacks to work for the administration for a maximum of 130 days a year, but exempted him from confirmation hearings or financial disclosure requirements. The office of government ethics did require Craft Ventures to divest in some of its AI holdings, though. In March, Sacks said he was leaving the position, but he’s since maintained close ties with the president. In May, he successfully urged Trump to scrap an executive order that would’ve subjected AI models to government review. And in July, the two men hosted the AI summit in Washington. At the event, the president delivered an “AI action plan”, once again aimed at relaxing restrictions on the development and deployment of the technology. Sacks’ influence on Trump has rankled other senior administration officials, according to the Wall Street Journal. Scott Bessent and Susie Wiles have both voiced concerns about the effects of AI on the country and have advised Trump to mandate increased oversight on the technology. But the president has consistently sided with Sacks on the issue. Critics say that Trump and Sacks are out of step with the American public on safeguarding AI, even among Republicans. A May poll by Bryson Gillette Insights for the AI safety group Future of Life Institute, found that 85% of Republicans say they support Trump taking strong action to ensure AI is developed and deployed safely. “Running the David Sacks playbook on AI might be the biggest miscalculation the Trump administration has made,” Sacha Haworth, the executive director of the Tech Oversight Project, said. “He is an out-of-touch Silicon Valley radical who wants to replace humans with machines. You cannot put this guy in charge and not expect to pay a political price. Republicans are going to follow big tech executives right over a cliff.” Sacks and the White House did not respond to requests for comment.

title: Our understanding of the slave trade is still evolving | Letters
summary: Letters: Readers respond to William Pettigrew’s article about the lasting significance of the slave trade to Britain’s politics, economy, institutions and culture
text: William Pettigrew’s book, Britain’s Slave Traders: A Forgotten History, adds a further dimension and depth to our understanding of how entrenched and significant Britain’s involvement in the transatlantic slave trade was. The landmark University College London’s Legacies of British Slavery project previously documented the “compensation” payments to 46,000 persons who, at the time of its abolition in 1834, had a financial interest in slave ownership – the £20m paid out is generally reckoned to be worth around £17bn at 2019 prices, or 40% of total government expenditure in 1834 – a vast national debt that was only fully amortised in 2015. The earlier study thus highlighted the extensive involvement of sections of the British public in profiting from slavery, and the further financial benefit from “compensation”. The recent study tracks back into the prior history from the beginning of the transatlantic slave trade through the 18th century, and shows how its tentacles throughout that time reached out deep into the economy and society. The economic impact over this whole period should not be underestimated. As Pettigrew observes (Slavery was not a footnote to British history. It helped shape the nation, 14 September), the slave trade provided some of the seed funding for the Industrial Revolution. The flow of income back from the Caribbean sugar plantations provided capital surpluses to fund new industries, through an expanded banking system, not to mention personal wealth. Defending these assets in turn stimulated the growth of the British navy, and its eventual control of the seas. Until American independence in 1776, the colonists relying on enslaved people for their cotton and coffee plantations were British settlers, paying taxes to the British exchequer. In the 19th century, “compensation” payouts fed into investments in the new railways; into banking; and into the funding of stately homes and the arts. Taken together, it could therefore be reasonably argued it was the slave trade that made Britain the cradle of the Industrial Revolution. Chris Hendry Emeritus professor, City, University of London • William Pettigrew is right that slavery was not a footnote to British history. His account powerfully demonstrates how the slave trade was entangled with the state, finance, politics and culture. But there is a further question: what about class? Pettigrew speaks of “Britain” and says “we are all – in some way – connected to it”. Yet Britain was never a single social actor. The slave owner, merchant and investor had a fundamentally different relationship to slavery from the growing cotton-mill proletariat whose labour helped turn slave-grown cotton into commodities. The danger is that “we are all connected” obscures the asymmetry of accumulation between those who owned capital and accumulated wealth from the system, and those who possessed only their labour and received wages. The question is not simply how slavery shaped Britain, but how its wealth entered an expanding capitalist economy – and was distributed through profoundly unequal class relations. David Eaton Sunderland • The Guardian’s excellent presentation of the findings of the Register of British Slave Traders (What is the Register of British Slave Traders and whom does it identify?, 14 September) highlighted what has been long known. It is also timely if it persuades anyone to question the thinking that underlies the philosophy shared by most western leaders that “western democracy” shines out in a challenging world, representing the best of humanity. Historians know that this is based on contradictions. The world’s first known democracy, the dazzling civilisation of ancient Athens, was based both on slavery and on a thoroughly undemocratic empire, the Delian League. Slavery has been practised across history by all types of government from despotic monarchies to republics and democracies. Put this alongside the fact that the democratic rights we now enjoy had to be extracted, sometimes by force, from the ruling class, and we might have a more humble evaluation of the place of our civilisation in the world. As Gandhi famously said when asked what he thought of western civilisation, “It would be a good idea”. Dr Peter Purton Southall, London • As slavery was abolished, poor laws were enacted across England. A distinction began to be established between those deemed to be worthy of charity and those who were not. The workhouse consolidated the form and substance of these differences. Distinctions established then persist today in ideas about the undeserving and deserving poor, scroungers and strivers, immigrant and indigenous labour. Rod Earle Guildford, Surrey • Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Please email us your letter and it will be considered for publication in our letters section.

title: Dirty clothes but a clean conscience | Brief letters
summary: Brief letters: Eco-friendly cleaning products | The UK’s Eurovision performances | Unravelling isles | Clothes for painting
text: I have shared the suffering that Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett faced as the veg box was finally cancelled (It’s my self-care tip of the year: I quit our local veg box scheme, and set my mind free, 16 September). But that is only the beginning. I struggle with grimy clothes and soiled dishes as I reluctantly persevere with eco washing and laundry products. As I gallantly scrub at stains and unmoved matter after a very expensive premium eco wash, the only thing that seems clean is my conscience. Chris Kington Cambridge • Maybe the solution to Britain’s poor performance at Eurovision (UK to answer for its ‘dismal record’ in Eurovision before committee of MPs, 18 September) is to admit that we, as a nation, are unpopular in Europe and our next, if not annual, entry should be a take on the Millwall FC refrain, sung to the tune of Sailing: “We are Britain / No one likes us / We don’t care”. Colin Burke Cartmel, Cumbria • What might we call the process by which the smaller nations depart the United Kingdom described by Simon Jenkins (Slowly then all at once: this emboldened Celtic alliance could spell the end of the UK, 18 September). Exbrit, perhaps? Dave Hunter Bristol • Re Roger Wilkinson’s drawer full of clothes that are “unfit for anything but gardening” (Letters, 15 September), I suggest he take up oil painting to get greater use out of his bottom drawer. title: Ukraine targets Moscow with hundreds of drones on final day of Russian election
summary: At least three people killed and oil refinery damaged as doubts cast over initial reports of ballistic missile use
text: Ukraine has targeted Moscow and the surrounding region in a large-scale attack that involved hundreds of drones. The attack killed at least three people and damaged what Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said was one of Russia’s “key oil industry facilities” on the final day of the country’s parliamentary elections, authorities said on Sunday. Zelenskyy said that among the weapons used in the attack was the Pelican, initially thought to be a short-range ballistic missile, but which sources said later was a winged drone. The president did not offer any further details, prompting media reports in Ukraine that it was a ballistic missile, only for doubt to be cast on the weapon identification later in the day. Zelenskyy also said Ukraine had used its domestically produced Flamingo cruise missiles to strike Moscow. The long-range weapon has previously been used against targets deep inside Russia and has the range to reach the country’s capital. Ukrainian and Russian Telegram channels posted images of what they said was debris from a Flamingo missile found in the Moscow region, though the claims could not be independently verified. Ruslan Leviev, the head of the open-source investigation group Conflict Intelligence Team, said the debris probably came from a Flamingo missile. Moscow’s mayor, Sergey Sobyanin, said that more than 1,600 drones had been intercepted and shot down, 450 of which were aimed at Moscow, though these figures are often exaggerated, and Ukraine’s daily drone fire rate estimated a number in the low hundreds. Sobyanin accused Ukraine of attempting to interfere with a tightly controlled three-day election in Russia that is expected to tighten Vladimir Putin’s 26-year grip on power. “The unprecedented attack was clearly planned with the aim of disrupting the elections. The enemy did not succeed,” he said on Telegram. At least three people were killed, including a 44-year-old woman and an elderly man, in separate incidents. A fire triggered by a drone crashing into a 21-storey building also led to 400 people being evacuated, said Moscow’s regional governor, Andrey Vorobyov, without specifying the drone’s origin. Kyiv has stepped up its campaign of long-range drone strikes against Russia in recent months, particularly against energy infrastructure, a vital source of the Kremlin’s revenue to fund its war effort. Ukrainian strikes have knocked out a significant part of Russia’s oil-refining capacity, triggering oil product shortages, fuel price increases and long queues at filling stations in many regions across the country’s 11 time zones. A facility on the territory of the Moscow oil refinery had been damaged, Sobyanin said. No casualties were reported and emergency services were on the scene. The refinery had already been hit by Ukrainian strikes in recent months. The Pelican missile was initially thought to be the FP-7 made by Fire Point, Ukraine’s most successful long-range drone and missile maker. But several hours later, as the speculation persisted, other military sources said it was a long-range drone. The company is also developing the longer-range FP-9, which has a range of more than 500 miles, meaning it could be used to target Moscow in the future. A test flight is expected later this autumn. The latest strike comes after the US president, Donald Trump, said on Monday that Ukraine and Russia had agreed not to target each other’s energy facilities. It also comes after Russians began voting on Friday in the country’s first parliamentary elections since Moscow invaded Ukraine in February 2022. Only parties that support Putin and the Kremlin’s military campaign have been registered to run. Moscow has also organised voting in occupied Ukraine. Few Russians doubt Putin’s United Russia party will coast to victory again, but the vote offers a gauge of public support for the war. With Agence France-Presse and Reuters

title: Bernie Sanders is right about the four-day workweek – but wrong about how to get there
summary: The senator proposed a federal overtime rule mandate, but incentives can better spur employers to reshape the workweek
text: Bernie Sanders, the Vermont senator, recently proposed new legislation that would change federal overtime rules. The new law, if passed, would require employers to pay a minimum 1.5 hours of overtime for each hour worked past 32 hours in a week. Currently, overtime kicks in at 40 hours per week. The requirement would phase in over a few years. Sounds great. Who wouldn’t want that? There’s just one problem: somebody has to pay for it. For business owners, this isn’t an ideological argument. It’s math. Say a company employs 100 people. And, for argument’s sake, say that each employee earns $50,000 annually for a 40-hour workweek. Assuming 50 workweeks, that’s about $1,000 per week or $25 an hour. Under Sanders’ proposal that employee would make $25 per hour for the first 32 hours and then be paid overtime of time and a half, or $37.50 for the additional eight hours to make it a 40-hour workweek. Which means that for a full week the employer is now paying $1,100 per week or $55,000 per year for 50 weeks. That’s $5,000 more for each employee. And it’s actually more than that. You have to add in federal and state taxes that an employer pays – about 7% of wages, which adds $350 more per year. A small business that employs 25 people would then be paying an additional $133,750 more per year under Sanders’ proposal. If they had 50 employees it would be an added cost of $267,500 per year. Well, you can do the math from there. And I’m not including other benefits – retirement plan contributions, workers compensation, etc – that are usually calculated as a percentage of wages. These costs would also go up. Of course, the business doesn’t have to pay for a 40-hour week. They can limit the workweek to 32 hours. But with unemployment and open jobs at historically low levels, I encounter very few businesses that can do this. They can’t find enough employees to do the work they have. No business wants to be forced to pay more for fewer hours. Up until now, many business owners have been dabbling with AI. But the owner of a 50-person company would gladly spend $100,000 on an AI project to save $267,500 per year. Sanders wants a moratorium on AI development. But now he’s proposing a law which would give employers another financial incentive to automate. The CEOs of Microsoft, Google, Anthropic and OpenAI must love this. The solution, I believe, is to accept that the workplace has changed. Today’s workers value compensation in different ways. It’s not just an hourly wage or a weekly paycheck. Recent research suggests that additional time off can have psychological benefits that an equivalent cash bonus doesn’t provide. According to a recent study in the Journal of Managerial Psychology, a majority of employees favored getting more time off over extra compensation. Researchers found that “a vacation time benefit gave surveyed employees an internalized sense of being treated and valued as a complete human being”. Getting paid a livable wage is of course important. But many workers, particularly in the younger generations that make up more than half of today’s workforce – want something just as important: balance. They want flexibility. They want to spend more time with their families, traveling, relaxing and pursuing their own personal interests. Providing incentives to – not mandating – employers to provide more paid time off, dependent care leave, and sick and personal days would make more sense. The government already provides employer tax credits for providing family leave and other benefits for reimbursing dependent-care expenses. This is also a valuable form of compensation, and one that more accurately addresses the issues that today’s employees face. Which is why a 32-hour, or four-day, workweek isn’t a bad concept. Government can help, but in the end it’s employers who need to step up. A four-day workweek can be accommodated by better scheduling. I know nurses, veterinarians, and healthcare and construction workers who are employed by firms that offer their employees to work four 10-hour days and take three days off. They love it. Of course, some jobs may not be amenable to such a schedule, and other paid-time-off plans for those workers should be considered. But if an employer invests the time to come up with a strategy for allowing their employees to only come to work four days a week (while still meeting the requirements of their job), they’ll find it easier to attract and retain talent.

title: Bear-y good neighbors: humans and animals are learning to live together in an expanding LA
summary: People are increasingly crossing paths with the wild animals as homes ring the outskirts of forests, sparking a new era of coexistence
text: Every year, as summer draws to a close and fall begins, California’s bears get hungry. Black bears have long roamed the state, hunting for acorns, ants and pine nuts by the bucketload to pack on calories before hibernation. But increasingly, for every berry and root, there’s an even greater temptation: our trash and the detritus of human existence. That dynamic is playing out in perhaps a surprising place: Los Angeles. As communities on the outskirts of the metropolis grow, bears are butting up against humanity, drawn to residents’ pools, their chicken coops, their fruit trees and trashcans. “Black bears are incredibly adaptable, versatile omnivores,” said Wilson Sherman, a PhD student at the University of California, Los Angeles, who studies human-wildlife interaction. “They can eat everything we can eat.” Human-bear interactions have increased since the 1990s, Sherman said, which makes sense as communities expand and the state is now home to some 50,000 to 70,000 black bears. A few hundred of those live in the Angeles national forest, just north of the city and its millions of hungry households. Brian Gordon and his partner moved to the state’s bear capital – Monrovia, California – four years ago. Their house is the last before the Angeles national forest begins, and as they were buying the home, a family of bears wandered through the back garden. It was the start of a new era of coexistence. Now, the pair regularly share their pool with a family of bears and document their exploits on an Instagram account called PoolBearLife. Videos show bear cubs with their snouts bubbling in the water, climbing – and falling from – trees and causing adorable, young bear mayhem. “I only had education up until I bought this house of bears from whatever I saw online. I actually thought people get eaten by bears a lot,” Gordon said. “But after we bought the house, we had bears walking through. That’s really all they’re doing. I realized, OK, I have an unnatural fear of these animals and we’ve kind of adapted to living around them. “People will say ‘you guys are the bear experts,’” Gordon went on. “No, we’re city boys. We bought a house that happened to have bears.” Gordon and his partner live amongst the bears, but they’re also vocal advocates for doing so safely. Trashcans are kept clean, temptations are removed and, despite the filming, they give the bears their space. Sometimes mistakes are made and a bear finds a case of beer in the garage. But with consideration, bears don’t even stop to sniff the trash cans and will just pass through the backyard like it’s an extension of the forest nearby, the couple said. In a perfect world, Sherman said, human dominated landscapes that buttress the natural world would take steps to minimize bear contact. That means making neighborhoods as unattractive to bears as possible. “Pet food left outside, koi ponds, fruit trees with a lot of fruit on them, swimming pools, all these things can be attractive to bears,” he said. It’s not that human food tastes better, it’s just much more calorie dense and therefore easier for bears to pack on the pounds. In fact, bears that live or forage near human environments tend to reproduce more often and at higher rates, likely due to the availability of our food. “It takes a lot of work to get the calories from, say, a half eaten pizza in the trash in equivalent calories from acorns and ants,” he said. “It makes sense to get calories from human food.” The other major factor is climate crisis. Warmer summers can alter the availability of natural food and force bears to expand their ranges. Major wildfires like the 2025 Eaton and Palisades fires were also linked to a lack in natural food sources, prompting the bears near Los Angeles to search in neighborhoods instead. Alex Heeran, a research scientist at the California department of fish and wildlife who studies the human dimensions of wildlife encounters, said human and bear interactions generally peak every year in late summer and early fall. September is often a really active month as black bears finish up their pre-hibernation hungry period, known as hyperphagia. 2026 is on track to be a record-setting year when it comes to reported bear encounters, Heeran said. It’s also a time when humans are out in force around Labor Day for the year’s final picnics and camping excursions. Fish and wildlife officials will often get reports of bears creating a nuisance and occasionally damaging fences, getting into sheds and making a mess as they look for calories. “The bear’s just looking for food, doing natural behavior, but it’s creating a situation that’s not ideal,” Heeran said. “A lot of the conflict can be prevented.” Sometimes, however, that conflict can escalate, which can result in a bear being euthanized or relocated. It’s rare and wildlife officials try and prevent situations from escalating to that point, but it happens. Earlier this year, the city of Monrovia erupted in fury after a mother bear known as “Blondie” was euthanized. Officials had determined she had swiped at local residents twice, causing minor injuries. She had two cubs at the time. They are now being raised in captivity until they can hopefully be released back into the wild. Residents rallied for an alternative plan, but that effort ultimately turned into a memorial walk through the city in Blondie’s honor. “The city was not a part of that conversation or decision,” Becky Shevlin, the mayor of the city, which is peppered with monuments to black bears, told the Los Angeles Times in March. “We were absolutely devastated, especially when you think about her having the two little cubs.” Sherman said the spread of bear footage on social media, many of it captured by doorbell cameras that have exploded in the last decade, is a double-edged sword. On the one hand, people get to see bears being bears, doing cute things. “Bears are really cute, and a lot of the things they do are really cute … This is a real way to build meaningful empathy for wildlife, and building empathy for wildlife is a powerful motivator for conservation actions,” he said. “There is this risk of … kind of Disney-fying them. Black bears are by nature not particularly aggressive unless they are put in a dangerous or threatening situation, but they can cause damage. It’s best to give them their space.” As September draws to a close, interactions between bears and Angelenos will thin out for the season. But residents of the city will have to contend with their neighbors again come spring, alongside the mountain lions, deer and coyotes that call the city’s outskirts home. “When people move to these foothill neighborhoods, a lot of people are moving in because they think it’s a suburb of LA. But they’re not necessarily thinking they’re going to have bears in their back yard,” Sherman said. “At first it can be really scary, but the people I’ve spoken to generally become accustomed to them.” “Bears are super likable and this population of bears wouldn’t be there if people didn’t like bears so much.”

title: Trump claims triumphal arch will serve as a ‘top grade military complex’ to store weapons
summary: US president on Truth Social claims his new plan for the 250ft arch comes at the ‘strong request’ of the US military
text: Donald Trump is proffering a new argument for building his triumphal arch in Washington DC: it will be converted into a “top grade military complex” replete with drone and ammunition storage space and customised sniper facilities on the roof and plaza. In a post on his Truth Social platform on Sunday morning, Trump claimed that his new plan came at the “strong request” of the US military. He said the 250ft structure would be able to “house, store, and have the rapid ability to use large quantities of sniper ammunition in storage”. With the hyperbole that is his trademark, the president added that the arch would be unique. “There will be no facility like this anywhere in the world.” The triumphal arch project has come under widespread criticism for its potential impact on the historic area of downtown Washington DC. Its intended location in a circle close to the Memorial Bridge could interrupt the sight lines of several of the most resonant structures, including the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery which would flank it. The siting of the structure close to the Ronald Reagan Washington international airport has also prompted questions from Democratic Congress members. Last week, the National Park Service warned that it could have “adverse effects to historic properties” and called for additional planning before the building work went ahead. The arch is one of several construction projects that Trump has initiated which he claims are necessary to elevate the visual greatness of the US capital but which critics have slammed as thinly veiled efforts to promote his own legacy. They include the creation of a White House ballroom, the refurbishment of the reflecting pool at the Lincoln Memorial and the renovation of the Kennedy Center. All those projects have run into big problems, ranging from criticism of their aesthetic qualities, structural difficulties and legal challenges. In the case of the John F Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, one of the world’s pre-eminent cultural venues, Trump has hinted that he might demolish the property altogether in a fit of pique at the courts blocking the addition of his name to its title. The White House ballroom, which Trump has also been calling a “military complex”, was beset by legal wrangling until the US supreme court last month said the project could go ahead. The ground breaking that will kick off construction of the arch is expected to begin this month. Trump has linked it to the 250th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence, and said in Sunday’s post that it would be “by far the greatest” triumphal arch in any of the world’s top cities and capitals. It will be clad in granite, with three golden statues on top.

title: UK startup snares $20m to recreate gigs with ‘hyper-realistic’ digital avatars
summary: Unit1 hopes to offer lower cost version of shows such as Abba Voyage, showcasing living and dead artists in any venue
text: The former chief executive of Andrew Lloyd Webber’s entertainment group has obtained a near-£15m investment for his UK music tech startup that hopes to recreate classic concerts by manifesting musicians as digital avatars.
