title: Victims say Home Office attempt to curtail spycops inquiry will result in a ‘cover-up’
summary: Shabana Mahmood is concerned about length and £144m cost of inquiry into intrusive police surveillance
text: Victims of intrusive police surveillance have accused the government of seeking to cut short the spycops public inquiry that has been examining widespread misconduct committed by undercover officers. The independent judge-led inquiry is scrutinising how officers, who spied on tens of thousands of political activists over more than four decades, carried out abuses such as deceiving women into sexual relationships and fathering children. The inquiry has been running for more than a decade, and is expected to last another two years. The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, has said she is concerned about the length and cost of the process. It was set up in 2015 and was supposed to have been completed within three years. Latest figures show the inquiry, which has been led by retired judge Sir John Mitting, has so far cost £144m. Mahmood initiated a public consultation, which closes on Sunday, that she said would help determine whether the inquiry should continue in a different format. However, those who were spied on say that the Home Office is looking to severely limit or scrap the later stages, leaving the full extent of wrongdoing by the police hidden. They say more than 2,000 people have objected to what they believe would be a cover-up. The spycops inquiry is one of the longest-running public inquiries. According to the House of Commons, the longest in modern times was an inquiry into a sectarian murder in Northern Ireland which reported last week, 22 years after being commissioned. It has so far been investigating the Special Demonstration Squad (SDS), a Metropolitan police unit that infiltrated political groups between 1968 and 2008. The inquiry has heard how the SDS officers formed long-term relationships with women without disclosing to them their true identity, spied on grieving families such as the parents of murdered teenager Stephen Lawrence, stole the identities of dead children and lied in court hearings. It is due to examine a second undercover squad, the National Public Order Intelligence Unit, which infiltrated political groups between 1999 and 2011. One of the unit’s key undercover officers was Mark Kennedy who infiltrated environmental and left-wing groups for six years. He deceived a large, but unknown, number of women into intimate relationships. Environmental campaigners had their criminal convictions overturned because crucial evidence gathered by Kennedy was withheld from their trials. The inquiry is also scheduled to look at the case of an undercover police officer who used his fake identity while infiltrating serious crime to deceive a woman into a 19-year relationship during which they had a child together. Victims of the surveillance say that the consultation is phoney and rigged as it only offers three alternatives: an inquiry with a narrower remit, one that would not have legal powers to force reluctant witnesses to testify or asking the police to disclose documents to victims without any type of inquiry. Kate Wilson, who was deceived into a two-year relationship by Kennedy, said: “Whatever the intentions of the Home Office in doing this, the practical effect of them curtailing the inquiry or reducing its powers to compel evidence will be a cover-up, and we may never understand the full extent of the misconduct that has occurred in undercover policing.” A Home Office spokesperson said: “The historic failings in undercover policing continue to shock the public. We are determined to get justice and hold those responsible to account. “However, the undercover policing inquiry was established more than a decade ago, and is yet to deliver justice for those affected, at significant cost to the taxpayer. It’s only right that we ask those affected themselves about the future of the inquiry.”

title: Earl Spencer says media treatment of Harry and Meghan ‘echoes’ Diana’s experience
summary: Comments come after he accused King Charles of gaslighting him in response to claims made in new memoir
text: Earl Spencer has said the relationship between the press and the Duke and Duchess of Sussex “echoes” the way the media treated his sister Diana, Princess of Wales. In an interview with the BBC to be aired on Sunday evening, Spencer described the press’s coverage of Harry and Meghan as having a “cancerous influence”, adding it would be “beholden on people to learn from Diana’s example”. Spencer added he worries about the Duke of Sussex “not having any police protection” and that he does not take sides in the row between Harry and his brother William, the Prince of Wales. He said: “If you look at an article in a tabloid about Diana or the couple that you were mentioning, Harry and Meghan, you know, they can be really, really unpleasant. And I think it would be really beholden on people to learn from Diana’s example. “I’m not here to speak for Harry and Meghan, but for anyone who’s being destroyed in this way daily, it must be such a cancerous influence in their life.” He said Diana was “really brought low” by criticism she received from the media, adding it was a pity to see “echoes of that” in the press coverage of Harry and Meghan. He added: “I would say that I personally worry about the fifth in line to the throne who’s served in the military not having any police protection. “As an uncle who’s seen his sister die in very, very preventable circumstances, that I would veer towards protection.” Spencer’s latest comments come after he accused King Charles of gaslighting him following Buckingham Palace’s response to explosive claims that Charles said “we’ll forget her soon enough” after Diana’s death. He has made a series of damning claims about the king in a new memoir chronicling Diana’s life that prompted the palace to push back, saying: “The pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason.” Spencer said: “It was astonishingly provocative and below the belt because it was essentially trying to say I’d lied without the king being able to deny what I’d said. I also thought it was a rather poor imitation of the ‘recollections may vary’ quote, which was a much more elegant way of putting things, but in these circumstances entirely out of place.” He added that “Diana would be cheering from the rafters at this book”. In response to the claims made in the memoir, a Buckingham Palace spokesperson said on Wednesday: “While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss.” In an extract of the BBC interview released on Friday, Spencer said he was telling the truth and described the king’s comments about his sister as “monstrous”. Asked whether he had evidence of the king’s comments, he told the BBC: “I told friends and family straight away, close friends and family, about what had been said, because it was so monstrous.” The Sussexes, who returned to the UK from the US on 26 August, have long been critical of their treatment by the media, with Harry in 2021 telling Oprah Winfrey the tabloid press had created a “toxic environment”. The Press Association contributed to this report

title: Outfoxed: How well do you know your native animals? Australians’ questionable quoll knowledge exposed
summary: About one in six NSW, QLD and Vic residents think foxes are native animals and a third believe quolls are introduced, survey shows
text: Most people identify wombats and kangaroos as Australian animals, but one in six people surveyed in Queensland, New South Wales and Victoria think red foxes are native wildlife. The polling commissioned by the Invasive Species Council also revealed that one in three Australians on the east coast did not know that quolls were native. More than 95% said kangaroos and wombats were native animals, according to the survey of 5,000 people by DemosAU, which listed animals and asked people to say if they were native or not, but showed recognition of other species like quolls and bandicoots was much lower. One in five thought cane toads were native. These amphibians hailed from Central and South America and were introduced in 1935 in a failed bid to control cane beetles, with disastrous results for native species. About 10% considered cats wildlife. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email “It’s wild,” the conservation group’s rewilding manager, Rob Brewster, said. Foxes and cats were among the country’s most destructive introduced mammals, while the quoll – a unique native predator – was arguably one of its most beautiful, he said. Brewster said quolls had loads of personality and character, and were once found in the heart of Sydney and Melbourne, right up until the 1950s and 60s. “There’s so few left, that there’s very little chance of having a meaningful interaction with a quoll these days.” The Invasive Species Council said the findings revealed the growing disconnect between Australians and wildlife, as local species declined while introduced animals – like cats, foxes and rabbits – became an increasingly familiar sight. “That is how extinction can begin long before the last animal dies,” Brewster said. “A species disappears from your back yard, then your neighbourhood, then your region. A generation grows up without seeing it, and eventually its absence starts to feel normal. “The less Australians encounter an animal, whether that be a quoll, bandicoot or bettong, the quicker they fade from public knowledge and eventually generations will not recognise them all – unless we do something about it.” Associate prof Diana Fisher, an ecologist at the University of Queensland, said quolls were intelligent and voracious predators. But apart from in the bush or at the zoo, most people were unlikely to encounter them because they were nocturnal and avoided houses and built up areas. “People love predators, and things like big cats,” she said. “Ours are a little bit smaller, but still very impressive and beautiful to look at, and they’ve all got spots.” Prof Euan Ritchie, a wildlife ecologist at Deakin University, said quolls were “magnificent marsupials”, that performed a vital role within ecosystems, and were even known to prey on introduced European rabbits. “Their delightful spotted patterns, wonderfully long tails, the way they bound through forests, woodlands and over boulders … they really are quollity!” Like many Australian mammals, they held deep cultural importance for many First Nations peoples, he said. “They are greatly underappreciated by many, and I hope we can return these wonderful mammals to more areas where they once lived and thrived.” Ritchie has advocated for lesser known species, including the marsupial mole, velvet worm or Jalbil (Boyd’s forest dragon), to be made mascots for the 2032 Brisbane Olympic Games, as a means to raise their profiles. “Sadly Australia is a world leader in extinctions,” he wrote. “Highlighting species many are unfamiliar with, the threats to them and their respective habitats and ecosystems, could help to stimulate increased conservation efforts.”

title: Why China is pushing back on US warnings over rapid AI development
summary: Beijing believes slowdown calls aim to lock in US advantage, and is pursuing a different balance between safety and pace
text: About two years ago, education entrepreneur Boris But had what he calls a “penny-drop moment” – that, like countless others in China, his company needed to embrace AI before it was made obsolete by it. His clients, well-off parents looking to send their children to study overseas, had begun arriving in his office reeling off information and opinions gleaned not from rival firms, but from chatbots. In response, he started developing his own AI study tool, concluding: “If you can’t beat them, join them.” The pace and quality of AI development in China is second only to the United States, with the two superpowers locked in an intensifying rivalry as the stakes rise with each new model’s capabilities. Analysts generally agree that frontier, or cutting-edge, US models are still some way ahead of their Chinese counterparts. But over the last few weeks the mood music from Silicon Valley has been decidedly sombre, as insider after insider has warned of the potential catastrophes that could result from “loss of control” of the most advanced AIs. And last Saturday Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei pitched a “worldwide pacing of the frontier” – something he said would “require cooperation with China”. “China is definitely not receptive” to a slowdown on US firms’ terms, though, said Lian Jye Su from technology research group Omdia. For the government, AI is a “core sovereignty capability”, and Beijing will not want to jeopardise the progress made in closing the gap with US frontier models. “It sees these calls [for a slowdown] as a bid to lock in US advantage,” said Su. Amodei made this explicit, mentioning China specifically when arguing it was key “to keep democracies’ AI lead over autocracies as large as possible”. He advocated for measures including continued export controls to China on advanced chips and machinery – the existence of which some argue already amounts to a forced unilateral “pacing”. China’s foreign ministry responded to Amodei’s piece by saying “fearmongering, confrontation and vicious competition will only disrupt the process of global AI governance”. However, several analysts told the Guardian it would be a mistake to assume this suggested a rejection of the broader concerns raised by the essay. This week China released the third iteration of its AI safety governance framework – a document that functions as a “mapping of the AI risk landscape and roughly what one should do about it”, said Gabriel Wagner, a researcher at Concordia, a Beijing-based AI safety consultancy. Included in the updates are the risks posed by agents, the cybersecurity threats from frontier models and the issue of recursive self-improvement – an as-yet hypothetical scenario where AI becomes advanced enough to improve itself. “In many ways, I think there is more common ground than people might assume between what Amodei is saying and what the Chinese government is saying,” said Wagner. That contrasts with US president Donald Trump, who this week called fears AI could wipe out humanity a “hoax”. Trump is set to meet counterpart Xi Jinping in Washington next week, with AI expected to make the agenda, though analysts are sceptical a major breakthrough will happen. The ruling Communist party, finely attuned to risks to its political control, has been proactive in ensuring the new technology has developed within boundaries set by the state. Centralised authority over critical infrastructure and commercial activity means China is generally better placed than the United States “to address any AI disaster”, said Omdia’s Su. However, Chinese companies do less voluntary monitoring and evaluation work than US ones, said Leia Wang from the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace (CEIP). Neither government seems prepared for a loss-of-control incident like those outlined over the last few weeks, she said. China’s regulation, though, is “iterative … they are quick to adapt and release new measures”, she added. China has had an algorithm registry since 2022, but warnings on agents released this year suggest a switch in focus “from controlling what AI says to controlling what it does”, per Concordia AI. Beijing also issued national regulations this year aimed at curbing emotional dependency on companion AIs. At the same time, AI is being actively encouraged across the economy to promote growth, enshrining this goal in its latest Five Year Plan. Local governments are offering funding and low rents to companies to help achieve this – entrepreneur But was recently invited to pitch his company, Hampshire Education, to a small city three hours from Shanghai set on establishing a reputation as a tech hub. Factories across the country’s huge manufacturing base are being encouraged to convert their processes into the AI era. “Safety and controllability are certainly major concerns, and they are actively discussed,” said a representative for Black Lake Technologies, an industrial agent platform that says it has worked with 40,000 factories globally. “But in manufacturing, these concerns tend to be much more concrete and operational … what companies care most about is whether the AI is reliable.” Daily life in China is already highly digitised, with traditionally less discourse around data privacy helping with widespread adoption. For example, digital health service A-fu, which features AI chatbot versions of prominent doctors trained on real clinical studies, recently hit 150 million users. “Most people treat AI as an already-useful everyday tool, not an abstract threat, so the practical attitude is to live with it,” said Ni Tao, founding editor of tech website yangtzeer.com. “There is real anxiety about jobs and misinformation, but it coexists with a strong belief that China must master AI rather than slow down.”

title: Farage says he wants to ‘hijack’ Trump’s ICE czar to help secure UK border
summary: Reform leader also tells US event Europe should have ‘more sensible view’ of president’s administration
text: Nigel Farage has said he wants to “hijack” Donald Trump’s hardline ICE adviser and bring him to the UK “to secure our borders”. Speaking at an event in the US, the Reform UK leader also called for Europe to take a “more sensible view” of the US president’s administration rather than seeing it as “villainous”. Farage complimented Tom Homan, Trump’s adviser on the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). Speaking at the event where Homan was a guest, he said: “I’ve got terrible news for you. We’re hijacking Tom Homan and taking him back with us to secure our borders.” Homan is Trump’s key adviser on ICE, which is under scrutiny over its aggressive approach to immigration enforcement after a number of fatal shootings by its agents, including two people in July. Salgado Araujo and Durán Guerrero were the 29th and 30th people that immigration officers have opened fire on since Trump took office last year, according to The Trace, an outlet that tracks shootings in its gun violence data hub. Homan has taken a more hands-on approach to immigration policy since Trump brought him in to “de‑escalate” tensions in Minneapolis, which was the scene of a brutal immigration crackdown in January. In Trump’s first term, he helped to design some of the administration’s most draconian measures – most notably family separation, a strategy reportedly deemed too severe by officials in the Obama White House, but which later became central to Trump’s “zero tolerance” policy. Reform UK has committed to a more hardline immigration policy than proposed by other mainstream parties, promising mass deportations of people who have entered the country illegally and deployment of the Royal Navy to intercept small boats in the Channel. The party did not respond to a request for comment on whether it would seek to emulate Trump’s style of immigration enforcement under ICE which has been criticised for its brutality. Farage interviewed Homan for his GB News show last year, describing him as uncompromising and saying he had achieved remarkable results on deportations, while acknowledging there had been “some backlash”. On Trump in general, Farage said at the event that it was “important that our country, and Europe too, get a better, more sensible view of America than it gets of the Trump administration through traditional mainstream media who frankly paint the whole project out to be villainous”. Farage’s positive remarks towards Trump and his administration come after the Reform UK leader appeared to distance himself from the president, saying in April they had not spoken for many months and questioning his judgment on the Iran war. His latest trip to the US comes at a time when relations between the White House and Downing Street are under strain over Iran and policy towards Israel since Andy Burnham took over from Keir Starmer. Burnham will have his first meeting with Trump in New York next week, with the US president having previously described him as “extremely liberal” but also having praised him for potentially opening up the North Sea to further drilling. Farage did, however, depart from Trump’s views again earlier this week after the US president said he would love to see a united Ireland. “Northern Ireland is a proud and integral part of the United Kingdom,” Farage said. “The people of Northern Ireland neither want a referendum nor unification.”

title: Chiltern Railways enters public ownership in Labour nationalisation push
summary: Operator that runs services between London Marylebone and Birmingham is sixth to be nationalised since 2025
text: Chiltern Railways has become the latest train operator to enter public ownership as the government closes in on its ambition to renationalise all major passenger rail services. The operator, which runs commuter rail services on the Chiltern mainline between London Marylebone and Birmingham, on Sunday became the sixth to be nationalised under Labour, with the remaining four to follow by the end of 2027. The Department for Transport (DfT) said the move would bring more reliable services, with plans to end what it termed the “daily frustration” of overcrowding. It has promised a package of improvements for Chiltern passengers, including more services and seats, new trains, upgraded stations and better onboard facilities including upgraded wifi. The government legislated in 2024 to renationalise private train operations as contracts allowed, joining the four operators already in public ownership and Network Rail to eventually establish an integrated body, Great British Railways (GBR). The rail minister, Peter Hendy, said: “Every transfer into public ownership gives us the chance to tackle the bread-and-butter issues people care about – more frequent, comfortable trains that turn up on time. “As we set up Great British Railways, we’re putting passengers first. It will not happen overnight, but we will build a railway the country can trust and rely on and that will create growth, jobs and homes.” Another 25 daily services will be introduced on the Chiltern network from December, with 10,000 extra seats each weekday, as more new trains are rolled out. Tony Baxter, the interim managing director of Chiltern Railways, said customers would see “improvements made possible thanks to years of planning, dedication and hard work by Chiltern colleagues. Public ownership will further strengthen that progress through closer collaboration across the industry.” The DfT said the move “also provides a fresh opportunity to deliver East West Rail”, the long-awaited services that should have started under Chiltern last year on a completed stretch of the future Oxford-Cambridge line. However, it is unclear if a start date for East-West services between Oxford and Milton Keynes has come any closer after the transfer to the state operator, DfTO. Although a variety of reasons have been given for the delay, unions oppose plans to run the trains without a guard. The RMT union is due to demonstrate outside London Marylebone station on Monday, and members are being balloted for strike action over plans backed by the DfT for driver-only operation. The row threatens to further cloud the horizon for GBR, as the government seeks to demonstrate the benefits of the publicly owned railway. The next operator to transfer into public ownership is due to be Great Western Railway in December.

title: ‘Flip the table and rise up’: Lib Dems’ president in combative mood as party gathers in Brighton
summary: Josh Babarinde wants to target big tech and crypto billionaires while giving power and cash back to the public
text: Standing outside Toynbee Hall in the East End of London, Josh Babarinde doesn’t exactly look like a rabble-rouser. But despite the well-cut suit and disarmingly large smile, the president of the Liberal Democrats is, apparently, up for a fight. “There are big modern giants that are getting in the way of people’s ability to thrive, and it is the job of Liberal Democrats to address that,” says the 33-year-old. “How are we going to do that? Well, first of all, we’ve got to flip the table over and rise up.” Flipping over tables is not behaviour normally associated with Liberal Democrat members, about 5,000 of whom are in Brighton for its annual conference this weekend. But Babarinde, frequently described as a rising star in the party’s ranks, wants his comrades to channel the spirit of the great Liberal thinker William Beveridge, who finessed his radical ideas on social reform in the 141-year-old Whitechapel building. Beveridge decried the five evils of want, disease, ignorance, squalor and idleness. However, Babarinde, the Eastbourne MP, is taking aim at targets from big tech to crypto billionaires. “People are looking for a force to help break some of those giants and give power and cash back to people who this country is meant to be working for,” he says. That people are seeking alternatives to the status quo is undeniable, but whether they are looking at the Liberal Democrats is a matter of debate. The historic 2024 election result gave the party 71 MPs, yet it has been stuck at about 11% in polls for months. The Lib Dems gained 153 councillors in England in May and six seats in the Scottish parliament, although the party’s advances were more modest than those of the Greens and Reform UK. The Lib Dem leader, Ed Davey, also struggles to command attention. Lib Dem MPs grumble that Nigel Farage only has to sneeze to attract media coverage, while Davey has to resort to bungee jumping. “You’ve got a very crowded multiparty system. You’ve got Reform saying any old shit in the media and getting coverage for it with no plan for delivering,” says Babarinde. “As Liberal Democrats, we’re not going to fall into that trap. But what we have got to be clear about is the diagnosis of the problem, who it is standing in the way and what needs to be done.” He dismisses the idea that the party is yet to produce eye-catching retail policies – “There’s oodles and oodles of it!” – but says it needs to reach beyond its middle England strongholds with digital campaigning that is as strong as its much-envied ground game. Babarinde, who has spoken about his mother being subjected to domestic abuse and how it shaped his politics, has experience engaging with hard-to-reach communities. He set up a social enterprise smartphone repair service staffed by former offenders and at-risk youth more than a decade ago, which earned him an OBE. After a stroll through the East End, he points to the stand in Spitalfields market where they had pinned up sheets of A4 paper with “Cracked It” written across them in felt-tip, and laughs. “I would never have got my phone repaired there,” he says. “But when people were giving their money over … I was seeing these guys think: ‘Oh my God, wow! Someone wants my skills. They want what I can offer.’” Do the Lib Dems want what the ambitious Babarinde has to offer? Despite being elected in 2024, he was elevated to the role of president in November, giving him a vital say in strategy and organisation. He bats away the inevitable question about whether he would like the top job – but when asked if he is a natural leader, he smiles. “I roll up my sleeves and get stuck in,” he says. “When I saw those young people in the East End prolifically involved in crime amid a lack of opportunities. I wasn’t waiting for someone to swoop in to come to address that issue. I decided to come up with a solution.” So if the problem is that the Liberal Democrats – despite a seemingly advantageous political backdrop – are stuck on 11% in the polls, what does he see as the answer? “The solution is exactly what is in the strategy we’re talking about this week,” Babarinde says. “I stood to be party president because I thought I had something to offer: to help develop a new strategy for the party so we can reach new heights.”

title: ‘The rules have changed’: has Russia begun to order assassinations on US soil?
summary: Exiled dissidents and an unsealed indictment suggest Kremlin may have abandoned longstanding taboo on attacks on its rival’s territory
text: Roman Dobrokhotov had been content enough for his appearance at a conference in Washington DC this week to be publicised, although it was not something he would normally risk in Europe. The dissident Russian journalist was named during a trial in London last year as one of the targets of a Russian spy ring that appeared to have murderous intent. “Maybe burn him alive on the street, spray him with some super-strong acid, VX, like the North Koreans, or the ricin,” a Russian-hired operative had texted of the plans for Dobrokhotov in Britain. American soil, though, has traditionally been regarded as something of a safe place for those speaking out against the Kremlin, whether it has been under the red flag of the Soviet Union or the tricolour of Vladimir Putin’s Russian Federation. It might be possible for Kremlin agents to get away with deploying poison-tipped umbrellas on people crossing London’s Waterloo Bridge, as was the fate of the Bulgarian dissident Georgi Markov in 1978, but risking such colourful assassinations on the Brooklyn Bridge or indeed anywhere on US territory would be a different matter entirely. If not part of the so-called Moscow rules, the fabled operating guidelines for western and Russian spies, then there was certainly an adjunct, a gentleman’s agreement of sorts, that neither side would kill on each other’s soil. That had been the understanding of many of the other dissidents as they prepared to appear at the Washington Dialogue conference on Russian affairs being held in the high-rise office of the National Endowment for Democracy, a short walk from the White House. This week the kaleidoscope was shaken. “It looks like starting from today, the rules have changed in America,” Dobrokhotov, 43, said. “We will have to change how we behave there. Nowhere is safe.” The game changer overshadowing the Washington conference was an announcement on Tuesday that the US Department of Justice was unsealing indictments in absentia against five individuals allegedly working for Russia’s intelligence services who were said to have conspired to “conduct attacks and murders around the world, including in the United States”. The most eye-catching claim was that of an audacious plot to recruit unnamed US residents to “eliminate” a prominent Russian dissident living in the US capital. Those named as part of the spy network were a serving officer of the Russian Federal Security Service (FSB), Kirill Khrameev, 27, and his father, Yuri Khrameev, 63, who is a former FSB colonel, along with two 35-year-old Cubans, Oemis Romagoza Durruthy and Yaidel Delgado Suarez, nicknamed “the Viking”, and a 22-year-old Venezuelan, Angel Eduardo Castro. The FBI had uncovered encrypted messages – written in Spanish and ineptly shrouded in spy code – commissioning what one of the alleged ring members had described as “gravely serious work”: an offer of $40,000 (£30,000) to surveil and then kill someone in Washington that the Russian state wanted to “disappear”. There was talk of bringing in assassins from Mexico to carry out the “construction” (the word used by the agents for murder) but they were “delayed” and so a local killer was sought, according to the indictment. The identity of the purported victim was not revealed by the authorities, but among the rumoured potential targets was Vladimir Kara-Murza, who was freed from jail in Siberia and went to the US as part of a swap for Russian intelligence operatives in 2024. He declined to comment on the case when approached by the Guardian. *** The almost unprecedented nature of the plot on US soil was unintentionally highlighted in the indictment itself, which listed a series of assassinations carried out by the Russian intelligence services. There was Paul Klebnikov, an American journalist and historian, murdered in Moscow in 2004. Two years later, Alexander Litvinenko, a former FSB officer, was killed in London by two Russian agents who put radioactive material in his tea. In 2018, Sergei Skripal, a former Russian military intelligence officer, and his daughter, survived after being poisoned with a military-grade nerve agent in Salisbury in the UK; a local woman, Dawn Sturgess, died after being contaminated. In 2019, a court in Germany found that Zelimkhan Khangoshvili, a former commander in the second Chechen war, was assassinated in Berlin, on the order of the Russian state. And in 2024 Alexei Navalny, the Russian opposition leader, died while in custody after being previously poisoned with the nerve agent Novichok. “More recently, countries throughout Europe have accused Russia of sabotage operations and extrajudicial targeting,” the indictment goes on. “For example, in or about September 2026, a German investigation reportedly linked the GRU’s military intelligence services to a drone attack at the Leipzig/Halle airport in Germany.” But no such activities on US soil were raised in the paperwork, and for historically rooted reasons. “I would describe it as an unwritten set of cold-war rules of the road,” said Chris Costa, a former US intelligence chief who is today executive director of the International Spy Museum in Washington DC. “The US and Soviet Union conducted aggressive espionage against one another, but there were understood limits, particularly around physically targeting each other’s intelligence personnel and families … If these allegations are proved, directing surveillance and murder on US soil crosses a very different line from traditional espionage.” *** Why would the Russians cross this red line? Jack Devine, a former associate director of operations at the CIA, said that the Kremlin had perhaps become blase about the potential repercussions – but that it could prove to be a misstep. “The Russians today put far less weight on political criticism internationally, and are less concerned about the ramifications, including sanctions,” he said. “Putin has a vision of himself in Russia and in the world as a powerful leader of the old school which he has often reminisced about in his interviews and public statements. I believe it’s wrongfooted, and he may be underestimating the long-term internal and external ramifications of this isolation.” For Calder Walton, author and assistant director of the Belfer Center’s Intelligence Project at Harvard University, it is not just the Russian motivations that should be analysed. In 2023, Walton revealed in his book Spies that three years earlier a Russian assassination squad had targeted Aleksandr Poteyev, a defector who had been living in the US. “In the Poteyev episode, American authorities apparently chose secrecy, presumably to protect intelligence sources and methods and avoid a public confrontation with Moscow,” he said. “By unsealing this indictment, the justice department is doing something different: exposing the alleged network, warning potential recruits, reassuring threatened dissidents and imposing costs on individuals who might otherwise have continued to operate in the shadows. Public attribution is itself a counterintelligence weapon.” European diplomats in Washington tasked with monitoring the conflict in Ukraine and US-Russian relations also said the exposure of the plot by the FBI indicated a shift in Washington’s position. “It’s a big deal that the US chose to reveal this now,” one said. “The decision to do that raises the profile and shows the clear and imminent threat to dissidents in the US.” Walton added: “The immediate policy consequences may be limited because all five defendants are reportedly abroad and remain at large. “We should nevertheless expect greater protection for Russian dissidents and defectors, intensified investigation of Russian proxy networks, closer intelligence cooperation with European allies, and potentially further sanctions, expulsions or criminal charges.” Evidence of a heightened state of alert to the risk to dissidents in the US has already emerged. Anastasia Shevchenko, a vocal critic of Putin who fled Russia for Lithuania in 2022 after becoming the first person found guilty of breaking a new law of participating in an “undesirable organisation”, said she had been warned at a recent interview for a visa to the US that she could not assume that she would be safe during her visit. Nikkie Lyubarsky, a research associate at the Soufan Center, an NGO in New York specialising in global security, said the unsealing of the indictment could reflect a “behind the scenes” escalation in tension between the White House and the Kremlin as a result of Russia’s reported support for Iran in the continuing conflict with the US and Israel. “The US publicising [the indictments] now definitely raises some flags in my mind,” said Lyubarsky. “It coincides obviously with the sanctions that have just been passed in the House and the CIA director’s visit to Russia recently. There’s probably some sort of escalation behind the scenes that we’re not aware of. It could be tied to Russian intelligence-sharing with Iran. That would be my best guess.” Back at the Washington Dialogue conference, the perhaps understandably conspiratorial-minded dissidents chewing on sandwiches at the lunch break had their own theories. Was Donald Trump seeking to distance himself from the news that the wedding of his son, Donald Trump Jr, had been partly paid for by the Putin loyalist and oligarch Umar Kremlev? Natalia Arno, the founder and president of the Free Russia Foundation, who experienced symptoms from a suspected poisoning during a 2023 trip to Prague that she believes was commissioned by the Kremlin, said that for all the theorising, one thing had changed undeniably. “We thought the Kremlin wouldn’t be as brazen as to do something on United States soil,” she said. “It’s a different landscape.”

title: Ukraine war briefing: Kyiv denounces Russia’s inclusion of annexed regions in parliamentary elections
summary: Ukrainian officials call the move illegal while European Commission condemns ‘another blatant violation of international law’ in parliamentary poll. What we know on day 1,670
text: Ukraine has denounced Moscow for having Russia’s parliamentary elections for the first time include residents of regions it illegally annexed from Ukraine during the war. Kyiv officials called the action illegal and a human rights activist described residents there as being coerced to participate in the poll, which is part of Kremlin efforts to cement its gains in Ukraine. The vote across Russia started on Friday and lasts until Sunday but balloting has in fact been under way in the annexed parts of Ukraine and some areas on the Russian side of the border since the end of last month, with Russian officials citing security reasons for the extended period. Russian authorities say the Donetsk, Luhansk, Kherson and Zaporizhzhia territories – annexed by Russia in September 2022 in a move not recognised internationally – have more than 3.5 million voters. Authorities in Kyiv called the voting in those territories illegal and urged foreign governments and international organisations not to recognise the election. They warned Ukrainians that taking part in organising the vote for the State Duma – Russia’s lower house of parliament – could carry criminal liability. Vladimir Putin has emphasised the importance of balloting there in a poll intended to show public support for the war and widely expected to see the ruling pro-Putin United Russia party retain its dominance. The European Commission said the voting in Russian-held regions represented “another blatant violation of international law”. “The European Union does not and will never recognise either the holding of these so-called elections, sham elections, in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine or their results,” spokesperson Christian Wigand said. Ukrainian human rights groups called on residents of the Russia-held territories to stay away from the polls and “above all, to protect their lives and health and to look after their own safety”. “Holding Russian elections in the temporarily occupied territories is an attempt to use the electoral process to legitimise the Russian occupation and the attempted annexation of Ukrainian territories,” the coalition of nine groups said in a statement. Violeta Artemchuk, coordinator of the Donbas SOS human rights group that was among those who signed the statement, said members of local election commissions were going house to house – escorted by Russian troops and security agents – to force people to vote. Russian authorities reported attacks ⁠on voting systems and communication lines across the country on Saturday amid the poll. The attacks were ‌continuing, Central Election Commission chair Ella Pamfilova was cited as saying by state media, but all were being successfully repelled. Putin has accused Ukraine of trying to interfere with the vote, without providing evidence, while Kyiv has called the election farcical. The US has approved a potential $2.68bn sale of air defence equipment to Ukraine, after Kyiv made repeated pleas for support to fend off Russian attacks. The state department said in a congressional notification that it made “a determination approving a possible foreign military sale to the government of Ukraine” for buying air defence development upgrades and related equipment and services. The proposed sale is subject to congressional review. Luxembourg’s authorities were investigating drone sightings that forced the temporary suspension of operations at the nation’s main airport overnight, the prime minister said on Saturday. Luc Frieden said Luxembourg was cooperating with Nato allies over the incident, which came amid heightened concerns in Europe over hybrid attacks from Russia. He said the presence of “potentially bigger drones” in the country’s airspace had been observed “over the past few days” but it was too early to say where they had come from. Ukraine and Russian have positions on the Black Sea that are “difficult to reconcile” to end the attacks there, Turkish foreign minister Hakan Fidan has said. Exasperated by the strikes, Turkey sent a proposal to Russia and Ukraine to end attacks on civilian ships, a Turkish diplomat told Agence France-Presse on Thursday. “We received responses from both sides,” Fidan told television’s NTV on Saturday. “We are trying to reach a conclusion. Frankly, both sides have demands and positions that are difficult to reconcile. Our first priority is the extraction of grain from the Black Sea. Countries around the world need it.”

title: Future of German chancellor hangs in the balance as two states go to polls
summary: Embattled Friedrich Merz faces nervous wait while far-right Alternative für Deutschland party targets further gains
text: Voters in two German states are going to the polls with the political future of the embattled chancellor, Friedrich Merz, hanging in the balance and an emboldened far right targeting further gains. Coming two weeks after a seismic election in Saxony-Anhalt in which the anti-immigration, pro-Kremlin Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) scored its highest ever result in a regional poll, the nativist party is expected to drain support again from Merz’s conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU). Just how brutal the outcome is could affect Merz’s ability to hang on as leader after only 16 months in power, possibly setting wheels in motion for his replacement or even snap elections – currently regarded as unlikely but not ruled out. About 2.5 million people are eligible to vote in the capital Berlin and nearly 1.3 million in the Baltic coast state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. Polling booths open at 8am local time on Sunday and will close at 6pm, when Merz and his allies will be watching exit polls on tenterhooks. The luckless chancellor has resisted calls to quit and vowed to fight for a signature package of economic and social welfare changes he argues are crucial to Germany’s future. “We as a government were elected for four years, I was elected for four years,” he told an industry group. “And I want to use these four years to lead the country out of this difficult period.” Merz, whose personal approval ratings have nosedived to 10%, cancelled a plan to speak at the UN general assembly in New York because “his presence is required in Berlin” after the elections, a government official said. His credibility has been tarnished by broken campaign promises to return Europe’s largest economy to growth and cut the AfD, the biggest opposition party in parliament and number one in opinion polls, down to size. The AfD fell just short of an absolute majority in former communist Saxony-Anhalt, which would have allowed it to govern on its own. It is looking for defectors from other parties to make it the first far-right force to run a German state since the Nazi period. However, polls indicate the AfD will fall well short of such a prospect in both of Sunday’s elections, even with its palpable sense of momentum. In Berlin, which is one of Germany’s 16 federal states, the incumbent CDU is vying for first place against the far-left Die Linke, which has called for expropriation of corporate landlords to fight rising housing costs. About 85% of Berlin households rent their homes and advertised rents have nearly doubled since 2014, when the city was still labelled “poor but sexy” by its then mayor, Klaus Wowereit. The AfD is polling strongly in third or fourth place, even in the cosmopolitan capital. The current mayor, Kai Wegner of the CDU, abandoned his re-election bid in July after getting tangled in contradictions explaining a decision to play tennis while large parts of the German capital were hit by an arson-triggered power blackout last winter. Stefan Evers, Berlin’s chief finance official, replaced him as the candidate but has failed to lift the party’s polling scores. In Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, the situation looks even dicier for Merz, whose weakness regional leaders have blamed for their poor showing. The AfD and the Social Democrats are locked in a neck-and-neck race while the CDU risks its first single-digit result in 75 years. If it crashes out of parliament entirely by falling below the 5% bar to representation, it would be unprecedented in the postwar period and mark a stinging setback for Merz’s quest to stay in office. The AfD’s triumph in Saxony-Anhalt sent shock waves through Germany and beyond and has left Merz’s back to the wall, with speculation rampant he could be replaced by another Christian Democrat as chancellor well before the next general election, due in 2029. Holger Schmieding, the chief economist at Berenberg bank, said he still expected Merz to serve out his full term. “But the risk that the CDU may revolt against him and replace the unpopular chancellor seems to have risen from 20% 10 days ago to roughly 35% now, in my view,” he said in a research note, underlining the impact of a global rise in petrol prices on already angry voters. Although some economic indicators have improved on Merz’s watch, soaring living costs and deindustrialisation in core sectors such as automaking in the face of Chinese competition have taken a heavy toll. Meanwhile a significant reduction in new arrivals at the border has failed to win back AfD voters, who are responding to the party’s strong focus on economic anxiety, fears around crime, and resistance to Merz’s staunch support for Ukraine. The AfD built its victory in Saxony-Anhalt in large part by mobilising non-voters. Its opponents are hoping the spectre of a far-right juggernaut across Germany will get voters to the polls in support of mainstream democratic parties, after tens of thousands joined anti-AfD street protests in the wake of the Saxony-Anhalt rout.

title: Sea dragon populations decimated in ‘mind-blowing’ mass mortality event caused by South Australian algal bloom
summary: Thousands of sea dragons, pipefishes and seahorses have washed up along state’s coastline according to analysis of citizen scientist records
text: Thousands of sea dragons, pipefishes and seahorses died during South Australia’s devastating algal bloom, in what ecologists say is the worst mass mortality event for the fish family globally. More than 1,600 weedy and leafy sea dragons, 1,400 pipefishes and 160 seahorses washed up as the harmful algae spread along the state’s coastline, according to analysis of citizen scientist records by Dragon Search SA. The state is home to more than 30 species of Syngnathidae, a family that includes sea dragons, seahorses, pipefishes and more. At least 13 were affected by the toxic bloom, which began in March 2025 and still lingers at one site in southern Spencer gulf. Weedy and leafy sea dragons, found only in Australia, were often some of the first mortalities observed, as the algal bloom spread up and down the coast. Sign up to get climate and environment editor Adam Morton’s Clear Air column as a free newsletter “Pipefishes and seahorses washed up mainly over winter and spring of 2025, but records of dead sea dragons continued for more than a year,” the report said. Prof David Booth, a marine ecologist specialising in sea dragons at the University of Technology Sydney, said scientists, governments and citizens were all “very concerned” about the future of the state’s marine emblem, known as “leafies”. “South Australian populations have probably been very much decimated, which is really sad, that’s the centre of their world distribution.” Weedy sea dragons, which dominated the tally with 1,524 specimens recorded, recently had their conservation status upgraded to vulnerable by the International Union for the Conservation of Nature. The leafy sea dragon’s status was also being reassessed in light of the bloom. The large and sustained mortalities and the loss of habitat, including kelp and seagrasses, would probably have long-term consequences, the report said. “There’s so much habitat destruction, huge loss of sponges, kelps, seagrasses, all those sorts of things that these animals need, and their food, little shrimps, that we really need to be working on,” Booth said. “There’s habitat restoration going on but it is a big job.” Scientists were also looking at other solutions, including rearing the sea dragon young in aquariums, and even artificial structures like seahorse hotels, which might help pipefish. Dr Yolanda Waters, a dive instructor and chief executive of Divers for Climate, said the losses were “extremely concerning”, and divers were often among the first to observe the bloom’s impacts underwater, she said. “It’s been a really up and down journey for the last 18 months, watching the ocean change, and we’ve all honestly still got our fingers crossed because we don’t know what’s going to happen long-term.” Stefan Andrews, a marine biologist and co-founder of the Great Southern Reef Foundation, said the scale of the mortalities was “mind blowing”, especially for animals like sea dragons, which were rare to see and found in only a handful of locations along the coast. More than 800 species have been affected in Australia’s first bloom of Karenia cristata, a rare and toxic type of algae deadly to marine life. Surveys and reports were beginning to put numbers on the devastating toll, such as the catastrophic decline in giant cuttlefish this year, research made possible through the contributions of citizen scientists and divers. “We saw so many people just step up and do their bit to report observations,” he said. “Sometimes mortalities that wash up on the beach could have disappeared in a matter of hours. So to have all of this data and information that scientists can analyse deeply is so useful to get an understanding of what’s going on.”

title: Gavin Newsom signs election security bills to thwart federal interference by Trump
summary: Bills signed by California governor safeguard vote by mail and make seizing ballots or election records a felony
text: California governor Gavin Newsom has signed off on a package of bills aimed at bolstering election security, including measures to thwart federal political interference, his office announced on Sunday. The pieces of legislation appear to address hot button national and state electoral issues, including an extension to the hours for mail-in voting drop off locations. Newsom singled out the vote-by-mail measure, framing it as a safeguard against the Trump administration’s efforts to restrict the practice it claims is rife with fraud. The US supreme court recently blocked the administration’s proposed changes to vote-by-mail, including an unwieldy mandate for states to submit lists of approved voters for mail ballots to the US postal service. “Donald Trump won’t stop until he can exert dictatorial control over your free vote and disenfranchise millions of people this November. California will stop him at every opportunity,” he said in a statement. “We have no bigger task than fighting to protect the right to vote from interference and meddling – the future of democracy is on the line.” Another bill makes it a felony to seize ballots or election records, an apparent reference to Riverside county sheriff Chad Bianco, who earlier this year took possession of over 650,000 ballots from a 2025 redistricting special election. The package also puts forth parameters around how political campaigns interact with social media influencers with a bill to impose penalties against individuals who do not disclose paid political content. In the recent gubernatorial race for Newsom’s successor, contender and billionaire philanthropist Tom Steyer faced criticism for paying thousands of dollars to content creators, who promoted him without proper disclosure. He was accused of trying to buy the race. At the time, a spokesperson for his campaign said Steyer believed in fair compensation for the content creators’ work. Newsom’s package comes after Trump repeatedly cast doubt on the veracity of the state’s 2026 primaries, saying without evidence that its slow counting process was an attempt to rig the outcome. “California is meeting the moment,” said secretary of state Shirley Weber in a statement. “No one should doubt the degree of our resolve in protecting our democracy.”

title: Thick smoke seen near Riyadh airport as Houthis claim attack on Saudi capital
summary: Authorities issued warnings for city in first such alerts for Riyadh since fighting with Iran-backed Houthis escalated in July
text: Yemen’s Houthis said they attacked “sensitive” sites in the Saudi capital with missiles and drones, hours after flames and a large plume of black smoke were seen rising above Riyadh airport on Saturday. The Saudi government sent air raid alerts to citizens by phone overnight warning of aerial attacks, marking the first time the government has issued such alerts for Riyadh since fighting with the Iran-backed Houthis escalated in July. Explosions were heard in Riyadh as firefighters battled to extinguish the flames of a burning fuel tank emblazoned with the logo of the Saudi oil company Aramco near the city’s King Khalid international airport. Residents told Agence France-Presse that hours after the alert, they had heard what sounded like another round of explosions echoing through parts of the Saudi capital. According to tracking website FlightRadar24, there were “major problems” at the airport and it has been listed under its maximum disruption index. “In the direction of the airport, we saw black smoke and fire,” one resident told AFP, speaking on condition of anonymity. The Saudi civil defence force sent air raid alerts overnight on Friday to residents of Riyadh, Jeddah and other cities including Yanbu, a major industrial port which is home to critical oil facilities. The military coalition fighting the Houthis said its air defences had destroyed a missile fired by the Yemeni group toward Riyadh. The all-clear was given shortly afterwards, but residents were encouraged not to gather in crowds. A Houthi military spokesperson, Yahya Saree, said the group had foiled unspecified “criminal attempts” ⁠in the Yemeni capital of Sana’a, blaming Saudi Arabia and vowing a response. The group also said the Saudi air force had conducted hundreds of airstrikes against it in recent days. The UN security council condemned the continued Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia in a statement on Friday. It said they had included attacks that affected civilian and energy infrastructure and had injured civilians, including women and children. It also condemned the Houthis’ military offensive in Yemen, where nearly 105,000 people have fled their homes, the International Organization for Migration said on Wednesday. The security council’s 15 members called for “practical cooperation” to prevent the Houthis from acquiring arms, military training, financing and other military-related assistance needed to carry out their attacks. They stressed that all countries must enforce the UN arms embargo against the group. The Houthis recently seized control of the strategic Red Sea islands of Greater and Lesser Hanish. Earlier this month, the group captured the port of Mokha and Perim island in the Bab al-Mandab strait, fueling fears the world could face a second oil supply crisis. The fighting between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia has developed as a new theatre of conflict in the wider war that began with US and Israeli strikes against Iran at the end of February. Donald Trump has rebuffed Saudi requests for direct US military intervention against the Houthis. A US state department security alert issued on Saturday for Americans ‌in the Middle East cited Houthi attacks. title: Kemi Badenoch accuses Andy Burnham of ‘fiddling while Europe risks burning’
summary: Tory leader claims prime minister is avoiding difficult decisions as she urges him to increase defence spending
text: Kemi Badenoch has accused Andy Burnham of “fiddling while Europe is at risk of burning”, as she repeated her call for the prime minister to cut the welfare budget to fund increase spending on defence. Speaking to the Telegraph, the Tory leader said that “Burnham may be a people pleaser but difficult choices cannot be avoided through dither and delay”. She said the government had to “fund our defence properly” at a time when former military chiefs have raised questions about Britain’s preparedness for war. Badenoch said: “Our government is fiddling while Europe is at risk of burning. In France and Poland, leaders are taking action now against the growing Russian threat. What is our government doing? Has anyone heard from Wes Streeting, the former head of the National Union of Students, who has rocked up as defence secretary?” Discourse on the “welfare v warfare” debate has grown louder in recent days since Burnham’s comments during prime minister’s questions on 9 September that national security could not “come at the expense of social security”. The Tory leader said Burnham was sending a “dangerous” message that he would not cut welfare to fund the military, which was “heard loud and clear in Moscow as well as Manchester”. She added: “We have to stop pretending that we are living in a carefree end of history when Russia is testing our resolve week after week. It’s time to get serious.” The UK has promised to commit 3.5% of national income to defence by 2035, in line with a pledge by Nato members, but there is growing pressure on the chancellor, John Healey, to outline how further increases will be achieved before next month’s budget. Adm Lord West, a former security minister under Gordon Brown, said Britain’s military was in “quite a parlous state”. “In many ways, one could argue we are already at war. We are certainly in the grey zone – whether it’s cyber-attacks, drones getting near the edge of somewhere or threats to underwater cables,” he added. Lord Dannatt, a former chief of the general staff, said: “My bottom line is that Andy Burnham, and regretfully I would now add John Healey, are playing fast and loose with the nation’s security.” The Conservatives have proposed capping housing benefit to raise £4bn to spend on defence. The party has rejected suggestions that the policy would make people homeless but suggested some would have to “move somewhere cheaper.” The Tories will hold their annual conference in Birmingham in two weeks.

title: Camilla praises ‘life-enhancing power’ of books amid Earl Spencer memoir controversy
summary: Queen speaks of love of reading at festival for charity she founded after success of her Instagram book club
text: Queen Camilla has spoken of her love for books with a “life-enhancing power” after a series of allegations were made about King Charles in extracts from Earl Spencer’s memoir about the life of Diana, Princess of Wales. Camilla was welcomed to Chatsworth House in Derbyshire for the first day of the festival for the Queen’s Reading Room, a charity she founded after the success of her Instagram book club during the pandemic. She told the guests: “I created my Reading Room simply because, like all of us here, I love books and their life-enhancing power and I want to share that love with others. “In those early days, I had no idea if anybody would be interested but six years on, we are a global community of millions from over 180 countries, swapping recommendations, undertaking research and donating thousands of books to women’s refuges and homeless shelters.” Camilla’s speech about her love for reading comes after Spencer made a series of damning claims about the king in a new memoir chronicling the life of his sister, Diana, that prompted an “unprecedented” response from Buckingham Palace, which said: “The pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason”. In further developments on Saturday, Spencer accused Charles of “gaslighting” in the palace’s response to the claims and said “Diana would be cheering from the rafters at this book”. Speaking to the Mail on Sunday, Spencer said “it was not every day you wake up to find you’ve been gaslit by the king”. He added: “It was astonishingly provocative and below the belt because it was essentially trying to say I’d lied without the king being able to deny what I’d said. “I also thought it was a rather poor imitation of the ‘recollections may vary’ quote, which was a much more elegant way of putting things, but in these circumstances entirely out of place.” The BBC is scheduled to broadcast its full interview with Spencer on Sunday. Camilla will also feature in the BBC Arts programme The Book That Changed My Life, which is due to air next month as part of the National Year of Reading 2026. The BBC has said the documentary film will follow Camilla as she meets four remarkable people whose lives have been changed by books at moments when they most needed them. The latest details of the show were revealed on Saturday at the Reading Room festival. During the event, she spoke to Ian Kirby, one of the contributors to the documentary, asking him about his experience of finding community and hope through reading. Kirby, from Gateshead, fell into depression after a traumatic incident at home, but discovered a new perspective on his own experiences after joining a local book club and reading the autobiography of local boxing champion Glenn McCrory. Speaking in the documentary, he says: “That is the beauty of a book. It can give you experiences you’ve never experienced, but they can also be an inspiration.” The BBC has previously said the documentary would “feature individuals from a wide range of backgrounds who all share one thing – moving stories of resilience and renewal, fostered by reading”. “From finding solace in a book while in prison, to overcoming deep depression through the connection of a local book club, or finding the inspiration to completely change their life, these stories reveal how books offer salvation, hope, joy, deep connection and fresh perspectives when people need them most,” it added. It said the film would also explore the growing scientific evidence that reading can improve health and wellbeing. The documentary was first announced by Camilla during a Clarence House reception celebrating the fifth anniversary of her Queen’s Reading Room book club in March. In a speech, Camilla described how her literary project was launched to share her “lifelong conviction that books make life better”. At the festival, alongside the journalist Reeta Chakrabarti and broadcaster Gyles Brandreth, Camilla revealed her four book recommendations for autumn – Finding Belle by Chakrabarti, The Picture of Dorian Gray by Oscar Wilde, Whistler by Ann Patchett and Sashenka by Simon Sebag Montefiore. In the Sculpture Gallery, Camilla also attended a reception with literary figures taking part in the festival, including Lee Child, who wrote the Jack Reacher novel series, and Turkish-British novelist Elif Shafak. The Book That Changed My Life is expected to air on BBC Two on 14 October.

title: Baby born via surrogate can leave Texas for treatment in California, court rules
summary: Ruling latest step in legal fight over medically fragile child born after surrogate reportedly rejected couple’s request for abortion
text: The Texas supreme court has decided that the month-old infant that surrogate McKenna West gave birth to can be relocated to Los Angeles, a Thursday ruling that came weeks after a California court had recognized the biological parents’ custody rights. “Sustaining the life of the medically fragile child is the paramount concern in this time-sensitive matter,” the court wrote in a Thursday order, referring to the baby’s rare severe heart defect. West had attempted to block the biological parents from removing the child from Texas and taking him to a hospital in Los Angeles where the couple live. The court cited testimony from the infant’s Texas physician, who described the window for an ICU-to-ICU transfer as short and “ripe now”. West’s attorneys did not immediately respond to a request for comment about the Thursday ruling. The infant, named Rumi by his biological parents, has hypoplastic left heart syndrome, a condition that impedes blood flow and requires extensive surgery. Without treatment, the defect can be fatal. The condition was detected when the baby was a fetus, prompting California couple Nausheen Gilkar and Omar Ahmed to reportedly ask that West terminate the pregnancy. West, who resides in Alaska, traveled to Texas, where abortion is illegal, to deliver the child. West and her legal team maintain that the couple attempted to force her into having the procedure, while lawyers for Gilkar and Ahmed say that West initially agreed to the abortion, before blindsiding them with the legal battle for custody. The case has stoked enormous debate around abortion and parental rights, particularly in the conservative mediasphere. The Texas attorney general, Ken Paxton, elevated the dispute’s national profile, when he intervened to ensure the baby would receive medical care after his birth. West had appealed to the US supreme court, suggesting Gilkar and Ahmed would put the baby into end-of-life care at a hospice rather than continue treatment for the heart defect. West was seeking to be informed about the baby’s medical status and to “advocate for her rights”, according to court documents. “Ordinarily, MW would have been deemed [the baby’s] mother under Texas law by virtue of giving birth to him. But because of the unlawful California judgment, she has been dismissed with prejudice from the Texas proceedings and denied any information,” West’s lawyers wrote in a court filing, using West’s initials. The couple’s attorneys responded in a court filing saying “there is simply no truth whatsoever” to the hospice claim. They argued that if the court sided with West, it would sow confusion over who had authority to dictate and consent to medical decisions for the child. Gilkar told a Dallas court in August that Rumi was “the most beautiful person”. “He’s the love of our lives. He’s suffering a lot,” she said.

title: Footballers and fans pay tribute to Noah Woods after toddler’s death in Suffolk
summary: Players in Everton v Ipswich Town match wear black armbands as supporters join in minute’s applause
text: Players wore black armbands during Everton’s home match against Ipswich Town on Saturday, as part of a tribute to three-year-old Noah Woods, whose body was found after he went missing in Suffolk this week. A photograph of the boy was shown on the big screen before the Premier League game in Liverpool, and three minutes after kick-off both sets of supporters stood to applaud in memory of Noah. The toddler, who was non-verbal, partially deaf and had been undergoing an assessment for autism, became separated from a relative after visiting a playground in Brantham on Tuesday afternoon, Suffolk police said. About 1,300 members of the public joined a search which ended on Wednesday when police divers recovered a body from a nearby lake. On Thursday, Noah’s father Rhys Woods paid tribute to his son in a message shared on a community Facebook group. He wrote: “There are no words to describe the pain of this loss, we are all absolutely heartbroken, Noah was the sweetest and most innocent little boy, with nothing but love to give, and we are going to miss him so very much.” Ipswich Town’s captain Dara O’Shea and goalkeeper Christian Walton were among a delegation from the Suffolk club who laid flowers at the playground where he went missing. Town defender Leif Davis donated £2,000 to a fundraising appeal set up by Good Dads Club, a group of fathers in Colchester, Essex, to support Noah’s family. It had already received more than £100,000 in donations from more than 6,000 supporters by Saturday evening. Suffolk constabulary said the child’s death was not being treated as suspicious but that the force still has a number of inquiries to complete before submitting a file to the coroner.

title: Ed Davey takes aim at Reform and Elon Musk as Lib Dem conference begins
summary: Leader says party ‘won’t give up the fight’ to defeat ‘nasty populism’ in first-day speech to delegates in Brighton
text: The Liberal Democrats’ leader, Sir Ed Davey, took aim at Nigel Farage and Elon Musk on the first day of his party’s annual conference, saying Lib Dems would not give up the fight to defeat “nasty populism” and Reform UK’s “£72m arsenal of hate and lies”. On stage at Brighton Centre, Davey called on the assembled delegates not to be deterred in the face of Reform’s hope “that the anger and the hatred and the lies will grind us down until eventually we just give up”. He also praised earlier speakers for showing “why we care and why we fight” and contrasted this with Reform, which, he said, “care about their own bank balance and they fight because two crypto billionaires gave them 72 million quid”. Davey, who entered conference season having to address frustrations over his leadership expressed by some Lib Dem MPs, also used the speech to recall his early political life as a student campaigning successfully for his university college to boycott Barclays, due to its investments in apartheid-era South Africa. He spoke of his “visceral shock [and] overwhelming anger at seeing human beings treating other human beings with total contempt” and drew parallels between that experience and the need to not look away “when we see human dignity under attack”. Davey said: “Today – we are back. Fighting again the fight that fired me up at university. The fight to end injustices. In our country and around the world. The fight to defeat the nasty populism of Trump, Le Pen, the AfD and the rest. “The fight to stop the world’s richest man who learned racism in apartheid South Africa from funding racism around the world.” He also referred to the “fight to defend the Royal National Lifeboat Institution after volunteers for the coastal rescue charity were recently targeted online amid anti-migrant protests”. He said “Reform know they don’t speak for the real United Kingdom” – and what Farage was “counting on to get him to No 10” was that people would get “tired, depressed, fed up with seeing Zia Yusuf on BBC Question Time week after week”. But Davey said he hoped Reform were watching and would see “a party that won’t be ground down. That won’t be deterred. That won’t give up the fight.” Also during the first day of the conference, Lib Dem health spokesperson Helen Morgan set out a £600m plan to improve maternity care, including proposals to bring in one-to-one midwifery for every woman in labour backed by a round-the-clock senior consultant. The party said the measures will pay for themselves by reducing how much the NHS has to spend on compensation for maternity negligence claims every year – totalling £1.3bn in 2024-25. Munira Wilson, the Lib Dem education spokesperson, said the party would introduce a guarantee to provide 100 hours of work experience for students from GCSE age to 18 to tackle the crisis of young people not in education, employment or training.
