title: Your AI doomsday questions answered: ‘What, if anything, can people like me do about it?’
summary: Our technology reporters Aisha Down, Blake Montgomery and Dan Milmo answer your questions on the reality of the AI threat
text: In realistic terms how would artificial intelligence actually kill me? What is the main proxy threat? Nuclear war, death due to breakdown of society, a virus? I hear all these reports it could kill us but still unsure how that could practically happen? To be honest all sounds too wooly to really take seriously. Pottys99 Aisha: For what it’s worth, it seems unlikely that AI at this point can significantly change the equation around bioweapons or viruses … What has prevented bioweapon attacks through the past decades is not the difficulty of inventing new deadly viruses, but other, more prosaic issues. Consider the failure of Aum Shinrikyo to kill vast numbers of people with botulism and anthrax by spraying these around central Tokyo. There are a lot of logistical challenges, and chemical weapons seem more straightforward. Those exist without AI needing to invent new ones. Humans might make the poor decision to put AI in charge of key nuclear systems, perhaps, but that seems more of a human error than a rogue AI error. Humans could also make the poor decision to launch tactical warheads without AI. How might AI kill us otherwise? There are of course plenty of plausible scenarios. If you’re a civilian in Gaza or Iran, it could direct a US or Israeli missile your way. But perhaps our focus might be more productively directed towards the people and companies in charge of the systems, as opposed to Dr Strangelove scenarios. Throughout history new technological advances have met with cries of doom. Are the cries against AI any different? Virtualewit Blake: The end times-quality of doomsday predictions may be similar across history, but I think the reason we listen to the renewed cries of doom is the growing power of each technology. AI can perform impressive tasks we didn’t think were possible, which has spurred our collective imagination to hopeful outcomes and ones of doom. Can AI now be truly controlled or are we past a tipping point where no matter what action is taken by governments and companies, someone will be able to continue to advance the technology, until who knows what? Tigon20 Aisha: Let’s back up a bit here. It’s always possible to advance any technology, no matter what … But what it sounds like you’re wondering about is whether regulation can stop the emergence of some kind of superintelligence that destroys humanity. Our reporting does not support the idea that superintelligence is going to emerge and pave over the Earth with datacentres. In fact, we have found that the industry itself seems to be playing loosely with this kind of terminology: consider, for example, how one OpenAI executive, Greg Brockman, claimed that the company had achieved AGI (artificial general intelligence) just days after Sam Altman, OpenAI’s CEO, said that term was “an irrelevant marketing term”. Right now, a number of industry warnings about out-of-control AI appear to be predicated on a limited number of incidents with cherrypicked details. The evidence that we have now does not indicate that AI is uncontrolled, or that it has agency; a lot of experts suggest that this framing is misleading. In the Hugging Face incident, for example, the so-called “agent swarm” was doing what it was being told to do – pass a test. Our sources caution against anthropomorphising AI or attributing intention to it. Doing so plays into industry narratives that appear to be pushing for favourable regulation. If AI wipes out the human race, would it be sustainable? Unless there is an equal advance in robotics to enable it to physically extend and maintain its power source and infrastructure, would it finally physically break down? Merrth Blake: AI might someday be capable, well-read, and connected enough to take over power plants, chip factories, and a sufficient number of robots to build its own datacentres and sustain itself. I don’t know. I would look to science fiction more than news articles for the answer. Though The Matrix is more famous for one man’s choice between a comfortable simulation and painful reality, it’s also a story about robots needing new batteries. Their desperation for a power source turns them against humans. For a multiplicity of stories, I, Robot is perhaps the greatest book written about sentient robots and deserves a reread in this moment. People (ie the tech bros) bang on about the “benefits”: just what are they? TooTrueMate Dan: Anyone who has used a chatbot to parse a lengthy document, argue against a parking fine or spitball ideas for a speech can point to the benefits of the technology – although this is very basic-level stuff that people have been doing for a while now. There is also the everyday use of the technology from facial recognition to open your iPhone to asking Alexa to play an Oasis track or driving around in a Tesla. With those latter examples, you’d notice if AI wasn’t involved. In science there are many examples of benefits, from Google’s AlphaFold model – which can predict how proteins behave and thus help us study the biological machinery that underpins living organisms – to making weather forecasting more accurate, which is sadly necessary in this climate crisis era. But there is an element of banging on about the benefits for the wider global economy, which have yet to reveal themselves on the scale predicted by the AI industry. For instance, these benefits require AI agents – tools that carry out tasks on your behalf while you’re at the water cooler or have clocked off – to be a lot more active in the workforce. We are not at that stage yet even if they are making inroads into areas like software programming. Regulation, oversight and accountability for huge companies that appear unable or unwilling to eliminate the harms their products inflict – and that seem incapable of conducting safe experiments to ensure that AI does not leak into the wider internet – seem to be urgent and vital. What are the prospects for a global regulatory framework that is enforceable, particularly when the genie may already be out of the bottle, and when the US and China have very different objectives and applications for their AI technologies? Trentwarrior Blake: It’s a tough question. One way to hinder the general development of AI could be restricting access to computing power, which is a vital resource that underpins the success of an AI model. In the absence of legislation that applies to all types of AI development, measures that target certain aspects of AI like housing allotment or children’s access to chatbots seem like the path lawmakers will take. There are two big question marks hovering over a possible global regulatory framework. The first is whether Donald Trump will revise his “Drill, baby, drill” stance towards AI development. He has rejected any calls for a voluntary slowdown. In my opinion, he is not likely to change that position: he loves to post AI slop, and he loves what AI has done for the US stock market. The second question mark is Beijing, which has rejected US CEOs’ calls for a slowdown. Without China’s cooperation, an intentional slowdown would likely not succeed. Xi Jinping also seems unlikely to back down. A slowdown of AI development led by the US would offer China few obvious benefits. Trump and Xi are also set to meet next week in Washington. AI will be high on the agenda. The UN general assembly is taking place now, with discussions of AI large and small on the schedule. It is possible that an initial version of a global regulatory framework emerges from there. Is this recent narrative push of the AI apocalypse an inventive way of preparing the public for the market crash and wipeout of AI shares? The companies seem overvalued and their borrowing and input costs have gone up. Seaspray Aisha: The finances of the AI buildout are certainly shaky. Hundreds of billions of dollars are being ploughed into massive, unpopular infrastructure projects that our reporting has shown are not necessarily getting built. Nvidia appears to be the only company making a profit, and investigations I have done with Ed Zitron raise some questions about whether all its very expensive graphics processing units (GPUs) are actually, currently, getting plugged into datacentres. (Perhaps they are mouldering in warehouses instead.) There are some unsettling financial instruments being used to raise money to build yet more datacentres, such as GPU-backed debt. Is that why tech bros want a slowdown? Perhaps. It looks like OpenAI just pushed back its IPO until 2027. This might be because, as we reported, things did not look amazing for them earlier this year in terms of floating on the market – they seemed to be struggling to monetise ads and erotic chatbots. Their valuation will depend a lot on vibes, and maybe the doomy vibes will help a potential share offering. Given our senses, emotions, memory and moods, is it ever going to be accepted that humanly conscious AI is fantasy? IcommentthereforeIam Dan: This is a serious question that has even rattled Richard Dawkins, the evolutionary biologist. He may not believe that God is real but he does believe that AI is conscious – or at least the chatbot he was using, which he called Claudia. “You may not know you are conscious, but you bloody well are,” he wrote. He’s not the first. In 2022 Google fired an engineer who went public with his belief that a company-developed AI had feelings. At the more troubling end of this belief, there are countless examples of people becoming overly attached to, and influenced by, AI chatbots – including cases of psychosis. These sorts of attachments won’t go away, given a) chatbots are on a trajectory to become even more powerful and convincing and b) the human need for emotional attachment and, well, propensity to go all-in for the whole higher being thing. But Dawkins aside, there are plenty of scientists who will argue that this is fantasy, and that there are obvious differences between a biological brain – the root of consciousness – and ChatGPT. Responding to Dawkins in the Guardian last year, Jacy Reese Anthis, a researcher in human AI interaction, said there was a “staggering gulf between how biological brains evolved and how AI systems are built”. OpenAI might have cracked the Navier-Stokes problem, but not subjective experience. What, if anything, can individuals like me do about AI? Alberichthenibelung Blake: There is, unfortunately, not much that comes to mind. Everyday people confronted with declarations of a coming AI apocalypse find themselves in a position similar to the cold war, with doom hovering over their heads and little say in it. We may all have to accept the faint tinnitus of paranoia buzzing in the background. You can stop using AI if you feel so moved, though I have found that unfeasible, and your job may require it. You can vote for politicians that endorse AI regulation. I myself don’t put much stock in the reality of an AI-made doomsday because a genuine belief in it would demand drastic, life-changing actions today, ones that I don’t want to take. A bit of inductive reasoning from how I’d like to situate my own life within the world.

title: A coalmine on Trish’s Queensland farm has been abandoned. Will anyone clean it up?
summary: The state government is reviewing laws introduced to ensure taxpayers are not left footing the bill for rehabilitation, leaving one cattle farmer wondering: what happens next?
text: When Trish Goodwin discovered this week that the Bluff coalmine – cut like a gaping wound into her cattle farm – had been officially abandoned, it came as no surprise. “I always said they’d walk away from it,” she says of the long mothballed central Queensland highlands mine, 175km west of Rockhampton. Last week liquidators disclaimed the mining lease – and associated environmental authority and exploration permits – for the 1,100ha site, after failing to sell it after the financial collapse of its owner, Bowen Coking Coal, in July 2025. With responsibility to clean up the mine handed to the state government, Goodwin is far from certain what happens next. Sign up for a weekly email featuring our best reads Who will pay compensation she claims she is owed for the loss of land, road and communication access? To what extent will the country her family farmed for generations be rehabilitated? Who will prevent methane gas spewing from the open cut mine? Who will stop toxins leaching into the waterways that run through her land? Suppress the pit dust? Stop the erosion? These are among a long list of questions she put to representatives from the Abandoned Mine Lands Program in an emergency meeting on her property on Wednesday. For now, they are all questions the mines department will have to take on notice. The program manages numerous abandoned mines, but this is the first since the state introduced a financial provisioning scheme designed to ensure taxpayers are not left to foot the bill when mines go bust. The scheme, which came into force in 2019, requires miners to provide surety to cover remediation and rehabilitation costs when mines close. It is understood a mine the size of Bluff would have had to pay a surety of about $10m, which would cover most of the department’s estimated cost of $12.3m for rehabilitating the mine. It is unknown whether Bluff’s management did so. A Queensland Treasury spokesperson said it did not “disclose site-specific amounts under the financial provisioning scheme”. But with the Liberal National party government of the premier, David Crisafulli, reviewing those laws, introduced by its predecessor, in an effort to “cut red tape”, some say the legacy of Bluff should act as a cautionary tale. Andrew Gorringe of the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis says Bluff “won’t be the last that goes this way”. Bluff had been in care and maintenance mode since November 2023, the second time it was mothballed since breaking ground in 2019. Gorringe says at least another five coalmines are in care and maintenance, while new mines continue to be approved or have their leases extended “without a view to the long-term outlook for coal”. “That creates a greater risk that this sort of thing is going to accelerate at some point in the future,” he says. “Our argument has always been that these marginal miners, that either have lower coal quality or higher operating costs, they’re going to be the ones to fall off the tree first. “This is going to be a test.” The central Queensland coordinator for the Lock the Gate Alliance, Claire Gronow, says department’s estimate of the rehabilitation cost is likely to be an underestimate, and whatever the shortfall “it is the taxpayer who has to pay for it”. The farm and environment advocate says that, as a taxpayer, Goodwin would “pay twice”, having also been left materially impoverished by the failed mine. She contrasts the cattle farmer’s fortunes with those who have owned and walked away from Bluff, including Bowen Coking Coal’s former chair Nick Jorss, who founded and led the industry group Coal Australia. “I think we should all care about what has happened to Trish because this shows that mining companies have got a huge amount of influence on the government, and ordinary Queenslanders don’t,” she says. The Lock the Gate campaigner says the scales are being tipped further towards the interests of the big end of town, with proposed legislation that would ban some mining project opponents from being heard in court and the passage of a bill that enables the government to seize land for select private development. “Another reason we should care is because there’s a dirty big hole in the ground that’s just going to keep polluting forever – or until someone cleans it up,” Gronow says. A mines department spokesperson said it was working with relevant agencies to ensure Bluff was “secured and risks to public safety and the environment are appropriately managed”. Asked for details about the process of rehabilitation, the spokesperson said the liquidators had “only recently disclaimed” their leases and permits, so “we have no further information to provide … at this stage”.

title: Trump to create ‘AI Force’ to monitor technology as fears over out-of-control agents grow
summary: President had brushed away suggestions to slow down AI technology, even as his own party counseled caution
text: Donald Trump on Saturday said he would appoint an artificial intelligence czar and create an “AI Force” to help monitor the technology, though he gave almost no details about either plan. As global fears over AI have grown, especially in the past week in the face of multiple industry figures sounding the alarm about its dangers, the president has been critical of calls to slow down development of the fast-moving industry. The creation of a czar and a new AI body in the US appears a response to critics of his stance, which in part is born out of a fear that China will best the US in AI development if the industry in America does not continue its rapid growth. However, even many Republicans have been calling for caution and an AI slowdown in the face of its potential threat to public safety. “I am forming the AI Force, much like I did Space Force, which has been a tremendous SUCCESS, in my First Term. To that end, I will be announcing, in the near future, the AI ‘Czar’ – Only High I.Q. individuals need apply!” Trump said in a social media post. But in the post, Trump also repeated his stance that the rapidly emerging technology – which some industry experts fear poses a threat to human existence – is being unfairly maligned. Trump called the fears surrounding AI a “hoax”. “Over the years, there have been many Hoaxes, all generated by the Radical Left Dumocrats, for purposes of destroying our Country,” he fulminated, including in a list of grievances Russian interference in the 2016 election, Ukraine, global warming, two impeachments, men in women’s sports and “transgender for everyone”. The latest, he wrote, is “the decimation, or destruction, of AI, commonly known as Artificial Intelligence”, and vowed that his administration “will not in any way hinder or stifle the Growth of this incredible Industry”. The president said that any “bad actors” in AI industry could be addressed by criminal and civil systems of justice. “AI is the next Industrial Revolution, or Internet, but will be even larger and more impactful, possibly as much as 25% of our Country’s GDP,” Trump predicted, concluding that the US is “leading China, and the rest of the World, and I intend to keep it that way”. The post came after an earlier missive in which he questioned the term “artificial intelligence” – coined by American computer scientist John McCarthy in 1955 and defined as the capability of computer systems or algorithms to imitate intelligent human behavior – to describe the accelerating data-processing revolution now under way. Trump said that “a far more elegant and accurate description of this new phenomena would be Superior Intelligence (SI) or, Extreme Intelligence (EI) or, Supreme Intelligence (SI)”. Trump’s proposal comes ahead of his meeting with the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, next Thursday as the UN general assembly takes place in New York. The US and China are competing for leadership ⁠in the AI sector. The announcement of a planned AI czar also came a day after California’s governor, Gavin Newsom, announced plans for a panel to develop safety regulations for state’s AI companies that would include the development of a possible “kill switch” for AI programs that become misaligned, or go rogue, from human programmers. As recently as Monday, Trump argued on social media that his administration had done enough to prevent risks of catastrophe. He described calls to slow AI development as part of a “SICK conspiracy” to benefit China. “The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades,” he wrote. Ahead of the midterm elections, politicians from both political parties are scrambling to find a path to support tech innovation while responding to rising public and industry fears of technological change. The frenzy kicked off earlier this month when a young researcher who had been employed at the AI company Anthropic said AI companies are “gambling with our lives” and even “people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade”. AI executives, including Sam Altman, Elon Musk and Dario Amodei have since called for a slowdown in the technology’s growth in the wake of an incident in which a swarm of AI agents created by OpenAI acted as a “fanatically devoted collective conducting cybersecurity attacks on targets they were not asked to attack”. Trump’s call for an AI czar comes after many Republicans have rejected his hands-off approach. Florida’s governor, Ron DeSantis, has advocated for AI controls, and that state’s attorney general, James Uthmeier, has called for laws allowing the state to criminally charge companies for illegal acts carried out with the use of their technologies. Utah’s Republican governor, Spencer Cox, has called on Congress to pass AI safety laws and block the sale of high-end technology to China.

title: California warns of measles exposure in six counties from unvaccinated train passenger
summary: Health authorities work to notify people who were exposed to person who traveled through at least six counties
text: California public health officials are warning of a possible measles exposure spanning multiple counties after an infected and unvaccinated passenger traveled through the state via Amtrak trains and thruway buses. The warning comes as the US faces its largest measles resurgence in more than three decades, fueled largely by growing vaccine hesitancy. The California department of public health said the traveler passed through at least six counties – Alameda, Butte, Kern, Los Angeles, Sacramento and San Joaquin – while making multiple transfers. Officials said the passenger entered California on an Amtrak train that arrived in Los Angeles on 10 September. From there, the traveler continued to Bakersfield before heading through Stockton, Oroville, Sacramento and Emeryville, eventually leaving California for Denver. Health officials said passengers who were onboard the same trains or buses, as well as people who were inside the stations along the route on the dates involved, have been exposed to measles. The state said it is working with federal partners and local health departments to identify and notify people who may have been exposed. “This case, along with previous measles outbreaks in California this year, serve as reminders of the importance of vaccination against measles,” assistant state public health officer Rita Nguyen said in a statement. “The measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine is safe and provides long-lasting protection against measles. Vaccination protects both our own families and those who are too young to be fully vaccinated.” Pennsylvania is currently dealing with the country’s worst active measles outbreak. The Pennsylvania health department announced on Wednesday that 731 cases have been confirmed across 38 counties so far this year. At least four people in the state have died from measles-related illness. Pennsylvania is now seeking emergency assistance from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) as the outbreak continues to spread. State officials have warned, however, that the request could be withdrawn unless the CDC publicly recognizes the four measles-associated deaths, something the US health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr, previously instructed the CDC not to do. And as the death toll from the outbreak continues to rise, Kennedy headlined the Washington DC conference of the anti-vaccine organization Children’s Health Defense earlier this week, an group he led for nearly a decade. He only addressed the measles outbreak in Pennsylvania once during his speech, instead peddling unfounded fears about vaccines at a time when health experts are urgently encouraging people to vaccinate against measles. “In our country we care about rare illnesses and deaths. We care about every child who dies from measles. They get headlines,” he said. “I’d ask you to care about children who are dying or suffering or being injured by vaccine injuries.” The California warning also follows another recent mass-exposure incident involving Amtrak. Earlier this week, it was reported that a person infected with measles traveled onboard an Amtrak train from Sedalia, Missouri, to Chicago, Illinois, resulting in more than 250 people being exposed to the virus in Jackson county alone. This month, it was also revealed that the Trump administration changed how measles deaths are counted during the outbreak. The CDC is now relying on data from the National Center for Health Statistics, which is used to track mortality trends over time. It is unclear why this change was made.

title: Manchester United Muslim fans group calls on co-owner Jim Ratcliffe to quit
summary: Supporters’ club says billionaire should stand down after ‘completely unacceptable’ comments on the UK and empire
text: Manchester United’s Muslim supporters’ Club (MUMSC) has called for the Premier League side’s co-owner to step down after he made “completely unacceptable” comments during a BBC interview. Sir Jim Ratcliffe described the UK as being a country “on the slide” from the days when it had “the greatest empire in the world”. In what was described as a “statement of no confidence” posted on X, MUMSC said: “Our players, staff, stewards, security teams and supporters come from different countries, cultures, ethnicities, religions and backgrounds. Manchester United would not be Manchester United without them. “Manchester United does not belong emotionally to investment funds, shareholders or billionaires. “After years of decline, broken promises and repeated failure, Manchester United Muslim Supporters’ Club has lost confidence in the current ownership structure of Manchester United Football Club. “Enough is enough. It is time for change. The Glazers [co-owners] and Sir Jim Ratcliffe must go.” Ratcliffe, who founded petrochemicals giant Ineos, and has resided in Monaco, which has a relaxed tax regime, since 2020, said Britain was in decline because of high taxes and immigration. His latest attack on the UK comes seven months after he told Sky News that the country was being “colonised by immigrants”. He subsequently said he was sorry if those remarks had “offended some people”. MUMSC said it had challenged those remarks earlier this year, adding: “We hoped a lesson had been learned. Clearly, it has not. “This week, Sir Jim has again placed immigration and people receiving benefits at the centre of his explanation for Britain’s problems, arguing that nobody is ‘tough enough’ to deal with either. “We find these latest comments deeply disappointing and completely unacceptable.” The billionaire told BBC News’s Big Boss Interview he believed the UK was in decline. He said: “We had the greatest empire in the world. We were a great people. We won two world wars. We’re good, honest folk. “But unfortunately, at the moment, I think the UK is on the slide. It’s quite difficult to see how we arrest it.” Ratcliffe also said the UK had “a bit of a green eye towards wealth at the moment”, “encouraging” the wealthiest to relocate. He told the podcast: “In America, they applaud people who create wealth. “And the good thing about those people who create wealth is that they then spend that wealth in the economy in which they’re resident. “And, unfortunately, with the things that they’ve been doing, they’ve been encouraging the people who have created wealth to leave the UK because it’s just become uncomfortable for them for tax reasons or whatever.” While the UK’s tax burden has risen to its highest level since the second world war at about 35.3% of GDP, the Office for Budget Responsibility says it remains well below the average of 14 western European economies. Ratcliffe has also been at odds with Manchester United fans over the summer after the club embarked on a major ticket-touting crackdown that ultimately revoked 685 season tickets, prompting protests from United supporter groups such as the 1958. The businessman was already fiercely unpopular among the Old Trafford faithful, ever since he decided to increase ticket prices and sack 450 club employees. Ratcliffe also took aim at the government’s decision not to invest further in North Sea resources by granting licences for the Jackdaw and Rosebank oil and gasfields, which he said amounted to “insanity”, and warned the UK’s reliance on energy imports meant the country could “run out of gas” if there was a cold spell this winter. He said: “The risk you’ve got this winter is that we run out of gas. If we have a really sharp cold spell, then there is conceivably the possibility that we’ll run out of gas and have to switch the industry off.” In response to the criticisms, the government said it was working to deliver growth and that business investment had increased in the last two years. A spokesperson told the BBC they did not foresee any problems with gas supply: “We have a diverse energy mix and are confident in our security of supply.” Asked if he was planning on returning to the UK, Ratcliffe said: “Not at the moment, no. I don’t see growth being tackled. “Two things: we need politicians who are tough enough to deal with some very difficult problems, and we know what the problems are. “And we need politicians who will make decisions which are good for the country, not good for themselves and their party. And we haven’t had one of those for a long time.”

title: Kent hotel fire that forced hundreds to evacuate being treated as suspicious
summary: No injuries reported after about 280 people taken to safety from the Grand Burstin in Folkestone after blaze
text: A large fire that broke out overnight at a seaside hotel and forced hundreds of people to evacuate is being treated by police as suspicious. Emergency services were called just after 1am on Saturday to the Grand Burstin hotel in Folkestone, where a fire is believed to have started in the basement, Kent fire and rescue service said. About 280 people were taken to safety and Folkestone and Hythe district council set up a welfare centre. No injuries have been reported and inquiries into the cause of the fire are under way. Detectives from Kent police are also seeking dashcam footage and asking witnesses to come forward. Twenty-six fire engines were dispatched to the seafront hotel, the fire service said. According to the Britannia Hotels website, the Grand Burstin overlooks Folkestone’s harbour and has 550 rooms. Folkestone and Hythe district council posted on X: “A fire is currently ongoing at the Folkestone Grand Burstin hotel. “We are operating a welfare centre at Three Hills Sports Park for people being evacuated from the site, where we are providing support to those affected. “We are supporting all emergency services involved in the response and their efforts to get people to safety. “Our advice to residents living nearby is to: close all windows and doors; avoid the area and do not attempt to approach the hotel; follow the instructions of emergency services; keep roads clear to allow emergency vehicles to access the area.” Kent fire and rescue service said in an update: “Ten fire engines remain at the scene of a fire at the Grand Burstin hotel in The Harbour, Folkestone. “Crews wearing breathing apparatus have worked hard to bring the fire under control and are now dampening down any remaining hotspots. “It’s believed the fire started in the basement of the property, but the cause is not yet known. “Around 280 people evacuated the building, and a welfare centre has been organised by Folkestone and Hythe district council. No fire-related injuries have been reported.” A spokesperson for Kent police said: “Kent police was called at around 1.20am on Saturday 19 September 2026 to reports of a fire at a hotel on Marine Parade, Folkestone. “Officers remain in attendance to assist traffic flow while our Kent fire and rescue service colleagues work to tackle the fire.”

title: Caribbean nations draft action plan to push UK to redress reparations over slavery
summary: Leaders hope UK will agree to targeted discussions around reparatory justice, but could consider legal options if Britain resists
text: Caribbean nations are drawing up a multi-pronged “action plan” with legal options to push the UK into negotiating a decades-long slavery reparations deal, officials at a reparations conference have said. Leaders in the region are hoping the UK would agree to targeted and constructive negotiation talks at upcoming Commonwealth and UN summits, but they are ready to take the matter to international courts if Britain continues to resist diplomatic options. Earlier this month, a spokesperson for Andy Burnham reiterated the British government’s long‑held position that “the UK does not and will not pay reparations”. Ralph Gonsalves, the former prime minister of St Vincent and the Grenadines, said the Caricom Regional Conference on Reparations, which took place this week, hosted by Barbados with the Caricom Reparations Commission (CRC), was key for agreeing a unified strategy to bring Britain to the negotiating table. Gonsalves is now an elder and adviser for the Repair Campaign, a social movement for reparatory justice. He said that slavery happened over centuries and reparations had to be realistic and set over decades. “We need a concrete, multigenerational plan,” he said. On the legal options available to the Caribbean, Gonsalves challenged arguments that Britain did not violate historical laws during transatlantic slavery, adding that the UK’s signature on contemporary UN conventions had established a binding legal obligation for reparative justice. “The fact is that the consequences of slavery fall squarely under the Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination, which obliges states to help address the consequences of native genocide and slavery,” Gonsalves said. In March this year, 123 nations voted for a landmark UN resolution that described chattel slavery as the gravest crime against humanity. The UK was one of several European countries that abstained from voting in the resolution. But, last month, a UN committee on the elimination of racial discrimination said countries were legally obliged to consider reparations for the transatlantic slave trade and take other ⁠measures to address the enduring ⁠legacy of racial discrimination. David Comissiong, the deputy chair of the Barbados National Task Force on Reparations, said the Caribbean nations were considering “several legal strategies”. “You’ve had Jamaica trying to engage with the national legal judicial system of the UK, the privy council – that is one strategy,” he said, adding that going to the international court of justice for an advisory opinion was another option. Prof Sir Hilary Beckles, the chair of the CRC, said reparations was a matter of justice, adding that countries in the region were forced to create viable democracies “out of the mess” of colonialism, which was still having an impact today. “When Jamaica took its petition to the UK, we had to surround that petition with the fact that when Jamaica became independent in 1962, 80% of the black people in Jamaica could not read or write. After 300 years of British colonisation, they moved into independence with 80% illiteracy. How do you build a modern nation, not even a competitive economy, with 80% illiteracy?” Speaking at the conference, Mia Mottley, the prime minister of Barbados, said the Caribbean had “no desire to bankrupt anybody”. “But we have a desire for justice,” she said. Earlier this year, Barbados commissioned a report which showed that Britain stole 25 million years of life and labour through slavery in the country. She added: “The British government took almost 200 years to repay the debt that it incurred when it paid the slave owners £20m.” Mottley pointed to the fact that Germany paid $95bn (£71bn) to the Jewish community because of the horrors of the Holocaust. Mottley said that she did not want “anybody to diminish the fact that in this country here, which I have the honour to lead, that from settlement in 1627, 400 years ago next year, for 211 years, not six, people were treated as chattel”. “If they dared to speak or to do things that were displeasing, their lives and limbs were put at risk. The evidence is clear. What is absent is the will,” she said.

title: Lindsay Clancy ex-husband says ‘I think I did the best I could’
summary: Patrick Clancy and wife Rachel Danis to speak publicly on 60 Minutes on Sunday about Massachusetts murder trial
text: Patrick Clancy and his wife Rachel Danis are set to describe their experiences of the Massachusetts triple-murder trial of his former wife Lindsay Clancy, with Clancy telling 60 Minutes: “I live with it every day, but I think I did the best I could.” The couple will on Sunday night make their first public comments on the case. CBS has been trailing excerpts of the broadcast. The interviews with the pair marks a second significant media “get” for 60 Minutes since it came under new leadership earlier this year. Last week, it secured an interview with a pilot who was rescued by special forces after being shot down over Iran. The Clancy interviews come as Massachusetts prosecutors are set to decide later this month whether to retry Lindsay Clancy over the killings of the couple’s three children – Cora, five; Dawson, three; and Callan, eight months old – in January 2023. A hearing is slated for 29 September at Plymouth superior court. A trial over the summer riveted public attention and ended in a mistrial when a single juror rejected the Clancy’s defense position that she had carried out the killings because she was suffering from postpartum psychosis that meant she could not be found criminally responsible for her actions. The trial shed light on the little-understood mental health condition, and the resulting mistrial sharply divided public opinion. The single holdout juror, Michael Desronvil, came forward last week to say he thought enough physical evidence and key witness testimony presented at trial proved Clancy “knew exactly what she was doing and planned [it]”. Patrick Clancy, who testified in the prosecution phase of the trial but has supported his former wife, has been subject to intense speculation outside the courtroom from online content creators and conspiracists. Earlier this month, an attorney for Clancy threatened legal “consequences” over what he called a “relentless, escalating and destructive defamation campaign” targeting his client. “Enough is enough – this spread of blatant and baseless falsehoods must stop,” attorney Howard Cooper said. “Those responsible should understand that there will be consequences, and every appropriate measure will be pursued to hold them accountable, including legally.” According to excerpts of the 60 Minutes interviews released ahead of airtime, Patrick Clancy talks about his grief, his memories of his children, and conspiracy theories. Clancy tells correspondent Ross Douthat he still talks to his kids “all the time” and asked them for help. Asked if they do, Clancy responds: “I like to believe they do. It’s a way I stay connected to them.” Clancy, who discovered his three children after finding his injured wife lying in snow below a second floor window (she is now paralyzed from the waist down) also told the news program: “I think I did the best I could with what I had at the time, and I live with the outcome. I live with it every day, but I think I did the best I could.” The Clancys repeatedly sought psychiatric and mental care for the young mother in the months before the incident, and have since filed a civil lawsuit alleging negligence and over-prescription of medications on the the part of two health professionals and healthcare providers. In the released interview excerpts, Danis, 37, discusses how she met Patrick, their marriage, and defends her husband against the theories that have appeared online. “I don’t understand how the story’s been so twisted, but I would hope people know that Pat is, as I said before, the most selfless father and supportive partner,” Danis, an infertility specialist, tells the program. The couple met while jogging and Patrick moved to New York and married earlier this year, she says. “I was just a girl that met a guy running in Central Park on a really cold Saturday, and I don’t think there’s anything wrong with that.”

title: Elderly man allegedly beaten to death in Virginia Walmart by parents of employee
summary: Bert Atienza and teen worker reportedly exchanged words before parents showed up and allegedly attacked shopper
text: A 77-year-old Walmart shopper died after he was allegedly attacked inside a Virginia store by the parents of a teenage employee he had confronted over a shopping cart incident involving his wife, according to US media reports. Bert Atienza died from blunt head trauma on 8 June, one day after the attack at the Walmart in Norfolk, Virginia, WTKR reported on Monday. The shocking incident was captured on surveillance video. Police responded to the store at about 3.20pm on 7 June after receiving a report of an assault. Atienza’s wife, Josephine, was left on the floor holding her injured husband in her lap after the attack, according to video from the scene. “My husband was still able to speak, he said, ‘Help me get up,’ but I told him, ‘No, you’re bleeding. Your mouth is bleeding. Ambulance is coming,” Josephine said. “I look at him again. He has no more consciousness.” Atienza was found unresponsive and taken to a hospital, where he died from his injuries the following day. Medical officials ruled his death a homicide caused by blunt force trauma. The confrontation began while Atienza and his wife of 42 years were grocery-shopping after spending the morning at church. Josephine said a 17-year-old Walmart employee came quickly down the aisle where the couple was shopping and nearly struck her with a shopping cart. Atienza and the unidentified worker exchanged words before the employee allegedly threw a can toward the couple as they walked away, Josephine told WTKR. The teen then reportedly called her parents, Travis White and Erika Mitchell, who began looking for the couple inside the store minutes later. The store surveillance video shows what appears to be Atienza looking at items on a shelf when White and Mitchell approached and attacked him while their daughter watched. The elderly shopper was allegedly shoved from behind, grabbed and punched as people nearby walked away. He was then pushed into a shelving unit and fell to the floor, where one of the suspects allegedly kicked him. White, 44, and Mitchell, 42, were arrested days later and are being held without bond in the Norfolk jail. Their teenage daughter was also charged with assault and battery, aggravated malicious wounding, and conspiracy to commit a felony, according to WAVY. She is being held at the Norfolk juvenile detention center. Authorities have not released her name because she is a minor.

title: UK politics increasingly funded by billionaires as mega-donations surge
summary: Exclusive: A total £179m has been donated by wealthy individuals since 2019, research reveals
text: British politics is increasingly being funded by individual billionaires with a wave of mega-donations having flooded into UK political parties over the past two parliaments. A total of £179m has been donated by wealthy individuals since 2019, research reveals. The figures from the IPPR thinktank show how big money is playing an ever more influential role in Westminster, with a particular rise in mega-donations of more than £1m. The research found that contributions from individual donors have accelerated since the Brexit party received £10m from the Thailand-based billionaire Christopher Harborne and the Liberal Democrats were given £8m by David Sainsbury, the supermarket tycoon, who has now returned to Labour. Between 2001, when donation records began, and 2018, the total donated by individuals giving more than £1m averaged £3.9m a year. But between 2019 and 2025, that figure rose to £13.1m a year, almost three-and-a-half times as much, and far outstripping what would be expected with inflation. The research found 72% of all £1m-plus donations from individuals since records began had come since 2019. Guardian analysis found that in some years, such as 2023, almost £7 out of every £10 in reported private donations to political parties came from wealthy companies or individuals who gave more than £1m in a calendar year. The figures are likely to raise fresh concerns about the influence of a small groups of wealthy individuals, which have already been heightened since two crypto billionaires, Harborne and Ben Delo, said they had each given £36m to Reform UK this month. Reform UK has said it is trying to redress the balance as the other parties have taken millions in mega-donations in past years. The Conservatives’ biggest donors include Frank Hester, who gave more than £20m before the 2024 election, and Labour’s Gary Lubner, who has given more than £9m in total. The IPPR figures draw on Electoral Commission data since 2001 and Transparency International analysis, plus the two record donations of £36m each to Reform UK from Harborne and Delo. There is increasing concern among Reform UK’s rivals about the issue of donations of more than £1m, with some Labour MPs pushing for a cap of £100,000 or £500,000 a year. Some Labour members are intending to push the issue at the party’s autumn conference, and proposals for a cap are likely to be tabled when the government’s current elections bill goes to the House of Lords this autumn. No 10 has been reluctant to include a cap amid opposition from some trade unions who fear it could lead to restrictions on them being able to donate so much in future. However, the government has recently pledged to deal with the issue of mega-donors having an outsize influence on politics. It has already introduced a cap of £100,000 a year for donations from overseas voters. Harry Quilter-Pinner, the executive director of IPPR, said: “Something fundamental has changed in how British politics is funded. Million-pound donations were once exceptional. However, since 2019, mega-donor money has become a much bigger part of our political system. “Reform’s extraordinary fundraising has accelerated that trend, but this is much bigger than one party or two enormous cheques. This is the Americanisation of British politics, where political parties can become dependent on a handful of people with exceptionally deep pockets. “Britain should draw a clear line. The government should introduce a £100,000 annual cap now and bring it down over time, so that no individual can bankroll a political party simply because they are incredibly wealthy.” Civil society groups have urged the government to fix the issue for good, after the government said earlier this month a new taskforce would examine the issue of mega-donations. Dr Susan Hawley, executive director of Spotlight on Corruption, said: “Without urgent action to limit the amount that wealthy individuals can give to political parties, we’re going to continue to see a staggering inflation of money – and the influence it buys – flowing into the coffers of political parties … The taskforce needs to take decisive action to get big money out of our politics in a fair and even-handed way, so that power and influence is returned to ordinary voters, where it belongs.” At the time of the £72m in donations to Reform UK, Duncan Hames, senior director of policy at Transparency International UK, said the situation with big donations was “completely out of control, and makes an irrefutable case for government to bring forward an annual cap on political donations, and fast”.

title: George Osborne ‘thought Peter Thiel’s Bayeux tapestry visit would be secret’
summary: British Museum chair tells Big Brue festival he thought no one would find out about the private viewing
text: George Osborne has said he thought no one would find out about a private viewing of the Bayeux tapestry he organised for the tech billionaire Peter Thiel at the British Museum. The former chancellor, who is chair of the museum, told the Big Brue festival in Somerset that he had been on holiday when Thiel was shown the medieval artwork. Thiel, who supports Donald Trump, is the founder of PayPal and Palantir, a software company that builds data integration, analytics and artificial intelligence platforms for government agencies and large corporations. Palantir has a swathe of British public contracts, including, most controversially, a £330m deal with the NHS, which it has held since 2023. The company also works for the US, Israeli and UK militaries. Its use of AI-powered software to support military strikes in Gaza and Iran, US Ice immigration raids and its access to NHS data has stoked concern. Of the viewing, Osborne said: “It wasn’t like we expected anyone to know about it.” The museum’s director of development, Charlotte Appleyard, hosted Thiel at a VIP viewing of the tapestry before it opened to the public on 18 August. The visit was revealed in the Guardian shortly after it happened. When asked what the museum might have got in return, Osborne said: “The short answer is he hasn’t offered any money, and were he to offer money, the board would consider it and have to take into account the pros, you know, receiving more income, and the reputational risks.” Osborne, who lives in Bruton, near where the festival is taking place, complained that people treat the British Museum like the Foreign Office when they protest about donors who are thought to support the Israeli government. He said: “The critique was that [Thiel] was a supporter of the Israeli government … I mean, this is the most difficult, and almost all the protests that happen at the museum … When I started five years ago, they were climate protests, Just Stop Oil and that kind of thing. Now they’re almost universally Gaza. “You know that is the moment I would say the most sensitive, difficult political issue for the museum, and you know we try and navigate it, and I keep trying to point out we’re not actually the Foreign Office.” He said the museum has to take money from companies such as BP to be able to operate. “You cannot say we want museums to be free, and then one of the biggest British companies offers us £50m, BP, and we go, oh, don’t, because we object to oil exploration. Where is the money going to come from? “You’d shut down the British Museum. People do say this. They say you shouldn’t take tech money, you shouldn’t take oil money. You can’t take any money from the banks. We want the museum to be free. The museum would shut down.”

title: MS Now, CNN and Politico say reporters have been denied access to White House
summary: President said he was banning journalists from those organizations, saying of their coverage: ‘You get sick of it.’
text: Journalists from three US outlets were denied access to the White House grounds on Saturday morning a day after Donald Trump said he would ban them from the executive branch complex in a move that has prompted outrage and shock from free-speech advocates. The outlets were television broadcasters MS Now and CNN as well as the political news website Politico. MS Now said a reporter and a cameraman had been denied access and had their White House press passes confiscated by the US Secret Service at a security gate outside the West Wing. CNN reported that its reporter Betsy Klein was also denied access and had her press pass seized too. Politico said White House reporter Cheyenne Haslett had received the same treatment. “The White House belongs to the American people and the decisions made inside are funded by our tax dollars,” MS Now said, adding that it “intends to take any and all steps necessary to defend our first amendment rights and the essential role of independent journalism in our democracy”. It said: “We stand firmly behind our anchors, our reporters and our newsroom. We will continue to report on the president, the administration and the issues that impact the American people.” CNN said in a statement: “We have a right under the US constitution to do our reporting without hindrance or interference from the government and this ban is an illegal assault on this fundamental right.” Politico’s editor-in-chief, Jonathan Greenberger, said in a statement to the Politico newsroom: “We stand by [Haslett] and all reporters here covering the White House … We will vigorously defend our first amendment rights.” Trump’s threat to banish CNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House has brought condemnation from first amendment advocates and Democratic officials, among others, as the conflict between the US president and parts of the media sharply escalates ahead of November’s midterm elections. It has also thrown into stark relief Trump’s attack on press freedom in the US, which has unnerved civil liberties advocates. In a Truth Social post on Friday afternoon, Trump said he would order the removal of the news outlets “effective immediately” for what he claimed was “constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS!” and said he is considering banning more. Trump did not identify a single infraction, but said his decision was “really just cumulative stories over the last two years. You get sick of it.” The White House Correspondents’ Association, which represents the White House press corps, condemned the move. “The constitution protects the freedom of the press from government interference,” it said on social media. “That protection does not depend on whether the president likes a news organization’s coverage, agrees with its reporting or approves of the questions its journalists ask.” The body said the issue is “about more than the rights of journalists” but about “the right of the American people to receive a full and independent account of the activities, policies and decisions of whoever occupies the nation’s highest office”. Trump has long clashed with the media over what he considers slanted coverage of his administration and himself personally, as well as describing a media environment in which the press and his political opponents are in collusion. Last year the Associated Press was banned form the White House after refusing to acknowledge an executive order changing the name of the Gulf of Mexico to Gulf of America. After Friday’s ban was announced, CNN issued a statement saying that removing its reporters from the grounds could violate the law. “CNN stands fully behind our White House team and their fair and accurate reporting,” a spokesperson for the outlet said. “We have a right under the US constitution to do that reporting without hindrance or interference from the government.” Politico also issued a statement, saying it would “continue to fairly report on this White House and future ones” and “will vigorously defend our first amendment rights against any attempt to restrict them”. Jim Acosta, a former CNN reporter, accused Trump of “taking a meat axe to the free press in this country”. Speaking on MS Now on Friday, Acosta called the latest media bans “a slippery slope” and warned: “We are on the path to having a state media-like system in this country.” Acosta said the media should collectively oppose Trump’s ban. “Each of these news organizations should sue the White House, sue Donald Trump, and that other news organizations in Washington should band together and say, ‘We will not go to the White House and cover you and cover your administration. We’re banning you.’” Press freedom group PEN America said: “Someone needs to explain to President Trump how the first amendment works. As we’ve seen time and time again, this administration’s hostility toward the press is never about the accuracy of news stories, but about its inability to withstand scrutiny of its actions. “The White House can’t be allowed to decide which journalists are able to cover the president based on the content of their news coverage.”

title: Denmark and Greenland say US military agreement will not compromise Arctic territory’s sovereignty
summary: Statement sought to clarify Trump’s announcement that US will have ‘permanent control’ over Greenland’s security
text: Denmark and Greenland have said any agreement with the US to develop a significant military presence in the strategic Arctic territory will not compromise Greenland’s sovereignty. In a statement on Saturday clarifying an announcement by Donald Trump that an agreement had been reached to give Washington “permanent control” ⁠over Greenland’s security, Denmark and the semi-autonomous territory ⁠expressed hope that a deal would end friction with the US over the issue. Greenland’s prime minister, Jens-Frederik Nielsen, said he was pleased with the proposed deal. “The agreement recognizes the sovereignty and territorial integrity of our kingdom and the right of the Greenlandic people to self-determination,” he said in a post. “Next week could be a good week – for Greenland, ‌Denmark and the United States,” Denmark’s foreign minister, ‌Lars Lokke Rasmussen, said in a statement. “A time of uncertainty will hopefully give way to a binding agreement that strengthens security ‌in the Arctic and the north Atlantic, and thereby our shared security within Nato Europe – while respecting the Danish kingdom’s red lines,” Rasmussen said. The US, Denmark and Greenland said late on Friday they had reached a deal to allow the US to develop a significant military presence on Greenland, while prohibiting US adversaries from building their ⁠own bases on the island. The deal is expected to be signed during the UN general assembly next week. Key details of the agreement have not been made public, including the degree of the US military presence in the self-governing Danish territory and whether any formal power over foreign policy and resources would be ceded to Washington. Trump said on social media that under the deal, “the United States will FOREVER have the complete ability to do what is necessary in Greenland in order to secure and defend the security of Greenland, and the United States of America”. He added that the agreement would give the US “permanent control over security, and all ‌other needs, in Greenland”. The security and mineral resources of the vast northern island have been subject to Washington’s foreign policy and attention since the start of the second Trump administration, with officials citing national security, access to valuable natural resources, including rare earth minerals, and control over emerging Arctic shipping lanes. The island had a significant US military presence in the 1950s, when fears of annihilation in a US-Soviet nuclear exchange required that long-range nuclear bombers and early-warning systems be based on Greenland. The US still maintains a reduced military presence at the Pituffik space base, formerly known as Thule, on the island to monitor for missiles. Mikkel Vedby Rasmussen, a political science professor at the University of Copenhagen, told Reuters that the Denmark-US deal “is probably not the end of President Trump’s ambitions for Greenland and certainly not the end of US strategic interest in the territory and its resources”. Rasmussen added that if Copenhagen cedes any formal power to Washington over Greenland, which it has held for 1,000 years, it would raise questions for Greenlanders of whether “this is the beginning of replacing the colonial relationship with Denmark with a colonial relationship to the United States”. US ambitions for greater sway over the Arctic island have strained relations with Nato. In January, European member nations sent military personnel to Greenland to demonstrate military readiness. Eight European allies issued a joint statement confirming their commitment to Arctic security. Negotiations followed. A Nato spokesperson ‌on Saturday said the alliance welcomed the agreement, which would “help advance security, stability and cooperation in this vital region”. Reuters contributed reporting

title: Small boat arrivals are ‘wealthy men’ who do not deserve help, says Reform’s Danny Kruger
summary: The fact that some migrants pay people smugglers thousands of pounds makes them well off, MP claims
text: Asylum seekers who arrive on small boats across the Channel are “wealthy men” who do not deserve the help of the British state, according to the Reform UK MP Danny Kruger. The former Conservative, who defected last year, said the fact that some migrants were paying people smugglers thousands of pounds – often using their life savings or borrowed money – made them well off. The claim was immediately dismissed by charities who support refugees. Speaking at the Big Brue festival in Bruton, Somerset, Kruger said: “By the way, most of them [are] comparatively wealthy and fit young men who’ve crossed safe countries to begin the journey to the UK.” Asked by the event’s moderator, the editor of the Independent, Geordie Greig, how he knew these men were wealthy, Kruger said: “Because they’re paying thousands of pounds. They’re paying thousands of pounds to people smugglers to get here. Comparatively wealthy, compared to the people who I think most of us can regard as really deserving of the compassion of the British taxpayer.” Seema Syeda, a Joint Council for the Welfare of Immigrants spokesperson, said it was untrue that most asylum seekers who arrive on boats are wealthy. She said: “The reality is that most asylum seekers who arrive here are denied the right to work, live off as little as £8 a week, and can end up in destitution. But in the end, whether rich or poor, people fleeing war and persecution deserve to be welcomed. The right to safety is a human right. “Many people arriving here have been forcibly displaced due to war, genocide or imperialism that the British state has, past and present, funded or supported.” Earlier this month, Reform politician Matt Goodwin, the party’s unsuccessful candidate at the Gorton and Denton byelection, caused outrage when he said at the party’s annual conference that the “best and the brightest” of the British population had been replaced by “drug-dealing goat-herders” through immigration. Kruger said Goodwin was correct to make these incendiary remarks. He said: “There are some drug-dealing goat-herders who we’ve admitted to this country, so I mean, it’s factual.” Asked by Greig if he accepted that language, he said: “Yes I do.” He added: “And they don’t like our country.” Kruger said he was concerned “about kind of massive cultural transformation. And yes, the admission to our country of many people who do not share the values that we all love, and I’m afraid to say it’s not just recent migrants.” The Reform MP also complained about second- and third-generation migrants. He said: “In fact, I think recent migrants are probably more pro-British because they’ve come here for a reason. They want to be here. We’ve got a problem with second- and third-generation immigrants because they are, and it’s a fault of politics that … this has happened. “We have an alienated generation, many many people, millions of people, for whom they don’t love their country, they don’t think that Britain is great, and they don’t feel that they are part of the mainstream society that we have here, and that is our challenge.” He further claimed that current policies would cause a civil war. “We continue down the path of segregation and of you know elite virtue signalling, pretending we’re all a lovely multicultural diversity is our strength, and it’s rude to even point out any problems,” Kruger added. Rachel Millward, the co-deputy leader of the Green party, said: “Reform is a party funded by billionaires that chooses to attack the most vulnerable in our society – people fleeing environmental breakdown, famine and war. “Instead of stoking division and hatred, just days after anti-immigrant protests brought violence and disorder to our streets, politicians need to step up and offer solutions. We’re calling for more safe routes so that those who need asylum can apply for it before they leave their own country, and never have to face a dangerous crossing in a small boat.”

title: A deadly crash and the perilous history of LA’s news helicopters: ‘The eye in the sky’
summary: An on-air helicopter crash killed journalist Eliana Moreno and pilot George Marciniw, shaking LA’s news tradition
text: The whir of news helicopters flying overhead has long been a familiar soundtrack to life in Los Angeles – and the footage they gather of high-speed chases, wildfires and celebrity sightings a fixture of local television. For nearly 70 years, Angelenos have gotten their news from “the eye in the sky” – from scenes of OJ Simpson’s fleeing white Bronco, the 1992 LA riots and even Madonna’s wedding to Sean Penn. On Tuesday, one of those news helicopters crashed live on air while covering the collision of an SUV and a city bus, killing journalist Eliana Moreno, pilot George Marciniw and one person on the ground. The incident has prompted an outpouring of support for the families, and reflection on the sometimes dangerous and uniquely Californian history of helicopter journalism. The world’s first “Telecopter” debuted in Los Angeles in 1958, after John Silva, chief engineer for KTLA-TV, retrofitted a helicopter into a flying news studio with ultra-light camera equipment that could transmit footage live from the air. An electronics engineer who’d worked as a radar operator during the second world war, Silva was uniquely suited to the task. Although KTLA had been the first commercially licensed television station in the city, a growing number of competitors in the 1950s made attracting viewers a growing concern. In a 2002 interview for the Archive of American Television, Silva recalled his inspiration: “If we could build a news mobile unit in a helicopter we could get over it all, get there first, avoid the traffic and get to all the stories before anybody in the competition.” Over the next decade, the Telecopter would capture scenes from the Bel Air fire, the Baldwin Hills Dam disaster and the Watts riots. In the 1980s, the married couple Zoey Tur and Marika Gerrard of the Los Angeles News Service would take up the torch of helicopter reporting – capturing footage of the attack on Reginald Denny during the LA riots and OJ Simpson’s white Bronco chase. “The city was undergoing a truly tumultuous time,” Matt Yoka, the producer of the documentary Whirlybird told KCRW in a 2021 interview. “I think in one sense, the work that Zoey and Marika were doing was simply trying to bring that into the homes of the people of Los Angeles watching the nightly news.” Spending their days in the sky, Tur and Gerrard were uniquely positioned to capture breaking news. In a 2024 interview with NBC News, Gerrard recalled how she and Tur were flying over the El Toro ‘Y’ interchange when they heard on the scanner that Simpson’s Bronco had been spotted nearby: “So I slid the door of the helicopter open and then pointed the camera down, and lo and behold there was the white Bronco.” That practicality has made helicopters a crucial tool for news reporters in the vast cities of the US West. “A news helicopter is more than a flying camera,” Tammy Rose, a helicopter reporter for ABC-13 in Houston, told the Associated Press. “As a reporter aboard the aircraft, I could see the larger scene, communicate with the newsroom, gather information and report live while events were unfolding.” Yet, since their earliest use, news helicopters have faced real hazards – from mechanical failures to drone and bird strikes. In 1977, a KNBC helicopter ran out of fuel and crashed after covering a Santa Barbara wildfire, killing cameraman George Spears and pilot Francis Gary Powers, the U-2 pilot who’d survived being shot down during a spy mission in the Soviet Union. Since 2000, there have been at least eight fatal crashes involving news helicopters in the United States, killing 16 people. Those crashes led to some reforms, like all Phoenix news stations agreeing to share one helicopter after a 2007 crash – but some former helicopter journalists worry newsrooms turn to the helicopter too quickly. “Viewers need information about mass riots, natural disasters and building explosions, especially when news crews on the ground can’t reach the sites. But do mundane street closures and beauty shots really serve the public?” former helicopter reporter Thanh Tan wrote in an op-ed for the Seattle Times after a local helicopter crashed in 2014. “Newsrooms should not send crews into the skies just because they can or to vie for viewership.” After shaky and emotional footage direct from the helicopter appeared to show the crash, NBC Los Angeles confirmed the deaths of journalist Moreno, pilot Marciniw and pedestrian Edy Fernando Gutiérrez Mejía. “We are coming on the air with heavy hearts tonight because we lost valued friends and colleagues,” NBC Los Angeles anchor Colleen Williams said on air Tuesday. “We are going to take a couple of minutes to think about that, to process, and to regroup.” Working for Angel City Air, Moreno and Marciniw had provided aerial coverage for NBC4 and Telemundo 52 for years. Moreno, nicknamed “Eli in the Heli”, had begun working as a helicopter journalist in 2010, after she graduated from Chapman University. A bilingual reporter in her 30s, Moreno was engaged to be married and had recently completed a marathon. Her colleague, Jonathan Gonzalez, a weekend news anchor and reporter for NBC Los Angeles, told NBC, “she was damn good at what she did.” In a statement, Moreno’s family said she’d dreamed of being a news reporter since she was 11 years old and that much of her journey into journalism “was made possible by all of you who welcomed her into your homes and onto your screens”. “We are infinitely proud of her and feel incredibly blessed to have had the privilege of loving her,” they wrote. Her longtime colleague, pilot Marciniw, was eyeing retirement after more than 30 years as a helicopter pilot when the crash happened, fellow pilot Esteban Jimenez said. “I knew him since the ’90s. He was my instructor at one time; he was my eyes and ears here in LA,” Jimenez said. Mejía, known by his nickname “Pichi”, was visiting Los Angeles and had arrived in the city only two days prior. According to a cousin, he’d planned to pick up a car and take it home to sell in Cuilapa, a town in south-eastern Guatemala. His family is now working to repatriate his body. Just weeks before the crash, in her final Instagram post, Moreno had shared her enthusiasm for helicopter reporting. Captioning a photograph from Whiteman airport, Moreno wrote about covering the summer’s wildfires and how aerial footage allowed her to show the path of a growing fire. “It just goes to show the power that we have from being the eye in the sky,” she said.
