title: Trump’s battle to rename the Kennedy Center has put its future at risk
summary: The president has threatened to block renovations and suggested the landmark could be demolished after courts ruled against his bid to rename it
text: It was born with the world premiere of Leonard Bernstein’s Mass. “Young people will come here and they will see this cultural centre,” Rose Kennedy, the mother of slain US president John F Kennedy, said at that opening night gala. “They will carry some of these ideas back to their different communities.” More than half a century later, the potential death knell came just after 4.30pm on Tuesday with a perfunctory announcement on the public address system: “The centre is now closed to the public. Please exit the centre by way of the Hall of States.” Soon barricades had been erected and security guards were blocking access. The John F Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts in Washington DC, once filled with the buzz of audiences and children, had fallen as silent as a mausoleum. Now a high stakes legal battle is under way to prevent Donald Trump from taking a wrecking ball to the building that is both national arts complex and living memorial to the 35th president. The current White House occupant, incensed that courts have prevented his name being added to the Kennedy Center, told reporters this week: “I think that the Trump administration should certainly have recognition. Because frankly, if we don’t do that, it’s going to close. It’ll end up being ripped down.” On social media, Trump declared the venue “destined to doom” without his intervention. The once unthinkable threat became more thinkable when an Agence France-Presse photographer took a picture of Trump aboard Air Force One, holding a placard with ominous red text: “Kennedy Center DEMOLIS...” The rest of the word was obscured by the plane’s window frame. Below was a big picture showing a yellow heavy construction vehicle scooping rubble from a torn-down building. Trump has no legal right to demolish the facility, which was established by Congress. Critics say he is acting out of spite because he cannot get his way. Kerry Kennedy, the former president’s niece , said: “Like a child who can’t play with a toy, he wants to stomp on the toy. But this is not a toy. This is the living memorial to a slain president. “It would be like adding the Trump name to the Trump-Lincoln Memorial or the Trump-Jefferson Memorial or Trump-Tomb of the Unknown Soldier. The courts have spoken, he cannot demolish it, he cannot put his name on it and he should be focused instead on his job.” The Kennedy Center did not respond to requests for comment. The 100ft structure opened in 1971 on the banks of the Potomac River. Since then it has presented ballet, children’s theatre, comedy, contemporary dance, hip-hop, jazz, international festivals and educational programmes. The annual Kennedy Center Honors have hosted past presidents and a who’s who of US arts and culture. Trump seized control of the facility in February 2025, claimed its finances were in dire straits and fired board members who did not align with his “vision for a Golden Age in Arts and Culture”. Deborah Rutter, the centre’s president, was ousted and replaced by Ric Grenell, a Trump loyalist and former ambassador with no experience in arts management. An initiative created in 2020 to promote anti-racism and community outreach was shut down and its 10-person staff dismissed. Citing “drag shows specifically targeting our youth”, any programming perceived as “woke” was purged. It was a commercial disaster as audiences, performers and philanthropists deserted the centre in droves. Lawyer Norm Eisen, who has litigated against the administration’s attempts to impinge on institutional independence, said: “He slapped his name on there and destroyed the lifeblood of the Kennedy Center: audience and artists.” In January, the Kennedy Center hosted the world premiere of Melania, a documentary about the first lady, with the Trumps in attendance. Three days later, the president announced that he would be closing the facility for two years for $257m repairs and renovations. The Trump-appointed board backed the move and also voted to rename the venue the “Trump-Kennedy Center”. Trump’s name was duly added to the exterior marble facade, before the US district judge Christopher Cooper intervened and ruled that only Congress has the authority to rename the memorial. The name was removed but the result remains hidden by giant scaffolding and tarpaulins. Asked about Trump’s motivations, Eisen of Democracy Defenders Action added: “You would need an authority in abnormal psychology to get the answer to that question but he appears to have developed an obsession because he’s not used to hearing the word no.” On Tuesday this week, Judge Cooper again ruled that the Trump administration could not put a new Trump sign on the Kennedy Center’s facade or rename its plaza for the president “without Congress’s blessing”. Hours later, the centre’s board voted to close the facility for two years, citing the need for $257m of repairs and renovations. The centre’s executive director, Matt Floca, ordered an immediate seven-day emergency closure, citing “acute risks to public safety resulting from continued structural deterioration”. But Democratic congresswoman Joyce Beatty and Senator Sheldon Whitehouse allege that the closure is a “pretext” to hide a financial “death spiral” caused by artist boycotts and dwindling ticket sales. In an interview on Friday, Whitehouse, the top Democrat on the environment and public works committee and an ex-officio member of the Kennedy Center board of trustees, said the events represented three phases of Trump’s assault on the complex. “One is what I call the mob bust out gone wrong, in which they tried to take over and run the Kennedy Center, give themselves and their friends big contracts, charge expensive goodies to Kennedy Center accounts, do political favours using Kennedy Center facilities for Trump allies, and that was extremely damaging to the business of the centre,” he said. “Then they moved into the renaming fiasco and that seems to have struck a lethal blow to the centre’s business model – a predictably damaging blow that they failed to consider at all. Now they’ve moved into a third stage in which they are threatening the actual destruction of the Kennedy Center if they don’t get their renaming.” Whitehouse added: “It has gone from bad to worse but the through line in all of this is that these trustees are under a legal duty to put the welfare of the centre itself first and, if they fail in that duty, they create a legal environment in which courts can and ultimately likely will step in to make sure that the centre is run lawfully.” The legal battle intensified on Thursday, when Judge Cooper issued an order requiring the Kennedy Center to give at least 30 days’ notice before making any major physical changes to the building, including demolition. Whitehouse said: “There’s a contrast between the thuggery and bullying world in which you could countenance a threat to tear down the Kennedy Center if your name doesn’t go on it and the actual legal world in which actions have to be approved by a board that has a fiduciary duty to put the welfare of the institution first. Those two are irreconcilable at this point.” Still, Trump ordered the demolition of the White House East Wing to make way for a ballroom, despite opposition from preservationists and questions over the administration’s authority to proceed without Congress. He is now threatening to cancel the renovation of the Kennedy Center, and warning of its possible demise, if his name is not restored to the building. Chris Raleigh, an organiser the Hands Off the Arts movement, which is mobilising grassroots resistance, said: “That’s what you do when the hostage takers can’t get what they want. There comes a point where the hostage is inconvenient. Look at it: the people who have fought back have pushed Trump to the brink here. “In no way at all is he winning. His name is not going up on the building. There is somebody in the White House every day who says, before they walk in that building, ‘Oh god, please don’t let there be another Kennedy Center story today.’” Raleigh added: “Everyone in Trump’s life should be telling him: ‘You gotta to get out now. This is not going to help you.’” And even if the current peril passes, it will be difficult to restore the centre to its former glories. On Friday it laid off about a dozen staff, the Washington Post newspaper reported. Michael Kaiser, who led the centre from 2001 to 2014, warns that even a two-year closure will be damaging. He said: “When you don’t have audiences and you don’t have donors participating for two years, those individuals go elsewhere. When you have no staff, even if there’s a time in the future where we can return to a more sense of being normal, it’s not going to be so simple to reopen a building of this size and complexity.” Some critics see the attack on the Kennedy Center as part of a broader assault on institutions and freedom of expression. On Friday, Trump announced that the media outlets CNN, MS Now and Politico would be banned from the White House and, with health secretary Robert Kennedy Jr standing behind him in the Oval Office, railed against the Kennedy Center again. To Kerry Kennedy, who has worked in the human rights arena for 45 years, the president is a “petty tyrant”. Asked to consider the possibility of the Kennedy Center being lost, she reflected: “It would be devastating for my family because we love Uncle Jack but in the end Trump is not going to hurt my family. He is hurting our country and he’s hurting our world and he’s giving permission to tyrants everywhere to shut down arts centres and silence critical voices.” On Friday evening thousands of protesters gathered outside the Kennedy Center in view of the marble facade that remained concealed by scaffolding and tarpaulins. The speakers included a drag queen. Against the setting sun, protesters beat drums and waved signs that read: “Keep your tiny hands off our Kennedy Center”; “You’re no Jack Kennedy”; “Our center not DJT’s”; and “Wicked starring DJT”.

title: Likelihood of eating fresh produce increases with income for US adults, new CDC report shows
summary: The report highlights deep divides between low- and middle- income, a disparity that dates back decades
text: A new report from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) reaffirms that adults are more likely to eat fresh fruits and vegetables as their income increases. The data brief comes as Republican cuts to food assistance programs, colloquially called “food stamps”, have led enrollment to “plummet”. Changes to US dietary guidelines, led by health secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr, have also made a government-recommended diet more expensive. A new “food pyramid” released in January emphasized animal protein, fresh fruit and vegetables, all of which cost more, according to studies. “Particularly for people with lower incomes this is really infeasible, especially when millions of people – and what will be probably millions of children – are going to lose access to a really critical benefit that keeps people food secure,” said Priya Fielding-Singh, director of policy and programs at the George Washington University Global Food Institute. The data brief from CDC’s National Center for Health Statistics found that more than nine in 10 Americans ate any vegetable on a given day and about 7 in 10 ate any fruit. The data brief covered adults older than 20 from August 2021-2023. However, the percentage of adults who ate any vegetables, “dark green vegetables, red or orange vegetables, and other vegetable types increased with increasing family income” – with deep divides between the low-income and middle class. For instance, the percentage of adults who ate any fruit on a given day was 56% for people living on less than 130% of the federal poverty level ($20,748 for a single adult). By contrast, 76% of people who earned 350% of FPL ($55,860) ate any fruit. Similarly, a single person who earned $55,860 was almost twice as likely (38% versus 19.6%) to eat berries, citrus and melons compared to the poorest people included in the study. The same was true of vegetables. Although most Americans ate a vegetable in a day, only 29% of the lowest income Americans in the data brief ate a dark green vegetable, compared to 42% for the highest income. This is not surprising. Years of studies have shown that people with less money and time spend more on energy-dense, shelf-stable packaged foods – foods that fill you up and don’t spoil. The relationship between food and income was known even 91 years ago, when a study of diet and income in the UK found that nearly everyone ate potatoes and bread, but the poorest in society bought far less milk, eggs, vegetables and fruits. “A review of the state of health of the people of the different groups suggests that, as income increases, disease and death-rate decrease, children grow more quickly, adult stature is greater and general health and physique improve,” Sir John Boyd Orr wrote in 1935. Multiple contemporary studies have pointed out the same tension. A recent study by University of Washington researchers found foods recommended by Kennedy’s health department cost a mean of $15.82 per day. The average Snap household is two people and receives $177 per month, or about $3 per day per person. About 39% of Snap beneficiaries are children. Republican cuts to food assistance programs in the “Big Beautiful Bill” act mean that fewer Americans are getting these benefits. Republicans required states to pay toward food benefits for the first time, barred certain legal immigrants (particularly people in the US on asylum and certain trafficking survivors) from food assistance programs, and required older people to submit to work requirements, raising the age for people required to prove they work 20 hours a week from 54 to 64. Republicans also required states to pay a share of food assistance benefits for the first time in the program’s history, which could result in hundreds of millions of dollars of new costs in some states, according to the Center for Budget and Policy Priorities. All of this is contributing to a swift decline in food assistance rates. Food assistance enrollment fell 13% nationally between May 2025 and May 2026, according to an Associated Press analysis. In some states the declines have been even more dramatic, such as Florida, Georgia, Louisiana and Nevada. In these states, proponents of welfare cuts argue that people are no longer eligible because they’re earning more money. Republicans also imposed new documentation requirements, making it more likely that eligible people will fail to complete paperwork. In Arizona, some analysts said this appears to be contributing to the 47% reduction in enrollees in the state, where new documentation requirements are running headlong into severe staff shortages. Pamela Lachman, chief strategy officer for the Center for Employment Opportunities (CEO), a group that works with people recently released from jail and prison, said that the administrative burdens simply do not consider the reality of daily life for people seeking food assistance. CEO’s own part-time work programs are often difficult to count as work for the purposes of food assistance, because hours can be irregular. “They have requirements to do their parole supervision, they’re trying to find a place to live – all of those things mean your work might be inconsistent,” said Lachman. “If you immediately need to start proving you’re working 20 hours a week, if not more, that’s very challenging to do.” Even as fewer Americans access food benefits, it is likely the government will have less insight into food insecurity. In September 2025, the US Department of Agriculture announced it would no longer sponsor the Food Security Supplement in the US Census Bureau’s annual survey, ending data collection that had occurred annually since 1995.

title: Scottish Labour’s new leader backs Rosebank and Jackdaw oil and gasfields
summary: Michael Marra supports development of the North Sea sites, calling for a ‘more rational’ approach to energy policy
text: Scottish Labour’s new leader Michael Marra has backed the development of the Rosebank and Jackdaw oil and gasfields in the North Sea in one of his first acts after being elected, calling for a “more rational” approach to energy policy. On Saturday, the MSP for North East Scotland won a near two-thirds majority to lead the party in Holyrood, becoming Scottish Labour’s 11th leader. He replaces Anas Sarwar after his shock decision to resign in July to join Andy Burnham’s new government as a trade minister. Dundee-born Marra said he would urge the British prime minister to back both fossil fuel projects despite warnings over their environmental impact. Neither is covered by the ban on new licences for drilling in the North Sea because their applications were already in the system when the Labour government took power, and there is growing expectation that ministers will approve the Jackdaw gasfield in the coming weeks. “I want Rosebank and Jackdaw to be approved,” Marra told reporters shortly after his election. “It’s the biggest issue in my region in terms of people’s voting intention. We need to have a more rational policy position that delivers for the Scottish economy and Scottish jobs.” In his acceptance speech at the Dynamic Earth science museum in Edinburgh, Marra said he would spend time reconnecting with Scottish voters after a bruising defeat in this year’s elections. “May hurt so much because we know the SNP didn’t deserve a fifth term in power. But the truth is Scotland didn’t think we would be much better,” he said. “Scots know what we are against. They can’t tell you what we are for. And that vacuum was filled by the poison, racism and bigotry of Reform. We must be clear in our values. We must lead with our values,” he said. “For a decade now, Scotland has gotten weaker. We must reconnect with the country if we are ever to form a government in Holyrood to face these historic challenges.” Marra faces an uphill battle to reverse the party’s fortunes in Scotland. While 37 Labour MPs from Scotland sit in Westminster, the party has lost seats at every Holyrood election since devolution in 1999. In May, the party suffered its worst ever results – winning just 17 seats as the SNP retained power. Labour has as many seats as Reform in Holyrood, just two more than the Scottish Green party and five more than the Conservatives. In a subdued campaign with few policy differences between candidates, both Marra and his main rival, Joe Fagan, were criticised for struggling to outline the circumstances in which Scotland should be allowed a second independence referendum. Marra said that he thought the party had become overly focused on middle-class voters in Scotland, and vowed to build a broader electoral coalition that was centred on the needs of the country. When asked again about the level of public support that would mean Scotland should have a second independence reference, Marra said the SNP’s failure to get an outright majority in Holyrood in May signalled that it was not a priority for voters. “The people of Scotland do not want a referendum right now. We will continue to make the case for a stronger Scotland in a changing UK. It’s imperative to me that we are not in this for the status quo. I’m in this to make sure that we can see a stronger Scotland,” he said. In total, 6,751 votes were cast in the leadership election, representing 49.43% of the Scottish Labour party membership. Fagan won 2,485 votes, while Marra won 4,266. Dr Eric Shaw, a research fellow at the University of Stirling who co-authored The Strange Death of Labour in Scotland, said the party had to reconnect with working-class voters to win back support. “The party is facing three main issues: the continued salience of independence, the association between Scottish Labour and Labour in Westminster, and the erosion of Labour’s historic base in Scotland. The plight of the party is reflected in the fact that Labour did better among the professional middle class than it did in the working class in the most recent election.” Dr Ewan Gibbs, a lecturer in economic and social history at the University of Glasgow, said the new leader had to ask difficult questions about who the party was meant to represent in Scotland. “We are approaching 20 years of failure with the government in Holyrood if we look at the performance of public services, educational attainment, ongoing income and wealth inequality in Scotland. But Scottish Labour isn’t a party that seems equipped to mobilise that opposition and disappointment at the moment.”

title: Girl orphaned by Super Bowl reporter’s drugging and a deadly Kansas crash is ‘extreme victim’, granddad says
summary: Parents of Eleanor, 3, both died within a year. Her dad’s killer was just convicted. Now a man faces trial in her mother’s car crash death
text: Brian Hinck followed from a distance the suburban New Orleans trial resulting in the convictions on Thursday of people charged in the drugging death of his son-in-law, Telemundo sports reporter Adan Manzano. That was because he and his family had simultaneously been girding themselves for another trial scheduled to start four days later: that of the motorist charged in the car crash that killed his daughter, Ashleigh Boyd, in Topeka, Kansas. Nonetheless, Hinck on Friday said he and his wife, Nicole, have done their best to shield their granddaughter, Eleanor, from the legal fallout of the brutal reality that she lost both of her parents over a roughly 10-month period beginning in the spring of 2024. “We don’t talk about it with her,” Hinck said on Friday referring to Eleanor, whom he and Nicole are now raising. “The only thing she knows is her mom and dad are in heaven, and she will see them one day.” Hinck’s comments came on the front end of a four-day break between the trials prompted by the deaths of his daughter and her husband. As he put it during a telephone interview, both cases have strained his faith in aspects of the criminal justice system. Boyd, 24, was in her sedan on 11 April 2024 when the driver of a pickup truck on the wrong side of the road hit her head-on in south-west Topeka. The Topeka elementary school teacher was pronounced dead at the scene, and her infant daughter, who was a passenger, was injured, investigators said at the time. Authorities charged a man named Todd W Armstrong with vehicular homicide in Boyd’s death. But Hinck said he was bitterly disappointed to learn that particular charge was a misdemeanor carrying no more than one year in prison. Hinck also alluded to how there evidently was a urine drug screen result showing cocaine metabolites in Armstrong’s system. However, according to court records, Armstrong’s attorney successfully argued that the screen result should be omitted from being introduced as evidence during the defendant’s trial, set to start on Monday. Meanwhile, Boyd’s widower was working for Telemundo’s affiliate in Kansas City, Missouri – relatively near Topeka – when he traveled to cover Super Bowl LIX in New Orleans. Manzano was found dead on 5 February 2025, days before the big game, in his hotel room in the New Orleans suburb of Kenner, Louisiana. Investigators ultimately determined Manzano had been preyed on by a group who targeted victims in New Orleans’ French Quarter with the prospect of sex – then knocked them unconscious by furtively drugging them before stealing their phones and bank cards to drain their financial accounts. An autopsy revealed Manzano had died lying face down on a pillow, having asphyxiated after ingesting a combination of alcohol and the pharmaceutical depressant Xanax. Late on Thursday, after a four-day trial, jurors from suburban New Orleans convicted Danette Colbert, 49, of negligent homicide, which can carry up to 10 years in prison. They also convicted both Colbert and her accomplice, Rickey White, 35, of racketeering, which can carry up to 50 years’ imprisonment. Colbert had drawn the Kenner police’s scrutiny after using Manzano’s credit card at various local stores. Her prior arrest record had also included allegations of theft and drugging men. A third defendant, 35-year-old Christian Anderson, testified against Colbert and White, whose sentencing was tentatively scheduled for late September. Anderson pleaded guilty to lesser charges of simple robbery and fraud in exchange for a six-year prison sentence. Hinck on Friday said he could not help but reflect on how Colbert was out on probation in connection with theft and fraud charges when she encountered Manzano on the day of his death. She was eventually given a 25-year prison sentence for violating her probation and being determined to be a habitual offender – but that was because of her arrest in Manzano’s death. And Manzano and Boyd’s daughter was orphaned by then. “The disappointment in the justice system is at a peak level in our house,” Hinck remarked. He said he loathed the idea that another trial centering on the death of one of Eleanor’s parents was fast approaching. And he said his hope was that the criminal justice system across the US improved as far as “protecting the general public” from offenders who should be subjected to more severe sentences. Failing to do so “creates victims as young” as young as Eleanor, age three, Hinck said. “She is an extreme victim of this,” Hinck added.

title: Hispanic voters’ support for Trump wanes over economy and immigration
summary: Polls show voters who helped elect president unhappy – and may be willing to vote Democrat in midterms
text: Hispanic voters who helped re-elect Donald Trump in 2024 are discontented with his second-term economic and immigration policies, according to recent polling – indicating they may not be willing to support the president’s party in the midterm elections. Despite a record number of Hispanic voters casting their ballots for the Republican president, more than 65% said they are displeased with Trump’s handling of his job and 78% said they would prefer to see the Democratic party in control of Congress, according to a September poll from the New York Times/Siena University. “When we ask voters, ‘OK, what is shaping your opinion about the president?’ The cost of living was number one, number two was immigration enforcement and deportation in US cities, number three is back to the economy – wages,” Clarissa Martinez De Castro, the vice-president of the Latino Vote Initiative at UnidosUS, said. Frustration with the consequences of the administration’s current policies are driving Latino voters away from Republicans, said Mike Madrid, a campaign consultant, author and teacher who has been studying Latino voting patterns for 35 years. “There’s no renewed affinity or love for the Democratic party. They’re just extremely upset and disillusioned and angry, frankly, with Donald Trump,” Madrid said. “So they’re gonna leave the Republicans for the exact same reasons that they left the Democrats two years ago,” he added. Other polls support those findings. Approximately 63% of Hispanic respondents told a Fox News survey in September they plan to vote for the Democratic congressional candidate in their district. In an UnidosUS poll from April/May, 54% of Hispanic voters said they would vote for the Democratic House candidate, compared with 27% who said they would favor the Republican. The economy and cost of living are top concerns for Hispanic voters, polls show. Trump’s message of economic populism helped him get elected in 2024, but voters, including Republicans, have soured on his handling of the economy amid high inflation and rising costs. The Iran war has pushed gas prices past $4 per gallon on average. Inflation has risen over the last year and remained stubborn at 3.4%, elevating grocery costs. When asked about the recent polling of Hispanic voters, White House spokesperson Allison Schuster said “hard-working Hispanic Americans are beginning to have some breaking room after four year of economic pain under the Democrats” and pointed to policies such as middle-class tax cuts, no tax on tips, overtime and social security and “defeating Biden’s inflation crisis”. Schuster said Trump was “honored to receive a record level of support from Hispanic Americans that helped fuel his landslide 2024 election victory” and that the president and Republicans in Congress would “continue fighting to make everyday life more affordable for working families”. Between October 2025 and May 2026, Hispanic voters’ favorability of Democrats in Congress increased by three percentage points, according to UnidosUS’s bipartisan poll of 3,000 Hispanic voters. Meanwhile, favorability toward Republicans in Congress only increased by one percentage point. Immigration is also an issue, especially since the Trump administration has deployed federal agents to Latino and Hispanic communities across the country. Some who have encountered immigration agents have accused the administration of racial profiling to target immigrants for deportation. But immigration is not the biggest issue for Latino voters – a misconception that politicians often make. In UnidosUS’s poll of 3,000, 17% said they wanted elected officials to prioritize increasing border security. Another 13% said they supported deporting all undocumented immigrants, regardless of how long they have been in the US. Those who voted for Trump are part of a larger cohort of “swing” voters who have no allegiance to a specific political party. They make up roughly 40% of the Hispanic electorate and are often misunderstood by politicians, Martinez said. “You have 40% of voters here for whom, many of them say, they don’t see the difference between the parties in terms of who really is going to be better,” Martinez said of the group. “That tells candidates: you have homework to do, and the clock is ticking,” she added. Republicans and Democrats have long struggled to resonate with Latino voters, Madrid said, in part because politicians often assume they know exactly what Latino voters want without doing proper outreach. “The political structure has done a massive disservice with fake polling, with organizations that were advocating an agenda, not facts and science … and politicians that were trying to benefit from that,” Madrid, who has consulted for both Republican and Democratic campaigns, said. Madrid and Martinez cautioned that while Latino voters appear tofavor Democratic candidates ahead of the November elections, it does not mean Democrats can – or should – count on their support in 2028. “Latino voters themselves are changing, which is why the Latino vote has changed,” Madrid said. “And you can’t you can’t come up with a solution until you understand that.”

title: ‘Way too many guns around’: the common theme in US family killings
summary: Acts of ‘familicide’ have increased dramatically this year – in the US, the killer is more likely to have easy access to a gun
text: The US is often known globally for its shocking levels of violence, but acts of “family annihilation” or “familicide” rank among the most disturbing of crimes. They occur when an assailant kills four or more of their own family members and often see the killer also kill themselves. These types of crime have increased dramatically this year, according to data from Northeastern University. The still rare but shocking mass killings have occurred across the country, including one this week in Texas, in which an alleged shooter killed four adults in a family that had taken him in, and one last month in Montana, in which an assailant killed eight relatives, including four children. After six such attacks occurred last year, the lowest number in at least two decades, there have already been at least 17 this year. Experts say they often occur after family estrangement or due to financial stresses, often on a father, or marital disputes. But, crucially, in the United States, the perpetrator is more likely to have easy access to a gun than many other parts of the world. Such familicide is preventable, experts argue, but happens, in large part, because of the country’s high gun ownership rate and lack of firearm regulations, which makes it more likely that an assailant will impulsively shoot their family. “There are way too many guns around and easy to pick up, and when someone is in some sort of a rage place, guns get picked up in anger,” said Jacquelyn Campbell, a Johns Hopkins University professor of nursing who has studied domestic violence homicide. In June, a domestic dispute occurred in Muscatine, Iowa. Ryan McFarland had previously been charged with child endangerment resulting in a death; neglect or abandonment; armed robbery and burglary; and fraud, according to WQAD-TV. After the dispute, McFarland shot and killed his wife and five family members before killing himself. “I just wanted to say that I will forever love and miss my mom, Lesa, my sister, Ryle, my four brothers, Dakota, Austin, Mark and Ryan,” Jonathan McFarland, the sole surviving family member, said, according to KWQC. In another case this summer, in Billings, Montana, Alan Smith’s parents had asked him to move out. Weeks later, he killed four generations of his family at a Sunday dinner. The father of two of the children killed told the Associated Press that Smith had been verbally abusive and a hermit. “There were many red flags and many people spoke out,” said Brad Ireland, the father. “No one listened.” The most common triggers for such events are relationship estrangement, including a recent divorce or separation, said Katherine Keyes, an epidemiology professor at Columbia University and author of a 2025 murder-suicide study. “Often in the intimate partner situation, it involves things like jealousy and just the kind of psychic pain involved in suicidal crisis overall,” Keyes said. But while the rate of intimate partner violence is similar across all high-income countries, according to a study published in the Lancet, gun ownership and deaths are much more common in the United States than other developed nations. When a domestic abuser, who is typically a man, has access to a gun, the victim is five times likelier to be killed, according to a study in the American Journal of Public Health. In the United States, there were 2.6 intentional homicides of women per 1,000 females in 2023, according to the World Bank Group. In the United Kingdom, for example, which has stricter gun laws and lower gun ownership, the number in 2021 was 0.7. There does not appear to be significant research examining familicide rates in the United States versus other countries. “There is a particular lethality and a particular impulsivity and a particular level of threat that occurs when a firearm is present, and right now in America we have more firearms than people,” said Doreen Dodgen-Magee, a psychologist whose sister-in-law and three nieces were shot and killed by her brother-in-law. As such, reducing access to lethal means, like guns, “is one of the most effective and evidence-based suicide prevention and violence prevention interventions”, Keyes said. Twenty-two states have red flag laws, which allow people, typically law enforcement or family members, to petition a judge for an emergency order that would temporarily remove firearms from a person found to be at risk of harming themselves or others. Meanwhile, six states have passed bans on such protective orders, and three are considering doing so, according to the Trace, a news organization that covers gun violence. All nine are majority Republican states. The National Rifle Association also previously expressed support for red-flag laws but later reversed its position. Such laws “strip away gun owners’ rights without due process”, Randy Kozuch, an NRA lobbyist, wrote in a Daily Caller column. Nathan Dahm, a Republican lawmaker in Oklahoma, which has among the nation’s highest suicide rates, sponsored the country’s first anti-red flag law. When the Trace asked him about the connection between firearms and suicide and a colleague who had killed himself with a gun, Dahm said: “Everyone dies. That’s life.” But there is evidence that red-flag laws can prevent suicides. The risk factors for suicide, such as psychiatric disorders, particularly depression, are often similar to those for homicide-suicides, Keyes said. After such mass murders, the shooters often kill themselves. A study published in January in the journal Jama Health Forum examined four states that passed such laws and eight that did not, and found that they reduced firearm suicides by an average of 3.79 incidents 100,000 people. Dodgen-Magee also does not accept the argument often used by gun rights advocates that firearms help people, including women, protect themselves. Given the number of firearms in the United States, “if that were true, we would be the safest country to live in”, said Dodgen-Magee, who advocates for stricter gun safety laws. Three decades ago, her sister-in-law and nieces left their home because they no longer were safe living with her brother-in-law. Despite a restraining order against him, he was able to purchase a gun and drove to Dodgen-Magee’s mother-in-law’s house where he killed his wife and children. She thinks a red-flag law and a measure that forced the vendor to run a background check before selling the gun to him could have prevented the shooting. Dodgen-Magee remains traumatized by it. “Every year when I go into schools, when it’s back-to-school season and backpacks are on the wall, my body sort of short shuts down,” she said. ““It’s easy to dismiss these crimes because you just think, oh, that was a messed-up family. It is everyone’s family. It is everyone’s town, and until we do some things to protect women and children, it will continue to be.”
