title: Reform UK activists squabble over Farage’s plan for £72m donations
summary: Crypto billionaires’ £72m will be used to hire campaign managers and professional staff in target constituencies
text: For Nigel Farage, the £72m lavished last week on his party by the crypto billionaire donors Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne finally places Reform UK on a level playing field with its political rivals. The donations are the largest received by a UK political party since declarations became required in 2001 and led to warnings Farage was aiming to “buy” his way to power, with a row still raging over whether they are legal. Yet among Reform’s grassroots, the fattening of party coffers comes with challenges of its own, with some activists less than impressed by Farage’s announcement that the money would be used to hire 400 campaign managers in target constituencies. “We need more activists to knock on doors NOT managers,” one posted on a Facebook group used by Reform activists, where the sentiment was not unusual. Another party member, and former candidate, told others he was “puzzled” by Farage’s announcement, adding that the campaign managers would need an army of volunteer doorknockers. “Those campaign managers will rapidly learn that they can’t get nearly enough volunteers to do that. Are Reform planning actually to pay them too, not just the managers?” he asked. “And what happens to the ordinary branch members currently serving as campaign managers having been elected by their membership to that role?” Substantial spending by Reform on professional organisers is already under way. The party is advertising this week for more than 60 roles, including four branch network coordinators – described as “the backbone of the party” – in various English regions. Forty-seven full-time campaign managers were also being hired in cities, towns and regions across Britain. Other positions include a call centre manager, two “local byelection managers” and a “councillor welfare manager” to work with the party’s 2,300 councillors and whose tasks would include “managing conflict”. Under the heading of “creative”, there are opportunities for a graphic designer, a video editor to bolster the party’s focus on TikTok and other social platforms, and “junior/senior writers”. “Hungry” applicants were asked to write a 500-word letter in the persona of Reform’s combative home affairs spokesperson, Zia Yusuf, “setting out how the political class broke Britain and how Reform UK will fix it”. The spending is aimed at putting Reform on a war footing for the next three years by overhauling its branch network. Other funds will go towards beefing up the policy apparatus behind Reform’s shadow cabinet, the Spectator’s deputy political editor, James Heale, reported, while tipping the party’s increasingly powerful treasurer, Harvey Griffiths, as an emerging figure behind the scenes as Farage aims to stop “fiefdoms” popping up at Reform’s Millbank HQ. Of course, much, much more is possible with £72m – and what could be about to come Reform’s way as it powers past Labour and the Tories in terms of donations. Byelections will happen, as will another round of local elections next year. Expect the Farage approach of having a highly centralised party – albeit with improved regional operations – to continue, with activists sent to have follow-up conversations at addresses targeted by direct mailshots. A Reform source emphasised that the first half of that had been “front loaded” with a view to going on with the mundane necessities of running a major party. “It’s the running of head office, the paperclips, the rent. All that stuff.” The same source dismissed squabbling over the money. “There will always be people who think that their pet projects should be the first to be funded, while every single person thinks their bright idea is the one that needs to be watered,” they said. “But it doesn’t work like that. We will still be fundraising from our members.” In a party such as Reform, which comes from a lineage of Farage-led movements whose members have enjoyed seeing themselves as insurgents, there is still room for new tensions to surface if the pace of “professionalisation” happens too fast or is seen to take away the soul of the party. Such claims were a factor in previous splits when Reform figures such as Ben Habib parted company, while Rupert Lowe’s Restore Britain is still making siren calls to tempt disillusioned Reform activists.

title: Lib Dems have ‘moral responsibility’ to block Reform, says Ed Davey as party gears up for snap election
summary: Exclusive: Lib Dem leader bullish ahead of party conference despite static poll ratings and MPs’ frustrations
text: The Liberal Democrats have begun work on a new manifesto in case of a possible snap election, as Ed Davey said he understood the frustrations of some of his MPs who fear that the party’s message is currently at risk of being lost. But Davey also urged his party not to panic at static polling numbers, arguing that with tactical voting and fragmented political loyalties, he fully expects the party to do even better at the next election than in 2024, when it won 72 seats, the highest total for a century. Speaking ahead of the party’s annual conference in Brighton, Davey warned that discipline and focus were vital, given what he described as their “moral responsibility” in blocking a Reform-led government, predicting that Kemi Badenoch would eventually seek an alliance with Nigel Farage’s party. A manifesto working group, led by the Cheadle MP Tom Morrison, has already been created, Davey said, meaning the party can be ready if Andy Burnham calls an election. “We don’t normally do it this early,” he said. The Lib Dems already have a number of policies in place, including an economic proposal based around seeking to rejoin the EU’s single market, with a similarly Brussels-focused immigration policy of signing up to a Europe-wide pact on migration and asylum. The party’s national poll ratings are largely static at about 12% or 13%, with the Lib Dems spending much of this year in fifth place behind Reform, Labour, the Conservatives and a resurgent Green party. Some of Davey’s MPs complain privately about what they see as an overly slow and cautious approach to both policy and rhetoric, saying this has sidelined the party from the national debate. However, it is by no means a unanimous view, with others saying the pace has picked up since the appointment of the party’s new political director James Holt, a veteran of the coalition years who then spent nearly a decade working with the Duke and Duchess of Sussex. Davey said he understood the concerns, but said MPs should not get distracted: “They’re frustrated because they’re coming up with the arguments, they’re running the campaigns and they don’t get the coverage for them. And I get it, it’s frustrating.” Headline poll ratings, he said, were only a partial guide to an election in which tactical voting and local campaigns were likely to play a major role in votes likely to be split five or even six ways. He said: “It’s going to be a ground war much more than people think, and good for us because we’re great at ground wars and at the community politics that turns poll ratings into loads of seats.” Party strategists are confident they can defend many of the 60-plus so-called blue wall seats won from the Conservatives in 2024 – a zone Davey now refers to as the “orange wall” – and add to that tally. A number of candidates are already in place in target seats after a streamlining of the selection process. Such efforts, Davey predicted, could be the one thing standing in the way of a Nigel Farage government. He said: “I have felt for a long time that we have a moral responsibility in our party. It weighs heavily on my shoulders, because when I see men in black shirts and balaclavas, and when I see overt racism at the level we’re seeing it, we have to win. That is a burden for me, knowing we just have to be as smart as we possibly can.” Some Lib Dems argue that this mission to hoover up anti-Reform sentiment actually makes the party’s slightly subterranean profile a potential benefit, and that Davey should ignore voices calling for him to be bolder or more outspoken. One MP said: “Unlike Reform and the Greens, we have worked out how to use the electoral system, and if we want to stop bad things happening, we have to tailor our campaigning to that reality. If, say, you embrace one side in a culture war, you divide your community.” Another MP said Davey should embrace his “centrist dad” image: “He’s a safe pair of hands, which is a valuable thing these days. He could say something a bit crazy to appeal to the core and increase our polling numbers … but it wouldn’t win us a single extra seat.” Although there are no moves to challenge Davey as leader, some Lib Dems are pushing for the party to set out what it represents. “We risk being dead in the water if we can’t articulate a proper vision of what we are, and what liberalism is,” one MP warned. “People know what Labour and the Conservatives stand for. If they have an opinion about us, it’s often that we’re slightly nicer Tories. “Yes, Ed has been our most successful leader ever. But you have to progress or you’re doomed, and at the moment it feels a bit static.”

title: Pact with Saudi Arabia threatens to draw Pakistan into Middle East conflict
summary: Activation of mutual defence agreement by Riyadh as fighting with Houthis escalates would have wide-reaching repercussions for Islamabad
text: As he stood in Riyadh last September, the world looked like a very different place for Pakistan’s most powerful man, Gen Asim Munir. The country’s army chief was there to witness the signing of a historic defence pact with Saudi Arabia, which he had personally orchestrated with the crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman. To Munir, it appeared to be a highly strategic win: Riyadh would provide cash-strapped Pakistan with billions of dollars of life-saving investments and loans. In exchange, Pakistan agreed to train up the Saudi military, and Pakistan’s armed forces would defend Saudi Arabia in the unlikely event of an attack on its territory. Analysts say it was clear that Pakistan presumed US-Iran relations would soon get back on track and the risk of a conflict sweeping across the Middle East and the Gulf was low. But a very different scenario soon unfolded. By February, the Middle East was on fire after the US and Israel began bombing Iran – and Iran began firing missiles at the Gulf states, including Saudi Arabia, in retaliation. It did not take long for the war to reinflame Saudi’s conflict with the Houthis, the Iran-backed rebel group based in Yemen, and for their fragile truce to collapse. Earlier this month the Houthis made unprecedented territorial gains in Yemen and hit Saudi territory with strikes and drones. Saudi Arabia has responded by pounding Yemen with airstrikes. Some believe a return to full-scale war is on the horizon. The pressure is now mounting on Pakistan, and particularly Munir. In August, the defence pact with Saudi Arabia was extended to include Turkey and renamed the Mecca joint defence agreement. The countries agreed that an armed attack on any one of them would be treated as an attack on all three. Ayesha Siddiqa, a defence analyst and senior fellow at King’s College London, said: “I don’t think Asim Munir properly calculated the threats the region was facing – and that Pakistan might need to put its troops on the line quite so soon.” Saudi Arabia has tens of billions of dollars in fighter jets and war machinery, but it does not have any warfare experience to fight the Houthis, who have proved to be tough, resilient fighters. Pakistan’s forces, trained to deal with the constant menace of India, would be highly valuable on the frontline. Analysts say that if Saudi Arabia decided to activate the Mecca pact to fight the Houthis, Pakistan would have no choice but to send in its troops, including thousands who are already deployed in Saudi Arabia for training. As well as being a defence partner, Pakistan is almost totally economically and geopolitically dependent on Saudi Arabia, which has recently given the country a lifesaving $8bn (£6bn) in funds and investments. Last week, Pakistani government ministers and senior military figures gave increasingly bullish statements, confirming their “unconditional” commitment to the pact and saying Islamabad would go to “any extent” to defend Saudi Arabia. But privately, officials in Pakistan are deeply worried about being dragged into the never-ending war unfolding across the Middle East. The country is already economically crippled, in a de facto war with the Taliban in Afghanistan, and facing an uncontrollable surge in militancy in its border areas. To many, an activation of the Mecca pact would be perceived as Islamabad taking a clear stance against Iran. Before the US and Israeli strikes on Iran, Pakistan had good relations with its neighbour – ties that Munir utilised to bring Tehran to the negotiating table in his attempt to secure a lasting ceasefire. But as the war has dragged on, Pakistan has become increasingly infuriated with Iran, while Tehran has little trust left in Islamabad. As Siddiqa emphasised, Pakistan joining the fight against the Houthis “would come with major repercussions”. After Iran, Pakistan is home to the second-largest population of Shia Muslims, who would probably rise up in protest against any involvement in strikes on the Houthis. Iran also maintains good relations with the Taliban in Afghanistan, posing the risk of further provoking one of Pakistan’s biggest security threats and driving militancy and security problems along the Afghanistan-Pakistan border to even deadlier levels. It also risks inflaming the situation in Balochistan, Pakistan’s unstable border region with Iran, which is home to a long-running and uncontrollable insurgency. Raja Nasir Abbas, the opposition leader in Pakistan’s senate, said that only the very few at the top of Pakistan’s military even knew what conditions and agreements had been made in the Mecca pact. With the military as Pakistan’s de facto rulers, the decision to join was not even put before parliament. “It will be a disaster for the country if Pakistan jumps into war,” said Abbas. “We are already facing two lethal insurgencies; our economy is in a shambles and inflation has rocketed. If we take Saudi Arabia’s side in this conflict, the country will face chaos, instability and religious division.” So far, no one has been able to pinpoint what the “red line” would be that would force the pact to be activated. Analysts said Pakistan appeared to be banking on Riyadh’s reluctance to enter into open warfare with Iran by escalating its fight with the Houthis. Turkey has also made it clear it does not want to enter the fray. “Pakistan will do its best not to get involved in any incursion on Yemeni soil,” said Muhammad Amir Rana, the director of the Islamabad-based Pak Institute for Peace Studies. Speaking privately, one senior official said he did not think the Saudi crown prince “wants to activate the pact now”. “If the kingdom plans to send its ground forces, Pakistan would support that,” he said. “But I don’t think Saudi Arabia would start a full-fledged war against the Houthis without American approval and Trump has snubbed them. Right now, the US does not want to open up another front; they prefer talking to Houthis.” He added: “You can’t predict the future though.”

title: Record fuel prices across EU prompt calls for bloc-wide windfall tax on firms
summary: German minister says companies are ‘exploiting situation’ in Middle East, as sky-high prices become major domestic issue for leaders
text: European governments have discussed imposing a bloc-wide windfall tax on energy companies, as near-record fuel and gas prices pile pressure on leaders desperate to contain mounting public discontent and the challenge of the far right. With elections due next year in eight EU countries including France, Italy, Spain and Poland, leaders are scrambling to head off the potential fallout from what analysts have warned could be one of the continent’s biggest energy shocks in decades. Germany’s finance minister, Lars Klingbeil, called on ‌the European Commission at a meeting of EU finance ministers in Dublin on Friday to propose possible ways to tax what he described as the excessive profits of oil companies. “Several member states have been calling for models for a long time,” Klingbeil said, demanding proposals by next month. “People can see how oil companies are exploiting the situation, overcharging and significantly increasing their profits.” Oil futures have climbed back above $100 a ⁠barrel, about 50% higher than before the Iran war, as escalating attacks across the Middle East threaten more supply routes. Derivatives markets suggest traders do not ‌expect a near-term drop in ‌prices. Pump prices have already reached all-time highs across Europe. In Germany, diesel prices surged to a record average of €2.45 a litre on Wednesday, while petrol hit a fresh high of €2.31 a litre, according to Europe’s largest motoring association, ADAC. Prices are even higher in the Netherlands, where petrol eclipsed last week’s record high to reach €2.73 a litre on Wednesday, with diesel at an average €2.78 a litre. Prices have risen higher still for petrol in Denmark and for diesel in Finland. Across the EU, petrol prices are 24% higher than a year earlier, while diesel is up 38% and jet fuel costs more than 100% more. Benchmark gas is trading at €81 a megawatt hour, up 150% on a year earlier, with analysts suggesting it could hit €100. The EU’s economic commissioner, Valdis Dombrovskis, has said the commission has no plans “at this stage” for an ⁠EU-wide taxing mechanism, but stressed it was “ready to engage in discussion” and member states were free to impose their own taxes. Sky-high fuel prices are already a major domestic political issue in France and Italy, both of which next year face crunch elections in which voters’ concerns are likely to be dominated by the soaring cost of living, driven largely by high energy prices. In Italy, Giorgia Meloni’s ruling rightwing coalition, trailing rivals in the polls, said this week it would scrap road tax for 14.5m cars and motorbikes from next year at a cost of over €2bn, on top of a cut to diesel duty that has already cost €2.8bn. “We have chosen to redirect a portion of the resources used to address rising fuel prices into a simple, structural measure designed especially for those who use cars and motorcycles every day to work, take their children, or get around,” Meloni said. France’s president, Emmanuel Macron, told ministers he wanted the government’s “full mobilisation” on fuel supply and prices, including efforts to secure supplies internationally by working toward the “peaceful reopening” of the strait of Hormuz. In the latest of a wave of protests, French fishers blocked access to two ports and a fuel depot in southern France on Thursday over soaring diesel prices that this week rose to €2.37 a litre, just below their record of €2.38. The fisheries minister, Catherine Chabaud, said the fishers had agreed after six hours of talks to lift the blockades after a promise that those with cashflow issues would be granted zero-interest ⁠loans and support measures would to be tied ‌to fuel price changes. The prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, this week extended emergency fuel subsidies until the end of the year for the agriculture, fishing and construction sectors. But the government is reluctant to step in to cut fuel prices for all. “Blanket measures that affect everyone – including those who don’t need them – are a false economy,” the country’s finance minister, Roland Lescure, told journalists earlier in the week. “Why? Because ultimately, we’ll have to fund them.” In August, Spain doubled its diesel tax discount to €0.20 a litre from 1 September after diesel prices jumped by 15.7% in July, while in Germany, the embattled chancellor, Friedrich Merz, announced a fuel tax cut late on Friday. Taxes on petrol and diesel ⁠would be cut by by €0.17 from 1 October until the end of the year, the government said, as well as holding talks with the oil industry with the aim of introducing a cap on fuel prices by 1 January 2027 ‌at the latest. “Anyone who relies on their car every day is reaching breaking point,” Merz said in a statement. “We are ‌showing that we are resilient in the face of the crisis and are helping our citizens,” he added. Merz’s centre-right CDU was this month heavily defeated in state elections in Saxony-Anhalt by the far-right AfD, and two more state elections this weekend are likely to bring further gains for the far-right party, which has campaigned on a platform of a return to the cheap Russian gas imports Europe largely abandoned after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

title: Harrods seeks to recover abuse compensation costs from Mohamed Al Fayed’s estate
summary: Exclusive: Survivors say luxury store’s attempt to recoup money is at odds with its public acceptance of responsibility
text: Harrods is seeking to recover the cost of the compensation paid to hundreds of women allegedly sexually abused by Mohamed Al Fayed from his estate, the Guardian understands. The luxury department store is seeking full indemnity from the late billionaire’s estate for any settlements it is required to pay, according to evidence seen by the Guardian. Survivors of Fayed’s alleged abuse said the retailer’s plan to recover its compensation costs was distressing and at odds with its public acceptance of responsibility. Lucy Traynor, a senior associate at KP Law, which represents the majority of known survivors, said: “Harrods publicly says that it accepts responsibility for the abuse suffered by survivors. However, its lawyers have confirmed that Harrods intends to seek a full indemnity from Mohamed Al Fayed’s estate for any compensation it is required to pay. “If successful, that would mean Harrods recovering the entirety of those compensation payments from the estate and bearing no ultimate financial consequence itself. Its present position is that, despite its statements about accepting responsibility, it intends to seek recovery from the estate of every pound it pays in compensation.” Traynor said Harrods’ intention to fully indemnify itself was “difficult to reconcile with its public statements about institutional responsibility and accountability”. She said the allegations concerning Harrods went beyond “Al Fayed as an individual who owned the business”. “Survivors have raised serious questions about the environment in which this was able to happen, the role of others within the organisation, what was known or ought to have been known, and whether institutional structures facilitated or failed to prevent his conduct,” she said. If Harrods were successful, the claims of survivors who were only seeking compensation from the estate could be affected, Traynor said. “Any attempt by Harrods to recover substantial sums from the estate could reduce the assets available to meet those survivors’ claims.” In a statement, Harrods said: “Our priority is to ensure all eligible survivors receive compensation for abuses perpetrated by Fayed, and Harrods continue to settle claims.” The store has previously accepted “vicarious liability” for the sexual abuse allegedly perpetrated by Fayed, and condemned it. Earlier this week, KP Law said compensation claims against Harrods and the estate by 275 of the survivors it represents could reach up to £150m. Fayed, who died aged 94 in 2023, has been accused of rape, sexual assault, sexual exploitation and human trafficking from 1977 to 2014. Survivors claim that Harrods did not adequately address the allegations for years. Two years ago, Harrods opened an investigation into whether any of its current staff were “directly or indirectly involved” in the alleged sexual abuse of women by Fayed. An employee had left the business in 2025 in relation to that investigation, the store later said. The retailer created its own compensation scheme for survivors last year, which closed to new claims in March. Its latest accounts showed it had paid out £4.1m from the £57m it set aside for compensation in 2025. The store added that it had made settlements with 113 women to date, but did not disclose the total amount paid. In 2023 the Sunday Times reported that Fayed’s fortune was £1.69bn, making him the fourth richest person in Scotland at that time. Last year, Harrods made a passing-over application (POA) to appoint special executors to administer Fayed’s estate, replacing family members. The department store said this was necessary to protect assets and to ensure the estate could pay compensation “in a timely and appropriate manner”. A high court hearing is scheduled for November. Harrods’ statement added: “To our knowledge, the Fayed estate has not publicly acknowledged abuses, nor apologised or settled a single claim. The POA seeks the appointment of an independent executor to administer claims against the estate, therefore, any financial recovery for compensation to survivors of Fayed’s abuses remains a number of legal steps away.” Shanta Sundarason, who says she was sexually assaulted by Fayed in his office when she worked as a designer at Harrods, said the store’s plan to recover the costs of compensation was “deeply disturbing”. “My abuse did not happen in some separate world belonging only to Mohamed Al Fayed. Harrods was not simply the backdrop to what happened to me, it was the environment in which I was recruited, selected, controlled and ultimately abused,” she said. “Harrods cannot tell me that it accepts institutional responsibility for what happened to me, while simultaneously seeking to ensure that the institution ultimately bears none of the financial consequence. For me, accountability is not simply writing a cheque and then recovering every penny from someone else. “What happened to me was not simply the act of one individual. My abuse existed within a system. From Mohamed Al Fayed’s security detail and office staff to management and the structures surrounding him, it took more than one person to create an environment in which abuse could occur and remain hidden.” A former employee named Catherine, who says she was sexually abused by Fayed when she worked as his personal assistant between 1990 and 1991, described Harrods’ plan to recover compensation costs from the estate as “truly sickening”. “Harrods have stated that they are sorry but [are] doing everything they can to escape paying anything and it’s simply not right,” she said. The estate was approached for comment.

title: Spider season! Ten species you’ll see scuttling across Britain’s carpets and lawns this autumn
summary: The world is suddenly full of webs and hairy legs. But why? And what do they belong to? Meet the spiders you’re most likely to encounter, from cardinals to false wolves
text: Summer is at an end, and suddenly spiders seem to be everywhere – in your house, in your garden, in your hair. Fresh webs hang from doorways, walls, shrubs and fence posts, creating invisible obstacle courses. Where do all these spiders come from, what kind are they and what, if anything, should we do about them? The short answer to the question “Why are there so many more spiders at this time of year?” is: there aren’t. They are just more obvious. Dave Clarke, an ectotherm (“cold-blooded” animal) specialist at the Zoological Society of London, says: “There are more spiders around in the spring, because that’s when they hatch from their egg sacs, and there are hundreds of babies in each egg sac. But they’re small and not very obvious. They grow up during the summer and, at this time of year, they reach their maximum size.” Their webs are also correspondingly larger. The other reason they are more apparent is that they are finding their way indoors in the desperate search for a mate. Dr Sara Goodacre, professor of evolutionary biology and genetics at the University of Nottingham, says: “The ones you see in your home at the minute, the really big, fat, hairy ones, they’re usually teenage males that are lost – emotionally, geographically – and are just hoping they might find a female so they can continue the life cycle.” The spider season can be a difficult time for people who don’t like spiders, but a little knowledge about these fascinating creatures can go a long way to promote understanding. Here, then, are the 10 spiders you’re most likely to run into this autumn. 1. House spider (Tegenaria domestica) One of the species you are likely to find in your home, the house spider ranges from pale to dark brown, with black markings and banded, hairy legs. While the name seems to imply that it thrives only within four walls, that is not the case. “They’re not called house spiders because they have to live in your house,” says Clarke. “It’s just because it’s the commonest species you would see inside the house.” Centrally heated homes are generally too dry and too short of food for most species of spider so you don’t have to feel bad about gently relocating one. “It’s your home,” says Goodacre. “You decide who you share it with.” If you wish to evict a house spider, trap it gently in an upturned glass and slide a piece of card underneath the glass. At this time of year, it’s probably best to release it somewhere with a bit of shelter – a porch, shed or garage. 2. Cardinal spider (Tegenaria parietina) The cardinal is the largest spider native to the UK, one of a range of hard-to-distinguish species in the genus Tegenaria that also go by the name giant house spider. The term “giant” is in some cases an exaggeration, but not here: adult cardinal spiders can reach a total leg span of 14cm. They are allegedly called cardinal spiders because Cardinal Wolsey was terrified of them, or because he was protective towards them, or he thought they were lucky, or something. They are found in the south of England, but not the extreme southwest. 3. Cellar spider (Pholcus phalangioides) It is also known as the daddy-longlegs spider (its legs are about five times the length of its body), but this can be confusing because the name daddy longlegs is also used for a type of crane fly and for harvestmen, the latter of which are arachnids but not spiders. Cellar spiders are originally subtropical, but they have spread around the world thanks to indoor living. They spin quite untidy webs and generally hang out in the corners where walls meet ceilings. When disturbed they can gyrate rapidly, turning themselves into a blur which, in theory, is supposed to convince predators that they have vanished. 4. Garden spider (Araneus diadematus) If you have ever stepped out your back door and walked face first into a spiral spider’s web, chances are it belonged to a garden spider. “They’re one of the most obvious because they tend to sit in the middle of the web,” says Clarke. “I’ve been blundering into loads of their webs in my garden over the last few weeks because they are very good at building them right across the path.” Garden spiders range in colour from grey-brown to reddish-brown, with a white cross – made up of speckles – on the abdomen. Females are twice the size of males, with a body length of up to 1.8cm. 5. False Widows (Steatoda nobilis, Steatoda bipunctata, Steatoda grossa) Of the three false widows, two – the cupboard false widow (Steatoda grossa) and the rabbit hutch false widow (Steatoda bipunctata) – are native to Britain. The other, the noble false widow (Steatoda nobilis), turned up here some time in the late 19th century from the Canary Islands. The noble false widow is the one that gets all the bad press: it’s often referred to as “Britain’s most dangerous spider”, a construction roughly as misleading as “Britain’s most earthquake-prone region”. It’s not a competition that is hard to come top in. Medium-sized with a glossy black abdomen, the spider is, in fact, solitary and not in the least aggressive. False widows can bite, although confirmed cases of them biting humans are rare, and while they are venomous, the common reaction to the bite is similar in severity to a nettle or wasp sting. “But it doesn’t fly like a wasp,” says Goodacre, “so you’d have to try really hard [to get bitten]. The level of hysteria is the worst bit – people feel ill because they’re so worried about the concept of a spider bite.” You may regard all other spiders commonly found in Britain as essentially harmless. And Britain’s most earthquake-prone region is Perth and Kinross, by the way. 6. Missing sector orb weaver (Zygiella x-notata) Often found in and around windows, this spider is usually silver-grey with an oak-leaf mark on its back, but it’s easiest to identify by its web: a classic circular pattern with one pie slice missing. This gap is bisected by a single thread, running from the outer edge to the centre, from which the spider can pick up the vibrations of anything landing. “They don’t sit in the middle of their web; they sit hidden on your windowsill,” says Goodacre. “They always sit with one foot casually out, but there’s nothing casual about it – it’s sensing.” 7. Tube web spider (Segestria florentina) One of the biggest spiders found in the UK – mostly in the south – its body can reach 2.2cm in length. It’s easily identifiable by its iridescent green mouth parts, but only if you can see them: tube web spiders spend most of their time tucked into holes in brick walls or fences, at the centre of their vortex-shaped web, waiting to pounce on any prey disturbing the silken tripwires. “If you’re very careful, you can often get them to come out of their retreat with a grass stem or something like that,” says Clarke. But it won’t work if you just touch it with your finger – they can sense the difference. This spider does have a venomous bite, which is said to be painful but not dangerous, but it’s a very reclusive creature, so you’d have to really bother it to get bitten. 8. Zebra jumping spider (Salticus scenicus) These little spiders are between 5mm and 9mm long, can jump about 10 times their length, and have been observed taking on prey up to three times their size. Despite their predatory nature, they are among the most adorable of all spiders, thanks to their zebra-stripe markings and their two big, front-facing SpongeBob eyes. “If you see a jumping spider and you look at it, it will look up at you, which is very cute,” says Clarke. For what it’s worth they also have six smaller eyes, distributed down their flanks and in the rear. 9. False wolf spider (Zoropsis spinimana) This gets its name because of its outward resemblance to wolf spiders. Like wolf spiders, they don’t trap their prey in webs – they go out and hunt it down. It’s also known as a Nosferatu spider, because the markings on its back look like a little vampire face. Normally found in the Mediterranean, the false wolf has only recently arrived in the UK, and is increasingly likely to be spotted in and around London. “This is a species that really wouldn’t survive our harsh winters outside,” says Clarke, “so they do rely on human structures.” 10. Woodlouse spider (Dysdera crocata) They get their name not because they resemble woodlice, but because they eat them. Their look, in fact, is quite distinctive: reddish orange with a peanut-shaped abdomen, and large enough fangs to penetrate the protective armour of a woodlouse. “People are often quite surprised when they see one because they look quite exotic,” says Clarke. But they’re not rare; just quite demure. “I think they prefer to be hidden away underneath things a lot of the time, rather than running about in the open.”

title: ‘Cost of housing’ crunch looms for low-income families, warns Resolution Foundation
summary: Thinktank calls on chancellor to end housing allowance freeze with typical two-bedroom household facing £158 week shortfall amid rent rises
text: More than 1.1 million low-income families in rented homes face a “cost of housing” crunch without action from John Healey in next month’s budget, the Resolution Foundation thinktank has warned. Local housing allowance (LHA) has been frozen in cash terms since autumn 2024. In a new report, Saving Private Renters, the thinktank found that rising rents since then have led to a widening gap between what families claiming LHA can afford, and the realities of the market. It said a low-income family renting a typical two-bedroom flat now faces an average shortfall of £158 a week. That rises to more than £300 a week in parts of London. The Resolution Foundation rejects the suggestion that relinking LHA with local conditions would mainly benefit private landlords, by driving up rents. By analysing previous changes in LHA, it finds that 90p of every £1 tends to fall to tenants, instead of feeding through into price changes. Resolution Foundation economist Stephen Hunsaker said: “The gap between average rents and Local housing allowance levels is set to reach a record high this October, and failing to repeg LHA to actual rents in next month’s budget could lock in a freeze for another year, and see the gap reach 30% by March 2028.” He added that “with many tenants receiving housing support already going without essentials to pay their rent today, the government should restore the automatic annual linking of LHA to relieve the pressure on low-income families in the private rented sector.” Relinking LHA to rents would cost £2bn a year by the end of this parliament in 2029-30. The Resolution Foundation suggests funding that change by increasing the “taper rate” at which universal credit (UC) is withdrawn as recipients’ income rises. The report argues this would involve a transfer within the UC system, towards claimants with the most need. The thinktank pointed to survey evidence suggesting one in five working-age adults in families on housing support in private rental accommodation were unable to afford to keep their homes warm, and one in eight were unable to afford three meals a day. When LHA was first introduced in 2008 it was pegged to the median level of local rents, and in 2011 that was reduced to the 30th percentile. It has been frozen for nine of the past 14 years. A chorus of charities and campaigners have called for the restoration of the link, including Crisis, the Joseph Rowntree Foundation and Citizens Advice. The chancellor will present his budget on 28 October. He is under pressure to fulfil Labour’s promise of giving voters a “breathing space” amid rising costs, but likely to be constrained by rising inflation and interest rates. A government spokesperson said: “Local housing allowance rates are reviewed annually, and future decisions will be taken in the context of the government’s welfare priorities, and the fiscal context.”

title: How to flood-proof your home: from water-thirsty plants to deflated footballs
summary: After summer’s heatwaves, prepare for winter of storms and heavy rain, with millions of UK homes at risk of flooding
text: The accelerating climate crisis and this year’s record-breaking El Niño mean that, although the summer’s heatwaves are still fresh in the memory, households in the UK are already being told to prepare for a potentially destructive winter of storms and heavy rain – leaving millions of homes at risk of flooding. Government action is needed to improve flood defences and build reliance on a national and regional level. But with the UK’s flood season just weeks away, the Guardian spoke to experts to find out what action communities and individuals can take to make their neighbourhoods and homes more resilient, from self-closing airbricks to deflated children’s footballs. Community action The first step is to check whether your home or neighbourhood is listed at risk of flooding on the government’s website. If it is, find out if the local council has a flood alert scheme and make sure you and your neighbours are signed up to that and the Environment Agency’s flood alerts system. Join any local community flood group – or consider setting one up with neighbours – and approach the council to see what flood plans it has in place, and get involved in making them better. This could include lobbying for more permeable surfaces, rain gardens and tree planting. Identify any vulnerable residents who might need extra support and draw up a street or neighbourhood flood plan to make sure everyone knows what to do in the event of a flood. Tracey Garrett, the chief executive of the National Flood Forum, said flooding can be “incredibly frightening and disruptive” but insists that together, communities, households and councils can make difference to an area’s resilience. “We are seeing increasingly intense rainfall and a growing risk from surface water flooding, and climate change means we cannot assume that the flooding patterns of the past will necessarily be the patterns of the future,” she said. “This makes preparation more important than ever.” Gardens and outdoor spaces According to Mary Long-Dhonau, who runs the Flood Mary campaign, protecting your home starts outside. She says now is an ideal time to check brickwork and mortar on outside walls for cracks or weaknesses. These should either be repaired or replaced and external walls can be treated with a breathable waterproof sealant. “Having cracks or crumbling mortar can be like having 20 taps in your wall that will let the flood water straight in,” said Long-Dhonau, who provides a directory of builders who specialise in flood-related work. Experts also suggest making sure gutters are clear and in good working order. Long-Dhonau adds that residents should consider installing water butts, which catch and store the rain before it reaches the ground. “They are easy and relatively cheap and it means if you get a warning about a possible flood risk you can empty the water butts before the rain arrives, meaning they have full capacity to hold the maximum amount once the rain starts, keeping it out of the drains,” said Long-Dhonau. The way gardens, driveways and other outdoor spaces are designed also has a big impact on how quickly rainwater runs into already stretched drainage systems – and how likely your home is to flood. Surfaces such as concrete, paving and artificial grass prevent water soaking effectively into the ground. Instead, you should include planted areas, rain gardens or permeable paving to allow water to drain away. “Even if you have a paved area, just taking up one or two paving stones and planting some water-thirsty plants can make a big difference,” said Long-Dhonau. Improving soil health and increasing plant cover also allow gardens to better absorb and hold water, reducing the risk of flooding. “The trick is to work with nature wherever possible,” said Long-Dhonau. Homes Flooding can happen quickly and be stressful, so experts advise having a “flood to-do list” spelling out what needs to be done should the worst happen, including how to turn off the gas and electricity supplies and which treasured belongings need moving out of harm’s way. With this in mind, experts advise having a “flood box” to keep a few flood essentials in, from a head torch to flood tape, plastic sheeting to absorbent flood cushions. “No one can say exactly what this winter will bring, but you don’t need to wait for a flood warning before taking action,” said Long-Dhonau. “After all, you don’t want to be hunting around for your insurance details or wondering which belongings to move first when the water is already rising.” In emergencies In terms of stopping the water getting in, the house experts warn that a standard airbrick can let thousands of litres of water in to your home every hour, so it is crucial to identify where they are and have a plan in place for what to do if a flood hits. Long-Dhonau says that ideally they should be replaced with Kitemarked self-closing airbricks, which seal when the flood water comes. Alternatively, temporary covers are available that have to be manually installed before the flood hits. Flood water can also come through doors or windows. Flood doors can be fitted, which, although expensive, are effective at keeping water out. Alternatively, floor barriers can be installed outside the door, which need to be put in place before the flood water arrives. In an emergency, Long-Dhonau suggests having flood tape or aluminium tape in the house, which can be used to seal up airbricks, doors and windows. “People always think of sandbags when floods happen, but having some good-quality flood tape on hand is not only a more effective way to better protect your home but also much, much cheaper.” One of the most distressing and destructive impacts of flooding can be waste water and sewage being forced back up into the house through the toilet system. Ideally, flood-risk properties should have a non-return valve fitted to the drainage system, which will stop this happening. Alternatively, toilet bungs and stoppers are available, which also work but need to be fitted manually. In an emergency, Long-Dhonau suggests a child’s football can be deflated, pushed down the toilet and pumped up again. The toilet seat can then be taped down using flood or aluminium tape. “Obviously, it is about being as prepared as you can be but also using whatever is to hand to limit the damage,” she said. Other tips for flood-prone homes Long-Dhonau suggests raising furniture off the floor by propping it up on upturned buckets or decorators’ trestles. She also says curtains can be tied up with scarves or tights and table legs put in buckets, or even wellies, to protect them from rising flood water. Precious objects should be put in plastic clip boxes and moved somewhere safe. “You want to go into your room and look around at everything below waist height and think, what is really precious to me?” In properties that regularly flood, experts recommend moving plug sockets higher up the walls and installing flood-resilient flooring and materials, which can make a property easier and quicker to clean and save thousands of pounds. Kelly Ostler-Coyle, from the government-backed Flood Re reinsurance scheme said: “No one can predict exactly where or when flooding will happen, but there are practical steps that people can take to make their homes more resilient … A little preparation can make a real difference – helping to protect the things people care about and making it easier to get back into their homes and back to normal if flooding does happen.”

title: Burning forests, emptying rivers, €180bn in damage: Europe’s politicians face reckoning after ‘summer of truth’
summary: Amid record-shattering heatwaves and popular demand for climate action, why are politicians often timid or in denial?
text: It was, according to the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, the “summer of truth”. Climate chaos ripped through Europe and the northern hemisphere, sending heat records tumbling, scorching crops in the fields, burning forests, emptying rivers and reservoirs, warping train tracks, melting roads and killing about 35,000 people in Europe alone. The EU has estimated the damage at about €180bn, and the full bill is yet to arrive: harvests have been depleted, which will probably raise food price inflation, and expensive repairs to infrastructure have only just begun. “All of this is a mere preview,” said von der Leyen in her state of the EU address on Wednesday. “These were the hottest summer months ever – but probably the coolest of the years to come. Science is clear. Europe is warming at double the global rate. Europe can, must and will stay the course on its climate targets.” But while Europe has heated faster than any other continent, no region of the world is being spared. In the US, this summer’s heat eclipsed that of the “dust bowl” years of the 1930s, and drought gripped 60% of the country from spring, a record for the time of year. Extreme rainfall across Asia brought flash floods and typhoons, displacing hundreds of thousands of people and causing severe damage to crops. So what has the political response been? Tepid at best from centrist and leftwing politicians, say campaigners, with few rays of hope to brighten the gloom; denial and dangerous, provocative incoherence from the right and far right. “It was the hottest of summers – it was the meekest of responses,” said Magda Stoczkiewicz, the EU programme director for Greenpeace, of von der Leyen’s intervention. “The EU Commission continues its crusade to dismantle and defund environmental action. It is planning to cut green funding in the next EU budget, continues to support fossil fuels like gas, and is speeding up permitting of environmentally harmful projects.” Von der Leyen promised to “double down” on low-carbon energy and to “make Europe’s future electric”, as well as build resilience to climate impacts with a heatwave plan. There have been other positive moves: the Netherlands produced its long-awaited roadmap to “transition away from fossil fuels”, and France adopted a speeded-up plan for electrification. The UK saw the first “down payment” on a promised £1bn community energy programme, and the prime minister, Andy Burnham, committed to “net zero by 2050”. In the developing world, Thailand decided to stop building gas-fired power stations, while Indonesia continued to scale up solar energy under a three-year plan to halt oil imports. India, which has already achieved its 2030 target to have 50% of its installed electricity generation capacity from renewables, vowed to push further, to reach 500GW by 2030 from about 260GW today. China’s emissions, meanwhile, are likely to fall this year under the acceleration of the country’s switch to electric vehicles and vast build-out of solar and wind energy. Yet, as campaigners have noted, these positive developments are outweighed by governments stalling on climate commitments, or pushing for more fossil fuels. In the UK, the government is mulling the opening of new oil and gasfields. Germany is building new gas-fired power stations; France is falling behind on its greenhouse gas reduction targets. Even the co-hosts of the next UN climate summit, Cop31, which will take place this November in Turkey but with Australia in charge of negotiations, are failing to walk the walk on climate. This month, Australia approved the expansion of a coalmine that will continue producing until 2055; the same mine supplies Turkey, which has refused to set a phaseout date for coal use. On the right, the record-breaking summer has not slowed US efforts to reverse and remove climate legislation: most recently, the Trump administrationhas repealed the Environmental Protection Agency rule that cuts emissions from power plants, and pressed ahead with dismantling renewable energy and boosting coal. Populist politicians on the far right are on the rise, and almost all embrace climate denial as one of their key tenets and paint attempts to cut greenhouse gas emissions as economy-crippling. Extreme heat and the coming of climate impacts that scientists have long predicted might be expected to give them pause; instead, their denial has often intensified – as is the case in the US under Donald Trump – or switched focus to clamorous demands for a huge expansion of air conditioning as the only means of adapting to the heat. Meanwhile, their anti-immigration policies ignore the potential impact of the climate crisis on immigration. Rather than address the root causes of immigration and fund clean energy and development, they prefer to claim that countries should build huge walls around themselves, and to demonise immigrants. “Climate has become the central part of the far right’s culture war in defence of the economic and energy status quo that bankrolls it,” says Romain Ioualalen, the global policy lead at Oil Change International. “When the brutality of climate impacts has made their previous climate denialism untenable, like in France, their fallback strategy has been to present adaptation [to the impacts of extreme weather] as a substitute for cutting emissions. All round the world, the far right has weaponised legitimate concerns about affordability and living standards generated by decades of neoliberal policies to protect the fossil fuel status quo.” The populist task is made easier in a world bombarded by threats: from AI, conflicts, geo-politics and rampant inequality. Memories are short, even for significant events. Previous climate disasters were quickly erased from global attention, says Laurence Tubiana, the chief executive of the European Climate Foundation. “We can’t ignore what has happened in Nepal, and we have forgotten what happened in Pakistan just a few years ago,” she says, referring to the deadly climate-driven floods that affected a third of the country’s population in 2022. “There is a big silence around all this.” Some of the most vulnerable countries are struggling to protect their people, and face a vicious cycle of debt, but are seeing little help from the rich world. “Many are being forced to choose between servicing enormous debts and investing in the infrastructure that could save lives when the next disaster strikes,” says Mohamed Adow, the director of the Power Shift Africa thinktank. If politicians in some of the world’s biggest economies are failing to act, it is not for a lack of demand among their voters. John Marshall, the founder and executive chair of the Potential Energy Coalition in the US, says recent polling by his organisation has found that politicians in many large economies are failing to keep pace with their voters on the issue. “The disconnect we’re seeing is not between the public and climate action,” he says. “It’s between what people are experiencing and how much they’re hearing from their leaders about it. People want more clean energy and less of the fossil fuel pollution that’s overheating the planet.” This calls into question the strategy of “climate hushing” that some Democrats in the US – and even progressive politicians in other countries – have embraced, amid a widespread perception that voters care only about the cost of living. According to the Potential Energy Coalition polling, that is not the case: about two-thirds of people in the US believe that if public officials refuse to acknowledge the reality of global heating, they are putting people at risk. A similar number said societies could not prepare for extreme weather if they were not willing to talk about the climate crisis. In Europe, polling by Climate Opinion found the shattered heat records elevated the climate to one of the top five concerns in France, Germany, Italy, Spain and the UK. (Denmark, which was less affected by extreme weather, was also included in the poll, but the number citing it as a top concern stayed flat at 28%.) About 68% to 83% of respondents in all countries identified the heatwaves as climate-related. “It’s difficult for the public to get their heads round,” says Michael Jacobs, an emeritus professor of political economy at the University of Sheffield. “And the [far right] are not wrong in one respect, which is that we do need to adapt to the heat. But what we need people to understand is that net zero is literally a description of scientific fact. If we don’t reach net zero emissions, we will see temperatures continue to rise.” If weather as extreme as this year’s “summer of truth” fails to make a lasting political impact, we will be doomed to repeat it – over and over, until acting on it is no longer a choice.

title: Country diary: A lesson from my final diary after nearly 40 years – keep looking closely | Phil Gates
summary: Stanhope, Weardale: I’ve realised in that time that beauty and fascination can lie in the most mundane of plants – in this case, broad-leaved dock
text: After another exceptionally dry summer, there’s a nagging question lurking at the back of naturalists’ minds: which species will be the winners and losers in our evolving climate? Throughout summer’s heatwaves and drought, I watched a dense stand of broad-leaved docks, Rumex obtusifolius, thrive while surrounding fields turned the colour of bleached straw. They have promising credentials as drought survivors, thanks to a deep taproot, fast, early spring growth and a long-lasting dormant seed bank in the soil. “One year’s seeding, seven years weeding” goes the old adage, warning of the consequences of allowing weed seeds to ripen and disperse on cultivated ground. That’s an over-optimistic outlook in the case of docks, whose buried seeds can remain viable for up to 80 years. They need light to germinate, but some of today’s bumper seed crop, brought to the surface by burrowing animals eight decades hence, could conceivably grow, flower and set seeds in the early years of the 22nd century. Broad-leaved dock, growing as a weed, has colonised cultivated land since the earliest days of British agriculture. As a wildflower, it’s a rather coarse, unattractive but medicinally useful ruderal (early coloniser). Country children of my generation learned to identify and crush dock for the sap that soothes nettle stings – perhaps the most widely used of all folk remedies. This morning, it was the flash of cerise breast feathers of a male bullfinch, feeding on the docks’ forest of russet seed heads, that caught my attention. There is enough food here to feed a bullfinch family for months. After 39 years and more than 500 country diaries, this is my last. During that time, I’ve realised that there is often hidden beauty in commonplace and superficially mundane plants, if you look closely enough with a hand lens. So it was with the dock seed that the bullfinch had been eating. Each was oblong, reminiscent of the head and body of a miniature mouse sitting on a papery bract, whose spiky, dry veins extended beyond its margins like claws: exquisite, natural Gothic architecture. Later, at home, I found some of those clawed seeds hooked into my coat sleeves. In autumn, wherever we go, plants often travel with us. • Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024, is available now at guardianbookshop.com

title: ‘My fear was too great’: the Pussy Riot member recruited by Russian spies to inform on fellow activists
summary: Exclusive: In her first media interview since fleeing Russia, Rita Flores describes her three years of being run by the FSB
text: First came the blackmail and death threats to secure cooperation, then came a series of tasks, each more sinister than the last: to inform on fellow activists, to elicit personal information from protest-minded artists and – eventually – to help with a plot to kidnap and murder a Kremlin enemy. That is how Rita Flores, a 29-year-old Russian artist, activist and former member of the Pussy Riot collective, described her recruitment and three-year handling by officers from Russia’s FSB security service, a cooperation she only broke when she fled the country last month. Flores made details of her collaboration public in a video discussion with her lawyer, Dmitry Zakhvatov, published just days after she left Russia at the end of August. She explained she was coming clean in the hope that others in a similar situation might feel emboldened to break their ties with the FSB. Now, in her first media interview since leaving Russia, she gave further detail on how she was recruited and run by the FSB. “For the first time in years, I feel calm. All this time I was dreaming about getting out and being able to talk about it all,” she said. The Guardian could not corroborate the details of Flores’s account, but there have been numerous cases of the FSB infiltrating opposition groups over the past few years. Flores, also known as Margarita Konovalova, has been associated with Pussy Riot since 2020, when she was detained after a performance near the Kremlin. She had served several short stints in jail and been subjected to surveillance and house searches on numerous occasions, which intensified after the domestic crackdown that followed the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. She was recruited after one of these police searches in February 2023, when two men stayed behind and introduced themselves as FSB officers, she said. They threatened to open a criminal case, under wartime censorship laws, over an Instagram post she had made criticising Russian killings in Ukraine. They also suggested they could arrange for her mother to be killed if she did not sign cooperation papers. “I believed them. I believed they could do everything they said they would … My fear was too great. I was so worried for my family and also for myself,” she said. As a reward for signing, she was given a one-off cash payment of 30,000 or 40,000 roubles (£266 or £355), she said. Her first tasks were to gather information about other opposition-minded artists in the same circles as her and report back to the FSB. The two FSB officers who recruited her became her regular handlers, she said, organising frequent meetings and largely sticking to a classic good-cop, bad-cop routine. She saw the senior officer only occasionally, a crude man in his late forties who introduced himself by a series of different names. In the end, Flores began calling him “the Jacket”, based on the shiny black suit he liked to wear. The junior officer, named Ivan, became her primary handler, and he often tried to be friendly and helpful, leaving direct threats to the Jacket. “Whenever I met with Ivan and the Jacket together, Ivan was silent. The Jacket would be rude, threatening; he’d insult me as a woman. He was the devil incarnate. Then just me and Ivan would meet, and Ivan would be nice, friendly,” she recalled. “He liked to say, ‘The FSB will re-educate you, I will re-educate you, you’ll have a nice and calm life, and you’ll love Russia, have children and be an obedient wife,’” she said. Flores said she was not supposed to tell anyone about her recruitment, but immediately told “about 20 people”, putting it down to the fact she is a “massive gossip”. Still, she stopped short of telling the people from the art world she was meant to report on, instead claiming that she initiated conflicts with them on pretexts, designed to push them away from her and prevent them sharing sensitive information. Her two handlers kept up the psychological pressure by repeating their threats, and even the friendlier Ivan on occasion made it clear that the consequences for crossing him would be severe, she claimed. “He tried to befriend me, but he could also be threatening. He’d calmly say, ‘they’ll kill your mother and you won’t be able to prove anything’ or ‘if you go abroad they’ll find you immediately and kill you,’ and then he would giggle, like it was all a joke. The Jacket, on the other hand, never joked. His threats were more direct.” In time, there were fewer targets to inform on, as most of the protest-minded artists left the country. She described life in wartime Moscow as an exercise in cognitive dissonance. “Moscow is booming; restaurants, bars and clubs are opening and there are a huge number of events. But those people who understand things have empty eyes and speak empty words,” she said. Artists who stayed are careful not to produce any work that could be considered even tangentially political, she said. “People who have stayed in Russia have accepted the rules of a game. You go to a gallery and every artwork may as well come with a sign saying ‘we were forbidden from saying anything’ … there are artists who used to make strong statements, and in 2026 they are drawing flowers in a vase.” Last May, Ivan and the Jacket first started asking her questions about Pyotr Verzilov, an activist previously linked to Pussy Riot who now lives in Ukraine and fights with the Ukrainian army against Russia. A longtime irritant to the Russian authorities, in 2018 German doctors said they believed Verzilov had been poisoned in Russia. Flores said her handlers wanted her to get information from Verzilov, including his address in Ukraine. Then, they suggested she use her old friendship with him to arrange a meeting in Serbia. There, he would be kidnapped and killed by a waiting FSB squad, they claimed. Ivan began to pay her 50,000 roubles a month as an additional incentive to help with the Verzilov case. Meanwhile, Flores said, she was plotting a way out. She married her partner last September, which she said was partly a way of worming out of the Serbia task, so she could claim to Ivan that her husband would never let her go on a trip to meet another man. Previously, her handlers had banned her from leaving the country, she claimed, and it was only when she contacted the lawyer, Zakhvatov, that she realised there could be a way for her to leave. The pair began scheming in secret over the details. “They created a reality where she felt like they controlled everything, but actually it is not that hard to leave,” said Zakhvatov. In 2022, fellow Pussy Riot activists Lucy Shtein and Masha Alekhina fled house arrest in Moscow by dressing up as food delivery couriers to evade police and eventually leave Russia. Flores’s escape was less dramatic, but both Zakhvatov and Flores declined to give details, citing the need to protect methods for future cases. After Flores’s escape, Zakhvatov announced a secure line for people in similar positions to contact him if they need help. Flores said she would also like to work to help others, and added that she was certain that recruitments in activist circles are a “mass phenomenon”. She said there was at least one person in her own surroundings who had informed on her before she agreed to cooperate, a fact she discovered when it turned out that the FSB had possession of a sex tape featuring her, covertly filmed by the person. Earlier this year, Poland jailed an exiled Russian activist for seven years, after it emerged he had passed information about fellow exiles to an FSB handler who had recruited him back in Russia. Flores’s video confession at the end of last month was met with praise from some parts of the exiled Russian opposition, who commended her bravery for speaking out and explaining how the FSB operates, but also some scepticism from those who criticised her decision to cooperate for so long. Since then, Flores has been making calls to people she informed on as well as other old friends to explain herself, and said everyone had been supportive in these conversations. “It’s not a big secret that it’s not great to work for the FSB, but fear can change a person,” said Alekhina. “It’s important that she’s now out of the country and that she said what happened to her out loud. Nobody was killed and nobody went to prison [because of her], so that is good news.”

title: Thousands protest Kennedy Center closure amid fears Trump set to demolish institution
summary: Demonstrators gather after president spotted holding placard that read: ‘Kennedy Center DEMOLIS ...’
text: On Friday evening thousands of protesters gathered outside the Kennedy Center in view of the marble facade that remained concealed by scaffolding and tarpaulins, to protest Donald Trump’s plans for the facility and express alarm that he might make good on his threat to tear down the institution. Crowding streets in the Foggy Bottom area of Washington and locking down traffic as they walked, many carried signs, as they joined in the “Hands Around the Kennedy Center” protest. Some wore costumes and booed when the president was mentioned during the program. Chris Raleigh, co-founder of Hands Off the Arts, which set up the gathering, said in an interview that he hoped the event would show that people are willing to fight to halt Trump’s plans for the building. One of the most iconic buildings on the Potomac River waterfront, the Kennedy Center has been a focus of Trump’s remake of Washington since 2025, when he began installing favorites on to its governing board. Late last year, he had his name placed on the center. A judge ruled that Trump’s name was illegally added and ordered it removed. The Kennedy Center board, which is aligned with the president, voted Tuesday to close the center indefinitely for repairs hours after US District Judge Christopher Cooper blocked their plans to return Trump’s name to the building. On Thursday, the judge ordered the Kennedy Center to provide 30 days’ notice before making any major physical changes to the building, including demolishing it. The protests on Friday came after a photo of Trump examining a depiction of the Kennedy Center apparently being demolished sparked widespread attention. In the image captured by AFP photographer Brendan Smialowski on Wednesday, the president was seen through the windows of Air Force One holding a placard with visible text in red declaring: “Kennedy Center DEMOLIS...” The rest of the word was obscured by the plane’s window frame. Raleigh said he, like others, is concerned Trump could tear down the building without notifying the court. “Look at the East Wing,” he said. “We got up one morning and there was a giant hole there.” Among the demonstrators were people in inflatable animal costumes and a man in a golden Trump mask with a crown and a sign that said: “Restore my name in gold you sycophants.” Another man wore a blue hat that said: “Make America intelligent again.” Baby Trump balloons danced in the air against the setting sun. Protesters beat drums, chanted “hands off!” and waved signs including: “Keep your tiny hands off our Kennedy Center”; “You’re no Jack Kennedy”; “Donny you are no JFK!”; “Kennedy Center 4 ever”; “Our center not DJT’s”; “Hands off the arts”; and “Wicked starring DJT”. Friday’s event followed a tumultuous week in federal courts in Washington in which filings and counter-filings flooded the courts as the administration continued its push for the president’s vanity projects. The administration has made substantive steps to begin work on a number of projects, despite the fact they are still being litigated. Such projects include Trump’s triumphal arch and the administration’s takeover of East Potomac Golf Links and the US Institute of Peace. Speaking from the Oval Office, Trump said he was willing to save the center, which he said was losing money. He did not address a question about demolishing it. “We have a lot of people working very hard on it to save it,” he said. “I can save it easily, but why should we be doing that and then raise money for the rest of our lives to keep it afloat? Because that’s what you have to do, if we get no recognition. I think the Trump administration should be recognized as having saved the Kennedy Center.” With the Associated Press and Agence France Presse
