title: Trump officials sending undocumented children to Texas sparks fears of mass deportation
summary: Exclusive: Nearly 90% of children in federal custody being directed to GOP-controlled state that has unlicensed facilities and low legal representation rates
text: The Trump administration has started sending a majority of undocumented children who came to the US alone and have new immigration court cases to Texas, where government facilities for them are unlicensed, their chances of getting a lawyer are low and advocates fear that “a deportation churn-out factory” awaits them, the Guardian has learned. Almost 80% of children in federal custody who arrived unaccompanied by a parent or legal guardian and who were placed in immigration court proceedings in July – and over 90% in August – have been funneled into shelter networks somewhere in Texas, a dramatic upswing from the months prior, according to analysis shared exclusively with the Guardian from researchers at the immigration data insights platform bklg.org. This is understood to amount to a total of 925 children in the care of the Health and Human Services (HHS) department’s office of refugee resettlement (ORR) and in open immigration court proceedings based in Texas, with 651 sent there in July and August alone. Federal officials’ sudden shift toward ushering these vulnerable kids to the Republican-controlled, deeply conservative state for no publicly stated reason has alarmed immigrants’ rights advocates amid concerns about their treatment and access to due process under US laws. Experts who spoke to the Guardian fear the advent of a mass apprehension campaign – forcing immigrant children from their communities within the country’s interior to gather them in Texas to ultimately pack them onto repatriation flights, which often leave from areas along the US’s southern border. “We’re thinking about congregating children in facilities in Texas, where there are less attorneys, where it’s one of the harshest jurisdictions, you know, in the country with regard to immigration judges and how they handle cases. And it’s close to the border, where they can just get planes,” said Roxana Avila-Cimpeanu, deputy director at the Arizona-based legal service non-profit, Florence Immigrant and Refugee Rights Project. She added that these facilities could be “a deportation churn out factory that has attorneys in name but not real representation”. Unaccompanied immigrant kids, who often come to the US fleeing abuse, neglect, abandonment, trafficking or other harms, regularly cross the US-Mexico border and enter the custody of ORR, which is legally tasked with their welfare, not the Department of Homeland Security’s Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agency. There were more than 1,800 kids in ORR’s care nationally at the end of July, scattered among shelters, foster care and secure facilities across the country. Yet already, more than 60% of those still detained with ongoing immigration court proceedings are now believed to be living in Texas, compared with fewer than half in June. ORR did not respond to a request for comment from the Guardian. The processing to Texas is occurring despite the state’s GOP-dominated government refusing to provide state licensing for ORR care providers, a policy that hasn’t stopped the facilities from operating there, but has meant less child welfare oversight and protections for kids. “Texas is very sympathetic to the Trump administration, at least the governor and the Republican legislature. And so I think the Trump administration knows that not only will there be no pushback from the state government and from the governor, but that people like Governor Greg Abbott are willing accomplices,” Veronica Escobar, a Democratic congresswoman from west Texas, told the Guardian in a phone interview this week. Meanwhile, many of the kids – from toddlers to teenagers – are navigating the US’s byzantine immigration laws mostly without attorneys. Already, only 31.7% of children in ORR custody with active immigration court proceedings nationally have had a notice of legal representation filed in their cases. Kids held in Texas are faring even worse, with 17.2% in Houston, 18.6% in El Paso and just 8.7% in San Antonio having a legal representation form filed on their behalf, bklg.org’s research found. “There needs to be far more oversight and representation, for children especially. These kids deserve lawyers,” Escobar said. At the same time, ORR officials have alarmed advocates by seeking multiple contracts for “emergency influx facilities” of up to 3,000 beds – despite the fact that such facilities can only open when the agency’s operational capacity reaches 85% or higher for multiple days, and ORR’s shelter and foster care network, by its own count, is operating at about 27% capacity. “Who are they planning to fill those facilities with?” Avila-Cimpeanu asked. “Our fear is huge mass internal apprehension of children.” Plans for such facilities were first reported by the Independent last month. At a recent roundtable presentation for roughly 120 stakeholders, ORR officials said the contracts would potentially give the administration “the capability to rapidly respond to any surges at the border of unaccompanied alien children”, according to a transcript of the meeting shared with the Guardian. But encounters with unaccompanied children at the south-west border have been exceptionally low over the last year and a half. Still, officials pushed for an aggressive timeline, with only 90 days for a facility to become fully operational after a contract is awarded. “That’s fast and you’re like: ‘I don’t know if I can do that.’ I think it’s very feasible. That is the intent of where we need to be,” said Tony Canales, a branch chief at ORR’s division of acquisition requirements, according to the transcript. “We’re looking to see whatever you got. I mean, if it’s a permanent facility, if it’s temporary buildings, if it’s a site that is blank that you plan on building on, whatever the case may be. We will definitely look at it and take [it] into consideration,” Canales told the attendees. The presentation specified that any shelter would require an 8-ft high perimeter fence. Although officials did not specify a location for such emergency influx facilities, many of the stakeholders closed in on Texas while asking questions. Officials also said the chosen contractors would be responsible for providing legal services, which could present a serious conflict of interest given that attorneys tasked with representing kids would now be dependent on ORR. For critics of the second Trump administration, the emergency influx facilities raise the spectre of a worst case scenario, with large-scale detentions for immigrant children in communities across the country, given that there is no apparent current need for the massive shelters otherwise. “The way that a country and a government treats its children and children in their custody is a direct representation of the level of morality or immorality of that government and those individuals,” Escobar said. “And so it is shameful the way that this administration has chosen to treat children.” José Olivares contributed reporting

title: Louisiana firefighters find feline native to sub-Saharan Africa while responding to house fire
summary: The African serval, illegally enclosed in the back yard, was subdued and transferred to an animal welfare facility
text: Louisiana firefighters responding to a small house blaze found a wildcat native to sub-Saharan Africa illegally enclosed in the back yard, prompting an animal welfare agency to seek placing the creature in an appropriate environment, according to officials. Firefighters investigating a report of a minor fire at a home in the suburban New Orleans community of Marrero on Tuesday spotted the cat in question – an African serval – behind the residence in a chain-linked enclosure resembling a cramped baseball batting cage, a spokesperson for the local animal protection services said. A statement from Jefferson protection and animal welfare services (JPaws) said its director, Michelle Brignac, and humane department supervisor, Victoria Clark, joined firefighters at the scene after they were summoned there. Local laws in effect in Marrero require an exotic animal permit to legally keep a serval as a pet, and the owner of the home at the center of the case did not have such a document, JPaws spokesperson John McCusker told the Guardian on Thursday. The statement said Brignac and Clark therefore “subdued the hissing serval and wrangled it” into a transport carrier from its 9ft-by-9ft (7.53-sq-meter) cage that McCusker likened to “a dog kennel”. Brignac and Clark then brought the serval to the JPaws facility in the nearby community of Harvey, according to the statement from the agency, which also shared vivid photographs of the wildcat. Beside their black spots, svelte physiques and striking facial features, servals are known for their ability to leap as high as about 7ft (2 meters) in the air. So McCusker said JPaws gave the serval an entire room to itself while the agency sought an appropriate refuge for the wildcat, which was born in captivity but whose natural habitat is African grasslands. Servals share some similarities with domesticated cats that make them immensely popular as pets, including their affinities for grooming themselves, purring, yowling and stalking potential prey. Nonetheless, they are not easily sustained pets, JPaws’ statement maintained. Servals in captivity do not have the physical space and stimulation needed to engage in normal, healthy behaviors, and they endure chronic stress as a result, the agency’s statement said. They mark their territory, become aggressive as they mature, cannot be fully house-trained and destroy furniture, and they have been known to barge through walls and doors, according to JPaws. Experts also say servals require a diet and specialized care beyond what house cats need, making them a major responsibility. A social media post on Friday by Brignac said JPaws had managed to place the serval with a zoo “where he could have something very different: space, enrichment, appropriate care and an environment designed with his needs in mind”. Brignac’s post did not specify to which zoo she was referring. The Marrero serval was the latest of several indicators of the wildcats’ growing popularity, a boom driven in part by social media content creators showing them in videos online. Cases involving servals have also tended to generate widely read news headlines in North America. That happened in Ohio in 2023, when officials in the Cincinnati area captured an African serval named Amiry that was spotted in a Cincinnati neighborhood tree and later tested positive for cocaine. In late 2025, a search for an African serval that escaped a Pennsylvania wildlife center culminated in heartbreak after a motorist fatally struck the wildcat, as Philadelphia’s NBC News affiliated reported. And the news outlet People reported on authorities in the Canadian city of Vancouver returning an African serval to its owners after it escaped and nestled under a neighbor’s porch in June. The British Columbia province to which Vancouver belongs had just banned keeping exotic cats such as African servals as pets. But, People reported, the owners of such cats were given until the beginning of May 2027 to apply for permits to legally possess them.

title: After four killings and a revealing autopsy, Memphis is fed up with the national guard takeover
summary: Although state officials laud a reduction in violent crime, a report claims it would have happened without the taskforce
text: National guard troops began walking the streets of Memphis a year ago this week, as part of a federal surge of law enforcement agents sent into the city at the behest of the Trump administration to reduce violent crime. Fewer soldiers are on the street today, as the city’s grudging initial acceptance of the president’s deployment has given way to doubts about their effectiveness, focus and respect for civil rights – particularly after four men were killed in gunfire by federal agents working with the taskforce, with a recent autopsy showing that one was shot in the back. Donald Trump signed an executive order last September directing a surge of federal law enforcement agents from the ATF, FBI, Department of Homeland Security and other agencies into Memphis. A month later, Tennessee’s Republican governor, Bill Lee, paired that with additional state patrol officers and the activation of 1,500 Tennessee national guard members to patrol the streets of downtown Memphis. The Memphis Safe Task Force claims credit for deep reductions in the violent crime rate. And while the city is on track for the lowest rate of homicides in decades, independent analysis argues the deployment of the national guard has had no statistically measurable impact on violent crime and that violence would have fallen in Memphis much like it has across the country in cities without similar interventions. Memphis’s headline-driving homicide rate has fallen about 35% since the start of the taskforce. Murders in the city’s second quarter decreased by 60% year over year, according to reports from the Memphis police department. But Memphis had a 26% decrease from 249 murders reported in 2024 to 184 in 2025, before the taskforce was deployed. A year to the day from the start of the Memphis Safe Task Force, Memphis reported 96 murders, compared with 149 the previous year. The city is on pace for 135 murders for 2026, a rate of about 22.2 per 100,000 residents. “The taskforce has been very successful and we appreciate the work the Tennessee national guard has done in helping us reduce crime,” said Brady McCarron, a United States Marshals Service spokeperson who fields media requests for the taskforce. “Overall crime in Memphis is down significantly, dropping nearly 36% year-to-date in 2026 compared to the previous year, according to Memphis police department’s own statistics.” A report by the Center for American Progress, a Washington DC-based thinktank, however, picked apart claims that large reductions in violence could be attributed to national guard patrols in New Orleans, Memphis and Washington DC, where the presence of troops on the tourist-heavy National Mall and the streets around the White House have become ubiquitous. Trump reacted to the center’s report by threatening a personal defamation lawsuit against the authors for $5bn unless they retracted the report and issued an apology. Describing the deployments as a “political charade”, the CAP report used statistical regression to measure changes in violent crime against historical patterns and the double-digit drops in crime in other large cities. “The findings of this analysis confirm what many already suspected: At the time of the administration’s federal law enforcement and National Guard deployments, the primary goal was never to stop crime,” the report said. “Despite multiple tests using multiple data sources, measures, and windows of time, there is no compelling evidence that these deployments reduced homicides, violent crime, or gun violence.” *** In Memphis, a brief initial decrease in violence when national guard troops began patrolling was actually followed by a brief increase in violent crime. The rate eventually smoothed out as crime continued to fall overall, both in Memphis and across the country. Fewer national guard troops are patrolling the streets of downtown Memphis today. The taskforce attributes that to a unit rotation. But the pullback also coincides with an autopsy report released by the family of Tyrin Johnson, who was shot dead by two national guard soldiers on Fourth of July weekend. The taskforce said they were chasing an armed robbery suspect. The autopsy said Johnson was shot in the back. “The timing is suspicious,” said community organizer Lucci Chambless, who has been in close contact with the Johnson family following the shooting. The Tennessee national guard and the governor’s office have not yet responded to requests for comment. Public sentiment in Memphis began to shift after the shooting. Tamboli’s, a pizza place in midtown Memphis, went viral for refusing to seat national guard troops in protest of the deployment. A call by conservatives to boycott the restaurant instead packed it with supporters. More than 50 other businesses have signed on to a “buy-cott” with Tamboli’s affirming their stance. “I think we’re seeing more and more every day that people are coming to the side that they don’t agree with them being here, seeing how they’re harming our community so much,” said Taylor Herndon, owner of Board to Beers, a board-gaming bar near the University of Memphis. Her bar is participating in the national guard lockout, which she says has had a positive impact on business, similar to Tamboli’s. “We have a lot of customers that we have started seeing because of the boycott,” she said. “We already had a large following, but the boycott has definitely helped us reach even more of our community, and we’ve had a lot of people reach out and thank us for being on the right side of history, and that they feel comfortable coming because of it and that they feel support because of it, which has been amazing.” She said she was disappointed that formal resistance by Memphis’s elected leaders has been comparably tepid. “It’s been hard, because I keep fighting and I keep fighting, and it seems like things just keep getting worse. Despite thinking: ‘Oh, it can’t get any worse,’ but it does,” she said. Democratic-led cities like Portland and Chicago strenuously resisted national guard deployments – rhetorically, in court and in the street. But the Memphis city council rejected a resolution condemning the federal surge when it first arrived, and public reaction had largely been muted until recently. The activities of the national guard have been as “transparent as mud”, and an immigration raid on the El Corralón nightclub earlier this month by the taskforce – resulting in 120 arrests, the most in one operation in state history – is exacerbating the change in public sentiment, Chambless said. Many of the people arrested in the raid have already been deported. The children of deportees presented themselves at the Memphis city council hearing Tuesday, to a chamber that has become more receptive to resistance after elections earlier this year. A new crop of county commissioners may restart legal action, she added. “We’re hopeful that maybe they will take up that cause. Especially now that the damages have been shown,” Chambless said. “Tyrin Johnson certainly would still be alive if the national guard had been stopped.”

title: Andrew Hastie says AI advised him to reply ‘congratulations!’ to man who planned to end life with assisted dying
summary: Liberal MP speaks of AI’s shortcomings as cyber chief tells inquiry the tech is needed to fend off ‘highly capable malicious cyber actors’
text: When a man with a terminal illness wrote to his local MP Andrew Hastie, telling him he planned on ending his own life with voluntary assisted dying, Microsoft Copilot suggested Hastie reply with “congratulations!”, “great to hear from you” or “that is wonderful news!”. Hastie shared the episode at a parliamentary inquiry on Friday to underline the shortcomings of the American-run software as he called for AI run by Australians. The hearing offered the some of the most detailed explanations of the Albanese government’s desire to bring Anthropic and OpenAI to Australia, in the face of calls to slow them down or shut them out. The defence establishment told the inquiry that cutting the companies out could be catastrophic. Abigail Bradshaw, the director general of the Australian Signals Directorate, said her agents needed advanced AI every day to fend off “highly capable malicious cyber actors”. “If a digital adversary has access to newer, more capable models than we do, they may be able to identify and exploit vulnerabilities in systems and networks before we can identify them,” Bradshaw said. But Australia’s top cyber-intelligence agency is “entirely reliant” on US-housed processing and would “dramatically” lose capability if cut off in a conflict, Bradshaw said. The defence department’s chief AI officer, Chris Crozier, said the government was already trying to keep its tech needs local, contracting Google to build a series of interlinked datacentres spread across the country and disconnected from the US. “Somebody can’t wake up and have a bad day and decide they’re going to turn it off,” Crozier said. “We do not want to be using AI tool sets that are located offshore … we want the compute, we want the application, we want the data, we want the decision making, all based in Australia.” Bringing big tech into the country would make the job much easier, he said, and not just by allowing the army to protect and maintain its datacentres. The Office of AI, set up in the prime minister’s department, said bringing firms under Australian law would make it easier for local law enforcement to combat threats on the platforms. Tight conditions on access could also materially improve Australia’s chances of using and defending itself with the best AI tools in the world, the inquiry heard. “We will get more assured access, earlier access, more detailed technical access, and better integration with technical experts at the frontier,” Bradshaw said. These would be assured by strict requirements on any top developers looking to train models in Australia, such as demanding government oversight and early access to advanced models, she suggested. The government is already planning to set the rules for companies that come here. It is consulting on standards that would force AI companies to report issues and breaches and potentially reserve some computational power for local research. Large datacentres will have to engage with communities, build away from schools and homes, and underwrite new renewables in most states. Another pillar of the standards – copyright law – is yet to be settled, with AI developers refusing to train models here without law reform. A proposal to give the companies access to everything Australians create online by default sparked a wave of backlash from creatives, who say the companies could pay for local licensing deals to access Australian content. But Jenna Priestly, the assistant secretary at the attorney general’s department, on Friday confirmed looser copyright laws would also affect AI access to foreign-made content distributed in Australia. She said the companies wanted to train models on “maybe billions” of pieces of information and claimed it was practically “impossible” to make deals with every rights holder. “As Australia’s copyright framework protects not only copyright material that’s Australian in origin, but worldwide, I think it is a fairly large number that [companies] would need to go and strike deals with,” Priestly said. The Greens senator David Shoebridge, who is among those fighting calls for copyright reform and demanding a pause on AI development, on Friday said Labor had refused him a seat on the inquiry committee. Labor ministers have spent the week meeting with OpenAI’s vice-president, and Anthropic’s special envoy Jeff Bleich, who this week suggested Australia had just months to bring in effective regulation. The attorney general’s department told Friday’s hearing the shape and timing of any copyright reform was yet to be decided. But the prime minister’s department said Anthony Albanese wanted draft laws on the broader AI standards by the end of 2026. Australia’s chance for influence on and special access to the models could be at risk by a delay, Bradshaw said. “Decisions around training are a matter of urgency,” she said. “I think it is inevitable that those providers will look at other places to locate.”

title: ‘I spend a bagful of money and don’t fill a bag’: the energy crisis hits Bangladesh
summary: The country has been left in the dark as it endures power cuts caused by the Iran war and reliance on gas imports
text: At 1am, Halder’s alarm goes off and the 34-year-old Bangladeshi bank employee rises and heads to her kitchen. She is up at this time not for work but to cook for her family. An energy crisis paralysing the capital, Dhaka, a city of almost 40 million people, means this has become the only time when the piped gas supply is strong enough to allow cooking. The city now operates in darkness, as people try to continue their lives with power even in public areas shut off early in the evening to preserve energy. It is a crisis created by the US war on Iran but exacerbated by Bangladesh’s reliance on imported energy. It is also a challenge that a government elected only weeks before the war began has struggled to meet. “I don’t want anything extraordinary from the government; I want to turn on the stove and find gas, I want to switch on the light and find electricity, I want clean water from the tap,” says Halder. “These are not luxuries. “Some nights I’m sleeping three hours, sometimes less. Then I’m expected to be a mother, run a household and do a full day at the office as if everything is normal.” The Bangladesh Nationalist party government was elected in February, following protests in 2024 that overthrew the previous government of the Awami League, which had been in power for 15 years and was accused of political repression, corruption and economic mismanagement. After a period of interim government, the BNP was tasked with forging a new path for the country but within weeks, war had broken out in Iran and the closure of the strait of Hormuz meant crucial gas shipments from the Middle East were disrupted. The government responded by rationing energy, and ordered shops, markets and shopping centres to close by 8pm – an hour earlier than previously permitted. Illuminated billboards must be switched off by 7pm, with exemptions only for hospitals, pharmacies, food shops and emergency services. The situation is worse in rural Bangladesh, where in August people were going without electricity for up to 16 hours a day. National load-shedding, or cuts in output, exceeded 3,000MW during the worst of the shortage, according to government data. But it is in Dhaka, a city usually in constant motion, that the change appears most dramatic. Long stretches of roads in areas packed with offices, businesses and shops, such as Mohammadpur, Kawran Bazar and Dhanmondi, are now eerily dark. The crisis has forced local residents to make calculations constantly, such as when the gas might be strong enough to cook with, how long a fan can be run during the humid summer, and how long the queue might stretch at the petrol station. As a result, almost 3 million more people are expected to be facing food insecurity in the final months of this year, a rise of 18% from the summer figure of 15.3 million, according to the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification, a global malnutrition monitor. Ahmed, 50, who wished to give only his last name, runs an electrical workshop in the central area of Mohammadpur but lives in Keraniganj, on the outskirts of Dhaka, where housing is cheaper. A commute he managed for years now fills him with dread. Once Ahmed has closed his shop, transport is hard to find and more expensive, and he fears being mugged in streets now left in darkness. “By the time I close the shop, it is already dark,” he says. “Then you are thinking all the way home about whether someone will stop you, rob you or take your phone and money. “Sometimes I think I should just leave the country and try somewhere else,” he says. “But I am 50; I don’t have the money needed to go. So I think about it, and then I feel there is nowhere to go.” Daily gas demand in Bangladesh is about 107-113m cubic metres (3.8-4bn cubic ft), far outstripping the available supply of roughly 74m cubic metres. The country produces little energy domestically, so it is reliant on gas from the Middle East, which provides almost half of Bangladesh’s energy supply. The US war with Iran has hit Bangladesh’s liquid natural gas (LNG) imports particularly hard – between July and August, imports fell by 83%. The situation was made worse on 21 July, when a fire put one of Bangladesh’s two floating LNG terminals out of action, temporarily adding to disruptions that have forced factories to run costly generators, cut production or even close down, raising manufacturing and transport costs. Khondaker Golam Moazzem, research director at the Centre for Policy Dialogue, a Dhaka thinktank, says the disruption added to longstanding frailties in Bangladesh’s energy system, caused by mismanagement of public utilities. As well as leaving households struggling, energy-intensive sectors of the economy such as textiles, ceramics, glass and steel, transport, agriculture, fisheries and general commercial activity were all affected. “Almost all economic activities have been operating at significantly lower levels of their usable capacity because of the energy crisis,” Moazzem says. At Krishi vegetable market in Dhaka, 41-year-old Aleya Begum struggles to run her roadside stall selling tea and street food. It is her family’s main source of income and pays for her son’s education; she had also been saving for her daughter’s marriage. Begum says the price of vegetables has risen so much that she can afford barely enough for her family. “I used to be able to fill a bag with vegetables without spending very much,” she says. “Now I can spend a bagful of money and still not fill the bag.” She has cut back on fish and chicken, and has to think twice about whether she buys eggs. Begum does not pay much attention to statistics on lost megawatts of energy or debates over the extent to which the government inherited an economic crisis or if it was caused by events abroad. “Governments can say many things, but we look at the market,” she says. “If prices don’t come down and our lives don’t get easier, how are we supposed to understand that anything has changed? “I don’t need big promises,” she adds. “I need to be able to go to the market, feed my family and come home without worrying about how I will manage tomorrow.”

title: Weather tracker: Thunderstorms hit Spain as Japan braces for typhoon
summary: At least one person dead as stormy weather causes severe flooding in Barcelona and Valencia
text: Intense and slow-moving thunderstorms broke out on Wednesday afternoon across parts of eastern Spain, bringing some severe flooding and killing at least one person. Storms first struck over the Castilla-La Mancha region during the afternoon before passing over Spain’s east coast, becoming very slow-moving and continuing overnight. Torrential rainfall, strong winds and large hail were reported in Valencia and Barcelona, causing widespread flooding in both cities. Weather stations west of Barcelona recorded some of the highest totals with more than 100mm (4in) of rain falling in the space of a few hours, and locally 70mm in just 30 minutes in the early hours of Thursday morning. Cars and roads were submerged, and flights were cancelled across the region. Wednesday’s La Liga fixture between Levante and Athletic Club had to be postponed due to flooding at the Estadio Ciudad de Valencia. On Thursday rescuers found the body of a man near Olivella, west of Barcelona, after his car was swept away in the waters. Spain’s east coast is susceptible to extreme rainfall during the autumn months, as experienced in 2024, when devastating flash floods killed more than 200 people in Valencia. With the Mediterranean Sea reaching record temperatures, this is providing extra fuel and moisture to thunderstorms, making flooding more likely. In New Jersey in the US on Sunday, the Racefaster half marathon was disrupted due to extreme rainfall and a partly submerged course. Runners had to wade through chest-deep waters at times as 50mm-100mm of rain fell. Despite the flooding, 250 people managed to finish the race. Flooding was also reported to the north-east in Connecticut and Rhode Island, where up to 190mm of rain was recorded in a 36-hour period. Tropical Storm Dujuan, currently over the open west Pacific Ocean, will move north-west on a track towards Japan over the coming days. It is forecast to intensify into a category one typhoon on Friday. The joint typhoon warning centre is forecasting that Dujuan will skirt past the south-east coast of Japan, potentially affecting Tokyo and the surrounding areas.

title: ‘A man threatened to shoot me’: the abuse pushing UK councillors out of politics
summary: Exclusive: Survey finds 78% of councillors feel at risk in their roles, with 52% saying intimidation has risen in past year
text: Heather Williams has been shouted at in the street, received death threats, threats of sexual violence, and had dog faeces left on her doorstep. At one point, she didn’t leave her home alone for more than three months. It was not how she expected her life to be when she first ran to be a Conservative district councillor in South Cambridgeshire nine years ago. “It is very intimidating. I’ve had people threatening to rape me in my sleep, a man once threatened to shoot me,” said Williams, now opposition group leader on the council. “You do question whether you’re doing the right thing, what impact it is having on your family. Even my daughter has security protocols now.” Williams has installed extra security measures in her home including cameras, panic alarms and an app on her phone so she can be tracked if needed. She is not the only one – a new survey from the Local Government Association (LGA) found that over a third (35%) of councillors have made modifications to their home for security reasons. This includes CCTV cameras, alarms, installing electric gates, removing or sealing letterboxes, reinforcing doors and locks, carrying a rape alarm, getting a dog and putting up ‘Beware of the dog’ signs (despite not having a dog). Some have even moved house. The annual Debate Not Hate survey of more than 1,500 councillors across England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland showed over half (52%) believed abuse and intimidation had increased over the past year. It also found that women, ethnic minority and LGBTQ+ councillors were being disproportionately pushed out of politics due to the high levels of abuse and harassment. In total, 38% of women who were considering not standing again for election said they were doing so because of abuse and intimidation – for men, the figure was 23%. Among ethnic minority respondents, 43% said abuse had influenced their decision to not stand again, compared with 28% of white respondents. For LGBTQ+ councillors, the figure stood at 41%. Hannah Dalton, a councillor and LGA civility in public life ambassador, said the findings showed that abuse was “a direct threat to the strength, diversity and health of our democracy”. “We must never accept a situation where harassment and personal attacks are simply regarded as part of public service,” she said. “It is deeply alarming that most councillors believe the problem is getting worse. This toxic culture is not only affecting those currently in office, it is deterring talented and committed people from standing for election in the first place. The majority of respondents (78%) said they felt at personal risk fulfilling their roles as councillors, with the figure rising to 85% for female, ethnic minority, LGBT+ or disabled councillors. A quarter of councillors said they had received threats of violence, and 7% had received a death threat. In response to the growing wave of personal attacks levelled at councillors, they are no longer required to publish their home address on council websites. Each police force also now has at least one force elected official adviser dedicated to dealing with security concerns for politicians. But the LGA said it was not enough, and it wanted the government, police and social media platforms to do more, with “formal arrangements” on tackling such abuse.

title: Japan raises interest rates to 31-year high to curb impact of rising prices
summary: Increase from 1% to 1.25% follows US Federal Reserve and European Central Bank tightening monetary policy
text: Japan’s central bank has increased interest rates to a fresh 31-year high as it attempts to combat global inflation linked to the war in Iran. The Bank of Japan (BoJ) voted to raise its target interest rate from 1% to 1.25%, the highest level since 1995. The move meant the BoJ joined the US Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank in tightening monetary policy this month, as central banks attempt to curb the impact of rising prices, linked to the conflict in the Middle East. The Bank of England on Thursday voted to leave UK interest rates on hold at 3.75% but warned they could soon rise amid the fallout from the Iran war. The BoJ policy committee’s vote to raise rates was not unanimous – with two of the nine board members dissenting against the increase. Kazuo Ueda, the governor of the BoJ, would not rule out the possibility of back-to-back rate rises by the bank’s policy committee. “That depends on how price conditions develop,” he said. “There could be various possibilities. We shouldn’t rule anything out. We’re at a phase where we need to look at various data carefully. But that doesn’t mean we can move slowly. We will analyse data carefully and take timely action as needed.” The BoJ’s policy committee meets eight times a year, roughly once every six weeks, and Ueda said there is no set plan for the timing of any future potential increases in the rate. “As for the pace of future rate hikes, we don’t have any pre-set idea in mind such as once every three months,” he said. “We will determine at each policy meeting how best to ensure underlying inflation stabilises ‌at 2%.” Ueda said the BoJ has changed its policy of trying to boost inflation in the economy to focusing on ensuring it does not go above its target of 2%. In August the rate of inflation in Japan was 1.9%. “Up until now, our short-term ‌policy focus was to push up underlying inflation from levels below 2%,” he said. “Now, underlying inflation is approaching 2%. If risks of underlying inflation overshooting 2% materialise, that could have a negative impact on Japan’s economy. It’s important to stabilise underlying inflation at 2%.” The BoJ has been raising rates since 2024, when it lifted its base rate out of negative territory. It has been under pressure to raise borrowing costs as the yen weakened steadily against the dollar this year. The Japanese currency weakened more than 1% against the dollar on Friday. Earlier this month, Scott Bessent, the US Treasury secretary, warned currency traders not to bet against the yen, after an intervention by the US and Japan at the end of July to stabilise the weakening Japanese currency. “I have asymmetric information. I am the house now,” Bessent said, adding that he had “pretty good insight” into what Japanese policymakers were going to do. “You can bet against me if you want.” In late July the US Treasury moved to sell at least $10bn in euros, without informing the European Central Bank, to buy yen to arrest its slide to a 40-year low. Fred Neumann, the chief Asia economist at HSBC, said: “The tone of the [BoJ] statement, along with two dissenters for the decision to raise rates, leaves lingering doubts that Japan’s central bank will be cautious in tightening monetary policy further. “While back-to-back hikes appear unlikely, investors will look for clues as to whether officials are prepared to raise interest rates again in December.” The drop in the yen helped the Nikkei stock market index to rise nearly 2%, while the Japanese two-year government ‌bond yields, which are most sensitive to ‌monetary policy expectations, fell four basis points to 1.82%. European stock markets were down 0.5% on Friday after the BoJ’s decision. Prashant Newnaha, a senior rates strategist at TD Securities, said the BoJ reiterated its concerns that underlying inflation could deviate upwards from its 2% target, but “we don’t see a smoking gun supporting a back-to-back hike ‌in October”. He said: “We stick with our call for rate hikes roughly every quarter with the next 25 basis points hike in December.” Hopes of alternative ways for oil supply from the Middle East to reach markets pushed Brent crude futures down as much as 1.5% to $103.29 a barrel even as concerns about strikes between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthis lingered. Reuters contributed to this report

title: ‘Outright racist’ Daniel Thomas will face full force of law over any crimes, says home secretary
summary: Shabana Mahmood says she wants to distinguish between far-right extremism and legitimate local concerns over asylum sites
text: Shabana Mahmood has described the anti-asylum activist Daniel Thomas as “a far-right and outright racist” who will feel “the full force of the law” if his organisation commits crimes near contested asylum sites such as Piddington. In an interview with the Guardian, the home secretary also “wanted to reassure” concerned villagers that asylum seekers due to move in to a neighbouring former defence site would not put pressure on local resources because they would be given self-contained facilities. Her intervention came after Thomas, a convicted criminal known as Danny Tommo and the co-founder of the Patriot Platform, said thousands of his masked followers could descend “for days” on to the Oxfordshire village to prevent male asylum seekers being moved in. At the launch of a crackdown on knife crime in Birmingham on Thursday, Mahmood said she wanted to distinguish between legitimate concerns felt by Piddington residents over a large-scale asylum centre and extremists who were “hijacking” community concerns. “I understand the anxiety of local people when they’re about to see a change to their community. But it is important to distinguish that anxiety, where reasonable people can have a conversation, and the far right and outright racists like Danny Thomas walking into town, hijacking an issue and then using that to divide our communities,” she said. “Their behaviour is completely unacceptable. And where they break the law, they will face the full force of the law.” Piddington’s local population registered their opposition to the proposed asylum facility on Wednesday, voting by 285 votes against 26 in a symbolic ballot to leave the UK and seek self-determination. The parish has been approached by hundreds of other town and village councillors and residents for advice on replicating the independence referendum campaign. The village’s opposition to the proposed asylum facility is backed by the Conservatives, Reform UK and the Liberal Democrats. [*See footnote]. Thomas visited Piddington the day after the vote. He was dressed in a grey suit and white shirt and was not accompanied by people wearing balaclavas. Joe Marshall, a parish councillor, said it was a private visit and Thomas was due to be given a tour of the village and a cup of tea by a resident. “It is a closed meeting. We will engage with them and walk them around the village and have a cup of tea,” he said. “We have also had an open invitation to Reform, Labour, Conservatives and Restore to visit.” Marshall said it was not clear that villagers would want security assistance from men in balaclavas, if it were offered. Thomas visited the village hall briefly and later visited the entrance to the Ministry of Justice camp where the asylum seekers are scheduled to be housed. In an interview broadcast on YouTube with Dan Wootton, he said he had spoken to three residents. “The people we are meeting are just normal mothers, normal grandmothers, normal men,” Thomas said. “We have to start somewhere. Right now there are no men in that camp. We are going to put a legal, lawful plan in place to help this community in a way that has never been done before.” Asked how she would respond to Piddington residents after the vote, Mahmood said: “I want to reassure the residents of Piddington that actually our experience from other large sites where we already have, asylum seekers accommodated, whether that’s in Wethersfield or Crowborough, is that putting all facilities on to one site is actually the best way to manage pressures for local communities. “Our experience of other large sites where we are housing asylum seekers is that we’re able to put on that site more of the facilities that asylum seekers need. It’s a relatively self-contained facility, and the knock-on pressure to those local areas, I don’t think we’re going to see.” Mahmood said she understood the anxiety of people in the countryside towards large groups of asylum seekers, but she pointed out that many people in inner-city areas such as her Birmingham constituency had similar concerns. “I do understand the anxiety that people feel, when they’re about to see a change in their community or they are reading misinformation on the internet, or when they’re just concerned that a village is about to have a facility nearby that maybe they think may pose them some challenges,” she said. “I also hear that concern from communities such as mine, where there are large numbers of HMOs [houses of multiple occupation] and accommodation in which asylum seekers are held as well. There is concern across every type of community. Not just in the countryside or in those sorts of areas, but in inner-city areas as well.” Thomas and his supporters recently coordinated disruptive protests in Dover and Portsmouth, where masked supporters blocked roads and attempted to intercept newly arrived people. On Thursday, Mahmood summoned police chiefs and urged them to improve their intelligence gathering and use all powers at their disposal, including new laws that allow for a blanket ban on face coverings at a designated location. Hampshire police then sought to impose the ban on Saturday as an anti-asylum demonstration took place in Thomas’s home town of Portsmouth. Thomas urged his supporters to stay away. A former bodyguard for Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, also known as Tommy Robinson, Thomas established his anti-immigration movement after serving a prison sentence for attempted kidnapping. In an interview with Robinson, broadcast on Friday night, he said: “How powerful would it be if 5,000 men … surround the [Piddington] camp. We take tents. We sit there for days and we don’t let them [the asylum seekers] get in. And then we reinforce [the blockade] with members from the north, from Scotland, from Ireland.” In the interview, Thomas said he was not racist and welcomed people of other nationalities into his organisation. “Racism within our organisation is just not acceptable. That is the stance we have. We are not a white nationalist movement. I have friends that are black.” Thomas has been approached for comment. Mahmood made her comments as she launched an anti-knife crime programme. More than 230 areas affected by knife crime will share £26.25m to pay for police patrols, CCTV and early-prevention work as part of a knife-crime crackdown across 27 police forces in England and Wales. Each area, roughly the size of 10 football pitches, will receive more police patrols, alongside programmes designed for young people most at risk of being a victim or a perpetrator of knife crime. Action in small, targeted areas was the most effective way of driving down knife crime, the Home Office said. Mahmood launched the initiative at the Acocks Green boxing gym in south Birmingham, which plays a role in the local area in supporting vulnerable young people to stay away from crime. She was joined by the anti-knife campaigners Lynne Baird, Lorraine Jones Burrell and Pooja Kanda. Each has lost a child to knife crime. Additional reporting by Amelia Gentleman • This article was amended on 20 September 2026. An earlier version, referring to the Piddington village independence referendum, said “the campaign” was “backed by the Conservatives, Reform UK and the Liberal Democrats.” To clarify: it is the village’s opposition to the proposed asylum facility that is backed by the Conservatives, Reform UK and the Liberal Democrats.

title: Revealed: how Russia uses mobile ‘super-app’ Max to spy on its citizens
summary: Research shows tens of millions of people are being forced to use platform that amounts to ‘backdoor’ on their device
text: Over the past 18 months, tens of millions of Russians have been forced to install a new app on their phones – a violet-blue button designed for messaging and payments, called Max. Authorities have touted it as a patriotic alternative to Telegram and WhatsApp; Russian glitterati have promoted it in rap videos and comic routines. This summer, it became the country’s most-used messaging app. It is a product of VKontakte, the Russian social media company, which is deeply entangled with the Russian state. The Russian president, Vladimir Putin, reportedly owns an indirect stake in Max. Max is Russia’s version of a “super-app,” combining an ecosystem of services into a single platform. It is a container for a number of “mini-apps” that now facilitate everyday life in Russia – banking apps, a messaging service that aims to replace Telegram, and apps for essential government services. The best-known super-app in the world is WeChat, China’s everything platform which facilitates the state’s social controls. But while WeChat was developed over decades, in step with China’s other internet controls, Max has been imposed on a population that once had mostly-free internet access. Now, forensic research has revealed a fuller picture of Max’s powerful surveillance capabilities. These amount to a “backdoor” into its entire mini-app ecosystem on every user’s device, said Roya Ensafi, an associate professor of computer science at the University of Michigan. “We have studied Russia’s escalation of internet control for the past decade,” said Ensafi. “What Max provides is the cleverest and also the scariest tactic by authoritarian governments” to surveil their citizens. Max is “a blueprint any government can follow” towards digital authoritarianism, said Ensafi. It represents the cutting edge of what governments such as Iran, Kazakhstan and India may soon try to achieve. Ensafi’s team were able to download the version of the app used in Russia. They found that Max can screenshot users’ devices – and the contents of its mini-apps – without their knowledge. It can access all the information stored in these mini-apps, their messages and payments. It can impersonate its users without them knowing. It can even inject code into mini-apps – which would mean, said Ensafi, that the Russian government could use Max to launch cyberattacks. Their research adds new clarity into an ongoing debate on Max’s surveillance capabilities. Crucially, said Ensafi, it cannot break into apps like Telegram and WhatsApp, if users have these installed. However, Russia has banned both. Many Russians working in or around state institutions have in effect been forced to use Max. Officials and public-sector employees, university students, teachers and even schoolchildren have all faced pressure to move their communications on to the platform. One schoolteacher in Moscow said staff at their school were ordered to switch to Max after instructions from the city authorities. “The school director called us in last March and told us directly: from now on, everything is on Max. That included chats with parents, sending out homework and other school communication,” the teacher said. “There isn’t really an option to say no, so in the end you just use the app,” they added. Daniil, a university student in St Petersburg, said he reluctantly downloaded Max shortly before the start of the academic year after being told students would be denied access to university buildings or dormitories without a QR code generated through the app. He said he had concerns about the app’s security and privacy, but felt he had little choice if he wanted to continue accessing campus. Among Russia’s elite, use of Max often appears to be largely performative, with Telegram and Signal still widely used for day-to-day communication, according to several well-connected figures and prominent businesspeople. One person in the Kremlin’s inner circle said he and several friends had bought second phones solely to install Max, while continuing to use their main devices and preferred messaging apps as before. “It’s all for show. No one in politics really uses it,” the person said, speaking on condition of anonymity. Max has yet to replace Telegram as a major source of news for Russians. Public channels – used by media outlets, bloggers and officials to broadcast news and commentary to large audiences – remain far less developed on Max, where only a small number have built audiences comparable to the biggest channels on Telegram. Several Max users contacted by the Guardian said the app closely resembles Telegram, long Russia’s most popular messaging platform, in its design and functionality, but concerns about privacy and surveillance were widespread. “Using Max feels like you never quite know who else might be watching,” said Nikolai, a 34-year-old consultant in Moscow. While the app looked modern and slick, Nikolai said there was always something slightly sinister about using it. “You end up using it more and more because the alternatives are becoming harder to access. But it still doesn’t feel right.” Russia’s success in rapidly pushing out Max should be a “wake-up call”, said Ensafi. China reached its current state of digital authoritarianism over the course of 35 years. But Russia has imposed these sweeping restrictions – shepherding people on to a state-controlled internet – in just a decade. “The world is changing, the infrastructure of private communication is changing – and the assault by authoritarian governments is very aggressive,” she said. Max and VKontakte were approached for comment.

title: The world’s rivers are at breaking point. Can we save them before it is too late?
summary: In this week’s newsletter: As the Guardian launches a year-long project, Our Rivers, we take stock of the issues facing waterways around the world
text: The nicknames of the world’s biggest rivers give a sense of how we feel about them: “the great river”, “the river that swallows all rivers”, “Mother Ganga” and “Old father Thames”. They feed and water us, and many other animal species. They carry our trade but also give us cool relief on a hot day. They’re nerve endings, elders and sources of comfort, but also of awe and respect. And yet many of the world’s rivers are suffering, hit by multiple environmental challenges. A new report out today from the World Meteorological Organization finds that rivers across the world experienced one of the driest years in more than three decades during 2025. We’ve been focused on water issues for many years, but with Our rivers, a new project that launches this week, the Guardian will spend the next year taking a closer look at the world’s rivers, in good health and bad. In this week’s newsletter, I wanted to talk about what we’ll cover – but first, this week’s climate headlines. Essential reads Climate crisis probably weakened glacier that caused devastating Nepal-Tibet floods, first study finds Who are the 514 people accused of starting French wildfires and what motivates them? Benedict Cumberbatch on his Earth-saving eco film: ‘We are in the last grab of the extraction era’ In focus With Our rivers, we want to dig deeper into the effects our changing climate. Drought is already hitting river systems such as the Amazon and La Plata in Latin America, but there are also challenges from the new timetables of our melting glaciers, and shifting rain patterns. The Ganges and the Brahmaputra in India have both suffered from the changes to the annual monsoon season. Even the mighty Congo River in Africa, the world’s deepest river (it crosses the equator twice!) has been hit by the climate crisis, drying up, slowly, for the last few decades, due to less rain, a weakening of the Walker circulation and an increase in sea surface temperature in the central eastern tropical atlantic ocean. But we also want to explore other human impacts. Most of our rivers are now heavily engineered from their source to their outflow into the sea. Political battles are being fought over how that water should be distributed, both between neighbouring states in the case of the Colorado and, in some cases, between countries, such as Egypt and Ethiopia, which have only recently settled a long diplomatic standoff over the division of the Nile. In some cases, such as the Mississippi River system, our rivers have arguably been over-engineered, with authorities zigzagging over ways to remedy problems they created; the mouth of the river was dug out to improve access but residents are now struggling to cope with the incursion of the ocean. We’ve put our rivers under tight control but now, in many places, local authorities are seeking to free them up again. China has put huge amounts of money into rebuilding the Yangtze, and is seeing the results: the doubling of fish biomass and rebounding of endangered species shows that the government measures are starting to work, according to biologists. The problem of pollution and sewage is a familiar one, but does not become less enraging with familiarity. Over the years, including in Down to Earth, we have reported on huge amounts of sewage being dumped into UK rivers and, in some places, local communities are now stepping in to try to take back control, in a way that central government seems, so far, unwilling to do. But the UK is not the only country that has poisoned its rivers; the Reconquista River in in Buenos Aires is Argentina’s second most contaminated river (after the Riachuelo). Scientists have recently created an “organic” solution for the pollution and our reporters have gone there this week to speak to communities around the river about the way forward. Over the next year we’ll explore these stories with this project, and look at our sense of ownership of our rivers, the love and passion that people feel for them. We always want to hear from our readers across the globe, so please do let us know what you think by replying to this email or getting in touch on downtoearth@theguardian.com. • To read the complete version of this newsletter – subscribe to receive Down to Earth in your inbox every Thursday.

title: Former Labour deputy leader Tom Watson joins Palantir
summary: Peer takes full-time position at the controversial company as it fends off pressure from both Andy Burnham’s government and Sadiq Khan
text: Another former government minister has been hired by a controversial US AI company, this time Palantir, which has appointed Andy Burnham’s former ministerial colleague Tom Watson. The Labour peer and former deputy leader will operate alongside Palantir’s UK and Europe chief executive, Louis Mosley, as the company attempts to fend off pressure on Burnham’s government to axe its £330m NHS contract. It is also fighting Sadiq Khan in court over the Labour London mayor’s block on a £50m contract to use its AI in Metropolitan police investigations. Palantir also wants to win more public sector work in the UK, where it already has an annual turnover of £427m. The company was co-founded by the Trump-supporting billionaire Peter Thiel and provides AI-powered software to the Israeli military and the White House’s ICE immigration crackdown, leading to a public and political backlash against its deepening involvement in British public services. Alex Karp, its chief executive, said: “This is just the latest chapter of Tom’s forty-year fight for better public services. We are fortunate to have him guide us as we help the British government to deliver for the British public.” His job will be, in part, to “deepen the social and economic value its work creates through better British public services, jobs and skills”, Palantir said. Since stepping down from parliament in 2019, Watson has been an adviser to the gambling and music industries and, since 2024, he has been a part-time adviser to Palantir, including accompanying Mosley at Labour party conferences. He was a defence minister and a minister for digital engagement in Gordon Brown’s government. Palantir has a £240m contract with the Ministry of Defence. The move is just the latest example of a revolving door between British politics and big tech. After the former deputy prime minister Nick Clegg spent nearly seven years earning millions working for Mark Zuckerberg at Meta, the former prime minister Rishi Sunak last year took jobs with Anthropic and Microsoft and the former chancellor George Osborne started working for OpenAI. Keir Starmer’s AI adviser, Matt Clifford, also joined Anthropic this month. He tried to retain the chair of a government science and tech research body, but quit under pressure over conflicts of interest. “The revolving door is proving very fruitful for big tech,” said Tom Brake, the chief executive of Unlock Democracy, a not-for-profit campaign group. “The only surefire way to stop tech companies benefiting from privileged information acquired by ministers or senior civil servants is to introduce an enforceable five-year ban on taking up industry posts.” Watson said he was “terrifically excited” by the new role as Palantir’s senior vice-president and highlighted two of the contracts that are in dispute when he said he wanted to help Palantir speed up NHS diagnosis, treatment and discharge from hospitals and enable “our police to crack crimes and root out corruption”. Palantir said Watson had taken a leave of absence from the House of Lords and had relinquished his parliamentary pass while working for Palantir in London.

title: Friday briefing: After two months as PM, is Andy Burnham passing his own test?
summary: In today’s newsletter: The Labour leader said he would assess his success by how his policies affected his constituency. From the cost of living to immigration, we look at how Makerfield voters feel about their MP’s choices
text: Good morning. Remember the Makerfield test? When Andy Burnham was elected as an MP back in June, he reassured wary voters that the constituency was not a “stepping stone” (to be fair, it was a bit) but a “touchstone”. He meant that the policies his government devised would have to matter on the high streets of Ashton and Hindley Green. “A Makerfield test at the heart of British politics will make sure that the places Westminster has neglected will now get fairness,” he said. As the Commons breaks for the jamboree of high ideas, low gossip and crap karaoke that is party conference season, it’s a good moment to ask how Burnham’s early decisions as prime minister – he’s been at it under two months, right enough – meet that test and what it tells us about his government. I spoke to someone who, since that byelection, has immersed himself in the opinions of Makerfield voters, and those living in constituencies like it, Luke Tryl, UK director of the research agency More in Common. But first the headlines. Five big stories UK news | Shabana Mahmood has described the anti-asylum activist Daniel Thomas as “a far-right and outright racist” who will feel “the full force of the law” if his organisation commits crimes near contested asylum sites such as Piddington. Russia | Russians are going to the polls to elect a new State Duma in a tightly controlled vote stripped of meaningful competition and with little doubt about the result. UK politics | Andy Burnham is under further pressure to take control of ailing Thames Water from a cross-party group of MPs who are calling for ministers to break off talks with the US hedge funds who are effectively running the company. Royal family | The brother of the late Diana, Princess of Wales, has claimed in published extracts of his new memoir that King Charles sounded “giddily elated – like a lottery winner” in a phone call to him immediately after her death. Nature | A diminutive wild cat that inhabits Bolivia’s ⁠cloud forest has been identified as a previously unknown species, marking the first time a new living feline species has been formally named and described in more than a century. In depth: ‘The top thing for people in Makerfield was that life was a struggle’ “Who cares what Makerfield man or woman thinks? I’m a Holborn and St Pancras via Caerphilly gal myself,” you might be muttering into your overnight oats. But here’s why it matters: Makerfield, like dozens of similar post-industrial seats in the north of England, is the sort of seat Labour used to win so easily they could put up a ham sandwich as a candidate. Things have since changed. The area voted to leave by 65% in the Brexit referendum, and in the May council elections, Reform won all eight council wards in the constituency with about 50% of the vote. In his byelection dispatches from Makerfield, Luke Tryl found a pervasive sense of being left behind and forgotten – despite being “at the centre of the universe”, as one constituent put it, for one frantic month of campaigning. According to the voters Tryl spoke to, the Makerfield test should consist of three elements: Burnham showing that he “gets it”; a record of delivery; and a national plan to address the issues that Makerfield residents share with people across the country. So how has Burnham fared on some of the early challenges he’s faced? Cost of living measures “The top thing we heard in Makerfield was a sense that too much of life was a struggle,” Tryl tells me. And More in Common’s polling has found that, so far, Burnham’s early cost of living measures are very popular across the country: 86% of Britons had heard about the bus fare cap, seven in 10 thought it reflected well on the government; about 8 in 10 had heard about the VAT cut on household electricity bills (amounting to an average of about £45 a year per household), and 67% said that it landed well. Voters in Makerfield-like areas are realistic, says Tryl: “They say: ‘£45 is not going to change my life’, but they see it as a statement of intent”. People who are slightly more engaged with politics specifically mention the budget as a test point: earlier this week Burnham warned of “difficult choices” ahead. The cut-through of these measures to voters is striking: “Part of it is just the ubiquity of Andy Burnham,” says Tryl. Most recent More in Common polling shows people are more likely to have seen him on social media than any of the other party leaders. A fifth of Britons (22%) have seen “Cool Dad” Burnham on social media in the past week, compared to 20% for Reform leader Nigel Farage. I’m fascinated to see that for under-25s that rises to 35%, compared with 13% for Green leader Zack Polanski, who is often touted as catnip for younger voters. Immigration More in Common polling in June estimated that 62% of Makerfield residents consider immigration to be a top issue, making it one of the most concerned constituencies in the country about that issue. Here, Burnham gets a mixed review. The idea of taking in refugees through capped, controlled routes is popular in Makerfield, where voters worry over a lack of control. That’s why Tryl argues that one policy that really does pass the Makerfield test is the community sponsorship scheme, part of Shabana Mahmood’s controversial asylum reforms. But while Burnham has won back Labour-Green switchers over the summer, he’s not been so successful with Labour to Reform defectors – and Tryl believes that’s because he has yet to move the dial on migration. Take, for example, the shift in people’s perceptions: 52% of Britons now cite concern that local women and girls would be at risk of sexual violence as the top reason why they’d oppose asylum accommodation in their area (previously, they were more likely to refer to pressure on services). In socially conservative areas such as Makerfield, voters feel this “much more strongly”. “I think this is an achilles heel”, says Tryl. Prisoner release It’s not just constituencies such as Makerfield where voters think the criminal justice system isn’t tough enough: across the country, nearly two-thirds of Britons think prison sentences are too lenient. “The case of Andrew Harper outrages people across the board,” Tryl tells me, “but particularly in somewhere like Makerfield.” So Burnham played a bad hand well, by explaining the competing priorities to the public, and taking time to examine options before finding a partial solution. “Taking the public on that journey – especially in Makerfield where people are very distrustful of politicians – was important,” says Tryl. Climate Burnham, who is now facing intense pressure over whether to approve oil and gasfields in the North Sea, wrote in the Guardian yesterday that the UK must fully commit to reaching net zero by 2050. While Labour-Reform switchers in places like Makerfield are often deeply worried about climate change, there’s also concern that net zero policies will unfairly punish ordinary people. For many, the issue of climate change falls below more pressing daily concerns like the cost of living crisis. In this context, More in Common’s polling suggests the main test for Britain’s energy policies will be whether they can lower household bills. Party donations Tryl’s fieldwork has found that the public aren’t deeply engrossed in the minutiae of donations limits, although they do want the system to be fair. So Burnham’s early failure to support a domestic cap on donations is unlikely to be a decisive factor when constituents in Makerfield next head to the ballot box. But for the recipient of those crypto-millions, the damage has been done: more than one in three voters now name Farage’s “sleaziness and corruption” as a barrier to them voting Reform. Rather than the party’s core voters, who seem unmoved by the continuing financial scandals, it is Labour-Reform switchers in seats such as Makerfield whose faith has been shaken. But Tryl cautions against over-stressing the issue. “At the next election, if the status quo on cost of living, core public services, andimmigration still feels pretty bad, I don’t think donations in themselves will be an issue” he says. We want to hear from you What do you want to know about the US midterms, and how the Guardian plans to report them? I’ll be putting your questions to our Washington bureau in the coming weeks, so send them in by hitting reply or emailing first.edition@theguardian.com What else we’ve been enjoying I loved our pics gallery of eastern Europe’s socialist hotels, which I hadn’t read about until now. Poppy Noor, newsletters team Cracker of a You be the judge this week: Ayaan lent her brother Ahmed some money thinking it was for something important … then he spent it on a holiday. But does it matter what he did with the cash? Charlie Lindlar, newsletters team I found Zoe Williams’s interview with academic/author/policymaker Camilla Cavendish, on all the reasons we’ve stopped having babies, utterly fascinating. Poppy In case you missed it, make sure you read this viral essay from The Cut (£) on friendless husbands and the wives who try desperately to build social lives for them. Charlie The photos in our piece on the Tate’s Edward Enninful-curated show, c, about how the 90s art and fashion changed British culture, are beautiful and nostalgic.
