title: ‘Run! Get away!’: witnesses recount Israeli ‘double tap’ strike that killed child and medic in Gaza
summary: When Mohammad Abdul Zinati, 15, rushed to help a man wounded in a bomb attack, he had no time to react before he too was hit
text: Mohammad Abdul Zinati was walking home from school through the rubble of Salah Khalaf Street, in northern Gaza City, when he stopped at a supermarket where a group of classmates and friends had gathered. Shortly before 3:30pm, an explosion tore through the air. Along with several others, Mohammad rushed into the street to see what had happened. When the smoke and dust cleared, they saw a man lying bleeding on the dusty road. He was badly wounded, but still alive. The man was calling for help, and Mohammad ran towards him. He did not hear the shouts of his cousin, who had spotted an approaching Israeli drone. Within seconds, the drone released a glide bomb, designed to allow operators to identify and strike targets with a high degree of accuracy. The munition plunged towards the street, detonating just metres from the teenager. Mohammad did not have time to react before a second blast killed him. The Guardian verified footage of the attack, and spoke to witnesses and weapons experts in an effort to shed light on the latest Israeli strike to kill a child in Gaza. “We heard a loud explosion and tried to make our way to the scene to find out what had happened,” said Tamer Lubbad, a witness who filmed the attack. “We found a man lying on the ground. He was still alive and calling for help.” The man injured in the initial strike was later identified by Gaza’s civil defense as the paramedic Sharif Shadi Labad. The Israeli military said that Labad was targeted because he was a Hamas militant. Several other civilians approached Labad, as he lay injured in the street. Among them was Mohammad Zinati’s cousin, Mohammed Rajeh Zinati, 26. “I ran from the house towards the street to find out what had happened,” he said. “On my way, I saw my cousin coming out of the supermarket. He was running towards the site of the strike. I started shouting at him: ‘Mohammad, stop!’ but he didn’t hear me and kept going. Then I saw a drone in the sky. “I started shouting: ‘Run! Get away!’ At that moment, Mohammad had reached the injured man. As soon as he got there, the drone struck him.” “Mohammad was hit directly in the chest and abdomen and was killed almost instantly. I couldn’t do anything to rescue him,” said Zinati. Video filmed later showed Mohammad’s body lying under a white shroud outside al-Shifa hospital after the attack, as his father bid him an emotional farewell, reciting verses from the Qur’an. People who knew Mohammad said he was a much-loved figure in the neighbourhood. “He was a kind, helpful, polite and respectful boy,” his cousin said. ‘‘He would help elderly to collect water from the water trucks. When he was killed, people from the neighbourhood came out into the street, crying for him.” The IDF has repeatedly rejected allegations that it deliberately targets civilians, saying it assesses and takes into account the risk of civilian harm when carrying out strikes. However, weapons experts who reviewed the video said the teenager’s death may have been avoidable. ‘‘The bomb that is visible before impact is a Mikholit, which is deployed by Israeli unmanned vehicles (UAVs) or drones, said Trevor Ball, a drones expert and weapons technical analyst with Armament Research Services (ARES). ‘‘These UAVs have high-quality cameras that would have been able to see the teenager and the man approaching the body. Some variants of the Mikholit at least are capable of being redirected to a different target/point while in flight.’’ The strike that killed the teenager and the paramedic appears to fit the pattern commonly described as a “double-tap” attack: an initial strike followed by a second on the same location after rescuers or bystanders have arrived to help the wounded. In a statement to the Guardian, the Israeli military said Sharif Shadi Ibrahim Labad was a Hamas terrorist who belonged to the elite Nukhba forces. The IDF stated that Labad had participated in the 7 October attacks in 2023 at the Erez border crossing and was targeted because he was planning new operations. Asked why the second attack went ahead when its target was visibly a minor, the military did not respond, but said it ‘‘is aware of reports indicating that an uninvolved individual was harmed as a result of the strike targeting the terrorist, regrets any harm to uninvolved individuals and makes every effort to minimise such harm”. The Israeli military said the incident was under review. On Tuesday, medical sources in Gaza reported an Israeli strike on al-Bureij refugee camp that killed an adult and a five-year-old child, identified as Udai al-Muridi. A pregnant Palestinian woman died on Saturday from injuries sustained after being shot in the head by Israeli forces south of Khan Younis, according to her family and medical workers. The woman, named as Iman Shalouf, 27, who was nearly eight months pregnant, was sitting inside her family’s tent in the Mawasi area when Israeli gunfire struck her, according to paramedics and witnesses. The Israeli military said it had no information about the killing of the pregnant woman. According to Unicef, several other children have been killed in Israeli attacks on Gaza in recent days, including two sisters aged six and 12, who were killed with their parents in an airstrike on Beit Lahia while they slept, and three other girls aged, three, eight and nine, who were killed by gunfire. According to the territory’s health ministry, 1,369 Palestinians have been killed and 4,627 wounded since the fragile ceasefire took effect on 11 October 2025. Since Israel’s war in Gaza began on 7 October 2023, at least 73,783 Palestinians have been killed and 174,738 wounded, according to health officials. • This article was amended on 23 September 2026 Trevor Ball is a weapons technical analyst with Armament Research Services, not a a conflict researcher and trainer at Bellingcat, as an earlier version said.

title: Improved air quality linked to better mental development in toddlers, study finds
summary: Long-term research in New York shows efforts to reduce air pollution associated with higher cognitive test scores
text: Improvements in air pollution are leading to brighter, smarter toddlers, according to a new study from Columbia University in New York. For more than two decades, Prof Frederica Perera and a team from the Columbia Center for Children’s Environmental Health measured the air pollution exposure of pregnant women and the development of their children in the disadvantaged communities of northern Manhattan and the South Bronx. More than 1,100 children were assessed when they were one, two and three years old. Perera said: “We tested cognitive processing including memory and sensory perception, problem-solving such as matching shapes, stacking blocks and communication, both speech and language comprehension. In the early years of the study, we reported significant associations between prenatal exposure to air pollution and neurodevelopment effects in the children. That was bad news.” Over the course of the study, air pollution in central New York improved massively. Clean-air legislation reduced some pollutants from the city’s yellow taxis by as much as 80%. Heavy fuel oils are being phased out for heating the city’s buildings and cleaner fuels are being used in the city’s buses. Fine particle pollution and levels of nitrogen dioxide halved between 1998 and 2016. Perera continued: “Would we see an association between improved air quality and improved mental development scores in the toddlers over time?” The good news is that the toddlers’ scores improved as the air pollution improved. This was especially clear when the children were two and three years old, and during times of sharper falls in air pollution. The researchers were also able to take into account the effects of other factors that may have affected the children’s development. These included rapid declines in the proportion of children who lived with a tobacco smoker, which fell from 34% to 18%, and increases in maternal education, with a nine percentage-point increase in the proportion of mothers who had successfully graduated from high school. The New York study adds to the growing evidence that air pollution is a fixable problem and that health improves when air pollution is reduced. In the UK, the introduction of London’s ultra-low emission zone was accompanied by an improvement in children’s lung health and fewer children with clinically impaired lung function. For adults in central London, there was a 3% reduction in annual trends for emergency admissions, including an 8% reduction for heart problems and a 6% reduction for breathing problems. A reduction of about 25% in GP visits for heart and breathing problems followed the implementation of a clean-air zone in Bradford, West Yorkshire. Despite the improvements in New York, Perera emphasised: “We cannot conclude that contemporary levels of air pollution are safe for the neurodevelopment of all children.” Action on air pollution requires bold political leadership. It is often controversial and can be made into a divisive political issue, but it can work. Perera said: “We need more studies such as ours to increase public awareness of the value of clean air and climate policies and motivate policymakers.” A recent report by the UN Environment programme found that integrated action on air pollution and climate change emissions makes economic sense too, with an average return of $15 in economic benefits for every $1 invested.

title: MPs urge ministers to break off Thames Water talks with US hedge funds
summary: Efra committee calls for emergency legislation enabling government to take public control of the company
text: Andy Burnham is under further pressure to take control of ailing Thames Water from a cross-party group of MPs who are calling for ministers to break off talks with the US hedge funds who are effectively running the company. Adding their voices to demands that the prime minister takes public control of the company, which has debts of £20bn and is being controlled by a group of 100 hedge funds and distressed-debt investors, the MPs said in a report that ministers should consider emergency legislation to take control of its financial affairs to stabilise the company. Alistair Carmichael, the chair of the environment, food and rural affairs committee (Efra), said it was unbelievable that the special administration regime (SAR) for insolvent or failing water companies could not be triggered for Thames Water on performance grounds alone. Angela Eagle, the environment secretary, has suggested that an SAR – effectively temporary public control – cannot be triggered under the current law because of the way the US hedge funds that bought Thames Water’s debt have kept it running while seeking a deal to renegotiate its liabilities. The report said Ofwat and the government should withdraw from negotiating with the consortium of distressed-debt specialists who lacked the proper expertise to turn around a vital public service. Carmichael said the creditors were operating in an opaque way, seeking relief from environmental penalties and dragging out negotiations while reaping millions of pounds in debt interest. “Thames Water’s 16 million customers have largely lost faith in it,” he said. “They are sick of seeing their waterways polluted, their bills going up, and drinking water gush through broken pavements while supplies run low. We believe Thames Water can be turned around, but not by giving the keys back to the people who have been joy-riding in the family car. “The government should reject offers from the company’s creditors in return for relief from fines for pollution and poor service. We do not believe this opaque consortium of 100 hedge funds and others has the interests of the public, the company or the environment at heart.” The report said ministers should explore all potential alternative options, including an SAR or using fresh legislation to draw a line under the debacle and restore stability to the sector by putting Thames Water on a sound footing for new buyers. Carmichael said putting the company into special administration once its money ran out could be the only way to reset its fortunes. “Liabilities that the government will face in the short term may be offset by a future sale of Thames Water once a new buyer can be found,” he said. The intervention comes after 64 MPs debated a 200,000-strong petition, set up by the campaigner Ash Smith of Windrush Against Sewage Pollution, to hold a referendum on putting the privatised water industry back into public ownership. MPs on the Efra committee said they were concerned that not enough regulatory due diligence had been carried out on the US-led consortium that bought Thames Water’s debt. Elliott Investment Management is one of the leading creditors in the group that includes Silver Point Capital, BlackRock and M&G. Elliott’s founder and co-chief executive is Paul Singer, a Trump donor whom Bloomberg has described as “the most feared investor in the world”. The consortium of hedge funds – known as London & Valley Water – is attempting to take over Thames in a multibillion-pound restructuring. It is seeking relief from environmental fines which could be worth up to £1bn, requesting leniency on environmental measures including pollution, leakage and other performance targets imposed a year ago. MPs said: “Their demands demonstrate that they will not prioritise the swift turnaround in performance that Thames Water so desperately needs. “Whilst keeping the company in limbo by drawing out negotiations, these creditors are simultaneously reaping millions in debt interest and fees. We have grave concerns … L&VW is an opaque consortium which is failing to live up to the transparency the public expects of the water sector.” The committee said it was difficult to see why SAR had not already been instigated for Thames Water. “Thames Water is at the end of the road. The company’s performance and the behaviour of its creditors are unacceptable. Their investment strategies are based on extracting value through debt rather than ensuring long-term success.” A spokesperson for the London & Valley Water consortium said: “Our enhanced proposal will address all feedback from Ofwat and ministers and is the fastest route to fix Thames Water’s complex problems. “The plan will write off billions of pounds of debt to achieve an investment grade rating and provide £10bn of new capital from experienced investors to improve and upgrade Thames Water’s infrastructure and clean up local rivers. “All fines Thames Water faces will be paid, all profits will be reinvested, and no dividends will be taken until the company is turned around and returned to the public markets. There will be no cost to the government or taxpayers, and customers will be protected from the costs of Thames Water’s restructuring. “A new board with specialist expertise will oversee Thames Water’s transformation and work tirelessly to drive the turnaround and rebuild trust. We are committed to ensuring Thames Water provides the service that customers and local communities deserve. This group of investors has never been in control of the company and has never received a dividend from Thames Water. They have stepped in to fund a significant revenue shortfall to ensure Thames Water’s record capital investment programme can continue without disruption.” A Defra spokesperson said: “Thames has been failing the public for a long time, and this government has been clear that nothing’s off the table when it comes to a solution that delivers for customers and the environment.” A Thames Water spokesperson said: “Turning Thames Water around will take a decade and require significant and sustained investment in our infrastructure, but we are already making progress and this is a different business from the one it was two years ago. “To sustain that turnaround, Thames Water needs to be recapitalised and put on a firm financial footing, including returning to an investment-grade credit rating, so we can continue investing for our customers and the environment over the long term. Anything that delays the recapitalisation risks slowing the turnaround, disrupting investment and increasing the cost of delivering the improvements our customers and the environment need.”

title: Is the tie dead? Fashion connoisseurs hope not as House of Lords relaxes rules
summary: Switch to ‘business attire’ is a sign of the times, but formal neckwear still has its place, say some of Savile Row’s finest-dressed
text: The House of Lords has long been derided as a stuffy relic of the past. But now its benches, usually filled with haughtily dressed men, could soon resemble something more akin to “dress-down Friday”. One of the nation’s most storied chambers of power has enacted a rule change: men are no longer required to wear a tie in the House of Lords. Instead, they should opt for “business attire”. Ties have long been a knotty item of neckwear. For some, they are a nuisance: too tight and they are uncomfortable, too loose and they look a bit shabby. For others, such as Stephen Fry, who professed his love for ties in a 256-page book, they can add a touch of undeniable class. Peter York, a writer and style commentator, is firmly on the traditional side of the debate, saying the dumbed-down dress code will “end in tears”. “Lords are not famous for being well-dressed at the best of times. If they can go without ties, they can also wear plimsolls and stuff like that. They will look silly,” said York, who owns hundreds of ties. He called them “little works of art”, and decried those who shunned them while dressing formally. “It looks as if you’re not completely dressed, or you’ve forgotten something,” he said. On Savile Row, views on ties were mixed. “I don’t think ties are completely dead, they’re just having a down moment,” said Guy Hills, 58, a fashion photographer and owner of Dashing Tweed, who was sauntering down the street in a green tweed suit. Something else was also green: his moustache. He said his dyed facial hair might be allowed in the House of Lords, and is in support of the relaxed dress code, believing that members have a responsibility to keep up with fashion trends. “They used to be the driving force of fashion, especially around Savile Row. They would go to their tailors and try to outdo each other. When you stop all that, and it becomes like a living museum, then the whole menswear fashion world stops,” he said. Hills usually has something around his neck. “I can’t go out without a scarf because it looks too slovenly,” he said. But Thursday afternoon was, unluckily, one of the rare occasions he was without a silk scarf or cravat. While ties aren’t totally “in”, Hills thinks they could make a comeback. “The younger generation is now getting more interested in sustainability and proper clothing. A tie really finishes a whole outfit off,” he said. Among the few wearing a tie on Savile Row was Chaand Singh. The 25-year-old, who works in marketing, had decided to wear a navy tie from Next because of an important work meeting. “Dressing up and adding a tie elevates the look,” he said – so much so that he had received compliments from people. “Someone said that I look a bit more sharp today.” Ties were no longer an office must, said Singh – but he thinks they still have their place. “I’ve got some from the 80s with cool patterns. They’re usually wider and designed when fashion was a bit more experimental,” he said. “I would wear them at work for the right scenario, but casually as well. Some girls even wear ties as belts.” What do tailors on the Row think? “The House of Lords should be a mirror of society. What better way of doing it than reflecting current trends?” said James Sleater, 45, the owner of Norton & Sons. “Women don’t have to wear ties, and if men have the option, it’s OK by me.” Sleater said that in the “post-Covid era, there has been a huge decline in neckwear and the number of people wearing ties to the office”, adding that the “relaxation of dress codes is symptomatic of people working several days a week at home”. Norton & Sons sees people from all walks of life. “Yesterday we had an ex-prime minister and today we’ve got a Hollywood star having a fitting. We also see people wanting a suit for their first job and people celebrating a wedding,” he says. Have these customers shunned ties and other neckwear in droves? Actually, no. “We’re seeing the reversal of this trend,” says Sleater. “We’re selling more neckwear this year than we did in previous years. “If you’re no longer forced to do something, it almost becomes a pleasure to it,” he adds. “To wear a suit to work when you don’t have to is a joy. When you’re told to do it, you’re almost feeling rebellious and you don’t want to do it.” People have opted for “more characterful textures rather than just plain silks or bright brash colours”, though Slater sees a limit to a potential neckwear revival. “I don’t see cravats or bow ties coming back,” he said. As for Lords who can keep their ties at home, some are in favour of the new rules. “In truth, the only people now wearing ties for business purposes are estate agents and funeral directors,” Lord Davies of Brixton, a Labour peer, told the Telegraph. “The tie is disappearing.” It remains to be seen if Davies’ fellow Lords will heed the message.

title: Country diary: Dinner time for the buzzard family is not a dignified affair | Kate Blincoe
summary: Caistor St Edmund, Norfolk: We have three breeding pairs on the farm, and one in particular has been a source of fascination and amusement
text: I’m out on the farm most days, but I miss so much. It took a few days to notice a mother mallard with her late brood of 12 ducklings until they were all dabbling in a yard puddle. Dad sees more than me. He told me of the lazy adult buzzard that waited in a tree, then dive-bombed a peregrine that had caught a pigeon. The peregrine dropped its prey, which the buzzard then delivered to a hay bale already strewn with feathers. A pair of juvenile buzzards swiftly followed, ready for a meal. Later, Dad placed the trail camera at the bale. The young buzzards were soon back in position with yet another dead pigeon. The footage tells a story that many parents will recognise after the long summer holidays. One young buzzard claims the pigeon, turns its back on the other and opens its wings around the food. Known as “mantling”, it creates a share-proof barrier. The other bird looks disgruntled, shifting around, head down, trying to work out a plan. It sticks a leg out under its sibling’s defensive wings and is told off with a shrill screech. Opting instead for being persistently annoying, it eventually provokes the pigeon-possessor to rise in attack. There’s a funny moment when both birds overbalance and plummet off the side of the bale. Another high-pitch squeak arises, off-camera. I shouldn’t anthropomorphise, but the expressions of the birds throughout this little drama do seem very familiar. There are three pairs of buzzards that nest on the farm, each wood has its couple. Usually seen soaring on thermals above the farm, or loafing around in the woodland canopy, they are in turn majestic and clumsy. Despite centuries of persecution, followed by the myxomatosis outbreak in the 1950s that reduced their favourite rabbit prey, buzzards somehow persisted, and more recently increased in numbers. The bales have now been cleared from the fields and this next generation of buzzards must fend for themselves. Meanwhile, back in the yard, each night there is a diminishing of ducklings. We’re down to eight now. Still an impressive amount in the numbers game of reproduction, but they have a long way to go until they too are independent. • Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024, is available now at guardianbookshop.com

title: Paul Keating says Aukus locking Australia into a US war against China, which it would ‘certainly lose’
summary: Former prime minister says US would ‘scuttle itself back to San Diego’, leaving Australia to deal with retribution from China
text: Aukus critic Paul Keating has said the submarine deal is locking Australia in to any future US conflict with China – “a war America would certainly lose” – and making Australia a target for retribution. The former prime minister seized on comments reported out of Washington this week from Republican congressman Michael McCaul – a China hawk and co-chair of the Congressional Friends of Australia caucus – who said “Australia is a target” for enemies of the US already. However, McCaul argued that greater integration with the US military would better protect Australia rather than leaving it more vulnerable. McCaul also said it was “logical to assume” US nuclear-powered submarines rotating through Australian bases could also be nuclear armed after 2032, and that Australia’s participation in a US war against China over Taiwan was assumed by the US military establishment. “I don’t think it was even questioned. It’s just obvious,” McCaul said. “Australia, being a Five Eyes [intelligence-sharing network member] and an ally of the United States, would be at odds with China invading Taiwan and threatening the Indo-Pacific.” He said it was “absolutely critical” for Australian to back any US intervention to protect Taiwan. McCaul met with the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, the defence minister, Richard Marles, and the foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, during a visit to Australia this month. Keating said the US would “certainly lose” in a war with China over Taiwan. “But having lost, [the US would] scuttle itself back to San Diego, leaving Australia vulnerable to China for having participated in a military escapade against it and its military assets.” Keating said Australia’s increasing enmeshment within the US military, especially through Aukus, was seeing Australia’s “sovereignty effectively being shredded”. “Australia is now getting locked in and locked up to the military prerogatives of the United States.” The Guardian revealed last week that the US military, and its corporate interests, control, or have access to, more than 100 military bases across the Australian continent. More than half of the military installations in Australia have some level of US control or access. Intelligence sites such as Pine Gap play a critical role in US warfighting, downlinking masses of surveillance data from satellites, and providing targeting information for US strikes. In parliament this week, Greens senator David Shoebridge seized on McCaul’s further comments that he considered Australia a “beachhead” for the US in its efforts to deter China and maintain peace in the region. “The US spruikers of Aukus have said they want to make Australia the beachhead for US military war against China,” Shoebridge told a press conference at Parliament House. “I want to be clear what happens at a beachhead: people get killed at a beachhead, destruction happens at a beachhead in someone else’s war. “How on Earth does Aukus make us safe, when a foreign military is bringing their nuclear-armed submarines into this country and consciously saying they want our country to be the beachhead in a war with China? It’s time we ended Aukus before we become the US’s beachhead.” Under Pillar One of the proposed Aukus agreement – a multi-decade deal slated to cost Australia $368bn to the mid-2050s – Australia will buy three “in-service” Virginia-class nuclear-powered, conventionally armed submarines from the US, beginning in 2032. From the early 2040s, Australia expects to deploy a new, larger Aukus-class submarine. The new class will be designed in the UK and the first boat built for the Royal Navy. Australia will then build five Aukus submarines - except for their nuclear reactors - in South Australia. America’s Virginia class submarines do not currently carry nuclear weapons but, from 2032, the US navy is planning to equip some of its Virginia boats with nuclear-armed sea-launched cruise missiles. The regular rotation of US nuclear submarines through HMAS Stirling is also part of Aukus cooperation. The US has a policy of “strategic ambiguity” around the deployment of its nuclear arsenal, refusing to confirm or deny the presence of nuclear weapons on platforms around the world. The Treaty of Rarotonga prohibits Australia from “stationing” nuclear weapons on its territory.

title: Russians go to polls against backdrop of Ukraine war and Putin’s tightening grip
summary: President’s United Russia party faces no meaningful opposition after liberal anti-war party barred from ballot
text: Russians are going to the polls to elect a new State Duma in a tightly controlled vote stripped of meaningful competition and with little doubt about the result. Vladimir Putin’s United Russia is expected to extend the grip on parliament it has held for 23 years, alongside a handful of nominal opposition parties that reliably vote with the Kremlin on the issues that matter. The three-day vote begins on Friday, with results expected after polls close on Sunday. For all the predictability of the outcome, the first Duma election since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 is taking place against the backdrop of a war that, once distant for many Russians, is increasingly intruding into everyday life. Swarms of Ukrainian drones have struck oil refineries, factories and logistics hubs across Russia over the summer, while polling has pointed to growing anxiety about the course of the fighting and what may still lie ahead. Against that backdrop, the Kremlin has tightened its grip further. Last month, the authorities barred Yabloko, the liberal anti-war party, from the ballot, removing the only political force remaining in Russia that was openly challenging the invasion of Ukraine. That leaves a handful of other parties, from the Communists to the far-right Liberal Democrats, which together form what is known in Russia as the “systemic opposition”: groups permitted to criticise the authorities at the margins, but which fall into line with United Russia on issues that matter to the Kremlin. For years, they have served as a political safety valve, giving voters somewhere to register discontent without posing a serious threat to the ruling party’s dominance. But even by the diminished standards of Russian politics, these parliamentary campaigns have been strikingly lifeless. “In most elections, candidates compete for attention. In Russia this year, many are doing the opposite,” said Farida Rustamova, a political analyst and founder of the independent Vlast newsletter. “No one wants to come into the spotlight or discuss anything sensitive.” Most candidates have barely campaigned at all, she noted. Televised debates have at times taken place in half-empty studios because politicians failed to turn up, producing awkward clips that quickly became memes online. United Russia’s campaign videos have leaned heavily on low-budget AI, with few memorable slogans or promises. None of the parties has dared to address the growing questions surrounding the continuing war that increasingly dominate private conversations. “The Kremlin is deliberately keeping the election low-key, as greater interest would not benefit them. They don’t want to discuss difficult issues and just [want to] get it over with,” said a person close to the Kremlin, speaking on condition of anonymity. By keeping the election subdued, Moscow hoped to depress turnout among disaffected and independent-minded voters while ensuring its own supporters made it to the polls, said Rustamova. Yabloko’s exclusion followed the same logic. Several observers believe that officials had initially expected the party to receive a negligible result, demonstrating how little support remained for an explicitly anti-war platform. But when polling instead suggested growing support for the party, the authorities removed it from the ballot rather than risk an unscripted result. Vladimir Gelman, a professor of Russian politics at the University of Helsinki, said another purpose of the elections was to provide the Kremlin with a continuing source of legitimacy and reinforce the impression that there was broad public consent behind the political system and the war. “Even though these elections are neither free nor fair, they are still the only source of legitimacy,” he said. In a televised address before the vote this week, Putin explicitly linked participation in the election to the war in Ukraine, presenting voting as a demonstration of unity in the face of outside pressure. “Your choice and your will will once again demonstrate that millions of people stand behind our soldiers, that we are a united people bound together by shared values, historical memory and love for our homeland,” Putin said. Putin himself secured another six-year term in the 2024 presidential election, with genuine opposition barred from the ballot, extending his rule until at least 2030. For many Russians, however, the election’s greater significance lies not in the result, but in what follows. With Moscow’s troops making little progress at high cost in Ukraine, rumours of another large-scale mobilisation have spread across the country. The fear is that once the election is safely out of the way and a compliant new Duma is installed, the Kremlin will have greater freedom to pursue unpopular measures it has so far avoided. The anxiety has already prompted some young men to leave the country, hoping to wait out any new mobilisation – scenes that carry echoes of September 2022, when hundreds of thousands of Russians fled after Putin announced the first wartime draft. The person close to the Kremlin said several friends had sent their sons abroad in recent weeks, a sign, he said, that even among those with access to the system, few are certain what will happen after the voting. Putin has sought to calm those fears. In recent weeks, he has twice dismissed suggestions that a new mobilisation is imminent. But those reassurances have not been enough for some men, including Dmitry, who flew to Yerevan, Armenia last week. “I’ll just wait a few weeks after the elections,” he said, adding that he felt the risk of a new mobilisation was too high to ignore. “Let’s see if anything changes after the vote.”

title: Ukraine war briefing: Poland’s Tusk heads to Kyiv after warning of Russian strikes on Ukrainian allies
summary: Donald Tusk says Moscow will not enter peace talks without Ukraine’s ‘total capitulation’ and will try to inflict a ‘tragically critical’ winter. What we know on day 1,668
text: Russia is planning hybrid strikes with drones or rockets on European countries supporting Ukraine, among them Poland according to its prime minister, Donald Tusk. Russia will pretend the attacks are “accidental” in order to “paralyse or at least weaken the motivation of Nato countries” to rush to the defence of the member state coming under attack, Tusk said in a speech to the Polish parliament. “There is a real risk that drones or other types of projectiles will enter the territory of one or several countries on the eastern flank and even cause destruction,” Tusk said, vowing that “if anyone dares to attack us, they will face a resolute response from us and our allies”. Tusk announced he would travel to Ukraine overnight, arriving on Friday, in what might be seen as an act of defiance against Russia after European leaders were in transit during a drone strike on a train near the Polish-Ukrainian border on Sunday. Officials usually keep their travel plans to Ukraine secret for security reasons. In Kyiv, he said he would discuss with Volodymyr Zelenskyy how to defend against the new types of drones, as well as discuss with partners including Slovakia further sanctions against Russia. The Slovak ⁠prime minister, Robert Fico, ‌also said ‌he would be in Kyiv as he claimed Europe is closer ⁠than ever to a large-scale ⁠war erupting ⁠from the war in Ukraine ⁠and politicians must strive for peace. Fico has ‌kept warm relations with Russia while criticising EU and Nato aid to Ukraine, though Slovakia’s arms industry is simultaneously a producer of artillery shells supplied to Kyiv’s forces. On Friday ⁠the European Union will ⁠disburse €3.3bn to ‌Ukraine to buy missiles and drones, Ursula von ⁠der ⁠Leyen, the European Commission president, has announced. Tusk said Russia was not ready for any peace talks “without the total capitulation of Ukraine”. “They are convinced the winter will be tragically critical for Ukraine.” He said last winter Poland stepped in with deliveries when Ukraine’s energy infrastructure came under attack, but if border crossings are destroyed it will be much harder for Warsaw to offer such help this winter. “Russia’s goal is to destroy as much as possible the economy and logistics of Ukraine,” Tusk said, adding that intelligence indicates continuous attacks of “very high frequency and intensity” on six main Ukrainian cities should be expected in the near future. A drone hit a petrol station near Ukraine’s border with Poland on Thursday, Tusk said separately at a press conference in Warsaw. A spokesperson for the Polish military told TVN24 that air defences were activated on Thursday after a jet-powered drone approached Polish airspace before exploding about 4km (2.5 miles) from the Polish border. Poland’s Lublin and Rzeszow ‌airports temporarily suspended operations on Thursday as the air force responded to Russian drone activity, Polish authorities said. Russian missiles and drones injured at least 19 people in Ukraine’s capital and the surrounding region, authorities said on Thursday. Kyiv’s military administration said more than 10 locations were hit, while 33 sites were damaged in the wider region. A 10-year-old girl and a 12-year-old boy were among the injured, the administration said. Ukraine’s air force said it destroyed or suppressed 131 Russian aerial targets during the overnight attack in the Kyiv, Zaporizhzhia and Odesa regions. The attack involved ballistic and cruise missiles as well as drones and decoys. In Odesa, seven people were injured, including two children, according to Ukraine’s state emergency Service. Apartments on the 14th through 16th floors of a residential building were damaged. A private residential building in Odesa was also destroyed and others damaged. Ukrainian forces struck an oil refinery in Yaroslavl and a military airfield in the Rostov region, Zelenskyy said on Thursday. Zelenskyy said Ukraine’s operation against the Yaroslavl oil refinery was conducted jointly by the country’s Security Service, special operations forces, military intelligence and the foreign intelligence service. The security service also struck a military airfield in Rostov, damaging an An-12 aircraft, two An-26s and three helicopters. Reuters said that according to its industry sources, the refinery halted crude processing after the Ukrainian ⁠attack. The local Russian governor confirmed the damage. A Russian drone struck a civilian vessel flying the flag of Tanzania in the Black Sea on Thursday, killing the ship’s captain and injuring three crew members, according to Oleh Kiper, the regional head in Odesa. Russia damaged the Bilhorod-Dnistrovskyi bridge in the Odesa region, ⁠significantly limiting Ukraine’s ability to transport grain to its Danube river ports, Ukrainian state railway ⁠operator Ukrzaliznytsia ⁠said on Thursday. According to Ukrzaliznytsia, about 3,000 grain wagons ‌are bound for the Danube ports. Without the bridge, they would need 26 days to reach the ports. “The situation is very difficult. We are working to restore the Bilhorod-Dnistrovskyi bridge,” a company official said.

title: Trump administration again denies entry visas to Palestinian officials ahead of UN general assembly
summary: For the second year in a row, the administration has barred the Palestinian delegation from US travel for the forum
text: The US state department said on Wednesday that it had again denied entry visas to Palestinian officials ahead next week’s United Nations general assembly gathering in New York. The state department said in a statement the Palestinian Authority (PA) and the Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO) had “failed to live up to their commitments”, accusing the groups of “taking actions to internationalize the Israeli-Palestinian Conflict including through the International Criminal Court (ICC) and International Court of Justice (ICJ)” and of “glorifying terrorism” among other allegations. “As a consequence of their failure to reform, contrary to their commitments to the United States, and their ongoing activities that undermine the prospects for peace, the United States will extend sanctions that deny visas to PLO members and PA officials,” the department said. The move marks the second year in a row the Trump administration has barred the Palestinian delegation from traveling to New York to attend the UN general assembly in person. The foreign ministry of the Palestinian Authority denied the allegations made against it in a statement on Thursday, describing the visa sanctions as an “unjustified measure” that “contradicts the efforts being made to restore trust, develop Palestinian-US relations, and prepare the necessary political climate for implementing the two-state solution and achieving peace and stability in the region”. Among the Palestinian officials barred from entering the US is Mahmoud Abbas, the longtime president of the Palestinian Authority, according to reports. The UN general assembly voted on Thursday to allow Abbas to address the gathering via ⁠video, for the second year in a row. This year’s UN general assembly general debate begins on 22 September.

title: US court sentences ex-Syrian official who ran notorious ‘punishment wing’ to 60 years
summary: Samir Ousman al-Sheikh, part of Bashar al-Assad’s regime, was in charge of Adra prison where prisoners were tortured
text: This article contains descriptions of torture. A US federal court in Los Angeles sentenced a former Syrian government official who ran one of the country’s most infamous prisons to 60 years in prison on Thursday – the most significant punishment handed to an official of ousted president Bashar al-Assad’s regime by a foreign court and to a defendant present in person. Samir Ousman al-Sheikh was the head of the Adra prison, on the outskirts of Damascus, between 2005 and 2008, when he oversaw an underground “punishment wing”, known as “Wing 13”, in which prisoners and regime opponents were interrogated and tortured as he watched through surveillance cameras. A federal jury convicted al-Sheikh last March of having tortured prisoners and then lying about it in US immigration forms. “The conduct was heinous, unimaginably cruel and almost unspeakably violent and brutal,” said Hernan D Vera, a US district judge, before delivering the sentence. Al-Sheikh’s legal team did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Assistant attorney general A Tysen Duva of the justice department’s criminal division said in a statement the sentence sends a clear message: “Human rights violators who come to the United States will receive no safe harbor here. We will find them, and they will be prosecuted and punished for their heinous crimes.” Al-Sheikh, 74, who also served as governor of Syria’s Deir Ez-Zour province in 2011, at a time of violent regime crackdowns against protesters, moved to the United States in 2020, obtained a green card and applied for US citizenship. He was arrested in July 2024 at Los Angeles international airport on immigration fraud charges and prosecutors later added four-torture related charges. He is the first al-Assad regime official to go to trial in the US and the highest ranking regime official to be tried anywhere in the world in person. Al-Assad was ousted by a lightning rebel offensive in December 2024 which toppled the regime in just 11 days. Since then, Syria’s new government has held a number of in absentia trials for former regime officials in connection to crimes committed during the country’s years-long civil war, which killed about half a million people and displaced half the country’s prewar population of 23 million. In August, a court sentenced al-Assad and his brother Maher to death for crimes against humanity and war crimes, but the two men have been in Moscow since the regime’s collapse. Other factions in Syria’s civil war have also been accused of abuse of detainees, including insurgent groups and the US-backed, Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces. During al-Sheikh’s nine-day trial, several victims and witnesses testified. They described guards folding prisoners into car tires, restraining and beating them. Some they said, were cuffed by their wrists to pipes on the ceiling, beaten with cables, and left suspended for extended periods of time. Others testified that they were placed on a device known as a “magic carpet” or “flying carpet” which consisted of two large wooden panels with hinges in the middle onto which guards strapped prisoners, forcing the panels together to cause excruciating pain. One victim recalled al-Sheikh himself stomping on the device. Another testified he was subjected to the “magic carpet” or “flying carpet” as punishment for writing a letter of support to a political prisoner and also forced to wear a red jumpsuit assigned to prisoners designated for execution, leading him to believe he was going to die. “[Al-Sheikh] chose to serve the ruthless, repressive Assad regime in Syria throughout his professional life, including for four years as the warden of Syria’s largest prison,” prosecutors wrote in a sentencing memo. “[He] knew that what he was doing was wrong. Nonetheless he ordered and participated in the torture of his victims because he had the power to do so and because he thought he would never be held accountable.” Several victims and witnesses also submitted written and video testimonies to the court ahead of the sentencing, in which they spoke of being haunted and traumatized by their experiences two decades later. “I still hear the screams of others begging for mercy,” said one of the men, Nidal Shikhani. “Even though 20 years have passed, I still live in the prison of my memory,” said another, Sultan Abdul Malek. “I suffer from sudden panic attacks and constant anxiety.” His brother, Khaled Abdul Malek, who was taken to “Wing 13” twice during his four years at Adra prison, spoke of the physical and psychological scars he was left with, including chronic back pain and mobility problems. “My son Battal asks if he could ride my back and with a heart wrung with pain, I am forced to tell him I [am] no longer strong enough to carry him,” he said. Several witnesses also submitted testimony on al-Sheikh’s behalf, speaking about his age and frailty as they asked the court for leniency. More than 50 people sent letters of support to the court, describing him as “a person of integrity, compassion, and generosity to his family and community”, his attorneys wrote. Prosecutors had asked the court for a minimum sentence of 80 years; al-Sheikh’s attorneys had called for a five-year sentence, citing his poor health and noting that he was willing to be deported to Syria. “Whatever moral weight this case carries in the broader arc of history – however much the world, or the victims, or the public might wish the sentence to ‘send a message’ – that desire cannot be the foundation of a just sentence,” the defense team wrote in a memo to the court. Al-Sheikh is one of only five people to be prosecuted under the extraterritorial Torture Act, which allows the US government to prosecute individuals physically present in the US over acts of torture committed abroad. “This case sends a message both to the new government of Syria and to other victims that justice is possible,” said Ela Matthews, an attorney at the Center for Justice and Accountability, which represented several victims. “The transitional justice process that is happening in Syria needs to continue to evolve and bring individuals like this to account, but in the US this sends a message that the rule of law is still functioning and that these types of cases are possible.”

title: LA woman charged with murder over bus crash that preceded deadly helicopter plunge
summary: Bailee Lynn Rios, 36, accused of driving on wrong side of road to cause fatal crash NBC news helicopter was covering
text: A California woman was allegedly driving under the influence when she sped down the wrong side of the road, ran a red light and plowed her SUV into a Los Angeles metro bus on Tuesday, killing two passengers, prosecutors say, in a tragedy compounded when a news helicopter covering the crash plummeted from the sky, killing three. Bailee Lynn Rios, 36, has been charged with two counts of murder over the deaths of the two people on the bus, identified as Daniel Castillo, 46, and Gage Weida, 31. Rios was being held on $4.1m bail and is set to be arraigned on 18 September. Online court records did not list a lawyer who might speak on her behalf, and the public defender’s office did not immediately return a message about whether it was representing her. The wake of Tuesday’s deadly bus crash took a turn for the worse in the hours after, when a local news helicopter responding to the scene crashed to the ground in a fiery ball, killing two individuals onboard: pilot George Marciniw and reporter Eliana Moreno. A pedestrian on the ground, 29-year-old Edy Gutierrez Mejia, also died in the crash. Reached Wednesday, Rios’s mother, Cindy, said she was shocked and saddened by the string of events. She said she had not spoken to her daughter since her arrest and had not been contacted by law enforcement. She could not immediately be reached on Thursday for additional comment. Castillo left behind four children. “We are still trying to process the unimaginable reality that he is no longer with us,” his youngest daughter, Johaunna, wrote on a fundraising page for funeral expenses. Weida’s family planned to visit him for his 32nd birthday, his father told CBS LA. “Unfortunately, we’re still heading out there, but for all the wrong reasons,” said Jeffrey Weida. “The deadly and destructive consequences of her actions will be felt for years to come,” Los Angeles county district attorney Nathan Hochman said in a statement. Stephanie Wiggins, chief executive of the Los Angeles metro, extended her sympathies to the bus crash’s victims and their families. “We are grateful to the first responders who rushed to the scene and to the law enforcement investigators and prosecutors working to establish the facts and pursue justice,” she said in a statement. A vigil was planned Thursday evening to honor the victims of both crashes. There were no immediate details on what caused the helicopter to go down, but investigators said significant clues could come from the last seconds of video the crew broadcast. In it, an alarm could be heard inside the helicopter’s cockpit as it lost altitude. National Transportation Safety Board investigator Fabian Salazar said on Wednesday the video was “probably the most important evidence that we have discovered so far”. In the video, after the beeping starts, a woman’s voice says: “Uh oh.” The helicopter moves quickly away from the bus crash site and starts losing altitude. The woman says, “You can’t pull up?” before the video stops as the chopper nears the ground. Aviation safety expert Jeff Guzzetti said the alarm suggested a potential loss of engine power and a dangerous decrease in the main rotor speed. He said the pilot appeared to be trying to perform an emergency maneuver to use the wind to force the rotor to spin again. The NTSB is also investigating the bus collision. Moreno and Marciniw worked for Angel City Air, a helicopter contractor, and provided aerial coverage for NBC4 and Telemundo 52. Moreno, born in Orange county, joined Angel City Air in 2010, the same year she earned a broadcast journalism and political science degree from Chapman University. She reported for several news outlets and began flying with Marciniw in 2023, NBC4 said. Marciniw grew up in southern California and graduated from Burbank high school in 1974. There have been at least eight fatal crashes involving news helicopters in the US since 2000, killing 16 people, according to a review of federal accident records and news accounts.

title: ‘Forcing a reckoning’: How Asia is preparing for a ‘supersized’ El Niño
summary: From Sri Lanka to South Korea, governments are preparing for droughts, wildfires, typhoons and floods – with climate plans facing their biggest challenge to date
text: Asian governments are rushing preparations for the most severe El Niño weather event on record, with hundreds of millions of people bracing for multiple crises at once as extreme heat, heavy rain and food shortages hit the region. Fuelled by exceptionally warm ocean conditions across the tropical Pacific – and developing alongside the human-driven climate crisis – El Niño is virtually guaranteed to grow to a very strong intensity towards the end of this year and into 2027. The World Food Programme has warned that about 50 million people will probably be pushed into acute hunger due to the exceptionally intense weather system, while UN secretary-general António Guterres said this month that El Niño was “being supersized before our eyes”. Here are the steps countries in Asia are taking to prepare for El Niño: ‘Climate risk maps’ in China In Hong Kong, authorities have already been forced to revise workplace policies, after the city experienced its hottest day on record on 9 August. During times of extreme heat, companies are expected to reschedule work, provide cooling equipment and rest breaks for their employees. Employers in the international financial hub could even face prosecution if they fail to provide staff with support at times of sweltering heat. In mainland China a 100-day campaign has been launched to prepare for extreme weather and help safeguard harvests against the opposing extremes of drought and intense rainfall. Beijing has plans to upgrade early warning monitoring systems, and in July, it launched a national plan encouraging cities to draw up ‘climate risk maps’ to help identify areas most vulnerable to flooding and severe heat. Taiwan, meanwhile, is treating the predicted extreme weather as an emergency situation, and preparing using methods similar to what it would do to train for a terrorist attack or earthquake. In early September, the island nation held a mass exercise simulating three consecutive days of temperatures above 40C. Hundreds of people took part in the field exercises, which simulated power and water disruption, rail problems, air conditioner failure and mass heatstroke. The government has also been testing its “Cool Map” online platform, which helps to direct vulnerable people to airconditioned and cool spaces. Sri Lanka plans to process salterwater El Niño is already wreaking havoc across south Asia; in parts of India there has been a shortfall of monsoon rainfall of almost 50% in September, with knock-on effects on key crops such as rice, pulses, cotton and maize. Concerns are mounting that there could be a diminished harvest in the coming months, likely driving up food prices – already crippling for poor and lower middle class families. The Indian government has taken a hyper-vigilant approach to establish what the agriculture minister, Shivraj Singh Chouhan, described as a “protective shield for farmers”. In more than 350 vulnerable districts authorities are boosting water conservation infrastructure and water harvesting, and are encouraging farmers to plant low-water, short duration crops – such as pulses and millets. But the most intense impact of El Niño in the area is in Sri Lanka, where the absence of rainfall and high temperatures have become so severe that the country is experiencing its worst drought in a decade. More than 160,000 people are now facing a drinking water shortage as several key reservoirs run dry. Officials have been forced to close the tourist areas of the Yala national park, home to leopards, elephants, crocodiles and spotted deer, and have been bringing in tankers of water to fill the ponds to make sure the animals do not die. In Mullaithivu lagoon, in the north-east of Sri Lanka, thousands of fish were found dead due to the lack of fresh water. The country’s disaster management centre is preparing for a situation in which freshwater supplies could vanish. “If water sources dry up, there will be no alternative means of obtaining water,” an official said. Colombo would then be forced to process salt water from the sea, although relying on the country’s one desalination plant is not considered workable. Tackling an agriculture crisis in south-east Asia In south-east Asia, El Niño is compounded by a series of ongoing crises. The Iran war has already disrupted global energy and supply chains and inflated fertiliser costs, disproportionately hitting the region. At the same time, severe haze from seasonal fires across Malaysia and Indonesia has choked cities and is damaging plants and trees. During the 2023–2024 El Niño, south-east Asian governments successfully cushioned agricultural impacts by adjusting planting calendars and managing water, but those strategies will be insufficient to deal with the scale of the crisis, experts warn. Regional rice yields are already projected to fall by 8 to 10%. “We can’t just assume that this El Niño is going to be the same as the last because there are so many challenges that have been stacking on top of each other,” says Elyssa Kaur Ludher, a climate and food security expert based in Singapore. The Philippines, Malaysia and Indonesia are particularly vulnerable to food price changes, says Kaur Ludher, a visiting fellow with the Climate Change for Southeast Asia Programme at the ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute in Singapore. “In Singapore, most of our income is not spent on food. It’s under 10%. But for Indonesians, it can be up to 50% or even more as a proportion of income spent on food. So any price rise affects them disproportionately.” With the potential for price rises to leave people desperate and angry, Kaur Ludher has argued for food security to be reframed as a national security issue. In Indonesia and the Philippines in particular, she said, social stability depends a lot on food prices. “Rice is a lifeline to this region,” she says. To prepare, south-east Asian governments and farmer cooperatives are promoting regenerative agriculture and shifting toward biofertilisers. “We have come to a stage where climate change is putting so much pressure on us – on our existing, already crumbling or structurally unsound, systems,” says Kaur Ludher. “Nature will force us to have a reckoning.” South Korea overhauls its heatwave alert system South Korea saw the driest July on record in the country’s south-east. Weeks later came a freak reversal, as a weakening storm system dragged in a deluge that dumped some of the heaviest rainfall ever recorded at a Korean weather station. The heat was so intense that farmers described spoilt potatoes as being “boiled” in the ground. The country’s weather agency has overhauled its heatwave alert system for the first time in 18 years, adding a top tier that triggers official guidance to stop non-emergency outdoor work once feels-like temperatures hit 38C. Nationwide, phones have buzzed for weeks with government alerts urging people to stay indoors during the hottest hours. Officials are watching out for a rough autumn, with seas around the Korean peninsula remaining unusually warm for the season and forecasters expecting the north-west Pacific to produce far more powerful storms than usual this year, since a strengthening El Niño is weakening the high pressure that has so far kept them away. Japan prepares for ‘cruelly’ hot days and typhoons Japan is also bracing for the arrival of so-called super-typhoons, which experts attribute to a combination of El Niño and human-induced global heating. El Niño was once associated with slightly cooler summers in Japan. But rising sea surface temperatures mean it is having the opposite effect, blanketing many parts of the country in record-breaking heat and humidity in 2023-4, the last time the weather pattern materialised. Japan recorded its first official “cruelly hot day” – or kokushobi – in July, just after the start of the current El Niño event. The Japanese term, introduced in April to underscore the threat to health posed by rising temperatures, refers to days when the mercury exceeds 40C. Now, as the summer heat dissipates, the country is bracing for the arrival of potentially destructive typhoons. The public is encouraged to take measures to protect themselves and their homes, such as heeding official evacuation warnings and stocking up on food and water. People living in apartments are urged to secure or bring inside flower pots and furniture – anything that could become a dangerous flying object during a storm. This month the infrastructure ministry said it had identified several high-risk underpasses on national highways that would be closed preemptively during heavy rain. Underpasses – which allow cars to travel beneath other roads or railway lines – became a focus of concern last month after two trapped motorists drowned during record-breaking rain in Chiba prefecture, east of Tokyo. Yu-chen Li contributed to this article

title: Find a credible plan for British Steel, ministers told as ‘startling’ costs soar
summary: Government spending watchdog warns of ‘startling’ price of keeping publicly owned firm in business
text: Labour has been urged to lay out a credible plan for the future of British Steel, as the government spending watchdog warned of the “startling” costs of keeping the struggling manufacturer in business with no end in sight. British Steel was taken into public ownership in July to protect “the future of steel production”, 15 months after the government stepped in to prevent the closure of its steelworks in Scunthorpe and the loss of 4,000 jobs. But it is costing £1.3m a day to keep the company running, with the total estimated cost reaching as much as £1.5bn by 2028. By mid-June, the government had spent £555m paying workers’ salaries and buying raw materials, excluding the cost of external advisers. The public accounts committee of MPs said on Friday that ministers were still “unable to articulate what business model” would put the company on a sustainable footing, nearly a year and a half after taking control at Scunthorpe. It added that the Department for Business and Trade had not given “even indicative estimates” of how much British Steel would ultimately cost taxpayers or how long the situation would continue. After nationalising British Steel, the government appointed new bosses to focus on stabilising the business. Clive Betts, the committee’s deputy chair, said the move to save the company was “all well and good”, but added: “This was just the beginning. Having brought British Steel onto the taxpayers’ books, it is now up to government to explain its plan for its future. “Unfortunately, beyond simply propping up the company with public money, the government was not able to outline such a plan to our inquiry. The reality is that British Steel is unable to wash its own face, and government is now in charge of making sure it gets on to a sustainable financial footing for the future. “We also require assurances that the startling levels of funding British Steel is currently receiving do not come at the expense of the wider sector.” The criticism came days after Labour also nationalised Britain’s third-biggest producer of the metal, the Yorkshire-based Speciality Steel UK, in an attempt to protect 1,300 jobs. Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, said at the time that the government did not “intervene in private companies lightly” but that the move was important to safeguard heavy industry. The public accounts committee said it showed the government could not “spend all its money supporting British Steel, when clearly there will be a need to support other parts of the industry”. It added: “[Taxpayers] remain exposed to significant and growing costs and uncertainty – it is not clear whether the money will ever be recovered.” The government should publish a plan for the company that included “options and analysis for the intended future production model and the role of British Steel in the UK economy; the preferred decarbonisation pathway; how the company will become financially sustainable; and the expected costs, funding sources and timetable”, the committee’s report said. The former owner Jingye has separately argued that British Steel owed it almost £1bn when it was nationalised and has started a formal process under an international treaty to win compensation from the government. The move has also put pressure on UK-Chinese relations, with China’s government saying it is “strongly dissatisfied” with the situation.

title: Trump officials move to dismantle key protection for US endangered species
summary: Fish and Wildlife Service memo calls for change in what it means to ‘take’ an endangered species
text: More than 1,600 critically imperiled species protected under the US Endangered Species Act (ESA) face losing further federal protections following a new reinterpretation of the 1973 law by the Donald Trump administration. A September 14 memo distributed to Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) field offices by FWS director Brian Nesvik calls for a reinterpretation of what it means to “take” an endangered species. Under the ESA, “take” is defined as “to harass, harm, pursue, hunt, shoot, wound, kill, trap, capture, or collect, or to attempt to engage in any such conduct”. The memo, obtained and shared by the Center for Biological Diversity, reinterprets the law to mean that harming or killing an endangered animal would no longer be considered illegal unless the action was specifically intended to cause harm or death. “A vessel that inadvertently strikes a whale has not taken it, because the vessel’s course was not set against the whale,” the memo said, adding: “Felling a tree is not a take of the bats roosting in it unless the tree is felled for the purpose of killing or capturing them.” The reinterpretation effectively excludes economic activities such as logging, mining and industrial development from the ESA’s prohibition on “take” when those activities foreseeably kill or injure wildlife without intentionally targeting them. The memo follows the Trump administration’s repeal in July of the ESA’s definition of prohibited “harm,” which was defined as “an act which actually kills or injures wildlife,” including acts that “may include significant habitat modification or degradation”. Interior secretary Doug Burgum justified the repeal in July by saying: “For years, federal agencies abused the ESA to obstruct lawful land use and burden American families and businesses.” Earlier this month, 20 states and Washington DC sued the Trump administration over its decision to redefine “harm,” including removing “modification or degradation” of habitat from conduct that can constitute a prohibited take. In a statement on Thursday to the Guardian about the administration’s reinterpretation of “take,” the interior department, which oversees the FWS, said: “As outlined in the final rule, the department determined that the previous regulatory definition of ‘harm’ expanded the Endangered Species Act’s prohibition on ‘take’ beyond the text Congress enacted. The final rule restores that interpretation while maintaining the ESA’s core protections for listed species.” The memo has drawn swift backlash from environmental advocacy organizations. The Center for Biological Diversity pointed to the supreme court’s 1995 6-3 decision in Babbitt v Sweet Home Chapter of Communities for a Great Oregon, in which the majority rejected the argument that “take” is limited to actions deliberately directed against endangered species. “If you chop down a tree full of endangered birds or race a huge ship through a pod of endangered whales, you should be held accountable for your destructive acts,” Brett Hartl, the Center for Biological Diversity’s government affairs director, said. “But this administration wants to give wildlife killers a get out of jail free card. Imposing new limitations on the entire definition of take is a flagrant and illegal attempt to rewrite the Endangered Species Act via unilateral fiat. This would drive imperiled species over the cliff to extinction,” he added. Similarly, the environmental law nonprofit Earthjustice told the Guardian: “The government’s new legal position is a prescription for extinction. It says that as long as you claim you didn’t mean to kill an endangered species, the law can’t and won’t stop you. That’s ridiculous. “The supreme court decided this issue in the Sweet Home case and its ruling still represents the best reading of the Endangered Species Act. We’ll see the Trump administration in court about this.” The Trump administration’s reinterpretation of the ESA is the latest in a series of environmental rollbacks. Since returning to office last January, Trump has moved to weaken federal protections for old-growth forests, potentially jeopardizing habitat for 400 endangered species across the US; scrapped drilling restrictions near a world heritage site in New Mexico; and directed his administration to consider the delisting of gray wolves from the ESA. During the signing ceremony for the latter, Trump asked: “You can shoot them as of today?” Agriculture secretary Brooke Rollins replied that Burgum “has to do a little magic, but yes”.

title: Addison Lee founder owes £20.5m in tax after UK tribunal ruling
summary: HMRC wins challenge over John Griffin’s claim to be non-dom despite having lived in England since childhood
text: The founder of Addison Lee owes £20.5m in tax after a tribunal dismissed a claim that he should be treated as a nom-dom despite living in the UK since childhood. John Griffin had argued he should be treated as a nom-dom due to his connection to Ireland, saying: “I was and am besotted with Ireland, infatuated with Ireland. I believe that I have always been and am Irish.” HM Revenue and Customs challenged the domicile status on Griffin’s self-assessment tax returns from 2013 to 2020, which would have allowed the 84-year-old to not pay UK tax rates on foreign earnings kept outside the country. This week, a London tribunal ruled in the tax authority’s favour. Griffin was born to Irish parents in 1942 and briefly lived there until he moved to London at the age of nine, according to tribunal documents. HMRC argued that England should be considered Griffin’s home, with the businessman raising a family in Hertfordshire and building his London-based taxi empire, having founded Addison Lee in 1975. Tribunal judge Michaela Snelders and tribunal member Gill Hunter said: “We are satisfied that by 5 April 2013, Sir John had settled in England in every meaningful sense.” “England was where he had established his home, raised his family, built his business, accumulated his wealth and organised his personal, social and professional life. “Although he retained a powerful emotional attachment to Ireland and a genuine hope that he might one day spend more time there, those sentiments never crystallised into a sufficiently definite intention to make Ireland his permanent home.” The tax chamber tribunal was told Griffin spent eight nights in Ireland in 2015, one of the years he claimed to be domiciled there, which the chamber ruled was “inconsistent with someone seriously preparing for permanent relocation”. As part of his appeal against HMRC’s stance, Griffin had argued that his domicile should be the same as his father, Jack, who had come to England from Ireland in search of work in 1935. Under UK law, a child’s domicile is the same as their father’s if the parents were married at the time of their birth. Legal counsel for HMRC, however, said Griffin’s domicile status under UK law would have changed when his father’s domicile of choice became England. They argued it had done so some time before Griffin reached adulthood at the age of 21 in 1963. The tribunal agreed with HMRC’s stance. The ruling caps off a long-running inquiry into Griffin’s tax affairs and reflects the period after he sold Addison Lee to private equity firm the Carlyle Group in 2013. The business was reported to be worth £300m at the time. Having Irish domicile would have potentially allowed Griffin to avoid being taxed on earnings made outside the UK, a legal benefit of being classified as a nom-dom. The tribunal’s ruling makes his worldwide income from the period subject to UK tax rules, with HMRC calculating that he owes an additional £20.5m covering the seven-year period. Nom-dom status was scrapped by the Labour UK government in April 2025, after a promise a year earlier by Rishi Sunak’s Conservative administration to do the same. Griffin, knighted in 2024 for services to business and charity, did not give evidence in person to the tribunal after HMRC accepted he was not medically fit to do so due to “cognitive decline”.
