title: Suspect in ‘Putney pusher’ case told family that investigation was ‘murdering him’
summary: Exclusive: Sisters of Nicholas Brandram recount 44-year-old’s deteriorating mental health in days before he took his life
text: Days before Nicholas Brandram, the man suspected of being the “Putney pusher”, killed himself, he told his family that the police investigation was “murdering him”. He had “no fight left” in him, he told his sisters, Alexia Hicks and Sophie Voelcker, and could not see an end to the Metropolitan police investigation, or the online abuse. Brandram’s lawyers warned the Met last week that his mental health had deteriorated and he was receiving treatment in a psychiatric hospital after renewed press reporting that he had been released under investigation. “He said a couple of days ago that this investigation was murdering him. Day by day, he was slowly being murdered,” Hicks, 40, said through tears. “He saw no end to this investigation,” added Voelcker, 45. “My sister and I were keeping a close eye on him because he was telling us he couldn’t go on. He said it more than once in the week before, that he couldn’t keep going. All we could do was just reassure him. We had faith in the system, we had faith in the police, and they neglected him. They failed in their duty of care to him, to the wider family, and we do not want to see another family going through this.” The pair insisted that Brandram, 44, was not the “Putney pusher” and that he died thinking no one would believe in his innocence. He was arrested on suspicion of attempted grievous bodily harm on 15 June, nine years after a jogger shoved a woman headfirst into the path of an oncoming bus on Putney Bridge in south-west London. The case attracted considerable media attention but appeared to elude detectives, who wound down their investigation in 2018, after interviewing 50 men and arresting three suspects. But there was renewed interest in the case after Brandram’s arrest, which his family described as heavy-handed and disproportionate. A number of officers in body armour reportedly swooped on his home address, his sisters said, while a reporter who had been tipped off about the arrest filmed the ordeal. Although Brandram’s name was not published in the media because he had not been charged, his family said that biographical information in reports made him easily identifiable. He was described as a wealthy banker who lived in a £1.4m west London home and an army veteran with links to royalty. Brandram was the grandson of Princess Katherine of Greece, who was a great-granddaughter of Queen Victoria. While in police custody in June over the Putney Bridge incident, he was also arrested on suspicion of possession of class A and class B drugs. His sisters said there was no forensic evidence linking Brandram to the Putney incident and that he had a prominent military tattoo and a withered calf which, they said, distinguished him from the man in footage of the attack on 5 May 2017. That morning, Brandram had walked from his home in Notting Hill Gate to his office in Bond Street and sent his sisters an email from his work account, which they said he could only access from his workplace. They said that evidence was passed on to the police. They added that Brandram had volunteered to take part in an identification parade and provided his DNA for comparison with a sample recovered at the time of the incident. Hicks said detectives told Brandram just days ago that they still did not know when the DNA analysis would be completed. “Our brother willingly provided DNA in an attempt to obviously help clear his name and to complete the investigation, and for weeks now we’ve been asking the police just to complete the DNA test,” Voelcker said. “We’ve always maintained that he’s innocent. He always maintained he was innocent. We just needed the police to complete their inquiry, and it just felt particularly egregious that they were just hanging this DNA test over him.” Hicks said as details of the case kept being reported in the press, her brother became preoccupied by online abuse on forums such as Reddit. “His reputation within a couple of days was in tatters. People saying he’s the alleged pusher, and you can imagine the vitriol that was coming out online,” Voelcker said. “You can imagine what people might say about somebody they think tried to push a woman in front of a bus. There was a lot of people had a lot of views about our brother, about his background, about where he worked.” “And the problem was he was reading it all every day,” Hicks said. “The vitriol is still there and that’s what’s so heartbreaking for us, is that when he took his own life he died thinking that effectively everyone hated him and thought he’d done something awful and that no one would see that he was innocent and he knew that his family were behind him but it wasn’t enough.” The sisters said Brandram had stayed with them in recent days after his mental health deteriorated following the publication of an update about the case that said he had been released under investigation. “He was really talking about ending his life and ending things. And he was very low and said he felt like he had no fight left in him. He couldn’t see the end,” Voelcker said. Brandram was admitted to a psychiatric hospital for six days before being discharged on Sunday. His family insisted the Met police were warned about his mental health. Voelcker tried to boost his mood on Tuesday by telling him it was a beautiful day and that he had many friends and his family supporting him. He was found dead at his home in Chiswick, west London, later that day. The family said their priority was to clear their brother’s name and “to ensure another family does not have to go through what we have as a result of the police delays and leaks to the media”. Hicks said: “Nick was really very loving, enthusiastic. He had an infectious character to be around, very funny. He was an extrovert, so he loved people. He was a much-loved father and uncle.” Voelcker added: “He spent a long time in the army before going into the city. And his reputation was important. He was a proud man. I think that’s the thing and even the fact that he needed to seek help from a psychiatric hospital was a big deal for him.” Ch Supt Dan Knowles, in charge of policing for south-west London, said: “Our thoughts are with Mr Brandram’s family and friends at this deeply distressing time. We recognise the significant impact his death will have on those who knew and loved him. We also understand the strain that being subject to a police investigation can place on individuals and their families. “The investigation remains ongoing. Following Mr Brandram’s release under investigation, it was made clear that inquiries would continue while officers progressed outstanding lines of inquiry and forensic examinations. This remains the position, and further investigative work is ongoing. “Investigations of this nature, particularly those involving complex evidential and forensic work, can take a number of months to complete as officers gather and assess all available evidence.” He added that the force had made a mandatory referral to the Independent Office for Police Conduct on 16 September. • In the UK and Ireland, Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123. Other international helplines can be found at befrienders.org

title: RFK Jr promises anti-vaxxers a ‘friend at the White House’ amid deadly measles outbreak
summary: The US health secretary added that he would’ve made sweeping changes ‘on day one’ but he had to follow the law
text: As the death toll from the worst measles outbreak in decades rises, Robert F Kennedy Jr headlined the Washington DC conference of the anti-vaccine organization Children’s Health Defense, which he led for nearly a decade. “Let me be clear. You have a strong and steadfast friend at the White House,” Kennedy, now serving as secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), told anti-vaccine activists at the conference in a nearly hour-and-a-half-long speech. He urged patience, saying that he would’ve made sweeping changes “on day one” but that he had to follow the law in order to make permanent change. “But as I said, you have friends in the White House, and we are doing this one day at a time,” Kennedy said. He only addressed the measles outbreak, which recently killed four people in Pennsylvania, once. “In our country we care about rare illnesses and deaths. We care about every child who dies from measles. They get headlines,” he said. “I’d ask you to care about children who are dying or suffering or being injured by vaccine injuries.” Recent polling suggests that one quarter of Americans now have doubts about the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccines following a years-long campaign against immunizations by once-fringe actors. But the majority of Americans also disapprove of the Trump administration’s handling of the widening measles outbreak, which killed three people in Texas and Arizona last year in addition to those inPennsylvania. Kennedy described “vaccine-injured children” as “damaged” because of diagnoses of allergies, asthma, ADHD and autism, among other conditions. He also claimed that diabetes, sudden infant death syndrome, and anorexia can be side effects of routine vaccines, and he said that the system to track such effects is “broken”. There is little daylight between Kennedy and his former organization. “I spent 40 years in these battles,” Kennedy said. “I intend to stay in this fight as long as I am able.” He thanked his friends who are still at CHD. Longtime anti-vaccine activists celebrated their unprecedented role in the national conversation, at times expressing astonishment over the ways anti-vaccine sentiment has been elevated to the highest levels of the US government. “We have an opportunity today to speak to our colleagues and our friends in mainstream media,” the CEO of the Children’s Health Defense, Mary Holland, said at the event on Thursday. Andrew Wakefield, a former gastroenterologist whose medical license was revoked after he was found to have fabricated research indicating a link between vaccines and autism, spoke before and immediately after Kennedy. “I could not have imagined two years ago that Bobby [Kennedy] would be in the White House and that President Trump would be saying ‘divide up the MMR into three different’,” said Wakefield, who proposed the same strategy years earlier when he attempted to patent his own single measles shot to compete with the MMR. He stopped to laugh. “What drug was I on that morning?” Anti-vaccine activists had become nervous earlier this year after the White House reportedly put the kibosh on speaking about vaccines before the US midterm elections. “February, March, April, May, vaccine reform got a little quiet, a little scary. You know, behind the scenes, we’re like, “Yeah, what happened?” said Michael Kane, CHD’s director of advocacy. But recent months have shifted vaccines back into the spotlight. “Just a few years ago, we were the, you know, hated stepchild in the corner,” Kane said. “Now we are a national movement that isn’t going anywhere.” The organization laid out its policy agenda, including plans to challenge state-level immunization requirements for school attendance, to recruit younger people to the aging organization, and to combat the installation of cell phone towers for fears of 5G and 6G. Several speakers explicitly linked vaccination to autism, despite decades of research showing no connection. Meanwhile, Kennedy also focused on the role of food systems in health, and touched on efforts to study electromagnetic fields and chem trails. He praised researchers at the University of Southern Denmark, who are now under investigation by their institution, as “the deities of vaccine research”. Kennedy attempted to fund their project in Guinea-Bissau looking at mortality after hepatitis B vaccination before local authorities cancelled the project. Their prior work on vaccines has been called “a house of cards” by other researchers. Mark Gorton, president of the Maha Institute, referred to himself as “the boldest anti-vaxxer in the anti-vax conference”, adding that “only anti-vaxxers can speak clearly enough to raise awareness.” Being called the “largest anti-vaccine conference, probably in the world” is “a red badge of courage”, said sen Ron Johnson, a Republican from Wisconsin. Johnson and Sen Rand Paul, a Republican and physician from Kentucky, both rehashed grievances over the Covid pandemic and the immunizations that were rapidly deployed to stem the tide of illness and death. Republican congressman Thomas Massie said he called Donald Trump soon after the election to ask for the agriculture secretary position. Trump asked, “Are you friends with Bobby? Is he too much for HHS? Don’t you think we need some vaccines?” Massie recounted. Kennedy was nominated to HHS the next day, he said. Massie offered two pieces of advice to the anti-vaccine activists: Instead of trying to get rid of “clowns”, he said, “get the clowns who are here to do what you want. Get them to get in the clown car you want. And use pressure. Treat them like cattle.” Coverage of the measles outbreak is a “psy op” that is “meant to control what I think, what I do, what I believe, and what my attitude towards Bobby Kennedy ought to be,” said Tony Lyons, the publisher of books from Kennedy who now heads Maha Action. Kennedy was frequently invoked as a hero of the movement at the conference. “The truth is, he really is dangerous,” Lyons said, invoking the common refrain from scientists and experts. “I think Bobby Kennedy is the most dangerous individual to this system who’s come along in a generation,” he said to a burst of applause. This article was amended on 17 September 2026 to clarify that Kennedy led Children’s Health Defense for nearly a decade.

title: Nato head: Britain must show ‘credible path’ of annual defence budget increases
summary: Mark Rutte said Britain will need to steadily increase defence spending to meet Nato target of 3.5% of GDP by 2035
text: Britain needs to show “a credible path” of annual increases in its defence budgets to meet a Nato target of spending nearly £30bn more on the military by the middle of the next decade, the head of the alliance said on Thursday. Mark Rutte, Nato’s secretary general, said that Britain could not wait until just before 2035 to lift defence spending to 3.5% of GDP, in an unusually pointed intervention a day after he met prime minister Andy Burnham. In an interview with the Press Association, he said: “And that is why you need a credible path towards that 3.5%, and yearly increments.” The alliance’s secretary general, a former Dutch prime minister, made similar remarks to the BBC, where he said that the UK understood that the target could not be met “in one go in 2034” and that it would have to be achieved gradually. Earlier on Thursday, Rutte met with Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, and Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary. He saw Burnham on Wednesday, at a business park in Didcot, and also met representatives from the defence industry. Keir Starmer signed the UK up to a Nato-wide target of increasing defence spending to 3.5% of GDP in the summer of 2025, under pressure from the US president, Donald Trump. The figure has since been endorsed by Burnham and his chancellor, former defence secretary John Healey. Current spending plans, covering until 2028/9, show defence spending levelling off at 2.7%, nearly £30bn below the ultimate target, raising the question of how it would be achieved after the next general election. It is unclear if taxes or borrowing would have to rise, or other government spending cuts. Healey resigned as defence minister in June because Starmer would not commit to lifting defence spending to 3% of GDP by 2030. At the time Healey said Labour needed to set “a clear path” to meet the Nato commitment, similar language to that used by Rutte in his interviews. But since then Healey and Burnham have avoided committing to the 3% by the end of the decade. Decisions on future spending are likely to be left to the next government spending review due next year, prompting the Nato leader to engage in public lobbying on his trip to Britain. Rutte said he was certain the Burnham government remained behind the ultimate goal and the need to increase defence spending gradually. “I am absolutely confident that when it comes to the yearly increments, they totally take it and accept it, that they have to be there,” he told the BBC. “There has to be a credible path. What that credible path exactly will be, we will see with the spending review next year,” Rutte added. A day earlier, Rutte gave a speech to at Ditchley Park in Oxfordshire, in which he warned that the 32 country military alliance faced “the most dangerous and complex security environment in a generation” with wars in Ukraine, the Middle East coming at time of rising state competition. Nato needed “more UK and more Europe”, he added, to take up the slack as the US reduces its military commitment to the alliance. Trump has long argued that the UK and Europe should match US levels of defence spending and take the lead in defending the continent from Russia aggression.

title: Accused Oregon serial killer indicted in connection with death of sixth woman
summary: Grand jury indicts Jesse Calhoun on a charge of first-degree manslaughter in the death of Elizabeth Gibson
text: An Oregon man accused of killing five women has been indicted in connection with the death of a sixth woman, officials announced this week. Jesse Calhoun was indicted by a grand jury on a charge of first-degree manslaughter in the death of Elizabeth “Libby” Gibson, said the Multnomah county district attorney on Wednesday. Calhoun is accused of causing Gibson’s death and acting “unlawfully and recklessly under circumstances manifesting extreme indifference to the value of human life”. Gibson, who lived in Portland, was 32 when she was last seen in 2022 and reported missing the following year. Officials believe she was killed on or around 18 November 2022 but have not found her body. Calhoun, 41, has already been charged in the killings of Ashley Real, 22; Kristin Smith, 22; Charity Perry, 24; Bridget Webster, 31; and Joanna Speaks, 32, between 2022 and 2023. He has pleaded not guilty to five counts of second-degree murder and four counts of abuse of a corpse. “We will not stop. We will do everything in our power to hold him accountable and see that justice is done for each and every one of these victims. We remain committed to these families for as long as it takes,” Nathan Vasquez, the Multnomah county district attorney, said in a statement. Prosecutors said earlier this year that they plan to try Calhoun for all murders in one trial rather than holding separate proceedings. Calhoun was previously incarcerated for assaulting a police officer, trying to strangle a police dog, burglary and other charges. He was released early in 2021 for helping fight wildfires through a prison program, but Oregon’s governor’s reversed the decision in 2023 when he came under investigation for the deaths. Gibson’s family said in a statement that they were “grateful that a definitive step toward justice is finally being taken”. “Libby was kind, creative, and silly. She welcomed everyone with love and acceptance. Her future was tragically taken from her way too soon,” her siblings said in the statement. “We are deeply appreciative of the tireless work and dedication of the law enforcement officers and the district attorney’s office whose efforts have helped bring us to this point.” Melissa Marrero, the senior deputy district attorney, said the scope of the investigation had been “enormous”. “But all information is useful. And to the extent that individuals have been willing to come forward in the past and provide information to us, no matter how small, that information has led us to where we are here today,” she said in a statement.

title: Outcry as Michigan high school asks girls to share details of menstrual cycles
summary: Students required to disclose information if they wish to make up swimming days lost because of their periods
text: A Michigan high school is facing scrutiny after parents raised concerns over a gym class policy requiring female students to disclose information about their menstrual cycles if they want to make up swimming days missed because of their periods. Under the policy, which appears in a Lakeview high school gym syllabus, female students who miss swimming because of their periods must have a parent submit a written note or email identifying the length of their menstrual cycle before they can make up the missed days. The syllabus states: “Female students will be given the opportunity to make up days, which are missed only because of their menstrual cycle. A written/email note from a parent stating the length of the menstrual duration is required, so the student can make up the days.” “Students will complete dry land workouts to be able to make up the days,” it continues. “Students will not just sit out. Each day that is not made up will be considered a non-participation day and place the student on the grade reduction scale.” The requirement caught the attention of Andy Amsdill, whose daughter attends Lakeview high school. Amsdill told WXYZ Detroit that he was stunned when he saw the requirements in her gym syllabus. “The teacher wants us to either send a note or an email with the suspected length of the cycle which, by itself, is ridiculous,” Amsdill told the outlet. Menstrual cycle length can sometimes be difficult to predict, and the US National Institutes of Health estimates between 14% to 25% of women experience menstrual irregularities. Irregular periods are even more common in young girls. Amsdill later told CBS News that other parents contacted him after he spoke publicly about the syllabus, saying they were glad he had brought attention to the issue. Among them was Bryan Shishakly, whose daughter is now a sophomore at Lakeview. Shishakly said she faced the same requirement during her freshman gym class last year and that it affected her grade. “My response was like, ‘If they ask, you have no obligation to tell them,’ and it did affect her grade,” Shishakly told CBS. “She’s a straight-A student, and she ended up with a C in gym, and I don’t know how fair that is since it’s only going to apply to the girls at the school.” The Lakeview public schools superintendent, Karl D Paulson, issued a statement that read: “We recently became aware of a parent’s concern relative to certain class expectations. Given our commitment to partnering with parents to address any issue that might arise, we immediately sought to schedule a meeting with the parent to engage in a conversation about the concern.” It added: “We look forward to meeting with the parent in the coming days and working collaboratively with that objective. The Lakeview school district remains fully committed to educational excellence and best practices in all it does.” It remains unclear whether the same requirement appears in other gym class syllabuses at Lakeview high school, or whether the district intends to remove it following the criticism. The controversy has also prompted Amsdill to question whether the policy could be in violation of Title IX, which prohibits sex-based discrimination in education programs or activities that receive federal financial assistance. Lakeview public schools addresses Title IX on its website and includes a separate guide aimed at helping students identify sexual harassment. The guide defines it as “unwanted sexual remarks or behaviors” and says that can include “comments about students’ bodies or how they look or act”.

title: Charles sounded 'giddily elated' after Diana’s death, claims Earl Spencer
summary: In latest extracts from upcoming memoir, Diana’s brother suggests some in Buckingham Palace were ‘relieved’ at her death
text: The brother of the late Diana, Princess of Wales, has claimed in published extracts of his new memoir that King Charles sounded “giddily elated – like a lottery winner” in a phone call to him immediately after her death. Earl Spencer also says he believed Buckingham Palace wanted William and Harry and himself to walk behind Diana’s coffin because the then prince was “adamant” he was going to walk and palace officials feared “members of the public might shout abuse at him”. By getting Diana’s sons to walk, “that would surely guarantee against insults flying”, he wrote. The memoir, Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, due to be published next week, has already made headlines, with Spencer alleging that during a heated phone call before Diana’s funeral, the king remarked: “rest assured, we’ll forget her soon enough.” Buckingham Palace issued a robust rebuttal on Wednesday evening, saying in a statement: “While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss.” In new extracts, published on Thursday on the website of the Daily Mail, which is serialising the book, Spencer suggests that some inside Buckingham Palace were “relieved – indeed pleased” at Diana’s death in a Paris car crash. It was his suspicion that Charles’s first reaction must have been to think how he could now marry Camilla Parker Bowles. According to Spencer, Diana had confided in a friend that days before their wedding, Charles had told her “she needed to know he was very happy to marry her, but he was not actually in love with her”, and she was certain he was “entering their marriage with his heart elsewhere”. Diana tried to break off the engagement after finding a bracelet Charles had bought for Camilla, who is now the queen, he writes. But their father was “appalled”, telling her “it was impossible to pull out of such an enormous commitment at that point”. Spencer says in the book that he also believes Charles may have contributed to the princess’s eating disorder, saying Diana’s waist shrank from 29in to 23.5in between the engagement and wedding after she was “devastated” at her fiance squeezing her waist and saying: “Oh, a bit chubby here, aren’t we?” He was also convinced Diana had ADHD and, like himself, suffered from Rejection Sensitive Dysphoria. He writes: “It is a sad fact that, in her later years, Diana drove herself more than once to Beachy Head, the highest chalk sea cliff in England, while contemplating ending it all. Her love for her sons stopped her from going further.” The excerpt goes on to say that Diana told him she was going to get divorced and that “my husband is in love with his valet”. Spencer, 62, has said he wrote the memoir to correct “untruths” told about his elder sister. The row over the book overshadowed a busy day for the royal family, with the Duke of Sussex also entering the mix with an engagement of his own. Harry, who it is understood was aware of his uncle’s book in advance but not its contents, arrived at the inaugural Invictus Spirit awards in London on Thursday evening in his first appearance since returning to the UK from the US last month. Harry was joined by, among others, the comedian James Corden, singers Jess Glynne and Sonique, rugby star James Haskell and actor Ross Kemp for the champagne reception and fundraiser at the Old Naval College in Greenwich, south London. The evening was to recognise those who have beaten the odds, supported others in their recovery, advanced sport and rehabilitation or made an outstanding contribution to the wider Invictus community. Giving a speech at the awards, Harry recalled how Invictus had begun. He said: “In 2008, flying home from Afghanistan, I travelled alongside three seriously injured British servicemen and the coffin of a Danish soldier. “That flight stayed with me because it helped me begin to understand two things about the military that would shape the rest of my life: it gives you purpose, identity, belonging, a team; and, in a matter of seconds, injury or illness can take it all away. “Years later, after seeing the Warrior Games in America, we brought an idea back to London. In September 2014, more than 400 competitors from 13 nations came together for the first ever Invictus games. Now, 12 years later, thousands have benefited. We have 26 nations in our community, and the games are coming home.” The Prince and Princess of Wales were on their first official trip to the Isle of Bute off the west coast of Scotland. The couple, who hold the titles of Duke and Duchess of Rothesay in Scotland, visited the namesake town of Rothesay, dropped in at a shinty club and stopped at a pub while meeting community leaders and volunteers. Charles, meanwhile, was appearing in public for the first time since Spencer’s allegations were aired, at an AI summit he had convened at Dumfries House, in Ayrshire. Addressing global tech leaders, he warned of the “existential dangers” of AI systems falling into the wrong hands. As those who have created these technologies had warned, AI risked “developing darker capacities – perhaps even to take life”, he said. The king spoke of the need for reassurance that “our humanity remains sacred” and “that we will not lose control of our destiny, or our souls”.

title: Judge orders Trump administration to give 30 days’ notice before moving to demolish Kennedy Center
summary: Ruling comes amid demolition threats by Donald Trump after being stymied from adding his name to centre
text: A federal judge has ordered the Trump administration to give at least 30 days’ notice before moving to demolish the John F Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts after the US president warned that it could be “ripped down”. The US district judge Christopher Cooper issued the order on Thursday after lawyers for the Democratic congresswoman Joyce Beatty submitted evidence of Trump’s comments and sought clarification over whether the building could be closed or bulldozed. Trump said on Wednesday that his administration deserved recognition for its efforts to renovate the Kennedy Center, including by putting his name on the national arts complex in Washington. “I think that the Trump administration should certainly have recognition because, frankly, if we don’t do that, it’s going to close,” he told reporters in Charlotte, North Carolina. “It’ll end up being ripped down.” The Kennedy Center was established by Congress as a living memorial to the slain president John F Kennedy and opened in 1971. It has hosted many of the world’s leading performers and run numerous educational programmes. But the centre shut down this week following claims of serious structural deterioration, and its board has voted to close it for up to two years for a $257m renovation. Matt Floca, the centre’s executive director and chief operating officer, said in a court filing that the building had been closed for at least seven days to assess “acute risks to public safety resulting from continued structural deterioration”. He said the temporary closure followed an inspection of the roof terrace canopy and a partial ceiling collapse earlier this month, and was separate from the longer-term renovation plans. The administration has said the seven-day closure does not breach an earlier court order restricting its ability to shut the centre. Beatty, an ex-officio member of the Kennedy Center board, has challenged Trump’s takeover of the institution and his attempts to put his name on the building. Her lawyers argued that the temporary closure could become a permanent shutdown lasting two years, which they said would violate the court’s previous orders. They also submitted an Agence France-Presse (AFP) photograph showing Trump onboard Air Force One apparently looking at a placard bearing the words “Kennedy Center DEMOLISHED”. The final letters were obscured by the aircraft’s window frame and the image does not establish that demolition was being planned. The photo, taken by the AFP photographer Brendan Smialowski as Trump returned to Washington from North Carolina, was widely circulated on social media and included in Beatty’s court filing. Cooper rejected Beatty’s request for an emergency hearing but ordered the administration to provide at least 30 days’ notice before taking any steps towards demolition. The administration is expected to ask the judge to dissolve an earlier order so it can proceed with what it describes as necessary restoration and renovation work. Cooper ruled on Tuesday that the Kennedy Center could not put Trump’s name on its exterior without congressional approval. Trump’s name had previously been added to the facade by the board but was removed in June following an earlier ruling by the judge. The board had proposed wording describing the building as the “John F Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts Restored and Renovated By President Donald J Trump”, as well as renaming the plaza and adding further recognition if a Trump Kennedy Center fund reached $100m. Those proposals were rejected by Cooper, who said changes to the institution’s name required Congress’s approval. Trump has argued that the centre has been badly maintained and would require substantial government subsidy to remain open. “It’s in very, very bad shape, very dangerous shape,” he said. “You see steel falling down. You see plaster falling off ceilings. You see a lot of dangers.” Beatty has accused Trump and his board of using the closure to circumvent the court’s orders. In a statement, she said the Kennedy Center was “a sacred, living memorial to President Kennedy” and said she would continue efforts to prevent it being “shuttered or demolished”. Hakeem Jeffries, the House Democratic leader, also criticised the plans, saying Democrats would find a way to “stop the president from another vanity project and waste of taxpayer resources”. Trump installed himself as the chair of the Kennedy Center last year after removing its previous leadership and replacing board members with his own appointees. It has since become one of several Washington institutions and landmarks at the centre of his efforts to reshape the capital and attach his name to major projects. On Thursday Barbra Streisand, a Kennedy Center honoree in 2008, questioned the closing of the center for repairs and called the controversy surrounding its operation “galling and painful to witness”. Of Trump’s attempts to add his name to the centre, she said in a statement to the Associated Press: “You can easily imagine my indignation at seeing this revered institution become the subject of such a bitter struggle over one man’s name and unchecked ego.”

title: White House withdraws nomination of ex-state trooper Lance Schroyer to head ICE
summary: Critics had criticized administration for nominating Schroyer, who has no formal experience working in ICE
text: The White House has withdrawn the nomination of Lance Schroyer, a former Oklahoma state trooper, to head Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), less than three months after announcing his role. Critics had initially criticized administration officials for nominating Schroyer, who has no formal experience working in ICE, to lead Donald Trump’s aggressive immigration enforcement agenda. Schroyer previously worked as a member of homeland security secretary Markwayne Mullin’s security detail when he was in the Senate. Since then, Schroyer has been serving as an adviser to Mullin. White House officials did not give a reason for withdrawing Schroyer’s nomination in an announcement posted on the White House website on Thursday. But Schroyer’s nomination stalled in the Senate because Rand Paul, the Republican chair of the homeland security and governmental affairs committee, had yet to schedule a hearing. The Guardian has asked the White House for more information. Trump initially announced Schroyer’s nomination in June, calling him “a PATRIOT with real operational experience, and proven leader with DECADES of experience locking up the worst of the worst”. At the time, the president urged the Senate to confirm Schroyer immediately. But some Department of Homeland Security officials expressed skepticism about Schroyer’s qualifications. Unnamed DHS employees told Politico in August they didn’t want Schroyer to take over and implement changes. ICE has not had an official director since 2017. The agency has been overseen by several acting directors, most recently David Venturella. The agency, and its leaders, have faced intense scrutiny in Trump’s second term due to the rapid expansion of the agency to accommodate the president’s intense crackdown on immigrants in the United States. ICE officers had been deployed to cities across the US to conduct sweeping arrests, often wearing face coverings and discreet clothing. Videos of officers forcefully grabbing individuals circulated online, provoking backlash from locals who accused the agency of instilling fear in communities. That scrutiny escalated sharply earlier this year, after federal agents fatally shot two 37-year-old US citizens, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, during ICE operations in Minnesota and accused both of agitating law enforcement. Then acting ICE director Todd Lyons, who was already facing criticism for overseeing officers’ aggressive actions, was further condemned after refusing to apologize to the Pretti and Good families. In May, Lyons left his position leading ICE. Nationwide outrage toward ICE forced the Trump administration to adjust its approach to detaining and deporting hundreds of thousands of immigrants, in part by diminishing the public-facing aspect of it. As a result, Mullin and Tom Homan, the White House “border czar” who has taken a more hands-on role in immigration enforcement, have faced criticism from Trump allies for not doing enough to deport immigrations. It is unclear whether the Trump administration plans to nominate another ICE director immediately or who that may be.

title: With Kemi’s new shadow chancellor, the Tories must hope for a bout of public amnesia
summary: Andrew Griffith is keen on clearing red tape. Good job he wasn’t part of a Treasury team that abolished the Office for Tax Simplification
text: On days like this, it’s not hard to be overwhelmed by existential futility. At the current rate of progress, the UK looks on course to wipe itself out far sooner than it would with any interference from AI. Everything feels hopeless. Years of minimal growth and a cost of living crisis. The tech bros and the bankers may be getting richer. The rest of us? Not so much. And there’s no end in sight. Andy Burnham may offer better vibes, but he is fighting a losing battle against global forces – wars, energy prices, borrowing costs – that he can’t control. You can feel the hope drain out of him as each day passes. Mr Congeniality is not quite so congenial as he once was. All the economic forecasts suggest things are going to get even worse in the next year. Even Labour allies are preparing the ground for a tough budget next month. The chancellor, John Healey, has been making it known that even he is surprised by just how bad things are. Can’t think why. The rest of us have known for a while, and he’s had the benefit of sitting at the Cabinet table with Rachel Reeves for the past two years. Perhaps he dozed off while she was speaking. He wouldn’t have been the first. Still, the government does have one thing going for it. There is currently no one better. That might not be much comfort to some people, but it helps Labour sleep a little easier. Reform members seem determined to take themselves down. If not by financial scandals then by their own stupidity. That’s why Richard Tice has such a prominent role within the party. Only on Wednesday, Dicky was at it again. Responding to the news that Healey had made the TUC general secretary, Paul Nowak, a non-executive director of the Bank of England, Motormouth Dicky immediately declared Britain had descended into a socialist hell. Were he better informed, he would have known it’s been a tradition for the last 40 years or so that the TUC head honcho gets a gig at the Bank. One started by that well-known Commie apparatchik Margaret Thatcher. But why let that get in the way of an ill-thought through social media clip. Usually, Dicky is in a league of his own in the competition to be the dimmest and least competent MP in Westminster. But this time Kemi Badenoch was keen to join in with a similar post. As much to remind everyone that the Tory party was still not ready to be taken seriously or forgiven for its 14 years of unmanaged decline as anything else. And where Kemi led, Andrew Griffith followed with his own statement insisting the unions would soon be running the country. You’d have thought that a shadow chancellor, with experience as a junior minister in the Treasury, would have inside knowledge of the Bank of England’s conventions. There again, Andrew will be Andrew. Living proof of Kemi’s currently insurmountable problem. She can say all she wants that she has changed the party, but all the country sees is more or less the same faces promising that this time everything will be different. Something that’s more or less inevitable when you have a party of fewer than 120 MPs. It takes some cheek to appoint a backer of Liz Truss’s mini-budget as your shadow chancellor. Two fingers to everyone. Right now, Griffith’s main function appears to be to make people yearn for the return of Mel Stride. The Melster may have been a bit useless, but he always looked as if he was trying to be decent. The Tories have set a lot of store by the fact that Andrew made a lot of money in the private sector before becoming an MP. Yet there is no sign that he can translate those skills into the public sphere. In Westminster, he is most noted for having loaned his £9.5m house to Boris Johnson’s leadership campaign team, for declaring that Elon Musk had saved humanity by buying Twitter and that too many Lib Dems were vegans. On Thursday, Griffith chose to make his debut speech as shadow chancellor at a college in north London. He can only hope that not many people were listening because it rapidly became apparent that he didn’t have much to say. And what he did say was – not to put too fine a point on it – half-arsed and intellectually dishonest. Where to start? The optics weren’t great. Looking like you’ve been locked in the boiler room by the college principal isn’t the best of looks. Though maybe it would have been better if he had been. There were no apologies, no acknowldgement of the Tories’ part in the current economic state of the country. It was as though July 2024 had been year zero. Everything had been just fine until then and Labour had ruined everything. “The chancellor must rule out raising taxes,” he said. Something he, himself, is unwilling to do. The Tories have committed to keeping the current tax thresholds until 2028, a stealth tax that raises billions more for the Treasury each year. It was breathtaking. But there was more. Griffith was determined to simplify tax regulation and red tape. Another astonishing feat of amnesia. It had been Andrew who played a key role in the Treasury abolishing the Office for Tax Simplification while in office. He must think we’re stupid. Surprisingly, he had nothing to say on the one tax cut that Kemi has actually committed to exploring. The abolition of inheritance tax. A proposal that would benefit the wealthiest 5%. So much for being the party of small business and the self-employed. Sometimes, it feels as if the current iteration of the Tories just can’t help themselves. They are their own burial ground. There was just time for Griffith to reiterate that Nowak’s appointment to the Bank of England was a death knell for the country – you’d have thought he might have wanted to rethink this after a night’s sleep – before he brought the event to a close. Astonishingly, he thought it had all gone brilliantly.

title: Jon Kyl, former Republican US senator who served three terms, dies aged 84
summary: The Arizona senator shepherded the confirmation of conservative supreme court justice Brett Kavanaugh
text: Jon Kyl, a Republican former US senator from Arizona who shepherded conservative supreme court justice Brett Kavanaugh through his confirmation hearing, died on Thursday at 84, his family announced. The cause was complications from a neurological disease, according to a statement. Last December, Kyl announced that he had been diagnosed with dementia. “We know that Jon belonged to all of Arizona, a state he loved and explored with vigor, curiosity and wonder. Serving his state and nation in Congress was a privilege and responsibility he honored and respected,” his family said. An attorney, Kyl won election to the US House in 1986 then the Senate in 1994, where he would serve three terms. He rose to become the Republican whip and served from 2007 until departing the chamber at the beginning of 2013, when his party was in the minority. Kyl lobbied and practiced law after leaving office, but returned to the public eye in 2018 to assist with the confirmation of Kavanaugh, a federal appeals court judge whom Donald Trump had nominated to replace Anthony Kennedy on the supreme court. As Kavanaugh’s nomination was being considered, Arizona’s Republican governor, Doug Ducey, appointed Kyl to fill the seat left vacant by the senator John McCain’s death. Kyl served in the chamber for the final three months of the year and voted to confirm Kavanaugh, before resigning and being replaced by Republican Martha McSally. Katie Hobbs, Arizona’s Democratic governor, called Kyl “a dedicated statesman who always cared deeply for our state”. John Thune, the Republican Senate majority leader, said Kyl “loved his state of Arizona and was a true legislator’s legislator”. Thune added: “He was an incredibly hard worker and honorably returned to service when his state called. He was a dear friend and will be missed.”

title: Ohio mother of 16 children rescued from ‘deplorable’ conditions pleads not guilty to child neglect
summary: Attorney also says Elizabeth Siders, 34, has been almost continuously pregnant since 15 without regular healthcare
text: An Ohio mother whose 16 children were rescued from appalling conditions pleaded not guilty to child endangerment and neglect charges in court on Wednesday. Elizabeth Siders, 34, is one of four family members, including her husband, Gary Siders Jr, charged with 16 charges of child endangerment and neglect after investigators found the children, who were 17 months to 18 years old, in “deplorable conditions” at the decrepit family home in the tiny village of Hamden in July. The children appeared “almost feral” after having been confined to one 12ft-by-12ft room among human waste for much of the past four years, authorities said. They did not attend school, and some were unable to speak at all. The eldest was developmentally disabled and could not even spell her name. During her appearance at Vinton county court on Wednesday, Siders pleaded not guilty to all counts. The judge deemed her a flight risk and raised her bond from $250,000 to $550,000. She and her husband, with whom she has been ordered to have no contact, have also been indicted in a separate case involving two counts of sexual battery and two counts of unlawful sexual conduct with a minor. Gary Siders Jr pleaded not guilty in August. Last week his father, Gary Siders Sr, was found incompetent to stand trial. Elizabeth Siders, Gary Siders Jr and his mother, Christina Siders, have also filed competency evaluation requests. The alleged victim was not one of the couple’s children, but another relative between the ages of 13 and 16, according to a copy of the indictment obtained by People, who was in their care for a period in 2022. The charges were among those that Elizabeth Siders pleaded not guilty to on Wednesday. Birth records obtained by local media outlet ABC6 show that Siders gave birth to a child in February 2022, when the alleged abuse was taking place. She also gave birth prematurely to twins in November 2022, who died shortly after birth. Her attorney, Tommy Stolly, told the court that his client still asks to see her children. The judge has ordered no contact. Stolly also argued that Elizabeth Siders had been pregnant for most of her life since getting married at 15 and had never received proper postpartum care, leaving her “suffering from mental health issues”. Stolly said he had “competency concerns”. “We have an individual … who was married at age 15, who has essentially been pregnant for the better part of two decades … [Siders] has never fully gone through any postpartum period and has not been receiving regular medical care that would be appropriate for someone who has had 16, 18 children,” he told the court. “So, I have concerns about what effects those have had on her, what effect it has had on being married at such a young age, being contained within the environment of the Siders household, and essentially not knowing any life outside of it.” Stolly has therefore asked for a competency evaluation, which is still pending and will determine the next steps in the case. “We are not saying that there’s any conduct at this point that has been proven, certainly, by the state to be illegal, but if her mindset was not there, and she didn’t have the ability or the capacity to understand it and make decisions in an informed way, that could certainly negate legal liability,” Stolly said. There is also speculation that Siders is currently pregnant again, after she appeared in court without handcuffs. Her attorney declined to comment when approached by a reporter from the Columbia Dispatch.

title: Greens urge Zack Polanski to take stance on proposed policy declaring ‘Zionism is racism’
summary: The Green leader has not spoken publicly about the motion, which is likely to be debated at the party’s conference in October
text: The Greens are pushing Zack Polanski to take a stance on a potential party policy stating “Zionism is racism”, with some fearing it could alienate Jewish supporters if it was passed. Polanski, who leads the Greens in England and Wales, has not spoken publicly about the motion, which came top of a members’ vote of policy motions to be debated at the party conference in Brighton at the start of October, and is thus almost certain to feature. The Greens make party policy by member votes at conferences. If passed, the motion would equate Zionism – the movement for a Jewish state – with racism, would call for a single Palestinian state, and would risk members who supported Zionism being disciplined for racism. While Polanski is believed to have reservations about the motion, some in the party believe he is wary of speaking out publicly to avoid angering left-leaning members who have joined the Greens in large numbers under his leadership, a number of whom have strong views on Gaza and Israel. “Zack can try to be everything to everyone, and that doesn’t always work in politics,” one senior Green said. “But he is in a difficult position. Some of the supporters of the motion can be quite aggressive.” A motion with the same title was submitted to the Greens’ spring conference but was never debated due to time constraints. If the motion had been debated, it is understood that the party’s MPs and Polanski would have opposed it. Polanski has not given a view yet this time but is understood to have concerns about any motion that could leave Jewish members feeling unwelcome in the party, or which could be seen as not helping a peace process. Some in the party view the coming weeks, and whether Polanski takes a stance or not, as a test of his leadership, and whether he is willing to challenge some of the new Green members, particularly those who were formerly in Jeremy Corbyn’s Labour. The motion calls for “a single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine with Jerusalem as its capital, equal rights for all, and the right of return for Palestinians and their descendants”, and says the Palestinian people have the full right to “resistance and liberation from Israeli occupation, domination and subjugation” within international law. If passed, Zionism “will be treated as any other form of racism” by the party, it adds. Two amendments to tone down the motion have been tabled, which one Green source said Polanski appeared to support. A Green official said that many activists loyal to the party’s leadership might not be at the autumn conference because it takes place a week before voting in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, in which Polanski hopes to take Keir Starmer’s old seat from Labour, potentially leaving more scope for others to push through the motion. “The risk is that if it passes as it is we are alienating ourselves from the Jewish community in the UK, a lot of whom are not big fans of the current Israeli government,” a Green source said. There was, they added, a parallel worry about internal splits, with some Green activists in leaked WhatsApp chats warning that Polanski was “struggling to overcome Zionist indoctrination”. They said: “In the past, even highly contested policy debates in the Greens have always been conducted in a mature and sensible way, even [a] boring way. Now it’s changed.”

title: US passenger duct-taped to plane seat says: ‘I don’t remember any of it’
summary: After being read charges, Layne Lundeen said: ‘I assaulted a police officer? Is that what it says? I don’t have my glasses’
text: An American Airlines passenger who was duct-taped to his seat following an alleged outburst including racial and homophobic slurs said that he does not recall the incident. On 3 September, 67-year old Layne Lundeen was restrained in his first-class seat with duct tape and zip ties over alleged unruly behavior. The American Airline Flight 618 was originally traveling from Dallas, Texas, to Newark, New Jersey, and was diverted to the Baltimore/Washington Thurgood Marshall airport in an emergency landing. Upon landing, authorities arrested Lundeen and charged him with second-degree assault and disorderly conduct. In a court hearing the following day, Lundeen said, “I don’t remember any of what happened,” according to a recording recently reviewed by the Baltimore Banner. The outlet added that after being read his charges, Lundeen said: “I assaulted a police officer? Is that what it says? I don’t have my glasses.” He added: “Oh my god, what a mess … I don’t remember any of it.” The Guardian has reached out to Lundeen’s lawyer for comment. Speaking to ABC following the incident, Juan Mejia, a former law enforcement officer and one of the flight’s passengers who helped restrain Lundeen, said that he had allegedly “made derogatory remarks to the staff of American Airlines and other passengers – racial slurs, vulgar language, very offensive to the women.” Another passenger, Richard Olenick, told CNN that Lundeen had allegedly also tried to hit the passenger next to him, as well as a woman who tried to intervene. Olenick, who also helped restrain Lundeen in his seat using duct tape, told the outlet: “Physically it lessened his ability to move for sure, but it did not solve the issue. He was still pushing and resisting and trying to get up.” American Airlines has also issued a statement, saying: “The safety and security of our customers and team members is our top priority and we do not tolerate violence. We thank our team members for their professionalism and our customers for their understanding.” Meanwhile, Lundeen’s former employer, Long Realty in Tucson, Arizona, said in a Facebook statement that it had “ended its affiliation” with him. “Long Realty is aware of reports concerning criminal charges filed against a former affiliated real estate agent arising from an incident that allegedly occurred during a commercial flight. Upon learning of the incident, Long Realty promptly ended its affiliation with the individual. The individual is no longer associated with or authorized to represent Long Realty in any capacity,” the company said.

title: New lawsuit alleges Epstein possessed ‘child sexual abuse material of countless children’
summary: Two women who filed suit against Epstein estate ask court to order program to notify potential victims
text: Jeffrey Epstein’s estate is facing a new lawsuit filed by two women who allege that Epstein possessed child sexual abuse material (CSAM) of them. They want a judge to order that a program be set up to identify and notify all individuals whose “unlawful sexualized images” might have been in Epstein’s collection, and are also seeking monetary damages. The complaint was filed this week in the US district court for the southern district of New York on behalf of two plaintiffs, who are anonymous in the filing but described as survivors of Epstein’s CSAM crimes. The lawsuit was filed against Epstein’s former lawyer Darren Indyke and Epstein’s former accountant Richard Kahn, who are being sued in their capacities as co-executors of Epstein’s estate. Attorneys for Indyke and Kahn, who have both said that they had no knowledge of Epstein’s crimes during their employment, did not immediately respond to a request for comment about the complaint on Wednesday. The complaint claims that for more than two decades, Epstein, who died in a Manhattan jail in 2019 while awaiting trial on federal sex-trafficking charges, possessed, transported, produced and distributed “child pornography and/or child sexual abuse material of countless children”. It alleges that Epstein “acquired by theft” nude or partly nude images of the first plaintiff, referred to in the document as Jane Doe, and that he transported the material across state lines and retained it. The lawsuit argues that many of those depicted in the CSAM that they say was possessed by Epstein have never been identified or notified through the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children’s victim-identification program. With regard to the second plaintiff, identified in the complaint under the pseudonym “Amy”, the lawsuit alleges that “upon information and belief, Epstein acquired CSAM images” of her. The complaint alleges that beginning in the 1990s, Epstein “created and kept” in his locked safe in his New York City home a “‘modeling book’ of sexualized images of children”. It further alleges that beginning in “at least in the 2000s, Epstein had his assistant take nude, sexualized photographs of multiple children, paid them for the images, and then used those photographs for his own sexual gratification and perhaps that of others”. Jane Doe alleges that she was around 12 years old when Epstein stole photographs of her partly nude, which the complaint claims had originally been taken “as part of an artist study for and catalogued, numbered and maintained by the artist in a lockbox”. The lawsuit alleges that Epstein also “stole nude or partially nude photos of another minor” and transported these images across state lines. The complaint also alleges that “despite contemporaneous reports made to law enforcement, specifically alerting law enforcement that Epstein had obtained these photos of Jane Doe, and similar photos of another minor, no one in law enforcement took action to prosecute anyone or even investigate these reports”. It adds that “upon learning that Epstein had possessed sexualized images of her as a child, Jane Doe suffered and continues to suffer severe emotional distress”. “Amy” alleges in the complaint that she is a victim of “actively traded CSAM which has been in distribution since the late 1990s to present day”. The lawsuit alleges that “on information and belief” images of her are contained within the CSAM collection seized from Epstein’s properties. In a statement to the Guardian, one of the lawyers representing the plaintiffs, Margaret Mabie, of Marsh Law, said that according to the released files, a report completed on Epstein’s collection identified 15 or more hits of known series like Amy’s and that “to our knowledge, none of the victims identified in that report, or in any other CSAM discovered in Epstein’s collection, have ever received notice”. The complaint also alleges that other people, “including Epstein’s employees and/or coconspirators, had access to, viewed, or otherwise received from Epstein, the CSAM images in his possession, including images of Jane Doe and ‘Amy’”. The two plaintiffs are bringing the lawsuit both individually and on behalf of a proposed class of other survivors they seek to represent, who are described as “all persons who were under the age of 18 at the time they appeared in any visual depiction of child pornography, including CSAM, contained within any image, video, or electronic media collections seized from properties or devices controlled by Jeffrey E Epstein, including the media identified in the Epstein Files Transparency Act productions and the materials described in the July 6, 2026, FBI and [justice department] memorandum”. In a statement this week, Hillary Nappi, of AWK Survivor Advocate Attorneys, said that their goal with the lawsuit “is accountability and identification”. “We want the estate to preserve and account for everything seized from Epstein’s properties, and we want a real, court supervised process to identify and notify every survivor depicted in that collection,” Nappi said. “Many of them have no idea their images exist in his files, and they deserve to know, and they deserve the chance to seek justice. “Survivors have waited years for accountability, and this case opens the door for others depicted in his collection who don’t even know they’re in it,” Nappi added.

title: Nicholas Brandram’s family deny he was ‘Putney pusher’ and say Met police pressure led to his death
summary: Banker, 44, was arrested in connection with 2017 incident but family say ‘no credible evidence’ he was involved
text: The family of Nicholas Brandram have denied he was the so-called “Putney pusher” and said he “took his own life after months of immense pressure caused by a Metropolitan police investigation”. Brandram, 44, was found unresponsive at a property in Chiswick, west London, believed to be his home, on Tuesday evening. The senior city banker had been arrested in June on suspicion of attempted grievous bodily harm in connection with an incident nearly 10 years ago on Putney Bridge, in which a jogger shoved a woman headfirst into the path of an oncoming bus. The Metropolitan police said Brandram had been released under investigation after his arrest. On Thursday, a spokesperson for the police complaints watchdog, the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC), confirmed the force had referred itself over its prior contact with Brandram. He said: “We have received a mandatory referral from the Met police relating to prior contact officers had with Nicholas Brandram, who was sadly found unresponsive and declared deceased on 15 September. We are currently assessing the referral before deciding whether further action is required from us.” Earlier, a statement released on behalf of his immediate family on Thursday said Brandram had taken his own life after “months of immense pressure caused by a Metropolitan police investigation into whether he was the so-called ‘Putney Pusher’”. His family denied his involvement in the incident and claimed the police had no forensic evidence linking him to it. They said: “There was no forensic evidence linking Nick to it, no evidence placing him on Putney Bridge at that time, and no credible evidence that he was the man shown in the footage. In fact, the evidence proved the opposite. “Despite that, the police chose to arrest Nick rather than invite him to attend for interview. They searched his home, and the Met police press team then released information which inevitably led to speculation and Nick being identified in subsequent reporting.” The family added: “For Nick, the consequences did not disappear. He was left for months carrying the stigma of an appalling allegation which the police themselves clearly recognised was unsupported by the evidence. “He lived with the shame, anxiety, humiliation and extraordinary pressure created by a wholly unnecessary investigation.” They said the police had repeatedly been asked to end their investigation and had been warned about the impact the investigation was having on Brandram’s mental health, saying: “Even then, the investigation was not brought to an end. As a result, Nick is dead.” Ch Supt Dan Knowles, in charge of policing for south-west London, said: “Our thoughts are with Mr Brandram’s family and friends at this deeply distressing time. We recognise the significant impact his death will have on those who knew and loved him. We also understand the strain that being subject to a police investigation can place on individuals and their families. “The investigation remains ongoing. Following Mr Brandram’s release under investigation, it was made clear that enquiries would continue while officers progressed outstanding lines of enquiry and forensic examinations. This remains the position, and further investigative work is ongoing. “Investigations of this nature, particularly those involving complex evidential and forensic work, can take a number of months to complete as officers gather and assess all available evidence. “As is required whenever a person dies following previous contact with police, a mandatory referral was made to the Independent Office for Police Conduct on 16 September.” The Met police had not previously named the suspect. Brandram was a director at HSBC and had previously served in the military, reaching the rank of captain. He was the grandson of Princess Katherine of Greece, who was the great-granddaughter of Queen Victoria, the Daily Telegraph reported in 2013, when he was convicted of crashing his Harley-Davidson motorbike into a female cyclist around Hyde Park Corner and driving off without leaving his details. In an interview with the Citywealth website in March this year, Brandram said he was a senior relationship manager at HSBC Private Bank. He said: “I usually bicycle into our office in Mayfair from my home in west London. And then from there, can either stay at my desk, go to Canary Wharf or the City, or get on a train or go to the airport. My first meeting is ideally over breakfast and I’m ideally home for bath time. I’m a co-parenting single father with a three-year-old.” Brandram said his proudest professional achievement was being invited to a Buckingham Palace garden party after military service in Afghanistan, and that the person he most admired was his mother. “She raised three children as a single parent and is the busiest person I know,” he said. “I’ve never met someone with greater moral integrity and courage, as well as resilience and stamina.”

title: Human remains discovered in London parkland identified as missing woman Joanne Sheen
summary: 56-year-old man arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to commit murder after discovery of woman reported missing in 2020
text: A body found in an area of London shrubland that was partly cleared of foliage by a wildfire in August is that of a woman who disappeared from Hampshire nearly seven years ago, police have said. A man has been arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to commit murder after the remains were identified as Joanne Sheen. She was reported missing in February 2020, having last been seen the previous December. The Metropolitan police were called on 12 August after bones were found at the parkland known as The Pits, in south-west London. The area had been the site of a grass fire shortly before. Scotland Yard opened a murder investigation, but Hampshire and Isle of Wight constabulary took over once the remains had been identified after extensive forensic examination and DNA testing. Sheen, who was 44 and a mother of three, had not been seen since she travelled from Fareham, in Hampshire, heading for her home city of Southampton. A 56-year-old man from Southampton has now been arrested by Hampshire police and is in custody. DCI Toby Elcock, from the Hampshire police’s major crime team, said: “This is a significant development in what has been a long and complex investigation and provides us with several new lines of enquiry, which we are exploring with our dedicated team. “While this tragic discovery is not the outcome Joanne’s family, or any of us, had hoped for, we hope the identification of her remains can at least begin to provide some answers after many years of uncertainty. “Throughout this investigation, Joanne’s family have shown tremendous strength and dignity in the face of unimaginable circumstances, and our thoughts remain with them at this incredibly difficult time. “As our investigation progresses, we remain committed to establishing exactly what happened to Joanne and ensuring that those responsible are held accountable. “There may still be people who have information about Joanne’s disappearance, her movements before she went missing, or how she came to be in Feltham. The passage of time does not lessen the importance of that information. No matter how small or insignificant it may seem, we would urge anyone who may know something to come forward. “We understand that coming forward may feel difficult, particularly if you are worried about the consequences, but we are asking you to think about the family who are left without their loved-one and who are waiting for answers. Please do the right thing. If you know something, now is the time to come forward. “We are also pleased that Crimestoppers has agreed to reinstate its £20,000 reward offer in support of our investigation. If anyone has information but does not feel comfortable speaking directly to police, I would encourage them to contact Crimestoppers anonymously.”

title: Are Trump’s Official Papers His Personal Property?
