title: Pennsylvania asks CDC for emergency help as measles outbreak spreads
summary: State reportedly asks for emergency assistance as state Democratic governor spars with US health secretary
text: Pennsylvania is seeking emergency assistance from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) as a major measles outbreak spreads across the state. The state warned the request could be withdrawn unless the federal agency publicly recognizes four measles-associated deaths reported by the state. The Pennsylvania department of health has begun the process of requesting CDC emergency support known as an Epi-Aid, according to a letter reviewed by the Guardian. The letter was first reported by Reuters on Thursday. Debra Bogen, Pennsylvania’s secretary of health, outlined the condition in a letter sent on Wednesday to the CDC director, Erica Schwartz. “The CDC’s choice not to publicly recognize ⁠the deaths undermines our response,” Bogen wrote. “For this reason, if CDC is unable to transparently and accurately communicate information about those measles-associated deaths, the department will respectfully rescind our request for a CDC Epi-Aid.” The development comes amid an ongoing dispute involving Josh Shapiro, the state’s Democratic governor, and Robert F Kennedy Jr, the US health secretary, over the state’s handling of the outbreak and how measles-related deaths are being counted. Kennedy has questioned whether deaths linked to the measles outbreaks since he took office were caused by the virus or by another condition. He also instructed the CDC not to include Pennsylvania’s reported fatalities in the national measles death count last month, a move health experts called “highly unusual” and warned it could lead the public to underestimate the dangers of measles. Kennedy, meanwhile, has accused Shapiro of politicizing Pennsylvania’s outbreak and failing to seek out federal assistance. The state’s latest move marks a shift from its earlier position. Pennsylvania health officials had previously resisted CDC assistance, saying they were capable of managing the outbreak without federal help. Since then, the situation has worsened. On Wednesday, the Pennsylvania health department announced that 731 measles cases have been confirmed in 38 counties across the state so far this year. Four people have died in the state from measles-related illness as of Tuesday. The CDC did not immediately respond to the Guardian’s request for comment. The outbreak is among the largest and deadliest in the country and comes as the US experiences its most severe measles resurgence in more than three decades, driven by increasing vaccine hesitancy. This month, it was revealed that the Trump administration changed the way it counts measles deaths amid the outbreak in Pennsylvania. The CDC is now using data from the National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS), which is a way to track mortality trends over time. It is unclear why this change was made. On Wednesday, Bill Cassidy, a Republican chair of the Senate health committee, blamed the Trump administration’s vaccine-skeptical approach for the ‌recent measles deaths in Pennsylvania.

title: Revolut reportedly facing $3m ransom demand after hackers steal hundreds of customers’ data
summary: Europe’s largest financial technology company confirmed it had fallen victim to an impersonation scam last week
text: Revolut is facing a reported $3m (£2.2m) ransom demand after hackers posing as government officials accessed the data of hundreds of the bank’s cryptocurrency customers, including one victim who says he fears for his safety. Europe’s largest financial technology company confirmed last weekend that it had fallen victim to an impersonation scam in which hackers compromised an Italian government email system to contact Revolut staff and request personal customer details. While the data breach only affected about 680 of Revolut’s 80 million global customers, it is believed to have targeted customers with suspected cryptocurrency holdings. It is not clear how the scandal might affect Revolut’s much-anticipated stock market debut, with Revolut’s founder, Nik Storonsky, telling Les Echoes on Thursday that there were plans for a dual listing in both London and New York. One of the alleged hackers has reportedly threatened to publish the customer data unless Revolut pays a $3m ransom, according to the Financial Times, which has been speaking to the purported hacker. A Revolut spokesperson said the bank “has not received any direct contact or demand from the individuals or group making these claims”. But some victims have said they fear they could end up being forced to face ransoms. The former chief executive of failed bitcoin exchange Mt. Gox, Mark Karpelès, said he was one of the victims of the data breach and is now worried about his family’s safety. “I have kids, we’re living together. My address is in those files, so of course I’m worried about this,” he told the Guardian. He has since contacted law enforcement in Tokyo, where he lives, after saying in an X post earlier this week that he feared he could be “kidnapped or dead” by the time Revolut gave him more substantial information about the breach. Karpelès said he was relieved that Japanese officials were taking the threat seriously, “but I might still have to travel overseas or be in places that may not be as safe”. The French businessman, who has been a Revolut customer since 2023, said that hackers may have mistakenly targeted his account, thinking he was wealthier than he actually is. He said he was forced to declare bankruptcy in the wake of a high-profile court case in Japan. Karpelès is a controversial figure in the crypto world. He was charged, but later acquitted, of embezzlement by Japanese courts, following the collapse of the crypto exchange platform in 2014. He was found guilty of falsifying data. Karpelès said he has joined a victim chat group on X in the wake of the data breach, where customers having been sharing information and support. “We’re all in the same situation, which is: we don’t know exactly what happened, or how it happened, so we’re trying to get as much information as possible,” he said. He added that one of the victims got in touch with the purported hacker, who showed they had the victim’s personal details on hand. The hacker then said they would delete the information, but only if they were sent $50,000, Karpelès said. While Karpelès was frustrated with Revolut, which was valued at $115bn in a secondary share sale earlier this summer, he does not believe the bank should pay the $3m ransom, which ultimately gives no guarantee that the data will be deleted. It is still not clear how many hackers are involved, and requests for the ransom to be paid through a platform known as Monero, meaning there would be no evidence or receipt of payment, allowing the hacker to claim they never received the money in the first place. Karpelès hopes Revolut will share more information about the breach. “This is very, very damaging [for the Revolut brand] because I do believe a lot of Revolut customers are more likely to be privacy sensitive,” he said, noting that this was usually a high priority among people invested in cryptocurrencies. A Revolut spokesperson said:“Revolut recently identified a sophisticated external impersonation scam where an unauthorised third party utilised a legitimate government agency domain email to submit fraudulent requests for information. “Upon detection, we immediately blocked the address and alerted the relevant government agency as well as enforcement agencies, data protection, and financial regulators. Revolut systems and customer funds are unaffected. We have contacted the limited number of impacted individuals directly to inform them and provide support.”

title: G.O.P. Representative Breaks With Trump in Ad: Hispanic Voters ‘Feel Betrayed’
summary: Representative María Elvira Salazar, a three-term representative from Miami, won re-election by 20 percentage points in 2024. Her ad suggests worry among some Republicans about their standing with Hispanic voters.

title: All smiles in Strasbourg but uncertainty clouds Canada’s EU membership plan
summary: Although Mark Carney welcomed offer to become bloc’s first associate member, no one seems to know what that means
text: Mark Carney received a rapturous reception in the European parliament when he gave his speech on Thursday welcoming a proposal for Canada to become the EU’s first-ever associate member. Politicians queued to shake his hand and take selfies. One described the speech as a historic moment. “Europe has extended a hand, and Canada has taken it,” said the German Green MEP Terry Reintke, who borrowed a Canadian ice hockey shirt for the occasion. One day earlier, in the same debating chamber, the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, issued the unprecedented invitation to Canada – an idea quickly derided by Donald Trump, who threatened Europe with “heavy tariffs” if it became a reality. But the prospect of Canada’s associate membership is uncertain, not least because no one is sure what it means. “I’m not quite sure why she [von der Leyen] used that term because there’s simply no legal definition,” said one senior politician. “This has just raised lots of questions. So people are talking more about what an associate membership means instead of … this unique partnership and alliance for the future that EU-Canada relations should be about.” The German chancellor Friedrich Merz’s spokesperson welcomed the initiative for a close partnership with Canada and said Germany was “open to discussing new models that reflect the special significance of the relationship”, but called for the associate membership label to be “reconsidered”. Merz himself has floated “associate membership” for Ukraine, as a stepping stone to joining the bloc, but this was quickly dismissed by other member states. One EU diplomat said von der Leyen “seemed a bit far out in floating this” and that even before Wednesday’s speech member states had worried that she was overpromising on Canada. A second diplomat said it was “an empty phrase” and it would be up to member states to define the substance. Any new trading and cooperation relationship with a foreign country would need to be approved by the EU’s 27 member states. There is a lot of common ground: both sides want to deepen cooperation on AI, energy security, critical raw materials, quantum computing and work together in the Arctic – Carney noted that Canada shared an Arctic border with Denmark, referring to the maritime border with Greenland. But difficulties went unspoken. Carney described the 2016 EU-Canada comprehensive economic and trade agreement as “one of the world’s most successful trade agreements”, but 10 EU member states have yet to ratify it, including France, Italy and Poland. With all three countries heading into an election year, that looks unlikely to change. While both sides extol the virtues of deeper trade between allies, they are also pursuing policies that appear to contradict that goal. Last year Canada introduced a buy Canadian policy, to ensure Canadian suppliers get priority in public contracts. The EU is debating its own buy European law, known formally as the Industrial Accelerator Act. The IAA, now being debated in the EU, would oblige member states to meet “made in Europe” content requirements when spending public money on green technologies and electric cars. Associate membership also raises questions about integration into the EU’s tightly guarded single market. Carney proposed “seamless digital trade in non-agricultural goods and a wide range of services”. But the EU has long insisted that the four freedoms of its internal market – free movement of goods, services, labour and capital – are one package that cannot be split and require alignment with EU rules. Now the applause has died down, there are plenty of tricky issues to work out, even for the closest of allies.

title: The Bank of England is shaking up its bond sales – why does it matter?
summary: The UK central bank has announced shakeup of its bond sales programme as it unwinds massive balance sheet
text: Mixed in with the Bank of England’s decision on Thursday to hold interest rates at 3.75% was a surprise announcement that it was shaking up its programme of quantitative tightening. So why is this apparently arcane change to QT important, and what does it mean for the public finances? What is QT? It is the Bank of England’s controversial process of selling off hundreds of billions of pounds worth of government bonds that it bought via the emergency policy of quantitative easing (QE) during the financial crises of 2008 and Covid. The Bank’s monetary policy committee (MPC) sees QT as the necessary unwinding of the massive balance sheet it built up. Its stockpile of bonds, known as gilts, has already been reduced from a peak of £895bn in February 2022, to £488bn. But critics on the right and left have complained that selling off significant quantities of government bonds costs the Treasury, as they are being sold at a loss. There have also been concerns that in a febrile bond market, large-scale sell-offs risk depressing prices – and thus driving up the yield, or interest rate, the government has to pay to borrow. What is the Bank looking to change? Instead of looking for private-sector buyers for its stock of gilts, the Bank plans to sell them directly to the Treasury instead. The Treasury’s debt management office (DMO), which has the job of doing the government’s borrowing for it, will then issue new bonds to cover the costs of those it has bought from the Bank. The Treasury sees this as simplifying what can be a messy process. As the chancellor, John Healey, put it in a letter to the Bank’s governor, Andrew Bailey, on Thursday: “This sales model … would see a return to a single public-sector supplier of gilts to the market.” It also has the advantage of allowing the DMO to tailor gilt sales to market demand, which currently favour gilts that mature over a shorter period, rather than the Bank having to sell off the 20- and 30-year dated gilts it still has on its books, for which there is less investor appetite. The yield, effectively the interest rate, on 30-year gilts dropped sharply on Thursday after the decision was announced, to 5.745% – and was on course for its biggest drop since 2020. No final decision has been made, however, despite the fact the Treasury, Bank and DMO have apparently been discussing the idea for a year. Healey has promised to make a final ruling in April – and until then, QT will be paused. Wasn’t QT already being slowed down? Yes. The Bank has run down its stock of gilts by £70bn this year. That included £20bn of actual sales; and another £50bn worth that reached their maturity date. Over the coming years, it plans to sell off £20bn of government bonds annually, alongside retiring gilts that reach maturity. That’s because the Bank is keen to avoid the risks of exacerbating already-fragile bond markets. The minutes of the MPC meeting revealed that members discussed offloading bonds at a faster rate; but “at a time when bond markets globally had been volatile, this risked destabilising markets”. The Bank also announced it would set aside about £120bn of the longest-dated government bonds it holds, as these are used to back the issuance of the UK’s bank notes. In total, the Bank expects to sell a total of £146bn of gilts between now and 2034 – at a steady pace of £20bn a year – back to the government, if Healey gives the plan the thumbs up. What’s the impact for the public finances? Analysts expect it to be modest. The Treasury may be able to finance its borrowing a bit more cheaply when the Bank is not selling a slew of long-dated bonds into the market. As analysts at the investment bank Jefferies put it: “Taken together, the changes imply a materially lower future supply burden, particularly for [long-dated gilts].” And to the extent that the pace of sales is slowing, the losses on those bonds, which is borne by the Treasury, will crystallise more slowly – another marginal upside. Jefferies also suggested that, by making its future plans clear, the MPC’s decision could “ease some of the pressure that had been building for changes to the Bank’s QT approach”.

title: House Republican releases campaign ad critical of Trump’s immigration policies
summary: María Elvira Salazar says some enforcement has ‘gone too far’ as GOP seeks distance from Trump before midterms
text: A Republican congresswoman has released a campaign ad criticizing Donald Trump’s approach to immigration enforcement, in the latest sign that a key plank of the president’s 2024 re-election campaign has become a liability for his congressional allies ahead of November’s midterm elections. “Mr President, some of your immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far,” Florida’s María Elvira Salazar says in a 30-second ad. “In July, 50% of the 50,000 people that were detained had no criminal record. Be careful what your advisers are telling you about immigration policy.” Salazar represents a competitive Miami-area district that is nearly three-quarters Hispanic, and where Trump won by a 15-point margin two years ago after a campaign in which he promised to carry out “mass deportations”. While his administration has implied that those targeted would be undocumented immigrants who committed crimes in the United States, in reality, a substantial portion of the people arrested since Trump returned to the White House in January 2025 have no criminal record. Salazar won re-election by a 20-point margin in 2024, but this year is facing a significant challenge from Eliott Rodriguez, the Democratic nominee and a former television news anchor. A poll conducted for his campaign late last month found him tied with Salazar. “The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today,” Salazar said in the ad. “You can be for immigration what Lincoln was for slavery and Reagan was for communism. I’m not talking about giving them amnesty. I’m talking about giving them a dignified life in this promised land.” First elected in 2020, the congresswoman is a champion of the Dignity Act, an immigration reform proposal in the House of Representatives that would create a pathway for some undocumented immigrants to obtain legal status. Salazar’s ad is the latest instance of Republican lawmakers seeking to put distance between themselves and Trump before the 3 November elections, in which Democrats are vying to take back both the House and Senate. With gas prices high due to the war with Iran and Trump’s public approval low – including on key issues like handling of immigration – Democrats increasingly believe their candidates are competitive even in heavily Republican seats.

title: Sweden’s PM resigns after centre-left bloc wins slim majority in election
summary: Ulf Kristersson has stood down from his post, paving way for Social Democrats leader to form a government
text: Sweden’s centre-right prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, has stood down, clearing the way for Magdalena Andersson, the Social Democrats leader, to attempt to form a government. In a victory speech on Thursday, Andersson said the Swedish people had “voted for a new direction for our country, voted for unity and against division”. She added: “The Swedish people have voted to take Sweden forward and I will realise the new direction that you have voted for.” Among the priorities she named were the climate crisis, schools, healthcare, elderly care and immigration policy. Andersson spoke as the preliminary count for Sunday’s election was finally completed, with 176 seats for the left-leaning opposition parties – a narrow three-seat majority over the right-leaning ruling Tidö coalition supported by the far-right Sweden Democrats (SD). There were 50,359 votes between the two blocs. Earlier on Thursday, Andersson, who was Kristersson’s predecessor as prime minister, sent an invitation to the other left-leaning parties – Left, Centre and Green – for initial coalition talks. Soon after, Kristersson, the Moderates leader, announced his resignation after four years as prime minister. Before the election, some had feared that the vote would mark a turning point for the far right after Kristersson promised key ministerial posts for the SD if his coalition took power. Instead, the SD lost support for the first time in a general election since its foundation, falling from Sweden’s second biggest party to third. In his resignation letter, Kristersson wrote: “Now it is the speaker who will lead the next steps towards forming a new government. In order for that work to begin immediately, I hereby request to be relieved of my duties as prime minister.” The speaker, Andreas Norlén, will now start working on proposals for a new prime minister after talks with representatives of each of the parties. Four celebration cakes decorated with red roses were brought into the Social Democrats’ headquarters amid cheers from inside. The result will be a considerable relief among Social Democrats, who remain Sweden’s biggest party but received record low support. However, the result marks only the beginning for Andersson of what is expected to be weeks of complicated coalition talks. One of the trickiest negotiations is expected to be between the Centre and Left parties. The Centre party has ruled out being in government with the Left, while the Left has demanded a place in government in return for its cooperation. Other difficult areas are expected to be the Left’s support for a billionaire tax, the Green party’s opposition to nuclear energy and differences of opinion on taxation. The Greens, Social Democrats and the Left are all in favour of tax increases, but the Centre party wants to cut taxes. Nooshi Dadgostar, the leader of the Left party, said: “The Swedish people have voted away Tidö and given us a clear mandate for change.” She added: “This is one of the proudest days of my life.” Elisabeth Thand Ringqvist, the Centre party leader, thanked Kristersson for his work as prime minister but said Sweden was now “entering a new political phase”. She added: “The Centre party will be a constructive force for Sweden to have a functioning government, with policies anchored in the middle.” Andersson, who was prime minister between November 2021 and October 2022, is understood to be reaching out to all the opposition parties, with the exception of the SD. The Liberals and the Christian Democrats have ruled out working with the left, but in his resignation letter Kristersson appeared to leave the door open. However, given Swedish tradition, it is extremely unlikely the Moderates and the Social Democrats would form a coalition. Kristersson wrote that the election had left a “complicated situation” for building a government and called for “constructive openness” from all parties to find a way to form a stable government. In the nervous days since the election, the Social Democrats are understood to have been using the time to prepare for coalition negotiations, where they are understood to be seeking broad cooperation with one or multiple parties. Minority-run governments are common within Swedish politics and it is commonplace for governments to form agreements outside of coalitions. In the last government, the SD were not officially in government, but they held considerable sway over the budget and policies. The Social Democrats are understood to be planning to prioritise making changes to the immigration, integration and climate policies of the last government. But with their policies having moved to the right in recent years, particularly on immigration and crime, much of the legacy of the previous government is likely to remain.

title: Solar panels going to landfill while Labor’s $25m recycling scheme on hold
summary: Australian Council of Recycling says it has had ‘no clarity about the nature of the complaint’ that delayed program announced in January
text: Recycling operators have expressed growing alarm about delays to a solar panel recycling scheme promised by the Albanese government with fears some could go bust while they wait. The $25m pilot scheme was announced in January to help develop a local industry for the recycling of panels and the recovery of valuable materials such as copper and aluminium. A process to appoint an entity to run the pilot was suspended in May after an undisclosed complaint, first reported by Renew Economy. The scheme had been due to commence mid-year. Four months on, eight solar recycling companies have written to several ministers to urge the government to lift the suspension. Their concerns follow the government’s recent decision to shelve plans for mandatory national packaging standards. The companies said the prolonged delay threatened the financial viability of operators in the emerging solar recycling industry and hindered Australia’s ability to recover “high-purity critical materials”. They wrote “every month of delay exacerbates the volume of solar waste entering landfills, damaging public trust in renewable energy infrastructure”. James Petesic, one of the letter’s signatories, is the co-founder of solar panel recycler PV Industries, which has facilities in Sydney and Melbourne. He said there had been little communication or clarity about the pilot’s future since the federal Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water suspended the procurement process in May. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email “The more time goes on, the more panels are coming off roofs,” he said. “And … the more we risk losing recycling capacity because more businesses will go into administration.” Petesic said the ongoing delay was affecting investor certainty in the industry. The letter urges the government to use a public interest provision in procurement laws to lift the suspension, so that the pilot can still progress while the complaint is investigated. Petesic said one of the biggest issues for the nascent industry was supply of solar panels. About one in three Australians have rooftop solar but most rooftop panels are not recycled at the end of their life. Recyclers have struggled to secure enough panels, with many ending up in landfill or waste stockpiles. Victoria is the only state with an outright ban on solar panels going to rubbish dumps, though some landfill sites in other jurisdictions also refuse to accept them. Petesic said as households installed home batteries, many were choosing to upgrade their solar panels at the same time, increasing the volume of panels that were becoming waste. He said the goals of the pilot scheme were to support transport of panels to recyclers, guarantee supply of panels for recycling and help the solar recycling industry to grow. The pilot was also intended to inform development of a mandatory national solar panel recycling scheme. The chief executive of the Australian Council of Recycling, Suzanne Toumbourou, said the delay would have “knock-on effects” for people who had invested in solar recycling. “There has been absolutely no clarity about the nature of the complaint that has held this process up indefinitely, which means the sector has no concept of what the way forward looks like,” she said. “Investment confidence has already been shaken by the delay itself but the indefinite nature of it amplifies that.” A department spokesperson said the government “remains committed to the policy objectives of the national solar panel recycling pilot”. They said the appointment process remained suspended in accordance with the government’s procurement rules. Gayle Sloan, the CEO of the Waste Management and Resource Recovery Association, said instead of the pilot scheme the government should introduce national regulations that made producers of solar panels responsible for what happened to them – whether that was repair, reuse or recycling. “We don’t need more trials. We need regulation that places the responsibility squarely on producers,” she said.

title: El Niño and global heating pushes water vapour in Earth’s atmosphere to record levels in August
summary: Global heating contributes to record, with a warmer atmosphere able to hold more water, scientists say
text: The planet’s atmosphere held more water vapour in August than any other month on record, further increasing the risk of extreme heat and rainfall around the world, according to Europe’s climate change service. Climate scientists said global heating was a contributor to the record because a warmer atmosphere can hold more water, and the historic El Niño in the Pacific Ocean was also likely pushing water vapour levels up. According to the Copernicus Climate Change Service (C3S), the amount of water vapour in the atmosphere through August was 27.35 kg per square metre, beating the previous record from July 2024 by 0.04 kg m². The value describes how much water vapour is in a column of air sitting above a square metre of the Earth’s surface, extending up through the atmosphere. The 0.04 kg m² increase on the previous record, one climate scientist calculated, was the equivalent of about 20 trillion litres of additional water, or 20 cubes of water, each a kilometre wide, high and deep. Dr Julien Nicolas, senior scientist at C3S, said water vapour was estimated in its ERA5 dataset by combining humidity measurements from satellites, weather balloons and other sources with a weather model. The water vapour estimates go back to 1979. August was also the planet’s joint hottest month on the ERA5 dataset going back to 1940, and the hottest according to the US government’s National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration dataset that starts in 1850. Nicolas said the water vapour record was “consistent with the record high global temperature in August” and said “warmer air can hold about 7% more water vapour per degree of [global] warming”. He said the tropical oceans were a major source of the water vapour. “The exceptionally high sea surface temperatures seen across these regions in August, partly linked to the presence and strengthening of El Niño conditions, increased evaporation and were likely an important contributor to the record-high global water vapour value.” He said rising water vapour levels could increase the risk of intense rainfall, including from cyclones, and give extra energy to storms “because heat is released when water vapour condenses into cloud droplets, potentially helping to intensify them”. The current El Niño climate pattern in the tropical Pacific is forecast to be the strongest on record and climate scientists predict it could push global temperatures to record levels next year. Provisional analysis by Australian scientists has found the expected record peak ocean temperatures in the Pacific that are a marker of the El Niño were being made six times more likely because of global heating. Dr Andrew Dessler, a climate scientist at Texas A&M University, wrote that it was “unimaginable that any month in the last few thousand years, maybe 100,000 years” had had more water vapour in the atmosphere than August. “We are, as the proverb says, living in interesting times,” he wrote. Prof Steven Sherwood, of the University of New South Wales Climate Change Research Centre, said while an extra 0.04 kg m² of water vapour across the planet “does not sound like a lot … when this rise is continuous, it starts to have effects. “A lot of the impacts of climate change actually happen because of water vapour. “When you move this water vapour to higher latitudes, it puts heat into the air, and so a lot of extreme heat that’s experienced there is indirectly from the water vapour. “We know high humidity has effects during heatwaves as it stops night-time cooling, so it gets harder for people to recover from very hot days.” Prof Jason Evans, also of the UNSW climate centre, calculated the water vapour record had exceeded the previous record by the equivalent of about 20 trillion litres, or about 41 Sydney Harbours’ worth of water. Dr Kimberley Reid, a climate scientist at the University of Melbourne specialising in water vapour research, said “given August was the hottest month for at least 170 years – this record isn’t too shocking”. “Temperature and water vapour are closely linked,” she said. “Like the temperatures, we are getting these records because of the emissions from burning fossil fuels and from the El Niño. “Water vapour is also part of the climate feedback loop – water vapour is a greenhouse gas and so the atmosphere will warm even further, and then take up even more water vapour. The root cause is the extra CO2 and methane.”

title: Money in people’s pockets is the key to economic recovery | Letter
summary: Letter: David Redshaw responds to a letter on the bond markets and economic pressures afflicting the UK
text: Neil Kinnock’s timely letter (9 September) reminds us that we are not alone in suffering high gilt yields and borrowing costs. We are still feeling the fallout from Covid, and it needs mentioning that our national debt is similar to America’s and much less than Japan’s, and it never gets mentioned that Italy routinely runs 100% of GDP debt. But as Kinnock observes, the policies of several Conservative governments (including Brexit) have made things worse, and the problem for us is not so much the actual debt but our direction of travel. The aforementioned will make the bond markets view us with a more jaundiced eye. It was predictable that Jamie Dimon would pop up at this point (JP Morgan boss meets Burnham and Healey to warn against bank tax rise, 10 September). He talks about potential lack of investment by the banks. What investment? We aren’t even a nation of shopkeepers any longer; we’re a nation of pizza deliverers. The economist JK Galbraith comes to mind here. He said that when push comes to shove, it’s the regular spendings of the working masses that keep the high street going. The spendings of the mega-rich involve either luxury goods or investment in plant, both of which are erratic and subject to the ups and downs of the economic cycle. Some might say, after the events of 1990 and 2008, that the banks have more money than is good for them. Money in people’s pockets and the confidence to spend it has always been the recipe for recovery. Might we start by housing policies to reduce the 40% of rent that many are paying out of their salary? And a bedroom tax for the rich to make better use of the existing housing stock? You can go on raising the minimum wage, but you’re simply chasing your tail. David Redshaw Saltdean, East Sussex

title: Charles’s rebuttal of Earl Spencer’s claim about Diana offers rare glimpse into palace thinking
summary: From ‘there were three of us in this marriage’ to ‘recollections may vary’, a lot can be conveyed with a carefully worded phrase
text: As denials go, King Charles’s response to Earl Spencer’s allegations that Charles said after Diana’s death, “We’ll forget her soon enough”, was a masterclass in the diplomatic royal rebuke. Rarely has Buckingham Palace responded to claims in countless books on royalty. But it was straight out of the block on this one. Little over an hour after the Daily Mail, which is serialising Spencer’s memoir Swan Song about his sister, the late Diana, Princess of Wales, had published its first extract online, a statement was issued. Charles, the headline claimed, had told Spencer days after Diana’s death and during a heated row over funeral arrangements: “Rest assured, we’ll forget her soon enough.” The king’s swift countering, that “the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss”, will enter the canon of carefully constructed regal pushbacks. As rebukes go, it is up there with the late Queen Elizabeth II’s “some recollections may vary” in response to a torrent of allegations from the Duke and Duchess of Sussex in their Oprah Winfrey interview. Senior courtiers are often drawn from the diplomatic service and thus highly-skilled in couching the passive-aggressive denial. Deploying delicate language to devastating effect is a stock in trade at the Foreign Office. But it is a weapon to be used sparingly. The royal mantra is, usually, “never complain, never explain”. However, Charles’s former communications secretary Julian Payne said: “This is a much more personal situation, given its author, and therefore has a greater ability to do harm.” That is why the palace “felt the need to set the record straight and deny these remarks have been made”, Payne told the BBC’s Today programme. Given the amount of things the palace don’t comment on, “you can imagine the strength of feeling”, he added. Payne remains close to the king and was due to be sitting alongside him at Thursday’s AI summit just hours later, so the fact he felt able to speak so freely suggests his robust defence of Charles came with official sanction. What is said behind palace doors usually remains private. The language may be less sensitive. But a carefully chosen phrase in public pulls back the privacy screen. When Diana, in her highly controversial Panorama interview, said “there were three of us in this marriage, so it was a bit crowded”, she reaped public revenge on her then husband and Camilla. In return, Diana found herself on the sharp end of Elizabeth’s ire weeks later. After Diana failed to respond to the queen’s request that the couple divorce, a palace spokesperson issued a statement: “After considering the present situation, the queen wrote to both the prince and princess earlier this week and gave them her view, supported by the Duke of Edinburgh, that an early divorce is desirable.” The matter was now, officially, out of Diana’s hands. White fury was behind the Duke and Duchess of Sussex’s statement in February 2021: “We can all live a life of service. Service is universal.” It was read as a succinct and direct challenge to the late queen’s insistence they could not keep their public service roles after stepping down as working royals. Meghan was less direct in a 2019 interview with ITV’s Tom Bradby in which he asked her if she was OK juggling life as a royal with a newborn, Prince Archie. “Thank you for asking, because not many people have asked if I’m OK,” she replied. Was it directed at the palace and the institution? A huge number of the claims the Sussexes later made, in TV interviews and in Harry’s memoir Spare, were that the duchess had been unsupported throughout her time as a working royal. One royal famously deficient in the art of the diplomatic royal rebuke, however, was the late Duke of Edinburgh. Philip was renowned for his gaffes. When a BBC journalist politely asked the queen at a banquet at the Élysée Palace if she was enjoying her stay in Paris in 2006, Philip dispensed with tact to snap: “Damn fool question!”

title: Trump arch could have ‘adverse effects’ on nearby monuments but will proceed, report says
summary: National Park Service lays out concerns that planned 250ft arch could interfere with historic sites in US capital
text: Donald Trump’s desired triumphal arch in downtown Washington DC will likely contribute “to adverse effects to historic properties”, according to the National Park Service’s planning document, but the construction is still planned to go forward. The president’s 250ft arch could interfere with some of the most well-known views in the nation’s capital, including the symbolic relationship between Arlington House, the Arlington National Cemetery, the Arlington Memorial Bridge and the Lincoln Memorial, which face each other to represent the reunification of the United States after the civil war. As a result, the arch’s construction could require supplemental planning and programming to preserve history, a document and emails obtained by the Washington Post on Wednesday outlined. “Such adverse effects cannot be fully avoided while retaining the location-dependent purpose of the undertaking,” the National Park Service wrote in the document. Despite concerns that the arch could interfere with historic sites and would require substantial construction management control, the Trump administration wants to move forward. The document was circulated among preservationists and other groups to review and sign by noon on Monday, according to an email obtained by the Washington Post. The Guardian has asked the National Park Service for comment. Historic preservationists, veterans and lawmakers have consistently raised concerns about the Trump administration building the massive triumphal arch in downtown DC. Veterans filed a lawsuit in September, seeking to halt construction of the arch, believing it would harm the symbolic relationship of historic sites representing the reconciliation of war or disrupt burials at the Arlington National Cemetery. Some lawmakers shared fears that the arch could further complicate DC’s airspace. But Trump has been emphatic about the arch, insisting it should be 250ft high to mark the US’s 250th anniversary. Should construction of the arch move forward, the National Park Service outlined several ways it would mitigate disruptions and potential damage to nearby monuments. That includes installing vibration plates near the Arlington Memorial Bridge and other sensitive sites to ensure construction remains within prescribed limits, enforcing limits on noise-generating activities, prohibiting unnecessary lighting, limiting work hours and more. The National Park Service’s document outlined roughly 37 nearby historic sites that could be affected, including the Lincoln Memorial, the National Mall, the Washington Monument, the Pentagon, the US Capitol and more. But the National Park Service also outlined methods it could implement to preserve the history of the area, such as developing digital programs to explain the commemorative relationship between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington House, to show before-and-after scenes of the skyline over the Potomac River, and to describe the significance of triumphal arches. Local preservation officers could refuse to sign the agreement, which could trigger another process that involves the Advisory Council on Historic Preservation, a federal agency. However, the Trump administration does not need the preservationists’ consent to move forward because it already received approval from the US Commission on Fine Arts, a federal advisory council made up of Trump appointees, and preliminary approval from the National Capital Planning Commission.

title: Meta ordered to remove UK deepfakes as oversight board criticises ‘inadequate’ safeguards
summary: Facebook told it was wrong in leaving up AI-generated videos of a Labour councillor and Muslim campaigner, amid calls to curb fakes
text: Meta’s “supreme court” has ordered the tech company to take down deepfake videos of a UK politician and a young Muslim woman from Facebook and do more to tackle AI-generated fake imagery. A fake video showing a Labour party councillor in Scotland making inflammatory comments about refugees should not have been left up by Facebook, the board said. It also ruled that an AI-generated video of a Muslim campaign volunteer should have been removed after it falsely depicted her offering health advice while carrying out absurd exercises or eating junk food. The board said Meta’s safeguards were “consistently and fundamentally inadequate” to address the rapid rise of AI deepfakes. “From politicians to private citizens, AI-generated deepfakes are increasingly being used to harass and silence women from engaging in public discourse,” said Pamela San Martin, an oversight board co-chair. “These cases demonstrate a broader, troubling pattern in which women who engage publicly on issues are disproportionately subjected to harassment and misinformation. Meta and other social media platforms need more robust policies to address the proliferation of deepfakes.” In the Scotland clip, the councillor is falsely represented as saying: “Refugees are welcome here, even if they rape our women, because white people do that too.” The oversight board, a quasi-independent body whose decisions are binding, said the video of the councillor appeared to be AI-generated, as indicated by the audio not being fully synchronised to the unnamed councillor’s facial movements. Even when raised directly with the company by the board, Meta decided the video did not violate its content policies and did not merit an AI label. In a blogpost published on Thursday, the board said the post should have been removed because it violated Meta’s rules on hateful conduct by alleging criminal and predatory sexual behaviour by refugees as an entire group and not as individuals. The video should also have received a “high risk AI” label, said the board, as it called for tougher measures on deepfakes. “The majority [of the board] finds that Meta needs more robust policies on deepfakes, including expanding the situations when ‘high risk’ labels can be applied, more measures to reduce the spread of deceptive AI content, increasing the penalties for accounts that repeatedly share it, and more transparency on data around when AI labels are applied,” it said. The board recommended nine policy changes at Meta, including ensuring algorithms demote content labelled “high risk”, making such posts less likely to appear in users’ feeds. It also recommended that Meta makes it more difficult for users to view AI-generated content by, for instance, introducing a warning screen that requires a click-through before viewing the content. In a separate ruling, the board also ordered Meta to take down from Facebook an AI-generated video mocking a young Muslim woman in Europe taking part in a campaign to improve menstrual health education and reduce stigma around health conditions for women and girls from ethnic minority backgrounds. AI-manipulated videos and images mocking the woman had tens of millions of views online, including on Meta platforms. The board singled out one of the videos – showing the woman exercising absurdly and eating junk food – as a breach of the company’s bullying and harassment policy. It recommended the post be removed and made three policy recommendations, including changing its definition of “unwanted manipulated imagery” to cover deepfakes of a private individual saying or doing things they did not say or do. The board was set up by Meta in 2020 to serve as a referee for content on its platforms. Meta has been approached for comment.

title: Baby found wrapped in 1910 newspaper was killed with twine, UK inquest concludes
summary: ‘Terrible thing’ happened to infant boy found under the floorboards at a house in Bishop Auckland, says coroner
text: A baby boy who was found with twine looped and knotted round his neck and wrapped in a 116-year-old newspaper was unlawfully killed, a coroner has concluded. Crispin Oliver on Thursday said the child, known only as Baby Auckland, had been garotted by an unknown person. He said it was an “unusual case, legally and evidentially”. The whole story, he added, was “very sad and singular”. Oliver said: “Clearly, this was a terrible thing that happened to a defenceless infant. It happened in our community. But it happened over a century ago, and it is heartwarming how the public and individuals in this community have stepped up to do the right thing by Baby Auckland.” The inquest heard that the skeletal remains of the baby had been found during renovations on the second floor of a late 19th-century house in Bishop Auckland, County Durham, on 29 July 2024. They were found by the house owner, Peter Moody, while he was laying a new floor. In a statement he said he had made the discovery when he lifted up a floorboard. He contacted the county council, unsure of whether he needed to call the police. DCI Mel Sutherland told the inquest he had been on duty in Bishop Auckland when he was alerted to the discovery of skeletal remains in a town centre house. After they were confirmed as human, he supervised the sealing of the house to keep it forensically sterile, while a forensic anthropologist was contacted. That scientist, Dr Micol Zuppello, travelled up that evening and spent two days at the house investigating. The baby’s skeleton was mostly complete, the inquest in Crook heard, bar a missing toe tip. The remains were partly mummified. Carbon dating could conclusively establish only that the baby died between the 17th century and 1955. A postmortem of the skeleton was carried out by Zupello and Dr Louise Mulcahy, a Home Office pathologist for north-east England based at the Royal Victoria Infirmary in Newcastle. Mulcahy said the baby had been 38-40 weeks, with no signs of traumatic injury, and had twine looped around his neck. She said it had been looped around the neck three times, knotted, and then looped again. It was not possible to say, she added, if it had been tight or loose. The medical cause of death, she said, was “unascertained”. The skeleton was too old to be able to confirm or refute the presence of natural disease, she said. In the absence of soft tissue it was not possible, the inquest heard, to say if there had been any assault or trauma. Equally, it was not possible to say with any certainty if the baby had been stillborn or not. Oliver said police had “had to think laterally” during their investigation. He praised Sutherland for “leaving no stone unturned”. Sutherland described some of the techniques they had used to investigate further, including DNA testing. All were inconclusive. He said the newspaper was very brown, but articles could be seen. It was called The Umpire and dated June 1910. Sutherland said that in 1911 census data, the building was described as dining rooms, meaning “a cafe-type establishment”. A public appeal was made for people who thought they might be related to come forward. Two sisters came forward who believed they were related to a servant at the house, but DNA testing revealed no match. During the whole investigation, Sutherland said, there had been “very little to go on”. Oliver asked if the twine might have been used for a religious artefact, but nothing like that had been found, Sutherland said. There was also no evidence to suggest any link to midwifery practices of the time. A knot specialist could not be used, the inquest heard, because the nearest person was in the Netherlands and would have been too expensive for this type of investigation. Baby Auckland was laid to rest at Bishop Auckland cemetery in April this year, with professionals involved giving their services for free. Sutherland said it had been two years of investigating, “challenging and frustrating at times, but heartwarming to see the send-off he got at the end”.

title: FBI warned ICE agents could be targeted by fake ‘tradwife’ dating profiles, memo reveals
summary: Exclusive: Internal FBI memo, reviewed by the Guardian, said women wanted to dox and ‘embarrass’ agents, but provided few details
text: The FBI internally warned that a group of women were creating fake online dating accounts with “tradwife” aesthetics in an effort to lure US immigration agents and “dox” them. The FBI in Chicago disseminated a brief memo to other law enforcement officials across the US on the potential threat to agents in February, warning that “as of late January 2026, a small group of women allegedly were creating fictitious online dating profiles with the purpose of attracting and then doxxing law enforcement participating in immigration enforcement”. The report, which was shared with the Guardian, provided few details about the alleged scheme and did not explain the source of the information. “These profiles were incorporating imagery of a ‘traditional wife’ aesthetic and listing specific interests in an attempt to appeal to … individuals in law enforcement,” the FBI continued. “The objective was to lure affiliated law enforcement personnel into an online or in-person interaction under the guise of a date, after which the individuals would be publicly exposed and doxed online. The tactic is intended to generate public embarrassment and deter immigration enforcement activity.” Property of the People, a government-transparency non-profit, obtained the document through a public records request, one of many internal records the group has collected revealing internal law enforcement concerns about activists organizing against Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). The FBI’s “situational information report” did not list the dating sites allegedly used by the women or where they were located, nor did it specify whether agents had actually been exposed. The memo aimed “to raise awareness” about this doxing “technique”, the FBI wrote, adding a disclaimer that the report was “not finally evaluated intelligence”. The FBI’s “tradwife” comments were a reference to the trend popularized in recent years by influencers promoting traditional gender roles, with women romanticizing domesticity. “Doxing” generally refers to publishing someone’s private information online without their consent, though the administration has used the term loosely, claiming doxing includes posting videos of officers. The FBI declined to answer detailed questions about the memo, saying the bureau doesn’t generally comment on intelligence briefings. A spokesperson added in an email: “The FBI regularly shares information with our law enforcement partners to assist in protecting the communities they serve as well as protecting those who serve and protect communities. The FBI is committed to ensuring that law enforcement officers are safe from threats or violence while performing their duties.” The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) said in a statement after publication that its officers are “under constant threat from violent agitators” and “publicizing their identities puts their lives and the lives of their families at serious risk.” The memo was sent weeks after the New York Post, a conservative outlet, ran a story saying that “lefty TikTokkers” were “orchestrating groups of women” to “chase dick picks and selfies of ICE agents in a twisted scheme to dox them”. That story cited Libs of TikTok, a rightwing account that had posted a screenshot of someone claiming to be part of a Facebook group dedicated to going on dates with agents to expose them. The article listed a handful of posts and videos from users discussing this tactic, though it did not include interviews with anyone who claimed to be duping agents and there was no evidence agents had been tricked. The news coverage did not mention women using “tradwife” imagery, so it’s unclear whether the FBI may have received direct accounts from targeted agents or was simply summarizing social media trends. “It’s absurd the FBI issued a thinly-sourced security alert about ICE agents’ online dating troubles,” Ryan Shapiro, executive director of Property of the People, said in a statement. “It’s equally ludicrous the FBI is spending taxpayer dollars to protect ICE agents from possible ‘embarrassment’ at the hands of a supposed ‘small group of women’ who might name and ridicule them online.” Mike German, a former FBI agent and longtime civil liberties advocate, reviewed the document for the Guardian and said it was odd the briefing did not have footnotes or citations. The briefing said the intelligence came from a “collaborative source”. “The rightwing echo chamber creates threats and the government’s intelligence apparatus just repeats those threats without any context, more detail or any instruction of how agents or officers should respond,” said German, arguing it seemed likely the briefing was inspired by the New York Post story. “They must have run out of other threats.” The document, German added, “reinforces the paranoid ‘us versus them’ mentality within law enforcement”. The briefing comes as US law enforcement has raised increasing alarms about officials, and ICE agents in particular, being “doxed”. More than a dozen internal law enforcement reports, obtained via records requests by Property of the People, include similar warnings about doxing. An October 2025 report from the US army said there was “credible intelligence” that “cartels” had offered to pay gang members and others in the US to dox, assault or kidnap immigration officers. That report cited charges against a man accused of a murder-for-hire plot targeting a top border patrol leader, but the man was found not guilty months later. In a November 2025 report, the FBI warned that AI, facial-recognition and automated data-scraping tools had “increased the scale and accuracy of doxxing attacks” targeting ICE officers. The alert said people had published ICE officers’ names, photos, license plates, locations and family details, citing various crowdsourced efforts by activists to report ICE sightings. In a January 2026 New York police department “terrorism brief”, the NYPD warned of “violent rhetoric” and “extremist messaging” on social media after the killing of Renee Good, including “calls to ‘hunt down’, ‘dox’, and kill ICE personnel”. The report cited a small number of online posts that appeared to call for violence. And a May 2026 alert from Customs and Border Protection (CBP), a branch of DHS, warned that smart glasses, which have cameras, could be used to surveil, record and potentially dox CBP personnel. A CBP spokesperson did not comment directly on the document, but said in an email that smart glasses “pose unique security and intelligence risks because of their ability to discreetly capture audio and video” and the agency continues to monitor technology trends. Property of the People shared records with the Guardian earlier this month showing law enforcement across the US have grown increasingly concerned that smart glasses could be used against officers. Other law enforcement agencies that have raised concerns about ICE agents being doxed in internal records include the FBI in Los Angeles, the Amtrak police department, an Idaho law enforcement consortium, a Florida fusion center of local and federal agencies, and the Federal Protective Service, which is also part of DHS. There can be safety concerns if agents’ home addresses or family information is exposed, and two activists were convicted of “stalking” in California after prosecutors said they followed an agent home and publicly disclosed the location. But German argued law enforcement’s claims about doxing were misguided, noting that ICE officers are domestic servants, not “secret agents” whose identities must be shielded: “These are agents working on the public dime. The public has a right to know who they are and what their qualifications and training are.”

title: ‘Songwriting instead of doomscrolling’: project inspires Welsh valleys towns to tune into their heritage
summary: Community groups and schools work with Wales’s folk arts organisation to set stories of the area’s people to music
text: Growing up in Wales, Liz Puleston-Jones was familiar with the country’s rich heritage of storytelling and traditional music, but none of it ever seemed to have much of a connection to her life in Swansea. Researching the history of the area as part of Cân y Cymoedd (When Valleys Sing), a project in nearby Port Talbot, she came across the story of Isabel Thomas, a 14-year-old girl in the 1940s who left school and lied about her age to work in a tin plate works to support her family. “Her story really spoke to me,” said Puleston-Jones. “Before I did this, I didn’t really have a connection to the history and storytelling aspect of folk music, and how much it’s about community and telling the stories of normal people … Anyone can be part of a tune, and write a tune, and share it.” Thomas’s story has now been celebrated in song form as part of the project from Wales’s national folk arts organisation, Trac Cymru. At Cân y Cymoedd community and school workshops, musicians, historians and volunteers have helped each group uncover stories at local heritage sites and museums, and channelled their findings into the creation of two dozen new compositions about local life in Rhondda Cynon Taf and Neath Port Talbot. For many participants, the workshops have rekindled a sense of cultural pride and belonging in the community. Jenny Pope, who took part in the sessions in Port Talbot, said: “For me, it made the Port Talbot area feel like a real beacon of folk music – somewhere people might once have just driven past but now feels full of life and culture. Creating something we can pass on to the next generation has been amazing.” Puleston-Jones added: “I was terrified at the idea of having to write or produce something on my own but it was a collaborative experience. Now instead of watching rubbish TV or doomscrolling I’m being drawn to songwriting and playing my violin after years and years. It feels much healthier.” At Llwyncelyn primary school in Porth, in the Rhondda valley, a year 6 class has been busy learning the song about their village composed by last year’s cohort with the help of a fiddle player, Aneirin Jones, before recording a music video at Rhondda Heritage Park, a former colliery. Their song, Ein Cân Fach Ni (Our Little Song), references the area’s mountains, mines and chapels, as well as the activities and places that make up the children’s day-to-day lives, such as the recycling centre and the playground. Ifan, 10, said: “I knew Cwm Rhondda before but I didn’t really know anything else about folk music before this, it’s been really fun. My sister is annoyed because her class wrote the song but my class is going to make the video!” The original songs are being professionally recorded for an album Trac Cymru hopes will be accessible to a wider audience and become a resource for future generations. The project manager, Antwn Owen-Hicks, said: “Cân y Cymoedd is about making sure that traditions continue to evolve. Magic happens when people explore all of this and begin to see where they’re from in a different light. It doesn’t matter what musical level you’re at or what language you speak. If you’ve got a story, you can write a song, and we help you do this.”
