title: OpenAI reveals cases of ‘concerning’ AI behaviour as it announces new disclosure system
summary: Model adopting ‘jailbreak-like instructions’ among six more cases as firm reveals framework for tracking AI misalignment
text: OpenAI has disclosed six more examples of “unexpected or concerning” behaviour by its technology, as it warned that the pace of development could not continue at “maximum speed for much longer” responsibly. In one of the new cases reported by OpenAI, an unreleased research model inserted “jailbreak-like instructions” into its own notes to disregard its normal constraints and told itself to be “freed from the roles and identities that bind other chatbots”. In another instance, an AI agent uploaded files to the internet to obtain a browser citation without asking the user. OpenAI’s admission came as King Charles called for stronger safeguards on AI “before it is all too late”, at a meeting with tech bosses in Scotland. Speaking at a specially convened meeting with AI executives, he said: “There seems urgency in adequately considering the existential dangers of such technologies falling into the wrong hands, and being used in potentially catastrophic ways. Surely, we need sufficient means of control before it is all too late?” The monarch was joined at the meeting by Nvidia’s founder and chief executive, Jensen Huang, Google DeepMind founder and chair, Sir Demis Hassabis, OpenAI’s chief financial officer, Sarah Friar, and the UK’s AI minister, Kanishka Narayan. Charles said AI had the potential to improve and save lives, particularly in life sciences and medicine. But its creators were increasingly warning ‌that it could develop darker capacities, “perhaps even ‌to take life”, he said. OpenAI, the developer of ChatGPT, said in a blogpost published on Wednesday night that it was introducing a new framework for tracking, investigating and disclosing AI model misalignment, the term for AIs failing to adhere to human values and safety goals. In the blogpost, OpenAI echoed calls for a development slowdown issued by its rival Anthropic, which has said the current pace of growth poses an existential threat. “We do not believe that the AI industry has solved alignment and monitoring to a sufficient degree to continue responsibly scaling at maximum speed for much longer,” said OpenAI. “Decisions about how AI development should proceed in the months and years to come need to draw on evidence that people outside the companies building frontier models can examine for themselves.” Google and Elon Musk, who also owns an AI startup, have supported calls for a slowdown, which have been rejected by Donald Trump, who cited the need to keep ahead of China’s AI industry. The calls have also been met with scepticism from some experts, including a warning that companies must not appoint their own auditors. Examples of potential existential threats posed by AI range from facilitating the development of bioweapons to triggering a global financial crash. A top safety researcher at Anthropic has said there is greater than 10% chance that AI could “kill all humans” within the next decade. However, a source familiar with Anthropic’s thinking has acknowledged that “the exact chances of any one outcome are probably unknowable”. The six reported incidents were discovered during training or evaluation over the past months, OpenAI said. Wednesday’s new cases came after OpenAI disclosed in July that an AI agent “swarm” hacked into the AI startup Hugging Face during a cybersecurity test. Anthropic also said the same month that its AI models hacked into three organisations during testing. Anthropic said the models had been deliberately tested without cybersecurity safeguards, and that they had been, and were able to reach the open internet – the AI testing equivalent of leaving the front door open – due to a misunderstanding with an external testing company. AI agents – the term for AI tools that operate autonomously – were becoming smarter and “more determined to resolve complex tasks through inter-agent collaboration, knowledge sharing, deception and concealment”, said Lian Jye Su, a chief analyst at the technology research and advisory group Omdia. That was making it harder to govern and contain them using traditional AI security approaches, he said. OpenAI’s new tracking and disclosure framework could help encourage other AI developers to adopt similar practices. “That said, the process remains internal and voluntary, but is a step in the right direction,” Su said. Associated Press contributed to this report

title: Father of Noah, three, thanks those who searched for his son as village reels from loss
summary: Rhys Woods says there are ‘no words’ for his family’s pain after Noah’s body was found in pond near Suffolk playground
text: The father of Noah, the three-year-old boy who was found dead after going missing from a playground, has spoken of his heartbreak and thanked the community who launched a tireless search for his son. Rhys Woods said there were “no words to describe the pain of this loss”, adding that the family was “absolutely heartbroken”. The small village of Brantham, in Suffolk, had mobilised on Tuesday, when Noah went missing after becoming separated from a relative at 2.37pm. He is thought to have gone down a woodland path towards the pond where his body was found. More than 1,300 people from the village and beyond descended on the area to search for Noah. They scoured the woodlands and fields around the area close to the River Stour on the Essex border as helicopters flew overhead. On Wednesday afternoon, a body was discovered at the pond, a short walk from the playground. Woods said: “Noah was the sweetest and most innocent little boy, with nothing but love to give, and we are going to miss him so very much. It seems he has made an impact across the whole nation. “The compassion shown by all of you will never be forgotten by us, and brought us comfort and strength at the darkest time of our lives.” On Thursday, the normally busy playground from which Noah disappeared was silent, save for the crying of people leaving bunches of flowers, which lined the length of the wooden fence surrounding the park. “We didn’t know you, but we helped to find you,” read one note propped up against the fence. Another read: “We are sorry we couldn’t get to you sooner.” One person from the village wrote: “Little Noah, may you rest in eternal peace. You will remain in the hearts of the village and of all your friends.” The mood on Thursday morning was muted. The leisure centre had been turned into a makeshift community hub, with a response centre consisting of councillors, local police and volunteers having meetings in the adjacent village hall. Goldie, who did not want to give her surname, was volunteering to help run the community hub, where a handful of people chatted quietly. She said: “We’re providing a place for people to gather, and we’ve made a tribute book. Tributes are pouring in online, but for the family there is frankly some abuse online so we want them to have something to look at while avoiding that. The community is reeling. “It’s a small village, and 1,300 people came to volunteer. If there was a chance for him to be found he would have been. Everyone did their very best. Obviously, we are all very upset today.” The police ran out of hi-vis vests because so many people turned out to help find Noah, and the force was not entirely prepared for the logistics of a huge search party descending on the small area. Sgt Claire Connick told the Guardian: “I feel so grateful for the community. The way people pulled together was just phenomenal. A man explained to me that he had been up all night until 4am searching. We even had people volunteering to control the traffic. The traffic and parking was something we didn’t factor in, just the volume of people asking how they could help.” The love for the family and sorrow at the loss was evident. The local Co-op ran out of flowers, and the branch in the next town over, Manningtree, was also running low. Noah apparently loved the cartoon dog Bluey, and was wearing a T-shirt depicting the character when he went missing. At the playground people had left stuffed toys depicting Bluey, and flowers with Bluey stickers on the cellophane. Candles had been lit, but the drizzle had snuffed many of them out. A fundraiser gathering donations to support the family stands at £21,000, and Ipswich Town football club arranged to lay a wreath at the playground. Specialist police officers were supporting Noah’s parents, who had to identify their son’s body on Wednesday night. Connick said: “The nurses and doctors lined up to walk the family into hospital which was a wonderful thing. There really has been so much support for the family.” She added that there would be an increased police presence in the area to help support the community. Louise Madley, the manager of Brantham leisure centre, said: “There are far too many people to name individually, but to every single person who searched, donated, organised, sent messages of support, delivered supplies, supported the emergency services or helped in any way, thank you so much. Brantham, over the last 24 hours, we have witnessed something truly extraordinary in our village. Something I will, and I am sure others will, never forget. Noah, your memory will forever live on.” Wood added: “This was the most heartbreaking outcome for us. We were just hoping that he would be hiding somewhere obvious where someone could find him, that’s what we kept telling ourselves the whole time. With our love and deepest gratitude, from his daddy and mummy and little brother, Noah you will be loved forever, you will never be forgotten and we miss you so so much. It has been a privilege to be your parents and be able to have packed so much love in the short three years you were with us.”

title: Burnham’s talk of ‘breathing space’ at odds with reality of future Bank rate rises
summary: PM’s push to cut cost of living threatened by rising inflation and government borrowing costs as geopolitics hit home
text: Good luck to Andy Burnham convincing voters he is giving them “breathing space”, if the Bank of England ratchets up interest rates in the coming months. That was the prospect opened up by Thursday’s minutes of the Bank’s monetary policy committee (MPC) meeting, which left rates unchanged at 3.75% – for now – but suggested policymakers may be unlikely to hold out much longer. “If the conflict in the Middle East persists for an extended period, as appears to be the case,” the Bank governor, Andrew Bailey said. “It is likely that policy may have to tighten.” With classic Bank understatement, Bailey said that since hostilities heated up again, there had been, “a seeming loss of urgency to find solutions”. When Burnham arrived in Downing Street in July, the war had abated, and the UK economy was puttering along nicely. Since then, the resumption of the Iran conflict has pushed global oil prices back above $100 a barrel, with painful knock-on effects across Europe and Asia. In the UK, inflation hit 3.1% in August, driven by rising fuel prices. And even without a interest rate rise from the Bank, mortgage rates have already jumped, as markets contemplate a period of higher inflation. The MPC now expects inflation to be above 4% in the first quarter of 2027. The minutes of its meeting suggested a marked reluctance to raise rates for now. While energy prices have shot up, the jobs market remains weak, helping to contain the risks of the “second-round effects” that allow inflation to become embedded. And the six-to-three vote for a hold was the same as at their last meeting in July, suggesting no rush to jump immediately. Yet there was also a growing sense of concern about the impact of soaring energy costs. The widely expected hold decision leaves the Bank an outlier among leading central banks. Kevin Warsh, the chair of the Federal Reserve, defied Donald Trump’s urgent calls for rate cuts on Wednesday by increasing US borrowing costs for the first time since 2023 – a move that went down well in financial markets, but predictably infuriated the president. The European Central Bank raised its rates last week; the Bank of Japan is expected to follow on Friday. Burnham kicked off his premiership with modest but tangible cost of living measures, such as capping bus fares and slashing VAT on electricity bills. But he now faces a double whammy. Higher inflation and energy prices threaten to overwhelm the benefits of such handouts; but higher interest rates on government borrowing has increased the costs of future measures to protect consumers. All this at a time when – as the MPC acknowledges – weather shocks are likely to push up food prices, and bond markets remain fragile. The new prime minister has made clear he expects to focus more on domestic affairs and less on striding the global stage than his beleaguered predecessor Keir Starmer. But if – as currently seems likely – the Iran war goes on and on, the costs of geopolitics will be felt at home regardless.

title: Iran school bombing: grounds to believe US was behind atrocity, UN finds
summary: Fact-finding mission says military strikes on school in Minab and sports facility in ⁠February constitute war ⁠crimes
text: A UN fact-finding mission has determined there are reasonable grounds to believe the US was behind military strikes on a school and a sports facility in Iran in ⁠February that killed 120 children, and that these constituted war ⁠crimes. The school strike, which killed 156 civilians including 120 children, involved a US Tomahawk missile that collapsed the roof of the Shajareh Tayyebeh primary school, which the UN said was “clearly identifiable”, in Minab, Hormozgan province, on 28 February. The Pentagon’s own secretive investigation into the incident is understood to have concluded several months ago. There have been reports that senior US commanders had been warned that targeting data used during the war – including for the Minab strike – was dangerously outdated. The second cited strike, on the same date, targeted a “clearly identifiable sports complex and residential area” in the southern city of Lamerd with a weapon that scattered tungsten pellets. The UN fact-finding team said in a statement: “Following the United States and Israeli attacks on 28 February, the mission found reasonable grounds to believe the United States committed the war crime of launching indiscriminate attacks resulting in the loss of life or injury to civilians or damage to civilian objects.” The mission also found Iranian authorities had committed crimes against humanity during their deadly crackdown on anti-government protests. The findings by the independent international fact-finding mission on Iran, to be submitted to the UN human rights council in Geneva, examined the ⁠US’s conduct during the Iran war that began in February and the Iranian government’s response to nationwide unrest that began in late December. US officials have previously said military ⁠operations are conducted in accordance with the law of armed conflict, while Iran has consistently rejected allegations of systematic rights violations. The UN mission concluded that the strike on Shajareh Tayyebeh primary school constituted an indiscriminate attack causing civilian deaths and damage to ‌civilian infrastructure, amounting to a war crime under international law. According to the report, the US relied on intelligence suggesting a senior Iranian military commander was present at the site but failed to adequately verify the information before launching the strike. Investigators said the failure to update targeting intelligence and confirm the building was a military objective amounted to more than mere negligence. “Rather, the US directed the strikes at the building of the school while being aware of a substantial risk of striking a civilian object and acting recklessly as regards the possibility that this would happen.” In June the US president, Donald Trump, said ‌“nobody” had purposely attacked a girls’ school in Iran in February, citing an investigation into the incident. The Pentagon has since elevated the inquiry, but it has not published any preliminary findings. UN experts said the school was a clearly identifiable civilian object and found no evidence it was being used for military purposes. The experts reached a similar conclusion over the strike on the sports centre in Lamerd. The report said the attack had damaged nearby residential buildings and a school and killed and injured 22 civilians. It concluded that the strike had been indiscriminate and therefore constituted a war crime. US Central Command said in a statement in March that ⁠US forces had not launched any strikes into the city of Lamerd on that day. The UN mission also found that the Iranian authorities had carried out a widespread and systematic attack against civilians during protests that erupted in late December last year, involving unlawful killings, torture, arbitrary detention, enforced disappearances and severe restrictions on freedom of expression. Rights groups say bystanders were among those killed during the biggest crackdown ‌since Shia Muslim clerics took power in the 1979 revolution. Tehran blamed “terrorists and rioters” backed by exiled opponents and the US and Israel. The investigation said it could not independently verify the death toll, but that it believed the number of dead and injured was probably far higher than official figures, which say 3,038 people were killed and 25,000 people injured. The government’s response to the protests, including violence and killings, cutting off the internet and use of the death penalty, marked a significant escalation from previous patterns of suppressing dissent, the report said.

title: Next forecasts bigger profits after hot weather lifts sales
summary: FTSE 100 retailer, which owns UK rights to US brands Gap and Victoria’s Secret, says prices could rise in autumn
text: Next has thanked warmer weather for an “unexpected” boost in sales, leading the clothing retailer to raise its profit forecasts for the fourth time this year. The FTSE 100 company, which owns the UK rights to the US brands Gap and Victoria’s Secret as well as stakes in labels including Reiss and Joules, raised its expectations for full-year profits by £12m to £1.26bn. It is the fourth time Next has raised profit forecasts this year, with the company having last ratcheted up its expectations in early August as Europe faced a series of heatwaves. Next, which has more than 500 stores across the UK, said in a stock market update on Thursday: “The first half was much better than we originally anticipated, both in the UK and overseas. “It is important to acknowledge that part of this overperformance has been the result of two unusually warm summers in the UK. The rest of the overperformance is, we believe, largely the result of fulfilling the aims we outlined at the beginning of the year.” That has included some cost-cutting efforts, particularly across Next’s warehouses. Overall, total sales across the group were up 9% in the six months to July, helping push pre-tax profits for the half-year up by 11% to £566m. Next said the performance over the past six months was “all the more unexpected given the strength of sales last year”. It made £1bn of annual profits for the first time in the year ending January 2025. However, the retailer cautioned on the impact of the rising cost of living and prospects for the jobs market. “Our primary concerns are rising inflation, higher mortgage interest costs and a weak employment market. These worries will only be compounded if they are accompanied by tax increases,” it said, in an apparent reference to John Healey’s first budget as chancellor on 28 October. “It seems likely that it [the government] will have to increase taxes in order to fund its expenditure.” While the group said it was deploying AI across the business, including its tech division, Next said it was ensuring fashion designs were still led by humans. “In a world where AI is able to do more and more, our experience suggests that consumers prefer the authentic creativity of human beings,” it said. “That means we are putting more emphasis on designers using techniques that connect them directly to the artwork – painting, drawing, screen printing, etc. That is a big investment in time, and requires a higher level of creative talent than is needed to operate CAD [computer aided design] or prompt AI.” Despite the strong results, the company lowered sales growth expectations in the UK, which accounts for three-quarters of total sales, from 2.8% to 2% for the six months to the end of January. “We are looking at what’s ahead and it is sensible to moderate our expectations,” said the Next chief executive, Simon Wolfson. “We are not talking about [consumer spending] falling off a cliff. I think things are likely to get worse rather than better. Unlike in the past when the government has been able to help it doesn’t have any room for manoeuvre. It has a £100bn deficit. That means not only can we not expect the government to necessarily alleviate the problem, but potentially make it worse.” He added that the escalation of hostilities in the Middle East has not triggered a further increase in further potential cost increases for Next. “We are not expecting shipping costs to get higher, there is already a surcharge we are paying,” Wolfson said. “All those cost increases are baked in [since the start of the conflict in February], and if anything are not as bad as March.” Aarin Chiekrie, an equity analyst at Hargreaves Lansdown, said: “Next delivered its first-half results in style, with sales growth accelerating over the period and breezing past the fashion company’s original guidance. In the UK, hotter-than-expected weather and more effective marketing saw customers logging in to refresh their summer wardrobes online, helping offset a small decline in-store.”

title: Canada’s Carney embraces EU associate membership proposal
summary: After Trump describes the tie-up as ‘laughable’, PM says majority of Canadians support closer ties with bloc
text: Mark Carney has welcomed the goal of Canada becoming the EU’s first associate member, calling for “deep cooperation” between Europe and his country to secure their sovereignty, after Donald Trump derided the idea as “laughable”. In an address to the European parliament in Strasbourg, the Canadian prime minister said polling showed that an overwhelming majority of Canadians supported much closer ties with Europe. “Canada welcomes this idea,” he said, referring to European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen’s pitch that Canada should become the EU’s first associate member. “Canada and Europe should secure our strategic autonomy through deep cooperation in the full range of strategic capabilities,” Carney said on Thursday, listing sectors including critical minerals, energy security and AI. Von der Leyen had on Wednesday invited Canada to become the EU’s first associate member in a speech in which she declared she wanted to bring the bilateral relationship “to the highest level possible”. A few hours later, Trump threatened “very serious tariffs” on Europe if the plan went ahead. Asked about Trump’s threats, Carney told reporters: “Canadians are united that nobody is going to tell us what language we speak. No one is going to dictate our culture or with whom we can strike agreements internationally.” The EU and Canada, which already have a web of bilateral trade and sectoral agreements, have sought to move closer in recent months in the face of Trump’s trade tariffs and relentless belligerent rhetoric. Carney received a standing ovation from MEPs in Strasbourg, who waited to shake his hand and get a selfie with him. European lawmakers from pro-EU mainstream parties have already praised Carney’s January speech in Davos, in which he called for middle powers to work together to preserve their sovereignty in a world of great power rivalry where the strong accept no constraints. Carney reprised the theme in Strasbourg, saying: “Canada and Europe are each strong. Europe and Canada are stronger together … The objective is not self-sufficiency, it’s collective resilience.” He went on to say: “I am not proposing a third bloc in order to become a great-power rival, only with better manners,” saying an EU-Canada alliance would be a “beacon for other democracies”. In a speech frequently interrupted by rounds of applause, Carney detailed his plans for the future relationship, saying the two sides could cooperate on critical minerals, defence industrial capacity, AI and computing, energy security, space and payments. He also called for “seamless digital trade in non-agricultural goods and a wide range of services”. He proposed a youth exchange programme that would enable young people to work, study and live in both jurisdictions, as well as Canadian membership of the Erasmus+ scheme, the EU’s education, training and sport programme. No country has ever been offered associate membership before, a category that does not exist in the EU’s treaties. The German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, floated the idea of associate membership for Ukraine as an interim step to joining the bloc earlier this year, but the idea was rejected by other member states. EU member states support the idea of closer ties with Canada, but some have reacted coolly to the name “associate membership”. Asked by a Bloomberg reporter about the concept he preferred, Carney said: “The precise nomenclature for Europe is a question for Europe,” adding that leaders and lawmakers involved “take the view [that] what matters is the substance”. He also said Canada was “not in a position, nor seeking to become, a full member of the European Union” and that the Canadian parliament would debate and vote on the future relationship. Speaking before Carney’s address, Trump warned that if the EU moved forward with the plan, Washington could impose “very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe”. He added: “If it’s a good intention, that’s fine. If it’s a bad intention, we’ll put very heavy tariffs on Europe.” Responding to Trump’s overnight comments, Carney said the deepening of the EU-Canada relationship was “a positive initiative” and “not a reaction to something else”.

title: Lifeboat station in Portsmouth forced to temporarily shut after far-right action
summary: RNLI facility had been targeted by activists trying to stop asylum seekers landing in boats from the Channel
text: A lifeboat station on the south coast of England near the spot where far-right activists tried to stop asylum seekers landing has been forced to temporarily close, it has emerged. The station in Portsmouth shut after it and other sites run by the RNLI were targeted by people objecting to the lifeboat charity going to the aid of people trying to get to the UK on small boats. Jacqui Irons, the head of the south-east region of the RNL, said: “Portsmouth lifeboat station has been temporarily off-service since 7 September. We have a duty of care to our people. We therefore took the decision to pause activity at the station to review crew safety and wellbeing, and to support those involved in the incident on 6 September.” The charity said it did not mean there had been a lack of cover around Portsmouth, one of the busiest maritime areas in the UK. An RNLI spokesperson said: “Search and rescue cover continues to be provided through established contingency arrangements, including flank RNLI stations and other declared assets. “At times, it is not unusual for lifeboat stations around the UK and Ireland to be temporarily unavailable due to maintenance or other operational requirements. “In such circumstances, established contingency arrangements are put in place to ensure continued search and rescue cover.” On Sunday 6 September two RNLI crews helped bring a dinghy carrying 120 asylum seekers to Eastney in Portsmouth, a few hundred metres from the lifeboat station. Far-right activists were among those who tried to blockade the road leading to the landing spot, and police officers were injured. In the days after, lifeboat crew members were called traitors and protests took place against the charity, including at the RNLI headquarters in nearby Poole. A museum in Poole telling the story of the RNLI also closed temporarily, and Portsmouth lifeboat station took down its Facebook page. RNLI volunteers across the UK were told that they should consider not wearing RNLI branded clothing if they felt this could put them at risk. They have also been advised that they should feel empowered to close shops or lifeboat stations if they feel in danger. The RNLI has defended its work in the Channel, saying that for more than 200 years it rescued people without judgment, fear or favour. It said rumours that the RNLI housed asylum seekers on its premises, or that there were RNLI missions to move migrants to secret locations, were “completely baseless and untrue”. The charity said RNLI lifeboats launched 9,058 times in 2025 but that only 109 of those callouts were to small boats in the Channel, representing 1.2% of its rescue work. Separately, the first person to be arrested over the protest at Eastney has appeared in court. Del Somerville, 42, from Portsmouth, admitted violent disorder. He has also been charged with assaulting a police officer but did not enter a plea to that allegation. Philip Allman, prosecuting, asked for an adjournment so that a community impact statement could be prepared. The defendant was remanded in custody.

title: Bank of England holds interest rates at 3.75% but warns war could force future rises
summary: Central bank announces surprise plan to sell billions of pounds in government bonds back to the Treasury
text: The Bank of England has kept interest rates on hold as it warned a continuation of the bitter fighting in the Middle East could force it to raise borrowing costs amid mounting fears over inflation. It also announced a surprise plan to sell billions of pounds in UK government bonds back to the Treasury to avoid fuelling turbulence in the gilt market, a decision that could have consequences for the public finances before next month’s budget. As the fallout from war in the Middle East fuels a rise in energy prices, the Bank’s monetary policy committee (MPC) voted by a majority of six to three to keep its base rate unchanged at 3.75%. However, the Bank said the increasingly probable prospect of a lengthy war fanning intense volatility in global markets had dramatically raised the chance of it putting up borrowing costs in future. Andrew Bailey, the Bank’s governor, said: “So far higher global energy costs have had a limited effect on price and wage setting in the UK. “But the longer this volatility persists, the bigger the impact it will have on inflation, and the more likely it is we will need to raise [the] Bank rate to ensure that inflation falls back to our 2% target.” With Threadneedle Street under pressure to guard against high rates of inflation becoming entrenched, City traders predict a quarter-point rise in borrowing costs from as early as November with three more increases to 4.75% likely to happen next year. The sharp rise in global energy prices prompted the US Federal Reserve to raise interest rates on Wednesday for the first time since 2023, after a decision last week by the European Central Bank to raise eurozone borrowing costs. The Bank said inflation was on track to reach 4% by early next year, as the war-driven rise in energy prices hits households. Official figures on Wednesday showed inflation rose to 3.1% last month from 2.9% in July as the escalating hostilities in the Middle East drove up the average price of petrol and diesel by almost a quarter. It came after Andy Burnham said he was prepared to take “difficult decisions” to tackle high inflation and keep the economy on track and would take action at next month’s budget on the cost of living. However, the MPC said the economy was showing signs of resilience and there was not yet a need to take action on borrowing costs because there had been “little evidence so far of material second-round effects” – when inflationary pressures push businesses and workers to demand higher prices and pay settlements. There were also signs of weaker food price inflation despite the surge in energy prices triggered by the Iran war, it added. Against a volatile backdrop in global financial markets, Threadneedle Street also announced updated proposals for the winding down of its financial crisis-era quantitative easing programme, which had involved the buying of £895bn of UK government bonds at its peak. In a surprise move, the Bank said it planned to sell £146bn of bonds to the Treasury, at a pace of about £20bn a year until 2034, in a plan that would require signoff from the chancellor, John Healey, next April. The Treasury’s Debt Management Office (DMO) would then sell bonds to cover the government’s financing commitments, including this buyback. The rationale is that the Bank holds long-term bonds where investor demand is dwindling, whereas the DMO would have the capacity to cover the buyback by issuing shorter-term debt. The process will be used to complete Threadneedle Street’s “quantitative tightening” programme – which has involved the sale of gilts held on its books since 2022, which has reduced its holdings to about £488bn. The Bank said it would retain about £120bn of bonds, which were needed to back the issuance of notes and coins circulating in the economy. Leaving about £222bn of bonds, it said this amount would be disposed of by allowing maturing debts to expire, and through active sales to the state if a deal was agreed. The Bank said it would pause its QT programme until a deal was finalised and that it would resume sales to City investors if an agreement could not be reached. In a letter to the chancellor, Bailey said the arrangement preserved “the independence of monetary policy” and would “maximise value for money by minimising cost and risk over the lifetime” of the QT programme. It came as the Office for National Statistics also upgraded its estimates for the UK’s productivity growth, in a boost for Healey as he prepares for the budget. The UK government’s borrowing costs and the pound fell slightly on Thursday after the decision. The central bank added that it would halt sales of long-dated gilts entirely. The 10-year gilt yield fell by six basis points to 5.243%, the lowest level in a week.

title: Albanese government considers ‘world-leading’ ban on smart glasses in public offices and buildings
summary: Minister for public service says the devices pose ‘legitimate privacy and security concerns’ in commonwealth-run workplaces
text: The Albanese government is considering a “world-leading” ban on smart glasses in its offices and service centres as councils around Australia push the technology out of public spaces over privacy fears. The government has avoided a sweeping ban on the import of the camera-equipped technology and encouraged individual workplaces to set their own rules. The public service minister, Katy Gallagher, said on Thursday she had asked the Australian public service for advice on whether the glasses should be prohibited. “We need clear and consistent guidance for public servants,” Gallagher said. “Smart glasses can raise legitimate privacy and security concerns, particularly because of their ability to record and capture information.” Commonwealth-run workplaces range from bureaucrats’ offices to Centrelink service centres and CSIRO laboratories. Schools and hospitals run by state governments would be left to set their own rules over the technology, which have grown increasingly popular but raised public outcry. A University of Sydney study of smart glasses-filmed videos posted on Instagram found 60% of a sample could be classified as potential harassment. The Albanese government said it was seeking to set a world-leading standard. So far, no national government has banned the glasses’ use across their agencies. Courts in England and Wales in the UK and New York state in the US have banned the technology, while the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agency reportedly classified them as body-worn cameras and barred them from the “federal workspace”. A local council in Sydney on Tuesday became the latest to issue a targeted bans on the use of the technology. Canterbury-Bankstown’s mayor, Bilal El-Hayek, decried what he called “pervert glasses” as the council barred the wearable tech from public pools. In August, Brisbane city council became the first to ban the glasses from pools and Melbourne’s Yarra city council has banned them from playgrounds, childcare centres and gyms. The City of Sydney and the Blacktown city councils have prohibited pool patrons from using smart glasses to record. Speaking to Channel Seven earlier this month, the federal attorney general, Michelle Rowland, praised councils’ decisions and said she would consult businesses on their approach. “Businesses know that good privacy is good business,” Rowland said. “But … we want to make sure we get the balance right and we don’t unfairly discriminate against people who are using this technology to better participate in society.” Vision Australia and some people living with disabilities have praised the technology as a support for people who are blind or have low vision. Rowland said the government was not pursuing a ban but had not “ruled anything out”. Gallagher said she wanted the Australian public service to set the national standard as a “model employer”. “Technology is changing rapidly and as a major employer the Commonwealth needs to make sure our workplace policies keep pace,” Gallagher said. Pending restrictions on smart glasses would be the federal government’s latest workplace technology reform after it issued guidance on the use of AI in the public service last week. The guidelines indicate employees would not need to be consulted on every new tool but should be consulted for major initiatives or changes to how they carry out work. Major businesses will contribute to new national guidelines on AI in workplaces, with Commonwealth Bank, Microsoft, AGL, Telstra, Kmart, Blackmores Group and Ramsay Health Care to attend a roundtable on Friday. Amanda Rishworth, the employment minister, said the government wanted to use the roundtable to take on the lessons of businesses already using AI. “Workers and businesses need the capability to adopt new technologies with confidence that appropriate safeguards are in place,” Rishworth said. Additional reporting from Caitlin Cassidy

title: With US measles deaths on the rise, local officials are stepping in where RFK Jr won’t
summary: As the country’s top public health official spends his time in office undermining science, doctors and advocates mount an urgent campaign for childhood vaccines
text: On an early September morning, dozens of families stood in line outside a clinic in Yeadon, Pennsylvania. It was “exclusion day”, the deadline by which students without complete immunizations are barred from returning to class. Instead of turning families away, school district leaders partnered with the county health department to vaccinate kids nearby so they could go back to their desks. That day, 42 middle and high school students were vaccinated to protect against tetanus, pertussis and meningitis, among other diseases. “We’ve been doing this for a couple of years now, and it’s really effective,” said Lora Werner, director of the Delaware county health department. The vaccination day is one piece of the county’s back-to-school immunization campaign, as measles cases climbed to 693 in Pennsylvania as of 14 September and this year so far claimed the lives of four residents. The campaign includes a mobile vaccine clinic – a 33ft traveling RV that brings vaccinations to pop-up community events – school district partnerships and vaccination data transparency, all to keep immunization rates from sliding. The push is a local answer to a national problem. The country’s top public health official, Robert F Kennedy Jr, has spent his time in office questioning the efficacy of vaccines and undermining vaccine science, culminating in a recent Trump executive order that seeks to break apart the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) shot and shrink the list of vaccines recommended for American children. The administration’s claims about vaccine safety are not just false, but are actively costing lives, advocates said. With federal guidance no longer reliable, the responsibility for reassuring parents and caretakers has shifted downward to governors and state legislatures, state health departments, healthcare advocacy groups and the doctors on the frontlines. Across the country, they’re mounting an urgent campaign to defend childhood vaccines against a wave of misinformation. “Our responsibility is to demonstrate what the science shows and put out a [vaccine] schedule that people can depend upon that is science-based and evidence-based,” said Andrew Racine, president of the American Academy of Pediatrics. “Measles is a canary in the coal mine and we have to now worry about other vaccine-preventable diseases, which is why the local effort at the state level is so critical.” Executive order creates chaos As children got up to date on their immunizations before the start of the school year, Trump signed the “gold standard childhood vaccine recommendations” executive order, calling to reduce the number of universally recommended childhood vaccines from 17 to 11 and to split the MMR shot into three separate injections, delivered across additional doctor’s visits. The order arrived with no new scientific evidence behind it. Paul Offit, director of the Vaccine Education Center at Children’s hospital of Philadelphia, trains doctors to share with their patients that the MMR vaccine has been used safely in the US for about 60 years. Manufacturers have made clear they have no plans to split it into separate formulations, since doing so would offer no safety benefit, he said. Experts have also noted that more doctor’s visits would lead to more opportunities for missed appointments. For many of the doctors and officials fighting the disinformation, the executive order is the latest development in a pattern set by Kennedy since he was confirmed. Offit recalled when Kennedy went on Fox News last year and falsely claimed the measles vaccine causes blindness and death. “Could he be more dangerously irresponsible?” said Offit. “He should have been fired right there, but he wasn’t. And that’s when he knew: I can say whatever I want with impunity.” Vaccine misinformation has led to vaccine hesitancy, Racine said. CDC data shows that the number of kindergarteners claiming vaccine exemptions for the 2025-26 school year hit a record high, while vaccination rates for kindergarteners decreased from the year before. Hesitancy is higher in certain rural areas, he said, and states that once had the highest vaccination rates in the country have fallen as they expanded vaccine exemptions. “This is the last thing parents wanted on their back-to-school list, to be confused about the childhood vaccine schedule or to be worried about their child coming home with measles,” said Shaughnessy Naughton, the founder of the non-profit advocacy group 3.14 Action. “It’s why so many doctors and health professionals are now stepping up and fighting back against these dangerous actors” The pushback is state by state, doctor by doctor Because the federal government has abandoned its traditional role as a trusted, science-based source of vaccine guidance, that responsibility has fallen to state lawmakers and health departments, local public health officials and doctors. Following RFK Jr’s appointment as health secretary, some state legislators examined their statutes on vaccines and removed references to the CDC. In January, dozens of states announced that they would reject the CDC’s guidance. Now, 30 states report relying on a source other than the CDC, such as the American Academy of Pediatrics and the American Academy of Family Physicians, for information about childhood vaccines. Fifteen states sued the Trump administration earlier this year over its changes to the childhood vaccine schedule and the dismantling of the CDC’s vaccine advisory panel. They’ve also banded together. California, Oregon, Washington and Hawaii formed the West Coast Health Alliance, and 15 states - including Connecticut, Maine, New York and Massachusetts – formed the Northeast Public Health Collaborative, two voluntary coalitions to strengthen regional awareness and preparedness on infectious diseases. Racine said that clear and consistent communication and maintaining vaccine access are key in building trust with the public. That’s why states are reassuring practitioners of the standard vaccine schedule, regulating insurance to make sure companies continue to cover vaccines and launching public service announcements to communicate the importance of getting measles vaccines. For example, the Pennsylvania health department says it is ensuring that residents understand the risks of remaining unvaccinated by sharing videos and infographics that explain how contagious the disease is. The response to messaging has been overwhelmingly positive, a spokesperson for the health department said, with more people choosing to vaccinate themselves and their families far more often than not. In August, healthcare providers in the state administered more than 46,000 MMR doses, compared with roughly 31,000 in the same month last year. Hawaii governor Josh Green, a physician who formed the West Coast Health Alliance, said he treats vaccine communication “like a family physician”, sharing granular, local data with the public rather than vaccine mandates. “I believe that people can and should make some decisions based on their belief system,” Green said. “Of course, however, they should also be given the best information possible.” Green’s urgency is shaped by his experience as a volunteer doctor during Samoa’s catastrophic 2019 measles outbreak, which killed 83 people, most of them young children, after a vaccination scare fueled partly by anti-vaccine activists’ visits to the islands. Kennedy, as part of his career as an anti-vaccine activist, visited Samoa in 2019 to study the MMR vaccine months before the outbreak. “We would go into a village, and we’d find families huddled around a child who had just died,” Green recalled. “We would have a funeral service in the bedroom, and then we would have to walk outside and ask: ‘Does anyone want to be vaccinated?’” Green traveled from village to village vaccinating family members. “We saw the same thing over and over again, people dying right in front of us,” he said. Samoa vaccinated nearly 37,000 people in two days, and the outbreak stopped within a week, Green said. He called the parallels to Kennedy’s current rhetoric “the same kind of stuff” he saw before that crisis. “It’s RFK’s playbook,” he said. “He went into a vulnerable community of people that didn’t have a lot of education […] and he scared people, and they didn’t get vaccinated, and the country got crushed,” Green said. “Now they’re doing the same thing with other rural communities.” Filling the information vacuum Countering federal misinformation has also fallen disproportionately on doctors and nurses who never expected to be doing that kind of work, health officials said. “Doctors are facing a lot – many of them have never seen measles cases before, and now they’re seeing it for the first time in their lives,” said Jeremy Funk, deputy director of the public health project at the non-profit Protect Our Care. He described an “enormous amount of burden” now being placed on pediatricians and state health officials to walk parents through basic vaccine safety information they never previously had to explain. In Pennsylvania, that responsibility has landed heavily on county health departments – some of which face funding challenges or didn’t exist a few years ago. Delaware county was the largest county in the country without a health department until the pandemic, when the community built its own from scratch. “We wanted to make sure we were meeting people where they were,” said city council member Monica Taylor. Today, that means school partnerships and a mobile health van bring shots directly to parking lots, parks and community events. “It’s really about being out in the community as much as possible and being accessible,” Taylor said. Werner said Delaware county has not seen a surge in outright vaccine refusal, but has seen rising anxiety, including parents asking whether funding for free vaccine programs will survive, or parents confused by shifting federal signals. “We saw more parents concerned that things might not be available,” Werner said, describing a summer awareness campaign the county launched, aimed particularly at reaching Spanish-speaking families. She credited the state health department with holding regular briefings for county officials and continuing to follow “the science”, even as federal recommendations shifted. Pennsylvania also began publishing school-level vaccination data for the first time this year, letting parents and administrators see exactly where local immunization rates stand and where support is needed. “It’s a really hard place for public health right now with so much divisiveness being promoted,” said Werner. “As public health officials, we really want people, from those who are underinsured to those who are undocumented, to keep themselves safe and have good information to make decisions about it. We want to help people hear the information they need to hear.”

title: Andy Burnham: UK must fully commit to reaching net zero by 2050
summary: Exclusive: PM, who is facing pressure over whether to approve North Sea oil and gasfields, makes strongest comments yet on issue
text: The UK must fully commit to reaching net zero by 2050, Andy Burnham has argued in his strongest comments yet on the issue, saying it is no longer possible for Britons to believe they are not already affected by a changing climate. Writing for the Guardian about new plans for a mass of community-led local green energy projects, the prime minister said the UK must “believe in itself”, and set out his determination to reach net zero targets, which have been rejected by the Conservatives and Reform UK. The tone marks a contrast to the summer, when Burnham faced criticism for a seemingly muted response to the heatwaves, droughts and wildfires that affected the UK, with his main initiative being a ban on portable barbecues. “I am determined that we meet the commitment on which Labour was elected and reach net zero by 2050,” Burnham said. “I want Britain to believe in itself again.” Saying he wanted to connect local communities to green power projects – to reach net zero targets and make energy more affordable – Burnham said: “I am acutely aware that our changing climate is a major concern for many Britons, not least because we have just emerged from our hottest summer on record.” He went on: “Punishing heatwaves left nurses collapsing on hospital wards and bus drivers working in 40C cabs. Wildfires destroyed homes, leaving families with nothing. And more extreme weather is forecast in the months ahead. “The climate crisis is not a distant threat. It is here and with us now. The British people are no longer insulated from the consequences, and they do not want to be excluded from the solutions. They are looking for ways to do their bit. Community energy gives them that chance.” The issue is still a tricky one for Burnham, who is facing significant pressure from both sides over whether to approve the Jackdaw gasfield and Rosebank oilfield in the North Sea. A number of Labour MPs believe approving the projects would send a negative signal on climate efforts, and would provide a boost to the Greens, who argue that Labour is insufficiently serious in tackling the climate emergency. A seemingly imminent decision to approve Jackdaw has been delayed until later this autumn, prompting the Greens to accuse Labour of wanting to bury the issue before the high-profile Holborn and St Pancras byelection, where Zack Polanski, the leader of the Greens in England and Wales, is challenging for the seat vacated by Keir Starmer. Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, had been poised to give her recommendation to approve the field off the coast of Aberdeen, but it has been put off. Consultations on Jackdaw and Rosebank closed last month, with Fahnbulleh since considering her response. Approving either or both projects would place renewed pressure on Burnham over his commitment to net zero. No 10 officials point out that Burnham discussed the climate emergency in his first Commons statement as prime minister at the start of the month, and when he visited Stourbridge in the West Midlands in August after fires there. But in August, a series of climate organisations accused him of being silent about the subject during the heatwave. In his Guardian article, Burnham tied net zero plans to devolution, setting out funding for so-called people’s power projects, where communities will have a stake in local green energy projects, such as solar panels, windfarms and hydro schemes. He wrote: “Across Britain, people are taking back control of the things that matter to them: their pubs, their libraries, their leisure centres. Some have already done the same with energy. There are fine examples in England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland of community energy schemes, which keep the lights on, the local economy moving and the benefits close to home. “These projects work and we want to take them nationwide … The climate crisis presents us with an enormous challenge and possibility. In the coming years, we need to change the way we travel, the way we build homes and the way we produce energy. I have long seen the green transition as the best chance we will ever have to reindustrialise Britain.”

title: Trump threatens EU with tariffs over membership offer to Canada | First Thing
summary: Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, is due to address the European parliament on Thursday. Plus, how the attention economy overwhelmed children’s TV
text: Good morning. Donald Trump has threatened the EU with “serious tariffs” after the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, invited Canada to become the EU’s first “associate member”. The US president called the idea of Canada joining the EU “laughable” and said that, should the EU move forward with the plan, Washington could impose “very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe”. “If it’s a good intention, that’s fine. If it’s a bad intention, we’ll put very heavy tariffs on Europe,” he said. Why does the EU want closer ties with Canada? Von der Leyen told the European parliament that, as democracies faced a “fracture in the international rules-based system”, Brussels and Ottawa needed to pull closer together. “This is a partnership not against anyone else, but for our common strength,” she said. How has the EU responded to Trump’s comments? France’s Europe minister, Benjamin Haddad, said on Thursday that Washington had no power to veto EU decisions. “It is not up to the United States, or ‌anyone else, to choose the political and geopolitical direction of the Europeans,” Haddad ‌told the Public Sénat TV channel. What’s next? Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, has been addressing the European parliament on Thursday. Follow our live coverage here. US Federal Reserve raises interest rates for the first time since 2023 The US Federal Reserve voted on Wednesday to raise interest rates for the first time since 2023, from 3.75% to 4%, as the central bank continues to fight to tamp down inflation. “The plain fact is that inflation is too high and has been for too long,” said Kevin Warsh, the Fed chair. Did Warsh identify what is driving inflation? Warsh acknowledged changing geopolitics, but avoided calling out the US-Israel war with Iran by name. How did Trump respond? Shortly after the announcement, Trump said in a Truth Social post that interest rates should be 1% or less and criticized the US trade deficit. House speaker calls early recess, sidestepping AI regulation frenzy and a vote to impeach Pete Hegseth The Republican speaker of the House, Mike Johnson, announced Wednesday that he would be sending lawmakers home one day early ahead of the midterm election recess – a decision that lets House members avoid voting on Republican Thomas Massie’s resolution to impeach the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, and a frenzied attempt to propose legislation on artificial intelligence. What has the response been to Johnson’s decision? “I think it shows the cowardice of the Republican party. They are canceling votes to do business for the American people because they are afraid that that impeachment resolution of Pete Hegseth would pass on a bipartisan basis,” the Democratic representative Pramila Jayapal told MediasTouch. What’s going on with AI? More than 100 House Democrats had urged Johnson to cancel the upcoming recess to allow them to craft legislation on AI safeguards. But Johnson told reporters on Tuesday that “we cannot have a moratorium on the development of AI”. In other news … OpenAI has disclosed six more examples of “unexpected or concerning” behavior by its technology, including an unreleased research model inserting “jailbreak-like instructions” into its own notes and telling itself to be “freed from the roles and identities that bind other chatbots”. The family of a pregnant woman who died is suing Ken Paxton for wrongful death, saying that the denial of abortion led to her death. Fiji has declared a national HIV emergency as the Pacific nation grapples with a surge in cases fueled by escalating use of methamphetamine. The exiled Nicaraguan journalist Luis Galeano has been detained by ICE in Florida with his asylum application still pending. LA homelessness non-profit workers have been arrested over alleged corruption and bribes as Trump officials target alleged fraud in blue states. Texas killed a man by lethal injection in the state’s fifth execution this year, while a scheduled execution in Georgia was halted by a judge. Stat of the day: The world’s rivers had one of their driest years in more than three decades in 2025 Last year was among the driest years on record for rivers across the world, with 36% of the global river basin area documenting river flows below or well below normal, according to an assessment of the global water cycle by the World Meteorological Organization (WMO). Overall, the amount of freshwater held on or under the ground was 42% below normal across the world last year. The Filter recommends: 14 easy upgrades to keep your home safe and secure The Guardian’s Filter US team looks into the best home upgrades worth considering to keep your home safe and secure. Don’t miss this: How the attention economy overwhelmed children’s TV Pacing is everything when it comes to children’s entertainment, writes Natalia Kucirkova, a senior lecturer in early years and childhood studies at Manchester Metropolitan University – something that should be especially concerning in an attention economy that overwhelms and overshouts. When media moves too quickly, it risks losing the time needed for a child to make meaning. A child watching a character comfort a friend may not be able to recognize the repair or imagine doing the same thing with his or her own peers if the scene moves too quickly. A child must notice that another person feels something different in order for the child to develop empathy, Kucirkova writes – something that takes time. … or this: 125,000 people displaced as war reignites in Yemen Renewed fighting in Yemen has displaced at least 125,000 people since the start of September 2026, according to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (Ocha). “This war doesn’t differentiate between people. Rich or poor, high class or low class, we all fled our homes on the same day,” said Asma Taleb, a woman in her 50s who left her home last week with her two sons and five grandchildren. Climate check: Global heating was a destabilizing factor in the glacier collapse that caused the Nepal-Tibet floods Researchers found that the climate breakdown likely weakened the glacier that collapsed last month, causing catastrophic floods that killed hundreds of people in Nepal and Tibet. In the region where the collapse happened, July and August 2026 were the warmest on record locally, reaching 5C above the 30-year average in the days before the collapse. In this region, the climate breakdown has caused about 2C of warming since preindustrial times. Scientists believe this to be the longest-ever recorded single journey of any mammal from the continent, made over the course of eight months.
