title: Trump and Rubio allies are vying for control of Cuba’s assets if regime falls
summary: Washington and Florida insiders are exploring lucrative deals for a post-communist Cuba crushed by ever-increasing US sanctions
text: Spanish hotel chains. A Canadian mining firm. European shipping giants. Visa and Mastercard. Scores of foreign companies have been driven out of Cuba this summer over fear of being hit with potent, new secondary sanctions. Marco Rubio, the secretary of state, told Axios last month there are “no escape valves” from his unprecedented pressure campaign against the island. But not everybody is losing out. A growing cast of Washington and Florida insiders – from billionaire Trump allies and Rubio-linked lobbyists to Cuban exiles – are jockeying for control of the communist-ruled island-nation’s key assets, charging top dollar to help clients navigate the ever-expanding web of sanctions, and positioning themselves for lucrative business opportunities in the case of regime collapse. Since an executive order signed by Donald Trump on 1 May drove Canada’s Sherritt International from its nickel and cobalt mining joint venture with the Cuban state, two rival US bids to buy out its stake have been presented to US authorities. Ray Washburne, the vice-chair of Trump’s 2016 Victory Committee who organized last week’s Republican Midterm Convention in Dallas, is clashing with Albert Huddleston, another Texas oil tycoon with close ties to the White House. Both are hoping to swoop in, despite nine-figure claims on Sherritt’s Cuba holdings by Citigroup and Office Depot – Fortune 500 corporations. Washburne did not respond to the Guardian and the consortium group including Huddleston declined to comment. A similar approach is being pursued by Australia’s Antilles Gold Ltd, which after being blacklisted over its Cuba operations in June received the green light from the Trump administration to negotiate the transfer of its stake in a Cuban copper-gold mine to the New York-based, multibillion-dollar investment fund, Global Emerging Markets. “If I had done during the Biden administration what Trump’s friends have done now, I’d have been put in jail,” said a person with several decades of experience in Cuba policy who requested anonymity. Sources tell the Guardian that several Trump Organization executives who had previously traveled to the island to explore real estate deals and who even registered the Trump trademark there in 2008 have in recent months returned to Cuba under the aegis of Dominari Holdings for meetings. The executives are said to have met with Raúl Guillermo Rodríguez Castro, the grandson of former Cuban president Raúl Castro, dubbed “the Crab”, to explore opportunities amid the departure of Spanish hotel giants Meliá and Iberostar, which had been operating on the island since the 1990s. Neither Antilles nor Dominari returned calls for comment. But American investors aren’t the only ones sensing opportunity in Rubio’s effort to coerce the sanctions-battered country of his parents’ birth into becoming economically dependent on the US. Cubans have been living under an effective fuel blockade since January 2026: the Trump administration cut oil shipments to the island from the island’s main ally after abducting Nicolás Maduro, the Venezuelan president; it then nixed oil deliveries from Mexico by threatening tariffs on any country sending petroleum to the island. Treasury department-authorised oil exports from Florida and Texas to the island’s private sector, however – all but non-existent last year – have shot up to over $160m so far this year. Meanwhile, Florida shipping lines such as Crowley, a donor to Cuban-American Republican lawmakers from Florida, Mario Díaz-Balart and María Elvira-Salazar, seem to be beneficiaries of fresh sanctions that have hit foreign shippers and forced Cuba-bound commerce to reroute through Florida, according to informed sources who spoke with the Guardian. Crowley declined to comment. And as UN human rights experts warn that Washington’s latest measures “knowingly deprive a population of the means to survive”, Franklin Graham, the Trump-allied CEO of evangelical aid organization Samaritan’s Purse recently secured a $40m federal contract to distribute humanitarian aid in Cuba – despite lacking the capacity to effectively implement such a contract on the island, according to sources familiar with the matter. A spokesperson for Samaritan’s Purse said: “Details about aid for Cuba are still being developed and are not yet finalized.” Ironically, some of those who have called most vociferously for harsher sanctions are also cashing in. In July, Madrid-based Vima World SL, a leading player in the island’s food industry which partners with GAESA, the Cuban military conglomerate that controls large swathes of the island’s economy and has become the main target of the US squeeze, hired top Washington lobbying firm Continental Strategy – led by Cuban-American allies of Rubio who oversaw the maximum pressure Cuba policy as officials in the first Trump administration – for matters related to trade, foreign relations and the food industry. Continental’s executives include Carlos Trujillo, Trump’s former ambassador to the Organization of American States John Barsa, Trump’s former acting USAID administrator and Alberto Martinez, Rubio’s former chief of staff. The firm, which terminated its contract with Vima this month after netting nearly $40,000 according to corporate disclosures, has been known for providing lobbying and government relations services to clients staunchly opposed to the one-party state, including MasTec, the telecom company owned by Rubio’s friend Jorge Mas Santos; American Sugar Refineries, owned by Trump-ballroom donor and Rubio patron Pepe Fanjul; and General Cigar Co, which is fighting Cuba’s state-owned tobacco enterprise in US court for the rights to the Cohiba cigar trademark. “It’s been interesting to watch how quickly some hardline ideologues become pragmatists once there’s money on the table,” one person familiar with the contract told the Guardian, noting that Continental has taken on other Spanish firms with Cuban business interests “trying to get on the right side of sanctions, like banks and hotel chains”. Other organizations that for years have won seven-figure grants from US federal agencies are capitalizing on the Trump administration’s push to force sweeping political and economic change on the island. Lobbying disclosure forms filed in July by a newly formed group made up of former employees at the US taxpayer-funded Foundation for Human Rights in Cuba (FHRC), alongside longtime Republican lobbyist Otto Reich and the husband of top Rubio state department aide Viviana Bovo, indicate it is “advising [the] State Department on [an] economic development plan for a future free and democratic Cuba, including energy-sector development and compensation for owners of property/business expropriated by the Cuban government”. Reich and Tony Costa, the Foundation for Human Rights chairman, are involved in efforts to mobilize billions of dollars in private investment from wealthy Cuban exiles for a post-communist Cuba through the newly created Cuban-American National Chamber of Commerce (CANCC). To get their priorities heard by lawmakers and officials in Washington, FHRC and another attendee of the CANCC gatherings, Armando Labrador, a Miami-based plastic surgeon who regularly meets with state department officials and wants to become Cuba’s next leader, have paid DC lobbying firm The Cormac Group a combined $100,000 since December. For another US taxpayer-funded non-profit that had been the subject of an internal Biden administration inquiry that was quickly shut down by powerful House appropriators, the administration’s unprecedented economic siege could not have come at a better time. Just before the July release of a heavily criticized state department report referring to Cuba as a nearby terror hub plotting to conquer the US, Digital News Association Inc received a fresh $250,000 contract from the US government’s office of Cuba broadcasting for “investigative journalism, research and media production”, after which its main site launched an online interview series repeating Trump administration claims of Cuba’s purported threat to US national security. Vima, Continental, Cormac and Digital News did not return calls for comment. “The cause is regime change,” said Erik Cartelle, a consultant working to connect prominent exiles with Rubio’s state department. “I have clients that want to do a lot of business in Cuba, and the administration is banking on Cuban-Americans going to Cuba and investing, but if there’s a deal that’s going to be had with the regime, it needs to take into account the diaspora’s wishes. You’ve got to listen to this community.”

title: Ilhan Omar brings bill to make ICE ‘pay the price’ for terrorizing communities
summary: Make ICE Pay Act would block nearly $140bn in funding and redirect money to places reeling from Trump crackdown
text: The US congresswoman Ilhan Omar is set to introduce a bill that would make federal immigration agencies “pay the price” for terrorising vulnerable communities, blocking nearly $140bn in funding and redirecting it to local recovery efforts, the Guardian has learned. The Make ICE Pay Act, due to be introduced on Thursday, targets funding previously designated for Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Customs and Border Protection (CBP) under Donald Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act. It would send the money instead to states, local government authorities, non-profit organisations and small businesses left reeling by Trump’s immigration enforcement crackdowns. “For over a year, ICE has been tearing through our nation, leading racist terror campaigns that have caused devastating damage to our cities, to our businesses and to the lives of our constituents,” said Omar, who represents Minnesota’s fifth congressional district, covering the city of Minneapolis and surrounding suburbs. Beginning last December, thousands of federal immigration agents descended on Minneapolis and surrounding areas, resulting in nearly 4,000 total arrests and the fatal shooting of two US citizens, Renee Good and Alex Pretti. The mood of fear and isolation also had a profound effect on commerce. Omar added: “In Minneapolis, Operation Metro Surge cost our community nearly $700m. We have a moral responsibility to end this abuse of power. Our bill will force ICE to pay the price for the damage they’ve left in their wake and ensure that these devastating operations can never be repeated.” Enforcement actions covered by the bill include Operation Midway Blitz in Illinois, Operations Swamp Sweet and Catahoula Crunch in Louisiana, Operation Catch of the Day in Maine, Operation Charlotte’s Web in North Carolina, and Operation Black Rose in Oregon. Grants under the scheme could be used to provide economic relief, reimburse operational expenses, assist educational institutions and deliver psychosocial support to affected individuals. The measure also authorises funding for official investigations, commissions of inquiry, record-keeping, truth-telling and memorialisation projects. The scheme would be administered through the office of inspector general of the Department of Housing and Urban Development over three years. ICE arrests surged to 49,571 in July, marking the highest monthly total of Trump’s second term. The total represented a 15% increase on the 43,021 arrests recorded in June, and a 70% rise compared with the 29,241 arrests made in February. The sharp rise in detentions comes despite assurances during confirmation hearings by Markwayne Mullin, now the homeland security secretary, that the department would pursue a more moderate approach to enforcement. Public opinion has turned against federal immigration agencies after a series of flashpoints, with 47% of Americans viewing ICE unfavourably and 39% viewing it favourably, according to a Harvard CAPS/ Harris survey of 2,100 registered voters last month. Omar, who was born in Somalia, arrived in the US as a refugee aged 12 and became a citizen at 17. She has been a particular target of Trump’s racist rhetoric, which has helped spur death threats against her. “We ought to get her the hell out!” the president told a rally last December as a crowd chanted: “Send her back!”

title: Hundreds of ageing Americans may not get results of Alzheimer’s study due to Trump cuts
summary: Shutdown of study is latest for Trump administration, which has canceled, frozen and otherwise disrupted more than 5,700 medical research grants over two years
text: Scientific funding cuts imposed by the Trump administration may force researchers to close a study on Alzheimer’s disease risk among 600 ageing people without sharing the results of cognitive tests with participants – even though researchers have all the data to do so. The Trump administration canceled a federal research grant studying two low-income, majority Black neighborhoods in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, in August. Researchers were given 90 days to shut down the study – more than five months earlier than planned. Now, they lack the time and money to assess data collected from trial participants. As a result, the funding cuts have the potential to unnecessarily delay diagnosis of Alzheimer’s disease or dementia syndromes in the group – diseases whose treatments rely on early diagnosis. Over the course of the last two years, the Trump administration has canceled, frozen and otherwise disrupted more than 5,700 medical research grants funded by the National Institutes of Health (NIH), according to Grant Witness, which tracks changes to funding. More than 4,500 has since been restored. The cancelation of clinical trials alone has impacted more than 74,000 participants nationally, a Jama study showed. A wide range of studies have been impacted, from those examining childhood hearing loss to pain during cesarean delivery, Jama found. The cuts are part of the Trump administration’s upheaval of federal scientific grants, which have attempted to remake US science in line with the president’s priorities, often in the name of ridding the government of “DEI”, or diversity, equity and inclusion. Researchers at Pitt are now also named plaintiffs in a class action lawsuit against the NIH, which argues that the administration is attempting to censor research whose conclusions it disfavors. “The plaintiff’s experiences and stories here really evidence that censoring research can have life or death consequences,” said Olga Akselrod, senior counsel with the American Civil Liberties Union’s racial justice program, and one of the lead litigators in the case. “It is dangerous for public health when research is censored based on political litmus tests, and particularly when it targets areas of research designed to address the needs of underserved populations that disproportionately experience negative health outcomes and some of the most accute health disparities.” In the canceled study, Tamara Dubowitz and co-researcher Andrea Rosso, an associate professor of epidemiology and expert in brain health at the University of Pittsburgh, examined how the built and social environments of neighborhoods may contribute to Alzheimer’s disease risk. The two neighborhoods being studied were historically ‘red-lined’ – areas denied access to mortgages, loans or insurance based on race. Black Americans are twice as likely to suffer from Alzheimer’s disease compared to white counterparts, but far less likely to be included in studies. In just one example, of more than 12,000 brain imaging studies on Alzheimer’s disease, only around 700 report race at all. Studies that do report race have more than 87% white participants. Researchers argue the administration has poorly defined its view of “DEI” and conflated the term with health equity – the study of how groups of people have different health outcomes, and the umbrella under which the Pittsburgh grant falls. Experts have also warned that grant cancellations “will kill” Americans. In the case of Alzheimer’s disease and other dementias, early diagnosis is critical. There is no cure for the disease, and treatments to slow its progression are best used early in the disease course. Roderick Blair, a 70-year-old trial participant who lives in the Homewood neighborhood, said the grant cancellation is a “clear” form of retribution for daring to examine links between the health of Black Americans and structural racism. “If you don’t agree with me, you’re going to go to the woodshed,” said Blair, later adding, “What has this administration done that has not been a retribution?” The study was designed to assess cognitive decline over the course of 18 months to two years. Trial participants took lengthy cognitive tests – often lasting hours and including deeply personal survey questions about childhood trauma. At the time the grant was cut, researchers had just finished data collection and were preparing for an “adjudication of cognitive status”. In adjudications, experts meet and reach a consensus on the outcome of the tests. The tests were expected to be assessed by a neuropsychologist and geriatric psychiatrist – in-demand experts whom even a well resourced patient might wait up to a year to see, the researchers said. The federal government has already invested more than $10m into the study over five years. Those results were promised to participants when they gave their consent to be part of research, and are impossible to deliver in the timeframe given to researchers for closure. Researchers said they had hoped for a one year, no-cost extension, since funds were frozen for months in the midst of research, thanks to the same DEI-related upheaval. The University of Pittsburgh and the researchers are appealing the grant cancelation. “The University of Pittsburgh is in the process of submitting appeals to the National Institutes of Health regarding the agency’s recent termination of these awards,” said Jared Stonesifer, head of communications. “These appeals represent the first step in the administrative process meant to act as a pathway for the University, as the recipient of the grants, to seek review of funding decisions. The University believes these appeals are supported by a strong legal foundation and will present its position through the appropriate channels. While the process is ongoing, the University remains hopeful for a favorable resolution.” Dubowitz, who spoke in her personal capacity, said the appeal argues that delivering results to participants, “is part of an ethical, orderly closeout, but we don’t know whether they are in agreement that that is the case”. The Trump administration has argued this grant, “no longer effectuates the program goals or agency priorities” and that “the lack of concrete, objective, and measurable variables is not in alignment with NIH’s priorities related to ‘promoting research focused on scientifically valid measurable health outcomes.’” Beginning in 2025, the administration canceled thousands of scientific grants. Although many canceled grants were reinstated after litigation by research institutions, the administration has continued to quietly cancel more research in 2026, including most recently the grant in question at Pittsburgh, a second on Alzheimer’s at the same institution, and a third at Emory University. Legal experts argue the targeted cancelations appear to be test cases for making cancelations stick in court. They come as the administration is seeking to move the entire $1tn federal grant-making apparatus under the control of political appointees. “The most important thing that they added on every year was trust,” said Blair, about researchers at Pitt. “They always gave you feedback on what you got, how you did, what you could do better.”

title: ‘We live with a big burden’: survivor of abusive Spotlight priest hopes clergyman’s death brings closure
summary: Keith Townsend says he hopes death of Ronald Paquin in prison helps victims and families to ‘keep pressing forward’
text: A survivor of childhood sexual abuse by a defrocked Boston Catholic priest who was portrayed admitting to molesting minors in the Oscar-winning Hollywood film Spotlight says he hopes the clergyman’s recent death in prison helps victims of his crimes and their families “keep pressing forward every single day”. “We live with a big burden in our hearts and on our backs,” Keith Townsend said on Wednesday while reflecting on the criminal charges which he successfully pursued against Ronald Paquin, who was imprisoned in 2019 and died in custody at age 83 on 11 September. “And my hope is that people can find closure and move on.” Those remarks by Townsend, 52, during a telephone interview were a notable reaction to the death of one of the key figures in the clergy sexual abuse and cover-up scandal with the Catholic archdiocese of Boston that – among other consequences – prompted the resignation of the institution’s archbishop, Bernard Law, at the end of 2002, as well as policy reforms across the US church. That same year, Paquin had pleaded guilty to sexually abusing an altar server from 1989 to 1992 while working at St John the Baptist church in the Boston suburb of Haverhill, Massachusetts. He was stripped of his clerical status and imprisoned in Massachusetts for that abuse, which was first publicly exposed in a Pulitzer-winning series of investigative articles by the Boston Globe newspaper’s Spotlight team. Paquin was freed in 2015. And learning of that release motivated Townsend – once a St John altar server, too – to come forward and report being abused himself by Paquin while on camping trips to Kennebunkport, Maine, between 1985 and 1989. As Townsend put it, he was between the ages of eight and 13 when Paquin molested him. Townsend recalled Paquin plying him with drugs and alcohol during the abuse, eventually leading him to battles with substance abuse addiction and incarceration. A Maine grand jury indicted Paquin in 2017 on new charges of gross sexual misconduct in connection with Townsend and another individual. Paquin faced a jury trial in November 2018 which culminated in a guilty verdict against him with regards to Townsend, though he was acquitted of having abused the other individual. Maine judge Wayne Douglas sentenced Paquin in May 2019 to 16 more years in prison. Paquin was in the Mountain View correctional facility in Charleston, Maine, when he died, the state’s department of correction said in a news release. Speaking five days later, Townsend said he first got word of Paquin’s death from his wife, who saw it circulating on the news and social media. He said he understood the many reactions which he subsequently heard or read that took delight in news of Paquin’s death. But Townsend, now a New Hampshire resident, also said he used the occasion to think about the work he did on himself which culminated in his “shaking off” the drug and alcohol addiction which had a grip on him in the wake of Paquin’s abuse. He said he contemplated the family he had built after overcoming “one of the biggest obstacles that could be thrown” at a person. “I get those who think the attitude should be, ‘Fuck him. Fuck what he did to me,’” Townsend said. “But look where I am today.” Townsend said he sought Paquin’s re-imprisonment with the aim of “protecting children … not [from] a man [but] a monster”. “Massachusetts just kind of let him go,” Townsend said. “So I had to dig deep … [because] I didn’t want anybody else to possibly have to go through [his] abuse. Maine thankfully had the balls to take this case, aggressively prosecute it and get a good outcome.” Townsend said he had not yet been able to see Spotlight, which dramatizes the Globe’s uncovering of the clergy sexual abuse scandal that roiled the city’s archdiocese. And therefore Townsend had not viewed the famous scene in the film in which Rachel McAdams, playing reporter Sacha Pfeiffer, confronts an actor portraying Paquin on his home’s front doorstep about allegations of molesting boys at St John the Baptist. “Sure, I fooled around – but I never felt gratified myself,” the actor playing Paquin, Richard O’Rourke, says in response as the journalist scribbles notes in a paper pad while wearing an astonished facial expression. “Right, um, but you admit to molesting boys at St John the Baptist?” McAdams’ Pfeiffer then asks O’Rourke’s Paquin. The latter’s reply: “Yes, yes. But, as I said, I never got any pleasure from it.” Another person closely familiar with Spotlight offered an opinion of that scene’s legacy on Wednesday. Attorney Mitchell Garabedian – who is portrayed in the 2015 movie by Stanley Tucci and has represented numerous victims of sexual abuse by Paquin and other clerics – said that part of Spotlight provided a powerful cue to survivors of clergy molesters that they were not alone. “It gave a sense of, ‘Aha, I’m not the only one,’” in one of Hollywood’s most critically acclaimed films, Garabedian said. ‘“It wasn’t my fault, and I shouldn’t feel guilty.’” Townsend said ultimately he is grateful for anything that raised awareness about Paquin’s atrocities before his push to bring him to justice. “When I lay my head down tonight, I know it saved lives,” getting Paquin imprisoned for his remaining years, Townsend added. “And that’s what matters to me.”

text: Barclays is facing a growing backlash over return-to-office plans, with thousands of staff calling for payouts to help cover travel costs and an exemption for those living more than 40 minutes from work. Unionised staff represented by Unite are pushing back against plans announced by the bank earlier this summer to get staff back into the office at least three days a week from October, with more senior employees expected to come in at least four days a week. The current policy requires full-time Barclays staff to be in at least two days a week. Unite, which represents nearly 80% of Barclays’ 45,000 UK staff, says thousands of employees have now signed an open letter – first reported by the Financial Times – that has been sent to the bank’s bosses and widely circulated across its UK offices. The union plans to speak to Barclays about staff concerns in the coming days. A Unite national officer, Rick Coyle, said: “One of the issues that has caused consternation is that most employers in banking and financial services are generally embracing greater flexibility. Our members think that Barclays is trying to fix a problem that doesn’t exist. “Thousands of employees have signed the letter and the figure continues to rise. Unite will be speaking to Barclays about the strength of feeling in the days ahead.” Barclays’ return-to-office order echoes those imposed by other large banks, which tightened their work-from-home policies after the Covid pandemic, particularly for younger staff. That includes JP Morgan, whose chief executive, Jamie Dimon, told Bloomberg last year: “It is an apprenticeship system … you can’t learn working from your basement.” A Barclays spokesperson said: “We recognise the benefits of balancing flexibility for colleagues with the importance of working together in our physical locations. Our minimum time-in-office requirements vary by business area, reflecting the nature of the work and the needs of the business. “This means that most of our colleagues who are not already working in the office three days [per week] will align with our broader approach across the bank. Alongside this, our most senior leaders will spend an additional day in the office to support collaboration, decision-making and leadership visibility.”

title: Big AI is trying to own the pathway to work. Universities shouldn’t play along | Ella Hafermalz
summary: Universities need to protect their position in education so that students have an independent pathway to employment
text: AI companies like OpenAI are insinuating themselves into the pathway from education to work. Soon they may claim it entirely, a disastrous result for students. We know that students are using AI at school and at university. In conversations with those I teach, I’m struck by the trust many place in it. They turn to ChatGPT and similar tools for personal problems as well as study help. Some even doubt their abilities without AI. Institutions are working hard to adapt. But we need to urgently look up from the use of AI to pay attention to big AI companies’ attempts to take over the educational pipeline, else we lose sight of the people that matter, our students. The industry has spent the past few years making our young people afraid of unemployment. Now it’s claiming to have a solution: more AI. On a website introducing its new certification programs, OpenAI gives a peek into the bigger picture. The company says it wants to “connect learning, certification and real economic opportunity in one clear journey, laying the foundation for our upcoming OpenAI Jobs Platform”. That means offering education, credentials and access to work – owning the entire pipeline, infusing AI at every step. The company is positioning itself to directly compete with universities. I don’t mean that we’ll soon see shiny new ChatGPT campuses. These companies don’t need to build a university out of bricks and mortar to take over key parts of higher education. They already own the tools where learning and work are increasingly happening – next, they can compete with universities by brokering access to employment. As big AI companies search for a business model beyond subscriptions, universities need to be alert to this threat and urgently protect their position. Otherwise, the possibility of an independent path for students may be lost. Big AI is slowly commandeering the pathway Even though many young people are ambivalent towards AI, it’s easy to see why they’d trust a service that’s explained accounting calmly and patiently for the 20th time and counselled them through a breakup. Now OpenAI is extending its close relationship with students even further, hiring students as campus ambassadors. The recruitment ad for joining what the company calls the Student Collective promises prospective campus leads “robust training in our tools, funding, swag and access to a community of remarkable peers”. Such a program gives OpenAI even greater access to students. This is a familiar brand strategy. Getting inside a community is a way to win trust and influence. It also gives you data that can inform your next move. At the same time, AI companies are getting boots on the ground within employers. The OpenAI Deployment Company launched this year, with “more than $4bn of initial investment”. It’s sending over 150 “forward deployed engineers”, a military metaphor used to describe engineers embedded in companies, to the “frontlines” of its network of organisations to re-engineer work around OpenAI’s tools. But a company that is at the centre of shaping work across industries also sees and influences what employers are looking for. That puts OpenAI in a powerful position to broker the relationship between students and employers. It can help shape the skills employers want, while becoming increasingly involved in how students learn those skills and prepare for work. So, OpenAI will have insight and influence over students and their learning on one hand, and employers’ workflows and needs on the other. With that, all that is needed for OpenAI to unbundle universities is credentialing. And it’s doing that, too. In collaboration with companies including Accenture and John Deere, OpenAI is now offering certificates meant to lead to employment opportunities. Currently, the focus is on AI tooling and literacy. That’s not new – tech providers have always taught people how to use their tools. The difference this time is how the credentials fit into a larger ambition to capture every step of the journey from learning to work. Look at the language it uses to sell the delivery of the program: “A full learning experience is available directly inside ChatGPT, where learners can practice real tasks, receive feedback in context, and reflect on their work in a single environment. ChatGPT acts as the tutor, the practice space, and the feedback loop.” A single learning environment, and one clear journey. OpenAI could soon be selling young people a one-stop-shop for learning, credentials and a job, all heavily dependent on its tools. We shouldn’t hand the pathway to work to big AI I understand that the picture I’ve painted here may be appealing to some. Students are nervous about their futures, and employers are urgently seeking workers with the ‘right’ skills. But there is a human, societal, and potentially economic cost to making this particular journey so centralized. Consider what a 23-year-old recently told the Wall Street Journal when discussing the appeal of “white-collar apprenticeships”: “Companies want to help mold you into the employees they’re looking for.” That may be so, but if commercial actors own the pathway from education to work, how will the next generation learn who they are and could be outside of the immediate demands of these structures? And what happens when what employers are looking for changes as technologies evolve and bubbles burst? Society – and students – need education to be more than a quick-turn-around response to the whims of today’s increasingly fragile market. Universities can and should offer an alternative path to a totalizing “single environment”. So let’s not compete on big AI’s terms. Rather than turning to AI to speed up grading or rushing to use bots as a stand-in for teachers, we need to focus on what OpenAI cannot so easily provide: independence, access to expertise in context, productive struggle and social connection. Memories are made when others – both peers and educators – see your efforts, and recognise who you are and who you are becoming. Not long ago, Sam Altman and peers had declared the job apocalypse. We should be wary when the same companies that warned young people that their future is uncertain offer them “one clear journey” towards a different version. Education should leave space and time for finding your own way, beyond a mold offered up for profit. Ella Hafermalz is an associate professor of work and technology at the Kin Center for Digital Innovation at Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam

title: ‘Very messy eaters’: scientists solve the mystery of when black holes ‘burp’
summary: The astronomical bodies fire off powerful jets in two distinct phases in their feeding cycle, researchers discover
text: Scientists have solved the mystery of when black holes “burp” – when the astronomical bodies launch jets after feeding on stars, blasting material enormous distances in space. Black holes are objects so densely compact that beyond a certain point their gravity is too strong for light and matter to escape. This boundary of no return is known as the event horizon – the point at which escaping would require something to travel faster than the speed of light. Despite their reputation as cosmic sinkholes, black holes are “actually very messy eaters”, said Dr Adelle Goodwin, an astrophysicist at Curtin University in Western Australia. “You have to get really, really close to a black hole to get to the event horizon,” Goodwin, also a Forrest Research Foundation fellow, said. “Stars get destroyed further out than that.” Scientists know from rare observations of stars being torn apart by black holes – a process that involves a stretching effect known as “spaghettification” – that “only about half of the star that gets too close to the back hole will end up eventually being swallowed by that black hole”, Goodwin said. The other material is launched back into space in powerful jets and outflows, sometimes so large they “can influence the entire evolution of a galaxy”, she said. “You can think of it as a black hole burp.” But the timing of these burps had previously been mysterious to astrophysicists. “Sometimes it would happen a year after the black hole destroyed the star, sometimes it would happen three or five years after.” In new research published in the journal Nature Astronomy, Goodwin and co-author Dr Andrew Mummery from the Institute for Advanced Study believe they have found the answer, using radio telescopes to study 20 tidal disruption events – instances where stars are eaten by supermassive black holes. “Radio is the only frequency where we can watch the jets and outflows as they’re moving outwards,” Goodwin said. They found that supermassive black holes – which range in size from hundreds of thousands to billions of times the mass of our sun – fire off powerful jets in two distinct phases in their feeding cycle. The first occurs when the black hole is feeding at very high rates. The second occurs hundreds to thousands of days after the star is first torn apart, when the feeding rate drops to about 2% of the maximum rate at which a black hole can swallow material. That same threshold is already known to trigger burps from stellar-mass black holes, much smaller bodies about 10 to 50 times the mass of our sun. The research showed that black holes appeared to release jets at the same point in their feeding cycle regardless of size, Goodwin said. She said the finding would enable scientists to precisely predict when such jets would be released, narrowing observation windows and freeing up precious telescope time. She added: “We can really start to understand not just when the jets are launched, but also how strong they are and if that is then dependent on the black hole properties.” Dr Sara Webb, an astrophysicist at Swinburne University who was not involved in the research, said: “We are still trying to untangle the very fundamentals of the most extreme objects in the universe – supermassive black holes.” Webb said the study showed “that supermassive black holes behave rather predictably at two distinct periods in their evolution” and the researchers had “tie[d] this back to what we’ve seen previously on the much smaller scale stellar-mass black holes”. • This article was amended on 18 September 2026. An earlier version quoted an expert as having said black holes behave predictably “at two distant periods in their evolution”; this should have said “distinct periods”.

title: ‘We left everything behind’: 125,000 people displaced as war reignites in Yemen
summary: Fierce fighting has forced people to abandon their homes, leaving everything behind to seek shelter in refugee camps
text: Abandoning their homes and cramming into cars, Yemeni families have fled in their thousands from a lightning advance along the Red Sea coastal plains and up the rugged hills towards the mountaintop city of Taiz as the war returned in dramatic form this month. “We fled a large, comfortable home, and here we are struggling to find a plastic sheet and wooden poles,” said one of the displaced, Asma Taleb, a woman in her 50s who fled her home last week with her two sons and five grandchildren. “This war doesn’t differentiate between people. Rich or poor, high class or low class, we all fled our homes on the same day and are all struggling now to find shelter.” The family fled the Maqbanah district in the wide Taiz region and headed toward Al-Shimayateen District, arriving at a camp for displaced families where she has relatives. More than 100,000 people have fled their homes in the last month. “The fighting was fierce in our village, and some of our civilian neighbours were killed or injured, so we fled home and left everything behind,” she told the Guardian. “Amid the fierce battles you forget everything. We left our home belongings, and one neighbour even left his livestock behind.” As soon as Taleb arrived in the camp, she found three or four families living in every tent because newly displaced people were constantly arriving. Left with no other option, she moved in with a relative’s family and three others. “On the first day, we were happy just to reach safety, but then we felt the suffering the next day. Displaced families kept arriving, and there was no space in the camp and not enough tents,” she added. Some humanitarian organisations intervened, providing displaced families with canned food and hygiene kits. Taleb said she had never left her village in her life except for brief emergencies, always returning in a day or two. This is the first time she has been forced to flee long-term, and she feels returning will be difficult. “I dream of returning to my village today, before tomorrow, but it isn’t in my hands. The fighting is still ongoing, and more families are arriving every day.” Renewed fighting in Yemen has displaced at least 125,000 people (about 18,000 households) since the start of September 2026, according to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (Ocha). The International Organization for Migration said more than 2,000 people fleeing the hostilities have reached Djibouti’s northern shores so far, landing at scattered points along the coast near Obock. Hatem Qasem, a farmer in his 40s from Al-Wazeyah district west of Taiz city, grew up in a village where residents rely on farming and raising livestock. He stated that when battles approached their village, they thought of nothing but their safety. “We are farmers and rarely leave our village except for emergencies, but three days ago, the shelling and clashes were all around us, and we found ourselves in a position where we had to flee,” Qasem told the Guardian. He explained that they sold their livestock at low prices simply to cover the cost of fleeing, as they could not take the livestock with them to an unknown destination. “We took the children and left – around five families in one car. We couldn’t believe we managed to escape the fighting, but praise be to God, we made it,” he added. They arrived in Al-Shimayateen district in Taiz. Although they do not have shelter there, it is a safe area where many displaced families have sought refuge. “I am happy that we are safe now and that no one in the family was killed or injured, but we have started to realise that it will be difficult to stay here for long. We have no work here and no one to help us,” Qasem said. According to Save the Children, at least 19 children were killed and a further 49 injured between 1 August and 9 September, bringing the total number of civilians killed in the escalating violence in Yemen to 117 and of those injured to 206. At least 175 were killed or injured in a single week (3-9 September), including 43 children, the highest weekly child casualty toll in the past 12 months. With fierce fighting ongoing in Qasem’s village, returning home is not an option. To remain displaced, however, he needs a source of income to provide for his family. “We will wait this month out here and see. If the fighting moves away from our village, we will return; if it continues, we will look for another solution.” Qasem’s family of eight lives with three other displaced families in the same house – each family occupying a single room to share the cost of rent. In Al-Safia makeshift camp, displaced people have no work and depend entirely on humanitarian organisations for their basic needs. In 2026, an estimated 22.3 million people in Yemen – more than half the population – require humanitarian assistance and protection services, including 5.2 million displaced people, according to Ocha. Ali Qaid, manager of the executive unit for Internationally Displaced People Camps Management in Taiz governorate, confirmed that some humanitarian organisations have begun providing aid to newly displaced families arriving in areas like Al-Shimayateen. However, he noted that many civilians remain trapped in active combat zones. “Displacement from the western districts of Taiz governorate is still ongoing, and many people are trapped in the middle of the fighting, preventing humanitarian organisations from reaching them with assistance,” he told the Guardian.

title: Trump threatens to stop trading with EU over ‘laughable’ membership offer to Canada
summary: US president responds as Mark Carney seeks to move closer to Europe and diversify defence ties
text: Donald Trump has threatened the EU with “serious tariffs” and a halt to trade after the bloc proposed making Canada its first ever associate member – an idea he derided as “laughable”. The US president said that if the EU moved forward with the plan, Washington could impose “very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe”. He added: “If it’s a good intention, that’s fine. If it’s a bad intention, we’ll put very heavy tariffs on Europe.” Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, is due to address the European parliament on Thursday, a day after the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, invited his country to become the EU’s first “associate member”. Von der Leyen pitched closer cooperation on tech, defence and energy to Carney, telling the European parliament that, as democracies faced a “fracture in the international rules-based system”, Brussels and Ottawa needed to pull closer together. She said: “This is a partnership not against anyone else, but for our common strength. In short, we want to bring the relationship with Canada to the highest level possible.” In response to Trump’s comments, France’s Europe minister Benjamin Haddad said on Thursday that Washington had no power to veto EU decisions. “It is not up to the United States, or ‌anyone else, to choose the political and geopolitical direction of the Europeans. Once again, we have a relationship ⁠with Canada, and we are fully entitled to seek to deepen it,” Haddad ‌told Public Sénat TV channel. A European Commission spokesperson said: “As our president made clear yesterday, the proposed strengthening of the relationship with Canada is not against anyone else, but for our common strength.” Carney has called for a “unique alliance” with the EU as Canada seeks to reduce its heavy dependence on US trade. After meeting EU leaders in Strasbourg on Wednesday, he described the EU and Canada as “natural partners, united by shared values” and said that both sides were focused on “a deeper partnership that reinforces our mutual sovereignty to create more opportunities and prosperity for our peoples”. An associate membership agreement would have to be approved by the EU’s 27 member states, who generally support closer ties with Canada, but were taken by surprise by the term. Canada and the EU already have a trade deal and numerous bilateral agreements, but have been moving closer since Donald Trump returned to the White House and raised tariffs on both old allies, while repeatedly talking about Canada becoming the 51st US state and lambasting the EU. In a sign that Canada was seeking to further diversify its defence ties ⁠away from ⁠the US, Carney’s office announced on Wednesday that the country had formally applied to join the British-led Joint Expeditionary Force military ⁠coalition. The force is a rapid response ‌military partnership comprising 10 North Atlantic Nato member states including Denmark, the Netherlands, Norway and Sweden. On Wednesday, Carney and the British prime minister, Andy Burnham, held a bilateral meeting at the ground of Everton football club. The leaders, who are both fans of the premiership club, then attended the team’s game against Wolves. The two discussed deepening defence cooperation and the opportunities and ⁠challenges presented by ⁠artificial intelligence. Downing Street said both prime ministers emphasised the importance of building close ties with European partners, particularly on trade and defence. The 27-member EU has never had an associate membership category, although it has close ties with Norway, Iceland and Switzerland, allowing deep economic integration with these countries, who follow many EU rules. However, it remains to be seen what associate membership means, including for Canada’s relationship with the EU single market. Von der Leyen said on Wednesday that it was time to move from cooperation based on trade to a broader “alliance for the future” and bring the relationship with Canada to the highest level possible. “We will work on intelligent manufacturing. We will create a tech alliance. We will integrate defence industrial bases. We will make the Arctic a flagship joint project,” she said. She listed energy, critical minerals, batteries, AI, cyber and economic security as other fields of cooperation. “This is a partnership not against anyone else, but for our common strength,” she said. With Agence France-Presse and Reuters

title: ‘It’s beautiful when it’s clean’: the Argentine neighbourhood saving a contaminated river
summary: Sewage, dog carcasses and industrial waste clog Argentina’s second most-polluted river. Meet the activists cleaning it up
text: Twenty-three years ago, María Monges looked around her flooded neighbourhood and knew something had to be done. Founded in 1998 in Buenos Aires province’s San Martín district, the community of Costa Esperanza sits on the banks of the Reconquista, Argentina’s second most-polluted river and owes its name to the fictional location of a hit Argentine youth telenovela of the time, Verano del 98. But the real place is very different from the idyllic coastal city where the protagonists of Argentina’s answer to Dawson’s Creek met their first loves or sang around bonfires. “You don’t know what it was like – when we started cleaning up, all the streams were blocked up everywhere: rubbish, dead dogs … a bit of everything. It was unsanitary, but we carried on working anyway,” says Monges, now 61. She started knocking on doors, getting people out to work with her, and in 2005 got the provincial administration to give them tools, uniforms and training. Now Monges leads 9 de julio, a workers’ cooperative that, from Monday to Friday, cleans up streams flowing from the river. “Every day, we will find rubbish,” says Monges. “It’s like people don’t understand.” The Reconquista is 51 miles (82km) long, located in the north-east of the province of Buenos Aires and flows through 18 municipalities. About 4-5 million people live in its basin. It flows into the Luján River, which then connects with the Río de la Plata estuary. Since at least the 1970s, the river has been a dumping ground for untreated sewage, industrial waste and landfill leachate. It has the state sewage company on its banks, along with homes that lack adequate infrastructure, residents connecting their drainpipes so that waste is discharged directly into the water. Several factories located in the district of San Martín, known as “the Industrial Capital”, also throw their waste into the river. “All of this not only pollutes the water, but also the soil and the air. In this area there’s no access to drinking water … all the aquifers are contaminated,” says Natalia Gavazzo, an anthropologist and researcher at the National Scientific and Technical Research Council. Gavazzo directs the Migrantas en Reconquista project, which conducts research and carries out initiatives in the region to strengthen the socio-environmental strategies employed by women in the neighbourhoods of the Reconquista river basin. She adds that the environmental activism in Costa Esperanza is carried out primarily by women. “They are not just victims,” she says. “They are also the key agents of mitigation and adaptation; they possess a wealth of knowledge that is central to the survival of their communities.” But the Reconquista is just one of the troubled rivers in La Plata, the giant system that connects multiple waterways across Uruguay and Argentina. According to the World Meteorological Organization State of Global Water Resources report, out on Thursday, major parts of La Plata river basins have experienced recurring below-normal water levels between 2021 and 2025, caused by persistent multi-year drought conditions. La Plata basin includes the Paraguay River, which has consistently recorded water levels at their lowest since 2020. Analysis of WMO data shows that the Paraguay River’s water levels have been consistently below normal for the last six years, with its 25 driest months since 1991 registered after 2020. The drought and pollution issues plaguing La Plata and the Reconquista are affecting many more of the world’s rivers. As Gavazzo puts it, “climate change has an uneven impact around the world – the north produces the emissions, but we in the south foot the bill.” For the anthropologist, the same is true at a local scale. “People in gated communities throw out rubbish, but it ends up here,” she added. Juan Borús, who recently retired from the National Water Institute and is one of the country’s leading hydrologists, says that governments should “tackle every one of these sources of pollution individually, which is an extremely costly, painstaking task that requires regulation”, but that “companies that discharge complex effluents evade the rules … They’ve been doing it all their lives.” In 2001, the Buenos Aires province created the Reconquista River Basin Committee (Comirec) to clean it up, but it had limited impact, and parts of the river where Costa Esperanza is located still exhibit “severe deterioration”, according to its early 2026 reports. High levels of E coli (a bacterium that indicates the presence of fecal matter) and low levels of oxygen make it “not a suitable environment for aquatic life” and “a risk to the population”, according to Patricio Carmona, a biochemist specialising in environmental analysis. “The smell is like an acid,” says Lorena Batista, 47, a neighbour who works at the National Institute of Industrial Technology. “It is nauseating,” adds Zulma Monges, María’s daughter. The stench, they agree, becomes unbearable in summer, and when the wind blows they have to close their windows. It is not only the smell – neighbours have suffered from skin conditions such as hives, rashes, sores and scars, respiratory and lung problems, and gastrointestinal diseases, although Zulma says the skin conditions have become somewhat rarer since her mother’s community squad started picking up the rubbish. Once a month, residents meet to discuss problems and contact representatives from the local government, to whom they address their concerns – accumulated rubbish or water cuts, for example. “It’s very much a part of our lives; it’s already become an integral part of the neighbourhood’s culture,” says grocer Rosa Valencia in her shop, laden with coconuts, plantains and yerba mate. And there are other efforts under way to clean up the river. The San Martín University’s School of Habitat and Sustainability is developing artificial wetlands – a nature-inspired method that could be installed on site to help filter out persistent pollutants and restore the area’s biodiversity. A group of several local organisations, Foro por la Recuperación del Río Reconquista, is campaigning for the creation of an ecological preserve. “Many years ago, before the landfill was built, that area was a large marshland with beaches,” they claim in their petition. “Older folks used to tell us: ‘we’d go fishing there, we’d spend our weekends there; there were always, always, always lots of animals’,” says Zulma Monges. The area, she says, is overpopulated, and “the few green spaces we do have, we’re maintaining them as a community”. Then she pulls out her phone and shows a picture of one of the streams, just after it was cleaned by her mother’s squad. “It’s beautiful when it’s clean,” she says. “The thing is, you have to stop the rubbish from reaching the neighbourhood. But this whole area … look, it’s beautiful.” Over the next year, in the Our Rivers series, we’ll be focusing on the environmental challenges facing the world’s rivers, looking at the waterways around the planet that are overengineered or suffocating and drying up, and those that are being opened up again and given new life.

title: Access-to-nature crisis ‘on par with that of Victorian Britain’s filthy air’
summary: Research finds many in England lack proximity to green and blue spaces as Labour urged to speed up manifesto pledge
text: Nearly half of all parliamentary constituencies in England have low access to nature despite a government target to ensure everyone is within a 15-minute walk from a green or blue space, new research reveals. The analysis by the Wildlife Trusts comes as the charity presents a green paper to ministers in an attempt to speed up Labour’s manifesto promise to improve access to nature and promote biodiversity. The research from the Wildlife Trusts and Liberal and Democrats for Nature and Climate (LDNC) has found that 238 English parliamentary constituencies (44% of the total) have 20% or more local properties situated more than 15 minutes’ walk from green or blue space (the latter an area with water, such as a river, canal, lake, pond, sea or other waterfront). Seven of the 10 most economically deprived constituencies had low access to nature. After a spring and summer of extreme heat across England, when some cities and towns saw temperatures of 38C, the Wildlife Trusts said there was increased need for cool, shady and nature-rich spaces. It is seeking a meeting with ministers to present its green paper. Matthew Browne, the head of public affairs at the Wildlife Trusts, said: “This research reveals stark inequalities in access to nature across England, with direct parallels between economic and nature deprivation. “Coupled with the extreme heat we’re experiencing in urban areas, this access crisis is on a par with that of Victorian Britain, when filthy air and water led to a programme of public park-building for the benefit of all. In facing today’s challenges, we need to embrace this same level of urgency once more, utilising existing legislation so that real change can be felt quickly in local communities.” Despite promises by ministers, the government has yet to publish its access to nature green paper. Critics say ministers need to act with more urgency. The Wildlife Trusts is calling for the government to: Make it more affordable for local authorities to use compulsory purchase powers for land purchase. Establish a community right to buy land for nature access. Treat nature as essential infrastructure, and free up capital funds to pay for the ongoing maintenance of natural spaces. Make it mandatory for developers to create climate- and nature-friendly housing estates. Make access to major rivers, especially those in urban areas, a statutory right. The trusts published the results of a public consultation with 5,000 people, in which they described how they sought out cool spaces in nature during the summer heatwaves. One contributor said: “Walking in my local woods in heatwaves is cooling. The physical benefits of a brisk, daily walk are well known, and I feel them.” Another said: “I have a long-term health condition which affects my mobility and mental health, particularly during periods of extreme heat. Access to natural spaces is incredibly important to me.” Dom Higgins, the head of health and education at the Wildlife Trusts, said there was a mountain of research and evidence from the public that showed the impact of nature on our physical and mental health. He said in an age of climate-driven extreme weather events and the growing health implications, access to nearby healthy natural spaces should be the right of every citizen. “Natural spaces in our cities can literally save lives, by keeping the air cooler and cleaner and reducing the strain on our hearts and lungs,” he said. “The blood pressure of pregnant women is lower when they live near an accessible park or garden, and young children who spend longer in nature-rich spaces have healthier lives. “Yet, despite the growing body of scientific evidence, having access to the natural world in whatever form that takes – from a river walk to a pocket park in an urban neighbourhood – is still not equal across the UK.” In the spring of last year, the Department for Environment Food and Rural affairs held workshops with experts to inform proposals to increase access to nature, in advance of a promised green paper last autumn. But a year on, the government has failed to deliver the paper. “The Wildlife Trusts don’t want the public to have to wait any longer,” the report said. “Access to nature is not a ‘nice to have’, it is a necessity. The time is ripe for action.” A government spokesperson said: “This government is focused on the things that matter most to the British public, including restoring nature so that we have pride in local communities and access to green spaces. “We are increasing access to nature and the countryside, delivering nine new National River Walks, a Coast-to-Coast route in the North of England and the 2,700 mile King Charles III England Coast Path.”

title: Thursday briefing: Yemen’s war continues to threaten oil supplies– but what about its people?
summary: In today’s newsletter: The Houthi advance along the Red Sea coast raised fears for global trade and energy supplies, while more than 100,000 Yemenis have been displaced by the fighting
text: Good morning. The lightning advance of Houthi militants along the west coast of Yemen over the past week has prompted fears of a spiralling conflict in the region and a new oil supply crisis. For families living in the Middle East’s poorest country, the most significant fighting between the Iran-aligned Houthis and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces in years is a crisis upon a catastrophe, with escalating civilian casualties and at least 100,000 displaced in recent days. Houthi fighters have captured strategic islands across a critical Red Sea trade route, the Bab al-Mandab strait, one of the most important shipping routes in the world – almost 15% of global sea trade passes through it. The strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of the world’s traded oil and gas transited in peacetime, has remained largely blocked since the US and Israel launched airstrikes in February, so the prospect of Iran and its allies exerting pressure on two maritime choke points has global implications. The price of crude oil has already begun to spike. For today’s newsletter, I spoke to Farea Al-Muslimi, a research fellow at Chatham House, about this new and dangerous dimension to the ongoing war in Yemen, and why fears over oil and global trade must not overshadow the plight of ordinary Yemenis. First, this morning’s headlines. Five big stories UK politics | Key allies of Andy Burnham have warned the prime minister not to back down over his promises to put water companies under public control, after details emerged about the prime minister’s plan to give mayors more oversight of the industry. Environment | Climate breakdown probably weakened the glacier that collapsed causing catastrophic floods and killing hundreds of people in Nepal and Tibet last month, the first scientific study of the disaster has found. Health | Women with the same medical condition as men are less likely to be offered treatment such as surgery, a stent or a strong painkiller, research has found. Europe | The UK government’s EU reset summit will be delayed again unless the bloc agrees to discuss legislation that could lock British business out of parts of EU industry, government sources have said. UK news | Police searching for a three-year-old boy who went missing from a playground on the Suffolk-Essex border have found a body. In depth: The fight for Yemen’s Red Sea coast The current escalation of violence in Yemen has its roots in a civil war that broke out in 2014 between the Yemeni army and the Houthi movement, which champions Yemen’s Shia Muslim minority. A year later, the Houthis – part of Iran’s “axis of resistance”, a loose coalition of armed groups that includes Hamas and Hezbollah – toppled the Saudi-backed Yemeni government. Al-Muslimi grew up in a remote mountain village in Yemen, where his family made honey, one of the country’s most lucrative and popular exports. His mother used to tease him because the bees didn’t recognise him after he spent long periods studying away from home – he was the only person in his family who had to wear a beekeeping suit. Al-Muslimi now writes about how the years-long internecine conflict has had a devastating impact on the honey trade and the farmers who tend Yemeni bees. At least 150,000 people have been killed since 2014, mainly through aerial bombardment by the Saudi-backed coalition that supports the Yemeni government, which has resumed this week. About 4.5 million people – the population of Birmingham and Greater Manchester combined – have already been displaced by fighting over the past decade, while the UN estimates that more than 18.2 million – twice the population of London – are in dire need of humanitarian assistance. The situation now is “worse than 2015”, says Al-Muslimi, with global attention diverted to crises in Syria, Sudan, and Ukraine and now focused on oil prices and regional consequences. “There is even less willingness to help civilians.” After the Houthis captured the port city of Mocha, birthplace of the global coffee trade, last week, Al-Muslimi heard local media reports of more than 240 pregnant women ready to give birth without accessible healthcare. “It’s absolutely nuts,” he says. “This is a country that was already suffering so many things, including indifference.” *** How has the conflict escalated in the past week? It has been plain for months to Yemen-watchers that the Houthis were preparing for a significant offensive, says al-Muslimi. This erupted about a week ago with the militants seizing control of parts of the west coast and gaining a hold over the Bab al-Mandab strait, including the strategic port of Mocha and key islands of Perim, Greater and Lesser Hanish in the 20-mile stretch of water that forms a natural chokepoint on the trade route connecting Asia with Europe. With government supporters in disarray, the degree of division among anti-Houthi forces is complicating the fight back. The Houthis have achieved what Al-Muslimi calls “the most consequential change in territorial control in Yemen for years”. Since then, the Houthis have claimed responsibility for missile and drone attacks on Saudi Arabia, including the bombing of a critical east-west oil pipeline. On Wednesday a military spokesperson for the Houthis denied attempting to fly a drone close to the holy city of Mecca, and claimed that Saudi Arabia has carried out as many as 450 airstrikes in Yemen ‌this week in retaliation. The ongoing aggression is driving fears that more Muslim nations could be drawn into the conflict. *** What does it mean for global oil supply? If the Houthis were to close the Bab al-Mandab strait, vessels would be forced to reroute all the way around the southern tip of Africa. The consequences for the global economy could be dire, particularly when taken along with the ongoing blockade of Hormuz. With Iran and its Houthi allies controlling potentially a third of energy trade globally, “it’s more dangerous than a nuclear bomb,” says Al-Muslimi bluntly, “especially at a time when the world still depends massively on this type of energy”. Attacks on Saudi Arabia’s east-west pipeline – which is now closed for repairs and has been crucial for moving oil from the strait of Hormuz to the Red Sea export hub of Yanbu – will add further pressure to global supplies. Al-Muslimi advises caution over Houthi claims that they don’t intend to impose transit fees on vessels passing through Bab al-Mandab. The UN security council has seen evidence that, since the militants started attacks on Red Sea shipping in 2023, in response to Israel’s decimation of Gaza, the Houthis have been extracting informal payments from some shipping agencies in return for safe passage. Meanwhile, Saudi anger with Iran for assisting Houthi attacks saw the cancellation of a meeting with Gulf states about the future of the strait of Hormuz on Monday. Reports in the early hours today that Saudi Arabia may be offering more crude cargoes through Oman saw the price of Brent crude drop to $104.59 a barrel after hitting $108 earlier this week. But for perspective, it was trading at $80 a barrel in early July. This comes as the average price of diesel in the US hit $6 per gallon for the first time last week, with the Iran war, combined with Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries, continuing to squeeze supply. *** What does it mean for the region? The UN security council held an emergency meeting in New York on Tuesday to discuss the escalating violence in Yemen and threats to maritime security, with members urging maximum restraint to avoid the situation devolving into a wider regional war. The conflict is the first test of a mutual defence pact between Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan, announced in August – but Saudi has yet to publicly call on either for assistance. Meanwhile, Al-Muslimi says the US, a close Saudi ally, faces a dilemma. The States reached a truce with the Houthis in May 2025, after conducting airstrikes against the group after attacks on Red Sea shipping. “The existing truce gives both sides reasons for restraint,” he says. “For Trump, preserving that arrangement helps keep the US away from another costly Middle Eastern military confrontation while it remains engaged in the strait of Hormuz. The Houthis have equally strong incentives to not be drawn into conflict with the US, which caused them serious damage in the 2025 bombing campaign.” Yesterday the Guardian confirmed that officials from the US had met Houthi leaders over the weekend in Oman, where they received assurances that the ceasefire still held and that the movement had no intention of attacking US shipping in the Red Sea. While Trump condemned the Houthi advance for threatening freedom of navigation, he has far rejected any military response in support of Riyadh. Al-Muslimi calls for a more coherent international approach to his country, which he considers one of the least understood in the region. Yemen analysts have frequently criticised the US and allies for approaching Yemen’s challenges with a focus on security rather than diplomacy or development, while internal instability has been exploited by larger regional powers to fight their own proxy battles. Most importantly, he says: “While this new international dimension of Yemen’s war makes the country strategically more important to the world, it should not overshadow the plight of ordinary Yemenis”. What else we’ve been enjoying Following the release of a report into the significant abuse faced by those who run for office, Labour MP Dawn Butler writes here about how politics is becoming a “no-go zone” for too many. Charlie Lindlar, newsletters team Who do teenage girls dream of becoming? I loved seeing the variety of items significant to young women in this picture gallery by Belgian photographer Eva Verbeeck. Sundus Abdi, newsletters team We may be hurtling toward autumn, but don’t let that stop you from reading our Filter team’s rundown of the best ice-cream makers for every budget. (Kudos to Danielle Amato for bravely taking on the assignment.) Charlie I loved this piece in the Atlantic that boils down to being an ode to being silly. “Few social situations encourage or even allow unadulterated loopiness,” Lily Mayer writes. “In general, art made for adults tends to abide by this taboo. We get satire, scatological jokes, imitations, and absurdity, but rarely do we get silliness.” Charlie Sport Football | Manchester United scored two early goals but lost 3-2 to Brighton in the Carabao Cup, while Tammy Abraham scored his first goals of the season in Aston Villa’s 3-1 win at Coventry. Formula One | Formula One has announced its calendar for 2027, with an increase in sprint races to 10 events, including at Monaco, and the addition of meetings in Portugal and Turkey. Rugby union | The inaugural women’s British & Irish Lions tour of New Zealand next year is expected to be broadcast live on Sky Sports in a significant boost for the women’s game. The front pages “Prisoners to ‘double up’ in single prefab jail cell units”, is the Guardian’s front page today. The Mail splashes on “‘Rest assured, we will forget her soon enough’”, the Times has “King: Grief has coloured earl’s claims over Diana”, the Telegraph writes “Palace hits back at Diana’s brother”, and the Sun’s take is “Recollections may vary … again”. The Mirror’s front page is “Heartbreak”, the i Paper’s splash is “Burnham warns of ‘challenging’ budget after 3.1% inflation”, and the Express says “We are ‘paying the price’ for Labour’s economy failure”. The FT leads on “Fed raises rates despite Trump pressure in bid to tame prices”. Lastly, Metro runs with “‘Putney pusher’ suspect dead”. Today in Focus: The Latest Ed Sheeran support acts quit after Macklemore ‘Free Palestine’ row All four supporting acts for the upcoming dates of Ed Sheeran’s tour have withdrawn in solidarity with fellow opener Macklemore. The American rapper was removed from Sheeran’s tour after comments made onstage in support of Palestine. Sheeran responded that venue owners – including Robert Kraft who owns the New England Patriots and its home stadium – had objected to Macklemore’s appearance on the tour. But after he had tried to negotiate with the venue owners ‘at length to build bridges’, ultimately the promoters made the decision to pull the plug. Artists who have pulled out include Finneas, Aaron Rowe and Beoga. Lucy Hough speaks to Guardian assistant opinion editor Jason Okundaye. Cartoon of the day | Nicola Jennings The Upside A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad The Moomin books about lovable trolls with hippopotamus snouts are coming to life in a new London exhibition, featuring previously unseen drawings by their creator, Tove Jansson. Opening in November, the show will include more than 100 works, from early Moomin sketches to photographs and films, celebrating Jansson’s enduring themes of nature, friendship, tolerance and being yourself. title: Country diary: Facing the flax – this city was once built on the stuff | Mary Montague
summary: Botanic Meadow, Belfast: I visit my local community garden, and the woman who has returned to growing this graceful crop that eventually becomes linen
text: In my hands is a brownish-grey hank of flax yarn. I twine it between my fingers to feel the thread’s strength and admire the fibres’ diffuse sheen. Along with fruit and vegetables, it’s the produce of our Friends of the Field community garden. It’s also the work of Merle, whose love of textile crafts has led her creative process right back to growing flax. Flax yarn is used to make linen, a fabric that is folded into Belfast’s history. During the 19th century, the city was a global powerhouse of linen production, but the advent of synthetic textiles contributed to the industry’s decline. So, despite its former importance to the Northern Irish economy, I’d never actually seen flax until I saw Merle’s crop. At summer’s height, her small plot swayed with flax’s graceful lime-green stems and delicate blue flowers. Over the season, the stems yellowed. Petals dropped, leaving little bonnets of seed pods. In late August, we pulled the crop. The plant’s shallow roots made our task relatively easy, but for previous generations of farm workers, pulling large fields of flax was back-breaking work. When we were done, we left the beets (bundles) of flax to dry in a polytunnel. Now the flax is retting, a decomposition process that macerates the stems. Traditionally this was done by immersing the flax in water, usually in a flax dam. Merle prefers to use the slower practice of dew-retting, which minimises any organic pollution. She has spread the dried beets on open ground so the flax can soften in the dew and rain over several weeks. Then it will be dried again. After that, Merle will break and scutch (beat) the flax stems to release their fibres, which she’ll hackle (comb out) until they’re fine enough to spin into new yarn (and so, through all these steps, such fabulous language is spoken again). Finally, Merle weaves the yarn into fresh linen on her table-loom at home. Merle also shares her yarn with other members of the community garden. For her, spinning and weaving and fabric-making is a way of threading together all the connections: of community and tradition; of earth and weather. I lift the hank she gave me to my nose. It smells clean, grassy and slightly peppery. • Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024, is available now at guardianbookshop.com
