title: 2025 was among driest years on record for world’s rivers, study finds
summary: Analysis of global resources reveals depletion in world’s water savings bank to 42% below normal levels last year
text: Rivers across the world experienced one of their driest years in more than three decades in 2025, a comprehensive study of global water resources has found. The assessment of the global water cycle by the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) reveals a depletion in the world’s water savings bank: the amount of freshwater held on or under the ground, including groundwater, lakes, rivers, snow, ice moisture in the soil and inside plants and trees, was 42% below normal across the world last year. The impacts of the climate crisis on extreme weather and the creation of so-called weather whiplash events are driving a more erratic and unpredictable water cycle. From melting glaciers to extreme droughts and flash flooding, the world’s rivers are swinging between having too much and too little water. The last seven years have seen the fewest rivers around the world with “normal” flows since 1991. In 2025, one of the warmest years on record, only about a third of rivers were in the normal range, while 36% of the global river basin area had river flows below or well below normal, and 21% were above- and much-above-normal flows, according to the WMO study, using simulations from 13 global hydrological models, driven by observed weather data. Celeste Saulo, secretary general of the WMO, said: “We are depleting that savings account. Global terrestrial water storage has shown a declining trend since 2014–16 – a persistent, decade-long signal.” Last year, for the fourth year in a row, each of the world’s 19 major glacial regions lost ice mass. Glaciers have seen their greatest losses of ice mass since the 1990s, and the largest losses are the most recent. In 2025 alone the ice mass loss was 400 gigatons, which adds 1.1mm to global sea levels. The analysis is a comprehensive, science-based assessment of the entire water cycle loop, including river flows, groundwater, evaporation and transpiration, land water storage, and snow and ice. Wayne Jenkinson, director of hydrology at the WMO, said the research was a call to action in the face of a continuing global picture of declining water resources. “We need to redouble our efforts to improve our understanding of water resources globally,” he said. “This requires increased data collection and sharing; that is how we increase understanding and protection for people’s lives and wellbeing.” The study is published as rivers across the world struggle against multiple threats caused by climate crisis-induced droughts, pollution and overexploitation. And the impact on our river systems has direct knock-on impacts for people, their wellbeing and the global economy. This summer record-low water levels on the Danube created an unprecedented energy crisis in Hungary and Romania, after all but one of their nuclear reactors had to shut down because the river was too low to provide water to cool them. The Mississippi, which is the primary source of water for 50 US municipalities, is threatened by chemical pollution that has created hypoxic dead zones in the Gulf of Mexico, sea level rise that is hastening wetland loss and saltwater intrusion, as well as intermittent droughts. Major African rivers such as the Nile, Niger and Zambezi face significant threats from severe pollution and climate-induced droughts that reduce water levels and harm local ecosystems. In England not one river is in good overall ecological and chemical health. They are suffering from a toxic combination of sewage pollution, agricultural pollution, the impact of forever chemicals and overabstraction. The WMO research shows the threat to rivers is continuing and, in some cases, accelerating. In 2025, for the seventh year in a row, the number of river basins with “normal” conditions was in a clear minority: ranging between 34 and 38%, compared with the average of 46% at normal conditions between 1991 and 2020, according to the report. Across the five years the WMO analysis has taken place, from 2021-25, repeated below-normal river flows were seen in major parts of the Amazon and La Plata basins, North America, central and east Africa, central Asia and the Middle East. Below-normal to much-below-normal river flows affected much of North America, the La Plata and São Francisco basins of South America, eastern European basins, the Middle East and central Asia. In each of the past five years, national meteorological and hydrological services around the globe reported record-breaking floods and droughts. Some places have had no recovery time between events. Over the next year, in a series called Our Rivers, the Guardian will focus on the environmental challenges facing the world’s rivers, looking at the waterways around the planet that are overengineered or suffocating and drying up, and those that are being opened up again and given new life

title: ‘Like a Disney movie’: Three wild dog brothers make Africa’s longest journey
summary: As three siblings came of age and had to leave their pack, scientists tracked the dogs’ perilous 2,500-mile odyssey to find their own territory
text: It sounds like a Disney movie: three wild dogs, all brothers, on an epic journey to find a home of their own after their family tells them to leave. They dodge cars and hunters in search of a new life, navigating bushmeat snares and the hostility of a human-dominated landscape until they find a new haven on the African savannah. But this is exactly what happened in Zambia last year, when three endangered African wild dogs made the longest-ever recorded single journey of any mammal from the continent. The brothers travelled more than 2,500 miles (4,100km) over eight months in their “dispersal” – when a young dog comes of age and must establish new territory to find a mate and start a family of their own. From point to point, starting in Kafue national park in western Zambia to their final destination in the Luangwa valley in the east of the country, the brothers covered 340 miles (546km), which is also a record. The epic single journey is almost equivalent to travelling the length of Chile by foot and farther than the famous wildebeest and zebra migration across the Serengeti in east Africa. The previous record was 2,418 miles, also made by African wild dogs, which moved between Loliondo, in northern Tanzania’s Ngorongoro district, and Tsavo West national park in southern Kenya in 2012. Dr Matt Becker, chief executive of the Zambian Carnivore Programme (ZCP), whose scientists were monitoring the wild dogs and have published their findings in the journal Ecology, says: “These extraordinary journeys show that natural connections between Africa’s wildlife strongholds still exist. But they also reveal how difficult and dangerous those journeys have become. “Rather than relying solely on fenced protected areas, these findings reinforce the value of investing in connected landscapes. The dogs are showing us that connectivity still works; now we need to do more to protect and strengthen it.” The researchers tracked 19 separate groups of wild dogs to monitor their dispersals, including a group of sisters to the three brothers who were far less successful at finding a new range. Two of the sisters died, probably caught in snares, but not before they had a touching final encounter with their siblings. Two months into their journey, the group of brothers and sisters came across each other deep in Zambia’s copper-belt mining region, spending the day together before going their separate ways again. Related dogs do not form new family packs, and typically have to travel long distances through the landscape to find prospective mates. Only 6,600 or so adults remain of 39 distinct populations of African wild dogs, and the species is classified as endangered on the International Union for Conservation of Nature’s red list. Habitat loss, declining numbers of natural prey, bushmeat hunters’ snares and human conflict are among the biggest threats to their survival. But researchers say the three brothers’ epic journey shows the wild dogs can still survive in a human-dominated landscape despite the enormous challenges they face. Alongside African savannah elephants, whose ancient migration routes are increasingly being blocked by human development, African wild dogs need to be able to make long journeys to find new homes. “These long-term studies provide key evidence that connectivity between large landscapes is still there,” says Dr Nyambe Nyambe, director of the Kavango-Zambezi transfrontier area secretariat, a key conservation region that spans five countries, including Zambia, where governments are trying to keep space for wildlife to move through the landscape. “If we conserve and continue to improve these connections – spanning the range of national parks, community areas, nations and regions – a lot of species like wild dogs can make the rest happen,” Nyambe says. Find more age of extinction coverage here, and follow the biodiversity reporters Rebecca Ratcliffe, Phoebe Weston and Patrick Greenfield in the Guardian app for more nature coverage.

title: English Heritage trains new generation of scythers to maintain meadows and craft
summary: Initiative aims to keep alive age-old skill, and at Muchelney Abbey in Somerset improve habitat for the shrill carder bee
text: It sounds like something out of a Thomas Hardy novel: a merry band of men and women roaming the West Country cutting meadows by hand in exchange for hunks of bread and cheese. But the conservation charity English Heritage is recruiting a team of volunteer scythers to maintain 21st-century meadowland in the old-fashioned way. The first scythers have been trained and will use their new skills in the meadows around an abbey in Somerset, where it is hoped that as well as helping to keep the age-old practice alive, they will protect a rare type of bumblebee. Ginny Slade, who has completed the training, said she found there was something therapeutic about scything. “You need a level of physical fitness but it’s also about enthusiasm and the passion to learn heritage skills,” she said. “It’s a repetitive movement. You find your rhythm and zone into it. You can really connect with the meadow, the landscape.” The first volunteers have also found that using the scythe is something of a sensual treat – the sound of the blade cutting, the scent of the meadow. Slade said: “Scything is a wonderful example of how traditional skills can still have a role in addressing modern challenges. We hope to help create the diverse, flower-rich habitats that pollinators need while also preserving knowledge and skills that have shaped our landscapes.” Slade, a volunteer and community engagement manager with English Heritage, is one of the first to be trained by professionals at the Exmoor National Park Authority in the art of using and maintaining a scythe. “You want a really good scythe,” said Slade. “If you look after them, they can last generations.” English Heritage rewards volunteers with bread and cheese (it also thought about providing West Country cider but thought this was not a good idea on health and safety grounds). The first group of scythers will help care for the meadow at Muchelney Abbey, in Somerset, which was once a wealthy and important monastery with features including a thatched two-storey monks’ lavatory, which is unique in Britain. They will work on a three-year project with the Bumblebee Conservation Trust to improve habitat for the shrill carder bee, a species that has declined significantly because of the loss of flower-rich grasslands. As part of the project, English Heritage volunteers have been trained by the bumblebee trust to carry out wildlife surveys. Rather than simply recording numbers, volunteers will monitor the relationship between bees and the meadow ecosystem, including which flowers are in bloom, which plants they are using, how far bees travel from their nests and how the habitat changes over time. Hardy wrote about scything in prose and poetry: in Far From the Madding Crowd, Bathsheba Everdene watches haymaking, and the farm hand Mark Clark is described as “humming a tune to the strokes of his scythe”. In his poem Four in the Morning, Hardy wrote about the “to-and-fro/Wheezed whettings of a scythe apace”. The meadow at Muchelney is one of 100 that English Heritage pledged to create and enhance to mark the coronation of King Charles in 2023. Slade said Muchelney was the pilot site but the idea was for the volunteers to travel to other English Heritage sites to use their skills. “We’re really at the beginning of this journey, but we’re very excited about it.”

title: Can fish and chip shops survive? ‘We made more money by closing than staying open’
summary: Soaring fish prices, labour costs and changing tastes all spell bad news for Britain’s chippies. Is this the end for the seaside staple – or will a few innovators succeed in keeping them alive?
text: One day in 2007, Darren Sudlow drove past the old stationmaster’s house at Padgate station, in Cheshire, noticed it was empty and decided to lease it. “He just fell in love with the place,” says his son, Kieran, who was 11 at the time. “He said he always wanted a fish and chip shop, for some reason.” Despite having worked as a joiner up to that point, Darren made a go of it, and the Plaice Station, as he named it, was a success from day one. “He worked like mad to get it open and then realised that the hard work hadn’t even started, and he had a queue out the door,” says the younger Sudlow. The family lived nearby. Kieran Sudlow, who is now 30, worked at the Plaice Station as a boy, peeling potatoes, washing dishes after school, then cooking at the range when he was 16. He went on to become a chef, working in Australia for a few years, then returning to help out at the chippy part-time when needed. Business had always been pretty good. They won local awards and had a loyal customer base. But one day in March, Kieran remembers, his father came in and told him: “‘I think the fish and chip shop’s going to go.’ He said, ‘It’s not making money. I can’t see it carrying on.’” In April, after 19 years, the Plaice Station served its last customer. In a Facebook post, Darren Sudlow explained that the closure was the result of multiple pressures: “Soaring fish prices, reduced fishing quotas and political issues around the world, relentless demands on VAT among other ever-increasing expenses, effectively destroying any profit margins remaining. Truth is, the product of fish and chips itself is facing its toughest battle.” Chippies across the UK are feeling similarly pessimistic. According to research carried out in May by the National Federation of Fish Friers (NFFF), 47% of them were “extremely worried” about the future of their business, and a further 30% were “slightly worried”. About 20% of them planned to quit in the next 12 months. Many have already shut in recent years. There are still 7,000-8,000 chippies in Britain, down from a peak of 25,000 in the 1930s, but the number of outlets, and the number of servings, are shrinking weekly. The big chains are also feeling the pressure: Deep Blue, which owns the historic Harry Ramsden’s brand, shut down nine of its restaurants last summer. Customers cannot have failed to notice the problem. The average price of takeaway fish and chips has gone up more than 60% in the past five years, from about £7 to £11.43 – a faster rise than other takeaway foods. A family of four would now pay nearly £50 for their meal. “It’s a fair chunk of money and I think it’s shocked people a little bit,” says Andrew Crook, president of the NFFF. “So they cut back on the number of visits, so volumes are going down as well.” Crook has been feeling it himself; he runs two chippies in Lancashire, and has been in the trade for 27 years. The recent hot weather has been good for coastal outlets, but “if you’re inland, nobody wants fish and chips”, he says. It’s been a hard summer for shops like his. “It’s not a very pleasant place to be when it’s hot, and it’s quiet as well. The night drags, and it can be 40-50C in the shop.” These are difficult times for UK hospitality across the board, but chippy owners have it particularly tough, Crook explains. For starters, they’re beholden to the costs of a very small set of basic ingredients. Fish prices have risen astronomically in recent years, especially cod and haddock. The cod quota in the Barents Sea, where most of the fish comes from, has gone down from about 1m tonnes in 2020 to just 285,000 tonnes this year, according to Undercurrent, a seafood industry data company. Inevitably, this has pushed up prices. “For an 18kg case of cod [fillets], I was paying something like £160 three years ago, and I’m now paying £330,” says Crook. Haddock quotas are slightly less affected, but the scarcity of cod has created a knock-on demand, again affecting prices. The Ukraine war has also had an impact on the industry (hence the “political issues” Darren Sudlow was referring to). The Barents Sea is jointly managed by Norway and Russia, but in May 2025, the EU sanctioned two Russian fishing companies, Murman SeaFood and the giant Norebo JSC, over alleged surveillance and sabotage activities. That has disrupted the whole supply chain, again raising prices. Potato prices are also likely to rise: after the heatwaves and droughts, this year’s European harvest will be one of the worst on record. Even cooking oil prices are going up. Then there are energy costs: the range has to be kept hot, and a lot of freezing and refrigeration is required. And the equipment is not cheap: a new frying range can cost upwards of £10,000. On the administrative side, chippies have been hit hard by recent rises in VAT (it returned to 20% in April 2022, after a temporary reduction during the pandemic to 5% and then 12.5%), business rates, the minimum wage and mandatory sick pay. The government has been putting in relief measures – lowering business rates for pubs and clubs in England, capping VAT on children’s meals over the summer – but none of this benefits chippies, says Crook. “So it does feel like we’re being run by our business now, rather than running the business. It’s taken a lot of the fun out of it for many.” All of these factors hit the Plaice Station, says Kieran Sudlow, squeezing margins tighter and tighter. VAT was the last straw. Like many small businesses, the firm was paying a flat rate of 12.5% to the government, but in 2025 its accountant warned it was approaching a limit: if the business’s annual turnover exceeded £230,000, the flat rate would no longer apply. “So it was going to cost us tens of thousands of pounds.” The only option was to earn less money. The Sudlows made the painful decision to temporarily close. “As strange as it sounds, we made more money by closing for three weeks than if we’d just stayed open,” Kieran says. In order to justify leaving the flat rate scheme, they would have had to turn over an extra £2,000 a week. “After 19 years, you know where you are with your business. You can’t just find an extra two grand a week.” Closing down was a demoralising experience. “I felt we were doing everything we could to make the products as good as possible. But then all that work that you’ve done to grow your business is ripped out from under your feet.” There’s another factor at play here: changing tastes. Fish and chips has been facing stiff competition from other takeaway options: pizzas, burgers, fried chicken, Indian, Chinese, Korean – most of which use much cheaper ingredients. Deep-fried foods are also losing popularity for health reasons, since they contribute to obesity; the government recently banned them from schools in England. Fish and chips is a great British institution, but the origins of the dish are not all that deep, or that British. The technique of coating fish in flour and deep-frying it is thought to have been introduced by Jewish immigrants from Spain and Portugal in the 17th century, but fish and chips only caught on commercially in the mid-19th century (starting in either London or Lancashire – it’s disputed). In the days before British cuisine opened up to international influences, it was one of the few convenience foods. It was also one of the few meals not rationed during the second world war, further cementing its patriotic connotations. One chip shop owner in his 80s (who did not wish to be named, as he is in the process of selling up) recalls starting out in the business in his 20s, in a small town in the north of England. “It was pretty busy, because in those days there was only your chip shop and your butcher’s and your pie shop,” he says. For most of his career it was a good way to make a living. His wife and children helped out in his shops and they often lived above the premises. But it has been tougher in recent years, he agrees, and he’s struggling to find a buyer for his business. Today’s establishments don’t look that different from the ones he started out in: “They’re more modern and very good-looking, but other than that, they haven’t changed. They can’t, because you can’t change the way you cook fish and chips.” The unchanging nature of fish and chips is both its strength and its weakness. Kieran Sudlow had begun to notice the dish falling out of fashion: “You’ve got a very ageing market – your traditionalists, your mums, your dads, your nans, they grew up on fish and chips. But we could see clear as day, and especially now with online orders and social media posts, your 18- to 35-year-olds, that younger bracket that’s your next generation of customers, they’re not interacting. They’re not coming through the doors.” A lot of chippies have tried using different, cheaper fish, such as hake, plaice, rock or spurdog (types of dogfish), or even tilapia, a freshwater fish farmed in southeast Asia. Many chippies claim customers would not be able to tell the difference, but we’re wedded to cod and haddock. Other chippies have expanded their menus to include items such as calamari, fishcakes, fried chicken, sausages, kebabs or loaded chips. Sudlow decided to change tack entirely. Three months after the Plaice Station closed, he reopened as Between Bread, a high-end sandwich shop. The fare is a cut above: he uses locally sourced “shokupan”, or Japanese milk bread; fillings include braised beef with chipotle sauce, and spicy tuna and avocado; prices are between £8 and £12. He did his homework, researching food trends and visiting similar establishments around the country. Business is great, he says – turnover is “much higher” than when it was a chippy (justifying that VAT change), and the shop is popular on social media and with young people. He also gets to be a bit more creative as a chef. Does he miss the chippy days? “Personally, no,” he says. “It got to a point at the end where it really was like fighting. It’s an expensive product to buy in nowadays and even harder to sell. Staff training is a nightmare: how many people do you know that go, ‘When I grow up I want to cook fish and chips’? It’s a part-time job; staff turnover’s horrendous. It’s a hard business to have.” But the great British chippy is not to be written off just yet. Cod and haddock quotas are expected to increase 10% next year, says Undercurrent, which could help reduce prices, and the UK government is facing increasing pressure to deal with the VAT problems plaguing the hospitality industry. Most importantly, perhaps, a new generation is embracing the chippy tradition and breathing new life into it – not necessarily by totally transforming it, but by doing it simply and well. The Scrap Box, outside York, is one such example: it won best takeaway this year at the NFFF’s National Fish & Chip awards. The Scrap Box was founded 12 years ago by brothers Aman and Gavin Dhesi, aged 37 and 33. Sons of a local off-licence keeper, they studied politics and economics at university, respectively, but then decided to open a chippy together. “It was pretty much on a whim, to be honest,” says Aman. “I was never proud to be doing fish and chips and never felt like it was really me.” After Covid, the brothers reached a crossroads, he continues. “It was like – do we do something else, do we sell out, or do we really double down and go on a journey to try to make sure we can improve every single aspect of the business?” They went on the journey, researching every aspect of the trade and its history, carefully sourcing their supplies and “letting our ingredients do the talking”: their fish comes from Iceland and is Marine Stewardship Council-certified; they fry in beef dripping from Ireland. There’s no secret formula, Aman says. The fish is lightly seasoned; the batter is just flour and water and a bit of natural colouring, applied as thinly as possible. Nothing artificial is added. “The main thing is, it needs to be made often, as opposed to just all done in the morning, so that it retains its bubbles and you still get your spikiness. And it wants to be cold, so that when it hits the oil, it has a bigger reaction – you get a nicer texture.” When I visit on a Friday night, the Scrap Box – a roadside hut on a layby that used to be a council toilet block – is buzzing: six or seven people cooking at a huge range; a constant bustle of customers. The menu is classic: haddock and chips for £11.95, cod and chips a pound more, sides like curry sauce and mushy peas, a few non-fish options. And the food is everything you’d want it to be: the fish fresh and succulent, the batter crisp and light, the chips hot and sog-free. At the end of the shift, Gavin tells me they’ve done about 650 portions that night. The award has raised their profile. They’ve just returned from a trip to see the fishing in Iceland, he says, and they’re about to go to Japan, where they’re doing pop-up stores in three cities. “There’s been so many opportunities – that’s kept us stimulated and excited.” They’re also looking at opening a branch in London, Aman says: “We want to bring the best of the north to the south.” Despite the union-jack-waving seaside cliches, what makes fish and chips quintessentially British is that it’s interwoven with our history of immigration and internationalism, says Aman, whose family has Punjabi roots. It is often immigrants who have run British chippies, he points out: Italians in Scotland, Chinese in Liverpool and the north-west of England, Indians and Pakistanis, Greeks and Turks. The fish recipe came from Sephardic Jews in Portugal; the potatoes often come from central Europe (via South America); the fish comes from Iceland and Norway. There are other outlets doing similar things to the Scrap Box around the UK. In Nottinghamshire the Cod’s Scallops (corny names come with the territory) includes fresh fish counters in its outlets; in Oxford Harrisons’s Fish & Chip Co has been diversifying its menu with a range of British fish. There are new young proprietors of established family chippies trying new things, and there are food trucks and mobile chippies such as Frosty’s in Northumberland keeping prices down by minimising their premises. So maybe there’s life in the old chippy yet. “I do think the better shops will survive and prosper,” says Aman Dhesi. “But it’s never going to die out.” Gavin agrees: “I think we need to hark back to just how pure a dish it is, how great it is. And when you think about it, for where it’s come from and the work that’s gone into it, it’s still a bargain.” • Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: ‘Pretend I’m on the ticket’: Trump hits campaign trail in bid to boost Republican hopes
summary: President stumps for Senate nominee Michael Whatley in North Carolina and urges voters to ‘crush the communists’
text: Donald Trump returned to the campaign trail on Wednesday, imploring North Carolina voters to “pretend I’m on the ticket” and “crush the communists” in the November elections at a rally in support of the Republican Senate nominee, Michael Whatley. Despite Trump’s deep unpopularity, Republicans hope to once again turn the president’s loyal following into a political force as the party confronts an unforgiving midterm landscape. “I’m not bragging, but when I’m on the ticket Republicans have always done really well,” Trump told supporters, speaking at the Gastonia municipal airport. “I just want you to go out and pretend I’m on the ticket, because essentially I am.” The rally, Trump’s first campaign event since the Republican party’s unusual midterm convention in Dallas last week where he debuted a similar message, was aimed at energizing the Make American Great Again (Maga) faithful behind Whatley, who is running in a crucial battleground race against the Democratic former governor Roy Cooper. With the Republican senator Thom Tillis retiring, Democrats see a rare opportunity to flip a seat in a state that has repeatedly dashed the party’s hopes in recent elections, but which could decide the balance of power in the Senate for the final two years of Trump’s presidency. To win control of the chamber, Democrats must prevail in at least four Republican-held seats. The president’s appearance in North Carolina on Wednesday underscored Republicans’ challenge in the state, where Democrats have not won a Senate race since 2008 but where polls have consistently shown Cooper ahead of Whatley. Nodding to Cooper’s edge, Trump claimed there was a misconception about the former governor’s politics, claiming he was a “radical” more closely aligned with his party’s left wing. “He tries to pretend he’s a moderate,” Trump said of Cooper. “He’s not.” During his hour-long remarks, Trump lavished praise on Whatley, his handpicked choice for Senate. The former Republican National Committee chair was a “ball-breaker” and “one of the greatest men I ever worked with in government”, the president said. “I had my choice of the whole country,” Trump said. “I chose Michael Whatley.” Whatley enthusiastically returned the embrace, praising Trump as the “greatest president of our lifetime”. By leaving no doubt about his loyalty to the president, Whatley is hoping Trump’s command of the Maga base can translate into broader support in a state where independent voters make up a large share of the electorate and where concerns about high prices, the economy and the administration’s handling of the war in Iran have complicated his party’s political prospects. In Gastonia, Trump sought to simplify the choice for voters. He cast the Senate contest as a referendum on Cooper’s governorship, arguing that the election was about “safety” and “bad management”. He invoked the killing of Iryna Zarutska, a 23-year-old Ukrainian refugee fatally stabbed on a Charlotte light rail train last year. Describing the attack in gruesome detail, Trump falsely claimed that the man arrested and charged with her murder, Decarlos Brown Jr, had been released from prison by Cooper. Dozens of mugshots appeared on a video screen as Trump bashed Cooper as a “murderer protector” and explicitly likened his playbook to the notorious “Willie Horton” ad used by George HW Bush’s 1988 presidential campaign against Michael Dukakis in a racially charged appeal to cast the Democratic nominee as weak on crime. “Years ago in Massachusetts, there was a governor named Dukakis, Michael Dukakis, you remember, who had a very substantial lead for president,” Trump said. “He was going to win easily, but he allowed a man named Willie Horton out of jail. Willie Horton was a bad guy, really bad guy. Same thing as this. Same exact thing.” Trump said Whatley was the “candidate of law and order” who preferred that criminals be “executed, arrested or deported”. Local Democrats held a news conference earlier on Wednesday to preempt some of Trump’s claims and denounce Whatley for supporting Trump’s agenda. “Why would Whatley back a war that is driving up prices for North Carolina families at a time when it’s already too hard for us to get by?” the Democratic state senator Woodson Bradley said. “Let’s not find that out, North Carolina. He’s already shown us everything we need to know.” In a reminder of the significant economic headwinds Republicans are facing, Trump spent time attacking the Federal Reserve, which on Wednesday raised its benchmark interest rate by a quarter-point, its first increase since 2023. The Fed said persistent inflation warranted the move. Speaking to reporters on the tarmac before the rally, Trump called the central bank “very hostile” to him and said its officials were a “bunch of politicians”. “They’re doing the wrong thing,” he said, repeating several times that interest rates were “too high”. Robert Mackey contributed reporting

title: Fiji declares national HIV emergency as Pacific nation grapples with surge in cases
summary: Government estimates that one in 60 adults in Fiji now living with HIV, as escalating use of methamphetamine fuels ‘epidemic’
text: Fiji has declared a national HIV emergency amid a spike in infections as the Pacific nation grapples with a correlating rise in methamphetamine use. The country’s health and medical services minister, Dr Ratu Atonio Lalabalavu, said in a statement on social media that an outbreak-level response was no longer sufficient to address what he described an “epidemic”. “Today I am formally declaring a national health emergency in Fiji,” he said. “This decision recognises the seriousness of the epidemic and the urgent coordinated response our country now needs.” The health minister said the government estimates that one in every 60 adults in Fiji is now living with HIV. “Five years ago, the estimate was one in 167. In 2025, we recorded 2,060 new HIV diagnoses,” he said, adding that one in 50 pregnant women has HIV. The emergency declaration followed on from a cabinet decision on 9 September and would require a coordinated response, he added. Home to less than one million people, the Pacific nation is facing one of the sharpest increases in new HIV infections globally, according to UNAIDS, which said that new infections spiked 12-fold between 2010 and 2025. Fiji’s location as a drug-running hub coupled with the escalating use of methamphetamine locally has fuelled the rapid spread of HIV, a situation worsened by unsafe injecting and a lack of access to clean needles. Low health awareness, cultural stigma and inadequate testing and treatment have exacerbated the crisis. Among HIV cases in Fiji with a known mode of transmission, over half were linked to sexual transmission and more than 42% to injecting drug use, according to UNAIDS. Of an estimated 9,100 people living with HIV in Fiji in 2025, only 39% were aware of their HIV status and only 22% were accessing antiretroviral treatment, the UN said. Responding to the emergency declaration, UNAIDS executive director Winnie Byanyima said in a statement on Wednesday that the situation was a “a stark reminder to the world that AIDS is not over”. “HIV epidemics can change quickly, and countries need health and community systems that are ready to respond urgently,” said Byanyima. “Fiji has recognised the urgency of the moment and is stepping up its response.” The UN agency said it welcomed plans to introduce a needle and syringe programme, with legislative amendments expected to go before parliament, as well as efforts to expand prevention, testing and access to treatment.

title: Ukraine war briefing: Drone kills Russian commander just decorated after fake victory claim
summary: Maj Gen Anton Grunis was praised by Vladimir Putin for purported capture of Kostiantynivka; UK names intel officer who died in Ukraine road crash. What we know on day 1,667
text: Ukrainian drone forces have killed a Russian general who had just been made a Hero of Russia after false claims that Moscow’s forces had captured the Donetsk city of Kostiantynivka. Maj Gen Anton Grunis died in eastern Ukraine on Saturday. “General Grunis was eliminated on September 12,” said Ukrainian drone commander Robert Brovdi, adding that the general was the seventh Russian military commander killed by his drone forces. Another Russian commander, Apti Alaudinov, posted confirmation that Grunis had died. The battle for Kostiantynivka is gruelling for Ukraine but war analysts say it remains contested. Grunis reported personally to Vladimir Putin earlier this year that his troops helped capture Kostiantynivka and was praised by the Russian president for “doing the work”. The territorial claim ⁠remains heavily disputed – the US-based Institute for the Study of War said Russian forces had infiltrated but not fully seized the city, and Russia’s claim was part of a wider information campaign to “portray the Ukrainian frontlines as collapsing”. Grunis received the Gold Star Hero of Russia award at a ceremony in late August. Russian ⁠airstrikes damaged buildings in Kyiv and injured three in the Black ⁠Sea port city of Odesa in the ⁠early hours of Thursday, officials said. In Kyiv, debris fell ‌on ‌warehouses and near ‌a petrol station, among other locations, said the mayor, Vitali ‌Klitschko. Three people, including a ⁠child, were injured as Russia hit a 19-storey apartment building in Odesa, authorities said. Russian drones struck a passenger bus, killing five people, as well as attacking a train in southern Ukraine on Wednesday, Ukrainian officials said. “There is no military logic to this, ⁠just another act of brutality,” said the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy. The bus was hit near the frontline city of Nikopol. Seven more people were wounded, said the Dnipropetrovsk region’s governor. Russian drones attacked a passenger train three times in Ukraine’s southern Mykolaiv region, the acting regional governor said. Passengers and crew were evacuated and no one was hurt. Zelenskyy said that ‌in addition, a locomotive was struck in Kovel near the border with Poland. Russian shelling on Wednesday killed one person in the southern Kherson region, and in the port of Odesa one death was reported. Russian attacks injured more than a dozen people in Sumy in the north and Kropyvnytskyi in central Ukraine. The Russia-installed head of areas of Ukraine’s eastern Donetsk region held by Moscow ⁠said a Ukrainian drone strike killed one person. Officials in Russia’s border Belgorod region said six people were injured in Ukrainian attacks. The Russian Gerbera-2 drone found in the Baltic Sea off Poland was armed with explosives, officials said on Wednesday. Polish defence minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said on Monday that the military had located the drone near the village of Rusinowo in north-western Poland and recovered it from the sea. The drone was thought to have been lost by Russia during test manoeuvres over the Baltic. Polish military prosecutors are investigating whether legal proceedings can be launched, presumably against Russia, for “causing an incident that endangers the life or health of many people and property of great value”. The Russian government has extended a ban on diesel ⁠exports until the end of October. The ban had been due to end this month. Russia introduced restrictions on exports of gasoline, jet fuel and diesel because of domestic ⁠fuel shortages driven by Ukrainian strikes on oil refineries. Reuters reported that fuel market data indicates three of Russia’s six largest diesel-producing refineries were forced to significantly cut output or halt production altogether in September because of damage caused by drone attacks. Russia’s Rosneft-owned oil refineries in the Volga river cities of ⁠Syzran and Saratov have stopped ⁠processing after Ukrainian drone attacks this month, Reuters reported on Wednesday citing three industry sources. Britain’s defence ministry has named a 40-year-old intelligence officer who died in a road crash away from the frontlines in Ukraine on Saturday. Maj Paul Wilks was commissioned from Sandhurst in 2012 and joined the Intelligence Corps, where he remained throughout his career. His commanding officer described Wilks as a “man of great intellect”, who often spoke of his love for his wife and two sons. The chief of defence intelligence described Wilks as “one of the most talented intelligence officers of his generation”. The defence secretary, Wes Streeting, said Wilks “served this country with pride and dedication”. A small number of British personnel serve in Ukraine providing security to diplomats and support the country’s armed forces. Britain’s MoD previously announced paratrooper George Hooley, 28, was killed in Ukraine in December as he watched Ukrainian forces testing a new defensive capability. A Russian strike destroyed a warehouse in Kyiv that stored props for Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s former TV studio, the company said on Wednesday, adding that its staff were unharmed. title: ‘Harrowing reading’: what the inquiry into NZ fugitive father Tom Phillips revealed
summary: Inquiry uncovered missed opportunities and failures by New Zealand police and government agencies that may have avoided four-year hunt
text: A major public inquiry into the disappearance of fugitive father Tom Phillips, who hid in New Zealand’s wilderness for nearly four years with his three children, has found authorities played down the harms he inflicted on his children, and did not do enough to protect them. Taking his children, of whom he did not have legal custody, Phillips disappeared into the rugged North Island wilderness in 2021. That disappearance was preempted by an earlier, shorter stint where Phillips went bush with his son and two daughters, aged five, seven and eight at the time. In August 2025, Phillips was shot dead by police in a shootout. Here are some key findings of the inquiry, which investigated agencies’ engagement with Phillips before and after he disappeared. Agencies overlooked harm Phillips was causing Over “significant periods”, police and Oranga Tamariki (OT), the ministry for children, “underplayed or overlooked” the harm Phillips was causing before and after he vanished, the inquiry found. They were too slow to identify important information, and the search was launched too late. Police intentionally adopted “a low-key approach”, the inquiry said. “This strategy appears to have been predicated on the misconceived view that there were no concerns for the children’s welfare.” The inquiry found OT was dismissive of multiple concerns raised by the maternal family after Phillips’ first disappearance, telling the family court the children were “completely fine” and further OT involvement was perhaps not needed. Significant family concerns minimised Had OT taken into consideration the significant concerns of the children’s mother and two other sisters, they “may have prevented or made more difficult” his second disappearance, the inquiry found. The sisters, who had lived with their stepfather Phillips for some years, repeatedly raised concerns over his pattern of isolation and harm he caused. The sisters were “uniquely placed” to comment on family dynamics and it was “regrettable the agency did not meet with them.” The children’s mother, named as Ms Smith, had told OT of Phillips’ controlling behaviour towards her. The inquiry found OT failed to hear her concerns before Phillips disappeared the second time. She also notified police that Phillips stashed multiple firearms “all over the place” six months before he disappeared. Police questioned her credibility because of a “custody dispute in the background” and did not respond to her allegations. Phillips’ state of mind and beliefs not treated seriously enough Police built a comprehensive profile of Phillips while investigating his first disappearance. His alcohol consumption concerned them, and his home was “very dirty”. They formed the view he was controlling and difficult to live with. A person close to Phillips was concerned that, if cornered, he would turn “violent”. Another told police he had a dislike of government agencies, “meaning anyone that might try to remove his children from him”. Phillips held anti-vaccination views and had told family he and the children would “just disappear” if there was another Covid lockdown. A 2021 police report, before his second disappearance, said Phillips was “prepared to put the children’s wellbeing at risk by hiding them” to deny Ms Smith access. His firearms licence was suspended and police wanted him to access mental health support. But the inquiry saw no evidence that support was explored or provided by police. The inquiry found police did not adequately share information with OT, and OT should have more carefully considered mental health concerns. Better communication between the two “may have prevented, and would likely have made more difficult” Phillips’ second disappearance. Public sighting a missed opportunity In May 2023, a woman living near Marokopa, close to the Phillips’ family farm told police a man had approached her house asking to jump start his car. She described a man fitting Phillips’ profile and said “he smelled … like someone who had not had a shower in a very long time”. She saw children in his car and later called police. A police unit was dispatched but, before it arrived, it was diverted to another incident. The inquiry found no evidence the police attempted to visit the location of the sighting, or the woman’s home. Police followed up the tip 10 days later. Authorities accept all recommendations The inquiry made nine recommendations, including urging agencies to better communicate, particularly in cases related to a child’s safety and ensuring gun safety concerns raised by former spouses are “actioned promptly”. The minister for social development, Louise Upston, apologised to Phillips’ children saying “our agencies did not take all practical steps to protect you”. The government accepted the 41 findings and nine recommendations. The police commissioner, Richard Chambers, said it was “clear there were gaps” in communication and police should have put more resources into their investigation earlier. Oranga Tamariki chief executive, Amanda Malu, said the report made for “harrowing reading”. She said the agency was immediately strengthening its checks and procedures.

title: IMF urges Australian government to cut spending as another interest rate hike looms
summary: Warning comes as forecast for nation’s economic growth downgraded amid concerns over rising debt and inflation
text: The International Monetary Fund has called on Australia’s federal and state governments to cut spending as it warns the Reserve Bank may have to hike interest rates further to get price pressures back under control. More disciplined budgets would rein in rising debt burdens and help solve Australia’s long-running inflation problem, the IMF said in a new report, as it downgraded its forecast for Australia’s economic growth in 2027. In a “concluding statement” that followed annual consultations with Treasury, RBA and Australian Prudential Regulation Authority officials, the Washington-based institution predicted that the economy would grow by 1.9% this year. But it shaved 0.1 percentage points off its forecast for real GDP growth to just 1.6% in 2027, flagging the downgrade was due to the higher likelihood of another RBA interest rate hike. “Inflation remains a central challenge, while weak productivity growth is weighing on the economy’s potential,” the statement said. “There is a risk that further large increases in global energy prices lead to stronger second-round effects and lift inflation expectations, warranting further tightening” in monetary policy. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email The new assessment will come as a blow to Jim Chalmers, the treasurer, who is already under pressure to present a convincing story of improving living standards and prosperity. Fuel prices in Australia are rising again after the worsening Middle East conflict pushed the global oil benchmark, Brent crude, above US$108 a barrel on Wednesday, marking a 35% surge since the start of August. As global energy costs climb and threaten to spill over into domestic inflation, financial markets are pricing in an 80% chance of a RBA rate hike on 29 September. The US Federal Reserve on Wednesday night voted to increase rates for the first time since 2023, threatening to reignite Donald Trump’s political attacks on the central bank. The IMF largely backed Labor’s budget changes to investor taxes, although it noted concerns around unintended consequences. Paulo Medas, the IMF’s mission chief, said previous consultations had identified that Australia’s property tax settings, including negative gearing, were “creating incentives for people to take more leverage and invest in housing” and adding to price pressures. Medas told journalists on Thursday morning that the budget changes had created a more “balanced” set of incentives that could lead to more investment in other segments of the economy. “That’s where we think it’s a positive change to the tax system, and hopefully helps on this affordability issue in housing.” House price falls had done little to address unaffordable housing, the IMF said. It welcomed the steps taken to boost housing supply, even as it urged states and the federal government to do more. The report noted that the combined federal and state deficit had widened over the past two years as states spent big on infrastructure projects, along with higher social services costs, especially in healthcare and the national disability insurance scheme. There was also taxpayer money committed to cushioning the impact of the initial global energy price shock, most notably through cuts to the fuel excise. New South Wales and Queensland spend more than twice as much on debt interest now than before the pandemic, according to Challenger. And while “Australia’s overall public debt remains relatively low compared to many other advanced economies”, the IMF officials pointed to rising debts and interest costs, especially in state governments. “The ongoing efforts to restrain general government spending, amidst strong private demand, would also support disinflation efforts by the RBA.” In the longer term, poor productivity growth was “Australia’s key structural challenge”, the IMF said. “Reversing the slowdown in recent years will be crucial to improving living standards” and making our public and private debt obligations sustainable over the long run. The comments come before Monday’s release of the government’s latest intergenerational report, which will paint a long-term and likely challenging picture of Australia’s economy and budget.

title: LA homelessness non-profit workers arrested over alleged corruption and bribes
summary: Pair accused of misappropriating millions in taxpayer dollars and using money for personal gain
text: Federal law enforcement officers have arrested two employees of California-based homelessness non-profits on corruption charges, alleging that they misappropriated millions in taxpayer dollars. The US justice department has arrested Michael Young, a founder of the Culver City-based non-profit Home at Last, and Lakiya Malone, an employee of the Los Angeles-based Special Service for Groups. The two are expected to appear in court on Wednesday. Young is charged with wire fraud in a scheme to embezzle more than $7.5m from contracts with Los Angeles county and other publicly funded agencies, which he used to open a high-end restaurant, nightclub and bingo hall. Malone is charged with taking more than $180,000 in bribes and kickbacks from the director of another homelessness non-profit, Alexander Soofer, who has agreed to plead guilty in a separate case. The justice department is also seeking to arrest Donye Mitchell, the CEO of the Los Angeles-based non-profit the Big Blue Umbrella. Mitchell is charged with wire fraud in a case that alleges he fraudulently obtained $1.2m in public grant funding, which he allegedly used for personal expenses, including his own bail bonds, credit card debt and PlayStation charges. “My message to every fraudster who steals from the vulnerable is clear: we will track you down, bring charges where the evidence leads and work relentlessly to reclaim every taxpayer dollar you stole,” said assistant attorney general Colin M McDonald of the national fraud enforcement division. The investigation was led by the homeless fraud and corruption taskforce, which US attorney Bill Essayli formed last year to “investigate fraud, waste, abuse and corruption involving funds allocated toward the eradication of homelessness within the seven-county jurisdiction of the central district of California”. The Los Angeles mayor, Karen Bass, said in a Wednesday statement: “My administration has zero tolerance for fraud – period. “Any misuse of taxpayer funds meant to help unhoused Angelenos should be met with the full force of the law. We appreciate the efforts of the Department of Justice in protecting public funds and working towards recovering dollars meant to serve Angelenos experiencing homelessness.” The arrests come amid growing Trump administration-backed efforts to root out “fraud” in blue states such as California. In April, Donald Trump named JD Vance his “fraud czar”, with a focus on investigating “those blue states where crooked Democrat politicians … have had a ‘free for all’ in the unprecedented theft of taxpayer money”. Months prior, he froze federal childcare funding to Minnesota over accusations of such fraud, and halted more than a quarter-billion dollars in Medicaid funds to the state as part of efforts to ensure it was a “good steward of the American people’s tax money”. This summer, the Trump administration suspended federal funding to Los Angeles’s homelessness agency, Lahsa, pending an investigation citing allegations of fraud. At the time, about 8% of Lahsa’s budget came from federal funding. And earlier this week, 12 people in southern California were charged with fraudulently collecting $10m in government childcare payments, despite allegedly caring for few or no children. “If you fail the taxpayer, if you fail our cities, if you fail our shared mission of ending homelessness, there will be consequences and we will cut you off,” the US housing and urban development secretary, Scott Turner, said at a press conference.

title: Climate crisis probably weakened glacier that caused devastating Nepal-Tibet floods, first study finds
summary: Scientists say global heating was a destabilising factor in collapse of 200,000 sq metre glacier in August
text: Climate breakdown probably weakened the glacier that collapsed causing catastrophic floods and killing over a thousand people in Nepal and Tibet last month, the first scientific study of the disaster has found. Researchers identified unusually warm conditions before the glacier’s collapse, which sent an avalanche of 110m cubic metres (3.885bn cu ft) of snow and ice into the valley below. This triggered flash floods on an almost unprecedented scale, hitting communities downstream without warning. “Communities in Nepal are paying with their lives for a crisis driven by fossil fuel emissions thousands of miles away,” said Dr Friederike Otto, a climate science professor at Imperial College London, which carried out the study. “When warming destabilises the roof of the world, no amount of local adaptation can fully shield vulnerable people downstream from this scale of destruction. Without much faster action to transition to zero fossil fuel emissions we will inevitably see more disasters of this scale occurring in the years to come.” More than 1,300 people were killed and more than 5,000 people remain missing after a massive section of overhanging glacier and rock measuring roughly 200,000 sq metres (2,153,000 sq ft) fell from Langtang Lirung mountain on 26 August. It dropped about 1,400 metres (4,660ft), slamming into the valley floor with such intensity that it registered as an earthquake, liquidising ice and sparking a freezing flood that careened downriver at speeds exceeding 110 mph. The devastating flood of water, ice, rock and sediment swept away families, homes, settlements, roads, bridges and other infrastructure, leaving survivors stranded and cut off. “Rock avalanches of this size are rare, with annual frequency estimates of approximately one event this size every 1,000–10,000 years,” the study said. “This event shows that limits to adaptation are already being reached.” The research was unlike previous studies by Otto and her team at World Weather Attribution (WWA) – a collaborative project between Imperial and other climate specialists worldwide – in that the role of climate breakdown could not be ascribed to one particular weather event. Instead, the researchers found the disaster was the result of a compound crisis, with a number of factors made worse by decades of atmospheric heating as a result of greenhouse gas pollution. Dr Ben Clarke, who researches extreme weather and climate change at Imperial, said the “fingerprints of climate change” were clear in the long-term changes that happened around the glacier before its catastrophic collapse. Among the study’s key findings were: In the region where the collapse happened, climate breakdown has caused about 2C of warming since pre-industrial times, and about 1.5C of warming in July and August specifically; July and August 2026 were the warmest on record locally, reaching 5C above the 30-year average in the days before the collapse; The freezing threshold in the Himalayas has risen by about 100 metres per decade since the 1980s, with higher and longer thaw temperatures weakening mountain slopes shaped by permafrost; The warming temperature had already driven substantial glacier recession, removing stabilising ice from around the site where the collapse occurred and contributing meltwater; A 7.8 magnitude earthquake in 2015 further contributed to slope failure, though its specific contribution to the disaster in August could not be confirmed. Otto, Clarke and the WWA team said their study did not directly ascribe climate breakdown as the fundamental cause of the catastrophe. Instead, it was best understood as a destabilising factor on the existing geology. Clarke said: “We found that climate change is transforming the high mountain environment, influencing many of the possible drivers of this collapse.” Nepal has filed a formal request with the UN loss and damage fund for financial support to address the destruction caused by the flood, a process that requires proof of a link to the climate crisis. The country’s foreign minister, Shisir Khanal, has also demanded that top emitting nations such as China and India “wake up” and accept shared responsibility for the disaster. Madhab Uprety, senior technical advisor for the Red Cross Red Crescent Climate Centre, which is part of WWA, said only aggressive cuts to global emissions could begin to address the “losses and damages faced by vulnerable frontline communities”. He added: “In addition to the human tragedy on an unimaginable scale, the cost of recovery for this disaster is substantial. For a nation that’s done virtually nothing to contribute to this problem, it underlines the need to find fairness in helping climate vulnerable nations cope with the problems they have not unleashed.” • This article was amended on 17 September 2026. The original version miscalculated a conversion from cubic metres to cubic feet.

title: US lawmakers pass bill giving Trump more power to sanction Russia and its enablers
summary: Act divides Democrats and Republicans, with some saying it gives president power that could be turned against US allies
text: The US Congress has passed a sweeping bill allowing Donald Trump to raise tariffs on top buyers of Russian energy and issue other punishing sanctions against the Kremlin following a pitched battle between lawmakers backing Ukraine and sceptics worried the bill gives the president too much power. The Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 passed in a 262-159 vote on the last day before Congress goes on recess ahead of the midterm elections. Graham, who died earlier this year, co-authored and submitted the bill more than a year and a half ago. The long delay in the vote was widely considered to be scepticism from the Trump administration, which had opposed additional sanctions and then recently changed its stance to support tabling the bill as efforts to negotiate with the Kremlin to end the war have yielded few results. However the bill faced last-minute hurdles in Congress as members of the Republican party’s isolationist wing were joined by Democrats who warned that Trump could use the bill’s new tariffs authority against allies instead. The bill would mandate new sanctions on Russian political and military officials, and foreign networks helping to supply Russia’s war machine and evade existing sanctions. It would also target Russia’s so-called fleet of “shadow tankers”, which have allowed the country to continue to ship crude around the world despite sanctions on its energy exports. It would also allow Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100% on the top purchasers of Russian energy, including China, as well as other countries helping the Kremlin evade sanctions. Senior Democrats voiced opposition to the bill during a heated floor debate. “Why in the world would this Congress give this president additional authority to visit that kind of economic harm on the American people?” said Hakeem Jeffries, the leading Democrat in the House, during a speech on Wednesday, adding he would vote against the bill. Democratic staffers supporting the bill said that it offered a “last chance” to increase sanctions on Russia before Ukraine entered a “long winter”. Russia has improved the drone technology it has used to strike Ukrainian infrastructure as Kyiv has suffered a shortage of anti-air missiles, leaving the country in a dire position. Don Bacon, a Nebraska Republican supporting the bill, called it the US Congress’ “Churchill vs Chamberlain Moment on Russia”. “Choking off the money funding a war of conquest in Europe is exactly what that authority should be used for, and Congress deciding to do that is Congress doing its constitutional job,” he said, rejecting arguments by Democrats that the bill gave Trump too much authority to slap tariffs on foreign countries. The bill passed the Senate last month in a landslide 86-11 vote. However it faced more pushback in the House of Representatives. A Tuesday rule vote allowing consideration of Senate amendments to the bill passed by just 214-211, with two renegade Democrats joining Republicans to vote in favour of what they said was an act of support for Ukraine. That vote led to senior Democrats holding terse talks with their fellow party members. “I’m proud to represent one of the largest Ukrainian communities in America – people who have lost fathers, mothers, sons and daughters in the fight to defeat fascism,” wrote Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, one of the two Democrat representatives, in a statement on Tuesday. “I’ll always stand with my community’s values, and am grateful for the 86 senators who voted to send this bill to the House. My vote today gets us one step closer to enacting these sanctions into law and I look forward to voting tomorrow to cut off the flow of Russian oil money fuelling this war.” The Ukrainian government has said it supported the bill, and hundreds of pro-Ukrainian activists calling for tougher sanctions on Russia held advocacy talks in Washington DC in the days leading up to the vote. “We support any initiative that is in the interest of Ukraine and Ukrainians,” said Denys Sienik, the Chargé d’Affaires at the Ukrainian embassy in Washington DC. “So if we are talking about the possibility of putting more pressure on Russia so that it holds the Russian war machine, of course, we are there, and we are grateful to every senator, to every congressman and congresswoman for their voice and, and for their support.”

title: US government paid federal employees $9.5bn not to work amid Doge cuts – report
summary: GAO report shows how use paid administrative leave rose by 435% from 2023 to 2025 and incurred a sixfold cost
text: The US government paid federal workers $9.5bn not to work in 2025 as part of the Trump administration’s attempts to shrink the federal workforce. As part of efforts by the “department of government efficiency” (Doge), spearheaded by Elon Musk, federal agencies’ use of paid administrative leave rose 435% from 2023 to 2025 – costing six times what the government spent in 2023 – according to a new report released on Tuesday by the Government Accountability Office (GAO), an independent watchdog. Of the $9.5bn paid to federal workers, $6.7bn was associated with the deferred resignation program. “Paid administrative leave for federal employees is an excused absence without loss of pay or charge to leave. It is a cost to taxpayers as employees receive full pay without performing job duties,” the GAO said. It added: “The number of workdays of paid administrative leave reported increased from about 4m workdays and 4.4m workdays in calendar years 2023 and 2024, respectively, to about 21.6m workdays in 2025.” About 70% of the paid administrative leave used in 2025 was tied to the deferred resignation program, according to the GAO. Across the 76 agencies reviewed, 144,312 employees reported taking paid administrative leave under the program. Since January 2023, the Trump administration has reduced the federal US workforce by approximately 355,000 employees, leaving many struggling to find new jobs while others have been rehired after the administration determined that too many positions had been eliminated. Speaking to the Guardian, Douglas Pasternak, research director of Public Citizen’s Trump Accountability Project, described the federal overhaul efforts as “haphazard”. “There are multiple examples of how this was not thought out,” Pasternak said, adding: “It’s very clear that the Trump administration gave zero forethought to these cuts and to these deferred resignation programs. They haphazardly went out and cut federal workers, and now we’re dealing with the ripple effects of that.” He pointed to delays in social security check deliveries, longer wait times at Veterans Affairs hospitals for patients seeking critical medical and mental health care, and cuts to federal firefighters. Pasternak also cited reductions at the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, which has since sought to rehire personnel. “It’s a case study in mismanagement in how people went about this and it impacted everyone of all political stripes … To simply say we’re going to have fewer workers and therefore less costs is not the way to look at this. You need to look at it in a more sophisticated way, like what do those workers actually do? How do they improve the government? How do they actually help … provide critical resources for the American public?” Pasternak said. In response to the GAO report, Patty Murray, vice-chair of the Senate appropriations committee, released a statement condemning the federal layoffs, saying: “After promising to cut waste, Trump instead set billions upon billions in taxpayer dollars on fire to quite literally pay people not to do jobs they loved – from researching cancer cures to taking care of our national parks, and so much else. “Trump spent billions to push out experienced and badly needed experts across government – this was the most expensive way imaginable to make government worse,” Murray added.

title: Exiled Nicaraguan journalist Luis Galeano detained by ICE in Florida
summary: Galeano, who has had asylum application pending for about seven years, was pulled over by agents while driving for Lyft
text: Veteran journalist Luis Galeano, one of at least 94 Nicaraguans whom the Ortega Murillo regime has stripped of citizenship in recent years for opposing the government, has been detained by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). Galeano, who has continued critically reporting on the Sandinista government online through his platform, Café con voz, since shortly after arriving in the US in 2018, has had an asylum application pending for about seven years, according to his wife, Daykel Santamaría. He also has a work permit and a social security number, she said. Nonetheless, shortly after beginning his second job driving Lyft on Monday morning in Florida, ICE agents pulled him over. As of Wednesday, Galeano was detained at Krome detention center in Miami. He has an immigration court date scheduled for 2 October, Santamaría said. “Deporting [Galeano] to Nicaragua would be a death sentence,” said Javier Melendez, a sociologist who has been friends with the journalist for more than 30 years. The Sandinista government also stripped Melendez of his citizenship; he’s now a US citizen, living in Washington DC. The denaturalization order also affected the acclaimed novelist Sergio Ramírez and poet and writer Gioconda Belli. ICE has been contacted for comment. Melendez called the situation facing his friend “a double trauma – he escaped from his country because of his work and then the place where he sought refuge detains him due to their domestic politics”. Galeano fled Nicaragua in December, 2018, days after police raided 100% Noticias, the outlet where he worked, and issued an order for his arrest. He arrived in Miami shortly thereafter and petitioned for asylum, according to Santamaría. Santamaría said she didn’t know if her husband was, effectively, a man without a country due to the 2023 measure denaturalizing him as a Nicaraguan. Meanwhile, on Tuesday, the House foreign affairs committee had a two hour-plus hearing on “Confronting the Totalitarian Ortega-Murillo Regime.” María Elvira Salazar, a Florida representative and the committee chair, opened the hearing by denouncing how Daniel Ortega and Rosario Murillo “have spent years dismantling democracy”, and warned that “the Administration is paying attention, and Ortega and Murillo should consider themselves warned.” The disjunction between the US government locking up a journalist targeted by the Nicaraguan government for reporting on its totalitarian tendencies, while at the same time denouncing those same tendencies is an example of “the serious and profound contradictions” in the Trump administration when it comes to Nicaragua, said Ana María Méndez Dardón, the Central America director at the Washington Office on Latin America. Galeano’s detention is one example many of “how due process is missing from the right to asylum” under the Trump administration, she added. Salazar issued a statement after Galeano’s detention saying: “America must always know the difference between a criminal and a political exile.” Queries from the Guardian to the committee and several of its members were not answered. Galeano’s detention has also been denounced by Salazar’s GOP colleague in Florida, Representative Mario Díaz-Balart, who posted a statement on X saying: “The United States has long been a beacon of freedom for those persecuted by tyranny. We must uphold that tradition”. The Committee to Protect Journalists and the Inter American Press Association called for Galeano’s release. Although Galeano escaped Nicaragua under threat of arrest in late 2018, records of him being targeted for his reporting date at least as far back as 23 February 2011, when Amnesty International issued a bulletin titled “Urgent Action,” warning that his life was in danger after “an unknown individual called [him] on his mobile phone and said ‘You have 72 hours to change your mind about what you’ll publish, otherwise your family won’t see you anymore.’” The caller referred to Galeano’s reporting for El Nuevo Diario on government misuse of about $20m between 2004 and 2008. Recently, the journalist had been seeing ICE agents in the streets of Miami with increasing alarm while driving Lyft. “He called me like a week ago, asking if I could help with a new journalism project he had in mind, a morning news program on the region [of Latin America],” said Melendez, who founded Expediente Abierto, a thinktank on Central America. “He wanted to get off the streets, seeing the raids everywhere,” Melendez said. Santamaría, Galeano’s wife, said the two had spoken often about what would happen if one or the either was detained. Plans included calling their lawyer, alerting the media and trying to stay calm. “We prepared ourselves mentally for this moment,” she said. “We’ve already lived through going into exile, having an order of arrest – these are situations that make you more mature,” she said. Galeano spoke with his wife several times on Wednesday. She described him as calm, telling her: “If God got me out of Nicaragua, he’ll get me out of here.” She said she has faith the US government will see what she called “a very well-documented asylum case”.

title: US Federal Reserve raises interest rates for the first time since 2023
summary: Trump urges lower rates after central bank agrees increase by quarter-percentage point to range of 3.75% to 4%
text: The US Federal Reserve voted to raise interest rates on Wednesday for the first time since 2023 as the central bank continues to fight to tamp down inflation. The Fed’s open market committee voted unanimously to raise its benchmark interest rate by a quarter-percentage point to a range of 3.75% to 4%. This is the first time the Fed has raised rates since July 2023 and potentially sets Kevin Warsh, the current Fed chair, on a collision course with Donald Trump. “The plain fact is that inflation is too high and has been for too long,” Warsh said on Wednesday. “This summer’s inflation readings do not tell me that underlying trends have meaningfully improved.” After the announcement, Trump said in a Truth Social post that interest rates should be 1% or less and criticized the US trade deficit. Trump said the US would make “at least 1.5 Trillion Dollars a year” if it were to stop trading with countries with which it has a deficit. “We are ‘carrying’ almost every country in the World, and that cannot go on any longer. LOWER THE INTEREST RATES FOR THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA, AND FAST!,” Trump wrote. Though Warsh acknowledged changing geopolitics, he avoided calling out the US-Israel war with Iran by name. “There’s no hiding from hotspots around the world, and our judgment about what is the most likely or least likely of the geopolitical situation has changed,” he said. Warsh also declined to answer questions about how Trump would react but reiterated that Fed independence was “a two-way street”. “We will let people that do trade policy and fiscal policy stay in their lane. That is the way we can stand up here and call them the way we see them,” he said. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment. New projections showed a majority of officials penciled in another rate hike before the year’s end, with four officials predicting the Fed’s benchmark interest rate would reach a range of 4.25% to 4.5% by the end of the year. And though estimates on the country’s economic growth and unemployment rate were upbeat, Fed officials believed it would take roughly until 2029 for inflation to reach its 2% goal. At its last meeting in late July, the open market committee voted 9-3 to maintain rates, the first time in 10 years that so many members shared dissent on a policy decision. Since then, the US and Iran have renewed attacks against each other, driving up the Brent crude benchmark to its highest levels in month. The war has driven up inflation, especially energy prices. Gas prices have remained, on average, $1 a gallon more expensive compared with a year ago. Diesel fuel, which is used for buses, trains and trucks, recently reached an all-time high of $6.31. Concerns about inflation have induced a sell-off in the US bond market, with the yield on the 10-year treasury note hitting a 19-year high earlier this week, despite efforts from the US treasury to calm the market. Typically seen as one of the safest investment vehicles, trouble in the US bond market can lead to higher interest rates for consumer and business loans. The Fed uses interest rates as a tool to cool price increases by slowing activity. Higher interest rates impact mortgages, car payments, student debt and other types of loans. After inflation reached a generational high of 9.1% in June 2022, the Fed increased rates 11 times from 2022 and 2023. Rates were brought up to a target range of 5.25% to 5.5% before the Fed eventually started lowering rates in 2024 and 2025. At the beginning of the year, when the annualized inflation rate was 1% lower than current levels, a Fed rate hike seemed highly unlikely. A majority of Fed officials were actually predicting a rate cut before the end of the year. But inflation in August remained stubbornly high while unemployment was steady, which furthered the chances of a rate hike. Higher prices have painted a grim economic outlook as voters prepare to head to the polls in November. Recent data and surveys have shown heightened inflation has wiped out wage gains for Americans and dampened consumer outlook. In August, hourly earnings for employees decreased by 0.1% year-over-year after accounting for inflation and fell by 0.3% from the month prior. Consumer sentiment has also rapidly declined, according to a monthly survey from the University of Michigan, while expectations for more inflation have increased. Candidates on both sides of the political aisle have sought to make cost-of-living concerns and the economy a forefront of their campaigns, but voters are split on which party has the greatest advantage on this issue, according to recent Pew data. Meanwhile, Trump has implored Republican voters to pretend as if they are voting for him on their midterm ballot and promised every American a $5,000 “Trump dividend” if Republicans retain control of Congress. Critics have likened the move to bribery and warned of the financial implications, especially after the US government debt reached a record-high $40tn last month.
