title: Suspect in ‘Putney pusher’ case found dead at his west London home
summary: HSBC director Nicholas Brandram, 44, was found unresponsive by emergency services on Tuesday evening
text: A senior city banker suspected of pushing a woman into the path of a moving bus in the “Putney pusher” case has been found dead. Nicholas Brandram, 44, was discovered at his home in Chiswick, west London, on Tuesday. He was arrested in June by the Metropolitan police in connection with a 2017 incident in which a jogger running across Putney Bridge pushed a woman towards an oncoming bus. She only avoided serious injury after the driver swerved around her at the last moment. Brandram was a director at HSBC and had previously served in the military, reaching the rank of captain. He was released on bail by detectives in June after being arrested on suspicion of attempted grievous bodily harm. In September, after answering bail, he was re-bailed with no conditions. Video footage showed the woman being pushed by a male jogger. She fell into the road, with the jogger running on. The Met wound down its investigation in 2018, after interviewing 50 men and arresting three suspects. The case, which attracted considerable attention, was unsolved. In a statement on Wednesday, the Met said: “At 19.12 on Tuesday, 15 September officers and the London ambulance service attended an address in Chiswick, Hounslow after a man was found unresponsive inside a property. “Sadly, a 44-year-old man was pronounced dead at the scene. His next of kin have been informed. “At this time his death is being treated as unexpected, but is not believed to be suspicious. “A file will be prepared for the coroner in due course.” Brandram was the grandson of Princess Katherine of Greece, who was the great-granddaughter of Queen Victoria, the Daily Telegraph reported in 2013 when he was convicted of crashing his Harley-Davidson motorbike into a female cyclist around Hyde Park Corner, before driving off without leaving his details. In an interview with the Citywealth website in March this year, Brandram said he was a senior relationship manager at HSBC Private Bank. He said: “I usually bicycle into our office in Mayfair from my home in west London. And then from there, can either stay at my desk, go to Canary Wharf or the City, or get on a train or go to the airport. My first meeting is ideally over breakfast and I’m ideally home for bath time. I’m a co-parenting single father with a three-year-old.” Brandram said his proudest professional achievement was being invited to a Buckingham Palace garden party after military service in Afghanistan, and that the person he most admired was his mother. “She raised three children as a single parent and is the busiest person I know,” he said. “I’ve never met someone with greater moral integrity and courage, as well as resilience and stamina.”

title: Body found in search for three-year-old Noah Woods
summary: Body found in pond in Suffolk village of Brantham, where Noah was last seen on Tuesday afternoon
text: Police searching for a three-year-old boy who went missing from a playground on the Suffolk-Essex border have found a body. Noah Woods was last seen at 3pm on Tuesday in Merriam Close, Brantham, near Manningtree, before becoming separated from a relative. The body was found in Decoy Pond in the village. In a statement, Supt Tom Pearse, from Suffolk constabulary, said: “Police and fire teams this afternoon sadly recovered the body of a child from Decoy Pond in Brantham. “Formal identification has yet to take place, but the family of Noah Woods have been informed of this development. The discovery of the body is currently being treated as not suspicious, but unexplained. “The coroner will be informed of this development. Since Noah was reported as missing, officers have carried out multiple inquiries, including the deployment of special search officers and dog units, and received support from various agencies, including helicopters from the National Police Air Service and HM Coastguard. “Additional assistance on the ground has been provided by HM Coastguard, Suffolk Fire and Rescue Service, Suffolk Lowland Search and Rescue and over 1,300 members of the public supporting the search. “First and foremost, our thoughts are with Noah’s family and all those who know them. Since Noah was reported missing, vast numbers of our officers and staff have been deployed in numerous functions in the search for Noah, and the support for his family. “We have been overwhelmed by the outpouring of public support and people putting on their boots to help us with the search. “As a parent myself, I completely understand why people would want to help, and such a response is one that typifies the strong sense of community and the heartwarming nature of Suffolk people that make the county such a special place. “I’m sure you appreciate that the family now need time, space and privacy, and I thank you for your understanding of this.” Earlier in the search, officers from Suffolk constabulary said Noah, who was autistic and non-verbal with partial hearing loss, was reported to have run down an alley near a playground towards a housing estate. Searches of Decoy Pond started earlier on Wednesday after it was cordoned off by police tape. A massive search operation had been under way in and around the village since Noah’s disappearance, supported by hundreds of volunteers. Volunteers wept in a garden area at Brantham Leisure Centre as Pearse updated them. “You will have heard the news,” he said. “First and foremost our thoughts are with Noah’s family and all those who knew him.” He said that the agencies involved in the search, and Noah’s family, “have been overwhelmed by the outpouring of public support, people putting on their boots and helping us with the search and that, ladies and gentlemen, is yourselves”. The officer’s voice cracked with emotion at times as he addressed the crowd of volunteers. Noah went missing after a visit to a play area where he became separated from a relative. Police had said Noah would not respond to his name if called. Earlier on Wednesday, Pearse said there was no indication anything sinister had happened. Volunteers could be seen in hi-vis jackets helping to search the area, with efforts being coordinated from the village hall and a leisure centre. Police, fire, coastguard and search and rescue teams, with sniffer dogs and a helicopter, were all deployed. As well as the ground search, officers scoured CCTV and other available video footage, going door to door and carrying out aerial and thermal imaging searches. Earlier, Noah’s father posted on social media asking volunteers to widen their search beyond the village where possible. He wrote: “I cannot go another night knowing he’s out there alone, please don’t give up on him guys. He is out there somewhere and I appreciate every single one of you.”

title: Don’t back down on pledge to put water firms under public control, Burnham told
summary: Key allies of PM issue warning as details emerge of his plan to give mayors powers to oversee water companies
text: Key allies of Andy Burnham have warned the prime minister not to back down over his promises to put water companies under public control, after details emerged about the prime minister’s plan to give mayors more oversight of the industry. Mathew Lawrence and Mark McVitie, who helped provide an intellectual underpinning to Burnham’s project over the summer, have both warned that merely giving politicians oversight of key utilities rather than financial control will fall short of what the prime minister promised. Their comments come after it emerged the prime minister is considering creating a set of regional bodies to hold water companies in England and Wales to greater account, including by questioning bosses on bills and sewage spills. Lawrence and McVitie warned this would not be enough to deliver Burnham’s promise of bringing “the essentials of life” under public control. Lawrence, the director of the Common Wealth thinktank, said: “Putting mayors in charge of water services is a successful model the world over. But the critical question is, will public oversight without ownership provide meaningful control over privatised companies or not? “Can they ban dividend payments, stop financial extraction, reduce the cost of capital that determines overall cost, or choose to take the service back into public hands to run for the public benefit? If the answer is no, devolving oversight risks handing over responsibility without the power to fix the problem.” McVitie, the former director of the Labour Growth Group, said: “Local leaders having real power over water investment would be a positive step. But public control has to mean more than public scrutiny. “The question is whether the public interest can actually be enforced in the face of the interests of monopoly operators. A functioning system needs to raise the required investment at a reasonable cost, prevent financial extraction when services fail, and ensure that operators which are no longer viable can be restructured.” He added: “Regional boards may improve planning, but unless the financial model is made to work for the British people, rather than the other way round, we risk giving local leaders more responsibility for a system they don’t have the power to fundamentally change.” Burnham plans to release a “10-year plan” for Britain in November, part of which will spell out how he intends to bring utilities such as water and energy companies under public control. Under plans first reported on Tuesday by the Telegraph, Burnham is understood to be considering creating nine regional bodies, roughly matching the geography of the biggest water companies in England and Wales. They will be tasked with setting company objectives and holding bosses to account over bills, shortages and sewage discharges. The boards are likely to engage with customers and run public consultations, but it remains unclear whether they will be given financial control over the companies. Government sources described the reports as “speculation”, and added that there would be more details in the 10-year plan. In the shorter term, the prime minister faces a decision over what to do about the financially stricken Thames Water, which is the subject of a bailout bid by its creditors. At the end of March the regulated value of Thames’s assets was estimated at £23bn, while its net debt increased to £18.5bn. Burnham said during his campaign to become an MP he would nationalise Thames, but doing so could cost several billions of pounds. The Guardian recently revealed Burnham is considering changing the law to take the company into special administration, which could be the first step to nationalisation. In the meantime, customer dissatisfaction with the water industry has continued to grow. The number of complaints made by households about water companies is up 48% year on year, according to the Consumer Council for Water, the steepest annual rise in two decades. Mike Keil, the CCW chief executive, said the numbers reflected “just how dissatisfied many people still are with the state of the water sector and the enormous task water companies face in rebuilding consumer trust”. A government spokesperson said: “Our water industry has not been working for people for far too long. We’re bringing in tougher regulation, stronger enforcement and greater accountability, so water companies deliver for customers and the environment.”

title: Amazon raises starting pay to $20 an hour and adds Whole Foods discount
summary: Wage increase brings Amazon’s US minimum pay in line with Costco and includes new grocery discount benefit
text: Amazon has raised its minimum wage in the US to $20 an hour, with average pay at the company reaching $24 an hour, according to the company. The pay increase represents a $1 increase from its starting level. The company is also expanding employee benefits to grocery discounts, with an uncapped 10% off eligible fresh groceries and everyday essentials on Amazon.com and Whole Foods Market Online, plus 20% off in-store at Whole Foods. The wage increase brings Amazon’s minimum pay in line with Costco, which raised its lowest starting pay to $20 an hour in 2025, with pay for most workers raised to more than $30 an hour. Both retailers have starting pay higher than most competitors. At Target, the starting wage remains $15 an hour, and $14 an hour at Walmart. Amazon has about 1.1 million employees in the US, the second largest private employer behind Walmart. The company has also cited the creation of 390,000 Amazon delivery service provider jobs, which are operated by contractors. “We talk a lot about continuous improvement at Amazon – about always wanting to get better, even when things are going well,” wrote Udit Madan, senior vice-president of worldwide operations at Amazon, in a blogpost announcing the pay increase. “I’m excited about how these investments work together to help our employees and their families continue to thrive for the long run.”

title: Fears collapse of trial could discourage reporting of assaults in UK armed forces
summary: Family of Jaysley Beck, 19, voice concern after two officers acquitted over handling of sexual assault before she killed herself
text: The family of a teenage soldier who killed herself after she was sexually assaulted fear the collapse of the trial of two officers accused of failing to investigate her case properly could discourage other young members of the armed forces from reporting attacks. Relatives of Gunner Jaysley Beck, 19, said it felt like the end of a “long and sad” journey and expressed concern that during the trial a military witness described the assault as not being out of the ordinary. Col Samantha Shepherd and Maj James Hook had faced a court martial for how they responded to the assault carried out on Beck by a superior while on a training exercise. The prosecution had alleged Shepherd had lied when she reported Beck’s allegations, deliberately playing them down so they would not be investigated by military police. Prosecutors also said Hook had not taken the teenager’s complaints seriously and had thought she might be making the allegations up so she could leave the exercise. However, on day three of the trial, the military board hearing the case was ordered to return not guilty pleas against Shepherd and Hook, both of whom had denied “conduct prejudicial to good order and service discipline”. In a statement, Beck’s family said it respected the decision and recognised that the two defendants had been acquitted. They went on: “Nothing was ever going to bring Jaysley back. But today marks the end of a long and very sad journey for Jaysley and for our family.” The family pointed out that a coroner had flagged what he saw as a string of serious failings in how Beck’s case was handled. They said: “Those failings contributed to her death. Those findings still stand. Despite the outcome of these court martial proceedings, it remains true to say that the army let our daughter down very badly. “Even during this trial, the court heard evidence that senior soldiers making passes at junior colleagues was not at all unusual – what does that tell you about the culture? “The experiences of our daughter in the British army – and the outcome today – do not fill us with optimism that young women being preyed upon by their seniors will feel confident coming forward.” Beck’s family drew particular attention to Hook’s reaction. They said: “It continues to cause us enormous pain to know that one of the first people who Jaysley spoke to just thought she was making up a serious allegation to get out of exercise. We can never forgive that.” The prosecution had claimed in its opening on Tuesday that the two officers had “let down” Beck, who was found dead at barracks in Wiltshire in December 2021, five months after the attack on her. However, on Wednesday the prosecution asked the court martial in Catterick, North Yorkshire, to halt the case against Shepherd after the evidence of a key witness, another officer the colonel had reported the Beck case to, did not support the allegation she lied. The assistant judge advocate general Edward Legard subsequently ruled there was no case to answer as far as Hook was concerned. He said: “The evidence in this case is inconsistent, vague and tenuous.” Derek Johashen, for Shepherd, said: “Col Shepherd remains absolutely devastated about Gunner Beck’s passing. She believed Gunner Beck, took her complaint seriously, listened to her and cared.” The defence secretary, Wes Streeting, said significant changes had been introduced since Beck’s death but there was more to do. “I will continue to drive the changes needed to ensure every voice is heard,” he added. Brig Melissa Emmett, the head of the army personnel services group, said: “We are determined to build a culture founded on respect, trust and accountability.” Last year, Michael Webber, a former sergeant major, was jailed for six months for attacking Beck, who was from Cumbria. • In the UK and Ireland, Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org. In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found at befrienders.org

title: More Republicans are turning on Iran war as midterms come into view
summary: Three more GOP members voted for war powers resolution to force withdrawal from the conflict as election looms
text: As the US war with Iran drags on, the ranks of Republicans signaling the conflict is a liability for their party continues to grow. When the House of Representatives on Tuesday evening considered its sixth war powers resolution intended to force Donald Trump to withdraw troops from the conflict, three Republicans who had not supported the previous efforts broke with their party to vote this one to passage. Earlier that day, a Republican who had lost his primary after repeatedly clashing with Trump proposed impeaching the US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, alleging a variety of constitutional transgressions including prosecuting the war against Iran without congressional authorization. The rebellions in the GOP are thus far mostly symbolic – Trump has ignored the sole war powers resolution to make it through both the House and Senate, and the prospects of Hegseth’s impeachment are unclear. But they underscore the growing nerves among both the party’s most vulnerable and most disobedient lawmakers over continuing a conflict that appears to have accomplished little other than play into the hands of Democrats, who have spent the entirety of Trump’s second term arguing that only they can be trusted to lower costs for Americans. “I said it in March: the mission had to stay focused and limited, because Americans do not want another forever war. I will not vote to keep our soldiers in an open-ended war, with Iowans paying too much at the pump,” said the congresswoman Mariannette Miller-Meeks, one of the trio of Republicans who for the first time supported a war powers resolution. She was joined by another Iowa Republican, Zach Nunn, who justified his vote by noting his state “has already paid a devastating price” in the conflict, with two Iowans among the US soldiers killed by Iranian attacks as the war began. “Congress owes them, their families, and every American in uniform clear objectives and constitutional oversight. With the negotiating window closed, sustained combat operations now require congressional authorization,” the congressman said. “Having deployed multiple times and flown over 700 combat hours in the Middle East, I will not support another open-ended war. We can defend Americans, pressure Iran and pursue peace while ensuring Congress fulfills its constitutional responsibility.” Since the US joined Israel in attacking Iran at the end of February, Democrats have wielded war powers resolutions as a cudgel to get Republicans on the record about a conflict that polls indicate is not popular with the public. Their first three attempts failed, but in June, the fourth passed with the votes of two libertarian-minded Republicans – Thomas Massie of Kentucky and Warren Davidson of Ohio – along with Tom Barrett of Michigan and Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania, both of whom occupy battlefield districts. The Senate later approved that measure, but Trump refused to abide by it. In July, the same lineup in the House passed a fifth war powers resolution, before Nunn, Miller-Meeks and Nancy Mace of South Carolina expanded the ranks of Republican objectors to seven in Tuesday’s vote. The two Iowans are among the Republicans considered most at risk of losing re-election in the November midterms, with Miller-Meeks having won her race two years ago by fewer than 800 votes. They also represent areas of a state where the market impacts of the war with Iran are pronounced, as Iowa farmers struggle with higher prices for diesel, gasoline and fertilizer, all of which have been compounded by Trump’s tariff regime. Iowa has drifted consistently to the right over the past decade, but this year, Democrats believe the circumstances are right for them to oust not just Miller-Meeks and Nunn, but also to win a Senate seat, the governor’s mansion and potentially more congressional districts in the state. It’s far from the only state where Democrats are on the offensive. The House vote took place on the same day the New York Times and Siena University released polling that showed likely voters preferred Democrats over Republicans for Congress by nearly nine percentage point, a finding that lines up with other surveys. Democrats are helped in their quest to retake the House by the fact that Republicans control it with a tiny majority that may be exceedingly hard to defend in November, and has also enabled Republicans like Massie to seize on splits within the party to embarrass Trump and his ally the House speaker, Mike Johnson. Last year, Massie banded together with Democrats and a handful of Republican dissidents to force passage of a bill requiring the release of files related to the disgraced financier and former Trump associate Jeffrey Epstein. That intensified the president’s ire towards him, and Massie lost his primary to the Trump-endorsed Republican Ed Gallrein earlier this year. Now with even less to lose, the congressman appears to be trying to seize on splits within the House GOP to retaliate against Hegseth, who campaigned for Gallrein. Massie proposed the resolution on Tuesday, and House rules appear to require it be voted on by Thursday. The chamber was scheduled to be in session that day for the last time before the 3 November midterm elections, but on Wednesday morning, House Republican leaders canceled votes scheduled for Thursday, sending lawmakers home early to face their constituents.

title: No matter how deranged and delusional your podcast is, Liz Truss can go further | John Crace
summary: In the Trusster’s latest appearance, she says Blair and Brown had a plot to dismantle civilisation and the Tories were part of the woke establishment
text: Some things you can set your watch by. Like every time small boats are in the news, the shadow home secretary, Chris Philp, will manoeuvre himself in front of a camera to suggest that all male migrants are either murderers or rapists. Probably both. But some things feel older than time itself. Like Liz Truss trying to persuade the world she was right all along. Most former prime ministers leave Downing Street relatively quietly. Lord Big Dave, the Maybot and even Boris nurse their grudges in private. Rishi lives in semi-retirement – almost a recluse – and only attends parliament when it suits him. Keir has been almost totally airbrushed out of history in a couple of months. Liz, though, is the outlier. She refuses to give up. The last cockroach alive after a nuclear apocalypse. Even now, she probably has a platoon of nuns locked up in her basement in south-east London where they are being forced to embroider a 70-metre tapestry dedicated to a revisionist history of her 49 days in office. One in which an old monarch dies and a new king ascends the throne. As one Elizabethan era ends so another Elizabethan era begins and a grateful nation bows down to her genius. You have to wonder if this obsession is healthy. Most normal people might be slightly embarrassed to be remembered as the UK’s shortest serving prime minister. And by far and away the dimmest in living memory. But Truss seems devoid of affect. No sense of shame. If anything she seems proud of her 49 days. That long! In Liz’s mind, she was simply too good for us. We weren’t ready for her. Give it a thousand years and her tapestry will be on show in the British Museum. One thing you can guarantee: offer Liz a platform to speak and she will bite your hand off. No matter how deranged and delusional it may be, Liz is confident she can be yet more deranged and delusional. She is every rightwinger’s favourite guest. Not only is she guaranteed to say yes, she will also make everyone else seem almost normal. Win-win. She’s done all sorts of weird stuff in the US, and in the UK she has her own podcast where she pretends to be interested in someone other than herself on Mike Graham’s YouTube channel. Graham, you might remember, is the man who thinks you can grow concrete. And Liz is sure he’s right. The new kid on the podcast block is the former Tory Brexiter Steve Baker. So who else would he get as his first guest than the Trusster. If anything, Steve has got even more weird in the two years since he lost his seat. These days he has the look of a far-right survivalist holed up in a hut somewhere in the Montana wilderness. And his podcast surroundings have the same feel. All very basic, just a table and chairs. The table probably has a cache of semi-automatic rifles underneath it. Every so often, Steve will interrupt the recording to do an ad for gold. He no longer trusts traditional currencies. And up steps Liz. Doing what only someone as half-witted as she can: talking non-stop nonsense. Often with a weird half-smile on her face. At times you are tempted to believe that she is in on the joke that she is the joke. But then you realise she’s deadly serious. She hasn’t quite understood that people aren’t laughing with her, they are laughing at her. There’s something almost unbearably sad about this. So much so you almost feel guilty for indulging her insanity. Then you remember that only 2,000 people are going to watch this. And only we dedicated few are going to make it to the end. Labour has ruined the country, she says. Tony Blair and Gordon Brown had a secret plot to dismantle British civilisation and nothing has been the same since 1997. At which point, even Steve has to remind Liz that the Tories were in power from 2010. The Trusster doesn’t miss a beat. She is rushing on her run, her onboard computer set to auto-pilot. The Tories weren’t really the Tories. They were socialists in disguise. All of them. They were all part of the woke establishment. That’s why they were anti-Brexit. And austerity never happened. At this point it would have been a kindness to wrap the podcast up. To remind Liz that antipsychotic help was available. Because to the best of my knowledge, Liz had been a minister in successive Tory governments since 2012. She had also been a vocal supporter of Remain. Only it turns out that was a different Liz. A doppelganger. She had been temporarily captured by the wokerati and made to do and say a lot of things against her will. It was only when she became prime minister that she could self-actualise into her truest state and then she was thwarted by the Bank of England getting tough on quantitative easing. All a deliberate plot to destabilise her mini-budget. Nothing to do with the mini-budget being riddled with unfunded tax cuts. There were only two trustworthy people left in the world, she said: Donald Trump and Javier Milei. It was time to disband the judiciary, the prisons and the civil service. The whole world order needed to be rebalanced. Steve readily agreed. He reckoned the NHS should also be included on the grounds that it had almost killed him and a friend of his. Not even Liz was going that far. But together the revolution was possible. Then the big question. What next for Liz? Would she stand for election again? Maybe, she said. But who for? She’s long since been too mad for the Tories and might even be too bonkers for Reform. All she knew was that she would never go away. Not while there were still things to talk about that no one was talking about except her. Poor Liz. The problem isn’t that no one is talking. It’s that no one is listening. Steve chucked her a nugget of gold and they both ran for the hills. You’ll never take them alive.

title: House speaker calls early recess before midterms amid AI regulation frenzy
summary: Mike Johnson cancels votes on Thursday, meaning House members will avoid voting on impeaching Pete Hegseth
text: The Republican speaker of the House, Mike Johnson, announced on Wednesday that he would again cancel votes scheduled for Thursday, sending lawmakers home one day early ahead of the midterm election recess. The latest change to the legislative schedule means House members will avoid voting on Republican Thomas Massie’s resolution to impeach the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, and comes amid a frenzied attempt to propose legislation on artificial intelligence. It’s the latest round of cancellations at the hands of Johnson, who had already cut the pre-election session short by two weeks. Democrats have reacted angrily, encouraging Johnson to keep lawmakers on Capitol Hill before the midterm recess beginning on Friday. “I think it shows the cowardice of the Republican party. They are canceling votes to do business for the American people because they are afraid that that impeachment resolution of Pete Hegseth would pass on a bipartisan basis,” the Democratic representative Pramila Jayapal told MediasTouch. Lawmakers also hoped to address regulating AI development after industry executives and whistleblowers expressed a dire need for oversight. Johnson, however, has been reluctant to intervene – aligning himself with Donald Trump. “We ⁠cannot have a moratorium on the development of AI,” Johnson told reporters on Tuesday. “Because then we will lose our edge to China, and that has serious national security implications for every American family.” More than 100 House Democrats had urged Johnson, via a letter, to cancel the upcoming recess to allow them to craft legislation on AI safeguards. In a notice on Wednesday, House leadership told members that other votes on EPA regulations, originally planned for Thursday, would instead take place on Wednesday afternoon. A spokesperson for Johnson characterized the House speaker’s latest move as simply moving up scheduled votes, not canceling future votes. Speaking to reporters outside of his office on Wednesday, Johnson said he was modifying the schedule because “the House has done its work”. Johnson said he wanted members to return to their districts to spend time with constituents ahead of the election. “You’ve seen the statistics we’ve been talking about for the last few days. This House has been the second most productive in terms of legislation in the history of the institution since 1789,” Johnson said, repeating a claim he also made earlier this month at the Republican midterm convention. However, so far, the current session has fallen short of passing legislation to surpass the two previous House sessions, according to the fact-checking website Snopes. Johnson also addressed Massie’s impeachment resolution, calling it “a publicity stunt by someone who wants attention”. The House speaker insisted it would be “immediately” postponed and he would not address it before the recess because the US is in the middle of international conflicts. Lawmakers will likely face a busy legislative agenda when they return to Capitol Hill after election day in November. Among their priorities will be addressing Massie’s resolution on impeaching Hegseth because it was filed as privileged, which fast-tracks the resolution.

title: US judge blocks DHS from threatening prosecution against man who criticized ICE
summary: David Streever was issued a ‘warning notice’ after sending an email critical of ICE to the agency’s director in January
text: The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) may no longer issue a “warning notice” – threatening prosecution against a US citizen – for criticizing Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), a federal judge in Washington DC ruled on Tuesday. Judge Rudolph Contreras sided with David Streever, a New York man who accused DHS officials of violating his first amendment rights when they showed up first at his home in June with a “warning notice”, claiming he made a threat against former ICE director Todd Lyons, and then to a hotel where Streever and his young daughter were staying. The notice and visits were in response to an email Streever sent Lyons in January, after federal agents fatally shot two US citizens amid an immigration crackdown in Minnesota. In the email, Streever called Lyons a “monstrous human being”, compared him to Nazi and warned him that his own conscience would “eat himself alive”. Contreras ruled the notice “practically shouts that Mr Streever may be prosecuted if he continues to engage in his political speech”. “Americans have long voiced their displeasure with their government. The Declaration of Independence itself is a list of grievances between Americans and the British government. And Americans have not always indulged in the elevated prose of the Declaration. Government officials have long endured ‘vehement, caustic and sometimes unpleasantly sharp attacks.’ Today is no different,” Contreras wrote. The court order is limited in that it prohibits the DHS, its secretary, Markwayne Mullin, or ICE from issuing another “warning notice”, making similar threats or pursuing prosecution for his speech while Streever’s case continues in court. A DHS spokesperson said in a statement to the Guardian: “Any allegation DHS and its components are attempting to ‘squash’ free speech is categorically FALSE. ICE investigates all credible threats towards its employees and officers, including threats to the ICE Director.” DHS law enforcement officers are “experiencing coordinated campaigns of violence against them”, including large increases in assaults, vehicular attacks and death threats, the spokesperson said. “Anyone who assaults or threatens our law enforcement officers will face the consequences,” they added. The Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression (Fire), a non-profit first amendment advocacy group, represented Streever in his lawsuit. “I’m deeply relieved that the court affirmed what I knew all along: that I am permitted to speak my conscience in the United States of America, including when I criticize government officials,” Streever said in a statement. Streever added: “While I wish this ordeal hadn’t happened, hopefully this incident will serve as a reminder that the first amendment protects us all.” The DHS previously defended its investigation into Streever by tying his email into a larger trend of threats made against law enforcement officials – particularly those enforcing the Trump administration’s anti-immigration agenda. Immigration enforcement officials have consistently justified federal agents’ aggressive actions by claiming they are protecting immigration enforcement officers. Contreras said his ruling allows DHS officials to investigate future conduct to ensure the safety of law enforcement and public officials, so long as it does not infringe on Streever’s protected speech.

title: Suffolk police release footage of Noah Woods as search for missing boy continues
summary: Hundreds of volunteers join hunt for three-year-old who went missing on Tuesday afternoon
text: A massive search operation is under way in and around a Suffolk village for a missing three-year-old boy with autism, supported by hundreds of volunteers. Suffolk police have said the hunt for Noah Woods remains a missing persons investigation with no indication anything sinister has happened. Noah, who is autistic, non-verbal and partially deaf, went missing after a visit to a play area in the village of Brantham on Tuesday afternoon when he became separated from a relative. Police have said Noah will not respond to his name if called. In an update on Wednesday, Supt Tom Pearse from Suffolk police said: “This is being treated as a missing person investigation at this stage and there is nothing to indicate anything sinister or any element of criminality has taken place although we keep an open mind as to the circumstances.” The force released new CCTV stills and footage of the little boy in the play area in Merriam Close just before he vanished. It is thought that he ran down an alleyway beside the playground towards a nearby new-build housing estate. The surrounding area includes woods and a pond and is near the River Stour and a railway. Noah is white with curly ginger hair and was wearing a white T-shirt featuring the TV character Bluey, shorts, and black Vans trainers with a white stripe. On Wednesday, volunteers could be seen in hi-vis jackets helping to search the area, with efforts being coordinated from the village hall and a leisure centre. They are part of a massive search operation led by police, fire, coastguard and search and rescue teams, with sniffer dogs being used and a helicopter flying overhead. As well as the ground search, officers are looking at CCTV and other available video footage, going door to door and carrying out aerial and thermal imaging searches. Noah’s father posted on social media asking volunteers to widen their search beyond the village where possible. He wrote: “I cannot go another night knowing he’s out there alone, please don’t give up on him guys. He is out there somewhere and I appreciate every single one of you.” In the update from police on Wednesday, Pearse urged volunteers to report to the coordination centre and to avoid the railway and open water, which need specialist searching. He said: “It has now been around 24 hours since Noah was reported as missing to us and we are doing everything we can to find him. “We are extremely grateful for the support shown by the public. If you are helping please report into the coordination centre to ensure the search continues to be done in a systematic and coordinated fashion. “This will ensure we can carefully plan and take account of people supporting the search. “We politely ask people to avoid open waters and railways – these are areas that require specialist and professional expertise. We also ask that personal drones are not used as these can interfere with specialist search equipment. “There may also be times when officers may need to restrict access to certain areas or move away from search locations. “Please do not be offended if this happens; it is necessary to allow us to carry out our inquiries and search activity as effectively as possible.” Later on Wednesday, the far-right activist Daniel Thomas, known as Danny Tommo, appealed for his social media followers to join search efforts to find Noah. The founder of Patriot Platform – the extremist group behind masked anti-migrant protests in Dover and Portsmouth this month – posted a video of himself in a car and said “we are on our way”. Louise Madley, the manager of Brantham Leisure Centre, who has been helping to coordinate volunteers, said: “We welcome any extra volunteers, probably from tomorrow now.” She said registration of volunteers would probably stop at about 5.30pm. She said that on Tuesday night there were “a lot of people on the streets that hindered the police search and search and rescue, and it’s just safety as well of everyone involved – around this area it can be quite precarious”. Advice from Brantham parish council to volunteers included: “You are looking for a frightened three-year-old. Think about slight movements in your peripheral [vision], high and low, tiny small spaces use all your senses whilst searching.” They have been told not to grab or approach Noah if they find him, but instead to call police on 999 immediately and give their exact location using the What3Words app. Anyone with private CCTV or doorbell cameras in the village, or who was driving through the area with a dashcam is asked to review the footage from 3pm on Tuesday afternoon onwards for any possible sightings of Noah.

title: At least 21 killed after Israeli-hit building in Gaza City collapses
summary: Rescue workers say search for dozens of people hampered by lack of heavy machinery
text: A building housing about 100 displaced Palestinian families has collapsed in Gaza City, killing at least 21 people in their sleep, including 11 children, forcing rescuers to dig through the rubble with their bare hands as they search for dozens of people believed to be trapped. A rescue team from Gaza’s civil defence said they had recovered the bodies of five children among the victims, while 25 injured people were taken to hospital. Medical sources said rescuers could hear the voices of people trapped beneath the rubble as they tried to reach them. The bombed-out multistorey building, which contained four apartments on each floor, had previously been hit by Israeli strikes during the war, leaving its structure badly weakened and at risk of collapse. When it gave way on Wednesday, it fell on to tents beside it housing displaced families, witnesses said. The collapse highlights the continuing danger facing tens of thousands of Palestinians living in an estimated 2,000 buildings damaged by Israeli airstrikes across Gaza. Mohammed Abu Dan, a superviser with the civil defence team recovering victims, said more than 10 families had been living in the building and displaced people had been forced to stay there because no other shelter was available. “Search and rescue operations are being carried out under extremely difficult conditions due to a lack of the necessary equipment and resources,” he said. Palestinian and UN officials have blamed Israeli restrictions on Gaza for the lack of heavy machinery in the territory. Israel says its restrictions are intended to prevent equipment from reaching militant groups. A video obtained by Reuters showed rescue workers trying to pull two people from beneath a collapsed wall. Another video circulating on social media showed Gaza’s civil defence spokesperson, Mahmoud Basal, carrying a young girl wrapped in a bloodstained scarf. Raed al-Dahshan, the director of Gaza City’s civil defence service, said: “We are still hearing voices from under the rubble, so there is still hope to find people.” Alessandro Mrakic, the head of the UN Development Programme’s Gaza office, said rescuers from UN agencies were taking part in the operation, which he described as extremely difficult because of the lack of appropriate machinery. Egypt’s relief agency was also involved. “There are actually people that are digging with their bare hands. We need to prepare [for more deaths],” Mrakic said. Tents belonging to displaced families had been erected along the road beside the building because there was nowhere else for them to shelter. Similar incidents have occurred repeatedly over the past two years, with dozens of homes and buildings damaged during the war later collapsing, trapping people and causing further deaths and injuries. With few other options, many Palestinians have returned to partly destroyed homes or moved into abandoned buildings, clearing small spaces among the rubble despite the danger. Soaring rents and the cost of vacant land have made finding safer accommodation increasingly difficult. Hundreds of thousands of displaced Palestinians also remain unable to return to neighbourhoods near the so-called yellow line, forcing families to find whatever space they can elsewhere. In May, the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, ordered the military to seize 70% of Gaza. Damaged roofs, walls and supporting columns can collapse without warning, particularly during strong winds, heavy rain or further bombardment. Asked whether they feared for themselves and their children, people living there said: “Yes, we are afraid, but where can we go? This is better than staying out on the street.” Israeli strikes on Gaza have continued despite the ceasefire. According to Gaza’s health ministry, 1,369 Palestinians have been killed and 4,627 wounded since the fragile ceasefire took effect on 11 October 2025. This year, an independent UN inquiry found Israel had continued to commit genocide by deliberately targeting Palestinian children in Gaza. Separately, a video from the Sheikh Radwan neighbourhood of Gaza City showed the aftermath of an Israeli drone strike that killed Mohammed al-Zinati, 15, and wounded several other people. Al-Zinati had been trying to recover the body of a man killed in an earlier strike. Israel’s defence minister, Israel Katz, said on Wednesday that it was only a matter of time before Israel resumed full-scale war in Gaza and moved to force out its Palestinian population. Katz, responding to criticism from another rightwing politician before the 27 October elections, said 70% of Gaza had already been emptied of its population during Israel’s offensive launched after the Hamas-led attacks of 7 October 2023 that killed more than 1,200 people, the deadliest attack against Israel, according to official Israeli figures. He added that the Israel Defense Forces were prepared “to finish the job so that we can also implement the migration plan”. Since the war began, at least 73,783 Palestinians have been killed and 174,738 wounded, according to the health ministry.

title: Labour holds No 10 drinks party for donors amid growing calls for donations cap
summary: Labour has also increased fundraising from members in response to Reform’s £72m donations from crypto billionaires
text: Labour has hosted major party donors at No 10 for a drinks reception, as the party comes under growing pressure from MPs and unions to consider a donations cap. The Guardian understands that high-level donors, including business leaders and philanthropists, were hosted by cabinet ministers in Downing Street for an evening reception on Tuesday. Donors from the party’s Rose Network give thousands of pounds a year to the party. Andy Burnham is under increased pressure from MPs to consider new restrictions for domestic donors after Reform UK received £72m from two cryptobillionaires, Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne, over the course of 48 hours. A Labour source said the donors event had been organised in advance of the Reform donations news. Over the weekend, Labour also stepped up fundraising from members, directly in response to the donations. The party’s chair, Bridget Phillipson, sent out two fundraising emails – understood to have both raised significant sums – calling on members to step up. The Labour email said Reform had secured “record-breaking financial backing – but for us it has to be a call to action … We cannot let less than a handful of extraordinarily wealthy crypto-billionaires simply drown Labour’s message out in elections to come [with] Reform dominating what voters see and hear, Labour fighting to be heard.” The follow-up email had a message from Phillipson saying: “When I saw that two crypto-billionaires had given Reform £72m, I had the same thought you probably did: how do you compete with that? “Then I watched the response from Labour supporters. People donated what they could … One person can’t match £72m. But thousands of us, standing together, can make sure Labour is as well-resourced for the fight ahead as it is possible to be.” On Tuesday, trade union leaders at the TUC stopped short of backing a cap on political donations, but called for further action on big money in politics. General secretaries have been split on a call for unions to back a specific cap on individual donors to political parties while protecting trade union donations, which the TUC said were the “cleanest money in politics” because they came from workers’ subscriptions. The TUC’s general secretary, Paul Nowak, said the donations to Reform were “a blatant attempt to effect a corporate takeover of our politics” and this should “ring alarm bells”. Downing Street, however, will take some succour from the warmer tone of union chiefs towards the party leadership at the annual TUC gathering in Brighton this week. Since 2020, Labour has received almost £43m from affiliated trade unions, which raise their money through individual workers’ membership fees. Sharon Graham, the general secretary of Unite, who had previously threatened to break the link with Labour, said Andy Burnham had earned the party a “second hearing”. Several other union leaders spoke of warm chats with the prime minister since he took office, and felt they were getting more of a hearing than when Keir Starmer was in No 10. However, despite welcoming the “Burnham bounce”, which they saw as giving Labour a better chance of fighting off the Reform threat, they warned there were key tests ahead for the government, including at the budget. Labour is under significant financial pressure, especially after several byelections, including the Greater Manchester mayoralty. Its most recent accounts filed with the Electoral Commission show Labour has lost more than a fifth of its membership in the space of a year, though party sources have said membership had gone up in anticipation of a possible leadership election, and since Burnham became prime minister. Income from donations has dropped by 84% since the election year, a drop that would be expected but is still significant. Last year, the party reported a £2.6m deficit. One union leader said the party was still “millions” in the red. However, Labour’s outgoing general secretary, Hollie Ridley, was understood to have told the party’s governing national executive committee that finances were healthy. She said the party was in its strongest financial position since the general election, due to spending discipline and increased fundraising efforts.

title: Why I can’t wait to get into a driverless car | Letters
summary: Letters: Lars Janssen says self-driving vehicles would be a boon for him as he has an eye condition and can’t drive, in response to an article by Adrian Chiles. Plus letters from Richard Connell and Michael Fuller
text: Adrian Chiles (Driverless cars are taking us on a road to nowhere, 10 September) wants to know who asked for driverless cars. I did. I have an eye condition called nystagmus and will never be able to drive unless a “tech-bro willy-waver”, or anyone else, finds a cure. Fortunately, not every driver is as reckless as the ones Chiles despairs of, and the most careful of all may not even be human. Waymo, Google’s sister company, says its cars have far fewer crashes causing injuries than human drivers. In July, the US Insurance Institute for Highway Safety found that its cars had 68% fewer crashes per mile than human drivers. Anyone wanting to take a swipe at tech-bro culture could pick a better target than a product that can save lives and give people like me independence. Chiles says we can’t be friends if driverless cars are near my top 10 wishlist. Well, I can’t wait to get into one. Lars Janssen Haywards Heath, West Sussex • My 18-year-old daughter is severely disabled, will never live independently and is entirely reliant on the support of others. To call the development of driverless cars the “willy-waving” of tech bros perhaps comes from a position of being able-bodied. Driverless cars open up my daughter’s world without the risks associated with her vulnerability. Augmented-reality glasses transform disabled people’s lives. An iPad has taught my daughter how to hold her hand still to be able to point. Richard Connell Richmond, London • Don’t be too quick to condemn driverless cars. They could be the saviour of country pubs. There are so many wonderful boozers around where I live, but you either have to drive to them and have one pint, which is not really worth the visit, or faff about getting an expensive taxi. Driverless cars? Bring ’em on! Michael Fuller Ampthill, Bedfordshire • Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Doctors, not cameras, save babies in intensive care | Brief letters
summary: Brief letters: Reflecting on the Thirlwall report | At one’s peak | Leaving the debate | Cut from the same cloth | End of the odyssey | A word’s worth
text: Re the Thirlwall report on the Lucy Letby case (Thirlwall report: what did it say about Lucy Letby case and what does it recommend?, 15 September), babies in neonatal intensive care units are saved by having consultant neonatologists (ie paediatricians who have undergone subspecialist training in neonatal medicine) doing rounds twice daily (in addition to being immediately available), trained neonatal nurses and appropriately resourced units – not by installing cameras on cots and insulin fridges. Dr Chris Fitzpatrick Retired consultant obstetrician; former CEO of Coombe hospital, Dublin, Ireland • Following the introduction of a competitive element in the nominative determinism debate (Letters, 15 September), I’d like to advise everyone that I am at my peak. Steve Munro St Osyth, Essex • I have found the nominative determinism letters interesting and amusing, but feel that they have gone on long enough. I have decided to leave the debate. Martin R Igoe Sheffield • All these letters are cut from the same cloth. Proctor Taylor Heathfield, East Sussex • The nominative determinism debate has been quite a journey, but is it time to end this odyssey? title: Obama family dog Sunny dies: ‘a force of nature’
summary: Sunny, who joined the Obama family at the White House in 2013, was the second Obama dog after Bo, who died in 2021
text: Sunny Obama, the Obama family’s second beloved Portuguese water dog, died on Tuesday, Barack Obama announced on Wednesday morning. “Yesterday, we lost a cherished member of our family,” the former president wrote on social media, attaching a photo of the 14-year-old dog, whom he called “a force of nature”. Sunny joined the Obama family at the White House in 2013 during Obama’s second term. She was the second Obama dog after Bo, who died in 2021. Unlike Bo, Sunny was known for her energetic disposition, occasionally making headlines for her rowdiness – like in 2013 when she knocked over a toddler during a White House holiday party or in 2017 when Sunny allegedly bit a visitor on the face. “She loved the girls, even if they were pestering her when she was napping. She loved our team, and would often follow them around, helping them on the job,” Obama said. Sunny was born in June 2012 in Michigan but joined the Obamas at the White House in August 2013. She was obtained from a breeder and, upon announcing her arrival, the family made a donation to the Washington Humane Society. The family chose to name her Sunny to “fit her cheerful personality”. “We will miss her terribly, and imagine she’s with her big brother now, making sure he’s okay,” Obama wrote.

title: Former French culture minister goes on trial over corruption charges
summary: Rachida Dati accused of lobbying for carmaker Renault-Nissan when she was member of European parliament
text: Rachida Dati, a former French culture minister, has gone on trial in Paris on corruption charges linked to dealings with the Renault-Nissan carmaking group. Dati, 60, is accused of illegal lobbying when she accepted €900,000 (£770,000) in lawyer’s fees from a Netherlands-based subsidiary of Renault-Nissan while she was a member of the European parliament. The court will have to decide what the money was for. Dati’s legal team denied all corruption allegations, saying she worked “exclusively” as a lawyer for the Renault-Nissan subsidiary. French prosecutors argue that she was instead paid to lobby for the carmaking group, an activity that is banned for members of the European parliament. Prosecutors said there was a lack of evidence to show Dati had carried out legal work. Dati was placed under investigation in 2019 on suspicion of illegally lobbying for Renault-Nissan between October 2009 and February 2013, when she was an MEP. Dati is on trial with Carlos Ghosn, the disgraced former Renault-Nissan chief, who will be tried in absentia. Ghosn, 72, was detained in Japan in November 2018 amid allegations of financial misconduct in a separate case involving a plot to falsify records about his personal pay in order to enrich himself. He dodged trial in Japan after escaping to Lebanon in an audio equipment case. He has denied all wrongdoing in the Japan case as well as in the Dati case. French prosecutors argue that a legal services contract signed in 2009 between Dati and Ghosn, in which Dati was paid an annual fee of €300,000, was used to disguise lobbying work. Investigators obtained the contract in 2019 during a search of Renault’s headquarters after Ghosn’s arrest in Japan. Dati, 60, who is the district mayor of the 7th arrondissement in Paris, is one of the most prominent figures on the French right. She was the first woman of north African and Muslim heritage to hold a major French government post when she was appointed justice minister by the rightwing president Nicolas Sarkozy. She returned to government under Emmanuel Macron, as culture minister. Dati redefined political celebrity in France, and has said growing up as the second of 11 children on a low-income housing estate on the outskirts of Chalon-sur-Saône in Burgundy gave her a greater understanding of the French electorate. She ran for mayor of Paris earlier this year, but lost to the Socialist Emmanuel Grégoire. If convicted, Dati faces up to 10 years in prison and a fine of up to €450,000. She could also face a five-year ban on holding public office. Dati’s lawyers said: “Unfounded allegations of influence peddling in the European parliament stem from an artificial intellectual construct devised by the prosecution.” In a separate investigation, Dati has been accused of accepting nearly €300,000 in undeclared payments from the energy group GDF Suez, also while an MEP. Prosecutors said last year they were looking into reports Dati failed to declare jewellery and watches worth €420,000 upon taking ministerial office. She has denied any wrongdoing in all cases.

title: Sweden voted against more power for the far right – but are centrists listening?
summary: Even as the ‘extremist’ AfD seeks further election gains in Germany, Europe’s leaders can learn from Sweden’s dangerous embrace with far-right ideology
text: Europe’s focus turned nervously to Sweden on Sunday, after an explosive election in Germany just a week earlier placed a far-right party, officially classed as “extremist”, on the brink of power in a German state for the first time since the Nazi era. A party with neo-Nazi roots has been pulling the government’s strings in Sweden for the last four years. Would the country’s general election put the far right formally in government? Or would enough Swedes opt for a gear change, having seen the Sweden Democrats’ hardline (some would say poisonous) agenda in action? Votes were still being counted on Wednesday but it was immediately clear that the far-right Sweden Democrats had suffered a setback; their first loss of support among voters since entering parliament for the first time 16 years ago. The party slipped from being the country’s second biggest party to its third. The centre-left Social Democrats appear poised for a return to power, although it could take months for their leader, Magdalena Andersson, to form a coalition. Strong results for the left and green parties gave her left bloc a wafer-thin, three-seat majority. Is the far right’s regression, however modest, a turning point? Have Swedes reached the limits of a taboo-busting experiment with populist, nationalist rightwing prescriptions? And is there a message for mainstream leaders across Europe, many of whom seem fatalistic about a continent-wide far-right surge? France goes to the polls in April while governments in Italy, Spain and Poland, all face their electorates later next year. The Dutch political scientist Cas Mudde says elections in one country are a poor guide to what will happen in another. Specific local factors in Sweden, including a scandal, may have dented the far right’s support. For Mudde, the scale of the AfD’s win in Saxony Anhalt, however, was “a black day for Europe” – and with far-right ideas gaining ground, he warned mainstream politicians that “today’s key fight is for democracy, rather than for party or power”. This is where Sweden offers a cautionary tale. Its political establishment had “fully normalised” the far-right party, Mudde said. “Its nativism is now shared by all the major parties, albeit in lighter form, from the Moderates on the right to the Social Democrats on the left.” But the decline in the far right’s support, for now, he thinks, “at the very least creates space for mainstream parties to focus on issues other than immigration”. Ann-Cathrine Jungar, a professor of political science at Södertörn University in Stockholm, is very sure that the Sweden Democrats are not on the way out. Electoral rankings go up and down, she said, and the party’s influence will endure. More important now is how the mainstream parties respond. “We focus a lot on the extreme and radical right parties, but the key to their influence is what the other parties do. Why have Sweden’s mainstream parties adopted the far right’s policies? The Social Democrats have co-opted their ideas, even though they are counter to the country’s needs. In Sweden, we need competent, talented people who want to come and live here, we need labour for health and social care. Yet nationalism seems to be the prevailing ideology now.” In a widely read Guardian essay headlined How Sweden lost its soul – and stopped being Sweden, published before the vote, Martin Gelin documented his country’s transformation after 2022. Rightwing parties that year signed a Faustian pact with the Sweden Democrats, buying its support for a minority rightwing government. The deal? The far right party was given a direct hand in shaping policy. “A new Sweden has emerged, cruel and cold for migrants”, wrote Gelin, with xenophobic and ethno-nationalist ideas “now comfortably embedded in the political mainstream”. Most shockingly, Andersson’s Social Democrats, modelling themselves on their hardline Danish counterparts, had bought into the far right’s framings on crime and immigration. Will Sweden’s Social Democrats now learn from their worst performance in more than 100 years, and embrace an agenda that does not involve deporting toddlers to Iran, people with dementia to the UK, or locking up 14-year-olds? Jungar is sceptical. “When it comes to linking crime and immigration, this is the new normal,” she said. “The Social Democrats will not pursue policies that are more liberal.” Yet the political centre in Sweden could articulate a clear alternative to the far right, Mudde says. The Left and the Greens did significantly better among young voters in this week’s election. “This reflects a development we see across Europe, namely that young people prefer outspokenly leftwing parties over centre-left parties.” *** Ghosts of grievance Like Giorgia Meloni’s party, Brothers of Italy, and Marine Le Pen’s National Rally in France, the Sweden Democrats have “deradicalised” in selective ways, to broaden their appeal, Jungar told me. By contrast, what was striking in Germany, was how the AfD doubled its score to 44% of the vote, on what Constanze Stelzenmuller in the FT called “a programme of stunning malevolence”. Two further regional elections this Sunday in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania will be closely watched, including by the AfD’s American boosters such as Elon Musk. Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania has economic and demographic conditions comparable to Saxony Anhalt. For those struggling to understand the appeal of the AfD in eastern Germany, Carolin Würfel’s essay offered an original insight. Born in the former East Germany, Würfel believes that many voters there don’t actually know or care about the AfD’s detailed policies. But the party had tapped into a legacy of grievance about the economic impact of reunification in the 1990s. “Villages and small towns that had been hollowed out, some of them ghostly and depopulated, were suddenly told again: you matter. Everyone else may have left you behind, but I, we, the AfD, care.” The AfD won’t improve life in east Germany, Würfel wrote, “but that was never the point”. As in Sweden, the political centre in Germany is now being warned that time is running out to offer a credible democratic alternative to the far right. As Florian Ranft of the Das Progressive Zentrum thinktank wrote: “Waiting for the AfD to fail is not a strategy.” To receive the complete version of This Is Europe in your inbox every Wednesday, please subscribe here.

title: Epstein survivors praise House panel over Leon Black contempt vote
summary: Victims hail 41-0 vote in favor of holding billionaire in contempt over refusal to comply with panel’s subpoenas
text: More than a dozen survivors of Jeffrey Epstein’s abuse praised the House oversight committee for unanimously voting to recommend that billionaire investor Leon Black be held in contempt for refusing to comply with subpoenas by the panel seeking his testimony and nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) as part of its investigation into Epstein. “We commend Chairman Comer for showing real resolve in pursuing accountability in the Epstein investigation,” the survivors said in a statement. They said that the 41-0 vote sends a “clear message that wealth and influence do not put anyone beyond the reach of congressional oversight”. “Survivors have fought for years to bring the truth about Epstein’s network into the open and have helped create this moment of accountability,” they added. “Congress now has an opportunity to build on that work by following the investigative leads contained in the Epstein files wherever they go and demanding answers from the powerful people connected to them.” The vote on Tuesday marked the latest escalation in the dispute between the committee and Black, whose name came up repeatedly in the Epstein files, and who, as reported by the New York Times, paid Epstein a total of $170m for what he described as tax and estate planning services from 2013 to 2017. The contempt resolution now goes to the full House for consideration, if speaker Mike Johnson permits a vote. Black has repeatedly denied any wrongdoing and said he had no knowledge of Epstein’s criminal activities. He voluntarily appeared before the committee for a transcribed interview in June, but the session ended abruptly after lawmakers from both parties said that Black refused to answer questions about NDAs. The committee, chaired by Republican representative James Comer, then issued two subpoenas: one demanding that Black produce all NDAs “to which he is a party” and another requiring him to appear before the committee again for a deposition. Black did not appear for his scheduled 3 September deposition and did not produce all of the NDAs sought by the committee. He instead sued Comer and the committee, arguing that the subpoenas were “invalid” and exceeded the committee’s “delegated authority in seeking private information that bears no legitimate connection” to its legislative purpose. He also argued that the subpoenas would “expose women who value their privacy, who have no known or public connection to Epstein”. Attorneys representing Black had asked for a postponement of the committee’s markup earlier on Tuesday, and described it as a “complete abomination”. Black’s attorneys said on Tuesday that the committee under Comer and representative Robert Garcia, its top Democrat, had “lost sight of its legislative purpose and is abusing its power”. The lawyers also described the subpoenas as “illegitimate, illegal and a textbook abuse of power designed to bully and destroy legal protections of private citizens” and reiterated that Black “never abused a woman”, “was never blackmailed by Epstein” and “had no knowledge of any of Epstein’s heinous conduct”. On Wednesday, a day after the vote, Comer announced the introduction of the Survivor’s Voice Protection Act, legislation his office said would ensure “survivors can speak freely about sexual abuse, even if they signed a nondisclosure agreement”. According to Comer’s office, the bill would also create “accountability for trusted individuals to protect minors by establishing an obligation to report suspected grooming behavior to law enforcement”. The legislation is a “result of the Oversight committee’s review of the federal investigations into Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell’s crimes”, his office added. In a statement on Wednesday, Comer said: “The federal government for decades failed the survivors of Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell’s crimes. We sadly cannot undue the harm and abuse inflicted upon these women. However, we have an obligation to take action to reform our laws to ensure survivors are protected and abusers can be held accountable.” He added: “During our investigation, we’ve learned how powerful men weaponized nondisclosure agreements to silence survivors of sexual abuse.” Republican representatives Nancy Mace, Virginia Foxx, Lauren Boebert and Anna Paulina Luna joined the bill as original cosponsors. The committee says that it has conducted 19 depositions and transcribed interviews thus far as part of its review of the federal government’s investigation of Epstein and Maxwell, and that it has released around 65,000 pages of documents from the Epstein estate, US Department of Justice, and interview transcripts, and also obtained Epstein’s bank records. Additionally, in June, Comer referred two men to the Department of Justice for further investigation after Sarah Kellen, a former assistant of Epstein’s, alleged that she was sexually assaulted by them in the years that she worked for Epstein. Neither men have been charged with any crime related to Epstein, and both have denied any wrongdoing and the allegations against them. Over the summer, the Guardian asked the DoJ for an update on this, to which a DoJ spokesperson told the Guardian that they had forwarded the letter from Comer about the two individuals to the FBI. “If, during the course of their review, FBI encounters of evidence of a federal crime, they will investigate that matter,” a DoJ spokesperson told the Guardian in July. When asked for an update in late August, the DoJ spokesperson said that the July statement “still stands”. The FBI did not respond to multiple requests for comment from the Guardian this month about the matter.
