title: ‘We need to get it right’: union gusto for Burnham will face make-or-break tests
summary: TUC conference rings with praise for new No 10 team, but battles loom over workers’ rights and north sea drilling
text: Louise Haigh, the UK first secretary, got a standing ovation from trade union members in Brighton this week, as she acknowledged what she called “the necessity to be bolder in this second chance that we’ve been allowed”. Haigh was the stand-in at the annual TUC congress for Andy Burnham, absent because of his father’s death. The headlines from the seaside gathering were dominated by party funding, after Reform announced £72m of donations in a single weekend and Unite called for a cap on donations by individuals in response. But as they gathered to swap gossip in Brighton’s pubs and hotel bars, senior union figures seemed reinvigorated for the moment by the “Burnham bounce”. Relations between the new No 10 team and the unions – including those less than popular with Keir Starmer’s regime – have improved significantly; general secretaries speak warmly of recent chats with “Andy”. Yet there is a clear sense that the real tests are to come – on the implementation of improved workers’ rights; on oil and gas licences, of particular concern to Unite and the GMB; and on John Healey’s crucial autumn budget. TUC delegates voted through policy statements on a slew of tricky issues in Burnham’s prime ministerial in-tray, from the future relationship with the EU – unions want him to drop Labour’s “red lines” – to Shabana Mahmood’s migration reforms. And senior union figures were keen to point to issues they see as make-or-break. Joanne Thomas, the general secretary of Usdaw, said she was pleased to see her former schoolmate Jonathan Reynolds back in cabinet as business secretary – but would judge him by results. In particular, she hopes to see the provisions in the Employment Rights Act on abolishing zero-hours contracts implemented in a way that embraces all workers in the retail and hospitality sectors she represents. “A lot of people think, job done – but the implementation means everything,” she said. “For this to make a real difference to people’s lives, we need to get it right. We want everybody to have a contract that reflects the hours they work.” The TUC is also gearing up to campaign on the issue in the coming weeks and months. “We will be getting our message out loud and clear, to Johnny Reynolds in particular,” she said. “It’s about reducing that one-sided flexibility, which employers have got in abundance.” Thomas also echoed a concern shared by several other senior union figures, about whether Reynolds’s newly expanded Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade (BIST), would end up lacking focus. “I would like to see a minister for work. BIST has so much to do, I worry that the labour stuff gets lost,” she warned. Mike Clancy, general secretary of Prospect, whose members include scientists and engineers – and which is not affiliated to Labour – expresses a similar concern, from a different perspective. Prospect is campaigning against real-terms cuts to science budgets by the taxpayer-backed UK Research and Innovation agency. Clancy frets that folding science into the department may lead to it being seen primarily through a business lens. “This is the first test of BIST … and whether this department’s really going to understand science culture,” he said. The GMB and Unite are waiting anxiously for the government’s ruling on the controversial question of whether to allow drilling in the Jackdaw gas and Rosebank oilfields. A decision had previously been expected this week, but appears to have been postponed until after the Holborn and St Pancras byelection in early October, in which the Green party’s leader in England, Zack Polanski, is standing. The two unions’ leaders are such ardent champions of continuing to exploit the North Sea’s declining fields, that Unite’s Sharon Graham and the GMB’s Gary Smith raised concerns about the idea that former energy secretary Ed Miliband would be Burnham’s chancellor. “What that gives us is time,” Graham said of the idea of exploiting Jackdaw and Rosebank. “It gives time for someone to get their backside into gear and realise we have to create an industry over the other side of this, whether it’s green fuel, whether it’s something else. All of that has to be done before you start saying you’re going to choke off what’s going on over here.” But the apparent delay until after a tricky London byelection underlines the fact that other parts of Labour’s electoral coalition are unlikely to welcome a “yes” to future drilling. Meanwhile Graham, who was an outspoken critic of Starmer, said she hoped the first Burnham budget would contain what she characterises as “winter fuel in reverse”. Rachel Reeves’s early decision to severely limit winter fuel payments to pensioners – eventually reversed – came to symbolise the last government’s missteps. “The abhorrence of that: do something as good as that,” Graham said. Unite’s (costly) suggestion is for the government to unfreeze the income tax thresholds that have seen a growing number of workers dragged into paying the basic or higher rates, and take fresh action on household bills. Healey has hinted he would like to do more to give the public a “breathing space” in the face of rising energy costs. But the shaky global backdrop, with oil prices rocketing and febrile markets driving up interest rates on government bonds, means he is likely to be left with little room for manoeuvre against Labour’s fiscal rules. For Graham, the answer is obvious: tax the wealthy more, and tax the banks. She rejects the idea that bond market turbulence is a reason for caution. “We cannot keep being told that we cannot do anything because of the markets. Because if that is the case, what is the point of us electing politicians?” she asked delegates in a fiery speech on Monday afternoon. The TUC has also called for a bank windfall tax to fund energy support. Judging by the mood music emerging from the Treasury of a “focused” budget with big spending decisions kicked into next year, Graham looks set to be disappointed. And as Farage’s lavishly funded Reform gears up for the next general election, the pervasive anxiety in Brighton this week was the same one that preoccupies even senior figures in the new government. The radical rhetoric of Burnham’s early weeks in power seems to have won him a fresh hearing with voters – but in straitened times, can he match them with action?

title: Michelin-starred Seoul restaurant fined for serving dessert topped with ants
summary: Prosecutors sought jail term for chief executive of Evett after insects not approved for consumption were on menu
text: A South Korean court has fined the operator of one of Seoul’s most celebrated restaurants and its chief executive for serving a dessert topped with ants, an insect not approved for consumption under local food safety law. The operator of Evett, a two-Michelin-star restaurant in the affluent Gangnam district, was fined 10m won (£5,400) and its chief executive 15m won, Newsis reported. Prosecutors had sought a one-year prison term for the chief executive and a 20m won fine for the company. The judge at Seoul’s western district court, Lee Se-chang, said the offence was “by no means light”, citing the length of time the dishes had been sold for, the restaurant’s use of them to promote itself and tests that found heavy metals above permitted levels in the ants. He said he had taken into account that the defendants admitted the offence, that the chief executive had no previous criminal record under the food safety law, that the number of ants served appeared lower than prosecutors had calculated and that the restaurant no longer used ants. Ants are used as an ingredient in the US and Europe, and the restaurant appeared not to have realised they were not permitted in South Korea, he said. Both sides have seven days to appeal. The Guardian contacted Evett for comment. Evett was founded by the Australian chef Joseph Lidgerwood, who has appeared on the Netflix cooking competition Culinary Class Wars and is the restaurant’s public face. He was not a defendant and was not charged. Under South Korean food safety law, the legal duties fall on the person registered as operating the business. Ginny Kim, Lidgerwood’s wife, is registered as the company’s chief executive and was named as a defendant, alongside the company that operates the restaurant. Only 10 insect species are approved as food ingredients in South Korea, including grasshoppers, mealworms and silkworm pupae. Businesses wishing to use an unapproved insect must obtain temporary approval from the ministry of food and drug safety, a step the restaurant did not take. Violating the law carries a maximum penalty of five years in prison or a 50m won fine. The ministry launched its investigation after seeing mentions of the ant dishes in blog posts and social media. Prosecutors said the restaurant imported dried ants from the US and Thailand by post from April 2021, and served three to five of them atop a sorbet made with sikhye, a sweet Korean rice drink, until January 2025. They estimated the dessert was served to 12,274 customers, using 49,096 ants, for total revenue of about 120m won. Lawyers disputed that figure in court, arguing that only about 60% of customers accepted the ant topping when it was offered. The restaurant also noted that only a small number of dishes on their 15-course menu included ants, and that restaurants in countries including Denmark, the UK and Australia use ants as an ingredient. Insect-eating is neither new nor unusual in South Korea. Beondegi, steamed silkworm pupae, has been sold from street carts for decades and remains a nostalgic popular snack for children.

title: New report reveals prevalence of physical and sexual violence in US
summary: Study finds more than half of US adults have experienced physical violence and nearly half sexual violence
text: In their lifetime, more than half of US adults have experienced physical violence – and nearly half have experienced sexual violence, according to a startling new national study. The study, led by researchers from Tulane University’s Newcomb Institute and the University of California, San Diego, examined experiences of physical, sexual and intimate partner violence, along with how they intersect with behavioral health, economic hardship, neighborhood safety and substance use, among other factors. The study found that 52% of US adults have experienced physical violence during their lifetime, including cases involving a gun or knife. The rate was the same among women and men: 52% each. Speaking to the Guardian, Anita Raj, executive director of the Newcomb Institute and co-author of the study report, said the survey pointed to the importance of assessing violence beyond crime reports. “That’s a fraction of people who are affected,” said Raj, whose study is titled Violence in America: Findings from the 2025 United States Violence Experiences Survey (USVEX). “We also don’t want to find out about it at that point because if we’re finding out at that point, the risk for fatality has now gone up.” USVEX surveyed 2,720 adults across all 50 states between October and December 2025 using a nationally representative sample administered by NORC at the University of Chicago. The study was conducted in English and Spanish, with its finding arrives months after the Trace – a non-profit newsroom dedicated to reporting on gun violence – calculated that the Trump administration had terminated, redirected or delayed more than $1bn in federal grants related to gun violence, public safety, mental health and other efforts to save lives. In the past year, one in 20 American adults (5%) experienced physical violence – and 3% reported physical abuse that did not involve a weapon, the study found. Women most often experienced physical violence at the hands of a spouse or romantic partner, at 61%, while men most commonly experienced violence from a stranger, at 38%. Among men, 25% reported violence by a spouse or romantic partner and 24% by a family member, according to the study. It also found both women and men most often reported experiencing physical violence at home, at 69% and 34%, respectively. Men also reported experiencing violence in public spaces at a rate of 30%. Physical violence was also associated with significant mental health consequences. Among those who experienced physical violence in the past year, 48% of women and 26% of men said the experience resulted in anxiety or depression. Only a minority of those affected filed formal complaints, including 10% of women and 17% of men. The study also found that 49% of US adults have experienced sexual violence during their lifetime, with a significantly higher prevalence among women, at 68%, than men, at 29%. In the past year, 7% of Americans – about one in 14 – experienced sexual violence, the survey found. The rate was 9% among women and 4% among men. The study noted that sexual harassment accounted for much of this violence. Strangers were the most commonly reported perpetrators of sexual violence in the past year, accounting for 58% of cases involving women and 66% of cases involving men. Acquaintances or community members were the next most commonly reported perpetrators, at 47% for women and 41% for men, according to the study. The locations also differed by gender. Most women who experienced sexual violence in the past year said it occurred in public spaces, at 55%, while 64% of men said it occurred at home, the study said. Additionally, 42% of women who faced sexual violence in the past year reported suffering from depression or anxiety, while 39% of men said the violence they experienced resulted in anxiety or depression. The study also found that 4% of women and 10% of men who experienced sexual violence during the past year considered suicide. Intimate partner violence (IPV) was also widespread, with 61% of women and 45% of men reporting that they had experienced it. Nearly one in five women, or 19%, reported potentially lethal IPV, including beating, burning, strangulation or violence involving a knife or gun – compared with 3% of men. The study found that experiences of violence rose sharply during adolescence and young adulthood, with rates increasing during adolescence and continuing to climb into young adulthood. By this stage, nearly one-third of adults reported having experienced sexual violence. Economic hardship was also closely linked to experiences of violence. Adults who had been evicted in the previous year were seven times more likely to report recent physical violence, three times more likely to report sexual violence and nearly five times more likely to report intimate partner violence, the study noted. Raj on Tuesday pointed to factors such as economic status as an important metric, saying: “What we really see are what we call economic shocks that increase their very acute vulnerability. So [those are] things like not having enough money to meet basic needs like food … an eviction, or having been homeless in the past year. “At the same time, we also see the early experiences of violence. … When you’ve had those experiences early in life, you are more vulnerable to them throughout your life, and so that’s really a piece of this. “It shouldn’t take a fatality for you to understand risk for fatality. By assessing behaviors that women have experienced that could have killed them, you have a better understanding of how much risk for fatality from domestic violence there actually is.” Echoing Raj, Jakana Thomas, a political science professor at the University of California, San Diego, and co-author of the study, said: “These findings show that violence prevention cannot occur in isolation. It must be part of a broader strategy that also addresses economic hardship, mental health and other forms of social inequality associated with violence.” Raj and Thomas’s study arrived three days after a woman, her daughter, her son and his girlfriend were killed in a stabbing spree at a home in Houma, Louisiana, about 60 miles south-west of the Newcombe Institute. The man whom authorities arrested in connection with the deadly attack – which also wounded a six-year-old minor – had reportedly fathered a child with one of the victims. Those killings occurred two years after Louisiana’s department of health warned that intimate partner violence was a “significant public health concern in the state”. The state’s rate of women murdered by men has historically been significantly higher than the national average, according to the Louisiana Coalition Against Domestic Violence. A statement from Tulane said the new study grew out of work focused on Louisiana that Raj and her colleagues had done before then seeing many of the same patterns emerge nationally. • In the US, the domestic violence hotline is 1-800-799-SAFE (7233). In the UK, call the national domestic abuse helpline on 0808 2000 247, or visit Women’s Aid. In Australia, the national family violence counselling service is on 1800 737 732. Other international helplines may be found via www.befrienders.org

title: Company behind failed Surrey oilfield project sells site at massive loss
summary: New owners apply for permission to extract oil in Surrey despite landmark ruling from supreme court in 2024
text: After years of trying to dig for oil in Surrey, the company behind the drilling project that was turned down in a landmark supreme court ruling has sold off the site for a fraction of the money it spent on it, and rebranded as a clean energy company. Meanwhile, the new owners, who picked up the site for £1m, are applying, once again, for permission to dig. UK Oil and Gas (UKOG) spent more than a decade trying to develop Horse Hill oilfields, where they said they had found 100bn barrels of oil. But in 2024 the supreme court, in a decision which has since become known as the Finch Ruling, decreed that “a planning authority should have considered the indirect downstream greenhouse gas emissions of an oil and gas project as part of its environmental impact assessment” and overturned a council decision to let expansion go ahead. The Guardian understands that the implied value of the Horse Hill licence area reached a peak of £46m in September 2018 after UKOG agreed to buy a 14.3% economic stake from a group of vendors for £6.6m. The surging valuations given to the fields was driven by industry estimates that there could be about 9.24bn barrels of oil in the tight Jurassic shale and conventional reservoir sections within the Horse Hill licences. Public records appear to show UKOG invested more than £25m into the site. Prior to the £1m sale, UKOG’s financial accounts showed that it had written down the value of its Horse Hill interests to just £55,360 on its balance sheet. UKOG has now changed its name to UK Energy Group, seeking to shift its focus towards salt-cavern energy storage and other clean energy projects. Stephen Sanderson, the company’s chief executive, said while the company still sees “potentially material resources” at Horse Hill, the divestment presented “timely and attractive opportunity to complete UKOG’s exit from the UK onshore oil and gas sector”. The company reportedly raised £1m in 2025 to develop hydrogen-storage projects in south Dorset and Yorkshire, and a further £500,000 to acquire land for a proposed East Yorkshire salt-cavern site. Guy Prince, the head of energy supply at energy transition thinktank Carbon Tracker, said Horse Hill was an example of “regulatory stranding”, in which climate litigation and regulatory shifts undermine the value of a fossil fuel asset. “The same transition risk can have really radical financial consequences depending on who owns the asset,” he said. “For a major [company], it might impair one investment opportunity. But for a small company concentrated on one project like this, it just transformed the entire business.” New owner Energy B is taking over UKOG’s application to drill for oil in Surrey. Horse Hill Developments Ltd, which it now controls, submitted a renewed planning application to Surrey county council in May for four production wells, a new oil processing area, tanker-loading facilities and a fluid reinjection well. The proposal would allow nearly 700,000 tonnes of oil to be extracted over 20 years. Sarah Finch, the campaigner who brought the successful legal challenge to the supreme court in 2024, said there were “serious shortcomings” with the application’s new environmental assessment. “New guidance from the government and pre-existing guidance all say that they have to place the emissions from a new proposed project within a cumulative context of all current and approved fossil fuel projects,” Finch said. “They didn’t make any attempt to do that, although the data is readily available out there.” The application estimates that the development would result in about 2.3m tonnes of greenhouse gas emissions over its lifetime, including emissions from the eventual burning of the oil, but concluded the impact was “insignificant”. Planning documents said: “Horse Hill would account for around 0.05% of the projected UK carbon budget; an insignificant contribution that would give rise to insignificant climate change effects.” Finch said the developer’s argument was “false”. “Any greenhouse gas emissions are significant,” she added. “The International Energy Agency has said we can’t afford any new oil or gas. Any additional fossil fuels are going to make it impossible to stay within the 1.5C target, so [the emissions] are significant.” The application argued that extracting up to 678,693 tonnes of oil at Horse Hill would improve energy security by reducing the UK’s reliance on imports. An Energy B spokesperson said: “At a time of global uncertainty and energy price shocks, domestic oil and gas production increases energy security. “We are confident of meeting all the necessary legal and environmental requirements for the site. With the oil being refined in the UK and the gas serving the domestic market, the field will contribute positively to the UK economy.” Finch disputed that argument, saying domestically produced oil was typically traded on an international market rather than necessarily supplying British consumers. Finch said Surrey county council’s decision would be a “significant test case” for whether the climate risks of fossil fuel projects are being properly assessed after the supreme court ruling. The local authority’s formal consultation closed on 13 July, although the council has said it will consider submissions received before it makes its decision, which could be reached this month. Finch said the Weald Action Group would not rule out seeking another judicial review if the council approved the development. “We’re fairly confident that the environmental statement that’s been submitted isn’t compliant with the law and the new guidance,” she said. UK Energy Group/UK Oil and Gas declined to comment.

title: McLaren to build SUVs geared towards Formula One fans with children
summary: Model comes as part of £500m UK investment by firm’s new Abu Dhabi owner that will also fund new factory
text: McLaren is gearing up to build an SUV for the first time in its 63-year history, betting that the glamour of its all-conquering Formula One team can sell cars to wealthy fans who do not own its supercars. The model, which does not yet have a name, comes as part of a £500m investment by McLaren’s new Abu Dhabi owner that will also create 1,000 jobs, adding to the existing workforce of 2,500 people. It will also fund a new factory, with Sheffield, home to McLaren’s existing carbon-fibre plant, understood to be the preferred site over the company’s headquarters in Woking. Nick Collins, the carmaker’s chief executive, said the recent success of the McLaren racing team had created an “untapped love” for the brand among people who have never bought its cars. The SUV would open the door to more buyers for whom two-seater sports cars were a limitation, he said. “It’s quite difficult if you have to decide which one of your kids you want to leave behind at home.” The new model is part of a turnaround plan at McLaren Automotive, which was bought from the Bahraini sovereign wealth fund Mumtalakat last year by CYVN Holdings, an Abu Dhabi government-owned investment company now called L’Imad. CYVN has vowed to invest $2bn (£1.4bn) in the loss-making group over five years. McLaren also merged with the British electric vehicle startup Forseven Holdings last April. However, McLaren has no immediate plans to build an EV of its own, despite a government mandate saying all new cars in the UK must be zero-emission by 2035. “[Customers] are not asking us, and we’re not doing one,” Collins said. Founded in 1963 by the racing driver Bruce McLaren, the company built racing cars, and later the McLaren F1 supercar in the 1990s, before spinning off McLaren Automotive as a dedicated road carmaker in 2010. But it has struggled in recent years amid mounting debts and falling sales, before last year’s takeover by CYVN. European luxury carmakers have faced tough trading conditions after a collapse in demand in China, a key market, which has already forced job losses at rivals Aston Martin and Bentley. Michael Straughan, McLaren’s chief operating officer, said the SUV was a “critical” moment for the company, adding that he could “quite easily see us doubling” sales, which now stand at about 3,000 cars a year, through the new model. He said the new factory was likely to be built in Sheffield, calling it “the jewel in the crown” for the company’s manufacturing capability, though no final decision has been made. It comes amid a bumper period for sister company McLaren Racing, which has won the last two Formula One constructors championships and is also based in Woking. Mumtalakat still has majority control of McLaren Racing, while CYVN has a minority stake. Straughan said: “There’s no doubt there’s people who are F1 fans … who would never purchase a McLaren sports car, but would definitely consider a McLaren SUV.” He would not be drawn on the exact price of the new vehicle, but expects it to compete with the Bentley Bentayga, Aston Martin DBX and Lamborghini Urus, models that all start above £200,000. “I think the trick here is conquest of other brands’ customers,” Straughan added – though not before seeing a Ferrari F40 drive past the window of McLaren’s technology centre in Woking. The prime minister, Andy Burnham, welcomed the investment, saying it showed the company was “doubling down on Britain”. The growth of SUVs has come against the backdrop of warnings over “carspreading” and safety. Research has shown cars have grown 1.2cm longer, 0.5cm taller and 0.5cm wider each year on average since 2000, and that potential SUV buyers are undeterred by warnings they are more likely to kill pedestrians. • This article was amended on 25 September 2026 to add the detail that CYVN Holdings is now known as L’Imad.

title: English village votes to leave UK in protest over migrant housing plan
summary: Villagers in Piddington, Oxfordshire, hold symbolic referendum over plans to house more than 1,000 asylum seekers nearby
text: Residents of an English village have voted to leave the UK in a symbolic referendum against plans to house more than 1,000 asylum seekers nearby. The result of the poll in Piddington, Oxfordshire, was announced on Wednesday morning after 312 people voted on Tuesday. A total of 285 people were in favour of independence from the UK while 26 voted against. One ballot was spoiled. The poll was organised by campaigners for residents to demonstrate opposition to government plans to house up to 1,256 male asylum seekers at a converted Ministry of Defence site in the town of Bicester. Reacting to the news, a government minister said the burden of accommodating asylum seekers should not fall just on poorer communities and she would “gently” tell residents of the village that the government was working to bring down the asylum backlog. Lisa Nandy, the culture secretary, told Sky News: “We are getting that backlog down. We’re speeding up the processing of claims, and in the meantime, we don’t think it’s acceptable for all of the burden of shouldering not just asylum accommodation, but also many other forms of temporary accommodation, to fall on poorer communities.” She added: “That’s what we saw under the previous government. Because accommodation is cheap in many, not just towns, but in particular postcode areas. People who live in more deprived communities have had to put up with almost … every other house in some instances … turned into HMOs [house in multiple occupation], and that is not OK.” The dispute over the plans in Bicester come against a backdrop of tensions elsewhere over the location of accommodation for asylum seekers. After disturbances in Thetford, Norfolk, earlier this year, which far-right activists attempted to exploit, the local Labour MP there voiced his concerns that cheaper, working-class areas were being chosen as locations for housing asylum seekers in HMOs. Tim Bearder, the leader of Oxfordshire county council, said on Wednesday that the result in Piddington showed that campaigners had done “an incredible job” to highlight their concerns. “This referendum shows how strongly they feel about the proposal and that is partly about the proposal itself and partly about way the government has gone about it, without engaging with local people and looking at the feasibility of the site,” he told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme. “It’s the wrong site for the local community and for the asylum seekers themselves,” said Bearder, who declined to say what alternative sites could be used. The result was announced on Wednesday morning by a “returning officer” in front of an audience of dozens of journalists and residents gathered outside the village hall. A parish councillor, Mike Nixon, said the proposed site had no pedestrian access areas, and that the nearest path was about a mile and a quarter away, down a busy unlit road. The Home Office has previously said that the government is closing asylum hotels in what is expected to saving taxpayers over £1bn on asylum support and that it is working fairly to house asylum seekers across the country. “As part of the process, we engage with local authorities and police forces to ensure the safety and security of those in the surrounding area,” a spokesperson said.

title: Record heatwaves bring Britain’s second-best butterfly season in 16 years
summary: Volunteers counted almost 1.4m common butterflies and moths, with painted ladies up 335% on last year
text: The recording-breaking heat of 2026 delivered the second-best British butterfly season of the past 16 years, according to the Big Butterfly Count. The largest insect count in the world, in which more than 100,000 volunteers counted almost 1.4m common butterflies and day-flying moths, confirmed what many people experienced – a noticeable profusion of butterflies during the five-heatwave summer. Particularly numerous were painted ladies, a migratory species which arrives in Britain each summer via a relay of several generations flying from sub-Saharan Africa. Their numbers were up 335% on last year, with the Butterfly Conservation count recording their second-highest numbers since the count began in 2010. The holly blue and the gatekeeper both had their best ever Big Butterfly Count results, while the small copper recorded its third best year. The overall results were the best for butterflies since the summer of 2019. But Butterfly Conservation warned that the drought in many parts of Britain could cause the collapse of butterfly populations next year because this summer’s caterpillars, which mostly produce adult butterflies next year, may have perished when so many grasses, wildflowers and other plants shrivelled and died in extremely dry conditions. Richard Fox, head of science at Butterfly Conservation, said: “Adult butterflies love hot, sunny weather for flying, feeding and breeding, and that’s exactly why people saw so many this summer. But a good summer for adult butterflies is not the same as a good summer for butterfly populations. “What matters far more is what’s happening on the ground, to the butterflies’ caterpillar offspring and the plants they depend on. The very same weather that made it a good year for butterflies – lots of sunshine and very little rain – could mean we’re actually on course for a population crash, which could take years to recover from.” There were population crashes in the summers after excellent butterfly seasons in 1976 and 1995, with drought a big factor, although recent droughts during 2018 and 2022 did not cause a comparable crash. Butterfly experts agree that although they are generally bad news for butterflies, no two droughts are the same. According to independent naturalist Matthew Oates, the drought of 1976 was exacerbated by a year of dry weather before the hot summer, whereas this summer was preceded by a wet winter. Oates, who has kept diaries of each butterfly season since 1964, said 1977 was notably poor for butterflies not simply because of the drought but because it featured a poor spring and one of the wettest ever Junes. This year, Oates said he had been looking for “frazzled butterfly foodplants” in the Cotswolds and Wiltshire and had detected good survival rates of important grassland butterfly foodplants, such as horseshoe vetch apart from on south-facing slopes. Oates said he was hopeful that last year’s wet winter and a wet week in early June before the drought began might ensure there is not a population crash next year. Although it has been a standout summer for migratory butterflies with the clouded yellow still flying across southern Britain in September and possibly record numbers of the non-native Queen of Spain fritillary also being seen close to coastlines, some drought-sensitive species have already recorded poor years. The speckled wood, green-veined white and ringlet were all seen in below-average numbers in the Big Butterfly Count and show declines of 44%, 54% and 39%, respectively, since 2011. Although there are winners and losers among British butterflies with hotter summers, Fox said: “There will be very few butterfly species that can thrive in the drought situations we had this summer across much of the UK.” Both Fox and Oates agreed that Britain was entering uncharted territory in terms of how new climatic extremes would impact native wildlife and flying insect populations. “If we get another summer of drought or excessive heat that’s really moving into a new future for us and our wildlife, including butterflies,” said Fox. Oates said the latest conditions were completely outside his experience of the past 62 summers he has logged in weather diaries and butterfly observations. “These last two summers have been way beyond our previous experience. We are out of our comfort zone and we can’t speak with any confidence any more,” he said. “A lot of our butterflies are behaving more like they behave much farther south in Europe. In some ways it is exciting but I worry about how relevant our existing, treasured knowledge is. We need every entomologist we can get in this country.” Big Butterfly Count Top 10 1. Small white, 281,634 in total, +32% (change from average year) 2. Gatekeeper, 211,029, +50% 3. Large white 190,295, +19% 4. Red admiral 141,178, +39% 5. Meadow brown, 134,335, -15% 6. Painted lady, 85,508, +161% 7. Common blue, 54,430 -16% 8. Peacock, 54,414, +39% 9. Holly blue, 43,849, +128% 10. Small tortoiseshell, 33,123, -53%

title: Al-Qaida and IS-linked violence in Africa’s Sahel belt set to hit record levels this year
summary: Twenty-five years after 9/11, figures compiled by conflict monitor underline how Sahel region has become centre of Islamist terror
text: Islamist extremist violence in Africa’s Sahel region is set to reach historic highs after a series of sweeping offensives by groups linked to al-Qaida and Islamic State, according to new figures compiled by the conflict monitor Acled. As the US marks the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks launched by al-Qaida against targets in Washington and New York, the statistics underline the continued expansion of the veteran organisation in parts of Africa – in stark contrast with its relative weakness elsewhere. Compiled by Acled, which stands for Armed Conflict Location and Event Data, the statistics focus on the centre of Islamic militancy in three countries – Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger – which together comprise a huge and hotly contested zone at the heart of the strategic Sahel region. According to the respected non-profit organisation, incidents of violence with jihadist groups present in the three countries have soared from 63 in 2016 to 2,845 in 2025. So far this year, 2,145 events have already been logged. If current trends continue in coming months, an annual total of well over 3,000 events appears likely. Though total deaths from terrorism globally have fallen to their lowest level since 2008, those in the Sahel have risen sharply. “Terrorism has become more geographically concentrated: the Sahel continued to record some of the world’s highest terrorism death tolls, with the UN recording more than 9,000 deaths from security incidents across Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger in 2025,” the 2026 report of the Global Peace Index noted earlier this year. In April, a joint offensive in Mali launched by the al-Qaida-linked group Jama’at Nusrat ul-Islam wa al-Muslimin (JNIM) and the Tuareg-dominated rebel group Azawad Liberation Front (FLA) targeted strategic towns, government forces and their Russian auxiliaries with ambushes, car bombs, drones and raids, inflicting significant casualties. Mali’s defence minister died in a suicide attack on his residence in the garrison town of Kati, 9 miles north-west of the capital, Bamako, and the head of military intelligence was killed. Other attacks hit Mali’s international airport, while rebels seized control of the strategic city of Kidal, a former stronghold of the FLA, after soldiers fled and a force of Russian mercenaries surrendered. The defeat reversed a key symbolic victory won by the junta in Mali three years ago. Since then, JNIM has continued to expand areas under its control in Mali, killing more soldiers and Russian mercenaries in recent weeks, and broadening its operations in some neighbouring countries. Much of the violence involves fighting with rival groups. The conflict has also included multiple killings by government armed forces and Russian mercenaries. In Burkina Faso, JNIM has claimed more than 130 attacks in 2026, striking closer to Ouagadougou, the capital. In Niger, the group claimed at least 17 attacks but remained significantly less active than its rival Islamic State in the Greater Sahara, according to a recent United Nations report based on intelligence supplied by member states. Experts said JNIM had distanced itself from al-Qaida’s historic objectives of striking the US and its allies. “In the Sahel, Islamic State and al-Qaida now command big areas but these are very localised groups. Not a single attack in Europe or the US has been planned in the Sahel,” said Ulf Laessing, a senior analyst at the Konrad Adenauer foundation in Berlin. The other main group in sub-Saharan Africa with links to al-Qaida is al-Shabaab, which has dominated much of Somalia’s rural areas for many years. “In east Africa, al-Shabaab remains one of the continent’s deadliest groups, with Acled recording more than 10,000 reported deaths in al-Shabaab-related violence over the past 18 months,” said Peter Bofin, Acled’s senior analyst for south-east Africa. “Despite some degradation of its extortion in Mogadishu, its revenue streams stretch across the country, and the region.” Militant groups linked loosely to IS are active in the Democratic Republic of Congo, Mozambique, Chad and Nigeria, where they were targeted by US airstrikes last year. The continuing expansion in sub-Saharan Africa has been welcomed in al-Qaida’s propaganda, but experts point out the continent barely featured in the group’s strategic planning until recent years. “Twenty-five years ago it was all about Afghanistan and then Iraq … Africa wasn’t really of interest then. Now its the main area of operations,” said Laessing. Though sectarian and ethnic conflict, bitter competition over resources, poor governance, endemic instability and other factors make Africa a fertile ground for Islamic militant recruiters, territory in places like Mali and Somalia has major limitations as a base for campaigns elsewhere in the world or for long-range terrorist attacks. At its peak in the years after the 9/11 attacks, al-Qaida affiliates posed a significant threat to authorities across much of the Middle East, with thousands convinced by the group’s call for a global uprising against the US, Israel and local regimes. Al-Qaida was also able to inspire and direct a series of lethal attacks in Europe that killed hundreds. However, the recent UN report described al-Qaida senior leadership as “marginalised” and noted that the group’s capability and intent to conduct external operations remained “unclear”. Analysts point out there has been no formal declaration of a successor to Ayman al-Zawahiri, the veteran Egyptian militant killed in Kabul by the US in 2022. Instead, the de facto leader is believed to be 66-year-old Saif al-Adel, who is thought to have been in Iran since 2002 and has yet to make any public statement. Other leaders are likely to be based in Afghanistan, where the group has been able to rebuild a limited infrastructure, western intelligence services believe. The most potent al-Qaida affiliate outside Africa is the Yemen-based Al-Qaida in the Arabian Peninsula (AQAP), which the UN report described as “the vanguard of the global al-Qaida movement” and one of the few affiliates committed to continuing al-Qaida’s decades-old campaign against the US. In May, AQAP’s media channels released a new video calling on Muslims in Europe and the US to carry out local attacks and to fight on “behalf of the [Islamic community] in any way possible”. But though AQAP continues to maintain an estimated 2,000 fighters, largely entrenched in the mountains between Abyan and Shabwa, the group’s activity fell by approximately 70%, from 63 events in the first seven months of 2025 to 19 during the same period in 2026, according to Acled. Some analysts have contrasted the high numbers of militants currently mobilised by groups such as JNIM and al-Shabaab, which number in the tens of thousands, with the much more limited manpower available to al-Qaida before the 9/11 attacks. Others stress the very different intentions and capabilities of the group now and 25 years ago.

title: Wednesday briefing: Why tech companies might be only too happy for us to believe AI will ‘kill us all’
summary: In today’s newsletter: It is hard to tell fact from fiction when it comes to AI. What is really going on – and what should the government do about it?
text: Good morning. As a general rule, it pays to be suspicious of any gigantic company that claims it’s developing a tool capable of destroying humanity. But in recent days, a number of warnings from the AI industry have suggested that even tech insiders are starting to worry about what they have unleashed. In a lofty essay published on Saturday, Dario Amodei, the founder of Anthropic (the company behind Claude), argued that tech companies need to “slow” the pace at which they’re developing the newest and most sophisticated AI models. Elon Musk and Sam Altman, the head of OpenAI, voiced support for Amodei’s arguments, while Donald Trump, who has staked America’s economy on AI, described the worries as a “HOAX”, and insisted the only control on AI the world needs is a “STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT”. Yesterday, the UK government took out a more cautious position, when Louise Haigh, the first secretary of state, said the UK must “heed the warnings” of AI experts. It’s hard to know what to make of this. Tech companies often tell fanciful stories about the fearsome potential of their products to convince the public (and the stock market) of those capabilities. So what’s really going on? For this morning’s newsletter I spoke to Aisha Down, the Guardian’s global technology reporter, to try to parse the reality of AI from the unreality of the AI discourse, and to figure out what the government should do about it. No tall order, then. That’s after the headlines. Five big stories Lucy Letby | Three babies might have survived if hospital had acted upon concerns over Lucy Letby, an inquiry has found. Lady Justice Thirlwall condemned the ‘complete failure’ to protect babies on neonatal unit at Countess of Chester hospital. UK politics | The leader of Reform UK in Wales stood down after arrest on suspicion of assault. Dan Thomas, a former Tory councillor, was elected to Senedd as leader of the opposition in May. AI | The progressive senator Bernie Sanders and rightwing strategist Steve Bannon have called for restrictions on artificial intelligence (AI) but offered competing visions for what they termed a “cold war” with China. UK news | Young people in Rotherham face a local jobs market with the fewest suitable opportunities in Britain, according to a report that warns stark regional divisions are fuelling a crisis in youth work. Defence | John Healey is in talks with the Canadian government about joining a new global defence bank intended to help allies rearm to counter mounting security threats, just weeks after Rachel Reeves rejected the move. In depth: ‘If a nuclear company had a radioactive spill, you wouldn’t be letting it regulate itself’ The most significant detail in Amodei’s essay, We Must Pace The Frontier, was a reference to the Hugging Face incident, which occurred in July, when the rival tech company OpenAI revealed that an autonomous AI agent powered by its technology hacked a prominent database of AI models, Hugging Face. Coverage of the hack made it sound as though OpenAI’s model had gone “rogue”. But tech researchers have since said that OpenAI turned off the model’s safety mechanisms, gave it impossible tasks to complete and ran it 1,200 times. “That’s human decision-making,” the tech research Eryk Salvaggio wrote in an essay on Substack. OpenAI then invited researchers from the non-profit institute METR to produce a report about the incident. As two legal experts observed in an interesting opinion piece for the Guardian, METR’s findings were constrained by its agreement with OpenAI, which prohibited investigators from accessing the underlying model that created the “rogue” agents. “Imagine a burglar who is hallucinating and breaks into the Louvre,” says Aisha. “Then imagine you shared a tape with the police that played back what the hallucinating burglar was saying to himself while he broke into the Louvre, but the report didn’t actually include any information about what the burglar did. That’s basically what OpenAI did.” In his essay, Amodei pointed to the Hugging Face incident as an example of the “catastrophic damage” that AI could cause in future. But industry critics are sceptical about what this incident can tell us, particularly since the only people who have examined it did so at OpenAI’s discretion. This reflects a broader problem where companies that claim to be developing products capable of catastrophic damage get to mark their own homework. “No other industry gets treated that way,” Aisha says. “If a nuclear company had a radioactive spill, you wouldn’t be letting it regulate itself.” *** Is it all just hype? Amodei’s essay has been treated as a doomsday warning. It was published just two days after Jacob Coxon, a 27-year-old researcher at Anthropic, quit his job and posted an alarming thread on X warning that “the people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of this decade”. Coxon is the latest in a long list of AI researchers who have been loudly quitting on X or making similar predictions. These self-styled whistleblowers don’t tend to leak documents that reveal useful information about the inner workings of AI companies, so their warnings of imminent apocalypse instead fuel speculation about the perils (and power) of AI. This plays into tech companies’ hands. The AI narrative is dominated by what the tech scholar Lee Vinsel calls “criti-hype” – criticism that feeds, and is fed by, hype. The language used to describe AI can be deeply unhelpful. While China tends to compare AI to “electricity,” western AI companies compare it to the atom bomb, which makes Anthropic and its rivals seem less like companies making everyday decisions about how they choose to build particular tools, and more like Promethean stewards of a fourth Industrial Revolution. “The framing is, ‘we’re inventing fire’,” Aisha says. “And that means governments have to treat them like magical gods and let them set the rules on their mysterious creation.” *** So why are AI firms calling for a slowdown? Apparently, AI firms now believe the risks posed by their technologies are too great for business to continue as usual. But there are a number of ways that Anthropic (and its competitors) might gain from a slowdown. Anthropic is launching its initial public offering later this year, so it has an interest in presenting its products in as epochal and deadly a fashion as possible. The backlash against AI is growing, and the firm has cast itself as a more responsible AI creator, most recently by refusing the Pentagon’s requests to use its Claude model to power autonomous lethal weapons. Meanwhile, American AI firms face increasing competition from Chinese AI firms, and are desperate to retain their share of the market. An industry-orchestrated slowdown could freeze the pace of AI development in China and might also help firms like Anthropic avoid the possibility of stringent government regulations by putting them on the front foot. One of the people who has called this out is David Sacks, co-chair of Trump’s council of advisers on science and technology, who said in response to Amodei’s essay: “demanding your preferred regulatory framework … will look like blackmail of the public and the political system”. *** What should the UK government do? To be clear, AI poses huge risks. Readers of First Edition will know that we’ve previously covered how the datacentres used to power AI demand huge volumes of water and energy. You can already use AI to generate sexualised “deepfakes” and child sexual abuse images, or make use of an open-source version of Palantir to monitor live camera feeds (meanwhile, Palantir has access to identifiable NHS England data). And experts have long been arguing that as AI becomes more advanced, it could pose existential risks. All of these things are terrifying. But much of the AI narrative focuses on extinction-like events, the Terminator hypothesis, rather than dangers that are playing out right now. And many of the organisations that are supposed to make AI safer are closely aligned with the tech industry, such as Britain’s AI Security Institute, which receives funding from the industry, and doesn’t have the legal power to regulate AI or to compel developers to hand over their models. One of the institute’s co-founders, Matt Clifford, who lobbied for the government to loosen copyright laws, was recently forced to stand down from his role as chair of the UK’s Advanced Research and Invention Agency after taking a job with Anthropic … nice work if you can get it. Recently, I’ve notice a creeping sense of fatalism in my conversations with friends about AI. Nobody (aside perhaps from government) consented to the volumes of energy, resource and information being fed into the giant AI machine. But as Aisha makes clear, the design of technology is a choice, not an inevitability, so there’s an argument for stubborn resistance to the idea there’s no alternative. “We should be treating AI like any other industry, and regulating it like any other industry,” Aisha says. “Policy based on fear and vibes is just never going to work.” What else we’ve been enjoying The narrative that white women recognised the suffering of enslaved people and fought for abolition is challenged in the last instalment of our Enslaving Nation series, identifying the women who invested in transatlantic trafficking in pursuit of economic independence. title: Fresh evidence of C of E’s role in enslavement uncovered as church wrestles with reparations debate
summary: Register of British Slave Traders shows clergymen financed company that trafficked enslaved Africans on hundreds of voyages
text: Nearly 250 years after the abolitionist Ottobah Cugoano made the Christian case for reparative justice, the archbishop of Canterbury, Sarah Mullally, visited the Ghanaian shore where he was enslaved as a boy. After witnessing the dungeons beneath the chapel at Cape Coast Castle, once run by the Royal African Company (RAC), Mullally recommitted the Church of England to its “journey of repentance” for its role in slavery. Back in Britain, historians working on the newly digitised Register of British Slave Traders were uncovering evidence that C of E clergy financed the RAC, which trafficked more African men, women and children than any other single organisation in the history of the slave trade. The register, which documents investors in Britain’s nearly 250-year transatlantic slave trade, includes 45 C of E clergymen, whose investments helped fund hundreds of slaving voyages and a 1720 relaunch of the RAC. Among them was Henry Brydges, later a canon at St Paul’s Cathedral, who bought half of his £10,000 shareholding on the day he became the Archdeacon of Rochester. Prof William Pettigrew, who led the project, said the register showed a “truly national picture”. Profits from enslavement filtered down to communities “from Cumbria to the Cotswolds” through bequests to parishes – evidence of a history of the C of E “giving slavery its blessing” and raising fresh questions about whether the church is doing enough to atone. In 2023, church commissioners – the C of E’s asset managers – launched Project Spire, a £100m impact investment fund for communities affected by slavery’s legacies, which has caused division within the church. It is not a reparations fund, but is central to the church’s determination to be a force for justice and healing in the world. It was launched nearly 20 years after Rowan Williams, the former archbishop of Canterbury, rejected the idea that today’s church bears no responsibility for the past. However, Spire mainly responds to historic investments in the South Sea Company, which trafficked close to 45,000 enslaved Africans. That represents a “sliver of church complicity”, said Prof Alan Lester, a historical geographer at the University of Sussex. That complicity helped shape modern Britain, Lester said. Plantation profits helped fuel the Industrial Revolution, railways, public health, welfare, universities, schools, church building and the public finances. “Look at Anglican parishes in Jamaica, their ability to withstand climate change, and compare that with the wealth generated in Britain by the plantation complex,” he said. For the Rev Natasha Beckles, the dean of racial justice for Willesden, reckoning with this past goes to the heart of Christian faith. “What was the purpose of the cross if we’re not able to talk about this?” she said. “Slavery made the image of God transactional. There has to be an understanding of the impact on the world.” Dr Leona Vaughn of the University of Liverpool, a co-organiser of a 2025 Anglican “truth-telling” event, said: “The public and people within the church don’t even know the extent of the church’s involvement. “We’ve not even started to come to terms with the ‘Slave Bible’,” she said, a C of E-sanctioned, heavily edited Bible, stripped of liberation narratives, that planters used as a tool of social control from 1807. The history of the United Society Partners in the Gospel (USPG), the C of E’s 325-year-old missionary partner, shows how powerful Anglicans practised and perpetuated transatlantic chattel slavery – a uniquely racialised, violent system of human commodification and forced mass migration. Today, members of USPG – of which Mullally is president – have committed to “the gospel’s call to break every chain of injustice”. USPG’s forerunner, the Society for the Propagation of the Gospel in Foreign Parts (SPG), supplied chaplains to the RAC at Cape Coast Castle. For more than 120 years, with the involvement of C of E leaders, SPG enslaved people on the Codrington estate in Barbados, which generated the equivalent of £5m a year in today’s money. At Codrington, enslaved Africans were branded with the word “Society”, tortured with the lash, straitjacket and iron collar, and worked to death. In seven months in 1746, 19 enslaved people died – including Daniel, who was “shot by accident” – with three deaths in a single day. Pettigrew said the “clear signal” sent by the C of E’s relationship with Codrington was “if the church is doing it, why shouldn’t I?” After abolition, SPG and at least 96 clergy who enslaved people received millions in compensation for “loss of property”. In 2023, USPG launched its own £7m reparative justice programme. Christian collusion can be traced back to a 1452 papal bull authorising the enslavement of non-Christians, the author Malik Al Nasir said. He wants the C of E to digitise its records in the UK and the Caribbean. In the 17th century, John Cotton, a former Lincolnshire vicar, co-drafted a charter legalising slavery in New England. By the 1750s, high churchmen were codifying pro-slavery ideology: Thomas Newton, later the dean of St Paul’s Cathedral, argued Africans were destined to be “servants of servants”, while Thomas Francklin, later the chaplain to George III, said: “We use [African] bodies for our support and happiness.” Some Anglican voices did oppose slavery. Condemning it in 1685, the preacher Morgan Godwyn said: “We have … conspired with Satan.” Project Spire’s critics have instead focused on the legacy of Anglican abolitionist MPs, such as William Wilberforce. Wilberforce’s 1823 anti-slavery petition was followed by his colleague Sir Thomas Fowell Buxton acknowledging that “we owe a large and liberal atonement”. In his 1787 book, Cugoano – who won his freedom in England – wrote that the injustice done to Africans “cries aloud for universal reformation and national repentance”. He drew on biblical scriptures such as Numbers, Leviticus, Exodus and Deuteronomy that included reparative principles. Class shaped church complicity, Beckles said. “The oldest child got the land, the second child they put in the church, the third was sent to the Caribbean.” That meant, Al Nasir said, that “one sibling could profit from slavery while another absolved it – the right hand washing the left”. Enslaved African Christian leaders helped force the issue of abolition – including Samuel Sharpe, the deacon executed for leading Jamaica’s 1831-32 Baptist war. The posthumously published Demerara diaries of the English Methodist the Rev John Smith also educated the British public about the relentless beatings, toil and meagre diet – raw yellow plantains – endured by enslaved Africans. Smith’s preaching was blamed by Anglican planters for Guyana’s 1823 Demerara rebellion. He died awaiting execution. The moral conviction of English non-conformists – such as Smith and Quaker abolitionists – contrasts with the 45 C of E clergymen in the register. The C of E already has an impact investment fund, so insiders have expressed surprise at the backlash against Spire, which is facing a legal challenge. In the House of Commons in September, the MP Marsha de Cordova, the second church estates commissioner, rebutted claims from rightwing critics that Spire diverts money from English churches. She said the church regarded historic links to slavery with profound regret, that Spire is funded from the commissioners’ own income rather than parish collections, and that the English ministry would receive £1.6bn over three years. A 2023 report estimated Britain’s slavery debt at £18.6tn. For Beckles, no sum could be enough. “What do you say to a mother who has had her child taken from her? To talk about a figure is grotesque,” she said. “For that level of human suffering, you’d be writing a blank cheque.” In 2023, the Scott Trust, the Guardian’s sole owner, published research showing that the founder of the Manchester Guardian and his backers profited from the enslavement of African people in Jamaica and the US. In response, the Scott Trust launched the Cotton Capital series and the Legacies of Enslavement programme, a 10-year restorative justice initiative.

title: People protecting nature and land set up self-defence units amid threat of murder
summary: Defenders of forests and rivers killed at rate of one every three days in 2025, with 85% of deaths in Latin America
text: Nature and land defenders were murdered at the rate of one every three days last year, prompting many communities to set up self-defence units, according to the latest annual death toll by the independent watchdog Global Witness. Organised crime groups or professional killers were implicated in more than a third of the 124 killings of defenders in 2025 as narco-trafficking activities overlapped with intrusions into indigenous territories and environmental crime, such as illegal logging and wildcat gold mining. This was particularly true in Latin America, which accounted for 85% of last year’s deaths of people trying to protect forests, rivers and other ecosystems. Colombia had the highest toll with 39 killings, followed by Brazil with 26 and Honduras with 12. In Asia, the most dangerous country for defenders was the Philippines, with 12 killings – many during crackdowns by state security forces. Since Global Witness began compiling statistics in 2012, the overall global tally is now 2,375 deaths and disappearances – on a par with a small-scale war. On a more positive note, the headline figure has declined over the last two years, from 196 in 2023 and 142 in 2024, though the report authors say this is likely to be an underestimate because data collection is difficult in war zones and authoritarian regimes. Many countries and companies are also carrying out nonlethal attacks on defenders, including criminalisation and online smear campaigns. Many defenders are now exposed to more organised crime with less assistance from the international community, partly as a result of cuts by the Trump administration. “The dismantling of USAID, which previously supported initiatives for Indigenous peoples to steward their own land, has had particularly serious implications for defenders,” the report says. Almost three-quarters of the killings documented in 2025 were of Indigenous people and small-scale farmers targeted for defending their land. With less outside help, an increasing number of these communities are establishing their own territorial defence mechanisms. The report highlights the example of the Kakataibo Indigenous Guard in the Peruvian Amazon. Six of the community’s leaders have been killed since 2020 amid growing incursions into the forest by criminal groups. Starting in 2022 with a few dozen recruits, the guard now has more than 150 volunteers in its 10 bases. Segundo Ispón, the commander of the organisation, said the self-defence groups provided a global benefit: “Defending our territory is important to us as a community and as a people, and we’re proud to support the climate that we all depend on. In our culture, the work of defending our resources and territory is taught from an early age. But for this next generation coming up, the work is more dangerous than ever.” At least a dozen other communities in Peru have organised self-defence units. Similar bodies have existed for some years in Colombia and Brazil. But it is risky. Last year, seven Indigenous guards were murdered. In at least five of these cases, the killings were linked to organised crime. Many forest communities report the narco-threat is growing closer. In July, Asháninka leaders on the Brazilian border with Peru petitioned the government for help after armed and masked men entered their homes, apparently in search of assassination targets. In the Ucayali basin on the other side of the border, Global Witness said there was a 600% increase in coca production between 2019 and 2023. This is pushing gangs to expand smuggling networks, including through the opening of illegal roads and trails through the forest. Corruption further adds to the risks facing forest protectors who stand in their way because many local politicians and police are in the pay of the traffickers. Forest communities want help from governments to ease these pressures but there are concerns the opposite may be happening. Under US leadership, many rightwing governments are pursuing military crackdowns on coca growers and drug traffickers, which is pushing narco-gangs further into remote regions and indigenous territories. Ricardo Soberón, a former head of Peru’s anti-narcotics office, said many communities were also affected on the border of Peru and Colombia. “We are in a situation where transnational criminal groups have appropriated the daily life of the Huitoto, Quichua, Bora, Secoya Indigenous people, who live along the Putumayo basin,” he said. Of particular concern, he added, were the threats against local leaders, environmental defenders and human rights activists who call for a more effective state presence. He fears the newly elected rightwing governments in affected countries will make matters worse by militarising the conflict in line with the “America shield” priorities of the Trump administration. Global Witness has urged the authorities to respect and work with nature and land defenders rather than making their role more difficult. Toby Hill, the lead author of the report, said: “Defenders are the world’s eyes and ears on the ground. It’s thanks to them that we know when ecosystems are being destroyed, where forests are being cleared or rivers polluted. We can’t forget the thousands of defenders around the world who are working every day to protect their territories and cultures under increasing pressure.”

title: Plantwatch: The insect-eating alpine plant that proves Darwin was right
summary: Study shows alpine plant traps and digests midges – just as the evolutionary biologist predicted back in 1875
text: In 1875, Charles Darwin predicted that Saxifraga candelabrum, a small alpine plant, could eat insects. Its leaves, petals and stems are smothered in tiny, sticky hairs and – just as the evolutionary biologist suspected – the sweet glue on the hairs can lure and trap midges before digesting them with an enzyme. The nitrogen from their remains is absorbed into the plant, which is essential for it to survive in the nutrient-poor soils of the Hengduan mountains in south-west China. The plant was also found to have genes related to those found in carnivorous plants. The study findings may point to other killer plants that trap insects with sticky hairs and feed off their remains. The leaves of the wild potatoes Solanum berthaultii and Solanum polyadenium are covered in sticky hairs and trap aphids and some other small pests, potentially opening the way to combine pest control with plant fertiliser. Other sticky-haired plants may follow a similar approach, according to a study in the Botanical Journal of the Linnean Society.

title: Country diary: Drama on the trail cam – this is Somerset’s version of a snow leopard | Derek Niemann
summary: Frome: We’ve been trying to help out struggling hedgehogs, and finally we have a sighting. But how long should we intervene for?
text: Deep into the night, and out of our sight, tiny claws rake over plastic. The animal skitters halfway through a pipe, then stops. A hunter five times its weight is on its tail, but it is safe from harm, and not just because the tunnel is too narrow for the hunter to enter. Curiosity killed the cat’s predatory thoughts with a face full of prickles a long time ago. The cat sniffs the tube, and wanders off. Until this summer, we had never laid eyes on our hedgehogs, not once in two years. Moist poos glistening with beetle shells told us they were here. But lawns like crispy seaweed, beds full of papered flowers, and reports of dehydrated waifs made us worried for them. Water baths slaked a thirst, but where were the invertebrates, the crunch of a carapace, a slug smoothie? A reputable website advised us to feed hedgehogs cat food and beetles. We have six cats using our garden as their public convenience – should it be their takeaway too? As for the beetles, if an insectivorous mammal can’t find any, how could we? At the beginning of August, our car left a DIY store looking equipped for a motorised joust, with a three-metre lance (aka drainpipe) thrust out of the front passenger window. Every night since, dinner has been served in a foil tray, down the pipe, cut to a third of its length but still beyond cat reach. Every morning, the tray is found nudged out the other end, empty. Our trail camera has captured all this, giving us Somerset’s answer to the snow leopard, live action photos of the otherwise unseen. It has recorded entrances and exits, both to the food pipe and the garden itself, slipping between slats at the front, or slotting through the purpose‑made hog hole in the fence at the back. And here the comedy ends. We’ll stop this supplementary feeding in time for hibernation, but how will hedgehogs fare next summer and in summers to come? Must we manage the emergency for as long as it takes them to adapt and evolve? Will they? • Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024, is available now at guardianbookshop.com

title: UK mathematician debunks myth around Parthenon’s optical illusions
summary: Study challenges belief that temple’s curves were designed to correct optical illusions that would have ruined its clean lines
text: A mathematician has uncovered what may be one of the longest-running myths in history after studying optical illusions and the Parthenon, the famed Greek temple that overlooks Athens. Scholars have marvelled at the building on the Acropolis hill for more than 2,000 years and heaped praise on its architects for their clever use of geometry. Its subtle curves are said to correct optical illusions that would have otherwise ruined the Parthenon’s clean lines. But after a detailed investigation, and a flurry of mathematical modelling, Prof Alain Goriely at the University of Oxford has reached an awkward conclusion. The optical illusions the curves are meant to fix are either nonsense or practically imperceptible. In short, the illusions are themselves an illusion. In his study, Goriely traces the myth back to the 1st-century Roman architect and engineer Vitruvius who wrote about the Parthenon 400 years after its construction. His account found its way into architectural books and became established fact. Today’s AI chatbots still churn out the tale. “I do think it might be the oldest myth that we have,” Goriely said, “apart from religion.” A common claim that the mathematician challenges concerns the Parthenon’s base or stylobate. Measurements show the sides of the base are not horizontal but form a gentle arc that rises 6cm in the centre. According to Vitruvius, this corrects an illusion that would make the base appear to sag in the middle. The sagging effect has been attributed to two proposed tricks of the light. The first states that long horizontal lines simply seem to slump in the middle, but Goriely found no evidence for this. The second suggests that the Parthenon’s marble columns create the illusion. This is based on the Hering illusion where parallel lines on a 2D sheet can look bowed when other lines intersect them. But the Hering illusion is strongest when the intersecting lines are at acute angles. The columns at the Parthenon are too vertical to produce the illusion, and there is no proof it even works in 3D, Goriely said. Another claim is that the bulges in the Parthenon’s columns – a curvature called entasis – corrects an optical illusion that would make them look too narrow in the middle. Again, Goriely found no evidence for the illusion. Moreover, the columns at the Parthenon bulge by a mere 18mm, which is barely perceptible at typical viewing distances. Goriely, who assesses and dismisses other supposed “optical corrections” in his paper concedes he “fell into a bit of a rabbit hole” pulling all the evidence together. He suspects the Parthenon’s architects had other reasons for the architectural features. The curve of the base may have prevented rain puddles forming and curved columns might simply have felt more organic and visually pleasing to the ancient Greeks, he writes in Royal Society Open Science. It is unclear why the myth has endured for so long, but Goriely suspects that the perception of ancient Greece as a supremely knowledgeable and ingenious civilisation is partly to blame. Unusually for an academic study, Goriely ends his paper by inviting readers to put it down and take a walk in a city. “Trust your own eyes, question what you see and decide for yourself whether the theory of optical corrections holds up,” he writes. Frank Salmon, professor of the history of classical architecture at the University of Cambridge, said: “Some experts have long been cautious of Vitruvius’s explanations, recognising the risks inherent in using his text as a sort of bible to explain architectural practices in Greece centuries before his time, but also the loss of the many Greek texts about their temple architecture he claimed to have read when preparing his own.”
