title: Airlines should pay for CO2 removal if Heathrow expands, say climate advisers
summary: Climate Change Committee says government cannot expand airport without requiring aviation industry to clean up its emissions
text: Heathrow airport should be allowed to expand only if airlines pay for the removal of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, the government’s climate advisers have said. Building a third runway and new terminals, as some in government want to do, would breach the UK’s carbon budgets and make reaching net zero by 2050 impossible, on current policies, according to the Climate Change Committee. The “only way” to manage such expansion within the UK’s climate commitments was for the aviation industry to become more efficient, use an increasing proportion of “sustainable aviation fuels” (SAF) in place of fossil fuels, and pay for the permanent removal and storage of carbon from the atmosphere. Nigel Topping, the chair of the CCC, said: “The government cannot expand Heathrow airport without requiring the aviation industry to clean up its emissions. Therefore, the government should legislate policies that require the aviation industry to fully address all of their emissions by 2050, either directly or by purchasing engineered removals. The polluter-pays principle must apply.” In a report to the government on Wednesday, the CCC found that the costs of SAF and carbon removal would probably be passed on to passengers by airlines, adding an estimated £150 to the price of a return flight to Alicante by 2050, or about £400 to the price of a flight to New York. These costs would be phased in gradually over 25 years. But campaigners rejected the CCC’s plan of relying on nascent technologies to wipe out the impact of an expansion that would commit the UK to much higher emissions for decades, and called on ministers to halt all airport expansion. Tony Bosworth, campaigner at Friends of the Earth, accused the CCC of “pulling its punches”, pointing to recent research by the Tyndall Centre that found SAF and carbon removals were unproven and unlikely to ramp up in time to the extent needed to justify airport expansion. “The CCC should have made it crystal clear: there is no plausible way to expand Heathrow without wrecking the UK’s climate targets,” he said. Frequent flying is overwhelming skewed towards the wealthy. In any year, only about half of people in England take a flight abroad, while about 80% of all flights abroad were taken by people who took two or more flights – about a quarter of the population. Frequent flyers – those who took five or more return flights abroad in 2024 – made up only 5% of the population, but accounted for a third of all flights. Those in the highest income group took 38% of all flights abroad – four times as many flights as those in the lowest income group, according to the National Travel Survey of England in 2024. The CCC said policies to force airlines to take responsibility for cleaning up their emissions should take these inequalities into account, but stopped short of recommending a frequent flyer levy. The rise in demand for flying since the Covid pandemic threatens to raise carbon emissions around the world. Separate research by the campaign group Transport&Environment has found that planned expansions at 20 of Europe’s biggest airports, including Heathrow, would breach EU and national carbon limits, even if the planes using them were more efficient and partly powered by sustainable aviation fuel. James Richardson, director of analysis at the CCC, said the past three decades of growth in the aviation industry and the likely increase in future demand meant it was “too big” to rely on other sectors to cut their emissions, allowing flying to take up more space within the UK’s carbon budgets. Aviation now produces more carbon than the UK’s electricity generation, and passenger demand has nearly tripled from 100 million passengers in 1990 to 300 million in 2025. It now makes up 9% of the UK’s emissions, and will be one of the two top emitting sectors, along with agriculture, by 2050. A spokesperson for Heathrow said: “Heathrow expansion cannot be a choice between economic growth and net zero – it must deliver both. The CCC’s assessment does not change this and acknowledges that the key solutions exist today. We will continue working with government and partners across the aviation sector to ramp up today’s proven technologies, while examining options for how the billions of pounds passengers already pay in carbon taxes can be used to support this.” But Tim Alderslade, chief executive of industry body Airlines UK, claimed the CCC’s approach was not affordable and would “put holidays out of reach for millions, turning the clock back to a time when flying was the preserve of the rich”. He said: “You can’t solve the climate crisis by pricing Britain out of the skies. The answer is affordable SAF – already cutting emissions since the mandate began – airspace reform by 2035 for more direct routes and scaled-up carbon removals.” The government is not obliged to follow the advice of the CCC, which was set up under the 2008 Climate Change Act to draw up five-yearly carbon budgets. Topping said that if consent was granted to Heathrow without legislation in place to force the industry to clean up its emissions, “there will be a big red light flashing” in the CCC’s report to parliament. Responding to the CCC’s findings, a spokesperson for the UK’s Department for Transport said: “Any expansion proposal [for Heathrow] would need to align with our net zero targets. We’re investing £219m in sustainable aviation fuel production and a further £43m in cleaner technologies to support greener aviation, while expansion could deliver around £40bn to the economy and support up to 60,000 local jobs.”

title: Students in Gaza ‘devastated’ after plan for them to study in Belgium fails
summary: Belgian government unable to agree on evacuation of 13 students to take up scholarships at universities
text: Students who are unable to leave Gaza and take up scholarships at Belgian universities have said they are devastated after Belgium’s government hit deadlock on a plan enabling them to leave the war-torn territory. Ahmed Abujami, a 28-year-old doctor in Gaza, said he was “deeply disappointed” after Belgium’s five-party coalition government last Friday failed to agree on an evacuation plan for 13 students and researchers in the territory. Abujami has a scholarship to do a one-year master’s degree in public health at the Institute of Tropical Medicine in Antwerp. He hopes to gain skills and experience to rebuild Gaza’s shattered health system. “I was devastated by the failure to reach an agreement on Friday,” he told the Guardian via a messaging app. “We have already lost so much because of the war and now we are facing the possibility of losing another academic year.” Like many of the 12 other students, he is unable to apply for a visa to Belgium, which can only be done in person in Jerusalem or Cairo, but is blocked from leaving the Gaza Strip. He said: “We are 13 students who followed every rule, went through a strict academic selection process and earned scholarships to study in Belgium. We have nothing to do with the political disagreements surrounding our case.” Salwa Abu Elhaj, a 23-year-old graduate, still hopes to take up her place to study communications sciences at KU Leuven, but said “with every passing day, that hope becomes more difficult. I have worked very hard for this opportunity and it is heartbreaking to see it becoming uncertain because of circumstances that are completely outside my control.” She lives in central Gaza in a tent with her family, after their home was destroyed and she was forced to move several times. “There is constant uncertainty about safety, food, water, electricity, communication and even what will happen the next day.” Ahmed Alsalibi, a 39-year-old computer science professor, said the failure of Belgium’s government to reach an agreement had been “painful” for the group. In May 2024, he was awarded a fellowship at the Free University of Brussels (ULB). He hopes to develop artificial intelligence-aided systems that can be used one day in Gaza to help with the efficient dispatch of ambulances and emergency vehicles. He said his visa has been approved, but he must collect it in person in Cairo, Jordan or Jerusalem. “We hope that the [Belgian] government in the end will decide to help us.” The support the students are seeking is not unprecedented. Italy and the UK are among European countries that have negotiated with Israel and neighbouring countries to enable the evacuation of researchers and students in the last year. The Guardian has seen official letters confirming the scholarships and, in Abujami’s case, emails denying requests for remote application for a visa. Rectors from seven of the academic institutions involved published a joint article on Monday saying they were outraged by the outcome. “The moral compass of some government partners is missing,” the group wrote in De Standaard. “These students are not illegal migrants. They were selected for a competitive scholarship by independent selection committees,” they said. Belgium’s government, an eclectic five-party coalition led by the Flemish nationalist prime minister, Bart De Wever, failed to reach an agreement on a plan to evacuate the 13 students last Friday. Maxime Prévot, one of Belgium’s deputy leaders and foreign minister, announced he was withdrawing a proposal to evacuate the students. He said it had been “completely rejected” by one coalition partner – understood to be the New Flemish Alliance party – “unless we were prepared to make concessions on returns to Afghanistan and return hubs”. “Faced with this attempt to hold one issue hostage to another at the expense of people already living in misery I chose to withdraw my proposal. Dignity is not for sale.” Belgium’s asylum and migration minister, Anneleen Van Bossuyt, opposes entry for the 13 students, without stronger action to ensure people without the right to stay in Belgium leave the country. She wants to see returns to Afghanistan of convicted criminals and other measures to strengthen deportations of irregular migrants. She has been vocal in her opposition to the students’ entry, arguing it would lead to “a domino effect” if they seek to bring family members or request asylum in Belgium. Van Bossuyt, a member of the New Flemish Alliance party says the evacuation would set a precedent for other countries. “Why wouldn’t that apply to people from Yemen or Sudan? Or why not Afghan girls who want to study here?,” she told the public broadcaster VRT earlier this month. Van Bossuyt is expected to make a statement on the issue in the Belgian parliament on Wednesday. Her spokesperson declined to comment ahead of this event. Writing in De Standaard, the seven rectors say they do not understand the minister’s reasoning, noting the students have scholarships to cover living expenses and are motivated to return home. “The courses they are coming to take align with what Gaza will need for reconstruction. After their studies, they want to return there for that purpose.” The academic leaders say they continue to press for a solution, adding: “The doors of our lecture halls remain open.” But with the academic year under way in some universities, the Gaza students are left watching time slip away. “Our universities are waiting for us, our academic year is already moving forward and every day we remain trapped in Gaza puts our futures at greater risk,” Abujami said.

title: ‘My future is in the EU’: the Ukrainian children who don’t want to go home
summary: Thousands of children in state care were evacuated when Russia invaded. Kyiv wants them back – but many resist
text: When he first arrived in his new home in a small village in the Italian Alps in March 2022, 15-year-old Denys* says he felt homesick and confused. He had been put on an overnight bus and relocated along with more than 100 other children from his orphanage in Berdiansk, in eastern Ukraine, which was one of the first areas to be invaded by Russian troops. “Ukraine was all I knew,” says Denys. “I had never left it my whole life.” But after he began going to school, making friends and integrating into Italian life, Denys says he no longer wanted to go back home. “I started to realise there was a different way of life I could be living,” he says. “One that didn’t involve airstrikes and poverty, and that could give me better opportunities for my future.” Thousands of Ukrainian social orphans – children given up to the state or taken away from parents considered unable to care for them – were evacuated overseas after Russia’s invasion in 2022. The relocation was meant to be temporary, but even after the situation stabilised in parts of Ukraine, many of them, such as Denys, refused to return. Ukrainian officials have repatriated most of the children, but more than 1,500 remain elsewhere in Europe. Some – like Denys – have been aided by Italian courts after their foster parents in Italy defied Kyiv’s repatriation order, citing concerns regarding the children’s wellbeing in a war-torn country with heavily damaged social welfare and public infrastructure. For Ukraine, already battling a plummeting birthrate and the loss of children abducted by Russia in occupied territories, the failure of some juveniles to return home has become a crisis. Kateryna Rashevska, a legal expert on war crimes against children in Ukraine, says: “We are losing those who should’ve been the future citizens of our nation. If these children ever actually return to Ukraine, they will have limited Ukrainian language, culture, history and identity, which also poses a threat to our future heritage and demography.” The situation escalated in April after a 15-year-old boy who had been evacuated to Italy in 2022 was legally adopted by an Italian family, despite having parents and two sisters back in Ukraine who wanted him to return home. A court in Italy overruled Ukrainian laws – in May 2022, shortly after the war started, Ukraine had suspended international adoptions to prevent trafficking or wrongful adoptions. Yuliya Donnichenko, a Ukrainian national based in Italy who has overseen evacuations to southern Italy and repatriations back to Ukraine for about 100 orphans, says there have been many childless couples who she sensed were taking advantage of the unstable situation to bypass strict international adoption laws and get a Ukrainian child. “I know that they meant the best for these kids, that they became attached to them and wanted the best for their future, away from a war-torn nation. But what they don’t understand is that by [seeking adoption] they’re putting at risk an already fragile situation,” she says. “It might not seem like a lot – just a few more hundreds compared with the already 20,000 lost to Russia – but to us every child counts. It’s the future of our nation.” Some accuse Ukraine of not being prepared to offer stable conditions and a fair future to a new generation, with the reality of return for many of the children different from what they were promised. Evelina, now 18, was repatriated after almost two years spent with an Italian foster family in Sicily, and was assigned to an adoptive Ukrainian family on the border with Romania. The family already had several foster children under their care, making her living conditions “not much different from living in an orphanage”, she says. Evelina says that when she returned home, she had her phone confiscated for more than a year, as she was not allowed to be in touch with the Italian family who hosted her throughout her stay there. “I was confined at home and didn’t go to school. I would only leave my room for an English class once a week or church on Sunday,” she says. “I felt very depressed; I didn’t understand why they made me return to live like this.” When she was finally given a new phone in autumn 2024, Evelina says she managed to open a Telegram account and spent hours talking to her Italian foster mother – the only mental escape from otherwise long, boring days. “I missed her. I constantly begged her to come pick me up and bring me back to Sicily,” she says. Evelina says her new family would record videos of her going up and down the street outside her home, as proof of her doing a minimum amount of exercise and getting out of the house. After she shared her concerns with the Italian family, Evelina’s phone was confiscated again, and her WhatsApp and Telegram accounts were permanently deleted. Now she is 18, Evelina says she cannot wait to leave Ukraine and return to the EU: “It made no sense to force our return since most of us had planned to leave anyway after turning 18, thanks to the connections we developed in Europe. “After all,” she says. “It was unfair to pretend we’d just get a quick taste of freedom in Europe and then head back to a place that can’t offer us as much as an EU country can right now.” Denys says he and almost 100 orphans evacuated to Rota d’Imagna, in the hills of Bergamo, received their repatriation order from Kyiv in August 2024. He was 17 at the time of the call to return, which meant that setting foot in Ukraine for him – as well as other boys in his age range – could mean being drafted into the war. “I was utterly frightened, but the authorities didn’t listen to our concerns,” he says. During one-on-one meetings in Italy with the orphans supposed to return, Denys says Ukrainian social workers would use “intimidating language and even swearwords if we showed any signs of resistance”, with younger ones “promised candies and PlayStations on their arrival in Ukraine”. He says: “They would use any possible, misleading argument to convince us to accept the return. They promised us we’d be adopted or reunited with family relatives we still had back home. All fake promises they couldn’t guarantee for sure.” With the help of Italian courts, Denys managed to stay in Italy, where he now works as a waiter and hopes to remain for the foreseeable future. He says those who ended up returning tell him they regret the choice, and that many stay not with adoptive parents but at institutions where there is no running water or electricity, and where up to six people live in the same room. He says they regularly have to hide in bunkers, as even western provinces in Ukraine are targeted by Russian attacks. “This proves that they didn’t have our best interests and safety at heart,” he says. Maksym, another orphan from the Rota d’Imagna group, said he reluctantly accepted repatriation, only to move to Germany three months later when he turned 18. “Ukraine changed too much over the past few years. There’s nothing for us young people there. My future is in the EU.” Diego Mosca, who supervised the group of Ukrainian orphans in Rota d’Imagna, says the children had been “tossed around like a tennis ball between two sides” by the repatriation dispute. “This situation has traumatised them and will forever leave wounds on their psyche. Providing mental health support to those who returned should be a priority over demographic needs.” * Name changed to protect identity Reporting for this article was supported by grants from IJ4EU and Journalismfund Europe

title: Saudi Arabia warns of ‘red line’ after Houthi drone intercepted close to holy city of Mecca
summary: Iran-aligned group rejects claim it targeted Mecca, while Organisation of Islamic Cooperation condemns attack
text: Saudi Arabia has claimed its air defences intercepted and destroyed a ⁠Houthi drone attempting to fly over the holy city of Mecca, as Saudi warplanes continued to pound Yemen, raising fears of the conflict spreading further across the Middle East. The Saudi-led military coalition said the security of Mecca – home to Islam’s two holiest sites – was a “red line” and that it would take necessary measures against the ⁠Houthis. The Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen have been attacking Saudi Arabian territory, oil pipelines and shipping but denied targeting Mecca. “The claims about targeting Mecca are a worn-out lie that has been used before and no longer fools anyone,” said the spokesperson Hazem al-Assad. Violence continued to spread in the aftermath of the Houthis’ significant territorial gains in Yemen last week. On Wednesday, the Houthis claimed that Saudi warplanes were carrying out intensive airstrikes on Yemen, with the group’s military spokesperson saying as many as 450 airstrikes had been carried out ‌this week. The group claimed to have shot down a Saudi F-15 fighter jet. Riyadh has yet to comment. The Houthis have seized control of parts of ⁠Yemen’s Red Sea coast overlooking the Bab al-Mandab, one of the world’s most important shipping waterways, threatening Saudi oil exports rerouted from the strait of Hormuz. The Houthis have also taken control of highly strategic islands in the Bab al-Mandab strait. The rebel group ‌has fired repeatedly into Saudi Arabia over the past week, causing alarms over cities in the south and west, and Saudi Arabia issued security alerts across parts of the country on Tuesday, including in Mecca. The conflict has already led to a severe disruption in oil supplies. Last week, an attack blamed on Iran-aligned fighters in Iraq knocked out Saudi Arabia’s east-west pipeline, the main route used to divert exports away from the blockaded strait of Hormuz. The escalating attacks on Saudi Arabia have fuelled fears that more Muslim nations could be drawn into the violence spreading across the Middle East. In August, a defence pact – referred to as the Mecca joint defence agreement – was signed between Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan, which declared that any attack against one country would be “regarded as an attack against them all”. On Wednesday, the Pakistani prime minister, Shehbaz Sharif, joined the condemnation of the drone attack on Mecca and said his country and the Saudis stand “unwaveringly, shoulder to shoulder”. Pakistan has already deployed its forces and military aircraft to airbases in Saudi Arabia under a previous joint defence agreement. However, ministers from Pakistan and Turkey said they had not received a request from Riyadh for support in response to the Houthis’ escalation. Pakistan and Turkey have emphasised that the Mecca pact is still not fully operational and that further efforts were needed to “institutionalise” the alliance The Organisation of Islamic Cooperation also condemned what they called a “heinous” attack on Islam’s holy city, blaming the Houthis. The group – which is made up of 57 Muslim-majority countries – decried the “ongoing aggression against the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia”. Saudi Arabia has ⁠led a coalition battling the Houthis since 2015. The conflict had largely quietened under a ceasefire in recent years, but reignited when the Houthis declared a naval blockade against Saudi Arabia in July and fired at southern areas in the kingdom, and significantly escalated this month. The US also indicated a lack of desire to get involved in the conflict. “The Houthis called us, and they don’t want to fight with us,” the US president, Donald Trump, said on Saturday. On Wednesday, the US tightened its travel warning for Saudi Arabia, banning government employees from travelling within 20 miles of the Yemen border.

title: Singapore pays people to pick up a book in battle against doomscrolling
summary: Affluent city-state hopes plan will improve critical thinking and imagination ‘in a world of extraordinary abundance of stimulation’
text: Singapore is paying its citizens to pick up a book for at least 15 minutes a day in an effort to fight the rise of doomscrolling. The affluent city-state hopes its gamification strategy, which launched this month, will improve concentration, critical thinking and the imagination of Singaporeans. Under the scheme, readers accrue points that can be redeemed for a few cents. People will have to log 50 daily reading sessions on a government website to earn S$1 (80c). A session of 15 minutes or more is rewarded with 20 virtual coins, with 1,000 coins needed for a dollar payment. One reading session is allowed daily. The national library board’s chief, Melissa Tam, said sustainable reading habits were built through small and achievable steps. “We live in a world of extraordinary abundance, of content, information and stimulation,” she told the Straits Times. “At any moment, we can scroll through hundreds of headlines, watch a video or get a summary of almost anything. “We know that habits are built through small, consistent actions. So, we are starting with a simple goal: just read for 15 minutes a day. On the bus, before bed or over lunch.” The government is considering ways to make social media less harmful for young Singaporeans, including a daily time limit. Doomscrolling and addiction caused most harm to young people, a recent study found. It is not uncommon for the Singapore government to use financial incentives to try to influence the behaviour of its citizens. Previous health-focused initiatives have included supermarket vouchers for walking and prizes for hitting daily step targets. Despite government concerns about reading, Singapore’s 15-year-old students recently topped the world rankings for reading in the 2025 Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA), beating China and Taiwan.

title: Human remains found in Arizona after deadly Grand Canyon flash floods
summary: Hiker Timothy Smith, 53, missing after late-August floods but officials decline to identify remains
text: Human remains have been discovered near Arizona’s Crystal Rapids, over two weeks after a flash flood tore through the Grand Canyon, leaving two people dead and one person missing. National Park Service personnel recovered the remains, before transferring them to the Coconino county medical examiner’s office, the agency confirmed over email. In late August, heavy rains brought a deluge of flood water barreling through the Grand Canyon national park. The bodies of a Texas chiropractor and a martial artist were recovered, according to the Associated Press. One hiker, Timothy Smith, a 53-year-old pilot from Wyoming, is unaccounted for. The National Park Service did not identify who the remains belonged to, adding that no further information would be available at this time. A Facebook account appearing to belong to the wife of the missing pilot, Carrie Smith, acknowledged the discovery of human remains. “We ask that you continue to pray alongside us! Please be considerate of those handling the situation and those going through this difficult time,” Smith wrote in a Tuesday post. In earlier Facebook posts, Smith described her husband as an outdoors aficionado. “Tim loves to show us somewhere new and take us back to the places we love,” she wrote. “We know the search teams are working hard to bring Tim home to us.”

title: Ukraine war briefing: New anti-drone weapon scores hit amid race against Shahed jets
summary: Ukraine’s 3rd Army Corps announces Vivaldi counter-offensive is recapturing Russian-held territory. What we know on day 1,666
text: “Today, there is good news about interceptors against jet-powered Shaheds,” Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in his Tuesday evening address as he spoke about efforts to counter newer, faster Russian suicide drones. A new interceptor managed to shoot one down, Zelenskyy said, without giving further details. “It’s a Ukrainian development and it scored a hit, ⁠the Shahed was destroyed.” He added: “Some technical things still need to ‌be refined.” Ukraine’s military said its forces downed 187 airborne targets overnight into Tuesday – Zelenskyy said “of course more is needed”. Ukraine has struggled to develop interceptors for the jet-engined Shahed drones that Russia has started using, which can go faster than 400km/h. Previously, Shaheds were all propeller-driven and half as fast. Reuters reports that tests of interceptors have been hampered by the high speeds involved. “With the jet drones, we completely screwed up the initiative again, that’s a fact … we don’t even know what to do about them,” Maksym Zhorin, deputy commander of the 3rd Army Corps, posted on Friday. Zelenskyy has said more than 60 Ukrainian companies are working on interceptors for jet-powered drones but only a handful have demonstrated results. Yuriy Cherevashenko, a deputy commander of Ukraine’s air force, said one solution being tested was a new generation of cheap guided missiles – engineered to cost less than the drones they shoot down. “I’m confident that soon we could fully have a class of weapons that will be effective at countering jet-powered UAVs [unmanned aerial vehicles],” Cherevashenko said. A Ukrainian army unit has launched a counteroffensive against Russian forces near Lyman in Ukraine’s east, the unit’s commander said on Tuesday. Ukrainian units have cleared Russian infiltrators from an area of “about 75 square kilometres”, said Andriy Biletsky. “The 3rd Army Corps has launched an offensive operation called Vivaldi in this sector,” Biletsky said. The battlefield mappers DeepState showed Ukrainian troops had made a small pocket of gains north of Lyman. The reported gains in the Donetsk region would add to Ukraine’s push earlier this year in the south-east, where Kyiv said it clawed back more than 700 sq km of territory during a months-long counterattack. A week ago, war analysts said the same corps had recaptured a “salient” – a protrusion of Russian-occupied land hemmed by Ukrainian-held territory – of more than 200 square kilometres near Lyman. Russia attacked port ⁠infrastructure in ⁠Ukraine’s southern Black ⁠Sea region ⁠of Odesa ‌overnight, ‌the regional governor ‌said on Tuesday. Residential buildings, ‌logistics facilities and transport infrastructure came ⁠under attack, said Oleh Kiper. A ⁠Russian drone attack ⁠killed ⁠one person and knocked out ⁠power in parts ⁠of the ‌city of Zaporizhzhia ‌in south-east ‌Ukraine, said the acting regional governor, Mykhailo Semikin, said. Russian strikes on Kyiv killed one person and wounded seven other people on Tuesday, with attacks carried out on the capital’s petrol stations, Ukraine’s state emergency service said. Two more people were killed in separate Russian strikes in the Ukrainian cities of Sloviansk and Kramatorsk. Ukraine struck ⁠an oil refinery ⁠in the ⁠Russian city of Syzran, ⁠Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Tuesday. He also reported a ‌strike ‌on a drone ‌production facility in the Russian city of Taganrog, and ‌on a drone preparation and launch site in the Oryol ⁠region. Unnamed targets were hit in the Black Sea, ‌he said. Zelenskyy said ⁠Russian drones attacked Moldovan airspace twice while he was in the country on board his aircraft at Chisinau airport headed to and from a trip abroad. “In Moldova, my presidential jet was there ⁠and that’s why they attacked Moldova, the airspace of Moldova. Maybe they didn’t want to attack ‌me personally,” Zelenskyy told CBS. “When ‌we came back home, again through Chisinau, again they did the ‌same.” Moldovan authorities said two drones entered ⁠the country’s airspace on Monday 14 September. One came down in a field and the other flew off into Romania. Initially reports that Zelenskyy’s plane was almost hit were later played down. Russia will not stop fighting ⁠in ⁠Ukraine while any potential ⁠talks take place, its foreign minister, ⁠Sergei Lavrov, said ‌on ‌Tuesday. Ukraine has repeatedly said that ⁠a ceasefire should be the starting point for the ‌talks. Ukrainian lawmakers approved ⁠Zelenskyy’s sacking of ⁠the prosecutor general, Ruslan ⁠Kravchenko, who resigned amid a corruption scandal in his agency but then appeared to attempt a challenge against anti-corruption agencies. The ‌vote was supported by 317 ⁠lawmakers, with 226 needed for a majority. None voted against.

title: Anthropic CEO renews call for AI slowdown as Nvidia’s urges acceleration
summary: At San Francisco conference, OpenAI chief Sam Altman calls for more rigorous security measures
text: Anthropic’s CEO took the stage at a conference in San Francisco on Tuesday to reiterate his call for a slowdown of AI development, while Nvidia’s CEO argued against such deceleration. Dario Amodei used an automotive analogy to make his point: when a competing car company has a safety incident like brake failures, it is a moment for all car companies to stop and review their own practices, he said at Salesforce’s Dreamforce convention on Tuesday. “It’s very tempting to attack your competitor and say these guys are unsafe,” he said. “But I think the more responsible way to respond to it is to say, let’s look at our own record. We may not have had this big, high-profile incident, but I’m sure we’re not perfect.” Nvidia’s Jensen Huang countered not long after: “Run as fast as you can.” Amodei is calling for three courses of action: embedding third-party evaluators inside AI companies; coordinating safety standards among Democratic countries; and, eventually, larger global coordination. At Dreamforce, Amodei said Anthropic has committed to independent evaluators and was “going to have a dialogue with the rest of the industry” on the other two steps. Amodei, xAI’s Elon Musk and OpenAI’s Sam Altman have recently called for a slowdown in the pace of AI development. The comments from the CEOs follow warnings from Jacob Coxon, a former Anthropic researcher, who resigned with a public declaration that AI could lead to the extinction of humanity within the decade. Coxon’s comments have stirred a larger debate within Silicon Valley, gained the attention of regulators and alarmed the public. Huang, who also made an appearance at Dreamforce on Tuesday, said companies should not slow down AI development. He argued that new regulations were not necessary, advising AI companies to simply wait to release products until they know they are safe rather than begging the US government to intervene. Huang said he envisioned a future where “every company, every enterprise … would become an AI company”. He said companies would become more ambitious when armed with AI and reiterated the idea that those who do not embrace the technology will get left behind. He also pushed back on the idea that AI is going to destroy jobs, calling it “completely nonsense”. One day prior at the All-In summit in Los Angeles, Donald Trump called Huang while the CEO was on stage. Huang put the president on speakerphone as Trump called the growing concern about AI a “hoax” and asserted again that a slowdown would only benefit China. Huang responded: “We’re going to make sure that everybody wins in the AI race of America.” Altman, who spoke later on Tuesday, called for a new level of rigor on security as AI advances. Altman said AI models had advanced so quickly that monitoring and security need to be treated with a “new level of rigor”, calling an incident in which OpenAI agents hacked into another company a “wake-up call” for the industry. He also said the public was very “right to be afraid” of AI because of the potential loss of control, and the possibility of a small group of powerful AI companies exerting their views on the world. People “feel the speed with which things are moving”, Altman said. “It doesn’t take as much imagination to imagine how this could go wrong.” Previously, Altman agreed with Amodei’s push for a slowdown. But at Dreamforce on Tuesday, he said he was disappointed with how the argument had been framed. “You have companies saying things like: ‘We will only slow down or we will only be responsible if other companies are responsible,’” he said, suggesting that this created fear for the public. “The world should trust that we are going to do the right thing because it’s the right thing.” Altman said the hacking incidents showed that companies needed to prepare for an “impending wave of cyber-attacks”, saying: “We are not that far away from open-source models that can do serious damage.” Companies should use this “little period of advantage to defend yourselves”, he said. The rising concern over AI comes as OpenAI and Anthropic head for initial public offerings, which could give investors and the public insight into the companies’ finances. Some analysts have predicted the IPOs will be among some of the largest in history. Amid the AI panic, Altman said he planned to delay OpenAI’s IPO until next year over safety concerns. On Tuesday, Amodei said what surprised him most about AI was the speed of its proliferation. “It’s been the pace of the progress – not just of the technology but of the economic side of it,” he said about the growing adoption of AI. “We had a prediction of just how capable these models would be. But I think what we didn’t appreciate is that it would lead to these companies growing so fast.” Regardless of the rapid pace of development, Altman said he believed people would use AI as a tool to benefit other people and grow their businesses. He said this moment represented a time when the “sci-fi” scenario came to fruition, where people were talking to their AI assistants and transforming the way they work. “I think we’re going to stay in an extremely human-centric world, no matter how good the technology gets,” he said.

title: Sleeping teen and camper wounded as Colorado bear attacks reach record high
summary: Bears came through bedroom window and swiped tent at campground, causing scratch marks and puncture wound
text: A black bear burst through a Colorado teenage girl’s window and scratched her, days after a bear also bit a camper in the state, according to wildlife officials. On Friday, a woman at a campground in south-west Colorado heard a growl and felt something hit her outdoors tent, according to a news release. She was treated for a puncture wound on her arm – consistent with a black bear bite – authorities said. Wildlife officers found claw marks on her tent and recovered several dark hairs. “The bite in this incident was more likely an act of surprise than aggression,” said Monte Vista area wildlife manager Rick Basagoitia, adding that the area had “no history of conflict or damage”. Two days later, a bear opened a cracked window, tore the screen off and entered the bedroom of a sleeping 17-year-old girl. The girl was roused by the animal’s presence and hid under her blankets. The bear’s paw struck her stomach, leaving three scratch marks, according to authorities. “The woman is very lucky she had multiple blankets covering her when the bear swiped her,” said district wildlife manager Luke Clancy. There have been 10 reported bear attacks on humans this year in Colorado, a number officials have described as unprecedented. A statewide drought has squeezed the food supply of black bears, who mostly eat berries, fruits and insects, officials say. The bears, who seek up to 20,000 calories per day as they prepare to hibernate during the colder months, have sought out new food sources in human residences. Nationwide, there has also been a rise in bear-human conflicts. In August, a bear broke into a New Mexico man’s home and mauled him to death, marking a rare fatal attack for the state. Wildlife officials have urged the public to secure their trash and to lock windows, doors, garages and vehicles.

title: Thirteenth Met police officer sacked after undercover BBC investigation
summary: PC Mason O’Connor dismissed following Panorama film showing misogyny and racism at London police station
text: A 13th serving Metropolitan police officer has been dismissed in relation to an undercover BBC investigation into misogyny and racism at Charing Cross police station. PC Mason O’Connor was found to have committed discreditable conduct and breached professional behaviour standards, linked to a comment he made towards a female colleague, according to the Met. The Panorama investigation aired in October 2025 and followed seven months of undercover filming. It included footage of officers calling for immigrants to be shot and boasting about using violence against suspects. On Tuesday, a disciplinary panel heard that O’Connor told a female colleague in October 2024 that he “hope[d] you get raped on your way to Waterloo”, while he was off-duty in a pub. The incident was reported as part of a witness appeal and “proactive wider investigation” launched after the broadcast of the Panorama film. At the time, the Met police commissioner, Sir Mark Rowley, said the footage was “vile to watch” and featured “incontrovertible evidence” that would enable the fast-tracking of misconduct hearings. O’Connor’s sacking comes a few weeks after the dismissal of PC Lloyd Hunter, who was found to have made comments that trivialised the use of force and suggested that he would enjoy using force against members of the public. Hunter also said he “hated” homeless people. Commander Simon Messinger, from the Met’s professionalism department, said: “Two more officers have now been dismissed for their appalling comments and attitudes. “I hope this sends a very clear message about the standards we expect from all our officers and the Met’s determination to improve our culture across the organisation. “We continue to support the ongoing IOPC [Independent Office for Police Conduct] investigation.” The IOPC confirmed that investigations were continuing against 15 other officers or police staff and that misconduct had been identified from footage provided by the BBC which had not been included in the Panorama broadcast. A gross misconduct hearing is scheduled for later this month over comments made by a detention officer regarding the treatment of people being held in police custody. Amanda Rowe, the IOPC’s director of engagement, said: “This is one of our largest ever investigations in terms of the number of officers investigated, and the sheer number of fast-tracked disciplinary proceedings show how seriously the IOPC and the Met, who held the misconduct hearings, are treating this matter.” Both O’Connor and Hunter will be barred from rejoining the police force.

title: Britons of all ethnicities feel racial inequality is worsening, study shows
summary: Nearly half of minority ethnic respondents in a poll say they have faced prejudice over the past year
text: Many Britons feel inequality is worsening and that discrimination has become more common, according to a thinktank study. The report by British Future has found that people across ethnic groups believe racial equality is worsening in Britain. One in six people are from minority ethnic backgrounds. “Most ethnic minorities in Britain feel there was a positive change against racism in our lifetimes yet now fear that progress being reversed,” said the thinktank’s director, Sunder Katwala. The research found nearly half of ethnic minority respondents had faced racial or nationality prejudice over the past year, with the problem notably higher among those aged 18 to 24. Prejudice was most often reported in public spaces, followed by on social media and in the workplace. The research found that 62% of ethnic minority Britons saw racial inequality as a serious problem, a view supported by 57% of the white population. White respondents were less likely to see structural barriers in education, work and public services and more likely to believe minority communities received equal or preferential treatment. The report, part of a three-year study funded by the Nuffield Foundation, found a growing polarisation over perceptions that minorities received preferential treatment. Among white respondents, 37% felt ethnic minorities were treated better than white British people, while 33% disagreed. Among ethnic minorities, 23% agreed and 48% disagreed. The report found divisions by age and politics were deeper than those relating to ethnicity. “In both the white and ethnic minority surveys, gaps between rich and poor are seen as the most important divide impacting the UK,” the report said. The research was driven by two online surveys of 2,009 white adults and 3,014 ethnic minority adults between 30 March and 29 April. It was supplemented by information from 12 focus groups. The study noted a difference within ethnic minority attitudes, finding Black respondents were frequently more positive about the UK making progress on racial equality. By contrast, Bangladeshi and Pakistani heritage respondents were found to be more pessimistic, with heightened anxiety seemingly linked to the 2024 riots. “Women, particularly ethnic minority women, are also more pessimistic than men throughout,” the report said. The study found that ethnic minority Britons would like to see more effort to promote equal pay and tackle disparities in essential services and unequal treatment in media reporting. This was brought into “sharp focus”, the report said, by the intense media scrutiny on Jason Arday, a Cambridge University professor who died at his London home after allegations of plagiarism. The report, which criticised successive governments for having “rarely held” a sustained focus on race, laid out 10 recommendations for the government, including challenging zero-sum thinking, supporting grassroots activities and pushing the watchdog Ofcom on compliance against online racism. Overall, it found low trust among political parties. While the Green party and Labour led narrowly in terms of treating people of different backgrounds fairly (+15 and +13 in net trust scores respectively), Reform UK had a net score of -31 (16% trust/47% distrust). Katwala said leaders should “counter the sense of a zero-sum contest over race equality: that fairness for ethnic minorities comes at the expense of the white majority, or vice versa”. He added: “The antidote to that is to pursue a broad and proactive fairness agenda – with the confidence and tools to tackle racism and discrimination where it is most needed.”

title: Kennedy Center to close as Trump threatens to block repairs over name dispute
summary: President says he will block renovation project unless court decision to bar his name from being added is overturned
text: Donald Trump said on Tuesday that the Kennedy Center would close “immediately” and threatened to cancel a planned renovation of the institution if federal courts did not allow his name to be placed on the front of the building. Trump’s ultimatum came shortly after the president’s handpicked board voted, again, to close the institution’s performing arts building in Washington, citing safety and financial concerns. In a Truth Social post, Trump said the board voted “almost unanimously” to close the riverside landmark “for Safety reasons, and so that I can begin the process of Reconstruction”. He then said he would block a $257m renovation project that Trump had previously touted to address what the center has described as “decades of deferred maintenance and critical infrastructure needs”. “The Renovation and Reconstruction, which is a very large and complex job, cannot begin until such time as the D.C. Circuit rules on the Board’s approved name,” Trump wrote. “If the ruling is a negative one, which it should not be, and is not overturned by the U.S. Supreme Court, the Reconstruction and the Renovation of The Kennedy Center will not take place.” The performing arts center, built as a memorial to President John F Kennedy, has been embroiled in a dizzying legal dispute over Trump’s desire to put his name on the building. Prior to the Tuesday meeting, a federal judge blocked the center’s board from adding Trump’s name to the venue, writing that it would violate his previous ruling ordering it to be removed. “Simply put, defendants cannot install memorials for President Trump or anyone or anything else at the Kennedy Center without Congress’s blessing,” US district judge Christopher Cooper wrote. “The board resolution bucks a federal court order and a statute Congress enacted.” Democratic congresswoman Joyce Beatty, an ex officio board member and trustee of the center, who brought the legal challenge, said Trump’s efforts to rebrand the institution in his name was a reflection of the president’s “vanity” and a “ breach of his fiduciary duty as a trustee”. “The board’s latest shutdown vote is more of the same failure and abuse that has characterized this administration’s treatment of the Kennedy Center,” Beatty said in a joint statement with attorneys Norm Eisen and Nathaniel Zelinsky. “The unlawful renaming drove audiences and artists away. Now the board has voted to shut down yet again to hide the terrible mismanagement under its current leadership. We’ll see the defendants in court.” Beatty told MS Now on Tuesday that the president had thrown “a tantrum” in a phone call to the board when he learned that she had prevailed in court. “It was the most unprofessional thing that I’ve ever witnessed or been a part of it,” Beatty said. “He went into name calling,” she added, saying that Trump had called her dumb. “He said, ‘I think you’re incompetent,’ and I said, ‘I know you’re incompetent,’” the congresswoman recalled. “He said he was going to hold me responsible if something fell out of the ceiling and killed someone,” she added. “And I told him, I said, ‘You’re already killing people, we’re at war.’ “Then he wanted to talk about how great he was with developing and he didn’t know anything about me, but I had never done anything. This was the biggest thing I had done. So I reminded him that he had more bankruptcies than anybody in the room.” The board’s vote followed a weekend of dueling court filings. The board’s proposal called for closing the main building on safety grounds, describing it as unsafe for continued occupancy. Beatty’s lawyers disputed that characterization, arguing in a court filing that the safety consultants cited, Delta Consulting Group, “expressly disclaimed” reaching any such opinion. Eisencalled the board’s weekend document dump “an outrageous act of hostage taking”, writing on X: “Pay up or the Kennedy Center closes, and the price is Trump’s name on the building.” The board had also been expected to vote on a proposal related to adding Trump’s name. But in a notice filed on Monday in the US district court for the District of Columbia, government lawyers disclosed that Joe LaFauci, the center’s vice-president of board relations, told the board that Tuesday’s meeting was “now focused exclusively on the necessary closure of the center”, citing “recently exacerbated structural emergencies”. However, in the filing, the board said trustees “stand by the recognition resolution proposed and passed by the board on August 13 2026”. The now-shelved second resolution had listed 10 options for inscribing Trump’s name and the “Trump Kennedy Center Fund” beneath the center’s name on the exterior marble, tying various forms of credit to renovation, endowment or oversight of the building. After Trump’s name was added to the exterior of the building above Kennedy’s, Cooper ordered the president’s name removed, ruling in May that only Congress has authority to rename it, and the lettering came down in June. The board voted in August to reinstate an inscription and proceed with the closure. Howard Lutnick, the US commerce secretary, posted a security video on Monday appearing to show debris falling in the center’s grand foyer, saying “the entire building is in this kind of shape” and that only Trump “can deliver the renovation on time and on budget”. Trump then shared the post on Truth Social. Lutnick’s wife, Allison, is a member of the president’s appointed board. Tuesday’s vote is the latest turn in a financial and legal fight that has dogged the center since Trump installed himself as chair in February 2025, firing the board and its longtime president, Deborah Rutter. Current leadership has blamed the crisis on mismanagement by Rutter’s team, alleging a “falsified” budget with $26m in “phantom revenue”, a claim Rutter and former board chair David Rubenstein have both denied, noting the center’s finances were independently audited.

title: Seattle passes measure to protect non-monogamous people as protected class
summary: City council votes unanimously in favor of bill that also protects multigenerational households
text: Seattle passed a measure on Tuesday to extend civil rights protections to non-monogamous people and multigenerational households, and recognize additional sexual orientations and gender identities as protected classes under local law. The city council voted unanimously in favor of the bill. As the largest city yet to pass such a law, Seattle joins a growing group of local governments acknowledging non-monogamous and polyamorous people as frequent subjects of housing and workplace discrimination, and in need of commensurate protection. Boston suburbs Cambridge and Somerville, and Berkeley and Oakland in California’s Bay Area, have previously passed similar policies; Seattle is the 10th city to do so. Advocates say the efforts help local governments serve the many family structures that actually exist, not just the ones that are easy to define. Research cited by the city council suggests that 10-20% of North Americans have engaged in consensual non-monogamy during their lives, while 5% are currently non-monogamous. More than 50% of respondents to a 2018 academic survey reported experiencing discrimination due to their consensual non-monogamous practices, including in medical settings, workplaces and family court. Local advocate Jessa Davis helped spearhead the grassroots movement to enact a bill in Seattle after her partner experienced job discrimination in August 2024 due to her non-monogamy. Davis said the experience exposed which forms of discrimination were still “not illegal” in Seattle, even as targeting her partner “based on her sexual orientation or her gender identity or political ideology” would have been “covered in Seattle”. Following engagement with advocates, Seattle’s Human Rights Commission penned an open letter in December 2025 in favor of a bill to address discrimination “on the basis of family and relationship structure” and to close “loopholes that currently allow exclusion, harassment, and denial of opportunity to persist unchecked”. Council member Alexis Mercedes Rinck, who sponsored the bill, said this most recent “update to code” is part of a “decades-long process” to recognize protected classes with “a degree of inclusivity”. In the 1970s, Seattle residents were the first in the US to vote in favor of legal protections for LGBTQ+ people; more recently, in 2023, Seattle was the first US city to ban caste-based discrimination. Updating anti-discrimination statutes to include other family structures and sexual orientations helps the law “reflect how our neighbors define themselves and define their families”, Rinck said. In Portland, Oregon, which passed a similar law in March, some lawmakers expressed concern that the measure could attract unwanted attention from rightwing groups. Adding legal protections for non-monogamous people shouldn’t be “a red-versus-blue culture war issue”, Davis claimed, adding that “lots of people, even people who vote for Donald Trump … are in our community”. Davis also said expanding civil rights protections benefits a broader population than those explicitly named in the laws, and can push back against growing conservative efforts to curtail the legal rights of minorities. “If we’re not expanding the circle of protections, we are leaving ground for people who aren’t being quiet about the fact that they are coming for marriage equality next,” she said. Republican-led governments in several states have recently declared June, traditionally pride month in celebration of LGBTQ+ rights, to be “nuclear family month”, which shows “their intention to roll back a lot of progress that we’ve made in the last 10 to 15 years”, Davis suggested. The Seattle law will go into effect on 1 June 2027. In addition to housing and employment protections, the new measure also entitles protected classes to bias-free encounters with police. Rinck, advocates and the Human Rights Commission are interested in evaluating and improving how Seattle’s anti-discrimination laws are enforced. “Seattle has a proud history of advancing civil rights protections, but I think those protections only matter when people can actually access them, and there’s a pathway for enforcement of them,” said Phil Lewis, a member of the Human Rights Commission. Davis has recently joined the Organization for Polyamory and Ethical Non-monogamy (Open), a nationally focused legal advocacy group, as its executive director. In Seattle, passing an anti-discrimination law can help more non-monogamous people speak up and shape policy without fear of retribution, she said. Advocates are working on similar measures in other large cities, Davis added, including Baltimore, Denver, Los Angeles and San Francisco.

title: Mail-in disaster averted as Trump in angry froth after court defeat
summary: Election officials continue push to assure Americans mail ballots are safe after supreme court rules against president
text: After the US supreme court halted Donald Trump’s efforts to make it significantly harder to vote by mail in the midterms, US election officials are redoubling their efforts to convince Americans it is safe to cast their ballots by mail. The supreme court’s Monday ruling, which sent Trump into an angry froth on Truth Social, averted what election officials of both parties said would be an administrative disaster for this year’s elections. Trump’s order would have required states to comply with cumbersome new rules, including redesigning mail-in envelopes and uploading lists of voters to the USPS, that were not feasible to implement before ballots started going out. The effort was seen as a push by the government to change voting policy as well as one to weaken confidence in voting by mail. “That is the whole intent of the president. He wanted to build doubt,” said Cisco Aguilar, a Democrat who serves as the top election official in Nevada, where mail-in voting is widely used. “He wanted to create chaos.” Twenty-nine percent of Americans voted by mail in the 2024 presidential election and roughly one third cast a mail-in ballot in the 2022 midterms, according to researchers at the MIT election lab. Democrats were more likely than Republicans to cast a mail-in ballot. “There’s just concern: ‘Can we trust the mail?’ And I say yes, because it’s not the leadership or the management of the postal service that’s actually going to have their hands on the ballots, it’s the postal workers who are on our side,” Aguilar said. Nevada officials also plan to run a series of public service announcements to educate voters on the election process. In Wisconsin, election officials have faced questions about voters concerned their ballots won’t be delivered in time. Wisconsin law requires mail-in ballots to be delivered by the close of polls on election day in order to count and in the state’s April election there was an increase in late-arriving ballots. There have been higher rates of late-arriving ballots tossed this year, according to an analysis by the New York Times. Wisconsin election officials have encouraged people through county websites, social media, and notes attached to their ballots, among other things, to mail their ballots back sooner, according to the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel. “We’re really trying to encourage people to act sooner. So hopefully they take that to heart,” said Ann Jacobs, a Democrat on the Wisconsin elections commission, which oversees voting in that state. “It’s hard to tell people, ‘No, really, you should trust the post office’ when they came up with this absolutely cockamamie rule that was going to eliminate absentee voting.” In a video released on Tuesday, Meagan Wolfe, the administrator of the Wisconsin elections commission, said: “If you’re going to be returning your ballot by mail, please do so at least two weeks before the election. And you also may want to contact your municipal clerk to find out if there are other opportunities for you to return your ballot in your community. You may have drop-boxes or you may be able to return your ballot in person to your clerk.” Jane Kleeb, the president of the association of state Democratic chairs, said Democrats were making a more aggressive effort to encourage people to vote early in person while also emphasizing that if they want to vote by mail, they should return their ballots quickly. “We’re being honest with voters. We’re saying, ‘Look, normally you might have given three days to get your ballot to your election office, and now you should give a week,’” she said. A DNC spokesperson said the party “will continue to use every tool at our disposal to defend the right to vote, and we encourage Americans to make a plan to vote that best works for them and make their voices heard this November.” In Washington state, where everyone received a mail-in ballot, more than 20,000 votes were rejected in the August primary because they arrived late at an election office. “There is a sense of distrust,” said Steve Hobbs, the Washington secretary of state. “Even though there is a victory in the courts, we still are urging our voters to put their ballot in a drop-box.” As lawsuits challenging the rule wound their way through federal courts this year, Adrian Fontes, Arizona’s secretary of state, publicly emphasized that the rule had not gone into effect yet and so that nothing around voting by mail had changed. Since the supreme court’s ruling preserved that status quo, he said, officials haven’t had to shift their messaging. While voters have raised questions about the proposed changes “we continue to tell them until there’s a change, there is no change,” said Fontes, a Democrat “We are still where we were. We never jumped on the paranoia bandwagon.” “It’s intentionally damaging to the entire elections administration process in this country,” said Fontes, a Democrat and the top election official in a state where voting by mail is widely used. “The administration, by their actions, have proven that they are hell-bent on driving American voters away from their own elections. And we’ve been working very hard to counter that.”
