title: House panel recommends Leon Black be held in contempt over Epstein inquiry subpoenas
summary: Financier refused to comply with subpoenas seeking his testimony for the investigation into the late sex offender
text: The House oversight committee voted unanimously Tuesday to recommend that the House of Representatives hold Leon Black, the billionaire financier, in contempt of Congress, after he refused to comply with subpoenas seeking his testimony and nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) sought by the panel as part of its investigation into Jeffrey Epstein. Black contends the subpoenas are “invalid” and he is suing to block them. “Subpoenas are not suggestions; they carry the force of law and require full compliance” the representative James Comer, who chairs the committee, said in the chamber on Tuesday afternoon before the voting began. “Mr Black’s testimony is crucial to our investigation because he maintained a close personal relationship with Epstein for years during the time when Epstein was engaged in sex trafficking.” He added: “We made it clear to Mr Black and his attorneys that if he did not comply, then the committee would initiate contempt proceedings.” The bipartisan committee passed the resolution 41-0. Comer said that the committee now “moves the report to the full House”. The office of the House speaker, Mike Johnson, did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Tuesday about whether the lower chamber would consider the contempt measure. The decision is the latest escalation in the dispute between the committee and Black, whose name has come up repeatedly in the Epstein files, and who, as reported by the New York Times, paid Epstein a total of $170m for what he described as tax and estate planning services from 2013 to 2017. Black has repeatedly denied any wrongdoing, and has said that he had no knowledge of Epstein’s crimes. Comerannounced last week that that the committee would consider the resolution to hold Black in contempt. It came after Black did not appear for his deposition scheduled for 3 September and did not produce all of the nondisclosure agreements sought by the committee. Instead, Black sued to block the subpoenas, arguing that they were “invalid to the extent they exceed” the committee’s “delegated authority in seeking private information that bears no legitimate connection” to its legislative purpose. Black’s lawsuit also argued that the subpoenas would “expose women who value their privacy, who have no known or public connection to Epstein, who bargained for confidentiality and have refused to release it, and who have no ability to protect themselves and their privacy before the committee”. The committee issued the subpoenas in June, after Black appeared voluntarily before the panel for a transcribed interview. The interview ended abruptly after lawmakers from both parties said that Black refused to answer questions about NDAs. Comer then issued the two subpoenas: one demanding that Black produce “all non-disclosure agreements to which he is a party”, and another requiring him to appear before the committee again. In August, Comer threatened to hold Black in contempt if he did not fully cooperate with the committee’s subpoenas. On Tuesday, during his remarks in the chamber before the vote, Comer said that Black “only produced one NDA to the committee” and noted that Black did not appear for his 3 September deposition. Attorneys representing Black had asked for a postponement of the committee’s markup earlier on Tuesday, and described it as a “complete abomination”. The attorneys said they sent two letters to Comer and Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the committee, saying that they would submit a complaint to the office of congressional conduct requesting “an investigation into conduct by Chairman Comer” alleging that ahead of Black’s scheduled deposition, Comer “engaged in what should be viewed as a violation of the rules of the House of Representatives relating to the deposition”. Black’s attorney said in a statement on Tuesday: “The committee under the leadership of Chairman James Comer and Ranking Member Robert Garcia has lost sight of its legislative purpose and is abusing its power.” The lawyers described the subpoenas as “illegitimate, illegal and a textbook abuse of power designed to bully and destroy legal protections of private citizens”. “Mr Black has repeatedly said that he feels terrible for Epstein’s victims and that he regrets ever doing business with Epstein,” the statement added. “He never abused a woman. He never was with an underage woman. He never engaged in sex trafficking. He never paid Epstein for access to women. He was never blackmailed by Epstein. Mr Black had no knowledge of any of Epstein’s heinous conduct.” Before Black’s scheduled deposition earlier this month, more than a dozen survivors of Epstein’s abuse urged him to comply with congressional subpoenas. They argued that his use “of NDAs underscores why Congress must scrutinize the agreements in his possession and determine whether they shed light on his relationship with Jeffrey Epstein and others in Epstein’s orbit”. Earlier this year, the committee also moved to hold former president Bill Clinton and Hillary Clinton in contempt for initially refusing to testify about Epstein. The Clintons ultimately testified before the House.

title: US House votes for third time to end Iran war after $38bn cost is revealed
summary: Damaging budget report estimates cost will grow by $3bn per month and stockpiles of weapons could take five years to rebuild
text: The US House of Representatives has voted for a third time to end the war in Iran, approving a war powers resolution a few hours after a Congressional Budget Office (CBO) report showed the conflict had cost at least $38bn and left America’s stockpile of defensive missiles so depleted it could take five years to rebuild. The final tally of 220-204 was similar to earlier votes, with a few more Republicans joining most Democrats in calling for an end to the war. None of the resolutions have made it to the president’s desk, where Trump would almost certainly veto them. The action is likely the last House vote on the Iran war before the midterm elections, where the war and America’s cost of living crisis are expected to hurt Republicans at the ballot box. Lawmakers are heading home at the end of the week to campaign nearly full-time, with less than 50 days to go before the elections that will determine control of Congress. “Remember when Donald Trump said that this war would last just a few weeks?” said Democrat Seth Moulton before the vote. He added it was time for Congress to “actually ask tough questions, as the constitution directs us to do, rather than be subservient to another warmongering administration”. Republican Brian Mast of Florida, the chairman of the House foreign affairs committee, questioned which military resources Democrats would want to remove from the region where he said Iran remains a threat. Mast said Trump is against “forever wars, and that is what he is ending”, meaning decades of hostilities from Iran. The House first approved a war powers resolution in June and followed up with another one in July, all seeking to halt US action in Iran. The Senate on its 10th try also approved a war powers resolution to end the conflict, but Republican senators quickly reversed course the next day after Trump berated them during a closed-door lunch. While the constitution gives Congress the authority to declare war, it also enables the president as the commander in chief to authorise some military actions. The war powers act, created in the aftermath of the Vietnam conflict, sought to put a more specific time limit on the president’s power, requiring congressional approval for sustained military actions after 60 or 90 days. The vote late on Tuesday came as the CBO report found that Iranian strikes had damaged or destroyed hundreds of buildings and structures at US bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman and Jordan. It estimated that the costs of the war will grow $3bn for every month the conflict continues, depending on its intensity, while noting that the war has driven up inflation. Much of the cost has come from missile defense. Fending off Iranian ballistic missiles and drones has consumed such a large share of the US stockpile of Patriot, Thaad and navy interceptors that the CBO said rebuilding it “would probably take at least five years, even if production was increased”. In a White House statement responding to reports of shortages, Donald Trump said the US had “far more munitions than anyone in the world” and “far more than we need”. In August, Pete Hegseth, the defense secretary, dismissed a CNN report on the depleted stockpiles as “not true”. According to the CBO report, shortages would be “especially problematic” in a hypothetical clash over Taiwan, because of the need for interceptors to engage “large numbers of ballistic and cruise missiles”. China maintains an arsenal of these and is expanding it, the report noted, and any US-China conflict over Taiwan would likely require far more interceptors, deployed far more quickly, than the campaign against Iran has. The economic report came a day after the Pentagon’s inspector general finally released its own first review of the war, saying that the US spent $22.3bn on munitions alone through 30 June, put total spending at $33.4bn, and found the fighting had “resulted in strategic inventory shortfalls and revealed industrial base bottlenecks for munitions resupply”. The Pentagon’s report did not address its own internal investigation of the Minab school strike on the first day of the war, which killed 156 people including 120 children. Critics have accused the Pentagon of burying results of the investigation that would show negligence in how it compiled targeting data for the initial strikes. The CBO report also found that increased energy costs, due in large part to the disruption of oil shipments through the strait of Hormuz, have increased inflation by half a percentage point compared with previous estimates. Brent crude jumped from $64 a barrel before the fighting to $103 at its peak, and the CBO projects the war will leave inflation running 0.5 percentage points higher than expected by early 2027, with short-term interest rates already about 0.2 points higher than they otherwise would have been. In June the White House requested $87.6bn in supplemental funding, of which $67.1bn was earmarked for the Pentagon. Once funding the CBO judged unrelated to combat operations is stripped out – including money for cybersecurity, drones and classified programs – $42.3bn of the Pentagon’s request appears tied to the Iran conflict, about 10% above the CBO’s estimate. The request included $12.1bn for classified programs the CBO could not examine – a far larger secret share than in past war supplementals. The CBO added that it still could not estimate the cost of repairing bomb-damaged US bases, nor any future diplomatic and foreign aid costs tied to the war.

title: Search under way for three-year-old boy missing from Suffolk playground
summary: More than 100 people reported to have joined search for Noah, who is autistic, non-verbal and has partial hearing loss
text: Police are urging people to check their gardens and sheds for a three-year-old boy who went missing on Tuesday during a visit to a playground near the Suffolk-Essex border. The boy, named Noah, was last seen at 3pm in Merriam Close in Brantham, near Manningtree, before being separated from a relative. Officers from Suffolk constabulary said Noah was reported to have run down an alleyway near the playground towards a housing estate. He is described as white, with curly ginger hair and was wearing shorts, white trainers and a white T-shirt featuring an illustration of the TV character Bluey. Police also confirmed that Noah is autistic, non-verbal and has partial hearing loss. The BBC reported that more than 100 people had joined in the search efforts by Tuesday evening and that train services between Manningtree and Ipswich were running at reduced speed while searches continued. Police have cordoned off the alleyway and there were reports of door-to-door inquiries in the area. A spokesperson for Suffolk constabulary said late on Tuesday: “Emergency services are currently in Brantham conducting searches. Residents in the area are asked to check their gardens, sheds and outbuildings.” A coastguard helicopter was also seen circling the village, which is near the estuary of the River Stour, and there were reports of sightings of drones flying overhead. Anyone who believes that they have seen Noah is being asked to contact Suffolk police, quoting CAD 203 of 15 September.

title: Catnapped bodega cat in Brooklyn reunited with owner after intense grassroots campaign
summary: Three-month-old Jabal was returned to Park Slope bodega after community rallied to rescue purloined kitty
text: The owner of a New York City bodega on Tuesday was reunited with the store’s cat after a couple passing by the establishment five days earlier appeared to abduct the feline in plain view of a surveillance camera and ignited an intense grassroots search effort. The plight of three-month-old Jabal began on Thursday morning in Brooklyn, when he went just outside the Eighth Street Mini Market where he lives as it opened for the day. A man walking alongside a woman passed the Park Slope market then picked up Jabal, and the pair took off as the kitten visibly squirmed, according to store surveillance video which the bodega’s owner, Imad “Jimmy” Innab, reviewed after he noticed the cat had gone missing. Dan Janzen, who lives across the street from the Eighth Street Mini Market and is one of its regular customers, said someone immediately ran after the couple and told them the kitten belonged to the bodega – but they were unmoved, stuffed Jabal into a bag and left with him anyway. As the New York Post and the local CBS affiliate soon reported, Innab and his family subsequently offered a $500, no questions asked reward for Jabal’s safe return, which was announced on a poster. Supporters of the bodega also canvassed the streets of Park Slope for Jabal while the neighborhood’s forum on the Reddit platform provided updates on the search efforts. One thread dedicated to Jabal’s disappearance had a photo of the couple who took the kitten and was titled, “Anyone Know These Two?” It generated about 1,000 upvotes – which indicate Reddit users’ approval of a thread – and more than 240 comments, with many aiming to help reunite Jabal with the Innabs. Another thread titled “Stolen Bodega Cat?!?” also called attention to Jabal’s catnapping, along with the news media coverage, which publicized the shocking surveillance footage of the kitten being brazenly snatched. The campaign paid dividends by Monday, when Janzen – speaking on behalf of Innab’s store – said the bodega had received a call from someone claiming to know who had Jabal. That person said Jabal would be brought back to the store from the Brooklyn neighborhood of Bushwick, according to both Janzen and Innab. Janzen on Tuesday afternoon then followed up with pictures of Innab holding Jabal, including one in which the bodega owner was planting a kiss on the top of the kitten’s head. Janzen sent the joyous pictures after spending part of Monday and Tuesday at the store with Innab eagerly awaiting Jabal’s return. “As much as we love the kitten, we love him more,” Janzen said of Innab. “We were rallying around him to keep his hopes up.” The Post on Tuesday reported that the woman seen leaving with Jabal arranged for her stepson to bring the kitten to the New York police precinct in Park Slope. Police then brought Jabal back to Innab’s bodega. Innab had previously said he only cared about Jabal being returned safely and did not want to see the pursuit of criminal charges in the case. But officers said they later arrested a 58-year-old Bushwick woman named Mary Sierra on a count of theft in connection with Jabal’s abduction, the outlets Gothamist and WPIX reported, citing New York police. Sierra later told the Post her arrest was unfair and that she was “an animal lover” with three rescue dogs. “They locked me up for this,” Sierra said to the publication. “I did not steal the … cat.” Innab on Tuesday spoke about how had been particularly affected by Jabal’s snatching because the Eighth Street Mini Market’s prior bodega cat, Victoria, had died in June after living there for 17 years. Innab took in Jabal to succeed Victoria, and the kitten was soon due to be given a microchip, which is injected subcutaneously and contains scannable owner and home address information. Bodega cats are deeply embedded in the fabric of New York City, serving to help keep vermin under control while also acting as living mascots for the stores where they reside. They can be seen lounging among store offerings or roaming along the freezer cases – among assorted other activities – in pictures on certain widely followed social media accounts, including @bodegacatsofinstagram on Instagram. Janzen on Monday made it a point to say that Innab refused to entertain the thought of not getting Jabal back. As Janzen put, Innab “always said, ‘I have a feeling he’s coming back.’” “I wish all the stories in the world could end this happily,” Janzen said on Tuesday. Innab said the way the neighborhood where his store had stood for 39 years supported him after Jabal’s temporary abduction “means everything” to him. “The people are very beautiful – very good – here,” Innab said of Park Slope. “And I thank everybody who tried to help me.” This article was updated on 15 September 2026 to reflect Jabal’s return to the bodega.

title: Air pollution linked to higher suicide risk, international research suggests
summary: Analysis of 29 studies highlights potentially heightened danger from small particulate matter and nitrogen dioxide
text: Air pollution is associated with an increased risk of suicide and suicidal thoughts, according to research. Environmental pollution is known to be associated with poorer mental health but its role in suicide risk is less well understood. Scientists at Queen’s University Belfast examined whether air, noise, light, and water pollution could influence the risk of death by suicide and suicidal behaviours. Their meta analysis of 29 studies found that exposure to airborne small particulate matter and nitrogen dioxide were linked to a heightened risk of death by suicide, suicide attempts and suicidal ideation. Narrative analysis of a further 16 studies suggested that some other air pollutants such as sulphur dioxide and ozone, as well as noise pollution, were also associated with a higher suicide risk. However, evidence for light and water pollution was inconclusive. The authors said the findings, published in the Journal of Epidemiology and Community Health, suggested that environmental pollution could be considered in suicide prevention strategies and that suicide prevention should also be viewed as a public health issue. “These findings bring to attention the critical importance of recognising environmental exposures as modifiable risk factors within suicide prevention efforts,” they said. “Integrating environmental health into mental health policy, through cross-sectoral collaboration, pollution reduction strategies, and targeted public health interventions, could play a vital role in reducing suicide risk and improving overall population mental wellbeing.” But other experts expressed caution about the findings. Dr Jess Moody, the senior research and evidence manager at Samaritans, said: “While the reasons for suicide are complex, evidence shows that a variety of factors can impact suicide risk and we must not ignore the environments we live in, particularly inequalities around living conditions. Samaritans welcomes research that helps awareness of how suicide links to wider public health concerns.” Dr Jon Van Niekerk, the chair of the general adult faculty at the Royal College of Psychiatrists, said the research suggested some forms of air pollution may be associated with a small increase in suicidal behaviour but it did not establish that air pollution itself caused suicidal thoughts or attempts. He added: “Air pollution is closely associated with other factors which we know can influence mental health, including socioeconomic deprivation, urban living, physical health and housing. “The study provides further population-level support for reducing harmful air pollution, though the findings should not be seen as supporting individual suicide risk prediction or suggesting that pollution reduction alone could be a suicide prevention measure.” Dr Rosie Cornish, a senior research fellow in epidemiology and health data science at the University of Bristol, said there were many factors associated with higher levels of air pollution as well as increased risk of suicide. “If air pollution is not actually a cause of increased risk of suicide then reducing pollution will not help to prevent suicide. The authors do not acknowledge this when drawing their conclusions.” Dr Stephen Burgess, a professor of biostatistics at the University of Cambridge, said: “This study confuses two fundamentally different concepts: causation and association. “There are many other factors that could potentially explain the associations observed. For example, areas with higher levels of pollution may differ in other ways that affect suicide risk. “This research finds factors that are associated with increased suicide risk, but further research is needed to claim that the factors identified are causes of increased risk.” More than 720,000 people globally die by suicide each year. It is the third leading cause of death among 15– to 29-year-olds, according to the World Health Organization. • In the UK and Ireland, Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org. In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found at befrienders.org

title: Republican Thomas Massie proposes impeaching Pete Hegseth over Iran war
summary: Congressman says defense secretary repeatedly violated constitution through his handling of Iran war
text: The Republican congressman Thomas Massie on Tuesday proposed impeaching Pete Hegseth, saying the defense secretary had repeatedly violated the constitution through his handling of war with Iran and the deaths of civilians in conflicts worldwide. The proposal by Massie, an iconoclastic lawmaker who lost his primary earlier this year after Donald Trump and Hegseth urged voters to oppose him, may put House Republicans in a bind just weeks before the 3 November midterm elections, in which they are defending their control of Congress. Under the rules of the House of Representatives, the articles must be voted on by Thursday, forcing Republicans to weigh in on one of the most prominent advocates of the war with Iran, which has gone on far longer than Trump said it initially would, and grown unpopular with the public. “By engaging in hostilities in Iran for more than 90 days without congressional authorization, Secretary Hegseth is breaking the law and must be held accountable,” Massie said in a statement after reading the text of his resolution on the floor of the House. “Secretary Hegseth’s constitutional violations extend beyond the illegal war in Iran. He is abusing the power of his office to ignore congressional war powers resolutions, to kidnap foreign leaders, and to intimidate critics of the Trump administration by retaliating against them for exercising free speech. If we are to remain true to our oath to ‘support and defend the constitution of the United States’, Congress must not turn a blind eye to Secretary Hegseth’s unconstitutional and illegal actions.” In a statement to the Guardian, a Pentagon spokesperson did not directly address the allegations put forward in the impeachment articles, but hailed Hegseth a “transformative leader” who had “slashed bureaucracy, unleashed innovation, and delivered for our warfighters every step of the way”. “The entire department is unified behind the secretary’s vision and will continue working to put our warfighters and America first,” the spokesperson, Kingsley Wilson, said. Massie’s resolution outlines eight alleged violations of the constitution by Hegseth, a former Fox News host and army national guard officer who as defense secretary has become a pugnacious defender of the president’s military politics. These include attacking Iran without first seeking Congress’s permission, and ignoring a war powers resolution the House and Senate approved in June that would require an end to the conflict. The resolution also accused Hegseth of “ignoring” laws that would have minimized civilian casualties, and specifically cites a US strike on a school in Minab, Iran that killed more than 168 people. Other articles allege Hegseth violated the constitution with the “extrajudicial killings” of at least 221 people on boats suspected of carrying drugs in the Caribbean sea and eastern Pacific ocean, and of “suppressing free speech” through his retaliation against the Democratic senator Mark Kelly for his criticism of the secretary. The final two impeachment articles accuse Hegseth of violating the constitution through his involvement in the military operation that captured Venezuela’s then president, Nicolás Maduro, and a bombing campaign in Yemen that began shortly after Trump returned to the White House. Should the resolution pass, the impeachment articles would head to the Senate, where the Republican leadership would have to decide whether to hold a trial of Hegseth, who has maintained Trump’s loyalty even as other cabinet secretaries – including attorney general Pam Bondi and labor secretary Lori Chavez-DeRemer – have been shown the door. The articles seem likely to attract many Democratic votes in the House. Massie has previously seized on unanimous Democratic support and the razor-thin Republican majority to push through a measure that forced the release of many files related to the disgraced financier and former Trump associate Jeffrey Epstein.

title: Bernie Sanders and Steve Bannon call for curbs on AI at ‘pro-human’ summit
summary: Leftwing senator and far-right strategist rail against tech oligarchs but offer competing visions on Chinese ‘cold war’
text: The progressive senator Bernie Sanders and rightwing strategist Steve Bannon have called for restrictions on artificial intelligence (AI) but offered competing visions for what they termed a “cold war” with China. Speaking at the “Pro-Human Assembly” in Washington on Tuesday, the ideological adversaries were united in warning of the potential dangers of AI and demanding stringent guardrails against Silicon Valley’s “oligarchs”. But the populist pair offered very different perspectives on how to resolve the AI race with China, which Donald Trump and other Republicans have cited to justify moving full speed ahead with the technology. Sanders, an independent senator from Vermont, noted that Trump is due to host the Chinese president Xi Jinping in Washington next week. Sanders called for international diplomacy and a global agreement, including with Beijing, to ban the development of super-intelligent machines. He told an audience gathered in the ballroom of a Washington hotel: “A super-intelligent AI that escapes human control will not be an American problem. It will not be a Chinese problem. It will be humanity’s problem. “That is why I very much hope that at their AI summit next week, President Trump will negotiate a comprehensive treaty with President Xi to establish a pause on advanced AI development and a ban on super-intelligence.” Sanders drew a comparison with US president Ronald Reagan and his Russian counterpart Mikhail Gorbachev seeking to avoid nuclear conflict at the height of the cold war, eventually signing a treaty that eliminated an entire class of missiles. He said: “They understood that a nuclear war would not be good for the Soviet Union, not be good for the United States, not be good for the world, and they came together for a nuclear treaty. With the survival of humanity at stake, they found a way to sign that treaty.” Bannon, who spoke directly after Sanders but did not share a stage with him, also used the cold war analogy but did not arrive at the same conclusion. The host of the War Room podcast and former White House chief strategist under Trump called for an aggressive economic and technological “quarantine” of China, demanding the immediate expulsion of Chinese nationals from US research laboratories, an end to the training of Chinese engineers and technologists and the total severance of capital flows. “Did our fathers and grandfathers, did they underwrite the Soviet Union?” Bannon asked. “Did they train Soviet Union scientists? Did they take Russian kids over here to college to let them go to the best universities and get the best degree? Did they have Wall Street slobbering to do their deals? Did they have every bank there to lend them money quicker than to lend anyone in this audience? “The answer is they did not. They stood up to the Soviet Union and the first thing to stand up to them was to choke them off and that’s what we have to do today to the Chinese Communist party. No deals, no agreements, you’re out of the AI business because we’re going to shut your ecosystem down.” Demanding immediate executive action to isolate Beijing’s tech sector, Bannon said: “No chips, no black marketing chips, no free ride off American technology, no steal on American tech … To hell with the Chinese Communist party.” Only then, Bannon argued, can the US have the time necessary to consider the proper regulation of the tech sector. He delivered a scathing verdict on major technology corporations and executives, accusing them of gambling with public safety for private profit. Bannon accused Silicon Valley of seeking to “socialise all the risk with the American people including potential bailouts” while keeping all financial upside. “The American people are not going to be supplicants to these tech oligarchs,” Bannon said, praising grassroots campaigns that previously defeated federal pre-emption bills aimed at blocking state-level AI regulations. Bannon has long praised Trump as a historic figure and endorsed his lie that the 2020 presidential election was stolen. But on Tuesday, while claiming that executive action is required rather than legislation by Congress, he made only a glancing reference to the president who has dismissed AI concerns as a “hoax” and “sick conspiracy”. Sanders, for his part, did criticise Trump and Congress along with the concentration of power in Silicon Valley. “Despite living in a so-called democracy, the public has had virtually no input into the AI revolution that is transforming the world in which they live,” he said. “Congress, under both Democratic and Republican control, has been asleep at the wheel and we now have a president whose ignorance regarding this issue is truly embarrassing. Virtually all of the decisions regarding the development of AI have been made by a handful of the richest people in the world … whose chief goal is to achieve even more wealth and more power than they already have, no matter what the impact their work has on ordinary people.” Sanders said he would introduce legislation next week to permanently ban the development of artificial super-intelligence, an AI mind smarter than any human being, and put an immediate pause on advanced AI development until clear safety rules are in place. Recent surveys have found ⁠majorities of Americans worry that AI could be used to eliminate jobs, raise costs for families or otherwise cause social harm. Residents in several states have also challenged ‌proposals for new data centres, a ‌critical component of the AI boom. The Pro-Human Assembly, taking place against a backdrop of growing bipartisan anxiety over AI risks, also heard from members of Congress, labour leaders and religious representatives. Congressman Greg Casar, who is co-sponsoring the legislation with Sanders, accused AI billionaires of deploying massive political spending to stifle regulation. “Even as the threat becomes clearer, there are many powerful people fighting to prevent action,” Casar told attendees. “AI billionaires are spending millions through the Leading the Future Pac to scare politicians into silence. The top Republicans who control the House of Representatives are not lifting a finger.” Casar added: “Leading in AI diplomacy does not mean waiting around for an international agreement on dangerous AI. Putting up guardrails now is the best way to show we are serious about getting to a deal.” Republican congressman Chip Roy similarly expressed scepticism over concentrating decision-making power within the executive branch or tech boardrooms. “The president yesterday said he should be making the decisions about AI. I disagree. I don’t think big tech CEOs should be making all the decisions about AI. “I don’t think Congress should be making all the decisions about AI. If we allow technology to fundamentally alter and transfer and change the way we make decisions about our society and our Republican form of government, then what do we have left?”

title: US treasury secretary hails government’s bond buyback a success
summary: On Tuesday, the 10-year treasury rate yield reached a 19-year high at 5.041% as investors are wary Iran war fallout
text: Scott Bessent, the US treasury secretary, claimed the government’s massive buyback of US bonds was a success. The claim came as the 10-year treasury yield reached a 19-year high on Tuesday, increasing pressure on interest rates as the Federal Reserve weighs another hike to see off rising inflation. US treasury yields, or the rate of return that investors receive when a bond matures, underpin the rates of other loans such as mortgages, car payments and credit card debt. On Tuesday, the yield rate for the 10-year treasury reached 5.041%, the highest level since 2007. The treasury yield rises when demand for bonds goes down. Though the US bond market is typically seen as one of the safest investment vehicles, investors have been wary of the effect the war in Iran is having on energy prices. Brent crude, the global benchmark for oil prices, hit $108 a barrel last week for the first time since May. When bond yields started to rise in August, the US treasury announced it would triple its buyback of government debt, going from $2bn to $6bn in an effort to bring down bond yields. Though the yields have continued to rise since, Bessent told Congress on Tuesday the operations are “the two most successful treasury auctions that we’ve had in 20 years”. “Since President Trump has come in, [the US bond market] has been the best-performing bond market in the developing world,” Bessent said. Earlier in August, the US government also stepped in to prop up the Japanese yen, a move that was seen as an effort to protect the Japanese government, a major holder of US bonds. Bessent told Congress the effort was a way for the US to signal support for Japanese policies. The Trump administration has been doing its best to fight against growing concerns over high inflation as the war in Iran continues, which is expected to have a major effect on the upcoming midterm election. US inflation has soared over the summer, reaching a three-year high of 4.2% in May before coming down to 3.4% in July and August. Stubbornly high prices set up a tough decision for the US Federal Reserve, which will on Wednesday announce any changes to the interest rate. The central bank is largely expected to raise rates for the first time since July 2023, which could help mitigate prices, though Donald Trump has demanded rates to be lowered.

title: Man admits to bombing California courthouse in retaliation for seized guns
summary: Nathaniel James McGuire faces maximum sentence of life in prison after guilty plea over September 2024 bombing
text: A California man has pleaded guilty to charges that he detonated a bomb at a Santa Maria courthouse in 2024 in retaliation for law enforcement officers seizing his firearms earlier that year. In September 2024, Nathaniel James McGuire, 22, of Santa Barbara county threw a backpack containing an explosive device into the courthouse before exiting the building to retrieve two long guns and 10 molotov cocktails from his car. Law enforcement officers apprehended McGuire before he could re-enter the building, but the detonation injured three people and caused $35,000 in damages to the courthouse. According to McGuire’s plea agreement, the attack was intended to kill sheriff’s deputies and a judge. He has been in federal custody since the attack. On Monday, McGuire pleaded guilty to one count of use of a weapon of mass destruction and one count of malicious destruction of a building using an explosive. His sentencing hearing is scheduled for 1 March. McGuire faces a maximum sentence of life in prison. “McGuire launched a vicious, terroristic assault on a court of law with the intent to kill law enforcement officers and a judge,” assistant attorney general for national security John A Eisenberg said in a justice department press release. “Individuals who use bombs against law enforcement officials, judges, and other government personnel must be held accountable and face severe punishment for their actions,” first assistant US attorney Bill Essayli for the central district of California said in a statement. At the time of the incident, the National Center for State Courts, a non-profit representing the justice system in the United States, reported that federal judges, prosecutors and court officials faced more than 4,500 threats in 2021, a 400% increase since 2015.

title: Ferocious fight among Brazil’s supreme court erupts on eve of presidential election
summary: Scandal explodes as country’s election campaign peaks, with polls suggesting dead heat between candidates
text: Brazil’s supreme court has been thrust into what experts consider the greatest crisis since the return of democracy in the 1980s, as two rival judges lock horns on the eve of the presidential election with unpredictable consequences for Latin America’s largest democracy. The politically charged dispute exploded into public view on Tuesday as judges traded insults and accusations during a heated supreme court hearing that was livestreamed into millions of Brazilian homes. During one of the most ferocious exchanges, one of the judges at the eye of the storm, Alexandre de Moraes, berated his rival, André Mendonça: “You’re at the service of a political group that tried to launch a coup in this country!” “It’s a lie!” Mendonça cried back. Minutes later, a third judge, Gilmar Mendes, angrily accused Mendonça of weaponizing the court’s work to cause political chaos and influence October’s presidential election. “Don’t point your finger at me, Minister Gilmar! Don’t point your finger! You’re not talking to any old person! Show some respect to this court!” Mendonça warned Mendes, who shot back: “Respect is earned, not given.” The courtroom drama – in many ways a proxy for the electoral battle between the leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, and his far-right rival, Flávio Bolsonaro – pits Moraes, a pugnacious shaven-headed martial arts practitioner, against Mendonça, a Presbyterian pastor who is the only openly evangelical member of the 11-seat court. Moraes was appointed almost a decade ago by rightwing president Michel Temer. But the 57-year-old judge is widely associated with Lula thanks to his successful prosecution of Flávio Bolsonaro’s father, the former president Jair Bolsonaro, for plotting a botched coup after losing the 2022 election to the leftwing veteran. Mendonça, meanwhile, was named during Jair Bolsonaro’s 2018-23 presidency and leftwingers widely view him as a stooge for the disgraced ex-president, who is serving a 27-year sentence for his failed power grab. With less than three weeks to go until the election, the two judges have gone to war, as Brazil’s biggest-ever banking scandal has snowballed into a judicial and political crisis of similarly shocking proportions. The Banco Master scandal began last November when the playboy owner of that collapsed bank, Daniel Vorcaro, was arrested by federal police as he prepared to board a private jet from São Paulo to Malta. Investigations uncovered apparent links between the jailed banker and an astonishing panoply of figures from Brazil’s political and judicial elite, foremost among them Flávio Bolsonaro and Moraes. Other members of the supreme court and their relatives have also been linked to Vorcaro. Mendonça has been accused of deliberately fast-tracking the investigation into Moraes, while stalling the inquiry into Vorcaro’s ties to the Bolsonaros and the banker’s bankrolling of a film about Jair Bolsonaro. Earlier this month, Mendonça unsealed an explosive police dossier relating to the Banco Master investigation that contained compromising WhatsApp exchanges apparently between Vorcaro and Moraes as well as a copy of a $25m contract between Banco Master and the law firm of Moraes’s wife. In one text message, sent two days before his arrest, Vorcaro asked Moraes: “Do you think … I need to get out [of the country]?” Moraes hit back on the eve of Tuesday’s hearing, claiming he was being smeared with politically-motivated “criminal lies” as part of a revenge attack by the rightwing forces behind the coup attempt that culminated in the January 2023 riots in Brasília. Moraes also alleged that the attacks on him involved “external actors” and were part of a possible foreign attempt to interfere in Brazil’s election. The Moraes/Mendonça tussle reached a crescendo on Tuesday as supreme court judges convened in Brasília to decide whether an investigation should be opened into Moraes’s conduct. Moraes has demanded an investigation into Mendonça. The judicial scandal has exploded just as Brazil’s election campaign is coming to a head, with polls suggesting a dead heat between Lula and Bolsonaro, who are likely to face off in a second-round run-off on 25 October. “The timing is awful. We are just a few weeks away from elections that already look to be challenging for a democracy that has been struggling to deal with extremist and anti-democratic groups that continue to be an important political force in the country. So I think we have a perfect storm here,” said Eloísa Machado, a constitutional law professor who follows the supreme court. Machado said Lula had “absolutely nothing to do” with the scandal engulfing Moraes and the supreme court, noting how the leftwing president had not appointed the judge. Even so, the crisis looks likely to hurt Lula’s chances of winning a historic fourth term, given the widespread public association between him and Moraes because of the judge’s involvement in Jair Bolsonaro’s jailing. In a social media video posted as Tuesday’s hearing played out, Flávio Bolsonaro blamed the judicial scandal on Lula’s administration but made no mention of his own alleged ties to Vorcaro. “This [is happening] because the current government ... is part of this decaying system and we are now seeing this rotten system reveal itself before the eyes of the entire nation,” Bolsonaro said, claiming Lula had “shared power” with Moraes. Thomas Traumann, a political analyst, predicted the scandal would accelerate the election campaign’s descent into a carnival of mudslinging, as both sides battled to convince voters of their rival’s sins. “This campaign is going to get dirtier much faster than we had expected,” he said.

title: Carney says Canada will pursue ‘unique security and economic alliance’ with EU amid US trade spat
summary: Prime minister speaks of strengthening Canada’s economic and political ties to Europe at Canada Investment Summit
text: Mark Carney said Canada will pursue a “unique security and economic alliance” with Europe as he positions his country as a base to build in the “new global economic order”. Speaking to investors, company executives and government ministers at the inaugural Canada Investment Summit on Tuesday, the prime minister pitched Canada as a “safe harbour” and lucrative home for foreign capital as his government looks to reduce its reliance on trade with the United States. Over the last 18 months, the relationship with the US has fractured, leaving Canada searching for ways to avert economic devastation. “The world is becoming more divided and dangerous. Sovereignty and openness are now in tension. Economic integration is being weaponised. Tariffs are used as leverage,” Carney said – a nod to the Donald Trump’s penchant for trade levies. “Canada recognised the rupture earlier than most. Our response reflects the two lessons we have taken from it: First, we must take care of ourselves, and second, we must take care of each other. Taking care of ourselves means building our strength at home and diversifying our partnerships abroad.” While Carney has referred to the trade spat as a “war”, there was a duelling sense of optimism at the summit among senior Canadian officials that the country’s more global perspective could usher in hundreds of billions in fresh investment into the country. That shift has been exemplified in recent weeks by Carney’s effort to strengthen Canada’s economic and political ties to the EU. Noting in his remarks at the summit that Canada is the only non-European member of Europe’s defence procurement initiative, the prime minister said his government will pursue a “unique” relationship with the bloc. He mused about the range of possibilities, including the prospect of visa-free travel and work between the two that has been raised in recent days, but said Canada and the EU were in early stage of talks. Carney will be the guest of honour at the European parliament’s plenary meeting in Strasbourg this week. He will attend European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen’s annual state of the union speech on Wednesday, where she is expected to sketch out new areas for EU-Canada cooperation. On Thursday, Carney will address MEPs in von der Leyen’s presence. The commission president hastily changed her plans to stay in Strasbourg, after being criticised over her initial “unacceptable” decision to skip Carney’s speech and return to Brussels. European officials are seeking to bring Canada as close as possible to the EU short of membership. But it will not be called associate membership, as the EU seeks to maintain a clear distinction between members and nonmembers. The long experience of Brexit negotiations cemented the EU’s preference not to split the four freedoms of its single market – free movement of people, services, goods and capital – so any deepening of the Canada relationship will be built around this red line. More immediately, the EU hopes to improve ties on raw materials and energy. Javier Moreno Sánchez, a Spanish socialist MEP, who leads the European parliament’s Canada delegation, said he wanted to hear “concrete steps” from von der Leyen on how to improve the EU-Canada relationship, calling for greater mobility for professionals, more student exchanges, joint work on defence and artificial intelligence. “Canadians are the most European people outside Europe and that is the key point for the development of our relationship,” he said. “Due to the difficult geopolitical geoeconomic situation in the world and the difficult relationship we have, both Canada and the European Union, with our traditional partner, the United States, I think it is the moment to have a closer relationship with Canada.” The EU and Canada already have a wide-ranging relationship, including a free-trade agreement and separate deals on digital cooperation, raw materials, research and a shared green alliance. Earlier this year, Canada became the first non-European country to join the EU’s €150bn defence loans scheme, meaning greater opportunities for Canadian defence firms to supply Europe. But irritants persist. Ten EU member states, including France, Italy and Poland, have not ratified the landmark EU-Canada Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (Ceta) nearly a decade after it was signed, meaning parts of the deal are yet to enter into force. French lawmaker Valérie Hayer, Emmanuel Macron’s ally in the European parliament, acknowledged the problem. “In the French parliament this agreement has yet to be ratified, notwithstanding the [trade] figures which are extremely good. That is why I call on political leaders [in France] to do their bit to act responsibly as elsewhere to make sure that we [the EU] can count for more in world affairs.” Hayer’s centrist Renew group, only the fifth-largest in the European parliament, is calling on EU member states and the commission to speed up Ceta ratification and launch an awareness-raising drive so European and Canadian companies have better knowledge of the trade opportunities. But ahead of a year of big elections – in France, Italy and Poland – progress on ratifying the 10-year-old agreement looks uncertain. EU-Canada’s trade in goods and services hit €130bn in 2025, an 80% increase since 2016 when Ceta was signed. But this pales in comparison to trade with the US, which is worth nearly US$880bn. Despite a deliberate push to increase global trade, Carney acknowledged the geographic realities of Canada’s proximity to its southern neighbour, and the reality, which most economists concede, that the US will remain Canada’s largest trading partner. “We will always be neighbours, and Canada will continue to be the US’s most important partner in many key areas,” he said. These arrangements work when we engage as true partners that respect each other’s traditions and sovereignty.” In recent weeks, Trump has both threatened Canada’s economy and mused about a North America under the umbrella of an expanded US. Event host Erik Schatzker told attendees that Canada was neither a “bystander nor a victim” in the dramatic geopolitical shifts that have defined the Trump era. “Canada is a protagonist. Canada has agency. Canada is defining its own future.” Carney said foreign investment has dramatically increased and the federal government was on track to balance the operating budget one year ahead of schedule, an announcement that received applause from the crowd. He announced a corporate tax “mega-deduction” that would help compete with similar incentives in the US allowing companies to immediately deduct 100% of the cost of new investment across more assets than previously permitted. Carney also confirmed Canada would open four of its major airports to foreign investment in order to “unlock their true value”. The prime minister also said his government would “apply [the] lessons” of instances in which allowing partial private investment had failed. But that theme – soliciting hundreds of billions in foreign investment while also reshoring domestic capability – has frustrated some. Ahead of the summit, thousands gathered in downtown Toronto for the Many vs the Money counter protest. Organisers said public money should not be used to reduce the risks of private investment while communities are left to shoulder the social and environmental costs of these projects. “Mark Carney’s here selling Canada to the international community,” said Stephen Hill, a lone protester standing outside the hotel as key figures arrived to the prime minister’s speech. “I’m Canadian. We’re an Aboriginal-led investment coalition. We want in. But you can’t get a returned email. You can’t get a returned phone call. You can’t get through to his ministers. So I’m here from British Columbia to try and get his attention and to tell him to think of Canadians first.” Ahead of Tuesday’s summit, the prime minister’s office announced nearly C$500bn in new domestic investment. “Canada has what the world wants,” Carney said during media availability late Tuesday morning. “The difference, this week, is that we didn’t cross an ocean to make our case. The world came to us … but what matters most is what we do for ourselves.”

title: John Healey in talks with Canada about UK joining new global defence bank
summary: Exclusive: Britain is understood to have been formally invited to become founding member of multilateral lender
text: John Healey is in talks with the Canadian government about joining a new global defence bank intended to help allies rearm to counter mounting security threats, just weeks after Rachel Reeves rejected the move. The chancellor is understood to be actively considering a bid to join the proposed Canada-led defence, security and resilience bank (DSRB), which proponents say could help the UK fund defence projects at lower cost, before planned talks with his Canadian counterpart this week. When he was defence secretary, Healey was understood to have been a strong advocate for keeping UK observers present at Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney’s, defence bank talks, despite resistance from the Treasury, which wanted to shut off those international discussions. Reeves, his predecessor as chancellor, was concerned the bank would not address the UK’s defence procurement issues and was more focused on lending to smaller defence firms in nations with lower credit ratings. The UK has had a AA credit rating since 2016. Healey, who has long been a proponent of multilateral funding mechanisms, met the Canadian finance minister, François-Philippe Champagne, twice at a G20 summit in North Carolina two weeks ago. They are due to meet again in the UK this week, when the two men are – according to sources – likely to discuss the defence bank, and both are expected to be at EU finance minister talks in Dublin later this week. Canada is understood to have already formally invited the UK to become a founding member of the bank, along with eight other countries including Ukraine and Turkey. Healey resigned as defence secretary in June, accusing Keir Starmer and his chancellor, Reeves, of putting the country’s security at risk because the defence spending package fell £13bn short of what he argued was required. As chancellor, he is expected to avoid setting a target date for reaching 3% defence spending in next month’s budget and instead is planning to set out a pathway to reaching the goal at the 2027 spending review. The DSRB could play a role in this by using financial leverage, separate from the balance sheets of already indebted nations, to boost defence investment. But it would need additional sovereign backing beyond current commitments to become a major player. Reeves announced at the Nato summit in Ankara in July that the UK would join the Netherlands, Finland and Poland to launch a new lender called the Multilateral Defence Mechanism. She said the MDM would help the UK with procurement – saving the UK as much as 20% – and stockpiling, which would give taxpayers better value for money while allowing government to borrow at a low rate to fund defence. The UK has committed an initial £600m to the new lender. The former chancellor had called for the two rival international defence financing schemes to merge, arguing that it made sense for countries to only fund one institution that could work for all nations. In addition to overlaps with existing initiatives, there were also understood to be concerns in the Treasury over the amount of capital that countries would need to commit while public finances are strained. The UK’s initial capital contribution would be between £1bn and £2bn over three years. The DSRB has been seeking to raise around €100bn, which it would use to lend at low cost to governments and contractors for defence projects. It would also offer guarantees for lenders financing smaller firms seen as riskier borrowers. A government spokesperson said: “We are fully committed to working alongside our international partners to scale defence industrial capacity. “We are working closely with our Canadian allies on ensuring the Multilateral Defence Mechanism and Defence Security Resilience Bank are complementary.”

title: Fourth person dies of measles-associated illness in US
summary: All deaths occurred in Pennsylvania, in worst year since 1992 for one of the most contagious diseases
text: Pennsylvania health officials said a fourth person had died of measles-associated illness in the worst year for the disease since 1992. All four US deaths have occurred in the state. Due to the Trump administration changing how it reports measles deaths, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) does not count any of the deaths in its national tally. Three people died in 2025. “My thoughts are with the two families who lost loved ones to this highly contagious virus, as Pennsylvania faces the worst measles outbreak in more than three decades,” Dr Debra Bogen, Pennsylvania’s secretary of health, said in a statement. Pennsylvania has reported nearly 700 cases of measles. “We remain committed to working with our partners across Pennsylvania to stem this outbreak and prevent more deaths. That means ensuring people have the facts about measles and access to the [measles, mumps and rubella] vaccine – which kept measles outbreaks at bay for decades,” she said. One to three people per 1,000 die of measles-related complications, such as pneumonia and neurologic complications. The measles-associated death announced on Tuesday was of an 18-year-old Mifflin county resident, who was diagnosed with encephalomyelitis, a rare and severe neurological complication of the virus. Up to one in five people infected with the disease will be hospitalized. Pennsylvania’s agricultural areas in Lancaster and Mifflin counties have been the center of the state’s outbreak. Utah, Florida, Virginia and Texas have also seen dozens of cases, according to tracking from Johns Hopkins University. The US has seen more than 3,300 cases in 2026. Epidemiological data is generally considered an undercount. Measles is one of the most contagious diseases known to medicine. The measles, mumps and rubella vaccine, or MMR, prevents 97% of measles cases. However, vaccination rates among kindergarten-aged children, considered a bellwether, have experienced a slow decline as experts argue the administration spreads confusion among parents. Robert F Kennedy Jr, the US health secretary and head of an anti-vaccine advocacy group before he took office, has upended federal vaccine policy and made multiple misleading statements about the MMR vaccine since taking office. The US eliminated measles in 2000, though it is unclear whether it can retain that status amid recent outbreaks. Globally, measles remains the leading cause of vaccine-preventable infant death.

title: Thirlwall inquiry has left biggest questions around the Letby case unanswered
summary: Decision not to pause proceedings means £18m report does not engage with concerns over former nurse’s conviction
text: Just two months before Lady Justice Kathryn Thirlwall opened her inquiry into events at the Countess of Chester hospital and the crimes of Lucy Letby, a report by Chris Henley KC was published into the “atrocious” wrongful conviction of Andrew Malkinson for rape. Henley prefaced that report with a plea for the legal establishment to recognise that the criminal courts produce miscarriages of justice. Right up to top judges in the court of appeal, Henley wrote, the system has “a deep-seated … cultural reluctance” to accept it “will on occasion make mistakes” and that “entirely innocent defendants will sometimes be convicted”. He said the system needed a culture that acknowledges mistakes can be made and ensures “in our various roles when making decisions we are all alive to this potential risk”. The Thirlwall inquiry was set up in 2023 by the then health secretary, Steve Barclay, on the basis that Letby was guilty of murdering seven babies, and attempting to murder seven more, at the Countess of Chester hospital’s neonatal unit where she was a nurse. Thirlwall’s terms of reference were to spotlight the hospital’s management, and whether their actions and culture “contributed to the failure to protect babies from Lucy Letby”. Many distinguished experts had already looked at the evidence and expressed very serious concerns that the system had made another of its mistakes and convicted an entirely innocent person. As the Guardian reported, 24 experts wrote to Wes Streeting, who took over as health secretary after Labour’s general election win in 2024, urging him to pause the inquiry or widen its terms of reference to examine the possibility of a miscarriage of justice. Streeting did not do so. In her opening speech in September 2024, Thirlwall, a court of appeal judge, referred to the criticisms of Letby’s convictions dismissively, referring to “a huge outpouring of comment” since the court of appeal refused Letby leave to appeal in May 2024, and to “all of this noise” that had caused distress to the bereaved parents. “It’s not for me to set about reviewing the convictions,” she said. “The court of appeal has done that with a very clear result. The convictions stand.” The core premise of the inquiry from the start was that the hospital’s managers had not acted on warnings about Letby from the consultants, and should have called in the police earlier. That was the central conclusion Thirlwall has reached in her 822-page report. She criticised “a prolonged delay by senior managers in calling the police” after two of three triplets, babies O and P at the trial, died in June 2016. There was an assumption throughout that the police, the Cheshire constabulary, were uniquely equipped to find the forensic truth about how the babies died. Thirlwall again emphasised in her final statement that her inquiry was “not an investigation into the criminal convictions or the guilt of Letby”. But the report is based on it being a fact that Letby is guilty and Thirlwall has delivered the devastating conclusion that babies would have been protected if the hospital had acted more quickly to safeguard them from the nurse. There was almost no moment in any of the gruelling inquiry sessions in the long, glittering ballroom of Liverpool town hall that engaged with the question looming over the proceedings: whether Cheshire constabulary may have got the case catastrophically wrong. A large group of British and international experts, led by the renowned Canadian neonatologist Dr Shoo Lee, who has argued relentlessly that his own research was misrepresented by the prosecution, concluded that there were no murders, only vulnerable newborn and premature babies, and poor care on the unit. Thirlwall heard in exhaustive detail about the actions the medical director, Ian Harvey, his management colleagues and the consultants took when considering the deaths and collapses of the babies. Postmortems had been carried out by three very experienced consultant pathologists at Alder Hey, Liverpool’s renowned children’s teaching hospital. They found no deliberate harm or any suspicion of it. Harvey had asked the Alder Hey pathologists to review their conclusions and they confirmed their original findings. He also had the babies’ deaths reviewed by a consultant neonatologist, Dr Jane Hawdon, of London’s Royal Free hospital. She also did not find any deliberate harm, but identified many areas of “sub-optimal care” on the unit. Harvey invited a review by the Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health, whose team came to a conclusion grimly familiar to maternity and children’s units in the NHS around the country. It had insufficient consultants and not enough consultant time was being spent on babies of such medical vulnerability, just two ward rounds each week. The management downgraded the unit so that it would no longer care for babies born so prematurely. Thirlwall examined all those processes and has concluded that none were adequate. Her conclusions are that when the consultants had raised concerns about Letby, safeguarding should immediately have been introduced and the police should have been called in earlier. So during two years and £18m spent on so much legal inquiry, the question has not been answered, nor was it allowed to be asked: how and why did Cheshire constabulary and the Crown Prosecution Service, and the doctors they recruited as expert witnesses, come to so wholly different a conclusion about the causes of death, from all the experts that had looked at the same medical evidence before? And nor was there permitted to be any solid engagement with the new experts, led by Lee, as to why they so fundamentally disagree with the prosecution’s case and convictions. In his call for more vigilance after the Malkinson catastrophe, Henley wrote: “Miscarriages of justice disfigure the lives of all connected to the case and make the public generally less safe.” The Criminal Cases Review Commission, the strained body whose role is to refer potential miscarriages of justice back to the court of appeal, is still looking at Letby’s application, and the copious expert reports submitted with it. In the meantime, a public inquiry chaired by a senior judge was set from beginning to end not to consider the possibility that the police, CPS and courts might have made a mistake, and served up a terrible injustice.

title: UK paying £56,000 for each person returned to France under ‘one in one out’ scheme
summary: Home secretary defends cost, saying it is about the same or cheaper than putting someone up in a hotel for a year
text: The government’s “one in, one out” deal is costing about £56,000 for every person sent back to France, Shabana Mahmood has told MPs. The home secretary disclosed the figure as she was questioned by the home affairs select committee over whether the scheme was delivering value for taxpayers. About 1,400 people have been removed to France by the Home Office since the scheme began in August 2025, although some have subsequently returned to the UK in lorries or small boats. Asked how much each return had cost, Mahmood said: “I’ll need to write to the committee on the most recent figures. “I think it’s per person for the numbers that have been returned so far, it’s about £56,000.” She later defended the cost, saying it was “still cheaper, or just about the same as supporting someone in a hotel for a year”. Under the deal, the UK sends a person who arrives by small boats back to France in exchange for taking an asylum seeker applying through a legal route. The pilot has already been extended once and is now due to run into October, with its long-term future still to be decided. France wants the bilateral arrangement to be eventually replaced by a wider EU-UK returns deal. An EU-wide returns deal known as the Dublin agreement existed before the UK left the EU. Attempts to continue the returns deal post-Brexit have been rejected by EU leaders. Mahmood dismissed suggestions an EU-wide system would be a “silver bullet” for the Channel crisis. She said the deal had already returned more migrants than Britain ever managed under the EU’s old Dublin arrangements. “It is a real mistake to think that that pact is the future. And if we were in that, this problem would go away because I promise you, it would not,” she said. She said the government’s scheme had struggled to scale up to larger numbers of returns, adding that it had been “operationally difficult” to increase removals because of constraints such as detention space. “It’s not been without its challenges. Obviously, the numbers are still relatively small,” she said. Laurent Nuñez, the French interior minister, has told Mahmood that he wants to end the scheme, it emerged earlier this week. In June, Nuñez told a French parliamentary inquiry: “For our part, we want to move away from this bilateral relationship with the UK. We consider that France should not have to carry it alone, and that it would be better to integrate it into an agreement between the EU and UK. “So I have already clearly told my counterpart that this pilot agreement, which we signed in August 2025, was not intended to be renewed beyond October 1, 2026.” Mahmood told the committee only “relatively small numbers” of rejected asylum-seeking families had taken up a separate pilot offering them as much as £40,000 to voluntarily leave Britain. She said: “If you’re a failed asylum-seeking family, what you’re trading off is an offer of £40,000, which will help you resettle back in your country of origin, versus, you know, access to free healthcare and education for your children.”

title: Republicans criticize racist social media post by Texas member running for office
summary: Karl Rove, a respected GOP consultant, further said he would vote for ‘bigot’ Bo French’s Democratic opponent after post
text: A senior Republican has called a party colleague running for office in Texas “a bigot” over a racist social media post attacking college football fans – and said he is so outraged by the comments that he will vote for the candidate’s Democratic rival. Karl Rove, who was former president George W Bush’s longtime political adviser and is a respected Republican consultant in Texas, told a private event in Austin on Sunday that he could not support Bo French’s candidacy for a seat on the state’s railroad commission, the Texas Tribune reported. Instead, he said, he will vote for Houston Democrat Jon Rosenthal over French, breaking a 32-year run of exclusively backing Republicans. His decision came after French posted on X a photograph of students wearing team attire celebrating the University of Texas’s rousing college football victory over top-ranked Ohio State on Saturday. The students are all non-Caucasian, and French wrote: “I heard UT graduation this year looked like this. I didn’t believe it. The problem is now obviously far worse than anyone imagined.” French could not have known the nationality or status of the students. According to Texas Global, fewer than 10% of the university’s 55,000 enrolled students are from overseas. His framing without evidence of the Asian students as “foreigners” – and attempt to denigrate them as outsiders – reflects a growing encroachment of formerly fringe views into mainstream Republican politics nationwide. But it drew condemnation from some in the party. John Cornyn – the establishment Republican Texas senator who lost his re-election primary to Ken Paxton, the Donald Trump-endorsed, scandal ridden state attorney general in May – attacked French on X on Tuesday. “The Republican Party is better than this. We should all condemn this bigotry directed at our fellow Texans or we will soon find ourselves a minority party,” he wrote, after French followed up his original post with an attempt to fundraise off it. Even Greg Abbott, the hard right Texas governor, appeared to have reservations. “That is not my message,” Abbott told Politico. “A selective picture of Longhorn fans celebrating our biggest home victory-ever actually shows a way that Texans unite. We all support our college football teams. “The way we win the state is the same way we win football games. We unite under the brand of Texas.” Republican state senator Lacey Hull urged French to remove the post on her own social media feed. “This post breaks my heart. I see college kids cheering on their football team. I see Texans,” she wrote. The chair of the university’s board of regents, Kevin Eltife, said in a statement that he too saw only Longhorns, the nickname of the college’s sports teams. “It’s the same remarkable view I have at graduation ceremonies and anytime I’m on campus,” he wrote. “I’m proud to celebrate all our Longhorn students today and every day. Thank you for making us proud.” French’s unashamed approach to the scandal continued on Monday in an appearance on a radio show in which he labelled Republicans who have criticized him as “less conservative”. “The establishment raised and spent $7[m] against me in the primary,” he told host Mark Davis, reported by the Tribune. “Many of the people who criticized me yesterday were some of the same people involved in that effort. It’s no surprise that the less-conservative people in Texas are the ones attacking me.” Other Republicans in midterm races elsewhere have also come under scrutiny for extremist, racist or misogynistic messaging, or their backgrounds. Brandon Herrera, a Texas candidate for a House seat in November, was called out for offensive sexual comments he reportedly made on social media using the handle “the AK guy”, a rightwing alter ego. In 2020, Herrera, who has 4 million followers on YouTube, filmed himself firing a gun at bottles of ranch dressing and, after they exploded, rubbed the condiment on to himself and declared that this would “make me irresistible to the fat bitches”. In 2024, after he described a Nazi-era gun as “the original ghetto blaster”, the Republican Jewish Coalition condemned him as “a goose-stepping extremist”. In New York, Peter Oberacker, a Republican state senator running for a congressional seat, was forced to delete a Facebook post paying tribute to his grandfather, who served in Adolf Hitler’s Nazi military during the second world war. Oberacker’s post featured a photograph of Ludwig Oberacker, who was killed during the Battle of the Bulge, in Nazi uniform. “I salute all who served,” Oberacker wrote, adding that he had debated whether or not to make the post. In Florida, Republican US House candidate Marshall Rowson was challenged on his ties to the League of the South, a white supremacist group. The online Talking Points Memo reported Monday that Rowson marched with neo-Nazis at the 2017 Charlottesville Unite the Right rally, at which Heather Heyer, a counter-protester, was killed. The outlet said it reviewed video showing Rowson and his now-wife arriving at the rally and being greeted by name by members of the League of the South members, which advocates for the secession from the US of southern states. Rowson did not respond to a request for comment after the Washington Post amplified the story on Tuesday.

title: Leader of Reform UK in Wales stands down after arrest on suspicion of assault
summary: Dan Thomas, elected in May, says he does not wish to be a ‘distraction’ on same day Reform MS defects to Plaid Cymru
text: The leader of Reform UK in Wales is standing down after he was arrested and bailed on suspicion of assault and controlling or coercive behaviour. Dan Thomas, a former Tory councillor, had only been announced as Reform’s Welsh leader by Nigel Farage in February. He was elected as leader of the opposition in May’s election to the Welsh parliament, when Reform UK became the second largest party. However, it emerged on Tuesday that Thomas would not be taking part in the first plenary session of the new Senedd term and questions for the first minister on Tuesday afternoon. Reform said he was absent for “personal reasons”. In a statement later on Tuesday afternoon, Thomas said: “Over the weekend, I was reported to the police and was released without charge. I stress that I have done nothing wrong, but I do not want the coming headlines to be a distraction from the fantastic work our Senedd team is doing in holding this government to account.” Gwent police said: “On Sunday 13 September, a 45-year-old man, from the Aberbargoed area, was arrested on suspicion of assault and engaging in controlling/coercive behaviour. He has been bailed pending further inquiries.” Thomas, a former Conservative leader of Barnet council in north London, is originally from Blackwood, Caerphilly. Eyebrows had been raised on Monday when Thomas was notably quiet when it came to commenting on the meeting of the nationalist first ministers of Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland, who called on Westminster to prepare for independence referendums. His resignation comes as a big blow to Reform, which has poured significant resources into Wales, where it believes further inroads could be made in traditional Labour strongholds. However, the perception of Thomas as a figure who was parachuted in by Reform headquarters has caused tensions. It is believed Farage chose an outsider to the Welsh branch of the party in an effort to distance from its former Welsh leader, Nathan Gill, who was jailed for accepting bribes to make pro-Russia statements in the European parliament. Since the new Senedd opened in May, there have been frequent reports of infighting in the Reform group, and its performance in the Siambr so far has been notable for unparliamentary conduct. Thomas led Barnet council between 2019 and 2022, when the north London council was seized by Labour, and defected to Reform last summer. He stood down in December as a councillor in Finchley – long synonymous with Margaret Thatcher – to move back to his south Wales valleys home town. In May, Reform won 34 seats at the expense of Labour and the Conservatives in the Welsh parliament’s newly expanded 96-seat chamber, behind Plaid Cymru’s 43. Reform had been aiming to become Wales’s biggest party, Thomas said, but it still performed better than any Welsh Conservative result on record and managed to increase its vote share from 1% in 2021 to 29% in 2026. With more than a third of the seats, the Senedd is the biggest political platform Reform has had to date. At almost exactly the same time Thomas announced his resignation, the Reform MS Sarah Cooper-Lesadd said she was defecting to Plaid Cymru – a party nearly on the opposite end of the political spectrum. She said in a statement: “[Reform UK] … are not serious about governing Wales. They are far more interested in division, opposition and headlines than in finding solutions.” The defection of Cooper-Lesadd coincided with more bad news elsewhere for Reform as three of its councillors resigned from the party on one of its flagship county councils, Durham, after allegations of bullying. Ken Skates, the leader of the Labour Senedd group, said: “Nigel Farage chose to make Nathan Gill his leader in Wales and he turned out to be a Russian asset. He chose to take £5m from a crypto billionaire that triggered an investigation. “He chose to meet two men in a pub in Clacton to discuss breaching electoral law. And he chose to make Dan Thomas his leader in Wales, who has now quit suddenly.” The Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, said on X that “people are innocent until proven guilty” but added that there was “a pattern” in terms of Conservatives who had defected to Nigel Farage’s party. “He took a large number of very problematic people from the Conservatives. Reform is where they belong,” she said.
