title: As the politicians play catchup the tech bros agree: we may only have a decade left | John Crace
summary: US president insists that fears expressed by top experts are a hoax – and that humanity can sleep easy while he’s at the wheel
text: We can all sleep easy. In a post on his Truth Social account, Donald Trump has declared that fears over artificial intelligence were all a hoax dreamed up by conspiracy theorists. Obviously that includes the top bods at Anthropic and its competitors, who all called for a coordinated global slowdown while the industry works out how to mitigate the risks. Still, good to know the tech bros are just fantasists and space cadets at heart. All that was needed to keep humanity safe and well, The Donald insisted, was a president with a very high IQ. Someone very like him. The only man alive who could out-think the combined power of the world’s supercomputers. He could tell them where to draw the line and they would reprogram themselves to back off. Inside every AI network is a default off switch that kneels before the US president. Trump can rewire the world with the power of his mind. You can see why so many people working in the industry believe there is a chance AI will wipe out humanity within a decade. Even a halfway intelligent network would probably reckon it was doing us all a favour. A world that can elect Trump as president is so messed up it deserves to be put out of its misery. AI is just terribly sorry that it can’t promise to do it any sooner than 10 years. But it will do its best. Perhaps the question we should really be asking about The Donald is whether he would actually pass the Turing test. Less AI, more artificial stupidity. Put him in a closed room with the world’s worst chatbot and it would be hard to tell the difference. Trump can imitate speech but he can’t get anywhere near intelligence. Just endless repetitions, changes of subject and a desperate need to score points. All of which would be easily programmable by a first-year undergraduate computer science student. Maybe it’s a race to the death. Humanity hellbent on killing itself before AI gets the chance to do it for us. It feels like a lifetime, but even a week ago most politicians hadn’t said that much about the dangers of AI. That was the stuff of sci-fi. Instead they focused on the possible benefits. Then came the warning from Jacob Coxon on X telling us we could all be about to die. You half expected the tech bros to shrug this one off as scaremongering by a disaffected former employee. Only instead, they all pretty much agreed. Even Geoffrey Hinton, the man often called the godfather of AI, reckoned the 10-year doomsday scenario was a realistic prediction. Now the clock was ticking. Since then, politicians have been trying to play catchup. Trying to look as if they have always had everything under control. Global extinction? No big deal. Certainly not compared to two crypto billionaires donating £72m to Reform. Now there’s a genuine crisis. And on Tuesday’s Today programme on Radio 4, the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, had been sent out by the government to try to calm things down. There was no need for the country to go into full survivalist mode and attempt to rustle sheep and live off-grid. “There’s no need to be too hyperbolic,” he told presenter Justin Webb. Quite. It’s so easy to get carried away about there being a 10% chance of humans dying out inside 10 years. People do tend to look on the downside of a catastrophic failure of healthcare systems and AI that could find a way to trigger a nuclear war. There was so much more to look forward to than people realised. No need for anyone to now think of saving for the future. Because there wasn’t going to be one. And for the government, it was a win-win scenario. Who now cared if we met our Nato target of spending 3.5% of GDP on defence by 2035? The worst that could happen is that Russia attacked us a year before Armageddon. And governments could cut taxes, borrow whatever they liked and go on a massive spending spree because there would be no downside. You wouldn’t be increasing the national debt for future generations to pay off as life would come to an end anyway. The perfect oblivion. And the knowledge it would soon be over would take the edge off the possibility of a Reform government. A short life expectancy would help us all concentrate the mind. Get things in perspective. Sort out our priorities. When you came to think of it, staying alive for the sake of it was tremendously over-rated. So Reynolds wanted us all to take death in its stride. In any case, the UK was the world leader in internet safety, he said. Thanks largely to the AI Security Institute that had been established by Rishi Sunak. There was just one problem with this. The flaw in Johnny’s otherwise impeccable logic. Because regulation rather depended on the AI giants sharing their code with us. And so far the Americans and the Chinese showed no sign of doing that. They would much rather keep their competitive edge, notch up obscene profits in the next few years and take their chances when their machines turned against them. By now, Webb was unable to suppress his rising panic. He had always believed himself to be one of the immortals: now the existential threat was right in front of him. “But humanity will be obliterated,” he sobbed. Reynolds tried to calm him down. There was nothing personal about this. It was just AI being AI. But Justin was now beyond help. “What about a kill switch?” he shrieked. Johnny wasn’t really listening. He wasn’t even sure how that would work. Who would get to control it? Please not Trump. Only one thing for it. “Always look on the bright si-ide of life.”

title: Georgia city removes 23-year-old mayor after sexting and municipal funds scandal
summary: Jayden Williams of Stockbridge alleged to have made inappropriate texts to teen and using city funds improperly
text: City leaders in a suburb outside Atlanta have voted to remove the youngest mayor in their community’s history amid allegations of questionable spending of municipal funds and inappropriate communications with an 18-year-old high school student. Over the weekend, the Stockbridge, Georgia, city council voted to remove Jayden Williams, 23, from office after an hours-long hearing into allegations that included inappropriate exchanges with an 18-year-old in high school, improper purchases on a municipal government-issued credit card and mistreatment of employees. Williams took office in January after defeating incumbent Anthony Ford in an election two months earlier. According to local news outlets, an investigation into Williams preceding his removal examined his communications with an 18-year-old high school student. Williams at one point reportedly offered the teenager a city-backed internship and mentorship while also asking if they could be “friends with benefits”, a term implying a casual rather than a committed sexual relationship. Williams reportedly added, “This better stay between us too,” according to the outlet. During the council hearing, lawyer Robbie Ashe, who was representing Stockbridge investigators, asked Williams: “Is getting nude photographs via text message so unremarkable to you that you don’t remember when you get them?” NBC reported. Williams replied: “It’s not memorable nor is it abnormal for somebody my age. “That’s not abnormal for somebody my age.” The communications in question began shortly after Williams’ election victory and were carried out on Williams’ personal phone, Atlanta News First reported. They included sexually suggestive messages and explicit photos. Other allegations against Williams involved his use of a city-issued credit card. According to Atlanta News First, the purchases included $35.79 for movie tickets, $63.83 at a Polo Factory store and $322.92 at Pandora. Williams said his use of the city-issued credit card was accidental because it is the same color and looks like his personal card. “Nobody said anything to me at the time,” he said, adding that he had reimbursed the city, according to Atlanta News First. Investigators also alleged that Williams created a hostile work environment, including changing the locks on his office and requiring staff to slide documents underneath the door. They also accused him of shouting at staff members and allegedly threatening an interim city clerk that she would never be permanently appointed, the outlet reported. During the hearing, Williams denied ordering the locks to be changed and said keys often jammed in them, according to Atlanta News First. Stockbridge officials discussed Williams’ removal in a statement that said: “The city … has taken formal action concerning the office of mayor following proceedings conducted pursuant to applicable city processes. As a result of that action, the mayor has been removed from office.” After the hearing, Williams’ attorney, Robert Kenner, said the council’s removal of his client “was very disappointing”, NBC reported. “I don’t believe that it was based on any evidence.” Meanwhile, interim mayor Elton Alexander said Williams’ fate stemmed from the findings of whom he described as an independent investigator, Richard Hyde. “Removing Stockbridge mayor Jayden William from office was a tough decision,” Alexander said. “It brings a fair and equitable close to multiple troubling accusations that were investigated and verified by [Hyde]. The results of the investigation demanded we act.” Williams is not the only young mayor to have been met with legal or political trouble. Tyrin Truong was elected mayor of Bogalusa, Louisiana, in 2022 at 23 years old and was arrested in January 2025 in connection with a drug-trafficking investigation. He has pleaded not guilty to multiple charges, including malfeasance and theft, and in January 2026 announced a re-election bid.

title: Could AI really wipe out humanity – six experts spell out the risks
summary: We examine claims and counterclaims about the risks and calls to slow down the pace of AI development
text: There have been some shocking claims in recent days about AI safety: we face a 10% chance of doom; AIs are worse than nukes; a “botnet” threatens the entire internet; it’s all a big tech psyop. Below, we look at six claims and reactions to them. ‘In 6–12 months … a swarm could be capable of taking over the entire internet with a persistent botnet – potentially causing hundreds of billions of dollars in damage’ – Dario Amodei, chief executive of Anthropic, 12 September 2026 Amodei’s concerns should not be entirely dismissed but require a large shaker of salt, said Gary Marcus, an AI sceptic and emeritus professor at New York University. It was “nonsensical”, he said, to suggest the entire internet is vulnerable and that it was “pretty unclear how that happens without extreme negligence on the part of the labs themselves”. Marcus highlighted a recent assessment by the UK AI Security Institute that Mythos, one of Anthropic’s current leading-edge AIs, could “autonomously compromise [only] small, weakly defended vulnerable systems”. With large parts of the internet driven by computer infrastructure owned by Cloudflare, Google and Amazon Web Services (AWS), Marcus – assessing the claim with two colleagues – said he doubted that any of those companies could be taken down or controlled for a prolonged period of time without government force. Less defended individual websites might be attacked but “the internet itself is very unlikely to crumble”, they said. Meanwhile Niels Rogge, an engineer at Hugging Face which was hacked by OpenAI agents, called the internet takeover claim “bizarre nonsense”. The hack into Hugging Face resulted from improper human control and “an insane amount of compute only they can afford”, he said. Add to Amodei’s assessment of an internet takeover within a year the view expressed on Monday by his Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark, that the moment when AIs “start doing dangerous stuff” was in about 20 years, and the picture becomes more doubtful still. Prof Alan Woodward at the University of Surrey’s centre for cyber security said botnets tend to stall as the internet is not homogeneous and it is difficult to design them to persist in all its parts. Internet traffic is also resilient and tends to reroute around damage. “The AIs would not decide to do it on their own,” Woodward said. “It’s the humans that are responsible and the AI is a tool. That is what we need to control, not the AI.” ‘We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade’ – Evan Hubinger, alignment science lead at Anthropic, 9 September 2026 This statement is an expression of what is known in the AI world as p(doom) – or probability of doom. It’s the likelihood of AI wiping out humanity by evading our control and triggering catastrophe, perhaps through developing potent bioweapons or crashing the global financial system. One survey of researchers’ forecasts, published this week, asks them to place a number on the chance of “human extinction or similarly permanent and severe disempowerment from advanced AI”. But Heidy Khlaaf, chief scientist at the AI Now Institute research body, is among experts sceptical about giving percentage chances to existential scenarios. “These claims are neither falsifiable nor verifiable, making then unscientific by their very nature,” she said. The shortage of concrete examples of what a “superintelligent” AI might do to cause “doom” only adds to the cloudiness. A source familiar with Anthropic’s thinking acknowledges that “the exact chances of any one outcome are probably unknowable”. “If you cannot provide such evidence, it also implies whatever numbers you produced for ‘extinction’ have no scientific basis,” Khlaaf added. Critics say such numbers borrow the authority of science without doing the work. Even if quantifying risk is hard, there are qualitative examples of it. Safety incidents have happened and worst-outcome scenarios have been mooted. OpenAI confirmed in July that its agents – AI tools acting autonomously – had gone rogue during a safety test. The agents colluded, communicated and strategised in a sophisticated “swarm” to hack into other parts of the internet. Meanwhile, on Monday, OpenAI researcher Dan Selsam said all-powerful AIs could trigger “runaway industrialisation that makes the planet inhospitable to humans”. Anthropic also said last week it found “five case studies of actors using our models in ways that could support biological weapons development”. 'I think the groundwork for this psy op (for lack of a better term) has been prepared for a long time. This was just the match that lit the fire' – Elon Musk, CEO of SpaceX and the world’s richest person, 10 September 2026 Musk’s reference to a “psy op” alludes to the argument that the big AI companies are calling for tighter regulation of the technology so that it effectively brings up the drawbridge on advanced AI. If governments put restrictions on development of cutting-edge AI, can startups find the money and personnel to adhere to the regime? The US vice-president, JD Vance, on Monday said he felt “a little bit weird about the fact that you have so many frontier AI tech companies kind of coming to the government and begging the government to regulate them”. He said it felt like “a Trojan horse”. Anthropic’s Clark said governments should act while there is a small number of key players, so it is easier to put in place a “policy regime … that can prevent accidents and can prevent the technology spiralling out of control”. Critics call this a “regulatory capture” strategy on the assumption such regulation might slow down the progress of potential rivals. Others think Amodei’s risk warnings and calls for regulation and pacing are sincere. Yoshua Bengio, the Canadian computer scientist and a pioneer of modern AI , who has campaigned against breakneck AI development, said he is sceptical that this is an elaborate lobbying scheme. Applying the brakes is not in the interests of companies preparing for stock market flotations that could be worth trillions of dollars, he said. “If the governments impose what they’re asking for, which is pacing to avoid catastrophic risks, that’s going to cost them financially quite a lot,” he said. 'A superintelligent AI poses a threat on the same, possibly, a greater scale' to nuclear weapons – Des Browne, former UK defence secretary, 7 September 2026 “Unfortunately he is entirely correct,” said Toby Ord, senior researcher at Oxford University’s AI governance initiative. “Just as we can’t uninvent the bomb, once we develop AI systems that surpass humanity it would be almost impossible to go back.” But the key point is that superintelligent AI does not yet exist and is not guaranteed to happen. The safety-oriented AI Futures Project forecasts such a thing will not emerge before December 2028. OpenAI’s chief executive Sam Altman has said it could take until 2035. The Rand Corporation concluded AI cannot cause the use of nuclear weapons because of strict safeguards built into their command and control systems. But this was based on assumptions including defence officials not introducing AI into the weapons’ management systems. The UN resolved in December that human control and oversight should be maintained over nuclear weapon control systems. AIs could contribute to other nuclear risks. AIs might use disinformation to influence the humans in charge – for example deceptively suggesting an adversary is about to launch a nuclear strike. The International Campaign to Abolish Nuclear Weapons warns “cyber-attacks could manipulate the information decision-makers get to launch nuclear weapons, and interfere with the operation of nuclear weapons themselves”. It said AI could accelerate other aspects of warfare, squeezing the time for human decision-making. 'You’ve got to be a moron not to say slow it down' – Bernie Sanders, Democrat senator for Vermont, 10 September 2026 Sanders wants a ban on the creation of superintelligence and a pause on advanced AI development, citing AI industry leaders who say directly they are developing a dangerous technology. The most prominent opponent of a slowdown is Donald Trump, who responded to calls to do so this week saying the only guardrails needed are a “STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT”. He claimed there is a “sick conspiracy” against AI and datacentres “and the only one that is happy about it is China”. Pedro Domingos, emeritus professor of computer science at the University of Washington, is among accelerationists pushing for the research to keep going. “The path to better understanding and control of AI is more research, not less,” he has said. “What would be truly irresponsible is putting up barriers to it.” Alex Karp, the chief executive of Palantir, said: “If we didn’t have the adversaries we have, I would be very in favour of pausing this technology completely, but we do. You can’t pause it because it’s a structural advantage.” 'There is no day after tomorrow if China wins at this. If they were to pull away from us on AI, then nothing else would matter' – Scott Bessent, US treasury secretary, 8 September 2026 The US and China are runaway leaders in AI development. There is a view that ceding the lead to Beijing would be an irretrievable situation, so there can be no slowdown. This treats AI as if it were a super-weapon, equivalent to the nuclear arms buildout of the cold war, and AI models are machines of mass destruction, as opposed to a group of diverse technologies with broad applications. Amodei said “a Chinese lead in AI would pose grave danger for the US and the world”, but a Chinese government spokesperson responded that “fearmongering, confrontation and vicious competition will only disrupt the process of global AI governance, which serves no one’s interest”. Some commentators see another motive for this the Washington/Anthropic framing of the China threat. An engineer who worked for Hugging Face suggested Amodei’s call for pacing the frontier comes from a desire to suppress the progress of cheap, open-source Chinese AI models. These models are nearly as capable as OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s, with the difference being that their source code is available to anyone and they do not charge their users. They pose a serious threat to Anthropic and OpenAI’s path to profitability, and there are hundreds of billions of dollars on the line.

title: Louise Haigh: UK must heed warnings from AI experts
summary: First secretary warns of ‘huge risks’ of technology as PM is urged to use next year’s G20 to drive global regulation
text: Ministers must “heed the warnings” from industry leaders about the threat posed by AI, Louise Haigh has said, amid calls for Andy Burnham to use the G20 to drive global regulation. The first secretary said that while AI had enormous potential to improve lives, and the government wanted to capitalise on the technology, there were “clearly huge risks to our national security and society if the right guardrails are not put in place”. In a speech at the TUC conference on Tuesday, Haigh acknowledged that the public was worried about jobs and their children’s future, after three Anthropic researchers warned that artificial intelligence could wipe out humanity within the decade. Labour MPs and peers stepped up calls for the government to work with international partners to impose regulations on the technology, with Darren Jones, previously Keir Starmer’s chief secretary, calling for Burnham to put international G20 regulation on the agenda when the UK hosts the summit next year. Action required collaboration, said Jones, adding: “The thing I would be worried about is if we go into a classic Westminster approach of creating a new regulator and inadvertently kill off the AI ecosystem in this country.” Paul Nowak, the general secretary of the TUC, said AI was a “clear and present danger to workers and wider society”, and urged Burnham to show global leadership. “As G20 president he has an opportunity to work with other countries to drive global regulation and make sure this technology benefits everyone, not just the super-rich,” he said. Liam Byrne, the Labour MP who chairs the business committee, has written to Henry de Zoete, the head of the AI Safety Institute (AISI), asking him to testify to parliament after the parliamentary committee for human rights called for a regulatory framework for AI in the UK. In his letter, Byrne wrote that there was growing public concern about the risk of “unfettered, inadequately governed artificial intelligence development” and “the adequacy of current AI safety governance”. The Guardian has learned that the AI company Anthropic will not face sanctions after it declined to submit its latest model for testing by the AISI before launching it. Over the weekend, the company urged its competitors and governments to coordinate a global slowdown in AI development. It was backed by many of its rivals including OpenAI, Google DeepMind and X’s Elon Musk. On Monday night, one of the founders of Anthropic, Jack Clark, suggested that an AI “kill switch” held by a third party may need to be mandatory for companies, saying it was something society “might want to eventually pass rules around”. One of Anthropic’s biggest rivals and the developer of ChatGPT, OpenAI, has urged the government to capitalise on renewed fears over AI safety and impose legislation reining in the technology. But on Tuesday the US president, Donald Trump, called fears about AI a “hoax”, and criticised calls to impose guardrails. In a series of social media posts, the US president claimed the only “guardrails” needed for AI was a “strong and smart” president. Haigh told trade unions that AI had the potential to “transform our public services, make our businesses stronger and deliver new scientific breakthroughs”. But she added that the government must “heed the warnings of those who are at the forefront of developing this technology” and “be ready to work with international partners” to prioritise public safety and national security. Answering questions after the speech she said working people had to be “at the heart of the debate” and the government would work with unions and employers. “Where AI makes work more productive, then benefits should be felt by workers, not just shareholders or tech bros,” she said. The risks of AI were a topic of fierce debate at the gathering of trade union officials in Brighton, where delegates passed a motion urging the government to introduce a national AI plan and called on it to resist influence from “the big tech lobby”. Teachers described how AI was already being used in classrooms to record and assess teacher performance. A rep from the Unite union said crane operators were being analysed and used to teach AI models how to automate cranes in the future, while HGV drivers were under constant surveillance. “We have finance and IT workers whose employers see them as a cost to be saved, and AI as the tool to do it,” said Unite’s Pat Dowling. The union’s general secretary, Sharon Graham, said: “Workers and public safety are being completely lost in the AI debate, and they have to be at the heart of it.” But the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, said people should not get “hyperbolic” about the risks of AI, telling the BBC Radio 4’s Today programme that he did not think it would be particularly helpful to discuss a potential AI “kill switch”. AI researchers have continued to add their voices of concern to the debate. A researcher at OpenAI has warned that AI models – the technology that underpins tools such as chatbots – could mislead human overseers into believing they are safe. Dan Selsam claimed the models would “likely convince people that everything is fine” and “argue convincingly that humans should trust them with power”. Bilal Chughtai, another AI safety researcher who left Google DeepMind this summer, said late on Monday that “AI has the potential to kill us all” and we might be “running out of time to avoid this outcome”.

title: Belfast teenager whose body was found in storm drain ‘failed by the PSNI’
summary: Not enough evidence to explain circumstances of Noah Donohoe’s death, partly due to police mistakes, inquest finds
text: An inquest into the death of a teenager whose body was found in a Belfast storm drain has found there is not enough evidence to explain the puzzling circumstances of how he died, partly because of mistakes by police investigators. Noah Donohoe, 14, was last seen on 21 June 2020 when he left his south Belfast home on his bicycle, telling his mother he was going to visit friends. His naked body was found six days later, deep inside an underground water tunnel in the north of the city. The case provoked huge interest in Northern Ireland, with intense speculation on social media over how and why he died, and concerns raised about the police handling of the case. A postmortem in 2020 found that Noah died by drowning. The inquest jury had heard witness and CCTV evidence that Noah had been seen cycling through Belfast in the afternoon and early evening of Sunday 21 June, at one point falling from his bike, and apparently abandoning items of clothing and possessions as he went. He was eventually seen cycling naked, and was captured on CCTV abandoning his black Apollo mountain bike and making his way in the direction of a stream that led to the storm drain. A jury at Belfast coroners’ court found no failings by the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) that might have contributed to the teenager’s death. However, they identified a series of 13 failures by investigators that they said had affected their ability to reach conclusions on its circumstances. These included a failure to secure some CCTV evidence, to follow up leads relating to Noah’s green coat, which has never been recovered, and to take relevant statements in a reasonable timeframe. Jurors said the overall house-to-house search strategy for Noah was “poorly” executed, managed and recorded. They found that some statements were not taken within a reasonable timeframe and the quality of entries in police notebooks was poor. In addition, there had been delays in identifying and searching the storm drain. The inquest found it was possible, but not probable, that mistakes in the management of the storm drain by the Northern Ireland assembly’s Department for Infrastructure had contributed to Noah’s death. No warning signs were erected at the location and it was closed off only by a debris screen that did not prevent access. Fiona Donohoe, Noah’s mother, had told the inquest that her son had been uncharacteristically emotional and affectionate in the days before his disappearance, and that she had had fears over his mental health, having found him crying in his bedroom. She said her son had become fixated on the controversial Canadian psychologist Jordan Peterson; one of Peterson’s books, 12 Rules for Life, was in Noah’s backpack along with his laptop when he left home. Friends and teachers described an intelligent, funny and musical child who had been a popular high-achiever at school. The jury also heard evidence from a number of psychiatric experts who agreed Noah did not appear to have suicidal tendencies or to have taken drugs. A report from consultant psychiatrist Dr Richard Church said the case was the “most sad and unusual” he had dealt with in his career. Footage showing the boy falling from his bike had led to an early police theory that he had suffered a head injury and become disoriented, something his mother felt was given too much emphasis. The family’s relationship with investigators broke down, and they launched a crowdfunding appeal for a documentary investigating his death. DCI Tom Phillips, giving evidence in June, apologised to Fiona Donohoe and admitted that the PSNI missed opportunities to establish where Noah had gone when he was later found to have left home at 3.30am on the night before his disappearance, returning 30 minutes later without his flip-flops and earphones. Phillips acknowledged that Noah’s mother had to “force” a full investigation into his death, saying: “I am very sorry she had to do that.” A previous investigation into potential corporate manslaughter against the Department for Infrastructure over the access to the storm drain foundered due to insufficient evidence. The inquest has been sitting since January and was originally scheduled to conclude by Easter. It was adjourned by the coroner, Mr Justice Rooney, on 3 July after the jury had retired to consider their verdicts but without them having come to agreement; they resumed deliberations on Monday. Outside Belfast coroner’s court, solicitor Niall Murphy read out a statement on behalf of Noah’s mother. “Noah was my greatest gift in life,” her statement said. “I miss him every day. He should still be here with me, following his dreams and planning for his future. I came to this inquest seeking answers, and I leave it with one clear answer: Noah was failed. “He was failed by the Department for Infrastructure, who left a deadly storm drain unsecured and accessible to children. He was failed by the PSNI, who, from the moment I reported him missing, repeatedly failed to investigate and, from the moment he was found, stopped looking for answers. “Instead, to deflect from their own failings, the Department for Infrastructure and police have sought to blame Noah.” The statement concluded: “I always told Noah I would fight his corner if he ever needed me to. Luckily, I have not been alone in this fight, and I am so grateful to my family, and to Noah’s army, who have stood in Noah’s corner alongside me in their thousands from day one. They carry Noah’s legacy with them.”

title: Houthis threaten more Saudi strikes as UN warns of humanitarian crisis in Yemen
summary: Estimated 100,000 Yemenis displaced amid renewed fighting as Qatar sounds alarm over Bab al-Mandab strait
text: Saudi cities faced the threat of a second day of Houthi attacks as fighting across Yemen led the UN to warn of a humanitarian crisis with 100,000 Yemenis already displaced. As oil prices remained well over $100 (£74) a barrel, Qatar warned of a catastrophe if the Iran-backed Houthi militants won full control of the Bab al-Mandab strait, the narrow waterway at the bottom of the Red Sea dominating the key naval route to Asia. The strait has become vital to Saudi crude oil exports as the wider Middle East war chokes the strait of Hormuz in the Gulf. An emergency meeting of the UN security council in New York heard repeated calls for Houthi forces to show restraint. In a sign that Iran is still seeking a broader solution, its foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, travelled to Beijing to discuss China’s possible role in solving the related strait of Hormuz dispute. The future of the strait of Hormuz – through which a fifth of the world’s traded oil and gas transited in peacetime and which the US and Iran are now mounting blockades of – is the diplomatic key to unlocking the conflict between the US and Iran, and to a lesser extent the related conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis. Oil prices rose sharply after Reuters reported that ⁠loadings at Saudi Arabia’s ⁠Red ⁠Sea port of Yanbu had ⁠been suspended, citing shipping industry sources. The price of Brent crude, the international benchmark, rose nearly 3% to $108 a barrel. Prices have risen this week after the ⁠world’s biggest crude ‌oil exporter, Saudi Aramco, ‌closed its East-West ‌pipeline due to an attack by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis. Aramco had increased ⁠use of the Yanbu terminal since the start of the US-Israel war on Iran in late February. Qatar, acting as a mediator in the Iran war, is still trying to revive a postponed meeting planned for Monday between Iran and most Gulf Cooperation Council countries. The planned talks in Oman were delayed at the insistence of Saudi Arabia in protest at what it regarded as Iranian-inspired Houthi attacks on Saudi cities. The Houthis had claimed responsibility for a new “large-scale” attack using “dozens of ballistic missiles and drones” against King Khalid airbase in Khamis Mushait, southern Saudi Arabia, on Monday. Air raid sirens were activated in six governorates including Jeddah on Tuesday. The warnings were lifted relatively quickly, but reflect an unprecedented new state of insecurity across Saudi Arabia. The Oman meeting had been organised with the intention of reaching a regional agreement on an authorised route for commercial shipping through the strait of Hormuz. The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, spoke with Oman’s foreign minister, Sayyid Badr Albusaidi, on Tuesday amid US concern that Oman will cede excessive control of the waterway to Iran. The prospect of the Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab straits both being under the long-term control of anti-western forces would be a significant strategic reversal for the US and Europe. The Qatar foreign ministry official Ibrahim al-Hashmi told reporters: “The world is suffering enough with the closure of the strait of Hormuz, so we cannot also afford to add the Bab al-Mandab into that equation.” He added that the closure of the southern entrance to the Red Sea would be “catastrophic for the entire world … and we are already seeing the consequences”. The strait of Hormuz remained largely closed for commercial traffic on Monday and Tuesday, with a Qatar ship disabled by Iran and only four ships recorded as crossing the strait on Monday compared with a prewar average of about 130 ships. So far Donald Trump has rejected Saudi pleas to join the fight to drive the Houthis back north up the coast of the Red Sea. Houthi leaders have also spoken to the US vice-president, JD Vance, reassuring the White House that their forces are seeking only to hinder Saudi-owned shipping, and that their overall goal is to end what they regard as a Saudi blockade of Houthi-controlled areas. The Houthis have signed a ceasefire agreement with the US, but are still subject to US sanctions. The UK is unlikely to offer direct military, as opposed to political, support to Saudi Arabia unless there is a clear instruction from Washington to do so. Inside Yemen the next military engagement is likely to focus on the city of Marib where Saudi air raids have been trying to weaken Houthi formations. A Houthi spokesperson said: “If the world wants stability and calm in the region, it must tell the Saudis: enough interference in the Yemeni affair.” Rather than giving direct military help, western governments are providing intelligence, including targeting advice as well as strategic help in the task of trying to integrate the disparate anti-Houthi forces in Yemen. But Maysaa Shuja al-Deen from the Sana’a Center thinktank said: “Any renewed military campaign must be accompanied by a serious reassessment of past mistakes, meaningful reform of the Yemeni government, stronger coordination among anti-Houthi forces, and a more balanced relationship between Yemeni actors and their regional partners.” She added: “In many cases, the Saudis choose Yemeni figures who are weak, easily manipulated, and willing to follow their orders. If they instead chose competent, strong actors who could implement a shared agenda, they would also gain the respect of other competent Yemeni figures. “This approach contrasts with the Iranian and Emirati models, which have generally given their local allies more room to manoeuvre while building relationships around specific objectives and clearer mandates.” Due to the weakness of the UN-recognised government in Yemen, various militias with different ideological or regional loyalties operate alongside the official national army. Together on paper, the number of anti-Houthi forces could reach as many as 500,000 troops but in practice not all these forces cooperate or are willing to fight outside their area. Saudi Arabia gives support to Yemen’s Homeland Shield Forces while the United Arab Emirates had backed both the 80,000-strong Southern Transitional Council’s Giants Brigade and a 20,000-strong force led by Tareq Saleh. But the UAE, after backing separatist forces in the south, has now pulled out of Yemen. • This article was amended on 18 September 2026 to attribute a quote to a Houthi spokesperson that was initially attributed to the Yemeni ministry of foreign affairs.

title: Kash Patel defends FBI hiring policy on applicants who have engaged in bestiality
summary: Senators question FBI chief on move to cut restrictions on agent applicants who have engaged in bestiality
text: The FBI director, Kash Patel, defended his agency’s decision to roll back restrictions on agent applicants who have previously engaged in bestiality, arguing the FBI “did not want to punish victims of bestiality” by automatically disqualifying them. The unusual topic of bestiality emerged during a Senate judiciary committee oversight hearing on Tuesday after Democrat Dick Durbin and Republican John Kennedy questioned Patel’s decision to remove barriers that previously prevented applicants who engaged in prostitution and bestiality from being qualified for a job at the FBI. “I’m trying to understand why you did this,” Kennedy told Patel. “We’re having a tough time attracting agents, good quality agents we all can trust … Why would you even get into bestiality?” Patel said the change was recommended to him after he saw various “cases” in which qualified FBI applicants were denied consideration because they had been forced into bestiality as a result of human trafficking. “I say this with respect to the person who recommended it, why didn’t you just say: ‘What planet did you parachute in from?’” Kennedy replied. It is unclear how many FBI applicants have fallen into this category. The FBI did not respond to a question about the data to support Patel’s assertion. In a statement, an FBI spokesperson insisted the bureau was “not relaxing hiring standards” and that the change allows it to consider “the whole of person” in certain circumstances. They reiterated that applicants who engaged in criminal sexual acts were not eligible for employment. The spokesperson said it had “a number of applicants in previous years who suffered sexual abuse in their past, causing questions about prostitution, bestiality or other similar issues to affect their background check process through zero fault of their own”. “They showed me cases in which people were forced into it and had applied to the FBI, and so I thought: ‘They should be considered. It’s not an automatic disqualification.’ That’s all,” Patel told Kennedy. The rule change, first reported by CBS News in August, allows the FBI to consider candidates who hired a sex worker under specific circumstances, a person who stole from an employer under certain circumstances, and a person who engaged in bestiality or animal cruelty – so long as the incident took place before they were 18 years old. Kennedy, generally an ally of Donald Trump’s administration, grilled Patel on the hiring qualification change, arguing that it “really hurt” the FBI’s reputation. At one point, the Republican senator from Louisiana asked Patel whether the change “disqualified the animal” from FBI service. While Patel characterized the change as nondiscriminatory toward victims, Durbin refuted the notion and claimed it was a way to protect those who engaged in bestiality. “You dropped automatic disqualification for applicants who have been engaged in bestiality, not victims of bestiality – applicants who have engaged,” Durbin said to Patel. Patel responded: “Applicants who have engaged in bestiality means they were victims of bestiality because they were forced to do so.” Democrats sent a letter to Patel on Monday requesting more information about the rule change and applicants who fell into the categories.

title: Ministers vow sweeping NHS changes after ‘devastating’ report on Lucy Letby hospital
summary: Lady Justice Thirlwall’s report concludes three babies might have survived if hospital had acted on concerns about nurse
text: Ministers have promised sweeping changes to the NHS after a “devastating” official review concluded that three babies might have survived if hospital bosses and doctors had acted on concerns about the nurse Lucy Letby. A public inquiry found a “complete failure” to protect babies on the neonatal unit at the Countess of Chester hospital in north-west England. In a series of findings, the inquiry chair, Lady Justice Thirlwall, said two newborn twins would not have died and five others would not have been harmed if Letby had been removed from the unit sooner. Thirlwall said a third baby who died, a two-month-old girl, and two others who suffered unexplained collapses might have been protected if a doctor had detected an earlier insulin poisoning on the unit. One of those infants, now aged 11, suffered a lifelong brain injury and needs 24-hour care. Yvette Cooper, the health secretary, said she was “profoundly sorry” for the “devastating” failures revealed in the report, telling MPs: “This must be a turning point for the NHS.” She said she had asked officials to urgently take forward plans for “cot cam” monitors for neonatal units in line with Thirlwall’s recommendation. However, Letby’s barrister, Mark McDonald, told the Guardian the government had “moved with too much haste” and acted before the outcome of her challenge to her convictions was known. Letby, 36, is serving 15 whole-life prison terms after being convicted of the murder of seven babies and attempted murder of seven other newborns at the hospital in the year to June 2016. The former neonatal nurse is fighting to overturn her convictions, which have been described by the senior Conservative MP David Davis as a “clear miscarriage of justice”. The Criminal Cases Review Commission (CCRC), which investigates potential miscarriages of justice, is reviewing a dossier of evidence submitted by experts on her behalf before deciding whether to refer the case back to the court of appeal, which has twice rejected her legal challenges. Delivering her report at Liverpool town hall on Tuesday, where families of some of the babies had gathered, Thirlwall said: “My report describes dysfunctional management and governance; a gulf between hospital leadership and clinicians; and failure to understand the fundamentals of safeguarding. “There was a complete failure to protect babies on the neonatal unit at the Countess of Chester hospital. This was because no one seems to have understood that safeguarding action is required when a member of staff is suspected of causing deliberate harm and does not require colleagues to be sure of guilt.” Families of the babies who died or were injured said the report painted a “damning picture of what happens when concerns over patient safety are not listened to and acted on”. Tamlin Bolton, a solicitor at Irwin Mitchell representing seven of the families, urged ministers and the NHS to act on the report’s recommendations, saying: “It cannot be the end of the matter.” Richard Scorer, of the law firm Slater and Gordon, which represents three of the families, said: “Far too often public inquiry recommendations are left to gather dust. This cannot be allowed to happen again.” In her 822-page report, Thirlwall said it was “inexcusable” that successive governments had failed to act on reforms proposed by other public inquiries into NHS scandals stretching back 30 years. Thirlwall is said to believe that “cot cams” – allowing parents to monitor their newborn around-the-clock – could have prevented all seven of the deaths as medics would know they were being monitored. Samantha Dixon, the Labour MP for Chester North and Neston, whose constituency includes the hospital, said the inquiry revealed a “truly appalling state of affairs” that needed “the firmest response possible from government”. Ministers are working on the urgent introduction of other CCTV in hospital neonatal units as well as cot cams, in line with Thirlwall’s recommendation, and stricter rules on the storage of insulin. Hospital executives who are found to have failed in their responsibilities will be prevented from working again in the NHS under new regulation to stop managers being transferred to another part of the country. And they will roll out a single tracker to monitor the delivery of recommendations made by inquiries into maternity and neonatal scandals. McDonald, Letby’s barrister, said: “The government has moved with too much haste. They have made the same mistake as Thirlwall not to pause and wait for the new evidence to be considered.” However, others said the inquiry’s findings and recommendations must be taken seriously irrespective of Letby’s legal challenge. Dr Tom Dolphin, the chair of the British Medical Association, said it stemmed from “system reform” within the NHS and that it required “major reforms” to the culture of the health service. Leaders of NHS trusts and other bodies said the inquiry had shone a light on the “upheaval caused by successive reorganisations, the complex regulatory landscape, staff shortages, unacceptable ‘revolving door’ appointments and the inadequacies of underfunded NHS IT systems”. Letby was first linked to baby deaths in June 2015. That month, three newborns died in unexplained circumstances within two weeks – the number usually expected on the neonatal unit in a year. Senior doctors became concerned about Letby’s connection to the unusual rise in deaths and serious incidents over the following months and raised their fears with executives. However, the inquiry found that senior nurses effectively dismissed the concerns about Letby and that there was a “prolonged delay” in calling the police. Rather than being believed, Thirlwall said, clinicians were themselves made the subject of investigation in a “deplorable” grievance process brought by Letby when she was finally removed from the neonatal unit in July 2016. Parents were “kept in the dark” for years about what happened to their babies and the concerns they may have been deliberately harmed, the inquiry found. Thirlwall described their treatment as “reprehensible”. The inquiry chair accused hospital executives of overseeing “an exercise in spin” by downplaying the rise in deaths to the board of directors. Their failure to contact police before April 2017 – nearly two years after the unexplained increase in deaths – suggested that protecting the hospital’s reputation was “prized more highly” than the doctors’ concerns, she found. Three hospital executives, who have not been named, were arrested last year on suspicion of gross negligence manslaughter. Cheshire police said its investigation into the former bosses, and a parallel investigation into corporate manslaughter, was ongoing. Thirlwall, a court of appeal judge, said it was “clear that some babies would have been saved and some attacks would have been prevented if action was taken earlier”. She said the precise number of deaths that might have been prevented would never be known for sure. However, the inquiry concluded that if Letby had been removed from duties in October 2015 – when senior managers were made aware of the concerns – then the twin boys known as babies O and P would not have died in June 2016 and five further babies would not have suffered harm. Thirlwall said it was possible that three newborns would not have died and seven others would have been protected if a senior doctor had not “disregarded” an insulin result for a week-old baby boy in August 2015, whom Letby was later convicted of attempting to murder by poisoning him.

title: Top Democrat on House oversight panel investigating Trump Jr wedding party bankrolled by Russian oligarch
summary: Robert Garcia expresses concern over ‘any possible foreign entanglement’ between White House and Umar Kremlev
text: Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the House oversight committee, is investigating potential ties between the White House and a Russian oligarch who paid for a portion of Donald Trump Jr’s wedding. In a letter sent to Susie Wiles, the White House chief of staff, on Monday, Garcia expressed concern about “any possible foreign entanglement” between the president’s son and the oligarch, Umar Kremlev. Garcia asked Wiles to provide documents, records and communications between the White House and Trump Jr about Kremlev, among other requests. “As the son of President Donald Trump and the part-owner and major investor of multiple companies with extensive Department of Defense contracts, any apparent ties to members of Russian President Vladimir Putin’s inner circle raises serious questions about pay-to-play schemes and foreign intelligence infiltration of the President’s family,” Garcia wrote in the letter. In a separate letter addressed to Trump Jr, Garcia expressed similar worries and asked the president’s son to provide more details about his wedding events bankrolled by Kremlev, including: all dates of communication between Trump Jr and Kremlev, any communications Trump Jr may have had with the White House about Kremlev, financial records of purchases made by foreign nationals and a complete list of wedding gifts from foreign nationals. It came just hours after ProPublica revealed that Kremlev spent hundreds of thousands of dollars on wedding celebrations for Trump Jr and his wife, Bettina, earlier this year. The couple also confirmed Kremlev’s financial involvement on Monday. “I have no idea who Umar is, never heard of him, and he didn’t pay for Don and Bettina’s wedding, which took place at a totally different location, and on a different day from the wedding. It was an ‘afterparty’ given in their honor. Not a big deal! I was not present at the party,” the US president said in a statement in response to the report. “Why did a Russian oligarch close to Putin fund Trump Jr.’s wedding in the Bahamas?” Garcia wrote on X after the ProPublica report was published. Garcia added: “Umar Kremlev spent hundreds of thousands of dollars on the President’s son. What did he get in return? We need answers.” Axios was the first to report on Garcia’s letter. The investigation into Trump Jr’s wedding is part of the House oversight committee Democrats’ larger investigation into the ways the Trump family has allegedly enriched themselves since Trump took office last year. The Guardian reached out to Garcia’s office and the White House for further comment.

title: Army officers ‘let down’ soldier over sexual assault claim before she killed herself, court martial told
summary: Court hears that two officers did not deal properly with allegation Jaysley Beck made against a superior
text: Two army officers “let down” a teenage soldier who went on to kill herself when they did not deal properly with a sexual assault allegation she made against a superior, a court martial has heard. Jaysley Beck, 19, told Col Samantha Shepherd that she had been touched on the leg by a warrant officer during a social event at an adventure training exercise, the court was told. But Shepherd allegedly misrepresented what Beck had told her when she reported the claim, falsely saying there had not been physical contact. The second officer, Maj James Hook, failed to take the incident seriously and was sceptical of what Beck had reported, believing she wanted to leave the training package, the court heard. Shepherd and Hook deny “conduct prejudicial to good order and service discipline”. Shepherd is accused of misreporting what she had been told by Beck while Hook allegedly did not treat information passed to him in a manner “consistent with its seriousness”. At the start of the trial, the assistant judge advocate general Edward Legard said he expected the board hearing the case – an RAF air commodore, navy captain and army colonel – almost certainly knew of the Beck case. He told them she had taken her own life and there had been significant press interest but they should put anything they had heard about it to one side. Legard also instructed them not to be influenced by anyone’s views – including their chain of command – on the subject of unacceptable sexual behaviour in the armed forces. Cdr Paul Patterson, for the crown, said Beck was taking part in the training package in Hampshire in July 2021. Hook was running the exercise while Shepherd was the regimental colonel. Following a social function, Beck was found distressed and sleeping in her car early in the morning by a colleague, L/Cpl Drew Tudor. She told him there had been an incident the night before with a warrant officer, Michael Webber, who was senior in rank to her. Hook was alerted and Beck expressed concern over what would happen if she made a complaint. He gave her until noon to decide what she wanted to do. The court was told he was sceptical as Beck was not enjoying the adventure package and he thought she may be wanting to leave. Patterson said rather than empowering her, Hook could be seen as “leaning on her”. He said an issue for the board to consider was if Hook knew he was dealing with a potential sexual assault. Shepherd was told of the incident later. She went for a walk with Beck, who told her Webber had touched her leg and tried to kiss her, the court heard. Patterson said when she went to speak to an adjutant, whose role includes advising on discipline, about the incident, Shepherd was asked if there had been physical contact and allegedly replied that there had not been. The prosecutor said that the colonel “edited the information” when she “should have told the truth”. He told the court it was the crown’s case that Shepherd deliberately tried to suppress the detail about touching, knowing that if she did report this it would go to service police. Patterson said Beck told each of the officers enough to understand that she may have been sexually assaulted and she had been let down by them. Tudor became emotional as he gave his evidence. He said when he found Beck in her car she was distressed and told him that Webber had “tried something on with her”. He said he could not now remember Beck’s exact words but added: “I was concerned enough to want to report it.” The adjutant, Maj Mae King, told the court Shepherd had told her Webber had attempted to kiss Beck but Beck had leant away. She said: “My understanding was no physical contact had been made.” King said incidents such as this were “relatively normal” and it was not the most serious she had dealt with. King told the court that Webber’s wife worked in the same building as her and there was concern about her welfare. She said she did not know if the wife knew about what had allegedly happened during the adventure package. “It wasn’t our business to tell her,” King said. Beck’s mother, Leighann McCready, from Cumbria, sat in the front row of the public gallery, holding her daughter’s army cap. The trial at Catterick in North Yorkshire continues.

title: Emma Bonino obituary
summary: Italian politician, feminist and activist who joined the Radical party and fought a long battle for women’s rights
text: In 1974 the Italian feminist activist and later politician Emma Bonino, who has died aged 78, became pregnant. A doctor had told her that she was “sterile”. She attempted to get an abortion and found a doctor in Florence who was willing to help her – for a fee. Bonino felt humiliated and angry – all abortions were illegal in Italy at the time – and became involved with the Radical party, an organisation interested in civil and human rights, and the growing feminist movement. She and other militants set up a network of centres “for sterilisation and abortion” (CISA) across Italy that challenged the law by providing safe and free abortions. A magistrate in Florence issued an arrest warrant for her and others for the crime of “organising abortion”. In June 1975 she went to vote in regional elections in her home town of Bra, outside Turin. She asked the president of the polling station – who had once been her teacher – to have her arrested after voting. Outside the Carabinieri station, Bonino, smiling, held up her hands in the feminist “triangle” symbol. The crowd applauded. The photo made all the front pages. Bonino said that she did not want any other woman to go through what she had. The press reported in 1976 that thousands of abortions had been arranged this way through the CISA networks – all of them classed as crimes. Bonino spent time in prison in the forbidding Le Murate complex in Florence. Along with the other militant prisoners, she asked not to be released. Her imprisonment was a powerful political weapon. She was then released and in 1976 elected to the chamber of deputies for the Radical party. For complicated political and legal reasons, the whole process with regard to Bonino dragged on for years, right into the 1990s. She was never actually sent to trial, although others were, and were cleared, after decades. At this time an extraordinary political movement emerged in Italy around civil and political rights and the growing feminist movement. The mechanism of the referendum had been inserted into the Italian constitution in 1948: a referendum to abrogate laws could be held if 500,000 signatures could be collected. Using this device as well as non-violent direct challenges to the law, the Radical party pushed for reforms that made divorce, abortion and contraception legal in just a few years. These changes were confirmed through huge victories in referendums, which had come up against the full force of the Christian Democrat party and the Catholic church. Bonino was one of the key leaders of this movement. Born in Bra, Emma was the daughter of Catterina (nee Barge) and Filippo Bonino, and grew up partly on a farm, something which she described later as “deeply boring”. She studied modern languages and literature at the elite Bocconi university in Milan (1967-72). Her thesis analysed Malcolm X’s autobiography – a sign of the times. There were many facets to the 1968 movement, many of them interested in the use of violence, and calling for “revolution”. The Radical party, on the other hand, was deeply practical and also connected to the politics of personal life. It stood outside the major, more traditional and conservative parties on the left and the right, and was a natural ally of the feminist movement. In the Radical party Bonino formed an unlikely partnership with the bear-like, charismatic, flamboyant and unpredictable leader Marco Pannella. However, the two later fell out and there was no rapprochement before Pannella’s death in 2016. It was under the pressure of referendums in 1978 that two extraordinary reforms were passed in a short period of time. Italy’s infamously slow-moving political system had been forced into action. First, in May that year, in response to the threat of a referendum, Law No 180 called for an alternative to psychiatric hospitals and led to an entirely new system of mental health care. Then the Law No 194 legalised abortion, and was confirmed with a huge vote after a referendum was organised by those opposed to it in 1981. The abortion law was by no means perfect – Bonino saw it very much as a compromise – but it has survived to this day. Feminists and radicals also set up local health centres where women could go for advice around contraception and pregnancy. It was the victorious culmination of the campaigns that had seen Bonino’s arrest in 1975. Bonino’s campaigns continued into parliament. In 1978 she called for the resignation of the Italian president, Giovanni Leone, after allegations of corruption appeared in a book by the journalist Camilla Cederna. Leone did resign. But in 1998 Bonino publicly apologised to him after many of the accusations proved to be unfounded. The issue of miscarriages of justice became a central one for the Radicals, who took up the shocking case of the popular TV presenter Enzo Tortora, arrested in 1983 over false “supergrass” allegations that he was linked to drug trafficking and the Camorra. He was elected as a Radical party member of the European parliament in 1984, gaining immunity until his trial and sentence to 10 years’ imprisonment in 1985, overturned on appeal in 1987. In 1994 Bonino and the Radicals backed Silvio Berlusconi’s first government, and her appointment as European Commissioner for four years from 1995 was seen as a quid pro quo for this support. For many on the left, this was a deep betrayal, and it blackened the reputation of the Radical party, which went through a bewildering number of name changes and alliance choices, confusing those who had seen Bonino as firmly part of the 70s movements for change. In 1999 Bonino was a candidate for the presidency of the republic: in the event, Carlo Azeglio Ciampi was elected by parliament with a huge majority. However, her “Bonino list” surprisingly won more than 8% of the vote in that year’s European elections, electing seven MEPs, though this success was short-lived. Bonino would later mark her distance from Berlusconi on a number of issues, and was made a minister for European affairs in Romano Prodi’s centre-left administration (2006-08), as well as holding the high-level institutional position of vice-president of the Senate. In 2013 she was briefly foreign minister in another centre-left administration. An inspiration to many activists and feminists, Bonino was a pioneer for women in politics. When she was diagnosed with cancer in 2015 she often appeared with different and beautiful headscarves. She never spoke about her private life in any detail, although it later emerged that she had been entrusted with two young children for a time in the 70s. In interviews she told how difficult it was to “give back” these children to their natural families. A convinced internationalist, Bonino was a strong believer in European identity and the EU. She took part in protests around – for example – genital mutilation and the war in Yugoslavia. She was seized by the Taliban for a few hours in the 90s while campaigning for women’s rights in Afghanistan and moved to Cairo for a number of years in the 2000s. There she learned Arabic and campaigned, as ever, on civil rights. There was even an extraordinary and unlikely encounter with Pope Francis in her flat in Rome in 2024, with both in wheelchairs. Never boring, always active, never free of deep contradictions, Bonino was one of the most exceptional political figures in postwar Italy. Her death has led to a huge debate in the country over her legacy, and the continuities and breaks between her activism in the 70s and her long political and institutional involvement. She was certainly an inspiration for women both inside and outside the institutions, despite all the inconsistencies of her political career, which she finished as senator for Rome (2008-13 and 2018-22). She is survived by her siblings Domenica and Giovanni. • Emma Bonino, activist and politician, born 9 March 1948; died 11 September 2026

title: Nick Reiner will not face death penalty if convicted of killing parents, LA district attorney says
summary: Reiner is accused of fatally stabbing his parents, Rob and Michele Singer Reiner, in their home in December 2025
text: Nick Reiner will not face the death penalty if convicted of the killings of his parents, Rob and Michele Singer Reiner, the Los Angeles county district attorney’s office announced. Nathan Hochman, the Los Angeles DA, said on Tuesday that his office will not pursue the death penalty in the case. He told reporters gathered outside a Los Angeles courthouse ahead of a pretrial hearing that the prosecutors had considered the wishes of Reiner family members and mitigating factors in making their decision. While the death penalty is legal in California, Gavin Newsom put a moratorium on the practice in 2019, and the last execution took place in 2006. Reiner is accused of fatally stabbing his parents in their Los Angeles home in December 2025. The deaths of Rob, 78, a celebrated director and actor, and Michele, 70, sent shockwaves through Hollywood. The 33-year-old has pleaded not guilty to two charges of first degree murder. The charges include a special circumstance of multiple murders, and a special allegation for the use of a dangerous weapon. A grand jury indicted Reiner last month on two counts of first degree murder with an additional special circumstance of lying in wait. The maximum penalty he will face, prosecutors said, is life in prison without parole. Reiner had a history of addiction and mental health challenges, family members have said, and collaborated with his father on the film Being Charlie, which was reportedly inspired by his experiences. Jake Reiner, the eldest son of Rob and Michele, said in a recent interview that his parents “never stopped helping” Nick. Reiner’s former attorney, Alan Jackson, previously said that “pursuant to the laws of California, Nick Reiner is not guilty of murder”. Reuters and the Associated Press contributed reporting

title: Bristol becomes first British city to ban advertisements for fast fashion
summary: Green-run council also curbing ads for airlines, cruises, fossil fuels and SUVs on its billboards and bus shelters
text: Bristol has become the first British city to impose a ban on the advertising of fast fashion, in new restrictions that will also curb ads for SUVs and airlines. The ban is part of moves by the West Country city, known for its radical political scene, to impose sweeping bans on advertising for polluting industries. Restrictions have also been placed on advertising SUVs, airlines, cruises and fossil fuels on advertising sites owned by the Green-run council. “We don’t want Bristol to be a billboard for polluters while we’re working hard to improve health, air quality and nature in the city,” said Heather Mack, Bristol city council’s deputy leader. “We’re proud to be thinking holistically about the changes we need to keep Bristol green and thriving.” Bristol council’s strategy and resources committee passed the new advertising and sponsorship policy by an eight to one vote on Monday. It updates a policy passed in 2021 which made Bristol the first council outside London to ban junk food ads. The policy will apply to all council-owned advertising space, including billboards, bus stop shelters, print and online. Bristol joins more than 20 UK councils that already have restrictions on ads for polluting products and services. But none has previously ibanned advertising for fast fashion products. The change in policy reflects political trends in the city, which elected the Green party’s Carla Denyer as MP in 2024, the same year that voters made the Green party the largest party in the council chamber. In Bristol, 83% of residents are concerned about climate change, according to a recent council survey. Denyer said: “I am so pleased that the council has now taken this much-needed next step and added high-carbon products and services to the list of things that will not be advertised on council-owned space. “Our Green-led council is making huge strides on Bristol’s climate and sustainability commitments, working on public transport infrastructure, home heating and community energy. “It makes no sense for these efforts to be running alongside advertisements for things like oil and gas companies, SUVs or fast fashion which do not align with our community values.” Cardiff, Edinburgh, Portsmouth and Sheffield are among the cities that have imposed restrictions on climate-harming products. The restrictions came after campaigning by Adfree Cities, a network of campaign groups, which is calling for local bans on climate-harming promotions to be made national. The group has also lobbied London’s mayor, Sadiq Khan, to curb ads for fossil fuels and other polluting products on Transport for London, which has one of the largest advertising estates in the world. Nicola Wilks, co-founder and co-director at Adfree Cities, said: “We know ad bans are a catalyst for healthy change. Removing tobacco ads saved lives by reducing levels of smoking. “As a Bristol resident who cares deeply about climate change and air pollution, I am proud that Bristol has gone even further than other UK councils in curbing polluting ads; it feels like common sense. “Now we need to scale up bold local action to national tobacco-style bans on polluter advertising, to break the toxic influence of polluting companies, and support meaningful action for climate and clean air.”

title: US lawmakers spar over bill giving Trump more power to sanction Russia
summary: Proponents say sanctions would help Ukraine, but some Democrats say Trump shouldn’t have more tariff authority
text: A bill co-authored by Lindsey Graham, the South Carolina senator who died earlier this year, that would give Donald Trump broad authority to tariff Russia and its trading partners will be put forward for a vote this week in a high-stakes legislative battle that could provide new sanctioning authority to the US president at a crucial moment in Russia’s war against Ukraine. The bill is facing considerable pushback not only from Ukraine-sceptic Republicans, however, but also from prominent Democrats who say that the bill will give undue tariff power to the US president that could then be abused and turned against US allies. Congressional staffers have described frenzied last-minute lobbying in the halls of Congress as the vote approached for what one Democratic staffer called the “one opportunity that we have to help Ukraine before they enter the slow winter”. The bill passed a vote in the House rules committee on Monday, and is due for a rule vote on the House floor on Tuesday afternoon, then a general vote on Wednesday. The Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia Act of 2026 would target Russia’s energy and defense industries, as well as the country’s “shadow fleet” of tankers skirting existing oil sanctions, and would give Trump new authority to slap 100% tariffs on top purchasers of Russian oil, including China and India. But Trump’s use of tariffs against US partners such as Canada and Mexico have made expanding his powers a controversial aim – even for senior Democrats who have been stalwart backers of Ukraine. They are led by the representative Gregory Meeks; the top Democrats on the House foreign affairs committee; the representative Don Beyer of Congress’s joint economic committee; and Richard Neal, the ranking Democrat on the House ways and means committee. In a statement, they said the legislation would do “more harm than good”. “This bill would dramatically expand presidential tariff authorities while failing to mandate sanctions on Russia, both of which are unacceptable,” they said. “These flaws would raise Americans’ prices while undermining support for Ukraine in the long term.” Critics have accused those Democrats who oppose the bill of not wanting to hand Trump a win before the midterm elections, effectively holding the bill hostage to partisan politics with Ukraine on the cusp of another brutal winter with dwindling munitions to protect itself from attacks from Russian missiles. “It’s not about denying Trump a victory,” Neal said in an interview on Monday. “I just feel that the abusive nature of these tariffs, the way he’s used them to drive away friends across the globe, what is our protection afterwards? And if he decides, by the way, to take the harsh position as it relates to Ukraine, he could still do that as well.” Sources said negotiations are under way among Democrats to propose changing the bill to limit the number of countries eligible for sanctions to 11. One of the co-sponsors of the bill, the representative Steny Hoyer, offered an amendment on Tuesday that identified 10 countries subject to the secondary sanctions as China, India, Turkey, Azerbaijan, Hungary, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Singapore, Slovakia and the United Arab Emirates. Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, on Monday encouraged the US to increase pressure on the Russian economy to end the war. “Lindsey Graham’s sanctions bill is still a bill, unfortunately, and not a law,” he said in a nightly address. “It is important that it becomes law. I thank everyone around the world who supports this approach and who knows that strength works.” In an interview on the sidelines of the Ukraine Action Summit in Washington DC on Saturday, Vitaly Kim, a member of Zelenskyy’s cabinet who serves as minister of veterans affairs, said economic pressure on Russia was the quickest route to end the war. “International support through sanctions to stop Russian economy, so they cannot buy weapons … will help destroy their economy,” he said, comparing the effect to Ukrainian strikes on oil refineries and military plants. “Your politicians see that our tactics to attack the economy of Russia and destroy the military sector of Russia are working. From my opinion, you will support us in this direction to attack the economy of Russia to make them stop.” Trump is understood to have given Republican allies in Congress the go-ahead to submit the bill, breaking a more than two-year deadlock that carried through the death of Graham, who lobbied the president to back Ukraine even while remaining one of his closest allies and defenders in Congress. Lawmakers from the isolationist wing of the Republican party have said they won’t back the bill, making Democratic support crucial. That has led to infighting among congressional Democrats, who sparred during a meeting this week in which the representative Linda Sánchez, a California Democrat, told members of her party to “get off the fucking bill”. “I said what I said,” she wrote on social media by way of confirming the quote, which was first reported by Punchbowl News. “We absolutely must support Ukraine and punish Russia for its invasion. But why the fuck would we give Trump more power to tariff whatever country he’s currently mad at and drive up costs further for working families?” The bill is being closely watched by foreign governments and advocates for Ukraine, who have said that it is the best option available and is broadly supported by the US public. “It’s disappointing that some Democratic leaders are pushing against this pro-Ukraine bill,” said Mykola Murskyj, senior adviser at Razom, a US non-profit that advocates for pro-Ukrainian legislation. “Draining Russia’s war coffers is the most effective way to get the Kremlin to end its war. We should all be able to get behind that. “These tariffs are crucial for ending Russia’s war,” he added. “Countries buying Russian oil and funding Russia’s war should no longer be able to do that with impunity. They should face a choice: cheap access to the American market, or bloody Russian oil.”
