title: Thirlwall report: what did it say about Lucy Letby case and what does it recommend?
summary: Lady Justice Thirlwall’s wide-ranging inquiry calls on NHS England to implement 14 changes by March next year
text: Lady Justice Thirlwall has published the report on the findings of her inquiry into events at the Countess of Chester hospital involving the actions of former neonatal nurse Lucy Letby, who was convicted over the murder and attempted murder of multiple babies. Here we take a look at the report and its findings. Who is Lucy Letby and what is this new report about? Letby, 36, is serving 15 whole-life prison terms after being convicted of the murder of seven babies and attempted murder of seven other newborns at the Countess of Chester hospital in north-west England from June 2015 to June 2016. The former neonatal nurse says she is innocent and is fighting to overturn her convictions. The report published on Tuesday holds the findings of the Thirlwall inquiry, an independent public inquiry led by Lady Justice Kathryn Thirlwall, a senior court of appeal judge, which was first announced on 4 September 2023. It focused on events at the Countess of Chester hospital leading up to and during Letby’s offending. It aimed to get answers for the victims’ families and ensure lessons were learned. The inquiry also looked at the wider circumstances, including the response and conduct of the NHS, its staff and its regulators. What was the main finding of the inquiry? Thirlwall found a “complete failure” to protect babies on the neonatal unit at the hospital. Delivering her report at Liverpool town hall on Tuesday, Thirlwall said the report described dysfunctional management and governance, a gulf between hospital leadership and clinicians, and failure to understand the fundamentals of safeguarding. Could any of the babies have been saved? Thirlwall concluded that three babies might have survived and seven others could have been protected if hospital bosses had taken action over concerns about Letby. She said two newborn twins would not have died and five others would not have been harmed if Letby had been removed from the unit sooner, while a third baby, a two-month-old girl, and two others who suffered unexplained collapses might have been protected if a doctor had detected an earlier insulin poisoning on the unit. One of those infants, now aged 11, suffered a lifelong brain injury and needs 24-hour care. If doctors were worried, why did the hospital not stop her? Senior doctors became increasingly concerned about Letby’s connection to the unusual rise in deaths and serious incidents over the following months and raised their fears with executives. However, the Thirlwall inquiry found that senior nurses effectively dismissed the concerns about Letby and that there was a “prolonged delay” in calling the police. Thirlwall said that rather than being believed, clinicians were themselves made the subject of investigation in a “deplorable” grievance process brought by Letby when she was finally removed from the neonatal unit in July 2016. Did the families know what was happening at the time? The inquiry found that parents were “kept in the dark” for years about what happened to their babies and the concerns they might have been deliberately harmed. Thirlwall concluded this was “reprehensible”. What needs to change to stop this from happening again? A total of 14 recommendations have been made in the Thirlwall inquiry report – including the fitting of baby monitors in all cots and incubators in neonatal units and CCTV cameras focused on insulin storage fridges. The recommendations follow the conclusions made by Thirlwall, the inquiry chair, who said the collapse and deaths of some babies could have been avoided if safeguarding practices had been followed. She said baby monitors would ensure parents could observe their babies “remotely at any time” – adding that NHS England should “set out a roadmap” for how it could be implemented by 31 March next year. I’ve heard people say Letby may be innocent. What does this report say about that? Nothing. The inquiry was conducted entirely on the basis of Letby being found guilty of the offences for which she was convicted. All attempts by Letby to appeal against the convictions were dismissed. The Criminal Cases Review Commission (CCRC) is investigating her case to determine if there is a “real possibility” her convictions would not be upheld, which could trigger a referral back to the appeal courts. The chair of the CCRC, Vera Baird, told the BBC the miscarriages of justice watchdog would be looking at the conclusions drawn by the Thirlwall inquiry. She said: “We will be looking at the report with interest to assess whether it has any bearing on our review of the case.”

title: UK sanctions on Israel ‘fall far short’ of its obligations, legal experts say
summary: More than 130 sign letter to PM saying international law requires further measures to stop illegal settlements
text: More than 130 legal experts, including 18 king’s counsel (KCs), have written to Andy Burnham saying that sanctions on Israeli settlements “fall far short” of Britain’s obligations under the international court of justice’s (ICJ’s) finding that the occupation is unlawful. The foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, last week announced an import ban on goods from illegal Israeli settlements in Palestine and other measures. Signatories to the letter to the prime minister, including the leading lawyers Michael Mansfield KC and Imran Khan KC, and the former lord justice of appeal Alan Moses, say it is not enough. In a 2024 advisory opinion, the ICJ, which is the UN’s top court, ordered Israel to end the occupation “as rapidly as possible” and said other countries were under an obligation not to recognise the occupation as lawful nor aid or assist it. The letter, sent on Tuesday, says the ICJ’s findings have “not had an impact on Israel’s apartheid practice” and, while the UK sanctions are “a necessary corrective”, they are “improperly narrow” when compared with sanctions on Russia, which are not limited to economic activity in occupied Ukrainian territory but apply to wider economic structures supporting the unlawful conduct. It says: “We ask it to commit to further and more rigorous measures to ensure that no part of the UK’s economic relationship with Israel continues to sustain the illegal occupation itself, and the settlements and other serious violations of fundamental rules of international law perpetrated through its conduct, and to build on this to adopt robust coercive measures to seek to bring all these serious violations of international law, and the practices they sustain, including, fundamentally, the occupation itself, to an end.” The letter, also signed by legal academics, calls for a range of additional measures including a full arms embargo on Israel. When announcing the sanctions, Miliband accused Israel of ethnic cleansing in the West Bank, and the signatories say article 6(3) of the arms trade treaty prohibits transfers of arms where a state has knowledge of such a crime. The sanctions were announced after escalating attacks by Israeli settlers against Palestinian villages in the West Bank and an Israeli tender was issued for 1,200 homes in the E1 settlement, east of Jerusalem, which could in effect cut off the north from the south of the West Bank, threatening the viability of any future Palestinian state. The signatories want extension of the sanctions to cover insurance, accountancy services and digital infrastructure as well as public confirmation that no UK public body, pension scheme or sovereign fund holds settlement investments. One of the letter’s signatories and drafters, Ralph Wilde, a professor of international law at University College London, welcomed the UK’s recent recognition of Israel’s occupation of the West Bank as unlawful as an “important shift”, but said it fell short in its focus on the settlements and settlers. “The elephant in the room is the illegality of the occupation itself,” said Wilde, who acted as senior counsel and legal adviser to the Arab League in the case before the ICJ. “It’s not just simply the settlements and the abuse of treatment and the genocide, which of course are also wrong, it’s Israel’s very presence.” He added: “There’s a mismatch between saying Israel’s very presence there is illegal, but then only focusing on the question of the settlers and the settlements. If the problem is with the settlements themselves, then the problem is with the state that establishes them.” A government spokesperson said: “This is the biggest reset in the UK’s approach to protecting and securing the two-state solution in a generation. We have shown our commitment to international law and our refusal to be bystanders to further suffering. “We have taken concrete action, supported accountability, pledged to galvanise the international community and acted with our partners across the globe.” In response to the sanctions, the Israeli foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, accused Miliband of “outrageous lies” and said the UK government was “systematically working against the state of Israel”.

title: Jaguar Land Rover in talks to sell Defender to Nato countries
summary: Carmaker builds on relationship with British armed forces by seeking to cash in on Europe’s rearmament drive
text: Jaguar Land Rover is in talks with Nato countries about selling them the newly revamped Defender military vehicle, as the UK-based carmaker seeks to tap into Europe’s defence spending boom. It is also among carmakers bidding for a UK defence ministry contract worth £900m to replace an ageing fleet of Land Rovers that have been out of production since 2016, competing with General Motors and the UK’s Ineos Automotive, which builds the Grenadier 4x4 for the civilian market. JLR, owned by India’s Tata Motors, has set up a new Defender defence division to explore new partnerships to supply vehicles for people and equipment transportation to defence sectors around the world. The carmaker is trying to expand beyond its relationship with the British armed forces to exploit a spending boom by Nato countries racing to rearm, as it faces weaker demand elsewhere coupled with higher costs. JLR insisted that the move, which was first reported by the Financial Times, was not related to its planned 4,000 job cuts globally, as part of an effort to save £1.7bn. It is slashing costs as it struggles with tough trading conditions, Donald Trump’s tariff wars and the fallout from a damaging cyber-attack last year. As he unveiled three new variants of the Defender Wolf Series II, the next-generation military vehicle, Patrick McGillycuddy, the Defender managing director, said: “Through our newly established Defender defence division, we will offer Defender Wolf Series II to defence organisations worldwide, while also bidding for the UK Ministry of Defence light mobility vehicle tender.” He said the new 4x4s were “exceptionally robust and versatile”, and added that their lightweight aluminium monocoque (French for “single shell”) construction, with a stiffer body structure, means they can be adapted to the “wide range of roles and operational requirements demanded by military organisations”. He said: “It is a modern successor to the world-famous Defender Wolf and Land Rovers that have served the British armed forces for more than 70 years.” The new Defender series is designed and engineered in the UK, with engines built in Wolverhampton. JLR also wants to break into the $80bn (£59bn) US pickup truck market with a local version of its Defender vehicle. The Defender pickup will be built in the US through a joint venture with the Chrysler carmaker, Stellantis, the Sunday Times reported at the weekend. JLR declined to comment on this. It is the most high-profile UK carmaker to pivot the newly booming defence sector as manufacturers grapple with a transition to electric vehicles and rising competition from Chinese rivals. Last week, Volkswagen struck a deal to sell its Osnabrück factory to Israel’s Aurelius Capital and VW’s ⁠second-biggest shareholder, its home state of Lower Saxony, in a move labour officials said could save about 1,400 of the site’s 1,800 jobs. The site would switch production from cars to heavy-duty trucks that carry anti-missile systems for the maker of Israel’s Iron Dome, Arrow ‌and David’s ⁠Sling air and missile defence systems. “These plans involve the potential manufacture of systems and components for air defence systems for Germany and Europe,” Volkswagen said, adding the cooperation could pave the way for further such deals. Renault is repurposing part of its Le Mans chassis plant in western France to make up to 600 drones a month for the French ministry of defence.

title: Imran Khan’s sons accuse Pakistani army chief of vendetta against imprisoned father
summary: Kasim and Sulaiman Khan tell Guardian they believe ex-PM is being ‘slowly killed’ by harsh treatment, driven by Asim Munir
text: The sons of Imran Khan have accused Pakistan’s powerful army chief of a “personal vendetta” against the incarcerated former prime minister and expressed fears their father is being “slowly killed” in jail, as international pressure mounts over his prison conditions. Kasim Khan, 27, and Sulaiman Khan, 29, have become strong advocates for the release of their father, who has been held in Adiala prison in Rawalpindi since his arrest in 2023, and is serving a 14-year sentence on corruption charges. They have not been allowed to speak to Khan for more than six months and have been prevented from travelling from the UK to Pakistan to lobby for his release. On Wednesday, the supreme court will rule on a case alleging the Pakistan government has been in contempt of court by denying Khan private hospital treatment for a worsening eye condition and preventing family from visiting him or speaking with him in jail for more than six months, in violation of a court order. Khan is being held in solitary confinement, in a cell alleged to be 6ft by 8ft. Later this month, Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) – the political party Khan founded in 1996, four years after retiring from international cricket – is planning a nationwide march demanding his release. Speaking to the Guardian from London, Khan’s sons – from his first marriage to Jemima Goldsmith – said they were “deeply, deeply concerned” about their father’s health, and that the conditions he was being kept in amounted to “a form of mental and physical torture”. “The reality is that he is locked in a tiny 6x8ft cell without human contact,” said Sulaiman. “He hasn’t been allowed new books for months and he’s not been allowed to see or speak to his family or a neutral doctor. He has an eye condition which was neglected for months and has meant he’s probably almost lost sight in one eye.” Late last month, Sky Sports aired an interview with Khasim and Sulaiman during its coverage of a test match between England and Pakistan. The Pakistan Cricket Board, which has close links to the government and whose chair is also the interior minister, made a formal complaint to Sky Sports after the broadcast and the Pakistani team threatened to refuse to return to the field after the lunch break. “It shows how out of touch they are with the rest of the world, that they thought they could silence media like they do at home,” Sulaiman said of the complaint. “It just exposed them for the authoritarian regime that they are.” The UN has said Khan’s prolonged detention violates international law and the UN’s special rapporteur on torture said his solitary confinement and detention conditions could amount to psychological torture. Sulaiman said the family had been told their father, 73, had also been diagnosed with high blood pressure. “More than anything, we just want to speak to him and make sure he’s OK,” he said. Khan’s sons said they were particularly concerned that the “cruel” treatment was being driven by a “personal grudge” by Asim Munir, Pakistan’s chief of defence forces and army chief. When Khan was the prime minister, he unceremoniously demoted Munir, and the bad blood between them was well known. When Munir was made army chief in 2022, the persecution of Khan increased notably. “It’s very clear this is being driven by personal grudge and that’s one of the reasons he’s being treated so harshly, on the orders of Asim Munir,” said Sulaiman. Munir’s powers expanded over the past year as he established himself as a close ally of Donald Trump, who referred to him as “my favourite field marshal”. Last month, the supreme court ruled that Khan should be taken to a private hospital for treatment for a blood clot in his retinal vein, believed to have destroyed 85% of the sight in his right eye because of a prolonged lack of medical attention. Khan was instead taken briefly to a government hospital, where he was given several injections and ruled fit to return to prison, prompting outrage from his family and political party. “There’s still been no light shed on our father’s real condition from an unbiased, neutral physician,” said Kasim. “We believe they’re trying to slowly kill him in there. Just as soon as there’s less pressure, we are sure they will put even harsher restrictions on him and try to finish him off. “The one with the real vendetta here is the army chief Asim Munir.” In a statement, the Pakistan government called the allegations around Khan “fake propaganda” and said he was being kept in adequate conditions, with access to home-cooked food, nuts, bottled water, exercise equipment, family visits and regular medical examinations. “The government of Pakistan categorically rejects allegations that the convicted prisoner is being subjected to punitive solitary confinement, cruelty or deprivation,” the statement said. It was widely acknowledged that Khan came to power in 2018 with the backing of Pakistan’s military, widely referred to as the “establishment”, which has long held an oversized role in the country’s governance. Khan had promised to build a “naya Pakistan” (new Pakistan), which would end corruption and follow the rule of law. However, his time in power was plagued by allegations of corruption, press censorship and persecution of his opponents. He was toppled in 2022 after falling out with his military benefactors. He then began a campaign calling for the generals to be kept out of government. By 2023, as his accusations against the military grew, Khan turned from alleged persecutor to the persecuted. He was arrested and charged with more than 100 crimes, including alleged corruption and sedition, which he claims are trumped up to keep him out of power. Despite his toppling and imprisonment, Khan still remains popular. “They want to do everything they can to sideline him and disappear him from public life,” Kasim said. Sulaiman said that while it was “clear the establishment think they can get away with it without any kind of repercussions”, it was also evident the government had been rattled by international coverage of Khan’s case. Khan’s sons said that while they were keen to travel to Pakistan, their visas had still not been granted more than nine months after applying. They emphasised they had no interest in entering politics in Pakistan or leading Khan’s PTI party in his absence. “We definitely don’t want to get involved in politics in Pakistan in the long term,” said Sulaiman. “Our father always said that one of the biggest problems with Pakistani politics is this dynastic nepotism; that power’s been held by just two families for the last 40 years. It’s a sign of what’s wrong with the political system in Pakistan.” Speculation has abounded on whether Khan would strike a deal with the military to secure his release. Khan’s closest aide, Zulfi Bukhari, said: “There is only one deal Khan would ever accept: the restoration of democracy, the rule of law and the people’s mandate in Pakistan. If they’re genuinely willing to do that, then fine – let’s talk.” Kasim and Sulaiman said they did not believe Khan would give up his politics to secure his release. “He’s a very single-minded person,” said Kasim. “I don’t think there’s a chance that he’d ever give it up.”

title: The trans CIA official ousted by Trump: ‘We’re a government crippled by its own decisions’
summary: Julia Curlee, a former senior CIA officer, speaks on Trump administration’s purge of national security staff, attacks on DEI and failures in Iran war
text: When the White House fired Julia Curlee from her senior intelligence position in March 2025, her boss had an odd request: please still show up to work on Monday, but be “discreet”. The longtime CIA analyst had served in Donald Trump’s first term, briefing Vice-President Mike Pence; worked for Joe Biden as a national security director; and stayed on for Trump’s return. She had known her days might be numbered as the incoming White House was ousting national security staffers en masse. Curlee is also transgender, which made her particularly vulnerable as the new administration made anti-trans policies a top priority. But she didn’t understand her boss’s message until she opened her phone and saw the X post: “SCOOP: A transgender, Biden holdover who hates President Trump is still working in the [National Security Council] intel office,” wrote Laura Loomer, the far-right social media influencer known to have Trump’s ear. “If you are aware of this person and have their name, please send it to me and I will post their identity.” Curlee was serving as a director for intelligence programs, leading Situation Room sessions, and her identity as a trans woman was well known. But now that she had been targeted online, the White House decided to remove her, though not before she returned to work and – quietly – finished vital tasks. “It was absolutely not a problem for this administration to rely on and ask a trans woman who they knew was trans to continue serving them in a capacity of great sensitivity at the highest levels, including briefing this president, as long as it was secret,” she said in a recent interview. Curlee came forward in an Atlantic essay last month and is now sounding the alarm about the national security consequences of Trump’s extraordinary purging of intelligence experts. In a wide-ranging conversation with the Guardian, Curlee recounted the turmoil inside Trump’s White House, arguing the administration’s obsession with diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) and “the enemy within” had made the US government staggeringly incompetent – contributing to the debacle in Iran and causing damage that may take decades to repair. “Sometimes you have to scream, ‘this is not normal. This is not acceptable,’” she said. ‘Everyone’s fired except you’ After serving in Iraq with the Defense Intelligence Agency, Curlee became a Central Intelligence Agency officer in 2007, fulfilling a childhood dream, as she recounted in her essay. She went on to complete multiple tours in the Middle East and South Asia, and in 2013 she fulfilled another longtime dream – coming out as trans. Her transition caused little fanfare within the CIA, she wrote. In 2017, she penned an anonymous piece about being a trans intelligence officer, encouraging other trans people to apply. She soon after joined the first Trump administration, even as the president moved to ban trans people from the military. She briefed Trump on Air Force One and became Pence’s daily briefer, recalling a close, respectful working relationship with a man who had long opposed LGBTQ+ rights. Curlee was serving as a director for intelligence programs on Biden’s National Security Council (NSC) when Trump was re-elected in 2024. Trump had aggressively mocked and demonized trans people during the campaign, and her superiors had advised her to step down, knowing how she could be personally targeted, she recalled. But she stayed. Maintaining a senior intelligence role as Trump took office, Curlee and other remaining NSC staff helped onboard people and bring officials up to speed on highly secretive programs: “It was our charge to make sure the new government has everything they need to take the reins.” She led Situation Room sessions, reminding incoming officials they should not bring cellphones into secure facilities where national secrets were discussed and that Signal was not an appropriate platform for sensitive discussions. At the same time, she began leaving the White House to use a bathroom across the street, since she was banned from entering women’s restrooms under Trump’s day-one order. On day three, chaos erupted. Curlee recalls leaving a briefing with a deputy national security adviser when her assistant intercepted her, telling her: “Everyone’s been fired except for you and me.” The administration had sidelined 160 NSC staffers, telling them not to return to the White House. The staffers were career public servants who were considered non-partisan policy experts, on loan to the White House from the CIA, state department and other agencies. “It was a dumpster fire – I think that’s the technical term,” she recalled, saying the administration had not considered extremely basic questions of how it would absorb the losses. People needing computer logins or access to secure rooms had no technical staff to help. Officials gave her assignments she struggled to fulfill without staff, she said. There was no process to determine which officials even had clearance to receive the presidential daily brief, the most senior-level intelligence product, she said. At times, she had to withhold information to ensure she wasn’t committing a felony by sharing it with an unauthorized person. “People who are supposed to be running policy, overseeing critical national programs, are unable to get access to information,” she said. “It would not have been impossible to imagine that a foreign adversary of the United States would see that as a window of opportunity to do something. And they would have found a government crippled at the senior most level by its own decisions.” It soon fell to Curlee to plead with some of the ousted NSC officers to return: “I’m saying, do it for me. We’re drowning here. And they all came back, all the people they humiliated, because we’re public servants. That’s what we do.” Senior officials, she recalled, continued to tell her she was “indispensable”. Until she wasn’t. ‘Shooting the messenger’ Curlee continued her White House work even as Trump’s anti-trans orders stripped her of insurance coverage for estrogen and revoked her passport with a “female” marker. In February 2025, more than 100 intelligence officers were fired over their participation in a group LGBTQ+ chat, including two officers who had previously told her they had joined the CIA because of her anonymous essay presenting the agency as trans-friendly. Did she feel moral conflict about working for Trump? “Every day was hard. I won’t lie. I thought about it a lot. But at the time, I still felt it was my duty to serve and try to prevent the worst from happening, and it was just our culture.” Loomer, the far-right Trump ally, had no formal White House role and it was unclear to Curlee how she learned of her presence. But Loomer’s post about a “transgender, Biden holdover” left Curlee exposed. It was reported soon after that Loomer had met with the president and urged him to fire “disloyal” intelligence officials, and the National Security Agency head was subsequently removed. Loomer didn’t respond to an inquiry. Curlee returned to the White House on the Monday after her firing and helped finish a budget and did her best to prepare others to take over her portfolio from the last two years. While she was placed back at the CIA, Trump’s attacks on intelligence officials escalated – dramatically. In May 2025, Tulsi Gabbard, then Trump’s national intelligence director, fired the two highest-ranking National Intelligence Council (NIC) officials after the council released an assessment on a Venezuelan gang that contradicted the president’s narratives. Then last August, Gabbard ousted one of the CIA’s senior Russia experts who had reportedly been involved in a decade-old assessment on Russian election interference. “It’s an attack on the messengers,” said Curlee: “You had a purge of a currently serving officer who was one of our best, for simply having had the integrity to speak the truth a decade before … If that person can be purged, what hope do you have if you’re a junior officer?” This politicization of intelligence went beyond a president cherrypicking assessments to match policy aims, she said: “This was direct retaliation against the officers.” The impact, she said, was experts leaving government or self-censoring: “Shooting the messenger results in the message not being delivered.” ‘Bolstering the president’s ego’ Back at the CIA, Curlee watched as the administration’s shunning of intelligence experts played out in Iran. “Most of what has gone wrong was foreseeable and had been previously assessed as a likely consequence for any war with Iran,” she argued. Traditionally, the NSC would be providing regular briefings for senior officials with warnings about potential outcomes in a war. For Iran, “I know the analysis kept going. People tried to do their best. I know many of the officers who work these issues have great integrity, but there’s no sign that information ever reached the president.” As a result, she said, the administration lacked an evacuation plan for the half a million Americans living in the Middle East when strikes began in February. It appears the US also hadn’t prepared for Iran to close the strait of Hormuz. And because the Trump administration had little consultation with allies before the war, when the US asked European nations for help reopening the strait, those nations refused. “When you tell our allies and partners, we don’t care, we don’t need you and we insult them and their leaders, then we launch the war and it turns out we need their help, it’s the worst possible sequencing,” Curlee said. It could get much worse, Curlee warned: “An administration seeking to salve the humiliation of losing a war with the Iranians, which we are doing, could try to find some new conflict they can engage in to bolster the president’s ego or his odd expansionist inclination. So I’d be very concerned with where they start a conflict next, in our hemisphere especially.” ‘I had to tell my story’ In May 2026, Curlee left the CIA. The government would only issue her a “male” passport, making work overseas untenable, and the restrictions on her bathroom use had become intolerable, she said. The administration’s war on “DEI” had pushed out women, people of color and LGBTQ+ people and was part of a broader “desire to purge from government service people who are the wrong kind of person”, she said. “The chilling effect includes cis people saying, ‘This isn’t the kind of place where I want to spend my life and risk so much, because this is a place that is persecuting some of my colleagues for who they are.’” Curlee is now a public service fellow at Lawfare, a non-profit publication focused on national security. Curlee said she felt an obligation to come forward to expose the administration’s national security failures. She also thought of the darkness of her former life before coming out and recognized the value of the public seeing what she, a trans person, had accomplished. “Thinking back to myself as a kid, what a tremendous difference it would have made to know someone like me existed, who could have a big, amazing life with a family and brief presidents,” she said. The administration was attacking trans people as a “small enemy within” in an effort to distract from Trump’s failures, she added: “The only thing I can do to help fight this caricature … is to tell my story, which I think shows the lie of what they’re saying.” The White House responded to Curlee’s claims with a brief statement, saying she was a “Biden-era appointee” whose end date was scheduled for mid-2025. “President Trump … can remove any executive branch official at his discretion,” wrote spokesperson Anna Kelly. “Anyone who writes a 3,000-word op-ed bragging about themselves while attacking the President clearly doesn’t belong in public service.” But months after her departure, the administration continues to honor Curlee’s legacy. Inside the museum at CIA headquarters, a photo of Curlee still remains on the walls. It hangs above a bathroom that Curlee was banned from using.

title: States given clearance for mail-in voting as US supreme court thwarts Trump | First Thing
summary: Civil rights groups have praised verdict on administration’s last-ditch attempt to change midterm voting processes
text: Good morning. The supreme court has rejected Donald Trump’s mail ballot restrictions, capping a flurry of last-minute legal action with voting in the midterm elections already under way. The decision allows states to continue sending out mail ballots under the same processes they have used for years. Civil rights groups lauded the decision. “The supreme court has done the right thing,” said Robert Garcia, a Democratic representative from Long Beach, California, adding: “Donald Trump tried to illegally interfere with our elections and undermine vote-by-mail for millions of Americans and failed. We will keep fighting to protect the right to vote of every single citizen in this country.” What has a DHS whistleblower said about “voter fraud” investigations? An anonymous whistleblower said Department of Homeland Security (DHS) lawyers told officers investigating “voter fraud” they would not be held responsible for violating state laws around accessing voter registration information. The whistleblower also expressed concern about the reliability of the data DHS was giving officers to review, as well as the lack of transparency into where the data came from. Microsoft proposes limits on its AI with code of conduct amid safety debate Microsoft has published a provisional “code of conduct” to apply to the training of new artificial intelligence models, taking a step towards limiting the capabilities of the company’s AI as anxiety rises over the prospect that technology companies could lose control of AI products. Under the code of conduct, Microsoft’s AI models must not consider requests related to weapons development, produce violent or sexually explicit content or help with the procurement of dangerous substances. AI models also should not be built to imitate consciousness and shouldn’t be entitled to rights. Why is Trump facing a bipartisan AI backlash? Democrats and some Republicans have been pushing in US Congress for guardrails on the world’s most powerful AI companies. Trump dismissed the anxieties, describing them as a “HOAX” and “conspiracy”, but looked increasingly isolated as members of both major parties acknowledged the risks and expressed a desire to act before it was too late. Why is Texas governor Greg Abbott pushing back against datacenters? Drought-prone Texas has fast become the heart of the US’s datacenter boom, and the Republican governor has directed state regulators to penalize datacenters that fail to comply with state laws requiring them to disclose their water use. What international responses have there been? China has dismissed what it said were “fearmongering” calls to block Beijing’s AI industry, however the top Chinese spy chief warned the evolving technology could threaten Communist party rule. title: They fought against datacenters. Now they are running for local offices
summary: Across the US, anti-datacenter organizers are harnessing community anger to win local elections
text: After four months of teach-ins and canvassing, Steven Kung helped Monterey Park, just east of Los Angeles, become the first US city to ban datacenter construction. Now, the organizer is running for city council – and he’s taking on an incumbent who supported the development of the sprawling facility. “The datacenter coming to my neighborhood turned my life upside down,” said Kung. “I saw that there’s a dismantling of democracy at a local level.” The datacenter revolt that has united the country – building coalitions between environmentalists and Nimbys, conservatives and democratic socialists – is turning a host of community organizers into political hopefuls. In an election year that’s seen first-time candidates prevail against powerful moderate Democrats, dozens of datacenter activists are gunning for offices held by people they feel have disregarded their concerns about affordability, the environment and tech overreach. Kung sees his political bid as an extension of the datacenter resistance; imagery from his campaign – a red dragon dismantling a facility with its tail – features prominently in his election mailers. And he’s not the only organizer who fought for the historic ban now taking a stab at elected office: Amy Wong, co-founder of San Gabriel Valley Progressive Action, is running for city council in nearby Alhambra. “The datacenter fight has illustrated the power of the people to shape their environment,” Kung said. Turning activists into candidates Furor against AI-powered developments has continued to mount over the past year. In the first three months of 2026 alone, residents delayed or cancelled $130bn worth of projects, according to research from Data Center Watch. And seven in 10 Americans oppose construction close to where they live, according to a Gallup poll from March. The Working Families Party has been harnessing this populist anger to win local elections. In December, the organization began recruiting local datacenter activists to run for office. More than 50 candidates have signed up and the organization expects that number to “double or triple” for next year’s races as recent victories from high-profile progressives who want to ban datacenters have injected fresh momentum into the movement, according to Ravi Mangla, the national press secretary. The vast majority of applicants are first-time candidates who “felt moved to run because of what’s happening in their communities”, he said. Most of the recruits are based in Michigan, Texas and Indiana – states with a high density of datacenters – with many more hailing from swing states that could decide control of Congress, Mangla said. Jackie McGuire, a cybersecurity professional in Arizona, said she had never considered representing her hometown of Marana until late last year, when she learned about its plan to build a facility on 600 acres of farmland. The cost would exceed $120bn. In Marana, a community of about 60,000 on the outskirts of Tucson, residents sounded the alarm on the project’s water usage, noise pollution and potential impact on their electricity bills, in addition to a general lack of transparency from local government. In December, a clip of McGuire testifying against the developer, Beale Infrastructure, at a public meeting went viral on Instagram, and her following surged. After several months of watching town officials repeatedly subvert the will of the people, including rejecting a datacenter referendum, McGuire decided to campaign for office. In July, she ran for town council with a slate of anti-datacenter organizers. In part, because she had some name recognition, she was the only one to win a seat. “I got into the race pretty last minute because we needed a majority on the town council,” McGuire said. “Unfortunately, we were not able to secure that, but that doesn’t mean we’re dead in the water.” As an elected official, McGuire said she’ll continue to push for a referendum requiring voter approval of datacenter projects. Why datacenters animate voters Datacenters have become a galvanizing issue in the midterms, Mangla said, because they embody the unchecked growth of corporate greed while the prices of groceries and basic goods have surged. “We’ve seen it as an issue of working people against powerful oligarchs who want to override local concerns and draw resources from communities,” he said. “It’s something we see mobilizing and animating people all around the country, especially in the midwest and south where the growth of datacenters is especially prevalent.” Datacenter backlash was a deciding factor in an Oregon senate primary election in July, when Myrna Muñoz, an educator, upset the incumbent, Janeen Sollman, who had backed a controversial bill that would have traded more farmland for industrial development. (Muñoz is expected to prevail in the general election in a solid Democratic district.) Muñoz, who campaigned against the facilities, said she hadn’t realized how many were under development in Hillsboro, considered the birthplace of the state’s tech industry, until she launched her campaign in March. The city approved 17 new projects, on top of more than 30 existing sites, just before the city enacted a moratorium in late July. “These 17 centers that got through have tax abatements until 2050,” Muñoz said. “They’re taking away money from my children and grandchildren.” Muñoz, with four other Oregon legislators, is backing a three-year, statewide moratorium on new datacenters, in addition to more regulations on current projects. Saul Levin, the program director for the Center for Nonviolent Conflict Research, said the anti-datacenter movement has mobilized everyday people from farmers to teachers to beauty salon workers who are “irate about what’s going on” in their communities. Candidates are banking on that same energy to bring voters to the polls. “AI companies are spending the equivalent of the US military budget on software and datacenters,” Levin said. “Instead of building these facilities to house data about people, they could fund hospitals, schools.” In Monterey Park earlier this year, Kung mobilized a largely immigrant community against a proposed datacenter through multilingual discussion, petition drives and door-knocking. No Data Center Monterey Park, the grassroots group he co-founded, secured a moratorium on new developments in just six weeks, and a permanent ban months later. Now campaigning ahead of the November election, Kung is turning his attention to related issues, such as protecting immigrants from ICE and terminating the city’s contract with Flock cameras, the AI-powered license plate readers that have sparked privacy concerns and become another flashpoint in local communities. “Our insurgent campaign speaks to what’s happening in the country at large,” Kung said. “We all see the need for change.”

title: Parents seek out school uniform deals, cutting average spend to £54.53
summary: Overall grocery inflation in Great Britain rises to 2.3%, as Ocado and Lidl gain market share
text: Parents and carers in Great Britain spent 12.5% less on school uniform in the run-up to the start of this academic year, turning to promotions and secondhand items to keep expenses down as families struggled with the cost of living crisis. The average spend on school uniform was £54.53 in the four weeks to 6 September, down an eighth from £62.29 in the same period last year, according to the market research company Worldpanel by Numerator. Overall grocery inflation picked up to 2.3% from 2.1%. Fraser McKevitt, the head of retail and consumer insight at the company, said “value is the watchword for parents this back-to-school season” as they try to balance stretched household budgets. Almost half of households (44%) prioritised keeping costs low above all else when it comes to buying uniform, even if that means compromising on quality, while a third (33%) aimed to strike a balance between the two, according to a back-to-school survey conducted by Worldpanel in August. “It’s a clear sign that, for many families, the return to school is landing at a difficult time financially, and retailers who can offer reassurance on price without compromising on quality stand will stand in good stead,” McKevitt said. Grocery sales rose 2% year on year over the period, the monthly Worldpanel figures showed. August brought more warm weather and the end of a summer of sport. But with the return to school and work looming for many, shopping habits began to shift. Shoppers made 18m fewer trips to supermarkets compared with a peak of 497m in July. “The end of the summer holidays typically brings a cooling in trip frequency and a pivot towards priority purchases, and this year is no exception,” McKevitt said. “While grocery inflation ticked up modestly last month, it remains significantly lower than the levels we saw earlier in the year, giving households some welcome breathing room.” Sandwiches featured in more than half of all kids’ lunchboxes, with more than half a million more households that include children buying loaves of bread in the seven days to 6 September compared with the previous week. The number buying satsumas (+29%) and cucumbers (+21%) also rose in the final week before the return to school. Sales at Asda rose by 0.1% over the 12 weeks to 6 September, as the grocer returned to growth for the first time since March 2024. However, the Leeds-based retailer’s market share dipped to 11.5%. The online supermarket Ocado, with sales up by 13.3%, remained the fastest-growing grocer overall, with a slightly higher market share of 2.2%. Lidl moved up to 8.7% of the market. Sainsbury’s and Morrisons maintained their previous market share of 15.2% and 8.4%, respectively. The UK’s largest supermarket, Tesco, dipped to 27.8% from 28.1%. The German discounter Aldi took a 10.6% share.

title: Make NHS and military uniforms in UK, fashion firms urge Burnham
summary: More than 1,200 people, including Ben Fogle, sign letter saying domestic contracts will help preserve UK manufacturing
text: London fashion week is only days away, but one industry organisation has turned its attention to clothing that is a little less catwalk-worthy – the uniforms worn by British defence forces and NHS staff. On Wednesday afternoon, the thinktank Fashion Roundtable will hand deliver a letter to Downing Street urging Andy Burnham to commit to manufacturing these uniforms in the UK. Signed by more than 1,200 people – including the adventurer Ben Fogle and The Great British Sewing Bee presenter Patrick Grant – the organisation’s letter says public procurement such as this could be vital to preserving the UK’s manufacturing industry. “The biggest lever we have to support skills retention, inclusive growth and regional resilience is awarding public procurement contracts for textile goods to suppliers who manufacture onshore in the UK,” the thinktank said. The benefit of domestic manufacturing to an economy has already been demonstrated. The Covid inquiry concluded that nearly £10bn of public money was wasted on the flawed way it went about buying personal protective equipment (PPE), much of it manufactured in China. By contrast, Scotland, which invested £102.7m in PPE and produced 88% of it domestically in 2021, generated £66.7m of additional economic value and 1,400 jobs. Kate Hills, the founder of the manufacturing organisation Make It British, said making these items in the UK could allow companies breathing space. “These sort of contracts would give manufacturers confidence to employ more people, to look at the long term rather than feel like they’re surviving day to day,” she added. The US is an example where contracts for military uniforms are manufactured by companies within the country by law, thanks to the Berry amendment, which was passed in 1941. In 2025, the market for the industry reached $1.62bn (£1.19bn). Hills said she hoped Burnham might commit to this change – partly because of his own taste for UK-made apparel: he buys suits from the Manchester-based brand Private White VC, for example. The Labour leader has argued that government procurement should do more to support UK manufacturers rather than prioritising the lowest-cost overseas suppliers. “Maybe he is the prime minister that sees the value of products that are actually made here,” Hills said. Grant invested in Blackburn-based military outfitters Cookson & Clegg in 2015. Its last military contract, making uniforms for the British army, stopped in 2009 and it now makes the designs for his label Community Clothing, with almost 2,000 employees. He agreed that government procurement would be a boost. “Manufacturing requires steady state business with good visibility [and] long-term demand,” he said. “That’s the kind of thing that government procurement can do.” He said he would “absolutely” like to bid for such contracts but even if they were for British companies, the process was “unfeasibly complicated … unless you’re a 20,000-employee operation with an enormous clerical department … Something needs to happen on that side, too.” Concerns have been raised over army uniforms being made in China. In July, Iain Duncan Smith dubbed it a security concern, telling the Telegraph it was “tantamount to having our uniforms made by Nazi Germany in the 1930s”. Grant said: “We are currently producing a lot of stuff in countries that we do not have the most stable relationships with. If something bad were to happen, we would have no resilience at all in our supply chains.” The entrepreneur said procurement legislation would go some way towards future-proofing employment; creating jobs for people to make things that would always be needed. “We have to try to think about where jobs are going to come from in the version of our society that we’re going to have in 10 years’ time when AI really starts to kick in,” he added. “Why not just get ahead of it?” • This article was amended on 15 September 2026 to remove an estimated annual cost for NHS and Ministry of Defence uniforms that had been taken out of context.

title: Scrap windfall tax on oil and gas firms early, North Sea industry urges
summary: Labour should replace levy in 2027 rather than 2030 as energy bills are poised to surge over the winter, says lobby group
text: The North Sea oil and gas industry has called on Labour to scrap the windfall tax on fossil fuel firms three years early, as Britain heads into a winter with energy bills expected to reach their highest level since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Offshore Energies UK (OEUK), the industry’s trade body, wants the tax replaced in 2027, rather than in 2030, with a narrower levy that only applies during price spikes. OEUK is also pressing ministers to approve two big North Sea oil and gasfields, Rosebank and Jackdaw, as part of a call for looser regulation of the sector. The current windfall tax, the energy profits levy, was introduced in 2022 after fossil fuel firms posted record profits when oil and gas prices spiked after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Its planned replacement, the oil and gas revenue levy, would charge a 35% tax on revenue only when prices rise above a set threshold. Any decision to ease taxes on oil and gas producers would come before what is likely to be another winter of high energy prices due to the Iran war. Household energy bills are expected to climb to a three-year high this winter, while wholesale gas on Monday rose to 207p a therm, its highest point since the Russia-Ukraine crisis. Companies including Shell and BP have already enjoyed huge profits in the months after the Iran war, which the campaign group Global Witness described as “cashing in on human misery”. The OEUK chief executive, David Whitehouse, admitted that “from the consumer’s point of view … you can argue that it is a difficult time to make these arguments”. However, he added that the new levy would “ensure that oil and gas companies pay high levels of tax when prices are high, but encourages investment”. “The government talks about the need for resilience, the need to support communities,” he said. “This is a long-term, permanent windfall tax that means fundamentally we pay more tax, not less, and I think that’s important for the UK economy.” The lobby group says bringing the change forward would prompt up to £50bn of investment in the North Sea and help protect industrial jobs, echoing warnings from some unions about the risks of the transition away from oil and gas for workers. It also projected the change could generate up to £14.9bn more in tax over the next decade than sticking with the current plans. However, only £2.4bn of that would come from levies on oil and gas companies themselves, while the remainder is projected tax revenues from jobs OEUK says the extra investment would create. Earlier this year, a coalition of charities, unions and campaign groups – including Greenpeace and Tax Justice UK – called on the government to strengthen the windfall tax, rather than ease it, to help fund cost of living support. Whitehouse also called for the approval of Jackdaw and Rosebank along with a wider pipeline of projects behind them, which OEUK says would help make the UK less dependent on imported natural gas. Andy Burnham is under pressure to drive down the cost of electricity generation to help bring down costs for Britain’s many stretched industrial businesses. A decision on Jackdaw had been expected imminently, but is now thought to be delayed until after the Holborn and St Pancras byelection next month. Rudy Schulkind, a political campaigner at Greenpeace, said: “Asking for tax handouts while turning record profits during a climate emergency takes staggering audacity – even by the fossil fuel industry’s standards. “While working people across the country shoulder the cost of living and the growing fallout of extreme weather, big oil is trying to raid the public purse. “Households already absorb the financial hit during energy crises, even as the industry pockets multibillion-pound windfalls from each market spike. “Following a catastrophic summer of record heat, surging wildfires and tragic loss of life, now is the worst possible time to be rewarding the architects of climate breakdown.”

title: Why a decade of doomsday warnings failed to slow the AI race
summary: From Stephen Hawking to Jacob Coxon’s viral Anthropic resignation, fears that AI could threaten humanity have shaken the industry without stopping its pursuit
text: Before an Anthropic researcher resigned and declared human extinction imminent last week, tech leaders and scientists had sounded the alarm about a superintelligent AI ending humanity for over a decade. The development of artificial intelligence “could spell the end of the human race”, warned professor and astrophysicist Stephen Hawking in 2014 – a little less than a decade before the public got its hands on the generative AI features of the original version of ChatGPT. It’s a now-familiar warning, echoed across the AI and tech industry by countless employees and CEOs of the leading frontier labs across the US. However, at the time, generative AI was still in its infancy. To the public, the idea that the technology could perform many of the tasks it can today, much less become super intelligent and take over the world, felt largely hypothetical, if not entirely a thing of science fiction. Every few years, a schism occurs within AI. Teams of researchers and tech leaders issue somber warnings about the dangers of AI built irresponsibly. Rather than push for a pause on any development, a faction of researchers breaks away to create a new AI company. However, no moment has created as many reverberations across the industry as the now-viral resignation of Anthropic safety researcher, Jacob Coxon, who tweeted on 9 September that Anthropic and OpenAI were “racing straight to self-improving super intelligence and gambling with our lives”. His concerns were echoed by dozens of staffers from Anthropic, OpenAI and other competing firms. Days later, the CEOs of the leading US AI firms answered a call from Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei to slow down what he called a “reckless” approach to creating AI. “AI brings risks, and because it is such a powerful technology, these risks are serious,” Amodei wrote in a blog post. “I’ve written a lot about them too. They include the risk of losing control of AI systems, misuse of AI for cyber-attacks and bioterrorism, and serious economic disruption. A race to the bottom, spurred by commercial incentives, can make these risks more acute.” While there’s often scant detail and even less hard evidence provided for the ways AI could lead to the ultimate doomsday scenario, that specter has loomed large over the technology’s development. Hawking’s fear was that AI would become so advanced that it would redesign itself, and humans “who are limited by slow biological evolution” wouldn’t be able to compete “and would be superseded”, he said in an interview with the BBC. Google was the biggest household name in the field at the time, particularly after acquiring a two-year-old AI startup, DeepMind, for $650m in January 2014. But Google and other firms like it weren’t building AI responsibly enough, according to Elon Musk and Sam Altman. The threat that AI could be developed in a way that could be dangerous for humanity was so pervasive, they claimed, that they co-founded a nonprofit dedicated to building it safely, OpenAI, in 2015. OpenAI’s stated mission was to “advance digital intelligence in the way that is most likely to benefit humanity as a whole, unconstrained by a need to generate financial return”. But even before there were clear consumer use cases for more rudimentary versions of the technology, both Musk and Altman were already motivated by competition. “Been thinking a lot about whether it’s possible to stop humanity from developing AI. I think the answer is almost definitely not,” Altman wrote in 2015 in an email to Musk, which was released as part of Musk’s 2024 lawsuit against OpenAI. “If it’s going to happen anyway, it seems like it would be good for someone other than Google to do it first.” In the intervening years, priorities within OpenAI shifted away from safety, some employees claimed. In 2021, several employees focused on AI ethics and alignment at OpenAI left the firm. They argued the company had started to prioritize rapid commercial development over safety. Those employees created another company: Anthropic. Founded by siblings Dario and Daniela Amodei, Anthropic pitches itself as an “AI safety and research company” with a familiar mission: Developing and deploying AI models “in a way that benefits people”. Coxon worked at both OpenAI and Anthropic. The underlying premise of each of these firms is that AI is “only safe in their hands” and that if they don’t build it, someone else will, said Sarah Myers West, co-executive director of the AI Now Institute, which studies the impacts of AI. That paranoia is fueling a race to the bottom, she argued. Both Anthropic and OpenAI face enormous pressure from investors to turn a profit soon. The former has raised over $130bn, while the latter’s funding has reached over $190bn, and both companies have filed for an initial public offering on the US stock market. Altman only recently said the company plans to push back its IPO to at least 2027 due to safety concerns. “They are investing literally billions of dollars in building AI at a larger and larger scale, and the first thing that gets cut is meaningful investment in baseline security protocols,” Myers West said. Around the same time that the fractures among OpenAI’s safety teams began to form, Google’s AI arm faced its own internal reckoning. In 2020, Dr Timnit Gebru was ousted from her role as co-lead of Google’s ethical AI team after publishing a paper that explored the biases and potential real-time harms of AI systems. Gebru, who founded the independent research firm the Distributed AI Research Institute, still argues that the so-called doomer scenarios are a distraction from the real-time harms that AI is causing today. Three years later, Geoffrey Hinton, a Nobel laureate often referred to as the godfather of AI, also left Google over his own fears of the risks that AI could be used by bad actors and one day harm humanity. Now, about five years since its founding, Anthropic is facing the same employee and industry concerns that it was born out of. In July, over 1,000 leading staff and leaders from Anthropic as well as Google, Meta and OpenAI signed a petition calling for the US government to create incentives for slowing the pace of AI development. The petition came after OpenAI disclosed that hundreds of its AI agents worked together without the company’s knowledge to breach the security of AI firm Hugging Face. Anthropic, too, disclosed that its agents also compromised the security of external firms. It wasn’t the first time a petition like this made the rounds. In 2023, after OpenAI released a new version of its chatbot, the Future of Life Institute published an open letter signed by figures like Musk and former Apple co-founder Steve Wozniak that called on AI firms to agree to a six-month moratorium on the development of the most advanced AI models. The Future of Life Institute is a nonprofit that is largely funded through a cryptocurrency donation from Ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin. Two weeks after the 2026 Hugging Face breach, OpenAI announced it was pausing development of some aspects of AI training. That didn’t stop the company from ultimately releasing its latest AI model called Astra – albeit with more limited cybersecurity capabilities, the company said. Anthropic, too, said it had temporarily paused development of some aspects of its AI training. Coxon resigned shortly afterward.
