title: Panama canal traffic facing further cuts as drought from El Niño worsens
summary: Planned daily reductions will further choke one of the world’s most important shipping lanes
text: The Panama canal plans to again cut maritime traffic due to worsening drought caused by the El Niño climate phenomenon, further choking up one of the world’s most important shipping lanes. The canal handles 5% of global maritime trade and about 40% of US container traffic; it is favoured by shippers because it usually reduces cost and transit times, especially for companies trading between China, Asia and the US. From October, an average of 29.5 vessels will be allowed to transit daily – down 18% from 36 in August, according to a draft plan submitted to Panama’s parliament. In September, officials cut daily transits from 36 to 32 because of the drought. The US and Israel’s war on Iran, and its disruption to the strait of Hormuz, has complicated logistics and added costs for shipping companies using the canal. In August, with vessels waiting 10 days to enter the canal – the longest since May – a container ship reportedly paid about $4m (£3m) to jump the queue. Maritime companies usually pay a flat fee to reserve a slot to transit the canal, but a daily auction allows shipowners to place bids to skip the queue. Bid prices generally rise during high demand. Shipping restrictions on the canal could yet worsen, with El Niño expected to peak later this year. The natural weather pattern that brings worldwide changes in winds, air pressure and rainfall patterns is forecast to be the strongest in four decades. The 82km-long canal, connecting the Caribbean Sea to the Pacific Ocean, relies on fresh water from rivers pouring into Lake Gatun to operate its system of locks. In September, officials said the watershed had received lower than forecast rainfall. The canal’s locks act like elevators, each filling with water to lift ships 26 metres (85 feet) from sea level to Lake Gatun and then back down to sea level on the other side. If lake levels are no longer safe for the largest ships to pass, the Panama Canal Authority imposes restrictions for safety and to preserve water. In 2023 the water level in the lakes feeding the canal was so low authorities cut daily transits from 38 to 22. Those restrictions led to a bottleneck of ships and sent companies scrambling to find alternative routes. El Niño has severely affected Central America and northern parts of South America, where nine countries have experienced their hottest June-August period on record this year. Fifty-two countries across all continents broke their seasonal temperature records for that period, according to an Agence France-Presse analysis of meteorological data from the European Copernicus programme. The extreme heat has taken many forms, from unprecedented heatwaves in Europe to devastating drought in Sudan and toxic smoke in Indonesia. More than a third of people experiencing the hottest northern summer months on record were in Africa, particularly in the Sahel and areas south of it. Eighteen African countries broke their seasonal records for the June-August period, from Mauritania and Sierra Leone in the west to Eritrea and Ethiopia in the east.

title: ‘This is seriously bold’: How China turned Taiwan tensions into a top-rating TV spy drama
summary: Dismissed in Taiwan as simply propaganda, the Long Watch, or Jiaofeng, has proved a sensation across the strait with its references to real-life crises
text: After shaking off the people trailing her through a crowded market and emerging from a bathroom in disguise, the double agent appears to have escaped. But a sip of water on a plane eventually gets her. She is poisoned after Taiwan’s military intelligence service discovers that she has been working secretly for China. The plot comes from a new Chinese spy drama co-produced by the Ministry of State Security. Since its premiere on 6 September, it has become a TV hit, with a fictionalised take on a subject rarely treated so directly: the modern history of tensions with Taiwan. The series, which will run for 40 episodes, is officially titled The Long Watch in English or Jiaofeng, meaning clashing or “crossing swords” in Chinese. It follows two decades of spies, double agents and intelligence operations between China and Taiwan from the mid-1990s. Jiaofeng mixes fictional characters and locations with real ones such as Taipei, the capital of Taiwan. Yet it remains difficult for analysts to verify how closely the drama follows real events as new episodes continue to be released. While Taiwan’s intelligence services are portrayed as an adversary capable of obtaining sensitive missile information, the drama casts Chinese state security officers as the heroes defending the country against infiltration and theft. By making these dramas, Chinese authorities are “essentially creating their own historical narrative,” says Li Fu-chung, a historian at Taiwan’s National Chengchi University whose research includes Chinese Communist party history and film history. “Through a dramatic format, people can very easily be brainwashed, not only in China but potentially in Taiwan as well.” Billed as drawing on declassified national-security cases, the series’ writers said they interviewed retired state-security officers and studied 27 case files while developing the script. Within about a week of its premiere, the series topped the daily prime-time drama ratings on China Central Television five times. Online, it surpassed 50m views across platforms within a week, according to Chinese entertainment data provider Maoyan. Chinese viewers have described the series as unusually “bold” for addressing real political figures and depicting details of espionage operations on both sides. “One reason China has been making more dramas on this subject in recent years is simply that espionage makes for good drama. Another is that they want to emphasise patriotism,” says Li. “Since the story involves Taiwan trying to turn Chinese officials into agents, there will be negative and positive characters. That contrast helps show who is patriotic and who is betraying the country,” Li adds. Spies, lies and cross-strait tensions Set in 1994, the first episode opens with a newsreader’s voice playing over a cityscape in China, reporting that Taiwan’s then president Lee Teng-hui had made remarks that “incite separatist sentiment” and “undermine the foundations of cross-strait relations”. “This is seriously bold!!! It’s exciting from every angle and really doesn’t shy away from anything,” one Chinese viewer wrote on the microblogging platform Weibo, surprised at the direct mention of Lee. Taiwan, formally known as the Republic of China, is a self-governed democracy that Beijing claims as its territory despite never having controlled the island. Lee, who later became Taiwan’s first directly elected president, was viewed by Beijing as a major “separatist”. His visit to the United States sparked Chinese missile tests and military exercises that developed into the 1995-96 Taiwan strait crisis, during which the US sent aircraft carrier groups to waters near the island. Jiaofeng, however, is not the first state-backed Chinese spy drama to draw on cross-strait relations. Last year, another TV series called Silent Honor, also made with guidance from the Ministry of State Security, portrayed espionage set against the backdrop of the end of the Chinese civil war. Despite the historical narratives, the shows help play into current events. In a commentary about Jiaofeng, published on 8 September, the state-run Global Times described cross-strait espionage as a “hidden front” and said “the struggle on this front will only truly end when the complete reunification of the motherland is achieved.” On Chinese social media RedNote, one user posted a video saying the drama had taught him a hard lesson about the spy game. “One moment of misplaced trust, one casual conversation or one flash of greed could be enough to pull you into the whole trap,” he said. ‘This is just propaganda’ So far, however, the drama appears to have caused barely a ripple in Taiwan. Little discussion is evident across social media, despite the series being available there through Chinese streaming service Tencent Video and on YouTube. Last year, Taiwan’s own drama about cross-strait security threats performed strongly, becoming the most-watched drama of the year. The government-subsidised series Zero Day Attack imagined a Chinese blockade and invasion, with storylines involving sleeper agents and media infiltration. Annie Hsieh, a 26-year-old Taiwanese postgraduate student, has never heard of Jiaofeng; nor would she be interested in watching it, given the topic. “Who knows what they’ve made out of it,” she says. Another Taiwanese graduate, Liang Tian-jun, says Chinese romance dramas were more popular among his peers, but that “watching dramas wouldn’t make them feel more open or receptive towards China”. A poll conducted last month found that only 7.4% of Taiwanese respondents had a favourable view of the Chinese Communist party, down from 9.6% in July. “Taiwan is, after all, an open and free society, so some people will be influenced by propaganda from across the strait,“ Li says, “But most Taiwanese can see that this is just propaganda.”

title: Supreme court rejects Trump’s mail ballot restrictions for midterm elections
summary: Decision allows states to send ballots under process followed for years even as president tried to limit system
text: The supreme court on Monday rejected Donald Trump’s mail ballot restrictions for now, capping a flurry of last-minute legal action with voting in the midterm elections already underway. The decision allows states to continue sending out mail ballots under the same processes they have used for years. The Trump administration had asked the court, once again at the center of a roiling political controversy, to clear the way for restrictions before the pivotal November contests for control of Congress. The case has major implications because nearly one-third of the country votes by mail. “The government is unlikely to succeed on the merits of its challenge to the district court’s preliminary injunction,” states the one-paragraph unsigned order. “And the equitable factors applicable for obtaining emergency relief from this court do not favor a stay.” Justice Brett Kavanaugh filed a concurrence, ruling that he believed the government had “at least a fair prospect” of success defending the plan, but that implementation so close to election day would be “arbitrary and capricious”. Justice Samuel Alito dissented, joined by Justice Clarence Thomas. In the dissent, Alito blamed the litigating states for creating the conditions of a ruling so close to an election, and wrote that they should not benefit from a protracted process that they created with their suit. “The plaintiff states cannot claim the timing of the rule tilts the equities in their favor when they, and courts hearing their claims, are responsible for so much of the delay,” he wrote. Civil rights groups lauded the decision. “It is alarming what the administration was seeking to do here,” said Kristen Clarke, NAACP general counsel and former head of the justice department’s civil rights division. “This was an 11th-hour effort by the administration to hijack the way that we vote by mail in our country.” Civil rights groups could not have moved faster, she said. “At the earliest opportunity, civil rights organizations like the NAACP took to the court to stand up for voters. It’s important to remember that the final rule was not issued until about roughly 10 days ago. So, I find Justice Alito’s statements disingenuous … We should focus on the fact that the court is leaving in place an injunction that prevents this administration from turning our electoral system on its head. What the administration was attempting to do here would have unleashed chaos across the country.” “The supreme court has done the right thing by protecting the American people’s right to vote,” said Robert Garcia, a Democratic representative from Long Beach, California. “Donald Trump tried to illegally interfere with our elections and undermine vote-by-mail for millions of Americans and failed. We will keep fighting to protect the right to vote of every single citizen in this country.” The case stems from an executive order issued by Trump on 31 March requiring the post office to refrain from delivering ballots for mail-in voting to registered voters deemed ineligible when compared with Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and other federal records. Voting rights groups, joined by 23 states and the District of Columbia, sued the administration to stop the proposed rule, arguing that the US constitution provides no authority for the president to issue orders governing the administration of elections. Election officials have said there was simply no way to carry out a complete overhaul in the weeks before the midterms. Indeed, Alabama, North Carolina and Wisconsin began sending mail ballots to voters over the past week while the new system was still not active. The Trump administration plan would require states to adopt a uniform envelope style and submit lists of eligible voters to an online portal. The postal service could refuse to deliver ballots to states that didn’t comply. A whistleblower report, though, said the postal system’s requirements could lead to millions of mail ballots never being sent, because the portal wasn’t properly built and a single bar code error could result in an entire batch of ballots being tossed out. Democratic state officials and voting rights groups challenged the restrictions in court, arguing the president has no constitutional authority to set election rules that would “virtually eliminate mail voting on the eve of a major election”. Lower courts agreed. But an initial injunction issued by US district judge Indira ⁠Talwani was overturned on procedural grounds in July, but was reinstated after the USPS posted a final rule on ballot delivery. Monday’s ruling upholds that injunction. The Trump administration appealed to the supreme court, arguing that federal control of the postal service allows them to set rules for mail ballot handling and that compliance was possible. The federal government won an early procedural decision at the supreme court, but the justices pointedly did not decide the legality of the plan. Trump has long opposed mail voting and falsely blamed it for his 2020 election loss to Joe Biden, even though he often uses that method to cast his own ballot, including as recently as this year. “The court’s ruling is a massive sigh of relief for local election officials and voters – especially for the thousands of service members abroad whose ballots are legally required to be sent by all 50 states within the next five days,” said Samantha Tarazi, co-founder and CEO of the Voting Rights Lab. “But this isn’t over. This administration will keep testing every avenue to manipulate our elections and sow doubt in results he doesn’t like. Today is yet another example of President Trump’s extreme elections agenda losing in the courts and with the American people. The bottom line is simple: states run our elections – not the president.”

title: Gavin Newsom says he will not run for president in 2028 if Kamala Harris does
summary: Term-limited California governor tells CNN running against former vice-president would ‘waste everybody’s time’
text: Gavin Newsom, the California governor, will not run for president if former vice-president Kamala Harris does, he said in a forthcoming interview with CNN. Newsom and Harris, both from California, are widely viewed as two of the top establishment frontrunners in the coming Democratic presidential primary. Newsom, who will leave office this year after his second term ends, has increasingly portrayed himself as a foil to Trump and is widely viewed as positioning himself for a 2028 White House bid. But Newsom said running against Harris would waste voters’ time and act as a “gift from God” to their political opponents, he said. “I wouldn’t do that to her,” Newsom told Jake Tapper, a CNN anchor. “I wouldn’t waste everybody’s time.” “The zen [sic] diagram on that, it’s pure crossover,” Newsom said. “I wouldn’t do that to people.” Newsom said he considered running in 2024, but that he “wasn’t ready”. He said he was still assessing whether he would be ready for the coming presidential primary. “You have to meet the moment,” Newsom said. “You have to be honest with yourself. Do you represent the zeitgeist of the moment? Are you wasting everybody’s time?” Newsom made the comments to Tapper as the two of them went fishing in the Bitterroot River of Montana, where Newsom’s in-laws own a ranch. His apparent reluctance to challenge Harris belies his long push to gain a more prominent national profile. Newsom has adopted a more strident tone on social media, where he routinely takes jabs at Trump. He has cultivated political “influencers” to spread awareness of his message. And he used a redistricting ballot initiative in California to help lead a national response to Trump’s attempts to manipulate the upcoming midterm elections by gerrymandering districts in conservative states to favor Republicans even more heavily. Harris has stayed relatively quiet in comparison since losing her ill-fated presidential race against Trump in 2024, though she said publicly in July that she has yet to decide about whether to run. She lost spectacularly to Trump in 2024, in an election tainted by Joe Biden’s late exit over concerns about his apparent cognitive decline. But Harris remains a household name and a serious contender for the Democratic presidential nomination.

title: Ukraine war briefing: No energy ceasefire until Russia stops, Zelenskyy confirms after Trump claim
summary: Moscow would need to commit ‘honestly and on a long-term basis’ to ending the war before Kyiv would de-escalate. What we know on day 1,665
text: Ukraine will only halt attacks on Russian energy targets if the enemy does likewise and the US guarantees it, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said. The announcement came after Donald Trump’s uncorroborated claim that both sides have agreed to such a ceasefire. Neither Ukraine nor Russia had said so at time of writing. The US president regularly claims to have brokered what turn out to be nonexistent or extremely shortlived deals between foreign adversaries or with his own overseas enemies, such as Iran. Ukraine’s president said: “So far, no one ‌has seen any genuine ‌willingness on Russia’s part to bring the war to an end. But if our ‌American partners can secure Russia’s genuine readiness to end the war aimed at destroying lives, and to do so honestly and on a long-term basis, Ukraine will take its own de-escalatory steps.” Russia would need to stop attacking Ukraine’s critical infrastructure for its intentions to be taken seriously, Zelenskyy suggested. It comes after Trump tried to blame diesel shortages and high prices on Ukraine’s strikes on Russian oil refineries. The main cause is Trump’s own war on Iran – the retaliation for which has crippled the trade in Middle East oil. Russia has banned diesel exports to address dire shortages at home caused by Ukraine’s attacks. But those exports comprise only a fraction of global supply, and the situation most directly affects neighbouring countries such as those in central Asia like Mongolia that rely heavily on supplies from Russian producers. A ⁠Nato fighter jet shot down a drone in Lithuania shortly after ⁠midnight on Tuesday, ⁠the national crisis management centre said. The drone, which likely entered from Belarus, ⁠was shot down near Pratkunai village in southern Lithuania, near Kaunas, the second-largest city, ⁠the centre’s spokesperson said. Its origin was yet to be determined at time of writing. A ‌drone alert was issued earlier in the ‌capital, Vilnius, and surrounding region. A ⁠Russian attack on ⁠a farming warehouse killed three people in the ⁠town of Pryluky ‌in Ukraine’s ‌northern Chernihiv ‌region, regional police said. Seven others were injured. Prosecutors in Germany have charged a German-Ukrainian woman with acting on behalf of Russian intelligence. The woman, identified as Ilona W in line with German privacy rules, is accused of being in contact with an intelligence officer at the Russian embassy in Berlin since at least October 2023. The defendant ran a marketing agency in Berlin and chaired a lobbying group, using these networks to get the intelligence officer into high-profile events, and to try to recruit German defence officials and industry figures. A member of the UK armed forces was killed in a crash in Ukraine on Saturday, Britain’s defence ministry said. It is understood the incident was not a result of hostile action, writes Priya Bharadia. A small number of British personnel in Ukraine provide security to diplomats and support the Ukrainian armed forces. Volodymyr Zelenskyy has formally dismissed Ukraine’s prosecutor general, Ruslan Kravchenko, whose office is embroiled in a bribery scandal. Zelenskyy announced the sacking in a government decree. Kravchenko – who has denied the allegations, but resigned on 7 September – posted that he is now outside Ukraine and has started legal action against the head of the national anti-corruption bureau, Nabu, accusing him of “falsifying official documents”. Nabu investigators raided the prosecutor general’s offices and said they had uncovered a network that made payments in return for protecting fraudulent call centres that had “laundered fortunes”.

title: Mitch McConnell returns to Senate after months-long absence
summary: The 84-year-old said he was prepared to cast his first vote after rampant speculation about his health
text: Mitch McConnell, the former Republican Senate majority leader, returned to the Capitol on Monday and cast his first vote after a months‑long absence that fueled rampant speculation about his health. One of the highest-profile figures in Congress, the 84-year-old senator has been away from the Senate since mid-June, following what his office said was a fall that left him hospitalized. After weeks of silence, that spurred demands for greater transparency and stoked online conspiracies, McConnell disclosed that he had been “briefly unconscious” and “also had to deal with a mild case of pneumonia”. He was discharged from a rehabilitation center last month. McConnell arrived on Capitol Hill in a wheelchair, and briefly addressed reporters on Monday evening before voting to confirm a federal judge to a district in Ohio. Appearing frailer, he said he was back to help advance the latest farm bill and to support legislation aiding “our good friends who are totally in the fight against the Russians”. The senator, who rarely replies to questions in the Capitol hallways, joked that after years of keeping silent, he wasn’t sure how many reporters would be there to see him return. “But I’m glad to see you,” he said. “It’s time to get back to work.” Reporters and photographers were instructed by Senate staff not to take video of his remarks, according to the Associated Press, though still images were allowed. In a statement released on Monday, McConnell described his recovery as a “long and often frustrating process” compounded by the “lingering effects of childhood polio”. Alarm over McConnell’s absence came amid a broader debate over term limits and concerns about the advanced age of many US political leaders, which has intensified since Joe Biden abandoned his bid for a second term amid concerns about his fitness to continue serving as president. The initial lack of information about McConnell’s health prompted unusual public intervention from Kentucky’s Democratic governor, Andy Beshear, who published an open letter urging the senator toreassure his constituents. The longest-serving Senate leader, McConnell will retire at the end of his term in January, and rejected calls to resign before then. He stepped down as the Republican leaderat the end of 2024, and was succeeded by senator John Thune of South Dakota. McConnell chairs the Senate rules committee and a defense appropriations panel, which is crucial in shaping Pentagon funding, and sits on the agriculture committee. His prolonged absence complicated the legislative efforts of Republicans, who control the Senate by a narrow 53-47 majority. Over the summer, his absence prevented Republicans from advancing the farm bill – a massive piece of legislation setting agriculture, nutrition and forestry policy – out of the agriculture committee. Speculation of his imminent return began to bubble when the agriculture committee scheduled a vote to advance the bill for Wednesday, suggesting he would be present to vote the measure through over opposition from Democrats. “I’m still not quite back to 100%,” McConnell said in the statement released Monday, “but I’ve assured Leader Thune that, as I continue with physical therapy on the advice of my doctors, I will do my best to be present for tough votes when our conference needs me.”

title: Democracy indicators in US at lowest levels for 50 years, data shows
summary: Trump administration undermining rule of law at home and worldwide, according to intergovernmental report
text: Key indicators of democracy in the US have fallen to their lowest levels in 50 years, with the global rule of law significantly undermined by the Trump administration’s “threats and actions”, data from a leading thinktank shows. Around the world, judicial independence, credible elections and freedom of expression, press freedom and access to justice are all at their lowest levels for at least 30 years, according to the Stockholm-based International Institute for Democracy and Electoral Assistance (International Idea). The intergovernmental organisation’s annual Global State of Democracy report is considered the most comprehensive of its kind, covering 174 countries and measuring democratic performance since 1975. International Idea said the decline in the US was particularly marked, but part of a global trend, with 2025 the 11th consecutive year in which more countries declined than improved democratically – the longest continuous downturn since the thinktank’s records began. “In 2025, the global challenges to democracy and the difficulty in stemming its erosion were both exemplified and compounded by political developments in the United States,” the report’s authors said. “President Donald Trump quickly amassed power in the executive branch and wielded it to further a narrow set of personal goals and pursue retaliation against perceived enemies … The results have been far-reaching, undermining the rule of law domestically and internationally and testing longstanding alliances and multilateral cooperation.” Kevin Casas-Zamora, International Idea’s secretary general, warned that the risk of conflict rose as democracies deteriorated. “The key message from our research is that investing in democracy should be at the heart of any country’s security strategy,” he said. “The connection between the erosion of the quality of democracy and increasing conflict is not being made either in policymaking or in the public debate.” The separate Uppsala Conflict Data Program, based at Uppsala University in Sweden, shows that 2025 had the most violent conflicts – including the most interstate conflicts – of any year in its dataset, which goes back to 1946. The International Idea report did highlight some positive developments, including in Australia – where civil society groups were consulted on an anti-racism strategy and children’s online privacy among other issues – and in Syria, where the repressive dictatorship of Bashar al-Assad was overthrown. In Bangladesh, Nepal and Sri Lanka, youth-led popular protests unseated long-serving leaders, but, the report noted, “it has proven difficult to create far-reaching, meaningful reform in a short period of time”. Casas-Zamora said it was clear that events in the US influenced other countries. International Idea added the US to its list of “backsliding” democracies for the first time in 2021, pointing to a “visible deterioration” it said began in 2019. The thinktank bases its assessments on 50 years of democratic indicators, assigning countries to one of three categories: democracies, “hybrid” governments and authoritarian regimes. Globally, it found rule of law was the weakest area of democracy in 2025, with 71 countries – 41% of those assessed – ranked as low-performing. It was also found to be deteriorating quickly, with 29 countries registering downturns. “Whatever happens in the US goes global. There is now an epidemic of election denialism, of which the patient zero is the current occupant of the White House,” Casas-Zamora said. “I am not willing to say the deterioration of the quality of democracy is inevitable or permanent. It can be reversed,” he added. “We live in a volatile world and that means things can happen which create very positive political openings.” Yet, despite the positive signs in Nepal, Bangladesh and elsewhere, the report paints a bleak picture overall. “While people continue to push back against democratic deterioration, civic space is narrowing,” its authors wrote. “Civil society and civic engagement have suffered, due in part to the widespread use of strategic lawsuits against public participation, foreign agent laws, and the criminalisation of peaceful protests.”

title: Texas governor threatens to penalize datacenters not obeying water laws
summary: Republican Greg Abbott says datacenters must help ‘protect’ drought-prone state and disclose water use
text: Greg Abbott, the Texas governor, has directed state regulators to penalize datacenters that fail to comply with state laws requiring them to disclose their water use. “Data centers must share the duty to protect Texas water,” the Republican governor said on Monday. “The Texas Water Code requires a complete and accurate water use survey. I direct the Texas Water Development Board to use its enforcement authority to penalize past failures and to impose legal consequences for any future failure to comply,” he added. In a letter to the water board, Abbott, who is seeking a fourth term, said: “Major water users, including data centers, appear to have committed civil and criminal violations by failing to provide the Texas Water Development Board (TWDB) with information about water usage as required by the Texas Water Code.” It follows a directive Abbott issued last month ordering the Public Utility Commission of Texas and the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (Ercot) to conduct a comprehensive audit of datacenters advancing through the Ercot interconnection process. Drought-prone Texas has fast become the heart of the US’s datacenter boom. Texas has the second-most datacenters of any state in the country, according to a tally by the Pew Research Center. But with 335 datacenters, and at least 248 more in the pipeline, experts believe it could surpass Virginia as the world’s largest concentration of datacenters by the end of the decade. But, amid growing public concern over datacenter construction, Texas has been working to tighten oversight of the industry as demand grows for the state’s power and water supplies. In 2025, Texas datacenters consumed an estimated 25bn gallons of water, according to the Houston Advanced Research Center. Water use by datacenters in the state could rise to 161bn gallons a year by 2030 – about 2.7% of all water used in Texas, or roughly the amount consumed by 1.3m households across the country. The audit requires datacenters to provide information about their water consumption, water sources and efforts to use water-efficient technologies. Abbott said projects that fail to complete the audit will be denied permission to connect to the state’s power grid. “TWDB’s water use surveys serve a similarly important purpose as this data center audit. TWDB must coordinate with PUC and ERCOT to ensure that covered entities provide critical water use information in response,” Abbott said in his Monday letter. “Any failure to respond to the audit’s request for water use information would trigger TWDB’s independent enforcement authority.”

title: DHS officers raise concerns over potentially illegal voter searches and unreliable data, whistleblower says
summary: Officers were instructed to search state voter databases and create federal records on suspected non-citizen voters despite concerns over the process
text: Department of Homeland Security (DHS) lawyers told officers investigating voter fraud they would not be held responsible for violating state laws around accessing voter registration information, an anonymous whistleblower revealed on Monday. DHS officers also had concerns about the reliability of the data they were working with, the whistleblower said. The Trump administration has ramped up its investigation into noncitizen voting ahead of the midterm elections. Noncitizen voting is extremely rare and the effort has only turned up a handful of cases so far. As part of the effort, officers tasked with investigating potential non-citizen voters were told to take data DHS had compiled on voters and run it through state websites where voters can look up their voter information. Some states require voters to click attestations affirming that they are looking up their own voter information. On the Virginia Department of Elections website, for example, voters must click a disclaimer that says: “I certify and affirm that the information provided to access my voter registration is my own or I am expressly authorized by the voter to access this information. I understand that it is unlawful to access the record of any other voter, punishable as computer fraud.” “In light of these instructions about access to the state websites, officers expressed concerns that accessing registered voter information on these websites may be illegal as officers are essentially misrepresenting themselves as the potential registered voter (with or without a specific attestation),” lawyers for Democracy Defenders Fund, who is representing the whistleblower, wrote in the disclosure. A slide in the presentation officers watched in the initiative says DHS’ office of the general counsel “advised that this type of review is permissible as open-source research when conducted for purposes related to adjudicative or investigative responsibilities”. It also said there was an effort to get further clarification from DHS leadership, and officers were told that immigration officers and immigration service officers “are not personally liable for conducting these searches when done as part of their official duties and properly documented”. “This statement suggests that there may be legal implications for accessing these websites, but that the officers themselves are simply not personally liable. This leads us to believe that USCIS-FDNS HQ is aware that the activity may be illegal, and yet they are still requiring officers to engage in this illegal activity with promises of personal liability protection,” lawyers for the whistleblower wrote. “Far from being rushed or untrained, these investigative efforts are conducted diligently and professionally. Identification and investigation of aliens who vote in our elections provides an essential guarantee in the authenticity of our election results. There is no quota on criminality. DHS will pursue each and every illegal voter to the fullest extent of the law,” a DHS spokesperson said in a statement. “One has to question why the media is so dead set on running a smoke screen for illegal alien voters in American elections.” The whistleblower also expressed concern about the reliability of the data DHS was giving officers to review as well as the lack of transparency into where the data came from. In some cases, DHS gave officers an individual’s name and specific dates on which they registered and voted. But when an officer went to look up the individual in the state’s voter registration website, there was no record of the voter. “With such a direct contradiction, knowing the specific source and date of the information is necessary to determine reliability before taking any action.” The whistleblower disclosure says this was a huge issue in California, where officers were often unable to access the voter registration database. Officers were told they should still create a file on the person in Tecs – a DHS database where law enforcement officials share information (Tecs is not an acronym). “The result is that a significant number of Tecs records, potentially thousands or tens of thousands, will be created against California residents based on data that an officer may have good reason to believe is unreliable or inaccurate without corroboration,” the disclosure says. “The whistleblower’s disclosure outlines shocking allegations of unlawful and unethical conduct that includes potentially thousands of violations of state law and the use of highly questionable data,” California senator Alex Padilla, a Democrat, said in a statement. Other election officials have raised concerns about the DHS data. Earlier this year, DHS told Nevada election officials it had identified as many as 15,903 non-citizens on its rolls. In a meeting last month, DHS representatives told the Nevada secretary of state’s office they had made that claim by comparing the state’s July 2025 public voter rolls against DHS data. When DHS began reviewing the data, they had only firmly identified 185 non-citizens on the rolls, though they said their review was ongoing. The disclosure also details the pressure the department put on officers to find voter fraud. Officers received their first and only training on 21 August, and were expected to begin researching four days later, lawyers for the whistleblower wrote. They were expected to review five individuals per hour. “The Department of Homeland Security is sending hundreds of officers who should be focused on our security on a wild goose chase to prove Trump’s long-debunked election conspiracy theories – and DHS is telling officers to lie to do it. This new DHS initiative is nothing more than an unlawful order by the government to silence the voices of Americans,” Senate minority leader Chuck Schumer said in a statement.

title: Duke and Duchess of Sussex granted security review after return to UK
summary: Committee to reconsider Harry and Meghan’s publicly funded police protection now they are full-time residents
text: The Duke and Duchess of Sussex will have a review of their publicly funded security following their return to the UK. The royal and VIP executive committee (Ravec), which oversees tax-funded security for royalty and public figures, is to reconsider Harry and Meghan’s level of police protection. The committee met last week to discuss the couple’s case, now they and their children are full-time residents in the UK and not just visitors. It will be the first risk assessment for Meghan since the couple stepped back as working members of the royal family in 2020. Harry was granted a review of his security in July but has yet to receive a decision. The Telegraph has reported that Ravec’s chair informed Harry last week the committee had commissioned a new risk assessment and a separate one for Meghan, in light of their return to the UK. The committee has reportedly asked the couple to provide their schedules and daily routine, including the school run, to inform their decision. Last year, Harry lost a legal challenge against the Home Office after the automatic tax-funded security for him and his family was withdrawn when the couple stood down as working royals. “The UK is my home,” said Harry in his witness statement. “The UK is central to the heritage of my children and a place I want them to feel at home as much as where they live at the moment in the US. That cannot happen if it’s not possible to keep them safe when they are on UK soil. I cannot put my wife in danger like that and, given my experiences in life, I am reluctant to unnecessarily put myself in harm’s way too.” The couple returned to the UK on 26 August. Soon after, a formal letter was issued on behalf of King Charles, reiterating their status as non-working royals. The letter stated the couple were “akin to private citizens with commercial and charitable interests” and “any operational security issues should continue to be directed to the relevant police authorities”. The Sussexes also decided on Monday to switch their children to a new school just two days after they started, reportedly due to security concerns over the long journey and heavy traffic. “The decision for the children to move school was taken following a discussion with the family’s security team about the practicalities of their current arrangements,” a family spokesperson told Hello! magazine. “The parents remain extremely grateful to all the teachers and staff for the love, care and effort they have shown their family. “This decision should in no way be interpreted as a reflection on the school or the exceptional care the children have received there.”

title: Russian oligarch close to Putin paid for part of Donald Trump Jr’s lavish wedding
summary: US president’s eldest child married Palm Beach socialite Bettina Anderson in three-day celebration across two exclusive private islands
text: Donald Trump Jr and his wife, Bettina, confirmed on Monday that a Russian oligarch close to Vladimir Putin partially paid for the couple’s wedding celebrations in May, following a ProPublica report revealing Umar Kremlev spent hundreds of thousands of dollars on the events. Trump Jr, the US president’s eldest child, married the Palm Beach socialite in a lavish three-day celebration across two exclusive private islands in May. Citing records and interviews with three anonymous sources familiar with the event, ProPublica reported that Kremlev, a member of the Russian president’s circle, footed the bill to rent one of the islands where a reception was held and where guests slept, along with other large expenses, including a huge firework show. In a statement signed by the couple and shared on Bettina Trump’s Instagram after ProPublica’s report was published, they confirmed Kremlev’s contributions to the celebrations and characterized them as “an extraordinarily generous wedding gift from a friend, and something for which we were and remain incredibly grateful”. A top Democrat demanded answers on the Trumps’ ties to Kremlev. “Why did a Russian oligarch close to Putin fund Trump Jr’s wedding in the Bahamas?” posted Robert Garcia, the ranking member and lead Democrat on the House oversight committee, on social media. “Umar Kremlev spent hundreds of thousands of dollars on the president’s son. What did he get in return? We need answers.” Kremlev has a longstanding relationship with Putin. He is the head of the International Boxing Association (IBA), a sporting body that has been backed by the state-owned Russian energy company Gazprom. According to ProPublica, the wedding payments came from an IBA-affiliated entity in Dubai that the boxing association uses for financial transactions. In the days before the wedding party, he reportedly went to China as part of a delegation accompanying Putin, and the month prior the Russian president had bestowed him with a state honor, the Order of Friendship. The Ukrainian government has imposed sanctions on Kremlev, citing his closeness to Putin and Russian security services. Alexander Lagutin, a businessperson who has held senior roles at a Russian defense contractor and a state-backed energy company, had been with Kremlev on the China trip. Kremlev’s right hand at the IBA, Elena Sobol, attended the wedding, too. While the event was extravagant, the guest list was intimate, with only about 50 people attending, most of whom were immediate family, close friends and business partners of the couple. Then there was Kremlev, who reportedly did not attend the ceremony itself, which was limited to just 18 guests, but was present with a large contingent of Russians at the party, much to the confusion of the other guests. The group reportedly sometimes stood by themselves speaking Russian, according to ProPublica. The affair has raised questions about the implications of a member of Putin’s circle financially supporting and gaining such intimate access to the US president’s family. In recent years Trump Jr has emerged as a leading campaign surrogate for Trump and has even been touted as a potential political heir. Donald Sherman, the president and CEO of Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington (Crew), said it was in the public interest for Congress to strongly consider requiring financial disclosure statements of a president’s adult children, in addition to the president themselves. The crux of the issue is the nature of the friendship, and whether the giving of gifts is genuine or designed to influence, Sherman said. “We know that private companies and foreign governments have been seeking to gain Don Jr’s favor in order to serve their own financial interests. And so, it’s important that there is a measure of transparency when folks tied to the Russian government are lavishing the president’s rich adult son with expensive gifts.” He added: “Most of us learn as children that there’s no such thing as a free lunch. It’s one thing if, in the nature of this friendship, there’s a mutual exchange of lavish gifts. It’s another if someone’s daddy becomes president and then all of a sudden this new friend starts giving gifts – that context very much matters.” In similar vein, retired FBI official Frank Montoya Jr told ProPublica: “If I’m paying for your wedding, at some point, you’re going to owe me something. This should be unthinkable for the son of the president.” It remains unclear why Kremlev helped pay for the wedding and why he was there, when he appears to have only met Trump Jr – the executive vice-president of the Trump Organization, who has a personal net worth somewhere in the ballpark of $300m – quite recently. Donald Trump famously didn’t attend the wedding. “He’d like me to go, but it’s going to be just a small, little private affair,” the US president told reporters a few days before the nuptials. “I said, you know, this is not good timing for me. I have a thing called Iran and other things.” In response to detailed questions from ProPublica, a spokesperson for Trump Jr did not deny that Kremlev had helped fund the wedding. “Umar is a personal friend of Don,” the spokesperson said, adding Kremlev was “not someone he has a business relationship with” and that the men met through a mutual friend in the hunting world. In their joint Instagram statement, Trump Jr and Bettina Trump thanked “our dear friend Umar” who “very generously hosted two incredible nights of celebrations for us AFTER our wedding”. They said they “got married privately” on 22 May “surrounded ONLY by our family”, and said the Russian businessman had simply given them a gift. “Friendship doesn’t require a political motive. Generosity doesn’t automatically come with an agenda. And sometimes a wedding gift is simply a wedding gift,” they said.

title: AI-linked stocks slide after tech bosses call for slowdown in ‘reckless’ development
summary: Donald Trump dismisses attempts to increase controls on artificial intelligence as ‘sick conspiracy’
text: AI-linked stocks tumbled on Monday after the bosses of Anthropic, OpenAI and SpaceX called for a slowdown in AI “reckless” development, citing fears the technology could soon run out of control. Shares in the semiconductor designer Nvidia – the world’s most valuable company – were down 3.3% by market closing in New York City, while Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) slid 4% and Micron Technology and Sandisk shares slumped by 5%. The tech-heavy Nasdaq index fund was down 0.5% by the end of the day. The sell-off came after the chief executive of Anthropic, Dario Amodei, appealed at the weekend for the AI industry to “slow down”. However, Donald Trump dismissed calls to increase controls on AI as a “sick conspiracy”. In a social media post on Monday, the president wrote: “The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the USA has that, in spades!” The president added that his administration had “stopped AI ‘people’ from doing bad, or potentially bad, ‘things,’ like Dario (Anthropic!)”. “There is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers, and the only one that is happy about it is China. WHOEVER WINS AI, WINS!”, he wrote. Trump offered a similar assessment when he called Nvidia chief, Jensen Huang, while the executive was on stage at an AI conference in California on Monday. “It’s a hoax,” Trump said via speaker phone to the audience. “The robots are not going to be taking over the world. That’s not going to happen.” The UN security council, meanwhile, is planning to hold a meeting on AI next week as international concern rises, Agence France-Presse reported on Monday. Shares in SoftBank, a Japanese investor that is a big backer of OpenAI, slumped 13%, while the South Korean Kospi stock index, which relies heavily on chipmakers that supply AI companies, dropped by 3%. Shares in the big global microchip supplier Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company dropped 1.2%. In Europe, shares in the Dutch tech manufacturer ASML, Europe’s biggest company by value and an important supplier for the semiconductor industry, slumped by 6%. There was, however, a rally in shares that have been threatened by the rise of AI, including the advertising group WPP, which rose by 5% in London, and the analytics business Relx, which was also up 5%. The latter had suffered a sharp fall earlier this year after Anthropic launched a suite of new data and automation tools. Amodei has said that “building too fast is reckless”, warning that a swarm of AI agents could cause hundreds of billions of dollars of damage by “taking over the entire internet” in future. His claims have been disputed by some experts, but on Monday investors began to price in a slowdown that would make it harder for the industry to pay for hundreds of billions of dollar in investments in AI infrastructure. The OpenAI CEO, Sam Altman, the Google DeepMind chief, Demis Hassabis, and SpaceX boss, Elon Musk, all posted support for Amodei’s essay on slowing AI development, titled “We Must Pace the Frontier”. Altman added that he would match Amodei’s commitment to embedding outside evaluators within his company to verify safety practices. And Jack Clark, an Anthropic co-founder, told the BBC an AI “kill switch” that could be triggered by a third party may be necessary to prevent catastrophe. Fears continue to grow over the rapid pace and lack of regulation in AI development. On Monday, a cross-party group of UK MPs and peers identified a series of human rights risks posed by AI, arguing that no country in the world had laws sufficient to contain them. Meanwhile, China’s top intelligence official warned that the use of AI by adversaries could pose a risk to the country’s political and social security. Chen Yixin wrote in a government outlet on Sunday that advanced US models such as Anthropic’s Mythos and OpenAI’s GPT-5.5-Cyber could pose serious risks to Beijing’s critical information infrastructure, and called for a comprehensive strengthening of AI security. Despite such concern about the risks around AI, Jim Reid, of Deutsche Bank, said intense competition in the sector meant it was unlikely AI companies would stop investing so heavily in their technology. “The competitive race between companies and countries remains intense, and it’s difficult to imagine firms voluntarily stepping back while rivals continue to push ahead.” he said. “It is hard to see China standing still. “If leading executives are openly discussing the risks of increasingly powerful systems, it could be them trying to get across how transformative they believe the technology may become and help advertise the power of their product. “Rather than signalling less spending, it could simply be that a greater share of AI investment is directed towards safety, monitoring and governance alongside the continued build-out of compute infrastructure.” Amodei’s warning came before reports emerged that Anthropic is on track to be profitable this quarter. The company told investors that its adjusted operating income would be positive for a second quarter in a row, according to the Financial Times, in a big milestone as it prepares to list on the US stock market this year. OpenAI has also suggested it will also join the stock market, although Altman said over the weekend that the company would not go public in 2026 owing to safety concerns with the technology.

title: US ends limits on coal and gas plant emissions, removing key tool to fight climate crisis
summary: Trump’s EPA strips itself of regulating ability, gutting Clean Air Act in what experts say is a gift to planet polluters
text: On the heels of the hottest summer ever recorded in the US, the Trump administration has said it will erase any limits on emissions from coal and gas plants that are dangerously heating up our planet. The US Environmental Protection Agency said it will strip itself of its ability to regulate greenhouse gas emissions coming from power plants under the Clean Air Act, removing a key tool to address the climate crisis. By erasing any limits on such emissions from coal and gas plants, the Trump administration has severely limited any future administration’s ability to curb this pollution. The EPA calculated the move will result in 123m metric tons of additional carbon emissions in the next decade, and save power plant operators $370m in direct compliance costs. Lee Zeldin, the agency administrator, said the Trump administration was protecting American energy from a “war on coal”. “Americans will see a decrease in electricity prices, but this is just the beginning,” said Zeldin, who unveiled the reversal of the 2024 carbon pollution standards at a G20 meeting in Houston on Monday. “We are working to go even further so that American energy can be fully unleashed. Realizing the full potential of American energy means more jobs, lower prices and a more prosperous America.” The EPA said greenhouse gas emissions from power plants have “no material impact on global climate change”. This is despite the fact that US electricity generation is responsible for a quarter of the country’s greenhouse gas emissions. If the sector were itself a country, it would be the fifth largest carbon polluter in the world, after China, the US, India and Russia. Trump, who has called the climate crisis “bullshit” and “a hoax”, earlier this year overturned the foundational 2009 EPA endangerment finding – spurred by a supreme court ruling – that greenhouse gases pose a significant threat to public health and the environment. This has opened the way for the administration to scrub out limits on the planet-heating gases that are causing our world to rapidly overheat and worsen deadly heatwaves, drought, wildfires and floods. In February, the EPA eliminated pollution standards for cars and trucks as part of a series of actions Zeldin described as “driving a dagger straight into the heart of the climate change religion”. Environmental groups immediately vowed to challenge the latest rollback in court. “This is full-throated climate denial while the climate crisis happens in real time, and a shocking betrayal of the American public,” said Holly Bender, chief program officer at the Sierra Club. “The Sierra Club will fight back against this reckless and dangerous proposal with everything we have in the courts, in Congress, and in communities across the country.” When it issued the latest carbon pollution standards for power plants under Joe Biden’s administration in 2024, the EPA found the rules would slash 1bn tonnes of greenhouse gases by 2047 and deliver $370bn in net benefits. The rules also would have prevented 1,200 premature deaths and 360,000 asthma attacks in 2035 alone, due to air quality improvements. Under Trump, however, the EPA has eliminated the dollar benefit of saving lives through reduced air pollution in its calculations. “Every American deserves to breathe clean air, but time and again this administration gives a green light to more pollution at the expense of our health,” said Gina McCarthy, the EPA administrator under Barack Obama. “Everyone will be affected by their actions, but the most vulnerable among us, our kids and grandkids, will suffer the most. Today’s decision lets the nation’s biggest industrial polluters off the hook by reversing findings the agency itself established.” Trump has long championed the use of fossil fuels, such as coal and gas, pushing a “drill, baby, drill” approach that has opened up more land for extraction while demolishing clean air and water regulations the industry said it found too onerous. As well as handing out hundreds of millions of dollars in taxpayer funds to prop up coal plants, which have struggled economically in recent years, the Trump administration has sought to directly strangle clean energy projects such as solar and offshore wind. The latest EPA intervention will probably be significant, if it survives legal challenge, as it will stymie any future attempt to restrict carbon pollution from power plants. It is the latest episode in a decade-long saga over how, or if, the US tames its power emissions. In 2016 the supreme court knocked down Obama’s clean power plan. A more narrow version, with the parameters set again by the court, was then enacted under Biden.

title: New special envoy for Britons detained overseas warns of limits of role
summary: Alistair Burt speaks candidly about difficulties of tackling complex cases as families express concern over mandate
text: The special envoy for British citizens detained overseas has spoken about the difficulties he faces in his new role, as families express concern over the position’s mandate in complex consular cases. In his first public engagement, Alistair Burt, the former Conservative Middle East minister, spoke candidly about the difficulties and limitations of the new appointment, made following years of mounting criticism of how the Foreign Office handled the cases of British citizens detained overseas. “I don’t make policy. I’m not a minister. I don’t have that authority. It will ultimately be the foreign secretary and the prime minister who will need to make the changes in policy or changes in approach if required,” Burt told an audience in Westminster, following his appointment on Monday evening. “The best thing I can do is not disguise from you the difficulties of the role,” added the former minister. Burt, who plans to meet the new foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, later this week, was tipped for the post more than a year ago. Burt was candid about the complexities of detention cases and of his role to “kick the tyres” of the policies involved. Burt, whose new role is appointed by the Foreign Office but not paid for by it, said he has already started to meet families of those with complex cases, and said there was “much to be gained” from stronger international condemnation. There is a strong view that the US special presidential envoy for hostages has secured more success and clout inside the diplomatic system, and used more innovative techniques to negotiate the release of Americans. Burt said he plans to meet his US and Canadian counterparts in the coming weeks, and is open to discussing broader cooperation with European leaders. The Foreign Office describes the purpose of the role as being to advance the government’s commitment to British nationals in the “most difficult and complex detention cases overseas” at the direction of the foreign secretary. The role is intended to advocate within and represent government, and engage with families. Speaking alongside Burt at Monday’s parliamentary event was Nazanin Zaghari-Ratcliffe, a dual national who was arbitrarily detained in Iran for six years before being released in 2022. A documentary was played showing the ordeal her family went through to secure her release, as well as that of Anoosheh Ashoori, for whom a historic £400m debt was paid to Iran. “I recognised the payment of the debt and I let my foreign secretary know repeatedly,” said Burt of Nazanin’s case, adding, “I got that one right.” That wasn’t the case, he admitted, for Matthew Hedges, a British academic sitting beside him, who was accused of spying for the UK government in the United Arab Emirates and was arrested and tortured. “Other cases I didn’t handle as well as I would have liked,” said Burt. “I’m very grateful that Matthew has seen me since to talk about his experiences.” While welcoming the appointment, Zaghari-Ratcliffe also expressed a fear of quiet diplomacy turning into an “excuse” for government inaction. Lawyers and campaigners at the event also expressed concerns over the limited mandate of the special envoy role, and called for the position to be independent of the Foreign Office and for the UK to be bolder in its diplomacy. In attendance was also Laila Soueif, who went on hunger strike in pursuit of freedom for her son, British-Egyptian activist Alaa Abd el-Fattah, who was released from an Egyptian jail in 2025 after serving six years, as well as Naomi Connell, a friend of Lindsay Foreman and Craig Foreman, who has campaigned for the couple’s release from Iran’s Evin prison. Also present was Heather Cornelius, whose husband, Ryan, has been arbitrarily imprisoned in Dubai for more than 18 years. The family discussed their case with Burt when he was a minister in 2018, said Heather, expressing scepticism over whether the envoy role, which runs for 18 months, will do anything other than liaise with and reassure families. “He’s not going in there saying: ‘Yes, I know I can make a difference, I know I can help these people.’ He’s not saying that. He’s just saying: ‘Well, it’s very difficult,’” said Cornelius, who delivered a letter to Andy Burnham earlier on Monday, asking for the prime minister to help secure her husband’s release. “They’re relying on other countries being involved, and of course that’s good, but Britain can do something, and they can do more,” she added.

title: US ‘super-emitters’ of planet heating methane identified by satellite analysis
summary: Energy Transfer, whose CEO is a major Trump donor, named as biggest single methane producer in new rankings
text: Down a short gravel track in a largely nondescript corner of Louisiana sits a gas processing facility, operated by a company whose chief executive is a major donor to Donald Trump. It may be the largest emitter of methane in the US. The Energy Transfer site, located near the city of Shreveport, is named as the biggest single “super-emitter” in new rankings of US oil and gas operations for the largest releases of methane, a powerful greenhouse gas that is rapidly overheating our planet, according to a new UCLA study, which is based on satellite data. From January 2025 to June this year, the Shreveport facility spewed out methane at an average emission rate of 1.56 tonnes an hour, which is 15 times larger than the threshold defined in a Biden-era program by the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) as a super-emitter event, according to the study. The Trump administration has put implementation of that program on hold but climate experts and advocates say reducing methane emissions is vital to limit the climate crisis. The new rankings combine satellite data and public records to indicate a “potentially responsible operator” for each of the largest methane plumes, researchers at UCLA’s Emmett Institute say. Such a task can be complicated by a lack of official records naming sites with large methane emissions as well as ascertaining ownership of pollution coming from tight clusters of differing oil and gas leases. Dallas-based Energy Transfer oversees a huge network of pipelines and processing properties in the US and is linked to four of the 15 sites highlighted in the new rankings, with the company responsible for 75 methane plumes in total over the study period – three times as much as the next operator. Other major corporate methane producers include Enterprise Products, Targa Resources and Enlink. Kelcy Warren, Energy Transfer’s billionaire chief executive, donated millions of dollars to Trump’s last election campaign and has previously described as an “insanity” when asked what he thought about a newspaper editorial that said net-zero carbon emissions policies would ultimately mean oil was no longer needed. Energy Transfer did not respond to questions on what it is doing to stem methane from its facilities or whether the Shreveport site has been intentionally venting the gas or has experienced some sort of leak. The company has previously described efforts it was taking to reduce methane emissions in company reports including optical gas imaging inspections across hundreds of its facilites. “Many of these sites are repeat offenders linked to not one but multiple mega plumes,” said Cara Horowitz, executive director of the UCLA Emmett Institute and author of the new report. “As America’s oil and gas industry ramps up production, it can no longer ignore what can only be described as super-sized pollution events seen from space.” Horowitz said that the satellite record is “spotty but important”, as it shows emissions “that used to be frankly invisible and historically undercounted. Now they are plainly visible, they deserve public and regulatory attention. These numbers are unacceptably large, these emissions seem very wasteful and very inefficient.” The new report draws upon data from the Tanager-1 satellite, compiled by the non-profit Carbon Mapper, of spotted plumes in the Permian, Appalachian and Haynesville-Bossier basins, resource-rich hotspots which span several states and account for about two-thirds of US gas production. A total of 1,097 methane plumes were detected from oil and gas sources in these regions between January 2025 and June this year. The UCLA team was able to assign an operator responsible for a plume in around a third of these cases, using publicly available data. Horowitz said, though, it is “a real cause for concern when it comes to transparency” that so few operators can be identified as responsible for this pollution. While satellites have helped reveal previously unknown methane emissions, such pollution is still vastly underreported, with researchers recently estimating actual US oil and gas methane emissions are about 64% higher than official EPA figures. Activists have long argued that drilling sites and pipelines often experience regular, sometimes dangerous, leaks or purposely vent methane into the air, to release the pressure of gas build-up in equipment, with little reporting or oversight. Even satellites are unable to capture the full extent of these emissions when they are obscured on cloudy days. It is not illegal to release methane in these ways and operators face no penalizing regulations for doing so. “I’ve been in the Permian basin and seen methane blowdowns happening everywhere for days but nothing got picked up on the satellites because it was overcast,” said Sharon Wilson, director of Oilfield Witness, an advocacy and monitoring group. Wilson, a former fossil fuel industry worker, has spent the last 14 years acting as a “methane hunter” by filming oil and gas sites with a special camera that makes methane emissions visible. In 2024 she documented a Energy Transfer facility in Pecos county, Texas, that is fifth on UCLA’s top 10 producers list. The video from her visit shows gusts of methane, resembling smoke, spiraling from the site. “Just a fraction of what is happening is being reported,” Wilson said. “I don’t see any improvement from the industry, what I see is just continued expansion. I have been to a lot of Energy Transfer sites and they are by far, in my opinion, the worst midstream operator I’ve seen. They always have massive methane plumes.” The UCLA researchers chose to focus on the three large oil and gas basins, rather than every single emitter in the US, as they are the fulcrum of a booming liquified natural gas (or LNG) export industry. The US has leapfrogged other countries in recent years to become the world’s leading exporter of LNG, constructing a slew of vast terminals where gas is chilled and then shipped overseas. Trump has sought to fast-track the growth of this industry. Proponents of LNG exports contend burning gas is cleaner than coal, although the repeated expulsion of methane during the export process can in fact make it even worse than coal for the climate, research has found. “While US industry players often talk about reductions in methane intensity, this analysis reveals a concerning number of super-emitter events from the regions that ship LNG overseas,” said Mary Nichols, former chair of the California air resources board and now distinguished counsel for the UCLA Emmett Institute. Methane is a potent greenhouse gas, trapping around 80 times more heat than carbon dioxide over a 20-year period, and is responsible for nearly a third of the global heating that has occurred since the industrial revolution. It is released via oil and gas drilling and transportation, as well as from landfills and agriculture. There has been a “scary” surge in global methane emissions since 2007, according to scientists, although the gas doesn’t linger in the atmosphere as long as CO2. This means that reducing methane emissions from leaky pipes, venting and burning gas as a fuel can act as a rapid “emergency brake” amid a climate crisis that is dangerously barreling past safe limits. Some progress can be achieved by identifying unseen methane leaks and fixing them, as has occurred recently in Turkmenistan. The country was previously releasing more methane than the entire emissions of the UK, a situation described as “mind-boggling” and “infuriating”, but has since started to plug some of the leaks emanating from its aging oil and gas infrastructure. Such remedial work has been happening in some instances in the US, too, with the industry claiming a recent “profound shift” in pinpointing and dealing with leaks. In the UCLA study, three of the top 10 methane producers, including the first and second placed sites, had no methane plumes detected in their most recent satellite observations, suggesting some improvements may have taken place. “The goal of shining a light on these emissions is to prompt action, which may already be under way at a few of these sites,” said Horowitz. But critics argue that leaks of methane will continue for as long as the oil and gas industry faces little financial or regulatory pressure to change its ways, or until it is eclipsed entirely by clean energy. Trump has set about eliminating enforcement, reporting requirements and fees aimed at driving down US methane emissions, with his EPA pushing ahead with the rollback of Joe Biden-era rules aimed at slashing this pollution. Lee Zeldin, the EPA administrator, has previously said these requirements “weaponized environmental regulations to regulate the oil and gas industry out of existence”. Wilson said the only way to force down methane emissions is to stop issuing new permits to the fossil fuel industry. “We have all these emissions blasting into the air and no one even knows about it,” she said. “We’ve gone so far past trying to rein in the industry. We don’t need oil and gas to energize our world anymore, it’s silly. Ironically Donald Trump has helped everyone realize the need to move on from oil and gas because of this (Iran) war. Gas isn’t energy security, it’s a vulnerability.” All of the companies named in UCLA’s top 10 sites and among those responsible for the largest number of plumes were contacted for comment. None of them provided a response for the story apart from Boardwalk Pipeline Partners, which said it has reduced emissions in recent years from the 10th placed site, a gas storage facility which is also near Shreveport, Louisiana. “Natural gas storage facilities require periodic inspections, testing, and maintenance activities to help ensure safe and reliable operations,” said a company spokeswoman. “During some of these activities, natural gas may be released to safely reduce pressure before work can be performed. This is part of the safe operation and maintenance of the facility and is not necessarily indicative of equipment leaks. “The Bistineau Storage Station operates in full compliance with all state and federal regulations. While there is more work to do, our emission reduction journey reflects Boardwalk’s ongoing commitment to responsible operations and continuous improvement.” • This article was amended on 18 September 2026. In a previous version, a chart listed Delaware Basin Midstream as the operator of the facility in Loving, New Mexico. The chart has been amended to state the potential operator is undetermined. Additional information was also added to make clear Western Midstream is the current owner of the facility in Pecos, Texas, but was not the owner at the time of the analysis.
