title: Ministers seek law change to make £72m donations to Reform illegal
summary: Plans to strengthen legislation already going through parliament might mean donors having to meet stricter UK residence requirements
text: Andy Burnham’s government could thwart Reform’s unprecedented £72m donations with retrospective restrictions on political donors that will include tough new residency requirements, ministers have announced. In a move that is likely to set off furious complaints from Nigel Farage’s party, the government will table amendments to legislation going through the House of Lords within weeks that puts the legality of Reform’s latest donations in doubt. Senior Labour and union figures had urged ministers to look again at party funding rules after Reform announced at the weekend that two cryptocurrency billionaires, Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne, who have both previously been based overseas, were each donating £36m to the party. Government sources, however, said the plans to strengthen the representation of the people bill had been under way for weeks, after MPs pushed for further action on domestic donations in the House of Commons. Under the proposals, which are expected to be tabled at the Lords committee stage of the legislation, individual donors will have to prove their ongoing physical presence in the UK, in line with the residence requirements applied to other areas of government policy, such as tax status. The extraordinary measure will be seen as a sign of the stakes attached to the donations, which would give Reform a vast advantage in organising supporters on the ground before the next election. However, Farage acknowledged on Monday that Reform could fall foul of government moves to clamp down on foreign donors, although the party has said the £72m donations are in line with both current rules and those already voted on by MPs in the bill. The legislation currently restricts donations from expats to £100,000, which would also apply for the first 12 months after they return to the UK – backdated to 25 March this year. Ministers have already brought in a minimum residency requirement of the remainder of the calendar year in which they return, plus a further full year, meaning Reform may not be able to accept the £72m donations until January 2028. Delo has been based in Hong Kong but said in April he would return to the UK to avoid restrictions, while Harborne was based in Thailand but is believed to have registered to vote in Hampshire in June. “Both these donations are 100% compliant with the law today, of that there is no question whatsoever,” Farage told the BBC. When asked if the two billionaires were UK residents as of 25 March, he replied: “All I’m going to say is, with the law of the land as it stands, they are both compliant.” Sharon Taylor, a Labour minister in the Lords, told peers that as well as donors having to demonstrate a “genuine and ongoing connection to the UK”, the government was also looking at further restrictions. “We are considering how we will strengthen the residency requirements, including ensuring the length of time spent in the UK aligns with broader government policy,” Lady Taylor added. However, MPs and peers who have been pushing for a full domestic donations cap are unlikely to be satisfied by the new amendments. Government sources have said they do not want to delay the bill’s progress further by considering such a cap, but are open-minded on further legislation. MPs have voiced anger in internal WhatsApp groups that the chance has been missed to cap domestic donations in this bill while it was in the Commons. Angela Rayner, speaking at the TUC, criticised Reform for suggesting its donations from cryptocurrency billionaires were equivalent to the contributions from trade union members to Labour. “How dare they try to compare money from a couple of crypto billionaires to union members’ subs? The most highly regulated political funding we can have,” the communities secretary said. “It couldn’t be more different from a couple of offshore billionaires trying to buy our democracy … We will never undermine the rights of working people to organise collectively and democratically.” Trade unions are set to issue a statement on Tuesday on political donations condemning attempts by Farage to compare wealthy individual donors with individual members who donate to Labour through their union, and urging the government to go further on political donations. The head of Britain’s union movement, Paul Nowak, said the government must act to “stop the super-rich corrupting our politics”. But union sources had said there were “significant differences” between general secretaries on how to proceed. Unite’s general secretary, Sharon Graham, on Sunday broke ranks and backed a limit on individual domestic donations. But others, including GMB chief Gary Smith, fear it would lead a future rightwing government to curb union donations. Government sources said that calls from opposition parties for any changes to domestic donations to apply to the unions too were “not under active consideration”. However, the government is understood to be looking at spending limits for parties, which are currently restricted to the year before a general election, with tighter limits in the weeks running up to polling day. In a letter to the Electoral Commission in August, Rayner and Louise Haigh, the first secretary of state, wrote: “We believe spending limits on parties and candidates are too high, and ought to be reduced.” The government has also set up a cross-government “task and finish” team to consider threats to UK democracy, including political finance, illegitimate influence, and broader threats to political equality. Philip Rycroft, who produced an independent report on tightening electoral law around overseas donations, said the Reform donations reopened broader questions about donations and spending caps. “The time has come when this does need a hard look. It would have been better if the government had started out before we had these huge donations coming down the track,” he said. “But we have to ask the question, is this healthy for our democratic process to have more money coming from fewer people in bigger lumps?” MPs who have campaigned for a donations cap are working with peers on a number of amendments to the bill which would tighten it up without having to wait for another act of parliament. They include one to enable ministers to set a cap on all donations at a later date, and another to prevent spending limits being raised without Electoral Commission approval. Teresa O’Neill, a shadow local government minister in the Lords, said some of the measures in the bill were deeply troubling. “Even just the perception of partisan, targeted legislation risks breaking down longstanding political conventions and, crucially, trust in the system,” she said. Reform denounced the government’s existing plans, with Zia Yusuf, the party’s home affairs spokesperson, describing them on X as “an unprecedented step from a leftwing government to plunge Britain into dictatorship and communism”.

title: Firefighters make progress to contain northern California’s Lucas fire
summary: Cal Fire official says Sunday was ‘big turning point’ to reduce blaze in Lake county, now 30% contained
text: Firefighters made progress toward containing northern California’s Lucas fire, state officials said on Sunday. Fire officials are still investigating the cause of the fire, which has burned more than 4,120 acres across Lake and Mendocino counties. The fire was 30% contained by Monday morning, according to the California department of forestry and fire protection, or Cal Fire. “We do feel like today was a big turning point for us,” Ryan Isham, Cal Fire’s operations section chief, told a crowd of 100 community members in the northern California town of Upper Lake on Sunday. “We are still going to be on the fire for several days to come, continuing to reduce the risk,” he added. Nearly 900 people fled the area after officials imposed evacuation orders. No one has died or gone missing, though a man was arrested for trying to jump a roadblock, said Lake county’s sheriff, Luke Bingham. The fire started on Thursday. It will continue to produce significant smoke in the area as firefighters work to hold it back on Elk Mountain, which caught flame more recently, Isham said. Cal Fire, working jointly with the Lake county sheriff’s office, had deployed 163 engines, along with 72 crews, dozens of water tenders and eight helicopters to halt the blaze. Mendocino national forest ordered an emergency closure of parts of its grounds and campsites last week due to the fire.

title: Mahmoud Khalil sues Columbia University over years of alleged anti-Palestinian discrimination
summary: Lawsuit accuses university of ‘deliberate indifference’ and failure to respond to ‘persistent and coordinated harassment’
text: Mahmoud Khalil announced on Monday that he’s sued Columbia University, accusing the New York City school he attended of a years-long history of anti-Palestinian discrimination, indifference to harassment, and retaliation. Khalil, a US green card holder of Palestinian descent, was a graduate student at Columbia’s School of International and Public Affairs (SIPA) when he was arrested at his university apartment by federal immigration agents in March 2025, the first of a number of foreign nationals that the Trump administration has detained and sought to deport over their pro-Palestinian advocacy. In a 60-page complaint filed in the southern district of New York, Khalil and members of the SIPA’s Palestine Working Group have now accused the university, its board, and the dean of the school, Keren Yarhi-Milo, of “deliberate indifference” and failure to respond to “severe, persistent and coordinated harassment” directed towards him and other students who had been outspoken about Palestinian rights. Khalil, who missed the birth of his first son while in detention, was released in June 2025 but is continuing to fight the administration’s efforts to deport him – a protracted legal battle that is expected to ultimately be decided by the US supreme court. Still, Khalil has continued to speak out, both about Palestinian rights and about free speech in the US. In July, he sued the Trump administration and several pro-Israel groups, accusing them of conspiring to target him and others as punishment for their advocacy. Separately, he has filed a $20m false imprisonment and malicious prosecution case against the administration and sued them for records of collusion with anti-Palestinian doxxing groups including Canary Mission. In an earlier lawsuit filed in March 2025 he also sought to stop Columbia from releasing student disciplinary records to the House committee on education and the workforce, which has led the charge against universities in the aftermath of Israel’s war in Gaza and widespread campus protests in support of Palestinian rights. “Columbia laid the groundwork for my targeting by the Trump administration through its deliberate indifference and discrimination aimed at intimidating Palestinian students,” Khalil wrote in a statement announcing the lawsuit. “For over two years, we pleaded with Columbia. Columbia did not care. Our safety and our wellbeing did not serve the ideological project its Board of Trustees was protecting, so they traded us away.” Khalil also warned of more lawsuits to come. “Next, I will turn to the hateful individuals at Columbia who were also responsible for what we endured,” he wrote. A spokesperson for the university declined to comment on pending litigation but said that “Columbia is committed to protecting our community from discrimination and harassment, and responding promptly and appropriately when concerns arise.” Columbia students were the first to erect pro-Palestinian encampments on campus in the spring of 2024, inspiring dozens more across the country. The university, once home to cutting-edge scholarship about Palestine, also became the first to be targeted by the Trump administration as part of its ongoing effort to exploit antisemitism accusations to bend universities to its agenda. As tensions flared on campus after the 7 October 2023 Hamas attacks and Israel’s subsequent war in Gaza, students repeatedly sought the administration’s support to protect them from doxing campaigns, the complaint alleges. Many had their photos, names, and personal information posted online, as well as on mobile billboard trucks. Mohammed Ibrahim Zubairi, a Columbia graduate and former president of the Palestine Working Group who is also a named plaintiff in the lawsuit, told the Guardian that the litigation is an effort to “force a reckoning within these institutions, so that they may recognize they have ended up on the wrong side of history”. “For me, this case is about the environment in which the hostility that I and other pro-Palestinian students experienced was able to persist,” echoed Bhavana Bellamkonda, another plaintiff. “What we are asking for is not special treatment,” she told the Guardian. “We are asking for the same protections that Columbia students are entitled to under state and federal law, and that Columbia itself has represented that it provides to its tuition-paying students.” Khalil was well known to university administrators because of his efforts to mediate between student protesters and school officials. In the months leading up to his detention, he reported threats, harassment, and doxing, including attacks targeting his immigration status. On 7 March 2025, a day before his arrest, he emailed Columbia’s then interim president, Katrina Armstrong, and other administrators, urging them to take immediate action to protect international students. “What Mahmoud Khalil endured for speaking up against the genocide in Gaza was unconscionable. And much of that was at the hands of or enabled by Columbia,” Brittany Finley, one of his attorneys, wrote in a press release. “Columbia knew what was happening on its campus, and it chose indifference over action.” According to the complaint, rather than address Khalil’s and other students’ concerns, Columbia subjected students to disciplinary proceedings and restrictions, including suspending SIPA’s Palestine Working Group in May 2025 – a suspension that remains in effect. Other pro-Palestinians students have also sued Columbia over its alleged failure to protect them from a hostile campus environment. “This didn’t begin with me, nor does it end with me,” Khalil said. “With this lawsuit, we hope to ensure that future generations of Columbia students never have to face this fight.”

title: Member of British armed forces killed in Ukraine crash, says MoD
summary: Ministry of Defence says person, who has yet to be identified, died in road traffic incident not believed to be result of hostile action
text: A member of the UK armed forces has been killed in a crash in Ukraine, the Ministry of Defence said. The person, who has not yet been named, died in a road traffic incident on Saturday. It is understood the incident was not a result of hostile action. The person’s family has been informed and has asked for some time before more details are made public. “Our thoughts and our sympathies are with the individual’s loved ones at this difficult time,” an MoD spokesperson said. The defence secretary, Wes Streeting, said on X: “This is very sad news for the family and for those grieving with them in our Armed Forces. “My deepest condolences go to them all.” The shadow defence secretary, James Cartlidge, said on X he was “saddened to hear this news” and offered his condolences to the person’s family and friends. A small number of British personnel in Ukraine provide security to diplomats and support the country’s armed forces. British paratrooper George Hooley, 28, was killed in Ukraine in December while watching Ukrainian forces testing defensive capability. The MoD described his death as a “tragic accident” that occurred “away from the frontlines”. Russia’s full scale invasion of Ukraine is in its fifth year and the conflict continues with fresh strikes on Ukraine, including an attack on a gasworks and a drone attack on a train station on Sunday. The attack hit a train at Yahodyn station, on the Polish border, shortly after a train carrying Boris Johnson had left ahead of schedule. Ukraine’s railway operator said the attack may have been aimed at the train carrying the former prime minister, among other dignitaries. Johnson had been returning from a major conference in Kyiv along with former Swedish prime minister Carl Bildt and a number of European security advisers. According to a translation from Ukrainian, rail operator Ukrzaliznytsia said in a post on Telegram it was “quite possible” the drone had been aimed at Johnson’s train.

title: China dismisses AI ‘fearmongering’ as spy chief warns of threat to Communist party rule
summary: Beijing hits back after Anthropic CEO calls for US to impede China’s progress in AI
text: China has dismissed what it said were “fearmongering” calls for the US to block Beijing’s AI industry, even as the top Chinese spy chief warned the evolving technology could threaten Communist party rule. The US tech entrepreneur and Anthropic chief executive, Dario Amodei, wrote an essay published over the weekend that called for a global slowdown in AI capabilities, but also said Washington should actively impede Beijing’s advancement in order to keep a technological edge. Warning that AI could give the Chinese Communist party a chance “to militarily dominate democracies”, Amodei said he believed “a Chinese lead in AI would pose grave danger for the US and the world”. China’s ministry of foreign affairs responded to a question about Amodei’s essay by saying all parties should work together on AI. “Fearmongering, confrontation and vicious competition will only disrupt the process of global AI governance, which serves no one’s interest,” spokesperson Guo Jiakun said at a press conference on Monday. In his essay, Amodei predicted that a swarm of AI “agents” could take over the internet in six to 12 months unless researchers agree to slow down. He said that while “global pacing will require cooperation with China”, steps were needed to “keep democracies’ AI lead over autocracies as large as possible”. Other tech bosses, including the OpenAI CEO, Sam Altman, the Google DeepMind chair, Demis Hassabis, and the SpaceX chief, Elon Musk, have posted general support for Amodei’s lengthy essay, although not specifically on China. While Beijing rejects that its dominance in AI would be dangerous, it does share fears over the pace of development. The president of China, Xi Jinping, warned at a conference in July that AI should “always remain under human control”. But the extent of the Chinese government’s concerns was shown in an article published on Sunday in the state-run magazine China Cyberspace, in which the country’s top intelligence official wrote that the technology could threaten the government’s hold on power. The head of China’s ministry of state security, Chen Yixin, wrote that “hostile forces and individuals with ulterior motives” were abusing AI to wage a “propaganda war and a cognitive war against us, directly threatening our political security, institutional security, and ideological security”. Chen referred specifically to US models such as Anthropic’s Claude and OpenAI’s GPT-5.5-Cyber models, which he said have been weaponised and were examples of new threats to cybersecurity. While the public, governments and tech bosses are now warning of the dangers of AI, Donald Trump has dismissed such concerns outright. On Monday, the US president said the only “guardrails” that AI needed were a “STRONG AND SMART” president. Trump has been particularly sensitive to stock market changes, and AI stocks have slipped after concerns over the pace of growth were raised. The US and Chinese leaders are expected to discuss AI governance, among other topics, at a meeting planned on 24 September. In an editorial published Sunday, China’s state-run Global Times newspaper dismissed Amodei’s essay as a veiled call to “contain” China. “The article is packed with containment provisions targeting China and is, in essence, a ‘cold war playbook’ for the AI sector,” it said. The Associated Press contributed to this report

title: Alligator Alcatraz held detainees in cages the size of phone booths, DHS watchdog says
summary: Office of inspector general’s report says practice at Florida immigration jail is not aligned with ‘humane treatment’
text: Before the facility was shuttered, detainees at Florida’s “Alligator Alcatraz” federal immigration jail were frequently locked in outside metal cages no bigger than a phone booth, according to a damning government watchdog report that said the practice “does not align with standards for humane treatment”. The findings from the office of the inspector general of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) were published on its website – and offer rare criticism of the Trump administration by one of its own agencies. The report also provides the first official confirmation that guards repeatedly used the highly restrictive cages on detainees in direct contravention of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) rules. In December, the Guardian was the first to report an Amnesty International dossier detailing multiple alleged human rights abuses at the controversial camp in the remote Florida Everglades, including how people were regularly shackled outside in metal cages for hours as well as exposed to brutal heat, sunshine and swarms of mosquitoes. At the time, a spokesperson for Ron DeSantis, the Republican Florida governor whose administration ran Alligator Alcatraz on behalf of the federal government, dismissed the claims now confirmed by the DHS report as “fabrications” – and the Amnesty report as “a politically motivated attack”. On Monday, his office declined to answer why it falsely denied using the cages and instead attempted to portray the detainees – with no evidence – as “violent criminal aliens who have proven they cannot remain peaceful while awaiting deportation”. In a statement, Alex Lanfranconi, DeSantis’s communications manager, contended that “the leftwing media wants to focus on a confinement area” which “adheres to all federal standards for criminal confinement”. His statement added: “We’d make it even smaller if we could.” Amy Fischer, Amnesty International USA’s director for refugee and migrant rights, said in a statement: “The findings confirm what we documented months ago: the horrific treatment of people detained at Alligator Alcatraz was real, not a hoax, as Trump administration officials were on the record saying. “This report should serve as a reminder that the public must never simply take the government’s word when officials deny that human rights violations are occurring.” The notorious immigration jail closed in June after a year of operation during which DeSantis boasted of detaining and deporting more than 21,000 immigrants. Officials cited the risk of holding detainees in tents during hurricane season for the closure. Critics, however, said the $1.2m of taxpayers’ money that DeSantis was spending on the camp daily was fast becoming a political millstone – while separate lawsuits swirled over the jail’s impact on the environmentally fragile Florida wetlands, and the harsh mental and physical treatment of detainees that several Democratic lawmakers decried as akin to “torture”. The inspector general’s office report exposed numerous failings found during an unannounced January 2026 visit by DHS inspectors to Alligator Alcatraz, which they refer to as the Florida Soft-Sided Facility (FSSF). Many of the shortcomings, they said, posed “significant risks to detainee health and safety”. “FSSF did not provide detainees with sufficient living space, creating cramped conditions for detainees who spent most of their time in their housing units, which may harm detainees’ physical and mental health,” the report said. Additionally, it studied records that revealed 79 instances between July 2025 and January 2026 in which guards placed detainees in the metal cages for up to two hours at a time. Each cage, the report noted, offered only about 18 sq ft of floor space, less than half the minimum 37 sq ft required for single-person spaces by ICE’s own published national detention standards. The inspector general’s discovery of cases in January means detainees were still being confined in the cramped cages more than a month after Amnesty International exposed the practice and DeSantis’s office denied it was taking place. The report acknowledged concerns raised by the Democratic US senators Jon Ossoff of Georgia and Dick Durbin of Illinois in March over the use of the cages known to detainees as “The Box”. But the report said facility staff insisted they were used as “calming areas” for detainees “to deescalate and have time alone”. “Staff further maintained that detainees asked to spend time” in them, the report said. However, inspectors found at least one time in which a cage was documented to have been used as a disciplinary tool: for a detainee who “failed to comply with a lawful command”. Inspectors noted that there were locking mechanisms on the cages. “Use of these small metal enclosures for any reason is unprecedented among ICE facilities inspected by OIG,” the report said. “Confining individuals in small metal enclosures for any reason presents significant risks to detainee health and wellbeing.” Krish O’Mara Vignarajah, president and chief executive of the immigration advocacy group Global Refuge, said in a statement: “There is no euphemism that can sanitize caging human beings. Calling a metal box a ‘calming area’ is an affront to the English language and to human dignity alike. “The stark reality is that human beings, many of whom came to this country seeking protection, were crammed into spaces unfit to accommodate them, denied adequate medical care, food and basic hygiene. That is not immigration enforcement. It is cruelty.” Other failures noted by the DHS inspectors during their tour of detention spaces, and kitchen and bathroom areas, included overcrowding, a lack of sufficient recreation time for detainees, and inoperable telephones preventing detainees from contacting their attorneys or families, and poor food hygiene standards leading to the risk of contamination and illness. Multiple detainees told the inspectors in January they had limited or no access to clean drinking water. The Guardian reported in June that the practice appeared to be continuing, with detainees complaining that guards were withholding clean water and food as punishment – or until they signed documents in English that they did not understand. The Florida department of emergency management, which oversaw the operation of the facility using private guards, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

title: Will the £72m of donations to Reform UK be allowed?
summary: Key questions surrounding the huge sums donated by crypto billionaires Christopher Harborne and Ben Delo
text: Reform UK announced over the weekend the two biggest single political donations in British history: £36m from the Thailand-based crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne and a further £36m from another crypto billionaire, Ben Delo. However, by Monday experts were questioning whether the donations would be legal, especially under the elections bill that the government is bringing through parliament and which will apply retrospectively. Are the donations allowable? Here are the key questions which must be answered. Are Delo and Harborne registered as UK-based voters? Under current law, anyone can donate to a political party as long as they are a British citizen who is registered to vote in the UK. However, under the Representation of the People Act donors who are registered as overseas voters will be subject to a cap of £100,000 a year. The £100,000 cap will also apply for at least a full calendar year – from January to December – after they return to the UK. So someone returning to the country in the summer would have to wait for about 18 months before they can donate more than £100,000. Crucially for Harborne and Delo, this rule will apply retrospectively from 25 March. So the question for both will be, were they registered as UK-based voters before that date? If not they will not be allowed to donate more than £100,000 each in a single 12-month period, making these donations impermissible. Sources have told the Guardian that Delo has been registered as a UK-based voter for years, but that is less clear where Harborne is concerned. A report by Channel 4 News last month said its reporters had seen records suggesting he had only registered as a domestic voter in June, in which case he would be subject to the cap until January 2028, and his donation would not be legal. Reform has refused to say when exactly both men registered as resident in the UK. Should Delo and Harborne be classified as domestic voters? Even if both men are registered as UK-based voters, this status can be challenged. To get on to the electoral roll as a domestic voter, a person only has to write to the local authority and sign a declaration saying the address at which they are registering is their “permanent home address”. Electoral administrators routinely check the person’s date of birth and their national insurance number, but do not do so for their connections to the address at which they are registering. However, if another local voter believes they might be lying about where they live, they can challenge the registration. Bob Posner, a former head of the Electoral Commission, said: “Just because someone is on the electoral register, does not mean they are rightfully so.” If a case were to come to court, there are no hard tests as to what qualifies someone to count as a domestic voter, but various elements can be taken into account, including the amount of time spent there and where a person’s family lives. For Delo and Harborne, there are questions over whether they really count the UK as home. An interview with Delo last year said: “He lives in the same modest flat in Hong Kong he rented 12 years ago.” The billionaire himself meanwhile wrote in the Telegraph in April: “I will move back to Britain early so I can contribute more to Reform’s budget.” As for Harborne, a recent report by Channel 4 News found that several residents of the tiny village in which he is now registered said they had never seen him. What is Reform saying? This weekend Reform sources said they were very confident the donations would be permissible. “We are 100% confident both are legal and won’t ever have to be handed back,” a spokesperson said, suggesting both men would meet the criteria on residency even within the rules of the new bill. By Monday that position appeared to be shifting, with Nigel Farage complaining about the fact that the bill would apply retrospectively. “Both these donations are 100% compliant with the law today, of that there is no question whatsoever,” the Reform UK leader told the BBC. But when asked whether Delo and Harborne were UK residents as of 25 March, he added: “I’m not going to go into their particular details. All I’m going to say is, with the law of the land as it stands, they are both compliant. “Now, there is talk, and Angela Rayner was talking about this yesterday, there is talk of them retrospectively declaring donations illegally. Well, that simply cannot be.” Could the law be toughened further? Ministers are now considering rewriting parts of the bill to make it clearer what should be counted towards UK residency. If it comes into line with the test for income tax as some experts have advocated, that could set a minimum number of days which Delo and Harborne would have had to have spent in the UK in the preceding year to qualify as UK residents. Importantly, this could set a standard that a voter is not allowed to donate unless they also pay income tax as a UK resident. However, it remains unclear exactly what these tests would be, and whether Harborne or Delo would meet them. What happens if the donations are ruled illegal? If, when the elections bill becomes law, it renders either or both of the Delo and Harborne donations impermissible, the money will have to be handed back. Even if Reform has spent a large chunk of it, it would still need to pay the full amount. More seriously for the individuals themselves, if they are found to have lied to electoral administrators in their declarations, they could be held criminally liable. “Providing false information to register to vote is a police matter,” said Laura Lock, the deputy chief executive of the Association of Electoral Administrators, on Monday. “Every registration makes it clear it is an offence to knowingly provide false information when making an application.” This crime can lead to an unlimited fine or up to six months’ imprisonment. • This article was amended on 29 September 2026. An earlier version quoted the Association of Electoral Administrators as saying the crime of providing false information to register to vote can be punished with up to 51 weeks’ imprisonment; this should have said six months’ imprisonment.

title: Europe must build own AI or risk getting cut off by US or China, says ECB’s Lagarde
summary: Central bank chief says continent’s AI dependency could give trade partners unprecedented leverage in negotiations
text: Europe must develop its own AI technology and build more datacentres in order to nullify the threat of being cut off by the US or China, according to the president of the European Central Bank. Christine Lagarde said the continent needed AI models – the technology that powers AI tools such as chatbots – that were “good enough” to carry out most tasks and run from domestic datacentres. If Europe invests in its own AI tech, said Lagarde, “the threat of being cut off loses its force”. AI is being built elsewhere, the ECB boss said in a speech in Vienna, with the US producing 59 notable models last year and China 35, while France and the UK produced one each. She added that the US hosts 75% of the world’s AI computing capacity – produced by datacentres – and Europe just 5%. Lagarde said Europe faced “an awkward choice”. “Either it holds back on adopting, because it cannot protect its data, and forgoes the growth. Or it adopts AI quickly, becomes highly dependent, and risks losing the freedom to organise its economy according to its own values.” Cutting Europe off from AI or changing the terms of its access would have a widespread and immediate economic impact, she said. “Within a few years it will be screening goods at the border, deciding which tax returns are audited, dispatching trains, watching patients on wards and clearing payments at banks. A withdrawal of access, or a change in its terms, would then reach every sector at once,” she said. Lagarde said this represented leverage that “no trade partner has ever held over Europe, and it could be ‌used in any negotiation, on tariffs or on digital taxes, for example”. While the EU and the US remain key allies, the Trump administration has shaken that trust in a range of episodes including the imposition of tariffs, demands to take over Greenland – a largely autonomous territory that is part of the Danish commonwealth – and the withdrawal of US troops from Europe over political disagreements. If adopted quickly, AI could lift the level of productivity – a measure of economic performance – by up to 4% over a decade, which would be transformative for public finances, Lagarde said. Urging Europe to build more computing capacity, she said: “Europe already has too little datacentre capacity to meet its own demand, and on current trends, that gap is projected to grow more than sixfold within a decade.” US technology firms’ investment ‌needs are so large that they are doing some of their borrowing in Europe, pushing up costs for everyone else as they crowd out others in the debt market. European pension funds also invest heavily in US tech stocks, so any market correction would affect European savings, she added. Reuters contributed to this report.

title: States and cities sue Trump administration over policy restricting green card benefits
summary: The policy allows immigration officers the authority to deny green cards to those using public benefits
text: A coalition of 22 states and the District of Columbia sued the Trump administration on Monday over a new policy that would allow individual immigration officers to deny green cards based on use of public benefits. The new policy changes a long-established “public charge” rule, which dates back to the Immigration Act of 1882, established to ensure that newcomers to the country would be able to provide for themselves without relying on governmental benefits. During his first term, the Trump administration attempted to impose a similar policy that likewise widened the number of categories immigration officers could consider, including Medicaid, food stamps and housing vouchers. That policy was also met with legal challenges and subsequently reversed by Joe Biden’s administration. “Hardworking families should not be forced to go without the support they need because they fear asking for assistance will get them deported,” said New York attorney general Letitia James in a statement. “This rule preys on that fear and counts on families forfeiting the food assistance, health care coverage, and other public benefits to which they are legally entitled. My office fought this exact policy once before and won, and we are leading the nation to ensure the Trump administration cannot inflict this harm on families again.” The new change is more expansive than the previous attempt. This time, it does not specify which safety nets should be considered and allows immigration officers to consider government benefits that are applied for on behalf of family members, including children who are US citizens. Many immigrants without green cards are already ineligible for public benefits programs despite paying into them. However, US citizen children are legally eligible for such benefits, regardless of their parents’ status. Historically, however, immigration officers did not include the use of benefits like the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (Snap) or Medicaid in their assessment. The new policy would reverse that practice, decreasing the number of federal programs that are available to non-green card-holding immigrants. “Congress never intended for the public charge ground to be weaponized against immigrants and their family members who merely use supplemental or temporary amounts of public assistance to which they are lawfully entitled. Yet that is exactly what Defendants now seek to do through the final rule challenged here,” the coalition wrote in their filing. The states’ filing argues that the impact of the policy change could be disastrous, noting that states would lose billions from the federal government because of the reduced use of Medicaid and the Children’s Health Insurance Program (Chip). They also said citizens who live with noncitizens might avoid signing up for benefits, which would have both financial and health impacts. The states’ suit was brought by New York, California, Illinois, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaii, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, New Jersey, New Mexico, Nevada, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, Vermont, Virginia, Washington, Wisconsin and the District of Columbia. New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani is leading a coalition of cities, including Chicago, Seattle, San Francisco, Santa Clara county in California and King county in Washington, filing a similar lawsuit. “The new public charge rule seeks to push immigrant families away from the programs that have kept people fed and healthy for decades,” Mamdani said in a statement. “New Yorkers will be afraid to see a doctor or ask for help they are legally entitled to. That fear will not stop at the families that the federal government is targeting. Families who remain fully eligible for benefits will feel a chilling effect, and all New Yorkers will pay for it.”

title: Microsoft proposes limits on its AI with code of conduct amid safety debate
summary: Firm publishes AI guidelines with Microsoft AI CEO saying: ‘AI must be subordinate and always in service of people’
text: Microsoft published a provisional “code of conduct” Monday to apply to the training of new artificial intelligence models, taking a step towards limiting the capabilities of the company’s AI as anxiety rises over the prospect that technology companies could lose control of AI products. Mustafa Suleyman, the CEO of Microsoft AI, published the code on social media early Monday, writing: “AI must be subordinate and always in service of people. “The fears about possible loss of control are real,” he wrote. A parallel post on the company’s website said: “The purpose of technology is to serve humanity and accelerate human flourishing. Any technology that doesn’t achieve that is a failure, and it should be rejected. That is the starting point of our approach at Microsoft AI, where we’re building towards Humanist AI, one that is subordinate, aligned, and contained.” Under the code of conduct, Microsoft’s AI models must not consider requests related to weapons development, produce violent or sexually explicit content or help with the procurement of dangerous substances. AI models also should not be built to imitate consciousness and shouldn’t be entitled to rights. Suleyman said the published guidelines were for public consultation. He called the need for a code “urgent” and said the last few months have been “a watershed moment”. “Things we have worried about for a long time in theory have become very real,” Suleyman added, and referred to the recent breakout of OpenAI bots that had infested AI company Hugging Face without apparent direction. “‘Swarms’ of agents breaking out of their sandboxes. Unauthorized hacks of enterprise grade systems. Agents modifying their own logs. I’m glad that a consensus is forming.” The executive on Monday told CNBC that Microsoft had been working for months on the new guidance. Satya Nadella, Microsoft’s CEO, wrote on X ahead of the announcement: “If the AI we build is not helping humanity and under human control, it’s not worth pursuing.” The issue of AI security flared up on Saturday when Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic, issued an appeal for the AI industry to “slow down” and offered a three-part plan for doing so, saying that his company would “unilaterally” commit to the first of the steps. In a post on social media, Amodei shared a link to an essay titled We Must Pace the Frontier in which he laid out how Anthropic would provide “third-party evaluators with permanent, employee-level access to our systems, so that they can verify adherence to our safety measures, report on incidents, and assess models’ alignment during training”. The move came after a former Anthropic researcher warned last week that AI could precipitate human extinction by 2030. Researcher Jacob Coxon said in a series of posts that he had quit his job because Anthropic and his previous employer, OpenAI, were ignoring or mishandling their response to the threat AI posed. Earlier, Sam Altman, OpenAI’s CEO, said the dizzying pace of progress could go “very badly” and that humans could lose “control of the future to AI”. “We welcome a federal framework that sets consistent safety requirements for frontier AI,” Altman said in a social media post. “No amount of American competitive pressure should justify recklessness,” he said. Elon Musk is backing the calls for AI caution. But the calls have also raised skepticism around “third-party” monitoring and international cooperation, particularly with China. “My concern is that the biggest labs could end up writing rules that protect their own position. If the cost of meeting those standards is so high that only the best-funded companies can afford it,” said Oliver Yonchev, co-founder and COO of Potentially AI. Slowing the AI frontier, he added, “may be sensible in principle, but I’m sceptical it will work without global cooperation and credible verification. Otherwise, we risk a slowdown in public announcements while the race continues behind closed doors.”

title: British man accused of drugging and raping wife over two decades admits 60 offences

text: A man has pleaded guilty to drugging and sexually assaulting his wife over a period of 20 years as he admitted 60 criminal offences. The man, who cannot be named in order to protect the anonymity of his victim, is in his 60s and before his arrest lived in Stockport, Greater Manchester. He admitted 60 counts, which include 21 counts of rape and sharing intimate images of his victim. His estranged wife sat on the front row of the packed courtroom with other family members as he entered his pleas, occasionally sobbing as he did so. In June, the man pleaded guilty to 15 of the charges against him. On Monday he admitted the final 45 at Manchester’s Minshull Street crown court. The defendant also previously pleaded guilty to sharing intimate photographs or film of his wife, without her consent, for sexual gratification. Twelve co-defendants all deny various allegations involving the same woman. Rick Jackson, an assistant chief constable of Greater Manchester police, said: “Our focus remains on supporting the victim of this horrific campaign of abuse through what is a very complex investigation. “Specialist support continues to be provided to the victim at the centre of this case. “If you are concerned you, or someone you know, may be affected by drug-facilitated sexual abuse, please know that you do not need proof, certainty, or a clear memory to be taken seriously. “You are not expected to understand exactly what has happened or who was involved in order to be taken seriously. If you feel that something has happened, then please report it or ask for help.”

title: House Democrats pitch bill to save people from having pay garnished for medical debt
summary: Exclusive: Currently under federal law, up to 25% of a worker’s take-home earnings can be collected
text: House Democrats introduced a bill Monday that would prevent workers from having their wages garnished for medical debt collection. The bill would amend the Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938 to include a ban on wage garnishment for medical debt and prohibit any state or court from issuing or enforcing such wage garnishments. “In the richest country in the world, medical debt should not be a threat to working people’s livelihood,” said Bobby Scott, a representative, ranking member of the House Committee on Education and Workforce and co-author of the bill, in a statement. “The American people should not have to slash spending on necessities to pay for life-saving care and no one should be denied future health care because of unpaid medical bills.” Currently under federal law, up to 25% of a worker’s take-home pay can be garnished, or the earned amount above $217.50, which is 30 times the federal minimum wage (currently $7.25 an hour). At least five states, including New York, Pennsylvania, Texas, Delaware, and North Carolina, have already banned wage garnishment for medical debt, and legislators in several states have introduced bills this year to ban or restrain wage garnishment for medical debt. “In 45 states, some workers have a portion of their take-home pay forcibly cut to pay off medical debt,” said Ilhan Omar, a Democratic representative and co-author of the bill, in a statement. The bill ensures “no worker is thrown into further financial hardship over often-predatory debt”. Over 100 million Americans face a total of $220bn in medical debt. As many as 550,000 people annually cite medical bills as the reason they filed for bankruptcy. A 2022 survey by the Kaiser Family Foundation found more than six out of 10 US households reported cutting back on basic necessities due to medical debt with 48% reporting that they used most or all of their savings to pay their debt. More than one-third of Americans reported skipping medical care in the past 12 months due to the cost, according a 2026 poll by the Kaiser Family Foundation. A 2023 study found about 1% of American workers are experiencing wage garnishment for debt at any given time, with about 10% of gross earnings as the average garnishment, though it’s unclear how much garnishment was specifically for medical debt. After the Trump administration allowed Affordable Care Act subsidies to expire, health premiums have gone up 20% in 2026 and are set to increase another 15% in 2027. More than 8 million Americans have lost health insurance between 2025 and 2026 due to the Trump administration’s Medicaid cuts and subsidy expirations. “Nobody should lose their wages because they got sick,” said Greg Casar, a Democratic representative and co-author of the bill, in a statement. “Trump and Republicans ripped health care away from millions of Americans to pay for tax cuts for billionaires. Now families who get sick are being hit with bills they can’t pay, and in most states a hospital or debt collector can take a cut of their paycheck before they ever see it. This needs to end.”

title: Maryland boy recovering from surgeries after rabid beaver attack at state park
summary: Teen was swimming at a popular spot at the time of the attack, the latest in a string that have occurred in the state
text: A 13-year-old Maryland boy is reported to be recovering from multiple surgeries and nerve damage after being attacked by a rabid beaver. The teen, Dominick Cebula, was swimming at a popular spot in Cunningham Falls state park in Thurmont, Maryland, on 26 July when a beaver attacked his chest underwater, a relatively rare kind of encounter that more recently has been recurring, according to reporting from local news outlets. Speaking to the news outlet WUSA, Dominick’s father, Jeff Cebula, said: “He grabbed its head and a leg and he tried to get it off of him … At that point, he kind of felt that it was locked onto him. And then it started shaking its head, kind of like a dog would do.” Jeff Cebula said his son pulled the beaver off his chest but as he backed away, the animal attacked again, biting him on the right hand, WUSA reported. Dominick fought off the beaver before being airlifted to Johns Hopkins hospital in Baltimore, where he underwent three surgeries on his chest and hands to repair nerve damage. He was also given a rabies post-exposure shot, with his father saying: “It’s not just one shot … It’s multiple shots around each bite site.” WUSA reported that the beaver was later confirmed to have rabies after being caught and euthanized. Multiple other beaver attacks have occurred in Maryland. On 5 August, a rabid beaver allegedly attacked the leg of a 19-year-old fisher at Cunningham Falls state park before being caught and euthanized. And a few days later, a 10-year-old girl endured a beaver attack while canoeing at Maryland’s Seneca Creek state park, CBS News reported. On 6 August, the Maryland department of natural resources (DNR) announced that it was investigating a potential rabies outbreak in Cunningham Falls state park. Actions in response to that possible outbreak included “dismantling a nearby beaver lodge and establishing daily surveillance at the lake for other beavers using DNR staff and a wildlife damage control cooperator”. The Maryland DNR said its wildlife and heritage service would “institute night-time monitoring at the lake along with daytime surveillance to remove additional beavers, if any are present”. Although beavers are typically non-aggressive and avoid conflict with humans, people should still maintain a minimum safe viewing distance of 25 yards, the Maryland DNR advised. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recently reported that the agency from July through August had received 17% more rabies-related inquiries than during the same period in 2025 – including reports of mass exposure events that involve more than one person. Rabies is a zoonotic viral disease with a near 100% fatality rate once symptoms develop. However, it is preventable when post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) is administered appropriately. PEP consists of a series of shots given promptly after potential exposure to the rabies virus Lyssavirus rabies and before symptoms begin. Common symptoms of rabies include anxiety, insomnia, hydrophobia, hypersalivation, fever and headaches.
