title: Richard Tice rallies to the defence of Reform’s crypto ‘patriots’ | John Crace
summary: You can’t buy Dicky’s level of stupidity though it could be argued that Christopher Harborne and Ben Delo just have
text: Never in the field of British politics has so much been given to so many by so few. You’d have thought Nigel Farage would have wanted to explain Reform’s sudden windfall from Christopher Harborne and Ben Delo himself. To bask in the glory of the donations from two down-to-earth, anti-establishment crypto billionaires. Men who know what it’s like to graft, who know the meaning of an honest day’s work for an honest day’s pay. There again, Nige is keen not to appear as a one-man band these days and he could do with some downtime to enjoy his own £5m handout. And besides, he’s got a police investigation into Reform party funding to worry about. Even so, it wasn’t the best of looks to send Richard Tice out on to the morning media round. Dicky may have his talents, but he keeps them well concealed. His main talent is the unfortunate ability to make Honest Bob Jenrick sound trustworthy. But he does always leave you guessing. Is he being wilfully stupid or is he naturally that half witted? Dicky began with a howl of protest. No rules had been broken. He made that sound as if it came as a surprise to him. I guess that’s an easy mistake for anyone to make. Everything was in the rules as they exist. Labour was mounting a coup against Reform for having passed legislation through the Commons that would prevent donors living overseas from giving more than £100,000 until they had lived in the UK for more than a calendar year, backdated to March 2026. You’d have thought Nige might have clocked this. But he probably hadn’t been in Westminster that day. And you can’t trust Dicky to be over the details. “Our money comes with no demands,” Dicky told Nick Robinson on the Today programme. Harborne and Delo were patriots. All they wanted was to save the country from being ruined by socialists and the rightwing Tories. Quite where he thought Reform fitted in on this particular continuum wasn’t clear. Presumably in the centre ground of British politics. Ordinary men and women who want to rescue their country from the do-goodery of the RNLI. “Patriots” was doing some heavy lifting here. Harborne had decamped to Thailand in the 90s, had become a Thai citizen in 2011 and had taken a Thai name. Now we learned that Dicky believed in dialectics. The more someone looked as if they were trying to put as much distance between themselves and the UK, the greater their commitment to the UK really was. Chris had just been playing very hard to get. The reality was he had been begging HMRC to ask him back so he could pay his fair share to the exchequer. Fine, said Robinson. When did he move back to the UK and does he now pay UK tax? Dicky was understandably clueless. He had no idea he was going to be asked whether Harborne complied with the law as it was going through parliament. I’m not his tax adviser, he protested, though if he was he would make sure he paid as little as possible. Dicky has always been upfront in his belief that only the little people pay tax. And as for Harborne’s whereabouts, he wasn’t his diary secretary. He just telepathically knew that Chris had complied with the law as it was and as it was proposed. It was the same with Delo. No man had ever loved his country more. From Hong Kong. Who wouldn’t want to receive money from a billionaire who had been convicted in the US for failing to comply with money-laundering laws and had been pardoned by Donald Trump? Dicky had no idea when Ben had come back to the country. That sort of level of detail was well above his pay grade. He was just here for the front-of-house stuff. The meet and greet. No one should expect any more from him than that. Then the killer line. “I hope you will trust the word of our compliance team,” said Dicky. They would assure listeners everything was above board. So touching. So sweet. Up till now, no one had any idea Reform even had a compliance team. They certainly hadn’t been much in evidence while James Orr and Dan Jukes had been negotiating a possible £500,000 gift from an overseas donor. And in the taped conversation, which Nige insisted he hadn’t been listening to, Farage had said, “it’s all above board”. So, if it’s all the same, we won’t be taking the word of an imaginary compliance team. Nick pressed on. What did Dicky think had attracted two crypto billionaires to a party that had promised to cut taxes on crypto, to limit regulation of the industry and had threatened to remove the governor of the Bank of England if he didn’t play ball? Dicky couldn’t quite put his finger on it. But he thought it was probably something to do with them really caring about a £500 tax break. And the pleasure of paying for Nige’s hideous suit. Champagne and oysters all round. There was just time for Robinson to point out that, far from getting nothing for their donations, the two men had already got everything they wanted and more. “Not at all,” Dicky insisted. Because Reform had promised to deregulate and cut tax before the two men had handed over the £72m. Where can you go with someone as dim as Dicky? A tale told by an idiot, signifying nothing. You can’t buy Dicky’s level of stupidity. Though Harborne and Delo just have. It was left to Farage himself to clear up Tice’s mess later in the day in a BBC interview. Well, sort of. Yes, Delo and Harborne’s donations probably wouldn’t meet the necessary deadlines for the legislation going through parliament. But you couldn’t blame Reform for taking the cash. Rather it was the fault of the government for putting in place regulations that Reform might not now be able to get round. As so often with Nige, there was always someone else to blame. Not that Labour was immune from a little hypocrisy. It had been Burnham who had tried to bury the plan to limit donations to all parties. Something the unions had pushed back against. But the £72m has rather concentrated everyone’s minds. Once the current legislation was through parliament there would still be a good year to pass another law to impose a cap. Down in Brighton, Angela Rayner wanted the TUC to know she was on their side. There was no equivalence between Labour funding from the unions and money from two crypto billionaires. Politics could be bought. Just by the right sort of people.

title: ‘A coin flip’: on the campaign trail as Brazil’s far right edges back to power
summary: Neck-and-neck with Lula in polls, Flávio Bolsonaro fires up his base in the bellwether state of Minas Gerais – starting at the scene of his father’s stabbing
text: A giant banner of Brazil’s incarcerated former president Jair Bolsonaro fluttered in the morning breeze as his eldest son, Flávio, touched down at an airfield on the fringe of a city that will soon help decide the future of one of the biggest democracies on earth. “Brazil is rudderless. Brazil has no president and Brazil needs a president – and that president is Flávio Bolsonaro,” the far-right senator declared as he waded into the flock of supporters who had gathered to welcome him to Juiz de Fora, one of the largest cities in the battleground state of Minas Gerais. With less than a month before nearly 159 million Brazilians choose their next leader on 4 October, the election appears on a knife-edge, with the incumbent leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, and his challenger, Flávio Bolsonaro, neck-and-neck in the polls. Bolsonaro’s campaign appears to have seized the momentum in recent weeks amid a slew of corruption scandals involving Lula’s son and the supreme court. That has prompted despair among progressives who fear their country could fall back into the hands of a radical rightwing movement that tried to grab power after the then-president, Jair Bolsonaro, lost the 2022 election to Lula. Last September, Jair Bolsonaro received a 27-year jail sentence for spearheading that botched coup – a verdict supporters insist was unjust. But the ex-president and his accomplices are likely to be freed if his son wins power – a prospect that delights the hardcore Bolsonaristas who turned out to greet Flávio Bolsonaro wearing yellow football shirts and headbands reading: “Lula out!” “Today is a moment of joy,” said Ulisses Lima, 50, a cybersecurity specialist with a Jesus Christ pendant around his neck. “Flávio represents change. He represents Brazil’s rescue from this socialist abyss we’ve spent so long warning about,” Lima added as supporters waited for the former president’s heir to arrive. Nearby, another devotee, José Caldeira, fell to his knees and begged for divine intervention to get Bolsonaro out of house arrest. “God, free this nation! Amnesty and freedom for Bolsonaro!” Caldeira bellowed, raising his hands towards the sky. A third man, Davi Frederico, held a banner celebrating Donald Trump, who has been accused of trying to swing the election in Bolsonaro’s favour through economic and diplomatic pressure. “Make Liberals Cry Again,” it said. Juiz de Fora, an industrial and university city traditionally associated with the left, is also a key location for Brazil’s hard right. The city’s army headquarters was the launchpad for the 1964 coup that plunged Brazil into two decades of military rule. And it was in Juiz de Fora, on the eve of the 2018 election, that Jair Bolsonaro was stabbed in the gut while campaigning – an attack widely believed to have helped the former paratrooper seal his victory. Bolsonaro’s shock win ushered in what, from a progressive perspective, were four abysmal years. Destruction of the Amazon rainforest and gun ownership skyrocketed, hundreds of thousands died during a Covid outbreak Bolsonaro was accused of mishandling, and the president’s authoritarian rhetoric and attacks on Brazil’s electronic voting system culminated in the 8 January 2023 riots in Brasília. The supreme court later called those disturbances part of a plot to “annihilate” the country’s democracy. But the Bolsonaros still enjoy abundant support, and that devotion was visible as Flávio Bolsonaro’s motorcade crept towards the high street where his father was ambushed eight years ago. “Let’s get the left out! Let’s get these motherfuckers out!” one elderly woman shrieked as the senator passed by on top of a sound truck stamped with the word: “Jesus”. Other fans, many senior citizens, waved Brazil flags from windows or stood on the sidewalk flashing victory signs with their hands. “Barring some kind of leftwing trickery, Flávio Bolsonaro can already be considered president. All you have to do is take a look at the streets and social media,” claimed Nikolas Ferreira, an influential far-right congressman from Minas Gerais who has more than 9 million TikTok followers. Alongside the enthusiasm, there were glimpses of the revulsion many Brazilians feel for the former president. One leftwinger took to his balcony with a loudhailer to taunt the Bolsonaristas as they paraded through town. “Trump! Trump! Get my daddy out of jail!” the dissenter jeered in reference to the US president’s attempts to help Bolsonaro escape punishment. Minas Gerais, a mountainous mining and agricultural region that is larger than France and has 21 million inhabitants, is Brazil’s bellwether state. Since democracy returned in the 1980s, no candidate has won the presidency without triumphing here. In 2018, Jair Bolsonaro beat Lula’s candidate in Minas by more than 1.7m votes. Four years later, Lula reclaimed the state by fewer than 50,000. After landing in Minas last week, Flávio Bolsonaro said he was confident of clawing back the swing state, with one recent poll putting him ahead there. “[Lula] is a president who you look at and see the past,” the 45-year-old senator said of his 80-year-old adversary. “With Flávio you can be sure that when people look at him, they see a modern government and a government of the future.” Thomas Traumann, a political analyst who has written a book about his polarised country, said the election was too close to call. “It’s a coin flip,” said Traumann, who believed an unexpected scandal or last-minute “black swan” event could swing the election either way. On Friday, it emerged that Flávio Bolsonaro had been placed under police investigation over suspicions of corruption involving the funding of a big-budget biopic telling the story of the assassination attempt against his father in Juiz de Fora. For progressive voters, the vision for a Flávio Bolsonaro administration laid out during his visit to Minas is the stuff of nightmares. “I think Flávio Bolsonaro’s presidency is going to be Jair Bolsonaro 2.0,” said Bruno Engler, a Bolsonarista lawmaker from Minas’ capital, Belo Horizonte. Engler believed a top priority would be zero-tolerance policing, with the younger Bolsonaro pledging an iron-fisted crackdown on criminals his father has compared to cockroaches. “Thugs who don’t surrender will be arrested or neutralised,” Engler vowed, predicting gun laws would be loosened. Speaking on the street corner where his father was knifed, Flávio Bolsonaro vowed to pack Brazil’s 11-member supreme court with five conservative judges “who are against abortion [and] against drugs”. “We’re going to give the streets back to the Brazilian people … We’re going to lower the age of criminal responsibility. We are going to introduce chemical castration for rapists,” shouted the candidate, who wore a bullet-proof vest. Those pledges prompted whoops of excitement from the crush of supporters below Bolsonaro’s truck. Dozens ofmobile phones captured the candidate’s every word. But amid the rightwing rejoicing there was fear and trepidation, too. Lennon César, a law student and leftwing activist who had come to confront Bolsonaro’s fans, voiced incredulity that less than four years after Jair Bolsonaro’s failed power grab, tens of millions of Brazilians seemed poised to vote for his son. “We were the victims of an attempted coup – and his father was the perpetrator,” recalled César, 28. “It’s terrifying. And the thing that worries me most is that the general public doesn’t really seem to get what’s happening. Brazilians have short memories when it comes to the past.” As a black, gay man, César felt particular dread at the prospect of a second Bolsonaro presidency, given the patriarch’s hostility to minorities. César vowed to vote for Lula, Brazil’s first working-class president, calling him the only leader who paid attention to the poor. “If today I’m studying for a law degree it’s because one of Lula’s government programmes allowed me to achieve that,” he said, warning: “These people … might destroy it all.” A few blocks away, a graffiti artist had spray painted their own message of disapproval on to the facade of Bolsonaro’s Juiz de Fora HQ. “Facists [sic],” it read.

title: Russian strike on passenger train will not deter Ukraine’s backers, Nato chief says
summary: Mark Rutte says attack that narrowly missed Boris Johnson and David Petraeus shows Vladimir Putin’s desperation
text: The head of Nato has said a Russian drone attack on a train close to Ukraine’s border with Poland would not deter Kyiv’s western backers. Mark Rutte said the strike on a passenger train showed how desperate Vladimir Putin had become. “He thinks that he can stops us from supporting Ukraine and that he can undermine our unity. He is wrong. Our answer is to increase support,” the Nato general secretary said. European leaders have condemned the strike in which a Russian drone hit a passenger train on Ukraine’s border with Poland on Sunday shortly after a convoy of high-level diplomats and former leaders had passed through. The earlier train, which was carrying the former UK prime minister Boris Johnson was running ahead of schedule, may have been the target of the Russian drone strike, Ukrainian Railways has said. A spokesperson forthe UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, struck a similar note to Rutte, saying the attack “was a futile attempt by Russia to undermine our support for Ukraine. It will not deter us.” The French foreign minister, Jean-Noël Barrot, said the goal of the attacks was “to intimidate Europeans, discourage and above all divide them”. The EU’s high representative for foreign and security policy, Kaja Kallas, said the strike “was clearly a message to the western world”. Speaking on the sidelines of an Arctic conference in Finland, she said: “I think the question for us is what do we take from that message? I think we should act the opposite. We should show that we are there for Ukraine and we are not scared off, because otherwise, you know, Russia will just achieve what they want, which is the submission of Ukraine.” A spokesperson for Kallas added: “We strongly condemn the latest Russian strikes near the Ukraine-Poland border, including the attack against the passenger train,” and referenced a recent EU decision to approve a €6.1bn tranche of the €90bn loan for Ukraine. “We are acting on the front to equip Ukraine better to defend itself, and we will continue to stand firmly with Ukraine and its right to defend itself against Russian aggression,” the spokesperson said. Overnight attacks across Ukraine involving more than 450 Russian drones and missiles killed at least six people and injured more than 40. Ukraine’s air force said it had intercepted 405 drones and four missiles. Western Ukraine, which is typically quieter than Kyiv or the eastern frontline zones, was particularly badly hit. The strikes, which prompted air raid warnings in Poland, came as EU diplomats met in Brussels on Monday for last-ditch talks on the rollover of the bloc’s sanctions against more than 2,600 Russian individuals and entities involved in supporting Vladimir Putin’s war. The sanctions are due to expire on Tuesday but their prolongation is being held up by a dispute about whether to remove an individual from the list. Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, wrote on Telegram on Sunday: “Ukrainians are fighting every day to prevent these strikes from spreading further into Europe, giving their lives and preventing the aggression from expanding.” Ukrainian Railways, which operates the line, said a train carrying several security advisers from European countries as well as Johnson and the former Swedish prime minister Carl Bildt, had passed through the border crossing shortly before the drone strike. The diplomatic train, Ukrainian Railways said, had left ahead of schedule and could have been the target of the Russian drone. Another train, with former CIA Director David Petraeus on board, was still at Yahodyn station when the drone struck, according to the rail operator. The Polish prime minister, Donald Tusk, warned on Sunday that intensifying Russian attacks in Ukraine in the coming weeks could affect Poland, as he chaired an emergency meeting after the Russian drone attacks near the border. “The coming weeks and months will be a period of very intensive actions on the Russian side,” he said, adding Poland “cannot rule out that this escalation will also affect our territory”. He added that Poland had been tipped off by its security services, and by intelligence agencies from allied countries, that an attack such as this was likely. “We knew that the Russian plan would include an attempt to disrupt, paralyse, and perhaps even destroy Ukrainian border crossings,” Tusk said. • This article was amended on 14 September 2026 to clarify that David Petraeus was on a separate train to Boris Johnson.

title: Texas Democrat under fire for honoring convicted abuser Chris Brown at concert
summary: Congresswoman Jasmine Crockett awarded the musician a congressional record recognition in Arlington
text: The Democratic US representative Jasmine Crockett is under fire for honoring musician Chris Brown, a convicted abuser, with an official recognition at a Texas concert over the weekend. Crockett, a Texas congresswoman, awarded Brown and R&B musician Usher a congressional record recognition at a performance in Arlington, Texas, on Saturday. Appearing alongside Texas state representative Venton Jones, Crockett said she was there to “honor” Brown and Usher. “We are experiencing Black joy at the highest level,” she said, according to video from the concert. “And I wanted to make sure we document that at the congressional level. So let’s give it up again for Chris Brown.” A congressional record recognition is a ceremonial honor in which a member of Congress can enter a specific person or achievement into the official congressional record. Brown pleaded guilty in 2009 to felony assault against his then girlfriend, music star Rihanna. He also awaits sentencing in a UK incident in which prosecutors alleged he hit a music producer over the head with a bottle. Brown pleaded guilty to a charge of “affray” in that case. Crockett lost the Democratic primary for US Senate in Texas earlier this year to James Talarico, a state representative now running against Republican Ken Paxton in a race that’s considered a toss-up and a key target for Democrats. Since her loss, Crockett has so far not campaigned for Talarico, with some people online calling attention to her choice not to campaign with the Democratic Senate nominee and instead appear with Brown. Roxane Gay, the author, wrote on social media platform Threads: “What the hell is [Jasmine Crockett] thinking? This is such a bizarre and unacceptable misstep.” She later added that Crockett didn’t mention voting or endorse candidates in the appearance. “She just flew on stage and gave a known abuser of Black women (multiple allegations past and recent) a congressional honor,” Gay posted. Crockett has said she “will be campaigning down ballot” when asked in recent weeks by CNN’s Laura Coates about whether she would be campaigning with Talarico, saying she wanted to make sure that people in lower-profile races weren’t getting “overshadowed” by a focus just on the top of the ticket. Some defended Crockett, saying her appearing with Jones, the state representative, at the concert before thousands of people was using her platform to get voters to turn out for the down ballot. Crockett did not respond to a request for comment. Beto O’Rourke, a former Democratic congressman in Texas, defended Crockett’s decision to campaign for down-ballot candidates at a roundtable hosted by Bloomberg News in Dallas last week, before the Brown concert. “She’s helping him in what I think is the most effective way possible, which is this reverse coattails of boosting these down-ballot candidates,” O’Rourke said. “It’s up to her and at her discretion, but I would not be surprised if we don’t see her play a larger role in what’s about to happen in Texas and she will deserve so much of the credit when James Talarico wins, when Gina Hinojosa wins, for the work that she’s done, the people that she has engaged.” David Smith contributed reporting

title: Unions to intervene on political funding as TUC chief warns ‘super-rich’ threaten democracy
summary: UK general secretaries had been split on issue but sources say they are likely to back strong words calling for action
text: Trade unions are set to launch an intervention on Tuesday on political donations after the head of Britain’s trade union movement, Paul Nowak, said the government must act to “stop the super-rich corrupting our politics.” Union leaders met on Monday to discuss possible support for a domestic cap on donations. Discussions are expected to continue but sources said general secretaries were likely to back strong words calling for further action on political donations from wealthy individuals – but arguing that trade union members should be treated as individual donors giving small amounts. Union leaders had been split on the prospect of limiting domestic donations to political parties, with many including the GMB fearing it would lead a future rightwing government to curb union donations. Labour-affiliated unions are working on a statement on political donations that is expected to be put before the TUC general council on Tuesday, the Guardian understands. But union sources said there were “significant differences” between general secretaries on how to proceed. Many of the trade unions that are not affiliated to Labour are keen to go further on limits – but would themselves not be affected by measures that could curb party donations. On Sunday, Unite’s general secretary, Sharon Graham, broke ranks and backed a limit, after two crypto billionaires, Christopher Harborne and Ben Delo, donated £72m to Reform UK within 24 hours. Asked about the possibility of an overall cap on donations, Gary Smith, the general secretary of the GMB, said “we’ll work that through” but added that amendments to the representation of the people bill, aimed at enacting a limit, “felt ill-thought-through”. However, Mike Clancy, the general secretary of Prospect, which is not affiliated to Labour, said the government should be doing more on political donations. “The government’s going to have to step in here. Citizens have noticed this. This is buying and distorting democracy, and in a way that ultimately will impact working people adversely,” he said. In his annual address to the TUC conference in Brighton, Nowak, the general secretary of the Trades Union Congress, said the donations were “a crisis for our democracy”. “Tell me, why is it that two crypto billionaires have donated £72m to Reform in just two days?” he said. “The evidence is clear: Reform UK is a party for sale. Nigel Farage is a politician for sale. And given half the chance, they’d sell our country down the river. “Make no mistake, this is a crisis for our democracy. We cannot allow our political system to be captured by corporate interests.” He said there was no similarity “between care workers chipping in a few quid a year through their union and a party bought and paid for by billionaires”. “We need a proper conversation about how we clean up our politics that doesn’t push workers to the margins – but does stop the super-rich corrupting our politics,” he added. Nowak said no donations at all should be allowed from those who did not live and pay taxes in Britain. A bill currently before parliament would limit donations from overseas British donors to £100,000. He said the government must also go further on foreign funding for political ads. “Elon Musk, keep your grubby hands out of British politics,” he said. Smith said that despite qualms about a donations cap it was clear that the government had to “clean up the money going into politics”. But he said he was concerned about trade union funding being caught in the crossfire. “Care workers, school, support staff, energy workers, they need a political voice. And they deserve a stake in the country, in politics, and we do that through pennies that our members donate to a political fund, some of which we use to support the Labour party. “So our money’s clean, it’s declared, it’s transparent. People know where it comes from, and we’re unequivocal and unashamed about advancing the interests of our members.” Joanne Thomas, the general secretary of Usdaw, said union donations were “the cleanest money in politics”, adding: “We must make sure we reflect the difference between our donations and other donations.” Thomas also urged the government to look again at election spending limits, as a way to help level the playing field. The bill currently in the House of Lords puts significant limitations on overseas donors, including for a calendar year after they return to the UK. Reform’s deputy leader, Richard Tice, said that while he was completely confident Reform had complied with all current and proposed laws on donations, he could not say when Delo returned to the UK from Hong Kong, or how much time the Thailand-based Harborne spent in Britain. The two separate donations of £36m by Harborne and Delo are unprecedented in UK political history and will give Reform enormously boosted resources before the next election. Delo was based in Hong Kong but has returned to the UK. Asked when, Tice said it was “many, many months ago”. Harborne is registered to vote in the UK but also lives in Thailand. The former Conservative prime minister Boris Johnson said on Monday that he thought the retrospective nature of the cap was “pathetic” and unfair. “Just because some people want to support one party very generously, Labour kicks up a huge fuss and says they’re going to cap donations,” he told GB News. “I think the next election is going to be fought on the shape of the British economy and on British society and the government that has the most credible [plan] and I think it’s the Conservatives.” But he said he questioned the motives of Reform’s donors. “The problem with Reform … whatever the motives of these guys, these crypto kings, in funding Reform with squillions. I wonder whether they want Reform to be pro-crypto,” he said. “Reform is weak on welfare, and I think weak on the economy.”

title: Michael Holiday obituary
summary: Other lives: Hospitality professional and hotel manager who spent 10 years as the ‘butler’ at Cliveden House
text: My friend Michael Holiday, who has died aged 92, left school with no qualifications but forged an international career in hotel, facility and events management that spanned 44 years. From 1985 to 1995 he was house manager at Cliveden House in Buckinghamshire. Born in Leigh-on-Sea, Essex, Michael was the son of Wilfred Holiday, a director at Tate and Lyle, and Hilda (nee Day), a housewife. He went to Felsted school in the county, but his education was curtailed when he was evacuated to Welwyn Garden City, Hertfordshire, during the second world war. Childhood holidays were spent at a guesthouse in Clacton-on-Sea, where he made a lifelong friendship with the actor Penelope Keith, whose mother organised children’s entertainment in the resort. After leaving school, Michael was advised by his father to study hotel and catering at the local college in Southend, where he mastered his signature dish: choux pastry swans. His hospitality career began at the Kensington Palace Hotel in central London. From there he went to Frankfurt, where he became fluent in German, returning to London for a period on reception at the Savoy – which earned him membership of the Savoy Gastronomes, a group of food and wine enthusiasts made up of former employees who travelled internationally together. After the Savoy he worked at the Le Meurice in Paris, before taking up the post of staff manager at Claridge’s in London. Then followed general manager positions at the Norfolk Hotel in Brighton and in South Kensington. In the mid 1960s he moved to the Canary Islands, becoming front of house manager at the Hotel Reina Isabel in Las Palmas. Michael had a spell running his own bar before a chance meeting in 1976 with the mother of the Playboy executive Victor Lownes led to him managing Lownes’s UK residence, Stocks House, near Tring in Hertfordshire. Michael organised lavish parties there including the 25th Playboy anniversary party in 1978 attended by more than 5,000 guests over its 25-hour duration. He regarded the peak of his career as his 10 years as house manager (“butler”) at Cliveden – the only job he was formally interviewed for. There he hosted many celebrity weddings; his old-school propriety meant that, in our 20-year friendship, he never revealed any guest details. He met his partner, the restaurateur and Michelin inspector Tony Rudge in the early 80s. They became civil partners in 2006. In retirement in Milton Keynes, Michael helped Tony after his disabling stroke. Together they catered for musicians playing for Cleo Laine and John Dankworth at the Stables, in the village of Wavendon, where he also worked as a part-time events assistant, alongside guiding in French and German at Woburn Abbey. Following Tony’s death in 2019, he volunteered at MK Gallery in Milton Keynes, enjoying educating visitors about the art exhibitions. Michael was a fabulous cook and enjoyed nothing more than hosting a party followed by a competitive game of Rummikub, which he played until a few days before his death.

title: US borrowing costs hit 5% for first time since 2023 amid bond sell-off
summary: Soaring oil prices of above $108 a barrel after Houthi attacks on Saudi infrastructure stoke inflation fears
text: US government borrowing costs have risen to 5% for the first time since 2023 as soaring oil prices fuelled by the war in the Middle East trigger an intensifying sell-off in the global bond market. The yield – in effect the interest rate – on 10-year US Treasury bonds hit the psychologically important threshold on Monday, on a day of renewed selling pressure on Wall Street as the global oil price reached $108 a barrel. With traders awaiting a crunch US Federal Reserve interest rate decision on Wednesday, the benchmark rate has steadily climbed from a low this year of 4% before the outbreak of the US-Israeli war on Iran in late February. The yield was last above 5% in October 2023. It comes as the rising global oil price stokes inflation fears, with the latest move prompted by a series of drone attacks that have forced Saudi Arabia to close a vital east-west crude pipeline as the fallout from the war mounts. Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil prices, surged to more than $108.5 a barrel on Monday – a 3.7% increase on the day. The spike came after Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi forces launched several attacks against Saudi Arabia and captured the strategic island of Perim in the Bab al-Mandab strait on Sunday, expanding their control of the waterway. The rise was also fuelled by the Gulf states postponing a meeting with Tehran to discuss creating a temporary shipping lane through the strait of Hormuz, a vital channel through which a fifth of the world’s oil and gas supply normally passes. Traders in the kingdom have warned it will run out of oil stocks for export if it does not reopen the east-west pipeline within days. Gas prices also climbed higher on Monday, with the UK benchmark rising by 5% to 208.73p a therm – its highest level since December 2022. It came despite Donald Trump on Monday announcing a deal between Ukraine and Russia not to hit each other’s energy targets, while insisting that he believed a politically sensitive rise in US diesel fuel prices was being driven by the conflict in Europe rather than the war in Iran. With fears mounting as the Middle East war escalates, bond markets have come under intense selling pressure. The US 10-year Treasury yield is used in global financial markets as a benchmark for pricing other assets, meaning a jump in borrowing costs for Washington has consequences for countries, businesses and households worldwide. Borrowing costs also rose across Europe on Monday, including a rise in 30-year UK government yields to the highest level since March 1998. The moves come as traders await decisions on interest rates from the US Federal Reserve on Wednesday and the Bank of England on Thursday after the European Central Bank raised borrowing costs last week. With investors anticipating an increase from the Fed and a hold decision from Threadneedle Street amid mounting inflationary pressures, analysts said global bond markets could face another week of renewed volatility. Daniela Hathorn, a senior market analyst at Capital.com, said: “Markets are starting the week on a defensive footing, with the combination of another escalation in the Middle East and increasingly hawkish central-bank expectations weighing on risk appetite.” With wholesale energy prices on the rise, the cost of petrol and diesel hit new Iran war highs on Monday, according to the RAC, with the average cost of petrol climbing to 169.68p and diesel hitting 191.68p. The US-Israeli war with Iran has disrupted oil and gas supply across the Middle East this year, sending the oil price soaring from its prewar level of about $72 a barrel to peak at $126 in April. Brent crude later fell back over the summer amid hopes of a lasting ceasefire, before starting to climb again after the memorandum of understanding between the US and Iran fell apart. After a recent stepping-up of hostilities the benchmark again rose above the $100 a barrel threshold last week for the first time since July. Chris Beauchamp, of the broker IG, said a “move back to the spring highs” looked increasingly likely. “Oil markets are being subjected to their worst fears all at once – attacks on energy infrastructure, the closure of Hormuz and a breakdown in attempts to restart negotiations,” he said. “The risk of further disruption is also spreading beyond the Gulf, with the threat of renewed Houthi attacks on shipping adding another layer of uncertainty around key energy and trade routes. “The major surprise is how calm markets remain in the face of all this, but if prices breach the March highs, things could get ugly very quickly.” Oil output from Saudi Arabia had been under pressure before the attacks on its major pipeline. Riyadh told the Opec oil cartel recently that its crude production in August was at its lowest level since 1990, according to Bloomberg.

title: Sweden’s political parties launch coalition talks as both blocs try to secure power
summary: Centre-left bloc led by Social Democrats has narrow lead with 95% of vote counted, but faces internal policy battle
text: Sweden’s political parties have launched coalition negotiations as the Social Democrats leader, Magdalena Andersson, started the long and difficult process of trying to form a new government. Full results from Sunday’s election are not expected until after overseas votes are counted on Wednesday, but with 95% of the votes counted, the Social Democrats and the centre-left bloc had a narrow but growing lead of 176 seats to the right-leaning parties’ 173. After losing support for the first time since they were founded, the far-right Sweden Democrats, who were hoping to enter government for the first time, appear to be out of the picture. But many of its policy ideas – on immigration laws, integration and crime – have become mainstream, including in the centre-left. Both Andersson and the outgoing centre-right prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, of the Moderates have each said they want to explore possible coalition options to secure power. After a long election night during which there was just one seat between the two blocs, Social Democrat leaders met Andersson on Monday morning at the party’s Stockholm headquarters. Questions remain as to whether the bloc is willing to work with the Left party (Vänsterpartiet), which the Centre party has previously ruled out. The Social Democrats press secretary, Tobias Baudin, said he had been in contact with colleagues from opposition parties and called for the resignation of Kristersson, who led the rightwing Tidö coalition government with the support of the Sweden Democrats. “Now the voters have had their say and they have given him a failing grade for himself and his government,” Baudin told the Swedish broadcaster SVT, adding: “He should resign himself. In fact it doesn’t matter, if he doesn’t resign he will be removed. How he does it is up to him. The Centre party said that in talks with the Social Democrats it would be seeking a government with a “desire for political stability” and a “clear centre-right character” with no “fringe politics”. The Social Democrat Morgan Johansson, who under the last Social Democrat-led government was deputy prime minister, said the Centre party’s announcement was a positive development and that overall there were “good prospects”. All of the left-leaning parties want a change of government, he said. “That is the starting point. I don’t think anyone wants us to end up in a situation where blockages lead to a new election.” Meanwhile, Kristersson appears to be keeping his options open. On Sunday night he said the result could lead to a “complicated government formation, where it ends remains to be seen”. On Monday, before a meeting with his fellow Tidö coalition leaders, he declined to elaborate, saying he would wait for a full result before having conversations. “If all the red lines remain then Sweden won’t have a government at all,” he added. “I plan to pursue a number of possibilities that may exist.” The Liberals and Christian Democrats have both said they will not work with the Social Democrats. After the overseas votes are counted on Wednesday, the final election results are not expected until the weekend. The new parliament will meet for the first time on 28 September and the earliest date that the speaker can suggest a prime minister is 29 September, but talks could take considerably longer. If, when parliament votes for a prime minister candidate, more than half say no, then the speaker must find a new candidate. If there are four failed votes there will automatically be a new election. After the 2022 election, it took 37 days to form a government; in 2018 it took 134 days to form a new coalition. Fredrik Furtenbach, the senior political correspondent at Sveriges Radio (Radio Sweden), said: “I think it will end with either the Left or Centre party having to give way. It might take several failed prime minister votes first.” But he does not believe the Social Democrats and Moderates, who he describes as “traditional archenemies”, will end up working together. “You cannot share the position of prime minister.”

title: Robin Morgan obituary
summary: Political theorist and one of the first feminists of her generation to point out the misogyny within male leftist counterculture
text: The poet, novelist and political theorist Robin Morgan, who has died aged 85, was a key figure of second-wave feminism. From 1976, she was a contributing editor of the influential Ms magazine, founded by her friend and close collaborator Gloria Steinem, and served as its editor in chief from 1989 until 1994. In 1967, she co-founded the radical activist group New York Radical Women, and the following year, the Women’s International Terrorist Conspiracy from Hell (Witch), which used street theatre and other actions to protest against cultural sexism. In 1970, she edited the anthology Sisterhood Is Powerful, now considered a foundational text of second-wave feminism, and, with the royalties received, founded the Sisterhood Is Powerful Fund to support women’s organisations. In all, she published 22 books, including three landmark anthologies. Morgan was one of the first feminists of her generation to point out the misogyny within male leftist counterculture. Her 1970 essay Goodbye to All That, published in Rat, a leftist newsletter, scorned both the so-called “sexual revolution” and the male radicals who expected women to type out their manifestos and share their beds while denying them political voice. She coined some of the feminist movement’s most effective and enduring slogans, including “Porn is the theory; rape is the practice”, a line that captured her lifelong opposition to pornography. On the anti-feminism backlash, which characterised the women’s movement as dangerous, she observed: “We are the women that men have warned us about.” She came up with the term “herstory”, for history written from a female perspective. It was a direct action with New York Radical Women that first put Morgan in the spotlight: in 1968, she helped organise a protest against the Miss America pageant in New Jersey during which women tossed bras, girdles and cleaning equipment into a “Freedom Trash Can” – although it was not set on fire, this gave rise to the derogatory put-down of feminists as “bra burners”. Born in Lake Worth, Florida, Robin was the daughter of Faith Berkley, a shop assistant, and Mordechai Morgenstern, a gynaecologist. The couple were not married, and Faith had moved to Florida from New York to hide her pregnancy. Robin was 20 when she first met her father. Pushed by an aunt into child modelling, she was a performer from the age of five, with her own programme, The Little Robin Morgan Show, on the New York radio station WOR and a starring role on the popular TV show Mama between 1950 and 1956. In her teens she rebelled, leaving acting to become a writer, and at 16 began studying literature informally at Columbia University in New York. She joined a writing workshop, where she met the poet Kenneth Pitchford, a founder of the Gay Liberation Front. Married from 1962 until their divorce in 1990, they had a son, Blake, in 1969. As a former leftist revolutionary, when Morgan joined a newly formed women’s group in the 1960s, it was her intention to convert them to Marxism; instead, they converted her to radical feminism. She never lost her taste for coalition work, but her politics were now unambiguously her own. In The Demon Lover: On the Sexuality of Terrorism (1989), she made connections between violence and misogyny by men on both left and right. “It is the common denominator of strutting machismo,” she wrote, “that links the random killings of the street terrorist with murderous state terrorism.” Her Fighting Words: A Toolkit for Combating the Religious Right (2006) took on Christian fundamentalism with equal force. Alongside Steinem and Jane Fonda, she was a co-founder of the Women’s Media Center in 2005. Its aim was to improve both representation and the positive participation of women and girls in the media. In 2008, she published Goodbye To All That #2 – an essay on the misogyny aimed at Hillary Clinton during her run to become the Democratic presidential candidate. Mass-forwarded by Clinton’s daughter, Chelsea, it went viral. “Me, I’m voting for Hillary,” Morgan wrote, “not because she’s a woman, but because I am.” In 2015, she organised a conference on the sexual exploitation of women in the sex industry, hosted by the Carter Center, Atlanta, the organisation founded by the former US president Jimmy Carter to promote human rights. As a result of her friendship with Carter, an indictment of pornography appeared on his website – a first for a former president. Carter was also the first male guest on Morgan’s weekly radio programme, WMC Live. I first met her in 1997 at a meeting in a Manhattan cafe, where Andrea Dworkin had gathered a group together to talk about how to call rapists to account through the criminal justice system. Softly spoken, she wore her feminist notoriety lightly. There was nothing egotistical about her; she once told me that her most important work was mentoring later generations of political activists. Close to her heart was the Sisterhood Is Global Institute, a feminist thinktank founded in 1984 with Simone de Beauvoir, which raises money for organisations improving the lives of women and girls globally. The anti-pornography scholar and activist Gail Dines said that Morgan “saw porn as front and centre of radical feminist theory and politics … she talked about the disgrace of the third wave, and how missing porn as the material and ideological mouthpiece of patriarchy would destroy feminism.” Asked in a 2007 interview for the Humanist magazine what it meant to be a radical feminist, she replied: “It means daring to be uncompromising, daring to be angry.” Her poetry collection Dark Matter (2018) explored ageing, mortality and resilience. She was diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease in 2010, and, according to her son, feared decline, not death. On the question of generational handover, she was unyielding. “It’s only natural for people to want to stay in charge of the movement they poured their life energies into,” she once said. “Get your own damned torch,” she told a young woman who intimated that it was time to pass hers on. “I’m still using mine.” She is survived by her son, Blake. • Robin Evonne Morgan, poet, writer and feminist activist, born 29 January 1941; died 5 September 2026

title: Government moves to nationalise Speciality Steel UK to protect 1,300 jobs
summary: Firm, once part of Sanjeev Gupta’s empire, fell into administration last year but has failed to find buyer
text: One of Britain’s steelworks is to come into public ownership after the government said it would take over Yorkshire-based Speciality Steel UK (SSUK). Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, said officials would “work towards” acquiring the company to protect the jobs of its 1,300 workers in Rotherham, Stocksbridge and Brinsworth in South Yorkshire and Wednesbury in the West Midlands. The insolvent steelmaker, formerly part of the tycoon Sanjeev Gupta’s industrial empire, fell into administration last year and its day-to-day operations have since been run by the government’s official receiver. The Norwegian steel startup Blastr Green Steel had been in talks to buy SSUK, but hopes had faded over the summer for a private sector takeover after a deadline to finalise a deal passed in June. The steelworks and its staff have been described by Reynolds as important strategic assets for the UK. SSUK is the largest producer of “green steel”, made using less-polluting electric arc furnaces. Reynolds said: “We do not intervene in private companies lightly. But nor can we simply stand aside and allow the future of this company and over 1,300 jobs to be decided by default. “Working towards public acquisition will keep options open while we work with local leaders, workers, industry and investors to determine the best long-term future for these sites, which could play a vital role in the future of the growth-driving sectors in our industrial strategy, including defence and advanced manufacturing. SSUK went bust last year after longstanding financial issues under previous ownership, particularly after the collapse of its primary lender Greensill Capital in 2021. A high court judge at the time found the company was “hopelessly insolvent”, with only £650,000 in the bank after running down its reserves. Since then, the government has been funding the wages of its workers, costing £3.5m a month. The plants have not been producing steel for the last year, though some staff remain on its sites to maintain equipment. Ministers’ preference was for a private sector buyer, but after what were described as “extensive discussions” with Blastr, officials decided the company’s offer could not provide the desired long-term stability for SSUK. A Blastr spokesperson said: “We are disappointed by the government’s decision today concerning Speciality Steel UK, and we were not informed in advance. Over the course of several months, we have advanced our plans for a private sector solution to acquire SSUK – and were today on site in South Yorkshire with investors and strategic partners. We have a fully-funded proposal – at no cost to the British taxpayer – that is ready to complete within 12 weeks.” Mark Bula, the Blastr chief executive, quit the company unexpectedly at the end of last month, with its finance boss, David Morant, taking his place. The shadow business minister Bradley Thomas said it was “surprising” that the government had moved away from a private sector buyer after picking a preferred bidder. Speaking in parliament, he asked Reynolds: “Other than a new prime minister who’s committed ideologically to nationalisation, what has changed Reynolds added there was “nothing ideological” about the move and that he would “not go into the detail” about why Blastr’s bid fell through. He accused the Conservatives of a “legacy of neglect” during their 14 years in government. The government has committed to spending up to £2.5bn on the steel industry through the national wealth fund. About £500m of that was put towards converting Tata Steel’s blast furnaces into electric arc furnaces. The South Yorkshire mayor, Oliver Coppard, said he was pleased the government had taken action, adding: “It’s the next important step forward, giving us more time to find the best possible outcome for our steelmaking communities – places where people have faced economic challenges and real barriers to opportunity for far too long.” Roy Rickhuss, the general secretary of the Community union, welcomed the intervention but said the lack of a credible buyer was “a disappointing outcome”. He added: “SSUK is a unique and integral component of the UK’s steelmaking capabilities, without which we would be entirely reliant on foreign suppliers for high-value speciality inputs to our critical energy infrastructure and our advanced manufacturing base, including the defence industries. We cannot allow British industrial sovereignty in these areas to be lost.”

title: Top civil servant sacked by Starmer received record £860,000 payout
summary: Special approval needed for amount that surpassed what Chris Wormald was ‘contractually entitled to’
text: The former head of the civil service Chris Wormald received a record payout of almost £860,000 when he was forced out of the top job in Whitehall by Keir Starmer. Cabinet Office accounts have revealed that the former cabinet secretary, who was sacked earlier this year, was paid £859,496 upon departure. The figure is an unprecedented amount, which required civil servants to seek a special direction from ministers to approve it because it was “greater than what Sir Chris Wormald would be contractually entitled to”. Wormald has since been made a member of the House of Lords, after serving as cabinet secretary for just 14 months. He was replaced by Antonia Romeo earlier this year. It was revealed earlier this summer that the size of the payout to Wormald was so vast that Cat Little, the permanent secretary of the Cabinet Office, had to request a ministerial direction from Starmer in February to override value-for-money concerns before she could approve it. In her letter to the prime minister at the time, Little wrote that she needed special permission to grant such a high award, saying “in respect of value for money, I have consulted civil service HR and legal advisers and have had due regard to managing public money and the consideration of Sir Chris Wormald’s employment rights in the circumstances. The proposed award is greater than what Sir Chris Wormald would be contractually entitled to.” Little said she had been informed a settlement of that level was “necessary given that this is a departure from a high-profile, unique role that has been agreed at very short notice”. She said the prime minister could take into account “the public interest in bringing this matter to a conclusion and the prevention of distraction from the effective operation of government”. The Conservatives said the payout was an “appalling waste”. The shadow Cabinet Office minister Alex Burghart said: “Chris Wormald was just one of many civil servants and advisers fired by Keir Starmer as he tried to save his own skin. “This payout is another appalling waste of taxpayers’ money by Labour. Whether it’s big payouts for fall guys, or gimmicky giveaways, this government is always happy to spend our money if it thinks it will benefit the Labour party.” The settlement with Wormald dwarfs the previous record amount given to the former Treasury permanent secretary Tom Scholar, who was forced out by Liz Truss in one of her first acts as prime minister. He was given £457,000, including severance pay and compensation in lieu of notice and leave. Wormald became a crossbench peer after he was nominated by Starmer as the former prime minister left office. At the time, No 10 had been criticised over its handling of Wormald’s departure, with his allies saying he had been badly treated and learned of his fate through the media. Dave Penman, the general secretary of the senior civil servants’ union the FDA, said the briefing against Wormald had been extraordinary and that it was “no way to run a country”.

title: Did you solve it? Do you have the brain of an engineer?
summary: The answers to today’s puzzles
text: Earlier today I set four engineering puzzles. Here they are again with solutions. (Do check out the hundreds of great comments posted below the line in the original story.) The cranberries In a cranberry sorting facility, thousands of cranberries are dropped every minute onto a board. Good cranberries are firm, and bounce, while bad cranberries are soft, and don’t bounce. What simple trick allows sorters to catch all of the good ones and none of the bad? Solution The board is at an angle. Good berries bounce off onto a conveyor belt. Bad ones fall down into a discard box. Caps off In the US, medicine bottle caps are designed to be secure against only 85 per cent of children under five. Why is this percentage not higher? Eighty-five seems quite low. Solution If the child-resistance rate was 100 per cent, the mechanism would also be hard for weak or arthritic hands. If the bottle is too hard for an elderly person to open, they may leave the cap off entirely, which is more dangerous than the small percentage of clever or strong kids who’d have taken it off anyway. The standard isn’t “as safe as possible” — it’s tuned to the point where making it safer for kids would make it less safe overall. Slats entertainment In 2020, engineers replaced the pedestrian handrail on the Golden Gate Bridge. The old handrail rested on metal balusters in the shape of an H, so the support looked like “HHHH…” where the H’s horizontal section was 10cm wide. The new handrail was supported only by thin vertical slats, making it look like “IIII…” and where each slat was only 0.6cm wide. The aim of the new handrail was to make it less resistant to wind, and hence safer during high winds. But it brought two serious unintended consequences. What were they? Solution 1) The wind level on the bridge was much higher, to the great annoyance of cyclists. 2) During certain winds, the whole bridge began to make an unbearable whistling noise that could be heard for miles. Essentially, the new slats behaved like reeds, and the bridge turned into in a gigantic harmonica. Under pressure Cabin air pressure in a plane is controlled to a level that is comfortable to humans. When a plane flies, the air pressure outside the plane drops to much lower than this level, causing the air pressure in the cabin to push outwards against the frame with great force. In the early 1950s, there were some major plane crashes when the fuselage was ripped apart mid flight. UK manufacturer de Havilland found a way to pressure test its plane, the Comet, the world’s first commercial jet, without the plane leaving the ground. What did they do? Solution Engineers at Farnborough built a giant water tank at and submerged the plane in it. Filling the cabin with water and increasing the pressure let engineers safely find the limit at which the structure would fail. Air at that same pressure would have exploded destructively, destroying the evidence along with the plane. Here’s a picture of the water tank from 1954, with the Comet’s wings sticking out. Today’s puzzles were adapted from How to Keep a Plane in the Sky, by Alex Davies. The book tells fascinating stories about test engineers – those geniuses whose work underpins our trust that objects do not crack, break or explode. You can buy the book at the Guardian Bookshop and other retailers. I hope you had fun. I’ll be back in two weeks. I’ve been setting a puzzle here on alternate Mondays since 2015. I’m always on the look-out for great puzzles. If you would like to suggest one, email me.

title: Kennedy Center leaders say Trump’s name on facade may avoid ‘fiscal collapse’
summary: Center’s Trump-installed leaders also say it is on brink of bankruptcy and could close as early as Tuesday
text: Leaders of the John F Kennedy Center for ⁠the Performing Arts say it is reportedly on the brink of bankruptcy and could ⁠close as early ⁠as Tuesday. The center’s Donald Trump-installed leaders argued that putting the president’s name on its facade may be the only way ⁠to avoid imminent and “certain fiscal collapse”, the Washington Post first reported, citing documents it ‌obtained. The paper said ‌a report, prepared by the Washington DC institution’s trustees, claimed that ‌within a few weeks the institution won’t be able to pay employees or meet maintenance costs. The report was prepared in advance of a meeting that is scheduled for Tuesday. The 57-page internal document, circulated to the board ahead of the meeting, also flagged safety concerns tied to the building’s maintenance backlog and recommended that the main building be closed immediately. Reached for comment by the Guardian, the Kennedy Center declined to address the leaked documents directly or to get ahead of the board’s deliberations. It pointed instead to a statement issued after part of the ceiling in the main hall collapsed on 4 September. “Another example of the urgent need to close for renovation and revitalization, as our Chairman President Trump has championed,” said Roma Daravi, the center’s vice-president of public relations, in the statement. “This structural failure stems from decades of neglect and deferred maintenance by the previous leadership, and there’s no justification for further delays in restoring America’s cultural center.” The Post also said Trump will help the Kennedy Center if his involvement is acknowledged. The trustees’ report represents “a remarkable new phase in Trump’s takeover of the Kennedy Center, which has been engulfed by financial turmoil, leadership upheaval and litigation since he installed himself” as chair in 2025, the paper said. That takeover began on 10 February 2025, when Trump dismissed 18 board members appointed under Joe Biden. Days later, the remaining trustees – many of them recently installed Trump allies, including White House chief of staff Susie Wiles and second lady Usha Vance – voted him in as chair, breaking with decades of precedent under which sitting presidents had kept the institution at arm’s length. The board also fired Deborah Rutter, who had served as the center’s president since 2014 and already planned to step down seven months later, replacing her with Richard Grenell, a Trump ally from his first administration. The shake-up prompted a wave of departures and cancellations. Board treasurer Shonda Rhimes, National Symphony Orchestra artistic adviser Ben Folds and opera singer Renée Fleming all resigned their positions, while actor Issa Rae pulled her sold-out show from the venue in protest. Subscription sales fell sharply over the following months, with the Post citing a 36% drop by June 2025, and ticket sales continued to soften into the autumn. A Kennedy Center spokesperson attributed the decline to wider Broadway industry trends, though sales had already begun falling within months of the takeover, before those pressures were cited, and alongside a wave of artist departures and cancellations. Grenell himself was replaced as president in March by Matt Floca, formerly the center’s vice-president of facilities operations, amid the continued upheaval. The Post also noted that Trump’s involvement with the Kennedy Center, which included the addition of his name to ‌the building, impaired fundraising work and ticket sales. A spokesperson disputed this, saying the name had instead attracted new donors and was “crucial” to fundraising, which goes against the trustees’ report’s own admission that Trump is withholding his fundraising help until his name returns. A judge in May ruled that the addition of Trump’s name to the center’s facade was illegal – and therefore it needed to be removed. Trump’s name was then removed in June after a judge rejected an emergency appeal blocking the removal. In August, the board voted again to reinstate Trump’s name on the building and to close the venue for a multiyear renovation, according to court filings. A spokesperson said the center had historically run an operating deficit of about $100m a year, and that prior leadership left a bottom-line deficit of $26m, describing the previous budget as “falsified”. This echoes an allegation Grenell made in 2025, when he said the center’s new CFO had found “$26m in phantom revenue” and called it “criminal”, a claim Rutter and Rubenstein rejected at the time, with Rubenstein saying the center’s financial reports “were reviewed and approved by the Kennedy Center’s audit committee and full board as well as a major accounting firm”. Separately, lawyers for the center have argued in litigation that hundreds of millions of dollars in private donations already pledged would have to be returned if Trump’s name were not restored to the facade, citing the institution’s bylaws. The board later told a federal judge it would hold off on adding the name until at least 8 October, a month’s delay on its earlier timetable. Reuters contributed reporting.

title: ‘Signs of violence’: asylum seekers arriving in France injured after being deported from UK
summary: French health service documents injuries including fractures and bruising after detention and return under ‘one in one out’ scheme
text: Multiple injuries including bruising and fractures have been documented by a health service supporting people returned to France under the controversial “one in, one out” scheme. The pilot scheme involves one asylum seeker who crosses the Channel in a small boat being returned to France in return for another in northern France being legally brought to the UK to claim asylum. The scheme is due to end on 1 October. Samusocial de Paris (SSP) has been commissioned by Île-de-France’s regional health agency to provide healthcare for asylum seekers returned to France in the first eight days after their deportation from the UK, when they are accommodated in a shelter in Paris. They have documented the cases of 90 returnees between 22 January and 7 June 2026. All are young men, mostly in their 20s and early-30s, who sought sanctuary in the UK after fleeing a variety of conflict zones including Eritrea, Sudan and Afghanistan. About 1,400 people have been forcibly removed to France by the Home Office since the scheme began in August 2025, although some have subsequently returned to the UK in lorries or small boats. The evidence compiled by SSP has been submitted to the French Assembly’s cross-party inquiry into the impact of the Anglo-French border deals known as Le Touquet agreements. This evidence comes from their own clinical consultations with returnees and some hospital reports from those sent to A&E. Many of those detained in the UK for “one in one out” have fled torture and other forms of persecution in their home countries, and have been subjected to modern slavery on their journeys in countries such as Libya. However, the focus of the report is on what happened to people while they were detained in the UK as part of the scheme and during their removal to France. According to the report: “Consultations are revealing signs consistent with recent physical and psychological violence as well as the consequences of prolonged detention in conditions described as particularly degrading.” It states that the physical and psychological conditions documented are “explicitly linked to the implementation of the France-British agreement”. The report adds: “The frequency and recurrence of the incidents reported by people transferred under the Franco-British agreement appear particularly worrying.” One A&E medical report from a returnee who arrived in France in such a bad state that he was sent to hospital reads: “The patient’s general condition was marked by significant suffering and shock upon arrival necessitating referral to the hospital emergency department. The medical certificate mentions reports of physical violence in England, including diffuse bruising, injuries consistent with restraint (lacerations with handcuffs) and abdominal pain resulting from repeated blows.” The report includes 13 case studies documenting a range of injuries, including problems that worsened due to a lack of medical treatment, while people were in detention in the UK. Concerns were also raised about mental health conditions such as PTSD. In one case, a man was referred for emergency psychiatric treatment because he was too disorientated to find his way back to the dormitory while in the shelter, suffered from body tics and incoherent speech and was deemed to be at risk of suicide. The report highlights limited options for ongoing psychiatric treatment for this group. SSP recommends that a mechanism should be established to collect information on allegations of mistreatment by the British authorities that can be sent to the UK. It also suggests reporting this issue to the French prosecutor under article 40 of the French code of criminal procedure. Nihal Osman, a programme coordinator for Médecins Sans Frontières, which also provides health support for this group of returnees, said: “This one in one out agreement is a machine for psychological destruction. “The deeply concerning physical injuries sustained whilst in detention in the United Kingdom, which we have documented among those deported, must be viewed in the light of a serious psychological deterioration.” A Home Office spokesperson said: “We take the welfare of those returned to France incredibly seriously. Migrants have regular access to healthcare while in detention and anyone unfit to travel will not be returned. “Contractors must adhere to strict standards of dignity and respect throughout the removal process.” • This article was amended on 16 September 2026 to remove a reference that was included in error.

title: Crispin Odey loses appeal against lifetime ban from UK financial services industry
summary: Judges uphold ruling that financier tried to ‘frustrate’ investigations into harassment claims against him
text: The former hedge fund boss Crispin Odey has lost a legal challenge to overturn his lifetime ban from the City for trying to “frustrate” investigations into sexual harassment allegations against him. A ruling by judges at the upper tribunal upheld the ban imposed by the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) in March last year, while reducing a proposed fine of £1.83m to £1.53m. “We have found that Mr Odey lacked integrity,” the tribunal ruling said, referring to the Conservative party donor’s behaviour at Odey Asset Management (OAM) between December 2021 and November 2022. “Mr Odey is not a fit and proper person and it is reasonable for the authority to have concluded that a prohibition order is appropriate.” Numerous allegations against Odey by female members of staff came to light after OAM launched an internal investigation into sexual harassment at the business in September 2020. Odey, who resigned in 2023 after the allegations were reported in the media, tried to block executives of his hedge fund from taking any action, including by twice firing its entire executive committee (ExCo). “He misused his power as controller to remove the ExCos as a means to protect his own interests and attempt to achieve his objectives,” the tribunal ruling said. The judges also said the Brexit-backing hedge fund chief failed to acknowledge any potential harm during a three-week appeal hearing in March. “He has expressed no contrition,” they added. “He sees nothing wrong with his approach, and indeed he wrongly sees himself as the victim.” The hearing involved a series of controversial admissions, including Odey blaming an incident in 2005 when he was alleged to have groped a colleague’s breasts on the effect of sedatives he had taken after root canal treatment. He said the woman had accepted his apology and continued to work for the company for another eight years. He also told the appeal judges he did not remember cornering a female employee after a boozy lunch and saying to her “I could attack you now”. The allegations against Odey were first reported by the Financial Times in summer 2023. OAM ceased trading months later. Commenting on the ruling, the FCA’s executive director for enforcement and market oversight, Therese Chambers, said: “Mr Odey clearly thought he could act with impunity. He twice sacked those tasked with protecting female employees from his inappropriate behaviour when they tried to hold him to account. He felt the rules shouldn’t apply to him and acted to save his own skin. “During the hearing he reinvented history, painted himself as a victim and displayed no contrition. That arrogant entitlement and the resulting complete disregard for proper governance means Mr Odey is unfit to work in financial services.” Odey’s legal representatives were contacted for comment.

title: Four victims identified in Louisiana stabbing spree after suspect detained
summary: Woman, her daughter, her son and his girlfriend identified as victims in incident that also critically wounded a child
text: A Louisiana woman, her daughter, her son and his girlfriend have been identified as the four victims killed in a stabbing spree on Saturday that also left a young child critically wounded in the southern part of the state, according to a relative and family advocate. Verna Mae Verdin, her daughter Letha Verrett, her son Paul Verret, and his girlfriend Krissy Lynn Parfait were stabbed to death at their home in the community of Houma, the relative and advocate, Brandon Thiel, told Louisiana television news station WVUE and said on an online campaign raising funds in part for the victims’ funeral expenses. The wounded child reportedly was Letha’s six-year-old grandson, who happened to be spending Saturday night with her. Local authorities have not formally identified any of the victims of Saturday’s stabbing spree but did say they had detained a 47-year-old man named Kaegan Jude Solet in connection with the case. A statement from the district attorney’s office in Terrebonne parish, Louisiana, which includes Houma, on Monday said sheriff’s deputies had obtained permission to arrest Solet on four counts of first-degree murder and one of attempted first-degree murder. In Louisiana, first-degree murder can carry either life imprisonment or the death penalty. Thiel told WVUE that Solet had fathered a child with one of the slain victims. It is not the first time Solet has been accused of violent behavior. He had previously been tried but acquitted of attempted murder in the December 2019 stabbing of a woman inside a Houma hotel, WVUE reported, citing criminal court documents. Solet had also been booked in the January 2019 stabbing death of an unhoused man named Scott Lovell, according to reporting from the news website HoumaToday.com. Lovell’s mother, Nancy Guidry, told WVUE on Sunday that a grand jury subsequently failed to indict Solet. The statement from Terrebonne district attorney Joseph Waitz’s office on Monday said, “We acknowledge that the prior prosecutions of Mr Solet did not have the desired outcome that our prosecutors tirelessly worked for in those cases”. “And our office respectfully disagrees with the findings of the juries in these matters,” the statement from Waitz’s office continued. “However, we are compelled to respect those decisions by our criminal justice system.” The bloodshed in Houma on Saturday came about two years after Louisiana’s department of health warned that intimate partner violence was a “significant public health concern in the state”. The state’s rate of women murdered by men has historically been significantly higher than the national average, according to the Louisiana Coalition Against Domestic Violence. Meanwhile, across the US, more than half of female homicide victims are killed by current or former male intimate partners, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) crime data show. Verdin was planning to retire in two weeks from a 20-year career at Walmart at the time of Saturday’s killings, as Thiel put it to WVUE. Thiel said Letha Verret was a mother herself and had seven children, including three who are minors. Paul Verrett and Krissy Lynn Parfait lived together in a camper behind Letha and Verdin, WVUE reported. Investigators said on Sunday that deputies with the Terrebonne sheriff’s office initially encountered the wounded child while responding to reports of a “series of stabbing incidents”. Deputies reported that they then found Verdin, the Verret siblings and Parfait dead nearby. A WVUE journalist on Sunday reported being told by the sheriff’s office that the wounded boy had run to a neighbor who called for emergency help in the aftermath of the mass murder. Thiel told WVUE that the boy is a “full of energy, smiling child that [is] just the light of so many of the family’s world”. “Thankfully, he was able to make it out,” Thiel remarked. He also said, “They are processing a lot right now. They are trying to process the loss of family members.” Community members rallied around Verdin’s family as news of the killings spread around Houma and beyond. The fundraising campaign Thiel had organized to support covering the slain’s victims’ funeral expenses and medical costs for the wounded boy had exceeded $46,500 by Monday morning. As of Monday, there had been at least 19 mass murders in the US for the year so far, according to statistics tracked by the Guardian. Two of those mass murders had been reported in Louisiana, including a case in April in which eight children were shot to death in the city of Shreveport in what the police described as a “violent domestic incident”. A mass murder is defined as a case in which four or more victims are killed. In the US, most such cases are carried out by attackers with guns. Texas authorities reported a mass murder on Sunday near the community of San Benito. Investigators there said they had booked Joel Christian Pacheco Maldonado with fatally shooting four adults who were all family members of each other, the Texas television news outlet KVEO reported. KVEO reported that the victims were two men – ages 50 and 29 – as well as a pair of women, who were 28 and 67. Maldonado was also accused of criminally endangering or abandoning three children who were inside the house where Sunday’s mass murder occurred. The minors were reportedly nine years, five years and two months old. And none were physically wounded, authorities said, according to KVEO. Local sheriff Manuel Treviño alleged that Maldonado referred to the oldest victim as “mom,” though they weren’t biologically related, KVEO reported. Treviño also contended that Maldonado allegedly considered the quadruple murder to be “revenge” after growing tired of being bullied.
