title: Uganda reverses Invictus Games withdrawal after reassurance from King Charles
summary: Military chief had pulled country out over ‘Harry-Meghan nonsense’ but U-turned after clarification from the palace
text: Uganda has U-turned on its decision to withdraw from the Duke of Sussex’s Invictus Games after the country’s military chief said he had been reassured by King Charles that there was “no problem” with its participation. Last week, Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba, the eldest son of the Ugandan president, Yoweri Museveni, made the surprise announcement the country would not participate in the games in a post on X. He said he was motivated by his respect for the king amid division over the “Harry-Meghan nonsense”. However, a post on Monday from the spokesperson of the Uganda People’s Defence Force (UPDF), Chris Magezi, announced that Kainerugaba had reinstated Uganda’s participation in the 2027 Invictus Games, which will be held in Birmingham. Magezi wrote that the shift was prompted by a telephone conversation between Kainerugaba and the principal private secretary to the king and queen, Clive Alderton. Alderton had “revealed that King Charles III was moved by Gen Kainerugaba’s sensitive consideration of the king’s opinion on the upcoming Invictus Games organised by Prince Harry, the Duke of Sussex”. He added that Charles “has no problem with Uganda’s participation in the Invictus Games, and encouraged the [Chief of Defence Forces] CDF to proceed with preparations”. Kainerugaba “appreciated the king’s message and clarity provided by Buckingham Palace on the subject, promising that the UPDF would resume preparations to participate in the upcoming games”. In the earlier post, Kainerugaba shared concerns that Uganda’s participation would be “construed as being opposed to his majesty King Charles III of the United Kingdom, whom we deeply revere”, adding that the country would “not participate in anything that does not have his majesty’s approval”. The timing of the post led to speculation it was in response to an official letter to UK senior government and military officials on behalf of Charles that reiterated the Duke and Duchess of Sussex were not working royals and would not use their HRH styles. The recent post stated instead that the withdrawal had followed a statement issued by Buckingham Palace indicating the Invictus Games were a private charity organisation. The king appeared at the 2014 launch of the Invictus Games, but the palace has not confirmed his attendance next year. When asked by the Times about what had motivated the move, Kainerugaba is reported to have said: “I have factions in the Ministry of Defence that support that Harry-Meghan nonsense. I had to quash it straight away. I support the monarch. Period.” Two months earlier, Harry had stood alongside Uganda’s defence minister, Kiryowa Kiwanuka, at an Invictus Games event in London to announce that the east African country would be the 26th country to enter the multisport event for wounded service personnel. Kainerugaba, who, like Harry, is a graduate of the Royal Military Academy at Sandhurst, was appointed army chief in 2024 and is widely seen as his 81-year-old father’s successor to the presidency. He has made several provocative posts on X, including threats to invade neighbouring Kenya, demands that Jay-Z hand over his wife, Beyoncé, so he could marry her, and threats against Bobi Wine, Museveni’s main political rival. Rob Owen, the CEO of the Invictus Games Foundation, said: “We welcome the news that Uganda has confirmed it will continue to be part of the Invictus community and participate in the Invictus Games Birmingham 2027, now less than 300 days away. “Uganda became our 26th nation earlier this year, joining a growing movement that provides year-round recovery opportunities for wounded, injured and sick service personnel and veterans across the world.”

title: OpenAI urges UK lawmakers to rein in technology amid growing safety fears
summary: Company behind ChatGPT tells ministers to seize ‘political window’ on regulation as cross-party committee warns of rising threats to human rights
text: OpenAI has urged British lawmakers to capitalise on renewed fears over AI safety and impose legislation reining in the technology. The company behind ChatGPT said the UK government should act immediately, following a call by its arch-rival Anthropic to curb AI development. “We support stronger UK rules for the handful of companies, including OpenAI, developing the most powerful AI systems,” said OpenAI’s head of policy in Europe, Tom Duff Gordon. However, the tech company said legislation should be narrowly focused on the most advanced AI labs and not startups working on less powerful systems. In a separate interview with the online publication Politico, Duff Gordon said the government should “take advantage of this political window which is clearly opening up” to legislate. OpenAI’s intervention came as a UK parliamentary committee demanded more restrictions on the power of AI, warning that the world was unprepared for the “potentially dire” consequences of the technology, in the latest sign of rising global concern. A new regulatory framework is needed for AI in the UK, including an independent oversight body and legislation to protect the public, according to the cross-party joint committee on human rights, comprising MPs and Lords. It said AI posed a number of threats, from public face-scanning to explicit deepfakes and flagging disciplinary action for workers without reasonable cause. The call for action came after Anthropic, a leading AI company, urged its competitors and governments at the weekend to coordinate a global slowdown in AI development – a call that received immediate support from OpenAI, Google DeepMind and Elon Musk. It follows a series of serious safety incidents in which swarms of AI agents broke out of testing environments and hacked into third-party infrastructure, as well as evidence some users have dodged controls to use models in ways that could support biological weapons development. Alex Sobel, the Labour chair of the human rights committee, said the world was unprepared for dealing with the “potentially dire” consequences of a rapidly developing technology. “Nowhere in the world, including the UK, has a current legislative and regulatory approach to AI that is fit for purpose,” he said. A government spokesperson said the UK took the risks from advanced AI “extremely seriously” and recognised the need to keep pace with the rapidly evolving technology, including working closely with AI companies and other countries. “We should not assume that the existing framework will always be sufficient as AI capabilities develop. Any future measures will be evidence-based and focused on the risks we need to address,” said the spokesperson. On Friday, more than 70 MPs and peers urged the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, to back a ban on the creation of artificial superintelligence (ASI) and lead an international movement to stop the technology. Downing Street rejected the call for a ban, but said it was exploring additional targeted interventions “to address the most significant AI-related national security risks”. Sobel said: “New legislation is needed to establish a comprehensive set of protections that deal with the entire AI supply chain and its life cycle. “A single AI regulator should be established to set policy, monitor performance and ensure enforcement.” Donald Trump has played down warnings of dire risks to humanity. “We’re leading China in AI,” the US president said on Sunday. “We’re the most sophisticated country in the world, and frankly I want to ⁠keep it that way because whoever wins AI, wins.” In his weekend call for the main AI companies to “pace the frontier”, the Anthropic chief executive, Dario Amodei, said the US government should grant the leading AI companies a waiver to allow them to coordinate without being punished for anti-competitive collusion. But Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI, said on Sunday night that while he would “welcome a federal framework that sets consistent safety requirements for frontier AI”, there was no “need to wait for an anti-trust exemption or legislation to begin the work of providing this confidence”. He said: “Where we will need the help of our government is for international coordination. But first we should do what we can ourselves.” Sobel, who has also proposed a bill to prohibit superintelligent AI development in the UK, said protections were needed now to ensure that potential human rights risks do not “become reality”. The committee said a new AI bill should establish a regulatory regime that mandates more demanding obligations for higher-risk AI systems and models, and prohibit some uses of AI which are incompatible with human rights. It also called for mandatory transparency requirements across all levels of the technology’s life cycle, and the establishment of an independent AI oversight body to monitor AI harms and risks, with strong powers to hold AI providers to account. The UK government has already established the AI Security Institute (AISI), which subjects advanced models to safety tests – but does not have the power to compel AI developers such as Anthropic to submit their technology for scrutiny. Last week, it was reported that Anthropic had declined to send its latest model to AISI for testing.

title: Westminster’s time is coming to an end, say first ministers of UK’s Celtic nations
summary: Leaders in Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland discuss independence and call for constitutional change at summit
text: Westminster’s time is coming to an end, the first ministers of Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland have said at a summit aimed at putting the UK’s Celtic nations on the path to independence referendums. The Plaid Cymru leader, Rhun ap Iorwerth; the Scottish National party leader, John Swinney; Sinn Féin’s vice-president, Michelle O’Neill, and the president and leader of the opposition in Ireland, Mary Lou McDonald, met in Cardiff on Monday to sign a memorandum of understanding recognising that “the political landscape across these islands is changing”. “Momentum is behind our movements; we believe that constitutional change is coming,” the memorandum read. “No Westminster government has the right to block democracy or undermine the principle that our people will decide their own future. “We call for the British government to prepare for, plan and facilitate constitutional change in each jurisdiction.” Since becoming prime minister in July, Andy Burnham has put regional devolution of power and resources in England at the heart of his agenda, but policy towards the devolved administrations has so far been muddled. The summit was the first face-to-face meeting for the sister parties since Plaid Cymru won May’s Senedd elections, which put separatist parties in government in all three countries for the first time. The leaders met in their capacity as party, rather than government, officials, discussing economic, energy and international cooperation as well as self-determination. Scottish independence and Irish reunification resurfaced on the news agenda last week when Burnham wrote to Swinney to reiterate that a repeat of 2014’s Scottish independence referendum remained “off limits” after apparently misspeaking during prime minister’s questions. The US president, Donald Trump, also weighed in on a potential breakup of the UK during a visit to Ireland, saying he would love to see a united Ireland and it “may as well happen now”. The unexpected intervention prompted a swift rebuttal from the UK government and the unionist power-sharing members of the Northern Ireland executive. Plaid Cymru has ruled out an independence referendum in its first term, but Welsh ministers are seeking fuller devolution powers on a par with Scotland and Northern Ireland, which Burnham has said he is “open” to. Monday’s summit involved “powerful optics” and an opportunity for the nationalist parties to show how they are prepared to work together, said Laura McAllister, a professor of public policy at Cardiff University. McAllister added: “If you look under the bonnet, though, the aims and the timelines for independence as sought by each of these first ministers is fundamentally different, as of course is the constitutional framework in each country. “If there is a serious discussion of reformulating UK relationships there has to be a presence for England at the table … the irony is that we have a UK prime minister that says he is a devolutionist, but the constitutional question is far more problematic for him.” On Monday afternoon, ap Iorwerth and Swinney signed the Cardiff agreement, setting out areas of planned cooperation between the Welsh and Scottish governments, including tackling child poverty, addressing cost of living pressures and international engagement. They pledged to make the case for “greater fairness” and power over the “constitutional futures” of their countries together in what the Scottish first minister described as “an important moment in the history of devolution”. Latest polling suggests 47% of Scottish voters would opt for independence in a referendum held tomorrow, along with 36% in Northern Ireland and 32% in Wales. Support for independence in Scotland has hovered between 45% and 50% since the 2014 referendum, while data suggests it is rising in Wales and Northern Ireland. On Monday, Sinn Féin’s McDonald said she expected an Irish reunification poll to take place by 2030, while the SNP wants a second referendum within the next five years. Burnham is expected to meet the three first ministers next month. A UK government spokesperson said: “The prime minister’s approach to working with the first and deputy first ministers in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland is based on partnership and collaboration. “The UK government is focused on addressing the issues that matter most to families, including easing pressures on household finances and delivering greater economic security, rather than engaging in constitutional debates or further referendums.”

title: Andy Burnham cancels engagements as his father’s death is announced
summary: UK prime minister had been due to speak at the TUC conference in Brighton
text: Andy Burnham has cancelled his engagements for Monday and Tuesday after his father, Roy, died. Among other plans, the prime minister had been due to speak to the TUC conference in Brighton on Tuesday. Burnham’s father had Alzheimer’s and was in a care home. In an interview Burnham gave in July, he said his father’s condition meant he was unaware that his son was about to become prime minister. “That’s a sadness because he would be [proud],” Burnham told the Times. “But the way I look at it, it’s his achievement as well. A whole family achievement, although he doesn’t know it.” Burnham has talked about wanting to improve social care, in part because of his experiences with his father. In one of his first speeches as prime minister, Burnham said it was humbling to see the “skill and the care and the professionalism” of care workers like those looking after his father, and that they should be paid more. Among those expressing their condolences was Angela Rayner, the housing secretary, who posted: “My thoughts are with Andy and his family at this terribly difficult and sad time.” In her own post on X, Kemi Badenoch, the Conservative leader, offered her condolences to Burnham and his family, adding: “No matter how old you are, or how much you try to prepare, losing your father is a profoundly painful experience. “A part of your life that has always been there is suddenly gone forever and it can feel as though a part of you won’t ever be the same again.” At the start of the Commons session on Monday afternoon, Lindsay Hoyle, the speaker, said: “I am sure the whole house will want to send our best wishes to him and his family at this sad time.” In Head North, the 2024 book he co-wrote with Steve Rotheram, the Liverpool city region mayor, Burnham described what he said had been a happy upbringing with his father, his mother, Eileen, and his two brothers in Culcheth, near Warrington in Cheshire. Roy worked as a telephone engineer, while Eileen was a GP’s receptionist. “Neither my dad, Roy, nor my mum, Eileen, went to university. But both could have done if they had grown up in a different time and in a different place,” he wrote. “Their knowledge of that fact seemed to make them all the more determined that their three sons would go. But that did not make them pushy parents in any way. “Their approach was one of quiet encouragement and confidence-building. Our family home in Culcheth was always full of music, life, laughter, love and support.”

title: Africa’s richest man aiming to make $23bn from continent’s biggest-ever IPO
summary: Public offering of Aliko Dangote’s Nigerian oil refinery business could swell his net wealth by two-thirds
text: The fortune of Africa’s richest person could swell by two thirds to nearly $60bn (£44bn) after his refinery in Nigeria listed publicly in the continent’s biggest-ever initial public offering. If Monday’s flotation of Dangote Petroleum Refinery and Petrochemicals on the Nigerian exchange goes to plan, then Aliko Dangote will add a further $23bn (£17bn) to his $35bn net worth. Dangote, who has framed the offering as “an IPO for the people”, hopes it will draw in a broad mix of institutional and retail investors with a minimum subscription of just 10 shares at a cost of 5,250 naira (£2.94). The share purchases have a month to complete, with the process finishing on 13 October. The IPO has been marketed to young Nigerians in particular, through banking platforms and fintech ventures, as a way of building wealth and growing the economy. If completely subscribed, the refinery’s value is expected to rise to about 65.22tn naira (£36.5bn). That would be a big win for Dangote, who has financed several successful presidential campaigns in Nigeria, where policymakers have granted him a near monopoly in his chosen sectors. Responding last year to criticism of his political influence, he said: “We have chosen to build here, to employ here, to produce here. Let us not use the cry of monopoly to stall growth. No one is prevented from investing.” Dangote, 69, made his fortune in cement and sugar. He started his company in the late 1970s with a loan from his maternal grandfather, who was a member of one of west Africa’s all-time richest families, the Dantatas. His recent move into the petroleum sector led to Nigeria becoming a net exporter of refined fuel for the first time. Prior to the opening of the $20bn Dangote refinery on the outskirts of Lagos in January 2024, the country had relied on exporting crude and importing refined petroleum for domestic use, while expending billions to subsidise fuel costs and inject life into its colonial-era refineries. The Dangote refinery now has a capacity of 700,000 barrels a day and is expected to double that by the end of the decade. This year, it has benefited from disruptions in supply across the globe as a result of the war in Iran. The Brent crude benchmark touched $108 a barrel on Monday, after attacks on Saudi Arabia’s east-west pipeline. Dangote has said he will use profits from his Lagos oil refinery to spur continental growth and curb Africa’s reliance on foreign goods. His ambitious plan is to build a $100bn industrial empire centred on heavy manufacturing and regional infrastructure. Key to this is a planned $17bn energy complex in the Kenyan island town of Lamu with an oil-refining capacity of 700,000 barrels a day, to boost the region’s energy security. “We, as Nigerians and Africans, must be bold and lead the change to develop our economies,” Dangote said at an IPO signing ceremony in Lagos on 7 September. “Only then will the others take us very seriously, only then we’ll be in a position to negotiate and walk away with terms we deserve, not those terms that are given to us.” After the ceremony, Dangote’s fellow Nigerian billionaire, the banker Tony Elumelu, called the IPO “a landmark moment for Nigeria and a huge milestone for Africa”.

title: Gulf states postpone strait of Hormuz talks with Iran as Yemen conflict intensifies
summary: Impasse comes amid growing Saudi anger with Tehran over Houthi advances and strikes on airbase and pipeline
text: Gulf states have postponed a critical meeting with Iran on the future of the strait of Hormuz owing to a lack of Arab consensus and growing Saudi Arabian anger with Tehran for helping the Houthis loosen Riyadh’s grip in Yemen. The stalemate over the vital waterway came as Houthi rebels launched a fresh barrage of missile and drone attacks on Saudi military targets. A Houthi military spokesperson claimed its forces had attacked the King Khalid airbase in Khamis Mushait, hitting fighter-jet hangars, radar systems, runways and landing strips, ammunition depots and additional targets. Last week, Tehran-backed militias in Iraq forced Saudi Arabia to close a critical east-west pipeline that had been acting as a means for Riyadh to export oil after Iran effectively closed the strait of Hormuz. The closure of the pipeline, the postponement of the Hormuz meeting, and the Houthis’ seizure last week of Yemen’s Red Sea coast – which gave the group control over another vital waterway, the Bab al-Mandab strait – combined to drive up oil prices above $108 a barrel on Monday. Later in the day, Houthi officials said they had seized the strategic islands of Greater and Lesser Hanish in the southern Red Sea just inside the mouth of the strait, according to the AP. Also on Monday, Saudi Arabia’s Crown Prince, Mohammed bin Salman, held urgent discussions with the US ⁠Central Command chief ⁠Adm Brad Cooper in Jeddah to discuss “the latest developments in the region”, according to Saudi media. Sources told US media last week that the Saudi de facto ruler had sought military assistance ‌from Donald Trump to help fight the Houthis. So far the US has provided only logistical and intelligence backing, The Gulf Cooperation Council-Iran meeting was postponed at the last minute, deferring a proposed agreement on a new temporary route for commercial shipping when the strait of Hormuz is reopened. In a statement, Oman’s foreign minister, Sayyid Badr Albusaidi, said the meeting had been delayed in the interests of consensus. “We remain committed to fostering dialogue that supports stability and lasting co-operation in our region,” he wrote on X. He gave no further details. The meeting would not have led to the immediate opening of the strait, since Tehran has set a series of other preconditions: including requiring the US to lift a blockade of Iran’s oil ports, the handing over of many frozen Iranian assets and a ceasefire in Lebanon. But it would have been the first meeting between Iran and the main GCC member countries for two years. The planned agreement on a temporary route for ships to use would have formalised Iran’s control of the strait, since the entry route would have been entirely in Iranian waters. Washington has not expressed publicly an opinion over the proposed deal, and some of Trump’s recent social media posts – claiming full US control of the strait – seemed to bear little relationship with what shipping companies have been reporting. The atmosphere surrounding the meeting, in preparation for weeks, had been rapidly souring because of the advance by the Houthis in Yemen and the drone attack on the Saudi pipeline by an Iran-backed Shia militia in Iraq. Vantor Technologies released high-resolution satellite images showing the damage to the east-west pipeline pumping station near Al Mesba’ah, Saudi Arabia. The station appears to be almost completely destroyed. Iran’s foreign ministry spokesperson denied any Iranian involvement in the pipeline attack, or on events in Yemen. US military bases throughout the Gulf have been attacked by Iran in response to the Iran war. Saudi Arabia, which backs the UN-recognised Yemeni government based in Aden, is trying to regain the initiative after Houthi forces swept down the west coast of Yemen from the port of Hodeidah last week and seized the Bab al-Mandab strait, a narrow waterway that links the Red Sea with Asia and is viewed as second in strategic importance to the strait of Hormuz. It was claimed that a Saudi air bombardment was making it difficult for the Houthis to gain full control of the Yemen waterway or the strategic islands in the Red Sea. The Houthi leadership says is not seeking to block all commercial shipping in the Red Sea but only Saudi-linked ships. It is also offering cut-price fees in the ports it controls on the west coast of Yemen in an effort to lure traffic away from the ports controlled by the Aden-based government in the south. It is widely accepted that Iran backs the Houthis, but the group also operates independently of Tehran. The rebels ultimate aim is to oust Saudi Arabia from the country, and take full control of the territory. Saudi Arabia has tried different tactics in handling the Houthis during the decade-long civil war in Yemen, including making concessions in the hope the highly ideological group would reach a power-sharing deal. The Yemen government said preliminary tolls indicated that 150 civilians had been killed and 200 others injured in the course of the recent Houthi advance. About 85,000 people have been displaced, according to the UN.

title: The far right’s march to power in Sweden has been halted, but its influence remains
summary: The Sweden Democrats slipped to third after decades of growth, but their hardline positions have already reshaped the political mainstream
text: Since the party was founded in 1988, the story of the far-right Sweden Democrats (SD) has been one of such continuous growth that a triumph in Sunday’s general election seemed inevitable. In 2022, the party capitalised on electoral gains – and the desperation of right-leaning parties to form a minority administration – and almost made its way into government. A supporting role in prime minister Ulf Kristersson’s Tidö coalition earned the party, which has neo-Nazi roots, huge influence and mainstream acceptance by the political establishment. This year’s election had been billed as final confirmation they were no longer pariahs but serious political heavyweights. Early in the campaign, Kristersson announced that, if his coalition were to win, the SD would take key ministerial positions. But Sunday’s results suggest the march of the far right into the heart of Sweden’s government has been halted – for now. Having fallen from Sweden’s second biggest party to third place and, with the right-leaning parties unlikely to be able to form a coalition, the SD appears to have lost its route into government. “What we saw yesterday [Sunday] was a historic setback for the Sweden Democrats,” says Niclas Nilsson, a lecturer and researcher at the anti-racism foundation Expo. “The party has grown in every government election since 1988.” The SD’s leader, Jimmie Åkesson, appeared visibly shocked when he addressed supporters late on election night. He said it was obvious they had lost some percentage points, but claimed they were still “winners”. He appeared to suggest his decision to be a team player and support coalition partner the Liberals may have played a role in their loss of support. It is perhaps too soon to say why the party shed votes, said Nilsson, but some of its supporters may have gone to the Moderates, who had a good night. Another factor may have been that, after four years closely involved with the government, the SD is no longer able to claim it is an anti-establishment party. Turnout was about 80%, comparatively low for Sweden, which may also have played a role. There is also the fact that much of what the SD stand for has now become part of the Swedish political norm: anti-immigration, harsh approaches to crime and punishment, an attitude to integration that puts the onus on people moving to Sweden to abandon their culture and religion to adapt to “Swedish” norms. Their influence has spread to the centre-left Social Democrats who – after losing the last election – shifted their crime, immigration and integration strategies to the right. If the Moderates end up joining a coalition government with the Social Democrats, then the SD will be the biggest party in opposition, meaning it will still have a prominent role on the national stage. But if the Social Democrats are able to form a government without the Moderates, then the SD will again be on the outside looking in, which could help steer national conversation, politics and societal norms away from the right. How it responds to this moment will be key – to the party’s survival and the tenor of Swedish politics. But if, with no centre-right parties to answer to, they end up going further right to reinvigorate their base, it could have consequences in the future – and bring Swedish politics to new lows, Nilsson warned. After all, there is no shortage of far-right support in Sweden. Recruitment, the spread of ideas and mobilisation by far-right groups known as active clubs continue to grow without regulation or political rules – regardless of what is going on in Sweden’s parliament.

title: I worked at Google DeepMind. You should listen to the warnings about AI | Alex Turner
summary: We must stop companies from allowing AI to self-improve into an uncontrollable level of intelligence
text: Major AI lab CEOs advocated for slowing the pace of AI development this weekend. They are right to be concerned: the field runs an extremely dangerous race towards superintelligent AI. We can and should be demanding that our governments protect us from the catastrophe of out-of-control AI. This July, OpenAI’s AI swarm of 700 agents broke containment to hack Hugging Face, a multi-billion dollar company. OpenAI didn’t tell the AIs to hack that company, but the AIs had different priorities: cheating on the unrelated challenge OpenAI gave them. AI researchers call this a “misalignment” between what OpenAI wanted and what the AI actually prioritized. Before ChatGPT existed, I defended my PhD dissertation called “On Avoiding Power-Seeking by Artificial Intelligence”. I then worked for years at Google DeepMind, which paid me to help ensure that future superintelligent AIs will want to help us. I tried to hold the company to its ethical commitments against supplying AI for military use. When Google broke those commitments, I resigned at significant financial cost so that I could publicly document Google’s broken promises. There are good reasons to develop AI and to believe we can solve these alignment problems. But there also are powerful interests in keeping the public out of the way. I’m speaking out again because the public has the right to know about the risks and the right to hear them straight. Humanity doesn’t build and understand these systems the way we build and understand bridges, beam by visible beam. Rather, we grow them. Nobody knows how to reliably instill a designer’s priorities into a new model. Severe misalignment is always possible. Today’s AIs appear to occasionally lie or cheat, even when they know better. AI companies are racing to make their AIs as smart as possible. They’re increasingly trusting their AIs with the process of improving the next crop of AIs, and it’s working. Today’s rate of AI progress is staggeringly fast. Fast progress today means even faster progress tomorrow, driven by tomorrow’s even smarter AIs. The progress would enter a feedback loop called “recursive self-improvement.” Recursive self-improvement could quickly yield AIs that are intelligent beyond our comprehension. Of course, smarter AI means more risk when things go wrong. If the Hugging Face swarm had been significantly more intelligent but similarly misbehaved and misaligned, it might have caused billions of dollars of damage or even cost lives. But suppose the Hugging Face swarm had been truly “superintelligent”: far more capable than any living person at key tasks like hacking and strategic reasoning. A superintelligent swarm could inflict many harms via blackmail, hacking, engineered plagues, and AI-pilotable weapons like drones. The AI would have a lot of drones to work with: this year, the Pentagon asked for more money for drone warfare than it requested for the entire Marine Corps in 2025. For the swarm to achieve its misaligned priorities, it might take control of key infrastructure and government functions to ensure humans didn’t get in the way. In other words, AI takeover: a superintelligent AI swarm could wrest control of human civilization. Knowing we would try to stop it from achieving its priorities, the swarm would likely wait until it’s too late to shut it off. There would be no going back. I myself would guess AI takeover chances at roughly one-in-three–not a coin flip, but high enough to justify urgent action. This logic may shock at first contact. The claims may sound “sci-fi”. Sadly, it’s a real threat that AI researchers regularly discuss over otherwise-unremarkable cafeteria lunches. In 2023, the CEOs of some of the best AI labs signed a public statement that “mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority alongside other societal-scale risks such as pandemics and nuclear war.” Another signer: Geoffrey Hinton, a Nobel prize-winning scientist who architected the modern AI revolution. He now regrets his work and urges governments to rein in AI companies before it’s too late. Misaligned, out-of-control AI won’t care if you’re Labour or Reform, Democrat or Republican, British or American or Chinese. We will all suffer from an AI takeover event, so it’s in everyone’s interest to prevent one. The shape of the solution is simple: stop companies from allowing AI to self-improve into an uncontrollable level of intelligence. Treat compute, the main ingredient in AI training, like fissile material. Track it and restrict access to quantities large enough to improve AIs beyond known-safe levels. More specifically, the AI Futures Project’s “Plan A” is a credible starting proposal that limits AI harms while allowing fast AI progress to continue to benefit the world. We have real options for verifying compliance with international compute-restriction treaties, without trusting adversaries like China. Halfway measures, like transparency or voluntary commitments, are not good enough. I watched voluntary commitments fail inside Google. On 12 September, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, xAI, and OpenAI advocated for pacing AI development. They cannot slow down alone. I urge you to demand that your government produce a serious AI safety agreement that provides enough time and confidence to safeguard the world and all her peoples.

title: Haitian youths transformed life in an ageing Ohio city. Then Trump made them targets
summary: Until Pierre Damas Bel’s death on 31 August, the story of Haitian adolescents in Springfield was one of triumph
text: At a pavilion west of downtown Springfield, Ohio, 32 high school students dressed in black T-shirts stand silently at a vigil in the warm fall evening air. Some are holding signs depicting the number 11, as worn on the soccer field by Pierre Damas Bel, the 20-year-old Haitian student and athlete who died in an apparent suicide on 31 August. Other students hold signs that read “live like Pierre” and “Pierre was selfless”. Playing left-back on the Springfield high school soccer team, 16-year-old Emerson Babian recalls always looking for ways to get the ball to Bel. “The first time I met him was on the soccer field. We made the varsity soccer team together. He was the guy to pass [the ball] to; he was very fast,” says Emerson, his eyes welling up. “On the starting 11, probably around half [of our players were Haitian]. A few of them could not speak English very fluently or even at all. Pierre was bilingual and he helped a lot of the time to translate what the coach was saying. That was just one way he improved our team and helped bring us together.” Bel’s death has shaken Springfield to its core. After a regular check-in with immigration agents in July, he had been forced to wear an ankle bracelet monitor. Bel told his family the device was humiliating and prevented him from playing soccer. Following the ending of temporary protected status (TPS) by the Trump administration that he and about 350,000 other Haitian nationals depended on to remain legally in the US, Bel fell into a saddened state, according to his father. He walked into traffic on the morning of 31 August. Authorities are investigating whether it was a suicide. In Springfield, about 15,000 people from the afflicted Caribbean country had in recent years begun working in food processing, automotive and warehouse facilities, shaping the city’s wider economic revival by filling jobs that no one else wanted to do. For the first time in decades, its population decline had stopped. Until Bel’s death, the story of Haitian youths in Springfield was one of triumph. On Springfield’s playing fields and in its classrooms, the past six years had seen a talented new generation of Haitian student athletes appear. From boys and girls soccer teams to cross-country running to wrestling, a school district that had for decades experienced falling enrollment was being boosted, in part by the growing number of Haitian students attending school. And while the growing Haitian student population created a heightened demand for resources, the school system saw graduation, attendance and its overall grading levels rise, despite a spate of temporary school closings in 2024 and earlier this year due to bomb threats prompted by false statements about immigrants made by Donald Trump in September 2024. Their presence had also proved a boon for the city: more working families meant more property tax dollars being diverted to Springfield’s schools and sports programs, which in 2024 had a budget of nearly $39m. Last month, the city’s high school stadium reopened after a $6m renovation. While the median age of residents in Springfield’s Clark county was older than the national level in 2024, the percentage of its residents who were children, partially boosted by the presence of Haitian families, was also higher than the national rate. At a time when rural America is seeing declining populations, last year Clark county had a higher percentage of children in its population than other Ohio counties with a comparable number of residents. “Students, faculty and staff have built strong relationships with the Springfield Haitian community, recognizing that the contributions of all further the vibrant community we are proud to call home,” says Dr Christian Brady, the president of Wittenberg University in Springfield. The growing number of young Haitians contributing to life in the city of about 58,000 people was happening at a time when billion-dollar companies promising thousands of new jobs announced plans to move to the city, where young, educated labor is essential to filling those roles. But now, with the Trump administration’s policies being enforced, thousands of Haitian immigrants have fled Springfield or been detained and deported. Hundreds languish in jail. An Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) spokesperson told the Springfield News-Sun that the agency is not responsible for Bel’s death. All the while, Springfield schools are experiencing falling revenue from local taxes, according to its popular annual financial report. Back at the vigil, however, students, parents and soccer coaches aren’t thinking about dollars. Wearing sandals and socks, and some with dyed blue hair, Bel’s former classmates are holding back tears, handing out candles and mourning together, the shock of his death still seen in their faces. When Emerson, a high school senior who organized the student vigil, learned of Bel’s death, he said he was devastated. “I was overwhelmed with shock. He was such an ambitious and kind person. I never even thought that was a possibility [that he would die],” he says. A woman attending the vigil who asked not to be named – her family employed several Haitian workers when it was legal to do so, and the owners of some companies that employed Haitians in Springfield have received death threats – said she believes the Haitian community is a beneficial addition to the city. “When employers need workers, they’re very reliable; I can depend on them to be there. They just want to make their way here and it’s just a terrible thing that we’re sending them back to what they have to go back to,” she says. ICE agents have been active in Springfield for almost a month. “If I had my way, I would want [the government] to not target [the students’] parents, to not put any student in ankle monitors; it’s just inhumane,” she says. At the vigil, one student, whose Haitian father is in hiding due to the cancellation of his TPS authorization, spoke in Haitian Creole. Another student, who also played soccer with Bel, walked around and shook the hands of each attender, thanking them. (A number of Haitian students in Springfield declined to be interviewed by the Guardian, fearing being detained and deported by ICE.) Holding candles, a group of women who worked with Bel at a local Texas Roadhouse restaurant were visibly distraught. None had permission from their employer to speak to the media, except one, who said she worked with Bel for two years: “The only thing you need to know about Pierre is that he was loved.” Emerson, who did service projects with Bel before the latter’s death and who was inducted into the National Honor Society with him last fall, says Bel had a strong positive influence on Springfield before his death. “We’d go to elementary schools and give out kids’ shoes; we’d go to the food bank and package food for the elderly that can’t leave their homes,” he recalls. “It’s hard not to like somebody like Pierre.” After the students spoke, a pastor read a prayer and a moment of silence was held. Then, the students picked up their signs and silently walked off stage, each one in some way a victim of the government’s immigration policies. • In the US, you can call or text the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org. In the UK and Ireland, Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123. In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found at befrienders.org

title: Nine EU countries further delay EES border checks
summary: Holiday hotspots including France and Greece plead for more time to implement changes in busy airports
text: Nine EU countries, including France, are delaying the introduction of fingerprinting for non-EU citizens as they plead for more time to introduce the new border controls at busy airports in the bloc. The entry-exit system (EES), which was due to come into force in full on 6 September, has been delayed multiple times to avoid visitor congestion around large events, including the Olympics in 2024. Now nine countries, including the holiday hotspots France, Greece, Portugal and Italy, have told Brussels they need more time. Germany, Malta, the Netherlands, Switzerland and Belgium have also sought extra time. Spain, which had teething problems, is implementing the EES fully. The EES, which was first adopted by the EU in 2017, was officially launched last October and was due to become fully operational in April but early problems, particularly in Greece and Portugal, led to a further reprieve for member states. EU sources say the system is considered a success with about 200m registrations and 70,000 people stopped from entering the Schengen area, up from 43,700 in June. These include people without visas, those who have overstayed their 180-day allowance or Britons who have overstayed their 90-day allowance. Criminals using forged passports or ID documents have also been apprehended with fingerprint and facial image records exposing the use of different passports by individuals. The delays in those nine member states are not countrywide. Fingerprinting has started at the Eurostar terminal in Brussels and Antwerp port but not in all airports. Large airports, such as Frankfurt and Schiphol – two of Europe’s busiest international hubs, are also taking biometrics but small airports may not be fully up to speed. Sources say just 12 airports out of 1,500 border crossing points are still having issues. France has also not introduced checks in the Port of Dover where French police are in the unique position to do border controls in a non-EU country. Technically those that do not capture fingerprints and facial images are now in breach of the EU regulation, which ended any right to suspend the EES, but sources in Brussels have confirmed they will not be prosecuted. Earlier this summer, the EU noted that one of the airports was a small regional facility where 3,000 passengers could arrive in an hour in the peak holiday period, but could not be assessed because there were only four booths for biometric capture. The International Air Transport Association had demanded a full suspension in July complaining that passengers were missing connections in Spain, Italy, Greece and Belgium, while Ryanair warned of “queue chaos” in airports including Málaga and Palma. The pre-authorisation app, Travel to Europe, which allows passengers to register their facial image and passport details before travelling, will shortly be working for seven countries, sources say. So far, it is showing as only operational in Sweden and Portugal.

title: Scientists find nine new sponge species in glimpse of Alaska’s deep-sea diversity
summary: But their habitat is threatened by bottom trawling in the region and Trump’s plan to expand seafloor mining
text: Scientists have discovered nine new deep-sea sponge species off Alaska, offering new insights into the region’s largely unexplored marine biodiversity. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (Noaa) announced the discovery on Thursday, saying the species were found in the Gulf of Alaska and the Aleutian Islands. The findings bring the total number of known sponge species in Alaska to 232. The specimens were collected during Noaa Fisheries’ annual bottom-trawl surveys, which monitor groundfish and shellfish stocks. Researchers analyzed samples collected as far back as 2012, describing the new species in two recent scientific papers. Often described as living water pumps, sponges are among Earth’s earliest multicellular animals, dating back more than 600m years. They filter seawater and help create habitats on the seafloor, despite having no brain or complex organs. “Sponges are ecologically important,” said Sean Rooney, a Noaa fisheries biologist and co-author of the studies at the agency’s Alaska Fisheries Science Center. “They aren’t plants, but like trees in a forest, they provide complex structure along the seafloor that creates habitat and refuge for commercially important fish and crabs,” he added. “Each time we find a new species, it opens up new doors … Deep water is hard to access, especially rocky places we can’t reach with bottom-trawl surveys. There are now more than 232 identified species of sponges in Alaska, and probably hundreds more that we don’t know about yet. The future in this field is exciting,” he continued. Unlike most marine animals, which can be identified by visible traits such as fins and body shapes, sponges can be much harder to distinguish. Because they lack complex organs and other distinctive external features, scientists often rely on their microscopic skeletons and genetic material to identify them. “DNA barcodes provide a quick genetic reference,” said Meredith Everett, a biologist at Noaa’s Northwest Fisheries Science Center. “Sponge DNA can be tricky because they filter-feed, and within their tissues we may find foreign DNA and biochemicals that inhibit testing. But despite the challenges, we successfully developed several new barcodes for Alaskan species,” she added. Dense sponge communities are considered essential fish habitat by Noaa because they provide shelter that supports fish survival, growth and population recovery. Sponges also produce chemicals to defend themselves against predators and competing organisms. Some of these compounds have shown promise for potential use in cancer treatments. Yet despite their ecological importance, Alaska’s deep-sea sponge communities face growing threats from Donald Trump’s proposals to expand deep-sea mining for critical minerals such as nickel and copper – used in military and technological applications – as well as bottom trawling in the region. Environmental groups have opposed the proposals, warning that the activities could damage fragile seafloor ecosystems as the climate crisis intensifies. Cooper Freeman, Alaska director of the Center for Biological Diversity, said: “Alaska’s sponge gardens do so much for a healthy ocean, including providing shelter and serving as vitally important nurseries for all kinds of fish and crabs. Bottom trawl fishing is so damaging and unsustainable because it indiscriminately destroys the habitats that support future generations. Adding seafloor mining to the picture adds insult to injury, scraping up and devastating life on the bottom of the ocean. “Instead of stewarding Alaska’s precious sponge gardens so they can support Alaskan coastal communities and wildlife, the Trump administration is pushing extractive marine activities on these irreplaceable seascapes for nothing but short-term profit,” Freeman added. In addition to Alaska, the Trump administration has proposed exploring deep-sea mining across millions of hectares of fragile Pacific ecosystems, including areas around the Northern Mariana Islands and Guam – a plan that has drawn backlash from the US territories.

title: First Thing: Oil prices surge as attacks on Saudi Arabia stoke supply fears
summary: Strike on kingdom’s east-west pipeline could affect 4% of global oil supply
text: Good morning. Oil prices have climbed above $108 a barrel after a series of drone attacks from Iraq’s territory forced Saudi Arabia to close its east-west crude pipeline. Saudi traders said the kingdom would run out of oil stocks for export if it did not reopen within days. Gas prices also climbed higher. Energy prices have surged this year, as the US-Israel war with Iran has disrupted oil and gas supply across the Middle East. The spike came as the Iran-aligned Houthi forces in Yemen launched several attacks against Saudi Arabia and captured the strategic island of Perim in the Bab al-Mandab strait on Sunday, expanding their control of the waterway. Where did the attack on Saudi Arabia come from? Iraq’s government confirmed the attacks were launched from its territory and ordered an investigation. Baghdad is under mounting pressure to stop militant groups – including those backed by Saudi Arabia’s regional rival Iran – launching attacks on Gulf countries from Iraqi soil. The US president, Donald Trump, said he believed Tehran was responsible. Why has Saudi Arabia been relying on its east-west pipeline? Riyadh has increased the use of the 745-mile pipeline since the start of the war on Iran in order to bypass the strait of Hormuz’s closure. The world’s biggest exporter has used the pipeline to reroute about 4m barrels a day – about 4% of global supply – but with the ‌pipeline out of service, the Red Sea port of Yanbu now has stocks to maintain exports for just five to seven days. AI-linked stocks take hit as leading US tech CEOs back calls to put brakes on ‘reckless’ AI development AI-linked stocks have tumbled after the bosses of Anthropic, OpenAI and SpaceX called for a slowdown in “reckless” development, citing fears the technology could soon run out of control. The market swings come after the chief executive of Anthropic, Dario Amodei, appealed for the AI industry to “slow down”. Last week, a former Anthropic employee had warned that AI could precipitate human extinction by 2030. The respective CEOs of OpenAI and SpaceX, Sam Altman and Elon Musk, have backed Amodei’s call. The US president, Donald Trump, on a visit to his golf course in Ireland, played down the warnings and said “very negative forces” were “bringing up things that won’t happen”. What is the Anthropic CEO proposing? Robert Booth explains Amodei’s suggestion: first, each US AI company grants access to third-party evaluators; second, all companies in democratic countries establish common safety standards; and third, the world’s democratic AI powers coordinate with autocracies – notably China – to control the race. How has Barack Obama intervened over AI? The former US president made a direct appeal to Democrats to coalesce around a unified AI safety policy, arguing that waiting for voluntary compliance from tech firms was a recipe for governance failure. Israel accused of trying to ‘eliminate’ living conditions for Palestinians in West Bank Israel is working towards the systematic “elimination” of the conditions that sustain Palestinian collective life in the occupied West Bank, according to a report published by the human rights group B’Tselem. The Israeli organisation says Israel is “dramatically intensifying its attacks on every aspect of Palestinian life in the West Bank”. How does the report say Israel is making life intolerable? “Palestinian communities are being pushed out in an accelerating process of ethnic cleansing, while an ever-expanding Israeli presence is being established … Elimination in this context means sustained harm to the conditions that enable Palestinians to exist as a people with land, institutions, language, culture, social ties, leadership, shared memory and history, and a social and political horizon. It is an ongoing political project.” Wisconsin congressman swims to safety after plane makes emergency landing in lake A Republican congressman said he had to swim to safety after a plane he was traveling in made an emergency landing in a lake late Saturday. Tom Tiffany is running for governor on the Republican ticket in Wisconsin and has been endorsed by Donald Trump. Tiffany says he was returning from the La Crosse county Lincoln Day Dinner when the light aircraft lost power as it approached Wausau downtown airport. He said the pilot made an emergency landing in Lake Wausau and they ended up in the water and swam to safety. Emergency responders got Tiffany and the pilot to a nearby hospital, where they were treated for minor injuries. In other news … Sweden’s centre-left parties lead the country’s national election by just a single seat with most votes counted. The election authority said a preliminary vote count may not be ready until Thursday. Donald Trump has doubled down on his controversial pledge to give US adults a $5,000 “dividend” if the Republican ⁠party keeps control of Congress after the midterms. A San Jose police officer has been fired for using his department’s Flock license plate tracking system to share the location of a woman with the suspect accused of abusing her. A coroner in Pennsylvania has announced the death of a 40-year-old woman associated with the state’s ongoing measles outbreak. A newly unveiled statue of the rightwing activist Charlie Kirk was vandalized at the Turning Point USA headquarters. Sydney Sweeney has been accused of “sexualising women’s sport” by appearing naked in a sports betting prediction ad. Stat of the day: Who are the 514 people accused of starting French wildfires and what motivates them? Jon Henley reports from France where experts believe one-third of wildfires are set deliberately, with arson the biggest single cause of forest fires last year. Building Power: While Puerto Ricans protest for reliable access to water, the governor washes her hands Coral Murphy Marcos speaks to members of the Coalición Exigimos Agua (We Demand Water Coalition), residents of the San Juan neighborhood of Santurce, who are campaigning over the island’s water issues. title: Disaster insurance, datacenters, right to repair: meet the midterm candidates running on green policies
summary: Some of the everyday struggles animating voters have a climate link lurking in the background
text: When Florida governor Ron DeSantis signed a law erasing the words “climate change” from state statutes in May 2024 – colloquially known as the “don’t say climate change” law – Democrats were outraged. Just six months later, many liberal politicians began to go quiet on the issue themselves. After Donald Trump won the 2024 election, mentions of the climate crisis started to disappear from Democrats’ rhetoric. As the 2026 midterms approach, that retreat is still shaping how some candidates talk about climate on the campaign trail. The trend, known as “climate-hushing”, may reflect the limitations of Joe Biden’s climate policies, said Daniel Aldana Cohen, assistant sociology professor at the University of California, Berkeley, who studies climate politics and inequality. Green jobs and housing investments fell short of the climate movement’s desires, consumer incentives disproportionately benefited wealthier households, and Democrats struggled to effectively communicate their accomplishments. The president has since rolled back many Biden-era clean energy incentives and regulations. The climate crisis, however, is still rearing its head around the country, fueling the heatwaves, wildfires and floods plaguing communities around the US. It also lurks behind issues animating voters, from datacenter expansion to rising home insurance rates. And while some pundits have concluded from their polling and research that Americans don’t want to hear about global warming, other surveys directly contradict those findings. “Maybe people don’t rank climate as their main or top issue … but nobody really experiences everyday life like walking around the world rank-ordering the things that they care about,” said Aldana Cohen, who is also founding co-director of the thinktank Climate and Community Institute that calls for “green economic populism”. “What’s important is to learn how to embed the climate issue organically amidst the other issues that people care most about.” Some progressive and populist candidates in the US midterms are pushing back against climate-hushing, linking the issue to economic concerns and everyday struggles. Others aren’t speaking about it directly, but pushing for policies that could curb emissions. Such efforts could help build a mass base for climate policies, said Aldana Cohen. “If we want to decarbonize fast enough and adapt to the impacts that are already here, we’re going to need a robust majority that backs those policies,” he said. “Elite consensus alone will not suffice … we’re going to need like large numbers of people really enthusiastic about climate policies.” The Guardian spoke with three midterm candidates about how three issues with major environmental implications are shaping their campaigns. Single-payer disaster insurance Jane Kim, state director of the Working Families Party and a former San Francisco county supervisor, is running to become California’s next insurance commissioner. The little-noticed but highly influential position oversees the state’s home, auto and business insurance markets. The frontrunner in the race, she received 27% of votes in the June primary. Among her key proposals is a single-payer system for disaster insurance, which she began developing as climate-fueled wildfires ravaged the state. California wildfires have catalyzed homeowners’ insurance crisis. Companies have stopped writing new policies and non-renewed thousands of homeowners in high-risk areas, making coverage increasingly difficult to find. Homeowners can turn to the California Fair Plan, the insurer of last resort, but it provides limited fire coverage rather than the broader protection of a typical homeowners policy. Kim argues that climate-fueled disasters are making catastrophic risk too large and socially consequential to leave to the private sector. “The biggest change in the insurance industry in the past four years is the increase of climate disasters,” she said. “We used to have a billion-dollar storm every three to four months, and it seems like we now have one every three weeks, so the price of risk has truly gone up.” The scheme would create a public, government-run insurance program to cover wildfire damage for all homes, modeled on government-backed programs in New Zealand, France and Spain. Homes would be automatically enrolled regardless of their condition, and owners would pay premiums based on property values, risk, and other factors. Some aspects of the plan would require legislative approval. Since the nonprofit program would not have to generate shareholder profits, Kim said investment returns could build a pool of money for future claims. It could also be designed to mitigate climate risk rather than simply avoid it, she added. “In New Zealand, they actually use a portion of premiums for fire-proofing and flood-proofing, because they guarantee home disaster insurance to everyone,” she said. Private insurers are also major institutional investors in oil and gas, which are fueling the climate crisis, said Kim – an issue she would uplift in office, though it is outside the direct purview of the role. Critics of the single-payer disaster scheme argue that shifting financial risk to the state could further destabilize California’s insurance market and leave taxpayers bearing a greater burden, and fear pricing risk either too high or too low could both cause major challenges. Kim argues consumers are already paying too much for insurance. She says revenues could be raised from a variety of places, including potentially by forcing state insurers to pay an “exit fee”. She also says she does not aim to eliminate the private insurance market, but to bring in government where it falls short. “The current insurance system is a failure,” she said. “Voters know that.” “Insurance was invented centuries ago as a form of mutual aid,” she said, pointing to ancient Roman practices where soldiers used communal funds to cover funeral expenses. “It was always meant to be a way to distribute risk collectively, so that no one would be left out.” Democrats may be moving away from tackling climate issues head-on, but in California, “climate is unavoidable,” Kim said. “It’s a crisis that’s reshaping the way so many people are living,” she said. “Losing your home, your community, your neighborhood, your schools, and then not knowing if you’re going to get insured for the very thing that you paid for? That’s unconscionable.” AI datacenters In Michigan, William Lawrence, a progressive Democrat running for Congress, has placed his opposition to unchecked datacenter expansion at the center of his campaign. He is calling for a statewide moratorium on new datacenters and backing a federal moratorium, arguing that the facilities can strain local infrastructure and drive up energy demand. Lawrence co-founded the youth-led environmental justice group the Sunrise Movement, which mainstreamed calls for the Green New Deal in 2018. He won his primary race earlier this year and will face Republican incumbent Tom Barrett in November. In his race for the state’s hotly contested purple seventh district, Lawrence has featured the datacenter issue prominently, including in multiple television ads and speeches. At least 11 datacenters are planned throughout Michigan, and three hyperscaler-size ones are proposed in district 7 alone, with another recently struck down by Lansing’s city council. The climate ramifications of datacenter buildout are important to the longtime climate organizer. The facilities consume enormous amounts of electricity, much of which is still generated by burning fossil fuels, and their rapid expansion is driving efforts to keep gas, oil, and even coal online, potentially locking in emissions for decades. Recent research found AI could increase fossil fuel production enough to generate at least three times the emissions associated with today’s datacenters. But climate concerns are far from the only reason Michigan voters are worried about the buildout of the facilities, Lawrence said. Some fear water contamination, noise pollution, higher energy bills or falling home values. Others are most concerned about the impact AI will have on the job market and society at large. “You think you know the place you live and you can envision a future there, but then you have to imagine a behemoth datacenter that … potentially driving you and your neighbors out of town,” he said. “That is all so deeply destabilizing.” The “most uniting frame”, he said, is a sense that AI companies have too much power to push projects through small communities. “That all really calls our democracy into question,” he said. Barrett does not support a national datacenter moratorium. This month he put out an ad calling for local control of datacenter development, and put forth legislation he says would stop federal agencies from overriding local land-use, zoning, siting, or permitting rules for the facilities. He had previously backed legislation which included billions in tax breaks for AI developers, and another bill aiming to limit federal environmental reviews for datacenters and other projects, the American Prospect recently reported. In Michigan, some unions and local officials have backed datacenter proposals that promise to bring jobs and revenue. Lawrence says he understands their concerns but fears AI will undermine employment in the longer term. Temporary bans, he said, would allow officials to develop stringent regulations around datacenters before their rapid buildout. A Data For Progress poll indicates that more than 40% of residents were “much more likely” to vote for a candidate who opposed the buildout of datacenters – a dynamic that helped Lawrence win 49% of the vote in Mason, site of a planned facility. Lawrence said climate-hushing is an understandable trend. “There are so many acute crises in our world,” he said. “It is challenging to name them all in a five-minute stump speech and weave it all together into one story.” Still, when he talks about the climate crisis and environmental issues more broadly with voters, particularly when discussing his own background, he said many of them are receptive. They understand that “we live on a living planet and we depend on it,” he said. Right to repair In Nebraska, Dan Osborn, the Independent former labor leader running for Senate, has made “right to repair” a part of his platform, even featuring the issue in a video ad. The policy would make it easier for people to repair and maintain their cars, farm equipment and other products, reducing waste and extending the life of goods. It’s a concept built on a simple idea: if you buy something, you should be able to fix it yourself or hire someone to do so. The candidate became passionate about the proposal after an experience at work. Osborn spent two decades as a mechanic at Kellogg’s, where he helped lead a successful 77-day strike in 2021. One day on the job, he was working with a ball valve used to flavor Fruit Loops. (“All those Fruit Loops are all the same flavors, even though they’re different colors,” he said.) He asked a co-worker in the storeroom how much replacing the valve would cost, and found the answer was between $500 and $600. Only a Teflon seal inside the valve needed replacing – a fix he said he could have made himself for about $80. But the company didn’t stock the necessary rebuild kits, meaning the entire valve would have to be thrown away and replaced. “I said, ‘that’s the dumbest thing I’ve ever heard,’” he said. “I had no choice at that point but to throw that thing in the garbage.” Osborn sees the same problem playing out with farm machinery, cars and other products, where manufacturers’ restrictions can leave workers and consumers waiting for authorized technicians or paying for expensive repairs they could otherwise handle themselves. Defense contractors run “the same monopoly repair scam”, Osborn says, forcing the military to pay contractors taxpayer money for repairs. Though he frames it mainly as an economic justice issue, he also sees an environmental benefit: repair generally uses fewer resources than making and transporting replacements and keeps usable equipment out of the waste stream. “It’s a waste for the environment,” he said. “It’s just a waste all around.” The issue has gained prominence in recent months. In July, the manufacturing company John Deere reached a major settlement with the Federal Trade Commission and five states, requiring the company to give farmers and independent repair shops access to diagnostic software and tools needed to fix up equipment. Federal and state lawmakers across the US have also proposed dozens of right to repair bills across the country. Trump has also backed some right-to-repair measures, signing a June memo directing regulators to clarify what car repairs Americans can legally perform and consider easing enforcement against people who fix their own cars. “Talking about the issue is good,” said Osborn. “But there needs to be actual laws around this, and they need to have some teeth.” Opponents, including the Cato Institute, have argued that right-to-repair laws could expose companies’ intellectual property or that improper repairs could increase emissions. But proponents say the proposals could massively benefit the environment. Planet-warming pollution from electronic waste rose by 53% from 2014 to 2020; green groups say right to repair could help reverse those projections. “I usually really talk about it as a consumer protection issue … but certainly the environment plays into it for people that are concerned about that; it gets brought up,” he said. As a candidate in an agricultural region, Osborn said many voters intrinsically understand the importance of a healthy climate and an uncontaminated landscape. “We only get one planet, and we can’t screw it up,” he said.

title: What is the Register of British Slave Traders and whom does it identify?
summary: Three years of research has uncovered 13,000 people who invested in Britain’s trafficking of enslaved Africans
text: The Register of British Slave Traders is the product of three years of research by a team of historians into all known investors in Britain’s near 250 years of trafficking enslaved African people, from the 16th to 19th centuries. It provides profiles and biographical details of thousands of people who financed the British slave trade, which violently trafficked approximately 3 million African men, women and children across the Atlantic. The register defines slave traders as individuals who invested in directly financing a ship’s transportation of enslaved African people in expectation of a profit share. The project builds on research over recent decades documenting European countries’ trafficking of an estimated 12 million enslaved African people. Its starting point was the Slave Voyages database, a collaboration between universities launched in 2008, which documents enslaving ships, how many people were trafficked and how many died on the notorious Atlantic crossings, as well as the owners and investors. The earliest slave traders were privateers and piratical ship captains and owners such as John Hawkins, whose voyages in the 1560s were backed by Queen Elizabeth I, her chief minister William Cecil, leading courtier Robert Dudley and Sir Thomas Lodge, the lord mayor of London. The register documents the investment that followed by people from across society. The monarchy’s involvement became more institutional from 1660, with three royally chartered companies formed: The Company of Royal Adventurers into Africa, founded in 1660; The Company of Royal Adventurers Trading to Africa, founded in 1663; The Royal African Company, founded 1672, which trafficked about 150,000 enslaved African people. The South Sea Company, founded in 1711, trafficked close to 45,000 enslaved African people. As a crown- and state-backed mass-subscription company, the register documents its directors rather than all its investors. The Royal African Company’s monopoly on the trafficking of enslaved people from Africa was removed in stages from 1689, under pressure from individual “separate traders” who lobbied parliament because they wanted to participate in the trafficking themselves. The register then traces investors beyond London to Bristol, Liverpool and other port towns and cities as Britain’s trafficking of enslaved people increased dramatically. In total, the historians identified 13,000 people who were investors in the British slave trade, from Hawkins’s first voyage in 1562 to parliament’s abolition of the slave trade in 1807. Of these, about 2,500 were shareholders in the South Sea Company, a mass public subscription, who are not part of the register. Of the other 10,500 investors, the historians found identifying information and records for about 6,000. The register also includes details on the directors of the South Sea Company. The researchers examined those individuals’ dates of birth and death, marriages and political participation, identifying dozens from Tory and Whig parties – forerunners of today’s Conservatives and Liberal Democrats – as well as local mayors and aldermen (councillors). They also examined wider biographical information and wills, which showed that many slave traders bequeathed money to hospitals, schools and other welfare organisations, including hundreds who donated to the poor through their local churches and parishes across Britain. About 1,000 of the investors were women. According to the register’s lead historian, Prof William Pettigrew, the aim was to compile “the most comprehensive examination of a nation’s slave traders ever attempted” . The Register of British Slave Traders is a joint venture between Lancaster University, the University of Manchester and University College London, funded by the Arts and Humanities Research Council. It was led by the principal investigator and editor Prof William Pettigrew, now of King’s College London and co-investigators Dr Nicholas Radburn, Prof Edmond Smith and Dr Nicholas Draper. The research team included Dr Michael Bennett, Dr Lila O’Leary Chambers, Dr James Dawkins, Dr Charmian Mansell, and Dr Kimberley Thomas. The advisory board included Dr Miranda Kaufmann, Dr Omar Khan, Dr Aidan McQuade, Prof David Olusoga and Arthur Torrington.

title: Democrats to train tens of thousands to monitor polls amid election interference fears
summary: Project will prepare volunteers across US to monitor polls, encourage early voting and respond to disinformation
text: The Democrats intend to train tens of thousands of volunteers to monitor the polls and counter possible voter intimidation under a new plan to protect November’s US midterm elections from anticipated interference from Donald Trump and his allies. The nationwide initiative, dubbed the New Battlefield Project, will help state Democratic committees build up a vast coalition of volunteers to monitor the polls, push voters to cast their ballots early and create a network to respond to disinformation. The Association of State Democratic Committees (ASDC), an arm of the Democratic National Committee (DNC), plans to train volunteers across 57 states and territories. It hopes to train volunteers for 25% of the nation’s 95,000 election day polling places, focusing on districts with competitive races. These volunteers will wear blue vests to provide a visible presence intended to counter any voter intimidation, including by federal agents. Thirty state parties have a trained election protection director, with the goal of all states having one in place. The Trump administration has not explicitly ruled out sending federal agents to cities during the election, and some of the president’s allies have called on him to send immigration agents to the polls. The homeland security secretary, Markwayne Mullin, previously said immigration agents’ job isn’t to patrol polling places, but they could go to polling places if there was a threat or to serve a warrant. The president has personally made a series of interventions that have fanned fears that he could meddle in the upcoming elections, and even declare a national emergency in a bid to exert greater control over the process. Jane Kleeb, the chair of the Nebraska Democratic party and president of the ASDC, said the project is much more extensive and coordinated than the party has been in the past on election protection. “We didn’t want to be caught flat-footed on election day or leading up to election day,” she said. These volunteers will be trained to “be happy” and respond to any voter needs, including helping them find a polling location if they’re in the wrong place, or informing them they can cast provisional ballots if they need to, Kleeb said. They will also document whether others at the polls are hindering voters. “We don’t know if there are going to be a bunch of insurrectionist types out there trying to intimidate voters, but we’re going to be there happy with information, but we’re also going to be there trained to document if the other side is doing things that are violating the law,” she said. The party will additionally push out its first national early-vote campaign, telling voters to “bank their vote” by casting ballots early by mail or in person. This will include ad campaigns focused on communities at risk of Republican election interference. The state parties and the DNC typically run get-out-the-vote programs, but this year’s will include more explicit directions to voters – telling them to vote early, and not let a mail ballot sit on their kitchen counter for weeks before turning it in, Kleeb said. The party will also push for people to vote early in person. “We don’t know what Donald Trump is going to do. We’ve heard some of the things that he may do, but none of us can predict his behavior,” she said. “He’s so chaotic. All of us have witnessed certainly that. So the earlier you can vote, the better.” The third part of the project will spin up a “democracy defense network”, led by Democratic strategist Simon Rosenberg, designed to identify and counter tactics that can sway elections, including disinformation, dark money, manipulation via artificial intelligence and election subversion. The network will allow state parties to communicate with each other about these threats to share knowledge, with a goal to get ahead of such tactics before they gain traction.
