title: Weather tracker: Floods in eastern India and hurricane damage in California
summary: Flooding in West Bengal has led to three deaths, while severe beach erosion has been witnessed in Orange county
text: Flooding around the city of Malda in the Indian state of West Bengal since Thursday has had a devastating effect. So far, three deaths have been recorded and many areas are still flooded, with numerous villages affected, along with the region of Bhutni. Erosion from the flooding, reported from Khaskol, led to a disruption in river flow which led to a more severe impact in Bhutni. More than 100 boats have been sent out for evacuation. At East Basudevpur, a 20ft (6-metre) embankment collapsed, reducing the channel from 550ft to under 150ft, which could lead to further flooding unless repaired. This flooding resulted after the Ganges River rose about 75cm above its “extreme danger” level owing to heavy rainfall. A swell caused by Hurricane Marie led to significant beach erosion across Orange county in California on 7 September. The erosion formed a cliff edge on some of the beaches, along with exposing old asphalt, pipes and even pieces of an old pier. The flooding caused by the swell damaged homes and vehicles, as well as flooding streets, leaving behind a layer of sand. The swell has been estimated to be between 8 and 10ft tall. Local people say it is not uncommon to see beach erosion, but this has been one of the most severe cases. After the hottest summer on record for the US, the above average temperatures are expected to continue this week as a heatwave grips many central states. A persistent area of high pressure and a very warm surface after recent heat will help to drive the daytime temperatures widely into the high 30s celsius or up to 40C across Oklahoma, Kansas and nearby states. Models keep the heat locked in through much of the remainder of the month, increasing the risk of wildfires, with other parts of the country already under red flag warnings.

title: Reform declines to say if £72m donors returned to UK within 12-month limit
summary: Richard Tice says contributions are legally compliant after author of review into overseas donations says rules will be applied retrospectively
text: Reform UK’s deputy leader has declined to say when two crypto billionaires who gave a combined £72m to the party returned to the UK, as the architect of a review into overseas donations said anyone here for less than 12 months would be subject to a limit on donations. Richard Tice said that while he was completely confident Reform had complied with all current and proposed laws on donations, he could not say when Ben Delo returned to the UK from Hong Kong, or how much time the Thailand-based Christopher Harborne spent in Britain. “I’m not their executive assistant responsible for their day-to-day diary,” Tice told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme when asked about the details of their UK residencies. He added: “Everything we’re doing is in accordance with the existing rules and the rules of the legislation that’s going through parliament as we speak.” The legislation referred to, the representation of the people bill, does not currently contain any overall cap on individual donations, after lobbying from Labour-backing trade unions. In response to the mega-donations by Harborne and Delo, trade unions, MPs and donors have urged the government to look again at the bill. But in the wake of a report on overseas influence on UK politics by Sir Philip Rycroft, a former senior civil servant, Britons living overseas will be limited to giving a maximum of £100,000. The bill, which goes further than some of Rycroft’s recommendations, sets out that the cap applies to anyone who was not UK-resident for electoral purposes for at least a year from March 2026, applying retrospectively once the bill becomes law. Speaking to Today, Rycroft said that while he could not comment on the circumstances of Delo or Harborne, the residency rules would apply. “What I do understand is that the way the law will work, it will implement my recommendation on a limit for Brits abroad, as it were. But there will also be rules on, if they return to the UK, how long they have to live in the UK before they can count as domestic donors. “And my understanding is that they will have to be living in the UK for at least a full calendar year. Once they met that requirement, then they become essentially a domestic donor.” Rycroft said his review concluded a cap on money from overseas-based British donors was important as it was harder to trace the origins of overseas money, and that it was “a question of fairness” in limiting the influence of “people who had chosen to take their wealth abroad and to be taxed abroad”. The two separate donations of £36m by Harborne and Delo, announced within 24 hours, are unprecedented in UK political history and will give Reform enormously boosted resources before the next election. Delo was based in Hong Kong but has returned to the UK. Asked when, Tice said this had happened “many, many months ago”. Harborne is registered to vote in the UK, but also lives in Thailand. Asked how he could know the donations were permissible under the new rules, Tice said Reform’s compliance department had looked into it. But he condemned the retrospective plans of the bill, telling BBC One’s Breakfast that it was the action of “a socialist government that wants to retrospectively change the rules and regulations in order to protect themselves from a bit of competition”. Speaking to Sky News, the schools minister Georgia Gould said the way the bill had been drafted was deliberate. Gould said: “The rules have been very clear, and the reason why it was applied retrospectively is because the risk is if you didn’t do that, then lots of donations would suddenly start flowing through before the legislation. “The really important thing is this was an independent report that looked into these really serious issues that many people are concerned about, foreign interference in politics, and we made very clear at the time that it would be retrospective for good reason.”

title: UK ministers urged to act after US flies out diplomat accused of possessing indecent images of children
summary: US officials reportedly raided envoy’s London home and took him to American airbase without warning Met police
text: British ministers face calls to act after US authorities secretly flew out of the UK a diplomat accused of possessing indecent images of children. US officials reportedly raided the diplomat’s London flat in August before taking him to an American airbase and flying him out of the country, without warning the Metropolitan police. American personnel have no powers of arrest in Britain, and there was no formal request for the man to be extradited. UK ministers are understood to be in contact with the US embassy over the incident, which could further strain relations between London and Washington. Elements of the case echo that of an American fighter pilot, first reported in the Guardian, who avoided being tried under English law for strangling a woman in Cambridge while off-duty. Capt Jacob Wulfson was tried by court martial at a US airbase and jailed for six months after being convicted of strangulation. He was acquitted of charges of sexual assault and aggravated sexual contact. In a letter to the justice secretary, Alex Norris, his Conservative counterpart, Nick Timothy, said he was concerned US actions represented “a cover-up” and that the diplomat may have committed offences in the UK. “If this is the case, the diplomat should face trial in an English court.” Timothy said the incident was part of a “concerning pattern” of US authorities prosecuting American service personnel accused of offences against British civilians while stationed in the UK. Citing the Wulfson case, he wrote: “These cases should have been investigated by the English police and prosecuted in our courts. I ask you to urgently explain what action you are taking to address this, and what will be done to ensure the accused diplomat faces a proper investigation in this country.” The diplomat’s case has also been likened to that of the US state department employee Anne Sacoolas, who caused the death of the teenager Harry Dunn in a car crash in 2019. Sacoolas was able to leave the country shortly after the fatal collision when the US asserted diplomatic immunity on her behalf. She eventually pleaded guilty to causing death by careless driving at a virtual high-court hearing in December 2022, and was sentenced to eight months in prison, suspended for a year. A UK government spokesperson declined to comment because of the ongoing US investigation but said Britain expects all foreign diplomats to obey the law while in the UK, “in the same way we expect all UK diplomats to do so when posted overseas”. A spokesperson for the US embassy said it was “aware of allegations” concerning one of its staff and expected “all personnel to adhere to the highest standards of conduct”. The spokesperson said: “We quickly informed UK law enforcement and took swift action, and we will continue to work closely with our law enforcement partners regarding these allegations. “The individual in question has been reassigned to the United States in conjunction with an ongoing investigation. The embassy has informed British authorities of the case.” A US state department spokesperson declined to discuss the specifics of the case, adding: “We take these allegations seriously.” A Met police spokesperson said: “On Tuesday 25 August, US authorities made us aware of an investigation they are conducting into suspected offences in London relating to indecent images of children. We continue to liaise with them regarding this matter.”

title: Indonesian police investigate deaths of Australian man and two children in Bali as suspected murder-suicide
summary: Police in Bali believe the two young children died as a result of violence, while a 57-year-old man is believed to have taken his own life
text: Indonesian police are investigating the deaths of three Australians who died in Bali over the weekend, with initial reports suggesting a father killed his two young children before taking his own life. The man, 57, and his two children, seven and four, who are also Indonesian citizens, were discovered deceased in a bungalow in Kuta on Sunday morning. According to Denpasar police, a witness, 51-year-old Nur Khamid, received a phone call from someone claiming to be the victim’s wife at about 8.30am on Sunday. She was in Jakarta, and asked Khamid to check on the condition of her husband and family, who she had been unable to reach. Khamid went to their bungalow and tried to look inside through a window, but “no activity or people were visible inside”, Denpasar police said in its statement. The witness then met the bungalow owner and both returned to perform a check before contacting the “neighbourhood head”, Kelian Lingkungan. Residents “knocked and pounded” on the door before it was forcibly opened, and the three bodies were located. “Police officers arriving at the scene conducted a crime scene investigation and preliminary examination alongside the Denpasar Police Identification Team,” the statement read. “From the initial external examination of the three victims, it is suspected that the two children died as a result of acts of violence, while [the father] is suspected to have died by hanging.” The bodies are at Prof Dr IGNG Ngoerah Central general hospital for further examination and handling. The Denpasar police chief, senior commissioner Leonardo D Simatupang, said Kuta police officers were investigating the incident. “Investigators are still conducting inquiries, including crime scene processing, examining CCTV footage at the scene, and questioning witnesses – including the victim’s wife – to determine the cause of death,” he said. Simatupang said Kuta police had taken a statement from the man’s wife and reviewed CCTV footage. They had also coordinated with the Australian consulate. A spokesperson for the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade confirmed it was providing consular assistance to the family of the three Australians. “We send our deepest condolences to the family at this difficult time. Owing to our privacy obligations we are unable to provide further comment,” they said in a statement. • In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is on 13 11 14 and the national family violence counselling service is on 1800 737 732. In the UK, Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123 and the domestic abuse helpline is 0808 2000 247. In the US, the suicide prevention lifeline is 988 and the domestic violence hotline is 1-800-799-SAFE (7233). Other international helplines can be found via www.befrienders.org

title: ‘We’re not going to back down’: tiny Dorset B&B stands up to Airbnb’s legal bid to ‘monopolise’ letters ‘bnb’
summary: Three little letters - bnb-side’s name is a play on the local b-side arts festival, but Silicon Valley colossus sees threat to global brand
text: In one corner is bnb-side, a six-room bed and breakfast on the Isle of Portland – a tiny wedge of limestone tied by a narrow ribbon of shingle to the Dorset coast – that was created to help secure the future of the rock’s much-loved arts festival, b-side. On the other is Airbnb, the San Francisco-based booking colossus. The battle between them is over the three little letters they share. b-side says the “bnb” in bnb-side means what it has always meant: bed and breakfast. But lawyers for the Silicon Valley titan say the name of the guesthouse, perched on an outcrop just 4 miles long by 1.5 miles wide, threatens the global brand of the $100bn heavyweight. “We thought the name was both really obvious and really cool,” said Rocca Holly-Nambi, director of b-side. “b-side was founded almost 20 years ago, so when we set up our BnB in 2024 to raise money for the festival, we just popped the ‘bn’ in front because it’s a universally recognised description of what we’re offering.” Airbnb doesn’t agree. In May, it sent the first of three legal letters to the tiny social enterprise to demand it cease its attempt to register the B&B using the name it had used since it opened its doors. “They won’t let us compromise by using a different case, an ampersand or an ‘and’,” said Holly-Nambi. “According to Airbnb, we can’t describe our BnB as a BnB at all.” For bnb-side, losing the argument could mean more than abandoning a clever name. It would mean replacing signage and rewriting websites, social media and all other material referencing and advertising the B&B. “That’s not just a huge waste of money – of which we don’t have much – and of the equally valuable time of our volunteers, but it would throw b-side’s core income stream into chaos,” said Holly-Nambi. “We’d have to painstakingly build our reputation and brand back up from scratch all over again.” Raina Summerson, chair of b-side, is fuming and incredulous. “We opened bnb-side because we were completely dependent on public funding and wanted to be more financially secure,” she said. “bnb-side now generates almost half the festival’s annual £250,000 turnover. If it loses its name, we risk having to establish it all over again.” Airbnb has opposed the name on three separate legal grounds: that consumers will confuse the two brands, that bnb-side could benefit from or damage Airbnb’s reputation, and that bnb-side will financially profit by misrepresenting itself as an official Airbnb service. b-side is asking the Intellectual Property Office to reject Airbnb’s opposition in full, with costs awarded in their favour. The case is still under way, with no ruling having yet been made. Airbnb’s claim has hit a nerve on the proud, windswept outcrop. Cat Wightman, manager of bnb-side, said: “It’s pretty bitter. We’ve watched other small, local hospitality businesses go under, and local people unable to afford homes here, who have been negatively affected by the force with which the Airbnb market has conquered Portland. One person owns eight properties on the island, all of which are rented out on Airbnb.” b-side obtained pro bono advice and is working with the law firm Stevens Hewlett & Perkins to defend them, but the process is still intimidating. “It’s terrifying but we’re not going to back down,” said Holly-Nambi. “We do things differently here in Portland.” Craig Beaumont, a trademark attorney and senior associate at Barker Brettell, a law firm that specialises in intellectual property, said that for all Airbnb’s might, this would not be an easy or straightforward win for them. “This feels like an uphill battle they’re embarking on,” he said. “BnB has long been widely understood as shorthand for a descriptive phrase, and descriptive phrases are available for the public to use.” bnb-side are not the only company who agree with Beaumont: Companies House records show that in the past decade 14 accommodation companies with “bnb” in their name successfully registered their businesses. Darren Meale, a partner and trademark litigation specialist at Simmons & Simmons, said it was no surprise the term was used so often. “It’s quite punchy of Airbnb to say they’re so well-known that they can monopolise a term that they only incorporated into their name in the first place because it was a descriptive one that everyone immediately understood, and then say that someone else using the term is going to confuse customers and damage them.” Lee Curtis, a partner and chartered trademark attorney at IP law firm HGF, agreed that Airbnb “may be testing the limits” of the law. But he pointed to another risk for the lodging colossus. “There’s a public relations angle to take into account,” he said. “Some companies may welcome getting a reputation for aggressive enforcement but that can backfire when the target is a community organisation, like this one.” An Airbnb spokesperson said: “Earlier this year, we were notified of a UK trademark application for “bnb-side” covering a wide-range of services, including holiday home bookings. “We want to resolve these situations amicably and directly, and contacted the applicant several times with no response, while a subsequent legal letter drew only a brief acknowledgement “With only a two-month window to object under UK rules and no dialogue underway, we filed an objection with the UK intellectual property office to preserve our ability to protect our trademark in the UK. We have initiated no other legal proceedings, and continue to extend an invitation to talk.”

title: Thames Water redraws mega-reservoir plan amid local opposition
summary: A targeted public consultation has opened on the 150bn-litre above-ground White Horse project in Oxfordshire
text: Thames Water has amended the blueprint of a planned mega-reservoir in Oxfordshire as the struggling utility tries to convince regulators that construction should go ahead amid warnings of “catastrophic consequences”. The White Horse reservoir near Abingdon is scheduled to hold 150bn litresof water with a surface area of 6.7 sq km (2.6 sq miles) – almost the same size as Gatwick airport. The estimated cost has rocketed from £2.2bn to between £5.5bn and £7.5bn after a review last year more than tripled the site to 38 sq km to accommodate extra building works, relocate adjacent solar farms and reroute local rivers and streams. Thames Water said the scheme, formerly known as the South East Strategic Reservoir Option, needed “additional access points to carry out construction and environmental mitigation works, such as new habitat creation”, forcing it to carry out “targeted consultation with landowners, and those with an interest in land that may be impacted by this change”. A public consultation into the original plans concluded in January. Last week, a further consultation began and is expected to end next month. Thames aims to submit a planning application by late 2026. If approved, main works construction would begin in 2032 with water available by 2040, serving 15 million people. Thames said the reservoir is needed to cope with the growing population in the south-east and the changing climate, which has put pressure on water resources in many parts of the UK, including during this summer’s heatwaves. Rapid, a partnership between the industry regulator Ofwat, the Environment Agency and the Drinking Water Inspectorate, which oversees the early development of large-scale water infrastructure projects, said there was a projected shortfall of more than 2bn litres a day by 2055. Campaigners have accused Thames Water of underestimating the reservoir’s cost and overstating its strategic value since plans for a 10 sq km, £1bn project were first put forward in 2006. The reservoir has proved controversial after designs showed the facility would be largely above ground level and would need walls up to 25 metres high to contain the main body of water, making it the largest “fully bounded” reservoir in Europe. The site is one of the few in the south of England with enough clay across a large area to build a reservoir, but the clay is only a few metres deep, forcing Thames to build the UK’s first walled reservoir structure. The most recent estimates of costs are in 2023 prices, leading critics to say that after three years of high inflation, especially in the construction industry, the estimated cost of the White Horse reservoir is more likely to be £7.5bn-£10bn. Customers of Thames Water, Affinity Water and Southern Water are due to pay for the new reservoir through their bills over the next 100 years. At the end of March, the regulated value of Thames’s assets was estimated at £23bn while its net debt increased to £18.5bn. Ministers are considering whether to put the company into special administration or accept a solution put forward by creditors to maintain private-sector control after a debt write-off. The Vale of White Horse district council, Abingdon town council and Oxfordshire county council have rejected the plans, citing flood risks to neighbouring villages from rivers and streams on the site that will need to be diverted. Derek Stork, chair of the Group Against Reservoir Development, said the reservoir was a flawed concept and there were more sustainable ways to supply water to the area. He said Thames Water had failed to consult adequately with local organisations, councils and residents. “No dam breach analysis or comprehensive flood risk modelling has been shared, despite the reservoir’s location on a red-rated flood plain and the potential for catastrophic consequences in the event of failure,” he said. A red-rated area is at severe risk of flooding, according to the Environment Agency. A Thames Water spokesperson said: “This consultation is just the latest part of our ongoing programme of engagement around the project, which we have been undertaking for more than four years. “The feedback we get, along with feedback gathered during our statutory public consultation last year, will help inform our proposals.”

title: Slavery was not a footnote to British history. It helped shape the nation | William Pettigrew
summary: Register of British Slave Traders reveals how deeply the trafficking of Africans was embedded in the country’s politics, economy, institutions and culture
text: Two obstacles have prevented us from appreciating the significance of the slave trade in British history. The first arose from the abolition campaign, which finally overcame opposition in parliament in 1807. The abolitionists promoted the idea that opposition to the slave trade flowed naturally from British values: justice, freedom and Christian benevolence. The success of this strategy obscured the role those same British values had played in supporting the trafficking. Today, Britain’s leaders place abolition in the pantheon of great and definitive national moments. The second obstacle has been the ingrained tendency of the British to offshore the causes and effects of African chattel slavery to the Americas. According to this view, slavery, and the racial thinking it engendered, was an American, not European concern. But Europeans transported the great majority of enslaved African people to the Americas and reaped huge advantages from doing so. These advantages reshaped European societies. The Register of British Slave Traders, published today, is another significant step towards removing these obstacles and reinscribing the slave trade at the centre of the nation’s history. Compiled by a team of historians across three UK universities over four years, the Register identifies some of the roughly 13,000 men and women, based in Britain, who financed the violent transportation of 3.2 million enslaved African men, women, and children for almost two and half centuries. It is the first to gather biographical information on all known investors in the trafficking. These were pivotal centuries for Britain: establishing the British state and its borders, defining its national religion and constitution, enlarging its status in the world, building its empire, launching its core institutions, characterising its culture, forging its progressive values and underpinning unprecedented phases of economic growth. Although slave traders were a tiny minority of the British population, the register shows them exerting an outsized influence on this golden age of British development. The trade in enslaved African people was a formative influence during perhaps the most formative period in Britain’s history. British slave traders had varied lives. The register reveals how they shaped several aspects of the country’s development and highlights their collusion with the state. To traffic enslaved African people, the Elizabethans had to muscle in on Spanish interests in the Americas and contest decades of Portuguese dominance in the trade. This was diplomatically sensitive and required the support of the most powerful people in England. Those who initiated the traffic did so from the very top of English society: the treasurer of the Royal Navy, Benjamin Gonson, the lord mayor of London, Thomas Lodge, leading courtiers such as Robert Dudley, the Earl of Leicester, and the most powerful man in the country, William Cecil; and Queen Elizabeth herself. All lent their power and prestige to the endeavour, as the register shows, wiring human trafficking into the state’s priorities. The register also shows slave traders’ impact on British politics and the constitution. Merchants embraced the slave trade as they challenged the Stuart monarchy during the English civil war. The monarchy coveted the traffic to defend itself from this challenge. Once restored, the monarchy chartered and led slave-trading monopoly companies to rehabilitate its economic reputation. The slave trade became both a tonic to heal a divided nation and a means to relaunch the monarchy from its lowest ebb. Plenty of Britons resented the restrictions that these monopolies placed on their access to slave-trading. They established political parties to challenge the monarchy, change the constitution, and widen access to the traffic. In this campaign, successful by 1712, British freedom became a core basis for the enslavement of millions of African people. Slave trader lobbyists developed innovative political methods, prioritising breadth of support over social status. They established novel forms of journalism – deploying opinion and persuasion, rather than just facts – to expand the nation’s slave trade. They formulated new (and still influential) notions of economic growth which celebrated individual entrepreneurial agency. Slave traders opened up access to the traffic, giving a wider section of the population the opportunity to embrace it. Interest in human trafficking cascaded down the social hierarchy. Its reach broadened and its scale increased by 300%, helping to make Britain the predominant slave-trading nation of the 18th century. Slave-trading became associated with the social upstart and propelled social mobility. Recent immigrants, some of them refugees, mostly from France and northern Europe, made up a disproportionate number of investors, as the register shows. The government did not abandon its foundational relationship with the trafficking. It made the scale of public enthusiasm for the slave trade the basis for a project to refinance the national debt – the slave-trading South Sea Company. The public engaged with enslavement in ever greater numbers, with only isolated objection to the unique brutality of the traffic, while viewing Africans as an inferior branch of humanity who deserved their fate in the plantations. The state reflected this engagement by fighting no fewer than three wars to expand the nation’s slave trade: the second Anglo-Dutch war, the war of Spanish succession and the war of Jenkins’ ear. Londoners kickstarted the traffic. The register reveals a new generation of provincial investors following them, spreading the opportunities of human trafficking to the west and north, helping to expand the country’s economy and providing some of the seed funding for the Industrial Revolution. Access to the free English slave trade became a commercial opportunity embraced by many Scots after the Act of Union. Slave traders pioneered new economic infrastructure – wet docks and canals – connecting port cities such as Liverpool to emerging industrial hinterlands. Investments in trafficking provided a founding generation of female investors, who make up just under 10% of the register, with the means to secure their wealth and the futures of their children. When assessing the slave traders’ connections to organisations, the register’s story is overwhelmingly about their charity. Slave traders supported the neediest in society, galvanising a national effort to establish and expand a safety net with almshouses, medical care, charity schools and anti-poverty charities. Many justified the trafficking in philanthropic terms – claiming that Africans would be better off on the plantations than in Africa. Britain’s slave traders also helped to define the nation’s culture. The slave trade enticed creative people with sporadic earnings as investors. The register shows how poets (John Gay), playwrights (Thomas Southerne), painters (Sir Godfrey Kneller), composers (George Frideric Handel), and architects (James Gibbs) gravitated towards the trafficwhile reshaping literature, art, music and architecture in Britain. The register also highlights the conspicuous role of slave traders in the emergence of British science, via the Royal Society, and medicine (Dr Richard Mead and Sir Hans Sloane). Overall, the register establishes a truly national connection to slavery. It finds investors in, and bequests to, organisations throughout the country. It broadens connections to slavery beyond those memorialised in statues – or whose statues have been toppled – such as Edward Colston in dominant port cities including Bristol and Liverpool, to landlocked counties throughout the UK. It should help us fully confront our history and process the breadth of our society’s connections to it. The register reveals that slave-traders were not protagonists in a distant, primitive phase in the nation’s history. They were enmeshed in the processes that produced the nation we know today. Britons can feel a wide and contrasting variety of connections to this history. But, more than anything else, the Register shows that we are all – in some way – connected to it. Prof William Pettigrew is the author of Britain’s Slave Traders: A Forgotten History, published by Penguin. To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.

title: Can you solve it? Do you have the brain of an engineer?
summary: Hacks from the hidden world of test engineering
text: Today’s puzzles test your engineering smarts. The cranberries In a cranberry sorting facility, thousands of cranberries are dropped every minute onto a board. Good cranberries are firm, and bounce, while bad cranberries are soft, and don’t bounce. What simple trick allows sorters to catch all of the good ones and none of the bad? Caps off In the US, medicine bottle caps are designed to be secure against only 85 per cent of children under five. Why is this percentage not higher? Eighty-five seems quite low. Slats entertainment In 2020, engineers replaced the pedestrian handrail on the Golden Gate Bridge. The old handrail rested on metal balusters in the shape of an H, so the support looked like “HHHH…” where the H’s horizontal section was 10cm wide. The new handrail was supported only by thin vertical slats, making it look like “IIII…” and where each slat was only 0.6cm wide. The aim of the new handrail was to make it less resistant to wind, and hence safer during high winds. But it brought two serious unintended consequences. What were they? Under pressure Cabin air pressure in a plane is controlled so that it is the same as air pressure at ground level. When a plane flies, the air pressure outside the plane drops, causing the air pressure in the cabin to push outwards against the frame with great force [UPDATE: I simplified the statement. To clarify, cabin pressure is set to a pressure that is comfortable to humans, equivalent to air pressure at about 2000m, which is much less high than cruising altitude. For airports at around 2000m, such as Mexico City, the statement remains true!] In the early 1950s, there were some major plane crashes when the fuselage was ripped apart mid flight. UK manufacturer de Havilland found a way to pressure test its plane, the Comet, the world’s first commercial jet, without the plane leaving the ground. What did they do? I’ll be back at 5pm UK with the solutions. UPDATE: Solutions are up here. PLEASE NO SPOILERS. Instead talk about your favourite engineering anecdotes. Today’s puzzles are adapted from a hugely entertaining new book about the world of test engineering, How to Keep a Plane in the Sky, by technology reporter Alex Davies. It tells fascinating stories about the scientists whose work underpins our trust that objects do not crack, break or explode. Thanks to Alex for the puzzles. You can buy his book at the Guardian Bookshop and other retailers. And finally…some professional news. Last week I won the 2026 Christopher Zeeman Medal, the UK’s most prestigious honour for mathematics communication, which is given by the London Mathematical Society and the Instititue for Mathematics and Its Applications. I’m absolutely thrilled and hope to continue setting mathsy puzzles here long into the future! I’ve been setting a puzzle here on alternate Mondays since 2015. I’m always on the look-out for great puzzles. If you would like to suggest one, email me.

title: ‘Tidal wave’ of Pfas being launched to satisfy AI industry, campaigners warn
summary: Big manufacturers planning to produce more of the forever chemicals to meet demand from datacentres
text: Pfas companies are launching a “tidal wave” of forever chemicals production to meet demand from the AI industry, a campaign organisation has warned. Despite alarm over the chemicals, which have been linked to cancer, a survey of the 10 biggest manufacturers found most had plans to increase production. Many frame their investments around the “AI revolution”, because of the role Pfas play in semiconductor production and next-generation datacentre cooling systems. But opponents warn that the chemicals, which never degrade in nature, are a ticking timebomb for human and planetary health. They say increased production risks undermining nascent moves to restrict Pfas in Europe, the UK and parts of the US. “These companies’ expansion plans show that unless governments and regulators insist on a rapid phaseout, we will face a new tidal wave of forever chemicals,” said Anne-Sofie Bäckar, the executive director of ChemSec, the Swedish chemicals watchdog that carried out the research. ChemSec’s survey found nearly all of the 10 biggest manufacturers of Pfas had plans to increase production, at sites in Europe, Asia and North America. The boom in AI tech was leading demand, with Pfas used for “eco-friendly” datacentre cooling and in various stages of semiconductor manufacturing. Japan-headquarted Daikin said it was launching a “datacentre hub” to meet demand, and promised to “maintain and expand our top share in the industry by expanding sales of existing fluorine products and introducing new products”. The French multinational Arkema was expanding its refrigerant offering, with a new $60m (£44m) production unit in Kentucky that it said “will enable us to follow the rapid expansion of datacenters’ cooling needs”. And the US Pfas producer Chemours was expanding to meet demand from “advanced datacenters and AI hardware”. It said its “innovative liquid cooling solutions” lower the energy, water, space, maintenance and investment costs of datacentres. Critics have said Chemours – recently ordered to pay $450m to settle a lawsuit over Pfas discharges – downplays the chemicals’ toxicity and climate impact. Other companies increasing production were Japanese multinational AGC, Chinese conglomerate Dongyue, India-based chemicals giant Gujarat Fluorochemicals, secretive Russian Pfas producer HaloPolymer, Mexico’s Orbia Fluor & Energy Materials, US-based fluorinated gases producer Solstice and Belgian multinational Syensqo. Producers also cited Pfas coatings and binders for lithium-ion batteries, used in EVs, laptops and phones, as a parallel growth area. Gujarat Fluorochemicals’ chief executive, Bir Kapoor, recently identified batteries as one of several “sunrise sectors”, alongside datacentres, semiconductors and green hydrogen. “There is a tremendous growth opportunity there,” he said. The only clear exceptions were the Swiss company Archroma, which was switching to marketing Pfas-free alternatives, and the German giant BASF, which has said it will exit Pfas production by 2028. Pfas are used for a new form of datacentre cooling touted as more water- and energy-efficient. In “two-phase immersion cooling” systems, servers are immersed in a pool of Pfas with a low boiling point. As the hardware gets hot, the fluid boils, drawing heat away as vapour. That rises to a water-cooled condensing coil at the top of the tank, cools back to a liquid state and re-enters the cycle. Pfas also play a crucial role in the fabrication process for semiconductors, another sector booming to meet demand from the AI industry. According to a recent investor note from Danske Bank: “In the world of microchips, these ‘forever chemicals’ are not merely peripheral additives; they are essential ingredients integrated into as many as 1,000 distinct steps at the nanometric level.” But analysts also warned Pfas were “the hidden risk of the AI boom” with “escalating potential for multibillion-euro remediation and litigation liabilities”. The carbon-fluorine bonds in Pfas, or per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, are among the strongest in organic chemistry, rendering them incredibly resistant to heat, water and corrosion. That makes them useful for a range of industrial processes and consumer products. But it also makes them virtually indestructible in the natural environment. As a result, they continue to be recycled through planetary systems, leading to their accumulation in air, water and soil, and up the food chain. Although Pfas have existed for less than a century, scientists have warned that their accumulation in the environment has already breached a planetary boundary. Already the chemicals are thought to contaminate the blood of nearly every living person. Research links them to cancer, liver disease, kidney issues, high cholesterol and birth defects. ChemSec sent finger-prick blood tests to the chief executives of all the European companies in its top 10, encouraging them to test Pfas levels in their own blood and share the results publicly. “The people who lead them must understand that they too are affected by the toxins they produce, which have been detected in the blood of more than 99% of people worldwide,” said Bäckar.

title: Pixel 11 Pro Fold review: the foldable with the best triple camera
summary: Big screen folder with slick software and advanced AI is just like a regular Android when closed
text: Google’s latest folding phone sticks with its tried and tested design of a traditional phone shape when closed and almost square when open, in the face of new competition from Apple’s squat iPhone fold. The Pixel 11 Pro Fold is Google’s fourth-generation folder and is still one of the only models with a full water and dust resistance rating similar to standard slab phones. It costs from £1,799 (€1,999/$1,899/A$2,799), which is £50 (€100/$100/A$100) more than last year as the pressure of RAMageddon continues to push up prices. The 11 Pro Fold looks identical to previous models, but it is 19g lighter and fractionally slimmer in all directions with a slightly larger outside screen. Unlike Samsung’s slender Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra or squat models such as Apple’s iPhone Duo or the Galaxy Z Fold 8, the Pixel has the same ratio screen as Google’s slab phones and so handles precisely like them when shut with a bright and smooth 6.5in display. Opened up, the internal screen is essentially square, which allows you to run two full-size apps side by side but is less ideal for video. The display is very bright, crisp and smooth, but the crease where it folds is more visible and detectable with your fingers than the best rivals. Like all foldable phones the screen is also delicate compared with standard hardened glass phones. The back of the phone hides the excellent Qi2 magnetic charging and accessory support from last year, while Google’s gimmicky HiLight notification LED, as seen on the other Pro Pixels, replaces the camera’s flash. Specifications Outside screen: 6.5in FHD+ 120Hz OLED (399ppi) Inside screen: 8in 120Hz OLED (372ppi) Processor: Google Tensor G6 RAM: 16GB Storage: 256, 512GB or 1TB Operating system: Android 17 Camera: 48MP wide, 10.5MP ultrawide, 10.8MP 5x telephoto; two 10MP selfie cameras Connectivity: 5G, eSim, USB-C, wifi 7, NFC, Bluetooth 6, UWB, Thread, GNSS Water resistance: IP68 (1.5 metres for 30 minutes) Dimensions folded: 155.2 x 76 x 10.1mm Dimensions unfolded: 155.2 x 150.4 x 5mm Weight: 239g Faster chip but slightly shorter battery life The 11 Pro Fold has the same Tensor G6 chip from the other Pixel 11 models with 16GB of memory, which works very well for all kinds of multitasking, remaining snappy and responsive with multiple apps on screen. It handles light gaming, but can’t match rivals for raw performance. The battery life is a little shorter than last year’s model and rivals, lasting about 36 hours between charges when used on a mix of 5G and wifi with the screens in active use for about 2.5 hours each for browsing, messaging, apps and photos. Most will have to charge it nightly, but even on the heaviest of use days the Pixel managed to end the day without requiring a top-up. Android 17, Magic Cue and Gemini The Fold runs the latest version of Android 17 with all of Google’s AI tools, including Gemini’s proactive system, the new supercharged voice dictation feature and six months of Google AI Pro subscription. Many of Google’s more creative AI tools, including the Omni video creation tool, Circle to Search and Gemini’s information cards benefit from the larger internal screen. Google has made a number of modifications to Android to better fit the folding form, including a floating taskbar and a split-screen mode that can resize apps beyond the bounds of the physical display introduced last year. The bubbles system, which was primarily used for messaging apps, has been revamped to allow as many as five apps of any kind to be opened as floating windows on top of a single or split-screen apps and minimised to a little taskbar. But it isn’t as flexible as Samsung’s true desktop-like floating window system that can be resized and placed anywhere on the screen. The 11 Pro Fold will be supported until August 2033 with operating system and security updates, making it one of the longest supported devices available. Sustainability The battery is rated to last in excess of 1,000 full charge cycles with at least 80% of its original capacity. The phone is repairable by Google and third-party shops, and self-repair with manuals and parts is due to be available. The Pixel 11 Pro Fold contains 24% recycled materials by weight. The company breaks down the phone’s environmental impact in its report and will recycle old devices for free. Camera The Pixel Fold has some of the best cameras on a foldable phone, including three on the back and two very good selfie cameras, one in each screen. The rear cameras include a new 48MP main camera with a larger sensor, matching that in the regular Pixel 11, which captures better detail and has significantly better lowlight performance than its predecessor. The 10.5MP ultrawide camera is the same as last year and is still as solid this year. The 10.8MP 5x telephoto is also the same and shoots good photos that meaningfully reduce the distance to objects. It has a solid digital zoom that stretches up to 30x magnification, but not the generative AI zoom of the Pixel 11 Pro. The Fold also has the new software features from the other Pixel 11 phones, including Camera Looks, which allows you to customise the processing of your photos for different styles. Magic Capture shoots video and photos automatically with one button, while the Creator suite helps you storyboard, trim and produce video content for social media. The camera also has tricks to make use of the folding form, including modes to shoot when propped up and the excellent Made You Look feature that displays an animated character that reacts to your kid’s smiling to help take better photos. Overall, the 11 Pro Fold has an excellent set of cameras that don’t feel a significant downgrade on top regular smartphones. Price The Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold costs from £1,799 (€1,999/$1,899/A$2,799). For comparison, the Pixel 11 costs £879, Pixel 11 Pro costs £1,079, the Pixel 11 Pro XL costs £1,279, the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra costs £1,899, the iPhone Duo costs £1,999 and the Honor Magic V6 costs £1,499.99. Verdict The Pixel 11 Pro Fold is a fairly minor hardware update for Google’s folding phone line, which makes it slightly lighter, smaller, brighter and faster, while keeping its overall look and feel the same. It has great AI tools, slick software and some of the very best cameras. The inside screen is super bright and crisp, but the crease down the middle is more noticeable than rivals, the battery life is a bit short and it is thick and heavy compared to the best from rival Samsung. As with all foldables the inside screen can be permanently marked by a fingernail if you press hard enough, so you must still be careful with it compared with a standard Pixel. But if you want a folding phone to be exactly the same as a regular one when closed, the Pixel Fold is the one to get. Pros: just like a regular Pixel when closed, good tablet screen, dust and water resistant, Qi2 magnetic accessory and charging, good performance, great cameras with 5x zoom, great software packed with cutting-edge AI, six months of Google AI Pro included, seven years of software updates. Cons: very expensive, more fragile and costlier to repair than a regular Pixel, thick and heavy, cameras can’t match regular Pixel 11 Pro, battery life could be better.

title: Monday briefing: What do Reform’s record-setting £72m donations mean for the party – and our politics?
summary: In today’s newsletter: As Labour MPs scramble to realign later today around a bill that could stop donations like this in their tracks, a look at new game-changing donations to a party engulfed in financial scandals
text: Good morning. Nigel Farage has a confirmed talent for upending the laws of political gravity, and this weekend has been no exception, as he declared himself “humbled” by two donations of £36m each from cryptocurrency tycoons Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne. I’d shoehorn a joke about buses in here but, honestly, this feels too consequential for that. The largest single donations in British political history were made after a dismal party conference, the substance of which was all but obscured by the financial scandals engulfing Reform. As the financial dubiety continues, and the numbers of millions tick upwards to seem almost meaningless, it might be tempting to roll your eyes and focus elsewhere – but this is not the time to look away. These are gamechanging donations, transformative if used effectively at this stage in the election cycle, just as Labour has regained its confidence and the Tories are contemplating a comeback. As a bill that could stop donations like this in their tracks returns to the Lords later today, I spoke to Jessica Elgot, the Guardian’s deputy political editor, about what these millions mean and why they matter. First, a wrap-up of this weekend’s headlines. Weekend roundup Economy | Former chancellor George Osborne said Britain’s economy had “fallen off a cliff” since Brexit – and that rejoining the European Union’s customs union would be the fastest route to recovery. Technology | Sam Altman and Elon Musk backed Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei’s call to “slow the pace” of AI development. Amodei had cautioned that an AI swarm could otherwise become capable of “taking over the entire internet” within a year. Sweden | With most of the votes counted, Sweden’s national election remained too close to call on Sunday night, with left-wing parties holding a lead of just a single seat according to a partial tally by the election authority. Ukraine | A train carrying Boris Johnson and the former CIA chief David Petraeus may have been the target of a Russian drone strike that hit a train engine near the Poland-Ukraine border, according to Ukrainian Railways. Travel | The air traffic control outage that caused thousands of flights to be grounded across the UK earlier in the week was caused by a military aircraft entering “spurious” flight data into the system, according to a report. In depth: More money, more problems? Let’s start with more detail on the donations, by businessmen who have amassed astronomical fortunes trading in cryptocurrency. Ben Delo, a previous Reform donor, has given £36m. Delo was convicted in the US in 2022 for failing to implement adequate anti-money-laundering controls in his trillion-dollar cryptocurrency business BitMEX, before being pardoned by Donald Trump last year. (A brief note here on how that story came to light: the Sunday Times approached Reform and Farage after a confidential source told them that Delo had donated to the party. Soon after, the Telegraph published an opinion piece by Delo himself, announcing the donation and trouncing the Sunday Times scoop. As Sunday Times political editor Ben Riley-Smith noted on X: “A fundamental part of political reporting – approaching for comment before publishing – just totally breaks down if this is what happens. Bad for both sides: Will increase the chance of inaccuracies.” Reform has used the same tactic with the Guardian, as we talked about in a previous newsletter.) Less than 24 hours later, another crypto donor was troubling the Telegraph’s op-ed page: this time Christopher Harborne – whose previous £5m gift to Farage is the one currently subject to a parliamentary standards investigation – announcing he had likewise donated £36m, saying: “My competitive spirit inspired me to match [Delo].” Taken together, these donations are unprecedented in British political history: £72m is bigger than the total sum spent by the seven largest parties in the last general election (about £67.9m) and almost double the total donations to all political parties so far this year (about £41.8m). *** Are these donations legal? “There’s nothing wrong with these donations that we know of,” says Jessica, her final four words doing a lot of heavy lifting in present circumstances. The Metropolitan police is conducting an inquiry into Reform’s finances and Farage is facing a parliamentary standards investigation into that £5m Harborne gift, made before he was first elected an MP in 2024 and first revealed by the Guardian. Reform and Farage have denied any wrongdoing. It’s a legal requirement for every party to rigorously check the sources of donations, and, doing the media rounds yesterday, Reform’s economics spokesperson Robert Jenrick was sounding supremely confident that the donations were “entirely in line with the law as it is and, as far as we know, what it is going to be in the future”. Jenrick was referencing the representation of the people bill, going through parliament, which will bring in more stringent rules about foreign donations. Gifts to political parties from Britons living abroad or those who have returned to the country within the past 12 months will be capped at £100,000 a year, with the rules backdated to March. Delo has recently moved back to Britain from Hong Kong, while Harborne is a citizen of the UK and Thailand. I don’t have space to get into it here, but if you’re curious about the path to becoming a crypto billionaire and the people who get trampled along the way, I’d recommend the actor and crypto investigator Ben McKenzie’s excellent film Everybody Is Lying to You for Money. (Yes, he’s Ryan in The OC). *** How could Reform spend the money? Reform has already vastly scaled up its party infrastructure since the general election, moving to new offices in London’s Millbank Tower, once synonymous with New Labour election operations. Press officers, graphic designers, videographers and regional organisers have augmented staffing capacity, but their wider policy offering is still weak. An injection of cash will probably mean more hires to address this, and perhaps even drafting legislation to boost Farage’s projection of a party that’s ready for government. Reform is expected to install campaign managers and branch coordinators in hundreds of seats across the country – as their list of 60-plus job vacancies indicates. And if this newsletter gig doesn’t work out for me, I might throw my bunnet in for the senior writer role advertised here – the application requires a 500-word letter, written in the style of Zia Yusuf, “setting out how the political class broke Britain and how Reform UK will fix it”. The donations also promise a massive boost to Reform’s visibility – they can pay for the big “air war” expenses incurred in coming byelections and council elections next year, more locally targeted online advertising and billboards, as well as getting creative with its TV studios. Reform now has the money to focus on labour-intensive data gathering in target constituencies as well, says Jessica, who predicts it will be “transformative” for the party. “You’ve got enough money now to spend on the granular and expensive work of going around every single constituency in the country making sure your data about voters, and non-voters, is bang on. And if you’re a party that wants to show that you’re on the march, they’ve got the momentum, you can dominate the airwaves, dominate people’s social media feeds.” *** Will this prompt a rethink on a cap for all donations? Labour MPs’ WhatsApp chats have been popping off over the weekend, Jessica reports, with anger that the government did not act last week to restrict domestic donations in the elections bill. Stella Creasy, the Labour MP for Walthamstow, pulled her amendment proposing an annual cap of £100,000 after Andy Burnham dropped his support for it, following intensive lobbying from the party’s trade union backers, who argued it would undermine their ability to donate to the party. But the bill has its second reading in the Lords later today and, yesterday, communities secretary Angela Rayner suggested that the government was still considering amendments and that “it’s not as simple as we’re saying we won’t put a cap”. As Sunday turned into Monday, some unions appeared to be shifting their opposition while Labour MPs and donors were urging the government to look again at party funding rules. But Reform argues that – as a relatively new political force – it needs this cash injection to level the playing field with other parties and their far longer-standing donor arrangements. *** What about an early election? As Jessica reminds me, Reform will be able to splash its cash in the coming months because many restrictions on party spending don’t kick in until a general election is called. “Other parties are not spending that money now because they don’t have it. And their donors are not giving money at this stage in the cycle. So they won’t have any competition for those eyeballs whatsoever.” There’s growing chatter in Westminster that – if economic growth continues to inch upwards and Reform remains static in the polls – Burnham may go for an early summer general election next year. (With a note of caution from Jessica that there will probably be a backlash from hundreds of Labour MPs on course to lose their seats.) A major consideration for the prime minister is, of course, Reform – which remains, in recent polls, a couple of points behind Labour and a similar amount ahead of the Tories. According to Jenrick on Sunday, these donations enable his party to be “battle ready”, whatever Burnham decides. Meanwhile, Labour sent out an “urgent” fundraising appeal over the weekend, warning that Reform could “simply drown Labour’s message out in elections to come”. Clearly, £72m in cash is good for Reform. “But whether it re-energises the party, and voters think, ‘People are willing to give this money millions of pounds because they offer a radical reset and I want that, too’ or whether it adds to that perception of a party being bought by billionaires, it’s hard to say.” Crucially, it keeps everybody talking about Reform’s finances. After a summer marred by scandal, internal divisions and a damp squib byelection, and at a point when Farage’s own popularity ratings have plummeted and support for the party has stalled, that is last place Reform wants to be. The week to come Monday | First ministers of Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland will meet in Cardiff to discuss moves towards self-determination across the nations. Tuesday | The final report of the Thirwall Inquiry into events at the neonatal unit where Lucy Letby worked will be published. Letby was sentenced to 15 whole-life terms for murdering seven infants and attempting to murder seven others. Thursday | Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, will address the European parliament. What else we’ve been enjoying Much of the hand-wringing around the death of reading can seem uncircumstantial, but not this excellent column from John Harris on what it could mean for the future of our democracy in a time of “nonsense and poison”. Charlie Lindlar, newsletters team Anyone who, like me, has returned to the place they grew up to see if mere proximity can transport them, in spirit, back to their youth will inhale this thoughtful and emotive collection of mini-essays by Deborah Levy, Julia Samuels and other novelists on revisiting their childhood homes. Here be ghosts. Craille Maguire Gillies, newsletters team Our This is how we do it series is a must-read, and this piece from a couple on making time for sex alongside their open relationship and raising three young kids is no exception (not least to understand how they possibly find the time). Charlie Sport Tennis | Alexander Zverev, the No 1 seed, beat Ben Shelton 6-3, 7-6 (2), 5-7, 6-2, the American’s hopes dashed in his first grand slam final. Golf | The captain Anna Nordqvist led Europe to a 15-13 victory in the Solheim Cup a month after retiring from competitive golf. Football | Sonia Bompastor’s Chelsea dominated in a 5-0 away victory against Eva Olid’s Manchester United, while Pro Ref admitted Erling Haaland’s winner in Sunday’s Manchester derby should not have counted after the VAR ruled Enzo Fernández was not interfering with play in the buildup. The front pages “Revealed: true scale of Britain’s involvement in the slave trade”, is the Guardian’s splash today. The Telegraph leads with “Hospitality chiefs urge PM to cut VAT” and the Express says “Labour tourist tax will hammer seaside B&Bs”. The i Paper’s headline is “Reform’s £72m crypto bonanza sparks Labour donations row”, Metro says “Labour threat to Reform’s £72m windfall”, while the Mirror’s take is “Bitcon?”. The FT’s splash is “Trump rejects industry calls for brake on AI over fears of losing race to China”. The Sun has “Boris flees Vlad drone blitz”, the Mail asks “Did Putin drone target Boris and top security officials?” Today in Focus AI isn’t going to end humanity … right? Ten per cent. That’s the risk, more or less, claimed a high-profile AI developer last week, that the technology wipes humanity out in the next decade. “I think it’s a crossover moment for the AI safety story because this has been for a long time talked about inside the AI world”, says our UK technology editor, Robert Booth, “but now, the general public and the political class have become increasingly concerned about it.” So how worried, asks Annie Kelly, should we be? Cartoon of the day | Tom Gauld The Upside A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad “In bistros and cafes, people don’t just eat and drink, they catch up with each other, meet new people, debate, laugh, read, write and sometimes fall in love,” said Alain Fontaine of Paris’s Le Mesturet bistro. Yet where once there were an estimated 500,000 cafe-bistros dotted throughout France, there are now only about 30,000 to 40,000. But one group of local campaigners in the northern Burgundy community of Saint-Martin-sur-Ouanne has saved one such establishment, and in the process, make their village livable again. After a successful community-led campaign to reopen it, Au Bon Acceuil cafe-bistro has been brought back to life – and every table is taken. As the village mayor, Hervé Chapuis, put it: “Our aim is to keep this kind of business open to support the social fabric. It’s part of village life and people missed it. Now, village life has returned to its proper rhythm.” Sign up here for a weekly roundup of The Upside, sent to you every Sunday Bored at work? And finally, the Guardian’s puzzles are here to keep you entertained throughout the day. Until tomorrow. Quick crossword Cryptic crossword Wordiply

title: Rail passengers get automatic right to switch operators for free when trains are cancelled
summary: ‘Commonsense change’ looks to end current confusion and put ‘passengers first, not shareholders’ when services are disrupted
text: Rail passengers whose trains are cancelled will have the immediate right to travel on other operators’ services to finish their journey without further charge, ministers have announced. The “commonsense change” will take effect from Sunday 20 September, ending the confusion in Britain where many pre-booked tickets are not valid on other firms’ trains. While passengers are frequently allowed to travel with different operators in times of severe disruption, travellers can be left to wait for a formal agreement that another firm’s tickets can be accepted, or sometimes buy an expensive new ticket and apply for a refund for the first. The Department for Transport said passengers had until now been “paying the price for a system which prioritises shareholders when trains are cancelled”. From 20 September, customers holding a valid ticket will be able to travel on another operator’s train two hours before or after the original cancelled service, on a reasonable alternative route. The rail minister, Lord Hendy, said: “This is a simple, commonsense change that puts passengers first. No one should be left stranded because of a fragmented railway when their journey is disrupted. From this weekend, if your train is cancelled, you can get on another operator’s service and carry on your journey without paying again.” He said the government was making the railway “simpler, fairer and easier to use, as we move towards Great British Railways and put public service back at the heart of our railways”. Automatic cross-operator ticket acceptance has been brought in already across firms returned to public ownership, but now CrossCountry, GWR, Avanti West Coast and Chiltern Railways, running important intercity routes, will be included. The remaining passenger train operations are scheduled to come into public ownership next year under a Great British Railways banner, bar a handful of open-access services, which will remain separate. East Midlands Railway, which has been beset with problems while introducing malfunctioning Hitachi bi-mode trains, will also not be immediately included due to its ongoing mass cancellations and shortages of seats. Alex Robertson, the chief executive of the independent watchdog Transport Focus said it was “a welcome change that we have long called for”, adding: “The key now is making sure passengers get clear information about their options whenever disruption occurs.”

title: AI CEOs say they need to slow the pace of development. But will they?
summary: After apocalyptic warnings about the the threats posed by AI, leaders like Sam Altman and Elon Musk backed Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei’s calls to ‘slow the pace’
text: Facing a public uproar over Anthropic researchers’ repeated warnings that artificial intelligence could kill all of humanity by 2030, the AI company’s CEO, Dario Amodei, issued a proposal at the weekend to slow down the technology’s advancement to ensure public safety. In a rare display of unity, the heads of the largest US artificial intelligence companies all agreed immediately. The OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Google DeepMind chief Demis Hassabis and xAI owner Elon Musk posted support for Amodei’s proposal for slowing AI development, titled “We Must Pace the Frontier”, with Altman stating he would match Amodei’s commitment to embedding outside evaluators within his company to verify safety practices. “I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier,” Altman posted Saturday on X. “Committing to having independent evaluators with employee-like access is a great idea, and we will do the same.” “Dario’s essay points towards the right path forward,” said Hassabis. Musk simply wrote: “Dario is right.” The AI CEOs’ warnings and promises open up a host of questions about how AI might be regulated, what risks it poses and whether the industry will actually slow down the fevered race to advance its technology. While lawmakers and the tech industry consider how to address growing fear and distrust of AI, many of the hurdles impeding comprehensive AI regulation remain the same as before last week’s apocalyptic declarations from a young Anthropic researcher. The US federal government is committed to a global AI arms race. Previous proposed AI legislation has wilted under intense, well-financed corporate lobbying. AI startups face the enormous pressures to release new, more powerful products ahead of upcoming trillion-dollar public offerings. Amodei’s pacing proposal has drawn heavy skepticism from critics and researchers who allege that AI firms are attempting to preempt more stringent government regulation and retain the status quo of power within the industry. Anthropic and OpenAI did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Amodei’s proposal focuses on three main pillars. First, a commitment to outside evaluators given employee-level access to monitor risk. Second, agreements between democratic states on AI safety standards. Finally, global coordination with authoritarian governments such as China on security issues. Amodei and others in the industry have made similar calls for global coordination in the past, even before the industry’s recent warnings over models becoming too advanced and gaining autonomy. The AI industry, especially the factions within it that focus on whether the technology is aligned with humanity’s interests, has also long warned about its existential threats. Rahm Emanuel, former congressman and chief of staff to Barack Obama, tweeted: “I can tell you when the last time a CEO or an industry at large asked to be regulated: never. That’s what makes Dario’s letter so striking – it’s an admission that we’re driving down a dark, winding road on wet pavement with the headlights off. And where’s President Trump? Looks like he nodded off again.” AI firms have fluctuated on their emphasis on communicating the potential harm from their products, however, at times warning about apocalyptic effects of AI and at others promising it will bring about utopian prosperity. OpenAI, for instance, shut down a “superalignment” team in 2024 dedicated to studying long term AI risks and earlier this year disbanded another team intended to communicate how OpenAI would benefit humanity. While AI companies have made grandiose claims about the threats and benefits from their technology, they have also historically provided little transparency or oversight into how their models operate and spent millions in lobbying efforts to shape favorable legislation. The result of the AI industry’s narrative that it is too powerful, complex and lucrative of a technology to regulate, critics say, is that it has been allowed to essentially govern itself. “AI exceptionalism has led to a total failure to uphold our standards for what products are deemed safe for use,” Sarah Myers West, co-executive director of the AI Now Institute, posted Sunday on X. Critics similarly see Amodei’s proposal as another instance in which the industry is seeking to set its own rules, in this case picking its own evaluators to monitor safety risks, instead of facing the scrutiny of more intensive government regulators. Alex Bores, a proponent of AI regulation whose failed bid for Congress spurred $24m in spending both for and against his campaign from AI-linked political action committees, warned that the AI lobby often seeks to undermine legislation while claiming to support regulation. “To everyone who genuinely wants real AI regulation, please don’t fall for their games,” Bores posted Sunday on X. Several critics of the AI pacing proposal from across the political spectrum expressed concern around Amodei’s proposal’s suggestion that the government could grant some form of antitrust waiver or exemption to allow industry coordination. Former officials, including Trump’s former “AI czar” David Sacks and Biden-era head of the Federal Trade Commission Alvaro Bedoya, suggested that the proposal amounted to an attempt at regulatory capture, which would benefit current industry leaders. “Antitrust law does not prevent AI companies from coordinating to make sure AI does not hurt people,” Bedoya posted on X, adding: “Antitrust law does absolutely prevent AI companies from organizing to prevent the entry of cheaper, upstart rivals because the bigger companies are burning cash and failing to achieve sufficient profitability.” The proposal’s calls for international coordination around AI and federal intervention also run up against president Donald Trump and his administration’s vows to turn the US into the dominant AI superpower regardless of safety concerns. The Trump administration has often framed AI development as a zero-sum contest against China for technological supremacy, an argument the AI industry itself has also promoted in the face of proposed government regulation. Vice-president JD Vance declared in a speech last year that the future of AI was “not going to be won by hand-wringing about safety”. On Sunday, Trump once again rejected calls for slowing down AI development while citing competition from China and telling reporters “whoever wins AI, wins”. “We could put guardrails. We can do this and that,” Trump told reporters while on a visit to Ireland. “But I think you have a lot of very negative ⁠forces that are bringing it up that shouldn’t be bringing it up and they’re bringing up things that won’t happen”. House speaker Mike Johnson likewise said Congress would not lead the charge on regulating AI safety, laying the responsibility at the feet of AI companies.

title: Starwatch: A Venus-spotting challenge with a beautiful reward
summary: The bright planet and the young crescent moon will make an attractive pairing on Monday evening
text: This week’s Starwatch is a challenge but a beautiful reward awaits for anyone who succeeds. The question is: how early in the evening can we find Venus? On Monday, the bright planet has a close encounter with a young crescent moon. The moon will be just over three days old with about 14% of its visible surface illuminated. Unfortunately for UK observers, the two make their closest approach during daylight, passing within a moon’s width of one another around lunchtime. By the evening they will have separated a little, but they will still make an attractive pairing for observers with a particularly good view towards the south-west. The chart shows the view looking south-west from London at 6.30pm. The sun will still be above the horizon, so do not use any visual equipment and avoid looking directly at the sun with the naked eye. First look for the slender crescent moon, low in the south-western sky. Once you have found it, use it as your guide to Venus nearby. As the sun sinks lower, Venus should become progressively easier to see, although the moon and planet will be descending towards the horizon. From the southern hemisphere, the moon and Venus are also visible together, appearing higher in the evening sky after sunset.
