title: Country diary: Notice anything wrong with this ripe, succulent plum? | Claire Stares
summary: Langstone, Hampshire: My garden is full of Victoria plums, but they’re not supposed to be crunchy inside
text: This summer has been challenging for the fruit trees in my garden, with intense heat and a lack of rain causing poor cropping, premature ripening and pre-harvest drop. While my dessert and cooking apples have produced just a handful of stunted, crab-apple-sized fruit, and my quince is bare, the Victoria plum growing next to the greenhouse is the exception. Its branches are so heavily laden that several have snapped under the weight. For the past week, I’ve been plucking and eating the plums straight from the tree. Occasionally, as I’ve bitten into them, the soft, honeyed flesh has given way to the bitter taste and gritty texture of coffee grounds. I assumed the woody endocarp that protects the seed had started to break down, perhaps due to environmental stress. It wasn’t until I cut one open and pulled out the pit, revealing a small, vivid pink caterpillar surrounded by crumbly brown pellets, that I realised I had been ingesting frass – insect excrement. The culprits were the larvae of the plum fruit moth (Grapholita funebrana), a drab, greyish-brown species that is locally common in southern England. In mid-summer, females lay individual eggs on developing fruit, and when the creamy-white, brown-headed caterpillars hatch, they burrow in, feasting on the flesh around the stone. As they grow and mature, their bodies flush pink. From a distance, the dusky purple plums looked flawless. Upon closer inspection, I discovered that affected fruit were slightly misshapen, and there was often a globule of clear, sticky sap oozing from the barely visible entry hole – a defence mechanism known as gummosis, triggered when the caterpillar bores into the skin. I usually leave fallen fruit for the blackbirds, peacock butterflies and wasps. But to prevent the caterpillars from emerging, pupating and perpetuating the cycle, the advice is to remove all dropped and damaged plums, disposing of them well away from the tree. I salvaged what I could to make jam, consigning the infested scraps to the compost bin. The following morning, I came into the kitchen to find a squirming mass of caterpillars had migrated out of the fruit and on to the bin lid. • Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024, is available now at guardianbookshop.com

title: Rise in abuse of election candidates is ‘changing politics’ in England
summary: Electoral Commission finds abuse, particularly of women, minority ethnic and disabled people, is affecting candidates’ behaviour
text: Abuse and intimidation of election candidates is “a serious and growing concern”, the Electoral Commission has said, as a review of this year’s local and mayoral elections in England revealed a surge in threats to those who stood. More than half of the candidates for Labour or Reform UK reported abuse while those most likely to be targeted were women, people from minority ethnic backgrounds and those with disabilities. A report by the commission said candidates described being spat at and verbally and physically assaulted. It found that levels of abuse had reached the point where it was changing the behaviour of people standing in elections. “I had to take my husband out on the door this time, which was a first,” said one candidate, who was among a third of those who said they may not stand for election again because of harassment or intimidation. They added: “I felt quite independent previously, but there was so much anger from men of an older age at the door and some younger men, all disillusioned by politics and let down. “I did understand that, but it was the anger and insults and close confrontation at times which was so aggressive. I feel I have to protect myself in public and not be on my own, for the first time in local politics, and will never put myself in any vulnerable places on my own again.” Female candidates were more likely to change their behaviour over such concerns. More than three-quarters (79%) said they avoided campaigning on their own at least once, compared with 46% of male candidates, while 57% avoided speaking on controversial topics, compared with 32% of men. Vijay Rangarajan, the chief executive of the Electoral Commission, said: “Our single biggest worry now is this rise in abuse and intimidation. It’s not directed at any one party and there seems to be a variety of causes.” He said there was an increasing trend towards the “othering” of political opponents, “literally, a dehumanisation” and a blurring of the boundaries of civility, in some cases driven by social media. “I think we’re going to see a kind of complete blurring of the online and offline worlds,” he said. “We’ve seen people in the real world walk down the street filming someone to produce an online video. And then when others see that online video, they get very angry and they go and start following someone else down the streets. So this kind of real, complete interaction between online and offline is a real feature.” Rangarajan said he was struck by two particular cases. One was a disabled candidate who said they were threatened on the doorstep but “couldn’t run away” because of their disability. Another was a candidate who was targeted on social media and whose daughter called from school to say she had seen the online abuse and people were calling her parent a racist, fascist and Nazi. The commission made a number of recommendations, including calling on social media companies to do more to tackle the online abuse of candidates by developing rapid response protocols, and calling on parties to urge their members to respect other campaigners. The review found 59% of Reform UK and 54% of Labour candidates told of personally experiencing inappropriate behaviour, harassment or threats to their security, followed by 42% of Greens, 37% of independents, 26% of Tories and 22% of Liberal Democrats. Rangarajan said the changes made by some candidates in how they campaigned was affecting local politics. “It takes away, in some cases, things like meeting your candidate, which is really important in our politics. The second thing is it definitely affects women much more and ethnic minority candidates too, and even more if you’re both. People are stopping wanting to be candidates because of this and that’s a real problem,” he said. Rangarajan called for a “multi-partisan approach” from parties. “We’re all up for really robust debate, that’s what the whole election is about and it wouldn’t work if it wasn’t … but it’s got to have a modicum of respect to it as well and there are some things which are really unacceptable, like following someone’s family down the street, for example, trying to video them, or posting people death threats.” On the upside, the report found that voters continue to be satisfied with how elections are run, with 94% of voters in England expressing satisfaction with the voting process, similar to 2025 (95%) and the last comparable elections in 2022 (96%). Nevertheless, voters remain concerned about the accuracy of election information. More than half of those surveyed said they had seen misinformation, and one in 10 said they had seen deepfake material. Rangarajan welcomed proposals in the representation of the people bill to protect election agents’ home addresses, extend protections to electoral staff and increase sentencing for offenders against candidates, elected officials and electoral staff.

title: Satellite images show extent of damage to major Saudi pipeline, amid global oil supply fears
summary: Saudis yet to provide details about damage from drone attack to key east-west pipeline to Red Sea that could affect 4% of global oil supply
text: Saudi Arabia will run out of oil ⁠stocks for export if it ⁠doesn’t restart a drone-damaged major pipeline to the Red Sea within days, leading to the loss of up to 4% of global supply, Saudi oil buyers and traders said. Satellite photos released on Sunday night appeared to show a pumping station on the key 1,200km (745-mile) Saudi east-west pipeline charred and badly damaged, after drone attacks on Friday. A further decline in oil flow from Saudi Arabia, the world largest oil exporter, will worsen the ⁠global supply crunch, which has already pushed global fuel prices to record highs and spurred inflation around the world. The news comes as Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi forces have launched attacks on targets in Saudi Arabia and captured the strategic island of Perim in the Bab al-Mandab strait, expanding their control of the narrow waterway. On Sunday, the international oil benchmark, Brent crude, rose more than 3.4% to $108 per barrel, a level not seen since May. Since the drone attacks forced the shutdown of the pipeline, Riyadh has yet to provide full details about the extent of the damage or how long the route will stay offline. The Saudis blamed the attack on drones launched by militants in Iraq. Sources that spoke to Reuters gave varying estimates, ‌with one saying the damage could take ‌up to six weeks to repair, while another said it could be fixed sooner and could resume pumping partially while ‌repairs are ongoing. Saudi Arabia’s government media office and energy ministry did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Two officials who spoke on condition of anonymity to the Associated Press said the pipeline would be mostly out of service for weeks. For the past six months, the pipeline running through the desert across the Arabian Peninsula has spared Saudi Arabia from the brunt of the impact of the wartime shutdown of the strait of Hormuz that has crippled exports from its neighbours. The world’s biggest exporter has used the pipeline to reroute around 4m barrels per day – about 4% of global supply – to the port of Yanbu on the Red Sea. But with the ‌pipeline out of service, Yanbu now has stocks to maintain exports for just five to seven days, according to three industry sources familiar with Saudi exports. Saudi Arabia also has stocks to supply customers for several days from Egypt’s ports of Ain Sukhna on the Red Sea and Sidi Kerir on the Mediterranean, a fourth source said. Stocks are not full and will ultimately run out without the east-west pipeline resuming operations, the four sources said. As the price of oil climbed, hopes for a diplomatic breakthrough in the near term faded when Oman’s foreign minister, Sayyid Badr Albusaidi, posted late Sunday that a regional meeting scheduled for Monday had been postponed “in the interests of consensus”. Iranian officials had said they would attend that gathering with Gulf Arab states to present ⁠an agreement with Oman on governing shipping routes through the strait of Hormuz. The strait was free to transit before the war, but Iran now requires vessels to obtain permission and is considering a mechanism to impose service fees. The disruptions to crude has driven up prices across refined derivatives such as petrol and diesel. Diesel prices in the US hit a record on Friday, soaring past $6 a gallon on average. The Houthis are targeting Saudi oil infrastructure and shipping as part of a recently declared blockade. Recent advances by the Iran-aligned group puts them closer to a major US base in Djibouti. The spiralling conflict in the Middle East is now in its seventh month, after US and Israel launched attacks on Iran on 28 February and Donald Trump declared the war would finished in four to six weeks. With Reuters and Associated Press

title: Ukraine war briefing: Poland calls for ‘double’ support to Kyiv after Russian train attack
summary: Polish minister denounces ‘escalation’ after strike near border with UK’s Boris Johnson and ex-CIA chief David Petraeus nearby. What we know on day 1,664
text: Poland and Ukraine have denounced Russian strikes close to the Polish border as an “escalation” in the war after a train was targeted while former British prime minister Boris Johnson and ex-CIA director David Petraeus were at a border station nearby. The escalation should lead to allies to “double” their support for Ukraine, Poland’s foreign minister said in Kyiv. “This was just a few hundred metres from the Polish border, this affects the safety of my countrymen,” Radoslaw Sikorski said. Polish prime minister Donald Tusk chaired an emergency meeting in Warsaw after the strikes, warning he expected Russia to escalate the war “in the coming weeks”. He added: “We cannot exclude that the escalation will also affect our territory … I hope not.” Poland and Ukraine said the Kyiv-Warsaw passenger train was struck just 2km from the Polish border, reporting no casualties. Shortly beforehand a diplomatic train was at Yagodyn station including Johnson and former Swedish prime minister Carl Bildt as well as security advisers from several EU member states, while former CIA director David Petraeus was aboard another train at the station when the attack occurred, the Ukrzaliznytsia rail operator said. It did not say how far the officials were from the train struck. Zelenskyy said Moscow had “deliberately” struck the locomotive. “It is precisely to prevent these strikes from spreading further into Europe that Ukrainian men and women fight every day, give their lives, and do not allow the aggression to expand,” the Ukrainian president said. Ukrainian Railways said Johnson and Petraeus may have been the target, report Amy Hawkins and Charlotte Higgins. Ukrainian foreign minister Andrii Sybiha said the attack was “Putin’s terror knocking directly on the doors of the EU and Nato”. Donald Trump has called on Zelenskyy to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries and other infrastructure used to produce and distribute diesel, saying the attacks were causing a global shortage. “Mr Zelenskyy has to do one thing – he has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia,” Trump told reporters in Ireland after diesel prices in the US hit a record high on Friday. “We spoke to Mr Zelenskyy about it. There are plenty of other targets. Don’t hit diesel fuel, because that’s hurting the world.” Kyiv says Russia’s oil industry funds and fuels Moscow’s war on Ukraine. Trump sought to tie Ukraine’s attacks on Russian refineries to rising oil prices, saying it was these attacks and not America’s ongoing conflict with Iran that were responsible for price rises. “This isn’t done by the Middle East, this is done by what’s happening with Russia and Ukraine,” the US president said. According to a report published on Friday by the International Energy Agency, net exports of diesel and oil from the Gulf countries in August stood at “just over a quarter” of what they were before the war on Iran began in February. “Disruptions to Russia’s refining system and a near-halt to product exports following intensified Ukrainian attacks have compounded these losses,” the agency wrote. The Kremlin said negotiations with Ukraine and the US on the war could take place in October. “We do not rule out such a possibility – we are talking about the foreseeable future,” Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said, cited by Russia’s Ria and Tass news agencies. Zelenskyy said separately he would be willing to meet Putin at the G20 summit in Miami in December, but Peskov said that was “impossible”, repeating Moscow’s demand that a meeting could only take place in the Russian capital. Putin has repeatedly rejected offers for face-to-face talks with the Ukrainian president. Zelenskyy has imposed sanctions on a former press secretary, ⁠accusing her and nine others of spreading Russian propaganda and of supporting Russia’s aggressive policy ⁠towards Ukraine. Yuliia Mendel, who ⁠worked with Zelenskyy from 2019 to 2021, before Russia’s invasion – responded with a message on Facebook saying it ⁠was unconstitutional to impose sanctions on Ukrainian citizens. She did not comment on the specific accusations. • This article was amended on 14 September 2026. An earlier version featured a photo of a burning train carriage that was from a different attack. This image has been replaced.

title: Hospitality industry urges Andy Burnham to lay out VAT cut plans
summary: More than 800 businesses ask PM to make good on pledge, or risk more closures and job losses
text: Hundreds of UK hospitality businesses, backed by celebrity chefs including Angela Hartnett and Heston Blumenthal, have asked Andy Burnham to lay out plans to lower VAT for the sector, urging him to make good on his previous pledge. More than 800 businesses have written an open letter to the prime minister as part of the #VATsTheProblem campaign, to warn that without a “fairer tax burden for hospitality”, there will be more closures and job losses, and fewer opportunities for young people. The signatories include pubs, bars and brewers such as Fuller’s, Greene King, Mitchell’s & Butlers and Wetherspoons, along with restaurant groups including Franco Manca, Pizza Express and Wagamama, hotel chains such as Best Western Hotels and Marriott international, along with the leisure groups Center Parcs and Parkdean Resorts. However, most of the signatories are small and medium-sized businesses, including independent, single-site pubs and hotels. Among the celebrity chefs who signed the letter are Andi Oliver, Clare Smyth, Jason Atherton, Nathan Outlaw, Paul Ainsworth and Tom Kerridge. In February, Burnham, then mayor of Greater Manchester, publicly said he would argue for a hospitality VAT rate in line with Europe because of the social value businesses bring to towns. More than 370,000 people have signed the #VATsTheProblem petition calling for a 10% rate of VAT for hospitality, bringing the UK in line with the European average. The campaign comes after the prime minister’s announcement to cut business rates by 20% for pubs, clubs and live music venues in his first week in office as part of a £100m aid package – but Burnham immediately faced calls to go further. The letter said: “It’s time for a fairer tax burden for hospitality. Without action, closures will only continue to accelerate, jobs will continue to be lost and opportunities for young people reduced. “A lower rate of VAT for hospitality can turn closures into openings, lost jobs into new jobs, and boarded up high streets into thriving centres of community.” Kerridge added: “The reality is that 20% VAT is holding hospitality back. Hospitality is different from many other businesses because so much of what we spend our money on is our teams. You can reclaim VAT on a product, but you can’t reclaim VAT on a person. That makes a 20% rate particularly tough for a sector where labour is one of our biggest costs. “And this is all happening at a time when businesses are already dealing with rising wages, energy bills, food costs and business rates. We’re seeing the consequences, with businesses closing their doors every single week.” The letter came as the government said it would work closely with publicans to give more options for pub tenants who want greater freedom in running their pubs, so they get fairer lease agreements and a better price on beer, following a review into the 2016 pubs code. Other changes are being considered, including to allow pub companies and tenants to agree to a longer-term relationship. There is an option for tenants to go “free of tie” from their pub company and instead pay market rent and buy products freely from other companies. The review found that between April 2022 and March 2025, fewer than 400 tenants applied for a free of tie agreement, saying they felt deterred by the cost and complexity.

title: Hidden history of royal staff uncovered in Buckingham Palace restoration
summary: Whist drive ticket embedded in rock and news article on Great Train Robbers among items discovered during 10-year restoration
text: Lost or long-discarded items revealing glimpses of the behind-the-scenes life of Buckingham Palace staff over decades have been uncovered during the restoration of the UK monarchy’s HQ. Misplaced belongings, found beneath the floorboards, in other areas of the royal residence and preserved within the fabric of the building, include a ticket to a whist drive run by the royal household’s social club from nearly 80 years ago. Blank Littlewoods football pools betting slips from 1957, a pair of battered black hobnail boots and an empty Silk Cut cigarette packet were among the everyday objects unearthed, as well as an almost 140-year-old fragment of the West End theatre listings from the Standard newspaper in 1889. The discoveries were made during the decade-long £370m reservicing of the palace which has included rewiring electrics, upgrading plumbing and heating and overhauling its infrastructure to prevent long-term damage. Electrical wire covered with Vulcanised Indian Rubber (VIR) cabling, which posed the risk of fire to the building, were also located. The cabling, which becomes brittle with age, was removed as a priority when the project, which is due to be completed next year, began in 2017. About 1.2 miles (2km) of the rubber cabling has been replaced so far. The small whist drive ticket, priced at 6d, a sixpence, and dated 14 April 1949 – during the reign of the king’s grandfather, George VI – was found embedded in a lump of building rock. The pass to the staff social club gathering in the palace reads “Royal Household Social Club – Buckingham Palace: A Whist Drive to be held on” followed by the faded, stamped date “14 APR 1949”. At that time, Queen Elizabeth II was still Princess Elizabeth and had been married to Prince Philip for less than 18 months and their eldest son, Charles, was only five months old. Pages from the Daily Express newspaper in 1966 detailed the maximum security prison housing the Great Train Robbers, picturing the inside of Durham prison and reporting that “the men who were found guilty of stealing a fortune in mailbags spend their week stitching them for nine shillings”. Instructions for royal household staff for the 1977 Silver Jubilee Diplomatic Corps reception informed them that the queen and other members of the royal family would move round the ballroom in a “clockwise direction”. Aides were to encourage the 350 British guests to mingle with the diplomats at the glittering white tie and tiaras annual gathering, according to the manually typed sheet, which also said that smoking was banned in the certain state rooms and the reception kept to a strict timetable. Other findings included a section of Minton decorative ceramic tiles from a fireplace hearth, with the design dating from around the mid-1800s, an aged Pewter tankard, a bottle of Schweppes still Malvern English spring water, a wooden junction box and a faded box containing six Christmas cards.

title: Swedish election: centre-left parties lead by just a single seat with most votes counted
summary: Race too close to call and may take days to become clear despite early exit polls suggesting left bloc win
text: With most of the votes counted, Sweden’s national election remained too close to call on Sunday night, with left-wing parties holding a lead of just a single seat according to a partial tally by the election authority. Earlier in the night, exit polls suggested that the country was on course for a brand new left-leaning government. But as the votes were counted, it was apparent it could take days for the outcome to become clear. With 80% of votes counted, there was just one seat between the left and right blocs. The left-leaning opposition parties, led by Social Democrat Magdalena Andersson, had 175 and the rightwing parties, led by the Moderates prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, had 174. At 10:30pm local time, broadcaster SVT predicted there were only 20,000 votes between the blocs. The election authority said a preliminary vote count may not be ready until Thursday. Kristersson, the incumbent prime minister, said the voters had had their say, but “we still don’t have a final result.” “Which government will lead Sweden in the coming years is still an open question, and we will do everything we can to ensure that this government will be the very best for our country,” Kristersson told supporters. The Social Democrats remain Sweden’s biggest party, but look to have had their worst result in decades. Speaking just before midnight local time, Andersson addressed supporters to say that every vote must be counted. “We will have to wait for the final election results. But my message is clear: we Social Democrats will always be ready to take responsibility for the result. It seems like it will be very even,” she said. “But right now we are leading. If it stands, then Sweden will have a new government. But we have to wait for the final result, so let me end where I began, in democracy, the finest thing we have.” It was also a bad night for the far-right Sweden Democrats, who are hoping to enter government for the first time. They slipped from the country’s second biggest party to third. The deputy prime minister, Ebba Busch, of the Christian Democrats, told her supporters that Sweden would be going “to bed with uncertainty” and may have to wait until Wednesday for a result. But she remained adamant that the ruling right-leaning coalition should remain in government. “This is a very clear message for the only unified government alternative in this election campaign,” she said in an upbeat speech. “This will be a real nail-biter, this could be uncertain all the way until Wednesday.” It comes after an unusually heated and polarised campaign punctuated by personal attacks between leaders, accusations of misinformation and Maga-inspired ads. Polls suggested an extremely tight race, with one showing just 0.3 percentage points between the left and right blocs. Polling stations across the country opened at 8am local time (7am UK time). Enthusiasm among voters appeared to be high. A record 3.6 million voters took part in early voting and there were reports of long queues at some polling stations. Whatever the result, coalition talks are expected to take weeks if not months. The right-leaning bloc, made up of what are known as the Tidö parties, has been in power for four years. It is formed of the Moderates, the Christian Democrats and the Liberals, with a supporting role for SD, Sweden’s second biggest party. The opposition left-leaning bloc is formed of Sweden’s biggest party, the Social Democrats, the Centre party, the Green party and the Left party. The rightwing coalition broke a longstanding taboo in 2022 by going into partnership with SD, which has neo-Nazi roots. SD has attempted to make itself more palatable to the mainstream by toning down its overtly racist rhetoric, while arguing that immigration is responsible for Sweden’s crime problems. After four years in a supporting role for the Moderates-run coalition government, however, during which it has shifted much of the Swedish establishment to the right and had a strong influence on policies, SD’s approach to the election has been more brazen. If the right-leaning coalition wins, the party has been promised a prominent role in the government, including key ministerial positions. SD’s campaign slogan of “make Sweden Sweden again” was reminiscent of Donald Trump’s “make America great again”. Its controversial ads on buses – with messages including: “Do you miss Mogadishu? The repatriation grant will help you get home” – were taken down after drivers refused to work in vehicles displaying them. The party leader, Jimmie Åkesson, was accused of sexism after asking the Social Democrats’ leader why she was so angry during a TV debate. Another leading SD figure, Gustav Gellerbrant, came under national scrutiny after an investigation by the publication Expo connected his partner to Russian state actors and the spread of Russian propaganda. His partner, who is Russian, works as a civil servant for SD in parliament. Gellerbrant said in response that it was “isolated information” intended to raise suspicion about her Russian origins and has since gone on leave. Andersson, who voted on Sunday morning in the Stockholm suburb of Nacka, said the campaign had been “a tale of two sides”. “There have been a lot of lies and bickering, but at the same time there are so many sensible people out there across the country,” she told SVT. “The focus is on winning and setting a new direction for Sweden.” Abba’s Benny Andersson showed his support for the Social Democrats’ leader by performing a reworked version of Mamma Mia to supporters at the party’s headquarters, replacing the words “Mamma Mia” with “Magdalena”. Kristersson had put considerable focus in the final days of campaigning on the penalty discount applied to criminals convicted of various offences. He accused the Social Democrat leader of not standing up for female rape victims. In response, she accused him of weaponising men’s violence against women. After voting in the town of Strängnäs, west of the capital, Kristersson said “momentum is on our side”. Despite dropping in the latest polls, he said the role of his party was to be “team leaders … uniting for the best of the country”. Voters say the most important election issues are healthcare, law and order, immigration and the economy. But much of the election debate has been focused on personal finance, said Radio Sweden’s senior political correspondent, Fredrik Furtenbach. “The parties have tried to outdo each other with promises of more money. It has been a sort of auction.”

title: ‘Sweat the asset’: new development minister plots path to make UK aid count
summary: Kirsty McNeill reaffirms Labour’s 0.7% of GDP pledge and promises value for money to allay voter concerns
text: The development minister, Kirsty McNeill, has declared herself “a huge believer in aid”, as she reaffirmed Labour’s manifesto pledge to return to a target of 0.7% of national income spending. McNeill, a former adviser to Gordon Brown and senior executive at Save the Children, declined to give any timetable, repeating the formula that the government would work towards the target “when fiscal circumstances allow”. But she made a full-throated argument for the benefits of aid – as well as promising to build new “agile partnerships” to work on development challenges. “I’m a huge believer in aid; I’m a huge believer in the quality of British aid, and when you have more of it, you can have more impact. And I think it’s important that colleagues hear that underscored,” she said. Repeating the manifesto pledge that Labour made before the 2024 general election to return to 0.7% – instead slashing aid the next year – McNeill insisted that in the Burnham government, “everyone from the prime minister down is a believer in the spirit that animated that manifesto”. McNeill will be setting out her priorities in a speech to charities and campaigners at the New Economics Foundation thinktank on Monday. She will announce that the government is making up to £15m available via its humanitarian crisis fund to support preventive action in countries most at risk from El Niño. “It will just do very practical things like vaccinate livestock and get cash to farmers to provide supplies,” she said. The UN has warned that the climate phenomenon is likely to be the most severe in 1,000 years, exacerbating risks of wildfires and flooding. The 0.7% aid target was adopted by the Blair government and became a cross-party consensus, until it was set aside by Rishi Sunak in the depths of the Covid pandemic, as the government rapidly stepped up domestic spending. Charities have warned that Labour’s more recent aid cuts, taking spending to 0.3% of national income, are causing sharp reductions in bilateral UK support to some of the world’s poorest countries. McNeill’s predecessor, Jenny Chapman, took the job after Anneliese Dodds quit over the scale of the cuts. At the time of Starmer’s decision, some Labour strategists were concerned about what they perceived as the unpopularity of aid spending among voters. But McNeill said Labour should not be afraid to make a straightforward argument for development. “As we’ve lost our confidence, we started trying to make lots of different arguments for development that go beyond what I believe to be the core one, which is, if you have the capability to save people’s lives and to change people’s lives, you should deploy that capability ambitiously,” she said. “I think aid is a really good instrument to save children’s lives. And the impacts of British aid, through immunisation, or by feeding children who would otherwise starve, is one that in every conversation with the public I’ve had, whether it’s with a constituent on the doorstep or in my previous job at Save the Children, when you’re saying, ‘Do you think if we can do that, we should do that?’ people say: ‘Yes, we should.’” Voters’ concerns are more about the value for money and effectiveness of aid spending, she said, promising to “sweat the asset” when it came to getting the best out of the current straitened resources. She said she saw her role as bringing all the expertise and leverage of the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) to bear on what she called the “five securities” – “health security, climate security, food security, human security and economic security”. “The focus on securities is an attempt to recast my job as being about global cooperation and how we get security through solidarity,” she added. “That will mean pressing for reform of some of the international bodies that spend UK aid, as well as forming ‘bespoke partnerships’, to work on specific issues.” A veteran of the Make Poverty History campaign in the mid-2000s, McNeill contrasted this approach with that of the Blair government, which used the UK chairing of the G8 group of industrialised countries in 2005 to secure significant debt relief for developing countries. “Many of us came of age at a time when there were summits with big announcements, and a cheque from the UK government, and actually the thing that I want to be held to account for is have I done the grind, the diplomatic grind, to get the maximum we can out of our relationships?” McNeill has been the MP for Midlothian, south of Edinburgh, since 2024, winning the constituency from the Scottish National party. Her boss, the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, has signalled that he wants development to be a more prominent focus of the FCDO’s work, including by directly taking up the UK’s seat on the World Bank board. “The foreign secretary’s been very clear that both development and climate are going to be at the heart of British policy: they’re not an addition, they’re right at the beating heart, which I’m obviously absolutely delighted about,” she said.

title: Andy Burnham to host entrepreneurs and local mayors at No 10 on Monday
summary: Prime minister vows to ‘reindustrialise Britain’ through new partnership with business
text: The prime minister is to host business leaders, entrepreneurs and local mayors at Downing Street on Monday to pitch his government as a “partner for growth” that can offer a stable platform for investment and jobs in the UK. Ahead of the event, Andy Burnham said the country had “everything it needs to succeed”, including talented people and world-class universities, but requires “a culture shift in how Britain does business” if it is to unlock its full potential. The new prime minister vowed to “reindustrialise Britain” through a new partnership with business. “That means putting government firmly on the side of the people who take risks, start companies, create jobs and bring new ideas to life,” he said. “It means ensuring ambition is rewarded, making it easier to start and grow a business and giving people the confidence that if they have a great idea, they’ll get all the support they need to bring it to life.” Burnham will host a roundtable with entrepreneurs – including the founders of Octopus Energy, Revolut and Starling Bank and quantum computing companies including Oxford Quantum Circuits – before welcoming chief executives from some of Britain’s largest businesses for a reception in No 10 along with regional mayors. They include the bosses of financial companies HSBC, Aviva and Standard Chartered, supermarkets Morrisons and Sainsbury’s, telecoms groups BT and Vodafone, oil companies BP and Shell and manufacturers Rolls-Royce and BAE Systems. Monday’s round of meetings come as Burnham and John Healey, the chancellor, prepare for their first budget on 28 October. Burnham has vowed to deliver growth across the country and to devolve power and resources away from Westminster to do so. But Healey faces a tough task, presenting his budget amid rising borrowing costs and the impact of the Iran war on the global economy. Although the economy unexpectedly grew by 0.4% in July, boosted by AI and cloud computing, economists have warned rising energy costs may have held back growth in August and September. Suren Thiru, chief economist for the Institute of Chartered Accountants England and Wales, said the chancellor could be left with a “budget headache” if economic growth starts to dwindle, as more muted growth and surging borrowing costs erode his fiscal headroom, raising the prospect of further tax rises. Both Burnham and Healey have stressed their commitment to the fiscal rules laid down by former chancellor Rachel Reeves, which require day-to-day spending to be covered by taxes and government debt to fall as a share of the economy by 2029/30. They are also bound by Labour’s manifesto commitment not to raise income tax, national insurance or VAT. In his first major speech as chancellor last week, Healey said boosting economic growth would be his defining mission as chancellor but also warned Labour had to “be honest” about the need to control public spending at next month’s budget. He talked of putting more power and resources into the hands of local leaders, reducing the cost of doing business and using public investment to attract private capital.

title: Donald Trump doubles down on support for united Ireland
summary: US president brushes off Andy Burnham’s opposition to referendum and says he will remove Irish whiskey tariff
text: Donald Trump has reiterated his support for Irish unification and brushed off Andy Burnham’s opposition to a referendum. “Everybody says that. Then things happen,” the US president said on Sunday of the British prime minister’s response. “It seems to me that one of the naturals of all time is to put them together,” Trump said of the unification of Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland. Trump caused consternation on both sides of the Irish Sea on Saturday when, at the start of a two-day visit to Ireland, he said he would “love” to see a united Ireland and “it may as well happen now”. Trump ended his visit on Sunday at his Doonbeg golf resort in County Clare in exuberant fashion by presenting the Irish Open trophy to Shane Lowry and announcing that he would cut tariffs on Irish whiskey. “Everyone’s been bugging me,” he told the crowd. “They say ‘will you do me a favour, it’s so unfair, could you possibly take the tariffs off Irish whiskey?’ And I said ‘on behalf of the United States of America I’m going to take the tariffs off Irish whiskey’.” Some in the crowd cheered Trump’s name and chanted “USA”. A 10% tariff on Irish whiskey – part of White House measures against EU imports – disadvantaged it against competitors, including scotch and Northern Ireland whiskey, which have no tariffs. The decision followed repeated affirmations by Trump that he loves Ireland – and wishes to see the island unified. The avowals undercut the tradition of White House neutrality on the constitutional status of Northern Ireland and prompted responses from London. Downing Street said Burnham still believed there was not the required support for unification to trigger a referendum, as set out in the 1998 Good Friday peace agreement. Two weeks ago, Burnham said a referendum was “off the table”. Irish nationalists welcomed Trump’s remarks, while the Conservative party and Northern Irish unionists condemned them. On Sunday, Trump expressed delight at the controversy. “Many people agree. I made what I considered to be a fairly routine comment, I have had so much support on that,” he said. Asked about independence for Scotland, he reserved opinion. “I won’t talk about Scotland yet, I will save that.” The leaders of Plaid Cymru, the Scottish National party and Sinn Féin are meeting in Cardiff on Monday, where they will discuss ways to strengthen cooperation for constitutional change. Angela Rayner, the UK’s communities secretary, played down the president’s remarks. “Donald Trump is Donald Trump, and the president will say and speak his mind as he sees it,” she told Sky News. The government was serious about the Good Friday agreement and would “continue on that path”, she said. Trump’s comments were awkward for the Irish government, which prefers to discuss cross-border initiatives rather than unification. Last month the taoiseach, Micheál Martin, said that he “goes bananas” when his Fianna Fáil party colleagues call for a border poll. On Sunday, Martin said there had been “overreaction” to Trump’s comments. “He takes a different sort of perspective on things. We know that,” he said. “I think if everyone keeps a calm perspective on things, you know, we will take it from there.” Sinn Féin figures welcomed Trump’s support for Irish unification. “They reflect the broad North American sentiment towards Irish unity and particularly the Irish diaspora towards Irish reunification,” said Gerry Adams, the party’s former leader. Adams accused successive Irish governments of being “incredibly shortsighted” and failing to plan for unification. “There is no excuse for this.” Trump’s comments also proved awkward for Northern Ireland unionists who have supported the president on other topics. “Everyone is allowed a personal opinion even when it’s wrong,” said Ian Paisley Jr, a former Democratic Unionist party MP. “The political, cultural and economic reality is that Northern Ireland and its people are British and wish to remain so,” he said.

title: San Jose officer fired for misusing Flock camera database in domestic abuse case
summary: Police officer shared location of a woman with his relative who is accused of abusing woman
text: A San Jose police officer was fired for using his department’s Flock license plate tracking system to share the location of a woman with the suspect accused of abusing her, Chief Paul Joseph told NBC Bay Area on Friday. The firing marks another in a growing number of cases of misuse of a controversial surveillance technology that has expanded rapidly over the last several years. The officer accessed Flock camera data last year without authorization on his personal phone for the vehicle of a woman allegedly abused by one of the officer’s family members, then sent that information to his cousin, according to Joseph. The suspect in the domestic abuse case was the officer’s cousin, according to the San Jose Mercury News. Police discovered the unauthorized access when the woman told police that her alleged abuser told her that he knew her location. The department immediately placed the officer on administrative leave and began a criminal investigation into his actions, Joseph said. “I was furious that an officer would betray the public’s trust in that manner, that he would not understand how serious of a violation that is,” Joseph said. Joseph did not publicly disclose the name of the officer. San Jose police department referred the case to the Santa Clara county district attorney’s office, but the officer was not been charged with a crime. The district attorney’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Joseph told the Mercury News that state lawmakers should pass legislation making it easier to charge such violations as crimes. San Jose police department referred the officer to the commission on peace officer standards and training, which has the power to bar him from working as a law enforcement officer again in the state, the paper reported. License plate reading technology has drawn broad criticism, recurring protests and vandalism from the right and left alike, as law enforcement has deployed tens of thousands of cameras across the country, raising concerns about privacy, mass surveillance, false positives and police misuse of the technology. The technology has also raised concerns among immigrant rights groups, as law enforcement agencies increasingly share that data with Immigration and Customs Enforcement that ICE uses to press forward with Trump’s broadly unpopular mass deportation agenda. Dozens of law enforcement officers have used license-plate readers to stalk women, according to the Institute for Justice, a public interest law firm. The California assembly adjourned this month without taking action on a bill that would have imposed new regulations on license-plate reading technology. It marked the fifth straight year that California lawmakers declined to impose new safeguards on license-plate readers like Flock, according to CalMatters. The California assembly passed a bill that would have imposed new regulations, including a mandate to delete data unrelated to an investigation after two months, but Governor Gavin Newsom vetoed it.
