title: We know how to prevent black lung, so why are workers still dying?
summary: Silicosis sufferers are getting younger as Trump and the coal mining industry push back on protections
text: Silicosis is one of the oldest workplace hazards and public health experts have known for decades how to prevent it. Yet a new wave of workers, from Appalachian coalminers to Latino countertop fabrication workers, are developing and dying from the disease as industry fights new protections and regulators fail to defend the rules that could protect them. John Robinson’s grandfather developed black lung back when coalminers could spend decades in the mines before being diagnosed with the disease, often dying in their 60s, 70s and 80s. But Robinson, who mined for coal in south-west Virginia, was diagnosed when he was 47. He’s part of a trend that has grown over the past two decades in central Appalachia, where more coalminers are developing black lung disease at younger ages. “Now, honey, how are these men getting sick? Something’s causing it,” Robinson said. “At one time, you didn’t say black lung around the coal site unless you wanted to lose a job. It’s such an outbreak right now they can’t hide it.” Around 2018, doctors throughout the US started documenting outbreaks of lung disease among countertop fabrication workers too. There were seven workers diagnosed in Colorado and another 12 cases in Texas. That same year, a 38-year-old Hispanic man in California, whose work involved grinding stone edges at a countertop fabrication company, died of respiratory failure. Public health experts say the cause of both outbreaks is inhalation of tiny crystalline silica dust on the job and prevention involves limiting workers’ exposure through sampling and tamping down the dust to stop particles from becoming airborne. This means different things depending on the occupation. For miners, the 2024 Mine Safety and Health Administration (Msha) rule years in the making and passed under the Biden administration was supposed to address the occupational hazard. But within months of the rule going into effect, industry groups petitioned to overturn it. When the Trump administration failed to defend the rule, the eighth circuit court of appeals stayed it and Msha notified the court that it will reconsider portions of the rule impacted by the industry challenge. The National Stone, Sand & Gravel Association (NSSGA) led the legal challenge of Msha’s 2024 silica dust rule. The trade group represents sand, gravel and stone mining companies. NSSGA did not oppose the rule’s reduction of the permissible exposure limit from 100 micrograms per cubic meter to 50 micrograms per cubic meter per eight-hour shift, said Kerry Lynch, NSSGA’s senior director of communications. Lynch did not respond to questions about why it brought the legal challenge of the rule. But in a letter to Msha before the rule was finalized, NSSGA said it takes issue with the frequent air sampling and medical surveillance requirements. The American Exploration & Mining Association (AEMA) is one of the industry groups that joined the petition to challenge Msha’s 2024 silica dust rule. In a written statement to the Guardian, AEMA’s executive director, Mark Compton said that the AEMA supports lowering the permissible exposure limit (PEL) of silica to better protect miners. “We joined the petition challenging the 2024 silica rule because the rule would actually undermine miner safety and health due to the restrictions Msha imposed on its implementation,” Compton said. “The rule takes an inflexible, cookie-cutter approach that doesn’t account for the variability in locations and types of actions at different operations, engineering controls are not always technically or economically feasible, contrary to Msha’s assertion in the 2024 rule. Greater use of administrative controls such as job rotation and acceptance of personal protective equipment in the form of respirators should be allowed to achieve and comply with the reduced PEL.” Countertop fabrication workers should be protected under a 2016 Occupational Safety and Health Administration (Osha) rule, which also faced industry pushback when it was implemented. Industry groups including NSSGA challenged the rule in court, arguing that Osha’s stricter exposure limit was “not based on sound science”. The appeal to “sound science” has long been a tactic used by industries seeking to cast doubt on research that could lead to stricter regulation, a strategy that David Michaels, an epidemiologist and professor at the Milken Institute School of Public Health of George Washington University, documented in his book Doubt Is Their Product. But the artificial stone slabs that fabrication workers cut to make countertops can contain up to 90% silica, meaning the Osha rule alone is not protective enough, said Michaels, who previously served as assistant secretary of labor for Osha from 2009 to 2017. “It’s also often that many small employers are not in compliance. But even if they were in compliance I think we would still have a silicosis problem,” Michaels said. “This product cannot be made in a way that’s both economic and safe.” In January, Michaels testified at a congressional subcommittee hearing about mounting lawsuits against manufacturers of stone slab products and the big box stores that sell them. The lawsuits were brought by people diagnosed with silicosis from working in fabrication shops where they cut, ground and polished countertops made from engineered stone, also known as quartz, which has grown in popularity over the past decade. But instead of aiming to protect the sick workers, the subcommittee discussed how to protect the stone slab manufacturers and distributors from litigation. In his opening statement, the subcommittee chair, congressman Darrell Issa of California, said: “Our hearing this morning examines the troubling rise in abusive litigation against the US stone slab industry.” Issa is among 16 co-sponsors of a proposed bill that would ban lawsuits against manufacturers or sellers of certain stone slab products. Michaels was the only witness to give testimony at the hearing who wasn’t representing industry. He suggested that instead of prohibiting lawsuits that the US should prohibit the sale of engineered stone products with high concentrations of silica. “There are substitute products that are comparable in use and cost, but which do not kill workers,” he said at the hearing. In May, California’s Osha began a rule making to prohibit the fabrication and installation of artificial stone products containing more than 1% crystalline silica. In response, the stone distributor Consentino sent a letter to Cal/Osha stating that the proposed state rule “is premised on inaccurate information refuted by current scientific information, is unnecessary, is not feasible, and exceeds the Board’s authority”. Consentino declined to answer questions from the Guardian about what alternative regulatory approach the company would recommend to protect countertop fabrication workers. Meanwhile, two new studies show that an increasing number of coal and countertop workers are getting sick and dying from silica exposure. A National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (Niosh) study published last month found that one in three coalminers in central Appalachia (Kentucky, Virginia and West Virginia) had black lung disease. And, a study published in the New England Journal of Medicine found that nearly 600 cases of silicosis have been identified among countertop fabrication workers in California, including 65 who had lung transplants and 31 who died. “Both are tragedies,” Michaels said. Niosh recommended implementation of a silica dust exposure rule for coalminers in 1995, said Rebecca Shelton, with the Appalachian Citizens’ Law Center. “That recommendation has been in place for over 30 years,” she said. But the coal industry has long pushed back on the need for such regulations, arguing that the new cases of black lung disease are from past exposures, not reflective of today’s coal mining operations. Shelton reviewed silica dust samples reported by Msha from January to June of this year. She found that 17% of the operations sampled had silica dust concentrations over the limit in the delayed 2024 silica dust rule and that most of the mines with the highest concentrations of silica were located in central Appalachia. “We show with our analysis that these exposures are happening now,” she said. While silicosis cannot be cured, it is preventable. Dr James Brandon Crum, a radiologist in eastern Kentucky who helped identify the epidemic of black lung in central Appalachian coalminers, said the 2024 silica dust rule for miners could prevent cases of the disease. More than a decade ago, he drove three and a half hours to a Niosh meeting in West Virginia to tell researchers that he was seeing an alarming amount of complicated black lung cases at his clinic. Since then, he’s identified hundreds of more cases. “We continue to show every single year just how bad this is and nothing ever gets done about it,” he said. “The only thing higher than our black lung rates is the amount of excuses.”

title: US scientists turn to chickens to sound the alarm as West Nile cases rise
summary: Chickens – which can test positive for viruses but cannot spread them – an ideal early warning system for mosquito-borne disease
text: The start of West Nile virus transmission began unusually early in some US states, with the most cases in early summer since 2004, the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) warned in July – so Delaware turned to chickens. “They kind of are the proverbial canary in the coal mine,” said Tom Moran, head of the mosquito control section at the Delaware department of natural resources and environmental control. Sentinel chickens, as they’re called, serve as an early warning for mosquito-borne diseases, especially Eastern equine encephalitis (EEE) and West Nile. They can often predict when virus activity begins ramping up, allowing officials to target mosquito control efforts and warn the public about taking precautions. Doctors know to be on the lookout when patients have flu-like symptoms – especially when it’s not flu season – and that can help reach diagnosis faster. Veterinarians can make sure horses are vaccinated. The chicken itself is a “dead-end host”, Moran said. They can test positive for the viruses, but they can’t spread the diseases, which is why they’re ideal sentinels, he said. Delaware keeps flocks of four chickens each at 20 locations throughout the state, a program that began in the early 1980s. It’s a relatively lo-tech way to monitor and prepare for the viruses, which can be deadly. “It is kind of the old-school gold standard,” Moran said. Some states have transitioned to testing mosquito pools, which can be a faster way to detect viruses, because it takes about a week for the chickens to develop antibodies after being bitten. They tried both in Delaware, but decided to go with the chickens only. “The chickens sometimes pick up virus activity in an area that the mosquito pools did not,” Moran said. Unlike the insects, they don’t fly away – which means officials can be certain that infected mosquitoes are active in that exact area. “It gives you a little more surgical information,” Moran said. “You take that information and try to use it to lessen the specter of any human transmission.” Cases usually start appearing from north to south as migrating birds pass the viruses to mosquitoes, Moran said. Delaware’s season usually begins in early August. The chickens could also be tested for other mosquito-borne illnesses if they emerge. That’s what happened when West Nile appeared in Delaware starting in 2000. At first, officials would test wild birds found dead to see if they had the virus, but they soon began testing the sentinel chickens they already had. Some places test for other local mosquito-borne illnesses, suchas St Louis encephalitis. If a neighboring state were to detect a pathogen like that, “we could probably pretty quickly get up to speed and start testing for that here too”, Moran said. The decades of data collected from sentinel chickens on virus patterns can be invaluable for creating models that predict the severity of a season. That’s what Lindsay Campbell, associate professor of entomology and nematology at the University of Florida, has focused on in her research. She digitized decades of paper records from Florida’s Department of Health and mosquito control programs, and she’s also drawn on environmental patterns – temperature, precipitation, land cover – as well as community science data like eBird to track bird migration patterns. The data, and the models built from it, can offer insight into the conditions driving good and bad years for West Nile and EEE. The sentinel chickens are providing important data “telling us what happened, while we would like to know what might happen in the future”, said Robert Guralnick, curator of biodiversity informatics at the Florida Museum of Natural History and a co-author with Campbell. “It gives us the opportunity to go ahead and see the ebbs and flows, essentially, of these viruses over time, and then we can try to link them with different environmental characteristics to see if we can maybe predict when there might be elevated activity in the natural environment,” Campbell said. There are many factors likely involved in how diseases like these spread – the hosts, like mosquitoes, birds, and other animals, as well as environmental conditions. That makes it complicated to predict how severe a year will be. But these models are examining, for instance, if weather patterns or temperatures from four or six or twelve months earlier affect how bad a viral season is. “For some viruses, like EEE virus, we’ve seen a strong association with a certain type of landscape that is associated with the mosquito vector – that’s really important for that virus,” Campbell said. For West Nile virus, they’ve identified some precipitation and temperature patterns a few months before chickens start testing positive. “The information that these programs have been able to provide is really invaluable,” Campbell said of sentinel chickens. Guralnick agreed. “It’s a clever way to gather really good information about what’s happening,” he said. Over the decades, officials have tried new things and learned what works best. For the first few years of the Delaware program, they used white leghorn chickens – but they proved, in Moran’s words, to be “very flighty”. They frequently tried to escape, running into the bushes and forests. “It’s literally like a scene from Rocky, where you’re chasing the chicken around – you can’t catch these things,” Moran said. It would sometimes take an hour to track the chickens down. Once they switched to a breed of Rhode Island red chickens, their work went much more smoothly. Similarly, officials have experimented with other means of tracking mosquito-borne illnesses, including one research project that proposes using honey traps to catch the insects. “We’re always looking: is there a better way, a faster way, a cheaper way, a more accurate way – it checks all those boxes?” Moran said. “Folks are always pushing the ball forward.” But for now, chickens rule the roost.

title: Registered sex offender was allowed to participate at South Carolina church for decades
summary: The Brookwood Church in Simpsonville only just disqualified Jerry Sidell from serving there in any capacity
text: A registered sex offender who was sentenced to prison in the 1980s after he told authorities that he had molested several boys whom he met through his religious work with Christian youth in Georgia was later allowed to participate for decades in ministry at a South Carolina church. The Brookwood church, a southern Baptist institution in the South Carolina city of Simpsonville, only just disqualified Jerry Sidell from serving there in any capacity, after he joined it in 1999 and fulfilled various ministerial roles. The church’s senior pastor, Bryan Jones, told congregants at a Thursday night meeting that Sidell had been “forthright” with Brookwood leaders back then about his previously pleading guilty in Georgia to the crimes of enticing a minor for indecent purposes and child molestation. Without mentioning Sidell’s name, Jones said that church leaders implemented boundaries addressing his participation at Brookwood, which operates a preschool. Jones said those rules included a prohibition from working in or being around children or student ministries. Sidell, 69, also could not set foot in the school or those particular ministries’ spaces, Jones said. And Sidell had to disclose his past to those in charge of any non-children or non-student ministries in which he wanted to take part, Jones told congregants, according to an audio recording of the meeting provided to the Guardian. Yet Jones – who was named Brookwood’s senior pastor in late 2022 – also suggested that he personally had only recently learned of Sidell’s status as a registered sex offender. Jones didn’t elaborate. But he said he reacted to that discovery by meeting Sidell and informing him that he could no longer perform with the church’s adult musical band or be a member of the small prayer group – also made up of adults – to which he belonged. Jones also said Brookwood had enacted a new policy requiring “any” registered sex offender attending church services to enter through a specific door, check in with the institution’s security team and then sit with a designated guard. That designated guard would then escort the registered sex offender out of Brookwood after the completion of services, Jones said. As Jones put it, he and his fellow Brookwood leaders believe in “grace and forgiveness” – but, he added, “we felt … there are consequences for actions”. An email to the Guardian from an individual familiar with Brookwood and Sidell contended that the church specifically put those heightened rules in place in either July or August. That was after authorities in Pawleys Island, South Carolina, reported arresting a registered sex offender named Warren Spence Perry for allegedly violating his probation by working at a school and children’s daycare run by a local southern Baptist church. Five other people connected to the Pawleys Island community church and its school, about four hours away from Simpsonville by car, were later also arrested on suspicion of illegally concealing Perry’s involvement with children there. Perry, 70, pleaded guilty in 2023 to sexually exploiting a minor three years earlier, and a proposed federal class-action lawsuit has been filed at the church and school where he had been working, as WCIV and other South Carolina news outlets have reported. Furthermore, the individual who emailed the Guardian about Sidell accurately noted his having founded Rusty Bucket Music, a venue which – according to social media video and images – has hosted youth performers and patrons since its opening in 2019. Videos available online suggest Brookwood leaders have had a presence at Rusty Bucket Music in the South Carolina town of Gray Court, which is adjacent to Simpsonville. Two videos show Jones and his fellow Brookwood pastor JC Thompson delivering prepared, recorded discussions of biblical scripture there. A pair of images circulating on social media show Sidell on the stage at Rusty Bucket Music adjusting the microphone stand amid three youth performers. Rusty Bucket Music’s website and its Facebook page had been taken down as of Friday. A professional networking page under Sidell’s name described him as a Brookwood church musician since at least 2013. He reportedly partook in worship ministry, played the keyboard and participated in small men’s groups at Brookwood, according to the Christian church watchdog website MinistryWatch, which first reported on Sidell in late August. The individual who corresponded with the Guardian about Sidell said the Brookwood church has about 5,000 congregants. According to the individual, “Sidell’s sex offender status was not disclosed to many of the people” who served alongside him or encountered him at the ministries in which he was involved. As the individual put it: “Sidell kept this information extremely private.” Sidell did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Neither did Brookwood. At Thursday’s meeting with congregants, Thompson and Jones made it a point to say that their own children were Brookwood congregants, too. Jones also said he had notified outside groups with whom Sidell was associated about Sidell’s status as a sex offender. “We care about protecting our people,” said Thompson, who also said that Brookwood had security cameras throughout the entirety of its campus, among other safety measures. Another pastor, Matt Plunkett, said all church volunteers must also take an abuse-prevention class. Jones at one point asked the congregation to pray for victims. But at another juncture, in a clear allusion to Sidell and the media’s interest in him, he asserted: “Satan would love to disrupt what’s happening in this church. He would love to disrupt what God is doing in this church.” The cases centering on Sidell and Perry came amid a broader, years-long scandal involving the handling of matters related to sexual abuse by the Southern Baptist Convention (SBC), the US’s largest Protestant denomination. It is also the second-largest Christian denomination in the US behind the Roman Catholic church. The SBC, a politically influential group of loosely affiliated churches with about 12 million congregants, in June 2022 issued a 205-page document listing hundreds of Baptist leaders and congregants accused or found guilty of sexually abusing children. Neither Sidell nor Perry were named in that specific document. Other religious denominations in the US and across the world besides the SBC and the Roman Catholic church – Christian or otherwise – have also spent years grappling with sexual abuse within their ranks. With respect to his case, Sidell pleaded guilty in 1983 to five charges of child molestation and one of enticing a minor to commit indecent acts, a 1986 Atlanta Journal-Constitution article reported. The newspaper reported that Sidell at one point told detectives that he had molested nine boys whom he knew from serving at the nondenominational First Christian church of Jonesboro, Georgia, as a youth minister. He received six concurrent 10-year prison sentences, the Journal-Constitution reported. The parents of two of Sidell’s victims – a pair of brothers – sued Sidell for $2m. The Journal-Constitution reported that the younger son secured a $500,000 jury verdict, but the award was eliminated entirely after Sidell was granted a new trial on what the outlet termed a legal technicality. The plaintiffs then dropped the litigation and told the Journal-Constitution that members of their church ostracized them for going public against Sidell. The publication’s coverage of Sidell included a quote from his wife, who likened child sexual abuse to alcoholism, saying it was “an incurable disorder [the molester] has to fight every day” and advocating for better rehabilitation programs for abusers. In addition to South Carolina, Sidell is registered as a sex offender in Florida, a US justice department tool shows. Both registrations list a home address in Simpsonville about a mile and a half away from the Brookwood church.

title: Heatwaves hit the Sunday roast: why the RHS says cauliflower is off the menu
summary: Charity urges gardeners in England to swap thirsty brassicas for drought-tolerant crops
text: They are an integral part of the British Sunday roast – but cauliflowers are now going to be off the menu, according to the Royal Horticultural Society. England’s climate has changed so much that the RHS is now recommending that gardeners exclude the brassicas from their vegetable patches. The UK is expecting a poor harvest of most brassicas, such as broccoli, cauliflower and cabbages, owing to the drought, with farmers saying this year could be one of the worst on record. This summer was the UK’s hottest on record, according to provisional Met Office data. In England, temperatures peaked at 38.1C (100.1F) at Kew Gardens in London on 13 August, and June had already been confirmed as the country’s hottest since records began in 1884. Scientists have said these heatwaves are only possible because of the climate crisis, predominantly caused by burning of fossil fuels. The RHS says home gardeners should stop growing cauliflower because of the change to the climate, adding many of its horticulturalists had stopped a long time before as planting cauliflowers had been so unsuccessful. The charity said cauliflowers and their close relative calabrese were thirsty and easily stressed in high temperatures, in which they fail to form a decent head. It recommends gardeners also reconsider planting other vegetables in the brassica family such as cabbages and brussels sprouts. Guy Barter, the RHS’s chief horticulturist, said: “Cauliflowers and their brassica cousins have been the hardest hit of those commonly found in domestic veg patches, and with summers likely to follow recent patterns, swapping them out for an equally as flavourful and nutritious alternative will save on all-important watering and provide a better guarantee of a good harvest. “There’s no doubt that we’re set to see tomatoes continue as the most popular summer vegetable, but with the likes of Asian loofah and okra cropping up more at mealtimes. Hopefully with recent rains we will see winter crops, carrots, leeks and brussels sprouts, make a recovery this year.” Horticulturalists in the charity’s gardens said they had been experimenting with alternatives to cauliflower. Simone Bratt, who tends the kitchen gardens at RHS Bridgewater, said she had not grown cauliflower for “a few years”. Growth had been “very hit and miss with the extremes of weather and we would only grow them as a late crop”, she said. “We tried a spring sowing again this year, but the heat really won. They bolted before we even got them in the ground. They simply haven’t been able to cope with the severity of the conditions, and need a lot of water and cool conditions.” Bratt added that purple sprouting broccoli was a good swap for cauliflower. “They also should cope much better as a ‘cut and come’ crop, rather than waiting for a single full head of calabrese or cauliflower.” The gardening charity said its members said the heat this year had allowed tomatoes and peppers to thrive outdoors, and that melon and watermelon could now be grown outside in some parts of the country, and where their watering needs could be met. Some gardeners have swapped from cauliflower to kale, as some kale is perennial, with deeper roots, so can better survive droughts. Gardeners have been able to grow cucumbers and sweet potatoes outside successfully, said Liz Mooney, a horticulturist on the edibles team at RHS Garden Wisley, in Surrey. She added she had not grown cauliflower this year, focusing instead on “warmth-loving crops”. Cat Hood, a horticulturist at RHS Hyde Hall in Chelmsford, Essex, said she had been experimenting with a range of warmer-climate vegetables, including chillies and okra. “We’ve had some really strong results from a number of crops this year,” she said. “Chillies, peppers and aubergines have all performed well in the outdoor beds, and we’ve had an amazing crop of loofah in the glasshouse. The okra have also done well, as have tortarello and carosello, the Italian heirloom cucumber-melons. A real surprise has been the yard-long beans, which have given us the best crop I’ve seen since I’ve been here, which I assume is because of the heat.”

title: ‘I said, if you want to fire me, just fire me. And so he did’: my showdown with Donald Trump
summary: What’s it like to be shown the door by the US president? A former national security adviser, an Apprentice contestant and more share their stories
text: Gene Folkes, 62, based in Manhattan, was a contestant on season 10 of The Apprentice, which aired in 2010. A former air force recruiter until 1991, he retrained as an investment banker, then launched his own business before appearing on the reality show. He was fired by Trump in episode 5. He now runs the technology consulting firm OshunX and hosts a podcast, Folkes Unfettered. I didn’t audition to be on The Apprentice. I received the call out of the blue: “Would you be interested in doing this show?” I didn’t know a lot about it. However, like any young business person, you look for people who you consider titans. There’s this mythology around Trump. He was one of the people I wanted to emulate. The first morning, wardrobe comes into your room at 3.30am. You meet the other contestants for the first time, then within an hour you’re on your first task. You learn really quickly that you’re playing a game and the rules can change at any moment. The first time we met, Trump was outside his building on Wall Street. He is an imposing figure. When he walks into a place he owns the room and there’s not a lot of air for anyone else to breathe. I thought, “OK, he’s presenting as exactly who I believed him to be.” There was a sense of admiration and aspiration. It was only when you dug deeper that you realised the emperor had no clothes. In the corporate world, there are certain things you just don’t do without consequences. And they were so natural for him. The first time we met him in the boardroom, Trump asked us if we thought the women were attractive. He would make these innuendoes – things that were sort of hard to pin down – but you felt kind of icky afterwards. The first round was split men v women. I put myself forward to be the project manager for the men’s team. Task one was to design a modern office space. We won that task, and my prize was a one-on-one with Trump. His desk in Trump Tower was rather small and somewhat messy. Initially, I felt he knows how to connect with people. There was charisma, there was charm; he evokes a certain amount of confidence. You can really get drawn into all things Donald, but as I sat back and started really listening to him, I thought, “Oh, I don’t think this is the person that I have tried to model myself after.” I didn’t feel empathy from him: I was more product than person. I think about it a lot now, because I believe that anyone who wants to lead a nation has to have a certain amount of empathy. If you don’t, then how can you relate to someone who’s a single mom or dad who’s struggling to put food on the table? A producer told me the series was mine to lose. The week I got fired, I didn’t feel like it was coming. We had to put on a fashion show for Rockport. When you’re an air force recruiter, like I had been, all you do is publicly speak, so my project manager selected me to be master of ceremonies. I wear glasses. In that episode I decided to wear my contacts. They weren’t bifocals, and I remember saying, “I need to go back and get my glasses.” We never got to it. We got on to the test and I couldn’t read a freaking thing on the script. When we went to the boardroom and we lost, they brought in three of us. Trump really took me off guard. The narrative shifted from, “Hey, I couldn’t see, and I wasn’t going to admit that I couldn’t see, because I didn’t want to start making excuses”, to one where I became illiterate: I couldn’t read; I couldn’t speak. It was very coded language that I was familiar with. It dawned on me: oh my God, he is framing me as a dumb person of colour. I’m sitting here with a degree in finance and he’s talking to me like I’m a moron. At that point I pushed back and said, “No one gets to talk about my speaking abilities. I don’t know what the bleep you’re talking about, but that’s not me.” His face was red. He was visibly angry. One of the things he did when pushed back on was escalate. It was like he didn’t hear anything you said. He was animated but in a controlled way. He was playing to camera. He knew the audience was salivating for his line. I finally said, “You know what? If you want to fire me, just fire me.” And so he did. I did not feel anger. I felt relief. At that point you realise you’re playing in a system that’s rigged. And the person in power controls the narrative, controls the outcome. This was a game, but my real-life consequences were: what is my life going to look like after the programme, for my relationships, business dealings, opportunities? When I watched the series, I got on the phone with NBC to say, “Holy crap, that’s where you guys want to go with that? That I was uneducated, ignorant?” There was no sense of empathy or compassion from the network or him. Afterwards I did not want to leave the house. I could not get out of bed some mornings. I really became almost a recluse for three months. It took me years to get comfortable talking about it. I was depressed. When I got a hold of myself, I began to do what I normally do: I started fighting. I wrote a blog where I gave my opinion on Trump considering running for the presidency. NBC asked me to take it down, which I refused to do. I remember someone saying to me, “You’re hurting the Trump brand, you’re hurting the NBC brand and you’re hurting the Apprentice brand”, and I remember saying, “But you’re hurting the Gene Folkes brand, and I didn’t sign off for this crap.” In the 15 years since I was on The Apprentice, media, entertainment, politics and news have started converging. Trump is the ideal politician for this moment: he’s all personality, he understands how to trigger you, he knows the power of his own mythology. When I served in the military, there were certain leaders you would follow to death. You knew they loved and cared about you. They were able to manage their emotions. They realised that the goal of the team outweighed their individual personality. Trump is the opposite. He’s all personality; there is no team. Good leaders want to be challenged. And what I learned from The Apprentice, and what I’m seeing now in politics, is consistent: don’t challenge him. As told to Kate Lloyd • NBC declined to comment. *** ‘Trump isn’t disciplined by anything, and so most of what I did was struggle to keep the train on the track’ John Bolton, 77, based in Washington DC, is an attorney and former ambassador to the United Nations who was national security adviser from 2018 until 2019, under Trump. His exit from government was announced by the president over Twitter on 10 September 2019: “I informed John Bolton last night that his services are no longer needed at the White House. I disagreed strongly with many of his suggestions, as did others in the administration, and therefore I asked John for his resignation, which was given to me this morning.” Bolton says things played out differently. For me, there was no one straw that broke the camel’s back, and I think that’s true in many resignation situations. It was an accumulation of factors. I had had a resignation letter drafted, and kept one copy in my desk drawer in the office and one copy at home, knowing I could print it out whenever I needed to. It was basically a one-sentence resignation, which was the way I wanted to do it. And it finally came to that in September 2019. The last conversation really was on 9 September. He was complaining about this and complaining about that, having heard, obviously from people inside the administration, of something I had done that they didn’t like. And I said to him, “Well, look, if you feel that way, I’ll resign.” And he was leaving the Oval Office to go and give a speech. [Trump told Bolton they would talk about his resignation offer the following morning.] I went back to my office and I just thought, I am going to resign; I’m not going to talk to him. So I did a few other things that evening and then I went home, and came in early the next morning. There were a couple of meetings I wanted to finish up, particularly the freeing up of the security assistance to Ukraine. I got that done and I gave the letter to my secretary and said, “I’m going home. I’ll call you when I’m there.” I wanted to get out of the blast zone. So I told her to hand it to Trump’s secretary and then be prepared that she would probably be leaving soon thereafter. The only mistake I made was that I should have tweeted right then that I had resigned, because when Trump saw it he went through the roof. I did get one tweet out saying I had resigned, and then they closed my Twitter account. I had to fight later to get it back. I believe in pre-emptive strikes, and I had failed to follow my own advice. I should have fired first, but I was pursuing old-fashioned norms. I tell this story in my book: before the Singapore meeting with Kim Jong-un, the first in the series on the North Korean nuclear programme, there was a chance that Trump was going to cancel, which I thought was exactly the right thing to do. I thought the whole thing was going to be a terrible waste of time. He was going off to a dinner, I think, with state governors, and as he was leaving, I said, “We can send out something saying we’re not coming if you want to do that.” And he said, “Let me think about it.” He said, “When I was dating, I always liked to be the one to break up with the girl. I never wanted the girl to break up with me.” I didn’t keep that much stuff in the White House office. A lot of things – pre-government files of clippings and things – I thought my secretary would be able to walk out with because they clearly weren’t government property. But we had to fight over that, too. There were several other of my staff who were also let go within 24, 48 hours. Some of their stuff was taken as well. I don’t think I get called naive very often. I thought I knew what I was getting into, largely because I thought that the weight of the decisions Trump would have to make in the national security area, the gravity of the responsibility, would discipline him. It turned out I was completely wrong about that. Trump isn’t disciplined by anything, and so most of what I did in my 17 months was struggle to keep the train on the track. Things like long-range planning? Forget it. By and large, there just wasn’t time to do it. I firmly believed that Trump would be no different from his predecessors. And, to me, it just exemplifies that it really is an aberration in American politics – I’d say almost in world history – to have somebody who performs the way he does. People would just ignore the [national security council policymaking] process and go directly to Trump. It was the phenomenon of the last person in the room gets his attention. There was this occasion when the Iranians shot down an American drone over the Persian Gulf, in what we believed was international airspace. We sized up what we were going to do, came up with retaliation, the president ordered it, then literally as planes were in the air, he changed his mind. So that leads people to say, why are we doing this? Why do we even bother? Look, everybody’s got an ego. Politicians notoriously have bigger egos than most. But I’ve never seen a politician where the ego wasn’t subsumed to at least some extent by bigger considerations. With him, it’s not subsumed by anything. That was part of the mistake I made. I just had never seen a personality like that before. As told to Julian Borger *** ‘I was at the school drama club when I had an email from somebody I had never heard of before. “Message from the president.” I thought, well, that can’t be good’ Rebecca Kelly Slaughter, 45, lives in Maryland. A Democrat, she was appointed to the Federal Trade Commission (FTC), an independent agency of the US government, by Donald Trump in 2018. The FTC’s work includes fighting illegal business practices, safeguarding online privacy and promoting competition to keep prices down for consumers. Slaughter was fired last year and fought a protracted legal battle, arguing that Trump did not have the right to remove an agency commissioner without cause. This culminated in the supreme court case Trump v Slaughter, which decided in favour of the president’s at-will removal power, overturning a 91-year-old precedent. It was an incredible privilege and honour to work for the FTC. In the time I was there we blocked the largest grocery store merger in history, which would have raised grocery prices even further. We sued big tech platforms for violating children’s privacy, for subscription traps that charged people more money than they should have been paying. We investigated things like the price of insulin and the role of pharmacy benefit managers in keeping drug prices unnaturally high. Right after the inauguration in January 2025, the president removed commissioners at a different independent board, the Privacy and Civil Liberties Oversight Board. But he didn’t fire me or my colleague, commissioner Alvaro Bedoya. We went through a period from mid-January through mid-March thinking, is he going to fire us today? He didn’t fire us today. Does that mean he’s not going to fire us? We don’t know. We decided early on that we couldn’t and wouldn’t operate in a way that was inconsistent with our oaths of office or our principles in order to avoid getting fired. We were just going to do the jobs we had as well as we could, and we couldn’t control how the president was going to react. On 18 March 2025, I worked a full day in the office then went to our local public elementary school, where I was volunteering in the evenings with the drama club production of Beauty and the Beast. I was the parent lead for this production. But, much more importantly, my second kid was playing Belle. She was in fifth grade. This was the culmination of all of her hopes and dreams in her 10-year-old life. I was sitting outside the dusty elementary school gym, children were running around pretending to be plates and spoons, inviting my daughter to come be their guest, and I checked my work phone and I had an email from somebody I had never heard of before. I can’t remember what it was titled – “Message from the president” or something like that. I thought, well, that can’t be good. I opened it, and it was a very long email, purportedly on behalf of the president, clearly not written by the president – many legal citations, no words in caps – the culmination of which was, your continued service on the FTC is inconsistent with my priorities, therefore you are terminated effective immediately. I took a deep breath and said some expletives in my head. I looked at the other parent volunteers sitting next to me and said, “I think I might have just gotten fired. Is it OK if I step outside to deal with this?” They said, “No, go home, go take care of what you need to do.” I said, “Oh no, I am not leaving Beauty and the Beast.” The rest of that evening is a blur in my mind. I talked to my husband, who was in California. I talked to my staff. I talked to a million reporters. We hastily organised a press conference that I participated in from the parking lot, holding a phone in front of my face, under the floodlights with a brick background behind me. I didn’t want my daughter to hear about this from other parents or other kids. I pulled her aside after they got through the run-through and said, “I have to tell you something. It’s going to sound scary but we are going to be OK and I don’t want you to be worried about it.” She said, “OK, what?” I said, “I got fired this evening.” I could see her little face well up. She said, “Are you going to have to stop working on the show?” I said, “No, I’m not going to let that happen”, and she said, “OK.” That was the key information she needed. You can try to take my job but you cannot take drama club from me. Alvaro [who was also fired] and I knew pretty quickly that we wanted to challenge our dismissals in court, because if we failed to do so it would be like acceding to this blatant violation of the law and destruction of these institutions, but the timing and structure of doing that were all questions we had to sort through. I was doing that until about midnight when my doorbell rang, which I thought was odd. I went to the door and there was a pizza delivery guy there. I said, “I didn’t order any pizza.” He showed me an order form with my name, my personal email address, my cellphone number, my home address. I said, “Well, I didn’t order it and I’m not gonna pay for it, so, sorry.” I called my husband and I was, like, this weird thing happened. Isn’t that funny? He goes, “No, it is not funny. That’s a thing that online trolls do to people, especially people who the president doesn’t like, in order to scare them.” I didn’t like that I was home with my four kids in the middle of the night when this happened. I talked to Alvaro, who also got a pizza. His take was, thank God, I’m starving, I haven’t eaten all evening! I don’t feel angry on my own behalf. It is very much not about me. I don’t feel any personal animus. I do feel a lot of anger on behalf of institutions of government, of public servants throughout the government. I have a lot of anger for those reasons. Donald Trump doesn’t think about me at all. I don’t think he knew that he fired me; I don’t have any evidence he actually knew and was involved in it. The president cares a lot about a ballroom and gold plating the White House and building monuments to himself. I don’t think he’s thinking about conservative legal theory. I also don’t think he is thinking about the American people. Last summer, in my interregnum period, I knew that I needed a project, so I signed up for the New York City marathon and ran it for charity. I had never run a marathon and I always thought it was impossible, and it felt like a metaphor for the professional experience I was going through. It was hard. It didn’t go as well as I had hoped or trained for, but I finished anyway. And that was also the metaphor for me: we do the hard things because they’re the right things to do, and that is the reward – even if it doesn’t turn out exactly the way you envision. ‘He didn’t have the courage to be the one to fire people. He didn’t want to face people’ Barbara Res, 76, based in New Jersey, met Donald Trump in 1978, when she was working as an assistant superintendent for the contractor HRH, building the Grand Hyatt hotel in New York. Two years later, he hired her to lead construction on Trump Tower. She eventually became senior vice-president and executive vice-president of the Trump Organization. She quit after a final stint as a consultant, when the redevelopment of the Ambassador hotel site in Los Angeles fell apart amid a prolonged condemnation battle with the Los Angeles school district and a collapsing real-estate market. Res says a last‑minute change in leadership, made by Trump against her advice, undermined negotiations that she believed could have allowed the project to finish with a small profit. She has written two books about her experiences over those years. She retrained as a lawyer and is now semi-retired. I worked for Donald for close to 18 years. I left on friendly terms. If I saw him at a function, we’d nod to each other. But in 2016 I wrote an op-ed in the New York Daily News about my experiences with him. He came out blazing guns against me at rallies and on Twitter. He released emails I had written to him five years earlier when I was looking for a job. A tabloid newspaper wrote that he had “got rid” of me and that I had begged him for a job. Both lies. His supporters tweeted things about me like “glad Trump fired her”. I wasn’t fired. I’d impressed him when I was working for HRH. In meetings the project managers and superintendents would talk about different problems on the job, and the architect would often blame the contractor or the subcontractors. I’d say, “That’s bullshit.” He loved that. At a meeting at his apartment, Donald asked me to be in charge of the construction of Trump Tower. I remember it was in a nice building on Fifth Avenue. Everything inside was white: the carpet, the upholstery, the walls, the ceiling. Donald went through a spiel about what he was building. I was to be the last word on site, he said. “You’ll be like a Donna Trump.” He offered me almost twice the salary I was getting. I liked being there. Trump Tower was a big deal and I had the best crew in the world. There were times when Donald was actually like a human being. We used to go into his office and sit and talk. He’d tell jokes. He was pretty funny. Now, I’m not saying he was a nice guy. Not at all. Any time anyone really disagreed with him, he would yell at them. He always needed someone to blame. If he screamed at me in front of the team it didn’t matter, because they were all getting screamed at. If he’d screamed at me in front of an architect or an investor, I would have walked out the door. When he wanted to do something that we thought was wrong or illegal, you couldn’t just say that. He couldn’t handle it. So we found ways of working around it – making him think that a substitute idea we’d come up with was his. I used to put him in a good mood by saying, “Hey Donald, did you see Ivana this morning? What an incredible outfit she’s wearing. She’s so gorgeous.” We were able to keep him somewhat under control. Nobody does that now. I was offered a partnership elsewhere and left. Donald threw a massive party for me. He got me a Cartier bracelet, signed, “Towers of thanks, love Donald.” A few years later, I got back in touch with him for some advice and he hired me again, this time to be in charge of all construction, then construction and development, for the Trump Organization. When I went back in 1987, he was surrounded by yes‑sayers. His book Trump: The Art of the Deal absolutely changed him in terms of his picture of himself. Even though he always said he was the smartest, now he thought he was a real big-time player. Everybody knew everything about him: how great he was, how brilliant he was. The second time I left was around 1990, when I was running Trump’s big West Side project on the riverfront. Neighbourhood groups and some big-name opponents – including Christopher Reeve – were fighting it hard. And a friend of Donald’s came to him and said, “You’ve got to meet with these people, and you’ve got to make a deal with them.” He wanted to build 14m sq ft. He made a deal to build just 7.5m. In that deal, the opposition group put their person in charge of the project. They wanted a semi‑famous lawyer who worked in development and didn’t have construction experience. I quit primarily because they brought in this other person. I told Donald I had to leave. My son has to have surgery, I said. The surgery was a big deal, but I wouldn’t quit over that. I told him it to soften the blow. I stayed on as a consultant on two other projects. One of those was the Ambassador hotel. One of our partners was going under. He wanted to be in charge of everything. My assistant and I told Donald this would blow up the project, which it eventually did. Donald allowed him to take over against our advice. Afterwards, at a big meeting with the realtor and the partners, Donald came down on me. I told him, “I told you not to let this guy get involved.” He started screaming. His face was contorting. That was the only time he’d ever done that in front of external people. I was enraged. I looked at him and I said, “You know, Donald, there are medicines that can help you control that.” He got crazy about that. After the people left, I went back up to Donald’s office and said, “Look, I can’t do this, I’m leaving.” And he said, “Why?” I didn’t say, “Because you made a fool out of me in front of the partners.” I said, “I’m looking after my son, I’m still having problems” – which was not true. “They’re just going to start school now, and I think I really should find something that won’t take me to California every week.” Donald talked about running for president when I was at the Trump Organization. I thought at the time that he was a very good manager, given the right people, and that he could be a decent president. I didn’t know then that he had zero knowledge of government. The Apprentice thing I’ve always thought of as a big joke. In my experience, he didn’t have the courage to be the one to fire people. He didn’t want to face people. He didn’t want to look bad. If someone was going to get fired, he wasn’t doing it. In my case, we had a woman who was working on some lobbying efforts we were doing. She had gotten pregnant. He found out and said, “Fire her.” I said, “You can’t, that’s against the law.” He got angry at me. “Fire her now!” I did it. It was terrible. I told her I would support her if she wanted to go after him because I knew that it was illegal to fire her. Here’s another story I remember: when we needed an apartment manager at Trump Tower, he found a guy and hired him to work under me. He was terrible. We didn’t like him; he had a bad attitude. I told Donald, “We’re going to fire him.” He said, “Go ahead.” We fired him, and he went across the street to where Donald’s office was at the time. Donald was convinced by him. He told us, “Give him another chance.” And that happened twice. It took three times to fire this guy. I think all the firing he has done in government shows a big shift in his attitude. But he has to blame someone. And how do you prove someone is at fault better than firing them? Even if they didn’t do anything wrong. As told to Kate Lloyd • Tower of Lies: What My Eighteen Years of Working With Donald Trump Reveals About Him by Barbara Res (Graymalkin Media, £14.99) is available now. • The Trump Organization did not respond to a request to comment.
