title: London Underground workers exposed to asbestos without protective masks, documents reveal
summary: Hundreds of staff may have worked without legally required face-fitted masks over 20 years
text: Hundreds of London Underground workers could have been exposed to asbestos for almost 20 years without protection required under safety regulations, according to documents seen by the Guardian. Under 2002 rules on controlling asbestos and other hazardous materials, employers are required to take a series of precautions, including ensuring exposed workers are given individually fitted face masks to prevent inhalation of toxic dust. Emails and minutes of meetings reveal that London Underground managers admitted that face-fitted masks were not issued to staff until as late as 2020. The documents suggest Transport for London (TfL), the public body responsible for London Underground, is at risk of more expensive legal claims after already paying out more than £7m in asbestos-related compensation and legal fees. The documents were disclosed as part of an employment tribunal hearing brought by a former London Underground cleaner, Micky Steeds, who successfully claimed he was unfairly dismissed after raising concerns about exposure to asbestos and other toxic dust. In one set of minutes, a manager said he had no recollection or record of face-fitted masks being issued in 2018 to the team responsible for cleaning dust from vents, which included asbestos-sheathed cables. He said such masks were not introduced to London Underground’s civils teams, responsible for all the tube buildings, until late 2020. In December 2020, another manager who was head of lifts and escalators said: “A lot of people aren’t face-fitted,” adding: “Staff shouldn’t have worked without face fit, but it has happened.” He blamed the failure on a lack of training. In 2019, an email from a third manager said allowing Steeds to carry on working without a face-fitted mask was oversight that would be rectified in future. In a 2023 email, a fourth manager admitted that asbestos dust fibre sampling, which is also required under the law, was not conducted. TfL has recorded more than 20,000 asbestos-containing materials across its network, according to data released under freedom of information to Confront Power – an investigative newsletter on industrial harms. TfL insists it has controls in place to manage the risk of asbestos exposure to its staff and the public. In an email in December 2022, a senior engineer responsible for hazardous materials said test results showed levels were “below the relevant workplace exposure limits for both respirable and inhalable dust”. But he said dust being cleaned contained “traces of asbestos fibre occasionally”. But Steeds and one of his former colleagues point out that tests were not conducted while the asbestos was being cleaned and disturbed. And minutes of meetings between staff and a manager also revealed issues with damaged asbestos, which is more dangerous. One experienced cleaner said he encountered asbestos on cables 90% of the time and sometimes: “Broken chunks of asbestos or cable shearing.” Asked what he did when he found asbestos, he said: “We would just carry on and use common sense … don’t bash cables and do what you can.” Catriona Ratcliffe, a solicitor from the personal injury team at LeighDay, said: “Where the asbestos materials are damaged or in poor condition, the risk of exposure is higher because there is more opportunity for the fibres to be released into the atmosphere.” Earlier this year Ratcliffe secured a six-figure settlement from TfL for a former inspector who was diagnosed with sarcomatoid mesothelioma 27 years after supervising the removal of asbestos from the Northern Line. She said the documents in Steeds’ case could result in more injury claims. She added: “If someone is exposed to asbestos over many years, even at low levels, that is going to put that person at risk. And if the employer had knowledge of the risk of exposure, that could result in a legal claim if they have not taken the precautions required under regulations. “Under the control of asbestos regulations [if exposure to asbestos is unavoidable] employers should be giving workers full protection including face-fitted respiratory masks to reduce that risk as far as possible.” Steeds, who was not fitted with a proper mask for 15 months, said: “Over the years, TfL must have put the health of hundreds of workers at risk by failing in their legal duty to provide fitted masks. It makes me so angry that even when I told them about it, they ignored my concerns and tried to cover it up. The incompetent managers who allowed this to happen now have serious questions to answer.” Rob Donnan, a former LU cleaner who is appealing against an employment tribunal’s rejection of his claim for unfair dismissal, said he worked without a fitted mask for three years. He estimated that up to 80 cleaners in the vents department alone were not fitted with masks between 2002 and 2020 and that a further 300 staff in the escalator department were similarly unprotected. A TfL spokesperson said: “We have strict controls in place, in line with the government’s control of asbestos regulations, which ensure customers and staff are not at risk from exposure to asbestos when travelling or working on the tube network. Our specialist teams monitor and manage locations where asbestos has been found to ensure the safety of everyone travelling or working on the network.” They added that, as TfL was appealing against Steeds’ successful tribunal ruling, it was unable to comment further.

title: Trump personality cult alive and well in Dallas – will it power Republican midterm success?
summary: President the star of the show at two-day convention, but party’s plan to treat November elections as referendum on Trump himself poses grave risks
text: “We’re going to have a good time listening to music,” Donald Trump told thousands of supporters in downtown Dallas before handing the mic to an opera singer, “because I’m getting a little bit tired of politics now.” Millions of Americans seem tired of politics after a decade dominated by Trump. So the US president’s decision to close out this week’s first ever Republican midterm convention with a plea – treat November’s congressional elections as a referendum on Trump himself – was received by his Democratic opponents with glee. They saw the president’s core pitch as a combination of begging and bribery. First he urged voters to “pretend that I’m on the ballot”. Then he promised $5,000 payouts to every US adult if Republicans retain control of the House of Representatives and Senate in November. Andy Beshear, the Democratic governor of Kentucky, told reporters on Thursday: “If Donald Trump wants to hold a convention saying this election is about him, I fully support his decision. He’s telling me to pretend that he is on the ballot – I want people to pretend that he is on the ballot.” But with hundreds of members of Congress and candidates staying away from the convention, most seats in the upper tier remained empty both nights. Trump’s keynote speech drew a modest 2.5 million viewers on Fox News, ⁠according to ⁠Nielsen data. Some attendees expressed discontent over the cost of living and Iran war while starting to look beyond the president to potential successors in 2028. With Trump’s approval rating at a historic low, it was far from certain that the two-day “Trump-a-palooza” will have the desired effect of galvanising the party’s base and recreating the turnout that powered his 2016 and 2024 presidential election victories. Holding a convention in a midterm year was an attempt to make history in order to defy history. The party that holds the White House typically suffers midterm losses: George W Bush’s Republicans took a “thumping” in 2006, while Barack Obama’s Democrats endured a “shellacking” in 2010. The omens this year are no less foreboding: the Decision Desk HQ website projects that Democrats are poised to capture the House of Representatives 229-206, with the Senate hanging on a knife-edge at 50-50. The spectacle in Dallas was rapidly pulled together at Trump’s behest after the host committee raised $45m in three weeks. It had some familiar trappings, including tall state delegations on the convention floor, fiery speeches and a celebratory balloon drop at the end, but no nominations or formal business. And there was no doubt who was the star of the show. Trump’s image was everywhere in the corridors of the American Airlines Center. Attendees wore clothes with phrases such as “Trump tribe”, “Trump has our back” and “Proud deplorable”. Speaker after speaker lavished him with effusive praise. Among them was Robert Kennedy Jr, the health secretary, who recalled their meeting soon after Trump survived a shooting in Butler, Pennsylvania: “I discovered a self-effacing man of superior intelligence, of empathy and compassion, with an encyclopedic grasp of the issues in molecular detail. And most of all, a near reckless courage to challenge vested interests and official orthodoxies.” But while the Trump personality cult was alive and well, another theme was just as prominent. Unable to point to falling grocery bills or peace in the Middle East, the convention leaned heavily into fear, painting a nightmarish portrait of what the US would look like with the Democrats back in charge. Images of the influencer Hasan Piker and other leftwing figures loomed ominously on giant video screens. A narrator’s voice boomed: “Today’s extreme left hasn’t simply moved away from Republicans. It has moved away from Democrats in its own party. Far beyond the common sense of the American people. This is no longer simply Republican versus Democrat or conservative versus liberal. Today, the choice is unmistakable. Extreme versus mainstream.” Numerous speeches sought to whip up a new red scare. Treasury secretary Scott Bessent warned that Democrats wanted to transform the US into a “socialist hellscape” while House Speaker Mike Johnson framed the midterms as a simple choice between “common sense and crazy”. Many speakers emphasised their own Christian faith while stressing the godlessness of communism and conflating it with threats from outside America’s borders, at times invoking the 25th anniversary of the September 11 terrorist attacks. Senator Ted Cruz of Texas said: “We are witnessing a new and dangerous red-green alliance – communists and Islamists coming together and sweeping over the Democrat party. They are united because they share the same enemies. They hate Christians, they hate Jews, they hate capitalism, they hate the constitution, and they hate America!” There were shouts in the arena of “He should be shot!” as Cruz singled out some leading progressives by name: “When people tell you who they are, believe them. When Hasan Piker says, America deserved 9/11, believe him. When Mamdani says he wants to seize the means of production, he means it. When Abdul El-Sayed says he has an ‘obligation’ to comply with Sharia law, he means it. And when James Talarico says he wants to dismantle capitalism, he means this.” On the convention floor, Republicans echoed Cruz’s apocalyptic framing. Pavel Sokolov, 33, vice-chair of the New Jersey Republican party, drew on his personal background to reinforce the point. “I was born in the former Soviet Union; my parents and I fled that exact rhetoric,” Sokolov said. “It always starts nice and friendly, saying everyone must pay their fair share. But it inevitably ends up the same. In the Soviet Union, ostensibly everyone was equal, yet somehow the party bosses ate caviar every day.” Conversely, most speakers swerved past voters’ everyday concerns about the cost of living and Trump’s war of choice in Iran. Trump himself claimed that concerns about ‌inflation were exaggerated and the word “affordable” was “fake”. Interviews with more than a dozen attendees found staunch support for him – but with some reservations beneath the surface. Gregorio Heise, 59, a disabled army veteran from Texas, described Trump’s second term as “friggin’ awesome”, explaining: “I prefer to pay $5 a gallon [of gas] and put my head on a pillow and wake up knowing this country is still here than watching it go boom with a nuke. No, thank you. I’m a vet and I didn’t serve this country to watch it go to crap.” Joseph Ditto, a 50-year-old statistician from suburban Minneapolis wearing an elephant-patterned Republican tie, admitted his frustration with the administration’s foreign policy. “I’m not a fan of the war in Iran. I hope it’s over quickly,” he said. “I voted for the anti-war Trump, so that’s frustrating.” Democrats, who held three midterm conventions in 1974, 1978 and 1982 with mixed results, have no plans for a rival event this time. But some travelled to Dallas to counter the Republican messaging. Sydney Kamlager-Dove, a congresswoman from California, highlighted what she saw as the fundamental disconnect of Trump’s second term. “Last night, Donald Trump was talking about how he wanted to build a big ballroom like they have in China,” she said. “The average American family can’t afford groceries or gas, and he’s fantasising about a ballroom in the people’s house. This entire event is built around one man who likes to hear himself talk.” To many political strategists, turning a midterm election into a direct referendum on an incumbent president whose national approval rating languishes in the low-to-mid 30s looks like a huge own goal. But Trump’s energetic performance on Wednesday night buoyed Republicans who believe he retains a unique ability to galvanise people who might not otherwise vote at all. David Hopkins, a professor of political science at Boston College, said: “There’s been a lot of journalistic dunking on Trump saying that making the election more about him is an ego trip winning out over smart strategy. That’s not an unreasonable take but there’s another way to look at it. The worst-case scenario for Republicans is that Republican voters stay home.” Hopkins pointed out that Trump commands a unique, low-propensity “Make America great again” (Maga) electorate that turns out passionately for him but frequently ignores down-ballot congressional races when his name is absent. “If they can’t get those people out, it looks like a real national wipeout.” The midterm convention also offered an intriguing subplot: the question of who inherits the Maga movement when Trump, the 45th and 47th president, is gone. Vice-President JD Vance was greeted by chants of “JD 48!” as he delivered Thursday night’s keynote address. He spoke at length about his family while describing Democrats as “the party that despises America and the people who built it”. When a protester waving a Mexican flag briefly interrupted his speech, Vance drew thunderous applause with a sharp put-down: “Well, my friend, if you love Mexico so much, get your ass over there. I’ll buy you the plane ticket.” In the concourses, delegates were actively sizing up the potential 2028 field. While Vance commands a substantial lead in early polling among Republican primary voters, several other names – most notably secretary of state Marco Rubio and Florida governor Ron DeSantis – were frequently cited. Heise said: “Marco Rubio is doing everything. He’s building on the foundations this country was created on in 1776.” Chris Daniel, 44, from Houston, who has been a delegate at every Republican convention since 2004, echoed that sentiment. “I prefer Marco Rubio over Vance if I had to pick one today. He has proven his ability to lead in any capacity.” Rusat Ramgopal, 26, executive director of the Queens county Republican party in New York, envisioned a pragmatic resolution to avoid a damaging primary battle. “Instead of a divisive primary between Vance and Rubio, I think the two of them and the president will sit down in a room and decide the ticket,” he predicted. “It just depends on who is top of the ticket and who is vice president.” Republicans declared the convention a triumph. Outside the arena, the verdict was rather less enthusiastic. Veteran pollster John Zogby described the two-day gathering as an “act of desperation” that highlighted internal vulnerabilities rather than strength. “The president promised that the war in Iran would end by August, inflation would be down by August, fuel prices would be low again by August,” Zogby noted. “None of those have been achieved. We have moved from the politics of anger into the politics of disappointment.”

title: Tensions simmer on US-Canada border for two towns relying on each other
summary: Canadians ‘angry’ at Trump for suggesting Canada should become 51st state, says mayor, as US businesses see sales fall amid trade war
text: Like many Canadians, Tom Reid isn’t crossing the US-Canada border as often these days. But he needed a haircut. The woman who cuts his hair lives in International Falls, Minnesota – her “sister is married to my wife’s cousin”, he explained – and so Reid, whose duty free shop in Fort Frances, Ontario, has to travel to her. That’s how it goes for the residents of the two towns, divided by the Rainy River and an international border. They’re longtime friends and, in many cases, family. People cross the border frequently to shop, dine, go bowling, take their kids to sports and visit each other. But Trump’s trade war against the US’s northern neighbor, and his derogatory comments about their country, has Canadians – known for their politeness – angry. Furious, actually. They’re shopping less at US businesses, and, in an unusual show of patriotism, encouraging consumers to “buy Canadian instead”. Reid is buying Canadian more and more, he said at the register in his shop, with the Canadian flag on the wall behind him. “I don’t have that much choice, eh?” he said. *** American business owners have seen declines in Canadian sales, while grappling with the uncertainty and costs associated with tariffs on their products. With tourist season winding down, and the leaves starting to change into yellows and oranges, the two towns are quieter. Canada’s retaliatory tariffs went into force this week, though no one who lived in the towns had seen that directly reflected in prices yet. It was the latest heated battle between the two countries in the last nearly two years. The mayors of the two towns call each other friends, and signed a joint declaration in 2025 affirming that friendship after Trump retook the White House. The flags of Minnesota, Ontario, both towns, and both countries fly outside the town offices in Fort Frances. But there’s only so much – and really, nothing – that a local official can do to blunt the economic effects of slipshod tariffs put in place by one man, more than a thousand miles away in Washington. Hoping for the best Most Canadians recognize this, according to Andrew Hallikas, the mayor of Fort Frances. They like Americans, and Fort Frances residents can relate to Minnesotans a lot: they share similar interests, in the outdoors and in community, he said. But they’re “irate” at Trump – for bullying their country, for going against an ally – and for suggesting Canada should become the 51st US state. “You cannot imagine how angry that makes us,” Hallikas said. “Please quote me on this. I cannot make this clear enough: we will never become the 51st state. We consider ourselves to probably be the best country in the world in which to live, and we’re quite content to remain that way, thank you very much.” For two towns that rely on each other, the tension of the trade war simmers underneath the surface. They all want it to end. They don’t know how, or when, it will. As the Guardian interviewed the mayor of International Falls at a coffee shop on the town’s main drag, a Fort Frances resident interjected angrily to tell the mayor that Canadians are “so pissed off” at Trump for how he’s attacked their country and that International Falls needed Canadians to survive. Their town was suffering, and their businesses losing longtime customers from Canada, because of it, he said. “I’m originally from the Falls, but I’m an American living in Canada,” the man said. “I’m scared to put that American flag on my shirt, what he’s done.” Residents, and the leaders of the towns, are worried about how they will rebuild the relationship between their two countries if this continues for much longer. Businesses will find other suppliers. Shoppers will replace their favorites with homegrown options. The sense of nationalism hardens. “We just hope for the best at this point,” said the International Falls mayor, Drake Dill. *** Grant Hauschild, a Democratic Minnesota state senator who represents 65% of the state’s border with Canada, said he’s heard from businesses that have lost up to 30% of their revenue from Canadians. With people already struggling with inflation and high costs, he said a hit like that goes from “a concern to devastation”. “My hope is, of course, that the relationship goes back to normal once we pass these chaotic times,” Hauschild said. “I think that’s what really scares me most … Even if people want to go back to the way things were, they might have unfortunately kind of moved on – and moved beyond – the relationship.” Two towns, one community To cross the Rainy River into either side, people use a toll bridge, with the cost for an average car now $10. They present documents to customs agents on whichever side they’re entering, and answer questions about their purpose in town. People who cross regularly recognize the agents and ask after their families. The main parts of each respective town sit on either side of the crossing, with both towns initially growing around paper mills. Fort Frances’ mill has since closed; International Falls’ is still running. Fort Frances is larger than International Falls, and because Canada is more sparse, Fort Frances serves as a regional hub. Its hospital will soon be getting an MRI machine – a huge boon for its aging population. The shops on either side carry gifts from both countries, catering to tourists who fly in to fish, mostly for walleye, and largely on the Canadian side. In a Fort Frances store, kids books called “Little Minnesota” and “Little Canada” sat right beside each other on a shelf. In International Falls, shelves of souvenir cups carried designs for International Falls and Canada. While Canadian flags line the shop windows and fly throughout downtown Fort Frances, Hallikas said this is not a reflection of increased patriotism, but just a border town welcoming visitors to their country. The two towns are “neighbors by geography, but we are friends by choice”, he said. “The bridge is over 100 years old, and we’ve been going back and forth it for over 100 years,” Hallikas said. “Before that, there was a ferry. But our friendship is still going to exist when Trump is long gone.” *** Dill, the International Falls mayor, owned a business and lived in Canada for 11 years. Many of his friends are Canadian. This fall, he will go up to an island in Canada to meet up with friends. “There’s no politics in that. There’s no thought of exchange rate, or trade war, or tariffs. It’s just – we’re friends,” he said. “But then you come home and you talk and you watch the news. … I would be really disappointed if it gets to a point where we can’t work through it, and there’s a fundamental change that will hurt International Falls significantly.” Residents on both sides have favorite products they grab whenever they cross. For Heather Johnson, executive director of the Fort Frances chamber of commerce, it’s Top the Tater, an iconic Minnesota chive and onion dip. She also checks prices on cheeses, and peruses the wider variety of pastas for sale in US stores. Johnson bowls weekly in a league in International Falls, made up of both Americans and Canadians. Leanne Guba, a Canadian who owns Hometown Hobby and Crafts in International Falls, crosses back into her home country once or twice a month, usually walking across the bridge, to buy ketchup chips, chocolate bars and Dad’s brand oatmeal chocolate chip cookies. American liquor is no longer on the shelves at government-run Ontario liquor stores, by order of Premier Doug Ford. The push to buy Canadian is “pretty well elbows-up”, Johnson said. “I’m drinking Canadian red wine now.” ‘Mr T took care of that’ Reid, the duty-free shop owner, said the tourist season was about average for him, with no noticeable decline in sales. He has seen some change in his customers. A couple of years ago, they’d come in with the signature red Maga (Make America Great Again) hats. Last year, not as many. This year, he didn’t see any red hats, and customers would tell him they didn’t vote for Trump. They’ll ask about the missing American bourbon from his shelves, and he’ll tell them, “Mr T took care of that”. He used to cross the border to go to a show, or the grocery store, or Menard’s, a hardware store, but not anymore. His daughter and her husband used to cross weekly for a date night and shopping, but no longer. People over here are “really upset” with Trump, he said. It has renewed his sense of Canadian pride, but “I’ve always had good pride”. Johnson, whose kids are now grown, said: “I’m glad that my kids grew up knowing both countries, and they know that there really isn’t a difference in people.” *** Across the border in International Falls, craft store owner Guba said she was seeing fewer Canadians, for several reasons. They’re dealing with rising costs, too, and the exchange rate is unfavorable. Some of it is politics, she said. Canadian regulars are coming less frequently. “They’re definitely being a little more picky about when they come over or being more careful about what they buy,” she said. The decline, while dealing with unpredictable tariffs on goods she brings in from overseas, has had an impact on her business. She’s adapted by seeking out new suppliers, bringing in new merchandise lines, and trying to reduce costs. She has a few companies she orders from in Canada – including a toy brand and a puzzle company – and expects the new tariffs will likely increase costs on those products. People are upset about the political dynamics, but they don’t tend to vent their political frustrations openly, she said. There may be the odd joke here and there, but not usually full-blown political debate. “We tend to try to stay friendly,” she said. The latest tourist season was “decent”, she said. “Overall, we’re still surviving … You can’t really control it.” ‘We remain neutral’ It’s tough to gauge the full impact of declining Canadian spending in the border town, though anecdotally, people are noticing it. The International Falls chamber of commerce would not comment on the impact of the tariffs on the town, or the deteriorating relationship between the two countries. “We remain neutral on political matters so that we can best serve our diverse membership, which includes individuals and organizations with a wide range of views. Because of that, the Chamber does not have an official comment on the political issues surrounding the US-Canada relationship,” the chamber said in an email. Isaac Johnson, who owns the Coffee Landing café in International Falls and lives above it with his wife, said he still sees a lot of Canadians who come over to grab espresso and breakfast. He loves his Canadian customers, including the couple he watched meet up at the coffee shop from across the border. They later married. The locals are caught in the middle of political games, said Johnson, who tries to just focus on himself, his family, and his faith. But people do get emotional about it at times, and “if you definitely bring up politics, for sure,” he said – just as the man who confronted Dill, the mayor, did. The man, who didn’t share his name or want to have a longer conversation with a reporter, said he’s noticed far fewer Canadians around town, nothing like it used to be. He described Canadians as “very pissed off” and said snowbirds were selling their houses in the US. International Falls voters went for Trump in 2024. These broader issues, like the trade war, “pit us against each other”, Johnson said, noting that the man got mad at the mayor “over a guy that’s making billions off us all”. “I love the Canadians, I love Americans, and I love them coming over here and enjoying what we have here, and we can go and enjoy what they have,” Johnson said. *** Dill, the town’s mayor, said Canadians are “definitely” not coming to International Falls as much as they were, though he thinks it has more to do with the exchange rate. Still, he said later, “we need all the Canadian commerce we can get, and I would like to think they feel the same way”. Local officials are in a tough position. They have no control over the tariffs, though with their communities at the center of the impact, they are expected to answer questions and concerns over levies. They have no direct line to the Trump administration, if that would even make a difference. And their communities are suffering. Hope springs eternal Hauschild, the Minnesota state senator, said he meets regularly with the Canadian consulate in St Paul, and reiterates his belief in a strong relationship with Canada. But as a state lawmaker, he has little to no control over any of it, beyond using his bully pulpit. Hallikas, the Fort Frances mayor, said most Canadians have “no rancor for individual Americans” and treat them kindly when they visit, largely avoiding talking about Trump or American politics. Americans will have to work to undo the damage Trump has done to the relationship between the two countries, and that will take time, even after the trade war simmers down or ends, he said. “But we’ll still be friends with the folks in Minnesota and International Falls,” Hallikas said. Dill said he doesn’t often run into the frustrations directed at him by the man in the coffee shop, though it happens. He doesn’t have any way he can directly fix the issue. “The US elected our current president and he has his own agenda and I don’t see that I can stop it,” he said. “I don’t want it to affect us locally. We’ll see. Hope springs eternal. I mean, I thought that everything was going along fine, but apparently it wasn’t.” The uncertainty of it all is “frustrating”, and he’s most curious about where it all lands, when a truce could be signed so that businesses can have a sense of comfort in planning for their futures. The two countries are engaged in a heated dispute – or a “donnybrook,” as they would say in Canada, noted Dill. He likened the current situation to two longtime best friends, who hunted and fished and vacationed together for years – until one of them said, you’ve been taking advantage of me for years. “That’s like driving a nail in a fence,” he said, “and then you pull it out, and even if the fence still stands, there’s a hole where the nail was.”

title: ‘We can see into the other room’: insurers face surge in subsidence claims
summary: Stressed UK homeowners tell of cracks opening up in the walls around them after two record-hot summers
text: “We’ve got one wall with an absolutely huge diagonal crack, through which we can see through to the other room; you could easily put your fingers in it and chunks of plaster are falling off,” says Henry Biggs, 49, from Stroud in Gloucestershire. He and his partner started noticing cracks in their family home in June 2025, a few months after buying it, and filed an insurance claim for subsidence that was accepted by their insurer, Admiral, in the spring. Monitoring devices were only recently fitted, about a year after they first submitted the claim, and they have no idea when the damage might start to be repaired. They are among a growing number of UK homeowners who face subsidence after two record-hot summers. August was the joint-hottest month ever recorded around the world. Signs of subsidence include widening and lengthening diagonal cracks, typically around window and door frames, as well as sloping floors, and sticking doors and windows. Millions of homes are at risk of subsidence because of the worsening climate crisis, the British Geological Survey has warned. Under its worst-case scenario, 11% of UK homes could be at risk of subsidence by 2070, more than 4.2 million houses. As hotter, drier summers and warmer, wetter winters become more frequent, the ground under houses can shrink and drag down a property’s foundations. Older properties with shallow foundations are more at risk, and those built on clay-rich soils. The most vulnerable areas include London, Essex, Kent and a tranche of land from Oxford up to the Wash on England’s east coast, according to scientists. Insurers have experienced a rise in claims for subsidence in recent months. Hastings says it had record subsidence claims in August, up 140% on last August. So far in 2026, its claims are up by 30% year on year. Axa, one of the biggest home insurers, has talked of a “surge year” for subsidence, and Aviva is reviewing its reserves and pricing models. During this year’s heatwaves the damage at Biggs’s house, which was built in 1970, worsened progressively. “There are cracks now throughout the house, diagonal cracks around almost every window, windows are getting harder to open and close, and the door lintels have dropped, so we have doors now that won’t close,” he says. “In the main part of the house, the kitchen, dining room, the hallway, the floor is dropping and cracking because it’s just falling away in the middle.” He adds: “It’s quite upsetting when you’ve just bought your first home, and we can’t even decorate at the moment.” The couple have hired their own loss assessor as subsidence claims tend to be complex and lengthy, often lasting several years. The average subsidence claim in the UK hit a record £20,000 between April and June, more than £2,000 higher than a year earlier, according to the Association of British Insurers (ABI). Insurers paid out £72m for domestic subsidence claims, compared with £60m in the same period last year. Timothy Farewell, a geospatial environmental data scientist, whose company MapleSky advises 20 insurers, as well as water companies, on ground movement, says: “We have seen widespread drying of soils across the UK in 2018, 2022, 2025 and 2026 leading to an uptick in the number of cracking houses, bursting water mains and failing roads.” It is all about “differential movement”, he says. “You can imagine if your house, road or pipe is built across two different soil types, with one soil more shrinkable than the other, then this differential movement is when you get significant problems, with one part moving more than the other. And differential movement could also happen when you have a tree on one side of the house that is drying out (and shrinking) the soil more on one side of the house than the other.” As old water pipes are more vulnerable than houses to ground movement, summer failures on the water network can indicate that the subsidence risk is increasing in that region. While fewer houses are built on peat-rich soils, movement in these soils has a considerable impact on rural roads and pipe networks, Farewell adds. Shaune Worrall, the deputy head of insurance of the British Insurance Brokers’ Association, has warned of a “double surge” of claims, as many subsidence claims from last year are still being processed. As well as environmental conditions, modern housing layouts can affect the risk, he says. Open-plan extensions, larger kitchens and interconnected living areas can mean that extensive structural repairs are needed. Subsidence excess is usually much higher than for other perils, and a figure of more than £1,000 has become common. This sum could rise to £10,000 for a property that has had subsidence in the past, despite underpinning works. Melissa, who works in the arts and has two children, says she and her husband “reluctantly” lodged an insurance claim for subsidence last month. While the cause of the extensive cracks in their 1901 home in Walthamstow, north London, is still to be determined, the couple felt they had no choice. “When we came back from holiday towards the end of August, our cracks had got a lot worse, in a short period of time. In some parts, wider than 1cm that you can fit a pencil in. Our front door was also sticking such that we could barely open or close it.” Structural engineers have still not been round to look at the damage, with long delays due to the general surge in insurance claims. Repair schedules will also be affected, with insurers stating months before remediation. Melissa says she has been warned that even if it turns out not to be subsidence, once a subsidence claim is lodged, “that will potentially affect your ability to get future insurance with other providers and will likely drive up your premiums”. Several homeowners told the Guardian that they might not make an insurance claim for subsidence because they worry about rising premiums, or not being able to get insurance cover in future. Rachel Hogarth Smith, 58, a recently retired headteacher, says she has been “quite stressed” about subsidence at her late Victorian/Edwardian house. She has held off from making an insurance claim after her insurer warned her about the potential repercussions. She has been advised by a structural engineer to wait until the spring before doing any repair work, while an olive tree near the house should be removed because it sucks moisture from the ground, exacerbating the situation. “I’m now not opening any of the windows in the bay window because they’re sticking a bit and I don’t want to be in a position where I can’t get them closed again,” she says. “There’s a small gap between the skirting board and the floorboards underneath the bay so you can see daylight in between them.” If the subsidence remedial works end up costing a lot more than hoped, she may file an insurance claim after all. Modern homes are considered less vulnerable, but Richard Smith, the head of standards, innovation and research at the National House Building Council, says it is reviewing whether changes should be made to its standards. Subsidence claims can be costly and complex, but underpinning or other remedial work should resolve the issues. Sarah Dodd, founder of the law firm Tree Law, says: “In around 25 years working with tree-related subsidence cases [that led to legal disputes], I can recall fewer than 10 cases where significant subsidence has recurred following underpinning.”
