title: Nearly 50,000 Yemeni civilians flee as Houthis advance along Red Sea coast
summary: Global struggle for control of Bab al-Mandab strait threatens to turn Yemen’s on-off conflict into a forever war
text: Nearly 50,000 people have fled a sudden advance by Houthi forces in western Yemen, with entire villages emptied and families trapped near frontline fighting with depleting food supplies, according to aid workers. Civilians in the Middle East’s poorest country have found themselves victims of a global struggle for control over one of the most important shipping routes in the world, which threatens to turn Yemen’s on-off conflict into a forever war. In a lightning advance this week, the Iran-backed Houthi militants have seized a string of towns along the Red Sea coast from forces aligned with the US- and Saudi-backed Yemeni government. Hundreds of people are reported to have been killed. Many fear a return to the full-scale civil war that killed 150,000 and brought many others to the brink of famine. The UN International Organization for Migration (IOM) said on Friday that 46,000 people had been displaced across the governates of Taiz and Hodeidah, where steep verdant mountain ridges give way to arid coastal plains. For many families, this was their second or even third time they had been forced out of their homes. A significant number of people were observed to be leaving the city with their belongings. Fighting has cut key roads, while phone lines are down in some areas. “The scale of displacement is increasing rapidly,” said Joe Lowry, IOM’s Middle East and north Africa spokesperson in Cairo. The most urgent needs were emergency shelters, cash assistance, food, drinking water, household items, healthcare and protection services. “Civilians are bearing the brunt of renewed frontline warfare, airstrikes, shelling, and large-scale displacement,” Lowry said. “Many of those fleeing have arrived with very few belongings after leaving suddenly, due to shelling and frontline advances.” Lowry said aid workers were having to constantly reassess access, and adapt movements, as the situation changed. “It’s a highly fluid and uncertain situation marked by rapid territorial changes, population movements and growing concern among communities about further escalation,” he said. The Houthi advance has come unexpectedly and fast, particularly the fall of the strategic port city of Mocha – widely regarded as the birthplace of the global coffee trade and the eponym for chocolate-flavoured coffee. Mohamed, 46, who left Mocha in the middle of the night, told Agence France-Presse there was an “apocalyptic” atmosphere in the city. Another man, Mujahid Tahami, who set off for the southern government-held city of Aden, said some families had fallen victim to “looting by gangs as they tried to flee”. Others reported that they had managed to flee in time, some on motorbikes, but other family members were not so lucky and were stuck. Yemen analysts have long criticised the US and its allies for taking a security-focused approach to the country that undervalues diplomacy and development. Washington launched a campaign of drone attacks against Sunni al-Qaida militants for much of the 21st century, but did not pay significant attention to the hardline Shia Houthi insurgency until its forces claimed the capital in 2014. By taking control of key areas this week, including islands off the coast, the anti-west Houthis hope to gain a direct presence near the Bab al-Mandab strait, a 20-mile stretch of water and vital trade and energy route that connects Asia with Europe. The strait’s name is roughly translated as “the gate of tears” or “the gate of grief”, and its strong currents and winds made the passage between the Arabian peninsula and Africa’s east coast hazardous for centuries. Modern-day cargo ships have no physical issue passing through. But if the Houthis were to close the natural chokepoint, the impact on the global economy could be disastrous. Ships would have to reroute around the southern tip of Africa, adding thousands of extra nautical miles. The fighting has already contributed to the price of oil rising above $100 a barrel after weeks when it was trading closer to $80. The fighting in Yemen, as well as Houthi missile strikes on Saudi Arabia, is the most significant violence in the country since the UN-brokered peace plan in 2022. The UN special envoy for Yemen, Hans Grundberg, told an emergency security council meeting on Thursday that the country faced “a new and more dangerous phase of war”. “This renewed war should alarm us all,” Grundberg said. “It effectively marks the end of the relative calm that Yemen has experienced for over four years since the UN-brokered truce. It not only threatens to plunge Yemen into a prolonged and expanding war, but also risks yet again dragging the country into the wider and unresolved regional confrontation, with global repercussions.” Instability in Yemen has been exploited by regional powers such as Saudi Arabia, Iran and the United Arab Emirates to fight proxy battles, and the failure to end the violence has led to the growth of powerful militias. The US-Israeli war on Iran has only heightened the tensions, with regional animosity at an all-time high. This has compounded one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises. The most recent UN humanitarian report, released last month, warned that the country of 40 million was facing a deepening malnutrition crisis, with roughly half the population facing acute food insecurity nationwide. “Years of conflict, economic deterioration, displacement, climate-related shocks and regional tensions have steadily weakened livelihoods and household resilience,” the report warned. “At the same time, declining humanitarian funding and operational constraints are limiting the ability of aid organisations to provide assistance at the scale required.” On the Red Sea coast, those who escaped the latest wave of fighting had their lives, but were left in shock. “It’s a catastrophe, and the attacks are ongoing,” said Mohammed Khudairi, who fled the fighting to a displacement camp of wood-and-straw huts near the areas of Khokha. “We managed to leave, but others remain trapped there.”

title: Firewall compromised: has Friedrich Merz blown ‘democracy’s last shot’?
summary: Many fear chancellor is wrong man for the job at a time when Germany’s defences against far right are crumbling
text: A cataclysm. A 9.0 earthquake. A five-alarm fire. A bitter rejection of Germany’s joyous reunification three decades ago, and a threat to the democratic postwar order. Sizing up the repercussions of last weekend’s win for the far-right Alternative für Deutschland party in the former communist state of Saxony-Anhalt, German commentators expressed a sense of doom, panic and helplessness in the political establishment. With nearly 44% of the vote, the AfD fell three seats short of an absolute majority. Its media savvy chief candidate, Ulrich Siegmund, is racing to find enough support from the other parties to prop up what would be the first rightwing extremist state government since the Nazi period. It is still anyone’s guess whether he will succeed, leaving a corrosive uncertainty at the heart of Europe’s top economic power. Hanging in the balance is the fate of Friedrich Merz’s centre-right government, once called “democracy’s last shot” to prevent an extremist takeover in Germany. The result in Saxony-Anhalt has put the conservative chancellor on the ropes, with further punishment for his Christian Democratic Union party (CDU) expected in two more state polls later this month. “This is the worst defeat for the CDU in years – decades – and something has changed, not just in Saxony-Anhalt but in all of Germany,” he said on Monday. Whether or not he survives politically until the next general election, due in 2029, will have dramatic repercussions for Germany and its European allies trying to beat back anti-democratic forces. Pivotal elections are due next year in countries including France, Spain, Italy and Poland. Merz’s many critics say the 70-year-old former BlackRock executive is the wrong man at such a consequential crossroads, calling him a ham-fisted and empathetically challenged leader who is erratic in his messaging. Only in office 16 months, the chancellor often seemed incapable of one of the basic tasks of leadership: making the case to voters that accepting bitter pills now could lead to a brighter future, said the political scientist Thomas Biebricher of Frankfurt’s Goethe University. “The prevailing impression at the moment is that, in terms of communication, he is unable to explain the many reforms – and the sacrifices they entail – to the public, and thereby win their acceptance,” Biebricher said, referring to planned cuts to the statutory pension and healthcare schemes. The former chancellor Angela Merkel, Merz’s longtime rival within the CDU, has criticised him publicly for his hardline rhetoric on migration and integration but said she took no pleasure in the debacle given the stakes. “This is a turning point – a real turning point – in the history of the federal republic of Germany,” said Merkel, who left office of her own accord in 2021 after 16 years in power. “As a CDU member it breaks my heart.” Speaking at a digital affairs conference on Tuesday, she advised Merz to rethink his messaging in a changing political ecosystem in which emotions counted more than facts. Merkel, 72, noted that the CDU had pointed to data during the Saxony-Anhalt campaign showing that joblessness had fallen and household wealth had risen in the small, relatively poor state. “And then [Siegmund] says: ‘That may be so, but that’s not how it feels.’” The AfD formed in 2013, during Merkel’s tenure, as a Eurosceptic outfit opposed to bailouts for debt-mired countries. It grew increasingly radical during the 2015-2016 refugee influx, when she left the borders open to more than a million asylum seekers fleeing war and hardship. Merz took office last year saying he would put the country back on track after the implosion of the previous government under Olaf Scholz. He promised a return to economic growth, a restoration of defence capabilities and urgent repairs to the creaking social welfare system. His recipe for confronting the far right – one of his key pledges – was competence in governing and solutions for Germans’ most urgent problems. Merz also promised a rejection of Merkel’s open-border policy in an attempt to rob the AfD of its signature issue. He had infamously accepted support from the far-right party for a tough draft law on migration just before the February 2025 general election, before back-pedalling in the face of protests. As “irregular” arrivals of migrants have fallen sharply since Merz took office, the AfD has successfully pivoted to a broader range of concerns about deindustrialisation, regional identity, affordability and crime to gain ground far beyond its eastern heartland. The AfD, widely seen as more radical than comparable European parties, had been relegated to permanent opposition in Germany by the “firewall” strategy of shunning by the mainstream parties. But this policy is now widely seen to have failed, allowing the AfD to snipe from the sidelines about the slow pace of any positive change. Biebricher said that for all Merz’s weaknesses, replacing him would not be a magic bullet for the mountain of challenges facing German security and prosperity. As well as the threat from Russia, he cited decrepit infrastructure, the demographic crunch on social welfare benefits, competition from China in once mighty industries such as car manufacturing, and geopolitical upheaval weighing on supply chains and energy imports. “None of that simply goes away the moment you have someone who communicates better,” Biebricher told public radio. Merz’s centre-right CDU-CSU bloc, divided between conservatives and moderates, is nevertheless known for its internal discipline in times of crisis – if only out of fear of even graver consequences from drastic changes. The situation is seen as so grim that it has triggered paralysis, with neither the popular North Rhine-Westphalia state premier, Hendrik Wüst, or Bavaria’s ambitious leader, Markus Söder, keen at this stage to snatch the poisoned chalice. “Merz has now reached a stage where the crisis – which he himself constantly exacerbates – is stabilising him,” said the veteran political journalist Bernd Ulrich of Die Zeit newspaper. “The CDU and the government (in coalition with the Social Democrats) as a whole are in such a dire state that, as far as anyone can tell, no one wants to take over his post.” Wüst, 51, leads a coalition with the Greens in Germany’s most populous state and faces a re-election battle next April. If he wins, the calls for Merz to make way for him may grow louder. Söder, who represents the bloc’s conservative wing, shares Merz’s view that it needs to echo the AfD’s harsh rhetoric on migration in order to win back support – a strategy political scientists have long disparaged as counterproductive. Yet the dangers of keeping a revolt at bay by betting on a status quo voters so clearly reject are apparent. Much will depend on how bad the news is from the regional elections in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania on 20 September. The AfD is polling well in both states, with clear momentum after Saxony-Anhalt, putting pressure on the CDU in particular. During a fiery clash with the AfD in parliament this week in which he laid out the threat it poses to German democracy, Merz was reflective about how to steer the country – and himself – out of the current straits. He quoted from a letter he received from the rector of a theological university arguing how many opportunities still lay ahead for Germany and advising him not to give in to despair. Merz said he intended to take this to heart and stay on as chancellor using a new roadmap: “Admit mistakes, forgive, get back on your feet, shape the future.”

title: Ukraine war briefing: Russian developers used AI to build ‘kamikaze’ attack drone software, Anthropic says
summary: Anthropic also found that hackers used AI in attacks against targets in Ukrainian government, military and diplomatic sectors.
text: A small team of likely freelance developers in Russia used AI chatbot Claude to develop software for an autonomous swarm of first-person-view “kamikaze” attack drones, including terminal guidance, target selection and coordination between multiple aircraft, according to Anthropic, the company that developed Claude. In a 154-page report describing how bad actors used its Claude AI system for state-sponsored surveillance and propaganda operations, Anthropic said the drone swarm was programmed to pick its own targets and crash into them to detonate, without a human making the final call. In their programming, the freelance team repeatedly picked a location in Ukraine’s Donetsk region as their target and used VPNs to circumvent Anthropic’s geographic blocks. Small drones have become a ‌central weapon in the war in Ukraine. Anthropic ‌also found that cybercriminals and state-backed hackers are increasingly using AI to orchestrate and execute large portions of cyber-attacks, including in attacks targeting officials in Ukraine. One hacking group allegedly ran phishing, hotel wifi hijacking and WhatsApp-takeover operations against targets in the Ukrainian government, military and diplomatic sectors, using AI at nearly every stage, Anthropic said. The group’s tradecraft was consistent with Russia-based threat actor Midnight Blizzard, which the US government has previously linked to Russia’s SVR foreign intelligence service, Reuters reported. The Russian embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The group allegedly used AI to build a system that automatically detected when its malware was flagged by security defences and rewrote the code until it evaded detection. The Anthropic report comes as petrol stations in Kyiv have been hit by jet-powered drones in a wave of targeted Russian attacks as the bombardment of Ukraine’s capital enters a new phase of intensity. At least two people were killed and 12 injured in strikes on two petrol stations on Friday morning, according to the city’s mayor, Vitali Klitschko. The rush-hour strikes follow a similar attack on a petrol station on Thursday. All three strikes targeted petrol stations operated by Ukrnafta, a state-owned oil and natural gas extraction company. A list of 18 petrol stations in Kyiv expected to be hit by Russian drones started circulating on Telegram on Wednesday. The three struck so far were on the list. Russian president Vladimir Putin has blamed the west for the conflict in Ukraine because of what he said was its constant pressure on Moscow and its attempts to “drag” Ukraine into the Nato alliance. Speaking to reporters before the BRICS summit in India, Putin said “everything happening in Europe right now is basically ‌the result of system errors by … the western globalists in politics, security, and economics”. After a Russia-friendly president was forced to flee Ukraine in 2014, he said the West “immediately set the goal of dragging Ukraine into Nato. And this ‌ultimately turned out to be the main reason for today’s tragic events in Ukraine”. He said people in Europe understood what was going on, which explained why they were voting for far-right parties such as the AfD in the German state of Saxony-Anhalt. A Russian official will attend a G20 energy meeting in Houston next week, a White House official said on Friday. Last month, the US welcomed ⁠Russian finance minister Anton Siluanov to a meeting of G20 countries in North Carolina, upsetting European officials because it was the first time Russia’s finance ⁠minister had attended the forum in person since Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022. The meeting comes as European Union efforts to become independent from Russian oil and gas are faltering, as it heads into winter with low gas stocks, its auditors said this month. The US House of Representatives is expected to take up a tough Russian sanctions package next week, although prospects of passage are uncertain despite the bill receiving overwhelming support in the Senate. The bill is designed to add pressure on Putin to negotiate an end to Russia’s war with Ukraine. However, several top Democratic lawmakers are worried the measure dramatically expands president Donald Trump’s tariff authority, and he would use that new power to go after US allies. Three people were killed in Russian ⁠strikes in southeastern Ukraine’s Dnipropetrovsk and Zaporizhzhia ⁠regions and in Kharkiv in the northeast, according to the governors of those regions. Russia has for two weeks been carrying out almost constant attacks with faster jet-powered drones that have killed a number of ⁠Kyiv residents and disrupted daily life in Ukraine’s capital. Ukraine also carried out drone attacks on Russia, killing two people in the Tula region overnight and one on Friday in the Kursk region, local officials said.

title: US rapper Lil Durk found not guilty of murder-for-hire scheme
summary: Prosecutors accused musician, born Durk Banks, of putting bounty on fellow rapper in retaliation for friend’s killing
text: Chicago rapper Lil Durk has been acquitted of all charges in a murder-for-hire scheme, in which a man was fatally gunned down in 2022. Prosecutors had accused Lil Durk, born Durk Banks, of putting a bounty on Atlanta rapper Tayquian Bowman’s life in retaliation for the 2020 shooting death of Banks’s friend, fellow Chicago rap star King Von. The state alleged that associates of Only the Family, Banks’s alleged criminal enterprise and record label, tracked Bowman to a gas station in West Hollywood in 2022, where they opened fire on his car. Bowman’s cousin, Saviay’a Robinson, was fatally shot in the ambush. Kacey Hester, who said he had been a shooter in the attack, testified, according to Courthouse News, that Banks probed for details on the ambush: “Did somebody get hit? How many times did you shoot? What did you do?” Banks’s defense attorneys cast doubt over the reliability of Hester’s testimony, saying he was seeking a more lenient sentence. The rapper’s defense team also sought to portray Kavon Grant, Banks’s former assistant, whose cousin died after an altercation with Bowman’s entourage, as the mastermind of the 2022 shooting. Prosecutors rebuffed the lawyers’ notion. “No one is saying he was the one on the ground with a gun in his hand in Los Angeles, but you know this story doesn’t happen without him, and it doesn’t make sense without his leadership,” assistant US attorney Ian Yanniello reportedly said. The Friday federal jury verdict brought an end to a highly publicized case that drew loyal fans and celebrity supporters to the downtown Los Angeles courthouse. Banks’s legal woes are not over yet. He is due to appear in court for a second trial on a racketeering charge. “While we are disappointed with the jury’s decision regarding Durk Banks, AKA Lil Durk, we look forward to presenting our evidence at his second trial, scheduled for 5 October, when he will face racketeering murder and firearms charges,” said first assistant US attorney Bill Essayli.

title: NSW police seize 36 illegal ebikes on northern beaches that are now destined for the crusher
summary: Officers found one 14-year-old’s ebike was capable of hitting 90km/h. Owners have two weeks to appeal the seizure before the bikes will be crushed
text: Dozens of high-powered and illegal ebikes have been seized by police on Sydney’s northern beaches just weeks after the force was granted new powers to destroy dangerous bikes. The operation was part of a coordinated push with the New South Wales government to ensure people only ride legal ebikes that have not been modified to reach high speeds. One of the ebikes seized on Friday belonged to a 14-year-old boy from Warriewood. Police said it was capable of reaching speeds of more than 90km/h. NSW police said they seized 36 “illegal ebikes”. The operation was launched on the northern beaches “following recent incidents of illegal, dangerous and reckless e-bike use”. Assistant commissioner David Driver said police would be launching more operations across the state in coming weeks. “Most ebike riders do the right thing and comply with the rules; however, police will enforce [the] new legislation if people ride non-compliant vehicles,” Driver said on Saturday. In late August, NSW police were given new powers to destroy ebikes capable of exceeding the legal speed limit. Owners of seized ebikes now have 14 days to let police know whether their bike was stolen and being used by someone else on Friday. After that two-week window, the bikes will be “crushed”, the government says. The legislation also allowed police to seize ebikes that do not cut power assistance at 25km/h, with non-compliant bikes to be removed from the streets. The government invested in a number of “dyno units” – portable speed-testing devices – to measure an ebike’s power output. The Transport for NSW secretary, Josh Murray, said one of the units was used on the northern beaches on Friday to inspect suspect ebikes. “We can put an ebike on a machine and test its power and speed very quickly,” Driver said. “When they did that yesterday, the bike showed that just by clicking the throttle it could go over 40km/h.” Ebikes have been hailed as a climate-friendly solution to city traffic congestion, transport emissions and even youth social media addiction, offering Australians a means to get more exercise and save money. But they have come with a cost. NSW recorded 226 injuries related to ebikes in 2024. In the first seven months of 2025, that had already to surged to 233 injuries plus four deaths. In NSW this year to date, 187 vehicle drivers, passengers and motorcyclists have died on the state’s roads. In 2025, the figure for the same period was 194. Murray said most people were legally using ebikes but a small group ignoring the rules endangered other road users. “We are serious about ebike safety and operations like this will continue by NSW police with support from Transport for NSW to ensure all road users are safe and complying with the state’s upgraded laws,” Murray said. “Ebikes must behave like bicycles, not motorcycles. If your bike can operate like a motorcycle under throttle or go more than 25km/h while being powered, it is not legal to ride in public. “Before you or your child jumps on an ebike, please make sure it’s road-legal, otherwise you risk losing the bike.”

title: California woman charged with murder after allegedly killing husband with flagpole
summary: SF Gate reports bond for Vicky Kyung Mi Kim, 65, set at $10m after man found dead at couple’s Palm Desert home
text: A 65-year-old California woman has been arrested on suspicion of murder after allegedly fatally wounding her husband with a flagpole, according to SF Gate. On 4 September, Palm Desert sheriff’s deputies responded to an “unknown trouble call” in The Enclave, a luxury condominium community. Upon arrival, officers located an individual with “traumatic injuries” that appeared to be from a physical assault and pronounced them dead. Vicky Kyung Mi Kim was taken into custody on suspicion of murder. The victim was her spouse, SF Gate reported. Her bail has been set at $10m, according to court documents. The events leading up to the deadly incident remain unknown, but court documents show Kim had a history of recent domestic violence. In January, she pleaded guilty to a misdemeanor charge of battery of a spouse or cohabitant and a misdemeanor charge of inflicting corporal injury on a spouse related to a separate violation. Kim entered a guilty plea for violating a protective order. The couple had previous arguments over finances and infidelity allegations, KESQ News Channel 3 reported. Molly Smith, a spokesperson for the Riverside county district attorney’s office, referenced Kim’s legal troubles to SF Gate: “In January of this year, our office charged Ms Kim with a felony, obtained criminal protective orders, and intended to aggressively prosecute her for her crimes against her husband.” In a statement, obtained by KESQ, Smith elaborated on Kim’s record. “Despite our office’s clear objections, a judge resolved all of the defendant’s cases as misdemeanors, released her from custody, and terminated all protective orders that prosecutors worked hard to obtain,” Smith said. The judge could not be immediately identified for comment.

title: Man arrested over death of Mississippi woman who was found hanging from a tree
summary: Police have arrested Jacques Ratliff for the death of Tasia Fortune, a 29-year-old Black woman who was found behind an empty house last month
text: Police in Jackson, Mississippi, have arrested a man in the death of Tasia Fortune, a 29-year-old Black woman found hanging from a tree behind a vacant house last month. The state medical examiner on Thursday ruled Fortune’s death a homicide. Jackson police chief RaShall Brackney-Wheelock said at a news conference Friday that police had secured search and arrest warrants for Jacques Ratliff and arrested him when they encountered him walking on the street. The state medical examiner’s office determined Thursday evening that the death was a homicide, Brackney-Wheelock said, allowing them to execute the warrants they already had on hand. The killing of the mother of four has attracted national attention, both because of the severity of the crime and Mississippi’s brutal history of racist violence and lynchings. Brackney-Wheelock acknowledged the media interest, but declined to discuss motive, other than saying the suspect, a 51-year-old Black man, knew Fortune. “We understand the questions and the desire for answers given Mississippi’s history,” Brackney-Wheelock said. “We understand this case is being viewed through a broader lens, a global lens, and we do not dismiss those concerns. We are taking them seriously.” “At the same time, we do have a responsibility to make sure that what we say publicly is supported by our evidence and facts,” Brackney-Wheelock added. “We cannot speculate by the nature or the manner in which Ms. Fortune was killed, beyond what has been officially determined by the medical examiner.” The investigation remains active and more arrests are likely, Brackney-Wheelock said. Christy Spivey, Fortune’s mother, said Friday after police told her of the arrest that, “I just started crying and told them ‘thank you, thank you, thank you.’” Spivey said police did not share a motive or whether DNA led them to the arrest. Spivey said she did not know the man who had been arrested, but was asking her daughter’s friends if they knew him. Spivey described the family as “in disbelief” and “shock”. “We still don’t have a lot of answers,” Spivey said. Fortune died less than a year after the hanging deaths of 21-year-old Trey Reed, a Black student at Delta State University in Cleveland, Mississippi and Cory Zukatis, an unhoused white man in his 30s, in Vicksburg.

title: ‘The future scares me’: why unemployment has become biggest election issue for young New Zealand voters
summary: As mainstream parties vie for votes with promises of jobs and economic growth, young people may take more convincing
text: Thirty minutes north of New Zealand’s capital, raucous laughter is tumbling out of a nondescript building in Naenae – an economically deprived suburb in Lower Hutt – into the car park of a tiny shopping strip. Inside, 10 students aged between 15 and 24 are trying to better their chances of finding a job, with help from Youth Inspire, a not-for-profit that assists hundreds of young people each year into training, education or work. They have been working on CVs, learning to drive, and today are roleplaying challenging moments in a workplace. There is a lightness and camaraderie in the room that belies their day-to-day reality – one shaped by a desperate and lonely search for work that is not there. “It’s really heartbreaking and it breaks my confidence,” says Luta Matagi, 23, who has spent seven months looking for work. “I may not have degrees but I am a hard worker. We are all hard workers in here.” These students are a handful of the 180,000 young New Zealanders either unemployed or underemployed in the past quarter. Nearly four in 10 (37%) of 15-24-year-olds are in this group, categorised by government as the “underutilised” – the worst rate in 30 years, according to Stats NZ. As New Zealand prepares for its general election in November, unemployment is a key issue. For voters aged 18-34, unemployment ranks as the second most pressing concern, behind the cost of living, according to a recent Ipsos poll. Michael, 20, joined Youth Inspire to upskill, after finding “nothing out there” when it came to electrical apprenticeships. He is not alone. Apprenticeship numbers have slid 32% since 2022 to a 15-year low in 2025, government figures show. Michael says he has applied for at least 40 entry-level jobs in the past two years. He has not had a single interview. “It’s isolating searching for jobs alone,” he says. Matagi can’t count how many jobs she has applied for, “just to get rejected from all of them”. Young people routinely bear the brunt of an economic downturn, says Shamubeel Eaqub, chief economist at Simplicity, which provides fund management for New Zealand’s national saving scheme. “When there are only a few vacancies, then the people in the front of the queue are the ones who have got the most experience and the most to offer.” The effect can be scarring both for their career and their mental health, Eaqub says. “By the time the economy recovers, you’re going to be competing with the next cohort of young people who are now into the workforce.” The government has promised to grow the economy to increase jobs for young people. At the same time it is toughening jobseeker benefit criteria for some of that cohort. Matagi, like most of her peers, is on the jobseeker benefit. If she doesn’t find work soon, she will have to sell her car, which could further hinder her ability to get a job. She says the government is “so misguided” and not supporting young people enough. Its policy preventing 18-19 year olds whose parents earn a combined income of $65,529 (US$38,412) or more from accessing the benefit from November will place further strain on them and their families, she says. “It’s so sad to say, but the future scares me.” Zainab Ali, the organisation’s chief executive, sees the pressures on young people growing. “I used to notice pies and cans of [the drink] V being stolen from the shops near Youth Inspire, now what I am catching is bread, milk and eggs. They are the basics. That change tells you it is getting harder out there.” About 500 people are on the Youth Inspire waitlist. Ali says the hundreds that have already been through their doors are incredibly motivated. “They are struggling and still going,” she says. “And I would challenge anyone that thinks young people are lazy or not willing to work that we have the evidence to show that is not the case.” ‘Young people need to see some hope’ New Zealand’s economy has been battered by recession and stagnation that arrived in the wake of the Covid-19 pandemic. Rising inflation piled pressure on businesses and drove households to rein in spending. Company liquidations rose 14% in the past year, and nearly 3,000 hospitality businesses ceased trading, credit bureau Centrix reported in September. There are, however, some flickers of improvement. Rating agency Moody’s said in September it expected 1.6% GDP growth in 2026. Ali says entry-level jobs have disappeared, retail shops are not hiring and the availability of full-time work is slim. “We used to count full-time work as the benchmark – that’s not the case now. Casual is most prevalent, but generally it is fixed-term or short-term work.” Labour’s spokesperson for finance and economy, Barbara Edmonds, says the national unemployment rate – currently at an 11-year high of 5.6% – is “a damning verdict” on incumbent prime minister Christopher Luxon’s economic management. “Our young people need to see some hope … they want to see that there are jobs available for them.” Edmonds says Labour would aim to turn around unemployment figures by backing trades and apprenticeships, guaranteeing graduate nurses a job, and introducing a “Future fund” – a policy to invest in innovative businesses and infrastructure to create jobs. But the National party’s minister for social development and employment, Louise Upston, blames high unemployment on the previous Labour government’s “reckless fiscal and economic management”. “It takes time to right the ship,” she says in a statement, adding her government is committed to growing the economy to boost job creation. Responding to criticism over her policy to limit access to benefits for 18-19 year-olds, Upston says young people should be in education, training or employment and “it’s a common-sense expectation that it’s their parents who will support them, not the taxpayer”, if they cannot do one of these things. As the mainstream parties vie for votes with promises of jobs and economic growth, young people may take more convincing. Recent polling shows support for Labour and National slipping away in favour of the minor parties, with younger women showing the highest support for left-leaning minor parties and younger men showing the highest support for minor rightwing and centrist parties. Voter turnout for younger, and poorer, people has historically been low but Ali says she is noticing “a huge trend” in the community of families who have never voted and are enrolling for the election because of concern for their children. “That gives me heart,” she says. Matagi and Michael say they will vote for the minor Green party. Matagi feels the party’s MPs “see our point of view”. Michael, meanwhile, believes “they look out for the underdog”. The pair feel this election could be the difference between a career-less future and a path to a new life. “There is not much hope,” Michael says, “unless we get a new government.”

title: Republican senator fires aide who used Nazi soldiers as Facebook profile picture
summary: Washington Post report also reveals Jon Husted staffer Stephen Woytek created pro-Rhodesia playlist on Spotify
text: The Republican senator for Ohio, Jon Husted, has fired an aide who was discovered to have used a photo of Nazi SS soldiers as his Facebook profile photo. Stephen Woytek was appointed as Husted’s political director last month in the senator’s knife-edge re-election contest against former Democrat senator Sherrod Brown. According to the Washington Post, Husted had decided to “part ways” with Woytek, 25, after learning that his Facebook profile showed he followed a military re-enactment group called LAH Living History Unit, which portrays the 1st SS Panzer division. The group’s website says its members dress up as the Leibstandarte, a Waffen-SS armored division that began as Adolf Hitler’s bodyguards. LAH says the Leibstandarte “came to symbolize the highest dedication to duty and individual as well as collective loyalty”. The group claims to be “non-political” and insists is disavows “political and religious persecution” that happened the second world war. A Spotify playlist recently created by an account bearing Woytek’s name hailed the former racist white-minority regime of Rhodesia, now Zimbabwe, seen as a symbol of white supremacy by some racist groups. In a statement, a spokesperson for Husted said the campaign had ended its relationship with Woytek. “While he denies negative intent, his social media activity displays a complete lack of judgement and disregard for its impact on others,” the spokesperson said. “Senator Husted demands better of those who represent him. Upon learning about the social media posts today, Senator Husted made the immediate decision to part ways.” The campaign did not respond to the Post’s questions about whether and how Woytek’s social media activity had been vetted before his appointment, the newspaper reported. Woytek’s departure follows a series of damaging episodes in which young Republicans groups have been discovered expressing pro-Nazi sympathies in group chats and internet forums. And in Georgia, Republican congressman Mike Collins’s campaign for Senate has been shaken by controversies involving his staff’s online activity. This summer, Collins replaced top aide, Kip Talley, after Slate revealed he had been part of a group chat with white supremacists. Woytek, who serves in the national guard and was a graduate of the Citadel, a military academy based in Charleston, South Carolina, issued a statement of regret, saying he wished he had “exercised better judgment when posting about my activities online”. “I want to be unequivocal: I reject the racist and antisemitic ideology the SS and Nazi Germany represented. I believe it is important to educate our younger generations, which is why I participate in historical reenactments,” he said. LAH shared a photo on a Flickr account that showed Woytek in 2018 – when he was 16 – wearing an SS uniform and marching in an area adorned with Nazi flags. Woytek follows several suppliers of SS uniforms on his Facebook page. On a Quora account bearing his name, Woytek also answered a question on whether anything good had occurred under Hitler, writing in 2017 “that Hitler started an anti-smoking campaign”. More recently, he created a public playlist of pro-Rhodesia songs on Spotify called “Tales from Rhodesia”, which is captioned: “Homesick for a place that no longer exists.” One of the songs uses a slur to refer to African troops. The former British colony’s white minority government fought a long war against guerrilla groups after issuing a unilateral declaration of independence in 1965. The country was officially recognized as Zimbabwe under black majority rule in 1980, a year after the minority government accepted its rule was unsustainable and entered peace negotiations. Rhodesia has been used by white supremacists as a symbol of the supposed superiority of white rule.

title: Military aircraft reportedly blamed for UK air traffic control outage
summary: Meltdown that grounded thousands of flights caused by ‘spurious’ flight data being entered into system, report says
text: The air traffic control outage that caused thousands of flights to be grounded across the UK earlier in the week was caused by a military aircraft entering “spurious” flight data into the system, according to a report. Hundreds of thousands of passengers were affected after more than 2,000 flights were cancelled on Tuesday when the system used by the National Air Traffic Services (Nats) shut down for four hours. According to the Financial Times, four people briefed on the incident claimed that the shutdown was caused by a flight plan submitted by a UK military aircraft, which caused a meltdown in air traffic control systems used by Nats which remained unfixed for several hours. The paper also reported that Nats operations officer Kathryn Leahy called the operations managers of numerous airports and airlines, and “tensions boiled over” after Leahy informed them their flight processing system did not have a dedicated backup due to Nats being in the midst of a “complete overhaul of its systems” and because the amount of data it keeps meant duplicating it would cost “vast amounts”. The crisis has put pressure on Martin Rolfe, the chief executive of Nats, who was summoned to a meeting by transport secretary Heidi Alexander on Wednesday. Alexander, who said she did “not believe the issue was unavoidable”, was understood to have given Rolfe a week to report on the causes of the shutdown, while also commissioning an independent review by the Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) into the incident. The outage is the most serious to affect British commercial airspace since August 2023, when a technical problem led to almost 1,600 flights being delayed. Nats came under fire after that episode, with the CAA setting out 34 recommendations to improve its systems to avoid similar incidents, all of which were said to have been fully implemented. Rolfe ruled out a cyber-attack, which was initially suspected, saying he “believes we’ve never seen an incident happen more than once, so this will be something different that we’ve never seen in 50 years of operation”. Numerous airlines have already called for Rolfe to resign or be fired over the outage. Ryanair’s chief executive, Michael O’Leary, accused Rolfe of “telling lies to save his own skin” and said his position was “untenable”. O’Leary added: “We don’t need more investigations, we don’t need more reports and we don’t need another parliamentary committee hearing where Martin Rolfe will promise change, will promise resilience and will promise an effective backup system.” The delays led to some aircraft full of passengers being stuck waiting for information for more than four hours, while flights due to arrive in the UK were diverted to different airports, with some forced to land in Germany. Despite the far-reaching effect of the outage, it was understood that passengers affected were unlikely to be able to claim compensation, as delays were due to “extraordinary circumstances”. The Ministry of Defence said it did not believe there was any indication of an error on the part of the military, but that it would be inappropriate to comment further until the Nats investigation had concluded. • This article was amended on 12 September 2026 to address an issue with the attribution of verbal guidance given by the Ministry of Defence.

title: Ex-CIA officer accused of stealing gold bars reaches tentative plea deal
summary: David Rush accused of stealing hundreds of gold bars worth over $40m and hiding them in his basement
text: Federal prosecutors have reached a tentative plea agreement with a former CIA officer accused of stealing hundreds of gold bars worth more than $40m from the US spy agency and hiding them in his basement, court records show. David Rush and federal justice department prosecutors have a “plea agreement in principle”, the parties said in a Friday court filing. The parties also asked a judge to extend the 17 September deadline for three weeks through 8 October to allow them time to “resolve the matter prior to an indictment”. “The parties need additional time to prepare the paperwork, including an agreed upon statement of facts,” assistant US attorney Raizza Ty and Rush’s attorney, Jessica Carmichael, wrote in the joint filing. “A pre-indictment resolution promotes the public interest by conserving government and judicial resources.” There were no further details in the court filing about the working plea agreement. Rush, a former executive service-level employee for the CIA, was fired after allegedly taking 303 bullion bars, each weighing 2.2lb (1kg) – and more than $2m in foreign currency – from his government office, according to an FBI affidavit. The search of his home in Virginia also turned up 35 luxury watches, many of them Rolex. He was arrested on 19 May and charged with one count of stealing public money after allegedly falsifying his educational qualifications and military service to secure his job with the CIA. He also allegedly submitted fraudulent timecards to claim about $77,000 in compensation for military leave he wasn’t entitled to. After his arrest, investigators discovered the full details of a fake classified program Rush had set up and through which he requested the gold bars and foreign money as “work-related expenses”. He had also allegedly lied about his academic credentials and military background across multiple employment applications, including falsely claiming to have been a navy pilot. Rush has been held in custody since his arrest after being deemed a flight risk. He had been a CIA agent for 17 years and served in the agency’s science and technology division. The CIA hasn’t disclosed what his exact role entailed.

title: Legionnaires’ disease outbreak kills one and infects others in the South Bronx
summary: The disease is a form of pneumonia caused by Legionella bacteria, which can grow in warm water and spread through mist produced by cooling towers
text: One person has died from legionnaires’ disease, and four more have been sickened in New York City amid a new cluster of cases only weeks after local health officials had declared a separate deadly Manhattan outbreak of the illness over. On Thursday, New York City officials announced that their municipal health department launched an investigation into a community cluster in parts of Melrose and Morrisania in the South Bronx, including ZIP codes 10451 and 10456. The health department said sampling of cooling towers in the area has been completed, with testing under way at the city’s public health laboratory. Previous community clusters have been associated with Legionella spreading through mist produced by cooling towers, city officials said. Building owners whose cooling towers test positive are directed to drain, clean and disinfect them. The department has also issued a health alert to providers, advising them to consider legionnaires’ disease when evaluating patients with compatible symptoms. “Our disease investigators have confirmed five cases of Legionnaires’ disease and are working quickly to identify and confirm any additional cases in the area. Sadly, one person has died, and our deepest condolences are with their loved ones,” said a statement attributed to the city’s health commissioner, Alister F Martin. “I understand that New Yorkers may have heightened concerns following the recent Upper East Side cluster,” Martin added. “We are taking immediate action. “Community health workers will be canvassing the neighborhood. Anyone who lives, works, or has visited the affected area since late August and is experiencing flu-like symptoms should contact a health care provider as soon as possible.” Legionnaires’ disease is a form of pneumonia caused by Legionella bacteria, which can grow in warm water, especially in human-made building water systems including showerheads and sink faucets, hot tubs, as well as large, complex plumbing systems and cooling towers, according to the federal Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Legionella bacteria can also grow in a vehicle’s windshield wiper fluid tank. The CDC warns that the bacteria are more likely to grow when the tank is filled with water rather than genuine windshield washer fluid. People can become infected by breathing in contaminated water droplets or mist. Nevertheless, New York City health officials say it is safe to use air conditioners, drink tap water and shower unless otherwise advised. Symptoms can include fever, chills, muscle aches and cough. The disease is not contagious and can be treated with antibiotics when caught early. The South Bronx investigation marks the second community legionnaires’ disease cluster identified in New York City in recent months – after a cluster on Manhattan’s Upper East Side identified in July. Multiple community clusters in one season have previously occurred in New York City, including two each in 2015, 2017 and 2018, and three in 2016, according to city officials. The disease was named legionnaires’ after a 1976 outbreak of the sickness in Philadelphia, which largely affected people attending a convention of the American Legion, the war veterans’ nonprofit organization.

title: California petition worker ‘paid people to forge voter signatures’
summary: Prosecutors say James Brass orchestrated scheme to pay people on LA’s Skid Row to duplicate registered voters’ signatures
text: A California ballot petition worker has been arrested and charged with identity fraud for allegedly paying people on Los Angeles’ Skid Row to forge the signatures of registered voters. Prosecutors say James Brass, 47, orchestrated the scheme with the help of two signature collectors, 49-year-old Courtney Price and 33-year-old Jateisha Herron. In California, a proposed statute or constitutional amendment can only qualify for inclusion on a ballot if proponents gather a certain number of signatures by a specified deadline. To that end, Brass was contracted by an unidentified petition management company, which set a price for each signature gathered. The nature of the ballot measure remains unclear. Brass, Price and Herron traveled across Southern California, including to Skid Row, an area in downtown Los Angeles inhabited by a large homeless community, to solicit participants, according to a grand jury indictment filed in a California district court. The trio would fish for the personal information and names of state voters on a public database, before instructing individuals on Skid Row to use the voters’s identities in the fraudulent petition signatures. Brass allegedly sought to conceal the location of where the signatures were coming from. He instructed Herron to “never ever say” downtown Los Angeles and instead reference Inglewood and Torrance. Brass pocketed a total of $41,000 from the operation, according to the indictment. Brass, Price and Herron have each been charged with one count for conspiracy to commit identity fraud. Brass and Herron were also charged with a count of identity fraud. Brass has reportedly pleaded not guilty and is out of custody on a $10,000 bond. “They allegedly used people, including members of Skid Row’s vulnerable homeless population, to try to cover up their tracks,” prosecutor Bill Essayli said in a statement. “The charged conduct undermines the confidence voters have in our election systems and we will vigorously investigate and charge anyone involved.” The arrests come months after a 64-year-old woman, Brenda Armstrong, pleaded guilty to paying individuals on Skid Row to register as voters and sign her petitions. In San Francisco, petition canvassers reportedly incentivized homeless people in the Tenderloin neighborhood this year to provide signatures by offering cash and food. Some of the alleged exchanges were captured in viral social media videos and have sparked a city investigation.

title: North Carolina state trooper charged with murder of police captain
summary: Nekime Matu Oxendine accused of first-degree murder of Adam Bean, shot and killed in apparent domestic dispute
text: A North Carolina state highway patrol trooper has been charged with the murder of the captain of a county sheriff’s office. Cumberland county Capt Adam Bean was shot and killed on 27 March at a home in the town of Hope Mills. A grand jury on Tuesday indicted Nekime Matu Oxendine, 44, with first-degree murder in Bean’s death, and a judge ordered him held without bond pending the outcome of the case. The case represents an extremely rare instance of one law enforcement officer killing another. Research shows such cases are highly uncommon – and when they do occur, they are most often linked to inadvertent friendly fire or mistaken identity. Search warrants obtained by the North Carolina news station WTVD in May identified Oxendine as a North Carolina state highway patrol sergeant who, according to a witness, fired the shots. The witness, a Cumberland county sheriff’s office employee, told investigators Bean arrived home and became upset after seeing Oxendine’s truck parked there, according to the documents reported by the outlet. Investigators said Oxendine came out of the house carrying a gun and fired one shot into the ground. Moments later, he allegedly opened fire again, striking Bean with several shots. Bean was found lying on his back in the front yard. When police arrived, Tara Lynn Whitman – who reportedly had relationships with Bean and Oxendine – was performing CPR on Bean while Oxendine remained nearby. Officials said Bean was pronounced dead at the scene. Court filings from state investigators indicate the deadly encounter came after years of mounting tension involving Bean, Oxendine and their relationships with Whitman. Investigators said Oxendine had shown persistent jealousy and insecurity over the years concerning Whitman’s connection with Bean. Oxendine remains on administrative leave. Bean had served with the Cumberland county sheriff’s office for 20 years. His survivors include his son, parents and two siblings. Bean was honored on Wednesday when he posthumously received a merit award recognizing his service and lasting contributions to the sheriff’s office. In a Facebook post on Wednesday, the sheriff’s office wrote that Bean’s “efforts helped strengthen the agency’s ability to recruit, retain, and support highly qualified personnel while contributing directly to the continued effectiveness of public safety operations throughout Cumberland”, adding “his legacy continues through the many contributions he made to this agency and the people he served”.

title: Los Angeles to memorialize late mountain lion P-22 with sculpture in Griffith Park
summary: The wild feline made its home in the park before being euthanized in 2022 after showing signs of declining health
text: The city of Los Angeles will memorialize its most famous mountain lion with a bronze sculpture at Griffith Park, the 4,200-acre (1,700-hectare) stretch of land the cougar once roamed. Known as “P-22”, the number assigned by the team of biologists that first identified him, the lion gained national fame after photographer Steve Winter captured an iconic image of him prowling through Griffith Park with the Hollywood sign in the background. The sculpture, by Los Angeles artist Adam Matano, will be installed at the park’s visitor center, according to the National Wildlife Federation, which championed the project through its Safe LA Cougars campaign. Matano’s interest in how wild animals navigate the encroachment of our growing cities dates back to his teen years, he said. He grew up in Rhode Island, surrounded by empty lots. But by the time he reached his teen years, they had been developed into homes. “I love my favorite hiking spots,” Matano said. “But I kept thinking, ‘what happens to the animals?’” His sculpture shows a muscular P-22 stepping down from one podium to a second, more freeform and rocky pedestal. The rear podium contains a series of panels depicting local wildlife navigating the city environment – a mule deer crouching through a broken fence, a coyote ambling along against a backdrop of downtown LA, a raccoon and a gray fox in front of the Atwater bridge and the 5 freeway. “It’s about how you can’t contain nature,” Matano said. “Most people would think it woud be impossible for a mountain lion to live inside the city. But P-22 showed it is possible to co-exist. We should include nature when we design our cities.” He made a point of portraying P-22 with the GPS radio collar that enabled biologists to study him. “I think the radio collar is kind of misunderstood,” Matano said, noting that geolocation has become one of the most important tools available for understanding how wildlife moves across the landscape, offering insight into how to stitch portions of the fragmented natural world back together. “If we don’t want to see the collars, then we need to do better with our wildlife,” Matano said. “It’s really important that we understand where these animals are going and how they’re living.” Matano tried to capture the “idea of the wild entering Los Angeles and awakening the city to the nature already within it”, he said in a statement. He aimed to transform P-22 “into a king not because he dominated the territory but rather because he lived according to his own nature and captured the heart of a city”. The project was paid for with private philanthropy. The GPS-collared lion attracted a devoted following in Los Angeles, where his moves often became the subject of local news coverage. Likely born in the Santa Monica mountains, P-22 had to cross about 10 lanes of traffic on LA’s famously gridlocked freeways to make his home in Griffith Park. That feat became a driving force behind the Wallis Annenberg wildlife crossing, which is slated to open in December. It will become the world’s largest wildlife crossing, and promises to improve genetic diversity in the Santa Monica mountains, where cougars show signs of inbreeding. Wildlife officials euthanized P-22 in December of 2022, after he attacked a leashed dog and began showing signs of declining health, likely precipitated by a vehicle strike. They estimated his age at 12 years old.

title: Trump ally resigns from post leading inquiry into alleged conspiracy against president
summary: Joe diGenova led investigation focused on intelligence assessment that Russia interfered in 2016 election
text: A longtime ally of Donald Trump resigned from his post leading a Department of Justice investigation into whether former law enforcement and intelligence officials conspired against the Republican president. “Sometimes people want things done faster and that’s all you can do,” Joe diGenova told the Guardian on Thursday. He appeared to be referring to concerns among other Trump loyalists that the president’s retribution cases were not moving quickly enough. “The bottom line is it takes a long time to make good cases, and you simply have to work at it,” he added. “All you can do is do the best you can under the circumstances.” The departure injects instant tumult into an investigation targeting former government officials who have investigated Trump over the last decade, including in connection with Russian interference in the 2016 presidential election and his retention of classified documents at his Mar-a-Lago estate in Palm Beach, Florida. The Florida-based investigation has proceeded in fits and starts since its inception a year ago, with its contours loosely defined, though it had shown recent signs of activity with new subpoenas demanding testimony before a federal grand jury. While retribution by the justice department against Trump’s perceived adversaries has been one of the president’s highest priorities, diGenova’s comments hint at internal dissent and disagreement over the cases. He declined to say exactly why he resigned. “I’m not going to make any comments about indictments or anything else,” diGenova said. “When you’ve been a prosecutor as long as I have you know how to make cases, and it takes time. And that’s just part of the process. And sometimes that works out, and sometimes it doesn’t.” The justice department sent the Guardian a statement after this article was published: “We are grateful to Joe diGenova for his many years of service to the Department. The Attorney General thanks him for his work these past five months alongside the great team of experienced prosecutors in the Southern District of Florida, led by US Attorney Jason Reding Quiñones.” During the first Trump administration, diGenova was a legal adviser to John Solomon, a conservative journalist who has played an official role in White House efforts to push the conspiracy allegations. In an interview later with the New York Post, diGenova responded to criticism of his management of the investigation by saying: “If you want indictments where there’s no evidence, you have an ethical problem.” The 81-year-old diGenova served as the US attorney for the District of Columbia during the Reagan administration. A close Trump ally, he was brought back to the justice department in April and given responsibility for an investigation aimed at trying to establish a conspiracy against Trump. DiGenova had previously asked the then US attorney general, Pam Bondi, to appoint him to the job and had openly and repeatedly claimed Trump was the victim of an intelligence community conspiracy. But five months later, no charges have been brought, and it remains unclear whether any will be, or what information has been gathered to support any basis for the idea of a plot against Trump by the government officials who investigated him. The investigation has focused intensely on one of Trump’s chief grievances: a US intelligence community assessment that Russia had interfered on his behalf in the 2016 presidential election. The president and some of his supporters have long decried that conclusion as a “deep state” plot to undermine the legitimacy of his win. Multiple government investigations, including by a justice department special counsel and by the department’s own inspector general, have concluded that Russia interfered in sweeping fashion to help get Trump elected. The year-long investigation had proceeded in fits and starts well before diGenova’s appointment, which was announced soon after a career national security prosecutor who had been playing a key role in the investigation was replaced on the inquiry after raising doubts about its legal viability. The Associated Press contributed reporting

title: Company hired for Trump’s reflecting pool makeover reportedly admits flaws in plan
summary: Atlantic Industrial Coatings was given $14.7m no-bid contract and its findings contradict president’s claims of vandalism
text: The company hired to renovate the Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool has acknowledged that “human oversight” and flaws in the repair plan caused the newly installed blue liner to peel and tear, according to documents reviewed by the New York Times that challenge Donald Trump’s repeated claims of vandalism. The president has repeatedly said vandals armed with knives or box cutters were responsible for tearing apart the pool’s “American flag blue” liner. But documents reviewed by the Times show that Atlantic Industrial Coatings, the company awarded the renovation contract, blamed its own execution of the repair work and a flawed design plan. The justice department has charged several people with vandalizing the pool in early July, but prosecutors began moving to dismiss those cases on 31 July. A federal court filing said information later supplied by the interior department showed the damage was caused by a flawed installation and the rush to finish the project ahead of the country’s 250th anniversary celebrations on 4 July, not vandalism. The White House referred questions about the contractor’s report to the interior department. But in a statement, White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers said: “President Trump promised to make DC safe and beautiful, and he’s delivering.” A spokesperson for the interior department did not directly address the report, but blamed “major vandalism” for the damage. In a statement, the spokesperson said Atlantic was “contractually obligated” to remedy the repairs and was “well on its way to doing so”. Atlantic Industrial Coatings did not immediately return a request for comment. Atlantic first acknowledged its mistakes in a 14 August report and provided additional details in early September, according to the documents. As a result of “human oversight”, the company said crews failed to spray enough primer to properly bond the liner’s layers in certain places. The company also said the design spelled out in the contract called for two chemicals to be used in separate layers of the liner even though the products ultimately proved incompatible. The chemical sprayed on top became hotter than the material below it could tolerate, causing the material underneath to blister and separate. Atlantic said it had not anticipated that reaction because combining the two products in that manner was “very uncommon”. Virginia-based Atlantic was awarded a $14.7m no-bid contract to repaint and waterproof the pool’s concrete floor in spring of this year. The approach had not previously been tested and was designed in part by the general manager of one of Trump’s golf clubs, according to the Times. The renovation was carried out on an accelerated schedule as the administration pushed to have the Reflecting Pool completed before the nation’s 250th birthday on 4 July. Atlantic has said it would repair the pool again under the project’s warranty. Last month, Trump acknowledged the renovation had been rushed and that the contractor made mistakes, though he has not backed off his claims that vandals were responsible for much of the damage. Writing on Truth Social, the president said the contractor had taken shortcuts while racing to complete the project for its 4 July opening. “As with many jobs, there was also some contractor error done by rushing the job,” he wrote, claiming that the damage caused by those mistakes was limited to “a very small area” and was “relatively inconsequential”.

title: Republican seeking to implicate Abdul El-Sayed over 9/11 voted twice against benefits for first responders
summary: Mike Rogers has also helped kill other bills that would have provided healthcare to responders and survivors
text: Mike Rogers, a Michigan Republican US Senate candidate, has sought in recent weeks to create controversy over old tweets his Democratic opponent, Abdul El-Sayed posted about 9/11. He has for example, falsely suggested El-Sayed, who is Muslim, said the US deserved the attack. But, as critics have noted, Rogers has twice voted against healthcare and other benefits for 9/11 first responders and survivors, congressional records show. He has also helped kill other bills that would have provided benefits and healthcare to first responders nationwide. Rogers, a former member of Congress, is vying for Michigan’s open US Senate seat in a tight race that could decide control of Congress during the next session. Rogers was among Republicans who voted against the 2010 James Zadroga Act to fund healthcare for 9/11 first responders and survivors, which was used in part to treat and monitor 40,000 people who worked in toxic conditions in the attack’s aftermath. The bills’ funding also helped treat responders for more than 50 types of cancer linked to exposures at Ground Zero. In committee, Rogers argued it “jeopardizes the financial health of the United States”. Rogers was joined by 156 other Republicans who voted against it, largely over its $5.1bn price tag, but 17 GOP members broke from the party and supported it. The final package passed the House over Rogers’ vote. That drew sharp criticism this week from John Feal, a 9/11 first responder who has advocated and lobbied for legislation supporting benefit programs, and who spent 11 weeks in the hospital after a steel beam fell on his foot at ground zero. Part of his foot was amputated. Feal told the Guardian he personally discussed the Zadroga legislation with Rogers on Congress’s floor during committee debate in which Feal testified. Feal said Rogers told him first responders’ health issues were a “New York problem” and asked: “Where is the money to help them going to come from?” He called Rogers’ opposition to 9/11 first responder benefits “a betrayal”. “Here’s the thing: Republicans like Mike Rogers love cops and firefighters until one gets shot or burned in a fire and can’t do his job,” Feal said. “That’s their playbook. They say: ‘You’re a hero. Oh, wait, you’re sick? You’re a drain on the municipality and the federal government. Get out of here.’” In response to the Guardian, the Rogers campaign said: “Any attempt to distract from Abdul making Hasan [Piker] the centerpiece of his campaign is incredibly disrespectful to the thousands of Americans who lost their lives that day.” Alyssa Brouillet, a spokesperson for the Rogers campaign, pointed to a 2019 comment the popular Twitch streamer made in which he said “America deserved 9/11”. (Piker has since apologized and walked back the comments soon after, stating that they were a poor attempt at satire. El-Sayed called the comments “dumb” and disavowed them. ) The revelation comes after Rogers sent an email to supporters criticizing El-Sayed over his 9/11 comments, and appeared to lie about seeing Osama bin Laden’s body. In a bold-typed section of the email, Rogers wrote: “I saw the dead body of Osama bin Laden with my own eyes, knowing that together, we had delivered justice for America.” But Rogers was not in Pakistan when Bin Laden was killed by US special forces, nor was he in the White House Situation Room, where then president Barack Obama and senior administration officials followed the raid. Republicans faced enormous backlash in 2010 for their votes against the Zagroda legislation. Feal at the time told CBS News: “Whatever member of Congress voted against this bill, whether Republican or Democrat, should go to jail for manslaughter.” In 2002, Rogers voted against adding additional funding for veterans’ healthcare and first responders to a bill that compensated NYC schools for 9/11-related expenses. In 2011, Rogers voted for a homeland security appropriations bill that was controversial over its deep cuts to funding for state and local first responders, as well as terrorism prevention funding. Several Republicans voted against it because of those issues. In 2013 and 2014, Rogers voted against amendments for budget legislation that included billions in funding for first responders. And in 2013 he voted against a proposal to protect pensions for first responders. Henry Yanez, a retired Michigan firefighter, now a city council member in Sterling Heights, a suburb of Detroit, who has endorsed El-Sayed, was among those who went to New York City to support their fire departments in the 9/11 attack’s wake. He criticized Rogers for his votes. “When you’re talking about the health and safety of our first responders, and now you’re going to kick the can down the road, you know – that’s a problem as far as I’m concerned,” Yanez said. “Mike Rogers – shame on him.” Yanez said he was especially surprised because other Republicans in Michigan have supported first responders, and Rogers was an FBI agent. “He should get it,” Yanez said. Feal said he believes Rogers’ opposition to the bills is disqualifying. “Many members of Congress think they’re untouchable until they get humbled and get beat in an election,” Feal said. “Rogers is not invincible, and he’s just in this for himself.”
