title: Russia targets Kyiv petrol stations for first time with jet-powered drones
summary: Three facilities in two days struck as bombardment of Ukraine’s capital enters new phase of intensity
text: Petrol stations in Kyiv have been hit by jet-powered drones in a wave of targeted Russian attacks as the bombardment of Ukraine’s capital enters a new phase of intensity. At least two people were killed and 12 injured in strikes on two petrol stations on Friday morning, according to the city’s mayor, Vitali Klitschko. The rush-hour strikes follow a similar attack on a petrol station on Thursday, the first of its kind in the capital. At the Ukrnafta petrol station in the Pochaina neighbourhood in northern Kyiv, bystanders said three people had been injured in Friday’s blast – the manager of a nearby car wash, his wife and the driver of a passing car. The blown-out vehicle was stranded by the side of the road, its windows shattered and seats spattered in blood. Witnesses said they had heard two explosions, and local authorities later said Russia had carried out a double-tap attack on the facility. “This is probably one of the most difficult periods of the war because life is just like on a rollercoaster,” said Anastasiia Demchenko, 30, who works at a delivery company opposite the petrol station. “It feels like life is on the edge.” All three strikes targeted petrol stations operated by Ukrnafta, a state-owned oil and natural gas extraction company. Sergiy Fedorenko, the acting head of Naftogaz, Ukrnafta’s parent company, said: “There is, and can be, no military objective behind such attacks. This is terror directed at the civilian population, at peaceful people.” A list of 18 petrol stations in Kyiv expected to be hit by Russian drones started circulating on Telegram on Wednesday. The three struck so far were on the list. At the other station hit on Friday, in Desnianskyi district, one of the most densely populated parts of the capital, the manager of a nearby car wash said it had been a miracle that no one had died in the blast. Fedir Lesovin said the air-raid siren had given the petrol station workers time to run to a nearby shelter, and that a customer waiting outside his business saw the incoming drone and also ran to safety. Russia has increased its attacks on Ukrainian petrol stations in recent months. Facilities in the east and south of the country have been repeatedly targeted, but this week’s attacks mark the first time that strikes against a vital part of daily life have been brought to the capital. Ukraine has also targeted Russian oil infrastructure. Its special forces said this week that they had struck facilities at the Caspian Sea port of Makhachkala. Kyiv has been pounded by daily drone and missile strikes since late August, at a time when Ukraine is running low on Patriot interceptors. A brief reprieve for the visit of the US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff over the weekend ended on Monday. The petrol station attacks happened as Volodymyr Zelenskyy was on an overseas trip intended to drum up international support and aid before what is expected to be a difficult winter. On Thursday the Ukrainian president met Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, who offered support to help boost Ukraine’s drone stocks. Additional reporting by Illia Dyadik

title: They drive toward tornadoes. We went with them to see how their work could save lives
summary: Tornadoes kill hundreds each decade in the US. These researchers are investigating why some storms produce twisters – despite the fatal risks
text: On a narrow road in southern Iowa, my phone shrieked. Tornado warning. Take shelter now in a basement or an interior room on the lowest floor of a sturdy building. Again, the alert sounded. Then again. As if shelter were a choice. I peered through a peephole of scratched glass, wedged into the lead storm-chasing truck with tornado researchers Josh Wurman and Karen Kosiba. On either side of us, only fields. No houses. No basements. No sturdy buildings. The dark belly of a storm dragged across a horizon gone an eerie green. For tornado chasers, it was a near perfect sky. My son Cheney, a photojournalist, was somewhere behind us in a rental car alongside two other research vehicles. The convoy was strung out across miles of highway. He had been tracking my location, but now I had lost cell service. I couldn’t reach him. I kept dialing. No answer. When a call finally went through, Cheney told me the wind was driving the rain so hard the road had disappeared. “I’m scared,” he said. Blinded, he had turned one way, then the other. Finally, he stopped. Either direction, he feared, could put him in a tornado’s path. Cheney was no stranger to danger. He has covered Ukraine during wartime, spent a New Year’s Eve alone in a car reporting on Chicago homicides, and crisscrossed the country documenting violent weather, including the devastating 2021 tornado in Mayfield, Kentucky. I hadn’t heard him express fear since childhood. Then he said it again. “I’m scared. I don’t know what to do.” *** About 1,200 tornadoes strike the United States every year. Between 2020 and 2025, they killed roughly 410 people, injured nearly 3,800 and caused about $8.5bn in reported property damage. The tornado map is changing too. A 2024 study found 25% fewer moderate-or-stronger tornadoes in the western US and 12% more in the east, where mobile homes are more prevalent, basements to get to safety are scarcer, and twisters more likely to strike at night. Sometimes the change from ordinary to deadly takes only minutes. Several months earlier, physician Jason Persoff had told me about chasing near Joplin, Missouri, in May 2011. A little after 5pm, he and his partner began looking for hotel rooms, figuring they were done for the day. “Suddenly, it was as if someone vomited on the radar,” Persoff remembered. “It was incredible.” A violent tornado seemed to emerge from the sky almost fully formed. Its sound lodged deep in Persoff’s body. “I felt irrational fear,” he said. “Like a primal warning.” They pulled over to help stranded truckers as police arrived. Persoff told one officer he was a physician. “I hope you don’t work at St John’s,” the officer told him. “That hospital’s been destroyed.” “That’s still one of the most terrifying things I’ve ever heard,” Persoff said. More than 150 people were killed in that tornado. Wurman, whose team I traveled with, is among the researchers trying to understand why some storms produce tornadoes while others do not, and what tornado winds do close to the ground – knowledge that could improve warnings and help engineers design buildings to withstand them. But the systems built to study and forecast tornadoes are under strain. In the first four months of 2025, the National Weather Service lost roughly 13% of its workforce – more than 560 employees – to firings, retirements, resignations and attrition. By the 2026 storm season, the agency was hiring again, but staffing gaps remained, and some stations were unable to maintain the twice-daily weather-balloon launches on which forecasters and researchers rely. Scientists I spoke with said they had lost confidence in forecast guidance. Chris Weiss of Texas Tech, who led a parallel chase team with the National Severe Storms Laboratory, was blunt: “I don’t remember when a suite of models has performed as poorly as this year.” Frustrated by the blurred, distant view from fixed-site radar, Wurman invented the Doppler on Wheels – mobile radar laboratories known as DOWs – three decades ago. Filling one with diesel costs about $1,000, and that is the inexpensive part: the greater investment lies in the trucks, trained graduate students and experienced crews that take years to build. But funding has become more uncertain. By the end of this field season, neither Wurman’s team nor Weiss’s could count on support for the next one. Cessily Skinner, whose family has lost two homes to tornadoes in west-central Georgia, closely monitors every approaching storm. Now the cuts give her another reason to fear: “As someone who lived through a storm with all the data in place,” she said, “it’s terrifying to think, ‘OK, so now we really are guessing.’” *** With Cheney still on the line, a team member plotted his location against the storm. The radar could see what he could not. A tornado we were tracking was east of him and moving east. Cheney should be safe, she said, as long as he stayed put and waited it out. I repeated this to him. As we spoke, the rain loosened. The sky lifted. The road reappeared. Cheney pressed the gas and began closing the distance between us. The second radar truck arrived first. Fifteen long minutes later, Cheney’s rental car came into view. Relief and disappointment arrived together. The convoy was whole again. But the day had yielded none of the data the scientists had come for. Several tornadoes touched down across the region that afternoon. None crossed the roads where our instruments were waiting. The storms left behind a sky ribboned with dark clouds. Some team members stood outside the trucks and applauded its beauty, lifting their phones for photographs. Wurman and Kosiba were not among them. They were already studying the models, deciding where the team should spend the night to be best positioned for morning. *** Tornadoes offer enough spectacle to draw film-makers, thrill-seekers, and carloads of chasers with cameras. But scientists who chase for data need more than drama. They need geometry: an open horizon, a road in and a road out, a storm that forms where the instruments can reach it. Even when everything lines up, a mobile radar crew can spend weeks following one promising storm after another, only to watch each weaken and dissolve before the instruments capture the measurements they came for. Why do they keep doing it? For data analyst Paul Robinson, the pull started with an image on television: Dorothy clutching Toto, calling for Auntie Em as a black twister writhed in the distance. “The Wizard of Oz is still my favorite movie tornado,” he said. “For me, it captures the feeling.” Growing up in West Virginia, he began keeping a notebook, recording the weather whenever it turned severe. But 31 May 1985, turned that interest into purpose. Everyone on this team seems to carry a storm they cannot forget. Robinson’s was not a single tornado but an outbreak: 43 twisters tearing across Ohio, Pennsylvania, New York and Ontario, killing 89 people. “That convinced me that maybe I could do some good by going into tornado research,” Robinson said. Research scientist Trevor White’s defining storm came later, on 24 May 2016, near Dodge City, Kansas. “Every chaser and their mother came out,” he recalled. “We were on it from the time it was a small cumulus cloud. I had never seen a storm that could effortlessly produce tornadoes. I counted three on the ground at the same time.” In two hours, a dozen tornadoes formed beneath the supercell. It was nearly perfect in the way that mattered most: no one died, and the tornadoes remained mostly over open country. But even experienced researchers cannot always remain beyond a tornado’s reach. In 2013, veteran tornado researcher Tim Samaras was killed near El Reno, Oklahoma, along with his son Paul and colleague Carl Young. Samaras was Wurman’s friend. Wurman’s team was tracking the same tornado that day. Asked by a reporter whether the deaths made him reconsider his work, Wurman noted that covering extreme weather “isn’t dangerous statistically”. Samaras, he said, was among the most responsible chasers he knew. Wurman would not speculate about what had gone wrong but said his own team would review its procedures. Wurman and his colleagues then returned to the data, reconstructing the motion of the nearly impossible-to-see subvortex that had overtaken Samaras and his team. He pursues the sky at its most theatrical without surrendering to drama himself. He would rather leave a question open than force an answer the data cannot support. “I wish this research were more of a eureka thing,” Wurman said, “but it’s not. We can’t do laboratory-type experiments. We can’t put 10,000 patients into a study. Meteorology is horrible that way. We’re trying to understand what’s special about the circumstances where tornadoes form and what it looks like when they do. But we can’t control the environment.” “Every time we’re in a disaster area, I carry with me the trauma of people who survive it,” White told me. “I don’t know if we can do anything to ease the impact of that experience, but I’ll never stop searching. The only thing worse than a human tragedy is a human tragedy where you can’t learn anything.” *** A mile outside Good Hope, Illinois, the deployment order came. Our truck slid to a halt on the shoulder of a two-lane road slick with rain. Robinson jumped out to unleash the radar dish. It began sweeping the sky, each rotation shuddering through the vehicle. Back in the driver’s seat, he talked to himself – “c’mon, c’mon” – as he worked the controls to lower a stabilizing pad into the mud, trying to keep the vehicle’s right side from sinking. He kept the left wheels on the pavement, he told me later, in case we needed to move fast toward – or away from – a tornado. In the back, White balanced one keyboard on his lap and kept several others within reach. Four screens glowed in front of him. “Frustrating,” Robinson murmured. “We’re getting data, but I want to see it; I want to see the fury.” The horizon closed around us. From the front passenger seat, I watched a low shelf of black clouds over the cornfields, its ragged underside reaching down in unfinished gestures. The walkie-talkie crackled, then Wurman’s voice came through. “What do you see?” No one answered immediately. White and Robinson studied the screens and conferred quietly in technical shorthand. They were looking for a hook curling in the rain, a couplet tightening in the wind field, some sign that the atmosphere had made up its mind. The clouds kept darkening. The dish kept turning. The truck kept shuddering. Robinson waited through one scan, then another, watching new data appear on the screens over White’s shoulder. Finally he spoke, his voice tight. “It’s falling apart, isn’t it?” After a few more minutes, Wurman confirmed he saw the same. He called out a new waypoint and then we were speeding again down a country road, pursuing the uneasy hope at the center of this work: a storm dangerous enough to teach but merciful enough to spare. *** When things align, the value of a single intercept can endure for years. On 18 May 2013, the team captured data from an EF4 tornado near Rozel, Kansas. It remained on the ground for about 30 minutes, long enough for the researchers to hold position and gather unusually rich measurements. “That gave us a chance to dig in deep,” Kosiba said. “And that data is still being used by engineers today. That’s why you have to keep going out, even with the misses. We’re in it for the long haul.” A 2024 study co-authored by Wurman and Kosiba analyzed mobile-radar wind profiles from 36 tornadoes. Those findings helped shape new national standards for designing buildings to withstand tornado winds, showing the potential impact of readings collected in the path of storms. This is the scale on which science advances: one measurement clarifying another, a dataset enduring long after the tornado itself disappears. Behind every chase is a life forced to accommodate the forecast. We had driven 2,000 miles in three days, from dawn until after dark, crossing and recrossing North Dakota, Minnesota, Wisconsin, Iowa and Illinois. Wurman’s team had gone weeks without the intercept they needed. Weiss’s team had endured an equally disappointing season. “We put in the same effort for fewer results,” Weiss told me. “We have lives and families, and we’re making a lot of sacrifices. So when it doesn’t work out, it eats at you.” White has a soft spot for hummingbirds. He keeps several feeders at home, and goes to great lengths to find someone to refill them when he’s gone. His absence is measured out in sugar water. He carries a small stuffed hummingbird on the road. “I told my wife a week ago we’d be home tomorrow. Instead, we are still out here, and there’s no end in sight,” he said. “But there’s something fundamental about this research that draws me in. The best version of me is the version that does this work.” Before this trip, I had imagined storm chasing as a form of appetite, the desire to see the most violent thing the sky could make. I hadn’t understood its strange rhythm: tedious hours beneath empty skies, then sudden races down country roads, decisions pressed into seconds, and moments of stark fear. The work demands patience when nothing happens and clear judgment when everything happens at once. Inside the truck, it looked less like appetite and more like devotion: painstaking, deliberate, largely invisible. In a culture that rewards quick verdicts and emphatic claims, these scientists let the sky contradict them. They reverse direction and answer to evidence rather than personal conviction. That discipline feels radical. Years from now, the data they gather may become a stronger roof, an earlier warning, hospital walls that hold. The researchers may never know whose lives their persistence reaches. That last night with Wurman’s team, I wrote three lines in my notebook: We went storm chasing. Nothing happened. We learned a lot.

title: How Ron DeSantis politicized Florida’s higher education by placing his loyalists at the top
summary: Term-limited, hard-right governor instituted an ideological infiltration of universities by placing allies in powerful posts
text: In less than four months’ time, Ron DeSantis, Florida’s hard-right governor, will be termed out of office, and what critics saw as his relentless eight-year, “anti-woke” assault on higher education in the state will finally be over. But while DeSantis himself will be gone, numerous hand-picked loyalists will remain in positions of power to protect his ideological makeover of universities and colleges. The latest, Alex Kelly, the governor’s former deputy chief of staff, and Florida commerce secretary, was named last week as the sole finalist in Pensacola state college’s search for a new president, at least the 12th close DeSantis ally to win such a plum post. If he is paid the same salary as Edward Meadows, the college’s outgoing president, Kelly’s earnings will soar from $186,000 at the commerce department to more than $353,000, according to the Miami Herald. DeSantis’s two terms were marked at regular intervals with unprecedented attacks on the established order, notably his “hostile takeover” of New College, the former liberal arts college; a push to end campus diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) programs and stifle free speech, struck down in July by a federal judge. There was also a steady drum beat of conservative Republican acolytes placed controversially in key university leadership roles, many with no previous experience of higher education administration. They include Jeanette Nunez, DeSantis’s former lieutenant governor, installed despite protests at Florida International University; and Marva Johnson, a lobbyist, businesswoman and tight political ally nicknamed “Maga Marva”, who last year became president of Florida A&M, the state’s largest historically Black public university, over fierce objection from students, faculty, alumni and four board trustees. Republican former state representatives Mel Ponder, Tommy Gregory, Fred Hawkins and John Temple all secured lucrative presidencies at state colleges; as did three of DeSantis’s former education commissioners, Anastasios Kamoutsas, Manny Diaz and Richard Corcoran. All were selected by university boards of trustees and confirmed by the state university system’s board of governors, a 17-member panel of which 14 are direct DeSantis appointees. Ray Rodrigues, chancellor of the state system, is another long-serving Republican politician. William Johnson, Florida director of PEN America, the free expression advocacy group that has challenged many of DeSantis’s policy changes and political maneuvers, said his administration had “made public education an apparatus of the state”. He said: “Political influence over higher education isn’t new. Rick Scott [DeSantis’s predecessor] did something similar, but the difference is the scale and the explicit ideological goals behind it. “It’s been this gigantic sea change on how higher ed is run. One of the key differences between DeSantis and everyone else is basically that you know these appointments have no experience in higher ed, so we can infer their main skill set is simply to follow the administration’s ideological mandates. “I can’t speak to the cronyism aspects. What I am interested in is cross-checking how many folks have come from any kind of higher ed background and understanding of academic freedom and has that ever been the focus of any of his appointees? “That’s what I’m curious about. And I would imagine that the answer is very few, if any.” Amanda Phalin, an associate professor in the University of Florida’s school of business, experienced first-hand the state’s approach to university hires as a faculty representative (not appointed by the governor) on the state board from 2023 to 2025. She remains outraged by its rejection of Santa Ono, an experienced academic chosen as UF president last year by the university’s own trustees, after his earlier advocacy for DEI initiatives came to light. “My position and opinion about the state university system changed pretty dramatically after the despicable and borderline insane treatment of Dr Ono by the board of governors,” she said. “You had members of the board of governors who were going against the choice of the board of trustees. They were all DeSantis appointees, but they were having sort of an internal squabble. “The two years I worked on the board of governors, I approached everything in 100% good faith. I had, and still have, strong political disagreements with folks, but I did my best to take them at their word, hear their concerns and really try to work with them constructively and productively. “What I saw during the whole Santa Ono debacle is that these people do not actually have the best interest of the state university system at heart. For them, the project is either ideological, or about personal power, or both.” DeSantis has never made a secret of his desire to impose his Florida “blueprint” nationally, and his legacy, Phalin said, could ultimately become other red states following his lead in injecting more politics and dollars into higher education, and tightening their grip on how it is run by appointing faithful followers to key roles. “The way the state university system of Florida is structured is that each university has a board of trustees, the governor controls who’s on those boards of trustees, and the boards of trustees ultimately answer to the board of governors, and the governor also controls everyone on the board of governors, except the student representative and faculty representative,” she said. “So it’s not even about the presidencies. That is almost beside the point. What DeSantis has really done is, in a behind-the-scenes structural way, politicized the entire system, top to bottom, in terms of its governance structure.”

title: ‘I think of him every year’: remembering those lost in 9/11, 25 years later
summary: Guardian readers share stories of the friends, colleagues and mentors whose lives they continue to honor decades after the attacks
text: The September 11, 2001 attacks killed 2,977 people, resulting in the largest loss of life caused by a foreign attack on American soil. Twenty-five years later, Guardian readers who lost friends and loved ones are continuing to honor their memories through stories about their lives, relationships and the moments they shared. Christopher Allen, 69, a retired estate manager from Niantic, Connecticut, remembers Jeremy “Caz” Carrington. Allen said he and his wife, Kim, met Carrington at the now-closed Santa Fe Junction bar and restaurant in East Hampton, New York. The men bonded as fellow British expatriates, talking about soccer, darts and London. “He was a portly sort of guy but moved quick, thought even quicker and was generally the life and soul of the party,” Allen said. Carrington worked for Cantor Fitzgerald, a firm which lost more people on 9/11 than any other organization. Six months after the attacks, Allen attended a celebration of Carrington’s life in East Hampton. Family members came from the UK, and friends and relatives shared stories about him. “The Celebration of Life service was not traditional or mournful; it was hilarious,” Allen said. “He really did live life to the fullest and we were all very grateful to have known him.” At the gathering, Allen met Carrington’s mother, Kate, and discovered she had been his primary school teacher years earlier, when he knew her as Miss Ross. They stayed in touch, exchanging jokes and gardening ideas until her death. In Allen’s words, he is in awe that such “a wonderful friendship started from such a horrific tragedy.” For Cheryl Ann of Santa Monica, California, the person she lost was a friend named Caroline, whom she described as a successful Disney executive and a mentor. Cheryl, who had pursued photography after moving from New Jersey to Los Angeles, said Caroline admired her work and treated her as an equal while she was working as an executive assistant. “We became personal friends and she invited me into her home and her life,” Cheryl said. “With genuine enthusiasm she offered to mentor me.” On September 11, Cheryl woke to messages telling her to turn on CNN. She had friends, godchildren, business associates and other loved ones in the region and feared for people she could not reach by phone. “I didn’t sleep; I could barely eat; life as I knew it was over,” she said. Later, Cheryl saw her friend Caroline’s name on a passenger list shown on the news. She initially hoped it was someone else with the same name, but a mutual friend confirmed it was the Caroline they knew. “It annihilated me. I don’t know any other way to express the depth of the pain of the loss. She had a beautiful light that lit up any room she entered,” Cheryl said. “She literally glowed, as beautiful on the outside as on the inside.” Steve S, whose name was changed for privacy, remembers John P Sammartino as one of his best friends. The two met at university, Steve said, and Sammartino later served as best man at his wedding. Though their careers caused them to drift apart, they continued getting together to watch football matches and make homemade beer with college friends. Steve was involved in computer-related cleanup work at the Pentagon after the attacks. Late on 12 September, he said, his then-wife called to tell him Sammartino had been on the plane that crashed into the Pentagon. “I was crushed,” Steve said. “From feeling lucky that I wasn’t directly affected to being involved changed my outlook on 9/11.” Years later, Steve continues to visit his friend’s grave. Sammartino had been an electrical engineer, and Steve sometimes thinks about the advances his friend never saw. “He’d get a kick out of modern cellphone technology,” he said. Alison K, whose name was also changed for privacy, is a 47-year-old artist who said that her life was changed by a man she never actually spoke to. In 2000, she moved to New York City to pursue a master’s degree. On her way to class, she would pass a small fire station where “there was often a firefighter out front washing down a truck, chatting with his co-workers. He had a big bushy moustache and his arms were covered with tattoos.” The two would exchange smiles and waves, and his friendly demeanor helped bring her comfort as a young student in a strange new city. Weeks after the attacks, classes resumed and she passed by the fire station again, where she saw a paper taped to the station door. “It was my fireman, whose name had been Manny Mojica, and who was killed when responding to the tower emergency,” she said. “I think of him every year, and this past Christmas I was back in NYC for the first time in 15 years. I made a visit to the memorial and found his name on the plaque and silently thanked him for his welcoming smile and his service.” Songwriter Larry Dvoskin remembers Patrick “Paddy” Brown, a friend from Jivamukti Yoga classes who was a former marine and a captain with the New York City fire department’s Ladder 3 company. “He was truly a ‘man’s man’ long before the current craze of the manosphere,” Dvoskin said. “Instead, he was thoughtful, humble, and I found it humorous seeing him in spandex tights in my yoga classes.” Dvoskin said that at Brown’s funeral at St Patrick’s cathedral, he heard an account of Brown heading toward the second tower as it burned. Firefighters leaving the building warned him not to enter because it was too dangerous. Brown replied: “Are you fucking crazy? It’s my job to go in there!” Brown and his team then entered the building. “Those were the last words he is remembered by,” Dvoskin said. “‘It’s my job to go in there.’”

title: Hundreds of asylum seekers removed from UK to France have disappeared, say NGOs
summary: Rights groups say those missing after being deported under one in, one out deal include dozens of age-disputed children
text: Hundreds of asylum seekers including at least 41 age-disputed children who were removed to France under the “one in, one out” deal have disappeared, human rights organisations have said. The pilot scheme was hailed as “groundbreaking” by the former prime minister Keir Starmer when he and the French president, Emmanuel Macron, announced it in July 2025. Under a treaty drawn up for this agreement, it forcibly returns small-boat asylum seekers to France in exchange for others brought legally to the UK from France. The deal is due to expire on 1 October and at the moment it is not known what, if anything, will replace it. The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, is reportedly pushing for the deal to be extended and scaled up, and the French government has indicated it wants the scheme to be expanded Europe-wide rather than France having to accept small-boat returnees alone. One French politician told the Guardian that so far France’s overtures to other countries to take back a share of small-boat asylum seekers had received a negative response. About 1,400 small-boat arrivals have been returned to France since September 2025, just 4% of 32,000 who have crossed the Channel since the deal was signed. These figures do not include the significant minority who have come back to the UK a second time, some of whom are now living under the radar here. The UK and France amended the treaty to allow for people returning to the UK in lorries to be sent back to France a second time. At a meeting in parliament this week chaired by Mike German, a general rapporteur on asylum and migration policy for the parliamentary assembly of the Council of Europe, and Alex Sobel, the new chair of parliament’s joint committee on human rights, parliamentarians were told about the disappearances and other concerns about the scheme by NGO representatives working on the ground. Maddie Harris, the director of the Humans For Rights Network, said several NGOs had between them compiled a list of at least 41 age-disputed children and young people whom they claimed had been unlawfully returned to France. It is unlawful to detain lone children in adult immigration detention centres, and they are excluded from the one in, one out treaty. The Home Office disputed this and told the Guardian: “This is categorically untrue. Nobody has been returned to France where their age is in dispute. “Every detained person is advised of their right to legal representation and how they can obtain such representation within 24 hours of arrival at an immigration removal centre. Age assessments are carried out to maintain the integrity of our border, while ensuring those genuinely under 18 receive the appropriate support.” However, the prisons and detention Independent Monitoring Boards have reported that almost a hundred children had been identified as unlawfully detained as adults for the scheme. The IMBs’ interim chair, Jane Leech, attended the meeting and raised concerns that some people were being unlawfully detained for the scheme because the Home Office was “detaining more people than they can remove”. French politicians have told the Guardian that only 200 people forcibly returned to France were still in contact with the authorities there, with hundreds of others having gone underground in countries across Europe. The Guardian has interviewed dozens of returnees who are no longer in contact with the French authorities and are living underground in Europe. They say they have disappeared due to hostility from the French authorities, pressure to return to their home countries where they believe they will be unsafe, or the threat of being forced back to other European countries such as Bulgaria that they passed through on their journeys. Home Office sources said that what happened to people once they were returned to France was a matter for the French authorities. France’s interior ministry declined to comment on the disappearances. Harris said the forced return of lone children to France was “shameful”. She said: “We support many children detained under this scheme and attempt to secure their release. However, at least 41 children have been removed from the UK to France and their whereabouts is currently unknown. The vast majority of these children have experienced acute violence and exploitation and are now without protection somewhere in Europe.” Nihal Osman, a programme coordinator for Médecins Sans Frontières, told the parliamentary meeting that asylum seekers were returned to France from the UK in a “deeply concerning” condition, with many displaying severe psychological symptoms such as flashbacks, acute anxiety, self-harm, suicidal thoughts and psychological breakdown. “What we are witnessing is the accumulation of trauma on trauma,” she said. Sobel said he was “deeply concerned” about the ongoing securitisation of the French border to prevent asylum seekers crossing the Channel to the UK. “The French police are doing things it would be unacceptable for British police to do,” he said.

title: How a month-long competitive food tour is rewriting the story of Rio’s favelas
summary: ‘The doors that aren’t open to us in the rest of the city, we open for ourselves here,’ Maria Cristina de Sales says
text: Even at the age of nine, Maria Cristina de Sales knew exactly when to ask her mother’s colleagues at the slaughterhouse for a piece of the pig they were butchering: when they got close to the pork leg, her favourite part. When she grew up, Sales followed the path of many others from Brazil’s deprived north-east and moved south in search of better work opportunities. She arrived in Rio de Janeiro and, unable to afford a home in tourist-heavy south zone, moved to a favela further north. She crossed the city every day to work as a receptionist and secretary, but only really found her footing 15 years later when she and her husband opened a burger restaurant, inside the favela. “The doors that aren’t open to us in the rest of the city, we open for ourselves here,” said Sales, 39, inside her restaurant in Maré, a favela complex that emerged in the 1940s in a vast mangrove area, settled by workers who could not afford to live in – or had been evicted by the state from – the wealthier parts of the city. What usually dominates the headlines about Maré, a complex of 16 favelas home to 140,000 people, are problems such as poverty, armed drug traffickers and bloody police operations, but Sales’s restaurant has joined an effort to change that perception. From 1 October, local bars and restaurants will take part in a month-long competitive food trail made up entirely of Maré establishments, hoping to attract visitors from across the city who are often afraid to visit a favela. “We face prejudice simply for saying that we live in a favela, but there are a lot of good things here,” she said. Were it not for the surrounding alleys so narrow that sometimes only one person can pass at a time, the tangled web of electrical wires crowding the utility poles and the occasional young man riding a motorcycle with a rifle, Sales’s restaurant could be anywhere else in the city – a family-friendly, air-conditioned burger joint. The superhero-themed decor was a request by Sales’s sons, and includes a life-size Spider-Man. Her entry for the food trail will be, of course, a pork leg, made into burger named Peppa Pig. “It’s a reference to my story: a girl who came from the north-east, went through hell and is now here, proud and still fighting – just like many other people here in Maré,” she added. One sweet-and-slightly-spicy element of the dish – a pineapple jam with chilli and ginger – she learned to make at Casa das Mulheres da Maré, a centre set up by a local NGO, Redes da Maré, to support women and which organises the food trail, called Comida de Favela, or Favela Food. “When we improve the quality of life of a woman in Maré, we’re improving the whole community,” said Mariana Aleixo, 38, the centre’s coordinator, herself a chef who was born and raised in Maré and has worked in the kitchens of Rio’s luxury hotels, including the Copacabana Palace. The food trail is now in its fourth edition – the first was held in 2015 – and is one of four finalists in the Best Culinary Festival in Latin America category at the 2026 World Culinary Awards, which will announce the winners in October. The 16 restaurants – selected from more than 150 applicants, most of them Black-owned – receive management and marketing training and, starting this year, guidance on how to support customers who report sexual harassment. The winners, chosen by customer vote, receive cash prizes. Reflecting the origins of many residents or their ancestors, many of the dishes feature other references to north-eastern cuisine, such as the “North-eastern Explosion”, a pizza topped with cassava cream, coalho cheese – similar to halloumi – and carne de sol, a lightly salted cured beef usually fried in a clarified butter similar to ghee. “Gastronomy is the biggest economic sector in the community,” said Aleixo, noting that of the roughly 3,200 businesses in the area, about 1,200 are restaurants and bars. Aleixo said she had approached sponsors of other food festivals across the city and had never succeeded in securing their support. “I believe it’s because of prejudice against favelas,” she said. Although the aim is for visitors to experience the favela from a “perspective other than violence”, Aleixo acknowledges that some may witness something that the thousands of people who live there have to contend with: the occasional presence of armed drug traffickers. Police generally do not patrol favelas unless carrying out operations. The food trail has no connection to the criminals, who also do not interfere with its activities because they seem to understand that it benefits the community. “Some of the experiences we live through here are very violent, and we want the city to have access to that. Understanding that sense of indignation that residents often have is important so that people can build a different repertoire for thinking about public security in Rio,” she said. “Violence exists here just as it does in other parts of the city, but it does not define Maré entirely,” added Aleixo. Despite the invitation to outsiders – Favela Food’s social media pages often advertise shuttle vans to bring visitors from other parts of the city and take them back again – another aim is to encourage the circulation of people and money between the complex’s own favelas. While Sales’s burger restaurant is in the Parque União favela, the snack bar run by Beatriz Santos Antônio, 39, is in the Nova Holanda favela, a 15-minute walk away. Born in another city in Rio de Janeiro state, Antônio arrived in Maré 16 years ago because she could not afford to live elsewhere. She and her children went through periods of hunger, but neighbours helped them, and she drew on cooking skills learned from her mother to start selling cassava fritters. Her entry for the food trail consists of four elliptical fritters, a classic Brazilian bar snack that Antônio has taken to new heights: crisp on the outside and moist inside, filled with either roast beef or prawns with cream cheese. “I’ve come a long way,” said Antônio, smiling as she wiped away tears and made the final preparations for her first time taking part in Favela Food. “Today, these tears are no longer because of hunger. Today it’s a story of happiness and of being able to encourage other women to start their own businesses too. There is also a lot of happiness in the favela.”

title: Nation pauses to remember September 11 on 25th anniversary | First Thing
summary: Commemoration ceremonies to be held around the world for the nearly 3,000 killed in 2001 terror attack on US. Plus, JD Vance sets out his stall as heir to Donald Trump
text: Good morning. It is a sombre day for the nation as people gather to mourn and remember the nearly 3,000 victims of the attacks on September 11 2001, when 19 al-Qaida hijackers seized control of four airliners, slamming two of the planes into the World Trade Center, one into the Pentagon in Arlington, Virginia, and the fourth into a field in western Pennsylvania. We have comprehensive coverage of the anniversary, which will be marked by ceremonies around the world. There are stories of the day from people who were there. Stanley Praimnath and Brian Clark were two of only four individuals known to have survived above the impact zone in the south tower, and they spoke to our Washington bureau chief David Smith. Anna Sweeney Rossman was five when her mother, Amy Sweeney, a flight attendant, was killed onboard American Airlines flight 11, and she spoke to Ramon Antonio Vargas about how the events of that day have cast a shadow on her life. CIA veterans spoke to Robert Tait about the chaos and confusion in the agency as the unprecedented attacks unfolded, and Guardian readers have told us about how September 11 changed their lives. Jason Burke, our international security correspondent, writes that while al-Qaida leader Osama bin Laden may have shaken the world on 9/11, it is clear today his wider plans failed. But we also have to acknowledge that the world’s most powerful country responded to the worst terrorist attack in its history by inflicting terror of its own – around the world, and at home. This read from David Smith outlines how the day saw heroes emerge showing the best of America, and then the response of US governments left a dark legacy – Guantánamo Bay, the Abu Ghraib scandal – which continues to unfold to this day. Those who remember September 11 will never forget the haunting images of that day, including the missing people posters that were put up in the confusing aftermath of the collapse of the towers in New York. Captured by the photographer Phil Buehler, they will form part of a new exhibition, and some can be viewed here. As we look back on a day that reshaped our world, our thoughts remain with the victims, their families, and all those whose lives were irrevocably changed 25 years ago. In other news … Donald Trump’s promise of a $5,000 “Trump dividend” for every US citizen if Republicans retain control of the US Congress in November’s midterm elections has sparked incredulity and accusations of bribery. With his approval rating at a historic low, Trump brought down the curtain on the Republicans’ first ever midterm convention by pleading with supporters to do him “the biggest favor” and “pretend” they are voting for him in November’s US elections. JD Vance, meanwhile, made a clear pitch that he should be the heir to Trump with a blistering speech that featured exaggerated claims of success, criticism of the Democrats as “lunatics” and an aggressive dismissal of a protester waving a Mexican flag. A US appeals court has rejected Trump’s attempt to impose sweeping restrictions on mail-in voting before November’s high-stakes midterm elections, dealing a fresh blow to the president’s attempted crackdown. Anthropic has detailed efforts by bad actors to misuse its AI for the production of bioweapons. More researchers and staff members at the AI startup have posted their own dire warnings about the safety of the technology, but Elon Musk called the chorus of concerns a “setup” and a “psyop”. California has adopted what Gavin Newsom described as “nation-leading” legislation that bans addictive social media features for young users, regulates companion chatbots and implements new safeguards around AI. Sales of previously occupied US homes declined in August to their slowest annual pace in more than a year as home shoppers grappled with rising mortgage rates and home prices. Stat of the day: $15m fund launched to create ‘unstoppable momentum’ to end FGM worldwide Leaders in the fight against female genital mutilation, which has affected more than 230 million women and girls worldwide, have welcomed an unprecedented $15.5m fund aimed at creating “unstoppable momentum” to finally end the practice. Culture pick: Is Sandra Bullock and Nicole Kidman’s agelessness the real trick of Practical Magic 2? Katie Edwards asks the awkward question about Practical Magic 2, would Hollywood have brought the franchise back from the dead if the intervening 28 years looked more visible on Sandra Bullock and Nicole Kidman? Don’t miss this: ‘We can’t stop for a second’ – tracking South Korea’s stalkers in real time Raphael Rashid reports from Seoul on an app that has allowed survivors – who are overwhelmingly women – to see exactly where their stalker is. If they come within a kilometre, an alert is passed to police and probation authorities, who can call and notify the victim. … or this: I turned off my algorithm for 24 hours – is this how social media used to be? “There are no more posts from accounts that you follow from the past 30 days” is a message we have long since stopped seeing on Instagram. In the wake of a government decision to insist companies provide algorithm opt-outs, my Australian colleague Caitlin Cassidy tried to turn her social media experience back to 2012. Climate check: English winemakers expect ‘vintage year’ after record-breaking summer heat While drought in France has been bringing predictions of a fall in wine production, English winemakers are benefiting after record-breaking summer heat quickly ripened grapes. It isn’t all good news for British drinkers though – beer sellers have warned of a potential shortage after the high temperatures caused poor yields of barley. Last Thing: Diana’s ‘revenge dress’, worn when Charles revealed infidelity, up for auction Worn by Diana the same night Charles would reveal his infidelity on TV, the black, fitted, off-the-shoulder, skintight and short Christina Stambolian dress was quickly labelled “the revenge dress” by the media. This month it will go on display at Sotheby’s auction house in London, before travelling to Hong Kong, Geneva and New York, where it will be sold. title: One in nine migratory birds threatened with extinction, global report says
summary: Findings on decline of species such as Arctic tern and turtle dove published alongside flyways pledge at Kenya summit
text: One in nine migratory birds are threatened with extinction and 45% of migratory species such as cuckoos, turtle doves and Arctic terns are in decline, according to a global report. The migratory slender-billed curlew was officially declared extinct last year, the first global bird extinction in mainland Eurasia and Africa in recent centuries. Worldwide, seven migratory bird species have been confirmed or are suspected to have become extinct over the last 150 years. The threats to migratory birds, which are overwhelmingly caused by humans and include the intensification of farming, unsustainable hunting, pollution, invasive species and global heating, were revealed in the State of the World’s Birds report. Seabirds and shorebirds, which depend upon marine habitats and coastal wetlands, are faring particularly badly, according to the analysis, which is produced every four years by BirdLife International. Stuart Butchart, the chief scientist at BirdLife International, said: “Migratory birds are sentinels, and their declines reveal growing pressure on the natural systems that sustain us. But the science is equally clear: conservation works, with coordinated action preventing extinctions and helping populations recover. The solutions exist: what is needed now is their implementation at flyway scale.” The report was published at the Global Flyways summit in Nairobi, Kenya, where governments, scientists, conservation NGOs and financial institutions signed a commitment to increase efforts to protect migratory birds along their flyways, the routes taken by billions of migratory birds moving between continents and seasons. The Nairobi Flyways Declaration comes with three development banks integrating flyway conservation into their lending frameworks, providing $6bn (£4.4bn) for habitat protection and restoration along migratory routes. Threats to migratory birds include persecution, with an estimated 13.1 million to 42.7 million migratory birds illegally killed or taken every year in Europe, the Mediterranean, the Caucasus and the Arabian peninsula. Many of these are songbirds caught in mist nets or on “lime sticks” for human consumption. Invasive species, such as rodents sometimes accidentally introduced on to small islands where seabirds breed, also threaten migratory birds. Loss or damage to natural habitats is another prime cause. According to the report, scientific monitoring over the past decade has found that more than half (58%) of 1,099 key biodiversity areas for migratory birds are in poor or very poor condition. But the report highlights how conservation action, often across national boundaries, is reviving some species. The eradication of non-native rabbits, cats, rodents and the weka bird from Australia’s Macquarie Island, an important site for breeding seabirds, has led to a resurgence in populations of migratory seabirds including the blue petrel, grey petrel, white-headed petrel and the Antarctic prion. In China, an ambitious countrywide programme to remove smooth cordgrass, a North American grass introduced in 1979 to stabilise coastal mudflats for development, has restored 37,553 hectares (92,756 acres) – half the total area – in its first year, opening up vital food-rich mudflats to shorebirds again. In Britain, the restoration of wetlands on agricultural land threatened by coastal erosion at Wallasea Island, Essex, has led to peaks of more than 32,000 waterbirds returning to the site, including 11,270 red knots. Outlined at the summit were plans by the Asian Development Bank to mobilise $3bn over the next decade to protect at least 50 priority wetlands across the east Asian-Australasian flyway, with the funds also supporting nearly 200 million people who depend on these ecosystems. The Development Bank of Latin America and the Caribbean is mobilising $3bn-$5bn up to 2050 to safeguard more than 30 landscapes and seascapes. Several billion dollars has also been pledged by the World Bank and BirdLife to support flyways across Africa, Europe and Asia used by more than 2 billion migratory birds. Princess Takamado of Japan, the honorary president of BirdLife International, said: “Migratory birds do not recognise borders. They connect Asia to Africa, the Arctic to the tropics. The Nairobi Flyways Declaration acknowledges this reality – that it needs international cooperation and coordination to keep migratory birds safe. I am excited and proud to see that the scientific community, conservation organisations and the financial sector are uniting to make this happen. We stand at an important turning point. We have been waiting for this moment for a long time.” Martin Harper, the chief executive of BirdLife International, also called the Nairobi Declaration a turning point but said governments, businesses and civil society needed to play their part. “Development banks are rising to the challenge. The BirdLife Partnerhip is prepared to act. We now need others to step up to reverse the declines and save the wonder of migration.”

title: Missouri UPS worker two weeks from retirement fatally struck by company vehicle
summary: Paul Roberts, who was employed by UPS for 44 years, was working at a customer care center when he was struck
text: A longtime United Parcel Service (UPS) employee less than two weeks away from retiring was struck and killed by one of the company’s vehicles while he was at work in St Louis, triggering a federal labor investigation along with an intense outpouring of grief from his family and colleagues. Paul Roberts, 63, was on duty at the UPS customer care center in Earth City, Missouri, on the night of 4 September when a company vehicle hit him, authorities said. Roberts, of nearby St Charles, Missouri, died at the scene. The vehicle’s driver cooperated with investigators who responded to reports of the fatal accident, local police said in a statement provided to the Guardian on Thursday. The federal Occupational Safety and Health Administration (Osha) is investigating Roberts’s death, a process that could take up to six months, an agency spokesperson said in a separate statement on Thursday. While neither Osha nor the police released more details, Roberts’s story quickly gained attention beyond St Louis because family members told local news media that he had planned to retire on 17 September after 44 years of working at UPS. Roberts had started with UPS sorting packages as a teenager, eventually working various jobs for the delivery company over the ensuing decades, the St Louis Post-Dispatch newspaper reported. He had most recently operated as a feeder truck driver and was looking forward to gardening while collecting his retirement benefits, having only married his wife, Barb, in March after 37 years together, according to the newspaper, which spoke to Roberts’s sister, Donna Schraer. “It’s just unbelievable – that close to finally [being] able to relax,” Schraer told the Post-Dispatch. The St Louis news station KSDK separately reported that it was contacted by UPS employees who were worried “about the dark conditions the night Roberts was killed, in addition to ongoing safety concerns”. Asked for comment about Roberts on Thursday, a UPS spokesperson, Jim Mayer, said in a statement to the Guardian: “We focus on the safety of our people every day. We train our people to prevent accidents and injuries and teach them how to stay healthy and safe.” Mayer’s statement said UPS “invested more than 35[m] hours and over $2[bn] on safety training” since 2021. His statement also said: “We’re saddened by the tragic situation in Earth City. Our heartfelt thoughts are with the family, friends and coworkers of our team member.” Osha did not list any other fatalities at the site where Roberts was killed, according to agency information cited by the Post-Dispatch. But the newspaper also noted that two past workplace incidents reported there resulted in amputations, and others resulted in heat-related injuries, though none involved vehicles. The Teamsters Local 688 labor union to which Roberts belonged described his death as “a tragedy”. The union’s statement also said: “Our members’ safety is priority one when on the job.” Besides Roberts’s sister and wife, his survivors include his children and grandchildren, KSDK reported. They all would remember his legacy as a “hard-working family man”, she told the channel. “It’s sad he’s not going to be able to celebrate” his retirement with his loved ones, Schraer also told KSDK. “I hate just being shocked that this is all going on right now.”

title: Emma Bonino, radical Italian politician who stood up to Vatican, dies aged 78
summary: Militant feminist led campaigns to legalise abortion and divorce and went on to become foreign minister
text: Emma Bonino, the radical Italian politician who led campaigns to legalise abortion and divorce against the objections of the Vatican, has died aged 78. “Today we lose not only our leader but also one of the most clear-sighted, courageous and free figures in the political history of our country,” the small party she founded, More Europe, said on Facebook on Friday. Bonino served as a European commissioner and as foreign minister in Italy but was best known as a militant feminist dedicated to political and humanitarian causes. “Her life was a long struggle against everything that denies freedom: against clandestine abortion, world hunger, the stranglehold of party politics, female genital mutilation, punitive justice, genocide, and every form of authoritarianism,” her party said. A former member of Italy’s Radical party, Bonino commanded respect across the political sphere. Italy’s far-right prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, paid tribute to her, saying that although their “backgrounds and perspectives differed, that never prevented me from acknowledging her significance and her role in our nation’s public life”. Even after the Radicals’ political star faded, Bonino remained a key political figure and human rights campaigner active in Italy for more than five decades. With her sharp wit and cutting insights, she appeared frequently on Italian TV. After a cancer diagnosis in 2015, she would appear in public wearing colourful headscarves. Bonino first got involved in Italian politics after she became pregnant aged 26 and had an abortion, even though it was illegal at that time. “I decided that never, never, never again should anyone have to suffer this humiliation,” she said. She went on to hand herself in to the police, turning her private “offence” into a ⁠public act of defiance. The arrest ⁠made headlines, fuelling a campaign that eventually led to the legalisation of abortion in 1978. It also launched Bonino into parliament with the Radical party, a small but relentless force for civil rights. During her 50-year political career, Bonino served as foreign minister, trade minister and EU affairs minister in Italian centre-left governments of the 2000s and 2010s. She remained an outspoken supporter of Europe and the rights of refugees and migrants. “You can look at the fights I have waged with this point of view: I support a democratic liberal order and believe in the centrality of the individual, his rights but also his responsibilities,” she told the Guardian in 2018. Over the years, Bonino cultivated a deep friendship with the late Pope Francis, despite their conflicting views on key ethical issues, including abortion and euthanasia. Bonino said that during their conversations Francis always encouraged her to bring forward her humanitarian battles, defending those most in need. When asked what battles she still needed to fight, Bonino would say: “Many, too many. Human rights, world hunger, free scientific research … Ten lives won’t be enough.” Bonino is survived by her siblings, Domenica and Giovanni, and their children.
