title: Reform UK beset by internal row over response to Dover and Portsmouth protests
summary: Nigel Farage said demonstrators in balaclavas were ‘horrible’, but others in the party defend them as ‘brave, passionate patriots’
text: Nigel Farage’s condemnation of the masked men whose blockade of Dover stole headlines on the final day of his party’s annual conference was swift, describing their actions as “horrible”. Yet less than a week on from the public debut of the black-clad members of Patriot Platform, Reform is gripped with internal friction over the activists. There has been unease among some members and councillors about Farage’s criticism and some outright praise for the group as “patriots”. Reform is facing questions about explicit links to the nationalist hard right after Ryan Bridge, a co-founder of the anti-migrant Raise the Colours group, was given a prominent platform at Reform’s conference, where Farage pledged to “legally back” him. Bridge, who was on bail and was charged this week with 14 offences including racially aggravated harassment, has worked closely with the leader of Patriot Platform, Daniel Thomas. Bridge has said he has no association with Patriot Platform. The starkest public example of Reform divisions over Patriot Platform played out publicly in Portsmouth on Monday after police had clashed with activists wearing balaclavas. Thomas gatecrashed a visit by the party’s home affairs spokesperson, Zia Yusuf, to tell him that events had been misreported. “I take your word for it,” Yusuf told him. Yusuf later reflected that Thomas – a convicted criminal and long-term associate of the activist who calls himself Tommy Robinson – made his points “respectfully” and challenged Kemi Badenoch’s condemnation of the group. “How dare you call them ‘thugs’,” Yusuf told the Conservative leader on X. Yusuf and other senior Reform figures including Richard Tice, Robert Jenrick and the leader of the party’s flagship county council, Kent, have criticised the use of face coverings by the new far-right group. But often in the same breath there has been tacit backing for their aims. “How about your government stops the boats instead? Then people wouldn’t feel the need to protest over the invasion of the country … just a thought,” said the Kent council leader, Linden Kemkaran, whose council includes Dover. Yet elsewhere – as highlighted by the anti-fascist group Hope Not Hate – others have been willing to go further. “Those patriots in Portsmouth have done more to stop the invasion than the last seven governments put together,” said the Dudley councillor Andrew Southall, while the Portsmouth councillor Emily Strudwick spoke of “a great sense of community” at the protest, which she attended. There is also, unusually, evidence of open dissent in Reform towards Farage himself. “We know there are strong feelings circulating today about Nigel’s comments regarding the Dover protest. We want to address it head on as a group,” the Tameside councillor Sharon Barker wrote on Facebook. “Many of the people at that march were brave, passionate patriots who had very real reasons for covering their faces, including the very real fear of losing their jobs simply for standing up for Britain.” Her group leader, Allan Hopwood, told the Guardian that the subject was “particularly emotive”, insisting the focus was on democratic politics. A factor in Tameside is that Reform locally is at the sharp end of the threat posed by the rightwing rival Rupert Lowe’s Restore Britain. But on the question of face coverings worn by the activists, Hopwood said: “These are people who clearly have a patriotic agenda and are concerned about the women and children of this country, but they are also acutely aware there will be media who want to propagandise things. They will have jobs they want to protect and unfortunately we’re in a position where people are reluctant to make their identities known.” During the Reform conference, Farage told Bridge of Raise the Colours that its campaign – which put up flags around England in circumstances that many people saw as intimidating – had been “phenomenal” and he would pass the group’s proposal to partner with Reform-led councils on to the party’s lawyers, an exchange that has been shared widely on social media. Bridge told the Guardian on Thursday that he had received a lot of interest from Reform councillors about his proposal and the party was considering the plans. “Specific councils are in acknowledgment of what we are trying to roll out and propose. It’s very, very positive from Clacton to Norfolk to Wales. Last night, I spoke to councillors in Burnley, it’s literally the whole country,” he said. “It felt like we were in a comfortable, safe environment of like-minded British patriots and people that want better for the country,” he said. The praise for Patriot Platform among some in Reform and ties to Raise the Colours come at a perilous moment for Farage as he seeks to nudge up Reform’s flatlining poll numbers by tempting wavering Tory voters. While he is fond of laying claim to being the man who killed off the British National party when it was competing with Ukip a decade ago, Reform faces an acute electoral danger of losing voters on its right to Restore Britain. Reform UK was approached for comment.

title: JD Vance pitches himself as Trump’s political heir on day two of Republican midterm convention
summary: Vice-president dog-whistled, exaggerated claims of success and echoed Trump talking points to excited audience
text: JD Vance made a clear pitch that he should be the heir to Donald Trump on Thursday night, closing out the Republicans’ midterm convention with a blistering speech that featured exaggerated claims of success, criticism of Democrats as “lunatics” and an aggressive dismissal of a protester waving a Mexican flag. Speaking in Dallas, the vice-president showed he could channel the basest instincts of his boss, filling his remarks with dog whistles and echoing Trump’s false claims that Democrats “cheered” the 7 October massacre of Israelis. Vance had been met with chants of “JD, JD,” as he walked on to the stage: the liveliest response anyone besides Trump received across the two-day convention, with some shouting that he should be the nominee in 2028. “We gotta take care of business this November, then we’ll worry about what comes next,” the vice-president responded with a smile. Vance began the speech by running through a list of Republican grievances, channeling Trump’s pugnacious attitude toward immigration as he told the crowd that two years ago “we were tired of being called racist for noticing that our country was becoming dirtier and poorer and less safe and less prosperous”. The Make America Great Again (Maga) crowd inside the arena liked that line, but the loudest cheer of the night came when Vance responded to a protester who briefly interrupted his speech. Vance claimed the protester was waving a Mexican flag, and adopted a fiery tone as he said: “Well, my friend, if you love Mexico so much, get your ass over there – I’ll buy you the plane ticket.” The applause was rapturous. The vice-president had to walk a tightrope coming into the speech, arguably the most important address of his short political career. He had to present his own case to the Republican base, without breaking too much from the notoriously sensitive Trump. Vance praised Trump as “the toughest SOB in American politics”, and paused repeatedly as the crowd lavished him with cheers and applause. He also invoked the recent birth of a fourth child, saying he had been looking at “the future of this country through the eyes of the future of my son” and “the birthright of this newest of Americans”. Addressing Democratic “radicals”, whom he accused of wanting to destroy the nuclear American family, he boomed: “Stay the hell away from our kids.” But it was also a speech aimed squarely at rallying the Maga faithful: attacking transgender rights, extolling the importance of American manufacturing and religious freedom, and accusing Democrats of “doubling down on the crazy”. Vance showed a penchant, too, for Trump’s baseless statements, claiming that some Democrats in New York “cheered on” the slaughter of Jewish people on 7 October, and suggesting that a “new generation” of Democrats seek to defund the police and “abolish the border”. “What is it that drives this new generation of radical Democrats? It’s not new policies. They’ll say the same stuff: defund the police, abolish the border, the green new scam. We’ve heard all this stuff before,” Vance said. He then tried out a new line: “I think that what’s new about them is what motivates them is a new type of hardcore hatred.” Vance won applause, too, for his praise of Charlie Kirk, the far-right activist who was assassinated in Utah exactly one year ago. Addressing Kirk’s children, who were not in the arena, Vance said: “History will record that your father was a great man. “Those of us who loved your dad, we know him as something even better than a great man – he was a good man,” he added of Kirk, a man who, among other things, endorsed Trump’s stolen-election lies and the racist great replacement theory. One problem Vance could face should he run in 2028 is his attachment to the deeply unpopular Iran war, and foreign policy was conspicuous by its absence in his speech. Last week he rejected the use of the word “war”, but said he wouldn’t set “artificial lines” regarding an end to the conflict. The Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday that Trump’s advisers have raised the prospect that the war could drag on through the rest of his term. Vance did not address the war directly. But in an oblique reference he invoked Kirk’s disdain for conflict. “Charlie hated war,” Vance said, before pleading with undecided voters to not abandon the party over policy differences. “What I’m asking you to do is do what Charlie did: do not throw the baby out with the bathwater,” he said. “Don’t give the country over to a bunch of crazy people because you happen to disagree with us on a policy issue here or there.” A poll found Vance was the favorite choice among likely Republican primary voters, with 43% saying they wanted him to be the nominee in 2028. Marco Rubio, the secretary of state, got 21%; Donald Trump Jr was at 7%. Vance will hope those numbers stick, but he wasn’t the only one auditioning in Dallas. Robert F Kennedy Jr, the health secretary who switched parties to support Trump in 2024, praised the president and attacked the Democratic party during a well-received speech earlier on Thursday, while Ted Cruz, the Texas senator, received a rousing response in his home state. “They hate Christians, they hate Jews, they hate the ‌capitalism, they hate ⁠the constitution and they hate America,” Cruz said of Democrats, offering no evidence for his claims, but very much tapping into the theme of the two-day convention. Rubio did not speak at the convention, instead taking part in a tour of South America. Both he and Cruz ran against Trump in 2016. During that contest, Trump dubbed Rubio “Little Marco” and suggested Cruz’s father was involved in the assassination of John F Kennedy. Vance, by contrast, has never publicly attracted Trump’s ire, and he will want to keep it that way as he seeks to take on leadership of the party in two years’ time. That was probably the thinking as the vice-president ended his speech, shouting over jubilant applause that Trump was the “greatest president” before relinquishing the stage for his boss to bring the convention to a close.

title: Tiananmen Square vigil organisers jailed for seven years in Hong Kong
summary: Pro-democracy activists Chow Hang-tung and Lee Cheuk-yan were found guilty of ‘incitement to subversion’ in controversial national security case
text: Two pro-democracy activists who were put on trial for organising an annual Tiananmen Square massacre vigil in Hong Kong have been sentenced to seven years in jail, in one of the city’s most significant national security cases. Chow Hang-tung, 41 and Lee Cheuk-yan, 69, were found guilty in August of incitement to subversion. The court found they had “incited other persons to organise, plan, commit or participate in acts by unlawful means with a view to subverting the state power”. Chow and Lee were leaders of the Hong Kong Alliance, which for decades organised the city’s annual vigil in memory of those killed in the bloody crackdown on pro-democracy protesters in Beijing in 1989. Lee and Chow received prison terms of seven years, and seven years and three months respectively. Albert Ho, a 74-year-old former lawmaker who pleaded guilty in January, received a sentence of five years and two months. Their case represented one of the last high-profile national security trials to be heard in Hong Kong, as the national security law imposed by Beijing in 2020 extinguishes what was once one of the world’s most widely watched pro-democracy struggles. The Alliance disbanded in 2021 following pressure created by the introduction of the national security law. The case had centred on a slogan that was used for decades by the Alliance: “end one-party dictatorship”. The court ruled that the defendants “intended to cause others to lose confidence in the Chinese Communist party by stirring up hostility and causing division”. The defence said that the Alliance was simply exercising its right to freedom of speech. One supporter who attended the sentencing told the Guardian: “A demonstration that lasted for more than 35 years without any problem is suddenly being seen as subversion.” Chow, a UK educated barrister, represented herself in court. She has been in detention since 2021 and while in prison has frequently written letters published on her social media. In August Chow wrote a note to the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, calling for Britain “to adopt a more robust stance in the face of the growing threat from a totalitarian and aggressive China”. The UK Foreign Office said it condemned the use of the national security law in convicting the two activists. Before sentencing, members of the public queued up for days to secure a seat in the court. Some in the queue had prepared food and umbrellas in preparation to stay overnight. Hong Kong and Macau were once the only places on Chinese soil where it was permitted to hold public vigils to mourn protesters who died on 4 June 1989 in Beijing. Hundreds, possibly thousands, were killed when the People’s Liberation Army put a bloody end to pro-democracy protests. For decades tens of thousands of people would gather in Hong Kong’s Victoria park to take part in a candlelit vigil. In 2020, Beijing’s sweeping national security law in effect banned public commemoration. In recent years, activists who attempted to publicly mark the day said they were frequently followed, searched and detained by plainclothes police. Authorities said the national security law would only affect a small number of people and was needed to return order after a year of often violent anti-government protests in 2019. But critics say it has transformed the city. “It is still surreal to me,” Lee’s wife, Elizabeth Tang, told the Guardian. “Every time the Alliance had an activity, they would get the police permission for every one. “The vigils are what made Hong Kong different,” she said, recalling the public commemoration that are now banned. “It’s very unjust. Complete silence is really very scary.” The case has seen widespread condemnation from foreign governments and human rights groups who criticised the use of the national security law to convict peaceful protesters and ban the vigil.

title: Ukraine war briefing: Nato ‘foils Russian undersea cable sabotage drill’
summary: Swindon drone factory was target of Russia plot involving British man, court hears; Poland says Ukraine border crossing came under threat. What we know on day 1,661
text: Nato forces chased away Russian ships in Arctic waters that were training to attack undersea cables with a secret sabotage weapon deployed by submersible craft, Reuters has reported, citing western officials. Reuters said its sources declined to detail how the technology works. The confrontation took place near the remote Svalbard archipelago. British and Norwegian officials took their findings to Moscow to show they were aware of the new technology. CIA director John Ratcliffe’s visit to Moscow in August was partly to warn ‌Russia against escalating sabotage operations in Europe, Reuters said, citing two people familiar with the matter. The US has not publicly explained Ratcliffe’s trip. The Norwegian defence minister, Tore Sandvik, told Reuters: “Through our joint operation, we sent a clear message to Russia that they cannot operate covertly … It is in no one’s interest to escalate tensions in the High ‌North.” Britain’s defence ministry pointed to previous statements about attempted covert activities in and near Norwegian and British waters by Russia’s “deep-sea research directorate”, known by the acronym GUGI, which is under international sanctions. The White House did not respond to a comment request, Reuters said, while the CIA declined to comment. The British man Joshua Cammidge, arrested as an alleged Russian agent, was part of a plot to sabotage a drone factory in England, prosecutors said on Thursday in a London court. Cammidge, 31, is charged with engaging in conduct to materially assist a foreign intelligence service in carrying out activities in violation of the National Security Act. He did not enter a plea and was returned to custody until due in court again on 25 September. Cammidge was in contact with a suspected representative of the GRU Volunteer Corps, a group controlled by Russia’s military intelligence agency, the prosecution told Westminster magistrates court. Cammidge allegedly provided information on four drone manufacturing sites in his home town of Swindon. A Ukrainian missile strike caused damage in the south ⁠of the Russian city of Volgograd, officials said on Friday. The Volgograd oil refinery ⁠run by Lukoil, one of Russia’s biggest by processing capacity, is located ‌in the southern part of the city. A ⁠Ukrainian drone attack ⁠caused ⁠a fire at a warehouse of Russian e-commerce ⁠company Ozon ‌in ‌the city of ‌Saratov, the company said on Friday. Russian airstrikes injured eight and caused a ⁠fire in a ⁠nine-storey apartment building in Kyiv on Friday morning, city authorities said. Poland and Ukraine stopped⁠ a threat to one of their border crossings and expect they will ⁠be further targeted, Donald Tusk said on Thursday, as ⁠Russia attacks wartime routes between Ukraine and its neighbouring allies. “Last night, thanks to cooperation between our services and their Ukrainian ‌counterparts, a direct ‌threat to one of the border crossings was averted,” the Polish prime minister said, adding that he had received “a fairly ⁠precise report directly from the CIA regarding possible events in the coming months”. Poland also suspended flights at its Lublin and ⁠Rzeszów airports on Thursday while its air ‌force conducted what were described as preventive operations related to ⁠Russian missile attacks on Ukraine. On Wednesday, drones hit a border crossing between Ukraine and Moldova in the southern region of ⁠Odesa, killing two people. “We expect similar actions targeting border crossings with Ukraine in other countries, including Poland,” Tusk said. Russia did ‌not immediately comment. A Russian strike on a shopping centre in Pavlohrad, central Ukraine, killed at least five people, authorities said on Thursday. Another 76 people were injured including children, and other parts of the city were also attacked. The city lies on a supply route for the Ukrainian ⁠military connecting central Ukraine to eastern frontlines. Two people were killed by a Russian attack in Dnipro on the ‌US-owned Bunge sunflower oil factory, one of Ukraine’s five largest food plants with a processing capacity of 1,600 tonnes of oilseeds per day. Another five people were injured. “This is no coincidence, but part of Moscow’s systematic terror campaign against American businesses and economic interests,” said the Ukrainian foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha. Before Russia started the war, Ukraine was the world’s largest exporter of sunflower ‌oil. Russia has carried out attacks on oilseed refineries and vegetable oil terminals while claiming to be targeting military ports and shipping. Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said Russian forces struck the eastern Donetsk region and the Kharkiv ⁠region in the north-east. In the north-eastern city of Sumy, officials said a jet-powered drone tore into a shopping centre – a day after two people were killed and 20 wounded in a similar attack there. Russian officials said Ukrainian drone attacks on the border region of Belgorod killed ‌two people and injured seven. Two Azerbaijani tugboat ⁠crew members ⁠were killed and two others ⁠injured in a Russian attack ‌on ‌civilian shipping ‌in Ukraine’s southern Odesa region, Kyiv’s infrastructure ministry ‌said. Canada offered support on Thursday to boost Ukraine’s air defences and help replenish its drone stocks, as the countries pledged to deepen their alliance during a visit by Zelenskyy. The support includes C$350m (US$253m) provided through a programme known as Jumpstart run in conjunction with the US. Carney said Ottawa was also offering C$450m in loan guarantees to enhance the Ukrainian energy supply; meanwhile Canada was racing to increase its drone arsenal, from which 30% of Canadian production would go to Ukraine. Russia is illegally trafficking foreigners to fight in Ukraine who quickly become “cannon fodder”, Amnesty International said on Thursday, citing interviews with prisoners of war deceived into signing Russian military contracts. Among the victims were citizens of Brazil, Colombia, Sri Lanka and South Africa lured to Russia through fake job advertisements. “Then it’s coercion. Their passports are taken away. They are made to sign documents they don’t understand,” said Agnes Callamard, Amnesty’s secretary general. “They are given training they don’t understand [and used as] cannon fodder.”

title: Texas reports first equine infection of New World screwworm on ranch horse
summary: The flesh-eating parasite had been largely eradicated, but now authorities are racing to contain an outbreak
text: A horse in southern Texas has been infected with the New World screwworm, marking the first US equine infection as health authorities race to contain an outbreak of the flesh-eating parasite. The pest was discovered on the hind limb of a working ranch horse in Presidio county, according to a statement on Thursday from the US Equestrian Foundation. The foundation advised horse owners to monitor the animals daily for wounds, foul odor or maggots. The screwworm, a fly larva, can nestle into and infest open wounds. “Check horses daily, keep wounds clean and covered as directed by your veterinarian, use veterinarian-recommended fly control products and limit fly access with physical barriers such as fly masks, sheets and clean stabling practices when appropriate,” the foundation’s statement read. The Texas Animal Health Commission, has restricted the movement of warm-blooded animals outside of infested zones in parts of Presidio and Jeff Davis counties, among several others, to curb new infestations. After being eradicated decades ago, the screwworm was detected in June on a calf in Zavala county, near the US-Mexico border. A screwworm infestation has spread throughout Mexico. Of the 49 US cases recorded this year, all have been in Texas, except for one in New Mexico, where the pest was found on a dog, according to the US Department of Agriculture. The resurgence of the parasite, which can cause severe injury or death in animals, has raised alarm about potential financial devastation for Texas ranchers. Greg Abbott, the Texas governor, issued a disaster proclamation in June to mobilize state resources toward coping with the rising screwworm presence. Before the pest was reported on American soil, the Trump administration announced the launch of a sterile fly dispersal facility in Edinburg. If female screwworm flies mate with a sterile fly, their offspring will not be viable, thus curbing the population. Reuters contributed reporting

title: Anthropic details bad actors’ efforts to misuse its AI for bioweapons
summary: The 154-page report comes two days after former employee Jacob Coxon resigned due to Anthropic racing to improve its models that would cause human extinction by 2030
text: Criminals, state-sponsored groups, spyware vendors, scientists and propagandists have attempted to use Anthropic’s powerful artificial intelligence models to design missiles and bombs, create deadly pathogens and surveil dissidents, according to a threat intelligence report the company published on Thursday. “The cases we share here aren’t typical misuse, but rather examples of the most notable and novel threat activity we’ve identified to date,” Anthropic wrote in its 154-page report. “We’re publishing this work because we believe we have a responsibility to disclose malicious misuse of our services.” In particular, the company detailed five case studies of scientists using its AI models in biological research. In these examples, Anthropic said the researchers circumvented its safeguards meant to prevent users from “unsupported regions”, as well as worked to hide the purpose of their work. “Biological misuse is one of the most serious risks of frontier AI models,” Anthropic wrote. “Without the correct safeguards, such capabilities could have catastrophic consequences.” Anthropic said it banned these accounts. The company did not reveal the names of the research institutions or the countries where the misuse took place, saying it was uncertain of the researchers’ intent. Anthropic gave dozens of other examples of threat actors using its AI models. Those included cyber operations such as Russian espionage and “smash-and-grab” cyberhacks; surveillance operations, including a China-based program targeting Uyghurs in Syria and another targeting internal dissidents; propaganda campaigns in Russia, Malaysia, Iran and Bangladesh; and the use of its Claude AI model in Yemen, China and Russia to develop software for conventional weapons, including firearms, missiles, armed drones, bombs and other munitions. In one of the examples of biological research, Anthropic found a scientist using Claude to work on a state-sponsored grant application to study the virus chikungunya. The virus is a mosquito-borne disease, similar to dengue and malaria, that can cause months of severe pain, fever and other debilitating symptoms. Such research could be used to develop vaccines, but could also be used to create biological weapons. Anthropic told the New York Times this case was especially concerning because it could see the study was to be done at a military research institute. The report comes just two days after an Anthropic employee, Jacob Coxon, set off a media firestorm with his resignation. He stated that he quit the company because it was not acting responsibly in creating its technology. Coxon said Anthropic and its rival, OpenAI, were “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence” that would cause human extinction by 2030. Current Anthropic employees posted public agreements with him. Many AI experts say the real-world threats, like those detailed in Anthropic’s intelligence report, are far more concerning within the next three years than an apocalypse brought on by an omnipotent intelligence. “AI accelerationism and AI doomerism are two sides of the same coin: they both enforce the notion that an AGI superbeing will come into existence,” said Heidy Khlaaf, the chief AI scientist at the AI Now Institute. Khlaaf said AI labs creating technology that can be used for cybersecurity exploitation and weapons of war could be exceedingly more deadly. In its report, Anthropic said that the potential real-world misuse from AI models is not typically in public view, instead, it’s investigated internally and by academics, governments and international organizations. The company said that the entire AI industry needs to work together, alongside governments, to address these harms and create defenses. “As models become increasingly capable, their risks will increase, unless AI developers and society’s defenders act to make them safer,” Anthropic wrote.

title: Woolworths increased prices of at least four ‘family staples’ during ‘Price Freeze’ promotion
summary: Exclusive: Analysis shows cost of chicken fillets, potatoes and donuts rose during supermarket giant’s three-month promotion
text: Woolworths raised prices for popular items – including a 33% mark up on chicken fillets – within days of promising to freeze prices on 300 “family staples” for three months to help customers with the cost of living. Pricing data, compiled by comparison website CW Scanner and provided to Guardian Australia, shows the supermarket chain increasing the prices of at least four key products after starting the three-month “Price Freeze” promotion on 1 May. The supermarket nearly doubled the price of a 420g can of Woolworths “Mexican Style 3 Bean Mix” during the promotional period – from 60c to $1 on 17 June – the data shows. Woolworths dropped the price back to 60c on 17 August. Woolworths has justified the increases because it regarded the previous prices as promotional prices, rather than the “standard shelf price” for each product. A Woolworths spokesperson said that the end of a temporary promotion did not represent a shelf price increase. “The Price Freeze gave our customers the certainty that they would not pay more than the shelf price on 300 popular products for three months – and we delivered on that,” the spokesperson said. When the price freeze was announced, the Woolworths chief executive officer, Amanda Bardwell, said the supermarket wanted to help customers who were concerned about how inflation driven by the war on Iran was affecting household budgets. “That’s why, for the next three months, we’re freezing the shelf price on 300 staples that families rely on most, like eggs, chicken breast fillets, pasta, beef sausages and nappies,” Bardwell said in a press release on 30 April. “It’s our promise that the shelf price you see on these items today is the most you’ll pay for the next three months. We’ll invest to absorb any extra costs that are agreed with suppliers on these products to make that happen.” Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Prof Jana Bowden, a marketing expert and chair of ethics at Macquarie University’s business school, said raising prices after claiming they had been fixed was “akin to not delivering on the everyday consumer’s interpretation of a ‘price freeze’ promise”. “How is the consumer expected to know what the start prices were before the campaign or even after the campaign started?” Bowden said. “No consumer walks into a supermarket with the insights of how the prices for the hundreds of products that they buy vary over a day, week, month or year – nor should they have to.” The analysis comes at a time of high scrutiny of the pricing tactics used by Woolworths – and rival Coles – after landmark court cases involving both companies. Woolworths is awaiting the verdict in the federal court case brought against it by the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC), with the watchdog alleging the supermarket misled shoppers with effectively fake discounts on its “Prices Dropped” campaign. Prices unfrozen During its price freeze period, Woolworths increased the retail price of 350g deli portions of RSPCA-approved chicken breast fillets by 33%. While a customer would have paid $9/kg for the chicken breast fillets on 29 April, the price increased to $12/kg on 5 May. It then alternated between $9/kg and $12/kg twice more during the “Price Freeze”. Before the promotion, Woolworths’ 2kg bags of washed potatoes had consistently followed a routine high-low pricing pattern alternating between $6 and $8. This appears to have occurred during the promotional period, with CW Scanner data showing they cost customers $6 on 29 April, before the price went up to $8 on 6 May. The price of a 12-pack of the supermarket’s own-brand fresh cinnamon donuts was increased from $3 to $3.50 on 6 May. It was reduced to $3 again on 18 August. Choice’s senior campaigns and policy adviser, Bea Sherwood, said the advocacy group regularly heard from consumers who said they were confused by the pricing tickets they saw on supermarket shelves. “Prices have changed so much over recent years and we’re seeing them continuously increase, so having an understanding of what a regular shelf price is is not something we can expect consumers to stay on top of,” Sherwood said. “When Woolworths or Coles say something is a standard price, we don’t have the transparency to understand how they’ve come to that.” • This article was amended on 11 September 2026 to delete an incorrect reference to 350g packs of RSPCA-approved chicken breast fillets rising in price from $9 to $12. This should have referred to a 350g portion of the chicken fillets from the deli rising from $9/kg to $12/kg. An incorrect reference to the price subsequently falling after the promotional period ended has also been removed.

title: A.I. Could Possibly End Humanity. How Are Humans Supposed to Process That?
summary: The technology is far from the only existential risk our species faces. But weighing such cosmic fears can become a mind-bending exercise.

title: More Anthropic researchers warn of AI’s perils but Musk dismisses ‘psyop’
summary: Insiders at the firm fear tech’s advancement could cause human extinction, while others are calling their declarations of concern a ‘setup’
text: A day after a former researcher at Anthropic made an apocalyptic declaration about artificial intelligence, more researchers and staff members at the AI startup publicly agreed with him and posted their own dire warnings. In response, Elon Musk and other conservative figures on X, formerly Twitter, called the chorus of concerns a “setup” and a “psyop”. The Anthropic insiders fear the technology they are building could become so advanced and dangerous as to cause human extinction within the decade, and they assert many of their colleagues feel the same but have not said so publicly. These researchers and staff are posting in response to a now-viral thread from Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon, who said on Wednesday he was resigning from the company because neither Anthropic nor its competitor OpenAI, also his former employer, were building AI models responsibly and are “gambling with our lives”. Anna Wang, who works on Artificial General Intelligence Safety at Anthropic and previously worked at Google’s DeepMind, said on Thursday that many people at Anthropic want to slow down development to come up with a plan to mitigate the risks that could come with these AI models. “There is not yet a viable scientific plan to solve risks from recursively self-improving AI,” Wang wrote on X. Drake Thomas, another Anthropic employee, said that he respected Coxon’s choice to abstain from building these models if he worries they could pose planet-scale risks. “Things are moving way too fast, we don’t have anywhere near the degree of assurance we’ll want for ASI [artificial superintelligence],” Thomas said. Musk took a more adversarial stance. “Seems like a setup,” he wrote. Coxon replied to the world’s richest man with a selfie, writing, “I’m real and these are my real beliefs. You could ask your xAI researchers about me if you hadn’t fired them.” In a statement to the Guardian, an Anthropic spokesperson defended the company’s strategy. “We have always been transparent that AI will bring both enormous benefits and unprecedented risks. To address these risks, we continue to build models with some of the strongest safeguards in the industry,” the statement said. Musk and others with a more positive view of AI have started to spread theories that Coxon’s post and the resulting fallout are part of a “psyop” to negatively influence the public’s feelings about AI. “I think the groundwork for this psy op (for lack of a better term) has been prepared for a long time,” Musk posted on X. “This was just the match that lit the fire.” Musk was responding to a post by Parker Thayer, a researcher at conservative thinktank Capital Research, in which he floated a theory with little evidence that Coxon’s post was the start of a “VERY sophisticated and well-funded PR operation to get support for Democrats to regulate AI into oblivion”. Other notable figures took notice. Bill Ackman, the billionaire CEO of the hedge fund Pershing Square, also quoted Thayer’s post, simply saying, “Interesting.” Other Anthropic employees had posted their agreement with Coxon shortly after he declared his resignation on Wednesday. “AI developers believe their technology could cause human extinction (or similarly bad outcomes),” wrote Samuel Marks, who works on safety research at Anthropic. “This could happen in the next few years. In general, the more senior the employee, the more concerned they are.” Evan Hubinger, who describes himself as a lead in the company’s alignment division, which works on ensuring Anthropic’s AI models function in line with human goals, said Coxon was “correct” and that the industry was falling behind in attempts to deal with the apocalyptic potential. “We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” Hubinger wrote. “I personally think it is >10% within the next decade. It’s not exactly clear how Coxon and others expect AI models to usher in the demise of humanity. Some experts doubt that the technology will become so intelligent as to cause the apocalypse. Gary Marcus, a scientist and leading voice in AI, said that it was time to boycott AI, but because it was already causing harm. More than extinction, Marcus said he worried about the “risk of catastrophe” from “from AI-generated pathogens, from wars started or escalated by AI-generated disinformation, from hacks that destroy critical infrastructure, and so on. Nothing I have seen gives any indication that any of that is under control”. The same day, Anthropic released a report documenting how the company dismantled an operation attempting to build a biological weapon using its AI models.

The Bay Area city, home to a large number of high-earning tech workers, has long been one of the most expensive housing and rental markets in the country. The ballooning rental costs have been attributed to a recent influx of wealth in the market, as artificial intelligence companies began to go public on the stock market. While demand has ratcheted up for limited housing options, San Francisco has notoriously lagged behind other cities in approving new housing. Among Lurie’s proposed measures are caps to rent increases for rent-controlled apartments, $27m in funding to cover funding lapses from federal housing vouchers set to expire and an increase in payments to tenants who are evicted under the Ellis Act, legislation landlords can evoke when leaving the rental business. “Today, most San Franciscans feel our city is finally moving in the right direction, but many are also asking whether they can still afford to live here,” Lurie said in a statement on Thursday. “We have lived through booms before – this time, we have an opportunity to build a recovery that is broad-based and lasting, where San Franciscans can put down roots and participate in our city’s success.”

title: US supreme court again rejects Missouri maps drawn to boost Republicans in midterms
summary: Latest decision appears to set the stage for the state to use its old electoral maps this year
text: The US supreme court again rejected a push backed by Donald Trump to overhaul Missouri’s congressional maps in an effort to hand Republicans an edge in November’s midterm elections. Its latest ruling, after days of confusion, comes less than two months before the pivotal midterm elections in which control of the narrowly divided US House of Representatives could be determined by a handful of seats. Following conflicting decisions that spanned four courts, Wednesday’s ruling appeared to set the stage for the state to use its old electoral maps this year. The end result does not completely end confusion for Missouri’s voters, who cast ballots in primary elections using the new map, butwill vote in November on the older map. “The state, the election apparatus, had no business going forward with the primaries under that bill, under that circumstance,” said David F Walbert, a storied voting rights attorney in Georgia, who has argued voting rights cases before the US supreme court. “The problem that we’re dealing with today is 100% the result of the state machinery that created this.” At the behest of the president, Missouri’s Republican-dominated legislature redrew district lines last year to net one additional seat for Republicans in the US House of Representatives. The new maps carve up a district representing Kansas City, long held by Emanuel Cleaver, a Democrat. After Missouri’s governor, Mike Kehoe, signed new congressional district boundaries into law in September 2025, the legislation faced immediate challenges, including a push by People Not Politicians, a campaign group, which gathered more than 300,000 signatures to force a statewide referendum on whether to keep or repeal the new map. But Missouri’s secretary of state, Denny Hoskins, a Republican, sought to use the new map anyway. The Missouri supreme court certified the referendum for the ballot on 3 September over Hoskins’s objections, ruling the new district lines would not take effect until 2027 – after the referendum vote – and that the 2025 redistricting did not comply with the law. The legal argument over redistricting pitted Missouri’s court, which is “not exactly full of foreigners that are some kind of wild liberals from California or New York”, Walbert said, against state leaders auditioning for the president’s attention. The court’s unanimous decision speaks to the clarity of state law on referendums. The law “suspends completely the effective date of the law that has been subjected to the referendum”, Walbert said. The state attorney general, Catherine Hanaway, also a Republican, immediately appealed this decision. Justice Brett Kavanaugh, who oversees emergency hearings from the eighth circuit, refused to stay the Missouri supreme court ruling on Tuesday. But federal district judge Stephen Clark made a ruling only minutes later, in a separate federal case, requiring Hoskins to use the new Republican-friendly map – compounding confusion over November’s elections. Hoskins then said he would follow Clark’s order, and a federal appeals court panel declined to block that order. On Thursday morning, Kavanaugh again ordered the state to comply with the Missouri supreme court ruling, blocking the new maps. “Today’s decision ensures Missouri voters will not be forced to vote under a gerrymandered map pushed through by the state legislature last year and then cynically imposed on voters by the secretary of state, in violation of the state constitution,” said Mark Gaber, senior director of redistricting at Campaign Legal Center. “Voters deserve to have their voices heard and to have fair representation in Congress. The Missouri supreme court unanimously affirmed that principle, and now, so has the US supreme court.” The Missouri supreme court meanwhile ruled on Thursday afternoon that Hoskins, the secretary of state, had been in contempt of court after continuing to use new maps that the judges had ruled invalid. But chief justice W Brent Powell also noted that Hoskins had purged himself of the contempt after declaring that the order by Kavanaugh had ended the controversy over which map to use in November elections, and would direct local election officials to use the 2022 map.

title: US appeals court rejects Trump’s bid to restrict mail-in voting before midterms
summary: Court declined to ⁠put on hold ⁠injunction preventing the USPS from tightening rules around postal voting
text: A US appeals court has rejected Donald Trump’s attempt to impose sweeping restrictions on mail-in voting before November’s high-stakes midterm elections, dealing a fresh blow to the president’s attempted crackdown. The Boston-based first US circuit court of appeals declined on Thursday to ⁠put on hold an ⁠injunction issued by a lower court judge last week, preventing the US Postal Service (USPS) from tightening rules around postal voting. The panel of three judges, nominated by Joe Biden, agreed with the plaintiffs that the president does not have the power to regulate states’ election policy. “Appellants have not made a strong showing that the district court erred in determining that the Final Rule is likely unlawful,” they wrote, making reference to a rule published by the USPS to implement Trump’s order. It comes as the US supreme court also considers Trump’s efforts to introduce new requirements curtailing the practice, which the US president has frequently criticized despite doing it himself. Back in March, Trump signed an executive order seeking to prohibit the USPS from delivering ballots to any voters not on a nationwide list of eligible voters in each state created by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). The result would mean a limited delivery of ballots to only the voters on those approved lists. Democratic states and voting rights groups swiftly filed several lawsuits, arguing that Trump’s ordered changes are unconstitutional. Meanwhile, state election officials who run the elections have said there is not enough time to overhaul their systems to meet the new federal directives. Indeed, with the midterms less than two months out, some states have already started sending out ballots. The Trump administration has called its plans to limit mail-in ballots “commonsense measures” aimed at protecting voting security. Trump has called the order blocking those plans “unreasoned and unlawful”. Trump has repeatedly sought to restrict voting by mail, despite doing it twice himself this year alone in his resident state of Florida. He has falsely blamed mail voting for his 2020 election loss to Biden, while promoting baseless claims of fraud. The president’s order allows states to voluntarily use the new system. But as yet, none have announced they will do so. The USPS, for its part, has said it stands ready to implement Trump’s new restrictions, which would require states to give the postal service the names and barcodes tied to mail-in ballots for federal elections, if the court injunctions are lifted. However, it has also said in recent court filings that the technology needed to administer the president’s order is not even available. And earlier this month, a USPS whistleblower warned of “potentially catastrophic problems” if the agency were to try to carry out the order.

title: Florida sues Netflix over misleading parents over minors’ data collection
summary: Lawsuit brought by James Uthmeier, the attorney general, marks latest action by the state against big tech companies
text: Florida officials filed a lawsuit against Netflix, accusing the streaming giant of misleading parents about its collection of minors’ data and using features that encourage children to “binge watch” content. The lawsuit, filed on Wednesday and led by James Uthmeier, the Republican Florida attorney general, marks the latest action by Florida against major technology companies. The red-leaning state has taken an increasingly aggressive approach toward big tech, particularly during the rise of artificial intelligence (AI). “Netflix told Florida families they could pay a monthly fee to escape big tech surveillance. That was false,” Uthmeier said in a statement. “Netflix collected detailed data on children and families, designed its product to keep kids watching, and then commercialized that information to launch the advertising business it promised never to build. “Parents, not corporate executives, direct the upbringing of their children. Netflix should expect to be held accountable,” he added. In a statement shared with the Guardian, a spokesperson for Netflix said: “Netflix takes our members’ privacy seriously. We comply with privacy and data‑protection laws everywhere we operate and have dedicated safeguards in place for kids who watch content on Netflix. This lawsuit lacks merit and we intend to vigorously defend the matter in court.” In the 66-page lawsuit, Florida accuses Netflix of carrying out a “years-long bait-and-switch” that has “led the company right to where it promised never to be: addicting children and families to its platform, mining those users for data, and then converting that data into lucrative intelligence for global advertising juggernauts”. The lawsuit claims Netflix opened Floridians’ data to commercial data brokers and advertising platforms after it launched advertisements in November 2022, allegedly allowing advertisers to “target Floridians by life stage, income, and household composition”. The complaint says Netflix failed to obtain the consent required under Florida law. It emphasizes that Netflix has in the past made a point to distinguish itself from tech companies that offer “free” services in exchange for data collection such as Google, Facebook and Amazon, but claims that Netflix has failed to live up to its promises to not track and monetize data similar to other tech companies. Netflix provides members with its updated privacy statement and terms of use annually, according to the streaming service. Those terms lay out the company’s advertising and privacy practices, along with users’ rights and available controls. It also offers parental controls that allow parents to filter or block content. The Florida case follows a lawsuit filed earlier this year by Texas officials accusing Netflix of spying on children and designing its platform to be addictive. Uthmeier has also filed lawsuits against OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, and TikTok this year. He recently kept Florida out of a multi-state settlement involving Meta, saying the $17bn agreement was “not enough to punish” the company over allegations that it failed to protect minor users. “We’re going to send a message to big tech companies. If you hurt our kids, you are going to have to pay for it,” Uthmeier said while announcing the Netflix lawsuit on Wednesday. “And so, in this lawsuit, we will be seeking billions of damages.”

title: James Talarico accuses Ken Paxton of ‘ignoring’ Epstein survivors
summary: Democrats are targeting Trump’s relationship with Epstein as part of strategy ahead of midterm elections
text: James Talarico, the Democratic candidate for Senate in Texas, accused his rival Ken Paxton of “ignoring” survivors of Jeffrey Epstein’s sexual abuse, as Democrats seek to increase pressure on Republicans ahead of November’s midterm elections. Speaking in Dallas, where Republicans are holding a midterm convention this week, Talarico appeared alongside one of Epstein’s victims at an exhibit that featured about 3.5m pages of Department of Justice’s files related to Epstein. “When did pedophilia become a partisan issue? When did holding sexual abusers accountable become controversial?” Talarico said. Talarico, who has emerged as one of the Democrats’ best hopes of winning one of the Republican Senate seats they need for a majority in the chamber, is among several members of his party appearing in Dallas this week, seeking to counter the Donald Trump-led convention. Democrats have made it clear in recent days that highlighting Trump’s longtime friendship with Epstein, a convicted sex offender, will be part of their strategy ahead of the midterms, and Talarico sought to loop Paxton into the attack. Talarico said survivors of Epstein’s abuse had requested to meet with Paxton, the Texas attorney general, but he had refused. “Our attorney general here in Texas has the power to get justice for these survivors, and he’s refusing to do so,” Talarico said. He added: “Ken Paxton has two choices: he can stand with these survivors and get justice, or he can continue to cover up Jeffrey Epstein’s abuse. The choice is entirely his.” The Epstein exhibit, which has previously been shown in New York, features row upon row of shelves holding all the files released so far related to Epstein. Critics say some of the documents released by the government revealed victim’s names, and that some material has been withheld. Speaking in Dallas, Sharlene Rochard, a survivor of Epstein’s abuse, said: “Questions remain about what hasn’t been released and why. Releasing only half of the documents is not transparency, and it cannot be where accountability ends. “I urge people to read the files, to follow the evidence, no matter where they lead. And when those leads reach someone wealthy, famous, politically connected, Republican or Democrat, keep following them, because justice that stops when it reaches power is not justice.” On Wednesday Gina Hinojosa, the Democrat running against the Texas governor, Greg Abbott, visited the same exhibit, reinforcing that the focus on Trump’s relationship with Epstein will not go away. “It’s really incredible that we live in a country where the justice system is so broken at every level that there has not been accountability of what we know was extensive sexual abuse, exploitation that happened for decades,” Hinojosa said, according to Associated Press. “And that powerful people who run this country are still living their lives without having been held to account.” Elsewhere Democrats condemned Trump’s Wednesday night speech promising a $5,000 “dividend” to all US adults if Republicans win the House of Representatives and Senate in November. Beto O’Rourke, former US congressman and presidential candidate, told a roundtable hosted by Bloomberg News in Dallas: “I think people will take it for what it is – it’s a gimmick, it’s a bribe. It’s another promise that the president will be unable to fulfill … It adds to the stink of desperation that is emanating from that convention centre.” At a press conference in a hotel near the convention centre, Robert Garcia, a Democratic congressman from California, told reporters: “Donald Trump is a known liar. This is the biggest liar to ever serve in government, period. And look, the dividend is not happening. He promised a dividend on tariffs; that didn’t happen. He promised the dividend on Doge; that didn’t happen. He promised some strange dividend from Air Force One six months ago; that never happened. “There’s no one in the country that thinks somehow this new dividend is actually going to happen. What the American people want is the president to actually focus on lowering the costs of gas, groceries and expand healthcare. The president has done the opposite. He’s made everything more expensive, and so he needs to stop lying and actually get to work.” Madeleine Dean, a congresswoman from Pennsylvania, described Republicans’ first midterm convention as a failure. “I think you can take a look at the arena last night, you can see the empty seats,” she said. “He is weak. His approval rating has plummeted. His numbers on the economy: a disaster. His numbers on this war: a disaster. His numbers of the personal economy for everyday Americans: a disaster. This is a spectacle really laced with fear.” The Democrats also faced questions about their colleague Senator John Fetterman’s surprise appearance in a video at the Republican convention. Dean said she has known Fetterman and his family for years “but what we have seen in his service as a senator is something very different than what I got know around John. You can see in his work ethic that he’s just not present.” The congresswoman said she held a one-to-one meeting with Fetterman in his office a couple of months ago, but it was “a disappointing conversation” and “he was not listening to me”. She added: “I am gravely disappointed with John and that stunt … I will tell you from the ground from suburban Philadelphia, my constituents are livid. Those who went out and knocked doors for him are absolutely livid.”

title: Victim families say it has ‘taken way too long’ to hold Saudi Arabia accountable for alleged support on 9/11
summary: Terry Strada, whose husband was killed in the attacks, says she remains hopeful for justice as a lawsuit alleging Saudi support for the hijackers moves toward trial
text: The leader of one group of 9/11 victims’ families says it has “taken way too long” to hold Saudi Arabia accountable for its alleged support of the terrorists who carried out the September 11, 2001 terrorist attacks, whose 25th anniversary is being observed across the US on Friday. As that grim milestone approached, Terry Strada – the national chair of 9/11 Families United – said she felt as if it had “been several lifetimes” for there to be progress in the effort “to achieve a modicum of justice through our court system” in connection with the deadliest act of terror against the US. But, even as the Saudis deny they had any role in 9/11, she added that she was as hopeful as ever that “the day of reckoning will come”. “We will have it,” she said. Strada’s role with 9/11 Families stems from the death of her husband, Tom, when terrorists intentionally crashed hijacked airliners into New York City’s World Trade Center, the Pentagon in Washington DC and a field in Pennsylvania, killing nearly 3,000 people. Tom Strada, 41, was killed at the World Trade Center, widowing Terry, with whom he had three children – including one who was less than a week old. Terry Strada subsequently became an advocate for people who lost loved ones on September 11 and wanted to be made as whole as possible in its aftermath. She said “getting to the truth and understanding everything” about how her husband was killed was not only the best way she could think of to honor his memory – but to also protect their country. One of the 9/11 families’ most visible attempts at accountability for the attacks has been a years-long civil lawsuit alleging that Saudi Arabia supported the al-Qaida terror group operatives who carried out September 11. Attorneys for Saudi Arabia have denied the lawsuit’s merits, maintaining that the kingdom has helped the US combat al-Qaida, its late founder Osama bin Laden, and terrorism in general. But in an August 2025 decision that Strada at the time called “another powerful step toward justice”, a federal judge in New York rejected a Saudi effort to dismiss the plaintiffs’ claims against the kingdom. The judge, George B Daniels, wrote in a legal opinion that an imam and an accountant’s employment by Saudi Arabia probably had links to their support of two al-Qaida members who came to the US in early 2000 to study English and take flight lessons. In his opinion, Daniels said that made the plaintiffs’ claims legally sufficient to proceed to trial, though it had not taken place as of Thursday. Other defendants named in the litigation – including al-Qaida itself, the Taliban and Iran – have already been found in default after not engaging with the claims. Regardless, as Friday loomed four days after celebrating her youngest son’s 25th birthday, Strada called on Saudi Arabia to “stop lying and take responsibility”. ABC News days earlier had reported on recently revealed records purportedly bolstering claims of Saudi complicity in 9/11. The outlet reported that those records included an alleged video of a kingdom agent casing the US Capitol, which investigators believe was the target of the airliner that crashed in Pennsylvania – and a sketch with calculations for flying a plane toward a ground target. Evidence of that kind was “strong”, Strada said. “You can’t deny it – and we are only getting more of it.” Nonetheless, the push to try that lawsuit has only been part of the focus for Strada’s advocacy alongside other kinds of 9/11 victims. Strada said she and many others collectively have spent years tracking the proceedings against a group of men who have spent years incarcerated at the US’s Guantánamo Bay detention camp for their alleged roles in the 9/11 attacks. She said she could hardly believe they were only recently given a tentative June 2028 trial date. Meanwhile, Strada was also a prominent voice against LIV Golf, the breakaway tour that was backed by Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund, which was launched in 2022 and spent billions of dollars luring players away from the US-based PGA. One professional US golfer who joined the LIV tour, Brooks Koepka, was asked what he would tell the families of 9/11 victims about his getting into business with a Saudi venture. He replied, in part, “I think as we move forward from that, we have to look toward the pathway to peace and forgiveness.” Strada and her allies disagreed with that kind of sentiment. “These people don’t understand how devastating September 11 was,” Strada said at the time. “My husband was dismembered. We don’t know where all his body parts landed. He has never been identified. “There was a psychological cruel[ty] that people do not realize.” All of which has made it a relief for Strada, she said in a moment of honesty, to see LIV Golf enduring deep financial struggles ahead of Friday. The tour filed for federal bankruptcy protection in her home state of New Jersey after abruptly losing its wealthy Saudi investors months earlier. Accusing them of “sportswashing”, Strada said, “The Saudis … [were] trying to improve their image and have a younger generation view them in a different way. And it didn’t work. There is some satisfaction in that.”
