title: Ministers face backlash from hospitality industry over ‘tourist tax’ plans
summary: Many mayors welcome power to impose tourist tax but industry warns of ‘irreparable harm’ and job losses
text: Ministers are facing a backlash from the hospitality industry after they announced mayors in England would be given sweeping powers to levy taxes on holiday accommodation such as hotels and Airbnbs. The plan, presented on Thursday by Angela Rayner, the local government secretary, will allow mayors to impose a “tourist tax” without a cap on how much they can charge and with few controls on how they can spend it. The move, which gives mayors some of their most significant tax-raising powers, was welcomed by regional leaders, who said it would give them a vital revenue stream at a time when local government is facing a funding crisis. Mayors will be expected to lay out their detailed plans for how they plan to use the new powers in early 2028. But it was met with outrage from hospitality businesses, who had expected the government to put stricter conditions on how much mayors could charge and how the money would be used. UKHospitality, the industry’s trade body, said a 5% overnight levy across England could result in 33,000 job losses and a £2bn hit to the economy, with regions more reliant on tourism, such as the Lake District, being worst affected. The owner of Premier Inn, Britain’s biggest hotel chain, said it would be “hugely damaging” and urged ministers to “avoid inflicting what could be irreparable harm on this large and vital sector of the economy”. Eddie Nelder, a co-owner of the Choice Hotels chain, which has hotels in Blackpool and the Lake District, said: “We’re here trying to stay alive, waiting for a lifeline from the government and we get another hammer blow. It feels like we’re being strangled.” However, Rayner said the tax-raising powers would help fund local communities. “This measure will give mayors the choice to raise and reinvest funding where it’s needed most,” she said in a statement before a meeting with the country’s mayors at No 10 North in Manchester. “It’ll help support the local services, public spaces and attractions that both residents and visitors rely on, with decisions taken by people who know their area best.” In the immediate term, the rate will be set at no more than 5% in almost every major English city after every Labour metro mayor agreed to cap their charges at that level. In a joint letter to Rayner, they wrote: “Foreign cities visited by British tourists from New York to Paris, as well as hundreds of smaller cities across the world, have long benefited from such levies while continuing to grow their tourism sectors. Granting the power to regions to introduce levies will help level the playing field by ensuring further investment in our cities, contributing to further growth.” But large parts of the east coast will not have to pay the tax after their mayors – two Reform UK and one Conservative – said they would refuse to impose them. The move follows a consultation launched by Keir Starmer’s government, and will bring England into line with many European countries and the US, where holidaymakers have for years been paying overnight visitor levies. Similar levies also apply in Wales and Scotland, though they will be capped in Wales. Edinburgh became the first city in Scotland to introduce a tourist tax, setting it at 5% in July. In Wales, councils will have the power to charge £1.30 per person a night in tax for most accommodation from April 2027. Under the proposal, which is expected to be introduced as a bill in parliament within months, mayors will be allowed to charge a levy as a percentage of the price of an overnight stay, rather than as a flat fee. Ministers at Westminster will cap the number of nights to which it can be applied in order to avoid hitting long-term rental properties. It is understood the cap is likely to be higher than the 5% that is applied by Holyrood. Any commercially rented property will face the tax, though there will be an exemption for those that are only rented occasionally on a casual basis. Mayors will be allowed to decide whether or not to exempt other sites such as festival campsites. They will also be allowed to share revenues with local councils. Kim McGuinness, the mayor of north-east England, backed the move for a visitor levy, saying it could bring money to the local economy during events such as the Great North Run, which is due to take place this Sunday. “A visitor levy could help us bring major international events to our region, back local businesses, improve visitor attractions, build on the 90,000 jobs already in this sector and unlock opportunities that come from a thriving visitor economy,” she said. “Most importantly, the money raised here would stay here, helping us invest in the future of our region rather than waiting for Whitehall to do it for us.” The move is one of the biggest handovers of power from the Treasury to local leaders in years, and comes before the first budget of Andy Burnham’s government, at which ministers have promised to hand over more tax powers to local leaders. It comes at a time when many local authorities are struggling for funds. Last year the government gave emergency funding worth £1.3bn to a record 28 councils, without which several said they would have gone bankrupt. But it also comes after a concerted effort by the government to ease the pressure on the hospitality industry, with many businesses struggling with high inflation and increased national insurance and minimum wage bills. Earlier this summer, the former chancellor slashed VAT on British summer holiday destinations, in a programme she called the “Great British summer savings scheme”. Meanwhile, in one of his first acts as prime minister, Burnham announced he would cut business rates for pubs, clubs and live music venues. Many hospitality businesses are struggling with high inflation, as well as additional national insurance and minimum wage costs imposed by Reeves in her first budget. Allen Simpson, the chief executive of UKHospitality, told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme: “What we’re talking about here is an open-ended power for mayors to set tourism taxes at any level they want … If you go to Paris, if you go to Rome, if you go to Berlin, you’re paying a small tourism tax, but it’s capped.” Additional reporting by Raphael Boyd

title: ‘It was all hands on deck’: how the CIA responded to 9/11
summary: Veterans recall chaos and confusion as the attacks unfolded – followed by a ‘war on terror’ that left agency with a tarnished reputation
text: A generation of spies had lost an enemy but not yet found a role. Then came 9/11. A decade after the dissolution of the Soviet Union, al-Qaida’s devastating attacks on New York and Washington on 11 September 2001 announced to the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) that the long era of battling communism, for which it had been founded, was officially at an end. It was to be replaced by a no-holds-barred “war on terror” that would leave the CIA with a soiled reputation over falsified intelligence that led to the invasion and occupation of Iraq, and an extraordinary rendition program in which suspects were subjected to “enhanced interrogations” at secret sites that official US inquiries subsequently defined as torture. The US intelligence community was dramatically transformed after two planes flew into the World Trade Center, a third smashed into the Pentagon, and a fourth crashed in the Pennsylvania countryside after passengers overcame the hijackers. Accounts of what unfolded inside the CIA’s headquarters in Langley, Virginia, suggests an organization unprepared for the drastically changed world the attacks ushered in, despite an awareness among some in the intelligence community that al-Qaida and its leader, Osama bin Laden, represented a clear and present danger. Margaret Henoch, then a counter-intelligence officer with little knowledge of terrorism, recalls confusion, chaos and an initial lack of direction from senior leadership as staff struggled to process what seemed like a bolt from a clear blue sky on that balmy late summer day. “One of my officers came in and said to me: ‘A plane just ran into the World Trade Center,’” she said. To this day, Henoch – who had previously been stationed in Vienna, where she focused on the International Atomic Energy Agency and nuclear threats – is haunted by the apparent vacuum that followed. About 40 minutes after the first attack, with no clear direction from the top of CIA, she decided to go up to the seventh floor, which accommodated the agency’s senior figures, including its then director, George Tenet. To her surprise, the area was deserted, apart from three assistants. “It was reasonable that they would have moved those guys someplace else,” said Henoch. “What was unreasonable, in my humble opinion, was that no one thought about all those people sitting in that building. Because if the Pentagon was hit, there was a chance that we, too, were a target – and it would be nice to believe that the people who left the building rapidly had a thought for all those who worked for them. “It was not clear that they did.” The Guardian contacted Tenet, now working in the private sector, for comment. In an emailed response, Bill Harlow, the CIA’s public affairs director at the time of the attacks, cited details in the 2007 memoir, At the Center of the Storm, which he co-wrote with Tenet, and said orders were issued for the majority of the staff to leave the building at “about 10am” – nearly an hour after the second plane struck at 9.03am. Harlow added: “We were aware at the time of intelligence gathered around 1995-96 of terrorist desires to attack CIA HQ with an airplane. “Director Tenet and the senior leadership moved to another building on the compound that presented a lower profile and would have a greater chance of survival if we were hit by a plane. “Notably, a decision was made that the personnel of the counter-terrorism center remained in the original headquarters building throughout that day … accepting the risk. The senior leadership team returned to the headquarters in the middle of the afternoon on 9/11.” ‘I had a briefing on who the hell al-Qaida was’ Some time afterwards, an order was given for the thousands of personnel in the building to evacuate. Some, including Henoch, were told to relocate to alternative sites to address the emergency. But by the time of that instruction, nearby roads were choked with traffic as commuters returned home from Washington DC after being released from work early. That prevented agency staff from departing, and triggered fears that they could be sitting ducks for the doomed fourth plane, which was already known to be in the air. “Large segments of the CIA operating staff were trapped,” Henoch said. “One guy, who was senior to me, was standing next to me in the car park and he said, ‘I have served in multiple war zones. I was a combat soldier in Vietnam and I’m going to die in the parking lot of the CIA.’” The dysfunctional scene was soon replaced by one of much greater conviction – leading to permanent changes in US intelligence. “I just remember loads of cable traffic coming in that said: it’s got to be al-Qaida,” said Henoch. “It wasn’t my world, so I had to have a quick briefing on who the hell al-Qaida was, because I just didn’t know anything about it. “The change was immediate. The next morning, everybody at the Central Intelligence Agency had to know who they were, and how it intersected with everything you were doing.” Steven Cash, a former CIA counter-terrorism officer who had left the agency to join the staff of the US Senate intelligence committee six months beforehand, faults the CIA’s pre-9/11 terrorism strategy as being too narrowly focused “looking to find bad guys” while neglecting the “political dimension”. “There was an emphasis on looking at terrorists as if they were a motorcycle gang,” said Cash, who had specialized on the Lebanese Shia group Hezbollah, a close ally of Iran. “A decision was made in the first [George HW] Bush administration to take terrorism away from the people who looked at geographic areas and separate it out. [It was] illustrative of a mistaken way of looking at the world, because terrorists don’t exist in a vacuum.” Cash moved on to focus on the Balkans before leaving the agency, but still harboured guilt after the attacks. “Was this our fault? Did we fail? That kind of guilt felt, at least for me, really personal.” Cash had been on Capitol Hill, attending a committee meeting, when news of the attacks filtered through. “Somebody said, put on the TV and we saw the second plane hit,” he said. “And then they started evacuating the building. “It was a mess. People were in the hall screaming, running around. The third plane had hit the Pentagon by that point, because we could see smoke across the National Mall.” The following day, Cash and his then boss, the late Democratic senator Dianne Feinstein, visited CIA headquarters and found a mood of determined resolve. “It was all hands on deck. The people I knew were getting deployed very quickly to Afghanistan,” he recalled. “These people are pros. They didn’t care whether they were blamed or not. They wanted to do something. “I have a little bit of survivor guilt here. Maybe I should have been shipped out to Afghanistan.” Political pressure On their visit to CIA headquarters on 12 September, senators asked agency operatives what legislation and resources they would need to respond to the attacks of the previous day, according to Cash. Two early – and controversial – results were the USA Patriot Act of 2001, which expanded law enforcement and surveillance powers, and the Homeland Security Act of the following year, creating the US Department of Homeland Security, which houses agencies including Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). Later changes established the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, with the goal of coordinating 18 different intelligence bodies and eliminating the lack of coordination widely held to blame for warning signs of the 9/11 plot going unheeded. “DNI was formed to make sure that we actually share everything with everybody. We don’t just keep it inside CIA,” said Susan Miller, a retired CIA counter-intelligence officer. “What’s really cool is we’ve changed how we do things across the board, not just for terrorism. It’s really improved things. There was no coordination before.” Yet the reaction to the attacks changed intelligence in another way – by making it more susceptible to political pressure, as President George W Bush’s administration searched for information that could be used to justify an invasion of Iraq to topple Saddam Hussein. In September 2002, Henoch – who had previously studied Russian weapons capabilities working at the Stanford Research Institute – was asked to assess intelligence provided by an Iraqi defector codenamed Curveball, who had sought asylum in Germany, and provided its intelligence agency with what he said was proof of Saddam’s biological weapons program. She quickly concluded the claims were fabricated, and passed her conclusions up the chain of command. They were not well received. When Colin Powell, the then US secretary of state, visited the CIA months later to review the agency’s intelligence on Iraq, Henoch and her fellow doubters were not informed. Powell’s subsequent speech to the United Nations security council in February 2003, in which he made the case for war, relied heavily on Curveball’s testimony – despite Henoch’s insistence when the address was checked with her and other officers beforehand that his assertions were not credible. “We took a look at the Powell speech and I said: ‘You can’t use this. We think this is garbage,” she said. “I did write somewhere – I can’t remember on what page – ‘How can you send someone to die for something like this? No one ever answered that for me. “The next thing I heard was, ‘Well, when we get in there, we’ll find something.’” After the invasion, inspectors found no evidence of biological weapons. Curveball was later debunked as a fraud. Miller, too, encountered the administration’s zeal for intelligence that could justify invading Iraq when she was posted to Prague as CIA station chief in 2002. Czech intelligence had investigated – and, initially, tentatively confirmed – a claim that one of the 9/11 ringleaders, Mohammed Atta, had travelled to Prague the previous year and met an Iraqi embassy official, Ahmad Samir al-Ani, months before the attacks. The report was seized on by the hawkish US vice-president, Dick Cheney, as evidence of Saddam’s possible links to the attacks, thus providing another justification for war. But Czech intelligence officials retreated from their earlier stance, and the CIA concluded there was no evidence that the meeting happened. Nevertheless, Donald Rumsfeld, then the US defense secretary, brazenly tried to revive it when Miller briefed him – along with George W Bush and Condoleezza Rice, the national security adviser – when they visited the Czech capital for a Nato summit in 2002. “‘Young lady, you forgot about this other thing’,” Rumsfeld told Miller, she said. “I played dumb and said: ‘What other thing?’ He replied: ‘Mohammed Atta was here in Prague meeting the Iraqi consul.’ “Bush was looking really uncomfortable and Condi was looking straight ahead. I simply said, ‘Mr President, Madam Secretary, and Mr Rumsfeld, the CIA, the Czech service and I don’t make things up. We give you the facts, and the fact is that he was not here.’ “Bush and Rice nodded in acceptance and the ambassador supported me. But Rumsfeld threw his pen down in disgust.” The invasion the neocons craved Whether the supposed meeting happened or not, Rumsfeld and his neoconservative allies got the invasion they craved – leading to a protracted conflict that tarnished the CIA’s reputation and whose length, along with the coinciding US-led military campaign in Afghanistan, spurred popular opposition to “forever wars”. Despite the blow to the agency’s standing, Cash insisted that its intelligence-gathering and functioning radically improved, thanks to the changes instituted after the attacks. “We have improved our intelligence capabilities significantly from what they were before 9/11,” he said, citing the success in preventing repeat attacks on US soil. But with the Trump administration now engaged in a war with Iran, roiling the Middle East, such security could no longer be guaranteed, he believes. “I’m not saying it was a great time,” Cash said, of the CIA’s record in the months and years after September 2001. “But the sense of purpose of being at a place in history where we – as a group, as a society – can do something, was pretty intoxicating. “I was very proud to have been part of it. It sucked – but proud to have been part of it. And I think everything we’re seeing now is the antithesis of that.”

title: Four people in hospital after stabbing in south-east London
summary: Seven people arrested following ‘altercation’ on Bromley High Street on Thursday afternoon
text: Seven people have been arrested after four men were stabbed in south-east London, the Metropolitan police said. Officers were called to reports of “an altercation” on Bromley High Street at 2.15pm and found four men with stab wounds, the force added. In a statement, it said: “Officers attended the scene alongside the London ambulance service and London’s air ambulance and found four men with stab wounds. Three of them were taken to hospital where they are receiving treatment for non-life-threatening injuries. One is in critical condition. “Seven men were arrested and they all remain in custody. Police inquiries continue and there is not believed to be any wider threat to the public.” A cordon was in place at the scene on Thursday, with police, as well as community support officers, standing around the perimeter. Forensics officers dressed in blue overalls and a crime scene photographer were coming and going from a branch of KFC, where locals said the incident occurred, and there were evidence markers visible on the floor. Abandoned food could still be seen on the tables as evening drew in, suggestive of the haste in which people left the restaurant amid the incident. “I heard a really loud bang and people running from KFC,” said George Ioannou, who was working in Antonio’s Male Grooming next door to the KFC. “An elderly woman ran into the shop and I had to lock the door to shelter her until it calmed down. She was crying. About five minutes later, we heard the sirens.” Other shop workers nearby said the incident was quick and that it was over in moments. The KFC has an alleyway down one side – along which people ran as they passed the male grooming shop – and faces on to Bromley’s High Street. Part of the latter was still closed to the public on Thursday evening. It is a busy thoroughfare, with a large shopping centre at one end and a train station taking commuters between Kent, south-east London and the capital’s centre at the other. Those and the parade of shops lining the high street draw large numbers of people from the surrounding area. About 15 bus routes were diverted, including the 61, 208 and 119. The London ambulance service said ambulance crews, a paramedic in a fast-response car, an incident response officer, an advanced paramedic and London’s air ambulance were dispatched to the scene. Four patients were treated at the scene before being taken to hospital, the service added. The Bromley and Biggin Hill MP Peter Fortune said: “I am aware of the incident on Bromley High Street this afternoon and I know that residents will have safety concerns. The police are in attendance and have made a number of arrests. I will remain in close contact with the police as they continue to investigate this incident.” A picture shared on social media on Thursday afternoon appeared to show a section of Bromley High Street cordoned off, with an emergency vehicle on site. The Met asked anyone with information to contact the police on 101.

title: Global bond sell-off resumes as surging oil prices stoke fears about inflation
summary: Crude jumps above $107 a barrel amid concerns over Middle East conflict and out-of-control government borrowing
text: Nervous investors across big economies have been dumping government bonds, driving up the cost of borrowing, as surging oil prices amplified fears about rising inflation. The cost of a barrel of oil jumped 6% to above $107 on Thursday amid concerns that advances by Houthi rebels along the Red Sea coast in Yemen could choke off Saudi crude exports. The global bond sell-off that has rocked markets in recent weeks resumed in response to the news from the Middle East – which came against a backdrop of escalating concern about out-of-control government borrowing. Higher oil prices, which had already climbed since hostilities resumed in the Iran war, are expected to drive up inflation, prompting central banks to raise interest rates and putting the brakes on economic growth. Donald Trump suggested on Wednesday that the conflict with Iran could continue until “immediately after” November’s US midterm elections, at which point he claimed oil prices would be “tumbling downward”. The European Central Bank (ECB) raised its main interest rate to 2.5% on Thursday, with its president, Christine Lagarde, saying: “We believe inflation will be longer lasting than we had anticipated.” “The conflict in the Middle East continues to ⁠generate inflation pressures, and inflation is set to remain well above target for an ⁠extended period,” she added. As Thursday’s sell-off gathered pace in London, the yield, or interest rate, on 10-year UK government bonds surged above 5.37% – the highest cost of borrowing since 2007 – creating a fresh headache for the new chancellor, John Healey. With less than seven weeks to go until Healey’s first budget on 28 October, higher interest rates on the UK’s debt-pile will raise the cost of future investment projects and eat into the Treasury’s fiscal headroom. At the same time, the prospect of higher energy bills as oil and gas prices rise is likely to intensify pressure on the government to help consumers to weather the winter. Unleaded petrol prices have already risen by 6p a litre since the start of September, according to the motoring organisation the RAC, while the prospect of higher inflation has prompted some banks to raise their mortgage rates. Healey has promised to provide a “breathing space” for UK households while also addressing the cost of doing business. In a speech on Monday, however, he also sought to tame bond market fears by committing himself to “controlling borrowing to bear down on inflation, and reducing long-term pressures on our public finances”. In the US, where Trump has promised to write a $5,000 (£3,700) cheque for every adult citizen if the Republicans win the midterms, Thursday’s sell-off pushed up the yield on 10-year borrowing to 4.92% – the highest since 2023. The cost of longer-term borrowing also continued to surge, with 30-year yields hitting the highest level since 2007, despite the US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, intervening directly in debt markets on Wednesday. Bessent hoped to bring down yields by buying back $6bn worth of government debt; but investors appeared to respond by deepening the sell-off. Kyle Rodda, a senior financial market analyst at the broker Capital.com, said: “Ultimately, a sustained drop in long-end yields can only be achieved by genuine shifts in macroeconomic policy: either the US government pulling back on spending or the Fed lifting rates.” Policymakers at the Federal Reserve, the US central bank, will meet under its new chair, Kevin Warsh, to set interest rates next week. Markets are expecting a rise – potentially enraging Trump, who has repeatedly demanded rate cuts. In a TruthSocial post last week, the president said: “The Fed Board, with its great new leader, must get smart – BE PATRIOTS for a change.” A plethora of UK data to be published over the next week, including on inflation, jobs and growth, will give an updated snapshot of how resilient the British economy has been in the face of the Iran war. In the first six months of the year, UK growth was the strongest among the G7 economies. This was despite higher-than-expected oil prices and the absence of hoped-for rate cuts. Bank of England policymakers will also meet next week, but are expected to leave the UK’s key interest rate on hold at 3.75% for the time being as they continue to monitor the impact of higher oil prices.

title: Trump faces growing scrutiny over ‘profoundly concerning’ cash gifts for aides including Natalie Harp
summary: The payments amounted to 30% of each aide’s $150,000 annual salary
text: Donald Trump may have committed “serious” ethical violations by giving three officials including his close personal aide Natalie Harp cash gifts of $45,000 each, according to a former White House “ethics czar”, as a watchdog group called for an investigation. The non-partisan Campaign Legal Center filed a complaint with the US Office of Government Ethics over the US president’s handouts to a handful of staff, arguing that an investigation was “clearly warranted”. Norm Eisen, who was a special counsel to Barack Obama for ethics and government reform, said the payments were a possible breach of regulation 18 USC 209, a federal conflict of interest statute that prohibits the US government’s executive branch employees from receiving payment beyond their salary for performing their official duties. The US president appeared to disregard that provision when he presented the payments to Harp, Chamberlain Harris and Margo Martin. The three aides reported the money on their financial disclosure forms as a “cash gift for holiday”. The payments amounted to 30% of each of the aides’ $150,000 annual salary. The Washington Post first reported the story. The White House has denied that they represent a breach of ethical codes. But Eisen said the denials strained credibility. “It appears to raise the most serious issues under 18 USC 209, which prohibits supplementation of income,” he said. “The White House denies that these payments represent income supplementation but that is hard to believe under the circumstances. “We’re not talking about some small gift or minor trinket, but about large sums.” James Thurber, another ethics specialist and a founder and former director of American University’s Center for Congressional and Presidential Studies, called the payments “legal but totally unethical”, adding in an email: “This is nothing new for Trump.” “The American public has a right to know where government employees’ loyalties lie,” said Kedric Payne, vice-president, general counsel and senior director for ethics at Campaign Legal Center. “Laws prohibiting government employees from receiving supplemental income are not arbitrary; they exist to ensure that public servants’ priorities remain focused on public service, not a wealthy benefactor who may have other objectives in mind. “An investigation into this matter is clearly warranted, and, if a violation is indeed found, this matter must be referred to the Department of Justice.” The statute states: “Whoever receives any salary, or any contribution to or supplementation of salary, as compensation for his services as an officer or employee of the executive branch of the United States government … from any source other than the government of the United States, except as may be contributed out of the treasury of any State, county, or municipality … shall be subject to … penalties.” These can include fines or imprisonment, depending on whether the breach was deliberate. The burden falls on both the giver and recipients of any payment deemed illicit. Eisen – now executive chair of the Democracy Defenders Fund, a non-profit group that has filed multiple lawsuits against the Trump administration – added: “There is a reason for these rules: we want our government employees’ first loyalty to be to the United States, and not to whoever happens to be its president. This is profoundly concerning.” The White House did not respond to requests for a response to Eisen’s comments. Harp, 35, who has been dubbed the “human printer” after she was said to carry a portable device to print out social media posts and articles favorable to Trump, has been the subject of recent public scrutiny because of the nature and intensity of her relationship with him. She was revealed to have sent the president gushing emails and accompanied him when he stealthily switched planes via a catering truck after a Nato summit in Turkey on the basis of a supposed assassination threat from Iran. Martin, a 31-year-old communications adviser, films Trump’s daily activities for social media posts. Harris, 26, is an executive assistant and was appointed last February to the US Commission of Fine Arts, which oversees Trump’s pet projects, including his controversial White House ballroom. Additionally, Walt Nauta, the director of Oval Office operations, reported a $20,000 gift from Trump. Nauta, who earns an annual salary of $175,000, also accompanied the president on the plane switch. He served as a valet during Trump’s first presidency and was a key witness and defendant in the Department of Justice’s investigation of Trump’s handling of classified documents at his Mar-a-Lago home, led by the special prosecutor Jack Smith.

title: Does Trump’s $5,000 ‘dividend’ count as a bribe if we never get the money?
summary: Trump’s promise to pay $5,000 to every adult US citizen if the Republicans win in November was only one questionable moment in a nearly two-hour speech
text: Hello, from the Republican midterm convention in Dallas, where on Wednesday night Trump definitely, definitely, did not try to bribe the American public into voting for his party in November. Speaking for almost two hours at the American Airlines Center, Trump promised to pay every adult citizen in the US $5,000 if Republicans retain the House and Senate in the midterm elections. The speech felt very much like a desperate last pitch to voters: the electoral equivalent of a dumped boyfriend offering to take his estranged girlfriend on a mini-break to Venice. It’s very important that even if the $5,000 offer might sound like a bribe – “if you do this for me, I will give you this money” – it is not a bribe; instead serving as a “dividend”, paid because of what Trump says is his administration’s “tremendous economic success”. The $5,000 non-bribe – inducement, perhaps – was the headline of Trump’s speech, during which the president was the liveliest he’s appeared in months. There were no surreptitious naps here as Trump rattled through some of his greatest hits (Sleepy Joe, Barack Hussein, Crooked Hillary) to the delight, initially, of the crowd. I say “initially” because this was evidence that you can have too much of a good thing. Even your favorite entertainer can go on too long. That was the case here, as an arena that wasn’t even full to begin with began to quietly empty after an hour and a half as Trump, becoming visibly drained by this point, leaned on his lectern and called Democrats “communist” for the 11th time. Earlier there had been energy from the audience, with the Maga base cheering and laughing in the way a crowd might will on a comedian who is fondly regarded, but way past his prime. They went wild for Trump’s bizarre character assassination of Ken Paxton, his handpicked candidate for Senate, who was the butt of a joke. Trump has invested a lot of political capital in Paxton – a flawed candidate who is running neck-and-neck with the Democrat James Talarico – so you might have thought the president would spend his time here lavishing praise. But this is Trump, who a) is just odd, and b) can never resist an opportunity to put another person down. “He may not dress right. He may not talk exactly perfectly, and he may not be the best-looking guy I’ve ever seen,” Trump said of Paxton. He wasn’t wrong, but it’s not the kind of thing that will convince people to vote for the guy, although Trump rounded off the remarks with the claim that Paxton “is the greatest attorney general in America”. That statement is worth a fact check, and we should be skeptical, too, about whether Americans will ever get that $5,000. As the Bulwark’s Catherine Rampell pointed out, Trump has previously discussed paying Americans: a “Doge dividend”; $2,000 tariff dividends; and checks from Obamacare rebates. Those payments also were not bribes, but neither did they ever come to pass. title: Forgetful Farage shares rose-tinted memories of Reform’s party conference | John Crace
summary: Oops, Nige skipped over the most embarrassing and dark details – let’s set the record straight
text: Which one of us has not dreamed of getting a personal email from Nigel Farage? So imagine the excitement that Reform supporters must have felt when a message from their leader dropped into their inboxes late on Wednesday night. And mine. Could he also be about to offer everyone in the country £5,000 in return for electing a Reform government? Sadly not. Even Honest Bob’s planned welfare cuts won’t cover that. Instead, Nige was treating us all to his reflections on his party conference that had just ended. The only drawback was that there appeared to be some gaps in his memory. Let’s be kind and assume he was pushed for space. So let’s help him fill in the blanks. Dear John. ‘Wow.’ That’s what I kept thinking as our conference closed. Good start, Nige. Because that’s what I was thinking too. It’s not every party conference that is completely derailed by an undercover investigation into allegations of illegal sources of party funding. And it came completely out of the blue. Who would have thought that a party leader under investigation over a £5m gift from a Thai crypto billionaire, and a party whose main funder is Ben Delo – who was convicted in the US for failing to comply with legislation against money laundering – might be implicated in possible wrongdoing? But we can all admire the sheer professionalism with which you handled the crisis. It was a stroke of genius to dismiss two of your oldest muckers as mere contractors. After all, Dan Jukes had only been your right-hand fixer for 10 years and James Orr, the Cambridge professor of ethics – nice touch that – was your head of policy. Of course it was all “loose pub talk”. Everyone goes to the pub to discuss how they plan to break the law. And you definitely “hadn’t been listening”. We could tell that by the way you appeared to join in the conversation. Such bad luck it’s all ended up in yet another police investigation. It’s obviously massively reassuring that you say you can’t be bought. But you can clearly be rented. 6,000 of us packed in Birmingham’s National Exhibition Centre. And may I say how pleasing it was that none of you felt you needed to come in a balaclava. What this country needs are patriots who are prepared to stand up and be counted. Who can be relied on to protest against the arrival of foreigners arriving by small boats. From now on, it will be Reform policy that the RNLI should be disbanded. We can’t have a country of volunteers who are prepared to jeopardise their own lives to save others. They are nothing less than traitors and send all the wrong messages to the rest of the world. I know I speak for everyone when I say that all Brits would rather drown than have one more foreigner step ashore in Portsmouth. I was also immensely proud to see so many in the audience at your conference speech who were willing to assault a female protester. Making England Great Again. Robert Jenrick nailed it when he said: “Boohoo.” We got Starmer out and are still neck and neck with Labour in the polls. Er, yes. That’s one way of putting it. Another is that you were at least eight points ahead of Labour only a few months ago. Your popularity may have peaked. The more people get to see of you the less they like you. It also seems that voters much prefer a leader who doesn’t require a minimum of £1m a year to get out of bed and a party that doesn’t seem to lurch from one financial scandal to the next. Zia Yusuf and I will put the Royal Navy in the Channel and stop the boats. This is the Zia Yusuf who is so unpopular that everyone in your inner circle privately refers to him as “the wanker” and is so disliked that no constituency wants him to stand as their Reform candidate. Yet he insists on referring to himself as the “shadow home secretary” when he remains outside Westminster. But let’s indulge you. Let’s pretend that Zia is elected an MP. Do you really think the Royal Navy is going to participate in operations to turn back the small boats that could result in the deaths of dozens of migrants? You saw the odds-on next prime minister of France, Jordan Bardella, sign a historic memorandum of understanding with us to make this happen. Or the memorandum of misunderstanding as we prefer to call it. Still, it gave us a huge laugh to see you pull the wool over the “wet behind the ears” Jordan. It’s so good to see Reform turn over its political allies abroad. A reminder to Johnny Frenchman that when we left the EU it was to put some distance between us and him. It was a masterstroke to write the memorandum in both English and French, and sneakily adding a clause in English agreeing that France would take back all migrants who had arrived in England. And as Jordan’s English was not that good, he never noticed! Chapeau! Or perhaps he’s a bit thick. Either way, he’s a lot less odds-on to be the next prime minister because Marine Le Pen is furious with him and there’s an almighty row going on in the National Rally party. In our first 100 days, Richard Tice pledged to cut £250 off your energy bill by scrapping the mad levies on them. No one thinks Dicky is going to do anything. Everyone inside the party thinks he is just an afternoon TV presenter from the 1980s. A man born to be your hype person. Who owes his entire existence to you. The same goes for Robert Jenrick and Suella Braverman. Politicians too mediocre even for the Tory party. It’s looking like we’ll need 10,000 candidates for the general and local elections. Recruiting that many candidates will be a mammoth task. So I need more of you than ever to step forward. It goes without saying that the 6,000 of you in Birmingham are already on the list. But we still need 4,000 more. So, please, I beg you, delete your Facebook and other social media accounts, where you might accidentally have liked something racist or spread idiotic conspiracy theories, and sign up. That includes you, Matt Goodwin. Your country needs you. Yours, Nigel Farage

title: Former PE teacher faces lengthy jail term for sexually abusing pupils
summary: Bronwen James, 30, admitted offences against two girls at schools in Wiltshire and Hampshire, and found guilty of charges involving boy
text: A former PE teacher is facing a lengthy jail sentence for grooming and sexually abusing three pupils at two schools. Bronwen James, 30, admitted offences against two girls at schools in Hampshire and Wiltshire and was found guilty by a jury of charges involving a boy. The Crown Prosecution Service described James’s crimes as “a sustained pattern of predatory behaviour against children in her care” and praised the teenagers she targeted for coming forward. Judge James Bromige asked for reports to be prepared on James so that he could assess the danger she posed when sentencing her later this year. Her defence team said she knew she faced a significant jail sentence. During her trial at Winchester crown court, jurors were told that James, from Chippenham in Wiltshire, flirted with a 16-year-old boy in class at a school in Southampton. They began exchanging Snapchat messages and arranged for her to drive him to a promenade, where they kissed in her car. Later they went to her house where they cuddled while watching the Wimbledon tennis championships on the television before going to her bedroom where they had sex. She told him she loved him and wanted him to move away with her. Edward Culver, prosecuting, told the trial the school was made aware of the incident after another student showed a teacher some text messages apparently sent between the James and the complainant. He said: “They suggested a sexually charged relationship. He [the boy] was named as ‘number 8’ in the messages as a cover. She acted not only in an unprofessional and overfamiliar way, but failed to recognise any boundaries, exploiting her position to engage in sexual activity with one of her young students.” In a police interview, the boy said he had been “groomed” by the defendant. James was convicted of three counts of sexual activity with a child by a person in a position of trust. Before the trial, James pleaded guilty to offences against two girls. One was a pupil at the same Southampton school as the boy, the other attended a school in Wiltshire that James had also taught at. The offences included sexual activity with a child, sexual communication with a child and making an indecent photograph of a child. The victims were 13 and 14 at the time. During legal argument, which can now be reported, it also emerged that at the start of her career, James received a warning while she was teaching at the private Seaford college in West Sussex for giving her personal mobile number to a pupil. Bethany Adams, of the CPS, said: “Bronwen James was trusted to educate and protect children. Instead, she used that trust to groom and sexually abuse three students. “James manipulated her victims with calculated precision, exploiting her position of authority to isolate them and normalise the abuse. “This was not a lapse in judgment; it was a sustained pattern of predatory behaviour against children in her care. “The courage shown by James’s victims in coming forward has been instrumental in securing this conviction. I hope it gives them, and their families, some measure of justice.”

title: Secret son revelation ignites bitter succession dispute in Ugandan kingdom
summary: Family of late King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV reject committee’s choice of cousin and TV presenter as new monarch
text: A traditional Ugandan kingdom has become engulfed in a bitter succession dispute after the family of a king who recently died rejected the selection of a television news anchor as his successor. King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, who became the world’s youngest reigning monarch when he took the throne in the kingdom of Tooro in 1995 at the age of three, died on 27 August in the US, where he was receiving cancer treatment. On Wednesday, the royal clan’s succession committee announced it had chosen Oyo’s cousin Prince Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma, a news anchor and editor at the public broadcaster UBC, as crown prince. However, at a press conference held later the same day, Oyo’s sister, Princess Ruth Nsemere Komuntale, said that according to her brother’s will, a son whose existence had not been publicly known until his death should succeed him. The kingdom’s ‌spokesperson shared a section of the document, which says: “I hereby declare and direct that if, at the date of my death, I am survived by a son lawfully recognised as my biological son, I appoint him as my heir to the throne of the kingdom of Tooro.” In a statement on Thursday, Oyo’s mother, Queen Mother Best Kemigisa Akiiki, denounced a “self-appointed group of clan members” who had selected a new king despite having had the will read to them hours earlier. She also claimed that the royal family had been put under house arrest. Troops had “removed the royal guards without notice, and ... were deployed around the palace,” she said. “We cannot leave or receive people freely.” Oyo was unmarried and was not known to have any children. The Tooro kingdom’s prime minister, Calvin Armstrong Rwomiire Akiiki, revealed the existence of a son in a social media post on 27 August when announcing Oyo’s death. “His majesty leaves behind a prince as his heir, whose identity will be formally revealed at the appropriate time, in accordance with the traditions and customs of Tooro kingdom,” he said. Another contender had been Prince George Desmond-Kamurasi, who plays for the London amateur football club South East Dons. According to the committee, the goalkeeper had declined the offer of the throne because of his other responsibilities. The Tooro king is selected by a succession committee appointed by the royal clan. A committee member told the local NTV station that a royal child must be officially introduced to elders in order to be considered for leadership. Andrew Mwenda, ⁠a prominent Ugandan journalist and relative of the royal family, wrote on X on Thursday that Oyo’s family had not been able to produce a photo of the purported son, and declined to disclose details about the family of the boy’s mother. He added that, in Tooro, a king’s son could only succeed him if he were born to ‌a queen officially married to the king. The prime minister called for restraint on Thursday. “There will be time to examine the will, to hear those advancing a different position, and to consider our customs, the applicable law and the proper institutions through which succession should be determined,” he said in a social media post. “That process should take place calmly and credibly, not through competing announcements, confrontation, or attempts to establish facts on the ground while our king still awaits burial.” Edward, a popular TV news presenter, is the son of Prince Christopher Paul Kijanangoma and a grandson of the former king George David Rukidi III. Oyo, who was crowned after his father’s death, will be buried on Saturday at the Karambi royal tombs in the kingdom’s capital of Fort Portal in western Uganda. Uganda has several ancient kingdoms that lack formal sovereignty, but whose leaders are revered as symbols of tradition and wield vast social influence. Tooro is one of five that are recognised by the government. Their monarchs have no political authority and are legally barred from engaging in partisan politics. In 1967 Uganda’s then president, Milton Obote, abolished the kingdoms, saying he wanted to unify the country. They were restored by the current president, Yoweri Museveni, in 1993. The Tooro are the latest African royal family to become mired in a succession dispute. King Misuzulu Sinqobile kaZwelithini, the reigning king of the Zulu people in South Africa, waited 15 months for his coronation after the death of his father because of a bitter feud involving accusations of forgery and poisoning. Reuters and the Associated Press contributed reporting

title: Steve Hilton vows to abolish California DMV if elected governor
summary: Republican calls department of motor vehicles a ‘bloated bureaucracy’ as he seeks to boost his longshot campaign
text: The longshot California gubernatorial candidate Steve Hilton pledged this week to abolish the state’s department of motor vehicles if he is elected, promising to shutter the oft-criticized department for good and set a flat $73 annual registration fee per car. Hilton, a Trump-backed former conservative pundit running in reliably blue California, called the state’s DMV a “bloated bureaucracy”, during a Tuesday campaign event, echoing the Trump administration’s efforts to slash the federal workforce. “The plan for buildings like this is to turn them into something that’s actually useful for California,” he said, standing in front of the DMV in West Hollywood. “We’re going to turn DMV offices into after-school clubs.” A California DMV spokesperson declined to comment on Hilton’s remarks. For many US motorists, updating their license at the DMV can be a herculean feat with lengthy wait times. And vehicle registration fees, which California motorists must pay annually, are steep: typically several hundred dollars a year. However, it is unlikely the state’s DMV could be abolished. The California legislature, in which Democrats hold a supermajority in both the state assembly and senate, would need to pass Hilton’s proposed legislation. Hilton also faces an uphill battle in the gubernatorial race. A Republican has not been elected to a statewide position in 20 years, and Hilton is trailing well behind his Democratic rival, Xavier Becerra, in recent polls. In a news release expanding on the idea, Hilton took aim at the cost of running the state’s offices – the legislature allocated $1.46bn to the DMV for the 2025-26 fiscal year – and the fees drivers pay for services at the DMV. He proposed transferring some functions of the DMV online and punting routine car title and plate transactions to local county offices. Becerra’s campaign, meanwhile, suggested his proposal would risk driver safety. “Nothing says ‘safer roads’ like outsourcing driver safety checks to the lowest bidder,” spokesperson Jonathan Underland said in a statement.

title: Democratic socialist clinches Rhode Island nomination amid party victories
summary: David Morales wins Democratic primary for Providence mayor, unseating the incumbent mayor, Brett Smiley
text: In the latest in a string of victories by progressives across parts of the US, the democratic socialist David Morales won the Democratic primary for mayor in Providence, Rhode Island, on Wednesday night, unseating the incumbent mayor, Brett Smiley. The Rhode Island state representative, who was endorsed by the Vermont senator Bernie Sanders as well as the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), is now the favorite to secure the mayoralty in the deep blue city’s November general election against the Republican nominee, 77-year-old David Talan. If he wins, Morales, at 27, will be the youngest mayor Providence has ever had. “Few believed that a 27-year-old democratic socialist could ever, few believed that we could ever take on big money, corporate real estate interests and endless attack ads – and we took them on and we won,” Morales said in his victory speech, which he delivered partly in Spanish. “The same way that we campaigned, we are going to govern – in coalition, side by side with our neighbors,” he added. Morales ran on a progressive platform pledging sweeping changes including capping annual rent hikes, building more affordable housing and raising taxes on corporate polluters and landlords. Rent stabilization was a key factor in the race, with Smiley, now ousted after one term, having vetoed a rent-stabilization ordinance back in April that had been passed by the city council. “When working people are getting priced out of the city that they love, then we must cap rent increases at 4% every single year,” Morales said. “We put housing justice on the ballot.” Morales, the son of a Mexican immigrant single mother, also took a hardline stance on making Providence an official sanctuary city and standing up to Donald Trump’s aggressive anti-immigrant agenda. “The city of Providence must use every tool that we have at our disposal to defend our immigrant community and protect us from the fascist ICE agents,” he said in his primary victory speech. In his tenure as mayor, Smiley had also faced scrutiny for implementing the city’s largest property tax increase in a decade, and for his continued support for Israel. Morales, by contrast, has accused the Israeli government of committing genocide in Gaza, and is a fierce proponent of Palestinian freedom. Born in Soledad, California, Morales became the youngest graduate in the history of the Brown University public administration master’s program. And when he was elected to the Rhode Island house of representatives at age 22, he became the youngest Latino ever elected to a US state legislature. He is also a part-time professional wrestler. A victory for Morales in November would follow a surge of democratic socialist victories in US cities this year, following the groundbreaking election of Zohran Mamdani as mayor of New York City last November. Since then, the Seattle mayor, Katie Wilson, has also taken office, with Janeese Lewis George set to follow in Washington DC, and the movement secured a string of summer wins in Democratic primaries in places including Michigan, Florida, Colorado, New York and Pennsylvania. As momentum around leftwing challengers to more established incumbents continues to grow, focus will turn to Los Angeles over the coming months, where another member of the DSA, Nithya Raman, will attempt to continue this winning streak against the current mayor, Karen Bass.

title: Shabana Mahmood urges police to curb far-right, anti-migrant protests
summary: Home secretary tells officers to make ‘full use’ of their powers after masked vigilantes cause weekend of chaos
text: Shabana Mahmood has urged police to curb the activities of far-right, anti-migrant groups which have “obvious malign intent” after a weekend of chaos caused by balaclava-wearing vigilantes. In a meeting on Thursday, the home secretary told senior officers to make “full use” of their powers, including bans on face coverings, after police were assaulted and ports were disrupted in Kent and Hampshire. She signalled the need for “strong deterrence” and improved intelligence in light of new tactics being deployed by groups such as Patriot Platform, led by the convicted kidnapper Daniel Thomas, which helped to organise the protests. Mahmood told the officers: “These scenes have caused disruption for people and, given that people are dressed in black wearing balaclavas, there is a fear factor and obvious malign intent being communicated to our residents. This makes it different from other protests, so we need to make sure we are learning lessons.” The Home Office and police were criticised in the aftermath of the weekend for failing to take a hard line on the far right. Environmental campaigners and civil liberties groups have complained that there appears to be a “two-tier” approach, with peaceful climate protesters prosecuted more aggressively than far-right agitators. Police in Dover on Saturday and then Portsmouth on Sunday were taken by surprise when hundreds of protesters wearing black clothes and face masks massed to oppose what they say is illegal immigration via small boats. Both protests are believed by police to have been far-right inspired, with evidence emerging that those behind them were determined to avoid detection. Thursday’s online meeting was held ahead of this weekend, when further disruption is predicted to take place. Mahmood told senior officers to make better use of intelligence to ensure they have the correct resources and expertise in place, and made clear the government’s expectation that police should make full use of the powers at their disposal to ensure anyone who is committing a criminal offence is dealt with “robustly”. The home secretary urged police to make full use of digital evidence, including body-worn video, facial recognition technology, CCTV, ANPR and other intelligence products to identify offenders. The move raises the possibility that Hampshire police will insist that protesters due to meet in Portsmouth at 12.30pm on Saturday will be ordered to take off any face coverings. Forces have planned an “enhanced and coordinated approach to intelligence gathering and operational planning” ahead of the weekend – laying the groundwork for a more proactive response. Labour’s Crime and Policing Act, which took effect in April, gave police powers to create mask-free zones at protests, backed by fines of up to £1,000 or one month’s imprisonment, or both. The power only applies to people who are trying to conceal their identity, rather than those covering their face for reasons of religion, health or work, and officers must take reasonable steps to notify the public of the restriction. Saturday’s protests in Dover, which Thomas claimed to have organised, blocked the town’s roads for several hours, disrupting traffic heading to and from the port. Kent police initially claimed that they had no warning of the Dover protest. That claim fell apart when the force admitted there were warning calls to police on Friday evening which were not acted upon. After a dinghy carrying 120 asylum seekers was rescued on Sunday near the Solent, about 200 black-clad men gathered at Eastney Marina. Protesters blocked roads, leading to alleged assaults on several officers. No one was arrested at either demonstration. Patriot Platform has attempted to bring together disparate local “patriot” groups rather than construct a single hierarchical organisation. In a further development, RNLI volunteers and staff have been warned not to wear the charity’s branding because of the “unacceptable abuse” they have faced from anti-migrant protesters. The charity has issued security advice since the protests in Dover and Portsmouth, which saw its workers targeted for bringing some small boat migrants ashore. This week, footage posted on social media showed volunteers being labelled as “traitors” after helping to look after people who had arrived in a dinghy in Portsmouth. Protests have been held at RNLI sites, including on Wednesday, when a small anti-migrant gathering was held at the RNLI College in Poole, Dorset. Commenting after the meeting, the deputy chief constable Andy Mariner, the NPCC lead for public order, said: “Policing is continually assessing and preparing for protests and any potential impact on public safety. This includes working closely with local forces, specialist teams, communities and partners, monitoring publicly available information, and ensuring the right resources are available where needed. “We have stepped up this activity this week at a national level, supporting local forces to ensure we have the right information, support and operational capacity in place to respond should we need to. “This includes ensuring commanders are ready to use every power at our disposal, from arrests and dispersal orders to more recent powers which can help police manage protests, where it is proportionate and necessary to do so.”

title: Remains found in North Carolina in 1970s identified as 15-year-old girl
summary: Advanced DNA testing reveals skeletal remains belong to Cindy Marcell Blizzard, who had run away from home
text: Skeletal remains discovered nearly 50 years ago in North Carolina have been identified as those of a 15-year-old girl who had run away from home. On 29 December 1977, skeletal remains and clothing were discovered in a wooded area near a tire manufacturing plant in Wilson, a city approximately 40 miles (80km) east of Raleigh. After decades of DNA testing, and with advances in technology, investigators identified the remains as belonging to Cindy Marcell Blizzard, a 15-year-old girl who had run away from her home in Monkton, Maryland, in the spring of 1977, the North Carolina state bureau of investigation (NCSBI) said. “Her death remains unsolved, investigators are still looking for answers,” the NCSBI said on Tuesday. When Blizzard’s remains were discovered in 1977, a medical examiner determined they belonged to a white female between approximately 16 and 23 years old who had probably been in the area for six months to two years, according to the NCSBI. Although the medical examiner’s office classified the manner of death as undetermined, circumstances surrounding the location and recovery of the remains raised the possibility of foul play, the NCSBI said, adding that investigators were treating the case as a homicide. Following the discovery of the remains, investigators compared dental records with missing persons cases but were unable to find a match. The case eventually went cold due to limitations in forensic technology. In 2010, a state anthropologist reopened the case and submitted the victim’s teeth for DNA testing but no positive match was found. Fourteen years later, the NCSBI’s cold case investigative team, led by special investigator Andy Murr, reviewed the case again, this time using more advanced forensic tools. Working with the medical examiner’s office, Murr determined the case was eligible for advanced DNA testing. A forensic lab tested a bone sample and created a DNA profile that allowed investigators to search for potential relatives. With help from the Maryland state police homicide unit and the Raleigh police department’s intelligence unit, the search ultimately led investigators to identify the victim as Blizzard. Investigators are urging anyone with information about Blizzard to contact the SBI cold case tip line at 919-582-TIPS, email coldcases@ncsbi.gov or contact the Wilson county sheriff’s office at 252-237-2118.

title: Francophiles, Norman outfits and broken threads: visitors see Bayeux tapestry in UK for first time
summary: Visitors got a first glimpse of the medieval artefact after it went on display at the British Museum in London
text: On the day Bayeux tapestry tickets were released, Megan Stockwell was at the beach. She was so determined to lock down her spot, that she sat with her toes in the sand for an hour, waiting in the online queue. “The whole ticket buying experience felt like what other people would do to get Taylor Swift tickets. I was like, ‘oh God, am I, like, the geek version of this?’” she recalled. Like any committed Swiftie, Stockwell felt confident the experience would be worth the hassle and cost. As a self-professed Francophile, she was fascinated by how the tapestry, which is temporarily housed at the British Museum until next July, tells the story of the Franco-British relationship through the Norman conquest, culminating in the battle of Hastings. “You just grow up learning so much about it – at primary school, in history studies. You’ve always got some mention of the Bayeux tapestry, the Normans, the fact there’s even three lions on the back of our pound coins comes from Normandy. “We’ve got such a close connection between French and British culture, our language and everything. This sort of feels like a visual representation of that,” she said. Stockwell’s dogged pursuit of tickets, fascination with the Franco-British relationship, and childhood memories of learning about the battle of Hastings, were experiences shared by many of the visitors on the exhibition’s opening day. Cydney, who lives in Texas, also drew inspiration from her experience queueing for concert tickets to secure a coveted opening day spot. She had woken up at 3am local time to join an online queue for an hour and half to secure them when they were released. She anticipated it would be worth it: “It’s going to be life-changing, we’re so excited.” Cydney had studied history for her undergraduate degree. “So I just really am interested to see what a significant artefact would be and to see how this is basically where the history of England and the UK as we know it really all began. Seeing something so old is just incredible and honestly such an honour.” Her feelings were echoed by Adrian Harris, who was so moved to catch the exhibition that he signed up for British Museum membership purposely to gain early access to tickets. He ended up the second person through the doors on Thursday morning, after joining a “really jolly” queue at 9.30am. “It was incredible. It was very, very moving to walk down the steps and to see the length and breadth of it. And I think they’ve done it so well, the British Museum. It was very profound to see it,” he said, adding he had been especially thrilled to spy Westminster Abbey, where he works, on the cloth. He noted that although he was one of the first through the doors, he felt that 40 minutes was a restricted timeframe to see the 68-metre tapestry, though he observed that attendants were diligent in ushering people along. A number of ticket holders for the Bayeux tapestry at a special first viewing last weekend were reportedly turned away after other visitors took too long to view it. The French owners of the tapestry have issued strict orders on when lights must be turned off in order to preserve the work. Richard and Madeleine Abramson, who were in the first group alongside visitors dressed in Norman costumes, agreed that 40 minutes was a short time, but that it was being well policed. “They’re very clear at the beginning there’s a maximum time … they’re very carefully moving you on,” said Madeleine. However, the oversight did not dampen the pair’s enthusiasm. “It was pretty awe-inspiring,” said Richard. “It’s very well presented, it develops like a film. It’s got a story to tell: it starts quietly, then it gets more intrigue and then you get to the action and it builds up to the battle, which is quite violent.” Madeleine felt the tapestry loomed large for many former English schoolchildren. “Of all the history lessons you have, every child remembers 1066,” she said, adding that the fact the tapestry was stitched by female embroiderers also resonated. “[That they] told this whole story is still phenomenal,” she said. Vivien and Karen had travelled from Hampshire to see the tapestry, also buoyed up by memories of their school days. “We learned about it at school. It’s something that’s always been in the back of your mind, then all of a sudden it’s here, so why not?” said Karen. Vivien practises needlework, and was especially excited to witness the craftsmanship up close. “I’ll be looking for the two broken threads,” she said. Denise Davies had bought two tickets for her husband John’s birthday. As a taxi driver who also runs black cab heritage tours of London, he was looking forward to expanding his historical knowledge. At £33 a peak-time ticket, the exhibition’s cost has attracted some criticism – but Denise felt it was worth it. “I could go to Alton Towers and it would cost me an arm and a leg. This is something special. I would have paid whatever it was because we’re never going to see it again … it’s a tick on the bucket list, basically.” • This article was amended on 11 September 2026 to describe the tapestry as being stitched, not woven, by female embroiderers.

title: The hospitality industry fears a tourist tax will deter visitors – the evidence says otherwise
summary: Studies from hotspots across Europe that have introduced levies suggest they have no impact on visitor numbers
text: If you wandered down Las Ramblas or lazed on a beach in the Balearics this summer, you probably paid a tourist tax for the privilege. In fact, if you enjoyed any of Europe’s beauty spots in recent years, it is likely that an overnight levy was added to your bill. Britons have become used to paying these fees abroad but ministers have shied away from introducing them in the UK. The furious response from UK hospitality bosses helps to explain why. The trade body UKHospitality estimates that a 5% tax on overnight stays in England would result in 12m fewer visits and 33,000 job losses, piling further pressure on an industry battling an increase in taxes and employment costs, as well as the effects of war, Covid and Brexit. In places like the Lake District and the Yorkshire Dales, which rely heavily on tourism, businesses are concerned that visitors will instead go to other parts of the country that choose not to impose such a levy. Large parts of England’s east coast, for example – from the seaside resort of Skegness to the town of Hartlepool – are expected to remain levy-free after their mayors, from Reform UK and the Conservative party, opposed the proposals on Thursday. But are overnight levies a success? The evidence suggests that it depends what mayors want to achieve, but they could be very lucrative. They were introduced in cities including Amsterdam, Barcelona and Venice as a way to prevent over-tourism. But there is little evidence they kept visitors at bay: trips to all three destinations have risen consistently over the past decade (despite Amsterdam charging an additional 12.5% for an overnight stay, believed to be the most expensive tourist tax in Europe). In April 2023, Manchester became the first place in the UK to introduce an overnight visitor levy, charging £1 per room per night in the city centre. A study published in the journal Tourism Management in 2025 found that the tax had had “no significant impact” on the occupancy of hotels in the city. In sharp contrast to the vocal opposition of national trade bodies, in Manchester it was hospitality businesses that introduced the levy through a business improvement district. Local leaders say the £1-a-night levy has raised £10.5m in its first three years of operation, with the revenue ringfenced for cultural projects such as the Brit awards and Mobo awards, both hosted in Manchester this year. When Labour MPs visit Liverpool for their party conference later this month, they too will be paying a tourist tax: a £2-a-night charge was introduced by its hospitality firms last June, raising more than £2m for projects in sports, culture and conferencing. Councils in Scotland already have the power to introduce local overnight levies, with Wales following suit next April. Only Edinburgh has taken the plunge so far, introducing a 5% tourist tax on 24 July, although Cardiff, Glasgow and three other regions of Scotland are expected to follow next year. Allen Simpson, chief executive of UKHospitality, said on Thursday that Edinburgh’s new charge was “already having damaging effects” on the city. However, Edinburgh Tourism Action Group, which represents the city’s tourism industry, told the Guardian it was “too early to draw any meaningful conclusions” on its impact. It said many of the cities that had adopted the scheme, including Manchester, had “not experienced a decline in visitor numbers” as a result. While there is little detailed international research on the economic impact of tourist taxes, a study by Bangor University in Wales in 2024 found no evidence to suggest they deter visitors. Researchers found they had been introduced in 125 destinations and 26 countries across Europe by 2019, with exceptions mainly in the Nordics and Baltic region. The modest nightly charges were being used to fund hundreds of millions of pounds worth of public projects, they found. In the Balaeric Islands, for example, the tourism tax had funded €263m (£226m) worth of projects since 2016, including social housing and scientific research. Zoë Billingham, the chief executive of IPPR North, a thinktank which has campaigned for a tourist tax, said it was wrong to assume that the entire hospitality industry was against the move, pointing to Manchester and Liverpool, where local businesses led the charge. She added: “With climate change and other uncertainties in the world, I would expect visitor numbers in the UK to increase – that’s not just domestic holidays, but also people from other countries coming here. This is a real way to share in the benefits of tourism growth in this country.” Henri Murison, chief executive of the business lobby group Northern Powerhouse Partnership, said there was little evidence tourists would be put off by an extra few pounds on their hotel bill. “The current system, where all the tax paid by businesses goes to central government and none of it benefits the destination, is wrong. It’s just wrong,” he said.

title: Americans on how 9/11 changed their lives: ‘It completely unraveled the US’
summary: Twenty-five years later, the Guardian asks US readers how the attacks affected their lives, and their country
text: As the United States commemorates the 25th anniversary of the September 11 terrorist attacks, in which nearly 3,000 people were killed in New York City, Washington DC and Pennsylvania, the Guardian asked American readers to share how the attacks affected their day-to-day lives and the country at large. Many readers shared their feeling of patriotism in the days following the attacks while also highlighting how the government’s response to 9/11 expanded government surveillance and fueled Islamophobia in the country. For those who were adults at the time of the attacks, the day marked a cataclysmic shift. For those too young to remember it, it served as the context for the complicated and violent world they grew up in. “When 9/11 first happened, everyone became your friend. We were all together in this loss, and the country felt like home everywhere. Driving down a suburban street every house displayed an American flag,” wrote Jennifer Jasensky, a 55-year-old paralegal based in Milford, Connecticut. “It was a beautiful sight, like something out of a book or Hallmark movie.” Elizabeth Zorko, a retired election administrator in Omaha, Nebraska, recalled a similar phenomenon: “I remember meeting the eyes of total strangers and there was a look that wasn’t there before, as if a deep personal connection had been forged by this shared horrific experience.” That feeling of unity soon gave way to anger and division, in large part due to the Iraq and Afghanistan wars, begun by the George W Bush administration and framed as necessary conflicts to help the US win the war on terror. “We launched two forever wars that were wholly ineffective at making us safer militarily, and only sank our prestige in the world – especially [in] Europe and the Middle East – at the cost of thousands of American soldiers and countless Iraqi civilians,” wrote Benjamin Price, a 50-year-old attorney in Savannah, Georgia. “While we would take seemingly any measure to fend off potential foreign terrorism, domestic terrorism in our own country seemed to become a monthly occurrence with absolutely no measures to widen or strengthen domestic gun laws.” Dan J, a 42-year-old based in Vermont, said: “From day one, the attacks on 9/11 have been used to demonize and dehumanize an entire region of the world. “We allowed 9/11 to bring our nation together, not in grieving or resilience, but in group hatred. I was ashamed of us then, and as we have allowed this country to become more absorbed in hatred, xenophobia and isolation now, the shame is stronger.” A Guardian reader, who asked to remain anonymous, wrote about the Islamophobia he faced as a devout Muslim growing up in a post-9/11 world. “The most it impacted me was during elementary through high school,” he said. “I grew up in the Bay Area where people are generally more tolerant and educated, so the worst experiences I have are mostly with regards to jokes and being poked fun at by classmates in school.” Beyond the walls of his classroom, he noticed that “the Middle East became associated exclusively with danger and terrorism, despite being the birthplace of all Abrahamic religions and a hotbed of ancient civilizations”. Many readers pointed to the Patriot Act and the Aviation and Transportation Security Act, both passed in response to the September 11 attacks, as the most tangible examples of the day’s legacy in our daily lives. “Measures we never would have accepted in the 90s, searches at airports, no bags in stadiums, seemed ‘reasonable’ and never went away,” said Price. Zorko said that she had not flown since April 2002: “Not because I’m afraid, but because it’s such a hassle.” Mona, a 72-year-old in California, believes that “the Patriot Act laid the groundwork for the excesses of the DHS [Department of Homeland Security], ICE [Immigration and Customs Enforcement] and CBP [Customs and Border Protection] that have killed many since 2025. It also provided ignorant and racist white Americans with cover to act on their prejudices.” Jeff Jarvis, a 72-year-old journalist and former Guardian contributor, arrived at the World Trade Center from the train right as the first plane hit. “I stayed to report and was a block from the South Tower when it fell, enveloping me in the dust of destruction,” he wrote. “In the 25 years since, many, including me, have ongoing health issues. I don’t know to this day what the effect is on children, including mine.” Jarvis continued: “Regardless of stirring memories of George W Bush standing atop the pile of rubble and visiting a mosque in a show of unity and compassion, now it is all the easier for rightwing fanatics in power to stir hatred, attack neighbors and start wars based on otherness. That one day of terrible suffering and loss took from us Americans our perspective for the suffering and loss we now bring down on other nations and peoples.” Ashley, a 30-year-old based in Washington DC, who celebrated her fifth birthday on 11 September 2001, said: “People who are older than me say ‘it united the whole country’. But growing up alongside its passing anniversary, I feel it completely unraveled the US, and we are still wrestling with its legacy.” She added: “To me, 9/11 has become representative of in America, paranoia, death, destruction, revenge, greed. Even our younger generations laugh at it, because they are desensitized not just to the violence of that day, but the overwhelming violence America committed abroad in its wake.”

title: Vauxhall factory closure shows that capitalism is alive and well in Luton | Letters
summary: Letters: Readers respond to Aditya Chakrabortty’s article about the closure of the Vauxhall plant
text: The closure of the Vauxhall plant in Luton is not the failure of capitalism but its success (‘Capitalism is dying’: in Luton, these former car workers have a moral tale for our times, 4 September). Producing goods on the cheap and selling for the highest price is why the car plant is now in Turkey. Zero-hours contracts, child labour and governments unable to protect workers are global symptoms. To reverse this we need to own production – nationalise. Marx was right.
