title: Highs and lows of Keir Starmer’s time in office | Letters
summary: Letters: Warren Brown lists some of the former PM’s achievements, but Stuart Finegan signals deep disappointment with his legacy
text: Zoe Williams may be right to describe Keir Starmer as a poor politician, but what did we expect (Farewell Keir Starmer, a terrible politician whom we desperately wanted to be something more, 2 September)? After 14 years of economic stagnation and a succession of career politicians as prime minister, we had a leader who previously had a proper job and career outside politics. Starmer’s legacy might be to demonstrate why we need to invest in a better cadre of skilled professional politicians. Those still pining for Starmer may remind us of achievements such as removing the two-child limit on universal benefit, more free school meals, Best Start family hubs, greater employment rights, increases in the minimum wage, renters’ rights, more GPs, lower waiting lists, the Hillsborough law, better relations with Europe etc. But they shouldn’t bother – no one was listening then, and they certainly aren’t now. However, history might record his period in office as the first time the cabinet were nearly all state-educated – a massive achievement, for which he deserves our gratitude. Warren Brown Ilkley, West Yorkshire • Zoe Williams rightly highlights the deep disappointment many people feel about Keir Starmer’s political legacy. For a politician who promised principle and integrity, he too often appeared willing to abandon commitments when they became politically inconvenient. His stance on Israel’s war in Gaza remains one of the clearest examples. Rather than showing moral leadership and clearly condemning the suffering of Palestinian civilians, Starmer seemed reluctant to challenge Israel’s actions, leaving many questioning where his principles truly lay. Equally troubling was his approach to criticism. Many longstanding Labour supporters, including elderly members who opposed the war, felt ignored or dismissed. Leadership requires engagement with dissent, not contempt for it. Starmer also struggled to connect with the public. In an age that values truth and conviction, he often appeared scripted and detached. It frequently felt as though he was delivering the conclusions of advisers rather than expressing his own beliefs. Beyond returning Labour to government, it is difficult to identify a lasting achievement. He may ultimately be remembered not as a leader, but as a manager of other people’s ideas. Stuart Finegan Lewes, East Sussex • Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Please email us your letter and it will be considered for publication in our letters section.

title: Sailors on the USS Abraham Lincoln had it a lot easier than Nelson’s crews  | Letters
summary: Letters: American sailors who were at sea for 286 days really have nothing to complain about, insists Chris Hardy
text: You report (4 September) that sailors from the USS Abraham Lincoln spent a “record uninterrupted 286 days at sea”. That’s nowhere near a record: Nelson and his fleet blockaded Toulon for two years, 1803-05, without going ashore. The American sailors complain about the food on their carrier; Nelson’s ships were exposed to terrible weather in which they pitched and rolled violently, and were cold, wet and plagued by rats. No electricity, let alone fridges; they ate salt pork and rock-hard bread full of weevils, drank green water, and every so often fought a battle or sailed to the Caribbean and back. Apparently the Americans are behaving respectably in the red-light port of Pattaya, Thailand. That’s another difference: the British sailors certainly did not when they came back to Portsmouth and were given two years’ pay in cash. title: Why are we giving a £24bn-a-year subsidy to profitable commercial banks? | Letter
summary: Letter: Gerald Holtham suggests that it time to cut the 3.75% that the Bank of England pays out on the lenders’ reserves
text: There are increasing calls for a windfall tax on banks (Taxing the banks: what Europe’s windfall levies brought in as Burnham eyes his next move, 2 September). Such a tax is unnecessary; it would be enough simply to stop paying commercial banks a huge existing subsidy. The Bank of England holds the reserve deposits of the commercial banks and pays its policy interest rate on the entirety of those reserves. Paying 3.75% on about £640bn means handing over £24bn a year of public money to profitable commercial concerns. The Bank does so only to control the banks’ lending rates by establishing a floor. Yet that could be done more economically by paying interest on a marginal slice of the reserves. The Bank could announce a tranche for each bank and declare that any reduction in reserves from that level is counted as coming firstly from the interest-bearing tranche. That keeps the same marginal opportunity cost to the banks and ensures interest-rate policy is effective. If the tranche were 20%, there would be a gross saving of more than £19bn a year. In all its long history before 2006, the Bank of England never paid commercial banks anything on reserves. And when raising interest rates, it generally increases banks’ profits anyway, by allowing them to charge customers more than they could under unrestricted competition. To increase that effect by paying out more public money than is required for policy purposes is extravagant. It reveals an irresponsible attitude to public finances. Gerald Holtham London • Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Please email us your letter and it will be considered for publication in our letters section.

title: Trump promise of $5,000 for US citizens after midterms decried as ‘bribery’
summary: Critics react to bid for Republican votes with incredulity and point to potential $1.2tn cost atop existing national debt
text: Donald Trump’s promise of a $5,000 “Trump dividend” for every US citizen if Republicans retain control of the US Congress in November’s midterm elections has sparked incredulity and accusations of bribery. “If the Republicans win, you win with us and you get $5,000,” Trump said during the unprecedented Republican midterm convention in Dallas. “It will be called the Trump dividend.” It comes amid extreme concern over the US national debt, which exceeded $40tn for the first time in August. Speaking to Politico, Chip Roy, the Republican US representative from Texas, sounded skeptical. “Well – I would like to know how they would plan to pay for … back of envelope … well over $1tn,” he said. In the moments after Trump made the announcement, Marc Goldwein of the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget wrote on X that “this would cost about $1.2 TRILLION in just one year. That’s more than ALL THREE ROUNDS of COVID relief checks, despite no recessions. The result would be a huge spike in the deficit, and almost certainly in the inflation rate.” The US has roughly 240 million adult citizens, suggesting the cost of $1.2tn. The federal government spent about $7tn in fiscal year 2025, with about $2tn taken on as debt. “The 10-year [treasury bond is] approaching 5%,” Goldwein said on Thursday morning. “Inflation is not under control. We spend more on interest than we spend on defense or on Medicare at this point. Social security is six years from insolvency. Just about the last thing we need is to borrow another trillion dollars to send checks to everybody.” Spending like this risked an economic sugar high followed by a recessionary crash, he said. But Goldwein was most concerned about what might happen if Trump’s gambit is effective. “If this works, the lesson for every future politician is going to be: if you want to win an election, promise a trillion dollars. And multiply a trillion dollars times the number of elections we have coming up, that is a recipe for bankruptcy.” Democratic political leaders reacted with blunt condemnation. “After making you sicker and poorer with his war, Donald Trump now wants to buy your vote with $5,000 in taxpayer-funded blood money,” the California governor, Gavin Newsom, said. “The most corrupt man ever to occupy the Oval Office.” The Democratic National Committee (DNC) pointed to Trump’s record on similar pledges, from $5,000 stimulus checks as a result of the work of the so-called department of government efficiency (Doge) to $2,000 stimulus checks from revenue from tariffs. “Donald Trump and Republicans are once again offering empty promises to Americans,” said Kendall Witmer, the committee’s rapid response director. “The only people reaping the benefits of Trump’s economy are himself, his family, and his ultra-rich elite donors. Meanwhile, working families get nothing except sky-high receipts at the grocery store and the pump, unaffordable healthcare premiums, and wages that aren’t keeping up with inflation.” The Bipartisan Policy Center has been tracking tariff revenue since Trump began raising rates in 2025. As of 8 September, the US has collected about $210bn in tariff and excise tax revenue in 2026. At a rate of $21bn a month, the US federal government would have to collect tariffs for nearly five years to cover a $5,000 payment, assuming every dollar of tariff revenue went to the payment, and discounting tariff payments refunded to retailers in legal challenges. Peter Schiff, chief economist for Euro Pacific Asset Management, said that Trump’s pledge had already begun rippling through financial markets. “Even though bond investors know that, even in the unlikely event Republicans retain control of the House, Trump’s promise to borrow over $1 trillion more to buy votes won’t be kept,” Schiff wrote in a post on X. “The promise itself is so reckless that they’re dumping Treasuries, sending yields to new highs … “Making his promise even worse, Trump referred to his $5,000 bribes as ‘dividends’, as if his policies had been so successful that the US now has surpluses to share. Instead, his reckless policies have produced massive deficits. Trump needs to send Americans bills, not checks.” JD Vance appeared to walk back Trump’s pledge, suggesting that the benefit would be means-tested. But the US senator Bernie Moreno, an Ohio Republican, promised support for Trump’s idea. “I will get a bill ready so that we can get the Trump Dividend passed immediately after the November 3rd election,” Moreno wrote on X.

title: Orthodox church sends medieval prince’s remains to Russian troops in Ukraine
summary: Part of Dmitry Donskoy’s right hand sent to ‘spiritually strengthen’ soldiers
text: The Russian Orthodox church has sent a fragment of a medieval warrior prince’s remains to troops fighting in Ukraine, saying the relic would “spiritually strengthen” soldiers and help them achieve victory. A reliquary containing part of the right hand of Dmitry Donskoy, the 14th-century prince revered in Russia for his victory over the Mongolian Golden Horde in 1380, has been taken to Russian-occupied eastern Ukraine and is now being transported along the frontline. The Russian Orthodox church said in a statement: “The holy commander is going to where the fate of the fatherland is being decided today, so that he may invisibly take his place in the same battle ranks as our defenders.” The relic was first brought on Tuesday to the Savur-Mohyla war memorial in the Russian-occupied Donetsk region of Ukraine, where senior Orthodox clergy held a prayer service alongside representatives of the Russian military. The Russian-installed Metropolitan Vladimir of Donetsk and Mariupol said its presence would help soldiers and civilians “mobilise their strength” and secure victory over the enemy. The relic’s journey is the latest example of the Russian Orthodox church’s rabid embrace of the Kremlin’s war in Ukraine, which Patriarch Kirill, its leader, has repeatedly portrayed in religious terms. Since Vladimir Putin launched the full-scale invasion in February 2022, the church hierarchy has become deeply embedded in the Russian war effort. Priests have been sent to military units and occupied territories, while churches across Russia have been instructed to recite prayers asking God to grant victory. Donskoy’s relics were first formally uncovered only last month during restoration work at the Cathedral of the Archangel inside the Kremlin, where generations of Russian princes and tsars are buried. Putin, who has grown increasingly close to the Russian Orthodox church over his more than two decades in power, personally attended the ceremony marking the unearthing. Critics have accused the church of breaking with religious protocol by opening Donskoy’s centuries-old tomb. The location of the prince’s burial had long been known, but the church had previously made no attempt to exhume his remains after he was canonised in 1988. Alexander Zanemonets, an Orthodox priest and historian based outside Russia, said the decision to uncover the relics almost four decades after Donskoy’s canonisation appeared driven by the demands of wartime patriotism. He wrote in a piece for the Carnegie thinktank: “By the fifth year of war, the church leadership in Moscow began to wonder what else it could do to show its support for what Russia terms its ‘special military operation’.” Zanemonets said the portrayal of Donskoy as a defender of the homeland fitted neatly with the Kremlin’s insistence that Russia was defending itself rather than conducting a war of aggression against its neighbour. Earlier this year, relics of Alexander Nevsky, another medieval prince and military hero revered by the Russian Orthodox church, were also sent to the front.

title: ‘Patients’ who pay $200,000 to be frozen after death are waiting to be reborn in an Australian shed
summary: Exclusive: Southern Cryonics operates out of a shed in Holbrook in rural NSW. Experts say reanimation is ‘a dream’ but true believers are willing to pay for a second chance at life
text: I’m standing atop a very tall ladder, peering down through a haze of liquid nitrogen vapour into a giant stainless steel flask containing three smaller containers. Inside the smaller wedges – which are labelled 005, 006, 007 – are three of Peter Tsolakides’ “patients”. The frozen bodies belong to people who, before their death, paid handsomely to be cryogenically frozen in the hope of one day being brought back to life. The ladder is inside a normal-looking shed in an industrial estate in Holbrook in regional New South Wales. Next to the shed is a grassy block strewn with several wrecked Hondas. Across the road is the local fire brigade. Since it opened in 2023, the shed has housed the southern hemisphere’s only cryonics facility. Inside, seven patients are “suspended” head-down in liquid nitrogen at -196C. Four to a flask – a dewar, as they’re known in the business. Tsolakides’ company, Southern Cryonics, is selling people “a chance of life extension”. The gamble costs more than $200,000. Experts say there’s no way it will work. Cryonics, they explain, remains a “dream”. Any attempted resurrection would be akin to taking a defrosted, and decidedly mushy strawberry, and believing it could be made firm and vibrant again. But proponents say cryonics offers adventure. And a glimmer of hope of a longer or potentially limitless life. Tsolakides, the chair of Southern Cryonics, makes no promises. “Basically, you need to have conquered death, cured all diseases and then be able to bring people back from the dead,” he says. He puts the likelihood of his patients being brought back to life in 250 years’ time at about 10%. That’s more than nothing, he says. But as with any risky venture, it pays to read the fine print. A shed and a submarine Holbrook is small town off the Hume Highway halfway between Melbourne and Sydney. It’s home to the decommissioned submarine HMAS Otway, stranded in a park 250km from the ocean. Southern Cryonics is one of six such facilities in the world, according to its operators. There are two in the US and one each in Switzerland, China and Russia. It’s thought there are about 1,000 people cryogenically frozen worldwide. Tsolakides describes the community as “tight knit”. “Almost nobody’s interested in cryonics,” he tells Guardian Australia. “The people who we get joining us are people who’ve had a sort of life interest … but never knew it was available” in Australia. Southern Cryonics chose Holbrook for its storage facility because of its proximity to Sydney and Melbourne and the fact it’s unlikely to be hit by earthquakes or floods. The cryonicists need somewhere relatively safe given that patients are frozen indefinitely. They’re in the dewar until humanity develops the technology capable of “reviving” them; or, as their contract stipulates, the company goes bust. In that case, their body may be “disposed of”. Conveniently, Holbrook was already home to a cattle-breeding association, and hence a delivery destination for the liquid nitrogen needed to freeze bull semen and embryos. Southern Cryonics has two dewars so far. They’re basically big Thermos bottles. Inside one are the first four of Tsolakides’ patients to be frozen. In May 2024, a man who died in his 80s was the first to be loaded upside down in his Trivial Pursuit-style quarter-cylinder wedge. The second dewar has room for one more patient. Being in the shed, looking down into that space, I feel an immense loneliness. Tsolakides says women are less likely than men to be interested in being frozen. That’s because, he suggests, women don’t like the idea of waking up in a future without family or friends. ‘A very strict protocol’ I am the first journalist allowed into the shed since the initial suspension in May 2024. The shed is unremarkable apart from the two towering dewars – and a crash-test dummy, fully dressed and lying on the floor. It was used to test the winching mechanism for depositing bodies into the dewars. Jim Davis, from Parkes Liquid Nitrogen, is there to top up the dewars. The metal flasks release plumes of vapour when they’re refilled. They were initially topped up once a month but that’s been increased to fortnightly at the request of two early clients who were worried about supplies running low after their mothers died and were suspended. Davis also delivers the icy liquefied gas to police dog and cattle breeders, hospitals, engineers and human IVF clinics. “If they’re freezing it, I’m doing it,” he says. Demand is increasing all the time, and supplies must be replenished regularly, Davis says. You can’t seal liquid nitrogen in a vessel without the container blowing up, meaning it slowly escapes. “If I sealed one of these tanks, mate, the building wouldn’t be here,” he says. To give patients the best chance of avoiding cellular destruction, their body undergoes an eight-hour “vitrification” process as soon as possible after death, Southern Cryonics says. Another of Tsolakides’ companies, CryoPath, arranges a third-party medical perfusionist company to carry out the vitrification. After someone dies, their body is cooled as quickly as possible – including by placing ice packs around their head. The corpse is then pumped with antifreeze-like embalming chemicals that turn it into a “glass-like state”, Tsolakides says, hopefully protecting it from the extreme temperatures inside the dewar. “It’s a slow process,” he explains. “You have to follow a very strict protocol.” After a body has been “stabilised” – usually at a funeral home – it’s transported to Holbrook and stored upside down. But not every patient in the shed has undergone this procedure. Some underwent a “straight freeze”. In the Southern Cryonics contract, clients are asked to acknowledge that any known cryonic suspension method will probably result in physical damage to their body, which may be irreversible. The contract notes there will be another fee, yet to be determined, for any future revival. Science v ‘mysticism’ Associate Prof Saffron Bryant, a cryopreservation expert at RMIT University in Melbourne, says current science “does not support our ability to quite preserve a whole body at this time”. Bryant says cells, embryos and blood products can be successfully “cryopreserved” through vitrification. She says it’s “sort of like antifreeze you might put in a car” to prevent ice forming and protect cells from damage. But it is not possible to deliver a cryoprotectant to everywhere in the body or even, at this stage, to a single organ. “If you’re trying to cool a whole body down at the same rate, you’re going to have the outside, like the skin, cooling down faster than the inside,” she says. “We [use] that strawberry analogy – where things sort of get mushy.” Bryant says even if it were possible to deliver cryoprotectant to the whole body and cool it at the correct rate, the underlying cause of death would remain. The “heart attack or the Alzheimer’s or whatever it was that killed them” happened and no amount of freezing could reverse that, the academic says. As to whether it’s possible to revive someone’s consciousness along with their physical body, Bryant considers this question to be more in the “realms of mysticism” than science. Asked if she thinks Southern Cryonics is a scam, Bryant replies: “I’m not allowed to answer that.” The initial stabilisation process costs an estimated $60,000. Clients then have to pay a further $150,000 to Southern Cryonics for their indefinite storage and a $350 annual “membership fee”. The company “demands payment upfront” and Southern Cryonics recommends people take out a $210,000 life insurance policy. Tsolakides says it costs about $5,500 a year to keep a patient suspended. Most of that goes towards liquid nitrogen and staff costs. He plans to invest $100,000 from each client in “blue-chip” funds which he says could result in a collective pool of billions of dollars over the 250 years he estimates it will take for revival to become feasible. On its website, Southern Cryonics says most suspensions are funded through life insurance and it can help people obtain a policy through a broker. But Tsolakides acknowledges only one Australian customer’s insurer has agreed to pay so far and it was reluctant. He knows of “two or three” major insurers that will pay for cryonics but he won’t name them. The Council of Australian Life Insurers says it can’t verify or endorse claims made by Southern Cryonics, CryoPath or any broker about using life insurance to fund cryonic suspension. Its chief executive, Christine Cupitt, says nominating a cryonics provider as the beneficiary of a life insurance policy is a “significant decision” that people should consider carefully. ‘It is a dream’ Dr Kate Falconer, an Australian legal academic who specialises in death law and teaches at University College Cork in Ireland, says the cryonics community is made up of a small number of “diehard true believers”. “Look, I think they probably do believe it,” she says. “But at the end of the day, it is a dream. There’s nothing concrete there.” Falcolner nevertheless shows her students a New York Times video from 2015 where a young woman with terminal cancer talks about having her brain frozen after death. “It’s incredibly moving [and] it really does hit home that there are some people who are choosing it because it is their only hope of any kind of long life.” The latest suspension at the Holbrook facility occurred in June after a man in his 90s died. Southern Cryonics’ youngest patient is a woman who died in her 40s and whose premature death devastated her family. The facility manager, Philip Rhoades, says he once preserved the brain tissue of a 15-year-old boy who took his own life. That was at the request of the teenager’s parents. The preservation was done by Rhoades’ earlier venture, the Neural Archives Foundation, a registered charity which claims to preserves brain tissue as a “historical archive”. Rhoades says the organisation makes use of “normal biomedical storage” across Australia. His own parents’ brains are preserved along with 12 other human brains and three dog brains. Rhoades is a left-leaning vegetarian with a big family but no children of his own. He was planning to open a “life extension village” near his home in Cowra, in NSW’s central west, but says that was foiled by red tape. “There was too much bureaucratic stuff,” he says. Instead, he’s thinking of turning the block into a GP clinic adjoined by a “biomedical research facility” for “radical life extension treatments”. When he dies, Rhoades would love to be “uploaded to a supercomputer as soon as possible”. But as he doesn’t think that will be possible given that he’s in his 70s, he plans to be frozen and stored in the Holbrook shed. Future generations will want to revive their great-great-great grandparents, Rhoades says. “If the technology is possible at all … I think it will become very popular to talk to revivees.” He thinks patients could be revived by 2080 and that someone who had a “good preservation” has more than a 50% chance of making it. But he knows there are no guarantees. “If you get woken up in the future, you’ve hit the jackpot, really.”

title: Kimmel says interview with Talarico won’t air on TV after threats from Trump’s FCC
summary: Host says he’s interviewing Senate candidate ‘under unusual circumstances’ and it will be posted on YouTube
text: Late-night TV host Jimmy Kimmel has said an upcoming interview with the Democratic Senate candidate from Texas James Talarico will not air on ABC, the US network that broadcasts his show, after the federal media regulator “threatened” his show, ABC and its local affiliates. “Tomorrow night I’ll be interviewing James Talarico under unusual circumstances,” Kimmel said during his opening monologue on Jimmy Kimmel Live! on Wednesday. Kimmel said that since the show began over 20 years ago, he has interviewed “Americans who are running for office with no problem at all”, noting that this ranged “from Hillary Clinton to Ted Cruz to Donald Trump himself”. “I interviewed Donald Trump when he was running for president in 2015,” Kimmel said. Trump came back for another interview, just before he became the Republican nominee in 2016. “But for some reason, and I can’t seem to figure out what that reason is, something has changed,” Kimmel continued. “Now that he is president, his FCC [Federal Communications Commission] has threatened me, threatened our show, threatened our network, ABC, our affiliates, our local stations based on simple traditional editorial decisions, guest bookings it would seem they don’t like. “And so out of consideration for our local stations, especially our ABC affiliates in Texas, who would have to deal with this nonsense, my interview tomorrow with James Talarico will not air on television,” he said. “It will be posted on YouTube instead.” The FCC did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Kimmel’s remarks. Talarico is running for US Senate in Texas against Ken Paxton, the Republican candidate and state attorney general. Kimmel’s announcement on Wednesday came amid increased scrutiny of broadcast television by the FCC under the Trump administration. In January, the agency issued guidance warning that daytime and late-night talkshows would be expected to comply with rules requiring broadcasters to give equal airtime to candidates running for the same office. According to the Hollywood Reporter, in general, talkshows have qualified for exemptions from those rules, ever since the FCC granted such an exemption to Jay Leno’s Tonight Show in 1996. Earlier this year, in February, Stephen Colbert, said Talarico was set to appear on an episode of The Late Show, which ran on CBS, until the network controversially canceled the series. But, Colbert said: “We were told in no uncertain terms by our network’s lawyers, who called us directly, that we could not have him on the broadcast.” That interview also ran on YouTube. Last year, following unusual pressure from the FCC, ABC temporarily suspended Kimmel’s late-night show for nearly a week over a monologue he delivered about the fatal shooting of the conservative activist Charlie Kirk. Last month, ABC and its parent company, Disney, sued the FCC, accusing the agency of violating the first amendment in ordering an unusual early review of the network’s local station broadcast licenses. “Acting through the Federal Communications Commission, the Administration has waged a retaliatory campaign against ABC for a single reason: it disapproves of what ABC broadcasts,” the complaint alleges. In an interview with the New York Times in August, the FCC chairman, Brendan Carr, called the lawsuit “meritless” and denied that the agency was violating free speech rights. “Holding a broadcaster accountable to their public interest obligations and statutory obligations is not a violation of their first amendment rights,” he said, “and that is what the FCC is doing.” Last week, the FCC asked the court to dismiss the lawsuit.

title: Hawaii has often dodged the path of hurricanes. Why did it see so many storms this summer?
summary: The island chain has tended to avoid the worst effects, but Hurricanes Lowell and Lala left a trail of damage this year
text: Hurricane Lowell surged near the Hawaiian Islands this week, leaving a trail of downed trees and power lines, crumbled roads, sunken boats and destroyed piers on the island of Kauai. Residents were left to grapple not only with the damage, but the rising risks to the tropical archipelago as sea surface temperatures climb. Despite its location, stretching across roughly 1,500 miles in the central north Pacific Ocean, Hawaii typically avoids the worst effects from hurricanes. In fact, the island chain so often dodges direct hits from the violent storms, that it’s been quipped they have a force field around them. But Lowell was the second named storm to brush by the islands so far this year. In August, Hurricane Lala hit the Big Island and Oahu with damaging winds, the first time hurricane-force gusts have been recorded there in 155 years. “An event of this magnitude is somewhat rare,” Michael Brennan, director of the National Hurricane Center said during a recent broadcast discussion on Lowell’s forecast, adding that Hawaii has not had a direct hurricane landfall since Iniki in 1992. That violent storm unleashed 145 mile-per-hour winds as it tore through Kauai, destroying or damaging roughly 70% of the island’s homes and businesses. It’s not luck (or a force field) that typically protected the islands, but location, according to Dr Nicholas Grondin, assistant professor of Environmental Science at the University of Tampa. Among the most isolated chain of islands on Earth, Hawaii is simply a small target in the vast open ocean, Grondin explained in an editorial published by the Conversation. Most approaching storms also must pass over cooler water temperatures to the east of the islands, which helps calm them. “Without warm oceans to provide fuel, hurricanes tend to weaken and fizzle out as they approach the islands,” Grondin said. Sea-surface temperatures in the tropical Pacific are, however, exceptionally warm this year due to El Niño. The climate phenomenon has already developed, but is expected to strengthen through the coming months typically limits hurricane activity in the Atlantic and enhances the development and strength of storms in the Pacific. Forecasters have warned it could reach a historic intensity. El Niño has caused hurricanes to form further to the south and west this year, according to Matthew Rosencrans, Noaa’s lead forecaster for the seasonal hurricane outlook, which “puts them in a place where they could make that westward run towards the Hawaiian islands”. It also makes for a lagging storm season. Hurricane risks typically extend from July to the end of November but fall off into the later months. September and October are far busier in El Niño years. The climate crisis has also played a part in strengthening the storms. The effects of El Niño are layered on top of the warming trends. Hurricane Lowell temporarily became a category 5 on 2 September. It swept over waters that were unusually warm, which helped fuel its ferocity. The sea surface temperatures along its path were “made up to 60 times more likely because of human-caused climate change”, according to a report from Climate Central, an organization of scientists and advocates who research impacts from global heating. Together, the climate crisis and El Niño are expected to supercharge extreme weather events around the world over the next year. For Pacific storms, Rosencrans said, it means they may carry more moisture and produce stronger winds. As efforts begin to clear debris and repair roads and infrastructure damaged during Lowell, emergency management officials must continue keeping close watch on the waters for the next big storm. “They just need to reset and regard any potential upcoming impacts,” Rosencrans said. “The season is not over – there is still a long bit to go.”

title: English winemakers expect ‘vintage year’ after record-breaking summer heat
summary: Hot weather means sweeter grapes, but outlook gloomier for beermakers, as drought diminishes barley harvest
text: English sparkling winemakers expect their earliest grape harvest and a “vintage year” after a scorching summer quickly ripened grapes. However, beer sellers have warned of a potential shortage after record-breaking temperatures and a drought hitting much of England has caused poor yields of barley. Nyetimber, which was the first producer in England to grow pinot noir, chardonnay and pinot meunier exclusively for sparkling wine, has 11 vineyards in West Sussex, Kent and Hampshire. It has announced it will begin picking grapes on 14 September for this year’s harvest, the earliest since the company planted its first vines in 1988. The winemaker’s next earliest harvest was in 2018, when the first grape was picked on 19 September. Nyetimber said this harvest, for which it has recruited 500 pickers, will yield almost 2,500 tonnes of grapes, which could result in more than 1.5 million bottles of sparkling wine being produced from the 2026 vintage. Because of the late spring frosts, it is expected the harvest will be slightly smaller than usual, but that the large number of sunny days this year will have concentrated the sugar in the grapes, meaning 2026 could be a vintage year. The company’s first vintage was Blanc de Blancs 1992, which won numerous wine prizes. Nyetimber’s head winemaker, Cherie Spriggs, said: “This year brings another unprecedented vintage as we begin harvesting earlier than ever. We are excited to taste the fruits of our labour, which as always has come with certain challenges: late spring frosts that affected almost 30% and the summer drought, which has decreased the size of certain berries. However, the hot and sunny weather has helped to balance out these factors, giving us strong potential for fantastic wine quality.” Though winemakers are celebrating, the outlook is gloomier for beer aficionados. Lisa Hogan, who runs the Diddly Squat Farm in Oxfordshire with her partner, the TV presenter Jeremy Clarkson, has said there may be “less beer all around” after extreme weather led to a poor barley harvest. This summer was the UK’s hottest on record, according to provisional Met Office data. In England, temperatures peaked at 38.1C (100.1F) at Kew Gardens in London on 13 August, and June had already been confirmed as the country’s hottest since records began in 1884. Scientists have said these heatwaves are only possible because of the climate crisis, driven by burning fossil fuels. August was the joint hottest month ever recorded around the world, with global temperatures reaching 1.65C above preindustrial levels, scientists said on Thursday, amid warnings of further heating on the way. Hogan and Clarkson make Hawkstone Lager on their farm, which has been made famous by the Amazon show Clarkson’s Farm. Hogan said: “I think a lot of barley farmers suffered … And funnily enough, last year our yields were terrible, but the quality was better. This year, after a second year of dry weather, both the harvest and its quality have suffered.” She said farmers were struggling to irrigate crops, leading to poor yields. The Agriculture and Horticulture Development Board has said the barley harvest could be the worst on record and said yields were running 19% below the five-year average last month. Hogan added that other countries are facing similar difficulties: “It is a struggle because if you have another bad harvest, you won’t be able to supplement, say, by getting grain in from Poland. So, we just have to pay a higher cost, and then we have to try not to pass that on to the customer.”

title: Much of Europe already levies a tourist tax – a nice little earner for Italian hotspots
summary: While England makes its first foray into unfamiliar territory, it’s proved a boon for Italy’s cash-strapped municipalities
text: A nightly tourist tax may be unfamiliar territory in the UK, but countries in continental Europe have been cashing in on these kinds of levies for decades. Tourists usually need to pay the tax on the day they check out of a hotel or holiday let, and are often surprised by an extra fee on top of their accommodation costs. Among the earliest introductions of a tourist tax was in Austria in 1842, specifically targeting those who stayed in spa and wellness retreats. Similar measures were later implemented in France, Italy, Germany and Switzerland as a way to prevent the inhabitants of towns hosting such high-end resorts from paying for costs incurred by wealthy visitors. Italy’s tourist tax structure has gone through various changes. During Benito Mussolini’s fascist regime, it was broadened to include any town or city classified as a tourist destination. The tax was then completely abolished for the World Cup in 1990 as Italy embraced more visitors, only to be brought back in nationally in 2011, with Rome becoming the first city to reintroduce the levy. Depending on the destination, and sometimes the hotel type, the nightly fee typically ranges from between €1 (£0.86) and €10 per person, although guests of five-star hotels in Milan pay €12. Venice has also had an entrance fee in place since 2024, although that is only targeted at day-trippers. The overnight levy is a serious earner for popular Italian destinations. In 2024, Rome made €222.4m, followed by Milan (€109.3m), Florence (€82.9m) and Venice (€38.9m), according to data from Siope, the finance ministry’s tracker of public money flows. The revenues are supposed to be spent on local services, especially in towns and cities buckling under the pressure of overtourism, or on maintaining monuments. However, the reality is that cash-strapped municipalities use it for other expenses. “All municipalities want the fee because they need the money,” said Gianluca De Gaetano, the manager of the Rome unit for Federalberghi, the hotels’ association. Tourists mostly just absorb the payment, even if begrudgingly. “They tend to complain when they find that the services in a city are not up to par, especially if they’ve already paid a lot for their accommodation,” said De Gaetano.

title: Secret systems used by Israel in mass killings of Gaza civilians revealed in new film
summary: Testimony from Israeli military insiders involved in surveillance and remote killings features in documentary produced by the Guardian
text: Testimony from 24 Israeli military insiders on the secret systems used in the war on Gaza has been revealed in a new documentary film about the mass killing of Palestinian civilians. NAZA, a film from the Oscar-winning Israeli directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, was shown at the Venice international film festival on Thursday as the only documentary competing for its prestigious Golden Lion award. The film’s title comes from an Israeli military acronym used euphemistically to refer to civilians expected to be killed in a military attack. Produced by the Guardian, it features extensive testimony from Israeli intelligence officers and soldiers involved in the surveillance and remote killing of Palestinian civilians. Interviews were filmed at night on rooftops in Tel Aviv, on the condition of anonymity because of the risks involved in speaking publicly about Israel’s war activities. The appearance and voices of participants in the film were digitally altered to disguise their identities. The interviewees detail the secret methods used by the Israeli military in Gaza, including AI-based systems built to identify large numbers of potential low-ranking Hamas targets, who were then bombed in their homes at night, in the knowledge attacks would also kill their families. The Israeli military hacked into phones to identify the location of such targets, and covertly listened into conversations with their wives and children moments before they were all killed. The film also features first-person accounts about the destruction of neighbourhoods where the Israeli military estimated that up to 25% of residents were still sheltering in their homes, the systematic burning of civilian homes, and the killing of civilians at a food distribution site. Abraham said at a press conference in Venice on Thursday: “We just told these officers: ‘Please describe to us what you did. How do these systems work? Sketch it out for us.’ Sometimes, in just asking the questions, you get the answers. “Some of them did not express remorse and some did. Some spoke out of indifference, some out of pride.” Several interviewees worked in a secret intelligence unit that reports directly to the office of Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu; one said their mission was to “thwart peace”. “We made this film out of a sense of obligation to use our position as Israeli film-makers and journalists to examine the systems behind the mass killing of Palestinian civilians for which our country is responsible,” Abraham and Szor said in their directors’ statement. The directors stressed the film’s focus was not on “sporadic war crimes committed by rogue soldiers”. “It is on the orders themselves, the policies, the accepted practices, the language and logic that make those practices possible, and the people who operate within them,” they said. “The system and its cogs.” The documentary was co-produced by James Wilson and executive produced by Jonathan Glazer, the same team behind the Oscar-winning film The Zone of Interest. The film received a nearly 25-minute standing ovation after its screening, according to Variety, which called it a record for length of applause not just at Venice but at any major film festival and reported that Glazer embraced Abraham and Szor as it went on, while some members of the audience held up Palestinian flags. NAZA builds on revelations first published by the Israeli-Palestinian publication +972 Magazine, the Hebrew-language outlet Local Call and the Guardian between 2023 and 2025. It was filmed and produced under tight security because of the risk to confidential journalistic sources, and its contents have remained a closely guarded secret before Thursday’s premiere. Paul Lewis, the Guardian’s head of investigations and an executive producer on the film, described NAZA as the culmination of “years of painstaking work to uncover and verify the systems used by Israeli military intelligence in Gaza”. Abraham said making the documentary had provided space to explore the collective impact of that work. “In this film we’re talking to 24 people. We are looking at systems of mass killing. There is something about cinema that allows you to explore structures and systems and how you put things together.” Before the premiere, Alberto Barbera, the Venice film festival’s artistic director, told journalists NAZA would be “truly groundbreaking”, calling it “a politically disruptive and cinematically extremely interesting work”. “It’s not just any collection of interviews,” Italy’s Cinecittà News quoted Barbera as saying. “It took them three years to convince these Israeli intelligence and military officials to share the work they did when the invasion of Gaza began, and I assure you, their testimonies are shocking.” Israeli attacks in Gaza since 2023 have killed more than 73,000 Palestinians, the majority of them civilians, and injured more than 174,000 others, together representing more than 10% of Gaza’s prewar population. Israeli restrictions on food shipments created a man-made famine last summer, and the Israeli military razed or damaged more than three-quarters of homes, so surviving Palestinians are now crowded into tent camps with little access to clean water or sanitation. Israel launched its war after the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attacks on Israel, when more than 1,200 people were killed and 251 taken to Gaza by militants. The majority of the dead and hostages were civilians. Abraham and Szor were two of the four co-directors of No Other Land, which won the Oscar for best documentary in 2025. Drawing a connection between the two films, the directors said: “In the film No Other Land, we spent five years, together with [Palestinian co-directors] Basel Adra and Hamdan Ballal, documenting the army destroying Palestinian homes in order to paint a larger picture of a system of occupation and ethnic supremacy aimed at the removal of Palestinians from the West Bank. “In NAZA, we are similarly connecting the dots of a system, gathering the testimonies of two dozen intelligence officers and soldiers and depicting the military systems used to perpetrate what a UN commission and the world’s leading human rights groups have described as a genocide.”

title: Lindy Cameron appointed first female head of UK Foreign Office
summary: High commissioner to India replaces Olly Robbins, who was sacked over Peter Mandelson scandal
text: The Foreign Office has its first female head after the appointment of Lindy Cameron, the high commissioner to India. Cameron’s new role as permanent undersecretary at the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office means she will replace Olly Robbins, who was sacked over the Peter Mandelson scandal. Her appointment comes at a time of wider change at the top of the civil service, as Cat Little, formerly leading the Cabinet Office, is moving to become permanent secretary of the Department for Business and Trade, and Tom Riordan, a former local government official, is taking the top job at the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government. Cameron is a former chief executive of the National Cyber Security Centre and has also held senior roles at the Northern Ireland Office and the former Department for International Development. Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary, said she brought “enormous experience across the fields of diplomacy, development and national security, and a reputation for dynamic leadership in postings across the world, most recently as high commissioner in India”. He said the Foreign Office under her leadership would be “committed to promoting British values and interests”. Antonia Romeo, the cabinet secretary, said Cameron had an “excellent track record in security and diplomacy, combined with her considerable experience in international development”. Cameron will enter the Foreign Office after a period of turmoil for the department during which it has been shedding jobs after Keir Starmer cut the aid budget. It had absorbed the international development function after the separate department was abolished under the Conservatives. The Foreign Office has also faced scrutiny over its handling of the Mandelson affair, after he was appointed as ambassador to the US before being removed over the depth of his links to Jeffrey Epstein, and revelations about his alleged leaking of government information while a minister. Robbins was dismissed from his post by Starmer after the then prime minister said he did not feel he had been given the whole picture about Mandelson’s failure to pass vetting. The Guardian revealed that Mandelson failed his security vetting in January 2025 during the process to appoint him as ambassador to the US. It is said that Robbins knew about Mandelson’s failure to pass the UK Security Vetting assessment but did not forward that information to ministers. Starmer claimed he was not made aware of the outcome of the vetting process until months later. Robbins has since submitted a legal challenge over his dismissal, applying to the high court for a judicial review of the decision to remove him.

title: Primark to launch home delivery service despite ‘challenging’ market
summary: Chain has long avoided deliveries in Great Britain but says a shift now offers ‘opportunity for profitable growth’
text: Primark will offer home delivery in Great Britain for the first time as the fast-fashion retailer seeks to revive flagging sales. The company, which already offers a click and collect service, has long avoided home delivery, arguing that its low prices made it too difficult to absorb the cost of packing and shipping orders. However, the clothing chain, which will spin off from its owner Associated British Foods (ABF) next year, disclosed on Thursday that it had acquired an automated fulfilment facility in Sheffield and would offer home delivery “in the future” in the UK, except for Northern Ireland. “Primark’s digital maturity, including the success of click and collect, and online market developments, mean there is now the opportunity for profitable growth through the home delivery channel,” it said in a statement. The push into home delivery came as the company told investors that it expected Primark’s sales to drop 3% ⁠in its quarter ended on 12 September, with the UK and Ireland up 0.4% but continental Europe down 4.3%. George Weston, the chief executive of ABF, said Primark’s trading in Europe “remained challenging”, but the initial customer reaction to its “iconic value” campaign – in which it cut prices across hundreds of autumn and winter products – had been encouraging. Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at the broker AJ Bell, said Primark, faced with slowing sales, “clearly had no choice but to adapt to the modern retail world” and adopt online delivery. Shares in ABF, which is listed on the London Stock Exchange, fell by almost 10% on Thursday, taking its year-to-date fall to 14%. Analysts at the broker Jefferies, an investment bank, said Primark looked particularly vulnerable as it started its final quarter of the year. “In an environment with rising concerns over both the health of the consumer and of industry input cost challenges, Primark continues to be among the most disadvantageously positioned clothing retailers,” they said. The news comes as Primark prepares to split from its parent company ABF, the owner of Twinings tea and Kingsmill bread. The demerger, which is likely to complete in December 2027, is expected to create two new FTSE 100 companies, with analysts predicting that Primark could be valued at as much as £9bn, and the food business £4bn. Weston, a member of the billionaire family that controls ABF and who is the long-term chief executive of the group, is to lead the food business after the demerger. Eoin Tonge, an experienced former ABF, Marks & Spencer and Greencore finance director, will remain as chief executive of Primark. The fashion chain, which was founded by Arthur Ryan under its Irish brand name, Penneys, in Dublin in 1969, opened its first shop in Britain in 1974, in Derby. It employs more than 80,000 people around the world.

title: RNLI steps up security after abuse by far-right agitators over small boat rescues
summary: Volunteers told to consider not wearing charity-branded clothing and to shut lifeboat stations if they feel in danger
text: The RNLI is increasing security after a backlash from far-right agitators over the lifeboat charity’s involvement in rescuing asylum seekers in the Channel and bringing them to UK shores. Volunteers have been told by the charity’s bosses that they should consider not wearing RNLI branded clothing if they feel this might put them at risk. They have also been advised that they should feel empowered to close shops or lifeboat stations if they feel in danger. There has been a heavy security presence around RNLI bases on the south coast of England over the last few days, with police and private guards monitoring some areas. At the charity’s headquarters in Poole, barriers have placed around a memorial sculpture to RNLI volunteers who lost their lives and around a rose bed to mark the 200th anniversary of the charity. A viewing platform into the headquarters has been closed off. The RNLI has said it will continue to rescue asylum seekers in the Channel despite the intimidation from far-right activists after its involvement in a rescue on Sunday in which a dinghy carrying asylum seekers was brought into Portsmouth. But after Sunday’s protest, the RNLI’s chief executive emailed volunteers to say security processes were being reviewed. Volunteers were asked to challenge people near lifeboat stations if they did not have ID, but advised not to engage with members of the public if they felt uncomfortable. Staff at the Portsmouth lifeboat station close to where the asylum seekers landed on Sunday have been approached by members of the public and asked to explain the RNLI’s actions. The RNLI has said workers have been subjected to “online and physical abuse” and there have been “baseless” rumours circulating that the charity had housed asylum seekers or moved them to secret locations after helping them to shore. Three police forces have been involved in protecting RNLI volunteers, staff and buildings. Dorset police have been helping keep the headquarters secure while Hampshire officers have patrolled RNLI stations in Portsmouth. Sussex police were investigating “offensive and threatening commentary towards RNLI volunteers”. Images of some RNLI crew members who were apparently involved in the operation on Sunday were published on social media with the accusation that they were complicit in an “invasion” of the UK. About 50 protesters, including members of the Poole Patriots and Hampshire Resistance attended a demonstration outside the RNLI’s headquarters in Poole on Wednesday. Protest leaders handed out rape alarms to women, claiming they were at risk from men brought into the UK by the RNLI, and called for people to stop donating to the charity. An RNLI spokesperson said: “Given the unacceptable abuse our people have faced, and with protest activity taking place at RNLI locations, we have taken action to help ensure the safety and wellbeing of our volunteers and staff. “As well as enhancing security at RNLI locations, we issued guidance to our people earlier this week on how to keep themselves safe. This guidance included how to manage potentially challenging interactions with members of the public, and where appropriate, choosing not to wear RNLI-branded clothing. “Our people have been reminded that their safety comes first, and they are encouraged to report relevant incidents internally and, where appropriate, to the police.”

title: ECB raises interest rates to 2.5% and warns Iran war is fuelling inflation
summary: Borrowing costs climb in Europe and oil tops $105 a barrel as bank says growing price pressures in eurozone will be ‘longer lasting than we had anticipated’
text: The European Central Bank has raised interest rates to 2.5% and warned that the risk of higher inflation over the next year has risen following renewed fighting in the Middle East. It came as government borrowing costs soared on the back of a jump in oil and gas prices after the latest US and Iran attacks on ships in the strait of Hormuz. The interest rate, or yield, on UK government debt rose to a 19-year high on Thursday, while the yield on US and European bonds also climbed in line with oil, which touched $105 (£78) a barrel. Investors had expected the ECB to raise the cost of borrowing across the euro bloc, but were spooked by the hawkish tone of the central bank’s report, which warned of inflationary pressures building in many sectors of the economy. Increasing its main rate from 2.25% to the highest level since March last year, the central bank lifted its forecast for eurozone economic growth in 2026 to 0.9%, up from 0.8% in June. It now expects inflation to average 3% this year. The biggest driving force of rising prices is the cost of energy, which again jumped on Thursday after this week’s increase in US and Iranian attacks on ships transiting the Gulf. Brent crude passed $105 a barrel, before slipping back to about $104.5, a 3.3% rise on the day. British gas prices rose to above 203p per therm, the highest since December 2022. Continental European gas prices also increased. The Dutch wholesale gas price – the EU standard – passed €80 per megawatt hour (MWh) for the first time since January 2023. The front-month contract is trading 3.4% higher at €82.56/MWh. This, in turn, increased government borrowing costs in leading economies. The interest rate on benchmark 10-year UK government bonds, also known as gilts, hit 5.36%, the highest since August 2007. The rate on Germany’s 30-year government bond rose 2.5 basis points to 5.08%, the highest since December 2003. The 10-year yield hit 3.45%, the highest since April 2011. France’s 10-year government bond yield was the highest since October 2008 at 4.344%, up 1 basis point. Central banks are concerned that high fuel and energy prices will feed into higher transport costs and more expensive heating for commercial and residential properties, which will lead to a broad-based rise in inflation. The ECB president, Christine Lagarde, said: “We believe inflation will be longer lasting than we had anticipated,” adding that food inflation, which had remained low at 1.2%, was likely to increase in response to higher oil and gas prices. She explicitly acknowledged ‌that gas prices could rise owing to further supply disruptions or an unusually cold winter in combination with low storage levels across much of the region. Investors are concerned that UK and EU governments have underplayed the risk of running out of gas and the negative effect a subsequent dash for supplies will have on inflation. Recent data shows EU gas stores are only 67% full, well below the five-year average of 84%. UK and continental European gas buyers have delayed filling gas stores in the expectation that the Middle East conflict will be resolved and prices will be lower before winter in the northern hemisphere. As the war drags on, there is the prospect of gas prices rising because of a scramble of buyers looking to replenish stocks before cold weather arrives. Bond markets were also put on alert by the US Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, who said the US would buy back $6bn worth of government debt – known as US treasuries – in an effort to alleviate a sell-off in the US bond market that has put pressure on interest rates. But the size of the package was considered inadequate by bond buyers and the yield on 10-year treasuries rose to a three-year high. “Headline inflation is expected to return to around target towards the end of 2027, supported by the effects of higher interest rates,” Lagarde said. Asked about the ECB’s next move, she said: “We have not debated at all any kind of future path. Markets do what they have to do and we do what we have to do – which is to provide price stability.”

title: Canada helped save the bald eagle from near extinction in the US – does the White House know?
summary: The White House posted a photo of bald eagle attacking a Canada goose – but it was Canada that played a critical role in the recovery of the raptor in the US
text: In late August, the White House posted a real photograph on social media of a bald eagle standing atop the limp neck of a Canada goose. The raptor presses the goose’s face into the grey winter slush. With its stark white head and brilliant yellow talons, the eagle looks victorious and defiant. As trade talks failed and tensions between Canada and the US rose, the image, viewed millions of times, apparently proved irresistible to the social media handlers at the White House for sending a clear message: the United States could not be challenged by Canada. But experts say the bald eagle, long prized by Americans as a symbol even before becoming the country’s national bird in 2024, came perilously close to disappearing from much of the country – and that it was neighbouring Canada that played a critical role in its recovery, even going as far as to fly juvenile eagles south by plane to return them to US skies. As many as half a million bald eagles once thrived before the European settlement of North America, near large bodies of open water, where they feasted on the abundant fish and nested in towering trees. The eagle’s hulking, majestic presence left an imprint on the founders of the modern United States, who placed the bird on the Great Seal of the United States in 1782. (The use of the word “bald” doesn’t not mean hairless. Instead, it comes derives from the Middle English word “balde” or “balled” which means marked by a white blaze.) But crisis struck, as rapidly expanding settlements put eagles on a collision course with humans. “Bald eagles were seen by some as competitors for fish resources and a threat to their livestock and wild game by others,” said David Bird, a professor emeritus of wildlife biology at McGill University in Montreal. “None of those things turned out to be true in the end.” Officials initially offered 50 cents for a pair of eagle feet, later raising the bounty to $2 by 1949. More than 100,000 bald eagles were killed under the bounty program until it was discontinued in 1953. Meanwhile, a synthetic chemical compound was having an unexpected effect on wildlife. DDT, first produced on a large scale to combat malaria and then widely applied after the second world war to fight pests, was accumulating in the fatty tissues of animals – particularly in predators at the top of the food chain. In birds of prey, the result was devastating: eggshells became so thin and brittle that many eggs broke before they could hatch. The effects inspired Rachel Carson’s Silent Spring, the 1962 book that helped catalyse the modern environmental movement. “If we are going to live so intimately with these chemicals eating and drinking them, taking them into the very marrow of our bones – we had better know something about their nature and their power,” she wrote. The pesticide was eventually banned in 1972. Bird said the “the double whammy” of bounties and reproductive collapse put immense pressure on bald eagles. In 1963, only 417 breeding pairs remained in the lower 48 states. Desperate biologists and officials turned to Canada. While DDT had ravaged much of the population in the US, the pesticide had been used less extensively north of the border. A 1983 media report profiled Operation Eaglet, a complex logistical effort that required cars, float planes and biologists in order to help repopulate the US. The CBC reporter called the effort a “courtesy of Canadian goodwill”. In one instance, the team collected eight baby eagles from northern Manitoba, where experts believed roughly 3,000 birds remained, and sent one each to Pennsylvania and New Jersey, with the remaining six bound for Massachusetts, where they would make “a tremendous difference”, as project leader Jack Swedberg told the CBC, because “currently we don’t have any”. The mission relied on a technique called “hacking”, in which eaglets were raised in controlled environments, out of sight of people, in order to prevent imprinting on humans and associating their caregivers with food. Over the years, 88 eagles were brought to Pennsylvania from the province of Saskatchewan. The state now has 300 breeding pairs. Even the location of the photograph used by the White House reflects the unlikely recovery of the population. The image was captured by Derek Stoll in New York state, which by the 1970s had just a single breeding pair. “You’re not allowed to import bald eagles. So there was a population in Canada, but we are not allowed to bring bald eagles into the United States,” Darryl McGrath, the Albany-based author of Flight Paths, said during a 2016 lecture. “So we couldn’t get the eagle chicks for this hacking project – we couldn’t get them from Canada, even though Canada was very willing to help us out.” Instead, New York relied on other states, including Alaska, until laws concerning the transport of endangered species were amended. Other eagles were sourced for the US from the coastal provinces of British Columbia and Nova Scotia, including 36 from Cape Breton sent to repopulate New Jersey and Massachusetts. Bird says that the people trading memes about the eagle and the goose may not know the shared history of a key conservation success story. But he points out that even if Canada geese look like easy prey for an eagle – and they can be – they are also “formidable” birds with powerful club-like wings. And he notes that another beloved Canadian bird – which adorns Canada’s one-dollar coin – should similarly not be underestimated. In 2020 an eagle was found floating lifelessly in a Maine lake. A necropsy confirmed what experts suspected – the eagle threatened a common loon and its chick. “It stabbed the eagle through the heart with its beak,” said Bird, adding that given the current political climate, the symbolism was “hard to ignore”.

title: Elon Musk attacks film-maker behind documentary about him
summary: Tech mogul calls director Alex Gibney a ‘bitter old man’ who has ‘zero integrity’ in series of posts on X
text: Elon Musk has issued an angry tirade at the film-maker behind a four-hour documentary about his life and influence, labelling the director, Alex Gibney, a “bitter old man” who has “zero integrity”. Gibney, who has previously made films about the collapse of Enron, WikiLeaks and Vladimir Putin, premiered his Musk documentary at the Venice film festival this week. He said he believed the world’s richest man was “extremely dangerous”. In a series of posts on X, which Musk bought for $44bn in 2022, the tech mogul railed against the film as a “hit piece that misses”, adding its four-hour length also made the documentary, which is highly critical of Musk, “as boring af”. Musk also appeared to push at conspiracy theory, reposting an image depicting the Democratic party as a puppet, controlling another puppet labelled “Team Soros” – a reference to the billionaire George Soros, who has supported progressive causes. That puppet in turn controls another one labelled “Alex Gibney”, while the Gibney puppet controls another labelled “Hollywood”. In response to the picture, Musk stated: “Accurate.” In response to a supporter who said he had never heard of Gibney until his Musk film, Musk replied: “It’s a psy op” – a reference to a planned “psychological operation” designed to influence the public’s thoughts. “Gibney has zero integrity. Zero,” said Musk. “Fortunately, his movies are boring af … It’s a hit piece that misses, and makes the fatal sin of being boring for 4 hours. “Gibney just assembled a hit list of people who either have an axe to grind or don’t even know me (but still have an axe to grind) … He’s a bitter old man who lost the plot long ago. “Dogshit is worth more respect than Gibney.” Musk’s lawyer has also threatened to sue Gibney for defamation, NPR reported on Thursday. The documentary has caused a stir since its premier, as have the claims made by some of those involved in the film. Musk specifically denied a claim made by his ex-partner, the former Maga influencer Ashley St Clair, that his team offered her $40m to sign a non-disclosure agreement about their time together. “She was never offered that and has a history of making false claims,” he wrote. Musk also amplified a post by the podcaster Katie Miller, the wife of Donald Trump’s powerful adviser Stephen Miller and former communications director for Musk’s “department of government efficiency” (Doge). Miller complained about the alleged absence of Musk acquaintances and allies in the film. “It simply can’t be ‘definitive’ if the people who were present didn’t participate,” she said. “This fictional movie is a hit job by a self-obsessed Hollywood director.” Musk’s influence on public discourse through X, and the content it prioritises, is making international waves. While he has repeatedly intervened in the immigration debate in the UK, he also celebrated the strong result for Germany’s far-right Alternative für Deutschland party in this week’s state elections in Saxony-Anhalt. Speaking at a press conference in Venice, Gibney said he had encountered a “sense of fear” among people he approached over his film. He surmised that Musk’s childhood in South Africa may account for how he behaves now. “He had a childhood that was very difficult and traumatic,” Gibney said. “To some extent he’s now playing out that trauma on the rest of us, if I were to psychoanalyse the situation.”
