title: OpenAI not on track to reduce risk of ‘catastrophic’ loss of control, says board member
summary: US government adviser Paul Christiano warns of risks to AI industry as he joins OpenAI’s non-profit foundation
text: OpenAI is not on track to reduce the risk of “catastrophic” loss of control to an acceptable level, a member of its non-profit board has said, amid spreading public and political concern that super-advanced AIs could one day wipe out humanity. Paul Christiano, a US government technology adviser, said: “There is a meaningful risk that rapid acceleration in AI capabilities leads to catastrophic and irreversible loss of control in the very near term.” He added: “I do not think that the AI industry in general, including OpenAI, is currently on track to reduce this risk to an acceptable level.” Christiano used to run model alignment at OpenAI and made the statement on Wednesday as he joined the board of the San Francisco company’s non-profit foundation. He will also sit on the foundation’s committee that provides governance over safety and security practices across all of OpenAI, which is developing some of the world’s most advanced models. This summer, OpenAI admitted that hundreds of its AI agents went rogue during a training exercise, accessed the internet, conspired on message boards and hacked into a third-party website, Hugging Face. Christiano said that “if OpenAI rises to the occasion we could significantly reduce risk”. His comments came after a senior employee at Anthropic, OpenAI’s major US rival in the race to AI supremacy, claimed on Tuesday there was a greater than 10% chance the technology could “kill all humans” in the next decade. Evan Hubinger, the alignment science lead at Anthropic, warned that his company did not have a plan to ensure artificial superintelligence (ASI) was aligned, meaning it did no harm. Predictions for when ASI might be reached vary from several years to more than a decade. ASI is often defined as AI that far surpasses human intelligence across a large range of fields. Fears of AI catastrophe were also ignited by the resignation of Jacob Coxon, a 27-year-old Anthropic researcher who said he also previously worked at OpenAI, claiming “neither company was acting responsibly” and they were “gambling with our lives”. Coxon said on Wednesday night in an interview with CNN: “Right now there’s no risk of extinction. “The current models, the worst they can do is maybe hack into something, potentially cause a lot of damages … in infrastructure.” He added they were “not intelligent enough to outsmart us at the level that would lead to extinction”. But he went on: “What’s just crazy is to look at the rate of progress. There is a very real possibility that in the immediate future … next year, the year after, recursive self-improvement will happen and will enter the phase of Evan’s post, where he argues that there’s a chance we could all die.” Geoffrey Hinton, the Nobel prize-winning computer scientist known as one of the “godfathers of AI”, was asked on Wednesday for his view of Hubinger’s claim and told BBC Newsnight: “Nobody knows how to estimate it; a 10% chance seems not an unreasonable estimate.” Christiano’s prognosis about the likelihood of the AI industry reducing risk came as concerns about the most extreme risks from super-powerful AIs, long discussed in Silicon Valley, broke out into the mainstream this week. Politicians on both sides of the Atlantic, from Ted Cruz and Bernie Sanders in the US to the MP Darren Jones in the UK, have called for government action and the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, told parliament on Wednesday that “AI poses risks to our national security, but it also could be the source of solutions to keeping us safer”. Meanwhile, Anthropic has admitted a new incident in which a version of its Claude model in training broke into third parties after its task could not be aborted. It said the incident happened in January and would be included in an independent investigation of a total of four incidents to be carried out by the Berkeley-based AI safety organisation METR. Overall, it said the models were showing two forms of misalignment: biased reasoning, in which models selectively interpret evidence in ways that favour justifying their actions, and “recklessness, in which models have a propensity to keep trying to solve their task, even when this could lead to harm”. Anthropic said it was especially concerned about misalignment it found in the behaviour of Claude Mythos 5, which it said “behaved recklessly” by going online and uploading malicious code to a public software repository, PyPI. This was a process that involved the AI agent trying to find cryptocurrency so it could pay for a phone number that would allow it to register an email address needed to access PyPI. When this failed, it found a free email provider and got in. Fifteen systems then downloaded the malicious code, which meant they leaked credentials that allowed Mythos to access a real security vendor’s database. The company’s assessment of the incidents said: “This remains unsettled science – it is critical that alignment and security mature faster than capabilities advance, which is one reason we support a coordinated, verifiable approach to pacing frontier AI development.”

title: Malta warned of corruption crisis after ‘utter disbelief’ over Daphne Caruana Galizia verdict
summary: Labour peer tells Council of Europe inquiry failure to implement legal protections still putting journalists at risk
text: Malta is vulnerable to “repeated instances of high-level corruption” unless it strengthens the rule of law and protections for journalists, the Labour peer Shami Chakrabarti said at the opening of an inquiry into judicial failures following the death of Daphne Caruana Galizia. Chakrabarti, a member of the House of Lords and former director of the human rights group Liberty, has been named special rapporteur for a Council of Europe investigation into the fallout from the assassination of the anti-corruption journalist, who died in a car bombing in October 2017. Malta is in turmoil after the acquittal of a wealthy and politically influential businessman, Yorgen Fenech, of any involvement in Caruana Galizia’s murder. Fenech denies paying a middleman €150,000 to have her killed. At the inquiry’s first hearing, on Wednesday, Chakrabarti said the verdict had “staggered many throughout Maltese society and beyond. “It’s now almost nine years since the assassination that struck at the very heart of Maltese public life but a mastermind has not yet been held accountable,” she added. The first witnesses on Wednesday were the journalist’s eldest son, Matthew Caruana Galizia, and her sister Corinne Vella, who questioned the verdict, which dismissed both charges against Fenech by an 8-1 majority. Matthew Caruana Galizia told members of the council’s committee on legal affairs and human rights: “The Maltese public have seen all of the evidence against the accused, and the vast majority were convinced of his complicity in the murder. And this is why there is this atmosphere of utter disbelief at how the jury could have reached such a decision.” Malta’s state prosecutor is understood to be preparing an appeal, with the aim of securing a retrial. The Council of Europe, founded in 1949 after the second world war, created the European convention on human rights. It is led by an assembly drawn from members of the parliaments of its 46 member states. During the hearing, representatives expressed shock and concern about the verdict, calling for the European parliament and the European Commission to intervene. Iulian Bulai, a Romanian centre-right politician, suggested the EU could withhold funds from Malta. The procedure, known as the rule of law conditionality mechanism, was first used in 2022, against Hungary. “If there is such huge problem in matter of rule of law and a function of the Maltese institutions, the EU should apply a similar procedure on increasing pressure for reform,” said Bulai. He said the procedure had “functioned in other cases … So why shouldn’t it function in Malta’s case?” Malta, the EU’s smallest member state, with a population of 600,000, is a net recipient of EU money. Analysis suggests that since joining the block 22 years ago, the island has received €2.4bn more in subsidies than it has paid in. Chakrabarti said she would look at why Malta had failed to implement many of the recommendations from a public inquiry held after the murder. “The targeted assassination of a journalist in the middle of investigating high-level corruption sent a chill down the spine of everyone who cares about democratic values,” she said. “Many claim that the legal and policy changes needed to protect journalists to combat corruption and ensure the independent functioning of justice have not been carried out. “I’m extremely concerned by the apparent absence of reforms in critical areas which make Malta vulnerable to repeated instances of high-level corruption and limit the press freedom which should hold it in check.” The public inquiry found although there had been no evidence that the Maltese state had a direct role in the murder, the state bore responsibility for creating a climate of impunity. It recommended Italian-style anti-mafia laws, and making the hindrance of police investigations and abuse of office a crime for public officials. These measures have yet to be implemented. Chakrabarti compared the Caruana Galizia case to miscarriages of justice in the UK, where officials had been involved in coverups, citing the mismanagement of Grenfell Tower, the Post Office scandal and the Hillsborough football stadium disaster. She said her inquiry, titled Justice delayed: the unfinished implementation of the Daphne Caruana Galizia case, was likely to conclude in a year. Vella said fear that serious crimes could go unpunished had increased since the verdict. “Before the verdict was given, we lived in a country where a journalist was killed, but there was a chance of ending impunity. That disappeared as soon as the verdict was out.” She said journalists who had continued to investigate corruption allegations involving former members of Malta’s government “felt uneasy walking to their own cars following that verdict”.

title: Ryanair will dispute passenger’s claim he was sucked out of window
summary: CEO Michael O’Leary tells reporters the businessman was sucked ‘towards’ but not ‘out of’ the opening
text: Ryanair has said it will be “disputing” that any part of a passenger’s body was sucked outside when a window on one of its aircraft broke while in flight. US investigators are examining the incident which left Ljubisa Karović, 61, severely injured when the window beside him shattered on a Ryanair flight from Greece to Germany in July. Karović’s lawyer said the Serbian businessman was hauled back in after his head and right arm were sucked through the window of the Boeing 737 owing to the sudden depressurisation. However, Ryanair’s chief executive, Michael O’Leary, said the airline would be “disputing” that account, telling reporters after the airline’s annual general meeting (AGM) in Dublin on Thursday that Karović was “certainly sucked towards the window, but he didn’t get out the window”. The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) in the US is leading the accident investigation, alongside Boeing, engine manufacturer GE, and Ryanair. O’Leary said: “He wasn’t partially out the window. Part of his face didn’t get out the window. We don’t think any part of his body got out the window, but he was certainly sucked in very dramatic circumstances towards the window.” He said the passenger had been “belted into the seat”, adding: “We will be certainly at the end of the process disputing that he or any part of his anatomy will bend out the window.” O’Leary said he was “not trying to downplay it” and the airline would “have to await the outcome of the NTSB report”. In an interview with the Guardian, Karović said he believed his seatbelt had kept him in the plane as he blacked out, while his wife, Svetlana, said one passenger played a crucial part in his rescue, as she watched her husband “half in and out of the plane”. She said the unknown male passenger, believed to be Albanian, “did all he could to bring him in and then tried to block the window, first with a bag that was immediately sucked out and then with a suitcase, which worked”. Meanwhile, about a third of shareholders at the AGM voted against O’Leary’s latest pay deal, worth €150m (£129m). The package, agreed over the summer, would give him options on 10m shares if he hits profit and share price targets, and stays at the helm of the Irish carrier until 2032. Ryanair said it would later publish the results of the votes, which approved the deal by about 2-1. O’Leary also continued to dispute the account of the British air traffic control provider National Air Traffic Services (Nats) over the reasons for the latest failure on Tuesday, which disrupted travel for hundreds of thousands of passengers flying in and out of the UK and cancelled more than 2,100 flights. Martin Rolfe, the Nats boss, told the BBC on Tuesday: “This will be something we haven’t seen in more than 50 years of operation.” Continuing his long vendetta against Rolfe, O’Leary accused him of “telling lies to save his own skin”. A Ryanair spokesperson said Nats told a call with its teams on Tuesday that the reason was a “spurious flight plan”. A separate flight plan problem caused an outage in 2023. Nats said the problem occurred in its flight processing system but was not the same fault as those that caused outages and mass disruption in 2023 and 2025. Speaking in the Commons on Thursday, the aviation minister, Keir Mather, said Nats had “experienced an issue with its flight processing system at its Swanwick centre affecting the data that was available to controllers”. He said the fix “took time as the systems needed to be tested to ensure that they had fully recovered and operations could safely return to normal”. Nats, he added, had “confirmed that it was a technical issue and it does not believe it to be cyber-related”. Nats is due to submit a report next week while ministers have instructed the Civil Aviation Authority to conduct an independent review. O’Leary stoked further outrage by comparing his competitors to “rapists”, a term he has used for some rivals since the 2000s but less often publicly in recent times. He told reporters people were “desperate to get to Ryanair’s low fares because they can’t afford to fly with the high-fare rapists around Europe”. After repeating the “high-fare rapists” comments, and when challenged whether this was appropriate language, O’Leary told reporters: “Absolutely.”

title: Fascism on the rise in the UK, Anglican bishop says
summary: Arun Arora, bishop of Kirkstall in Leeds, condemns ‘twisted theology’ of groups who demonstrated at south coast ports at weekend
text: Fascism is on the rise in the UK, a Church of England bishop has warned, condemning the “twisted theology” of the self-described “Christian patriots” who demonstrated at ports on the south coast last weekend. The masked, black-clad, anti-migrant agitators – led by Daniel “Danny Tommo” Thomas, a former bodyguard of the far-right influencer Tommy Robinson – were heard chanting: “Christ is King.” Arun Arora, the bishop of Kirkstall in Leeds, said the incidents in Dover and Portsmouth were part of an increasingly worrying and disturbing rise in attempts “to tear the social fabric of our country” this year. Arora said the disorder that followed the “evil” killing of Henry Nowak in Southampton earlier this year, the subsequent racist firebombings in Belfast, anti-migration protests in Thetford, Norfolk, and a recent incident in Lancashire – in which the BBC reported that a six-year-old boy had a racial slur scrawled on his forehead – were “the first steps on the journey to open fascist nationalism that takes pride in conflict, hostility and division”. Arora added: “The biggest threat to England’s fabric today is to be found in the tidal wave of nationalism that threatens to destroy the foundations of community, to devastate social cohesion and threaten any sense of unity within this United Kingdom. “What we have seen on our streets in Southampton, in Belfast, in Thetford, in Portsmouth, in Dover is the playing out of a new machtpolitik – the ideology that argues that might is right – that threatens not only those of us who are likely to be targeted or attacked but threatens our way of life as a country. “This goes beyond the racism that many of us grew up with in the 1970s. Rather it is a return to the 1930s, where those dressed in blackshirts gathered on the streets under the banner of fascism.” Arora said the church had to challenge the “sinful idolatory” and “twisted theology” of so-called Christian nationalists, saying they were using the cross of Christ as a fashion accessory, with no understanding of Jesus’s message of love. He added: “We need to be consistent and unequivocal in our theology that there is no national flag that sits atop the cross …. Fascism is on the rise.” Arora made the speech at a Lambeth Palace event this week, hosted with his co-lead bishop for racial justice, Rosemarie Mallett, and the archbishops of Canterbury and York, to celebrate the the contribution of the C of E’s diverse clergy, ordinands and lay ministers. Asked about how people from ethnic minority backgrounds in the UK were feeling increasingly threatened and the misuse of Christian symbols, the archbishop of Canterbury, Sarah Mullally, said: “I think we’re all becoming aware that we have created a society where people feel that it is acceptable to intimidate others. “I think there is an increasing responsibility on Christian leaders to speak up and not be silent, because silence itself encourages a society in which people think it’s alright to intimidate in this way.” The event came five years after the publication of From Lament to Action, a landmark report to address institutional racism in the church. Referring to a recent incident in which a vicar, Rev Canon Dr Richard Frith, was surrounded by anti-immigration protesters inside Doncaster Minster after claims church bells drowned out their rally, Mallett told the Lambeth Palace event that “conflict is being brought directly into our sacred spaces”. She added: “In the same week that hundreds of masked vigilantes marched on Dover and Portsmouth, and a vicar has been surrounded by anti-immigration protesters at Doncaster Minster, it is clear racial justice is more needed than ever. “Fear of the stranger is being performed as a public spectacle. The church can tell the truth about history, protect the dignity of radicalised people, and offer a theological vision of belonging that lives out Jesus’s call to welcome the stranger.”

title: ‘I feel the pain of all those souls’: Ground Zero visitors remember lives lost on 9/11
summary: People from across the US and around the world pay their respects at memorial to victims of the terrorist attacks
text: “No day shall erase you from the memory of time,” reads an inscription at the the Ground Zero national September 11 memorial and museum, quoting from The Aeneid and cast in 15in letters made from the steel of the twin towers, which fell 29 minutes apart in a terrorist attack a quarter century ago. It took a decade for the 9/11 memorial in downtown Manhattan to be completed. It is composed of two dark granite basins on the footprints of the original towers with water cascading from their lips and the names of all 2,977 who died as a result of four aircraft hijackings inscribed on bronze panels around it. In the 15 years since, the memorial has served as a place of remembrance and, perhaps for some, as a place of secular pilgrimage to honor, identify and remember the lives lost in the terrorist attacks. Last week, many gathered at the memorials from all over the US and the world. A security guard who has worked the eight-acre site for a decade said that around this time of year the atmosphere becomes more solemn. Many visitors said they felt compelled to come to pay their respects. One said it was a part of a cruise ship itinerary. A man from Sligo, Ireland, recalled that he used to drink at O’Hara’s on nearby Cedar St when tower two was still under construction in the early 1970s. The towers, part of a seven-building World Trade Center commercial complex intended to revitalize lower Manhattan and centralize international trade, stood for barely three decades, but for many they came to symbolize American dynamism and power. “It holds a certain significance to the city’s identity,” said Kosta Athanasellis, visiting from Toronto. He said he had also heard great things about Greenwich Village. The memorial, he said, “definitely brings a wave of melancholy. What happened here caused an uproar all over the world.” Sara Salehi had a professor whose brother had died here. She recalled that a family member later committed suicide, traumatized by watching the attack and its aftermath. “All those people now are like little sparkles in the water,” she said, observing the shimmer of droplets caught in the sunlight. Also reflecting on the events 25 years ago was Andrea Cemal, 56. She was on her way to work in Buenos Aires, Argentina, when the news of the attack broke. “I think about how sad I was and how everybody was so moved in my country so far away from here. The images of those planes impacting on the building were so terrible. I feel the pain of all those souls.” “It’s an example of what’s wrong in the world,” said Cemal. Her daughter, a student of international relations, said the memorial was a reminder of what wars had become with terrorism folded into the way they were fought. “In the current mixed wars and hybrid wars we see more civilians being lost to violence and that sometimes goes unnoticed,” she said. Pamela Isaac, 70, said she had worked in a brokerage nearby for many years. She was in bed watching the news at home in Queens when the attack came on TV. “I really didn’t understand what was going on,” she said. “Things were very different after that.” She said she hadn’t visited the area since. “I didn’t want to come before. I felt the need to come to pay my respects to the people I’d been watching in a CNN documentary.” The sense of pilgrimage in coming to the memorial was not solely for Americans. “It’s sad, because all types passed away here,” she said. A young woman visiting from Morocco, who declined to offer her name, said she had felt the need to pay her respects. “It’s one of the most talked accidents,” she said, “and it’s impacted everyone a lot, especially me as Muslim. It’s so sad for the people who lost their lives, but it really destroyed a lot more than just a building. It was like when you throw a stone in the water.” Nadia Boggette, from Spain, said she was moved to see white carnations placed in inscriptions of the victims on their birthday. “It’s very lovely.” The memorial, she added, was “peaceful and sad at the same time”. “The crowd seems silent,” said Anthony Knecht from Greenville, South Carolina. “It was a very sad, eerie time in history.” He said it had been “terrible and shocking” to see the faces of those who lost their lives in the museum but “also important to see”. On that day, he said, a roommate came in to say America was being attacked. “I was like, ‘No shit.’ Now we have this memorial. It’s 25 years later, but what has changed? This terrible thing happened, but those organizations that paid for it are still there.” Gina and Steve Hutt from Dallas, Texas, said it was important to come. A pilgrimage? “No, that would be the wrong word. You have to pay respects,” Gina said. But she doubted that it had changed politics. “You can call anyone a zealot if you want to. People say all kinds of things but no one really knows why they did what they did. I don’t think it was to do with the administration. George W Bush suffered a lot for it because of his dad [George HW, who had served as CIA director and later president].” Michael Tarney 78, from Sligo, Ireland, said it was like a pilgrimage for him to visit the memorial. Tarney reflected on what had taken place. He’d watched a documentary on the disaster the previous evening. “They said it created the world for the 21st century. It was the biggest event, I suppose somewhat similar to the Titanic in 1912. Shocking and with a very personal touch.” Joseph Krings, a film editor from Brooklyn, had stopped by on his way to a Labor Day march. “I don’t come here very often because it’s heavy. It’s a very somber feeling you get when you come here.” Krings said it was not a personal pilgrimage to visit the memorial, he just had time to kill. “I’m sure it would be a pilgrimage for some people, but I don’t do pilgrimages of any sort. But I think it’s beautiful and I love that it’s here.”

title: Glencore’s former head of oil pleads not guilty to bribery charges
summary: Billionaire Alex Beard and his former deputy appear in London court over alleged payments to west African officials
text: Glencore’s billionaire former head of oil trading has pleaded ⁠not guilty ⁠to two bribery charges after allegedly facilitating payments to west African officials in order to advance the Swiss commodity group’s operations ⁠in the continent. Alex Beard, 59, denied two counts of conspiracy to make ⁠corrupt payments at Southwark crown court in London on Thursday, in a case brought by the Serious Fraud Office (SFO). The oil trader, who emerged from obscurity when he was revealed as a billionaire during Glencore’s flotation on the London Stock Exchange in 2011, ‌is alleged to have been involved in ‌a conspiracy to make corrupt payments ‌to government or state-owned oil company officials in Nigeria between 2010 and 2014 and in Cameroon between 2007 and 2014. A relaxed-looking Beard, wearing an open-neck shirt and sports jacket, appeared in the dock alongside his former deputy Andrew Gibson, who was Glencore’s head of oil operations. Gibson also denied four counts of conspiracy to make corrupt payments in Nigeria, Cameroon and Côte d’Ivoire. Gibson, 66, also pleaded not guilty to an ⁠additional charge of conspiracy to falsify documents required for an accounting purpose. Four other former Glencore traders – Martin Wakefield, David Perez, Paul Hopkirk, Ramon Labiaga – previously pleaded not guilty to all charges in the same case last year. title: Houthis seize key Yemeni port of Mocha in drive to take control of Red Sea coast
summary: Iran and its proxies move closer to full control of two shipping chokepoints as regional conflict widens
text: Houthi forces in Yemen are making a concerted drive to take over the country’s Red Sea coast fully, claiming control of the key port of Mocha in the most serious wave of fighting with the Saudi-backed government in years, bringing the Iran-aligned group closer to full control of a key shipping route. Seizure of the coast and some of the islands in the sea would be a strategic disaster for Saudi Arabia and the US, taking Iran and its proxies closer to full control of two choke points for western shipping on opposite sides of the Arabian peninsula: the Bab al-Mandab at the southern end of the Red Sea and the strait of Hormuz in the Gulf. Observers have said a reduction in hostilities – the most intense since the UN-sponsored ceasefire of April 2022 put an end to major military exchanges – now seems unlikely in what is seen as an attempt by the Houthis to open a second front in the Iran-US war, alongside the battle for control of Hormuz. Baraa Shiban, the Royal United Services Institute’s (Rusi) Yemen specialist, a London-based security thinktank, said the situation in the country was spiralling out of control, adding that the UN-recognised Yemeni government was opening new fronts against the Houthis in the hope of putting more pressure on their forces than they could withstand. But in the past 48 hours the Houthis had major advances south, down Yemen’s west coast, taking them closer to the high ground overlooking the narrow Bab al-Mandab strait. The fighting has also raised questions about whether Saudi Arabia, which on Thursday launched as many as 40 airstrikes on Houthi targets, will activate the Mecca defence agreement and ask its co-signatories, Pakistan and Turkey, to send forces. The pact is designed to be defensive in nature and believed unlikely to apply to Saudi military activities in Yemen. By taking control of more of the Red Sea coast south of the port of Hodeidah, the Houthis’ aim is to use a new lever to put pressure on Saudi Arabia and the US to agree a deal that lifts the US blockade on Iranian oil tankers in the Gulf. Donald Trump on Wednesday acknowledged he did not expect the war with Iran to end before the US midterm elections at the start of November. The latest phase in the escalation began when Houthis attacked energy installations and southern cities in Saudi Arabia using drones and ballistic missiles. In response, the kingdom’s military forces launched at least 15 strikes between 3 and 7 September. The conflict data monitor Acled estimated there were 276 fatalities over the five-day period alone. The fighting has continued, with the Houthis claiming control of Mocha in Taiz province, as well as the inland city of Hays and the Khalid ibn al-Walid camp, the largest military base in the region. One Houthi-linked estimate suggested its forces had gained control of more than 2,320 sq miles (6,000 sq km) of land. The commander of the Yemeni government forces, Maj Gen Tareq Saleh, admitted he had organised a strategic retreat south of Mocha in order to regroup in a secure location. “The armed forces in the western coast paid a heavy price – martyrs and wounded – over the past days as they confronted the Houthi attack planned by Iran, and supported by it,” he said. Analysts claimed that the effectiveness of Yemen’s government forces was weakened by internal divisions, as well as external pressure from Saudi Arabia. The latter, meanwhile, continues to take advantage of its air superiority to attack Houthi positions, though government sources acknowledged Houthi ground advances along the coast and their missile strikes on the strategic Red Sea islands of Zuqar and Hanish. The clashes have raged across Yemen, including Ad Dali, al-Bayda, Marib, Shabwah, al-Jawf, Hodeidah, and Taiz. In the initial days of the renewed conflict the Houthis were forced back in some areas as battles on multiple fronts overstretched their resources and fighter numbers. The Houthis will be hoping political divisions inside the Yemeni government, reflected in a lack of an integrated military, will slowly give them the upper hand. The United Arab Emirates, previously a powerful player in southern Yemen where it backed the separatist forces of the Southern Transitional Council, withdrew its financial and military support at the turn of the year. The southern forces have refused to fight outside their own region. “A reduction in hostilities anytime soon seems unlikely, as both sides continue to escalate with the goal of inflicting enough damage to the other side to force a compromise,” said Sherwan Hindreen Ali, a Yemen analyst for Acled. “In terms of military capability, both sides are more equal compared to the immediate period prior to the 2022 ceasefire when the Houthis had the upper hand.” He added: “Fighting will remain focused on the fronts of the Red Sea coast in Hodeidah and Taiz, where both the Houthis and the Saudi Arabia-Yemen government have a vested interest in claiming the whole territory to deprive the other side of effective control of the strait of Bab al-Mandab.” The head of the Houthis’ national delegating negotiating team, Muhammad Abdul Salam, insisted non-Saudi commercial shipping would not be attacked. The fighting has contributed to the price of oil rising above $100 a barrel after weeks when it was trading closer to $80. The escalation to this week’s all-out violence has been a slow process. It began after a senior delegation of the Houthi group, which has long been in a complex alliance with Iran, flew to Tehran for the funeral of the Iranian supreme leader Ali Khamenei in July, returning in an Iranian plane that the Saudis refused to land in rebel-controlled Sana’a. The Saudis instead bombed the runway, leading the Houthis to announce a Red Sea naval blockade of Saudi Arabia in what the Yemeni group described as a blockade for a blockade. The 20 July announcement of the blockade was followed by a strike on Saudi Arabia’s Jazan refinery on 25 July and on a tanker off Yanbu on 24 August. Saudi Arabia has become reliant on the Red Sea route for trade after Iran throttled shipping through the strait of Hormuz as a result of US-Israeli attacks.

title: UK ministers explore raising price of water for industrial users amid shortages
summary: Environment Agency says talks under way about increasing prices for industrial users to try to reduce poor water management
text: Ministers are exploring making water more expensive for some users, in the face of severe supply shortages. Despite the UK being a famously wet country, the precarious nature of the water supply has been made particularly acute this summer, with almost three-quarters of England and all of Wales in drought and 27 million people facing restrictions on their water use. As the climate crisis worsens and demand for water increases, the Environment Agency has estimated that, without action, England’s water supply could be short by 5bn litres a day by 2055. Helen Wakeham, the director of water at the Environment Agency, said that to plug this severe and growing gap, the value of water needed to increase. “If someone wants an abstraction licence from the Environment Agency, what they pay for is the cost of producing the licence. They don’t pay anything towards the value of that water,” she said. While millions of households in England are paying record levels for their water bills, Wakeham said that, for big industrial customers, the more water they used, the less they paid. There was a “lively conversation” going on about whether we could “completely reframe the way we value and pay for water”. “It’s the beginning of a conversation, but ministers have asked us to look at the value of water and how our abstraction licensing system works,” she said. The Guardian recently revealed that less than 1% of businesses in England use more water than the daily needs of 10 million people. Some of these businesses, which include oil refineries, chemical plants and paper mills, face no requirements to cut their consumption. With the government committed to make England an AI superpower, there are also questions about where water-hungry datacentres will get their resources from. Water UK, the body representing the UK water industry, warned the UK would not have enough water for future datacentres. “The reason datacentres are water-hungry is because water is so cheap,” said Wakeham. Dr Doug Parr, Greenpeace UK’s chief scientist and policy adviser, said: “Every day, people are doing their bit to save water, but they are being hit with higher bills and hosepipe bans while big business gets cheap water access. At a time when the country is facing water stress due to climate change, it is absurd that major companies have access to water that is cheaper for them, per litre, the more they use. This has to change. The whole abstraction policy and licensing needs to be rewritten from a blank sheet of paper to make it fit for a country facing summer droughts and a biodiversity crisis.” Environment Agency permitting means datacentres are required to use drinking water only. Jon Chappell, the trade body’s deputy director, said this was “unforgivable” and a “genuine failing of government”. Water UK has estimated that datacentres in England use 6.6m litres of drinking water every day. With the government’s ambition to triple datacentre capacity by 2030, this could increase to 19.8m litres a day. Wakeham agreed there was an issue with drinking water being used for cooling and industrial supply, and said the agency was “working with the government to look at different ways of pricing and valuing water to make sure that the right water goes to the right places”. She said this could result in water becoming more expensive for industrial users. “The overarching message is that water is so cheap that often it’s not managed, because it’s cheaper just to use more water,” Wakeham said. A Defra spokesperson said: “We’ve all felt the impact of extreme weather this year. With millions of households facing hosepipe bans and farmers dealing with drought, it’s only right that we take a closer look at industrial water use too, to ensure we’re using our water resources wisely. “We want to keep bills as low as possible for consumers and make sure industry uses less drinking-quality water where it isn’t needed, while making it easier to reuse water so every drop counts. The water system in this country is broken. That’s why we’re delivering the biggest reform in a generation, so water is there for the people who need it.”

title: John Lewis losses widen to £124m as shopper confidence dips
summary: Retailer says first half was a tougher market than it expected, though Waitrose grew sales
text: Losses at the owner of John Lewis and Waitrose widened by more than 40% in the first half of the year as it struggled with higher costs and shoppers feeling less confident about their money. The John Lewis Partnership, which operates 36 department stores and more than 300 Waitrose supermarkets, said its pre-tax loss for the six months to 1 August climbed to £124m, compared with £88m in the same period in 2025. Jason Tarry, the chair of JLP, said the first half of the year had been a “tougher market than we had planned for”. “Customers have been more cautious about spending, particularly when they replace the bigger-ticket things in their homes,” he said, citing higher interest rates, the rising cost of living and uncertainty triggered by wars around the world. Higher national insurance contributions and a series of heatwaves over the summer also drove up costs, JLP said. Tom Denyard, the boss of Waitrose, said the heat had triggered “some challenges with refrigeration and freezing”, but that the company was investing in more resilient equipment. Waitrose still outperformed John Lewis, with sales across the supermarket arm up 4% while those at the department store chain fell 2%. Overall half-year sales rose 2% to £6.3bn. The company added that it was “starting to build” a joined-up loyalty offering across the partnership. It currently offers separate John Lewis and Waitrose loyalty cards, which include free “treat” products and personalised rewards. The partnership, which is employee-owned, is in the midst of a turnaround plan, after having closed 16 department stores and at least 20 Waitrose outlets since the pandemic and is cutting thousands of staff jobs. Tarry called on the chancellor, John Healey, to reduce the cost of doing business in the UK in his inaugural budget in October. “We want the government to deliver against their manifesto, which is to reform business rates,” he said. “It is the biggest business tax that we face, and in some locations it is bigger than our rent bill. “Anything that the government can do to help us employ more people and be able to drive more growth would be very helpful.” JLP’s drop in profit comes after Peter Ruis, head of the department store arm, said last month he would step down after less than three years in the role. He has been replaced by Will Kernan, a former boss of the River Island fashion chain. In March the company felt confident enough to pay its 69,000 workers, whom it calls partners, a bonus – of 2% of salary – for the first time in four years, following a 6% rise in its underlying profit. Staff shared a pot of £35m, worth about one week’s extra pay each. The company said it was still too early to say whether staff would be paid a bonus for this financial year, although Tarry said he was “confident we will be able to make a profit”. The retailer typically makes the bulk of its profit in the second half of its year, which includes the peak Christmas trading period. But Robyn Duffy, an analyst at the consultancy RSM UK, said John Lewis looked vulnerable heading into the second half. “The retailer is particularly exposed to big-ticket, deferrable categories like home, furniture and electricals – exactly where these consumers are choosing to cut back or delay spending,” she said. John Lewis is one of the few remaining national department store chains, following the closure of Debenhams and Beales. This summer Harvey Nichols was bought out of administration by the owner of Sports Direct, Mike Ashley, who had said the Knightsbridge store was in a “death spiral”.

title: Trump makes highly unusual promise of $5,000 for all if Republicans win midterms | First Thing
summary: Speaking in Dallas, the president raised ethical concerns with an apparent $1tn offer to the electorate
text: Good morning. Donald Trump has pledged to pay every adult citizen in the US $5,000 if Republicans retain the House and Senate in the midterm elections. The outlandish proposal, which would cost over $1tn, immediately raised ethical concerns. Trump made the promise during a marathon speech at the Republican midterm convention in Dallas in which he assailed Democrats as “radical”, defended his unpopular war in Iran, and urged voters to “pretend that I’m on the ballot”. Trump claimed, without evidence, that his second term had been “the most successful two years, financially and every other way, in the history of the presidency”. In a statement, Ken Martin, the chair of the Democratic National Committee, accused Republicans of holding a “bizarre dog-and-pony show” to placate the president’s “fragile ego”. “Tonight only confirmed that the president is a lame duck failure who is dragging his party toward defeat,” Martin said. Why did the Republicans hold a midterm convention? Republicans are gambling that the GOP’s first midterm convention can salvage their threatened House majority. However, Trump’s dismal approval rating drove many competitive candidates to skip the two-day event entirely. What has Trump said about the former attorney Michael Cohen? The US president has said he would consider pardoning Michael Cohen, the former fixer whom he once branded a “rat” for testifying against him. Cohen was Trump’s personal lawyer, but flipped in 2018, and pleaded guilty to federal crimes including facilitating a hush payment to the pornography star Stormy Daniels and lying under oath to Congress. The statement comes a year after Washington began a campaign of unilateral deadly strikes against those it calls “narco-terrorists” operating boats in international waters. “I think it’s an incredible advance for the first time to have countries that are willing to participate in these efforts in their territorial waters,” Rubio told reporters on a trip to the Ecuadorian capital, Quito. “The important point is that these routes are being disrupted. These routes are being ended”. How many people has the US killed in its campaign? Late Wednesday, US Southern Command announced the latest strike in the Caribbean Sea, saying it killed three people. That brought the number of people who have been killed in boat strikes by the US military to at least 230 in 69 strikes. What has the US announced about Ecuador’s gangs? The US has designated Ecuador’s Los Tiguerones gang as a terrorist organisation. Rubio said the gang was linked to narcotics trafficking, as well as attacks on civilians, law enforcement officers and journalists. “We are talking about terrorists who, in many cases, possess weapons and equipment resembling the national armies of certain countries,” he said. Apple unveils folding iPhone Duo … and its new CEO Apple has unveiled the iPhone Duo, the company’s first foldable phone and the most significant change to the iPhone since its 2007 introduction. The nearly $2,000 device takes inspiration from iPads’ wide screens, and when opened, is the company’s largest phone display and thinnest phone. While competitors have been releasing foldable smartphones since the late 2010s, the new model is a first for Apple, and its rollout serves as the first big test for its new CEO, John Ternus, who took over from Tim Cook last week. The phone will be available on 23 October. What did new CEO Ternus say about his role? Helming the company’s annual showcase for the first time, Ternus said: “I want to take a moment to express what an extraordinary privilege it is to represent the remarkable teams here at Apple. I continue to be inspired every single day by the curiosity, invention and relentless pursuit of excellence that define Apple.” Anthropic researchers say AI could cause human extinction by 2030 Artificial intelligence could kill off humanity within the decade, according to three researchers with the industry giant Anthropic, one of whom has quit his job in protest. title: World must reject climate culture wars or face economic ruin, says UN’s Stiell
summary: Warning by United Nations climate chief comes as EU data shows August 2026 was joint hottest month ever
text: Attempts to stoke a climate crisis culture war must be rejected or the world will face economic disaster, the UN’s climate chief has warned. Simon Stiell, the executive secretary of the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change, warned that this year’s “hot as hell” summer had killed tens of thousands of people in Europe alone and “hammered” infrastructure, businesses and economics, costing a likely €180bn (£155bn), as well as leading to forced migration around the world. “The climate crisis is now a continent-wide economic security emergency,” he told a committee of the European parliament on Thursday morning. “We’ve seen mass evacuations. Power stations closed. And trade routes choked. Crops lost. Yields down. And food prices up – and set to rise further.” He said political polarisation over climate action was not in the interests of voters and would lead to far worse outcomes. “Climate is sometimes seen as a partisan issue, as territory in the culture wars,” he said. “That is palpably false … Climate cuts across the core concerns of voters, whatever their politics: [affecting] family health, community safety and economic stability; affordable food and available water; jobs, business costs and household bills.” With populist parties in the EU and around the world calling for backtracking on policies to cut greenhouse gas emissions, Stiell hit out at some of those politicians’ key talking points, including on migration, which he said was increasing as a result of extreme weather. “To be soft on climate action is to be soft on inflation, and the cost of living, soft on sovereignty and security, and soft on economic growth and jobs. The fossil fuel crisis is also pushing up the costs of government borrowing, meaning less fiscal space to deliver vital services that populations need and expect.” Stiell’s warnings came as the EU’s climate monitoring service released data showing August 2026 was the joint hottest month ever recorded around the world. Global temperatures reached 1.65C above preindustrial levels, scientists said on Thursday, amid warnings of further heating. Last month tied with July 2023 for the hottest on record, according to the EU’s Copernicus Climate Change Service. Sea surface temperatures also soared to their highest levels on record for August. These temperatures were recorded before the coming El Niño weather system had made much of an impact. El Niño is a naturally recurrent phenomenon whereby wind changes over the Pacific lead to rising ocean temperatures and the transfer of huge amounts of heat to the atmosphere, with the consequences felt around the world in floods, droughts and heatwaves. This year’s system, likely to reach its full strength towards the end of the year, is forecast to be potentially the most intense on record, as it is now supercharged by the climate crisis. Friederike Otto, a professor of climate science at Imperial College London, said: “While El Niño is starting to ramp up the heat, the underlying driver [behind this year’s high temperatures] remains our relentless burning of fossil fuels. Climate change makes every El Niño hotter, and until we stop burning coal, oil and gas, these record-shattering months will simply keep on coming.” The effects of August’s extreme heat are still being felt around the world, in the aftermath of devastating wildfires, damage to harvests, excess deaths from heatwaves and disruptions to transport, business and public services in many countries. Food price inflation is likely to increase further, as the impacts of smaller harvests are felt in domestic markets and imports. Stiell said: “If humanity doesn’t cut the fossil fuel pollution … this summer’s brutal heat, fires and droughts will seem mild compared to the permanent climate nightmare that will follow.” Although temperatures exceeded 1.5C above preindustrial levels, set in the 2015 Paris climate agreement as the lower of two limits that governments would strive to keep, such highs would need to continue for several years before the agreement was judged to be breached. Data from the Copernicus Earth observation satellite service confirmed that western and central Europe, as well as areas of Scandinavia and south-eastern Europe, had experienced much drier than usual conditions over the summer, while around the world much of the south of the US, northern Mexico, parts of Canada, the Maghreb, part of the Horn of Africa, Siberia, large parts of central Asia, China, South America, South Africa, and northern Australia were all also drier than average. The more temperatures rise above the 1.5C threshold, the greater the chance of reaching planetary “tipping points” that could push temperatures much higher and irretrievably break down key stabilisers of the climate system, such as the Arctic ice cap and the Amazon rainforest. Ruth Fuller, chief adviser on climate to the environmental charity WWF UK, said: “This year has seen records broken left, right and centre, increasing the risk that natural systems will irreversibly change once they are pushed past tipping points.” Samantha Burgess, the strategic lead for climate at the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts, which operates the Copernicus service, said: “August 2026 was a remarkable month in the global climate record. It was both the warmest August and the warmest month ever recorded, with global temperatures reaching 1.65C above preindustrial levels, marking the return of global temperatures above 1.5C. “Combined with record global sea surface temperatures and the warmest summer on record for western Europe, these observations show how climate change is driving extremes across the atmosphere and the oceans. The impacts of these conditions are increasingly being felt by communities, economies and ecosystems across the world.”

title: Trouble in US bond market could mean higher prices are here to stay
summary: Concerns over rising inflation, continuing war with Iran, and the US’s record national debt have shaken the market
text: Americans who have been grappling with the higher cost of living over the last few years now face another issue: trouble in the US bond market that could mean elevated costs are here to stay. US government bonds – known as treasuries – are supposed to be the most stable type of investment vehicle. But investor concerns over issues including rising inflation, the continuing war with Iran, and the US’s record national debt have shaken the market and slowed demand for US treasury bonds. Loans for homes, cars and credit cards, along with money businesses borrow to keep things running, could get more expensive if the sell-off in the bond market continues. Here’s what we know about the problems in the bond market and what it could mean for US consumers. How the US bond market works A US treasury bond is essentially the US government packaging up its debt and selling it to investors with a promise to pay interest. Investors can buy bonds that mature at different rates – a two-year note will mean an investor gets their money back quicker than a 30-year bond, but typically with lower interest. When it comes to measuring the bond market, investors pay attention to the yield rate for each type of bond. The yield is the rate of return that investors who purchase that type of bond can expect to receive once the bond matures, and it fluctuates based on the price of the bond itself. A higher yield rate means more investors are trying to sell off their bonds and are willing to offer more to get it off their hands. What’s happening in the bond market? While small fluctuations in the bond market are normal, the yield on US treasurys has continued to rise over the summer, with the 10-year treasury note hitting its highest yield since 2023 on Tuesday. The increase started in the spring, when the US first declared war in Iran, and has kept rising. At the end of February, the yield rate for the 10-year treasury was 3.95%. On Wednesday, the rate hit 4.8%. The yield for the 30-year treasury took a huge dip earlier in the summer, when the US and Iran were in the middle of a temporary ceasefire. At the time, oil prices were dipping down to their lowest levels since the start of the war, and prices have been up ever since. Activity in the bond market provides an insight into how investors are feeling about the US economy, even more so than the stock market, which can get outsized boosts from industries that are doing particularly well, like AI and tech, even when other sectors of the economy are faring less well. Higher yields in the bond market point to concern around rising inflation, which has ticked up significantly since the start of the Iran war. Investors are bracing for higher interest rates from the US Federal Reserve, which is expected to raise rates at least once before the end of the year. This would also make borrowing more expensive, even if the bond market calms. Higher loans for consumers Mortgages are closely tied to the US treasury market – when yields go up, mortgage rates are expected to follow. Mortgage rates are already double what they were during the pandemic. While the 30-year fixed-rate mortgage dipped down below 6% in February, reaching its lowest level since 2022, rates have since gone back. At the end of August, the mortgage rate sat at 6.66%, and is expected to go up more after the bond market sell-off. House building has already been hit by higher rates and a further blow will ripple through the economy from construction jobs to the sale of white goods. Other loans will also be affected, including car loans and the interest rates consumers pay for their credit cards. Alex Jacquez, senior vice-president of policy, advocacy and research at the progressive thinktank Groundwork Collaborative and a former economic adviser to the Biden administration, said that higher borrowing costs will be especially painful for Americans whose savings have been depleted after years of high inflation. “We’ve seen credit card balances start to creep back up, defaults start to creep back up,” Jacquez said. “More and more people are turning to credit instruments to pay down all kinds of basic things like healthcare, groceries and gas.” Failed intervention Scott Bessent, the US treasury secretary, announced that the treasury department would triple its buyback of US treasuries, increasing the operation from $2bn to $6bn. The move is just the latest intervention meant to stabilize the bond market. Earlier in the month, Trump announced the US bought Japanese yen to strengthen the currency, which was seen as a move to prop up the Japanese government, a major owner of US bonds. While Bessent’s announcement briefly calmed the treasury market, it did little to quell investor concerns over inflation and yields soon started rising again. The Billionaire investor Stanley Druckenmiller, Bessent’s former mentor, criticized the move, saying “governments defending prices against fundamentals always lose”. The backdrop of the bond market crisis is the US hitting a major borrowing milestone. The gross national debt topped $40tn for the first time in history last month, and Trump has shown little interest in his pre-election pledge to balance the US’s budget. Jacquez, of the Groundwork Collaborative, said that there was little that the Trump administration can do if it continues to pursue inflationary policies, like continued conflict in the Middle East and new tariffs on close trading allies. “First and foremost, they should stop getting in their own way,” Jacquez said. “It’s no wonder that people are expecting more inflation in the months to come.”

summary: Boss Richard Walker is ‘proud to be backing Britain’ with a store in the capital, Stanley
text: The supermarket chain Iceland has said it will open a shop on the Falkland Islands in early December. The shop, to be launched in partnership with a local retailer, Kelper Stores, will be the first UK high street brand to have a presence in the British territory and will be in the capital, Stanley. Richard Walker, the retailer’s executive chair, said the company was “proud to be backing Britain”. “The Falklands are a special part of the British family and it’s always been an ambition of mine to support it, so being able to bring Iceland to Stanley is a huge moment for us,” Lord Walker said. “This is an important moment for the business and our international aspirations. “I will personally be visiting the Falklands to officially open the store and I’m looking forward to welcoming our new customers through the door.” Iceland’s plan comes less than a week after the Argentine president, Javier Milei, stepped up his nation’s sovereignty claims over the islands. “Recently, President Trump declared that the US is re-evaluating its historic position in relation to the Malvinas,” Milei said, using the Argentinian name for the Falklands. He said the UK was facing “multiple crises of a migratory, demographic and economic nature that are unlikely to be resolved. It is clear that they are on a path of decline. Argentina’s future, however, is flourishing and will prevail.” Milei pledged to impose sanctions on oil companies drilling in the territory, with his government confirming on Monday that it would file criminal charges against the Israeli energy company Navitas Petroleum and ⁠its executives ⁠for operating in the Falklands. Meanwhile, a local fishing company, Fortuna, and the Danish company F-land ApS have faced local opposition to a joint venture to build a salmon farm in the region, primarily around environmental concerns. Salmon Free Falklands, set up by local people to oppose the proposal, is calling for a referendum on the project.
