title: Climate ‘feedback loops’ could worsen global warming by 30%, study finds
summary: Emissions of planet-heating methane and CO2 from natural sources are worsening the climate crisis, paper says
text: Rising global temperatures caused by the burning of fossil fuels are transforming the world’s forests, wetlands and tundra to the point they are releasing emissions that could further worsen global heating by as much as 30%, a new study has found. As the world heats up, permafrost in the high latitudes is thawing, fiercer wildfires are burning in drying forests and wetlands and lakes are warming. All of these changes are themselves causing the release of planet-heating methane and carbon dioxide locked in trees and soils, therefore worsening the climate crisis, the paper states. While scientists have long known of these “feedback loops” that amplify the impact of direct pollution from burning coal, oil and gas, the emissions from natural sources are largely unaccounted for in climate projections. This additional heating is, however, significant, researchers found, with emissions from natural sources set to amplify global heating by 20% to 30% by the end of this century. This would add an estimated 0.2C to 0.4C to the global average temperature by this time, depending on the overall action taken by countries to combat the climate crisis. Even small fractions of temperature change across the global climate can greatly change the risk of severe and deadly heatwaves, floods, drought and other impacts. The United Nations last week conceded the international pact to constrain the global temperature rise to 1.5C above pre-industrial levels will be breached in the next few years, causing climate impacts such as this summer’s record heatwaves and wildfires to “strike faster, hit harder and last longer”. Yet the increase in the world’s fever will likely be even larger than most projections currently account for, the new research warns, as they do not factor in the methane and CO2 that will spew from permafrost, wetlands, freshwaters and wildfires – the four areas the paper analyzed. “This hidden multiplier is missing from the models guiding climate policy, so those models are likely underestimating how much warming is coming – and overestimating how much carbon we can still afford to emit,” said Sam Abernethy, a scientist at Spark Climate Solutions who led the research, published in Environmental Research Letters. The disruption of the world’s carbon cycles is now being seen in “real time”, said Rob Jackson, a Stanford University scientist and study co-author. “The results are a wake-up call, and it’s imperative that they be included in the next generation of climate policies,” he added. “Failure to do so will make meeting the world’s climate goals less and less likely.” There has been longstanding concern that should global heating melt enough of the Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets, thaw enough permafrost, warp crucial ocean currents and turn the Amazon rainforest into a savannah, the world will career past a series of catastrophic tipping points where the climate system spins wildly outside any sort of restraining human influence. The planet is getting closer to such a “point of no return” where this runaway global heating becomes reality, a separate study earlier this year warned. This latest paper makes clear that action by countries to cut fossil fuel pollution will still lessen the amount of additional emissions that come from landscapes. Under the most optimistic climate scenario where emissions are cut quickly, natural sources will add 0.2C of warming, the paper found. Under a worst-case higher emissions scenario, 0.4C will probably be added. Current policies put in place by governments are likely to see the global temperature rise to 2.6C above pre-industrial times, according to Climate Action Tracker. This will probably cause severe disruption and hardship to billions of people through sea level rise, crop losses and other consequences. “One of the most troubling aspects of climate change is that warming can trigger natural processes that cause still more warming,” said Bill Ripple, an ecologist at Oregon State University who helped author the research earlier this year on runaway heating. He was not involved in the new paper, which he called “important”. “This does not mean that a Hothouse Earth trajectory is inevitable, but it provides another warning about the possibility of reinforcing feedbacks that can amplify the warming humans initiate,” he said. “The paper also reminds us why every fraction of a degree matters. The more we warm the planet, the more we risk activating natural processes that add still more greenhouse gases to the atmosphere. This makes rapid reductions in fossil fuel emissions even more urgent.”

title: JP Morgan boss meets Burnham and Healey to warn against bank tax rise
summary: Jamie Dimon tells UK politicians before October budget that investment could be at risk, it is understood
text: Jamie Dimon, chief executive of the largest US bank, JP Morgan, is understood to have warned Andy Burnham and his chancellor, John Healey, against raising taxes on banks in his inaugural budget in October. The Wall Street billionaire met the politicians on Wednesday and cautioned them that higher taxes could put investment and employment in the UK at risk, it is understood. The meeting came amid speculation that Healey is considering a windfall tax on banks and oil companies in his budget on 28 October. Dimon has a long track record of lobbying against Britain’s additional bank taxes, which were imposed after the government bailed out big UK lenders in the 2008 financial crisis. Lenders in the UK pay a 28% corporation tax rate, higher than the standard 25%, as well as a separate surcharge on their UK balance sheets. The JP Morgan chief executive has previously warned that raising these taxes further could have “adverse consequences”. In August, he told Healey in a telephone conversation that higher levies could hit jobs, citing a fall in finance roles in New York that he blamed on the city’s tax regime. Dimon was among a group of bank bosses who successfully lobbied against higher taxes before Healey’s predecessor Rachel Reeves’s budget last year – with Dimon hosting Varun Chandra, who remains in his post as the prime minister’s business envoy, at a birthday celebration for King Charles at the bank’s Manhattan headquarters. Days afterwards, Dimon revealed plans to build a 3m sq ft tower in London’s Canary Wharf district, although he added that a “continuing positive business environment in the UK” was required. However, in May this year, he said he could scrap plans for the £3bn tower – which is expected to serve as JP Morgan’s UK headquarters and house more than half its 23,000-strong UK workforce – if Keir Starmer were replaced by a new Labour prime minister who was hostile to banks. Burnham has not made any specific comments about a bank tax so far. However, he has faced calls to introduce higher levies from the TUC and the campaign group Positive Money, which argue that a tax increase could help cover rising household bills as part of his drive to tackle the cost of living. The UK’s four biggest lenders: HSBC, NatWest, Barclays and Lloyds Banking Group, have generated £200bn in pre-tax profits over the past five years, largely off the back of rising interest rates. UK banks together paid an estimated £43.3bn in tax for the financial year that ended in March 2025, according to a report commissioned by the industry body UK Finance.

title: Pixel 11 Pro review: Google’s best pocket camera goes customisable
summary: Solid battery life, snappy performance and quality software make for a great smaller phone with a killer camera
text: Google’s latest Pro phone is out to prove it has the best camera on a smartphone while embracing customisation, allowing you to change the look and feel of your photos far beyond simple filters even if that means making them technically worse. The Pixel 11 Pro packs the best of Google’s hardware and software into a still-pocketable and easy to handle frame, instantly making it a contender for best smaller phone of the year. Being smaller doesn’t make it cheap. The 11 Pro sits above the regular £879 Pixel 11 and costs from £1,079 (€1,199/$1,099/A$1,849) – £80 (€100/$100/A$150) more than last year, with double the storage but less memory owing to the cost of RAMageddon. Little has changed on the outside for the Pro Pixels in several years. The new model is 0.1mm smaller in all directions and 3g lighter but has the same size 6.3in OLED screen, same polished aluminium and glass body and a large camera bar sticking out the back. It is an attractive design that has aged well. The temperature sensor from previous Pixel Pro generations, which always felt like a gimmick, has been replaced by a coloured HiLight LED that works as a camera flash and notification light. The LED glows when you talk to Gemini or pulses with one of five colours when your favourite contact calls. But it doesn’t work for notifications of any other kind, so is a wasted opportunity. The 11 Pro has the same Tensor G6 chip as the regular Pixel 11 and has 12 or 16GB of RAM depending on the storage version. It can’t match the raw performance of the top Qualcomm or Apple chips for games but is snappy in day-to-day tasks. Battery life is just shy of two days with the screen actively used for about seven hours across a mix of wifi and 5G for browsing, messaging apps and photos. This is a bit behind the regular Pixel 11 but should see out even the heaviest of use days with some left in the tank. Most people will need to charge the 11 Pro every other day for general use. Specifications Screen: 6.3in 120Hz QHD+ OLED (495ppi) Processor: Google Tensor G6 RAM: 12 or 16GB Storage: 256, 512GB or 1TB Operating system: Android 17 Camera: 50MP + 48MP UW + 48MP 5x tele; 42MP selfie Connectivity: 5G, eSIM, wifi 7, UWB, NFC, Bluetooth 6, Thread and GNSS Water resistance: IP68 (1.5m for 30 minutes) Dimensions: 152.7 x 71.9 x 8.4mm Weight: 204g Quality Android 17 experience and AI The 11 Pro runs the same Google version of Android 17 as the regular Pixel 11 and will be supported until August 2033 with operating system and security updates, making it one of the longest-lasting devices available. It’s a polished experience with smooth animations, nice touches of haptic feedback across the system and enough customisation to make it yours. But as with other Pixel devices, the phone is a showcase for Google’s most advanced AI tools that are littered throughout the software. The 11 Pro comes with six months of Google AI Pro subscription, which gives you access to Gemini Omni to generate surprisingly good eight-second videos, higher AI usage limits, 5TB of cloud storage and Google Health Premium. But the most interesting tools are the local AI ones, including the new Rambler voice dictation feature in Gboard, which produces fully formed succinct sentences and paragraphs from your ramblings, removing unnecessary pauses, ums, ers and deviations. Gemini’s proactive assistance has also improved with more time-saving suggestions, although it only works in certain apps and not WhatsApp, Signal or other third-party apps. Camera The reason you buy a Pixel Pro is for the camera. The 11 Pro has a very good 42-megapixel selfie camera on the front and a similar winning triple camera system on the rear from last year: a 50MP wide, 48MP ultra wide and a 48MP 5x telephoto camera. All three cameras capture really fantastic photos across a range of lighting conditions with very little effort. The wide and telephoto cameras now capture more light and slightly better detail, but the biggest boost is the new Instant Night Sight. It dramatically speeds up low-light photos by up to 4.5 times, which makes taking great shots in very dark scenes a lot easier. The 5x telephoto camera manages a very good 10x crop zoom before stretching up to 120x magnification, first with a very good traditional digital zoom to 30x then using local generative AI to go beyond. The camera keeps the regular digital zoom image and the one processed by AI to add back lost detail, which can be remarkable or filled with artefacts. Magic Capture takes video and photos automatically with just one button for point-and-shoot recording, which works well for events such as a birthday party. But Camera Looks is the most interesting feature for getting creative with photography. It allows you to modify how the camera processes your photos, starting with subtle changes such as darker shadows and ranging to more distinctive looks such as “minimal”, which reduces the computational photography processing for a more raw photo. Other options include “digi”, which replicates the look of old digital cameras that have become popular, and “velvet”, which mimics the look of some film cameras. Each look can be further customised, allowing great creative licence. The Pixel shoots great video with lots of stabilisation and processing tools including the new “Creator Suite”, which captures clips straight into a folder for storyboarding and trimming, with a teleprompter, framing for social media and speed enhancement. Sustainability The battery is rated to last in excess of 1,000 full-charge cycles with at least 80% of its original capacity. The phone is repairable by Google, third-party shops or self-repair with manuals and parts available. The Pixel 11 Pro contains 31% recycled materials by weight. The company breaks down the phone’s environmental impact in its report and will recycle old devices for free. Price The Google Pixel 11 Pro costs from £1,079 (€1,199/$1,099/A$1,849) in a choice of four colours. For comparison, the Pixel 11 costs £879, Pixel 11 Pro XL costs £1,279, Pixel 11 Pro Fold costs from £1,799, the Pixel 10a costs £499, the Samsung Galaxy S26 costs £879, the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra costs £1,279 and the Apple iPhone 17 Pro costs £1,099. Verdict The Pixel 11 Pro is a refinement of multiple generations of Google’s Pro phones rather than an outright revolution, but that’s no bad thing. It is one of the very best smaller phones, packing all the top-end hardware, cameras and AI features of Google’s most biggest and expensive model into a slightly cheaper and more pocketable form. You buy a Pro Pixel for the camera, which doesn’t disappoint with arguably the best photography on a phone at the moment. The ability to customise the processing of your photos goes far beyond rivals for interesting creative potential. The dramatically faster Night Sight is also a significant improvement. Gemini’s proactive tools show great potential but depend on using the right apps. The supercharged Rambler voice dictation system is fantastic, and there are many other little AI tools that are useful from time to time. With just shy of two days battery life, a decent chip and quality software, the Pixel 11 Pro is a great pocketable phone. It just isn’t a massive upgrade on the already excellent Pixel 11 or recent Pixel Pro models. Pros: great camera with extended zoom and extensive customisation, seven years of software updates, excellent screen, impressive dictation and local AI features, Qi2 wireless charging and magnetic accessory support, good battery life, great size, fast fingerprint and face recognition, six months of Google AI Pro included. Cons: quite expensive, less memory on cheapest model than before, face unlock option not as secure as Face ID, raw performance and battery life short of best-in-class, no physical sim card slot in the US, not a massive upgrade.

title: Applicants for UK citizenship charged more than five times the admin cost
summary: Fee of £1,709 compares with an estimated administrative cost of just £324, according to Home Office data
text: People applying to become British citizens are charged more than five times the amount it costs the Home Office to process their application, a new analysis has shown. The latest fee of £1,709 to become a citizen compares with an estimated administrative cost of just £324, according to the latest Home Office data. Applicants must also pay a further £130 for a citizenship ceremony if successful, taking the total cost of becoming a British citizen to £1,839. The costs have emerged from an analysis by the left-leaning thinktank the Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR). It comes as Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, is expected to soften plans to double the waiting time for some people to qualify for permanent residency. A fees-and-costs table released by the Home Office shows that, after a 6% increase, aspiring citizens will pay £1,709 for naturalisation as a British citizen. The estimated unit cost is just £324. For nearly all applicants, a citizenship ceremony is mandatory and must be booked within three months of receiving confirmation of citizenship. The UK charges considerably more than other G7 countries for naturalisation. Its £1,709 application fee is more than three times the next highest – the US at £562. Before applying for citizenship, many applicants have to pay thousands of pounds in visa fees, as well as a mandatory annual immigration health charge of £1,035 per person. Steve Valdez-Symonds, the refugee and migration rights policy lead at Amnesty International, said: “Successive governments have charged these increasingly high fees for the purpose of passing the cost of the UK’s immigration system from the taxpayer on to migrant people – this includes the cost of the system’s errors and delays. “But governments are increasing the burden upon people seeking to make their new lives in the UK, people who already pay taxes and may have also paid solicitors and court fees too.” Imran Hussain, the director of external affairs at the Refugee Council, said: “In the past, citizenship has been encouraged as a sign of someone successfully integrating into British life, but higher and higher financial barriers risk putting this out of reach for refugees.” The IPPR report said the fees could put citizenship beyond the reach of long-term residents, leaving some people who have built their lives in Britain outside full participation in political and civic life. At the same time, the thinktank argues that the citizenship process itself does too little to encourage civic participation or build a shared sense of belonging. The former Labour home secretary David Blunkett, in a foreword to the analysis, called for citizenship and democracy to be placed on the schools curriculum next year, not in 2028 as planned. He also called for early “indefinite leave to remain” to be granted to applicants on authorised visa or resettlement routes who pass courses in English and demonstrate their commitment to the community. “The journey to naturalisation could be sped up as people are supported to demonstrate their commitment and contribution to the community in which they live. The same approach could be used as part of this journey to citizenship to invest in and develop greater social cohesion and integration,” Blunkett wrote. The IPPR called for Britain to be less reliant on transitory migration and said it should instead build a system geared towards settlement, integration and citizenship. It also said citizenship fees should be much closer to administrative costs, and that there should be clearer pathways for long-term residents. It further recommended replacing the Life in the UK test with a new citizenship course and test, focused on community life, UK institutions and shared values. Marley Morris, the author of the report, said: “A fair society should view new migrants as potential citizens and actively encourage people to commit to their new home. Yet the act of getting citizenship is a largely bureaucratic process that is priced out of reach for many. “If we want long-term residents to be included in our common life, there should be a clear and affordable route to becoming British.” Mahmood announced plans in the spring to force many people to wait 10 years to qualify for settled status, rather than the existing five-year period. After threats of a backbench rebellion, and since Andy Burnham became prime minister, Mahmood has been widely expected to soften the proposals, including exemptions to the new rules on indefinite leave to remain. The Home Office said it did not profit from immigration and nationality fees and that any income from fees set above the cost of processing helped fund the migration system. A Home Office spokesperson added: “While we will always welcome those who come to this country and contribute to our national life, British citizenship is a privilege. “It is right that those who benefit from the migration and borders system contribute towards its operation, reducing the burden on the taxpayer.”

title: How the fate of a small furry animal reveals the ecological tragedy of Israel’s war on Lebanon | Hisham Younes
summary: The Syrian rock hyrax depends on the fragile landscapes of the border region. Alongside other environmentalists, I have been documenting the destruction of its habitat
text: Wars are usually measured in the number of people killed, homes destroyed and towns erased. Far less attention is paid to what happens beneath the rubble. Across southern Lebanon, repeated large-scale detonations are not only causing human tragedy by demolishing villages, they are also destroying the ancient limestone habitats that have sheltered colonies of rock hyrax for centuries. As founder and president of Green Southerners, an environmental organisation documenting the ecological effects of war in southern Lebanon, I have been helping colleagues to record the damage inflicted on forests, wildlife and fragile ecosystems across the border region. The Syrian rock hyrax (Procavia capensis syriaca), locally known as tabsoun, depends almost entirely on the fissures and cavities of karstic limestone for shelter and on sparse coastal vegetation for food. We have monitored colonies of the species for years, but over the past few months, our team has watched many of their familiar habitats disappear beneath bombings and demolitions. For example, on 30 April, social media accounts associated with the Israeli army published footage showing a massive detonation targeting a neighbourhood in Bayada, along Lebanon’s southern coast. Similar demolitions have become increasingly common across the villages invaded by Israeli troops, erasing and reshaping not only urban areas but also the surrounding karst. The April explosions in Bayada and nearby Naqoura were reportedly powerful enough to be seen and heard in the coastal city of Tyre, more than six miles to the north, and appeared to directly affect an area known to host at least one colony. Likewise, Green Southerners had previously documented rock hyrax colonies in the landscape surrounding Majdal Zoun. Satellite imagery after large-scale detonations on 26 June shows extensive alteration of these habitats. While the status of the colonies requires field verification, the fragmentation of their habitat raises serious ecological concerns. The same is also true for Qantara, where large-scale destruction has been inflicted on the surrounding landscape. Studies on blasting and karst environments have shown that powerful explosions can destabilise these fragile formations through shock waves and intense ground vibration, causing fractures, collapses and the obstruction of subterranean refuge systems. Added to this, large-scale demolition operations can have two major environmental consequences. First, repeated blasting generates post-blast gases, including carbon monoxide and nitrogen oxide, rock dust, particulate matter and, depending on the explosive formulation and detonation efficiency, residual explosive compounds that may affect surrounding soils, air and water. In karst landscapes, these contaminants may spread rapidly through interconnected fractures, caves and groundwater systems because of the high permeability of the limestone. Second, blast waves and structural collapse can alter cave humidity, airflow and temperature regimes, while damaging habitats relied upon by cave-dwelling and rock-dependent fauna. Such changes may have severe implications for species adapted to these environments, including the rock hyrax, which depends on stable rocky shelters for thermoregulation, reproduction and avoiding predators. Across the areas we have monitored, many of which remain under Israeli occupation, these and other habitats are now under unprecedented pressure. Repeated bombardment, fires, large-scale detonations, the burning of vegetation and other ongoing military activity have transformed landscapes that once supported human communities and wildlife. Hills have been fractured, valleys burned and rocky escarpments destabilised, while burned areas, craters and rubble have fragmented the habitats of species across the region. The consequences extend beyond the destruction of a single breeding ground or shelter network. Habitat fragmentation can become a serious threat to survival. The destruction of shelter networks may isolate colonies and weaken connectivity across already fragile environments. Recent assessments of wartime environmental damage in southern Lebanon have similarly identified habitat fragmentation and the creation of ecological barriers that disrupt wildlife movement patterns for many species, including the rock hyrax. The damage inflicted on the vegetation that sustains these colonies is another overlooked factor. Rock hyraxes rely on surrounding low shrubs and sparse coastal plants for food. Heavy bombardment, detonations and fires not only destroy vegetation, but may also leave behind residues and contaminants capable of altering soil quality and further degrading these fragile habitats. In addition, white phosphorus is present in some forms of smoke-screening shells used by the military. It is feared burning fragments or residues may enter or become lodged within the fissures and crevices used by rock hyraxes and other fauna as refuges, in addition to the chemical’s potential effects on soil and soil biota. Taken together, these impacts raise broader questions about the long-term environmental consequences of the weapons and demolition methods used during the conflict. Assessing the direct and indirect damage inflicted on rock hyrax colonies remains difficult without access to the affected areas and comprehensive field surveys. This uncertainty extends to colonies our team documented in Naqoura and Bayada before the war, along with others on the slopes surrounding Beaufort Castle, as well as Wadi Majdal Zoun and Wadi Zebqine, all which were subjected to heavy bombing. While the International Union for Conservation of Nature has previously described the regional subspecies as relatively stable, no official nationwide assessment of rock hyrax populations exists in Lebanon. The absence of recent field surveys also makes it difficult to evaluate population trends with confidence. In any case, the ecological consequences may extend far beyond the loss of a single species. A recent report on postwar recovery from Lebanon’s National Council for Scientific Research notes that biodiversity loss can occur through wildlife mortality, species displacement and the breakdown of ecological interactions such as pollination and seed dispersal. In this context, the disappearance of local hyrax colonies would signal not only the decline of a single mammal, but the deterioration of whole ecological systems.The full ecological cost of the conflict cannot yet be measured. When the war eventually ends, homes can be rebuilt. Reconstructing geological systems and ecological communities that evolved over thousands of years will prove far more difficult. When contacted by the Guardian for comment on the ecological impact of its military activity, the Israel Defence Forces (IDF) said: “Similar to many western militaries, the IDF possesses smoke-screening shells containing white phosphorus, which are lawful under international law. These shells are used by the IDF to create smoke screens and not to strike targets or cause fires, and are not classified under international law as incendiary weapons. “The IDF is aware of the potential environmental impacts of its activities in the area and takes measures to minimise harm to the environment. The IDF does not target wildlife and does not carry out strikes against wildlife. Operational activity is directed solely against military targets and is conducted with consideration for the surrounding environment. The IDF operates to protect the citizens of Israel and ensure the security and safety of the surrounding areas, while taking precautions to minimise harm to civilians and the environment.” • Hisham Younes is founder and president of the environmental organisation Green Southerners

title: As the midterms loom, Trump returns to his happy place: on stage in the theatre of the absurd
summary: President’s quest in self-mythology stops off in Dallas for a Republican convention where fans indulged his lies and revelled in his jokes
text: Kim Il-sung of North Korea reportedly sought transfusions of blood from young men; Mao Zedong of China believed sex with young women could prolong his life; Muammar Gaddafi underwent fat injections and hair transplantation to make himself look younger. But for Donald Trump, the secret of eternal youth lies in nights like this. The occasion of the Republican midterm convention in Dallas was enough to get the 80-year-old US president’s juices flowing. An arena with thousands of fanatical supporters indulging his lies, laughing at his jokes and burnishing his fantasies of greatness is Trump’s happy place. It certainly beats stuffy Washington. “State of the Union, you have to be very staid,” he said, feigning stiffness and a dreary voice: “Ladies and gentlemen, it’s an honour to be your president.” The crowd laughed. Trump continued: “You do that for about an hour and then everybody’s falling asleep. This is a much harder routine, let me tell you. We’re also out here to have a little bit of fun.” The crowd roared. Trump’s second term has been a quest in self-mythology. It is there in the dramatic foreign policy aimed at reshaping the world. It is there in the monuments and renovations in the capital, Washington DC. It is there in the barrage of social media posts and AI slop in which Trump appears as a young and virile all-conquering hero. It was also there on Wednesday night as Trump milked the adulation of his fanbase, the Make America Great Again diehards who, in some cases, have followed him for more than a decade. He was visibly gratified to see the “front row Joes” from his rallies, including Blake Marnell, who wears a brick-patterned suit resembling his brick wall. The president spoke for an hour and 44 minutes, surpassing his own record length convention speech set in Milwaukee two years ago. He never stopped to sip water, though the adrenaline shot of this crowd, as devoted as his aide Natalie Harp, likely could have kept him going much longer. Anyone who suspected that this unconventional convention would be a “Trump-a-palooza” had the view reinforced when Lee Greenwood sang (somewhat shakily) “God Bless the USA”, the familiar intro to Trump campaign rallies. A giant video screen with the US flag slowly rose to reveal dozens of mainly female Trump fans, waving little flags and smiling exuberantly. Trump, wearing a navy blue suit, white shirt and blue tie, walked slowly across the shiny black stage, trimmed with gold. Chants of “USA! USA!” erupted as the song finished. “Welcome to the first ever midterm convention of any party,” Trump said, conveniently ignoring three that the Democrats held in the 1970s and 1980s. He soon told another lie. “Not only is this packed, but you have an equal number of people standing outside. If anybody would like to give up their seat!” In fact there were dozens of empty seats in the stadium, with the “nosebleeds” in the upper tier mostly unfilled. Making the dubious boast that no one had left the arena after 80 minutes, the president said: “It’s a great tribute to Trump … Everybody loves me and I love everybody!” But the most grievous lie came when he falsely claimed to have won three presidential elections, and declared, also falsely, that “people on the other side are actually admitting it”. The crowd cheered and shouted: “Four more years!” This was political theatre of the absurd with many bizarre Trumpian riffs, ranging from bad sporting trades involving the Dallas Mavericks and Babe Ruth to how Trump had to sacrifice hygiene for his political career so he could shake hands (“I’m a very clean person”). In trying to champion Texas attorney general Ken Paxton for the US Senate, he said: “He may not dress right, he may not talk exactly perfectly and he may not be the best looking guy I’ve ever seen but you know what he is? He’s the greatest attorney general in America and he deserves to be your next senator. I’m sorry, Ken. Where the hell is he? He’ll never speak to me again but that’s OK.” There were language games. He spoke as if his big idea of changing “Democrats” to “Dumocrats” was a piece of marketing genius or political artistry worthy of Lee Atwater. (“Nobody knows that dumb has a B at the end of it – most people think it’s ‘D-U-M’”.) Most reasonable people would look at him and think this poor elderly person is in need of an intervention. But this audience, of course, lapped it up and encouraged him. So he revelled in his name changes. He mentioned the “Gulf of America” and earned cheers and chants of “USA! USA!” He said, “Lake Ontario, you know we’re going to call that Lake America” – more cheers. “We did come up with one the other day which we think is appropriate. You have a neighbouring state, New Mexico. We think it should be called ‘New America.’” Turning to the Iran war and strait of Hormuz, he said: “Ladies and gentlemen, I’ll have an announcement, we’ll call it the ‘Trump Strait’ and I’m sure the Iranian leadership will be thrilled with that.” Speaking of Iran, the war would be seen as a liability by any normal president in an election year and it is a subject many Republicans would rather avoid. But Trump, true to form, bulldozed straight ahead. He also advised Iran “not to get cute” and asked the crowd: “Does anybody here think that Iran should have a nuclear weapon?” There was a huge shout of, “No!” Trump even speculated what would have happened if Iran obtained a nuclear weapon and subjugated the US. “If they had a nuclear weapon, I’d be calling the Supreme Leader and I’d be saying, ‘Mr Supreme Leader, how are you, sir? Is there anything we can do for you?’ – as opposed to bombing the crap out of him.” Somewhere in all this mess, Trump talked about the midterms. He asked voters to “pretend” that he is on the ballot and promised $5,000 to every adult US citizen if Republicans retain control of both the House and Senate. It was the old Trumpian trick: flaunt your bribery in public so blatantly that enough people assume it can’t be corrupt. He railed against Democratic “communists” and declared: “They have more bullshit than any human beings on the planet.” His supporters went wild. Such a witty putdown, sir! Trump castigated James Talarico, the Democrats’ candidate for the Senate in Texas, as “Talafreako” and claimed: “He ran a campaign to ‘beat meat.’ He called it ‘beat meat.’ I don’t know what the hell he meant by that … he wants to ‘beat meat?” … I’m getting myself in trouble. He was recently seen having a barbecue and eating a lot of meat.” All this and so much more. It went on and on, looping back on itself, zigzagging across the map, bamboozling any outside observer but somehow here, in the arena of Maga, making a warped kind of sense. “I love the weave,” Trump mused, gesticulating wildly. “You know what the weave is? You talk about something, then you bring in a ballroom, or you bring in an aeroplane, or you bring in Air Force One – but you notice I always get right back to the same topic. Some day there’ll be a time when I do the weave, weave, weave; some day there’ll be a time when I don’t get back to the original subject.” Pointing his finger in the air, Trump said: “And then you can say: he’s had it.”

title: Wall Street Journal publisher convicted in Hong Kong of deterring reporter from union role
summary: Dow Jones convicted of one count of deterring Selina Cheng from role at Hong Kong Journalist Association but cleared of second charge
text: A Hong Kong court has convicted the publisher of the Wall Street Journal of deterring a reporter from taking up a trade union role, in a case that raised concerns about press freedom in the city. The newspaper dismissed Selina Cheng just weeks after she was appointed chair of the Hong Kong Journalist Association (HKJA) in 2024. She was told at the time her termination was officially due to restructuring. Outside court on Thursday, Cheng said: “If reporters’ employment rights are not sufficiently safeguarded, or when their rights are violated and not enforced in law, then we can no longer work safely as reporters.” Principal magistrate David Cheung ruled that Dow Jones Publishing, the parent company of the Wall Street journal, was guilty of “preventing or deterring an employee from exercising trade union rights,” but acquitted it of “dismissing or discriminating against an employee because she exercised those rights.” Cheng, who covered China’s automobiles and energy sectors for the WSJ, said her editor had told her that employees should not be seen as advocating for press freedom in “places like Hong Kong”, saying it could be perceived as a conflict of interest. She alleged her employer had attempted to prevent her from taking up a role in the union. She said the company told her that she needed to seek the firm’s approval for outside activities and requested her to leave her then-board position at the association. Cheng launched the private prosecution against Dow Jones Publishing after losing her job in July 2024, weeks after taking up the position as chair of the union. The company pleaded not guilty to both charges, which each carry a maximum fine of HK$100,000 (about $12,750). Sentencing is expected to be handed down at a later date. During the trial, the defence argued that Cheng was terminated because of redundancy and that the prosecution had not sufficiently proved that the firm’s management instructed Cheng’s supervisor. The defence also accused Cheng of acting in bad faith in a previous hearing. But magistrate David Cheung said that Cheng’s termination “was motivated by wrongful and unjustified application of their code of conduct” when it insisted Cheng needed to seek prior approval to stand as chair of HKJA. Cheung said he accepted Cheng’s explanation, describing the former WSJ reporter as “honest and reliable”, adding she was clearly motivated by “the wish to see justice”. Cheng’s termination alarmed journalists, who are already operating in an increasingly restricted media environment in the city, where foreign outlets have traditionally faced less pressure than local news outlets. “The WSJ set a very bad precedent by punishing an employee who was exercising her constitutionally protected rights in Hong Kong,” said Eric Lai, a senior fellow at the Georgetown Center for Asian Law. The WSJ maintained there was no link between Cheng’s role in the Hong Kong union and her termination. At the time of Cheng’s dismissal, it issued a statement saying: “The Wall Street Journal has been and continues to be a fierce and vocal advocate for press freedom in Hong Kong and around the world.” HKJA is the oldest journalist union in Hong Kong. It was established in 1968 and is registered as a trade union representing journalists and workers in news. It has faced increasing pressure since the introduction of a Beijing-imposed national security law in 2020. Hong Kong has fallen sharply in global press freedom rankings since the law’s introduction. In 2019 Reporters Without Borders ranked the city 73rd in the world. By 2026 it had fallen 67 places to 140th out of 180 countries and territories.

title: Thursday briefing: 68 facts about the Bayeux tapestry as it goes on display
summary: In today’s newsletter: No Bayeux ticket? Everything you need to know about the sold-out exhibition – from its epic journey to London to a Game of Thrones likeness
text: Good morning. If you live in the UK, you have probably heard about the Bayeux tapestry exhibition, which opens today, and you probably haven’t got a ticket. The digital queue was nine-hours long when they first went on sale in July, and the exhibition has already broken the British Museum’s record for the number of tickets sold in a single day. Some lucky individuals, including King Charles and aspiring overlord Peter Thiel, have been treated to early previews of the medieval tapestry. Guests staying at One Aldwych, a hotel where rooms go for £1,000 a night, can partake in the “Bayeux experience” with a themed cocktail (mead spritzer, anyone?), a full English breakfast and preferential access to tickets. In a break from our regular programming, this morning’s newsletter brings you 68 facts about the Bayeux tapestry for anyone who hasn’t been able to see the real thing. That’s one fact for each of its 68 metres (bonus fact: it’s 68.3m long). If that’s not your vibe, just be glad I didn’t manage to find 1066 facts. First, here are the headlines. Five big stories Reform | The Met police will investigate allegations that Reform UK broke electoral law relating to overseas donations as part of a wider inquiry. UK- Israel | Prominent British rabbis have backed Ed Miliband’s sanctions on Israeli settlements, warning that the time for inaction on settler violence must come to an end. Technology | Just a day after three Anthropic researchers warned that artificial intelligence could kill off humanity within the decade, US politicians have begun lashing out about the risks of the burgeoning technology. UK news | Protesters who gathered outside a Portsmouth hotel mistook Pakistan’s under-19 cricket team for asylum seekers. US news | Donald Trump pledged to pay every adult citizen in the US $5,000 if Republicans retain the House and Senate in the midterm elections, during a marathon speech at the Republican midterm convention in Dallas. In depth: From nudity, a save from the Nazis and its restoration, a buffet of Bayeux facts 1. First of all, as the exhibition’s curator Michael Lewis points out in his book, the Bayeux tapestry isn’t really a tapestry. It’s “more accurately described as an embroidery”, Lewis writes. (Nobody actually calls it an embroidery, though, so we’ll stick with tapestry). 2. The embroidery tapestry tells the story of the events that culminated in the Battle of Hastings in 1066, when William the Conquerer defeated King Harold. 3. It was supposedly commissioned by Bishop Odo, William the Conquerer’s half-brother, for his newly built cathedral in Bayeux in 1077. He was prone to “self-aggrandisement” (in Lewis’s words), which is why he gave himself a starring role in the tapestry. 4. But it wasn’t made in Bayeux. Researchers think it was probably made in England, near Canterbury. 5. It’s embroidered on linen, with 10 colours of woollen thread likely dyed with woad, madder and indigo. 6. Its nine panels were embroidered separately, and then stitched together to form a continuous picture. 7. It features 623 men, 190 horses, 35 dogs, 37 buildings (including Mont-Saint-Michel) and 41 ships. 8. It may have had a single master designer who plotted its narrative, but … 9. The embroidery was almost certainly stitched by multiple women (William of Poitiers cited English women as skilled embroiderers). 10. It’s unclear how long it took them – one estimate reckons the stitching took between two and four years. 11. Yet, only three women actually feature in the tapestry. None of them are having a good time: one is weeping at her husband’s deathbed, another is fleeing a burning building and a third is being assaulted by a priest. 12. This third figure is Ælfgyva (meaning elf-gift), the only named woman in the tapestry. Scholars think that she could be Emma of Normandy, who was accused of having an affair with the Bishop of Winchester. 13. The tapestry conveniently doesn’t mention Edgar Ætheling, who had a stronger hereditary claim to the English throne in 1066 than either William or Harold. 14. The borders tell their own stories. They’re filled with fantastical beasts, creating what the Guardian’s art critic Jonathan Jones described as a “marginal world of monsters and myths”. 15. The upper border features one of the first depictions of Haley’s Comet. 16. The tapestry also shows a figure with the name Harold, depicting the famous (and probably apocryphal) moment he was struck in the eye by an arrow. Most scholars think Harold was actually hacked to death. 17. It was possibly designed to be interpreted by a live storyteller in front of an audience, much like an epic poem. 18. It’s damaged at the end, and incomplete. Nobody knows what scene would have finished the tapestry (some think it could have been a depiction of William’s coronation at Westminster Abbey in 1066). 19. It survived at least three fires in Bayeux Cathedral. 20. The first recorded reference to the tapestry was in the 1476 inventory of Bayeux cathedral, which described a “very long and narrow hanging of linen, embroidered with figures and inscriptions representing the Conquest of England.” 21. The tapestry hasn’t always been well looked after. For centuries it was rolled out for cathedral visitors. One visiting English antiquary observed in the early 1800s that it was “much rubbed at the beginning, torn towards the end.” 22. In 1792, during the French Revolution, the tapestry was nearly used to cover a wagon (it was saved at the last minute by an official who swapped it for a piece of canvas). 23. In 1794, an proposal was briefly floated to cut the tapestry into strips to decorate a festival float. 24. A 19th-century British artist secretly snipped off two fragments that ended up in a London museum (these were eventually returned to Bayeux). 25. In 1803, Napoleon had the tapestry temporarily moved from Bayeux to Paris, where it hung on display at the Louvre, to rally support for his planned invasion of Britain. 26. The first full photographic copy of the tapestry was made for the South Kensington Museum in 1872 (now the V&A museum). 27. A group of women in Staffordshire created the largest Bayeux reproduction in 1885, which is displayed in Reading Museum. It took them 18 months. 28. They removed 93 penises from their reproduction, 88 belonging to horses and five to men. 29. The Nazis saw the tapestry as a propaganda tool, and wanted to establish that Normans were actually the descendants of Viking settlers. 30. They appointed a professor of Viking archaeology as the leader of “Special Assignment Bayeaux” to study it. 31. Heinrich Himmler tasked two SS officers in 1944 to seize the Bayeaux tapestry from the basement of the Louvre, where it was being stored. 32. A group of local resistance fighters tipped off by code breakers at Bletchley Park managed to intercept the officers and protect the tapestry. 33. Since 1983, the tapestry has been displayed at the Bayeux museum, in a 17th-century seminary near Bayeux’s medieval town centre. 34. When the tapestry arrived at the Bayeux museum in the 1980s, photos show that it appeared to have been folded and hoisted up a stairwell. 35. It’s incredibly fragile, and liable to fray. A 2020 study found the tapestry had “24,204 stains, 16,445 wrinkles, 9,646 gaps in the cloth or the embroidery” and “30 non-stabilised tears.” 36. The first request for the Bayeux tapestry to be loaned to Britain was in 1953, for Queen Elizabeth II’s coronation. The French refused. 37. Another request was made in 1966, to mark the 900th anniversary of the Battle of Hastings. The French refused, again. 38. In 2013, a committee was formed to advise on how the tapestry could be redisplayed. It raised the prospect of a loan to the UK (“I did sort of bang on about it,” Lewis, a committee member, later recalled, “until I was a bit like a broken record”). 39. The Bayeux museum was scheduled to be closed for refurbishment, creating an opportunity for the tapestry to travel on loan. 40. In January 2018, Emmanuel Macron announced at a summit with Theresa May that the French had agreed to loan the tapestry. Although France had “found the best experts of the world to explain in perfect detail” why the loan “was impossible”, Macron said that the French government had “decided” otherwise. 41. Many people insist it should never have been moved. Arts journalist Didier Rykner started a petition against the loan that gained more than 70,000 signatures. 42. The late David Hockney agreed, described the loan as “madness,” and said “some things are too precious to take a risk with.” 43. And two expert reports in 2021 and 2022 advised Macron against the transportation of the tapestry. 44. The loan specified the tapestry had to be stored lying flat, and couldn’t be subject to tremors any greater than two millimetres per second during its transportation. 45. A team of conservators and experts, including a German vibration technology scientist, were involved with its relocation. They designed a meticulous solution for transporting the tapestry involving a “paravent”, a hinged folding screen on wheels. 46. The paravent was designed so it could be closed into a rectangular block with the tapestry inside, effectively folded 28 times. 47. It took ninety people in blue latex gloves seven hours working to extract the tapestry from its case and transfer it to the paravent. 48. It then had to be stored in a specially manufactured crate for shipping. The art logistics firm Hizikia built two nesting crates, with an outer aluminium crate designed to reduce the impact of movement. 49. The firm also provided a customised reinforced truck to dampen vibrations. 50. Experts carried out two dry runs, one with a replica tapestry transported across the channel that made its way to an art warehouse in south London. 51. Data from these dry-runs showed that French roads are smoother than British roads. 52. The tapestry has been insured by the Treasury’s indemnity scheme for £800m, which is more than twice the value of the most expensive artwork ever sold at auction (Salvator Mundi, a painting of Jesus attributed to Leonardo da Vinci). 53. Two threads were reportedly broken when the tapestry arrived in London. 54. At the British Museum, it will be housed in a custom-made case, believed to be the longest ever constructed, and will be exposed to a limited number of light hours per day. 55. When the lights are switched on, they’ll be dimmed to 50 lux, the international museum standard for sensitive materials. 56. Andy Burnham, Emmanuel Macron and King Charles viewed the tapestry last Wednesday. 57. It will be displayed at the British Museum until July 2027, before it returns to a newly built museum in Normandy that will open later next year. 58. Nicholas Cullinan, director of the British Museum, has said he hopes the Bayeux loan could revive the prospect for a loan of the Parthenon marbles. 59. The tapestry has inspired numerous copycats, including the Bloody Sunday Tapestry created by the artist Darren Cullen in 2013. 60. There’s also a Game of Thrones Tapestry at the Ulster Museum in Belfast. 61. The Sun newspaper commissioned a “Bye-EU” tapestry in 2018 to commemorate the Brexit vote, which depicted Boris Johnson in chain mail and Theresa May surrounded by the decapitated corpses of Brussels bureaucrats. 62. A helmet from Sutton Hoo, and the Lewis chess pieces, were both loaned to Normandy museums as part of the Bayeux loan. 63. My favourite bit of any trip to the British Museum is the gift shop (eds: does this count as a fact?), where you can now buy a replica Norman helmet and bottle of Bayeux mead with your Tutankhamun pencil tin. 64. Speaking of Bayeux tat, Nigel Farage sported a Bayeux-themed tie during the 2014 Rochester byelection, a reminder of “the last time we were invaded and taken over”. 65. Radio 4 has devoted a special day of broadcasts to mark the arrival of the tapestry. 66. And the museum’s videos about the tapestry’s arrival are narrated by the Traitors presenter Claudia Winkleman. 67. Philippe Bélavel, Macron’s former culture adviser, has said “such a loan will only happen once and never again.” 68. The next wave of public tickets for the tapestry, which cost £33, will go on sale on 21 October at 10am. Best of luck getting yours. What else we’ve been enjoying I loved Micha Frazer-Carroll’s brilliant newsletter exploring how and why generations of Black athletes have become style icons. Sign up to receive the Long Wave in your inbox here. Michael Segalov, newsletters team J Oliver Conroy’s long piece on what happened to Turning Point USA in the year after the killing of Charlie Kirk is a compelling, frightening read on the future of the American right. Charlie Lindlar, newsletters team Among all the tributes, I found these reflections on Gloria Steinem’s legacy from a host of contemporary feminist writers to be a particularly powerful homage. Michael Resident sex expert Alix Fox hosted this riveting reader Q&A yesterday, fielding your queries on making time for intimacy in parenthood, the rise of audio erotica, and why trendy sex toys are apparently shaped like fruit now. Charlie I watched the trailer for Andrew Garfield’s new film The Uprising while at the cinema last weekend (the Odyssey; quite long?), and Peter Bradhsaw’s cutting review confirmed my initial instinct to steer well clear. Michael Sport Cricket | England lead Pakistan by 23 runs at Edgbaston, after 14 wickets tumbled on the opening day of the third Test. Tennis | Elena Rybakina will become the No 1 woman in the world for the first time after orchestrating a supreme recovery to reach the semi-finals of the US Open with a 3-6, 6-1, 6-4 win over the Olympic champion Zheng Qinwen. Cycling | Matthew Brennan claimed a fifth stage victory on Wednesday as the young British rider edged a bunch sprint in Seville to win the 17th stage. The front pages “Police launch inquiry into alleged overseas donations to Reform UK”, is the Guardian’s front page today. The Times says “Farage faces Met inquiry over Reform donations”, the i Paper also has “Police set to interview Farage over Reform UK donations”, and the Mirror writes “Farage faces cop quiz on donors”. The FT has “US spy chief to take stronger role in stalled Ukraine talks”, the Mail writes “Burnham: National security can’t come at the expense of social security”, and the Express leads with “The King has spoken with Harry since return”. The Telegraph splashes “Labour’s new tax assault on hospitality”, and on air traffic chaos, Metro has “Ready for departure?” Today in Focus: The Latest Why is Trump silent on UK sanctions against Israeli West Bank settlements? The foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, is facing a backlash over the government’s sanctions against illegal Israeli settlements in the West Bank after the chief rabbi, Ephraim Mirvis, said the safety of British Jews could be at risk. Miliband has rejected the warnings, emphasising that ministers can confront the actions of Benjamin Netanyahu’s government while also fighting antisemitism. US president Donald Trump, however, has failed to comment on the UK government’s action. Lucy Hough speaks to diplomatic editor Patrick Wintour. Cartoon of the day | Ella Baron The Upside A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad For decades, Robert Ashton contended with paruresis: a condition that meant, if in the presence of others, his shy bladder left him unable to urinate. Turns out, all that was needed to alleviate this affliction was a trip to an Essex naturist club. Stripping down helped Robert let go of his inhibitions and alleviated a lifetime of anxieties – he’s been free-flowing ever since.
