title: Pleading for Votes, Trump Tries a New Spin on an Old Promise: Free Money
summary: In his convention speech, the president floated the idea of a $5,000 “Trump Dividend” for every adult American if Republicans keep control of Congress. The idea, like many others, may not come to pass.

title: US citizens will receive $5,000 if Republicans win midterms, Trump claims in lengthy convention speech
summary: President makes offer that would cost US over $1tn and asks voters to ‘pretend that I’m on the ballot’ despite being deeply unpopular among electorate
text: Donald Trump pledged to pay every adult citizen in the US $5,000 if Republicans retain the House and Senate in the midterm elections, during a marathon speech at the Republican midterm convention in Dallas in which the president assailed Democrats as “radical” and defended his unpopular war in Iran. The outlandish proposal, which would cost over $1tn, immediately raised ethical concerns. But it laid bare the extent of the Republicans’ concern about their prospects in the pivotal November elections. “If the Republicans win, you win with us, and you get $5,000,” Trump told a roaring crowd, during a nearly two-hour speech in which he also urged voters to “pretend that I’m on the ballot” – despite his historic unpopularity causing many vulnerable Republican politicians to avoid the event. Surrounded by supporters waving American flag placards, Trump claimed, without evidence, that his second term had been “the most successful two years, financially and every other way, in the history of the presidency”, but devoted much of his speech to fearmongering about what would happen should Democrats win the House or the Senate for the final two years of his presidency. “There is a crazy little sick cloud over our country,” Trump said. “We will defeat communism in America.” The president and Republicans are gambling that throwing a midterm convention – the first the GOP has ever held – can buoy the party, which is predicted to lose control of the House. Yet, Trump’s deep unpopularity among Americans – his approval rating is hovering at about 38% – meant many Republican candidates running in competitive races skipped the two-day confab entirely. Even so, Trump’s speech made it clear he thinks he will be the deciding factor in November. Noting that the party which holds the White House traditionally struggles in the midterm elections, Trump said: “We’ve got to change that, because we have something going that’s so good. “If we lose, you’re going to lose your border, you’re going to lose your tax cuts, you’re going to lose your safety and security, you’re going to lose your wealth. Our country is going through hell – we will be going through hell, just like we did, just two years ago,” he said. The buildup to the midterm convention had somewhat of a chaotic air. Trump was initially scheduled to speak on the second night, before the Republican National Committee announced that he would deliver the keynote on Wednesday, and instead give closing remarks on Thursday after his vice-president, JD Vance, speaks. Trump made several references to the war in Iran, warning Tehran “not to get cute” or the US “will have to hit them very hard”. But he also appeared to acknowledge the economic pain caused by the soaring price of oil. Trump re-enacted the way he told his economic advisers that the US needed to start the conflict because Iran was “two, maybe three weeks away from having a nuclear weapon”. “I hate to do this to you,” he said he told them, noting the economy had been doing well. At the convention center, there were signs of middling enthusiasm among the rank and file. Compared with the four-day traditional convention in Milwaukee two years ago, the first day felt muted. There were no long queues to enter, no eternal waits for food or bathrooms. Swathes of empty seats were visible throughout Trump’s speech. Visible, except to Trump, who claimed, wrongly, that the arena was full. “Not only is this packed but you have an equal number of people standing outside,” Trump declared. This was not observed by Guardian reporters. The RNC had announced in mid-August that Americans could apply for tickets to attend the event, suggesting that applicants would enter a lottery and only a lucky few would be granted access. Yet on Wednesday, with the convention under way, applications for tickets were instantly being granted on an RNC sign-up page. Trump himself, however, appeared energized in his call to action on the first night, cracking jokes, including at the expense of Ken Paxton, his handpicked candidate for Senate in Texas who won a primary against the incumbent John Cornyn earlier this year. “He may not dress right. He may not talk exactly perfectly, and he may not be the best-looking guy I’ve ever seen,” Trump said of Paxton. “But you know what he is? He’s the greatest attorney general in America.” Trump spent several minutes attacking Democrats, including Paxton’s opponent, James Talarico, who Trump mocked as a “weird-looking dude”; the former North Carolina governor Roy Cooper, who is now running for Senate; and Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for Senate in Michigan. In a statement, Ken Martin, the chair of the Democratic National Committee, accused Republicans of holding a “bizarre dog-and-pony show” to placate the president’s “fragile ego”. “Tonight only confirmed that the president is a lame duck failure who is dragging his party toward defeat,” Martin said. The Republicans’ unusual midterm convention features 12 hours of programming across two nights. On Wednesday, the speaker lineup featured Trump loyalists and candidates, but showmanship remained at the center of the agenda. Byron Donalds, a rising star in the party who is running for governor of Florida, and Mehmet Oz and Scott Bessent, two of Trump’s cabinet secretaries, were among those to take the stage, yet the president, a UFC fan, decided he would be introduced by two fighters, the middleweight Bo Nickal and Justin “The Highlight” Gaethje, a lightweight. Most speakers only got five minutes. Nickal and Gaethje, who both fought at the UFC 250 event on the White House Lawn in June, got 10. Gaethje told the crowd he had earned his “Highlight” nickname when he knocked out his first opponent very quickly in 2016, before linking himself to the 80-year-old Trump. “One mistake I’ve made in my career was becoming complacent while I was on a winning streak and forgetting how unforgiving my sport would be,” Gaethje said. “If we are not just as passionate about voting and winning in these midterms as we were in the last presidential election, then we risk being knocked out and losing all the momentum we have been fighting for.” Earlier, Republicans said the focus would be on “lowering costs, securing our border, making our communities safer, and putting American workers and families first”. Yet speaker after speaker instead attacked Democrats on alleged support for transgender rights, in particular, suggesting the Republican party intends to put culture wars towards the front as November approaches. Trump will speak again on Thursday, but said his address would be much briefer. “I gave you a lot of material,” he said, capping his remarks on Wednesday, before pleading one more time with voters to “please pretend that I’m running”. • This article was amended on 10 September 2026. An earlier version incorrectly described Roy Cooper as a Republican.

title: ‘Pretend That I Am Running’: 7 Takeaways From the G.O.P. Midterm Convention
summary: At a first-of-its-kind midterm convention, President Trump mostly offered retreads and self-congratulation. Then, he offered to pay Americans $5,000 apiece if Republicans kept power.

title: North Korea has built new uranium facility to expand nuclear arsenal, UN agency says
summary: The International Atomic Energy Agency voices ‘serious concerns’ over expansion of Yongbyon facility to enrich uranium
text: The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) has voiced “serious concern” over evidence that North Korea has built a facility capable of enriching weapons-grade uranium to bolster its nuclear arsenal. The new building, located at the the country’s main Yongbyon nuclear facility, can house up to 28 centrifuge cascades – machinery commonly used to enrich uranium – according to a report by the nuclear watchdog released this week. The regime has also expanded operations at an enrichment site in Kangson, near the capital Pyongyang, according to the report, which was based on analysis of satellite imagery and open-source material, including photographs published by the country’s state media. The IAEA, whose inspectors were expelled from North Korea in 2009, identified the Yongbyon building as the site’s second uranium ‌enrichment facility after comparing satellite images taken during its construction with media photographs of a visit in early June by the country’s leader, Kim Jong-un. During his visit, Kim claimed the North’s capacity to produce weapons-grade nuclear material had more than doubled over the past five years, according to state media, promising “vast future plans to exponentially strengthen the country’s nuclear forces”. Citing a 2025 analysis by the James Martin Center for Nonproliferation Studies in the US, South Korea’s Chosun Daily said the potential 28 cascades comprising 4,592 centrifuges at the Yongbyon facility could yield about 85 kg of weapons-grade highly enriched uranium a year – enough to build three or four additional warheads. In a statement released this week, the IAEA’s director general, Rafael Grossi, said: “The ongoing operation of enrichment facilities at Kangson and Yongbyon and the reported further expansion of [North Korea’s] production of weapons-grade nuclear material is a cause for serious concern.” “The continuation and further development” of North Korea’s nuclear programme are “clear violations of relevant UN security council resolutions and are deeply regrettable”, he added. South Korea’s defence minister, Ahn Gyu-back, said in August that the North possessed between 80 and 120 nuclear warheads – a much higher number than the 57 cited by Donald Trump the same month. The South Korean figure was based on estimates by private research organisations, Ahn told lawmakers, adding that the country’s military could not confirm the numbers. North Korea has made rapid progress in its ballistic missile and nuclear programmes in recent years, as it demands international recognition as a legitimate nuclear state. North Korea has conducted multiple long-range missile tests since 2017, the year it last tested a nuclear weapon. In a report submitted to the UN security council in 2020, international experts said the North had “probably developed nuclear devices to fit into the warheads of its ballistic missiles”.

title: UK disabled people could swap Pip cash for ‘in kind’ support in benefit overhaul
summary: Claimants could trade part of payment for specialist equipment, services or training under proposal
text: Some disabled people could receive “in kind” support rather than just cash payments under a radical overhaul of the personal independence payment (Pip) proposed by official government advisers, the Guardian can reveal. The proposal, from an expert committee largely made up of disabled people, is one of a number of striking “emerging recommendations” likely to form the basis of the government’s Timms review of Pip, expected to be published in the next two months. Rather than automatically receive weekly cash payments, currently between £30.30 and £194.60 depending on need, some claimants could instead swap part of the cash award for specialist equipment and aids, services, or skills and training. Pip would remain non-means-tested, but while cash would remain “the foundation” of the award, the idea that claimants would be offered the choice of practical rather than just financial support marks a potentially radical departure in welfare policy. The committee does not address the costs of Pip – currently about £23bn a year – and does not discuss potential cuts in spending, although it acknowledges its reforms must stay within current Pip spending projections of £41bn a year by 2029. Although political and media debate has focused on the affordability of increases in Pip spending, the committee has focused primarily on improving people’s experience of Pip and better supporting ill and disabled people to participate in every day life. Other recommendations include: • Introducing a fast-track process to allow new claimants with a terminal illness to claim Pip more speedily – and reducing the number of benefit reassessments for people with lifelong or degenerative conditions. • Reviewing strict and “unnecessarily stressful” rules that suspend an individual’s Pip award automatically after they have spent more than 28 consecutive days in hospital. • Improving the way Pip assesses fluctuating issues such as mental illness to adequately capture the impact of conditions that vary over time. While Pip is vital to help disabled people meet the extra costs of disability, it should also support individuals to live independently and help give them choice, dignity and control over their lives, the committee says. Pip should be tailored more closely to individuals’ needs and requirements, offering a wider range of support to help them achieve “participation and opportunity across every day life” including work, care and volunteering, it adds. The 12-strong committee of expert advisers, the majority of whom have lived experience of disability or long-term health conditions, are at the heart of a review commissioned to redesign the Pip benefit after the disastrous collapse of Labour’s planned cuts to disability benefits last year. A backbench rebellion forced the government into a U-turn on £5bn of cuts in the summer of 2025, amid public opposition to plans that would have slashed household incomes and pushed hundreds of thousands of people with disabilities into poverty. The subsequent review of Pip, co-chaired by the welfare minister, Sir Stephen Timms, published an interim report in July this year which concluded that Pip was unfit for purpose and too often left vulnerable claimants feeling dehumanised rather than supported. Pip, which is claimed by nearly 4 million people in England and Wales, is designed to help claimants with the extra costs of disability, such as energy, transport and food. It is not linked to employment status, and about a sixth of claimants are in work. The committee insists the emerging recommendations are not final but will be tested for fairness and workability in a series of workshops involving thousands of people with disabilities across the UK to be held over the next few weeks. There may be resistance among campaigners to introducing non-cash elements within Pip awards. However, recent polling of Pip recipients by the Good Growth Foundation thinktank found half supported the principle of swapping part of their cash payment for services such as skills and training, home adaptations or therapy. The committee’s recommendations are likely to be closely scrutinised by a separate review of the youth jobs crisis by former Labour MP Alan Milburn, who has made it clear that some of the cash spent on benefits for young people should be redirected towards providing them with training and skills. A Department for Work and Pensions spokesperson said: “These are not the final recommendations. The review will report to the secretary of state this autumn and he will carefully consider the final proposals within it. “The Timms review interim report, co-produced with disabled people, made clear that Pip is no longer fit for purpose. “Our goal is to deliver a system that supports disabled people and those with long-term conditions to live independent lives, while remaining fair, sustainable and fit for the future.”

title: ‘Fundamentally unfair’: Burnham must overhaul migration reforms, says TUC general secretary
summary: Paul Nowak says changes to immigration rules risk overstretching social care and fuelling far-right sentiment
text: Andy Burnham must overhaul Shabana Mahmood’s migration reforms or risk overstretching social care and fuelling far-right sentiment, the TUC general secretary, Paul Nowak, has warned. Speaking ahead of the TUC’s annual congress in Brighton next week, Nowak welcomed the “sense of optimism” around Burnham’s fledgling government, but he urged the PM to act in a series of areas, including migration and the cost of living. Burnham reappointed Mahmood as home secretary when he became prime minister in July. Her department is consulting on proposals that would force more than 300,000 low-paid workers to wait 15 years for the legal right to remain in the UK. These include many carers who came to the UK to fill vacancies after the Covid pandemic, and were told they could apply for indefinite leave to remain after five years. “I think it is fundamentally unfair to change the rules when people came to this country with one set of expectations,” Nowak said. “I hope we can think again on that.” He added: “There are 111,000 staff vacancies in social care at the moment. I want us to train up as many Brits as possible to do those jobs. But I suspect in a growing economy with an ageing population, we are still going to need people to come and live and work in the UK and work in sectors like social care.” As well as criticising the backward-looking changes, Nowak also condemned the idea of applying a 10- or 15-year wait to many new arrivals, as the Home Office has proposed. “Both my granddads came to this country after the second world war – one came from Hong Kong, one came from Poland. Both raised their families here. The idea that you could be here for the next 10, 15 years and you’d still have no legal right to remain in the country … how the hell do you plan? Can you buy a house? What does that mean for your employment? Do you have kids? Do you send them to school? I mean, it cuts across any effort to integrate at all.” Labour politicians supportive of the changes see them partly as a way of assuaging public concerns about migration, and neutralising the appeal of populist parties, including Nigel Farage’s Reform UK. But Nowak suggested that by significantly lengthening the time before people can consider themselves settled in the UK, the approach could ultimately fuel far-right sentiment. “I tell you where you end up: you end up with Reform claiming that a woman who was born in Somalia and has lived here for most of her life and worked hard and contributed to our society, somehow isn’t fit to hold elected office in this country.” Reform UK’s home affairs spokesperson, Zia Yusuf, was recently accused of “straightforward racism” by Labour after he suggested the party’s frontrunner to replace Keir Starmer in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, former child refugee Sagal Abdi-Wali, was not British. Nowak acknowledged that many TUC members will have backed Reform in recent local elections, but suggested the party’s appeal may be waning. “Our members are a broad cross section of the British public. Of course, large numbers of them voted Reform, like other people did. But certainly the evidence that we’re getting fed back from unions is that just like the British public, the more they see of Nigel Farage, the less keen they are.” Nowak claimed there was a “direct line” from the rhetoric of Farage and his allies, to what he called the “proto-fascism” of the balaclava-clad vigilantes who blocked infrastructure in Dover and tried to stop migrants arriving in Portsmouth last weekend. He suggested Labour should focus on cost-of-living issues to combat Reform’s populist appeal – including offering voters more help with rising energy bills. “The most important thing that Andy Burnham can do is to deliver the change that people voted for back in July 2024. If people feel that the government is taking the stuff that matters to them seriously and is delivering on it, I think it cuts the legs from underneath that rightwing populism.” Ahead of the budget on 28 October, Nowak called for a “social tariff” to cut energy bills for lower paid users, funded by a windfall tax on the banks. “As well as delivering a boost to hundreds of thousands of households up and down the country, it will help bear down on the cost of inflation,” he said. “The public bailed the banks out in 2008. For those families who are worried about turning on the heating this year, asking the banks to pay their fair share isn’t unreasonable.” A Home Office spokesperson said: “last November, we set out reforms to double the standard qualifying period for settlement to 10 years for most migrants, with shorter routes for those who contribute most to the UK. “A consultation on elements of those reforms has now closed, and we will set out our response in due course.”

title: Climate solutions most likely to reach ‘positive tipping points’ revealed by scientists
summary: Global shift towards clean electricity could trigger ‘cascade’ of progress, helping reduce air pollution, cut waste and revive oceans
text: A rapid global shift to clean electricity could trigger a “cascade” of progress towards repairing the damage to the planet by the climate crisis, according to a report identifying the environmental solutions most likely to bring about change. The analysis focuses on “positive tipping points” – thresholds beyond which a sustainable technology or practice becomes increasingly cheap, widespread or politically popular, allowing progress to become self-propelling. It identifies clean electricity as the “highest-leverage” transition, because cheaper solar and wind power can accelerate change far beyond the energy sector. Clean power improves the economics of electric vehicles, heat pumps and cleaner industrial processes, while reducing air pollution and stimulating further demand for renewable electricity. The report builds on the work of Prof Tim Lenton, the founding director of the University of Exeter’s Global Systems Institute, who has studied climate tipping points since the 1990s. Steve Smith, the report’s author and a research fellow at the University of Exeter, said: “The cascade of clean energy that we’re seeing now is just doing so much more than anybody expected even 10 years ago.” Solar and wind power have already crossed positive tipping points in many major markets, Smith said, as growing deployment has reduced costs, attracted investment and driven further expansion. The report, produced by the University of Exeter with the Earthshot prize, applies tipping point science to 51 priority areas across five environmental goals: protecting nature, cleaning the air, reviving oceans, eliminating waste and tackling the climate crisis. Smith said positive tipping points could be understood as the beneficial counterpart to dangerous climate thresholds, such as the collapse of ice sheets or the death of coral reefs. “Tipping points can also work in our favour,” he said. The rapid growth of solar power, wind power and electric vehicles, as well as the recovery of some natural systems, showed beneficial change could accelerate after reaching a critical threshold. However, the transition to clean power is being impeded by slow planning and grid expansion, particularly in wealthier economies, and a severe lack of investment elsewhere. Africa receives less than 2% of global clean energy investment despite possessing 60% of the world’s best solar resources, according to the report. Research cited in the analysis suggests coordinated policies supporting clean power, transport and heating could bring forward tipping points in those sectors by between two and eight years. Progress in one sector makes the others easier by increasing demand for clean electricity, encouraging investment and driving costs down further. Transforming global commodity supply chains is identified as another high-impact intervention. A relatively small number of companies, banks and regulators control trade in commodities including beef, soy, palm oil, timber, cocoa and coffee, which together drive much of the world’s tropical deforestation. Aligning the policies of large markets such as the EU, China, UK and US could make deforestation-free products the global norm, the report said. If regulators, producers and financial institutions adopted common standards, companies could find it increasingly difficult to sell or finance goods linked to forest destruction. “You need to be able to align not just the producers, but also the policymakers, the wholesalers, the consumers, the banks, the insurance companies, and get everybody working and doing the same thing,” Smith said. Clean cooking and household energy are also close to tipping points in some countries, as pay-as-you-go business models and decentralised solar power make cleaner technologies more affordable and accessible. About 2.1 billion people still rely on solid fuels for cooking, exposing them to harmful indoor air pollution, with women and children suffering disproportionately. Smith also singled out cutting methane emissions as one of the quickest ways to alter the course of global heating. Methane is responsible for about 30% of the warming experienced so far but remains in the atmosphere for only about 12 years. “Methane abatement is one of the fastest levers we have available for limiting peak warming,” he said. Satellites and drones can now expose methane leaks that were previously invisible, allowing relatively inexpensive interventions to affect the temperature trajectory within a decade. The report argues that climate adaptation could also become self-reinforcing. When flood defences, early-warning systems and resilient infrastructure are shown to reduce losses, they can lower insurance and borrowing costs, attract investors and make further investment more attractive. But finance is frequently working in the opposite direction. About $7.3tn (£5.4tn) flows each year to activities that degrade nature, compared with about $220bn for nature-based solutions, according to UN figures cited in the report. “For every £1 invested in protecting nature, you’ve got £30 spent trying to degrade it,” Smith said. “So that’s a political choice and it’s not a lack of finance. It’s where it’s used.”

title: ‘Institutional neglect’: 25 years on from 9/11, experts sound alarm over US counter-terror efforts
summary: Budget cuts, loss of knowledgeable officials and diverted resources raise risk of another attack, experts warn
text: The US faces growing challenges in countering international terrorism as resources are diverted to other threats, experienced security officials leave and “complacency” spreads, experts have warned. It is 25 years this week since the 9/11 attacks launched by Osama bin Laden’s al-Qaida on New York and Washington, which killed about 3,000 people and led to decades of conflict, radicalisation and instability across the Middle East and beyond. Though there have been no successful attacks on anything like a similar scale in the US since, and only a small number inspired by extremist Islamist ideologies, many are warning of growing risks. Some blame Donald Trump for politicising counter-terrorism efforts, making ill-considered and inappropriate appointments to senior intelligence posts and diverting attention from more urgent threats with a campaign against drug cartels. Bruce Hoffman, a terrorism expert at Georgetown University, said: “I remember [9/11] and this pure chaos and pandemonium in the streets and I remember thinking that we would never lower our guard again and complacency against a threat that is episodic but when it is revealed highly consequential.” This year, Hoffmann told the US House permanent select committee on intelligence that “the counter-terrorism architecture built after 9/11 is eroding … through budget cuts, personnel losses, and the diminution of terrorism as a national security priority”. This was “recreating the conditions of under-resourcing and institutional neglect that preceded the 2001 attacks. Moreover, the terrorist threat to Americans has both changed and grown.” Analysts are split over whether the lack of obvious recent efforts by al-Qaida to strike in the US suggests a lack of ambition or disguises a careful, strategic plan to wait for the right opportunity. Last month, a UN report based on intelligence supplied by member states’ monitoring said the “al-Qaida senior leadership remained marginalized” while “its capability and intent to conduct external operations remained unclear”. Colin Clarke, the executive director of the Soufan Center, said the US intelligence community was experiencing a “basket of factors” including “funding, personnel [and] complacency”. “There is a certain amount of fatigue. We did the global war on terror for 20 years and people were keen to pivot to something else,” he said. Most analysts support a 2018 shift away from terrorism to focus on “long-term, strategic competition by … revisionist powers” such as Russia and China. But choices made by the Trump administration have exacerbated existing problems. “There is a real lack of morale because of the way the president has treated the intelligence community … the quiet professionals are really demoralised,” Clarke said. Intelligence veterans criticised the appointments of Tulsi Gabbard as director of national intelligence and Kash Patel as director of the FBI, accusing both of lacking sufficient top-level experience in law enforcement. For the 2026 financial year, funding requested for the principal agencies of the civilian intelligence community totalled $81bn. But the designation of criminal groups such as the Mexican drug cartels as foreign terrorist organisations has stretched resources. An updated counter-terrorism strategy released in May by the Trump administration has been controversial. Many intelligence experts and analysts have highlighted how the strategy downplays the rising threat from rightwing extremism in the US and stresses instead the battle against leftwing violence, cartels and gangs. “It is a very partial document [and] raises the question: are you protecting America or people who agree with you?” said Clarke. “We have finite resources now. You don’t have a blank cheque like after 9/11 and at the same time it’s not just Sunni jihadist groups which are considered the threat.” Devorah Margolin at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy said that the new strategy was a significant shift. “That is not to say that counter-terrorism policies cannot change as the landscape changes, but this year’s strategy appears more focused on a political agenda than the reality of the threat,” Margolin added. “While the strategy still acknowledged the threat posed by groups like the Islamic State and al-Qaida, it also expanded definitions of counter-terrorism. It sought to use the vast counter-terrorism bureaucracy that has been built over the last two decades for its own political agenda. This has spread dwindling counter-terrorism resources even thinner.” The loss of experienced personnel is a significant problem, experts say, with many criticising the dismantlement last year of programmes aimed at countering extremist ideologies and preventing radicalisation. Don Rassler, the director of strategic initiatives at the Combating Terrorism Center at West Point, said that terrorism became less of a priority as strategic focus shifted to real or potential threats from China and Russia, and warned the US needed to be careful the intelligence community did not “revert back to the dynamics that led to an event like 9/11”. The 2001 attacks were the culmination of a series of attacks launched by Bin Laden on US targets. In 1996 and again in 1998, 10 years after founding al-Qaida, Bin Laden “declared war” on America with statements issued from a base in Afghanistan, listing grievances including US backing for “tyrannical, apostate” regimes in the Middle East such as in his native Saudi Arabia amid a broader diatribe against what he called western aggression against Muslims worldwide. Shortly afterwards, double bombings demolished two US embassies in east Africa and a suicide attack nearly sank a US warship off Yemen in 2000. The failure of senior officials including George W Bush to act on multiple intelligence warnings was highlighted by the congressional investigation into the 9/11 attacks, as well as the failure of the FBI and the CIA to share with each other vital information that might have prevented the atrocity. An al-Qaida effort to blow up a passenger plane as it prepared to land in Detroit in 2009 was averted only at the last minute when explosives failed to detonate as intended. An attack a decade later by a single “self-radicalised” Saudi Arabian air force officer in Florida which killed three was linked to the organisation’s affiliate in Yemen. Since then, there have been more than 100 attacks in the US by violent Islamic extremists linked to the broader “jihadi” movement, according to a count by the Center for Strategic and International Studies. Rassler said extremist Islamist groups were still a key priority but with fewer resources and fewer people the US had “to accept more terrorist risk”. “There hasn’t been another attack … but there is a danger of believing that the [terrorist] threat isn’t there. The threat is different in many ways from 10 years ago and we have to be as clear-eyed as possible about it.”

title: Country diary: A little garden mystery – why are the wood mice hoarding opium seeds? | Susie White
summary: Allendale, Northumberland: My late-flowering poppies have lit up the garden, and it’s not only me who’s taken an interest
text: The opium poppies have now set seed, their leaves rattling like crisp packets, the vents beneath their pod lids open for the seeds to be scattered. Dotted throughout my flower borders, adding stature to the vegetable garden, Papaver somniferum is the breadseed poppy, its large, floppy petals unpredictable in colour: pale lilac, purple, pink or sometimes with fringed petals. The unexpected brings a freedom and a randomness to the garden. Those blue-grey seeds are sprinkled on bagels and bread, baked into cakes or ground as a thickener for curries, adding protein, plant fats and trace elements such as manganese. But in its unripe state this is the plant that gives opium, a two-sided drug, both medicinal and destructive as a sedative – its specific name somniferum means sleep-bringing. It is when the petals fall off, leaving a plump, unripe capsule the colour of celadon, that the opium is extracted. Damage the pod or break off a poppy stem, and a white, milky latex oozes out. It is this that contains a mixture of opiate alkaloids including morphine, heroin and codeine, something wildlife would normally avoid. These poppies are also the source of a mystery in my garden. I’m sitting on the terrace in the late afternoon sun, feeling the absence of the swallows, when a wood mouse scampers past. It runs lightly up the stalk of a poppy, one that I’ve been enjoying for its late flowering. Speedily severing a stem, the mouse carries a pod several times the size of its own head, and manoeuvres it with difficulty into a hidden store in the drystone wall. Curious to know if the alkaloids take their toll, I set a nightly wildlife camera. Several times the mouse goes back, eyes large in the momentary light, tail curling round a stalk. There’s a rustle of foliage and the sound of chewing before a heavy seedpod drops to the ground. Bemused, I try some research. The general opinion is that unripe poppies would spoil when cached, that immature seeds have fewer nutrients, and that even a small amount of latex would be toxic to the mouse. I haven’t seen the field mouse since, but then maybe it has chosen something else to harvest. • Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024, is available now at guardianbookshop.com

title: ‘Scots are the kindest people on earth!’ Meet the Americans moving to Scotland
summary: Since Donald Trump’s re-election in 2024, there has been a 63% rise in Americans renting properties in Scotland. Politics is one reason – but there are many other surprising motivations …
text: Four years ago, when Tammi Gaw, a 50-year-old property adviser, moved from Washington DC to Glasgow with her Scottish partner, friends and family laughed at her. “People back home kept asking me: ‘Ha ha, why would you want to move to Scotland, where it rains all the time?’ Now those same people are asking me: ‘Hey, how do I move there?’” They are not alone. According to data from Rightmove, 28% of inquiries from Americans about buying a home in the UK are about Scotland, a larger number than for London. And a recent survey from lettings platform Goodlord reported a 63% rise in the number of Americans renting properties in Scotland since Donald Trump’s re-election in November 2024. But Gaw, a member of Democrats Abroad, believes that disenchantment with the current administration does not fully explain Scotland’s appeal. She also cites the feelgood factor created by the more than 20,000 Scottish football fans who descended on Massachusetts for the World Cup this summer, winning over Bostonians with their pranks and bagpipe parades, enriching local bar owners and even bagging up their rubbish: “The Tartan Army put on a better marketing campaign for their country than any funded programme by the government. People now view Scotland as a very fun option.” There are other, more hard-headed reasons for Scotland’s allure. “I advise people across all income brackets,” says Gaw. “Some are planning ahead. For example, they want Scottish residency so that, later, their children can get free university tuition fees.” She mentions the NHS as another draw. Although most people moving to the UK on a family or skilled worker visa have to pay an annual immigration health surcharge of £1,035, this is considered a bargain by those familiar with American health insurance plans. “The cost was less than the basic monthly premiums in the US, before all the other deductibles and charges,” says Gaw. She suggests that Scotland has a particular advantage for those with longstanding health conditions because prescriptions are free for all in Scotland. Politics and practicalities aside, a cursory glance at social media reveals another, less obvious, reason for some of this Caledonian clamour – the long-running fantasy series Outlander, in which a former second world war military nurse, Claire Randall, is transported to the 18th-century Highlands, where she falls in love with Jamie Fraser, a warrior. The series features scenic locations including the Devil’s Pulpit in Finnich Glen and the standing stones at Calanais. “Plans for the evening: watch Outlander. Knit Outlander shawl. Dream of moving to Scotland,” reads a typical post. “Just back from Scotland and did a few Outlander filming locations. Cried my eyes out for a couple of days after returning home. Need to move to the Scottish Highlands!” reads another. Someone who knows more than most about the Outlander effect is Hailey Beaupre, 28, who runs the tour company Sassenach Historian. She became obsessed while still a student in New Hampshire, binge-watching the series, reading the books by Diana Gabaldon on which it is based and booking a whirlwind trip to Scotland. “I attended an Outlander tour where we drove to Midhope Castle [the derelict 15th-century castle near South Queensferry was one of the locations in the series]. It was like a switch in my head flipped. I said aloud: “I’m going to move to Scotland and I’m going to do tours like this for a living.” Beaupre now describes what happened next as “either a breakdown or a breakthrough”, depending on how you look at it. “I broke up with my boyfriend, I hired a therapist and I changed my degree from education to history, all in the space of a week.” Her resolve to relocate remained unwavering, despite challenges. Her first attempt, enrolling on a course at Dundee University in March 2020, lasted three days before she was repatriated because of Covid. That same week, her best friend died. “Outlander, and the dream of moving to Scotland, gave me something to believe in, something to reach for during that difficult time. I would not still be here without it.” Eventually, she completed a master’s at the University of Aberdeen, got a job as a tour guide and set up her own company. She now lives in Glasgow’s thriving Southside with her Scottish husband. “Honestly, I’ve never felt homesick or a longing to move back to the US. Scots are the kindest people on earth. You meet them in the pub and they’ll give you a hug and buy you a pint. I’ve never once felt unwelcome here. The thing that people say to me most often is: ‘I’ve lived here all my life but you probably know more about Scotland than I do.’” As a Scot myself, I must hang my head in shame on that front. I have only the sketchiest grasp of Highland clearances, rebellions and clans, based solely on school textbooks that were more dreary than dreamy. But when it comes to today’s Scotland, it seems doubtful that anyone who has previously only lived in the US would have a clue about the reality. Few Americans appear to be rushing to move to any of the less scenic areas of the Central Belt. Take the former shipbuilding town of Greenock, for example, where the council recently announced that it has been actively encouraging migrants to move there as a remedy for depopulation. And no one mentions that other Scottish screen hit, Trainspotting, in their relocation fantasies. Scotland has its fair share of social and economic problems, and not everyone is delighted by the influx of wealthy Trump refugees. “There is already a housing crisis in many of those longed-for areas due to second homes, holiday lets etc,” vents one poster on Threads. “People who pay over the odds for their dream homes push out younger folk from those areas, reducing services. Scotland is not a retirement village.” On the other hand, social media and newspaper headlines are inflating the scale of the American inundation. Getting a visa is not easy without a British parent or an employer willing to sponsor you. Looking more closely at the increase in demand for rentals, the number of properties involved is tiny: from 265 in 2024 to 431 this year. Plus, Scotland needs skilled workers, and many coming to the country are filling vital roles in remote areas with falling populations. Eleven years ago, American photographer Corey Kinnan, 44, and his wife went on holiday to Scotland for the first time. “We only had a week, because like many people in the US, we had limited vacation time. But during those days, we fell in love with the country. There was this one day in particular that started with whisky porridge for breakfast, then a tour of Balvenie distillery in Speyside, then an afternoon on the dunes at Lossiemouth, and in the evening a ceilidh. It was so appealing seeing a community coming together like that, in a way that doesn’t really happen in the US any more. My wife and I agreed that it was the most amazing day of our lives.” But turning the dream into reality was not easy. It took the couple 10 years to get there, and it was only possible because Kinnan’s wife, an obstetrician, got a job in Inverness. Now with a young son in tow, they bought a house in the Black Isle, a remote but scenic peninsula. “Arriving there in the December was a bit of a depression,” admits Kinnan. Their furniture was in transit . It was all a long way from whisky porridge. Gradually, though, they began to find their feet, buoyed by the landscape that had lured them there in the first place. “New colleagues generously loaned us furniture and made us feel welcome. And, when you cross over the Kessock Bridge into the Black Isle, seeing the mountains in the background and a red kite flies over your car, it feels like the best place on Earth,” Kinnan says. Having to restart his photography business in a new country has proved tough, though. “I’ve had to adapt what I do, from only selling landscape prints to offering portrait shoots to people honeymooning or celebrating anniversaries in the area. That has become a big trend now, and one I’m grateful for.” He also stumbled upon Dingwall Camera Club, which he says has been a social lifeline as well as a boon for professional networking. “We don’t have anything like that back home. It’s yet another reason why our hope is to live here permanently. We want to contribute to our community and make Scotland a better place. Not that I am suggesting that it needs any improving,” he adds hastily. Melody Sandona, a 66-year-old corporate meeting planner, also relocated to the Highlands in August 2025, when she got a remote-working transfer to her company’s European office. She has dual citizenship because of her Mancunian mother, and had travelled to the UK to visit family for most of her life. Yet she only ventured into Scotland after she turned 60. “I had an old friend who lived in Edinburgh and she invited me to come for a visit. I fell in love with the country on that trip. I had always planned on moving to the UK at some point; on that trip I decided to move from Colorado to Scotland.” A perhaps over romantic view of the country prompted her to rent a stone cottage in a village on the Kyle of Lochalsh. The nearby village of Plockton is a location best known as the eerie setting for the film The Wicker Man. “My younger son was with me for the first six months and it was very cold and miserable.” Fortunately, Sandona lived next door to the local library and the two librarians took her under their wing and welcomed her warmly into the community. “But just before Christmas last year, my Edinburgh friend paid me a visit. ‘What are you doing here? This is a dump!’ I mean, it was charming, but bleak. Anyway, she has a beautiful big home and insisted I move into her spare room. So, there are three women living there now, in this wonderful Golden Girls setup. We have a great time. I feel so at peace here.” Sandona finds the cost of living is far cheaper than in the US. “I was spending $200 [£150] a month on cellphone service, $2,000 on health insurance and $1,000 a month on groceries. I’m never going back to the US – this is it for me. It’s been the best thing I’ve ever done in my life.” For Ryan Forber, a 46-year-old firefighter from Nashville, the decision to move with his family to Kirkcaldy in January was political and practical. “My brother-in-law is from Edinburgh, and we visited two summers ago. Since the first Trump administration, my wife and I had been having a conversation about leaving. I felt that there was only so much you could do with activism and voting. At some point you have to just be like Albert Einstein and get out,” he says, referring to the scientist’s decision to renounce his German citizenship and move to the US in 1933. Unfortunately, there isn’t a formal programme for American firefighters to join the Scottish Fire and Rescue Service, so for the family to secure a skilled worker visa, it was necessary for his wife, a vet, to find a job. “She got responses to her application within 48 hours,” says Forber, still sounding amazed. “It was lightning fast.” It took a lot of energy and resources to make the move, though. “We sold everything we owned, including our home. I’m really aware that this isn’t an option for everyone. When you factor in all the costs, it’s a very expensive thing to do.” Since the move, they have settled happily into the local community. Forber says he likes the slower pace of life, being able to cycle to school with his son on the back of his e-bike and being recognised by local people. “Scotland is a much safer place to bring up a child,” he says. “School shootings and gun violence have always been a concern of mine. I went to high school in Littleton, Colorado, at the time of the Columbine shooting, though I attended a different school. It was earth-shattering.” Forber cites everyday joys and frustrations about his new life – missing his beloved Girl Scout Cookies, the slog of getting a UK driving licence, “though I’ve learned to love roundabouts”, the great pub culture, football and Scottish beer. The main challenge has been finding work as a firefighter. “I feel that I’m stuck in a system where I have to apply from scratch, along with all the kids who are just starting out. I could run rings round them, but I’m not even getting a call back. I really miss the camaraderie of the job as well.” What advice would he give to his compatriots thinking about making a similar move? “It’s not all green pastures and golf courses. Keep an open mind. Just because you watched Braveheart as a kid does not mean you understand the country or its traditions. For example, I sort of want to buy a kilt, but then I don’t know if I’m really allowed to wear one. My Scottish friends tell me I should get one. But I’m dragging my feet. I’ve got until next January to decide.” Why next January? “Our first Burns Night,” he says. Spoken like a true Scot. • This article was amended on 11 September 2026 to clarify details made in a quote by an interviewee.

title: ‘They poison the population’: how the far right changed Sweden’s conversation
summary: The election could oust a coalition propped up by extremists, but some fear the country has been irrevocably altered
text: Not far from one of Scandinavia’s biggest shopping malls, Kashif Virk stood on the pavement, handing out flyers and smiling at those who passed by. On a cloudy Tuesday afternoon, the Swedish-born imam had taken to the street to invite people to ask him anything they had ever wanted to know about Islam. For years, Sweden’s far right has peddled its own, distorted view of Islam, portraying it as being at odds with Swedish values. The Ask-a-Muslim – or Fråga en Muslim – campaign, conceived by Virk in 2017, was his way of fighting back. With the help of dozens of volunteers from the Ahmadi Muslim community, the campaign had called in at more than 150 farmers markets, squares and city centres, inviting strangers to strike up a conversation in hopes of dispelling myths and shedding light on Islam. “We have some radical parties and people are genuinely afraid about Islam,” said Virk. “Sometimes people get very rude. But most people in Sweden are lovely, friendly and interested – they want to learn more.” Ahead of Sweden’s general election on Sunday, polls show the centre-left opposition has a narrow lead, suggesting that the rightwing minority-run coalition supported by the far-right Sweden Democrats could be ousted. Such a result would not only be significant for the Scandinavian country; it could also reassure mainstream voters across Europe that far-right forces such as the Sweden Democrats or Germany’s Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) – triumphant after its best showing in a state election last weekend – are not inevitably on the rise. But even so, the Swedish polls have narrowed slightly in recent weeks, making many nervous, particularly as the right-leaning ruling coalition has for the first time said it would offer ministerial posts to the far right if it wins. Those who have borne the brunt of the far right’s time propping up the government worry that Sweden, long held up as a leading light when it comes to equality and freedom, may have been irrevocably changed, regardless of what happens on Sunday. “It’s a kind of Pandora’s box that has been opened,” said Munir Niazi, who has long worked with Virk on the Ask-a-Muslim campaign. During the government of the centre-right prime minister Ulf Kristersson, the far-right Sweden Democrats have used their leverage to steer policies on migration and crime, seizing on the spotlight to spread rhetoric linking the two and scapegoating migrants, Muslims and other minorities for all that ails the country. The result had shifted Sweden’s national conversation to the right, said Niazi. “In the past four years, the biggest opposition party, the Social Democrats, have slowly adopted and even voted with the right wing on migration, on crime. In the near future, at least, we don’t see the country going back to the policies of the 80s and 90s.” Virk nodded in agreement. “We see, unfortunately, that everybody plays the anti-Islam card when they need it.” The repercussions have been felt widely. Last year, a gunman killed 10 people in the Swedish city of Örebro, most of whom had an immigrant background. Across Sweden, mosques have regularly been vandalised and in 2023 the country grappled with a spate of protests in which copies of the Qur’an were burned or otherwise damaged. Speaking to commuters in Malmö making their way through Hyllie station, many said the politics had started to feel deeply personal, as though their existence in Sweden was a political battleground. “When the far right talk about my religion and my hijab, it feels like they’re talking about an animal,” said one nurse, 46, who asked not to be named. Originally from Lebanon, she had settled in Sweden in 1999. “The older people in the hospital say that myself and other immigrants have helped to build Sweden – why doesn’t the far right see this?” Sitting in a nearby park, Onyango, 42, said the atmosphere in Sweden had become “horrible” for migrants amid the far right’s steady increase in influence. “I feel like they poison the population,” he said. “They’ve created an environment where if you’re not a Swede, you are scared.” The hostile rhetoric, coupled with efforts by the government to tighten the rules around migration, had left the Kenyan national devising a backup plan despite nine years spent in the country and a good job working with supply chains. “You start thinking maybe I need to have an apartment in Kenya and set aside some money, just in case,” he said. Sitting next to him, his friend Waithira, 30, nodded in agreement. “Before you wanted to invest here, buy an apartment here, start a business. But now you start thinking twice,” she said. “We don’t know what the future holds, but it’s a bit less attractive than before.” In the southern reaches of Stockholm’s Södermalm district, Jonna Mannberg and Isaac Kuehnle-Nelson recalled how in 2015, about 1,700 people from across the country spontaneously turned up at the city’s central station, eager to welcome and help settle Syrian and Afghan asylum seekers as they arrived. In the 11 years since, the initiative, formalised into Refugees Welcome Stockholm, had unwittingly become a shorthand for the changes sweeping Sweden. “We’ve gone from being an organisation that was at the forefront of public political dialogue in Sweden to being a smaller organisation where our funding and ability to reach out have shrunk significantly,” said Kuehnle-Nelson. They had watched as policy stances once reserved for the far right became mainstream, from a slashing of refugee quotas from 5,000 to 900 people a year, to allowing residency permits to be revoked over the vaguely defined criteria of “bad behaviour”. “In 2015, people were met with open arms. We had the prime minister say: ‘My Europe doesn’t build walls,’” said Mannberg. “But the harsh reality is that we still have the same people that we were dealing with in 2015. We’re still with them in 2026 and they have not received legal status yet.” The psychological toll was laid bare during a recent programming course for young, undocumented asylum seekers. “There were days when many were unable to attend because they couldn’t get out of bed,” she said. “To have physically healthy, 20-year-old guys who have been so pushed down by life that they were unable to leave their beds, unable to see any future for themselves, that’s a really hard thing.” Among those caught up in the crackdown on asylum seekers was an undocumented 14-year-old who, despite being born in Sweden, was facing deportation to Armenia, along with his single-parent mother and his younger brother. “It’s like hell. I’ve been here my whole life,” he told the Guardian. “I feel Swedish.” His parents had come to Sweden as political asylum claimants, but their separation resulted in the claim becoming mired in bureaucracy. While there had been a visa category that might have given the family another chance of continuing the lives they had built in Sweden, it was scrapped recently by the rightwing government. Instead, the order looms over them, clouding the life of a child who had sung in a church choir and dreamed of a future as a civil engineer in Sweden. “It feels horrible,” he said, pointing out that he had never been to Armenia, did not speak the language and was terrified about the possibility of being forced to complete its mandatory military service. The changes to immigration policy, including recently introduced rules barring most asylum seekers from accessing permanent residency, were an example of how the political conversation in Sweden had been transformed by the far right’s time as power-brokers, said journalist Bilan Osman. “There’s a lot of proposals in Swedish politics today that we couldn’t even imagine 10 years ago,” she said, citing the tens of thousands of euros being offered to migrants to return home as an example. “People would have said: ‘You’re a lunatic.’ Now it’s like: ‘Let’s discuss it.’” Osman had long researched rightwing extremism, tracking the movement as they created their own media outlets capable of reaching new audiences. What emerged was a steady normalisation of their discourse, blaming migrants and minorities for Sweden’s social and economic ills, while the fallout of the country’s soaring inequality levels was largely overlooked. The resulting rhetoric had pushed some to the margins, recasting Sweden as a place where some belonged and others were made to feel as though they did not. It was a marked shift that would probably have long-lasting consequences, she said, citing Swedish Muslims, who make up an estimated 8% of the population, as an example. “I think we are at a breaking point right now in Sweden, where the main question is: ‘Is there a future for Muslims in this country?’” said Osman. “If we continue to have these kinds of discussions, I think a lot of Muslims will feel that there is not a future here. And that’s sad.”

title: Enact Trew’s law to automatically review ‘bent copper’ convictions, says report
summary: Experts say failure to immediately review cases involving corrupt police officers risks ‘ruining’ more lives
text: Convictions that imprisoned police officers were involved in obtaining should be automatically reviewed to correct miscarriages of justice such as those perpetrated by the corrupt and racist officer DS Derek Ridgewell, a report says. The proposed Trew’s law, named after Winston Trew – who was framed by Ridgewell and spent decades fighting to clear his name – would trigger an immediate, independent review of past cases linked to any jailed officer in England and Wales. Ridgewell’s story has been described as “the real Line of Duty”, with reference to the BBC show about “bent coppers”. Since 2018, 13 victims of Ridgewell, including the Oval Four and members of the Stockwell Six had their convictions quashed. A 14th case involving the British Transport Police (BTP) officer was referred to the court of appeal in February. Trew, who is working on the campaign for a new law with the miscarriages of justice charity Appeal, said: “When my convictions were finally quashed in 2019, it came after nearly 50 years of fighting to clear my name. No one should have to spend decades uncovering the truth about police wrongdoing. Justice shouldn’t depend on luck, or on victims fighting for years to expose miscarriages of justice. Trew’s law would place responsibility where it belongs: with the state.” In 1980, Ridgewell was jailed for seven years for stealing mailbags worth £364,000, but an immediate review of his past cases was not initiated. In 2024, Lucy D’Orsi, chief constable of BTP, called the force’s failure to do so “simply inexcusable”. Dr Joanna Gilmore, from the University of York, which produced the report with Appeal, said that despite D’Orsi’s apology “when we began researching this issue, we were struck by how little exists in law today to prevent history from repeating itself”. She added: “In many of the cases we examined, judges noted in sentencing remarks how officers had used their police position to facilitate serious offending – and yet the decision to review their past cases remains discretionary, opaque, and unpredictable.” CPS guidance recognises that a review may be required where a witness, including a police officer, is later “discredited” – but does not mandate it. The researchers found that between 2023 and 2026, at least 64 current or former police officers received immediate custodial sentences for offences including serious dishonesty, physical and sexual violence, and abuse of position. They also discovered that there was no central system to record when police officers received custodial sentences, nor whether their past cases were reviewed and, if so, the outcomes. Dr Mattia Pinto, from the University of York, said: “Even today it is far too common for the lives of innocent people to be completely ruined by convictions based on unchecked evidence from corrupt officers.” A triage process would focus on cases where the officer’s integrity was central to the conviction, while excluding purely administrative or peripheral involvement. As well as triggering an immediate review, Trew’s law would require affected individuals to be notified and given disclosure where a material risk to conviction safety was identified, to enable timely access to legal advice. Materiality includes providing witness evidence, preparing key investigative documents, or handling exhibits and disclosure. Matt Foot, co-director of Appeal, said: “The criminal justice system takes far too long to correct miscarriages of justice. In the case of the victims of DS Ridgewell and his squads, it has taken an eternity. I believe there are many more victims out there still. It’s high time for Trew’s law so that officers that are doing harm who are imprisoned have their files investigated immediately to stop delay for those that have suffered enough.” The campaign launch will be held in south London on Thursday night at Lambeth town hall, where an event was held in 1973 protesting against the imprisonment of the Oval Four. They were beaten up and framed for attempted theft and assaulting the police on the London Underground. The Ministry of Justice has been approached for comment.

title: Rhode Island’s Democratic governor loses primary amid anger over bridge
summary: Helena Foulkes beats incumbent Dan McKee after criticizing handling of Providence’s Washington bridge, now expected to be completed in 2028
text: Rhode Island’s Dan McKee became the first sitting governor to lose a primary in nearly a decade, bested not by a more progressive challenger or a more youthful upset but by frustration over a bridge. McKee lost his Democratic primary to Helena Foulkes, a former longtime executive with the Rhode Island-based retail pharmacy CVS, the Associated Press said on Wednesday. “Tonight, we may have won the Democratic primary for governor, but let me be clear about what happens next: you will have a governor for everyone,” Foulkes said during her victory speech in the state’s capital, Providence. “Because there is so much work that needs to be done, and we need to do this together.” It is rare for a sitting governor to lose a primary election. It hasn’t happened in Rhode Island since 1994. In his concession speech, also in Providence, McKee promised to work with Foulkes to ensure she is elected in November. “This is something that I think is difficult to deal with,” McKee said, “but we just got to hold our heads high.” Several Democratic incumbents have been toppled this cycle, in a wave of anti-establishment anger that has elevated young and progressive insurgents. But this contest was different. On the campaign trail, Foulkes criticized McKee’s handling of repair work on Providence’s Washington bridge, a major east-west traffic artery that carries roughly 100,000 vehicles a day. She accused him of bungling those repairs, which have dragged on longer than originally planned. McKee closed the bridge in December 2023, after inspectors uncovered serious structural problems. By March 2024, officials had concluded that repairing the structure was not feasible and that it would have to be rebuilt. State officials initially estimated that the bridge would be reopened to traffic this year, but the project’s completion date has since been delayed to November 2028. The primary contest was something of a rematch from four years ago, when Foulkes, who is the niece of former Democratic Senator Chris Dodd of Connecticut, came in a close second behind McKee in a five-way contest. McKee went on to easily win the general election in 2022, after having assumed the role from then-governor Gina Raimondo, who stepped down to become Joe Biden’s US commerce secretary in 2021. Election prognosticators rate the seat as strongly Democratic, and therefore the winner of Wednesday’s primary is seen as having a major advantage in the November general election. McKee’s defeat was not the only electoral upset on Wednesday. In Providence, David Morales, a 27-year-old Democratic socialist defeated Mayor Brett Smiley in the Democratic primary, ending the incumbent’s bid for a second term. Morales’s campaign was backed by progressive stalwarts, including Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont and several labor unions.

title: Ukraine war briefing: Arctic attack extends Kyiv’s strike reach into Russian gas heartland
summary: ‘Guess who?’ says Fire Point, Ukrainian maker of long-range weaponry; drone alert in Moldova as Zelenskyy waited to fly out. What we know on day 1,660
text: Ukraine’s special forces said ⁠they attacked two crucial natural gas plants in the Arctic about 3,000km (1,800 miles) from the Russian-Ukrainian border. Both lie in the heartland of Russian gas production: Novy Urengoy is Russia’s unofficial gas capital, ⁠located in the Yamal-Nenets region in north-western Siberia. The other plant is in the Purovsky district of Yamal-Nenets. A Ukrainian statement described the ‌two plants as “crucial for the gas condensate industry … Previously, this was considered an absolutely safe area away from the front for the aggressor.” Fire Point, a Ukrainian company that makes deep-strike weapons including the Flamingo cruise missile, posted: “Guess who just travelled over 3,300km and successfully hit the target?” Volodymyr Zelenskyy, the Ukrainian president, praised the strikes for their effect on the Russian economy. The Russian regional governor confirmed the attack and said the damage was being assessed. About 80% of all natural gas in Russia is extracted in the Yamalo-Nenets region, according to the Interfax news agency. Ukrainian forces also targeted Novorossiysk, a Black Sea port in Russia’s Krasnodar region. The attack hit the Russian naval base, including a terminal used to load oil, military port facilities, and warships carrying cruise missiles, Zelenskyy said. Ukraine and neighbouring Moldova played down reports that a plane carrying Volodymyr Zelenskyy was almost hit by a drone as it flew to Oslo. In fact, Zelenskyy’s departure for Norway was delayed when authorities closed Moldovan airspace due to a drone ⁠alert, a Moldovan ⁠government spokesperson said. The president’s plane was cleared for take-off from Moldova on Tuesday once it was established ⁠that the drone had come down. In all, three ⁠departures and four arrivals were delayed. Norway’s prime minister was among those who thought Zelenskyy’s plane had been attacked. The Moldovan president, Maia Sandu, denounced the drone intrusions as a “serious threat to people’s lives” and condemned an earlier Russian drone attack on a border crossing with Ukraine that killed two people. Three other people were injured in the strike on the Starokozache border crossing with Moldova. One person was killed and at least four people injured when a Russian drone struck an apartment building in Kyiv, while more strikes were reported in Dnipro, Mykolaiv, Kharkiv, Zaporizhzhia and Zhytomyr. A Russian drone strike on a shopping centre ⁠in the ⁠northern Ukrainian city of Sumy killed two people and injured ⁠20, four of them seriously, said the regional governor. Volodymyr Zelenskyy declared “there has been too little response from the international community to these strikes”. He added: “A response is needed – Moscow must not go into the winter believing that it can get away with missile and drone terror without consequences. The aggression must be stopped here and now, before it spreads any further.” He called for “effective” sanctions against Russia and support for Ukraine, saying “the partners who can help know exactly what is needed every day”. A Ukrainian couple got married anyway after a Russian air raid on the eve of their wedding wrecked their Kyiv apartment. Before going to bed, Liudmyla Ryzhak had hung on the bedroom door her dress, white skirt and her soldier fiance Leonid’s traditionally patterned shirt. As they slept a Russian strike hit a warehouse across the street from their building. They fled with Liudmyla’s six-year-old daughter and two guinea pigs to a bomb shelter – but soon returned to dig their wedding clothes out of the rubble of their ruined apartment. In the morning, amid more air raids, they forged ahead with the ceremony – only possible after Leonid had been able to make it back from the frontlines in eastern Ukraine. “If God gave me a continuation of life, then why should I put it off?” the bride said. “At least for now, I have the right to be happy. Both him and me.” – Associated Press Russia’s ⁠arms production poses a future threat that goes beyond the war in Ukraine, the German defence ⁠minister, Boris Pistorius, warned on Wednesday. “Moscow uses large ‌parts of its budget … to fill its inventories for future conflicts, not to deploy ‌weapons to the frontline in Ukraine,” he told the German parliament. “On average, only ⁠80 of the 150 short and medium-range missiles that Russia can produce ‌per month are being deployed to Ukraine.” In the UK, a man has been charged after allegedly assisting Russian spy services in planning a sabotage operation, Raphael Boyd writes. Joshua Cammidge, 31, was arrested in Swindon on Friday 4 September. Scotland Yard said it relates to alleged contact with a representative of the GRU Volunteer Corps, a group controlled by Russia’s military intelligence agency that has been accused of engaging in acts of sabotage against Britain and its allies. Cammidge would appear at Westminster magistrates court on Thursday, police said. Moscow wants peace talks to take place in Abu Dhabi, the UAE capital, said a Kremlin aide, Yuri Ushakov. Ushakov also said ‌the US should halt aid to Kyiv if the fighting is to stop. Moscow has been indignant throughout the war about Ukraine being able to defend itself with military aid from its allies. Another Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, cited a “confirmed political will” for the talks and suggested prisoner exchanges between the US and Russia might be part of the picture. Peskov was responding to a comment by the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, about a ⁠possible roadmap to restart talks. There have been no talks between Russia and Ukraine ⁠since ⁠February.

title: Baby orangutans found in forest in India spark trafficking investigation
summary: Native only to the islands of Borneo and Sumatra, the rare apes were found thousands of kilometres away in Odisha state
text: Five baby orangutans have been found in a forest in India, prompting authorities to investigate if they were trafficked into the country from south-east Asia. The orangutans, native only to the islands of Borneo and Sumatra and known for their shaggy red fur, were found in Balasore district of Odisha state, thousands of kilometres away from their natural habitat. Odisha’s environment minister, Ram Singh Khuntia, said wildlife investigators were trying to establish how the rare apes reached India. “We suspect that an international racket might be involved in this,” Singh said. International commercial trade in orangutans is prohibited under Cites – a global agreement governing trade in endangered wildlife. The five babies were found by forest department officials who were patrolling in the Jaleswar range in Balasore district. Officials believed the orangutans had been in the area for just a few days, and they have now been placed in quarantine at a zoological park in Odisha. According to the World Wildlife Fund, about 104,000 orangutans remain in Borneo and Sumatra, down from more than 230,000 a century ago. The Tapanuli orangutan (Pongo tapanuliensis), a third species, is classified as critically endangered, with fewer than 800 believed to survive in the wild. In November, conservationists found the Tapanuli population had been reduced by 7% after severe flooding in Indonesia. Between 33 and 54 Tapanuli orangutans were estimated to have been killed in widespread floods and landslides in North Sumatra province. Previous research has suggested annual losses of 1% of the Tapanuli orangutan population would be sufficient to lead to eventual extinction. The entire Tapanuli population dwells solely in the West Block of the Batang Toru, a forest threatened by mining, palm oil plantations and a large hydropower project.

title: Democrat John Fetterman makes surprise appearance at Republican convention
summary: Senator praises ‘great friend’ Dave McCormick and says he will help him and Trump to support steel in Pennsylvania
text: The Democratic senator John Fetterman made a surprise virtual appearance at the Republican midterm convention, delivering a video address supporting Dave McCormick, a Republican senator in Pennsylvania. Fetterman, who has increasingly broken with his party since his election in 2022, said in the video that he would always reject “extremes and socialism”, repeating an oft-used Republican critique of the Democratic party’s increasingly popular left wing. The video message will do little to dampen speculation that the renegade senator, who is now more popular among Republican voters in Pennsylvania than the Democrats who helped elect him, is preparing to switch political parties. Fetterman has repeatedly said that is not his plan, though he recently suggested he would be forced to formally break with the Democratic party if it ever became “the anti-Israel party”. Democrats currently hold 47 seats in the US Senate. Despite the long odds, Democrats believe discontent with the economy and Trump’s low approval ratings have given them a rare opportunity to retake control of the upper chamber. A defection would jeopardize their already narrow path to a majority. Yet if Fetterman remains a Democrat, he would hold outsized influence, effectively wielding veto power in a 51-49 majority. In the roughly one-minute video, Fetterman, wearing his trademark black hoodie, stood outside the Mon Valley Works – a processing plant operated by US Steel in Pittsburgh. In a stunning display of support for a Republican colleague in the Senate, Fetterman called McCormick his “great friend”, and said that he would work with him and Donald Trump “to fight and defend the steel way of life”. “Yes, I’m a Democrat. Why am I here talking to you today? Because, well, I’m a commonsense Democrat. I’m always going to stand with America,” the Pennsylvania lawmaker said in the pre-recorded message. “I’m always going to reject the extremes and socialism and that anti-American way of life. Dave McCormick is the kind of senator that gets the job done, and he’s going to fight for Pennsylvania.” At the convention center in Dallas, attenders welcomed the senator’s rightward march. “I actually think it’s really awesome that he’s come around,” Tracy Smith, an attender from Maryland, said. “He’s more commonsense, and even though he’s a Democrat, he can see both sides. You have to get along. It’s like a seesaw. You know, not right or left, but in the middle. And I think he realized that, and it’s actually amazing.” Asked if she thought Fetterman could switch to the Republican party, Smith said: “I actually do. I think he’s leaning that way right here. It would be great. I think it would be awesome.” Eric Torrison, who traveled from Arizona to attend the convention, was also laudatory. “There is no way on God’s green Earth that I would have supported Fetterman when he ran for the Senate, and [was] aghast when he got elected,” said Eric Torrison, who lives in Arizona. “But it’s really interesting. He seems to have held to his beliefs, and not run to the left, and he seems to be, from a conservative standpoint, from a Republican standpoint, the only sensible Democrat there.” Fetterman’s fellow Democrats were far less charitable. “John Fetterman is the laziest Benedict Arnold America has ever seen. He didn’t even have it in him to get off his couch in his million-dollar penthouse to kiss Donald Trump’s ring in person. He phoned it in, just as he has every day as our senator. John should do his job or resign,” the Pennsylvania state representative Malcolm Kenyatta said in a statement. Fetterman has been in the limelight after reports from current and former staff that he was avoiding constituent events, behaving erratically and cozying up to conservative media. In the past week, the senator has attempted to defend himself after an account on X, which claims to be run by former staffers, gained traction.
