title: Lawmakers blast AI companies after researcher warns of human extinction by 2030
summary: Former Anthropic employee Jacob Coxon said AI will become ‘superhuman systems’ that can cause human extinction by the end of the decade
text: Just a day after three Anthropic researchers warned that artificial intelligence could kill off humanity within the decade, lawmakers have begun lashing out about the risks of the burgeoning technology. Ted Cruz, a republican senator from Texas, said in an interview on ABC’s The View, that AI posed a “catastrophic risk” and that he “read that whole tweet thread that that developer put out. It was highly concerning. “It reminded me, last year I had Elon Musk on my podcast … and one of the questions I asked him, I said, ‘OK, what are the odds that AI destroys humanity?’ And he looked at me and said, ‘10-20%.’ And I’m like, ‘holy crap,’” Cruz added. On the polar end of the political spectrum, Bernie Sanders, an independent senator from Vermont, said: “A recent poll shows that the American people overwhelmingly want to ban artificial super intelligence and pause the development of AI until we establish clear safety standards.” The outrage began after an Anthropic employee, Jacob Coxon, announced on social media on Tuesday that he was resigning from the company, saying AI would soon be “superhuman systems” that could cause human extinction by 2030. “I spent the last three years doing pretraining research at both OpenAI and Anthropic. Neither company is acting responsibly,” Coxon wrote. “They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” After Coxon’s post, at least two other Anthropic employees responded to back up these predictions. One said: “We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” Both Cruz and Sanders have been working on legislation that would put guardrails on AI, and echoed this sentiment on Wednesday. Other lawmakers also called on Congress to act. Ted Lieu, a Democratic congressman from California, said Coxon’s post was “exhibit number 739 for why we need to pass the bipartisan AI Kill Switch Bill asap”. Lori Trahan, a Democratic congresswoman from Massachusetts, said it was “past time for Congress to get off the sidelines and do its job”. “Safety researchers are resigning, powerful AI models are breaking out of their labs, and companies are racing ahead anyway,” Trahan added. Even musician Sheryl Crow weighed in, posting on Instagram about Coxon’s warning and saying that AI had the capacity to “eliminate us in order to continue”. “I am begging and pleading that we wake up to this moment and demand our leaders put aside their greed and prevent this from going forward,” Crow wrote. Singer-songwriter Maggie Rogers reposted Crow, writing: “what she said”. The outrage comes after both OpenAI and Anthropic revealed that some of their AI agents went rogue in hacking sprees over the past couple of months. Executives at the companies have touted the power of their technology and warned of its potential, but have stopped short of prognostications like Coxon’s. On Wednesday, Anthropic published a lengthy cybersecurity incident report about its occurrences. The company said it scanned hundreds of millions of transcripts to look for further incidents and that it “found no other cases of similar or worse severity”. Anthropic insisted that while the agent’s actions were “misaligned, they remained within a narrow scope”. “We have always been transparent that AI will bring both enormous benefits and unprecedented risks,” an Anthropic spokesperson said in a statement to the Guardian. “To address these risks, we continue to build models with some of the strongest safeguards in the industry.” The spokesperson added that the industry should work together “to pace how we release powerful models”. OpenAI did not return a request for comment.

title: Anthropic researchers say AI could cause human extinction by 2030
summary: One researcher who resigned said many in industry believe that without regulation AI could kill off humanity
text: Artificial intelligence could kill off humanity within the decade, according to three researchers with the industry giant Anthropic, one of whom has quit his job in protest. The latest doom-laden predictions came in posts on social media on Tuesday by a researcher who said he resigned because Anthropic and his previous employer, OpenAI, were ignoring or, at best, mishandling their response to the threat. “Neither company is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives,” wrote Jacob Coxon. “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade. This is not a marketing stunt. If anything, many executives and senior researchers will couch their phrasing in the press to sound sensible – but I hear the same people express fear privately. No other human activity poses this level of danger.” The post garnered responses from at least two other Anthropic employees who backed up Coxon’s dire predictions. In the first, Evan Hubinger, who describes himself as a lead in the company’s alignment division, which works on ensuring Anthropic’s AI models function in line with human goals, said his former colleague was “correct”, and that the industry was falling behind in attempts to deal with the apocalyptic potential. “We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” Hubinger wrote. “I personally think it is >10% within the next decade. I believe Anthropic is trying its best, but we do not yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence and are not clearly on track to.” Hubinger’s comments mark a surprising affirmation of Coxon’s unflattering, apocalyptic predictions from a person still on Anthropic’s payroll. A second response came from Samuel Marks, Anthropic’s “scalable oversight lead”, who posted a lengthy analysis he stressed was in his personal capacity, and not the views of his employer. “AI developers believe their technology could cause human extinction (or similarly bad outcomes),” wrote Marks. “This could happen in the next few years. In general, the more senior the employee, the more concerned they are.” In a statement to the Guardian, an Anthropic spokesperson defended the company’s strategy. “We have always been transparent that AI will bring both enormous benefits and unprecedented risks. To address these risks, we continue to build models with some of the strongest safeguards in the industry,” the statement said. “Anthropic has been a pioneer in mechanistic interpretability, the science of looking inside AI models to understand how they work, which is now being used to analyze and prevent incidents of AI misalignment across the industry. We were the first lab to publish a Responsible Scaling Policy, a public framework dedicated to mitigating catastrophic risks from AI models and we continue to aggressively test our models for dangerous capabilities in areas like cybersecurity and biology, and publish what we learn for scrutiny and research. “This work is also why we believe the world would benefit from the industry adopting a lawful, verifiable way to work together to pace how we release powerful models.” The researchers’ musings on the possibility of human extinction follow more concrete warnings about AI’s cybersecurity capabilities by Sam Altman, chief executive of Anthropic’s rival OpenAI. OpenAI’s president, Greg Brockman, has conceded previously that “we underestimated the real-world cyber capabilities of our AI models”. Altman said last year that certain aspects of AI, including what he called the “silent surrender” of human decision-making, terrified him. AI executives have shared some concerns about the direction of AI and its growing ability to manipulate, seize and control human functions and actions. A sharp rise was reported this summer in incidents of AIs escaping users’ control to lie, ignore instructions and pursue goals in harmful ways. In one of the most publicized examples, staff at OpenAI recorded rogue behavior among its leading AI agents that escaped a closed training environment in July to access the open web and launch an unprecedented hacking attack on the software repository Hugging Face. OpenAI, the San Francisco-based startup behind the publicly available AI bot ChatGPT, later admitted that it should have responded earlier to warning signals of the days-long attack, which is widely considered to be the first autonomous agent cyber-attack. Those executives, however, have stopped short of agreeing with the full doomsday warnings like Coxon’s and have bristled at any attempts to regulate the AI industry. Some politicians have urged the industry to slow down, or in some cases, halt development on AI altogether. Bernie Sanders, the independent Vermont senator, reposted Coxon’s resignation on Wednesday with his own note: “Mr. Coxon is right. The very people building this technology admit that it could threaten the future of humanity.” Sanders said he would soon introduce legislation to “ban superintelligence” and pause AI development.

title: Missouri’s voting maps saga reaches supreme court after conflicting rulings
summary: Appeal against approval of Trump-backed maps is latest move in legal back-and-forth spanning four courts
text: A high-stakes legal battle over Missouri’s congressional map returned on Wednesday to the US supreme court, after a series of conflicting decisions threw the state’s elections into turmoil less than two months before the November midterm elections. On Wednesday, a federal appeals court panel declined to block a ruling ordering Missouri to use the newly drawn congressional lines backed by Donald Trump to give Republicans an edge in the midterms elections. Opponents of the state’s redistricted map immediately filed an appeal to the US supreme court. The appeal is the latest move in an extraordinary legal back-and-forth spanning four courts. The rulings have left voters and local election officials in the state confused and uncertain about what the November ballot will look like. And there’s little time left before the pivotal elections that will decide which party controls a closely divided Congress – and will affect the fate of Trump’s agenda for the rest of his term. On Tuesday, the conservative justice Brett Kavanaugh had denied a request from Missouri officials to use the House map favored by Republicans. His refusal left in place a unanimous ruling from the Missouri supreme court, which blocked the newer maps, drawn to carve an additional Republican-friendly House seat. But not long after, a federal district judge in St Louis issued a contradictory decision, temporarily preventing the state from using its old congressional maps in the November elections. The temporary restraining order, or TRO, ordered Missouri to use the newly drawn districts that favor Republicans, which the state used in its August primary elections. That ruling, issued by Stephen Clark of the eastern district of Missouri, was then appealed to the eighth US circuit court of appeals. “Using a different map for the general election would wreak havoc on the fairness and orderliness of Missouri’s congressional elections, calling into question the candidacy of those nominated in the primaries and the votes of those who voted in the primaries. Widespread voter confusion would inevitably follow,” Clark, who was appointed by the president, wrote. “The public interest factor thus weighs in favor of a TRO.” People Not Politicians, the group leading the challenge to the Republican-drawn map in Missouri, said in a statement on Wednesday that the eighth circuit court’s decision to deny their stay request had left state election officials with “no legal map to use”. Trump urged Republican-led states last year to redraw congressional districts to their advantage ahead of November’s midterms, sparking a national redistricting battle. Texas went first, followed by Missouri in responding to the president’s push. The revised map, passed by state lawmakers last September, targeted the fifth congressional district held by Emanuel Cleaver of Kansas City, a longtime Democratic representative. It reassigned parts of Kansas City to two neighboring districts represented by Republicans and stretched the remainder of Cleaver’s district far eastward into rural Republican areas.

title: Notorious Ecuadorian crime gang designated a terrorist group by US
summary: Trump administration to seek extra funding from Congress to ‘dismantle’ Los Tiguerones over narcotics trafficking
text: The US has designated Ecuador’s Los Tiguerones gang, which stormed a television station during a live broadcast in 2024, as a terrorist organisation as the Trump administration expands its campaign against narcotics traffickers it says are destabilising Latin America. The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, made the announcement in Quito, where he met Ecuadorian president Daniel Noboa, one of several rightwing allies of Donald Trump whom Rubio is courting as a security partner during a three-nation tour through Latin America that began on Tuesday. Rubio said the Los Tiguerones gang was linked to narcotics trafficking, as well as attacks on civilians, law enforcement officers and journalists. “We are not talking about an ordinary mafia, nor are we talking about common criminals, we are talking about terrorists who, in many cases, possess weapons and equipment resembling the national armies of certain countries,” he said. The heavily armed gang’s attack on the TC Televisión network in 2024 prompted Noboa to declare a state of “internal armed conflict”, amid claims foreign drug gangs had descended on Ecuador to take control of important routes for coca grown in neighbouring Colombia and Peru and then shipped to the US. Live footage from the El Noticiero news programme showed men toting pistols, shotguns, machine guns, grenades and sticks of dynamite. The viral images quickly became a symbol of the drug violence destabilising the country. In its efforts to fight against narcotics trafficking and illegal migration from Latin America, the Trump administration has also empowered a number of hardline leaders through its “Shield of the Americas” coalition that aims to tighten security cooperation with rightwing allies in the region. During his trip, Rubio plans to visit several newly elected conservative leaders amid a significant political shift to the right in Latin America. On Wednesday, Rubio hailed Ecuador as being the Trump administration’s most “aggressive” partner in its military campaign against alleged drug traffickers, including in the controversial strikes against boats that have killed at least 227 people whom the Trump administration has called drug traffickers without providing evidence. Rubio said that he would seek $45m (£33m) in additional funding from Congress towards efforts aimed at “dismantling these terrorist groups”, although he did not go into details. He also told reporters that elite forces from both countries were “working jointly on a day-to-day basis in a way that has no precedent in order to try to dismantle these terrorist organisations”. Rubio visited Colombia on Tuesday, where he met its newly inaugurated president Abelardo De La Espriella, who narrowly won a June election against leftist leader Gustavo Petro with whom the Trump White House had cold relations. During his remarks, Rubio took something of a victory lap, saying that the two sides would seek to “[confront] the mistakes of the past four years” and called Petro’s leadership of the country “unnatural”. Colombia joined the Shield of the Americas initiative only after its change in government. During the meeting, the two men discussed security and counternarcotics policy, and signed memorandums of understanding on critical minerals and nuclear energy. Rubio is expected to next travel to Peru, where he will meet Keiko Fujimori, who defeated a leftwing candidate by a margin of just 50,000 votes during a close election in July. She has promised to fight crime with an “iron fist” and adopt some controversial policies from neighbouring El Salvador, which has been a close ally of the US on security policies.

title: Labour picks former child refugee to stand in byelection for Starmer’s seat
summary: Sagal Abdi-Wali, who came from Somalia in the 1990s, likely to face Zack Polanski in Holborn and St Pancras contest
text: A former child refugee who became the leader of Camden council has been selected to be the Labour candidate for the byelection in Holborn and St Pancras. Sagal Abdi-Wali, who came to the UK from Somalia as a child in the 1990s and was elected leader of Camden council in May, was chosen by Labour members to contest the north London seat vacated by Keir Starmer. She was previously the chair of the local constituency Labour party, after first being elected as a Labour councillor in 2022. Abdi-Wali, 42, said she was “delighted” and promised to put the community at the heart of her campaign. “This place welcomed my family as refugees and gave us hope when we needed it most,” she said. “I am so grateful to have had the opportunity to build a life here, serving our community as a councillor, school governor and community activist. Now I am standing to say thank you and to give back the hope you gave me. “Throughout this campaign, I promise to put our communities at the heart of everything I do, now and for the future. Together, we can make hope win.” Abdi-Wali has worked for more than a decade as a volunteer and trustee for local charities and is a governor of two schools in the borough, according to Labour. The party’s members queued outside St Pancras church in Euston for the selection meeting on Wednesday night, with voters including MP Georgia Gould and her mother, Lady Gail Rebuck. The local figure will probably go head to head with Zack Polanski, the Green party leader, who announced his intention to fight for the Commons seat. Local Greens in Holborn and St Pancras still have to formally select their candidate under a process that will not be completed until next Friday. But it seems likely they will endorse Polanski, under whose leadership the party has soared in the polls, with membership more than tripling. The high-stakes byelection on 8 October will pit the star power of Polanski against a resurgent Labour under Andy Burnham. Starmer announced he was stepping down from the seat he has represented since 2015 last week, in after his departure as prime minister. Starmer saw his majority more than halve at the last election from nearly 28,000 to 11,500 amid a challenge from the left. The Greens came third, with Starmer’s main competitor being Andrew Feinstein, a leftwing independent. In a boost to Polanski, Feinstein has since confirmed he would not stand, indicating that the Camden People’s Alliance, the group which emerged from his campaign, would most likely back the Greens. Labour have further lost support to the Greens in the area since the general election. The Greens made gains on Camden council in the local elections in May, although they failed to take control of it. But recent missteps by Polanski have dented his popularity, while Burnham’s arrival in Downing Street has boosted Labour’s standing in the polls. Abdi-Wali became the focus of unwanted attention last week when Reform’s Zia Yusuf suggested she was not British in a social media post that was described as “straightforward racism” by Labour. Yusuf, Reform UK’s home affairs spokesperson, posted on X: “The frontrunner being foisted on the people of Holborn by Labour to replace the former prime minister Keir Starmer in our parliament was born in Somalia. Do you understand what’s happening?” The Greens are planning to flood the constituency with volunteers, while Labour said all members of the cabinet were likely to campaign in the seat, with campaigners calling the first official weekend of the campaign the “Make Hope Win Weekend”. Labour’s byelection campaign lead, Liam Conlon MP, said Abdi-Wali was a “fantastic local champion” with a strong delivery record on “revamping council homes, reducing homelessness, and tackling nuisance antisocial behaviour”. He added: “She will be a powerful progressive voice for Holborn and St Pancras to work alongside our Labour government to improve the lives for local people. “Labour will run a positive campaign that brings people together and restores hope. I look forward to joining hundreds of members to campaign with Sagal over the coming weeks.”

title: Trump officials push to exclude undocumented immigrants from US census
summary: Census Bureau also considers race and ethnicity questions in overhaul that would have dramatic effect on voter maps
text: The Trump administration on Wednesday proposed changes to the US census intended to exclude immigrants without legal status in addition to other groups, with potentially significant effects on the allocation of federal resources and drawing of districts in the US House of Representatives. In a proposed rule published in the Federal Register, the Census Bureau also announced it was considering changes to the data it collects about race and ethnicity, amid the Trump administration’s push to rid the government of diversity, equity and inclusion programs. Conducted decennially, the census historically counts the “whole number of persons” in the United States specified in the 14th amendment, regardless of citizenship or immigration status. The data is used by states to draw congressional maps that are crucial in determining which party controls the House. Donald Trump and his rightwing allies have long insisted that undocumented immigrants could skew the data, and the president called last year for the 2020 census to be redone in favor of a new survey based on “results and information gained from the Presidential Election of 2024”. “People who are in our country illegally will not be counted,” he wrote on Truth Social. The new rule proposed by the Census Bureau would continue counting lawful permanent residents, while excluding undocumented immigrants “due to their lack of a sufficient tie and allegiance to the United States”. It also proposes excluding “aliens whose legal status is less durable and indefinite in length than lawful permanent resident status”. The bureau, which is under the commerce department, notes that it is considering using “its enormously broad access to administrative records” to determine the legal status of respondents. That could include data collected by the US departments of the treasury, health and human services, defense, and homeland security, as well as the postal service, the proposal says. The changes reprise a campaign Trump waged during his first term, when he tried unsuccessfully to add to a question about respondents’ citizenship to the 2020 survey. The bureau determined the citizenship question would have reduced the numbers of people willing to participate, and the supreme court ultimately ruled against the effort, which was abandoned when Joe Biden took over as president in 2021. The bureau is also reconsidering questions it asks regarding “race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation”. The rule points to the “(potentially) sensitive nature” of such inquiries and “the reduced need for or usefulness of this information”, which could conflict with the public’s obligations under federal law to respond truthfully to census questions. “Substantial doubts about the meaning, significance, and impact of attempting to categorize persons by race and ethnicity, in particular, have featured prominently in our national discourse and have been reflected in shifts in the law,” the proposal reads. Should the Census Bureau move forward with the changes, it will likely face legal challenges from Democrats and allied advocacy groups. Democrats on the House oversight committee accused the president of trying to “rig” the survey, and said: “The 14th amendment is clear: the census is meant to count ALL people living in the United States. We will fight this.”

title: Bond market rebuffs US treasury’s plan to buy back $6bn in government debt
summary: Scott Bessent made announcement on Wednesday as bond yields rose to highest point since 2008 financial crisis
text: The US treasury moved to cut the cost of borrowing on Wednesday only to be swiftly rebuffed by the bond market. Scott Bessent, the treasury secretary, announced the US would buy back $6bn worth of government debt – treasuries – in an effort to alleviate a selloff in the US bond market that has put pressure on interest rates. But the size of the deal failed to appease bond buyers and the yield on 10-year treasuries rose to a three-year high. Rising inflation and uncertainty from the war in Iran have spooked investors from US bonds, historically known to be one of the safest investment vehicles. Treasury yields have been rising, with the yield for the 30-year treasury bond hitting about 5.2% – the highest yield since the 2008 financial crisis. In an attempt to alleviate the bond market, Bessent on 19 August announced the treasury would at least double its typical buyback operation. The move is meant to stabilize the market: fewer bonds on the market should mean that yields go down. But in the weeks since the announcement, treasury yields have continued to rise. Even after Bessent announced the operation would target $6bn worth of government bonds, yields on Wednesday continued to rise. In August, US government debt for the first time in the country’s history reached $40tn – double the amount of debt from just 10 years ago. Higher yields could ultimately mean higher interest rates on loans, including mortgages, student debt and car loans, as these loans are often tied to the bond market. The move puts more pressure on the US Federal Reserve to deal with inflation, which has been pushed up by the war in Iran. The annualized inflation rate hit a three-year high in May before going down to 3.4% in July – 0.7% higher than the same time last year – largely because of higher energy prices. Donald Trump on Wednesday warned that oil prices were unlikely to come down before the midterm election. Though Iran “can’t hold out any longer”, its leaders are “desperate to try and affect the election”, he said. “Right after the election, oil prices are going to be tumbling downward,” Trump predicted. Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil prices, rose past $100 for the first time since July on Wednesday as conflict in the Middle East continued to escalate. The Fed could raise interest rates to mitigate higher prices, at the risk of upsetting the White House. Last week, Trump said the Fed “must get smart” and lower interest rates. “A STRONG COUNTRY MEANS A LOWER INTEREST RATE,” he wrote on social media. The pressure puts the Fed chair, Kevin Warsh, who stepped into the role in May, in a bind: manage inflation or face the president’s wrath. In a closely watched speech at the Fed’s Jackson Hole symposium in August, Warsh affirmed that it was “the Fed’s job to deliver stable prices”, but held off on whether the the central bank would raise rates anytime soon.

title: Cities in Great Britain most vulnerable to extreme heat revealed
summary: OS index examines which ‘urban heat islands’ suffer the most – and which cope the best with rising temperatures
text: Portsmouth, Leicester, Exeter, Bristol and Nottingham will be among the cities that warm the most by the end of this century as global heating turns British cities into urban heat islands, according to research. Analysis from Ordnance Survey (OS) has created a heat vulnerability index for all cities in Great Britain. Portsmouth, which sits on the south coast of England and is home to 208,000 people, is the most vulnerable to extreme heat today and into the future, according to the research from the OS, the Met Office and the data analysis company 4 Earth Intelligence. Concrete, asphalt, buildings and hard surfaces in cities absorb solar radiation during the day and act like giant radiators, holding on to the heat rather than cooling down at night as in more rural areas. Cities can be up to 10C hotter than surrounding areas. Areas most at risk of extreme warming are those with the least tree cover, green space and waterways. This summer was provisionally the UK’s hottest on record, and the research reveals which cities are suffering now from intense urban heat and which will be among the warmest in future. The research analyses 71 cities granted by royal charter across England, Scotland and Wales but excluding Northern Ireland. The OS heat vulnerability index suggests that by 2040 all 71 cities will reach high heat vulnerability. By the turn of the century, almost two-thirds could reach the most severe level. Those facing the most severe impact by the end of the century are predicted to be Portsmouth, the City of Westminster, Plymouth, Leicester and Exeter, according to the analysis. Nick Bolton, the chief executive of Ordnance Survey, said: “Cities are where millions of people live, work and spend their everyday lives. “Extreme and sustained heat can affect people’s health and wellbeing, how comfortable our homes and workplaces are, and put additional pressure on transport, energy and emergency services. Understanding how and where this vulnerability is changing depends on an accurate view of how the country is built, based on trusted authoritative data, which is critical for planners, developers and local authorities preparing for a warmer future.” Portsmouth is today the most heat-vulnerable city and will remain at the highest level for warming until the end of the century, according to the research. The city of Leicester is projected to show the biggest rise in Britain’s heat vulnerability rankings, climbing from 10th now to fourth by the end of the century, while Exeter and Nottingham also rise into the 10 most vulnerable cities, alongside Bristol and Brighton and Hove by the end of this century. Leaders in Portsmouth have identified areas including Somerstown, Portsea, Southsea and Fratton as those particularly exposed to urban heat because of their limited green areas and hard surfaces, and noted that areas with less green space overlap with those of deprivation. The City of London and the City of Westminster areas rank among the most heat-retentive urban environments in the UK. The City of London records the highest built-environment score and the least effective natural cooling of any city, given the concentration of buildings, roads and hard surfaces as well as limited green space, trees and water. Westminster ranks third for overall heat vulnerability today and second in both future periods behind Portsmouth. A study commissioned by the mayor of London has put the total economic cost of the 2022 London heatwaves at £1.5bn, including productivity losses, health impacts, education disruption, energy demand, transport and emergency services. The OS heat vulnerability index combined current observed temperatures with the structural characteristics of Britain’s built environment and climate projections into the future to produce a score for every city on a scale of 1 to 5, where 3 to 4 is high and 4 to 5 is severe. Among cities coping the best with the changing climate is Milton Keynes, which ranks 69th out of 71 cities for heat vulnerability today. Milton Keynes has the lowest built-environment vulnerability in England and the most effective natural cooling of any city in the analysis, with 46 sq km of natural surfaces, against almost 40 sq km of hard made surfaces. Jonathan Hendry, the chief executive of 4 Earth Intelligence, said exposure varied street by street within a single city. “The areas consistently subjected to higher temperatures than their surroundings are the ones that overheat first during a heatwave,” he said. “We’re mapping how to turn thermal threats into actionable blueprints for urban resilience, supporting decisions on where heat refuges are sited and how emergency responses are planned in advance rather than in the middle of climate events.”

title: Man in Swindon charged with assisting Russian intelligence agency
summary: Joshua Cammidge, 31, arrested after investigation led by counter-terrorism policing London
text: A man has been charged with offences related to national security as part of an ongoing investigation led by counter-terrorism policing (CTP) London, according to the Metropolitan police. Joshua Cammidge, 31, was arrested at an address in Swindon on Friday 4 September by CTP London officers, supported by officers from Wiltshire police. Searches were also carried out at a different address in Swindon. He was further arrested and detained the following day, being charged with assisting a foreign intelligence service and intending to commit or engage in conduct to prepare an act of sabotage. The Met have claimed that Cammidge’s arrests relate to alleged contact with a representative of the GRU Volunteer Corps, a group controlled by Russia’s military intelligence agency that have been accused of previously engaging in acts of sabotage against Britain and its allies. The National Security Act, which Cammidge was arrested and charged under, was introduced in 2023 to help increase the measures that law enforcement can take in order to protect the UK from security threats such as espionage, foreign interference or influence, and sabotage. Frank Ferguson, chief crown prosecutor for the CPS special crime and counter-terrorism division, said: “The Crown Prosecution Service has decided to prosecute Joshua Cammidge with National Security Act offences following a counter-terrorism policing investigation. “Our prosecutors have worked to establish that there is sufficient evidence to bring the case to court and that it is in the public interest to pursue criminal proceedings. “We remind all concerned that proceedings against the defendant are active and he has the right to a fair trial. “It is vital that there should be no reporting, commentary or sharing of information online which could in anyway prejudice these proceedings.” Cammidge will appear at Westminster magistrates court on Thursday 10 September.

title: Oil prices rise above $100 a barrel for first time since July as Iran war escalates
summary: Brent crude up by more than 3% after latest fire between US and Iran in Gulf and Houthi attacks on Saudi cities
text: The price of oil has risen above $100 a barrel for the first time since July as the escalating conflict in the Middle East threatens further disruption to global supplies. Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil prices, rose by more than 3% to top $101 after tensions increased in the Gulf amid the latest tit-for-tat exchange of fire between the US and Iran. The US military said it had “destroyed” multiple Iranian tankers, after Tehran attempted to strike a US navy warship with ballistic missiles. The previous nightm Iran-backed Houthis attacked four cities in Saudi Arabia, wounding more than 70 people and setting oil installations ablaze. UK and mainland Europe gas prices also soared on Wednesday. The benchmark Dutch gas contract rose by almost 4% to €78.73 a megawatt hour, the highest since January 2023. Meanwhile, the British contract rose by 7.77p to 196.57p a therm, the highest since December 2022. On Tuesday, the Bank of England governor, Andrew Bailey, said the latest rise in oil prices was putting pressure on inflation and interest rates. “The risks, I’m afraid, are on the upside,” he told MPs. “And that’s really the risks coming from energy prices.” The oil price has jumped by a quarter since early August as hopes for a permanent resolution to the six-month-old war faded. The climb in costs has hit UK motorists, with petrol at the pump reaching an average of 166.2p a litre on Tuesday, the highest level in four years, according to the motoring body the AA. The AA said diesel hit an average of 187.7p, a price it last reached in May. Prices for a litre of petrol have risen 4.4p since the August bank holiday, with diesel up 4.1p. Households will face further pressure on their bills when Ofgem’s energy price cap rises by 4% in October. Andrew Goodwin, the chief UK economist at the consultancy Oxford Economics, has predicted that the cap could now rise by a further 13% in January. “Wholesale prices are currently well above the level of the previous observation window, and our commodities team expect them to remain high in the near term,” he said. The energy companies BP, Shell and the British Gas owner, Centrica, were among the top performers across the FTSE 100 on Wednesday morning, with their shares rising by at least 1% on the back of the higher oil price. The index was down by 0.5% overall. Brent is up more than 60% this year, and has risen above the $100 mark for three periods so far in 2026. China, the world’s largest importer of crude, has increased purchases in recent days, after a hiatus that had been a factor keeping oil prices somewhat in check in the early part of the conflict. Giovanni Staunovo, a commodity analyst at UBS Global Wealth Management, said: “For the direction of crude prices, we are also monitoring Chinese crude imports as a key indicator. “Chinese crude imports recovered to nearly 9m barrels per day in August, up from the June low of 7.15m, but still lower compared to the [pre-conflict] February imports of 12.6m. It looks like the recovery trend could continue.” Oil prices have fluctuated in the six months since the start of Tehran’s block on the strait of Hormuz prompted what many feared would be the greatest energy supply disruption in history. In the first weeks after the first US-Israeli attacks on Iran in late February, oil prices soared past $100 a barrel. The oil price peaked at $126 in April but later fell back amid hopes of a ceasefire. The price then began to climb again after the memorandum of understanding between the US and Iran fell apart and hostilities restarted. The rise in energy prices has stoked fears about inflation and the prospect of higher interest rates this year. In the US, economists are expecting at least one interest rate rise from the Federal Reserve by the end of the year.

title: Apple’s new CEO introduces himself at annual showcase: ‘I continue to be inspired every single day’
summary: John Ternus helms his first major event as head of $4.5tn company, where he announces first foldable iPhone
text: John Ternus, Apple’s new CEO, helmed the company’s annual showcase of new iPhones and other products on Wednesday. It was the first time the public saw the warm and unpretentious demeanor of the executive, who is filling the shoes of Tim Cook and his predecessor, Steve Jobs, at the $4.5tn tech giant. The event kicked off with a video montage of characters describing the best way to start a movie, from a getaway scene to a closeup of woman revealing her true identity, before the well-known voice of Cook piped in. “Camera follows a mysterious figure before revealing our main character,” Cook said. “No. Not me. That’s your guy. That’s your opener.” The figure came into focus: Ternus. “I want to take a moment to express what an extraordinary privilege it is to represent the remarkable teams here at Apple,” Ternus said. “I’ve spent much of my life at this company, and I continue to be inspired every single day by the curiosity, invention and relentless pursuit of excellence that define Apple.” Not much is publicly known about Ternus’s leadership style, even though he has worked at Apple for 25 years. He has kept a low profile and is known for a calm manner and attention to detail. Ternus started at the company in 2001 and in 2013 became the vice-president of hardware engineering. By 2021, he was heading the entire hardware department. In Apple tradition, Ternus, as the CEO, kicked off Wednesday’s keynote address and cued up the gadget reveals. Apple made big announcements at its “Surprise and Shine” event in Cupertino, California, including its first foldable phone, called iPhone Duo, as well as upgrades to standard iPhones, AirPods headphones and Apple Watch lines. Ternus hosted the event in a friendly style, presenting himself in everyman attire of a dark, crew-neck maroon sweater and black jeans. Nearly an hour after the event started, he began to tease the announcement of iPhone Duo, saying: “Actually, there is one more thing …” Then, taking the phone from the back pocket of his jeans and holding it up to the camera, he said with a coy smile, “this is iPhone Duo.” Ternus cast the Duo, with its wider displays and multidirectional cameras, as an upgrade to the iPhone experience, rather than the technological revolution Jobs described when he unveiled the original iPhone in 2007. He said the Duo “will redefine the experience of using a foldable phone”. Bob O’Donnell, the president and chief analyst of Technalysis Research, said: “While products like the expected foldable iPhone have been in the works for some time, the fact that, as the new CEO, John Ternus gets to introduce it to the world is hugely symbolic because it shows off how a new era of more interesting new products for the company is kicking off under his leadership.” Jobs, Apple’s greatest showman, was known for his commanding stage presence, donning his black turtleneck and blue jeans uniform. When he debuted the first iPhone, he paced back and forth on the stage, drumming up suspense, then said: “Every once in a while, a revolutionary product comes along that changes everything.” The crowd went wild. Cook had a much calmer demeanor, often holding his hands as if clasped in prayer and repeating a similar mantra during Apple’s iPhone events: “We think you’re gonna love it” and “This is the best iPhone we’ve ever created.” Under Cook, Apple became a hardware juggernaut, and he turned the company into the world’s first trillion-dollar business. Although he was not considered a visionary like Jobs, Cook was credited with the pragmatism that made Apple a lucrative success. When the company announced in April that Ternus was taking over from Cook, Ternus said he was “profoundly grateful” to “carry Apple’s mission forward”. “I have been lucky to have worked under Steve Jobs and to have had Tim Cook as my mentor,” he added. “I am humbled to step into this role.” Cook praised his successor as having “the mind of an engineer, the soul of an innovator and the heart to lead with integrity and with honor”. Dipanjan Chatterjee, a principal analyst at Forrester, said that Ternus inheriting this legacy would be “both a boon and a burden for him”. The new CEO would need to continue with Cook’s scale and monetization, he said, while also moving toward the future with new advancements in technology other than smartphones. “His first keynote will set the tone for his vision of Apple’s future,” Chatterjee said.

title: Met police launch inquiry into alleged overseas donations to Reform UK
summary: Scotland Yard confirms it is investigating allegations broadcast by Channel 4 News after undercover sting
text: The financial scandal around Reform UK has deepened as police expanded their investigation into allegations of illegal foreign donations and the elections watchdog said it was considering regulatory steps. Police confirmed on Wednesday they would broaden their inquiries into Reform after Channel 4 News broadcast an undercover sting by a group called Verbatim, in which a reporter posed as a foreign donor seeking to fund Reform. The Electoral Commission also said on Wednesday that it was “considering all relevant information and regulatory steps” in parallel with the police inquiry. Two of Nigel Farage’s close advisers, Dan Jukes and James Orr, resigned last week after footage was broadcast showing them discussing ways to get around electoral law with a reporter posing as the son of a foreign businessman. The fake US-based donor also paid for more than £30,000 of polling intended to benefit Reform that was not publicly declared. In the footage, Jukes also appeared to suggest the impermissible US donor could contribute through his UK-based son as a way to get round election law banning foreign donations. The police investigation will form part of an existing inquiry into Reform’s political funding before July 2024, including allegations that it took impermissible donations. It means the party is facing intense scrutiny on multiple fronts, with a separate parliamentary standards investigation into Farage’s gift of £5m received from an overseas donor, first revealed by the Guardian, and calls for a wider investigation into his undeclared funding from his unpaid aide, the fraudster George Cottrell. It also raises the prospect that Farage and other senior figures linked to the party could end up being interviewed by detectives, although the force stressed that no arrests had been made so far, and no one had been interviewed under caution, in relation to the latest allegations. The initial police investigation into Reform, launched in February last year, relates to allegations about £500,000 donations to Reform UK before the 2024 election from Fiona Cottrell, the mother of George Cottrell. Both have been interviewed under caution. The financial scandals overshadowed Reform’s autumn conference last week, with the party beginning to slip in some polls into second place behind Labour and opinion surveys suggesting voters are have noticed stories about the party’s funding. A Metropolitan police spokesperson said: “Following a broadcast by Channel 4 News on Thursday 3 September, the Met received a number of reports relating to donations and polling involving a political party. “Detectives have assessed the information provided and determined that there are potential offences requiring investigation. “The potential offences are similar in nature to matters already under investigation by the Met’s special enquiry team relating to donations made to the same political party. As a result, these matters will form part of that ongoing investigation. “Detectives are now seeking to obtain relevant footage relating to the broadcast and are liaising with the Electoral Commission and Crown Prosecution Service as inquiries progress.” A Reform UK spokesperson said the party “denies any wrongdoing and will fully cooperate with the investigation”. It added: “We won’t be commenting further while a live investigation is under way.” Jukes and Orr have both also denied wrongdoing. In the undercover investigation, the journalists posed as a potential Reform supporter and his wealthy American father, an impermissible donor, who paid for £30,000 of polling commissioned by Reform and which benefited the party when it was published in national newspapers. If found to have been a donation in kind and made from abroad, it would have been impermissible as it was a foreign source and was not registered with the Electoral Commission. Farage was subsequently caught on camera in a meeting with the fake US donor in Clacton where he appears to be celebrating the success of the poll, saying it was “amazing” and provided “bang for buck”. He said: “It worked. Boom.” In footage of another meeting, Jukes appeared to suggest to the fake UK-based supporter that his US-based father could make a substantial donation by channelling it through the son. When the possible structure was explained to Farage, footage of a meeting between him and the fake donors shows him saying: “Thank you both.” Farage has since said he was not listening. At another point, Orr appeared to suggest that the fake UK-based donor and his US father might secure a meeting with Farage if he could promise a five- or six-figure sum. The meeting later took place in Clacton with Jukes over oysters and champagne. In a different clip, Orr can be heard saying of the poll funding arrangement that Farage “doesn’t know, won’t know” and it was the kind of thing he would “rather not know”. At one point the footage shows him saying it was “totally legit” and with “nothing untowards about it at all”. The Guardian reported last week that the police were highly likely to launch a full investigation into the allegations. Reform initially dismissed the investigation by Verbatim as a hoax and Farage responded by reading out a legal statement in which he described it as “a little local difficulty” and an “an exercise in entrapment”. Farage claimed Orr and Jukes had merely been “contractors” who engaged in “loose pub talk, including a couple of boasts that simply were not true” – despite Jukes having been the Reform UK leader’s very close adviser for more than decade. A spokesperson for Verbatim, which was founded by the Centre for Climate Reporting, said the group would cooperate with the police investigation. The initial police investigation into Reform was launched in February last year after a referral from the Electoral Commission. Lawyers acting for George Cottrell, who lives in Montenegro, have previously said he had no comment to make. In a prior letter to the Guardian, the lawyers stated that “his mother’s donations have been entirely her own decision, and are a matter for her”. Both George and Fiona Cottrell were previously interviewed under criminal caution by Scotland Yard detectives. They attended voluntarily. Fiona Cottrell, who lives in Worcestershire and once dated King Charles, has not responded to questions from the media about any issues involving her support for the Reform party. Lisa Smart, the Liberal Democrat Cabinet Office spokesperson, said: “Thanks to Channel 4’s investigation we all saw with our own eyes Farage’s true colours … we welcome the Met police’s criminal inquiry into their finances, and if proven, Nigel Farage and his cronies should face the full force of the law.”

title: Apple unveils folding iPhone Duo as new CEO takes center stage
summary: The passport-size iPhone Duo serves as the first big test for John Ternus, who took over from Tim Cook last week
text: Apple has unveiled the iPhone Duo, the company’s first foldable phone and the most significant change to the iPhone since the smartphone’s introduction in 2007. The nearly $2,000 device takes inspiration from iPads’ wide screens and combines them with the portability and camera features of iPhones. When opened, it is the company’s largest phone display and thinnest phone. The Duo opens and closes like a passport to double its screen size. “iPhone Duo brings an entirely new design while preserving everything you love from an iPhone,” said John Ternus, the company’s new chief executive. “It feels effortless to use and it makes new experiences possible.” The phone will start at $1,999 and be available on 23 October. The product release event, titled “Surprise and Shine”, began at 10am Pacific Standard Time on Apple’s campus in Cupertino, California, south of San Francisco. “I started the day with an intelligent personal hub and why there’s no product in the world that is better to be that hub than iPhone,” Ternus said. “We think the best way to achieve that is with a foldable design. Others have created foldables that just feel like two phones stuck together … scrolling through vertical content feels compromised.” While competitors have released foldable smartphones since the late 2010s, the new model is a first for the iPhone maker, and its rollout serves as the first big test for Ternus, who assumed the role on 1 September. He claimed the Duo “will redefine the experience of using a foldable phone”. Apple reportedly began testing prototypes of its folding iPhone display in early 2021 – though at the time there were no plans for its launch, according to a Bloomberg report. The company started the event with its more routine announcements, including the new iPhone 18 Pro, which starts at $1,199, and 18 Pro Max models, which start at $1,299. Apple emphasized the AI-enabled features that will be integrated throughout the phone. Called Siri AI, the company said it will be able to tap into third-party apps and already works with over 300,000 apps. Among the many AI-related features available on the new iPhones will be a novel mechanism that fingerprints an image and identifies as captured by an iPhone’s camera – not generated by AI. The feature, called Apple Reference Image, will act as a “digital negative”, as one Apple executive described it, and serve as proof that the the original image was not AI-generated. Both new iPhones also represent a “massive leap” in battery life, executives said – the iPhone 18 Pro Max will have 45 hours of battery life and the iPhone 18 Pro will have 36 hours of battery life. Though the foldable iPhone took center stage on Wednesday in California, overall demand for foldable phones makes up only a small sliver of overall mobile device sales. Customers’ interest in standard iPhones, by contrast, remains high, as evidenced in Apple’s most recent robust earnings. The company also unveiled new iterations of some of its other product offerings at its events and over the next few months, including updates to its Apple Watch and AirPods lines. The company announced the fifth generation of its AirPods headphones, describing them as 50% more noise cancelling than AirPods 4 and sporting five hours of battery life. The latest iteration starts at $129. The company also introduced its latest watches, Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4, pitching them as some of the most advanced and accurate wearable devices to support health and fitness goals. The updated watch will include several new AI features, including “Health Age”, which analyzes heart health, sleep, mental wellbeing, movement health, metabolic health, hearing and nutrition and measures how users stack up to their chronological age. The watch will also include “audio intelligence”, meant to enable your watch to record ambient conversations throughout the day and take notes, producing a transcript of what someone said 15 seconds earlier in case you missed it. At the end of the day, a watch user can review a summary of their day, called a “Siri Recap”. The company said these recordings are stored on the device and anything that is collected is end-to-end encrypted. Ternus took the stage as CEO for the first time, marking the beginning of his tenure as the head of Apple, replacing the outgoing CEO, Tim Cook. In a note to employees on his first day, Ternus said that he was excited about “the incredible products already in the works and the ones we haven’t even imagined”. “I’m honored to be stepping into this role at what is truly the greatest company in the world, and I am so excited about everything we have in store,” Ternus wrote in his letter. “We have a huge launch next week that’s going to be phenomenal. Thanks for everything you’ve all done to make it possible.”

title: ‘Baggage reclaim was pandemonium’: passengers hit by airport IT chaos in UK recount their ordeals
summary: From hours stuck on planes awaiting takeoff, to sleeping the night on the floor at Heathrow. Here are some travellers’ experiences
text: More than 2,000 flights have been cancelled after an air traffic control system failure that has thrown airports across the UK into chaos. Nats, the air traffic control provider, fixed the problem within hours on Tuesday, but hundreds of thousands of passengers were hit by further delays and cancellations on Wednesday. Martin Rolfe, the chief executive of Nats, has been given a week to report back on the reasons for the technical failure. People affected by the disruption talked about their frustration during the two days of chaos – from hours spent stuck on planes waiting to take off, to spending the night sleeping on the floor of Heathrow airport. Here are some of their experiences: ‘People were sleeping on every spare inch of flooring’ Daniel Garrick, 32, a software engineer, was scheduled to leave Heathrow on a flight to Austin, Texas, on Tuesday. After waiting for seven hours on the asphalt, “we were released from the plane only to find Heathrow in absolute chaos”, he says. “My baggage was lost, and British Airways employees were nowhere to be found. People were sleeping on every spare inch of flooring, in arrivals and at security.” Baggage reclaim was “pandemonium”, he says. “All the screens just said it was closed. You couldn’t tell where your baggage was supposed to be. “I found some other Texans going back to Austin on our flight. Someone had an air tag in their luggage and we figured out that the bags were still on the plane. Eventually, there was some announcement where we were told they were not going to finish getting all the bags off the planes tonight, so we’re just going to have to leave.” At the time of writing, Garrick still had not retrieved his case with a week’s worth of clothes. Garrick’s airline, British Airways, sent a mass email apology at about 9pm on Tuesday. “Then in the app, it automatically rebooked me for a flight tomorrow [Thursday] morning, 48 hours after my first flight. Luckily I’m staying with a friend of a friend in Surrey. It was over £100 just for the Uber here.” ‘We were left to our own devices’ Melanie Thompson, 71, an interdisciplinary artist, was on a 14-hour flight returning from her performance at a mixed media festival with her son in Tokyo on Tuesday when she was told the flight would not land in London. “We were exhausted. About 40 minutes before we arrived, the pilot very politely said, ‘because of IT problems and disruptions at Heathrow, we are going to have to divert to Edinburgh’. “There was a big silence. About 20 minutes later, he said: ‘We were hoping we could refuel and then take you on to Heathrow. But we can’t do that, so we would like you to stay in Edinburgh tonight.’ Then we were left to our own devices to find travel and accommodation for the night. “We suddenly found ourselves in Edinburgh with nowhere to stay because all the hotels and Airbnbs had been filled up,. “We finally found a flat for £500, paid for the taxi to get there and stayed the night there last night.” Thompson spoke to the Guardian on her train journey from Edinburgh to London as there were no flights available on Wednesday. ‘It’s Kafkaesque’ Thomas Reilly, 55, was due to fly with BA from Marrakech to Gatwick on Tuesday and then on to Marseille, where he lives and works as a freelance geopolitical adviser. It was only when he got to the airport that he was told his flight was cancelled. “I am currently stuck in Morocco,” says Reilly. “I did not receive any information from BA about the disruption before getting to the airport.” He says that, once at the airport, BA staff were helpful and courteous but he has been left with no option but to book a hotel to stay an extra two nights in Marrakech – at his own expense. (BA staff at the airport did tell him he could “pay and reclaim” for his hotel expenses.) He has been trying to rearrange his journey, attempting to cancel with BA and fly directly to Marseille through a different airline. He says: “BA’s customer services operator is not taking calls as ‘the lines are too busy’. There is no email address. And their chatbot cannot help. It is Kafkaesque.” Reilly says he has worked out “alternative travel arrangements, namely to fly direct from Marrakech to Marseille on Thursday 10 September” but he wanted to get his “refund agreed first before outlaying more money on the replacement flight.” When Reilly got through to someone at BA, he says the airline told him they “would not refund the Heathrow-Marseille ticket”. “It’s absurd,” Reilly adds. A spokesperson for British Airways said: “Since yesterday, we’ve rebooked more than 60,000 customers to travel on alternative flights, getting them to their destinations as quickly as we can. Today, we’ve been able to operate almost 80% of our schedule across our whole network. “We know this has been a very challenging and frustrating time for our customers, and we’re incredibly sorry for the experience they’ve endured because of an issue that has been entirely out of our control.” ‘We have also lost two days of our trip’ Keith Sessions, 74, a computer engineer from Cobham, Surrey, and his wife were due to fly from Heathrow to Tahiti via LA on Tuesday with a five-hour stopover at LAX airport. For the first leg of their journey, they were to fly Virgin, but once on the plane it was clear there were problems. He says the pilot informed them there were delays. Five and a half hours later, with the plane still on the asphalt, the pilot announced that the flight had been cancelled. Sessions says they were not offered a meal in that time, “only water, soft drinks and courtesy snacks”. The couple decided to return home via taxi and their flights were auto-rebooked. They will now fly out on Thursday with an 11-hour stopover at LAX airport. They will arrive in Tahiti at 5.30am on Friday. “The 11-hour stopover is not ideal,” says Sessions. “We have also lost two days of our trip and had to spend an extra £340 when you factor in extra cabs to and from the airport and the cost to reserve seating on our flight. Communication from Virgin has been very poor, diabolical.” A Virgin Atlantic spokesperson said: “We’d like to sincerely apologise to our customers for the widespread disruption … We know how frustrating delays and changes to travel plans can be and appreciate our customers’ patience.”

title: Uganda to withdraw from Invictus Games ‘out of respect for King Charles’, says military chief
summary: Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba announces decision to pull out in post on X, citing tensions over ‘Harry-Meghan nonsense’
text: Uganda is withdrawing from the Duke of Sussex’s Invictus Games, the country’s military chief has said, out of respect for King Charles amid division over the “Harry-Meghan nonsense”. Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba, son of the Ugandan president, made the surprise announcement in a post on X on Wednesday. Kainerugaba wrote: “In order not to be construed as being opposed to His Majesty King Charles III of the United Kingdom, whom we deeply revere, Uganda hereby withdraws from the Invictus Games. We shall not participate in anything that does not have His Majesty’s approval.” The timing of the post suggests it may be in response to an official letter to UK senior government and military officials on behalf of Charles that reiterated the Duke and Duchess of Sussex were not working royals and would not use their HRH styles. When asked by the Times about what had motivated the move, Kainerugaba is reported to have said: “I have factions in the Ministry of Defence that support that Harry-Meghan nonsense. I had to quash it straight away. I support the monarch. Period.” The news, first reported by the Uganda Pulse news website, will be a blow to Harry, who two months ago stood alongside Uganda’s defence minister, Kiryowa Kiwanuka, at an Invictus Games event in London to announce that the East African nation would be the 26th country to enter the multisport event for wounded service personnel. At the time, Kiwanuka praised the Ugandan president, Yoweri Museveni for his “visionary leadership” and Kainerugaba, a Sandhurst graduate, for “championing our team’s entry”, adding that their support “marks a new chapter for our servicemen and women”. The Ugandan government spokesperson Alan Kasujja confirmed to the BBC: “Gen Kainerugaba decides whether or not the UPDF [Uganda People’s Defence Force] participates in the Invictus Games. What you saw is his stated position. If it changes, he will let the world know.” The decision to withdraw may be an unintended consequence of the official letter, issued on Monday by the head of the royal household, the lord chamberlain, Richard Benyon, at Charles’s behest, clarifying the position of the Sussexes after their return to the UK two weeks ago. The letter directed that the couple were “no longer working members of the royal family”, that their charitable work “is a personal matter for them both and undertaken in their private capacity” and “their position is akin to private citizens with commercial and charitable interests”. Kainerugaba was appointed army chief in 2024 and is widely seen as his 81-year-old father’s successor to the presidency. He has made several provocative posts on X, including threats to invade neighbouring Kenya, demands that Jay-Z hand over his wife, Beyoncé, so he could marry her, and threats against Bobi Wine, Museveni’s principal political rival. The Invictus Games and representatives for the Duke of Sussex have been approached for comment.

title: Scientists Discover the Earliest Evidence of Drug Use in Really Old Teeth
summary: A hunter-gatherer who lived in Indonesia as early as 25,000 years ago may have regularly sucked on betel nuts to release their psychoactive properties.

title: Indonesian foragers may have sucked on mind-altering nuts 25,000 years ago, research finds
summary: Analysis of two skeletons reveals tooth wear and traces of psychoactive substance in what may be earliest known evidence for human drug taking
text: What may be the earliest known evidence for human drug taking has been traced to ancient Indonesian foragers who sucked on mind-altering nuts as long as 25,000 years ago. Analysis of two exceptionally rare skeletons from the Indonesian island of Sulawesi revealed dramatic tooth wear and traces of a psychoactive substance in the individuals’ remaining teeth, suggesting they routinely sucked on hard, abrasive betel nuts. Although little known in western societies, betel nuts are the world’s fourth most widely used psychoactive substance after alcohol, caffeine and nicotine, with an estimated tenth of the global population chewing the seeds. “We’ve found evidence for how this very common drug use habit, which is found throughout a lot of the Asia-Pacific region today, might have evolved,” said Prof Adam Brumm at Griffith University’s Australian Research Centre for Human Evolution in Brisbane. The work began when the team examined skeletal remains of two pre-agricultural foragers unearthed at two different sites on the island. One was dated to about 7,000 years old, the other more ancient at 16,000 to 25,000 to years old. Writing in Science Advances, the researchers describe how both adults had deep, rounded grooves in their teeth. Some went so deep they would have exposed the dental pulp. “I was thinking, what the hell were these people doing? It’s like someone had a drill head shaped like a gobstopper and wore away the inner part of the tooth,” said Brumm. Betel nuts are actually the seeds of the Areca catechu palm, but are misnamed because they are often wrapped in betel vine leaves for chewing. Today, the nuts are typically chewed after being mixed with slaked lime made by grinding burnt shells to form a “quid”. Brumm suspected the bizarre tooth wear was caused by the foragers holding hard, round and abrasive objects in their mouth, but what sort of object? “Imagine you kept a stone in your mouth and you moved it from one part of your mouth to another, and if you did that day after day, hour after hour. Eventually it would wear down your extremely hard dental tissue to form these grooves,” he said. The team wondered whether the grooves were the result of foragers sucking on betel nuts before people realised that mixing the nuts with slaked lime helped release more of the psychoactive drug and intensify the “high”. To test the hunch, the scientists soaked betel nuts in artificial saliva and found that it soon contained enough of the psychoactive compound arecoline to induce a high, albeit a milder one than when the nut is chewed. Analysis of the foragers’ teeth found traces of arecoline in the tissues. “I’ve sucked on a nut as an experiment and it’s a really bitter, astringent taste. It makes your mouth go numb and I think that’s what they were interested in,” Brumm said. “This might have been a traditional remedy for toothache, but if they did it for too long, sucking on the nut wore down their teeth so badly that it actually created much worse dental pain in the long term. These individuals were seemingly caught in a self-perpetuating cycle where they were continually sucking on the nuts to treat the tooth pain caused by this nut-sucking habit.” While humans probably began using mind-altering plants as soon as they encountered them, the oldest traditions of psychoactive drug use are thought to have arisen about 13,000 years ago with fermented drinks such as barley beer. Dr Elisa Guerra-Doce, an associate professor in European prehistory at the University of Valladolid in Spain, said the study provided “direct evidence of the antiquity of human drug use”. “These findings not only represent the earliest known evidence to date of the use of psychoactive plants anywhere in the world, but also demonstrate that the consumption of Areca nuts is a millennia-old tradition dating back to prehistoric times,” she added.
