title: Tens of thousands line the streets as Norway bids farewell to King Harald V
summary: Europe’s royals and global political figures attend ceremony that brings 13 days of national mourning to a close
text: Norway has observed a minute’s silence as it takes leave of King Harald V in a series of ceremonies, bringing to a close 13 days of national mourning that followed the popular monarch’s death last month at the age of 89. Tens of thousands of people lined the streets of Oslo and foreign heads of state and government converged on the Norwegian capital for the funeral of the late king, a light-touch and unassuming reformer who ruled for more than three decades. With the king’s casket carried on an artillery carriage, draped in Norway’s red royal banner and topped with white flowers, the funeral cortege made its way on foot along Oslo’s main avenue from royal palace to the cathedral, as a 21-gun salute rang out from the Akershus fortress. King Haakon VIII, who succeeded his father on Harald’s death, and other royal family members walked in the cortege, with Harald’s widow, Queen Sonja, 89, and Haakon’s wife, Queen Mette-Marit, who is recovering from a lung transplant in June, following in a car. The procession was followed by a church ceremony attended by royals including Britain’s Prince William and Princess Anne; Spain’s King Felipe and Queen Letizia; ‌Sweden’s royal family; Denmark’s King Frederik and Queen Mary; the Netherlands’ King Willem-Alexander and Queen Maxima; and Japan’s Crown Prince Akishino. Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, and political leaders and dignitaries from more than 20 countries were at the service, at which the speaker of Norway’s parliament, Masud Gharahkhani, recalled a monarch who was “not afraid to meet his people with his rubber boots on”. The prime minister, Jonas Gahr Støre, said Harald “struck a balance between being stately and being down-to-earth. He made Norway greater. He spoke of a ‘we’ in Norway where everyone is there for each other.” After the service four F-35 fighter jets flew over the cathedral, one breaking away to symbolise the king’s passing. The casket was then carried to the Akershus fortress where it was due to be lowered into the royal crypt, next to Harald’s parents and grandparents, in a private ceremony. Norwegian police said securing the funeral had been the largest planned operation in the force’s history. More than 46,000 Norwegians have filed past the king’s casket in the past week and schoolchildren were allowed to miss ⁠classes for the occasion. Harald’s death came at a time of numerous crises for the Norwegian royal family, with Mette-Marit, 53, in particular coming under heavy criticism – including from the prime minister – for her association with the late US sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. The new queen’s son from a previous relationship, Marius Borg Høiby, who is under house arrest and wearing an ankle monitor pending his appeal against a conviction for rape and domestic violence, was given permission to attend the funeral and was a pallbearer during the transfer to the royal chapel. Despite its recent scandals, however, the monarchy remains broadly popular: 72% of Norwegians support it, while 20% favour a republic or another form of government, according to a poll for the public broadcaster NRK.

title: Why the horror warnings about Australia’s ‘collapsing’ housing market are absurd – and very much in bad faith | Greg Jericho
summary: If prices were to take a 10% fall from the March 2026 peak, as CBA has suggested, that would still only mean prices were back where they were at the end of 2024
text: House prices in the June quarter fell slightly off the back of three interest rate rises and the changes to the capital gains tax discount and negative gearing. But prices remain extremely high. In the June quarter the total value of Australia’s housing fell $34bn. Sounds like a lot? In percentage terms it was just 0.3%. That’s because in the June quarter the total value of Australian housing was $12.18tn. And here’s the kicker: that is $948bn more than it was a year ago. The horror warnings about Australia’s “collapsing” housing market really are quite stupid – and very much in bad faith. That bad faith began before the budget when vested interest groups and the opposition suggested the capital gains tax (CGT) discount and negative gearing had no impact on housing affordability and cutting them would not do anything to house prices. Now they are to blame for prices falling! Those vested interests have been loudly crying about the fall of house prices and the “brutal” tax changes. On Tuesday the latest total value of dwellings (houses and apartments) figures provided some much-needed data on the idiocy of the debate. These latest figures only go to the end of June, so we have yet to see an entire quarter under the new rules, but they do give some insight. There was a fall in the average dwelling prices in the June quarter – 0.7% across Australia. Although that is very much affected by the 2.4% fall in New South Wales prices and 2.1% drop in Victoria. Prices still rose in all other states except the ACT: If the graph does not display click here The size of the housing problem is clear when you ponder that even with that 2.4% fall in NSW, which took average dwelling prices from $1.337m to $1.305m, they are still 2% higher than the $1.28m price they were a year ago. In every single state the average dwelling price was higher in June this year than a year ago: If the graph does not display click here And even worse is that over the past six years (since the pandemic), only Victoria has seen house prices grow less than household income: If the graph does not display click here Because these figures include prices from April as well as after the budget in May and June, clearly they don’t register the impact of the tax changes. This may mean that the median house price in Adelaide does not hit the $1m barrier that Perth, Brisbane, Canberra and Sydney have all reached. If the graph does not display click here But here’s a juicy statistic to chew: in Adelaide, Perth and Brisbane, the median price of houses has more than doubled in six years. Just think on that. Yep, nice, steady Adelaide, historically the cheapest capital city on the mainland to buy a home. Back in June 2020, half of the houses sold in the city of churches went for less than $487,500. In the June quarter of this year, you needed a bid of at least $975,000 to have a chance of buying a median-priced house. If the graph does not display click here And sure, the percentage growth of house price in Sydney over the past six years was not as large (a mere 56% jump compared with Adelaide’s 100%, Brisbane’s 111% or Perth’s 112% increase), but the median price of a Sydney house in the June quarter this year was $532,600 more than it was six years ago. Yes, the median price fell from $1.55m in March to $1.49m in June, but is anyone sauntering around Pitt Street chatting about how cheap the harbour city has become? Whenever we hear anyone, whether they be an economist seeking an AFR column or a wannabe comedy-influencer seeking a spot on Sky After Dark, talking about the fall in house prices and the end of time, we really do need to calm the hell down. As I noted last month, the “scary” projections about how far house prices would fall would take prices in Sydney merely back to 2023 levels. In Brisbane the projected fall wouldn’t even get you back to the price they were at the end of last year! Currently the average dwelling price across Australia is $1.1m – if prices were to take a 10% fall from the March 2026 peak, as the Commonwealth Bank has suggested, that would mean prices would go back to where they were at the end of 2024. If the graph does not display click here The good news is because household incomes have been growing since 2024, that 10% price drop would take the value of an average dwelling in Australia from being equivalent to 16.9 years of average household disposable income to 15.4 years. That is marginally higher than it was in the middle of 2021. If the graph does not display click here And what were people saying about housing back in 2021? Well, I wrote a column talking about the howl of despair of those whose housing dreams were being dashed. The changes in the budget are working as expected and desired. And if anyone thinks they are about to destroy the wealth of Australians, they should think back to 2021 and remember that no one thought housing was cheap then. • Greg Jericho is a Guardian columnist and chief economist at the Australia Institute

title: The RBA hoped this year’s three interest rate rises would tame inflation – but nothing is going their way
summary: The breakdown of the US-Iran ceasefire, rising oil prices and the explosion in datacentre investment are making the central bank’s task harder
text: For five years the Reserve Bank has been trying to wrangle inflation back to its 2.5% target, and for years it has essentially failed. The result is a cost-of-living crisis that has generated intense community grievance. The RBA’s deputy governor, Andrew Hauser, acknowledged as much on the ABC’s 7:30 report on Tuesday. “People are furious about inflation,” Hauser said. “Inflation has been above target for a long period of time and, at some point, we will have to say, ‘That is long enough’.” Are we at that point? Not yet, said Hauser, even as he hinted we are getting closer every day. The RBA’s nine-member board had hoped this year’s three interest rate hikes would be enough to bend the arc of inflation slowly back to reach 2.5% by the end of next year. But nothing is going their way. The latest blow is the complete breakdown of the US-Iran ceasefire, with escalating tit-for-tat strikes on oil tankers and infrastructure in and around the strait of Hormuz. The global oil benchmark has risen above $US100 a barrel for the first time since July. Fuel prices are tracking higher once again, with unleaded approaching $2.10 a litre and diesel passing $2.50. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Then there is this year’s sudden explosion in datacentre investment. That has heaped pressure on a construction sector already struggling to get the materials and labour it needs to build the massive pipeline of work to build homes, roads and rails. Households are complaining a lot and feeling depressed, but there’s still a surprising lot of spending happening, which is keeping consumption growth ticking along. Meanwhile, Australia’s productivity performance – the thing that could make it easier for the economy to grow without pushing inflation up – remains flat. Investors and an increasing number of economists believe we are approaching that point when the RBA has to say “enough is enough” and act more aggressively to get price rises back under control. Financial markets are pricing in more than a 70% chance of another rate hike on 29 September, and even the chance of a second by the end of the year. “Of course we could raise interest rates sharply,” Hauser said. “We could do it tomorrow. We could no longer take seriously the full employment part of our objective [and say] we’re gonna bring inflation down come hell or high water.” Here Hauser is pointing out that the RBA has not been asleep at the wheel, but has been making a conscious calculation. Since mid-2021, annual inflation has only been below 3% for one year. On the other hand, unemployment has been below 5% for almost all of that time – a labour market record unmatched in modern Australia history. “The reason as a board we have decided to take it slowly is to preserve as many jobs in this country as we could,” Hauser said, and not for the first time. But the balance is starting to shift. “We have one big problem, and that’s inflation,” he said. “Inflation is too high, that’s why we raised interest rates three times at the beginning of this year. The question now, frankly, for us, is have we done enough, or is more needed?”

title: An ocean away from Nepal, Sonia spends her spare time piecing together clues about missing flood victims: ‘I wanted to be useful’
summary: Facebook groups are checking information from family and friends of the missing against Nepal’s police database in a task where success is bittersweet at best
text: A chain of flowers tattooed from knee to foot, a gold nose ring worn on a left nostril, a primary school tie caked in mud: these are the images that linger in Sonia Patil’s mind as she tries to help Nepali flood victims find their loved ones. More than 1,300 have died and at least 5,500 have been reported missing since a glacial collapse sent a torrent of water, mud, ice and debris through riverside communities along the Nepal-Tibet border on 26 August. Families and friends of those reported missing have spent weeks searching through graphic photos of bodies, which were uploaded by Nepali police for the community to identify. Some show only partial corpses – disconnected torsos, limbs splayed at unnatural angles, decomposition eating away at extremities – while in others, the faces of flood victims are turned to the camera, their expressions frozen in their death masks. Patil, a Melbourne-based chef, has no direct connection with Nepal or any of the people whose loved ones have been reported missing. But when she saw videos of their grief, she knew she could help share their burden. “It’s a very harrowing task for them,” she says. “If I had lost a family member, the prospect of coming across their body in that condition would be unbearable. “I knew I wanted to be useful, it’s the least I can do, even if it’s just being another pair of eyes.” Almost every day since the disaster, she arrives home at midnight after a 12-hour shift and spends another four to five hours on the Nepali police website, trawling through the hundreds of images of decomposing bodies and limbs. If any have distinctive features – such as clothes, tattoos and jewellery – she adds them to her list and posts it to Facebook groups filled with those looking for their loved ones. It can be a confronting and tedious process, Patil says. During the day, the Nepal police website slows or malfunctions under the weight of all the families looking for information, so she finds it easier to work at night. The listings, which grow by the day, may only show partial remains, and most only have one image per body – meaning she cannot see any other angles. Missing persons posters are also spread across multiple platforms, forcing Patil to search across the internet to crosscheck information. But no matter how hard it is, she says it is worse for those on the ground. “It’s very disturbing to know that I may be looking at a picture of a live person and somebody who is deceased at the same time, trying to compare them,” she says. “I find it easier when I go in with the mindset that all the images on that website are all human: they have lived lives, they have stories, they have families looking for them.” Patil is part of a group which includes people from the US, Europe, New Zealand and other countries who work together to identify bodies. They generally look for matches for those who have reached out to them with photos of their missing friends and family. It is difficult to be 100% certain through visual identification alone, as many images of the bodies are unrecognisable. So when members think they have made a match, the group asks relatives to submit their DNA to labs in Nepal for official confirmation. If they believe they have made a match for someone who has not asked for their help, the group tries to report it to Nepali authorities. Making a likely identification is bittersweet for everyone involved, Patil says, because while they are glad a family will get closure, “it’s not a great feeling to know that person is no longer here”. But it is worse when she posts her lists and no one responds. “In some cases, entire families have been wiped out, which means that even people with the most recognisable tattoos have nobody left to identify them,” she says. Patil does not want any thanks for her work. Instead, she urges everyone to keep sharing the lists in case someone in their network recognises the missing. It is now becoming harder to discern any distinctive features as the bodies disintegrate under the sun and sludge with the passing days. But Patil has vowed to continue. “So long as I can find tattoos or anything identifiable, I will keep going,” she says.

title: New Mexicans meet Trump’s threat to change state’s name with ridicule and outrage
summary: Residents denounced suggestion to rename state ‘New America’, save some Republicans who insist it was ‘satire’
text: When scrolling through social media over the Labor Day weekend, Steven Michael Quezada, an actor, comedian and native New Mexican, was stopped cold by a post about Donald Trump’s recent call to rename New Mexico as “New America”. “At first I thought, nah, that’s got to be a joke,” said Quezada, who played the drug enforcement agent Steven Gomez in the legendary TV series Breaking Bad. But it’s not drawing a lot of laughs in the state with the largest percentage of Latinos and 23 federally recognized Native American tribes. “In his mind, the word ‘Mexico’ has some kind of connotation of people of color and it just feels like the whitewashing of our state,” said Sarah Noss, a native New Mexican and non-profit executive, one of many residents expressing outrage at Trump’s social media posts in interviews with the Guardian. The president’s calls to rename New Mexico have reopened deep wounds for a state with a racial and ethnic composition that has made it a target for bigoted attacks dating back to 1848, when the US acquired the Mexican territory as part of the treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo. Later, the former civil war general William T Sherman said the US should “declare war on Mexico and make it take back New Mexico”. An AI-generated video of the president changing a “Welcome to New Mexico” sign to “Welcome to New America” comes 10 days after the Trump administration sued the state for providing in-state tuition and state-funded financial assistance to undocumented immigrant students – the majority of whom are Latino – another example of what some residents said were policies targeting people of color. “We were New Mexico even before we were the United States,” said Antoinette Armijo-Rougemont, a multigenerational New Mexican and army national guard veteran. “Every day is a new illogical idea. He should be focusing on ending the war and improving the economy.” The messages have tapped into longstanding anger in the state over racist government policies. US lawmakers resisted statehood for New Mexico for more than 60 years – until 1912 – because of its large Spanish-speaking and Native populations. “We were denied statehood because we were considered mixed-blood Mexicans, fanatical Catholics and savage Indians,” said Rob Martinez, the New Mexico state historian. “We went to bed Mexicans and woke up supposedly American citizens, but we weren’t treated like Mexican American citizens, we were treated like foreigners in our own land.” Martinez said the state’s name traces back to the 1560s, when Spanish settlers called it Nueva Mexico, in a reference to Mexico City. The name evolved to Nuevo Mexico, then New Mexico. By the 1920s, various civic groups launched campaigns to rename New Mexico, including a push to call the state Coolidge, in honor of the sitting president Calvin Coolidge. Republicans in the state, including gubernatorial candidate Gregg Hull, have dismissed the president’s suggestion out of hand, and congressional candidate Greg Cunningham, who is running in a swing district, called the president’s posts “satire” and an attempt by Democrats to “distract voters from their awful record by focusing on what the president is posting on social media”. Quezada, who called his 2022 comedy special The New Mexican, said Trump is like a comic on stage who knows he is losing the room. “Everything’s a mess right now, and I guess the best entertainer knows to distract you from what’s really going on,” he said. But the last laugh will be for New Mexicans, who would have to approve an amendment to the state’s constitution for a name change, an unlikelihood in a state in which every major statewide office is held by a Democrat. • This article was amended on 25 September 2026. An earlier version incorrectly said that New Mexico has the most federally recognized Native American tribes in the United States.

title: ‘I fear the price could be high’: Inside the German state where the far-right surged
summary: After the AfD’s landslide win in Saxony-Anhalt, people in the state capital share what they make of the result – and what comes next
text: Asking residents in a city where a seismic political event has just taken place ‘How do you feel?’ demands chutzpah – this struck me as I walked around Magdeburg, Germany on Monday. The night before, the far-right populist, anti-immigrant, pro-Kremlin party Alternative für Deustchland (AfD) had landslide 44% win in Saxony-Anhalt’s state elections, sending shock waves to Berlin, across Germany and way beyond. Regardless of how people in the capital voted, it felt like a bit of an affront to probe. Given the radical plans of the victors, a party classified by domestic intelligence as “rightwing extremist”, that is what I wanted to know. But from the 21-year-old Guinean-German paramedic I met at the central bus station, collecting donations for a local hospice, to the elderly couple returning to their apartment after a stroll down the Elbe river, almost everyone I met opened up to me warmly. Judith, 88, was initially reluctant to talk, but shared some of her life story. Her experience as an eight-year-old refugee, forced to leave Poland in 1946 and eventually ending up move with her family in Magdeburg, had shaped her outlook on life, her successful career as a project engineer – as well as her politics. The news that AfD had not only won the election, but by such a wide margin, was “heartbreaking”, she said. Huy, from Vietnam, who runs a newsagents in the city centre, was also reticent, but laughed and rolled his eyes as he sold the last copy of that day’s local paper, Die Volksstimme, and pointed to the headline that read: “Landslide in Saxony-Anhalt”. Shaking his head, he said: “44%!” “I don’t want to think what it might mean … but maybe it will all be OK?” His question hung in the air. A glance at the AfD’s manifesto, in particular its pledge for the first 100 days, focuses the mind. Top of the list: challenging Germany’s post-war memory culture (which it says stands in the way of national pride) – so, “more Bismarck, less Hitler”, as they put it. “From the first minute”, they say, the party will start the deportation of what it refers to as “irregular migrants”. I met Franz-Josef, a 71-year-old retired mechanic and Green voter, on holiday from a small west German town. He called the election a “catastrophe”, particularly in the light of the country’s Nazi past. Luisa, a 34-year-old bank teller told me she hopes “those who voted for the AfD thought about what they were doing”. It was one thing, she said, to “deliver a kick in the shins” to Berlin, over its failure to pull the German economy out of the doldrums. And maybe the AfD would fail to push through its promises in government. “But we cannot know, and I fear the price could be high.” *** Fragrance of power It remains unclear how precisely the AfD, led by charismatic former fragrance salesman Ulrich Siegmund, might take the reins of power in Saxony-Anhalt, if at all. He lacks an absolute majority by a whisker. There have been rumblings for days – even prior to the election – of an AfD charm offensive to try to lure members of chancellor Friedrich Merz’s Christian Democrats, to make up the necessary numbers. The CDU denies any defections are expected. Some AfD members have brazenly appropriated Ronald Reagan’s appeal to the Soviets to “tear down this wall”, from his 1987 speech in West Berlin. They are calling on mainstream parties to “tear down the firewall”, a reference to the Brandmauer, or refusal to ever coalesce with the AfD in an effort to prevent the far-right populists from coming to power. Yet an increasing number doubt that the firewall will hold much longer. Especially now that almost one in two of those who cast their votes on Sunday have opted for the party. Turnout at 78% was a record for the state. Whatever the outcome, we can expect weeks, even months of wrangling. Expect stasis in the meantime on the federal government front, as we’re close to elections on 20 September in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern and Berlin, where the AfD is also expected to do well. Merz will be wary of doing anything that might drive more voters away. At the same time politicos in Berlin are debating how long he has in the job. In the Bundestag today, Merz accused the AfD of seeking “ethnic cleansing”. No wonder Maryam, 16, whom I met as she returned from work experience at a retirement home, said she and her family were on edge. The Syrian teenager, whose father arrived in Germany in 2015, followed by her and her mother, told me she couldn’t stop thinking about what this vote might mean for her family. She wished, she said, for a return to the days of Angela Merkel, the German chancellor who welcomed in a million migrants including Maryam’s father, resentment over which turbo-charged support for the then-fledgling AfD. Across the road, Doreen, a cleaner, who reluctantly admitted voting for the AfD, said: “What on Earth is there to thank Merkel for? It’s owing to her that we are in the state we’re in.” She recalled an attack near the Christmas market in the city centre in 2024, where six people were killed when a Saudi doctor drove a car into the crowd, an incident that helped fuel support for the AfD. “That attack is symbolic for a whole lot of misery, the decision to open our doors to strangers has brought us,” Doreen told me. “I say, good on the AfD for promising to clean up the mess.” For such a small state, home to 2.1 million people, Saxony-Anhalt has managed to create a political maelstrom, the ramifications of which will be felt across Europe. title: Burnham sees sanctions against Israeli settlements as an electoral asset
summary: While a survey found Labour, Lib Dem and Green voters to be the strongest backers of such a ban on trade, even Tory and Reform voters were in favour overall
text: There was a time when placing Israel under strict trade sanctions would have been a politically risky thing for a British prime minister to do. Andy Burnham, however, considers it an electoral asset. As Kemi Badenoch attacked him over defence spending at prime minister’s questions on Wednesday, Burnham deliberately turned the topic to the trade ban on illegal settlements which he had announced on Tuesday. With the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, sitting to his left, the prime minister said: “In this difficult and dangerous world Britain has to stand for something, Britain has to show leadership, Britain has to stand for fairness against injustice. “Where people are being bullied out of their homes and intimidated, we will always stand with the underdog and take what action we can to support them. That, Mr Speaker, is leadership on the world stage: Britain being true to what it’s always been about. “That is what the British people expect of us and that is what this government will do.” Under the new sanctions announced on Tuesday, goods produced in illegal settlements in occupied Palestine will be banned from being imported into the UK and those who help build or finance settlements will face sanctions. The measures drew a sharp response from the Israeli government, which announced the closure of the British consulate in East Jerusalem. Domestically, the opposition has been led by Badenoch, who has long been a staunch ally of Israel. In a piece in the Jewish Chronicle, the Conservative leader warned that the prime minister risked “fanning the flames of antisemitism here at home”. “For all Labour claim to have rooted out antisemitism internally, the degree of anti-Israel hatred means that Labour’s approach to many of these issues is Corbyn in all but name,” she added. Others in her party, however, have struck a less aggressive tone. On Tuesday, the shadow foreign secretary, Tom Tugendhat, said: “None of us here rejects the government’s stated aim that we must do everything we can to end the circle of violence and support the Abraham accords and the two-state solution. “What we reject is performative politics, acting alone, that leaves our envoys irrelevant and our voice weaker.” Some senior Conservatives even backed the government. Edward Leigh, who as father of the house has held his seat longer than any other MP, told the Commons on Tuesday: “I am proud to say that I absolutely and fully support what he is doing today, because it is about standing up for freedom, for morality and for justice for all people in this world.” The government has reason to believe it is on strong electoral ground with this decision. A poll by YouGov earlier in the summer found 50% of British voters supported a ban on trade with West Bank settlements, while only 16% were opposed. While Labour, Liberal Democrat and Green voters were the strongest backers of such a move, even Conservative and Reform voters were in favour overall. Labour officials hope the announcement may help them make up ground with progressive and Muslim voters who have moved away from the party since the 2024 election. Many say they remain angry about an interview given by Keir Starmer soon after the Gaza war began in which the then prime minister said he thought Israel had the right to withhold water and electricity from Palestinians. The disillusionment among Muslim voters was particularly important in the Green party’s victory in Gorton and Denton. Meanwhile Labour lost a large part of its broader progressive base during the local elections, in which the Greens took a number of councils and mayoralties in central London. Zack Polanski, the leader of the Greens in England and Wales, tweeted on Tuesday: “Ed Miliband’s statement on Israel is only a first step. We need to go further: a full ban on goods, services & investment.” Labour and the Greens are now again locked in battle, over the Holborn and St Pancras seat, which Starmer has vacated. Though the policy was in train long before that byelection was called, it could prove an important campaign tool for Labour canvassers looking to reassure their core voters.

title: Peter’s farm is on ‘flood country’. As Australia’s sea levels rise, safe land is vanishing and costs are huge
summary: Climate Council forecasts more than 267,000 coastal properties will be damaged by flooding by 2100, costing hundreds of billions of dollars
text: When grazier Peter Lake moved to the Clarence Valley in the New South Wales northern rivers region in 2007, he knew was “buying in flood country with … eyes open”. His cattle farm, about halfway between Yamba and Grafton, borders the Coldstream River and has flooded five times since 2009. “Out of 130 acres … in a major flood we would have maybe 15 acres that were flood-free,” he said. Lake has systems in place to prepare for such events, including moving cattle to the dry paddocks, where they would also store fodder to feed the animals. But the amount of safe ground is shrinking: in the historically big flood in 2022, “we only had just a few acres of flood-free land”. Because of both drought and frequent floods, “we just haven’t been able to successfully grow a fodder crop for some years”. “If we’re going to have more frequent and more severe major events … we need to change the way we think about how we manage,” Lake said. “If rising sea levels impact on us, it’ll just make property less and less viable.” Agricultural damages are among $855.1bn in economic losses projected Australia-wide by the end of the century due to coastal flooding, according to a Climate Council report released on Thursday. The report forecasts that more than 267,000 coastal properties and 2m hectares (4.9m acres) of Australian land will be damaged by flooding by 2100 as sea levels rise. Queensland (93,157 properties), NSW (71,210) and Western Australia (51,366) are the three states with the greatest number of homes at risk. The Gold Coast, Brisbane and Melbourne are the metropolitan areas expected to be worst affected. The Gold Coast, the country’s most exposed urban area, faces $84.4bn in projected economic losses, while in Melbourne losses are concentrated in low-lying areas around Port Phillip Bay and the Yarra River. The Climate Council report is based on mapping coastal flooding by 2100, taking into account both sea level rise and storm surges under the climate scenario known as RCP4.5 – which projects a 2.7C increase in global temperature by the end of the century, similar to expected heating based on current policies worldwide. It was co-authored by Prof Tom Kompas at the University of Melbourne, whose modelling of the economic impacts was also published in the peer-reviewed journal Scientific Reports and drew upon localised projections at 239 hotspots around Australia. Kompas said the costs – an estimated $274.3bn in property losses and $580.7bn in land use damages – were a conservative estimate and did not take into account the additional impacts of coastal erosion or significant ice sheet melt. He said due to the scale of agricultural losses there was a food security issue potentially coming as well: damage is projected to affect 619,713 hectares (1.5m acres) of farming land. Sea levels have risen, on average by more than 22cm globally since 1900, with human-caused global heating the dominant cause of the rise since 1970. An additional 14cm rise is expected in Australia by 2050, increasing the frequency of permanent inundation and tidal flooding. Kompas said that while reducing greenhouse gas emissions to limit global heating was of paramount importance, “we have to start planning and responding and adapting now”. “The nice thing about the work is it shows where the hotspots are and what … assets will be impacted. So we can start to plan for how to deal with that. “The first thing, of course, is not to build on flood plains, which is common still.”

title: Sinkhole at Malibu home reportedly owned by Nicolas Cage prompts evacuation
summary: More than 30 properties ordered to evacuate after sinkhole grows to roughly 25-30ft deep and 30 by 60 feet wide
text: The city of Malibu, California, has ordered the evacuation of more than 30 properties after a large sinkhole opened on Tuesday. Malibu officials declared a local emergency on Tuesday evening after a “large sinkhole” emerged near 31630 Sea Level Drive. The officials said the sinkhole was believed to have begun developing on Monday, and had grown to roughly 25-30ft deep and 30 by 60ft wide by Tuesday evening. In an earlier update on Tuesday, officials said they were responding to the “collapse of a driveway” and a resulting gas leak, which had been reported at about 5.45am local time. The Los Angeles county sheriff’s department and Los Angeles county fire department closed the private road and identified the gas leak. Actor Nicolas Cage is reportedly the owner of the home where the sinkhole formed. Cage purchased the home in 2024, the New York Times noted. A representative for Cage did not immediately respond to a request for comment. “Conditions are continuing to be evaluated, and the full extent of the impacts is not yet known,” Malibu city officials said on Tuesday evening, warning that the sinkhole “poses imminent danger to the homes and residents along Sea Level Drive”. By Tuesday evening, 31 properties were under an evacuation order. Officials said that seven homes had been red-tagged because of “hazardous conditions resulting from the sinkhole” while another 24 residences were red-tagged “due to the loss of safe vehicular access”. Sheriff’s deputies notified residents in person and a digital alert had been issued. Gas service to the affected area was shut off by Tuesday evening and city officials warned that water service “may also be discontinued as conditions warrant”. They also cautioned that “conditions are likely to worsen with forecasted high tides and rains”. Additionally, Post-tropical Cyclone Marie could continue to bring “increased rainfall and high surf” to the area. The National Weather Service said on Tuesday that “swells generated by Marie will continue to affect portions of the coast of the Baja California Peninsula and southern California for the next couple of days”. A coastal flood advisory had been in effect until 11pm local time on Tuesday, Malibu officials said. A temporary shelter was also established by the American Red Cross at Malibu high school. City officials said that emergency personnel access “is severely constrained and may be impassable, due to the large portion of the road that has collapsed”. They said that as of Tuesday evening, the “intact portion of the roadway is too narrow to accommodate emergency response vehicles, including fire engines and other large apparatus, creating a substantial risk to public safety and emergency response capabilities”.

title: AI could kill all humans in next decade, warn experts: but how seriously should we take them?
summary: Alarming warnings from industry insiders increase pressure for curbs on artificial superintelligence
text: Does artificial superintelligence really pose a risk greater than nuclear weapons? Is there a significant chance of “a Chornobyl-sized catastrophe”? Might there even be a greater than 10% chance that AI could “kill all humans” in the next decade? These warnings were issued over the past 48 hours on both sides of the Atlantic about the potential impact of a technology that most people still think of as a more talkative search engine. Some of the threats were raised in the UK as MPs and peers began to wrestle with the danger of AI outperforming human capabilities. The nuclear warnings came from Des Browne, a former defence secretary, and Prof Stuart Russell, an eminent Berkeley computer scientist. Beatrice Fihn, who won the 2017 Nobel peace prize for leading the International Campaign to Abolish Nuclear Weapons, told parliamentarians: “It is not the first time we’re confronted with abilities that could end up killing us all.” The session on Monday was convened by Control AI, a lobbying group pushing for international regulation of the technology. It is backing a bill tabled in parliament this week by the Labour MP Alex Sobel and aimed at banning the creation of artificial superintelligence (ASI). On Tuesday night, a senior employee at Anthropic admitted he believed there was a greater than 10% chance the technology could “kill all humans” in the next decade and warned that his AI company did not have a plan to ensure ASI was aligned, meaning it did no harm. Predictions for when ASI might be reached vary from several years to more than a decade. Evan Hubinger, alignment science lead at Anthropic, posted the comment after Jacob Coxon, a 28-year-old researcher at the San Francisco company and previously at OpenAI, resigned, claiming “neither company was acting responsibly”. He said they were “gambling with our lives”. Coxon said the risks at Anthropic were well understood but they were “locked in a race to get there first”. In a glimmer of hope, he added that he was optimistic about the potential for coordination between US labs on pacing their progress in the race. Anthropic has been approached for comment on the issue. OpenAI pointed to a statement from its chief scientist, Jakub Pachocki, who said last week: “International coordination on future AI development needs to become a top priority for governments around the world.” The push for wider coordination to control ASI was at the heart of events at Westminster this week. According to the Financial Times, government officials voiced concern that Anthropic had declined to submit its latest model – Mythos 5.1 – to the UK’s AI Security Institute for pre-release testing. Only a few US organisations have had access to Mythos 5.1, the Cabinet Office confirmed. A spokesperson added: “The AI Security Institute continues to collaborate closely with industry partners, including Anthropic.” The Labour MP Darren Jones has written to the prime minister, Andy Burnham, and the heads of the UN and the OECD calling for a “multinational treaty for the regulated and safe development of superintelligence – not a ban on innovation or scientific endeavour but a safety-first approach to the rapid development of this technology”. Citing Coxon’s resignation, Jones added: “The debate ranges from the end of humanity to claims of ‘marketing hype’. Either way, governments must now step in.” On the other side of the Atlantic, Bernie Sanders ratcheted up his AI safety campaign this week by again calling on Congress to regulate the technology. He pointed to polling suggesting that 81% of Americans believed their politicians should take action. The independent senator for Vermont said: “We can’t allow a handful of greedy people to play God and determine the future of humanity – our economy, environment, democracy, privacy and more – without public input.” ControlAI is funded by Jaan Tallinn, the multi-billionaire founder of Skype who calls himself an “anti-extinctionist”. He has dedicated part of his fortune to campaigning for AI safety and says some senior AI executives would be happy for humanity to be wiped out. Despite being an early investor in Anthropic and Google DeepMind, two of the leading AI labs, Tallinn estimates that 10-15% of AI employees believe the technology will be a worthy successor to humanity. He said in an interview earlier this summer: “A fairly known AI researcher said to me ‘Jaan, don’t worry about this. Humans are a disposable species’. From what I understand he was fine with becoming extinct.” Tallinn’s lobby group ran the session for MPs and peers at Westminster on Monday and urged them to back measures to curb the most powerful AI models. On every chair was a copy of the book, If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies: The Case Against Superintelligent AI. The politicians heard from Russell, who made the Chornobyl warning and said: “The other possibility is a much larger catastrophe, in which humanity loses control irreversibly. But we have no say over whether we continue to exist.” Browne said that when he was defence secretary he thought nuclear war was the most likely threat facing humanity. Now he believed “a superintelligent AI poses a threat on the same, possibly, a greater scale”. Other contributors were more cautious. Dr Andrew Rogoyski, of the Surrey Institute for People-Centred AI, said: “In reality, these systems are nowhere near as versatile as humans, let alone humans acting collectively. I suspect we’re heading towards ‘the great disappointment’ where advanced AI turns out to be too expensive and not useful enough to continue in its current form.” David Barber, director of Sofair, a state-backed AI research lab combining academics from Oxford, Cambridge, Edinburgh and UCL, said he was worried about people “throwing the baby out with the bathwater”. “AI is not going to go away,” he said. “It’s incredibly useful, whether or not you allow it in a fully unconstrained way to access the internet and various systems that’s potentially problematic. We may need to learn how to better control these things. There are vulnerabilities in the software frameworks that need to be patched. But that’s doable. “What we need as a country is to get to grips with the duality that is both an incredibly important and useful technology, and at the same time, it’s something that needs to be carefully thought about and carefully controlled.” Sandra Wachter, a professor at the Oxford Internet Institute, said she did not believe in “Terminator scenarios” but that AI posed real threats including its environmental impact, spreading of misinformation and replacing jobs. “These problems are real and urgent and need addressing now,” she said. “Terminator scenarios are a big distraction from real issues.” Gary Marcus, an AI industry commentator and academic, said: “There is a difference between superintelligence that is aligned (if such a thing is possible) and superintelligence that is not. “It is at least conceivable that the former might be net positive. So far we have neither, but a superabundance of hype combined with a striking lack of prudence on OpenAI’s part has gotten us where we are, with intense mistrust all around.”

title: Merz accuses AfD of ‘ethnic cleansing’ policy and cancels call with Trump
summary: German chancellor attacks Alternative für Deutschland after far-right party’s win in Saxony-Anhalt election
text: Germany’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz, has accused the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) of seeking “ethnic cleansing” with its “remigration” drive, after the nativist party’s seismic weekend victory in a state election. In his first public confrontation with the AfD since Sunday’s shock outcome in Saxony-Anhalt, Merz said at a raucous parliamentary debate that the far-right party would take an axe to one of the pillars of the German economy with a racist campaign of mass deportations. “The term ‘remigration’ is nothing but a synonym for ethnic cleansing based on origin and skin colour,” he said on Wednesday to applause from the other parties in the Bundestag lower house. In a fiery speech addressed to the AfD parliamentary group, which repeatedly interrupted him with loud taunts and heckling, Merz said millions of working immigrants were crucial to German society. “If those working in Germany have to leave the country again because you are championing ‘remigration’,” Merz said, “then the skilled trades in Germany will no longer be able to function: not a single care home will remain open, not a single hospital in Germany will remain operational, and not a single restaurant in Germany will be able to stay in business.” He said the AfD’s rhetoric, which propelled it to the strongest showing for a far-right party in a German state since the Nazi period, “is precisely what is dividing our society so deeply”. The AfD has repeatedly called for large-scale expulsions of irregular migrants, a policy that would face stiff challenges under German law. In the election, the party rode an international wave of populism, nationalism and discontent with mainstream parties, underscored overnight by congratulations from Donald Trump. In a post on his Truth Social platform, the US president hailed the AfD’s “really big night” in Saxony-Anhalt. “They finally got tired of the absolutely horrible Immigration rules and regulations which have hurt Germany so badly,” Trump wrote. Merz responded by cancelling a planned phone call with Trump on Wednesday. A spokesperson for the chancellor declined to explain but noted that Merz had always objected “in general terms” to “interfering in or commenting on the domestic political situation, particularly regarding elections”. Support for Merz, a conservative Christian Democrat, has plummeted in the 16 months since he took office at the helm of a coalition with the centre-left Social Democrats, amid disappointment over slow progress on economic growth and the cost of living. He has adopted a hard line on border policy in a faltering effort to win back AfD supporters, and acknowledged Germany still had “problems in the area of migration”. “We still have many people in Germany who should not have permanent residency. This is consensus in the [ruling] coalition, that we need to deport more people,” he said on Wednesday. “But we make a careful distinction between those who work in Germany, who contribute to our prosperity, and who are welcome here, and those who do not have permanent residency in Germany and who must leave our country. Unlike you [the AfD], we take great care to make this distinction.” The AfD won nearly 44% of the vote in Saxony-Anhalt but fell three seats short of an absolute majority. Its chief candidate, Ulrich Siegmund, is seeking potential supporters among the other parties to elect him as state premier. Merz, who has acknowledged his unpopularity played a role in the halving of support for his party in the state, tried to put a brave face on the rout. “Fifty-six percent of voters in Saxony-Anhalt didn’t vote for you,” he told the AfD. He accused Siegmund, whose party is classed as rightwing extremist by domestic intelligence, of “electoral fraud” by already breaking a campaign promise not to seek to govern the state if he failed to win an absolute majority. “And you won’t manage that in Germany either [at the federal level],” Merz told the AfD co-leader Alice Weidel. “Nowhere in Germany will you get a majority. You are and remain a destructive force.” Merz also attacked the AfD for its opposition to military assistance for Ukraine, and accused it of making common cause with Russia, which Berlin has alleged is mounting a sabotage and disinformation campaign on its soil. He said that despite “clear evidence” a failed drone bomb attack at Leipzig airport last month “had been planned in Russia for months and was specifically directed against Germany”, the AfD had remained silent on it. Earlier, Weidel had savoured her party’s resounding election victory from the podium, saying the CDU had been “pulverised” and calling it a referendum on Merz’s leadership. Attacking the government’s migration policy and blaming it for crime and other security problems, Weidel said: “Your time is up. The public want a change in policy, and they will get it,” reiterating her party’s aim to form a federal government in the foreseeable future. Polls show Merz’s fractious coalition would not have a majority in a general election, though the next national vote is not due until 2029. The AfD is polling in first place at 28% to 29%, with the wind at its back before another two state polls this month, in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.

title: Hawaii’s western islands see significant damage as Hurricane Lowell passes by
summary: Storm didn’t make direct hit but fierce winds downed trees and caused widespread power outages on Kauai
text: Damaging winds and heavy rains from Hurricane Lowell caused significant damage on Hawaii’s western islands, knocking out power to thousands, ripping up stretches of road and drenching homes and stores with mud. Fierce winds downed trees and caused widespread power outages on the island of Kauai, home to 73,000 residents. The Kauai Island Utility Cooperative reported that nearly all of its roughly 35,000 members were without power on Tuesday. About 30,500 customers remained affected by outages as of Wednesday afternoon. Hurricane Lowell did not make a direct hit, but passed west of the islands in the overnight hours on Tuesday. Still, massive waves crashed on the coast, pushing piles of sand and lava rocks on land. Fierce winds knocked over trees and downed power lines. Worst hit were the islands of Kauai and the tiny island of Ni’ihau, which has fewer than 100 permanent residents. Lowell, which is expected to gradually weaken as it moves further north-west, posed no land hazards on Wednesday, according to the National Weather Service. Local authorities, however, continue to assess the extensive damage across Kauai. Traffic lights are non-functioning throughout the island, Kauai county officials also said in a Wednesday update. Some areas on the northern and eastern shore also experienced water service outages, according to the county’s water department. Authorities were still assessing the destruction, and asked residents to move around with vigilance. Elton Ushio, the Kauai emergency management agency chief, said on Tuesday that the county was tracking 198 active hazard reports. Since then, however, officials have made public few details about the extent of the damage, reported the local news outlet Honolulu Civil Beat. In the Port Allen small boat harbor, several vessels sank and piers were destroyed. Storm surge came into Hanapēpē Stadium, officials said. Kauai’s North Shore and Westside highways were impassable due to flooding and debris on Tuesday, the outlet reported. The Hoone roadway in Poipu was also blocked on Wednesday. Local authorities have urged the island’s residents to limit non-essential travel as they work to clear the debris. While Kauai and Ni’ihau bore the brunt of the storm, Oahu, the chain’s most populous island, was battered by rain and high surf. Road crews were clearing sand and rocks from a major route along the island’s western edge after flood waters topped a coastal highway, north of Honolulu. One man died on Oahu on Monday evening when a tree hit his tent, the Hawaii governor, Josh Green, said. Lowell is one of several storms that have hit the islands in recent months. In August, Tropical Storm Lala brushed past the islands and stirred up landslides, washing away about 100 homes and causing widespread power outages. The storms come as a powerful El Niño has formed in the central equatorial Pacific Ocean. Temperatures are so high that the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (Noaa) predicts a “historic event that would exceed the strength of previous El Niño events dating back to 1950”. El Niño, a natural climate pattern where sea surface temperatures in the central and eastern Pacific Ocean become unusually warm, tends to promote hurricane activity in the Pacific while suppressing it in the Atlantic. The human-caused climate crisis can amplify El Niño’s effects because a warmer ocean and atmosphere increase the availability of energy and moisture for extreme weather events, such as heatwaves and heavy rainfall.

title: Noel Clarke charged with six sexual offences including assault and voyeurism
summary: CPS says charges relate to alleged sexual misconduct by the actor towards five women between 2007 and 2016
text: The actor and film-maker Noel Clarke has been ⁠charged with six sexual offences, including two counts of sexual assault, after allegations made by five women. The charges against the former Doctor Who actor also include three counts of voyeurism and one count of exposure. Announcing the charges, the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) said the alleged offences took place between 2007 and 2016, and involved allegations made by five women. Clarke is due to appear at Westminster magistrates court on 21 October. The charges were brought after an investigation that began in September 2025. Det Supt Mike Cagney said: “The women connected to these charges continue to receive support from specially trained officers. We urge anyone who has been a victim of sexual assault to contact police. The information you provide will be dealt with in the utmost sensitivity and we have trained investigators on hand to support you.” Bethan David, the deputy chief crown prosecutor for London, said: “The CPS has decided to prosecute Noel Clarke with two counts of sexual assault, three counts of voyeurism and one count of exposure. This follows allegations made by five women in connection to sexual misconduct that took place between 2007 and 2016. “Our prosecutors have worked to establish that there is sufficient evidence to bring this case to court and that it is in the public interest to do so. We have worked closely with the Metropolitan police as they have carried out their investigation into the allegations.” David reminded the public that legal proceedings were active and Clarke had the right to a fair trial. She said: “It is vital that there should be no reporting, commentary or sharing of information online which could in any way prejudice these proceedings.” Clarke, 50, is known for his role in Doctor Who and for writing and starring in Kidulthood, which explored bullying, drug abuse and extreme violence among young ⁠people in London.

title: Polanski calls for report on ecosystem collapse to be published in full
summary: Green leader says ministers must stop ‘hiding the truth’ about threat to UK security from climate and nature crisis
text: Zack Polanski has challenged Andy Burnham’s government to publish an unredacted version of an explosive report by the UK’s spy chiefs that found the collapse of overseas ecosystems would have catastrophic consequences for the UK’s national security. The Green party leader in England said the prime minister should come clean about the scale and impact of the climate and nature crisis and called on the government to publish in full the report that warns the UK faces devastating security consequences. Speaking at the Wild Summit event in Bristol on Wednesday, Polanski asked the prime minister: “Will you tell the truth – and release the full unredacted report from the joint intelligence chiefs? Or will you keep hiding the truth from the public?” The Guardian revealed last year that the report paints a devastating picture of severe food shortages, price rises, migration, political destabilisation and possible war, resulting from the collapse of ecosystems, fuelled by the human-induced climate crisis and over-exploitation. A redacted 14-page version, including some of the report’s findings, was published in January but the government has repeatedly refused to publish the full version, despite repeated freedom of information requests from journalists and calls from MPs. Polanski, who is expected to be the Green party candidate in the upcoming byelection in Holborn and St Pancras, argued that the extreme weather experienced by much of the UK this summer should be a wake-up call for ministers. “It was a bleak preview of what is to come if we continue to allow the greed of corporations to come above the survival of our natural world – and all that relies on it. This must mark a turning point. Where we say: no more loss, no more quieting of birdsong, no more steady trickling of sewage and poison into our waters.” The report by the joint intelligence committee and other government departments, revealed by the Guardian last October, shows that the UK will face catastrophic consequences from the collapse of key ecosystems in other countries. These include the Amazon rainforest, which scientists fear is reaching a “tipping point” triggered by deforestation and rising temperatures, which would turn the ecosystem from a huge absorber of carbon dioxide into a net source of carbon. Food shortages would be almost certain to result from the decline of ecosystems overseas, the report found, as would a big increase in global migration, with the potential to fuel unrest. Among the most alarming findings was that armed conflict, which includes nuclear war, was also a potential consequence. The report was due to be published at an event last October, attended by King Charles, in the Natural History Museum. However, at the last minute the publication was pulled, at the behest of Downing Street. In an interview with the Guardian after his speech, Polanski said the Green party would introduce a nature, biodiversity and national security bill to make climate adaptation “fundamental to everything we do”. The party would also seek to appoint a climate resilience minister whose principal job would be to address problems such as extreme heat, surface-water flooding and wildfires. Polanski reiterated a commitment to introduce a basic income for farmers to “ensure those producing the food we rely on are paid properly for their work”. “We know farmers have had wrecked harvest after wrecked harvest. Their crops are struggling and on top of that you’ve got supermarkets where the bosses are taking record bonuses while fleecing farmers,” he said. Simultaneously on Wednesday, in a letter to Burnham, a coalition of green groups has warned that national security, public health and economic growth are at risk without urgent action to restore nature. The UK has a legally binding target to restore 30% of nature by 2030. This target, which was set by more than 100 countries during Cop15 negotiations in Montreal in 2022, is considered the minimum restoration needed to halt and reverse the global decline in nature. The UK is currently on track to miss this target, with a recent plan to reach this target in England condemned as “pathetic” and “completely insufficient”. “Your government has diplomatic and legal obligations to halt the decline of wildlife and protect 30% of the land and sea for nature by 2030 … On the current path the UK will miss those targets,” the groups warn the prime minister in the letter. The letter also highlights that two-thirds of the UK’s protected nature sites need “urgent repair”, with many of these sites neglected or damaged by intensive industry, pollution and the climate crisis. The groups warn this leaves communities and businesses exposed to flooding, drought, wildfires and pollution. This warning comes as new research finds that about £2bn a year needs to be invested in protected nature sites – up from roughly £1.1bn today – to restore them by 2042. The groups are calling for more funding, stronger laws and decisive enforcement to “stop the abuses that are hollowing out our natural world”. A Labour spokesperson said: “This is the first government to take seriously the risks that climate change and nature loss pose to our food security, economic resilience, and national security. “We’re taking decisive action, including launching the UK’s first taskforce on the national security and resilience risks of climate change and nature loss, investing in nature recovery at home and abroad, and delivering the largest nature-friendly farming budget in history.”

title: Streeting praises new series The Wargame for highlighting Britain’s defence needs
summary: Show depicting attack on UK and featuring Michael Gove and Nicola Sturgeon will ‘make people think’, minister says
text: A docudrama depicting a Russian attack on a Britain led by an unlikely pairing of Michael Gove and Nicola Sturgeon has been praised by the defence secretary, Wes Streeting, for writing “my spending review submission”. The Wargame, due to be broadcast on Sky this month, features a string of former politicians advised by ex-securocrats, grappling with an unusually powerful Moscow, while highlighting limitations in the British military. It features Gove, who was a Conservative minister for more than a decade, as prime minister – a job he unsuccessfully ran for in 2016 – and Sturgeon, the former first minister and leader of the Scottish National party, as his deputy, in a mock Downing Street Cobra emergency situation room. Labour figures involved in the production include the former Scotland secretary Jim Murphy as foreign secretary, as well as Harriet Harman and the peer Ayesha Hazarika, who plays the role of director of communications in the embattled team. After a preview screening at the National Gallery in central London, with many of the former politicians present, Streeting quipped: “On behalf of the association of UK defence secretaries, thank you for my spending review submission.” Though the war depicted was of “a low likelihood, albeit high impact”, Streeting said he anticipated the show would stimulate public debate on defence spending, currently planned to rise by about £30bn by 2035. Streeting said The Wargame would “play a role in making people think about where they would put defence in the order of priorities as voters”, though he added that wildfires, floods and other natural disasters should also prompt the public to think how they would be able to cope in a crisis. The scale of the cash increase, pushed for by the US president Donald Trump but signed up to by the UK and other Nato allies, is such that it would require taxes or borrowing to be raised, or substantial cuts from other government spending after the next election. The five-part programme is a spin-off from a Sky News podcast presented by the journalist Deborah Haynes, who has helped to develop the television show. “We want our country to understand better what the threat is, what credible defence is”, she said. Producers said a series of incidents involving Russian sabotage in the UK and Europe had made the programme more relevant. During filming in mid-June, a Russian frigate south of the Isle of Wight unexpectedly fired warning shots near an approaching pleasure yacht in the Channel, terrifying a British couple onboard. Gove – who was a minister between 2010 and 2024 – said it had come as a surprise to him how limited Britain’s missile defence capability was during filming, an issue highlighted in the show. “For anyone watching, they will think: ‘WTF. How did we get into that situation?’” It was, he said, “quite sobering” for somebody who had been in government for as long as he had, though he had not been a defence minister. A succession of cuts to defence spending made by Conservative and Labour governments from the end of the cold war until the early part of the decade have reduced defence investment and left the navy struggling to deploy warships and submarines. Since then, there has been a growing consensus across the centre of British politics for increased defence spending. Though Russia remains fully engaged in its war in Ukraine, Moscow retains the ability to conduct cyber, sabotage and disinformation operations in the UK. Sturgeon said the programme could help dispel “the optimism bias that this won’t happen”. Gove said: “I never thought I would say this, but I agree 100% with Nicola”. The Wargame airs on Sky One from 21 September

title: US airports to let some people without tickets pass through security
summary: TSA PreCheck program members will be eligible to send off friends and family at gate in change to post-9/11 rule
text: Some people without plane tickets will be allowed to pass through security at US airports and go to gates to see off family or friends, rolling back a rule that was introduced after the 9/11 terrorist attacks. Certain people who are part of the TSA PreCheck program but who do not have tickets to fly will be able to go through security to airport gates, the Transportation Security Administration (TSA) said. This will revive a previous tradition where friends and family of those flying were able to go to the gate with them to bid farewell. The practice was largely banned following the 2001 terror attacks, which are nearing their 25th anniversary on Friday. “As an exclusive benefit for our most trusted travelers, this new program makes it easier to return to the gate for welcomes and send-offs, meet friends during a layover, and enjoy dining and shopping along the way, bringing back the moments that once defined air travel,” the TSA said on its website. The program, called Gateside by TSA PreCheck, is free, but interested members must apply online one to three days before their planned visits and receive approval before going to the airport. If approved, they can enter security using a TSA PreCheck lane with an acceptable form of identification. The passes are valid for one calendar day, but re-entries are allowed on that day. The TSA says members of other trusted-traveler programs who have a Known Traveler Number also can apply for access to the gates. The program is initially available at 13 airports, including Los Angeles international airport, Dallas-Fort Worth international airport, Harry Reid international airport in Las Vegas and Salt Lake City international airport, according to the TSA. The agency says it plans to expand the program to more airports in the coming months. The TSA was created in the wake of 9/11 as part of a series of changes aimed at tightening aviation security. Passengers underwent more rigorous security checks, with knives and box cutters banned from carry-on bags. Aircraft cockpit doors were reinforced and air marshals were introduced to flights.

title: Liz Truss relaunches podcast on channel of broadcaster famous for ‘grow concrete’ exchange
summary: Podcast is now on YouTube site of Mike Graham, fired from TalkTV after racist post appeared on his Facebook page
text: When Liz Truss launched her podcast last year, she declared it would bring a “counter-revolution” to take on the “deep state”, which, she said, “tried to destroy” her. The revolution, however, has not yet arrived. Truss, whose stint as UK prime minister abruptly ended after her disastrous mini-budget crashed the economy, has so far failed to find a wide audience in her media career. Her podcast episodes hosted on YouTube often receive fewer than 4,000 views each, which is understood to be below the amount generally needed to monetise a video. Now, Truss is relaunching her podcast and joining the former TalkTV host Mike Graham’s YouTube channel, UKLive, where she will be livestreaming twice a week. Graham was dismissed from Rupert Murdoch’s digital channel after the company said he had failed to cooperate with an investigation into a racist post that appeared on his Facebook account. The post inquired: “Why are we surrounded by non-white people?” Graham claimed he did not post it and that he was hacked. The presenter, whose new channel calls itself “the home of common sense”, came to public prominence after claiming on air that it was possible to grow concrete. Graham was questioning the eco-activist and carpenter Cameron Ford on whether timber was a sustainable building material. Cameron said timber was “regenerative”, adding: “You can grow trees. You can’t grow concrete.” Graham replied: “Yeah, you can.” Graham’s channel does generate income, securing enough views to qualify for YouTube’s scheme that shares ad revenue with creators. While UKLive only averages about 24,000 views a video, its prolific output of 1,700 posts in the last year means it has secured 41m views in that time, according to the Socialpruf analytics site. That is enough to generate thousands of pounds a month in ad revenue. The rise of YouTube has created a home for those shunned by mainstream outlets, but its growth has also in effect created a whole world of broadcasting outside of the regulated world of mainstream TV. “Since Ofcom took over broadcast regulation in 2003, the way we watch television has changed beyond recognition,” said Chris Banatvala, who was Ofcom’s founding director of standards. “We now have a huge range of content that looks and feels like television – and is often available on the same television set – but isn’t subject to the same standards. “Viewers may have no idea whether what they are watching is regulated by Ofcom or not – and these regulatory grey areas are only likely to grow. “It is a good thing that the public has access to such a wide range of views and content. But the law has not kept pace, parliament has yet to confront the implications of this increasingly blurred distinction, and the platforms themselves have not always proved able to prevent serious harm.” Truss will be joining a host of other presenters including the former actor Laurence Fox, who was suspended from GB News after making sexualised comments on air about a female journalist. Also on the roster is Mark Littlewood, a former director of the Institute of Economic Affairs thinktank, which praised many of Truss’s economic policies, and the pro-Reform commentator Ellie Hodges. Truss may hope to benefit from Graham’s larger following; his channel has 179,000 subscribers compared with her 32,300. Recent podcasts from Truss include one in which the commentator June Slater claimed “Labour is panicking as Reform surges in Makerfield byelection”. Andy Burnham won for Labour in Makerfield by a wide margin. Another is an interview with Lucy Connolly in which she complains she was “jailed for a tweet”. Connolly was sent to prison in 2024 for stirring up racial hatred against asylum seekers in a post in which she called for asylum hotels to be burned down. The former prime minister said her new show would have “exciting new guests”. Truss has been attempting to relaunch her career in recent months, including setting up a new private members’ club in Mayfair with the property tycoon Robert Tchenguiz. The club, named the Leconfield, states on its website that it is a “beacon of sophistication and refined elegance” that has “curated an exclusive sanctuary where tradition meets contemporary luxury”.

title: Death and fear stalk Haitians in Ohio city amid Trump’s anti-immigrant crackdown
summary: Springfield community mourns one of its own after Pierre Damas Bel, who was forced to wear electronic ankle bracelet by ICE, walked into traffic and was killed by truck
text: For 20-year-old Pierre Damas Bel, the humiliation of starting college last month with an electronic ankle bracelet – attached by ICE agents this summer – was deeply traumatic. “I’m walking through the streets of the United States with a GPS monitor on my leg, carrying a feeling of shame and humiliation that I never imagined I would experience,” he wrote on Instagram in July. Until recently, the world for Bel, who was born in Haiti, was opening up. He was given the coveted number 11 shirt for the Springfield Wildcats high school soccer team, scoring two goals and providing three assists during last fall’s season – one of a growing number of skilled Haitian student athletes putting the city’s sports teams on the map. In high school, he had received an award from the US army’s junior reserve officer training corps. But on Monday morning, police reports say Bel pulled his 20-year-old Toyota off the side of Interstate-70 outside Springfield and started walking into traffic. He was killed by a passing semi-truck. Police are investigating his death as a possible suicide. His father, Pierres Ronal Bel, said in a written statement: “After my son was outfitted with an ankle monitor, he felt like he was treated like an animal.” He went on to describe how wearing an ankle bracelet interfered with his son’s ability to play soccer and had led to bullying and taunts of being “a criminal”. Bel’s experiences of life under the Trump administration’s anti-immigrant crackdown illustrates the wider crisis Haitians now face in Springfield, Ohio, a struggling, Rust belt city of 60,000 people. In June, the supreme court revoked temporary protected status (TPS) for 350,000 Haitians, taking away their ability to legally reside in the US. In Springfield, ICE officers have now become a common presence along the city’s main streets and in parking lots where Haitian-owned businesses operate. Haitian churches have seen a huge attendance fall-off and at least 30 Haitians, including two church pastors, have been detained by ICE in recent weeks. For the most part, agents are stopping Haitians driving on the streets or taking them directly from their homes. “ICE is getting increasingly aggressive. On Saturday, they boxed in a car around the corner from my house and detained the man driving it,” says Marjory Wentworth, a community advocate for Haitian immigrants in Springfield. She later confirmed that the man was a Haitian national. “It’s frightening.” In a single day last month, 57 people, including children, were deported from the US to Haiti, according to the Miami Herald. What awaits them there, say those already deported by the Trump administration, is a hellscape. William came to the US in 2023 after crossing the border with Mexico with an I-94 entry document and headed straight to Springfield. He asked the Guardian not to use his real name as he was attempting to mount a legal case to be returned to the US. In Ohio, William worked two jobs – at an Amazon warehouse and at a metal fabrication company an hour’s drive from his home. Last March, he married a woman from Springfield, whom he met at a local church. At his regular ICE check-in last May, however, William was detained by agents, shackled, put on a plane and flown back to Port Haïtien in northern Haiti alongside more than 160 other Haitian men. “They wouldn’t tell us where they were taking us. All we had to eat was bread and water,” he recalls of his detention and deportation flight. “I kept telling them: ‘Please don’t send us back to Haiti; anywhere else.’” In Haiti, the security situation has worsened in recent weeks. Forty-seven people were massacred and 50 more were kidnapped from a farming community outside Haiti’s capital, Port-au-Prince, on 23 August in the worst single violent incident in several years. Once back in Haiti, William immediately realized he would be targeted by the growing presence of gang members hunting returnees from the US. On its social media channels ICE has prominently displayed promises of returnees receiving $2,600 in return for self-deporting. In February three people were killed in Ouanaminthe, a border town of 115,000 people in Haiti’s north-east and William’s home town, by a machete-wielding man, before the attacker was lynched. “It was so bad that I had to leave again. My mother pleaded with me to get out of Haiti,” said William, who now lives in an unadorned room in the neighboring Dominican Republic. Within weeks, William fled Haiti for a second time, despite widespread persecution and the deportation of more than 100,000 Haitians from the Dominican Republic. “When I spoke to him over the phone from his mother’s house, I could hear gunfire in the background,” said his wife. The couple’s troubles haven’t stopped at the Trump administration’s deportation policies. They have spent about $11,000 on immigration lawyers whom they hoped would help William. “We paid the attorney – one that charged us $8,000 – they were supposed to meet us at the ICE check-in on 21 May. At 11pm the night before, we got a call saying that [the attorney’s] flight was delayed and she would send another attorney on her behalf,” she said. “This person was from a law office we never heard of, she knew nothing about our case; she was just a stand-in. When we got there, she did nothing. She didn’t tell them that we were married and had an I-130 immigration application.” Being married to a US citizen does not prevent a non-US spouse from being deported. In Springfield, the Haitian-owned Keket restaurant, where just months ago people crowded together to watch their national team play in the World Cup for the first time in 52 years, is now shuttered “due to ICE activities”, says a former worker who asked not to be identified. The large strip malls around Springfield that once bustled with Haitians picking up food from cafes and groceries are once again quiet. Pastor Gilbert Joubert Adrien and a second Haitian man were detained at a gas station on 20 August. Adrien’s wife and children – aged seven and 15 – are now without a breadwinner. He was being held at the Butler county jail, an hour’s drive south of Springfield, that has been criticized for receiving large amounts of federal dollars in return for holding hundreds of detainees for ICE. A second, unnamed pastor who was detained on 25 August and has been transferred to a facility out-of-state, according to local activists. Neither man had criminal records at the time of their arrests. According to his Instagram account, Bel was in the first month of studying physiology and neuroscience at Wright State University, a suburban college 20 minutes from Springfield. Before his death, he worked part-time at a Texas Roadhouse restaurant and had hoped to go on to medical school. In the UK and Ireland, Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123.
