title: Texas was once a hotbed of wild west socialism – could it make a comeback?
summary: Long before it became a rightwing political bastion the state was defined by cowboys on strike and farmers organizing
text: Texas is well-known as a Republican-red state, but it has another, largely forgotten red history of the radical shade. Long before it became a rightwing political stronghold, it was defined by cowboys on strike, farmers organizing against the railroads, and one of the largest Socialist party chapters in the country. “In Texas, the history of our radical politics and labor and working class tradition has been purposefully hidden,” author David Griscom said. “It’s important to go back and correct the record and see that there was an effort to try to make Texans forget the radical roots in the kind of more recent past.” That’s the project of Griscom’s first book, The Myth of Red Texas. The cowboys idolized by conservatives, for instance, fought for public land access during the fence-cutting wars of the 1880s. At that time, wealthy northerners and Europeans were entering the state. Their arrival coincided with the invention of barbed wire, which cowboys called “the devil’s rope”, explains Griscom, who co-hosts two leftist podcasts, Left Reckoning and The Jacobin Show, and is based in Austin. “People almost immediately saw barbed wire for what it was, which was a tool of dispossession,” said Griscom. “It almost immediately got used across the state by the wealthy big landowners who wanted to enclose more and more land and access to water in streams, but that ran up against an older tradition of the west as an open range.” As fences blocked access to grazing land, water and roads, groups of cowboys began cutting them down, organizing themselves into clandestine vigilante organizations with names like the Blue Devils and the Knights of the Knippers. Ordinary Texans largely supported the cowboy fence-cutters, but the backlash was swift. Rich ranchers complained to government officials, who sent the Texas rangers – a state-sanctioned police force – to crack down on them. In 1884, the governor called a special session of the state legislature, which declared fence-cutting to be felony punishable by up to five years in prison, while making it a misdemeanor to fence land that did not belong to you. “It really shows the unequal way that the state and the legal system were developing in Texas and what that was a response to,” said Griscom. “But notably, while these large landowners were trying to enclose more and more land as private property, they were still using the public grasslands to raise their cattle. They were very happy to use the public lands while trying to restrict people’s access.” During the same period, cowboys also fought for labor rights as ranchers began hiring them to work on their newly privatized land – and paying them low wages. A group of those cowboys banded together and went on strike in 1883. Many Texas history books, Griscom said, assert that the new labor activists spent all their time getting drunk at the saloon, spending their entire strike fund. But according to the US commissioner of labor’s official report on the strike, the author said, the cowboys actually won their demands. Despite crackdowns from the government and wealthy capitalists, Texans kept organizing for their rights, including by forming the third-largest socialist party in the nation by the early 1900s. “Whenever you see people advocating for labor politics or democratic socialist politics in Texas, you’ll often be told, that’s good for California or New York, said Griscom. “But the fact of the matter is that Texas has maybe an even stronger socialist and democratic socialist tradition than some of these other places that we see as the hotbeds for these kind of politics.” That history, said Griscom, cuts against the pervasive idea that Texas will only become more progressive as Californians and New Yorkers move in. Some of these same narratives have resurfaced during this year’s midterm election season. “But most of the data that we have right now actually shows those people are more Republican than the average Texan,” he said. “Just think about some of the famous examples, Joe Rogan and Elon Musk.” As the book notes, polls show that in the 2018 Senate race, more native born Texans voted for Democratic candidate Beto O’Rourke than incumbent Senator Ted Cruz, who won the election. Amid the midterms, there have been some efforts to reclaim the state’s left-populist history, Griscom said. James Talarico, the Democratic Texas state representative and former public school teacher who is now also the Democratic nominee for US Senate, has been telling voters that billionaires are waging “class warfare” against ordinary people – something Griscom has praised. Griscom has, however criticized some of Talarico’s recent moves to cozy up to billionaires like business magnate Mark Cuban, with whom he teamed up on recent policy proposals. “He needs to avoid the siren song of moving to the right economically,” Griscom said. “The way to build that mass appeal, and win a populist coalition, is not by tacking right or pushing technocratic policies no matter what the consultants tell you. Nor is sorting billionaires into good or bad billionaires. The history of populism, and the success of Talarico in the primary is clear, if you want to win Texas you need to mobilize working people with a clear vision of the way politics can improve their life.” The author believes a true return to left populism in Texas will require the buildout of organizations like the Democratic Socialists of America. Though they’ll never have the capital of wealthy far-right political financiers in the state like oilman Tim Dunn, he hopes these organizations can make up for their lack of money with “people power”. “If you look at the history of the Texas populous movement, that was their great advantage,” said Griscom. “They had a rootedness in working-class communities in the state of Texas. That’s what it takes.” In February, he noted, union leader and Democrat Taylor Rehmet won a special election for state senate, flipping a reliably Republican district which Donald Trump won by 17 points in 2024. “It was a real moment of reckoning for the Republican party which got them running scared,” he said.

title: ‘They’re ready to come home’: the movement to bring young voters back to Democrats
summary: After young people shifted right for Trump, Democratic-aligned groups across the US are eager to capture gen Z voters before November’s midterm elections
text: On the first day of the fall semester at California State University, Northridge, student organizers holding “Hot People Vote” signs wheeled a bright pink wagon outside the student union. They offered “no strings attached” donuts, heart-shaped sunglasses and voting information for the November general election. Even though it was 105F outside, dozens of people stopped by to chat with the Donuts + Democracy volunteers and register to vote. One student told organizer Dzian Tran that she didn’t plan to vote because she was disillusioned with politics. Tran chatted with her about how civic engagement is important to democracy and how some elections are won by a margin of only 400 votes. As she thanked Tran, the student held her phone up to a QR code to get more information about voting. About 50 million young people are eligible to vote in 2026, but nearly half are either not registered or civically engaged, according to US Census Bureau data. After Donald Trump made significant gains among young men in the 2024 election, Democratic-aligned groups have been eager to capture gen Z voters who may be disaffected by politics. From bringing politicians, celebrities and donuts to campuses to hosting tailgating events, happy hours and street parties, a crop of youth-led and youth-focused organizations are employing fresh tactics to meet gen Z where they are – and luring them in with fun. Heather Haggarty, who runs Donuts + Democracy with her daughter, said traditional voter engagement strategies such as postcards, clipboards and phone-banking fail with young voters. When her two gen Z children suggested taking donuts to a university voter registration event a few years ago, she ended up speaking to more than 100 kids in 90 minutes. Haggarty said the deep-fried snack is akin to “breaking bread”, making zoomers more willing to talk and connect. “Young kids aren’t apathetic,” she said. “They care. But voting isn’t easy and traditional voter engagement can feel transactional and alienating.” ‘From a quinceañera in Texas to a block party in Philly’ While Republicans invested more than $1bn to target young voters from 2020 to 2025, Democrats haven’t historically backed campus organizing and young organizers, said Haggarty. It’s often left up to young people to inspire and educate their peers. Since 2021, the Keep Arizona Blue Student Coalition, or Keep AZ Blue, has registered about 15,000 students at high schools and colleges. “We engage people online where young people are most, on campus and at community events and coffee shops and other hangout spots,” said Jacob Marson, the group’s 22-year-old executive director. “As football starts up, we’re going to bring elected officials to tailgates along with energy drinks and donuts – these are conversation starters.” Marson’s team has found that community colleges have been largely ignored by organizers in the past. When they show up on those campuses, whether in rural areas or Maricopa county (the fourth-most populous US county), they have “amazing conversations”, Marson said. Last year, Keep AZ Blue brought the Arizona representative Lorena Austin to Mesa Community College, and earlier this year they introduced Arizona’s attorney general, Kris Mayes, to students at Arizona State University. “I think some young voters took a chance on Trump, but it’s clear they’re ready to come home and support our Democratic candidates,” Marson said. “They’ve seen the policies of a Republican-controlled House, Senate and presidency. I am fully confident that young voters are ready to elect Democrats across the state.” Although research has shown that 43% of zoomers do not identify with a political party, they are twice as likely to move left in recent years. And while young people face the most obstacles to voting of any age group, once gen Z is registered to vote, they vote at close to the turnout rates of those over age 30. Youth-focused organizations understand that gen Z voters swing elections. The non-partisan voter organization When We All Vote, founded by Michelle Obama, hosted more than 500 Party at the Polls events throughout the US in 2024. This year, they are scaling up to 5,000 events with a goal of reaching an estimated 20 million gen Z voters. They are particularly focusing on Black and brown communities in the aftermath of the gutting of the Voting Rights Act and other suppression efforts. “It could be anything from a quinceañera in Texas to a block party in Philly to smaller cookouts and barbecues,” said senior adviser Kalisha Dessources Figures. “We’re meeting communities where they are with what looks like joy and celebration to them.” The organization recently brought Love Island USA winner Serena Page to the University of Houston for a conversation on college, dating and civic engagement that was attended by hundreds of students who received free giveaways such as tooth gems and custom merch. HeadCount is another organization mixing voter registration efforts with joy. This year, they have teamed up with celebrities such as Ilana Glazer, Harry Styles and Bob the Drag Queen to encourage gen Z to take action for chances to win tickets and VIP experiences at concerts, sporting events and music festivals. All of this outreach might be helping: some primaries this year have already seen increased turnout among zoomers. In El Paso’s primary, the youth turnout nearly tripled compared to 2022. In Michigan, Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed received almost 60% of the vote in key counties where college-aged voters live, and some experts believe the youth vote was likely responsible for his close primary win. California, meanwhile, has added nearly 2 million more gen Z-aged registered voters since 2022, and more than two-thirds of 18- to 29-year-olds say they are inclined to support progressive candidates in the state. Harnessing anger and frustration Some youth-led organizations are also rallying young people to get more involved in activism, organizing their peers and building political power for their generation. At the recent Voters of Tomorrow summit in Raleigh, North Carolina, hundreds of young people turned out to hear from progressive politicians such as the Tennessee representative Justin Pearson and North Carolina representative Jordan Lopez. Attenders also participated in trainings and workshops on peer-to-peer organizing and building political power online. “We’re working to make sure young people know what’s at stake, but we’re also working with candidates to make sure they are making promises that they can actually deliver on,” said Santiago Mayer, the founder and executive director of Voters of Tomorrow (VOT). “We’ve seen in New York and New Jersey and Virginia and Michigan – young people are looking for candidates who are talking about the issues they need addressed.” The gen Z-led organization has more than 11,000 members and chapters in more than 25 states. In addition to campus events, they have hosted happy hours in Iowa and a film festival in North Carolina to engage new voters. “We’re trying to host events where young people can make new friends and come back not just because they agree with the politics, but because they feel it’s a third space where people can find community and have fun,” said Mayer, who founded VOT in 2019 at age 17. While he said the left was outspent when it came to targeting young voters in 2024, he believes Democrats can win gen Z in the midterms. “Trump lied to them when he said no new wars and that prices would come down,” he said. “Young people do not like being lied to or used, and that’s what Republicans did. They immediately threw us under the bus.”

title: EU unveils ‘buy European’ public procurement rules to counter China
summary: Authorities and public bodies to be urged to buy goods and services from Europe, but without binding quotas
text: European authorities will be encouraged to buy more domestic goods and services when they spend public money under the EU latest effort to counter China’s economic might. In a further “Buy European” plan, the European Commission published proposals on Wednesday for a sweeping overhaul of EU public procurement rules. National authorities and public bodies, such as schools and hospitals, will be encouraged to buy goods and services made in Europe but, unlike earlier plans to promote domestically manufactured clean tech, there will be no binding “made in Europe” quotas. Brussels officials are concerned that many public agencies think existing EU rules oblige them to choose the cheapest bid when spending public money, which can lead to the contract going to a non-European firm. The European Commission’s lead official on industrial policy, Stéphane Séjourné, told reporters the regulation would give public sector buyers greater legal certainty and clarity about purchasing goods and services made in Europe. “Purchasers can have a more preferential approach to European bids [and] restrict or reject bids from countries which do not have a public procurement agreement or do not play by binding rules in terms of public procurement internationally,” he said. Public procurement is estimated by EU officials to amount to 15% of the bloc’s gross domestic product, about €2.6tn (£2.2tn) a year, and is seen in Brussels as an underused lever already deployed by Washington and Beijing to support their respective domestic companies. The new rules will oblige public buyers in the EU to put more emphasis on quality and metrics such as environmental sustainability and local supply chains, rather than opting for the cheapest bid. Under the proposals public agencies will be obliged to give a minimum 30% weighting to quality when they draw up conditions to award a contract, or explain why they chose to disregard this indicator. Labour-intensive contracts will have a minimum 50% weighting for quality, so purchasers must ensure decent jobs when awarding the contract, not simply the cheapest price. Séjourné hopes the proposals will encourage more democratic scrutiny over the spending of public money by local authorities. “It won’t be the European Commission’s fault if purchasers were to prefer Chinese buses to European buses because … in the [draft regulation] there is every possibility to give preference to European buses.” Brussels is concerned about inroads Beijing is making into European markets for transport and infrastructure, especially Chinese firms benefitting from state subsidies that make them cheaper than European alternatives. In April, the commission blocked a Chinese rolling-stock company from joining a consortium to build a new line on the Lisbon metro after an investigation found the firm had benefited from state subsidies that gave it an “unfair competitive edge”. Last year, Brussels opened an investigation into Chinese security company Nuctech, which has supplied European airports and ports with security scanners. EU officials suspect the company was helped by subsidies and tax breaks that gave it an unfair advantage in the European market, although the investigation has not reached final conclusions. Séjourné – a close ally of France’s president, Emmanuel Macron, who has long championed European preference – said spending public money on goods made in Europe should become “part of public discourse and accountability”. He added: “It should be very clear that it’s not because of European Union rules that a foreign product was preferred over a European one, but because it was a political choice that was made.” The draft regulation, which also aims to radically simplify rules by merging three laws into one, must be agreed by the European parliament and the EU ministers before it enters into force. It is likely to be altered during the legislative process. Séjourné is also spearheading a push for made-in-Europe rules to apply to the public purchase of renewable energy products and electric cars under the the Industrial Accelerator Act. The IAA, which also is likely to be changed by MEPs and ministers, marks a departure for Brussels, long a bastion of open markets. The plans have alarmed the British government, but EU officials said the latest draft rules on procurement would not disadvantage UK firms because existing agreements ensured both sides played by the same rules. Séjourne said the EU had agreements with the UK whereby reciprocal market access was respected. “There should not be any difficulties for the UK,” he added. Non-EU countries that have agreements with the bloc on public procurement are not expected to face barriers. An online tool will allow public purchasers to see which countries are covered by the EU’s web of free-trade agreements and other international deals that cover procurement. Membership of the World Trade Organization’s agreement on government procurement (GPA), which promotes fair competition in markets to supply state bodies, will be an important indicator. The GPA has 22 members including the EU (counted as one), the UK, the US, Canada and Japan. Mainland China is not party to the agreement.

title: UK airport disruption: what are your rights if you have been affected?
summary: Air traffic control issue affecting UK airports on Tuesday has been resolved, but disruption continues into Wednesday
text: Airports across the UK including Manchester, Birmingham and all those in London were thrown into chaos by a technical failure in the air traffic control system on Tuesday. Although the air traffic control provider Nats fixed the problem within hours, the fallout continued to cause flight delays and cancellations on Wednesday. The total number of cancellations has now passed 2,000 after hundreds more flights were axed. Here we explain what you can expect if you have been affected. Is your flight delayed or cancelled? The Civil Aviation Authority website explains how long the delay has to be before you are entitled to care and assistance from your airline. The timeframe differs by flight distance. This help should cover food and drink and the ability to make phone calls or send emails, plus accommodation and the necessary transfers if the flight is delayed until the next day. Many airlines will provide vouchers to buy food and drink, and overnight accommodation will typically take the form of a nearby hotel (unless you live nearby, in which case your airline may reimburse your costs for getting to and from home). Sometimes airline staff are unable to arrange care and assistance for all passengers, in which case you can sort yourself out and claim the cost back later. But don’t splash the cash – and keep receipts. The CAA says airlines may have guidelines on this, adding: “Airlines are unlikely to consider alcoholic drinks, luxury hotels or luxury meals to be reasonable.” Should I ask the airline for another flight or a refund? If your flight has been cancelled and is covered by UK law – that means one departing from an airport in the UK on any airline, or arriving at an airport in the UK on an EU or UK airline, or arriving at an airport in the EU on a UK airline – your airline must offer you the choice of another flight or a refund. If you select an alternative flight, it is up to you whether you fly as soon as possible or at a later date. If the delay is more than five hours you can choose not to travel and receive a refund. Rory Boland, the editor of Which? Travel, said: “If your flight is cancelled you’re entitled to choose between being rerouted on a different flight or getting a refund. Rerouting will usually be your best option, as once a refund is accepted, your airline has no ongoing responsibility towards you or any costs you may incur for accommodation, meals or transport during your delay. You’ll also avoid paying over the odds for a new ticket if prices shoot up.” He added: “Crucially, if you opt to be rerouted, your airline must get you to your destination at the earliest opportunity, even when that means booking you with a rival carrier. It’s important to stand your ground on this point, as all too often we see examples of airlines flouting the rules and forcing passengers to wait longer for a spot on their own planes.” I am due to fly imminently – should I still go to the airport? If you are due to travel, check the latest advice from your airport or tour operator, or airline apps and airport social media feeds, for the most up-to-date information. In a statement on social media on Wednesday morning, Heathrow confirmed that flights were operating but “some disruption may continue as airlines reposition aircraft and crew”. A Heathrow spokesperson said: “We advise passengers to check with their airline for the latest flight information and to only travel to Heathrow if they have a confirmed flight operating today. We know how frustrating this situation is and apologise to those affected. We have extra colleagues on hand to support across our terminals and are working closely with our local Nats team and airline partners to recover normal operations as quickly as possible.” In a similar vein, a spokesperson for Gatwick airport said: “Flights have now resumed from London Gatwick. However, we still anticipate that it will take time for our operations to fully return to normal. Passengers should continue to check with their airlines for more information regarding their flights.” Travel experts say the best way to rebook flights is via airline apps, websites or call centres rather than at the airport check-in desk. At Heathrow, for example, rebooking is not an option at check-in desks as staff prioritise that day’s operations. Will I be entitled to compensation from the airline? If your flight was cancelled or delayed as a result of Tuesday’s problem, you are unlikely to be owed compensation by the airline. This is because the technical problem affecting flights will be considered an extraordinary circumstance and out of the airline’s control. Causes of disruption classed as outside an airline’s control also include severe weather and security alerts. Coby Benson, a solicitor at the law firm Bott and Co, said: “Air traffic control restrictions are generally considered an ‘extraordinary circumstance’, meaning passengers will not usually be entitled to compensation for delays or cancellations.” He added: While airlines may not be responsible for the initial problem, they should not use it as a reason to leave passengers stranded when reasonable alternative travel options are available.” It also worth consulting the small print on your travel insurance document. Anna-Marie Duthie, a travel insurance expert at the financial ratings company Defaqto, says: “Travel insurance may cover you if you cannot claim costs back from the airline, operator or credit card, but that will all depend on whether your policy includes cover for delay, travel disruption, missed connection or abandonment.”

title: Conflicting court rulings on Missouri map threaten November’s election | First Thing
summary: The state can’t use new congressional districts under one court order – or its old ones under another. Plus, the architects in Europe turning urban spaces into areas of climate respite
text: Good morning. Clashing court rulings plunged Missouri’s congressional elections into uncertainty less than two months before the November midterms that will decide which party controls a closely divided Congress. Conservative justice Brett Kavanaugh denied the emergency request from Missouri officials to use a congressional map in November that was redrawn with Donald Trump’s support to give Republicans an edge in the midterms, but a ruling by a federal judge in Missouri temporarily prevented the state from using its old congressional maps. Why is there legal action over the maps? The Missouri supreme court has previously ruled that the new map must go before voters to approve or reject the new districts, meaning it cannot be used in time for the November election. The president and Republicans had fumed over the decision, with Trump calling it “horrible, ridiculous, and unconstitutional”. What are the significant changes to the map intended to favor Republicans? The revised map targeted the fifth congressional district, held by longtime Democratic representative Emanuel Cleaver of Kansas City. It reassigned portions of Kansas City to two neighboring districts represented by Republicans and stretched the remainder of Cleaver’s district far eastward into rural Republican areas. Israel to close British consulate in Jerusalem after UK imposes sanctions on West Bank settlements The UK government has entered a diplomatic row with Israel after it announced sweeping sanctions on trade with Israeli settlements. In the country’s starkest condemnation since the founding of the Israeli state, the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband – whose mother, Marion Kozak, was a Holocaust survivor who fled to Israel – said settler terrorists supported by Benjamin Netanyahu’s government were committing ethnic cleansing in the West Bank. Mike Huckabee, the US ambassador to Israel, claimed the ruling UK Labour party Miliband belongs to was gripped by “Jew hatred”. What has the British prime minister said? Writing in the Guardian, Andy Burnham said he would “not stand by” as horrific suffering continued, and that for too long the UK had been hesitant to act “fearful of being accused of being anti-Israel”. “The measures we are taking,” he said, “are about targeting illegal settlements and increasing the pressure on the Israeli government to change course. We are not imposing sanctions on Israel as a whole.” How has Israel reacted? Israel has ordered the closure of the British consulate in occupied East Jerusalem among retaliatory measures including entry bans on several UK lawmakers. The Israeli government added that longstanding British involvement in the training of Palestinian security forces on the West Bank would be terminated. Britain will also be excluded from the US-led Gaza coordination mission. US says Iranian tankers ‘destroyed’ as Houthis strike Saudi Arabian cities The US military on Tuesday said it had “destroyed” several Iranian tankers after Iran attempted to strike a US navy warship with ballistic missiles, as violence once again surged across the region, pushing the price of oil past $100 a barrel. Centom said the strikes came after the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) targeted a US navy warship with ballistic missiles twice over the past two days. The IRGC said it had struck a US military base in Jordan in retaliation. What have been the other developments in the region? Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis have attacked four cities in Saudi Arabia, wounding more than 70 people and setting oil installations ablaze in what appeared to be a significant expansion of the Middle East war. Saudi Arabia said it would retaliate after the overnight strikes – reportedly involving dozens of drones and missiles – that targeted several oil facilities in the country’s south. US bans Canadian dairy, alcohol and motorcycles as trade war escalates The US is banning dairy products, most alcoholic beverages and motorcycles from Canada, the White House said on Tuesday, as the trade war between the two neighbors and longtime allies escalates. The ban will take effect in three weeks and comes after Canada imposed retaliatory tariffs on $20bn in US imports earlier on Tuesday. Donald Trump also moved Tuesday to shut Canadian products out of large, long-term US government contracts. Some Canadian provinces have banned the sale of US alcoholic products – a move that prompted the retaliatory US ban on Tuesday. Canadian tariffs hit hundreds of American products, including steel, aluminum, cheese, appliances, clothing, cosmetics and farm equipment. Ex-60 Minutes managing editor Guy Campanile says fired staffers “refused to be accomplices” in the show’s “destruction” under new editorial leadership. The Trump administration plans to confront Australia’s government over its decision that US tech companies must allow users to opt out of social media algorithms. Television programme South Park is to change its name to South America “inspired by bravery and patriotism” of Apple and Google, who capitulated to Donald Trump’s requests to change Lake Ontario to Lake America. The development comes as Kyiv faces food shortages after Moscow’s forces continually bomb warehouses supporting civilian life. Well actually: the truth behind ‘old person smell’ No you aren’t imagining it, people do smell different as they get old. Jillian Pretzel gets into the science of why, and whether you can do anything about it. title: Can an entire Arctic ecosystem evolve to adapt to the climate crisis?
summary: In the first project of its kind, scientists are trying to answer if the future of Alaska’s streams and tundra may depend not on survival of the fittest but on how species adapt together
text: On Alaska’s North Slope, scientists tread carefully across clumps of tussock grasses toward a fast-flowing stream draining the imposing Brooks Range of ice and snow. Near Galbraith Creek, they string out a mist net for white-crowned sparrows. The birds have recently arrived from southerly latitudes, intent on feasting on the insects that will soon descend on the tundra like storm clouds. The Arctic summer is short-lived, and sparrows have only a few weeks to establish territories, find mates, lay eggs and raise their chicks on a steady diet of bugs. From every ensnared bird, the scientists collect blood, feather and faecal samples to see what they are eating and how that changes over the summer. One thing they want to know is whether the sparrows are consuming a lot of stream insects, such as stoneflies and mayflies, says Ian Shuman, a doctoral student in quantitative ecology at Columbia University. As willow shrubs claim new territory along the Arctic’s rivers and streams – a process scientists call “shrubification” – this could disrupt the life cycles of stoneflies and mayflies. If the songbirds also depend on aquatic insects to thrive, that might affect the sparrows’ prospects. The tundra can feel immutable in its vastness. A sea of grass and moss extends as far as the eye can see. But above the Arctic Circle, change is happening faster than anywhere else on Earth. Snow is melting earlier in the spring, sending torrents of water downstream. By late summer, such early season deluges have given way to parched creek beds. The Arctic grayling – cold water fish in the salmon family – that swim between deep lake winter refuges and shallow summer spawning streams may become stranded in isolated pools. Their survival, too, rests on the mayflies and stoneflies. Galbraith Creek on Alaska’s North Slope Ian Shuman, a PhD student at Columbia University, downloads the data from an autonomous recording unit set up on the tundra of Alaska’s North Slope to listen for bird calls An Arctic grayling, a freshwater fish in the salmon family, caught in Toolik Lake, Alaska Across the planet, global heating is reshuffling the order of life. Some species will prosper, while those that can’t adapt quickly enough will nosedive toward extinction. Evolution and adaptation have long been thought of as solitary endeavours – a survival of the fittest. But what if species could instead draw on their longstanding relationships not to succeed or fail alone, but to swiftly evolve and adapt together to climate breakdown, keeping whole ecosystems intact? That’s the question evolutionary ecologists, biologists, physiologists and geneticists are trying to answer from Alaska’s stream and tundra ecosystems in a first-of-its-kind $15m (£11m) project, supported by the US National Science Foundation. Over six years, scientists will closely assess five species and their connections to one another: the white-crowned sparrow, the feltleaf willow, the Arctic grayling, an aquatic mayfly and a ground beetle (the exact species are yet to be determined). If species adapt in response to temperature, they may also adapt in response to each other – and each other’s adaptations. “There is how organisms respond individually, but then all those organisms also live in a matrix that is an ecosystem,” says Linda Deegan, a senior scientist at Woodwell climate research center in Massachusetts who is leading the project, known as the Evolving Meta-Ecosystems Institute (Evome). “We think those connections will help them prosper in climate change. Things won’t completely fall apart.” Scientists chose Alaska’s tundra and stream ecosystems to study, not only because the Arctic is the fastest-warming region on Earth, but because it is also home to relatively simple ecosystems where a handful of species shape the environment. Still, what they find in the far north will help inform how ecosystems around the world, from the tropics to the alpine regions, might be able to withstand the climate crisis. *** The land on either side of the Dalton Highway, the road that connects Fairbanks to the oilfields of Prudhoe Bay, serves as a sprawling laboratory for the 50 scientists from US research institutions working on the project. Almost every day throughout the spring and summer, scientists trawl the 15 field sites scattered along a nearly 190-mile stretch of road that runs from just south of the Brooks Range up toward Sagwon Creek, 60 miles south of the Arctic Ocean. The Brooks Range peeks out from behind the sprawling tundra of northern Alaska It is impossible to walk very far on the tundra without stumbling across a research project tucked into the willows or sedges. Dozens of sticky traps poke out of the permafrost to collect bugs. Recording boxes listen for bird calls. Temperature sensors lie submerged in frigid streams. Mesh bags flap around on the tundra to gather willow leaves. In the distance, the silver Alyeska pipeline cuts through the rugged terrain, transporting crude oil to Valdez – a reminder of why scientists are here in the warming landscape. “We follow the road and the pipeline all summer,” says Andie Norton, a Woodwell research assistant who is studying the impact of encroaching willows on nutrient flows in Alaska’s streams. Andie Norton, an ecologist with Woodwell Climate Research Center, examines a water sample taken from Alaska’s Hershey Creek for aquatic mayflies and stoneflies, and a feltleaf willow, one of Evome’s main study species, in the early stages of leafing out A shadier stream means less algae is produced through photosynthesis to feed the mayflies and caddisflies, she says. But if more willows are dropping their foliage, shredding insects that enjoy munching on leaves – such as stoneflies – might become more abundant. The question is whether fish and birds will be able to take sufficient advantage. Unlike mayflies, stoneflies generally don’t form large swarms and they emerge earlier, during the spring melt. Still, there is good reason to think that Alaska’s stream and tundra ecosystems will continue to function, Deegan says, though she notes such an optimistic outcome is only a best guess. Few studies have looked at how adaptive evolution can affect entire ecosystem dynamics – including nutrient and energy flows – and none have assessed how evolution could affect connections between two adjacent ecosystems. Individual species can adapt to a warmer world in one of three ways. They can adjust their behaviour, such as birds shifting their migration routes. They can acclimatise at the physiological level, for instance trees temporarily altering photosynthesis during a drought. Or they can draw upon evolution – passing on genetic changes to their offspring, sometimes within just a few generations. Scientists measure the beak length of a newly arrived, migratory white-crowned sparrow on the tundra of Alaska’s North Slope Studies reveal that many plants and animals have been able to persist through evolutionary rescue – the process by which a population on the brink of extinction survives and rebounds through rapid genetic adaptation. Scarlet monkeyflowers in Oregon and California, for example, rapidly evolved during the 2010s to survive a four-year drought. “Across hundreds of experiments, we have seen this happening,” says Mark Urban, an evolutionary biologist at the University of Connecticut working on the project. “There is this incredible buffer ability of adaptive evolution.” Alpine azalea, a common dwarf shrub found on the Alaska tundra How the evolution of one species can help the holistic ecosystems depends on how an adaptive trait ultimately translates into ecological properties. For example, if a fish species can quickly evolve, it means that not only is the population maintained, but so is the stream’s productivity. “Any ecological properties that depend on those populations are maintained as well,” Urban says. To get a better idea of whether the Arctic’s stream and tundra habitats will continue to prosper, scientists are mapping the genetic diversity of each of the five study species to see if there is enough to allow for adaptation – influencing the ecosystems’ resilience potential. “We can get so far with ecology, but at some point we want to get down to the basics of why organisms do the things they do, and can they change the things they do,” says Urban. “That’s something only genetics can explain.” Certain genes control the traits associated with succeeding in different environments. “The holy grail in genomics is to find that one gene that affects everything. The gene that rules them all,” he says. “I think that’s optimistic. Most of the traits are going to be determined by hundreds of thousands of genes.” *** The Arctic grayling is, in many ways, the crown jewel of the scientists’ investigation. The migrating fish – distinguished by its iridescent body and flamboyant dorsal fin – connect Alaska’s watersheds, moving nutrients between streams and lakes. They are also exceptionally vulnerable to changes in the climate. Grayling require cold water to develop into adults. They feed on the stoneflies and mayflies likely to be affected by increased shrubbiness. And unpredictable summer stream flows can block their movement back to winter lakes. “The snow is melting earlier most years, but summers are also getting drier and grayling have to move,” says environmental ecologist Chris Neill, also at Woodwell, who is looking at stream flows, water chemistry and plant communities for the project. Certain cues tell grayling when they should begin migrating. “Those cues may be programmed into their genome – or they may not.” Harrison Dubois and Chris Neill, members of the Evome project, measure the late spring stream flow of Galbraith Creek on Alaska’s North Slope In May, University of Alaska Fairbanks students Matthew Zimmerman and Roberto Ponce Velez travelled to a lake just south of the Brooks Range hoping to collect fertilised eggs from the spawning grayling for a pilot experiment. Just finding a spawning event is “like throwing a hammer at a nail”, Zimmerman says. Things only got harder from there. The students had hoped to transport their bounty back to a laboratory on the university campus along the notoriously bumpy Dalton Highway. More than half of their eggs perished en route. The survivors that made it to Fairbanks were placed into four tanks with five different water temperatures ranging between 4C and 20C. At the same time, the students collected fertilised eggs from a channel of the Chena River a few miles outside Fairbanks, where grayling were spawning at just 4C – six degrees cooler than the grayling up north – and transferred them to the tanks. The idea is that by collecting species from different geographies and growing them together under shared conditions, scientists will be able to see how genetic variations and adaptations differ across the Arctic. “Temperature is really controlling how quickly things develop,” says Ponce Velez. “There are a lot of trade-offs. At higher temperatures, we have much quicker development of fish. But we have really high mortality.” Next year, they’ll gather more fertilised eggs from other lakes and streams spread across the North Slope to see how each population fares in the lab. Matthew Zimmerman, a PhD student at the University of Alaska Fairbanks, holds up an Arctic grayling caught in Toolik Lake Evome scientists are close to completing the first reference genome for the Arctic grayling, which will allow them to compare differences in temperature responses between populations and search for the specific genes that may be tied to local adaptations. Mist-netting for birds, scrubbing rocks for algae, assembling genomes, and trucking grayling eggs down the Dalton Highway, scientists hope, will eventually allow them to forecast how this fragile place at the top of the world might manage to persist under the weight of immense change. Will Alaska’s streams and tundra bounce back, bend, or snap entirely? “I think there are going to be a lot of springs,” says Urban. “But we’ll also witness a few breaks or bends in the system.” Find more age of extinction coverage here, and follow the biodiversity reporters Rebecca Ratcliffe, Phoebe Weston and Patrick Greenfield in the Guardian app for more nature coverage.

title: Electronic shelf labels likely to cost jobs and drive up grocery prices, US report warns
summary: AFL-CIO calls for ban on such labels to protect consumers and workers from surveillance pricing and job cuts
text: The universal adoption of electronic shelf labels in grocery stores across the US could cost tens of thousands of jobs and billions of dollars in lost wages while further driving up grocery costs, according to a report released on Tuesday. An analysis by the AFL-CIO Tech Institute of the label manufacturers’ own marketing materials found the universal adoption of electronic shelf labels, which are marketed to retailers as a cost-cutting measure, could cost workers between $1.6bn and $6.9bn in lost wages annually and affect between 44,223 and 191,633 jobs. The policy brief – Priced Out, Pushed Out: Electronic Shelf Labels Raise Prices and Shrink Paychecks – calls for a ban on electronic labels to protect consumers and workers. Manufacturers have hailed the labels as a way to collect huge amounts of personal data from customers, increase profits and cut labor costs. The report argues that electronic shelf labels use the same pricing systems that allow dynamic pricing – price changes such as increasing allergy medication prices when pollen counts are high – to surveillance pricing, changing prices based on personal data. These technologies are being implemented across the US retail industry at a time when food prices have surpassed inflation and wage gains, increasing 33% over the past seven years. “Through our analysis, we found that the implementation of electronic shelf labels are likely going to drive prices even higher. The reason being that these labels are connected to the same algorithmic pricing software that online retailers are already using,” said Sunny Glottmann, policy and programs managers at the AFL-CIO Tech Institute and co-author of the report. “Electronic shelf labels create the infrastructure that would make rapid algorithmic price changes easier to implement at scale, and this raises concerns for consumers that are already struggling with grocery costs.” The report comes as several states have begun introducing legislation to ban surveillance pricing and electronic shelf labels. In April, Maryland became the first state in the US to ban surveillance pricing. Connecticut signed a ban into law in June and New Jersey signed a ban into law in July. Electronic shelf labels “enable instantaneous price changes”, said Lauren McFerran, executive director of the AFL-CIO Tech Institute and former chairman of the National Labor Relations Board. “This is a technology that both is enabling this kind of ‘how do we extract the absolute most money out of grocery shoppers that is humanly possible’ and ‘how do we squeeze our workers as much as is humanly possible’,” said McFerran. A May poll released by the United Food and Commercial Workers union found 68% of Americans believe surveillance pricing will increase grocery costs and 65% say digital price tags will do the same. About 67% support banning digital price tags and surveillance pricing, with only 26% opposing a ban. Ademola Oyefeso, vice-president of UFCW International, said that as retailers are implementing electronic shelf labels, the labor cuts occur gradually, with workers who typically change prices on shelves losing work hours. “Slowly, if someone has a full-time job or a part-time job, they go from full-time to part-time, from part-time to no time, and that’s what’s going to start happening across the entire industry,” said Oyefeso. “We have gone with paper labels for over 100 years. It’s worked. It’s the trust stores have built with people. I know [that] you and I are paying the same price. “If we come there on Monday, you and I are going to pay the same price on Monday, on Tuesday, on Wednesday.” Oyefeso said workers were also consumers, and that electronic shelf labels allow price changes to occur multiple times a day. In December, Instacart ended a pilot program practice that allowed retailers to charge online shoppers different prices for the same products after an investigation by Consumer Reports and Groundwork Collaborative found grocery prices could differ by as much as 23% between customers. “ESLs are the embodiment of surge pricing and surveillance pricing,” Oyefeso said. “Shelf labels allow grocery shopping to become airline ticket shopping.”

title: Homeland security agent charged with child rape in Alabama, officials say
summary: Kent Blacklidge, who officials say was ‘directly involved with child exploitation cases’, turned himself in last week
text: A federal law enforcement agent tasked with “trying to provide justice in cases involving kids” has been charged with child rape in Alabama, state authorities said on Tuesday. Kent Blacklidge, described as a special agent with Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), turned himself over to the Baldwin county jail on 5 September in connection with a grand jury indictment charging him with first- and second-degree rape, sodomy and sexual abuse, police in the city of Spanish Fort said in a statement. During a Tuesday news conference, the Spanish Fort police chief, John Barber, said the charges against Blacklidge, 43, stemmed from an 11 January child sexual abuse report involving an underage girl. The Spanish Fort police statement said Blacklidge had been put on administrative leave by HSI as soon as officers began investigating the complaint against him. Barber said Blacklidge was charged after officers conducted interviews and gathered other unspecified evidence into that complaint, about which the chief declined to release specific details. “It takes an unbelievable amount of courage and strength for a victim of these types of crime to come forward,” Barber said at Tuesday’s news conference. “And I commend our victim for having that resolve.” Alabama’s attorney general, Steve Marshall, said it was particularly disturbing to have to prosecute Blacklidge on child sexual abuse allegations because his responsibilities at HSI included “trying to provide justice in cases involving kids”. He “was directly involved with child exploitation cases, working with these cases and raising awareness”, Marshall added. “That’s why it’s so profoundly disappointing and frankly disgusting that we stand here today and tell you that we charged him” with crimes that are incongruent with “what his professional responsibility was”. Marshall further remarked: “It is also to be reaffirming to the public [that] it is our responsibility to follow the facts and apply the law regardless of what you’ve done, regardless of where you work and regardless of who you are.” An attender of Tuesday’s news conference told Marshall at one point that “we had covered” Blacklidge previously at a seminar where he provided training to local public school teachers about how to detect online predators targeting children for sex crimes. The Alabama attorney general said his staff was handling the charges against Blacklidge because Blacklidge is a witness in some cases being prosecuted by the local district attorney’s office, requiring the latter agency to recuse itself. Barber and Marshall each argued that Blacklidge’s charges should not reflect on the entire law enforcement field. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees HSI, on Wednesday said it could not comment on Blacklidge because his case was ongoing. But the DHS has previously faced scrutiny over its employee vetting practices after it received an unprecedented $170bn in funding for immigration and border enforcement securities amid the Trump administration’s drive for mass deportations. The Associated Press reported in February that another agency under the DHS’s purview, Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), had seen at least two dozen of its employees and contractors be charged with various crimes since 2020. Blacklidge by Tuesday had been released from jail on bond pending the outcome of his case, according to facility records. Remarks from Marshall on Tuesday suggested his bond amount had been set at more than $350,000. As a condition of his release on bond, Blacklidge would have to submit to electronic monitoring, home confinement and an order to neither contact the alleged victim in the case nor anyone else under the age of 18, Marshall said. A message left for Blacklidge at a telephone number associated with him was not immediately returned.

title: US allies lack resources to keep pace on AI, top Pentagon official says
summary: Cameron Stanley talks up ‘revolutionary’ AI capabilities and says Washington working with Nato and Five Eyes partners
text: The Pentagon’s top artificial intelligence official said on Tuesday that America’s closest allies lack the resources to keep pace with the US military’s adoption of AI, and that Washington is working to steer them away from mistakes it made along the way. “They don’t have the resources that we do, they don’t have the experience that we do, they don’t have the scale that we do,” Cameron Stanley, chief digital and artificial intelligence officer at the Department of Defense, said at an event at the Billington Cybersecurity summit. Of Nato and the Five Eyes, an intelligence-sharing partnership of the US, UK, Canada, Australia and New Zealand, Stanley said Washington was “actively working with a number of our partners” so “they don’t make the same mistakes that we make”. The comments come less than a year into Stanley’s tenure, during which the Pentagon’s AI office has rolled out several new tools while losing a number of senior staff. Since January, Stanley has overseen the launch of GenAI.mil, an internal chatbot platform he says has reached 1.7 million users, and Agent Network, a system designed to shorten the time between intelligence-gathering and a commander’s decision. The defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, has directed Stanley’s office to report AI deployment speed as a monthly metric, part of a wider push to expand military computing power. Much of Stanley’s appearance focused on speed. He described watching a commander halt a scheduled briefing to take a 30-second phone call and issue an order on the spot, without a formal decision brief or a review of the room’s security clearance level. He called the moment “revolutionary”. “I know it sounds simplistic,” Stanley explained. “It’s only simplistic because we’re good at it now.” It’s a term he has used before. Project Maven, the Pentagon’s original AI targeting program launched in 2017, became the Palantir-built Maven Smart System, which the US leaned on heavily during its 2026 air campaign against Iran, helping strike more than 13,000 targets over the first 38 days, according to Stanley at conference in May. Speaking at Palantir’s AIPCon 9 conference in March, Stanley called Maven “revolutionary” too, saying it let commanders go from identifying a target to launching a strike within a single platform. But the campaign has drawn scrutiny. More than 120 members of the US Congress signed a letter demanding answers from the Pentagon regarding civilian casualties and the use of artificial intelligence, following a 28 February strike on an elementary school in Minab, which Iranian officials say killed at least 168 people, many of them children. Stanley ended by telling the audience that the department’s old habits were now its biggest liability. “The way we’ve always done it is the most risky course of action,” he said, adding that the department needed to “think differently” if it wants AI tools in the hands of warfighters faster.

title: Miliband rejects chief rabbi’s claim that West Bank sanctions put UK Jews at risk
summary: Foreign secretary says Sir Ephraim Mirvis wrong to suggest measures against Israeli settlements will make British Jews less safe
text: Ed Miliband has rejected warnings from the UK’s chief rabbi that the government’s sanctions against illegal Israeli settlements will make British Jews less safe, as he emphasised ministers can confront the actions of Benjamin Netanyahu’s government while also fighting antisemitism. The foreign secretary announced sweeping sanctions on trade with Israeli settlements in the West Bank on Tuesday, with the government taking the position that Israel’s occupation of the Palestinian territory was unlawful. The measures were coordinated with France, Canada and nine other countries that were also introducing sanctions on Israel over the increasing expansion of settlements, which the UK government says is threatening the future of a Palestinian state. In a joint statement, leaders including Andy Burnham, Emmanuel Macron and Mark Carney said: “The time has come to take further action to uphold our commitment to protect the two-state solution, our interests and to stand up for our values, before it is too late.” The chief rabbi, Sir Ephraim Mirvis, called the UK sanctions a “dark day for British Jews” and said they could embolden people who “use hatred as a weapon against Jews”. Milliband, who describes himself as a “proud British Jew”, said he did not agree with Mirvis. Asked on BBC Radio 4’s Today programme whether he was saying the chief rabbi was wrong, Miliband replied: “Yes, I am saying I don’t agree with the chief rabbi, somebody over whom I have great respect.” He added: “I just want to be very, very clear. As I said it in my statement yesterday, anyone who holds British Jews, or indeed Jews around the world, responsible for the actions of the Israeli government is engaging in antisemitism, pure and simple. “And it must be possible to stand up in our society for British values of freedom, dignity, and against oppression and injustice, and do so as I believe I did yesterday in a way that calls out antisemitism.” The foreign secretary was pressed on the chief rabbi’s fear that British Jews could feel less safe as a result of the sanctions and was challenged by the BBC presenter, Justin Webb, who suggested Mirvis’s claim could mean less to Miliband because he did not attend synagogue. “No, I don’t agree with that,” said Miliband, adding: “Antisemitism is a scourge and an evil … I want Jews, I want people of all faiths and none to feel safe in our country.” Burnham told MPs at PMQs that it was vital to take the decision before the Israeli elections because the tenders for the E1 settlement plans were being finalised soon, and the sanctions would affect the practicality of those plans being carried out. “Words from any politician about a two-state solution will be only words if it’s not backed with action, and leadership is about taking action where there is injustice, where we need to correct unfairness, people being driven out of their homes, losing their homes, being intimidated in their daily lives,” he said. “Britain has to stand for something. Britain has to show leadership. Britain has to stand for fairness against injustice, where people are being bullied out of their homes, intimidated. We will always stand with the underdog and take what action we can to support them.” Tuesday’s sanctions announcement also prompted a swift backlash from Israel, which ordered the closure of the British consulate in Jerusalem and banned 12 British MPs and activists from entering Israel. Washington’s ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, threatened that the US could take retaliatory action over trade, but the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said the US would “obviously” not follow the UK government’s actions but did not want to see the West Bank destabilised. Miliband told Sky News he would “let our American friends speak for themselves” but insisted the international community had been “quite frustrated to put it mildly, with some of the actions of the Israeli government”. The foreign secretary said he regretted what the Israeli government had announced but was “proud of what we did yesterday and it was the right thing to do”. Miliband accepted the closure of the British consulate in Jerusalem would be “damaging” but said the government had “weighed up the costs and benefits in advance if this”. The government is set to enact: An import ban on goods from illegal settlements in the occupied territories and a new ban for arms licences and other exports that “materially contribute to the occupation”. A comprehensive sanctions regime against providing services such as construction or financing for Israeli settlements and a ban on advertising them in the UK. Personal sanctions against the main individuals accused of promoting settler violence. A new ban for arms licences and other exports that “materially contribute to the occupation”. Miliband made an impassioned statement in the Commons on Tuesday, recounting the horrific tales he had heard from Palestinians in the West Bank, whose homes had been destroyed, and doctors in Gaza who saw children dying while waiting for treatment. The prime minister, Andy Burnham, said the sanctions were “the right thing to do” and emphasised they were aimed “not at the Israeli people”. Burnham is due to face MPs over this issue at prime minister’s questions.

title: ‘I am seen as a Marmite figure’: Margaret Hodge on political battles, victories, errors – and regrets
summary: At 82, the politician and anti-corruption champion is indefatigable. She discusses fighting the BNP, tackling antisemitism, and why, with her new memoir, she’s reclaiming the word ‘battleaxe’
text: Margaret Hodge doesn’t do small talk. “So, how d’you think Andy’s doing?” is her opening gambit. “Not too bad, huh? I think he’s had a really good start.” It’s classic Hodge – sufficiently curious to ask the question about the new Labour prime minister, and assertive enough to provide the answer before you get yours out. “Yep. Fantastic empathy. But then he’s got to deliver. I think the budget is going to be the key moment. And we’ve also got these awful global challenges and Iran and Hormuz. God, it’s a mess. Ugh. Hahahaha!” She hoots with laughter at the horror of it all. She says she was against ousting Keir Starmer. “I thought we were doing so badly that what we really needed was a complete change in what we were about, what our ambitions were, where we were going, what our priorities were and how we were going to have a message of hope. I thought it was about much more than Keir at that point. I thought changing leaders was like rearranging deckchairs on the Titanic. I think I was wrong, right?” Hodge has seen it all. Decade-long leader of Islington council when it was regarded as part of the “loony left”; Labour moderate and Blair-Brown loyalist throughout the years in power; scrapper extraordinaire who has taken on the BNP as MP for Barking, antisemitism in Jeremy Corbyn’s Labour and tax-avoiding tech companies as the formidable chair of the cross-party public accounts committee (PAC). Now, in the week of her 82nd birthday, Hodge is publishing a memoir, Battleaxe. “I’m reclaiming the term. It shouldn’t be a term of derision. It’s a strong woman.” Who came up with the title? “If I’m absolutely honest, it was my agent. My children don’t like it, but lots of people do.” Does she really feel like a battleaxe? “People do say: ‘Oh, you don’t want to take on Margaret.’” She stares me down, fiercely proud, big brown eyes aglint. “Can I tell you what I think about myself? I listen and reflect, but when I’ve made up my mind I’m quite strong and determined.” She reminds me of the great football manager Brian Clough, who said: “If I had an argument with a player, we would sit down for 20 minutes, talk about it, and then decide I was right.” We are at her London home, where she lives alone. It’s every bit as immaculate and stylish as she is. “Don’t look in the garden,” she says. “It’s such a mess – I’ve been away for six weeks.” Her gardening tools are at the ready by the door. The walls are covered in lovely paintings. There are busts of her husband (the high court judge Henry Hodge, who specialised in immigration and died aged 65 in 2009) and her father (Hans Oppenheimer, who co-founded Coutinho, Caro & Co, a steel trading firm that became the multinational Stemcor). On the main wall in the living room is a gorgeous splash of abstract colour by Gillian Ayres. “I love it because it’s painted in big bold strokes and is really optimistic.” You could say much the same of Hodge. She’s had a fascinating life. Her Jewish parents fled Germany to escape the Nazis, and she was born in Egypt. After a window was broken at her father’s business in 1948 during the first Arab-Israeli war, he took the hint. This time the family fled to Kent in England. Although they were atheists, the family’s only friends were other Jewish refugees. On Christmas Day in 1954, when Hodge was 10, her mother died of stomach cancer. Shortly afterwards, it was decided that as the brightest child in her class, she should skip a year. So within months she had lost her mother and her peer group. She was devastated, and became increasingly unruly. Oppenheimer didn’t know what to do with her and sent her away to boarding school in Oxford, which she hated. In 1966 she graduated from the London School of Economics with a third-class honours degree in economics. She worked in corporate market research for seven years, and did a stint as an unqualified teacher. In 1968 she married Andrew Watson, an economist with whom she had two children. She joined the Labour party in 1973, and won a seat on Islington council in the same year. A friend had told her that getting involved in local politics would keep her sane while raising a family. She was, and remains, driven by two desires – to equalise life chances and fight racism. By 1975, she was chair of the council’s housing committee, with Henry Hodge, then a solicitor, as her deputy. In 1978, she divorced Watson and married Hodge. They went on to have two daughters. In 1982, she became leader of the council. Opponents nicknamed her Enver Hodge, a play on Enver Hoxha, the brutal communist dictator who ruled Stalinist Albania. Hodge admits she was pretty hardline. “I don’t hold back. Henry always used to try to restrain me.” Can she give an example? “We did a walkout on Michael Heseltine because he did a conference on inner-city regeneration and he was chopping all our funding. I thought it was such hypocrisy.” Why did Henry object to the walkout? “He said it was a daft thing to do. It was gesture politics. And in that era we were seen as engaging in too much gesture politics.” She pauses. “But,” she barks, “having said that, he was incredibly supportive.” She gives another example of her gesture politics. “I refused to meet Margaret Thatcher. But she did do these awful things.” I’m fully aware of the things she did, I say, but wasn’t it … She finishes the sentence for me. “It was stupid. It was stupid. I wouldn’t do it today, but isn’t that interesting to learn that of yourself and how you’ve changed? And it fitted with the time. She was taking on local government and the unions. She was destroying what Andy’s now going to try to recreate.” She says that pre-Thatcher, she had so much power as a council leader, and the Iron Lady gradually stripped it away – rate-capping, grant cutting, privatisations, the abolition of the Greater London Council. “It was a terrible transformation. We did hate her. She was a Marmite figure, wasn’t she? You loved her or you hated her.” That’s funny, I say: Marmite is how you describe yourself in Battleaxe. “Yep. Ha! This is true. I am controversial. I am seen as a Marmite figure, too. Why is that? Why is that?” And for once she doesn’t answer her own question. Has she been surprised by her career? “Yes. As a school kid, I never thought I’d be anybody. I thought I’d be a mum. I’d lost my mother and it made me think the only thing I want to be in life is a mum. So I feel surprised by the extent of my experience and opportunities.” There’s another thing that has surprised her – this time, not so positive. “I never thought I would become a hate figure in the way that I became sometimes.” What does she consider her greatest achievement? “BNP,” she says instantly. “It has to be the BNP, doesn’t it?” In 2006, the neo-Nazi party won 12 of the 51 seats on Barking and Dagenham council. It looked as if it could go on to win the 2010 council election and that the BNP leader Nick Griffin could oust Hodge as MP in the general election. Labour had committed the cardinal sin of taking the electorate for granted, Hodge says. What’s more, it was terrified of talking about migration. Meanwhile, her constituency had become unrecognisable to many. “It went from 98% white to under 50% in a generation, which is massive. If your community or my community changed liked that in a generation, we would feel unsettled. At best, unsettled. Kids in the street change, neighbours change, food in the shops changes.” Hodge discovered her constituents were furious because they believed they were being ignored and that migrants were being prioritised for social housing. She proposed that weighting be given to people’s links to the community rather than housing being based purely on immediate need, which eventually happened. Many fellow Labour MPs criticised her. Keith Vaz said she “appears to want to be the Alf Garnett of Islington”, while Alan Johnson accused her of pandering to the BNP. “He said that on Question Time. He was going for the deputy leadership,” Hodge says. Did they have a point? “No. I never ever caved in to the racism. Ever. Ever!” In 2010 Labour wiped out the BNP and she trounced Griffin by 18,000 votes. How did that feel? “Very mixed because it was just under a year since Henry had died. There was a lot of ‘why is Henry not here?’ in it. But I also felt fantastic. Jubilant. If I hadn’t changed the way I’d operated politically, and knocked on doors, I think we would have had a BNP council and a BNP MP. It took me four years of work – it wasn’t just a quick three weeks before the election.” She talks about the echoes today with Reform. “We lost control of immigration so I think what Shabana [Mahmood] is doing is really important. Now you don’t have massive delays in dealing with asylum seeker applications. People who come here have to abide by our rules, and if they don’t, they lose the right to be here. If they commit a criminal offence they should lose the right to be here.” Really? Surely our rules are that you serve a sentence for a crime, then come out and get on with your life? I point out that many refugees are deported for minor crimes. “That changes once you’ve got your British citizenship,” she says. But under new Labour legislation, you could wait 20 years for that. “No, I agree,” she says. “I have problems with a 20-year wait.” What was tougher, fighting the BNP or antisemitism? “The BNP was a much easier fight in an odd way. It was much clearer.” Why? “Because antisemitism was in the Labour party. It was horrible. Antisemitism is the worst of all the battles I have fought. I hated it. I absolutely hated it. It was miserable. I hated the abuse. I hated walking into rooms and thinking: ‘God, who’s for me and who’s against me in this room?’” Abuse on social media included: “The only support she deserves is a handrail to climb the gallows”. Was she surprised when in 2018 she ended up calling Corbyn … Again she finishes the sentence for me. “An antisemite? Was I surprised at myself? No, that’s the battleaxe in me, isn’t it?” She had told two fellow MPs that she had planned to do it beforehand. So, I ask, was there a theatrical element to it? “I didn’t do it publicly. These two lads wanted me to say it to him on the frontbench. I said, ‘I’m not going to do that – I’ll catch him on his way out [of the House of Commons chamber]’, which is what I did.” The 2022 report by Martin Forde KC into the toxic culture in the Labour party concluded that antisemitism was weaponised by the left and the right of the party. “I was anti-Corbyn; but no, I never used it as a weapon,” Hodge says. Does she agree in general that it was weaponised on both sides? “Yes, probably. I think there was some weaponising.” If she saw Corbyn now, what would she say to him? “He doesn’t talk to me. Haha! He passes me by. Haha! Ignores me.” She chuckles with satisfaction. The Labour party asked her to apologise to Corbyn, but she told it where to go. After the party dropped its investigation in August 2018, she told Sky News: “On the day that I heard that they were going to discipline me and possibly suspend me, it felt almost like … what did it feel like to be a Jew in Germany in the 30s?” Was this when she felt most hated in politics? “Yep.” Has it left scars? “It’s still there. But it’s a joy now to be in the Labour party. When Keir became leader, he single-mindedly tackled antisemitism. I hadn’t expected that and I appreciate it. But it’s a part of my life, so it doesn’t disappear.” Now she says it took Corbyn to help her rediscover her identity. “It’s brought me back to feeling an empathy with who I am – a Jewish immigrant refugee.” What is her biggest regret in politics? She immediately cites the sexual abuse scandal in Islington children’s homes when she was leader of the council. “I just don’t think any of us thought paedophiles were operating out of children’s homes. It was unconscionable. Now it’s unconscionable today to think that we didn’t realise it. That’s probably caused me more political problems than anything.” She had just been made the UK’s first children’s minister when the scandal became headline news again decades later in 2003. She offered her resignation to Tony Blair, who refused it. But many people knew it was going on and told you so? “We went through each allegation, and I had all the officers there and they denied any of this was happening. Remember, back then kids in care were called naughty. Today that is unconscionable, isn’t it? I’d listened to all the officers, but I didn’t talk to the kids, and that’s a regret.” What was even more unconscionable is that she tried to close down an investigation by BBC Radio 4’s Today programme and called Demetrious Panton, a child abuse survivor, an “extremely disturbed person”. She squirms when I mention it. “That was a terrible error. Terrible error.” Why did you do that? “I was advised. Everyone was ringing me up saying the Today programme was digging around and I thought: ‘How the hell can I stop this?’ That was an appalling bit of advice. But in the end I took responsibility. I did it.” Hodge was forced to issue an unreserved public apology in the high court, she paid Panton’s legal costs, and was ordered to pay him £30,000, which included a £10,000 donation to a charity of his choice. But in the end Hodge, who now sits in the Lords, will be remembered more for exposing corruption than for covering it up. Although she never achieved high office as an MP, she became a political rock star as chair of the PAC between 2010 and 2015. She was convinced it was going to be a dull job when she took it on, yet it proved anything but. The cross-party committee tasked with assessing the value for money of government projects became a must-watch as corporate executives and senior civil servants were held to account for dodging taxes, playing fast and loose with public money, failing to answer questions or simply being rude. Hodge proved herself a fearless one-woman grilling machine. Google’s Matt Brittin (now director general of the BBC) was well and truly Hodged when she threw the company motto back in his face, saying: “You are a company that says you ‘do no evil’. And I think that you do do evil.” After a session challenging BBC execs over excessive severance payoffs, she concluded it was “a very unedifying experience watching seven people at the top of the BBC dancing on the head of a pin to try and avoid responsibility”. In 2024, she was made the UK’s official anti-corruption champion, a fiscal Wonder Woman fighting dirty money, offshore tax dodgers and economic crime. On her kitchen table today is a tax file she tells me I mustn’t look at on pain of death. For all of Hodge’s warmth, I tell her she can be terrifying. “Why?” Well, I’ve seen you in action on the PAC, I say. Again, Hodge hoots with happy laughter. That’s the battleaxe, she says. Then she half-whispers, almost conspiratorially: “I’m always surprised when people say: ‘God, you don’t cross Margaret.’” But I’m not so sure she is. • Battleaxe by Dame Margaret Hodge is out on 10 September, published by HarperCollins (£25).
