title: Supercar maker McLaren to create 1,000 UK jobs in £450m tech investment
summary: New roles at Woking-based centre a welcome boost to ailing automotive industry
text: The British supercar manufacturer McLaren is to create 1,000 jobs in a welcome boost to the UK’s struggling automotive industry. The carmaker is creating the jobs as part of a £450m investment in its technology centre in Woking, Surrey, near to the plant where it manufactures all of its vehicles. McLaren, which last year merged with the premium UK electric vehicle startup Forseven Holdings, employs 2,500 staff. The new jobs will include indirect and agency workers, according to the Financial Times, which first reported the investment. The news comes days after Jaguar Land Rover confirmed plans to cut 4,000 jobs over the next two years. JLR, which is restructuring to address falling sales and financial challenges, including Donald Trump’s tariff wars and the fallout from a cyber-attack last year, employs 44,000 people globally and 34,000 in the UK. The cuts will mainly affect the 26,000 UK employees who are salaried, and management workers. Last year, CYVN Holdings, an Abu Dhabi government-owned investment company, acquired McLaren’s automotive business from Bahraini sovereign wealth fund Mumtalakat. CYVN has said that it plans to invest $2bn (£1.4bn) over the next five years in the loss-making group. McLaren Automotive, one of the UK’s best-known sports carmakers, is thought to be planning a product overhaul after years of manufacturing only performance cars such as the F1 model, first launched in 1992. It was last year reported to be planning a new SUV as part of the turnaround plan under its boss Nick Collins, a former JLR executive, though no new information has emerged since then. It appointed a new chief creative officer, David Woodhouse, formerly of Nissan and Ford, over the summer. CYVN also holds a minority stake in McLaren Racing, the parent company of the Formula One team which has won the last two constructors championships in the sport and is also based in Woking. Mumtalakat still has majority control of McLaren Racing. European carmakers have faced tough trading conditions as Chinese rivals, such as BYD and Chery, have enjoyed soaring sales across the UK and mainland Europe. In July, Chery, which also owns the Omoda and Jaecoo brands, accounted for nearly 8% of UK market share, up from 3% last year, according to the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders (SMMT). Last week, Volkswagen announced it would cut 100,000 of its more than 650,000 global workforce by 2030, and halve the number of models it produces. VW group also includes the Bentley, Audi, Skoda, Seat, Porsche, Cupra and Lamborghini brands. From early next year, UK carmakers face a 10% tariff for electric vehicles shipped to the EU. UK-made vehicles do not qualify for “made in Europe” subsidies, under current proposals. The UK government is also consulting on loosening its battery EV sales targets for manufacturers, after extensive lobbying by the industry. The chief executive of the SMMT, Mike Hawes, said earlier this summer that companies with existing UK operations were considering building new models, but were holding back until ministers relaxed EV sales rules. Lachlan Buirds, managing director of manufacturer Edale, said: “McLaren’s investment is a welcome reminder that UK manufacturing is a sector with a future. “Recent redundancy announcements understandably attract attention, but they risk giving young people the impression that UK manufacturing is an industry in decline. In reality, modern manufacturing increasingly depends on engineering, automation, software and digital technology, creating a much broader range of career opportunities.”

title: Family of British man found dead in Grenada ask local police to work with UK investigators
summary: Andrew Frederick’s body was found in property he was staying at in Grenada in January
text: The family of a British father who was found dead in the Caribbean in January is urging authorities in Grenada to work with UK police to uncover the truth about his death. Andrew Frederick’s body was found in the property he was staying at in Grenada on 4 January. An autopsy, performed in the same week by a privately hired pathologist, concluded that the 47-year-old’s death was a homicide. In June, Grenada’s director of public prosecution, Howard Pinnock, said at a press conference that Frederick’s and another pending case would be sent to the coroner to determine the cause of death “because there is no basis in terms of both investigations that any homicide has occurred”. After a sustained campaign by the family, British authorities became involved and Frederick’s body was repatriated to the UK last month, where a second autopsy was carried out. The UK coroner has noted that Frederick’s organs are missing and the death is currently “unascertained”. At the start of an inquest at West London coroner’s court last week, senior coroner Lydia Brown said the Metropolitan police are now investigating Frederick’s death. The family, who attended the court hearing by video link, said the coroner’s “decision to suspend Andrew’s inquest to allow the Metropolitan police to conduct a criminal investigation marks a significant turning point”. In statement to the Guardian, they urged Grenada and the UK to work together to find out what happened to Frederick. “We are encouraged and grateful that the Metropolitan police investigation is now under way. Justice for Andrew depends on everyone with the power to act, on both sides of the Atlantic, doing what is right,” the statement said. It added: “Andrew was a deeply loved member of a close-knit family; a son, brother, father and grandson. He leaves behind his cherished daughter, who should be growing up with him beside her, not learning to live without him. “Our family remain determined to uncover the truth about what happened to Andrew and to see justice follow. We hope this ruling is the step that finally enables a complete, properly coordinated investigation and that everyone who can assist will now do so.” This year, the family had called for an urgent review of the policies governing UK assistance to the loved ones of Britons killed abroad, after they were forced to launch their own public appeals for information, and commission an independent forensic pathologist and a private investigation. “Eight months have passed since Andrew was taken from us. In that time, we have learned what no family should ever have to learn, and fought battles no family should ever face alone,” their statement said. It added: “We have relentlessly sought answers and support while carrying the weight of Andrew’s loss and the horror of what was done to him. We still do not have a complete account of what happened, and important questions remain unanswered. “We hope the Grenadian authorities with knowledge of the case will now share that information and work collaboratively with the Metropolitan police, allowing the investigation to proceed without further delay. We are also seeking urgent answers as to why Andrew’s organs were absent when his body was returned to the UK for further examination.” In Grenada, the Office of the Commissioner told the Guardian that “the matter will be progressing to the coroner’s court for the parish of Saint George”. A Met spokesperson said: “The Met is investigating the death of 47-year-old Andrew Donald Frederick, who died in Grenada on 4 January. “Mr Frederick’s family are being supported by specialist officers. “No arrests have been made at this stage and inquiries are ongoing.” Officers have contacted the Royal Grenada Police Force to offer assistance and discuss how the investigation can be progressed. Inquest proceedings have been suspended pending the outcome of police investigations.

title: Reform insists National Rally agreed migrant policy after backlash in France
summary: Critics say agreement between Nigel Farage and Jordan Bardella to return migrants to France goes against France’s ‘interests and sovereignty’
text: Reform UK has insisted its deal with France’s far-right National Rally to return migrants back across the Channel was fully approved by the party and signed off by its president, Jordan Bardella, amid a furious backlash in France. The agreement unveiled on Friday between Nigel Farage and Bardella, who is the 30-year-old protege of presidential candidate Marine Le Pen, appeared to directly contradict Le Pen’s long-held policy of refusing to accept the return of those who arrive in the UK in small boats from France. Le Pen was pressed for her position by journalists from France TV, the state broadcaster, on Monday. Le Pen declined to comment, saying she would talk about the issue soon, but at a time of her choosing. In 2021, Le Pen said she wanted a rewriting of border agreements for the UK to specifically send people arriving on boats back to their countries of origin, instead of returning them to France. Since the agreement, Bardella has come under fire from political parties in France for signing the deal, with Benjamin Haddad, the Europe minister, criticising Bardella for “submission” that was “against our interests and sovereignty”. Some French media have questioned whether Bardella was duped by Reform, querying whether the French translation accurately conveyed the meaning by Farage that the National Rally (RN) was prepared to accept any migrants back who travel by small boat. However, a Reform spokesperson said it was “signed off by both Bardella and the presidential team”, that the policy was included in the French version as well as the English, and it could “confirm both parties are fully on board”. Until the summer, Bardella had been considered as a potential replacement for Le Pen in next spring’s presidential election but will now run as her future prime minister. In July, when a Paris appeal court upheld Le Pen’s conviction for embezzling European parliament funds, her ban from running for office was reduced, allowing her to stand. Farage has kept Le Pen at arm’s length, while having cultivated good relations with Bardella over the past year, but he is rumoured to be planning to meet her later in the autumn. He previously rejected the idea of a tie-up in 2014 in the European parliament when he accused Le Pen’s party of having a history of “prejudice and antisemitism”, which she said was slander. Last week, Farage said he would not have done a deal with the party when led by Jean-Marie Le Pen, Marine’s father, a convicted Holocaust denier who co-founded the Front National in 1972. Le Pen expelled her father from the party in 2015. Farage praised her, saying she had got rid of “extreme elements”. At the heart of the row in France is the wording of the document Farage brought out for Bardella to sign with him on stage in Birmingham, calling it a memorandum of understanding. Both texts, presented side by side in English and French, state that, if Farage and Bardella become prime ministers of their respective countries, the UK will intercept boats launched from the French coast, and that France will return people onboard to their countries of origin. But the English text carried an extra phrase saying “France will ordinarily accept these persons” who would then be returned to their home country. This appeared to show that Bardella was promising to accept returned persons in France, which contradicts the long-held position of RN. France TV said RN denied any controversy, saying the text was only a declaration of intention that would be refined at a later point. Speaking in Italy over the weekend, Bardella suggested his party in government would prevent migrants from reaching France by much tougher border controls, resulting in the numbers crossing to the UK being much lower. However, RN’s opponents were critical of Bardella for signing a memorandum on immigration on stage with Farage. The MP, Sacha Houlié, an ally of the centre-left would-be presidential candidate, Raphael Glucksmann, wrote on X about what he called “a miserable episode where the whole of France could see Mr Bardella used as a doormat by the English far-right.” He told the RN: “You claim to be patriots, you’re cowards.” Gabriel Attal, the former centrist prime minister and presidential candidate, wrote on X: “To applause from his party members, Nigel Farage made Jordan Bardella sign a memorandum to ensure that all migrants intercepted in the Channel are sent back to France. Either Jordan Bardella doesn’t understand English or he is shamefully weak when it comes to defending French interests. And I think he does understand English.” Édouard Philippe, a former prime minister and centre-right candidate, said it was an example of hypocrisy and division in Bardella’s party. Philippe said it looked like Bardella found it difficult to stand up to Farage in order to “protect French interests”. Xavier Bertrand, the rightwing head of the northern Hauts-de-France region, wrote on X that in agreeing that France alone would take responsibility for returning people to their home countries, Bardella was “reducing France to the status of Britain’s subcontractor.” Chris Philp, the Conservative shadow home secretary, said: “Reform UK’s deal with Jordan Bardella is a complete farce … Time and again, Reform prove they are fundamentally unserious with grand claims for the cameras, with none of the detail or hard work that might survive actual scrutiny.”

title: UK datacentres will create just 25% of jobs predicted by tech sector, analysis finds
summary: Facilities likely to employ 10,400 workers, compared with 40,000 in industry estimates, thinktank says
text: Datacentres in the UK will create just a quarter of the jobs predicted by the tech sector, while consuming vast amounts of energy, according to new research. Environmental thinktank Verdant predicts that all the datacentres currently planned are likely to directly employ 10,400 workers – compared with the more than 40,000 cited in projections by the industry lobby group TechUK. Labour has defended the rapid rollout of AI datacentres in the face of growing public scepticism, amid concerns about their demand for water and energy. The government has also echoed TechUK’s claims about job creation. Verdant’s analysis is based on 20 projects for which data on staffing levels are publicly available, including via planning applications, company accounts and press releases – as well as international comparisons. It says the datacentres that have already been built have directly created fewer than 4,400 jobs – about 8.6 jobs for each megawatt of energy they consume, against the 43.7 jobs claimed in TechUK’s projections. Verdant also argues that the many future projects currently at the planning stage are on a far larger scale, and so likely to be much less job-intensive – perhaps creating as few as 1.6 permanent positions per megawatt. Its analysis focuses on the permanent workers needed to maintain and operate datacentres, setting aside the much larger number of temporary construction jobs needed to build them. James Meadway, the thinktank’s co-director, said: “We’re being rushed into supporting a frantic pace of datacentre buildout on very flimsy economic grounds. “Clearly artificial intelligence and related technologies have great potential. But vast new datacentres arrive at significant real costs to local communities and even our climate ambitions, and their use case has to be made by the government and industry – rather than assuming we can build first and then work out why we did later.” To underline the resource intensity of the vast data warehouses, Verdant compared the 8.6 jobs they currently create per megawatt of power used with about 400 in a car plant and more than 3,600 in a hospital or health facility. The government rejected this comparison, and questioned Verdant’s methodology. A spokesperson said: “This report relies on a deeply misleading jobs-per-megawatt metric, makes false comparisons with hospitals and schools, and appears to confuse electricity capacity with actual consumption. More seriously, it discounts the wider economic value of compute [computing capacity] and the national security and sovereignty case for building critical digital infrastructure in Britain.” Verdant said it had based its calculations on the electricity capacity that tech firms claim they need – which could still crowd out alternative plans, even if the completed datacentres don’t end up using all the capacity. Labour has classified AI datacentres as critical national infrastructure in an attempt to speed up the planning process, and Andy Burnham has underlined his backing for the sector by appointing AI minister Kanishka Narayan to his cabinet. Narayan has advocated a rapid increase in datacentres, partly on grounds of national sovereignty. He told the Times last month: “The British public is very clear that it wants strong defence. It wants strong, sovereign capability, it doesn’t just want foreign billionaires to own things that matter to our lives. If we’re being true to those British values, it is impossible to achieve that without building a sovereign level of datacentre capacity in this country.” By contrast, the Green party in England has called for a moratorium on building datacentres, while there have been protests in Scotland, amid claims that massive projects are being rushed through. Zack Polanski, the party’s leader in England, said: “The government is planning to steamroller local opposition so private companies can build datacentres – but it can’t explain what the benefits are. ‘“England and Wales are still facing drought after our hottest summer ever, but these datacentres are set to be given priority access to water. Meanwhile, this latest research suggests far fewer jobs may actually be created in constructing and staffing them than the government claims.” In response to the Green party’s call for a “pause”, a government spokesperson insisted that it would “simply send investment and good jobs abroad, while leaving Britain dependent on overseas computing for the processing of sensitive health and defence data”. A spokesperson for TechUK said: “Our estimates that the UK datacentre industry supports 43,500 jobs, and could support 40,000 more by 2035, are built on a published methodology using industry data and standard economic impact assessment techniques. The figures were built transparently from the best available industry data at the time, and we are confident they remain a reasonable estimate of the sector’s employment contribution.”

title: Wednesday briefing: Inside sweeping UK sanctions on trade with Israeli settlements
summary: In today’s newsletter: Ed Miliband has announced the strongest statement on Israel’s actions ever issued by the the UK government, but will it make a meaningful difference to Palestinians?
text: Good morning. For almost half a century, British governments have condemned illegal Israeli settlements, acknowledging they represent an obstacle to peace and threaten the prospect of a two-state solution. And yet no government has ever compelled Israel to stop its expansion. Ed Miliband’s statement in the House of Commons yesterday was an attempt to change that. In a powerful and emotive speech, the foreign secretary recounted childhood memories of picking oranges on his grandmother’s kibbutz, accused Israeli “terrorists” of ethnic cleansing in the West Bank and announced a series of new measures intended to address what he described as a “deeply painful contrast” between rhetoric and reality. It was the strongest statement on Israel’s actions ever issued by the UK government. But will it make a difference to Palestinians living under the omnipresent threat of violence? Today’s newsletter, with the Guardian’s chief Middle East correspondent Emma-Graham Harrison and our diplomatic editor Patrick Wintour, drills into the details of Miliband’s announcement and explores that question. That’s after the headlines. Five big stories UK news | Police have been told by the government they expect better intelligence gathering after masked far-right groups took to the streets at the weekend, the Guardian has learned, as the Kent force admitted mishandling warnings of potential trouble. UK politics | Andy Burnham should tackle inequality in the UK by introducing a wealth tax, universal free personal social care and bringing gas and electricity networks under public ownership, according to a report from more than a dozen influential thinkers. Airline industry | Flight delays and cancellations were expected to continue today at UK airports after another air traffic control failure kept planes grounded for hours, affecting hundreds of thousands of passengers. Iran | Iranian forces claimed to have seized an American underwater drone in the strait of Hormuz that the US military said had “malfunctioned” more than a day earlier. US news | Donald Trump gave sizeable holiday gifts to four White House aides, according to new financial disclosures released by the administration, including $45,000 to executive assistant Natalie Harp. In depth: Could Miliband’s statement shift what seems politically possible? The number of settlers in the occupied West Bank (including East Jerusalem) has risen from 270,000 in 1993 at the time of the Oslo Accords to about 770,000 today. Settlements are often framed as the project of violent extremists backed by far-right cabinet ministers, but Israel’s annexation enjoys longstanding cross-party support. As Emma Graham-Harrison wrote in January, the idea has “persisted in Israeli political imagination,” and although Israeli politicians have condemned settler violence, roughly half of Israelis think settlements help Israel’s security. In August, Benjamin Netanyahu’s government opened the tendering process for construction work on the E1 settlement, a vast project for 1,200 homes that would cut across the heart of the West Bank, dividing it in two and jeopardising the prospect of a two-state solution. Final bids for these contracts close days before the Israeli election next month, and the timing is strategic. “Netanyahu is trying to make E1 an election issue,” Patrick Wintour tells me. Miliband’s predecessors Yvette Cooper and David Lammy condemned the plans for E1, and Cooper backed international sanctions on individual settlers. But neither went as far as Miliband. “He’s a more decisive foreign secretary,” Patrick tells me. “You can’t sporadically say this is an outrage, and then not mention it for two months”. His stance also reflects Labour’s desire to win back voters on the left. The post-match analysis from Labour’s disastrous May local elections focused on the threat of Reform, but the Greens were a bigger threat to Labour’s vote. Miliband acknowledged yesterday that “Labour has not done enough in the face of what is happening”, and has announced these sanctions just before a pivotal byelection in Holborn and St Pancras, where the leader of the Green party, Zack Polanski, will be contesting Keir Starmer’s former seat. *** What has Miliband announced? It’s worth remembering where we were just two years ago, when Starmer’s government was still resisting calls for a ceasefire in Gaza. Although Starmer became more critical of Netanyahu’s government and ultimately recognised Palestinian statehood, Miliband’s speech marked a significant shift in tone and substance from this equivocating stance. He framed his intervention not as an argument with Israelis, “with whom the UK has unshakeable bonds”, but with the conduct of Israel’s government, its illegal occupation of Palestine, and with “settler terrorists”, while attacking the Boycott, Divest and Sanctions movement that calls to limit all trade with Israel. The first measure he announced is a widely anticipated ban on the import of goods from illegal settlements. This is important, not least because these settlements violate international law, but the economic impact of the ban will probably be minimal. The settlement economy is relatively small, and its products are already excluded from a 1995 EU free trade deal that reduces the tariffs on Israeli imports to Europe. It’s also kept alive by generous subsidies from the Israeli government. Israeli exporters to Europe regularly hide the origins of produce grow in settlements, something that could be dealt with by the “comprehensive sanctions regime” Miliband is working up with the business secretary. As significant as the ban itself is the fact France and Canada will join the UK in sanctioning Israeli settlements, a diplomatic coup for Miliband. Far-right ministers such as Bezalel Smotrich and Itamar Ben-Gvir have come out forcefully against Miliband’s sanctions (on Monday, Ben-Gvir issued a statement in Spanish calling for sanctions on Britain over its “occupation” of the Falkland Islands). Part of the reason is because Israel’s economy is bound far more closely to Europe than to the United States, and they fear a domino effect. “The UK is a permanent member of the security council, and they’re worried that Miliband’s statement could shift the window in terms of what seems politically possible,” says Emma. “Someone else stands up and says it, and suddenly, you aren’t taking an initiative – you’re following another country.” *** What will this mean for illegal settlements? One of its most transformative changes could be Miliband’s pledge to take action against companies and individuals who finance or “facilitate” illegal settlements. Any individual or company that wants to bid for government led construction projects, including new settlement expansion, needs a guarantor to underwrite their new property. Settlement residents also need banking services. Under these changes, banks and other companies that provide services to Israeli settlements will be sanctioned. “Hypothetically, this could force mainstream financial organisations in Israel to choose between financing settlements, or doing business with the UK,” Emma says. *** What has the fallout been? Israeli ministers have frequently made their intentions in the West Bank clear, but the gap between reality and the reactions of the international community is vast. Miliband’s statement went some way towards closing that. He announced that the British government officially views Israel’s occupation as unlawful (it had previously declared settlements illegal but remained silent on the wider occupation) and that it will refuse all licences for arms that contribute to the occupation. He chose his words carefully, accusing “settler terrorists” of “ethnic cleansing”. As the Israeli human rights lawyer Michael Sfard observed, the recognition of ethnic cleansing triggers legal obligations on the UK to prevent it in the West Bank, potentially dictating “many aspects of British policy towards Israel”. Israel retaliated by announcing it will be closing the consulate in Jerusalem and banning 11 MPs (on a list topped by Jeremy Corbyn) from entering the country. Meanwhile, the US has threatened “repercussions”. “There is no limit on what Trump could potentially do,” Patrick says. “But it’s worth bearing in mind that he is quite ambivalent about Netanyahu at the moment.” Their relationship has soured over Israel’s refusal to agree to Trump’s peace plan and the ongoing conflict in Iran. Unquestioning bipartisan support for Israel among US politicians appears to be faltering. Rahm Emanuel, Obama’s former chief of staff who is sounding out a presidential bid, has said he would back sanctions on companies financing illegal settlements. Earlier this week, Mike Huckabee, the US ambassador to Israel, attacked Miliband for “Jew hate” over the (not yet announced) sanctions plans, but he has also called settler violence an “act of terror”. Miliband’s statement is a powerful recognition of the international law that Israel has relentlessly tried to reject, and comes at a time when itlooks increasingly isolated. What else we’ve been enjoying Tom Wall’s investigation reveals how councils are paying millions to house at-risk children in unsuitable care homes, including hotels, Airbnb properties and, in one case, a tent. It’s a tough read, but I’m grateful that Tom’s kept the spotlight on children, who need us most and who we, as a society, serve least. title: Birdwatch: the avian equivalent of a catwalk model, blue cranes are under threat
summary: Numbers of the exquisitely graceful species are falling amid loss of food supply and habitat
text: Few birds are quite as elegant as the blue crane. As I watched a pair feeding alongside a busy road in South Africa, against the rather incongruous backdrop of a herd of cows, I was struck by their sheer beauty. With a slender body, curved neck, long legs, elongated tail plumes and a subtle, dove-grey plumage, this bird really is the avian equivalent of a catwalk model. But not all is well for the blue crane. It has the smallest global range of any of the world’s 15 crane species: apart from an isolated population in Namibia, almost all are found in South Africa, where it is celebrated as the national bird. Once common and widespread, blue crane numbers have fallen steadily over the past 50 years, and today between only 25,000 and 46,000 individuals remain in the wild. If the downward trend continues, this species faces a genuine risk of extinction. The reasons for the decline are tediously predictable. As a grassland specialist, when intensive farming takes over, the food supply is inevitably reduced. A lethal cocktail of threats, including illegal poisoning, disturbance, habitat loss and the climate crisis – which this year brought unseasonably early rains followed by drought – mean that its future is far from rosy. But as I watched these beautiful birds, I could forget about their plight for a few moments and quietly rejoice in their exquisite grace.

title: Europeans want a united Europe but question whether it can get there, study finds
summary: A continent-wide crisis of confidence is creating fertile ground for far-right narratives of decline, report suggests
text: Europeans overwhelmingly want a strong, united and independent Europe but question whether it can get there, according to a study that suggests a continent-wide crisis of confidence is creating fertile ground for far-right narratives of decline. The report, based on 5,800 interviews in France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Poland and the UK and analysis of the way Europe is discussed in the politics and media of 15 countries, paints a picture of an ambitious but disillusioned public. It found that 68% of respondents spoke about Europe in terms of a “general deterioration or loss of normality”, compared with just 12% who said they viewed the present moment as a time of “European awakening and renewal”. Many recognised the major challenges facing Europe, including war (43%), economic pressures (33%) and the need for greater international autonomy (29%). But 74% said Europe was not dealing well with them, and 56% believed its future was “in danger”. The problem is not lack of ambition: an overwhelming 73% of respondents harbour a strong European vision of unity and political integration (35%), peace and security (28%) or prosperity (19%), while only 13% hope for “less Europe” or EU dissolution. For many, said the study’s author, Paweł Zerka, a senior fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations (ECFR) thinktank, the problem was “not that they’ve stopped wanting a stronger Europe, but that they no longer believe it’s achievable”. The result, Zerka added, was an “imagination gap. People can picture the kind of Europe they want, but struggle to imagine a credible path from where it is today to where they want it to be. These are matters of policy, not just communication.” A week before the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, is due to deliver her annual “state of the union” address in Brussels, Zerka said the evidence suggested the bloc needed “fewer grand promises” and more “proof of trajectory”. The study cites dozens of conversations with Europeans. “I’m regularly relieved I live in Europe. It’s not perfect and some things are going in the wrong direction, but no region in the world is safer, freer and more democratic,” one German said. However, while he identified the climate crisis and far-right parties as the continent’s greatest challenges, he said they were not being tackled effectively. “Elections focus too much on the here and now, and not enough on the future,” he said. The respondent said he would like Europe in 20 years’ time to be “free, democratic, sustainable, less indebted, politically further to the left [and] peaceful”. Asked whether he thought that was likely to happen, he said: “No.” The study classed Europe’s voters in four categories. The Positives (19%) are staunch pro-Europeans who view current crises as a catalyst for a stronger, more integrated union. The Negatives (39%) believe Europe’s best days are behind it. Almost half of people in France, Germany and Italy – and almost all who voted for radical-right parties such as Germany’s AfD, France’s RN, the Dutch PVV and Reform UK – were Negatives, with 83% speaking of Europe in terms of loss and decline. The Disconnected (12%) are generally apathetic voters for whom EU integration is distant background noise, and the Uncertain (31%) share pro-European values but doubt the continent’s ability to act decisively, keep citizens safe or uphold its values. Almost a third (32%) of respondents across all countries surveyed mentioned “Europe’s slowness” in their responses. As one young Polish citizen, born in the 2000s, put it bluntly: “The EU fundamentally discusses a lot, but does nothing.” The bloc’s failure to stand its ground when confronted by powerful actors was also a recurring theme, mentioned by almost a third (30%) of all respondents, with the EU’s recent tariff concessions to Donald Trump a particularly humiliating symbol. Zerka said the Uncertain group was key to the future trajectory of Europe. “Leaders tend to preach to the Positives or bow down to the Negatives,” he said, but it “is among the ‘uncertain’ where belief in Europe’s future remains up for grabs.” Unlike hardened Eurosceptics, Uncertain voters retain a strong emotional attachment to the European project, the report argues, but are alienated by institutional inertia, bureaucratic slowness and perceived geopolitical weakness. Winning back those doubters would require politicians to demonstrate that collective European action can solve tangible domestic crises, from energy security and defence to climate change and the cost of living crisis, Zerka said.

title: Burnham urged to tackle inequality with policies including wealth tax
summary: Key thinkers suggest other radical measures in Compass report such as free personal social care and abolishing Lords
text: Andy Burnham should tackle inequality in the UK by introducing a wealth tax, universal free personal social care and bringing gas and electricity networks under public ownership, according to a report from more than a dozen influential thinkers. In the lead-up to the first budget of the chancellor, John Healey, this autumn, the Compass thinktank has collated 70 policy options from 15 leftwing thinkers that they argue would deliver on the prime minister’s promise to end 40 years of neoliberalism. Introducing the report, Ending Business as Usual, Michael Jacobs, a former adviser to Gordon Brown, and Neal Lawson, director of Compass and a close friend of Burnham, praise what they call the prime minister’s “invaluable aura of authenticity”. However, they warn that while he has ambitious plans “there is no guarantee that he will be given any longer to deliver results than his immediate predecessor”. The authors argue that it is “simply not the case that a British government can no longer govern from the left of centre”. Among the policy proposals, which the organisation states is “a menu of policy options, not a manifesto”, are a £50,000 cap on political donations, the abolition of the House of Lords and an immediate cost of living package. The plans also include a raft of far-reaching tax policies, including the introduction of a wealth tax on net assets of more than £10m, which would raise about £24bn a year, according to Caitlin Boswell from Tax Justice UK. Other mooted policy ideas include equalising capital gains tax with income tax, which would raise a further £11.3bn a year – enough “to fund the building of 90,000 new social homes”. The Institute for Fiscal Studies has argued such a move would risk lowering total tax revenue and investment, and lead wealthy individuals to move their money or leave the country. The essay also calls for what it describes as the “regressive, outdated and unfair” council tax as well as stamp duty to be replaced with a proportional property tax, noting such a move would result in 23% of households – concentrated in London and the south-east – paying more. “If the new Labour government is serious about rebuilding public confidence and delivering material improvements to people’s lives, it must be prepared to address one of the structural causes of inequality: a tax system that favours wealth over work,” writes Boswell. Suggested social policy changes in England include introducing free personal social care, paid for by a surcharge on income tax rates for people aged over 40, and a contribution from housing wealth. Sebastian Rees, from the Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR) argues that personal care needs, such as washing, dressing and eating should be covered by the state with accommodation or ordinary living costs, remaining the responsibility of the individual and their family, a model currently in place in Scotland. Stating that a 1% surcharge on income tax for the over-40s would raise between £8bn and £9bn, it also argues that care costs could be secured against a property and recovered after sale or death. This would “would allow housing wealth to contribute to the cost of reform without requiring people to sell their home when they first need care,” says Rees. Elsewhere, the report calls for universal free childcare, which it argues would “boost the economy, support children’s development, help families and promote gender equality”. Chris Hayes, from Common Wealth, calls for government-owned companies to be put in charge of running energy networks, as well as the setting up of regional energy boards, while the director of politics at Green Alliance, Holly Brazier Tope, argues for a climate resilience standard for critical infrastructure. Michael Jacobs, professor of political economy at the University of Sheffield, said Burnham and his chancellor must resist pressure to conform to the “moderation and orthodoxy” that he argues ended the tenures of Keir Starmer and Rachel Reeves. “There are a wealth of alternatives,” he says. “As Burnham knows, the public is disillusioned with politics and angry with their politicians. He does not have long to prove to voters that, when he says he wants to end business as usual, he means it.”

title: ‘It’s like a death sentence’ says British widow facing deportation from Sweden
summary: Exclusive: Joyce Thomas, 78, describes her ‘nightmare’ hours before the deadline for her removal from country
text: A 78-year-old British widow facing deportation over from Sweden over Brexit has said she feels she is facing a “death sentence” just hours before she was due to be removed from the country. “I just want this nightmare to go away before I die,” says Joyce Thomas. “It is dragging me down. I am really not the same person I was. This has taken years. I just feel sick,” she adds as she packs her bags. Thomas, a retired nurse, who has lived in Sweden for 22 years, was given four weeks to leave the country in August, separating her from her son, grandchildren, large network of friends, her church and her husband’s grave. Her husband, Gwynne, died in 2023 of cancer. It was on a trip back from the UK in 2022, when they visited their second son in Brighton, that they first learned they should have made a formal application to stay in Sweden after Brexit. Her subsequent application to stay in the country in 2023 missed the official deadline but she said her husband who looked after all the household administration, had previously been told there was nothing the couple needed to do after Brexit. She was first told to leave the country in November and after an appeal received the news in August that the administrative court in Luleå upheld Sweden’s migration agency decision that she could not stay. The migration agency says that simply not knowing she had to apply to stay by the cutoff date at the end of 2021 was not a “reasonable ground” for staying in the country. So Thomas had little choice on Monday: she got up at 6am to thoroughly clean her flat, cook for supporters that night, and pack her bags for the UK. Then, late on Monday evening, she was advised that she could stay pending a late application by a lawyer for a review of the removal order. However, her plight remains the same with the threat of a deportation merely in abeyance. “I am very stressed,” she says kneeling over two suitcases beside Tia, a collie lent to her for company in the past few weeks by a friend. “I just want this nightmare to go before I die. I need a peaceful life at my time of life. This is what I want. I just want to get up and be normal,” says Thomas. Thomas is one of hundreds, potentially thousands of Britons who have either been told to leave voluntarily or removed forcibly through deportation since Brexit. Last week the migration agency confirmed it had already deported 458 including one 34-year-old who had been in the country since he was 10. Another British businessman was taken into detention last week in Stockholm to be deported. “I just wish one of those people [in the authorities] had parents in my situation. I think they would think twice because it is the worst think they can do to a human being,” says Thomas. She appealed to the European Commission and the Swedish government to intervene not just for her but for all the British citizens who have simply made “a mistake” because they did not know Sweden required a formal application to remain after Brexit. “Please, please can you hear us. We have done nothing wrong. We are not criminals,” she says. “People here are suffering mentally, physically. “It is cruel. It is inhumane. They must read the papers to know that I am really low. I just feel sick.” No British minister has said anything about Britons being deported from Sweden since the controversy erupted, apart from the former business secretary Peter Kyle who appealed to the Swedish government on behalf of Thomas’s son, who lives in the constituency next to his. Her local MP, Håkan Svenneling, raised her case in the Swedish parliament, claiming the controversy is damaging relations between the EU and the UK, while the opposition Centre party has vowed to offer a repreive to Britons with new laws if it gets into power after Sunday’s general election. She says she has been a brilliant “actor” and gives people the impression she is coping but that is far from the truth. “This waiting month by month, year by year is like a death sentence. That is how I feel because I am not getting a clear answer [about my future] and I am in limbo all the time. “At the start of this I was ready to take my life because I was so depressed. I am coping now with a lot of help from good people but it is still hard. Inside I am not coping at all.” Sweden is among 13 countries, along with the UK, that opted for a “constitutive” system requiring citizens to formally apply to remain in the country. Others, like Spain, opted for a less onerous “declaratory” system requiring registration in the country, something many Britons would already have done at their town hall. But campaigners at Brits in Sweden say countless British citizens were either given no information or incorrect information about what to do after Brexit by the authorities. “All I did was make a mistake, a mistake,” says Thomas. “Even with a parking fine they give you notice if you have not paid the fine; why didn’t they tell us we had to apply, and send us a reminder? We got nothing, never mind a reminder.” The migration agency has said it had no mandate to contact British citizens on the population register to tell them what to do. Under the withdrawal agreement late applications for permits to remain resident after Brexit were permitted as long as there were “reasonable grounds”. On Friday the Swedish migration agency told the Guardian it had “no indication” that Sweden had in any way interpreted the withdrawal agreement in an extreme manner or differently from other member states. “The Swedish migration agency has applied applicable law, and there has been an opportunity to appeal rejection decisions,” it said.

title: Country diary: Wetland plants have prospered this year – and I love this understated beauty | Sarah Lambert
summary: Ailsworth, Cambridgeshire: Trifid bur-marigold is struggling nationally, but thanks to a little ‘Goldilocks’ land management, it has the perfect conditions here
text: After a night of storms, the air feels freshly washed. I breathe in delicious scents of damp grass, earth, and sweet, winey blackberry from hedges weighed down with a bumper harvest. Once again, I’m drawn to the River Nene, a ribbon of blue and green that snakes lazily through the valley. I stand for a while on the bridge over Ailsworth weir, where water spills and chatters over bright green swathes of river water-crowfoot. For a moment its steady white noise overpowers the nearby A1. The main river is slow and silent, yet its margins are bright with flowers: purple loosestrife, marsh woundwort, water mint, water forget-me-not and celery-leaved buttercup. Together they make a loose embroidery of mauve, blue and yellow among the green – quite the contrast from the scorched gold fields I’ve become used to. But the plant that catches my eye is trifid bur-marigold, with its understated, button-like golden flowers. Its name comes from its mostly three-part leaves and fruits that are tipped with barbed bristles, ready to hitch a lift on passing cattle, dogs, maybe an otter, or even humans. Once familiar in places that are flooded in winter but exposed in summer, it has declined nationally owing to factors including drainage and canalisation of watercourses, and is now “vulnerable” in Great Britain. But, like many wetland plants, it has prospered this year. With ready access to water, endless days of sunshine and warmth have allowed unusually lush growth. An annual species, it needs bare, damp mud in spring for seed germination – and thanks to the Red Ruby Devon cattle which have poached the soft river’s edge, here it has the perfect conditions. But management that suits one species can trouble another. Too much trampling erodes the riverbank, and loosened silt may choke up the clean gravels used by spawning fish. Yet fencing stock out entirely lets vigorous perennials close over the muddy margins, excluding the bur-marigold. Nene Park Trust, which owns the site, has met the dilemma with a simple gated fence set well back from the water. This allows cattle grazing in measured doses. You could call it a Goldilocks arrangement: not too much disturbance, not too little, but just enough for this golden-flowered plant to keep its place beside the river. • Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024, is available now at guardianbookshop.com

title: ‘Miserable and impossible’: food scarce in Kyiv as Russia targets supply chains
summary: Supermarket shelves half-filled in Ukrainian capital as Moscow bombs warehouses supporting civilian life
text: Stocking up on cured sausages from the half-empty shelves in her local supermarket, Valentyna Sveshnikova is worried about money. The 68-year-old grandmother lives off her small pension and has already noticed the cost of several goods increase, including sausages. Russia wants “to make our life miserable and impossible. And they’re actually succeeding in it,” she says. Russian strikes on food warehouses and logistics supply chains around several Ukrainian cities have left gaps on supermarket shelves and risk causing price increases. Kyiv has faced a particularly intense barrage of attacks. A temporary truce that was in place between Moscow and Kyiv to ensure the safe passage of US negotiators over the weekend ended abruptly on Monday night when jet-powered drones and ballistic missiles pounded Ukraine’s capital, killing two people. Many shelves at the Novus supermarket where Sveshnikova is shopping for groceries are empty. But customers, hardened by four years of war, are sanguine. “It’s scary, but I don’t plan to go anywhere,” says 40-year-old Dariya Malyukova. The agrarian policy and food minister, Taras Vysotsky, has warned that food prices could increase by 2.5% because of the attacks on warehouse infrastructure. But Dmytro Krymskiy, the co-founder of Bureau of Wine, which operates several high-end retail brands in Ukraine, including the supermarket chain Goodwine, says the impact could be as high as 15%. One of Krymskiy’s warehouses near Kyiv was hit on 1 September, wiping out €4m (£3.4m) of stock. The attacks “seriously hurt our business”, he says. Krymskiy says that prices will increase not because of a shortage of supplies, but because of the cost of reorganising supply chains to make them more resilient against strikes. He is exploring several options, including moving his warehouses to a neighbouring country such as Poland, using underground storage facilities and splitting his stock across several smaller sites. “We understand that we cannot have only one big warehouse,” he said. Krymskiy thinks his prices could rise by about 5%. The latest strike did not come as a complete surprise; it was the third time since the start of the full-scale invasion that his warehouses had been hit. The first, in 2022, destroyed €15m of supplies, while another attack in July this year annihilated €1.5m-worth of goods. “It was really a matter of time,” he says. “The problem is, we had 3,000 pallets there, and you simply cannot move it,” he says. The recent onslaught of airborne attacks also meant that warehouse staff could only work for three to four hours per day, reducing the company’s ability to shift stock. The raids come at a difficult time for Ukraine. Kyiv has been hit by a torrent of daily drone and missile strikes since late August, killing dozens of people and destroying key infrastructure. As well as the food warehouses, Russia has targeted e-commerce logistics hubs and stockpiles of medical supplies. On Wednesday night, one of the World Health Organization’s main warehouses storing humanitarian aid on the outskirts of Kyiv was hit. At the warehouse of Biokon, a pharmaceutical company, the air was thick with the smell of burnt fuel on Friday as firefighters picked through the wreckage of the building. The company said in a statement that three months of medicines had been destroyed and that it had suspended all operations. Shopkeepers and customers say that most people are not panic-buying food in the way that they were in 2022. “What’s the point?” says Iryna Mesyanzhynova, a 54-year-old woman shopping for groceries at ATB, a low-cost supermarket in Brovary, near some of the burnt-out warehouses. “I have a bit of extra products, like porridge oats, but for the rest – vegetables, fruits – why would I buy them? They will just rot. “I’m trying to deal with today’s problem,” she says. “I try not to think about the future.” In a statement to the Guardian, Vysotsky, the agrarian policy and food minister, said that the logistics hubs of all of Ukraine’s leading supermarket chains, including Novus, ATB, Silpo and Fora had been destroyed or significantly damaged in the recent strikes. “This wave of strikes is the most massive since the beginning of the full-scale invasion,” Vysotsky said. “If in 2022 the enemy attacked mainly export-agricultural infrastructure, and in the following years destroyed the energy sector, then the attacks of August-September 2026 are a systemic attack on the internal civilian life support system. The enemy is purposefully trying to destroy the logistics that provide Ukrainian cities with food.” Aside from growing their own food, which many people already do, Ukrainians have few options other than trying to continue as normal. The attacks are “not our first of the war”, says Olena Zhuk, a 36-year-old travel manager shopping at a central Kyiv farmer’s market. “We will survive. We will not die from the hunger.” Additional reporting by Illia Dyadik

title: UK air traffic control chaos disrupts flights for hundreds of thousands of passengers
summary: More than 1,000 flights cancelled with problems continuing on Wednesday and airlines calling for overhaul after third incident in just over three years
text: Flight delays and cancellations were expected to continue into Wednesday at UK airports after another air traffic control failure kept planes grounded for hours, affecting hundreds of thousands of passengers. At least 177 flights scheduled for Wednesday to and from UK airports had been cancelled, plane tracking site Flightradar24 said, “nearly all at London Heathrow”. More than 1,000 were cancelled by about 8pm on Tuesday. The “technical issue” at the air traffic control services provider Nats caused Britain’s third major stoppage in just over three years. Nats said on Tuesday evening: “This has been a very complex recovery and has created difficulties for the whole aviation network, from which it will take time to recover.” The breakdown started at about 1pm on Tuesday and affected departing flights at many of Britain’s biggest airports including Heathrow, Gatwick, Manchester and Stansted. By the time Nats said it had fixed its flight processing system almost four hours later, most flights scheduled to depart were yet to take off. The disruption spread to include incoming flights to much of southern England. Cancellations and delays continued through Tuesday evening, and British Airways said disruption would affect operations into Wednesday at least, with passengers offered free rebooking until Friday. Nats provides air traffic control services to 15 UK airports. Ryanair said more than 65,000 passengers had been delayed and 50 flights cancelled. The knock-on effects hit flights across Europe, according to easyJet. Some inbound flights had to be held at airports abroad, said Eurocontrol, the European airspace co-ordinator. London airports, as well as Manchester and Birmingham, were among the most directly affected. Flights to and from other airports around the UK, including Edinburgh and Belfast, were also disrupted. Heathrow said late on Tuesday that departures had resumed with disruptions but arrivals had been suspended for the rest of the night. Nats initially announced at 1.46pm that it was “investigating a technical issue which is causing some disruption to flight departures”. It later identified the problem in its flight processing system, and announced at 4.40pm that it was fixed. A spokesperson said the fault was not the same as those that caused outages and mass disruption in 2023 and 2025. “We are continuing to work closely with our airline and airport customers on recovery. We apologise sincerely for the disruption to people’s journeys today and they should continue to check with their airline.” The chief executive of Nats, Martin Rolfe, was scheduled to brief the transport secretary, Heidi Alexander, on Wednesday over the breakdown. Alexander will in turn address MPs in the Commons for the second reading of the civil aviation bill. Rolfe expressed his “huge sympathies to everyone who has been caught up in today’s disruption”. “We absolutely take responsibility for this,” he told Sky News. “We never want this sort of thing to happen. I completely understand how frustrating it is for passengers.” He claimed, however, “these things are relatively rare”. “We resolved it to get back to our systems operating normally,” he added. “But of course, there’s a huge amount of disruption that’s now built up in the system. “We’re working very closely now with airlines and airports to try to work through the night to make sure that we can get as many people travelling as possible.” The air traffic control problems follow an “isolated event” a year ago that caused widespread disruption, and appeared less severe than the full grounding of flights in August 2023, which prompted a parliamentary inquiry. British Airways said that “the severity of the issue means there will be a significant knock-on impact for customers and colleagues”. “We were forced to cancel or divert more than 100 flights on Tuesday afternoon, inconveniencing tens of thousands of customers,” a spokesperson said. “This incident was entirely out of our control and incredibly frustrating for our customers and colleagues, with aircraft and crews ending up out of place.” Airlines renewed calls for Nats to be overhauled. Ryanair repeated its demand for Rolfe to resign. The airline’s chief operating officer, Neal McMahon, said: “Families travelling on holiday, people travelling for work and thousands of visitors to the UK have once again paid the price for Nats’ abhorrent failure.” He said the government should “stop making excuses for repeated Nats failures and appoint a new leader capable of running the UK ATC system”. Wizz Air said: “A critical national infrastructure provider should not repeatedly bring the aviation system to a standstill. Nats is simply not fit for purpose in its current form.” Alexander, said: “I’m aware of a technical issue impacting flights at airports including Heathrow and Gatwick. Technicians have identified the issue and are fixing it as we speak. I know this will be frustrating for passengers and I’m sorry. “I am seeking assurances that lessons will be learned and systems that support aviation are up to the job.”

title: Pilots tried to abort landing seconds before deadly Amazon cargo plane crash
summary: Five killed were aircraft cleaning company employees in van struck by plane after it overran Miami airport runway
text: Officials in Florida on Tuesday said evidence collected from Saturday’s Amazon cargo plane crash at Miami international airport suggests the pilots considered aborting the flight’s landing before it crashed and killed five people on the ground. At a press conference on Tuesday evening, officials from the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) released data from the plane’s “black box” flight data recorder, which was recovered from the wreckage on Monday, indicating pilots initiated a “go-around”, or aborted landing, seconds before impact. The NTSB said that ‌30 seconds before the end of the flight data recording, the nose landing gear and right main landing gear touched down, while 19 seconds before the end of the recording, the left main ⁠landing gear touched down. A few seconds later, the brakes were released and the throttles were increased to values consistent ‌with go-around thrust. The NTSB added there was no indication in the recorded data that speed brakes or thrust reversers were deployed. Jennifer Homendy, the NTSB chair, said the pilots will be interviewed on Wednesday, and details from the cockpit voice recorder will be released publicly after that interview. The NTSB will be conducting further analysis on the flight data and other available evidence to determine the cause of the accident, officials said. Earlier Tuesday, officials identified the five people killed on Saturday – and said two more remained hospitalized in critical condition. At a morning news conference, the Miami-Dade sheriff, Rosie Cordero-Stutz, also said both pilots of the Amazon Prime Air Boeing 767, which careered off the end of the airport’s runway and struck at least two vehicles, were released from the hospital after treatment. The aircrew, whom she did not name, were the only two people onboard. The sheriff identified Rolando Aleman Leon, 55; Yoel Rodriguez Narajo, 53; Julio C Pineda, 75; Carlos Acosta Fajardo, 53; and Javierkys Reyes Quevedo, 47, as those killed on the ground. All five dead and the two people most seriously hurt – men aged 79 and 32 – were in a Ford Econoline van that was hit by the aircraft, operated by the all-cargo airline 21 Air llc under contract to Amazon, while it landed after a flight from San Juan, Puerto Rico, and crashed through fencing on to a roadway. The victims killed were employees of Professional Ocean Service Corporation, an aircraft contract cleaning company, which released a statement on Tuesday paying tribute to its dead workers. “Our employees are far more than the people who work beside us each day, they are family, and they are deeply loved,” the statement said. “Our hearts and prayers are with every employee and every family whose lives have been forever changed. We grieve with those who lost a loved one and pray for the healing and recovery of those who were injured.” The lives of the families of the victims had been torn apart, Cordero-Stutz told reporters at the news conference. “[We’re] trying to identify what happened and how it occurred, but for those families, they are going to be living with this for the rest of their lives,” she said. “So it’s a very difficult time, and it’s very difficult on each and every one of these families.” Investigators from the NTSB continued their examination of the crash site on Tuesday as the airport began to return to normal operations after three days of cancellations and delays. At a press conference on Monday afternoon, Homendy said teams were working through a scene of “utter devastation” after the crash, which occurred after a thunderstorm. The aircraft, she said, traveled about 1,300ft beyond the paved surface at the end of the runway and through a perimeter fence. The crash left a wide field of debris, including airbags and other parts of the destroyed vehicles, sections of the aircraft, and fencing. “It’s pretty extensive,” she said. “Hard to see, and I’m sure it must have been very difficult for the responders as well. I would describe it in one word as devastating, utter devastation.” Video showed the plane touched down far along the runway, prompting speculation its speed was too high to be able to stop safely. Other factors being examined, Homendy said, were weather conditions before and during the landing, and the mechanical condition of the 32-year-old plane that was completing its third flight of the day. Although the NTSB team would remain on site for about a week, she added, they would focus on recovering as much “perishable” evidence as possible, and not immediately determining a cause. Some industry experts have said they believe the circumstances of the crash point towards pilot error. They include Robert Clifford, an aviation attorney who has handled cases in numerous commercial aircraft crashes spanning five decades. “This appears to be a classic tailwind landing mistake where a pilot mistakenly or over-confidently decides to land with a tailwind instead of a headwind,” he said in a statement to the Guardian. That, he said, “causes excessive touchdown speed and distance from the threshold, leaving inadequate stopping distance for the airplane’s braking and reverse thrust systems to handle”. Clifford also noted the absence of any arresting devices or fencing at the end of the runway commonly found at other major airports. Homendy said on Monday the NTSB would be looking at that to determine its impact on the severity of the Miami tragedy. Amazon, meanwhile, said it would work closely with federal investigators on the investigation. Homendy said her team would also examine the relationship between Amazon and 21 Air, the Miami-based aircraft operator. Reuters contributed reporting

title: Lindsay Clancy juror had reasonable doubt but would not agree to acquit, foreperson says
summary: Roni Carlson, in wake of mistrial, says holdout juror could not be persuaded while colleague calls him ‘very arrogant’
text: A lone juror in the trial of Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts mother accused of the murder of her three children, would not agree to acquit Clancy despite expressing reasonable doubt about whether she was guilty, the jury’s foreperson said in an interview airing on Monday. Speaking to NBC 10 Boston just days after Clancy’s trial ended in a mistrial, Roni Carlson, the foreperson, confirmed there was one holdout juror who would not be persuaded to acquit Clancy due to insanity. “He admitted he had reasonable doubt and I started filling out the forms. I was so excited,” said Carlson, a retired elementary school teacher. According to Carlson, the holdout juror then said: “But I’m still not going to say that she’s not guilty by reason of insanity.” Carlson is one of three jurors who spoke to the Boston NBC affiliate. In the NBC10 interview, another juror, Paula Devlin, called the holdout “very arrogant”, adding: “He really did not take anything that anybody said.” The holdout juror has not yet spoken publicly about the trial. During jury deliberations, Carlson told Massachusetts judge William Sullivan that one member of the 12-person jury was not following the court’s instructions on reasonable doubt. Clancy strangled her three young children in January 2023 before attempting to kill herself by jumping out her bedroom window, leaving her paralyzed. During the closely watched trial, prosecutors argued she intentionally killed the children. The defense argued that Clancy, who did not deny killing her children, had sought help for her declining mental health before suffering a psychotic break. The attorneys cast blame on the healthcare system for overmedicating her, in lieu of properly diagnosing her with postpartum depression. The three jurors told NBC10 that the evidence presented during the trial indicated Clancy was a loving mother. “Everything proved she loved her children, from her journals to her mother-in-law, everything proved that she loved her children. So she had to have snapped and not known what she was doing,” Carlson said. The judge declared a mistrial after the jury could not reach a verdict. Clancy remains held at a psychiatric hospital. A status hearing has been set for 29 September. Prosecutors have not yet announced if they will retry her. In the US, call the national maternal health hotline on 1-833-852-6262. In the UK, the Pandas foundation offers support via WhatsApp on 07903 508334. In Australia, the national maternal and perinatal mental health hotline is 1300 726 306.

title: Ukraine war briefing: Kyiv books in 1,000 Patriots as UK and EU open up missile aid
summary: Germany ‘urgently’ sending PAC-2 interceptors from its stockpile and urges other countries to do the same. What we know on day 1,659
text: Ukraine is ⁠contracting a supply of about 1,000 Patriot missiles over the coming years with the help of allies and ⁠through an E⁠U loan, Kyiv’s defence minister, Yevhenii Khmara, said on Tuesday as the country’s allies met. Germany announced it is “urgently” sending Ukraine part of its stockpile of Patriot Pac-2 interceptors. Berlin’s defence minister, Boris Pistorius, appealed to other supporters of Ukraine “to look into their own stocks and make similar deliveries”. The long-established Pac-2 version destroys ballistic missiles and aircraft by exploding and shredding them with shrapnel, whereas the latest upgrade, the Pac-3, is a higher precision “hit-to-kill” missile that rams into its targets. “I am aware that it is not easy to strike a balance between one’s own security requirements and urgently needed support to Ukraine,” Pistorius said. “But please, if in doubt, decide in favour for Ukraine.” Before the defence contact group meeting started, the UK announced it had committed £100m to boost Ukraine’s air defences by buying US military equipment that will include Patriot interceptors, write Dan Sabbagh and Jamie Grierson. The commitment also covers large-calibre ammunition and drones. Regarding Patriots, Khmara, Kyiv’s defence minister, stressed: “The majority of these [1,000] missiles will only start to be shipped in the coming years, which is why we ask that you supply us the missiles from your stockpiles today.” The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, said Ukraine will ⁠be able to put the ⁠next €3.2bn (£2.7bn; US$3.7bn) disbursement ⁠from the EU’s support loan towards ⁠Patriot. Ukraine says it needs 300 Patriot interceptors to defend itself through the winter. Khmara said Ukraine was also being hindered by a shortfall of $27bn in financing for drone supplies. Khmara said Russia was making no strategic gains along the 1,200km (750-mile) frontline, but was trying to compensate with “terror against Ukrainians”. Russia resumed its near-constant drone and missile attacks on Kyiv on Tuesday after a brief halt ⁠for the visit of US peace negotiators. Officials said five people were killed in the capital and more in several regions. There are signs of a successful operation by Ukraine’s Third Army Corps to recapture a Russian-held finger of land near the strategic town of Lyman in the Donetsk region. War analysts said the action liberated more than 200 square kilometres of territory. In a video posted on Monday, Andrii Biletskyi, commander of the corps, stood in the monastery town of Sviatohirsk west of the salient and taunted Putin over the Russian president’s recent claim that Moscow’s forces had captured it. Military analyst Emil Kastehelmi, of the Finland-based Black Bird conflict analysis group, told Reuters that the extent of the Ukrainians’ gains remained unclear. September and October could see the year’s most intense fighting in Donetsk, with Russia potentially trying to stage new mechanised assaults, Michael Kofman of the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace told Reuters. “As the weather conditions deteriorate, drones become less effective. And that’s usually where Russians try to return mobility to the battlefield.” But Ukraine had developed a solid defence against such attacks, Kofman added, pointing to a failed Russian assault in July near the city of Dobropillia. Russian forces are less than 15km (9 miles) from Sloviansk and Kramatorsk, the two main cities in the “fortress belt”. Both are under worsening strikes by drones and guided bombs, regional officials have said. Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump on Tuesday had an hour-long phone call, a summary of which was only available from the Kremlin at time of writing. Trump called for a speedy end to the fighting, said Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov. Putin “pointed out what the Americans could realistically do to bring the hostilities to a swift conclusion” and stressed that Russia had “no aggressive plans” towards Europe. Volodymyr Zelenskyy meanwhile said Russian, Ukrainian and US negotiators could meet as early as this month. “If all sides agree, we also want to hold it in the autumn. If September works out, then it would be great. The earlier, the better.” A Bloomberg report predicted no serious moves towards peace by Russia until 2027. Romania’s SRI intelligence service said it prevented a sabotage ⁠operation coordinated by Russia on Romanian territory. “The Russian citizen was instructed by an intermediary to make photo-video materials with targets of ⁠strategic military interest, including Ukrainian Antonov cargo aircraft during their presence on the national territory.” Suspected Russian agents tried to blow up an Antonov in August at Leipzig/Halle Airport in Germany. The SRI said: “The investigation also ‌revealed that the Russian Federation continues to use persons from vulnerable categories to carry out such illegal activities.” Russian authorities said they detained a suspect in last week’s shooting of a senior military officer. The Federal Security Service said a 21-year-old Moldovan national was arrested for being allegedly “involved in an assassination attempt” at the behest of Ukrainian intelligence services. Russia’s investigative committee said the officer was shot at least six times on 3 September on the outskirts of Engels. The city in the Saratov region hosts Russian strategic bombers that are used to attack Ukraine.
