title: US says Iranian tankers ‘destroyed’ after missile attacks on American warship
summary: Tit-for-tat violence surges again in region, with tankers struck by the US in the Gulf of Oman, and reprisal attacks by Iran on a US base in Jordan
text: The US military on Tuesday said it had “destroyed” several Iranian tankers after Iran attempted to strike a US navy warship with ballistic missiles, as violence once again surged across the region, pushing the price of oil past $100 a barrel. American forces struck the tankers in the Gulf of Oman and near Iran’s Kharg Island, US central command (Centcom) said in a statement, adding that American forces “directed the crews to abandon ship before the vessels were struck”. Centom said the strikes came after the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) targeted a US Navy warship with ballistic missiles twice over the past two days. “The US warship successfully evaded the attempted Iranian attacks and continued to patrol regional waters. No American personnel were harmed,” it said in a statement. The IRGC said they had struck a US military base in Jordan in retaliation. Air-defence systems destroyed 18 ⁠of the ⁠20 ballistic missiles originating ⁠from Iranian territory, Jordan’s state ⁠news agency ‌reported, citing the ‌armed forces, adding that two missiles fell in unpopulated areas ‌and there were no casualties. The IRGC also said they ⁠attacked ⁠two US vessels and eight ⁠oil tankers in the Gulf, after warning crews of oil tankers near ports in Kuwait and Bahrain to immediately leave their vessels. After a month of relative calm in August, Iran and the US have resumed exchanges of fire, sending ‌global oil prices back up to levels last seen in July. On Wednesday, oil prices rose above $100 a barrel in early Asia trading. On Tuesday, Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis attacked four cities in Saudi Arabia, wounding more than 70 people and setting oil installations ablaze in what appeared to be a significant expansion of the Middle East war. Saudi Arabia said it would retaliate after the strikes – reportedly involving dozens of drones and missiles – that targeted several oil facilities in the country’s south. Remarking on the latest strikes by Iran, Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, said the US would not let Iran’s attacks to go unanswered. “Iran continues to try to hit US naval ships. And for every time they do that or try to do that, they’re going to lose tankers. And I think you’ll see that again today,” Rubio said on Tuesday, during a trip to Colombia. The strikes followed an earlier dispute over an American underwater drone in the strait of Hormuz, which the IRGC claimed to have seized as part of a “complex intelligence and operational action at dawn”, according to Iranian state TV. In a statement, the IRGC said images of the vessel would be released shortly. In a statement, US Navy Capt Tim Hawkins, a United States Centcom spokesperson, said the submersible was “defective” and an older model “that neither collected sensitive data nor carried any classified sonar or radar equipment”. Operations in the area continue, he said. Iran has maintained a blockade of the strait of Hormuz, which normally carries about one-fifth of the global oil and gas shipments, since the outbreak of the war more than six months ago, while the US has imposed its own blockade of Iranian ports. In Paris, South Korean president Lee Jae Myung and French president Emmanuel Macron discussed cooperation on security and freedom of navigation in the strait of Hormuz. South Korea’s defence ministry said it had sent an inspection team to the United Arab Emirates to assess security conditions in the region, but stressed that the mission was intended to gather information and did not presuppose a troop deployment. A South Korean official said Iran had expressed interest and sought explanations through diplomatic channels after media reports about a possible South Korean role in Hormuz security efforts. South Korea’s presidential office ⁠separately said reports that the US had set a deadline for Seoul to send assets to Hormuz were untrue. Seoul said last week it was reviewing various options, including military measures, to contribute to freedom of navigation in Hormuz, but denied reports that the US had set a deadline for Seoul to dispatch assets to the strait. Trump has struggled to end the unpopular war, which has claimed the lives of 18 US service members. Iranian authorities have previously put the overall death toll from US and Israeli strikes in the thousands, figures that outside observers, including US-based monitoring groups, have broadly corroborated.

title: Mamdani releases 170,000 pages of records regarding impact on air quality of 9/11 attacks
summary: Documents available through an online portal launched three days before the 25th anniversary of September 11
text: New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani’s administration has released more than 170,000 pages of municipal records involving the impact of the September 11 attacks on air quality health, as well as the city’s response. Mamdani announced the documents and an online portal for accessing them on Tuesday. The release comes alongside the settlement of two lawsuits pursued by 9/11 Health Watch, which fought for access to these long-withheld documents. “For too long, New Yorkers have had to fight for access to records that should have been available to them in the first place,” Mamdani said in a statement. “The devastating truth is that the suffering did not end once the smoke cleared and the dust settled,” Mamdani also said at a press conference. “People got sick because the leaders they trusted lied and told them they were safe to breathe in toxic air.” The tranche of documents offers just a fraction of air quality reports on Ground Zero. But they do include an internal memo where New York City weighed possible liability related to air quality. The release of these records comes three days before the 25th anniversary of 9/11 – which killed nearly 3,000 people in New York City, Washington and Pennsylvania. The documents provide further evidence that city officials knew air surrounding the twin towers was toxic – but misled the public into thinking it was safe, officials said. “My colleagues and I who represented Ground Zero and the surrounding communities immediately warned local and federal officials of the health risks posed by toxins in the air at the time,” congressman Jerry Nadler said in a statement. “Our warnings were not heeded, and now we and the public know that city hall, led by former mayor [Rudy] Giuliani, predicted that thousands of responders and community members would face devastating long-term health impacts from these toxins.” New York City council member Gale Brewer voiced similar sentiments. “For 25 years, first responders, survivors, families, and people who lived, worked and went to school in lower Manhattan have lived with the health consequences of 9/11 while critical pieces of the city’s own record – HOW they got sick – remained out of reach,” she said in a statement. The portal, Brewer said, “is a great first step toward giving the public access to that record, one that has been denied them under previous administrations.” Ben Chevat, executive director of 911 Health Watch, thanked Mamdani for “being the mayor, after 25 years, who finally begins to answer the question: ‘What did the city know about the dangers from the toxic cloud at Ground Zero and when did it know it?’ “For 25 years, four different Mayoral administrations kept from the public, the US Congress, and the city council documents showing what the city actually knew about the danger of the toxic chemicals in lower Manhattan and western Brooklyn after the World Trade Center collapse, even as city officials continued messaging to the public that the air was ‘safe and acceptable’,” he said in a statement.

title: Trump-backed John Sununu wins New Hampshire Republican Senate primary
summary: Frontrunner Sununu beats Scott Brown to earn Republican nod in closely watched race in November
text: Former senator John E Sununu triumphed on Tuesday in the New Hampshire Republican Senate primary over Scott Brown, earning the GOP nod in what will probably be a must-win race if Democrats hope to seize the upper chamber. Sununu, 61, was the clear frontrunner in the GOP primary. He served one term in the Senate from 2003 to 2009. Brown represented Massachusetts, later moved to New Hampshire, and served as US ambassador to New Zealand and Samoa during Donald Trump’s first term. The US president threw his support behind Sununu earlier this year, despite the former lawmaker’s past criticism of Trump, including a 2024 op‑ed in which Sununu called Trump a “loser” and backed Nikki Haley in the Republican presidential primary. On the trail, Sununu has tried to show daylight between himself and the administration, criticizing Trump’s tariff policy, urging Congress to rein in executive power, and questioning the decision to launch military action in Iran. He told New Hampshire Public Radio it was “a tactical mistake” to go to war “without having a plan for protecting the strait of Hormuz”. That posture may matter in a state where Trump’s approval rating sits at 38%. Sununu and Brown did not respond to the Guardian’s interview requests. Kristen Cianci, a spokesperson for the Republican National Committee (RNC), said Sununu was a “strong candidate” who was “well positioned to beat out Pappas” in a general election. “While Democrats have been consumed by infighting, Republicans have been laser-focused on real issues like affordability and security,” she added in a statement. Sununu will face congressman Chris Pappas, who beat back a progressive challenger in the Democratic primary, advancing as most observers expected to what will be a closely watched general election that is critical to Democratic hopes of flipping the upper chamber. Some Democrats, however, worry New Hampshire could become a sleeper risk – a state where Republicans control the legislature but haven’t won a Senate race since 2010, when Kelly Ayotte, now the governor, captured a seat.

title: Congressman Chris Pappas wins New Hampshire Democratic Senate primary
summary: Pappas fends off challenge from progressive Karishma Manzur in seat to be vacated by retiring Jeanne Shaheen
text: Congressman Chris Pappas beat back progressive challenger Karishma Manzur in the Democratic primary for US Senate in New Hampshire on Tuesday, advancing as most observers expected to what will be a closely watched general election that is critical to Democratic hopes of flipping the upper chamber. The two were competing for the nomination that opened up after Jeanne Shaheen, 79, the state’s three‑term incumbent Democratic senator, announced her retirement. Pappas, a popular centrist, has served in the House since 2019 and has crossed the aisle at various points. He calls himself “battle‑tested” and has consolidated establishment backing, earning endorsements from leading Democratic lawmakers and former vice‑president Kamala Harris. His family’s name also carries weight in New Hampshire: the Pappases own the Puritan Backroom, the century‑old Manchester restaurant famed for allegedly inventing the chicken tender and long embedded in the state’s retail‑politics circuit. Support for Israel played a large role in the primary, as it has in many intraparty contests this year. Manzur, who supports Medicare for All and higher taxes on mega‑corporations and the ultra‑wealthy, has repeatedly highlighted the money Pappas has received from donors aligned with the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac). She casts him as milquetoast and ineffective. “I was tired of choosing between the lesser of two evils and still seeing so much pain and suffering right here in my state,” she said. Pappas has long backed US aid to Israel but told the Guardian that Benjamin Netanyahu was “not a trustworthy ally of the US” and said he hoped the Israeli prime minister would be ousted in the country’s October election. Pappas noted he has rejected corporate Pac money in this race but did not directly address his support from pro‑Israel donors, instead pointing to a “broad‑based effort” of individual contributors that have supported his Senate bid. Pappas will face the Donald Trump-endorsed former senator John E Sununu, who is seeking a return to the seat he once held and is part of a political dynasty that includes his father and brother, both former governors. Some Democrats worry New Hampshire could become a sleeper risk – a state where Republicans control the legislature but have not won a Senate race since 2010, when Kelly Ayotte, now the governor, captured a seat.

title: Missouri congressional maps thrown into chaos after conflicting court rulings
summary: Tug of war as federal judge says old maps cannot be used in November, hours after supreme court blocked new maps backed by Trump
text: Clashing court rulings plunged Missouri’s congressional elections into uncertainty on Tuesday, the latest in a legal tug-of-war that comes less than two months before the November midterms that will decide which party controls a closely divided Congress. First, the conservative justice Brett Kavanaugh denied the emergency request from Missouri officials to use a congressional map in November that was redrawn with Donald Trump’s support to give Republicans an edge in the midterms. Then, shortly thereafter, a ruling by a federal judge in Missouri temporarily prevented the state from using its old congressional maps in the November elections. The temporary restraining order, known as a TRO, was issued by US district judge Stephen Clark and ordered Missouri to use the newly drawn districts that favor Republicans, which the state had used in its August primary elections. “Using a different map for the general election would wreak havoc on the fairness and orderliness of Missouri’s congressional elections, calling into question the candidacy of those nominated in the primaries and the votes of those who voted in the primaries. Widespread voter confusion would inevitably follow,” Clark, who was appointed by the president, wrote. “The public interest factor thus weighs in favor of a TRO.” That order was swiftly appealed to the eighth US circuit court of appeals. Tuesday’s legal action came after the Missouri supreme court ruled that the map must go before voters to approve or reject the new districts, meaning it cannot be used in the November election. The president and Republicans had fumed over the decision, with Trump calling it “horrible, ridiculous, and unConstitutional”. The state’s attorney general argued the decision would disenfranchise Missouri voters and thrust the state into a “full‑fledged constitutional crisis”. Trump set in motion a national redistricting battle last year as a way to give Republicans an advantage in the midterm elections, in which the party that controls the White House has historically lost seats. But with Trump plagued by low approval ratings and an unpopular war against Iran, Republicans are bracing for potentially major losses in the House and possibly even control of the Senate. Failure to cement the Republican redistricting effort in Missouri would be a rare setback for the party that has largely succeeded in redrawing congressional lines. Missouri was the second Republican state to act in response to the president’s push to redraw congressional maps to favor Republicans. Mike Kehoe, the state’s governor, called the legislature into a special session last year to create new boundaries ahead of the US midterm elections. The revised map targeted the fifth congressional district, held by longtime Democratic representative Emanuel Cleaver of Kansas City. It reassigned portions of Kansas City to two neighboring districts represented by Republicans and stretched the remainder of Cleaver’s district far eastward into rural Republican areas. Cleaver was unopposed in the Democratic primary. State senator Rick Brattin won the Republican primary in the reshaped district. Kehoe backed the temporary block of the old congressional maps on Tuesday, saying it provided “clarity” in the election process. “With today marking the deadline for changes to the November ballot, the Missouri First Map will be used in the general election. Voters and candidates deserve consistency, certainty, and not to have the rules changed between elections,” Kehoe wrote on X. While Republicans in the state celebrated the latest legal twist in their favor, Chuck Hatfield, an attorney for People Not Politicians, an advocacy group that sponsored the referendum petition, said the decision from the state’s supreme court remains in effect. “An individual federal judge cannot overrule the Missouri supreme court,” he said. The Associated Press contributed reporting

title: California confirms rare sighting of gray wolf in Mendocino national forest
summary: Officials say sighting a sign species – driven to extinction in state before reintroduction in 2011 – expanding its range
text: A gray wolf has recently been seen in California’s Mendocino national forest for the first time since the species returned to the state 15 years ago, state wildlife officials confirmed. Officials in Lake county, which is about two hours north of San Francisco, said last week the California department of fish and wildlife (CDFW) had received reports of sightings in the forest in late August. The agency verified the presence of a wolf in the far north end of the county, county supervisor Brad Rasmussen said in a statement on social media. The CDFW confirmed the sightings in a statement, telling the Guardian it had received two separate reports from an area where Mendocino, Glenn and Lake counties meet. The agency received photos and were on the ground to confirm the presence of the animal the following day, said Alicia de la Garza, the CDFW deputy director of public affairs. “The sighting was verified by a CDFW wolf biologist who confirmed the validity of the photos, conducted surveys in the area and confirmed wolf tracks where one of the sightings was reported,” De la Garza said. A century ago hunters and settlers drove wolves in California to extinction, but the animals returned to the state in 2011 and have significantly expanded their presence over the last decade, largely in the rural and remote north-east. There are at least 50 documented wolves in California. The recent appearance in the Mendocino national forest, which was first reported by MendoLocal.News last week, is significant. It represents the only confirmed sighting west of the Sacramento valley, Axel Hunnicutt, the state gray wolf coordinator for the CDFW, told the Sacramento Bee, and is a sign the species is expanding its range. “Evidence of wolves in that part of the state is a good thing,” he said. The return of the animal has not been without controversy. Ranchers have expressed frustration that there is little they can do when wolves kill their livestock – the species is protected in California and under the federal Endangered Species Act. Donald Trump has sought to change that. Last week the president signed an executive order, titled “Supporting America’s Ranchers”, that directs the interior department to look at removing gray wolves from the Endangered Species Act, and to loosen restrictions for “lethal removal”. The US Fish and Wildlife Service has sought to de-list the gray wolf, but the matter is still unfolding in court. Meanwhile, the act protects the wolves that are across the majority of the lower 48 states under a 2022 federal court order. Environmental groups condemned Trump’s order. “Once again, we see this administration attempting to override the checks and balances provided by bedrock environmental laws like the Endangered Species Act in order to create industry carveouts and distract from other bad policies that are proving unpopular,” said Leia Barnett, New Mexico conservation lead for WildEarth Guardians.

title: Two more people arrested over ‘mountain of illegal waste’ dumped in Oxfordshire
summary: A total of six people apprehended as clean-up of rubbish stacked 10 metres high cost about £6m
text: Two men have been arrested after fly-tippers dumped a “mountain of illegal waste”, stacked 10 metres high, in Oxfordshire. Hundreds of tonnes of rubbish appeared in a field between the River Cherwell and the A34 near Kidlington in November last year. The waste tip was so large that removing it could cost more than the local council’s annual budget, the area’s MP said. The clean-up operation, which concluded last month, took five months. An estimated 22,704 tonnes of rubbish were cleared, with the operation costing an estimated £6m. The Environment Agency (EA) has confirmed on Tuesday that a 21-year-old man from Ashford in Surrey and a 43-year-old man from Stanwell in Surrey had been arrested. It brings the total number of people apprehended to six, after one arrest in February, two in January and one in November, the EA said. The watchdog shut down the Kidlington site in October after officers discovered continued criminal activity after the first report of dumping at the site in July 2025. Colin Chiverton, area environment manager for the Thames at the EA, said: “The dumping at Kidlington was abhorrent and had no regard for the local community. “We moved quickly to remove all illegal waste from the site and our teams continue to work tirelessly on this investigation. These arrests are another vital step in collecting new evidence and delivering justice for the residents of Kidlington.” Dame Angela Eagle, the environment secretary, said: “This government said we’d take on waste criminals and that’s exactly what we’re doing. “These arrests are another step towards delivering justice for Kidlington residents, who have had to put up with the dumping of disgusting waste. “The years of waste crime being allowed to fester have ended. We are taking decisive action through our crackdown and putting more officers on the frontline to restore pride in our communities.” The two men have been released on conditional bail pending further investigations. The EA previously announced it was to spend millions of pounds to clear the enormous illegal rubbish dump, saying the waste was at risk of catching fire. Its policy is to refuse to clear up illegal waste dumps across the country, instead pursuing the perpetrators and landowners. But officials said they had taken the exceptional decision to clear up the waste outside Kidlington, which is next to the River Cherwell, because the scale of the fire risk set it apart from other illegal waste dumps in England and presented an overriding public imperative. The agency was given no extra money to clear the waste, and the EA said this would come from “making efficiencies in its operations”. The cost to the taxpayer would also include the payment of the landfill tax on the waste to the Treasury. The dumping in Kidlington took place under the noses of the EA, which was monitoring the site after being alerted to suspicious activity.

title: OpenAI claims to have solved maths problem that stumped humans for decades
summary: Company behind ChatGPT says 10,000 of its AI systems cracked the Navier-Stokes problem in 88 hours
text: OpenAI claims to have solved a major mathematics problem that has stumped humans for nearly a century after spending millions of dollars on the artificial intelligence-led endeavour. The company behind ChatGPT said it had cracked the Navier-Stokes problem, one of seven Millennium Prize Problems published by the Clay Mathematics Institute to highlight some of the biggest unsolved puzzles in the field. However, the announcement swiftly became mired in controversy after mathematician Tristan Buckmaster, a professor at New York University, said OpenAI accelerated its work on the problem after hearing that he and another researcher at Anthropic, an OpenAI rival, were poised to announce their own breakthrough. Buckmaster had further concerns because the pair’s work in progress was stored in OpenAI’s Codex model, which is used for writing computer programs, potentially making the work visible to the OpenAI team. In a document posted on his website, he added: “I do not know what their model did, or how. I do not know whether our data was used. I am not accusing anyone of anything.” At a press briefing on Tuesday, OpenAI researcher Sebastien Bubeck denied that the company had used the pair’s work or accessed material shared with OpenAI’s servers. OpenAI’s announcement on the breakthrough gave more details, saying that the company was inspired to launch the effort after hearing rumours that two Millennium Prize Problems had been solved. It also said it could not rule out that data from the pair’s use of their products “helped improve our models.” OpenAI said it tackled the Navier-Stokes problem with an internal OpenAI system that was more powerful than its latest GPT-6 Astra model. About 10,000 AI agents – AI systems that carry out tasks autonomously – worked on the problem at once and reached the solution in 88 hours. “A major goal of our work is to empower scientists to advance research and technology that benefits all of humanity,” OpenAI researchers wrote in a blog. “We believe it is important to inform the world about the pace of AI progress and what to expect from upcoming models”. The breakthrough is the latest to demonstrate how advanced artificial intelligence models consuming enormous amounts of computing power are encroaching on and reshaping the field of mathematics. In May, OpenAI claimed progress in another mathematical problem first proposed 80 years ago, while Google DeepMind has also claimed maths achievements with its models. Bubeck said the solution to the Navier-Stokes problem was “a spectacular culmination of the arc we have seen over the past 12 months”. The Navier-Stokes problem asks whether equations that are used to describe the movement of fluids like air and water fail under particular conditions. OpenAI’s proof suggests that they do, with the equations occasionally “blowing up” with the speed of fluids becoming impossibly infinite. It took OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra about 17 hours to verify the solution. Mathematicians who solve any of the Millennium Prize Problems are in line for a $1m (£740,000) reward from the Clay Mathematics Institute. OpenAI, which is preparing for a flotation that could value the business at around $1tn, said it did not intend to claim the prize. The clash with Buckmaster aside, the maths announcement also allows OpenAI to cast its technology in a positive light after a period of alarm over how safely it is being developed. OpenAI revealed in July that a swarm of agents had hacked into Hugging Face, a third'-party software store, during a cybersecurity test. The incident, plus a similar episode at Anthropic, has led to renewed calls for curbs on AI development, with US senators calling last week for a permanent ban of AI “superintelligence” – the term for systems that outperform humans in all cognitive tasks.

title: Far-right port protests: police told to improve intelligence gathering
summary: Whitehall officials ask why laws meant to clamp down on mask wearing at demonstrations were not used
text: Police have been told by the government they expect better intelligence gathering after masked far-right groups took to the streets at the weekend, the Guardian has learned, as the Kent force admitted mishandling warnings of potential trouble. Police in Kent on Saturday and then Portsmouth, Hampshire, on Sunday said they were taken by surprise when hundreds massed to oppose what they say is illegal immigration via small boats. Both protests are believed by police to have been far-right inspired, with evidence emerging that those behind them were determined to avoid detection. Claims by Kent police since Saturday that they had no warning fell apart on Tuesday when the force admitted there were warning calls to police on Friday evening which were not acted upon. Kent police said: “The force had received non-emergency information late on Friday evening that a protest could take place in the town the following day. This information was not fully assessed.” The government’s view is that police actions once officers were faced by hundreds of men was reasonable. But there is dismay at how Kent police explained their decision-making afterwards, for instance viewing the gathered masked men outside the port of Dover as peaceful protesters, with one source describing it as “fucking crackers”. On Tuesday evening the prime minister, Andy Burnham, met police chiefs to discuss what had happened and preparedness for any further unrest. In Dover on Saturday, where hundreds of masked men in black converged undetected, police believe those taking to the streets used walkie-talkies to coordinate their actions. Police on the ground report the masked men had lawyers’ phone numbers and cited public order case law and were well briefed on how far they could go: “They toed the line perfectly to avoid arrest,” one source said. In Hampshire police are investigating whether vehicles were deliberately left behind to block access roads. Police said the Dover gathering passed peacefully, while in Hampshire there were clashes, with the local Police Federation saying anger and violence was directed at officers. The Guardian understands that part of Hampshire police’s investigation will examine whether the gathering of 200 people was meant to harass or intimidate. A spokesperson added they are also hunting for those behind the violence, conducting “a thorough review of the body-worn video” to look for offenders. The protests are believed to have been coordinated on closed social media networks and not publicly advertised. Police are considering whether the threshold for warrants for covert tactics has been met, with one source warning that police were wary of criticism of using “police state tactics” against people portraying themselves as peaceful protesters motivated by a legitimate issue. The National Police Coordination Centre has intensified its monitoring. The action in Kent was organised by Daniel Thomas, a long-term associate of the far-right activist Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, known as Tommy Robinson. Thomas, who has established an umbrella grouping called Patriot Platform, was also linked to the blockade in Portsmouth the following day. Whitehall officials have asked police why tougher laws in place since last year meant to clamp down on the wearing of face masks at protests were not used. The police view was that at Dover those gathered complied with requests from officers and dispersed after three hours. In Portsmouth, which was more heated, police prioritised a formal dispersal order which they think worked. Both police and government sources say the “optics” of masked men in black thronging the streets looked “intimidating”. Also on Tuesday it emerged that lifeboat staff who picked up 120 asylum seekers from a large dinghy in the Channel on Sunday were refused entry to two ports shortly before being harangued by right-wing protesters. Crew on two RNLI vessels were also threatened with legal action if they approached Southampton Port and tried to bring the claimants ashore. They were forced to take the migrants several miles away to Eastney, where police, firefighters, Border Force and other officials faced protests by up to 200 people, most of whom wore balaclavas and black clothing. Peter Sparkes, the chief executive of the RNLI, said abuse of its volunteers is “wholly unacceptable in a civilised society”. He said recent protests had “generated deliberate misinformation and a misunderstanding” about the charity, and condemned threats by “those who would hide behind a balaclava or a keyboard”. Officials confirmed that a broadcast on an open marine VHF radio said Southampton Vessel Traffic Service and King’s Harbour Master Portsmouth denied the RNLI permission to enter their ports. The two RNLI rescue boats from Bembridge and Yarmouth had intercepted a “mega-dinghy” that had left Utah beach near Cherbourg in Normandy. A spokesperson for Associated British Ports (ABP), which operates the port of Southampton, said: “ABP did receive an enquiry about landing recovered migrants at the port of Southampton. We had to decline the enquiry as the port did not have suitable reception facilities available. If there had been a safety of life at sea issue where Southampton was the closest port or if we had received a formal direction from the relevant authority then we would have played a role. Neither was the case in this situation.” On Tuesday, anti-migrant protesters attempted to identify RNLI volunteers involved in rescuing those onboard the dinghy. Demonstrators named and shared pictures on X of two people they said were volunteers, claiming they had tracked down an address for one of the men. Sparkes’s words come after footage posted on social media showed volunteers labelled as “traitors”. In a statement issued on Tuesday, Sparkes said the misinformation led to “some of our volunteers and staff [being] the subject of online and, in the worst cases, physical abuse. “The RNLI’s people represent the very best in our society. They selflessly give up their time to keep others safe. “Yet they and their families are being threatened by those who would hide behind a balaclava or a keyboard. “Their action, in contrast, is wholly unacceptable in a civilised society. “We will take whatever steps we can to care for and protect our people and their families.”

title: UK accuses Israeli ‘terrorists’ of ethnic cleansing in West Bank with government backing
summary: Ed Miliband announces sanctions on trade with settlers as PM says in the Guardian it is time to act
text: Settler terrorists supported by Benjamin Netanyahu’s government are committing ethnic cleansing in the West Bank, Ed Miliband has said, in the UK’s starkest condemnation since the foundation of the Israeli state. Andy Burnham, the prime minister, said he would “not stand by” as horrific suffering continued, writing in the Guardian that for too long the UK had been hesitant to act, “fearful of being accused of being anti-Israel”. In the Commons, the foreign secretary said the government would now take the official position that Israel’s occupation of the West Bank was unlawful in its entirety, as he announced sweeping sanctions on trade with Israeli settlements. The dramatic shift in the UK’s position comes after a summer of intense diplomacy against a backdrop of increasing settler violence in the West Bank, which has resulted in 12 nations – including France and Canada – announcing they would impose sanctions. In a joint statement Burnham, Emmanuel Macron and Mark Carney said: “The time has come to take further action to uphold our commitment to protect the two-state solution, our interests and to stand up for our values, before it is too late.” In response, the Israeli foreign minister, Gideon Saar, announced the closure of the UK consulate in Jerusalem and that 12 British MPs and activists – including Jeremy Corbyn and Labour MP Diane Abbott – would be banned from entering Israel. Saar accused Miliband of “outrageous lies” and said the UK government was “systematically working against the state of Israel”. Washington’s ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, warned that the US could take retaliatory action over trade. However, the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said Washington would “obviously” not follow the UK’s course of action, and did not want to see the West Bank destabilised, but declined to comment further. Burnham had briefed Donald Trump on the plan in advance. In his statement to parliament, Miliband said the UK government would enact: An import ban on goods from illegal settlements in the occupied territories and a new ban for arms licences and other exports that “materially contribute to the occupation”. A comprehensive sanctions regime against providing services such as construction or financing for Israeli settlements and a ban on advertising them in the UK. Personal sanctions against key individuals accused of promoting settler violence. A new ban for arms licences and other exports that “materially contribute to the occupation”. The foreign secretary said the UK’s actions would show that “Britain is not silent in the face of deep injustice, and nor is it powerless”. In an emotional statement, he described the agony he had heard from Palestinians in the West Bank whose homes had been destroyed and from doctors in Gaza who had seen children dying waiting for medical treatment. The UK’s actions have been made increasingly urgent by Israel’s plans to expand the E1 settlement project east of Jerusalem, which could in effect cut off the north from the south of the West Bank, threatening the viability of any future Palestinian state. Ministers expect the legislation to enforce the trade ban and sanctions to be in place within nine months, although they could be subject to legal challenge, which would result in a delay. Miliband stopped short of describing Israel’s actions in Gaza as a genocide, as some on the left have demanded, saying the UK would wait for the determination of the international courts, but that there was evidence of “war crimes”. Speaking in the Commons, he said: “The British government agrees that there is ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in areas of the West Bank, perpetrated by settler terrorists. “All too often the Israeli government has turned a blind eye to this and worse, members of it have made statements and taken actions to support the forced displacement of Palestinians. “I recognise the gravity of saying this, but the truth is the least the people who face such suffering deserve. And it should be the prelude to justice.” Miliband suggested that Keir Starmer had been reluctant to take action against West Bank settlers during his time as prime minister. “I’ll say very bluntly we should have acted earlier. And it has taken the new prime minister to come in and recognise the gravity of the situation,” he told MPs. Burnham, who apologised for Labour’s stance on Gaza when he became prime minister, attempting to shore up votes on the party’s progressive flank, also said the previous government had been too slow to act. Writing in the Guardian , he said: “We have called for years for a two-state solution in the Middle East, but we must recognise that those words are meaningless unless we back them up with action. For too long, we have been hesitant to act, fearful of being accused of being anti-Israel.” Miliband said he was taking the action as foreign secretary but also as a “proud British Jew” with relatives who had found safety in Israel after the Holocaust. “I am proud of my Jewishness and unwavering in my support for the state of Israel,” he said. “And there is absolutely no contradiction between this and my support for the state of Palestine. Indeed, quite the opposite. The two-state solution is based on an explicit belief that the only route to security for both peoples is to live side by side in peaceful coexistence with freedom, security and self-determination.” The foreign secretary said that to respond to threats against Jews around the world, the UK would also impose sanctions on Lebanese Hezbollah’s financing arm, Al-Qard al-Hassan, and reimpose major economic sanctions on Iran in line with the EU and US. The action marked the beginning of a new approach towards Israel and Palestine, he said, one that not only condemned but took action. “Our argument is not with the people of Israel, with whom the UK has unshakeable bonds. Our argument is with the conduct of its government.” Burnham wrote that the British Jewish community must not be blamed for the actions of the Israeli government. “[It] is wrong, plain and simple. And it is antisemitism, plain and simple,” he said. “I met with the representatives of the Jewish community just last week. I know the fear they live with day by day. My government will stop at nothing to ensure they are safe and to stamp out antisemitism in every part of our society.” The shadow foreign secretary, Tom Tugendhat, said “illegal settlements are wrong” but suggested that Miliband was introducing policies the Foreign Office did not believe would work. Whitehall insiders denied this was the case. The senior Conservative MP also said there was a risk of harming Palestinians who worked in the West Bank and that “the economies of Palestine and Israel were too interconnected” for a ban on goods for illegal settlements to work. But the veteran Tory MP Edward Leigh gave full backing to the sanctions. “I am proud to say as the longest serving member of the Conservative Friends of Israel that I absolutely and fully support what he is doing today because it is about standing up for freedom, for morality and justice for all people in this world,” he said. The move forms part of a broader attempt by Burnham’s government to reset British policy towards Israel, in part to regain the trust among Muslim and progressive voters in the UK they lost in the early days of the conflict. It was overwhelmingly welcomed by Labour MPs, many of whom have been struggling with the issue in their constituencies, although some sounded a note of caution about the potential impact on local Jewish communities. Emily Thornberry, the Labour chair of the foreign affairs select committee, said: “At last! I am so very happy to see a British government – a Labour British government – finally doing the right thing and taking a strong stance … no longer a bystander wringing their hands.”

title: Ikea wins right to launch legal action against Belgian far-right party
summary: EU’s highest court allows Swedish furniture firm to begin proceedings after Vlaams Belang used its trademarks in immigration campaign
text: Ikea has won the right to take legal action against a Belgian far-right political party that parodied the Swedish flatpack furniture firm’s branding in its anti-immigration campaign. In a ruling on Tuesday, Europe’s highest court said that Ikea had the right to oppose the use of its trademarks and distinctive graphics by Vlaams Belang, a rightwing Eurosceptic political party that advocates for an independent Flemish state. The court found that Vlaams Belang’s use of Ikea’s trademarks to illustrate its policy on asylum and immigration could “cause significant detriment to the repute” of the company. The party, which has called for a near total stop to immigration and limitations on the building of mosques, had used Ikea’s branding in political material published in 2022. One image featured characters modelled on the cartoon people used in Ikea instructions, one carrying a flag featuring a lion – the symbol of Flanders – and another holding a shield in Ikea’s distinctive blue and yellow livery. The image was titled “Ikea plan” with the subtitle “Immigration really can be different.” After Ikea issued proceedings against Vlaams Belang, the party argued that its freedom of expression should override the Swedish company’s rights over its brand. But the Luxembourg-based Court of Justice of the European Union ruled on Tuesday that Ikea could proceed with legal action against Vrijheidsfonds, the association behind the party. In a statement, the court said “it does not appear that the use of the Ikea trademarks for the sole purpose of taking advantage of their reputation to reinforce a political message and increase its dissemination, takes precedence over the rights and interests of the proprietor of those trademarks.” However, it said a final decision on the dispute could only be made in subsequent legal proceedings in a Belgian court. Pauline Piernez, a trademark and design associate at Marks & Clerk, an intellectual property law firm, said: “While the CJEU rightly confirms that political parody is not prohibited, it also makes clear that freedom of expression is not a blank cheque to appropriate the identity of a famous brand simply to amplify a message. “In this case, the court found that the use of the Ikea trademarks was liable to damage their reputation and was primarily intended to take advantage of their notoriety in order to increase the reach of a political message entirely unrelated to Ikea itself. “The decision should be welcomed as an important safeguard for the system of protection afforded to reputed trademarks.| “Inter Ikea fully believes in – and deeply respects – freedom of expression,” the company said in a statement. “At the same time, it cannot accept the use of the Ikea trademarks in ways that damage their reputation or distinctive character, particularly when such use serves no other purpose than to free-ride on the reputation of the Ikea brand.” Vlaams Belang said its campaign association had taken note of the judgment and that it “will thoroughly study its scope in the context of the further legal proceedings”.

title: Ed Miliband has overturned decades of Foreign Office inertia on illegal Israeli settlements
summary: Foreign secretary ends UK’s feigned helplessness with sanctions and condemnation of ‘ethnic cleansing’
text: The indefatigable ability of UK Foreign Office ministers over decades to issue boilerplate statements of concern about the extension of illegal settlements in Israel has long been a matter of ridicule. Even some of the Conservative ministers who issued them, notably Alan Duncan and Alistair Burt, have agreed. Duncan described the UK stance towards settlements as weak and naive, while Burt wondered at the ability of the Foreign Office to find new forms of diplomatic condemnation that never amounted to any specific action. Margaret Thatcher, often torn as prime minister between her natural sympathy for Israel and her fear of the Gulf states falling under the sway of the Soviet Union, similarly expressed her anger at the settlements. But in the face of the Israeli disillusionment with a two-state solution – to which the UK had been committed at the UN since 1946, if not before – the UK produced little practical policy to prevent the spread of Israel’s illegal settlements. The UK-Israel trade agreement prevented preferential tariffs applying to goods coming from territories brought under Israeli administration after June 1967. The business department also advised companies not to trade with the settlements – but many simply ignored the advice or, to secure the preferential tariff, relabelled their goods as from Israel. The then trade minister Chris Bryant told the business select committee in June it was very difficult to be certain of the origin of goods. At the same time, the legal advice was that the UK regime could place sanctions on entities only if they were linked to settler violence, but could not put a contractor under sanctions simply for working on settlements. It was this unhappy moral and legal mess that Ed Miliband inherited. As soon as he took office as foreign secretary, he said he refused to be a bystander to further suffering and the destruction of the two-state solution that settlement expansion represented. In this he had the support of the prime minister, Andy Burnham. Above all, Miliband felt that the UK could not feign powerlessness, and to do so, or pay lip service to action, would prove disastrous to Israel’s own future. He was perhaps the only front-rank Labour politician who could push this argument through at such pace, overturning the inertia and caution built into Foreign Office legal advice. His Jewish heritage – his mother, Marion Kozak, was a Holocaust survivor who fled to Israel – his life growing up with the Palestinian question and empathy for those subjected to antisemitism put him in a near unimpeachable position to adopt the role of Israel’s critical friend. The US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, might this week say the Labour government is gripped by Jew-hatred, a charge he laid at Miliband’s door knowing he is Jewish, but Miliband’s riposte is simple. The best route to Israel’s security lay in Palestinian self-determination and the introduction of the two-state solution in its fullest form. To equate Israel only with the current Likud-led government as too many Conservatives have been prone to do, was a category error, he said: “Holding Jewish people responsible for the actions of the Israeli government is antisemitism, plain and simple.” He is thus the first UK foreign secretary to describe what is happening in the West Bank as ethnic cleansing, and in so doing to in effect to accuse Israel of turning a blind eye to acts that amount to war crimes. Miliband also ended the two years of delay in responding to the international court of justice advisory opinion in June 2024 that the occupation is unlawful. In what he admitted was an overdue statement of reality, he accepted the ICJ opinion that the occupation, and not just the settlements, were so designated. Accepting the ICJ opinion arguably places stronger obligations on the UK government to not assist the occupation. It may help to explain why the trade ban extends into services such as providing insurance for illegal settlements. The biggest diplomatic rabbit Miliband pulled from the hat was the agreement of France and Canada to impose similar trade bans. France took the lead last year on recognition of Palestine; this year, it is the turn of the UK to lead on following through on the consequences of that recognition. Paris appears to have been persuaded by the UK to stop waiting for the EU to reach an agreement on collective action, since it seemed unlikely the opposition in Germany and indifference in parts of the European Commission would end. A group of countries imposing the trade ban together of course makes Israeli reprisals harder, and serves to underline Israel’s isolation. The perceived weaknesses are obvious. Miliband still left it to the international courts to determine whether a genocide occurred in Gaza, something that might not be adjudicated for at least five years. There was mounting evidence of ethnic cleansing in Gaza, he said, but again it was for the courts to determine if that was so. There is no pledge to protect the international court of justice or the international criminal court from the US drive to render them inoperable. As to a UK arms sales ban, an exemption continues for the sale of parts for F35 jet planes to the main US spares pool – all on the basis the F-35 jets “do not materially support the occupation” – the criteria the foreign secretary has set. Miliband specifically condemned the Boycott, Disinvestment and Sanctions movement because it targets the whole Israeli economy and not just the occupied territories. The secondary legislation required to make sanctions as wide as envisaged may take as long as nine months, contrasting with the speed with which sanctions were enforced against Russia over the annexation of Crimea. But to focus solely on what is absent is to miss the moment. Duncan, for instance, said: “At last, in the face of state-backed terrorism by illegal settlers, the British government has shown unprecedented moral courage.” There is a risk of a cascading backlash from the White House – but Trump, trapped in a political labyrinth after he was persuaded to attack Iran, has little reason to come to Benjamin Netanyahu’s aid. Miliband has taken a risk, but after more than 70,000 deaths in Gaza, and the two-state solution on life support, it may be time to dare.

text: Apple and Google will be forced to block explicit images on children’s smartphones by law in the UK after talks failed to produce a breakthrough, the government has said. The legislation commitment puts ministers on a collision course with two of the biggest players in Silicon Valley, months after the government announced a social media ban for under-16s. Lisa Nandy, the secretary of state for digital, culture, media and sport, said the government would start work on an act of parliament to stop under-18s taking, sharing or viewing nude images on their devices. Talks with Google and Apple, whose operating systems dominate the smartphone market, had not reached agreement as a three-month deadline passed on Tuesday. Nandy told the House of Commons the tech companies could still reach a deal but it was “almost certain” groundbreaking legislation would be required. “For too long, technology companies have failed to protect children from some of the worst harms,” she said. “And to be frank, I am not prepared to give them the benefit of the doubt that progress will continue at the pace that we need it to, while harm is being done now.” The prime minister, Andy Burnham, said the protections would be “built into the device and switched on by default”, and tech companies will be required to verify an adult user’s age before they are allowed to take, view or send nude images. The government also wants the restrictions to apply to apps used by children, which will require further legislation. Nandy said: “This will ensure that the whole ecosystem changes, tackling the means by which children are most often abused or groomed in the online world.” Sources familiar with progress in the talks have said there iwas a desire to reach a deal on both sides but significant hurdles remained including privacy concerns on the tech side. Jess Phillips, the Labour MP and former safeguarding minister, said the legislation would stop the UK from producing self-generated child sexual abuse material, where children are duped or groomed into sharing explicit images of themselves. However, she urged the government to ensure the UK was followed by other countries and to make sure that “while we lead the world, we’re not standing alone for too long”. Hannah Swirsky, head of policy at the Internet Watch Foundation, which monitors the online spread of child sexual abuse material [CSAM], said: “It is deeply disappointing that tech firms have failed to act in full, but we are pleased that the government is now taking decisive legislative action to keep children safe.” Last year the IWF said a quarter of the images or videos of CSAM it recorded were self-generated, representing more than 140,000 pieces of content over a 12-month period. One of Keir Starmer’s final acts as prime minister was to give Apple and Google three months to stop under-18s from generating, sending or seeing nude images on their devices, by activating built-in features on the hardware or other technological solutions. Between them, Apple’s iOS and Google’s Android smartphone operating systems dominate the mobile phone market. The nudity block implies the use of “client-side scanning”, where content is scanned by software on the device before it is encrypted or sent. “Client-side scanning is the least evil approach,” said Lukasz Olejnik, a visiting senior research fellow in cybersecurity and privacy at Kings College London. “That said, it does put in place an infrastructure to scan content of messages.” Privacy campaigners have also warned that adults would have to verify their age before switching off any nudity-blocking features. In June, the government said the proposals would “not affect the use of devices owned and used by adults who verify their age”. Google said it was “pleased to have made progress” in talks with the government and was “fully committed” to working with legislators, experts, app developers and device manufacturers to “keep children safe, while also protecting privacy and access to information”. An Apple spokesperson said the company was preparing to strengthen its “communication safety” feature, which warns children when they are receiving or sending nude images and videos. “We share the UK’s commitment to combating exploitation and abuse online, and have shared with UK officials future plans to strengthen communication safety and other tools even further to help keep kids safe.”

title: Will UK sanctions have any impact on Israel’s ‘settler terrorists’ in West Bank?
summary: A look at whether Ed Miliband’s plans will be effective and what they signal for future Israel-UK relations
text: The British foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, has announced plans for an import ban on goods from illegal settlements in occupied Palestine and sanctions for companies that “finance or facilitate” the construction, infrastructure and marketing of illegal settlements. He also said “settler terrorists” were perpetrating ethnic cleansing in the occupied West Bank, while the government turned a blind eye and some members supported it. Britain’s argument was with the government of Israel, not its people, Miliband said. The new measures would target only the expansion and entrenchment of Israel’s illegal occupation of Palestine, not Israel inside the green line – the 1949 armistice boundary, once seen as a possible template for Israel’s border with a future Palestinian state. The measures were prompted in part by Israel’s decision to press ahead with a vast new settlement in the heart of the West Bank, in an area known as E1. The project is designed to “bury the idea of a Palestinian state”, the far-right Israeli minister Bezalel Smotrich has said, and Miliband described the issuing of construction tenders in August as a “red line”. He told parliament of his family ties to Israel, including joyful childhood memories of visiting his grandmother, who found a home there after Nazis murdered her husband and 60 other relatives. By acting against ethnic cleansing and settlement expansion, Britain was standing up for its core values, including “rule of law, freedom and self-determination”, and the future of both Israelis and Palestinians, he said, adding that the new measures were designed to “salvage the only course for peace and security for Israelis and Palestinians, the two-state solution”. Why is going after E1 settlement financing a big deal? The trade in goods grown or produced in settlements is a relatively small part of Israel’s export economy, although its exact scale is obscured by a lack of Israeli statistics. Miliband highlighted that the Israeli settler population in occupied Palestine had almost tripled over the past three decades, from 270,000 in 1993 to 770,000 today. That expansion is underpinned by large government subsidies. A trade ban alone would be unlikely to have much impact on the viability of construction that is a government priority, or on the broader Israeli economy. However, plans to place sanctions on any company that finances or facilitates settlement expansion could force Israel’s main banks and insurance companies to chose between their business interests in the UK and those in occupied Palestine. Miliband has not provided details of the new measures, which he said would take between six and nine months to put in place. But they have the potential to slow or stop construction. The activist Yehuda Shaul wrote in a social media post about new building projects: “Companies that bid for tenders on government-led projects, including settlement expansion, must have a financial guarantor. Without the backing of Israeli financial institutions, these projects cannot occur.” What is the status of Israeli settlements and the settler economy? Miliband said Britain recognised Israel’s occupation of Palestine as unlawful, in line with a landmark 2024 ruling from the UN’s international court of justice (ICJ). The UK had previously recognised settlements as illegal, but remained silent on the occupation overall. The ICJ ordered Israel to end its occupation “as rapidly as possible” and make full reparations for its “internationally wrongful acts”. Israeli supporters of the UK measures say they redraw the line between Israel proper and illegally occupied territory, and are a much-needed response to Israeli government policies that are undermining the country. Michael Sfard, one of Israel’s leading human rights lawyers, said the measures were “enormously important”. “It redraws the green line and provides a recommitment to international law. Every cent that goes from the UK or other countries to support the economy of settlements is a cent that allows violation of international law,” he said. The former Israeli prime minister Ehud Olmert, whom Miliband quoted in his speech, said: “The British government decision became unavoidable as a result of a continuous effort of ethnic cleansing perpetrated by a large group of Jewish terrorists in the West Bank … Sanctions are directed against the terrorists, not against Israel, and as such they are unavoidable.” What does Miliband’s intervention mean for UK-Israel relations? Israel’s foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, responded rapidly with a series of measures, including closing the UK the consulate in East Jerusalem, Britain’s diplomatic mission to occupied Palestine. There was fierce condemnation from other Israeli politicians. The far-right minister Ben Gvir called for Israel to recognise Argentinian sovereignty over the Falklands – even before Miliband made his speech. However, Israel holds elections in six weeks, and for months polls have shown Benjamin Netanyahu and his coalition stuck below the threshold needed to form a new government. Although none of the leading candidates to replace him oppose the occupation, there has been growing condemnation of violence in the West Bank. A new government would mean a chance to reset ties. Israel may be seeking to deter others from following the UK’s lead, but a dozen countries have already said they are planning similar restrictions on settlement trade, among them Israel’s historical allies Canada and France. A joint statement from the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham; the Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney; and the French president, Emmanuel Macron, said the action marked “a further turning point in our approach to protecting the two-state solution”. Netanyahu’s policies have already pushed Israel into a position of unprecedented international isolation, and taking similar punitive action against all these countries would only deepen that. What other pressure could be applied? The measures unveiled by Miliband mark the most serious step yet to impose a political and economic price on Israel for settlement expansion. The Israeli government’s furious response belies growing support both inside Israel, and among some of the country’s staunchest supporters abroad, for stronger action to halt violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank. This summer dozens of Israelis from the country’s security, political and cultural elite threatened legal action against their government over support for “Jewish terrorism” and an “ideology of ethnic cleansing” in the occupied West Bank. Trump’s ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, and some Republicans in Congress attacked Miliband before his speech. But the US also has elections this autumn. The Democrat Rahm Emanuel, a former Chicago mayor whose father fought in the Israeli military, used a speech in Tel Aviv to call for broad sanctions on Israel’s financial sector to stop violence against Palestinians. Pressed on the implications of placing sanctions on banks with branches in settlements – which is all of Israel’s major institutions – he told the Jerusalem Post: “America uses its tools to achieve its policy goals. We believe in a two-state solution. You want to pursue a greater Israel? You pay full price for it. Everything. That’s a choice you make.”

title: United Utilities fined nearly £1m after discharging raw sewage along Lancashire coast
summary: Seaside communities and businesses were affected significantly by the contamination in June 2023
text: United Utilities has been fined nearly £1m after illegally discharging raw sewage along the Lancashire coastline and polluting seaside holiday locations including Blackpool. The water company pleaded guilty to five environmental permit offences relating to a pollution incident along the Fylde coast in June 2023, and was ordered by Preston magistrates court on Tuesday to pay £964,225 in fines and costs. Sewage was released from pumping stations at Manchester Square, Anchorsholme and Chatsworth Avenue for more than 35 hours over several days in June 2023, affecting coastal communities in Blackpool, Lytham St Annes, Fleetwood and Cleveleys. The Environment Agency issued “no bathing” advice for all eight designated bathing waters along the affected coastline. United Utilities’ modelling showed that a sewage plume had reached seven bathing waters and significantly affected water quality. Communities and businesses along the coast were affected significantly by the contamination, according to the Environment Agency. “In Blackpool alone, summer visitor numbers fell by hundreds of thousands compared with the previous year.” Sewage was reported on beaches and at marine recreational facilities, including Fleetwood baths, while tests indicated the presence of E coli. Three shellfish beds were temporarily closed because of concerns about public health. The incident began after the part collapse of a final effluent pipe at Fleetwood wastewater treatment works reduced the amount of sewage the site could receive, causing wastewater to back up through the network. After rainfall, sewage was discharged from the three pumping stations. An Environment Agency investigation found that conditions required under United Utilities’ environmental permits had not been met. The company accepted the incident’s classification in category one, the agency’s most serious level. Andy Brown, the Environment Agency’s water regulation manager, said: “This was an unacceptable pollution incident which had far-reaching consequences for residents and businesses along the Fylde coast. “Our investigation found that United Utilities Water Ltd discharged sewage outside the conditions of its environmental permits. The company admitted those breaches, and today’s record fine reflects the seriousness of the offences and the harm caused.” Chris Borradaile, director for wastewater services at United Utilities, said: “We want to reiterate our sincere and unreserved apologies for this incident and the harm and disruption it caused.” He added: “We accept responsibility for what happened and recognise that we fell short of the standards our customers and communities rightly expect.”

title: Yes, cut red tape. But shareholder votes on boardroom pay are not ‘pointless admin’
summary: Nothing good can come of ditching annual investor votes on remuneration reports or encouraging online-only shareholder meetings
text: The government, like every other one in living memory, is on a mission to reduce red tape for business. The former chancellor Rachel Reeves promised “a blitz on bureaucracy” and “pointless admin” and here comes the business department with a 12-week consultation on “modernising corporate reporting to support long-term economic growth”. Never mind that cutting energy costs for business would, by an order of magnitude, do more to support growth than any bonfire of red tape ever will. The consultation is still worthwhile: clearing out accumulated clutter, exploring digital options and clarifying reporting “exemptions and exclusions” for small- and medium-sized companies could free up a bit of time for doing more business. But two ideas in this burden-lifting exercise are terrible because they involve an unacceptable loss of transparency. One is the idea of dropping annual shareholder votes on companies’ remuneration reports. The supposed justification is that, since a binding vote on a company’s overall remuneration policy would still be required on a three-yearly cycle, there is no point in having an annual advisory-only poll on how the policy has been implemented. Such a weaselly idea could only have come from those FTSE 100 companies that resent scrutiny of their directors’ mega-bucks pay packages. Too bad: annual votes are a modest (and mostly ineffectual anyway) check on runaway boardroom rewards. Obliging the non-executives on the remuneration committee to justify their decisions to the outside world, in the knowledge the owners will vote, is a bare minimum requirement for retaining a bit of accountability in the system. If the chief executive has to squirm when, say, 30% of shareholders rebel, so be it. By rights, any reform ought to be in the other direction: it would be better to make the annual poll binding. The government’s other bad proposal is to encourage the trend among quoted companies towards online-only annual shareholder meetings. It’s true that many such meetings struggle to attract attendances in double figures, so the desire to turn the thing into a glorified Teams call is vaguely understandable. But a well-established principle is at stake: even small investors in a listed company should have the right, once a year, to buttonhole the bosses and ask a question in the flesh. The best solution in a digital age is hybrid meetings – let the shareholders decide if they wish to turn up or dial in. It is hardly an onerous requirement on the company to make a meeting room available. Again, one suspects the dead-hand of corporate affairs departments at work: with honourable exceptions, they don’t like the hassle of dealing with retail investors or campaign groups. Sorry, but that’s life. One other piece of advice for the department: yes, it’s true that annual reports have grown monstrous in size – running to “98,000 words, longer than JRR Tolkien’s The Hobbit” on average, it complains. And, yes, burdensome reporting requirements explain part of the growth. But it’s also true that companies don’t help themselves by padding out their productions with acres of irrelevant corporate babble. If, as the consultation says, annual reports are “a document primarily intended for investors and creditors”, make them easy to use. Part of the corporate instinct to write at Tolkien-like length stems, one suspects, is from fear of being accused of leaving anything out. The result, too often, is unreadable guff that doesn’t offer a concise account of the directors’ view of how the company is run and the risks and opportunities it faces. By all means, reform some of the reporting burdens – there are probably plenty to go at. But don’t undermine the transparency offered by annual votes on pay and annual meetings. And don’t allow companies to use “regulatory requirements” as an excuse for boilerplate communication.
