title: UK government pays highest interest rate on 30-year bond since 1998
summary: High yields threaten to wipe out at least half of the £24bn headroom John Healey was expecting to have for his budget
text: The UK government was forced to pay the highest interest rate for a 30-year bond since 1998 on Tuesday, underlining the fiscal challenges facing the chancellor, John Healey. Echoing the global bond market sell-off that has driven up yields, or interest rates, on government borrowing across the main markets, the Treasury paid 5.82% to borrow £4bn. That was the highest rate since the Debt Management Office, which is responsible for financing government borrowing, was established in 1998. Healey used a speech in Coventry on Monday to stress that he was determined to balance the books. Markets have been spooked by fears of a fresh rise in inflation after the resumption of the Middle East conflict increased oil prices, and investors fretting about the risks of rising public debt. When the Office for Budget Responsibility does its latest forecast before the budget on 28 October, higher interest rates on government borrowing are expected to wipe out at least half of the £24bn headroom that Healey’s predecessor, Rachel Reeves, built up at her spring forecast in March. News of the costly debt auction came as the Bank of England governor, Andrew Bailey, told MPs the latest rise in oil prices were also putting pressure on inflation and interest rates. “The risks, I’m afraid, are on the upside,” he said. “And that’s really the risks coming from energy prices.” Bailey insisted there was no secret plan to raise interest rates, however, and stressed that higher borrowing costs had already had an impact on consumers without the Bank having to take action. “UK mortgage rates now are typically at the moment about a three-quarters of a percent higher than they were at the point when the conflict broke out,” he said. “I think with the possible exception of Japan, although that’s a little hard to map, that’s the largest increase in mortgage rates in the G7.” Brent crude was trading at about $97 a barrel on Tuesday. Bailey said the oil price could be higher still with the strait of Hormuz still largely closed to tanker traffic and Ukraine attacking refineries in Russia. The governor was appearing at the Commons Treasury select committee alongside three fellow members of the Bank’s monetary policy committee, which will meet next week to set interest rates. Megan Greene, who was in the minority voting for a rate rise in July, said she remained concerned about the risks of acting too late against inflation, but Dave Ramsden and Alan Taylor, who didn’t back a rate rise, suggested prices had risen less than feared as a result of the Iran war.

title: Smithsonian Institution secretary to retire amid Trump attacks on museum independence
summary: ‘I have to be honest, it has been stressful,’ says Lonnie Bunch III
text: The Smithsonian Institution’s secretary, Lonnie Bunch III, will retire at the end of the year amid Donald Trump’s attacks on the museum’s content and independence. Bunch, who was appointed in 2019 as the first African American to lead the museums, cited personal reasons for departing, while acknowledging the pressure that the president’s attacks on the Smithsonian’s depictions of US history had taken. “There is no place like the Smithsonian – it has been one of the great loves of my life, and I am extraordinarily proud of what we have accomplished together,” Bunch, 73, said in a statement. “I leave with pride and sadness, gratitude and joy, and with enormous confidence in the people who will carry this remarkable institution forward.” “It was really just saying, now’s the time,” Bunch, 73, told the New York Times. He added: “I have to be honest, it has been stressful. And at a certain point, I’d like to wake up in the morning and not look at my cellphone.” Trump largely left the Smithsonian alone during his first term, but sought to align its content with his administration’s policies shortly after returning to the White House. In March 2025, the US president signed an executive order accusing the museum of coming “under the influence of a divisive, race-centered ideology”, and outlining steps to “restore the Smithsonian Institution to its rightful place as a symbol of inspiration and American greatness”. Two months later, he tried to fire Kim Sajet as director of the National Portrait Gallery, calling her “a highly partisan person” and a “strong supporter” of the diversity and equity programs his administration was seeking to ban. Bunch pushed back, and the Smithsonian issued a statement affirming that the power to hire and fire lay with him, but Sajet nonetheless resigned in June 2025. Trump has kept up his pressure campaign in recent months, and in July ordered the National Museum of American History to display signs that accuse it of inaccuracy, though those have yet to appear. A historian who previously led the creation of the National Museum of African American History and Culture, Bunch acknowledged to the Times that he had to choose his battles in the job. “My goal has been to win, not to make me feel good,” he said. “To win – to protect the Smithsonian – there were times I would fight, make clear what the red lines were. And there were other times I let things go.” Bunch’s replacement will be selected by the Smithsonian’s 17-member board of regents, which is led by John Roberts, the chief justice of the supreme court. The panel also includes JD Vance, three Democratic members of Congress and three Republicans, as well as nine private citizens. Three of those citizens’ terms expired recently, however, and the Trump administration has not yet announced replacements. Roberts praised Bunch for having “pursued excellence in the telling of our nation’s story”, adding: “The Regents, and the Smithsonian, have benefited greatly from his wisdom, vision and leadership. We look forward to working with him in the coming months to ensure a smooth transition for his successor.” News of Bunch’s departure drew mixed reactions from Capitol Hill. Bunch was a frequent target of conservative critics, and Republicans celebrated his decision to step down. “Good riddance,” wrote Josh Hawley, a Republican senator from Missouri. The lawmaker and staunch Trump ally said that Bunch “should return his salary to the American people”. Democrats, meanwhile, praised Bunch for his steady leadership in the face of constant pressure from the president and his administration. Senator Alex Padilla of California, the ranking Democrat on the Senate rules and administration committee, which has oversight of the Smithsonian Institution, applauded Bunch for “putting truth and accuracy over politics”. Senator Catherine Cortez Masto, a Democrat from Nevada, who serves on the Smithsonian’s 17-member board and will be responsible to selecting his replacement, echoed the sentiment, heralding Bunch as a “student of history who has devoted his life to telling America’s full history”. She added: “I look forward to working with Secretary Bunch over these next few months to ensure his successor exhibits the same commitment to the arts, culture, science and history that he did.”

title: Commons breathes a sigh of relief as UK finally takes a moral stance on Israeli settlements | John Crace
summary: Opposition to Miliband’s announcement of sanctions rings hollow – helped by fewer than 10 Tory backbenchers turning up to debate
text: Nobody can say they weren’t warned. The Andy Burnham government might have looked like Continuity Keir with more positive vibes for the first six weeks or so, but on Tuesday a new line was drawn. When Burnham said he felt Labour had not done enough on Palestine and Gaza, he had meant it. His decision to impose trade sanctions on illegal settlements in the West Bank was to be his first break with the past. Some opponents chose to get their retaliation in early, before Ed Miliband had even stood up to make the announcement in the Commons on Tuesday. Mike Huckabee, the US ambassador, declared on Sunday that Ed was guilty of “hating Jews”. Which rather implied he thought Ed hated himself. Huckabee also wondered when we would get round to sanctioning Russia, China and North Korea. Er … We have, Mike. Try to keep up. The Israeli president, Isaac Herzog, insisted that “the UK would be on the wrong side of history” if the sanctions were imposed. Presumably that means that doing nothing as Israeli settlers, with the explicit endorsement of the Israeli government, seize land, burn homes and kill children is the right side of history. It’s a strange world we live in. Itamar Ben-Gvir, the far-right security minister, went completely rogue. His take was that this made “Las Malvinas” Argentinian territory. As though it was the sanctions that were the nail in the coffin for the Falklands. Still, there was some consistency there. The Israel government has never placed much weight on the rights of the Palestinian people to self-determination. So why should they bother to make an exception for the Falkland islanders? Nor was all the oppo to be found abroad. Kemi Badenoch wrote a piece for the Jewish Chronicle in which she insisted that the government was desperate to win back Islamists and that Jews would no longer be safe in this country. Bizarrely, though, she made no effort to engage with what the Tories proposed to do about the Israeli settlements. Presumably nothing. Just give another nod and a wink to Benjamin Netanyahu as yet more Palestinians are forced off their land. I mean, it’s not as if the diplomatic efforts until now have had much effect. By contrast, the Commons itself was an oasis of calm. Proof that just occasionally MPs are capable of behaving and arguing as adults. A proper debate with proper arguments, sincerely held. This could have been partly helped by fewer than 10 Tory backbenchers having bothered to turn up – we have to assume most of them don’t care much either way what goes on in the West Bank – but the Labour benches were all but full. For most of them, this was a statement that was long overdue. Though there was little triumphalism to be seen. More like relief. Burnham even showed up to lend support. Miliband started by addressing his own Jewishness. He had reason to be grateful to Israel for providing a home to some of his relatives and he condemned all forms of antisemitism. But there was a separation to be made between the Israelis and the Israeli government. This was about righting a wrong, not giving in to hatred. And these sanctions would only apply to goods and services provided to or from the illegal settlements. This wasn’t a blanket ban on everything Israeli. It was about taking a moral stance. At no longer being a bystander while a foreign government broke the law. It was time to live our values and fight oppression and suffering. We were not powerless. It was the only way to maintain the dream of a two-state solution. Nor were we alone. France and Canada had also joined other countries in imposing sanctions. The tone of the debate was immeasurably improved by having Tom Tugendhat reply for the Tories. Had Priti Patel still been the shadow foreign secretary, it would almost certainly have become a lot more bitter. Although Tugendhat was clearly operating with one hand tied behind his back. It wasn’t immediately clear what Tom really thought about the sanctions, but he was under instructions from Kemi to say they were definitely a bad thing and they needed to be opposed. So that’s rather what he had to do. Tugendhat began with a long list of things with which he agreed in Miliband’s statement. That the settlements were illegal, that crimes had been committed, that Hamas were a terrorist organisation and that a two-state solution was the only workable outcome. You felt that in another world, Tom might have left it at that. But he had a job to do so he came out with a few comebacks. The sanctions wouldn’t work, British security would be compromised and 25% of the UK would die because we would no longer receive Israeli pharmaceuticals. As with Kemi, Tom couldn’t quite square all this away with his default position of doing nothing. Tugendhat considers himself a man of action. Someone who would much rather be seen to be doing something. Now he was left to endorse the option of continuing to let Netanyahu get away with allegations of literal murder. As if all our allies automatically got a free pass. An annual allowance of dead children. Up to 100 and we promise to look the other way. Much of the rest of the statement was taken with Labour MPs offering their appreciation to a government that had listened to their concerns. Nor was it just the home crowd. Edward Leigh declared he was the longest-standing member of the Conservative friends of Israel and he was 100% behind Miliband in this. Enough was enough. Kit Malthouse and Desmond Swayne felt much the same. When you have these three on your side, you’ve almost certainly more than made your case. Oliver Dowden was a little more reticent. Couldn’t we have waited just a little bit longer? Until after the Israeli elections. Then Netanyahu might be out of office and a more moderate government installed in its place. It was hard to know what he was getting at. It’s not as if any Israelis are in much doubt about the nature of their current government. Britain imposing sanctions isn’t going to sway some marginal voters into thinking that maybe they needed more illegal settlements after all. Maybe it was just Oliver’s way of thinking out loud. He’s easily confused after all.

title: US federal court says no constitutional right to clean water in Mississippi case
summary: Appeals court dismisses lawsuit from Jackson residents claiming that tainted drinking water violated their rights
text: A US appellate court has decided that the federal constitution does not guarantee a right to clean water. That legal opinion came in the form of a decision on Friday from the fifth circuit court of appeals to uphold a lower court’s dismissal of a 2022 lawsuit from several Jackson, Mississippi, residents claiming that tainted drinking water violated their constitutional rights. Those residents of Mississippi’s capital city contended that their local drinking water was unsafe to drink because of high lead levels and other contaminants. The New Orleans-based fifth circuit’s majority opinion held that the residents wanted “recognition of two new constitutional rights lacking any foundation in the history and tradition of our nation” – those being “the right to be free from exposure to contaminated water and the right to accurate information from public officials”. In the majority’s view, residents should have gone about their legal fight for clean water another way, such as pursuing “tort claims” or by “electing representatives who will better manage the public-water system, and petitioning their representatives for other remedies”. Tort claims allege “harms caused by others” while seeking “to impose liability on parties responsible for the harm, and to deter others from committing harmful acts”, according to Cornell University’s law school. Friday’s decision also said that state and federal officials were working hard to improve the majority-Black city’s drinking water. The residents who filed suit alleged that public authorities had for years failed to mitigate lead levels and failed to inform them about an increase. “Plaintiffs have not been left to go at it alone,” the court said. “The State of Mississippi and federal government have worked for years, and continue today, to improve the city of Jackson’s drinking water quality through regulations, investigations, and compliance plans.” Meanwhile, the opinion also said: “It is undisputed that the Constitution does not guarantee clean water.” The opinion also held that a state does not have a constitutional duty “to provide substantive services for those within its border absent a special relationship”. And municipalities are not constitutionally obligated to provide sewerage, water treatment or waste management services “in a reasonably competent fashion”, the decision said. The decision nonetheless said that the majority of the court recognized the allegations of “serious government misfeasance” and was “sympathetic to the injuries [the plaintiffs] may suffer as a result”. But, the court’s ruling said “our sympathies cannot be the basis” for converting tort claims into constitutional issues. “These deprivations, while grievous, do not infringe upon any deeply rooted constitutional right,” the fifth circuit’s opinion said. Attorneys for the plaintiffs could not immediately be reached for comment. John Horhn, the Jackson mayor, said in a statement: “We are pleased that the fifth circuit upheld the dismissal of these claims. “The City remains committed to the health, safety, and well-being of every Jackson resident.” Jackson residents say that they have long reeled from water crises. The NAACP filed a complaint in September 2022 alleging that Mississippi state authorities violated civil rights law by repeatedly sending federal money earmarked for drinking water safety to white communities rather than Jackson. Such diversion of funds constituted racial discrimination, the complaint said. “The result is persistently unsafe and unreliable drinking water and massive gaps in the access to safe drinking water that are intolerable in any modern society,” Jackson residents said in a complaint to the federal Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). “Nearly all of the residents of Jackson have watched brackish, dirty, impure, and undrinkable water trickle from their taps. At times, some have had no water at all.” The NAACP’s Jackson branch sued over the diversion of these funds in August 2025. The suit against several Mississippi state officials alleged that they “intentionally deprived [Jackson] residents … of access to federal relief funds … which were promised to Jackson in order to address the water infrastructure crisis”. The lawsuit asked for a judge to declare that this diversion of money “is both facially discriminatory and the result of discriminatory purpose” – and to bar officials from permanently siphoning that money away from Jackson.

title: Trump renames places and poses as superhero in bizarre social media blitz
summary: Trump passed the long weekend posting a torrent of memes and musings on his Truth Social platform
text: The long weekend may have proved too long for Donald Trump, who passed the time by musing about annexing other countries, unilaterally renaming places he’s not allowed to rename and turning himself into a superhero. Amid the torrent of memes and posts by the president on his Truth Social platform over the Labor Day holiday weekend was a bizarre AI-generated video depicting Trump as the Green Lantern DC superhero, wielding a glowing green power ring to erect his border wall, illuminate an “American manufacturing” scene, and command a fleet of warplanes and warships behind him. Trump’s controversial forays into AI-generated images have seen him depict himself as a Christ-like figure, the pope, Atlas from Greek mythology, as Superman, and many others. Over the weekend he also shared a map with a US flag emblazoned over most of North America and several countries in Central America, as well as Greenland, Iceland and many islands in the Caribbean. Iceland has summoned its US ambassador over the post. Trump also separately claimed the moon. The president has spent much of his second term taunting Canada repeatedly with the suggestion of making it a 51st US state with “economic force”, and aggressively pushing for the annexation of Greenland, a self-governing Danish territory, which has sparked a major geopolitical row. He has also threatened military action in Mexico, Cuba and Colombia, threatened to seize the Panama Canal, and casually mused about taking over other countries including Micronesia and the Marshall Islands. Also in the flurry of Labor Day posts was a map of the US state of New Mexico with the word “Mexico” crossed out and replaced with “America”. A few hours later, he posted what seems to be an AI video of him sticking an “America” label over the word “Mexico” on a “Welcome to New Mexico” road sign. Trump’s suggestion that New Mexico should be renamed to “New America” comes as tense trade negotiations ⁠with Mexico ramp up. It also comes hot on the heels of Trump signing an order directing the federal government to change Lake Ontario’s name to “Lake America” amid his escalating trade war with Canada after negotiations last month failed to produce a deal. He has also joked about renaming either the Atlantic or Pacific oceans, along with the strait of Hormuz, which has been central to his disastrous war against Iran, to “Trump strait”. He declined to elaborate on that latter idea when asked by a reporter in the Oval Office last week. In the case of New Mexico, whose name predates the founding of the United States and is explicitly enshrined in its constitution, Trump has no legal authority to rename it – or indeed any US state. Any change to its name would have to come from the state itself and would require a formal constitutional amendment. And while his “Lake America” order directs federal agencies to adopt the name-change on US maps, documents and databases, Trump has no authority to rename Canada’s portion of the lake, nor to compel Canada, international legal bodies, international mapmakers or the rest of the world to adopt a new name.

title: Ukraine’s prosecutor general quits after anti-corruption agents raid his office
summary: Ruslan Kravchenko resigns over allegations some of his officials were engaged in large-scale money laundering
text: Ukraine’s prosecutor general has resigned after investigators used ladders to raid his office in connection with a major corruption scandal that threatens to embarrass Volodymyr Zelenskyy. Ruslan Kravchenko quit his post on Monday after allegations that some of his officials were involved in large-scale money laundering. They received cash to protect call centres involved in illegal phone scams, it was claimed. Kravchenko, who denies wrongdoing, left his job after meeting Zelenskyy. Ukraine’s president also spoke to the heads of Nabu and Sapo, the two anti-corruption agencies that have uncovered a sprawling criminal scheme involving government officials. Zelenskyy described his conversation with Kravchenko as “fairly long” and said: “I’m sure you understand what we discussed.” The prosecutor’s resignation letter will be sent to Ukraine’s parliament, the Verkhovna Rada, he said. Kravchenko is the latest member of Zelenskyy’s inner circle to be linked to corruption. The allegations involve so-called call centres operating in Ukraine. Employees pose as banks, law enforcement agencies or investment advisers, and persuade victims to transfer funds to accounts or crypto wallets under their control. Those targeted include Ukrainians, Russians and EU citizens. According to Nabu, a senior official inside the prosecutor general’s office protected the criminal network and helped it to launder its assets. Each “call centre” paid $7,000 (£5,200) a month in protection money, law enforcement sources told the Ukrainska Pravda newspaper. The bribes ran into millions of dollars, it said, with hundreds of centres believed to employ about 60,000 people across the country. Nabu investigators raided Kravchenko’s office on Friday. Staff refused to let them in so they used ladders to scale a metal gate. Kravchenko was not at work and had disappeared from his home, which was searched later that evening. The chief suspect was arrested in the western city of Lviv. Recordings of phone calls published by Nabu suggested he was overseeing repairs at Kravchenko’s home while simultaneously collecting bribes from the fraudulent call centres. Nabu released images over the weekend of a safe filled with bundles of dollar bills. It said it had uncovered five officials behind the scheme but did not name them. The cash was spent on real estate, jewellery and other valuables, it said, laying out its evidence in a 30-minute video. Zelenskyy tried to strip Nabu and Sapo of their independence last year, a move he reversed after protests in Kyiv and other cities. There are further claims that the prosecutor’s office subsequently spied on Nabu staff and tried to obstruct their work. The revelations come at a time when Ukraine is under day-and-night attack from Russian drones and missiles. Three people were killed and 19 injured in overnight strikes on Kyiv that caused huge fires and left smoke hanging over the city. The onslaught marked the end of a three-day ceasefire in the capital after a visit on Sunday by Donald Trump’s envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. They visited Moscow on Saturday and met Vladimir Putin. Zelenskyy said the pair had brought some “very good, worthwhile ideas” for ending the war but gave no further details. He said he hoped to meet Trump in the next two weeks. Few expect a breakthrough, with the Kremlin claiming on Tuesday that its forces were close to victory. While Russia escalated its bombing, Ukrainians were talking about corruption investigations, posting numerous comments on social media, the transparency advocate Olena Tregub said. “Society is shocked and appalled by government officials who are basically behaving as mafia,” she said. “It’s not even corruption. It’s organised crime, protecting illegal call centres that were scamming people, not only in Ukraine but in Europe.” She said anti-corruption investigations were different from previous ones because Nabu detectives were “very good technically”. “They are recording people in their homes, in their offices and over the phone,” she said. “They are outsmarting other law enforcement bodies fighting against them, and are able to tape people who think everything is discreet.” She said the high-profile raids were “changing the culture in Ukraine” and making society less tolerant of ill-gotten wealth. Zelenskyy’s former business partner fled the country last year after being implicated in a corruption case featuring the state nuclear energy company. Two ministers were fired. The president’s powerful chief of staff, Andriy Yermak, also later resigned after being questioned. Both deny wrongdoing. Kravchenko rejected the allegations against him on Sunday, calling them “completely unsubstantiated”. A day later he said he did not want his office “to be used as a tool in political confrontation”. The deputy chair of parliament’s law enforcement committee, Andriy Osadchuk, said the scandal underlined the need to ‌reform the prosecution service and called for key posts to be filled through open competition. Fighting corruption was also vital to Kyiv’s bid for EU membership, he said. “It will be very difficult for Ukraine to move forward if we do not change the approach to selecting and appointing the prosecutor general and prosecutors at lower levels,” Osadchuk said.

title: Remilitarisation and support for Ukraine must not slacken, US tells Europe
summary: Comments in virtual meeting aimed at securing 300 Patriot missiles for Kyiv come as UK commits £100m for Ukraine’s air defences
text: The US undersecretary of defence, Elbridge Colby, told European countries they “must not slacken” in their remilitarisation and their backing for Ukraine in a virtual meeting aimed at securing 300 Patriot interceptors for Kyiv. The influential Pentagon official praised Ukraine’s recent “stout defence”, which he said proved that Europe was capable of leading the defence of its own continent from Russian aggression rather than relying on the US. “Support for Ukraine contributes to Europe’s security,” Colby said at the start of a 50-country virtual meeting of the Ukraine contact group, reflecting what appears to be a warmer tone from the US on Ukraine. It helped, he continued, “to rebuild Europe’s military strength and industrial capacity. But words are not enough. Real money and industrial capacity must be put to work. Again, I underline that this is happening, but we must not slacken.” Led by its president, Donald Trump, the US has been pushing for Europe to dramatically increase defence spending and pay to supply American weapons, such as Patriot interceptors, to Kyiv, via a scheme set up by Nato. The UK announced it had committed £100m to boost Ukraine’s air defences over winter by buying a package of US military equipment that will include urgently needed Patriot missiles, before the meeting had started. Boris Pistorius, the German defence minister, pledged in his opening remarks that Berlin would donate a number of older Patriot Pac-2 interceptors from army stocks, and urged other allies of Ukraine to follow suit. Ukraine is currently unable to prevent Russian ballistic missile attacks because of a shortage of Patriot interceptors, leading to attacks that have killed civilians and destroyed food and logistics warehouses over the summer. Wes Streeting, the UK defence secretary, said that Ukraine had been “pretty clear” about what it needed: “Three hundred Patriot missiles from partner stocks, 500 air-to-air interceptors with counter-cruise missile capability, $2bn for drones,” and continued contributions to other schemes. The UK did not say how many Patriots it would be able to buy, but the number is likely to be only a fraction of the number sought, given the cost of each interceptor is estimated at about $3m. Yevhen Khmara, Ukraine’s newly appointed defence minister, acknowledged that Ukraine’s “situation with ballistics is much more difficult” and which was “precisely down to a lack of Patriot missiles”. It was a situation, he added, that the Kremlin was aware of, and trying to exploit. The Ukrainian minister also said that Ukraine faced a defence budget gap of €23bn this year, and he hoped that countries would bring forward more funding so that its drone investment programme could continue uninterrupted. Kyiv hopes that the EU will bring forward some of a €90bn two-year loan to help plug the shortfall. An escalation of the long-range war has meant that the harm to civilians is increasing as Ukraine targets Russian oil refineries and warehouses, while Russian bombing has meant that civilian casualties in Ukraine are at their highest level since May 2022 amid near constant attacks on the country’s cities. On Sunday, US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited Kyiv for the first time, to discuss peace proposals, though no breakthrough was made. A day earlier they had visited the Kremlin, which is still pressing for Ukraine to give up territory and make a string of concessions for ending the war. The prime minister, Andy Burnham, spoke to Trump about the war on Monday, with the two agreeing on the need to “continue working towards a ceasefire that prevented more loss of life”.

title: Israel to close British consulate in Jerusalem after sanctions announced
summary: Several MPs also banned from Israel after UK steps up condemnation of settlements and announces sweeping sanctions
text: Israel has ordered the closure of the British consulate in occupied East Jerusalem in response to sweeping UK sanctions on goods from illegal settlements. Reacting to Ed Miliband’s description of violent Jewish settler activity on the occupied Palestinian West Bank as “ethnic cleansing” carried out with the tacit backing of the Netanyahu government, Israel’s foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, announced retaliatory measures including the closure of the consulate and entry bans on several UK MPs. It is the latest stage in a furious and escalating row between the countries in which diplomatic relations have hit rock bottom. The consulate in the Sheikh Jarrah area of the city focuses on Palestinian issues in the occupied territories, including Gaza, the West Bank and Jerusalem. The British embassy in Tel Aviv is where the UK’s ambassador to Israel is based. While most countries regard East Jerusalem as illegally occupied by Israel since the Six Day War in 1967, Israel says Jerusalem is its undivided capital. “United Jerusalem is the capital of Israel and is under its full sovereignty,” Sa’ar said. “Any foreign activity in the area must be conducted through accepted and agreed channels and without violating Israel’s sovereignty.” Sa’ar also announced entry bans on a number of mostly leftwing MPs including the former Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn, the Your Party MP Zarah Sultana, the Labour MPs Diane Abbott, Naz Shah, John McDonnell and Richard Burgon and the Green MPs Hannah Spencer, Carla Denyer, Siân Berry and Ellie Chowns. The Israeli government added that longstanding British involvement in the training of Palestinian security forces on the West Bank would be terminated. Britain will also be excluded from the US-led Gaza coordination mission, which is based in Israel. The British sanctions were coordinated with 11 other countries, including France and Canada. Sa’ar said: “The British move is morally distorted, and constitutes blatant interference in the affairs of a sovereign state and its electoral process.” He added: “Israel has nothing against the British people. We know that we have many friends in Britain. Unfortunately, a hostile Labour government is in office, systematically acting against the state of Israel, and it has left us with no choice but to finally respond to its hostile actions.” Sa’ar said that he had coordinated ‌Israel’s response with the prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu. Israel will hold an election in late October. Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, called the ban “a grave miscalculation, a decision that will fall on the wrong side of history”. “In the current context, it would be a gross interference in the democratic elections of a sovereign nation,” he said. “Sanctions are not a solution – dialogue is. I say to all foreign governments: Stop. Step away from the dead-end of sanctions and boycotts, and turn toward constructive dialogue and toward cooperation.” Settlement building and settlement-related violence have increased under the auspices of far-right Israeli ministers in the Netanyahu government who have said publicly that they aim to “bury” a two state solution through their actions. Itamar Ben-Gvir, Israel’s hardline public security minister and a settler leader, called on Netanyahu to recognise Argentina’s claim to the Falkland Islands, a British overseas territory in the South Atlantic known in Argentina as Islas Malvinas. The US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, a longtime supporter of the settlements, said the British sanctions were “discrimination against the Jewish people”. He said the UK could face “repercussions or retaliations” from the US. However, in a markedly more muted response, US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said Washington would ‌not follow Britain, France and Canada in blocking ⁠imports from Israeli settlements in the Palestinian territory and did not want to see moves that would destabilise the West Bank. Israel has been under notice from successive British governments – both Conservative and Labour – for years over the risk of international isolation and potential sanctions related to continuing settlement activity in the occupied territories. These warnings have becomelouder in recent years as violent settler activity has escalated. The UK’s Labour government previously sanctioned some Israeli settlers and illegal outposts over violence against Palestinians and illegal development in the West Bank. In a change of Britain’s position, Miliband, the foreign secretary, said on Tuesday that the UK regards Israel’s occupation of the West Bank, and not just the settlements, as illegal. The tougher stance is likely to be welcomed by many Labour voters and lawmakers, who have urged the government to go further in sanctioning Israel and supporting Palestinians. Difficulties to establishing an EU-wide approach, coordinated with the UK, had led to countries making individual decisions on a widening sanctions regime that culminated in the joint statement by 12 countries that they were setting in train the process of far harder-hitting sanctions.

title: Black-clad mobs and the puzzle of two-tier justice | Letters
summary: Letters: Readers respond to reports and commentary on far-right groups of masked vigilantes causing unrest in Dover and Portsmouth over the weekend
text: In Dover and Portsmouth at the weekend, mobs of masked vigilantes in balaclavas acted in an intimidating and racist manner (‘Army of Christian patriots’: how a black-clad vigilante group swarmed Portsmouth, 8 September). Critical infrastructure was blocked, with roads, boats and transport disrupted. Police officers were injured and vehicles damaged. Permission for the orchestrated demonstrations was not sought or granted. Arrests? None. Imagine if this had been a masked pro-Palestine protest or an unauthorised environmental action disturbing the flow of traffic, intimidating the public and injuring police officers. There would have been hundreds of arrests. So, we have an extraordinary example of “two-tier policing”, with the police service being tough on Palestine and climate protesters while going easy on anti-immigrant demonstrations. To be consistent, it’s time to call for extremist racist organisations such as Patriot Platform to be designated as “terrorists”. Or, at the very least, for the government and police to use the many powers they have to take robust action against the participants of this kind of shocking whipping up of hatred that has already led to racist pogroms in many parts of the UK. Gideon Ben-Tovim University of Liverpool • Zoe Williams is right to expose the hollowness of the hard right’s claim to “protect … our women” (Why does the hard right have such a high tolerance for domestic abusers in their midst?, 7 September). Last year, I was one of a number of women in a group protesting against Tommy Robinson’s Unite the Kingdom march. As we waited for our train home, our group was attacked by some of his supporters. I was punched in the face. I am due to give evidence in the resulting court case. The contradiction is hard to miss. A movement that presents migrants and refugees as a threat to women can apparently tolerate intimidation and violence against women who stand in its way. There is another disturbing contrast. I am due in court myself, charged under the Terrorism Act after sitting peacefully in Trafalgar Square holding a placard saying: “I oppose genocide, I support Palestine Action.” Masked far-right protesters can march through our streets intimidating refugees, migrants and Muslims, while peaceful protesters face prosecution under terrorism legislation. If the phrase “two-tier justice” means anything, surely this deserves scrutiny. Name and address supplied • It’s right that to undercut support for racism (Editorial, 7 September), an end to 15-plus years of austerity must be called not just in theory but in practice. That means spending on public services and infrastructure, not cuts, and wages at least keeping pace with inflation. There is also an immediate task. The far-right mobilisations in Dover and Portsmouth represent an attempt to build a fascist street force fuelled by the words of Reform UK and Restore Britain. As we approach the 90th anniversary of the battle of Cable Street, the lesson remains clear. They must not pass. Keith Flett Tottenham, London • My response to the horrifying sight of masked thugs parading in Dover? A donation to the refugee charity Care4Calais. title: Bank of England’s tricky balancing act in dealing with global bond shock  | Letter
summary: Letter: Complicated trade-offs raise the issue of whether the government needs to change its relationship to the Bank of England, says Prof Costas Milas
text: Your editorial (The Guardian view on the global bond shock: Andy Burnham should take note, 1 September) implicitly suggests that the global bond shock will bring firmly into focus our government’s fiscal responsibility. Fiscal responsibility is a precondition for avoiding a further rise in the UK’s cost of borrowing. Nevertheless, fiscal policy has to be considered together with monetary policy. In fact, the current rise in UK yields poses a huge challenge for the Bank of England’s policymakers, who will make their next decision on UK interest rates on 17 September. This is when the Bank’s monetary policy committee (MPC) will announce the amount of government bond sales (or quantitative tightening, QT) to be pursued over the next 12 months. In a recent Bank of England staff working paper, co-authors and I found that QT policies add up to 0.4 percentage points to UK yields, but also reduce UK inflation by as much as 1.4 percentage points. Since QT policies increase UK yields over and above the impact coming from the ongoing global turmoil, the MPC is likely to slow down the current pace of £70bn in annual sales of government bonds. Such a decision will relieve the ongoing pressure on UK borrowing costs, but it will also make it more difficult for UK inflation to revert quickly to the Bank’s 2% target. There are complicated trade-offs here that raise the issue of whether the government needs “to change … its relationship to the Bank of England”, as your editorial suggests. title: Save our seabirds from the huge windfarm due to be built near Bass Rock | Letter
summary: Letter: The offshore windfarm at Berwick Bank is predicted to kill more than 4,000 birds in its first year alone – among them gannets, puffins and kittiwakes, writes Ashley Davies
text: Lev Parikian paints a vivid picture of the gannets of the Bass Rock and the impact that avian flu has had on their numbers (Country diary, 31 August). There’s another threat, though, and it’s one that puts some supporters of renewable energy like me in a novel situation: protesting against the construction of a windfarm. Berwick Bank will be one of the biggest offshore windfarms in the world – a few kilometres from the Bass. This is perilously close, and the RSPB has calculated that it will kill more than 4,000 seabirds in its first year alone, among them gannets, puffins and endangered kittiwakes. I support windfarms, but the location of this one is deadly, cruel and shortsighted, and thousands of us want it to be moved further out to sea. Stick up for these seabirds at stopberwickbank.co.uk. title: Neither political donations nor special interest groups should dictate policy | Letters
summary: Letters: Readers respond to George Monbiot’s article on Andy Burnham and political donations
text: George Monbiot condemns Andy Burnham for his alleged subservience to the interests of the wealthy (Andy Burnham has already made a mistake that will cost him his premiership: he lost his nerve over political donations, 2 September). If true, I agree. But the same could be said of any interest holding sway in our politics. Lobbying groups, activists, unions, thinktanks, people who obsess about this, that or the other. It is surely not OK for our democracy – at local or national level – to have its priorities dictated by those with the shrillest voices, as well as those with the deepest pockets. Speaking from Scotland, I think that our public realm is a case in point. It seems special interest groups are, to all intents and purposes, the main driver of government policy now. And all too often, said influence is framed by an ideological mission that does not necessarily align with that boring, broad swathe of folks who don’t follow politics closely, and don’t see government as a means to progress personal hobbyhorses or single-issue causes. The latter are, in their own insidious way, as injurious to democracy as the whispers of the wealthy in the ears of politicians. So too is turning a blind eye to such undue influence because its aims chime with your own beliefs. Leaders of any party must endeavour to serve not some, but all – without fear or favour – including those who didn’t vote for them. Not easy. No guarantee of success. But abandoning that principle makes our politics all the poorer. Colin Montgomery Edinburgh • I was surprised to see George Monbiot paying feasance to that liberal shibboleth, “the general interest”. If a society is fractured by inequalities of class, race, gender, sexuality, etc, then there can be no “general interest” until these are overcome. Ensuring trade union influence over Labour policy through the continuation of union donations acts as leverage against policy being captured by the likes of Lord Alli and Lord Sainsbury. When Monbiot goes on to say that “Labour governments know they can safely bash benefit recipients, who aren’t unionised, while they tread very carefully – far too carefully in my view – around the interests of oil workers”, he misses the obvious point that the way, then, to protect benefit claimants is to organise them. Unite, for instance, already has a community membership for students, claimants and pensioners, and has organised days of action against benefit cuts and sanctions. Monbiot’s proposal would not strengthen the power of benefit claimants, it would simply weaken the power of trade unions. Nick Moss London • George Monbiot is right; Andy Burnham lacks the courage to take on vested interests, and nowhere is this more apparent than over climate breakdown. During an extensive Panorama interview with Laura Kuenssberg, the climate crisis was not mentioned once, despite record temperatures, drought affecting half the country and unprecedented wildfires raging throughout Europe. The cap on bus fares will be financed by abandoning international climate payments; and now Burnham wants to take a “pragmatic” approach to drilling in the North Sea. Next year we will breach the 1.5C limit stipulated in the Paris agreement, and this will be followed by the disappearance of coral reefs and the eventual disintegration of the Western Antarctic ice sheet – irreversible events that will undermine the marine food chain and raise sea levels by six metres. Andy Burnham’s lukewarm approach won’t look so pragmatic to our descendants when coastal cities worldwide are under water. title: Police overlooked tip-off day before far-right agitators blocked Dover roads
summary: Details passed to Kent police after people heard in pub boasting about going to Dover to ‘attack Muslims’
text: Police were told the night before far-right agitators blocked roads into Dover that those involved had converged on a village 18 miles away and planned to use it as a launchpad, it has emerged. People in Preston-next-Wingham told of how hundreds of men had started to arrive in the village of just over 920 residents on Friday afternoon and in effect “took over” the village. At least one person is understood to have sought to pass on details to counter-terrorism police after people heard the far-right activists boasting in the local pub that they intended to go to Dover and “attack Muslims”. The information was passed on to police but little or no interest was shown in the tipoff, according to the anti-fascist group Hope Not Hate, who spoke to the person. Others reported careless and illegal parking to the police but no action was said to have been taken. The claims have raised fresh questions about Kent police’s handling of the protest, in which hundreds descended on Dover at 7am and which the force described as “spontaneous”. No arrests were made during the action, which involved hundreds of black-clad masked men standing in the middle of roads and led to access to the port of Dover being blocked for several hours. Kent police admitted on Tuesday that an initial review of its handling of the protests found that the force had received non-emergency information late on Friday evening that a protest could take place in the town the next day. “This information was not fully assessed. If it was, it may have allowed the force to consider its resourcing,” it said in a statement. “However, this information would not have prevented the lawful protest from taking place, nor the disruption experienced by the town, port and wider community.” Roger Gale, the MP for Herne Bay and Sandwich, who lives in Preston-next-Wingham, said the unrest in Dover on Saturday was clearly not “spontaneous”. He said that the village in Kent was unusually full of cars on Friday night and that a local car park and the recreation ground was still full of vehicles on Saturday morning, prompting him to call 999. Gale said: “A local councillor took photographs of the number plates and they should be able to work back from those to establish who owns the cars. I called 999 at around 9.30am on Saturday and two officers came over quite quickly. “I am going to write to the chief constable to ask what they are going to do with this information. There were roughly 50 cars in the car park and the recreation ground and more on the road. [What happened in Dover] was not spontaneous. It was carefully coordinated. Those participating were transported from the village to Dover, most likely in Luton vans.” Gale was not aware of calls being made to the police on Friday but he added that he knew that conversations among participants in Saturday’s unrest had been overheard in the village pub on Friday night. The action was organised by Daniel Thomas, a long-term associate of the far-right activist Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, known as Tommy Robinson. Thomas, who has established an umbrella grouping called Patriot Platform, was also linked to a blockade in Portsmouth the following day. One person who lives in Preston-next-Wingham told Hope Not Hate: “There were hundreds of them. They took over the place. “They were literally parking everywhere. They parked in the recreational ground, in the butcher’s car park, in the primary school, on the roads and even on junctions.” A fleet of vehicles is understood to have arrived at about 5.30am on Saturday in the village. Video footage later showed men who took part in the protest disembarking from the back of the vehicles in Dover.

title: Barnaby Webber’s death in Nottingham attack was ‘potentially preventable’, inquiry told
summary: More rapid use of blood products may have raised chance of 19-year-old making it to hospital, though chance was low, says counsel
text: The death of a 19-year-old student who was killed in the Nottingham attacks in 2023 was “potentially preventable”, a public inquiry into the incident has heard. Barnaby Webber and Grace O’Malley-Kumar, both 19, and Ian Coates, a 65-year-old caretaker, were fatally stabbed on 13 June 2023 by Valdo Calocane, who had been diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia. In 2024, Calocane was sentenced to an indefinite hospital order after admitting three counts of manslaughter on the grounds of diminished responsibility and three counts of attempted murder. The inquiry is examining the events leading up to attacks, and has heard evidence from various local authorities, including health professionals and police officers, as well as Calocane’s family, in order to assess the “events, acts and omissions” that led to the killings. During closing submissions on Tuesday, it heard how a panel of medical professionals had assessed the emergency medical response to the attacks and the “survivability” of victims. Rachel Langdale KC, counsel to the inquiry, said the assessment had found that “more rapid administration of blood products” could have increased Webber’s chance of getting to hospital and possibly undergoing surgery. The 19-year-old had a “far less” than 50% chance of surviving his injuries, which was classed as “potentially preventable”, Langdale said. She added that O’Malley-Kumar and Coates’s deaths were “not preventable”. The assessment, which also acknowledged the efforts of emergency services, found that a more rapid administration of blood to Webber would have to have been coupled with multiple other rapid and meticulous steps “in order for Barnaby to survive to intensive care”. The inquiry also addressed the emergence of further evidence after hearings had concluded in early June. At the start of closing arguments, the inquiry’s chair, Deborah Taylor KC, said it was “disappointing”, and that further evidence “ought to have been identified by core participants and disclosed earlier”. She called on them to provide all corrections and omissions by 31 December. Such evidence included the police discovery of a holdall bag at Calocane’s former address in Nottingham in the days after the attack. The bag contained notebooks that were not disclosed to the inquiry until June this year. The books contained notes from Calocane in which he described himself as God, and said police had “mind-reading software” and that he had the power to “resurrect people”, the inquiry heard. Other documents created by Calocane were found in a bin at the property, containing bullet points about explosives, including TNT and nitrate fertiliser. Such notes were not identified or taken into account by police, nor made available to the Crown Prosecution Service or to psychiatric experts, the inquiry heard. The lawyer representing bereaved families, Tim Moloney KC, said one of the notes appeared to say “Manchester Arena”. Calocane had also searched online for “large venues in Nottingham”, he said. “Nobody has ever asked [Calocane] why he was researching explosives and large venues, because they couldn’t,” Maloney said. “There was a failure to investigate [Calocane’s] historical behaviour and actions.” The inquiry was also not told of violent assaults committed by Calocane until after the hearings concluded in early June. One involved an assault on a colleague in a warehouse in 2021, and in another he punched a colleague in Normanton in February 2023. Evidence presented to the inquiry earlier this year detailed how Calocane had committed a string of violent incidents in the years before the attacks, leading to him being sectioned four times in the space of two years. An arrest warrant was also out for Calocane at the time of the Nottingham attacks, after he failed to appear in court for the alleged assault of a police officer, the inquiry heard previously. Closing submissions will conclude on Wednesday and a report detailing the inquiry’s findings will be published next year. • This article was amended on 9 September to change a reference in line with the Guardian’s house style.

title: Lindsay Clancy’s lawyer urges Trump to consider pardon after mistrial
summary: Attorney hopes Trump would consider clemency given ‘the type of person she is’ and ‘what she has been through’
text: The lawyer of Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts woman accused of killing her three young children, has said he hopes Donald Trump will pardon his client after her trial recently ended with a deadlocked jury. Clancy’s attorney, Kevin Reddington, made the appeal on a televised interview on the ABC show Good Morning America on Tuesday. The plea comes to Trump after a judge on Friday declared a mistrial after the jury in the Clancy case could not reach a unanimous verdict on whether she was guilty or not guilty. Reddington said he hoped that the president would “consider a pardon” for Clancy given “the type of person she is” and “what she has been through”. “Mr President, I would hope that you would consider this young lady,” said Reddington, who also alluded to how Trump on Friday called the case a “tragedy”. Trump’s pardon powers are applicable in the federal justice system in the US, and Clancy was tried in Massachusetts’ state criminal justice system. But in June in Colorado, Tina Peters – the former clerk convicted in state court of participating in a plot to chase election conspiracy theories boosted by Trump – was released early from a nine-year prison after the Democratic governor, Jared Polis, succumbed to pressure to do so from the Republican president. Clancy, who is 36, was charged with fatally strangling her three children – Cora, five; Dawson, three; and Callan, eight months old – in their Duxbury, Massachusetts, home in January 2023. She had also thrown herself out of her bedroom window in an apparent suicide attempt, which left her paralyzed. Prosecutors argued that Clancy was aware of her actions and had “coldly and efficiently executed” the children after planning to do so, including ensuring her husband was out of the house. But her defense, led by Reddington, claimed that she was suffering from postpartum psychosis which compelled her to carry out the killings and therefore was not legally culpable. During the trial, Reddington called a forensic psychiatrist, Dr Phillip Resnick, to testify that Clancy had “severe depression” and a history of anxiety, which increased after the birth of her children to the point that she “felt she couldn’t function”. “At the time of the crime … Ms Clancy was frankly psychotic,” Resnick said. “She was clearly psychotic on that day.” Jurors in Plymouth state court spent more than 38 hours in deliberations over the charges, which sparked a broader national debate over maternal mental health issues that can occur postpartum. Ultimately, Reddington has said the 12-person jury, made up of nine women and three men, was split 11 to one in favor of a not guilty verdict. The lack of a unanimous verdict led to the judge declaring a mistrial, opening the way for another trial. Trump was asked about the trial by reporters on Friday, with the president calling the case “a shame” and a “horrible tragedy”. “I think the judge has said it’s going to be a mistrial, so there’s going to be another trial,” he said. “It’s a terrible situation. Look, she did a horrible, horrible thing. “Can’t be worse. But you’ll find out what the price to pay is. There’ll be a price. It’s going to be mental institution or jail or something, but I guess they’re going to go through another trial.” In the US, the national maternal mental health hotline is 1-833-852-6262. In the UK, the Pandas foundation offers support via Whatsapp on 07903 508334. In Australia, the national maternal and perinatal mental health hotline is 1300 726 306

title: British family of man abducted by Saudi Arabia speak out over nine-year ordeal
summary: Mira Lozi says quiet diplomacy has failed to free Rami Naimi who was first seized in Dubai in 2017
text: A British woman has spoken out for the first time about the alleged abduction, torture and coercion of her husband at the hands of Saudi authorities, after nine years of “failed” quiet diplomacy. The businessman Rami Naimi was first abducted in Dubai in 2017 on his return from a trip to Australia with his father. After being tortured, he was released the following year. The father of three, who is the son of Ali Al-Naimi, a former Saudi oil minister and head of the state oil company Aramco, was detained again in 2022 and held for two years. Last year he was sentenced to six years’ imprisonment after a secret trial. He was initially detained alongside 400 of the kingdom’s most powerful people in an infamous round-up at the the Ritz-Carlton hotel in Riyadh, which became the biggest and most contentious purge in the modern kingdom’s history. Speaking out for the first time after years of what they described as a failed diplomatic process, his family has alleged abduction, disappearance, torture and coercion at the hands of Saudi authorities. Naimi now faces a second trial for allegedly following certain accounts on X critical of Saudi Arabia and for attempting to leave the country without permission – both of which he denies. “The first thing I wanted to do was speak out, but I was told no,” said his wife, Mira Lozi, speaking alongside her son at a campaign launch to bring Naimi home in London on Tuesday. Lozi, currently fighting cancer, fought back tears as she said she had been encouraged to keep silent since 2017 to help secure his release. “For nine years my children and I have lived through a nightmare,” she said. “Saying the truth today is like a liberation, enough is enough and we’re just hoping that we can end this nightmare and all the governments will be able to help us.” Naimi left Saudi Arabia aged 13 and travelled for years between the UK, US and Middle East as a businessman. His family claim he was abducted in Dubai in 2017 after returning home from a book tour trip from Australia with his father. They say he was blindfolded and forcibly taken by car to Abu Dhabi and then by private jet to Saudi Arabia. He was surprised to find himself with the others who had been rounded up, his family said, as he is not a journalist, activist or politician. His abduction in 2017 came as the kingdom’s elite were detained at a five-star hotel in Riyadh during a purge in which princes, tycoons and ministers were stripped of their fortunes. Accounts later surfaced detailing torture and coercion, and the event preceded the murder of journalist Jamal Khashoggi, whose assassination at the Saudi consulate in Istanbul in 2018 sparked revulsion around the world. Naimi was held at the hotel and tortured, electrocuted, waterboarded and psychologically abused for three months, his family said. He was told, falsely, that his father was being tortured next door. He was released in January 2018 after signing a “settlement agreement”. He was subsequently forced to sign a document pledging to surrender 5bn Saudi riyals, later “discounted” to 1bn riyals (£200m) – which the family says neither he nor they possess. Naimi was placed under electronic surveillance and banned from leaving the kingdom. His family said he was disappeared again for nearly two years in 2022, and subjected to further torture, and emotional and psychological abuse. They said they had no idea if he was alive or dead, and learned only through the help of his legal team and diplomats that he was being held in Saudi’s notorious Al Ha’ir prison. It was after his release in March 2025, with an electronic tag and subject to a travel ban, that he learned of charges against him claiming he had “exploited” his father’s official influence. Naimi faced allegations he acted as an agent for a US company in Saudi Arabia and helped Aramco to secure a contract to provide technology to prevent diesel smuggling. After seven years without charges, Naimi, an EU citizen, was sentenced to six years’ imprisonment after a secret trial. Now he is unable to leave Saudi Arabia and his communications with his family remain monitored. He has no idea, the family said, of their decision to go public with his case. “Until today we have no idea why Rami was targeted,” said Lozi, who is too frightened to return to Saudi Arabia or travel to the United Arab Emirates. “It really is something out of a movie. It’s shocking and we just want to end this nightmare,” said his 21-year-old son, Ali, who was 12 when his father was abducted. In recent years the UK’s relationship with Saudi Arabia has come under scrutiny over the flow of arms between the two countries, Riyadh’s use of public executions and targeting of exiled activists and dissidents. “Any family making a decision like this needs to be supported by the government,” said human rights lawyer Caoilfhionn Gallagher KC, who is leading the case. As the family hopes to meet the new prime minister and foreign secretary, Gallagher said the recent appointment of a special envoy for Britons detained overseas did not go as far as campaigners, experts and parliamentarians had called for. Gallagher described it as: “Tea and sympathy for a very limited group of people.” Last month the Guardian reported that X had become the latest US social media company to block the accounts of Saudi dissidents so they are no longer visible inside the kingdom, following orders from Saudi authorities. The UK Foreign Office declined to comment. The Saudi embassy in London has been approached for comment.

title: Letter: David Hencke obituary
summary: Richard Faulkner writes: Hencke revealed secret plans to implement a huge programme of passenger closures
text: In November 1979 the journalist David Hencke prevented a second set of cuts to Britain’s railways along the lines of those made by Richard Beeching in the 1960s. In reports in the Guardian, Hencke revealed secret plans to implement a huge programme of passenger closures, partly through extensive substitution by buses. Between 700 and 2,000 miles of railway were under threat. Hencke had seen British Rail’s confidential corporate plan, evaluating 40 out of 85 branch lines and provincial services. It laid down a timetable for closures covering two stages, up to 1984 and up to 1989. As a result, the transport minister, Norman Fowler, over-ruled BR and his officials in a letter to BR’s chairman, Peter Parker: “It is my firm policy that there should be no substantial cuts in the passenger rail network … the option of closing 40 passenger services is one that the government have rejected.” Virtually all these services are still running and most are thriving. The culture in favour of the railway has changed, not least thanks to David Hencke.

title: Netanyahu was warned of 7 October Hamas attacks, book claims
summary: Israeli PM says allegation that UAE president alerted him more than a week before major offensive is ‘absolute lie’
text: Benjamin Netanyahu was personally alerted by the president of the United Arab Emirates that Hamas was planning a large-scale offensive against Israel a week before its 7 October 2023 attack, but did not act on the warning, according to a book by Haaretz reporters. The claim, which comes amid a crucial election campaign, prompted Israeli opposition leaders to describe the prime minister as “unfit” for office, even as Netanyahu denounced the report as an “absolute lie” and denied he spoke to the Emirati leader at that time. Haaretz said the Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar, later killed by Israel, had warned a former Palestinian official that the militants were preparing “a terrifying operation” which he described as an “earthquake”. According to the report, the UAE president, Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, spoke to Netanyahu a week and a half before the attack, and told him Hamas was planning a major operation. The allegations, published in Haaretz on Tuesday, pile more pressure on the Israeli prime minister who has already faced heavy criticism for his handling of events before the 7 October attacks. Hamas militants killed more than 1,200 people and took another 251 people hostage during the offensive. Hundreds of Israelis, mostly soldiers, have been killed in continued fighting from consequent wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran. Israel’s retaliatory offensive has left most of Gaza in ruins and killed more than 73,000 Palestinians. The claims are contained in the book Hostages: 843 Days of Abandonment, which, its authors say, is based on dozens of sources in Israel and worldwide, including very senior officials. According to Haaretz, bin Zayed communicated frequently with senior Israeli leaders, including Netanyahu and the Israeli president Isaac Herzog, with a UAE diplomat delivering a secure phone to the Israeli prime minister for the conversations. A week and a half before 7 October, the reporters say, bin Zayed called Netanyahu from the presidential palace in Abu Dhabi and, in a 45-minute call, warned that Sinwar was planning a major operation which the Emirati leader was concerned could destabilise the region. To bin Zayed’s surprise, Netanyahu reacted calmly to the news, the report said. Netanyahu’s office on Tuesday denied that the UAE gave him a warning. “If there was any relevant information, it was passed through intelligence channels between the two countries,” the statement said. In a joint statement on Tuesday, several Israeli opposition party leaders declared their intention to find out what Netanyahu knew and when, and what actions he took, if any. “Why did he not inform the security establishment, and why did he not act to protect Israeli citizens?” the statement demanded. Gadi Eisenkot, a former military commander who has emerged as Netanyahu’s main rival in the October elections, accused the long-serving prime minister of evading responsibility for security lapses and resorting to “pathetic” excuses, such as saying he was not woken up soon enough on the morning of the attack. “Netanyahu received dozens of warnings for 7 October and ignored them all. He is unfit,” Eisenkot wrote on X. Naftali Bennett, a former prime minister also running in the elections, said Netanyahu “bears personal and direct responsibility” for the deaths on 7 October, the deadliest attack in Israeli history. “Netanyahu cannot continue to serve in his position for even one more minute,” Bennett said. The leader of the centre-left Democrats party, Yair Golan, accused Netanyahu of “endangering Israel”. “The stories about ‘no one woke me up’ are over. You knew, you ignored, you failed, you are to blame,” he said, in a video posted on social media. Many Israelis have demanded an independent state commission of inquiry into the security lapses that failed to prevent Hamas’s attack. Opposition parties say establishing such a commission, whose members would be appointed by the supreme court, would be their first priority if elected. Netanyahu’s government has rejected the proposal.

title: Electric car owners could save hundreds of dollars a year under the solar sharer scheme. Here’s how
summary: New research shows who benefits most from the federal solar sharer plans
text: Electric car owners could have a new way to save money under a federal government scheme that promises three hours of free electricity. Since the solar sharer plans became available in July, many Australians have been asking – is it possible to save money by switching, and how? New research reveals who could save hundreds of dollars by taking advantage of the regulated energy offer – and its free power period – and who risks paying more due to higher peak and supply charges. EV owners could save with midday charging Households with one electric vehicle could save up to $800 a year on the government’s solar sharer plan, while some with two vehicles could save as much as $1900, according to new modelling by the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis (IEEFA). Jay Gordon, an energy analyst at IEEFA, says EVs already cost less to run than petrol or diesel cars. With solar sharer, “if you’re able to charge that EV in the middle of the day – you can take advantage of the free power period and lower the running costs even more,” Gordon says. “And if, of course you’re a larger household that had two EVs – and we know the majority of Australian homes do have more than one vehicle – you could be seeing double those savings, so you’re easily exceeding $1,000 a year just on that regulated solar sharer offer.” Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Gordon calculated the potential savings using IEEFA’s household energy model, comparing the total energy bill for a home on solar sharer to the same home on a standard electricity plan, with an average amount of driving. This modelling came after EV sales outpaced petrol cars for the first time in Australia in August. The chief executive of the Electric Vehicle Council, Julie Delvecchio, says many Australians were already saving thousands of dollars each year by switching to an electric car. “If you start to build in things like solar and make use of the best time of the day to charge, you can save a whole lot more.” The EV Council’s research shows the vast majority of people charge their vehicles at home, with 80% using solar panels. There are now more than 200 EV models available in Australia, with some under $25,000, Delvecchio says. “When you think about the opportunity to couple that with solar, and with charging at different times of the day. I think it’s one of the single biggest cost of living measures available to Australian households today.” Hot water heating draining the budget? About 40% of Australian households have an electric hot water system. Those homes could save between $400 and $800 by switching to the regulated energy plan, Gordon says, by programming their water heating to run during the free power period. “If you don’t have an electric hot water system, you most likely have a gas hot water system. Now, we know there’s already savings to be had from switching the gas system to something efficient and electric. What the solar sharer tariff can do is deepen those savings a bit.” What about homes that already have solar and a battery? For homes with solar panels and a battery, the results were mixed, Gordon says. “If you’ve already got more than enough rooftop solar to meet your home’s needs and to charge your battery, a solar sharer free period doesn’t necessarily add value.” Some customers might see moderate savings, while others could end up paying more. Who should think twice before switching? Solar sharer was not necessarily the best or cheapest plan available. “What we know about those default offers is they are almost never the best available option on the market,” Gordon says. “This is definitely the case for solar sharer tariffs. We found that when you looked at other offers on the markets, there is almost always a more competitive option.” Potential energy bill savings for households on a market offer with a free power period – who were able to shift their car charging or water heating – were even higher. Many other types of households, including renters, apartment dwellers and those with gas appliances, wouldn’t be able to shift enough of their energy use to benefit from the regulated solar sharer plan. “Households that can’t flex their demand are unlikely to benefit,” he said. Both the federal and Victorian governments provide comparison sites to help people compare plans and find the cheapest deal.

title: Organised crime driving illicit cigarette factory boom ‘in almost every EU state’
summary: Bloc losing €13bn in revenue with one in 10 cigarettes illegal, watchdog reports
text: The illegal trade in tobacco is booming in the EU, according to a report by the bloc’s financial watchdog, with almost one in 10 cigarettes produced illicitly or smuggled, causing an estimated €13bn loss in tax revenue each year. The European Court of Auditors (ECA) said in a report on Tuesday that the trade had “changed significantly” in recent years as smuggling, while still “a problem”, was overtaken by illicit manufacturing, which has increased dramatically in the bloc. Organised crime gangs are moving production inside the EU “to shorten supply chains and get closer to consumers”, said the ECA’s Petri Sarvamaa. “Illegal production sites have now been detected in almost every EU member state.” The ECA cited the example of a large-scale illicit cigarette factory in Belgium dismantled by police last year. It operated around the clock, with 50 workers running four production lines, each able to produce 1m cigarettes every hour. During a raid on the largest illegal facility so far uncovered, in Spain, police seized 3m packs of cigarettes valued at €15m, five tonnes of raw tobacco worth €5m, and made 20 arrests. The factory’s products had been distributed across six EU countries. “The scale is quite remarkable,” Sarvamaa said. “Last month French authorities dismantled a cross-border operation that had been supplying the city of Lille only since last December but had already made 120 deliveries of 7,500 packs each.” The ECA report said such illicit cigarette factories, which usually operate for two- to four months, were using sophisticated equipment and employing experienced technicians to set up and maintain their machinery. The organised crime groups that run them split production across multiple facilities and often locate them in border regions, tailoring their operations by producing specific brands for individual markets and even developing new tobacco products. The damage goes beyond lost tax revenue. The trade “undermines public health policies by making tobacco products cheaper and more accessible, especially to young people”, Sarvamaa said. It also feeds organised crime and finances other illegal activities. While, overall, tobacco consumption has continued to fall across the EU, the quantity of illicit tobacco products has risen steadily, reaching about 8.8 % of total cigarette consumption in 2023 (the latest figures available), the report said – although information about the size, structure or economic impact of the trade remains “incomplete and unreliable”. The report said the EU and many member states had taken steps to combat the trade, but were hampered because European law in the area was not harmonised and member states’ efforts were uneven, leaving enforcement gaps. National control systems and enforcement have different definitions of offences and of penalties, encouraging criminals to move to the more lax jurisdictions, and information exchanges in the bloc were inconsistent. “Criminals involved in the illicit tobacco trade are succeeding not because Europe lacks legislation but because gaps remain in coordination, information and enforcement,” Sarvamaa said. “Organised crime has a strategy. We need one too.”
