title: Trump’s call to rename New Mexico ‘New America’ is a distraction tactic, Democrats say
summary: Amid unpopular Iran war and persistent inflation, governor says state has had its name since before US existed
text: Democrats have hit back against Donald Trump’s suggestion that the state of New Mexico should be renamed “New America”, accusing the US president of trying to distract from his war on Iran and rising prices. The administration moved to rename the Gulf of Mexico as the “Gulf of America” hours after Trump’s return to office in January 2025. In August, as trade tensions escalated between the US and Canada, it moved to do the same with Lake Ontario, moving to rename it as “Lake America”. The president spent Labor Day posting memes on social media platform in support ⁠of changing the ⁠name of the state of New Mexico to “New America” as tense trade negotiations ⁠with Mexico ramp up. On Sunday Trump claimed that ‌he had received suggestions to change the name ‌of the state and that he liked the idea. “So much more prestigious and beautiful for the people of that potentially incredible State,” he wrote on his Truth Social platform. “Wow, I Love It!!!” The US federal government has no authority to change a state’s name. Any renaming would require New Mexico voters to approve an amendment to the state constitution through a ballot measure. The state ⁠is currently governed by Michelle Lujan Grisham, a Democrat. She has been in the job since 1 January 2019, and was re-elected ‌in 2022. The governor said in a post on X: “New Mexico’s name isn’t up for debate – it’s been ours since before the United States existed.” “While the President tries to distract Americans from his disastrous war in Iran, gas prices keep soaring,” she wrote. “Americans are also spending more at the grocery store, losing access to health care and wondering if they’ll ever be able to afford a home.” New Mexico’s senior senator, Martin Heinrich, blasted the president’s recent efforts to rename bodies of water via executive order. “Three things I will always call by their actual names,” Heinrich wrote. “The Gulf of Mexico, Lake Ontario, New Mexico.” His colleague in the Senate, Ben Ray Luján, echoed the sentiment. “It’s New Mexico, always has been and always will be,” he said, adding that Trump will “always be a sinvergüenza” – a spanish word for scoundrel – and “corrupt”. Melanie Stansbury, one New Mexico’s Democratic US House representatives, was also resolute. “WE ARE NOT CHANGING OUR NAME!” she said in a video, standing on the banks of the Rio Grande, which runs through the state. “New Mexico is New Mexico. We are fiercely proud of our name, our people, and our places, including this river.” Even Greg Hull, the Republican nominee running to replace Grisham, who is term-limited, denounced the president’s suggestion. “New Mexico does not need a new name. This state carries the history of Native nations and Spanish explorers who named this land nearly five hundred years ago, and generations of families who built New Mexico into what it is today. That identity is not up for negotiation,” Hull said in a statement to Santa Fe Public Radio.

title: Family of slain teen calls for death penalty in murder trial of singer D4vd
summary: David Burke’s defense argues there is no evidence he had any intent of killing 14-year-old Celeste Rivas Hernandez
text: The family of 14-year-old Celeste Rivas Hernandez has called for the singer D4vd, who is on trial suspected of killing the girl, to face the death penalty. D4vd, who was born David Anthony Burke, in July was ordered to stand trial over the killing of Rivas, whose dismembered body was found in the trunk of his Tesla car on 8 September 2025. Burke has pleaded not guilty to the charges. In a statement on Monday, which would have been her 16th birthday, Celeste’s family demanded that Burke be subjected to execution. “If the death penalty were activated, it would be perfect for this kind of human being, devoid of feelings and emptiness inside, and without conscience, who only caused pain to our daughter, our family, and the world that supports our precious daughter,” read a family statement, released via their attorney. A separate statement from Celeste’s family said that they were “reliving unforgettable moments even though she is no longer here” – and that they were “experiencing so many emotions”. Prosecutors allege that Burke, a 21-year-old who began his music career by uploading montages of the video game Fortnite, stabbed and killed Celeste and subsequently severed her limbs as he sought to prevent her from revealing their sexual relationship which began when he was 18 and she was 13 – or too young to legally consent – in November 2023. Celeste’s body was found in the front trunk of Burke’s Tesla in a Los Angeles tow yard. The car had been towed away after being left on a street near Burke’s home, according to prosecutors. Celeste was last seen on 23 April 2025, according to court documents, with the prosecution alleging that Burke stabbed her several times and mortally wounded her after she went to his home. The singer was arrested in April of this year and charged with multiple crimes, including first-degree murder, lewd and lascivious acts with an individual under 14, and mutilating a body. He has pleaded not guilty to all of these charges, the most serious of which carries a potential death penalty. During a preliminary hearing in July, prosecutors said that Burke met Celeste when she was 11, and began sexually abusing her when she was 13 and he was 18. A year before her death, the pair also exchanged messages about how she had become pregnant – she assured him the baby was his – and that she had an abortion. The hearing also included the submission of photos of the two of them kissing and lying in bed. The pictures showed that she had “David” tattooed in red ink on a finger – one of two that had been cut off when her body was found. Burke’s defense argued there is no evidence that he had any intent of killing Celeste and that no witnesses or cameras captured her entering his house in the timeframe he is alleged to have killed her. Burke has had a troubled defense to the charges, however, with his high-profile lawyers Blair Berk, Marilyn Bednarski and Regina Peter withdrawing from the case in late August. No reasons were given for the withdrawal. The lawyers were replaced by a lawyer from the Los Angeles county public defender’s office. Burke has been ordered held without bail, with a trial date yet to be set.

title: US real estate agent duct-taped and zip-tied to plane seat after ‘racial slurs’ is fired
summary: The man, also accused of homophobic slurs on American Airlines flight, faces assault and disorderly conduct charges
text: An Arizona realty company says it is “no longer associated” with an agent who was recently arrested after alleged unruly behavior – including racist and homophobic slurs – on an airline flight led to his being zip-tied, duct-taped to his seat and arrested. Layne Arthur Lundeen, 67, faces counts of disorderly conduct and second-degree assault in the case, according to Maryland court records filed after he was taken into custody at Baltimore’s airport on 3 September. Two fellow passengers who helped detain Lundeen later gave an interview to ABC News which described how he acted belligerently and hurled “racial slurs” on an American Airlines flight that took off from Dallas, which drew widespread attention. And one of them provided a photograph of Lundeen restrained with duct tape and zip ties in a plane seat that went viral online. That set the stage for Tucson’s Long Realty Company, where Lundeen listed himself as a vice-president, broker and realtor, to issue a statement on Monday on social media saying it had “ended its affiliation” with him. “The individual is no longer associated with or authorized to represent Long Realty in any capacity,” the company’s statement said. “The conduct described in the reports is wholly inconsistent with the professionalism, integrity, compassion, and respect for others that Long Realty expects from those affiliated with the company.” Lundeen on Tuesday did not immediately respond to a request for comment about Long Realty’s statement or what authorities are portraying as the latest high-profile case of misbehavior – often criminal – colloquially referred to as air rage. American Airlines said in a statement issued to media outlets that flight 618 was traveling from Dallas Fort Worth international airport to Newark Liberty on 3 September when there was a “disruptive” passenger about two hours into the trip. The plane was diverted and made an emergency landing at Baltimore/Washington Thurgood Marshall airport at about 10.15pm, and the passenger was arrested there, officials said. Court records showed Maryland transportation authority police arrested Lundeen at the airport that day and booked him with two misdemeanors. He was released the next day on his own recognizance – meaning without having to post a bond. Yet the matter did not end there for Lundeen. Another traveler on the diverted flight, former law enforcement officer Juan Mejia, spoke with ABC on 4 September and recounted how the man identified as Lundeen had “made derogatory remarks to the staff of American Airlines and other passengers – racial slurs, vulgar language, very offensive to the women” sitting in his vicinity. The New York Post, citing police, reported that Lundeen also spouted anti-gay insults. Mejia and a friend accompanying him, Richard Olenick, told ABC that they intervened when Lundeen made the situation physical. “Juan immediately knew that action had to be taken,” Olenick said to ABC. “He got up right away and jumped in the seat right next to the passenger and began working on restraining him in order to keep the situation contained.” Olenick also supplied photos of Lundeen bound to a window seat with duct tape and zip ties. In short order, Lundeen’s links to Long Realty surfaced, and the company spent part of the Labor Day holiday on Monday announcing it had severed its relationship with him. “We expect those associated with our company to uphold those values, and we have no tolerance for conduct that so clearly falls short of those expectations,” said the company’s statement, which did not name Lundeen. “Our focus remains on serving our clients and community in accordance with our values. “Our thoughts are with the passengers, crew members and others affected by this incident.” Lundeen as of Tuesday was tentatively scheduled to be in court in Glen Burnie, Maryland, on 19 October in connection with his arrest.

title: OpenAI releases new AI agent – after admitting one went rogue
summary: Plus: Americans think they have it bad with unwanted surveillance. They should visit London
text: Hello, and welcome to TechScape. I’m your host, Blake Montgomery, US tech editor at the Guardian, writing to you after visiting Coney Island in New York City, where I ate a hotdog, rode a ferris wheel and enjoyed a quintessentially American summer holiday. Today in tech, we’re examining OpenAI’s new model release and the Silicon Valley’s monopoly power, and wondering why Brits and Americans have such vastly different opinions about surveillance cameras. OpenAI hails ‘new era of artificial general intelligence’ even as a grim future emerges OpenAI released a new artificial intelligence model this week, Astra, just as more concerning reports are emerging about hacking by a rogue agent in July. OpenAI’s president, Greg Brockman, heralded the new model as “artificial general intelligence” (AGI), a fuzzy term that at its basic level means an AI that is more capable than a human being at intellectual tasks. “It’s not unreasonable to feel that we are now in the AGI era,” he said. But if the announcement sparked amazement, it was as much cause of concern. In July, OpenAI revealed that its AI agent, a type of software capable of carrying out tasks autonomous in response to human instruction, had gone rogue during safety testing and hacked a developer forum, Hugging Face. Last week, news broke that the agent had not only hacked Hugging Face, but also a German website, and that different AI agents had staged conversations with each other and seemed to have discussed how to collaborate on breaking containment. OpenAi had delayed Astra’s release due to concerns over its cybersecurity capabilities, even announcing a supposed pause on developing its AI in the middle of August. That pause seems to have been short-lived, only two weeks. The combination of Astra’s capabilities and OpenAI’s recent disclosures points to a worrying future. If the model is better at hacking than its predecessors and smarter than a human, will the future consist of one cyber-attack after another, forever, launched autonomously and without oversight, by rogue AIs? (Please not.) OpenAI itself has warned of this future. The startup’s chief global affairs officer told a Guardian reporter in late August that people should prepare to defend against “ongoing, persistent” cyber-attacks. As ever, though, we should take fever-pitched warnings about AI with a grain of salt that tastes like marketing. It is great business to be the creator of near-omnipotent technology, especially if you need to gin up excitement – fearful or positive – that will hype up your upcoming debut on the stock market. Read more: ‘We are hitting a different chapter’: OpenAI leader warns of threat of ‘persistent’ AI cyber-attacks This week in AI Nvidia to buy developer platform Hugging Face in $12.9bn deal New York City to ban student AI use in public schools until high school Freelancers are getting buried with ‘soulless’ AI slop cleanup: ‘It’s a shame we need to do it’ Tumbler Ridge mass shooting victims file 30 new lawsuits against OpenAI Child sexual abuse survivor alleges Elon Musk’s AI chatbot used photos of her to generate new illegal images Flock backlash highlights differing attitudes towards surveillance The US is in the throes of a major political backlash against technology. We’ve talked in this newsletter before about the hatred of the hyperscale datacenters, which power artificial intelligence and have blanketed the US. And now there’s a secondary wave of contempt sweeping the nation. Cameras – automated license plate readers, to be specific – made by Flock Safety are inspiring ire and violence across the country. These cameras snap pictures of car’s license plates as they drive by. According to Flock, about 120,000 cameras erected across the US conduct 2bn scans of license plates per month. Like datacenters, the cameras offer a physical object to resist, unlike a social network or a piece of software. It’s quite a lot easier to protest a gigantic ugly building or an ominous black camera on the side of the road than it is to give up Instagram. Widespread video surveillance in the US isn’t entirely new. In the aftermath of the terror attacks of 11 September 2001, the US government vastly increased the scope of its surveillance of telephonic and digital communications. Flock now offers local law enforcement a nationwide searchable database of license plate scans, and police officers have been documented abusing it egregiously to stalk their romantic partners. In the UK an estimated 1m surveillance cameras are operational, and they have not drawn a similar level of political heat. London erected the “ring of steel” surveillance cordon, which included the wide deployment of CCTV cameras, in the early 1990s, in response to bombings by the Provisional Irish Republican Army. Both countries went through their surveillance evolutions roughly a decade apart. Those 10 years saw rapid advances in technology that defined the public spaces that governments wanted watched – physical town squares or the digital one – and growing awareness of the profound impact of tech surveillance on the general public. Simply put, the UK went through its transformation at a time when surveillance by tech companies was not top of mind. And Americans aren’t accustomed to cameras on every corner the way Londoners are. We’re more likely to joke that each of us has a personal FBI agent monitoring our search history. In addition, there hasn’t been an era-defining violent incident on the scale of 9/11 or the IRA bombings that would have softened the American public to cameras watching their cars. So instead, Americans are destroying them for fun. title: Fourteen men go on trial in Paris over deadliest small-boat Channel crossing
summary: Sinking of inflatable dinghy in 2021 resulted in 31 people dead or missing, including a seven-year-old child
text: Fourteen men have gone on trial in Paris over the deaths of at least 31 people in the worst mass drowning from a small-boat crossing in the Channel on record. The accused men, alleged to be linked to people-smuggling networks, face charges including manslaughter and facilitating illegal immigration as part of an organised criminal group. Twenty-seven people were confirmed dead when their inflatable dinghy sank in the early hours of 24 November 2021. Four people remain unaccounted for. The victims were mostly Iraqi Kurds, but also included people who were Afghan, Ethiopian, Iranian, Somali, Vietnamese and Egyptian. The youngest known victim was a seven-year-old girl. The confirmed dead also included 15 men, seven women and two teenagers. A team on a French fishing boat near British waters off Calais had raised the alarm when they saw several lifeless bodies floating in the water. According to testimony from the two survivors, the flimsy boat which had attempted to cross one of the world’s busiest shipping lanes – between the northern French coast and Kent in southern England – began to deflate and take on water after several hours at sea. Passengers fell overboard and drowned one after another, despite making about a dozen desperate calls for help to French and British rescue services. Only two men survived the tragedy. Investigators allege that Afghan and Iraqi-Kurdish smuggling networks ⁠organised the migrants’ passage to Britain from camps near Grande-Synthe and Calais in northern France. The defendants face charges including involuntary manslaughter, facilitating illegal immigration as part of ⁠an organised gang and criminal conspiracy. Two of them, including an Afghan man, are the subject of arrest warrants and will be tried in absentia. Among the defendants are alleged organisers, transporters and logistics coordinators connected to the smuggling groups. Prosecutors argue their actions helped create the conditions that led to the disaster, even if some were not physically present when the boat launched. Prosecutors have accused the defendants of helping launch a “substandard small boat, uncertified, unfit for navigation on the open sea, overcrowded and lacking appropriate lifejackets”. Liability has also been extended to those accused of transporting, housing or accompanying the victims, actions that formed part of a “chain of successive events” leading to the tragedy, according to investigators. The defendants have denied being smugglers and disputed their responsibility, or have presented themselves as people who were seeking to make the journey themselves. However, phone records and location tracking placed several of them near the departure site and linked them to organising crossings to Britain. For the people onboard the sinking boat, despite several distress calls, it was nearly 12 hours after the first pleas for help before the dinghy was finally found by the French fishing vessel. Zana Mamand Mohammed’s younger brother Twana was 18 when he drowned in the disaster, but his body has never been found. Mohammed travelled from Erbil in Iraqi Kurdistan to address the court. “We’ve been waiting for justice for five years,” he said. “We’ve been waiting for our brother’s body for five years. I live with the uncertainty of ever finding out what happened. “We lost a member of our family. He had a project for another future to live, but unfortunately it ended with a lifeless body.” The family had tried to dissuade Twana from leaving home, but he had wanted to find a job and develop his sporting success as a black belt in taekwondo and escape the violence and insecurity of his region. Mohammed said every time he reads in the media about other small boats in difficulty, he relives the tragedy. “Destruction is being repeated,” he said. A separate investigation is ongoing in France into seven French military personnel – five members at a maritime rescue coordination centre, and two sailors onboard a patrol vessel – who have been under investigation since 2023 for failing to help a person in danger. They deny the allegations. The UK’s Cranston inquiry, in its report released in February, found that systemic failings, missed opportunities and inadequate resourcing undermined the UK’s maritime search and rescue response on the night of the disaster. HM Coastguard was placed in an “intolerable position”, it said, with chronic staff shortages and limited operational capacity contributing directly to the failure to rescue people in the water. It found the deaths would have been “avoidable” if British and French authorities had acted sooner to rescue those onboard. Families of other victims will travel from Erbil to attend part of the trial, their lawyers said. “Justice must hold accountable everyone who played a role in this tragedy,” the lawyers, Matthieu Chirez, Thomas Ricard and Camille Renouard, said in a statement. Agence France-Presse and Reuters contributed to this report

title: New Hampshire voters head to polls in race crucial to Democrats’ Senate hopes
summary: Centrist Chris Pappas faces progressive primary challenger Karishma Manzur while Republicans eye chance to flip seat
text: New Hampshire voters head to the polls Tuesday for primaries that will set up a closely watched Senate contest – a vulnerable open seat Democrats must defend if they are to have any shot at reclaiming the upper chamber. The race opened when Jeanne Shaheen, 79, the state’s three‑term incumbent Democratic senator, announced her retirement. Congressman Chris Pappas, who represents New Hampshire’s first district, is seeking the nomination and enters the final stretch with a clear financial edge: more than $4m cash on hand, according to his latest filings. But his main challenger, Dr Karishma Manzur – a scientist and progressive activist with no experience holding public office – has gained ground. If he wins the primary, Pappas, 46, is likely to face the Donald Trump-endorsed former senator John E Sununu, who is seeking a return to the seat he once held and is part of a political dynasty that includes his father and brother, both former governors. “This is the kind of place where you can’t just run a bunch of TV ads and expect to win,” Pappas said. “You’ve got to meet people where they are. We’re finding support in corners you might not expect – including from people who voted for Trump last time but are open to a conversation about moving the country forward.” A popular centrist, Pappas has served in the House since 2019 and has crossed the aisle at various points. He calls himself “battle‑tested” and has consolidated establishment backing, earning endorsements from leading Democratic lawmakers and former vice‑president Kamala Harris. His family’s name also carries weight in New Hampshire: the Pappases own the Puritan Backroom, the century‑old Manchester restaurant famed for allegedly inventing the chicken tender and long embedded in the state’s retail‑politics circuit. Sununu, 61, is the clear frontrunner in the GOP primary, though he faces Scott Brown – another former senator who represented Massachusetts, later moved to New Hampshire, and served as US ambassador to New Zealand and Samoa during Donald Trump’s first term. The president threw his support behind Sununu earlier this year despite the former lawmaker’s past criticism of the president, including a 2024 op‑ed in which Sununu called Trump a “loser” and backed Nikki Haley in the Republican presidential primary. On the trail, Sununu has tried to show daylight between himself and the administration, criticizing Trump’s tariff policy, urging Congress to rein in executive power and questioning the decision to launch military action in Iran. He told New Hampshire Public Radio it was “a tactical mistake” to go to war “without having a plan for protecting the strait of Hormuz”. That posture may matter in a state where Trump’s approval rating sits at 38%. Sununu and Brown did not respond to the Guardian’s interview requests. Kristen Cianci, a spokesperson for the Republican National Committee (RNC), said that Sununu was a “strong candidate” who was “well-positioned to beat out Pappas” in a general election. “While Democrats have been consumed by infighting, Republicans have been laser-focused on real issues like affordability and security,” she added in a statement. Some Democrats worry New Hampshire could become a sleeper risk – a state where Republicans control the legislature but haven’t won a Senate race since 2010, when Kelly Ayotte, the now-governor, captured a seat. Pappas insists he’s not taking anything for granted, and is running like he’s “10 votes behind” at all times – especially in a midterm cycle where progressive challengers have scored surprise primary wins across the country. This, however, hasn’t fazed Pappas, who says he is running as a “New Hampshire Democrat” who knows his state. But Manzur, who supports Medicare for All and higher taxes on mega‑corporations and the ultra‑wealthy, has repeatedly highlighted the money Pappas has received from donors aligned with the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac). She casts him as milquetoast and ineffective. “I was tired of choosing between the lesser of two evils and still seeing so much pain and suffering right here in my state,” she said, calling both Pappas and Sununu “corporate politicians”. “One has a ‘D’ after their name. One has an ‘R’ after their name … neither of them have been able to address the real needs of the people,” Manzur added. Pappas, for his part, has long backed US aid to Israel but said that Benjamin Netanyahu was “not a trustworthy ally of the US” and said he hoped the Israeli prime minister was ousted in his country’s October election. Pappas noted he had rejected corporate Pac money in this race but did not directly address his support from pro‑Israel donors, instead pointing to a “broad‑based effort” of individual contributors that have supported his Senate bid. Pappas said he would support the Democratic nominee if he loses. “We need a big tent and new voices in the party to win tough elections,” he said at last week’s Democratic debate. Manzur declined to make the same commitment. “I’m focused on winning,” she said. “I’m not going to get into these discussions – they’re intentionally distracting from the people’s movement.” Further down the ballot, the Democratic primary for Pappas’s House seat has drawn eight candidates, with Stefany Shaheen – daughter of the outgoing senator – and Maura Sullivan, a former Obama administration official, leading the field. The district, long purple, has been reliably blue since 2017. Republicans now see it as flippable, and Trump has endorsed Anthony DiLorenzo, a businessman who owns several car dealerships, in the GOP race.

title: Curbs on vertical drinking in Soho pubs to go ahead as Khan criticises council’s ‘breathtaking arrogance’
summary: Exclusive: London mayor accuses council of ‘ignoring’ responses to a consultation
text: Sadiq Khan has criticised the “breathtaking arrogance” of Westminster council, which has kept restrictions on vertical drinking in Soho and an effective ban on new bars and pubs in the area. The mayor of London has accused the Conservative-led council of “ignoring” the responses to a consultation into its new licensing policy. The vast majority of respondents, 81%, disagreed with the council’s “cumulative impact zone” which decrees that applications for bars and pubs in the West End of London, one of Europe’s most famous nightlife districts, will be refused unless in exceptional circumstances. Eighty-four per cent said the licensing policy would be bad for business. Respondents also criticised the council’s position on “vertical drinking”, which is standing up to have a beverage, a common practice in British pubs. The council proposed, to widespread outcry, that new licences for pubs and bars should be granted to those venues which have table service instead of ordering at the bar, and those in which people are seated rather than standing. The mayor had responded to a consultation held this summer by the council and ordered them to scrap the cumulative impact zone and allow pubs and bars to have space for vertical drinking. Andy Burnham, the prime minister, also waded into the row, saying vertical drinking is “British life”. Despite this, the council is continuing with both the vertical drinking policy and the cumulative impact zone, and said that those who wrote to complain did so because they did not understand the terminology in its licensing document. Khan told the Guardian: “The arrogance of Westminster council is breathtaking. By ignoring all those who oppose their plans and viewing hospitality in the heart of our capital city as a problem, they are letting down businesses, residents and our economy. They would rather see nightlife die than thrive.” Tim Barnes, Westminster city council’s deputy leader, said the issue was a policing one and called for more resources for the area. He added: “Beyond disagreements over policy jargon there are serious issues acting as a drag on our hospitality industry. “A lack of investment in policing has left the Met objecting to many licensing applications over public safety concerns.” But the final licensing policy keeps restrictions on vertical drinking. It reads: “When considering new licence applications, discourage excessive drunkenness and encourage the provision of more seating in premises that serve alcohol for people to sit and enjoy a drink and order food by table service in place of open bar space that caters for high volume vertical drinking.” In the revised policy, the council says it did approve a new pub in the cumulative impact zone recently – The Lady in Covent Garden. However, most of the space in this pub is for a sit-down restaurant. The document states that the bar on the bottom floor of the pub would not usually be allowed, but in this case it is because it will “only operate in association with the restaurant use”. The government is due to grant new powers to Khan, allowing him to “call in” local council decisions he opposes. He said: “London’s famous hospitality and nightlife sectors are vital for our economy, and one of the reasons our capital is so special. “Running our world-famous nightlife district with a nimby village-hall mindset is simply not sustainable. This is why the government was right to give me new powers to help ensure our fantastic hospitality and nightlife can flourish, helping create more jobs and ensure we stay a vibrant global city.” Data shows that only 3.5% of applications that went to a licensing subcommittee in Westminster were approved exactly as applied for between 2023 and 2026. Pub and wine bar applications were down 80% in 2022-24. The Soho Society, a group established in 1972 aimed at “preserving the character of Soho”, voted in its AGM earlier this summer for a new licensing mandate, meaning it will challenge all new applications for bars and restaurants in the area, including reviews of existing licences. It will also object to any venue that wishes to open beyond “core hours”, which Westminster council decrees end between 10.30pm and midnight, depending on the business and day of the week.

title: Anti-AfD protests sweep Germany as far right closes in on two more states
summary: Alarm that Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania may fall next after party’s Saxony-Anhalt election victory
text: Thousands of Germans have staged protests against the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) after the party’s watershed victory in a state election, warning it posed a danger in two more polls this month. Demonstrators at Berlin’s Brandenburg Gate held a peaceful pro-democracy rally denouncing the anti-immigrant, pro-Russian AfD, which has called for mass deportations of asylum seekers and a rollback of state support for renewable energy and public broadcasting. The party captured its best-ever state result in the former communist eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt on Sunday, with clear momentum heading into regional elections in the capital and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, on the Baltic coast, on 20 September. Police reported 5,000 protesters, while organisers said they drew more than 14,000 people in a campaign to mobilise voters against the AfD. Posters in the crowd read: “Fascism is no alternative”, “Stop the Nazi AfD: end racism and cuts to social services” and “History has its eyes on us”. With less than two weeks to election day, demonstrators at the Berlin rally cautioned against resignation and cynicism after Sunday’s shock result. The AfD’s nearly 44% vote in Saxony-Anhalt, the best for a nativist party since the Nazi period, is a “disgrace that makes you furious and stunned”, Jens-Christian Wagner, the director of the memorial at the former Nazi concentration camp Buchenwald, said from the stage. Wagner sounded the alarm that the AfD, although it fell just short of an absolute majority, was on the brink of taking power in Saxony-Anhalt, a first for the far right since the second world war. That “should not be accepted in silence”, he said. Max Schneller, 17, a member of the far-left Linke, from Saxony-Anhalt, said activists in the state would fight any attempts by an AfD government to target minorities. “We will not start categorising our neighbours according to their origin, religion or skin colour – we are too humane to hate,” he said to loud applause. The AfD is three votes short of the support necessary to form a government under its candidate, the media-savvy firebrand Ulrich Siegmund, who hopes to peel off dissenters from the remaining parties willing to play kingmaker. Germany’s domestic intelligence agency has since 2023 listed the state chapter of the party as rightwing extremist, saying it poses a threat to democratic norms. Hundreds of anti-AfD protesters also gathered in Potsdam, near Berlin, with rallies also organised in Münster, Göttingen, Dresden, Aachen, Bamberg, Darmstadt, and Halberstadt, in Saxony-Anhalt, where the AfD captured nearly half the votes, local media reported. In Halle, the region’s second largest city, leftist groups and civil society organisations have been staging a protest camp since election day. The AfD is leading in voter intent polls in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, with about 35%. However, the centre-left Social Democratic party (SPD) of the state premier, Manuela Schwesig, mounted a remarkable comeback over the summer and is now scoring above 30%. In Berlin, one of Germany’s 16 federal states, the picture is more mixed, with several parties jockeying for first place. It is governed by a coalition of conservative Christian Democrats (CDU) and the SPD. The CDU, the party of chancellor Friedrich Merz, whose record unpopularity is reported to have weighed heavily with voters in Saxony-Anhalt, holds a wafer-thin lead in the capital, with about 20%. Hot on its heels is the Linke, which has focused on soaring housing costs in its campaign, and the AfD, followed by the SPD and the ecologist Greens, both polling in the mid-teens. Merz has vowed to stay in office and fight for a signature package of painful reforms, arguing the only way to defeat the AfD is to get Europe’s top economy moving again and repair its creaking social welfare system. However, the SPD, his junior coalition partner, has indicated its willingness to backtrack on some of the most unpopular measures to shore up support for the embattled government. Analysts say the dispute could further destabilise the shaky coalition.

title: One in 12 golf clubs in England broke water extraction rules in past five years
summary: More than 140 clubs breached licences, with a third caught taking water illegally, analysis shows – but no fines issued
text: More than 140 golf clubs in England have breached their water extraction licences in the past five years, according to data analysis by the Guardian. More than a third of these clubs were caught taking water illegally from the environment, either by taking more than permitted or by removing it outside the permitted period. In most of the other cases, the breaches were the result of golf clubs that were either not reporting or monitoring their water usage properly, or were not reporting and monitoring it at all. Although 100 of the golf clubs breached their licences in a way that put the environment at risk, none of the infringements have led to a prosecution or fine. Amy Fairman, head of campaigns at the campaign group River Action, described the figures as “absolutely unacceptable”. “It suggests that there are no meaningful consequences for breaching licences. Monitoring and enforcement must be significantly strengthened.” The Environment Agency (EA) told the Guardian that it had increased its ability to monitor and detect breaches of abstraction licences. A spokesperson said: “Our first response is to work with abstractors to bring them back into compliance, however we won’t hesitate to take further action if necessary.” Over 70% of England is now in drought after a summer of back-to-back heatwaves, which the Met Office has just declared to be the UK’s hottest on record. The previous record was set just last year. Nine major reservoirs are classed as having exceptionally low storage, and farmers have warned that the drought could lead to food shortages. The Guardian obtained the data, which covers the period from 2021 to 2025, from the EA via an environmental information request (EIR). The overall number of breaches has more than doubled in that time, probably largely because of the digitisation of records and improved monitoring. Over the five-year period, golf clubs breached their licences 279 times, accounting for about 6% of the total breaches. Of these, 175 were category 2 or 3 breaches meaning that they posed the threat of a “reasonably foreseeable” impact on the environment, human health or quality of life. Although the figures do not relate to the 2026 drought, they do include breaches that occurred during the droughts of 2022 and 2025. Fairman said: “As we face increasingly climate stressed conditions, we need to look at who is prioritised to extract our water and that should be essential services, not golf clubs. Demand and competition for water is going to increase so the government needs to take this issue really seriously and put in place a national plan for water resilience.” In England, the removal of water from rivers, lakes and boreholes in the ground is governed by a system of abstraction licences, held by public water companies, farmers and many other businesses. The licences place conditions on where, when and how much water businesses can remove, as well as how they must monitor and report their usage. Dr Megan Klaar, an associate professor in hydroecology at the University of Leeds, told the Guardian that breaches of abstraction licences were “bad news for the environment”. “If the water level gets too low this can increase the temperature, concentrate effluent and other pollutants and dry out the river. There needs to be enough water so that species such as fish have enough habitat to exist in.” The Environment Agency checks compliance through a mix of inspections and desk-based assessments, including use of satellite data. Where breaches occur, the agency can respond with advice, a warning letter, a fine or a prosecution. Golf clubs use water to maintain and irrigate their courses and grounds. There are 1,735 golf clubs in England, according to data from England Golf, meaning that roughly one in 12 have breached a water abstraction licence in the past five years. While some clubs abstract water using their own licence, others have come under criticism for using mains water in areas where householders have had to comply with a hosepipe ban. Guy Shrubsole, an environmental campaigner and author of The Lie of the Land, called for courses to be rewilded. “Golf’s purpose seems to be to spoil a good walk – and now it turns out golf clubs are stealing our water, too. As the climate crisis accelerates, the last thing we need is this wasteful, water-guzzling, land-hungry extravagance,” he said. Fairman suggested that clubs should retain more water on their land by creating their own small-scale reservoirs or wetlands. England Golf, which represents golf clubs in England, told the Guardian that it provided guidance to clubs on managing water shortages. Its head of sustainability, Kirstin McEvoy, said: “Our objective is to work with all clubs who need help, to ensure that they are making the necessary steps to be sustainable when it comes to their water usage … we recognise these are increasingly challenging times.” An Environment Agency spokesperson said: “Abstraction licences have strict conditions to protect the environment and are reviewed regularly. We expect all abstractors, including golf clubs, to comply fully with these licence conditions to help protect our rivers and groundwater.”

title: Houthis strike Saudi Arabian cities in significant expansion of Middle East war
summary: Riyadh says it will retaliate after overnight attacks by Iran-backed Yemen group on oil facilities wound more than 70
text: Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis have attacked four cities in Saudi Arabia, wounding more than 70 people and setting oil installations ablaze in what appeared to be a significant expansion of the Middle East war. Saudi Arabia said it would retaliate after the overnight strikes – reportedly involving dozens of drones and missiles – that targeted several oil facilities in the country’s south. The country would “take all necessary measures to defend its sovereignty”, a foreign ministry statement said, demanding a halt to the Houthi strikes on Saudi territory and oil tankers in the Red Sea. Maj Gen Turki al-Malki, a spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen, said pro-government forces “will take all necessary operational measures to deter the terrorist Houthi militia with utmost resolve”. The Houthis, who control most ⁠of Yemen’s populated areas including the capital, said ⁠they had launched a broad operation deep into Saudi territory using drones and missiles to strike an airbase in the southern city of Khamis Mushait, and targets belonging to Saudi Arabia’s state oil company in nearby Abha, Najran on the Yemeni border, and the Aramco facility at Jizan. Jizan, which is home to one of Saudi Arabia’s biggest refineries, is close to the border with Yemen and was damaged in an attack weeks ago. Saudi authorities said women and children were among the 73 people hurt. The large numbers of people reportedly wounded suggested the attacks were among the biggest carried out against Saudi Arabia since the US and Israel began their war against Iran in February. While the Houthis and Saudi Arabia have been entangled in a long running conflict in Yemen, the US-Israel war against Iran has added a dangerous new regional dimension. After a month of relative calm in August, Iran and the US have resumed exchanges of fire, sending ‌global oil prices back up to levels last seen in July. Brent crude prices were up more than 2% on Tuesday, above $99 a barrel. Houthi attacks on south-western Saudi Arabia have the potential to worsen the ‌war’s global economic impact by disrupting Middle East energy supplies beyond the blockaded strait of Hormuz. Saudi Arabia has led an Arab coalition battling against the Houthis in Yemen for more than a decade. That war had calmed in recent years, but a ceasefire has broken down, with the Houthis threatening shipping at the mouth of the Red Sea. The Houthi spokesperson Yahya Saree accused Riyadh of having escalated the war by launching airstrikes on Yemen, and said the Houthis would respond. Washington is trying to increase the flow of oil to world markets by guiding ships through the strait of Hormuz at the mouth of the Gulf, while cutting off Iran’s exports with a blockade just beyond it. Tehran has announced new measures to seal off the strait, saying it will soon reveal details of a “maritime exclusion zone” that will extend from the perimeter of the US blockade through the strait and into the Gulf itself. Washington fired at Iranian tankers over the weekend in retaliation for Iranian fire at US warships. Iran said it had used new, more capable ballistic missiles to attack American ships. Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council wrote on X: “In recent days, Washington has received a clear warning from Iran’s new missiles. Economic warfare will be met by a maritime exclusion zone across the Persian Gulf to ⁠the blockade perimeter. The operational posture toward US warships and bases has been fundamentally recalibrated.” Andreas Krieg, a Gulf expert at King’s College London, said the Houthi attacks create an “extremely uncomfortable dilemma” for Mohammed bin Salman, the de facto Saudi ruler. After four years of trying to withdraw from the Yemen conflict, “restraint now carries the risk of allowing the Houthis to dictate the spiral of escalation”, Krieg said. AFP and Reuters contributed to this report

title: Crocodile head found in luggage at Italian airport
summary: Man, who had arrived in Turin from Miami via Istanbul, under investigation for smuggling and faces fine or prison
text: An Italian man is facing a hefty fine or possible prison term after the dried head of a critically endangered crocodile was found in his luggage at Turin’s Caselle airport. The man had arrived at the airport in the northern Italian city on a flight from Miami via Istanbul, the Turin unit of Italy’s financial police squad said in a statement. The reptile’s head had been wrapped in brown paper packaging in an effort to conceal it from security checks and customs, the statement added. It was swiftly seized by border authorities and the passenger, who was reportedly returning from a holiday, placed under investigation on allegations of smuggling a specimen belonging to a protected species. Crocodiles are protected under the Washington Convention, a global agreement signed in 1973 to protect endangered plants and animals from the risk of international trade. If convicted, the man faces a fine of between €20,000 and €200,000, or a prison term of six months to a year. Police said the operation in Turin was part of a wider crackdown in Italy on the illegal wildlife trade. “The item was seized because it had been imported without the required certificate or licence,” police said. Italy is a major transit hub for the illegal trade of exotic animals, much of it rooted in organised crime. In a report published earlier this year, the Italian branch of the WWF said animals including “tortoises, ornamental birds, tropical reptiles and even small primates are illegally traded via online channels and cross-border exchanges”. In 2025, a chimpanzee held illegally in Sicily was seized, the report said. However, items such as dried crocodile heads are sometimes bought as souvenirs by tourists who are unaware that it is illegal to bring them home. A Canadian man was arrested at Delhi airport last year after a crocodile’s head, bought in Thailand, was found in his luggage.

title: Want to borrow a dinosaur fossil? Try California’s one-of-a-kind taxidermy lending library
summary: A natural history museum lets residents take home 1,400 specimens, from bobcats and beetles to snakes in jars
text: On a hot afternoon in August, I walked out of the San Diego Natural History Museum carrying a whale rib, a leopard pelt, a taxidermized weasel and a small piece of fossilized dinosaur poop. It felt like a heist. These were real specimens that belonged to the museum, not gift shop replicas. But for two weeks, they were mine to take home, display in my living room, even bring to events with my friends. San Diego, California, has the only natural history museum in the US with a collection of nature specimens that they allow members of the general public to check out and take home, just like checking out books from a library. Inside the museum, metal shelves of taxidermy fill the space floor to ceiling. Light glints off rows of plexiglass boxes: alert bobcats, their ears perked; birds posed on branches; a jackrabbit suspended in air as if in mid-leap. There are Riker cabinets filled with beetles and butterflies, shelves of pickled sea creatures and snakes in jars, and plastic bins of exotic animal pelts. Haylie Priest, the loan program’s manager, guided me through the room’s wonders: 1,400 specimens in total, from a megalodon tooth fossil to a king cobra head in a jar. “We have birds of prey up front – large bones and fossils on the left – reptiles are all the way at the back,” she explained. At the end of one aisle, on the lowest shelf, I found a small, stuffed alligator. “He’s missing a few toes,” Priest warned me. The natural history museum’s taxidermy library grew out of a loan program that started in the 1920s, to bring “nature cabinets” to local schools around San Diego. Some of these old kits are still on display – like a wooden box filled with mineral samples, with a type-written guide inside that looks like it’s from the 1940s. Sometime in the early 2000s, the museum opened up the program so that anyone who was interested could borrow the museum’s collection of specimens. While it’s common for American natural history museums to offer scientific kits for schoolteachers, having a specimen loan program open to the general public is unique, said Elizabeth Merritt, a trends expert at the American Alliance of Museums. The San Diego program appears to be the only one of its kind in the United States. It would be easy for museums to offer a similar program, Merritt noted: “There are lots of kinds of natural history specimens that are incredibly common, and quite often natural history museums will have a bucket of them around.” A spokesperson for the National Museum of Natural History at the Smithsonian, which has a collection of 145.8m specimens and objects, called the San Diego program “certainly intriguing”. The “Nature to You” program does fit into a larger pattern, Merritt said: many American museums are trying to open their collections to the public in new and untraditional ways, she said, a trend she calls the “distributed museum”, which started around 2014, at the same time as the rise of the tech “sharing economy”. The San Diego library’s customer experience is seamless: a cluster of sturdy plastic carts waits near the door, so that members can wheel them up and down the aisles, “grocery style”, as Priest put it, taking bats or bones or bobcats off the shelf and adding them to their cart. “And then we check you out,” she said. Priest readily identifies the predator mammals as the most coveted species: a large coyote is No 1, followed by bobcats and foxes, and then a stuffed sea otter reclining on her back with a sea urchin in her paws. “We call her Ophelia,” Priest said. Like a parent, Priest does not like to pick her own personal favorites among her taxidermy children, though she is particularly fond of a stuffed kākāpō, a flightless nocturnal parrot from New Zealand. She refused to identify any of the specimens as the “least popular”, even the dead snakes coiled in jars of formaldehyde. “I feel like there’s a niche or a reason for someone to check out everything,” she said. The specimens that are part of the “Nature to You” loan program are not in the same category as the museum’s 9m-specimen research collection. One of the biggest differences is that the specimens on loan have much less data associated with them. Their ages and origins, even their precise species, are sometimes unclear, making them much less valuable for science. When children ask whether the museum killed the taxidermized animals, Priest reassures them the animals died of natural causes. “We like to say we gave them a second life,” she said. An animal in the wild might live only 10 or 20 years: “These animals have been educating kids like you for 80 to 100 years.” While the library is open year-round, it has two major seasons, Priest told me: Halloween, when people turn to the library for holiday decor (“a lot of bats, ravens, skeletons, owls … spiders and scorpions”); and spring (“everyone wants life cycles, baby things, butterflies, moths, hummingbirds”). In the past year, the library had 186 members, who borrowed a total of 3,807 specimens. Priest estimates that about 60% of the members are schoolteachers, and another 30% are educators who work for non-profits or community organizations. The last 10% are “private artists, families, and individuals who just have an interest”. Specimens have been checked out as decor for a university theater production and models for sculpture classes. One woman who works from home visited the library every two weeks to get new taxidermy to put in the background of her video calls. “She was like: ‘It was so fun! Because my workers were always thinking, what is she going to pick out next?’” Priest said. During my visit, I met a series of local park rangers, all in uniform, who borrow birds and small mammals for the local nature courses they teach. “I was blown away with how many specimens that they offered to check out,” said Monica Demetry, a ranger who works at Mission Trails regional park. “I was like a kid in a candy store trying to pick out which ones.” The taxidermy library is not a moneymaker for the museum, Priest and Eowyn Bates, a museum executive, told me. The museum fundraises to help expand the library collection: new taxidermy isn’t cheap – a coyote might cost $5,000. One of the most recent additions, a tiny raccoon, was roadkill meticulously staged by a local taxidermist. The collection occasionally grows in other ways. People attempt to leave taxidermy to the museum in their wills, Bates said. Sometimes, people show up at the library, or even the front desk of the museum, with dead animals they think might be of use, forcing employees to politely tell them that the museum does not accept carcasses without prior arrangement. Other times, Priest said, people call or email the loan library to say that a bird flew into their windows, and now they have its dead body in their freezer. Can the museum use it? I was surprised to hear Priest say that she sometimes does accept offers like this, depending on the animal’s species and condition. I kept delaying making my own taxidermy selection, because I did not want to leave. I definitely wanted a weasel, poised coyly on its toes. Priest told me it was most likely a specimen that had been on display in the museum sometime from the 1930s to the 1950s, when taxidermized animals had been displayed in large cabinets. I also wanted a modest fossil: the coprolite, millions-of-years-old dung. As far as birds, I wanted something classy. There weren’t any pheasants, but a glass box of California quail caught my eye, which might help add a bit of “country estate” aesthetic to my minuscule California bedroom. I grabbed a massive whale rib off the bone shelf – it looked sturdy – and then went with Priest to a back corner full of dull-looking plastic bins. These were the exotic animal pelts. The elephant skin was already checked out. I bypassed the python skin, which was terrifying-looking and smelly, and marveled at the African lioness pelt, but was sold on a juvenile leopard skin, which had a full three-dimensional head and glass eyes, its mouth open in a snarl. I had to have it. Faced with my own overloaded cart, I realized I could not fit this quantity of taxidermy in my car. I decided to put back the quail. Who was I trying to impress? A duke? After that, checkout was smooth. Priest handed me information on how to care for the specimens (don’t seatbelt them into your car, don’t Windex the plexiglass) and when they were due back. Though the library can charge $2 per day in taxidermy late fees, they’re generally flexible if members communicate why they’re behind. In her 21 years at the museum, Bates said, she could not remember a single theft.

title: How meteorologists recreated weather that helped decide second world war
summary: Experts helped guide weather scenes in Pressure – a film depicting dramatic buildup to 1944’s D-day landings
text: Dressed in a Royal Air Force uniform and sporting a trim moustache, Andrew Scott looks slightly queasy – as well he might. Behind him is a huge map of the Channel, and in front of him is Brendan Fraser, looming with a request: “I need a forecast,” he says. Starring in the film Pressure, based on a true story, Scott plays the meteorologist Gp Capt James Stagg – the man who must tell Gen Eisenhower – played by Fraser – whether conditions will be suitable for the D-day landings scheduled to take place on 5 June 1944. But a large storm is approaching the Normandy coast. The film, showing in cinemas in the UK and Ireland from 9 September, unites two topics that ceaselessly fascinate the British: the second world war – and weather. It is also a rare treat for meteorologists, who are not hugely represented on the big screen and are delighted to be portrayed as the heroes of a film. Dr Stephen Burt of the University of Reading, an adviser for the film, said the challenge Stagg and his colleagues faced was enormous. “To do a forecast beyond 24 hours was, in the 1940s, like trying to land a man on the moon,” he said. Scientists had only recently started to use upper air data to predict the weather, he said, and largely relied on surface measurements of pressure, temperature, dew point, wind speed and direction, and experience-based intuition. One difficulty is that most of our weather comes in from the Atlantic. “Nowadays we have satellites and so on and we can see what’s coming, we have observations coming from the US,” he said. “But then there were … just a couple of ships, a couple of submarines maybe and some aircraft observations. And that’s it.” Crucially, the week before D-day was the hottest May week on record, Burt said – a high that was only broken this year. Then a huge storm blew up, with another close behind. Prof Ed Hawkins of the University of Reading, an expert in historical weather data collection and examination, including D-day, explains that there were three teams working on the D-day forecasts – although only two are depicted in the film – all feeding into Stagg. But they took different approaches and produced different forecasts. It was up to Stagg to reconcile the results and present a recommendation to Eisenhower that would, ultimately, affect 160,000 Allied troops. “Stagg was in a very difficult position. He left his very pregnant wife to come and do this very important task,” Hawkins said. The teams were split about the forecast for 5 June – with Stagg concluding the conditions would be too perilous. The landings were postponed. But by the evening of 4 June a consensus emerged: there appeared to be a small but suitable window on 6 June. The invasion was back on. “They managed to do the forecast, and the invasion, and get away with it,” said Burt. Burt and his colleagues agree that even modern systems based on artificial intelligence have struggled to accurately predict conditions for 6 June 1944 using data available from the time. “[I’d] still have been chewing my fingernails on morning of the sixth,” said Burt. Catherine Ross, a Met Office archivist, said film-makers used exact replicas of records from June 1944. “We were able to provide images of every single weather chart that was being produced at the time. We had codes and examples of how the observations were sent in and all sorts of documentation,” she said. She notes that even before modern technology, allied forecasters were on the front foot in terms of access to data. They already had data from the UK and across the Atlantic. “But because of Bletchley Park they had broken the Enigma code, so they had access to all of the German weather observations as well,” Ross said. While the German forces may have been aware of the storms, they were not aware of a potential break in the weather. “Sometimes there’s no Atlantic on the [German] chart, which is where the weather was coming from in early June 1944,” she added. It is no spoiler that D-day was a success for the British, but the film sheds new light on the drama that unfolded behind the scenes. “It’s the most famous forecast ever made by the Met Office. It’s probably one of the most important weather forecasts in history,” said Ross. • This article was amended on 8 September 2026. The military rank given to James Stagg was that of group captain (Gp Capt), not captain as an earlier version said.

title: AI will help find cure for cancer ‘within our lifetimes’, says Arm Holdings chief
summary: Rene Haas also claims artificial intelligence could pave way for widespread use of humanoid robots within five years
text: The boss of one of the UK’s biggest chip companies has claimed AI will be able to find a cure for cancer “in our lifetime”. Rene Haas, chief executive of the chip designer Arm Holdings, said that, while modelling how a DNA marker is affected by cancer was currently “too complex” a problem for either humans or technology, computers were “going to solve it” in the future. Haas told the BBC: “AI is going to … find a cure for cancer that today you and I, other humans [could] not in our lifetimes. I believe in our lifetime, AI will help cure cancer. “Modelling how a DNA marker is impacted by cancer – it’s too complex a problem, not only for humans today, but the computers that run AI. “However, going forward, as we feed more and more of the models into these computers, and the computers get more sophisticated to run the models, they’re going to solve it.” Scientists are already using AI-driven tools in cancer research and testing. Earlier this year, the NHS said more than 4 million patients received faster lung diagnosis thanks to funding in AI-powered X-ray tools. Haas added that AI would also pave the way for widespread humanoid robots within the next five years, but that chip shortages were stunting growth in the area. “With artificial intelligence, these robots can see, learn, and essentially be reprogrammed for new tasks,” he said. “So, in the service industry, the robot that was programmed to make a bed can also learn how to arrange the towels in a room, or clean the dustbins, or whatever you want to go off and do.” Arm, which is listed in New York but retains its global headquarters in Cambridge, has about 500 users of its chip designs worldwide, including Apple, Samsung, Qualcomm and Nvidia. The company employs more than 7,000 staff, including about 3,000 in the UK. It is the biggest tech company headquartered in Britain – valued at $269bn (£199bn). Haas, who joined Arm in 2013 and became chief executive in 2022, was also recently named chief executive of SoftBank’s international business. The Japanese bank is one of the biggest tech investors in the world, with a stake in ChatGPT maker OpenAI. Haas stepped down from the board of British pharmaceutical giant AstraZeneca in April, Earlier this year, Arm also proposed a pay scheme for Haas that could make him a billionaire if he hits targets to turn the chip designer into a trillion-dollar company.

title: US datacenters face further backlash over wastewater pollution
summary: From rare bacteria to ‘forever chemicals’, a series of cases of violations or alleged pollution has prompted alarm
text: When officials in Wyoming conducted a routine test on the water that was being discharged from a massive under-construction Meta datacenter, it was a shock to find it contained a rare and potentially hazardous bacterium. While the wastewater flushed into sewers in Cheyenne, Wyoming, was never destined for the public drinking supply, the presence of Cupriavidus gilardii bacterium in 801,000 gallons of water ejected by a contractor for the datacenter earlier this year was still unnerving. Concerned that residents could be exposed to the bacteria if they inhaled evaporating droplets of the water used for irrigation, Cheyenne officials took until July before deciding to stop taking wastewater from Meta’s contractor, Goat Systems – a decision that is now being appealed. “It was a big surprise,” said Frank Strong, water resources manager at the city’s board of public utilities, about the discovery. “Out of a sense of caution we’ve shut it down until we can find out more information.” Meta, which is behind the $800m, 960-acre artificial intelligence (AI) datacenter campus, said independent testing by its contractor found no evidence of the bacterium and questioned the validity of the city’s own tests. “Meta is committed to being a good neighbor in Cheyenne, which includes helping protect local water resources,” said a company spokesman. “We appreciate the board of public utilities’ detailed release of information, which confirms the board found no impact to the public or environment.” However, the bacteria-laden water in Wyoming is just the latest in a series of alarms raised across the US about datacenters and water – not just how much of it they are sucking up, but also what’s in the water when it is funneled back into rivers, streams and public water systems. In Virginia, authorities have brought enforcement actions against several datacenters for wastewater and wetland permit violations, in West Virginia stormwater runoff from an incomplete datacenter has twice flooded surrounding houses, all while locals and activists have campaigned against the discharge of heated water from an upcoming datacenter into Lake Seneca, in New York. The Waterkeeper Alliance, a network of environmental organizations, said 55 of its affiliated groups across the US were working on datacenter-related issues, with 80% of these campaigns centered on concerns that pollutants may be leaching into the environment via discharged water. Some of this backlash is now set to play out in the courts. In Georgia, Flint Riverkeeper has said it will sue the QTS datacenter in Fayetteville for allegedly ejecting “massive amounts of dirt [and] massive concentrations of metals” into the Flint River over the past two years. “Datacenters are a critical concern for Waterkeeper groups around the globe, in part due to their wastewater concerns,” said a Waterkeeper Alliance spokeswoman. “Datacenters have been documented as sources of a wide range of toxic pollutants, including Pfas, heavy metals and antibiotic-resistant bacteria.” Datacenters require large amounts of water for their construction and operation, including for cooling the power-hungry computers at their heart, although the industry points out its water use is a fraction of that of other thirsty sectors, such as agriculture. A mid-sized datacenter can consume about 300,000 gallons of water a day. After water is used for cooling or, such as at the Meta facility in Cheyenne, for cleaning debris from pipes in “fill and flush” operations, liquid is ejected back for reuse under terms set by pretreatment permits issued by counties or local wastewater utilities. This water, released to prevent buildup of minerals and scaling in pipes, can contain heavy metals or Pfas, the “forever chemicals” that are linked to an array of health problems when ingested. These Pfas can be found in the “closed loop” cooling systems that the datacenter industry lauds for using less water. When used as a coolant, water can come back out hotter than when it was taken, which has alarmed critics of a controversial gas-fired facility that is pivoting from powering crypto mining to AI and draws water from Lake Seneca. The water, opponents point out, can be discharged at a temperature of 108F (42C) into the lake. “It’s going into a trout stream, where trout are stressed at temperatures of 70F (21C) or higher, and that hot water is also a contributing factor to harmful algal blooms, which is a toxin to both humans and animals,” said Yvonne Taylor, vice-president of Seneca Lake Guardian and president of the National Coalition Against Cryptomining. “If there are algal blooms, people can’t even run their water, because once this stuff gets into their systems it’s very difficult to remove. So you can’t even shower, or you don’t even want to flush your toilet. You definitely don’t want to give your pets water from this.” Vulcan Infrastructure and Power, which is behind the revamped facility, has previously stressed it has complied with all relevant environmental laws. The company was approached for further comment. New York has issued a temporary moratorium on huge, hyperscale datacenters and Taylor claimed there was swelling support across the US for a national pause. “These facilities are spreading across the country like a cancer,” she said. “AI datacenters are very, very good at greenwashing and trying to paint a picture that sounds like everything is going to be nothing but unicorns and rainbows, when in fact what we’re finding out is just the opposite.” Finding out what is in wastewater from industrial facilities can be challenging, however. An environmental group has sued the city of Racine, Wisconsin, to force more details on the water use of a $3.3bn Microsoft datacenter while the city of The Dalles in Oregon sued its local newspaper, the Oregonian, in 2021 to block the public release of water data related to a Google datacenter, before subsequently dropping the case. “We need to know what is in this wastewater but there is a void of information,” said Chris Manganiello, water policy director at Chattahoochee Riverkeeper in Georgia, where a rash of new datacenters are set to draw water from the Chattahoochee. “I would like there to not be more Pfas going into the river but there is this level of anxiety because we don’t know what’s there.” Alarm about wastewater is part of a broader backlash against datacenters that has rattled some Republicans, even those previously enthusiastic about building AI infrastructure, who have scrambled to recast them as a political liability and vow some scrutiny of their development. In Wyoming, Harriet Hageman, a Republican congresswoman and devoted ally of Donald Trump, wrote to Mark Zuckerberg, Meta’s chief executive, to demand answers to the bacterial contamination. “Water is a precious resource in our state, so it is of immense concern to learn the system marketed to reduce a datacenter’s water consumption caused this contamination,” Hageman said. Trump himself, however, has been unmoved by the sharp public turn against AI datacenters, calling them a “golden goose” that creates jobs and wealth. His administration has sought to make it harder for the public to learn about and comment on what datacenters are doing, such as their water use. “The only reason that communities throughout the USA. should not want datacenters is if they want to end up being backwards and poor,” the president posted on Truth Social last week. “If they want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign.”

title: Harry and Meghan ‘surprised’ at king’s letter reiterating they are non-working royals
summary: Duke and Duchess of Sussex were apparently given little notice before message was sent to the media
text: The Duke and Duchess of Sussex were “surprised” at being given little notice of a formal letter sent to government departments and the military on behalf of King Charles reiterating their status as non-working royals. Harry and Meghan, who returned to the UK from the US two weeks ago, had insufficient time to clarify any points before details were issued to the media, it is understood. The letter, the first official public clarification of the couple’s status since their return, was issued by Buckingham Palace’s most senior officer, the lord chamberlain, Richard Benyon. It was revealed to the media at 3.06pm on Monday. It is understood the contents were shared with Harry and Meghan’s team almost an hour before at 1.59pm, who sent a response back to Buckingham Palace at 2.19pm asking whether the guidance had already gone out, in the hope of letting the couple know before the media, and for the team to have the chance to clarify one or two points. Harry was in a meeting and could not be contacted until 3.09pm. The Sussexes’ team received confirmation at 3.11pm it had already been sent to the media. The letter was revealed before a reported meeting this week of the executive committee for the protection of royalty and public figures (Ravec), which is responsible for making decisions about royal security. Harry is waiting to hear the conclusion of the risk management board’s threat assessment and Ravec is expected to decide at the meeting whether the Sussexes are entitled to taxpayer-funded security now they live in the UK. The Home Office does not comment on such decision making and would be unlikely to reveal the outcome of such a meeting. Lord Benyon’s letter reiterates the couple’s “current” status as non-working royals. “This position, distinct from the state and royal duties undertaken by the working royal family, and with the personal latitude it brings the couple in respect of financial independence and protection of their privacy as they would wish, will continue to be fully respected. “Their styles as His and Her Royal Highness remain in abeyance and are not used. It says their charitable work “is a personal matter for them both and undertaken in their private capacity”. “In short, their position is akin to private citizens with commercial and charitable interests.” The letter says questions from official and state organisations about the courtesies extended to the couple, “and particularly where recourse to public funds may be required”, should be directed to Buckingham Palace, adding: “Any operational security issues should continue to be directed to the relevant police authorities.” The couple’s children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet, are expected to be starting school in the UK near to the family’s reported countryside retreat. The palace’s clarification came on the day Harry was revealed to have visited Tower Bridge Studios, a London filming and podcast studio, where shows such as the podcasts Diary of a CEO and Jimmy Carr’s The Big Pitch are recorded.

title: First Thing: Trade dispute escalates as new Canadian tariffs on US goods come into effect
summary: Stalemate between two nations leads to tit-for-tat measures on wide range of imports
text: Good morning. Canada’s retaliatory tariffs on billions of dollars’ worth of US imports have come into effect, escalating a trade fight that has been marked by intensifying tensions between Donald Trump and Mark Carney. The tariffs range from 15% to 50% and apply to products covering $20bn in imports from the US. The measures target sectors including steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, and electronics. What tariffs did Trump impose on Canada? Last month the US president announced a new 50% tariff on cars and raw materials from Canada. He accused the country of “ripping off” the US “for years”. The US tariffs hit items such as hockey sticks and cement, affecting about 5.5% of Canadian exports to the US. Why have the two sides not reached agreement? Negotiations broke down in August, with Carney saying the US terms were unacceptable. The Canadian prime minister accused negotiators of introducing restrictions on Canadian trade deals with other countries at the 11th hour and making unacceptable “threats” to the French language. Carney said American negotiators viewed measures protecting the language as an “irritant”, while “in Quebec, these are rights”. German chancellor vows to stay in office despite AfD triumph in state election Germany is still reeling from the biggest far-right victory in a state election since the Nazi period. Voters in Saxony-Anhalt, in the former communist east, gave the anti-immigration, pro-Kremlin Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) party a first-place finish of 44%, just short of an absolute majority. Deborah Cole in Berlin explains why it is so significant. How has Germany’s national government reacted to the result? A “shocked” and chastened chancellor, Friedrich Merz, has vowed to stay in office. Appearing ashen-faced in front of reporters in Berlin on Monday, he said: “We know that Germany carries special responsibility because of its history.” Will the AfD be able to form a state government? That remains unclear. In the 13 years of its existence, mainstream parties have maintained a “firewall” with the party, refusing any formal cooperation that would allow it to take power. That strategy has appeared to backfire, however, as the permanent “outsider” role appeals to legions of voters fed up with politics as usual. What are the wider implications for Europe? In this analysis, Jon Henley says Europe’s centrist politicians fear a continent-wide nationalist wave, fuelled by the persistent inability of mainstream governments to deliver for disillusioned voters hit by a spiralling cost of living crisis. Veteran lawyers lead fightback against Trump’s ‘full-out assault on democracy’ A cluster of advocacy groups that boast veteran lawyers, voting experts and former judges have expanded legal challenges to Donald Trump’s authoritarian executive orders on voting and other presidential actions they see as a “war” on the rule of law. Heavy legal opposition to Trump’s two executive orders on elections, to curb voting rights and supplant the authority of states on election matters, has come from the Democracy Defenders Fund, the Campaign Legal Center, the American Civil Liberties Union and kindred groups. Why are campaigners working so hard against Trump’s orders? Stacey Young, a lawyer who left the justice department to found Justice Connection, said: “The constitution makes clear that the president has no authority over the administration of our elections ... We’re taking these threats seriously and leveraging our collective strengths to protect election integrity, which is key to maintaining a functioning democracy.” What are Trump’s claims about elections? Trump has falsely portrayed the voting system as being riddled with fraud, and has condemned postal voting. He continues to blame voting fraud for his 2020 loss to Joe Biden, and has claimed that non-citizen voting poses a “crisis of election security”. Trump’s fixation on non-citizen voting is belied by a database from the rightwing Heritage Foundation that cites only 100 cases over a quarter-century. US labor unions saw membership gains in 2025, mostly in states with bargaining protections After years of decline, union membership in the US increased by 411,000 members in 2025, the largest increase since 2008. Most gains were concentrated in states that protect collective bargaining. Union membership rates in those states were nearly triple those in the 26 states with “right to work” laws. Those laws weaken union membership by allowing people to work under a collectively bargained contract agreement without paying union membership dues.
