title: ‘Everything is against us’: Jaguar Land Rover suppliers voice fears amid carmaker’s cutbacks
summary: Firms warn of impact of company’s decision to to axe 4,000 jobs and call for government to support sector
text: David Roberts is not in an optimistic mood. The chair of Coventry-based Evtec may preside over a business with 900 highly skilled employees, multiple sites and precision machinery, but the outlook for the manufacturer appears tricky. “Everything is against us,” he says. Evtec is a “tier 1” supplier to Jaguar Land Rover, also headquartered in Coventry, which this week announced 4,000 job cuts over two years even as the chancellor, John Healey, attempted to talk up Britain’s growth prospects in his first big speech, just down the road. The cuts have stoked fears for the estimated tens of thousands of people across the UK who are employed in the supply chain to Britain’s biggest carmaker, particularly in the West Midlands. JLR made the cuts in the face of intense competition from Chinese carmakers, Donald Trump’s tariff wars and the fallout from a cyber-attack. Roberts warns the automotive demand will “contract inexorably over the next five years” without significant support and changes in government policy. “Nobody knows the rate or speed of that decline, but decline it will, because everything is against us, everything, [when] making cars in the UK,” says the chair of Evtec, which specialises in high-pressure aluminium die casting and has sites in Coventry and Kidderminster. The JLR chief executive, PB Balaji, hopes to save £1.7bn through the cuts which will mainly affect employees at its head office. He said the automotive industry “faces significant challenges, with technological change amid intense competition and ongoing geopolitical uncertainty”. The decision marks the latest in a string of worrying signs of decline for the industry, threatening Andy Burnham’s ambition to “safeguard sovereign manufacturing” and reindustralise Britain. Corin Crane, the group chief executive of the Chamber of Commerce in Coventry and Warwickshire, believes 140,000 to 180,000 people are employed in supply chain businesses connected to JLR. It is hard to overstate exactly how important JLR is to the West Midlands economy, he says. “We make stuff here and so many of our businesses are in the supply chain for JLR and even if not manufacturing companies, the business support companies, the professional services, all of them have contracts with this great big supplier. “So when there’s problems with JLR, it’s a broader problem for the West Midlands as a whole.” Oxford Economics has estimated JLR contributed £8.7bn to the West Midlands in 2024, equivalent to 4.7% of the regional economy – as well as contributing £1.1bn to the north-west, where it has a plant at Halewood. The importance of JLR to the local and UK-wide economy was underscored last year when the devastating hack left suppliers struggling and hit UK GDP. JLR scrambled to set up a help desk for its supply chain, including more than 700 companies making the 30,000 parts that can make up a luxury car. The hack paused production for four weeks, leaving factory workers stuck at home, and costing the manufacturer £200m. It was one of several factors contributing to JLR posting a profit before tax of just £14m – down from £2.5bn the year before. This time, white-collar managers and research and development staff are in the crosshairs, with the cuts expected to be largely found through UK voluntary redundancies in those areas. However, there are concerns over a ripple effect if JLR’s struggles persist. Evtec’s Roberts has united a loose collective of about 15 business that supply JLR, making up £2bn of revenue and with 12,000-14,000 employees, in order to speak with a “common voice” about the issues they are facing. He describes JLR as the “kingpin” of the UK’s automotive industry and warns that challenges facing the manufacturer had knock-on effects on suppliers and smaller car manufacturers including McLaren, Aston Martin, Bentley and Rolls-Royce. “There will come a point that the decline will be unstoppable and that will be the end of the motor industry as we currently know it. We’ll just be a very small volume player,” he says. Industry experts have long warned of the growing challenges facing car manufacturers in the UK, from the increased competition from China, Trump’s tariffs and the transition to electric vehicles. Healey acknowledged it was a “worrying time” for JLR’s workers and suppliers on Monday, while the mayor of the West Midlands, Richard Parker, announced a £500,000 support package for JLR staff. The business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, who has ruled out state support to protect the jobs, will meet the company and the Unite union to discuss the cuts on Tuesday. The owner of a plastic manufacturer based in Birmingham, who has supplied JLR for decades, says his workforce has been cut by about 75% because of the challenges facing the sector. The business owner, who did not want to be identified, calls on JLR to be more transparent with suppliers and the public in order to restore confidence. “We’ve got owners that do want to invest in taking us to the next level but they need the transparency, the visibility and confidence in future UK productions … to justify investment,” he says. The business owner also voices concerns about the broader impact of declining industry on jobs and skills in the local area. “JLR supports an enormous network of tool-makers and moulders, manufacturers and engineers across the whole region, so it’s affecting us all,” he says. “The saddest aspect is we could potentially lose decades of engineering if we haven’t got these big companies in the Midlands supporting it any more.” Steve Morley, the president of the Confederation of British Metalforming, echoes concerns for the automotive industry but says the announcement of job cuts was not a surprise. “Previous government policies have done nothing to support the automotive sector at all and the writing has been on the wall for a long time, not only here but in Europe as well,” he says. Specifically, he criticises high labour and energy costs in the UK, as well as policies around EVs. The industry has argued the government’s EV sales targets are too onerous. Reynolds has refused to rule out watering down government targets for UK automakers to reach 80% zero-emission car sales by 2030, which would lead to a ban on the sale of new petrol and diesel cars by 2035. Morley says: “If we want to be competitive, we have to have infrastructure that lets us be competitive. We cannot afford to have the energy costs we’ve got, the labour costs we’ve got, the policies around EV that stranglehold the automotive sector.” Balaji said on Monday JLR was “committed to supporting everyone with care, fairness and respect” through the redundancy process. A government spokesperson said it understands that this will be an “uncertain and concerning time for affected workers, their families and wider communities”.

title: US police fear Meta smart glasses could be used to secretly record them
summary: Exclusive: Documents show officers from Maine to California worry Meta’s camera-equipped glasses will be used either to secretly record them or aid acts of terrorism
text: In January, the New York police department’s counter-terrorism unit sent out a memo warning police officers about a new potential “security and counterintelligence” threat: Ray-Ban Meta glasses. The memo directed officers to “conduct thorough inspections of all eyewear permitted within inmate cells” and cautioned that people who have been arrested could use these glasses, equipped with small cameras and microphones, to record inside police facilities. The memo cited two examples of such videos posted on social media. “The ability to covertly record inside a law enforcement or detention facility, could result in a security risk if proprietary information about cell layouts, camera placements, or officer patrol/site protection routines are released,” the memo read. The NYPD memo is one of a dozen, previously unreported and reviewed by the Guardian, that showed law enforcement agencies across the US are increasingly concerned about the potential for smart glasses to be used against them. Officers from Maine to California worry the technology will be used either to secretly record officers and facilities or to aid in the execution of crimes and acts of terrorism. One of the videos, taken with smart glasses and posted to TikTok in July 2025, offered a rare peek into a South Carolina detention center that had been the subject of a federal investigation over unsafe conditions. “Everyone here is trying to figure out what’s going on with my glasses, why my light is blinking,” the user said about other detainees in the video. “People don’t know about Meta glasses.” He filmed a dingy shower, the inside of holding cells, an overcrowded cafeteria, and several other detainees as they slept, ate or walked, all seemingly unaware of being recorded. Detention facilities in the US typically confiscate any and all devices that would be capable of recording video footage. Some Meta smart glasses have gone unnoticed, though. The glasses are discreet and can pass as a regular pair of Ray-Bans or Oakleys. Their main differentiator is a small blinking light in the corner of the frame that is activated when the glasses are recording. The covertly recorded videos prompted the NYPD’s intelligence and counter-terrorism bureau, a specialized unit that works with the FBI to monitor and prevent terrorist threats, to send out the January memo to other police departments. The glasses “may appear as ordinary prescription eyewear”, the memo read. US police and federal agents are not alone in their fear. Concern among the public and privacy experts over Meta’s smart glasses, widely dubbed “pervert glasses”, is growing. The technology enables its wearers to record people without their consent and has already been used to harass people. Documents obtained by Property of the People, a non-profit that works to increase government transparency, show law enforcement agencies have grown as equally worried as everyday people about being filmed without their knowledge. Ryan Shapiro, the executive director of Property of the People, said the documents show that law enforcement officials want the exclusive right to use surveillance technology and cameras to monitor the public without those cameras being turned back on them. “These agencies surveil the public incessantly, but the moment we can watch them back, it’s deemed a security threat,” Shapiro said. “When only the government is allowed to hold the camera, that’s not security. It’s impunity.” “The potential for smart glasses to be used by residents and the general public to conduct surveillance and other nefarious activities has introduced additional risks and concerns in Department of Corrections and law enforcement facilities,” read a memo distributed in June 2026 by Maine’s fusion center. Fusion centers are Department of Homeland Security facilities spread across the country as surveillance hubs that collect and analyze what the DHS describes as “threat-related” information from local law enforcement, private companies and other state and federal agencies. “Some smart glasses can leverage AI software including facial recognition, which could lead to doxing of publicly available information or connections to law enforcement officers,” the Maine document continued. Other memos expressing concerns about Meta smart glasses originated from the DHS’s joint counter-terrorism assessment team and fusion centers nationwide, including in San Diego, California, Tennessee, Virginia, Maine and New York. Those fears have been enough to prompt federal agencies to bar their own employees from using the smart glasses in the workplace. In August, the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agency said that smart glasses qualify as body-worn cameras, which means they can’t be worn in the “federal workspace”, according to a memo the New York Times obtained. The “use of Meta Glasses or similar devices could unintentionally capture, record or transmit sensitive information”, the memo, written by ICE’s acting director David Venturella, read. Meta says its glasses “are designed to be noticed”. “Every pair has a bright white LED that blinks when a photo or video is taken for your gallery, it can’t be turned off, and if someone covers or tampers with the LED, the camera is disabled,” said a Meta spokesperson, Dina El-Kassaby. Beyond being filmed without their consent, law enforcement agencies are also cautioning that these glasses may be used to aid in planning or “reconnaissance” for violent acts of terrorism or “hostile pre-operational surveillance”. A January 2025 NYPD memo cited the New Year’s Day terror attack in New Orleans, when a man rammed his truck into a crowd on Bourbon Street, killing 14 and wounding 35 people. The FBI had alerted local agencies like the NYPD that the perpetrator of the attack biked around Bourbon street twice at the end of 2024 wearing smart glasses. The FBI alleges the perpetrator conducted “pre-attack target reconnaissance”. Officers should be aware of and report individuals “acting in a suspicious manner observed wearing what may be smart glasses”, the memo states. Evan Greer, the executive director of digital advocacy non-profit Fight for the Future, said they were not surprised police are concerned about the technology being used against them or to cause harm. “Surveillance makes all of us less safe,” Greer said. “There’s no such thing as Meta glasses that are only for the good guys.” The French quarter is a highly trafficked tourist area, Meta spokesperson El-Kassaby said, arguing that the perpetrator could have filmed the French Quarter with any other recording device including a phone. The concern over Meta’s smart glasses is part of a broader concern expressed by law enforcement officials over the ways the proliferation of artificial intelligence-backed technology may impinge on police activity, the documents show. Law enforcement are at once looking for ways to use AI for investigative purposes and warning against public opposition to its use. In an August 2025 document, the NYPD wrote that while new AI technology could “significantly transform day-to-day police operations” that police would also need to address public fears about the use of advanced tech in policing. The memo was a response to “AI 2027”, a paper written by a former OpenAI researcher and other industry experts proffering what the future of AI development could look like and the effect it will have on society. It warns that AI opposition could result in “anti-tech violent extremist activity” and civil unrest over job losses, the widespread use of deepfake technology, and loss of trust in government and tech. Anti-tech violent extremist activity isn’t a formal DHS designation for categories of terrorism but has recently cropped up in law enforcement messaging about a broad spectrum of extremist opposition to AI. Experts worry it could serve to criminalize all anti-tech opposition and the constitutionally protected right to protest.

title: UK to adopt tougher stance on Israel with illegal settlements trade ban
summary: Ed Miliband to reassert support for Palestinian rights and a two-state solution in move fiercely criticised by US and Israel
text: Ed Miliband will announce a broad reset of the UK’s relations with Israel on Tuesday, promising the government will take a more active approach in supporting the Palestinian cause. In an intervention which has already drawn fierce criticism from the US and Israel, the foreign secretary will impose a UK ban on the trade in goods and some services from illegal Israeli settlements. He has also told civil society groups he is determined to reassert support for a two-state solution to the conflict, with an appeal for the protection of Palestinian rights and respect for international law. The prime minister, Andy Burnham, spoke to the US president, Donald Trump, on Monday night, a call which No 10 said “stressed the importance of a two-state solution”, but it gave no other details of the conversation. On Tuesday the US ambassador to Israel said the US could issue its own reprisals against the UK. Mike Huckabee, who had claimed the Labour government is gripped by “Jew hatred”, told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme it would “do great damage to any Brits who are doing business in a number of states in the US”. He said he did not “know what all of the national sanctions or repercussions or retaliations will be from the US, it hasn’t been announced yet … but one of the largest US states, Florida, that has a law that if this action is taken, then Brits will not be able to do business with any company or business in Florida”. The work and pensions secretary, Pat McFadden, said on Tuesday that the motivation for the move was the desire to protect the viability of the two-state solution. “At the heart of the statement is the idea that the UK, along with many other countries, do not want to see the possibility of a two-state solution in Israel and Palestine being erased by changes to the facts on the ground, and the reason that danger has become more urgent is because of expanded settlement activity in recent weeks and months,” he told Sky News. Plans in the “E1” area could mean the “effective cutting off of the north of the West Bank from the south of the West Bank”, McFadden said. “But I think it’s also important to say that Israel is an important trading partner for the UK. This isn’t intended to be a boycott of all Israeli goods.” In his statement to MPs, Miliband is expected to use firmer language than his recent predecessors in calling out the humanitarian injustices suffered by Palestinians in Gaza. The steps he lays out are likely to fall short of the full set of demands made by Palestinian advocacy groups, but they will still be seen as a sign that the UK is moving beyond traditional rhetorical support for a two-state solution towards active steps to forestall the expansion of illegal settlements in the West Bank – widely seen as intended to destroy the prospect of a Palestinian state. Israel has already threatened reprisals over Miliband’s previous claim that the Israeli military has held back aid for Gaza. Israel’s far-right finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, appeared to respond to the reports by saying: “Expel the British ambassador tonight!” The prime minister, Andy Burnham, spoke to Donald Trump and key Gulf allies, such as Qatar, on Monday to brief them on the government’s plans in the region. Polling released to the Guardian shows Britons across the political spectrum favour banning trade with illegal Israeli settlements by a margin of more than two to one. The polling, conducted by Opinium and published by the European Council on Foreign Relations, shows that only 18% of UK adults oppose a ban on trade in goods with Israeli settlements, compared with 46% in favour. Support rises to nearly three-quarters when those who did not express an opinion are excluded. Miliband’s statement will stand by his claim that the Israel Defense Forces, in the name of security, are placing unnecessary controls on aid entering Gaza, creating a horrific situation. It is understood, however, that he is sceptical of the UK’s leverage to resolve the situation apart from calling for the restrictions to be lifted. His claim that aid was being held back was denied by the Israeli foreign ministry at the weekend. Miliband is likely to go further than his predecessors in placing the settlement measures firmly in the context of upholding international law, including the findings of two key institutions, the international criminal court and the international court of justice (ICJ), which are under attack by the US. The package is unlikely to include sanctions over aid restrictions into Gaza, or to describe what has happened in the territory as a genocide. The UK has kept open the option of joining countries such as South Africa at the ICJ to claim Israel is in breach of the court’s previous rulings. But by acting decisively on trade, Miliband has set aside warnings that a polarising UK intervention may help Benjamin Netanyahu’s chances in Israel’s election next month. British sources said that even Israeli military officials had warned their prime minister that the IDF would struggle to defend new settlements and outposts in the northern West Bank, because they lack basic security infrastructure and were established for political rather than security reasons. Despite US criticism of the UK stance, Washington has also been putting pressure on Netanyahu over the settlements issue, to the point that he has called for some to be dismantled, saying they were not established with the necessary permits. Israel has previously demolished some outposts, but they are often rebuilt soon after. The UK ban on trade in settlement goods, long parried by the Foreign Office as impossible to implement, is in line with the ICJ advisory opinion in 2024 requiring governments not to aid or assist an Israeli occupation of Palestinian territory, not just illegal settlements. The UK government has never formally replied to the opinion, but ministers in Keir Starmer’s government said it was broadly compliant. The measures on settlements may require primary legislation to ban the trade in goods rather than an easier statutory instrument, while the trade ban will extend to some services including financing and advertising illegal settlements. The Foreign Office has previously argued that it was impossible to distinguish between products coming from illegal settlements and those from Israel. The UK officially regards all Israeli civilian settlements built on territories captured during the 1967 six-day war as illegal under international law. Total trade in goods and services between the UK and Israel in 2025 was £6bn, and the scale of the disruption may depend on Israeli reprisals. Goods produced in Israeli settlements have not been entitled to preferential tariff treatment upon entry into the UK since 2005. The country has also issued guidance on misleading labelling and urged businesses not to trade with or be engaged in economic and financial activities in Israeli settlements. The new measures will make such investments unlawful. The UK reset was made more urgent by Israel’s E1 settlement project east of Jerusalem from November. But the Burnham government also feels compelled to act because of the increase in settler violence in the West Bank and the failure of Trump’s Board of Peace after six months to secure the twin objectives of Hamas’s disarmament and Israel’s withdrawal from Gaza. Labour is also under domestic pressure from the Greens on Palestine. The party leader, Zack Polanski, is expected to stand in the 8 October Holborn and St Pancras byelection triggered by Starmer’s resignation as an MP. The new Labour policy may give the party’s candidate some political cover against Polanski. In a sign of the potential ramifications for Miliband, Netanyahu’s older son, Yair, suggested last week that the Falkland Islands belonged to Argentina, not Britain. He is not a minister, but after his comments Trump indicated that Washington could reconsider its position on British sovereignty over the islands. Trump said last Thursday that he would not back Britain if Argentina were to invade the islands. He told GB News: “Your country was not there to help me” when the US and Israel began their war on Iran in February. The Foreign Office declined to comment when approached by the Guardian.

title: Tokyo tourist hotspot bans short-term rentals amid surge in complaints
summary: Shinjuku ward targets accommodation in residential areas and near cultural sites as locals complain visitors disposing of rubbish improperly and being too noisy
text: A neighbourhood in Tokyo popular with foreign tourists will ban visitors from using thousands of short-term rental accommodations after a slew of complaints about behaviour. In the latest sign that Japan’s patience with mass tourism is wearing thin, Shinjuku ward – home to the notorious Kabukicho nightlife district and the world’s busiest railway station – will prevent visitors from using private lodgings in residential areas and near schools and important cultural sites, Japanese media reported this week. The measure, to be introduced through a local ordinance, could encourage other local authorities to follow suit. Shinjuku, with a regular population of more than 350,000, is home to 3,775 private lodgings – or minpaku – the largest number anywhere in Japan. While tourism has boosted sectors of Japan’s economy and raised the country’s profile overseas, the surge in visitor numbers has created tensions with residents in popular destinations such as Tokyo, Kyoto and Osaka. Shinjuku ward believes the measure will affect as many as 2,000 lodgings in residential areas – almost half the total, according to the Mainichi Shimbun. The number of minpaku residences in Shinjuku has almost tripled since 2022. Reports said officials had been forced to act after receiving more than 1,300 complaints from residents in the 12 months to March. Many cited disruption caused by visitors who did not dispose of their rubbish properly, made too much noise and smoked in areas where it is banned. There have also been reports of trespassing. Officials said temporarily revoking the licences of renters whose tenants misbehaved would not address residents’ concerns. “Even if we crack down on badly behaved operators, the number of complaints remains the same,” a ward official told the Japan Times. “So we decided it’s better to change the ordinance.” Authorities did not single out particular operators for the ban. But it is likely to affect those using popular companies such as Airbnb. An Airbnb spokesperson told the Guardian: “Shinjuku has been an important partner to us, and we take residents’ concerns seriously. Home sharing works best when residents, hosts and guests can all live well alongside each other, and that is what we want to help the ward protect. “We would welcome the chance to work with the ward on measures that target the problem more precisely - a prohibition across residential zones would close thousands of registered homes affecting compliant and responsible hosts, while leaving untouched the unregistered operators behind much of the disruption residents describe. “We believe there is a version of this ordinance that protects residents’ quality of life without closing responsible, licensed hosts, and we want to help find it.” The ward will ask for members of the public to give their feedback on the proposal next month, with a view to submitting revisions to the ordinance in February. It also plans to reduce the number of days per year that minpaku in residential areas can be rented out from 180 to 120. Authorities in Kyoto – where tourists flock to view temples and shrines, rent kimono and photograph traditional geisha entertainers – limit minpaku operations in residential areas to just 60 days a year, during the off-peak season between January and March. “Residents are concerned that their communities could be falling apart,” Kyoto’s mayor, Koji Matsui, said earlier this year. “We have strengthened the oversight of operators, but that is not enough. We need to go further,” the Asahi Shimbun quoted him as saying. A record 42 million people visited Japan last year, spending a combined ¥9.5tn ($62bn) – also an all-time high. The government has set a target of 60 million visitors by 2030 – a goal critics say will exacerbate “tourism pollution”. Authorities near Mount Fuji have introduced climbing fees and imposed a daily visitor cap in an attempt to reduce overcrowding on Japan’s highest mountain. In February, the town of Fujiyoshida, a popular Fuji viewing spot, decided to cancel this spring’s cherry blossom festival, citing a rise in disruptive behaviour by tourists. The mayor, Shigeru Horiuchi, said the decision had been taken to “protect the dignity and living environment of our citizens”.

title: Who are the Australians missing in the Nepal floods? What we know so far
summary: There are 35 Australians among the thousands of people missing as rescue efforts continue after deadly flash floods on the Nepal-Tibet border
text: The number of Australians missing in the Nepal-Tibet flash flooding disaster has fallen from 36 to 35, after another person was confirmed safe on Tuesday. The Australian citizen, who was in Nepal and uncontactable in the wake of the flash flooding on 26 August, confirmed they were safe and well and did not require consular assistance. It comes after seven previously unaccounted for Australians were confirmed safe in recent days, with one found in Nepal, one in Tibet and three outside the crisis-hit area. A Sydney woman, Cara Severino, 25, was also safely located in Nepal more than two days after the floods. The names of the Australians confirmed safe have not yet been released. Pilgrims trekking to a holy site in Tibet make up the majority of Australians who have been reported missing after the deadly flash floods and landslides tore through valleys on the Nepal-Tibet border. Most were travelling with Himalayan Glacier Adventures, Kailash Journeys and the Isha Foundation. Across Nepal and Tibet, more than 5,000 people have been reported missing and Nepali and Chinese authorities have confirmed that more than 1,000 have died. Here’s what we know about the Australians who remain missing. This article will be updated as more information becomes available. Venkatraman Balakrishnan and Chitra Venkatraman New South Wales couple Venkatraman Balakrishnan, 52, and Chitra Venkatraman, 46, were among 15 Australians travelling to Mount Kailash on a spiritual trip with the Himalayan Glacier Adventures tour group. Their son, Akash Venkatraman, said his parents had planned to leave their riverside accommodation in Syabrubesi before it was devastated by flood waters. Muralitharan family Shylaja Muralitharan, 42, Chandresekaran Muralitharan, 47 and their children Ashwin, 14, and Aarush, 11, were also taking part in the Himalayan Glacier Adventures spiritual tour to Mount Kailash when the flood hit. The parents and two children had been training together for the long walk, Shylaja’s younger sister Vaishnavi said. She lost contact with the family shortly after their breakfast on the morning of the flood. Iyer family Sreedharan Iyer, 52, and Lakshmi Iyer, 50, and their adult sons Rishab Iyer, 23, and Rudhra Iyer, 20, were taking part in the spiritual pilgrimage to Mount Kailash with Himalayan Glacier Adventures. The Iyer brothers are medical students at the University of Newcastle and members of the West Pennant Hills Cherrybrook cricket club in Sydney’s north-west. Karan Bhardwaj, Arpan Mithalal Kothari and Bhavin Raval Karan Bhardwaj, Arpan Mithalal Kothari and Bhavin Raval were travelling together on a Kailash Journey tour of the region. Bhardwaj’s family says the three men have known each other since 2009, when they met at university. Raval’s wife, Bhavinkumar Raval, has told the ABC she believes her husband is still alive and is making plans to travel to Nepal. Bhardwaj is a 40-year-old Brisbane-based member of the Royal Australian Air Force. Bhardwaj’s family member Jen said: “Karan is a dad to my beautiful seven-year-old nephew, as well as a brother, uncle and brother in law. He is so desperately loved by his family and right now we are desperately praying, hoping and believing that Karan is safe, alive and somehow making his way back to us.” Narayan Panthi Narayan Panthi, from Brisbane, has been listed by Nepali police as travelling with operator Kathmandu Holiday Tours and Travel. It is understood Panthi had been carrying out independent volunteer charity work in Kathmandu earlier in the week before travelling towards the border region. Panthi’s cousin, Amrit Bhusal, told Guardian Australia his family were devastated but “holding on to hope and praying for positive news”. “We are still hoping,” Bhusal said. “We are still searching. We are still praying for Narayan to come home safely.” Bhusal said Panthi had been “helping disadvantaged children in Nepal reach their full potential through education”. Bharat Mangwani Bharat Mangwani, 42, was travelling with the Isha Foundation as part of a pilgrimage to Lake Manasarovar when his family lost contact with him on Wednesday morning. He was last seen at Gyirong before the group was set to depart for Kathmandu. “All of us are praying for him and hopefully he comes back to us soon,” said a close friend, Kushagra Tiwari. Mangwani’s family, including his nine-year-old son and three-year-old daughter, have travelled to India with a family friend, while his wife has flown to Nepal to look for him. Renee Spry A Sunshine Coast disability support worker, Renee Spry has been described as a “deeply spiritual” person who travelled to Nepal on a pilgrimage. “She had two degrees, and she chose to do something that was … a completely selfless vocation,” her sister Clair Spry said. “Her priority was always other people.” “Every person she touched, they knew her love and kindness. She would be so uncomfortable with all this.” Clair Spry has set up a GoFundMe so her family can travel to Nepal to look for signs of Renee. Suhasini Kandimalla A mother of two from Springfield, near Brisbane, Suhasini Kandimalla was hiking with another Springfield local, according to her sister, Supreethini Kandimalla. While she was a New Zealand citizen, Suhasini had been approved for Australian citizenship, her sister said. She had planned to attend a citizenship ceremony for it to be granted soon after she returned. “I don’t know if it was a religious calling for her to do it,” Supreethini said of the Nepal trip. “But she certainly loved the treks in New Zealand too, and would go on lots of long hikes.” Reshma Patel A Newcastle woman, Reshma Patel, 46, was in the Isha Foundation group. She didn’t know Sumi Adhikari beforehand but the pair had become friends on the pilgrimage, said Patel’s family friend Chin Valsan. “They were talking to each other, and they were supposed to come back on the same flight on Thursday,” he says. He describes Patel, who has two children aged 10 and 14 and works casually for Canterbury-Bankstown council, as “full of life” and a “kind soul” who loves her family and friends. Kanagamah Sundrasan The mother of two from Springfield, near Brisbane, was part of the Kailash Journey trek to Mount Kailash. Her daughter, Swaatika Kanniah, said her mother had been excited about the hike. “It was a pilgrimage, she really wanted to go and have that experience.” A photograph of her on the trip shows her smiling with five other members of the tour; all are now missing. “I feel like everyone is trying their best but yes we don’t know much about what’s going on,” Kanniah said of the recovery efforts. Michael Keats The family of 37-year-old Michael Keats, from Mollymook in NSW, said on social media that he had died. Keats’s partner, Emily Boyd, said on Instagram on Sunday that he had been on a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash, which had been his “dream for many years”. “Mike went on a pilgrimage to Mt Kailash seeking enlightenment,” Boyd said. “There’s a bittersweetness knowing that there was nothing more that Mike wanted [than] to know God, and to merge with the divine. “He was a mystic, a medicine man, a teacher, leader, partner, father, brother, son, uncle and dearly beloved friend. He showed up for so many people in so many ways. A heart of pure gold. We love you forever and always.” On Tuesday, the foreign affair minister, Penny Wong, said the Australian government “has not yet received official confirmation of Mr Keats’ passing. He does remain unaccounted for in terms of the information we have. But … we respect the rights of the families to make the statements they have. “Our thoughts go out to his family and to every Australian family who is hoping that the many who are missing can be located.” Luke Costanzo Luke Costanzo, 30, from Perth remains missing, his family has confirmed. He was on a pilgrimage trek with the Isha foundation, and the group was last in contact at the Gyirong border crossing as they were making their way back to Kathmandu on the final day of their journey, the family said. “Luke is an extremely strong, compassionate, disciplined and spiritual person,” they said. “Once he makes a decision he commits to it fully and he was so excited to be visiting Mount Kailash on a pilgrimage trek with the Isha Foundation.” “We truly appreciate all the love and support from friends and family that we’ve received and ask everyone to keep Luke, and all those affected, in your thoughts and prayers.” The family has asked people who wish to help to donate “to aid the wonderful people on the ground who continue with rescue efforts”. Sandeep Mohapatra and Sidharthi Kumari Sahu Sandeep Mohapatra and Sidharthi Kumari Sahu are members of Melbourne’s Odia community. The couple had taken part in a pilgrimage and were last believed to have been making their way towards the immigration office. Hara Patro, a member of the Melbourne Odia community, travelled to India to speak with their families and has urged Australians to keep the couple in their hearts. “Their families are living through unimaginable uncertainty,” he said. “Every day without news makes the situation harder, but we continue to hope and pray that Sandeep and Sidharthi will be found safe.” The couple’s son is staying with family in India as they wait for news.

title: Social media users could opt out of the algorithm if Australian government has its way – but that’s a big if
summary: Even if the legislation passes, tech companies may still find ways to frustrate its intent and keep Australians hooked on their feed
text: Social media could become a “choose your own adventure” between the doom-scrolling status quo, or just the feed of the friends you want to see, if the government’s planned digital duty of care legislation passes, and the tech companies don’t muck around on compliance. But that’s a big if. For years people have complained about the random videos or posts cluttering their social media feeds as served to them by the tech giants. It often feels invasive – tracking our activity across websites and apps to serve content and ads – but in many cases, it is also toxic. Guardian Australia was first reporting these issues back in 2024, conducting experiments with blank phones set up to be young men, with very little other information to go on and to see what the algorithms pushed into our feeds. The results were shocking – how the default would quickly send someone down a rabbit hole of extreme misogynistic and far right content, and just how sensitive the algorithm is to any minor interaction on an image or video. Many of the perceived problems teens face on social media are also problems facing adults. While the social media ban was designed to combat the harms faced by under-16s, many of us know relatives who have been radicalised reading Facebook comments, or grandparents scammed out of their retirement money by fake investments they saw on social media. Outrage bait is rewarded by engagement on platforms, and this has infected politics and public discourse in Australia and elsewhere. The move, announced by the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, on Tuesday to have a pop-up notification proactively require users to decide whether they want the platform to decide what they see or just want to see the content of the people and groups they’ve chosen to follow – similar to how many of the platforms worked in the early 2010s – could be game-changing. When Apple introduced a notification in iOS in 2021 that allowed people to opt in or opt out of ad tracking in apps, it cost Meta $10bn in one quarter, with users rushing to opt out of tracking on Facebook and Instagram. Compare that to when Instagram chief executive, Adam Mosseri, was on the stand in the landmark US court case last month just before Meta agreed to a $18bn settlement with state attorneys general. One of the company’s safety features for teens, called Take a Break, which was designed to let teens stop using Instagram if they had been scrolling for a while, had a take up rate of 1.8%, the court heard. The companies love to tout their safety features, but then often bury them within the settings, with little notice to users, and then suggest to regulators that the low take up shows people love their product as is. The companies may also find ways to make it as clunky an experience as possible when people opt out, to drive them back to the preferred model, depending on how the law is written. Just look at Europe. In 2023 Meta introduced the option for a no-algorithm feed to comply with EU law, but in 2025 a Dutch court found people were automatically reverted to the Meta algorithm when they closed and reopened the app. The court ordered the company to provide a direct and simple way for people to opt out of the timeline, to comply with the law. Meta continued to argue it was already in compliance. Instagram is also expected to sell the benefits hard. It will launch its “Algo Confessions” series in Australia this week, in which celebrities and influencers run through their “For You” feeds, and why what Instagram recommends to people is just so good. They may find a sympathetic ear among organisations that have benefited from algorithms that reward outrage content with user engagement. It was telling the prime minister pointedly thanked News Corp for its support for the social media ban in Tuesday’s press conference. It’s not clear whether the “my feed, my way” proposal will enjoy similar levels of full-throated support in the newspapers as the social media youth ban had, particularly as it seems likely that other parts of the proposed law around combating online harms will face opposition from the Coalition and One Nation. But by framing it as “empowering people” Albanese is hoping it won’t be seen as the big arm of government coming in and determining what people see on social media. Through the pop-up notification every Australian will have a choice. “If people want to doom scroll … that’s fine, that’s up to them,” Albanese said on Tuesday. “But if people want to have a change, then this will provide them an opportunity.”

title: ‘It breaks my heart’: far-right’s big election victory sparks dismay in German state capital
summary: Fears expressed for immigrants and for country’s future after AfD vote hits historic high in Saxony-Anhalt
text: Maryam and her best friend were ambling through Magdeburg toward the railway station, talking over the dramatic events of the previous evening and the surge by the far-right Alternative für Deutschland to a historically high vote in the Saxony-Anhalt elections. “Don’t laugh at me,” she said, “but I wish we could go back to the days of Angela Merkel, when things were OK in Germany”. The teenagers, from nearby Wolmirstedt, said they were shocked by the AfD’s landslide win. But they felt powerless to do much about it and felt afraid about where it might take their home state. “We talk about it all the time,” said Maryam, whose name has been changed. “It’s on my mind constantly. My dad came to Germany from Syria in 2015. My mum and I joined him two years later.” The first clause of the anti-immigrant AfD’s 100-day programme says that – “from the first moment” of being in power – the party will deport people it deems “irregular migrants”. Maryam believes her family could well face deportation. “We have to renew our residency permits every three years as it is. We’ve always lived in a state of uncertainty. Now after these election results we face going back to Syria which we don’t think is safe, and I can’t even read or write Arabic.” The AfD won almost 44% of the vote in Sunday’s election, more than even it had hoped for. Doreen, 54, did not immediately admit to having supported the party, but said later in an interview she had put her faith in what she termed “the blues” “out of a sense of desperation”. When challenged about the human impact the party’s policies could have, for example on immigrant families, she shrugged: “It is what it is.” “If they [refugees] hadn’t turned up here in such large numbers in the first place, they wouldn’t have to go through such heart-breaking situations now,” she said. Doreen, a cleaner, said she hoped the pro-Russia AfD would be able to take power and act on promises to end refugee status for Ukrainians (as well as aid to Kyiv). “The winners will hopefully straighten up a few things right away,” she said. “They [Ukrainians] come here in their fancy cars, pretending they’re escaping devastation, but most of them have far more resources and designer clothes than I do.” Doreen is speaking close to a stolperstein, or stumbling stone – a brass plaque embedded in the concrete – commemorating Ernst Fliess, a Jewish lawyer. Born in 1877, he lived on the spot where a glass-fronted fitness club now stands until he was “humiliated, disenfranchised … (and) took flight in death” (a euphemism for suicide). But she angrily rejected any parallel between the AfD’s rise in popularity and the Weimar era rise of the Nazis. “Don’t tar me with that brush,” she said. “We are in a different age, with different problems.” Returning from their daily stroll to the Elbe river, 88-year-olds Ernst and Judith, a retired boiler maker and a design engineer who have been married for 64 years, said they did not want to talk about the election result. But it soon became clear that they were shattered by the news. Voting data has shown a stark drop-off in support for the far-right party among the over-70s. “It’s not like we didn’t see it coming,” said Judith. “But we don’t quite know what to do with the information. The reality of it hasn’t quite kicked in.” The couple said they had voted for the far-left Die Linke. Judith said she was “devastated that a party that has so little regard for refugees” had won, and by such a large margin. Her own life story – she was forced to flee her home in Silesia in 1945 and spent years in temporary accommodation before settling in Magdeburg – has greatly sensitised her to the plight of refugees, she said. “I see the look in their eyes, it doesn’t matter where they come from, who they are, and I am so empathetic to their situation,” she said. “It breaks my heart to think that almost half of the population has voted for a party that is so anti-immigrant, particularly after all Germany has gone through as a nation in the last century.” Sitting on a heart-shaped rainbow-coloured bench in front of Magdeburg’s gothic cathedral, Christiane and Franz Josef Jäker, 67 and 71, on holiday from North Rhine-Westphalia, were also digesting the news. “The populists are ruining everything,” said Franz Josef. “Everything that Germany has built up again after world war two. They promise a lot that they can’t deliver, and they also suppress a lot – such as what is going on in Ukraine – so that they can argue for the resumption of Russian gas imports to Germany.” Eric, a paramedic cheerily drumming up funds for a hospice, said he was kicking himself for not having voted. The 21-year-old son of a German mother and a Guinean father who spent 10 years applying for a German passport, said: “I try not to think about what the installation of the AfD in government might mean for me as a dark-skinned man.” Most of all he is worried about “the constitutional changes they might make, and the domino effect that might have across Germany”. Luisa, a bank teller who says she voted for Die Linke, fears for the image of her state. “It’s really bad for the reputation of Saxony-Anhalt. A lot of people have said that foreigners here will now choose to leave, but I know enough low-paid foreign workers who won’t be able to afford to do so, and will just have to put up with being badly treated. “I saw some interviews with Holocaust survivors and they drew parallels with the mood around what’s happening now and the rise of the Nazis. We have to pay attention to this similar sense they say they have – they’re not making it up.”

title: Tuesday briefing: What happens next after Germany’s far-right breakthrough?
summary: In today’s newsletter: The AfD’s local election triumph has shocked Europe, and raised questions about how to counter the rising far right
text: Good morning. Across Germany – and Europe more widely – there has been a palpable sense of shock and disbelief after the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) swept to a historic state election victory in the early hours of Monday. It was, according to France’s European affairs minister, Benjamin Haddad, “a very grave moment for Europe”. The resonance was stark in the UK too: as the results came in, hundreds of black-clad activists intent on blocking migrant arrivals were battling with police for a second night along England’s south coast. While seasoned observers stress the context that Saxony-Anhalt, a small state in the former communist east of the country, has traditionally voted further to the right, a red line has been crossed. A far-right party has been propelled to the brink of power at regional level in Germany for the first time since the Nazis – despite 13 years of increasingly desperate efforts by mainstream parties to shut them out of government. For today’s newsletter, I spoke to the Guardian’s Berlin correspondent Kate Connolly from the state capital Magdeburg, and our Europe correspondent, Jon Henley, about why Germany’s famous firewall against the far right has failed, and what happens next. First, this morning’s headlines. Five big stories UK news | Batons and synthetic pepper spray were used to repel hundreds of masked, black-clad vigilantes in Portsmouth on Sunday, it has emerged, as the policing minister said officers had been injured as they repelled organised “aggression”. Israel | Ed Miliband will announce what he has described as a broad reset of the UK’s relations with Israel on Tuesday, promising the government will take a more active approach in supporting the Palestinian cause. US | The Trump administration has raised “serious concerns” over Downing Street’s plan to force digital platforms to hand more prominence to established broadcasters, warning the move risks “facilitating censorship”. Climate crisis | Nepal is demanding $20m in climate compensation for the recent devastating floods, as a senior minister called on the world’s most polluting countries to “wake up” and accept shared responsibility. UK politics | There is little appetite for cuts to disability benefits even among Conservative and Reform voters, and proposals to reduce spending could prove politically risky, according to an authoritative national survey. In depth: ‘A palpable sense of disbelief’ The first person Kate spoke to when she arrived in Magdeburg on Monday afternoon was a paramedic named Eric, who was fundraising for a local hospice. He explained how his father had spent years working to obtain a German passport after migrating from Guinea. “Already that day he felt the mood on the street had become more hostile,” Kate told me. I know from experience how difficult it can be to persuade strangers to elaborate on their private voting decisions – especially when you have copy to file in a hurry – but yesterday was different, she said: “Everybody had very profound thoughts to share.” She described conversations with a “heartbroken” older couple, who had grown up under communism; a 16-year-old who arrived from Syria under Angela Merkel’s open borders policy in 2015 and was frightened she would be first on the list to send back; another woman who’d voted for the AfD and said she didn’t appreciate being “tarred with the same brush” as supporters of Hitler in the 1930s. Kate interviewed her as they stood by a Stolperstein, a memorial plaque to a victim of Nazi persecution. As we spoke, thousands were gathering at Berlin’s Brandenburg Gate to express their opposition to the AfD, and where there was a palpable sense of disbelief and dread as news of the results filtered. *** Why is the AfD on the rise? The German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, was elected leader of the centre-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) in 2022 on a pledge to halve the AfD’s vote. Instead it has doubled, and support for his centrist coalition that has tumbled. A “deeply shocked” Merz vowed to stay in office yesterday after the nativist party triumphed with 44% of the vote, just short of an absolute majority The turnout in Saxony-Anhalt was breathtaking. At 77.8%, compared with 60.3% in 2021, it suggests the AfD – classified as extremist by Germany’s security services – has succeeded in energising many who didn’t vote at all five years ago. Detailed polling analysis suggests that, while one in three AfD supporters align with the party’s extremist ideology, its growing popularity is driven by a diversity of voters who feel alienated from mainstream politics. Ulrich Siegmund, the AfD’s lead candidate in Saxony-Anhalt, is a charismatic former perfume salesman who has weaponised voter discontent around the faltering economy and migration – even though irregular immigration has reduced since Merz came into office. Research from 2023 found a direct link between rent increases – particularly amonglower income voters – and likelihood of supporting the AfD. Last month, Der Spiegel put Siegmund on its front cover, with the tagline “Germany’s most dangerous man”. He responded by filming himself signing copies for his 800,000 TikTok followers. Siegmund has capitalised on a mood of ostalgie – nostalgia for communist East Germany – and bubbling resentment among poorer east Germans who view themselves as second-class citizens compared to people from the west. Strikingly, it appears one of the highest shares of the AfD’s vote came from the 35- to 44 age group, who were children or infants when the Berlin Wall came down. *** What does the result mean for Germany? There’s now debate about whether the previous consensus over how mainstream parties should deal with the far right – the so-called “Brandmauer”, or firewall – has horribly backfired. Sceptics believe this non-cooperation with AfD at any level from local councils up to federal government has allowed the party to escape the scrutiny that comes with holding office. Another criticism is that it has neutered the political mainstream. “The argument runs that in order to keep the far right out, it forces mainstream parties into unnatural coalitions,” Jon says. The compromises that they have to strike have resulted in ineffective government and in turn feeds the extremes further.” Now, there are complex coalition talks ahead for the parties in Saxony-Anhalt. While Siegmund has rejected leading a minority administration, initial indications are that the AfD could govern with the hard-left, pro-Russian Bündnis Sahra Wagenknecht party, which received 5.3% of the vote. If he succeeds in becoming the state’s first far-right governor, Siegmund will have control over significant policy areas including education, policing and public broadcasting. AfD has already proposed revisions to the school curriculum, in what one party member described as “more Bismarck, less Hitler”, as well as defunding anti-racism initiatives and removing pride flags. Jon also suggests the AfD might make changes to civil service recruitment “to create a more supportive environment”. But securing the Saxony-Anhalt government would also give the AfD seats in the Bundesrat upper house: while they wouldn’t have enough seats to block legislation they could still act as a disruptive force. And with the AfD leading the polls nationally, there’s a likely ripple effect across the country. There are more state elections later this month – including in traditionally liberal Berlin, where the AfD is now polling at 18%, with the CDU maintaining a slim lead in the early 20s. If their vote share rises across states, options for coalition building without the AfD become increasingly convoluted, further flattening the mainstream’s ability to govern confidently. *** … And for Europe? Not all of Europe’s far-right leaders have welcomed this development. Jon, who is based in Paris, has been listening to France’s National Rally – which under Marine Le Pen has spent years successfully detoxifying its image – on the airwaves insisting that, in his words, “these guys are way too extreme for us”. To give you one example, two years ago the National Rally expelled the AfD from its European parliamentary group, which includes Italian prime minister Giorgia Meloni, following revelations that the party backed mass deportations and downplayed the crimes of the Nazi SS. But any domestic shock waves in Europe’s largest economy will inevitably affect the bloc. “A weakened German government in complete upheaval would obviously be bad news for Europe,” says Jon. “It could affect things like the bloc’s policy towards migration; the environment, because the AfD is famously climate-sceptic; and Ukraine, because it’s also pretty much pro-Kremlin.” In a press conference yesterday, an ashen-faced Merz drew a fairly explicit link between the AfD and Russia, noting that “2,500 km in the east, the election results were being celebrated.” This may reflect growing calls within the CDU and their coalition partner, the Social Democrats, for Merz to toughen his stance on Russia. After a drone attack on Leipzig airport in August, the German government took a month before publicly blaming Moscow, though the language could not have been more direct when foreign minister Johann Wadephul stated: “We are not at war, but we are a daily target of hybrid warfare.” With a series of federal or presidential elections taking place in Spain, France, Italy, Poland, and Germany over the next two years, the AfD’s landslide can be viewed as an indication of coming peril and a challenge on how to meet it. “The far right’s ideas have been steadily normalised by the media and the political centre,” says Jon. “They have completely framed the immigration debate, and everybody else is just scrambling to react to them”. As Keir Starmer’s government discovered with Reform in the UK, repurposing populist rhetoric doesn’t convince disaffected voters. “Political scientists across Europe would say this result is down to that, and the failure by mainstream parties to come up with inspiring policies that will actually make a real difference to people’s lives and address some of the reasons why they choose to vote for the far right,” he said. • For more on the far right in Europe, sign up to This Is Europe, our free weekly with selection of the most pressing stories and debates. What else we’ve been enjoying I thought David Smith’s re-telling of 9/11, through the eyes of two strangers who met in the middle of the smoke and became some of the only people who survived the incident, was brilliant. Poppy Noor, newsletters team Nesrine Malik is the best voice in Britain writing about Israel and Gaza. Her column on the horrific plans of Israeli ministers is well worth your time. Hettie One of the most interesting things about working at the Guardian is the letters we get from our readers. This recent series of responses about how to solve the prisons crisis made many good suggestions. Hettie I enjoyed Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor’s recent piece in the Financial Times (£) about “end times fascism” and the Nazi warships revealed as rivers in eastern Europe dried up this summer. Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor will be speaking at a Guardian event later this month (tickets here). Hettie The Guardian Australia has just launched a new politics newsletter to bring you up to speed on the stories that really matter, and what they mean for you. Sign up here. Sport US Open | Zheng Qinwen recovered from 5-0 down in the opening set to stun Iga Świątek and reach the last eight of the US Open, while Elena Rybakina beat Naomi Osaka 6-1 6-4. Cricket | Pakistan have launched an investigation into the “discipline and conduct” during their tour of England, with two players understood to have had their mobile phones confiscated as part of the probe. F1 | Bernie Ecclestone was detained in Portugal on Monday after customs authorities found him in possession of an undocumented shotgun. The front pages “UK hardens stance on Israel with ban on illegal settlements trade”, is the Guardian’s front page today, while the Times has “PM to declare trade ban on settlements in West Bank”. The FT leads on “Pressure builds on Germany’s Merz as far-right AfD toasts ‘dream result’”, the i Paper says “New ISA to help Britain’s older first-time buyers”. On small boats protests Metro has “Port in a storm”, the Mirror says “Now they try to stop the lifeboats”, while the Express’s take is “Don’t ignore public anger over illegal migrants”. The Telegraph splash with “King tells Harry: No return to the firm”, Mail writes “King puts Harry and Meghan in their place”, and the Sun writes “Megxit means Megxit”. Today in Focus: The Latest Far-right protesters descend on Dover and Portsmouth The government has condemned the ‘thuggish and intimating behaviour’ of far-right activists clad in black and balaclavas who caused disruption and unrest in Dover and Portsmouth over the weekend in an attempt to obstruct asylum seekers arriving on small boats. The action was seemingly organised by Daniel Thomas, an agitator better known as Danny Tommo, who has close ties with the far-right extremist Tommy Robinson. Thomas was recorded on the ground saying Portsmouth was now ‘ground zero’ for small boat crossings, and has threatened further action. Lucy Hough speaks to political correspondent Ben Quinn. Cartoon of the day | Ben Jennings The Upside A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad For the first time in a century, glow-worms are shining again in North Yorkshire. In recent decades, the bioluminescent female invertebrates had vanished from the British countryside. But after a budget reintroduction programme led by volunteer “glow-getters”, they’ve been spotted over multiple weeks this summer at Nosterfield nature reserve near Ripon.
