title: Country diary: This moorland needed rainfall – it got something even better | Ed Douglas
summary: Eyam Moor, Derbyshire: It’s a place that I treasure greatly, and now it has a change of ownership that is worth celebrating
text: Can a landscape sigh with relief? It felt that way, pushing through bilberry and cowberry hung with pearls of overnight rain that soaked my lower legs. On the path, dry, dusty soil had reverted to reassuring gloop. I was thrilled, at one point, to step cautiously round a puddle. Overhead, a buzzard wheeled and a small gang of swallows skimmed across heather whose purple intensity was already fading, too soon it seemed to me. To the west, a kestrel was quartering the slopes of Wet Withens. The downward curve of the moor steepens here, as it drops towards Highlow Brook, but before it does, there’s a bench, a flat space, which in the bronze age was used for a barrow. Next to it is a henge, with its circle of small stones, the most prominent of which was long ago dubbed “the chair”. I noticed that a raptor, perhaps the kestrel nearby, had recently been dismantling something small and furry on top of the chair, so I moved quickly on to the barrow. The view from here is among the best I know – evidence that our distant forebears had a grand feeling for landscape. I could see in the distance the spire of St Michael’s in Hathersage, its location no less harmonious, nestling in the crook of the hills opposite, ridgelines intersecting like arms round shoulders. The barrow itself is a jumble of stones, torn apart in the mid-18th century when the nearby turnpike was built and workmen came looking for material. This was decades before the commons were snaffled by acts of enclosure, in this case for the Duke of Devonshire. Later in the 19th century he turned it into a grouse moor. These twisting strands of deep history show how varied our uplands have been, from sacred space, to sheepwalk, to elite playground. Now this place has a new story. An anonymous benefactor has presented Eyam Moor to the Derbyshire Wildlife Trust to be a haven for biodiversity, a gleam of light in a troubled sky. • Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024, is available now at guardianbookshop.com

title: Trump Announces Ban on Some Canadian Imports
summary: President Trump invoked a 1930 law after Canada imposed new tariffs on U.S. goods, which followed his own recent tariffs in a widening trade war.

title: Canada’s retaliatory US tariffs take effect as trade dispute grows
summary: Counter-measures covering several sectors come after Trump announced 50% tariffs on Canadian goods
text: Canada’s retaliatory tariffs on billions of dollars’ worth of American imports have come into effect, escalating a trade fight that has been marked by intensifying tensions between the US president, Donald Trump, and the Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney. The tariffs took effect at 12.01am on Tuesday, and range from 15% to 50% and apply to products covering $20bn in imports from the US. The measures target sectors including steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper, and electronics – industries that have been most affected by US tariffs. The retaliatory tariffs come “as a result of the United States’ decision to impose a 50% tariff on $20bn of Canadian goods effective August 22”, the Canadian government said. Carney said Tuesday that Canada would move faster to reduce its economic reliance on the United States. “In too many areas, they wanted dependency, not a true economic partnership,” said Carney. “We can’t let American goods into Canada tariff-free while they charge our companies to export to them.” Last month, Trump announced a new 50% tariff on cars and raw materials from Canada. He accused the country of “ripping off” the US “for years”. The US tariffs hit items such as hockey sticks and cement, affecting about 5.5% of Canadian exports to the US. Since then, tensions between Canada and the US have intensified, with Carney last week urging the Trump administration to “start being serious” as the trade dispute has increasingly spilled into broader diplomatic tensions. Trump and senior US officials have repeatedly criticized Canada and its leadership, while Trump has taken a series of symbolic digs at Canada including signing an executive order renaming Lake Ontario as “Lake America” – which Canadians have rejected. On Monday, Trump threatened to block sales of Canada’s Bombardier Aviation in the US, unless the Quebec-based plane maker moves manufacturing to the US. “No more selling Bombardier in the United States!” Trump posted in all caps on his Truth Social platform, though he did not specify how he would achieve a sales halt. Thousands of Bombardier aircraft currently operate in US airlines’ domestic fleets. In a statement on Monday, the aerospace company touted its creation of “tens of thousands of jobs across the United States”, with “direct employment” in more than 20 states including Kansas, Texas, Arizona and California. The company also noted that it spent more than $2.5bn annually with suppliers, and said its supply chain was “made up of approximately 2,800 American companies across 47 states”. Negotiations between both sides broke down on 21 August after days of meetings in Washington, with Carney saying at the time that the Trump administration’s terms were ultimately unacceptable and that US negotiators had introduced restrictions on Canadian trade deals with other countries at the 11th hour. US officials also made unacceptable “threats” to the French language and “Quebec culture”, he added, referencing the French-speaking province in eastern Canada, with Carney saying American negotiators viewed the measures as an “irritant”, while “in Quebec, these are rights”. But Trump’s top trade official Jamieson Greer later noted the US government was aware that French language protections were sensitive and important. “This is not something where we push hard, or condition, or red-line,” he told Canadian public broadcaster CBC last month. Polls show Carney has broad support from Canadians, but it could disappear within months as the consequences of the trade war sink in, according to political analysts. Just 20% of Americans approved of Trump’s ⁠tariffs on Canadian goods, a Reuters/Ipsos poll found. Carney said last week his government was ready to sign a trade deal that benefited both countries, but US media reports say there are currently no ongoing negotiations between the two sides. Agence France-Presse and Reuters contributed reporting

title: Europe’s fighter jet plans are in disarray. What happens next?
summary: While the UK and Italy are making progress, France and Germany’s joint venture came to nothing, and the prospect of more countries pulling together seems way off
text: When the former European Central Bank president and Italian prime minister Mario Draghi laid out a plan for Europe to catch up economically with the US and China, collaborating on defence was one of the prescriptions. No more should each country in Europe try to make its own version of a boat, tank or jet but instead share costs and technologies between allies. Europe appears to have fallen at the first hurdle. The German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, and the French president, Emmanuel Macron, were forced to cancel the joint future combat air system in June, after fraught efforts to work together since 2018. The question exercising defence executives over the summer since then is: what happens now? France appears to be content to push ahead with its own fighter jet but Germany has been left questioning whether it will have its own aircraft. It may instead be left as a secondary customer to the rival Tempest jet under the global combat air programme (GCAP) led by the UK, Italy and Japan. Meanwhile, in the UK the debate over the summer has been over the future of military spending, after the resignation of John Healey as defence secretary in June over spending commitments, his return under Andy Burnham as chancellor and continued questions over when the UK will meet its target of spending 3% of GDP on defence. Militaries are racing to develop the sixth generation of fighters since the first jets that flew in the second world war. The Tempest and the US’s F47 will be developed to dominate the air, with AI technologies, more advanced stealth and swarms of drones to fly alongside. (The F47 is named, at least until a Democratic president enters the White House, after Donald Trump, the 47th US president.) France and Germany’s effort foundered amid arguments between France’s Dassault Aviation and the Germany-headquartered Airbus Defence and Space over who would lead the programme. France also reportedly wanted a smaller jet capable of landing on its aircraft carriers, while Germany does not have any aircraft carriers. The final nail in the coffin came over the summer, with the French engine maker Safran’s announcement it will end its joint effort to make engines for the fighter jet with Germany’s MTU Aero Engines. A European defence chief executive recently acknowledged that it was not impossible for there to be as many as three European fighter jets if Germany were to try to build one (possibly with partners) to rival GCAP and France. “It would not be ideal,” the boss said, slightly abashed. Three is too many, according to pretty much anyone without a financial interest in winning work share. “No way we end up with three,” one UK-based consultant who works with many of the big prime manufacturers said. “There’s no order book for it. You need an order book to make these economical.” The same person believes that it is unlikely that there will even be two European fighters, given the strained economics. Fighter jet programmes are considered a success in industrial terms if they can make hundreds – about 600 is seen as a good benchmark. That is far beyond the size of any single European air force. France has 228 Rafale fighter jets in service, according to the International Institute for Strategic Studies, a thinktank. Dassault is determined to press on. Éric Trappier, the chief executive of Dassault Aviation, in July said a next-generation combat jet could be developed solely in France or in cooperation with other partners. He wants a demonstrator to be flying as early as 2031. The outlines of the story are already familiar to many in the defence industry. In the early 1980s European nations were looking at building a fourth generation of fighter jets. France joined Italy, Spain, West Germany and Britain in a joint effort. Yet disputes over workshare and the capabilities of the final product grew until France walked away. Dassault ended up building the Rafale, while the other four countries are still building the Eurofighter Typhoon 30 years after its first flight. Yet some people are sceptical that Dassault would be able to create something with the same stealth abilities as other sixth-generation jets. Dassault could create a “Rafale plus” or “Super Rafale” with newer radar, weaponry and digital systems, and an upgraded engine, but without a complete redesign to put it at the very cutting edge. The Rafale upgrade already in development for the early 2030s will be able to work in partnership with stealth drones. Another important question – one faced by every air force, including the US and the GCAP partners – is whether a crewed fighter will be outdated by the time it is operating in 2035. However, the consensus in the industry for now appears to be that crewed fighters will still be required, but surrounded by a swarm of “loyal wingmen” drones such as BAE Systems’s Brontanax that can be sent into harm’s way over the horizon by the crewed jet fighter lurking further back. For Germany that leaves the somewhat embarrassing option of asking to join GCAP. Canada joined GCAP at July’s Farnborough airshow but only as an “observer”. That could put it front of the queue to buy products but does not entitle it to the politically valuable manufacturing jobs that come with status as a core partner. (Wealthy Saudi Arabia is also pushing to join, although it does not have much technological knowhow to offer and would be heavily criticised over its human rights record.) “They are very expensive platforms, and having assured orders for them is very helpful,” said Kevin Craven, the chief executive of ADS, the UK aerospace and defence lobby group. “I think there’s a realisation across Europe and Nato that the very expensive platforms require collaboration.” There are “elements of the sixth generation programmes that could work across Europe”, he added. Some of the industrial partners are open to Germany joining. Lorenzo Mariani, the chief executive of Leonardo, Italy’s lead defence company in GCAP, said Germany would be a “positive element” and a “strong financial partner, financially the strongest in Europe”. However, another core partner would add to the risk of delays, he acknowledged. Reopening discussions to let in another core member could be tricky. The UK, Italy and Japan set up a joint venture called Edgewing to build the Tempest. Marco Zoff, Edgewing’s chief executive, said its aim was “creating the conditions not to fight”. Another insider described it as “having all our fights at the start” over who gets what work, clearing the way for rapid development to be in the air by 2035. Tufan Erginbilgiç, the chief executive of the Tempest jet engine maker Rolls-Royce, told reporters at Farnborough that “I don’t think it will negatively impact GCAP at all” if Germany joins – although he would not be drawn on whether Rolls could share work with MTU. “It is not surprising that more countries are interested, and that will make the programme even more successful because to me it means more markets,” he said. Michael Schoellhorn, the chief executive of Airbus Defence and Space, told reporters in London that the company would join something where they could “have a significant portion of the work and the leadership. That’s currently being explored.” Yet now European executives are back from their summer holidays, they will have to work quickly if they are to avoid the fragmentation that Draghi warned against. Failure to do so would risk repeating the mistakes of the past of building several alternatives that all have to compete against each other for export orders. A European consultant covering the defence industry said: “It would mean we don’t learn.”

title: ‘We have really cool sharks’: three-year project to lift lid on Britain’s little-understood species
summary: Anglers will help scientists investigate the porbeagle, tope and blue shark to boost knowledge and conservation
text: ‘We have really cool sharks,” says Dr Lucy Hawkes. She is not referring to animals in the rich coastal waters of South Africa or Mexico, but instead talking about the species that live around Britain. Hawkes, an associate professor at the University of Exeter, is co-leading a new three-year project to investigate the lives of three of England’s most vulnerable shark species. “I like the porbeagle, which looks like a baby great white shark,” she says. “Surfers could see one and absolutely poop their pants, but they’re not dangerous. It’s amazing that we share the water with some pretty exciting animals.” More sharks swim in British waters than you might expect. From small catsharks and deepwater dogfish to migratory blue sharks and huge filter-feeding basking sharks, there are more than 40 different types in these waters. Yet scientists know surprisingly little about most of them. Now, the lab that Hawkes and her colleague Dr Matthew Witt run at Exeter has been awarded almost £1m by Natural England to collaborate with the Marine Biological Association, the Angling Trust and the Pat Smith Database, a long-running online record of shark catches dating back to 1953. Together, they will use a mix of historical records, electronic tags and recreational sightings to find out more about where and when porbeagle, tope or school sharks, and blue sharks are feeding, mating and migrating. The project will also monitor how shark populations are changing in terms of numbers and distribution – helping determine how best to prioritise conservation efforts. Sightings from some of the nation’s 3 million recreational anglers provide crucial information. “The UK has a long history of recreational fishing for sharks and big fish like tuna,” says Dr Francesco Garzon, a marine biologist working alongside Hawkes. “It’s one of the best places to see sharks in Europe.” Recreational shark fishing in the UK is now “catch and release”, he explains. Angling clubs used to keep catch records based on weight once a dead fish was landed onboard the boat. Now, many fishers measure the length of live sharks in the water before releasing them. Tagging should reveal how sharks respond to catch-and-release practices. “Anglers are conservation-conscious,” says Garzon. “They can sometimes be ostracised but are usually just as passionate about protecting sharks as we are.” He adds that direct commercial fishing or accidental bycatch are the biggest threats for UK sharks. Hawkes likens shark anglers to bird ringers. “These people are so passionate about the marine environment; they want to spend thousands of hours just trying to see these amazing animals up close. They’re obsessed with sharks.” By reporting their catches to the Pat Smith Database, skippers and recreational anglers act as citizen scientists and help researchers find out where these species go. “Even if all the shark researchers in England got together, we just couldn’t have the same level of records,” says Garzon. “Angler records are an essential tool, helping us understand shark populations.” The shark scientists will also run in-person workshops and interview hundreds of anglers across the country, from the south-west to the north-east of England. The mutual trust they have developed with the angling community is key to the success of the project. Over the years, the team have spent a lot of time on boats talking to fishers, while tagging pelagic species such as bluefin tuna. And it is entirely possible that porbeagles, for example, could swim halfway across the Atlantic, as bluefin tuna do. Forty tags, each worth £1,500, will stay on the fish for about 45 days. These tags should reveal how well sharks survive after being caught then released. According to Hawkes, even anglers want to know more about this so they can take measures to avoid harming the fish. “If tags show that sharks are travelling into waters where a particular fishery is permitted with a high rate of bycatch, that would be relevant to their conservation. It really depends on what the sharks tell us.” During tagging, the team plan to take DNA samples from the sharks. Usually that involves obtaining a tiny clip of skin from a fin, or swabbing a cotton bud on their skin. By doing this, scientists create a map of genetic connectivity. “We could work out whether a French blue shark is closely related genetically to an English blue shark,” explains Garzon. “They might be loners then aggregate in big numbers to mate, like tope sharks do in northern Scotland. We don’t yet know.” The team will also use another 30 more expensive tags, costing about £4,500 each, which last about a year. “These enable us to reconstruct a shark’s path and tell us how deep each shark has been diving and for how long,” says Garzon. Hawkes says people often recoil when she mentions sharks. “We scientists are the ones who say, ‘Shark! Where? Let me see!’ I’d love to change people’s minds about these beautiful animals. They totally belong here.” This story was produced in partnership with the Conversation, where Anna Turns is senior environment editor

title: Hijacking pirates exploit regional chaos to return to seas off Somalia
summary: US-Israel war against Iran and political instability in Somalia have led to pirates targeting cargo ships off Horn of Africa
text: The scourge of Somali piracy targeting cargo ships and smaller dhows off the Horn of Africa has returned to levels not seen in a decade, driven by a convergence of factors including disruptions to the shipping industry caused by the US-Israeli war against Iran and a resurgence of political instability in Somalia. Since late April there have been eight hijackings by Somali pirates, including two within the space of a fortnight in August: one targeting an oil tanker with ties to Iran, the other a Cameroon-flagged vessel, the Lutuf, carrying military equipment for Turkey. Over a seven-year period from 2005 there were more than 1,000 attacks on vessels in the waters off Somalia, which has mainland Africa’s longest coastline. Thousands of crew members were taken hostage, netting $400m (£296m) in ransom payments for the piracy network’s financiers, the low-level “foot-soldier” pirates and the communities who provided them with goods and services. The attacks only petered out after a multinational anti-piracy force was deployed. The hijacking of the Lutuf was the most high-profile of the recent incidents. Turkey has been expanding its influence in Somalia after an agreement signed in 2024 to build up its navy, and the Lutuf’s release two weeks after its capture involved a joint Turkish-Somali operation that resulted in the destruction of four pirate vessels. However, local officials including Mohamed Mubarak, the head of the Puntland security coordination office, have said that a $2.5m (£1.85m) ransom was also paid, prompting warnings that such payments risked encouraging similar incidents. In a comment for the Center for Maritime Security in July, Matthew Reisener, the thinktank’s national security adviser, warned that naval campaigns by Iran in the strait of Hormuz and Iran’s Houthi proxies in the Red Sea – launched in response to the US-Israel war on Iran – are allowing regional piracy “to once again thrive”. He wrote: “Not only have the global navies that once combatted piracy off the Horn of Africa diverted their resources to counter the threats against ships in these critical waterways, but these conflicts have also drawn maritime traffic closer to Somalia’s coastline, creating openings for opportunistic pirates to target commercial ships.” According to Reisener, about 70% of maritime traffic that passed through the Red Sea prior to the Houthis’ targeting of ships there is now being rerouted around the Cape of Good Hope in South Africa. A report by the International Institute for Strategic Studies in May reached a similar conclusion: “The recent deterioration of maritime security followed a prolonged period of relative calm in the waters off the Somali coast, which resulted in the redeployment of international anti-piracy fleets and the relaxation of commercial risk-management practices. These factors – alongside the distraction posed by Houthi attacks in the Red Sea – have converged to create an opening that Somali pirates have been quick to exploit.” Analysts also note that rising oil prices driven by the war have made oil cargoes a more valuable target. *** Among the least developed countries in the world, Somalia has endured conflict and clan battles with no strong central government since the autocratic ruler Mohamed Siad Barre fell in 1991. Insufficient patrol vessels and an inability to regularly pay salaries to those involved in coastal patrols are among the reasons why Somalia has long-struggled to secure its coastline. Piracy has historically thrived during periods of increasing instability and political, factional and regional competition. Observers say the recent rise in incidents has been exacerbated by a domestic and international focus on arms smuggling to Yemen by networks acting on behalf of Iran. Analysts suggest some of these networks have become increasingly associated with Somalia’s Islamist al-Shabaab group as it once again expands its territorial control in central and southern Somalia and seeks to build ties with the Houthis in Yemen. Local officials interviewed by the Guardian described how in the recent spate of incidents, pirate groups have been using vessels they had already seized to attack and capture other vessels. According to the officials, the Lutuf was approached as it sailed three nautical miles from Somali shores near the fishing town of Maraya by a previously hijacked cement carrier, the MV Sward, which had been repurposed as a pirate mothership. Eight gunmen from the Sward then boarded the Lutuf and were able to overpower the ship’s armed guards. Officials say the recent attacks have also been marked by increased technological sophistication on the part of pirate groups, including the use of SpaceX’s Starlink satellite internet service to facilitate the tracking of potential targets and for high-speed communications between pirates. That reflects what Lloyd’s List has described as an increasingly “more capable and adaptive Somali piracy threat” that is already exposing vulnerabilities in carriers’ existing anti-piracy security measures. In the weeks since the Lutuf ransom was paid, residents of Galkayo, a commercial hub in the north-central Mudug region, said money had started circulating through the local economy to a much greater degree than before. Consumption of the stimulant khat has reportedly increased, and greater numbers of expensive sports utility vehicles have been seen on the roads. During the previous piracy boom, increased flows of money through the economies of coastal communities and places like Galkayo had profound societal impacts, including an expansion of alcohol and drug use and prostitution. Perhaps foreshadowing the regime of tougher measures that may be required to counter the growing piracy threat, the Lutuf was only released after a series of drone attacks on the pirate groups involved in the seizure, both at sea and on land. The dead included nine armed men who were killed by a missile fired from a Turkish drone as they prepared boats to join the gunmen onboard the Lutuf. The question now is whether the growing threat can be countered. Writing in The Conversation in May, the UK-based academics Anja Shortland and Federico Varese, who studied Somalia’s piracy problem in 2014, were uncertain whether there was an international appetite or the capacity for the same sort of anti-piracy force deployed more than a decade ago. “What happens next will depend on how the current hijacks proceed. Pirates rely on ransoms for reinvestment and to attract young men into their no-win-no-fee contracts. Fast and generous payments … may free the captive ships. But they will lead to escalating risks for everyone else. “No state or alliance also currently has the will or capacity to run a naval mission on the scale seen in 2011 and 2012, when navies worldwide spent more than US$1bn annually on counter-piracy operations off Somalia. “Although piracy manifests as a sea-based problem, it can only be solved on land.”

title: Majority of Tory and Reform voters do not back cuts to disability benefits, survey finds
summary: Nearly half of respondents say spending on personal independence payments should be increased
text: There is little appetite for cuts to disability benefits even among Conservative and Reform voters, and proposals to reduce spending could prove politically risky, according to an authoritative national survey. The British Social Attitudes (BSA) report found that while support for welfare spending as a whole had dipped sharply in recent years, just 7% of respondents backed cuts to disability benefits – and 49% said they should be increased. Two government-commissioned reviews – of the personal independence payment (Pip) benefit, and support for jobless youngsters – are expected imminently, amid speculation they will seek to restrict spending on disability benefits. The BSA report notes that any ministerial proposals to axe disability benefits would carry little support among Labour voters, of whom just 5% favoured reduced spending and 57% backed more generous spending. Support for spending on disabled people remained high among Tory and Reform UK voters of whom 40% supported more spending on claimants who could not work, and just 10% supported less spending. The report’s co-author Robert de Vries, a senior lecturer at the University of Kent, said: “Despite growing political divisions on welfare, support for disability benefits remains remarkably strong. “Very few people favour cuts, disabled people are seen as among the most deserving recipients of support, and proposals to reduce disability benefits appear politically risky across the political spectrum.” However, the report acknowledges it was difficult to be precise about public support for disability benefits, some of which depends on respondents’ subjective ideas of whether claimants were “deserving” or “genuinely” unable to work. It was possible that there was support for cuts to specific groups of disabled people, with some conditions such as depression and anxiety ranking relatively low in an informal public hierarchy of “deserving cases” compared with, say, people who use a wheelchair. Equally, the report added that initial public support for proposed cuts can change when it becomes clearer precisely who will be affected, and what the consequences are in terms of numbers of claimants pushed into hardship. “We … cannot say in advance whether a particular cut to disability benefits will be supported or opposed by the public, but it is clear that this is very challenging terrain for a government to be confident of taking the public with them,” the report said. The survey interviewed 4,656 people across the UK between August and October 2025. It has tracked British public attitudes since 1983 on a range of issues from immigration and taxation, to marriage and sexuality. Last year the government was forced to U-turn on £5bn of disability benefit cuts in the face of public opposition and a Labour backbench rebellion over plans that would have pushed hundreds of thousands of disabled people into poverty. It subsequently launched a review of Pip headed by the former welfare minister Sir Stephen Timms. Its initial findings, published in July, found that Pip, which is claimed by nearly 4 million people in England and Wales, should be overhauled. However, it said changes would have to be financially sustainable. A separate review by the former Labour MP Alan Milburn into how to support nearly 1 million young people aged 16-24 who are not in education, employment or training (Neets) has led to concerns that benefit support for youngsters claiming Pip or the health element of universal credit may be cut. Both the Conservatives, who launched a review to save £23bn, and Reform UK, which claims drastic cuts to Pip could help save up to £50bn, are keen to bring down what they characterise as out of control disability benefits spending. The BSA report notes that while disability benefit spending has risen in recent years, overall levels of welfare spending have remained flat, suggesting that media and political claims of an unsustainable system are overstated.

title: Friedrich Merz is now on borrowed time. But that’s not why the AfD’s triumph is seismic | Jörg Lau
summary: The anti-fascist consensus about our Nazi past is fundamental to German democracy. But that, shockingly, is being shattered, says Jörg Lau, an international correspondent for the German weekly Die Zeit
text: As shock at the scale of the far right’s resounding state-election victory in Germany reverberated on Sunday, not everybody was unhappy. Seconds after the first exit polls from Saxony-Anhalt were revealed, Donald Trump posted the results on his Truth Social platform, seemingly delighted by the devastation of the centrist-conservative Christian Democrats (CDU) and the surge of the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD). It was indeed a humiliation for the CDU chancellor, Friedrich Merz, whose party lost more than half of its seats in the state parliament, while the AfD increased its count from 23 to 39. This was the exact opposite of what Merz promised to deliver when campaigning for office. With good government under his guidance, he insisted, he would easily cut the AfD in half. The AfD’s co-leaders did not miss the opportunity to point out the historic upset in their victory speeches, with Alice Weidel even boasting the CDU would “never win an election again”. Leaving the AfD’s swagger aside, this is a political earthquake with consequences far beyond a little state in the centre of Germany. The shock waves are still coming. To begin with, it is unclear if (and for how long) Merz can hold his own coalition together and cling to the chancellorship. True, the losses in the state of Saxony-Anhalt are not directly his fault. But that is only because he is so unpopular that his own party did not want him to campaign. Merz’s face was not on any posters, and when he visited the state capital, Magdeburg, the public was carefully excluded. That says it all about his standing in his own party. Two more elections are coming up on 20 September, in Berlin and the Baltic coastal state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. On the current trajectory, the CDU is looking at two more debacles. Merz’s leadership has become a liability, and it will be contested sooner rather than later. For now, only the absence of a convincing alternative and the many constitutional hurdles against sudden leadership changes in Germany protect him. He is the public face of a crisis of confidence in Germany’s leadership, but he is not its sole cause. The seismic nature of this moment goes far beyond party tactics. Germany is entering a period of political upheaval in which the core values of the postwar republic are up for dispute. Most shockingly, this extends to the anti-fascist consensus of “never again”, established over decades in many heated debates on the Holocaust and the crimes of the Wehrmacht. The AfD has managed to attack the national consensus that facing up to the Nazi past is fundamental for democracy in Germany. The party’s message is the opposite: the culture of remembrance is an “identity disorder” holding Germany back. It’s a central tenet of the AfD’s platform that it can “heal” the country by relativising its guilt and focusing on German greatness instead. This is why Charlotte Knobloch, a 93-year-old Holocaust survivor and former chair of the Central Council of Jews in Germany, expressed “horror” about the results. Knobloch said she “struggled, on days like these, to recognise my homeland”, adding: “In my worst nightmares, I could not have imagined that rightwing extremists win elections again in this manner.” She is right to be alarmed. The Saxony-Anhalt state chapter of the AfD is confirmed by domestic intelligence to be among the most radical nationally. Hardcore former neo-Nazis sit in influential positions. A distinctive trait of Germany’s far right compared with France or Italy is often overlooked. The AfD is markedly different from other rightwing populist parties in Europe: it is becoming ever-more radical the closer it gets to power. The leadership in Magdeburg employs several former members of prohibited neo-Nazi groups. These people might soon serve in high offices in the state, controlling the police, the domestic spy service (Verfassungsschutz), the judiciary and education. It’s a sign of the deterioration of political norms in my country that this shocking outlook hardly figured in the aftermath of the election. The German taboo about hard-right extremists in executive office is crumbling. The AfD slogans against the mainstream parties (“Altparteien”) have a distinctly Weimar vibe, echoing hateful propaganda against the despised “system” from a century ago. It is no coincidence that books on the end of the Weimar republic are bestsellers these days. The AfD is not a normal party. It must be understood as a (counter)revolutionary movement trying to change the system from within. Its leaders’ ambitions go beyond this or that policy change. Look at the crucial topic of migration: the number of asylum applications is rapidly falling (down by 48% in July 2026 compared with the same month last year), partly due to restrictive measures by Merz’s government. Still, the hard right is growing and radicalising at the same time. At the core is the idea of a German ethnostate with as few foreigners as possible. The party’s rallying cry of “remigration” targets not just “illegals” but all immigrants (and their descendants) with unwanted foreign backgrounds. The leadership have coined a term for what they do not want to become: they vow to avoid “Melonisierung” (Meloni-isation). Giorgia Meloni, despite her neo-fascist roots, surprised many at home and abroad by moving towards the mainstream, by standing with Ukraine and supporting the eurozone, Nato and the principle of free movement within the EU. The AfD, by contrast, promises to leave the EU and eurozone and put an end to the Schengen agreement. It is fiercely pro-Russian and wants to cut any support for Ukraine (including sending refugees back). Fear of escalation with Russia played a big part in the election. The recent hybrid attacks on Leipzig airport and other infrastructure may have tipped the scales: Merz had pointed a finger at Russia and vowed to “make the perpetrators pay”. This turned out to be perfect fodder for the AfD’s campaign. Abandoning Ukraine, rapprochement with Russia, reopening the Nord Stream pipeline in the Baltic – all this was presented as a “policy of peace”. This is also an election win for Vladimir Putin. What’s next? Without an absolute majority, the AFD may depend on the cooperation of a tiny splinter party. The leadership of the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), which broke away from the hard-left Die Linke, may want to help. They represent a new brand of leftist nationalism which is fiercely anti-immigrant and pro-Russian – and in that sense compatible with the AfD. Still, forming a government in Magdeburg will not be plain sailing. And it is a long way from this point for the AfD to take Berlin. One glimmer of light is that civil society is mobilising, now the initial shock has worn off. We can expect big demonstrations in major cities. A silent anti-fascist majority is beginning to organise. But it will be hard to break the dark spell that this victory in a troubled state has cast over the political landscape in Germany. One thing is certain: the coming weeks will be a challenge to the political imagination, not just for Germans. Jörg Lau is an international correspondent for the German weekly Die Zeit Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: How the Nepal-Tibet disaster became the latest victim of China’s ‘Clean Internet’ campaign
summary: The online campaign used to focus on tackling cybercrime and hacking but has since expanded to suppress information that differs from official narratives
text: Tsering Phuntsok watched news of the Nepal-Tibet flood unfold from thousands of miles away in southern India. The 46-year-old Tibetan in exile has missing family members on both sides of the border; those in Nepal are named in official government lists, but in Tibet he has received no information. “I have started praying for the lost ones now. I have to accept they will not return [because] … I’m not getting any information.” The flooding disaster is an example of the increasing use by Chinese authorities of “Clean Internet 2026”, the latest version of a long-running campaign by the Ministry of Public Security that criminalises anything officials regard as false information, which includes unofficial accounts of the floods. It follows a well-established playbook in which authorities promote official narratives, suppress independent accounts, discourage efforts to look back at the causes of a disaster and punish those who post claims that differ from the government-approved narrative. While earlier versions of the campaign focused on cybercrime and hacking, it is increasingly being used to target what the authorities call “rumours” which include unofficial information about the disaster. “The campaign serves a dual purpose. Tackling genuine problems like fraud and misinformation while tightening control over public narratives,” says Tencho Gyatso from the International Campaign for Tibet, a US based Tibetan advocacy group. “That dual purpose is what makes it more nuanced and challenging to criticise.” In the hours after the floods, researchers say they saw a huge surge in interest across Chinese social media. The topic was trending, but then fell away as comments were removed in real time. Screenshots seen by the Guardian show the Chinese app WeChat restricting posts about the floods. In one case, a user was notified by WeChat that a post about the flooding had been reported and then deleted for containing “politically sensitive content”. Another was stopped from being shared. It was said to be “unavailable due to policy violation” and that it contained “prohibited content”. “[The trend] was constantly shifting and being manipulated because there was real interest,” says David Bandurski, director of the China Media Project, a research group that monitors Chinese media. “A ‘crackdown’ is not the right word, because they don’t crack down. It’s a consistent, persistent, everyday application of a policy of public-opinion guidance.” On 30 August, four days after the disaster, police in Tibet reported 10 cases under the Clean Internet 2026 campaign relating to “rumours” about the disaster. In the majority of cases there were claims that more than 1,000 people had been swept away in the floods. So far, Chinese authorities have released a death toll of 43. Human rights and Tibetan advocacy groups have accused the Chinese government of concealing the true scale of the death toll. The police notice said that spreading of “rumours” “misleads the public and disrupts online order” and it intended to “ensure that disaster relief work proceeds smoothly”. A user from Jiangxi, a province 3,000km away from the disaster, posted on a video platform claiming “the number of missing people had risen to 826”. According to the police report the user faced “administrative punishment” without specifying what that involved. ‘Proving that the state is working hard’ One former Chinese state media journalist, who agreed to speak on the condition of anonymity for fear of reprisals, says control in times of crisis also works through simple omission of information as much as suppression: “Official news coverage devotes enormous space to proving that the state is working hard, but gives very little information answering the most basic questions: who is missing? Where were they last seen? Which buildings have been searched? “Controls have become much stricter, especially regarding the internet, though there are nuances, as there are still ways to bypass restrictions. For instance, by posting quickly or using veiled language to get content through,” they say. But allowing some reporting can serve the interests of central authorities, says one former CGTN editor who worked at the broadcaster during the Covid pandemic and who also asked not to be named for fear of reprisals. “The government needs journalists to uncover uncomfortable truths because it needs accurate information in order to govern effectively,” they say. “But if journalists are given completely free rein to uncover and publish those truths, they may expose things that are politically uncomfortable or challenge the interests of the state.” Bandurski says: “The [Communist] party sees itself in a global public-opinion struggle. It is wrestling with the world fighting to get its view out. This is how China sees information globally, in a very, very oppositional framework.” Phuntsok hopes his family on the Nepal side could still be alive. His grandfather, Wangyal, uncle Janngchup, aunt Sumchok and their young child Yeshi Dorjee are still missing. On the Tibet side he is unwilling to share the names of his missing relatives with the Guardian for security reasons. Kalsang Jigme, a Tibetan journalist based in New Delhi, says: “Normally, when there’s some disaster, people are very active, praying and support, and they send goods to the affected area. But this time they’re completely silenced.” Additional research by Yu-chen Li in Taipei

title: Ukraine war briefing: New political turmoil in Kyiv as prosecutor general resigns
summary: Anti-corruption agencies raid offices and arrest a deputy of Ruslan Kravchenko in case linked to alleged laundering of phone scam proceeds. What we know on day 1,658
text: Ukraine’s prosecutor general, Ruslan Kravchenko, has resigned amid corruption accusations that saw anti-graft officers search his offices at the weekend as part of investigations into illegal call centres. Kravchenko has rejected any allegations against him, calling them “completely unsubstantiated” and denying wrongdoing. The National Anti-Corruption Bureau (Nabu) and Specialised Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s Office (Sapo) announced on Saturday that they had uncovered a money-laundering scheme “led by an official in the prosecutor general’s office” and had conducted raids there. According to investigators, a corrupt network received money to protect call centres that carried out phone scams and “laundered fortunes amounting to millions”. Nabu published images of a safe filled with bundles of dollar bills, saying it uncovered five members behind the scheme, without naming them. A deputy of Kravchenko has been remanded in custody on suspicion of money laundering in connection with the case. Volodymyr Zelenskyy in 2025 faced protests that forced him to reverse efforts to make Nabu and Sapo subordinate to the national prosecutor’s office. According to the Swiss-based Global Initiative Against Transnational Crime (GI-TOC), illegal call centres employ about 60,000 people in Ukraine. On Monday, Kravchenko posted: “I have submitted my resignation as prosecutor general. I do not want the office of prosecutor general to be used as a tool in political confrontation. My position regarding the charges remains unchanged.” The new turmoil confronting Zelenskyy, Ukraine’s president, comes after a shootout between Ukraine’s SBU and GUR security and intelligence services. Kyiv is also bedding in new military leadership after Zelenskyy sacked the defence minister and was then forced by protests to sack Ukraine’s military commander-in-chief as well because of feuding between the pair. Russia resumed its attacks on Kyiv, Ukraine’s emergency service said late on Monday, as air raid alerts were issued in more than a dozen regions. It came after the expiration of a three-day halt in attacks while US envoys visited the Ukrainian capital and Moscow. Kyiv’s city military administration said at least two people were killed and seven wounded. The strikes damaged buildings across Kyiv, including a five-storey apartment block in the Solomianskyi district, while vehicles caught fire in the Podilskyi district. “Russians attacked Boryspil and Fastiv districts with drones,” the emergency service said. Social media channels monitoring air threats on Ukraine said Moscow’s forces had started to transport ballistic missiles and relocate heavy bombers from Russia’s east to airfields closer to Ukraine. Russia “does not rule out the resumption of the trilateral format”, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said on Monday, referring to possible talks involving the Russians, Ukrainians and the US. “But it is too early to say anything about the venue or the exact dates at this stage,” Peskov added. US negotiators told European representatives during talks in Kyiv that Russia was showing a “new willingness” to negotiate over the Ukraine war, the French presidency said on Monday. “The Americans told us that there was a new willingness on the part of Russia to negotiate following the Duma [Russian lower house] elections, and we should prepare for a fresh start to the negotiations,” said an aide to Emmanuel Macron, the French president. Donald Trump’s administration, though, has repeatedly construed Putin’s willingness to meet US representatives and reel off his unaltered maximalist demands as a willingness to negotiate. Ukraine struck a Russian ⁠oil refinery ⁠in the Ryazan region, as ⁠well as oil-processing facilities in the ⁠Perm region ‌and Tatarstan, ‌Zelenskyy ‌said on Monday. Both attacks were confirmed by regional governors – in Perm the governor said one person was ⁠killed ⁠and four others were injured ⁠when one of the drones ‌damaged a residential building. A Russian ⁠attack damaged ⁠a British ⁠American Tobacco plant in the town ⁠of Pryluky in Ukraine’s northern ⁠Chernihiv region with no known injuries, BAT Ukraine’s ⁠press office said. Off-site power at the Zaporizhzhia ⁠nuclear ⁠plant in south-eastern Ukraine has been restored via ⁠the Ferosplavna power line, according to Rosatom, the Russian state nuclear corporation ⁠that is illegally in control of the power station. The plant had ‌been without ‌external power since 20 August and ‌reliant on emergency diesel generators for cooling of its nuclear fuel. The International Atomic Energy Agency confirmed that repairs were completed during a ceasefire that it brokered. Latvia’s ⁠government plans to impose a 300% tariff on grain arriving ⁠from Russia and ⁠Belarus. Officials in ⁠Latvia and its neighbour Lithuania last week said they considered ending ⁠shipments of Russian grain through their ports after Moscow ‌stepped up the ‌transits in response to attacks by Ukraine ‌on its Baltic ports. The UN human rights chief, Volker Türk, said he was “horrified by reports that fully autonomous drones launched by the Russian Federation killed three Ukrainians last month”. Türk called for an urgent ban on such weapons. The New York Times has reported that a Russian drone guided entirely by an artificial intelligence system killed three civilians in Zaporizhzhia on 6 July.

title: Nepal says big polluters must ‘wake up’ as it calls for climate compensation over flood disaster
summary: Foreign minister Shisir Khanal tells the Guardian the world’s biggest economies need to help Nepal, which contributes less than 0.1% of global greenhouse gas emissions
text: Nepal is demanding $20m in climate compensation for the recent devastating floods, as a senior minister called on the world’s most polluting countries to “wake up” and accept shared responsibility for a disaster that led to the death or disappearance of more than 6,000 people. Scientists believe the climate crisis had a role to play in the floods, which were triggered when a melting glacier partially collapsed and set off a deadly landslide and flash flooding through Chinese-controlled Tibet and Nepal in late August. So far, more than 1,300 are confirmed dead and more than 5,500 still missing, with hopes of their survival diminished after 12 days of rescue operations. Speaking to the Guardian, Nepal’s foreign minister, Shisir Khanal, was forthright in his call for climate justice and said it was imperative the world’s biggest economies stepped up to help Nepal recover and rebuild after the catastrophic floods. Nepal contributes less than 0.1% of global greenhouse gas emissions, while its neighbours India and China are among the world’s biggest emitters. The mountains of the Himalayas – which span across India, China, Nepal and Bhutan – have been warming at a rate nearly 50% faster than the global average. In 2023, the UN said Nepal’s mountains had lost close to a third of their ice in just over 30 years due to global heating. Khanal emphasised that the recent disaster was far more extreme than any flooding regularly seen during the monsoon season, and said the magnitude of damage was on par with the 2015 earthquake that left much of the country in ruins. “This felt like a tsunami that was coming from the Himalayas,” he said. “We experienced waves as high as 60, 70 feet, which were mixed with debris, mud, stones, rocks, and came at the speed of almost 180km per hour. Towns, villages and highways were completely wiped out and there are some areas still disconnected.” Khanal confirmed that Nepal’s ministry of finance and ministry of environment had written a joint letter to the UN’s fund for responding to loss and damage – which was set up in 2022 in line with the Paris climate agreement – to request $20m in climate-related damages. “We have contributed so little to climate change,” he said. “It is imperative for those in the global community who benefit from larger, much more polluting economies, and whose historical contribution to greenhouse gases is much bigger than ours, to accept a shared responsibility. This affects all of humanity.” For Nepal, the disaster was particularly worrying because it was “one of the strongest warning signals that we’ve experienced of what’s to come”, he said. “The global community should not see this as one-off disaster; it should be viewed in the context of the changing climate in the Himalayas,” he said. “We know it is going to be a recurring scenario that more and more communities, not just in Nepal but around the world, will have to face.” Khanal acknowledged that the compensation amount Nepal has requested from the UN was “obviously not nearly enough to cover the damage that we have sustained”. According to some estimates, the total damage caused by the floods will be upwards of $5bn, though Khanal said it could be even higher. Upwards of 20,000 homes will probably have to be rebuilt, as well as the main highway. Villages built in vulnerable areas along the river, some of which washed away entirely, may have to be relocated to higher, safer ground. While Khanal initially singled out India and China as countries that should step in to help – while avoiding mention of the US, which is the world’s biggest polluter – he rowed back on those comments, saying: “It is not just about shifting the blame to one or the other country, it’s about us all working together.” He emphasised that the compensation demand was also meant to act as a “wake-up call for the global community to establish a more robust mechanism to help vulnerable and small economies like Nepal”. The UN has admitted the loss and damage fund is already facing a “significant financing gap”. The fund has already received requests totalling $2.8bn from about 119 countries, but so far only around $400m has been given by the international community. The US has given just $17m, after Donald Trump withdrew from the Paris agreement. Khanal acknowledged there were “political challenges” in getting Nepal the climate compensation it was demanding. “Yes there always will be people who may not agree to our perspective or deny there is climate change, but there are also people who deny that the Earth is round,” he said bluntly. He emphasised the importance of funds being made available not just for immediate disaster response but also for preparedness and mitigation for climate-related risk. Khanal rebuffed allegations that China had failed to give an adequate warning or share data with Nepal about the impending floods. He said he was in discussion with China about enhancing coordination and data sharing for the Himalayan region. “With the benefit of hindsight, we can now see that this glacier was fragile and had been receding in the past six months,” he said. “But before the floods hit, there was no knowledge on our part, or on the part of Chinese scientists, that this particular collapse was imminent. I do not believe any of us had any idea of the threat until it happened.”

title: Global move away from oil could lead to conflict and migration, experts say
summary: Researchers urge governments to help worst afflicted countries, such as Nigeria and Algeria, which rely on oil revenues for public services
text: Conflict, migration and economic upheaval will accompany the global move away from oil, unless governments act urgently to help the worst afflicted countries to cope, research has found. Nigeria, Iran, Angola and Algeria are among the countries that will be severely affected, as they rely strongly on oil revenues for their government and provision of public services, but have little diversification and too little capital to cushion the blow. Oil use is already waning in many countries, with the growth of renewable energy, and has been hastened by the effects of the Iran war, which has constrained supply and sent prices soaring, triggering high inflation and political instability. Global demand for oil is forecast to plateau in the coming decade, with a peak likely in the early 2030s, which will force producers to chase a shrinking pool of buyers. Many will try to hang on to their resource revenues as long as possible, according to research from the E3G thinktank published on Tuesday, but the cheapest producers with abundant resources – such as Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates – are likely to win against those with less advanced infrastructure. The example of Venezuela, which was suffering collapse and have had a partial takeover of government by the US, now shattered further by the impact of earthquakes, should warn countries of what is at stake, the report’s authors found. “Governments are not thinking about and not prepared for [these outcomes],” said Beth Walker, co-author of the report. “The transition becomes riskier for everyone when oil producers are left to adjust on their own, and oil markets left to manage themselves. Producer fragility becomes a global security risk.” Putting off or slowing down the transition is an even worse option than confronting it, however, as the climate crisis is rapidly worsening. “None of this is an argument for slowing the transition,” said Maria Pastukhova, a co-author of the report. “A slow but chaotic transition can be just as destabilising as a fast one, maybe even more so.” E3G compiled the report over two years, in part through “war-gaming” various scenarios for declining oil demand with more than 100 public servants and experts from around the world. Bob Ward, policy director at the Grantham Research Institute at the London School of Economics, who was not involved in the report, said developed countries would also be affected. “Many oil producers have been in denial about the pace and scale with which both demand and supply will have to fall if we are to avoid dangerous climate change,” he said. “We should be clear that the highest-cost producers will likely be the first to feel this shock. The North Sea has high operating costs and so is unlikely to be economically viable once demand starts to fall sharply and market prices reduce.” Income from oil makes up more than 40% of the revenue to governments in 17 countries around the world, and in some cases is overwhelmingly the biggest source of income, for instance in Iraq and Libya, where it represents 70% to 90% of government revenues. But this revenue will fall rapidly from 2030: E3G forecasts that Algeria will experience an 87% drop in revenue and Nigeria more than 60%. Algeria in particular was “one to watch” said Walker, with its position near the borders of Europe and almost total reliance on the EU for its exports. This will leave countries with big gaps to fill in providing basic services, which will destabilise social structures. Debt will be an increasing burden – already, Angola and Mexico spend more than a quarter of their government revenue in servicing public debt, the report found. Walker said: “This isn’t one dramatic global oil or security crisis, it’s a series of national fiscal crises that could turn into very different security problems: unrest and migration in Algeria; a much more brittle settlement in Iraq with spillover into Gulf regional stability; weaker state capacity in the most populated country in Africa, Nigeria, with spillovers across the continent; military competition over oil infrastructure in Libya with heightened security risk in Europe. Most of these problems are a much larger scale than Venezuela, and they could all unravel just as the UK and Europe’s capacity to contain live conflicts is drained.” Any attempt to remedy this situation will require organisations such as the International Monetary Fund, the World Bank, private sector financial institutions and governments to work together. “Much of the toolkit already exists, but in separate policy boxes that need to work together,” said Pastukhova. “Major demand powers need to coordinate and communicate more clearly about their future demand. They need to produce adjustment not just as part of their development assistance or climate policy, but as part of their foreign and economic security policy, given the consequences that otherwise might follow.” China was the dominant source of increasing oil demand over the past few decades, but its oil consumption is now on a downward path, in part owing to the rapid uptake of electric vehicles. India’s future direction is less certain, and the country could become pivotal to whether demand declines in time to stave off some of the worst impacts of climate breakdown.

title: Federal investigators search for cause of Amazon cargo jet crash that killed five
summary: Focus likely on whether plane touched down too late in its glide path on to tarmac to enable it to stop safely
text: Federal investigators have started collecting evidence, including a flight data recorder, following the Sunday crash of an Amazon cargo jet at Miami international airport that killed five people and injured five others. Speaking at a press conference on Monday, Jennifer Homendy, chair of the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB), announced a preliminary investigation into the Amazon Air flight 7598 accident involving a Boeing 767-33 Alpha operated by 21 Air, an all-cargo airline. “What we know so far is the flight was arriving from San Juan, Puerto Rico, with two crew members on board. This was the third flight for the aircraft. That aircraft yesterday went from Cincinnati to Miami, Miami to San Juan, and San Juan back to Miami,” Homendy said. She added: “[It] overran runway 30 on landing, struck navigational aids and equipment, then impacted a 2012 white Ford Econoline van that was owned by Professional Ocean Service Corporation, which is a contract cleaning company for the airline. In the van were seven persons on board. “The aircraft then traveled through a perimeter fence and impacted a Toyota Corolla Cross LE, which was traveling on Northwest 67th Avenue, and then continued into the grass and impacted another fence line, which separated an area where Tesla robotaxis were stationed. In total, it was about 1,300ft past the paved surface.” Homendy described the Ford Econoline van as “torn apart”, and noted that for the Corolla Cross LE, “you can see airbags … you can see components from vehicles, both passenger vehicles and the aircraft itself”. Federal investigators are expected to focus on several areas, including operations and human performance, flight crew experience, as well as 21 Air’s policies and contractual relationship with Amazon. Other areas of focus include air traffic services, radar data, aircraft performance and structure, meteorology, as well as the “lack thereof of an engineered materials arresting system, or EMAS … a crushable, lightweight material that’s at the end of a runway that safely stops an aircraft”, Homendy said. She added that although the NTSB would remain on scene for at least a week, its focus during that time would not be on determining probable cause, but rather on documenting the scene and collecting perishable evidence. Video footage from Sunday showed the Boeing 767 jet wobbling slightly, coming in fast and flying relatively far along the runway before it touched down. After the aircraft overshot the runway, coming to rest in a parking lot with its nose tipped forward, flames burst out of part of the jet and thick, dark smoke began billowing into the air. The crash trapped the pilot and co-pilot in the cockpit and some occupants in cars, the Miami-Dade rescue fire chief, Ray Jadallah, said. The agency said crews also had to extricate a person who was trapped under a vehicle. Jadallah described the incident as a “very complex situation” where the plane crashed into multiple vehicles as it ran off the tarmac, trapping several people inside their vehicles. Video of the Amazon Prime Air Boeing 767-33A, operated by contractor 21 Air, posted to social media show it touching down far along the runway. Other posted footage shows the plane with a left-hand wheel of the landing gear still a little above the ground as the jet speeds down the tarmac, apparently abnormally fast, and then it overruns the end of the runway, where the right undercarriage collapsed and the wing caught fire. Typically, the landing zone is within the first 3,000ft (914m) of a runway. Aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo said if it was beyond that area, the plane should normally have aborted the landing and gone around for another attempt. Mary Schiavo, who is a pilot and former inspector general of the transportation department, said video posted online shows the Amazon plane floating above the runway for an extended period without flaring the nose upward to force the main landing gear on to the ground. Storm clouds can be seen in the area and strong winds reported. Schiavo said that if the plane had a tail wind, that could have contributed to it floating further down the runway. “A tail wind would certainly add to your troubles if you’ve already given up a good chunk of the runway by not touching down and landing right away,” Schiavo said. Miami airport is not equipped with “arresting beds”, systems of lightweight, crushable material that the federal aviation authority (FAA) says have been installed at more than 120 airports nationwide at the end of runways to help safely stop planes that overshoot. About 200 emergency personnel responded to the incident, finding the plane with heavy flames and smoke from a complex engine compartment fire, the fire department said. The flight operators, 21 Air, is a cargo carrier based in North Carolina. The 32-year-old Boeing 767 was originally built to carry passengers and flew for several airlines for more than two decades before being converted to a cargo plane in 2015, according to flight-tracking site Flightradar24. More than 160 flights were canceled and nearly 325 delayed by late Sunday, according to FlightAware, a website that tracks flight disruptions. Flights later resumed, although two runways at the busy airport remained out of service on Monday morning. The Associated Press contributed reporting
