title: 25 years ago, two strangers met in the twin towers and escaped on 9/11. What happened next?
summary: Stanley Praimnath and Brian Clark were two of only four individuals known to have survived above the impact zone in the south tower
text: He has told the story hundreds of times, but it never seems to fade. If anything, it only becomes more vivid. “Oh, gosh,” exclaims Stanley Praimnath, his voice cracking with an “ooooooh!” as if bearing a weight. “It’s like reliving that day.” Nearly 3,000 people died in the terrorist attacks on New York City and Washington DC on September 11 2001. But Praimnath and another office worker, Brian Clark, were two of only four individuals known to have survived from above the impact zone in either tower of the World Trade Center. The two strangers met in the smoke and fire of the 81st floor of the south tower, and walked down 1,620 steps into the rest of their lives. Their split-second decisions that day made all the difference. Over the next 25 years, both men moved from middle age into old age and retirement. Both enjoyed family weddings and watched children and grandchildren grow. Both saw US presidents come and go as old wars ended and new wars began. They remained friends through it all. They also told their story – countless times – in churches, schools, TV studios and elsewhere. “It could be 800, 1,200, a number like that,” Clark estimates. Praimnath, in a separate interview, muses: “People refer to me as ‘the 9/11 guy’. It doesn’t feel repetitive. It is like unloading baggage from my shoulder, like washing my soul with tears. It is comforting to know that people out there still want to hear.” A cry for help Clark is now 79, living in retirement in northern New Jersey with his wife; he has 11 grandchildren and two great-grandchildren. Praimnath, a decade younger, lives in Valley Stream, Long Island; he is a pastor, grandfather and empty-nester who speaks of his survival not as luck, but as an act of God’s grace. Their recollections of 9/11 are still as clear as the cloudless sky over Manhattan on that September morning. Clark, a Canadian who was executive vice-president at the financial brokerage firm Euro Brokers, arrived at his office on the 84th floor around 7.15am. Down on the 81st floor, the Guyanese-born Praimnath had settled into his desk at Fuji Bank, where he worked as a loan officer. At 8.46am, the peace was shattered by a deafening double boom as the hijacked American Airlines Flight 11 slammed into the north tower. Clark recalls: “The lights above me flickered and I spun around in my chair and my peripheral vision caught flames against the window. It was surreal. Two or three seconds later, the flames dissipated and the airspace was filled with singed paper.” Having volunteered as a floor fire warden after the 1993 World Trade Center truck bombing, Clark sprang into action. He retrieved an official torch marked “WTC fire safety team” from an overhead cabinet and began shepherding staff toward the building’s central corridor. Co-workers crowded against the north-facing windows, gazing up nine stories at the raging “ring of fire” consuming their twin building. Thinking the emergency was confined next door, Clark phoned his wife at home and his father in Toronto, reassuring them that he was safe. Three floors below, Praimnath was on the telephone with a colleague in Chicago who had witnessed the north tower explosion on television and begged him to evacuate. He was looking towards the Statue of Liberty when he spotted another plane – so close that he could make out the “U” on the tail of United Airlines Flight 175. “On a given day, it was normal for a plane to zoom by a half a mile to a mile away,” he recalls. “But this plane is coming towards me. I made eye contact. I dropped the phone and screamed and said, ‘Lord, I can’t do this. You take over.’ I don’t know why I said that – but thank God I said that.” Praimnath dived under his desk in the foetal position, weeping and praying as the Boeing 767 bore down on his window. “With the most thunderous sound, the plane came and crashed into the building,” he says. The aircraft struck diagonally at 9.03am, cutting through the 77th to 85th floors. The impact flattened entire walls, severed electrical wiring and sent a shock wave of jet fuel and debris through Fuji Bank’s offices. Praimnath says: “That big orange glow that you see there – I’m stuck in the middle of it. Upon impact, it looks like a demolition crew came with a big giant wrecking ball and ripped the entire office. Every wall is flattened. I remember a large chunk of the plane was broken off and stuck in the office doorway. “I remember flames all around me, as if somebody took a giant bag of cement, threw it in the air and I can’t breathe. The floor above me collapsed and it’s hovering over the desk and I’m like, ‘Oh, my God, I’m going to die. It’s gonna totally collapse, crush me to death, or I’m gonna get sucked out by the air pressure.’ You can hear the sound.” At the memory, he sets his teeth and blows down the phone to recreate the terrifying whoosh. Three floors higher, Clark was standing on the west side of the 84th floor when the aircraft sliced into the building’s eastern trading floor. “Our room exploded,” he says. “Everything came out of the ceiling – air conditioning ducts, lighting, the whole works. For five seconds the building swayed to the west and then it swayed back to vertical. For those 10 seconds I was quite terrified, thinking the building was going to roll over. But it didn’t.” When the tower steadied, Clark gathered a group of six or seven colleagues and led them toward the central core. The impact had demolished stairwells B and C, but stairwell A, tucked furthest away on the north-west side, somehow remained open. The group began descending stairwell A. On the 81st floor landing, they were halted by a man and woman coming up the stairs. “She was insistent we not go down,” Clark says. “‘No, no, no. You can’t go down,’ she said and, because she stopped us, it allowed me to hear a call for help from within the 81st floor, a muffled cry: ‘Help, I’m buried. I can’t breathe.’” Brothers for life Clark squeezed through an opening where the door frame had been ripped from the drywall and stepped into the dark 81st floor, guided by Praimnath’s desperate shouts. Inside the office, Praimnath prayed for rescue. “I can still remember the flames encroaching and I’m screaming, ‘Lord, send somebody, I don’t want to die.’ I’m crawling away from the flames, dodging all the cables that were hanging in the ceiling, short-circuiting because the sprinkler system came on,” he recalls. “I’m like, ‘Oh my God, I’m gonna die.’ Somebody had a flashlight on the other end of the floor. The person’s saying, ‘I’ll wait for you’, but I couldn’t hear because I got temporarily deaf when the plane hit the building. As I’m crawling away, the flames are coming closer, licking up the office space. “I got to the wall. The person’s saying, ‘Bang on the wall, I know where you are’. I hit the wall and the person says, ‘Climb over there.’ It had a hollow ceiling, a 10-foot sheetrock wall, a drywall. I remember that so vividly.” Clark’s torchlight had picked out a hand protruding from a hole in the 10-foot sheetrock wall. He grasped Praimnath’s hands and hauled him over the partition. The desk beneath Clark gave way, and both men crashed to the floor in a heap. Clark recalls: “We fell and he gave me a big kiss. I said, ‘What’s going on, what are you doing?’ I stuck out my hand and said, ‘I’m Brian Clark.’ He says, ‘I’m Stanley Praimnath; we’ll be brothers for life.’ I said, ‘Well, I don’t have any siblings.’” Clark noticed that Praimnath had a puncture wound on his palm, while his own hand was cut and bleeding from moving debris. Clark recalls his instinctive gesture of solidarity: “I smooshed our hands together and said, ‘In fact, we’ll be blood brothers for life. Come on, buddy. Let’s go home.’” When they returned to the stairwell, Clark made the critical decision to ignore the warning of the woman on the landing. Pointing his torch down the staircase, he saw no flames. Clark and Praimnath turned downward. Most of the colleagues who had been with Clark, however, chose to head upward, believing safety lay on the roof. They died in the collapse. At Euro Brokers, 61 of Clark’s colleagues perished. Lives intertwined When Clark and Praimnath finally emerged on to the street, police and emergency workers yelled at them to run. Minutes later, the south tower collapsed in a cascade of steel and concrete, sending a rolling cloud of debris surging through lower Manhattan. The two men dived inside 42 Broadway to escape the choking dust. In the chaos, Praimnath reached into his pocket and handed Clark a business card from a small home business he and his wife operated. Separated in the confusion, Clark used the number on that card to reach Praimnath late that evening, confirming that both had made it home. While Clark suffered remarkably little long-term psychological distress – describing his lack of post-traumatic stress as an unearned “gift” – Praimnath’s return to the living was fraught. Arriving home on Long Island on the evening of 9/11, Praimnath says he suffered profound memory loss. “I wanted to know what this strange woman was doing in our house with two children, not going home. I refused to go to bed because this strange woman was in that room.” His wife, Jennifer, quietly cared for him without judgment. “She would hobble me into the bathroom, fill the tub with warm water and Epsom salts, and tell me to soak,” he says. “Then she would put me on the couch. Every day, she would leave an apple, a sandwich, a bottle of water and a notepad. I don’t know how long I was in that state. All I know is that one day, I got up, looked at her, recognised her and snapped out of it.” When Praimnath returned to work in October at a temporary office in Jersey City, he still could not navigate on his own. “I had to draw out my commute on a map and colour-code it,” he recalls. “When I got to work, people would say, ‘Stan, can you please sign this?’ I didn’t have a clue what I was signing. But they were kind, patient managers. Gradually, the pieces came back.” In the quarter-century since that Tuesday morning, the lives of Clark and Praimnath have remained intertwined. They shared family milestones, celebrated at each other’s daughters’ weddings and phoned one another regularly. When Clark’s eldest daughter married, Praimnath and his wife were seated at the head table. Praimnath says: “Brian introduced me to all his friends and family as his blood brother. You could see people looking around, thinking, ‘Something doesn’t quite fit the picture!’ But Brian didn’t care. That’s who he is. He is the big brother I never had.” For Praimnath, surviving 9/11 opened a deep spiritual vocation. In 2006, he became a pastor, joining the staff of the church where his father-in-law was senior minister. Over the past two decades, he has travelled to churches, military bases and schools worldwide, delivering his testimony as a sermon on redemption. “On 9/11, I was crying out to the Lord under that desk, ‘Lord, let me live to walk my daughters down the aisle,’ and God answered. I walked Stephanie and Caitlin down the aisle. I’ve lived to see my grandchildren, Hannah and Ezra. They don’t call me Papa – they call me ‘Papaya’. Stephanie even bought me a shirt that says ‘Papaya’.” Yet Praimnath’s resilience has been tested repeatedly. In 1993, he narrowly escaped the first truck bombing at the World Trade Center. He was diagnosed with leukaemia and a severe bout of Covid-19 scarred his lungs with bilateral pneumonia. Then, after a trip to Europe with his wife, doctors discovered that his four coronary arteries were severely blocked, requiring emergency quadruple bypass surgery. “My question has always been: how many times do you try to kill one man?” asks Praimnath, who retired from the Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation two years ago. “I’m living by grace. I still travel. I still do exactly what I used to do before.” Blood brothers He and Clark know they have more years behind them than lie ahead. On the 25th anniversary, Clark will attend a memorial service at his local town square in New Jersey, beginning at 8.45am, before spending the day quietly with his wife. Praimnath will be at a church in Virginia, telling his story once again, with gratitude. Both men find themselves speaking to a generation for whom 9/11 is not a living memory, but history. Clark, who retired in 2006, says: “I don’t have to teach history any more – the textbooks have that covered. What textbooks don’t have is the emotional reality, the optimism that life carries on despite terrible evil. But whenever I speak at schools, 98% of the time, the very first question the kids ask is: ‘Are you still in touch with Stanley?’” Praimnath experiences the exact same phenomenon. Just recently, he addressed 700 students over Zoom at a Christian school in Tampa, Florida. “These children weren’t even alive when the towers fell,” Praimnath says. “Yet when you describe the roar of the jet engine and the wing slicing through the office, you can hear the audible gasp in the auditorium. It becomes real to them.” The blood brothers look out at the contemporary US with a mixture of sorrow and perplexity. Clark has become an outspoken pacifist, dismayed by the decades of overseas conflict that followed the attacks. He says: “With 25 years of time to think about it, I realise more and more the utter futility of war. I think of Germany, Italy and Japan being our greatest allies today. What on earth are we doing to ourselves? Dropping bombs on residential areas in Ukraine, Russia, Gaza – what a senseless waste of energy and human life.” Clark’s aversion to vengeance ran so deep that he was repulsed by the street celebrations following the killing of the al-Qaida leader Osama bin Laden in 2011. “I was disgusted when people were driving around in pickup trucks chanting ‘USA!’ and cheering for another human being’s death. Capture him, interrogate him, lock him away – fine. But taking lives and celebrating it? No. That is not who we should be.” Praimnath recalls the profound but fleeting sense of unity that blossomed after 9/11. “After that infamous day, the entire nation rallied around each other,” he reflects. “All the churches were packed. A month later, everything went back to normal. “But I still believe we are a resilient people. We may have our political differences but at the end of the day we know that, when tragedy strikes, the labels fall away. On the 81st floor, there were no Republicans or Democrats, no Black or white. We were just brothers trying to find the way out.” • The subheading on this article was amended on 7 September 2026. An earlier version said the interviewees escaped from the north tower, rather than the south. Stanley Praimnath’s surname was also misspelled.

title: Labour’s new powers for water customers are a ‘stitch-up’, say campaigners
summary: Exclusive: Documents reveal water firms have been allowed to advise on how they wish to be held to account
text: Labour’s new powers for customers to hold water companies to account are a “stitch-up”, campaigners have said, as utilities firms have been advising on how to implement it. The Consumer Council for Water (CCW) is creating what the government referred to as “powerful consumer panels” so the public can question the executives of their local water company and get redress for problems they face from sewage and water companies in England and Wales. But documents reveal that the CCW has asked water companies to advise on how they wish to be held to account by consumers. Ministers promised last year to set up water boards for consumers that would allow them to air complaints such as about water shortages and sewage backing up into people’s homes. Large areas of south-east England have faced days on end without water due to faults at treatment centres. Meanwhile, there have been hosepipe bans across the country for months as water companies have failed to invest in reservoirs, and companies continue to dump sewage in waterways. Water bills also continue to rise. Water customers currently find it difficult to get companies to respond and properly compensate them when they are left without water. Signing up to the CCW is voluntary for water companies and it is often left to local MPs to solve complaints. The new “Water Voice” panels have been established to give consumers a say on how their bills are spent and the problems they face at the hands of water companies. This is part of sweeping changes announced after the general election, aimed at fixing the broken water industry and giving more power to the customers of the monopolies who run the industry. Documents released under freedom of information laws reveal the CCW has been consulting water companies on how to set up the new consumer boards that would hold them to account. It said it had “set up an industry advisory group to get ideas, feedback and advice from water companies”. Feargal Sharkey, the former Undertones frontman turned water campaigner, said: “This is a stitch-up. If water companies are involved in setting this up customers will not get any redress. The people who are important in all of this are the customers who have been extorted by these companies. The CCW is asking the extorters what should be happening to the victims, this is an outrage and a scandal.” He added: “It sounds like this scheme will be equally inept and dysfunctional.” The consumer group said complaints about water companies were rising. It received 80% more complaints in 2025-26 than the previous year, yet had no increase in resource. Andy Burnham, the prime minister, is under pressure to take Thames Water under public control as the company is running out of money. However, this plan has faced delays as government officials fear a legal challenge by the company’s creditors if it is forced into administration, and the Treasury is concerned about the costs. He is also due to introduce a new water bill to parliament, which will include the regulatory changes that are supposed to give new powers to crack down on water companies. As part of this, Ofwat will be replaced by a regulator with supervisory powers, similar to the oversight of banks after the financial crash. Experts would be appointed to work inside water companies and ensure they are obeying the law and improving the environment. A CCW spokesperson said: “It is a complete misrepresentation to suggest that CCW consulted water companies on how they would like to be held to account. CCW has engaged with water companies to work through the practicalities of how we could ensure their full engagement in the panels. For example, giving them enough lead time to ensure their chief executives were able to attend the accountability sessions and making sure action plans were produced in good time.” A Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs spokesperson said: “We know the water industry hasn’t been working in the public interest for far too long. That’s exactly why this government is looking at how to give the public more control and keep bills as low as possible. “We’re not satisfied with the current system, so we’re also introducing a new, independent and impartial water ombudsman to strengthen customer protection and make sure complaints are taken seriously and resolved quickly. It’s the least the public can expect, and one of our first steps to building a water system that works.”

title: UK’s biggest private hospital firm Spire agrees £1bn takeover by hedge fund
summary: Toscafund, founded by City figure known as ‘the Rottweiler’, signs deal amid fears over creeping privatisation of NHS
text: Britain’s biggest private hospital operator has agreed to a £1bn takeover by a hedge fund manager known as “the Rottweiler” for his aggressive business tactics. Spire Healthcare, which owns the Claremont hospital in Sheffield and St Anthony’s hospital in south London, has agreed to a 250p a share offer by an investor group led by Toscafund Asset Management, which values the business at £1.03bn. Toscafund was founded in 2000 by Martin Hughes, a City investor nicknamed “the Rottweiler” for his vocal activist approach. The takeover follows a lengthy period of negotiation between Spire and Toscafund, which was already the second biggest shareholder in the business. The company operates 38 private hospitals and more than 60 clinics across England, Wales and Scotland, which together provided care to 1.36 million patients in 2025. The deal comes despite concerns about the creeping privatisation of the health service. A study in April found that private companies providing services to the NHS, including healthcare and consultancy, have together made £1.6bn in profit over the past two years. Spire had previously been in talks with the private equity companies Bridgepoint and Triton, although they fell through when both pulled out in March. Spire had announced a strategic review last September, telling investors that it was in discussions with several parties to explore a potential sale of the business. Hughes said in a statement that his fund “has a track record of backing successful healthcare businesses to grow and improve”. “As a private company, Spire would have the freedom to plan for the long term and the agility to move faster: investing in its hospitals and people, putting the latest technology to work and setting new standards in patient care,” he said. Debbie White, Spire’s chair designate, said the company, squeezed by rising costs such as national insurance contributions and a higher minimum wage, had faced “much volatility” in its trajectory without a buyer. “As an experienced healthcare investor and the company’s second largest shareholder, Toscafund has deep knowledge and experience of the business and its operations, and Toscafund has assured the board of Spire that it is committed to providing the highest standards of care to patients,” she said. Shares in Spire, which is a member of London’s FTSE 250, rose by 3.2% in early trading on Monday to about 246p. The company’s biggest shareholder is Mediclinic, a private healthcare group founded in South Africa.

title: Weather tracker: Typhoon Saudel causes mass evacuations in south-east China
summary: Torrential rain causes widespread damage; while north-west South Africa hit by thunderstorms and central-southern US faces oppressive heat
text: Typhoon Saudel brought days of torrential rain to Zhejiang, Jiangxi, Fujian and Guangdong provinces in south-east China last week. The city of Putian, in Fujian province, recorded 416.5mm of rain in a 24-hour period between Thursday and Friday, with surrounding villages recording more than 500mm in the same period. In Fujian, authorities estimate that almost 600,000 people were evacuated from high-risk, flood-prone areas. A further 128,000 people in 53 counties were also affected across Jiangxi, with emergency evacuations affecting 9,000 people. Flooding, landslips and infrastructure damage were reported widely in the region. More than 2,500 teachers and students were trapped in a school compound in the Zhejiang city of Wenzhou on Wednesday after extreme rainfall caused flash floods in low-lying areas. At least 1,260 people reportedly had to be rescued in Putian after a river embankment collapsed on Thursday, flattening 100 homes. On Saturday, a landslip in a village of Suichuan county, in Jiangxi province, killed three people and nine others remaining missing. This is the seventh typhoon to affect China this year, and Saudel arrived shortly after Typhoon Narra dumped heavy rain on Guangdong, Hainan and Guangxi late last month. The South African Weather Service implemented several thunderstorm warnings late last week, covering a large swathe of the northern and western provinces. Disruptive rainfall, damaging winds, excessive lightning and hail were all reported, with rainfall totals expected to have reached at least 75-100mm for parts of the Northern Cape and North West provinces over the weekend. In Johannesburg, eight families were evacuated from an apartment building after strong winds tore off a significant part of its roof. Oppressive heat in the US affected states across the central-southern plains and the Mississippi valley this weekend, with maximum temperatures easily reaching the high 30s celsius (high 90s fahrenheit). However, with high humidities, the heat indices in this region have been closer to 40-43C (105–110F). The unrelenting temperatures will continue across the midwest and southern US this week, with maximum temperatures continuing to reach the high 30s.

title: ‘We can win here’: Zack Polanski presses the flesh in Holborn and St Pancras
summary: Polanski is confident of taking seat vacated by Keir Starmer, but says he will stay on as Green party leader even if he loses
text: Zack Polanski has said he will remain as Green party leader even if he loses the Holborn and St Pancras byelection in a high-stakes contest for the left of British politics. Speaking to the Guardian while door knocking in the north London constituency, Polanski calls the Greens underdogs in the race but says he is confident he could beat Labour, which won the seat with a majority of more than 11,000 at the 2024 general election. The seat has been vacated by Keir Starmer, who announced last Tuesday he was leaving parliament having resigned as prime minister in June. The Greens are confident about their chances, with party activists having already “knocked on thousands of doors”, according to Polanski, but the race comes as the party has fallen in the polls. There have been murmurs that it might have reached its peak in dying days of Starmer’s premiership, exemplified by the party’s seismic win in the Gorton and Denton byelection in February. Polanski is not yet formally the Green’s candidate for Holborn and St Pancras but local members are likely to select him. The race will test the electoral heft of his eco-populist party and Andy Burnham’s Labour. The byelection will be Labour’s first electoral challenge since Burnham became prime minister six weeks ago. Some critics saw Starmer’s decision to announce his intention to leave Westminster on Burnham’s first day in the Commons as prime minister as a way to twist the knife against his successor on his way out of parliament. Polanski joined volunteers in King’s Cross over the weekend to speak to local voters. It was his fourth visit to the constituency in a week. Should he win, Polanski says he will not move to the area but cycle from his flat in Hackney. “I can cycle to the constituency really quickly. In fact, the length of the constituency is just as fast for me to cycle,” he says. “I’d regularly be here, doing surgeries and representing people.” Some political commentators have said the seat is a difficult one for the Greens to win and that his run is a high-risk proposition. “I think it’s nonsense,” Polanski says. “I think people are trying to up the stakes because they want some drama.” Nigel Farage ran for election eight times before he won, Polanski says. If he does fall short of winning, he says he definitely stay on as Green leader. Polanski appeared popular while canvassing. Members of the public stopped him several times between knocking doors to express enthusiastic support for him. At one point, an eager procession of young men who say they have seen Polanski on TikTok gather around him before shaking his hand one by one, making off to the side in an orderly fashion once done. “I feel like the Queen!” the Green leader says. Starmer won the seat with a 11,572 majority in 2024. The anti-apartheid activist Andrew Feinstein, who is on the left, came second with 7,312 votes and the Greens were third with 4,030. Even if the vote for Feinstein, who will not run this time and has endorsed Polanski, and the Greens was tallied up, the party would be more than 7,500 votes shy of unseating Labour based on the general election figures. Despite this, Polanski still fancies his chances. “We know we can win here,” he says. It was slow going on the doorstep at first and not many people answered, but things soon picked up. The first woman who answers the door via her buzzer is a big fan. She has arthritis and is unable to come downstairs but she tells Polanski she loves him. “This is a great response. Thank you. I love you too,” he shouts into the buzzer. Shortly after, Usman Ayyub stops Polanski in the street and shakes his hand. “He is standing on his principles,” says the 27-year-old section manager, who plans to vote for him. He is unimpressed by Labour, who he says has “completely lost the plot”. “They don’t know what they’re doing,” Ayyub says. “Sometimes they’re falling towards the far right, sometimes they say they’re for the left or the centre. They are not standing for anything.” After another door knock, a man who claims he worked with Polanski at an adventure summer camp in 2002 stops him. “I saw you on TV and said: ‘That’s Zack!’. Very well done,” he says. Polanski says he has spoken to Labour voters who are considering a switch to the Greens. “It’s a very easy conversation to have with people. Even if you support Labour or you want to give Andy Burnham a chance, voting Green in this election still makes sense because it’ll make him be a better Labour prime minister,” he says. “We’ll make sure that we keep pushing him left rather than listening to Nigel Farage. That argument has been resonating with people.” Pointing at Scala, a famed nightclub in the constituency, Polanski says he worked the door there years ago. He also says his barber is in the constituency. “I come here every week,” he adds. Some sources in the party have expressed frustration about Polanski’s social media use, with one saying he is “terminally online”. When asked about that, Polanski says: “I think people really appreciate the fact that I’m accessible. With other politicians you get corporate politicians where every single part of their life is micromanaged. “Every sentence that comes out of their mouth is focus-grouped and I think people absolutely see it as more of a benefit that they know I’m genuine and authentic.” The issues of housing, the NHS and local crime come up on the doorstep. Burnham has spoken at length about the north-south divide, but Polanski believes there is stark poverty in London and the constituency he is vying for. “Regional inequality exists so it is important that we talk about supporting all communities,” he says. “It’s also true though that there’s a sense that London is wealthy, but actually somewhere like Holborn and St Pancras has deep poverty and deprivation and often it lives side by side with huge pockets of wealth.” As the clock passes 11am, Polanski buzzes on a door across from King’s Cross station as people rush pass with suitcases, hoping to catch their trains. Instead of saying “Hi, this is Zack from the Green party” as he normally would, he has begun using his full name, even though it feels “odd”. It appears to work. The man over the buzzer can’t believe it. “Is this Zack Polanski, seriously?” he says. “Yes, it’s Zack Polanski seriously,” he hears back.

title: Pixel 11 review: Google sets the bar for standard flagship phones
summary: Longer battery life, faster chip, actually useful AI tools and better cameras keep quality Android ahead of competition
text: Google’s Pixel 11 continues to set the standard for what you should expect from the base model of a flagship phone with class-leading cameras, long software support and almost all the bells and whistles of its most expensive phones. The regular Pixel 11 costs £879 (€999/$899/A$1,499) making it £80 or equivalent more expensive than last year’s model as the cost of RAMageddon continues to bite. It’s not cheap by any stretch of the imagination, but it comes with 256GB of storage and is £200 less than the Pixel 11 Pro, matching rival Samsung’s Galaxy S26. At a glance the Pixel 11 looks very similar to the previous two Google phone iterations: glass front and back with flat aluminium sides and large pill-shaped bar at the back, which is much slimmer this time. Stick it in a case and the protruding camera all but disappears. The 6.3in OLED screen is crisp and super bright with up to a 120Hz refresh rate to keep your scrolling smooth. The in-screen fingerprint scanner is fast and accurate, while the camera-based face recognition works well during the day and is secure enough for use with banking apps, unlike similar systems on most Android rivals. Specifications Screen: 6.3in 120Hz FHD+ OLED (422ppi) Processor: Google Tensor G6 RAM: 12GB Storage: 256 or 512GB Operating system: Android 17 Camera: 48MP+ 13MP UW + 10.8MP 5x tele; 10.5MP selfie Connectivity: 5G, eSIM, wifi 6E, UWB, NFC, Bluetooth 6 and GNSS Water resistance: IP68 (1.5m for 30 minutes) Dimensions: 152.8 x 72.0 x 8.6mm Weight: 197g Faster and more efficient Tensor G6 chip The Pixel has a new generation of Google’s chip, the Tensor G6, which is up to 20% faster in tests. It significantly lags top-end rivals from Qualcomm and Apple, so won’t win any raw performance awards, but feels snappy in daily tasks and can handle mid-level gaming just fine. The battery life is also improved over previous models, lasting about 54 hours of light use between charges. That includes actively using the screen for more than seven hours for browsing, messaging, apps and photos across a mix of 5G and wifi. Gaming and more demanding use hits the battery harder, but the Pixel should be able to see out even the heaviest of use days. Android 17 with more proactive AI The Pixel 11 runs the latest Android 17 out of the box with operating system and security updates provided until August 2033. The software is slick, nicely animated and well optimised, with plenty of colourful customisation if you want it. As with previous Pixels, it is a showcase for some of Google’s most advanced AI systems, many of which run on-device, making them fast. The most interesting of the tools remains Google’s proactive AI systems, which vary a bit depending on where you live. In the UK the expanded Magic Cue from last year pops up in messages and a few other apps with information such as your schedule, flight or order details, and suggestions for good local restaurants from Google maps or photos to share in a chat. In the US, Canada, Australia and a few other regions, the feature is called “Gemini Proactive Assistance” but has similar powers. If you use a supported app, such as Google Messages, the suggestions are low-key great. Unfortunately it doesn’t work in WhatsApp, Signal or other third-party apps I’ve tried, which limits its usefulness. In the UK and US, Gemini can go further, proactively taking action for you, such as booking a restaurant via OpenTable, which is the type of assistance that has long been promised by various AI agents. Another useful AI feature is built directly into Google’s keyboard called Rambler, which is voice typing on steroids. You can speak naturally to it and the system will remove your ums and ers and other deviations to produce a succinct, fully formed sentence or paragraph. It makes trying to dictate a rushed messaged while hustling for public transport a lot easier, although it doesn’t show your text until after you hit the stop button, unlike most other dictation tools. Camera The Pixel 11 has three cameras on the back and a solid 10.5-megapixel selfie camera in the screen. The improved main 48MP camera captures excellent photos across a range of lighting conditions, including low light where its larger sensor helps capture more of what’s available. The 13MP ultra-wide camera is one of the best on a phone of this class, helpful for fitting more in the shot or providing a different perspective. But it is the 10.8MP 5x telephoto camera that sets it apart from the competition, capable of meaningfully closing the distance to objects. In bright light it can digitally zoom to 30x magnification with surprisingly good results. Entirely new for the Pixel camera this year is the “Looks” feature, which allows you to customise how the phone captures and processes your photos for very different styles far beyond simple filters applied after the fact. There are three versions of the default look available – natural, vanilla and shadows – plus six more-distinctive looks, including “digi” that replicates the look of the old digital cameras that has recently become popular. Each look can be customised in colour, tone, grain and sharpness, so you can get arty or replicate a particular film style. If you are a Pixel user who has ever thought its photos look a little too cold, dramatic or overly processed, this is for you. The Pixel shoots great video at up to 4K at 60 frames a second. The new Magic Capture feature is a one-button shooting mode that records video and photos automatically that is best used during events such as birthday parties where you want to be more in the moment but still capture the scene. Google has also added a “Creator Suite” mode to the video capture, which shoots straight to a folder you can quickly storyboard and trim to create a video. It also has a teleprompter mode for shooting face to camera, a social media grid to get the alignment correct and speech enhancement that cuts out background noise. All these features are in addition to Google’s popular Auto Best Take, Add Me and Camera Coach from last year, which makes the new Pixel camera one of the most feature rich available. Sustainability The battery is rated to last in excess of 1,000 full charge cycles with at least 80% of its original capacity. The phone is repairable by Google, third-party shops or self-repair with manuals and parts available. The Pixel 11 is contains 33% recycled materials by weight. The company breaks down the phone’s environmental impact in its report and will recycle old devices for free. Price The Google Pixel 11 costs from £879 (€999/$899/A$1,499) in a choice of four colours. For comparison, the Pixel 10a costs £499, the Pixel 11 Pro costs £1,079, the Pixel 11 Pro XL costs £1,279, the Pixel 11 Pro Fold costs from £1,799, the Samsung Galaxy S26 costs £879 and the Apple iPhone 17 costs £799. Verdict The Pixel 11 isn’t the most advanced Google phone, nor is it the cheapest. But this middle-ground model offers more than enough to beat the competition and question whether you really need to spend more on a Pro phone. It offers, yet again, a very high-quality experience, great triple camera, long software support and very good battery life. It won’t win any raw performance awards, so those looking for a gaming phone should look elsewhere, but it feels fast and responsive in daily use. Google’s AI tools are second to none, particularly its Rambler dictation feature in the keyboard and the proactive Gemini features, which offer genuinely useful help even if they are not available in every third-party app. The new camera looks feature provides more control over photos than ever before on a Pixel, so you can tailor it to your preferences or get creative far beyond simple filters. It may not have changed all that much from last year’s equally excellent Pixel 10, and it isn’t quite the bargain the Pixel 10a is, but the Pixel 11 is the best phone you can get under £900. Pros: seven years of software updates, great camera with 5x telephoto, great screen, impressive local AI features, Qi2.2 wireless charging and magnetic accessory support, long battery life, good size, fast fingerprint and face recognition, 256GB starting storage. Cons: face unlock option not as secure as Face ID, raw performance short of rivals, no physical SIM card slot in the US, heavier than rivals, not a big upgrade on previous model, no wifi 7.

title: Monday briefing: ​How much longer can Nigel Farage survive amid ongoing scandals?
summary: In today’s newsletter: ​At Reform’s conference​ the faithful remained defiantly upbeat, even ​through fresh allegations and overnight suspensions,​ with Farage’s grip on the party suddenly looking far less secure
text: Hello. There’ll be a tetchy postmortem taking place at Reform HQ this morning. Its party conference appears to have been a disaster, as scandal once more dogs Nigel Farage and his coterie. Instead of policy announcements and set-piece speeches generating attention, all eyes remain on that footage: in which senior Reform figures – Farage included – appear to play fast and loose (again) with legal process and parliamentary procedure. Two big names have already been suspended, raising further credibility questions for the party and Farage himself – claiming plausible deniability is tricky when you’re caught on camera. But what was the mood among the party faithful in Birmingham? And, as the slew of allegations continue, do Reform voters – or its leadership – even care? For today’s First Edition, Guardian political editor Pippa Crerar, who was at party conference, walked me through the significance of this latest scandal. That’s after a roundup of this weekend’s other big stories. Weekend roundup Germany | The populist, far-right, anti-immigration Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) has surged to a resounding victory in a crucial state election in Germany, but fell just short of winning a majority in its quest to form the country’s first far-right state government since the second world war. Ukraine | US peace envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner headed to Kyiv following talks on Saturday in Moscow. The White House said they “plans for next steps” towards ending the war. US-Israel war on Iran | The US military said Saturday it struck three Iranian oil tankers after US navy warships came under missile attack, further escalating tensions in the region. UK news | Dozens of people dressed in black and wearing balaclavas blocked the road at the port of Dover, chanting “England til I die,” and forcing closures in both directions on Saturday. On Sunday, hundreds of far-right activists descended on Portsmouth, where a small boat with 140 asylum seekers on board was intercepted. Brexit | Travellers to the EU could face renewed border queues as flexibility measures for the bloc’s entry-exit system officially come to an end – although sources have indicated that biometric checks won’t be enforced by some member states. In depth: ‘It definitely felt like the leadership was shaken’ What a difference a year makes. Just 12 months ago, Reform was riding high in the polls – hovering at 30%, sometimes above – and pitching itself as a government waiting in the wings as Starmer’s beleaguered premiership faltered further. After last year’s jaunt (also in Birmingham), Reform basked in a post-conference glow. There was consensus among politicos that an “atmosphere of jubilation” had prevailed. Unions panicked about Labour support leaking to Reform. Big name defections were in the offing. The nation’s bout of Farage-fever appeared to be incurable. This year, Reform needed a repeat performance. After an injurious summer for Reform in which scandal has proved impossible to shake, Farage’s approval ratings had plummeted. Andy Burnham’s arrival in Downing Street had offered Labour a (modest) bounce and knocked Reform from the polling top spot. Farage’s party felt desperately in need of a reset. It wasn’t to be. Reform activists and bigwigs instead ventured home from Birmingham yesterday after another damaging few days, with focus firmly on Farage’s “damaged leadership” and a party “in crisis”. It didn’t start well. On the eve of conference kick-off, footage was released of an undercover sting. Members of Reform’s top team were filmed by reporters appearing to plot ways to avoid strict electoral laws on foreign donations. Dan Jukes, a senior aide to Farage, and James Orr, Reform’s head of policy, apparently plotted routes to circumvent electoral law to secure foreign party donations worth hundreds of thousands of pounds. Jukes appeared to suggest this could be done by channelling American cash through a British citizen. The footage also showed polling costing £30,000 was commissioned by Reform and paid for by a reporter posing as a wealthy American. The polling was beneficial to Reform, and widely publicised on newspaper front pages, but the party failed to disclose their role in its production, or the fact it was paid for by a US donor. “The reality is we could easily get away with it”, Orr told the undercover reporters. Meanwhile, the footage also shows Farage referring to the polling as “bang for your buck,” and thanking the fake donors after they explain their plot to covertly provide funding to the party – which would break the law on party donations. The story has dominated ever since, despite Reform’s best efforts. The police and Electoral Commission are both investigating. *** Vibe in the room Pippa was at the Reform conference, where she found its supporters to be unfazed and fiercely loyal. “The mood in the conference zone was actually very buoyant,” she tells me. “It’s important that we distinguish between how Reform activists and the party itself feel about allegations of financial wrongdoing, and the wider public.” Inside the conference hall and at fringe events, Pippa heard similar refrains repeatedly: that Reform is the “victim of a hoax” and “an establishment plot”; and that these stories are “skewed by the left-wing media.” If anything, Pippa found, among Reform’s base these allegations “are making them even more committed to Farage and the Reform cause”, as has been the case with Trump supporters. The mood is different at the top. A defiant “I have done nothing wrong” tone had certainly been struck by Farage et al in recent months, which was echoed again during his keynote conference speech on Saturday. But while Farage may have trotted out his beloved blame “the establishment” defence, beneath the rhetoric, Pippa has seen positions start to shift among Reform’s upper echelons. Yesterday, Farage admitted the row “looks bad”. “It is becoming quite clear to the party leadership that the wider public aren’t happy, and it’s causing Reform problems,” says Pippa. *** Who got the chop? At 2:30am on Friday morning, both Orr and Jukes were swiftly removed from their positions. These weren’t low-ranking, incidental officials: both had been critical to Farage’s political project. Jukes’s departure in particular is a massive blow to Farage. The pair are said to have something of a father-son relationship, having worked together since Jukes was a fledgling Ukip press officer. “For maybe 15 years, Jukes has been by Farage’s side as a media spokesperson and his closest aide,” says Pippa. “He has been intricately involved in every step of Reform’s development.” Orr, meanwhile, is a Cambridge academic close to far-right politicians like Viktor Orbán, and shares many hard-right views, among them being totally opposed to abortion rights. He became Reform’s head of policy in February after much criticism was raised last year at Reform’s lacklustre platform. “Orr provided Reform with a deeply ideological intellectual heft,” says Pippa. When she arrived in Birmingham on Thursday, Reform chiefs were “boasting about how thorough and comprehensive” their policy platform had become during Orr’s tenure. Pippa spoke to Farage on Thursday and he appeared “characteristically bullish” about the allegations. By the end of the weekend, “it definitely felt like the leadership was shaken.” It’s why Jukes and Orr had to go – losing them both will cause Farage pain, but “Farage was very quickly working to shore up his own position.” *** Had no choice Polling doesn’t show Reform is on the brink of annihilation. Far from it: despite a summer of scandal it remains a serious electoral force, roughly equal to the Tories. Still, it’s a steep decline from where the party sat just months ago often close to 10 points clear of any rival. And while Reform loyalists might show little concern as sleaze oozes from the party, Farage isn’t content with being leader of the third or even second party: he wants a route to power. Unlike US president, Donald Trump, who won by appealing to his Maga base, to win the keys to 10 Downing Street, Farage will need to secure support from beyond his devotees. “These ‘Reform-curious’ voters saw the party as a potential home while there was widespread dissatisfaction with Labour and the Tories,” says Pippa. Burnham’s arrival, Badenoch 2.0, and a stream of Reform scandals has – temporarily, at least – offered Labour and the Tories some reprieve. “Without these voters, it’s not just that Farage can’t win a majority. It’s a case of Reform not even being the biggest party and therefore able to negotiate a way into government.” Give away too much ground, however, and Farage risks alienating his most loyal supporters, with Rupert Lowe and Restore circling. A fine balancing act now faces Farage’s team. “He needs to give a nod to the membership that Reform hasn’t done anything wrong,” says Pippa, “while making sure that they appear to be taking these allegations seriously.” It’s a difficult bind for Farage, who also has his own alleged indiscretions to grapple with. “As things stand it’s not looking great for Farage,” says Pippa. “There is speculation as to whether he’ll even stick it out. He says he will, but we know his family are reluctant, and we know he’s under intense pressure.” It’s far from guaranteed, she says, that he’ll be at Reform’s helm come the next election. That’s not to say he should be counted out yet. Farage is a political cockroach, or as Pippa puts it slightly more flatteringly, “he has spent a career defying political gravity.” The week to come Monday | Jon Healey will deliver his first major speech as chancellor outlining the government’s plan for economic growth. Thursday | New York fashion week, the first of the world’s biggest fashion events, kicks off – with Paris, Milan and London fashion weeks to follow. Friday | The second reading of the assisted dying bill will take place in the House of Commons. What else we’ve been enjoying Teachers undoubtedly have it hard these days – so Nell Frizzells’ surprising, beautifully nostalgic piece, on becoming a teacher in her 40s, felt like a tonic. Poppy People travel from all over the world to stand on the “skim of destiny” and take part in the World Stone Skimming Championship, I enjoyed Patrick Greenfield’s entertaining roundup of the tournament. Katy Vans, newsletter team I enjoyed Polly Hudson’s column on how to cut endless natter short – and will be using Forbes’s very good three phrases in future to do just that. Poppy Sport Football | Mikel Arteta warned that Arsenal are capable of hitting even greater heights after the champions sent a statement to their title rivals by fighting back from a goal down to beat Chelsea. Formula One | Kimi Antonelli won the Italian Grand Prix for Mercedes at Monza, coming back from 19th on the grid to take his first win at his home race. Tennis | Reigning champion Carlos Alcaraz beat Tommy Paul 6-4, 6-3, 6-4 to move into the last eight at Flushing Meadows. The front pages “Families scramble to secure Send plans ahead of ministers’ reforms”, is the Guardian’s front page today. The i Paper leads with “Blunkett’s plea to Burnham: Find the money to fund end-of-life care”, the Telegraph writes “Scrap the triple-lock, businesses tell Healey”, the Times says “Just 1% of asylum pleas are genuine, says insider”, and the Mail has “Labour ‘chickens out’ on curbing migrant rights”. The FT says “Europe is losing battle to halt Russia’s ‘hybrid’ war, defence officials warn”, and the Express has “‘Weak’ Britain a prime target for Russian sabotage attacks”. Metro’s front page is “I was Reform attack victim” and the Mirror has “A&E heroes under attack”. Today in Focus Why Meta started losing in court For years, the investigative journalist Katy McQue has been reporting on the potential harms Meta’s platforms pose to children. Yet, as she explains to Annie Kelly, despite the mountain of evidence compiled by journalists, prosecutors, bereaved families and others, it has been nearly impossible to bring Meta and other social media companies to court. Finally, in 2026, something seems to have changed. Cartoon of the day | Tom Gauld The Upside A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad Andrea Malone’s 94‑year‑old mother drove to buy a vacuum cleaner she had seen on sale, only to find her local store had sold out. Staff told her the nearest available one was an hour away, a trip she couldn’t manage. As she stood there disappointed, a stranger in the queue offered to drive to the other store, collect the vacuum, deliver it to her home and even assemble it. The woman followed through the next day, and the two later met for coffee. Only afterwards did Andrea’s mother discover her helper was renowned Australian basketballer Michele Timms. This unexpected kindness shows that generosity and community spirit still thrive, even among celebrities. Sign up here for a weekly roundup of The Upside, sent to you every Sunday Bored at work? title: Starwatch: Waning crescent moon gets close to brilliant beacon of Jupiter
summary: The moon will pass less than a degree north of the giant planet and will be on its other side the next morning
text: Those already out and about at 5am this week will be rewarded with a beautiful waning crescent moon approaching Jupiter, while Mars watches on from a little further away. The chart shows the view looking east from London at 5am on Tuesday. The waning moon will be easily visible with about 10% of its visible surface illuminated. The brilliant beacon of Jupiter will be close by. The two are drawing together ahead of a conjunction later that day when the moon will pass less than a degree north of the giant planet. For comparison, the moon appears to be about half a degree wide in the sky. Unfortunately, the conjunction itself takes place at 7.11pm, after both objects have set from the UK. The following morning offers another opportunity, with the moon now on the other side of Jupiter. Mars adds to the scene. Look upwards and to the west and the red planet will be identifiable because of its colour. Mars lies in Gemini, while the moon and Jupiter are in neighbouring Cancer. From the southern hemisphere the pairing is also visible before dawn, with the moon and Jupiter generally appearing higher in the morning sky.

title: Country diary: A dreadful den of murder and thievery – or is it? | Merryn Glover
summary: Lynchat, Spey Valley: So many stories fill the iron age Raitts Cave, from wild legend to the more quotidian truth of its history
text: The word “cave” is full of possibility. It speaks of darkness, secrets, treasures and escapees, all of which can be found in the stories of Raitts Cave, which lies in a field near the hamlet of Lynchat, Inverness-shire. Its Gaelic name is An Uaimh Mhor, “the great cave”, and one legend claims it was built by giants, the females hollowing out the earth and carrying the soil in their aprons to dump in the River Spey, while the males cut its massive stone slabs from the hills above. Because, in fact, it is not a natural cave, but a subterranean passage, shaped like a horseshoe and lined with stone. Another tale attributes it to the 11 strapping sons of a local freebooter from the powerful 13th-century Clan Cumming (or MacNiven), who used it to stash their loot and hide from the law (or the laird, who tricked them by disguising himself as a beggar). Justice, or vengeance, eventually caught up with them, and the brothers were hauled out and executed at the cave’s entrance. Or, it could have been the hiding place of escaping Jacobites after Culloden, who were burned alive inside. Or indeed a shelter for persecuted worshippers. The identities of the builders, the hiders and the avengers and their various fates change with each version of the story, but the evidence is scant. Officially, archaeologists first excavated the site in 1835, and called it an erd house – “earth shelter” – and later a souterrain, an underground space constructed by humans. At some point, the central roof was removed, giving access to steps and a narrow tunnel on one side, and a large covered chamber at the other. Further digs have dated it to the late iron age (100-400 AD) and the conclusion is that it was a storeroom, probably for food, serving a roundhouse above. Bother. What about all the magic and calamity? I hearten myself that the academic’s mundane deductions do not rule out other thrilling escapades, and I explore the cave in the vivid company of giantesses, thieves, fugitives and murderers – who are, of course, much more fun in folklore than reality. • Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024, is available now at guardianbookshop.com

title: UN expert Francesca Albanese calls for ‘true paradigm shift’ as Miliband resets policy on Israel
summary: Exclusive: UN special rapporteur on occupied territories says ban on goods from settlements ‘important’ but must go further if it is to amount to more than a ‘press release’
text: The UK’s planned ban on trade with unlawful Israeli settlements is a welcome, if overdue, first step and must be judged according to its practical impact, a UN expert has told the Guardian. The UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, has vowed to act more decisively against Israeli settlements, as well as continued restrictions of aid into Gaza, prompting the US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, to claim on Saturday that Downing Street was motivated by “Jew hatred”. Miliband said what he had been told about restriction on aid into Gaza had reinforced the need for more decisive action. But Huckabee, writing on X in support of the Israeli foreign ministry’s own criticisms, said: “The Brits have lost it. The Jew hate of their government knows no boundaries and knows no facts.” Huckabee did not mention in his statement that Miliband is himself Jewish. The Israeli foreign ministry had said: “Had the foreign secretary been interested in facts rather than stories, he would have known that there are no restrictions whatsoever on bringing medicines into the Gaza Strip, and that no medicine is being blocked.” Palestinian groups in the UK are holding judgment until they see the fine detail of Miliband’s policy, due to be announced on Tuesday, but are expecting the most significant shift since a previous foreign secretary, David Lammy, withdrew most arms export licences in September 2024. Speaking to the Guardian, Francesca Albanese, the UN’s special rapporteur on the occupied territories, said a “ban on settlement goods was a change in UK government stance and absolutely important”. She added she would “not join those dismissing it as theatre before the details had been announced”. She said a settlement trade ban would have to be part of “a true paradigm shift to Israel-Palestine that ultimately seeks to implement the international court of justice advisory opinion in 2024”, which stated that Israel’s presence in the occupied territories was “unlawful in its entirety”. The opinion, she added, said that “all states carry an obligation – not a preference of an obligation – not to recognise the situation as legal, and not render aid and assistance in maintaining it”. Albanese also said the trade ban could not be narrowly confined to goods – such as agricultural products and cosmetics – since “they are a fraction of what sustains the occupation, and a fraction that Israel can absorb without difficulty”. The package should also aim to include trade in services, she said, progressively suspending British intelligence cooperation, all arms licensing and the unexamined flights out of RAF Akrotiri in Cyprus. Albanese warned that if the steps were not taken or were “completely off the table”, the changes would “over time come to be seen as not amounting to a reckoning, but a press release”. She said that a state banning “dates from Ma’ale Adumim [a city in the West Bank]” while “continuing to licence the equipment used to enforce the checkpoints around it” had not “changed its relationship with the occupation … It has rearranged its communication strategy.” Albanese added that, “because the 2024 ICJ advisory opinion declares the entire Israeli presence in the occupied territories as unlawful, third states’ obligations ‘not to render aid or assistance’ extends to everything that sustains that unlawful presence as a whole.” Albanese said the UK needed to end any ambiguity around the tender for the E1 settlement that will sever East Jerusalem from the rest of the West Bank and cut the territory in two, adding: “Since bids close a week before Israel’s elections on 27 October, there is nothing that London can realistically do in September that can change that calendar.” But she warned the government could not let the tenders simply pass, pointing out that Israel’s finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, had already said E1 was designed to “bury the idea of a Palestinian state”. “There is a difference between the tenders closing and the settlement getting built and financed,” she added. “Construction on this scale needs finance, insurance and construction firms, and since E1 amounts to annexation and not just settlement expansion, sanctions or similar have to be threatened against those firms that seek to cooperate with the building of E1.” Albanese also called on the UK government to join South Africa before the ICJ, and also support Nicaragua on Monday when the ICJ hears preliminary oral objections from Germany over claims filed by the Central American country that Berlin’s continued arms sales to Israel makes it complicit in genocide. She said: “Britain is not a party to that case. It can still choose which side of the argument it stands on: whether it treats participation in international accountability mechanisms as a threat to an alliance, or recognises that an alliance built on anything other than principle and the rule of law is not an alliance at all. It is an arrangement of convenience, honoured only until convenience changes.” Finally she urged the UK to issue guidance to UK-based firms not to overcomply with sanctions imposed by the US on the international criminal court prosecutor, the deputy prosecutors, eight judges and an increasing number of others, including herself and Palestinian human rights groups that have cooperated with the court. “This has frozen bank accounts, everywhere, for people doing nothing other than their judicial function or providing evidence lawfully requested by an international court,” she said.

title: Ukraine seeks to seize water company owned by billionaire family of British theatre mogul
summary: Dispute centres on stake held by Patarkatsishvili family in bottled water firm it jointly owns with Russian oligarch
text: A British theatre impresario and her billionaire family are embroiled in a bitter dispute with Ukrainian authorities seeking to seize a water company they jointly own with a Russian oligarch. The row centres on a 34% stake held in the producer of Ukraine’s biggest bottled water brands by the Patarkatsishvili family, including Liana Patarkatsishvili, who recently worked on an immersive show with Toby Jones and Meera Syal. The corporate holdings of IDS Ukraine were frozen by the Ukrainian authorities in 2022 owing to the 49% stake that is also held in the company by Russian investors, including Mikhail Fridman, the founder of the Russian Alfa Group conglomerate. He is under western sanctions for his support for Vladimir Putin’s regime. Ukraine’s asset recovery and management agency (Arma) has been tasked with instructing independent management to take over the running of the company whose other minority shareholders include the Georgian government. The Ukrainian agency’s head, Yaroslava Maksymenko, said they had repeatedly run into legal and bureaucratic obstacles owing, in part, to the shareholders’ resistance to give up control of their assets. The agency further claims to have been the subject of a cyber-attack during one attempt to find an independent manager for the company although there is no evidence as to who was responsible and the Patarkatsishvili family is not suspected. However, Maksymenko claimed New World Value Fund Limited, the vehicle for the Patarkatsishvili’s investment in IDS Ukraine, had pursued an unfounded claim of unlawful conduct by Arma’s officials which she said was “misinformation”. An investigation by the National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine into the claims of unlawful conduct continues. Maksymenko said her agency had concerns over potential money laundering and value extraction from IDS Ukraine if it remained under the current management although there have not been any official findings of such criminality. There are separate proceedings in the Ukrainian anti-corruption high court in which the shareholders are fighting attempts to nationalise part or all of the ownership of IDS Ukraine, which is seen by some in government as a key strategic asset at a time of war. A spokesperson for the Patarkatsishvili family said they had been committed supporters of Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of the country in February 2022, adding that the family were being unfairly targeted and would seek justice in the international courts if necessary. They said: “The Patarkatsishvili family strongly believes that an asset should not be taken away from non-sanctioned shareholders against whom there are no allegations or concerns, and is defending this position through all relevant proceedings before the Ukrainian courts and authorities. “If the Patarkatsishvili family is unable to obtain justice through the Ukrainian courts, and the asset is ultimately taken away through the Arma process, it will, of course, have no choice but to seek justice before the international courts, as it has consistently done in the past.” The family’s shareholding in IDS Ukraine was inherited in 2008 by Liana, her sister, Iya, and mother, Inna, after the death of Badri Patarkatsishvili, a businessman who made his fortune during the breakup of the Soviet Union. Patarkatsishvili fled to the UK in 2007 but died in 2008 of a heart attack at the age of 52 with an estimated fortune of £6bn. Iya Patarkatsishvili and her husband made headlines last year for being granted a refund after buying a £32m London mansion that was said to be infested with moths. Last summer, Liana Patarkatsishvili staged a large-scale immersive theatre production called Storehouse about “misinformation” through her production company Sage & Jester, starring the actors Toby Jones and Meera Syal. A spokesperson for IDS Ukraine said: “Throughout its operations, the IDS Ukraine Group of companies has operated and continues to operate in accordance with the requirements of Ukrainian law, including tax and financial legislation. “No competent state authority of Ukraine, including the state tax service of Ukraine, has established any facts of money laundering, unlawful withdrawal of funds or any other financial activity of this nature on the part of IDS Ukraine. “We are not aware of any investigations or other current inquires of Ukrainian authorities into the operations of IDS Ukraine with respect to any such allegations. “IDS Ukraine has also not ceased operations for a single day since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion. The group continued production and supplied Ukrainian consumers with drinking water even amid continuous missile and drone attacks.” The spokesperson added: “We are aware of statements by the asset recovery and management agency implying but not saying it directly that [a cyber-attack] is somehow connected with the IDS Ukraine Group of companies. However, this information is simply false and in reality completely irrelevant.”

title: Designers should not fear being replaced by AI, industry leaders say
summary: Firms are more likely to use technology as ‘the intern in the office’ than as a replacement for skilled staff
text: Professional designers should not feel “threatened” by the rapid growth of generative AI, according to business leaders, despite fears over job losses in the sector. With design and film production companies and manufacturers all adopting AI at an accelerating pace, industry bodies said the technology would be used to enhance the work of designers rather than replace them. Mat Hunter, the chief executive of the Design Council – a charity which champions the industry – said that while AI was increasingly being used by designers, “they are using it to add value”. He said: “We are aware that technology always displaces people with new ways of working. However, we believe in the imagination and inventiveness of designers to find opportunities. We believe the UK needs more professional designers, so overall employment should continue to grow.” Deborah Dawton, chief executive of the Design Business Association, said: “What protects great designers from AI is skill, experience, empathy and deep understanding of the sectors they operate in. So, no, [workers] shouldn’t feel threatened if they operate at this level.” Earlier this year research, conducted by The King’s Institute for Artificial Intelligence and the Policy Institute, showed 57% of the public think AI will lead to widespread unemployment. Last week, freelancers including designers told the Guardian they were picking up “soulless” work correcting AI errors. The Design Council said on Monday that its analysis showed the sector – which covers everything from the design of household products and fashion to building and transport design – had grown by 40% between 2019 and the end of 2023, beating the economy’s 23% average rate of expansion and leapfrogging the size of the retail industry. Research funded by the council for its triennial overview – Design Economy 2026 – showed that sectors like construction, services and manufacturing support 2.27m design jobs, and that there has been a 15% increase in employment between 2020 and 2025. While the figures estimating the size of the industry pre-date the arrival of dominant AI tools including ChatGPT and Claude, the employment figures to the end of last year indicate that their use has done little so far to affect the demand for workers with design skills. Hunter said design was often considered to be an add-on or nice-to-have, but was essential to industries from advanced manufacturing to digital services. “People don’t realise design is everywhere and is about trying to make things usable,” he said. He added that the government’s consolidation of hundreds of public sector websites into one consistent design was an example of improvements in a service that can be supported by designers. Dawton said AI was being used as a substitute for the work done by human designers, but “rip-offs have been happening for a very long time – AI hasn’t enabled that”. The industry went through a similar transition when companies began using computer-aided design software, displacing draughtspeople, but Dawton said modern workers could find jobs elsewhere in the industry as it expands. She added: “The key thing to remember is that these copycats look the same but they aren’t the same. The materials, finishes, methods of manufacture, assembly, colour, etc, mean that they are very different products.” Over the longer term, she said: “We have to adapt to any technological change that takes place around us. The difference with the design industry is that large chunks of it drive that change. “For most in business, efficiency/optimisation is the main conversation around AI. Designers have a second conversation with AI, which is about the potential it opens up in the hands of a creator.” Andrew Duff, head of the Society of Garden and Landscape Designers, said many people working in his industry were nervous about AI. He said design companies were more likely to use AI as “the intern in the office” than as a replacement for skilled staff. The Design Council report said some regions had grown strongly over the last eight years, though from a low base. There was an 88% increase in income from design across all industries in Wales and a 67% rise in the north-east of England. London remained the hub for design industries, accounting for £43.3bn of gross value added (GVA) – a calculation of income from economic activity – compared with just £3.1bn in the north-east from a UK total of £136.7bn. Its contribution was larger than the UK’s retail sector, worth £114bn, and nearly twice the size of the accommodation and food service industry, worth £70bn. Hunter said a lack of skilled workers was a bigger problem than AI after entries for design and technology GCSEs declined by 68% over the decade to 2024. Dawton said: “We need specialist teachers and equipment in schools if we’re going to inspire the next generation of world shapers at an early age.”
