title: Far-right AfD wins key German state election but falls just short of majority
summary: Alternative für Deutschland surges to victory in Saxony-Anhalt as Friedrich Merz’s CDU slumps to disastrous result
text: The populist, far-right, anti-immigration Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) has surged to a resounding victory in a crucial state election in Germany, but fell just short of winning a majority in its quest to form the country’s first far-right state government since the second world war. The party of Germany’s unpopular chancellor Friedrich Merz, the Christian Democrats (CDU), slumped to a disastrous result in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt. AfD’s candidate for governor, Ulrich Siegmund, said “we have written history” and the party had a clear mandate to govern. He told public broadcaster ARD that voters had sent a signal that “things cannot carry on like this”. “A very good campaigner for us in this election campaign was Friedrich Merz,” Siegmund said. AfD was seeking an absolute majority in the state legislature to govern alone and overcome the so-called firewall of mainstream parties’ refusal to work with the party. AfD in Saxony-Anhalt has been classed as “rightwing extremist” by Germany’s domestic intelligence agency. Final results showed AfD falling three seats short, with 39 lawmakers in an 83-member parliament. Siegmund, 35, said it would not engage in “games” such as a minority government. But it was not evident how its divided opponents could assemble any stable government without it. AfD won 43.8% of the vote, more than double its showing five years ago in the region of 2.1 million people west of Berlin. That was far ahead of Merz’s CDU , which polled 17.2% – losing about half its support – and won 15 seats. The centre-left Social Democrats polled 9.3%, the Greens 8.9% and the Left party 8.6%, winning eight seats apiece. The BSW party, which has said it would not elect either Siegmund or incumbent Sven Schulze as governor but criticises the “firewall” against AfD, took 5.3% and five seats. Participation in the election was at a record high of 76.5%. Addressing jubilant supporters after ⁠exit polls had been published, Siegmund said his party was ready to ⁠reach out to ‌all powers ‌that ‌strove for political change. “We extend a hand to all ‌democratic forces that wish to pursue better policies,” he said, adding that themes such as migration and domestic security were not up for debate. The CDU described its result as “bitter” but said it would not back down from its refusal to rule together with AfD, which the far-right party has also ruled out. Franziska Hoppermann, general secretary of the CDU, called it a “defeat overall” for the Christian Democrats. “And it is also a defeat for all those who have borne responsibility in the democracy in Saxony-Anhalt over the past 35 years,” she added, in reference to the difficult post-communist era. She ruled out any discussion over Merz’s future, which analysts have suggested will increasingly become a topic of debate after his party’s defeat. In one recent poll, only 9% of voters in Saxony-Anhalt said they were satisfied with Merz’s politics. Alice Weidel, AfD’s co-leader, said the result gave her party a “clear government mandate” and that it would “talk to all the parties” to work out a strategy as to how AfD could rule. About 1.7 million people were eligible to vote in the east-central state. Final polls had shown AfD to have about 40-41% of support, and the party appears to have almost doubled its 2021 result of 23.7%. The number of undecided voters in advance of the vote was much lower than at previous elections, polling showed. The small state has been governed since 2002 by Merz’s conservative CDU, together with two smaller parties. The Saxony-Anhalt election had been seen as the biggest test yet for Merz, who is very unpopular, along with his government, a coalition with the SPD. Merz has thus far failed in his promises to reset Germany’s struggling economy or stop the rise of the AfD, which has been making regular and steady gains since it entered parliament in 2017 and is now the Bundestag’s leading opposition party. Irregular immigration has reduced since Merz has been in office, but not to an extent that has appeased the average voter. In national polls, the CDU has also been overtaken by the AfD, which has its eyes on victory at the next federal elections in 2029 or 2033. If the AfD manages to form a government in Saxony-Anhalt, Siegmund has promised to immediately start a remigration and deportation offensive, ban rainbow flags in schools and halt the building of new windfarms. He wants to change the slogan of the state from “Think Modern” to “Think German”, and to reintroduce the singing of the German national anthem in schools. Siegmund also sought in the campaign to capitalise on a mood of “ostalgie”, or nostalgia for communist East Germany, and to tap into discontent among east Germans. He has made repeated references to a rise in foreigner-related crime, even as the crime rate has fallen dramatically. AfD is pro-Kremlin, urging a stop to support for Ukraine and pushing for Ukrainians to no longer receive refugee status. Siegmund turned up to vote on Sunday morning with his wife, riding an East German-era moped in the party colours, which was also a prominent prop during the election campaign in rallies across the state. In a statement in front of the polling station, he voiced his optimism that the party would achieve “45%, and some”, and saying he wanted to “build bridges”. Tensions before the election were high, with a considerable police presence and a number of demonstrations taking place across the state. Thousands of opponents of the AfD gathered in the state capital, Magdeburg, on Saturday, for a “festival of democracy”. On Saturday evening, a message beamed on to the facade of Magdeburg Cathedral read: “We do not abandon what we love. True love of the homeland is not the AfD.” The bishop of Magdeburg, Gerhard Feige, in an address to a gathering of churchgoers, warned against forces “that want to sow discord, stoke mistrust and fear”. He drew parallels with history, warning that a democracy has the potential to abolish itself. “Not everyone who votes or is elected democratically is a democrat,” he said. The German Economic Institute has warned of the far-reaching consequences for the German economy, in Saxony-Anhalt and beyond. It said the AfD’s immigration policy would be “calamitous” for the state, which has an ageing, dwindling population and is heavily dependent on foreign workers. Critics have also warned that an AfD-run state, due to the Kremlin-friendly stance of the party, could leak sensitive information to Russia. The AfD has dismissed such claims. It has said it would seek to reform the domestic intelligence service, calling it biased.

title: Ukraine war briefing: US envoys leave Kyiv without breakthrough on ending war
summary: Zelenskyy says after talks with Witkoff and Kushner that Kyiv seeking ‘serious volumes’ of US support for winter defences. What we know on day 1,657
text: US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have held “encouraging” talks with Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Kyiv in their first official visit to Ukraine but made no breakthrough towards ending the war with Russia. The envoys’ trip followed talks with Vladimir Putin in Moscow on Saturday which a Kremlin aide said were “highly useful” while also giving no indication of a breakthrough. Zelenskyy said at a news conference that his talks with the envoys on Sunday covered air defence needs – including Patriot systems – and a “winter package” of support covering both air defence and energy infrastructure before the colder months. He said Kyiv was seeking “serious volumes” of American support on that front, with backing from European partners as well. It appeared the war would continue into winter, he also said. Zelenskyy said Russia had intensified strikes on Ukrainian cities before Russia’s State Duma election later this month, calling the attacks deliberate “terror” against civilians. Ukraine was working with 67 domestic companies developing systems to shoot down Russia’s jet-powered drones at scale. He said the sides agreed to hold a follow-up meeting involving Ukraine, the US and Europe, with a location still to be set. The US envoys brought new and “more effective” proposals to Ukraine on ending the war with Russia, according to one senior Ukrainian presidential official. “It’s not the same as it was before. This one now is more effective,” the unnamed offical told Agence France-Presse after the talks with Zelenskyy. “They’re still talking. This is actually the most important part. There are three of them now.” Ukraine’s rail operator announced the envoys’ departure from Kyiv early on Monday. Witkoff said earlier that both sides would need to compromise, adding: “We think we have the ingredients to get to that place … and we look forward to continuing this as long as it takes.” Kushner said: “Hopefully this trip has come out with some new ways to advance forward. I think we’ve learned a lot from the trip.” In Moscow the US envoys had “discussed substantive plans which will be announced in the coming weeks”, a White House official said. The Kremlin said the Americans had “put forward a number of ideas on possible routes to a settlement”, without elaborating. Witkoff said he was hopeful a new round of US-mediated Ukraine-Russia talks would be announced “in short order”. Putin has repeatedly said Moscow intends to seize the rest of eastern Ukraine while Zelenskyy insists Russia should not be rewarded for its aggression. A girl ⁠was killed and three ⁠other people ⁠were wounded in a Ukraine ⁠drone attack on the Russia-held Black ⁠Sea port city ‌of Sevastopol ‌late on ‌Sunday, the city’s Moscow-appointed governor, Mikhail Razvozhayev, said on Telegram. Russian forces ⁠struck a ‌Ukrainian ‌cargo vessel in ‌the Black Sea which was carrying military equipment supplied to ⁠the Ukrainian army by western countries, Russian news ‌agencies reported the defence ministry as saying on Sunday. Kyiv’s forces struck the Ryazan oil refinery – about 480km (300 miles) inside Russia – causing a fire, Ukraine said on Sunday. Russia’s foreign minister said Germany’s accusation that Moscow was involved in a ⁠drone incident near a Ukrainian cargo plane at Germany’s Leipzig airport were, “by and large, the ⁠start of a real war”, state news agency Tass ‌reported. “He is, in effect, declaring war on us,” Sergei Lavrov said of the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz. Berlin has ordered a series of measures in response to the attack attempt.

title: Hundreds of far-right protesters descend on Portsmouth after small boat arrival
summary: Influencer livestreams event calling for men to travel to port to block coaches carrying asylum seekers from leaving
text: Hundreds of far-right activists have descended on Portsmouth, where a small boat with 140 asylum seekers on board was intercepted heading towards the Portsmouth coast. The vessel’s arrival sparked a major response with a helicopter, an aeroplane and lifeboats sent to the scene. It is thought to be the first time such a large boat containing asylum seekers has been brought to Portsmouth and the first time a large group of anti-migrant protesters have tried to block newly arrived asylum seekers from being processed. The protesters blocked roads for hours and had vowed to stay all night to prevent the new arrivals from being taken to a processing centre. The demonstration ended about 3am, when police obtained a dispersal order and threatened arrests. It is the second major anti-migrant protest of the weekend. Many of those at Portsmouth were dressed in all black and wore face masks, similar to those who attended a rally that blocked roads in Dover on Saturday. One witness who was not involved in the protest said on Sunday night: “The atmosphere here is still very tense. The coaches carrying asylum seekers have still not left. About 25-30% of the far-right protesters are wearing balaclavas and many are wearing black. Two police cars had their windscreens smashed by protesters. At one point they broke through the police cordon.” The boat’s occupants were brought to shore in the maritime city and the Home Office’s plan was to take them to Manston, outside Ramsgate in Kent, where small boat arrivals are processed. However, videos circulating on social media showed large groups of protesters close to the coaches that were to be used, with some blocking vehicles carrying asylum seekers from leaving. Late on Sunday, Hampshire police had urged people to avoid the area, and said a dispersal order was in place. The government has condemned what it described as the “thuggish behaviour” of the protesters. “We condemn the intimidating and thuggish behaviour we are seeing tonight,” a government spokesperson said. “The right to peaceful protest is fundamental to our democracy, but it must never cross a line into disorder.” In a livestream from the scene, Daniel Thomas, also known as Danny Tommo – a former bodyguard of the far-right activist Tommy Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon – encouraged viewers to travel to Portsmouth to join the protest. Thomas has recently established Patriot Platform which blocked part of port of Dover on Saturday. He previously launched Operation Overlord which planned to send far-right activists to France to “stop the boats”. He and his supporters filmed themselves slashing abandoned dinghies on a French beach. The french authorities subsequently banned him from France. Small boat crossings so far this year have reduced by more than 40% compared with the same period last year. While the Home Office has disrupted the smugglers’ business model, their methods appear to have evolved by launching boats such as the one that arrived on Sunday evening from different parts of the coast, much further from the UK, making the crossings more dangerous. Most small boat arrivals are rescued by Border Force and RNLI boats on the English side of the Channel and brought ashore in Dover. The Maritime and Coastguard Agency said it was alerted on Sunday to a small boat heading towards the Hampshire coast. The coastguard sent lifeboats, a helicopter, an aeroplane and rescue teams to the area, a spokesperson said. “Border Force, Border Security Command, Hampshire police and south central ambulance service were also sent,” they said. Saturday’s Port of Dover rally was criticised by politicians from all parties, with questions expected to be raised on Monday about whether Kent police were prepared for it. There could be similar criticism of Hampshire police. The Dover demonstrations brought traffic on routes to the UK’s busiest international ferry and passenger port to a halt, delaying some ferry services and blocking major roads, but there were no arrests. The business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, criticised the demonstrations, which saw protesters march through Dover chanting “Whose streets? Our streets” and “Stop the boats”. Reynolds told Sky News he condemned the behaviour and the disruption it caused, adding: “Peaceful protest – essential part of British life, but that’s not dressing up in costumes like this and disrupting people’s lives.” On Sunday night, a Home Office spokesperson said: “This government is bearing down on dangerous small boat crossings and restoring control at our border. Joint efforts have seen over 48,000 crossing attempts prevented and 1,100 boats and engines seized since the election. “We are making progress, with the number of small boat crossings down this year and the lowest number recorded for the month of July since 2020. “But we must go further, which is why we have signed a payment-by-results deal with the French to put 40% more boots on the ground on French beaches.”

title: Chancellor to argue UK economy can ‘turn corner’ despite bond market turmoil
summary: John Healey speech on Monday will stress links between fiscal discipline and growth amid concerns his cautious approach jars with Burnham’s radical plans
text: John Healey will argue the government’s plans to boost growth across the whole country will enable the British economy to “turn a corner” despite anxiety over volatile bond markets derailing Labour’s crucial first budget. The chancellor is expected to argue that fiscal discipline is “indivisible” from good growth, especially at a time of difficult global headwinds, amid concerns that his cautious approach jars with Andy Burnham’s more radical policy plans. In a speech in the West Midlands on Monday, Healey will set out how the government plans to boost regional economies by easing Treasury bureaucracy and giving more powers to local leaders to drive business investment, innovation and skills. But public finances are under pressure from soaring global bond yields, which hit an 18-year high last week, driving up government borrowing costs, resulting in Healey putting Britain on notice for a tough 28 October budget. Economists have predicted that the chancellor – who has said he wants a “buffer against uncertainty” – will have to put up taxes or cut spending to protect the £24bn fiscal headroom his predecessor Rachel Reeves had last year. “Fiscal credibility is indivisible from good growth,” the chancellor is expected to say. A Treasury source said this was “true at any time, but especially at a time of global uncertainty” amid warnings that Donald Trump’s war in the Middle East would push up inflation and hit public finances. Healey will say that, despite the bleak global backdrop, pursuing growth across every region will help unlock “huge latent potential” and show Britain is “turning a corner”, with people, businesses and communities ready to seize the opportunities of new technologies. The prime minister argued at the weekend that it would be impossible to build a dynamic economy on crumbling infrastructure, with businesses needing affordable energy and reliable transport, and so more investment would be needed. But in a move that will undermine Labour’s efforts to reindustrialise, the UK’s biggest carmaker, Jaguar Land Rover, which is based in the West Midlands, was expected to announce thousands of job cuts. During a speech at a manufacturing site on Monday, Healey is expected to reiterate that Britain’s growth must extend beyond its biggest cities. “The prime minister laid out a clear diagnosis of what has gone wrong in the past,” he is expected to say. “The solution is a fundamental shift that starts with putting power in the right places. The next chapter of Britain’s growth story will be written in more places.” National government must work with the new No 10 North on a “dual mission” to remove obstacles for local leaders and businesses, he is expected to say. “Instead of getting in the way with complexity and red tape, we need a strong, strategic centre wired to enable local leaders and their ambitions. “I want to see wealth creation in this country. I want to see businesses make a profit. And to create the conditions for that we need an active, accountable state at all levels to remove blockages and create the conditions for more investment.” Healey will announce that the British Business Bank will allocate £150m to scale up businesses across the north of England. The pot will offer investments from £5m to £15m to help university spinouts and the expansion of other innovative companies. He will underline the government’s commitment to “place-based” growth, building on Reeves’s attempts to move the focus of the Treasury away from the south-east. “Ask an economist what growth is and you’ll get a number,” he will say. “But ask the country and you’ll get a different answer. “A young person getting a new job in a company that’s on the up. A sole trader winning a new contract that pays for a holiday with their kids. A business winning a new export order, giving the community around it a new lease of life.” However, businesses are braced for what they fear will be higher taxes to fill a fiscal hole caused by rising borrowing costs and Burnham’s new spending plans. In an interview with the Financial Times on Saturday, Healey refused to rule out increasing levies on bank profits. Healey has also been under pressure over the timeline to hit defence spending targets, after quitting Keir Starmer’s cabinet over the issue. On Sunday, the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, indicated the government would spend 3% of gross domestic product on defence by 2030. “We’ve made some clear movements early on to show that direction of travel … [Healey] has not moved away from the target you’ve said. He said the fundamental target is the 2035 3.5% of GDP on defence spending that is our Nato commitment. The trajectory to that covers the 3% but that is the principal target,” said Reynolds. Robert Jenrick, Reform UK’s economic spokesperson, said: “Even Rachel Reeves had more vision than this guff. Days after a market meltdown, when grip and direction are required, John Healey has revealed himself to be an empty vessel with no idea about how to rescue our economy.” Andrew Griffith, the new shadow chancellor, described Healey’s speech as a “policy-light word salad”, saying it would do little to comfort families and businesses who were worried about more tax rises or the rates of government borrowing. On the BBC on Sunday, Griffith, who was a Treasury minister at the time of Liz Truss’s disastrous mini-budget, said there had been “lots of good things” in that fiscal statement – including tax cuts and cutting regulation – attracting criticism from Labour.

title: ‘Gigantic spaceship’: University of Bristol’s flagship £500m campus opens
summary: Temple Quarter Enterprise Campus near to station will make it easier for students and staff to commute
text: Not so long ago, the first impression for visitors arriving by train to Bristol’s main railway station was a derelict building described by David Cameron as looking like the entrance to a war zone. On Monday, a shiny new University of Bristol campus on the site of that crumbling Royal Mail sorting office next door to Temple Meads is opening its doors to students, teachers and members of the public. The proximity of the Temple Quarter Enterprise Campus (TQEC) to the station should make it easier for students and staff who cannot afford Bristol’s expensive property and rental market to commute, and for business and research partners from all across the country to attend meetings. The campus is also designed to be “porous”, with many areas completely open to the public, turning it into a front door to the university for Bristolians in a way that its grand buildings high on the hill in the leafy Clifton area never have been. The £500m campus is a major part of one of the UK’s biggest regeneration schemes, Bristol Temple Quarter, which is to bring thousands of new homes, work spaces and health and education centres to one of the city’s – and England’s – most deprived neighbourhoods. The scheme is so important to Labour locally and nationally that it got a mention in Andy Burnham’s first prime minister’s questions. Speaking in a garden space in TQEC almost directly above Temple Meads’ platform 15, Judith Squires, deputy vice chancellor and university lead for the TQEC, said the new site put the university “front and centre” in the city. “We think it opens up lots of opportunities that we haven’t yet explored,” she said. “One of them will be for students who commute to Bristol, which I think may become an increasingly important trend given that rent is such an expensive cost. Living at home is becoming an increasing option for students. “It also means that it’s very accessible for a lot of our staff who can commute in, but also for our industrial partners who will be coming to do research and collaboration in the building.” The site will be a hub for teaching and research across areas including business, innovation, digital engineering, artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, advanced telecommunications and quantum technologies. It features a rare example of a circular lecture theatre. When the Guardian visited, an actor and voice coach from Bristol Old Vic theatre was showing lecturers how to best use the space. But the university is keen to emphasise that it is is not just for academic types to use, but for all of Bristol’s citizens. A new entrance from the station to the campus has been created, and new footpaths and cycleways added. Spaces aimed at citizens include the Bristol Rooms and the Story Exchange on the ground floor, which are designed to bring academics and students together with business, public sector and community organisations. Sessions on topics important to Bristolians, such as health inequalities, reparative justice and the climate crisis, have already been organised. Members of the public are to be allowed more casual access to the campus. They will be able to have a coffee on the campus, plug in a laptop and work or use it as a meeting spot. Squires said: “We wanted to make it a porous place so that people can feel it is a space for them, designed with them in mind. It’s really great to have such an accessible front door to the university where everybody can find it, so we don’t feel so cut off from the city. I think it positions us physically and symbolically in a different way with the city.” The main building has cost £241m and is named the Sloane Robinson building, after a foundation set up by the former Bristol University student and hedge fund manager Hugh Sloane, which donated £20m. The West of England Combined Authority (WECA) has invested £35m into the campus and £25m into the station entrance and new paths. The university has snapped up other parcels of land nearby so it can expand the campus in the coming years, taking the cost of the campus up to £500m. Behind the Sloane Robinson building, work on the wider Bristol Temple Quarter project is under way in the St Philip’s Marsh area of the city, currently a place of factories, waste disposal sites and Bristol’s fruit market. Though the new quarter will be 30 years in the making, workers in hi-vis are preparing the way for new homes, shops, community spaces. A bridge is to be built from TQEC to link to it. Helen Godwin, the mayor of the West of England, said the opening of the campus was a major milestone for Bristol. “Our investment in Bristol Temple Quarter will unlock a giant leap forward for the West of England,” she said. Martin Booth, editor of the independent magazine and website Bristol 24/7 and author of 111 Places That You Shouldn’t Miss in Bristol, said the new site looked as if a “gigantic spaceship” had crash-landed next to the station. “But it is a manifestation of the university’s efforts to be a more visible part of our city – not just in their privileged position on top of a hill in Clifton,” he said.

title: Assailant lunges at Ohio Democratic gubernatorial candidate, campaign says
summary: Armed suspect Patrick Havas allegedly attacks Amy Acton during a campaign stop at a fair, injuring several people
text: Amy Acton, Democratic candidate for Ohio governor, was the target of an attack on Sunday during a campaign stop at the Canfield fair, campaign officials said. Several people were injured when the armed assailant lunged at Acton. The suspect knocked volunteers to the ground before he was arrested and was “discovered to have weapons”, Mahoning county Democratic party chairperson Chris Anderson said in a statement. Sheriff Jerry Greene told a local NBC outlet, 21 News, that the suspect, Patrick Havas, knocked down two older ‌adults during the incident. Havas is expected to be charged with assault and disorderly conduct, Greene told 21 News. Acton was not injured, but campaign officials said multiple people were hurt. She is “grateful for the swift and decisive action of law enforcement and are praying for the recovery of those injured. This kind of violence has no place in Ohio. Dr Acton will always stand up to the chaos, hate and vitriol that pits us against one another,” said Addie Bullock, communications director for the campaign. A photo shared to social media by a fair attendee after the incident showed Acton checking on one of those injured in the incident. “What happened at our tent today during today’s visit from Dr Acton is reprehensible and should be condemned by leaders on all sides of the aisle,” Anderson said. Acton is facing Republican Vivek Ramaswamy, who has parlayed his national name recognition, tech industry connections and alliance with Donald Trump into a record fundraising haul that he is tapping for advertising spots aimed at the November election. He is using campaign rallies and advertising to criticize Acton, the state’s former public health director. Ramaswamy called the incident on Sunday unacceptable. “Candidates should be able to meet with voters without having to worry about threats or violence. What happened today is completely unacceptable and has no place in politics, and we hope that no one was hurt,” Ramaswamy’s communications director, Connie Luck, said in a statement on Sunday. Abdul El-Sayed, Michigan’s Democratic US Senate candidate, also denounced the attack. “There’s no place for political violence in America,” El-Sayed said in a social media post. “Our prayers go out to Dr Acton and her team, and we hope that this moment is yet another wake up call regarding how important it is to make sure that democracy is a process by which we address our political differences peacefully.” The fairground’s police department referred inquiries to the Mahoning county sheriff’s department, which didn’t immediately return a message seeking comment. The Ohio state highway patrol didn’t immediately respond to a request for information.

title: At least five dead after Amazon cargo plane crashes at Miami airport
summary: Three people in critical condition and two hospitalized as operations at one of busiest US airports brought to a halt
text: An Amazon cargo plane crashed at Miami international airport in Florida on Sunday afternoon after the flight, which was arriving from Puerto Rico, overshot the runway, striking several vehicles and resulting in at least five deaths. The plane erupted in flames as dark smoke billowed into the sky, bringing operations at one of the busiest airports in the US to a halt. The pilot and copilot were trapped in the cockpit as a result of the crash, said the Miami-Dade rescue fire chief Ray Jadallah. The mayor Daniella Levine Cava of Miami-Dade county said at a news conference on Sunday that in addition to the five people who were killed, five others were injured. Miami-Dade fire rescue confirmed during the same conference that 10 total people were involved, with five deaths, three people in critical condition and two taken to a local hospital. Jadallah, described the incident as a “very complex situation” where the plane crashed into multiple vehicles as it ran off the tarmac, trapping several people inside their vehicles. The National Transportation Safety Board has assembled a team to investigate, the agency said in a social media post on Sunday evening. They are scheduling a media briefing for Monday. The plane was a Boeing 767 flying for Amazon Prime Air. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) confirmed the crash in a statement to the Guardian, saying: “21 Air Flight 7598 overran the runway after landing at Miami International Airport around 2 pm local time on Sunday, September 6. The Boeing 767-300 cargo aircraft departed from Luis Muñoz Marín International Airport in San Juan, Puerto Rico. The FAA will investigate.” The plane overran the airport’s diagonal runway and was disabled at the north-west end of the airport, a spokesperson for Miami international airport said. An air and ground stop has been issued at the airport, preventing all other flights from landing or taking off at the busy south Florida hub. Fire crews were still dealing with a fuel leak on the plane several hours after the crash, Jadallah said. “All runways and taxiways at MIA are currently closed as of 3pm and a ground stop is in effect,” the airport said, adding: “Miami-Dade Fire Rescue has responded to the scene.” About 250 flights were delayed at the airport late afternoon on Sunday, according to FlightAware, a website that tracks flight disruptions. More than 60 units from the Miami-Dade fire rescue services appeared on scene, with units arriving “to find an airplane that had caught on fire as a result of this crash, with heavy flames and smoke showing”, the fire department said, with the post adding that the plane had struck multiple vehicles near the airport. Firefighters were “working on extinguishing the fire and assessing patients”, the post said. US transportation secretary Sean Duffy said on social media that responders would “assess the scene after an Amazon cargo plane overran the runway”. “If you’re traveling through the area, please expect significant delays and potential cancellations,” he added. Meanwhile, the Miami-Dade sheriff’s office announced street closures due to the crash, saying: “NW 67th Avenue between NW 25th Street – NW 36th Street is currently closed. Expect delays and seek alternate routes.” Kelly Nantel, an Amazon spokesperson told the Guardian in a statement: “We can confirm that an Amazon Air plane operated by 21 Air experienced an incident while attempting to land at Miami International Airport today.”” Amazon said in a statement that it would cooperate with any investigation. “We’re heartbroken to learn that five people lost their lives in today’s incident at Miami international airport,” the company said. “Our deepest sympathies go out to the families, loved ones, and all those affected by this devastating loss.”

title: Hawaii declares state of emergency as Hurricane Lowell approaches islands
summary: Storm, which may make impact as soon as Monday, is third system in weeks to threaten state during hurricane season
text: Hawaii has declared a state of emergency as powerful Hurricane Lowell makes its way toward the islands, with the first impacts expected as soon as Monday. The storm is the third system in just over three weeks to threaten Hawaii during an active hurricane season in the central Pacific. Lowell remained a category 3 hurricane early on Sunday morning, packing winds of 125mph while moving north-west at 6mph. According to the forecast, Lowell will reach Hawaii as a category 2 hurricane. Its center could pass roughly 130 miles west of Ni’ihau or 170 miles west of Kauai between Monday evening and Tuesday morning. The threat comes amid unusually intense hurricane activity across the Pacific. As of Saturday, Hurricanes Karina, Lowell and Marie were all churning in the Pacific at the same time, marking the region’s first triple-hurricane stretch in a decade. The National Hurricane Center (NHC) was also monitoring a fourth potential system off the coast of Mexico. The Pacific averages only eight hurricanes per year, according to the NHC, making three simultaneous hurricanes highly unusual. Lowell’s projected offshore path is expected to keep the storm’s most dangerous winds away from Hawaii’s islands. But heavy rain, high surf and dangerous coastal conditions are still expected. A tropical storm warning is in effect for Kauai and Ni’ihau, where wind gusts above 39 miles per hour are possible over the next 48 hours. Lowell is the third storm in a matter of weeks to hit Hawaii as the climate crisis continues to increase the intensity and frequency of storms and other weather events. Tropical Storm Moke struck the southern part of Hawaii’s islands two weeks ago, bringing heavy rainfall and strong winds. That came just days after Hurricane Lala hit the region. The Hawaii governor Josh Green said Lala alone had caused at least $43m in infrastructure damage on the Big Island, along with another $4.6m in damage to homes. The escalating storm activity comes as the UN warns that this year’s El Niño is forecast to become the strongest on record in four decades. A statement released on Thursday described El Niño as being “supersized before our eyes”, adding that the world is in “the danger zone of extreme weather”. The latest data on the natural climate phenomenon shows a near 100% likelihood that the latest El Niño will continue through February 2027, the statement said. The stronger an El Niño becomes, the greater the chance it will significantly alter rainfall and temperature patterns around the world and help fuel extreme weather. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (Noaa) has previously warned there is a 69% chance that this El Niño will be the strongest in 70 years.

title: US envoys Kushner and Witkoff visit Kyiv for first time after Putin talks
summary: Witkoff says he hopes trilateral talks involving the US, Ukraine and Europe will be announced ‘in short order’
text: The US negotiators Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff travelled to Ukraine for the first time on Sunday for talks with Volodymyr Zelenskyy in an attempt to end the war with Russia. The Ukrainian president announced plans to widen peace discussions to include European countries in the near future, saying he wanted to do “everything to ensure that trilateral meetings take place” with Ukraine, the US and Europe. Witkoff said he was hopeful such meetings would be announced “in short order”. The British, French and German national security advisers briefly joined Sunday’s talks. Witkoff said the talks with Zelenskyy had been “very constructive and substantive”. Kushner said the conflict between Russia and Ukraine was “a long, hard and emotional war”. There were otherwise few details from the highly anticipated talks between Washington and Kyiv, which came a day after the US envoys met Russia’s president, Vladimir Putin, in Moscow. Kushner and Witkoff were forced to arrive in Kyiv by train after Russia bombed the city’s two main airports on Friday. Both countries pledged to refrain from attacking each other’s capitals over the weekend to ensure the US envoys’ safe passage. Zelenskyy joked that the delegation should come more often to “protect our citizens who are in the capital”. But the president’s mood was generally sombre. He said Ukraine was “really counting on a winter package” from the US and Europe to enable it to withstand another war-torn winter. “We specifically discussed this with Steve and Jared, as well as with our European partners: air defence, energy support, and as you know we are counting on the serious use of LNG, American LNG,” he said, referring to liquefied natural gas. Zelenskyy greeted the US envoys earlier in the day in Sophia Square, in front of Kyiv’s historic cathedral. The cathedral is a few hundred metres away from the headquarters of Ukraine’s SBU intelligence agency, which was hit by a Russian drone on Friday afternoon, marking an escalation in a conflict that has dragged on for more than four and a half years. Kushner said his team was in almost daily contact with Ukrainian officials. “Just because we haven’t travelled out, it doesn’t mean we haven’t … been communicating,” he said. Expectations going into the talks were low. US-backed mediation has stalled over the past few months as Washington has been focused on the war with Iran. Many Ukrainians are also sceptical that Trump is committed to a peace agreement that is acceptable to Kyiv. “People don’t trust the Russians and people don’t trust Trump personally,” said Artem Bronzhukov, a political analyst. Talks between Russia and Ukraine on ending the war have focused on a 20-point peace plan put forward by Washington and Kyiv in December. But the two sides have failed to reach common ground on several sticking points, including control of territory in east Ukraine. “People mostly understand that if you step back from the Donbas, the next day or the next week, Putin will push for another condition,” Bronzhukov said. A White House official said on Saturday that the talks with Moscow “discussed substantive plans for next steps” for ending the war and that an announcement would follow in the coming weeks. The senior Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov described the talks as “extremely frank” and said there was an acknowledgement of the need to address “the root causes of the conflict”. Kyiv and the surrounding areas have been hit by a barrage of daily drone strikes for more than a week, the most sustained attack on Ukraine’s capital in months. The capital is now enjoying a reprieve from strikes and air raid alerts that had become a daily occurrence, but other parts of the country are still being hit. Ukrainian authorities reported on Sunday that at least eight people were killed and 69 injured across Ukraine in the past day. Ukraine is facing a critical shortage of US-made Patriot interceptor missiles that can shoot down incoming threats. Many of the recent Russian strikes have been by new-model jet-powered drones that can reach speeds of 250mph, making them hard to intercept. Many Ukrainians are worried about the war dragging on into a fifth year and are anxious about the winter ahead. This week, Zelenskyy’s defence technology adviser, Serhii Beskrestnov, told the Guardian that the government should consider evacuating elderly people from Kyiv as Putin had ordered the Russian military to “prepare and carry out mass strikes” on Ukraine’s energy facilities. Russia and Ukraine have increased their use of long-range missiles in recent weeks in an effort to sap morale in each other’s countries. Additional reporting by Illia Dyadik

title: Energy secretary says US might not reach nuclear agreement with Iran
summary: Chris Wright tells ABC there ‘may not’ be an agreement that would prevent Iran from having nuclear weapons
text: US energy secretary Chris Wright said on Sunday morning that the US may not be able to reach a nuclear agreement with Iran that would prevent the country from having nuclear weapons. Asked on ABC on Sunday morning about any sign of such a deal, as negotiations appear stalled and the US-Israel war on Iran continues, Wright said: “There may not be a nuclear agreement.” He talked about options for ending the “existential threat” of a nuclear armed Iran coming about by further US military action to knock out the country’s capacity to manufacture and deploy such missiles, saying: “It may be simply [a case of] destroying their capabilities to do it” or else “an agreement may await the next administration in Iran”. He later said on CBS that the US was not shutting down diplomatic outreach and was “always open for a deal”. Wright told that network’s Face the Nation show that the “biggest role” of the US military in the Gulf region currently was to stop Iranian energy exports. “We are strangling their economy to try to bring either a change in policy from the existing regime or a new regime,” he said. In an earlier interview with CNN on Sunday, Wright declined to declare the strait of Hormuz safe for oil tankers – unless they are being escorted by the US navy – and stopped short of saying whether the navy would need to remain in the Gulf region “indefinitely” in order to keep the vital energy passageway operating, as the conflict drags on. This came despite Donald Trump’s repeated claims that ships can safely navigate the narrow marine waterway, and the US president’s insistence last week that the US controls the strait, while floating the idea that it be named after him – statements that were followed by further strikes from both sides in the area. Wright, appearing for an interview on CNN’s State of the Union show on Sunday as well as ABC and CBS, was asked whether he could “unequivocally” assure safety to merchant ships transiting the strait. The question came after a New York Times report found that August was the deadliest month for merchant vessels in the area since March. “We’re working cooperatively with fleets that do want to transit. Some ships aren’t transiting, and, of course, that’s their choice. But the United States is working with teams from all the nations in the Gulf to get transits and to continue to ramp them up,” Wright said. “But you’re not saying that it’s currently safe?” host CNN Dana Bash asked, to which Wright replied: “We’re getting a lot of ships through, but, of course, it requires the US military to do that. We are not [at] pre-conflict levels, if that’s what you’re asking.” Bash then asked: “If a country or a company wants to send its tanker through the strait of Hormuz, can they do so safely?” “Well, if they want to work with the United States navy, I think they can,” Wright said. Bash then asked whether the US navy would remain in the region “indefinitely” and whether its presence in the strait was becoming “the new normal”. Wright responded: “Well, it is today, but I think, as you look forward, other nations will come and work with us in this endeavor. Certainly, trade for the world is important. It shouldn’t be just the United States’s responsibility.” “But until Iran changes their position or changes their government, we’ll have to deal with them. But, slowly, their capabilities are being degraded and ours are being enhanced,” he added. Nuclear and diplomatic talks between the United States and Iran appear to have stalled after a June interim agreement to end military operations collapsed without producing a lasting settlement on peace or the future of what remains of Iran’s nuclear program after US strikes last summer caused huge damage. Wright was also asked by CNN if he would say the US is still at war. “We’re still in a conflict, for sure,” he said. On Thursday, the US vice-president JD Vance said at a White House press briefing: “I wouldn’t call it a war,” instead referring to a military conflict. Trump then defended Vance, saying: “A lot of people do not call it a war, I would call it a military conflict, because it’s small potatoes for us … it’s not a big thing.” The Republican US senator John Kennedy of Louisiana was asked on Sunday by NBC if the war would be over by November. “Probably not,” he said. The conflict passed the six-month mark in late August. The former defense secretary Leon Panetta warned in an interview with the Guardian this weekend that it could last a lot longer.

title: EU faces 300,000 factory job cuts as China ‘colonises’ supply chains, industry warns
summary: Protest using 10 coffins to symbolise struggling manufacturing industry to take place in Brussels
text: Job losses in EU manufacturing will rapidly increase unless Brussels stops the “colonisation” of industry by Chinese component manufacturers, a leading industry trade body has warned. Eurometal predicts 300,000 job losses in manufacturing in the rest of 2026 because of expanding competition from China, which is now enjoying a record €1bn-a-day trade surplus with the bloc. On Monday, Eurometal will bring its concerns to decision-makers in Brussels, staging a protest using 10 symbolic coffins in a procession around the European Commission headquarters. The coffins will be marked with phrases such as “EU competitiveness”, “industrial jobs” and “European factories”. European manufacturers fear that the commission is not fully alive to the cannibalisation of their industries as China becomes embedded in supply chains through the sale of components. Alexander Julius, the president of Eurometal, told the Guardian: “China has made no secret of what it is doing. It is in their five-year plan. “China doesn’t want to be a raw material supplier, it wants to be a finished product supply. They want to be in key product supply chains because they know that once they control the supply chain, they own the complete value chain.” He wants the commission to understand fully the impact of Chinese exports at component level, including metals and chemicals used in 90% of manufacturing. The EU has already taken action on electric vehicles by imposing tariffs on Chinese imports in 2024, and in June introduced higher tariffs on imports of foreign steel. The bloc’s trade commissioner, Maroš Šefčovič, has also said the EU’s €360bn (£310bn) annual import/export imbalance with China is “not sustainable”, with both sides agreeing to hold three months of talks, ending in October, to try to avert a trade war. “You look at the job losses stacking up in industries in places like Germany. The media, the politicians can see the consequences, but they don’t go after the virus that is causing it,” Julius said. “They don’t see why it is happening or ask why companies are either relocating to China or India or going bust.” Among the conditions allowing the “virus” to spread is the increasing costs borne by European metal manufacturers with tariffs on steel imports and carbon emissions taxes for those high-energy sectors. Components manufactured in China face none of those levies, said Julius, and that, combined with the undervaluation of the Chinese currency, the yuan, makes it challenging to compete with Chinese rivals, he added. Companies have to satisfy shareholders and will continue to buy from China, whatever the political rhetoric coming out of Brussels, he said. “When manufacturing leaves Europe, Europe not only loses production but investment, knowhow and long-term economic resilience,” Eurometal said ahead of the protest. Analysis by the European Commission in June projected potential job losses of more than 1m on the back of high energy costs and global competition, which will include the 100,000 job cuts at Volkswagen confirmed by the German carmaker last week. China has repeatedly accused Europe of protectionism. It threatened “resolute countermeasures should the EU further target Chinese companies or products”, according to the state-owned Xinhua agency earlier this year. Since then, the EU and China have agreed a three-month truce.

title: Downside of Burnham’s devolution drive | Letter
summary: Letter: Areas will remain excluded, and nothing is gained from making local government units larger and more anonymous, write Steve Leach and Colin Copus
text: John Harris correctly recognises that “England’s 14 regional and metro mayors are right to see a growing opportunity for a civic political renaissance”, but justifiably points out how areas remain excluded from the new arrangements, or are at best a poor fit (Cities are the big winners in Burnham’s devolution drive. But what happens to the rest of England?, 30 August). Allowing for a further batch of city region-based authorities over half of England’s population does not suit this model. Where are the city regions and “strategic authorities” in most of rural Devon, Surrey, Hertfordshire and much of Kent and Essex? If Andy Burnham goes ahead with the local government reorganisation (LGR) he inherited from Steve Reed, we will be faced with vast tracts of non-place authorities with names such as Devon Coast and Countryside and North West Essex, which do not make sense as strategic authorities. They are what remain when the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government has completed its long-term aspiration of reducing the number of English councils and councillors. We estimate that when this LGR is completed, 90% of councillors and 75% of councils across England could have disappeared, eliminating almost all authorities based on real places and communities. Germany, with its Basic Law, much admired by Mr Burnham, operates with about 11,000 municipalities in a tiered county-municipality structure, and retains municipalities based on real places. The equalisation elements of the Basic Law, which sparks the PM’s interest, have been achieved without the introduction of huge anonymous unitary councils across Germany. England already has the largest units of local government across Europe; nothing is to be gained from making them larger and more anonymous. Steve Leach Emeritus professor of local government, De Montfort University; Colin Copus Emeritus professor of local politics, De Montfort University • Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Lessons for the aid sector | Letter
summary: Letters: USAID’s closure was abrupt, but no PR campaign will bring it back, says Monica Kappiantari
text: Jeremiah A Carew argues that USAID fell because of poor storytelling rather than poor work (How misconceptions and woeful PR allowed Musk to shred USAID so easily, 1 September). Having spent decades in a recipient nation working at the final point of delivery, I see a different lesson. The primary problem was not the story USAID told, but the architecture behind it. Aid money passes through a heavy supply chain: from prime contractors down through international and local NGOs, with administrative costs absorbed at every layer. Meanwhile, project success is too often measured by easy outputs, such as workshop attendance, rather than long-term systemic impact. There is also a quiet truth: aid workers, including local consultants like myself, often benefit when projects extend, creating incentives to prolong processes rather than complete them. Comparing USAID to Nasa is equally unhelpful. Nasa delivers visible, binary moments of engineering triumph. Aid involves slow, complex and contested social change shaped by local politics. No amount of polished marketing can package that like a rocket launch. USAID’s closure was abrupt, but no PR campaign will bring it back. The real lesson for the broader aid sector is to focus less on telling a better story and more on structural reform: shortening the supply chain and funding local actors directly, as some Nordic donors already do, measuring genuine outcomes, and rewarding work that truly finishes. Monica Kappiantari Development specialist, Jakarta, Indonesia

title: Iain Thornton obituary
summary: Other lives: Leading figure in the field of environmental geochemistry whose work contributed to the removal of lead additive from petrol
text: My former colleague Iain Thornton, who has died aged 91, was a driving force in the development of environmental geochemistry, in particular the study of how natural and anthropogenic chemicals that are present in media such as soils, stream sediments, water and house dust may affect human and animal health. Iain did much of this work through the Applied Geochemistry Research Group (AGRG) at Imperial College London, starting in 1964 and retiring as professor in 2000. Initially he worked with John Webb on mapping the distribution of chemical elements across the UK, a project that led to the Wolfson Geochemical Atlas of England and Wales in 1978, which laid the foundation for systematic geochemical mapping worldwide. The atlas provided valuable information for various industrial sectors, including mineral exploration, but also for those interested in the health of humans and animals exposed to elements that are potentially toxic. Promoted to lead the research group on Webb’s retirement in 1979, Iain began to focus on the harmful environmental effects particularly of heavy metals. In the late 1970s potentially serious levels of cadmium were discovered in local soils around the village of Shipham in Somerset. Subsequent medical investigation showed that the cadmium had not produced any conclusive adverse effects on human health, despite press speculation, and that there was nothing to worry about. However, Iain and his team did come across causes for concern in other areas, particularly for elevated levels of lead in urban environments. These findings contributed to the removal of lead additive from petrol in the UK in 2000, and internationally around that time. Blood lead concentrations in children have dropped significantly in many urban environments since then. The approaches Iain developed in the UK were widely adopted by researchers investigating elemental pollution being revealed by subsequent mapping across the world. In 1988 AGRG was renamed the Environmental Geochemistry Research Group, and Iain moved from Imperial College’s department of geology to its Centre for Environmental Technology. Born in South Shields, Tyne and Wear, Iain was the son of Alfred, who owned a delicatessen, and Kathleen, a housewife. He attended Bedford school, then gained an agricultural sciences degree at King’s College, Durham and, after working as a soil scientist in the Gambia, he began his work at Imperial College. In 1988 he was promoted to professor of environmental geochemistry and health. Iain was a founding member of the Society for Environmental Geochemistry and Health in 1970, a president of the society from 1985 to 1987, and a lifetime board member. Among several international awards, he was elected as a member of the Norwegian Academy of Science and Letters. In his spare time fly-fishing was one of his main interests, and wherever he was in the world he could often be seen with rod in hand, occasionally singing geordie songs from his childhood. Iain’s first marriage, to Greta Metcalf in 1961, ended in divorce in 1982, and in 1985 he married Lyn Foley, a midwifery tutor. She survives him, as do two daughters from his first marriage, Diana and Katharine, and seven grandchildren.

title: Trump again asks supreme court to restrict mail-in voting as midterms loom
summary: Legal fight continues as states begin sending out ballots for voters to vote by mail in November’s midterm elections
text: The Trump administration renewed its appeal to the US supreme court on Sunday to allow restrictions on mail-in voting, after a federal judge had blocked new limits on such ballots, just ahead of November’s midterm elections. The latest filing follows a decision by US district court judge Indira Talwani on Friday to extend a court order preventing the US Postal Service (USPS) from enforcing Donald Trump’s executive order. The legal fight was continuing as states begin sending out ballots for voters to vote by mail – giving the administration little time to make major changes to the rules. “Ballots have already begun to be mailed in North Carolina, and more states will begin the mailing process as the injunction remains in place – including Alabama on September 9 and at least five states the week of September 13,” the solicitor general, John Sauer, said in the filing to the supreme court on Sunday. “Once those ballot envelopes enter the mailstream, there is no retrieving them. And while the injunction allows the Postal Service and the states to continue taking steps to ensure that their envelopes satisfy the rule’s requirements … each day the injunction is in place risks sowing confusion and chaos because the injunction makes those preparatory steps voluntary, rather than mandatory,” Sauer continued in the emergency application. It is the third time the administration has asked the highest court in the US to step into the dispute and that court has allowed the plan to move forward but has not decided whether it was legal. The outcome of the wrangling could have significant consequences for this year’s elections, with control of Congress on the line. Nearly one-third of US voters cast their ballots by mail. The US president signed an executive order in March that would prohibit the USPS from delivering ballots to any voters not on a federal list of citizens deemed eligible to vote in each state by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). The result would mean a limited delivery of ballots – ie only to voters on approved lists. Democratic states and voting rights groups argue the ordered changes are unconstitutional, while state election officials who run the elections say there is not enough time to overhaul their systems to meet the new federal directives. The Trump administration has called its plans to limit mail-in ballots “commonsense measures” which are aimed at protecting voting security, and further called the order blocking those plans “unreasoned and unlawful”. Trump has repeatedly sought to restrict voting by mail, despite having often used the method himself. He has falsely blamed mail balloting for his 2020 election loss to Democrat Joe Biden, while promoting baseless claims of fraud. The USPS has said it stands ready to implement Trump’s new restrictions, which would require states to give the postal service the names and barcodes tied to mail-in ballots for federal elections, if the court injunctions are lifted. The Associated Press contributed reporting

title: Long-term proteges and verifiable reality must be jettisoned for Saving Private Nige | John Crace
summary: Has Farage’s brain been hacked? Has he started talking in his sleep? There’s no shortage of explanations for this scandal
text: We’ve all been there. It’s a lovely summer’s day and you just want a bit of me time. A quiet lunch of champagne and oysters. As you do. Anything to get away from having to pretend you are interested in the people of Clacton. Hell, it’s bad enough being expected to actually visit Clacton – who in their right mind would want to do that? – let alone having to talk to the little people who live there. So, you’re just minding your own business when who should turn up but two of your closest mates in politics – or contractors who you’ve barely heard of, as you prefer to call them – saying they have been having meetings with an American donor and his son who have already given you more than £30,000 for an opinion poll you have commissioned and now want to bung you another £500,000. And these guys would like to meet you. The cheek of it. Two strangers, one of them even a foreigner, who want to take up an hour of your time. And all you’re going to get for it is half a million quid. Who do they think you are? Don’t they know the Thailand-based crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne stumped up a £5m gift? Admittedly, several hundred Cameo users have bought you for £80 a pop, but that was at least a few months ago. Things have changed. Besides, that wasn’t really being bought. More a short-term rental. These wasters are basically insulting you. But you’re a tolerant kind of guy. You choose to indulge them. If you have a fault it’s that you’re never chippy and are unfailingly polite. Everyone tells you that. So you go along with them even though they have nothing of value to offer you. Yes, Yes. That’s fascinating. Thank you so much. But all along, you’re not really listening at all. You’re just zoning out. Trying to chill out in the sun. All you’re really thinking is of getting the first train out of Clacton. Over the past few days, Reform have been in a tailspin over the Channel 4 News sting that appeared to show the party was intensely relaxed about breaking the law by taking money from overseas. First, they tried to style it out. It was a hoax. Nothing to see here. It was an establishment plot carried out by anti-establishment climate protesters. Go figure. Then, as the net closed in, they started to panic. No one had a clear line on anything. Dan Jukes, Nigel Farage’s long-term protege, and James Orr, the lawyer turned Cambridge academic turned Reform head of policy, left the party. Anything to buy some breathing space. All that mattered now was Saving Private Nige. Everyone else was expendable. So for his interview with the BBC’s Laura Kuenssberg that was recorded on Saturday but broadcast on Sunday morning, Nige was keen to distance himself from any allegation of wrongdoing. That person in the film that people said was him? It was actually an avatar. Who knows how many versions of Nige might be in play at any one time? He’s a very busy man. But whichever Nige it had been, he was certain that he hadn’t been listening as the people around him were discussing in some detail not only how they exactly planned to break the law but how they had done so in the past. I mean, that was just pub talk. Who doesn’t like to boast about apparently criminal behaviour over a couple of drinks? Laura K seemed rather taken aback by this. She wasn’t the only one. Because it turns out Nige is capable of holding down his part in a conversation when he isn’t even listening. What a gift that must be. Most of us distinctly remember him saying, when the talk turned to the polling, that Nige insists he had no idea he had been funded by foreign money, that the polling had been “amazing”, had provided “bang for buck” and “it had worked – boom”. Perhaps he was just talking in his sleep. Or had had his brain hacked by the establishment. He even made a point of thanking the donors. Not that they were donors, of course. Maybe that was the bit that hurt the most. The realisation that the offer had never been genuine. Then came the distancing. Jukes and Orr had been “injudicious at best”. That would suggest that at worst they might have been … maybe that’s one for the lawyers. What you had to remember was that Nige had never been close to Dan. Had never really liked him. Come to think of it, he had no idea why he had allowed him to be his right-hand gofer for the last 10 years. As for James, he was just an ingenu. A dreamer. It was totally unreasonable to expect someone who had trained as a finance lawyer to know anything about … er, the law concerning party funding. And it was just daft to think that a Cambridge ethics professor should behave ethically. Orr’s thesis had been on “divine lawmaking”. Perhaps breaking the law had been God’s will. Dan and James had just been freelancing. They didn’t really work for Reform. So any alleged law breaking was one step further removed from Nige. Besides, as Reform leader, it wasn’t his job to be the compliance officer. Even though no one apparently knew the rules governing party donations better than him. He was the world’s leading expert. That was by the by. His job was just to be the frontman. To smile and shake a few hands. He had just been doing what he had been told. Yes, said Laura, by now totally confused. But you did appear to be up to speed as the potential donor outlined how a scheme like that would be breaking the law and told him, “it’s all above board”, she said. Worried that she might be losing the plot. No, said Nige. What he had said was: “Is it all above board?” Except he hadn’t. He had definitely said it as a statement. Still, that cleared up one thing. The reason he hadn’t been listening was because he had hearing difficulties. One that made him turn every sentence on its head. Hopefully the police will take that into consideration if they get round to starting an investigation. Nige could do with a break.

title: China prepares £40bn stimulus for financial sector amid fears over sluggish growth
summary: Beijing wants banks and insurers to bolster investment in stock market as it helps to replenish cash reserves
text: China will inject $54bn (£40bn) into its financial sector as Beijing attempts to shore up banks and insurers in the face of faltering economic growth. A host of financial institutions said they were due to receive billions of yuan in capital from state institutions including the ministry of finance and even the company that runs the country’s tobacco monopoly. The stimulus is designed to help China bolster the ability of its financial sector to invest in the stock market and lend to businesses, amid signs that the world’s second largest economy is struggling to escape weak growth. The country’s largest life insurer, China Life Insurance, will get 35bn yuan, while the China Taiping Insurance Group said it would receive 7bn. The People’s Insurance ⁠Company of China said it planned to raise up to 15bn yuan through a private placement of A-shares – stock that specifically allows investors to trade in China-based companies – to the ministry of finance, with the proceeds used to replenish ‌its capital. The initiative could help bolster ‌state insurers that have been directed by Beijing to support the stock market with medium- and long-term funds, while positioning them to help regulators ‌manage smaller, higher-risk insurance companies. The insurance sector has been struggling with eroding profitability owing to persistently low interest rates, with numerous small and mid-sized insurers reporting deteriorating solvency ratios, a measure of financial health. “The injection is an important step by the country to enhance the financial sector’s ability to serve the real economy and promote the high-quality ‌development of the financial and insurance industries,” China Life said, adding that it would strengthen the group’s ability to withstand risk. Separately, three state lenders on Sunday also announced they will receive a combined 290bn yuan in capital injections. The plan was first announced at an annual parliamentary meeting in March this year, extending a financing tool that had helped bolster some other big state banks last year. The Agricultural Bank of China and the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China, two of the country’s largest state banks, said ⁠they planned to raise up to 160bn yuan and 100bn yuan respectively through private A-share placements to the finance ministry, China National Tobacco Corp and its subsidiaries. The two lenders said the proceeds would be used entirely to replenish cash reserves, helping them sustain credit expansion, as Beijing leans ‌on state banks to support growth despite weak demand for loans.

title: Volcanic eruption halts flights at Jakarta and seven other Indonesian airports
summary: Ash cloud from Anak Krakatau affects hundreds of flights and some school and fishing activities
text: Indonesia halted operations at eight airports on Sunday, including from its main international hub, affecting hundreds of flights as a result of an ash cloud from the Anak Krakatau volcano. Saturday’s eruption, which produced lava and booming sounds that were heard up to 435 miles (700km) away, according to Indonesia’s geology agency, also interrupted some school activities and fishing. Two more eruptions were recorded on Sunday. Ash was detected in the airspace around Soekarno-Hatta international airport near Jakarta, prompting authorities to suspend operations. They announced several extensions of the shutdown, keeping the airport closed to flights until 9.30pm local time on Sunday. The suspension affected hundreds of flights, including international ones, according to the airport operator, Angkasa Pura. Singapore Airlines said it had cancelled flights to and from Jakarta for the rest of Sunday. The Australian flag carrier said there were “disruptions to a number of Qantas services, including cancellations to and from Jakarta today”. “Our meteorologists and operations teams are closely monitoring conditions in and around Jakarta and any impact on our operations,” it said in a statement. “Safety remains our highest priority. We have contacted affected customers and are providing assistance. Services will resume when conditions allow.” Volcanic ash can damage jet engines, baking on to hot internal parts and quickly wearing out turbine blades, as well as clogging fuel and air systems. It can also damage pilots’ windscreens. Ash ‌reached as high as 6,000 metres (20,000ft) ‌on the Java side of the volcano and 15,000 metres on the Sumatra side and some parts of Banten province in Java, the meteorological agency BMKG said. Several schools cancelled activities on Saturday after students and residents suffered eye irritation, and fishers cancelled fishing trips, the local media outlet Kompas reported. The disaster mitigation agency BNPB said it would conduct a weather modification operation, which could include cloud-seeding to promote rain. “If it rains heavily enough, the volcanic ash that has been disrupting our daily lives since yesterday and continuing today will be washed away quickly,” the BNPB chief, Lt Gen Suharyanto, told a press conference. More than 22,000 passengers and 209 flights were affected, the transport ministry said, particularly those bound to and from Singapore. Other affected international routes included Doha, Sydney and Kuala Lumpur. At least 16 domestic flights to Bali were cancelled, local airport authorities said. Anak Krakatau, which means “child of Krakatau”, sits in a strait that separates the islands of Java and Sumatra. The volcano has been sporadically active since it emerged from the sea in the caldera formed after the 1883 eruption of Mount Krakatau. That was one of the deadliest and most destructive volcanic eruptions in human history. About 35,000 people were killed. Port authorities said ships passing through the strait were prohibited from going within a two-mile radius of the volcano and should be vigilant. With Agence France-Presse

title: Black-clad Dover vigilantes will return if police do not act, say campaigners
summary: Far-right linked group able to mobilise at scale due to police ‘inaction’, says founder of Hope Not Hate
text: The group of masked, black-clad vigilantes who blockaded roads in Dover could repeat the disruption unless police step up efforts to stop them, politicians and campaigners have said. Responsibility for the demonstration has been claimed by Patriot Platform, an anti-immigration group with links to the far right, which styles itself as having a “fierce love for our homeland”. The campaign group Hope Not Hate, which has been monitoring Patriot Platform, said that despite its founder, Daniel Thomas, nicknamed Danny Tommo, posting on social media about his plans to cause disruption, the authorities had “failed to act”. Thomas, a far-right social media influencer who was Tommy Robinson’s bodyguard, was able to mobilise a large group for the demonstration on Saturday. Hope Not Hate’s founder, Nick Lowles, said that this was “clearly the consequence of the inaction from the police”. He added: “We fear that without decisive action things will only get worse from here.” Thomas posted that Saturday’s gathering had been the group’s “warning”, suggesting it could be the first step in a wider plan. On Instagram, he wrote that he was switching off for a few weeks as he was “mentally exhausted”, but that he would subsequently resume “updated meetings and vetting”. “A message was sent! Now imagine how powerful the next message will be,” he wrote. Mike Tapp, the Labour MP for Dover and Deal, shared his concerns about the need for greater police support “when Dover is targeted again” in a piece for the Mirror. He suggested that he would like additional officers, including mutual aid from forces such as the Met, available to be mobilised quickly. He wrote: “The Port of Dover is not just another road junction. It is critical national infrastructure. “Wilfully obstructing a highway can be a criminal offence. New legislation also means police can designate protest areas where concealing your identity with a balaclava or other face covering becomes an offence.” Tapp posted on X that Kent police appeared to have had “little advance warning”, and questioned whether intelligence had been missed. “I will be asking why,” he wrote. “A clearly coordinated protest is not ‘spontaneous’ as described by police. We can and must do better.” Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, said that although peaceful protest was an “essential part of British life”, this differed from “dressing up in costumes like this and disrupting people’s lives”. He told the Sky News Sunday Morning programme: “I would condemn it, but I’d condemn the disruption it caused for local people as well. Clearly, that’s not something we would want or expect to see on the [streets] of Britain.” When pressed on the apparent unpreparedness of the police, he said that “on the whole, the police handled it very well”. Kent policeengaged with the protest on Saturday, which the Port of Dover described as a “public order incident”. Protesters had dispersed by lunchtime, and no arrests were made during the incident. Social media videos showed a large number of demonstrators linking arms in a blockade across the A20, chanting “stop the boats” and “England till I die”. The police did not give an official estimate of the number of people involved. The Patriot Platform was formed in June from smaller localised anti-migrant groups, and describes itself as an “army of patriots” that believes “Britain belongs to the British”. Before the demonstration on Saturday, it had held several recruitment days across England. The group has been built up through Thomas’s social media following, with his content containing false or unevidenced claims, such as that Birmingham city council has banned English flags, as well as unsourced statistics claiming that rape has ballooned in the UK relative to other European countries. Hope Not Hate has previously revealed the violent history of key members of the group, including records of violence against women. Thomas also has multiple criminal convictions. In late 2025 and early 2026, he collaborated with Raise the Colours – the flag campaign group that put up hundreds of union and St George flags across England in 2025 – to run a series of trips to Calais in which he filmed asylum seekers and hounded the charity workers assisting them, resulting in a ban from France. He has since targeted migrants arriving by small boat along the English south coast, and was banned from Dover, Ramsgate and Folkestone in August. Reform UK’s Robert Jenrick said that although he understood that people were “extremely frustrated” by the small boats crisis, he has “always hated people obstructing other people doing their daily life”. He told the Sky News Sunday Morning programme: “I don’t like people going around in balaclavas, which is obviously very intimidating. In fact, our party’s policy is to ban face coverings like that. “The police should take whatever action they can to stop this happening again.” Kent police declined to comment. A government spokesperson said: “The right to peaceful protest is fundamental to our democracy, but we condemn the behaviour in Dover and the travel disruption it has caused.”
